title: Same Execution fee is used for different Settlement tokens Submitted by Aamirusmani1552, also found by BengalCatBalu
description: As per the sponsors, any ERC20 could be used as a settlement token. But in the ExecutionFeeHandler, the max execution fee is set to 1e7 which is in USDC token. And there is no way to update this fee. That means, if some other token except USDC is used as a settlement token, the protocol will only be able to charge upto 1e7 of that token. Which would be just a dust amount for most of the tokens. Because of that, protocol might suffer a huge revenue loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the protocol calculates and enforces the execution fee for actions that can be settled with any ERC‑20 token. The ExecutionFeeHandler contains a hard‑coded maximum fee of 1e7, a value that was chosen for USDC (which has 6 decimals). Because this constant is not tied to the specific settlement token, the same numeric fee is applied regardless of the token’s decimal layout or market price. The root cause is the absence of a configurable, token‑aware fee mechanism – the contract does not expose any function to update the fee nor a mapping that could store distinct fees for different tokens. Consequently, when a user selects a settlement token other than USDC, the protocol attempts to charge at most 1e7 units of that token. For most tokens, 1e7 units represent a negligible amount (dust) that is far below the intended compensation for executing the action. An attacker can therefore exploit this by submitting transactions that settle with a non‑USDC token, paying only the tiny dust amount while still receiving full execution privileges. The impact is an economic drain: the protocol collects far less revenue than expected, potentially reducing its ability to fund operations, cover oracle costs, or sustain incentives. This condition manifests whenever the system processes a request that uses a settlement token other than USDC, and it affects all participants that rely on fair fee collection, including the protocol owners, token holders, and users who might be overcharged in a different scenario. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s documented fee model with the actual implementation. It can be difficult to notice because the fee check does not outright fail – the transaction succeeds, but the fee collected is unexpectedly small, which may not be visible in the UI or may be dismissed as a rounding artifact. From the user’s perspective, actions that should incur a meaningful cost appear to cost almost nothing, leading to a discrepancy between the expected fee (e.g., "I should pay 0.1 WETH") and the reality ("only 0.00000001 WETH was taken"). This bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded monetary constants and insufficient configurability, often resulting in under‑payment or fee bypass. To remediate, the execution fee should be made dynamic: either expose an admin‑controlled variable that can be updated per token, or maintain a mapping of token addresses to their respective fee amounts, ensuring that each settlement token is charged an appropriate, market‑aligned fee.

title: When calling _recalfs from dctstake, the calculated fs may be incorrect Submitted by cccz
bug_full:
The vulnerability concerns an inconsistent accounting flow between the shareCommission routine and the _reCalFs function that is invoked after a DCT stake operation. In the contract, shareCommission updates two critical state variables for a pool owner: the amount of earnings that have already been distributed (_sharedA) and the maximum earning threshold (_maxEarningOf). This update is performed only when the function is explicitly called. However, the staking pathway (dctStake) calls _reCalFs directly after minting new staking power, without first invoking shareCommission. As a result, when a pool owner has earned commission that has not yet been shared, the stored _maxEarningOf value remains stale – it reflects the earnings that were known before the most recent commission, not the true current maximum. The stale value is then used by _reCalFs to compute the "fs" (the factor that determines the amount of staking power or reward). Because the contract assumes the maximum earning is up‑to‑date, the calculated fs may be lower (or potentially higher) than intended. This mis‑calculation can lead to an under‑allocation of minted power for the pool owner, meaning the user receives fewer staking tokens than they are entitled to, or conversely, an over‑allocation that distorts the protocol’s reward accounting.

The issue is triggered only when the pool owner has pending, unshared earnings at the moment of staking – a condition that can naturally arise in a live protocol where commissions accrue continuously. The bug is subtle because the functions involved are separate and the code paths appear unrelated; a reviewer may not notice that _reCalFs relies on a variable that is normally refreshed by shareCommission. Moreover, the symptoms manifest at the user interface level as an unexpected balance change: a user who stakes DCT may see a smaller than expected increase in their staking power or rewards, or may later notice that their overall earnings accounting does not match the on‑chain events. The discrepancy does not raise an explicit error, making it difficult to detect without detailed state tracing.

The root cause is a missing ordering dependency – the contract fails to guarantee that the latest commission earnings are accounted for before any reward‑related calculation is performed. The recommended mitigation is to invoke shareCommission for the pool owner immediately before calling _reCalFs (and _reCalBooster if applicable) in the staking flow. By pulling the latest earnings, the contract ensures that _maxEarningOf holds the correct, up‑to‑date value, and the subsequent fs computation reflects the true economic state. Conceptually, the fix enforces a consistent accounting sequence: first settle all pending commissions, then recalculate any reward factors. This eliminates the stale‑data class of bug, restores correct reward distribution, and aligns the protocol’s on‑chain accounting with user expectations that staking yields the correct amount of power and earnings.

title: Invalid Slippage Control in FlashProtocol::flashStake()
bug_full: The FlashProtocol contract implements a flashStake() function that combines staking, minting of fTokens, and immediate burning of those fTokens to claim yield in a single transaction. The routine queries the expected yield by calling IFlashStrategy(_strategyAddress).quoteBurnFToken() before approving the strategy to spend the newly minted fTokens and then invokes IFlashStrategy(_strategyAddress).burnFToken() with three parameters: the amount of fTokens, the quoted return, and the address that should receive the yield. The core problem is that the quoted return is treated as a slippage limit, but the burnFToken implementation does not enforce any minimum‑return check; it simply burns the fTokens and transfers whatever yield is currently available. Because the quote is taken before the burn, a malicious actor can front‑run the transaction, modify the strategy’s internal accounting (for example by withdrawing yield or executing other operations) between the quote and the burn, causing the actual amount returned to be smaller than the quoted value. The flashStake caller therefore receives less upfront yield than expected, potentially as little as zero, even though the user interface or documentation promises a specific return. This vulnerability manifests only when an adversary is able to insert a transaction in the same block that changes the strategy’s state after the quote but before the burn, a condition that is common in permissionless blockchain environments. Users, stakers, and the protocol itself are affected because funds that should have been credited instantly are silently lost, breaking the economic assumptions of the flashStake feature and eroding user trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of flashStake and identified the missing validation of slippage. It is difficult to notice because the function appears to protect the user by passing a quotedReturn value, yet there is no on‑chain assertion that the actual return meets this quote, and the loss can be hidden within normal transaction variability. To remediate the problem, the contract should either enforce a minimum‑return check inside burnFToken (reverting if the actual payout is below the quoted value), compute the quote after any state‑changing operations, or employ a commit‑reveal scheme or oracle that guarantees the quoted amount cannot be altered by a front‑runner. In short, the flashStake implementation suffers from an unchecked slippage control that enables front‑running attacks, leading to unexpected reduced yields or missing refunds for users.

title: Improved Validation Of Function Arguments
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a set of helper functions used by the FireBirdRouter contract to obtain pool state information for token swaps. Specifically, the function that retrieves the reserves and weight parameters of a pair, referred to as getFactoryReserveAndWeights, assumes that the caller‑supplied token address (tokenA) is always one of the two tokens that compose the pool. The implementation checks only whether tokenA matches token0; if it does not, the function unconditionally treats tokenA as token1 and returns the corresponding reserve, weight and the other token address. When tokenA is neither token0 nor token1 – for example, an attacker supplies an arbitrary address that is not part of the pair – the function still returns a set of values that are unrelated to the actual pool state. These incorrect values are subsequently fed into the getAmountOut formula used by _swapSingleSupportFeeOnTransferTokens to calculate the amount of tokenOut that should be received for a given tokenIn amount. Because the calculation is based on bogus reserves and weights, the router may compute an amount that is far higher or lower than the true market rate. In practice, the swap can either fail the require check ("Router: INSUFFICIENT_OUTPUT_AMOUNT") or, more damagingly, complete with a dramatically reduced tokenOut amount, causing the user’s balance to be lower than expected. The bug manifests only when a token address that is not part of the targeted pair is passed to the router – a scenario that is not covered by normal usage but can be triggered maliciously through crafted transaction data. The affected parties are any user of the router who attempts a swap with a mis‑specified token address, the protocol that relies on the router for accurate pricing, and ultimately the funds that may be unintentionally lost or left unreceived. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit in which the code flow was examined and the absence of an explicit validation check for tokenA was observed. It is easy to miss because the function behaves correctly for legitimate inputs, and the wrong values are not flagged by any require statement; the error propagates silently into the pricing calculation. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce an early validation that tokenA equals either token0 or token1 and revert with a clear error if the check fails. This change prevents the function from returning mismatched reserve and weight data, thereby preserving the integrity of the swap calculation and ensuring that users receive the expected amount of output tokens. In summary, the bug is a classic case of insufficient argument validation leading to incorrect state retrieval, which violates the fundamental accounting assumptions of the swap mechanism and can cause funds to disappear or refunds to be incorrectly calculated.

title: Rejected deposit transaction to DepositHandler will cause the funds stuck in the Vault Submitted by Aamirusmani1552, also found by KupiaSec, Roberto, BengalCatBalu, silverologist, aua-oo7, Bigsam, 0xEllipticCurve, CasinoCompiler, ZoA and zxriptor
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in the deposit‑withdraw workflow of the Vault contract. When a user calls Vault.deposit(...), the contract first transfers the requested token amount to the Vault and immediately generates a requestId that will later be used to increase the user’s collateral in the AssetService. The transfer is performed before the sequencer has a chance to approve or reject the request. If the sequencer decides to reject the deposit – for example because the user’s account is liquidatable – the DepositHandler executes the reject branch. In this branch the contract emits a LogDepositRejected event and, crucially, marks the requestId as processed (isProcessed[_requestId] = true) without performing any compensating action such as returning the transferred tokens or clearing the request flag. Because the request is considered processed, the subsequent WithdrawHandler sees no collateral associated with the user’s sub‑account and therefore reports a withdrawable amount of zero. When the user later calls Vault.withdraw(...), the function reverts with an ExceedWithdrawableAmount error, even though the tokens physically reside inside the Vault contract. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears successful – the transaction does not revert, a Deposit event is emitted and the token balance in the Vault increases – yet the expected outcome (an increase in usable collateral) never materializes, and the user cannot retrieve the assets. The issue was discovered during an audit test where a deposit was intentionally rejected and the subsequent withdrawal failed. It is difficult to notice because the deposit path does not revert and the contract emits a normal Deposit event, so users and external monitors may assume the operation succeeded. The root cause is the misuse of the request lifecycle: the system consumes the requestId and flags the deposit as processed regardless of the outcome, and there is no fallback or emergency withdrawal function to recover the locked funds. This class of bug is a “rejected operation handling” flaw, where assets are transferred before final approval and the contract does not correctly roll back or expose a recovery path when the operation is rejected. The impact is that user funds become permanently stuck in the Vault, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that every successful deposit must correspond to a proportional increase in collateral. To remediate, the contract should either (i) postpone the token transfer until after the sequencer’s approval, (ii) avoid flagging the request as processed on rejection, and/or (iii) provide an emergency withdrawal mechanism that lets users retrieve tokens that were transferred but not credited as collateral. Implementing any of these fixes would restore the logical invariant that deposited assets are either credited as collateral or remain withdrawable by the depositor.

title: Withdrawal transactions can get stuck if out-
description:
Withdrawal transactions may never be executed if the L2 output root for the block,
for which the withdrawal was proven, is challenged and reproposed.
Withdrawal transactions can be reproven in the case that the output root for their
previously proven output index has been updated. This can happen if the L2 output
root was removed by the challenger. However, to circumvent malicious users from
reproving messages all the time and resetting the withdrawal countdown, reproving
can only be done on the same L2 block number (and if the output root changed).
If the challenger deletes the block with the withdrawal transaction and the
proposer proposes a different block that does not have the withdrawal transaction,
the withdrawal transaction can never be finalized - even if a future block includes
the legitimate withdrawal transaction again, as reproving it is bound to the old
provenWithdrawals[withdrawalHash].l2OutputIndex.
Legitimate withdrawal transactions will never be finalized if the proposed block was
challenged and replaced with a different one not having the withdrawal transaction.
As this call fails on the "lowest level", the OptimismPortal, these transactions also
cannot be replayed or be issued refunds. In case the withdrawal transaction was a
token bridge transfer, the tokens are stuck on the other chain and cannot be
recovered by the user.
Optimism L2 block derivation has a long list of validation steps performed on
the validations in a different order than the spec lays out.
There is an error in the order which is described in the spec versus the one in the
implementation.
According to the specs, the following check comes first:
batch.timestamp > batch_origin.time + max_sequencer_drift -> drop:
i.e. a batch that does not adopt the next L1 within time will be
dropped, in favor of an empty batch that can advance the L1
origin. This enforces the max L2 timestamp rule.
After it comes this check:
batch.timestamp < batch_origin.time -> drop: enforce the min L2
timestamp rule.
However, in code in batches.go executes in reverse:
if batch.Batch.Timestamp < batchOrigin.Time {
log.Warn("batch timestamp is less than L1 origin timestamp", "l2_timestamp",
batch.Batch.Timestamp, "l1_timestamp", batchOrigin.Time, "origin",
batchOrigin.ID())
,!
,!
return BatchDrop
}
// If we ran out of sequencer time drift, then we drop the batch and produce an
empty batch instead,
,!
// as the sequencer is not allowed to include anything past this point without
moving to the next epoch.
,!
if max := batchOrigin.Time + cfg.MaxSequencerDrift; batch.Batch.Timestamp > max {
log.Warn("batch exceeded sequencer time drift, sequencer must adopt new L1
origin to include transactions again", "max_time", max)
,!
return BatchDrop
}
In practice this should not lead to any issues because both are drop rules and are
right next to each other.

When creating a contract from L1 (mainnet) to L2 (optimism) the nonce of the
sender is kept at 0 in the context of the transaction receipt and thus the existing
infrastructure (Etherscan) will incorrectly interpret the address of the new contract
(creating a collision).
It is possible to create a contract in Layer 2 from Layer 1 by sending a transaction to
the optimism portal. This is the function of interest:
function depositTransaction(
address _to,
uint256 _value,
uint64 _gasLimit,
bool _isCreation,
bytes memory _data
) public payable metered(_gasLimit)
To create a contract the "_to" address needs to be set to "address(0x0), " the
"_isCreation" needs to be set to "true" and the bytecode needs to be passed in the
"_data" field.
• The contract is then created through the "create" opcode, therefore the
address is computed by hashing the nonce and the address of the sender.
If the nonce is kept at 0 during some time of the execution, the new contract
address will always be the same (nonce is always 0).

Incorrectness in computing block signing hash allows cross-chain replay attacks
The sequencer signs over a message: keccak256(domain ++ chain_id ++
payload_hash). The chain_id is included to prevent replaying the same message
over another chain. However, SigningHash function fails to ensure the chain_id is
included in the message.
func SigningHash(domain [32]byte, chainID *big.Int, payloadBytes []byte)
(common.Hash, error) {
,!
var msgInput [32 + 32 + 32]byte
// domain: first 32 bytes
copy(msgInput[:32], domain[:])
// chain_id: second 32 bytes
if chainID.BitLen() > 256 {
return common.Hash{}, errors.New("chain_id is too large")
}
chainID.FillBytes(msgInput[32:64])
// payload_hash: third 32 bytes, hash of encoded payload
copy(msgInput[32:], crypto.Keccak256(payloadBytes))
return crypto.Keccak256Hash(msgInput[:]), nil
}
If you look at this line:
copy(msgInput[32:], crypto.Keccak256(payloadBytes))
/p2p/signer.go#L36
It is supposed to copy the encoded payload hash to the third 32 bytes of
msgInput. However, it start from 32nd byte which would overwrite the second 32
bytes allocated for the chain_id.
Any block signed by the sequencer in any chain is valid for other chains. For
example, a malicious verifier can pick a message signed for a test chain and gossip
it out for P2P on main chain.

bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a situation where a withdrawal that has been proven on Optimism can become permanently unfinalizable when the L2 output root associated with the block that originally contained the withdrawal is later challenged and replaced. In the Optimism design, a withdrawal is first proven by referencing a specific L2 output index; the contract records the output root and the block number at which the withdrawal was included. The protocol permits a challenger to delete a range of L2 output roots and propose a new set, but reproving a withdrawal is only allowed if the new proof refers to the same L2 block number and the output root has changed. Because the reproving logic ties the withdrawal hash to the original output index, once the challenger deletes the block that contained the withdrawal and a proposer submits an alternative block that does not contain the withdrawal, the stored reference still points to the now‑missing output index. Subsequent attempts to finalize the withdrawal fail because the contract checks the stored output root against the current one at the same index, which no longer matches. Consequently, the withdrawal transaction remains stuck forever: the OptimismPortal call that would finalize the withdrawal reverts, the transaction cannot be replayed, and the bridge does not issue a refund. Users who initiated a token bridge transfer see their tokens disappear from the destination chain, receiving no balance update or confirmation, while the L1 side shows the withdrawal as pending indefinitely. This condition can be triggered whenever a malicious or faulty challenger removes an L2 output that includes a pending withdrawal and the system allows a proposer to replace it with a block that omits the withdrawal. The impact is loss of access to bridged assets, violation of the expectation that a proven withdrawal will complete, and erosion of trust in the roll‑up’s finality guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal flow, where the auditors noted that the reproving guard only compared the current output root at the original index and did not account for the case where the index itself becomes invalid after a challenger‑driven deletion. The bug is subtle because the protocol still emits events indicating a proof was submitted, and the UI may display a pending withdrawal, making it appear as though the process is simply delayed. The fix involves decoupling the reproving condition from a fixed output index, allowing a withdrawal to be reproved against any newer valid output root when the original root changes, or alternatively preventing challengers from deleting outputs that still have pending withdrawals. Aligning the contract logic with the specification—where the withdrawal proof should reference the current valid output rather than a stale index—will restore the guarantee that a proven withdrawal can always be finalized.

title: PositionUtils.validatePosition() usesisIncrease
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the position validation routine of the protocol. The function PositionUtils.validatePosition is responsible for ensuring that a trader's position respects collateral limits, minimum size requirements and, crucially, that the position is not already liquidatable. To determine liquidatability the routine calls isPositionLiquidatable and forwards the caller's isIncrease flag. The flag indicates whether the surrounding operation is an increase (e.g., a market increase order). Liquidation, however, is always a decrease of the position, regardless of the trade type that triggered the validation. By passing the isIncrease flag unchanged, the validation mistakenly treats a liquidation as if it were an increase when the surrounding operation is an increase order. This leads to a double‑counting of the price‑impact effect: the price impact of the increase is calculated once during order execution and a second time inside the liquidation check, effectively inflating the impact value. The inflated impact can cause the position to be incorrectly judged as safe when it should be flagged as liquidatable, or conversely to reject a legitimate increase because the computed impact appears excessive. The bug manifests only when validatePosition is invoked with isIncrease set to true – typical after a LimitIncrease or MarketIncrease order – and does not affect decrease or liquidation orders directly. Users submitting increase orders may see their position accepted while the underlying risk metrics are wrong, leading to unexpected liquidations later, loss of collateral, or protocol state inconsistencies. Auditors discovered the issue during a code review and confirmed it with a proof‑of‑concept that showed the priceImpactUsd value being doubled after an increase order. The problem is hard to notice because the negative price impact appears plausible and no explicit error is thrown; only a detailed log of the impact calculation reveals the discrepancy. The correct mitigation is to treat every liquidation check as a decrease operation by always passing false to isPositionLiquidatable, thereby aligning the logic with the business rule that liquidation reduces position size. Conceptually, the fix decouples the liquidatability test from the trade direction, ensuring accurate price‑impact accounting and reliable enforcement of collateral requirements.

title: A malicious lender can freeze borrower’s ERC1155 tokens indefinitely because the guard can’t differentiate between rented and non-rented ERC1155 tokens in the borrower’s safe.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the reNFT Gnosis Safe guard that governs ERC1155 token transfers. The guard intercepts calls to the ERC1155 `safeTransferFrom` selector and checks whether the token is currently rented, but it does not distinguish between tokens of the same contract address and token ID that are part of an active rental and tokens that belong to the borrower outside the rental. As a result, when a borrower holds both rented and non‑rented ERC1155 tokens with the same ID, any attempt to transfer that ID – even the borrower’s own tokens – is blocked by the guard. The problem can be abused by a malicious lender who supplies the rented tokens from a contract that deliberately reverts in its `onERC1155Received` callback. The `stopRent` function, which finalises a rental by calling `safeTransferFrom` on the lender’s contract to reclaim the rented tokens, will also revert because the lender’s hook forces the callback to fail. Since the guard treats the revert as a failure to stop the rental, the rental state remains active indefinitely. Because the guard continues to flag the token ID as rented, the borrower’s pre‑rental balance becomes permanently untransferable, effectively freezing those funds. The issue manifests whenever a borrower’s safe contains ERC1155 tokens of a particular ID before entering a rental for the same ID, and the lender is able to control the receiver hook. Users of the protocol who rent ERC1155 assets are affected, as their own assets may become immovable without any indication in the UI other than transaction failures or missing balances. The bug was discovered during a static audit of `Guard.sol` (line 242) and confirmed with a proof‑of‑concept that deploys a malicious lender contract with a reverting `onERC1155Received` function. The flaw is subtle because the guard’s selector‑based check appears to protect against unauthorized transfers, yet it silently groups all tokens of that ID together, making the freeze non‑obvious until a transaction fails. To remediate, the guard must maintain a per‑rental record that includes the specific token IDs and amounts currently rented and only block transfers that would affect those exact rental holdings. Additionally, `stopRent` should be designed to succeed even if the lender’s receiver hook reverts, for example by using a low‑level call with a fallback or by separating the reclamation logic from the safe’s transfer guard. Proper accounting and separation of rental and native balances would restore the expected behaviour where borrowers can freely transfer their own ERC1155 assets while the protocol still protects rented assets.

title: A malicious borrower can hijack any NFT with `permit
description:
1. ERC-4494: Permit for ERC-721 NFTs : ERC721-Permit is very similar to ERC20-permit (EIP-2612). ERC721 Permit adds a new `permit()` function. It allows user can sign an ERC721 approve transaction off-chain producing a signature that anyone could use and submit to the permit function. When permit is executed, it will execute the approve function. This allows for meta-transaction support of ERC721 transfers, but it also simply gets rid of the annoyance of needing two transactions: `approve` and `transferFrom`. Additionally, ERC721-Permit, just like ERC20 permit, prevents misuse and replay attacks. A replay attack is when a valid signature is used several times or in places where it’s not intended to be used in.

You can find an implementation of it here, by uniswap: <https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/main/contracts/base/ERC721Permit.sol>

ReNFT doesn’t account for ERC721 implementing the `permit()` function, allowing a malicious borrower to hijack the token by producing a signature and feeding it to the `permit()` function requesting it to approve his address to transfer the token

Exploitation Steps

  1. The attacker rents the NFT token in his rental safe
  2. The attacker creates a signature which he will need to feed to the `permit()` function. The signature is a signed data including info like: 1. the deadline (until when the signature would be valid), 2. the token ID he wants to approve his address to spend, 3. the spender, in this case it’s the attacker’s address (Look at the PoC to see how it’s generated)
  3. The attacker calls `permit()` funtion and gives it the signature along with the deadline, approved address and the spender.
  4. The `permit()` function will reach out to the attacker’s rental safe (since it is the owner of the token and since it’s a smart contract verifying the signature (EIP-1271) ), asking it if the signature is valid
  5. The rental safe will verify the signature and confirm that it’s the attacker (owner of the safe) who signed the transaction
  6. `permit()` will approve the attacker’s address to spend the token on behalf of the attacker’s safe (token is owned by the safe)
  7. Attacker will then transfer the token out of his safe.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a permission‑escalation bug that stems from ReNFT’s failure to recognise the ERC‑721 `permit()` function defined in the ERC‑4494 standard. ReNFT assumes that the owner of an NFT is a simple externally‑owned account (EOA) and that all approvals are performed on‑chain via the traditional `approve()` call. When a borrowed NFT is held inside a Gnosis Safe (the rental safe), the safe validates signatures through EIP‑1271. Because the ERC‑721 implementation (Uniswap’s `ERC721Permit`) supports off‑chain signatures, a borrower who controls the safe can create a valid `permit()` signature authorising himself as an approved spender for the token ID he is renting. The protocol never checks whether the NFT contract implements `permit()`, and it does not restrict the use of `permit()` during the rental lifecycle. Consequently, the borrower can call `permit(spender=attacker, tokenId, deadline, v, r, s)` from the safe, causing the NFT contract to record the attacker as an approved operator for that specific token. After the approval is in place, the attacker simply calls `transferFrom(rentalSafe, attacker, tokenId)`, moving the NFT out of the rental safe and into his own address.

Why it happens: ReNFT’s rental logic records the safe as the token owner but never validates or disables the `permit()` entry point on the NFT contract. The `permit()` function itself is designed to be a meta‑transaction shortcut that is safe for ERC‑20‑style tokens, but it also permits a signature‑based approval without any additional on‑chain guard. Because the safe is a contract, the signature verification falls back to EIP‑1271, which the safe implements, making the signature appear legitimate.

How it can be exploited: An attacker first rents an NFT through the ReNFT protocol, which places the token into his own Gnosis Safe. He then constructs the EIP‑712 digest required by the NFT’s `permit()` method, signs it with the private key of the safe’s owner (which he controls), and submits the signed data to the NFT contract via `permit()`. The contract updates its internal approval mapping, allowing the attacker’s address to transfer the token. Finally, the attacker calls `transferFrom(rentalSafe, attacker, tokenId)`, extracting the NFT from the rental pool.

Impact: The borrower, who was supposed to only have temporary usage rights, can permanently hijack the underlying NFT, resulting in loss of ownership for the lender. From the user’s perspective the rented NFT disappears from the rental safe, the safe’s balance for that token drops to zero, and the attacker’s wallet shows an unexpected increase in NFT balance. The protocol’s accounting and security guarantees are broken, as the lender’s asset is effectively stolen.

When it occurs: The exploit can be performed whenever a rental involves an ERC‑721 token that implements ERC‑4494 `permit()` and the renter’s safe is the token holder. The attack does not depend on timing other than the signature deadline, which can be set far in the future. It requires the attacker to be the owner of the rental safe (i.e., the borrower) and to have the private key of that safe.

Who is affected: The primary victims are the lenders who list NFTs on ReNFT, the borrowers who unintentionally gain the ability to steal assets, and any users of the protocol who rely on the assumption that rental does not transfer ownership rights. The protocol itself suffers reputational and financial damage.

Discovery: The issue was uncovered during an audit of the ReNFT codebase by Code4rena. The auditors noticed that the protocol’s rental contracts did not contain any logic to detect or block the `permit()` function on the NFT contract. A proof‑of‑concept test exploiting the oversight was built, confirming that a malicious borrower could approve himself and transfer out the token.

Why it may be hard to notice: From an external viewpoint the `permit()` call looks like a normal approval and does not emit any unusual events beyond the standard `Approval` event. Because the Safe validates signatures via EIP‑1271, the approval appears as a legitimate contract‑based signature, making it difficult for simple monitoring tools to flag. Moreover, the token does not change ownership until the final `transferFrom`, at which point the loss may be attributed to a user error rather than a protocol flaw.

Suggested fix: ReNFT should explicitly check whether the NFT contract implements the ERC‑4494 interface and, if so, either disable calls to `permit()` during the rental period or require that the safe’s owner be an EOA that cannot produce a valid EIP‑1271 signature. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce that only the safe itself can call `approve()` on the token, rejecting any off‑chain signature‑based approvals. Adding a guard that re‑validates the owner after any approval change and disallows approvals to addresses different from the protocol’s designated transfer agent would also mitigate the issue. In short, the rental logic must treat `permit()` as a potentially unsafe entry point and block or audit it before allowing token transfers.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The DCAv2 protocol grants a single externally owned account (EOA) the TIME_LOCKED_ROLE, which authorises it to call privileged configuration functions such as setSwapFee, setLoanFee and setPlatformFeeRatio. This privileged account can arbitrarily modify protocol‑wide parameters that directly affect the cost and distribution of user funds. The root cause is the concentration of administrative authority in an unguarded EOA without additional safeguards such as multi‑signature control, timelock delays, or DAO‑based governance. An attacker who gains control of this admin key, or a malicious insider acting as the admin, can invoke the privileged functions at any time, set fees to the highest possible values, or alter the platform fee ratio beyond the intended limits, thereby increasing the cost to users or diverting a larger share of assets to the admin. The impact is that users may experience unexpectedly high swap or loan fees, see a sudden reduction in the amount of assets they receive, or notice that the platform retains a larger portion of their trades than advertised. From the user’s perspective the UI may show normal transaction confirmations but the returned amount is lower than expected, or the fee breakdown displayed in the wallet does not match the protocol’s published fee schedule, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The vulnerability manifests whenever the privileged account sends a transaction to any of the configuration functions; there is no additional timelock or quorum requirement to prevent immediate execution. Because the functions are publicly visible and the role check is the only gate, the issue can be subtle for auditors who might assume that a role name such as TIME_LOCKED_ROLE implies a delay or community control, when in reality it is held by a single private key. The problem belongs to the broader class of centralised‑admin or privileged‑key risks, where critical protocol parameters are mutable by a single party, violating the expectation of trust‑less, transparent governance. To remediate, the protocol should transfer the TIME_LOCKED_ROLE to a decentralized governance contract, optionally protected by a timelock, replace the single EOA with a multi‑signature wallet, and ensure that any proxy‑admin privileges are also governed by the same decentralized mechanism, thereby aligning on‑chain parameter changes with community consensus and reducing the counter‑party risk to users.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The DarkNess Dollar protocol relies on two privileged accounts – an owner and a strategist – to perform critical administrative actions such as adding or removing liquidity pools, updating oracle addresses, changing fee structures, and modifying protocol‑wide parameters. This centralisation creates a trust issue because the owner or strategist can unilaterally execute these functions without any on‑chain veto or delay. The root cause lies in the use of simple access‑control modifiers (onlyOwner, onlyStrategist) that grant absolute authority to a single externally owned account (EOA) or a contract with no multi‑sig or timelock protection. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting intentionally, can invoke functions like setStrategistStatus, setTreasuryPolicy, setOracleDollar, setOracleDark, setOracleShare, setOracleCollaterals, setOracleCollateral, setCollateralReserve, updateProtocol, addPool, and removePool. By removing an existing pool, the contract’s redeem() and collectRedemption() calls in that pool become impossible and will revert, resulting in users being unable to withdraw their assets and potentially losing value if the pool’s balances become stranded. Similarly, changing oracle addresses can redirect price feeds, allowing the privileged party to manipulate minting or redemption fees, inflate or deflate the dollar price, and indirectly affect the amount of collateral users receive. The vulnerability is exploitable whenever the privileged account is active; it does not require a special transaction sequence beyond calling the exposed administrative function. The impact includes loss of user funds, denial of service for pool participants, erosion of trust in the protocol’s claimed decentralised nature, and regulatory concerns around custodial control. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the Treasury contract where the privileged functions were highlighted and their potential misuse examined. It may be hard to notice because the functions appear benign and are typical in many contracts; however, their consequences become apparent only when an admin action, such as pool removal, triggers a revert in user‑facing calls. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are abrupt transaction failures, unexpected zero balances after a redemption attempt, or missing funds after an admin changes an oracle. The expected behaviour – successful redemption and stable fees – is violated, leading to a scenario where “my funds disappear” or “my redemption reverts”. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an admin‑key centralisation or privileged‑account risk, where over‑trusted roles break the trustless guarantee of smart contracts. The recommended remediation is to replace the single owner and strategist roles with a community‑governed DAO, introduce time‑locked governance for critical parameter changes, and, if a proxy pattern is used, ensure the proxy‑admin role is also governed by a multi‑signature or timelock mechanism. By distributing authority and adding delays, the protocol can mitigate the risk of immediate malicious actions and align with its intended decentralised governance model.

title: Deposit transactions / events may mixed in case of chain re-org and lead to double deposit Submitted by BengalCatBalu
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way deposit transactions are identified and processed across two contracts – a Vault contract that emits a LogDeposit event with a requestId, and a separate DepositHandler that consumes that requestId to adjust collateral. The handler stores a simple boolean flag isProcessed[requestId] to ensure a request is not handled twice, but it never verifies that the requestId originated from the Vault or that it is unique within the broader system. Because the flag is not bound to the Vault’s state, a chain re‑organization (re‑org) can cause the same requestId to be generated again in a later block. In a normal execution, a user makes a deposit, receives requestId 1, the sequencer forwards the deposit to the handler, the handler processes it once and marks requestId 1 as processed. However, if a re‑org occurs after the handler has marked requestId 1, the block containing the original Vault deposit can be replaced by a new block that includes a different deposit that also generates requestId 1 for another user. The handler will reject the second transaction because requestId 1 is already marked, but a subsequent block may contain a new deposit from the first user that now generates requestId 2. Since the handler only checks the boolean flag, it treats requestId 2 as fresh and processes it, effectively crediting the first user’s balance a second time while the second user’s deposit fails. This double‑deposit scenario arises only when (i) a re‑org happens, and (ii) another transaction that increments the request counter is included in the same block as the sequencer’s deposit. The impact is that a user can receive twice the amount they deposited, inflating their collateral, while another user’s deposit is lost or reverted, leading to inconsistencies in protocol accounting and potential fund leakage. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of requestId handling and noticed the lack of cross‑contract validation. It is hard to notice because the LogDepositProcessed event appears exactly once per handled requestId, and typical blockchain explorers do not expose re‑org events unless explicitly examined, so the double credit may only be observed through anomalous balance changes. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of replay/re‑org vulnerabilities caused by insufficient nonce or identifier binding across contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an unexpected second credit – “my balance increased twice after a single deposit” – or a failed deposit with no refund, contradicting the expectation that each deposit yields exactly one credit. To remediate, the DepositHandler should verify that the requestId being processed was indeed generated by the Vault (for example, by maintaining a mapping of valid requestIds issued by the Vault, or by storing the originating transaction hash) and should ensure that the identifier cannot be reused across forks. Adding a deterministic, per‑subaccount nonce or tying the processing flag to the Vault’s state would prevent the double‑deposit condition and restore confidence in the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the concentration of privileged authority in a single administrative account, called Operator, within the DarkCrypto protocol. This account is granted exclusive access to a set of setter functions in the Treasury contract that can re‑configure core system parameters such as the Boardroom contract address, the DarkOracle address, the acceptable Dark token price ceiling, and the operator role of the Boardroom itself. Because the Operator is implemented as a plain externally owned account (EOA) rather than a multisignature wallet or a community‑governed DAO, the root cause is an over‑reliance on a single private key to perform high‑impact state changes. An attacker who compromises that private key, or an insider who misuses it, can invoke the privileged functions at any time, bypassing any timelock or collective decision‑making process. By changing the Boardroom address, the attacker can redirect reward distribution; by swapping the Oracle address, they can feed manipulated price data; by setting a malicious price ceiling, they can force price‑based mechanisms such as liquidation or minting to behave incorrectly, potentially causing users’ balances to be reduced or preventing withdrawals. The impact therefore ranges from subtle economic distortion—users receiving lower rewards or unexpected liquidations—to outright loss of funds if the altered parameters enable the diversion of assets controlled by the Treasury. This scenario materialises whenever the Operator key is active and there is no additional governance safeguard; it affects all token holders, liquidity providers, and any participant relying on the protocol’s promised trust‑less behaviour. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the access control modifiers and noticed that the only restriction on these critical functions is the ‘onlyOperator’ check, without any multi‑party approval or time delay. The problem can be hard to notice because the setter functions perform simple assignments and emit no special warning events, so observers may assume the parameters are immutable or governed by a decentralized process. To remediate the risk, the privileged role should be transferred to a DAO‑style governance contract that enforces proposal voting, timelocked execution, and possibly a multi‑signature scheme for emergency actions. Additionally, the contract should replace the single‑address operator pattern with a role‑based access control system that can be upgraded to a more decentralized model, thereby aligning the implementation with the protocol’s stated trust‑less philosophy and preventing a single point of failure that could cause funds to disappear or rewards to be unexpectedly zero.

title: Inconsistent Dark Amount Calculation in getBurnableDarkLeft() and redeemBonds()
bug_full: The Treasury contract contains two functions that calculate how much DARK token can be extracted when a holder redeems their bonds, but the formulas used in each function are not aligned. The viewer function getBurnableDarkLeft() determines the maximum amount of DARK that can be burned for the current epoch by taking the smaller of the remaining contraction allowance and a value derived from the current DARK price multiplied by the number of bonds that could still be minted. Specifically, it computes _maxBurnableDark as _maxMintableBond multiplied by the current DARK price divided by 1e18. In contrast, the state‑changing function redeemBonds() calculates the amount of DARK to transfer to the redeemer as _bondAmount multiplied by a premium rate returned by getBondPremiumRate(), again divided by 1e18. Because the premium rate may differ from the raw market price of DARK, the amount reported by getBurnableDarkLeft() can be higher than what redeemBonds() will actually dispense. This inconsistency creates a situation where the contract claims, via the view function, that a certain quantity of DARK is available for redemption, yet the execution path may revert due to insufficient balance or may deliver less DARK than the user expects based on the view calculation. The root cause is the use of two independent accounting formulas – one based on market price, the other on a premium rate – without a shared constraint that guarantees they produce compatible limits. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or regular user can query getBurnableDarkLeft() and see a large available amount, then attempt to redeem bonds expecting to receive that amount. If the premium rate is lower, the transaction either fails with a "treasury has no more budget" error or transfers a smaller amount, violating the user’s expectation of a full refund. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the displayed redeemable amount and the actual received DARK; users may see their bond balance disappear while the DARK balance they receive is zero or unexpectedly low. This bug is most likely to appear when the DARK price is below the ceiling threshold, there exists a positive bond premium rate, and the contract still has a positive epochSupplyContractionLeft. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of the view function against the redeeming workflow and identified the divergent calculations. It can be hard to notice because both functions compile and run without error, and the view function alone does not enforce the premium rate, so naive UI components may present misleading figures. To remediate the problem the contract should consolidate the calculation of the maximum redeemable DARK into a single, consistent formula that incorporates the same rate used for actual redemption, or adjust getBurnableDarkLeft() to reflect the premium rate and enforce that the treasury never promises more DARK than it can deliver under the premium calculation. Aligning these calculations restores the invariant that the reported burnable amount is always a safe upper bound for actual bond redemption, thereby preserving accounting integrity and user trust.

title: Proper Refund of The Excess ETH
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the addLiquidityETHTaxFree convenience function of the TaxOffice contract in the DarkCrypto system. The function accepts a payable amount of ETH from a user, forwards the entire msg.value to the UniswapV2Router's addLiquidityETH method, and receives back three values: the actual amount of Dark tokens used (resultAmtDark), the amount of ETH actually consumed by the liquidity addition (resultAmtFtm), and the liquidity token amount. The router is designed to automatically send any unused ETH back to the calling contract (TaxOffice). However, the TaxOffice implementation fails to forward this excess ETH from itself to the original caller. As a result, the difference between the originally supplied ETH (msg.value) and the amount reported by the router as used (resultAmtFtm) remains locked inside TaxOffice. This occurs whenever a user supplies more ETH than strictly needed for the desired liquidity, which is a common case when the user provides a maximum acceptable amount to protect against slippage. From a user’s perspective, the transaction appears successful: the expected liquidity is added, the Dark token refund (if any) is correctly returned, but the user’s wallet shows a larger-than-expected reduction in ETH balance, and no visible refund is received. The root cause is a missing transfer statement that should move the surplus ETH (msg.value - resultAmtFtm) from TaxOffice back to msg.sender. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit by Peckshield, who noted that while the token side of the refund logic is correctly implemented, the ETH side is omitted. This bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, emits no error, and the contract’s balance simply increases; typical UI metrics display the correct amount of liquidity added, masking the hidden loss of ETH. The impact is medium severity: over time, repeated deposits can accumulate significant amounts of unintentional ETH holdings in the contract, effectively stealing users’ excess funds. The affected parties are any users who interact with addLiquidityETHTaxFree, as well as the protocol, which may be held liable for the misplaced funds. To remediate, the function should be revised to explicitly transfer the surplus ETH back to the caller, for example by adding a payable call such as (msg.sender).transfer(msg.value - resultAmtFtm) after the router call, or by using a low‑level call with proper checks. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that excess ETH must be refunded, restoring correct accounting and preventing money from disappearing.

title: Lack of slippage control in llido.sol::swapexactinputsinglehop Submitted by erictee, also found by Lefg, b0g0, Auditism, walter, 0xrex, jesjupyter, 0xRajkumar,
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent slippage protection mechanism in the LLido contract’s swapExactInputSingleHop function. The function builds an ExactInputSingleParams struct for the Uniswap V3 router and deliberately sets the amountOutMinimum field to zero, which removes any lower bound on the amount of destination tokens that must be received. This design choice eliminates the contract’s ability to reject a trade that yields an unfavorable price, thereby exposing the swap to front‑running, sandwich, and other miner extractable value (MEV) attacks. An attacker who can observe the pending transaction can insert a preceding trade that moves the price unfavorably, then allow the victim’s transaction to execute at the manipulated rate, resulting in the victim receiving far fewer tokens than anticipated. From the user’s perspective, the expected outcome – a reasonable amount of tokenOut corresponding to the input amount – is replaced by a significantly reduced or even negligible amount, often perceived as a sudden loss of balance or a missing refund after a swap. The issue manifests whenever swapExactInputSingleHop is invoked, regardless of the token pair, because the slippage check is hard‑coded to zero. It affects any user or protocol component that relies on this function to perform token swaps, potentially draining funds or skewing accounting if repeated over time. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit of the codebase, where the absence of a minimum‑out constraint stood out as a logical oversight. Because the swap still completes successfully, the problem may not be obvious without comparing expected versus actual output values, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should calculate a dynamic amountOutMinimum based on an acceptable slippage percentage (for example, 5%) and a reliable price feed such as Chainlink or a time‑weighted average price (TWAP). This value would be passed to the router, ensuring the transaction reverts if the received amount falls below the threshold. Alternatively, access to the swap function could be limited to trusted actors who can supply appropriate slippage parameters. In essence, the bug is a classic example of missing slippage validation, a class of vulnerabilities that break the economic guarantees of decentralized exchanges by allowing trades to execute at arbitrarily bad rates, thereby violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations of fair value.

title: The lack of slippage protection leads to capital loss Submitted by Bauer, also found by 0xRajkumar and Bauchibred
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the earnings‑pull routine of the protocol’s Controller contract. When a user other than the account that triggered the pull (bountyPullerTo_) requests a reward, the contract calculates a portion of the contract’s wrapped stETH (wstETH) balance, swaps that amount for WETH on Uniswap V3, converts the WETH to native ETH, and finally transfers the ETH to the bountyPullerTo_ address. The swap is performed with a Uniswap router call that sets amountOutMinimum to zero and omits a deadline, meaning the transaction accepts any amount of output token regardless of the price impact. Because there is no slippage protection, a malicious actor can execute a sandwich attack: the attacker places a large trade that moves the pool price just before the protocol’s swap, causing the protocol to receive far fewer WETH (and thus less ETH) than expected, and then reverses the price manipulation after the protocol’s transaction completes. The protocol therefore loses value on the conversion step, delivering a reduced ETH payout to the bounty puller while still deducting the full wstETH amount from its balance. This results in capital loss for the protocol and for the user who expected a full reward; the user may observe that the transferred ETH amount is unexpectedly low or even zero despite the contract indicating a successful pull. The issue manifests whenever earningPulls() is invoked with a non‑self bountyPullerTo_ address and a non‑zero _bountyPullEarningPercent, i.e., any time the protocol performs the wstETH‑to‑ETH conversion. It affects all participants who rely on the earnings pull mechanism, including bounty pullers, token holders, and the overall liquidity pool. The defect was identified during a security audit that inspected the swap parameters and noted the absence of a minimum‑out constraint. It is difficult to detect in normal operation because the transaction does not revert; the contract’s balance updates appear normal, yet the economic outcome is degraded. The proper remediation is to introduce explicit slippage protection by setting amountOutMinimum to a reasonable bound derived from market prices (for example, a 0.5‑1 % tolerance) or by using a time‑limited deadline, and to consider integrating a price oracle or TWAP to verify expected output before executing the swap. By enforcing a minimum acceptable output, the protocol can reject swaps that would cause excessive loss, thereby preserving user expectations of receiving the correct reward and maintaining the integrity of the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: Pool owner can sandwich deposits into his pool to keep their fs at 1 while being able to withdraw ETH earnings Submitted by Aslanbek Aibimov, also found by cccz
description:
The trust Score depends on three factors: total ETH staked in the pool, Booster, and financial stability.  
Financial stability is the ratio of current ETH earnings to max ETH earning, so the reason why pool owners would not claim their ETH earnings is to not decrease their financial stability.  
The purpose of FS formula is to impose a temporary penalty on pool owners for withdrawing ETH earnings; however, this penalty can be bypassed: a pool owner would monitor the mempool for ethStake's into their pool, and withdraw as much ETH as they are going to receive in owner fees from the upcoming ethStake.  
Likelihood: Many of the pool owners could be interested in this exploit, as it would allow them to withdraw liquid ETH for any purpose without affecting their financial stability.
poc:
1. Bob signs a ethStake transaction that is going to stake 50 ETH into Alice's pool.  
2. Alice frontruns Bob and withdraws 1 ETH from her EthEarnings, decreasing her financial stability.  
3. Bob's transaction makes Alice 1 ETH in owner fees, so Alice's FS is instantly back to 1.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a sandwich‑style manipulation of the pool owner's earnings withdrawal logic that allows the owner to keep the financial stability (FS) metric at its maximum value while still extracting ETH from the pool. The FS score is calculated as the ratio of current ETH earnings to the maximum possible ETH earnings, and it is intended to impose a temporary penalty on owners who withdraw earnings, thereby discouraging frequent cash‑outs. However, the formula does not take into account pending ETH stake transactions that are still in the mempool. An owner can monitor the pending ethStake call that will increase the pool's total ETH stake, then front‑run this call by withdrawing their accrued owner fees before the stake is mined. After the stake transaction is confirmed, the newly added ETH increases the pool’s earnings, instantly restoring the FS ratio to 1. From the user’s point of view the pool’s trust score remains unchanged, giving the illusion that no penalty was incurred, while the owner’s wallet receives the withdrawn ETH. This exploit can be performed whenever the owner can observe a pending stake transaction targeting their own pool and is able to submit a competing transaction with higher gas price. The attack scenario is: (1) a participant signs an ethStake transaction that will add a certain amount of ETH to the pool; (2) the pool owner detects this pending transaction and submits a withdrawal of the amount they will earn as fees; (3) the owner's withdrawal reduces the current earnings and would normally lower the FS, but the subsequent stake restores the earnings balance, bringing the FS back to its maximum. The impact is that the incentive mechanism designed to penalise frequent withdrawals is effectively bypassed, granting the owner an unfair advantage and potentially eroding confidence among other participants who rely on the FS metric for rewards or reputation. Because the FS number appears unchanged on the UI, the problem can be hard to notice; the protocol reports a stable trust score even though liquidity has been drained. The issue was identified during a security audit by observing the logical relationship between the FS calculation and the ordering of state‑changing transactions. To mitigate the flaw, the protocol should incorporate pending deposits into the FS computation, enforce a lock‑up period after a withdrawal before new stakes can affect the FS, or redesign the penalty mechanism to be atomic and impossible to reverse with a single subsequent transaction. In essence, this is a class of state‑dependency bug where the order of transactions can be manipulated to hide the effect of a withdrawal on a derived metric, leading to money disappearing from the pool without the expected decrease in the trust score.

title: Abuser can vote twice by voting, withdrawing dct and staking it on another account Submitted by Auditism
description:
When a user stakes DCT, they will be granted some dp2pTokens. These tokens will allow user to vote against or for the attacker when someone gets challenged. The present issue is that an abuser is able to withdraw his DCT, transfer it to another account, stake it, receive voting power (dp2pTokens) and vote again.  
Impact: Abuser of this loophole are able to stake twice with the same amount of DCT, influencing votes in forbidden ways.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a governance voting mechanism that derives voting power from dp2pTokens minted when a user stakes DCT. When a stake is created, the contract calculates a staking power amount and mints an equivalent amount of dp2pTokens, which are later read by the Voting contract to determine how much influence a voter contributes to a challenge. The core of the issue is that once a voter has cast a vote, the contract records the contributed power in the challenge’s state (vote.attackerPower, vote.defenderPower and vote.powerOf) but never clears or adjusts this recorded power when the voter subsequently withdraws or transfers the underlying DCT. The unstake function burns the dp2pTokens and returns the DCT, yet it does not modify the previously stored voting power. Consequently, an attacker can stake DCT, obtain voting tokens, vote, then call lockWithdraw to retrieve the DCT, transfer the tokens to a new address, stake again, receive a fresh batch of dp2pTokens and cast a second vote on the same challenge. Because the contract does not check whether a voter still holds any votingPower before allowing unstaking, and because the voting contribution is never removed, the same amount of DCT can be leveraged to generate multiple votes. This double‑voting can be repeated as long as the challenge remains open, allowing the abuser to amplify their influence and potentially sway outcomes in a forbidden manner. The impact is that the integrity of the challenge resolution is compromised: the protocol’s accounting assumptions that one unit of DCT corresponds to one unit of voting power are broken, leading to inflated vote tallies, misrepresented attacker/defender power, and a risk that malicious participants can overpower honest voters. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the voting logic where the auditor observed that the burn routine does not invoke any cleanup of the vote’s power mapping. It is difficult to notice because the token balance of the voter becomes zero after the burn, which gives the impression that voting influence has been removed, while the internal vote state still retains the original contribution. The recommended mitigation is to prevent users from unstaking while they have a non‑zero votingPower in an active challenge, or to explicitly subtract or clear the voter’s recorded power from the challenge before burning the dp2pTokens, ensuring that the voting contribution cannot persist after the stake is withdrawn.

title: max_supply will not be reached as there is an early return that does set ismintingfinished to early Submitted by 0xWeiss, also found by Haxatron, cccz, Rotciv Egaf, Tripathi, Auditism, walter, jesjupyter, er-ictee, merlin, Aslanbek Aibimov, nmirchev8, 0xumarkhatab, Bauchibred, Chad0, sashik-eth, Said, ast3ros, Victor Okafor and tutkata
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the publicMint function of the DCT token contract, where an early return is used to mark the minting process as finished once the projected amount of newly minted tokens would push the total supply above the defined MAX_SUPPLY. The code first calculates the pending amount of tokens that could be minted based on the elapsed time (_tps * pastTime) and stores it in mintingA. It then checks if totalSupply() + mintingA exceeds MAX_SUPPLY; if so, it sets the boolean flag isMintingFinished to true and returns without performing any minting. The root cause is that the flag is set before the contract attempts to mint the remaining tokens needed to reach the cap, and the pendingA view function deliberately returns 0 whenever isMintingFinished is true. Consequently, any tokens that were still owed at the moment the condition became true are never minted, because subsequent calls to publicMint see isMintingFinished as true, pendingA as 0, and therefore skip the minting logic entirely. This situation can be triggered simply by a lapse in calling publicMint for a period long enough that the pending amount would have exceeded the remaining supply – in the example, 953 seconds (under 15 minutes) without a publicMint call leaves 6,666 tokens permanently unreachable. The impact is that the token’s supply will never actually reach the promised MAX_SUPPLY, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol, potentially affecting price, scarcity, and any downstream contracts that rely on the exact token count. Users who attempt to mint after the flag has been set receive no tokens, contrary to the expectation that they would receive the remaining supply; from a user‑interface perspective this appears as a silent failure where a mint transaction completes but the balance does not increase. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the minting routine and noticed that the early return prevents the final minting step. It may be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error – it simply stops minting, making the supply appear capped while still being short of the maximum. To remediate, the minting logic should cap mintingA to the exact amount needed to reach MAX_SUPPLY (MAX_SUPPLY – totalSupply()) before setting isMintingFinished, ensuring that the last batch of tokens is minted and the flag accurately reflects the completion of minting. This adjustment aligns the contract behavior with its tokenomics, guarantees that the maximum supply can be attained, and removes the scenario where tokens disappear from the minting schedule.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Unlimited Centralized Controls
description: Throughout the codebase critical values are allowed to be set without appropriate limits on the configured values. Some of these critical values include: collateralFactor FEE_TAKEN_PROFITS deltaCutoff withdrawFee limitProcess interestRateParams
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of unchecked configuration parameters that can be modified by privileged callers without any bounds checking. The contract exposes functions that allow the central authority to adjust critical economic variables such as the collateral factor, the fee taken from profits, the delta cutoff for position adjustments, the withdrawal fee, the processing limit, and the interest‑rate parameters. Because there is no validation of the supplied values, an attacker who gains access to the privileged role (or a malicious insider) can set these variables to extreme or nonsensical numbers. For example, setting the collateral factor to zero would render all user positions instantly under‑collateralized, triggering liquidations and causing users to lose their deposited assets. Similarly, inflating the withdrawal fee to 100 % would cause every withdrawal request to return no funds, effectively freezing user balances. An excessively high interest‑rate parameter could generate uncontrolled accruals, breaking the protocol’s accounting logic and leading to a mismatch between on‑chain balances and expected values. The impact manifests as loss of user funds, incorrect accounting, and a breach of the economic guarantees promised by the protocol. This flaw appears whenever a privileged account invokes the setter functions; the condition is not tied to any specific transaction pattern, making it difficult to detect during normal operation because the transactions succeed and emit no error. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the codebase, where the auditor noted the absence of any require statements or clamping logic around these setters. The problem is subtle because the functions themselves look benign and the parameters are expected to be mutable for governance, yet the lack of limits creates a hidden backdoor for arbitrary economic manipulation. To remediate the issue, each mutable parameter should be constrained by explicit lower and upper bounds that reflect the intended economic model, and any attempt to set values outside these ranges should cause the transaction to revert. By introducing sensible caps and rigorous input validation, the protocol can maintain its financial invariants and prevent a privileged actor from arbitrarily disabling withdrawals, draining funds, or breaking the liquidation logic.

title: BIN-1 | Option May Have Time Value But Zero Premium
description: An option’s premium is calculated to be Premium = Time Value + Intrinsic Value. Consequently, even if an option is out-the-money (no intrinsic value), if there is still time until expiration the premium should be non-zero. Due to the specific 15 periods and volatility factors used for binomial calculation, it is possible for all of the terminal payoffs to be zero and result in the option’s premium to be zero. Trader may buy a contract for 0 premium and then sell it as price moves in their favor allowing for nearly risk-free trades. Health Ratio Not Validated Correctly Put-Call Parity Equation Is Invalidated
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the option‑pricing routine in a binomial model implementation. The contract calculates an option's premium as the sum of intrinsic value and time value, expecting a non‑zero price whenever the option still has time to expiry. However, due to the fixed choice of fifteen pricing periods together with certain volatility inputs, the algorithm can produce a scenario where every possible terminal payoff is zero. When this happens the binomial backward induction yields a premium of exactly zero even though the option retains time value. The root cause is an insufficient discretisation of the price lattice and an unchecked volatility parameter range, which together cause the payoff tree to collapse to a flat zero line. An attacker can exploit this by purchasing an option for a zero premium and then selling the same contract after the market moves in his favour, effectively creating a near risk‑free arbitrage. The impact is that a trader can obtain profit without risking capital, eroding the economic guarantees of the platform and potentially allowing large scale fund extraction. This condition arises only under specific market settings—particularly low volatility combined with the limited number of binomial steps—but it can be triggered unintentionally by normal market fluctuations. All participants who rely on the option pricing—users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the pricing inconsistency undermines the intended risk/reward balance. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the security team observed that the Health Ratio check and the put‑call parity relationship were violated, indicating that the pricing model did not preserve basic financial invariants. Because the premium appears as a legitimate zero value, the bug can be hard to notice in the UI where a $0 cost may be interpreted as a promotion rather than a calculation error. To remediate, the pricing algorithm should be revised to use a finer granularity of time steps, enforce a minimum premium floor, and validate volatility inputs against bounds that guarantee a non‑zero time value. Additionally, the contract should re‑implement the put‑call parity check and health‑ratio validation to detect when the payoff tree collapses. In summary, the flaw is a discretisation‑induced zero‑premium bug in the option pricing logic that allows arbitrage by buying "free" options, breaking accounting assumptions, and exposing the protocol to financial loss.

title: DIEM-6 | PNL Always Decreased By borrowedAmount
description: In the _calculatePnl function, for expired buy trades the PNL is decreased by the entire borrowedAmount no matter the closedUnits provided. This is fine during the _closeTrade function call as the _amountContracts is set to the entire trade.contractsOpen, however other functions that rely on the _calculatePnl function do not make this adjustment. For example the calculatePnl function does not make such an adjustment and therefore can give results that may be used to manipulate systems interacting with IVX and relying on the returned value.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the profit‑and‑loss (PNL) computation for expired buy positions within the IVX smart contract suite. The core of the issue is a mis‑scaled deduction: when an expired trade is evaluated, the internal routine _calculatePnl always subtracts the full borrowedAmount from the PNL, regardless of how many contract units are actually being settled (closedUnits). This behaviour is acceptable during the _closeTrade flow because that path forces closedUnits to equal the total contractsOpen, effectively matching the full borrowedAmount. However, other entry points—most notably the public calculatePnl view function—may invoke _calculatePnl with a closedUnits value that is smaller than contractsOpen. Because the routine does not proportionally scale the borrowedAmount by the ratio closedUnits / contractsOpen, the resulting PNL is artificially reduced. The root cause is an arithmetic oversight: the code applies a flat subtraction (structured.PNL -= int256(_trade.borrowedAmount)) instead of a proportional one (structured.PNL -= int256(_trade.borrowedAmount.mulDivUp(closedUnits, _trade.contractsOpen))). As a consequence, any system that relies on the PNL value—such as off‑chain accounting dashboards, reward calculations, margin checks, or liquidators—may receive a value that is lower than the true economic outcome. An attacker could exploit this discrepancy by querying calculatePnl for a subset of contracts, causing the protocol to report a loss where none exists, potentially triggering unwarranted liquidations or manipulating incentive mechanisms. The impact is therefore a distortion of accounting logic that can lead to loss of funds, incorrect incentive distribution, or denial of service for legitimate traders. The condition manifests whenever an expired buy trade is evaluated through a path that does not close the entire position, i.e., when closedUnits < contractsOpen. Users, traders, and any third‑party service integrating with IVX are affected, as they may see their PNL incorrectly reported as negative or missing expected profit, leading to confusion when a UI shows a zero or reduced balance after a trade should have settled positively. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit, where the auditors noticed that the view function returned inconsistent values compared to the on‑chain closing path. It is subtle because the primary execution path (the actual trade close) masks the error; only alternative read‑only calls expose the miscalculation, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. To remediate, the subtraction must be scaled by the proportion of closedUnits to contractsOpen, either by using the mulDivUp formula or by adjusting the closedUnits internally to equal contractsOpen when the option is expired in the view function. This correction restores the linear relationship between borrowedAmount and the portion of the position being settled, preserving accurate PNL reporting and preventing manipulation of downstream systems.

title: DIEM-7 | Borrowing Fees Extend Past Option Expiry
description: When a trader closes a trade their borrowing fees are computed based on the period from the trade.timestamp to the current block.timestamp. However, when an option expires the trader will be closing the trade at a timestamp that is past the expiry time of the option. Therefore borrowing fees accrue for the option even past it’s expiry, when the result has already settled and cannot change. The segment of time between the option expiry and the timestamp of the block in which the trader closes the trade should not be factored when the borrowing fees are computed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of borrowing fees for option trades on the DIEM protocol. When a trader decides to close a position, the contract computes the fee based on the elapsed time from the trade's original timestamp up to the current block.timestamp. This logic does not take into account that an option may have already expired before the closing transaction is mined.
