From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a trade they believed would execute at or below a certain price instead settles at a slightly higher price, leading to a perceived “funds disappear” or “unexpected loss” situation where the balance after the trade is lower than expected. The correct mitigation is to move the slippage validation to compare the userMaxPrice against the price that already incorporates the position fee (the adjustedPrice), ensuring that the user’s maximum price bound truly reflects the total cost of execution. By doing so, the contract restores the intended invariant that the trader cannot be charged more than the price they approved, preserving the accounting integrity of the protocol.

title: M-25 | Closed Amt Not Seized If Its Value Is < 0
description:
The _validateClosePositionWithAction function checks if the position is liquidatable and if so seizes its closeBoundedPositionValue and gives it the vault.
This check happens with the neutral price and later on, it calculates the value of the position with the price rounded down by the pyth interval and reduced by the position fee.
Therefore the value of the position could be < 0, and in that case the closeBoundedPositionValue is not seized and nothing happens as the rest of the function is only executed if (data.positionValue > 0). In this case, the closeBoundedPositionValue is stuck in the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the position‑closing routine of the Smardex USDN protocol. When a trader requests to close a leveraged position, the contract calls a validation function that first determines whether the position can be liquidated. If liquidation is possible, the function is supposed to seize the amount represented by the closeBoundedPositionValue and transfer it to the vault as a liquidation penalty. The amount to be seized is calculated using a neutral price, then adjusted by rounding the market price down to the nearest Pyth interval and finally subtracting the position fee. Because the rounding step can reduce the price enough that, after the fee deduction, the computed position value becomes negative, the subsequent conditional check `if (data.positionValue > 0)` fails. Consequently the contract skips the seizure logic, leaving the closeBoundedPositionValue permanently trapped inside the system. From a user’s perspective, a trader who expects to receive a liquidation payout sees no funds transferred and may notice that their balance in the vault does not change, even though the protocol has recorded the position as closed. The issue is triggered only when the price rounding combined with fee subtraction pushes the calculated value below zero, a scenario that can occur during volatile market conditions or when the Pyth interval is relatively large. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the auditor observed that the condition guarding the seizure only allowed positive values and did not account for zero or negative outcomes. It is subtle because the contract still marks the position as closed, giving the impression that the process completed successfully, while the underlying assets are silently locked. This class of vulnerability can be described as an accounting mismatch caused by an incomplete edge‑case check, leading to fund‑locking or loss of capital. The impact is that affected users lose the expected liquidation compensation, and the protocol’s total locked value may become inconsistent with its accounting records, potentially eroding trust. To remediate the problem, the seizure step should be executed for any non‑positive position value, i.e., the condition should be changed to `if (data.positionValue >= 0)` or the logic should explicitly handle negative values by still transferring the closeBoundedPositionValue to the vault. This ensures that no assets remain stranded and that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.

title: M-26 | User Can’t Close Rebalanced Position
description:
The protocol has specific logic to ensure that any user can fully close their position if the position is apart of the rebalancer. The logic is intended to ignore the min long position amount if the user is coming from the rebalancer and the close amount is the full amount from that user.
However, the check fails to take into account any change in the users position value. So when the rebalancer is in profit the close amount will be greater than the position amount used in the check and visa versa for when the rebalancer is at a loss.
Because of this users will not be able to close their position if any pnl is experienced and there is only a small amount of assets in the rebalancer. Given that the rebalancer is a long position that can face liquidation having only a small amount in it is a real possibility.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract logic that governs the closing of leveraged positions that participate in the protocol’s rebalancer. The intended design allows a user to fully close a position that is part of the rebalancer without being blocked by the generic minimum‑long‑position check. However, the implementation validates the close request against a stale snapshot of the user’s position size, ignoring any profit or loss that has been realized since the snapshot was taken. When the rebalancer is in profit, the user’s current position value exceeds the stored amount used for the check, causing the validation to fail; conversely, when the rebalancer incurs a loss, the current value falls below the stored amount, also triggering the failure. As a result, any user who tries to close their entire position after the rebalancer experiences PnL, especially when the rebalancer holds only a small amount of collateral, will be unable to do so. From the user’s perspective, the transaction either reverts with a ‘minimum position not met’ error or simply does not change the on‑chain balance, leading to a confusing experience where the UI shows a pending close request but the funds remain locked. The impact is a form of denial‑of‑service: users cannot retrieve their capital, the rebalancer may become under‑collateralized and face liquidation, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are breached because the expected invariant – that a user can always unwind a full position – no longer holds. This flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that inspected the closing path and identified that the condition `if (isFromRebalancer && closeAmount == userPosition)` incorrectly references a pre‑PnL position variable. The bug is subtle because the check appears to protect against tiny residual positions, yet it only fails under the specific circumstance of dynamic PnL, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should recompute the user’s current position amount at the moment of closure and, when the requested close amount equals the full current position, bypass the minimum‑position restriction entirely. In conceptual terms, the fix aligns the validation with the real-time accounting state rather than a stale snapshot, restoring the guarantee that any participant can always exit a rebalanced position.

title: M-27 | Liquidatable Positions Can Be Opened
description:
In the validate open position flow if the maximum leverage is exceeded with the new startPrice the position and it's tick is recalculated. This new tick could be liquidatable in edge cases if the price between init and validate changed drastically but the position is still created.
The primary instance where this becomes a problem is when the liquidation tick actually increases when modified. In these situations a once healthy position can become liquidateable resulting in prior liquidation safeguards not being triggered and allowing liquidatable positions to be opened.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the position‑opening routine of the protocol, where a check for maximum leverage is performed before a new position is created. When the submitted start price would cause the leverage to exceed the configured maximum, the contract recalculates the position’s tick (the internal price index used for liquidation checks) and proceeds with creating the position. In edge cases where the market price changes dramatically between the initial price submission and the validation step, the recalculated tick can move into the liquidatable range. Because the contract does not re‑evaluate the liquidation condition after the tick has been adjusted, a position that was healthy at the moment of submission can become instantly liquidatable without triggering the built‑in liquidation safeguards. This flaw allows an attacker, for example, to manipulate the oracle price or trigger a large price swing right before the validation, open a position that is already under‑collateralised, and then be liquidated (or force others to liquidate) immediately after creation. The impact is that users may lose their collateral without the protocol’s protective checks intervening, and the protocol’s risk model is effectively bypassed, exposing it to capital loss and undermining trust. The issue is observed only when the price movement between the init and validate phases is extreme enough to raise the liquidation tick after the leverage adjustment, which makes it hard to reproduce in normal testing and easy to miss during code review. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the position‑opening flow, where the logic sequence was examined and the missing post‑adjustment liquidation check was identified. To remediate the problem, the contract should perform a liquidation eligibility test after any modification of the position’s leverage or tick, and if the position is found to be liquidatable, it must be liquidated immediately or rejected before creation. This adjustment restores the intended accounting invariants that a position must always remain above the liquidation threshold when it is opened, preserving user funds and protocol safety.

title: M-08 | removeBlockedPendingAction Extractable Value
description:
In the _removeBlockedPendingAction function when a ValidateClosePosition pending action is removed the entire closeBoundedPositionValue amount is added to the vault.
This means the trader loses their entire position value in the event that their close position action is stuck, even if they were nowhere near close to liquidation. This could cause significant loss for a trader which has a large position.
Furthermore, this creates a potentially large arbitrage opportunity. If a removal of a ValidateClosePosition pending action for a large position close is sitting in the mempool it would be potentially significantly profitable for an actor to front-run this transaction and initiate a deposit into the vault right before the removal takes place.
Because vault deposits only vary based on price action between initiation and validation the malicious actor would realize their corresponding value of the immediate vault balance increase from the removal of the pending close position action.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the logic of the _removeBlockedPendingAction routine that handles the removal of a ValidateClosePosition pending action. When such a pending close action is cleared, the implementation adds the entire closeBoundedPositionValue – the full notional value of the trader’s position – to the protocol vault instead of returning any portion to the trader or handling it according to the intended accounting rules. The root cause is an incorrect accounting step: the contract treats the pending action removal as a total liquidation and credits the vault with the full position value, regardless of whether the position was close to liquidation or whether the trader expected a partial refund. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who observes a pending ValidateClosePosition transaction that is stuck in the mempool. By front‑running the removal transaction and depositing funds into the vault immediately before the removal executes, the attacker can capture the sudden increase in vault balance that originates from the mis‑attributed position value. The impact is twofold: the affected trader loses the entire value of the position they intended to close later, effectively seeing their balance drop to zero or a large unexpected reduction, and the attacker gains a potentially large arbitrage profit equal to the mis‑credited amount. The issue manifests whenever a pending close action is removed while the position is not actually being liquidated, which can happen for large positions that become stuck due to network congestion or other delays. All traders with pending close actions and the protocol’s overall fund safety are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the pending‑action removal pathways and identified the unconditional transfer of the full position value to the vault. Because the vault balance increment appears to be a normal deposit, the bug can be subtle and may not be immediately visible without tracing the source of the credit. To remediate, the contract should redirect the position value to the trader’s specified address, allowing the protocol to decide how much, if any, should be donated to the vault via a dedicated donate function. In broader terms, this is a mis‑allocation of assets caused by an incorrect handling of pending actions, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and user expectations that a pending close does not automatically forfeit the entire position value.

title: M-09 | Tick Liquidation Penalty Cannot Be Reset
description:
In the _removeAmountFromPosition function the liquidationPenalty is not reset on the tick data after all positions have been removed.
Additionally, during the initiate open flow, the existing tick's liquidation penalty as the result of getTickLiquidationPenalty(s, data_.posId.tick) is used to re-assign the new liquidation penalty.
Thus even after all positions have been cleared from the tick, the latest configured liquidation penalty cannot be assigned to this tick.
bug_full:
The vulnerability concerns the persistence of a liquidation penalty value inside a tick data structure of the Smardex USDN protocol. When a user removes all positions from a tick via the internal _removeAmountFromPosition function, the contract fails to reset the tick's stored liquidationPenalty field to zero. Consequently, the stale penalty value remains attached to the tick even though no positions remain. Later, during the initiate‑open flow, the contract reads the existing tick’s liquidation penalty through getTickLiquidationPenalty and reassigns it to the newly opened position. Because the stale penalty was never cleared, the new position inherits an outdated penalty that does not reflect the current configuration. This is a classic state‑cleanup bug where leftover data leads to incorrect business logic.

The root cause lies in the omission of a reset operation after the last position is withdrawn. The code removes the amount but does not include a conditional branch that checks whether the tick has become empty and, if so, clears the penalty field. The bug manifests only after a tick becomes empty and is subsequently reused, which can be hard to notice during routine testing because most test scenarios keep positions open or do not reuse emptied ticks.

An attacker or a careless user can exploit the issue by deliberately emptying a tick that currently carries a high liquidation penalty and then immediately opening a new position in the same tick, expecting the penalty to be at its default (typically zero) or at a lower configured value. Instead, the contract will apply the previous high penalty, causing the new participant to over‑pay liquidation fees or suffer reduced returns. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is an unexpectedly high liquidation fee or a reduction in net profit where the protocol documentation promises a lower or configurable penalty. The impact includes financial loss for users opening positions after a tick reset, distortion of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, and erosion of trust because the fee model no longer behaves as advertised.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the tick management functions, where the auditor noted that the liquidationPenalty variable was never cleared after a full position sweep. The bug may escape detection in functional testing because the state appears correct when positions are continuously held, and the penalty remains consistent; only the edge case of empty‑then‑reuse reveals the fault.

To remediate the problem, the _removeAmountFromPosition function should include logic that detects when the tick’s total position size drops to zero and then explicitly writes a zero value to the liquidationPenalty field. This ensures that subsequent calls to getTickLiquidationPenalty return the default penalty, aligning the contract’s state with the intended business rules and preventing stale data from influencing new positions. In broader terms, the fix is to enforce proper cleanup of mutable state variables whenever they become irrelevant, a best practice for preventing similar accounting‑related bugs in decentralized finance contracts.

title: M-10 | Incorrect pendingBalanceVault Correction
description:
In the _removeBlockedPendingAction function the _pendingBalanceVault is corrected by computing the withdrawal amount without accounting for fees.
However upon the initiation of the withdrawal the _pendingBalanceVault was decremented by the withdrawal amount less fees.
As a result when a withdrawal action is removed with the _removeBlockedPendingAction function using cleanup as true the _pendingBalanceVault experiences an invalid net increase by the withdrawal fee amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the contract’s pending‑balance vault. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract reduces the _pendingBalanceVault by the net amount (withdrawal amount minus the protocol fee). Later, if the same withdrawal action is removed via the _removeBlockedPendingAction function with the cleanup flag set to true, the function adds back the full withdrawal amount without subtracting the fee that was already excluded from the original decrement. Consequently, the vault receives an extra credit equal to the fee that should have been retained, producing an invalid net increase in the pending balance. This defect arises because the fee component is omitted from the correction calculation, creating a mismatch between the debit performed at withdrawal time and the credit performed during cleanup. The flaw can be exploited by repeatedly triggering withdrawals that are subsequently cancelled, each time inflating the vault’s accounting by the fee amount. Over time, this artificial inflation may allow an attacker to withdraw more funds than legitimately owed, or cause the protocol’s internal accounting to diverge from the real token balances, potentially leading to liquidity shortfalls or inaccurate user balances. The issue manifests only when a withdrawal is both executed and later removed as a blocked pending action; normal successful withdrawals do not exhibit the problem. All participants who rely on the pending‑balance vault – including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the vault’s state no longer reflects the true amount of funds locked for pending withdrawals. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the withdrawal lifecycle, where the auditor noticed that the pending vault’s value increased after a cleanup operation, a behavior inconsistent with the intended fee retention logic. Because the fee is usually a small percentage, the discrepancy may be hidden in normal UI displays and only become evident after many cancellations, making it difficult to spot through casual testing. To remediate the issue, the correction applied in _removeBlockedPendingAction must mirror the original debit logic: the vault should be increased by the net withdrawal amount (withdrawal amount minus fee) or, alternatively, the fee component must be explicitly subtracted from the amount added back. This aligns the vault’s state with the contract’s accounting rules and eliminates the double‑counting of fees. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑handling or accounting bugs where state updates are not symmetrically applied, leading to double counting or loss of funds, and it violates basic financial invariants that the total of locked balances plus accrued fees must remain constant.

title: M-11 | _calcPositionSizeBonus Errant Token Amount
description:
The position size bonus for liquidator remuneration is computed with the _calcPositionSizeBonus function.
The bonus is based upon a difference in the current price and the liquidated ticks price and the documentation for the _calcPositionSizeBonus indicates that the resulting value is denominated in native ether.
However when the asset is wstEth and the WstEthOracleMiddleware is used the price will be for wstEth and thus the _calcPositionSizeBonus function will return a wstEth amount.
However this returned value is treated as native ether and converted to wstEth redundantly on line 108: wstETHRewards_ = _wstEth.getWstETHByStETH(totalRewardETH);
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the liquidator remuneration bonus for positions involving the wrapped staked ETH (wstETH) asset. The contract uses the internal function _calcPositionSizeBonus to compute a bonus that, according to the documentation, should be expressed in native ether (ETH). When the liquidation involves wstETH, the price supplied by the WstEthOracleMiddleware is denominated in wstETH, causing the _calcPositionSizeBonus function to return a quantity measured in wstETH instead of ETH. The subsequent code mistakenly treats this wstETH‑denominated amount as if it were ETH and invokes getWstETHByStETH(totalRewardETH) to convert it back to wstETH. This redundant conversion leads to a mismatch between the intended reward amount and the actual amount credited to the liquidator. Under the specific condition that a liquidated position contains wstETH, the protocol may credit liquidators either an inflated or incorrectly sized reward, effectively allowing the protocol’s treasury to lose funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of value through the liquidation pathway and noted the inconsistency between the documented units and the runtime units. The bug is subtle because the function signatures do not expose the underlying unit and the extra conversion appears syntactically correct, making the error easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should recognize that _calcPositionSizeBonus already yields a wstETH amount when the underlying asset is wstETH and should add this value directly to the liquidator’s reward without invoking getWstETHByStETH. Additionally, the maximum reward cap must be applied to the resulting wstETH amount to prevent over‑payment. This adjustment aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the bonus should be calculated in the same denomination as the collateral asset, preserving accounting consistency and preventing unintended fund drainage.

title: M-12 | Inaccurate Imbalance Check In _checkImbalanceLimitOpen
description:
The function _checkImbalanceLimitOpen inaccurately calculates the imbalance when initiating the opening of a new position because it does not account for the position fees deducted. This miscalculation could allow the system to enter a state where it is unbalanced beyond what should be possible after the action is validated.
This is because _checkImbalanceLimitOpen calculates the imbalanceBps by assuming that the balance of the vault is equal to just s._balanceVault + s._pendingBalanceVault and that the balance of the long side is equal to s._balanceLong + openCollatValue where openCollatValue is equal to params.amount.
However, openCollatValue does not reflect the true position value and should be instead equal to data_.positionValue (params.amount minus the position fee paid). On the other hand, currentVaultExpo should also include the position fee which can be calculated as params.amount - data_.positionValue. Do notice that this update is performed after _checkImbalanceLimitOpen check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate imbalance validation performed when a new position is opened. The contract checks that the vault’s long‑side exposure does not exceed a predefined limit, but the check calculates the exposure using the raw collateral amount supplied by the user instead of the net position value after the protocol fee has been deducted. Because the fee is subtracted from the user’s collateral only after the imbalance test, the test assumes the vault balance equals the sum of the stored vault balance and pending deposits, and that the long‑side balance equals the stored long balance plus the raw collateral amount. In reality, the true long‑side exposure should be the position value (collateral minus fee), and the vault’s total exposure should also include the fee amount. This mismatch can be exploited by opening positions with just enough collateral to pass the imbalance check while the hidden fee pushes the actual exposure over the limit. An attacker could repeatedly open such positions, causing the vault to become over‑exposed on one side, potentially leading to insufficient liquidity for opposite positions, failed liquidations, or loss of users’ funds. The issue surfaces only during the opening of a new position and only when the fee amount is sizable enough to tip the balance beyond the allowed threshold. All participants that rely on the vault’s balance invariants – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting guarantees are broken. The flaw was discovered during a code audit that examined the imbalance‑checking logic and identified that the fee contribution was omitted from the calculation. It may be hard to notice in normal operation because the vault’s recorded balances still appear consistent and the fee is small relative to typical positions, so the over‑exposure manifests only after many borderline openings. To remediate, the imbalance check should be updated to use the net position value (collateral minus fee) for the long‑side balance and to add the fee amount to the vault’s exposure calculation before the comparison. In broader terms, this is a classic accounting‑logic bug where a fee or tax is applied after a safety check, causing the system to think it is within limits while it is not, leading to potential fund disappearance or protocol instability.

title: M-13 | Exposure During Closure Unaccounted
description:
During the initiation of a close action, the position, or the portion of a position being removed, is effectively removed from the protocol as it is deducted from its corresponding tick and the cumulative balance and exposure accounting. However the USDN vault still serves as a counterparty for any PnL realized by the position in the period: [initiateClose, validateClose] and the user is still exposed to this price action as well. This may present an issue as the system will technically be more exposed to the long side than the imbalance tracking accounts for. As a result the corresponding imbalance mechanisms may not be used when they ought to.
Extracting value from a vault withdrawal (assuming 0 protocol fees):
1. Bob initiates close position. Bob provided empty Pyth data so Pyth.getPriceUnsafe() is called retrieving the price of Ether 59 minutes ago (price manually updated on-chain by Bob 59 minutes ago). The price retrieved is 1750 even though the current Ether price is 59 minutes later/now 1925. 14 minutes passes and Bob has not validated yet.
2. Alice initiates a withdrawal providing the actual current Pyth price of (1925 Ether price). We are assuming a 10% increment of Ether price in 1 hour 14 minutes.
3. Bob validates its position closure, and balanceVault is decreased based on the size of the long position closed and on the 10% price increase.
4. Alice validates withdrawal, but she still gets the assets respective to the vaultBalance at the time of the initiation. As the vaultBalance was higher, Alice unfairly gets more assets than she deserves. As at minute 60 + 14 the position value of Bob was already determined (it was already determined at minute 60 + 24 seconds) but Bob decided to delay his validation and because of this Alice received a higher amount of assets.
assetsReceivedWithExploit ................................... 1821845730818816586
assetsReceivedWithoutExploit ................................ 1813360204002626022
Increment of ................................................ 46794/10000000 (0.47%)
Value of the position closed compared to total long value ... 2%
Price change ................................................ 10% increment of Ether price
Extracting value from a vault deposit (assuming 0 protocol fees):
1. Bob initiates close position. Bob provided empty Pyth data so Pyth.getPriceUnsafe() is called retrieving the price of Ether 59 minutes ago (price manually updated onchain by Bob 59 minutes ago). The price retrieved is 1750 even though the current Ether price is 59 minutes later/now 1575. 14 minutes passes and Bob has not validated yet.
2. Alice initiates a deposit providing the actual current Pyth price of (1575 Ether price). We are assuming a 10% decrement of Ether price in 1 hour 14 minutes.
3. Bob validates its position closure, and balanceVault is increased based on the size of the long position closed and on the 10% price decrease.
4. Alice validates her deposit, but she still gets the shares respective to the vaultBalance at the time of the initiation. As the vaultBalance was lower, Alice unfairly gets more shares than she deserves. As at minute 60 + 14 the position value of Bob was already determined (it was already determined at minute 60 + 24 seconds) but Bob decided to delay his validation and because of this Alice received a higher amount of shares.
sharesReceivedWithExploit ...................................
sharesReceivedWithoutExploit ................................
Increment of ................................................ 45872/10000000 (0.46%)
Value of the position closed compared to total long value ... 2%
Price change ................................................ 10% decrement of Ether price
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from a mismatch between the protocol’s position‑closing logic and its exposure accounting. When a user initiates a close action, the smart contract immediately removes the position (or the portion being closed) from the tick‑level book and updates the cumulative balance and exposure counters as if the position no longer exists. However, the USDN vault that acts as the counter‑party for any profit‑and‑loss (PnL) remains exposed to the price movement of that position until the close is actually validated. Because the vault’s exposure is not reduced during the interval between initiateClose and validateClose, the imbalance tracking mechanisms, which rely on the current exposure, underestimate the protocol’s net long exposure. This creates a window in which an attacker can manipulate the timing of deposits or withdrawals to capture a larger share of the vault’s assets. In a typical exploit scenario, an attacker (Bob) initiates a close with stale oracle data, deliberately postpones the validation step, and meanwhile a second participant (Alice) performs a vault withdrawal or deposit using up‑to‑date price data. The vault balance used to calculate Alice’s share is still based on the higher (or lower) value recorded at the time of Bob’s initiation, causing Alice to receive more assets or shares than she is entitled to. The effect is a small but measurable profit – on the order of half a percent per transaction – that can accumulate over many closures. The issue is triggered only when the closing validation is delayed and another user interacts with the vault before that validation completes, and it can also affect liquidations that occur during the validation window because the liquidation logic values the position at the block of initiation, while the normal close values it at the current price. All participants who rely on fair accounting – depositors, withdrawers, long‑position holders, and the protocol itself – are impacted because the accounting invariants are violated and the vault may gradually lose funds. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the exposure counters did not reflect positions that had been logically removed but not yet validated. The bug is subtle because the discrepancy is hidden inside the accounting layer and does not surface as an obvious error in user‑visible balances; only a detailed comparison of vault state snapshots reveals the over‑allocation. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should either (a) include pending closures in the imbalance calculations until they are validated, ensuring that exposure is accurately reflected throughout the entire close lifecycle, or (b) compute the exact PnL at the moment of initiation and remove the position’s exposure entirely for the duration of the pending validation. Additionally, liquidation logic should be aligned with the closing logic so that both treat exposure consistently. By closing this accounting gap, the protocol will restore correct exposure tracking, prevent unfair enrichment of users, and protect the integrity of the vault’s asset pool.

title: M-14 | Innacurate isLiquidationPending Check In ValidateOpen
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the validation routine that determines whether a newly opened position should be marked for liquidation. The routine extracts a liquidation price that ignores the protocol‑defined liquidation penalty and then compares the market's last price against this incomplete price. If the last price is lower, the position is flagged as pending liquidation; otherwise the validation proceeds. The root cause is the use of an ineffective price calculation – the liquidation price without the penalty – rather than the full liquidation price that incorporates the penalty factor. Because of this mismatch, a market price that lies between the penalty‑free liquidation price and the true liquidation price (including the penalty) will not trigger the liquidation flag. Under those conditions a position that is, by protocol rules, already under‑collateralised remains unmarked, allowing it to stay open. An attacker or a trader can exploit this by timing a price move to land in that narrow window, thereby avoiding the intended liquidation. The impact is two‑fold: users may believe their position is safe while it is actually liquidatable, leading to unexpected loss when the price later crosses the true liquidation threshold; and the protocol's risk controls are weakened, potentially exposing the system to under‑collateralised positions and inaccurate accounting. The issue appears only when a non‑zero liquidation penalty exists and the last traded price falls between the two calculated thresholds. All participants who open leveraged positions are affected, as are the protocol’s liquidation engine and any downstream users relying on correct risk assessment. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the logic of the `_prepareValidateOpenPositionData` function. It can be difficult to notice because the price range where the error manifests may be small and price movements can be volatile, making the incorrect flagging appear as a rare anomaly. To remediate the problem, the validation should compute the effective liquidation price using the tick that includes the penalty (or otherwise apply the penalty factor) and compare the last market price against this corrected value. By doing so, any position that meets the true liquidation condition will be properly flagged, restoring the intended risk protection and preventing unexpected fund loss.

title: M-28 | Validate Deposit Ignores Funding
description:
The _validateDepositWithAction function uses either the available vault balance at init for the share price calculation or applies the PnL of the current price on it, whichever is bigger, but does not take funding into account.
Therefore, if the longs paid funding fees to the vault between initiation and validation of a deposit the user receives more assets than the user should and the other way around.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the deposit validation routine of the vault contract, specifically in the _validateDepositWithAction function. This routine calculates the number of assets a depositor should receive by comparing the vault's initial balance with the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) derived from the current price, and then selecting the larger of the two values. However, the calculation completely ignores any funding fees that have been accrued by the vault between the moment the vault was initialized and the moment a new deposit is being validated. Funding fees are typically paid by long position holders to the vault over time, and they represent a reduction in the vault’s net asset value. By omitting this component, the contract can allocate more assets to a depositor than the economic reality justifies when funding fees have been collected, and conversely can allocate fewer assets when the vault has incurred negative funding. The flaw is rooted in the assumption that the vault’s balance alone accurately reflects the value that should back new deposits, without adjusting for the dynamic funding adjustments that are integral to the protocol’s accounting model. An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by timing deposits to occur immediately after a large funding payment to the vault, thereby receiving an inflated amount of shares or tokens relative to the amount actually contributed. Conversely, a depositor who acts after the vault has suffered a funding loss may receive fewer assets than expected, effectively incurring an undisclosed loss. The impact includes mis‑allocation of economic value, potential over‑minting of shares, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants, leading to user confusion, inadvertent dilution of existing participants, and possible financial loss for the protocol if over‑minted assets are later withdrawn. The condition under which this occurs is any deposit operation that triggers _validateDepositWithAction after a funding fee event has been recorded but before the vault’s internal accounting is reconciled with that fee. All participants—depositors, existing token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the error distorts the share price and the perceived value of holdings. The issue was discovered during an audit review of the vault’s accounting logic, where the lack of a funding adjustment in the deposit path stood out as a logical inconsistency. It may be hard to notice because the discrepancy only manifests when funding events are sizable, and the contract typically reports only the number of assets minted, not the underlying funding balance, making the bug invisible in normal operation. To remediate, the deposit validation should incorporate the latest funding state—i.e., the net funding amount that has been added to or subtracted from the vault—into the asset‑allocation formula, ensuring that the number of shares issued accurately reflects both the vault’s balance and any recent funding adjustments. Conceptually, this classifies as a “funding‑aware accounting error” or “deposit mis‑allocation due to omitted state variables,” a pattern common in financial smart contracts where fee accruals are not reflected in user‑visible calculations. From the user’s perspective, the symptoms may include receiving more tokens than the deposited amount would suggest, seeing unexpected zero or negative balances after a deposit, or observing refunds that do not match the expected amount. The expectation that a deposit yields a proportional share of the vault’s assets is violated, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual token allocations.

title: FeeTaker is not accounting for unwrapWeth Feature
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the FeeTaker (and the related IntegratorFeeExtension) contract’s post‑interaction routine, which assumes that the asset received from the limit‑order protocol is always an ERC20 token. When a maker creates an order with the takerAsset set to WETH and enables the unwrapWeth flag, the protocol unwraps the WETH and forwards the taking amount as native ETH directly to the FeeTaker contract. The postInteraction function, however, unconditionally calls safeTransfer on the IERC20 interface of the takerAsset and therefore attempts to move WETH that no longer exists in the contract’s balance. Because the contract does not hold any WETH after the unwrapping, the ERC20 transfer reverts, leading to a transaction failure. In addition, the FeeTaker contract lacks a receive() payable fallback, so it is unable to accept the incoming ETH at all. This mismatch between the expected token type and the actual native‑currency flow causes the order execution to abort, the maker (or fee recipient) receives no funds, and users observe a silent loss of expected ETH or a reverted transaction with an ETHTransferFailed error. The issue manifests only when the unwrapWeth feature is active and the takerAsset is WETH; it does not affect orders that keep the asset as an ERC20 token. The affected parties include makers, takers, fee recipients, and any integrators that rely on the fee‑extraction logic. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the post‑interaction code, where the auditor noted that the contract never handles native ETH and that the unwrap logic in the order executor is not mirrored in the fee‑collection routine. The bug is a classic example of an asset‑type mismatch or improper accounting of wrapped versus unwrapped token flows, a class of error that often surfaces when contracts treat ETH and its ERC20 wrapper as interchangeable without explicit conversion handling. From a user perspective the symptoms are orders that revert despite providing sufficient ETH, makers receiving zero tokens, and feeRecipient addresses never getting paid. The root cause is the missing conditional branch for ETH and the absence of a payable receive function. To remediate the issue the contract should be extended to detect when the takerAsset has been unwrapped, accept ETH via a receive() function, and transfer ETH directly to the intended receiver and feeRecipient instead of attempting an ERC20 transfer of WETH. This change restores correct accounting, prevents transaction failures, and aligns the fee‑distribution logic with the actual asset type delivered by the protocol.

title: FeeTaker is incompatible with fee-on-transfer tokens
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the FeeTaker contract when it processes a taker asset that implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism. The contract's postInteraction function assumes that the full takingAmount specified in the order will be available in its token balance after the taker transfers the asset to the contract. However, fee‑on‑transfer tokens automatically deduct a portion of the transferred amount as a fee, so the contract actually receives only takingAmount minus the token's transfer fee. The code then attempts to forward the original takingAmount minus any protocol fee to the designated receiver using a safeTransfer call. Because the contract's balance is lower than the amount it tries to send, the safeTransfer reverts, causing the entire order execution to fail. This mismatch stems from the root cause that the contract does not verify the token balance before performing the outbound transfer, nor does it adjust the expected amount to account for transfer‑fee deductions. An attacker or any user can exploit this by submitting an order that uses a fee‑on‑transfer token as the taker asset, causing the contract to revert on every execution path that involves the postInteraction routine. The impact includes failed trades, potential lock‑up of user funds within the contract, and a degradation of protocol reliability, as users expecting a successful swap receive no tokens and may see their balances unchanged or erroneously reduced. The issue occurs whenever the FeeTaker contract receives a fee‑on‑transfer token, regardless of the specific fee amount, and it affects any participant who tries to execute orders with such tokens, including takers, makers, and the protocol itself. This bug was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the unconditional assumption about token balances. It can be hard to notice because fee‑on‑transfer tokens behave like standard ERC‑20 tokens from the interface perspective, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings before the revert; the failure only surfaces at runtime when the transfer amount is insufficient. To remediate, the contract should first read its token balance after the incoming transfer, compare it to the intended takingAmount, and cap the outbound transfer to the actual available balance, or otherwise reject fee‑on‑transfer tokens at the input validation stage. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of “incorrect handling of tokens with transfer fees”, a common accounting flaw where expected token amounts are not reconciled with actual on‑chain balances, leading to unexpected zeros, missing refunds, or funds that appear to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: MJR-1 Decrease in the amount of tokens during exchange due to arithmetic
description:
At the lines:
UnoswapV3Router.sol#L166 и
UnoswapV3Router.sol#L175
a number with the type uint256 is converted to a number with the type int256. This number is passed in the function parameter and, after conversion, is sent to the UniswapV3Pool contract.
But, if the value of the number is greater than the maximum value for the type int256, an arithmetic overflow will occur.
This is demonstrated by the following example: https://gist.github.com/mixbytes-audit/b471cc82105f856d1546ba638de20f4e.
For example, if you take the number 57896044618658097711785492504343953926634992332820282019728792003956564819970, then after the conversion you get the value-
We see a decrease in modulus of the initial value of the variable.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked type conversion in the UnoswapV3Router contract. A 256‑bit unsigned integer representing the amount of tokens to be exchanged is cast to a signed 256‑bit integer before being forwarded to the UniswapV3Pool. Because Solidity does not automatically guard against overflow when converting a uint256 to an int256, any value that exceeds the positive limit of int256 (2^255‑1) will wrap around to a negative or smaller positive number. This arithmetic overflow reduces the effective magnitude of the amount that the pool receives. When the router later uses this truncated value to calculate the amount of output tokens, the result is smaller than the user’s original request. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a swap transaction appears successful but the received token balance is unexpectedly reduced, sometimes to zero, even though the input amount was large. The issue is triggered only when the input amount crosses the int256 ceiling; typical small swaps are unaffected, making the bug hard to notice during routine testing. It affects any participant who attempts to swap large token quantities through the router, potentially causing loss of funds or incorrect accounting for the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a static analysis audit that flagged the implicit conversion and reproduced the effect with an extreme payload (e.g., 57896044618658097711785492504343953926634992332820282019728792003956564819970). Because the overflow manifests as a silent reduction of the transferred amount, it may be misinterpreted as a normal slippage or fee, especially when users are not monitoring the exact output. The underlying class of bug is an unchecked integer cast leading to overflow, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the amount sent to the pool equals the amount specified by the caller. The recommended mitigation is to insert an explicit bounds check before the conversion, ensuring that the unsigned amount is always less than or equal to the maximum positive value of int256. This prevents the overflow and preserves the intended token economics of the exchange.

title: MJR-2 Increase in the amount of tokens during exchange due to arithmetic
description:
At the lines:
UnoswapV3Router.sol#L170 и
UnoswapV3Router.sol#L179
the number with the type int256 is converted to the number with the type uint256. The number is taken with a minus sign.
But before that, there is no check that the number is less than 0.
If we take a small positive value and apply the transformation uint256(-amount) to it, we get a very large value due to arithmetic overflow.
This is demonstrated by the following example https://gist.github.com/mixbytes-audit/b471cc82105f856d1546ba638de20f4e.
For example, if you take the number 1000, then after conversion you get the value 115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457584007913129638936.
We see an increase in the initial value of the variable.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token exchange logic of the UnoswapV3Router contract where an amount stored as a signed 256‑bit integer (int256) is unconditionally cast to an unsigned 256‑bit integer (uint256) after applying a negation operator. Because there is no validation that the signed value is non‑negative before performing the conversion, a positive input amount is transformed into its two's‑complement negative representation and then reinterpreted as an extremely large unsigned number. For example, converting the positive integer 1,000 with uint256(-amount) yields a value on the order of 1.15e77, effectively inflating the amount by many orders of magnitude. This arithmetic overflow can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a small, seemingly innocuous amount to a swap function; the router will then calculate that it must transfer the gigantic unsigned amount, causing the contract to either attempt an impossible transfer, drain liquidity, or revert with out‑of‑gas errors. The impact includes potential theft of assets from the liquidity pool, denial of service for legitimate users, and incorrect accounting that violates the protocol’s financial guarantees. The condition occurs whenever the router processes a swap that involves the flawed conversion path, typically in the functions at lines 170 and 179 of UnoswapV3Router.sol. All participants interacting with the router – end‑users, liquidity providers, and downstream protocols – are affected because the bug can be triggered by any caller providing a malicious amount. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors observed that the code performed a signed‑to‑unsigned cast without a sign check and demonstrated the overflow with a concrete example. The problem is subtle because the conversion itself compiles without warnings, and the resulting huge number may not be immediately visible in logs, especially if the transaction reverts before observable state changes. To remediate, the code should explicitly verify that the amount is non‑negative before applying the negation and casting, and should skip the conversion entirely when the amount is already positive. This class of bug falls under unsigned‑integer overflow caused by improper handling of signed values, a common source of accounting errors where the system’s assumptions about non‑negative balances are broken, leading to situations where users expect a correct refund or token amount but receive either an astronomical value or none at all.

title: MJR-3 No validation of the value of the variable msg.value
description:
At the lines ClipperRouter.sol#L57-L68 processing of the input data is done before the exchange procedure.
ETH is not required to work with WETH and regular tokens. But the user can inadvertently transfer it.
In this case, the user will lose these ETH.
To prevent this from happening, you need to add checks before lines 60 and 67:
```solidity
require(msg.value == 0, "CL1IN: wrong msg.value");
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the omission of any validation on the amount of Ether supplied with calls to the aggregation router functions that are intended to operate solely with wrapped Ether (WETH) or standard ERC‑20 tokens. Because the contract does not enforce a zero‑value requirement (msg.value == 0) before processing the input data and initiating the exchange, a caller can unintentionally or maliciously attach Ether to the transaction. The router treats the incoming Ether as if it were part of the intended swap, but the subsequent logic never consumes or forwards that Ether, effectively leaving it locked in the contract or otherwise unrecoverable. This scenario violates the accounting assumptions of the protocol, which presumes that no raw Ether will be transferred during these calls. From a user perspective, the symptom is a reduction in the sender’s Ether balance without receiving any corresponding token or refund, leading to a perception that "funds disappeared" or that a "refund calculation error" has occurred. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit by MixBytes, which noted that the code processes input data before the exchange procedure but lacks a safeguard against accidental Ether transfer. The flaw can be hard to notice because the function’s purpose does not involve Ether handling, so developers may assume that the payable fallback is implicitly disabled, and no explicit revert is triggered when Ether is sent. The root cause is an input‑validation omission: the contract does not check that msg.value equals zero, which is required for functions that are supposed to be non‑payable. Exploitation is straightforward – any user (or an attacker) can submit a transaction with a non‑zero Ether value, and the contract will accept the Ether without error, resulting in loss of funds. The impact is a direct loss of the sender’s Ether, undermining user trust and potentially allowing malicious actors to trick users into sending Ether to a router that will not return it. To remediate the issue, developers should introduce an explicit require statement (require(msg.value == 0, "CL1IN: wrong msg.value")) before any state‑changing logic in the affected functions, thereby guaranteeing that the contract rejects any transaction that attempts to transfer Ether. This fix aligns the implementation with the intended business logic, restores proper accounting, and prevents accidental or intentional Ether loss.

title: M-29 | Sandwich Liquidations
description:
When liquidations happen a stepwise jump in the value of shares happens. Either the liquidated value will increase the share value or the liquidation reward and/or bad debt will decrease it.
As the init call of deposit/withdraw saves the current balances and calculates the share/asset amt received based on that, users are able to sandwich liquidations to make proﬁt or avoid losses.
Deposit for proﬁt:
• LP sees that a liquidation call will increase the vaults balance
• LP front runs the transaction and initiates a deposit to mint shares based on the old balance
• The liquidation call goes through
• The LP validates the deposit and is in instant proﬁt without price changes
Withdraw to avoid loss:
• LP sees that a liquidation call will decrease the vaults balance (bad debt)
• LP front runs the transaction and initiates a withdraw to burn shares based on the old balance
• The liquidation call goes through
• The LP validates the withdraw and avoided paying for the bad debt and socialized more loss to the other LPs by doing so
bug_full: The vulnerability is a sandwich‑type manipulation around vault liquidation events. The root cause lies in the way the vault computes share value: when a deposit or withdraw transaction is initiated, the contract records the current asset balance and uses that snapshot to calculate how many shares should be minted or burned. This calculation is performed before the liquidation logic is executed, and the resulting share price is not re‑evaluated after the liquidation changes the vault's total assets. Consequently, an attacker who can observe an upcoming liquidation can front‑run the vault by depositing just before the liquidation (to mint shares at the pre‑liquidation price) or withdrawing just before the liquidation (to burn shares at the pre‑liquidation price). In the first scenario, the liquidation inflates the vault's asset balance, so the attacker receives more assets for the same number of shares, turning an instant profit without any market price movement. In the second scenario, the liquidation would create bad debt and reduce the vault's assets; by withdrawing beforehand, the attacker avoids absorbing that loss, shifting the burden to remaining liquidity providers. The impact is a misallocation of value: the attacker gains assets they are not entitled to, while other participants suffer reduced balances or increased exposure to bad debt. This condition occurs whenever the protocol allows external liquidation calls to modify the vault's total assets between the snapshot taken at deposit/withdraw initiation and the final share accounting. It primarily affects liquidity providers who trust the vault's share accounting to reflect true proportional ownership. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state updates and identified that the share‑valuation step does not account for pending liquidation effects. The bug is subtle because the vault’s external interface shows correct balances after each transaction, and the profit or loss avoidance manifests only for participants able to front‑run, making it difficult to notice without analyzing transaction ordering. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “price‑manipulation through state‑snapshot inconsistencies” or “front‑running sandwich attacks on share‑minting/burning logic.” From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected profit on a deposit (receiving more tokens than expected) or an unexpected reduction in loss on a withdraw (receiving a full amount while the vault’s balance has dropped). The protocol’s business logic, which assumes that each share always represents a proportional claim on the vault’s assets, is violated because the share price is artificially decoupled from the actual asset pool during a liquidation. To remediate, the share‑valuation step should be performed after any operation that can change the total assets, or the contract should lock the vault’s state during a liquidation, preventing deposits and withdrawals from being processed until the liquidation completes, thereby ensuring that share minting and burning always reflect the true post‑liquidation asset balance.

title: M-30 | Validate Withdrawal Ignores Funding
description:
The _validateWithdrawalWithAction function uses either the available vault balance at init for the share price calculation or applies the PnL of the current price on it, whichever is less, but does not take funding into account.
Therefore if the vault paid funding fees to the longs between initiation and validation of a withdrawal the user receives more assets than the user should.
In certain edge cases this can also lead to a underﬂow DoS of the _validateWithdrawalWithAction function as this calculated withdrawal amount is later decreased from the _balanceVault where funding was applied to.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal validation routine of a vault contract. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the _validateWithdrawalWithAction function calculates the amount of assets to be returned based on the vault's balance at the time of initiation and the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) of the current market price, selecting the smaller of the two values. However, the calculation completely ignores any funding payments that the vault may have distributed to long positions between the moment the withdrawal request is created and the moment the withdrawal is validated. Because funding fees are subtracted from the vault’s total assets, omitting them from the share‑price computation can cause the contract to credit the withdrawing user with more tokens than the vault actually holds. In the opposite edge case, when the funding fee is larger than the amount that the algorithm would otherwise deduct, the computed withdrawal amount can become negative, triggering an arithmetic underflow that aborts the function and effectively disables further withdrawals (a denial‑of‑service condition). The flaw originates from an incomplete accounting model: the contract assumes that the vault balance remains static with respect to funding, which is not true for perpetual‑style markets where funding is applied continuously. An attacker or any user who times a withdrawal request to coincide with a large funding payout can exploit the bug by receiving an inflated payout, while honest users may experience failed withdrawals if the underflow path is taken. The impact includes unintended loss of assets from the protocol (over‑payment) and potential service interruption (withdrawal lock‑out), affecting all participants who hold positions in the vault, including liquidity providers and traders. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting flow with the actual implementation and identified that funding adjustments are never reflected in the withdrawal share‑price formula. The problem can be subtle because the contract still appears to honor withdrawal requests and the discrepancy may only manifest when funding events are sizable, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the withdrawal calculation should incorporate the latest cumulative funding amount (or the net funding delta since the withdrawal request) when determining the user’s entitled share of the vault assets, ensuring that the accounting remains consistent with the actual balance. Alternatively, the protocol could explicitly document that withdrawals are calculated without funding considerations, but this approach would require clear communication to users. In short, the bug is a classic case of “incorrect accounting for external state updates” that leads to over‑payment or underflow, violating the core economic guarantees of the vault and causing funds to disappear or withdrawals to fail unexpectedly.

title: M-1 Possible arithmetic overﬂow
description:
At the line UserAccounting.sol#L29 the number with the type int256 is converted to the number with the type uint256. The number is taken with a minus sign.
But before that, there is no check that the number is less than 0.
If we take a small positive value and apply the transformation uint256(-amount) to it, we get a very large value due to arithmetic overﬂow.
For example, if you take number 1000, then after conversion you get value 115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457584007913129638936.
bug_full: The issue is an unchecked conversion from a signed 256‑bit integer (int256) to an unsigned 256‑bit integer (uint256) that can produce an arithmetic overflow. In the examined contract, a variable called amount is stored as an int256, but the code later casts it to uint256 without first verifying that the value is non‑negative. Because two's‑complement representation is used, a negative signed integer is interpreted as a very large positive unsigned integer when converted. For example, casting the signed value 1000 with a unary minus (‑1000) to uint256 yields the number 115792089237316195423570985008687907853269984665640564039457584007913129638936, which is essentially the maximum uint256 value minus 999. This overflow can be exploited by an attacker who can supply a small positive amount that, after the erroneous negation and cast, becomes a massive token amount. If the contract subsequently uses this inflated value for accounting, token transfers, or reward calculations, the attacker may receive far more tokens than intended, or the protocol’s accounting can be corrupted, leading to loss of funds, inaccurate balances, or denial of service. The vulnerability manifests whenever the function that performs the conversion is called with any amount that could become negative after the internal logic (e.g., a subtraction that makes the amount negative) and the code does not guard against that condition. Users of the protocol, token holders, and any downstream contracts that rely on the accounting logic are affected because they may see unexpected balance increases, erroneous payouts, or the protocol’s token pool being drained. The flaw was discovered during a manual review of the contract’s arithmetic operations, where the auditor noted the missing sign check before the cast. It can be hard to notice because the conversion compiles without error and the resulting value, although large, may not immediately cause a revert; instead, it silently skews the accounting. The appropriate remediation is to add an explicit require or assert that the signed value is >= 0 before casting, and to avoid performing a negative‑to‑unsigned conversion altogether. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of unchecked signed‑to‑unsigned type conversions that lead to integer overflow or underflow bugs. From a user perspective, the symptoms could appear as a sudden, inexplicable jump in token balance, a refund that is far larger than expected, or a transaction that seems to succeed while the protocol’s total supply is suddenly inflated. The bug violates the protocol’s financial logic, which assumes that amounts are always non‑negative and that conversions preserve the intended magnitude. Correcting the check restores the invariant that only non‑negative amounts are represented as unsigned integers, preventing the creation of unintended token quantities.

title: M-2 Gas overﬂow during iteration (DoS)
description:
Each iteration of the cycle requires a gas ﬂow.
A moment may come when more gas is required than it is allocated to record one block. In this case, all iterations of the loop will fail.
Affected lines:
• ERC20Farmable.sol#L70
• ERC20Farmable.sol#L117
• ERC20Farmable.sol#L121
• ERC20Farmable.sol#L137
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service condition that arises from an unbounded iteration over dynamic arrays in the ERC20Farmable contract. Each iteration of the reward‑distribution loop consumes a fixed amount of gas, and the contract does not enforce any upper bound on the number of elements that may be stored in the arrays it traverses. When the number of farm entries grows large enough that the cumulative gas required for a single call exceeds the block gas limit, the transaction runs out of gas and all loop iterations revert. This situation can be triggered when an attacker or a large number of legitimate users add many farming positions, inflating the array size beyond what can be processed in one block. The result is that any subsequent attempt to claim, harvest, or otherwise interact with the farming logic fails with an out‑of‑gas error, effectively locking users out of their rewards and preventing the protocol from performing its accounting. The issue is observed only after the array reaches a size that pushes the total gas consumption over the per‑block limit, so it may not be noticed during early testing when the array is small. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor identified loops at lines 70, 117, 121 and 137 that lack checks on the maximum possible number of elements. From a user’s perspective, transactions that previously succeeded start reverting with "out of gas" messages, the UI shows no reward being returned, or the balance appears unchanged despite a claim attempt. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded loop or iteration‑related gas exhaustion vulnerabilities, which violate the business logic assumption that reward calculations can be performed atomically for all participants. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a hard limit on the array length or redesign the logic to process entries in bounded batches, possibly using a pagination scheme or a pull‑based model where each user claims their own reward individually, thereby guaranteeing that any single transaction stays within the gas budget.

title: M-31 | Remove Pending Position Price Can Be Stale
description: The _removeBlockedPendingAction uses the _lastPrice to calculate the value of the stuck open long position. As this function does not update the price before performing this action it can potentially be stale.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way a smart contract calculates the value of a pending long position that becomes blocked and must be removed. The internal helper function _removeBlockedPendingAction relies on a variable called _lastPrice, which stores the most recent price that was recorded at a previous point in time. Because the function does not query the price oracle or otherwise refresh the price before performing the removal calculation, it may use a stale price that no longer reflects the current market value. This stale‑price usage is a classic instance of a time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) or stale‑data bug, where the contract’s accounting logic is based on outdated information. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the removal of a blocked pending position after a significant price movement. When the contract computes the position’s value with the stale _lastPrice, it may either credit the user with more assets than they are entitled to, or, more commonly, credit them with less, leading to an under‑payment. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a missing or reduced refund: a user expects to receive the value of their open long position after it is cleared, but the amount returned is unexpectedly low or, in edge cases, the balance may even appear to drop to zero. The issue impacts any participant who holds pending positions, the protocol’s accounting accuracy, and ultimately the integrity of funds managed by the contract. It was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the function never updates the price before using it, a logic oversight that is easy to miss because price values are stored internally and not exposed to the UI. The bug is difficult to observe in normal operation because the discrepancy only appears after the price has changed notably and the removal function is called, which may be infrequent. The recommended remediation is to fetch the current market price from the trusted price source at the start of _removeBlockedPendingAction and use that fresh price for all subsequent calculations, ensuring that the protocol’s financial logic always reflects the latest market state. By guaranteeing price freshness, the contract will correctly honor refunds, maintain accurate accounting, and prevent users from experiencing unexpected loss of funds due to stale data.

title: M-32 | Neutral Price Used In Init Functions
description:
All init functions use the lastPrice (the latest neutral price) for calculations, while the validation functions use prices that were adjusted by the pyth interval up or down to round against the user.
Therefore all the checks and temporary state updates at init are most likely wrong at validation time.
Here are a few examples:
• Slippage checks
• Imbalance checks
• The temporary position between init and validate open position
• SDEX calculations
• When a stuck open position action is removed by the admin the user receives the position value based on a unadjusted start price
These examples will lead to users entering a position at a price they explicitly did not agree too, Protocol reaching an imbalanced state and Incorrect amount of SDEX being burned.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a mismatch between the price that is used when a trade is initially recorded (the init functions) and the price that is later verified during validation. All init functions rely on the contract's stored lastPrice, which represents the most recent neutral price supplied by the oracle. In contrast, the validation functions apply the pyth interval adjustment—an upward or downward rounding step that aligns the price with the user's expected execution range. Because the init phase does not incorporate this adjustment, every check that is performed immediately after a user opens or modifies a position—such as slippage limits, imbalance detection, temporary position accounting, and the calculation of the SDEX token amount to be minted or burned—uses a price that is subtly different from the one the validation phase will later enforce. When the validation step runs, it compares the user‑provided parameters against the adjusted price, causing the previously stored temporary state to be inaccurate. This mismatch can lead to several concrete problems: a user may believe they are opening a position at a price they approved, yet the contract will settle the position at a slightly worse price, effectively taking away the user’s expected slippage margin; the protocol’s internal accounting may become imbalanced because the recorded position size does not match the validated price; the amount of SDEX that is burned or minted can be computed on an incorrect basis, resulting in token supply drift; and when an administrator forces the removal of a stuck open position, the refund calculation uses the unadjusted neutral price, so the user receives less value than they are entitled to. From the user’s perspective this manifests as unexpected zero or reduced balances, refunds that are lower than anticipated, or transaction reverts due to failed validation checks that were not visible at the time of submission. The issue is difficult to spot because the UI typically displays the neutral price, and the discrepancy only becomes apparent after the contract internally applies the interval adjustment during validation, a step that is not exposed to the front‑end. The root cause is a logical inconsistency in the contract’s price handling strategy: two distinct code paths consume different price representations for the same logical operation. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the code paths of the init and validation functions and identified that the adjusted price was never propagated to the init logic. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute and store the adjusted price in the init functions whenever that same price is later used for validation, thereby guaranteeing that all checks, temporary state updates, and token accounting are performed against a single, consistent price reference. This change restores the intended business logic that users’ trade parameters are evaluated against the price they actually consented to, preserves protocol balance, and ensures accurate SDEX accounting.

title: M-33 | Funding Rate Affected By Updates
description:
In the _fundingPerDay function the resulting _fundingPerDay value is a function of the current imbalance added to the existing EMA value. This resulting _fundingPerDay value is then factored into the EMA.
The additive nature of the current skew to the current EMA for the resulting _fundingPerDay value means that the more updates occur in a given timeframe the higher the funding will be.
In the attached PoC shows that in a week period the funding is 34% greater if there is an update every day versus if there are only updates at the beginning and end of the period.
This is unexpected as the amount of updates should not affect the funding amount paid or the funding rate and instead this should be based purely on the skew experienced and the time of imbalance.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract calculates the daily funding rate using an exponential moving average (EMA) of market imbalance. Instead of feeding the current imbalance as a single new data point into the EMA, the implementation adds the current skew directly to the existing EMA value before computing the fundingPerDay amount. Because the additive term scales with the number of times the funding function is called, each additional update in a given period artificially inflates the resulting funding rate. A simulation showed that when updates occur daily over a week, the funding paid out is roughly 34 % higher than when updates happen only at the start and end of the same period, even though the underlying imbalance and elapsed time are identical. This discrepancy arises from a logical flaw: the skew is double‑counted—once in the EMA update and again in the funding calculation—making the funding amount a function of update frequency rather than solely of the magnitude of the imbalance and the time elapsed. An attacker or any participant who can trigger frequent updates (for example by submitting small trades or synthetic transactions) can exploit this behavior to cause the protocol to overpay funding, draining the funding pool or causing unintended redistribution of funds. The impact is that users may receive larger or smaller funding payments than contract specifications dictate, breaking the economic guarantees of the protocol and potentially leading to loss of capital for the pool or other participants. The issue manifests whenever the fundingPerDay function is invoked multiple times within a short interval, which is common in contracts that update funding on every block or trade. It affects all users who hold positions that are subject to funding payments, as well as the protocol itself, because the accounting assumptions about fair, imbalance‑based compensation are violated. The flaw was discovered during an audit by analyzing the relationship between update frequency and funding outcomes and observing a systematic deviation from expected values. It is subtle because the funding rate still appears to move in the correct direction; only a detailed comparison of scenarios with differing update counts reveals the inflation, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The correct remedy is to treat the term derived from the current imbalance (numerator² × _fundingSF / denominator²) as the latest observation fed into the EMA, without adding it to the EMA for the intermediate fundingPerDay calculation. The EMA should then be used directly to compute the funding amount, eliminating the double‑counting and ensuring that the funding rate depends only on the actual skew and time, not on how often the function is called. This class of bug is an EMA misuse that leads to double‑counting of stateful metrics, a common pattern where aggregations are incorrectly combined, resulting in time‑dependent inflation of financial calculations.

title: M-34 | Old Vault Validations Swing USDN Price
description:
https://github.com/GuardianAudits/usdn-1/blob/7462fc4d1b886129a4091dfc91ff5304d1d3a970/src/UsdnProtocol/libraries/UsdnProtocolVaultLibrary.sol#L576
The behavior of the deposit ﬂow is such that a user’s shares are not minted and their deposited amount is not added to the vault balance until validation time. This however causes several issues related to funding and the price of USDN. The minting of shares is an activity that changes the price of shares when the ratio used to mint is stale.
