<https://github.com/vetherasset/vaderprotocol-contracts/pull/159/commits/2f69f8317ce98846fbe227a3bf6ca1b644d01ff2#diff-5de3130299a0ddc914d7a906802a4cc093ed18d7a89c52a4aafefc8a11ac3f54R193>
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the `deploySynth()` function of the Pools contract, where a guard is intended to prevent the core tokens VADER and USDV from being used as parameters for synthetic token deployment. The guard uses a `require` statement with the logical expression `token != VADER || token != USDV`. Because the disjunction (`||`) evaluates to true for any possible token value—since a token can never be equal to both VADER and USDV simultaneously—the check always passes. Consequently, an attacker can supply either VADER or USDV as the token argument and successfully invoke the factory’s `deploySynth()` function. This logical error violates a fundamental protocol invariant that synthetic assets must be distinct from the underlying native assets. When a synth is created for VADER or USDV, accounting logic that assumes synths represent non‑core assets becomes inconsistent, leading to incorrect balance calculations, potential double‑counting of value, and scenarios where funds become unreachable or are inadvertently transferred to the wrong contract. The exploit can be performed at any time an authorized or malicious user calls `deploySynth()`, requiring no special privileges beyond the ability to invoke the function. The issue was identified during a security audit by Code4rena, where the logical condition was flagged as incorrectly using the OR operator instead of the AND operator. The bug is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the require statement appears to perform a validation, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate the problem, the condition should be rewritten to `require(token != VADER && token != USDV);`, ensuring that both core tokens are explicitly rejected. In generic terms, this is a classic case of an improper logical condition leading to an authorization bypass, which may cause protocol‑wide state corruption and fund loss. From a user’s perspective, attempts to interact with a synth that was mistakenly deployed for VADER or USDV may result in unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or failed trades, contradicting the expectation that the newly created synth would be functional and tradable.

title: Allowing duplicated anchors could cause bias on anchor price.
description:
In `Router.sol`, the setup of the five anchors can be interrupted by anyone adding a new anchor due to the lack of access control of the `listAnchor` function. Also, duplicate anchors are allowed. If the same anchor is added three times, then this anchor biases the result of `getAnchorPrice`.

Referenced code: [Router.sol#L245-L252](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader/blob/main/vader-protocol/contracts/Router.sol#L245-L252)

PoC: [Link to PoC](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1W3jhlWIIh7FxTLZET3z49yA0DBvlbcPg?usp=sharing) See the file `200_listAnchor.js` for a PoC of this attack. To run it, use `npx hardhat test 200_listAnchor.js`.

Recommend only allowing `listAnchor` to be called from the deployer by adding a `require` statement. Also, check if an anchor is added before by `require(_isCurated == false)`.

Deployer will list the anchors, seems highly unlikely they will get griefed in practice. Severity: 1
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the router contract that maintains a list of price anchors used to compute the reference price for the protocol. The function responsible for registering these anchors, listAnchor, lacks any form of access control, allowing any external account to invoke it and append a new anchor to the internal array. Moreover, the implementation does not verify whether an anchor has already been added, which means the same oracle address can be inserted multiple times. When the price is later derived through getAnchorPrice, the contract aggregates the values of all stored anchors, typically by averaging them. Because duplicate entries are counted separately, an attacker who adds the same anchor repeatedly can overweight that oracle’s quote, biasing the resulting price upward or downward depending on the attacker’s intent. This bias can manifest as users receiving unexpectedly high or low trade rates, refunds that are smaller than expected, or balances that appear to shrink after a transaction. The issue becomes exploitable whenever the router is in its initialization phase or when anchors are later updated, as there is no restriction preventing malicious parties from flooding the list with duplicated entries. The affected parties include any user or liquidity provider that relies on the protocol’s price feed, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer from distorted accounting, loss of trust, and potential financial loss. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined function visibility and state‑mutation patterns and identified that listAnchor is public and that the contract does not enforce uniqueness of entries. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the price deviation may be subtle, especially if the duplicated oracle’s price is close to the median; only a systematic analysis of the anchor array reveals the redundancy. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict listAnchor to a trusted role (e.g., the deployer or an admin) using an access‑control modifier, and it should include a check that prevents an anchor from being added more than once, for example by maintaining a mapping of already‑registered addresses and requiring that a new entry is not already curated. By enforcing these constraints, the protocol restores the intended unbiased price calculation and aligns the observed outcomes with user expectations of fair pricing.

title: Transfer fee avoidance
description: The `Vether4.addExcluded()` function on mainnet (0x4Ba6dDd7b89ed838FEd25d208D4f644106E34279) allows a user to exclude an address from transfer fees for a cost of 128 VETH. By exploiting the conditions in which fees are taken, it is possible to set up a contract for a once-off cost in which all users can use to avoid transfer fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an fee‑avoidance flaw in the token contract that permits any user to add an arbitrary address to a fee‑exempt list by calling a public function that costs a fixed amount of 128 VETH. The root cause is the contract’s fee‑exclusion logic, which does not restrict who can invoke the addExcluded() routine nor enforce any access control beyond the one‑time payment, and the transfer routine simply skips fee calculation for any address present in the exemption list. An attacker can therefore create a contract that calls addExcluded() once, pays the 128 VETH, and then advertises the newly exempt address to other participants; any user who transfers tokens through that address will see the usual fee deduction disappear. Exploitation proceeds by (1) paying the exclusion fee, (2) registering the attacker's address as fee‑free, (3) forwarding or allowing other participants to route their token transfers through the exempt address, and (4) observing that the protocol’s fee mechanism does not deduct the expected percentage, effectively diverting revenue away from the token’s economic model. The impact is a loss of expected fee revenue, distortion of tokenomics, and potential erosion of trust because users may notice that their transfers no longer incur the advertised fee, while the protocol’s fee collector receives less than intended. This condition manifests whenever a transfer originates from or is routed through an address that has been added to the exemption list, which can happen at any time after the one‑off payment. All token holders, especially those relying on fee‑based funding for the protocol’s sustainability, are affected. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the fee handling code, where the auditor observed that the addExcluded() function lacked the usual role‑based restrictions and that the transfer path did not re‑validate fee eligibility. The flaw can be subtle because the lack of a fee appears only in the transaction logs; the transfer succeeds and the balance updates as normal, but the fee field is simply omitted, making it easy to miss without detailed event analysis. To remediate, the contract should restrict the addition of fee‑exempt addresses to a privileged role (such as governance), enforce a per‑address or per‑transaction verification before bypassing fees, and possibly remove the public, paid‑for exemption mechanism altogether. In essence, this is a classic example of an "unrestricted privilege escalation" within a fee‑collection module, where an openly callable function grants a financial advantage that contradicts the intended accounting logic of the token system.

title: Init function can be called by everyone
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unprotected initialization function that can be invoked by any external account after the contract has been deployed. Because the init routine is declared as public and lacks any access‑control restriction, a third party can call it before the intended deployer runs the same call. The root cause is the missing check that the caller is the contract owner or that the function has already been executed, which results in a classic initialization race condition. An attacker who manages to submit a transaction to the init method in the narrow window between deployment and the legitimate initialization can supply arbitrary constructor‑like parameters, effectively locking the contract into an unusable state or configuring it with malicious addresses. Once the contract is initialized with incorrect data, subsequent calls to the protocol’s public functions either revert, return zero values, or operate with wrong routing information, making the system appear broken from a user’s perspective – users may see their balances unchanged, withdrawals failing, or “no response” from the contract UI. The impact is that the deployed instance becomes dead and must be redeployed, incurring additional gas costs and potentially disrupting the overall protocol if the compromised contract is a core component. In extreme scenarios, where the attacker can set privileged addresses (for example, a vault or router), they could divert funds or prevent proper accounting, leading to significant financial damage. The condition under which the bug manifests is the brief period immediately after contract creation, before the authorised deployer executes the initialization. Any account with the ability to submit a transaction in this window could exploit the flaw; the likelihood is low because it requires precise timing and coordination, but the damage can be critical. The issue was identified during a formal audit by the Code4rena team, who noted that all contracts in the repository expose an init function without restrictions. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the init function appears to follow a typical pattern, making it easy to overlook the absence of an ownership check. To remediate, the init function should be guarded by an access‑control modifier that permits only the deployer (or a designated admin) to call it, and it should enforce a one‑time execution guard (e.g., an initialized flag) to prevent re‑initialization. This class of bug, often termed an “unprotected initializer” or “missing initializer access control,” violates basic design assumptions that initialization is a privileged, single‑use operation and can cause the protocol’s accounting logic to be bypassed or corrupted.

title: Pool functions can be called before initialization in _`init_`
description:
All the external/public functions of `Pools.sol` can be called by other contracts even before `Pools.sol`contract is initialized. This can lead to exceptions, state corruption or incorrect accounting in other contracts, which may require redeployment of said contract.

Recommend using a factory pattern that will deploy and initialize atomically to prevent front-running of the initialization,

OR

Given that contracts are not using `delegatecall` proxy pattern, it is not required to use a separate `init()` function to initialize parameters when the same can be done in a constructor. If the reason for doing so is to get the deployment addresses of the various contracts, which may not all be available at the same time, then consider rearchitecting to create a “globals” contract which can hold all the globally required addresses of various contracts. see [Maple protocol’s](https://github.com/maple-labs/maple-core/blob/develop/contracts/MapleGlobals.sol) for example.

OR

Prevent external/public functions from being called until after initialization is done by checking initialization state tracked by the inited variable.

**[strictly-scarce (vader) dipsuted](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader-findings/issues/114#issuecomment-830598388):**

<https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader-findings/issues/39>

Same general comments apply to this issue as with issue #18, but it is a separate type of exploit that would be slightly less detectable. This increase in risk is balanced against the exploit being much harder to effect and the likely impact being lower.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a pool contract whose external and public functions are callable before the contract’s initialization routine has been executed. Because the contract separates the deployment step from an init() function and does not enforce a guard that blocks any state‑changing calls until the init flag is set, an adversary can interact with the pool during the narrow window after deployment but before the intended initialization transaction. This premature interaction can trigger unexpected exceptions, corrupt internal bookkeeping, or produce incorrect accounting results, because the contract’s internal variables (such as address references, fee parameters, or balance mappings) are still in their default, uninitialized state. When a function that assumes those variables are set is executed early, it may read zero or garbage values, write to the wrong storage slots, or revert due to failed require checks. The impact includes denied service for legitimate users, potential loss or misallocation of funds, and the need to redeploy the affected pool contract to restore correct operation. The issue manifests only when the contract has been deployed but not yet initialized, which is typically a short period that can be targeted by front‑running bots or malicious contracts that observe the deployment transaction. All participants that rely on the pool – users, liquidity providers, and downstream protocols – are affected because the pool’s accounting logic is foundational to the protocol’s financial guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the contract’s lifecycle management and noted the absence of an initialization‑state check on every external entry point. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the contract behaves correctly after a proper init call; the problem only appears under the specific timing condition of premature calls. To remediate the issue, the contract should either perform all required setup inside the constructor, eliminating the need for a separate init function, or enforce an atomic deployment‑and‑initialization step using a factory pattern that guarantees the init call cannot be front‑run. Alternatively, a simple modifier that checks a stored boolean (e.g., `inited`) before allowing any external call can be added, or the architecture can be re‑designed to centralize address configuration in a globals contract. In each case the core fix is to prevent any external interaction before the contract’s critical state variables have been deliberately set, thereby restoring the expected invariant that the pool’s accounting logic only operates on fully initialized data.

title: `changeDAO` should be a two-step process in Vader.sol
description:
`changeDAO()` updates DAO address in one-step. If an incorrect address is mistakenly used (and voted upon) then future administrative access or recovering from this mistake is prevented because `onlyDAO` modifier is used for `changeDAO()`, which requires `msg.sender` to be the incorrectly used DAO address (for which private keys may not be available to sign transactions). See [finding #6 from Trail of Bits audit of Hermez Network](https://github.com/trailofbits/publications/blob/master/reviews/hermez.pdf).

Recommend using a two-step process where the old DAO address first proposes new ownership in one transaction; and then, accepts ownership from the newly proposed DAO address in a second transaction. A mistake in the first step can be recovered by granting with a new correct address again before the new DAO address accepts ownership. Ideally, there should also be a timelock enforced before the new DAO takes effect.

A lot has to go wrong to get to this point, so disagree with severity (funds not at risk).

Two step-process seems wise though.

Risk lowered because of the extremely low probability
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the governance control flow in the Vader smart contract, specifically the `changeDAO()` function that updates the DAO address in a single transaction. The function is protected by an `onlyDAO` modifier, which requires the caller to be the current DAO address. Because the address update occurs in one step, an erroneous address can be introduced through a mistaken vote or input. If the new address is wrong – for example, an address for which no private key is known – the contract will thereafter require that address to call `changeDAO()` for any future update. Consequently, the protocol loses the ability to change its administrative authority, effectively locking out any further DAO‑controlled actions such as upgrades, parameter changes, or emergency shutdowns. This situation can occur only after a governance proposal that mistakenly sets an invalid DAO address is executed, and it remains hidden until an attempt is made to modify the DAO again. The impact is a loss of governance control, which may prevent recovery from bugs, upgrade paths, or security incidents, and could ultimately erode user confidence in the protocol. The issue was identified during an external audit that referenced similar findings in the Hermez Network review, where the same single‑step address change pattern was highlighted. The problem is difficult to notice because the function executes successfully and does not emit an error; the contract appears normal until a later administrative action fails due to the missing private key. The recommended mitigation is to replace the one‑step process with a two‑step handover: the current DAO proposes a new DAO address in the first transaction, and the proposed address must explicitly accept ownership in a second transaction, optionally after a timelock. This design allows the old DAO to correct an erroneous proposal before the new address finalizes control, preserving the ability to recover administrative rights. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of governance handover flaws where immediate address replacement without confirmation can lead to irrevocable loss of control, violating the protocol’s assumption that DAO governance remains always reachable and updatable.

title: Copy-paste bug leading to incorrect harvest rewards in Vault.sol
description:
The conditional in `calcReward()` function uses the same code in both if/else parts with repeated use of `reserveUSDV`, `reserveVADER` and `getUSDVAmount` leading to incorrect computed value of `_adjustedReserve` in the else part.

This will affect harvest rewards for all users of the protocol and lead to incorrect accounting. Protocol will break and lead to fund loss.

Recommend changing variables and function calls from using USDV to VADER in the else part of the conditional which has to return the adjusted reserves when synth is not an asset i.e. an anchor and therefore base is VADER. L144 should be changed to: `uint _adjustedReserve = iROUTER(ROUTER).getVADERAmount(reserveUSDV()) + reserveVADER();`

Funds are not at-risk, just that some users will get less rewards, some will get more.

Recommend: 2

Our decision matrix for severity:

0: No-risk: Code style, clarity, off-chain monitoring (events etc), exclude gas-optimisations 1: Low Risk: UX, state handling, function incorrect as to spec 2: Funds-Not-At-Risk, but can impact the functioning of the protocol, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements 3: Funds can be stolen/lost directly, or indirectly if a valid attack path shown that does not have handwavey hypotheticals.

Recommended: 2
bug_full: The vulnerability is a copy‑paste logic error in the reward calculation routine of the Vault contract. The function that determines how much a user can harvest, calcReward(), contains a conditional that should treat two scenarios differently: when the synthetic asset is an underlying asset and when it is an anchor (non‑asset) whose base token is VADER. Because the same code fragment was duplicated in both the if and the else branches, the else branch mistakenly continues to use the USDV reserve and the getUSDVAmount helper instead of the VADER equivalents. This results in an adjusted reserve value (_adjustedReserve) that is calculated with the wrong token amounts, producing an inaccurate reward figure. The root cause is a developer oversight during code reuse, where the necessary substitution of USDV‑related variables with VADER‑related ones was omitted. The bug can be exploited indirectly: any user who harvests rewards while the contract is in the else branch will receive a reward that is either higher or lower than what the protocol’s accounting rules dictate. Over time, this mis‑allocation skews the overall reward pool, potentially causing some participants to lose expected earnings while others gain undeserved extra tokens. The impact is primarily on the protocol’s economic integrity – users see unexpected reward amounts, the accounting ledger diverges from the intended model, and the protocol could become financially unsustainable if the error persists. The condition triggers whenever the synth token is not an asset (i.e., when an anchor token is used), which is a normal operational path for many vaults. All participants in the protocol, including liquidity providers and harvesters, are affected because the reward distribution logic underpins their expected returns. The issue was uncovered during a formal code audit conducted by the Code4rena team, who noticed that the two branches of the conditional were identical despite needing distinct calculations. Because the duplicated code looks syntactically correct, it can evade standard unit tests that only verify that a function returns a value, making the defect hard to spot without a targeted review of the business logic. To remediate the problem, the else branch must be rewritten to compute the adjusted reserve using the VADER amount function and the VADER reserve (i.e., replace getUSDVAmount(reserveUSDV()) with getVADERAmount(reserveUSDV()) and add reserveVADER()). This aligns the calculation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the base token in the anchor scenario is VADER, restoring correct reward distribution. In user‑facing terms, a participant expecting a proportional harvest may instead receive an unexpectedly low or high amount, leading to confusion when balances appear to shrink or grow without explanation. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic or accounting miscalculations caused by incorrect variable substitution, which undermines the trust model of the protocol even though it does not directly expose funds to theft.

title: `Vader.redeemToMember`
description:
The USDV balance of the Vader contract is vulnerable to theft through the `Vader.redeemToMember()` function. A particular case is through USDV redemption front-running. Users can redeem USDV for Vader through the `USDV.redeemForMember()` function or the `Vader.redeemToMember()` function. In the case of `Vader.redeemToMember()`, a user would need to send their USDV to the contract before redemption. However, as this process does not happen in a single call, the victim’s call is vulnerable to front running and could have their redeemed USDV stolen by an attacker.

User’s redeem USDV could be stolen by an attacker front running their `Vader.redeemToMember()` call.

The steps are as follows:

  1. User sends USDV to Vader contract to be redeemed
  2. User calls `Vader.redeemToMember()`
  3. The `Vader.redeemToMember()` call is detected by an attacker, who front-runs the call by calling `Vader.redeemToMember()` specifying their own address as the member parameter.
  4. The full USDV balance of the Vader contract is redeemed and sent to the attacker.

Note that while this particular case is front running a redemption call, any USDV balance could be stolen in this manner. Please find the POC showing the above steps here: <https://gist.github.com/toastedsteaksandwich/39bfed78b21d7e6c02fe13ea5b2023c3>

Recommend that the `Vader.redeemToMember()` function should be restricted so that only the USDV contract can call it. Moreover, the amount parameter from `USDV.redeem()` or `USDV.redeemForMember()` should also be passed to `Vader.redeemToMember()` to avoid the need to sweep the entire USDV balance. In this way, the member’s redemption happens in a single tx, and would only be allocated as much Vader as redeemed in USDV.

Vader complies with a monetary security policy of “money in, money out”. Contracts will only send out funds if they are first sent funds.

This is the case for the entire system, not just `Vader.redeemToMember()`, such as swaps and adding liquidity. Vader is not designed to be interacted with directly, it should be wrapped. In this case, users should convert and redeem only thru the USDV contract, which first sends funds.

Incidentally this is the same mechanism that uniswap employs for withdrawing liquidity, or syncing funds to balances. You can also get front-runned if you do it in two tx, it should be wrapped in 1 tx.

Our decision matrix for severity:

0: No-risk: Code style, clarity, off-chain monitoring (events etc), exclude gas-optimisations 1: Low Risk: UX, state handling, function incorrect as to spec 2: Funds-Not-At-Risk, but can impact the functioning of the protocol, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements 3: Funds can be stolen/lost directly, or indirectly if a valid attack path shown that does not have handwavey hypotheticals.

Recommended: 0
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the two‑step redemption flow of the Vader contract when a user invokes Vader.redeemToMember() to exchange USDV for Vader tokens. The design separates the transfer of USDV into the contract and the actual redemption into two distinct external calls. An attacker watching the mempool can detect the second call, Vader.redeemToMember(), and front‑run it by issuing the same function with their own address as the member parameter before the victim’s transaction is mined. Because the function does not restrict who may call it and it redeems the entire USDV balance held by the Vader contract, the attacker’s front‑run captures all available USDV, effectively stealing the victim’s funds. This issue arises only when users redeem directly through Vader.redeemToMember() rather than through the USDV wrapper, which would perform the transfer and redemption atomically. The affected parties include any user attempting to redeem USDV via this path, the protocol’s overall token reserves, and any downstream liquidity that relies on accurate accounting of redeemed amounts. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after sending USDV they receive no Vader tokens and their USDV balance is reduced to zero, contrary to the expectation of a successful redemption. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external interface appears to work – the transaction does not revert – yet the funds are silently redirected to the attacker, making the loss difficult to detect without detailed event analysis. The root cause is the lack of proper access control on Vader.redeemToMember() and the reliance on the contract’s total USDV balance instead of an explicit amount passed from the caller, which together allow the redemption to be manipulated in a non‑atomic fashion. To remediate, the redemption function should be restricted so that only the trusted USDV contract can invoke it, and the exact amount to redeem must be supplied as an argument, ensuring that the redemption happens within a single transaction and only the intended amount of Vader tokens is minted for the specified member. This adjustment restores the “money in, money out” invariant, prevents front‑running theft, and aligns the implementation with standard atomic swap patterns used by other protocols.

title: User may not get IL protection if certain functions are called directly in `Pools.sol`
description:
Functions `removeLiquidity()` and `removeLiquidityDirectly()` when called directly, do not provide the the user with IL protection unlike when calling the corresponding `removeLiquidity()` function in `Router.sol`. This should be prevented, at least for `removeLiquidity()` or highlighted in the specification and user documentation.

Recommend adding access control (e.g. via a modifier `onlyRouter`) so `removeLiquidity()` function of Pools contract can be called only from corresponding Router contract’s `removeLiquidity()` function which provides IL protection. Alternatively, highlight in the specification and user documentation about which contract interfaces provide IL protection to users.

User should use the Router, as designed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity pool contract where the public functions that remove liquidity, namely removeLiquidity() and removeLiquidityDirectly(), can be invoked directly by any user. These functions are intended to be called only through the router contract, which applies an additional calculation to protect liquidity providers from adverse price movements, commonly referred to as impermanent loss (IL) protection. Because the pool contract does not enforce any access control, a caller can bypass the router and execute the removal logic without the IL‑protective adjustment. The root cause is the lack of a restriction such as an onlyRouter modifier, leaving the functions publicly accessible despite the protocol’s design that assumes they are internal to the router workflow. An attacker or an unaware user can therefore call the pool’s removal functions directly, receive the raw token amounts based on the current pool state, and potentially suffer a worse outcome than if the router’s protective algorithm had been applied. This situation manifests when a liquidity provider initiates a withdrawal through a custom UI, a script, or a contract that interacts with the pool contract instead of the router. From the user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that the router will calculate a safe redemption amount that mitigates impermanent loss; however, the reality may be that the user receives fewer tokens, experiences unexpected slippage, or sees a sudden drop in the value of the withdrawn assets. The impact is a financial loss for liquidity providers, a breach of the protocol’s advertised safety guarantees, and erosion of trust in the platform’s documentation. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the behavior of the router‑mediated removal path against the direct pool calls and noted the absence of any protective checks. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because both functions appear to work correctly and there is no explicit UI warning; the only clue is the missing IL protection, which is not obvious without inspecting the contract code or the specification. To remediate, the pool contract should restrict calls to its removal functions so they can only be invoked by the authorized router, for example by adding an onlyRouter modifier or by making the functions internal and exposing them exclusively through the router’s interface. Alternatively, the protocol’s documentation and user guides must clearly state that only the router’s removal functions provide IL protection, warning users against interacting with the pool contract directly.

title: Incompatability with deflationary / fee-on-transfer tokens
description:
The `DInterest.deposit` function takes a `depositAmount` parameter but this parameter is not the actual transferred amount for fee-on-transfer / deflationary (or other rebasing) tokens.

The actual deposited amount might be lower than the specified `depositAmount` of the function parameter.

This would lead to wrong interest rate calculations on the principal.

Recommend transferring the tokens first and comparing pre-/after token balances to compute the actual deposited amount.

While this is true, we have no plans to support fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit workflow of the DInterest contract, where the function that records a new deposit accepts a numeric argument representing the amount the caller intends to transfer. For standard ERC‑20 tokens this argument normally matches the actual tokens that arrive in the contract, but for fee‑on‑transfer (also called deflationary) or rebasing tokens the protocol automatically deducts a portion of the transferred amount as a fee or as a balance adjustment. Consequently, the balance that the contract receives can be lower than the value supplied in the depositAmount parameter. The root cause is the absence of any verification step that compares the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer, so the contract assumes the declared amount is the true principal. An attacker or any user who deposits a fee‑on‑transfer token can therefore cause the accounting logic to record a higher principal than was actually received. The interest‑rate calculation later uses this inflated principal, which leads to an inaccurate interest accrual: either the protocol may over‑pay interest because it believes it holds more capital than it does, or it may under‑pay because the rate is derived from a distorted principal‑to‑supply ratio. The impact is a breach of the financial guarantees of the protocol – users may observe unexpectedly high or low interest, and the protocol’s overall accounting can become inconsistent, potentially endangering its solvency if many such deposits occur. This condition only manifests when the contract is used with tokens that implement a transfer fee or automatic rebasing; standard tokens behave correctly. The affected parties include any depositor of such tokens, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and downstream users who rely on correct interest calculations. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined the handling of token transfers and identified that the deposit function does not perform a balance‑difference check. It can be difficult to notice because the UI typically displays the amount the user entered, not the amount that actually arrived, and token contracts do not emit an explicit event describing the fee taken. The proper mitigation is to treat fee‑on‑transfer tokens as unsupported, or to amend the deposit routine to first transfer the tokens without assuming the amount, then read the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer to compute the exact amount received, and finally use that real amount for all subsequent interest calculations. This class of bug is generally known as a token amount mismatch or fee‑on‑transfer incompatibility, where the contract’s internal accounting diverges from the true token flow, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that "what you input is what you receive".

title: Unchecking the ownership of `mph` in function `distributeFundingRewards` could cause several critical functions to revert
description:
In contract `MPHMinter`, the function `distributeFundingRewards` does not check whether the contract itself is the owner of `mph`. If the contract is not the owner of `mph`, `mph.ownerMint` could revert, causing functions such as `withdraw`, `rolloverDeposit`, `payInterestToFunders` in the contract `DInterest` to revert as well.

Recommend adding a `mph.owner() != address(this)` check as in the other functions (e.g., `mintVested`).

Fixed in [this commit](https://github.com/88mphapp/88mph-contracts/commit/026dde3d30bddedbc1eeca6c87bce4bc5b5c7ee5).
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the MPHMinter contract where the function distributeFundingRewards calls mph.ownerMint without first confirming that the MPHMinter contract itself is the current owner of the MPH token. This missing ownership check creates an unchecked external call: if the MPHMinter contract is not the token owner, the call to ownerMint will revert. Because distributeFundingRewards is invoked by the DInterest contract as part of its reward‑distribution cycle, a revert propagates to higher‑level functions in DInterest such as withdraw, rolloverDeposit and payInterestToFunders. Consequently, users attempting to withdraw their deposits or receive accrued interest experience transaction failures, and the protocol’s accounting appears to stall – balances remain unchanged, expected interest is not credited, and the interface may show generic error messages. The issue surfaces whenever distributeFundingRewards is executed while the MPHMinter contract does not hold ownership of MPH, for example after an ownership transfer, an upgrade that changes the owner, or a malicious actor deliberately reassigns ownership. All participants who rely on DInterest – depositors, funders and the protocol itself – are affected because their ability to move or earn funds is blocked. The flaw was identified during a systematic audit that compared function implementations and noticed that other mint‑related functions (e.g., mintVested) include an explicit mph.owner() == address(this) guard, whereas distributeFundingRewards does not. The problem can be hard to detect in normal testing because the contract is usually deployed with the correct owner, so the function succeeds under typical conditions; only edge cases where ownership changes expose the bug. To remediate, a simple require statement checking that mph.owner() equals the MPHMinter address should be added before invoking ownerMint, mirroring the pattern used in the other mint functions. This correction restores the expected control flow, prevents unexpected reverts, and ensures that reward distribution and subsequent user actions behave as intended, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Undefined behavior for DAO and GRANT vote proposals in `DAO.sol`
description:
Given that there are only three proposal types (GRANT, UTILS, REWARD) that are actionable, it is unclear if ‘DAO’ type checked in `voteProposal()` is a typographical error and should really be ‘GRANT’. Otherwise, GRANT proposals will only require quorum (33%) and not majority (50%).

Recommend changing ‘DAO’ on L83 to ‘GRANT’ or if not, specify what DAO proposals are and how GRANT proposals should be handled with quorum or majority.

Also, check and enforce that `mapPID_types` are only these three actionable proposal types: GRANT, UTILS, REWARD.

DAO not yet fully implemented
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the DAO contract’s vote handling logic, specifically in the function that validates a proposal’s type before determining the required voting threshold. The contract defines three actionable proposal categories – GRANT, UTILS and REWARD – each of which should be subject to either a quorum (33% of voting power) or a majority (50% of voting power) depending on its semantics. In the current implementation a literal string check for a fourth category labelled ‘DAO’ is performed inside the voteProposal() routine. Because no proposals are ever created with the type ‘DAO’, this condition never matches legitimate GRANT proposals. As a result, GRANT proposals fall back to the quorum rule (33% approval) instead of the intended majority rule (50% approval). The root cause is a typographical or design error where the contract checks for the wrong identifier and fails to enforce a whitelist of allowed proposal types. An attacker who can submit a GRANT proposal can therefore succeed with a far lower level of community support, potentially causing funds to be allocated without genuine consensus. The exploit scenario is straightforward: a malicious actor creates a GRANT proposal, gathers only enough votes to satisfy the 33% quorum, and the contract treats the proposal as passed because it never evaluates the majority condition for GRANT proposals. The immediate impact is a breach of the DAO’s governance guarantees – funds may be transferred to unintended recipients, the token‑holder base loses confidence, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because the expected majority threshold is not enforced. This flaw manifests whenever voteProposal() is invoked for a GRANT‑type proposal, which under normal operation is a frequent event. All DAO participants, token holders and any downstream contracts that rely on the DAO’s grant logic are affected. The issue was discovered during a third‑party audit that compared the documented proposal types against the actual checks inside the contract and noticed the mismatch. It is hard to spot in routine testing because the contract compiles and the check passes syntactically; the incorrect identifier does not raise an exception, and the quorum threshold is a legitimate value, so the behavior appears to work albeit with weaker security. To remediate the problem the contract should replace the ‘DAO’ identifier with ‘GRANT’ in the voting logic, and additionally enforce that the mapping of proposal identifiers (mapPID_types) only ever contains the three sanctioned types. This change restores the intended majority requirement for GRANT proposals and eliminates the undefined behavior caused by the stray ‘DAO’ check, thereby re‑establishing the correct governance guarantees and preventing unauthorized fund transfers.

title: Lack of input validation in `replacePool`
description:
There is no input validation in `replacePool()` function to check if `oldToken` exists and is curated. Using a non-existing `oldToken` (even 0 address) passes the check on L236 (because `Pools.getBaseAmount()` will return 0 for the non-existing token) and `newToken` will be made curated. This can be used to bypass the `curatedPoolLimit` enforced only in `curatePool()` function.

Recommend checking if `oldToken` exists and is curated as part of input validation in `replacePool()` function.

Valid
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the replacePool function, which is intended to substitute an existing curated token pool with a new token. The implementation fails to verify that the supplied oldToken address actually corresponds to a currently curated pool. It calls Pools.getBaseAmount(oldToken) and proceeds under the assumption that a zero return value is acceptable, allowing the function to continue even when oldToken does not exist or is the zero address. Because the curatedPoolLimit, a restriction on the total number of curated pools, is enforced only in the curatePool function, an attacker can invoke replacePool with a non‑existent oldToken and a malicious newToken, causing the new token to be added to the curated list while bypassing the limit. This missing‑validation or unchecked‑existence bug breaks the protocol’s accounting assumption that only existing curated pools may be replaced and that the total count of curated pools cannot exceed a predefined limit. Exploitation involves calling replacePool with any arbitrary or zero address as oldToken; the transaction succeeds, the newToken becomes curated, and the protocol may later accept swaps or other interactions with this token, exposing users to potential loss, unexpected behavior, or manipulation of pool economics. The impact includes the ability to inflate the curated pool set beyond its intended capacity, introduce malicious assets, and undermine trust in the pool whitelist, affecting any participant who trades or relies on the correctness of the curated list. The condition is triggered whenever replacePool is invoked, regardless of the caller’s identity, because there is no access control or existence check. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where the control flow was examined and the absence of a validation step for oldToken was noted. The problem may be hard to detect because the function does not emit a distinct error for an invalid oldToken; users see a successful transaction and may not notice that the curated pool count has grown unexpectedly, while the UI may simply display the replacement as completed. To remediate, replacePool should first confirm that oldToken is currently curated, for example by checking a curated‑status mapping or ensuring that getBaseAmount(oldToken) returns a non‑zero amount, and then apply the same curatedPoolLimit checks used in curatePool. This correction restores the intended business logic that only existing curated pools can be replaced and that the total number of curated pools cannot be exceeded, thereby preserving protocol integrity and user safety.

title: `flashProof` is not flash-proof
description:
The `flashProof` modifier is supposed to prevent flash-loan attacks by disallowing performing several sensitive functions in the same block.

However, it performs this check on `tx.origin` and not on an individual user address basis. This only prevents flash loan attacks from happening within a single transaction.

But flash loan attacks are theoretically not limited to the same transaction but to the same block as miners have full control of the block and include several vulnerable transactions back to back. (Think transaction _bundles_ similar to flashbot bundles that most mining pools currently offer.)

A miner can deploy a proxy smart contract relaying all contract calls and call it from a different EOA each time bypassing the `tx.origin` restriction.

The `flashProof` modifier does not serve its purpose.

Recommend trying to apply the modifier to individual addresses that interact with the protocol instead of `tx.origin`.

Furthermore, attacks possible with flash loans are usually also possible for whales, making it debatable if adding flash-loan prevention logic is a good practice.

Flash loans with the help of miners _was not intended to be countered_ , although a check for `msg.sender` AND `tx.origin` will be applied.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in a contract modifier that is intended to make certain functions resistant to flash‑loan attacks by checking the origin of the transaction. The modifier relies on the global variable tx.origin, assuming that if the originating address is the same as the caller then the call must have occurred within a single transaction. This assumption is flawed because tx.origin reflects only the original externally owned account that started the transaction, not the individual calls that may be made within the same block. Miners or other actors with block‑building control can submit a series of transactions in the same block, each invoked from a distinct EOA that forwards calls through a proxy contract. Because each transaction has a different tx.origin, the modifier’s check passes for each call, allowing the protected functions to be executed multiple times within the same block. Consequently, an attacker can perform the same sequence of actions that a flash‑loan exploit would perform, but spread across several back‑to‑back transactions bundled in a single block, effectively bypassing the intended protection. The impact is that the protocol’s critical state‑changing functions can be abused to manipulate prices, drain funds, or otherwise violate the protocol’s accounting assumptions, leading to users seeing unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or other loss of assets. This condition occurs when a miner includes a bundle of transactions that interact with the vulnerable contract, each using a different origin address, or when a colluding party controls transaction ordering. The affected parties include any user of the protocol whose assets are managed by the contract, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage and financial loss. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the logic of the flashProof modifier and recognized that checking tx.origin does not provide block‑level isolation. It can be difficult to notice because the code appears to defend against flash‑loan attacks, and tx.origin is often used mistakenly for authentication, leading developers and reviewers to assume the check is sufficient. To remediate the problem, the contract should track usage on a per‑address basis across blocks, for example by storing the last block number in which a protected function was called for each address and rejecting subsequent calls within the same block, or by combining checks of both msg.sender and tx.origin along with a reentrancy guard. The core fix is to replace the global tx.origin check with a mechanism that enforces that a single address cannot invoke the protected functions more than once per block, thereby truly preventing flash‑loan style or miner‑bundled attacks and preserving the intended business logic of protecting user funds and protocol integrity.

title: Interest debt is capped after a year
description:
The `Utils.getInterestOwed` function computes the `_interestPayment` as:
    
    uint256 _interestPayment =
      calcShare(
          timeElapsed,
          _year,
          getInterestPayment(collateralAsset, debtAsset)
      ); // Share of the payment over 1 year

However, `calcShare` caps `timeElapsed` to `_year` and therefore the owed interest does not grow after a year has elapsed.

The impact is probably small because the only call so far computes the elapsed time as `block.timestamp - mapCollateralAsset_NextEra[collateralAsset][debtAsset];` which most likely will never go beyond a year.

It’s still recommended to fix the logic bug in case more functions will be added that use the broken function.

Recommend using a different function than `calcShare` that does not cap.

A member who doesn’t interact with the contract for more than a year misses out on some rewards, so severity:1
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interest‑calculation routine of the contract. The public function Utils.getInterestOwed determines the amount of interest owed by first calling calcShare with three parameters: the elapsed time since the last era, a constant representing one year, and the per‑year interest payment for the given collateral and debt assets. Inside calcShare the elapsed time argument is deliberately limited to the value of the year constant, meaning that any time greater than one year is truncated to exactly one year. As a consequence, when more than twelve months have passed since the last interaction, the computed interest payment no longer reflects the additional time; the interest amount stays fixed at the one‑year share. This logical error arises because the developer reused a generic share‑calculation function that was designed for proportional distribution over a fixed interval, without adapting it to a scenario where the interval can exceed one year. Exploitation does not require an attacker to submit malicious transactions; the contract itself will under‑pay interest to any user who remains inactive for longer than a year. The impact is a loss of expected reward: users see their accrued interest stop growing, leading to a discrepancy between the amount they anticipate (based on continuous accrual) and the amount actually credited. From the user’s perspective the interface may display a static interest balance, or the user may notice that after a year no additional rewards are added, despite the passage of time. The issue manifests only when the elapsed time calculation (block.timestamp minus the stored next‑era timestamp) exceeds the one‑year threshold, a condition that is unlikely in the current code path because the stored timestamp is typically reset within a year, but the bug remains present and could affect future functions that reuse getInterestOwed with longer intervals. This problem can be difficult to spot during testing because normal test cases often cover periods shorter than a year, and the contract still returns a sensible interest figure for those cases; the error only appears in edge‑case timelines. The appropriate remediation is to replace the call to calcShare with a function that computes the proportional share without capping the elapsed time, or to modify calcShare to accept the true elapsed duration. By doing so the contract will correctly accumulate interest for any length of inactivity, preserving the economic expectations of participants and aligning the implementation with the intended accounting model that interest should increase linearly over time.

title: Canceled proposals can still be executed
description:
Proposals that passed the threshold (“finalized”) can be cancelled by a minority again using the `cancelProposal` functions. It only sets `mapPID_votes` to zero but `mapPID_timeStart` and `mapPID_finalising` stay the same and pass the checks in `finaliseProposal` which queues them for execution.

Proposals cannot be cancelled.

Recommend setting a cancel flag and check for it in `finaliseProposal` and in execution.

Valid
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance workflow of the contract, where a proposal that has already reached the "finalized" state – meaning it satisfied the voting threshold – can still be cancelled by a minority of participants using the `cancelProposal` function. The cancellation routine only resets the vote tally stored in `mapPID_votes` to zero, but it leaves the proposal's start timestamp (`mapPID_timeStart`) and its finalising flag (`mapPID_finalising`) untouched. Subsequent calls to `finaliseProposal` rely solely on the timestamp and finalising flag to determine eligibility for execution, and therefore the cancelled proposal passes those checks and is queued for execution despite having been marked as cancelled. This inconsistency between the visible state (zero votes) and the internal lifecycle flags enables an attacker who opposes a proposal to invoke `cancelProposal` after the proposal has been finalized, and then allow the proposal to be executed as if it were still active. The impact is that governance decisions that were intended to be aborted can still be carried out, potentially resulting in unauthorized state changes, fund transfers, or other protocol actions that contradict the community's intent. The issue manifests whenever a proposal moves to the finalized state and a minority participant subsequently calls `cancelProposal`; under these conditions the contract's logic fails to enforce the intended cancellation semantics. All participants, including token holders, protocol operators, and any downstream contracts that rely on the outcome of proposals, are affected because the governance process no longer guarantees that a cancelled proposal will be inert. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit that examined the proposal lifecycle and identified that the cancellation flag was not persisted or checked during finalisation. The bug can be subtle to detect because the UI or external observers may display a proposal as having zero votes, leading them to assume it is effectively dead, while the contract internally still treats it as executable. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce an explicit cancellation flag that is set when `cancelProposal` is called, and both `finaliseProposal` and the execution pathway must verify that this flag is not set before proceeding. This ensures that once a proposal is cancelled, it cannot be queued or executed, restoring the intended invariant that cancelled proposals remain inert. In generic terms, the flaw belongs to the class of state‑machine inconsistencies where a transition (cancellation) does not update all relevant state variables, allowing forbidden actions to occur later in the workflow. From the user's perspective, a proposal that was believed to be withdrawn may still appear in execution logs, causing confusion such as "I cancelled the proposal but it still executed" or "my vote count is zero yet the proposal runs". This breaks the expectation that cancelling a proposal prevents any future effect, thereby violating core governance and accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: Completed proposals can be voted on and executed again
description:
A proposal that is completed has its state reset, including the votes. Users can just vote on it again and it can be executed again.

Completed proposals should most likely not be allowed to be voted on / executed again. This could also lead to issues in backend scripts that don’t expect any voting/execution events to be fired again after the `FinalisedProposal` event has fired.

Recommend adding an `executed` flag to the proposals and disallow voting/finalising on already executed proposals.

It might be intended to have repeated proposals.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s handling of proposal lifecycle state. When a proposal reaches the completed (finalised) state, the contract resets the vote tally and clears the voting flag, but it does not permanently lock the proposal. As a result, any user can submit additional votes on the same proposal after it has already been finalised, and the proposal can be executed a second time. The root cause is a missing "executed" or finality flag that should prevent any further interaction once the FinalisedProposal event has been emitted. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker observes a proposal that has just been finalised, then calls the vote function again to add new votes, and finally triggers the execution path a second time. This double‑execution may lead to unintended state changes, such as issuing rewards, transferring assets, or updating protocol parameters twice, effectively allowing double spending or governance manipulation. The impact is medium‑severity because it can corrupt accounting logic, give malicious actors extra voting power, and cause backend services that rely on the FinalisedProposal event to misbehave, for example by processing duplicate execution events. The bug manifests only after a proposal has been marked as completed; under normal operation it is invisible, which makes it hard to notice unless test cases explicitly verify that a completed proposal is immutable. Users may see a proposal that appears to be finished on the UI, yet their subsequent votes are still accepted and the execution can be triggered again, leading to confusion such as "my vote was counted again" or "the same proposal executed twice". The affected parties include all token holders who vote, the governance protocol that assumes a one‑time execution, and any off‑chain services that track proposal finality. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that reviewed the proposal state transitions and noticed that the vote‑reset logic was performed without an accompanying guard that checks whether the proposal has already been executed. To remediate, the contract should introduce a persistent boolean flag (e.g., `executed`) that is set when the FinalisedProposal event is emitted and never cleared. All voting and execution functions must check this flag and reject any call on a proposal that has already been executed. This change restores the intended one‑time finality of proposals, prevents double execution, and aligns the contract’s behaviour with governance and accounting expectations.

title: Divide before multiply
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the ordering of arithmetic operations in a Solidity function that calculates a token amount. The code first performs a division to derive an intermediate value (_units) and then later multiplies this intermediate value by a slip‑adjustment factor before dividing again by a scaling constant (10**18). Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the initial division truncates any fractional part, potentially reducing _units to a very small integer or even zero when the numerator is smaller than the denominator. When the subsequent multiplication is performed, the small _units value may be multiplied by a factor that is later divided by the same scaling constant, but the lost precision cannot be recovered. As a result, the final returned amount can be zero or otherwise incorrect, even though mathematically the expression should yield a non‑zero result. This mistake is a classic case of loss‑of‑precision due to performing division before multiplication, sometimes referred to as a "divide‑before‑multiply" bug. The flaw can be triggered whenever the inputs (P, part1, part2, part3) produce a numerator that is less than about 10**9, causing the intermediate _units to be less than one when scaled by 10**18. Under these conditions, users who expect to receive a token allocation, a refund, or a slippage‑adjusted amount instead receive nothing, seeing a zero balance appear in the UI. The affected parties are any end‑users of the protocol that rely on this calculation, as well as the protocol itself because accounting invariants are violated and total supply may become inconsistent. The issue was identified during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the arithmetic flow and noticed that the division was placed before the multiplication, leading to potential truncation. It is hard to spot because the code superficially appears mathematically correct and the constants used (both 10**18) suggest a cancel‑out, masking the integer truncation effect. To remediate the problem, the calculation should be reordered so that multiplication is performed before division, or a library such as FullMath should be used to handle fixed‑point arithmetic without intermediate truncation. Alternatively, the function could be rewritten to use a higher‑precision intermediate type (e.g., uint256 with unchecked overflow protection) and ensure that any division occurs only after all necessary scaling operations have been applied. By preserving precision throughout the computation, the protocol will return the expected non‑zero amounts, maintain correct accounting, and prevent users from seeing inexplicable zero balances.

title: Incorrect use of `_addTribute` instead of `_addGovernanceTribute`
description:
As part of the `purchaseMembership()` function, the `addRegistrationTributeGovernance()` function is called by the FSD network to update tribute when 7.5% is contributed towards governance. However, this function incorrectly calls `_addTribute()` (as is also done in `addRegistrationTribute`) instead of `_addGovernanceTribute()`.

The impact of this is that `governanceTributes` never gets updated, rendering all of the tribute accounting logic incorrect.

Recommend using `_addGovernanceTribute()` instead of `_addTribute` on L140 of FSD.sol

The second of the two easter eggs!

Fixed in [PR#20](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/20).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error that occurs in the membership purchase flow of the FairSide protocol. When a user calls purchaseMembership, the contract is supposed to allocate 7.5 % of the contributed amount to the governance tribute pool by invoking the internal function that updates governance‑specific bookkeeping. However, the implementation mistakenly calls the generic _addTribute function, which records the amount in the general tribute ledger instead of the dedicated governanceTributes structure. The root cause is a simple but critical misuse of an internal helper: the code references the wrong function name, and because both functions have similar signatures the mistake is not obvious during casual review. An attacker or honest user can trigger the purchaseMembership path, and the governance tribute will never be recorded, meaning the protocol’s accounting for governance funding is permanently out of sync. Consequently, any downstream calculations that depend on the governanceTributes balance—such as voting weight, reward distribution, or fee redistribution—will use stale or zero values, leading to inaccurate governance decisions and potentially misplaced funds. This error manifests only when the specific 7.5 % governance contribution path is executed; ordinary tributes that do not target governance are unaffected. All members who contribute toward governance are impacted because their expected governance credit disappears from the protocol’s state, even though they have transferred the funds. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors inspected the call chain of addRegistrationTributeGovernance and observed the incorrect internal call. The bug is hard to notice because the UI does not display the internal tribute balances, and the naming similarity of _addTribute and _addGovernanceTribute masks the defect. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or zero governance credit after contributing, while the user expects a positive governance balance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of "incorrect internal function dispatch" leading to accounting mismatches. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the call to _addTribute with a call to _addGovernanceTribute at the indicated line, ensuring that governance tribute amounts are recorded in the correct storage variable and that all downstream accounting reflects the true contributions.

title: Call to `swapExactTokensForETH` in `liquidateDai`
description:
`liquidateDai()` calls Uniswap’s `swapExactTokensForETH` to swap Dai to ETH. This will work if `msg.sender` (i.e., the FSD contract) has already given the router an allowance amount that is at least as much as the input token Dai.

Given that there is no prior approval, the call to UniswapV2 router for swapping will fail. This is because `msg.sender` has not approved UniswapV2 with an allowance for the tokens that are attempting to be swapped.

The impact is that, while working with the Dai stablecoin, `updateCostShareRequest()` will fail and revert.

Recommend adding FSD approval to UniswapV2 with an allowance for the tokens that are attempting to be swapped.

Fixed in [PR#19](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/19).
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a missing ERC‑20 token allowance when the FairSide (FSD) contract attempts to liquidate Dai by calling Uniswap V2’s swapExactTokensForETH function inside the liquidateDai() routine. The contract assumes that the Uniswap router already has permission to transfer the required amount of Dai from the FSD contract, but no explicit approve() transaction is performed beforehand. Because ERC‑20 tokens enforce that a spender must be approved for the exact amount to be transferred, the router’s call to transferFrom fails, causing the swap to revert. This failure propagates back to the updateCostShareRequest() function, which relies on a successful swap to calculate and distribute ETH proceeds. As a result, any liquidation request that involves Dai ends in a transaction revert, leaving the user with no ETH receipt and an unchanged Dai balance. From the user’s perspective, a call to liquidate their position appears to succeed at the UI level, but the transaction later fails, and the user sees no ETH refunded, often seeing a "transaction reverted" or "insufficient allowance" error in the wallet logs. The impact is limited to operations that require Dai-to-ETH conversion; other token paths that include proper approvals continue to work. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s liquidation flow, where the auditor observed that the code issued a token swap without a preceding allowance grant. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and the function signatures are correct; only at runtime does the ERC‑20 transfer check reject the operation, making it easy to miss without executing the specific code path. This is an instance of the classic "missing token approval" class of vulnerability, where business logic assumes a pre‑approved token transfer that is never established, violating accounting assumptions that the contract can freely move assets on its own behalf. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit call to the Dai token’s approve() method (or increaseAllowance()) for the Uniswap router before attempting the swap, ensuring the router has sufficient allowance for the intended input amount. Proper error handling should also be added to surface allowance‑related failures to the user rather than allowing silent reverts. Once the approval step is introduced, liquidateDai() will be able to perform the swap, the ETH proceeds will be correctly calculated and distributed, and the protocol’s liquidation mechanism will function as intended.

title: Conviction totals not updated during tokenization
description:
`_updateConvictionScore()` function returns `convictionDelta` and `governanceDelta` which need to be used immediately in a call to `_updateConvictionTotals (convictionDelta, governanceDelta)` for updating the conviction totals of conviction and governance-enabled conviction for the entire FairSide network.

This updating of totals after a call to `_updateConvictionScore()` is done on Line70 in `_beforeTokenTransfer()` and on Line367 in `updateConvictionScore()` of ERC20ConvictionScore.sol.

However, the return values of `_updateConvictionScore()` are ignored on Line284 in `tokenizeConviction()` and are not used to update the totals using `_updateConvictionTotals(convictionDelta, governanceDelta)`.

The impact of this is that when a user tokenizes their conviction score, their conviction deltas are updated and recorded (only if the funds locked are zero, which is incorrect and reported separately in a different finding), but the totals are not updated. This leads to incorrect accounting of `TOTAL_CONVICTION_SCORE` and `TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE`, which are used to calculate tributes, and therefore will lead to incorrect tribute calculations.

EXAMPLE:
Alice calls `tokenizeConviction()` to convert her conviction score into an NFT. Her conviction deltas (as returned by `_updateConvictionScore()`) are ignored. Furthermore, `TOTAL_CONVICTION_SCORE` and `TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE` values are not updated. As a result, the tributes rewarded are proportionally more than what they should have been. This is because the conviction score totals are used as the denominator in `availableTribute()` and `availableGovernanceTribute()`.

Recommend using the return values of the `_updateConvictionScore()` function (i.e. `convictionDelta` and `governanceDelta`) on Line284 of `ERC20ConvictionScore.sol`, and then use them in a call to `_updateConvictionTotals(convictionDelta, governanceDelta)`.

Fixed in [PR#17](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/17).
bug_full:
The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatch that occurs when a participant tokenizes their conviction score. The contract provides a private function `_updateConvictionScore()` that calculates two deltas – `convictionDelta` and `governanceDelta` – which represent the incremental change to the network‑wide totals `TOTAL_CONVICTION_SCORE` and `TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE`. In the normal execution paths, these deltas are immediately fed into `_updateConvictionTotals(convictionDelta, governanceDelta)` so that the global counters stay consistent with each user’s balance. However, in the `tokenizeConviction()` workflow the return values of `_updateConvictionScore()` are silently discarded, and the subsequent call that would update the totals is omitted. As a result, a user’s personal conviction balance is reduced (the deltas are recorded on the user’s side) while the aggregate totals remain unchanged. The root cause is a missing function call after the score‑updating step, i.e. a logical oversight in the tokenization path of the ERC20ConvictionScore contract.

Exploitation is straightforward: any holder who invokes `tokenizeConviction()` causes the global totals to become stale. Because the tribute distribution formulas (`availableTribute()` and `availableGovernanceTribute()`) divide by these totals, the stale denominator inflates the proportion of tribute that each participant receives. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after converting conviction to an NFT they receive a larger than expected tribute, or that the protocol appears to over‑reward tokenized users. The impact is an economic imbalance: the protocol may distribute more rewards than intended, potentially draining reserve funds or unfairly advantaging certain participants. This condition manifests only when the tokenization function is used; all other transfer pathways correctly update the totals.

The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s state‑mutation logic. The auditor noticed that the line where `_updateConvictionScore()` is called in `tokenizeConviction()` does not forward its outputs to `_updateConvictionTotals`. The problem can be subtle because the contract’s internal events still fire and the user’s balance changes, giving a false impression that the overall accounting is correct. Only by tracing the global variables `TOTAL_CONVICTION_SCORE` and `TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE` through the code does the discrepancy become evident.

To remediate, the missing call should be added: capture the two delta values returned by `_updateConvictionScore()` and then invoke `_updateConvictionTotals(convictionDelta, governanceDelta)` before completing the tokenization. This ensures that the network‑wide totals stay in sync with individual user actions, preserving the correctness of tribute calculations. The fix aligns with the intended design of the contract, where every change to a participant’s conviction score must be reflected in the aggregate counters, thereby preventing inflated reward distribution and maintaining the protocol’s economic integrity.

title: Eth may get stuck in contract
description:
The Istanbul hardfork increases the gas cost of the SLOAD operation and therefore breaks some existing smart contracts.

In file `withdrawable.sol`, contract uses `transfer()` to send eth from contract to EOA due which eth can get stuck.

The reason behind this is that, after the Istanbul hardfork, any smart contract that uses `transfer()` or `send()` is taking a hard dependency on gas costs by forwarding a fixed amount of gas (2300). This forwards 2300 gas, which may not be enough if the recipient is a contract and the cost of gas changes.

Recommend using `call()` to send eth.

Although I am fine with the severity, perhaps it may not be applicable given that even after EIP-3074, transfers will not fail with proper access lists, and I highly doubt the transfer method will fail to work altogether anytime soon.

Fixed in PR#8.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the contract’s reliance on Solidity’s built‑in transfer() function to move Ether from the contract to an external address. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient, an assumption that was safe before the Istanbul hardfork. Istanbul increased the gas cost of the SLOAD opcode, which in turn raises the amount of gas required by many fallback or receive functions in contracts. When the recipient is a contract whose fallback logic now needs more than 2300 gas, the transfer call reverts. Because the contract does not handle the revert, the Ether intended for withdrawal remains locked in the contract’s balance. This situation can occur whenever the withdrawable.sol contract invokes transfer() or send() to an address that may be a smart contract, especially after the hardfork when gas pricing changed. The affected parties include any user who expects to receive a refund or payout, the protocol that relies on correct fund disbursement, and the contract owner who may be unable to retrieve accumulated Ether. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the auditor noted that the fixed‑gas stipend creates a hard dependency on the gas schedule, making the behavior fragile under future hardforks. It is difficult to notice because transfer() traditionally succeeds for externally owned accounts, and the failure only manifests when the destination is a contract with non‑trivial fallback logic, which may be rare in normal testing. The impact is the potential loss of user funds: a user may see a zero or unchanged balance after a withdrawal attempt, and the contract may display an unchanged Ether reserve despite successful execution of the withdraw function. Conceptually, this is a classic “gas stipend” or “transfer‑stuck” bug, where the contract’s accounting assumes successful Ether transfer but the underlying EVM semantics prevent it. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer() with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a calibrated amount) and checks the returned success flag, or alternatively adopt a pull‑payment pattern where the recipient pulls funds instead of being pushed. This change removes the hard dependency on a fixed gas amount and ensures that Ether can be moved safely regardless of future gas cost changes.

title: Bug inside ABDKMathQuad library
description:
The `FairSideFormula` library is using the `ABDKMathQuad` library underneath. According to the `ABDKMathQuad` README, the range of values is the following:

The minimum strictly positive (subnormal) value is 2^−16494 ≈ 10^−4965 and has a precision of only one bit. The minimum positive normal value is 2^−16382 ≈ 3.3621 × 10^−4932 and has a precision of 113 bits, i.e., ±2^−16494 as well. The maximum representable value is 2^16384 − 2^16271 ≈ 1.1897 × 10^4932.

Using Echidna, a fuzzing tool for smart contracts, I found some edge cases in which some of the operations do not work as expected. This is the test code I ran using `echidna-test contracts/TestABDKMathQuad --contract TestABDKMathQuad`. see [issue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-fairside-findings/issues/32) for more details.

If we check in Remix, we can see that there is a small difference when converting from UInt to Bytes16 (and vice versa). This issue is probably the same with all the other operations.

Recommend using some fuzzing tool like [Echidna](https://github.com/crytic/echidna) to verify that there are no edge cases.

I am slightly mixed about this finding. We did employ fuzz tests during the audit we had gone through, and they were unable to pinpoint any issues in the value range we expect the curve to be utilized in. This is definitely a good suggestion and one we will assimilate. However, I am not sure how one would judge the severity of this.
bug_full:
The vulnerability originates from the use of the ABDKMathQuad library inside the FairSideFormula library, where the library’s handling of quadruple‑precision floating‑point numbers exhibits subtle rounding and precision errors at the boundaries of its representable range.
