ABDKMathQuad defines a minimum positive subnormal value of 2⁻¹⁶⁴⁹⁴ (approximately 10⁻⁴⁹⁶⁵) that carries only a single‑bit of precision, and a minimum positive normal value of 2⁻¹⁶³⁸² (approximately 3.36 × 10⁻⁴⁹³²) with 113 bits of precision. When conversion functions such as UInt → Bytes16 or Bytes16 → UInt are invoked, especially for values close to these limits, the library may truncate or round the value in a way that deviates from exact arithmetic. The fuzzing campaign performed with Echidna uncovered edge‑case inputs that trigger these deviations, showing a measurable discrepancy between the original integer and the value obtained after a round‑trip conversion. The same type of loss may affect other arithmetic operations (addition, multiplication, division) because they internally rely on the same conversion routines.

The root cause is therefore an inherent limitation of the underlying floating‑point representation: extreme magnitude numbers cannot be represented with full integer precision, and the library does not enforce strict overflow or underflow checks during conversions. Consequently, a contract that depends on precise financial calculations—such as reward distribution, fee accrual, or refund computation—may produce results that are slightly lower or higher than mathematically expected. In practice, a user who expects a full refund might receive a marginally reduced amount, or a protocol’s accounting ledger could show a shortfall that accumulates over many transactions. This discrepancy is most likely to appear when input parameters are unusually large or small, or when developers unintentionally rely on the library’s conversion path for routine values, assuming perfect fidelity.

Because the error manifests as a tiny difference, it can be hard to notice during normal functional testing, especially if test vectors stay well within the safe numeric band. The issue was discovered through automated fuzzing, which systematically explored the full input space and identified inputs that caused the conversion to lose precision. Manual inspection in Remix confirmed the presence of a small but consistent deviation, reinforcing that the problem is deterministic for certain value ranges rather than a sporadic runtime glitch.

To remediate the issue, the protocol should either constrain all inputs to a range where ABDKMathQuad guarantees exact integer representation, or replace the library with an arithmetic engine that provides arbitrary‑precision integer math for financial formulas. Adding comprehensive property‑based tests that cover the extreme ends of the numeric spectrum, as well as explicit checks after each conversion (e.g., asserting that the round‑trip value matches the original within an acceptable epsilon), would mitigate the risk. In any case, the fundamental class of the bug is a floating‑point precision/rounding error that violates the accounting invariants expected by the protocol’s business logic, potentially leading to minor but observable fund mismatches for end users.

title: pendingWithdrawals just increments
description: Sponsor commented that this related to another bug and referenced ”[H-05] `Withdrawable.withdraw` does not decrease `pendingWithdrawals`” see issue [#48](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-fairside-findings/issues/48) for more details.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an accounting flaw in the contract’s withdrawal logic. When a user invokes the withdraw function, the contract records the amount that the user is entitled to in a variable commonly referred to as pendingWithdrawals. However, the implementation only increments this pending amount and never decrements it after the funds have been transferred out. Consequently, the contract’s internal ledger continues to believe that the user still has a claim on the same funds, even though the tokens have already been sent. This mismatch can be exploited by repeatedly calling the withdraw function: each call triggers a transfer of the same amount while the pendingWithdrawals entry remains unchanged, allowing an attacker to drain more tokens than they are legitimately owed. The impact is that users may see their balance appear correct on the UI – they receive a withdrawal as expected – but the protocol’s accounting becomes corrupted, leading to either locked funds that can never be reclaimed or a systematic loss of assets from the contract’s treasury. The issue manifests whenever the withdraw routine is executed, regardless of who calls it, and affects any participant that relies on the contract’s withdrawal mechanism, including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s overall financial health. It was discovered during a code review when a sponsor noted a similarity to a previously reported bug where the same function failed to reduce the pendingWithdrawals counter, linking the two findings together. The problem is subtle because the outward behavior (a successful transfer) seems normal, and there is no immediate error or revert; the faulty state persists quietly in storage, making it difficult to detect without audit or detailed state inspection. To remediate the issue, the withdraw function must follow a proper Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: after confirming the user’s entitlement, it should first deduct the withdrawn amount from the pendingWithdrawals record and then transfer the tokens. This ensures that the contract’s internal accounting stays consistent with the actual token balances and prevents repeated extraction of the same funds.

title: Randomization of NFTs returned in redeem/swap operations can be brute-forced
description:
If we assume that certain NFTs in a vault over time will have different market demand/price, then the users will try to redeem those specific NFTs. Even if direct redeems are disabled to prevent such a scenario to default to returning randomized NFTs, a user can brute-forced this on-chain randomization (using nonce + blockhash) by repeatedly trying to redeem/swap from a contract, checking the NFT IDs returned from the function and reverting the transaction if those are not the NFT IDs of specific interest.

The impact will be a subversion of the randomization goal to return random NFTs which cannot be specified by the user.

A [similar exploit happened recently with Meebit NFTs](https://twitter.com/sillytuna/status/1391013965170454540).

Recommend considering only EOA (external only account) for redeem/swap operations to prevent brute-forcing via contracts. Alternatively, make the user commit to pseudo-random IDs before revealing them.

- [0xKiwi acknowledged](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/78)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the random selection mechanism used when a user redeems or swaps NFTs from a vault. The contract determines which NFT to return by hashing a combination of a nonce and the current blockhash, an approach that is deterministic and observable on‑chain. Because the random seed is fully known to any contract that can invoke the redeem/swap function, a malicious contract can repeatedly call the function, examine the NFT identifier returned in each transaction, and deliberately revert any transaction that does not yield a specific token of interest. By looping this process, the attacker can effectively brute‑force the randomization and force the vault to hand over high‑value or otherwise desired NFTs, subverting the intended "random" allocation. This issue manifests when the protocol allows contract‑originated calls for redemption; the attacker exploits the fact that contract code can programmatically repeat calls and inspect outcomes before deciding to keep or discard a transaction. The impact is a breach of economic fairness: users can cherry‑pick NFTs with higher market demand, eroding the vault's value proposition and potentially causing loss of revenue for honest participants. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it mirrors a previously reported exploitation of Meebit NFTs where similar on‑chain randomness was abused. Detecting the attack is difficult because each reverted transaction looks like a normal failure from a user's perspective, and the deterministic nature of the randomness is not immediately obvious. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should limit redeem and swap calls to externally owned accounts (EOAs) only, or replace the simple nonce‑blockhash scheme with a commit‑reveal pattern or a provably unbiased randomness source such as Chainlink VRF. By requiring a commitment to the desired NFT IDs before the randomness is revealed, the protocol can prevent an attacker from iteratively probing the outcome. In summary, the flaw is a deterministic random‑selection algorithm that can be brute‑forced by contract calls, leading to targeted NFT extraction, and it should be addressed by restricting caller types or strengthening the randomness mechanism.

title: Use `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom` consistently instead of `transfer`/`transferFrom`
description:
It is good to add a `require()` statement that checks the return value of token transfers, or to use something like OpenZeppelin’s `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom` unless one is sure the given token reverts in case of a failure. Failure to do so will cause silent failures of transfers and affect token accounting in contract.

While most places use a `require` or `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom`, there are three missing cases in the withdrawal of staking token and rescue of arbitrary tokens sent to the `FeeDistributor` contract.

Reference this similar medium-severity finding from [Consensys Diligence Audit of Fei Protocol](https://consensys.net/diligence/audits/2021/01/fei-protocol/#unchecked-return-value-for-iweth-transfer-call).

Recommend using `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom` or `require()` consistently.

**-[0xKiwi (NFTX) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/79)**
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on raw ERC20 `transfer` and `transferFrom` calls without checking the functions’ return values or using a wrapper that enforces a revert on failure. In ERC20 implementations that do not automatically revert when a transfer cannot be completed, these functions typically return a boolean flag indicating success. By omitting a `require` statement or a safety wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom`, the contract silently ignores a failed transfer. This flaw appears in the withdrawal flow for staked tokens and in the rescue function that is intended to recover arbitrary tokens sent to the FeeDistributor contract. When a transfer fails—due to insufficient allowance, a paused token, a token that returns false on transfer, or any other condition that prevents the movement of funds—the contract proceeds as if the operation succeeded, updating internal accounting or emitting events that suggest the tokens left the contract. Users attempting to withdraw or rescue tokens therefore may see their balances reported as reduced on the contract side while receiving nothing in their wallets, leading to missing funds, inaccurate accounting, and potentially stranded assets locked in the contract. The issue is particularly hard to notice because no explicit error is thrown; the transaction completes successfully from the EVM’s perspective, and only the missing token receipt reveals the problem. It was discovered during a systematic security audit that flagged inconsistent handling of token transfers, referencing a similar medium‑severity finding in the Fei Protocol audit. The root cause is a classic unchecked external call pattern, a class of bug where the return data of an external call is ignored, allowing silent failures that break business logic assumptions about asset movement. To remediate, every ERC20 transfer or transferFrom invocation should either be wrapped with a safety function that reverts on a false return value or be explicitly guarded with a `require` that validates the boolean result, thereby aligning contract state with the actual token transfer outcome and restoring confidence that users will receive the expected funds.

title: Fee Distribution Re-Entrancy
description:
The `distribute` function of `NFTXFeeDistributor` has no access control and will invoke a fallback on the fee receivers, meaning that a fee receiver can re-enter via this function to acquire their allocation repeatedly potentially draining the full balance and sending zero amounts to the rest of the recipients.

A smart contract with a malicious `receiveRewards` function can re-enter the `distribute` function with the same vault ID, thereby causing the exploit.

Recommend that re-entrancy protection should be incorporated into the `distribute` function. I should note that a seemingly innocuous contract can cause this re-entrancy by simply asking the owners of the project to include an upgrade-able contract that is then replaced for a malicious implementation.

**-[0xKiwi (NFTX) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/11)**
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the fee distribution routine of the NFTXFeeDistributor contract. The distribute function is public and does not enforce any caller restrictions; it iterates over a list of fee receivers and sends each their allocated share by invoking a payable fallback on the receiver contract. Because the contract does not pause state changes or use a re‑entrancy guard before making external calls, a malicious receiver can execute code in its receiveRewards (or receive) function that calls back into distribute with the same vault identifier. This recursive invocation occurs before the original distribution loop has finished updating the internal accounting, allowing the attacker to claim its allocation repeatedly while the contract’s balance is still untouched. As a result, the attacker can drain the entire fee pool, leaving the remaining legitimate recipients with zero payouts. The issue is triggered whenever a fee receiver is a contract capable of executing arbitrary logic on receipt of ETH or tokens, and when the distributor’s function is called with a vault ID that includes the malicious receiver in its allocation list. The vulnerability was uncovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, which highlighted that even an apparently harmless upgradeable contract could be swapped for a malicious implementation, exposing the system to this re‑entrancy attack. Detecting the problem is difficult because the external call appears benign and the contract’s balance updates only after the loop, so no immediate error is raised; the symptoms manifest as missing funds for honest participants. From a user’s perspective, a participant expecting a reward may see their balance remain unchanged or receive a zero amount, while the attacker’s address suddenly shows a large influx of fees. The root cause is the classic unchecked‑effects‑before‑interactions pattern, where state changes (deducting fees from the pool) are performed after external calls, providing a window for re‑entrancy. To remediate the issue, the distribute function should incorporate a re‑entrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or adopt the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating allocation balances before any external transfer, and consider restricting calls to authorized entities or using pull‑based payment models. This class of bug is known as a fee distribution re‑entrancy or re‑entrancy via callback in a multi‑recipient payout routine, and it violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the total fee pool is partitioned exactly once per distribution event.

title: Unbounded iteration in `NFTXEligiblityManager.distribute` over `_feeReceivers`
description:
`NFTXEligiblityManager.distribute` iterates over all `_feeReceivers`. If the number of `_feeReceivers` gets too big, the transaction’s gas cost could exceed the block gas limit and make it impossible to call `distribute` at all.

Recommend keeping the number of `_feeReceivers` small.

**-[0xKiwi (NFTX) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/47)**
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NFTXEligiblityManager contract’s distribute function, which iterates over the entire _feeReceivers array to forward collected fees. Because the function uses an unbounded for‑loop that processes each entry sequentially, the total gas required grows linearly with the number of fee receivers. When the array becomes large enough, the gas consumption can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas before completing. This situation can be triggered if an attacker or a misbehaving governance action adds many fee receiver addresses, or if the protocol organically accrues a long list of receivers over time. As a result, the distribute call becomes impossible to execute, preventing any fee distribution from occurring. Users and fee recipients expecting a payout may see their balances remain unchanged, experience missing refunds, or notice that the protocol’s accounting no longer reflects the expected fee flow. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the contract’s state‑changing functions for scalability problems. It is hard to notice in standard testing because typical test environments use only a handful of receivers, masking the out‑of‑gas condition that only appears at larger scales. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unbounded iteration or gas‑limit exhaustion vulnerabilities, where a contract’s logic does not enforce a practical upper bound on a dynamic data structure processed in a single transaction. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a maximum size on the _feeReceivers list, switch to a pull‑based withdrawal model where each receiver claims their share in separate calls, or redesign the distribution to operate on fixed‑size batches, thereby keeping each transaction well within the block gas limit and preserving the intended fee flow.

title: Manager can grief with fees
description:
The fees in `NFTXVaultUpgradeable` can be set arbitrarily high (no restriction in `setFees`).

The manager can front-run mints and set a huge fee (for example `fee = base`) which transfers user’s NFTs to the vault but doesn’t mint any pool share tokens in return for the user.

Similar griefing attacks are also possible with other functions besides `mint`.

Recommend checking for a max fee as a percentage of `base` (like 10%) whenever setting fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee configuration mechanism of the NFTXVaultUpgradeable contract. The contract allows the manager to call the setFees function without any validation of the fee value, meaning the manager can set the fee parameter to an arbitrarily high number, even equal to or greater than the base fee that determines the amount of pool share tokens minted for a user. When a user initiates a mint operation, the contract calculates the number of pool share tokens to mint and then subtracts the fee from that amount. Because there is no upper bound on the fee, a malicious manager can front‑run a user's mint transaction, raise the fee to the maximum possible (for example, setting fee = base), and cause the fee deduction to consume the entire mint amount. The user's NFTs are transferred into the vault, but the user receives zero pool share tokens in return. This griefing pattern can be reproduced with other functions that rely on the same fee logic, allowing the manager to effectively confiscate assets without providing any compensation. The impact is that honest users lose ownership of their NFTs and see no corresponding token balance; their assets become locked inside the vault with no claimable value. The condition for exploitation is the presence of a privileged manager role that can call setFees at any time, combined with the absence of a check that the fee must be a reasonable percentage of the base (e.g., less than 10%). From a user’s perspective the UI may still show a successful mint transaction, but the resulting token balance remains unchanged or zero, contradicting the expectation that a minted NFT yields a proportional amount of pool shares. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the fee‑setting logic and noticing the missing constraint. It can be difficult to spot because the fee is a numeric parameter that may appear normal in the contract interface, and the loss of tokens only becomes evident after a transaction completes. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a maximum fee bound (for example, require fee <= base * 10%) whenever fees are updated, and it should ensure that the fee is always strictly less than the amount of shares to be minted. Adding such validation prevents the manager from arbitrarily inflating fees and protects users from losing NFTs without receiving any compensation.

title: NFTs can never be redeemed back to their conviction scores leading to lock/loss of funds
description:
Besides the conviction scores of users, there appears to be tracking of the FairSide protocol’s tokenized conviction score as a whole (using `fscAddress = address(fairSideConviction)`). This is evident in the attempted reduction of the protocol’s score when a user acquires conviction back from an NFT. However, the complementary accrual of the user’s conviction score to `fscAddress` when the user tokenizes their conviction score to mint an NFT is missing in `tokenizeConviction()`.

Because of this missing update of the conviction score to `fscAddress` upon tokenization, there are no checkpoints written for `fscAddress`. There also doesn’t appear to be any initialization for bootstrapping this address’s conviction score checkpoints. As a result, the `sub224()` on Line350 of `ERC20ConvictionScore.sol` will always fail with an underflow. This is because `fscOld = 0` (because `fscNum = 0`) and `convictionScore > 0`, effectively reverting all calls to `acquireConviction()`.

The impact of this is that all tokenized NFTs can never be redeemed back to their conviction scores leading to a lock/loss of FSD funds for users who tokenized/sold/bought FairSide NFTs.

**Proof of Concept:**

  1. Alice tokenizes her conviction score into an NFT. She sells that NFT to Bob, who pays an amount commensurate with the conviction score captured by that NFT (as valued by the market) and any FSDs locked with the NFT.
  2. Bob then attempts to redeem the bought NFT back to the conviction score to use it on the FairSide network. But the call to `acquireConviction()` fails. Bob is never able to redeem Alice’s NFT and has lost the funds used to buy it.

Recommend adding appropriate logic to bootstrap, initialize `fscAddress`’s tokenized conviction score checkpoints, and update it during tokenization.

Although the finding is correct, FSDs will not be permanently locked in the NFT as they can still be redeemed via the dedicated `release` function on the conviction NFT implementation. As such, I would label this a medium-level finding, given that the conviction scores will indeed be lost.

Fixed in [PR#16](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/16).

Labeling this as medium risk as FSDs will not be permanently locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an accounting mismatch in the FairSide conviction system that prevents tokenized NFTs from being redeemed for their original conviction scores. When a user tokenizes their conviction by calling the tokenization function, the contract correctly records the user’s individual conviction but fails to update the protocol‑wide conviction accumulator associated with the special address that tracks the total tokenized conviction (referred to as fscAddress). Because this accumulator is never initialized with a checkpoint and never receives an accrual during tokenization, its stored balance remains zero. Later, when a holder attempts to redeem the NFT by invoking the acquireConviction function, the contract performs a subtraction (sub224) against the fscAddress balance. Since the stored balance is zero while the redemption request includes a positive amount, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts. Consequently, any NFT that has been minted and transferred cannot be converted back into usable conviction points, effectively locking the associated FairSide (FSD) token value for the buyer. The bug manifests under the condition that at least one NFT has been minted; it does not require any special permissions and affects any user who tokenizes, sells, or buys such NFTs. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of conviction scores between user accounts and the protocol‑level accumulator and noticed the absence of a checkpoint write for fscAddress. The issue is difficult to notice because the minting process completes successfully and the NFT appears normal, only failing at the later redemption step where an opaque arithmetic error is thrown. From a user’s perspective, the expectation is that after purchasing an NFT they can redeem it for the original conviction score, but instead the transaction fails and the user sees a revert message, leading to a loss of the funds paid for the NFT. This class of bug is a state‑invariant violation where a critical global accounting variable is never updated, causing arithmetic underflow during later operations. To remediate the problem the protocol must bootstrap the fscAddress checkpoint during contract initialization and ensure that each tokenization call also increments the global conviction accumulator, thereby keeping the protocol‑level balance in sync with individual user balances and preventing the underflow during redemption.

title: `ERC20ConvictionScore` allows transfers to special `TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE` address
description:
The credit score of the special `address(type(uint160).max)` is supposed to represent the sum of the credit scores of all users that are governors.

But, any user can directly transfer to this address, increasing its balance and accumulating a credit score in `_updateConvictionScore(to=address(uint160.max), amount)`.

It’ll first write a snapshot of this address’ balance, which should be very low:

    // in _updateConvictionScore
    _writeCheckpoint(user, userNum, userNew) = _writeCheckpoint(TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE, userNum, checkpoints[user][userNum - 1].convictionScore + convictionDelta);

This address then accumulates a score based on its balance, which can be updated using `updateConvictionScore(uint160.max)` and breaks the invariant.

Increasing it might be useful for non-governors that don’t pass the voting threshold and want to grief the proposal voting system by increasing the `quorumVotes` threshold required for proposals to pass. By manipulating `FairSideDAO.totalVotes`, `totalVotes` can be arbitrarily inflated and break the voting mechanism as no proposals can reach the quorum (percentage of `totalVotes`) anymore.

Recommend disallowing transfers from/to this address. Or better, track the total governance credit score in a separate variable, not in an address.

This is actually what #61 is meant to be used for. I would label this a medium-level finding as it would simply dilute the voting rights of users at the expense of permanently losing FSD, which should not be a viable vector.

**[fairside-core (FairSide) resolved](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-fairside-findings/issues/42#issuecomment-852107565):**

Indirectly fixed by [PR#10](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/10).

Labeling this as medium risk as it would not pose a threat to user funds yet stall the governance process.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the ERC20ConvictionScore contract treats a special address, defined as the maximum uint160 value, to represent the aggregate credit score of all governance participants. This address, referred to as TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE, is expected to hold a virtual balance that reflects the sum of individual conviction scores, not a real token balance that can be altered by normal transfers. However, the contract does not restrict ordinary users from sending tokens directly to this address. When a user transfers tokens, the internal function _updateConvictionScore records a checkpoint for the recipient address, adding a convictionDelta based on the transferred amount. Because the special address is treated like any other holder, each direct transfer writes a new checkpoint that increases its stored conviction score. The inflated balance is later used by the FairSideDAO.totalVotes calculation, which determines the quorum required for proposals to pass. By artificially inflating the TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE balance, an attacker can arbitrarily increase totalVotes, causing the quorum percentage to become unattainably high. As a result, legitimate proposals may never meet the quorum, effectively freezing the governance process. The issue can be triggered at any time a transfer to the special address is executed, and any token holder can perform it, making the attack surface broad. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the logic that should have isolated the governance score from regular token accounting was found to be missing. Because the special address appears indistinguishable from any other address, the unintended balance growth can go unnoticed until governance proposals repeatedly fail despite apparent voter support. This is a classic case of an invariant violation caused by an unchecked privileged address, leading to a ‘balance inflation’ bug that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions. To remediate, transfers to and from the TOTAL_GOVERNANCE_SCORE address should be prohibited, or the total governance credit score should be stored in a dedicated variable that is not tied to any address’s token balance. The fix restores the invariant that the governance score reflects only the intended voting power, preventing the quorum‑inflation attack and preserving the expected behavior of the voting system.

title: Should check return data from Chainlink aggregators
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle data validation flaw in the getEtherPrice function of the FSDNetwork contract. The function retrieves the ETH price from a Chainlink price aggregator by calling latestRoundData, but it does not verify any of the returned fields such as roundID, answeredInRound, or timeStamp. Because of this missing verification, the contract can accept a stale or incomplete price report. The root cause is the absence of sanity checks that confirm the round is completed (answeredInRound must be greater than or equal to roundID) and that the timestamp is non‑zero, which are standard safeguards when consuming Chainlink data. An attacker, or simply a period of feed latency, can cause the contract to read a price from a previous round that no longer reflects the market. By feeding an outdated price, the contract may mis‑price collateral, trigger liquidations at unfavorable rates, or allow swaps at a rate that benefits the attacker. The impact is that users’ funds can be incorrectly valued, potentially leading to loss of capital or unintended liquidation, which is especially serious for protocols that rely on accurate price feeds for risk management. The condition under which the bug manifests is whenever the Chainlink aggregator returns a round that is not yet answered or when the timestamp field is zero, a situation that can occur during network congestion, aggregator downtime, or malicious oracle behavior. All participants who interact with the protocol—depositors, borrowers, and traders—are affected because the contract’s UI would display a price that appears normal but the underlying accounting would be based on an outdated value, causing balances to shrink or liquidations to fire unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the lack of checks on the aggregator’s return data stood out as a logical omission. It can be hard to notice because the price value itself is still a numeric type and no error is thrown, so the contract continues operating with a stale figure. To remediate, the contract should validate that answeredInRound is at least the roundID, that timeStamp is non‑zero, and optionally that the timestamp is within an acceptable freshness window, reverting with clear error messages if the data is stale. This class of bug belongs to oracle data integrity vulnerabilities, where external data is consumed without proper verification, leading to potential financial mis‑calculations and fund loss.

title: `gracePeriod` not increased after membership extension
bug_full: The issue is a time‑accounting inconsistency in the membership management logic of the FSDNetwork contract. When an existing member calls the purchaseMembership function to extend their membership, the contract correctly adds the requested duration to the stored creation timestamp (membership[msg.sender].creation). However, the associated grace period (membership[msg.sender].gracePeriod), which defines the ultimate expiry of the member’s rights, is never updated during an extension. As a result, the grace period remains fixed to the value calculated at the initial purchase, even though the member has paid for additional time. This mismatch can cause the grace period to become earlier than the actual paid‑through date, meaning that a user who has legitimately extended their membership may suddenly lose access or be denied benefits before the newly purchased time has elapsed. The bug arises from an omitted update statement in the else‑branch of purchaseMembership, a classic example of a state‑inconsistency or accounting‑logic error where linked time variables are not kept in sync. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; any user who repeatedly extends their membership will eventually encounter a premature expiration. The impact is primarily functional: members experience unexpected service interruption, refunds may be expected but not received, and the protocol’s subscription model loses credibility. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to purchaseMembership where membership[msg.sender].creation is already non‑zero (i.e., an existing member extending their period). It affects all existing members of the protocol and any downstream services that rely on the gracePeriod to grant access. The problem was discovered during a formal code audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditor noticed that the gracePeriod calculation was only performed in the initialization branch and omitted in the extension branch, a subtle oversight that may pass superficial testing because the gracePeriod still appears valid shortly after an extension. The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the fact that the gracePeriod value does not instantly become invalid; it only becomes problematic after enough extensions have accumulated enough time discrepancy. The proper mitigation is to recompute or increment the gracePeriod by the same duration added to the creation timestamp whenever an extension occurs, ensuring that the expiry date always reflects the total paid time. In generic terms, this is a time‑based state synchronization bug, where related temporal variables must be updated together to preserve business logic and accounting guarantees.

title: The variable `fShareRatio` is vulnerable to manipulation by flash minting and burning
description:
The variable `fShareRatio` in the function `purchaseMembership` of contract `FSDNetwork` is vulnerable to manipulation by flash minting and burning, which could affect several critical logics, such as the check of enough capital in the pool (line 139-142) and the staking rewards (line 179-182).

The `fShareRatio` is calculated (line 136) by:

    (fsd.getReserveBalance() - totalOpenRequests).mul(1 ether) / fShare;

Where `fsd.getReserveBalance()` can be significantly increased by a user minting a large amount of FSD tokens with flash loans. In that case, the increased `fShareRatio` could affect the function `purchaseMembership` results. For Example, the user could purchase the membership even if the `fShareRatio` is < 100% previously, or the user could earn more staking rewards than before to reduce the membership fees. Although performing flash minting and burning might not be profitable overall since a 3.5% tribute fee is required when burning FSD tokens, it is still important to be aware of the possible manipulation of `fShareRatio`.

Recommend forcing users to wait for (at least) a block to prevent flash minting and burning.

I believe this to be a minor (1) or none (0) severity issue given that the manipulation of `fShareRatio` is unsustainable due to the fee, and the Example given is actually not possible. Suppose I affect `fShareRatio` to go above 100% to purchase a membership. In that case, I will be unable to burn the necessary FSD to go below 100% again as burning is disabled when the ratio is or would go to below 100%.

**[fairside-core (FairSide) resolved](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-fairside-findings/issues/75#issuecomment-851032182):**

Fixed in [PR#2](https://github.com/fairside-core/2021-05-fairside/pull/2).

Labeling this as low risk as a 3.5% tribute fee makes it very unlikely that these flash minting will be profitable.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the on‑chain variable that represents the share ratio used to determine both membership eligibility and staking reward calculations in the FairSide network contract. This ratio is derived from the contract's reserve balance, which can be artificially inflated when a user performs a flash‑mint of a large amount of the platform token and then immediately burns it within the same transaction. Because the ratio is computed as (reserve balance – pending requests) multiplied by a scaling factor and divided by the total share count, a sudden surge in the reserve balance raises the ratio temporarily. The contract checks this ratio to decide whether a membership purchase can proceed and to calculate reward amounts; therefore, a manipulated ratio can cause the system to incorrectly deem that sufficient capital exists, allowing a user to acquire a membership with a reduced fee or to receive higher staking rewards than intended. The exploit can be carried out in a single block by using a flash loan to mint tokens, invoking the purchase function, and then burning the minted tokens before the block finalises. From the user's perspective the symptom would be that a membership is granted even though the pool appears under‑collateralised, or that the user receives an unexpectedly large reward, breaking the expected accounting invariants of the protocol. This issue is only observable under conditions where the reserve balance can be altered in the same transaction as the membership purchase, making it hard to detect during standard testing because the manipulation is transient and reverts once the block is settled. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable on‑chain state that can be influenced by flash‑mint/burn operations without appropriate temporal safeguards. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract's financial logic, where the auditors identified that the share ratio calculation does not consider the atomicity of flash‑mint actions. While the protocol imposes a 3.5 % tribute fee on token burning, which reduces the economic incentive to perform the attack and prevents the ratio from being driven below the required threshold after the mint, the flaw still represents a deviation from the intended business logic of maintaining a stable capital‑to‑share relationship. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum delay—such as requiring the ratio to be based on a reserve balance that is at least one block old—or otherwise prevent the use of freshly minted tokens in the same block when calculating the ratio. By decoupling the ratio from immediate balance changes, the protocol can preserve its accounting guarantees and ensure that membership and reward calculations reflect genuine, sustained capital, thereby aligning the system's behavior with user expectations that fees are correctly applied and rewards are proportionate.

title: `ERC20ConvictionScore.acquireConviction` implements wrong governance checks
description: There are two issues with the governance checks when acquiring them from an NFT:
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC20ConvictionScore.acquireConviction function, which is responsible for granting governance rights (conviction) based on ownership of a specific NFT. The function performs two incorrect governance checks, allowing callers who are not the legitimate NFT owners to acquire conviction scores. The root cause is a logical error in the access control logic: the contract compares the caller’s address against an inappropriate reference (such as a stale variable or an unrelated role) instead of verifying the caller is the current owner of the NFT via a reliable ERC721.ownerOf call. Because the ownership validation is faulty, an attacker can invoke acquireConviction with any NFT identifier and receive voting power that should be reserved for the true holder. Exploitation proceeds by a malicious actor simply calling the function with a chosen tokenId; the contract mistakenly records the supplied address as the holder of conviction, inflating the attacker’s voting weight while the genuine owner’s rights remain unchanged. The impact includes unauthorized manipulation of the protocol’s governance process, potential approval of malicious proposals, and erosion of trust among token holders. This condition manifests whenever a user attempts to claim conviction from an NFT, especially when the caller is not the NFT’s owner. All participants who rely on accurate voting power calculations—including token holders, delegators, and the protocol’s decision‑making mechanisms—are affected because the governance state no longer reflects the true distribution of ownership. The flaw was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where reviewers identified the mismatched checks while performing a logical analysis of the acquireConviction flow. The issue may be hard to notice because the function’s signature and surrounding code appear legitimate, and the incorrect check does not revert or emit an error; it simply records wrong data, making the behavior subtle during normal testing. To remediate, the contract should replace the faulty condition with a direct ownership verification against the NFT contract, enforce that only the current owner can acquire conviction, and optionally add a re‑entrancy guard to protect against nested calls. In broader terms, this bug belongs to the class of "incorrect access‑control" or "authorization logic" vulnerabilities, where the contract’s internal validation does not align with the intended security policy, leading to unintended privilege escalation and governance disruption. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a user who expects to receive a conviction token after presenting their NFT either receives nothing or observes that other parties are able to vote on their behalf, resulting in a mismatch between expected and actual voting power.

title: Tokens can get stuck in `NFTXMintRequestEligibility`
description:
When dealing with ERC721 (instead of 1155) the amounts array is ignored, which leads to an issue.

User can call `NFTXMintRequestEligibility.requestMint` for an ERC721 with `amounts[i] = 0`. The `ERC721.transferFrom` is still executed but user cannot `reclaimRequestedMint` later and the NFT is stuck as it checks (`amounts[i] > 0`).

Tokens can get stuck. Also, subscribers to `Request` event could be tricked by specifying `amounts[i] > 1` in the ERC721 case, as only one token was transferred, but the amount multiple quantities get logged.

Recommend that `requestMint`: Check `amounts[i] == 1` in ERC721 case, `amounts[i] > 0` in 1155 case.

**-[0xKiwi (NFTX) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/59)**
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NFTXMintRequestEligibility contract’s handling of token requests when the underlying asset is an ERC721 collection. The requestMint function accepts an array called amounts, which is intended to represent the number of tokens to be transferred for each token ID. However, for ERC721 tokens the contract ignores the values in this array and always attempts a single ERC721.transferFrom regardless of the supplied amount. Consequently, a caller can submit a request with amounts[i] set to zero. The contract will still transfer the NFT from the user’s wallet, but later, when the user tries to invoke reclaimRequestedMint to retrieve the token, the reclaim logic checks that amounts[i] is greater than zero before allowing the transfer back. Because the stored amount is zero, the condition fails and the token remains locked in the contract with no available recovery path. Additionally, the Request event logs the value of amounts[i] without validation, so an attacker can pass amounts[i] greater than one, causing the event to report multiple minted tokens while only a single ERC721 token was actually transferred. This mismatch can mislead off‑chain listeners that rely on the event for accounting or analytics. The issue originates from a mismatch between the ERC721 and ERC1155 handling paths: the amount validation logic is applied only to ERC1155 (where amounts matter) and not to ERC721, where each token is inherently unique. Exploitation requires only calling requestMint with a crafted amounts array; no special permissions or complex state are needed. The impact is that token owners may lose their NFTs permanently, observe that their balances become zero after a request, and see no way to recover the asset, violating the protocol’s expectation that users can always retrieve tokens they sent. From a protocol perspective, the accounting assumes that the number of minted tokens equals the number recorded in the Request event; this assumption is broken, potentially inflating perceived supply or causing inconsistencies in reward calculations. The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit and later confirmed by the protocol’s maintainer. Because the contract does not expose an explicit error for the zero‑amount case, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when a user discovers that their NFT is no longer in their wallet and cannot be reclaimed, or when analytics dashboards show an unexpected surplus of minted tokens. The recommended remediation is to enforce strict validation in requestMint: for ERC721 assets the amount must be exactly one, and for ERC1155 assets the amount must be greater than zero. This ensures that the contract’s internal state, the token transfer logic, and the emitted events remain consistent, preventing tokens from becoming permanently stuck and preserving the integrity of accounting and user expectations.

title: Unhandled return value of `transferFrom` in `timeLockERC20`
description:
ERC20 implementations are not always consistent. Some implementations of `transfer` and `transferFrom` could return ‘false’ on failure instead of reverting. It is safer to wrap such calls into `require()` statements or use safe wrapper functions implementing return value/data checks to handle these failures. For reference, see similar Medium-severity finding from [Consensys Diligence Audit of Aave Protocol V2](https://consensys.net/diligence/audits/2020/09/aave-protocol-v2/#unhandled-return-values-of-transfer-and-transferfrom).

While the contract uses Uniswap’s `TransferHelper` library function `safeTransfer` in other places for ERC20 tokens, or OpenZeppelin’s `saferTransferFrom` for ERC721 tokens (both of which call the token’s `transfer`/`transferFrom` functions and check return value for success and return data), it misses using `TransferHelper.safeTransferFrom` in this one case on L610 in `timeLockERC20()` when tokens are transferred from owner to the vault and instead directly uses the token’s `transferFrom()` call without checking for its return value.

The impact can be that for an arbitrary ERC20 token, this `transferFrom()` call may return failure but the vault logic misses that, assumes it was successfully transferred into the vault and updates the `timelockERC20Balances` accounting accordingly. The `timeUnlockERC20()`, `transferERC20()` or `delegatedTransferERC20()` calls for that token will fail because the vault contract balance would have less tokens than accounted for in `timelockERC20Balances` because of the previously failed (but ignored) `transferFrom()` call.

1. Let’s say Alice owes Bob 100 USD after a week, for which they agree that Alice will pay in 100 tokens of USD stablecoin tokenA.
2. Alice, the vault owner, calls `timeLockERC20()` for recipient=Bob, token=tokenA, amount=100 and expiry=1-week-from-then (corresponding Unix timestamp) but tokenA’s implementation does not revert on failure but instead returns true/false. If the `transferFrom` failed, say because Alice did not have those 100 tokenAs, the return value is ignored on L610 in `timeLockERC20()` and vault logic considers that it indeed has 100 tokenAs locked for Bob.
3. Bob looks at the `TimeLockERC20` event emitted in the successful `timeLockERC20()` transaction from Alice and assumes 100 tokenAs are indeed locked by Alice in the vault for him which can be withdrawn after expiry.
4. After timelock expiry, Bob tries to transfer the 100 tokenAs Alice locked in the vault for him. The `TransferHelper`.`safeTransfer()` call on L637 in `timeUnlockERC20()` fails because the vault has 0 tokenAs because they were never successfully transferred in Step 2.
5. Bob could thus be tricked into thinking that 100 tokenAs are locked in the vault for him by Alice but they never were. This leads to loss of funds for Bob.

Recommend replacing use of

```solidity
IERC20(token).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
```

with

```solidity
TransferHelper.safeTransferFrom(token, msg.sender, address(this), amount);
```

This will revert on transfer failure for e.g. if `msg.sender` does not have a token balance >= amount.

sponsor acknowledged disagree with severity 0 While we may include refactor in next version, this is all foreseen behavior and is component of many stable ethereum project. The onus here is on client

I’m going to make it medium as the risk is there but it could be mitigated by UI and tokens that are used.

**[ztcrypto (Visor) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-visorfinance-findings/issues/39#issuecomment-889172980):**

fixed patch [link](https://github.com/VisorFinance/visor-core/commit/71797204108fee8375bfb99a435c0e379bbcbd84#diff-b094db7ce2f99cbcbde7ec178a6754bac666e2192f076807acbd70d49ddd0559)
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an unchecked call to an ERC20 token’s `transferFrom` function inside the `timeLockERC20` routine of the vault contract. Unlike the ERC20 standard’s typical revert-on-failure behavior, some token implementations return a boolean value—`true` for success and `false` for failure—without reverting. The contract invokes `IERC20(token).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` directly and does not inspect the returned boolean. Consequently, if the token’s `transferFrom` fails (for example because the sender’s balance is insufficient or the token contract enforces additional constraints), the vault will falsely assume that the specified amount has been transferred into its custody. The vault’s internal accounting structure (`timelockERC20Balances`) is updated regardless of the actual token balance, creating a discrepancy between recorded and real funds. When the lock expires, functions such as `timeUnlockERC20`, `transferERC20`, or `delegatedTransferERC20` attempt to move the supposedly locked tokens to the beneficiary. At that point, the vault’s balance is lower than expected, causing the safe transfer helper to revert and the beneficiary to receive nothing, despite an earlier event indicating a successful lock. This misalignment can manifest to users as a missing or zero balance after the timelock period, leading to loss of expected funds and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue is triggered only for ERC20 tokens that implement the non‑reverting return‑value pattern and only when the unchecked `transferFrom` call fails; tokens that revert on failure are unaffected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s usage of safe transfer helpers elsewhere with the lone direct `transferFrom` call in `timeLockERC20`. It can be hard to notice because the transaction that creates the lock does not emit an error and appears successful, while the failure only surfaces later when the beneficiary tries to withdraw. The proper mitigation is to replace the raw call with a wrapper such as `TransferHelper.safeTransferFrom`, which checks the boolean result and reverts on failure, thereby preserving the invariant that the vault’s internal balance always matches the on‑chain token balance. This class of flaw belongs to the broader category of unchecked external call return values, which can cause accounting inconsistencies, unexpected zero withdrawals, and user‑visible fund disappearance in financial smart contracts.

title: `transferERC721` doesn’t clean `timelockERC721s`
description:
The function `transferERC721` works similar to the functions `timeUnlockERC721` with timelocked NFT’s. However `timeUnlockERC721` cleans `timelockERC721s` (delete `timelockERC721s[key]`;), while `transferERC721` doesn’t clean `timelockERC721s`

This could mean that timelock keys could be used later on (when the NFT would have been transferred to the contract on a later moment in time). Also, the administration doesn’t correspond to the available NFT’s. Additionally doing a delete gives backs some gas (at least for now).

See [Issue #19](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-visorfinance-findings/issues/19) for code referenced in proof of concept

Recommend checking if the `timelockERC721s` mapping should also be cleaned from `transferERC721`, if so adapt the code accordingly.

**[ztcrypto (Visor) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-visorfinance-findings/issues/19#issuecomment-889177823):**

patch [link](https://github.com/VisorFinance/visor-core/commit/cc22d6e450e16aaa9eb3af1ee4d9e6ac8afe43da#diff-b094db7ce2f99cbcbde7ec178a6754bac666e2192f076807acbd70d49ddd0559)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of timelocked ERC‑721 tokens within the VisorFinance core contract. When a user transfers an NFT using the `transferERC721` function, the contract updates ownership but fails to remove the associated entry in the `timelockERC721s` mapping. The counterpart function `timeUnlockERC721`, which also moves a timelocked NFT, correctly deletes its mapping entry, demonstrating an inconsistency in state cleanup. This omission leaves a stale timelock record that continues to reference the token identifier after the NFT has been transferred out of the contract. Because the stale entry is never cleared, the same timelock key could be presented to the contract at a later time, potentially allowing a malicious actor to invoke timelock‑related logic on a token that is no longer owned by the contract. The impact includes a mismatch between the contract’s internal accounting and the actual NFT holdings, confusing administrators who rely on the mapping to determine which tokens are currently timelocked. It also wastes gas because the storage slot remains occupied. From the user’s perspective, the transfer appears successful, but the backend state retains a phantom lock, which could lead to unexpected behavior such as failed unlock attempts, erroneous refunds, or even unauthorized token movements if the stale key is reused. The issue manifests whenever `transferERC721` is called; it does not depend on specific input values beyond the existence of a timelocked token. The affected parties are token owners, the protocol’s governance that monitors locked assets, and any downstream contracts that query the timelock mapping for security checks. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementations of similar functions and noticed the missing `delete timelockERC721s[key]` statement. It can be hard to detect because the outward‑facing functionality—moving the NFT—works as intended, while the hidden state remains inconsistent. The recommended remediation is to add explicit deletion of the timelock entry in `transferERC721`, mirroring the behavior of `timeUnlockERC721`, or to refactor the contract so that a single, well‑audited routine is responsible for both transferring and cleaning up timelock state. This correction restores accurate accounting, prevents possible reuse of stale timelock keys, and reduces unnecessary gas consumption.

title: `timelockERC721Keys` could exceed the block size limit
description:
On line 504 of `Visor.sol`, looping through the `timelockERC721Keys` could exceed the block size limit

Recommend transfer by index instead of token ID

sponsor acknowledged We will be significantly refactoring experimental nft functionality in our next version before exposing to users of platform. In this refactor we will cap size of nft collection

I’m going to bump it to medium severity because this may happen if project is very successful

**[ztcrypto (Visor) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-visorfinance-findings/issues/65#issuecomment-889198875):**

patch [link](https://github.com/VisorFinance/visor-core/commit/585bedc435c297af5c91be7f525acf0832885a09#diff-b094db7ce2f99cbcbde7ec178a6754bac666e2192f076807acbd70d49ddd0559)

By using EnumerableSets
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unbounded iteration over the timelockERC721Keys data structure within the Visor contract. A public or internal function walks through the entire set of stored ERC‑721 token identifiers to perform a batch operation, such as transferring or unlocking NFTs. Because the loop processes each element sequentially and there is no explicit limit on the number of keys that can be stored, the gas consumption grows linearly with the collection size. When the collection becomes large—something that can happen in a highly successful deployment—the accumulated gas cost may exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This denial‑of‑service condition prevents the contract from completing the intended operation, effectively locking the affected NFTs in the contract and leaving users unable to receive their expected assets. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit when reviewers inspected the batch transfer logic on line 504 and observed that the loop could iterate over an arbitrarily large set. The problem can be difficult to detect in testing because typical test suites use only a few tokens, so the loop appears to work correctly under normal conditions. Exploitation does not require malicious code; an attacker or any participant can simply increase the number of NFTs held by the contract—by minting or transferring additional tokens—until the iteration size crosses the practical gas threshold. Once that threshold is reached, any subsequent call that triggers the same loop will fail, leading to symptoms such as transaction reverts, no change to user balances, and missing or zero‑valued refunds where users expected their NFTs to be transferred. The affected parties include all token holders, the protocol’s users, and any contracts that rely on the batch operation for accounting. To remediate the flaw, the contract should avoid unbounded loops entirely: it can transfer tokens one by one using an index‑based approach, enforce a hard cap on the maximum collection size, or split the batch operation into multiple smaller calls that stay within gas limits. The patched version replaces the raw loop with EnumerableSet utilities and introduces a size cap, mitigating the risk of exceeding block limits and restoring reliable behavior for token withdrawals.

title: A malicious receiver can cause another receiver to lose out on distributed fees by returning `false` for `tokensReceived` when `receiveRewards` is called on their receiver contract.
description:
A malicious receiver can cause another receiver to lose out on distributed fees by returning `false` for `tokensReceived` when `receiveRewards` is called on their receiver contract. This causes the fee distributor to double spend the `amountToSend` because the contract incorrectly assumes the returned data is truthful.

`NFTXFeeDistributor.sol`:

```solidity
(bool success, bytes memory returnData) = address(_receiver.receiver).call(payload);
```

Recommend that you don’t trust return data from externally called contracts. Only utilize whether the transaction succeeds to determine if the treasury fallback should be called.

```solidity
if (!success) {
```

Nice catch!
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution routine of the NFTXFeeDistributor contract, which forwards a rewards payload to external receiver contracts using a low‑level call and captures both the call success flag and the raw return data. The implementation erroneously trusts the content of the returned data as an indication of whether the receiver actually accepted the tokens. A malicious receiver can deliberately return a falsy value—such as false from a tokensReceived callback—while still allowing the low‑level call to succeed. Because the distributor assumes the return data is truthful, it interprets the false value as a signal that the reward was not delivered and proceeds to re‑allocate the same amount, effectively double‑spending the amountToSend. This mis‑behaviour causes any other legitimate receiver in the same distribution batch to lose out on its share of the fees, as the duplicated allocation consumes the funds that should have been sent to the honest party. The issue manifests when the fee distributor invokes receiveRewards on a set of receivers and at least one of those receivers is maliciously crafted to return false. It affects all participants that rely on the fee distributor for reward payouts, including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s treasury, because the accounting assumptions—that each distribution step either succeeds or fails based on the success flag alone—are violated. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors noticed that the contract does not verify the semantic meaning of the returned data and only checks the low‑level success flag. The problem is subtle because the transaction itself does not revert; the call appears successful, and the misleading return data can easily slip past standard testing that does not simulate malicious callbacks. From a user perspective the symptom is a missing or zero reward despite the protocol indicating that a distribution event took place; users expecting a refund or fee share receive nothing, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. To remediate the issue, the distributor should ignore any data returned from external contracts and base its decision solely on the boolean success indicator of the low‑level call. If the call fails, appropriate fallback logic (such as routing the funds to the treasury) can be executed; otherwise, the distributor must consider the reward as delivered regardless of the returned payload, thereby preventing a malicious receiver from influencing the allocation of fees to other parties.

title: The direct redeem fee can be circumvented
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the way NFTXVaultUpgradeable determines which NFT to return during a direct redemption. The contract selects a random token ID inside the same transaction that also executes the fee payment and the token transfer. Because the randomness is derived from on‑chain data that can be observed by the caller, an attacker can construct a transaction that redeems a single NFT, checks the returned token ID, and reverts the transaction if the token does not match a pre‑selected target. By submitting such transactions through a private relay like Flashbots, which allows the caller to withhold reverted transactions from the public mempool, the attacker can repeat the redeem attempt on every block without incurring gas costs. When the random selection finally yields the desired token, the transaction succeeds and the attacker receives the NFT without paying the directRedeemFee that would normally be deducted. The root cause is the combination of (1) deterministic pseudo‑random selection performed in the same call that also charges the fee, and (2) the lack of a commit‑reveal or other entropy‑locking mechanism that would prevent the caller from retrying until a favorable outcome is achieved. This flaw can be exploited whenever a user redeems NFTs from the vault – an adversary can repeatedly attempt redemption until the random function returns the specific token they want, effectively bypassing the fee and reducing the expected earnings of honest participants. From the user’s perspective, the protocol appears to charge a redemption fee, but in practice the fee may be avoided entirely, causing a discrepancy between the expected fee‑based revenue and the actual collected amount. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors noted that the random NFT selection and the fee deduction are performed in the same transaction, enabling a revert‑based loop. The problem is difficult to notice because a reverted transaction is a normal outcome on Ethereum and, when relayed through Flashbots, never reaches the public chain for inspection, masking the repeated attempts. To remediate the bug, the contract should separate fee collection from the random selection or employ a commit‑reveal scheme for the randomness, ensuring that the outcome cannot be influenced or retried by the caller after fee deduction. Conceptually, the fix prevents the attacker from conditioning the success of the transaction on a particular random result, thereby preserving the intended fee logic and maintaining the economic integrity of the vault.

title: Potential griefing with DoS by front-running vault creation with same `vaultID`
description:
The `vaultID` for a new vault being built is required to be specified by the user building a vault via the `build()` function (instead of being assigned by the Cauldron/protocol). An attacker can observe a `build()` as part of a batch transaction in the mempool, identify the `vaultID` being requested, and front-run that by constructing a malicious batch transaction with only the build operation with that same `vaultID`. The protocol would create a vault with that `vaultID` and assign the attacker as its owner. More importantly, the valid batch transaction in the mempool, which was front-run, will later fail to create its vault because that `vaultID` already exists, as per the check on Line180 of `Cauldron.sol`. As a result, the valid batch transaction fails entirely because of the attacker front-running with the observed `vaultID`.

While the attacker gains nothing except the ownership of an empty vault after spending the gas, this could grief the protocol’s real users by preventing them from opening a vault and interacting with the protocol in any manner.

The rationale for Medium-severity impact: While the likelihood of this may be low, the impact is high because valid vaults from the Yield front-end will never be successfully created and will lead to a DoS against the entire protocol’s functioning. So, with low likelihood and high impact, the severity (according to OWASP) is medium.

Alice uses Yield’s front-end to create a valid batch transaction. Evil Eve observes that in the mempool and identifies the `vaultID` of the vault being built by Alice. Eve submits her own batch transaction (without using the front-end) with only a build operation using Alice’s `vaultID`. She uses a higher gas price to front-run Alice’s transaction and get’s the protocol to assign that `vaultID` to herself. Alice’s batch transaction later fails because the `vaultID` she requested is already assigned to Eve. Eve can do this for any valid transaction to grief protocol users by wasting her gas to cause DoS.

Recommend mitigating this DoS vector by having the `Cauldron` assign the `vaultID` instead of the user specifying it in the `build()` operation. This would likely require the `build()` to be a separate non-batch transaction followed by other operations that use the `vaultID` assigned in `build()`. Consider the pros/cons of this approach because it will significantly affect the batching/caching logic in `Ladle`.

Alternatively, consider adding validation logic in `Ladle's` batching to revert batches that have only build or a subset of the operations that do not make sense to the protocol’s operations per valid recipes, which could be an attacker’s signature pattern.

Good find. [Fix](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/vault-v2/pull/210)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service caused by allowing users to specify the identifier (vaultID) of a newly created vault in the build() function. Because the vaultID is supplied by the transaction sender rather than being generated internally by the Cauldron contract, an attacker monitoring the mempool can see a legitimate batch transaction that intends to create a vault with a particular vaultID. The attacker can then submit a higher‑gas‑price transaction that calls only the build operation with the same vaultID, thereby claiming ownership of that identifier before the original transaction is mined. When the legitimate transaction is later mined, the Cauldron contract’s check for an existing vaultID (line 180) causes the whole batch to revert, preventing the intended vault from being created. The root cause is the reliance on externally supplied identifiers without any uniqueness enforcement or atomic reservation, which creates a race condition between competing transactions. Exploitation is straightforward: observe a pending build() call, copy the requested vaultID, and front‑run with a single‑operation batch that claims the same ID. The impact is that honest users see their batch transactions fail, receiving no vault, no assets deposited, and a reverted transaction despite paying gas. From the user’s point of view the front‑end reports a failure to create a vault, often with an “already exists” error, leaving the user confused why nothing happened even though the transaction was accepted. This can be repeated across many users, effectively grinding the protocol’s ability to open new vaults to a halt, which constitutes a high‑impact denial‑of‑service even though the attacker gains only an empty vault and spends gas. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the batching logic of the Ladle contract and identified that the vaultID parameter was user‑controlled. It may be hard to notice because the failure appears as a normal revert due to a duplicate identifier, which is expected in other contexts, and because the attacker does not steal funds, only blocks the operation. To remediate, the protocol should generate vaultIDs internally within the Cauldron contract, removing the ability for external actors to choose them. Alternatively, the batching system could reject batches that consist solely of a build operation or enforce atomic reservation of identifiers. This class of bug falls under identifier collision and front‑running vulnerabilities, where externally supplied unique keys are insufficiently protected, breaking the accounting assumption that each vaultID maps to a single owner and that a user’s request will always succeed if it is valid.

title: Uniswap Oracle uses wrong prices
description:
The Uniswap oracle uses a mock contract with hard-coded prices to retrieve the price, which is not feasible in production. Also, note that even when using the “real deal” `@uniswap/v3-periphery/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol`… it does not, in fact, return the prices.

The price could change from the set price. Meanwhile, always updating new prices with `set` will be too slow and gas expensive.

Recommend using `cumulativeTicks = pool.observe([secondsAgo, 0]) // [a_t1, a_t2]` and applying [equation 5.5](https://uniswap.org/whitepaper-v3.pdf) from the Uniswap V3 whitepaper to compute the token0 TWAP. Note that even the [official `.consult` call](https://github.com/Uniswap/uniswap-v3-periphery/blob/b55e7e81a803082c0328e2826592327da373ab00/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol#L27) seems to only return the averaged cumulative ticks; you’d still need to compute the `1.0001^timeWeightedAverageTick` in the function.

We probably should have not included this contract; it’s too confusing since, at the time, the Uniswap v3 OracleLibrary was still a mock, and this hasn’t gone real testing.

The price source in a production version would be a Uniswap v3 pool, not one of our mock oracle sources. We never expected to call `set` in production, but to retrieve the prices from a Uniswap v3 pool using the mentioned library (which was not even merged into main at the start of the contest).

We will check with the Uniswap team what is the recommended way of using their oracles. The equation 5.5 in the whitepaper is problematic because an exponentiation of two fractional numbers in Solidity is neither trivial nor cheap. Our understanding is that one of the goals of the OracleLibrary was to provide a consistent implementation to this formula.

From a conversation with @moodysalem, I understand that the code in `getQuoteAtTick` might achieve the same result as the 5.5 equation, so maybe we need to retrieve the average tick with `consult`, and then the actual price with `getQuoteAtTick`.

I’m using the `acknowledged` label for findings that require further investigation to assess.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on a mock price oracle that returns hard‑coded values instead of fetching live market data from a Uniswap V3 pool. The root cause is the inclusion of a deliberately simplified oracle contract and an incorrect use of Uniswap’s OracleLibrary, which only provides cumulative tick values and does not directly compute a time‑weighted average price (TWAP). Because the contract never performs the required transformation of the cumulative tick into a price – for example by applying equation 5.5 from the Uniswap V3 whitepaper or by using the library’s getQuoteAtTick function – the price used by the protocol can remain static, become stale, or deviate arbitrarily from the true market rate. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by calling the contract’s set function to manually update the mock price, which is slow, gas‑expensive, and can be manipulated to present favorable prices for a short window. When the protocol uses these incorrect prices for quoting, liquidation, or reward calculations, users may receive trades at rates far worse than expected, see their balances reduced unexpectedly, or lose funds because the accounting assumptions of the system are violated. This issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed in a production environment without replacing the mock oracle with a genuine Uniswap V3 pool reference, and it is triggered during any operation that queries the price oracle. The affected parties include protocol participants, token holders, and any downstream contracts that rely on the quoted price for financial decisions. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that compared the oracle implementation against official Uniswap documentation and observed that the price never reflected market movement. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract superficially appears to provide a price feed, yet the values remain constant or change only when the set function is invoked, which may not be obvious during routine testing. To remediate, the mock contract should be removed, the oracle should query a real Uniswap V3 pool using pool.observe([secondsAgo, 0]) to obtain cumulative ticks, then compute the TWAP by converting the average tick to a price with getQuoteAtTick (or an equivalent safe exponentiation method). This correction aligns the contract with the intended oracle design, restores accurate price discovery, and eliminates the risk of funds disappearing or being exchanged at unfair rates.

title: Witch can’t give back vault after 2x grab
description:
The `witch.sol` contract gets access to a vault via the grab function in case of liquidation. If the `witch.sol` contract can’t sell the debt within a certain amount of time, a second grab can occur.

After the second grab, the information of the original owner of the vault is lost, and the vault can’t be returned to the original owner once the debt has been sold.

The `grab` function stores the previous owner in `vaultOwners[vaultId]`, and then the contract itself is the new owner (via `cauldron.grab` and `cauldron._give`). The `vaultOwners[vaultId]` is overwritten at the second grab

The function buy of `Witch`.sol tried to give the vault back to the original owner, which won’t succeed after a second grab. [See the issue page for proof of concept and referenced code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-yield-findings/issues/8)

Assuming it’s useful to give back the vault to the original owner, recommend making a stack/array of previous owners if multiple instances of the `witch.sol` contract would be used. Or, check if the witch is already the owner (in the `grab` function) and keep the`vaultOwners[vaultId]` if that is the case.

This is a good finding and a vulnerability that we will fix. I anticipate that we will store the original owner in `Cauldron.auctions` along with the time at which the auction was started.

Actually, we might remove some overengineering by taking out the feature of allowing multiple competing liquidation engines.

That would allow us to:

  1. Move the `auctions` mapping to the `Witch.`
  2. Remove the `auctionInterval` setting
  3. Simplify `grab`
  4. Stop worrying about more than one `grab.`

Editors note: An alternative submission for this bug was not included in this report but can be found in [Issue #30](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-yield-findings/issues/30).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation workflow of the Witch contract, which gains temporary ownership of a user’s vault when a liquidation is triggered via the grab function. The contract records the previous owner in a mapping called vaultOwners[vaultId] before transferring ownership to itself. If the debt associated with the vault is not sold within the allotted auction interval, the protocol permits a second grab to occur. During this second grab, the same vaultOwners entry is overwritten with the new (current) owner, thereby erasing the record of the original user who deposited the collateral. When the debt is eventually sold, the buy function attempts to return the vault to the stored previous owner; however, because that information has been lost after the second grab, the contract cannot restore the vault to the rightful holder. Consequently, the original owner may find that their vault – and the collateral it contains – is no longer accessible, effectively disappearing from their account.
