Consequently, any operation that depends on fresh price data—such as collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or token swaps—cannot proceed, resulting in a halt of protocol functionality and potentially freezing user assets. From the end‑user perspective, interactions that normally would display a quote or allow a trade instead show no price, display an error, or simply do nothing, leading to confusion as “my transaction won’t go through” or “the price is missing”. The condition manifests whenever the deprecated endpoint is no longer serviced, which could happen abruptly after a Chainlink upgrade or policy change. All participants who rely on the protocol—traders, lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s own governance—are affected because their funds become inaccessible until the contracts are redeployed with a supported price‑feed interface. The issue was discovered during a third‑party audit that reviewed external oracle calls and identified the use of the outdated function. It can be hard to notice because the contract may work correctly for an extended period before the upstream API is turned off, giving a false sense of stability. The appropriate remediation is to replace all calls to `latestAnswer()` with the current V3 interface methods (e.g., `latestRoundData()`), update the contract’s oracle adapter to use the new ABI, and redeploy the updated contracts. This change aligns the protocol with the maintained API contract, ensuring continuous price availability and protecting the system from sudden service disruption. The bug belongs to the class of "deprecated external dependency" or "unstable oracle integration" vulnerabilities, where reliance on legacy interfaces can cause silent failures that break critical business logic such as price calculation and fund movement.

title: No check `transferFrom`
description:
The smart contract doesn’t check the return value of `token.transfer()` and `token.transferFrom()`, some erc20 token might not revert in case of error but return false. In the [TracerPerpetualSwaps:deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/TracerPerpetualSwaps.sol#L151) and [Insurance:deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/Insurance.sol#L51) this would allow a user to deposit for free. See issue page for other places.

Recommend wrapping the call into a `require()` or using openzeppelin’s [SafeERC20 library](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked return value from ERC20 token transfer functions (transfer and transferFrom) within the deposit routines of a perpetual swaps contract and an insurance contract. The root cause lies in the assumption that ERC20 implementations will always revert on failure, while the ERC20 standard permits a function to return false instead of reverting. Because the contract does not evaluate the boolean result, a token that signals failure by returning false will be treated as if the transfer succeeded. An attacker can exploit this by calling the deposit function with a non‑standard token that deliberately returns false on transferFrom; the contract will record the deposited amount in its internal accounting, but no actual tokens are transferred from the attacker’s wallet. Consequently, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent: the attacker’s on‑chain balance appears increased for free, while the protocol’s real token reserves remain unchanged. This mismatch allows the attacker to later withdraw the credited amount, effectively draining funds from the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a deposit function invokes token.transfer or token.transferFrom without checking the returned value, and it is triggered specifically with ERC20 tokens that do not revert on failure. All users and the protocol itself are affected because the internal ledger may show balances that do not correspond to real token holdings, undermining trust and financial integrity. The flaw was discovered during an external audit that reviewed the code paths for token handling and identified the missing require statements. The problem is subtle because most popular ERC20 tokens do revert on failure, making the bug invisible under standard testing; only when a token that returns false is introduced does the discrepancy surface, often only observable through mismatched UI balances or unexpected zero token movement after a successful deposit. To remediate the issue, each external call to transfer or transferFrom should be wrapped in a require statement that validates the boolean result, or the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library should be employed, which automatically reverts on false returns. This aligns the contract’s accounting with actual token transfers, restoring the invariant that a recorded deposit corresponds to a real token movement, and prevents attackers from inflating balances without providing assets. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of unchecked external call return values, leading to accounting errors and potential asset loss.

title: Deflationary tokens are not supported
description:
There are ERC20 tokens that may make certain customizations to their ERC20 contracts. One type of these tokens is deflationary tokens that charge a certain fee for every `transfer()` or `transferFrom()`.

The `deposit()` functions of `Insurance` and `TracerPerpetualSwaps` assume that the external ERC20 balance of the contract increases by the same amount as the `amount` parameter of the `transferFrom`.

The user is credited the full amount without the taxes (`userBalance.position.quote`).

Recommend as one possible mitigation, measuring the asset change right before and after the asset-transferring functions.

Most likely not a medium risk as you can do a lot more nasty things than just use rebasing tokens. Since the owner of a market can set their own quote token, this token could be a token they control the supply of allowing them to arbitrarily transfer tokens between accounts, etc.

As such, this sort of falls outside of our trust model. Market creators should use tokens that behave as “standard” ERC20s. We will make a not that rebasing and deflationary tokens should not be used as quote tokens without weird behaviour.

Would be better as a low or informational issue due to this.

Marking this as low risk as it seems to fall outside of the trust model, yet important enough to communicate to users explicitly.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the assumption that ERC20 tokens behave in a strictly transfer‑for‑exact‑amount manner. In the `deposit()` functions of the `Insurance` and `TracerPerpetualSwaps` contracts, the code calls `transferFrom` with a user‑specified `amount` and then credits the caller’s `userBalance.position.quote` with that exact `amount`. This logic works for standard ERC20 tokens that transfer the full amount, but it fails for deflationary (or rebasing) tokens that deduct a fee or automatically adjust the supply on each transfer. Because the contracts never verify the actual token balance change after the call, they credit users with a higher quote balance than the contract really received. When the fee is, for example, 5 %, a user who deposits 100 tokens will see a credit of 100 tokens while the contract’s token balance only increases by 95. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful deposit and the expected balance, yet later withdrawals or position settlements may fail or result in the protocol owing more tokens than it holds. The root cause is a missing balance‑verification step and an implicit trust that the quote token complies with the vanilla ERC20 specification. The issue manifests whenever a quote token that imposes a transfer fee is used – typically when a market creator selects a custom deflationary token as the quote asset. The affected parties include depositors, who receive an inflated balance; the protocol, which may become under‑collateralized; and market creators, who could deliberately exploit the discrepancy to siphon tokens by repeatedly depositing and withdrawing inflated balances. The flaw was discovered during a static audit that compared expected versus actual token flows and noted that the contracts never read the token balance before and after the transfer. It is difficult to notice because the `transferFrom` call succeeds and emits no error, and the ERC20 standard does not forbid fee‑charging implementations, so developers may incorrectly assume that the transferred amount always matches the input. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "incorrect accounting for transfer fees" or "missing post‑transfer balance validation". The exploitation scenario is straightforward: an attacker deploys or selects a deflationary token, sets it as the quote token, makes deposits, receives full credit, and later withdraws or settles positions for more tokens than the contract actually holds, effectively draining the protocol’s reserves. The recommended mitigation is to measure the token balance of the contract immediately before and after each `transferFrom` (or use `safeTransferFrom` with return‑value checks) and credit the user based on the observed delta rather than the requested amount, or simply restrict quote tokens to standard fee‑free ERC20s. This aligns the on‑chain accounting with business logic that expects a one‑to‑one correspondence between deposited amount and balance, preventing money from disappearing or accounting from breaking.

title: Underflow problems occurring when a token has >18 decimals
description:
The contracts assume that all tokens will have <=18 decimals. This isn’t necessarily a problem if the Tracer team is the only people deploying the contracts and they keep it in mind. But, If the contracts are to be deployed by other people, this assumption should be made explicit and hard-coded.

We can see that the scaler computations will underflow and be defined when it should not be In [L220-L232](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/lib/LibBalances.sol#L220-L232).

Recommend writing a require check that ensures `tokenDecimals <= 18` before running the above functions.

Valid issue and makes sense as a medium.

Suggested mitigation will be implemented.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an implicit assumption in the contract library that all ERC‑20 tokens interacting with the system have a decimal precision of at most 18 places. This assumption is baked into scaling calculations performed in the LibBalances.sol functions around lines 220‑232, where token amounts are multiplied or divided by a factor derived from 10ⁿ, with n representing the token's decimals. When a token with more than 18 decimals is supplied, the derived scaling factor exceeds the range that can be safely represented in the unsigned integer type used, causing the arithmetic to underflow. The underflow produces values that are dramatically smaller than intended, often collapsing to zero. As a result, balance accounting, fee distribution, or refund logic that relies on these computed values becomes incorrect; users may see their balances disappear, refunds return zero, or fees be mis‑allocated. The issue manifests whenever a third‑party token with >18 decimals is accepted by the contract – a scenario that can occur if the platform is open for deployment by external developers or if new token integrations are added without explicit validation. The affected parties include any user who deposits or receives such tokens, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer accounting inconsistencies and potential loss of funds. The flaw was identified during a formal audit where the auditor examined the scaling logic and observed that the computation would underflow for higher‑precision tokens. Because the problem resides in a low‑level arithmetic operation, it may not be immediately visible in the UI; users may simply notice that their balances become zero or that expected payouts are missing, without a clear indication of a mathematical error. To mitigate the issue, the contract should enforce an explicit requirement that tokenDecimals be less than or equal to 18 before any scaling operation is performed, or it should adopt a more robust arithmetic approach that can safely handle larger decimal values, such as using larger integer types or a library that performs overflow‑safe scaling. This preventive check aligns the implementation with the business logic that assumes a maximum decimal precision, thereby preserving the integrity of balance calculations and preventing unintended loss of funds.

title: Add reentrancy protections on function `executeTrade`
description:
As written in the to-do comments, reentrancy could happen in the `executeTrade` function of `Trader` since the `makeOrder.market` can be a user-controlled external contract. See [L121-L126](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/Trader.sol#L121-L126) in `Trader.sol`.

Recommend adding a reentrancy guard (e.g., the [implementation from OpenZeppelin](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/security/ReentrancyGuard.sol)) to prevent the users from reentering critical functions.

This means that at worst you could directly use...
What the finding also implies, is that if...

Marking this as medium risk as, regardless of being noted by the team, still poses a security threat.

Duplicate of [#72](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer-findings/issues/72)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy weakness located in the executeTrade function of the Trader contract. The function interacts with a market contract that is supplied by the caller, meaning the market address can be an arbitrary external contract controlled by a malicious user. The root cause is that executeTrade performs an external call to the market contract before finalizing its own internal state, such as updating order status or balances. Because control is transferred to an attacker‑controlled contract, the attacker can invoke executeTrade again (directly or indirectly) before the first invocation finishes, thereby re‑entering the critical section. An exploit would consist of the attacker deploying a malicious market contract whose fallback or called function re‑calls executeTrade, perhaps with crafted parameters, causing the function to run multiple times in a single transaction. Each re‑entered call could, for example, trade the same order repeatedly, withdraw more assets than intended, or manipulate accounting variables that have not yet been locked. The impact is the potential loss of funds or incorrect accounting: users may see their balances reduced unexpectedly, trades may be executed multiple times, or the protocol’s internal ledger could become inconsistent, leading to money disappearing from the contract. This condition occurs whenever a trader submits an order that targets a market address that the attacker controls, and the contract does not employ a reentrancy guard or the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The affected parties include any user of the Trader contract, the protocol operators, and any downstream contracts that rely on the correctness of trade execution. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit where TODO comments highlighted the possibility of re‑entrancy and the external call was identified in the source lines. The bug can be hard to notice because the external call is legitimate for the intended functionality, and the contract may appear to work correctly under normal market contracts; only a malicious market reveals the flaw. To remediate, the contract should adopt a reentrancy protection mechanism such as OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard, or restructure the code to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: perform all state updates before making any external calls, and, if an external call is unavoidable, lock the function during execution. In user‑visible terms, a trader might place an order and later observe that their balance drops to zero or that they received no trade confirmation, even though the transaction succeeded. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each order is settled exactly once, and therefore breaks the financial integrity of the protocol.

title: Single-step process for critical ownership transfer
description:
The `Tracer Perpetuals Factory` contract is arguably the most critical contract in the project given that it deploys all the markets. The ownership of this contract is transferred to `_governance address`, i.e. TracerDAO, in the constructor. This critical address transfer in one-step is very risky because it is irrecoverable from any mistakes.

The impact is that, if an incorrect address (e.g. one for which the private key is not known) is used accidentally, then it prevents the use of all the `onlyOwner()` functions forever, which includes the changing of various deployer contract addresses and market approvals. This use of an incorrect address may not even be immediately apparent given that these functions are probably not used immediately. When noticed, due to a failing `onlyOwner()` function call, it will force the redeployment of the `factory` contract and require appropriate changes and notifications for switching from the old to new address. This will diminish trust in markets and incur a significant reputational damage. See [issue page](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer-findings/issues/43) for proof of concept.

Recommend retaining the deployer ownership in the constructor and then using a two-step address change to `_governance` address separately using setter functions:

1. Approve a new address as a `pendingOwner`
2. A transaction from the `pendingOwner` (TracerDAO) address claims the pending ownership change.

This mitigates risk because if an incorrect address is used in step (1), then it can be fixed by re-approving the correct address. Only after a correct address is used in step (1) can step (2) happen and complete the address/ownership change.

Correct that having the owner be set to a wrong address could be detrimental, however for the first deploy of the factory, this will be owned by the DAO and will be easy to validate on deployment.

Subsequent ownership transfers will be done via DAO proposal, and will have many eyes across them (due to them being a public Tracer DAO proposal) before function execution happens.

For this reason it seems like a lot of overhead to have a two step process for this. Not withstanding that the issue you mention could still be possible
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the Tracer Perpetuals Factory contract assigns its owner during deployment. In the constructor the contract immediately transfers ownership to a hard‑coded governance address (TracerDAO) in a single, irreversible step. This design is risky because the ownership transfer is performed without any verification or opportunity to correct the address after the transaction is mined. The root cause is the absence of a two‑step ownership handover pattern – there is no pendingOwner state that must be claimed by the new owner. Consequently, if the address supplied to the constructor is mistyped, points to an address for which no private key is known, or is otherwise incorrect, the contract becomes permanently locked. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; the mere mistake of providing a wrong address renders every function protected by the onlyOwner modifier unusable, including the ability to update deployer contract addresses, market approvals, and any future governance actions. The impact is that the factory can no longer create new markets or modify existing ones, effectively halting the protocol’s core functionality and potentially causing loss of trust among users and market participants. This condition may stay unnoticed for some time because the onlyOwner functions are typically invoked only during governance or upgrade events, so the failure does not manifest immediately after deployment. When the problem is finally observed, the contract will reject all calls that require ownership, forcing the developers to redeploy a new factory contract, migrate state, and announce the change – a costly and reputation‑damaging process. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s initialization logic and ownership management. It can be hard to spot because the constructor call appears normal; the address assignment succeeds on‑chain, yet the logical error is hidden until an owner‑only action is attempted. The recommended mitigation is to retain ownership with the deployer at deployment time and then adopt a two‑step transfer: first, set a pendingOwner address; second, require a transaction from that pendingOwner to claim ownership. This allows the deployer to correct an erroneous address before it is finalized, protecting the protocol from irreversible lockout. In summary, the flaw belongs to the class of "single‑step ownership transfer" bugs, where critical control is handed over without confirmation, leading to potential loss of administrative capabilities, halted market creation, and erosion of stakeholder confidence.

title: Malicious owner can arbitrarily change fee to any % value
description:
The Tracer protocol like any other allows market creators to charge fees for trades. However, a malicious/greedy owner can arbitrarily change fee to any % value and without an event to observe this change or a timelock to react, there is no easy way for users to monitor this via front-end or off-chain monitoring tools.

The impact is that, if the users are trading on a market with 0.1% fees and the owner suddenly changes this to 100%, the users realise this only after their trades are executed. Market loses confidence. Protocol takes a reputational hit.

See similar Medium-severity finding in [ConsenSys’s Audit of 1inch Liquidity Protocol](https://consensys.net/diligence/audits/2020/12/1inch-liquidity-protocol/#unpredictable-behavior-for-users-due-to-admin-front-running-or-general-bad-timing)

Recommend implementing an `Emit` event, and providing a timelock for users to react and establish an upper threshold for fees that is decided across markets by governance.

Like the idea of having a timelock for any update parameter update that immediately affects traders
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted administrative control over the trading fee parameter of the Tracer protocol. The contract stores the fee as a mutable percentage value that can be modified by the owner through a privileged function. Because the function does not emit any event, does not enforce a timelock, and lacks a governance‑defined upper bound, the owner can set the fee to any arbitrary percent, including extreme values such as 100%. This design flaw originates from the absence of a mechanism that publicly announces fee changes and from the missing delay that would give market participants time to react. An attacker who controls the owner address can invoke the fee‑setting function, change the fee instantly, and then users who submit trades will be charged the newly‑set fee without prior notice. The impact is that traders expecting a modest fee (for example 0.1%) may find that their trades incur an unexpectedly high charge, effectively draining a large portion of their assets. From the user’s perspective the UI may still display the old fee or no fee information at all, leading to a situation where a trade completes and the user receives far less output than anticipated, sometimes perceiving that “their funds disappeared” or that a “refund is missing”. The protocol suffers a loss of confidence and reputational damage, as market participants cannot trust that fee parameters are stable or transparent. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the fee‑adjustment logic and noting the lack of event emission and timelock. It is difficult to detect in production because off‑chain monitoring tools typically rely on emitted events to track parameter updates; without such signals, the change remains invisible until after a trade is executed. To remediate the problem, the contract should emit a dedicated FeeChanged event whenever the fee is altered, introduce a timelock that enforces a minimum delay between proposal and activation of a new fee, and enforce a maximum fee ceiling defined by governance or a multi‑sig process, thereby aligning the implementation with standard best practices for updatable critical parameters.

title: Missing events for critical parameter changing operations by owner
description:
The owner of `TracerPerpetualSwaps` contract, who is potentially untrusted as per specification, can change the market critical parameters such as the addresses of the `Liquidation`/`Pricing`/`Insurance`/`GasOracle`/`FeeReceiver` and also critical values such as `feeRate`, `maxLeverage`, `fundingRateSensitivity`, `deleveragingCliff`, `lowestMaxLeverage`, `insurancePoolSwitchStage` and whitelisting.

None of these setter functions emit events to record these changes on-chain for off-chain monitors/tools/interfaces to register the updates and react if necessary.

The impact of this is that, if a malicious owner changes the critical addresses or values that significantly change the security posture/perception of the protocol. No events are emitted and users lose funds/confidence. The protocol takes a reputation hit.

See similar high-severity finding in [OpenZeppelin’s Audit of Audius](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/audius-contracts-audit/#high) and medium-severity finding [OpenZeppelin’s Audit of UMA Phase 4](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/uma-audit-phase-4/).

Recommend to consider emitting events when these addresses/values are updated. This will be more transparent and it will make it easier to keep track of the status of the system.

Duplicate of #66

Opening this issue as the event emission seems to be separate from the arbitrarily changing of the values.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of emitted events for a set of privileged setter functions in the TracerPerpetualSwaps contract. The contract’s owner – which the specification treats as potentially untrusted – can alter critical parameters such as the addresses of the Liquidation, Pricing, Insurance, GasOracle and FeeReceiver contracts, as well as numeric values that govern feeRate, maxLeverage, fundingRateSensitivity, deleveragingCliff, lowestMaxLeverage, insurancePoolSwitchStage and the whitelist configuration. Because the setter functions do not fire any events, changes to these values are invisible to off‑chain monitoring tools, indexers, user interfaces and any external services that rely on log‑based notifications. This lack of transparency creates a situation where a malicious or compromised owner could silently redirect the protocol to a contract under their control, lower fee rates to attract unsuspecting traders, raise leverage limits to increase liquidation risk, or otherwise manipulate the economic parameters without any on‑chain audit trail. Users interacting with the protocol would continue to see the old configuration in the UI, believing that the system is operating under the previously displayed parameters, while the underlying state is different. When such a hidden change leads to loss of funds – for example, a user sends a trade to a newly set malicious liquidation address and their position is liquidated under unfair terms – the protocol suffers both financial damage and a severe reputation hit. The issue manifests each time the owner calls any of the setter functions; it does not depend on any particular transaction pattern beyond the privileged call. The affected parties include all traders, liquidity providers, and any third‑party services that rely on accurate protocol state, as well as the protocol itself, which may be blamed for negligent governance. The problem was uncovered during a formal code audit that flagged the missing event emissions as a best‑practice violation. It can be hard to notice because the state changes are still recorded on‑chain; without logs, developers and auditors need to manually inspect storage changes or compare before‑and‑after contract state, which is cumbersome and prone to oversight. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of "missing transparency for critical state changes" and is often reported as an event‑emission omission for privileged setters. To remediate, each function that updates a critical address or parameter should emit a well‑named event containing the old and new values, ensuring that any off‑chain observer can detect and react to the change. Adding events also aligns the contract with industry‑standard practices for governance‑related state mutations and improves auditability, user confidence, and overall security posture.

title: Wrong funding index in settle when no base?
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the funding‑rate accounting logic of the TracerPerpetualSwaps contract. When a user without an open position (base amount equals zero) calls the settle function, the contract records the user’s last funding index as the current global funding index. However, the surrounding comment and the logic used for users with a saved rate indicate that the last updated index should reference the most recently *fully established* funding period, which is the global index minus one. By storing the current index instead of the previous index, the contract incorrectly marks the user as already having accounted for the most recent funding period. The check that determines whether a user needs to settle funding compares `accountLastUpdatedIndex + 1` with `currentGlobalFundingIndex`. Because the stored index is already equal to the current index, the expression evaluates to false, and the funding settlement is skipped for that user. Consequently, a first‑time depositor can open a position, avoid paying the first funding fee, and later benefit from the accrued funding without having been charged. This leads to an under‑collection of protocol fees and creates an unfair advantage for attackers who deliberately open a zero‑base position to skip the initial funding charge. The bug manifests only when a user’s base position is zero at the time of settlement, which is a legitimate state for new depositors, making it easy to miss during functional testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when reviewers compared the implementation against the documented intention in the source code comment. The issue is hard to notice because the contract continues to operate normally for users with existing positions, and the off‑by‑one discrepancy does not produce an immediate revert or obvious error; it merely results in a subtle accounting deviation. To remediate the problem, the contract should align the stored `lastUpdatedIndex` with the last fully established funding period, i.e., set it to `currentGlobalFundingIndex - 1` (or adjust the subsequent comparison logic accordingly) so that the funding settlement check correctly triggers for new depositors. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that every user must pay funding for each completed period, preserving protocol revenue and preventing users from receiving a free funding period.

title: `prb-math` not audited
description:
The library [`prb-math` documents](//%20https://github.com/hifi-finance/prb-math#security) have not been audited by a security researcher. This means its more risky to rely on this library.

Recommend considering (crowdsourcing) an audit for `prb-math`.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a smart‑contract system that imports and relies on the external arithmetic library prb‑math without an independent security audit. The root cause is the trust placed in a third‑party code package whose internal functions (e.g., fixed‑point multiplication, division, rounding, overflow checks) have never been examined by a dedicated security researcher. Because the library implements core financial calculations, any hidden flaw—such as an unchecked overflow, an incorrect rounding rule, a division‑by‑zero edge case, or a subtle precision loss—can propagate into the contract’s state. An attacker who discovers such a flaw can craft inputs that cause the library to return a wrong result, which in turn may lead the contract to credit or debit amounts incorrectly, lock funds, or allow a user to withdraw more than entitled. The impact manifests as mis‑accounted balances, unexpected zero refunds, or funds disappearing from the protocol’s treasury, thereby breaking the accounting assumptions of the business logic. The issue becomes active whenever the contract calls any prb‑math routine, which is typically during token swaps, interest accrual, fee calculation, or any price‑determination step. All participants—users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the correctness of any monetary transfer hinges on the underlying math. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit that noted the library’s documentation explicitly states it has not been audited, highlighting an elevated risk. This kind of omission is hard to detect in functional testing because the library’s outputs may appear correct for common cases, while edge‑case inputs that trigger the bug can be obscure. To remediate, the protocol should obtain a formal security audit of prb‑math, replace it with a vetted alternative, or implement its own arithmetic with comprehensive unit tests and overflow/underflow checks. In essence, the contract suffers from an unaudited external dependency that can cause financial miscalculations, violating the expected invariant that balances always reflect the true economic state.

title: Claim liquidation escrow
description:
A liquidator can always claim the liquidation escrow in the following way:

* create a second account
* setup a complimentary trade in that second account, which will result in a large slippage when executed
* call `executeTrade` (which everyone can call), to execute a trade between his own two accounts with a large slippage
* the slippage doesn’t hurt because the liquidator owns both accounts
* call `claimReceipt` with the receiptId of the executed order, within the required period (e.g. 15 minutes)

[L67](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/Trader.sol#L67)

```solidity
function executeTrade(Types.SignedLimitOrder[] memory makers, Types.SignedLimitOrder[] memory takers) external override {
```

[L394](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-tracer/blob/main/src/contracts/Liquidation.sol#L394)

```solidity
function claimReceipt( uint256 receiptId, Perpetuals.Order[] memory orders, address traderContract) external override {
```

Recommend to perhaps limit who can call `executeTrade`.

Valid issue which would allow someone to get reimbursed for slippage against themselves.

The Trader contract will have whitelisted relayers added to prevent issues like this (similar to #119)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted trade execution path that enables a liquidator to claim the liquidation escrow without incurring any real loss. The root cause is that the contract's `executeTrade` function is public and does not enforce any restriction on who can invoke it or on the relationship between the maker and taker orders. Because of this, a liquidator can create a second account, place a complementary limit order on each account, and then call `executeTrade` to match the two orders. By deliberately configuring the orders to generate a large slippage, the liquidator ensures that the trade would normally require a reimbursement from the protocol. However, since the slippage is internal – both sides of the trade are owned by the same entity – the liquidator does not actually lose any assets. After the trade is settled, the liquidator proceeds to call `claimReceipt` with the receipt identifier of the executed order within the permitted claim window (for example, fifteen minutes). The `claimReceipt` function does not verify that the slippage incurred originates from an external counter‑party, allowing the liquidator to collect the full liquidation escrow as if the trade had been against an unrelated trader. This can be exploited at any time after a liquidation event whenever the liquidator has the ability to create an auxiliary account and execute a self‑trade before the claim period expires. The impact is a draining of escrow funds that are meant to compensate genuine liquidations, reducing the protocol's collateral pool and potentially harming other participants who rely on proper liquidation incentives. The issue affects the integrity of the liquidation mechanism, the protocol's financial safety, and any users whose positions could be under‑collateralized as a result. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between `executeTrade` and `claimReceipt` and noticed that the former is callable by anyone without restriction. The flaw can be difficult to spot because the trade appears syntactically valid, the slippage is recorded, and no immediate on‑chain error occurs; the loss is only reflected in the unexpected escrow payout. To remediate the problem, the contract should restrict `executeTrade` to a whitelist of trusted relayers or enforce that maker and taker orders belong to distinct accounts that cannot be owned by the same entity. Additionally, `claimReceipt` should verify that the slippage reimbursement is justified by an external loss and not by a self‑matched trade. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of "unauthorized self‑trading with reward claim" or "lack of access control leading to reward abuse" and violates fundamental accounting assumptions that escrow payouts must be funded by genuine counterparties, not by the claimant themselves.

title: avoid paying insurance
description:
It’s possible to avoid paying insurance in the following way:

* once per hour (at the right moment), do the following:
* using a flash loan, or with a large amount of tokens, call `deposit` of `Insurance.sol` to make sure that the pool is sufficiently filled (`poolHoldings` > `poolTarget`)
* call the function `executeTrade` of Trader.sol with a minimal trade (possibly of value 0, see finding ”`executeTrade` with same trades”)
* `executeTrade` calls `matchOrders`, which calls `recordTrade`
* `recordTrade` calls `updateFundingRate()`; (once per hour, so you have to be sure you do it in time before other trades trigger this)
* `updateFundingRate` calls `getPoolFundingRate`
* `getPoolFundingRate` determines the insurance rate, but because the insurance pool is sufficiently full (due to the flash loan), the rate is 0
* `updateFundingRate` stores the 0 rate via `setInsuranceFundingRate` (which is used later on to calculate the amounts for the insurances)
* withdraw from the Insurance and pay back the flash loan

The insurance rates are 0 now and no-one pays insurance. The gas costs relative to the insurance costs + the flash loan fees determine if this is an economically viable attack. Otherwise it is still a grief attack. This will probably be detected pretty soon because the insurance pool will stay empty. However its difficult to prevent.

See issue page for code referenced in proof of concept.

Recommend setting a timelock on withdrawing insurance.

Really like this exploit idea. Currently this is possible since the Trader is not whitelisted (eg there is no whitelisted relayer address). With this added, this exploit is no longer possible as only off chain relayers can place orders with the trader.

Disagree with the severity mainly due to the fact that executing this exploit once would only cause insurance funding to not be paid for a single hour. For insurance funding to never be paid, you would have to time this transaction as the first transaction on each and every hour. This would quickly be noticed. The only affect on this would be insurance depositors miss interest payments for a few periods.

Marking this as medium risk as a front-runner could keep doing this for not paying any funding using a bot.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation and setting of the insurance funding rate in a decentralized trading protocol. The protocol determines the insurance rate each hour by reading the current insurance pool balance (poolHoldings) and comparing it to a predefined target (poolTarget). The function that updates this rate, updateFundingRate, is invoked indirectly during the execution of any trade via the executeTrade → matchOrders → recordTrade → updateFundingRate call chain. Because the contract does not restrict who can call executeTrade, an attacker can manipulate the pool balance immediately before the hourly update. By obtaining a large amount of tokens through a flash loan (or using an existing large balance) and calling the deposit function of the Insurance contract, the attacker can temporarily raise poolHoldings above poolTarget. When the subsequent minimal trade triggers updateFundingRate, the insurance calculation perceives the pool as sufficiently funded and returns a rate of zero. The zero rate is then stored via setInsuranceFundingRate and used for the upcoming insurance fee assessment. After the rate is recorded, the attacker withdraws the deposited tokens, repays the flash loan, and the protocol records an hour in which no insurance fee is collected. The impact is that insurance depositors miss the expected interest or fee for that hour, reducing the pool’s funding and potentially undermining the protocol’s risk coverage if the attack is repeated. The issue manifests only when the attacker can time the deposit, trade, and withdrawal within the same hourly window before any other legitimate trade updates the funding rate. It affects all participants who rely on the insurance mechanism, including depositors and the protocol’s security model. The flaw was identified during a security audit that examined the call flow of the Trader contract and noticed that the funding rate update does not guard against artificial pool inflations and that the Trader contract lacks a whitelist for authorized relayers. The problem is difficult to notice because the deviation lasts only for a single hour and may look like normal variance in insurance earnings, especially if the attacker does not repeat the attack frequently. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that the insurance funding rate cannot be reduced to zero solely by a temporary balance increase, such as by introducing a timelock on withdrawals, restricting who can trigger the funding rate update, enforcing a minimum non‑zero rate, or using a snapshot of the pool balance taken before any trade in the hour. These measures would prevent an attacker from exploiting the timing window to avoid paying insurance, preserving the intended economic incentives and ensuring the insurance pool remains adequately funded.

title: Trader orders can be front-run and users can be denied from trading
description:
The `Trader` contract accepts two signed orders and tries to match them. Once they are matched and become filled, they can therefore not be matched against other orders anymore.

This allows for a griefing attack where an attacker can deny any other user from trading by observing the mempool and front-running their trades by creating their own order and match it against the counter order instead.

In this way, a trader can be denied from trading. The cost of the griefing attack is that the trader has to match the order themselves, however depending on the liquidity of the order book and the spread, they might be able to do the counter-trade again afterwards, basically just paying the fees.

It could be useful if the attacker is a liquidator and is stopping a user who is close to liquidation from becoming liquid again.

This seems hard to circumvent in the current design. If the order book is also off-chain, the `executeTrade` could also be a bot-only function.

Marked as a dispute as this is not really an issue. Tracer will initially maintain an off chain order book that is the entry point for users to make orders (and for market makers to interact with).

Orders only get propagated on chain once they have been matched, and they will only be propagated on chain by whitelisted relayers. As such nobody can arbitrarily frontrun the orders with their own.

Currently not seeing a whitelisted relayer functionality, so marking this a valid medium risk issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Trader contract processes trade orders. The contract is designed to accept two cryptographically signed orders, match them, and then mark both as filled so that they cannot be matched again. Because the matching logic does not enforce any ordering or protection against earlier submissions, an attacker who monitors the mempool can observe a pending user order and create a competing order that matches the same counter‑order first. By submitting their own order and causing the match to be recorded on‑chain before the legitimate user’s transaction is mined, the attacker effectively front‑runs the trade. Once the attacker’s order is matched, the user’s order is considered already filled and is rejected, preventing the user from executing the intended trade. This constitutes a grief‑or‑denial‑of‑service attack rather than a direct theft of funds; the attacker does not steal the user’s assets but forces the user to either accept an unwanted fill or lose the opportunity to trade. The impact is that traders may experience missing or zero‑filled orders, see their balances unchanged despite attempting a trade, and may be forced to pay additional gas and fee costs to re‑enter the market. The condition under which this occurs is when the order book is maintained off‑chain and any order is only recorded on‑chain after a match, combined with the lack of a whitelisted relayer or ordering mechanism that could enforce first‑come‑first‑served semantics. The affected parties include any user trying to trade through the platform, market makers who rely on predictable order execution, and protocol operators who might face reputational damage if users perceive the system as manipulable. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the matching flow and considered possible malicious actors observing the mempool. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct error for a front‑run; from a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails or appears to be silently ignored, leading to confusion when expected trades never materialize. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of front‑running and order‑matching race conditions where the system lacks atomicity guarantees for order settlement. To remediate, the design should enforce a deterministic ordering of order submissions, restrict who can call the matching function (e.g., via whitelisted relayers or a bot‑only executor), or move the order book on‑chain with proper sequencing to eliminate the time window that an attacker can exploit. By ensuring that only authorized entities can propagate matched orders and that matches are processed in the exact order they are received, the platform can mitigate the griefing vector and align actual trade execution with user expectations of fairness and reliability.

title: Signatures use only tx ID instead of entire digest
description:
The signature check in `recoverFulfillSignature()` only uses transaction ID (along with the relayer fee) which can be accidentally reused by the user, in which case the older signatures with the older relayer fees can be replayed. The signature should be on the entire digest `hashInvariantTransactionData(txData)` as indicated in the comment on L306.

The impact is that, If the user signatures are indeed on the digest as indicated by the comment, the signature/address check in `fulfill()` will fail. If not, they may be accidentally/intentionally replayed with same transaction ID, which also appears to be an outstanding question as indicated by the comment on L12.

`recoverCancelSignature()` similarly uses only tx ID.

Unless there is a good reason not to, it is safer to include `hashInvariantTransactionData(txData)` in signatures so that they cannot be replayed with different txData (but same tx ID) whose `preparedBlockNumber` is > 0.

Recommend evaluating if the signature should contain only tx ID, or the entire digest, and then changing the logic appropriately.

User should be able to break up large transfers across multiple routers using the same `transactionId` to keep the transaction unlocking atomic. For example, say I want to transfer $100K, but there are only 8 routers who each have $60K available. I should be able to break up the single transaction into $20K transactions split across 5 of the routers. When unlocking this, I should only need to broadcast a single signature, so all of the transactions can be unlocked simultaneously.

Bumping to medium risk as replay attack can have significant consequences
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract validates cryptographic signatures for transaction fulfillment and cancellation. Instead of signing the complete transaction digest, which includes all invariant data such as the amount, destination, and prepared block number, the implementation only includes the transaction identifier (txId) together with the relayer fee in the signed message. This limited signing scope creates a replay surface: an attacker who obtains a valid signature for a particular txId can reuse that signature for a different transaction payload that shares the same identifier. Because the contract’s `recoverFulfillSignature()` and `recoverCancelSignature()` functions reconstruct the signed message from only the txId, they are unable to detect that the underlying transaction data has been altered. The flaw appears when a user or a relayer submits a fulfillment request with a different `txData` (for example, a larger amount or a different prepared block) but reuses the original signature. If the original signature was intended for the full digest, the contract will reject the request; however, if the signature was generated only over the txId, the contract will accept the malformed request, effectively allowing an older signature to be replayed with newer transaction parameters. The impact can be severe: funds may be transferred under unauthorized terms, the relayer fee may be manipulated, or the transaction may be unlocked with unintended amounts, leading to loss of assets for the protocol or its users. The condition arises whenever the same transaction identifier is reused across multiple sub‑transactions—an intended feature for atomic unlocking across many routers—but the signature does not bind those sub‑transactions to the identifier. Users attempting to split a large transfer into several smaller router‑specific transfers expect a single signature to unlock all parts simultaneously; under the current scheme, an attacker could capture that signature and replay it with altered amounts, causing the user to receive less than expected or to pay an incorrect fee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s signature verification logic, where comments indicated that the full digest should be signed, yet the code only used the txId. The bug is hard to spot because the function signatures appear correct and the contract still enforces a signature check; however, the semantic mismatch between the intended signing domain (full digest) and the actual signing domain (txId only) is subtle and does not raise obvious compiler warnings. To remediate the problem, the signature verification should be updated to include the hash of the invariant transaction data (`hashInvariantTransactionData(txData)`) in the signed message, ensuring that any change to the transaction payload invalidates previously issued signatures. This change closes the replay vector, forces each sub‑transaction to be signed explicitly, and aligns the implementation with the documented security intent. In summary, the flaw is a replay‑able signature design where signing only the transaction identifier permits malicious reuse of signatures across different transaction contents, compromising the integrity of fund transfers and potentially leading to unauthorized asset movement.

title: Malicious router can block cross-chain-transfers
description:
The agreement between the `user` and the `router` seems to already happen off-chain because all the fields are required for the initial `In variantTransactionData` call already. A router could pretend to take on a user’s cross-chain transfer, the user sends their `prepare` transaction, locking up funds on the sending chain. But then the `router` simply doesn’t respond or responds with a `prepare` transaction of `amount=0`.

The user’s funds are then locked for the entire expiry time, whereas the router does not have to lock up anything as the amount is 0, even no gas if they simply don’t respond. In this way, a router can bid on everything off-chain without a penalty, and take down everyone that accepts the bid.

Recommend that maybe there could be a penalty mechanism for non-responsive routers that agreed off-chain, slashing part of their added liquidity. Could also be that the bid signature already helps with this, but I’m not sure how it works as the off-chain part is not part of the repo.

This is true, and we are building penalty mechanisms outside of these contracts. For now we are considering adding in a permissioned launch, see #49
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a denial‑of‑service style attack on cross‑chain transfers that rely on an off‑chain agreement between a user and a router. When a user initiates a transfer, the protocol expects the router to later supply a signed "prepare" transaction that contains the amount to be moved on the destination chain. Because the agreement and the router's commitment are handled off‑chain, the smart contract does not enforce that the router actually locks the corresponding amount of liquidity. A malicious router can therefore accept a user's request off‑chain, allow the user to submit the on‑chain prepare transaction that locks the user's funds on the source chain, and then either never respond or respond with a prepare transaction that claims an amount of zero. In this situation the user’s funds remain locked for the full expiry period while the router incurs no on‑chain cost or collateral, effectively blocking the transfer. The root cause is the lack of an on‑chain escrow or penalty mechanism that ties the router’s off‑chain promise to a verifiable on‑chain stake. The attack can be carried out simply by a router that advertises willingness to forward any transfer, receives the user’s request, and then disappears or returns a zero‑amount prepare, leaving the user’s balance frozen and the destination chain never receiving any assets. The impact is a loss of usability and potential financial loss for users, who see their balances locked and may not receive the expected funds; the protocol suffers from a denial‑of‑service vector that undermines trust in the bridge. The issue appears only after the user’s prepare transaction is mined, making it difficult to detect beforehand because the malicious behavior happens off‑chain and is not recorded on the blockchain until the expiry timeout expires. The vulnerability was identified during a code audit that examined the interaction flow between users and routers and noticed that the router’s obligations are not enforced by the contract. It is hard to notice in normal operation because no on‑chain event signals a router’s intent to refuse service; only the missing outcome (no funds on the destination chain) and the persistent lockup on the source chain reveal the problem. The proper mitigation is to require routers to post a security deposit or to lock a matching amount of liquidity on‑chain before they can be selected, and to implement a slashing or penalty for routers that either fail to respond within the agreed timeframe or submit a zero‑amount prepare. Such a mechanism would make the router’s off‑chain commitment economically enforceable, ensuring that users’ funds are either transferred or released back to the sender in a timely manner, thereby restoring the intended business logic of trustworthy cross‑chain asset movement.

title: Use of `safeApprove` will always cause `approveMax` to revert
description:
Unlike `SwappableYieldSource` which uses `safeIncreaseAllowance` to increase the allowance to `uint256.max`, `mStableYieldSource` uses OpenZeppelin’s `safeApprove()` which has been documented as (1) Deprecated because of approve-like race condition and (2) To be used only for initial setting of allowance `(current allowance == 0)` or resetting to 0 because it reverts otherwise.

The usage here is intended to allow increase of allowance when it falls low similar to the documented usage in `SwappableYieldSource`. Using it for that scenario will not work as expected because it will always revert if current allowance is != 0. The initial allowance is already set as `uint256.max` in constructor. And once it gets reduced, it can never be increased using this function unless it is invoked when allowance is reduced completely to 0. See issue page for referenced code.

Recommend using logic similar to `SwappableYieldSource` instead of using `safeApprove()`.

This issue has been fixed in the following commit: <https://github.com/pooltogether/pooltogether-mstable/pull/3/commits/156a990901e6ddff543897905e3ea3d09c78d817>
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of OpenZeppelin’s safeApprove function within the mStableYieldSource contract to raise an ERC‑20 token allowance to the maximum value (uint256.max). SafeApprove is deprecated for allowance updates because it enforces a strict rule: the function may only be called when the current allowance is exactly zero, otherwise it reverts. In the constructor the contract pre‑sets the allowance to the maximum, but once the external token spender consumes part of that allowance the remaining value becomes non‑zero. Any subsequent attempt by the contract to increase the allowance back to the maximum—intended to mimic the safeIncreaseAllowance pattern used in SwappableYieldSource—triggers a revert, because the current allowance is no longer zero. This logic error means the contract cannot restore a depleted allowance, causing calls that depend on a fresh allowance (such as depositing, withdrawing, or harvesting yield) to fail. From a user’s perspective, attempts to interact with the pool may result in transactions that revert with no obvious error message, leading to symptoms like “my withdrawal returns zero” or “the transaction fails without moving any funds”. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any participant whose actions cause the allowance to be partially spent; funds that should be transferable from the mStable pool become effectively locked until the allowance is manually reset to zero, an operation that the contract itself cannot perform automatically. The problem is discovered during a code audit that compared the allowance‑handling logic with the reference implementation in SwappableYieldSource and identified that safeApprove was being misapplied. The issue can be subtle because the initial state (full allowance) works correctly, and only after a reduction does the bug manifest, making it easy to miss in basic unit tests. The correct mitigation is to replace the unsafe safeApprove call with a pattern that either uses safeIncreaseAllowance to add the missing amount, or resets the allowance to zero before setting a new maximum, mirroring the approach taken in the sibling contract. By aligning the allowance‑management logic with the recommended OpenZeppelin usage, the contract will maintain the ability to replenish its token allowance and avoid unintentionally locking user funds.

title: Inconsistent balance when supplying transfer-on-fee or deflationary tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way SwappableYieldSource handles token deposits in its supplyTokenTo function. The contract assumes that the value passed to safeTransferFrom will be the exact amount that arrives in its balance, and it forwards this amount to the underlying yield source. This assumption fails when the deposited token implements a transfer‑on‑fee mechanism, a deflationary burn, or a rebasing supply model. In such cases the token contract deducts a fee, burns a portion of the transfer, or adjusts the total supply during the transfer, so the quantity that actually reaches SwappableYieldSource is lower than the amount specified by the caller. The code does not verify the post‑transfer balance, therefore the internal accounting records a higher supplied amount than was really deposited. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a fee‑on‑transfer token, causing the protocol to think it has received, for example, 100 tokens while it only holds 95. This discrepancy can be used to manipulate yield calculations, over‑issue tickets, or create a shortfall that later users cannot redeem, effectively causing funds to disappear or be mis‑allocated. The impact is medium‑severity: users may see their balances or expected refunds reduced, the protocol’s accounting may become inconsistent, and the overall trust in the system can be eroded. The condition occurs whenever a user deposits a token whose transfer logic deviates from the standard ERC‑20 model, especially when the token is intentionally designed to charge a fee on each transfer. The affected parties are depositors, the PoolTogether protocol itself, and any downstream contracts that rely on the reported supply amount for reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit where the auditors identified that the contract does not capture the actual received amount after the safeTransferFrom call. It is subtle because the transfer does not revert and the transaction appears successful, making the shortfall easy to overlook during normal testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should measure the token balance before and after the transfer and use the difference as the true received amount when calling the yield source’s supply function. This change ensures that the protocol records the exact amount of tokens it controls, preventing accounting drift and protecting users from unexpected loss of funds.

title: Old yield source still has infinite approval
description:
After swapping a yield source, the old yield source still has infinite approval. Infinite approval has been used in large attacks if the yield source isn’t perfectly safe ([see furucombo](https://github.com/pooltogether/swappable-yield-source/blob/89cf66a3e3f8df24a082e1cd0a0e80d08953049c/contracts/SwappableYieldSource.sol#L268)).

Recommend decreasing approval after swapping the yield source.

PR: <https://github.com/pooltogether/swappable-yield-source/pull/3>
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑management defect that occurs when a protocol replaces its external yield source but fails to revoke or reduce the previously granted ERC‑20 token allowance. Specifically, the contract continues to hold an infinite (max uint256) approval for the old yield source after the swap operation. This situation arises because the swap logic only updates the reference to the new source without adjusting the token allowance granted to the previous contract, leaving a persistent permission that can be exercised at any time. An attacker who can control, compromise, or replace the old yield source can invoke its transfer functions using the retained infinite allowance, thereby pulling any amount of tokens that the protocol holds. The impact of such an exploit includes unauthorized draining of user deposits, resulting in balances that appear to vanish, refunds that never arrive, and a breach of the protocol’s financial accounting guarantees. The condition manifests immediately after a governance or administrative action that swaps the yield source, affecting all token holders who rely on the protocol to safeguard their assets. The issue was identified by the Code4rena audit team, which recognized the pattern of infinite approvals as a known attack vector cited in previous incidents such as the furucombo exploit. The bug is hard to notice because infinite allowances are sometimes used deliberately for convenience, and the allowance state is not visible through the user interface; only the unexpected loss of funds reveals the problem. To remediate, the contract should explicitly set the allowance for the previous yield source to zero or to the minimal required amount during the swap, or employ a safe allowance pattern that updates permissions atomically with the source change. This class of bug falls under the broader category of "authorization persistence" or "unrevoked token allowance" vulnerabilities, where residual permissions enable unauthorized asset movement, violating the protocol’s business logic that assumes only the active yield source can access deposited tokens.

title: Single-step process for critical ownership transfer/renounce is risky
description:
The `SwappableYieldSource` allows owners and asset managers to set/swap/transfer yield sources/funds. As such, the contract ownership plays a critical role in the protocol.

Given that `AssetManager` is derived from `Ownable`, the ownership management of this contract defaults to `Ownable`’s `transferOwnership()` and `renounceOwnership()` methods which are not overridden here. Such critical address transfer/renouncing in one-step is very risky because it is irrecoverable from any mistakes.

Scenario: If an incorrect address, e.g. for which the private key is not known, is used accidentally then it prevents the use of all the `onlyOwner()` functions forever, which includes the changing of various critical addresses and parameters. This use of incorrect address may not even be immediately apparent given that these functions are probably not used immediately. When noticed, due to a failing `onlyOwner()` or `onlyOwnerOrAssetManager()` function call, it will force the redeployment of these contracts and require appropriate changes and notifications for switching from the old to new address. This will diminish trust in the protocol and incur a significant reputational damage.

See similar [High Risk severity finding](https://github.com/trailofbits/publications/blob/master/reviews/hermez.pdf) from Trail-of-Bits Audit of Hermez.

See similar [Medium Risk severity](https://github.com/Uniswap/uniswap-v3-core/blob/main/audits/tob/audit.pdf) finding from Trail-of-Bits Audit of Uniswap V3:

Recommend overriding the inherited methods to null functions and use separate functions for a two-step address change:

1. Approve a new address as a `pendingOwner`
2. A transaction from the `pendingOwner` address claims the pending ownership change.

This mitigates risk because if an incorrect address is used in step (1) then it can be fixed by re-approving the correct address. Only after a correct address is used in step (1) can step (2) happen and complete the address/ownership change.

Also, consider adding a time-delay for such sensitive actions. And at a minimum, use a multisig owner address and not an EOA.

This isn’t a security issue but an improper use of the `initialize` function. We do check for address zero so at least the risk of deploying the contract with address zero is excluded. Also, these contracts will be deployed by a multi sig owned by governance so the risk of a single human error is almost null.

Disagree with sponsor. A two step process would be a safer implementation. A multi-sig does not remove human error or the potential risk here. It may be an acceptable risk to the team, but still worth highlighting with the given severity.

We have studied this solution and decided to not implement it since it would make it a pretty tedious process to deploy a swappable yield source, especially through the use of our builder which would mean that a user would have to manually `claimOwnership` after deploying a pool. Plus, this contract will be owned by governance so it will be very difficult to transfer it to another owner or renounce ownership.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the use of a single‑step ownership transfer and renouncement mechanism in a contract that inherits the standard Ownable pattern. The contract’s critical functions, such as setting or swapping yield sources, are protected by the onlyOwner or onlyOwnerOrAssetManager modifiers, which rely on the address stored in the owner slot. Because the inherited transferOwnership() and renounceOwnership() functions are invoked directly without any additional validation or confirmation, an erroneous address can be written to the owner slot in a single transaction. This situation typically occurs when a developer mistakenly supplies an address whose private key is unknown, a zero address, or a contract that does not implement the required interface. When the incorrect address is set, any subsequent call to an onlyOwner‑protected function reverts with an ownership‑related error, effectively locking out all privileged operations. From the user’s perspective, the user interface may appear to stop responding to administrative actions: attempts to change parameters, withdraw funds, or update asset managers fail silently, and the console logs display “caller is not the owner” messages. The impact is operational: critical protocol parameters become immutable, maintenance tasks cannot be performed, and the protocol may need to be redeployed, causing loss of trust, potential reputational damage, and financial disruption for participants. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s initialize function and ownership management flow, noting that while a zero address check prevents deployment with an empty owner, there is no safeguard against inadvertent assignment of any other incorrect address. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the contract continues to function for non‑owner actions; the failure only surfaces when an owner‑only call is attempted, which may not happen immediately after deployment. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “single‑step privileged role assignment” weaknesses, where insufficient confirmation allows irreversible state changes. The recommended mitigation is to replace the one‑step transfer with a two‑step handover: an owner sets a pendingOwner, and the pendingOwner must explicitly claim ownership, optionally with a time‑delay and multisig enforcement. This design permits correction of a mistaken pending address before finalization, reducing the risk of permanent loss of control while preserving the ability to manage the contract safely.

title: Incorrect internal balance bookkeeping
description:
The sherlock smart contract system uses internal bookkeeping of arbitrary ERC20 token balances. It doesn’t assert that the ERC20 doesn’t implement some non-standard behavior. For example, deflationary tokens, or tokens with a transfer fee, will result in incorrect internal balances. In summary, an attacker can perform stake and deposit actions without actually depositing the amount that sherlock assumes. As a result, an attacker is unduly rewarded balance and yield.

Balancer had a similar vulnerability in their system <https://blog.1inch.io/balancer-hack-2020-a8f7131c980e>.

An example location where such internal bookkeeping happens can be found [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-07-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/facets/PoolBase.sol#L271)

Mitigating the issue is possible by requiring the amount to be added to the contracts’ balance. Alternatively, it’s possible to update the pool based on actual balance changes.

2 med-risk, as extensive research will be done before adding certain tokens. This finding could even be noted a 0 non-critical if only ‘standard’ ERC20s are being used.

med-risk because certain popular tokens are up-gradable and could potentially implement non-standard behavior

since there will be a curation process, I agree with sponsor, this is medium risk
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect internal balance bookkeeping mechanism used by the Sherlock smart‑contract system for arbitrary ERC20 tokens. The contract records deposits and stakes based solely on the amount specified in the function call, assuming that the token transfer will move exactly that amount. This assumption fails for non‑standard ERC20 implementations such as deflationary tokens, fee‑on‑transfer tokens, rebasing tokens, or any token that alters the transferred amount during a transfer. Because the contract does not verify the actual amount received after calling transferFrom, its internal ledger can credit a higher balance than the real token balance held by the contract. An attacker can exploit this by selecting a token that deducts a fee on transfer, depositing a smaller amount while the contract records the full nominal amount. The attacker then participates in staking or yield‑earning operations with an inflated internal balance, receiving rewards that exceed the true contribution. This discrepancy leads to misallocation of yield, potential loss of funds for honest participants, and overall accounting breakage for the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a token with non‑standard transfer behavior is added to a pool, which is likely given the protocol’s token curation process that may allow up‑gradable tokens to change their logic after deployment. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include seeing unexpectedly high rewards, balances that appear larger than the amount actually deposited, or, conversely, seeing the pool’s real token holdings shrink while internal numbers stay high. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s bookkeeping logic and noted the lack of checks on transferred amounts, a pattern previously exploited in the Balancer hack. The bug is hard to notice because all external calls succeed and no transaction reverts; only a comparison of the contract’s internal ledger against the real token balance reveals the drift. To remediate, the contract should verify the actual amount received—e.g., by recording the token balance before and after the transfer, using safe transfer functions that return the transferred amount, or by updating pool state based on observed balance changes rather than declared amounts. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce a whitelist of ERC20 tokens that conform to the standard and reject any token that implements transfer fees or rebasing. In summary, the flaw is a classic accounting inconsistency caused by trusting non‑standard token behavior, leading to inflated internal balances, undeserved yield, and potential fund loss for legitimate users.

title: `_doSherX` optimistically assumes premiums will be paid
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the `_doSherX` function calculates the amount of underlying assets to return to a user who redeems SherX tokens. The function relies on `LibSherX.calcUnderlying(totalSherX)`, which produces an optimistic view of the protocol’s cash balance by assuming that all accrued premiums—effectively a debt owed by the protocol—have already been paid. To avoid transaction reverts, the code only invokes `LibPool.payOffDebtAll(tokens[i])` when the calculated amount for a token exceeds the protocol’s recorded SherX underlying balance (`ps.sherXUnderlying`). For the majority of tokens, where the amount is less than or equal to the underlying balance, the debt‑pay‑off step is skipped. If the protocol does not actually have sufficient funds to settle the outstanding premiums, the pay‑off call would fail, but the conditional guard prevents it from being executed. Consequently, the optimistic `calcUnderlying` result is used unchanged, leading to an inflated payout that exceeds the real value of the user’s holdings. An attacker or any user can exploit this by redeeming SherX tokens when the protocol’s premium debt is under‑collateralized, receiving more underlying tokens than entitled. The impact is a loss of funds for the protocol, as the over‑issued assets drain its reserves, potentially compromising solvency. This condition occurs whenever there is accrued premium debt that the protocol cannot fully cover and the redemption amount does not trigger the defensive `payOffDebtAll` branch. All users who interact with the redemption function are affected, as they may receive more assets than expected, while the protocol suffers a financial shortfall. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that inspected the flow of premium settlement and noticed the optimistic assumption embedded in the calculation routine. The bug is subtle because the code appears to protect against reverts, masking the fact that an insufficient balance can silently produce an over‑payment. Conceptually, the fix requires that the protocol either (1) settle all outstanding premium debt for every token before performing the underlying calculation, (2) recompute the payout after any successful debt settlement, or (3) reject the redemption if the required premium payments cannot be satisfied, thereby ensuring that the returned amount never exceeds the true available balance. This class of bug belongs to optimistic accounting or unchecked debt‑settlement vulnerabilities, where the system assumes a favorable state without verifying it, leading to incorrect financial outcomes such as "funds disappear" for the protocol or "refund calculation error" for users expecting a correct payout.

title: reputation risks with `updateSolution`
description:
`GovDev.sol` has a function `updateSolution` to upgrade parts of the contract via the Diamond construction. Via `updateSolution`, any functionality can be changed and all the funds can be accessed/rugged. Even if this is well intended the project could still be called out resulting in a reputation risk, see for [example](https://twitter.com/RugDocIO/status/1411732108029181960).

Note: there is a function `transferGovDev` which can be used to disable the `updateSolution`

```solidity
function updateSolution(IDiamondCut.FacetCut[] memory _diamondCut, address _init, bytes memory _calldata) external override {
    require(msg.sender == LibDiamond.contractOwner(), 'NOT_DEV');
    return LibDiamond.diamondCut(_diamondCut, _init, _calldata);
}
```

Recommend applying extra safeguards for example to limit the time period where `updateSolution` can be used.

Fair point, although we are not anonymous, we still want to mitigate this risk.

I’m thinking something like this
  * update is pushed, everyone can review the code changes
  * 14 days of waiting, people are able to get their funds out
  * update is executed.

Downside is that it doesn’t allow us to fix potential critical issues fast.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in a privileged upgrade function called `updateSolution` that is part of a Diamond proxy architecture. This function allows the contract owner to invoke a low‑level `diamondCut` operation, which can replace, add, or remove any facet of the contract logic.
