The fix restores the intended business logic that each market’s accounting and liquidity must be isolated, preventing funds from disappearing or markets from being incorrectly configured.

title: Incorrect balance computed in `getUsersConfirmedButNotSettledSynthBalance`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the view‑only function that reports a user's confirmed but not settled synthetic token balance. The function determines the value to return by selecting a price snapshot indexed with the current market update index, even though the user’s pending position was created at an earlier update index (the userNextPrice_currentUpdateIndex). When the oracle produces multiple updates after the user has shifted a position but before the outstanding next‑price settlement is executed, the condition that checks userNextPrice_currentUpdateIndex <= currentMarketUpdateIndex passes, yet the code subsequently reads syntheticToken_priceSnapshot[marketIndex][isLong][currentMarketUpdateIndex] instead of using the snapshot from the user’s stored index (x+1). This off‑by‑one price selection causes the reported balance to be calculated with a price that does not correspond to the user’s actual position, leading to an inaccurate figure shown in the UI. Although the core protocol logic uses the settlement function (_executeOutstandingNextPriceSettlements) and therefore the on‑chain state remains correct, the erroneous view can mislead users who rely on the displayed pending balance for hedging or liquidation decisions, especially in volatile markets where a sharp price move may cause unexpected loss if the user acts on the wrong number. The issue was discovered during a code audit when the auditor noticed that the price snapshot reference did not match the intended update index. The bug is subtle because it affects only a read‑only helper and does not alter contract state, making it easy to overlook in functional testing. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of accounting mismatches or stale data usage where a calculation references a more recent market snapshot than the one governing the pending position. From a user perspective the symptoms can be a dashboard showing a higher or lower pending synth balance than expected, sometimes even zero, leading to confusion and potentially costly trades. The proper fix is to compute the balance using the price snapshot associated with the user’s stored next‑price update index, or to enforce settlement of outstanding next‑price adjustments before exposing the balance, thereby aligning the reported figure with the actual accounting state.

title: Missing events/timelocks for owner/admin only functions that change critical parameters
description:
Owner/admin only functions that change critical parameters should emit events and have timelocks. Events allow capturing the changed parameters so that off-chain tools/interfaces can register such changes with timelocks that allow users to evaluate them and consider if they would like to engage/exit based on how they perceive the changes as affecting the trustworthiness of the protocol or profitability of the implemented financial services. The alternative of directly querying on-chain contract state for such changes is not considered practical for most users/usages.

Missing events and timelocks do not promote transparency and if such changes immediately affect users’ perception of fairness or trustworthiness, they could exit the protocol causing a reduction in liquidity which could negatively impact protocol TVL and reputation.

There are owner/admin functions that do not emit any events in `LongShort.sol`. It is not apparent that any owner/admin functions will have timelocks.

See similar High-severity [H03](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/audius-contracts-audit/#high) finding in OpenZeppelin’s Audit of Audius and Medium-severity [M01](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/uma-audit-phase-4/) finding OpenZeppelin’s Audit of UMA Phase 4

See issue page for referenced code.

Recommend adding events to all owner/admin functions that change critical parameters. Add timelocks to introduce time delays for critical parameter changes that significantly impact market/user incentives/security.

We will manage timelocks and multi-sigs externally to these contracts.

I would consider this a duplicate of #84 in many ways. (or at least #84 is a sub-issue of this issue)

duplicate of #84 as both offer solutions for dealing with privileged functionality (including the transfer of ownership). Leaving severity as 2 based on the potential risks associated with an incorrect admin change or similar.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of owner‑only and admin‑only functions that modify critical protocol parameters without emitting any events and without any timelock protection. The root cause is the omission of standard governance safeguards during contract development: privileged functions directly update storage variables, but they neither broadcast a change through an event nor enforce a delay that would give participants time to react. Because there is no event, off‑chain monitoring tools, explorers, and user interfaces cannot automatically detect that a fee, collateral ratio, or other economic parameter has been altered. The lack of a timelock means the owner can execute the change instantly, removing any window for users to evaluate the impact or to withdraw, redeploy capital, or otherwise protect their positions. An attacker who gains control of the owner key could therefore change parameters in a single transaction, causing immediate and potentially adverse effects such as increased fees, tighter margin requirements, or altered liquidation thresholds. Users would notice only after the fact, for example by seeing their expected returns drop, their positions liquidated unexpectedly, or their balances becoming lower than anticipated. The impact is primarily on trust and financial safety: participants may lose confidence, withdraw liquidity, and the protocol’s total value locked may shrink, damaging reputation and long‑term viability. The issue is triggered whenever an admin calls any of the privileged functions that change critical settings; there is no conditional guard that would prevent execution, nor a delay that forces a proposal‑then‑execute workflow. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the LongShort.sol contract, where the auditors observed that several admin functions lack both event emission and any timelock pattern, mirroring similar findings in other audited projects. The flaw is subtle because the contract will still operate correctly from a functional perspective, and the state changes are visible only through direct reads of storage, which most users do not perform regularly. To remediate, each privileged function should emit a clearly defined event that records the parameter name, old value, and new value. Additionally, a timelock mechanism—such as a delayed execution contract, a proposal‑then‑vote period, or an external multi‑signature schedule—should be introduced so that any change to critical parameters requires a waiting period before it becomes effective. This combination restores transparency, allows users to monitor governance actions, and provides a safety buffer against sudden, potentially malicious changes, aligning the contract with standard best practices for admin‑controlled financial protocols.

title: Staker.sol: Wrong values returned in edge cases of `_calculateFloatPerSecond`
description:
In `_calculateFloatPerSecond()`, the edge cases where full rewards go to either the long or short token returns

`return (1e18 * k * longPrice, 0);` and

`return (0, 1e18 * k * shortPrice);` respectively.

This is however `1e18` times too large. We can verify this by checking the equivalent calculation in the ‘normal case’, where we assume all the rewards go to the short token, ie. `longRewardUnscaled = 0` and `shortRewardUnscaled = 1e18`. Plugging this into the calculation below,

`return ((longRewardUnscaled * k * longPrice) / 1e18, (shortRewardUnscaled * k * shortPrice) / 1e18);` results in

`(0, 1e18 * k * shortPrice / 1e18)` or `(0, k * shortPrice)`.

As we can see, this would result in an extremely large float token issuance rate, which would be disastrous.

The edge cases should return `(k * longPrice, 0)` and `(0, k * shortPrice)` in the cases where rewards should go fully to long and short token holders respectively.

Fix:

```solidity
-return (1e18 * k * longPrice, 0);
+return (k * longPrice, 0);
```

and

```solidity
-return (0, 1e18 * k * shortPrice);
+return (0, k * shortPrice);
```

**[DenhamPreen (Float) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-floatcapital-findings/issues/6#issuecomment-897480501):**

Resolved <https://github.com/Float-Capital/monorepo/pull/1085>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑rate calculation performed by the private function `_calculateFloatPerSecond` in the Staker contract. This function is responsible for converting unscaled reward amounts for long and short positions into a per‑second issuance rate for the protocol’s float token. In the normal execution path the calculation divides the product of the unscaled reward, the protocol’s multiplier `k`, and the price of the respective token by the constant scaling factor `1e18`. However, in the two edge cases where the entire reward allocation is intended for either the long side or the short side, the implementation returns `(1e18 * k * longPrice, 0)` or `(0, 1e18 * k * shortPrice)` respectively. Because the unscaled reward in these scenarios is already equal to `1e18`, multiplying again by `1e18` inflates the resulting float‑per‑second value by a factor of one quintillion. The root cause is an incorrect handling of the fixed‑point scaling factor: the code applies the scaling factor twice instead of once, violating the arithmetic invariants used throughout the contract. An attacker can exploit this by triggering a state where all rewards are allocated to a single side—such as by driving the market price or position balances to a condition that makes `longRewardUnscaled` equal to `1e18` and `shortRewardUnscaled` equal to zero, or vice‑versa. When the edge‑case branch executes, the contract will calculate an astronomically high issuance rate, allowing the attacker to mint an excessive amount of float tokens in a single block. The immediate impact is uncontrolled inflation of the float token supply, which can drain the protocol’s reserve pool, devalue existing holdings, and break the accounting guarantees that depend on a bounded reward rate. This bug manifests only when the reward distribution is fully skewed to one side; under normal mixed‑reward conditions the calculation appears correct, making the flaw subtle and easy to miss during routine testing. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which examined the contract’s edge‑case logic and identified the over‑scaling error. Because the erroneous branch is rarely exercised, developers might not notice the discrepancy unless they deliberately test scenarios where one side receives the entire reward. To remediate the problem, the extra `1e18` multiplier must be removed so that the edge‑case returns `(k * longPrice, 0)` and `(0, k * shortPrice)`, aligning the calculation with the normal case and preserving the intended fixed‑point semantics. The bug belongs to the class of “fixed‑point scaling errors in financial contracts”, where an arithmetic constant is applied more than once, leading to overflow‑like inflation and breaking business logic that assumes a proportional reward distribution.

title: Wrong aave usage of `claimRewards`
description:
Aave yield manager claims rewards with the payment token. According to aave’s document, aToken should be provided. The aave rewards would be unclaimable.

YieldManager’s logic in [L161-L170](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-floatcapital/blob/main/contracts/contracts/YieldManagerAave.sol#L161-L170)

Reference: <https://docs.aave.com/developers/guides/liquidity-mining#claimrewards>

Recommend changing to

```solidity
address[] memory rewardsDepositedAssets = new address[](1);
rewardsDepositedAssets[0] = address(aToken);
```

Great catch!

This contract is going to be upgradable but really applicable within this context 👍

Oof yeah! Good one :)

Devil in those documentation details :)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20556729/129041188-b712e09a-f735-44d4-922f-328b156e2461.png)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an incorrect call to Aave's liquidity‑mining function `claimRewards` in the FloatCapital YieldManager contract. Instead of supplying the aToken address that represents the deposited asset, the contract passes the payment token address (the reward token) as the asset identifier. Aave’s documentation specifies that the first argument of `claimRewards` must be an array of aToken addresses for which the caller wishes to claim accrued rewards. Because the wrong address type is provided, the Aave protocol does not locate any reward balance for the supplied asset, and the call silently returns zero tokens. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the Aave API and a mismatch between the contract’s internal accounting (which expects rewards for the aToken) and the external call signature. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; any user invoking the YieldManager’s reward‑claiming function will receive no rewards, effectively making the earned incentives unclaimable. This situation manifests when the YieldManager’s `claimRewards` method is executed, typically after a period of accrued yield. Affected parties include all users of the FloatCapital Aave yield strategy, as they anticipate receiving reward tokens but observe empty balances or missing refunds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction while the reward amount displayed remains zero, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a formal code audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the contract implementation against Aave’s official documentation and identified the mismatched parameter. Detecting the bug is difficult because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the only symptom is the absence of expected reward tokens. To remediate the flaw, the contract should construct the assets array with the correct aToken address—e.g., `address[] memory rewardsDepositedAssets = new address[](1); rewardsDepositedAssets[0] = address(aToken);`—and pass this array to `claimRewards`. This change aligns the call with Aave’s intended usage, ensures that accrued rewards are correctly transferred to users, and restores the accounting invariants of the protocol. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of API‑misuse or parameter‑validation errors where a contract interacts with an external protocol using an incorrect identifier, leading to silent loss of value and broken business logic.

title: Prevent markets getting stuck when prices don’t move
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a market‑state‑update mechanism that relies exclusively on detecting a change in the reported asset price to advance the internal market counter (marketUpdateIndex). In the contract, the function _updateSystemStateInternal fetches a new price from an oracle, compares it with the previously stored price, and sets a boolean flag assetPriceHasChanged. Only when this flag is true – or when the caller is the designated staker – does the function proceed to increment marketUpdateIndex and trigger the settlement logic that processes pending mints, redeems and token shifts for each user. If the price never changes, assetPriceHasChanged remains false, the early return prevents the counter from being increased, and the subsequent function _executeOutstandingNextPriceSettlements never observes a higher marketUpdateIndex. Consequently, all pending settlement actions are indefinitely postponed, leaving the market effectively "stuck". This situation can arise in legitimate scenarios such as a synthetic stable‑coin that is deliberately pegged to a constant value, or a binary option market after the underlying event has resolved and the price becomes static. The root cause is the absence of a time‑based or admin‑driven fallback that would advance marketUpdateIndex even when the price remains unchanged. The impact is an availability issue: users attempting to trade or withdraw may see their balances unchanged, pending orders never settle, and the UI may display zero or stale positions despite transaction confirmations. No funds are directly lost because the contract does not overwrite balances, but the inability to process settlements creates a denial‑of‑service condition that can erode user trust and affect protocol liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that traced the flow from price update to settlement execution and identified the hard dependency on price movement. It is subtle because the contract behaves correctly when prices fluctuate, and static prices are a relatively rare edge case, making the bug easy to overlook in standard testing. To remediate, the update logic should be enhanced with a timeout mechanism – for example, after a configurable period (e.g., one day) without a price change, the function should still increment marketUpdateIndex and invoke the settlement routines, or provide an administrative function that can manually force the market index forward. This change would ensure that markets continue to process user actions even when price feeds are temporarily static, preserving availability while retaining the intended accounting guarantees.

title: TokenHandler.sol, L174 - `.transfer` is bad practice
description:
The use of `.transfer` in [`TokenHandler.sol` L174](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/4b51b0de2b448e4d36809781c097c7bc373312e9/contracts/internal/balances/TokenHandler.sol#L174) to send ether is now considered bad practice as gas costs can change which would break the code.

See [stop using soliditys transfer now](https://consensys.net/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/), and [istanbul hardfork eips increasing gas costs and more](https://chainsecurity.com/istanbul-hardfork-eips-increasing-gas-costs-and-more/).

Recommend using `call` instead, and make sure to check for reentrancy.

This should be `0 (Non critical)`. ETH transfers still work as of today. This is a best practice recommendation. In the case that there is a hard fork that breaks ETH transfers the protocol can be upgraded to support the use of `call()`

I aline with warden on this one. `.transfer` will not work if the account is a smart contract. Keeping as is.

**EDITORS NOTE:** Additional conversation regarding this vulnerability can be found [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional-findings/issues/38)
bug_full: The contract uses Solidity's built‑in .transfer method to send ether to an address. .transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient and reverts the whole transaction if the call fails. This practice is now discouraged because the Ethereum protocol can change gas costs for operations, as happened with the Istanbul hard‑fork, which increased the gas required for certain opcodes. When a contract receives ether and its fallback or receive function needs more than the 2300 gas stipend—perhaps due to logging, state changes, or calls to other contracts—the .transfer call will run out of gas and revert. Consequently, any logic that depends on a successful ether transfer will fail, potentially locking funds or halting a protocol operation. The vulnerability manifests when the contract attempts to send ether to another smart contract, especially after a hard‑fork that raises gas consumption. Users, protocol operators, and any party relying on the contract’s ability to distribute ETH are affected because a transfer that previously succeeded may now silently fail, leading to unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or failed withdrawals. The issue was identified during a security audit that flagged the usage pattern as a known anti‑pattern. It may be hard to notice because .transfer behaved correctly for many contracts before the gas‑cost changes, and the failure appears only under specific conditions that are not evident in regular testing. The root cause is the rigid gas stipend and lack of a mechanism to handle the possible revert, which violates the assumption that a simple ether transfer will always succeed. To remediate, the contract should replace .transfer with a low‑level call, e.g., (bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: amount}(""), and explicitly check the returned success flag. The call should be placed after state changes (Checks‑Effects‑Interactions) and protected by a re‑entrancy guard to avoid further vulnerabilities. This change aligns the contract with current best practices for external ETH transfers, ensuring that the protocol remains functional even when gas costs evolve.

title: `.latestRoundData`
description:
The method `.latestRoundData()` on an oracle returns the latest updated price from the oracle, but this is not the current price of an asset. To get an accurate current price you need to query it by calling the oracle and waiting for a callback to fulfill the request.

Inaccurate price data could quickly lead to a large loss of funds. Suppose the price of an asset changes downward 5% but your oracle is not updated. A user could deposit funds (credited with an extra 5% since the oracle isn’t updated), wait until `.latestRoundData()` updates (or update it himself) and becomes accurate. He then withdraws to the same asset he put in for an extra 5%. [`ExchangeRate.sol` L84](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/4b51b0de2b448e4d36809781c097c7bc373312e9/contracts/internal/valuation/ExchangeRate.sol#L84)

Recommend not fetching the latest price (having to call the oracle to update the price instead), and then waiting for the callback.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the `.latestRoundData()` function of a price oracle to obtain the asset’s valuation. This function returns the most recent price that the oracle has *published*, not the real‑time market price. Consequently, if the market price moves before the oracle updates its feed, the contract will continue to use a stale price for calculations such as deposits, withdrawals and exchanges. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the oracle’s data freshness guarantees: the contract assumes that the latest stored price is always an accurate reflection of the current market value, ignoring the asynchronous nature of the oracle’s update cycle. An attacker can exploit this by waiting for a significant price shift (for example a 5 % drop), depositing assets while the oracle still reports the higher stale price, and then either triggering the oracle update himself or waiting until it occurs naturally before withdrawing the same amount of assets. Because the contract credits the deposit based on the inflated stale price, the attacker extracts the price differential as profit, effectively stealing value from the protocol. The impact is a direct loss of funds proportional to the price discrepancy, with the user‑facing symptom that a withdrawal yields more of the underlying asset than was originally supplied, or that a balance appears unexpectedly higher after a transaction. This condition occurs whenever the oracle feed is out‑of‑date – typically after market volatility, during network congestion, or when the oracle’s update interval is longer than the contract’s transaction frequency. All participants that rely on the contract’s valuation – depositors, lenders, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the accounting invariant that deposits equal the value of assets no longer holds. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that compared the oracle’s documented behavior with its usage in the `ExchangeRate.sol` contract, noting the mismatch between expected real‑time pricing and the static value returned by `.latestRoundData()`. Detecting this flaw can be difficult because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a price is stale, and normal operation may appear correct during periods of low volatility, masking the underlying risk. To remediate, the contract should avoid using `.latestRoundData()` for critical pricing decisions; instead it must submit a fresh price request to the oracle, wait for the asynchronous callback that delivers a verified current price, and only then perform valuation logic. This change aligns the contract’s accounting with the oracle’s intended security model and eliminates the opportunity for profit extraction through stale price exploitation. The bug belongs to the broader class of “oracle staleness” or “price feed lag” vulnerabilities, which break the assumption that on‑chain price feeds are instantly up‑to‑date and can lead to mispricing, fund loss, and broken economic guarantees.

title: Allowance checks not correctly implemented
bug_full:
The contract implements a two‑layer allowance model for token transfers: a whitelist allowance that is always consulted first, followed by a currency‑specific allowance. The vulnerability lies in the way these two allowances are combined. The code deducts as much as possible from the whitelist, stores the remaining amount in a variable called requiredAllowance, and then attempts to satisfy the rest using the currency‑specific allowance. However, due to an incorrect conditional structure, the check that verifies the second allowance is performed regardless of whether requiredAllowance is zero or not, and the logic that should fall back to the currency‑specific allowance is never reached when the whitelist allowance is insufficient. Consequently, a transaction reverts with an "Insufficient allowance" error even though the user’s currency‑specific allowance would have covered the full transfer amount. The root cause is a misplaced or missing block;
that makes the require statement execute unconditionally, effectively treating the whitelist as the only source of allowance. An attacker does not need to act actively; any honest user who relies on the secondary allowance will experience failed transfers. The impact is that legitimate users cannot move tokens they have approved, leading to a denial‑of‑service for token holders and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the allowance handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the fallback path was never exercised. It can be hard to spot because the code superficially appears to check both allowances, and the failing condition only manifests when the whitelist allowance is lower than the transfer amount—a scenario that may not be covered by basic unit tests. To remediate, the conditional should be rewritten so that the second allowance check is executed only when requiredAllowance is greater than zero, and the required allowance should be satisfied from the currency‑specific allowance before updating the state. In broader terms, this is an instance of improper access‑control logic where multiple authorization sources are not correctly combined, resulting in an erroneous "insufficient allowance" revert. From a user’s perspective, they initiate a transfer expecting the protocol to honor their approved balance, but the UI shows a transaction failure or a message stating "Insufficient allowance" even though their allowance balance is non‑zero. Expectations of a successful transfer clash with reality, where the funds appear to disappear from the user's perspective because the operation cannot be completed.

title: `CompoundToNotionalV2.enableToken` ERC20 missing return value check
description:
The `enableToken` function performs an `ERC20.approve()` call but does not check the `success` return value. Some tokens do **not** revert if the approval failed, returning `false` instead.

The impact is that, tokens that don’t actually perform the approve and return `false` are still counted as a correct approve.

Recommend using [OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/release-v4.1/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol#L74) versions with the `safeApprove` function that handles the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token‑enable routine that calls the ERC20 approve function without checking the boolean return value. In the ERC20 specification, approve should return true on success, but some tokens deviate from the standard and instead return false while leaving the transaction unchanged, without reverting. Because the contract does not verify this return flag, it proceeds under the false assumption that the allowance was granted. This logic flaw shows up whenever a user attempts to enable a non‑standard token: the enableToken call reports success, the UI indicates the token is approved, yet the contract’s allowance mapping remains zero. Subsequent operations that rely on the allowance—such as deposits, withdrawals, or trades—fail or silently lose the ability to move the user’s tokens, resulting in user‑facing symptoms like “my balance didn’t change after approving”, “withdrawal returns nothing”, or “the token appears enabled but I cannot transfer it”. The impact is a medium‑severity breach of accounting expectations: the protocol believes it can debit the user’s balance, but the token transfer cannot be executed, potentially locking funds or causing failed transactions that confuse users. The condition occurs only with tokens that do not revert on a failed approve, making it hard to notice because many mainstream tokens behave correctly and the contract emits no explicit warning. The issue was identified during a formal security audit where the lack of a success‑check in the approve call was flagged as a logical oversight. Fixing the problem involves replacing the raw approve call with a wrapper that validates the return value, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeApprove, which reverts on false returns and also handles non‑standard tokens, thereby restoring the invariant that an approved token truly has a non‑zero allowance before any accounting operation proceeds.

title: `nTokenERC20Proxy` emits events even when not success
description:
The `nTokenERC20Proxy` functions emit events all the time, even if the return value from the inner call returns `false`, indicating an unsuccessful action.

An off-chain script scanning for `Transfer` or `Approval` events can be tricked into believing that an unsuccessful transfer was indeed successful. This happens in the `approve`, `transfer` and `transferFrom` functions.

Recommend only emitting events on `success`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the nTokenERC20Proxy contract, where the public functions approve, transfer and transferFrom emit the standard ERC20 events (Approval and Transfer) unconditionally, without checking the boolean return value of the delegated call to the underlying token contract. The root cause is a missing verification step: the proxy forwards the request, receives a success flag, but proceeds to fire the corresponding events regardless of whether the inner call returned true (indicating a successful state change) or false (indicating that the operation was rejected). This behavior can be exploited by an off‑chain observer, such as a block explorer, indexer, or wallet UI, that relies solely on emitted events to infer token movement. An attacker can trigger a transfer that fails at the token level, yet the proxy still logs a Transfer event, leading the observer to believe that funds have moved. Consequently, users may see a successful‑transfer notification, while their balances remain unchanged, causing confusion, erroneous accounting, and potential financial loss if downstream logic (e.g., automated payouts, audits, or reputation systems) trusts the event feed. The issue manifests every time any of the three functions is called, irrespective of the actual outcome of the inner call, and therefore affects all token holders, dApp developers, auditors, and any third‑party service that parses ERC20 events for state reconstruction. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the proxy’s source code, where the event‑emission statements were found to be placed before—or independent of—the success check. The problem is subtle because the transaction itself does not revert, and the presence of correctly formatted events gives the false impression of compliance with the ERC20 specification, making it easy to overlook without direct state validation. To remediate, the contract should emit Approval and Transfer events only after confirming a true return value from the underlying token contract, or alternatively revert the whole call on a false result, thereby aligning event emission with actual state changes and restoring trust in the event‑driven accounting model.

title: `TokenHandler.setToken` ERC20 missing return value check
description:
The `setToken` function performs an `ERC20.approve()` call but does not check the `success` return value. Some tokens do **not** revert if the approval failed but return `false` instead.

The impact is that tokens that don’t actually perform the approve and return `false` are still counted as a correct approve.

We recommend using [OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/release-v4.1/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol#L74) versions with the `safeApprove` function that handles the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s `setToken` function, which invokes the ERC20 `approve` method without verifying the boolean return value. In standard ERC20 implementations the call either reverts on failure or returns true on success, but a number of tokens deviate from the specification by returning false while not reverting. Because the contract does not inspect this return flag, it proceeds under the false assumption that the allowance was successfully set. This logical oversight allows a token that silently fails to grant an allowance to be treated as approved, breaking the contract’s accounting and permission model. An attacker or a careless user can supply such a non‑standard token to the `setToken` routine; the contract will record the token as approved, yet the actual allowance in the token contract remains zero. Subsequent operations that rely on the presumed approval—such as transfers, withdrawals, or fee collections—will either revert unexpectedly or silently fail, leading to a situation where users see a transaction marked as successful but their funds remain unmovable or are never transferred. From the user’s perspective, the UI may display a successful approval message, yet later attempts to withdraw or trade result in “no funds received” or a zero balance, contradicting the expectation that the token was authorized. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the lack of a return‑value check was noted as a deviation from best practices. It can be difficult to notice because most popular tokens conform to the ERC20 spec, so the failure mode does not surface during routine testing unless a misbehaving token is deliberately used. The proper mitigation is to employ a wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20.safeApprove`, which automatically checks the return value and reverts if the approval did not succeed, thereby enforcing the intended permission model across both standard‑compliant and non‑standard tokens. In abstract terms, this is a classic case of “unchecked external call return values” that compromises contract logic and can result in lost or locked funds, broken accounting, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s token handling mechanisms.

title: Attackers can force liquidations by borrowing large amounts of an asset.
description:
Consider an attacker who borrows enough to greatly increase the oracle rate. It is claimed that arbitrageurs will come in and fix this discrepancy before the attacker has a chance to profit off of his price manipulation:

“This means that at worst you could directly use...
What the finding also implies, is that if...”

In my opinion, this incentive is not sufficient to prevent an attack. This assumes that:

  1. There is sufficient volume to notice a manipulation like this
  2. The arbitrageurs would be willing to deploy capital for a short amount of for a slightly increased rate
  3. The arbitrageurs would now know that this is a manipulation, and not a natural market movement (For example, lets say an asset lending rate goes up 10% in value, is it being manipulated or is the rate actually worth 10% more for some reason? An arbitrageur needs to make this before he deploys capital). Since notional is the only market to offer something like this, it is difficult to discern what the response should be.
  4. The arbitrageurs don’t join in on the attack, and try to liquidate accounts with the attacker

Proof of concept is based off of the formula and text [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/internal/valuation/_README.md).

Uncertain what the recommendation should be.

This is a fair point. With a timeWindow value that is under an hour, it’s not clear whether capital will flow in to take advantage of artificially inflated yields before the oracleRate catches up to the lastImpliedRate and accounts are potentially eligible for liquidation at this early stage in Notional’s lifespan before there are lots of eyes on the system and its market dynamics are widely understood.

However, it’s worth noting that there are several mitigating circumstances which make such an attack unlikely:

  * The necessary conditions for a profitable attack to exist are quite narrow
  * The capital required to execute such an attack is substantial
  * The sunk cost of executing this attack prior to any payoff is significant
  * The payoff of the attack is not guaranteed


First let’s examine what this attack would have to look like.

  * With the current fCash market parameters, interest rates top out at about 25%, so the most that an attacker could push interest rates from their natural level is ~20% (assuming a starting interest rate of 5%).
  * With the current active maturities (longest dated maturity is one year), a 20% change in interest rates could decrease the collateral value of an account’s fCash by a maximum of ~20%.
  * Pushing the interest rate to the top of the range requires the attacker to borrow all of the cash sitting in the liquidity pool. If you assume there is $100M sitting in the pool, then the attacker would have to borrow $100M. At worst, if they execute the borrow all in one shot, their realized borrow rate would be 25%. At best, if they execute the borrow in pieces (increasing the time taken and risk of the attack), their realized borrow rate would be ~15%. This implies that the attacker has placed at least $15M at risk (his total interest owed) as there is no guarantee that he can exit his position in profit or at cost.
  * In order for this to be a profitable attack, the attacker needs to offset their borrowing by executing an fCash liquidation that would allow them to lend at the artificially inflated interest rate. This means that there must be an account, or set of accounts, which have borrowed against their fCash, are 20% away from under collateralization, and have enough fCash such that the attacker can offset his borrow by liquidating their fCash. In other words, there would need to be $100M+ of fCash held in the system that is being used as collateral and is close to liquidation.
  * These conditions are possible, but improbable. It would imply that the amount of outstanding loans that are being borrowed against (and are close to under collateralization) is greater than the total liquidity in the pool. This strikes me as unlikely for two reasons:
  * For there to be more fCash outstanding than liquidity in the pool, there would have to be a lot of two-way trading. We expect this to happen eventually, but in the initial stages we would be very surprised by this because lenders do not earn NOTE incentives, only liquidity providers earn NOTE incentives. It would be very surprising to see more lending than liquidity given this fact. We expect more lending than liquidity once Notional is more mature, but by then there will be more eyes on the system which would make this attack less likely as arbitragers and/or automated yield aggregators really would come in to push rates back down to their natural level.
  * Only a percentage of fCash will actually be used as collateral, and probably not a large percentage. So if you specifically need fCash used as collateral (and close to liquidation) to be a multiple of liquidity in the pool, this would imply that the amount of total outstanding fCash would be like an order of magnitude greater than the liquidity in the pool. That strikes me as highly unlikely.


Ultimately we don’t think this is a significant risk because the necessary conditions are unlikely to obtain in the early stages of Notional’s growth, the attack involves substantial sunk costs and capital committed, and the risk of an unsuccessful attack is significant. To further mitigate against this unlikely risk, we will skew the timeWindow to a longer time / larger value.

This attack requires a lot of things aligned and for that single reason I’ll give it medium risk.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol derives its oracle interest rate from recent borrowing activity within a short time window. Because the oracle rate is updated directly from the average rate of newly borrowed assets, an attacker who can borrow a large amount of the underlying asset can artificially inflate the reported rate. When the rate is pushed far above its natural level, the valuation of collateralized fCash positions drops proportionally, causing some healthy accounts to become under‑collateralized. The protocol’s liquidation engine then treats these accounts as eligible for liquidation, allowing the attacker to trigger liquidations and capture the excess value. The attack does not rely on a coding error but on a design assumption that market participants will quickly arbitrage away any abnormal rate. That assumption fails when (1) the volume needed to notice the manipulation is not present, (2) arbitrageurs are unwilling to commit capital for a short‑lived, modest rate increase, (3) they cannot instantly distinguish manipulation from a legitimate market move, and (4) they might even join the attacker rather than counteract the manipulation. Exploitation proceeds as follows: first, the attacker borrows a substantial portion of the pool’s liquidity, pushing the oracle rate upward; second, the inflated rate reduces the market value of fCash used as collateral by roughly the same percentage; third, accounts that were previously safe now appear under‑collateralized; fourth, the attacker initiates liquidation calls against those accounts, receiving the collateral at a discount. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a previously funded account is suddenly liquidated, resulting in a loss of deposited collateral or a zero‑balance warning, even though market conditions have not changed dramatically. The impact is loss of funds for honest borrowers and lenders, erosion of confidence in the protocol’s pricing oracle, and potential systemic risk if many accounts are liquidated simultaneously. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the valuation formulas and the interaction between the oracleRate, timeWindow, and liquidation thresholds. It is difficult to notice because the price deviation may be modest (e.g., a 10–20 % rate rise) and the oracle updates are trusted by the system, so front‑end dashboards often show normal rates while the underlying valuation is already compromised. To remediate the problem, the protocol should decouple the oracle rate from immediate borrowing activity, introduce a longer observation window or smoothing mechanism, add safeguards that prevent rate changes from instantly affecting collateral valuations, and implement checks that reject liquidation when the rate shift exceeds a reasonable bound within a single window. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “oracle manipulation leading to forced liquidation” vulnerabilities, where a financial protocol’s reliance on a self‑referential price feed allows an attacker to distort collateral values and trigger punitive actions against honest participants.

title: Uninitialized Variable `marketWhitelist` in `RCTreasury.sol`
description:
The variable, `marketWhitelist`, is never initialized in the contract `RCTreasury.sol`. As a result, the function `marketWhitelistCheck()` does not perform a proper check on whitelisted users for a restricted market. Additionally, the function will always return `true`, even if a market wishes to restrict its users to a specific role.

The initial state variable is defined in [`RCTreasury.sol` L75](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards/blob/main/contracts/RCTreasury.sol#L75).

The state variable `marketWhitelist` is accessed in the function `RCTreasury.marketWhitelistCheck()` at [`RCTreasury.sol` L269-L281](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards/blob/main/contracts/RCTreasury.sol#L269-L281).

The function `RCTreasury.marketWhitelistCheck()` is called in `RCMarket.newRental()` at [`RCMarket.sol` L758-L761](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards/blob/main/contracts/RCMarket.sol#L758-L761). The comment indicates that there should be some ability to restrict certain markets to specific whitelists, however, there are no methods in `RCTreasury` that allow a market creator to enable this functionality.

Recommend ensuring this behavior is intended. If this is not the case, consider adding a function that enables a market creator to restrict their market to a specific role by whitelisting users.

I think the severity could be double-checked on this one. It’s a close one but I’d be tempted to put it under 1 (low risk) as a “Function incorrect to spec”. Regardless, this will be fixed.

Edit: I notice the duplicates were both marked as 1 (low risk).

based on ” but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted” in the code4 docs, I am going to agree with warden and leave this as a 2. The function of the protocol is certainly impacted in a case where the whitelist if not working correctly.

**[Splidge (Reality Cards) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards-findings/issues/18#issuecomment-914175471):**

Fixed [here](https://github.com/RealityCards/RealityCards-Contracts/commit/1515f87e97be1ed09316340e19caea5c12242c17)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a whitelist bypass caused by an uninitialized state variable named `marketWhitelist` in the `RCTreasury` contract. The contract is supposed to restrict access to certain markets by checking whether a caller is present in a whitelist before allowing actions such as creating a new rental. However, because `marketWhitelist` is never assigned a concrete mapping or list, its default value remains empty, and the internal function `marketWhitelistCheck()` always returns `true` regardless of the caller's actual permissions. This mismatch between the intended business logic (restricting a market to a specific role) and the implemented logic (always allowing) originates from a missing initialization step and the absence of any external method for a market creator to populate the whitelist. When a user calls `RCMarket.newRental()`, the code invokes `RCTreasury.marketWhitelistCheck()`. Since the check indiscriminately passes, any address—including those that should be blocked—can successfully register a rental in a market that was advertised as restricted. The impact is a violation of access‑control guarantees: market creators lose the ability to enforce exclusive participation, potentially exposing premium or limited‑supply assets to unauthorized users, eroding trust, and opening avenues for economic abuse such as frontrunning or draining of market‑specific incentives. The flaw manifests whenever the whitelist validation is executed, i.e., during each new rental creation, and affects all participants that rely on the whitelist promises, as well as the protocol itself because the advertised market restrictions are effectively non‑functional. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit where the auditors compared the contract comments with the actual code paths and noted that no setter exists for the whitelist and that the check always returns true. Detecting this bug can be difficult because the function does not revert or emit an error; it silently succeeds, making automated tests that do not cover negative whitelist scenarios pass unnoticed. To remediate, the contract should initialize `marketWhitelist` to a proper data structure (e.g., a mapping of market IDs to address sets), provide controlled functions for market owners to add or remove addresses, and modify `marketWhitelistCheck()` to return false when the whitelist is empty or when the caller is not authorized. This would align the implementation with the intended specification, restore proper access control, and prevent unauthorized users from exploiting the market’s restricted status.

title: Parameter updates not propagated
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of parameter‑update functions that only modify values stored in a single, top‑level contract while failing to propagate those changes to dependent contracts that rely on the same parameters. Functions such as setNftHubAddress, setOrderbookAddress, setLeaderboardAddress, and setMinRental modify storage variables inside the RCFactory or RCTreasury contracts, but they do not inform the contracts that interact with these variables (for example, market contracts, order‑book logic, or payment handling contracts). The root cause is the absence of a notification or synchronization mechanism after a parameter is altered, resulting in a stale reference being used by downstream contracts. An attacker or a careless admin can trigger the update, after which the system continues to operate with mismatched addresses: the top‑level contract points to a new NFT hub while the market contract still calls the previous hub, or the treasury continues to enforce an old minimum rental divisor. Exploitation is straightforward – an authorized party changes a parameter while the protocol is live, and because the change is not broadcast, subsequent transactions invoke outdated logic, leading to failed rentals, misplaced orders, or incorrect leaderboard updates. The impact includes loss of expected functionality, user‑facing symptoms such as orders not being recorded, rentals being rejected despite meeting the new criteria, or leaderboards showing stale data. In worst‑case scenarios, funds may become locked if the market contract cannot interact with the correct NFT hub, effectively making user assets inaccessible. The condition under which this issue appears is any time a parameter is updated on an active deployment without a coordinated migration of dependent contracts. All participants that interact with the affected contracts—users, market makers, and the protocol’s treasury—are potentially impacted because the business logic they rely on is no longer consistent across the system. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when reviewers observed that the setter functions lacked any event emission or cross‑contract call to inform other modules of the new values. It is subtle because the setters themselves succeed without error, and the contract state appears correct when inspected in isolation, making the inconsistency hard to notice without end‑to‑end testing. The recommended fix is to introduce a propagation mechanism: emit events that downstream contracts listen to, or directly invoke update functions on the dependent contracts within the setter, ensuring that all references are synchronized. This class of bug is commonly known as “state desynchronization across contracts” or “parameter propagation failure,” and it violates the fundamental accounting assumption that all components of a system share a single source of truth for configuration values. From a user perspective, the UI might show a successful update message, yet subsequent actions such as renting an asset, placing an order, or viewing the leaderboard behave incorrectly – e.g., a user expects their rental request to be accepted but receives a silent rejection, or the leaderboard displays zero points despite earned activity.

title: Deposits don’t work with fee-on transfer tokens
description:
There are ERC20 tokens that may make certain customizations to their ERC20 contracts. One type of these tokens is deflationary tokens that charge a certain fee for every `transfer()` or `transferFrom()`. Others are rebasing tokens that increase in value over time like Aave’s aTokens (`balanceOf` changes over time).

The `RCTreasury.deposit()` function will credit more deposits than the contract actually received:

```solidity
erc20.safeTransferFrom(msgSender(), address(this), _amount);
user[_user].deposit += SafeCast.toUint128(_amount);
```

Recommend ensuring that the `erc20` token does not implement any customizations. Alternatively, a mitigation is to measure the asset change right before and after the asset-transferring routines

The issue that [keeps on giving..](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-06-realitycards-findings/issues/152)

![takemymoney](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/73956628/130954991-f6f29f54-926f-4e68-b4cb-f73ed1dc3c95.jpg)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit routine of the treasury contract, which assumes that the amount specified by the caller is the exact quantity of tokens that will be transferred into the contract. The function executes a safeTransferFrom call and then unconditionally adds the requested _amount to the user's internal deposit balance. This logic is flawed for tokens that modify the amount transferred during the call, such as fee‑on‑transfer (deflationary) tokens that deduct a percentage as a transfer fee, or rebasing tokens whose balance changes after receipt. Because the contract does not verify the actual change in token balance, it can credit a user for more tokens than were physically received, or conversely credit less when a token’s balance expands after the transfer. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a fee‑on‑transfer token, receiving credit for the full _amount while the treasury only receives a reduced amount after the fee. The inflated internal accounting can later be used to withdraw a larger quantity of tokens than the attacker originally contributed, effectively draining funds from the treasury. The flaw manifests whenever any user calls the deposit function with a token that implements custom transfer logic, and it affects all participants who rely on accurate accounting of deposits, including the protocol’s treasury and its downstream financial mechanisms. The issue was identified during a manual audit that reviewed the token handling code and recognized the missing balance verification step, a subtle problem because the ERC20 safeTransferFrom call returns successfully even when the token contracts deduct fees internally. The problem is hard to notice because the contract’s external behavior—accepting a deposit—appears to succeed, and the internal accounting discrepancy only becomes evident during withdrawals or audits of token balances. To remediate the issue, the contract should measure the token balance of the treasury before and after the transfer and use the actual delta as the amount to credit, or restrict deposits to tokens that conform strictly to the standard ERC20 behavior without transfer fees or rebase logic. Implementing such a check ensures that the internal ledger reflects the real asset received, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting and preventing illicit extraction of funds.

title: `SettV3.transferFrom` block lock can be circumvented
description:
The `SettV3.transferFrom` implements a `_blockLocked` call to prevent users to call several functions at once, for example, `deposit` and then `transfer`ring the tokens.
    
```solidity
function _blockLocked() internal view {
    require(blockLock[msg.sender] < block.number, "blockLocked");
}
```

However, as the block lock only checks `msg.sender`, an attacker can circumvent it using `transferFrom`:

  * Attacker owns accounts `A`, `B` and `C`
  * A deposits, `_lockForBlock(msg.sender) = _lockForBlock(A)` is called and `A` is locked.
  * A approves B.
  * B calls `transferFrom(from=A, to=C, amount)`. This passes the `_blockLocked() = _blockLocked(B)` check.
  * C calls `withdraw()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an ineffective block‑locking mechanism in the SettV3 token contract. The contract intends to prevent a user from performing multiple state‑changing actions, such as depositing and then transferring tokens, within the same block by storing a lock timestamp in a mapping called blockLock and checking it with a private function _blockLocked that contains the statement require(blockLock[msg.sender] < block.number, "blockLocked"). However, the lock check is performed only against msg.sender, i.e., the address that initiates the transaction, and not against the token holder whose balance is being moved. As a result, an attacker who controls several addresses can deposit funds from address A, causing A to be locked for the current block, then approve address B to spend A's tokens, and finally have B call transferFrom(A, C, amount) in the same block. The _blockLocked call inside transferFrom validates B’s block lock status, which is still clear, so the transfer succeeds despite A being locked. The attacker can then have C withdraw the tokens immediately, effectively circumventing the intended protection. This flaw belongs to the class of authorization‑bypass or improper origin validation bugs, where access control logic uses the caller context (msg.sender) instead of the resource owner. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit any explicit warning about the misuse of transferFrom and the lock appears to function correctly for direct calls; only indirect calls through an approved spender reveal the problem. The impact is that users who rely on the block lock to ensure that their deposited assets cannot be moved in the same block are exposed to unexpected balance reductions or total loss of funds, violating the accounting assumption that a lock guarantees exclusivity for the locked address for that block. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which identified the logical mismatch between the lock’s target and the token transfer flow. To remediate the problem, the lock function should be refactored to accept an explicit address parameter representing the token holder and enforce blockLock[holder] < block.number for any operation that moves tokens from that holder, including transferFrom. This change would align the lock’s scope with the actual asset owner and close the bypass vector. Until the fix is applied, any user may experience a situation where they deposit funds expecting a block‑level freeze, yet see their tokens disappear or be withdrawn by an approved third party within the same block.

title: `CvxLocker.setBoost` wrong validation
description:
The `CvxLocker.setBoost` function does not validate the `_max, _rate` parameters, instead it validates the already set **storage** variables.
    
```solidity
// @audit this is checking the already-set storage variables, not the parameters
require(maximumBoostPayment < 1500, "over max payment"); //max 15%
require(boostRate < 30000, "over max rate"); //max 3x
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CvxLocker.setBoost function, which is intended to limit the boost parameters that control how much additional payment a user can receive and how much the boost rate can be multiplied. Instead of validating the function arguments _max and _rate, the implementation erroneously checks the already‑stored maximumBoostPayment and boostRate values. As a result, the require statements that are meant to enforce a maximum boost payment of 15 % and a maximum boost rate of three times are applied to stale state rather than the new inputs. This logic flaw allows a caller with permission to setBoost to pass arbitrarily large values for _max or _rate without triggering a revert, because the stored variables still satisfy the original limits. An attacker who gains access to the privileged role (e.g., admin or governance) can therefore invoke setBoost with a _max far above 1500 or a _rate exceeding 30000, causing the strategy to calculate excessively high payouts. The impact is that the protocol may over‑pay users, drain the vault, or break the accounting assumptions that the boost is bounded, leading to a situation where users receive far more tokens than expected or, conversely, the contract runs out of funds and cannot honor legitimate claims. The issue manifests whenever setBoost is called with out‑of‑range parameters; it is not prevented by the existing checks because they reference the previous values. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers noted that the require statements were commenting on the wrong variables. Because the function still contains require statements, the problem can be subtle and may not be evident during normal testing until extreme values are supplied. To remediate the issue, the contract must validate the incoming parameters directly, replacing the current storage‑based checks with require(_max < 1500) and require(_rate < 30000). Adding an administrative wrapper that enforces these limits before delegating to setBoost can also mitigate the risk. This class of vulnerability is known as improper input validation, where stale state is used to enforce constraints, leading to potential financial loss and violation of business logic that expects bounded boost calculations.

title: No ERC20 safe* versions called
description:
The `claim` function performs an ERC20 transfer `rewardsToken.transfer(to, claiming);` but does not check the return value, nor does it work with all legacy tokens.

Some tokens (like USDT) don’t correctly implement the EIP20 standard and their `transfer`/`transferFrom` function return `void` instead of a success boolean. Calling these functions with the correct EIP20 function signatures will always revert.

The `ERC20.transfer()` and `ERC20.transferFrom()` functions return a boolean value indicating success. This parameter needs to be checked for success. Some tokens do **not** revert if the transfer failed but return `false` instead.

Tokens that don’t actually perform the transfer and return `false` are still counted as a correct transfer and tokens that don’t correctly implement the latest EIP20 spec, like USDT, will be unusable in the protocol as they revert the transaction because of the missing return value.

Recommend using OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20` versions with the `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` functions that handle the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.

True, thanks for spotting it!

**[alcueca (Yield) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield-findings/issues/31#issuecomment-899365841):**

[Fix](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/yield-utils-v2/commit/3715140ab7d6fbde593257c7542a661bc9191d8c)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s claim function invoking a raw ERC20 transfer via rewardsToken.transfer(to, claiming) without verifying the returned success flag or handling tokens that deviate from the EIP‑20 specification. Standard ERC20 contracts are required to return a boolean indicating whether the transfer succeeded; however, many legacy tokens, such as USDT, implement transfer and transferFrom with a void return type, causing calls that use the standard signature to revert. Additionally, some compliant tokens may return false on failure instead of reverting. Because the claim function ignores the return value, it proceeds as if the transfer succeeded even when the token contract either reverts silently (in the case of non‑standard tokens) or returns false. Consequently, the protocol records the reward as claimed while the user’s balance remains unchanged, leading to rewards that are never delivered, accounting mismatches, and the potential for repeated claims that drain protocol accounting without moving any funds. This condition manifests whenever a user invokes claim with a token that does not adhere to the standard return‑value convention, affecting all reward claimants, the protocol’s token accounting, and any external parties relying on the correctness of reward distribution. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the lack of a return‑value check and the absence of safe ERC20 handling were identified as logical oversights that may not trigger obvious transaction failures, making the problem hard to spot because the transaction does not revert and appears successful on‑chain. To remediate, the contract should replace direct calls to transfer and transferFrom with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library functions safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom, which internally handle missing return values, revert on failure, and provide compatibility with non‑standard tokens, thereby aligning the implementation with the expected business logic of guaranteed reward delivery.

title: `TimeLock` cannot schedule the same calls multiple times
description:
The `TimeLock.schedule` function reverts if the same `targets` and `data` fields are used as the `txHash` will be the same. This means one cannot schedule the same transactions multiple times.

Imagine the delay is set to 30 days, but a contractor needs to be paid every 2 weeks. One needs to wait 30 days before scheduling the second payment to them.

Recommend also including `eta` in the hash. (Compound’s `Timelock` does it as well.) This way the same transaction data can be used by specifying a different `eta`.

Funny, [BoringCrypto was quite negative about including the eta in the txHash](https://twitter.com/Boring_Crypto/status/1425401221091762189). At the time I couldn’t think of a reason to repeat the same call with the same data, but you are right that sometimes it might make sense, and storing off-chain the expected eta of each timelocked transaction is something you should do anyway.
 
I’ll confirm this issue, and will bring it for public discussion once the contest is over.

**[alcueca (Yield) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield-findings/issues/27#issuecomment-921487023):**

I ended up [refactoring the Timelock](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/yield-utils-v2/blob/main/contracts/utils/Timelock.sol) so that the eta is not included in the parameters, but repeated proposals are allowed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a Timelock contract that computes a transaction identifier (txHash) solely from the arrays of target addresses and calldata payloads supplied to the schedule function. Because the identifier does not incorporate the execution timestamp (eta), any attempt to schedule two transactions that have identical targets and identical data produces the same txHash. The contract treats this as a duplicate entry and reverts, preventing the second scheduling. This design flaw originates from an overly strict uniqueness check that assumes a transaction is uniquely defined by its call parameters alone, ignoring the scheduled execution time. An attacker or a legitimate user who needs to repeat the same call—such as a recurring contractor payment, periodic token distribution, or any scheduled action that uses identical calldata—will be unable to do so until the original lock expires or is cancelled. In practice, this means that a payment intended every two weeks cannot be queued while the global delay is set to a longer period, for example 30 days, because the second attempt to schedule the same call will be rejected. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on scheduled operations: funds that should be released on a regular cadence remain locked, users see missing or delayed payments, and the protocol’s business logic that assumes regular payouts is broken. The condition occurs whenever the same combination of target contracts and calldata is reused, regardless of the intended execution time, and it affects any role that relies on the Timelock for automated or recurring actions, including contractors, token holders, and protocol governance participants. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the scheduling logic and identified that the txHash calculation omitted the eta field. It can be hard to notice because the contract simply reverts with a generic error, offering no clear indication that the failure is due to a duplicate hash rather than, for example, insufficient gas or a permission problem. To remediate the problem, the contract should include the eta (or another unique nonce) in the txHash computation, thereby allowing identical calls to be scheduled at different times, or it should redesign the uniqueness check to allow multiple pending entries with the same call data. This class of bug can be described as a transaction‑uniqueness constraint flaw that leads to a functional denial‑of‑service for recurring operations, violating the expectation that identical calls can be queued with distinct execution timestamps.

title: Rewards squatting - setting rewards in different ERC20 tokens opens various economic attacks.
description:
Users essentially have an option to either claim currently earned reward amounts on future rewards tokens, or the current rewards token.

Although stated on line 84, it does not take into account the implications the lock in this contract will have on the future value of new tokens able to be issued via rewards.

Smart users will monitor the mempool for `setRewards` transactions. If the new reward token (token b) is less valuable than the old reward token (token a), they can front run this transaction by calling claim. Otherwise, they let their accrued ‘token a’ roll into rewards of of the more valuable ‘token b’.

Given loads of users will likely hold these tokens from day 1, there will potentially be thousands of different addresses squatting on rewards.

Economically, and given the above, it makes sense that the value of new reward tokens, i.e. ‘token b’ should always be less than that of ‘token a’. This is undesirable in a rewards token contract, as there is no reliable way to start issuing a more valuable token at a later stage, unless exposing yourself to a major risk of reward squatting.

i.e. You could not issue a more valuable token in future (for example, if we wanted to run a rewards period issuing an asset like WETH rewards for 10 days) after first initially issuing DAI as a reward. This hamstrings flexibility of the contract.

P.s. This is one of the slickest contracts I’ve read. Love how awesome it is. Just believe this should be fixed, then its good to go.

It is true you could probably write a script to manually go call `claim` on thousands of squatting token addresses but this is a poor solution.

Recommend instead, that a simple mapping pattern could be used with an index mapping to a reward cycle with a reward token and a new accumulative etc. Users would likely need to be given a period a to claim from old reward cycles before their token balance could no longer reliably used to calculate past rewards. They would still be able to claim everything up until their last action (even though this may be before the rewards cycle ended).

Thanks! I agree that allowing to change the rewards token is just too troublesome.

**[alcueca (Yield) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield-findings/issues/64#issuecomment-899270061):**

[Fix](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/yield-utils-v2/commit/6df51f81a36e8f9b26b4946ac1aeda90eff6ffda)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of a rewards contract to change the ERC‑20 token used for future reward distributions without restricting or accounting for the economic value of the new token relative to the previously distributed token. The contract offers users a choice to claim accrued rewards either in the currently active reward token (token a) or to let those rewards roll over into the next reward cycle where a different token (token b) may be used. Because the contract does not enforce any relationship between the market value of token a and token b, an attacker who monitors pending transactions can front‑run the owner’s call to setRewards. If token b is expected to be worth less than token a, the attacker can submit a claim transaction immediately before the setRewards execution, thereby harvesting the higher‑valued token a before it is replaced. Conversely, if token b is expected to be more valuable, users may deliberately defer their claim so that their accrued token a balance is converted into the higher‑value token b, effectively allowing market‑value arbitrage. This economic attack is termed “reward squatting” because a large number of addresses can pile up on the contract to claim or defer rewards based on anticipated token price changes. The impact is a distortion of the intended reward distribution: funds that should be allocated to legitimate participants are captured by opportunistic actors, leading to lower overall payouts, loss of trust, and a broken accounting model where the contract can no longer guarantee that total rewards equal the sum of contributions. The vulnerability manifests whenever the contract owner calls a function that updates the reward token (often called setRewards) while the contract still holds unclaimed accrued balances. Any user holding the reward token from the beginning of the reward program is exposed, but the most affected are those who have not yet claimed and thus have a large pending balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑cycle logic and recognized that the contract’s state transition does not consider token valuation, allowing front‑running and economic exploitation. The flaw is subtle because the contract’s code functions correctly from a purely functional standpoint—claims succeed and token balances update—but the financial consequences are hidden unless one analyses token price dynamics and transaction ordering. To remediate the issue, the contract should treat reward token changes as a distinct reward cycle, requiring users to claim all pending rewards before a new token becomes active, or enforce a lock‑up period during which claims are disabled while the token is being switched. An indexed mapping of reward cycles, each with its own token address and accumulation state, can prevent the value‑mismatch arbitrage by ensuring that users can only claim rewards for the token that was active when they earned them. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is that after a token change, attempts to claim may return zero or an unexpectedly low amount, contradicting the expectation of receiving previously accrued rewards. This breach of the business logic violates the fundamental accounting assumption that rewards are token‑agnostic and should retain their economic value regardless of the token used for future distribution.

title: Use `safeTransfer` instead of `transfer`
description:
Tokens not compliant with the ERC20 specification could return `false` from the `transfer` function call to indicate the transfer fails, while the calling contract would not notice the failure if the return value is not checked. Checking the return value is a requirement, as written in the [EIP-20](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20) specification:

Callers MUST handle `false` from `returns (bool success)`. Callers MUST NOT assume that `false` is never returned!

See [ERC20Rewards.sol L175](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield/blob/main/contracts/utils/token/ERC20Rewards.sol#L175).

Recommend using the `SafeERC20` library [implementation](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol) from OpenZeppelin and calling `safeTransfer` or `safeTransferFrom` when transferring ERC20 tokens.

[Fix](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/yield-utils-v2/commit/3715140ab7d6fbde593257c7542a661bc9191d8c)
bug_full: The contract transfers ERC‑20 tokens by calling the standard `transfer` function and ignores the Boolean value that the function returns. According to the ERC‑20 specification, a token implementation may legally return `false` to indicate that the transfer failed, and callers are required to check that return value. Because the contract does not examine the returned flag, a transfer that silently fails is treated as successful. This situation can be triggered when the contract interacts with a non‑compliant token that deliberately returns `false` (or a token that simply fails due to insufficient balance, paused state, etc.). An attacker can exploit the weakness by providing a malicious ERC‑20 that always returns `false`, causing reward or payment calls to appear to succeed while no tokens are actually moved. From the protocol’s perspective the accounting state is updated as if the tokens were transferred, leading to a mismatch where the protocol believes it has paid out rewards or fees, but the user’s balance remains unchanged. Users may notice that they receive no tokens after a claim, that their reward balance stays the same, or that a transfer event is emitted without a corresponding balance change. The vulnerability manifests every time the contract executes a token transfer via the raw `transfer` method without checking the Boolean result, which is a common pattern in many DeFi contracts. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the source code and identified a direct call to `transfer` at line 175 of `ERC20Rewards.sol` without any return‑value verification. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert, no exception is thrown, and no on‑chain error message is produced, making it difficult to detect through normal testing or monitoring. To remediate the flaw, the contract should replace raw `transfer` and `transferFrom` calls with the OpenZeppelin `SafeERC20` library’s `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` wrappers, which automatically revert when the token contract returns `false` or fails to return a value at all. This ensures that any failed token movement aborts the transaction and prevents the protocol from recording an illusory successful transfer, thereby preserving correct accounting and protecting user funds.

title: No minimum rate in the auction may break the protocol under network failure
poc: [Black Thursfay for makerdao 8.32 million was liquidated for 0 dai](https://medium.com/@whiterabbit_hq/black-thursday-for-makerdao-8-32-million-was-liquidated-for-0-dai-36b83cac56b6) [bug-impacting-over-50-of-ethereum-clients-leads-to-fork](https://www.theblockcrypto.com/post/115822/bug-impacting-over-50-of-ethereum-clients-leads-to-fork)
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the auction settlement logic that computes a new ibRatio without enforcing any lower bound.
