Conceptually, the fix is to apply a re‑entrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) to the createBasket function, ensuring that any re‑entrant call will be rejected while the first execution is still in progress. This aligns the function with the generic class of re‑entrancy bugs where untrusted external calls are made without a protection pattern. From a user’s perspective, a basket may appear to be created successfully but later show missing or altered token balances, leading to confusion such as "my basket shows zero tokens after creation" or "the protocol reports my funds have disappeared". The expectation that creating a basket will securely lock the specified tokens is violated, and the actual outcome can be a silent loss of assets or corrupted accounting records.

title: `regerralFeePool` is vulnerable to MEV searcher
description:
`claimRewardAsMochi` in the `ReferralFeePoolV0` ignores slippage. This is not a desirable design. There are a lot of MEV searchers in the current network. Swapping assets with no slippage control would get rekted. Please refer to <https://github.com/flashbots/pm>.

Given the current state of the Ethereum network, users would likely be sandwiched. I consider this is a high-risk issue.
poc: [ReferralFeePoolV0.sol#L28-L48](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/feePool/ReferralFeePoolV0.sol#L28-L48) Please refer to [Mushrooms Finance Theft of Yield Bug Fix Postmortem | by Immunefi | Immunefi | Medium](https://medium.com/immunefi/mushrooms-finance-theft-of-yield-bug-fix-postmortem-16bd6961388f) to see a possible attack pattern.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ReferralFeePoolV0 contract’s claimRewardAsMochi function, which transfers the entire Mochi token balance held by the pool to the caller without any verification of the amount that will actually be received after a market swap. Because the function does not enforce a minimum‑received‑amount parameter or otherwise check slippage, a malicious miner or MEV searcher can observe a pending claim transaction, insert one or more trades that dramatically worsen the price, and then let the victim’s transaction execute at a far worse rate. In practice, the victim expects to receive their full reward in Mochi tokens, but after the sandwich attack the swap yields only a fraction of the expected amount, or possibly zero tokens if the price impact is extreme. The attack works by front‑running the claim with a large buy order that pushes the price up, then back‑running with a sell order that pushes the price down, capturing the spread while the victim’s claim is executed in between. This exploit is possible whenever the network contains active MEV searchers and the contract is called without a slippage guard, which is the default state. Users, token holders, and the referral fee pool protocol are all affected because the pool’s accounting assumptions—namely that the full balance will be transferred to the claimant—are violated, leading to lost rewards and inaccurate fee distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the reward‑claim flow and compared it to known MEV attack patterns, such as those described in the Flashbots documentation and the Mushrooms Finance post‑mortem. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds on‑chain, emits no error, and the pool’s balance simply decreases, which may be attributed to normal operations rather than an exploit. The recommended mitigation is to add a minReceivedAmount argument and a require check that ensures the contract’s Mochi balance after the swap is at least the expected minimum, and to have the front‑end compute this minimum based on the current market price. By incorporating slippage protection, the contract aligns its behavior with the intended business logic—guaranteeing that users receive at least the promised amount of reward—and prevents sandwich attackers from profiting at the expense of honest participants.

title: A malicious user can potentially escape liquidation by creating a dust amount position and trigger the liquidation by themself
description:
In the current implementation, a liquidated position can be used for depositing and borrowing again.

However, if there is a liquidation auction ongoing, even if the position is now `liquidatable`, the call of `triggerLiquidation()` will still fail.

The liquidator must `settleLiquidation` first.

If the current auction is not profitable for the liquidator, say the value of the collateral can not even cover the gas cost, the liquidator may be tricked and not liquidate the new loan at all.

Considering if the liquidator bot is not as small to handle this situation (take the profit of the new liquidation and the gas cost loss of the current auction into consideration), a malicious user can create a dust amount position trigger the liquidation by themself.

Since the collateral of this position is so small that it can not even cover the gas cost, liquidators will most certainly ignore this auction.

The malicious user will then deposit borrow the actual loan.

When this loan becomes `liquidatable`, liquidators may:

1. confuse the current dust auction with the `liquidatable` position;
2. unable to proceed with such a complex liquidation.

As a result, the malicious user can potentially escape liquidation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a liquidation‑flow logic error that allows a malicious borrower to evade liquidation by creating a tiny, or “dust”, under‑collateralised position and then re‑using the same account for a larger loan. The root cause is that the protocol marks a position as liquidated but does not prevent that position from being used again for deposits and borrowing while a liquidation auction is still pending. The function that triggers a new liquidation (triggerLiquidation) is blocked until the previous auction is settled (settleLiquidation). Because the dust auction yields no profit – the collateral value does not even cover the gas cost – rational liquidators will simply ignore it, leaving the auction open. An attacker can therefore open a dust position, force a liquidation, and leave the unprofitable auction unresolved. Afterwards they open a normal‑sized loan, which later becomes under‑collateralised. When a liquidator attempts to liquidate the new loan, the protocol still sees the earlier dust auction as active, causing the triggerLiquidation call to fail or be confused, and the liquidator may be unable to process the correct liquidation. The impact is that the attacker’s larger loan can escape liquidation, potentially resulting in lost collateral for the protocol and unfair loss for lenders. The condition occurs whenever a liquidation auction is open and the protocol does not enforce settlement before re‑using the position, especially when the auction’s collateral value is too small to be economically viable for liquidators. All participants who rely on the liquidation mechanism – borrowers, lenders, and liquidators – are affected because the safety guarantees of the lending pool are broken. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by examining the state transitions of liquidated positions and noticing that the contract allows deposit/borrow calls after a liquidation flag is set but before the auction is settled. It is hard to notice because normal usage does not involve dust‑size positions, and the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the transaction simply fails silently, giving the impression that the system is functioning. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that a liquidated position cannot be reused for any deposit or borrowing action until the associated liquidation auction is fully settled, or automatically settle unprofitable dust auctions, or impose a minimum collateral threshold that prevents dust positions from being created in the first place. By treating the liquidation state as a hard lock on the account, the protocol restores the intended accounting invariant that every under‑collateralised loan can be liquidated and that no loan can hide behind an unfinished auction, thereby protecting user funds and preserving protocol integrity.

title: Unchecked ERC20 transfer calls
description:
ERC20 `transfer` and `transferFrom` calls normally return `true` on a succesful transfer. In DutchAuctionLiquidator the call `asset.transfer(msg.sender, _collateral);` is made. `asset` refers to whichever ERC20 asset is used for the vault of that auction. If `asset` is an ERC20 token which does not comply with the EIP-20 standard it might return `false` on a failed transaction rather than revert. In this case it would count as a valid transaction even though it is not. If a vault would be making use of USDT the transfer call would always revert as USDT returns `void` on transfers.

There are a few more transfer(From) calls which are unchecked, these are however all on a predetermined asset (mochi, usdM and crv) and unlikely to cause problems.
poc: See [issue page](https://github.com/code-423n4/reports/blob/mochi/mochi/2021-10-mochi-findings-DRAFT.md) for referenced code.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on ERC20 transfer functions without verifying their return values. In the DutchAuctionLiquidator the statement asset.transfer(msg.sender, _collateral) is executed assuming that a successful transfer will always return true, as defined by the standard EIP‑20 interface. However, not all tokens adhere to this specification; some, such as USDT, implement a transfer function that returns no value (void) and instead revert on failure, while others may return false to signal an unsuccessful transfer without reverting. Because the contract does not check the boolean result or handle a missing return value, it proceeds as though the token movement succeeded even when the underlying call failed. This creates a logical inconsistency: the auction logic credits the caller with collateral that was never actually transferred, or it believes that collateral has been taken from a user when the token remained in the user’s wallet. The impact is that funds can disappear from the protocol’s accounting, enabling an attacker to claim assets without providing the corresponding ERC20 tokens, or causing honest participants to lose expected refunds or collateral. The condition occurs whenever the auction interacts with a non‑standard ERC20 token, particularly if the token’s transfer or transferFrom functions return false or do not return a boolean at all. Users who participate in the auction expect to receive their collateral back after a successful bid; instead they may see their balance unchanged while the protocol records a deduction, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the audit team identified that the contract makes unchecked calls to external token contracts and that the standard safety wrappers (cheapTransfer and cheapTransferFrom from the mochifi cheapERC20 library) are not used. This bug can be subtle because transactions may appear to succeed on-chain, emitting no error, while the internal accounting diverges from reality. To remediate the problem, every external ERC20 transfer should be wrapped in a utility that checks for a true return value or, if the token does not return a value, verifies that no revert occurred. Replacing raw transfer calls with cheapTransfer or cheapTransferFrom ensures that the contract either receives a confirmed success or reverts, preserving the integrity of the auction’s accounting and preventing undisclosed loss of assets. The class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked ERC20 return value, which violates the assumption that all tokens follow the EIP‑20 standard and breaks the business logic that relies on accurate token movement.

title: Chainlink’s `latestRoundData` might return stale or incorrect results
description: Chainlink’s `latestRoundData` might return stale or incorrect results
poc:
[`ChainlinkAdapter.sol` L49](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/8458209a52565875d8b2cefcb611c477cefb9253/projects/mochi-cssr/contracts/adapter/ChainlinkAdapter.sol#L49)

The `ChainlinkAdapter` calls out to a Chainlink oracle receiving the `latestRoundData()`. If there is a problem with Chainlink starting a new round and finding consensus on the new value for the oracle (e.g. Chainlink nodes abandon the oracle, chain congestion, vulnerability/attacks on the chainlink system) consumers of this contract may continue using outdated stale or incorrect data (if oracles are unable to submit no new round is started).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the contract retrieves price information from a Chainlink aggregator by calling `latestRoundData()` without performing any validation on the returned fields. Because the call returns a tuple that includes the round identifier, the raw price, the timestamp of the update, and the round in which the answer was actually supplied, the contract implicitly trusts that these values are fresh and correct. In practice, if the Chainlink network experiences node abandonments, network congestion, or an attack that prevents a new round from being produced, the aggregator can continue to emit the data from the most recent successful round. When this happens the fields `rawPrice` may be zero or otherwise invalid, `updateTime` may be zero indicating an incomplete round, and `answeredInRound` may be lower than the current `roundId`, signalling that the price is stale. The contract does not check any of these conditions, so it may use outdated or incorrect pricing data in downstream calculations such as collateral valuations, loan interest, or token swaps. An adversary who can influence the timing of oracle updates—or simply wait for a period of network delay—can cause the protocol to execute trades or liquidations based on a stale price, potentially resulting in users receiving far less value than expected, liquidations occurring prematurely, or funds being transferred at an unfavorable rate. From a user perspective this manifests as unexpected zero refunds, balances that suddenly drop after a transaction, or trades that appear to have been executed at wildly different rates. The issue was identified during a security audit where the lack of sanity checks on the oracle response was noted as a logical oversight. It is difficult to notice because the call itself succeeds without reverting, and the returned values look syntactically correct, hiding the fact that the data may be obsolete. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient oracle data validation, where contracts fail to verify freshness, positivity, and consistency of external price feeds. To remediate the problem, the contract should explicitly check that the price is greater than zero, the update timestamp is non‑zero, and that `answeredInRound` is at least as recent as `roundId`. These checks ensure that the contract aborts if the oracle provides stale or incomplete data, restoring confidence that the business logic operates on up‑to‑date market information.

title: Debt accrual is path-dependant and inaccurate
description:
The total `debt` in `MochiVault.accrueDebt` increases by the current `debt` times the debt index growth. This is correct but the total `debt` is then _reduced_ again by the calling _user’s_ discounted debt, meaning, the total debt depends on which specific user performs the debt accrual.

This should not be the case.
poc:
Assume we have a total debt of `2000`, two users A and B, where A has a debt of 1000, and B has a debt of 100. The (previous) `debtIndex = 1.0` and accruing it now would increase it to `1.1`.

There’s a difference if user A or B first does the accrual.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the debt‑accrual routine of the MochiVault contract. When the function accrueDebt is called, the contract first multiplies the current total debt by the growth factor of the global debt index, which correctly reflects interest accrual. Immediately after this, it subtracts the discounted portion of the debt that belongs to the caller of the function. Because the subtraction is performed only for the calling user instead of for the entire portfolio of lenders, the resulting total debt becomes dependent on the order in which different users trigger the accrual. In other words, the same global debt index change can lead to two different total‑debt values depending on whether a large creditor or a small creditor initiates the transaction. This path‑dependent behavior violates the accounting assumption that total debt should be a deterministic function of the debt index and the aggregate of all users’ balances, independent of who updates the state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed that calling accrueDebt with different user accounts produced inconsistent total‑debt figures. It can be hard to notice because the contract still updates the debt index and the per‑user balances, so ordinary balance queries appear reasonable; only a comparison of total‑debt before and after different callers reveals the discrepancy. An attacker could exploit this by deliberately ordering calls: a user with a large discounted debt could invoke accrueDebt first, causing the contract to subtract a big discount from the freshly increased total, thereby artificially lowering the reported global debt. This could reduce collateral requirements or enable the attacker to withdraw more assets than justified, potentially leading to loss of funds for other participants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may manifest as unexpected zero or reduced refunds, missing interest accrual, or balances that appear lower than expected after a transaction that should have increased them. The affected parties include all lenders who rely on the vault’s accounting, the protocol’s risk model, and any downstream contracts that depend on the reported debt figure. To remediate the flaw, the contract should either eliminate per‑caller discounts from the total‑debt update or, more robustly, maintain a weighted‑average discount that represents the sum of discounts across all users and subtract that aggregated value when the debt index grows. This ensures that total debt evolves solely based on the debt index and the collective state, restoring deterministic accounting and preventing manipulation through caller order.

title: Changing engine.nft contract breaks vaults
description: Governance can change the `engine.nft` address which is used by vaults to represent collateralized debt positions (CDP). When minting a vault using `MochiVault.mint` the address returned ID will be used and overwrite the state of an existing debt position and set its status to `Idle`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates fromthe protocol’s ability to replace the address of the NFT contract that represents collateralized debt positions (CDPs) in the MochiVault system. Vaults rely on the external NFT contract to issue unique token identifiers, which are then used as keys for storing each CDP’s state, including its debt amount, collateral, and status. The contract permits governance to update the `engine.nft` address without imposing any constraints on the identifier space of the new NFT contract. When a user mints a new vault via `MochiVault.mint`, the function obtains a token ID from the currently configured NFT contract and directly writes the new CDP data to the mapping keyed by that ID, overwriting any existing entry that shares the same identifier. Because the new NFT contract may start issuing token IDs from zero or from any value that collides with IDs already used by existing vaults, the mint operation can unintentionally replace the state of a previously created debt position, resetting its status to `Idle` and discarding its associated debt and collateral information. This flaw can be exploited by any party that can trigger a governance change to the NFT address, or by an attacker who can persuade governance to point to a malicious NFT contract that deliberately reuses identifiers. The exploitation flow is: (1) governance updates the `engine.nft` address to a new contract; (2) a user (or attacker) calls `MochiVault.mint`; (3) the mint function receives a token ID that matches an existing vault; (4) the vault’s storage entry for that ID is overwritten, wiping the original CDP’s data and setting its status to `Idle`. From a user’s perspective, the vault suddenly appears empty or idle, the previously deposited collateral may no longer be accounted for, and attempts to repay or withdraw may fail. The impact includes loss of visibility into one’s position, potential loss of collateral if further actions rely on the corrupted state, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only after a governance action changes the NFT address and subsequently any minting operation occurs, making it hard to notice because the token IDs themselves are not directly exposed in the UI, and the overwritten state may not generate explicit errors. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the logical dependency between the NFT address and the uniqueness of its identifiers was identified as insufficiently guarded. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid changing the NFT contract address after deployment or enforce strict monotonicity of token IDs, ensuring that a new NFT contract can only issue identifiers that are higher than any previously used ID. A more robust solution would involve decoupling CDP identifiers from external NFT token IDs, storing a separate internal counter, or validating that a newly supplied NFT address does not introduce identifier collisions before allowing the change. By eliminating the possibility of ID overlap, the vault’s state integrity and the accounting guarantees of the protocol can be preserved.

title: `UniswapV2/SushiwapLPAdapter` update the wrong token
description: The `UniswapV2LPAdapter/SushiswapV2LPAdapter.update` function retrieves the `underlying` from the LP token pair (`_asset`) but then calls `router.update(_asset, _proof)` which is the LP token itself again. This will end up with the router calling this function again recursively.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑update mechanism of the UniswapV2LPAdapter/SushiswapV2LPAdapter contract. When the public update function is invoked, it extracts the address of the underlying asset from the LP token pair supplied as _asset, but then mistakenly forwards the same LP token address to the router’s update method instead of the underlying token. This erroneous call causes the router to invoke the same update function again with the identical LP token, leading to a recursive loop. The recursion continues until the transaction runs out of gas, at which point the call reverts. The root cause is a simple mix‑up of variables: the contract uses the LP token identifier where a base token identifier is required. Exploitation is straightforward – any actor who can trigger the update function, either directly or indirectly through a router that forwards price‑update requests, can cause the contract to exhaust gas and fail to complete the price refresh. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for price updates: the exchange ratio for the underlying asset will not be refreshed, causing stale or incorrect price data to be supplied to downstream protocol components. Users who rely on accurate pricing for trades, liquidation triggers, or reward calculations may see unexpected behavior such as trades executing at out‑of‑date rates, liquidation thresholds being missed, or apparent loss of value. From a user‑interface perspective, the symptom could appear as a token price that remains unchanged despite market movement, or a balance that seems to be valued incorrectly, leading to confusion when expected refunds or reward payouts appear too low or zero. The issue manifests whenever the update function is called – either through an explicit external transaction or as part of the router’s routine price‑feed updates – and only when the supplied asset is an LP token. All participants that depend on the router’s price information, including liquidity providers, traders, and protocol governance, are potentially affected. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, where static analysis highlighted the mismatched argument in the router.update call. It may be hard to notice because the recursion does not produce a distinct error signature; the transaction simply runs out of gas, which can be mistaken for a normal failure or an unrelated gas‑limit issue. To remediate the problem, the contract should pass the underlying token address – the asset that actually represents the price pair – to router.update, i.e., replace router.update(_asset, _proof) with router.update(underlying, _proof). This change ensures that the router updates the correct price feed without triggering recursion, preserving the integrity of the exchange ratio calculation used in _getPrice and restoring reliable price data for all downstream consumers.

title: `UniswapV2TokenAdapter` does not support Sushiswap-only assets
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token adapter that determines whether a given asset is supported by checking the liquidity of the asset's pair on UniswapV2. The adapter’s `supports` function invokes an internal `aboveLiquidity` routine which queries the UniswapV2 router for the pair’s liquidity, converts it to a value using the current price feed, and compares the result against a configured `minimumLiquidity` threshold. If the returned value is below the threshold, the routine returns `false` immediately. The implementation never attempts to query the same asset on Sushiswap, even though the surrounding `try…catch` block has code prepared to perform a secondary lookup. As a result, assets that have sufficient liquidity on Sushiswap but insufficient or non‑existent liquidity on UniswapV2 are incorrectly marked as unsupported. The root cause is an early return after the UniswapV2 check, which prevents the fallback Sushiswap query from executing. An attacker or a mis‑configured asset can exploit this by deploying a token that only has a healthy Sushiswap pair; the adapter will reject the token, causing the protocol to refuse deposits, trades, or other interactions involving that asset. From a user’s perspective, the UI may indicate that a token is not supported or that a deposit fails, even though the token’s market on Sushiswap is active and liquid. This discrepancy can lead to loss of trading opportunities, confusion, and potentially reduced confidence in the platform. The condition occurs whenever the UniswapV2 liquidity for the token‑paired asset is below the required minimum, regardless of the existence of alternative liquidity sources. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the control flow of the `aboveLiquidity` function and noting that the catch block for Sushiswap is unreachable after a false return from the Uniswap check. Because the failure manifests as a logical false return rather than a runtime error, it may be difficult to notice without explicit tests that cover assets exclusive to Sushiswap. To resolve the problem, the `aboveLiquidity` routine should be modified so that when UniswapV2 liquidity is insufficient, it proceeds to query the Sushiswap router and applies the same minimum‑liquidity check, returning the result of that secondary evaluation. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an incomplete fallback logic or missing "or" condition in a multi‑source liquidity verification routine, where a premature exit prevents alternative data sources from being considered, thereby breaking the intended accounting invariant that an asset is supported if any recognized DEX provides sufficient liquidity.

title: griefing attack to block withdraws
description:
Every time you deposit some assets in the vault (via `deposit()` of `MochiVault.sol`) then “lastDeposit[_id]” is set to `block.timestamp`. The modifier `wait()` checks this value and makes sure you cannot withdraw for "`delay()`" blocks. The default value for `delay()` is 3 minutes.

Knowing this delay you can do a griefing attack: On chains with low gas fees: every 3 minutes deposit a tiny amount for a specific NFT-id (which has a large amount of assets). On chains with high gas fees: monitor the mempool for a `withdraw()` transaction and frontrun it with a `deposit()`

This way the owner of the NFT-id can never withdraw the funds.
poc:
* [`MochiVault.sol#L47` L54](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/806ebf2a364c01ff54d546b07d1bdb0e928f42c6/projects/mochi-core/contracts/vault/MochiVault.sol#L47-L54)
  * [`vault/MochiVault.sol` L171](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/806ebf2a364c01ff54d546b07d1bdb0e928f42c6/projects/mochi-core/contracts/vault/MochiVault.sol#L171)
  * [`profile/MochiProfileV0.sol` L33](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/806ebf2a364c01ff54d546b07d1bdb0e928f42c6/projects/mochi-core/contracts/profile/MochiProfileV0.sol#L33)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (griefing) flaw in the withdrawal logic of the vault contract. Each time any address deposits assets for a given NFT identifier, the contract records the current block timestamp in a mapping called lastDeposit[_id]. A modifier named wait() reads this timestamp and prevents a withdrawal until a fixed delay, expressed in seconds (default three minutes), has elapsed. Because the timestamp is overwritten on every deposit, an attacker who can repeatedly deposit a tiny amount for the same NFT identifier can constantly reset the timer, meaning the owner of that NFT will never satisfy the waiting period and therefore cannot withdraw the funds that belong to them. The root cause is that the contract treats all deposits equally, regardless of the depositor, and it does not differentiate between recent deposits that should be locked and older balances that should be freely withdrawable. The exploit can be carried out in two ways: on a low‑fee chain the attacker can simply submit a tiny deposit exactly every three minutes, extending the lock indefinitely; on a high‑fee chain the attacker can monitor the mempool for a pending withdraw transaction and front‑run it with a deposit, again resetting the timer before the withdrawal is processed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the NFT owner attempts to withdraw and receives either a transaction revert or a silent failure, seeing no funds transferred even though the vault shows a large balance associated with their identifier. The impact is a permanent loss of access to the locked assets for the legitimate owner, effectively freezing their capital and breaking the economic guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the logic of the wait() modifier was inspected and its interaction with the deposit function was traced. It is hard to notice because the delay mechanism appears legitimate and the contract does not emit any warning when the timer is refreshed by an external actor; only the lack of a successful withdrawal reveals the problem. The appropriate mitigation is to restrict who may call deposit for a particular NFT identifier, typically limiting it to the NFT owner, or to record separate timestamps for each depositor and only block withdrawals of the newly deposited portion while allowing older balances to be withdrawn. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “timestamp‑based lock‑griefing” vulnerabilities where an unrestricted state variable governing a time lock can be manipulated by any participant, violating the intended accounting assumption that only the rightful owner’s actions affect their withdrawal eligibility.

title: borrow function will borrow max cf when trying to borrow > cf
description: Borrow function in `MochiVault` will borrow to max cf when trying to borrow > cf instead of revert with “>cf” as specified in the supplied test. The difference in behavior may cause user to borrow at dangerous collateral level, and receive less than the amount requested.
poc: * [`MochiVault` sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/vault/MochiVault.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the borrow routine of the MochiVault contract. When a caller requests to borrow an amount that exceeds the vault’s calculated maximum Mintable amount (the maximum collateral factor, or maxCF), the function does not revert as the test suite expects. Instead, the implementation silently caps the borrowed amount to the maximum allowed value and proceeds with the loan. The root cause is an inadequate validation check: the contract adds the requested amount to the current debt, compares it to the maxMinted limit, but then uses the lesser of the two values rather than aborting the transaction when the request is too large. This logic flaw allows a borrower to obtain a loan that is larger relative to their collateral than intended, while also receiving less than the amount they asked for. An attacker can exploit the condition by submitting a borrow request that is intentionally higher than the maxCF; the contract will grant the maximum permissible loan and update the user’s debt to that capped value. Consequently, the borrower may believe the transaction succeeded as requested, but in reality the protocol has issued a loan at a dangerous collateralisation level, increasing the risk of liquidation. The impact is two‑fold: users may unknowingly receive a smaller amount than requested, and the protocol’s risk parameters are violated, potentially leading to loss of funds through forced liquidation or reduced trust in the system. This behavior manifests only when the borrow request exceeds the maximum mintable amount; under normal requests the function behaves correctly. All participants that interact with MochiVault – lenders, borrowers, and the overall protocol – are affected because the accounting invariant that debt must stay within the collateral factor is broken. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when a test case that expected a revert with the message “>cf” passed a transaction that instead succeeded and returned a truncated amount. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not fail; it appears successful, and the only symptom is that the borrowed amount is lower than requested, which may be overlooked in routine UI checks. To remediate, the contract should enforce a strict pre‑condition: if the sum of existing debt and the desired borrow amount exceeds maxMinted, the transaction must revert with a clear error (e.g., “>cf”). This restores proper input validation and prevents silent truncation, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that borrowers cannot exceed the collateral factor. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of missing or incorrect bounds checks that lead to silent value capping rather than explicit rejection, which can compromise financial guarantees in decentralized lending protocols.

title: anyone can create a vault by directly calling the factory
description:
In [MochiVaultFactory.sol#L26-L37](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/vault/MochiVaultFactory.sol#L26-L37), there’s no permission control in the `vaultFactory`. Anyone can create a vault. The transaction would be reverted when the government tries to deploy such an asset.

As the protocol checks whether the vault is a valid vault by comparing the contract’s address with the computed address, the protocol would recognize the random vault as a valid one.

I consider this is a medium-risk issue.
poc:
Here’s a web3.py script to trigger the bug.
```python
vault_factory.functions.deployVault(usdt.address).transact()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted factory function that allows any external account to deploy a new vault contract without any permission checks. The root cause is the absence of an access‑control modifier or explicit require statement in the vaultFactory’s deployVault method, which means the contract does not verify that the caller is the authorized engine or governance component. An attacker can exploit this by invoking the factory directly (for example, using a web3.py script that calls vault_factory.deployVault(tokenAddress).transact()), thereby creating a vault whose address is computed by the protocol’s address‑derivation logic. Because the protocol later validates a vault solely by comparing the stored address with the computed address, the maliciously created vault is mistakenly accepted as a legitimate vault. When the government role later attempts to register an asset that references the expected vault, the transaction reverts, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for the asset registration flow. This issue manifests whenever the governance module calls registerAssetByGov with a token that relies on a vault that has been preemptively created by an unauthorized actor. The affected parties include the protocol’s governance participants, asset issuers, and ultimately end‑users who would be unable to register or interact with the affected assets. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the factory contract and noted the missing msg.sender check, and it is subtle because the contract does not throw an error on vault creation; the problem only surfaces later when the registration transaction fails, which can be mistaken for a generic bug. The impact is a medium‑risk disruption of the asset registration process and a potential vector for an attacker to inject a vault that could be later used for malicious logic, though the current code only checks address equality. To remediate, the factory should enforce that only the designated engine or a whitelisted address can call deployVault, for example by adding require(msg.sender == engine, "!engine") at the start of the function. This change restores the intended trust model and prevents unauthorized vault creation, ensuring that only vetted vault contracts are recognized by the protocol’s validation routine. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a transaction that reverts during asset registration, with the unexpected outcome that a newly added token appears to have no vault or that the registration silently fails, contrary to the expectation that the asset should be accepted after providing a valid token address.

title: Improper Validation Of `create2` Return Value
description: The `BeaconProxyDeployer.deploy()` function is used to deploy lightweight proxy contracts that act as each asset’s vault. The function does not revert properly if there is a failed contract deployment or revert from the `create2` opcode as it does not properly check the returned address for bytecode. The `create2` opcode returns the expected address which will never be the zero address (as is what is currently checked).
poc: * [`BeaconProxyDeployer.sol` L31](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-library/contracts/BeaconProxyDeployer.sol#L31)
bug_full:
The vulnerability concerns an improper validation of the result returned by the CREATE2 opcode when deploying lightweight proxy contracts that serve as asset vaults. The BeaconProxyDeployer.deploy() function attempts to detect a failed deployment by checking whether the returned address is the zero address. However, CREATE2 never returns the zero address; it always returns the deterministic address calculated from the sender, salt, and init‑code hash. If the contract creation reverts or the bytecode fails to be stored, the address returned is still non‑zero, but the deployed address will contain no contract code (extcodesize == 0). Because the function only checks for a zero address, it does not revert on such failures and proceeds as if a functional proxy were deployed. This logical flaw originates from a misunderstanding of CREATE2’s return semantics and results in a missing‑code detection bug, a classic case of improper post‑deployment validation.

An attacker or any user can exploit this by supplying a salt or init‑code that triggers a revert during deployment (for example, by causing out‑of‑gas or using a constructor that deliberately fails). The deployer will still emit the expected address, but the address will be empty. Subsequent interactions with the supposed vault – such as deposits, withdrawals, or balance queries – will either revert or silently do nothing because there is no contract code to execute. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a vault address and even allow a transaction to be submitted, yet the user receives no confirmation, the balance appears unchanged, or funds seem to disappear. The impact is that assets intended to be stored in the vault may become inaccessible, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that each asset has a functioning vault) are violated, potentially leading to loss of funds or a denial‑of‑service condition for affected users.

The bug manifests whenever BeaconProxyDeployer.deploy() is called, i.e., during the creation of any new asset vault, which is a core operation of the protocol. All participants who rely on these vaults – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the missing proxy breaks the expected business logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, which noted that the function’s error handling did not match CREATE2’s behavior and that the check used (iszero(result)) was insufficient.

Detecting this problem can be difficult because the deployment transaction may appear successful on‑chain, the address is non‑zero, and there is no immediate revert or error event. Only by inspecting the bytecode size at the deployed address (extcodesize) can one see that the contract was not actually created. The symptom – a vault that does nothing – may be attributed to other reasons, making the bug subtle.

To remediate the issue, the deployment function should verify that the deployed address contains code by checking extcodesize(result) > 0, and revert if it is zero. Conceptually, the fix requires a proper post‑deployment validation that ensures the contract bytecode exists before accepting the deployment as successful. Updating the check from iszero(result) to iszero(extcodesize(result)) resolves the logical gap and restores the guarantee that each vault address points to a functional proxy contract.

title: `MochiTreasuryV0.withdrawLock
description: `withdrawLock()` does not prevent users from calling this function when locking has been toggled. As a result, withdraws may be made unexpectedly.
poc: * [`MochiTreasuryV0.sol#L40` L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/treasury/MochiTreasuryV0.sol#L40-L42)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the treasury contract's withdrawLock() function, which is intended to enforce a lock on token withdrawals when a specific lock flag (often represented as a boolean such as lockCrv) is enabled. However, the implementation does not include any check to verify that the lock is currently active before allowing the function to be executed. Consequently, callers can invoke withdrawLock() even after the protocol has toggled the lock flag, resulting in withdrawals that should have been prohibited. This omission originates from a missing require statement that would normally revert the transaction if the lock flag indicates a locked state. An attacker, or any user aware of the missing guard, can trigger withdrawLock() during a period when the lock is supposed to be in effect, thereby extracting tokens from the treasury or re‑locking tokens in a malicious manner. The impact is that funds intended to be frozen may be moved unexpectedly, leading to potential loss of assets for token holders and compromising the protocol's accounting assumptions about locked balances. The issue manifests whenever the lock flag has been set to true but withdrawLock() is called without restriction; it affects all participants who rely on the lock mechanism for security, including users, the treasury itself, and downstream contracts that assume locked funds remain immobile. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logic of the function was examined and the absence of a lock check was noted. Because the function name suggests a protective operation, developers and auditors might overlook the fact that the actual state is not enforced, making the problem subtle and easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify the lock status at the beginning of withdrawLock(), typically with a statement such as require(!lockCrv, "!lock"), ensuring that the function reverts when the lock is active. This change restores the intended business logic: withdrawals should only be possible when the lock is disabled, preserving the integrity of the treasury's locked balances and preventing unexpected fund movement.

title: `MochiTreasuryV0.sol` Is Unusable In Its Current State
description: `MochiTreasuryV0.sol` interacts with Curve’s voting escrow contract to lock tokens for 90 days, where it can be later withdrawn by the governance role. However, `VotingEscrow.vy` does not allow contracts to call the following functions; `create_lock()`, `increase_amount()` and `increase_unlock_time()`. For these functions, `msg.sender` must be an EOA account or an approved smart wallet. As a result, any attempt to lock tokens will fail in `MochiTreasuryV0.sol`.
poc:
* [`VotingEscrow.vy` L418](https://github.com/curvefi/curve-dao-contracts/blob/master/contracts/VotingEscrow.vy#L418)
  * [`VotingEscrow.vy` L438](https://github.com/curvefi/curve-dao-contracts/blob/master/contracts/VotingEscrow.vy#L438)
  * [`VotingEscrow.vy` L455](https://github.com/curvefi/curve-dao-contracts/blob/master/contracts/VotingEscrow.vy#L455)
bug_full: MochiTreasuryV0.sol is designed to interact with Curve’s VotingEscrow contract in order to lock USDM‑derived Curve tokens for a minimum period of ninety days, after which a governance role may withdraw them. The intended behavior is that the treasury contract calls the escrow’s create_lock, increase_amount and increase_unlock_time functions so that the Treasury’s holdings become vote‑escrowed assets, earning protocol incentives and securing the treasury’s value. In practice, the escrow contract contains a hard check that requires the caller (msg.sender) to be either an externally owned account (EOA) or an explicitly approved smart wallet; regular contracts are rejected. Because MochiTreasuryV0.sol is itself a contract, any attempt to invoke these three functions reverts, meaning the lock never succeeds. This restriction is the root cause of the vulnerability – a mismatch between the escrow’s caller‑type enforcement and the treasury’s expectation that a contract can act as the lock holder. Exploitation occurs simply by invoking the treasury’s lock‑related entry points; the transaction will fail, leaving the caller with a reverted state and no locked tokens. The impact is that the treasury cannot perform its core function of locking assets, effectively rendering the contract unusable for its stated purpose. Users who expect their deposited USDM to be locked for ninety days see no change in balances, may observe that the treasury’s locked‑balance view stays at zero, or experience missing refunds that were supposed to be generated from escrow rewards. This condition manifests whenever the treasury’s lock functions are called, i.e., any time the governance role or an automated script attempts to lock or extend a lock. The affected parties include the protocol’s governance, token holders who rely on the treasury’s asset management, and any external integrators that assume the lock will succeed. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that reviewed the interaction with Curve’s VotingEscrow and identified that the contract does not satisfy the escrow’s caller restrictions. It can be hard to notice because the compile‑time type checks pass, and the failure only appears at runtime when the external call reverts, often without an obvious error message in higher‑level UI components. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "caller‑type enforcement" or "restricted external call" vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes it can act as a privileged actor in another contract but the target contract imposes a stricter sender requirement. From a user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected zero or unchanged balance after initiating a lock, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. To remediate the problem, the treasury should either be rewritten to use an escrow service that permits contract callers, or replace the external escrow mechanism with an internal locking contract that holds USDM directly, thereby eliminating the need to call functions that reject contract senders and reducing exposure to external token price risk.

title: liquidation factor < collateral factor for Sigma type
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an incorrect configuration of the risk parameters for the Sigma asset class in the MochiProfileV0 contract. Specifically, the liquidation factor – the percentage of collateral at which a position becomes eligible for liquidation – is set to 40%, while the maximum collateral factor – the percentage of collateral that a user is allowed to borrow against – is set to 45%. This inverted relationship creates a situation where a borrower can obtain a loan that is already beyond the liquidation threshold. The root cause is a logical error in the contract’s parameter definitions, likely introduced by a copy‑paste mistake that left the two conditions identical and the numeric values mis‑ordered. When a user deposits Sigma collateral and requests the maximum allowed loan (45% of the collateral value), the protocol immediately flags the position as under‑collateralized because the liquidation factor is lower (40%). As a result, the position can be liquidated instantly, causing the user’s collateral to be seized or transferred to a liquidator. The impact is that users experience unexpected loss of funds, see their balances drop to zero, or receive error messages indicating that their loan has been liquidated right after approval. This condition occurs whenever a loan is taken at or near the maximum collateral factor for Sigma assets, which is a normal user action rather than an exotic edge case. The affected parties include borrowers of Sigma assets, lenders who rely on the protocol’s risk model, and the protocol itself, which could suffer reputational damage and reduced trust. The issue was discovered during a third‑party audit when the auditors compared the documented safety buffer requirement – that the liquidation factor must be strictly lower than the collateral factor – with the actual implementation and identified the mismatch. The problem is subtle because both parameters are expressed as percentages in similar code blocks, making the inconsistency easy to overlook without a detailed review of the business logic. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated so that the liquidation factor remains strictly lower than the collateral factor, restoring an appropriate safety buffer (for example, setting the liquidation factor to 40% and the collateral factor to a higher value such as 45% or more). This aligns the implementation with the protocol’s design principles, prevents immediate liquidation on maximum loans, and preserves user funds. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of configuration or parameter ordering bugs where safety thresholds are improperly set, leading to violations of accounting assumptions and financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective the failure mode appears as a loan that is approved but then instantly triggers a liquidation event, leaving the user with no remaining collateral and possibly an unexpected transaction revert. Expectations that a maximum loan is safe are contradicted by reality, where the protocol’s internal checks deem the position liquidatable immediately after creation.

title: Users can avoid paying fees for ETH swaps
description: Users can call `Swap.swapByQuote()` to execute an ETH swap (where they receive ETH) without paying swap fee for the gained ETH. They can trick the system by setting `zrxBuyTokenAddress` to an address of a malicious contract and making it think they have executed an ERC20 swap when they have actually executed an ETH swap. In this case, the system will give them the ETH they got from the swap (`boughtETHAmount`) without charging any swap fees for it, because the systems considers this ETH as “refunded ETH” that wasn’t part of the “ERC20” swap.
poc:
The steps of the attack are:

  1. Deploy a malicious contract (denoted by `M`), that will be used for `zrxBuyTokenAddress`.
  2. Call `Swap.swapByQuote()` with `zrxBuyTokenAddress=M` and `minimumAmountReceived=0`. The rest of the arguments should specify our ETH swap, nothing special here.
  3. Define `M` to return `0` and `1` at the first and second times when `fillZrxQuote` calls `zrxBuyTokenAddress.balanceOf(address(this))`, respectively.
  4. As a result, `boughtERC20Amount` now equals `1` and the function will “return any refunded ETH” to the caller, without charging any swap fees on it. This ETH is actually the output of that ETH swap.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the Swap.swapByQuote() function, which is responsible for executing token swaps on behalf of users. The contract distinguishes between two output types: ERC20 tokens and native ETH. When the function processes an ERC20 swap, it calculates a swap fee based on the amount of ERC20 tokens received (boughtERC20Amount). The fee logic, however, assumes that any ETH returned by the swap is "refunded ETH" that originated from a previous over‑payment, and therefore it does not apply a fee to that ETH. By supplying a malicious contract address as the zrxBuyTokenAddress, an attacker can trick the system into believing an ERC20 swap has taken place while the actual swap is for ETH. The malicious contract manipulates the balanceOf() calls so that the first call reports zero balance and the second reports a non‑zero balance, causing boughtERC20Amount to be non‑zero even though the swap outcome is ETH. Consequently, the protocol treats the ETH obtained (boughtETHAmount) as a refund and returns it to the caller without charging any swap fee. This fee‑bypass can be exploited by any user who can deploy a contract and invoke swapByQuote() with carefully crafted arguments, resulting in the protocol losing the fees it would normally collect while the user receives the swapped ETH for free. The issue manifests only when the swap is an ETH‑for‑ETH operation that is falsely reported as an ERC20 swap and when the attacker controls the contract used as zrxBuyTokenAddress. The problem is subtle because the UI and typical accounting logs show a successful swap with a zero fee, which matches the expected behaviour for a refund scenario, making it easy to overlook. The vulnerability was discovered during a code audit that included a proof‑of‑concept where a malicious contract returned manipulated balances, exposing the fee calculation flaw. To remediate the issue, the fee logic should be extended to also charge fees on any ETH that is returned in a transaction where boughtERC20Amount is greater than zero, or the contract should enforce that boughtETHAmount must be zero for ERC20‑type swaps. By ensuring that fees are always applied to the net value transferred to the user, the protocol can prevent the leakage of fee revenue while preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the swap engine.

title: `exitTempusAMM` can be made to fail
description:
There’s a griefing attack where an attacker can make any user transaction for `TempusController.exitTempusAMM` fail. In `_exitTempusAMM`, the user exits their LP position and claims back yield and principal shares. The LP amounts to redeem are determined by the function parameter `lpTokensAmount`. A final `assert(tempusAMM.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0)` statement checks that the LP token amount of the contract is zero after the exit. This is only true if no other LP shares were already in the contract.

However, an attacker can frontrun this call and send the smallest unit of LP shares to the contract which then makes the original deposit-and-fix transaction fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a grief‑or‑Denial‑of‑Service (DoS) condition in the TempusController.exitTempusAMM workflow. When a user calls the controller to exit their liquidity‑provider (LP) position, the internal function _exitTempusAMM redeems the amount of LP tokens specified by the caller and then checks, with an assert statement, that the contract’s LP token balance is exactly zero after the redemption. This check assumes that no other LP tokens are ever held by the contract at that moment. An attacker can violate this assumption by front‑running the legitimate transaction and transferring a single unit (the smallest possible share) of the same LP token into the contract before the user’s call is executed. Because the contract now holds a non‑zero balance, the assert(tempusAMM.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0) condition fails, causing the entire transaction to revert. From the user’s perspective, the exit transaction simply fails – the UI may display a generic error, no funds are returned, and the user sees that their expected principal and yield shares are not credited. The impact is that any user attempting to withdraw LP shares can be blocked, effectively freezing their capital in the AMM and preventing them from claiming accrued yields. The bug occurs only when an attacker can submit a preceding transaction that adds any amount of LP token to the contract, which is feasible on public blockchains where transaction ordering can be manipulated. The affected parties include all LP providers, the Tempus protocol’s reputation, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful exits. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the exit function’s state assumptions. It is subtle because the assert looks like a harmless sanity check, yet a single token – far smaller than typical user balances – is enough to trigger it, making the failure appear sporadic and hard to reproduce. The root cause is an improper reliance on an invariant (zero balance) without accounting for external interactions, leading to a deterministic denial‑of‑service vector. The bug belongs to the class of front‑run‑able balance‑check failures and improper state assumptions that enable griefing. To remediate, the contract should either remove the assert, replace it with a safe accounting mechanism that accounts for any pre‑existing balance, or restructure the exit logic so that the contract can correctly handle residual LP tokens without reverting. This would restore the ability of all users to exit their positions regardless of malicious token transfers.

title: `depositAndFix` can be made to fail
description:
There’s a griefing attack where an attacker can make any user transaction for `TempusController.depositAndFix` fail. In `_depositAndFix`, `swapAmount` many yield shares are swapped to principal where `swapAmount` is derived from the function arguments. A final `assert(yieldShares.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0)` statement checks that the yield shares of the contract are zero after the swap. This is only true if no other yield shares were already in the contract.

However, an attacker can frontrun this call and send the smallest unit of yield shares to the contract which then makes the original deposit-and-fix transaction fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (griefing) flaw in the TempusController.depositAndFix workflow. The function _depositAndFix swaps a calculated amount of yield shares for principal and then asserts that the contract’s yield‑share balance is zero. This assertion is based on the assumption that no yield shares are owned by the controller contract before the call. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate user’s depositAndFix transaction by sending a minimal amount of yield shares to the controller contract just before the user’s call is executed. The presence of these extra shares violates the assert condition, causing the transaction to revert. The exploit does not steal funds; instead, it blocks the user from completing the deposit, resulting in a failed transaction and no state change. The issue occurs whenever the contract’s yield‑share balance is not strictly zero at the point of the assert, which can be triggered by any external address that can transfer yield shares. It primarily affects users trying to deposit and fix their positions, as well as the protocol’s availability, because repeated front‑running can effectively deny service to all participants. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the controller’s logic and identified that the assert relied on an implicit invariant that could be broken by external token transfers. The problem is subtle because the assert appears to be a safety check, yet it creates an exploitable precondition that is not enforced elsewhere. From a user’s perspective, attempts to deposit result in a transaction that reverts with no obvious error, leading to confusion as the UI may display “transaction failed” while the user’s balance remains unchanged. The business logic of guaranteeing a successful deposit‑and‑fix operation is broken, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that the controller holds no residual yield shares during the operation. To remediate the issue, the assert should be removed or replaced with logic that correctly accounts for any pre‑existing yield‑share balance, such as safely handling surplus shares or restricting external transfers before the operation. This change eliminates the exploitable dependency on a zero‑balance invariant and restores the expected deposit functionality.

title: Wrong keeper reward computation
bug_full:
The vulnerability stems from an incorrect handling of numeric units in the keeper reward calculation of the pool contract. The function that determines the keeper tip, keeperTip, returns an integer where the value 1 corresponds to 1 percent and 100 corresponds to 100 percent. The auditor discovered that the contract immediately converts this integer into a Quad fixed‑point value and stores it in the variable _tipPercent, but the accompanying comment mistakenly claims that the value is expressed in WAD units (18‑decimal fixed point). Consequently, later code treats _tipPercent as if it were a WAD‑scaled percentage (where 100 % would be 1e18) and combines it with another Quad value representing the keeper gas cost. The reward formula attempts to compute `_keeperGas + _keeperGas * _tipPercent` and performs a division by a constant called fixedPoint (1e18 as a Quad). Because _tipPercent is actually a plain percentage, the division should be by 100, not by 1e18. This unit mismatch causes the multiplication term to be dramatically reduced, resulting in keeper rewards that are far lower than intended.

The root cause is the mixing of two different fixed‑point representations—WAD (18‑decimal) and Quad (128‑bit floating point)—without a consistent conversion strategy. The comment that annotates the code is misleading, and the subsequent arithmetic misinterprets the scale of the percentage variable. This subtle error can easily go unnoticed because both representations are nominally “fixed point” numbers, and developers may assume the comment is correct without verifying the actual unit semantics.

An exploit scenario involves a keeper who calls the keeper function expecting a reward calculated from the advertised tip percentage. Due to the faulty division, the contract pays out only a fraction of the promised amount. From the keeper’s point of view the UI may display a normal transaction, but the balance after the call shows a much smaller increase than anticipated, or even appears unchanged when the tip is high. Over time, this under‑payment can erode the economic incentives for keepers, potentially degrading the protocol’s reliability. The issue affects any participant that relies on the keeper reward mechanism—typically the pool’s maintainers and the broader ecosystem that depends on timely keeper actions.

The problem was identified during a manual code audit where the auditor compared the documentation comment with the actual conversion logic and noted the inconsistency. Because the reward discrepancy manifests only in the final monetary outcome and not as an outright failure, it may be hard for a non‑technical user to detect without examining on‑chain balances or detailed transaction logs. The recommended remediation is to avoid mixing WAD and Quad arithmetic altogether. Either use a single fixed‑point library throughout, or adjust the keeperTip function to return a Quad value where 1 represents 100 percent (i.e., `ABDKMathQuad.fromUInt(1)`). The reward formula should then multiply the keeper gas amount by the percentage and divide by a Quad constant representing 100, eliminating the erroneous division by 1e18. This change restores the intended reward amount and aligns the contract’s economic model with its specifications.

title: Deposits don’t work with fee-on transfer tokens
description: There are ERC20 tokens that may make certain customizations to their ERC20 contracts. One type of these tokens is deflationary tokens that charge a certain fee for every `transfer()` or `transferFrom()`. Others are rebasing tokens that increase in value over time like Aave’s aTokens (`balanceOf` changes over time).
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s assumption that the amount of ERC20 tokens transferred into a deposit function is exactly equal to the amount specified by the caller. This assumption is violated by fee‑on‑transfer (also known as deflationary) tokens that deduct a fee on every transfer, as well as by rebasing tokens whose balance can change independently of explicit transfers. When a user attempts to deposit such a token, the contract calls the token’s transfer or transferFrom method and then records the supplied amount as the user’s deposited balance. Because the token contract reduces the transferred amount, the protocol records more tokens than it actually receives. The same problem appears with rebasing tokens: the balance that the protocol reads after the transfer may differ from the balance before the transfer, breaking the accounting invariants that the pool relies on for rewards, withdrawals, and safety checks. The impact is that a user may see a successful deposit transaction while their on‑chain deposited balance is lower than expected, leading to missing rewards, failed withdrawals, or even a scenario where the protocol believes it holds more collateral than it actually does, potentially exposing the pool to under‑collateralisation. This issue manifests any time a fee‑on‑transfer or rebasing token is used with the deposit function, i.e., when the contract attempts to move tokens into its custody. The affected parties are the end‑users who deposit these tokens, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any downstream components that rely on correct balance information, such as reward distribution and emergency shutdown mechanisms. The flaw was identified during a manual audit of the pool’s token handling code, where the lack of validation of the actual amount received after a transfer was noted. The bug can be hard to notice because the token transfer call returns a success flag and the transaction does not revert, giving the impression that the full amount was transferred. From a user perspective, the UI may report a successful deposit, yet the displayed balance remains lower than the deposited amount, or the user may later receive fewer rewards or be blocked from withdrawing the full amount they thought they had deposited. The issue belongs to the broader class of “incorrect token amount handling” bugs, specifically those involving fee‑on‑transfer or rebasing token mechanics. To remediate, the contract should measure the token balance of the protocol before and after each transfer and credit the user with the actual delta, or explicitly reject tokens that implement transfer fees or rebasing behavior. Conceptually, the fix requires the protocol to stop trusting the input amount and instead verify the net change in token holdings, ensuring that deposited balances accurately reflect the true amount received.

title: `PrizePool.awardExternalERC721`
description: The `awardExternalERC721()` function uses solidity’s try and catch statement to ensure a single tokenId cannot deny function execution. If the try statement fails, an `ErrorAwardingExternalERC721` event is emitted with the relevant error, however, the failed tokenId is not removed from the list of tokenIds emitted at the end of function execution. As a result, the `AwardedExternalERC721` is emitted with the entire list of tokenIds, regardless of failure. An off-chain script or user could therefore be tricked into thinking an ERC721 tokenId was successfully awarded.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the prize‑distribution routine that awards external ERC‑721 tokens. The contract attempts to transfer each tokenId inside a try/catch block so that a single failing transfer does not abort the whole operation. When a transfer reverts, the contract correctly emits an ErrorAwardingExternalERC721 event that contains the revert reason, but it fails to remove the offending tokenId from the collection that will later be reported in the AwardedExternalERC721 event. Consequently, the final event lists every tokenId that was originally supplied, regardless of whether the transfer actually succeeded. This discrepancy creates a false‑positive signal: off‑chain scripts, monitoring dashboards, or users watching the event will assume that all listed tokenIds have been successfully awarded, while in reality some tokens remain with the contract or the original owner. The root cause is a logical oversight in the post‑error handling path – the list of successful tokenIds is never filtered after a catch, so the emitted accounting data does not reflect the true state. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can deliberately cause a transfer to revert (for example by sending a malformed token contract, using a token that implements a failing onERC721Received hook, or by revoking approval) and then rely on the misleading AwardedExternalERC721 event to convince a user or an off‑chain service that the token was delivered. Users may see their UI report "Token awarded" or a dashboard may mark the prize as paid, while the token never arrives, leading to lost or unclaimed rewards and broken trust in the prize‑pool protocol. The issue manifests whenever at least one token transfer fails during the batch award process, which can happen under normal blockchain conditions such as insufficient approvals, token contract reverts, or malicious token implementations. All participants who depend on the event – token recipients, protocol operators, auditors, and any automated reward‑distribution scripts – are affected because they may make decisions based on inaccurate event data. The problem was uncovered during an external audit that reviewed the prize‑pool’s awardExternalERC721 logic and noticed the mismatch between error handling and event emission. It can be difficult to spot because the transaction itself does not revert, and the contract still emits a success‑type event, giving the appearance of a normal execution path. To remediate, the contract should maintain a separate list of tokenIds that actually succeeded, pushing only those that pass the try block, and emit that filtered list in the AwardedExternalERC721 event. Alternatively, the function could rebuild the list after the loop, excluding any tokenIds that triggered a catch, ensuring the on‑chain event accurately reflects the real state of token distribution. This class of bug falls under inaccurate event emission and accounting inconsistency, where emitted data does not match the underlying contract state, violating the protocol’s guarantee that awarded prizes are truly transferred.

title: `initialBalance` for native token is wrong
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the trade‑execution routine that calculates the amount of output tokens a user should receive after a series of swaps. The routine records an `initialBalance` by calling an internal balance‑query helper with the destination token address (`toToken`). The helper, `_getTokenBalance`, distinguishes between native blockchain currency (e.g., ETH) and ERC‑20 tokens: for the native currency it returns the ether balance of the execution contract, while for ERC‑20 tokens it returns the token balance of that contract. Later in the same function, when the destination token is the native currency, the code reads `finalBalance` from the balance of the wrapped native token contract (e.g., WETH) instead of from the native ether balance. Consequently, `initialBalance` and `finalBalance` are taken from two different sources – ether versus wrapped ether – and the difference (`finalOutputAmount`) is computed on mismatched units. The root cause is an inconsistent handling of native currency: the initial snapshot uses the raw ether balance, while the final snapshot uses the wrapped token balance. This inconsistency can be exploited by an attacker who first sends a small amount of ether to the execution contract, thereby inflating the recorded `initialBalance`. When a user swaps into the native token, the contract will calculate a smaller `finalOutputAmount` than the actual amount of wrapped ether received. The user may receive less than expected or the transaction may revert because the `finalAmountMin` constraint cannot be satisfied. In practice, the attacker can deposit ether into the execution contract (or any other means of increasing its ether balance) before a victim’s trade, causing the victim’s trade to miss its minimum‑output guarantee, resulting in a loss of funds or a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue is observable from the user interface as a missing or reduced refund: a user who expects to receive, for example, 1 ETH after swapping may instead receive 0.75 ETH, or the transaction may simply fail with an “output too low” error despite sufficient market liquidity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the balance‑tracking logic and identified that the same token type was not used consistently for both the pre‑trade and post‑trade snapshots. Because the discrepancy only manifests when the contract already holds ether, it can be subtle and easy to miss in normal testing where the execution contract starts with a zero ether balance. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where inconsistent state queries lead to erroneous arithmetic, often called “balance‑snapshot mismatches” or “native‑token handling bugs”. To remediate the problem, the balance‑query helper should return the balance of the wrapped native token when the requested token is the native currency, ensuring that both `initialBalance` and `finalBalance` refer to the same underlying asset. By aligning the source of truth for the native token throughout the trade flow, the protocol restores correct accounting, prevents inadvertent fund loss, and eliminates the opportunity for an attacker to manipulate the balance snapshot.

title: Trades where toToken is feeOnTransferToken might send user less tokens than finalAmountMin
description: Slingshot’s `executeTrades` checks that the trade result amount (to be sent to the user) is bigger than `finalAmountMin`, and _after that_ sends the user the amount. But if the token charges fee on transfer, the final transfer to the user will decrease the amount the user is getting, maybe below `finalAmountMin`.
poc: Slingshot requires `finalOutputAmount >= finalAmountMin` before sending the funds to the user: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-slingshot/blob/main/contracts/Slingshot.sol#L93:#L98> So if the token charges fees on transfer, the user will get less tokens than `finalOutputAmount`. The check of `finalOutputAmount` against `finalAmountMin` is premature.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way Slingshot’s `executeTrades` function validates the outcome of a token swap before the final transfer to the user. The contract checks that the calculated `finalOutputAmount`—the amount that the protocol intends to send to the caller—meets or exceeds the user‑provided `finalAmountMin`. This check is performed immediately after the trade execution, but it does not take into account that the destination token (`toToken`) may implement a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism, whereby a portion of the tokens is burned or redirected on each transfer. Because the validation occurs before the actual `sendFunds` call, the contract can report a successful trade even though the subsequent transfer will be reduced by the token’s tax, potentially causing the user to receive fewer tokens than the promised minimum. The root cause is the premature assumption that the amount calculated by the trade engine is the exact amount the user will end up with, ignoring the possibility of transfer fees enforced by the token contract. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker (or merely a user) selects a fee‑on‑transfer token as the trade output, the protocol executes the swap, the internal check passes because `finalOutputAmount >= finalAmountMin`, and then the protocol transfers the tokens to the user. The token’s transfer fee deducts a portion of the amount, so the user’s actual receipt falls below `finalAmountMin`. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a trade that appears successful in the UI, but the received balance is lower than expected, sometimes even zero if the fee is high enough, leading to confusion or perceived loss of funds. The impact is medium: users do not get the minimum output they were promised, which violates the economic guarantee of the trade, but the funds remain within the protocol’s control and are not directly stolen. The issue occurs only when the output token implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism, a property that is not enforced by the ERC‑20 standard and therefore can be easily overlooked during testing. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the post‑transfer amount could be less than the pre‑transfer check due to token tax logic. The bug is subtle because the contract’s internal accounting shows the expected amount, and the transfer succeeds from a contract‑level perspective, making it hard to spot without simulating fee‑on‑transfer tokens. To remediate, the contract should capture the recipient’s token balance before the transfer, execute the transfer, then capture the balance again, and assert that the net increase meets or exceeds `finalAmountMin`. Alternatively, the protocol could explicitly document that fee‑on‑transfer tokens are not supported for guaranteed minimum output, thereby aligning user expectations with protocol limitations.
