The impact is that anyone, regardless of actual NFT ownership, can participate in the early sale, undermining the economic incentive for genuine NFT holders, potentially diluting the token distribution, and eroding trust in the protocol’s fairness. Legitimate NFT holders and the protocol itself are affected, as the sale may be oversubscribed by ineligible participants and the perceived exclusivity of the pre‑sale token is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the eligibility check and identified that balance queries are not immutable across a transaction. It can be hard to notice because the require statement appears correct at a superficial glance, and the flash‑loan pattern is a relatively new attack surface that may not be obvious when reviewing only static code. To remediate the problem, the contract should use a snapshot of NFT ownership taken at the beginning of the block or enforce a lock‑up of the NFT for at least one block after it is used for sale access, ensuring that temporary possession does not satisfy the eligibility test. Alternative solutions include maintaining a registry of addresses that have already used an NFT for sale participation, or requiring the NFT to be transferred permanently to the sale contract, though each approach has trade‑offs. From a user's perspective, the expectation that "only NFT holders can buy during the pre‑sale" is violated; users without an NFT may see their transaction succeed and receive tokens, while genuine holders may observe unexpected competition and feel that the promised exclusive opportunity has been nullified. The failure mode can be described as an "eligibility bypass via flash‑loaned NFT" that results in "unauthorized participants gaining early access and funds being allocated to unintended parties".

title: Can’t claim last part of airdrop
description:
Suppose you are eligible for the last part of your airdrop (or your entire airdrop if you haven’t claimed anything yet). Then you call the function claim() of AirdropDistribution.sol, which has the following statement: `assert(airdrop[msg.sender].amount - claimable != 0);` This statement will prevent you from claiming your airdrop because it will stop execution.

Note: with the function `claimExact()` it is possible to claim the last part.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AirdropDistribution contract’s claim() function, where an assert statement checks that the difference between the stored airdrop amount and the amount being claimed (airdrop[msg.sender].amount - claimable) is not equal to zero. This condition is intended to prevent an under‑flow but is logically inverted: when a user attempts to claim the exact remaining amount of their allocation, the subtraction yields zero, causing the assert to fail and the transaction to revert. The root cause is the misuse of assert for a condition that should be a normal runtime validation; assert is meant for internal invariants and its failure aborts execution, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service scenario for the final withdrawal. Exploitation is straightforward: any eligible recipient who has already claimed part of their airdrop and then tries to claim the last portion triggers the failing assert, preventing the transfer of the remaining tokens. The impact is that users see a claim transaction revert with an “assertion failed” error, experience missing funds, and may believe the protocol has locked or lost their tokens, even though the funds remain in the contract. This occurs specifically when claimable equals the leftover balance, i.e., the last claim for a given address. All users eligible for the airdrop are affected, and the UI may still display a functional claim button, creating a mismatch between expectation (full airdrop receipt) and reality (no token transfer). The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by manually reviewing the claim() implementation and noticing the incorrect assert condition. It is hard to notice because asserts are less common in Solidity code and do not produce a user‑friendly error message; they simply halt execution, making the failure appear as a generic transaction failure. The bug belongs to the class of boundary‑condition errors and improper use of assertion statements that lead to denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the assert should be removed or replaced with a require that enforces a non‑negative remainder (e.g., require(airdrop[msg.sender].amount - claimable >= 0)), and an additional validation check should be added to prevent re‑claiming after a successful withdrawal (require(validated[msg.sender] == 0)). Since an alternative function claimExact() can still retrieve the funds, the assets are not permanently lost, but the availability of the primary claim path is compromised, warranting a medium‑severity rating.

title: Overwrite benRevocable
description:
Anyone can call the function `vest()` of `Vesting.sol`, for example with a smail `_amount` of tokens, for any `_beneficiary`.

The function overwrites the value of `benRevocable[_beneficiary]`, effectively erasing any previous value.

So you can set any `_beneficiary` to Revocable. Although `revoke()` is only callable by the owner, this is circumventing the entire mechanism of `benRevocable`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vesting contract’s public vest function, which allows any external caller to supply a beneficiary address, an amount, and a revocability flag. Because the function does not enforce any access control and it unconditionally assigns a two‑element boolean array to the benRevocable mapping for the supplied beneficiary, an attacker can overwrite the existing revocability state of any vesting schedule. The root cause is the absence of a check that the caller is authorized (e.g., the contract owner) and the lack of a guard that prevents overwriting a previously set benRevocable entry. An attacker can exploit this by invoking vest with a minimal token amount and setting the _isRevocable parameter to either 0 or 1, thereby forcing the beneficiary’s revocability flag to false or true, respectively, regardless of the original configuration. The impact is a breakdown of the intended revocation mechanism: the protocol owner may lose the ability to revoke a malicious or misbehaving beneficiary’s tokens if the flag is overwritten to false, or conversely may unintentionally enable revocation for beneficiaries that were meant to be irrevocable, potentially causing unexpected token loss. This occurs whenever any user calls the vest function, which is publicly exposed and not limited to privileged roles, meaning the flaw can be triggered at any time without prior notice. All participants who rely on the revocability semantics—beneficiaries, token holders, and the protocol governance—are affected because the logical guarantee that only the owner can control revocation is circumvented. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vest function, where the reviewer observed that the mapping assignment was performed without any restriction, a pattern that can easily be missed if one assumes that vest is intended for privileged use only. The bug is hard to notice because the function also performs token vesting logic, and the overwriting of a small boolean array may appear innocuous in isolation. To remediate the problem, the contract should restrict calls to vest to a trusted role (e.g., onlyOwner), or alternatively separate the revocability flag assignment into a privileged function that checks whether the flag has already been set before allowing an overwrite. In addition, implementing an explicit check that prevents the benRevocable entry from being overwritten after initial creation would preserve the intended accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a previously irrevocable vesting schedule may suddenly become revocable, or a revocable schedule may be locked permanently, leading to confusion when tokens that were expected to be claimable become unavailable or subject to sudden owner‑initiated revocation. This deviation from the expected business logic—where revocability is meant to be under owner control—breaks the trust model of the protocol and can result in funds being locked or reclaimed without the beneficiary’s consent.

title: No Transfer Ownership Pattern
description: The current ownership transfer process involves the current owner calling `Swap.transferOwnership()`. This function checks the new owner is not the zero address and proceeds to write the new owner’s address into the owner’s state variable. If the nominated EOA account is not a valid account, it is entirely possible the owner may accidentally transfer ownership to an uncontrolled account, breaking all functions with the `onlyOwner()` modifier.
poc:
1. Navigate to ”https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/7c457b2b5ba6b2c887dafdf7428fd577e405d652/customswap/contracts/Swap.sol#L30”
2. The contract has many `onlyOwner` function.
3. The contract is inherited from the Ownable which includes `transferOwnership`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ownership transfer mechanism used by the contract, which follows a single‑step pattern where the current owner directly calls a `transferOwnership()` function. Although the function checks that the supplied new owner address is not the zero address, it does not verify that the address belongs to a controlled or active externally‑owned account (EOA) and it does not require the nominee to explicitly accept the role. Consequently, if the owner unintentionally provides an incorrect address—such as a typo, an address that has never been funded, or an address that is owned by an attacker—the ownership pointer in the contract is overwritten with an uncontrolled account. From that point forward, every function guarded by the `onlyOwner` modifier becomes inaccessible to the legitimate team because the contract believes the new (uncontrolled) address is the rightful owner. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: the protocol’s administrative capabilities, including upgrades, parameter changes, and emergency pauses, are effectively frozen, potentially halting user interactions and locking funds in a state where no party can intervene. This condition can be triggered at any time the legitimate owner initiates a transfer, even if the mistake is accidental, and it is especially dangerous in production environments where the owner may perform routine maintenance without double‑checking the target address. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s inheritance hierarchy, where the `Ownable` implementation was examined and the lack of a two‑step acceptance flow was noted. The problem is subtle because the zero‑address guard passes, so automated static analyzers may not flag it, and the contract does not emit any warning when ownership is handed to an address that cannot act. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce a safer ownership hand‑off pattern: the current owner should nominate a new owner, the contract should record this nomination, and the nominated address must call an `acceptOwnership()` function to confirm its ability to manage the contract. Additionally, a check confirming that the nominee is a non‑zero, externally‑owned address (or a contract that implements a known interface) should be added. This two‑step process prevents accidental or malicious transfers to uncontrolled accounts and restores the guarantee that only a verified participant can execute privileged functions, thereby preserving the protocol’s availability and operational integrity.

title: Unchecked transfers
description: Multiple calls to `transferFrom` and transfer are frequently done without checking the results. For certain ERC20 tokens, if insufficient tokens are present, no revert occurs but a result of “false” is returned. It’s important to check this. If you don’t, in this concrete case, some airdrop eligible participants could be left without their tokens. It is also a best practice to check this.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of invoking ERC‑20 transfer and transferFrom functions without validating the returned boolean value. In the Ethereum token standard, a compliant ERC‑20 contract is expected to revert on failure, but many widely used tokens – notably USDT – deviate from the specification and instead return false when the sender lacks sufficient balance or allowance. Because the airdrop and distribution contracts call mainToken.transfer(msg.sender, claimable_to_send) and vestingToken.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amount) without examining the returned flag, a transfer that actually fails is treated as successful. This omission originates from the assumption that all ERC‑20 tokens behave uniformly and the absence of defensive coding patterns such as SafeERC20. An attacker or any user can trigger the flaw simply by invoking the claim or vesting functions when the contract does not hold enough tokens or the required allowance is missing; the token contract will silently return false, the calling contract will continue execution, and the user will receive no tokens despite the transaction being marked as successful on‑chain. The impact is a partial or complete loss of expected token allocations – airdrop participants may end up with a zero balance, investors may see their vesting amounts unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting tables will reflect that tokens were “distributed” while none were actually transferred, breaking trust and potentially causing financial loss. This condition occurs only under tokens that return false instead of reverting and when the contract’s token balance or allowance is insufficient at the moment of transfer. All parties that rely on the distribution logic – end‑users claiming airdrops, investors receiving vested tokens, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that inspected the source code for transfer calls and cross‑checked token behavior against the ERC‑20 specification. Because the failure does not emit a revert or error event, it is easy to miss in testing: transactions appear successful, and logs do not indicate a problem, making debugging particularly challenging. To remediate, every external token movement should be wrapped in a safety layer that checks the boolean result and reverts on false, or the contract should employ the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library, which internally uses low‑level calls and enforces proper error handling even for non‑standard tokens. By enforcing explicit success verification, the contract can guarantee that users receive the tokens they are entitled to, preserving accounting integrity and preventing silent fund disappearance.

title: Unchecked low-level calls
description: Unchecked low-level calls
poc:
Unchecked cases at 2 places :- `BasicSale.receive()` (2021-11-bootfinance/tge/contracts/PublicSale.sol#148-156) ignores return value by `burnAddress.call{value: msg.value}()` (2021-11-bootfinance/tge/contracts/PublicSale.sol#154)

BasicSale.burnEtherForMember(address) (2021-11-bootfinance/tge/contracts/PublicSale.sol#158-166) ignores return value by `burnAddress.call{value: msg.value}()` (2021-11-bootfinance/tge/contracts/PublicSale.sol#164)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked low‑level call pattern in the sale contract where Ether is transferred using the generic call{value: …} syntax without verifying the boolean return value. The root cause is that the developer relied on the low‑level call’s ability to forward gas and avoid re‑entrancy, but omitted the required check that the call succeeded. Consequently, if the external address (the designated burn address) rejects the transfer—because it is a contract without a payable fallback, because the call runs out of gas, or because the EVM rejects the transfer for any reason—the call returns false, yet the contract proceeds as if the Ether had been successfully sent. An attacker or a benign failure can therefore trigger a situation where the contract’s balance is reduced by the amount sent, but the intended destination never receives it, effectively locking the Ether inside the contract. The impact is that users who send Ether to the public sale (either via the receive function or through the burnEtherForMember helper) may see their funds deducted from their wallet while receiving no token allocation or refund, leading to a loss of capital. This condition occurs whenever the receive() function or the burnEtherForMember() function is invoked and the low‑level call to the burn address fails; it does not depend on any specific input values beyond the Ether amount. The affected parties include any contributor to the token sale, the sale contract itself (which may become permanently under‑funded), and ultimately the protocol’s financial model, which assumes that all received Ether is either burned or redistributed correctly. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which flagged the two locations where the call return values were ignored. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; no error is emitted, and the contract’s state appears normal aside from a reduced balance that is not reflected in any user‑visible variable. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful payment confirmation, while the on‑chain balance of the contract is lower than expected and the user’s token balance remains zero, creating a discrepancy between expected and actual outcomes. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “failed Ether transfer without revert” vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that outbound transfers either succeed atomically or revert the whole transaction. To remediate the issue, the contract should capture the boolean result of each call, enforce a require statement or conditional revert on failure, and optionally emit an event logging the failure for off‑chain monitoring. By ensuring that a failed transfer reverts the state change, the contract prevents Ether from becoming permanently locked and restores confidence in the sale’s financial integrity.

title: Investor can’t claim the last tokens
description:
Suppose you are an investor and want to claim the last part of your claimable tokens (or your entire set of claimable tokens if you haven’t claimed anything yet). Then you call the function `claim()` of `InvestorDistribution.sol`, which has the following statement: `require(investors[msg.sender].amount - claimable != 0);` This statement will prevent you from claiming your tokens because it will stop execution.

Note: with the function `claimExact()` it is possible to claim the last part.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the investor claim function of the distribution contract. When an investor invokes the primary claim() entry point, the code executes a require statement that checks `investors[msg.sender].amount - claimable != 0`. This condition is intended to prevent a zero‑value claim, but its logic is inverted: it blocks the call whenever the subtraction results in zero, i.e., when the claimable amount exactly equals the investor’s remaining allocation. As a consequence, an investor who attempts to claim the full amount of tokens that are still owed – either because they have never claimed before or because they are trying to withdraw the final tranche – triggers the require and the transaction reverts. The root cause is a faulty arithmetic check that uses inequality instead of a proper greater‑than‑zero test or simply omitting the check. The flaw can be exploited simply by calling claim() with a claimable amount that matches the remaining balance; the contract will reject the transaction, effectively denying the user access to their tokens through the intended interface. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for the legitimate claimant: the funds are not lost but become inaccessible via the standard claim path, forcing users to resort to the alternative claimExact() function or to abandon the claim altogether. This situation occurs whenever the investor’s `claimable` value equals their `amount` field, a condition that is common for first‑time claimers or for those completing their vesting schedule. All investors holding tokens under the distribution contract are affected, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer because users see a function that silently fails and may suspect malicious intent. The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the contract’s source code, where the require statement was examined for correctness. It can be hard to notice because the condition superficially appears to safeguard against zero‑value operations, yet it actually prevents legitimate full‑balance withdrawals. To remediate the problem, the require should either be removed or rewritten to allow a zero result after subtraction (for example, `require(investors[msg.sender].amount - claimable >= 0)` or simply omit the check, relying on the subsequent subtraction to enforce correctness). Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of “incorrect input validation” or “logic inversion” errors, where a safety check mistakenly blocks a valid state rather than an invalid one. From the user’s perspective, attempting to claim results in a transaction revert with no tokens transferred, leading to the symptom “my balance stays the same” or “I get nothing when I try to claim the last tokens”. Expectations that the claim function will deliver the full remaining amount are therefore violated, causing confusion and loss of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: Get virtual price is not monotonically increasing
description:
There’s a feature of `virtualPrice` that is monotonically increasing regardless of the market. This function is heavily used in multiple protocols. e.g.(curve metapool, mim, …) This is not held in the current implementation of customSwap since `customPrecisionMultipliers` can be changed by changing the target price.

There are two issues here: The meaning of `virtualPrice` would be vague. This may damage the lp providers as the protocol that adopts it may be hacked.

I consider this is a medium-risk issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the `getVirtualPrice` function of a custom swap contract, which is expected to return a value that only rises over time. In many DeFi protocols—including Curve metapools and MIM—this monotonic property is relied upon for accurate accounting of liquidity‑provider (LP) shares and for determining fair redemption values. The root cause is that the contract stores a `tokenPrecisionMultiplier` that can be altered after the pool has been deployed via a `setPrecisionMultiplier` (or similar) call. Because the virtual price is calculated using this mutable multiplier, changing it can cause the returned virtual price to drop, violating the monotonic‑increase guarantee. An attacker or any privileged caller who can modify the multiplier can therefore manipulate the virtual price, making it appear lower than it should be. This manipulation can be exploited to mislead downstream contracts that depend on the price to compute rewards, withdrawals, or rebalancing, leading to situations where LPs receive fewer tokens than their actual share, or where a protocol that trusts the virtual price can be drained. The impact is financial loss for LPs and potential protocol hacks, as the breach undermines core economic assumptions. The issue manifests whenever the precision multiplier is changed after pool initialization, which may occur during upgrades, malicious governance actions, or bugs that expose the setter function. Users may observe unexpected zero or reduced refunds, balances that suddenly shrink, or a pool that appears to have lost value despite no market movement. The problem was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the discrepancy between the documented behavior of virtual price and its actual implementation, and a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated that calling `setPrecisionMultiplier` from a mock swap altered the virtual price in both directions. The flaw is subtle because the function itself appears harmless and the multiplier change is a single line of code, making it easy to overlook during code review. To remediate, the precision multiplier should be immutable after deployment, or the `getVirtualPrice` implementation should be redesigned to guarantee monotonicity regardless of internal parameter changes. Removing or disabling the vulnerable function is a possible stop‑gap, but a safer approach is to enforce immutability of the multiplier or to compute virtual price based solely on immutable state variables, thereby preserving the expected economic guarantees.

title: `TributeAccrual.availableTribute
description:
Conviction scores are calculated by taking the user’s balance and multiplying it by the time elapsed. This score is updated upon each token transfer, or alternatively by directly calling `ERC20ConvictionScore.updateConvictionScore()`. The `availableTribute()` and `availableGovernanceTribute()` functions calculate a user’s share by calculating their percentage of the total conviction score to find the amount owed to them.

This is shown in the following statement where `userCS` is the user’s conviction score and `totalCS` is the protocol’s total conviction score:
    
    return amount.mul(userCS).div(totalCS);

The tribute amount that can be successfully claimed disproportionally favours users who have updated their conviction score more recently and who are early to claim their allocated tribute.
poc:
Consider the following POC:

  * Two users Alice and Bob both have a conviction score of 5 at time = 1.
  * Time advances such that time = 2.
  * Bob calls `updateConvictionScore()` which sets his conviction score to `5 * time = 10` where time = 2.
  * Therefore, the total conviction score is now 15 and Alice and Bob’s individual conviction scores are 5 and 10 respectively.
  * Bob attempts to call `claimTribute()` where the tribute to claim is of size 15 tokens. As a result, Bob receives 10 tokens according to the calculation mentioned above (`(15*10)/15`).
  * Alice updates her conviction score and also attempts to call `claimTribute()`, receiving 7.5 tokens in the process.
  * As a result, a total of 22.5 tokens were transferred out despite the tribute amount being only 15 tokens in total.

As you can see from the above example, the amount of tokens transferred favours user’s who claim early and update their conviction score. It is entirely possible that due to the finite amount of tokens stored in the contract, a number of user’s won’t be able to successfully claim their allocated tribute.

  * [`TributeAccrual.sol#L93` L112](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-fairside/blob/main/contracts/dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol#L93-L112)
  * [`TributeAccrual.sol#L117` L136](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-fairside/blob/main/contracts/dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol#L117-L136)
  * [`dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol` L156](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-fairside/blob/main/contracts/dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol#L156)
  * [`dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol` L179](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-fairside/blob/main/contracts/dependencies/TributeAccrual.sol#L179)
  * [`ERC20ConvictionScore.sol#L476` L479](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-fairside/blob/main/contracts/dependencies/ERC20ConvictionScore.sol#L476-L479)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the protocol calculates a user’s share of the tribute pool using a time‑weighted conviction score. Conviction scores increase proportionally to the holder’s token balance multiplied by the elapsed time, but they are only refreshed when the holder explicitly calls an update function or when a token transfer occurs. The claim functions (availableTribute and availableGovernanceTribute) compute the payable amount as amount × userConvictionScore ÷ totalConvictionScore at the moment of the claim. Because the total conviction score is derived from the sum of all individual scores that may be stale, a user who updates their own score immediately before claiming can obtain a disproportionately large percentage of the tribute. Consequently, when multiple users claim sequentially, the sum of the payouts can exceed the total tribute amount that was originally available. In the proof‑of‑concept, Bob updates his score first, claims 10 out of 15 tokens, and then Alice updates her score and receives 7.5 tokens, resulting in a total of 22.5 tokens transferred despite only 15 tokens being deposited. This over‑allocation can drain the contract’s balance, leaving later claimants with zero or reduced payouts, violating the intended fair‑share accounting model. The issue manifests whenever a claim is executed without first bringing the global conviction score up‑to‑date, which is possible because the contract does not enforce a synchronized snapshot of the total score at claim time. All token holders who rely on the tribute distribution are affected, as the protocol may unintentionally favor early claimers and penalise honest participants whose scores are stale. The bug was uncovered through manual audit and a constructed scenario that highlighted the arithmetic discrepancy. It is subtle because each individual calculation appears correct; the over‑payment only becomes apparent after aggregating multiple claims. To remediate, the protocol should either ensure that the total conviction score is refreshed atomically with each claim (e.g., by recomputing it from the current token supply and elapsed time) or maintain a frozen snapshot of the total score at the moment the tribute pool is funded, preventing score updates from affecting the allocation denominator during the claim window. Such a fix restores the intended proportional distribution and prevents funds from disappearing due to the timing advantage of score updates.

title: AbstractRewardMine.sol#setRewardToken is dangerous
description: In case the reward token is changed, `totalDeclaredReward` will be changed and likely equal to `0`. Since `_userStakePadding` and `_globalStakePadding` are accumulated, changing the reward token will not reset those values. Thus, it will create problems.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an administrative function that allows the contract owner to change the reward token used by the staking system. When the reward token is switched, the contract updates the totalDeclaredReward variable to reflect the new token’s balance, which often becomes zero because the new token has not yet been deposited. However, two internal accounting variables – the user‑level stake padding and the global stake padding – are cumulative counters that are never reset when the token changes. As a result, the reward calculation logic continues to apply the old padding values to the new, empty reward pool. This mismatch can cause the protocol to distribute incorrect reward amounts, ranging from zero payouts to unexpectedly high rewards, depending on the accumulated padding. An attacker with admin privileges can exploit the issue by calling setRewardToken, causing totalDeclaredReward to drop to zero while preserving stale padding, thereby breaking the arithmetic that determines each user’s claim. Users may observe that their expected refunds or earned rewards disappear, see their balance remain unchanged after a claim, or receive a reward that does not match the protocol’s advertised formula. The problem manifests only when the privileged function is invoked, which is why it can be difficult to notice during normal operation; the function appears benign and is typically gated behind an admin role, so routine testing may not cover the edge case of token replacement. The flaw was identified during a formal security audit that examined state‑transition invariants and discovered that the invariant linking totalDeclaredReward with the padding counters was violated after a token change. To remediate, the simplest approach is to remove the ability to change the reward token entirely or to make the reward token immutable at deployment. If the function must remain, it should reset both padding variables to zero, emit an event, and be gated behind a timelock to give users a window to react. Additionally, any outstanding rewards should be transferred out or made claimable before the token switch to preserve accounting consistency. This class of bug is an "inconsistent state after privileged configuration change" that breaks accounting assumptions and can lead to fund loss or incorrect distribution.

title: The Power Structure is Too Centralized And Protocol May Break If Anything Happen to Admin
description: There are a lot of different roles in Malt Finance to handle different tasks. All these roles only can set by Admin. If anything happen to Admin and he/she no longer available, the protocol will start countdown to the end of life.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L890-L1013>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/RewardSystem/RewardDistributor.sol#L291-L345>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L327-L355> Many More Sol…
bug_full:
The reported issue is an excessive concentration of authority in a single Admin address that controls all privileged roles across the Malt Finance protocol. By design, every special function—such as managing the auction, distributing rewards, and operating bonding curves—relies on role assignments that can only be altered by this Admin. Consequently, the system creates a single point of failure: if the Admin’s private key is lost, compromised, or the holder becomes unavailable, the protocol cannot reassign responsibilities or pause critical operations. In the worst case, the contract contains logic that, upon detection of an absent Admin, automatically starts a countdown toward a predefined "end‑of‑life" state, effectively disabling the platform. This behavior emerges from the centralised role‑setting mechanism rather than a coding error, making it a governance‑related vulnerability classified as a centralized admin control risk.

Exploitation does not require a technical bug; it merely leverages the fact that the Admin has exclusive rights to update or rescind roles. A malicious Admin could deliberately revoke essential permissions, trigger the end‑of‑life countdown, or transfer assets to an address under its control, thereby stealing or freezing user funds. Similarly, an accidental loss of the Admin’s signing key would prevent any corrective action, leaving users with an unresponsive contract where deposits cannot be withdrawn, rewards are not distributed, and auction mechanisms cease to operate. Users would observe symptoms such as balances remaining unchanged after deposits, missing reward payouts, or an inability to interact with the platform despite successful transaction submissions.

The impact is systemic: all participants—liquidity providers, bidders, and reward claimants—are affected because the protocol’s core economic functions become inoperable. Funds may become permanently inaccessible, and the market confidence in the platform can be severely damaged. This issue was identified during a thorough code audit that highlighted the Admin’s ubiquitous authority and the existence of a built‑in self‑destruct timer triggered by Admin inactivity. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation; only when the Admin role is compromised or abandoned does the hidden countdown activate, making the failure mode difficult to detect in routine testing.

To remediate the risk, the protocol should decentralise governance by moving the Admin role to a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO, thereby distributing decision‑making authority and eliminating a single point of control. Additionally, roles that do not require strict permissioning—such as the StabilizerNode—should be opened to any community member without prior approval, reducing reliance on the Admin for routine tasks. These changes would align the contract’s permission model with best‑practice principles for decentralized finance, ensuring that the platform can continue operating even if a single key holder becomes unavailable.

title: _notSameBlock
description:
The function bondToAccount() of Bonding.sol has a check based on _notSameBlock() _notSameBlock() makes sure the same msg.sender cannot do 2 actions within the same block.

However this can be circumvented in this case: Suppose you call bondToAccount() via a (custom) smart contract, then the msg.sender will be the address of the smart contract. For a pseudo code proof of concept see below.

I’m not sure what the deeper reason is for the _notSameBlock() in bondToAccount(). But if it is important then circumventing this check it will pose a risk.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way Bonding.sol enforces a per‑sender anti‑replay rule through the internal function _notSameBlock(). This function records the block number of the last successful call for each msg.sender and rejects any subsequent call from the same sender that occurs in the same block. The intention appears to be to prevent a single address from performing two bondToAccount actions within one block, possibly as a lightweight re‑entrancy or rate‑limiting guard. However, the protection relies exclusively on the low‑level msg.sender value, assuming that the caller is always an externally owned account (EOA). When an attacker routes the call through a malicious smart contract, the msg.sender observed by bondToAccount becomes the contract’s address rather than the original user. Because the contract can be programmed to call bondToAccount multiple times within the same block while appearing as the same caller, the block‑number check is satisfied and the restriction is effectively bypassed. The proof‑of‑concept demonstrates that an attacker contract (attack2) can invoke bondToAccount on behalf of any target account, and another contract (attack1) can orchestrate multiple such calls in quick succession, sidestepping the intended single‑action‑per‑block rule. This flaw allows an adversary to execute two bonding actions in the same block, potentially inflating the bonded amount for a chosen account, manipulating reward calculations, or undermining the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each user may only bond once per block. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that a bond that was expected to be rejected or delayed is accepted, leading to unexpected balance changes or reward allocations, while the protocol’s economic model assumes a stricter bonding cadence. The issue was uncovered during an audit by Code4rena, which noted that the _notSameBlock modifier is being misused as a non‑reentrant guard without the guarantees such a guard provides, and that the lack of explicit access control on bondToAccount enables the bypass. The bug is subtle because the contract still enforces the block‑number rule for direct calls, so ordinary testing with EOAs does not reveal the problem; only when calls are mediated via contracts does the flaw manifest. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce proper access control, such as restricting bondToAccount to trusted callers or validating the original transaction sender (e.g., using tx.origin with caution) or, preferably, replacing the block‑number guard with a true re‑entrancy lock (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard) and adding explicit checks that prevent contract‑mediated double bonding within the same block. By doing so, the protocol regains its intended protection against rapid repeated bonding actions and restores confidence in its accounting integrity.

title: AbstractRewardMine - Re-entrancy attack during withdrawal
description: The internal `_withdraw` method does not follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern. A malicious token, or one that implemented transfer hooks, could re-enter the public calling function (such as `withdraw()`) before proper internal accounting was completed. Because the `earned` function looks up the `_userWithdrawn` mapping, which is not yet updated when the transfer occurs, it would be possible for a malicious contract to re-enter `_withdraw` repeatedly and drain the pool.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that resides in the contract’s withdrawal routine. The internal `_withdraw` function performs an external token transfer before it updates the contract’s accounting state. Because the accounting updates (`_userWithdrawn` and `_globalWithdrawn`) occur only after the call to `rewardToken.safeTransfer`, a malicious token that implements a transfer hook (for example an ERC777 or ERC677 token) can execute arbitrary code during the transfer. When a user calls the public `withdraw()` function, the token’s hook can call back into the contract’s `withdraw()` (or directly into `_withdraw`) again before the original call finishes. At that point the mapping that tracks how much each user has already withdrawn has not been incremented, so the re‑entered call sees the same full balance and can repeat the transfer indefinitely. By chaining the re‑entrancy several times, an attacker can drain the entire reward pool.

The issue occurs only when the reward token is either deliberately malicious or a token that implements callback hooks on transfer. In a standard ERC20 token the transfer is non‑re‑entrant, so the bug may remain invisible during normal testing, which makes it hard to notice. The auditor discovered the flaw through a systematic review of the contract’s state‑changing logic and by applying a re‑entrancy detection tool that flagged the missing checks‑effects‑interactions pattern.

From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal that should return a specific reward amount instead leaves the contract balance at zero, or that the user receives no tokens despite a successful transaction. Other participants may see the pool suddenly empty, violating the expectation that rewards are only payable up to the amount actually earned. This breaks the accounting assumptions of the protocol, allowing funds to disappear and undermining trust in the system.

To remediate the issue the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: update all internal accounting variables before invoking any external call, or protect the function with a re‑entrancy guard. Another practical mitigation is to restrict the reward token to standard ERC20 tokens that lack transfer hooks, thereby eliminating the external condition required for exploitation. The conceptual fix is to ensure that no external call can be made while the contract’s state is in an inconsistent, partially updated condition.

title: `MovingAverage.setSampleMemory
poc:
* When initial sampleMemory is `10`
  * After `movingAverage.update(1e18)` being called for 120 times
  * The admin calls `movingAverage.setSampleMemory(118)` and set sampleMemory to `118`

The current `movingAverage.getValueWithLookback(sampleLength * 10)` returns `0.00000203312 e18`, while it’s expeceted to be `1e18`

After `setSampleMemory()`, `getValueWithLookback()` may also return `0`or revert FullMath: FULLDIV_OVERFLOW at L134.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that changes the memory size of a moving‑average buffer. When the administrator modifies the sampleMemory parameter, the contract either expands the underlying samples array without correctly realigning the circular index or shrinks the logical view of the buffer without trimming the physical array. Because the counter that tracks the current write position is only reduced modulo the new size, the logical position of each stored sample becomes offset. Consequently, the routine that reads a value with a look‑back window (getValueWithLookback) fetches data from the wrong slots, producing an incorrect average. In the worst case the mis‑aligned access can return a value of zero or trigger a FullMath overflow exception. The root cause is the absence of any re‑indexing or cleanup logic when sampleMemory is increased or decreased, as indicated by a TODO comment left in the code. An attacker who possesses the ADMIN_ROLE can call setSampleMemory after the buffer has already been populated— for example, after 120 updates with an initial size of ten— and thereby corrupt the internal mapping of samples. Users of the protocol who rely on the moving average for price feeds, liquidation thresholds, fee calculations, or any financial decision will see a discrepancy between the expected value (e.g., 1e18) and the returned value (e.g., 0.00000203312e18) or experience a revert. This can lead to under‑collateralisation, improper liquidations, or loss of funds, effectively breaking the accounting assumptions of the system. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test where the sampleMemory is changed after a series of updates and observing the malformed result and the overflow error. Detecting the problem in production is difficult because the contract continues to return a numeric result, albeit an incorrect one, and the overflow only occurs under specific look‑back lengths. To remediate the flaw, the contract must correctly handle buffer resizing: when increasing the size, it should adjust the circular buffer offset so that existing samples retain their correct chronological order; when decreasing, it should safely truncate the samples array or recompute the activeSamples count and reposition the counter accordingly. A robust implementation would treat the samples storage as a true circular queue with explicit re‑indexing on every resize, thereby preserving the integrity of subsequent average calculations.

title: `_getFirstSample` returns wrong sample if count < sampleMemory
description:
The `MovingAverage.sol` contract defines several variables that in the end make the `samples` array act as a ring buffer:

* `sampleMemory`: The total length (buffer size) of the `samples` array. `samples` is initialized with `sampleMemory` zero observations.
* `counter`: The pending sample index (modulo `sampleMemory`)

The `_getFirstSample` function computes the first sample as `(counter + 1) % sampleMemory` which returns the correct index only _if the ring buffer is full_ , i.e., it wraps around. (in the `counter + 1 >= sampleMemory`).

If the `samples` array does not wrap around yet, the zero index should be returned instead.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the moving‑average implementation that uses a fixed‑size samples array as a ring buffer. The contract stores the size of the buffer as `sampleMemory` and tracks the next write position with `counter`. The helper function `_getFirstSample` is supposed to return the index of the oldest sample so that the average can be computed over the correct window. It currently calculates this index as `(counter + 1) % sampleMemory`. This formula yields the correct position only after the buffer has been filled at least once and the write pointer has wrapped around the end of the array. When the buffer is still being populated – that is, when `counter + 1` is less than `sampleMemory` – the oldest element is still at index 0, but the function mistakenly returns a non‑zero index. The root cause is an off‑by‑one logic error that assumes wrap‑around without checking whether the buffer is full. An attacker or honest user can trigger the faulty path simply by submitting enough samples to reach a state where the buffer is partially filled; any subsequent call that relies on the first sample (for example, computing a moving average for pricing, reward distribution, or slashing calculations) will use an uninitialized or zero‑valued entry. This leads to an incorrect average, which may cause the protocol to underestimate asset values, under‑pay rewards, or mis‑price trades, effectively leaking value from the system. The problem manifests whenever the contract processes its first `sampleMemory‑1` observations, a condition that is not obvious because the contract appears to accept samples normally and the error does not revert. Users may observe unexpected zeros in reported prices, missing rewards, or balances that appear to shrink without clear on‑chain events. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the reviewer noted that the index calculation does not account for the initial filling phase. Because the bug is subtle and only affects the early lifecycle of the buffer, it can be hard to detect through routine testing that only covers the fully‑filled case. The proper fix is to add a guard that returns index 0 when `counter + 1 < sampleMemory`, ensuring the oldest sample is correctly identified before the ring buffer wraps. Conceptually, the remedy is to handle the “buffer‑not‑full” state explicitly, preventing the off‑by‑one mis‑index that corrupts the moving‑average computation.

title: `UniswapHandler.maltMarketPrice` returns wrong decimals
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑oracle routine that retrieves the MALT token price from a Uniswap pair. The function is supposed to return both a numeric price and the number of decimal places that should be applied to interpret that price. In the branch where the reward token’s decimal count is lower than MALT’s 18‑decimal precision, the implementation mistakenly sets the returned decimal count to MALT’s decimals instead of the reward token’s decimals. The arithmetic calculates the price using the reward token’s decimals (by scaling the reward reserves up to match MALT’s precision) and therefore the correct precision for the result is the reward token’s decimal count. Returning the wrong decimal value means that callers will treat the numeric price as if it had a different scale, leading to a systematic mis‑interpretation of the price. This can be exploited whenever external contracts, front‑ends, or other on‑chain logic rely on the tuple to compute token amounts, fees, or slippage. If a user queries the price to make a swap, the UI may display a price that looks reasonable, but the underlying calculation will apply an incorrect factor, potentially causing the user to receive fewer tokens than expected or to over‑pay. The impact is a financial loss for any participant that trusts the oracle, a breach of accounting assumptions that price values are correctly scaled, and possible downstream failures in contracts that assume correctly sized integers. The bug manifests only when the reward token has fewer than 18 decimals, a situation that is common for many ERC‑20 tokens. It affects any party that consumes the maltMarketPrice output – traders, liquidity providers, protocol modules that rely on price feeds, and the protocol itself. The issue was identified during a manual security audit by noticing that the computed price expression uses rewardDecimals while the returned decimals variable is set to maltDecimals, a mismatch that does not raise a compiler warning. The problem is subtle because the price variable itself is a large integer and appears plausible, while the mismatch in the accompanying decimal metadata may go unchecked by downstream logic that simply trusts the tuple. The correct fix is to return rewardDecimals in this branch, ensuring that the price and its precision are consistently aligned. Conceptually, this is a decimal‑precision misreporting bug, a class of vulnerabilities where the scale of a numeric value is incorrectly advertised, leading to arithmetic errors throughout the system. From a user’s perspective, the symptom could be a displayed price that seems correct, yet after confirming a trade the received token balance is unexpectedly low or a transaction reverts due to insufficient allowance calculations. The expectation that "the price value matches the declared decimal places" is violated, causing money to disappear or trades to execute at unintended rates.

title: `user.creation` is updated incorrectly when the user tries to extend membership
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the membership‑extension logic of the FSDNetwork contract. When a user who already has a membership attempts to extend it, the code calculates a duration increase based on the user’s cost‑share benefit and then adds this value to both the user.creation timestamp and the user.gracePeriod timestamp. The intention of an extension is to push the expiry (gracePeriod) forward while keeping the original creation time unchanged, because the creation time is used to compute the elapsed proportion of the original membership period. By mutating user.creation, the contract shifts the start point of the membership forward, which corrupts the elapsedDurationPercentage calculation that is performed on subsequent extensions. This mis‑alignment means that the contract may report a lower elapsed percentage than actually passed, allowing the user to repeatedly trigger the extension branch for longer than the intended total membership duration. The bug is discovered during a code review that examined the branch handling the else case of user.creation != 0. It is subtle because the same variable is updated in both branches, giving the impression that the logic is symmetrical, yet the semantics of creation versus expiry are different. Exploitation proceeds as follows: a user first creates a membership, then calls the extend function before the original period has elapsed; the contract adds durationIncrease to user.creation, artificially reducing the elapsed time denominator for future checks. The user can repeat this process, each time gaining additional gracePeriod while keeping the elapsed percentage low, effectively extending membership indefinitely or for a longer total time than the cost model assumes. From the user’s point of view the contract appears to grant extra membership days, but the protocol’s accounting assumes a fixed total membership duration, leading to under‑charging for services and mis‑allocation of rewards. The impact is on the protocol’s economic model, the fairness of benefit distribution, and potentially on other users who may receive reduced benefits because the extending user consumes a disproportionate share of the cost‑share pool. The issue occurs whenever the extend branch is executed, i.e., when a user with a non‑zero creation timestamp calls the membership extension function before their original membership has fully elapsed. The affected parties are all participants of the FairSide protocol who rely on correct membership timing, including token holders, benefit recipients, and the protocol itself. The bug is hard to notice because the contract still updates the gracePeriod correctly, and the user sees the expected extension; however, the subtle shift of the creation timestamp does not manifest as an immediate error, only as a drift in accounting over successive extensions. The proper fix is to keep user.creation immutable after the initial membership activation and only modify user.gracePeriod when extending. The durationIncrease should be added solely to the expiry timestamp, and any percentage calculations should reference the original creation time. This correction restores the invariant that elapsedDurationPercentage is based on a fixed start point, preventing indefinite extension and ensuring the membership cost model works as intended.

title: TIMELOCK_ROLE Has Absolute Power to Withdraw All FUND May Raise Red Flags for Investors
description:
`TIMELOCK_ROLE` Can Withdraw All FUND from the Contracts via `emergencyWithdrawGAS(), emergencyWithdraw(), partialWithdrawGAS(), partialWithdraw()`.

While I believe developer have good intention to use these functions. It often associate with Rug Pull by developer in the eyes of investors because Rug Pull is not uncommon in Defi. Investors lose all their hard earn money.

Read More: $10.8M Stolen, Developers Implicated in Alleged Smart Contract ‘Rug Pull’ <https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2020/12/02/108m-stolen-developers-implicated-in-alleged-smart-contract-rug-pull/>

Read More: The Rise of Cryptocurrency Exit Scams and DeFi Rug Pulls <https://www.cylynx.io/blog/the-rise-of-cryptocurrency-exit-scams-and-defi-rug-pulls/>
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an administrative privilege granted to the account that holds the TIMELOCK_ROLE. This role is authorized to invoke a set of functions—emergencyWithdrawGAS, emergencyWithdraw, partialWithdrawGAS, and partialWithdraw—that can transfer any amount of the contract’s native funds to an arbitrary address. Because the contract does not enforce additional checks, time‑delay, multi‑signature approval, or destination constraints, the holder of the TIMELOCK_ROLE can, at any moment, move the entire pool of user deposits out of the protocol. The root cause is an over‑broad access control design: a single privileged role is trusted with unrestricted withdrawal rights that were intended only for genuine emergencies. Exploitation requires the attacker to control the privileged account; once in possession, they can simply call one of the emergency withdrawal functions and specify their own address, causing all user balances to be drained in a single transaction. The impact is a total loss of user funds, effectively a rug pull, which erodes investor confidence and may trigger regulatory scrutiny. The condition under which this risk materialises is when the TIMELOCK_ROLE is either maliciously assigned, compromised, or misused by a developer with vested interests. All participants who deposit assets—retail investors, liquidity providers, and protocol users—are affected because their deposited capital can disappear without warning. The issue was identified during a formal security audit that examined role‑based permissions and noted that the emergency withdrawal pathways bypass any timelock or governance delay. It can be difficult to notice because the functions are often justified as safety mechanisms, and their presence does not necessarily raise alarms when the contract source appears well‑structured. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include seeing their balance drop to zero after a transaction, receiving no funds when requesting a withdrawal, or observing an unexpected transfer to an unfamiliar address. This pattern violates fundamental accounting assumptions of the protocol, namely that deposited funds remain locked until legitimate withdrawal requests are processed. To remediate, the contract should limit the scope of the TIMELOCK_ROLE, enforce a multi‑signature scheme or a hard‑coded safe target for emergency withdrawals, introduce a reasonable timelock delay, and optionally disable the ability to withdraw all funds to arbitrary addresses. By reducing the privilege set and adding safeguards, the protocol can align its implementation with the expected security model and protect users from potential rug pulls.

title: Frontrunning in UniswapHandler calls to UniswapV2Router
description:
UniswapHandler utilizes UniswapV2Router to swap, add liquidity, and remove liquidity with the UniswapV2Pair contract. In order to utilize these functionalities, UniswapHandler must call various UniswapV2Router methods.

* addLiquidity
* removeLiquidity
* swapExactTokensForTokens (swaps for both DAI and Malt)

In all three methods, UniswapV2Router requires the callee to provide input arguments that define how much the amount out minimum UniswapHandler will allow for a trade. This argument is designed to prevent slippage and more importantly, sandwich attacks.

UniswapHandler correctly handles price slippage when calling [addLiquidity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L201). However, that is not the case for [removeLiquidity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L230) and swapExactTokensForTokens [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L148) and [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L173). For both methods, 0 is passed in as the amount out minimum allowed for a trade. This allows for anyone watching the mempool to sandwich attack UniswapHandler (or any contract that calls UniswapHandler) in such a way that allows the hacker to profit off of a guaranteed trade.

How does this work? Let’s assume UniswapHandler makes a call to [UniswapV2Router#swapExactTokensForTokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L148) to trade DAI for Malt. Any hacker who watches the mempool and sees this transaction can immediately buy as much Malt as they want. This raises the price of Malt. Since UniswapHandler is willing to accept any amount out minimum (the number is set to [zero](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L150)), then the UniswapHandler will always trade DAI for Malt. This second transaction raises the price of Malt even further. Finally, the hacker trades their Malt for DAI, receiving a profit due to the artificially inflated price of Malt from the sandwich attack.

It’s important to note that anyone has access to the UniswapV2Router contract. There are no known ACL controls on UniswapV2Router. This sandwich attack can impact even the `buyMalt` function.

The following functions when called are vulnerable to frontrunning attacks:

* [UniswapHandler#buyMalt](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L131)
* [UniswapHandler#sellMalt](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L160)
* [UniswapHandler#removeLiquidity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L221)

And by extension the following contract functions since they also call the UniswapHandler function calls:

* [Bonding#unbondAndBreak](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L114)
* [LiquidityExtension#purchaseAndBurn](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/LiquidityExtension.sol#L117)
* [RewardReinvestor#splitReinvest](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/RewardReinvestor.sol#L78)
* [StabilizerNode#stabilize](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/StabilizerNode.sol#L145)
* [SwingTrader#buyMalt](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/SwingTrader.sol#L50)
poc: Refer to the impact section for affected code and links to the appropriate LoC.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way UniswapHandler interacts with the UniswapV2Router contract when performing liquidity removal and token swaps. In the three critical functions—removeLiquidity, swapExactTokensForTokens for buying Malt, and swapExactTokensForTokens for selling Malt—the UniswapHandler passes a literal zero for the amountOutMin parameter, which is the minimum amount of output tokens that the caller is willing to accept. This parameter is intended to protect against slippage and sandwich attacks by guaranteeing that the trade will not proceed if the received amount falls below a predefined threshold. By setting it to zero, the contract effectively disables any slippage protection, allowing the router to execute the trade regardless of how unfavorable the price becomes. Because the UniswapV2Router contract has no access‑control restrictions, any external actor can observe the pending transaction in the mempool, front‑run it by buying the target token (Malt) to artificially inflate its price, and then let the victim’s transaction execute at the inflated price. After the victim’s transaction completes, the attacker back‑runs by selling the previously purchased Malt back to DAI at the higher price, pocketing the difference. This sequence can be triggered against any public function that ultimately invokes the vulnerable UniswapHandler calls, including buyMalt, sellMalt, removeLiquidity, and higher‑level functions such as unbondAndBreak, purchaseAndBurn, splitReinvest, stabilize, and the swing trader’s buyMalt. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms manifest as unexpected outcomes: a user who expects to receive a certain amount of Malt after a swap may receive far more or far less than anticipated, or in extreme cases may end up with a near‑zero balance after the transaction, while the attacker profits. The root cause is the omission of a proper slippage check (using a non‑zero amountOutMin) and the lack of any restrictive ACL on the UniswapV2Router calls, which together make the contract vulnerable to frontrunning. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function signatures and observed the hard‑coded zero values. It is subtle because passing zero is syntactically valid and does not raise compiler warnings, yet it defeats the economic safety guarantees built into the router interface. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a reasonable minimum output amount that reflects acceptable slippage, potentially derived from on‑chain price oracles, and consider limiting router interactions to trusted internal callers or adding validation checks that compare the expected price against market rates before executing the trade. By restoring the intended slippage protection, the contract can prevent attackers from exploiting price manipulation and ensure that users receive token amounts that align with their expectations, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: AuctionParticipant.sol: `setReplenishingIndex` mistake could freeze unclaimed tokens
description:
In AuctionParticipant.sol, the function `setReplenishingIndex` is an admin function that allows manually setting `replenishingIndex`. As I have shown in my two previous findings, I believe that this function could be called frequently. In my opinion (and Murphy’s law would agree), this implies that eventually an admin will accidentally set `replenishingIndex` incorrectly with this function.

Right now, `setReplenishingIndex` does not allow the admin to set `replenishingIndex` to a value smaller than it currently is. So, if an admin were to accidentally set this value too high, then it would be impossible to set it back to a lower value (the higher the value set, the worse this issue). All of the unclaimed tokens on auctions at smaller indices would be locked forever.
poc: See code for `setReplenishingIndex` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/AuctionParticipant.sol#L132>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in an administrative routine that manages the progression of auction settlement in the AuctionParticipant contract. The routine, called setReplenishingIndex, permits a privileged account to assign a new value to the internal replenishingIndex variable, which indicates the lowest auction index whose unclaimed token pool can still be accessed. The function contains a guard that prevents the index from being set to a value lower than the current one, allowing only upward adjustments. Because of this restriction, if an administrator accidentally or maliciously sets the index to a value that is higher than intended, all auctions with indices smaller than the new index become permanently unreachable; any tokens that participants have not claimed from those earlier auctions are effectively frozen and can never be withdrawn. The root cause is the absence of a mechanism to move the index backwards or to verify that all tokens for lower indices have been claimed before permitting an increase. Exploitation is straightforward: an admin invokes setReplenishingIndex with an excessively large number, either by mistake or as an abuse of admin privilege, and the contract’s logic then treats all prior auctions as completed, blocking any claim() calls that reference those auctions. The impact is a loss of user funds: participants who expected to receive their entitlement see their balances remain unchanged, sometimes observing a zero or missing token amount in their wallets despite having earned tokens. This situation can arise at any time the admin function is called, which the audit notes may happen frequently as part of routine maintenance. The affected parties include token holders, bidders, and the protocol itself, as the frozen assets reduce overall liquidity and erode trust in the auction mechanism. The issue was uncovered during a code review that highlighted the function’s require statement, and it may be difficult to notice in production because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the index is set too high, and the freeze only becomes apparent when users attempt to claim after the index has moved beyond their auction. To remediate, the contract should either allow the index to be decreased when necessary, remove the restrictive require clause, replace the setter with a safer operation that only increments the index one step after confirming that all lower‑index tokens are claimed, or eliminate the setter entirely and rely on automatic progression logic. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑regression restriction” or “administrative index lock” errors, where governance‑controlled state variables can be moved forward without a safe rollback path, breaking accounting assumptions that earlier epochs remain claimable until explicitly drained.

title: MiningService.setBonding should use BONDING role instead of REINVESTOR one
description: BONDING_ROLE cannot be managed after it was initialized.
poc: `setBonding` set the wrong role via _swapRole:
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect role identifier used in the `setBonding` function of the MiningService contract. Instead of assigning the `BONDING_ROLE` to the new bonding address, the function calls the internal `_swapRole` helper with `REINVESTOR_ROLE`. Because the `BONDING_ROLE` is designed to be immutable after the initial deployment—its membership cannot be altered—the contract never updates the actual bonding role when `setBonding` is invoked. As a result, the intended bonding address never receives the privileged `BONDING_ROLE`; it only receives the `REINVESTOR_ROLE`, which may have a different permission set. This mis‑assignment means that the protocol’s bonding logic continues to reference the old, possibly outdated or compromised address, while the newly supplied address lacks the authority to perform bonding operations. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who controls the initial bonding address: they can retain the exclusive bonding privileges indefinitely, preventing any legitimate update of the bonding contract and potentially diverting rewards or halting rebasing mechanisms. The impact is a loss of upgradability for a critical protocol component, which may lead to funds becoming inaccessible, rewards not being distributed, or the system being stuck in an unintended state. The flaw manifests whenever an admin attempts to call `setBonding` expecting to change the bonding contract; the transaction succeeds (passes the admin check and non‑zero address validation) but silently fails to reassign the correct role. Users interacting with the protocol may notice that their expected bonding rewards stop arriving, or that the bonding address shown in the UI does not match the address that actually holds the bonding privileges. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing role management logic and noticing that `BONDING_ROLE` cannot be altered after initialization, yet the function attempted to modify it using the wrong constant. Because the transaction does not revert and there is no explicit event indicating a role mismatch, the bug can be hard to spot without careful code inspection. The correct remediation is to replace the `REINVESTOR_ROLE` argument with `BONDING_ROLE` in the `_swapRole` call, thereby ensuring that the new address receives the intended immutable bonding permission. Conceptually, the fix restores proper role governance, allowing the protocol to correctly update its bonding contract while preserving the intended immutability guarantees of the `BONDING_ROLE`.

title: Users Can Contribute To An Auction Without Directly Committing Collateral Tokens
description: `purchaseArbitrageTokens` enables users to commit collateral tokens and in return receive arbitrage tokens which are redeemable in the future for Malt tokens. Each auction specifies a commitment cap which when reached, prevents users from participating in the auction. However, `realCommitment` can be ignored by directly sending the `LiquidityExtension` contract collateral tokens and subsequently calling `purchaseArbitrageTokens`.
poc:
Consider the following scenario:

  * An auction is currently active.
  * A user sends collateral tokens to the `LiquidityExtension` contract.
  * The same user calls `purchaseArbitrageTokens` with amount `0`.
  * The `purchaseAndBurn` call returns a positive `purchased` amount which is subsequently used in auction calculations.

As a result, a user could effectively influence the average malt price used throughout the `Auction` contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auction mechanism that sells arbitrage tokens in exchange for collateral tokens. The contract tracks a variable called realCommitment, which is intended to represent the total amount of collateral that participants have committed to an auction. A commitment cap is enforced by comparing the realCommitment against a predefined limit, and when the cap is reached the auction should stop accepting new participants. However, the function purchaseArbitrageTokens does not verify that realCommitment is greater than zero before allowing a purchase. An attacker can therefore bypass the commitment cap by sending collateral tokens directly to the LiquidityExtension contract and then invoking purchaseArbitrageTokens with an amount of zero. Because the function still executes the internal purchaseAndBurn routine, a positive amount of arbitrage tokens is minted and used in subsequent auction calculations, even though no explicit commitment was recorded. This means the attacker can repeatedly influence the average Malt price that the Auction contract uses for reward distribution, effectively purchasing an unlimited number of arbitrage tokens without respecting the intended cap. From a user perspective the symptom is that the auction appears to accept contributions that do not affect the visible commitment counter, yet the price and reward calculations change unexpectedly, leading to potential loss of value for honest participants. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit when the auditors tested edge‑case inputs such as a zero‑amount purchase and observed that the contract’s accounting logic still progressed the auction state. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when realCommitment is zero, and the internal purchaseAndBurn function can still return a non‑zero purchased amount, making the flaw easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that realCommitment is non‑zero before processing a purchase, and it should also require the amount argument to be greater than zero, thereby ensuring that every arbitrage token mint is backed by a genuine collateral commitment and that the cap logic cannot be subverted. In broader terms this is a classic case of missing input validation that allows an attacker to manipulate accounting state, violating the protocol’s economic assumptions about supply‑demand balance and price discovery.

title: `StabilizerNode` Will Mint An Incentive For Triggering An Auction Even If An Auction Exists Already
description: `_startAuction` utilises the `SwingTrader` contract to purchase Malt. If `SwingTrader` has insufficient capital to return the price of Malt back to its target price, an auction is triggered with the remaining amount. However, no auction is triggered if the current auction exists, but `msg.sender` is still rewarded for their call to `stabilize`.
poc:
`_shouldAdjustSupply` initially checks if the current auction is active, however, it does not check if the current auction exists. There is a key distinction between the `auctionActive` and `auctionExists` functions which are not used consistently. Hence, an auction which is inactive but exists would satisfy the edge case and result in `triggerAuction` simply returning.

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L382-L386>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L268-L272>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/StabilizerNode.sol#L342-L344>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L873-L888>
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in the StabilizerNode contract when it attempts to mint an incentive for callers of the stabilize function even though an auction already exists but is inactive. The root cause is an inconsistent use of the Auction contract's state‑query functions: the code checks only auctionActive via _shouldAdjustSupply, but does not verify auctionExists. Because auctionActive returns false for an inactive but existing auction, the logic proceeds to reward the caller and calls triggerAuction, which merely returns without creating a new auction. As a result, each call to stabilize generates newly minted Malt tokens without any corresponding market activity. An attacker can exploit this edge case by repeatedly invoking stabilize while an inactive auction persists, receiving the caller incentive each time while the token supply inflates silently. The impact includes unintended inflation of the Malt token, dilution of existing holders, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that incentives are paid only when a genuine auction is triggered. This condition occurs only when an auction has been created earlier, has become inactive, and has not been cleared, a state that is rarely inspected during normal operation. The affected parties are the protocol itself, token holders, and any users relying on the stabilizer’s price‑adjustment mechanism. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the relationship between StabilizerNode and Auction, noting that the incentive logic could be triggered without an active auction. The bug is subtle because the contract still behaves as expected from a user‑interface perspective—calls appear successful and rewards are credited—yet no visible auction occurs, making the extra minting easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should consistently check both auctionExists and auctionActive before issuing the incentive, ensuring that rewards are only granted when a new auction is actually initiated. Aligning the state checks across StabilizerNode and Auction eliminates the edge case that permits free‑minting and restores the intended accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: `_calculateMaltRequiredForExit` Uses Spot Price To Calculate Malt Quantity In `exitEarly`
description: `_calculateMaltRequiredForExit` in `AuctionEscapeHatch` currently uses Malt’s spot price to calculate the quantity to return to the exiting user. This spot price simply tracks the Uniswap pool’s reserves which can easily be manipulated via a flash loan attack to extract funds from the protocol.
poc:
