* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/AuctionEscapeHatch.sol#L65-L92>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/AuctionEscapeHatch.sol#L193>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L80-L109>
  * <https://shouldiusespotpriceasmyoracle.com/>
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the early‑exit mechanism of the AuctionEscapeHatch contract, specifically the internal function that calculates how many Malt tokens must be returned to a user who invokes exitEarly. The function obtains the current Malt price directly from a Uniswap‑style liquidity pool by reading the pool’s reserves – a so‑called spot price – and then uses that value to determine the Malt quantity. Because the spot price is an instantaneous snapshot of the pool’s state, it can be aggressively altered by an attacker who performs a flash‑loan‑backed swap on the same pool immediately before calling exitEarly. By injecting a large amount of the paired asset, the attacker can drive the reserve ratio in their favour, making the spot price appear either dramatically higher or lower than the true market value. When the manipulated price is used for the calculation, the protocol may dispense an excessive amount of Malt for a comparatively small amount of underlying assets, effectively extracting value from the system. This exploit can be carried out in a single atomic transaction: the attacker takes a flash loan, performs the price‑distorting trade, invokes exitEarly with the now‑biased price, and repays the loan, leaving the protocol with a net loss of funds or an inflated Malt supply. The impact is loss of protocol assets, erosion of token economics, and reduced confidence for users and sponsors. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts an early exit while the underlying liquidity pool is vulnerable to manipulation – typically in environments where pools are permissionless and lack safeguards against flash‑loan attacks. All participants who rely on the exit functionality – regular users, token holders, and the protocol’s sponsor – are potentially affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that the spot price reflects a fair market rate) are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit conducted by Code4rena, when reviewers noted that the contract uses the Uniswap pool’s reserve ratio directly without any averaging or sanity checks, a pattern known to be exploitable with flash loans. The problem can be difficult to spot because the reserve values appear normal at a glance, and there is no explicit protection against short‑term price manipulation. To remediate the issue, the calculation should be based on a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or an external, manipulation‑resistant oracle, and optionally include slippage limits or a delay between price observation and token redemption. By decoupling the exit logic from a volatile spot price, the protocol can restore its intended accounting guarantees and prevent attackers from draining funds through flash‑loan‑driven price distortion.

title: `addLiquidity` Does Not Reset Approval If Not All Tokens Were Added To Liquidity Pool
description: `addLiquidity` is called when users reinvest their tokens through bonding events. The `RewardReinvestor` first transfers Malt and rewards tokens before adding liquidity to the token pool. `addLiquidity` provides protections against slippage by a margin of 5%, and any dust token amounts are transferred back to the caller. In this instance, the caller is the `RewardReinvestor` contract which further distributes the dust token amounts to the protocol’s treasury. However, the token approval for this outcome is not handled properly. Dust approval amounts can accrue over time, leading to large Uniswap approval amounts by the `UniswapHandler` contract.
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the liquidity‑addition routine that is invoked when users reinvest their rewards through a bonding event. The routine, called addLiquidity, is designed to protect against slippage by allowing a 5 % margin and to return any leftover (“dust”) token amounts to the caller. In the current implementation the caller is the RewardReinvestor contract, which forwards the dust to the protocol’s treasury. However, the function does not adjust the ERC‑20 allowance that was previously granted to the UniswapHandler contract. When the supplied amounts of malt or reward tokens are not fully consumed (i.e., maltUsed < maltBalance or rewardUsed < rewardBalance), the excess tokens remain in the RewardReinvestor’s balance and the original approval value stays unchanged. Over successive reinvestments this leads to the allowance on the UniswapHandler growing arbitrarily large, because each call adds more dust without resetting the allowance. The root cause is the missing reset or reduction of the approval after a partial liquidity addition.

An attacker who can trigger addLiquidity indirectly, or who gains control over the UniswapHandler contract, can then call transferFrom using the inflated allowance to pull more tokens from the RewardReinvestor than were intended for the specific liquidity operation. Because the allowance is recorded on‑chain, the exploit does not require a bug in the token contract itself; it merely takes advantage of the unchecked leftover approval. The practical impact is the potential loss of user‑funds that were meant to be reinvested, the creation of an unchecked spending channel for the protocol treasury, and possible incompatibility with tokens that enforce strict allowance semantics (for example USDT, which may revert on repeated approvals). Additionally, the failure to clear the allowance prevents the gas‑refund mechanism that would normally be triggered by resetting allowances to zero.

This condition manifests only when the slippage protection causes the router to request slightly less than the supplied token balances, leaving a non‑zero dust amount. It is therefore invisible to a user who sees a successful reinvestment transaction and may not notice that a large approval persists behind the scenes. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the RewardReinvestor’s reinvest flow, where the code path handling the dust return was examined and found to lack any allowance management.

From the user perspective the symptom is that after a reinvest transaction the expected token balance is correctly reduced, but the protocol later appears to “spend” additional tokens without any apparent action from the user, resulting in missing funds or unexpected treasury withdrawals. The user expects the reinvested amount to be fully accounted for, yet the contract retains an oversized permission that can be abused.

To remediate the problem the approval should be explicitly reset (e.g., set to zero and then to the exact needed amount) whenever the function detects that not all supplied tokens were used, or the contract should use the safe‑approve pattern that always overwrites the previous allowance. This ensures that the UniswapHandler can only pull the exact amount required for the current liquidity addition and that no residual permission remains to be accumulated over time.

title: `_distributeRewards` Does Not Reset Approval If Not All Tokens Were Allocated
description: `_distributeRewards` attempts to reward LP token holders when the price of Malt exceeds its price target. Malt Finance is able to being Malt back to its peg by selling Malt and distributing rewards tokens to LP token holders. An external call to `Auction` is made via the `allocateArbRewards` function. Prior to this call, the `StabilizerNode` approves the contract for a fixed amount of tokens, however, the `allocateArbRewards` function does not necessarily utilise this entire amount. Hence, dust token approval amounts may accrue from within the `StabilizerNode` contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution routine that is triggered when the Malt token price surpasses its target. The routine, named _distributeRewards, first grants a fixed token allowance to the StabilizerNode contract before invoking the external Auction contract through allocateArbRewards. The root cause is that the code assumes the entire approved amount will be consumed, but allocateArbRewards can legitimately spend only a fraction of the allowance, leaving a residual "dust" approval on the StabilizerNode contract. This leftover allowance is never cleared or reduced, meaning the StabilizerNode remains authorized to transfer more tokens than were actually intended for the reward round. An attacker or a malicious contract that gains access to the approved spender address could later call transferFrom using the leftover allowance to siphon additional Malt tokens, effectively draining funds that were supposed to stay in the protocol. Even when no attacker is present, the stale approval can cause transaction reverts with tokens that enforce strict allowance checks, such as USDT, because subsequent attempts to transfer more than the current balance will fail. The issue also forfeits a potential gas refund that would have been available if the allowance had been reset to zero before being set again. From a user perspective, a liquidity provider expecting a full reward may see a missing or reduced payout, or may notice that their balance appears unchanged after an apparent reward event. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit of the Malt Finance code base, where the logic of the approval handling was examined and the discrepancy between the approved amount and the amount actually spent was identified. Because the leftover approval is a subtle state that does not manifest as an immediate error, it can be hard to notice without a targeted review of allowance management. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly reset the allowance to zero (or to the exact amount used) whenever the amount actually transferred is less than the pre‑approved amount, ensuring that no excess approval remains and that future calls start from a clean state. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected accounting model where each reward round consumes exactly the tokens that were approved, preserving both security and gas efficiency.

title: AMM pool can be drained using a flashloan and calling `stabilize`
description: All of the `rewardToken` in a given AMM pool can be removed from the AMM pool and distributed as LP rewards.
poc:
In the `stabilize` method in the `StabilizerNode` the initial check to see if the Malt price needs to be stabilized it uses a short period TWAP: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/StabilizerNode.sol#L156>

However, if the price is above the threshold for stabilization then the trade size required to stabilize looks at the AMM pool directly which is vulnerable to flashloan manipulation.

Attack:

  1. Wait for TWAP to rise above the stabilization threshold
  2. Flashloan remove all but a tiny amount of Malt from the pool.
  3. Call `stabilize`. This will pass the TWAP check and execute `_distributeSupply` which in turn ultimately calls `_calculateTradeSize` in the `UniswapHandler`. This calculation will determine that almost all of the `rewardToken` needs to be removed from the pool to return the price to peg.
  4. Malt will mint enough Malt to remove a lot of the `rewardToken` from the pool.
  5. The protocol will now distribute that received `rewardToken` as rewards. 0.3% of which goes directly to the attacker and the rest goes to LP rewards, swing trader and the treasury.

The amount of money that can be directly stolen by a malicious actor is small but it can cause a lot of pain for the protocol as the pool will be destroyed and confusion around rewards will be created.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a stabilization routine that is intended to keep the price of a native token close to a predefined peg by interacting with an automated market maker (AMM) pool that also holds a reward token. The routine first checks a short‑term time‑weighted average price (TWAP) to decide whether stabilization is required. If the TWAP indicates that the price is above the threshold, the contract then computes the trade size needed to bring the price back to the peg by reading the current reserves of the AMM pool directly. Because the calculation uses the instantaneous pool state, an attacker can manipulate those reserves with a flash loan. By borrowing a large amount of the native token, draining almost all of it from the pool, and leaving only a tiny residual balance, the attacker creates a false view of scarcity. When the attacker subsequently calls the stabilization function, the TWAP check still passes (the average price remains high), and the trade‑size calculation now determines that an enormous amount of the reward token must be removed from the pool to restore the peg. The protocol then mints additional native tokens, executes the trade, and distributes the fetched reward tokens as LP rewards, of which a small fraction (approximately 0.3%) is sent directly to the caller. This sequence effectively drains the reward token balance from the AMM pool, destroys liquidity, and distorts the intended accounting of rewards. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service and economic grief: liquidity providers see their pool balance drop to near zero, expected reward payouts become absent, and the protocol’s treasury and swing‑trader allocations receive far less than intended. Users may notice that their LP positions no longer earn rewards, that reward balances on the UI remain at zero, or that the pool appears empty after a stabilization event. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the stabilizer contract, where the interaction between the short TWAP guard and the direct pool‑state read was examined. It is difficult to spot because the stabilization function appears benign and the direct profit for the attacker is small, making the exploit look like a minor rounding or accounting error rather than a systemic flaw. The underlying class of bug is a flash‑loan‑driven price manipulation caused by reliance on unprotected on‑chain state for critical economic calculations. To remediate, the design should replace the direct reserve read with a longer‑period TWAP or other oracle that cannot be altered within a single block, add slippage and maximum‑trade‑size limits, and possibly enforce a delay between price detection and trade execution to prevent instantaneous manipulation. These changes would ensure that the stabilizer operates on a price signal that reflects genuine market conditions rather than a temporarily emptied pool.

title: No max for advanceIncentive
description:
The function setAdvanceIncentive of DAO.sol doesn’t check for a maximum value of incentive. If incentive would be very large, then advanceIncentive would be very large and the function advance() would mint a large amount of malt.

The function setAdvanceIncentive() can only be called by an admin, but a mistake could be made. Also if an admin would want to do a rug pull, this would be an ideal place to do it.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unbounded parameter in the DAO contract that controls the amount of token minted as an advance incentive. Specifically, the function setAdvanceIncentive allows an account with the ADMIN_ROLE to assign any uint256 value to the internal variable advanceIncentive, but the contract does not enforce a maximum limit on this value. When a user later invokes the advance function, the contract multiplies the stored advanceIncentive by 1e18 and mints that many MALT tokens to the caller. Because the incentive can be set to an arbitrarily large number, an admin can cause the advance function to mint an excessive supply of tokens in a single transaction. This effectively dilutes existing token holders and enables an exit‑scam scenario where the admin creates a massive token supply that can be sold or withdrawn, draining the protocol's economic value. The issue is triggered only when an admin deliberately calls setAdvanceIncentive with a large number and subsequently calls or allows others to call advance. All token holders, participants who expect a modest reward, and the overall protocol security are affected, as the uncontrolled minting can collapse the token price and undermine confidence in the platform. The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the absence of a cap on a privileged variable was flagged as a logical oversight rather than a direct code error, making it easy to overlook in testing because the function appears harmless on its own. Detecting the problem may require reviewing the governance model and the range of values that privileged functions can accept, which is not always part of standard unit tests. To remediate the bug, the contract should enforce a reasonable upper bound on advanceIncentive, preferably tied to the protocol’s token economics or governance voting, and should include safeguards such as multi‑sig approval for changes that affect token supply. By limiting the maximum incentive or requiring additional checks before minting, the protocol can prevent arbitrary dilution and protect users from unexpected token inflation and potential rug pulls.

title: Permissions - return values not checked when sending ETH
description: On lines 85 and 101, ETH is transferred using a `.call` to an address provided as an input, but there is no verification that the call call succeeded. This can result in a call to `emergencyWithdrawGAS` or `partialWithdrawGAS` appearing successful but in reality it failed. This can happen when the provided `destination` address is a contract that cannot receive ETH, or if the `amount` provided is larger than the contract’s balance
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of ETH transfers performed with a low‑level .call in the emergencyWithdrawGAS and partialWithdrawGAS functions. The contract forwards the entire balance (or a requested amount) to an address supplied by the caller, but it does not verify the boolean value returned by the call. Because a low‑level .call only indicates success or failure through its return flag, any situation in which the destination address cannot accept ETH—such as a contract with a non‑payable fallback or a contract that deliberately reverts on receipt—will cause the call to return false while the surrounding function continues as if the withdrawal succeeded. The root cause is the omission of a require statement that checks the returned flag, a common mistake when developers rely on the fact that .call does not automatically revert on failure. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by providing a malicious contract as the destination address; the contract will reject the transfer, the call will return false, and the funds will remain locked in the Permissions contract. From the user's perspective the withdrawal transaction completes without error, yet the expected refund never arrives, leaving the user’s balance unchanged or zero. This issue manifests whenever the caller supplies an address that is unable to receive ETH or when the amount requested exceeds the contract’s current balance, both of which cause the low‑level call to fail silently. The affected parties include any user who relies on the emergency withdrawal functions, the protocol that promises safe fund recovery, and any downstream contracts that may assume the withdrawal succeeded for accounting or composability purposes. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s source code and identified the missing success check after the .call invocation. Because the function does not emit an event or revert on failure, the problem can be hard to notice in routine testing; standard unit tests may only verify that the function executes, not that the funds actually moved. To remediate the issue the contract should capture the boolean result of the .call, require that it is true, and optionally use a library such as OpenZeppelin’s Address.sendValue which encapsulates this pattern. By enforcing the check, any failed transfer will cause the transaction to revert, preventing the appearance of a successful withdrawal when funds have not been moved, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees and user expectations of receiving their ETH.

title: Reducing the epoch length results in leaking value from advancement incentives
description: Unintended advancement incentives being paid out to third party
poc:
`DAO.sol` incentives outside parties to advance the epoch by minting 100 MALT tokens for calling the `advance` function. This is limited by checking that the start timestamp of the next epoch has passed.

This start timestamp is calculated by multiplying the new epoch number by the length of an epoch and adding it to the genesis timestamp.

This method makes no accommodation for the fact that previous epochs may have been set to be a different length to what they are currently.

In the case where the epoch length is reduced, `DAO` will think that the epoch number can be incremented potentially many times. Provided the `advanceIncentive` is worth more than the gas necessary to advance the epoch will be rapidly advanced potentially many times paying out unnecessary incentives.
bug_full: The contract implements a time‑based epoch system in which a privileged function called advance() can be invoked by any caller and rewards the caller with a fixed amount of newly minted tokens. The eligibility to call advance() is gated by a check that the start timestamp of the next epoch has elapsed. This start timestamp is computed by multiplying the current epoch index by a globally stored epoch length and adding the immutable genesis timestamp. The vulnerability arises because the epoch length is mutable by an administrator, yet the calculation of the next epoch’s start time continues to reference the original genesis timestamp without accounting for the moment at which the epoch length was altered. Consequently, when the epoch length is reduced, the contract’s view of the timeline contracts, causing the condition that the next epoch start time has passed to become true for many successive epoch numbers. An attacker with admin rights can therefore change the epoch length to a shorter value and subsequently invoke advance() repeatedly, each invocation satisfying the time check and triggering the caller incentive. The exploitation flow is: (1) admin reduces the epoch length; (2) the contract believes that many epoch boundaries have already been crossed; (3) any user can call advance() multiple times in quick succession; (4) each call mints the incentive amount, draining the token supply allocated for rewards. The impact is a systematic leakage of value: a potentially large quantity of tokens is minted and transferred to arbitrary callers, reducing the protocol’s token reserves and undermining the economic model. The issue manifests only after the epoch length is modified and the subsequent calls to advance() occur; it does not affect epochs that retain their original length. All participants who rely on the integrity of the incentive distribution – including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected because the unexpected minting dilutes existing balances. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between epoch timing and incentive payout logic, noting that the epoch length variable is used directly in the time calculation without persisting the moment of change. The problem may be difficult to notice because the contract still enforces a timestamp check, so on the surface the calls appear legitimate, and the excessive minting only becomes evident when the token supply depletes faster than expected. To remediate the issue, the contract should store the block timestamp of the most recent epoch‑length modification and compute future epoch start times relative to that stored point, or alternatively make the epoch length immutable after deployment. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “parameter‑driven time calculation errors” where mutable configuration values are used in deterministic time‑based formulas without proper versioning, leading to incentive leakage and accounting inconsistencies. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a seemingly normal transaction the caller’s wallet receives a sudden influx of tokens, while the protocol’s reserve balance shrinks unexpectedly, contradicting the expectation that rewards are only paid once per epoch.

title: Wrong permissions on `reassignGlobalAdmin`
description:
The `Permissions.reassignGlobalAdmin` function is supposed to only be run with the `TIMELOCK_ROLE` role, see `onlyRole(TIMELOCK_ROLE, "Only timelock can assign roles")`.

However, the `TIMELOCK_ROLE` is not the admin of all the reassigned roles and the `revokeRole(role, oldAccount)` calls will fail as it requires the `ADMIN_ROLE`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a mis‑configured access‑control flow in the contract that manages role reassignment. A function intended to change the global administrator, called reassignGlobalAdmin, is guarded by a modifier that only allows callers holding the TIMELOCK_ROLE. The function internally revokes a specified role from the current holder and grants it to a new account by invoking revokeRole and grantRole. However, the TIMELOCK_ROLE is not set as the admin of the roles that are being revoked, and the revokeRole operation requires the caller to possess the ADMIN_ROLE of the target role. As a result, when the timelock – the only entity that passes the onlyRole(TIMELOCK_ROLE) check – attempts to execute the function, the internal revokeRole call fails and the transaction reverts. This mismatch between the role used for the external access check and the role required for the internal state change creates a dead‑end path whereby the global admin cannot be reassigned. The issue can be triggered whenever governance or any timelock executor tries to rotate the admin, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for admin‑level upgrades, parameter changes, or emergency actions that depend on the ability to replace the admin. Users of the protocol may observe that expected admin actions simply do nothing or revert, causing confusion when a governance proposal that should update permissions appears to fail silently. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the permissions module, where the auditor noted that the onlyRole check did not align with the role hierarchy used by revokeRole. Because the function’s interface suggests that the timelock can perform admin reassignment, the problem can be hard to spot without tracing the internal require statements of revokeRole. To remediate the issue, the contract should either grant the TIMELOCK_ROLE the ADMIN_ROLE for the affected roles, modify the function to perform the revocation with an account that holds the proper admin rights, or redesign the role hierarchy so that the external access check matches the internal permission requirements. In essence, this is a classic role‑misconfiguration bug where the caller’s permission is insufficient for the internal state transition, violating the protocol’s intended governance flow and potentially leaving the system without a viable way to update critical administrative controls.

title: Bonding doesn’t work with fee-on transfer tokens
description: Certain ERC20 tokens make modifications to their ERC20’s `transfer` or `balanceOf` functions. One type of these tokens is deflationary tokens that charge a certain fee for every `transfer()` or `transferFrom()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a bonding mechanism that assumes a token transfer will deliver exactly the amount specified in the call to the contract. The contract executes a standard ERC‑20 `transfer` or `transferFrom` and then records the amount that was transferred based solely on the value supplied by the caller, without validating how many tokens actually arrived in its balance. Certain ERC‑20 implementations – commonly referred to as fee‑on‑transfer or deflationary tokens – deduct a fee on every transfer, meaning the recipient receives less than the amount requested. Because the bonding logic does not measure the token balance before and after the transfer, it mis‑calculates the bonded amount. When a user attempts to bond with such a token, the contract may either record a lower bonding amount than intended or, if it performs a sanity check that the received amount matches the requested amount, the transaction will revert. This situation occurs whenever the bonding contract interacts with any token that modifies the semantics of `transfer` or `balanceOf`, i.e., tokens that charge a fee, rebalance balances, or otherwise change the transferred quantity. The affected parties are token holders who try to bond their assets, the protocol that relies on accurate bonding for staking, rewards or governance, and any downstream contracts that assume the bonded amount is correct. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s token handling logic and noticed that it never verifies the net token inflow. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and functions correctly with standard ERC‑20 tokens, and the fee‑on‑transfer behavior is only visible at runtime when the token’s transfer logic reduces the amount. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful bonding request, but the on‑chain state reflects a smaller bond, or the transaction may simply fail with a revert error, leaving the user confused as to why their funds do not appear bonded. The bug belongs to the class of "incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens" or "mis‑accounted token transfers", where the contract trusts the caller‑provided amount rather than the actual change in balance. To remediate, the bonding contract should record the token balance of the contract before invoking the transfer, perform the transfer, then read the balance again and compute the difference; this delta is the true amount received and should be used for bonding calculations. By basing the bonded amount on the observed balance change, the contract becomes compatible with fee‑on‑transfer tokens and prevents unexpected reverts or under‑bonding, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: theft of system profit
description: System profit comes from the stabilize function when the price of malt is above 1. Therefore it should not be allowed for anyone to take a part of the system profit when the price is above one. Right now, anyone can take a part of the investors’ profits, even if they don’t own any malt at all.
poc:
suppose that the price went up to 1.2 dai; the investors should get the reward for this rise. instead, anyone can take a part of the reward in the following steps: The price of malt is now 1.2 dai. Take a flash loan of a large amount of malt. Sell the malt for dai. Now the price went down to 1.1 dai because of the enormous swap. Call stabilize in order to lower the price to 1 dai. Buy malt to repay the flash loan at a lower cost with the bought dai. Repay the flash loan, and take the profit.

It is a sandwich attack because they sold malt for a high price, then they called stabilize to lower the value, then repurchase it for a low price.

The user made a profit at the expense of the investors.

If a user already has malt, it’s even easier: just sell all malt at a high cost.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an unintended extraction of system profit from the price‑stabilisation mechanism of a token whose value is anchored to a peg of 1 DAI. The protocol is designed to generate profit for liquidity providers when the market price of the token rises above the peg; this profit is meant to be distributed only to holders of the token. However, the contract permits any participant, even one that holds no token, to capture a portion of that excess value by exploiting the stabilisation routine. The root cause is a missing access control check in the transfer‑verification hook that allows a flash‑loan borrower to trigger the stabiliser after selling a large amount of the token at an inflated price. Because the stabiliser unconditionally reduces the price back toward the peg, the attacker can then repurchase the token at a lower price, repay the flash loan, and keep the spread as profit. This flow can be executed whenever the price is above the peg (plus a small tolerance) and sufficient liquidity exists to absorb a large sell order. The attack can be carried out without owning any of the token beforehand, meaning that ordinary investors who see the price rise and expect to receive the associated reward may instead witness their accrued earnings being siphoned away. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after a price spike the expected increase in their token balance or reward does not materialise, and the overall pool value appears to shrink despite a prior price increase. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit when the security team examined the PoolTransferVerification logic and identified that the stabiliser could be invoked by any transfer, including those originating from a flash‑loan arbitrage. The problem is subtle because the stabiliser is intended to protect the peg, so its execution is not immediately flagged as malicious; the profit loss only becomes apparent when investors compare expected versus actual reward allocations. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce that the stabiliser is only invoked when the recipient of a transfer is the designated liquidity pool and that the transfer originates from a legitimate holder, or otherwise embed a guard that prevents profit‑extraction paths that involve flash‑loan‑driven price manipulation. In other words, the system must restrict who may trigger price‑stabilisation and ensure that any profit generated by a price above the peg is allocated solely to token holders, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Auction collateralToken won’t work if token is fee-on-transfer token
description:
There are several ERC20 tokens that take a small fee on transfers/transferFroms (known as “fee-on-transfer” tokens). Most notably, USDT is an ERC20 token that has togglable transfer fees, but for now the fee is set to 0 (see the contract here: <https://etherscan.io/address/0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7#code>). For these tokens, it should not be assumed that if you transfer `x` tokens to an address, that the address actually receives `x` tokens. In the current test environment, DAI is the only `collateralToken` available, so there are no issues. However, it has been noted that more pools will be added in the future, so special care will need to be taken if fee-on-transfer tokens (like USDT) are planned to be used as `collateralTokens`.

For example, consider the function `purchaseArbitrageTokens` in Auction.sol. This function transfers `realCommitment` amount of `collateralToken` to the liquidityExtension, and then calls `purchaseAndBurn(realCommitment)` on the liquidityExtension. The very first line of `purchaseAndBurn(amount)` is `require(collateralToken.balanceOf(address(this)) >= amount, "Insufficient balance");`. In the case of fee-on-transfer tokens, this line will revert due to the small fee taken. This means that all calls to `purchaseArbitrageTokens` will fail, which would be very bad when the price goes below peg, since no one would be able to participate in this auction.
poc:
See `purchaseArbitrageTokens` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L177>

See `purchaseAndBurn` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/LiquidityExtension.sol#L117>
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the assumption that an ERC‑20 token transfer will deliver exactly the amount specified to the recipient. In the Auction contract, the function purchaseArbitrageTokens sends a value called realCommitment of the collateralToken to a LiquidityExtension contract and then immediately calls purchaseAndBurn(realCommitment). The first line of purchaseAndBurn checks that the contract's balance of the collateralToken is at least the amount requested using require(collateralToken.balanceOf(address(this)) >= amount). This check is safe for standard tokens that transfer the full amount, but it fails for fee‑on‑transfer tokens, such as USDT, which deduct a small fee on each transfer. When a fee‑on‑transfer token is used as collateral, the amount actually received by the LiquidityExtension is lower than realCommitment, causing the balance check to revert. As a result, every attempt to execute purchaseArbitrageTokens aborts, preventing participants from buying arbitrage tokens during a price‑below‑peg auction. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the auction flow with only DAI (a fee‑free token) in the test environment, overlooking tokens that charge transfer fees. It is difficult to notice because the contract works correctly with regular tokens and the fee is not evident from the external interface. The impact is that users cannot participate in crucial auction rounds, potentially leaving the protocol unable to restore peg and exposing funds to stagnation. The affected parties include any user trying to commit collateral, the auction mechanism itself, and ultimately the protocol’s stability. To remediate, the contract should not rely on the transferred amount matching the input but instead compute the actual tokens received—e.g., by measuring the recipient’s balance before and after the transfer—or explicitly reject fee‑on‑transfer tokens. This class of bug belongs to improper handling of fee‑on‑transfer token mechanics, a common pitfall when contracts presume a 1:1 transfer relationship. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful transaction submission but the auction never processes, balances remain unchanged, and expected refunds or token purchases never occur, creating confusion and loss of trust.

title: AuctionParticipant.sol: `purchaseArbitrageTokens` should not push duplicate auctions
description:
In AuctionParticpant.sol, every time `purchaseArbitrageTokens` is called, the current auction is pushed to `auctionIds`. If this function were to be called on the same auction multiple times, then the same auction id would be pushed multiple times into this array, and the `claim` function would have issues with `replenishingIndex`.

Specifically, even if `replenishingIndex` was incremented once in `claim`, it is still possible that the auction at the next index will never reward any more tokens to the participant, so the contract would need manual intervention to set `replenishingIndex` (due to the if statement on lines 79-82 that does nothing if there is no claimable yield).

It is likely that `purchaseArbitrageTokens` would be called multiple times on the same auction. In fact, the commented out code for `handleDeficit` (in ImpliedCollateralService.sol) even suggests that the purchases might happen within the same transaction. So this issue will likely be an issue on most auctions and would require manual setting of `replenishingIndex`.

NOTE: This is a separate issue from the one I just submitted previously relating to `replenishingIndex`. The previous issue was related to an edge case where `replenishingIndex` might need to be incremented by one if there are never going to be more claims, while this issue is due to duplicate auction ids.
poc:
See code for `purchaseArbitrageTokens` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/AuctionParticipant.sol#L40>

Notice that `currentAuction` is always appended to `auctionIds`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way AuctionParticipant.sol stores references to auctions that a participant has interacted with. Each call to the function purchaseArbitrageTokens unconditionally appends the current auction identifier to an array called auctionIds. The contract does not check whether the same auction identifier has already been recorded, so repeated invocations of purchaseArbitrageTokens on the same auction result in duplicate entries. This duplicate‑entry condition interferes with the logic of the claim function, which iterates over auctionIds using a cursor called replenishingIndex. When the array contains the same auction ID several times, the claim routine may advance the replenishingIndex once, but the next entry may refer to an auction that no longer yields any claimable yield. Because the claim code contains a guard that simply returns when no yield is available, the replenishingIndex can become stuck on a non‑rewarding duplicate entry. As a consequence, participants who have purchased arbitrage tokens may see their balance remain unchanged, the UI may display zero pending rewards, and the contract requires manual intervention to reset replenishingIndex. The issue occurs whenever purchaseArbitrageTokens is invoked more than once for a given auction, which is a realistic scenario given the surrounding comment in ImpliedCollateralService.sol that hints at multiple purchases within a single transaction. The affected parties are token holders and any user that expects to claim arbitrage tokens after making a purchase; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each auction contributes a single, distinct reward stream are violated. This flaw was discovered through a manual code audit that examined state updates around auction tracking. It is subtle because the array itself appears to function correctly and the duplicate entries do not cause immediate reverts; the problem only surfaces later when claims yield zero tokens, a symptom that can be easily missed without thorough testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce uniqueness of auction identifiers, for example by replacing the mutable array with a mapping that records whether an auction ID has already been stored, or by adding an explicit duplicate‑check before pushing to auctionIds. Ensuring each auction ID appears only once restores the intended sequential claim flow and prevents the replenishingIndex from becoming dead‑locked, thereby guaranteeing that users receive the arbitrage tokens they are entitled to.

title: Dutch auction can be manipulated
description:
When malt is under-peg and the swing trader module do not have enough capital to buy back to peg, a Dutch auction is triggered to sell arb token. The price of the Dutch auction decrease linearly toward endprice until _endAuction() is called. <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L589>

_endAuction() is called in

1. When auction.commitments >= auction.maxCommitments

2. On stabilize() -> checkAuctionFinalization() -> _checkAuctionFinalization()

3. On stabilize() ->_startAuction() -> triggerAuction() -> _checkAuctionFinalization()

It is possible manipulate the dutch auction by preventing _endAuction() being called.
poc:
Consider someone call purchaseArbitrageTokens with auction.maxCommitments minus 1 wei, `_endAuction` won’t be called because auction.commitments < auction.maxCommitments. Further purchase would revert because `purchaseAndBurn` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L184>) would likely revert since swapping 1 wei in most AMM will fail due to rounding error. Even if it does not revert, there is no incentive to waste gas to purchase 1 wei of token.

As such, the only way for the auction to finalize is to call stabilize(). However, this is not immediately possible because it require `block.timestamp >= stabilizeWindowEnd` where `stabilizeWindowEnd = block.timestamp + stabilizeBackoffPeriod` stabilizeBackoffPeriod is initially set to 5 minutes in the contract

After 5 minute, stabilize() can be called by anyone. By using this exploit, an attacker can guarantee he can purchase at (startingPrice+endingPrice)/2 or lower, given the default 10 minute auctionLength and 5 minute stabilizeBackoffPeriod. (unless a privileged user call stabilize() which override the stability window)

Also note that stabilize() might not be called since there is no incentive.
bug_full: The contract implements a Dutch‑style auction that sells a synthetic arbitrage token when the protocol’s main token falls below its target peg. The auction price is designed to fall linearly from a starting price to an end price over a fixed auction length, and the auction is supposed to close automatically once the total amount of committed purchases reaches the predefined maximum commitment (auction.maxCommitments). In practice the auction finalises only when the internal function _endAuction is invoked, which happens either when the commitment threshold is met or when a stabilisation routine reaches a specific time window. The vulnerability arises because the contract does not lock the price for each individual buyer at the moment of commitment and because the finalisation condition can be avoided by deliberately leaving one wei of commitment unfilled. An attacker can purchase arbitrage tokens up to auction.maxCommitments − 1 wei, leaving the commitment counter just below the required threshold. The remaining 1 wei purchase cannot be performed because the swap on the underlying AMM (e.g., Uniswap V2) reverts when the output amount rounds to zero, triggering an INSUFFICIENT_AMOUNT error. Consequently, the automatic trigger for _endAuction never fires. Since the auction can only be closed by calling stabilize() after a back‑off period of five minutes, the attacker can wait for the price to drift down to its lowest point and then either wait for any user to call stabilize or use a privileged call to close the auction. By doing so the attacker secures a purchase price that is roughly the average of the start and end prices, often representing a 50 % discount compared to the intended market price. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that the auction appears to be stuck, the price keeps falling, and legitimate participants receive either no tokens or an unexpectedly low amount of arbitrage tokens for the gas they spend. The protocol’s revenue model, which expects the auction to capture the discounted price and return the remaining value to the system, is violated because the discount becomes predictable and exploitable, effectively draining value from the protocol. The issue was identified during a formal audit by observing that the auction finalisation logic depends on a strict equality of commitments and that the swap function can revert on minimal amounts due to rounding. Because the failure occurs only when an attacker precisely leaves a single wei of commitment, it is subtle and may not be revealed by standard functional tests that use larger purchase quantities. The root cause is a combination of missing price‑locking per buyer, reliance on a single numeric threshold for termination, and the AMM’s behaviour on sub‑unit swaps. To remediate the problem the contract should either make _endAuction callable by anyone without restriction, incentivise callers to finalize the auction, or record the price at each buyer’s commitment so that later price movements do not affect already‑committed purchases. Additionally, the auction should enforce a minimum remaining commitment buffer or reject purchases that would leave the commitment counter within a rounding‑error margin, thereby preventing the attacker from creating the 1‑wei edge case. Implementing these changes would restore the intended economic guarantees of the Dutch auction and prevent the systematic discount manipulation observed in the proof‑of‑concept attack.

title: FeeSplitter: Unbounded number of shareholders can cause DOS
description: There is no limit to the number of shareholders. It is therefore possible to set a large number of shareholders such that `_sendFees()` will run out of gas when adding shares to each shareholder. This will cause denial of service to all NestedFactory functions, especially the ones that will remove funds like `withdraw()` and `destroy()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic list of shareholders in the FeeSplitter component. Because the contract does not enforce any upper limit on how many shareholders can be registered, an attacker can add a very large number of entries. The internal function _sendFees iterates through the entire shareholder array to allocate each share of the collected fees. When the array grows beyond what can be processed within a single transaction’s gas limit, the call to _sendFees runs out of gas and reverts. This gas exhaustion propagates to all public functions that invoke _sendFees, notably withdraw() which is used to pull accumulated fees and destroy() which is intended to clean up the contract. As a result, legitimate users who attempt to withdraw their entitlement experience a transaction that fails with an out‑of‑gas error, effectively locking their funds and rendering the contract unusable. The denial‑of‑service condition occurs whenever the shareholder count exceeds the practical gas capacity of the EVM, a situation that may not be evident during normal testing because the list can be grown gradually until the limit is reached. The issue impacts any participant who relies on fee distribution, including token holders, protocol operators, and any role with permission to invoke withdrawal or destruction. It was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the recursion depth and gas consumption of batch operations. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to function correctly with a modest number of shareholders, and only fails when the list becomes excessively large, a state that may only be reached through malicious manipulation. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “unbounded loop DoS” where a contract’s logic iterates over an unbounded data structure, allowing an attacker to force a gas limit breach. From a user’s perspective, the UI would show a request to withdraw or close the contract, but the transaction would revert silently or with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving the user with a zero balance and no explanation. The expected behavior—receiving a proportional fee share or confirming contract termination—is violated, resulting in funds that appear to disappear or become inaccessible. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a sensible maximum number of shareholders, either by capping the array size at the time of addition or by redesigning the fee distribution mechanism to use a pull‑based model, mappings, or incremental processing that does not require iterating over the entire list in a single transaction. By limiting the number of entries or changing the accounting approach, the contract can avoid the gas‑limit bottleneck and restore reliable fee distribution and contract lifecycle operations.

title: isResolverCached
description:
While there is no loss of funds, removing an operator will cause the cache functionality to be permanently broken. If there was a function that had a modifier which requires the cache to be synced before the function can be called, it would not be callable as well.

The underlying issue is how the `bytes32` operator is removed from the array when `removeOperator()` is called. Its value gets deleted (set to 0x0), but isn’t taken out of the array.
poc:
For ease of reading, we use abbreviated strings like `0xA`, `0xB` for `bytes32` and `address` types.

1. Import 3 operators by calling `OperatorResolver.importOperators([0xA, 0xB, 0xC], [0x1, 0x2, 0x3)`.
2. Call `NestedFactory.addOperator()` 3 times to push these 3 operators into the `operators` state variable.
3. Call `NestedFactory.rebuildCache()` to build the cache.
4. Let’s say the second operator `0xB` is to be removed. Taking reference from the `removeOperator.ts` script, `OperatorResolver.importOperators([0xA, 0xB, 0xC], [0x1, 0x2, 0x3)` is called first. This works because OperatorResolver uses a mapping(bytes32 ⇒ address) to represent the operators. Hence, by setting `0xB`’s destination address to be the null address, it is like as if he was never an operator.
5. Call `NestedFactory.rebuildCache()` to rebuild the cache. `resolverAddressesRequired()` will return `[0xA, 0xB, 0xC]`. `0xB` will be removed from `addressCache` because `resolver.getAddress(0xB)` returns 0x000 since it has been deleted from the OperatorResolver.
6. Call `NestedFactory.removeOperator(0xB)`. The `operators` array now looks like this: `[0xA, 0x0, 0xC]`.
7. When you try to call `NestedFactory.isResolverCached`, it will always return false because of the null `bytes32` value, where `addressCache[0x0]` will always return the null address.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a stale cache condition caused by an incorrect removal operation in a contract that manages a list of operator identifiers (bytes32). When an operator is removed via the removeOperator function, the implementation deletes the element by setting its slot to the zero value (0x0) but does not shift the remaining elements or shrink the array. Consequently, the operators array retains a placeholder entry with a zero identifier. The contract later builds a resolver cache based on the contents of this array; during cache reconstruction, the zero identifier is included, producing an entry in the addressCache mapping that always resolves to the null address. Any downstream function that checks the cache – for example, a modifier that requires the resolver to be cached before execution – will encounter a missing address and consequently reject the call. The flaw originates from the array‑deletion pattern that neglects to maintain a dense array, a common pitfall when using dynamic arrays in Solidity. Exploitation follows a straightforward sequence: an attacker (or any user with permission to remove an operator) removes an operator, causing the array to contain a zero entry; the cache is then rebuilt, embedding the zero entry; subsequent calls to functions protected by a “cache‑synced” modifier always fail because the cache lookup for the zero identifier returns the null address. The impact is functional – legitimate users cannot invoke actions that depend on a synchronized resolver cache, effectively freezing parts of the protocol that rely on operator management. No direct loss of Ether or tokens occurs, but the protocol’s expected behavior is broken, leading to a denial‑of‑service‑like condition for any role that depends on the affected functions. The issue surfaces whenever an operator is removed and the cache is later rebuilt, which can happen at any time during the contract’s lifecycle. All participants that interact with the affected functions – contract owners, operators, and end‑users relying on those functions – are affected because the contract silently reports a cache miss and returns false, causing transactions to revert or be ignored. The problem was discovered during a systematic security audit that inspected array manipulation logic and cache‑building routines; the auditor observed that the array entry remained at zero after deletion and traced the resulting false cache state. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract does not throw an explicit error when the zero entry is created; it merely leads to unexpected “cache not synced” responses that appear as logical failures rather than outright crashes. To remediate the issue, the removal routine should preserve array density by swapping the element to be removed with the last element and then popping the last slot, thereby eliminating the zero placeholder. This approach restores the integrity of the operators list and ensures that subsequent cache rebuilds contain only valid identifiers, allowing cache‑dependent functions to operate as intended. In broader terms, the flaw falls under the class of "array element deletion without compaction" bugs, which can corrupt auxiliary data structures that rely on the array’s contents, leading to logical inconsistencies such as missing refunds, failed authorization checks, or, as in this case, a broken resolver cache.

title: `NestedFactory.sol#_submitInOrders`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the order‑execution routine of the NestedFactory contract. When a user supplies a certain amount of an input token ( _inputTokenAmount ) to be spent across a batch of orders, the contract calculates the total amount actually spent ( amountSpent ) and the protocol fee ( feesAmount ). The business rule for the system is that any portion of the input token that is not consumed by the orders should be returned to the caller. However, the implementation incorrectly treats the leftover tokens as part of the fee. After the loop that aggregates amountSpent, the contract computes feesAmount and asserts that amountSpent does not exceed the input amount minus the fee, which prevents overspending. It then calls _handleUnderSpending with the arguments (_inputTokenAmount - feesAmount, amountSpent, _inputToken). Because the first argument already subtracts the fee, the function receives a value that includes the unspent tokens together with the fee, and the internal logic of _handleUnderSpending does not separate the two. Consequently the unspent tokens are retained by the contract and counted toward the fee, so the user receives less than the expected refund. This flaw can be exploited simply by submitting orders that deliberately spend less than the supplied amount; the attacker does not need any special privileges, only to craft an order list with a low total cost. The impact is a direct loss of user funds: the user’s balance is reduced by the amount that should have been returned, and the protocol may appear to charge higher fees than advertised. The condition occurs whenever the order batch results in under‑spending, which is a common scenario when market prices move unfavorably or when the caller over‑estimates the required input. All users of the factory, including those who rely on reserve‑based funding, are affected because the bug is in the shared private function _submitInOrders. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors examined the fee‑handling logic and noticed that the assertion only checks overspending, leaving the under‑spending path unchecked. It is subtle because the contract does not explicitly emit an event or revert when funds are retained; the loss is silent and may only be observed as a missing balance after execution. The proper fix is to redesign the under‑spending handler so that it first computes the true leftover amount as (_inputTokenAmount - amountSpent - feesAmount) and then transfers that exact remainder back to the caller, while ensuring that feesAmount is calculated solely from the amount actually spent. In generic terms, this is a miscalculated refund bug, falling under the class of accounting or asset‑return errors where the contract’s bookkeeping does not faithfully return unspent assets to the originator. From a user perspective, the UI would show that a trade was executed, but the user’s wallet would reflect a lower token balance than expected, or a refund transaction would appear missing, leading to confusion such as "I expected to get X tokens back but got zero". The flaw violates the protocol’s economic model, which assumes that all supplied capital is either spent on the intended orders or returned to the user after fee deduction.

title: Ensure on-chain that cache is synced
description: Currently, many core operations (like `NestedFactory.create()`, `NestedFactory.swapTokenForTokens()`) are dependent on the assumption that the cache is synced before these functions are executed however this may not necessarily be the case.
poc:
1. `OperatorResolver.importOperators()` is called to remove an operator.
2. A user calls `NestedFactory.create()` that uses the operator that was being removed / updated.
3. `NestedFactory.rebuildCache()` is called to rebuild cache.

This flow is not aware that the cache is not in synced.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an implicit reliance on a synchronization mechanism, called the cache, within a suite of core contract operations such as creating a new nested contract instance or swapping tokens through the NestedFactory contract. The contract assumes that before any of these functions execute, the internal cache of operator data is up‑to‑date, but there is no explicit enforcement of this condition. Consequently, when the operator registry is altered – for example by calling OperatorResolver.importOperators() to remove or update an operator – a user can invoke NestedFactory.create() or NestedFactory.swapTokenForTokens() before the cache has been rebuilt with the new operator set. The cache rebuild is performed by NestedFactory.rebuildCache(), which may be scheduled or triggered later, leaving a window where the contract logic consults stale operator information. An attacker or an unfortunate user can therefore interact with a contract that still references a removed or outdated operator, leading to unexpected execution paths, failed swaps, or creation of contracts that rely on invalid operators. From the user perspective, this may appear as a transaction that completes but results in no token transfer, a zero‑amount receipt, or an outright revert without a clear reason, because the underlying operator validation fails silently. The impact is medium severity because funds may become temporarily locked or lost if the stale operator directs assets to an address that is no longer authorized, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that each operation uses a current, vetted operator – are violated. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that reviewed function pre‑conditions and noted the absence of a cache‑synced guard. It is difficult to notice in routine testing because the cache eventually synchronizes and the bug only manifests under the specific timing sequence of operator removal followed by immediate user interaction. To mitigate the risk, each external‑facing function that depends on operator data should be protected by a modifier that checks the cache state and forces a cache rebuild or rejects the call when the cache is out of sync. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of "state‑inconsistency" or "cache‑stale" vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal view of external data can diverge from the source of truth, breaking business logic and potentially causing funds to disappear or operations to behave incorrectly.

title: Passing multiple ETH deposits in orders array will use the same `msg.value` many times
description: Contract holdings can be emptied as malicious user will do deposit/withdraw to extract value. This is possible because after `transferInputTokens` system uses contract balance for user’s operations, assuming that equivalent value was transferred.
poc:
`msg.value` persist over calls, so passing `'Order[] calldata _orders'` holding multiple ETH deposits will use the same msg.value in each of them, resulting in multiple deposits, that sums up to much bigger accounted value than actually deposited value, up to contract’s ETH holdings.

create / `addTokens` -> `submitInOrders` -> `transferInputTokens`

* [`NestedFactory.sol` L103](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested/blob/main/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L103)
* [`NestedFactory.sol` L119](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested/blob/main/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L119)

`sellTokensToWallet` -> `submitOutOrders` -> `transferInputTokens`

* [`NestedFactory.sol` L172](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested/blob/main/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L172)

`sellTokensToNft` -> `submitOutOrders` -> `transferInputTokens`

* [`NestedFactory.sol` L152](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested/blob/main/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L152) `transferInputTokens` uses msg.value:

[`NestedFactory.sol` L462](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested/blob/main/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L462)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the NestedFactory contract processes ETH deposits when multiple orders are supplied in a single transaction. The contract inherits from a Multicall library that permits batching of internal calls, and the function transferInputTokens reads the global msg.value to determine how much ether should be transferred for each order. Because msg.value is a transaction‑level property, it remains unchanged across all sub‑calls made through multicall. Consequently, if an attacker includes several orders that each request an ETH deposit, the same msg.value is applied to each order as if the full amount had been sent repeatedly. The contract’s accounting logic assumes that the ether transferred with the transaction will be consumed once per order, but it never deducts the used amount nor validates that each order receives a distinct portion of the funds. This mismatch allows the attacker to claim a larger total deposit than actually provided, leading to an inflated internal balance. By later invoking withdraw or settlement functions, the attacker can extract ether up to the contract’s total ETH holdings, effectively emptying the contract if it holds any funds. The issue manifests only when the contract holds ether and when a batched call contains more than one order that involves ETH, a condition that may be overlooked in normal testing because single‑order scenarios work correctly and the contract’s balance appears consistent. The problem was discovered during a code audit that traced the flow from create/addTokens through submitInOrders and submitOutOrders to transferInputTokens, revealing that msg.value persists across calls. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings and the accounting discrepancy only appears under specific multi‑order usage patterns. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that includes multiple ETH deposits may result in the user receiving no refund, seeing their balance unchanged, or observing that the contract’s ether balance has decreased unexpectedly after a withdrawal. The bug violates the fundamental business assumption that each deposit corresponds to a distinct amount of ether, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To remediate the issue, the contract should be re‑designed to treat ETH operations as non‑batchable, enforce that only a single ETH‑related order can be processed per transaction, or explicitly track and deduct the used portion of msg.value for each order. Alternatively, removing the Multicall inheritance eliminates the possibility of reusing msg.value across calls, thereby restoring correct accounting and preventing the over‑withdrawal scenario.

title: Slippage checks when adding liquidity are too strict
description:
When adding liquidity through `UniswapHandler.addLiquidity`, the entire contract balances are used to add liquidity and the min amounts are set to 95% of these balances. If the balances in this contract are unbalanced (the ratio is not similar to the current Uniswap pool reserve ratios) then this function will revert and no liquidity is added.

See `UniswapHandler.buyMalt`:

```solidity
(maltUsed, rewardUsed, liquidityCreated) = router.addLiquidity(
  address(malt),
  address(rewardToken),
  maltBalance, // @audit-info amountADesired
  rewardBalance,
  // @audit assumes that whatever is in this contract is already balanced. good assumption?
  maltBalance.mul(95).div(100), // @audit-info amountAMin
  rewardBalance.mul(95).div(100),
  msg.sender, // transfer LP tokens to sender
  now
);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the UniswapHandler contract adds liquidity to a Uniswap pool. When a user calls the addLiquidity function, the contract supplies the entire token balances it holds as the desired amounts and sets the minimum acceptable amounts to 95 % of those balances. This logic implicitly assumes that the contract's token holdings are already proportional to the pool's current reserve ratio. If an attacker or any external party transfers an uneven amount of one of the tokens to the contract, the internal balances become misaligned with the pool reserves. Because the slippage check is hard‑coded to a strict 95 % threshold, the router call reverts as soon as the actual amounts that would be deposited deviate from the expected ratio, preventing any liquidity from being added. The exploit is a simple griefing attack: by deliberately unbalancing the contract’s token balances, an adversary can cause legitimate users’ add‑liquidity transactions to fail, resulting in a lost gas fee and a denial‑of‑service for the protocol’s liquidity provisioning feature. From the user’s perspective the transaction reverts with no LP tokens received, often appearing as if the funds have “disappeared” or the refund calculation is wrong, while the underlying token balances remain locked in the contract. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the code was examined for assumptions about token ratios and the hard‑coded slippage tolerance was flagged as overly strict. It is difficult to notice because normal operation with balanced deposits succeeds, so tests that only cover the happy path do not trigger the failure. To remediate the problem the contract should no longer rely on its entire balance as the desired input, should calculate the desired token amounts based on the current pool reserves, and should accept explicit amounts and slippage parameters from the caller. The slippage tolerance should be configurable and derived from off‑chain price data rather than a fixed 95 % value, and the contract should protect its balances from external manipulation or rebalance them before attempting to add liquidity. Implementing these changes restores the intended business logic that liquidity can be added as long as the user provides adequate amounts, eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector and aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations of successful LP token minting.

title: Bonding.sol _unbondAndBreak does not account for edge case where no tokens are returned
poc:
See `_unbondAndBreak` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L226>

Notice how the edge case where `amountMalt == 0 || amountReward == 0` is not considered in this function, but it is considered in the Uniswap handler’s `removeLiquidity` here: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/c3a204a2c0f7c653c6c2dda9f4563fd1dc1cecf3/src/contracts/DexHandlers/UniswapHandler.sol#L240>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function _unbondAndBreak of the Bonding.sol contract. This function is responsible for transferring a user's staked tokens to a dexHandler and then invoking removeLiquidity on that handler to retrieve the underlying assets. The Uniswap handler, which implements removeLiquidity, contains explicit logic to handle the edge case where the router returns zero tokens for either the malt or reward asset. In that situation, the handler returns the LP tokens back to the caller (Bonding.sol). However, Bonding.sol does not contain any corresponding check to detect that the returned amounts are zero. Consequently, when the router fails to deliver any malt or reward—due to insufficient liquidity, price impact, or a paused pool—the LP tokens are sent back to Bonding.sol and become permanently locked because the contract has no subsequent path to forward them to the original user or to revert the transaction. This flaw originates from an implicit assumption that removeLiquidity always yields a non‑zero amount, a premise that is violated in real‑world market conditions. An attacker or a benign user can trigger the failure by causing the router call to return zero tokens, for instance by withdrawing a large amount of liquidity when the pool cannot fulfill the request. The exploit manifests as a successful unbond transaction that appears to complete, yet the user receives no malt or reward and the LP tokens remain trapped inside the Bonding contract. From the user's perspective, the UI may display a zero refund or a missing balance update, leading to confusion or panic as funds seemingly disappear. The affected parties include any holder who attempts to unbond their LP tokens through the Bonding contract, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage and loss of capital. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that compared the edge‑case handling of the Uniswap handler with the corresponding logic in Bonding.sol, revealing the missing safeguard. The defect is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply transfers assets to an address that has no mechanism for recovery, making the problem hard to detect without detailed code review. To remediate, the _unbondAndBreak function should incorporate logic mirroring the handler’s zero‑output check, either by forwarding the LP tokens back to the user or by reverting the call when no malt or reward is obtained. This adjustment restores the expected accounting invariant that unbonding either returns the correct assets or fails without leaving value stranded, aligning the contract’s behavior with its financial intent.

title: User can bypass Recovery Mode via UniswapHandler to buy Malt
description: One of the innovative feature of Malt is to block buying while under peg. The buy block can be bypassed by swapping to the whitelisted UniswapHandler, and then extract the token by abusing the add and remove liquidity function. This is considered a high severity issue because it undermine to protocol’s ability to generate profit by the privileged role as designed and allow potential risk-free MEV.
poc:
1. User swap dai into malt and send malt directly to uniswapHandler, this is possible becuase uniswapHandler is whitelisted

`swapExactTokensForTokens(amountDai, 0, [dai.address, malt.address], uniswapHandler.address, new Date().getTime() + 10000);` 2) User send matching amount of dai to uniswapHandler 3) User call addLiquidity() and get back LP token 4) User call removeLiquidity() and get back both dai and malt
bug_full: The vulnerability allows an attacker to circumvent the protocol’s recovery‑mode restriction that is intended to block purchases of the Malt token when its price is below the peg. The root cause is that the public functions addLiquidity() and removeLiquidity() are callable by any address even while the system is in recovery mode, and the contract that mediates these operations – the UniswapHandler – is explicitly whitelisted to operate during recovery. Because the buy‑block logic is only enforced on direct purchase functions, an adversary can acquire Malt at a discount by performing a swap, sending the resulting Malt tokens to the whitelisted UniswapHandler, then adding liquidity with an imbalanced pair of DAI and Malt and subsequently removing that liquidity. The removal returns the attacker’s original DAI together with the discounted Malt tokens, effectively providing a risk‑free MEV opportunity. This exploit is triggered only when the protocol is in recovery mode, the UniswapHandler remains whitelisted, and the addLiquidity function is not disabled. It affects the protocol’s economic model, the privileged role that relies on the buy‑block to protect revenue, and any user who expects that buying Malt is prohibited under the peg condition. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between recovery‑mode controls and the liquidity‑management contracts; it can be easy to miss because the liquidity functions appear benign and the whitelist mechanism is intended for legitimate recovery operations. The flaw violates the business assumption that recovery mode fully prevents discounted purchases, allowing funds to be extracted without selling Malt. To remediate, the protocol should prevent liquidity addition (and optionally removal) while in recovery mode, or embed the same price‑guard checks within the liquidity functions and restrict the UniswapHandler’s privileges during a blocked‑buy state. In practice, a user could notice that they are able to acquire Malt even though the UI indicates that purchases are disabled, receiving tokens and DAI back after a single transaction flow that should have been rejected by the protocol’s rules.

title: Malt Protocol Uses Stale Results From `MaltDataLab` Which Can Be Abused By Users
description: `MaltDataLab` integrates several `MovingAverage` contracts to fetch sensitive data for the Malt protocol. Primary data used by the protocol consists of the real value for LP tokens, the average price for Malt and average reserve ratios. `trackMaltPrice`, `trackPoolReserves` and `trackPool` are called by a restricted role denoted as the `UPDATER_ROLE` and represented by an EOA account and not another contract. Hence, the EOA account must consistently update the aforementioned functions to ensure the most up-to-date values. However, miners can censor calls to `MaltDataLab` and effectively extract value from other areas of the protocol which use stale values.
poc:
Consider the following attack vector:

* The price of Malt exceeds the lower bound threshold and hence `stabilize` can be called by any user.
* The `_stabilityWindowOverride` function is satisfied, hence the function will execute.
* The state variable, `exchangeRate`, queries `maltPriceAverage` which may use an outdated exchange rate.
* `_startAuction` is executed which rewards `msg.sender` with 100 Malt as an incentive for triggering an auction.
* As the price is not subsequently updated, a malicious attacker could collude with a miner to censor further pool updates and continue calling `stabilize` on every `fastAveragePeriod` interval to extract incentive payments.
* If the payments exceed what the `UPDATER_ROLE` is willing to pay to call `trackMaltPrice`, a user is able to sustain this attack.

This threatens the overall stability of the protocol and should be properly handled to prevent such attacks. However, the fact that `MaltDataLab` uses a series of spot price data points to calculate the `MovingAverage` also creates an area of concern as well-funded actors could still manipulate the `MovingAverage` contract by sandwiching calls to `trackMaltPrice`, `trackPool` and `trackPoolReserves`.

`trackMaltPrice`, `trackPool`, and `trackPoolReserves` should be added to the following areas of the code where applicable.

* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L159>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L173>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Bonding.sol#L177>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L881>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/Auction.sol#L710>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/StabilizerNode.sol#L156>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/StabilizerNode.sol#L190>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-malt/blob/main/src/contracts/ImpliedCollateralService.sol#L105>
bug_full:
