When the `initialize()` method is called on the newly cloned `Basket` contract, a method called `approveUnderlying(address(auction))` is called, which would trigger the reentrancy, call `initialize()` again, passing in altered critical values such as `auction` and `factory`, and then removes its self from `proposal.tokens` and `proposal.weights` so it doesn’t appear in the token list to basket users.

[Basket.sol#L44-L61](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/main/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L44-L61)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Basket contract’s initialize function, which is invoked when a newly cloned basket is set up. During initialization the contract calls approveUnderlying(address(auction)), which forwards an approve call to each ERC20 token listed in the proposal. If an attacker supplies a malicious ERC20 token whose approve implementation contains a reentrancy callback, the external call can re‑enter the initialize function before the original call finishes. Because the contract does not use the initializer modifier from ERC20Upgradeable, there is no reentrancy guard protecting the execution. An attacker can therefore invoke initialize a second time with crafted arguments, overwriting critical storage variables such as the auction address and the factory address. After the re‑entered call completes, the malicious token removes itself from proposal.tokens and proposal.weights, making it invisible to users while the basket’s internal accounting now points to attacker‑controlled contracts. This flaw occurs whenever a basket is initialized with a proposal that contains at least one token whose approve function can trigger external code, i.e., any ERC20 token that is not trusted. The affected parties are creators of baskets, users who rely on the basket’s listed tokens, and any downstream contracts that trust the basket’s auction or factory addresses. From a user’s perspective the basket may appear to contain the expected assets, but interactions that depend on the auction or factory (such as trading, withdrawals, or fee collection) could be redirected to attacker‑controlled contracts, potentially leading to loss of funds or unexpected behavior. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the logical flow of approveUnderlying revealed the missing reentrancy protection. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the reentrancy occurs only during initialization and the malicious token can hide itself after the attack, leaving no obvious trace in the token list. The recommended fix is to apply the initializer modifier (or an equivalent reentrancy guard) to the initialize function, which sets an internal initializing flag preventing the function from being entered recursively. By ensuring that initialize can only be executed once per deployment, the attacker cannot overwrite the auction or factory addresses, and the token list will remain consistent, preserving the integrity of the basket’s accounting and preventing hidden malicious tokens from being introduced.

title: Change in `auctionMultiplier/auctionDecrement` change profitability of auctions and factory can steal all tokens from a basket abusing it
description: When factory changes `auctionMultiplier` or `auctionDecrement` profitability of bonded auctions change. There is no protection against this behaviour. Furthermore, factory owners can decide to get all tokens from baskets where they are bonded for the auction.
poc:
1- Factory owners call `bondForRebalance` for an auction.

2- Factory owners sets `auctionMultiplier` as 0 and `auctionDecrement` as maximum value

3- `settleAuction` is called. `newRatio = 0`, since `a = b = 0`. All tokens can be withdrawn with this call, since `tokensNeeded = 0`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ability of the factory contract to modify the parameters that govern auction profitability, specifically the auctionMultiplier and auctionDecrement values, without any access control or governance protection. Because these parameters are used directly in the calculation of the new price ratio during the settlement of bonded auctions, an attacker who controls the factory can set auctionMultiplier to zero and auctionDecrement to its maximum allowed value. When the auction is settled under these manipulated settings, the internal formula produces a newRatio equal to zero, which in turn causes the contract’s token‑required check (tokensNeeded) to evaluate to zero. As a result, the settlement function permits the withdrawal of the entire token balance from the basket, effectively allowing the factory owner to drain all assets that were bonded for the auction. This exploit can be triggered whenever a factory owner initiates a rebalance through the bondForRebalance function, adjusts the multiplier and decrement to the malicious values, and then calls settleAuction. From the user’s perspective, after an auction appears to have concluded normally, their balance may abruptly drop to zero, or they may receive no tokens despite expecting a refund or payout, creating a symptom of “funds disappear” or “refund missing”. The issue occurs only when the factory contract is controlled by a malicious party; however, the lack of protection means the protocol’s economic assumptions about auction profitability and token accounting can be subverted. The flaw was uncovered during a formal security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept sequence demonstrating the parameter manipulation and the resulting zero‑ratio settlement. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the auction logic itself functions as intended under normal parameters, and the zero‑ratio condition may only appear briefly during settlement, making it easy to miss in routine monitoring. The core problem belongs to the class of “parameter tampering leading to accounting bypass” vulnerabilities, where mutable governance variables are used in critical financial calculations without safeguards. To remediate, the contract should store the auctionMultiplier and auctionDecrement as immutable or globally protected variables that cannot be altered by the factory after deployment, and a timelocked governance mechanism should guard any changes to these values. Additionally, the settlement routine should enforce a non‑zero ratio and verify that tokensNeeded reflects the actual required collateral, preventing arbitrary withdrawals. Implementing these controls would re‑align the protocol with its intended business logic, ensuring that users receive the correct payouts and that no party can unilaterally invalidate the auction’s accounting model.

title: Basket can be fully drained if the auction is settled within a specific block
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the auction settlement routine of the basket contract, where the amount of each pending token that must remain in the basket after an auction is calculated by multiplying the total supply, a pending weight, and a variable called `newRatio`. The `newRatio` is derived from the auction multiplier, the basket’s internal‑balance ratio, the elapsed blocks since the auction started, and an auction decrement constant. Because the contract allows a caller to specify the block number (`bondBlock`) at which the `bondForRebalance()` function is executed, an attacker can deliberately wait until `bondBlock` equals `auctionStart + 20000` (approximately three and a half days for the default parameters). At that exact block the expression `a - b` that defines `newRatio` evaluates to zero. When `newRatio` is zero, the product that forms `tokensNeeded` becomes zero, and the subsequent `require` statement only checks that the basket balance is greater than or equal to zero – a condition that is always true. Consequently, the `settleAuction()` function does not enforce any token retention requirement and permits the caller to specify arbitrary output tokens and weights, effectively draining the entire basket of its assets. The impact is that all assets held in the basket disappear, users who expected their holdings to be preserved after the auction find their balances empty, and the protocol loses the economic value it was meant to protect. This scenario can only be triggered when the auction’s settlement window remains open long enough for an attacker to wait the required number of blocks and when the contract does not enforce a strictly positive `newRatio` or a minimum internal‑balance ratio (`minIbRatio`). The issue was uncovered during a security audit by examining the loop that validates the basket’s token balances and realizing that the formula could produce a zero requirement. The bug is subtle because the check appears to guarantee sufficient basket funds, yet it never validates that the required amount is non‑zero, making the flaw easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce that `newRatio` never becomes zero (e.g., by requiring `newRatio > 0` or by guaranteeing `minIbRatio` is positive), add an explicit check that `tokensNeeded` is greater than zero before proceeding, and possibly tighten the time constraints on when `bondForRebalance()` and `settleAuction()` may be called. This class of vulnerability falls under arithmetic edge‑case bypasses where a zero‑valued multiplier disables a critical accounting check, leading to a complete drain of funds and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: `Auction.sol#settleAuction`
poc:
Given:

  * `bondPercentDiv` = 400
  * `basketToken.totalSupply` = 40,000
  * `factory.auctionMultiplier` = 2
  * `factory.auctionDecrement` = 10,000
  * `basket.ibRatio` = 1e18
  * `pendingWeights.minIbRatio` = 1.9 * 1e18
  * Alice called `bondForRebalance()` `2,000` blocks after the auction started, paid `100` basketToken for the bond;
  * Alice tries to `settleAuction()`, it will always fail because `newRatio < minIbRatio`;
  * a = 2 * 1e18
  * b = 0.2 * 1e18
  * newRatio = 1.8 * 1e18;
  * Bob calls `bondBurn()` one day after, `100` basketToken from Alice will been burned.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect placement of the safety check that guarantees the new interest‑bearing ratio (newRatio) stays above the minimum acceptable ratio (minIbRatio) during an auction rebalance. In the current design the contract computes newRatio inside the settleAuction() function and immediately requires newRatio >= minIbRatio. If, at the moment of settlement, newRatio has fallen below minIbRatio, the require statement reverts and settleAuction() cannot complete. Because there is no alternative path for the bonder to cancel the bond or retrieve the deposited basket tokens, the bond amount becomes permanently locked. The root cause is a post‑condition validation that is executed only after the bond has been taken, rather than a pre‑condition check performed when the bond is created. An attacker, or even an honest participant, can trigger the failure by allowing the auction decrement to reduce newRatio below the threshold – for example by waiting many blocks after the auction start or by manipulating the minIbRatio value through an authorized timelock update. Once the condition is violated, any attempt to settle the auction will revert, leaving the bonder’s tokens stuck in the contract. Subsequently, when the protocol executes bondBurn(), the locked tokens are burned, effectively destroying the user’s funds. The impact is that honest users who bonded tokens expecting to receive a refund or a proportional share of the rebalanced basket end up with no refund and may lose the full value of their bond. The issue manifests only after the bonding transaction has succeeded and the auction has progressed enough for the ratio to drop; it is invisible during the bonding step because no validation is performed there. Users are affected because the UI will show a successful bond transaction, but later the settlement transaction fails with a generic "require" error, and the user sees no balance change or refund – the token balance remains unchanged while the protocol’s accounting assumes the bond was settled. The problem was uncovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the misplaced require statement and the lack of a cancel or refund mechanism. It is difficult to detect in normal testing because the failure occurs only under specific timing conditions (e.g., many blocks after auction start) and the revert message does not explain the underlying economic reason. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑condition validation leading to locked funds” and “missing abort path for financial operations”. To remediate, the ratio check should be moved to the bonding function (bondForRebalance) so that a bond is rejected if newRatio is already below minIbRatio, or a separate cancel function should be introduced that allows the bonder to retrieve their tokens when the condition cannot be satisfied. In either case, the protocol must guarantee that a user either successfully settles the auction or can safely unwind the bond, preserving the expected invariant that deposited funds are either returned or correctly accounted for.

title: Lost fees due to precision loss in fees calculation
description: In fees calculation, division is being used in the midst of the calculation, not at the end of it. This leads to lost precision in fee amount (as solidity doesn’t save remainder of division). Division should happen at the end to maintain precision.
poc:
Division in the midst of a calculation:
```solidity
uint256 feePct = timeDiff * licenseFee / ONE_YEAR;
uint256 fee = startSupply * feePct / (BASE - feePct);
```
[Basket.sol#L140:#L145](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/main/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L140:#L145)  
It’s a little hard to share a POC script as it involves changing the .sol file so I tested it manually. But after moving the division to the end using the mitigation below, I saw 1%-7% increases in fees minted. Usually 1%.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a loss of precision in the protocol’s fee‑calculation routine caused by performing an integer division before all multiplicative terms have been applied. In Solidity, division discards any remainder, so when the code computes an intermediate fee percentage with `timeDiff * licenseFee / ONE_YEAR` and then uses that intermediate value in a subsequent multiplication and division, the remainder from the first division is permanently lost. This truncated intermediate value propagates through the rest of the formula, leading to a systematically smaller fee amount than the economic model intends. The issue can be exploited simply by invoking any function that triggers the fee calculation – typically minting or rebalancing operations – because the protocol will mint fewer fee tokens than it is owed, effectively leaking value from the system. The impact is a reduction of protocol revenue ranging from about one to seven percent per operation, as observed during manual testing, which accumulates over many transactions and erodes the treasury. The condition under which it occurs is any execution path that calls the fee‑calculation code while `timeDiff`, `licenseFee`, `startSupply`, and the constant `ONE_YEAR` are non‑zero, which is the normal operational state of the contract. All participants that rely on the fee – the protocol itself, token holders, and any downstream contracts that depend on the fee revenue – are affected because the expected accounting balance is lower than it should be. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where auditors rewrote the calculation to move the division to the end of the expression and observed an increase in the minted fee amount, confirming the precision loss. The problem is hard to notice because the user‑facing UI typically displays the fee as a rounded number, making the small discrepancy appear as normal rounding variance rather than a systematic under‑payment. To remediate the issue, the calculation should be reordered so that all multiplication is performed first and division is applied only once at the final step, for example `uint256 fee = startSupply * licenseFee * timeDiff / ONE_YEAR / (BASE - licenseFee);`. This eliminates intermediate truncation, preserves full precision, and aligns the on‑chain accounting with the protocol’s economic design, ensuring that fees minted match the intended amount and that no inadvertent value is lost.

title: `Basket:handleFees` fee calculation is wrong
description: The fee calculation on L141 is wrong. It should only get divided by BASE and not (BASE - feePct)
poc:
This shows dividing only by BASE is correct:  
Assumptions:

  * BASE is 1e18 accordign to the code
  * timeDiff is exactly ONE_YEAR (for easier calculations)
  * startSupply is 1e18 (exactly one basket token, also represents 100% in fee terms)
  * licenseFee is 1e15 (0.1%)

If we calculate the fee of one whole year and startSupply is one token (1e18, equal to 100%), the fee should be exactly the licenseFee (1e15, 0.1%),

```solidity
uint256 timeDiff = ONE_YEAR;
uint256 feePct = timeDiff * licenseFee / ONE_YEAR;
```
=> therefore we have: feePct = licenseFee which is 1e15 (0.1%) according to our assumptions  
```solidity
uint256 fee = startSupply * feePct / BASE; // only divide by BASE
```
=> insert values => fee = 1e18 * licenseFee / 1e18 = licenseFee

This shows the math is wrong:

Assumptions:

  * BASE is 1e18 according to the code
  * timeDiff is exactly ONE_YEAR (for easier calculations)
  * startSupply is 1e18 (exactly one basket token, also represents 100% in fee terms)
  * licenseFee is 1e15 (0.1%)

If we calculate the fee of one whole year and startSupply is one token (1e18, equal to 100%), the fee should be exactly the licenseFee (1e15, 0.1%), but the fee is bigger than that.

```solidity
uint256 timeDiff = ONE_YEAR;
uint256 feePct = timeDiff * licenseFee / ONE_YEAR;
```
=> therefore we have: feePct = licenseFee which is 1e15 (0.1%) according to our assumptions

```solidity
uint256 fee = startSupply * feePct / (BASE - feePct);
```
insert the values => fee = 1e18 * 1e15 / (1e18 - 1e15) => (factor out 1e15) => fee = 1e15 * 1e18 / (1e15 * (1e3 - 1)) => (cancel 1e15) => 1e18 / (1e3 - 1)

math: if we increase the divisor but the dividend stays the same we get a smaller number e.g. (1 / (2-1)) is bigger than (1 / 2)  
apply this here => 1e18 / (1e3 - 1) > 1e18 / 1e3 => 1e18 / (1e3 - 1) > 1e15 this shows that the fee is higher than 1e15

[Basket.sol#L133](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/205d3766044171e325df6a8bf2e79b37856eece1/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L133)  
[Basket.sol#L141](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/205d3766044171e325df6a8bf2e79b37856eece1/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L141)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee calculation performed by the Basket contract when handling fees. Instead of dividing the product of the token supply and the fee percentage by the constant BASE (which represents the scaling factor 1e18), the implementation erroneously divides by the expression (BASE - feePct). Because feePct is a small positive number, subtracting it from BASE yields a denominator that is slightly smaller than BASE, which mathematically results in a larger fee than intended. The root cause is a misuse of the denominator in the fee formula, leading to an over‑estimation of the amount to be charged. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the code; any user who interacts with the contract during fee handling will automatically be charged the inflated fee. The impact is that users pay more than the advertised license fee, causing their balances to decrease faster than expected, potentially eroding trust in the protocol and reducing adoption. This condition occurs whenever the handleFees function is called with a non‑zero fee percentage – essentially every time fees are calculated for a given time interval. The affected parties include token holders, liquidity providers, and any participant relying on the basket token’s accounting, as they receive less value for the same amount of underlying assets. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit when the auditors compared the on‑chain arithmetic against the theoretical fee model and observed a discrepancy in the divisor. The bug is subtle because the denominator expression looks plausible and the difference is only noticeable under careful numerical analysis, making it easy to overlook during casual testing. To remediate the problem the fee calculation should be simplified to divide only by BASE, aligning the on‑chain math with the intended economic model and preventing fee over‑charging. This class of bug is a miscalculated financial formula, where an incorrect denominator leads to a systematic over‑collection of fees, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and violating user expectations that the fee should equal the license fee proportion of the supplied tokens. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a fee period their basket token balance is reduced by more than the expected 0.1% (or whatever fee rate is configured), often presenting as an unexpected zero or a missing portion of their holdings, contrary to the expectation that only the precise license fee would be deducted.

title: Fee calculation is slightly off
poc:
[Basket.sol#L133](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/205d3766044171e325df6a8bf2e79b37856eece1/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L133)

While this is technically true, the actual precision loss should be very negligible.

I think any precision loss or value leakage qualifies for a `medium` severity issue. This seems like it would lead to an inconsistent fee calculation and is probably worthwhile fixing long-term.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the contract’s fee‑calculation routine, which attempts to compute a proportional charge based on elapsed time using integer arithmetic. The code first determines the time delta (block.timestamp ‑ lastFee), multiplies this delta by a fixed annual fee rate, and then derives a percentage (feePct) by dividing by the number of seconds in a year. Finally, the fee amount is calculated as startSupply * feePct / (BASE ‑ feePct). Because each arithmetic operation is performed with Solidity’s integer division, any fractional component is truncated at every step. This truncation introduces a small precision loss that becomes noticeable when the fee is collected frequently, i.e., when timeDiff is small. In that scenario the intermediate feePct value is reduced more aggressively by floor division, causing the final fee to be slightly lower than the theoretical value defined by fee/(supply+fee) = %fee. Conversely, when fees are collected after a longer interval, the larger timeDiff yields a larger feePct, partially compensating for the earlier loss, but the overall accounting remains inconsistent. The root cause is the use of a naïve, non‑compounding interest formula combined with integer‑only math, which fails to preserve the intended proportional relationship across varying collection intervals. An attacker or merely an honest user does not need to actively exploit the bug; the protocol itself will under‑collect fees whenever it schedules fee collection more often than anticipated. The impact is a gradual revenue leakage for the protocol’s treasury, a deviation from the economic model that assumes a constant fee rate, and potential distrust from stakeholders who expect fees to be calculated precisely. The issue manifests under the condition that the contract’s fee‑withdrawal function is called repeatedly with short intervals, a pattern that could arise in automated strategies, user‑initiated withdrawals, or testing environments. It was discovered during a formal code audit where the auditors compared the on‑chain fee amounts with the expected values derived from the fee formula and observed a systematic shortfall. Because the discrepancy is small, it may go unnoticed in casual inspection, especially when reviewing only high‑level balances rather than per‑transaction fee details. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that the protocol appears to charge marginally less than advertised; users might see a slightly higher net balance after a fee event, while the protocol’s revenue reports show a tiny deficit. This bug belongs to the broader class of "integer‑division rounding errors in financial calculations" and violates the assumption that fee calculations are mathematically exact. The conceptual fix is to redesign the fee logic to either use a higher‑precision arithmetic library (e.g., fixed‑point with more decimals) or to rearrange the formula so that division occurs only once after all multiplications, thereby minimizing truncation. Alternatively, the contract could adopt a cumulative accounting approach that tracks owed fees over time and settles them in a single rounded operation, ensuring that the total fee collected matches the intended rate over the long term.

title: `Basket:handleFees`
description: The fee calculation is based on the totalSupply of the basket token. But some amount of the totalSupply represents the fees paid to the publisher/ protocol owner. Therefore the fees are “overcharged”: because the fee amount is calculated on a part of already “paid” fees, should only take into account what is “owned” by the users and not the publisher/protocol owner.
poc:
L141: the fee percent is multiplied by startSupply (=basket token total supply)  
L144 & L145: publisher / protocol owner receive basket tokens as fees payment  
[Basket.sol#L141](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-defiprotocol/blob/205d3766044171e325df6a8bf2e79b37856eece1/contracts/contracts/Basket.sol#L141)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the fee calculation routine of the Basket contract. The contract determines the fee amount by multiplying a fee percentage with the current totalSupply of the basket token. However, a portion of that totalSupply already represents fees that have been paid out to the publisher or protocol owner. Because the algorithm does not subtract the previously distributed fee balance, it charges fees on top of fees that have already been collected. This double‑counting causes users to be overcharged: the effective fee taken from a user’s deposit is larger than the protocol intends. The flaw occurs whenever the fee routine reads the totalSupply before the newly minted tokens for the owner are accounted for, which is the normal execution path of the contract. Users who interact with the basket – for example, by depositing assets and receiving basket tokens – will notice that the number of tokens they receive is lower than expected, effectively seeing their balance shrink or a higher-than‑advertised fee. The protocol owner, on the other hand, receives a slightly larger fee payout due to the over‑calculation. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the mathematical logic of the fee function and observed that the variable representing the startSupply was derived directly from totalSupply without excluding the fee‑tracking amount. Because the overcharged portion is generally small, it can be difficult to detect through routine testing or by users monitoring their balances, especially when the protocol’s fee rates are modest. The bug belongs to the class of “fee double‑counting” or “accounting inflation” errors, where a formula incorporates a value that already includes the component being calculated, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that fees should be computed on the net user‑owned supply only. To resolve the issue, the contract should maintain a dedicated storage variable that records the cumulative fee amount distributed, subtract this value from the totalSupply (or startSupply) before applying the fee percentage, and adjust the tracker whenever fees are burned or transferred. This conceptual change ensures that fees are calculated solely on the portion of tokens owned by regular users, preserving the intended economic model and preventing inadvertent fee inflation.

title: Bad redirects can make it impossible to deposit & withdraw
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the vault contract redirects token balances between internal sub‑vaults. When a deposit is processed, the internal function _push() reads a redirects matrix supplied in the strategy parameters. For each vault index i, the code adds the amount stored in amountsByVault[i][j] to the target vault indicated by redirects[i] and then immediately resets amountsByVault[i][j] to zero. The same logic is mirrored in the _pull() function for withdrawals. If the redirects array is configured incorrectly – for example, if an index points to itself, or two indices point to each other, creating a cycle – the amounts are moved to the target vault but the source vault is cleared regardless of whether the target will later be cleared as well. In a cyclic or self‑redirect situation, all balances can end up being set to zero, effectively making the pool unusable. Users attempting to deposit will see their funds disappear from the UI, and attempts to withdraw will revert or return zero, violating the expectation that a deposited amount can be retrieved. The issue emerges only when the redirects matrix contains self‑loops or circular references, a condition that is not currently validated when the contract is deployed or when the strategy parameters are updated. Because the code does not raise an explicit error, the malfunction can be subtle and may only be observed when users experience failed deposits or withdrawals. The root cause is a lack of validation on the redirects configuration, allowing an invalid graph topology that breaks accounting invariants. To remediate, the contract should enforce that redirects[i] ≠ i for all i and that the overall redirects mapping forms an acyclic directed graph, rejecting any configuration that would introduce self‑references or cycles. This will preserve the invariant that total deposited amounts are conserved across vaults and ensure that users can always retrieve their assets.

I’m updating this [from a low] to a medium. Reentrancy represents a real and significant risk (as evident by ETC existing) and should be protected against regardless of if you can foresee the external event that causes lack of protection to be an issue.

`2 — Med (M): vulns have a risk of 2 and are considered “Medium” severity when assets are not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements.`
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a systematic omission of a reentrancy guard (typically a nonReentrant modifier) on a large set of public and external functions across multiple contracts in the NFTX ecosystem. The core issue is that these functions perform state‑changing operations—such as receiving Ether, minting or redeeming vault tokens, adding liquidity, updating fee receivers, or executing flash loans—while also invoking external calls or transferring assets. Without the nonReentrant protection, an attacker-controlled contract can invoke one of these vulnerable functions, trigger an external call (for example, a token transfer or a fallback function), and then re‑enter the same function before the original execution finishes. This re‑entrancy loop can cause the contract to process the same state transition multiple times, leading to double spends, unauthorized allocation changes, or corruption of accounting variables. The impact ranges from users seeing unexpected zero balances or missing refunds, to the protocol’s fee distribution and liquidity mechanisms being manipulated, potentially resulting in loss of funds or degraded availability. The condition under which the bug manifests is when a malicious contract is able to interact with any of the affected functions that involve external calls or payable receive logic. All participants who interact with the affected functions—depositors, withdrawers, liquidity providers, and protocol administrators—are potentially exposed. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which compared the presence of the nonReentrant modifier across similar functions and flagged the inconsistencies. Because no concrete exploit was demonstrated, the flaw can be subtle and may not produce immediate observable failures, making it easy to overlook during routine testing. To remediate the problem, each vulnerable function should be wrapped with a proven reentrancy guard such as OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier, ensuring that any re‑entrant call is rejected until the first execution completes. This correction restores the intended single‑execution contract invariant and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s security assumptions, thereby preventing fund disappearance, refund calculation errors, or other accounting anomalies that arise from unchecked re‑entrancy.

title: NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor#addReceiver: Failure to check for existing receiver
description:
The `addReceiver()` function fails to check if the `_receiver` already exists. This could lead to the same receiver being added multiple times, which results in erroneous fee distributions.

The receiver would receive more than expected (until the duplicate entry has been removed).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution contract’s addReceiver() function, which does not verify whether the address being added already exists in the list of fee receivers. Because there is no check for duplicate entries, the same receiver can be inserted multiple times. The root cause is insufficient input validation: the contract treats the receiver list as a plain array without maintaining a set‑like invariant or a mapping that records membership. An attacker or any privileged caller with access to the permissioned addReceiver() function can repeatedly invoke it with the same address, causing the contract’s internal distribution loop to allocate a share of the collected fees to that address for each occurrence in the array. Consequently, during each fee distribution cycle the duplicate receiver receives a multiplied portion of the total fee pool, while the remaining legitimate receivers obtain a reduced share. From a user’s perspective this manifests as unexpectedly high payouts to one address, missing or reduced refunds for others, and a rapid depletion of the contract’s fee balance. The issue is discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the implementation logic, and it can be hard to notice because the distribution still succeeds and the overpayment may only be observable through detailed accounting or abnormal balance changes. The impact is medium severity: funds may be unintentionally drained, fee accounting is broken, and trust in the protocol’s fairness can be eroded. The problem can be mitigated by enforcing uniqueness when adding receivers, for example by maintaining a mapping address => bool (isReceiver) or using a set data structure that rejects duplicate inserts, and by emitting an event when a duplicate addition is attempted. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of duplicate‑entry or insufficient‑validation vulnerabilities that violate business‑logic assumptions about exclusive participation in fee sharing.

title: `NFTXMarketplaceZap.sol#buyAnd***`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a marketplace zap function that is intended to purchase ERC‑721 tokens on behalf of a caller and then forward the acquired assets to a designated recipient. The function accepts a parameter called maxWethIn, which represents the maximum amount of WETH the caller is willing to spend. It transfers the full maxWethIn from the caller to the contract before performing the purchase. After the purchase, any leftover WETH that was not required for the actual cost is sent to the address supplied in the “to” argument, regardless of who originally supplied the funds. Consequently, when the caller specifies a recipient that is different from themselves, the contract refunds the excess to the recipient instead of the payer. This logical mis‑routing of funds creates a scenario where a user can unintentionally lose the unused portion of their payment. An attacker could exploit the flaw by calling the function with a high maxWethIn and setting the “to” address to an address they control; the contract would then forward the surplus WETH directly to the attacker while the original caller sees no refund. The impact is a loss of up to (maxWethIn – actual cost) for any transaction where the actual cost is lower than the supplied maximum and the recipient differs from the caller, which can be a substantial amount of capital. The issue manifests whenever the function is used for "buy‑and‑swap" operations with slippage protection that relies on an over‑estimation of input funds and when the caller does not set the recipient to themselves. Users of the protocol, especially those who employ the zap to acquire NFTs for a third‑party, are affected because they may see their balance reduced by the full maxWethIn even though the purchase required less. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected refund behavior against the implementation logic. It is subtle because the transaction completes successfully, emits a Swap event, and does not revert, so developers might assume the refund was handled correctly. The bug belongs to the class of "incorrect refund destination" or "mis‑allocated excess funds" errors, which violate the accounting assumption that any overpaid amount should be returned to the entity that supplied it. To remediate, the contract should either (1) return the surplus to msg.sender, (2) allow the caller to specify a separate refund address, or (3) calculate the exact amount needed before pulling funds, thereby ensuring that only the required WETH is transferred in the first place. By aligning the refund flow with the payer's expectations, the protocol would avoid unintended fund loss and restore trust in its financial logic.

title: NFTXStakingZap and NFTXMarketplaceZap’s transferFromERC721 transfer Cryptokitties to the wrong address
description: `transferFromERC721(address assetAddr, uint256 tokenId, address to)` should transfer from `msg.sender` to `to`. It transfers to `address(this)` instead when ERC721 is Cryptokitties. As there is no additional logic for this case it seems to be a mistake that leads to wrong NFT accounting after such a transfer as NFT will be missed in the vault (which is `to`).
poc:
NFTXStakingZap: transferFromERC721 <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXStakingZap.sol#L416>

NFTXMarketplaceZap: transferFromERC721 <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXMarketplaceZap.sol#L556>

Both functions are called by user facing Marketplace buy/sell and Staking addLiquidity/provideInventory functions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ERC‑721 transfer helper function `transferFromERC721(address assetAddr, uint256 tokenId, address to)` used by the NFTXStakingZap and NFTXMarketplaceZap contracts. The function is intended to move an NFT from the caller (`msg.sender`) directly into the vault specified by the `to` parameter. However, when the asset being transferred is the CryptoKitties contract, the implementation mistakenly encodes a call to `transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId)`, which routes the token to the Zap contract itself rather than to the intended vault address. This discrepancy stems from a hard‑coded destination address that was introduced under the false assumption that the Zap contract must temporarily hold the NFT for custody checks. Because the Zap contract does not implement any follow‑up logic to forward the token to the vault, the NFT becomes stranded in the Zap’s balance, resulting in an accounting mismatch: the vault’s inventory no longer reflects the deposited token, while the Zap contract holds an unexpected NFT. Exploitation occurs when a user invokes a marketplace buy/sell operation or a staking add‑liquidity/provide‑inventory function that internally calls `transferFromERC721` with a CryptoKitties token. The user expects the NFT to be deposited into the vault and receive the corresponding share tokens, but the transfer silently deposits the token into the Zap contract, leaving the user’s balance unchanged or reduced and the vault under‑counting its assets. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show the transaction as successful, yet the expected NFT is missing from the vault, and subsequent actions that rely on the vault’s inventory (e.g., withdrawing shares) may fail or return incorrect values. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the static analysis of the Zap contracts highlighted the hard‑coded destination address for the CryptoKitties case. The bug is subtle because the function otherwise behaves correctly for other ERC‑721 contracts, so the incorrect address is not obvious without tracing the specific code path for CryptoKitties. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of "incorrect destination address" or "misrouted asset transfer" bugs, where a contract forwards assets to an unintended recipient, breaking accounting invariants and potentially causing loss of assets. To remediate, the encoded call should pass the `to` argument supplied by the caller instead of `address(this)`, ensuring that the NFT is transferred directly into the vault as originally intended. This conceptual fix restores correct accounting, prevents NFTs from becoming trapped in the Zap contract, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the protocol’s business logic that the vault should own the deposited NFTs.

title: User deposits don’t have min. return checks
description:
The `LPIssuer.deposit` first computes _balanced amounts_ on the user’s defined `tokenAmounts`. The idea is that LP tokens give the same percentage share of each vault tokens’ tvl, therefore the provided amounts should be _balanced_ , meaning, the `depositAmount / tvl` ratio should be equal for all vault tokens.

But the strategist can frontrun the user’s deposit and rebalance the vault tokens, changing the tvl for each vault token which changes the rebalance. This frontrun can happen accidentally whenever the strategist rebalances.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing minimum‑return checks on LP token deposits. When a user calls the deposit function, the contract first calculates a balanced amount of each underlying token based on the current total value locked (TVL) and then mints LP tokens proportional to the user’s contribution. The calculation assumes that the TVL remains unchanged during the operation. However, a strategist or any privileged actor can execute a rebalance of the vault’s token holdings immediately before the user’s transaction is mined, thereby altering the TVL for each token. Because the contract does not verify that the amount of LP tokens minted meets a user‑specified minimum, the deposit can be performed with a lower-than‑expected exchange rate. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the LP token balance received may be substantially lower than anticipated, or may even be zero in extreme cases. The impact is that users lose part of the intended ownership share of the pool, effectively receiving less value for their deposited assets while the protocol’s accounting remains internally consistent. This issue is triggered whenever a rebalance happens in the same block or shortly before a deposit, which can occur unintentionally as part of regular strategy execution or intentionally as a front‑running attack. It primarily affects depositors, LP token holders, and ultimately the credibility of the protocol because users cannot rely on the quoted share they are purchasing. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where reviewers noted that the deposit routine lacks any slippage protection or minimum‑return assertion, making it difficult to notice without comparing expected versus actual LP token amounts after each deposit. To remediate the issue the contract should accept a user‑provided minimum acceptable LP token amount and revert the transaction if the minted amount falls below this threshold, thereby enforcing a slippage guard similar to those used on decentralized exchanges. This class of bug falls under front‑running and slippage‑protection failures, where the absence of a minimum‑return check allows an attacker to manipulate the pricing oracle (the TVL) and cause users to receive a lower-than‑expected token amount, violating the protocol’s economic assumptions and user expectations of fair value exchange.

title: Withdraw from `AaveVault` will receive less than actual share
description: `AaveVault` cache `tvl` and update it at the end of each `_push` and `_pull`. When withdrawing from `LpIssuer`, `tokenAmounts` is calculated using the cached `tvl` to be pulled from `AaveVault`. This will lead to user missing out their share of the accrued interest / donations to Aave since the last `updateTvls`.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-mellow/blob/6679e2dd118b33481ee81ad013ece4ea723327b5/mellow-vaults/contracts/LpIssuer.sol#L150>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-mellow/blob/6679e2dd118b33481ee81ad013ece4ea723327b5/mellow-vaults/contracts/AaveVault.sol#L13>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the AaveVault contract records and uses the total value locked (TVL) for accounting purposes. The vault keeps a cached TVL value that is only refreshed after each internal push or pull operation. When a user initiates a withdrawal through the LpIssuer contract, the amount of tokens to be returned is calculated based on this cached TVL rather than the current, up‑to‑date TVL that includes the most recent interest earnings or donations received from the Aave protocol. Because the cached TVL may be stale, the withdrawal logic under‑estimates the user’s proportional share of the accrued earnings that have accrued since the last update. An attacker or any user who times their withdrawal to occur after interest has been credited but before the cache is refreshed can therefore receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to. The impact is a systematic shortfall of funds for withdrawing users, effectively siphoning accrued interest away from them and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This condition manifests whenever a withdrawal is processed while the vault’s TVL cache is out of sync with the actual balance – a situation that can happen frequently in a live system where deposits, interest accruals, and withdrawals interleave. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by examining the sequence of state updates in the AaveVault and LpIssuer contracts and noticing that the `withdraw` function relied on a stale TVL variable. The problem is subtle because the withdrawal transaction still succeeds and appears to transfer tokens, but the amount received is slightly lower than expected, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should refresh the TVL at the beginning of the withdrawal path (for example by invoking `updateTvls`) or compute the user’s share directly from the current vault balance, thereby ensuring that the calculation always reflects the most recent interest earnings. In broader terms, this is a classic example of a caching‑state bug where financial calculations depend on outdated accounting data, leading to fund discrepancies and violating the core business logic that users receive their full entitled share of earnings.

title: Users can avoid paying vault fees
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑charging mechanism of the vault contract that mints additional liquidity provider (LP) tokens to collect protocol, management, and performance fees during deposit and withdrawal operations. The contract invokes an internal function that inflates the total LP supply, but this minting step is bypassed when the time elapsed since the last fee charge is smaller than a configurable parameter called `managementFeeChargeDelay`. Consequently, if a user makes a deposit immediately after a fee‑charging event and then withdraws before the delay period expires, the contract omits the fee minting entirely, allowing the user to exit with the full amount of their deposited assets and any accrued interest without paying any of the expected fees. This scenario can be reproduced by timing a deposit to follow a fee charge (or a large interest harvest) and then withdrawing within the same block or within the delay window, effectively sandwiching the fee‑charging logic. The impact is primarily economic: the protocol loses the fees it would normally collect, reducing its revenue and potentially distorting the incentive model. Users who are unaware of the fee‑avoidance opportunity see their balances behave as expected, but the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that each deposit or withdrawal contributes a proportional fee—are violated. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s fee logic, where the conditional early‑return based on `managementFeeChargeDelay` stood out as an edge case that could be abused. Detecting the problem in practice is non‑trivial because the fee‑charging code executes correctly for the majority of interactions, and the delay parameter may be perceived as a benign optimisation rather than a security control. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce fee collection on every deposit and withdrawal regardless of the elapsed time, or alternatively set the delay to zero so the conditional guard never triggers. If gas costs are a concern, the protocol could consider alternative designs such as aggregating fee charges off‑chain or adjusting the fee schedule, but the core requirement is that the fee‑minting path must not be conditionally skipped, ensuring that users cannot evade fees by timing their actions. This class of bug falls under "fee‑evasion through timing manipulation" and illustrates how subtle state‑dependent conditions can open economic attack vectors even when direct fund loss is not observed.

title: `ChiefTrader.sol` Wrong implementation of `swapExactInput`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ChiefTrader contract’s handling of token swaps through its swapExactInput and swapExactOutput functions. When a user invokes swapExactInput, ChiefTrader forwards the call to a sub‑trader contract using ITrader(traderAddress).swapExactInput, but it does not first approve the input ERC20 token for the sub‑trader nor does it transfer the tokens from the original caller into ChiefTrader. Consequently, the sub‑trader attempts to pull the input token from msg.sender, which at that point is the ChiefTrader contract itself. Because ChiefTrader has never been granted an allowance for that token, the ERC20 transfer reverts, causing the entire swap transaction to fail. The same omission exists in swapExactOutput, where the function also forwards the call without performing an allowance or a safeTransferFrom from the user. This flaw is a classic missing‑approval/incorrect‑caller bug that stems from a misunderstanding of the msg.sender context across contract boundaries. It can be exploited simply by calling the swap functions; the attacker does not need to craft any special payload—any call will trigger the revert, effectively denying service to legitimate users. The impact is a denial‑of‑service at the protocol level: users attempting to swap tokens through ChiefTrader receive a transaction revert, pay gas fees, and see no token movement, leading to a mismatch between the expectation of a successful trade and the reality of a failed operation. The issue manifests whenever a user calls either swapExactInput or swapExactOutput with any supported token path, regardless of token type, as long as the token has not been pre‑approved for the sub‑trader. The affected parties are all users of the protocol that rely on ChiefTrader as an entry point for swaps, as well as the protocol itself, which suffers from reduced functionality and potential loss of user confidence. The problem was uncovered during a code audit that examined the flow of token approvals and transfers in the swapping functions. It is subtle because the function signatures appear correct and the contract compiles without warnings; only runtime behavior reveals that the token allowance is missing, which may be overlooked if tests do not cover the exact call‑stack involving ChiefTrader and its sub‑traders. To remediate the issue, the contract must either explicitly approve the input token for the sub‑trader and perform a safeTransferFrom from the caller before delegating the swap, or the swapExactInput and swapExactOutput entry points should be removed from ChiefTrader entirely to avoid an incomplete implementation. In conceptual terms, the fix restores the expected token flow: the user’s tokens are moved into ChiefTrader, ChiefTrader grants the sub‑trader permission to spend them, and then the sub‑trader executes the swap, ensuring that the business logic of token exchange and accounting remains sound.

title: Admin can break `_numberOfValidTokens`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract that tracks the number of tokens permitted by the protocol. A counter variable, `_numberOfValidTokens`, is meant to represent the current size of the token whitelist. However, the `removeFromTokenWhitelist` function decrements this counter every time it is called, regardless of whether the token address passed was actually listed as allowed. The function only clears the `_tokensAllowed` flag and checks a separate flag `_tokenEverAdded`, but it never verifies that `_tokensAllowed[addr]` was true before applying the decrement, nor does it reset the `_tokenEverAdded` flag. As a result, an administrator can invoke the function repeatedly for the same address, driving `_numberOfValidTokens` down to zero even when no tokens have been removed from the whitelist. This creates a mismatch between the logical whitelist (which may still contain many tokens) and the reported count, breaking any protocol logic that relies on the counter for validation, allocation, or fee calculation. Users may experience legitimate tokens being rejected by the system, deposits failing, or unexpected zero‑balance errors because the protocol believes there are no valid tokens available. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the missing guard around the decrement operation. Because the counter is used internally and not directly exposed to users, the bug can be subtle and only manifest under certain administrative actions, making it hard to notice during normal operation. The proper fix is to decrement `_numberOfValidTokens` only when the token being removed is actually present in the whitelist—i.e., when `_tokensAllowed[addr]` is true—ensuring the counter always reflects the true number of allowed tokens and preserving the protocol's accounting invariants.

title: UniswapV3’s path issue for `swapExactOutput`
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect manipulation of the Uniswap V3 path encoding within the `UniV3Trader.swapExactOutput` function. Uniswap V3 represents a multi‑hop swap as a byte array that concatenates token addresses (20 bytes each) and pool fee values (3 bytes each) in the order (tokenA, feeAB, tokenB, feeBC, tokenC). When performing a `swapExactOutput`, the contract attempts to reverse this path so that the router can process the hops from the desired output token back to the input token, i.e., (tokenC, feeBC, tokenB, feeAB, tokenA). The implemented helper `_reverseBytes` reverses the entire byte array byte‑by‑byte rather than reversing each logical element. Consequently, each token address is byte‑reversed, turning the original address into a completely different, invalid address, and fees are also mis‑ordered. This malformed path is then supplied to the Uniswap V3 router, which may either revert the transaction due to an unknown token address or route the swap through unintended pools. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the exact amount of the target token – may not materialise; instead the transaction may fail silently, return zero tokens, or swap through a pool with unfavorable rates, effectively causing funds to be lost or stuck. The issue is triggered whenever `swapExactOutput` is called with a multi‑hop path, i.e., any scenario where the trader needs to specify more than one pool hop. It affects any user or protocol that relies on this function to obtain a precise output amount, including automated market makers, token aggregators, or end‑users executing trades through the contract. The bug was uncovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by inspecting the path‑handling logic; it is subtle because the path is an opaque bytes object and the reversal operation does not produce an obvious syntax error, making it easy to miss during manual testing. The class of bug is a data‑encoding reversal mistake—specifically, a byte‑order manipulation applied at the wrong granularity, leading to invalid address encoding. To remediate, the path should be parsed into its constituent token and fee segments and then reconstructed in the opposite order, preserving each segment’s internal byte order. This element‑wise reversal restores the intended routing logic and prevents malformed token addresses, ensuring that the swap either succeeds as intended or fails with a clear, predictable error, thereby protecting user funds and preserving the contract’s business logic of exact‑output trading.

title: Pool Manager can frontrun fees to 100% and use it to steal the value from users
description: Pool Manager can front-run entry fee to 100% and users could lose all their deposits.
poc:
Considering:  
The pool manager is the creator of the pool.  
Anyone can create a pool.  
Manager is not a trusted actor.

Anyone can create a pool and get people to join. If there is a big deposit admin could front-run the transaction and set the fee to max which is uint(1 ether) = 10**18 (100% as this is a per token fee).

Function that set fees : <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/194073f750b7e2c9a886ece34b6382b4f1355f36/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXVaultUpgradeable.sol#L119> Max fees are 1 ether : <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/194073f750b7e2c9a886ece34b6382b4f1355f36/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXVaultFactoryUpgradeable.sol#L122>

The manager could benefit from this by having other pool assets deposited in staking so he would receive fees in Vtokens and could use them to withdraw the nfts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑manipulation and front‑running issue in the pool manager component of the NFTX vault system. The contract allows the pool manager, who is the creator of each vault, to set the entry fee for deposits via a public function without any delay or governance restriction. Because the fee is expressed as a per‑token amount and the contract caps the maximum at 1 ether (representing 100 % of the deposited value), a malicious manager can submit a transaction that changes the fee to the maximum immediately before a user’s deposit is processed. This can be done by observing a pending deposit transaction (or by anticipating a large deposit) and then executing a fee‑update transaction that front‑runs the deposit. The root cause is the lack of a time‑locked or otherwise delayed mechanism for fee changes, combined with the fact that the manager role is not a trusted, immutable entity and that the fee‑setting function is callable by anyone who holds the manager role for a given vault. When the fee is set to 100 %, the contract deducts the entire amount from the user’s deposit, effectively returning zero tokens to the depositor and crediting the full amount to the manager’s fee balance. The impact is that users who interact with a vault whose fee has been maliciously raised lose all of their deposited assets; from a user’s perspective the UI may show the transaction succeeded but the resulting token balance is zero, leading to confusion and financial loss. This condition can only occur when a vault is not yet finalized – that is, when the vault’s fee parameter is still mutable – and when the attacker can observe or anticipate a user deposit transaction. The vulnerability was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which identified the missing timelock as a logical flaw allowing direct front‑running of fee updates. The issue is subtle because the contract enforces a maximum fee limit, which may give the impression that fees cannot be set to extreme values, and because the UI already warns users about un‑finalized vaults, potentially masking the severity for inattentive users. To remediate, the fee‑setting function should be protected by a timelock or a multi‑step governance process that forces a delay between the fee change announcement and its activation, thereby giving users visibility into the new fee and preventing immediate exploitation. This class of bug is commonly known as a “parameter front‑run” or “fee manipulation” vulnerability, where privileged yet untrusted actors can alter economic parameters on‑chain without sufficient notice, breaking the expected accounting invariants of the protocol and leading to loss of user funds.

title: Return variable can remain unassigned in _sendForReceiver
description:
The `_sendForReceiver()` function only sets a return function in the “if” code block, not the “else” case. If the “else” case is true, no value is returned. The result of this oversight is that the `_sendForReceiver()` function called from the `distribute()` function could sucessfully enter its `else` block if a receiver has `isContract` set to False and successfully transfer the `amountToSend` value. The `ditribute()` function will then have `leftover > 0` and send `currentTokenBalance` to the treasury. This issue is partially due to [Solidity using implicit returns](https://github.com/ethereum/solidity/issues/2951), so if no bool value is explicitly returned, the default bool value of False will be returned.

This problem currently occurs for any receiver with `isContract` set to False. The `_addReceiver` function allows for `isContract` to be set to False, so such a condition should not result in tokens being sent to the treasury as though it was an emergency scenario.
poc: The `else` block is missing a return value <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/194073f750b7e2c9a886ece34b6382b4f1355f36/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor.sol#L167-L169>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑distribution routine where the internal helper function _sendForReceiver is expected to return a boolean indicating the success of a token transfer. In its current implementation the function only assigns a return value inside the conditional branch that handles contract receivers; the else branch, which is taken when the receiver is flagged as a non‑contract (isContract == false), performs the transfer but does not explicitly return a value. Because Solidity automatically returns the default value for a missing explicit return, the function yields false even though the transfer may have succeeded. The calling distribute function interprets this false as a failure, calculates a leftover amount greater than zero and, as a fallback safety measure, forwards the entire current token balance to the treasury address. Consequently, tokens that should have been delivered to a legitimate non‑contract receiver are instead redirected to the treasury, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations. This defect manifests whenever a receiver is added with isContract set to false—a condition that the _addReceiver function permits—so any such receiver can trigger the erroneous treasury transfer. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers observed that the else block lacked a return statement and that the implicit false return caused unexpected leftover calculations. It may be hard to notice because the transfer itself succeeds and no revert occurs, making the loss of funds appear as a normal treasury sweep rather than a failed transaction. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful distribution event while the expected balance of the receiver remains unchanged or drops to zero, and the treasury balance unexpectedly spikes. The bug belongs to the class of implicit‑return mis‑use and faulty control‑flow errors that break business‑logic invariants. To remediate the issue, every execution path of _sendForReceiver should explicitly return true after a successful transfer, or the contract should enforce that only contract receivers can be registered, thereby preventing the else branch from being exercised.

title: No access control on assignFees
description:
If the Vault owner decides to set factoryMintFee and factoryRandomRedeemFee to zero, any user could call the function NFTXVaultFactoryUpgradeable.assignFees() and hence all the fees are updated.

This function is left over from some upgrades. It will be removed. Thank you.

**[0xKiwi (NFTX) resolved](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx-findings/issues/50)**
bug_full: The vulnerability is an uncontrolled public function that updates the fee parameters of the NFTX vault factory. The function assignFees() is callable by any address because it lacks any access‑control modifier (e.g., onlyOwner). Consequently, anyone can invoke it and set the factoryMintFee and factoryRandomRedeemFee to arbitrary values. The root cause is that the function was left in the contract after a series of upgrades without restricting who may call it. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker simply sends a transaction to assignFees() with the desired fee amounts. Because the function directly writes to storage variables that govern how much users are charged when minting or redeeming NFTs, the attacker can raise the fees to extremely high percentages, causing users to lose a large portion of their deposits, or lower them to zero, depriving the protocol of revenue. The impact is financial loss for users and a break of the protocol’s economic model; users may see unexpected high costs, refunds that are lower than expected, or a sudden disappearance of funds from their balances after a transaction that should have been cheap. The condition under which this can be triggered is any time the contract is live with assignFees() present; the vulnerability becomes especially exploitable when the vault owner initially sets the fees to zero, because then the contract’s state appears harmless and any external observer may not suspect the function can be abused. All participants who interact with the vault – token holders, liquidity providers, and the contract owner – are affected because the fee values are globally applied to all mint and redeem operations. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s upgrade history, where the auditor identified residual functions that no longer have appropriate modifiers. It may be hard to notice because the function does not emit any events, does not revert, and its presence does not affect normal operation unless someone intentionally calls it; therefore, it can remain unnoticed in code reviews that focus only on core logic. The appropriate remediation is to remove the function entirely, as intended by the developers, or at minimum protect it with a strict access control such as onlyOwner or a multi‑signature guard, and emit an event whenever fees are changed so that any change is observable. In generic terms, this is a classic example of an "unrestricted external setter" vulnerability, where a public function that mutates critical financial parameters lacks proper authorization checks, leading to potential fee manipulation and loss of funds. From a user’s perspective, the symptom could be that after attempting a mint or redemption the wallet shows a much lower returned amount than expected, or the protocol suddenly charges an unusually high fee, making the transaction appear to "steal" funds. The expectation that only the protocol owner can change fees is violated, and the accounting assumptions that fees are static or only owner‑controlled are broken.

title: Malicious receiver can make distribute function denial of service
bug_full: The NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor contract implements a fee distribution routine that iterates over a list of registered fee receivers and attempts to transfer a proportional share of the collected token balance to each receiver. For contract‑type receivers the routine approves the token amount, builds a payload that calls the external contract’s receiveRewards function via a low‑level call, and then checks whether the call succeeded and whether the allowance was cleared. The vulnerability arises because the distributor trusts the external receiver to honour the call without any safeguards. If a malicious receiver implements receiveRewards so that it always reverts, the low‑level call returns false and the allowance remains unchanged. The distributor records the unreleased amount as "leftover" and proceeds to the next receiver, but the leftover is never forwarded to the treasury or any other safe address. Consequently the tokens that should have been distributed remain locked inside the distributor contract, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for fee distribution. This condition occurs whenever the feeReceivers array contains a contract that can deliberately cause the receiveRewards call to fail, which can be triggered by anyone who can add or replace a receiver (or by the DAO if it mistakenly registers a malicious address). The impact is that token holders and the protocol treasury do not receive the expected rewards; users may see their expected refunds or fee payouts disappear, balances shown in the UI may remain unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fee distribution are broken. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of the distribute function and identified that a revert in an external call does not propagate but still prevents the intended transfer. The problem is subtle because the contract does not outright revert the transaction, so the failure can go unnoticed while funds stay idle in the contract. To remediate, the fee distribution should adopt a pull‑based model where the allocated amount is recorded in a state variable and each receiver can claim its share via a separate function, or the distributor should enforce that a failed external call results in a safe fallback such as sending the amount to the treasury. This eliminates the reliance on external contracts executing correctly during the distribution loop and prevents a malicious receiver from blocking the entire fee distribution process.

title: transfer return value is ignored
bug_full: The issue originates from the contract’s reliance on the standard ERC‑20 `transfer` and `transferFrom` functions without verifying their return values. Although the ERC‑20 specification states that these functions should return a boolean indicating success, many deployed tokens deviate from the standard: some, such as USDT, return no value at all, while others may return `false` instead of reverting on failure. The contract assumes that a failed transfer will automatically revert, and therefore proceeds to update internal accounting and emit events as though the token movement succeeded. In reality, when a non‑compliant token silently fails or returns `false`, the contract’s state is updated while the actual token balance remains unchanged. This discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a malicious token that always returns a success flag (or no flag) regardless of the real transfer outcome. By calling the vulnerable functions, the attacker can cause the contract to believe a transfer succeeded, while no funds are moved, effectively allowing the attacker to drain or lock user assets. The impact is that users may see a transaction receipt indicating success, yet their token balance stays the same, leading to funds appearing to disappear or refunds not being issued. The problem manifests whenever the contract interacts with any ERC‑20 token that does not strictly adhere to the specification, which includes a wide range of popular tokens used in the staking and flash‑swap logic of the protocol. All participants—token holders, stakers, and the protocol itself—are potentially affected because the accounting assumptions of the protocol are broken. The flaw was uncovered during a Code4rena audit that inspected the contract’s source code and identified calls to `transfer` and `transferFrom` that lack any return‑value checks. Detecting this issue can be difficult in practice because the transaction does not revert and the blockchain explorer shows a successful status, providing no immediate indication that the token transfer failed. The proper mitigation is to replace raw `transfer`/`transferFrom` calls with a safe wrapper, such as OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` and `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom`, which perform low‑level calls and explicitly verify that the operation succeeded, reverting otherwise. By ensuring that token movements are confirmed before any state changes, the contract regains the expected invariant that internal balances match actual token holdings, thereby restoring the intended business logic of accurate accounting and reliable refunds.

title: `xToken` Approvals Allow Spenders To Spend More Tokens
description: The `approve` function has not been overridden and therefore uses `xToken` shares instead of the equivalent rebalanced amount, i.e. the underlying vault token amount.
poc:
The approved spender may spend more tokens than desired. In fact, the approved amount that can be transferred keeps growing as rewards continue to be distributed to the `XTokenUpgradeable` contract.

Many contracts also use the same amount for the `approve` call as for the amount they want to have transferred in a subsequent `transferFrom` call, and in this case, they approve an amount that is too large (as the approved `shares` amount yields a higher rebalanced amount).
bug_full:
The vulnerability originates from the way the xToken contract handles ERC‑20 approvals. The standard approve function is left untouched, meaning that the allowance mapping stores the number of xToken "shares" that a spender is permitted to move, instead of the equivalent amount of the underlying vault token that those shares represent after rebalancing. Because the value of each share changes over time as rewards are distributed to the vault, the same share allowance can correspond to an ever‑increasing amount of underlying tokens. Consequently, a spender that has been granted, for example, 1,000 shares may later be able to transfer a larger quantity of the underlying asset without any explicit increase in the stored allowance. The transferFrom implementation also relies on the share count when decreasing the allowance, further compounding the discrepancy.

An attacker can exploit this by first obtaining an allowance of a modest share amount from a token holder who expects the spender to be limited to a comparable amount of the underlying token. After the contract distributes rewards and the share‑to‑token conversion rate rises, the attacker calls transferFrom and withdraws more underlying tokens than the holder intended, effectively draining funds beyond the original consent. This scenario is especially likely when contracts approve exactly the amount they intend to transfer in a subsequent call, assuming a one‑to‑one relationship between shares and underlying tokens; the implicit inflation of the allowance goes unnoticed because the UI typically displays the raw share allowance, not its current token value.

The impact is a loss of value for any user or protocol that relies on the approval mechanism to enforce spending limits. The issue manifests only after the token has accrued rewards or otherwise rebalanced, so it may be invisible during initial testing and can be difficult to detect in production because the allowance value itself does not change. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the approve and transferFrom logic and identified that the allowance bookkeeping does not account for the dynamic share valuation.

To remediate the problem, the contract should override approve so that the allowance mapping records the rebalanced amount of the underlying token rather than raw shares. TransferFrom must also be overridden to subtract the spent amount in terms of underlying tokens, converting the requested token amount back into the appropriate number of shares based on the current exchange rate. By aligning the allowance semantics with the economic value that users expect, the contract will prevent the effective allowance from unintentionally growing, restoring the intended security guarantees.

From a user's perspective the bug looks like a normal approval transaction, but later the user observes that more tokens are transferred than they approved – balances drop unexpectedly, or a refund that should return a certain amount comes back as zero. The expectation that "the spender can only move the amount I approved" is violated, leading to potential fund loss. Although the risk is classified as medium because the attacker must be a malicious spender contract, the economic effect can be significant if the allowance is large and the token accrues substantial rewards.

title: Rewards can be stolen
description:
The `NFTXInventoryStaking` contract distributes new rewards to all previous stakers when the owner calls the `receiveRewards` function. This allows an attacker to frontrun this `receiveRewards` transaction when they see it in the mem pool with a `deposit` function. The attacker will receive the rewards pro-rata to their deposits. The deposit will be locked for 2 seconds only (`DEFAULT_LOCKTIME`) after which the depositor can withdraw their initial deposit & the rewards again for a profit.

The rewards can be gamed this way and one does not actually have to _stake_ , only be in the staking contract at the time of reward distribution for 2 seconds. The rest of the time they can be used for other purposes.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution mechanism of the NFTXInventoryStaking contract. When the contract owner invokes the receiveRewards function, the contract allocates the newly received reward tokens to every address that currently holds a stake in the contract, without distinguishing between long‑term stakers and addresses that have just entered the contract. Because the contract enforces only a very short lock period of two seconds (DEFAULT_LOCKTIME) on newly deposited funds, an attacker can monitor the mempool for a pending receiveRewards transaction, submit a deposit transaction that lands just before the reward distribution, and thereby qualify for a proportional share of the rewards. After the two‑second lock expires the attacker can immediately withdraw both the original deposit and the freshly received rewards, netting a profit while other legitimate stakers receive a smaller share of the same reward pool.
