This attack does not require the attacker to actually stake for any meaningful duration; merely being present in the staking contract at the moment of distribution for a brief window is sufficient. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit that examined the logical flow of reward allocation and identified that the reward calculation does not filter out deposits that occur in the same block as the distribution. The problem can be subtle because the contract appears to function correctly for ordinary users – rewards are credited, balances update, and no error is thrown – yet the profit extracted by the attacker is effectively stolen from the pool of other stakers, violating the intended accounting assumptions of proportional, time‑based reward sharing. The impact is a reduction of expected returns for honest participants and a potential loss of value for the protocol, as the reward pool can be drained by repeated front‑running attacks. The exploit is feasible whenever the owner’s receiveRewards call is observable in the transaction pool and the locktime remains as short as two seconds. To remediate the issue, reward distribution should be amortized over time (e.g., streamed per block or per second) rather than issued as a single lump sum, or the contract should exclude deposits that occur within a defined window before a reward payout from receiving that payout. Additional mitigations include extending the lock period, introducing a minimum staking duration before eligibility for rewards, or redesigning the reward accounting to use cumulative per‑share accrual that inherently prevents instant capture of newly arrived rewards. By adopting a streaming or accrual‑based model, the protocol can ensure that rewards are earned proportionally to the actual time that capital remains staked, restoring the intended fairness and protecting users from profit‑stealing front‑run attacks.

title: Low-level call return value not checked
description: The `NFTXStakingZap.addLiquidity721ETHTo` function performs a low-level `.call` in `payable(to).call{value: msg.value-amountEth}` but does not check the return value if the call succeeded.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a liquidity‑adding function that forwards leftover Ether to an external address using a low‑level .call operation. The contract constructs the call as payable(to).call{value: msg.value‑amountEth} but never inspects the boolean success flag returned by the call. Because the low‑level call does not automatically revert on failure, any error in the recipient—such as a revert in its fallback function, a rejection of Ether, or an out‑of‑gas condition—will cause the call to return false while the surrounding transaction continues as if the transfer had succeeded. This omission creates a situation where the contract assumes that the excess Ether has been refunded to the caller, yet the funds remain locked in the contract or are silently discarded. An attacker controlling the recipient address can deliberately cause the call to fail, preventing the refund and leaving the user’s balance unchanged while the transaction reports success. The impact is that users who add liquidity with ETH may see their expected refund disappear, leading to a loss of funds or an inconsistent accounting state where the contract believes it has transferred Ether that never left its balance. The problem manifests only when the function is invoked with a non‑zero surplus (msg.value > amountEth). Users observing the UI will notice that after adding liquidity, their wallet balance has decreased by the full amount sent, but they receive no corresponding refund, contradicting the expectation that only the exact amount needed for the liquidity operation is deducted. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, and because the failure does not emit events nor revert the transaction, it can easily go unnoticed in standard testing. To remediate, the contract should capture the boolean returned by the .call, verify that it is true, and revert the whole transaction if the refund fails, thereby preserving the atomicity of the operation and ensuring that users either receive the correct refund or the transaction is rolled back. Conceptually, this is an unchecked low‑level external call—a common class of bugs where error handling is omitted, leading to silent failures and potential fund loss.

title: Bypass zap timelock
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the timelock mechanism used when staking NFTs through the NFTX protocol. The contract responsible for minting staked tokens, XTokenUpgradeable, implements a private function that records a lock expiration timestamp by simply adding the supplied lock length to the current block timestamp and storing the result in a mapping. This calculation is performed unconditionally, regardless of whether the account already has a lock that expires later. The protocol defines two default lock durations: a seven‑day lock for the NFTXStakingZap contract and a two‑millisecond lock for the NFTXInventoryStaking contract. When a user who already possesses a longer lock (for example, the seven‑day lock set by the zap) later calls the deposit function of NFTXInventoryStaking, they can supply the minimal two‑millisecond lock value. Because the minting function overwrites the existing lock entry without a comparison, the previously longer lock is replaced by an almost immediate expiry. Consequently, the user can claim their newly minted staking tokens immediately, bypassing the intended waiting period. This flaw arises from the absence of a safeguard that ensures a new timelock can only extend, not reduce, an existing lock, combined with inconsistent default lock parameters across related contracts. The exploit can be carried out by any participant able to invoke the deposit function with a custom lock length, which the contract permits. Under these conditions, the attacker’s funds become withdrawable far earlier than the protocol’s economic design anticipates, potentially undermining reward schedules, token emissions, and overall trust in the staking system. The issue was identified during a formal security audit that compared the default lock constants and inspected the timelock‑mint logic for proper handling of existing locks. It may be difficult to spot in routine testing because the function appears to behave correctly for first‑time deposits, and the overwrite of a longer lock with a very short one does not raise an immediate error or revert. To remediate the flaw, the timelock‑mint routine should be modified to update the stored lock only when the new calculated expiration is later than the current one, preserving the maximum lock duration for each account. This change ensures that an attacker cannot reduce an existing lock and that the protocol’s intended lock‑up periods remain enforced. In user‑facing terms, the bug manifests as a situation where a user expects their staked assets to be locked for days but can withdraw them almost instantly, creating a discrepancy between the expected and actual behavior of the staking UI, and potentially leading to loss of protocol revenue or confidence.

title: NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor._sendForReceiver doesn’t return success if receiver is not a contract
description: Double spending of fees being distributed will happen in favor of the first fee receivers in the `feeReceivers` list at the expense of the last ones. As `_sendForReceiver` doesn’t return success for completed transfer when receiver isn’t a contract, the corresponding fee amount is sent out twice, to the current and to the next fee receiver in the list. This will lead to double payments for those receivers who happen to be next in the line right after EOAs, and missed payments for the receivers positioned closer to the end of the list as the funds available are going to be already depleted when their turn comes.
poc:
`distribute` use `_sendForReceiver` to transfer current vault balance across `feeReceivers`: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor.sol#L67>

`_sendForReceiver` returns a boolean that is used to move current distribution amount to the next receiver when last transfer failed. When `_receiver.isContract` is `false` nothing is returned, while `safeTransfer` is done: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor.sol#L168>

This way `_sendForReceiver` will indicate that transfer is failed and leftover amount to be added to the next transfer, i.e. the `amountToSend` will be spent twice: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor.sol#L64>
bug_full:
The NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor contract contains a logic flaw in its internal fee distribution routine. The routine iterates over a list of fee receivers and, for each entry, calls a helper function to transfer the allocated amount of the vault’s ERC‑20 token. The helper function determines whether the recipient is a contract or an externally owned account (EOA). When the recipient is a contract, the function returns a boolean indicating success or failure of the transfer. However, when the recipient is an EOA, the function executes a safe ERC‑20 transfer but does **not** return a true value. The caller interprets a false return as a failed transfer and therefore adds the un‑sent amount to the next receiver’s payout. Because the transfer to the EOA actually succeeded, the same amount is sent a second time to the following receiver in the list. This double‑payment behavior benefits the early receivers in the list and starves later receivers, whose allocated funds may have already been exhausted by the duplicated transfers.

The root cause is the missing success flag for non‑contract recipients, which breaks the contract’s accounting invariant that each receiver should be paid exactly once. The failure is subtle because the ERC‑20 transfer itself succeeds and no revert occurs; only the boolean return value is incorrect. As a result, the contract’s external state (the token balances of the receivers) diverges from the intended distribution logic, leading to an imbalance where total distributed funds exceed the available vault balance.

An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; the vulnerability is triggered by simply listing an EOA before other receivers in the feeReceivers array. When the distribution function is invoked—either by a regular user or by an automated keeper—the contract will automatically double‑pay the first EOA and any receiver that follows it, while the last receivers receive less or nothing. The impact is monetary: legitimate fee recipients later in the list lose expected payouts, and the protocol may appear to over‑distribute fees, potentially exhausting the vault and causing subsequent operations that rely on those funds to fail.

The condition under which the bug manifests is any fee distribution run where the feeReceivers list contains at least one EOA followed by another receiver (contract or EOA). The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit by Code4rena, which traced the boolean return path of the helper function and observed that the safeTransfer call for EOAs lacked a corresponding "return true" statement. The problem is hard to notice in practice because the transaction does not revert and there is no immediate error event; only the downstream accounting discrepancy becomes visible after multiple distributions, often only when a later receiver reports missing funds.

To remediate the issue, the helper function should return a success flag for **all** successful transfers, regardless of the recipient type. By explicitly returning true after a safeTransfer to an EOA, the calling distribution loop will correctly recognize the transfer as completed and will not re‑allocate the same amount to the next receiver. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that the sum of all transferred amounts never exceeds the vault balance and that each receiver is paid exactly once.

In summary, the vulnerability is a classic example of an "incorrect return value" or "missing success indicator" bug in a payment loop, which leads to double‑spending of fees, incorrect accounting, and potentially lost payouts for downstream receivers. Users may observe that their expected refunds or fee shares are either duplicated for early recipients or missing for later recipients, violating the protocol’s promise of fair fee distribution.

title: NFTXVaultFactoryUpgradeable implementation can be replaced in production breaking the system
description: `NFTXVaultFactory` contract holds information regarding vaults, assets and permissions (vaults, _vaultsForAsset and excludedFromFees mappings). As there is no mechanics present that transfers this information to another implementation, the switch of nftxVaultFactory to another address performed while in production will break the system.
poc:
`setNFTXVaultFactory` function allows an owner to reset `nftxVaultFactory` without restrictions in the following contracts:

NFTXLPStaking <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXLPStaking.sol#L59>

NFTXInventoryStaking <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXInventoryStaking.sol#L51>

NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor.sol#L135>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NFTX protocol’s auxiliary contracts that store a reference to the NFTXVaultFactory implementation. The factory contract maintains critical mappings that describe which vaults belong to which assets and which addresses are excluded from fee collections. The auxiliary contracts expose a public `setNFTXVaultFactory` function that can be called by the contract owner to replace the stored factory address at any time without any safeguards or migration logic. Because the factory holds state that is not automatically transferred to a new implementation, changing the address after deployment causes the auxiliary contracts to point to a fresh, empty factory instance. Consequently, calls that rely on the factory for vault lookup, asset association, or fee exemption will either return default values (often zero addresses) or fail outright. This breaks essential business logic: users attempting to deposit, withdraw, or claim fees may find their vaults invisible, balances appearing as zero, or fee calculations yielding unexpected results. The root cause is the absence of immutability or one‑time initialization for the factory reference and the lack of a data‑migration procedure when the reference is altered. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who gains ownership privileges—or a malicious owner—invokes `setNFTXVaultFactory` on any of the affected contracts (NFTXLPStaking, NFTXInventoryStaking, NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor) and supplies a new address. After the switch, all subsequent protocol operations that depend on the factory retrieve empty mappings, effectively rendering vault functionality unusable and potentially locking user funds. The impact is medium‑severity because it compromises the availability and correctness of the protocol’s core accounting, though it does not directly enable arbitrary asset theft. The issue manifests only after the owner performs the address change; prior to that the contracts behave as expected, making the bug difficult to notice during normal operation. The affected parties include all protocol participants—vault owners, liquidity providers, and users who rely on fee distribution—because their interactions with the system may silently fail. The problem was uncovered during a professional security audit, where the auditors noted the unrestricted setter and the lack of any migration pattern. To remediate, the factory reference should be made immutable or restricted to a single initialization, for example by requiring the stored address to be zero before it can be set, or by moving the setter behind a timelock and adding explicit migration functions that atomically transfer the factory’s state to the new implementation. This ensures that any change to the factory preserves the essential mappings and maintains protocol integrity.

title: `buyAndSwap1155WETH` Does Not Work As Intended
description: The `buyAndSwap1155WETH` function in `NFTXMarketplaceZap` aims to facilitate buying and swapping `ERC1155` tokens within a single transaction. The function expects to transfer `WETH` tokens from the `msg.sender` account and use these tokens in purchasing vault tokens. However, the `_buyVaultToken` call in `buyAndSwap1155WETH` actually uses `msg.value` and not `maxWethIn`. As a result, the function will not work unless the user supplies both `WETH` and native `ETH` amounts, equivalent to the `maxWethIn` amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the NFTXMarketplaceZap contract’s buyAndSwap1155WETH function, which is intended to let a user purchase ERC‑1155 vault tokens using WETH that has been transferred from the caller’s address. The function first pulls the specified maxWethIn amount of WETH from msg.sender via transferFrom, but when it later calls the internal _buyVaultToken helper it incorrectly passes msg.value – the amount of native ETH sent with the transaction – instead of the previously supplied maxWethIn. As a result, the purchase operation attempts to spend ETH rather than the WETH that the caller has approved. When the caller supplies only WETH and does not send an equivalent amount of ETH, msg.value is zero, causing _buyVaultToken to execute with a zero‑value input. The swap therefore yields no vault tokens, yet the function proceeds to attempt an ERC‑1155 swap and finally returns any remaining WETH balance to the caller. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed (no revert), but the expected tokens are never received and the user’s balance may show an unexpected zero‑output or a refunded WETH amount, contradicting the expectation of acquiring new assets. The issue stems from a logical mix‑up between an ERC‑20 payment token (WETH) and the native cryptocurrency (ETH), a class of bugs where the wrong currency variable is used in a payment flow. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the call parameters and noticing the mismatch. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and does not revert; the symptom is simply a missing token receipt, which can be easily overlooked in UI testing. The impact is medium: users waste gas and may be confused by a transaction that completes without delivering the purchased assets, and any leftover WETH is merely returned, so no direct fund loss occurs, but the business logic of “buy and swap in one step” is broken. To correct the flaw, the code should replace the msg.value argument with the maxWethIn variable when invoking _buyVaultToken, ensuring that the transferred WETH amount is the one used for the purchase. This aligns the payment source with the contract’s intent and restores the expected behavior of the marketplace zap function.

title: Dishonest Stakers Can Siphon Rewards From `xToken` Holders Through The `deposit` Function In `NFTXInventoryStaking`
description:
`xTokens` is intended to be a representation of staked vault tokens. As the protocol’s vaults accrue fees from users, these fees are intended to be distributed to users in an inconsistent fashion. `NFTXInventoryStaking` is one of the ways users can stake vault tokens. Deposits are timelocked for `2` seconds by default, essentially rendering flash loan attacks redundant. However, it is more than likely that the same user could withdraw their `xToken` deposit in the next block (assuming an average block time of just over 13 seconds).

Hence, if a well-funded attacker sees a transaction to distribute rewards to `xToken` holders, they could deposit a large sum of vault tokens and receive a majority share of the rewards before withdrawing their tokens in the following block. Additionally, the attacker can force distribute rewards in `NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor` as there is no access control on the `distribute` function.

This issue allows users to siphon user’s rewards from the protocol, intended to be distributed to honest vault token stakers.
poc:
Consider the following exploit scenario:

  * Currently there are 1000 `shares` and 1000 `base tokens` in the `XTokenUpgradeable` contract.
  * Honest actor, Alice, calls `distribute` in `NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor` which attempts to send 200 `base tokens` as rewards for `xToken` holders accrued via protocol usage.
  * Bob sees a transaction to reward `xToken` holders and frontruns this transaction by staking vault tokens, minting 1000 `shares` and 1000 `base tokens`.
  * Rewards are distributed such that `XTokenUpgradeable` has 2000 `shares` and 2200 `base tokens`.
  * Bob unstakes his tokens and exits the pool, redeeming his 1000 `shares` for 1100 `base tokens`.
  * As a result, Bob was able to siphon off 100 `base tokens` without having to stake their tokens for the same time period that Alice had staked her tokens for.
  * This unfair distribution can be abused again and again to essentially reward dishonest actors over honest staking participants such as Alice.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution mechanism of the NFTXInventoryStaking system, specifically in the interaction between the deposit function of the XTokenUpgradeable contract and the publicly callable distribute function of the NFTXSimpleFeeDistributor contract. The contract is designed to represent staked vault tokens (xTokens) and to allocate protocol fees as rewards to holders of those xTokens. However, deposits become eligible for reward calculation immediately after they are made, and the reward distribution routine reads the current total supply and balance at the moment of execution without any historical averaging or lock‑up period. Moreover, the distribute function lacks any access control, allowing any external actor to trigger a distribution at any time. Because the deposit timelock is only two seconds, an attacker can observe a pending transaction that intends to call distribute, front‑run that transaction by depositing a large amount of vault tokens in the same block (or the next block, given the ≈13‑second block time), and thereby obtain a disproportionate share of the newly minted rewards. After the distribution, the attacker can immediately withdraw their stake, redeeming the inflated share of the reward pool while the honest staker, who deposited earlier, receives only a reduced portion of the intended reward. The impact is a direct siphoning of fees that should have been shared fairly among all participants; honest users see their expected refunds shrink or disappear, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional reward allocation are broken. This flaw manifests whenever a reward distribution transaction is visible in the mempool and the attacker possesses sufficient capital to out‑scale the existing pool balance, which is feasible because the protocol does not enforce a sufficient delay between deposit and reward eligibility and does not restrict who can trigger a distribution. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by examining the logical flow of reward calculations and noticing the absence of a time‑weighted balance or role‑based guard on the distribution entry point. It can be difficult to detect in production because the total reward amount transferred appears correct, while the individual allocation is subtly shifted, leading to only a modest loss per exploit that may be masked by normal fee variance. To remediate, the protocol should impose a meaningful deposit delay (e.g., a 20‑block lock‑up) that exceeds the typical block propagation time, replace the instantaneous balance snapshot with a time‑weighted‑average‑balance (TWAB) or similar accounting method, and restrict the distribute function to a privileged role so that only authorized contracts or governance can trigger reward payouts. These changes would ensure that rewards are calculated based on holdings over a defined period, preventing front‑running attacks and preserving the fairness of the fee‑distribution model.

title: No checks if given product is created by the factory
description:
An attacker can create a fake product. `Collateral` contract does not check whether the given product is created by the factory. A malicious product can return arbitrary maintenance amounts, therefore they can make any deposit to fake product stuck (simply return collateral - 1 as maintenance) and fake product owner can change the maintenance and liquidate whenever wanted and claim full collateral.

This is a serious attack vector, since by only interacting with `Collateral` contract the user can lose funds. Furthermore, this vulnerability poses big risks in combination with web vulnerabilities. Users always have to check the product address to avoid getting scammed, but likely most users will only check the contract address.

Furthermore, if another protocol would want to add perennial protocol for its use case, the other protocol has to be careful with this behaviour and keep track of whitelisted products. This complicates adoption of perennial protocol, since whitelist has to be managed manually or else this vulnerability will likely be exploitable.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Collateral contract of the Perennial protocol, which accepts an arbitrary product address from callers without verifying that the product was instantiated by the authorized factory. Because the contract does not enforce a whitelist or any provenance check, an attacker can deploy a counterfeit product contract that implements the required interface but returns malicious values for the maintenance calculation. In a typical user flow, a participant supplies the address of a seemingly legitimate product and deposits collateral. The counterfeit product can report a maintenance amount that is deliberately set to collateral minus one, effectively locking the user’s funds inside the Collateral contract. Later, the attacker, acting as the product owner, can modify the maintenance value or trigger the liquidation function, causing the contract to release the entire collateral amount to the malicious product owner. The impact is a direct loss of user funds, with the victim seeing their balance reduced to zero or receiving no refund after a deposit that appeared successful. This flaw is triggered whenever a user interacts with Collateral functions that take a product address as a parameter; the contract does not discriminate between genuine factory‑created products and arbitrary contracts. All participants who rely on the Collateral contract—regular users, integrators, and other protocols that might whitelist products—are potentially exposed. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit that inspected the authorization logic of the Collateral module. The problem can be difficult to spot in a UI because users typically see only the product contract address and may assume that any address accepted by the protocol is safe, overlooking the need to verify the factory source. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control or unchecked external address vulnerabilities, where a trust boundary is improperly assumed. To remediate the defect, the Collateral contract should maintain a mapping of approved product addresses that is updated by the factory, or it should directly query the factory to confirm that a given product was created by the authorized source before accepting it. This adds a small gas overhead but restores the intended security model, ensuring that deposits cannot be hijacked by a fake product and that users receive the expected refund or balance after interacting with the protocol.

title: `cancelPromotion`
bug_full: The contract contains a logical flaw in the cancellation flow for promotions that have not yet started. The function `cancelPromotion()` internally calls `_getRemainingRewards()`, which in turn invokes `_getCurrentEpochId()`. The epoch calculation in `_getCurrentEpochId()` subtracts the promotion's `startTimestamp` from the current `block.timestamp` and then divides by the epoch duration. Because both timestamps are stored as unsigned integers, when the promotion's `startTimestamp` is in the future (i.e., the promotion has not begun), the subtraction `block.timestamp - _promotion.startTimestamp` underflows, causing the transaction to revert. This revert prevents the cancellation logic from executing and consequently blocks the refund of the promotion's allocated tokens. The vulnerability arises from the missing guard that checks whether the promotion has already started before performing the subtraction. An attacker who is the promotion owner can trigger the failure by calling `cancelPromotion()` before the scheduled start time, resulting in a denial‑of‑service situation where the promotion's tokens become permanently locked in the contract. Users observing the UI will see that the promotion cannot be canceled and that the expected refund of tokens never arrives, possibly showing a zero balance or a stuck promotion state. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the call stack of `cancelPromotion()` and identified the unsafe timestamp arithmetic. It is difficult to notice because the code appears to correctly compute remaining rewards for active promotions; the edge case of a future `startTimestamp` does not surface during normal operation. To resolve the problem, the contract should first verify that the promotion has actually started (`_promotion.startTimestamp <= block.timestamp`) before performing any subtraction, and in the case of a pre‑start cancellation it should directly refund the full amount of `tokensPerEpoch * numberOfEpochs` to the caller, bypassing the epoch calculation entirely. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a promotion can be cancelled before it begins and that the promoter should recover their deposited tokens.

title: getRewardsAmount doesn’t check epochs haven’t been claimed
description:
In ITwabRewards.sol, it is claimed that `getRewardsAmount` should account for epochs that have already been claimed, and not include these epochs in the total amount (indeed, there is a line that says `@dev Will be 0 if user has already claimed rewards for the epoch.`)

However, no such check is done in the implementation of `getRewardsAmount`. This means that users will be shown rewardAmounts that are higher than they should be, and users will be confused when they are transferred fewer tokens than they are told they will. This would cause confusion, and people may begin to mistrust the contract since they think they are being transferred fewer tokens than they are owed.
poc:
See the implementation of `getRewardsAmount` here: <https://github.com/pooltogether/v4-periphery/blob/b520faea26bcf60371012f6cb246aa149abd3c7d/contracts/TwabRewards.sol#L209>

Notice that there are no checks that the epochs have not already been claimed. Compare this to `claimRewards` which _does_ check for epochs that have already been claimed with the following require statement:
```solidity
require(!_isClaimedEpoch(_userClaimedEpochs, _epochId), "TwabRewards/rewards-already-claimed");
```
A similar check should be added to `getRewardsAmount` so that previously claimed epochs are not included in the sum.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑view function of the TwabRewards contract. The function that calculates the total pending rewards for a user – getRewardsAmount – is documented to return zero for any epoch that the user has already claimed, but the implementation does not actually verify whether each epoch in the sum has been claimed. The root cause is the omission of a check against the user's claimed‑epoch bitmap, a check that is present in the state‑changing claimRewards function. When a user invokes getRewardsAmount, the function iterates over the requested epoch range and adds the raw epoch reward amounts without filtering out those that have already been paid out. Consequently, the returned figure can be inflated, showing a higher reward amount than the user is truly entitled to. An attacker does not gain direct financial advantage from this bug, but the inflated number can mislead honest users: they are shown a reward amount that appears correct, they proceed to claim, and the contract transfers fewer tokens than the earlier view indicated. This discrepancy creates confusion, erodes trust in the protocol, and may lead users to suspect that the contract is intentionally short‑changing them. The issue manifests whenever a user queries pending rewards for epochs that include at least one previously claimed epoch – a common scenario for regular participants who claim rewards periodically. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when the auditors compared the logic of getRewardsAmount with the logic of claimRewards and noticed the missing require statement that rejects already‑claimed epochs. Because getRewardsAmount is a view‑only function, the mismatch does not raise an exception and can silently pass unnoticed until a user compares the displayed amount with the actual transfer. To remediate, the contract should incorporate the same claimed‑epoch verification used in claimRewards, ensuring that only unclaimed epochs contribute to the calculated sum. This correction aligns the function’s behavior with its documentation, restores accurate reward visibility, and prevents user‑perceived loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state‑dependent checks are omitted from read‑only calculations, leading to inconsistent UI data and broken business assumptions about reward entitlement.

title: Dust Token Balances Cannot Be Claimed By An `admin` Account
description: Users who have a small claim on rewards for various promotions, may not feasibly be able to claim these rewards as gas costs could outweigh the sum they receive in return. Hence, it is likely that a dust balance accrues over time for tokens allocated for various promotions. Additionally, the `_calculateRewardAmount` calculation may result in truncated results, leading to further accrual of a dust balance. Therefore, it is useful that these funds do not go to waste.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the permanent accumulation of dust token balances in promotion reward contracts that cannot be reclaimed by an administrative account. The root cause is two‑fold: first, the reward calculation routine uses integer division or truncates fractional values when determining each participant's share, which discards any remainder smaller than the token's smallest unit; second, the contract does not expose any function that permits an admin to withdraw or skim these leftover tokens after a promotion becomes inactive. When a user attempts to claim a reward that is smaller than the gas cost required to execute the transaction, the claim either fails or returns zero, leaving a tiny amount of tokens locked in the contract. Over time, as many users claim small rewards, the unrecoverable remainder aggregates into a dust balance that is invisible to the UI because the displayed reward amount rounds down to zero. This issue was identified during a manual audit of the reward distribution logic, where the auditor noted that the `_calculateRewardAmount` function returns truncated results and that no admin withdrawal path exists for dormant promotion pools. The problem is subtle because the amounts involved are small, making it easy to overlook in testing and during normal operation, and because the contract correctly records the balances on‑chain even though they cannot be accessed. The impact is that protocol funds are effectively lost, reducing the economic incentive for users, breaking the accounting assumption that all allocated promotion tokens will eventually be distributed or reclaimed, and potentially undermining trust in the fairness of the promotion system. The vulnerability manifests when a promotion has been active long enough for most users to claim their rewards and only fractional leftovers remain, or when the promotion becomes inactive without a cleanup mechanism. Affected parties include end‑users who expect to receive a reward (but see a zero payout), the protocol that earmarks tokens for promotions, and any admin or governance participant who cannot recover the residual dust. To remediate, the contract should implement a controlled admin “skim” or “sweep” function that can be invoked after a configurable inactivity period, allowing the protocol to reclaim and possibly re‑allocate the dust balances. This function must be gated by proper access control and emit events for transparency. Additionally, the reward calculation should be revised to handle fractional amounts more accurately, for example by using a higher‑precision arithmetic library or by rounding up small remainders to the nearest claimable unit, thereby minimizing the creation of dust in the first place. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of "dust accumulation" and "rounding/truncation" vulnerabilities where leftover token amounts become permanently inaccessible due to missing administrative withdrawal paths, leading to unexpected loss of funds and a mismatch between expected and actual reward outcomes.

title: Multiple initialization of Collateral contract
description: The attacker can initialize the contract, take malicious actions, and allow it to be re-initialized by the project without any error being noticed.
poc:
The `initialize` method of the `Collateral` contract does not contain the `initializer` modifier, it delegates this process to check if the factory is different from address(0) in the `UFactoryProvider__initialize` call, however the `factory_` is other than address(0), so an attacker could use front-running by listening to the memory pool, initialize the contract with a `factory=address(0)`, perform malicious actions, and still allow it to be started later by the project without noticing any error.

Source reference:

  * Collateral.initialize
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑initialization flaw in the Collateral contract where the initialise routine can be executed more than once because it lacks the standard OpenZeppelin `initializer` guard. The root cause is the absence of a state flag that records whether the contract has already been set up, combined with a weak check that only verifies that the supplied factory address is non‑zero for a particular internal call. As a result an attacker – either the original deployer or a front‑runner listening to the mempool – can invoke `initialize` with a deliberately crafted set of parameters, for example setting `factory` to the zero address and supplying a malicious token reference. This first initialisation creates a temporary state in which the contract believes it is attached to a token that the attacker controls, allowing the attacker to perform privileged actions such as issuing tokens, moving collateral, or manipulating accounting values. Because the contract does not prevent a second call to `initialize`, the legitimate project can later call the same function with the correct factory address and the transaction will succeed without reverting, effectively overwriting the previous factory address while leaving the malicious state‑changing actions already performed in place. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken – depositors may see their balances reduced, refunds become zero, or tokens appear immutable while actually being swapped behind the scenes. Users expect that once collateral is set up the underlying token cannot change, but the flaw allows that expectation to be violated, leading to potential loss of funds or a rug pull on future depositors. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed without an initialization guard and the initialise function is called more than once, which is plausible in upgradeable or factory‑based deployments where the contract is expected to be initialised exactly once. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Perennial protocol when reviewers noticed that `Collateral.initialize` does not carry the `initializer` modifier and can be called repeatedly. The problem is subtle because the second, legitimate initialisation does not produce an error, making the earlier malicious state hard to detect from the outside. To remediate the flaw, the contract should be modified to include an `initializer` modifier or an equivalent one‑time‑only check that marks the contract as initialized and rejects any further calls, and it should enforce that the factory address cannot be the zero address. This change restores the invariant that the collateral token and factory are immutable after deployment, preventing the class of re‑initialisation attacks that compromise accounting and user funds.

title: Chainlink’s `latestRoundData` might return stale or incorrect results
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract reads price data from a Chainlink oracle using the `latestRoundData` function without validating that the returned round is fresh and reliable. The function returns a tuple that includes the round identifier, the price, a timestamp, and an `answeredInRound` field that indicates which round actually provided the answer. Because the contract does not check any of these fields, it may accept a price that is stale, zero, or otherwise incorrect. This situation can arise when the oracle has not updated its price for a number of blocks, when the answer is being carried over from a previous round, or when the round is still incomplete and the timestamp is zero. An attacker or a market participant could exploit the oversight by waiting for a period in which the oracle data is outdated and then submitting transactions that rely on the stale price, causing the protocol to compute collateral values, liquidation thresholds, or trade settlements based on inaccurate information. The impact includes potential under‑collateralization, unintended liquidations, loss of funds for borrowers or lenders, and a general erosion of trust in the protocol’s pricing logic. The issue manifests whenever the `sync` function is called and the oracle returns data that fails to meet freshness criteria; the contract will still accept it, push it into `priceAtVersion`, and emit an event, giving the appearance that a new, valid price was recorded. Users interacting with the UI may see a price update on the screen but, in reality, the underlying value has not changed, leading to situations where a user expects a refund or a trade at a current market price but receives an amount based on an old price, effectively “money disappears” from the user's perspective. The bug belongs to the class of oracle‑staleness or data‑integrity vulnerabilities where external data sources are trusted without verification. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by cross‑referencing Chainlink’s documentation on historical rounds and the FAQ that explicitly advises checking the `answeredInRound` and timestamp fields. The problem is subtle because the function call succeeds without reverting, and developers often assume that `latestRoundData` always returns the most recent round, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should validate that the returned price is positive, that `answeredInRound` is greater than or equal to the round ID (indicating the answer is not carried over from a previous round), and that the timestamp is non‑zero and within an acceptable delay window. Adding these checks aligns the implementation with the recommended Chainlink usage pattern and restores confidence that price updates reflect fresh market data.

title: Unsafe uint64 casting may overflow
description: The `_calculateRewardAmount` function casts epoch timestamps from uint256 to uint64 and these may overflow. The epochStartTimestamp value is a function of the user-supplied `_epochId` value, which could be extremely large (up to 2**255 – 1). While Solidity 0.8.x checks for overflows on arithmetic operations, it does not do so for casting – the OpenZeppelin SafeCast library offers this. The overflow condition could cause `_epochStartTimestamp > _epochEndTimestamp`, which the Ticket.sol getAverageBalanceBetween may not be expected to handle. The `_epochStartTimestamp` could overflow to have a value before the actual start of the promotion, also impacting the rewards calculation.
poc: There are 4 uint64 casting operations in the `_calculateRewardAmount` function of `TwabRewards.sol`: <https://github.com/pooltogether/v4-periphery/blob/b520faea26bcf60371012f6cb246aa149abd3c7d/contracts/TwabRewards.sol#L304-L312>
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unsafe cast of large unsigned integers to a 64‑bit type within the reward‑calculation routine of a token‑staking contract. Specifically, the function that determines a participant’s reward converts epoch timestamps, which are stored as uint256, into uint64 values. Because the epoch identifier supplied by a caller can be arbitrarily large – up to 2**255‑1 – the product of the epoch duration and the epoch identifier may exceed the maximum value representable by uint64 (2**64‑1). Solidity 0.8.x automatically checks for arithmetic overflows, but it does not enforce overflow checks on explicit type casts. Consequently, the cast silently truncates the higher bits, causing the derived start timestamp to wrap around to a much smaller number. This wrap‑around can make the calculated start timestamp appear earlier than the actual promotion start or even earlier than the end timestamp, violating the assumption that _epochStartTimestamp < _epochEndTimestamp that downstream accounting functions rely on. When the contract later invokes the average‑balance calculation with these malformed timestamps, the logic may treat the period as negative or extremely long, leading to an incorrect reward amount – either zero reward for legitimate participants or an inflated reward that can drain the contract’s funds. The issue manifests when a malicious actor submits a fabricated epoch identifier or when an unusually large epoch duration is configured, both of which are technically possible under the current public interface. The affected parties are any users of the staking protocol who expect to receive correctly calculated rewards, as well as the protocol itself, whose economic model depends on accurate accounting. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by a security research team that examined the casting logic and identified that SafeCast was not used despite the known risk of overflow on down‑casting. The problem is subtle because the contract will still compile and pass basic tests; the incorrect timestamps may only surface under edge‑case inputs that are not exercised by typical unit tests, making the bug hard to notice without targeted analysis. To remediate the issue, the contract should avoid casting from uint256 to uint64 without safety checks; the most robust approach is to store epoch timestamps directly as uint64, eliminating the need for a cast, or to employ OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library and add explicit require statements that enforce _epochEndTimestamp > _epochStartTimestamp after casting. These measures prevent the timestamp overflow, restore the correctness of reward calculations, and protect user funds from unintended loss or over‑payment.

title: Missing Check When Transferring Tokens Out For A Given Promotion
description:
The `claimRewards` function is called upon by ticket holders who parse a set of `_epochIds` they wish to claim rewards on. An internal call is made to `_calculateRewardAmount` to calculate the correct reward amount owed to the user. Subsequently, the `_updateClaimedEpoch` function will set the epoch bit of the tracked `_claimedEpochs` mapping, ensuring an `epochId` cannot be claimed twice for a given promotion.

However, there may be inaccuracies in the `_calculateRewardAmount` function, which results in more tokens being sent out than allocated by a promotion creator. This severely impacts the ability for users to claim their owed tokens on other promotions.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming flow of a promotion contract. When a ticket holder invokes the claimRewards function, the contract iterates over the supplied epoch identifiers, checks that each epoch has not been claimed before, calls an internal routine to calculate the reward amount for that epoch, updates the claimed‑epoch bitmap, and finally transfers the accumulated token amount to the caller. The core issue is that the contract does not verify that the sum of rewards calculated for a promotion remains within the total token balance that the promotion creator allocated for that promotion. Consequently, if the internal _calculateRewardAmount routine returns a value that is larger than the entitlement – for example because of a rounding error, incorrect formula, or a deliberately crafted promotion with a fake ticket – the contract will happily transfer the excessive amount. Because there is no ceiling check, the promotion’s token reserve can be exhausted, which in turn prevents other legitimate users from receiving their rightful rewards on the same or different promotions. The bug manifests whenever a user claims rewards against a promotion whose calculated rewards exceed the remaining allocation, which can be triggered by supplying a crafted set of epoch IDs or by exploiting a promotion that was created with insufficient safeguards. The affected parties include promotion creators (who lose allocated tokens), regular users (who may later receive zero or reduced rewards), and the protocol itself, which suffers a breach of its accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the logical flow of reward distribution and identified the missing total‑allocation check. It is subtle because the contract does not revert on over‑payment; the transaction succeeds and the user receives tokens, making the over‑payment appear legitimate until the promotion balance is unexpectedly depleted. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected large payouts on the first claim followed by missing or zero payouts for subsequent claims, violating the expectation that a promotion’s reward pool is finite and evenly distributed. This class of bug falls under unchecked accounting or supply‑cap violations, where a contract fails to enforce that the total disbursed amount does not exceed a predefined budget. The recommended remediation is to introduce a guard before the safeTransfer that ensures the cumulative claimed rewards for a promotion never exceed the promotion’s allocated token balance, and to enforce per‑epoch or per‑claim caps where appropriate. By adding this check, the contract preserves its invariant that the sum of all rewards paid out is bounded by the promotion’s funding, thereby preventing attackers from draining funds and preserving fairness for all participants.

title: AaveYield: Misspelled external function name making functions fail
description:
In `AaveYield.sol` the functions:

  * `liquidityToken`
  * `_withdrawETH`
  * `_depositETH`

Make a conditional call to `IWETHGateway(wethGateway).getAWETHAddress()`

This function does not exist in the `wethGateway` contract, causing these function to fail with the error `"Fallback not allowed"`.

The function they should be calling is `getWethAddress()` without the “A”.

Small yet dangerous typo.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misspelled external function call in the AaveYield contract. The contract attempts to retrieve the wrapped Ether (WETH) address by invoking a function named getAWETHAddress on the WETHGateway contract. The actual WETHGateway implementation, however, provides a function called getWethAddress – the extra "A" in the called name makes the selector point to a non‑existent function. Because the WETHGateway contract does not implement a fallback function (the fallback is explicitly disabled), the call reverts with the error "Fallback not allowed". This mistake is present in three entry points: the public liquidityToken view, the internal _withdrawETH routine, and the internal _depositETH routine. Whenever a user or another contract tries to deposit ETH, withdraw ETH, or query the liquidity token, the contract executes the faulty call, causing the entire transaction to fail. From a user perspective the UI may report that a deposit or withdrawal cannot be completed, that no tokens are received, or that the operation appears to have stalled despite the user having approved the transaction. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any workflow that depends on ETH handling, effectively preventing users from adding or removing liquidity with ETH and potentially halting revenue generation for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit when the auditor compared the interface definition (IWETHGateway) against the deployed WETHGateway contract and noticed the mismatched function name. It can be difficult to spot because the Solidity compiler does not verify that an external call matches the runtime contract’s ABI; the error only surfaces at execution time. The bug belongs to the class of interface mismatch or incorrect function selector errors, where a typo in the function name leads to an unintended call to a non‑existent selector. To remediate the problem, the contract should be updated to call the correct function name getWethAddress, or the IWETHGateway interface should be modified to reflect the actual gateway API. An alternative defensive measure is to wrap the external call in a try/catch block and provide a graceful fallback, or to add a permissive fallback function in the WETHGateway contract that returns a sensible default. By aligning the function name with the gateway’s ABI, the contract will be able to retrieve the WETH address correctly, allowing ETH deposits and withdrawals to succeed and restoring the intended business logic of liquidity management.

title: Missing approve
description: There are 3 instances where the `IERC20.approve()` function is called only once without setting the allowance to zero. Some tokens, like USDT, require first reducing the address’ allowance to zero by calling `approve(_spender, 0)`. Transactions will revert when using an unsupported token like USDT (see the `approve()` function requirement [at line 199](https://etherscan.io/address/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#code)).
poc:
* [CreditLine/CreditLine.sol:647](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/CreditLine/CreditLine.sol#L647)
  * [CreditLine/CreditLine.sol:779](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/CreditLine/CreditLine.sol#L779)
  * [yield/AaveYield.sol:324](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/yield/AaveYield.sol#L324)

Note: the usage of `approve()` in yield/CompoundYield.sol ([lines 211-212](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/yield/CompoundYield.sol#L211-L212)), in yield/YearnYield.sol ([lines 211-212](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/yield/YearnYield.sol#L210-L211)), and in yield/AaveYield.sol ([lines 297-298](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/yield/AaveYield.sol#L297-L298)) do not need modification since it they already use the recommended approach. Additionally the usage of `approve()` in [yield/AaveYield.sol:307](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/9df1b7c4247f8631647c7627a8da9bdc16db8b11/contracts/yield/AaveYield.sol#L307) likely does not need modification since that approve function only handles ETH.
bug_full: The contract contains an allowance‑setting flaw that stems from the way ERC‑20 approvals are performed. In three places the code invokes the standard IERC20.approve(spender, amount) function without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. Certain token implementations, most notably USDT, enforce a non‑standard rule that requires the allowance of a spender to be cleared (approved with a value of 0) before it can be set to a new non‑zero amount. The root cause is an assumption that all ERC‑20 tokens follow the original OpenZeppelin specification, which permits a direct change of allowance, whereas the actual token contract includes a guard that reverts the transaction if the current allowance is not zero. As a result, when a user attempts to interact with the protocol using an unsupported token such as USDT, the approval transaction fails and the subsequent operation that depends on that allowance—typically a token transfer, deposit, or yield‑generation step—reverts. The exploitation scenario is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft any special payload; they simply trigger a legitimate user flow (e.g., opening a credit line or depositing into a yield strategy) with a token that enforces the zero‑allowance rule. The protocol’s contract attempts to approve the token for a spender, the token contract reverts, and the user experience degrades to a transaction that appears to have been submitted but never completes. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a pending transaction that never confirms, or it may display an error message indicating a failure to approve the token, leading to symptoms such as “no funds were deposited”, “balance remains unchanged”, or “deposit failed without a clear reason”. The impact is primarily on availability: legitimate users cannot use certain popular stablecoins, reducing the protocol’s usability and potentially driving users away. No direct theft of assets occurs because the failure happens before any token transfer, but the loss of functional access can be significant for a DeFi product that relies on broad token support. This issue was discovered during a manual security audit where the auditors reviewed the approve calls and compared them against known token standards, noticing the missing zero‑allowance reset for USDT. The problem can be hard to notice because most ERC‑20 tokens accept a direct allowance change, so the contract appears to work correctly with the majority of tokens, masking the edge case. To remediate the vulnerability the contract should adopt the two‑step approval pattern: first call approve(spender, 0) to clear any existing allowance, then call approve(spender, desiredAmount). This pattern aligns with the ERC‑20 token reference implementation and satisfies tokens with stricter allowance rules. Implementing this change across all approval sites restores compatibility with USDT and similar tokens, eliminating the revert scenario and re‑establishing expected functionality for users who expect their deposits or credit line openings to succeed after approval.

title: Ether can be locked in the `PoolFactory` contract without a way to retrieve it
description:
If a borrower calls the `createPool` function with a non-zero value, but also includes an ERC20 token address for `_collateralToken`, then the Ether value sent will be locked in the `PoolFactory` contract forever.

  * [createPool L260-317](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/main/contracts/Pool/PoolFactory.sol#L260-L317)

In the `_createPool` function, a `_collateralToken` address other than the zero address will set the `amount` variable to zero. That `amount` variable will be passed to `create2` which will send 0 wei to the newly created `Pool` contract.
    
```solidity
uint256 amount = _collateralToken == address(0) ? _collateralAmount : 0;
```
poc: A borrower reuses a script they made to create a pool and deposit collateral. They intend to deposit Ether as collateral so they send value with the transaction, but forget to change the `_collateralToken` address to address(0). The `Pool` contract will be deployed using the `_collateralToken`, and will lock the Ether sent in the `PoolFactory`
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the pool creation flow of the protocol's factory contract. When a borrower invokes the createPool function, they may optionally supply an ERC20 token address as the collateral token (_collateralToken) and also attach native Ether (msg.value) to the transaction. The implementation contains a conditional that sets the variable amount to the provided collateral amount only if the collateral token address is the zero address; otherwise, amount is forced to zero. This amount is later used as the value sent to the newly deployed Pool contract via CREATE2. Consequently, if a caller sends Ether while also specifying a non‑zero ERC20 token address, the factory forwards zero wei to the new pool, leaving the sent Ether trapped in the factory's balance. The root cause is a missing cross‑validation between the presence of Ether and the choice of collateral token, allowing user error to translate into an irreversible asset lock.

An attacker does not need to exploit a traditional security flaw; the issue is triggered simply by honest users who mistakenly combine Ether with an ERC20 collateral token. Once the transaction is mined, the Ether is no longer accessible because the factory contract does not provide any withdrawal mechanism for that balance, effectively disappearing from the user's perspective. Users experience symptoms such as their wallet balance decreasing while the newly created pool shows no received funds, or the UI indicating a successful pool creation but their deposited Ether never appearing in the pool's balance. The impact is limited to loss of the specific amount of Ether sent in the erroneous transaction; no other assets are compromised, but the protocol's usability and trustworthiness are degraded.

The condition occurs only when msg.value > 0 and _collateralToken != address(0). It is a classic example of an asset‑locking logic error caused by inadequate input validation, falling under the broader class of "fund‑locking" or "mis‑configuration" bugs. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the createPool logic and identified the discrepancy between the collateral token selection and the Ether forwarding path. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the contract does not emit an explicit error; the funds simply become inaccessible, which may only be observed later when users query balances or notice missing refunds.

To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a sanity check that either (i) requires _collateralToken to be the zero address whenever msg.value is non‑zero, or (ii) rejects transactions that attempt to send Ether while also specifying a non‑zero token address. Additionally, providing a withdrawal function or a rescue mechanism for stuck Ether could mitigate the impact of user mistakes. By aligning the business logic—where Ether can only be used as collateral when no ERC20 token is supplied—the protocol restores its intended accounting guarantees and prevents inadvertent loss of user funds.

title: CreditLine.liquidate doesn’t transfer borrowed ETH to a lender
description: Funds that are acquired from a liquidator and should be sent to a lender are left with the contract instead. The funds aren’t lost, but after the fact mitigation will require manual accounting and fund transfer for each CreditLine.liquidate usage.
poc: ETH sent to CreditLine.liquidate by an external liquidator when `autoLiquidation` is enabled remain with the contract and aren’t transferred to the lender: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-sublime/blob/main/contracts/CreditLine/CreditLine.sol#L1015>
bug_full: The CreditLine contract contains a liquidation logic error that prevents the borrowed amount of native ETH from being transferred to the lender when a liquidator calls CreditLine.liquidate with autoLiquidation enabled. The function correctly calculates the excess ETH (msg.value minus the amount needed to cover the borrower’s debt) and returns that excess to the liquidator, but it never sends the borrowed ETH that should compensate the lender. This omission is caused by a missing transfer statement in the ETH‑specific branch of the liquidate implementation; the code only contains a conditional that refunds the surplus to msg.sender and lacks a call to transfer the borrowed tokens to the _lender address. An attacker (or any external liquidator) can trigger liquidation as intended, and the transaction will appear successful – no revert or error is emitted – yet the lender’s balance remains unchanged while the contract’s internal ETH balance increases by the amount that should have been paid out. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful liquidation event, but the expected receipt of ETH by the lender does not occur, leading to symptoms such as “my loan was liquidated but I received no payment” or “the contract’s ETH balance grew unexpectedly”. The bug is hard to notice because the funds are not lost; they are merely retained in the contract, and no explicit error flag is raised. This breaks the protocol’s accounting assumptions that liquidation fully settles the borrower’s debt and compensates the lender, potentially causing mismatched accounting, delayed manual fund transfers, and increased operational risk for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation path for native assets and compared it with the ERC20 path, where a proper transfer to the lender is performed. To remediate, the liquidation logic should include an explicit call that transfers the borrowed ETH amount to the lender before any surplus is returned to the liquidator, mirroring the behavior of the ERC20 branch and ensuring that the lender is correctly paid and the contract’s balance reflects only transient surplus funds.

title: Collateral can be deposited in a finished pool
description: Collateral can be deposited in a finished pool.
poc: The depositCollateral function doesn’t check the status of the pool so collateral can be deposited in a finished loan. This can happen by mistake and all funds will be lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing status check in the function that accepts collateral deposits for a loan pool. The contract allows users to call the depositCollateral method without verifying that the loan is currently in an active or collection state. Because the loan lifecycle includes a finished state—when the loan has been repaid, defaulted, or otherwise closed—the function should reject any further deposits at that point. The root cause is a business‑logic validation omission: the contract does not enforce the invariant that collateral can only be added while the loan is open. An attacker, or a careless user, can therefore send assets to the depositCollateral endpoint after the loan has been marked finished. The transaction will appear successful on‑chain, but the protocol’s internal accounting will treat the pool as closed and will never provide a path to withdraw the newly added assets. From the user’s perspective the funds disappear: the transaction receipt shows a successful deposit, yet the user’s balance in the protocol remains zero and no withdrawal function is available. This scenario can happen whenever a user interacts with the UI after the loan has been settled, or if a malicious actor deliberately calls the function with a finished loan identifier. The impact is primarily financial loss for the depositor; the protocol itself does not expose direct asset risk, but the incident undermines confidence in the system’s correctness and could affect its availability if many erroneous deposits accumulate. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the loan lifecycle functions and noticed the absence of a status guard in depositCollateral. It is difficult to notice because the function does not revert or emit a warning; the only symptom is the silent loss of funds after a seemingly normal transaction. This type of bug falls under the class of insufficient state validation or business‑logic access control errors, where functions accept inputs that should be prohibited by the contract’s state machine. To remediate, the depositCollateral implementation should include a require statement that checks the loan’s current status and only permits deposits when the loan is in an "active" or "collection" state, rejecting any attempts otherwise. By restoring the intended state invariant, the protocol can prevent accidental or malicious collateral loss and align on‑chain behavior with user expectations that deposits are only possible while a loan is open.

title: Unlinked address can link immediately again
description:
After a master calls unlinkAddress() to unlink an address, the address that has just been unlinked can directly link again without permission. The address that is just unlinked can call linkAddress(masterAddress) which will execute because pendingLinkAddresses is still set. Assuming the master has unlinked for a good reason it is unwanted to be able to be linked again without any permission from the master.

Note: a master can prevent this by calling cancelAddressLinkingRequest(), but this doesn’t seem logical to do
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract manages the pending linking state for address relationships. When a master address calls unlinkAddress() to remove a linked address, the contract correctly deletes the stored linked address information, but it fails to clear the corresponding entry in the pendingLinkAddresses mapping. Because pendingLinkAddresses[msg.sender][_masterAddress] remains true after the unlink operation, the previously unlinked address can immediately call linkAddress(masterAddress) and satisfy both the check that it is not already linked and the pending‑request check. This logical oversight allows the unlinked participant to re‑establish the link without any explicit approval from the master, effectively bypassing the intended permission model. The exploit can be carried out in a single transaction: the attacker first triggers the unlink (or waits for the master to do so), then invokes linkAddress with the same master address, and the contract will execute the internal _linkAddress routine while leaving the pending flag untouched. The impact is a breach of the master’s authority over its linked addresses; a master may think it has revoked a relationship for security or compliance reasons, yet the revoked address regains full privileges instantly. This situation can lead to unauthorized actions such as asset transfers, role‑based function calls, or any business logic that assumes a revoked address no longer has access. The issue manifests only after an unlink operation; if no unlink occurs, the pending flag behaves as intended. It primarily affects masters who rely on the unlink mechanism to enforce policy, as well as any users or auditors who monitor address relationships for correctness. The flaw was discovered during a code audit that inspected the unlinking flow and observed that the pendingLinkAddresses entry was never cleared, a condition that can be easily missed in functional testing because the contract still allows a link but the UI or logs may not immediately show the inconsistency. Because the pending flag lives in a separate mapping, the bug is subtle and does not raise an exception, making it hard to notice without a targeted review of state changes. The appropriate remediation is to delete the pendingLinkAddresses entry for the address that is being linked after a successful link, or to clear it as part of the unlink routine, ensuring that the pending state cannot be reused unintentionally. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of "state‑invalidation" bugs where a flag governing future actions is not reset after a state transition, leading to unauthorized re‑use of stale permissions. From a user perspective, the symptoms may appear as a previously removed address still being able to perform actions, balances remaining unchanged despite revocation, or a UI indicating that the address was unlinked while the contract still permits linking. The expectation that an unlink permanently disables the address’s ability to re‑link is violated, breaking the accounting assumption that permissions are strictly monotonic unless explicitly re‑granted by the master.

title: Extension voting threshold check needs to rerun on each transfer
description: The `Extension` contract correctly reduces votes from the `from` address of a transfer and adds it to the `to` address of the transfer (in case both of them voted on it before), but it does not rerun the voting logic in `voteOnExtension` that actually grants the extension. This leads to issues where an extension should be granted but is not:
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance Extension contract where vote balances are transferred between addresses during a token transfer, but the contract fails to re‑evaluate the extension‑granting threshold after the transfer. When a user moves tokens, the contract correctly subtracts any votes attached to the sender (the `from` address) and adds them to the recipient (the `to` address) if both parties had previously voted on the same extension. The root cause is that the function responsible for applying the voting threshold – the logic inside `voteOnExtension` that decides whether the accumulated support reaches the required level to activate the extension – is not invoked after the vote balances have been updated. Consequently, a situation can arise where the total support for an extension actually exceeds the required threshold after a transfer, but the extension remains inactive because the threshold check was never re‑run. An attacker or any participant can trigger this condition by transferring tokens from an address that does not contribute votes to an address that does, thereby increasing the overall vote count without causing the contract to recognize that the threshold has been met. The impact is a logical dead‑lock: extensions that should become available – for example, new protocol features, fee rebates, or permissioned actions – stay disabled, breaking the intended governance flow and potentially preventing users from accessing promised functionality. This issue emerges on every token transfer that moves voting power and is especially pronounced when the recipient’s vote weight pushes the total over the required level while the sender contributed none. It affects all token holders who rely on the extension mechanism, the protocol’s governance process, and any downstream contracts that assume extensions are granted once the threshold is satisfied. The flaw was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it may be difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an error or revert; the UI will still display the updated vote totals, yet the extension’s state does not change, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual behavior. To remediate the issue, the contract should invoke the same threshold‑checking routine used in `voteOnExtension` after adjusting votes in the `removeVotes` (or equivalent) path, ensuring that any increase in total support immediately triggers the extension grant if the threshold is met. This change restores the invariant that a sufficient vote tally always results in the extension becoming active, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic and governance expectations.

title: `NoYield.sol` Tokens with fee on transfer are not supported
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s token‑locking routine, which treats every ERC‑20 transfer as a fee‑free operation. When a user calls the lock function, the contract blindly records the requested amount as the number of shares to be issued, assuming that the exact same token quantity will be received. However, a class of ERC‑20 tokens implements a transfer fee (often called fee‑on‑transfer or deflationary tokens) that deducts a portion of the amount during the transfer. As a result, the contract actually receives less than the amount declared by the caller, but it still credits the user with the full amount in shares. Later, when the unlock routine attempts to return the original amount to the user, it tries to transfer more tokens than are held in the contract. This mismatch triggers a revert due to insufficient balance, effectively locking the user’s funds inside the contract. The issue is manifested when a user deposits a fee‑on‑transfer token, receives a confirmation that the deposit succeeded, but later observes that their withdrawal either fails or returns zero tokens, contrary to the expectation of receiving the full amount they deposited. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the lock and unlock pathways and identified the missing accounting for transfer fees. Because the transfer itself does not revert and no explicit error is thrown at deposit time, the discrepancy can remain hidden until the withdrawal attempt, making it difficult for users to spot the problem early. The impact is limited to users who interact with tokens that charge a fee on transfer; they may lose access to their deposited assets or only retrieve a fraction of them. The contract should not assume a 1:1 transfer relationship. A correct mitigation would involve measuring the token balance before and after the transfer to compute the actual amount received, or requiring that only fee‑free tokens be used, or adjusting the share calculation to reflect the net received amount. This class of bug falls under “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens” and violates the business logic that a user’s deposited amount equals the amount they can later withdraw, breaking the accounting guarantees of the savings mechanism.

title: No way to remove `GasThrottle` from `VaderPool` after deployment
description: Potential DOS on swaps on `VaderPool`.
poc:
BasePool makes use of a `validateGas` modifier on swaps which checks that the user’s gas price is below the value returned by `_FAST_GAS_ORACLE`.

Should `_FAST_GAS_ORACLE` be compromised to always return zero then all swaps will fail. There is no way to recover from this scenario.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permanent, non‑removable gas‑price throttling mechanism embedded in the VaderPool contract. During each swap, the contract executes a `validateGas` modifier that queries a fast gas oracle (`_FAST_GAS_ORACLE`) and aborts the transaction if the caller’s gas price exceeds the value returned by that oracle. Because the contract has no administrative function or governance toggle to disable this check, the throttling logic cannot be turned off after deployment. The root cause is the design decision to hard‑code the gas‑price validation without a fallback path or a control switch, effectively coupling the pool’s core functionality to an external oracle that can be influenced or corrupted.
