An attacker who can compromise the oracle, or who can force it to return a value of zero, will cause every swap call to fail the validation step, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where no user can execute a swap. From a user’s perspective, attempts to trade result in immediate reverts, balances appear unchanged, and expected swaps never happen, giving the impression that the pool is broken or that funds have vanished. The impact is that liquidity providers are unable to withdraw or swap their assets, traders cannot execute orders, and the protocol’s revenue stream is halted. This scenario surfaces only when the oracle returns an unexpected low value; under normal network conditions the pool behaves correctly, making the bug difficult to detect through routine testing. The issue was identified during a formal audit (Code4rena) that inspected the swap logic and noted the lack of a governance‑controlled escape hatch. To remediate the problem, the gas‑throttle contract should either be removed entirely or a governance‑controlled function should be added that can disable the `validateGas` check, similar to the implementation in VaderPoolV2.sol. This would restore the ability to perform swaps even if the oracle misbehaves, aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic of allowing continuous trading and liquidity access.

title: `VaderReserve.reimburseImpermanentLoss` improperly converts USDV to VADER
description: IL isn’t properly converted from being in terms of USDV to VADER, resulting in reserve paying out incorrect amount.
poc:
`VaderReserve.reimburseImpermanentLoss` receives an `amount` in terms of USDV and converts this to an amount of VADER to send to `recipient`.

However as shown in the link if there is a previous price stored for USDV, the amount of VADER tokens to be sent to the `recipient` is `amount / usdvPrice`.

`usdvPrice` is the total USD value of foreign assets divided by the total amount of USDV in a number of pairs. It’s then some measure of the inverse of the price of USDV in USD, nothing to do with converting into VADER.

The reserve will then improperly calculate the amount of VADER to pay out once there is a single reading of the USDV price.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the impermanent‑loss reimbursement routine of the VaderReserve contract. The routine is intended to accept a loss amount expressed in USDV, convert that amount into its monetary equivalent in USD, and finally exchange the USD value for VADER tokens that are sent to the liquidity provider who suffered the loss. Instead, when a historical price for USDV has been stored, the contract uses the stored value (usdvPrice) as a divisor directly on the USDV amount (amount / usdvPrice) and treats the result as the number of VADER tokens to transfer. The stored usdvPrice represents the inverse of the USDV price (total USD value of foreign assets divided by the total USDV supply) and therefore does not represent a USD‑to‑VADER conversion factor. As a result, the contract skips the required USD conversion step and applies an incorrect formula, causing the reserve to reimburse an amount of VADER that is either too low or, in some edge cases, excessively high. This mis‑calculation occurs only after the contract has recorded a USDV price reading, i.e., when the if‑branch that uses usdvPrice is taken. Any user who expects a full reimbursement of their impermanent loss will receive a smaller VADER balance than justified by their USDV loss; from the UI perspective the user may see a zero or unexpectedly reduced VADER credit after a loss claim. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the logic of the conversion was examined and the relationship between usdvPrice and the required USD‑to‑VADER conversion was found to be inconsistent. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to perform a conversion and the divisor operation looks mathematically plausible, yet the semantics of the variable are misunderstood, and no explicit tests verify the correctness of the reimbursement amount. To remediate the problem the conversion must be performed in two explicit steps: first multiply the USDV amount by the true USDV price to obtain a USD value, then divide that USD value by the current VADER‑per‑USD price (or use a reliable oracle) to calculate the exact number of VADER tokens owed. Alternatively, the contract should store the USDV price in a direct USD‑per‑USDV format and apply it correctly. Implementing proper validation of the conversion path and adding unit tests that compare the expected VADER reimbursement against the actual transfer will prevent the reserve from paying out an incorrect amount and restore the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Users can lock themselves out of being able to convert VETH, becoming stuck with the deprecated asset
description: I’ve put this as a medium issue as we’re leaking value as users are stuck with assets which are likely to be worth much less as they are deprecated. It could also be low as it’s not exploitable by outside parties and the loss isn’t taken by the protocol but the user.
poc:
Should a user have a zero allowance of VETH on the converter, no VETH will be taken and no VADER will be paid out as L147 will set the amount to zero.

There is a `minVader` check on L153 to enforce a minimum output of VADER but should this be improperly set the transaction would succeed with the user receiving much less VADER than they expect.

Crucially, the merkle proof that was used in this transaction will be marked as invalid so the user will not be able to try again once they have set the proper allowance. Someone can then lose the opportunity to convert their VETH and are left with a worthless deprecated token if they are inattentive.

It seems like this is trying to handle the case where a user doesn’t have the full amount of VETH as they are entitled to convert (by setting their allowance equal to their balance?). This is a pretty suboptimal way to go about this as it’s extremely implicit so users are liable to make mistakes.

I’d recommend decoupling the merkle proof from conversion of VETH to VADER:

  1. Change the merkle proof to set an `amountEligibleToConvert` value in storage for each user (which would be initially set to `amount`).
  2. Allow a user to then convert VETH to VADER up to their `amountEligibleToConvert` value, subtracting the amount converted from this each time.

For gas efficiency we can use a sentinel value here to mark a user which has claimed their full quota already distinctly from someone who hasn’t provided a merkle proof yet (to avoid having to track this separately in another storage slot)

These two steps could be chained in a single transaction to give a similar UX as currently but would also allow users to recover in the case of partial conversions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the conversion workflow that allows holders of the deprecated VETH token to exchange it for VADER. The contract first checks the caller's allowance for VETH and then consumes a Merkle proof that records the caller's entitlement. If the allowance is zero, or insufficient for the full entitled amount, the conversion logic sets the amount to transfer to zero and still marks the Merkle proof as used. Because the proof is invalidated even when the transfer amount is zero, the user cannot retry the conversion later; the contract no longer recognises any further claim for that address. Consequently, the user ends up holding VETH that cannot be converted to VADER, effectively locking the value of a deprecated asset. The root cause is an implicit coupling between allowance validation and proof consumption, and the lack of a recovery path when the conversion amount is zero or when the minimum‑output check (minVader) is mis‑configured. The bug is triggered when a user interacts with the converter manually, for example by setting an allowance lower than their eligible balance or by attempting a partial conversion, which causes the contract to record the proof as spent while returning no VADER. Affected parties are any VETH holders attempting to claim their VADER entitlement; from their perspective the UI may indicate a successful transaction, yet their token balance remains unchanged and no VADER is received, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the conversion routine and observing that a zero‑allowance path leads to a zero output without reverting, while the proof flag is permanently cleared. This behavior is subtle because the transaction does not revert and therefore does not raise an obvious error, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑consumption bugs where a claimable right is consumed without delivering the promised asset, resulting in a lockout of the user’s funds. To remediate, the conversion logic should be decoupled from the Merkle proof: the proof should only record the maximum eligible amount, stored in a dedicated variable, while allowing repeated conversions up to that amount. The contract must ensure that the proof is not marked invalid unless the actual token transfer succeeds, and it should permit users to retry with corrected allowances. Additionally, the minimum‑output check should be verified to prevent unintentionally low payouts. Implementing these changes restores the ability of users to recover their VETH value and aligns the contract behaviour with the expected business logic that every entitled VETH can be exchanged for VADER.

title: Oracle can be manipulted to consider only a single pair for pricing
description: Loss of resilience of oracle to a faulty pricing for a single pair.
poc:
In the oracle we calculate the TVL of each pool by pulling the reserves and multiplying both assets by the result of a supposedly manipulation resistant oracle (the oracle queries its previous value for USDV and pulls the foreign asset from chainlink).

This value can be manipulated by skewing the reserves of the underlying pair with a flashloan attack. An attacker can then make a pool appear with an arbitrarily large `currentLiquidityEvaluation` which will result in all other pairs contributing negligibly to the final result of the oracle.

This doesn’t result in loss of funds by itself afaict but should there be an issue for the chainlink price feed for the asset in any pool then an attacker can force the oracle to only use that pool for pricing USDV/VADER

Medium risk as “Assets not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements.” External requirements being a malfunctioning or deprecated chainlink pricefeed for any used asset.

Calculating TVL of the pool is equivalent to value of all LP tokens so for more information see this post: <https://blog.alphafinance.io/fair-lp-token-pricing/>
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an oracle design that aggregates the total value locked (TVL) across several liquidity pools by multiplying each pool's on‑chain reserves with a price fetched from a supposedly manipulation‑resistant source. The price source is built from two parts: the previous block’s USDV price and a Chainlink price feed for the foreign asset. Because the oracle treats the TVL of each pool as a weight in a single‑pool average, an attacker who can dramatically inflate the reserves of any one pool can cause that pool to dominate the weighted average. This is possible through a flash‑loan attack that temporarily skews the pool’s reserves without changing the underlying token balances after the loan is repaid. Once the inflated TVL is recorded, the oracle’s computed "currentLiquidityEvaluation" becomes extremely large for the manipulated pool, while the contributions of all other pools become negligible. If, in addition, the Chainlink feed for the foreign asset used by the manipulated pool is faulty, deprecated, or deliberately corrupted, the oracle will effectively price USDV/VADER using the manipulated pool’s distorted data alone. The root cause is the reliance on a single weighted‑average calculation that does not enforce a minimum diversity of price inputs or protect against extreme reserve outliers. The issue manifests whenever an attacker can flash‑loan enough capital to temporarily flood a pool with one side of the pair, causing the on‑chain reserve reading for that block to be far from the true market depth. The affected parties include any user of the protocol who relies on the oracle for pricing, the protocol itself because mispricing can lead to incorrect minting, burning, or liquidation logic, and potentially external markets if arbitrageurs exploit the temporary price distortion. The flaw was uncovered during a static audit that examined the oracle’s TVL aggregation logic and identified that the calculation only pulls a single price per asset and does not cap the influence of any individual pool. It is hard to notice because on‑chain TVL numbers look superficially correct and the price feed for the foreign asset may appear legitimate, while the manipulation only persists for a single block and the overall protocol state may not immediately show a loss of funds. The exploit does not directly steal tokens, but it can cause the protocol to make incorrect economic decisions, such as issuing USDV at an inflated value or rejecting legitimate deposits, which can erode confidence and potentially lead to value leakage. To remediate the issue, the oracle should compute fair reserves using the pool invariant and incorporate both assets’ fair prices, ensuring that no single pool can dominate the weighted average. Additionally, the design should enforce diversification constraints, apply outlier detection, and fall back to a secondary price source if the primary feed deviates beyond a safe threshold. By recalculating TVL with a mathematically sound invariant that balances the two assets and by limiting the impact of any single pool, the protocol can restore resilience against flash‑loan‑induced reserve manipulation.

title: `VaderPoolV2.mintFungible` exposes users to unlimited slippage
description: Frontrunners can extract up to 100% of the value provided by LPs to VaderPoolV2 as fungible liquidity.
poc:
Users can provide liquidity to `VaderPoolV2` through the `mintFungible` function.

This allows users to provide tokens in any ratio and the pool will calculate what fraction of the value in the pool this makes up and mint the corresponding amount of liquidity units as an ERC20.

However there’s no way for users to specify the minimum number of liquidity units they will accept. As the number of liquidity units minted is calculated from the current reserves, this allows frontrunners to manipulate the pool’s reserves in such a way that the LP receives fewer liquidity units than they should. e.g. LP provides a lot of `nativeAsset` but very little `foreignAsset`, the frontrunner can then sell a lot of `nativeAsset` to the pool to devalue it.

Once this is done the attacker returns the pool’s reserves back to normal and pockets a fraction of the value which the LP meant to provide as liquidity.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the VADERPoolV2 contract’s mintFungible function, which allows a liquidity provider (LP) to add tokens to the pool in any proportion and then mints a corresponding amount of pool‑share tokens based on the pool’s current reserves. Because the function does not require the caller to specify a minimum acceptable amount of LP tokens, the amount minted is calculated solely from the reserves at the exact moment of execution. This design flaw opens the function to front‑running attacks: an adversary can observe a pending liquidity addition, then trade against the pool just before the mintFungible transaction is mined, temporarily skewing the reserve balances. By selling a large amount of the asset that the LP is contributing, the attacker depresses the pool’s price for that asset, causing the contract to compute a smaller share of liquidity units for the LP. After the LP’s transaction is processed, the attacker can reverse the price manipulation, restoring the reserves to their original state while retaining the value that the LP intended to contribute. The root cause is the absence of slippage protection or a minimum‑mint constraint, which permits the minting calculation to be arbitrarily influenced by external trades. Exploitation requires only that the attacker can place a transaction ahead of the LP’s add‑liquidity call, a realistic scenario in any public mempool where transaction ordering is not enforced. The impact can be severe: the LP may receive far fewer liquidity tokens than expected, potentially as low as zero, resulting in the loss of up to 100 % of the contributed value. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction but the LP token balance increases only marginally or not at all, contrary to the expectation that their deposited assets are fully represented by newly minted pool shares. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit by Code4rena, where the logic of mintFungible was examined and the lack of a minimum‑output parameter was noted. The problem can be subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; only the post‑transaction token balance reveals the discrepancy, making it easy to overlook. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce a slippage guard comparable to Uniswap’s “minimum amount out” parameter: the caller must provide a lower bound on the number of LP tokens they are willing to accept, and the transaction should revert if the calculated amount falls below this threshold. Alternatively, the minting logic could incorporate price validation against a time‑weighted average price oracle or require that the ratio of assets supplied matches the current pool price within an acceptable tolerance, thereby preventing manipulative front‑running trades from affecting the minting outcome.

title: Adding pair of the same `foreignAsset` would replace oracle of earlier entry
description: Oracles are mapped to the `foreignAsset` but not to the specific pair. Pairs with the same `foreignAsset` (e.g. UniswapV2 and Sushi) will be forced to use the same oracle. Generally this should be the expected behavior but there are also possibility that while adding a new pair changed the oracle of an older pair unexpectedly.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the contract's design where price oracle addresses are stored in a single mapping keyed by the foreign asset identifier, without taking the specific trading pair into account. Because the mapping uses only the foreign asset as the unique key, adding a new pair that references the same foreign asset overwrites the previously stored oracle address for any existing pair that also uses that asset. This mutable, shared state is the root cause of the issue; the contract assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between a foreign asset and its oracle, which is not guaranteed when multiple liquidity sources (for example, UniswapV2 and SushiSwap) share the same underlying token. An attacker or even a well‑intentioned maintainer who adds a new pair can unintentionally replace the oracle for older pairs, or a malicious actor can deliberately add a pair with a counterfeit oracle address. Once the oracle for an existing pair is replaced, all price‑dependent calculations such as swap rates, collateral valuations, or liquidation thresholds for that pair will be performed using the attacker‑controlled feed. This can lead to users receiving far‑worse exchange rates than expected, their balances being drained, or liquidations being triggered erroneously. The exploit is triggered at the moment a new pair is added to the protocol while the foreign asset of that pair is already present in the system. Anyone who has permission to register pairs – typically a contract admin or a governance function – can cause the overwrite, affecting all users of the previously registered pair. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pair‑registration logic and noticed that the oracle mapping key omitted the pair identifier. It can be difficult to notice in normal operation because the UI displays the correct oracle for the most recently added pair, masking the fact that earlier pairs are silently using a different, possibly malicious, feed. To remediate, the oracle should be bound to the unique pair identifier (e.g., using a mapping from pair ID to oracle address) or a composite key that includes both the foreign asset and the source exchange, ensuring that each pair retains its own dedicated price source. By separating the oracle storage per pair, the protocol preserves the integrity of price calculations, prevents accidental or malicious oracle replacement, and aligns with the expected business logic that each market operates with its own price feed.

title: Fee not decayed if past `decayTime`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑decay routine of the ThreePieceWiseLinearPriceCurve contract. The function calculateDecayedFee is designed to reduce the lastFeePercent proportionally to the elapsed time (decay) up to a configured maximum period (decayTime). In the intended logic, when the elapsed time is less than decayTime, the fee should be lowered by the ratio decay/decayTime, and when the elapsed time reaches or exceeds decayTime the fee should be reset to zero, reflecting that the fee has fully decayed. However, the implementation treats the case decay > decayTime the same as decay == 0, returning the unchanged lastFeePercent instead of zero. Consequently, after the decay window has passed, the fee remains at its previous non‑zero value indefinitely. This occurs because the else branch unconditionally assigns fee = lastFeePercent, disregarding the fact that decay may be larger than decayTime. The bug was identified during a manual audit of the code base, where the reviewer noticed the contradictory comment and the mathematical mismatch. It can be hard to spot in testing because the function still returns a sensible fee for short intervals, and the unchanged fee does not trigger a revert or an explicit error; it merely deviates from the economic model. An attacker or a regular user interacting with the protocol after a long idle period will be charged a higher fee than the protocol’s specification expects, effectively overcharging participants. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a fee that should be zero or minimal, but the transaction incurs a noticeable cost, causing balances to drop unexpectedly. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that fees decay to zero after a certain time – are violated, breaking the intended incentive structure. To correct the issue, the decay logic should explicitly check whether decay is less than decayTime and compute a proportional reduction, otherwise set the fee to zero when decay >= decayTime. This change aligns the code with the documented business rule and prevents fees from persisting beyond their intended lifetime.

title: Wrong `lastBuyBackPrice`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the buyBack function of the protocol’s token contract, where the variable lastBuyBackPrice is calculated by dividing the first element of the amounts array (the amount of YUSD sold) by the second element (the amount of YETI received). This calculation assumes that the swap always returns exactly two amounts ‑ one for each token in a direct YUSD‑>YETI pair. In practice, the function accepts an arbitrary swap path supplied by the caller. When a multi‑hop path of length three or more is used, the amounts array contains intermediate values for each hop, and the second element no longer represents the final YETI amount. Consequently the stored price reflects a ratio of YUSD to an intermediate token rather than YUSD to YETI. The logic also implicitly trusts that every router sorts token pairs in the same order as Uniswap/Sushiswap, which is not guaranteed for all routers. An attacker who controls the owner account (or compromises it) can invoke buyBack with a crafted path that produces a misleading lastBuyBackPrice. Because later protocol components may rely on this price for accounting, rewards distribution, or protective thresholds, the wrong price can cause the system to underestimate the cost of buying back YETI, leading to over‑issuance of YETI, unexpected dilution of token holders, or loss of treasury funds. The issue manifests only when the path length exceeds two or when a router orders pairs differently, conditions that are not obvious from the UI and may go unnoticed because the contract emits the raw amounts in an event but does not expose the computed price to users. The bug was identified during a formal audit when the auditors noted the hard‑coded price calculation and flagged it as potentially incorrect for non‑direct paths. Fixing the problem requires validating that the first and last tokens in the provided path correspond to YUSD and YETI respectively, and then using the first amount (YUSD sold) and the last amount (final YETI received) to compute the price. Additional checks should enforce that the router’s pair ordering matches expectations or that the contract explicitly retrieves the correct token amounts from the router’s output. By correcting the price computation, the protocol restores accurate accounting, prevents inadvertent token over‑minting, and aligns on‑chain price data with the economic assumptions of the system.

title: Should check return data from Chainlink aggregators
description:
The latestRoundData function in the contract PriceFeed.sol fetches the asset price from a Chainlink aggregator using the latestRoundData function. However, there are no checks on roundID.

Stale prices could put funds at risk. According to Chainlink’s documentation, This function does not error if no answer has been reached but returns 0, causing an incorrect price fed to the PriceOracle. The external Chainlink oracle, which provides index price information to the system, introduces risk inherent to any dependency on third-party data sources. For example, the oracle could fall behind or otherwise fail to be maintained, resulting in outdated data being fed to the index price calculations of the liquidity.

Example Medium Issue : <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional-findings/issues/18>
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a price‑feed contract that calls the Chainlink aggregator’s latestRoundData function but fails to validate any of the returned fields. Specifically, the contract does not check that the roundID is non‑zero, that the answeredInRound value is at least the current roundID, that the timestamp is non‑zero and not in the future, or that the price value itself is positive. Chainlink’s documentation states that when an aggregator has not produced an answer for a given round, the function returns a price of 0 and may carry over data from a previous round, while still reporting a valid roundID. Because the contract trusts the data unconditionally, a stale or uninitialized round can silently feed a zero or outdated price into the protocol’s PriceOracle. This unchecked data can be exploited when the external oracle lags, is paused, or otherwise fails to update; an attacker who can influence the oracle’s state (or simply wait for a natural outage) can cause the price feed to return zero or a stale price, leading the protocol to compute incorrect valuations for liquidity, collateral, or liquidation triggers. The impact is that users may experience unexpected liquidations, withdrawals that return no funds, or balances that appear to disappear because the protocol’s accounting uses an inaccurate market price. The bug manifests whenever the Chainlink aggregator does not have a fresh answer—i.e., during network delays, oracle maintenance, or failure of the data source. All participants who rely on the price feed—borrowers, lenders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by Code4rena, which observed that the contract only checks for a successful call but omits all semantic validation of the data payload. The problem is difficult to notice because the contract does not revert on a zero price; it proceeds with calculations that may produce plausible‑looking results on‑chain while the UI may still display the last known good price, masking the inconsistency until a financial operation fails or results in loss. To remediate, the contract should enforce explicit checks on the price (price > 0), ensure answeredInRound ≥ roundID, validate that the timestamp is non‑zero and not beyond the current block time, and revert with clear error messages when any of these conditions are violated. This pattern belongs to the broader class of insufficient validation of external oracle data, where unchecked return values enable stale or malformed inputs to corrupt downstream logic, violating the fundamental business assumption that price data always reflects the current market state. From a user’s perspective, the symptom can be described as “my transaction failed with a zero price”, “my balance became zero after a trade”, or “my position was liquidated at an unexpected price”, all of which contradict the expectation that the protocol provides accurate, up‑to‑date pricing.

title: Unwhitelisted token can cause disaster
description: Contract instability and financial loss. This will happen if one of the allowed contract calls sendCollaterals with non whitelisted token (may happen with user input on allowed contract)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatch that occurs when the ActivePool contract processes a collateral transfer for a token that is not present in the system's whitelist. The root cause is the use of whitelist.getIndex(_collateral) without verifying that the token is actually whitelisted. When an unapproved token is supplied, the whitelist implementation returns a default index of 0, which the contract then treats as the index of a legitimate, whitelisted asset. Consequently, the internal accounting variable poolColl.amounts[0] is decremented by the transferred amount even though the pool never held that token, and the same erroneous index is later incremented for the recipient when the protocol’s receiveCollateral hook is invoked. This leads to a situation where the pool’s recorded balance for a whitelisted token is reduced while a non‑whitelisted token is silently moved to the recipient, breaking the invariant that the sum of pooled collaterals matches the actual token holdings. An attacker can exploit this by calling sendCollaterals from an allowed contract (e.g., BO, Trove, TML, or SP) and passing an arbitrary ERC‑20 address that is not in the whitelist together with a small amount. Each call corrupts the accounting state, and repeated calls can drain the pool’s reported collateral, potentially causing loans to become under‑collateralised and exposing the protocol to financial loss. The bug manifests under the condition that user‑controlled input reaches the allowed contract’s call to sendCollaterals, which the auditors found during a logical review of the code base. Because the function does not revert on a missing whitelist entry, the error is subtle: users may see their balances appear correct on the UI, but the underlying accounting is wrong, leading to missing or negative collateral reports, unexpected zero balances, or refunds that never arrive. The issue belongs to the class of whitelist enforcement failures and improper index handling. To remediate, the contract should enforce that every collateral token passed to _sendCollateral is verified against the whitelist before the index is retrieved, for example by adding require(whitelist.isWhitelisted(_collateral)) or by making whitelist.getIndex revert on unknown tokens. Additionally, sendCollaterals should reject calls that contain non‑whitelisted assets, ensuring that the protocol’s accounting invariants cannot be violated.

title: Out of gas.
description: There is no upper limit on `poolColl.tokens[]`, it increments each time when a new collateral is added. Eventually, as the count of collateral increases, gas cost of smart contract calls will raise and that there is no implemented function to reduce the array size.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unbounded dynamic array that stores collateral token identifiers (poolColl.tokens[]) inside the protocol. Each time a new collateral type is deposited, the contract pushes an entry onto this array without checking a maximum length, and there is no function provided to remove or shrink the array. Because many contract functions – especially withdrawal and accounting routines – iterate over the entire token list, the gas required for those calls grows linearly with the number of collaterals. When the array becomes sufficiently large, the gas needed to complete the loop can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert with an out‑of‑gas error. An attacker or even a benign user can trigger the condition simply by adding many distinct collateral types; the protocol does not enforce a cap, so the array can expand indefinitely. As a result, legitimate users attempting to withdraw or perform any operation that traverses the token list may see their transactions fail, the UI showing a correct balance while the withdrawal returns zero or reverts, effectively locking funds in the contract. The issue was identified during a manual audit where the code path that iterates over poolColl.tokens[] was examined and the absence of bounds checking was noted. The problem can be hard to detect in testing because gas consumption increases gradually and only manifests after a large number of collaterals have been added, which may not occur in short‑term test environments. Conceptually, this is a classic unbounded array denial‑of‑service bug that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all deposited funds remain withdrawable. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable maximum size for the collateral list, provide mechanisms to safely remove unused entries, or replace the array with a more gas‑efficient data structure such as a mapping combined with an indexed list that can be pruned. Implementing these controls will prevent gas exhaustion, keep withdrawal functionality reliable, and preserve user confidence in the protocol’s safety.

title: Reentrancy in contracts/BorrowerOperations.sol
description:
There are several potential re-entrant functions in contracts/BorrowerOperations.sol:

=> Function addColl() on line 346 is potentially re-entrant as it is external but has no re-entrancy guard declared. This function invokes _adjustTrove() which potentially impacts user debt, collateral top-ups or withdrawals.

* Same applies to

-- withdrawColl() on line 373 -- withdrawYUSD() on line 389 -- repayYUSD() on line 406 -- adjustTrove() on line 420

=> Function openTrove() on line 207 is potentially re-entrant as it is external but has no re-entrancy guard declared. This function invokes _openTroveInternal() which potentially impacts trove creation, YUSD withdrawals and YUSD gas compensation.

=> Function closeTrove() on line 628 is potentially re-entrant as it is external but has no re-entrancy guard declared. This function invokes troveManagerCached.removeStake(msg.sender) and troveManagerCached.closeTrove(msg.sender) impacting outcomes like debt, rewards and trove ownership.
poc: <https://solidity-by-example.org/hacks/re-entrancy/>
bug_full: The vulnerability is a set of re‑entrancy weaknesses present in several external functions of the BorrowerOperations contract. The root cause is that functions such as addColl, withdrawColl, withdrawYUSD, repayYUSD, adjustTrove, openTrove and closeTrove are marked external and can be invoked by any address, yet they do not employ a re‑entrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard) to prevent recursive calls. Because each of these functions ultimately calls internal routines that modify critical state – for example, adjusting a trove’s collateral balance, updating a user’s debt, withdrawing YUSD, or removing a stake – an attacker can re‑enter the function before the state changes are finalized. In a typical exploit scenario, the attacker would call a vulnerable function, trigger an external call (such as a token transfer or a callback), and during that callback invoke the same vulnerable function again. By doing so, the attacker can manipulate the accounting logic, for instance withdrawing collateral multiple times before the contract records the reduction, or creating a trove with inflated collateral while the debt calculations are still pending. This may lead to the loss of funds, unintended reduction of a user’s debt, or the acquisition of rewards without proper stake removal. The issue manifests when a user or attacker interacts with any of the listed functions; normal users may observe symptoms such as a collateral balance that drops to zero after a withdrawal attempt, a YUSD repayment that appears to succeed while the debt remains unchanged, or a trove that seems to close but still carries debt or rewards. The vulnerability was uncovered during a static analysis audit performed by Code4rena, which flagged the absence of a re‑entrancy modifier on the functions. It can be difficult to notice because the contract’s external interfaces behave as expected on a single call, and the erroneous state only appears when a malicious contract orchestrates a nested call sequence, a situation that typical unit tests may not cover. To remediate the issue, each external entry point that mutates trove or collateral state should be protected with a re‑entrancy guard, ensuring that any re‑entrant call is rejected until the first invocation completes. Adding the OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard or an equivalent custom non‑reentrant modifier will enforce a single‑active execution context, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended accounting rules and preventing funds from disappearing or being mis‑allocated.

title: Collateral parameters can be overwritten
description: It’s possible to repeatedly add the first collateral token in `validCollateral` through the `Whitelist.addCollateral` function. The `validCollateral[0] != _collateral` check will return false and skip further checks.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the collateral whitelist management function that allows the contract owner to repeatedly add the same collateral token as the first entry in the validCollateral list. The function attempts to prevent duplicate entries by checking that validCollateral[0] != _collateral before performing a require that the collateral has not been registered yet. However, when the caller supplies the address that is already stored at index 0, the inequality comparison evaluates to false, causing the whole conditional block—including the require that would reject an existing token—to be skipped. Consequently, the function pushes the duplicate address onto the validCollateral array and overwrites the CollateralParams mapping entry for that token with the newly supplied parameters. This logical flaw constitutes an insufficient uniqueness validation bug in a whitelist management routine, which permits overwriting of critical protocol configuration such as the minimum collateralisation ratio, oracle address, decimal precision, and price‑curve contract for the first listed collateral. The impact is that a malicious or compromised owner can modify these parameters at will, potentially lowering the required safety margin, redirecting price feeds to manipulated oracles, or otherwise breaking the accounting assumptions that keep loans properly collateralised. When the altered parameters are used by downstream borrowing and liquidation logic, borrowers may experience unexpected liquidations, their collateral value may appear to disappear from the UI, or loans may be approved under insecure conditions, leading to loss of funds for users and undermining confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the addCollateral function is called with a collateral address that already occupies the first slot of the validCollateral array; calls with any other address are correctly guarded. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the whitelist implementation and identified that the existence check was inadvertently bypassed for the first element. The bug can be subtle because the require statement is present and appears to enforce uniqueness, yet the surrounding logical condition renders it ineffective for the specific case of the first entry, allowing duplicate entries to go unnoticed in the array while silently overwriting parameters. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a proper uniqueness check that does not rely on a single positional comparison. A robust solution is to verify that the collateral address is not already present in the whitelist regardless of its position, for example by checking that collateralParams[_collateral].index is zero (indicating an unregistered token) or by maintaining a dedicated mapping of registered tokens and rejecting any attempt to add an already‑registered address. This ensures that collateral parameters cannot be overwritten and that the whitelist remains invariant, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Cannot use most piecewise linear functions with current implementation
description: The `ThreePieceWiseLinearPriceCurve.adjustParams` function uses three functions `f1, f2, f3` where `y_i = f_i(x_i)`. It computes the y-axis intersect (`b2 = f_2(0), b3 = f_3(0)`) for each of these but uses **unsigned integers** for this, which means these values cannot become negative. This rules out a whole class of functions, usually the ones that are desirable.
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the implementation of a piecewise‑linear price curve used by the contract’s ThreePieceWiseLinearPriceCurve.adjustParams function. The function receives three linear segments f1, f2 and f3, each defined as y = f_i(x). In order to stitch the segments together the code calculates the y‑axis intercept for the second and third segments ( b2 = f2(0) and b3 = f3(0) ) and stores those values in unsigned integer variables. Because unsigned integers cannot represent negative numbers, any segment that would naturally have a negative intercept – for example a decreasing line that crosses the y‑axis below zero – cannot be expressed. As a result the contract only supports a limited subset of piecewise‑linear functions, excluding the class of functions that are typically required to model price drops or discounts after a certain volume threshold.

The root cause is the choice of an unsigned integer type for the intercept values, which forces the compiler to treat the calculated result as a non‑negative number. When the true mathematical intercept is negative the value underflows, wrapping around to a very large positive number, or the calculation is simply prevented by the type system. This logical flaw is not caught by the compiler because the code type‑checks, but it silently changes the intended pricing logic.

Exploitation is indirect: a protocol developer configuring the curve may select a function that mathematically requires a negative intercept, assuming the contract will respect it. The contract, however, records a large positive intercept, causing the second and third price segments to be shifted upward. Users interacting with the contract will therefore see higher prices than expected after crossing the first cutoff point, or they may observe that a discount never materialises. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the correct initial price, but subsequent purchases cost more than advertised, or refunds calculated with the curve return zero or an unexpectedly small amount. The discrepancy can lead to over‑charging, loss of trust, and potential economic damage to token holders.

The issue manifests whenever the adjustParams function is called with parameters that imply a negative y‑intercept for any segment – a fairly common situation when modeling decreasing price curves or incentive structures. All participants who rely on the price curve – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the pricing logic no longer matches the intended business model.

The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit of the Yetifinance codebase. The auditor identified the unsigned declaration while reviewing the mathematics of the curve composition, recognizing that the type choice prevents negative intercepts. The problem is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the contract still behaves as a piecewise‑linear function, just with an incorrect domain of acceptable functions. Detecting the issue requires understanding the intended mathematical properties of the curve rather than just testing for crashes.

To remediate, the intercept values should be stored in a signed integer type, allowing both positive and negative results. Alternatively, the curve can be evaluated without explicitly calculating the absolute y‑intercept: for the middle segment, the price can be expressed as f(x) = f1(cutoff1) + f2(x - cutoff1), and similarly for the final segment, eliminating the need for a separate intercept. This approach is illustrated in Compound’s JumpRateModel implementation and was applied in the upstream pull request that introduced signed support. By fixing the type or redesigning the evaluation, the contract regains the ability to represent the full class of piecewise‑linear pricing functions, restoring correct economic behavior and preventing inadvertent over‑charging of users.

title: Wrong comment in `getFee`
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between documentation and implementation in the ThreePieceWiseLinearPriceCurve.getFee function. The comment for this function indicates that when a dollar cap is defined (dollarCap != 0), the sum of the current total collateral value and the new user‑provided collateral input must not exceed the cap. However, the actual Solidity code only verifies that the individual input amount (_collateralVCInput) is less than or equal to the cap, completely ignoring the already accumulated total. This logical discrepancy allows a scenario where the protocol’s global collateral cap can be bypassed: an attacker or any user can submit a small amount that satisfies the input‑only check while the combined total of existing collateral and the new input pushes the overall balance past the intended cap. The issue becomes exploitable whenever the cap is active and the current total is close to the limit; the contract will accept additional deposits that technically breach the economic constraint. From a user perspective, the UI may still display the cap as a hard limit, but deposits that should be rejected are accepted, leading to unexpected token minting or fee calculations that appear inconsistent with the protocol’s published rules. The impact is a violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: the cap, which is meant to control inflation or risk exposure, can be exceeded, potentially diluting token value and undermining investor confidence. This bug was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewer compared the function comment with the code and noted that the economic auditors had also flagged the inconsistency. Because the check exists only in comments, automated tests that focus on input validation may not catch the problem, making it subtle and easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should either update the comment to reflect the actual behavior or, preferably, modify the require statement to enforce the intended rule – verifying that currentTotal + _collateralVCInput <= dollarCap when a cap is set. Aligning documentation with implementation restores the intended economic safeguard and prevents unintended over‑collateralization.

title: Tolerance is not enforced during a flash governance decision
description:
Most of the functions with a `governanceApproved` modifier call `flashGoverner.enforceTolerance` to ensure the provided parameters are restricted to some range of their original values. However, in the `governanceApproved` modifier, `flashGoverner.setEnforcement(true);` is called after the function body is executed, and thus the changed values are not restricted during the function execution.

An attacker can exploit this bug to change some critical parameters to arbitrary values by flash governance decisions. The effect will last until the community executes another proposal to correct the values. In the meanwhile, the attacker may make use of the corrupted values to launch an attack.
poc:
1. An attacker executes a flash governance decision, for example, the `adjustSoul` function of `Limbo`, and sets the `fps` of a soul to an extremely large value.
2. During the flash governance decision, some of his assets, for example, EYE, are locked in the `FlashGovernanceArbiter` contract.
3. He calls `claimReward` to get his rewards on the corresponding soul (assume that he has staked some number of the token before). Because of the manipulated `fps`, he gets a large number of Flan tokens as the reward.
4. Surely, he will lose his EYE tokens because of the malicious flash governance decision. However, as long as the attacker gets large enough Flan tokens, he is incentivized to launch such an attack.

Referenced code: [DAO/Governable.sol#L46-L57](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Governable.sol#L46-L57) [Limbo.sol#L380-L381](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/Limbo.sol#L380-L381) [Limbo.sol#L327-L329](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/Limbo.sol#L327-L329) [Limbo.sol#L530](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/Limbo.sol#L530) [Limbo.sol#L628-L630](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/Limbo.sol#L628-L630)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a missing tolerance enforcement during the execution of a flash governance decision. In the contract, functions protected by the governanceApproved modifier are expected to call flashGoverner.enforceTolerance so that any parameter changes introduced by a proposal are limited to a predefined range around their original values. However, the modifier sets flashGoverner.setEnforcement(true) *after* the protected function’s body has run, which means that the tolerance check is disabled while the function is executing. As a result, an attacker can submit a flash‑governance proposal that temporarily overrides critical protocol parameters with arbitrary values. For example, the attacker can invoke the adjustSoul function to set the fps (parameter that determines reward calculation) to an extremely large number. While the flash decision is in effect, the attacker’s assets (such as EYE) may be locked in the FlashGovernanceArbiter, but the manipulated fps inflates the reward calculation in claimReward, allowing the attacker to withdraw a disproportionate amount of Flan tokens. The corrupted state remains until the community submits another governance proposal to restore the correct parameter values, giving the attacker a window to exploit the inflated rewards. The impact is economic: honest users see their expected rewards reduced or vanish, the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, and trust in the governance process is eroded. This flaw occurs only during the first flash‑governance execution after enforcement is turned on; subsequent proposals are correctly bounded, which is why the issue may be hard to observe in routine testing. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit when the interaction between the governanceApproved modifier and the flashGoverner tolerance enforcement was examined. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to enforce limits, yet the ordering of the enforcement call nullifies the protection during the critical code path. To remediate, the enforcement flag must be cleared before the function body runs and restored only after the call, as illustrated in the recommended rewrite of the _governanceApproved function and the governanceApproved modifier. By ensuring the tolerance check is active throughout the execution, arbitrary parameter manipulation via flash governance decisions is prevented, restoring the intended safety guarantees.

title: All the scxMinted is at risk of being burnt.
description:
If one of the variables that calculate adjustedRectangle is a zero value, it will impair the calculation of excessSCX which would equal to all of the scxMinted on line 219. Nothing will be deducted from scxMinted on line 229 since adjustedRectangle = 0 putting all of the former at risk of being burnt(line 230).

Also, the check on line 224 would not pass for high value migrations since scxMinted would always be greater than the adjustedRectangle. No scx would be avaliable to be sent to the AMM helper nor would there be any LP minted.

Furthermore, since SCX is needed to ensure the proper functioning of the protocol, ie, to provide liquidity and influence the value of Flan, it would be imperative that the correct value of excessScx is accounted for.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting calculation that derives an adjusted rectangle value used to compute the excess SCX amount during token migrations. If any of the inputs that compose the adjusted rectangle—most notably the community‑controlled inflation factor—evaluate to zero, the adjusted rectangle itself becomes zero. Because the contract does not guard against a zero adjusted rectangle, the subsequent excessSCX calculation divides by or multiplies with this zero value, causing the excessSCX variable to be set to the full amount of scxMinted. The protocol then attempts to deduct excessSCX from scxMinted, but since the excess amount equals the entire minted supply, no deduction occurs and the whole scxMinted balance is left exposed to a burn operation that follows line 230. Additionally, the check that ensures excessSCX does not exceed the adjusted rectangle fails for high‑value migrations, preventing any SCX from being transferred to the AMM helper and blocking the minting of new liquidity provider tokens. From a user perspective, this manifests as unexpected loss of tokens: a user who expects to receive a refund or newly minted LP shares instead sees their balance remain unchanged or be reduced to zero, and the protocol may report that no LP tokens were minted. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit while reviewing the migration logic; it is subtle because the zero‑value condition only occurs under an edge case where the inflation factor is deliberately set to zero, a scenario that might not be exercised in regular testing. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑edge‑case vulnerabilities where unchecked zero or null inputs propagate into critical financial formulas, breaking accounting invariants and causing funds to disappear. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the adjusted rectangle is non‑zero before it is used in any calculation, typically via a require statement, and should include fallback logic that safely handles the zero case without allowing a full‑supply burn.

title: user won’t be able to get his rewards in case of staking with amount = 0
description:
If a user has a pending reward and he calls the `stake` function with `amount = 0`, he won’t be able to get his reward (he won’t get the reward, and the reward debt will cover the reward)

That’s happening because the reward calculation is done only if the staked amount (given as a parameter) is greater than 0, and it updates the reward debt also if the amount is 0, so the reward debt will be updated without the user will be able to get his reward

Good catch! I’d be interested in your mitigation step being provided.

To me, it looks like the simplest solution is just to remove that if statement. Users who stake zero will pay unnecessary gas costs but the contract shouldn’t have to optimise gas consumption for undesired behaviour.

Upgraded to `Med` as users can lose their rewards.
bug_full: The contract contains a reward‑claiming flaw that appears when a staker invokes the staking entry point with a zero amount while there is an outstanding reward balance. The logic that updates a user’s pending reward is wrapped inside a condition that checks if the supplied stake amount is greater than zero. When the amount is zero the function skips the reward‑distribution calculation, but it still executes the code that updates the user’s reward debt. As a result the reward debt is increased to cover the previously earned reward without any transfer of the reward tokens to the user. From the user’s perspective the call succeeds, gas is spent, and the UI still shows a non‑zero pending reward that never arrives; the balance may appear to drop to zero after the transaction. This issue can be exploited simply by submitting a stake(0) transaction for any account that has accrued rewards. The exploitation does not require any special privileges, only the ability to call the public staking function. The impact is the loss of earned rewards, which effectively disappears from the user’s account and reduces the overall incentive model of the protocol. The bug manifests only under the specific condition that a user with pending rewards attempts to stake with an amount of zero; normal staking with a positive amount works as intended. All participants who rely on the contract’s reward accounting—including regular stakers, delegators, and any downstream applications that display reward balances—are affected. The flaw was uncovered during a formal security audit when the auditors inspected the reward‑calculation path and noticed that the zero‑amount branch omits the reward transfer while still mutating the reward‑debt state. Because the function call does not revert and there is no explicit error, the problem can be subtle and may go unnoticed in routine testing, especially if test cases never invoke the zero‑amount path with pending rewards. The vulnerability belongs to a class of accounting and state‑inconsistency bugs where a contract updates internal accounting variables without performing the corresponding external effect. To remediate the issue the contract should either remove the amount‑greater‑than‑zero guard around the reward‑distribution logic, or separate the reward‑claiming mechanism from the staking function so that a user can always harvest pending rewards regardless of the stake amount. Ensuring that the reward debt is only adjusted after a successful reward transfer, or adding an explicit early‑return that preserves pending rewards when amount is zero, would bring the implementation back in line with the intended business logic of rewarding participants for their stake.

title: Incorrect `unlockTime` can DOS `withdrawGovernanceAsset`
description: `unlockTime` is set incorrectly.
poc:
1. Navigate to contract at <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol>
2. Observe the assertGovernanceApproved function

```solidity
function assertGovernanceApproved(
    address sender,
    address target,
    bool emergency
  ) public {
  ...
  pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime += block.timestamp;
  ...
}
```

3. Assume assertGovernanceApproved is called with sender x and target y and pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime is 100 and block.timestamp is 10000 then

```solidity
pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime += block.timestamp; // 10000+100=10100
```

4. Again assertGovernanceApproved is called with same argument after timestamp 10100. This time unlockTime is set to very high value (assume block.timestamp is 10500). This is incorrect

```solidity
pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime += block.timestamp; // 10100+10500=20600
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect update of the unlock timestamp used by the flash‑governance mechanism. When the function assertGovernanceApproved is executed, the contract adds the current block.timestamp to the stored pendingFlashDecision.unlockTime (using the += operator) instead of setting it to a fixed offset from the present time. Because the stored value already contains a previous timestamp, each successive call accumulates the full block.timestamp value, causing the unlockTime to increase far beyond the intended delay. As a result, the subsequent withdrawGovernanceAsset function, which checks that block.timestamp is greater than or equal to pendingFlashDecision.unlockTime, will never satisfy the condition once the timestamp has been inflated. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: users who have deposited governance assets and then participated in a flash decision find their assets permanently locked, seeing zero withdrawable balance despite having a positive stake. The issue manifests whenever a flash governance decision is approved more than once for the same target and sender pair, which can happen in normal protocol operation or be triggered by an attacker repeatedly invoking the approval function. It affects any participant that relies on the ability to withdraw their governance tokens after a flash decision, effectively breaking the accounting assumption that funds become withdrawable after a predictable lock period. The bug was identified during a manual audit by reviewing the function implementation and reasoning about the arithmetic of the timestamp update; its impact is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit errors, only silently prevents withdrawals, making it hard to notice during routine testing. The proper remediation is to replace the additive update with an assignment that adds a constant unlock period to the current block.timestamp (e.g., pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime = block.timestamp + CONST_UNLOCK_TIME). This ensures the unlock time reflects a single, well‑defined delay rather than an ever‑growing value, restoring the expected withdraw functionality and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Reentrancy on Flash Governance Proposal Withdrawal
description:
The function [withdrawGovernanceAsset()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol#L142) is vulnerable to reentrancy, which would allow the attacker to drain the balance of the `flashGoverananceConfig.asset`.

Note: this attack assumes the attacker may gain control of the execution flow in `asset.transfer()` which is the case for many ERC20 tokens such as those that implement ERC777 but will depend on which asset is chosen in the configuration.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawGovernanceAsset function of the FlashGovernanceArbiter contract. The function allows an authorized user to retrieve a previously locked governance asset after an unlock time has passed. However, the implementation performs the external token transfer before it clears the pendingFlashDecision mapping that records the user’s entitlement. Because the external call (asset.transfer) is made prior to any state update, a malicious token that executes code during its transfer – for example an ERC777 token with a token hook – can re‑enter the withdrawGovernanceAsset function before the pending entry is deleted. This re‑entrancy permits the attacker to invoke withdrawGovernanceAsset repeatedly within the same transaction, each time draining the contract’s balance of the configured asset until the stored amount exceeds the remaining contract balance. The root cause is the violation of the check‑effects‑interactions pattern: the contract checks the conditions, then executes an external call, and only afterward performs the effect (deleting the pending record). The issue is only exploitable when the asset used in the withdrawal is a token that can execute arbitrary logic on transfer, which the audit notes includes many ERC777‑compatible tokens. It is discovered during a manual security review that flagged the ordering of operations as non‑standard. The flaw can be subtle because a regular ERC20 token, which does not invoke callbacks, would not exhibit re‑entrancy, leading developers to assume the function is safe. From a user’s perspective, a participant who expects to receive their previously locked governance token may instead see their balance reduced to zero, while the contract’s internal accounting no longer reflects the withdrawn amount, effectively disappearing funds. The impact is a medium‑severity loss of governance assets, potentially undermining the protocol’s decision‑making process and compromising user trust. To remediate, the contract should adopt the check‑effects‑interactions pattern by deleting the pendingFlashDecision entry before making the external transfer, or by applying a non‑reentrant modifier, and it should enforce that only known safe assets (e.g., native tokens without transfer hooks) can be used for withdrawals. These measures eliminate the window for a re‑entrant call, restore proper accounting, and align the contract with established secure design practices.

title: Burning a User’s Tokens for a Flash Proposal will not Deduct Their Balance
description: The proposal to burn a user’s tokens for a flash governance proposal does not result in the user losing any funds and may in fact unlock their funds sooner.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting logic of a flash‑governance mechanism that is supposed to burn a user’s tokens when a flash proposal succeeds. The contract’s `burnFlashGovernanceAsset` function calls the external token’s `burn` method, but afterwards it overwrites the user’s pending decision record with a static configuration object (`flashGovernanceConfig`). This configuration contains the original amount that the user deposited and a lock‑up duration expressed as a plain number of seconds, not as an absolute timestamp. Because the overwritten record replaces the user’s actual balance with the unchanged config amount, the contract never deducts the burned tokens from the user’s on‑chain balance. Moreover, the lock‑up check in `withdrawGovernanceAsset` compares the stored `unlockTime` against `block.timestamp`. Since `unlockTime` holds a duration (for example 7 days) instead of a future timestamp (now + 7 days), the condition `unlockTime < block.timestamp` is true almost immediately after the burn call, allowing the user to withdraw the tokens straight away. The bug is a classic state‑overwrite/incorrect‑time‑calculation flaw that breaks the intended accounting invariant: after a burn, the user’s locked balance should be reduced and remain locked for the configured period. Exploitation proceeds by a malicious or careless user submitting a flash proposal, triggering the burn, and then calling `withdrawGovernanceAsset` to retrieve the same amount of tokens that were supposedly destroyed. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the tokens were burned, yet the wallet still shows the same balance and a withdrawal can be performed instantly, contradicting the expectation that the funds are gone or locked. The impact is that the protocol’s token supply accounting is corrupted, token‑locking guarantees are violated, and the system may suffer from inflated effective supply or loss of security guarantees that rely on locked tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state updates inside the flash‑governance arbiter contract and noticed that the pending decision struct was replaced wholesale rather than updated incrementally. It is subtle because the external `burn` call succeeds, giving the impression that tokens have been removed, while the internal ledger remains untouched; the mis‑interpreted unlock time further hides the problem because the lock condition appears to be satisfied. To remediate, the contract should either delete the user’s pending decision entry after a successful burn (preventing any later withdrawal) or, if partial balances are allowed, subtract the burned `amount` from the stored `pendingFlashDecision.amount` and recompute `unlockTime` as `block.timestamp + config.lockDuration`. This ensures the internal accounting reflects the token destruction and that the lock‑up period is enforced correctly.

title: The system can get to a “stuck” state if a bad proposal
description:
The LimboDAO contract has a variable that indicates the current proposal - every time there can be only one proposal. The only way a proposal can be done and a new proposal can be registered is to finish the previous proposal by either accepting it and executing it or by rejecting it. If a proposal that can’t succeed, like for example an `UpdateMultipleSoulConfigProposal` proposal that has too much tokens and not enough gas, will stuck the system if it will be accepted. Thats because its time will pass - the users won’t be able to vote anymore (because the `vote` function will revert), and the proposal can’t be executed - the `execute` function will revert. So the proposal won’t be able to be done and the system will be stuck because new proposal won’t be able to be registered.

When trying to call the `executeCurrentProposal()` function that activates the `updateCurrentProposal()` modifier, the modifier will check the balance of fate, it will see that it’s positive and will call `currentProposalState.proposal.orchestrateExecute()` to execute the proposal. the proposal will revert and cancel it all (leaving the proposal as the current proposal with `voting` state).

When trying to call `makeProposal()` function to make a new proposal it will revert because the current proposal is not equal to address(0).

To sum up, the system can get to a “stuck” state if a bad proposal (proposal that can’t be executed) is accepted.

I’m so glad someone finally noticed this. So many issues logged skirted around this issue. A lot of issues were logged about adding too may token to the updateMultipleSoulProposal but the crux of the matter is that the proposal.execute() should be replaced with a call that returns a success boolean so that the DAO doesn’t get stuck on broken proposals. Congratulations on spotting this.

This is a good one, but I’m still going to downgrade this to `medium` as there is no fund at risk afaics.

@jack-the-pug There is a funds risk. Limbo can be paused via flash governance. When paused, funds can’t be withdrawn. The only way to unpause is with a proposal. If the DAO gets jammed up with a broken proposal contract then an attacker can pause Limbo and all staked funds will be locked permanently.

Yeah, I agree that funds can be at risk indirectly, like the vector you described above, but only when the warden made a clear and persuasive presentation about how the funds can be at risk, then it can be a `High`.

Furthermore, this attack vector requires the community to misbehave or at least be imprudent, to pass a malicious proposal, which already lowers the severity of it.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the DAO’s proposal management logic, which assumes that a proposal can always be either executed or rejected once it has been accepted. The contract stores a single active proposal identifier and only clears this slot when the proposal reaches a terminal state. If an accepted proposal contains code that cannot be executed—such as an UpdateMultipleSoulConfigProposal that requires more gas than is available or attempts to transfer more tokens than the contract holds—the execution step reverts. Because the execution function returns no status, the surrounding modifier leaves the proposal in the “voting” state even though voting is no longer possible; the vote function itself reverts due to the stale state. Consequently, the DAO cannot register a new proposal because the currentProposal address is still non‑zero, and the system becomes effectively dead‑locked. This dead‑lock can indirectly put funds at risk: the protocol can be paused through flash governance, and the only way to un‑pause is via a new proposal, which cannot be created while the contract is stuck. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined edge cases around proposal execution and noticed that the orchestrateExecute call does not return a success flag, allowing a malicious or malformed proposal to freeze the DAO. The problem is subtle because the proposal appears to be accepted and voting may appear to be open, yet any interaction with the vote or execute functions fails, leading to confusing error messages for users who see “transaction reverted” without obvious cause. From a user’s perspective, attempts to vote result in immediate reverts, new proposals cannot be submitted, and the UI may show a proposal stuck indefinitely in a voting state, contrary to the expectation that proposals either pass or are cancelled. The class of bug can be described as an irreversible state lock or dead‑lock caused by unhandled execution failures in governance contracts. A proper fix would involve redesigning the execution pathway so that it returns a boolean indicating success, and if execution fails the contract should automatically clear the current proposal slot or move the proposal to a rejected state, thereby restoring the ability to submit new proposals and preventing the DAO from becoming permanently stuck.

title: flan can’t be transferred unless the flan contract has flan balance greater than the amount we want to transfer
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the token transfer routine where the contract checks its own balance instead of the caller's balance before performing a transfer. The function safeTransfer reads the balance of the contract address (address(this)) and caps the transfer amount to that value. If the contract holds less flan than the amount requested, the calculated transfer amount becomes zero and the internal _transfer function is invoked with an amount of zero. Because the function does not revert on a zero‑value transfer, the transaction is reported as successful even though no tokens move from the sender to the recipient. This flaw originates from using the wrong balance source – the contract's balance rather than the sender's balance – which violates the expected accounting logic that a user should be able to transfer any amount they own, regardless of the contract’s holdings. The issue can be exploited by any participant who triggers a transfer when the contract’s balance is insufficient; the call will silently succeed while the user’s tokens remain unchanged, leading to a perception that the transfer succeeded while the funds never left the sender’s account. The impact is primarily a usability and trust problem: users may see a transaction receipt, expect their balance to decrease and the recipient’s balance to increase, but instead both balances stay the same, causing confusion, potential loss of confidence, and possible financial disagreement if the user believes the transfer was executed. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to safeTransfer where the contract does not already hold at least the requested amount of flan, which can happen even when the sender has sufficient personal balance. All token holders and any protocol component relying on safeTransfer are affected, as the bug prevents legitimate transfers and may be mistaken for a scam or a broken contract. The problem was discovered during an audit that examined the function’s logic and identified the misuse of balanceOf(address(this)). It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert nor emit an obvious error; it merely results in a zero‑value transfer that may still generate a Transfer event with amount zero, appearing normal on chain explorers. The proper fix is to replace the contract‑balance check with a check against the caller’s balance (balanceOf(msg.sender)) or to remove the manual cap entirely and rely on the underlying _transfer implementation to revert when the sender lacks sufficient funds. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect balance verification” or “zero‑value transfer due to wrong source account” errors, where business logic assumes a user can move their own tokens, but the implementation incorrectly ties the operation to the contract’s own holdings, breaking accounting invariants and causing funds to appear to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: Consistently check account balance before and after transfers for Fee-On-Transfer discrepencies
description: Wrong fateBalance bookkeeping for a user. Wrong fateCreated value emitted.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the burnAsset function of the LimboDAO smart contract. The function accepts an amount of an asset to be transferred from the caller to the contract using ERC677.transferFrom, a token interface that can implement a fee‑on‑transfer (FOT) mechanism. Because the code does not verify the actual amount received after the transfer, it continues to calculate the fateCreated value based solely on the user‑provided amount parameter. For assets other than the native eye token, the calculation derives an implied amount of eye per unit of the burned asset, but it still uses the original amount instead of the net amount that arrived after the FOT deduction. Consequently, the contract may credit the caller with an inflated fateBalance and emit an event containing an incorrect fateCreated value. This discrepancy can be triggered whenever a user burns a fee‑on‑transfer token, i.e., any token that deducts a percentage on transfer. Users expect that burning a certain number of tokens yields a proportional amount of fate tokens; however, due to the missing balance check, they may receive more fate tokens than the protocol’s economic model intends, effectively creating unearned value. The impact includes inflation of internal accounting, potential over‑distribution of rewards, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants, which could be exploited by repeatedly burning fee‑on‑transfer tokens to accumulate excessive fate tokens. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit where the auditor noted the absence of a pre‑ and post‑transfer balance verification (the “FOT not taken into account” annotation). It is difficult to detect in testing because fee‑on‑transfer tokens silently reduce the transferred amount, making the arithmetic appear correct at first glance. To remediate the flaw, the contract should record the contract’s token balance before the transfer, perform the transfer, then measure the difference to obtain the exact amount received. All subsequent calculations of fateCreated and the emitted event must use this actual received amount. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens” or “failure to account for token transfer fees in accounting logic,” which can lead to over‑minting, mis‑reporting, and financial leakage.

title: Calling `generateFLNQuote` twice in every block prevents any migration
description:
<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/71d8e0cfd9388f975d6a90dffba9b502b222bdfe/contracts/UniswapHelper.sol#L138> In the Uniswap helper, `generateFLNQuote` is public, so any user can generate the latest quote.
