If you call this twice in any block, then the two latest flan quotes will have a `blockProduced` value of the current block’s number.

These quotes are used in the `_ensurePriceStability` function. The last require statement here is key: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/71d8e0cfd9388f975d6a90dffba9b502b222bdfe/contracts/UniswapHelper.sol#L283-L285>

This function will revert if this statement is false:

```solidity
localFlanQuotes[0].blockProduced - localFlanQuotes[1].blockProduced > VARS.minQuoteWaitDuration
```

Since `VARS.minQuoteWaitDuration` is a `uint256`, it is at least 0

```solidity
localFlanQuotes[0].blockProduced - localFlanQuotes[1].blockProduced > 0
```

But, as we’ve shown above, we can create a transaction in every block that will make `localFlanQuotes[0].blockProduced - localFlanQuotes[1].blockProduced == 0`. In any block we can make any call to `_ensurePriceStability` revert.

`_ensurePriceStability` is called in the `ensurePriceStability` modifier: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/71d8e0cfd9388f975d6a90dffba9b502b222bdfe/contracts/UniswapHelper.sol#L70>

This modifier is used in `stabilizeFlan`: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/71d8e0cfd9388f975d6a90dffba9b502b222bdfe/contracts/UniswapHelper.sol#L162>

Lastly, `stabilizeFlan` is used in `migrate` in `Limbo.sol` <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/71d8e0cfd9388f975d6a90dffba9b502b222bdfe/contracts/Limbo.sol#L234>

Therefore, we can grief a migration in any block. In reality, the `minQuoteWaitDuration` would be set to a much higher value than 0, making this even easier to grief for people (you only need to call `generateFLNQuote` every `minQuoteWaitDuration - 1` blocks to be safe).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the public function generateFLNQuote in the UniswapHelper contract. This function returns a quote that includes the current block number (blockProduced). Because the function is unrestricted, any user can invoke it multiple times within the same block. When two calls are made in a single block, the contract stores two consecutive quotes whose blockProduced values are identical. Later, the internal routine _ensurePriceStability retrieves the two most recent quotes and checks that the difference between their blockProduced fields exceeds VARS.minQuoteWaitDuration. The require statement reads localFlanQuotes[0].blockProduced - localFlanQuotes[1].blockProduced > VARS.minQuoteWaitDuration. Since minQuoteWaitDuration is a non‑negative uint256, the condition collapses to requiring a positive difference. If the two quotes share the same block number, the subtraction yields zero, causing the require to fail and the transaction to revert. This check is performed inside the ensurePriceStability modifier, which protects the stabilizeFlan function, and stabilizeFlan is subsequently called by the migrate function in Limbo.sol. Consequently, an attacker who can submit two generateFLNQuote calls every block (or every minQuoteWaitDuration‑1 blocks if the parameter is larger than zero) can deliberately cause every call to migrate – and any other function guarded by the same modifier – to revert. From a user’s perspective, migration attempts appear to fail silently: the UI may show a generic “migration failed” message, no tokens move, and balances remain unchanged, even though the user has sufficient funds and the transaction is otherwise valid. The root cause is the reliance on block numbers as a measure of temporal separation without enforcing a minimum interval or restricting who may generate quotes. The design assumes that each quote will be produced in a distinct block, which is not guaranteed when the function is publicly callable. This flaw is subtle because normal usage – where quotes are generated at a slower pace – satisfies the condition, so the defect may not surface during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the UniswapHelper contract by analyzing the flow of data from generateFLNQuote through _ensurePriceStability. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that can lock user assets in the migration process, effectively preventing the protocol from completing essential state transitions. To remediate, the contract should replace the block‑based freshness check with a time‑weighted average price oracle, restrict generateFLNQuote to trusted callers, enforce a mandatory waiting period between successive quotes, or impose a penalty (e.g., burning EYE tokens) for calls that violate the minimum interval. These measures would eliminate the ability for an attacker to manipulate quote timing and restore the expected behavior of migrations and price‑stability checks.

title: You can grief migrations by sending SCX to the UniswapHelper
description:
The attack here allows the attacker to prevent migrations.

The attack here is recoverable because we can just call `buyFlanAndBurn` (if it worked as expected) with SCX as the input token to buy Flan with the extra SCX, then run the migration again.
poc:
The attack here is simple:

1. Get some SCX
2. Send it to the UniswapHelper contract
3. Any migration called will revert

My proof of concept test. You should be able to use this directly in the thig <https://gist.github.com/CamdenClark/b6841ac7a63e868d90eff7d9a40e3e0a>

`localSCXBalance` is the SCX balance of the uniswap helper. <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/cedb81273f6daf2ee39ec765eef5ba74f21b2c6e/contracts/UniswapHelper.sol#L163>

But, the caller of `stablizeFlan` assumes that the `rectangleOfFairness` parameter is going to be equal to the amount of SCX that was sent <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/cedb81273f6daf2ee39ec765eef5ba74f21b2c6e/contracts/Limbo.sol#L234>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migration mechanism that uses the UniswapHelper contract to stabilize the Flan token. During a migration, the caller of the `stablizeFlan` function in the Limbo contract passes a parameter called `rectangleOfFairness` that is assumed to represent the exact amount of SCX tokens that have been transferred to the UniswapHelper contract. Inside the helper, the contract checks that the on‑chain SCX balance (`localSCXBalance`) is exactly equal to the supplied `rectangleOfFairness` value using a strict equality (`==`). Because the equality check does not consider the possibility of external token transfers, an attacker can simply send additional SCX tokens directly to the UniswapHelper contract before a migration is initiated. The extra tokens increase `localSCXBalance` without the caller’s knowledge, causing the equality test to fail and making the migration revert. This enables a griefing attack: the attacker does not need to control the migration logic, only to deposit a modest amount of SCX to the helper contract, after which any migration transaction will fail until the extra tokens are removed. The impact is that legitimate migrations are blocked, delaying the intended token migration and potentially affecting the price dynamics of both Flan and SCX, as the protocol relies on timely migrations to rebalance incentives. Users expecting their migration to succeed will see the transaction revert, receiving no token updates, and may observe their balances remain unchanged or experience temporary price distortions. The issue affects all participants of the protocol – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – because the migration process is a core economic function. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditor attempted to execute a migration after sending SCX directly to the helper contract and observed a revert caused by the equality condition. The problem is subtle because token contracts allow arbitrary external transfers, and developers often overlook that balance checks based on caller‑provided values can be violated by such transfers. The root cause is the use of a strict equality comparison instead of a more permissive inequality (e.g., `>=`) and the reliance on an externally supplied parameter that should be derived from the contract’s actual token balance. To remediate the issue, the migration logic should validate that the helper’s SCX balance is at least the amount claimed (`>=`) and should compute the expected amount internally rather than trusting the caller’s input. Alternatively, the contract could lock the helper’s balance during migration or prevent direct token transfers to the helper contract. By fixing the balance verification, the protocol would prevent the griefing scenario while preserving the intended economic behavior of migrations.

title: You can flip governance decisions without extending vote duration
description: The impact here is that a user can, right at the end of the voting period, flip the decision without triggering the logic to extend the vote duration. The user doesn’t even have to be very sophisticated: they can just send one vote in one transaction to go to 0, then in a subsequent transaction send enough to flip the vote.
poc:
<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/608cec2e297867e4d954a63fecd720e80c1d5ae8/contracts/DAO/LimboDAO.sol#L281> You can send exactly enough fate to send the fate amount to 0, then send fate to change the vote. You’ll never trigger this logic.

On the first call, to send the currentProposalState.fate to 0, `(fate + currentFate) * fate == 0`, so we won’t extend the proposal state.

Then, on the second call, to actually change the vote, `fate * currentFate == 0` because `currentFate` is 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a governance voting mechanism that attempts to protect against sudden flips of a proposal outcome by extending the voting period whenever a vote would reverse the current net sentiment. The implementation checks whether the product of the incoming vote weight (fate) and the existing net vote (currentFate) is non‑zero to decide if a flip has occurred. Because this condition only fires when currentFate is non‑zero, an attacker can exploit the edge case where the net vote is exactly cancelled to zero. By submitting a first transaction that casts a vote equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to the existing net vote, the attacker drives the net vote to zero without triggering the flip‑extension logic. In a second transaction—sent immediately after, often within the same block—the attacker casts a vote of the opposite direction, thereby flipping the proposal outcome. The contract treats the second vote as a normal vote because currentFate is now zero, so the multiplication test fails and no extension is applied. This sequence can be performed by any holder with sufficient voting power and does not require sophisticated contract interaction; simply calculating the exact amount needed to nullify the current tally is enough. The impact is that the governance process can be subverted at the last moment, allowing malicious actors to approve or reject proposals that would otherwise have been decided fairly, breaking the protocol’s assumed democratic consensus and potentially leading to unauthorized changes in protocol parameters or fund allocations. The issue manifests only at the tail end of a voting window when the net vote is non‑zero but can be brought to zero, making it easy to miss during routine testing because normal voting scenarios rarely produce a perfect zero balance. The flaw was identified during a formal audit by reviewing the flip‑detection condition and confirming that a zero‑state bypass existed, then demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept that precisely zeroed the fate and immediately flipped the decision. To remediate, the voting logic must treat a transition to zero as a potential flip and still extend the voting period, or enforce that any vote that changes the sign of the net outcome—regardless of intermediate zero state—triggers extension. More robust designs could require that the absolute value of the new vote squared does not equal the current net vote, ensuring that a vote intended solely to cancel out others cannot be used to stealthily flip the decision, or implement explicit checks for sign changes before and after each vote. Overall, the bug belongs to the class of “vote manipulation through edge‑case bypass” where business rules about timing and outcome reversal are incorrectly implemented, leading to unexpected loss of governance integrity.

title: Lack of access control in the `parameterize` function of proposal contracts
description: Most of the proposal contracts have a `parameterize` function for setting the proposal parameters, and these functions are protected only by the `notCurrent` modifier. When the proposal is proposed through a `lodgeProposal` transaction, an attacker can front-run it, modify the proposal parameters, and let the community vote it down. As a result, the person proposing loses his `fate` deposit.
poc:
1. A benign user Alice wants to make a proposal, so she deploys one of the proposal contracts and sets the intended parameters. Her proposal is approved by the `ProposalFactory` and is ready to be proposed.
2. Alice calls the `lodgeProposal` function of `ProposalFactory` to propose her proposal.
3. An attacker Bob, who listens to the mempool, notices Alice’s transaction and front-runs it. He calls the `parameterize` function to change the parameters to undesirable ones.
4. Alice’s proposal becomes the current proposal. However, the community rejects the proposal because of the changed parameters, causing Alice to lose her deposit.

Referenced code: [DAO/Proposals/BurnFlashStakeDeposit.sol#L25-L37](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Proposals/BurnFlashStakeDeposit.sol#L25-L37) [DAO/Proposals/SetAssetApprovalProposal.sol#L21-L24](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Proposals/SetAssetApprovalProposal.sol#L21-L24) [DAO/Proposals/ToggleWhitelistProposalProposal.sol#L22-L28](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Proposals/ToggleWhitelistProposalProposal.sol#L22-L28) [DAO/Proposals/UpdateMultipleSoulConfigProposal.sol#L40-L61](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Proposals/UpdateMultipleSoulConfigProposal.sol#L40-L61) [DAO/Proposals/WithdrawERC20Proposal.sol#L26-L32](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/Proposals/WithdrawERC20Proposal.sol#L26-L32) [DAO/ProposalFactory.sol#L74-L78](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/ProposalFactory.sol#L74-L78)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a class of DAO proposal contracts where the function that sets or updates the proposal parameters, commonly named `parameterize`, is protected only by a generic `notCurrent` modifier. This modifier merely prevents the function from being called on the proposal that is already active, but it does not restrict who may invoke the function. As a result, any external address can call `parameterize` on a freshly deployed proposal contract before the proposal becomes the current one in the DAO's voting cycle. The root cause is the absence of proper access control that ties the ability to modify parameters to the original proposer or to a privileged role. An attacker monitoring the mempool can observe a legitimate user’s transaction that calls `lodgeProposal` on the `ProposalFactory`. By front‑running this transaction and inserting a call to `parameterize` with malicious values, the attacker changes the proposal’s configuration to undesirable terms. When the proposal is later accepted as the current proposal, the altered parameters cause the community to vote it down, which triggers the protocol’s penalty logic that slashes the proposer’s `fate` deposit. Consequently, the honest proposer loses a financial stake without receiving any benefit, effectively experiencing a loss of funds. The issue manifests only during the narrow window between the `lodgeProposal` transaction being broadcast and the proposal being recorded as current, making it difficult to notice in normal operation because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about unauthorized parameter changes, and the transaction ordering on the blockchain can obscure the attacker’s front‑run. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a proposal that was correctly configured by the user is rejected, and the user’s deposited collateral disappears, contradicting the expectation that once a proposal is lodged with the intended parameters, those parameters remain immutable. This class of bug is an access‑control flaw often referred to as “unauthorized state mutation” or “front‑run mutable configuration”. It violates the accounting assumption that a proposer’s submitted parameters are immutable after submission, breaking the trust model of the governance process. The appropriate remediation is to enforce that only the original proposal creator—or an explicitly authorized governance role—may invoke the `parameterize` function, typically by adding an `onlyCreator` or similar access‑control modifier. Additionally, the contract could emit events on parameter changes and reject any attempts to modify parameters once a proposal has been submitted for voting, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that proposals are immutable after lodging.

title: UniswapHelper.buyFlanAndBurn is a subject to sandwich attacks
description:
Trades can happen at a manipulated price and end up receiving fewer Flan to be bought than current market price dictates.

For example, at the time a user decides to call `buyFlanAndBurn` Flan trades at 0.8 in the input token terms at the corresponding DEX pool. If the input token holdings are big enough to compensate for pool manipulation costs, the following can happen: Flan buy order will be seen by a malicious bot, that buys Flan, pushing it to 0.9 before UniswapHelper’s order comes through, and selling it back right afterwards. This way, given a cumulative impact of the trades on Flan’s market price, the input token will be overspent.

This yields direct loss for the system as input token market operations have lesser effect than expected at the expense of contract holdings.
poc: `buyFlanAndBurn` doesn’t control for swap results, executing swaps with exchange pool provided amounts, which can be manipulated:
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniswapHelper contract function that purchases FLAN tokens and immediately burns them. The function initiates a token swap on a Uniswap‑style pool but does not enforce any bounds on the amount of FLAN that must be received. Because the swap proceeds with the pool’s current price without checking a minimum output or slippage limit, a malicious actor can observe the pending transaction, execute a front‑running trade that pushes the FLAN price upward, and then let the victim’s transaction execute at the manipulated, higher price. The attacker then reverses the price impact by selling FLAN back to the pool. As a result, the calling contract spends more of the input token than necessary to acquire the intended amount of FLAN, leading to a net loss of value for the protocol. This attack can be launched whenever the function is called with a token that has a relatively shallow liquidity pool, which is typical for tokens not listed on Limbo that nonetheless have a FLAN pair. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the swap logic and observed that the function does not verify the actual amount received against an expected threshold. The problem is subtle because the transaction still completes successfully, returns no error, and the contract’s state appears consistent; only the economic accounting shows that more input tokens were consumed than justified by market prices. The impact is that the protocol’s treasury or users who trigger the function see their funds depleted, the contract’s FLAN balance may not increase as expected, and the overall accounting of token inflows versus outflows becomes skewed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or sandwich attacks caused by missing slippage protection. From a user’s perspective, a call to buyFlanAndBurn that should have purchased a certain amount of FLAN may end up receiving less FLAN, while the input token balance drops more than anticipated, appearing as an unexplained loss or a zero‑return on a burn operation. To remediate, the function should accept a parameter that defines the minimum acceptable amount of FLAN (or a maximum acceptable price) and must revert the transaction if the actual swap result falls below this threshold. Adding a relative slippage parameter tied to a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle would further protect against short‑term manipulations. Such controls align the contract’s behavior with its business logic that expects a predictable exchange rate and ensure that the protocol does not suffer inadvertent losses due to front‑running price manipulation.

title: The value of LP token can be manipulated by the first minister, which allows the attacker to dilute future liquidity providers’ shares
poc:
Given:

* The `Pool` is newly created;
* The market price of `baseToken` in terms of `quoteToken` is `1`.

The attacker can do the following steps in one tx:

1. `addLiquidity()` with `2 Wei of baseToken` and `100e18 quoteToken`, received `14142135623` LP tokens;
2. `removeLiquidity()` with `14142135622` LP tokens, the Pool state becomes:
3. totalSupply of LP tokens: 1 Wei
4. baseTokenReserveQty: 1 Wei
5. quoteTokenReserveQty: 7071067813 Wei
6. `baseToken.transfer()` 7071067812 Wei to the Pool contract;
7. `addLiquidity()` with no baseToken and `50e18 quoteToken`;
8. `swapBaseTokenForQuoteToken()` with `600000000000000 baseToken`, the Pool state becomes:
9. totalSupply of LP tokens: 1 Wei
10. quoteTokenReserveQty 591021750159032
11. baseTokenReserveQty 600007071067801
12. `baseToken.transfer()` 999399992928932200 Wei to the Pool contract;
13. `addLiquidity()` with no baseToken and `1e18 quoteToken`, the Pool state becomes:
14. totalSupply of LP tokens: 1 Wei
15. quoteTokenReserveQty: 1000000000000000013
16. quoteTokenReserveQty: 985024641638342212
17. baseTokenDecay: 0

From now on, `addLiquidity()` with less than `1e18` of `baseToken` and `quoteToken` will receive `0` LP token due to precision loss.

The amounts can be manipulated to higher numbers and cause most future liquidity providers to receive fewer LP tokens than expected, and the attacker will be able to profit from it as the attacker will take a larger share of the pool than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the exchange pool establishes the initial pricing curve and mints liquidity provider (LP) tokens for the first minter. Because the contract allows the first depositor to set the reserves without any lower bound on the amount of LP tokens minted, the attacker can artificially inflate the value of a single wei of LP token. The attack proceeds by minting a large amount of LP tokens, immediately burning nearly all of them so that only one wei of LP token remains, and then transferring a sizeable amount of the base token directly into the pool. When the attacker subsequently calls addLiquidity in the single‑asset entry mode, the contract calculates the new LP token amount using a square‑root or proportional formula that now treats the single wei of LP supply as a denominator, causing the minted LP tokens for subsequent deposits to be dramatically over‑issued. Due to integer division and rounding, future liquidity providers who add relatively small (dust) amounts receive far fewer LP tokens than the protocol’s accounting logic expects, often receiving zero tokens for deposits below a certain threshold. From the user’s perspective this manifests as deposits that appear to be accepted by the contract but result in no LP tokens being credited, or in a share of the pool that is far smaller than anticipated, effectively siphoning a larger portion of the pool’s assets to the attacker. The impact is a dilution of all later providers’ ownership, meaning the attacker can claim a disproportionate share of the underlying base and quote tokens and extract value whenever other users interact with the pool. The condition under which this occurs is when the pool is newly created, the attacker is able to perform the initial mint‑burn sequence, and subsequent users add liquidity in amounts that trigger the precision loss. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit of the protocol, with similar patterns observed in earlier audits of comparable systems. It can be difficult to notice because the abnormal behaviour only surfaces after the pool has been compromised and typically affects only very small deposits, which may be dismissed as normal rounding errors. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “initial‑state manipulation combined with integer‑division rounding errors” that allow an adversary to distort the accounting of share tokens. A proper mitigation involves enforcing a minimum amount of LP tokens to be minted for the first liquidity addition, locking a small fraction of those initial tokens in a trusted address, and adding checks that prevent the total supply from falling to a level where division by a near‑zero value can cause inflation. These measures restore the invariant that each LP token corresponds to a predictable proportion of the pool’s reserves and prevent an attacker from exploiting the arithmetic handling of tiny token quantities.

title: repayDebt in Vault.sol could DOS functionality for markets
description:
Any user can pay the debt for any borrower in `Vault.sol`, by using `repayDebt()`. This function allows anyone to repay any amount of borrowed value, up-to and including the `totalDebt` value; it works by setting the `debts[_target]` to zero, and decreasing `totalDebt` by the given amount, up to zero. However, all debts of the other borrowers are left untouched.

If a malicious (but generous) user were to repay the debt for all the borrowers, markets functionality regarding borrowing would be DOSed: the vault would try to decrease the debt of the market, successfully, but would fail to decrease `totalDebt` as it would result in an underflow
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the repayDebt function of Vault.sol, which permits any address to repay the debt of an arbitrary borrower. The function accepts a caller‑supplied amount that can be up to the global totalDebt value and then sets the target borrower’s individual debt entry to zero while decreasing the contract‑wide totalDebt by the exact amount supplied. Because the repayment amount is not constrained to the actual debt owned by the specified borrower, a malicious user can submit repayment calls that collectively clear the debts of many borrowers while still deducting the full supplied amount from totalDebt each time. When the sum of the supplied repayment amounts exceeds the true aggregate of individual debts, totalDebt is forced below zero, triggering an arithmetic under‑flow (or a revert in modern SafeMath implementations). This mismatch between per‑borrower debt clearing and the global debt accounting disables the market’s ability to correctly update its debt state; subsequent borrowing operations fail because the vault can no longer reconcile the debt reduction, effectively resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition for the entire borrowing market. The issue manifests when an external actor invokes repayDebt with a target borrower that is not themselves, providing an amount larger than that borrower’s outstanding balance, and repeats this for multiple borrowers. All users who rely on the borrowing functionality—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the market becomes unusable. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit, where the auditors noted that the function lacks proper access control and does not validate that the repayment amount does not exceed the borrower’s actual debt. Because the function appears to simply “repay a loan” and does not emit obvious error messages, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught through casual testing. To remediate the issue, the function should be rewritten to either restrict repayment to the caller’s own debt or, if third‑party repayments are intended, to clamp the repayment amount to the borrower’s outstanding debt and to reduce totalDebt by exactly the amount of debt that is being cleared rather than by the caller‑provided value. This adjustment aligns per‑borrower accounting with the global debt counter, eliminates the possibility of under‑flow, and restores the expected behavior where users can repay their loans without jeopardizing the market’s operability. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic and improper authorization vulnerabilities that break invariant relationships in financial smart contracts, leading to symptoms such as “borrow function always reverts”, “available borrowing capacity appears as zero”, or “my balance shows no change after a repayment”.

title: Owner can call `applyCover` multiple times in `PoolTemplate.sol`
description:
The owner could potentially extend the insurance period indefinitely in the `applyCover` function without ever allowing the market to resume. This is because there is no check in `applyCover` to ensure that the market is in a `Trading` state.

This can also allow the owner to emit fraudulent `MarketStatusChanged` events.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing state validation in the PoolTemplate contract’s applyCover function, which permits the contract owner to invoke the function repeatedly without the market being in the expected Trading state. Because the function does not verify that the market is currently active, the owner can repeatedly extend the insurance covering period, effectively keeping the market in a paused or halted condition indefinitely. This allows the owner to prevent the market from ever resuming normal trading, which defeats the protocol’s intended lifecycle of opening, trading, and closing. Additionally, the owner can emit MarketStatusChanged events that claim a status transition even though no real state change has occurred, creating the appearance of legitimate market activity while the market remains stalled. The exploit can be carried out simply by the privileged account calling applyCover multiple times in succession; no special permissions, re‑entrancy, or external contracts are required. The impact is that users attempting to trade will see the market remain inactive, receive no execution of orders, and may observe confusing or contradictory status events. Funds that would otherwise be accessible for trading remain locked in the pool, and participants may experience zero returns or missed opportunities. This condition occurs whenever the owner decides to misuse the privileged function, and it is observable under any normal market operation where a trader expects the market to be in Trading state but finds it permanently paused. The affected parties include all token holders, liquidity providers, and traders who rely on the market’s availability, as well as the protocol’s reputation and reliability. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where reviewers noticed the absence of a state check and recognized that the owner could manipulate the market lifecycle. The flaw is subtle because the function signature appears harmless and the contract does emit status events, which can falsely reassure observers that the market is transitioning correctly. From a developer’s perspective, the bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization or state validation” vulnerabilities, where privileged functions are not guarded by appropriate pre‑conditions. To remediate the issue, the applyCover function should require that the market’s current status is Trading before allowing a new coverage period to be applied, and it should restrict the emission of MarketStatusChanged events to genuine state transitions only. By enforcing the proper state check, the protocol restores its intended flow, prevents indefinite market halts, and aligns emitted events with real status changes, thereby protecting users from silent fund lock‑ups and misleading UI indicators.

title: Signature replay
description: Signature replay in `PoolTemplate`.
poc:
The `redeem` method of `PoolTemplate` verifies the data stored in `incident`, and the verification logic of this process is performed as following:
    
```solidity
require(
    MerkleProof.verify(
        _merkleProof,
        _targets,
        keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(_insurance.target, _insurance.insured)
        )
    ) ||
        MerkleProof.verify(
            _merkleProof,
            _targets,
            keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_insurance.target, address(0)))
        ),
    "ERROR: INSURANCE_EXEMPTED"
);
```
As can be seen, the only data related to the `_insurance` are`target` and `insured`, so as the incident has no relation with the`Insurance`, apparently nothing prevents a user to call `insure` with high amounts, after receive the incident, the only thing that prevents this from being reused is that the owner creates the incident with an `_incidentTimestamp` from the past.

So if an owner create a incident from the future it’s possible to create a new `insure` that could be reused by the same affected address.

Another lack of input verification that could facilitate this attack is the `_span=0` in the `insure` method.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a signature replay flaw in the PoolTemplate contract that allows an attacker to reuse an insurance claim in order to extract additional funds from the pool. The root cause is insufficient validation of the incident timestamp and the insurance span parameters. When the contract’s applyCover function creates an incident, it does not verify that the provided _incidentTimestamp is earlier than the current block timestamp, nor does the insure method enforce that the _span argument is greater than zero. Consequently, a malicious owner can publish an incident with a future timestamp, and an attacker can call insure with a large amount, receiving a Merkle‑based proof that only includes the target and insured addresses. Because the incident’s timestamp is not part of the proof, the same insurance data can be presented again after the future timestamp becomes current, enabling a replay of the claim. The replay can be repeated as long as the incident remains in effect, effectively draining pool assets or causing multiple payouts for a single insured event. This condition occurs whenever the contract relies solely on the Merkle proof of target and insured and no additional time‑bound checks are performed, which is typical for insurance‑type protocols that expect incidents to be created only with past timestamps. The affected parties include any user who purchases insurance, the pool’s liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, as its assets may be siphoned without proper compensation. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors identified that the incident creation logic does not protect against future timestamps and that the span validation is missing. The flaw can be hard to notice because the Merkle verification appears to succeed, and no explicit error is thrown when the timestamp is in the future; the contract’s UI may simply show that a claim is pending, while in reality the claim can be replayed later. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that _incidentTimestamp < block.timestamp when an incident is created, and that _span is strictly greater than zero (or meets a minimum duration). Additionally, the incident timestamp and span should be incorporated into the data covered by the Merkle proof so that any replay attempt would fail verification. By tightening these checks, the protocol can ensure that each insurance claim is bound to a single, time‑restricted incident, preserving the intended accounting and preventing funds from disappearing due to replay attacks.

title: System Debt Is Not Handled When Insurance Pools Become Insolvent
description:
If an incident has occurred where an insurance policy is to be redeemed. The market is put into the `MarketStatus.Payingout` mode where the `_insurance.insured` account is allowed to redeem their cover and receive a payout amount. Upon paying out the insurance cover, any user is able to resume the market by calling `PoolTemplate.resume()`. This function will compensate the insurance pool if it is insolvent by querying `IndexTemplate.compensate()` which in turn queries `CDSTemplate.compensate()` to cover any shortage.

In the event none of these entities are able to cover the shortage in debt, the system accrues the debt. However, there is currently no mechanism to ensure when `transferDebt()` is called in `PoolTemplate.resume()`, the accrued system debt is paid off. Therefore, the system may incorrectly handle insolvency on an extreme edge case, generating system instability.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of system‑level debt that can arise when an insurance market transitions from a paying‑out state to a trading state after an incident. In the normal flow, when a claim is settled the market enters `MarketStatus.Payingout` and the insured party redeems their cover. After the payout, any user may call `PoolTemplate.resume()` to reactivate the market. The `resume()` function attempts to compensate any shortfall by invoking `IndexTemplate.compensate()` and `CDSTemplate.compensate()`. If those layers cannot fully cover the deficit, the contract records a residual shortfall as system debt and subsequently calls `vault.transferDebt(_shortage)`. However, the code does not contain any enforcement that the transferred debt is actually settled – there is no minting, repayment, or other mechanism that guarantees the shortage is cleared from the system’s balance sheet. As a result, when the insurance pool is insolvent and the shortage exceeds the compensation that can be drawn from the index and CDS layers, the protocol may accrue unchecked debt. This edge‑case can be triggered whenever an extreme loss event occurs, the market status is `Payingout`, and the `resume()` function is executed while the calculated `_shortage` is greater than zero. The affected parties include policyholders who expect a payout, market participants who rely on the market to resume trading, and the protocol itself, which may become financially unstable or unable to open new markets due to lingering debt. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of funds in `resume()` and identified that the call to `vault.transferDebt()` does not have a corresponding repayment path. The problem is subtle because the function appears to perform a debt transfer, and no immediate revert or error is raised – the protocol can continue operating while silently carrying an unrecovered liability. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may manifest as a market that never truly restarts, missing or zero payouts, or a sudden drop in reported liquidity that cannot be explained by normal trading activity. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unhandled debt accumulation” or “incomplete financial settlement” vulnerabilities, where accounting invariants are violated and the protocol’s balance sheet no longer reflects reality. The recommended remediation is to introduce a deterministic mechanism that clears the system debt, such as minting a dedicated token (e.g., `INSURE`) to cover the shortfall, or implementing an explicit `repayDebt()` flow that can be triggered automatically during `resume()`. Ensuring that the debt is either fully compensated or explicitly reclaimed will restore the accounting guarantees and prevent the protocol from entering an unstable state.

title: `Vault.sol` Tokens with fee on transfer are not supported
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the Vault contract's addValue function, which assumes that the amount of ERC20 tokens transferred from a user to the vault is equal to the amount specified in the function’s _amount parameter. This assumption holds for standard ERC20 tokens that transfer the full amount, but it fails for fee‑on‑transfer (also called tax or deflationary) tokens, which deduct a percentage or fixed fee on each transfer. Because the function calls safeTransferFrom with the caller‑specified _amount and then directly adds that same _amount to its internal balance and uses it to compute attribution shares, the contract records a higher received value than the actual token balance. The root cause is the lack of verification of the net amount received; the contract does not compare the vault's token balance before and after the transfer, nor does it query the transfer return value (which is often absent for fee‑on‑transfer tokens). An attacker can exploit this mismatch by depositing a fee‑on‑transfer token, causing the vault to credit the attacker with attribution points based on the nominal amount while the vault only holds a smaller amount. When the attacker later redeems or claims a share of the vault’s assets, they receive more tokens than they actually contributed, effectively draining the vault's value and reducing other users’ proportional shares. The impact includes inaccurate accounting, over‑allocation of shares, potential loss of funds for honest participants, and a breach of the protocol’s financial integrity. This condition manifests whenever the vault is configured to accept a token that imposes a transfer fee, which the current implementation does not guard against. All users who deposit such tokens, as well as the protocol itself, are affected because the internal balance diverges from the true on‑chain token balance, leading to erroneous share calculations and possible fund loss. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the logical flaw of assuming a 1:1 transfer was identified. It can be hard to notice because the transfer call succeeds, no error is thrown, and the vault's internal accounting appears consistent; only a discrepancy between the contract’s recorded balance and the actual token balance reveals the problem. To remediate, the addValue logic should measure the vault’s token balance before and after the safeTransferFrom call and use the observed delta as the true received amount, or the vault should restrict accepted assets to fee‑less tokens such as USDC until a more gas‑efficient multi‑currency solution is implemented. This class of bug is known as a “fee‑on‑transfer token misaccounting” or “incorrect transfer amount assumption” and violates fundamental accounting assumptions that deposited value equals recorded value, resulting in user‑visible symptoms such as deposited funds appearing to be missing, zero or reduced shares after a deposit, and unexpected token balances after withdrawals.

title: Index compensate is 0 when totalLiquidity
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the compensation routine of the IndexTemplate contract. The function compensate is designed to calculate a payout amount (denoted as _compensated) that should be used to offset a user’s debt in the vault. The logic correctly assigns _compensated when the requested amount (_amount) is less than or equal to the available value (_value). However, when _amount exceeds _value but is still less than or equal to the total liquidity of the pool (totalLiquidity()), the code enters the else branch and never sets the _compensated variable before calling vault.offsetDebt. Because Solidity initializes unsigned integers to zero, _compensated remains zero, and the contract proceeds to call vault.offsetDebt(_compensated, msg.sender) with a zero value. This means the vault records a debt‑offset operation without actually transferring any funds. The root cause is a missing assignment or fallback handling for the case where _amount > _value yet totalLiquidity() can cover the request, resulting in an unintended default value.

An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by deliberately requesting a compensation amount that is just above the underlying value but still within the pool’s total liquidity. The contract will then record a successful offset of debt while the user receives no compensation. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a claim was processed successfully, but the balance or refund remains unchanged – the user expects to receive a payout, but receives zero. This discrepancy can lead to funds effectively disappearing from the protocol’s accounting, as the vault’s internal state believes the debt has been settled whereas the actual token balances have not been moved. The issue is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it completes normally, making it easy to miss during testing or code review unless the developer checks the value of _compensated before the offset call.

The impact is medium severity: it undermines the financial integrity of the protocol, can cause users to lose expected refunds or premiums, and opens the possibility for malicious actors to manipulate debt accounting to their advantage. The bug was discovered during a static analysis audit (Code4rena) that flagged the missing assignment path. The difficulty in detection arises from the fact that the function does not contain an explicit else clause that sets a non‑zero value, and the offsetDebt call is unconditional, so the flaw is hidden behind the control flow.

To remediate the issue, the compensation function should explicitly handle the scenario where _amount exceeds _value but is still covered by totalLiquidity(). It must compute a proper _compensated amount—likely the difference between totalLiquidity() and the amount already accounted for, or by redeeming the pending premium—as the intended business logic suggests. The function should ensure that _compensated is never left at its default zero before invoking vault.offsetDebt, and it should add a guard that reverts or returns an error if a zero compensation would be applied. This corrective measure aligns the contract’s accounting with its intended financial guarantees and prevents silent debt offset without actual fund transfer.

title: `requestWithdraw` without obligation to withdraw allow underwriter to avoid payout
description: To prevent withdrawal front-running, a lockup period is set between withdrawal request and withdrawal. However, there are no obligation to withdraw after the lockup period and the capital will keep earning premium during lockup. A strategy for underwriter is to keep requesting withdrawal every `lockup period` to keep their average lockup to `lockup period/2`.
poc:
Assuming

  1. Reporting DAO vote last for 24 hours (according to docs) plus there will be delay between the hack and vote creation
  2. the `lockup period` is set to 86400 (24 hours) in the supplied test cases

It is very likely an underwriter can avoid payout by such strategy since their effective lockup would be 12 hours only. They will continue to earn yield in the pool and only require some extra gas cost for the `requestWithdraw` every 24 hours.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a withdrawal mechanism that imposes a lockup period after an underwriter calls the `requestWithdraw` function, but does not enforce any obligation to actually execute the withdrawal once the lockup expires. As a result, the contract only delays the transfer of capital without guaranteeing that the funds will leave the pool. An underwriter can exploit this by repeatedly submitting a withdrawal request at the end of each lockup interval. Because each new request resets the lockup timer, the effective time that the capital remains locked averages to half of the configured period. During this reduced lockup the retained capital continues to accrue premiums and yield from the insurance pool, allowing the underwriter to earn additional income while avoiding the intended payout obligations. The exploit is possible whenever the lockup period is relatively short (e.g., one day) and there is no automatic or forced withdrawal after the timeout. It affects any policy holder or claimant who expects the underwriter’s funds to be available for claim settlements, as well as the overall solvency of the protocol. From a user’s perspective the platform may display a pending withdrawal request, yet the underwriter’s balance does not decrease and the pool’s available capital remains unexpectedly high, contradicting the expectation that withdrawing should reduce the underwriter’s exposure. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic surrounding withdrawal requests and identified that the lockup was implemented solely as a front‑running mitigation, without any subsequent enforcement. The problem can be subtle because the UI shows a normal withdrawal workflow, and the extra gas cost of repeatedly calling `requestWithdraw` is minimal, making the malicious behavior inexpensive and hard to detect through ordinary monitoring. To remediate, the contract should either double the lockup duration so that the average locked time cannot be reduced below a safe threshold, or, more robustly, require the underwriter to actually withdraw its funds immediately after the lockup expires—either by making the withdrawal mandatory or by disabling further requests until the pending withdrawal is fulfilled. This change restores the intended economic guarantees of the insurance protocol and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business logic that underwriters must eventually release their capital for claim payouts.

title: Unbounded iteration over all indexes
description: The transactions could fail if the array get too big and the transaction would consume more gas than the block limit. This will then result in a denial of service for the desired functionality and break core functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic array that is performed on‑chain without any limit on the number of elements processed. The root cause is the contract’s design of looping through every index of an array to perform a core operation, while the array can grow indefinitely as users add entries. When the array becomes large enough, the gas required to complete the loop exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This failure mode can be triggered by simply adding more items to the array, so it occurs under the condition that the array length surpasses the amount of gas that can be supplied in a single block. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users attempting to invoke the affected function see their calls fail, the expected state changes (such as reward distribution, claim processing, or policy updates) do not happen, and from a user’s perspective the UI may display an error, a transaction that “runs out of gas”, or simply no response while the user expects a successful operation. Funds that should have been transferred or updated remain unchanged, effectively locking protocol functionality. The issue was identified during a professional security audit where the auditors noted that the function iterates over the entire array and warned that the gas consumption grows linearly with the array size, a pattern that is often missed in unit tests that use only small data sets. It is hard to notice because the problem only surfaces after the array reaches a certain size, which may not be encountered in early testing or on testnets. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded loop” or “out‑of‑gas DoS” vulnerabilities common in Ethereum smart contracts that use naïve O(n) iteration over storage arrays. To remediate the problem, the contract should avoid processing the whole array in a single transaction. Recommended mitigation strategies include replacing the array with a mapping and processing entries individually, implementing pagination or batch limits, using a pull‑based pattern where users claim their own data, or explicitly capping the array size. By ensuring that any on‑chain function processes a bounded number of items, the protocol can maintain availability and prevent transaction reverts caused by excessive gas usage.

title: Usage of deprecated ChainLink API in `EIP1271Wallet`
description:
The Chainlink API (`latestAnswer`) used in the `EIP1271Wallet` contract is deprecated:

This API is deprecated. Please see API Reference for the latest Price Feed API. [Chainlink Docs](https://web.archive.org/web/20210304160150/https://docs.chain.link/docs/deprecated-aggregatorinterface-api-reference)

This function does not error if no answer has been reached but returns 0. Besides, the `latestAnswer` is reported with 18 decimals for crypto quotes but 8 decimals for FX quotes (See Chainlink FAQ for more details). A best practice is to get the decimals from the oracles instead of hard-coding them in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of a deprecated Chainlink price‑feed interface, specifically the `latestAnswer` function, within the `EIP1271Wallet` contract. This function was originally designed to return the most recent price but has been superseded by `latestRoundData`, and its continued use introduces several subtle risks. The root cause is that `latestAnswer` does not revert when the oracle has not produced a valid answer; instead it returns a zero value. Moreover, the function reports prices with a mixed decimal precision: 18 decimal places for cryptocurrency quotes and only 8 for fiat‑currency (FX) quotes. Because the contract hard‑codes the expected number of decimals, it mistakenly interprets the returned value, leading to a miscalculation of the asset price. An attacker or an unfortunate market condition can trigger the oracle to return a stale or missing answer, causing the contract to read a zero price or a price with the wrong scale. This mispriced data can be exploited to bypass or manipulate economic checks such as collateralisation ratios, fee calculations, or settlement amounts. In practice, a user may see their transaction revert unexpectedly, receive an incorrect amount, or notice that the protocol’s accounting appears off – for example, a refund that should be several dollars comes back as zero, or a collateral requirement is calculated far too low, allowing an under‑collateralised position to be opened. The issue manifests whenever the contract queries the price feed, especially during periods of low oracle activity or when the feed switches between crypto and FX assets. All participants that rely on the contract’s price‑validation logic—depositors, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the financial guarantees of the system become unreliable. The flaw was identified during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted the deprecated call and the absence of sanity checks on the returned data. It is easy to overlook because the function appears to return a numeric value, and a zero may be interpreted as a legitimate price if the surrounding code does not explicitly validate it. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace `latestAnswer` with the modern `latestRoundData` interface, retrieve the oracle’s declared decimals dynamically, and add explicit checks that the round is complete, the timestamp is non‑zero, and the returned price is within an acceptable freshness window. These safeguards restore confidence that the protocol receives accurate, up‑to‑date pricing data and prevent the silent acceptance of zero or mis‑scaled values that could otherwise cause severe financial loss or protocol downtime.

title: `sNOTE.sol#_mintFromAssets`
description:
```solidity
BALANCER_VAULT.joinPool{value: msgValue}(
    NOTE_ETH_POOL_ID,
    address(this),
    address(this), // sNOTE will receive the BPT
    IVault.JoinPoolRequest(
        assets,
        maxAmountsIn,
        abi.encode(
            IVault.JoinKind.EXACT_TOKENS_IN_FOR_BPT_OUT,
            maxAmountsIn,
            0 // Accept however much BPT the pool will give us
        ),
        false // Don't use internal balances
    )
);
```

The current implementation of `mintFromNOTE()` and `mintFromETH()` and `mintFromWETH()` (all are using `_mintFromAssets()` with `minimumBPT` hardcoded to `0`) provides no parameter for slippage control, making it vulnerable to front-run attacks.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the minting functions of the sNOTE contract, specifically the internal helper _mintFromAssets that is used by mintFromNOTE(), mintFromETH() and mintFromWETH(). These functions invoke Balancer's joinPool operation with a JoinKind of EXACT_TOKENS_IN_FOR_BPT_OUT, but they hard‑code the minimumBPT (the minimum amount of Balancer Pool Tokens that the contract is willing to receive) to zero. Because there is no parameter that limits slippage, an attacker who can observe the pending transaction can submit a front‑running transaction that moves the pool’s price just before the victim’s joinPool call is executed. The victim transaction will still succeed – the Balancer Vault does not revert when the amount of BPT received is lower than expected – but the caller will obtain far fewer BPT (sNOTE) than anticipated, effectively losing value. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the mint operation succeeded while the resulting sNOTE balance is unexpectedly low or even zero, contradicting the expectation that the supplied assets will be exchanged for a proportional amount of pool tokens. The issue manifests whenever any of the three minting entry points is used, i.e., whenever a user provides NOTE, ETH or WETH to receive sNOTE. It affects all users of the Notional protocol who rely on accurate, predictable minting, and it also harms the protocol’s economic guarantees because the accounting assumption that the amount of BPT received is at least proportional to the assets supplied is violated. The problem was identified during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the joinPool call and noticing the missing slippage protection. It can be difficult to detect in testing because the transaction does not revert; only the returned BPT amount is lower, which may be overlooked if the test does not assert the exact output. The appropriate remediation is to introduce a slippage bound: callers should be able to specify a non‑zero minimumBPT that reflects the worst acceptable price, or the contract should compute an on‑chain minimum based on a trusted price oracle and revert if the pool would deliver less. Adding this guard restores the invariant that users receive at least a predictable amount of sNOTE for the assets they provide, preventing front‑run exploitation and preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity.

title: No upper limit on `coolDownTimeInSeconds` allows funds to be locked sNOTE owner
description: Inability for sNOTE holders to exit the pool in the case of ownership over SNOTE contract being compromised/malicious.
poc:
sNOTE works on a stkAAVE model where users have to wait a set cooldown period before being able to reclaim the underlying tokens. This cooldown period can be set to an arbitrary uint32 value in seconds by the owner of the sNOTE contract.

Below in the `startCooldown()` function, it’s possible for the owner of the sNOTE contract to choose a value for `coolDownTimeInSeconds` which always causes this function to revert (`_safe32` will always revert if `coolDownTimeInSeconds = type(uint32).max`).

Should ownership over sNOTE become compromised then all of the users’ assets may be locked indefinitely.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unbounded cooldown period in the sNOTE staking contract, which allows the contract owner to set the `coolDownTimeInSeconds` parameter to any uint32 value. Because the function `startCooldown()` contains a safety check that reverts when the provided cooldown exceeds the maximum value that fits in a uint32 (`_safe32` will always revert if `coolDownTimeInSeconds` equals `type(uint32).max`), a malicious or compromised owner can deliberately set the cooldown to the maximum possible value. When this occurs, any attempt by a user to initiate the cooldown and later claim the underlying tokens will instantly revert, preventing the user from ever exiting the pool. The root cause is the lack of an upper bound on a time‑locking parameter that is controlled solely by the contract owner, combined with a hard revert on overflow rather than graceful handling. Exploitation is straightforward: the owner (or an attacker who gains control of the owner’s privileges) updates the cooldown variable to the maximum uint32 value, after which the `startCooldown()` function cannot succeed for any user. As a result, sNOTE holders find that their transactions to withdraw funds revert, their balances remain unchanged on the UI, and they receive no tokens even though they have waited the expected period. From the user's point of view the interface shows a normal cooldown timer, but when the timer expires the “claim” button triggers a transaction that fails with a revert, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have vanished. The impact is not a direct theft of assets, but a denial‑of‑service on user funds: assets are effectively locked indefinitely, undermining the protocol’s availability and eroding trust. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the contract’s parameter handling, and it can be difficult to notice because the cooldown mechanism works correctly for typical values; only extreme values cause the hidden revert. To remediate, the contract should enforce a sensible maximum cooldown duration (for example, no more than 30 days) or use a fixed, immutable cooldown period. This constraint prevents the owner from setting an arbitrarily large lock time, ensuring that users can always eventually withdraw their underlying assets, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: L1Migrator.migrateLPT` can be used to take away protocol’s access to LPT tokens in BridgeMinter
description:
Same thing as the ETH issue I reported earlier. I wasn’t sure if those are supposed to be a single issue or not. The concept is the same. But, now you lose LPT tokens.

The `L1Migrator.migrateLPT()` function can be called by **anyone**. It pulls all the LPT from the `BridgeMinter` contract and starts the process of moving the funds to L2. First of all, this function is only executable once. The RetryableTicket created with the first call is the only chance of moving the funds to L2.

The attacker can call the function with [parameters](https://developer.offchainlabs.com/docs/l1_l2_messages#parameters) that make the creation of the RetryableTicket on L2 fail. Thus, the LPT sits in the L1Migrator contract with no way of moving it to L2 or anywhere else. Effectively, the funds are lost.
poc:
The function is only executable once because it uses the `amount` returned by `IBridgeMinter(bridgeMinterAddr).withdrawLPTToL1Migrator()` to specify the amount of LPT to be sent to L2: <https://github.com/livepeer/arbitrum-lpt-bridge/blob/main/contracts/L1/gateway/L1Migrator.sol#L342>

After the first call to `migrateLPT()` that function will always return 0 since the `BridgeMinter` won’t have any more LPT: <https://github.com/livepeer/protocol/blob/streamflow/contracts/token/BridgeMinter.sol#L107>

So after the attacker called `migrateLPT()` with insufficient funds to create a RetryableTicket on L2 we have the following state:

  * BridgeMinter has 0 LPT
  * L1Migrator has X amount of LPT that is not accessible. There are no functions to get the LPT out of there.
  * 1 failed RetryTicket

The same thing can also be triggered by a non-malicious caller by simply providing insufficient funds. The whole design of only being able to try once is the issue here.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L1Migrator contract’s migrateLPT() function, which is intended to move the entire LPT balance from the BridgeMinter contract to Layer 2. The function is callable by any address and can be executed only once because it relies on the amount returned by the BridgeMinter’s withdrawLPTToL1Migrator() call to specify how many tokens to transfer. After the first successful call the BridgeMinter holds zero LPT, causing subsequent calls to return an amount of zero. An attacker can exploit this design by invoking migrateLPT() with carefully crafted parameters that force the creation of the RetryableTicket on L2 to fail. When the ticket fails, the LPT that was pulled into the L1Migrator contract becomes locked in that contract with no further mechanism to forward it to L2 or any other destination. From a user’s perspective, the expected outcome – the migration of their LPT to the L2 escrow – does not occur; instead the token balance appears to disappear, and the UI may show a zero or missing balance despite the contract holding the tokens. The issue affects all participants relying on the bridge, including token holders, the Livepeer protocol, and any downstream applications that assume successful L2 migration. It was uncovered during a security audit when the auditor examined the call flow of migrateLPT() and identified that the function’s one‑shot nature combined with unrestricted access allows an adversary to deliberately cause a retryable ticket failure, effectively DoS‑ing the bridge. The problem is subtle because the contract does not expose any function to withdraw the trapped LPT, so the loss may not be immediately evident beyond the missing funds. Conceptually, this is a classic case of an access‑controlled, single‑execution bridge function that fails to handle retry failures and does not provide a recovery path. The recommended mitigation is to base the transferred amount on the actual token balance of the L1Migrator (or escrow) rather than the amount reported by the BridgeMinter, and to restrict callers to a privileged role (e.g., only the protocol’s governance or a designated bridge operator). Additionally, implementing a fallback mechanism that allows the contract to retry the migration or to pull the tokens back from the escrow would prevent permanent loss of funds.

title: [WP-H3] `L1Migrator.sol#migrateETH`
description:
```solidity
uint256 amount = IBridgeMinter(bridgeMinterAddr).withdrawETHToL1Migrator();
```

`L1Migrator.sol#migrateETH()` will call `IBridgeMinter(bridgeMinterAddr).withdrawETHToL1Migrator()` to withdraw ETH from `BridgeMinter`.

However, the current implementation of `L1Migrator` is unable to receive ETH.

```solidity
(bool ok, ) = l1MigratorAddr.call.value(address(this).balance)("");
```

A contract receiving Ether must have at least one of the functions below:

  * `receive() external payable`
  * `fallback() external payable`

`receive()` is called if `msg.data` is empty, otherwise `fallback()` is called.

Because `L1Migrator` implement neither `receive()` or `fallback()`, the `call` at L94 will always revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L1Migrator contract used by the Livepeer Arbitrum bridge. When the migrateETH function is executed, it invokes withdrawETHToL1Migrator on the BridgeMinter contract, which attempts to transfer the contract's ETH balance to the L1Migrator using a low‑level call that supplies value. In Solidity, a contract can only receive Ether through a payable receive() function or a payable fallback() function. L1Migrator implements neither of these entry points, so the call that carries value always triggers a revert. As a result, any attempt to move ETH from BridgeMinter to L1Migrator fails, leaving the funds locked in BridgeMinter and preventing the migration process from completing. This failure can be triggered whenever migrateETH is called—typically during token withdrawals or bridge migrations—so the issue manifests under normal operational conditions. Users and protocol participants expect the bridge to transfer ETH and reflect the new balance in the UI, but instead transactions revert and balances appear unchanged, giving the impression that funds have vanished. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the ETH transfer path and identified the missing payable entry point. Because the contract simply reverts on receipt of value, the symptom may be subtle: no explicit error is emitted beyond the transaction failure, making it easy to overlook in casual testing. The impact includes a potential denial‑of‑service where the bridge cannot process ETH migrations, and a risk of funds being effectively inaccessible unless the BridgeMinter contract is instructed to point to a new L1Migrator that does contain a receive() function. The class of bug is an "unpayable contract" or "missing payable fallback" vulnerability, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a contract designated as a recipient will actually accept incoming Ether. The correct remediation is to add a payable receive() (or fallback()) function to L1Migrator so that it can accept ETH transfers, thereby restoring the intended migration flow and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Fund loss when insufficient call value to cover fee
description: Fund can be lost if the L1 call value provided is insufficient to cover `_maxSubmissionCost`, or stuck if insufficient to cover `_maxSubmissionCost + (_maxGas * _gasPriceBid)`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L1LPTGateway contract's outboundTransfer function, which forwards tokens to an escrow on L1 and initiates a retryable ticket for L2 execution without verifying that the Ether attached to the call (msg.value) is sufficient to cover the required submission cost and the gas fee for the ticket. The root cause is the absence of a check that the supplied call value equals the sum of _maxSubmissionCost and the product of _maxGas and _gasPriceBid, a validation pattern that is present in Arbitrum's L1GatewayRouter. Because this validation is missing, a user (or an attacker) can submit a transaction with an insufficient Ether amount. If the Ether provided is less than _maxSubmissionCost, the retryable ticket creation fails immediately, causing the deposited LPT tokens to remain locked in the escrow while the Ether sent with the transaction is lost to the failed ticket. If the Ether is between _maxSubmissionCost and _maxSubmissionCost + (_maxGas * _gasPriceBid), the ticket is created but cannot be executed automatically; it must be manually executed, effectively freezing the funds in the escrow and leaving the user unable to retrieve them without additional steps. This defect can be exploited by any party that can craft a call with a deliberately low msg.value, leading to a scenario where users see their LPT balance reduced to zero on L1, receive no corresponding L2 tokens, and notice that the Ether they sent appears to have vanished. The impact is high because both LPT tokens and Ether may be irretrievably lost or stuck, violating the bridge's accounting assumptions that each outbound transfer is fully funded and that the escrow will always be reimbursed. The issue occurs under conditions where users interact with the bridge directly, bypass an application‑level fee calculator, or where a malicious front‑end misreports the required fee. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it emits a DepositInitiated event, yet the user receives no assets on L2 and the L1 escrow holds the tokens. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the flow of funds and identified the missing require statements. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that msg.value matches the expected total cost (maxSubmissionCost plus gas cost) and that maxSubmissionCost is non‑zero, mirroring the safety checks used by the official Arbitrum gateway. This ensures that any outbound transfer is either fully funded or rejected before token escrow occurs, preventing accidental fund loss or indefinite locking.

title: [WP-M0] `MINTER_ROLE` can be granted by the deployer of L2LivepeerToken and mint arbitrary amount of tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the minting mechanism of the L2LivepeerToken contract. The contract exposes a public mint function that can be called by any address possessing the MINTER_ROLE. Because the deployer of the contract is granted the ability to assign this role, the deployer – or any address to which the deployer subsequently delegates the role – can invoke mint() and create an arbitrary amount of new LPT tokens. This design creates a centralization risk: if the private key of the deployer or any current minter is compromised, an attacker gains the capability to mint unlimited tokens at will. The impact is two‑fold: the attacker can inflate the token supply, diluting existing holders and potentially crashing the market price, and the protocol’s monetary policy assumptions are violated because token issuance is no longer tightly controlled. The issue manifests whenever a transaction is sent from a compromised minter address; the network will accept the newly minted tokens and credit them to the attacker’s balance, while honest users may see their relative share of the supply shrink, leading to unexpected balance changes and loss of confidence. The flaw was identified during a formal audit of the contract’s access control logic, where the role‑based permissions were examined and found to be overly permissive. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the mint function itself appears legitimate and emits the expected Mint event, making unauthorized token creation indistinguishable from legitimate minting without close monitoring of role assignments. To remediate, the MINTER_ROLE should be eliminated or at least restricted to the contract owner, and the owner should be set to a dedicated L2Minter contract that implements the intended supply schedule. This change would ensure that only a trusted, auditable component can issue new tokens, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s economic model and reducing the risk of supply manipulation.

title: [WP-M1] `BURNER_ROLE` can burn any amount of L2LivepeerToken from an arbitrary address
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L2LivepeerToken contract’s burn function, which is guarded only by a BURNER_ROLE modifier but does not restrict the source address of the tokens being destroyed. As a result, any account that holds the BURNER_ROLE privilege can invoke burn(_from, _amount) and specify an arbitrary _from address together with an arbitrary amount, causing the contract’s internal _burn routine to reduce the balance of that arbitrary address and emit a Burn event. The root cause is the combination of an overly permissive access control (the role check) and the absence of a check that _from must equal msg.sender or be otherwise authorized, which deviates from the usual ERC‑20 burn pattern where only the token holder may destroy their own tokens. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious or compromised address with the burner role calls burn() with the address of a liquidity pool or any user’s wallet and an amount equal to the full balance, effectively removing those tokens from circulation. This can be done without any on‑chain acknowledgement from the victim, making the loss appear as a silent token disappearance. The impact includes loss of user funds, potential draining of Uniswap liquidity pools (e.g., the LPT‑WETH pool), and a centralization risk where a single privileged role can unilaterally erase token balances, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that token supply changes only reflect legitimate minting or holder‑initiated burning. The issue surfaces whenever the BURNER_ROLE is assigned, which is typical in the bridge’s outbound transfer flow where the role is used to destroy L2 tokens after they are moved to L1. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the role‑restricted functions and noted the inconsistency with standard burn semantics. Detecting the problem may be difficult because the presence of a role check can give the impression of a safe privileged operation, and the function signature itself mirrors common burn interfaces, hiding the arbitrary‑source flaw. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the BURNER_ROLE from the burn function entirely and restrict burning to the caller’s own balance, i.e., replace the existing function with one that calls _burn(msg.sender, _amount) and emits the event accordingly. Additionally, any outbound transfer logic that currently calls Mintable(l2Lpt).burn(from, _amount) should first transfer tokens from the user to the bridge and then burn only the transferred amount, ensuring that no third‑party address can be targeted for token destruction.

title: [WP-M2] `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` can approve arbitrary address to spend any amount from the `L1Escrow` contract
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a public function that permits any address holding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to call an external token contract’s approve method on behalf of the L1Escrow contract. The function does not enforce any constraints on the token address, the spender, or the amount being approved; it simply forwards the caller‑provided parameters to the token’s approve function and emits an event. This design creates a centralization risk because the admin can grant an unlimited allowance of any ERC‑20 token held by the escrow to an arbitrary external address. If the admin key is compromised, an attacker can invoke this function, set an allowance for the attacker’s address equal to the total token balance, and subsequently transfer the entire escrowed token supply to themselves. The impact is the complete loss of funds that users have deposited into the escrow, violating the protocol’s guarantee that assets are safely locked until a legitimate governance action occurs. The issue manifests whenever a holder of the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE interacts with the approve function, which may happen during routine governance operations or, more dangerously, after a key compromise. It affects all participants who rely on the escrow to safeguard their tokens, as well as the protocol’s reputation and financial integrity. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the contract’s access control and token interaction patterns; the presence of an unrestricted approve call can be easily overlooked because the function resembles a standard administrative utility. Detecting the problem requires understanding that an ERC‑20 allowance granted by a contract can be used by the approved spender to move tokens out of the contract without further checks. To remediate, the approve function should be removed entirely or tightly restricted: the contract should only grant allowance to the designated L1Gateway for the specific LPT token during deployment, and any future allowance changes should be mediated by a multi‑signature governance process. By eliminating the ability for a single admin to approve arbitrary spenders, the protocol restores the intended trust model where only authorized bridge components can move escrowed assets, thereby preventing unauthorized fund extraction and preserving user confidence.

title: [WP-M4] Unable to use `L2GatewayRouter` to withdraw LPT from L2 to L1, as `L2LPTGateway` does not implement `L2GatewayRouter` expected method
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an interface mismatch between the Arbitrum L2GatewayRouter contract and the Livepeer L2LPTGateway contract that is responsible for moving Livepeer Token (LPT) from Arbitrum (L2) back to Ethereum (L1).
