The router is designed to invoke a six‑parameter function outboundTransfer(address token, address to, uint256 amount, uint256 maxGas, uint256 gasPriceBid, bytes data) defined in the ITokenGateway interface. In the Livepeer implementation, however, L2LPTGateway only provides a four‑parameter overload outboundTransfer(address l1Token, address to, uint256 amount, bytes data). Because the router forwards calls using the six‑parameter signature, the call reaches a contract that does not expose that exact function selector, causing the low‑level call to fail silently or revert. Consequently, a user who follows the documented workflow – initiating a withdrawal through the L2GatewayRouter – receives no transaction receipt confirming a successful transfer, sees no change in their L1 balance, and may incorrectly conclude that the withdrawal succeeded while the funds remain locked on L2. The bug manifests only when the withdrawal is performed via the router; direct calls to L2LPTGateway using the four‑parameter version still work, which makes the problem subtle and easy to overlook during testing that only exercises the direct path. The issue was discovered during a static audit that compared the official withdrawal guide with the actual contract ABIs, revealing that the expected method signature was absent. From a security perspective the flaw does not open a path for theft, but it constitutes a functional denial‑of‑service: users cannot retrieve their LPT using the standard router interface, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees that deposited tokens should be withdrawable on demand. The failure mode can be described as a “withdrawal‑router mismatch” or “missing outboundTransfer overload”. To remediate, the L2LPTGateway contract should implement the full outboundTransfer function with the six parameters, either by delegating to the existing four‑parameter implementation or by adding the additional gas‑related arguments as no‑ops, thereby satisfying the ITokenGateway interface expected by the router. After the amendment, calls routed through L2GatewayRouter will correctly forward to L2LPTGateway, enabling users to see their LPT move from L2 to L1 as documented, restoring confidence in the bridge’s reliability.

title: Admin can rug L2 Escrow tokens leading to reputation risk
description:
The `L1Escrow` contract has the function `approve` that is callable by the admin to approve an arbitrary spender with an arbitrary amount (so they can steal all of the escrow’s holdings if they want). Even if the admin is well intended, the contract can still be called out which would degrade the reputation of the protocol (e.g. see here: <https://twitter.com/RugDocIO/status/1411732108029181960>). LPT is valuable on the Ethereum mainnet, so this rug vector should be mitigated. It would be best to restrict this function’s power by only allowing approvals to other trusted protocol contracts (like L1LPTGateway, which I believe uses the escrow’s approval).

NOTE: Even if the admin is under a timelock, this is still an issue, as users have to wait a whole week to withdraw from L2 -> L1 due to the dispute period.
poc: See the `approve` function [here](https://github.com/livepeer/arbitrum-lpt-bridge/blob/ebf68d11879c2798c5ec0735411b08d0bea4f287/contracts/L1/escrow/L1Escrow.sol#L21)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the escrow contract that holds LPT tokens destined for the L2‑to‑L1 bridge. The contract implements an `approve` function that can be called exclusively by the admin address and permits the admin to set an arbitrary allowance for any spender of any amount. Because the function does not validate the target spender or limit the approved amount, the admin – or an attacker who gains control of the admin key – can grant themselves or a malicious contract permission to transfer the entire token balance from the escrow. Once the allowance is set, the attacker can invoke the underlying ERC‑20 `transferFrom` to move all escrowed LPT to an address of their choosing. This attack can be carried out at any time, even if the admin role is protected by a timelock, because the withdrawal process from L2 to L1 includes a mandatory dispute period of one week; during that window the malicious approval can be executed and the tokens will be unavailable when the user finally attempts to claim them. The primary impact is the potential loss of valuable LPT tokens and a corresponding reputational damage to the protocol, as users would see their bridge withdrawals fail or their balances disappear without warning. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit and highlighted by external community discussion about rug pulls on similar bridges. It is hard to notice because the `approve` function mirrors the standard ERC‑20 pattern and is expected to be harmless; users do not see the internal allowance changes, and the presence of a timelock can give a false sense of security. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include a missing LPT balance after a claimed withdrawal, a transaction that appears successful but results in zero tokens being received, and an overall loss of confidence in the bridge’s safety. The flaw belongs to the class of privileged‑approval or admin‑controlled allowance bugs where a contract grants unrestricted token spending rights. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict the `approve` operation to a whitelist of trusted protocol contracts (for example, the designated L1 gateway) or remove the admin’s ability to set arbitrary allowances entirely, possibly replacing it with a more granular role that only permits approvals to known components. Implementing such a whitelist will ensure that even a compromised admin cannot direct escrowed tokens to malicious addresses, preserving both funds and the protocol’s reputation.

title: MAX _SHORTFALL_ WITHDRAW limit on BTP extraction is not enforced
description:
The function `extractTokensForCollateralShortfall()` allows the owner of the sNote contract to withdraw up to 50% of the total amount of BPT.

Presumably, this 50% limit is in place to prevent the owner from “rug-pulling” the sNote holders (or at least to give them a guarantee that their loss is limited to 50% of the underlying value).

However, this limit is easily circumvented as the function can simply be called a second, third and fourth time, to withdraw almost all of the BPT.

As the contract does not enforce this limit, the bug requires stakers to trust the governance to not withdraw more than 50% of the underlying collateral. This represents a higher risk for the stakers, which may also result in a larger discount on sNote wrt its BPT collateral (this is why I classified the bug as medium risk - users may lose value - not from an exploit, but from the lack of enforcing the 50% rule)
poc: See above. The code affected is here: https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-notional/blob/main/contracts/sNOTE.sol#L100
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the withdrawal logic of the sNote contract’s extractTokensForCollateralShortfall function. The contract is supposed to limit the owner’s ability to pull collateral to a maximum of 50 % of the total BPT balance, a safeguard meant to protect sNote holders from a full rug‑pull. However, the implementation only checks the amount on a per‑call basis and does not keep any record of how much has already been withdrawn within a given time window. Because of this missing cumulative accounting, the owner can invoke the function repeatedly in the same period – second, third, fourth calls – each time withdrawing up to the 50 % per‑call ceiling, ultimately draining almost the entire BPT pool. The root cause is the absence of state that tracks the total withdrawn amount against the 50 % cap over a defined interval (e.g., per week). An attacker who controls the contract’s owner role can therefore exceed the intended limit simply by calling the function multiple times before other participants have a chance to react. The impact is that stakers may see their sNote value dramatically depreciate, experience unexpectedly low redemption amounts, or find that the underlying collateral is insufficient to back their tokens, effectively losing up to the full value of their investment. This condition occurs whenever the contract owner decides to invoke the extraction function, and it relies on the trust that governance will respect the informal 50 % rule, which is not programmatically enforced. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented intent (a 50 % cap) with the actual code, noticing that the limit is only enforced per transaction and not cumulatively. The bug is subtle because the per‑call check passes, giving the appearance that the safeguard is functional, while the overall system invariants are broken. To remediate, the contract should introduce a time‑bound state variable that records the total amount withdrawn during each period and reject any call that would cause the cumulative total to exceed 50 % of the current BPT balance. A cooldown or weekly reset would give users time to withdraw their share before any further extraction. This class of vulnerability is generally known as a ‘cumulative withdrawal limit bypass’ or ‘insufficient state tracking for rate‑limited operations.’ From a user’s perspective, the symptom may appear as a sudden reduction in the displayed collateral, a zero or much‑smaller refund when attempting to redeem sNote, or an unexpected loss of value that contradicts the promised 50 % safety net.

title: anti-flashloan mechanism may lead to protocol default
description: There is a price check to avoid flash loan attacks which significantly moved the price. If current price is 5% lower than the stored twap price, the liquidation will fail. This design can be dangerous as it is to openleverage’s benefit to close under-collateralized position ASAP when there is a huge market drawdown. When the market keep trading downward, it is possible that the spot price keep trading 5% lower than the twap, which prevent any liquidation from happening and causing the protocol to be under-collateralized.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a protective price check that is intended to mitigate flash‑loan manipulation during liquidation. The contract compares the current spot price of an asset against a short‑term time‑weighted average price (TWAP). If the spot price is more than a configured threshold (approximately 5%) lower than the TWAP, the liquidation function reverts with the error code ‘MPT’. While this guard can stop a malicious flash‑loan attacker from forcing an artificial price drop, it also creates a situation where legitimate, rapid market drawdowns trigger the same condition. When the market continues to trade below the TWAP for a period longer than the TWAP window (which is only one minute), every liquidation attempt fails because the price check repeatedly triggers the revert. As a result, positions that are genuinely under‑collateralised remain open, the protocol cannot recover the outstanding debt, and the system accumulates bad debt that may lead to a default. The impact is that lenders’ funds can become unrecoverable, users see their positions frozen while the protocol’s overall health deteriorates, and the expected liquidation‑based risk‑mitigation mechanism becomes ineffective. This issue was discovered during a formal security audit of the OpenLev V1 library, where the auditor observed that the ‘isPositionHealthy’ logic uses an OR combination of three price checks, and that the TWAP‑only condition can be the sole blocker for liquidation. The problem is subtle because the same code path also protects against flash‑loan attacks, so test cases that only simulate normal liquidations may pass, while extreme market conditions reveal the failure mode. To remediate the issue, the contract should avoid using a hard revert based on the TWAP deviation for liquidation decisions. Instead, the TWAP should be used as a reference for assessing position health, while allowing liquidation to proceed using alternative safeguards (such as slippage limits or a secondary oracle) so that genuine under‑collateralised positions can be closed even when the spot price remains substantially below the TWAP. This adjustment restores the intended economic guarantees without exposing the protocol to flash‑loan price manipulation.

title: `sNOTE` Holders Are Not Incetivized To Vote On Proposals To Call `extractTokensForCollateralShortfall`
description:
As `sNOTE` have governance voting rights equivalent to the token amount in `NOTE`, users who stake their `NOTE` are also able to vote on governance proposals. In the event a majority of `NOTE` is staked in the `sNOTE` contract, it doesn’t seem likely that stakers would be willing to vote on a proposal which liquidates a portion of their staked position.

Hence, the protocol may be put into a state where stakers are unwilling to vote on a proposal to call `extractTokensForCollateralShortfall`, leaving Notional insolvent as stakers continue to dump their holdings.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a misalignment of incentives between the governance system and the economic stake of sNOTE holders. In Notional, users who lock NOTE tokens to receive the rebasing token sNOTE automatically gain voting power proportional to the amount of NOTE they have deposited. A critical protocol function, extractTokensForCollateralShortfall, allows the contract owner to withdraw a bounded portion of the pooled Balancer BPT tokens in order to cover a collateral shortfall. The withdrawal, however, can only be executed after a successful governance proposal is passed. When a large majority of the total NOTE supply is staked in the sNOTE contract, the very voters who must approve the proposal are also the owners of the assets that would be liquidated. Because the proposal would reduce the value of their own staked position, rational stakers have little incentive to vote in favor of the extraction, and may even actively vote against it or abstain. As a result, the protocol can become stuck in a state where a collateral shortfall exists but the governance proposal required to trigger the rescue function cannot obtain the necessary majority. This creates a scenario where the protocol’s collateral pool is insufficient, users attempting to withdraw or redeem their holdings receive nothing or see their balances unexpectedly drop to zero, and the overall system may become insolvent. The issue was identified during a manual code audit that examined the interaction between token staking, voting rights, and the emergency extraction mechanism. It is difficult to detect because the smart‑contract code for the extraction function itself appears correct; the problem lies in the economic and governance design, which is not immediately obvious from static analysis. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should redesign the incentive structure so that voters are compensated or otherwise motivated to approve rescue proposals, for example by allocating a portion of protocol fees to an insurance fund that can be used to cover shortfalls without requiring stakers to sacrifice their own collateral. Conceptually, the fix decouples the voting power from the direct loss of value caused by a rescue action, thereby aligning participants’ interests with the health of the protocol and preventing a situation where funds disappear due to governance deadlock.

title: `getVotingPower` Is Not Equipped To Handle On-Chain Voting
description:
As `NOTE` continues to be staked in the `sNOTE` contract, it is important that Notional’s governance is able to correctly handle on-chain voting by calculating the relative power `sNOTE` has in terms of its equivalent `NOTE` amount.

`getVotingPower` is a useful function in tracking the relative voting power a staker has, however, it does not utilise any checkpointing mechanism to ensure the user’s voting power is a snapshot of a specific block number. As a result, it would be possible to manipulate a user’s voting power by casting a vote on-chain and then have them transfer their `sNOTE` to another account to then vote again.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance module that derives a user’s voting power from the function `getVotingPower`. This function computes the power on the fly by reading the current on‑chain balances of the underlying sNOTE token and the price oracle at the moment the call is executed. Because it does not incorporate any historical snapshot or checkpointing mechanism, the returned value reflects the present state rather than the state at the block where a vote was cast. The root cause is the absence of a per‑block voting‑power ledger, which allows the reported power to change between the time a proposal is submitted and the time the vote is tallied. An attacker can exploit this by first voting with a certain amount of sNOTE, then immediately transferring the same sNOTE to another address (or using a flash loan) and voting again in the same proposal, because the governance contract will query `getVotingPower` each time and obtain the updated, higher balance. The impact is a distortion of the intended one‑vote‑per‑stake rule, leading to inflated voting influence, potential passage of malicious proposals, and erosion of protocol trust. The flaw manifests whenever a governance vote is processed without a prior‑state snapshot, i.e., for any on‑chain voting that relies on `getVotingPower` during the tally phase. All participants of the Notional protocol, including token holders, delegators, and the broader ecosystem, are affected because the governance outcome can be manipulated, potentially resulting in decisions that do not reflect the true distribution of economic stake. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which examined the logic of the voting‑power calculation and noticed the lack of a checkpointing scheme. It can be difficult to notice because the function appears to return a reasonable numeric value, and normal operations (e.g., a single user voting) show no obvious discrepancy; the problem only surfaces under rapid, repeated voting actions that a typical user would not perform. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a snapshot‑based query such as `getPriorVotingPower(blockNumber)` that records each account’s effective voting power at the block when the vote is cast and stores it in a checkpoint data structure. This would enforce that voting power is immutable for the duration of a proposal, preventing double‑spending of stake. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "state‑changing calculations without historical anchoring," similar to missing checkpointing in token voting systems, which can lead to double‑voting and governance manipulation. From a user’s perspective, the symptom would be that a proposal passes despite a relatively small amount of sNOTE being legitimately held, or that the same stake appears to count multiple times, contradicting the expectation that each unit of stake should only be able to vote once per proposal. The discrepancy violates the fundamental accounting assumption that voting weight is a static representation of a holder’s stake at the snapshot moment, thereby breaking the integrity of the governance process.

title: `_validateOrder` Does Not Allow Anyone To Be A Taker Of An Off-Chain Order
description:
The `EIP1271Wallet` contract intends to allow the treasury manager account to sign off-chain orders in 0x on behalf of the `TreasuryManager` contract, which holds harvested assets/`COMP` from Notional. While the `EIP1271Wallet._validateOrder` function mostly prevents the treasury manager from exploiting these orders, it does not ensure that the `takerAddress` and `senderAddress` are set to the zero address. As a result, it is possible for the manager to have sole rights to an off-chain order and due to the flexibility in `makerPrice`, the manager is able to extract value from the treasury by maximising the allowed slippage.

By setting `takerAddress` to the zero address, any user can be the taker of an off-chain order. By setting `senderAddress` to the zero address, anyone is allowed to access the exchange methods that interact with the order, including filling the order itself. Hence, these two order addresses can be manipulated by the manager to effectively restrict order trades to themselves.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the EIP1271Wallet contract that is used by the TreasuryManager to sign off‑chain 0x orders on behalf of the protocol. While the _validateOrder function checks several critical parameters such as feeRecipient, makerToken, takerToken, price oracle availability and slippage limits, it neglects to verify that the takerAddress and senderAddress fields of the order are set to the zero address. In the 0x order format, a non‑zero takerAddress restricts order execution to that specific address, and a non‑zero senderAddress restricts who may call the exchange methods that interact with the order. Because the contract assumes these fields will be zero, the treasury manager can craft an off‑chain order that lists his own address as the taker (or sender), thereby granting himself exclusive rights to fill the order. Combined with the flexible makerPrice calculation and the ability to maximise allowed slippage, the manager can execute the order at a price that favours him, effectively extracting value from the treasury’s harvested COMP assets. The exploit can be carried out whenever the manager creates an off‑chain order, signs it with the EIP1271 wallet, and then fills it or allows only his address to fill it. Users attempting to fill the same order will be rejected because the contract does not enforce a open‑taker policy, leading to a symptom where a user sees "order cannot be filled" or receives no tokens despite offering appropriate balances. The impact is a loss of treasury funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that any user should be able to act as taker of off‑chain orders. This issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewer noticed that the validation routine omitted checks for takerAddress and senderAddress, a subtle omission that can be easily missed because the rest of the validation logic appears sound. The vulnerability belongs to the class of order‑access‑control bugs where insufficient validation of permission fields enables privilege escalation. To remediate, the contract should explicitly require both takerAddress and senderAddress to equal address(0) before allowing the order to be processed, thereby ensuring that any user can act as the taker and that the exchange methods remain open to the public. Implementing these requires statements such as require(takerAddress == address(0), "manager cannot set taker"); and require(senderAddress == address(0), "manager cannot set sender"); which will close the loophole and restore the intended trust model.

title: `UniV2ClassDex.sol#uniClassSell
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token‑sale helper function that swaps a sell token for a buy token on a Uniswap‑V2‑style AMM. The function calculates an expected output amount by calling a deterministic pricing routine (getAmountOut) based on the current reserves and then immediately checks that this calculated amount meets the caller‑provided minimum (minBuyAmount). However, the function never validates the actual amount of tokens that the payee receives after the swap. It only returns the difference between the payee's balance before and after the swap (bought) for later use, but the require statement still uses the pre‑computed buyAmount. Because the AMM may deliver fewer tokens than the formula predicts – for example when the token implements a transfer fee, when the pair reserves are altered by a preceding transaction, or when an attacker front‑runs the call and reduces the output – the require condition can be satisfied while the user actually receives less than the guaranteed minimum. Consequently, the seller (payer) may lose value, the payee receives a shortfall, and the protocol may suffer systematic value leakage. This flaw manifests whenever the swap involves a token whose on‑chain transfer semantics differ from the pure constant‑product model assumed by getAmountOut, or in any scenario where the reserves change between the sync call and the actual swap execution. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the implementation of the complementary uniClassBuy function, which correctly validates the actual received amount, with the uniClassSell logic that relies on the theoretical output. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the UI will typically report a successful trade, making the shortfall easy to miss. To remediate, the function should record the payee's balance before the swap, perform the swap, then recompute the real increase (bought) and compare that to minBuyAmount, reverting if the received amount is insufficient. This aligns the check with the true accounting outcome and prevents inadvertent slippage or fee‑on‑transfer token manipulation from causing loss of funds.

title: Missing payable
description:
The following functions are not payable but uses msg.value - therefore the function must be payable. This can lead to undesired behavior.
    
        LPool.sol, addReserves should be payable since using msg.value

Nice find! The warden has identified a function which is missing the `payable` keyword. Preventing any users from adding reserves using native ether.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing payable modifier on a smart‑contract function that nevertheless reads the amount of Ether sent with the transaction via msg.value. Because the function is not declared payable, the Ethereum Virtual Machine will reject any call that includes a non‑zero value, causing the transaction to revert before the contract’s logic can be executed. The root cause is a mismatch between the function’s intended behaviour—accepting native Ether to add reserves—and its visibility declaration, which defaults to non‑payable. An attacker or any regular user can exploit this by attempting to fund the contract through the affected function; the call will fail, leaving the caller with a reverted transaction and no Ether transferred to the protocol’s reserve pool. The impact is that legitimate participants are unable to add reserves using native Ether, which effectively blocks a core economic operation of the protocol. This condition manifests whenever a user sends Ether together with a call to the affected function, for example the addReserves method in LPool.sol. Both end‑users and the protocol itself are affected: users experience failed transactions and may lose gas, while the protocol suffers from missing liquidity, potentially affecting loan issuance or other services that depend on adequate reserves. The issue was identified during a manual audit where the reviewer inspected the source code and noticed that the function accessed msg.value without being marked payable. It can be hard to notice because the function may compile without warnings and the developer might assume that the presence of msg.value implicitly allows payments, which is not the case in Solidity. The appropriate remediation is to add the payable keyword to any function that reads msg.value or otherwise expects Ether, ensuring that the EVM permits value transfers. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "incorrect function visibility" or "missing payable modifier" errors, where the contract’s public interface does not align with its intended financial logic. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a “Submit” button to add funds, but after confirming the transaction the user sees a generic revert error and their balance remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation that the protocol would accept the deposit. The failure mode is effectively a silent denial of service on the reserve‑adding path, leading to “funds disappear” in the sense that the user’s attempt to transfer funds does not reach the contract, even though the contract’s code seems to intend to receive them.

title: Eth sent to Timelock will be locked in current implementation
description: Eth sent to Timelock will be locked in current implementation. I came across this problem while playing around with the governance contract.
poc:
* Setup the governance contracts (GovernanceAlpha, Timelock)
  * Send eth to timelock contract
  * Setup a proposal to send 0.1 eth out. Code snippet in ether.js below. proxy refers to GovernorAlpha.

    await proxy.propose(
        [signers[3].address],
        [ethers.utils.parseEther("0.1")],
        [""],
        [ethers.BigNumber.from(0)],
        "Send funds to 3rd signer"
    );

  * Vote and have the proposal succeed.
  * Execute the proposal, the proposal number here is arbitrary.

    await proxy.execute(2);  // this fails
        await proxy.execute(2, {value: ethers.utils.parseEther("0.1")})  // this would work
        0.1 eth will be sent out, but it is sent from the msg.sender not from the timelock contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of Ether (ETH) within the governance system that relies on a Timelock contract to enforce delayed execution of proposals. In the current implementation, when a proposer includes a non‑zero ETH amount in a proposal, the governance contract (GovernorAlpha) calls the Timelock's executeTransaction function without forwarding the Ether value. As a result, the ETH that was previously sent to the Timelock becomes locked because the transaction that should transfer the funds is executed by the caller (msg.sender) rather than by the Timelock itself. The root cause is the missing value forwarding in the GovernorAlpha execute() method: it iterates over proposal targets and calls timelock.executeTransaction with only the target, value, signature, calldata, and eta, but the value field is not passed on as msg.value, nor is the call made with the required Ether attached. Consequently, an attacker (or any user) must manually supply the Ether when invoking execute(), which defeats the purpose of the Timelock, undermines trust, and enables scenarios where funds are effectively frozen. The exploit is straightforward: a user deposits ETH into the Timelock, creates a proposal that intends to withdraw that ETH, votes the proposal to succeed, and then attempts to execute it. The execution reverts or sends no Ether unless the executor also includes the Ether value in the transaction, meaning the Timelock never disburses the funds on its own. From a user perspective, the UI shows a successful proposal but the expected ETH transfer never occurs; balances appear unchanged, and users may see "0 ETH transferred" or an empty receipt despite a positive vote. The impact is that protocol funds become inaccessible, governance cannot move capital, and token holders may lose confidence because the system cannot enforce its own delayed transfer guarantees. This issue was discovered through manual testing of the governance contracts, where sending ETH to the Timelock and executing a proposal resulted in a failed transfer unless the extra value was manually supplied. It can be hard to notice because the Timelock contract itself includes an executeTransaction function that appears capable of moving ETH, and developers may assume the GovernorAlpha wrapper will automatically forward the value. To remediate, the GovernorAlpha execute() function should be modified to forward the Ether amount specified in each proposal element, either by passing proposal.values[i] as the msg.value parameter in the call to timelock.executeTransaction or by redesigning the flow so that the Timelock itself holds and releases the ETH without requiring external value forwarding. The conceptual fix is to ensure that any ETH attached to a proposal is transferred by the Timelock during execution, preserving the intended delayed‑execution security model and preventing funds from becoming permanently locked.

title: OpenLevV1.closeTrade with V3 DEX doesn’t correctly accounts fee on transfer tokens for repayments
description:
The amount that OpenLevV1 will receive can be less than V3 DEX indicated as a swap result, while it is used as given for position debt repayment accounting.

This way actual funds received can be less than accounted, leaving to system funds deficit, which can be exploited by a malicious user, draining contract funds with multiple open/close with a taxed token.

In the `trade.depositToken != longToken` case when `flashSell` is used this can imply inability to send remainder funds to a user and the failure of the whole closeTrade function, the end result is a freezing of user’s funds within the system.
poc:
`trade.depositToken != longToken` case, can be wrong repayment accounting, which will lead to a deficit if the received funds are less than DEX returned `closeTradeVars.receiveAmount`.

As a side effect, `doTransferOut` is done without balance check, so the whole position close can revert, leading to inability to close the position and freeze of user’s funds this way:

I.e. if there is enough funds in the system they will be drained, if there is not enough funds, user’s position close will fail.

V3 sell function doesn’t check for balance change, using DEX returned amount as is:
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OpenLevV1 contract’s closeTrade workflow when it interacts with a Uniswap V3 style decentralized exchange to sell a token that charges a transfer fee (often called a fee‑on‑transfer or taxed token). The contract assumes that the amount reported by the DEX call (closeTradeVars.receiveAmount) exactly matches the tokens that will be deposited into the contract’s balance after the swap. In reality, because the token deducts a fee on each transfer, the actual balance increase can be smaller than the reported amount. OpenLevV1 subsequently uses the DEX‑reported amount as the basis for repaying the position’s debt without verifying the real incoming balance. This mismatch creates an accounting deficit: the protocol records that a larger repayment has been made than the funds actually received. When the deficit grows, the protocol’s global fund pool becomes negative, allowing a malicious actor to open and close multiple positions with a taxed token and effectively drain the contract’s assets. Additionally, in the specific case where the deposit token differs from the long token and the flashSell path is taken, the contract attempts to transfer out the presumed remainder without checking whether sufficient balance remains. If the net received amount is lower than expected, the doTransferOut call can revert, causing the entire closeTrade transaction to fail and leaving the user’s position funds permanently locked in the system. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that inspected the UniV3Dex.uniV3Sell implementation and observed that it calculates the received amount solely from the DEX’s return value, ignoring the before‑and‑after balance delta that is required for fee‑on‑transfer tokens. The bug is subtle because transfer fees are not visible in the transaction logs and the contract’s internal accounting appears consistent at a superficial level. From a user perspective, an expected refund or liquidation payout may be zero or the transaction may simply revert, resulting in frozen funds and a loss of confidence in the protocol. To remediate the problem, the contract should measure the token balance before and after the swap, derive the true net received amount, and adjust the repayment bookkeeping accordingly. Moreover, any outbound transfer should be guarded by a balance check to ensure that the contract does not attempt to send more tokens than it actually holds. This change aligns the accounting with the real economic flow of fee‑on‑transfer tokens and restores the integrity of the liquidation and repayment processes.

title: Late users will take more losses than expected when the underlying contract
description:
Even though it’s unlikely in practice, but in theory, the underlying contract (`EthAnchor`) may suffer investment losses and causing decreasing of the PPS of AUST token. (There are codes that considered this situation in the codebase. eg. handling of `depositShares > claimerShares`).

However, when this happens, the late users will suffer more losses than expected than the users that withdraw earlier. The last few users may lose all their funds while the first users can get back 100% of their deposits.
poc:
// ### for deposits: d1, d2, d3, the beneficiary are: c1, c2, c2
    depositAmount          claimerShares
d1: + 100e18           c1: + 100e36
d2: + 100e18           c2: + 100e36
d3: + 100e18           c2: + 100e36

    depositAmount of d1, d2, d3 = 100e18
    c1 claimerShares: 100e36
    c2 claimerShares: 200e36
    total shares: 300e36

    // ### when the PPS of AUST drop by 50% 
    totalUnderlyingMinusSponsored: 300e18 -> 150e18

    // ### d2 withdraw
    c2 claimerShares: 200e36
    d2 depositAmount: 100e18
    d2 depositShares: 300e36 * 100e18 / 150e18 = 200e36

    Shares to reduce: 200e36
    c2 claimerShares: 200e36 -> 0
    c2 totalPrincipal: 200e18 -> 100e18
    totalShares: 300e36 -> 100e36

    underlying.safeTransfer(d2, 100e18)
    totalUnderlyingMinusSponsored: 150e18 -> 50e18
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract calculates a user’s withdrawal amount when the underlying investment strategy suffers a loss that reduces the price per share (PPS) of the protocol’s token. The contract stores a single global variable representing the total underlying assets and derives a user’s entitlement by multiplying the user’s share balance by the current PPS. When the underlying value drops, the PPS shrinks, but the contract does not keep any record of the loss that has already been absorbed by the system. Consequently, the share‑to‑underlying ratio is recomputed for each withdrawal based only on the reduced underlying balance. Early withdrawers, who act before the loss propagates, receive an amount that matches their original principal because the share conversion still reflects the higher PPS at the time of their deposit. Later withdrawers, however, are forced to exchange the same nominal amount of shares against a smaller pool of underlying assets, which means they receive a proportionally smaller payout. In extreme cases, the last few participants may end up with zero funds even though they deposited the same amount as earlier users. The impact is a violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees: users expect to recover at least a proportional share of their deposits, but the flawed accounting can cause disproportionate loss, effectively “money disappearing” for late participants. The issue is triggered only when the underlying contract experiences a loss that lowers its PPS, a scenario that is unlikely in normal operation but possible under adverse market conditions or faulty strategy execution. All depositors, regardless of role, are affected because the share accounting is global. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the handling of `depositShares > claimerShares` and simulated a 50 % drop in the PPS, revealing that the withdrawal logic does not adjust for accumulated losses. The bug is subtle because the contract still functions correctly when the underlying value is stable; the incorrect behavior only manifests after a loss event, which may not be observed in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a state variable that tracks the cumulative loss (e.g., `totalLoss`) and compute an adjusted underlying balance (`adjustedUnderlying = underlying + totalLoss`). This ensures that the share‑to‑underlying conversion remains consistent with the total value that depositors collectively own, preserving proportionality across all withdrawals. In other words, the contract must maintain invariant accounting that decouples individual share balances from transient fluctuations in asset value, thereby preventing late users from receiving less than their fair share or losing all funds.

title: No setter for exchangeRateFeeder, whose address might change in future
description: EthAnchor’s docs state that “the contract address of ExchangeRateFeeder may change as adjustments occur”. BaseStrategy does not have a setter to change exchangeRateFeeder after deployment.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an immutable reference to the ExchangeRateFeeder contract inside EthAnchor's BaseStrategy implementation. The documentation for EthAnchor explicitly states that the address of the ExchangeRateFeeder may change over time as adjustments are made to the protocol, yet the BaseStrategy source code does not provide any setter function that would allow the contract owner or governance to update the stored exchangeRateFeeder address after deployment. Because the investedAssets() view function relies on exchangeRateFeeder.exchangeRateOf() to convert aUst balances into the underlying asset value, an outdated or incorrect feeder address will cause the conversion to use stale data, return zero, or even revert if the contract at the old address no longer implements the expected interface. This mis‑calculation propagates to share minting, redemption, and any accounting that depends on the reported total assets. The impact is that users may see their vault share price diverge from the actual value of the underlying assets, leading to situations where a user expects to receive a correct amount of ETH or aUst on withdrawal but receives less, zero, or an unexpected amount. The error only manifests after the ExchangeRateFeeder contract is upgraded or its address changes, a condition that is not detectable during normal operation because the function works correctly with the initially deployed feeder. Consequently, the issue can remain unnoticed until a protocol upgrade occurs, at which point the accounting logic silently breaks, potentially eroding trust and causing financial loss for investors. The flaw was discovered during a code audit that compared the contract's stated behavior in the official documentation with the actual implementation and noticed the absence of any mechanism to modify the feeder address. It is difficult to spot in routine testing because the contract behaves as intended with the original feeder address; only a change in external dependencies reveals the bug. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a controlled setter—restricted to an appropriately authorized role such as governance or the contract owner—that allows the exchangeRateFeeder address to be updated safely, thereby keeping the asset valuation logic aligned with the current protocol configuration and preserving correct share accounting.

title: Changing a strategy can be bricked
description:
A vault wouldn’t let the strategy be changed unless the strategy holds no funds.

Since anybody can send funds to the strategy, a griefing attack is possible.
poc:
`setStrategy` requires `strategy.investedAssets() == 0`. [(Code ref)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/Vault.sol#L113:#L116) `investedAssets` contains the aUST balance and the pending redeems: [(Code ref)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/strategy/BaseStrategy.sol#L271)
    
```solidity
uint256 aUstBalance = _getAUstBalance() + pendingRedeems;
```

So if a griefer sends 1 wei of aUST to the strategy before it is to be replaced, it would not be able to be replaced. The protocol would then need to redeem the aUST and wait for the process to finish - and the griefer can repeat his griefing. As they say, griefers gonna grief.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in a vault contract that only permits a strategy to be replaced when the strategy reports zero invested assets. The invested assets are calculated as the sum of the strategy’s raw aUST token balance and any pending redemption amounts. Because the check uses the on‑chain aUST balance directly, an attacker can send a tiny amount of aUST (for example, 1 wei) directly to the strategy contract. Once any external aUST resides in the strategy, the investedAssets value becomes non‑zero, so the vault’s setStrategy function reverts and the current strategy cannot be swapped out. This creates a griefing scenario where the protocol becomes effectively bricked: the intended upgrade or replacement of the strategy is blocked, and the vault is forced to attempt a redemption of the offending aUST. However, EthAnchor, which the vault interacts with, does not accept redeems of less than 10 aUST, meaning the tiny amount cannot be redeemed either. The attacker can repeat the injection of minimal aUST, keeping the balance above zero and preventing the vault from ever meeting the zero‑balance precondition for strategy change. The impact is that the protocol’s governance or operators lose the ability to upgrade the strategy, potentially freezing user deposits and impairing withdrawals, which harms token holders and any parties relying on the protocol’s correct operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by checking the logic of setStrategy and the definition of investedAssets in the base strategy contract; the indirect reliance on raw token balances made the bug subtle and easy to overlook in testing, especially because normal operation rarely involves external token transfers to the strategy. From a user perspective the UI may still display an option to change the strategy, but the transaction will revert with an error, leading to confusion as funds appear to be stuck and no new strategy can be deployed. The root cause is the mismatch between internal accounting (deposits and pending redeems) and external token balances, combined with the lack of a mechanism for the strategy to return aUST to the vault. To remediate, the contract should maintain an internal accounting of aUST held by the strategy, update this accounting on every deposit and redemption, and use the internal figure—not the raw token balance—to decide whether the strategy is empty. Additionally, the strategy should be given the ability to transfer any aUST it holds back to the vault so that accidental or malicious external deposits can be cleared, ensuring that the zero‑balance requirement can be satisfied and the vault remains upgradeable.

title: `investedAssets
description:
The `investedAssets()` function is implemented by the vault’s strategy contracts as a way to express a vault’s investments in terms of the underlying currency. While the implementation of this function in `BaseStrategy.sol` and `NonUSTStrategy.sol` is mostly correct. It does not account for the performance fee charged by the treasury as shown in `finishRedeemStable()`.

Therefore, an attacker could avoid paying their fair share of the performance fee by withdrawing their assets before several calls to `finishRedeemStable()` are made and reenter the vault once the fee is charged.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the vault’s strategy contracts report their total assets through the `investedAssets()` view function. The function aggregates the underlying token balance and the value of aUST holdings, but it does not take into account the performance fee that is deducted later by the `finishRedeemStable()` routine. This omission creates a discrepancy between the amount reported to the vault and the actual net value that will be left after the fee is applied. The root cause is an accounting oversight: the strategy calculates invested assets based purely on on‑chain balances and exchange rates, ignoring the conditional fee that is only realized when a redemption operation is finalized. An attacker can exploit this by withdrawing their position before the vault processes the pending redemption operations that trigger `finishRedeemStable()`. By doing so, the attacker receives a larger amount than they would have after the performance fee is taken, then they can immediately re‑enter the vault once the fee has been collected, effectively paying a reduced share of the fee. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol’s treasury and a distortion of the economic model, because the fee‑paying mechanism can be bypassed. The problem manifests only when there are pending redeems and the `finishRedeemStable()` function has not yet been called; under normal deposit‑withdraw cycles the discrepancy may go unnoticed because the on‑chain balances appear correct. Users of the vault—depositors, withdrawers, and anyone interacting with the strategy—are affected, as they can unintentionally or deliberately receive more assets than intended. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the asset accounting logic in `investedAssets()` with the fee logic in `finishRedeemStable()`. It is subtle because the reported balance matches the raw token holdings, so developers and auditors may assume the accounting is sound without cross‑checking the fee deduction path. To remediate the bug, the `investedAssets()` calculation should be amended to subtract the expected performance fee that would be charged if the strategy’s assets were fully withdrawn, or otherwise incorporate a net‑after‑fee view of the holdings. By aligning the reported assets with the net value after fee, the protocol prevents users from gaming the fee mechanism and restores the intended financial guarantees. This class of bug falls under “fee‑calculation omission” or “accounting inconsistency” where a public view does not reflect hidden state changes, leading to potential fund leakage.

title: Incompatibility With Rebasing/Deflationary/Inflationary tokens
description: The Strategy contracts do not appear to support rebasing/deflationary/inflationary tokens whose balance changes during transfers or over time. The necessary checks include at least verifying the amount of tokens transferred to contracts before and after the actual transfer to infer any fees/interest.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/strategy/BaseStrategy.sol#L239>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/strategy/BaseStrategy.sol#L221>
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the strategy contracts assuming that ERC‑20 token balances remain unchanged during a transfer, which is true for standard fixed‑supply tokens but not for rebasing, deflationary, or inflationary tokens. The root cause is the absence of any verification of the actual token balance before and after a transfer operation, meaning the contracts never detect that a token’s supply or balance may be altered by mechanisms such as automatic rebasing, transfer fees, or interest accrual. An attacker or unsuspecting user can exploit this by supplying a token that reduces its amount on transfer (for example, a token that charges a 2 % fee) or that changes its total supply between the moment it is deposited and the moment the strategy records the deposit. The strategy records the intended amount based on the transaction parameters, but the vault actually receives a different amount, leading to a discrepancy in accounting. Over time, these discrepancies can accumulate, causing users to see lower balances than expected, refunds that are smaller or missing entirely, and in worst‑case scenarios, permanent loss of funds that are locked in the strategy under an incorrect accounting state. The issue manifests whenever a user interacts with the protocol using a token whose balance can change without explicit notification – during deposits, withdrawals, or any internal rebalancing that involves token transfers. All participants that rely on accurate accounting – the end‑users depositing assets, the protocol’s treasury, and any third‑party integrations that read vault balances – are potentially affected. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that compared the code paths of the strategy contracts with known patterns for handling fee‑on‑transfer and rebasing tokens, noting the lack of balance snapshots that are present in other well‑audited systems. Because the token interface still conforms to ERC‑20, the bug can be subtle and may only be observed as unexpected zero balances, missing rewards, or a mismatch between the amount a user approved and the amount actually credited. To remediate, the contracts should be updated to either reject tokens that do not conform to a “non‑rebasable, fee‑free” model or, preferably, to implement a safe‑transfer pattern that records the token balance of the contract before the transfer, executes the transfer, then records the balance after the transfer and computes the actual delta. This delta should be used for accounting and emitted in events, ensuring that any rebasing or fee logic is captured. Additionally, explicit documentation of supported token types and runtime checks on token behavior should be added to prevent future accidental acceptance of incompatible assets. By treating this as a generic “token balance manipulation” class of vulnerability, developers can apply a consistent mitigation strategy across all contracts that interact with external ERC‑20 tokens.

title: A Single Malicious Trusted Account Can Takeover Parent Contract
description:
The `requiresTrust()` modifier is used on the strategy, vault and factory contracts to prevent unauthorised accounts from calling restricted functions. Once an account is considered trusted, they are allowed to add and remove accounts by calling `setIsTrusted()` as they see fit.

However, if any single account has its private keys compromised or decides to become malicious on their own, they can remove all other trusted accounts from the `isTrusted` mapping. As a result, they are effectively able to take over the trusted group that controls all restricted functions in the parent contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted privilege revocation mechanism in contracts that rely on a simple trusted‑account mapping. A modifier called requiresTrust checks only that the caller’s address is present in the isTrusted mapping before allowing execution of privileged functions such as setIsTrusted. Because any address that is already trusted can call setIsTrusted with an arbitrary boolean value, a single trusted account that becomes compromised or decides to act maliciously can invoke setIsTrusted to set false for every other entry in the mapping. By removing all other trusted accounts, the attacker gains exclusive control over every function protected by the requiresTrust modifier, effectively taking over the parent contract’s administration. This takeover can be used to alter contract parameters, pause or disable functionality, or transfer assets held by the protocol, leading to loss of funds or a complete disruption of service. The condition for exploitation is simply the existence of at least one trusted address whose private key is exposed or whose owner is untrusted; no additional permissions or multi‑signature approval are required. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the trust management design and identified that the trusted set lacks a hierarchical owner or quorum, making the revocation logic overly permissive. The problem is subtle because the setIsTrusted function appears benign and the contract emits an event for each change, so basic tests may not reveal that an attacker can empty the trusted set. The vulnerability belongs to a class of admin‑role revocation bugs where any privileged user can remove other privileged users, resulting in a single point of failure and a privilege‑escalation path. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may include an inability to perform expected actions such as withdrawals or upgrades, unexpected contract pauses, or the sudden disappearance of funds after an apparently legitimate transaction. The contract’s business logic assumes that the set of trusted accounts is collectively managed and that no single member can displace the others; this assumption is violated by the current implementation. The recommended remediation is to introduce a dedicated owner role, preferably controlled by a multisignature wallet or DAO, that is the only entity authorized to add or remove trusted accounts. Using a vetted authentication contract such as Rari Capital’s Auth.sol enforces this hierarchy, preventing any single trusted address from unilaterally revoking the rights of its peers and thereby eliminating the takeover risk.

title: Check _to is not empty
description: functions `claimYield`, `_withdraw`, and `_unsponsor` should validate that `_to` is not an empty 0x0 address to prevent accidental burns.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from three contract functions—claimYield, _withdraw, and _unsponsor—that accept an external address parameter called _to but do not verify that the supplied address is non‑zero. Because the code lacks a require(_to != address(0)) guard, an attacker or a careless user can intentionally or unintentionally pass the null address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) as the destination for transferred assets. When the contract attempts to send tokens, ETH, or any other value to this address, the transfer succeeds but the funds are effectively burned, removing them permanently from the protocol's balance sheet. The exploit can be triggered whenever a caller is able to invoke any of the three functions with a custom _to argument; no additional conditions are required beyond the function’s normal access controls. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a missing payout: a user who expects to receive a yield, a withdrawal, or a sponsor refund instead sees a zero balance or receives no tokens, often without an explicit error message. The impact is a loss of funds for the affected user and a reduction of the protocol’s total assets, potentially breaking accounting assumptions such as total supply, sponsor balances, or yield distribution totals. This issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit when reviewers noted the absence of an empty‑address check, a common defensive pattern in Solidity contracts. The problem can be hard to notice because a zero‑address transfer does not revert and the UI may simply show a successful transaction with no visible indication that the assets have been destroyed. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit validation that the _to argument is not the zero address before any transfer logic is executed, thereby preventing accidental burns and preserving expected financial flows. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or unchecked address parameters, which can lead to unintended asset loss and violate core business logic that assumes funds are always transferred to a legitimate recipient.

title: `NonUSTStrategy.sol` Improper handling of swap fees allows attacker to steal funds from other users
description:
`NonUSTStrategy` will swap the deposited non-UST assets into UST before depositing to EthAnchor. However, the swap fee is not attributed to the depositor correctly like many other yield farming vaults involving swaps (`ZapIn`).

An attacker can exploit it for the swap fees paid by other users by taking a majority share of the liquidity pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NonUSTStrategy contract that converts deposited non‑UST assets into UST before allocating them to the EthAnchor protocol. The core issue is that the contract does not correctly attribute the swap fee incurred during the conversion to the depositor. Instead of deducting the fee from the incoming amount and issuing new shares based on the net UST received, the contract issues shares as if the full pre‑fee amount were transferred. This mis‑allocation creates a gap where the fee is effectively paid by other users of the vault. The problem becomes exploitable when an attacker can obtain a controlling stake in the underlying Curve pool that performs the FRAX‑UST swap. By adding a large amount of liquidity to the pool, the attacker can acquire more than fifty percent of the pool’s share. When a victim deposits FRAX, the strategy swaps the tokens, paying a small fee (for example 0.04%). Because the fee is not charged to the depositor, that portion of the fee is deposited back into the pool and is subsequently claimable by the liquidity provider – the attacker. After the victim’s deposit, the attacker withdraws their position from the vault, removes the liquidity they added, and collects the accumulated swap fees, effectively stealing value that should have been part of the victim’s balance. From a user’s perspective, a depositor expects that the amount they deposit will be fully accounted for after the swap, but instead sees a shortfall where part of their funds are missing, leading to a situation where “my balance is lower than expected” or “the refund I receive is zero”. The impact is a reduction of other users’ effective share value and a loss of funds that are not directly at risk for the attacker but erode the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This flaw only manifests under specific conditions: the pool must have low liquidity so that an attacker can become a majority provider, and the contract must allow share issuance based on pre‑fee amounts. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that identified a mismatch between fee handling logic and typical vault implementations that incorporate a ZapIn pattern. It is difficult to notice because the fee percentage is tiny and the vault’s normal operation masks the discrepancy, making the loss appear as normal slippage or market movement. The recommended mitigation is to calculate the number of new shares using the net UST amount received after the swap (i.e., amount out divided by total underlying UST), thereby ensuring that each depositor bears both the swap fee and any slippage. Adding slippage controls and avoiding low‑liquidity pools further reduces the attack surface. In summary, this is a classic case of improper fee attribution in a token swapping strategy, leading to an economic drain that violates the expected accounting invariants of the vault and can be exploited by an attacker who controls a majority of the liquidity pool.

title: Centralization Risk: Funds can be frozen when critical key holders lose access to their keys
description:
The current implementation requires trusted key holders (`isTrusted[msg.sender]`) to send transactions (`initRedeemStable()`) to initialize withdrawals from `EthAnchor` before the users can withdraw funds from the contract.

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/a90ad3824955327597be00bb0bd183a9c228a4fb/sandclock/contracts/strategy/BaseStrategy.sol#L214-L223>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/a90ad3824955327597be00bb0bd183a9c228a4fb/sandclock/contracts/strategy/BaseStrategy.sol#L163-L170>

This introduces a high centralization risk, which can cause funds to be frozen in the contract if the key holders lose access to their keys.
poc:
Given:

  * `investPerc` = 80%
  * 1,000 users deposited 1M UST in total ($1000 each user in avg), 800k invested into AUST (`EthAnchor`)

If the key holders lose access to their keys (“hit by a bus”). The 800k will be frozen in `EthAnchor` as no one can `initRedeemStable()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk that stems from the contract’s reliance on a set of trusted key holders to perform a critical step before any user can withdraw their assets. Specifically, the strategy contracts require an address flagged as trusted (isTrusted[msg.sender]) to call the initRedeemStable() function, which triggers the redemption process in the external EthAnchor contract where the protocol’s invested funds are held. The root cause is the hard‑coded trust model: only the privileged key holder can initiate the redemption, while ordinary depositors have no direct method to request it themselves. If the trusted address loses access to its private key – for example, due to loss, death, or a compromised environment – the required initRedeemStable() call can never be executed. Consequently, the funds that have been moved into EthAnchor remain locked, because the contract’s withdrawal path is blocked waiting for a state transition that never occurs. This situation can be exploited indirectly; there is no malicious actor needed, but the unavailability of the privileged key holder effectively freezes user balances. The impact is that users see their deposited amounts unchanged, or even a zero balance after a withdrawal request, because the underlying tokens are still stuck in EthAnchor and cannot be transferred back to the user. The condition under which this occurs is when the protocol has invested a portion of the vault’s capital (e.g., 80% of deposits) and the trusted key holder is unable to act. All depositors, the protocol’s availability, and any downstream applications that rely on timely withdrawals are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BaseStrategy contract, where the auditor identified the single‑point‑of‑failure pattern in the initRedeemStable() call sequence. It is hard to notice because the code looks functional under normal conditions; the bug only surfaces in an edge case where the privileged key becomes inaccessible, a scenario that is not covered by typical tests. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the single‑trusted‑key dependency: either allow users to invoke the uninvest (redeem) function themselves under defined constraints, or replace the single externally owned account with a multisignature controller or a decentralized governance mechanism that can act if one signer is unavailable. By providing an alternative path for redemption, the protocol can preserve its accounting guarantees, ensure that user‑expected refunds are delivered, and avoid a situation where "funds disappear" or "withdrawals fail" due to centralization of authority.

title: unsponsor, claimYield and withdraw might fail unexpectedly
description:
`totalUnderlying()` includes the invested assets, they are not in the contract balance.

when a user calls withdraw, claimYield or unsponsor, the system might not have enough assets in the balance and the transfer would fail.

especially, force unsponsor will always fail, because it tries to transfer the entire `totalUnderlying()`, which the system doesn’t have:
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch between the value reported by the contract's totalUnderlying() function and the actual token balance held by the contract. totalUnderlying() aggregates both the assets that are currently held in the contract and those that have been delegated to an external investment strategy, but the function does not differentiate between liquid and invested portions. When a user invokes withdraw, claimYield, or unsponsor, the implementation attempts to transfer an amount equal to totalUnderlying() (or a portion of it) directly from the contract's balance. Because the invested assets reside off‑chain in the strategy and are not available in the contract's token holdings, the transfer can fail due to insufficient balance. The failure is most evident in the forceUnsponsor path, which unconditionally tries to move the entire totalUnderlying() amount, guaranteeing a revert whenever any portion of the assets is invested. This flaw may remain unnoticed during normal operation because the contract's public view functions continue to report a healthy totalUnderlying value, leading users to believe that sufficient funds are on‑hand. Exploitation does not involve stealing funds; instead, an attacker or a cascade of legitimate users can trigger a “bank‑run” scenario where repeated calls to withdraw or unsponsor cause multiple transactions to revert, effectively freezing the protocol's ability to release assets. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition: users may see their withdrawal or claim attempts fail, balances in the UI may appear unchanged or zero, and the protocol’s advertised availability is compromised. This condition occurs whenever the contract holds a non‑trivial proportion of its assets in the external strategy, which is a common configuration for yield‑generating DeFi protocols. The affected parties include all users attempting to retrieve funds, the protocol operators responsible for maintaining liquidity, and any third‑party integrators that depend on successful withdrawals. The issue was identified during a code audit that highlighted the discrepancy between accounting totals and actual cash flow. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s state variables correctly reflect the total value, masking the underlying liquidity shortfall until a transfer is attempted. To remediate, the contract should separate the notion of total underlying value from the immediately spendable balance, perform a balance check before any external transfer, and, when necessary, trigger a synchronous redemption from the strategy or impose a withdrawal limitation based on available liquid assets. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “insufficient liquidity transfer” or “accounting‑vs‑cash‑flow mismatch” and violates the fundamental expectation that a reported total balance can be fully withdrawn on demand.

title: Add a timelock to `BaseStrategy:setPerfFeePct`
description: To give more trust to users: functions that set key/critical variables should be put behind a timelock.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the ability of the contract administrator to modify the performance fee percentage through the setPerfFeePct function without any enforced delay or community oversight. This design flaw originates from the missing timelock on a critical parameter that directly influences how much of the generated yield is retained by the protocol versus distributed to users. Because the setter can be called instantly, a malicious or compromised admin could raise the fee percentage at any moment, for example immediately before a large batch of users attempts to withdraw or claim rewards. The exploitation scenario involves the admin submitting a transaction that updates the fee to a higher value, which is then applied to subsequent accounting calculations, causing users to receive less than the amount they anticipate. The impact is a reduction in user earnings, potential loss of trust, and financial harm to any participant who relied on the previously advertised fee structure. This condition can occur anytime the admin chooses to execute the setter, meaning all token holders, delegators, and any downstream contracts that depend on the fee calculation are affected. The issue was identified during a systematic audit of the contract’s governance and parameter‑update mechanisms, where the absence of a proposal‑and‑delay pattern for critical variables stood out. It can be hard to notice because fee changes are legitimate administrative actions, and unless one monitors the on‑chain events closely, the increase may appear as a normal protocol upgrade. To remediate, the function that changes the performance fee should be wrapped in a timelock contract that requires a predefined waiting period after a proposal is submitted before the new fee takes effect, optionally coupled with a multi‑signature or governance vote. This class of bug is commonly referred to as “instant admin control over critical parameters” or “missing timelock on governance variables,” and it violates the accounting assumption that the fee rate remains stable over a reporting period. From a user’s point of view, the symptom may be a withdrawal that yields less than expected, an unexpectedly low net reward, or even a situation where the net return appears to be zero because the fee has been set to an extreme value. Users expect the fee to be predictable, but the current implementation allows it to be altered without warning, breaking that expectation and creating a vector for financial loss.

title: `totalUnderlyingMinusSponsored
poc:
* Underlying token = USDT
  * Swap Fee = 0.04%
  * Sponsor call `sponsor()` and send 10,000 USDT
  * totalSponsored = 10,000
  * `NonUSTStrategy.sol#doHardWork()` swapped USDT for UST
  * pendingDeposits = 9,996
  * totalUnderlying() = 9,996
  * Alice tries to call `deposit()`, the tx will revet due to underflow in `totalUnderlyingMinusSponsored()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked subtraction in the public view function that reports the net underlying asset balance after accounting for sponsor contributions. The function returns the result of totalUnderlying() minus totalSponsored without first verifying that the sponsor total does not exceed the underlying total. Because the contract permits a sponsor to contribute an amount larger than the current underlying balance – a situation that can arise when a sponsor deposits a large sum and the underlying assets are later reduced by swap fees or market movements – the subtraction can underflow. In Solidity versions that automatically revert on arithmetic underflow, this operation throws a runtime exception, causing any downstream call that relies on the net balance to fail. The underflow is triggered when a user attempts to deposit after a sponsorship that leaves totalSponsored greater than totalUnderlying, as demonstrated by a scenario where a sponsor adds 10,000 USDT, the underlying balance drops to 9,996 after a swap, and a subsequent deposit call reverts. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate depositors see their transactions revert with no obvious reason, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s core accounting functions become inaccessible, effectively freezing new capital inflows. The issue affects all participants who interact with deposit‑related functions after an oversized sponsorship, including liquidity providers and end‑users, while the sponsor’s funds remain locked but usable for existing positions. It was discovered during a systematic security audit that evaluated the contract’s arithmetic safety and identified that the view function could produce a negative result when totalSponsored exceeds totalUnderlying. The bug can be hard to notice because the function is a view accessor and does not emit events; the failure only surfaces when another function reads its value, leading to unexpected revert messages that may be misinterpreted as network or gas issues. The appropriate remediation is to add a defensive check that returns zero when totalSponsored is greater than totalUnderlying, thereby preventing the underflow and preserving the contract’s ability to calculate a non‑negative net balance. This class of flaw falls under arithmetic underflow bugs, where insufficient validation of subtraction results in runtime reverts and functional disruption, violating the business logic that assumes the net underlying balance can never be negative. From the user’s perspective, the UI would display a transaction error, the deposited amount would not be reflected in their balance, and they would receive a message such as "transaction reverted" despite having sufficient funds, contradicting the expectation that a deposit should succeed.

title: Vault can’t receive deposits if underlying token charges fees on transfer
description:
Some ERC20 tokens charge a fee for every transfer. If the underlying token of a vault is such a token any deposit to the protocol will fail.

Some tokens have the possibility of adding fees later on, e.g. USDT. So those have to be covered too.

Generally, the user would also receive fewer tokens on withdrawing in such a scenario but that’s not the protocol’s fault.

I rated the issue as medium since part of the protocol become unavailable in such a situation.
poc:
`_transferAndCheckUnderlying()` is used to deposit and sponsor the vault. It checks that after a `safeTransferFrom()` the same exact amount is sent to the balance of the vault. But, if fees are enabled the values won’t match, causing the function to revert. Thus, it won’t be able to deposit or sponsor the vault in any way.

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/Vault.sol#L162>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/Vault.sol#L266>
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the Vault contract’s assumption that an ERC20 token transfer will move the exact amount requested from the sender to the Vault. During a deposit, the internal function _transferAndCheckUnderlying() calls safeTransferFrom() and then checks that the Vault’s token balance has increased by the same number of tokens that were specified in the deposit request. This check fails when the underlying token implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism, where a portion of the transferred amount is retained by the token contract as a fee. Because the actual amount received by the Vault is lower than the requested amount, the balance check does not match and the function reverts, preventing any deposit or sponsorship operation from succeeding. The issue also applies to tokens that may add such a fee in a future upgrade (for example, USDT, which historically has been fee‑free but can be upgraded to charge fees). The impact is that users attempting to deposit or sponsor the Vault with a fee‑on‑transfer token experience transaction reverts, see no change in their on‑chain balance, and are unable to participate in the protocol’s core functionality. From a business‑logic perspective the protocol’s accounting model assumes a 1 : 1 correspondence between the amount a user inputs and the amount credited to the Vault; fee‑on‑transfer tokens break this invariant, violating the accounting assumptions and rendering part of the system unavailable. The bug was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the deposit logic and noticing the strict equality check on the token balance after transfer. It can be hard to notice because many commonly used stablecoins (e.g., USDC, DAI) do not charge transfer fees, so the code appears to work in typical test environments, and the revert is presented as a generic error without exposing the underlying cause. To remediate, the protocol should either restrict accepted tokens to those that guarantee fee‑free transfers or modify the deposit logic to handle fee‑on‑transfer tokens by accounting for the net amount received, for example by reading the actual transfer event or by using a pull‑payment model that does not rely on an exact balance increment. In generic terms, this is a transfer‑amount‑mismatch vulnerability affecting contracts that interact with fee‑on‑transfer ERC20 tokens. From the user’s perspective, a deposit transaction fails with no token balance change, and a withdrawal may return fewer tokens than expected if the same token imposes fees on outgoing transfers, leading to the symptom of "funds disappear" or "refund is missing" despite the contract behaving as programmed.

title: Medium: Consider alternative price feed + ensure _minLockPeriod > 0 to prevent flash loan attacks
description: It is critical to ensure that `_minLockPeriod > 0` because it is immutable and cannot be changed once set. A zero `minLockPeriod` will allow for flash loan attacks to occur. Vaults utilising the nonUST strategy are especially susceptible to this attack vector since the strategy utilises the spot price of the pool to calculate the total asset value.
poc:
