Assume the vault’s underlying token is MIM, and the curve pool to be used is the MIM-UST pool. Further assume that both the vault and the strategy holds substantial funds in MIM and UST respectively.

  1. Flash loan MIM from the [Uniswap V3 MIM-USDC pool](https://etherscan.io/address/0x298b7c5e0770d151e4c5cf6cca4dae3a3ffc8e27) (currently has ~$3.5M in MIM at the time of writing).
  2. Convert half of the loaned MIM to UST to inflate and deflate their prices respectively.
  3. Deposit the other half of the loaned MIM into the vault. We expect `curvePool.get_dy_underlying(ustI, underlyingI, ustAssets);` to return a smaller amount than expected because of the previous step. As a result, the attacker is allocated more shares than expected.
  4. Exchange UST back to MIM, bringing back the spot price of MIM-UST to a normal level.
  5. Withdraw funds from the vault. The number of shares to be deducted is lower as a result of (4), with the profit being accounted for as yield.
  6. Claim yield and repay the flash loan.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from allowing the immutable constructor argument `_minLockPeriod` to be set to zero. Because this parameter cannot be changed after deployment, a zero value leaves the vault without any enforced lock‑up period for deposited assets. The vault’s accounting logic, particularly for strategies that rely on the spot price of a liquidity pool (such as the non‑UST strategy), uses the current pool price to compute the total value of assets and to determine how many vault shares are minted for a deposit. When `_minLockPeriod` is zero, an attacker can execute a flash loan that temporarily skews the spot price of the pool, deposit the loaned assets during the manipulated window, and receive more shares than the true value of the deposited capital would warrant. After the price normalises, the attacker withdraws the inflated share balance, effectively converting the price distortion into unearned yield while repaying the flash loan. This attack vector is feasible whenever the vault employs a price feed that can be influenced by on‑chain swaps, and it is especially relevant for pools where the underlying token pair’s price can be changed with modest capital, such as the MIM‑UST Curve pool. The impact is that honest users may see their share of the vault’s earnings diluted, and the protocol can suffer a loss of assets equivalent to the amount of profit extracted by the attacker. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit through analysis of the vault’s constructor and the strategy’s reliance on spot pricing, highlighting that a zero `_minLockPeriod` creates a missing safeguard against rapid price manipulation. Detecting the exploit in live operation is difficult because the price distortion can be brief, leaving transaction logs that appear legitimate; the vault itself reports normal deposit and withdrawal events, while the underlying accounting silently awards extra shares. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce `_minLockPeriod > 0` at deployment, ensuring that any deposited assets remain locked for a non‑zero duration, thereby preventing immediate withdrawal after a price swing. Additionally, using a more robust, manipulation‑resistant price oracle—such as a time‑averaged TWAP or an external trusted feed—would reduce reliance on volatile spot prices and further mitigate flash‑loan‑induced reward inflation. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of "lock‑period bypass" and "price‑oracle manipulation" vulnerabilities, where missing temporal constraints enable attackers to profit from transient market conditions, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that shares represent a proportional claim on the vault’s true asset value.

title: no use of safeMint
description: In `Vault.sol` the `deposit()` function eventually calls claimers.mint() and depositers.mint(). Calling mint this way does not ensure that the receiver of the NFT is able to accept them. `_safeMint()` should be used with reentrancy guards as a guard to protect the user as it checks to see if a user can properly accept an NFT and reverts otherwise.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/Vault.sol#L470>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock/blob/main/sandclock/contracts/Vault.sol#L256>
  * <https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L248>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Vault contract mints ERC‑721 tokens during a deposit. The deposit() function forwards the call to two internal contracts, Claimers and Depositors, and invokes their mint() functions directly. The Claimers contract uses the standard ERC‑721 mint routine, which transfers the newly created token without performing the ERC721Receiver safety check that _safeMint() provides. Consequently, if the recipient of the minted NFT is a smart contract that does not implement the onERC721Received callback, the token will be transferred but the receiving contract will be unable to acknowledge it, leading to a situation where the NFT is effectively lost or locked. In addition, the deposit() function lacks a reentrancy guard, so a malicious contract could recursively call deposit() before the first call finishes, potentially corrupting the internal accounting of deposited assets. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who deploys a contract that either rejects ERC‑721 safe transfers or re‑enters the deposit logic. The attacker triggers a deposit on behalf of a user, causing the vault to mint an NFT to the malicious contract via mint(). Because the safe check is omitted, the transfer succeeds even though the contract cannot handle the token, resulting in the user receiving no NFT despite a successful transaction. If the attacker also re‑enters the deposit function, they may manipulate balances or cause double‑minting, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The impact is that depositors may lose their NFTs, see their balances remain unchanged, or experience silent failures where the protocol’s state diverges from expected values. This problem manifests only when the intended NFT recipient is a contract that does not conform to the ERC721Receiver interface, making it difficult to detect during routine functional testing that only involves externally owned accounts. The affected parties include any user depositing into the Vault, the Claimers and Depositors contracts, and the broader protocol that relies on correct NFT distribution for its asset management. The flaw was identified during a manual audit of Vault.sol, where the reviewer noted the direct use of mint() in Claimers and the absence of a nonReentrant modifier on deposit(). The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the fact that the transaction does not revert and appears successful, while the user’s wallet simply never shows the NFT. To remediate the issue, the Claimers contract should replace the insecure mint() call with OpenZeppelin’s _safeMint(), which performs the recipient check and reverts if the contract cannot receive the token. Additionally, the deposit() function should be protected with a reentrancy guard (e.g., the nonReentrant modifier) to prevent recursive calls that could corrupt state. This class of bug – unsafe ERC‑721 minting combined with missing reentrancy protection – violates the protocol’s business logic that assumes every deposit results in a correctly delivered NFT and reliable accounting of user balances.

title: `SherlockClaimManager`: Incorrect amounts needed and paid for escalated claims
description:
When escalating claims, [the documentation](https://docs.sherlock.xyz/claims/claims-process) states that the protocol agent is required to pay and stake a certain amount for the process. If the covered protocol is proven correct, then the amount specified by the claim will be paid out. **They will also receive the stake amount back in full.** If the covered protocol’s escalation is not successful, then the amount specified by the claim is not paid out and the stake amount is not returned.

The protocol agent is reasonably expected to pay the following:

  * The stake (`BOND`) and
  * UMA’s final fee

In reality, the protocol agent will end up paying more, as we shall see in the proof of concept.
bug_full: The SherlockClaimManager contract contains an economic inconsistency that causes protocol agents to lose a portion of the stake they provide when escalating a claim. According to the official documentation, an agent must pay a bond (BOND) and UMA's final fee, and if the claim is resolved in the agent's favor, the full bond amount should be returned along with the final fee. In practice, the contract forwards the BOND value to UMA's SkinnyOptimisticOracle as the request bond, but UMA's internal logic automatically burns half of the bond at settlement and also treats the final fee as part of the total bond. Consequently, when an escalation succeeds, the agent receives only BOND minus the burned portion (approximately 50 % of BOND) plus the final fee, not the full BOND as documented. The root cause is a mismatch between the documented economic model and UMA's actual bond handling, compounded by the fact that the requestAndProposePriceFor parameters were set without accounting for UMA's _computeBurnedBond logic. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; the vulnerability is triggered simply by using the existing escalation flow under the documented assumptions. The impact is a systematic reduction of the returned stake for any successful escalation, leading to unexpected loss of funds for protocol agents and potentially discouraging participation. This condition occurs every time an escalated claim is disputed and resolved in favor of the reporting agent, because the UMA oracle will burn half of the bond regardless of the external expectations. The affected parties are the agents who submit escalated claims, the protocols that rely on Sherlock for coverage, and ultimately the end users who trust that their stakes are fully refundable. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that compared the protocol's white‑paper description with the actual Solidity calls to UMA, and verified the discrepancy through a proof‑of‑concept transaction that showed the burned bond amount in the settlement trace. The bug is hard to notice because the documentation explicitly promises a full bond return, masking the subtle internal fee calculation performed by UMA, and because the burned bond is not emitted as a separate event. To remediate the problem, the parameters passed to UMA should be adjusted so that the bond argument is set to a minimal value (e.g., 1) and the intended BOND is used as a reward rather than a bond, ensuring that the agent's economic exposure matches the documented model. Alternatively, the documentation should be corrected to accurately reflect the actual burned‑bond behavior. This class of vulnerability falls under "documentation‑implementation mismatch leading to incorrect financial accounting," where an on‑chain protocol enforces a different bond and fee model than what users are told to expect, resulting in missing refunds, reduced balances, and a violation of the assumed accounting invariants of the system.

title: `tokenBalanceOfAddress` of `nftOwner` becomes permanently incorrect after `arbRestake`
description:
Successful `arbRestake` performs `_redeemShares` for `arbRewardShares` amount to extract the arbitrager reward. This effectively reduces shares accounted for an NFT, but leaves untouched the `addressShares` of an `nftOwner`.

As a result the `tokenBalanceOfAddress` function will report an old balance that existed before arbitrager reward was slashed away. This will persist if the owner will transfer the NFT to someone else as its new reduced shares value will be subtracted from `addressShares` in `_beforeTokenTransfer`, leaving the arbitrage removed shares permanently in `addressShares` of the NFT owner, essentially making all further reporting of his balance incorrectly inflated by the cumulative arbitrage reward shares from all arbRestakes happened to the owner’s NFTs.
poc:
`arbRestake` redeems `arbRewardShares`, which are a part of total shares of an NFT:

[Sherlock.sol#L673](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/Sherlock.sol#L673)

This will effectively reduce the `stakeShares`:

[Sherlock.sol#L491](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/Sherlock.sol#L491)

But there is no mechanics in place to reduce `addressShares` of the owner apart from mint/burn/transfer, so `addressShares` will still correspond to NFT shares before arbitrage. This discrepancy will be accumulated further with arbitrage restakes.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an accounting inconsistency in the token balance reporting of NFT owners after the arbitrage restake operation (arbRestake). The contract maintains two correlated variables: stakeShares, which represents the total shares attached to each NFT, and addressShares, which aggregates the shares owned by a particular address and is used by the tokenBalanceOfAddress function to report the user’s token balance. When arbRestake successfully calls the internal function _redeemShares to extract the arbitrager reward, it reduces the stakeShares of the targeted NFT by the amount of arbRewardShares. However, the implementation neglects to adjust addressShares for the NFT owner during this partial redemption. Consequently, tokenBalanceOfAddress continues to return the pre‑redeem balance, which is inflated by the amount of shares that have been removed from the NFT but not from the owner’s aggregate accounting. This mismatch persists even after the NFT is transferred; the transfer logic in _beforeTokenTransfer subtracts the new (reduced) stakeShares from the recipient’s addressShares, while the previously removed reward shares remain stuck in the former owner’s addressShares, causing a permanent overstatement of that address’s balance. The defect is a classic state‑synchronisation bug where related accounting fields are not updated atomically during a partial share redemption, violating the protocol’s core assumption that an address’s total shares equal the sum of the shares of its NFTs. The issue manifests whenever arbRestake is executed and the reward is partially redeemed, which can be repeatedly triggered by an attacker to accumulate inflated balances. An adversary could repeatedly call arbRestake on NFTs they control, then transfer the NFTs to other parties, leaving the inflated share credit in their own addressShares and potentially withdrawing or leveraging those phantom tokens. Affected parties include the NFT owners, arbitrage participants, downstream contracts that rely on tokenBalanceOfAddress for accounting, and any users interacting with the UI that displays balances. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the arbRestake logic, where the auditors observed that _redeemShares only modifies stakeShares and not addressShares. The bug is subtle because the UI may still show a plausible balance, and typical unit tests might not cover the partial‑redeem pathway or the subsequent transfer scenario, allowing the discrepancy to remain hidden until a transfer or a deep balance reconciliation is performed. To remediate the problem, addressShares must be updated in lockstep with stakeShares during a partial redemption, for example by introducing a flag (e.g., isPartialRedeem) that triggers a subtraction of the redeemed amount from addressShares, or by refactoring the contract so that any change to stakeShares automatically mirrors on addressShares. Alternatively, the partial redemption feature could be removed entirely if its benefit does not outweigh the added complexity. Correcting the synchronization restores the integrity of tokenBalanceOfAddress, ensuring that users see a balance that truly reflects the underlying shares held in their NFTs.

title: `updateYieldStrategy` will freeze some funds with the old Strategy if `yieldStrategy` fails to withdraw all the funds because of liquidity issues
description:
Part of the funds held with the strategy can be frozen if the current strategy has tight liquidity when `updateYieldStrategy` is run as this function makes an attempt to withdraw all the funds and then unconditionally removes the strategy.

The Sherlock to YieldStrategy link will be broken as a result: Sherlock points to the new Strategy, while old Strategy still allows only this Sherlock contract to withdraw.

This way back and forth switches will be required in the future to return the funds: withdraw all from new strategy and switch to old, withdraw all from old and point to new one again, reinvest there.
poc:
In peer-to-peer lending protocols it is not always possible for the token supplier to withdraw all what’s due. This happens on high utilization of the market (when it has a kind of liquidity crunch).

This way yieldStrategy.withdrawAll is not guaranteed to obtain all the funds held with the strategy:

[Sherlock.sol#L286](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/Sherlock.sol#L286)

The worst case scenario here seems to be the remainder funds to be left frozen within the strategy.

For example, AaveV2Strategy `withdraw` and `withdrawAll` have `onlySherlockCore` modifier:

[AaveV2Strategy.sol#L78-100](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/managers/AaveV2Strategy.sol#L78-100)

While Sherlock core is immutable for the Strategy by default:

[Manager.sol#L26-41](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sherlock/blob/main/contracts/managers/Manager.sol#L26-41)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract function that updates the yield strategy, called updateYieldStrategy. The function first attempts to withdraw all assets from the currently active strategy by invoking its withdrawAll method, and then it unconditionally replaces the reference to that strategy with a new one. If the active strategy is unable to return the full amount—typically because it is experiencing a liquidity crunch, high utilization, or other constraints—the withdrawAll call silently returns only a partial amount. Because the function proceeds to replace the strategy reference regardless of the withdrawal result, the linkage between the core contract (Sherlock) and the old strategy is broken: Sherlock now points to the new strategy while the old strategy still retains the remaining funds and only permits withdrawals by the original Sherlock core. Consequently, the leftover assets become effectively frozen, inaccessible to users and the protocol, and can only be recovered by performing a series of back‑and‑forth strategy switches—withdraw from the new strategy, switch back to the old one, withdraw the remaining balance, and then re‑switch. This scenario can occur whenever the current strategy has tight liquidity, such as in peer‑to‑peer lending markets under high utilization, and it is not prevented by any checks in the updateYieldStrategy implementation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of funds during strategy migration and noted that the withdrawAll function does not revert on partial failure, allowing the subsequent strategy pointer change to create a dangling reference. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error or revert; the partial withdrawal simply reduces the balance silently, making the frozen funds invisible at first glance. From a user’s perspective, after a strategy update they may observe that their deposited tokens are not fully returned, or that their balance appears unchanged despite the protocol indicating a successful migration, leading to confusion and concern that funds have disappeared. The impact includes potential loss of user capital, reduced protocol liquidity, and the need for manual, complex remediation steps, which could erode trust. To mitigate the issue, the update routine should verify that withdrawAll has indeed transferred the complete expected amount and should revert if any remainder remains. Alternatively, the contract could provide a flexible withdrawal mechanism that allows the owner to withdraw from any strategy, not only the current one, and rename the unconditional version to something like forceUpdateYieldStrategy to indicate its riskier nature. By ensuring that strategy switching only occurs after a successful full withdrawal, the protocol preserves accounting integrity and prevents funds from becoming trapped.

title: Reenterancy in `_sendSherRewardsToOwner`
description:
This is a reentrancy vulnerability that would allow the attacker to drain the entire SHER balance of the contract.

Note: this attack requires gaining control of execution `sher.transfer()` which will depend on the implementation of the SHER token. Control may be gained by the attacker if the contract implements ERC777 or otherwise makes external calls during `transfer()`.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw located in the internal function that distributes SHER token rewards to an NFT owner. The function first reads the reward amount, then calls `sher.safeTransfer(_nftOwner, sherReward)`, an external call that may execute code supplied by the token contract. Only after this transfer does the function delete the entry in the `sherRewards_` mapping. If the SHER token implementation supports callbacks—such as ERC‑777 hooks or any other mechanism that can invoke external code during `transfer`—an attacker can craft a malicious token or a malicious receiver contract that re‑enters the reward‑sending routine before the mapping entry is cleared. By re‑entering, the attacker can cause the same reward balance to be transferred multiple times, eventually draining the whole SHER balance held by the contract.

The root cause is the ordering of operations: the external token transfer is performed before the contract’s internal state (the reward mapping) is updated. This breaks the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and gives the attacker a window where the contract’s accounting still reflects the original reward amount. The attack can be triggered through any public entry point that eventually calls `_sendSherRewardsToOwner`, such as the `ownerRestake()` function, which is external and therefore callable by an attacker contract.

Exploitation proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker deploys a contract that implements a token callback or uses an ERC‑777‑compatible SHER token; (2) the attacker stakes a minimal amount to obtain a reward entry; (3) when the reward is about to be paid, the attacker’s contract receives the SHER tokens and, within the callback, calls back into `ownerRestake()` (or directly invokes the internal reward function via the external entry point); (4) because the reward mapping has not yet been cleared, the second call transfers the same reward again; (5) the attacker repeats the re‑entrancy loop until the contract’s SHER balance is exhausted. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the contract’s reward pool suddenly becomes empty, legitimate owners receive no tokens, and the protocol appears to lose funds without any on‑chain error messages.

The impact is a loss of all SHER tokens allocated for rewards, effectively draining the economic incentive mechanism of the protocol. The vulnerability is medium‑severity because it depends on the SHER token exposing a callback interface, which the current SHER implementation does not provide, but the risk rises if the token were upgraded or swapped for a token with such hooks.

The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors inspected the reward‑distribution code and identified the unsafe order of operations. It can be hard to notice because the function is internal and the external call appears safe (using `safeTransfer`), leading developers to assume no re‑entrancy risk. However, the underlying token contract’s behavior is not verified, so the re‑entrancy surface remains hidden.

To remediate the flaw, the contract should either (a) apply a re‑entrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s `nonReentrant`) to the external entry points that trigger reward distribution, or (b) reorder the logic to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: perform all validation, update the `sherRewards_` mapping by deleting the entry, and only then call the external `safeTransfer`. Both approaches eliminate the window where the contract’s accounting can be manipulated. Updating other functions that perform external token transfers (e.g., `_redeemShares`, `initialStake`, `SherClaim.add`, and `depositToActiveBalance`) to follow the same pattern further reduces the attack surface.

title: `burn
description: The CollateralizedDebt.sol contract is a ERC721 token. It has a `mint()` function, which uses the underlying `safeMint()` function to create an ERC721 token representing a collateral position. The `burn()` function in CollateralizedDebt.sol should reverse the actions of `mint()` by burning the ERC721 token, but the ERC721 `_burn()` function is never called. This means a user can continue to hold their ERC721 token representing their position after receiving their funds. This is unlike the `burn()` function found in Bond.sol, Insurance.sol, and Liquidity.sol, which all call the `_burn()` function (though note the `_burn()` function in these other Timeswap Convenience contracts is the ERC20 `_burn()`).
poc:
The problematic `burn()` function is found in CollareralizedDebt.sol <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/CollateralizedDebt.sol#L80-L88>

Compare this function to the `burn()` functions defined in the other Timeswap Convenience contracts, which contain calls to `_burn()`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CollateralizedDebt smart contract, which implements an ERC‑721 token to represent a user’s collateralized debt position. When a borrower repays the loan, the contract’s public burn() function is expected to reverse the minting process by destroying the ERC‑721 token that encoded the position and by releasing the locked collateral. However, the implementation fails to invoke the internal ERC‑721 _burn() routine, so the token’s record remains on‑chain even after the underlying debt and collateral have been cleared. The root cause is a missing call to the token’s destruction logic; the function only updates internal accounting for the debt but does not remove the NFT representation. An attacker can exploit this discrepancy by retaining a token that falsely signifies an active position, potentially confusing downstream contracts or off‑chain services that rely on token ownership to infer outstanding liabilities. The impact includes mismatched state between the protocol’s balance sheet and the token registry, misleading users who still see an NFT in their wallet, and the risk that other contract functions may treat the stale token as valid, opening avenues for double‑withdrawal or unauthorized actions if any logic assumes token existence implies outstanding collateral. The condition occurs every time a user calls burn() to close a position; the contract will emit events indicating repayment while leaving the NFT untouched. All participants who hold or rely on the ERC‑721 representation – borrowers, lenders, and any third‑party analytics or risk engines – are affected because the visible token no longer reflects the true financial state. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the burn implementation across similar convenience contracts, revealing that the other contracts correctly call their respective _burn() methods. The bug is subtle because the repayment succeeds and funds are transferred, giving the appearance of a normal closure; only a careful inspection of token metadata or a query of token ownership reveals the lingering NFT. To remediate, the burn() function should be amended to invoke the ERC‑721 _burn(id) call after the debt and collateral are cleared, thereby removing the token from the owner’s balance and restoring consistency between on‑chain accounting and token representation. This class of bug falls under incomplete state cleanup or token lifecycle mismanagement, where an asset’s logical destruction is not mirrored by its on‑chain token counterpart, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and user expectations that a closed position disappears from their wallet.

title: safeDecimals can revert causing DoS
description:
The `safeDecimals()` function, found in the SafeMetadata.sol contract and called in 3 different Timeswap Convenience contracts, can cause a revert. This is because the safeDecimals function attempts to use abi.decode to return a uint8 when `data.length >= 32`. However, a data.length value greater than 32 will cause abi.decode to revert.

A similar issue was found in a previoud code4rena contest: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-05-nftx-findings/issues/46>
poc:
The root cause is [line 28](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/libraries/SafeMetadata.sol#L28) of the `safeDecimals()` function in SafeMetadata.sol

The following link shows the `safeDecimals()` function in the BoringCrypto library, which might be where this code was borrowed from, uses the strict equality check `data.length == 32` <https://github.com/boringcrypto/BoringSolidity/blob/ccb743d4c3363ca37491b87c6c9b24b1f5fa25dc/contracts/libraries/BoringERC20.sol#L54>

`safeDecimals()` is used in multiple functions such as

  * CollateralizedDebt.sol [line 50](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/CollateralizedDebt.sol#L50) and [line 54](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/CollateralizedDebt.sol#L54)
  * Bond.sol [line 34](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Bond.sol#L34)
  * Insurance.sol [line 36](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Insurance.sol#L36)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a helper routine named safeDecimals() that is intended to retrieve the number of decimal places from an ERC‑20 token’s metadata. The routine calls a low‑level staticcall to fetch the token’s decimals and then attempts to decode the returned calldata with abi.decode(data, (uint8)) only after checking that the returned data length is at least 32 bytes (data.length >= 32). Because abi.decode expects the exact size of the encoded type, any response whose length exceeds 32 bytes – for example a token that returns a 64‑byte padded value or includes extra data – causes abi.decode to revert. This off‑by‑one style length check therefore allows a legitimate but non‑standard token response to trigger an exception. The function is invoked by three Timeswap convenience contracts (CollateralizedDebt, Bond, and Insurance) whenever they need to read a token’s decimals, so a revert propagates up the call stack and aborts the whole external transaction. When the condition occurs, users attempting to open a position, mint a bond, or purchase insurance experience a failed transaction with no state change, often seeing a generic “execution reverted” error. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that no value was returned, showing a zero or empty decimal field, and the expected operation – such as receiving a loan, issuing a bond, or confirming insurance coverage – simply does not happen. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: any token whose decimals getter returns data longer than 32 bytes can render the affected contract functions unusable, effectively freezing user interactions that depend on that token. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which matched a similar bug previously reported in a Code4rena contest. It can be hard to notice because the revert occurs only for a subset of tokens with non‑standard ABI responses, and the surrounding code does not log a detailed reason for the failure. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of input‑validation errors where assumptions about external contract data size are incorrect, leading to an unhandled exception. The proper fix is to tighten the length check to require an exact match (data.length == 32) before decoding, or to use a safer decoding method that can handle variable‑length responses. By ensuring that only correctly sized data is decoded, the routine will return a sensible default or propagate a controlled error instead of aborting the whole transaction, thereby restoring expected functionality and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: `safeName
description:
The `safeName()` function, found in the SafeMetadata.sol contract and called in 4 Timeswap Convenience contracts in the `name()` functions, can cause a revert. This could make the 4 contracts not compliant with the ERC20 standard for certain asset pairs, because the `name()` function should return a string and not revert.

The root cause of the issue is that the `safeName()` function assumes the return type of any ERC20 token to be a string. If the return value is not a string, abi.decode() will revert, and this will cause the `name()` functions in the Timeswap ERC20 contracts to revert. There are some tokens that aren’t compliant, such as Sai from Maker, which returns a bytes32 value: <https://kauri.io/#single/dai-token-guide-for-developers/#token-info>

Because this is known to cause issues with tokens that don’t fully follow the ERC20 spec, the `safeName()` function in the BoringCrypto library has a fix for this. The BoringCrypto `safeName()` function is similar to the one in Timeswap but it has a `returnDataToString()` function that handles the case of a bytes32 return value for a token name: <https://github.com/boringcrypto/BoringSolidity/blob/ccb743d4c3363ca37491b87c6c9b24b1f5fa25dc/contracts/libraries/BoringERC20.sol#L15-L47>
poc:
The root cause is [line 12](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/libraries/SafeMetadata.sol#L12) of the `safeName()` function in SafeMetadata.sol

The `safeName()` function is called in:

  * [Bond.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Bond.sol#L20-L25)
  * [CollateralizedDebt.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/CollateralizedDebt.sol#L22-L36)
  * [Insurance.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Insurance.sol#L20-L27)
  * [Liquidity.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Liquidity.sol#L22-L29)
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the `safeName()` helper that is used by four Timeswap convenience contracts to implement the ERC20 `name()` view function. The helper assumes that any ERC20 token implements `name()` with a return type of `string`. It calls the external token contract, receives the raw return data, and attempts to decode it as a string using `abi.decode()`. For tokens that deviate from the ERC20 specification and return a `bytes32` value instead of a string—such as Maker’s Sai token—the decoding step fails and triggers a revert. Because the `name()` functions in the Timeswap contracts directly forward the result of `safeName()`, the revert propagates outward, causing the entire `name()` call to revert. This behavior violates the ERC20 standard, which requires `name()` to always return a string and never revert, and therefore renders the Timeswap contracts non‑compliant for any asset pair that includes a non‑standard token.

The issue can be exploited simply by invoking the `name()` function on a Timeswap contract that references a non‑standard token. The call will revert, preventing callers—such as user interfaces, other contracts, or off‑chain services—from retrieving the token name. From a user’s perspective, the UI may display an empty name field, show an error, or cause a transaction that queries the name to fail. While the bug does not directly cause loss of funds, it can disrupt workflows that rely on token metadata, potentially leading to failed trades, misreported balances, or a degraded user experience. The problem manifests only when the underlying asset’s `name()` returns a bytes32 value; compliant tokens that return a string are unaffected.

The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors observed that the `safeName()` implementation lacks handling for alternative return types. The bug is subtle because the `name()` function is a view that does not affect state, so developers may not notice the revert unless they explicitly query token names for every supported pair. Moreover, the contract’s reliance on a utility library that mirrors the flawed logic makes the issue repeat across multiple contracts, magnifying its impact.

To remediate the vulnerability, the `safeName()` implementation should be replaced with a version that gracefully handles both `string` and `bytes32` return formats. The BoringCrypto library provides such a function, employing a `returnDataToString()` routine that converts a `bytes32` value to a human‑readable string before returning it. Incorporating this logic eliminates the revert, restores ERC20 compliance, and ensures that users receive the expected token name without encountering unexpected errors.

title: `safeSymbol
description:
The `safeSymbol()` function, found in the SafeMetadata.sol contract and called in 4 Timeswap Convenience contracts in the `symbol()` functions, can cause a revert. This could make the 4 contracts not compliant with the ERC20 standard for certain asset pairs, because the `symbol()` function should return a string and not revert.

The root cause of the issue is that the `safeSymbol()` function assumes the return type of any ERC20 token to be a string. If the return value is not a string, abi.decode() will revert, and this will cause the `symbol()` functions in the Timeswap ERC20 contracts to revert.

Because this is known to cause issues with tokens that don’t fully follow the ERC20 spec, the `safeSymbol()` function in the BoringCrypto library has a fix for this. The BoringCrypto `safeSymbol()` function is similar to the one in Timeswap but it has a `returnDataToString()` function that handles the case of a bytes32 return value for a token name: <https://github.com/boringcrypto/BoringSolidity/blob/ccb743d4c3363ca37491b87c6c9b24b1f5fa25dc/contracts/libraries/BoringERC20.sol#L15-L39>
poc:
The root cause is [line 20](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/libraries/SafeMetadata.sol#L20) of the `safeSymbol()` function in SafeMetadata.sol

The `safeSymbol()` function is called in:

  * [Bond.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Bond.sol#L27-L31)
  * [CollateralizedDebt.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/CollateralizedDebt.sol#L38-L42)
  * [Insurance.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Insurance.sol#L29-L33)
  * [Liquidity.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/bf50d2a8bb93a5571f35f96bd74af54d9c92a210/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/Liquidity.sol#L31-L35)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SafeMetadata.sol library used by four Timeswap convenience contracts (Bond, CollateralizedDebt, Insurance and Liquidity). These contracts expose a public symbol() function that is expected, by the ERC‑20 specification, to return a string and never revert. The implementation forwards the call to a helper called safeSymbol(), which unconditionally decodes the returned data as a string via abi.decode(). This assumption is flawed because not all ERC‑20 tokens implement the symbol() view with a string return type; some legacy tokens return a fixed‑size bytes32 value or even an empty payload. When such a non‑standard token is queried, abi.decode throws, causing safeSymbol() – and consequently the contract’s own symbol() – to revert. The root cause is therefore an unchecked type assumption in the metadata extraction routine. The bug can be exploited simply by interacting with the affected Timeswap contract using a token whose symbol does not conform to the expected string format; the call to symbol() will revert, breaking UI components that display token names, causing transaction receipts that rely on symbol() (for instance events or off‑chain indexing) to fail, and rendering the contract non‑compliant with ERC‑20. From a user’s perspective the most visible symptom is a missing or empty token symbol in wallets or dashboards, sometimes accompanied by a generic “call reverted” error when trying to query the token. The issue is not apparent during normal operation with compliant tokens, which is why it can go unnoticed until a divergent token is introduced. It was discovered during a static analysis audit by Code4rena, which identified the unsafe abi.decode usage and linked it to known problems in other libraries such as BoringCrypto’s safeSymbol implementation. The problem is hard to spot because the symbol() function is typically called only for display purposes and its failure does not affect core financial logic, leading developers to overlook the necessity of handling alternative return types. To remediate the issue the safeSymbol logic should be replaced with a more robust version that detects the length of the returned data and, when it is 32 bytes, converts it to a string (as performed by BoringCrypto’s returnDataToString function). This change ensures that both string and bytes32 symbols are handled gracefully, keeping the contracts ERC‑20 compliant and preventing unexpected reverts that could confuse users or break integrations.

title: users might pay enormous amounts of gas
description:
When a user mints new liquidity, if the pair doesn’t already exist, it deploys it.

Deploying a new contract on ethereum is super expensive, especially when it’s such a large contract like TimeswapPair, it can cost thousands of dollars.

<https://medium.com/the-capital/how-much-does-it-cost-to-deploy-a-smart-contract-on-ethereum-11bcd64da1>
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an implicit contract‑creation step that is triggered when a user attempts to mint new liquidity and the requested token pair does not yet have an associated pool contract. The core logic automatically deploys a fresh TimeswapPair contract in the same transaction. Deploying a large contract on Ethereum is extremely gas‑intensive; a single deployment of TimeswapPair can require thousands of dollars worth of gas at typical network prices. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour is to supply assets and receive liquidity tokens, yet the transaction also pays a massive, unexpected fee for the underlying contract creation. This discrepancy arises because the contract assumes that the cost of deployment is acceptable and does not give the caller an opportunity to confirm or reject it. The root cause is a design decision that couples a business‑level operation (minting liquidity) with a low‑level operation (contract deployment) without exposing the cost to the caller or providing a way to opt‑out. An attacker could exploit the situation by repeatedly requesting liquidity for new, previously non‑existent pairs, forcing victims to bear the prohibitive deployment gas each time; however, the issue is not an active attack vector in the current implementation, as the transaction will simply fail if the sender cannot afford the gas. The impact is primarily financial: users may see their transaction revert due to out‑of‑gas, or they may complete the transaction and see a huge gas bill that dwarfs the value of the minted liquidity, leading to loss of funds in the form of fees. This condition occurs whenever the mint function is called for a pair that has not yet been instantiated, which can happen at any time a new market is created. All participants that rely on the mint interface – regular users, liquidity providers, and integrators – are affected because they cannot predict the hidden cost. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the mint workflow and identified the unexpected contract‑creation call. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the function appears to work correctly after successful deployment, and the high gas cost may be attributed to network congestion rather than a contract bug. The recommended remediation is to change the logic so that, if a pair does not exist, the transaction reverts with a clear error message, requiring the caller to explicitly invoke a separate deployment function that they can run when they are prepared to pay the associated gas. Conceptually, this separates the concerns of pool creation and liquidity provision, aligns with the principle of least surprise, and allows documentation to warn users about the expense. By treating the hidden deployment as a distinct operation, the protocol avoids unintentionally draining users’ gas balances and restores confidence that the mint action only performs the intended accounting of liquidity.

title: Failed transfer with low level call could be overlooked
poc: See `_safeTransferAVAX` [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/a1579f6453bc4bf9fb0db9c627beaa41135438ed/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L620). See how this function is called with `_to` as `rocketJoeFactory.penaltyCollector()` [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/a1579f6453bc4bf9fb0db9c627beaa41135438ed/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L371), but this contract’s existence is not verified, which is a problem as described above.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a helper function that performs a native AVAX transfer using a low‑level call. The function invokes `_to.call{value: _value}(new bytes(0))` and only checks the boolean `success` flag returned by the call. According to Solidity’s semantics, a low‑level call reports `true` even when the target address does not contain contract code – for example, when the address has been self‑destructed or was never deployed. Consequently, the function may consider the transfer successful while the AVAX is either not delivered to an executable contract or is sent to an address that the protocol no longer recognises as a valid recipient. This logical gap can be triggered whenever the contract reads a destination address from external sources, such as `rocketJoeFactory.penaltyCollector()`, without first confirming that the address still corresponds to a live contract. If the penalty collector has been removed (via `selfdestruct`) or was never deployed, the low‑level call will still return `true`, the `require` statement will not revert, and the AVAX will be transferred to an address that cannot execute any expected logic. From a user's perspective the protocol appears to have deducted the penalty amount, but the intended recipient never receives it, leading to missing balances, zero refunds, or unexplained loss of funds. The impact is a breach of accounting assumptions: the protocol believes the penalty has been collected, while in reality the funds are either locked in a dead address or simply sit idle, breaking the incentive model and potentially causing users to receive no compensation. The issue was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, which noted the discrepancy between the documented behaviour of low‑level calls and the contract’s reliance on the `success` flag alone. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the only symptom is an unexpected reduction of the contract’s AVAX balance without a corresponding receipt. To remediate the flaw, the transfer routine should explicitly verify that the destination address hosts contract code (using `extcodesize` or Solidity’s `Address.isContract` utility) before attempting the call, or alternatively employ a higher‑level transfer pattern that reverts on failure regardless of contract existence. By ensuring that the address is verified, the protocol can prevent silent loss of funds and maintain correct economic invariants.

title: possibility of minting rJOE tokens before ownership is changed to RocketJoeStaking
description: There is a possibility of the rJOE tokens in RocketJoeToken.sol to be minted by original owner without staking any JOE, before the ownership is transferred to RocketJoeStaking.
poc: Contract: RocketJoeToken.sol Line: 37 function mint(address _to, uint256 _amount) external onlyOwner { _mint(_to, _amount); }
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of the original contract owner to mint new rJOE tokens in the RocketJoeToken contract before the ownership of the token contract is transferred to the RocketJoeStaking contract. The mint function is guarded only by the standard onlyOwner modifier, which means that any address that is the current owner – initially the deployer or a privileged account – can call mint without providing any JOE stake. Because the ownership transfer to the staking contract is intended to be the moment when token minting becomes linked to a staking mechanism, the premature minting bypasses that economic safeguard. An attacker who retains ownership can invoke the mint function, specify an arbitrary recipient address, and supply an arbitrary amount of tokens, thereby inflating the total supply. The inflated supply dilutes existing token holders, reduces the value of legitimate stakers' rewards, and can be used to extract value from the protocol by selling the newly minted tokens on the market. This issue manifests only during the window between contract deployment and the successful execution of transferOwnership(address) that points to the RocketJoeStaking contract. All participants who rely on the token’s accounting – users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the token’s supply no longer reflects the amount of JOE actually staked. The flaw was identified during a formal code audit that traced the minting logic and noted the absence of any additional gating condition tied to the staking contract. It can be difficult to notice in normal operation because the mint function looks conventional and the contract’s ownership change is a one‑time administrative action that may be performed off‑chain, so the possibility of pre‑transfer minting is not obvious from the UI or transaction logs. To remediate the issue, the contract should override the inherited transferOwnership function and ensure that the totalSupply is zero (or that no further minting is permitted) before allowing the owner to be changed, or alternatively replace the onlyOwner restriction with a role that is permanently assigned to the staking contract, thereby eliminating any chance for the original owner to mint tokens after deployment. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unauthorized minting before ownership handoff” or “privileged token inflation prior to role transfer”, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that token issuance is exclusively linked to staking activity.

title: withdrawAVAX
description: In LaunchEvent.sol the withdrawAVAX() function makes an external call to the msg.sender by way of _safeTransferAVAX. This allows the caller to reenter this and other functions in this and other protocol files. To prevent reentrancy and cross function reentrancy there should be reentrancy guard modifiers placed on the withdrawAVAX() function and any other function that makes external calls to the caller.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the withdrawAVAX() function of the LaunchEvent smart contract. The function transfers AVAX to the caller by invoking an internal helper, _safeTransferAVAX, which in turn performs an external call to msg.sender. Because the contract does not employ any reentrancy protection, an attacker can craft a malicious contract that receives the AVAX transfer and, within its fallback or receive function, call withdrawAVAX() again—or any other external‑call‑making function in the same or related contracts—before the original execution finishes. This cross‑function reentrancy allows the attacker to repeat the withdrawal logic multiple times, potentially extracting more AVAX than entitled. The issue manifests when a legitimate user initiates a withdrawal and the contract sends funds back; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal while the balance of the protocol unexpectedly drops, or the user may see their own balance increase repeatedly in an unintended way. Conversely, a victim may observe that after a withdrawal their remaining contract funds have been drained, or that refunds appear to be missing despite the contract reporting a successful transfer. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit, where the auditors noted that the external call to msg.sender was not guarded by a reentrancy check or the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to follow a straightforward transfer flow, and the external call is hidden behind an internal helper, giving a false sense of safety. The root cause is the lack of a reentrancy guard (e.g., a non‑reentrant modifier) and the absence of state updates before the external call, violating the principle that state changes should precede any untrusted interaction. The impact ranges from loss of AVAX funds for the protocol to erosion of user trust, as malicious actors could repeatedly invoke the vulnerable function to siphon assets. To remediate the issue, the contract should be refactored to update internal accounting before performing the external transfer and should apply a reentrancy guard modifier to withdrawAVAX() and any other functions that make external calls to msg.sender, thereby enforcing the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern and preventing recursive entry. This mitigation aligns the contract with standard defensive coding practices for handling external calls in Solidity.

title: LP Tokens May Be Locked in Contract Due to `allowEmergencyWithdraw`
description: The function [allowEmergencyWithdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L520) may be called by the `rocketJoeFactory.owner()` at any time. If it is called while the protocol is in Stage 3 and a pair has been created then the LP tokens will be locked and both issuers and depositors will be unable to withdraw.
poc:
If `allowEmergencyWithdraw()` is called `stopped` is set to `true`. As a result functions [withdrawIncentives()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L468) and [withdrawLiquidity()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L438) will revert due to the `isStopped(false)` modifier reverting.

Additionally, [emergencyWithdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L494) will revert since all the `WAVAX` and `token` balances have been transferred to the liquidity pool.

Thus, depositors and issuers will have no methods of removing their LP tokens or incentives.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the emergency withdrawal control flow of the LaunchEvent contract. The function allowEmergencyWithdraw() can be invoked by the RocketJoeFactory owner at any moment, regardless of whether a liquidity pair has been instantiated. When this function is called during Stage 3 after a pair has been created, it flips the internal stopped flag to true. This change activates the isStopped(false) modifier on both withdrawIncentives() and withdrawLiquidity(), causing these functions to revert. At the same time, the emergencyWithdraw() routine also reverts because the contract’s WAVAX and token balances have already been transferred to the liquidity pool, leaving no assets that the routine can move. Consequently, issuers who minted LP tokens and depositors who supplied liquidity are unable to retrieve their LP tokens or any pending incentives. From a user perspective, the UI may still display a withdraw option, but attempts to execute the withdrawal result in transaction failures, giving the impression that funds have vanished or that the refund mechanism is broken. The root cause is the lack of a guard condition that ensures a pair exists before allowing the emergency stop, which creates a denial‑of‑service scenario for LP owners. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined state transitions and function accessibility. It can be difficult to notice because the allowEmergencyWithdraw() function appears benign and is intended for emergency scenarios, yet it silently disables all withdrawal paths without warning. To remediate, the contract should require that the pair address be non‑zero before permitting an emergency stop, or redesign the emergencyWithdraw() path to still allow extraction of LP tokens and incentives even after the stop flag is set. This class of bug falls under improper access control leading to asset lockout, breaking the accounting assumption that users can always retrieve their deposited liquidity or earned rewards.

title: `createPair`
description: The LaunchEvent.sol `createPair()` function calls router.addLiquidity() with a amountADesired == amountAMin and amountBDesired == amountBMin. Because there is no allowance for slippage, if the zero slippage requirement is not met then the addLiquidity() function [will revert](https://github.com/traderjoe-xyz/joe-core/blob/5c2ca96c3835e7f2660f2904a1224bb7c8f3b7a7/contracts/traderjoe/JoeRouter02.sol#L52-L57) and prevent users from using the createPair() function. This could be caused either by frontrunning the createPair call or in a situation where the liquidity pool exists but does not allow for zero slippage with the assets it is holding.
poc: The zero slippage addLiquidity call is found [in LaunchEvent.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/a1579f6453bc4bf9fb0db9c627beaa41135438ed/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L411). This code may have been written with the assumption that only Rocket Joe will have a balance of the new token, so no other user could call the addLiquidity function with both assets, since the whitepaper states “Rocket Joe liquidity launch will complete before launchpad public sale release any tokens to the public”. However, the new token contract should be considered untrusted and Rocket Joe cannot guarantee where all the new tokens are before phase 3 of the Rocket Joe launch event, which is when `createPair()` is called. The token creator who has control over the token allocation is not controlled by Trader Joe, so an attacker who has early access to the new token can break the outlined assumptions.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LaunchEvent contract’s createPair() function, which forwards a call to the router’s addLiquidity() method with the parameters amountADesired set equal to amountAMin and amountBDesired set equal to amountBMin. This design implicitly enforces a zero‑slippage condition: the router will only accept the liquidity addition if the market price does not move between the moment the desired amounts are specified and the moment the transaction is executed. The router implementation reverts the transaction when any slippage is detected, as documented in its addLiquidity() logic. The root cause is the assumption that the newly launched token will have no external holders and that the price will remain perfectly stable during the call. In practice, an attacker who obtains early access to the token, or a front‑runner who modifies the pool’s price just before the transaction, can introduce even minimal slippage. When this happens, the addLiquidity() call reverts, causing the whole createPair() transaction to fail. The failure prevents the creation of the token pair, effectively locking the launch process and denying users the ability to provide liquidity or receive the expected trading pair. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a transaction that appears to have been submitted but then ends with a generic “transaction reverted” error, leaving their token balances unchanged while they expected the new pair to be created and their tokens to be deposited. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the launch event, potential loss of confidence in the protocol, and a situation where funds intended for liquidity are not locked into the pool, possibly leading to project delays or financial loss if the launch cannot be resumed. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which examined the contract logic and identified the unrealistic zero‑slippage requirement as a logical flaw. Because the revert only triggers under specific market conditions, it may not be evident during normal testing and can be hard to detect without simulating adversarial price movements. To remediate the problem, the createPair() function should be modified to accept a slippage tolerance parameter, allowing amountAMin and amountBMin to be set lower than the desired amounts. This change aligns the call with common liquidity‑addition patterns that protect against price movement, and it mitigates the risk of front‑running or unexpected token distribution. Additionally, the contract should avoid trusting that the new token has no external holders and may incorporate checks or time‑locks to ensure that only the intended party can invoke the liquidity addition during the launch phase.

title: Use safeTransfer/safeTransferFrom consistently instead of transfer/transferFrom
description: It is good to add a require() statement that checks the return value of token transfers or to use something like OpenZeppelin’s safeTransfer/safeTransferFrom unless one is sure the given token reverts in case of a failure. Failure to do so will cause silent failures of transfers and affect token accounting in contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on the raw ERC20.transfer and ERC20.transferFrom functions without verifying their return values or using a safe wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s safeTransfer / safeTransferFrom. According to the ERC20 specification, a token transfer may fail by returning false instead of reverting, especially for non‑standard tokens that implement fee‑on‑transfer, pausable, or blacklisting logic. Because the contract does not include a require statement that checks the boolean result, a failed transfer is silently ignored. Consequently, the contract’s internal accounting – for example, balance bookkeeping or fee calculations – is updated as if the transfer succeeded, while the external token balance of the recipient remains unchanged. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a token that deliberately returns false under certain conditions, causing the protocol to believe funds have been moved when they have not. The impact includes incorrect user balances, potential loss of funds when the protocol later attempts to use the presumed‑received tokens, and a breach of the protocol’s financial integrity. This condition occurs whenever the contract interacts with arbitrary ERC20 tokens that do not strictly revert on failure, which is common in DeFi ecosystems where many third‑party tokens are accepted. Users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because expected token transfers (e.g., withdrawals, rewards, or swaps) appear successful on‑chain but result in missing or zero balances on the user side. The issue was discovered during a security audit that flagged the missing require checks and the absence of safeTransfer usage. It can be hard to notice because transaction receipts show no error, events are still emitted, and the only symptom is a discrepancy between the contract’s internal state and the actual token balances – a situation that may only surface when a user reports receiving no tokens after a successful transaction. To remediate, the contract should replace all raw transfer calls with safeTransfer / safeTransferFrom or wrap each call in a require statement that reverts if the function returns false, ensuring that any failure aborts the transaction and preserves accounting consistency. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an "unchecked ERC20 return value" or "unsafe token transfer" and violates fundamental business logic that token transfers must be atomic and reliably reflected in both contract state and external balances.

title: Re-enterable Code When Making a Deposit to Stake
description:
Note: this attack requires `rJoe` to relinquish control during `transfer()` which under the current [RocketJoeToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/RocketJoeToken.sol) it does not. Thus this vulnerability is raised as medium rather than high. Although it’s not exploitable currently, it is a highly risky code pattern that should be avoided.

This vulnerability would allow the entire rJoe balance to be drained from the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit function of the staking contract, where an external token transfer is performed before the contract updates the user’s staking balance and reward accounting variables. Because the contract calls the rJoe token’s transfer method (_safeRJoeTransfer) and only afterwards adjusts the user.amount and user.rewardDebt state fields, a malicious contract that can gain execution control during the token transfer could recursively invoke deposit again. Each re‑entry would calculate the same pending reward as the previous call, because the accounting variables have not yet been refreshed, and the contract would consequently transfer the pending amount to the attacker multiple times. By repeating this loop, an attacker could exhaust the entire rJoe balance held by the staking contract. The root cause is a classic re‑entrancy pattern violation: the contract does not follow the checks‑effects‑interactions principle and does not protect the function with a re‑entrancy guard. Under the current implementation of the RocketJoeToken, the transfer function does not hand control back to the caller, so the issue cannot be exploited today; however, any future change to the token that allows a callback (e.g., via a malicious ERC777 hook or a custom token implementation) would make the attack feasible. From a user’s perspective, a depositor might see their deposited tokens disappear from the contract, receive no rewards, or notice that the contract’s total staked balance drops unexpectedly to zero. The impact is severe because it allows complete draining of staked funds, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that deposited assets are safely locked until withdrawal. The finding was uncovered during a security audit that examined the flow of external calls and identified the misplaced state updates. The flaw can be subtle to detect because the code appears to handle rewards correctly at a glance, and the external call is encapsulated in a private helper, masking the re‑entrancy window. The recommended remediation is to either apply OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard to the deposit function, which serialises calls and prevents nested entry, or to restructure the logic so that all state changes (updating user.amount and user.rewardDebt) occur before invoking any external token transfer, thereby adhering to the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern.

title: Pair creation can be denied
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the creation of a liquidity pool for the WAVAX‑token pair during a launch event. The contract function responsible for initializing the pair checks only that the factory returns address(0) for the given token pair at the moment of execution. Because the underlying factory allows any address to create a pair without permission, an external actor can call the factory’s createPair method in an earlier phase of the launch (phase 1 or 2). When the launch event later attempts to run its own createPair function, the require statement fails because the pair already exists, causing the transaction to revert with the message “LaunchEvent: pair already created”. This situation effectively denies the creation of the pair needed for the token launch. The root cause is a race‑condition / front‑running denial‑of‑service: the contract assumes that no one else can create the pool, but the permissionless nature of the factory invalidates that assumption. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by simply invoking the factory’s createPair function before the launch event reaches phase 3, thereby preventing the launch contract from provisioning liquidity. The impact is not a direct loss of funds—assets remain safe—but the protocol becomes unavailable for the affected pair: users attempting to participate see errors, no liquidity appears, and the launch may have to trigger an emergency state to allow withdrawals. This issue surfaces when the launch event is in its early phases and the pool has not yet been created; the affected parties include the token issuer, prospective liquidity providers, and any users expecting to interact with the newly launched market. The flaw was identified during a security audit that noted the mismatch between the expectation that the pool is unique to the contract and the reality of a public factory. It can be difficult to notice because the require statement appears to guard against duplicate creation, yet it does not account for external creation paths. To remediate, the launch function should be designed to handle the case where the pair already exists—by checking for existing liquidity, applying a slippage or minimum‑LP check, and restricting the call to privileged accounts (e.g., the issuer). Alternatively, the function could skip pair creation entirely and focus on adding liquidity with proper price checks. By enforcing permissioned access or incorporating robust validation of the pool’s state, the denial‑of‑service vector can be mitigated, ensuring that the launch proceeds as intended and that users receive the expected liquidity without encountering “pair already created” errors.

title: ERC20 return values not checked
description: The `ERC20.transfer()` and `ERC20.transferFrom()` functions return a boolean value indicating success. This parameter needs to be checked for success. Some tokens do **not** revert if the transfer failed but return `false` instead. Tokens that don’t actually perform the transfer and return `false` are still counted as a correct transfer.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract's interaction with ERC20 tokens without verifying the boolean return value of the token's `transfer` and `transferFrom` functions. According to the ERC20 specification, a successful token transfer should return `true`; however, some token implementations do not revert on failure but instead return `false`. The affected contract assumes that a token transfer always succeeds and proceeds as if the tokens have been moved, even when the function returned `false`. This omission creates a silent failure path: when a user invokes any of the withdrawal‑related functions—such as `withdrawLiquidity`, `withdrawIncentives`, `emergencyWithdraw`, or `skim`—the contract calls `token.transfer(msg.sender, amount)` and does not check the returned value. Consequently, if the token contract refuses the transfer (for example because of insufficient allowance, a paused state, or an internal rule) and returns `false`, the call will appear to have succeeded on‑chain, no revert will be triggered, and the caller will receive no tokens. From the user’s perspective the transaction receipt shows success, the UI may display a confirmation, yet the expected balance increase never occurs, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual funds. This problem is especially acute because the launch event token can be any ERC20 token, meaning an attacker could deliberately supply a malicious or non‑standard token that always returns `false`, causing withdrawals to be silently ignored. The impact includes loss of user funds, failed incentive distribution, and inaccurate accounting that can undermine the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue surfaces whenever the contract interacts with an external token without performing a `require(success)` check or using a safe wrapper like OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20`. It was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of return‑value validation in several functions. The flaw is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no events indicate the failure, and the contract’s state does not reflect the missing transfer, making debugging rely on manual balance comparison. To remediate, each ERC20 call should capture the returned boolean and enforce it, e.g., `require(token.transfer(recipient, amount), "Transfer failed")`, or employ the `SafeERC20` library which automatically reverts on false returns. This change ensures that any unsuccessful token movement aborts the transaction, preserving funds and maintaining correct accounting across the protocol.

title: DOS pay function
description:
In the `pay()` function users repay their debt and in line 364: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Core/contracts/TimeswapPair.sol#L364> it decreases their debt.

Let's say a user wants to repay all his debt, he calls the `pay()` function with his full debt. An attacker can see it and frontrun to repay a single token for his debt (since it’s likely the token uses 18 decimals, a single token is worth almost nothing) and since your solidity version is above 0.8.0 the line: `due.debt -= assetsIn[i];` will revert due to underflow.

The attacker can keep doing it every time the user is going to pay and since 1 token is basically 0$ (18 decimals) the attacker doesn’t lose real money.
poc:
From solidity docs:

Since Solidity 0.8.0, all arithmetic operations revert on over- and underflow by default, thus making the use of these libraries unnecessary.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the debt repayment routine of the Timeswap V1 Core contract, specifically in the `pay()` function that reduces a borrower’s outstanding debt by the amount of assets supplied in the transaction. The function blindly subtracts `assetsIn[i]` from the stored debt variable `due.debt` using the expression `due.debt -= assetsIn[i]`. Because Solidity version 0.8.0 and later automatically reverts on arithmetic underflow, the subtraction will fail if `assetsIn[i]` exceeds the current debt balance. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate repayment transaction. The attacker first submits a minimal‑value repayment (for example, one token with 18 decimals, effectively a negligible amount) that reduces the borrower’s recorded debt by a tiny fraction. When the victim’s transaction later attempts to repay the full original debt amount, the stored `due.debt` is now smaller than the repayment amount, causing the subtraction to underflow and the transaction to revert. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the borrower is unable to clear their debt, their balance remains unchanged, and subsequent protocol operations that depend on a cleared debt (such as liquidation avoidance or interest accrual) may be disrupted. The issue surfaces only under a specific ordering of transactions – a malicious front‑run preceding a legitimate repayment – making it difficult to detect through ordinary testing because normal repayment calls succeed when they are the first to modify the debt. The affected parties are any users who hold debt positions on the Timeswap pair contract, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer from stalled repayments and potential loss of confidence. The root cause is a missing validation that the repayment amount does not exceed the current debt, allowing the arithmetic operation to revert. To remediate, the contract should cap the repayment amount to the outstanding debt, for example by setting `assetsIn[i] = min(assetsIn[i], due.debt)` and then assigning `due.debt = 0` when the cap is reached, or by explicitly checking `require(assetsIn[i] <= due.debt)` before performing the subtraction. This defensive pattern prevents underflow, eliminates the front‑run vector, and restores the intended business logic that a borrower can always pay down or fully clear their debt without being blocked by a malicious actor.

title: Convenience contract fails to function if asset or collateral is an ERC20 token with fees
description: There are ERC20 tokens that collect fees with each transfer. If the asset or collateral used in a pair is of that type, the Convenience contract fails to function. It always sends the flat amount specified in the function’s parameter. If the token collects fees, the amount the Pair contract receives is less than it expects to get and reverts the transaction.
poc:
The function used to trigger the callback function and verify the received value: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Core/contracts/libraries/Callback.sol#L50>

Convenience contract’s callback function uses the amount specified in `collateralIn` in the transfer function: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Convenience/contracts/TimeswapConvenience.sol#L535>

If the token collects fees, the value the Pair contract receives will be less than `collateralIn`. The following require statement will fail: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Core/contracts/libraries/Callback.sol#L52>

The same thing applies to all the other callback functions in the library.

This issue doesn’t impact the Pair contract itself. Because of the safety checks for each callback, the contract always receives the amount it expects or the transaction is reverted. Meaning, the user has to adapt and cover the fees themselves. The convenience contract doesn’t do that and thus always fails.

The only issue would be outgoing transfers. For example, if a borrower pays back their debt, the pair contract receives the correct amount. But, the borrower will receive less collateral because of the fees. Since there’s no such check in those cases: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-timeswap/blob/main/Timeswap/Timeswap-V1-Core/contracts/TimeswapPair.sol#L374>

Hi what projects out there are using this fee mechanism in their transfer function? And what do you think is the mitigation for this? 

Almost all tokens don’t have this fee implementation. If someone wants to utilize this, they can create their own convenience contract to interact with Timeswap V1 Core.
