Would be worth documenting the behavior for fee on transfer tokens and also expected behavior for rebasing tokens as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the convenience layer of the Timeswap V1 protocol, which assumes that a token transfer will deliver exactly the amount specified in the function call. This assumption is violated by ERC‑20 tokens that levy a fee on every transfer, commonly known as fee‑on‑transfer or tax tokens. When such a token is used as either the asset or the collateral in a pair, the convenience contract forwards the flat amount defined by the caller (the collateralIn parameter). Because the token deducts a portion as a fee, the receiving Pair contract gets less than the expected amount. The Pair contract contains a safety check that compares the received balance with the announced amount; when the actual amount is lower, the check fails and the transaction reverts. Consequently, any operation that relies on the convenience contract – for example opening a leveraged position, adding collateral, or executing a repayment – cannot complete when a fee‑on‑transfer token is involved. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails, often with a generic revert message, while the user’s funds remain locked in the contract. In addition, the outbound paths of the convenience contract do not perform a similar balance verification. When a borrower repays a debt, the Pair contract receives the correct net amount, but the fee taken on the outgoing collateral transfer means the borrower receives less than intended, creating an unexpected shortfall in the returned collateral. The issue was discovered during a static audit of the Callback library, where the auditors observed that the contract relied on the ERC‑20 transfer function’s return value rather than measuring the pre‑ and post‑transfer balances. Detecting this problem can be difficult because most ERC‑20 tokens do not implement transfer fees, leading developers to overlook the edge case. The class of bug is an improper handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens, a form of accounting mismatch where the contract’s internal accounting assumes a 1:1 transfer ratio. To remediate the problem the convenience contract should be refactored to verify the actual amount received after each transfer (e.g., by reading the token balance before and after the call) or to adjust the expected amount based on the token’s fee model. An alternative mitigation is to restrict the convenience contract to fee‑free tokens only, documenting the incompatibility with fee‑on‑transfer and rebasing tokens. By ensuring that the contract accounts for the real transferred amount, the protocol can preserve its invariants, avoid unexpected reverts, and guarantee that users receive the collateral or refund they expect.

title: Improper Upper Bound Definition on the Fee
description: The `rJoePerSec` does not have any upper or lower bounds. Values that are too large will lead to reversions in several critical functions.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked configuration parameter that controls the per‑second emission rate of the reward token, referred to as rJoePerSec. This variable is intended to represent the fee or reward amount that the protocol distributes over time, but the contract’s updateEmissionRate function does not enforce any upper or lower limits on the value supplied by the contract owner. Because of this missing validation, an owner—or a malicious actor who gains ownership—can set rJoePerSec to a value that exceeds the safe arithmetic range used by several core pool functions. When the emission rate is excessively large, internal calculations that multiply or divide by rJoePerSec overflow or trigger division‑by‑zero guards, causing those functions to revert. The affected functions include pool updates, reward claims, deposits and withdrawals, all of which rely on the emission rate to compute accrued rewards or fees. As a result, users attempting legitimate actions such as depositing liquidity, withdrawing, or harvesting rewards may encounter transaction reverts and see their balances appear unchanged, leading to the perception that funds have disappeared or that refunds are missing. The issue surfaces only when an extreme emission rate is set; under normal operating values the contract behaves as expected, which makes the bug difficult to notice during standard testing. The problem was discovered during a security audit when testers supplied unusually high numbers to the updateEmissionRate function and observed systematic reverts in downstream calls. Exploitation does not require sophisticated code injection—simply invoking updateEmissionRate with a huge value is sufficient to lock the protocol’s core accounting pathways. This breach of business logic violates the fundamental assumption that reward calculations remain within a bounded numeric domain, breaking the accounting invariants that guarantee users receive the correct amount of tokens. To remediate the issue, the contract should define explicit minimum and maximum bounds for rJoePerSec and enforce them with require statements in the updateEmissionRate function, ensuring that any attempted update outside the safe range is rejected before it can affect the system’s state.

title: Owner of LaunchEvent token has the ability to DOS attack the event
description:
The owner of the token for which the LaunchEvent was created, has the ability to DOS attack the event. They can prevent the LaunchEvent from creating a JoePair which in turn limits the access to the following two functions: `withdrawLiquidity()` & `withdrawIncentives()`. Thus, stopping anybody from withdrawing their LP tokens.

The owner of the RocketJoe platform has the ability to enable the emergency withdrawal allowing the depositors to take back their AVAX. But, they lose their burned rJOE tokens and the gas fees.

The dev team might use this attack vector if they think the price of their token is too low. In that case, they can DOS attack the LaunchEvent. If the RocketJoe owner enables the emergency withdrawal, the dev team is able to take back their initial deposit. Thus, they don’t lose anything but their reputation.
poc:
When `createPair()` is called, the function checks whether a pair already exists. If it does, the transaction is reverted: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L382-L389>

Anybody is able to create a new JoePair using the existing TraderJoe contracts. If someone owns both AVAX and the LaunchEvent token, they are able to create a new pair and deposit a small amount of liquidity. Thus, the `totalSupply` will be `> 0`. Meaning, at that point, the call to `createPair()` fails. Per design, the LaunchEvent will be used to issue a token to the public market. So only the dev team and its trusted parties have access to the necessary tokens to create a pair and provide liquidity.

Since `createPair()` can’t be executed the `pair` state variable is never initialized: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L422>

Thus, the following two functions are not reachable any more: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L439>

If the emergency withdrawal is enabled, the token issuer can take back their deposit: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-trader-joe/blob/main/contracts/LaunchEvent.sol#L510-L516>
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that can be triggered by the token owner or any party that controls both the native AVAX token and the LaunchEvent token. The LaunchEvent contract is designed to create a new Trader Joe liquidity pair (JoePair) during the event; this pair is required for the functions withdrawLiquidity() and withdrawIncentives() to operate. The createPair() function first checks whether a pair for the given token already exists and reverts the transaction if it does. Because the check is performed without restricting who may call createPair(), an adversary can pre‑emptively create a bogus pair – even with a tiny amount of liquidity – causing the pair’s totalSupply to be greater than zero. Once such a pair exists, the subsequent call from the LaunchEvent contract fails, leaving the internal pair variable uninitialized. As a result, the two withdrawal functions become permanently inaccessible, preventing participants from retrieving their LP tokens or any accrued incentives. From the user’s perspective, a depositor who expects to see their LP balance grow and later be able to withdraw finds the balance frozen, receives no incentive payouts, and may see the UI show a zero or missing withdraw button. The impact is that funds deposited into the launch event are effectively locked until the platform’s owner invokes an emergency withdrawal mechanism. This emergency path refunds the deposited AVAX but burns the corresponding rJOE tokens and requires the depositor to pay gas fees, resulting in a partial loss of value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LaunchEvent contract, where the logic of createPair() and its lack of access control were identified as a design flaw. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly when the pair is created as intended; only under the specific condition where a prior pair exists does the failure manifest, making it easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, the ability to create a JoePair for a token that is undergoing a LaunchEvent should be limited exclusively to the LaunchEvent contract itself, or a dedicated factory should enforce that only the authorized contract can call createPair(). This change would prevent external actors from pre‑creating a pair and thereby close the DoS attack surface. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of “unrestricted initialization” or “access‑control‑less state‑set” bugs, where a critical contract state can be set by anyone, violating the assumed business logic that only the platform should control liquidity pair creation and subsequent withdrawals.

title: `createRJLaunchEvent`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RocketJoeFactory contract’s createRJLaunchEvent function, which permits any externally‑owned account to invoke the routine as long as it can supply a positive token amount (greater than zero). The root cause is the absence of any access‑control check – the function does not verify that the caller is the contract owner, an authorized issuer, or a privileged role. Because the only gating condition checks that the token address is non‑zero and that a minimal token amount is transferred, a malicious actor can approve a transfer of a single wei of the target token, call createRJLaunchEvent, and cause the factory to record a launch event for that token. The exploit proceeds by the attacker submitting a tiny transfer, triggering the internal require statements, cloning the launch event implementation, and moving the token amount into the newly created event contract. This effectively reserves the token identifier in the factory’s getRJLaunchEvent mapping, preventing the legitimate token issuer or the platform itself from later creating a proper launch event for the same token. The impact is a denial‑of‑service scenario: legitimate users lose the ability to launch token sales, potentially locking a small amount of funds in an event that no one controls, and eroding trust in the protocol’s onboarding flow. The issue manifests whenever any user with the capability to approve a token transfer interacts with the factory; it does not require large capital, making it cheap to execute. All parties that rely on the factory – token issuers, the platform operators, and downstream investors – are affected because the expected workflow (“issuer creates a launch event, deposits tokens, and users can participate”) is broken; users may see a launch event appear but receive no allocation, or may find that their token balances are reduced to zero without any visible purchase. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that examined function visibility and parameter checks, noting that the external function lacked ownership or role restrictions. It can be difficult to spot because the code otherwise appears logically sound: it validates non‑zero addresses, ensures the token amount is positive, and checks that no existing liquidity pair exists. These checks give a false sense of safety, masking the missing privilege verification. To remediate, the function should be guarded by an onlyOwner modifier or an explicit require that the caller matches the intended issuer, using OpenZeppelin’s Ownable or AccessControl patterns. In broader terms, this is an instance of an “missing authorization” or “unrestricted external function” bug, which can lead to privilege escalation and denial‑of‑service attacks. From the user’s perspective, the UI may display a newly created launch event with the correct token name, yet the user receives no participation rights, and the token balance they attempted to deposit appears to have vanished, violating the expectation that the contract will only accept deposits from the authorized issuer.

title: Uninitialized `RocketJoeStaking.lastRewardTimestamp` can inflate `rJoe` supply
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the staking contract’s reward‑tracking variable `lastRewardTimestamp` being left at its default value of zero. In normal operation the function `updatePool` is called before any deposits are made, and when the contract’s Joe token balance (`joeSupply`) is zero the timestamp is set to the current block time, preventing any erroneous reward calculation. However, because the timestamp is not initialized during contract deployment, an attacker can exploit the contract by sending a small amount of Joe tokens directly to the contract address before any call to `updatePool`. When `updatePool` is finally invoked, the expression `block.timestamp - lastRewardTimestamp` evaluates to the full current block timestamp (a large number) instead of a short interval, and this inflated multiplier is multiplied by the per‑second reward rate `rJoePerSec`. The result is a massive `rJoeReward` that is minted to the contract itself via `rJoe.mint(address(this), rJoeReward)`. These newly minted rJoe tokens are not allocated to any user; they simply increase the total rJoe supply, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially diluting the value of existing rJoe holders. The flaw appears only under the specific condition where tokens are transferred to the contract before the first pool update, a scenario that is not covered by the typical deposit workflow and therefore can be overlooked during testing. The issue was discovered by the Code4rena audit team while reviewing the staking logic and noting that `lastRewardTimestamp` lacked an explicit initialization. Detecting the problem is difficult because the contract behaves correctly when interacted with through its intended `deposit` function, and the supply inflation does not manifest as an immediate loss of user funds, only as an unexpected increase in total token supply. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain an explicit storage variable representing the total amount of deposited Joe tokens and use this value for reward calculations, decoupling the reward logic from the raw token balance and ensuring that unsolicited token transfers cannot affect the reward timestamp. Initializing `lastRewardTimestamp` at deployment or in the first `deposit` call would also close the window for exploitation. By correcting the accounting mechanism, the protocol restores its intended economic model where rewards are proportional to genuine user deposits and the total rJoe supply accurately reflects distributed incentives.

title: Incompatibility With Rebasing/Deflationary/Inflationary tokens
description: The TraderJOE protocol do not appear to support rebasing/deflationary/inflationary tokens whose balance changes during transfers or over time. The necessary checks include at least verifying the amount of tokens transferred to contracts before and after the actual transfer to infer any fees/interest.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the TraderJOE protocol’s implicit assumption that any ERC‑20 token transferred to its contracts will retain the exact amount specified in the transfer call. This assumption fails for tokens that implement rebasing, deflationary fees, or inflationary mechanisms where the token balance can change during the transfer or as a result of time‑based supply adjustments. The root cause is the lack of any verification step that compares the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer; the protocol simply relies on the transfer function returning success and does not check that the post‑transfer balance matches the expected amount. Consequently, when a user deposits a token that charges a fee on transfer, or a token that automatically reduces its supply (rebases down) at the moment of the transaction, the protocol records the deposit as successful while actually receiving fewer tokens than intended. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately using a fee‑on‑transfer or rebasing token to cause the protocol to accept a reduced amount, thereby creating a discrepancy between the reported deposited amount and the actual token balance held by the contract. The impact is that users may see their deposits appear to succeed in the UI, but the contract’s internal accounting shows a lower balance, leading to missing funds, failed refunds, or an inaccurate representation of liquidity in the pool. This situation occurs whenever a token’s transfer logic modifies the sender’s or receiver’s balance beyond the nominal amount, such as when the token implements a transfer tax, burns a portion of the tokens, or automatically adjusts supply during a launch event. All users who attempt to trade, provide liquidity, or withdraw using such tokens are affected, as are the protocol’s overall financial integrity and trustworthiness. The issue was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, which noted that the missing balance checks constitute a medium‑risk flaw because the protocol does not revert the transaction when the token’s balance diminishes, and there is no safeguard against accidental loss of funds. The problem can be difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert, no error is emitted, and the standard ERC‑20 interface appears to behave normally; the only symptom visible to the user is a discrepancy between the amount they sent and the amount reflected in their on‑chain balance or UI display, such as a zero or reduced balance after a successful deposit. To remediate, the contract should implement explicit balance snapshots before and after each token transfer, enforce that the difference equals the intended amount, and either reject tokens that do not preserve the transferred amount or whitelist only tokens known to be fee‑free and non‑rebasing. This correction aligns the implementation with the generic class of bugs known as “insufficient validation of token transfer amounts” and restores confidence that the protocol’s accounting matches business logic expectations.

title: Lack of input checks
description: If penalties are set to 0 the protocol would be vulnerable to price manipulations like the one described in the contest documentation.
poc:
The protocol uses economic penalties to punish withdraws to protect against economic price manipulation attacks. If these penalties are set to 0 in the creation of a token launch the sale would be vulnerable to this kind of attack. The penalties should never be 0 for any token sale.

The economic attack that could be done with 0 penalties is detailed on page 7 of the whitepaper.

I consider this to be a medium risk since it could completely invalidate a token launch but it’s still unlikely (but possible) the creators will set penalties to 0. This could be done by mistake or by the creators of the launch event to exploit it themselves.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient validation of the economic penalty parameter used during token launch configuration. The protocol relies on a non‑zero penalty to discourage strategic withdrawals that could manipulate the token price during a sale. Because the contract does not enforce that the penalty value be greater than zero at initialization or when created through the factory, an attacker – or an unwary deployer – can set the penalty to zero. When the penalty is zero, the economic deterrent disappears, allowing an adversary to execute a price‑manipulation attack as outlined in the protocol’s whitepaper (page 7). The exploit works by withdrawing large amounts of the token or performing coordinated trades without incurring any cost, thereby distorting the market price and potentially draining funds or invalidating the entire token launch. The impact can be severe for the token launch participants: users may see their expected refunds or token allocations disappear, balances may be reduced to zero, and the launch may be rendered economically meaningless. The issue manifests only when the launch parameters are configured with a zero penalty, which can happen by mistake during deployment or be deliberately set by a malicious launch creator. Because the parameter is a numeric field without explicit bounds, the flaw can be easily overlooked during code review or testing, especially if the default value happens to be zero. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors noted that the lack of a >0 check contradicts the protocol’s security model. To remediate, the contract should enforce a constraint that the penalty value must be strictly greater than zero either in the initializer function or within the factory that creates launch contracts, ensuring that the economic safeguard is always active. This type of bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or unchecked parameter constraints, which can undermine business logic that assumes a minimum economic cost for certain actions.

title: `_safeMint` Will Fail Due To An Edge Case In Calculating `tokenId` Using The `_generateNewTokenId` Function
description:
NFTs are used to represent unique positions referenced by the generated `tokenId`. The `tokenId` value contains the position’s score in the upper 128 bits and the index wrt. the token supply in the lower 128 bits.

When positions are unlocked after expiring, the relevant position stored in the `positionOf` mapping is deleted, however, the NFT is not. The `merge()` function is used to combine points in unlocked NFTs, burning the underlying NFTs upon merging. As a result, `_generateNewTokenId()` may end up using the same `totalSupply()` value, causing `_safeMint()` to fail if the same `amount_` and `duration_` values are used.

This edge case only occurs if there is an overlap in the `points_` and `totalSupply() + 1` values used to generate `tokenId`. As a result, this may impact a user’s overall experience while interacting with the `XDEFI` protocol, as some transactions may fail unexpectedly.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the XDEFI distribution contract constructs a unique token identifier (tokenId) for each minted NFT. The tokenId is built by concatenating a 128‑bit score (derived from the amount and duration of the locked position) with a lower 128‑bit sequence number generated as totalSupply() + 1. Because the contract burns NFTs during the merge() operation, totalSupply() decreases, meaning the low‑order part of the tokenId can repeat. If a user later attempts to lock a new position with the same amount and duration (thus the same score) after such a burn, the calculation may produce an identical tokenId that already exists. When _safeMint() is called with this duplicate identifier, the ERC‑721 library rejects the minting, causing the transaction to revert. This edge case only manifests when the points component of the new tokenId matches the points accumulated from a previous merge and the current totalSupply() value aligns such that the lower 128‑bit suffix repeats. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a failed lock or merge transaction, often reported as “_safeMint failed” or a generic revert, leaving the user unable to receive the expected NFT and potentially causing confusion about why their funds appear to be locked without a receipt. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the tokenId generation logic and identified that relying on a mutable supply counter does not guarantee uniqueness after token burns. The problem is hard to spot because the failure only appears after a specific sequence of operations (burn then mint with identical scoring parameters) and the revert message does not explicitly point to an identifier collision. Conceptually, this is a classic case of non‑unique identifier generation caused by using a state variable that can decrease, violating the assumption that tokenId values are monotonically increasing and therefore always unique. The impact is limited to transaction failures and degraded user experience; no direct loss of funds occurs because the minting simply does not happen, but users may be prevented from creating or merging positions, effectively a denial‑of‑service for certain parameter combinations. The appropriate remediation is to replace the totalSupply‑based suffix with an internal counter that only increments on each mint and never decrements, ensuring that every tokenId remains globally unique regardless of burns. This change restores the invariant that token identifiers are unique and monotonic, eliminating the edge case that leads to _safeMint reverts.

title: Oracle data feed is insufficiently validated
description: Price can be stale and can lead to wrong `quoteAmount` return value
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from insufficient validation of external price oracle data used to compute token swap quotations. The contract fetches the latest price values from Chainlink feeds for DAI, USDC and USDT but does not verify that the returned price data corresponds to a recent, completed round. Consequently, if a price feed is stale, has not been updated, or the round is incomplete, the contract may still accept the stale value and use it in the quote calculation. This happens because the code only checks that the numeric price is greater than zero, without asserting that the timestamp is recent, that the round identifier matches the answered round, or that the round has been marked complete. An attacker or simply a lagging oracle can therefore cause the contract to return an incorrect quoteAmount. From a user's perspective the symptom is that a trade yields an unexpectedly low or zero amount of the target token, or that their balance appears to have been reduced more than anticipated. The impact includes financial loss for users, distortion of the protocol's pricing invariants, and potential drain of liquidity if malicious actors trigger large trades under incorrect pricing. The condition occurs whenever the Chainlink price feed does not update within its expected interval, which can happen during network congestion, oracle node failure, or deliberately manipulated feed latency. The affected parties are all participants who rely on the contract for price quotes, including end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle integration and identified the missing staleness checks. It is subtle because the contract functions correctly under normal feed operation, so the bug may only surface during rare feed outages, making it hard to detect through standard testing. Conceptually, this is a classic “oracle staleness” or “unchecked external data” flaw, where the contract trusts out‑of‑date information without verifying freshness. The proper mitigation is to add explicit validation of the reported round data: ensure the answeredInRound is at least the current roundID, confirm the timestamp is non‑zero and recent (e.g., within a configurable threshold), and reject any price that does not meet these criteria before proceeding with the quote calculation. Once those checks are in place, the contract will no longer accept stale or incomplete price data, aligning the on‑chain pricing with the intended business logic and protecting users from incorrect trade outcomes.

title: Rewards distribution can be disrupted by a early user
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution routine that updates the cumulative reward integral stored in a 128‑bit unsigned integer (uint128). The routine computes an increment based on the amount of newly received reward tokens divided by the total supply of the underlying token. When an attacker, or any early participant, mints or wraps only a single wei of the underlying token, the total supply (_supply) becomes equal to one. If the contract subsequently receives a large amount of reward tokens – for example 5e18 wei – the expression ((bal - rewardRemaining) * 1e20) / _supply evaluates to a value that exceeds the maximum representable value of uint128 (2^128‑1). Because the code casts the intermediate result back to uint128 without overflow protection, the reward_integral variable wraps around, silently overflowing. This overflow breaks the accounting logic that assumes reward_integral grows monotonically. As a result, later calls that calculate each user’s entitled reward based on the difference between the current integral and the user’s last recorded integral will produce incorrect, often zero, reward amounts. From a user’s perspective, balances that should increase after a claim remain unchanged, refunds appear to be missing, or the UI shows that no rewards have been earned despite the contract holding a substantial reward token balance. The issue manifests only when the contract holds reward tokens and the total supply is extremely low – a condition that can be deliberately created by an early user or inadvertently by a deployment sequence that allows a single‑token supply before reward funding. The bug was discovered during a static audit that identified the narrow type used for reward_integral and the unchecked arithmetic. It may be hard to notice because the overflow does not revert the transaction; it merely produces a wrapped value, so the contract continues to operate but with corrupted accounting. The bug belongs to the class of integer overflow/underflow vulnerabilities caused by inappropriate type sizing and missing safety checks in financial accounting formulas. To remediate the issue, the implementation should either store reward_integral in a 256‑bit type, add explicit overflow checks before casting, or redesign the calculation to avoid large intermediate results, ensuring that the cumulative reward integral cannot exceed its storage capacity.

title: Basis points constant BPS_MAX is used as minimal fee amount requirement
description:
Base fee modules require minimum fixed fee amount to be at least BPS_MAX, which is hard coded to be 10000.

This turns out to be a functionality restricting requirement for some currencies.

For example, WBTC (https://etherscan.io/token/0x2260fac5e5542a773aa44fbcfedf7c193bc2c599, #10 in ERC20 token rankings), has decimals of 8 and current market rate around $40k, i.e. if you want to use any WBTC based collect fee, it has to be at least $4 per collect or fee enabled follow.

Tether and USDC (https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7 and https://etherscan.io/token/0xa0b86991c6218b36c1d19d4a2e9eb0ce3606eb48, #1 and #3) have decimals of 6, so it is at least $0.01 per collect/follow, which also looks a bit tight for a hard floor minimum.
poc:
BPS_MAX is a system wide constant, now 10000:

[FeeModuleBase.sol#L17](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/FeeModuleBase.sol#L17)  

[ModuleGlobals.sol#L20](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/ModuleGlobals.sol#L20)  

This is correct for any fees defined in basis point terms.

When it comes to the nominal amount, 10000 can be too loose or too tight depending on a currency used, as there can be various combinations of decimals and market rates.

The following base collect module implementations require fee amount to be at least BPS_MAX (initialization reverts when amount < BPS_MAX):

All collect module implementations use the same check:

FeeCollectModule: [FeeCollectModule.sol#L72](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/FeeCollectModule.sol#L72)  

LimitedFeeCollectModule: [LimitedFeeCollectModule.sol#L79](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/LimitedFeeCollectModule.sol#L79)  

TimedFeeCollectModule: [TimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L81](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/TimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L81)  

LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule: [LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L86](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L86)  

FeeFollowModule also uses the same approach: [FeeFollowModule.sol#L62](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/follow/FeeFollowModule.sol#L62)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of a single hard‑coded constant, BPS_MAX, which is defined as 10 000 basis points and is employed by all fee‑related modules as a minimum fee amount requirement. In practice this means that when a collect or follow module is initialized, the supplied nominal fee amount must be greater than or equal to BPS_MAX, otherwise the transaction reverts. Because BPS_MAX is intended to represent the maximum possible basis‑point value (100 %), repurposing it as a lower bound creates a hidden floor on the fee that can be expressed in any token. The root cause is a logical misinterpretation of the constant’s semantic purpose and the lack of a separate, token‑agnostic minimum fee parameter. Exploitation is straightforward: a developer or user attempting to configure a fee for a token with low decimal precision or a modest market price—such as USDC (6 decimals) or WBTC (8 decimals)—will find that the required minimum fee translates into an unexpectedly large monetary amount (for example, at current prices the minimum fee for WBTC becomes roughly $4, and for USDC or USDT it becomes $0.01). When the fee amount supplied is lower, the contract’s constructor checks fail and the transaction reverts, preventing the creation of the fee‑collecting module. From the user’s perspective this manifests as an inability to set a reasonable fee, error messages on deployment, or the absence of a collect/follow option for certain tokens, leading to a mismatch between the expected low‑cost fee and the actual blocked operation. The impact is functional rather than a direct loss of funds: it restricts the protocol’s ability to support a wide range of assets for fee collection, potentially reducing revenue, discouraging user engagement, and breaking business logic that assumes fees can be set arbitrarily low. The issue was identified during a systematic audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed that the same BPS_MAX constant was used across multiple modules for both maximum and minimum fee calculations, a pattern that is easy to overlook because the constant’s name suggests an upper‑limit rather than a floor. The problem is hard to notice in testing because the revert only occurs when a fee below the hidden floor is attempted, a scenario that may not be exercised in typical test suites that use higher‑value tokens. To remediate, the contract should introduce a distinct constant representing the minimal nominal fee amount (e.g., a fixed value of 1 or 10 of the token’s smallest unit) and adjust the initialization checks to compare against this new parameter rather than BPS_MAX. This decouples the basis‑point ceiling from the fee floor, allowing each token’s decimal precision and market price to be respected and restoring the intended flexibility of the fee modules.

title: Inappropriate handling of `referralFee` makes collecting Mirror fails without error when `referrerProfileId` is burned
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the collect module processes referral fees for mirrored publications when the profile that originally published the mirror has been burned. In the current implementation, the collect function attempts to resolve the referral recipient by calling the ERC‑721 `ownerOf(referrerProfileId)` on the Hub contract. If the `referrerProfileId` corresponds to a burned (non‑existent) ProfileNFT, the `ownerOf` call reverts with the standard "ERC721: owner query for nonexistent token" error. Because the revert occurs inside the fee‑handling block, the entire collect transaction fails even though the underlying content is still valid and should be collectible. This failure manifests only when a Mirror is collected and a non‑zero `referralFee` has been configured on the original publication. Users trying to collect such a Mirror experience a transaction that either reverts silently or fails without an explicit error message indicating the cause, leading to a situation where they receive no funds, see no change in their balance, and may be left uncertain about why the collect did not succeed. The impact is limited to collectors of mirrors that reference burned profiles; the protocol’s treasury and the original publisher are not directly affected, but the user experience is degraded and revenue that should have been routed to a referrer is lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the `FeeCollectModule` where the control flow around `_processCollectWithReferral` was examined and the interaction with `ownerOf` was identified as unsafe for burned IDs. It can be hard to notice because the revert originates from an external ERC‑721 call rather than the collect module itself, so developers may not anticipate that a burned profile can cause the entire collect to abort. The proper fix is to treat a missing referrer as a non‑existent participant: the contract should attempt to read the referrer address using a `try/catch` (or equivalent) and, on failure, skip the referral fee logic and optionally emit an event such as `LogNonExistingReferrer`. Conceptually, this aligns the bug with the class of "invalid external call handling" where a contract assumes the existence of an external token ID without guarding against its absence. By handling the error gracefully, the collect operation can proceed, the adjusted amount is transferred to the treasury, and no unexpected revert occurs, preserving the expected user flow where a collector receives the content and any applicable fees are correctly accounted for.

title: Profile creation can be frontrun
description:
[PublishingLogic.sol#L50](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/aaf6c116345f3647e11a35010f28e3b90e7b4862/contracts/libraries/PublishingLogic.sol#L50)  

The `LensHub/PublishingLogic.createProfile` function can be frontrun by other whitelisted profile creators.  
An attacker can observe pending `createProfile` transactions and frontrun them, own that handle, and demand ransom from the original transaction creator.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the profile‑creation routine of the Lens protocol, specifically the PublishingLogic.createProfile function that is accessible to any address whitelisted by governance. When a user submits a transaction to mint a new profile handle, the contract does not reserve the chosen handle until the transaction is actually executed. Consequently, an attacker who monitors the mempool can see the pending createProfile transaction, craft their own transaction with the same handle, and submit it with a higher gas price. Because the protocol simply checks for handle availability at execution time, the attacker’s transaction may be mined first, thereby claiming the handle that the original user intended to obtain. The original transaction then either fails or proceeds without the desired handle, leaving the user without the expected profile. This front‑running scenario can be exploited by any whitelisted profile creator, does not require any special contract privileges, and is feasible on public chains where private transaction relays such as Flashbots are not enforced. The impact is primarily a disruption of the user experience – the user expects to receive a specific handle but receives none or a different one – and a loss of trust in the naming system, as handles can be hijacked for ransom or resale. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the PublishingLogic library, where the lack of a commit‑reveal or other anti‑front‑running mechanism was noted. It may be hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds from a blockchain perspective; the failure is manifested only as an unexpected UI outcome (e.g., “profile creation failed” or “handle unavailable”), which can be mistaken for a benign error. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should adopt a commit‑reveal scheme for handle registration, enforce private transaction submission via MEV‑resistant relays, or redesign the handle allocation to include an auction or other deterministic reservation process. In generic terms, this is a front‑running vulnerability in a name‑registration function where the uniqueness check is performed only at execution, allowing an adversary to pre‑emptively claim a resource that should be reserved for the original requester.

title: Name squatting
description:
[LensHub.sol#L142](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/aaf6c116345f3647e11a35010f28e3b90e7b4862/contracts/core/LensHub.sol#L142)  

Creating profiles through `LensHub/PublishingLogic.createProfile` does not cost anything and will therefore result in “name squatting”.  
A whitelisted profile creator will create many handles that are in demand, even if they don’t need them, just to flip them for a profit later.  
This ruins the experience for many high-profile users that can’t get their desired handle.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the unrestricted registration of user handles in the Lens protocol, specifically within the createProfile function of the LensHub contract. Because the contract allows any whitelisted address to create a profile at zero cost and imposes no limitation on the number of profiles that can be minted per address, an actor can register a large number of desirable handles without incurring any economic penalty. This design flaw creates a classic name‑squatting scenario: the attacker registers high‑value or popular handles, holds them, and later attempts to sell or transfer them for profit. The root cause is the absence of a fee, auction, or any scarcity‑enforcing mechanism for handles, combined with a whitelist that only checks that the caller is authorized to mint, not that the handle is being used responsibly. Exploitation is straightforward – a malicious whitelisted contract or externally owned account simply calls createProfile repeatedly, passing in the desired handle strings, and thereby exhausts the pool of attractive handles. The impact is primarily economic and reputational: legitimate users who wish to claim a recognizable handle encounter a "handle already taken" error, experience frustration, and may be forced to choose an inferior identifier. High‑profile users, brands, or projects may be unable to secure their preferred names, undermining user experience and potentially eroding trust in the platform. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s createProfile function is invoked without a monetary cost or a rate‑limiting rule, which is the default state of the current deployment. All participants of the Lens ecosystem—end users, developers building on the protocol, and token holders—are affected because the perceived scarcity of handles is a core part of the platform’s identity model. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor observed that the payable modifier and any fee‑related logic were missing from the profile creation path. It is easy to overlook because the function works as intended for creating profiles, and there is no immediate loss of ether from the contract; the damage is indirect and appears only as a usability issue. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a cost model for handle registration – such as a fixed fee, a staking requirement, or an auction mechanism – and possibly enforce per‑address limits or a cooling‑off period to deter bulk registration. This aligns the vulnerability with the broader class of "free name registration leading to squatting" bugs commonly found in domain‑name services and other on‑chain naming systems. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is a failed attempt to claim a desired handle, receiving an error indicating the name is already owned, even though no malicious contract activity is visible on‑chain. Users expect to be able to register a handle they like without competition, but instead the platform may silently allocate those names to an unknown party, effectively causing the handle to disappear from the marketplace.

title: Cashback on referral
description:
[FeeCollectModule.sol#L99](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/aaf6c116345f3647e11a35010f28e3b90e7b4862/contracts/core/modules/collect/FeeCollectModule.sol#L99)  

In the fee collect modules like `FeeCollectModule` there is no prevention of someone submitting a second profile they own as the `referrerProfileId` in `processCollect` to receive back part of the fees paid.

The referral system is essentially broken as all rational agents will submit a second profile they control to get back part of the fees. One could even create a referrer smart contract profile that anyone can submit which automatically refunds the fee received. A [similar royalties/referral fees issue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-nested-findings/issues/30) was judged high-severity recently.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the referral mechanism of the fee‑collect module. When a user calls the `processCollect` function they may supply any `referrerProfileId`, and the contract does not verify that the referrer is independent from the collector. Consequently, a rational actor can create a second profile that they also control, or deploy a contract that automatically registers itself as a referrer, and then submit that profile identifier as the referrer when collecting a publication. The contract treats the declared referrer as an external party and awards it a portion of the collected fees, effectively returning part of the fee to the collector. This self‑referral loop creates a value‑leakage bug: the protocol’s intended revenue sharing model is subverted, curators receive less compensation, and the overall fee pool is reduced. The issue manifests whenever the `processCollect` call is executed with a referrer profile owned by the same entity that initiates the collection, which can happen in any transaction that bypasses the front‑end’s safety checks. It affects collectors, curators, and the protocol’s economic assumptions, as users can obtain a discount on fees without any explicit permission. The flaw was uncovered during a systematic audit of the referral logic, where the absence of any owner‑or‑whitelist validation was noted as a logical oversight rather than a runtime error, making it easy to miss in normal testing. Exploiting the bug does not produce visible contract reverts; the transaction succeeds and the fee rebate is silently transferred to the attacker’s own profile, which is why the problem can remain unnoticed. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that the referrer profile either belongs to a whitelisted set of infrastructure accounts or, at a minimum, that the owner of the referrer profile differs from the collector’s address. Additional safeguards such as requiring explicit consent from the original publication creator before crediting a referrer could also close the self‑referral loop. In abstract terms, the bug is a classic case of a self‑referral or royalty‑loop vulnerability where incentive alignment is broken, leading to unintended fund redistribution and reduced protocol earnings.

title: Imprecise management of users’ allowance allows the admin of the upgradeable proxy contract to rug users
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an imprecise handling of ERC‑20 allowances in a system where users must approve a fee‑collect or fee‑follow module to spend an unlimited amount of tokens on their behalf. The module’s processFollow function invokes safeTransferFrom with the address supplied in the follower argument, rather than the caller (msg.sender). Because the LensHub contract is implemented as an upgradeable proxy, the contract’s logic can be replaced by any code the proxy admin chooses. A malicious or compromised admin can therefore upgrade the implementation to a contract that forwards calls to the original module but passes an arbitrary user address as the follower. When the upgraded contract invokes processFollow, the unlimited allowance that the user granted to the module is abused to transfer the approved amount from the user’s wallet to arbitrary recipients, such as the admin’s treasury address. This attack vector can be triggered whenever a user has granted a high or unlimited allowance to a fee module and the protocol’s governance permits the proxy admin to replace the implementation without further checks. From a user’s perspective, the UI shows a successful follow or collect action while the token balance of the user unexpectedly drops, sometimes to zero, and no funds are received by the intended recipient. The impact is a direct loss of user‑controlled assets, effectively “money disappears” from the user’s wallet, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit that highlighted the combination of unchecked follower parameters and the upgradeable proxy pattern. It is hard to notice because transferFrom is a standard ERC‑20 operation and developers often assume allowances can only be spent by the contract that received the approval, not considering that the contract’s internal logic may be swapped later. The root cause belongs to the class of allowance misuse coupled with unchecked upgradeability, where the from‑address of transferFrom is not constrained to the transaction sender and the contract holding the allowance is upgradeable. To remediate, the payment‑processing logic should enforce that the source of transferFrom is always msg.sender, and the contract that holds user allowances should be made non‑upgradeable or protected by a multi‑sig governance that prevents unilateral admin upgrades. Alternatively, a dedicated non‑upgradeable payment hub can be introduced so users approve only a single trusted contract, eliminating the need for multiple modules to hold unlimited allowances.

title: It’s possible to follow deleted profiles
description:
[InteractionLogic.sol#L49](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/libraries/InteractionLogic.sol#L49)  

When someone tries to follow a profile, it checks if the handle exists, and if it doesn’t, it reverts because the profile is deleted. The problem is that there might be a new profile with the same handle as the deleted one, allowing following deleted profiles.
poc:
Alice creates a profile with the handle “alice.” The profile id is 1.  
She deleted the profile.  
She opens a new profile with the handle “alice”. The new profile id is 2.  
Bob tries to follow the deleted profile (id is 1).  
The check  

```solidity
if (_profileIdByHandleHash[keccak256(bytes(handle))] == 0)
    revert Errors.TokenDoesNotExist();
```

doesn’t revert because there exists a profile with the handle “alice”.  
Therefore Bob followed a deleted profile when he meant to follow the new profile.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an identifier‑reuse flaw in the Lens Protocol’s follow logic. When a user attempts to follow a profile, the contract checks only whether the handle associated with the requested profile still resolves to a non‑zero profile identifier. The check does not verify that the identifier returned for the handle matches the specific profile ID supplied in the follow request. Consequently, if a profile is deleted and a new profile is created later using the same handle, the mapping from handle hash to profile ID points to the newly created profile. The follow function still sees a non‑zero entry for the handle and therefore does not revert, even though the caller supplied the ID of the deleted profile. An attacker can exploit this by recreating a previously deleted handle and then causing other users to inadvertently follow the stale profile ID, effectively directing their follow action to a profile that no longer exists or to an unintended account. The impact is that users may believe they have followed the intended, newly created profile, while the protocol records a follow relationship with an old, deleted profile, leading to misplaced social graph edges, confusion in activity feeds, and potential privacy concerns. This bug manifests whenever a profile is deleted and its handle is later re‑registered; it affects all participants who rely on the follow operation to connect with a specific profile ID, including the profile owner, followers, and any downstream services that index follows. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by analyzing the logic in InteractionLogic.sol and observing that the existence test only compares against zero rather than ensuring the handle‑to‑ID mapping matches the provided ID. The problem is subtle because the UI shows the handle as existing, so users see a successful follow transaction and have no immediate indication that the target profile is actually the old one. To remediate, the contract must compare the stored profile ID for the given handle with the caller‑supplied profile ID (or use a dedicated exists() query) before allowing the follow, thereby guaranteeing that the handle and profile ID are consistent. This change prevents the accidental following of deleted profiles and restores the expected business logic that a follow should only succeed for a currently existing, correctly identified profile.

title: Missing whenNotPaused
description:
[LensHub.sol#L929](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/LensHub.sol#L929)  

All the external function of LensHub have whenNotPaused modifier.  
However, LensHub is erc721 and the transfer function doesn’t have the whenNotPaused modifier.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing pause protection on the ERC‑721 token transfer path of the LensHub contract. LensHub is built as a Pausable contract where every external function is guarded by the whenNotPaused modifier, ensuring that an emergency pause stops all state‑changing interactions. However, the standard ERC‑721 transfer functions (transferFrom, safeTransferFrom, etc.) delegate the actual state change to the internal hook _beforeTokenTransfer, and this hook does not include the whenNotPaused check. As a result, even when the contract owner or governance has activated a pause, users can still move NFTs between addresses. The root cause is the reliance on an internal hook that was not modified to respect the Pausable state, creating an unintended bypass of the emergency stop mechanism. An attacker, or even a regular user, can exploit this by initiating a token transfer while the protocol is paused, thereby contravening the expectation that all activity is frozen. The impact is that the pause, which is meant to protect assets during an emergency, no longer guarantees the safety of token ownership; NFTs may be transferred without consent, leading to potential loss of value, confusion among holders, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions. This condition occurs anytime the pause flag is set to true; the contract’s external state‑changing functions are blocked, but the ERC‑721 transfer path remains active. All token owners, lenders, and any parties relying on the pause for security are affected because their assets can be moved despite the pause. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that verified the presence of the whenNotPaused modifier on public functions but did not initially check internal token transfer hooks. It can be difficult to notice because the UI typically only shows a paused indicator for the main contract functions, while transfers continue to work silently, leading users to believe their assets are frozen when they are not. To remediate the problem, the whenNotPaused modifier should be added to the _beforeTokenTransfer hook (or directly to the transfer functions), ensuring that any token movement is blocked while the contract is paused. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that pausing the protocol halts all token transfers, preserving user balances and preventing unauthorized asset migration. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is that after invoking a pause, attempts to transfer an NFT still succeed, contrary to the expectation that the transfer would revert or be rejected. Users may notice that their NFTs can still be sent or sold, or that balances change when they believed the system was frozen, which constitutes a clear violation of the protocol’s safety guarantees.

title: Collect modules can fail on zero amount transfers if treasury fee is set to zero
description:
Treasury fee can be zero, while collect modules do attempt to send it in such a case anyway as there is no check in place. Some ERC20 tokens do not allow zero value transfers, reverting such attempts.

This way, a combination of zero treasury fee and such a token set as a collect fee currency will revert any collect operations, rendering collect functionality unavailable.
poc:
Treasury fee can be set to zero:

[ModuleGlobals.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/ModuleGlobals.sol#L109)  

Treasury fee transfer attempts are now done unconditionally in all the collect modules.

Namely, FeeCollectModule, LimitedFeeCollectModule, TimedFeeCollectModule and LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule do not check the treasury fee to be sent, `treasuryAmount`, before transferring:

[FeeCollectModule.sol#L176](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/FeeCollectModule.sol#L176)  

[LimitedFeeCollectModule.sol#L194](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/LimitedFeeCollectModule.sol#L194)  

[TimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L190](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/TimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L190)  

[LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L205](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/collect/LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule.sol#L205)  

The same happens in the FeeFollowModule:

[FeeFollowModule.sol#L90](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/modules/follow/FeeFollowModule.sol#L90)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the collect modules of the Lens Protocol, where a treasury fee amount of zero is not checked before attempting an ERC‑20 token transfer to the treasury address. Because the code unconditionally calls `safeTransferFrom` with the calculated treasury amount, a zero‑value transfer is still executed. Certain ERC‑20 implementations reject zero‑value transfers and revert the transaction. When the protocol’s configuration allows the treasury fee to be set to zero and a token that disallows zero transfers is selected as the fee currency, any collect operation—whether from a FeeCollectModule, LimitedFeeCollectModule, TimedFeeCollectModule, LimitedTimedFeeCollectModule, or the related FeeFollowModule—will revert. This makes the collect functionality unavailable for users, who experience transaction failures, see no tokens transferred, or receive UI messages such as “collect failed” or a generic revert error. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit by examining the module source code and noticing the missing condition that guards against a zero treasury amount. It is difficult to notice because a zero fee is a legitimate configuration in many contexts, and developers may assume the token transfer will succeed regardless of amount. The bug falls into the class of missing input validation or improper handling of edge‑case token behaviours, specifically zero‑value transfer reverts. Exploitation does not require an attacker; any user or contract can trigger the failure simply by configuring a zero treasury fee with a non‑zero‑transfer‑rejecting token. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the collect feature, potentially reducing protocol revenue and harming creator incentives. The recommended fix is to add a guard that only performs the treasury transfer when the amount is greater than zero, thereby preventing unnecessary zero‑value transfer calls and restoring normal collect operation.

title: Zero collection module can be whitelisted and set to a post, which will then revert all collects and mirrors with `PublicationDoesNotExist`
description:
In case when zero collection module be whitelisted and then zero collection module set to a post (done by different actors), its functionality will be partially broken: every collecting and mirroring of it will be reverted with Errors.PublicationDoesNotExist, while getPubType will return its type as a Mirror.

Setting severity to Medium per ‘function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted’, as either the behavior of rejecting collects/mirrors is desired and to be implemented explicitly, or such a scenario shouldn’t exist in a system, i.e. now zero address absence in white list cannot be guaranteed as its setting is manual and possible.
poc:
Collect module isn’t checked additionally on init, any whitelisted address can be set:

[PublishingLogic.sol#L308-309](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/libraries/PublishingLogic.sol#L308-309)  

While zero address also can be whitelisted:

[LensHub.sol#L128-135](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/LensHub.sol#L128-135)  

If zero address is whitelisted and then set as collectModule for a post, a getPointedIfMirror helper function called on it will revert with Errors.PublicationDoesNotExist:

[Helpers.sol#L47](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/libraries/Helpers.sol#L47)  

This way all attempts to collect and mirror this post will also revert:

[InteractionLogic.sol#L108](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/libraries/InteractionLogic.sol#L108)  

[PublishingLogic.sol#L258](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/libraries/PublishingLogic.sol#L258)  

Also, getContentURI view will fail with the same error:

[LensHub.sol#L785](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/LensHub.sol#L785)  

And getPubType will return Mirror as a publication type:

[LensHub.sol#L829](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/main/contracts/core/LensHub.sol#L829)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Lens protocol manages the whitelist of collect modules. The whitelist logic permits any address, including the zero address (0x000…000), to be added without additional validation. When a post is later created, the author can assign a collect module that has been whitelisted, and if the zero address has been whitelisted, it may be set as the collect module for that post. The contract’s internal helper functions, such as the getPointedIfMirror routine, assume that a non‑zero collect module represents a valid publication and attempt to resolve its type and content. Because the zero address does not correspond to an existing publication, any call that traverses this path reverts with the generic Errors.PublicationDoesNotExist error. Consequently, every attempt to collect the post, mirror it, retrieve its content URI, or query its type results in a revert. From a user perspective, the publish transaction may appear successful, but later interactions—clicking the “collect” button, trying to mirror the post, or viewing its content— either fail silently or return an error stating that the publication does not exist, effectively making the post unusable. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any post that inadvertently or maliciously receives the zero collect module: users cannot collect, mirror, or view the post, and the protocol’s availability is reduced. This scenario can be triggered when a malicious or careless governance participant whitelists the zero address and an attacker (or the same participant) assigns it to a post. The issue was discovered through static analysis of the PublishingLogic, LensHub, and Helpers libraries, noting that the initialization step does not enforce a non‑zero collect module and that the whitelist function does not filter out the zero address. The bug is subtle because the zero address looks like a regular address in the whitelist and the failure only surfaces during later interactions, which may be interpreted as a generic platform error rather than a specific contract flaw. To remediate the problem, the protocol should forbid the zero address from being whitelisted as a collect module, and should include an explicit validation check when setting a collect module on a post, rejecting zero addresses with a clear error message. Alternatively, if the intention is to allow posts that reject collections, the contract should provide a dedicated error path that conveys the intended rejection rather than relying on an implicit failure. This class of vulnerability can be described as an "unvalidated input leading to improper handling of sentinel values" and manifests as a functional denial‑of‑service bug that breaks business logic around content collection and mirroring.

title: Approvals not cleared when transferring profile
description:
[ApprovalFollowModule.sol#L32](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-aave-lens/blob/aaf6c116345f3647e11a35010f28e3b90e7b4862/contracts/core/modules/follow/ApprovalFollowModule.sol#L32)  

The `ApprovalFollowModule.approve` function is indexed by both (`owner = IERC721(HUB).ownerOf(profileId)`, `profileId`) in case the profileId NFT is transferred.  
However, upon transfer, the old approvals are not cleared.

This can lead to similar issues as OpenSea not cancelling their sale offers upon NFT transfer.  
When the NFT is at some point transferred back to the original owner, all the old approvals are still intact which might not be expected by the owner.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ApprovalFollowModule's handling of profile ownership changes. When a profile is represented as an ERC‑721 token, the module stores follow approvals in a mapping that is keyed by the address of the current owner (obtained via IERC721(HUB).ownerOf(profileId)) together with the profile identifier. The contract does not clear or revoke these stored approvals when the profile NFT is transferred to a new address. As a result, the permission data that was granted by the previous owner remains active after the transfer. This stale authorization state can be exploited by an attacker who either regains ownership of the profile or who is able to trigger actions through the still‑valid approvals. For example, if a profile is sold to a buyer, the seller's previously granted follow approvals continue to be honored; should the profile later be transferred back to the seller (or a compromised address), the seller can invoke follow actions that were intended to be limited to the original owner. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that transferring a profile resets all associated permissions, yet in practice the approvals persist, leading to situations where a user may see unexpected follow actions or find that other addresses can still interact with their profile. This issue was identified during a formal security audit that examined the lifecycle of profile ownership and noticed that the module lacks a transfer hook to reset state. The bug can be difficult to notice because the approvals are stored off‑chain in the UI and the contract does not emit any event indicating that stale approvals exist; the protocol’s documentation does not explicitly state that approvals survive transfers, so developers and users may assume the opposite. The impact is a breach of the intended access control model: the protocol’s business logic assumes that only the current owner can manage follow approvals, but this assumption is violated, potentially leading to unauthorized actions, reputational damage, or loss of trust. The class of bug is a permission‑state leakage across asset transfers, commonly seen in systems that fail to invalidate or re‑initialize authorization data when ownership changes. To remediate the issue, the module should reset or completely clear all stored approvals whenever a profile NFT changes hands, either by integrating a transfer hook or by providing an explicit function that the new owner can call to purge stale approvals. Alternatively, a configurable option could be introduced to retain certain approvals if desired, but the default behavior should favor revocation to preserve security guarantees.

title: Ineffective Whitelist
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an ineffective whitelist controlling the creation of user profiles in the Lens protocol. The contract checks only whether the caller of the profile creation function is listed in a whitelist mapping, but it does not enforce any limit on how many profiles a whitelisted address can mint. Because the check is performed solely on the caller’s address, a single whitelisted account can invoke the creation routine repeatedly and assign each newly minted profile NFT to any arbitrary address. This design flaw allows an attacker who controls a whitelisted account, or a compromised whitelisted contract, to generate an unlimited number of profiles on behalf of unsuspecting users. The root cause is the absence of a per‑account or per‑transaction cap and the lack of any validation of the intended recipient, which means the whitelist only guarantees that the caller is allowed to call the function, not that the number of calls is bounded. Exploitation is straightforward: the malicious actor calls the profile creation method in a loop, each time specifying a different recipient or even the same recipient, thereby flooding the system with synthetic profiles. From the user’s point of view, unexpected profile NFTs may appear in their wallet without any request, or the platform may become populated with a large number of low‑quality or spammy profiles, violating the expectation that only a controlled set of creators can issue profiles. The impact includes erosion of trust in the reputation model, possible denial‑of‑service through gas‑heavy spamming, and a dilution of the value of legitimate profiles. The issue manifests whenever a whitelisted address is able to call the internal validation function, which occurs on every profile creation transaction; there is no conditional logic to stop repeated calls. It was discovered during a manual audit of the LensHub contract when the validation routine was examined and found to lack any quantitative restriction. Because the problem does not produce an explicit error, it can be difficult to spot in normal testing—transactions succeed, and the contract behaves as coded, yet the business rule that profile creation should be limited is silently broken. The proper mitigation is to treat the whitelist as a gate *and* enforce a numerical cap per whitelisted account, introduce a separate governance‑approved quota, or redesign the system so that only a tightly controlled set of contracts (with embedded caps) can create profiles. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of "unbounded minting permissions" where access control is present but resource limits are missing, resulting in a mismatch between the intended policy and the actual on‑chain behavior.

title: Reentrancy allows commenter to overwrite own comments
description:
Since the Lens platform is a blockchain-based social media platform, it’s important that information relevant to users be emitted so that light clients need not continually refer to the blockchain, which can be expensive. From the docs:

`Events are emitted at every state-changing function call, in addition to standard ERC721 events. Events often include the timestamp as a specific parameter, which allows for direct consumption using a bloom filter without needing to fetch block context on every event.`

As such, it is important that the content of emitted events matches what direct lookups of publication data shows.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the comment creation flow of the Lens social media protocol. When a user creates a comment, the contract fetches the next publication identifier (pubCount + 1) and immediately passes it to the reference module via PublishingLogic.createComment. The contract only increments the profile's pubCount after the external call returns. Because the external reference module can execute arbitrary code, a malicious module can re‑enter the comment function, invoke comment again with the same publication identifier, and overwrite the stored contentURI of the original comment. As a result, the event emitted for the first comment contains the intended, benign URI, but the on‑chain storage for that comment is replaced with a malicious URI controlled by the attacker. Users browsing the platform or light clients that rely on events will see a comment that appears to link to harmless content, while reading the comment or following the URI will actually direct them to a phishing or malware site. The issue manifests only when a reference module with re‑entrancy capability is whitelisted, which may happen through governance error or a compromised DAO upgrade. It affects any profile that can publish comments and any follower or reader that consumes the comment, leading to potential exposure to malicious links and loss of trust in the platform. The bug was uncovered during a security audit that added a mock malicious reference module and observed that the contentURI stored after the re‑entered call differed from the one logged in the CommentCreated event. The problem is subtle because the event appears correct, making the inconsistency hard to detect without explicit state checks or manual verification of stored data. The class of bug is a re‑entrancy‑induced state overwrite, where external calls are made before the contract’s internal state is safely updated, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. To remediate, the contract should capture the new publication identifier in a local variable before invoking any external module and should increment the profile's pubCount before the external call, ensuring that subsequent re‑entered calls cannot reuse the same identifier. Additionally, the reference module interface could be limited to non‑re‑entering functions or guarded by a re‑entrancy lock. This fixes the root cause by preventing the external module from influencing the same storage slot during the same transaction, restoring consistency between emitted events and on‑chain data, and protecting users from hidden malicious content.

title: The Owner and Proxy Admin can make users lose funds
description:
The contest explicitly asks to analyze the contract for “Rug Vectors”, so that is what this issue is about.

I have classified this issue as “high risk” - although the vulnerability is considerable, the attacks themselves are not very likely to occur (they depend on the owner and/or the proxy admin to be compromised). The main reason why I believe the vulnerabiity is “high” is because the very fact that all these factors exist can make the sale fail, as informed users will avoid the contract completely one they realize the extent in which the contract is manipulable.

In the current implementation, there several ways that investors can lose funds if the owner of the contract is not well behaved. These risks can be divided into two kinds:

  * owner becomes unable to act (for example, owner looses her private key, or the owner is a wallet or a DAO and signers cannot agree on the right action to take)
  * owner is malicious (for example, the owner account gets hacked or the signers turn bad), and wants to steal as much as the funds as possible (“Rug Vectors”), or executes a griefing attack (i.e. acts in such a way to hurt the buyers and/or the project, without immediate financial gain)

The contract is vulnerable to all three types of vulnerabilities (“rug pull”, “griefing” and “inactivity”).

(1) Loss of funds due to owner inactivity: (1a) If the owner does never funds the contract, the buyers will not receive their tokens, and have no recourse to get their investment back (1b) If the owner does not call `finalize`, buyers will not receive their tokens, and and have no recourse to get their investment back

(2) Griefing attacks by the owner (attacks that that have no immediate gain for the attacker, but are either annoying or lead to loss of funds) (2a) the owner can change many essential conditions of the sale: for example, the price, the start time, the duration, the guest list, and the total amount of tokens that are allowed to be sold. The owner can do this at any moment, also **while the sale is in course**. This allows for all kinds of griefing attacks. It also voids the whole point of using a smart contract in the first place. (2b) Owner can pause the contract at any time, which will freeze the funds in the contract, as it also disallows users to claim their tokens

(3) Rug pull by owner (attacks with financial gain for the attacker, buyer loses money) (3a) The Owner can call `sweep` at any time and remove all unsold CTDL tokens while the sale is in progress. Future buyers will still be able to buy tokens, but the sale can never be finalized (unless the owner funds the contract) (3b) Owner can front-run buyers and change the price. I.e. the owner can monitor the mem pool for a large `buy` transaction and precede the transaction with her own transaction that changes the price to a very low one. If the price is low enough, `getAmountOut` will return `0`, and the buyers will lose her funds and not receive any CTDL tokens at all.

(4) Rug pull by proxy Admin (4a) Although no deployment script is provided in the repo, we may assume (from the tests and the fact that the contracts are upgradeable) that the actual sale will be deployed as a proxy. The proxy admin (which may not be the same account as the owner) can change the implementation of the contract at any time, and in particular can change the implemention logic in such a way that all the funds held by the contract can be sent to the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of owner‑controlled and proxy‑admin‑controlled privileges that allow the sale contract to be manipulated in ways that can cause investors to lose their funds.
