The root cause is the overly broad access control: the contract’s owner (or a separate proxy admin) can change critical sale parameters, pause the contract, withdraw tokens, or upgrade the implementation at any time, including while a token sale is in progress. Because these actions are not constrained by any time lock, quorum, or multi‑signature check, an attacker who gains control of the owner key or the proxy admin can execute a range of attacks. An inactive owner or a compromised owner can simply abandon the sale, leaving deposited ETH or stablecoins locked forever, while buyers receive no tokens and have no recourse. A malicious owner can grief participants by arbitrarily changing the sale start time, duration, price, token caps, or by pausing the contract, which freezes funds and prevents users from claiming their allocations. The owner can also call a sweep function to remove all unsold tokens during the sale, rendering finalization impossible and effectively stealing the remaining token supply. Moreover, because the price can be updated on‑chain, an owner who monitors the mempool can front‑run a large purchase, lower the price just before the transaction is mined, cause the pricing formula to return zero, and make the buyer’s transaction revert with loss of the paid amount. If the contract is deployed behind an upgradeable proxy, the proxy admin can replace the implementation with malicious code that redirects all held funds to an arbitrary address, achieving a classic rug pull. The impact is that users may see their balances disappear, receive no tokens after contributing, or be unable to withdraw their investment, violating the fundamental expectation that a crowdsale contract safely holds and disburses funds according to a predetermined schedule. The issue was discovered during a security audit that focused on “rug vectors” and was identified by reviewing the access modifiers on administration functions and the lack of constraints around mutable sale parameters. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to function correctly when the owner behaves benignly; only under adverse conditions does the hidden power surface, making it hard for non‑technical participants to notice until funds are already lost. To remediate the issue, the contract should eliminate owner‑only mutable state after the sale starts, enforce that the token supply is locked before opening the sale, remove the sole‑owner restriction on finalization so any participant can trigger settlement, restrict or time‑lock price changes, ensure that pause does not lock user withdrawals, limit sweep functionality to post‑finalization, and avoid using an upgradeable proxy for a single‑purpose sale. Using a well‑audited, battle‑tested crowdsale implementation from OpenZeppelin would also mitigate many of these risks. In summary, the contract suffers from an over‑privileged owner and proxy admin that can cause inactivity, griefing, or outright rug pulls, leading to lost investments, unreceived tokens, and a loss of trust in the protocol.

title: `saleRecipient` can rug buyers
description:
In `TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#buy()`, `tokenIn` will be transferred from the buyer directly to the `saleRecipient` without requiring/locking/releasing the corresponding amount of `tokenOut`.

This allows the `saleRecipient` to rug the users simply by not transferring `tokenOut` and finalizing the sale.
poc:
Given:

  * tokenIn: `WBTC`
  * _tokenOutPrice: `1e8`
  * tokenOut: `CTDL`
  * Alice `buy()` with `100e8`;
  * Alice `buy()` with `200e8`;

A malicious `saleRecipient` can just not transfer any `CTDL` to the contract and `finalize()` and keep `300e8 WBTC` received.

As a result, Alice and Bob can not get the expected amount of `tokensOut`, and there is no way to retrieve the WBTC paid, in essence, lose all the funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper escrow and premature fund release pattern in the token sale contract. When a buyer calls the buy() function, the contract transfers the incoming payment token (tokenIn) directly to the address designated as saleRecipient without first ensuring that the corresponding amount of the offered token (tokenOut) is already deposited or locked in the contract. This design flaw means the saleRecipient can finalize the sale without ever delivering tokenOut, effectively keeping the transferred tokenIn. The root cause is the absence of a settlement step that checks for sufficient tokenOut before releasing tokenIn, combined with the ability of the saleRecipient (or contract owner) to invoke finalization at will. An attacker can exploit this by simply calling buy() on behalf of users, receiving the payment tokens, and then calling finalize() while withholding tokenOut. As a result, buyers see their payment balances reduced (e.g., WBTC is debited) but receive zero or no amount of the purchased token (e.g., CTDL), leading to a loss of funds with no on‑chain recovery path. This issue manifests whenever the buy() function is executed and the saleRecipient chooses not to provide tokenOut before finalization; it does not require front‑running or additional market manipulation beyond the malicious control of the recipient address. All participants who intend to purchase tokens—individual users, the broader protocol, and any downstream applications—are affected because the contract violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a purchase must be settled atomically: payment is taken only when the purchased asset is delivered. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the flow of funds and noticed that tokenIn is transferred directly to an external address without any escrow or verification of tokenOut availability, a pattern that can be subtle because the transfer itself appears legitimate and no explicit error is thrown. The issue is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract does not emit warnings when tokenOut is missing, and the balance of the buyer may simply show a reduction with no incoming token balance change, which can be mistaken for a normal transaction fee or a delayed delivery. To remediate, the contract should first receive tokenIn into its own address, hold it in escrow, and require that a sufficient amount of tokenOut be deposited into the contract before releasing tokenIn to the saleRecipient. This ensures that payment is only transferred after the sale is settled, restoring atomicity and preventing the saleRecipient from rug‑pulling funds. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “premature fund release” or “missing escrow” vulnerabilities that allow a privileged party to keep user funds without providing the promised assets, breaking trust and economic guarantees of the token sale.

title: Owner can steal input tokens
description:
[TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L299-L309](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-badger-citadel/blob/main/contracts/TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L299-L309)  
[TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L311-L324](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-badger-citadel/blob/main/contracts/TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L311-L324)  
[TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L211-L224](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-badger-citadel/blob/main/contracts/TokenSaleUpgradeable.sol#L211-L224)

Owner is in full control over the `saleRecipient` address. When a `buy()` transaction enters the mempool, an owner can frontrun the buy with a transaction that calls `setTokenOutPrice()` and sets the price to a very high value, effectively making bought tokens close to (if not usually equal) zero and consuming the tokens to the owner-selected address - `saleRecipient`. Thus, an owner has incentive to perform such attack as they may cause little or zero additional indebtnees to the contract and all tokens to the owner.

This can also be seen as a coincidence - an owner sets a price while a user broadcasts a `buy()` transaction. The user may buy for a significantly different price than they intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an admin‑controlled price manipulation bug in the token sale contract. The contract allows the owner to change the variable that determines how many sale tokens a buyer receives for each unit of payment (the token out price) at any time, even after the sale has started. Because the owner can set this price to an arbitrarily high value, a malicious owner can front‑run a legitimate buy transaction by submitting a transaction that raises the price just before the user’s transaction is mined. When the user’s buy transaction is finally executed, the inflated price causes the contract to calculate an almost‑zero amount of sale tokens to transfer to the buyer while still forwarding the buyer’s payment to the address stored in saleRecipient, which is controlled by the owner. From the user’s perspective the UI will show that the purchase was successful, but the received token balance will be unexpectedly low or zero, contradicting the expectation that they receive a proportional amount of tokens for the amount paid. This issue occurs only while the sale is active and the price‑changing function remains callable, making it exploitable whenever a buyer broadcasts a transaction that has not yet been mined. The affected parties are all participants who attempt to purchase tokens during the sale, as well as the protocol’s reputation because funds are effectively stolen by the owner. The flaw was uncovered during a formal audit, where the code path that permits price updates was examined and the interaction with the buy logic was identified as a front‑running vector. The problem can be subtle because price updates are legitimate in many sales, so a sudden price spike may be attributed to market conditions rather than malicious intent, especially when the front‑run transaction executes in the same block. To remediate the issue, the contract should lock the token price once the sale begins, prohibit any further modifications to the price or the sale start flag, and ensure that token transfers to buyers are performed after the payment settlement rather than before. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an “admin‑controlled pricing oracle” vulnerability where the privileged actor can manipulate a pricing parameter to cause a loss of value for users, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that the price used for a transaction is fixed at the moment the user initiates it.

title: `StakingRewards.sol#notifyRewardAmount
bug_full: The contract implements a staking reward mechanism where a designated rewardsDistribution contract calls notifyRewardAmount to announce a new reward amount. The function validates the announced amount by checking that rewardRate does not exceed the current balance of the rewards token divided by the rewards duration. This check assumes that the entire token balance belonging to the contract is freely available for distribution. However, the contract also holds rewards that have already been earned by stakers but not yet withdrawn. Because the balance check does not subtract these outstanding obligations, a situation can arise where the rewardsDistribution announces a new reward amount that, together with the previously accrued but unclaimed rewards, exceeds the actual token holdings. The contract therefore records a rewardRate that is higher than the real available supply. When a staker later attempts to claim their accrued rewards via getReward, the transfer fails due to insufficient token balance, leaving the user with an earned balance that cannot be redeemed. This flaw was discovered during a formal audit where the auditors demonstrated a concrete proof‑of‑concept: after a first funding round of 100 reward tokens and an unclaimed balance, the rewardsDistribution called notifyRewardAmount again with another 100 tokens without transferring any additional tokens to the contract. The contract accepted the call, the earned amount for the staker doubled to 200, but the subsequent claim transaction reverted because the contract’s token balance was only 100. The vulnerability is difficult to notice because the require statement passes – the balance appears sufficient when measured against the newly announced rate, obscuring the fact that part of that balance is already promised to other users. The issue belongs to the class of reward‑allocation accounting bugs where future allocations are not reconciled against pending liabilities. It affects any staker who has not yet claimed their rewards and can lead to loss of expected yield. To mitigate the problem, the notification function should be redesigned to transfer the exact reward amount into the contract (e.g., using safeTransferFrom) and to compute the new rewardRate based on the incoming tokens plus any leftover rate from the current period, ensuring that only freshly supplied tokens are counted toward future rewards. This prevents the contract from over‑committing rewards and preserves the ability of all users to claim what they have earned.

title: Users Will Lose Rewards If The Shelter Mechanism Is Enacted Before A Recent Checkpoint
description:
The shelter mechanism aims to protect the protocol’s users by draining funds into a separate contract in the event of an emergency. However, while users are able to reclaim their funds through the `Shelter.sol` contract, they will still have a deposited balance from the perspective of `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol`.

Because users will only receive their rewards upon depositing/withdrawing their funds due to how the checkpointing mechanism works, it is likely that by draining funds to the `Shelter.sol` contract, users will lose out on any rewards they had accrued up and until that point. These rewards are unrecoverable and can potentially be locked within the contract if the reward token is unique and only belongs to the sheltered `_pid`.
poc: [ConvexStakingWrapper.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol)
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a reward‑loss bug that occurs when the emergency “shelter” mechanism of the protocol is triggered before a user’s latest reward checkpoint is performed. The ConvexStakingWrapper contract keeps a per‑user accounting of accrued rewards that is only updated during explicit deposit, withdrawal, or a call to the internal `_checkpoint` function. When the owner activates the shelter, all deposited LP tokens and any associated fund balances are transferred to a separate Shelter.sol contract for safekeeping. However, this transfer does not invoke the reward‑checkpointing logic, so the wrapper continues to record the user’s balance as if the funds were still staked, while the internal reward index for that user remains stale. Because users receive their pending rewards only when the checkpoint is executed (which normally happens on the next deposit or withdrawal), the act of moving the funds to the shelter effectively freezes the reward calculation at the last checkpoint. As a result, any rewards that accrued between the previous checkpoint and the shelter activation become unrecoverable; they are neither claimable through the shelter contract nor credited to the user’s account. This problem is especially severe when the reward token is unique to the sheltered pool identifier (`_pid`), because the orphaned reward balances may be permanently locked in the wrapper contract.

The exploit scenario is straightforward: an owner with the privilege to trigger the shelter can, either intentionally or unintentionally, cause all current depositors to lose the yield that had been earned since the last checkpoint. From the user’s perspective, the UI may still display a positive deposited balance, but when they later try to claim or withdraw, they receive no rewards and may even see a zero payout despite having earned yield previously. The discrepancy is subtle because the contract’s balance view does not immediately reflect the missing rewards, making the issue hard to notice without detailed accounting checks.

The impact is a loss of earned yield for every affected depositor, potentially reducing the economic incentive for users to stake and eroding trust in the protocol’s safety guarantees. The bug is classified under the broader class of “stale accounting” or “reward checkpoint bypass” vulnerabilities, where state updates tied to financial incentives are not triggered by a critical state‑change operation.

The flaw was identified during an audit by Code4rena, where the researchers simulated the shelter flow and observed that the reward index was never updated after the emergency transfer. The difficulty in spotting the issue stems from the fact that the emergency transfer itself succeeds, and the user’s deposited balance remains unchanged from the wrapper’s perspective, hiding the underlying reward discrepancy.

To remediate the problem, the contract should allow users (or a trusted component) to invoke a public `_checkpoint` after funds have been moved to the shelter, ensuring that pending rewards are calculated and made claimable before the balance is considered frozen. Alternative mitigation strategies include moving to a global reward index that can be compared against individual accruals, or modifying the shelter’s logic to explicitly account for and transfer any pending rewards to the user’s address. Any solution must balance the need to prevent post‑withdrawal reward harvesting against guaranteeing that users receive the full amount of yield they earned prior to the emergency transfer.

title: `ConvexStakingWrapper.enterShelter
description: The shelter mechanism provides emergency functionality in an effort to protect users’ funds. The `enterShelter` function will withdraw all LP tokens from the pool, transfer them to the shelter contract and activate the shelter for the target LP token. If this function is called again on the same LP token, the `amountInShelter` value is overwritten, potentially by the zero amount. As a result its possible that the shelter is put in a state where no users can withdraw from it or only a select few users with a finite number of shares are able to. Once the shelter has passed its grace period, these tokens may forever be locked in the shelter contract.
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the emergency shelter mechanism of the ConvexStakingWrapper contract. The function `enterShelter` is intended to protect users by withdrawing all LP tokens from a pool, transferring them to a separate shelter contract, and flagging the token as under shelter. Internally, the contract stores the amount of tokens placed in shelter in a mapping called `amountInShelter`. However, each invocation of `enterShelter` overwrites the entry for a given LP token with the freshly withdrawn amount, using a plain assignment (`amountInShelter[lpToken] = amount`). This design flaw means that if the function is called more than once for the same LP token—whether accidentally, due to a distracted admin, or deliberately by a malicious owner—the previously recorded shelter balance is lost. In the worst case, the second call may transfer a zero amount (if the wrapper holds no tokens at that moment) and consequently set `amountInShelter[lpToken]` to zero. The shelter contract later relies on `amountInShelter` to compute each user’s share during withdrawal. When the stored amount is zero, the withdrawal logic believes there are no sheltered tokens, preventing any user from reclaiming their funds. After the shelter’s grace period expires, the locked tokens become effectively irretrievable, resulting in permanent loss of user capital.

The root cause is the use of an overwriting assignment instead of an additive update or a guard that prevents re‑entering the shelter for the same token. The issue can be exploited by an attacker with owner privileges who calls `enterShelter` a second time for a token that is already under shelter, supplying a zero or otherwise incorrect amount. The exploit does not require complex calldata; a single transaction from the contract owner suffices. Once triggered, the impact is that users see their balances unchanged on the front‑end, may observe that the shelter is active but the reported total share is zero, and any attempt to withdraw results in a no‑op. From the user’s perspective, funds appear to disappear: a user expects to be able to claim a refund after the emergency period, but the UI shows a zero balance or a failed transaction, creating confusion and loss of trust.

The condition for the bug to manifest is the repeated execution of `enterShelter` on the same LP token, which can happen during routine maintenance, upgrades, or a malicious admin action. Because the contract does not emit an explicit event indicating that the shelter amount was overwritten, and because the total share is read from the same mapping, the problem may remain hidden until users attempt withdrawal.

The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the ConvexStakingWrapper code, where the reviewer noted that the mapping update used a simple assignment and that the accompanying comment in `totalShare` would return zero when the shelter is not activated, inadvertently masking the overwritten state.

Remediation involves changing the logic to accumulate the sheltered amount (`amountInShelter[lpToken] += amount`) or, alternatively, preventing the function from being called again for an already‑sheltered token. Adding proper event logging and access controls would also improve observability. By preserving the original shelter balance, the withdrawal calculation remains correct and users retain the ability to recover their funds after the grace period.

title: `USDMPegRecovery.provide
description:
The `provide` function does not take a `_steps` argument and will instead calculate `addingLiquidity` by truncating amounts under `step`. As a result, if there is an excess of `usdm` such that the truncated amount exceeds the contract’s `pool3` truncated balance, then the function will revert due to insufficient `pool3` collateral.

This will prevent guardians from effectively providing liquidity whenever tokens are available. Consider the following example:

  * The contract has `500000e18` `usdm` tokens and `250000e18` `pool3` tokens.
  * `addingLiquidity` will be calculated as `500000e18 / 250000e18 * 250000e18`.
  * The function will attempt to add `500000e18` `usdm` and `pool3` tokens in which there are insufficient `pool3` tokens in the contract. As a result, it will revert even though there is an abundance of tokens that satisfy the `step` amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a liquidity‑provision function that attempts to add equal amounts of two tokens (USDM and pool3) to a Curve pool. The function calculates the amount to be added, called addingLiquidity, by truncating the contract’s USDM balance down to the nearest multiple of a fixed step size. It then assumes that the same amount of pool3 is available, builds a two‑element array with the identical value, and calls the Curve pool’s add_liquidity method. Because the calculation only inspects the USDM balance, it completely ignores the actual pool3 balance held by the contract. When the contract holds a large surplus of USDM relative to pool3, the truncation may produce an addingLiquidity value that exceeds the pool3 token balance. In that situation the add_liquidity call reverts with an insufficient‑collateral error, even though the contract possesses enough USDM to satisfy the step amount. The root cause is a logical fallacy: the code treats the two assets as if they were always available in a 1:1 ratio and fails to validate the pool3 side of the trade. This flaw can be triggered whenever the USDM balance divided by the step size, multiplied back by the step, results in a number greater than the pool3 balance. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service for the guardian role that is authorized to provide liquidity; their transaction reverts, preventing any new liquidity from being added to the pool. Consequently, the protocol’s liquidity pool may remain under‑funded, users may experience higher slippage or reduced swap capacity, and the expected revenue from liquidity provision is lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted an inconsistency between the amount of USDM approved and the amount of pool3 actually present. It is difficult to notice because the function’s code appears to approve both tokens and there is no explicit balance check for pool3, so the revert only manifests at runtime during the Curve call. To remediate the problem, the provide function should accept a step count (or a custom amount) as an input, and it must compute the maximum addable liquidity based on the minimum of the truncated USDM balance and the actual pool3 balance after applying the same step granularity. Alternatively, the function could query both token balances, apply the step rounding to each, and ensure that the amounts array never exceeds either balance before invoking add_liquidity. This correction restores the intended business logic that liquidity can be provided whenever both tokens are available, eliminating the inadvertent reversal and allowing guardians to fulfil their role reliably.

title: `StakingRewards.recoverERC20` allows owner to rug the `rewardsToken`
description:
[StakingRewards.sol#L166](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/StakingRewards.sol#L166)  

`StakingRewards.recoverERC20` rightfully checks against the `stakingToken` being sweeped away.  
However, there’s no check against the `rewardsToken` which over time will sit in this contract.

This is the case of an admin privilege, which allows the owner to sweep the rewards tokens, perhaps as a way to rug depositors.
poc: Calling `StakingRewards.recoverERC20(rewardsToken, rewardsToken.balanceOf(this))` enables the `owner` to sweep the token.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the public recoverERC20 function of the staking rewards contract. The function is intended to allow the contract owner to rescue any ERC20 token that might have been accidentally sent to the contract, but it only checks that the token being rescued is not the staking token that users deposit. There is no analogous safeguard for the rewards token, which accumulates over time as the contract distributes incentives to stakers. Because the contract does not enforce a rule that the rewards token cannot be withdrawn, a malicious or compromised owner can invoke recoverERC20 with the address of the rewards token and an amount equal to the contract's full balance, effectively sweeping all pending reward funds. This flaw is a classic example of an unauthorized token withdrawal backdoor caused by an incomplete validation check on privileged functions. Exploitation is straightforward: the owner calls recoverERC20(rewardsToken, rewardsToken.balanceOf(this)), and the contract transfers the entire rewards pool to the owner’s address. The impact is that stakers who expect to receive periodic reward distributions will see their pending balances drop to zero, receive no payouts, and may notice that the contract no longer holds any reward tokens while their staking balances remain unchanged. The issue manifests whenever the contract holds a non‑zero rewards token balance, which is the normal operating condition for any staking rewards system. All participants who have deposited staking tokens are affected, because their entitlement to future rewards is erased without any on‑chain indication other than the missing token balance. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the author noticed that the protective require statement only compared against the staking token and omitted the rewards token. The bug can be hard to detect in runtime because the function is only callable by the owner, and there is no visible event or warning that the rewards pool has been emptied; users typically observe only the absence of expected reward payouts. The proper remediation is to extend the validation in recoverERC20 to reject any attempt to withdraw the designated rewards token, for example by adding a require statement that the token address is not equal to the rewards token address. Conceptually, the fix aligns the function with the principle that privileged recovery mechanisms must never be able to drain assets that are integral to the contract’s economic model. By preventing the owner from extracting the rewards token, the contract preserves its accounting guarantees and ensures that reward distribution behaves as advertised.

title: Deposits after the grace period should not be allowed
description:
[Shelter.sol#L34](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/Shelter.sol#L34)  
[Shelter.sol#L54](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/Shelter.sol#L54)  

Function donate in Shelter shouldn’t allow new deposits after the grace period ends, when the claim period begins.  
Otherwise, it will be possible to increase savedTokens[_token], and thus new user claim amounts will increase after some users might already have withdrawn their shares.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the donation routine of a token‑shelter contract that separates a grace (rescue) period from a subsequent claim period. The contract tracks the total amount of tokens saved for a given asset in a variable (savedTokens) and later distributes that balance to users who have previously contributed. The implementation does not enforce a time‑based restriction on the donate function, allowing anyone to add new deposits after the grace period has expired and the claim period has begun. The root cause is an absent check that compares the current block timestamp with the activation timestamp of the token plus the predefined GRACE_PERIOD. Because of this omission, an attacker can invoke donate during the claim phase, inflating savedTokens after some users may already have withdrawn their proportional shares. The inflated pool changes the arithmetic that computes each user’s claim amount, potentially granting extra tokens to later depositors or altering the distribution ratios for earlier claimers. The impact is an economic distortion: users who expect a fixed share based on the amount saved at the start of the claim period may receive a different (often larger) amount, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and undermining fairness. The issue manifests only when the contract is in the claim stage – that is, after block.timestamp exceeds activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD – and it affects all participants who rely on the claim calculation, including donors, claimers, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit that reviewed the lifecycle of the shelter contract and noticed that the donate function lacked any temporal guard. The problem can be subtle because the function appears to work normally during the grace period, and no immediate error is thrown when deposits are made later; the only symptom is an unexpected change in payout amounts, which may be attributed to normal reward variation. To remediate the flaw, the donate function should include a require statement that enforces the condition block.timestamp <= activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD, thereby preventing any new deposits once the claim period starts. This aligns the contract with the intended economic model, ensures that the savedTokens total remains immutable during settlement, and restores trust that users receive the correct share of the originally saved pool.

title: Unconstrained fee
description:
[MasterChef.sol#L86-L101](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/MasterChef.sol#L86-L101)  

Token fee in `MasterChef` can be set to more than 100%, (for example, by accident) causing all `deposit` calls to fail due to underflow on subtraction when reward is lowered by the fee, thus breaking essential mechanics. Note that after the fee has been set to any value, it cannot be undone. A token cannot be removed, added, or added the second time. Thus, mistakenly (or deliberately, maliciously) added fee that is larger than 100% will make the contract impossible to recover from not being able to use the token.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unconstrained deposit fee in the MasterChef contract that can be set to a value greater than 100 %. The root cause is the absence of any validation when an admin updates the fee parameter; the contract stores the fee as an unsigned integer and later subtracts it from the reward amount without checking for underflow. When the fee exceeds the total reward, the subtraction underflows, causing the entire deposit transaction to revert. Because the fee is stored in a permanent, admin‑only variable and the contract does not allow the token to be removed, re‑added, or the fee to be cleared, a fee greater than 100 % permanently disables deposits for that token. An attacker or a careless administrator could therefore set an excessive fee, either accidentally or maliciously, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where users are unable to deposit, earn rewards, or withdraw their staked assets. The impact is that the protocol’s core staking mechanics become inoperable for the affected token, effectively locking user funds and breaking the economic model. This condition occurs whenever the admin calls the fee‑setting function with a value above the logical maximum; it is triggered at the moment a user attempts a deposit after the fee has been set. All participants who interact with the affected token – liquidity providers, stakers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their expected reward flow is interrupted and no further deposits can be processed. The issue was discovered during a code audit that highlighted the admin privilege to adjust the fee and the lack of an upper bound check. It can be difficult to notice in routine testing because typical fee values are well within expected ranges, and the underflow only manifests when the fee surpasses the reward, a scenario that may not be exercised in standard test suites. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a maximum fee limit (e.g., 100 % expressed in the contract’s fixed‑point scale) at the point of fee assignment, optionally allow the fee to be decreased or cleared, and employ safe arithmetic checks that revert on underflow. This fix restores the intended invariant that fees never exceed the total reward, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and preventing the loss of functionality and user funds.

title: `USDMPegRecovery.sol#withdraw
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw function of the USDMPegRecovery contract, which relies exclusively on internal bookkeeping to determine a user’s entitlement while pulling the actual tokens from the contract’s on‑chain balance. The function records the total and per‑user liquidity in storage variables and, when a withdrawal is requested, it first checks that the USDM withdrawal is allowed (the unlockable flag) and then attempts to transfer the requested amount directly from the contract’s USDM and pool3 token balances. The root cause is the mismatch between the accounting state and the real token holdings after the contract’s provide() method moves the majority of the deposited assets into an external Curve pool (usdm3crv). Because the contract does not verify that its current token balances are sufficient before performing the safeTransfer calls, a withdrawal can fail with an out‑of‑gas or ERC20 transfer revert when the internal ledger still shows a positive balance but the external pool holds the funds. An attacker—or even an honest guardian—could trigger provide() to shift all assets, effectively locking user deposits; users would see their UI display a non‑zero balance yet receive no tokens, leading to a situation where funds appear to be available but are unretrievable. This scenario was uncovered during an audit test where a user deposited USDM and pool3 tokens, the guardian called provide() moving those tokens to the Curve pool, and a subsequent withdraw call from the same user consistently reverted due to insufficient contract balance. The issue is hard to notice because the internal state remains correct, hiding the liquidity shortfall until a withdrawal is attempted. The impact is that legitimate depositors may be unable to withdraw their funds, violating the protocol’s financial guarantees and potentially eroding user trust. To remediate, the contract should either (a) query the actual token balances before transferring and fallback to withdrawing liquidity from the external pool when the contract balance is insufficient, or (b) redesign the accounting model to use share tokens or vault shares that represent a claim on the pooled assets, ensuring that withdrawals can be satisfied either from on‑hand liquidity or by redeeming shares from the external pool. Implementing proper liquidity checks and a dual‑path withdrawal mechanism would align the accounting state with real asset availability and restore user confidence.

title: `USDMPegRecovery.sol#provide
bug_full: The contract USDMPegRecovery contains a logic flaw in its provide() function that can cause liquidity provision to fail unexpectedly. The function is intended to add USDM and 3pool tokens to the Curve 3pool at a 1:1 ratio, but it calculates the amount of liquidity to add (the variable addingLiquidity) using only the USDM balance of the contract, rounded down to the nearest multiple of a fixed step (250,000 tokens). It then reuses this same value for the 3pool token amount without checking whether the contract actually holds enough 3pool tokens. Because the contract’s USDM balance can be larger than its 3pool token balance, the add_liquidity call may be supplied with a 3pool amount that exceeds the available balance. When this occurs, the Curve pool contract reverts the transaction, causing the entire provide() call to fail. From a user’s perspective, attempts by the guardian to replenish liquidity result in a transaction that reverts, leaving the contract in a state where no new liquidity is added and the USDM peg recovery process stalls. This issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the calculations performed in provide() with the behavior of related functions, revealing the mismatched token handling. The bug is subtle because the function does not directly read the 3pool balance when determining the liquidity amount, so the mismatch does not surface until a specific imbalance occurs, which may be rare in normal operation. The impact is medium: it does not directly result in loss of funds, but it can prevent the contract from executing its intended recovery mechanism, effectively locking funds or causing prolonged downtime. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect token accounting” or “imbalanced liquidity provision” bugs, where assumptions about token ratios are hard‑coded rather than derived from actual balances. To fix the issue, the function should first compute the minimum of the USDM and 3pool token balances, then truncate that shared amount to the step size, ensuring both token amounts are guaranteed to be available before calling add_liquidity. This change aligns the logic with the intended 1:1 ratio and prevents revert failures caused by insufficient 3pool tokens.

title: USDM locked unless guardian remove liquidity
description:
In README.me:

 USDM deposits are locked based on the KPI’s from carrot.eth

However, USDM deposits are also locked until guardian remove liquidity because there are no mechanism to remove deposited USDM in `withdraw`.

[USDMPegRecovery.sol#L90](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/72b5216bfeaa7c52983060ebfc56e72e0aa8e3b0/contracts/USDMPegRecovery.sol#L90)  

The warden has identified Admin Privilege in that the deposit contract is controlled by the admin and liquidity LPd into the Curve Pool cannot be withdrawn by user (although code for redemption is present).

Ultimately a refactoring that transforms this contract in something similar to a Yield Bearing Vault would solve for accounting while allowing an easier time adding and removing liquidity.

Personally I’d recommend the sponsor to denominate the deposit token in the CRV_LP token to avoid issues with Single Sided Exposure, which other findings in this contest already discuss.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a smart contract that accepts deposits of USDM and is supposed to lock those deposits based on external KPI metrics. In practice, the contract also locks the funds indefinitely because the public withdraw function does not contain any logic to retrieve the deposited USDM from the Curve liquidity pool. The only entity capable of extracting liquidity from the pool is a privileged admin role, referred to as the guardian, which can call an internal function to remove the LP tokens and thereby release the underlying USDM. Consequently, a regular user who deposits USDM and later attempts to withdraw finds that their request either does nothing or reverts, leaving the balance appearing unchanged or being reduced to zero without any compensation. This situation arises because the withdraw implementation fails to redeem the LP tokens for USDM and to transfer the resulting USDM back to the caller, while the contract does contain code for redemption that is never invoked by the public interface. The root cause is a design flaw: the accounting logic and the withdrawal path are decoupled, and the only withdrawal mechanism is gated behind an admin‑only function, effectively giving the guardian exclusive control over users’ funds. The impact is that users’ assets become trapped; from a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal transaction but the balance remains unchanged, or the user receives nothing when expecting a refund. This breach of the contract’s economic assumptions violates the promise that users can retrieve their deposited USDM after the KPI conditions are met. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noted that the withdraw function lacks any calls to the LP‑to‑USDM conversion routine and that the admin role is the sole party able to invoke the liquidity removal function. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and includes a redemption function, giving a false sense of completeness, yet the public interface never exposes it. To remediate the bug, the contract should be refactored so that the withdraw entry point performs the full redemption flow: it should convert the stored Curve LP tokens back into USDM and transfer the resulting amount to the withdrawing user, or otherwise provide a permission‑less exit path. An alternative design is to remodel the contract as a yield‑bearing vault where accounting and liquidity management are transparent and not dependent on a single privileged actor. Implementing proper access control, emitting events on successful withdrawals, and adding unit tests that verify that a depositor can retrieve the exact amount of USDM will prevent the funds‑lock scenario and restore confidence in the protocol’s honesty and safety.

title: `StakingRewards.sol` `recoverERC20
bug_full: The contract includes a privileged recoverERC20 function that permits the contract owner to transfer any ERC20 token held by the contract to their own address, provided the token is not the staking token. The intended safeguard is a require statement that blocks withdrawals of the staking token, but the function fails to also block the rewards token, which is the primary asset used to pay staking rewards. This omission creates a logical flaw: a malicious or compromised owner can invoke recoverERC20 with the address of the rewards token and move an arbitrary amount of those tokens to themselves. Exploitation is straightforward – the attacker calls recoverERC20, passes the rewards token address and a chosen amount, and the safeTransfer call sends the tokens directly to the owner's address. The impact is a loss of reward funds, meaning that stakers will receive reduced or no rewards, breaking the protocol's economic guarantees and eroding user trust. The vulnerability manifests only when the owner role is exercised; it does not affect regular users directly, but any user relying on the reward distribution mechanism can suffer. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s admin functions, where the auditor noted the missing guard for the rewards token. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to protect the most obvious asset (the staking token) and the additional check for the rewards token is subtle. To remediate, the recoverERC20 function should include a require that rejects both the staking token and the rewards token, and optionally allow the caller to specify a destination address for the transfer, emitting an event that records the recipient. This change restores the intended security guarantee that no core protocol token can be withdrawn by the owner, preserving the integrity of reward accounting and preventing unauthorized fund siphoning.

title: Fee-on-transfer token donations in `Shelter` break withdrawals
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the Shelter contract when handling fee‑on‑transfer ERC‑20 tokens. The donate function records the intended transfer amount (_amount) in the internal savedTokens mapping before the actual token transfer occurs, assuming that the full amount will be received. However, fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred value as a protocol fee, causing the contract to receive less than the recorded amount. As a result, savedTokens[_token] becomes an over‑estimate of the real token balance held by the contract. When a participant later calls withdraw, the contract computes the withdrawable share using the inflated savedTokens value multiplied by the caller's share percentage. This calculation may produce an amount that exceeds the contract's actual token balance, leading to a failed transfer for the last withdrawer or an under‑payment for earlier participants. From a user perspective, a donor expects their contribution to be fully accounted for, and a beneficiary expects to receive their proportional share, but instead may see a zero payout, a reverted transaction, or a balance that appears to disappear. The issue manifests only when the donated token implements a transfer fee, which is not apparent from the standard ERC‑20 interface, making it easy to overlook during testing. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the mismatch between stored token totals and on‑chain balances. The impact is medium severity: it can cause denial‑of‑service for the final claimant, lead to inaccurate accounting, and potentially lock funds that are perceived as lost by users. To remediate, the contract should update savedTokens[_token] based on the actual amount received, for example by recording the token balance before and after the safeTransferFrom call and adding the difference, or by using a token interface that returns the net amount transferred. This ensures the internal accounting reflects the true contract balance, preserving correct share calculations and preventing unexpected transfer failures. The class of bug can be described as an "incorrect accounting of fee‑on‑transfer tokens" or a "misaligned bookkeeping for tokens with transfer taxes", which violates the core business logic that each donor's contribution is fully counted toward the pool of withdrawable assets.

title: Donated Tokens Cannot Be Recovered If A Shelter Is Deactivated
description: The shelter mechanism can be activated and deactivated on a target LP token. The owner of the `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` contract can initiate the shelter whereby LP tokens are sent to the `Shelter.sol` contract. However, if the owner decides to deactivate the shelter before the grace period has passed, all LP tokens are transferred back to the `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` contract. Donated tokens are also sent back to the contract. As a result, these tokens do not actually belong to any user and will effectively be lost in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in the interaction between the shelter mechanism of the ConvexStakingWrapper contract and the donation functionality of the Shelter contract. When the contract owner activates a shelter, LP tokens belonging to the wrapper are transferred to the Shelter contract and the amount transferred is recorded in the mapping amountInShelter. Separately, anyone can donate additional LP tokens to the shelter via the donate function, which simply increments a stored balance savedTokens and transfers the tokens to the Shelter contract, without creating a separate accounting entry for individual donors. If the owner decides to deactivate the shelter before the intended grace period has elapsed, the exitShelter function resets amountInShelter for the corresponding LP token to zero and calls shelter.deactivate, which causes the Shelter contract to send *all* LP tokens it holds back to the ConvexStakingWrapper contract. Because the donated tokens are indistinguishable from the originally shielded tokens in the contract’s balance, they are also sent back, but there is no mechanism for the wrapper to credit any user or the donor with those tokens. As a result, the donated tokens become stranded in the wrapper with no recorded owner, effectively disappearing from the system. The issue can be exploited by a malicious owner who deliberately deactivates the shelter early, thereby confiscating any contributions that were meant to be charitable or incentivized. The impact is a loss of funds for donors, a breach of the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol, and potential loss of trust in the platform. The condition under which the loss occurs is the execution of exitShelter while the Shelter contract holds an excess balance beyond amountInShelter, i.e., when donations have been made. Affected parties include token donors, protocol participants who rely on accurate balance reporting, and the wider community that expects donated assets to be safely retained. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that traced the flow of tokens through the activation and deactivation functions and observed that the donation bookkeeping does not differentiate between core and donated assets. The problem is subtle because the UI typically shows only the shelter activation state and does not expose the hidden donated balance, making the disappearance of tokens appear as a normal contract operation. To remediate, the contract should separate donated token accounting from the core shelter balance, prevent the deactivation logic from returning tokens that exceed amountInShelter, or explicitly route excess tokens to a designated owner or burn address. In any case, the fix must ensure that donated assets cannot be involuntarily reclaimed by the wrapper, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the shelter mechanism.

title: Owner can steal Concur rewards
description:
[MasterChef.sol#L78-L80](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/MasterChef.sol#L78-L80)  
[MasterChef.sol#L157-L180](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/MasterChef.sol#L157-L180)  

Owner can steal Concur rewards by adding a depositor and inflating other depositors’ assigned balance of the token within the contract. Thus, the owner-managed depositor can get most (all but one wei) of the created tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an owner‑controlled inflation of internal reward balances in a staking contract. The contract allows the contract owner to add new depositor addresses at any time, even after other participants have already deposited tokens. Because the contract’s accounting for reward allocation is based solely on a mapping of deposited balances and does not verify that the added depositor actually holds the claimed amount of the underlying token, the owner can register a malicious depositor and artificially inflate its recorded balance to an extremely large value. The reward distribution mechanism mints new reward tokens in proportion to each depositor’s recorded balance. By inflating the malicious depositor’s balance, the owner causes the vast majority of newly minted reward tokens – effectively all but a single wei – to be assigned to the owner‑controlled address. This exploitation can be carried out by an admin who triggers the add‑depositor function, sets the inflated balance, and then harvests the rewards. The impact is the theft of reward tokens that should have been earned by legitimate participants, reducing their expected returns to near zero and compromising the economic integrity of the protocol. The condition for the attack is that the contract’s owner retains the privilege to add depositors after the initial configuration and that there is no safeguard preventing the assignment of arbitrary balances without a corresponding token transfer. All participants who rely on the contract to fairly distribute rewards – including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit where the logic of the depositor‑management functions was examined. It can be difficult to notice because the inflated balance is stored in an internal mapping and no external token movement occurs, so front‑end dashboards may still show normal deposit amounts while the reward calculations are silently skewed. To remediate the issue, the contract should either prohibit the owner from adding depositors after the initial setup, make the set of approved depositors immutable, or enforce that any balance increase is backed by an actual transfer of the underlying token. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “privileged balance inflation” or “admin‑controlled accounting manipulation” bugs, where an actor with excessive rights can corrupt internal accounting to appropriate assets that should be distributed fairly among users.

title: Transfer to treasury can register as succeeded when failing in `_calcRewardIntegral`
description:
[StakingRewards.sol#L126](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/72b5216bfeaa7c52983060ebfc56e72e0aa8e3b0/contracts/StakingRewards.sol#L126)  

If the transfer of the reward token fails to the treasury (due to insufficient funds for example), the function `_calcRewardIntegral` will still update accounting and cause devastating accounting discrepancies in the contract.
poc: Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked token transfer to the treasury that is followed by accounting updates in the internal function that calculates the reward integral. The contract calls the ERC20 transfer method without verifying the returned boolean or without surrounding it with a require statement. Because some ERC20 implementations do not revert on failure but instead return false, the call can silently fail— for example when the treasury does not hold enough tokens or the token contract deliberately rejects the transfer. Despite the failed transfer, the subsequent logic in _calcRewardIntegral proceeds to update the reward accounting as if the transfer had succeeded. This mismatch creates an accounting discrepancy: the protocol records that a reward has been paid out while the treasury’s balance does not reflect the payment. An attacker or a malicious contract can exploit this by forcing a transfer failure (e.g., by draining the treasury’s token balance) and then invoking the staking reward function, causing the contract to credit future rewards based on an inflated reward integral. The impact includes over‑issuance of rewards, depletion of the treasury, and a breach of the fundamental accounting invariant that rewards paid out must be deducted from the treasury. The flaw manifests whenever the reward token does not revert on error, which is common for older or non‑standard ERC20 tokens, and when the treasury lacks sufficient balance. All participants who rely on accurate reward distribution— stakers, token holders, and protocol owners— are affected because the protocol’s promised payouts become unreliable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of token transfers and the reward‑integral calculation; the auditor noted that the transfer result was ignored, a pattern often referred to as “no safeApprove” or unchecked transfer. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error event is emitted, so the user interface may still display a successful reward claim while the underlying balances are inconsistent. From the user’s perspective, a staker may see a reward claim transaction succeed, yet receive no tokens, and later notice that the protocol’s reward rates appear unusually high or that the treasury is depleted. The bug violates the business logic that a successful reward claim must correspond to an actual token movement. The recommended remediation is to enforce a check on the transfer outcome, for example by wrapping the call in a require statement that validates the returned boolean, or by using a safe‑transfer library that reverts on false returns. Ensuring that the reward token adheres to the ERC20 standard’s revert‑on‑failure semantics or explicitly handling non‑standard tokens will restore the accounting integrity and prevent future reward‑integral mismatches.

title: Rewards distribution can be disrupted by a early user
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward accounting logic of the ConvexStakingWrapper contract. The contract maintains a cumulative reward variable called reward.integral as a uint128 and updates it with the expression reward.integral = reward.integral + uint128((d_reward * 1e20) / _supply) whenever a reward token is transferred and there is a non‑zero total supply of LP tokens. Because reward.integral is stored in a 128‑bit unsigned integer, the addition can overflow if the product (d_reward * 1e20) divided by the total supply (_supply) exceeds the maximum value representable by uint128 (2^128‑1). An attacker can trigger this situation by front‑running the pool, making a minimal deposit of exactly 1 wei of LP token, which forces _supply to equal 1, and then causing a large amount of reward token (for example 5 e18) to be transferred to the contract before any other user deposits. Under these conditions the term ((d_reward * 1e20) / _supply) becomes astronomically large (on the order of 5 e38), causing reward.integral to wrap around silently. The overflow corrupts the accounting of accrued rewards, so subsequent users receive incorrect or zero rewards even though they deposited LP tokens. In practice the pool may enter a denial‑of‑service state because the broken integral prevents proper reward distribution and may block further deposits. The issue affects all liquidity providers and the broader protocol that relies on accurate reward calculations, leading to a mismatch between expected earnings and actual payouts. It was discovered during a formal audit by the Code4rena team, who noticed that the combination of a tiny total supply and a large scaling factor (1e20) could cause the uint128 addition to overflow. The bug is hard to detect because the overflow does not revert; instead it silently wraps, making the UI appear normal while rewards disappear. To remediate, the contract should either use a 256‑bit integer for reward.integral, reduce the scaling factor to a value that guarantees the intermediate product fits in 128 bits (e.g., 1e12), or initialise the wrapper with a non‑zero synthetic total supply that prevents the denominator from ever being 1. Adding explicit overflow checks before the addition, or rejecting deposits that would cause the total supply to fall below a safe threshold, would also close the attack surface. By fixing the arithmetic precision and ensuring the denominator never becomes too small, the protocol can maintain correct reward distribution and avoid the DOS condition caused by this overflow.

title: `ConvexStakingWrapper#deposit
poc:
When `_amount` = `uint256(type(uint192).max) + 1`:

* At L235, `uint192(_amount)` = `0`, `deposits[_pid][msg.sender].amount` = `0`;
* At L241, `uint256(type(uint192).max) + 1` will be transferFrom `msg.sender`.

Expected results:

`deposits[_pid][msg.sender].amount` == `uint256(type(uint192).max) + 1`;

Actual results:

`deposits[_pid][msg.sender].amount` = `0`.

The depositor loses all their invested funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit function of the ConvexStakingWrapper contract, where the amount supplied by a user is cast from a 256‑bit unsigned integer to a 192‑bit unsigned integer without any range check. This unsafe type conversion truncates any value that exceeds the maximum representable value of uint192 (2^192‑1). Consequently, when a caller invokes deposit with an _amount larger than type(uint192).max, the contract still transfers the full token balance from the user to its own address, but the internal accounting variable deposits[_pid][msg.sender].amount stores only the lower 192 bits of the supplied value. In the worst case, the truncation yields zero, meaning the protocol records that the user has deposited nothing while actually holding the user's tokens. The root cause is the unchecked casting operation (uint192(_amount)) that silently overflows. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) can deliberately provide an amount just one unit above the uint192 ceiling; the contract will accept the transfer, record a truncated (often zero) balance, and later allow withdrawals based on the recorded balance, effectively confiscating the user's funds. The impact is a loss of deposited assets for any affected participant and a breach of the accounting invariants that the protocol relies on to calculate rewards and withdrawals. The bug manifests only when the deposit amount exceeds the uint192 limit, a scenario that may be rare in normal operation but becomes possible with tokens that have large supplies or when an adversary purposely crafts the input. All users who interact with the wrapper are potentially at risk, and the protocol’s reputation suffers because the contract’s state no longer faithfully reflects the real token holdings. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that exercised the contract with extreme input values; it is difficult to notice in routine testing because typical deposit amounts are far below the overflow threshold and the Solidity compiler does not emit a warning for the explicit cast. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce an upper bound on _amount (e.g., require(_amount <= type(uint192).max)) or, preferably, avoid down‑casting altogether by storing the amount in a uint256 or by using a safe casting library that reverts on overflow. By aligning the storage type with the input type and adding explicit validation, the accounting logic remains consistent with the actual token transfers, preventing silent loss of funds.

title: `StakingRewards.setRewardsDuration` allows setting near zero or enormous `rewardsDuration`, which breaks reward logic
description: notifyRewardAmount will be inoperable if rewardsDuration is set to zero. If will cease to produce meaningful results if rewardsDuration is too small or too big.
poc:
The setter does not control the value, allowing zero/near zero/enormous duration:

[StakingRewards.sol#L178-185](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/StakingRewards.sol#L178-185)

Division by the duration is used in notifyRewardAmount:

[StakingRewards.sol#L143-156](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/StakingRewards.sol#L143-156)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking rewards contract’s administrative function that sets the rewards duration. The function accepts an arbitrary unsigned integer and stores it in a state variable that is later used as the divisor in the reward‑rate calculation performed by the notifyRewardAmount routine. Because there is no validation of the supplied value, an administrator (or any entity that can invoke the privileged setter) can set the duration to zero, a value that is extremely close to zero, or an excessively large number. When the duration is zero, the division performed in notifyRewardAmount either reverts due to a division‑by‑zero exception or produces an undefined reward rate, rendering the reward notification mechanism inoperable. When the duration is set to a very small positive number, the computed reward rate becomes astronomically high, causing the contract to drain the allocated reward pool almost instantly. Conversely, an extremely large duration makes the reward rate negligible, so stakers receive virtually no reward despite having deposited tokens. The root cause is a missing input‑validation check on the rewardsDuration setter, allowing any value to be written to a critical accounting parameter that directly influences reward distribution logic. The bug can be exploited by an attacker who either gains control of the privileged account or compromises the admin key and then updates the duration to an inappropriate value before calling notifyRewardAmount. Under these conditions the contract either halts reward issuance, over‑pays rewards, or under‑pays rewards, breaking the economic assumptions of the staking system. All participants who rely on the contract for earned rewards—regular users, delegators, and the protocol treasury—are affected because they may see their expected payouts disappear, be inflated unexpectedly, or become zero. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the lack of bounds checking on the setter and its downstream impact on a division operation. It may be difficult to notice in normal operation because the UI typically only shows the configured duration as a number, and extreme values may not trigger visible errors until reward distribution is attempted; a zero duration often manifests as a transaction failure that can be misattributed to other causes. To remediate the problem, the setter should enforce a minimum duration greater than zero and a sensible maximum that reflects the intended reward horizon, rejecting out‑of‑range inputs with a clear revert message. Additionally, emitting an event when the duration changes can aid monitoring. Conceptually this class of bug is a parameter‑validation flaw that leads to arithmetic errors such as division by zero or extreme rate calculations, breaking the contract’s accounting guarantees and resulting in missing or incorrectly sized reward payouts for users.

title: `MasterChef.sol` A `depositor` can deposit an arbitrary amount without no cost
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the role‑based deposit mechanism of the MasterChef contract. The contract owner can designate any address as a "depositor" through the addDepositor() function, which merely writes the address into a mapping without any additional validation or constraints. Once an address is marked as a depositor, the deposit() function can be called by that address with an arbitrary _amount parameter. The function does not require the caller to transfer any tokens, nor does it enforce any maximum deposit size, fee verification beyond the optional depositFeeBP, or balance checks against the underlying token contract. Consequently, a malicious or compromised depositor can invoke deposit() with an extremely large amount, inflate its internal user.amount balance, and thereby capture an overwhelming share of the pool's accConcurPerShare value. Because pending rewards are calculated as user.amount multiplied by the pool’s accumulated per‑share metric, the inflated balance leads to the attacker receiving nearly 100 % of all future reward distributions, effectively draining the reward pool from honest participants. This exploit becomes possible when the owner adds a malicious address as a depositor or when the depositor role is compromised; it does not depend on any external token transfer, making it difficult to notice in normal operation. From a user’s perspective, funds that were expected to be distributed proportionally appear to vanish: users may see their pending rewards drop to zero, their balances remain unchanged while the pool’s reward token accrues to a single address, and the UI may show that a deposit was made but no corresponding token movement occurred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined role privileges and deposit logic, highlighting that the depositor role grants unchecked authority over reward accounting. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted amount injection” and “missing source‑of‑value verification” vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts an internal accounting entry without confirming the underlying economic transfer. To remediate, the depositor role should be eliminated or tightly constrained, the deposit function must enforce that the caller actually transfers the specified amount of the underlying token (e.g., by pulling tokens via ERC20 transferFrom), and reasonable caps or validation checks should be introduced to prevent excessively large deposits that could distort reward calculations. Additionally, the contract could limit the number of depositor addresses to a trusted single contract, implement role‑based access control with multi‑sig governance, and ensure that reward distribution logic accounts for potential abuse scenarios.

title: During stake or deposit, users would not be rewarded the correct Concur token, when MasterChef has under-supply of it
description:
During stake or deposit, users would not be transferred the correct Concur token, when MasterChef has under-supply of it.

There is an assumption that MasterChef contract would own enough Concur tokens so as to distribute to users as reward, during deposit or withdraw. But say, due to excess user activity, MasterChef runs out of Concur tokens. All deposits & withdraws that happen after that, would have zero transfer of Concur token to the user. This will continue until the MasterChef contract is replenished again.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked assumption that the MasterChef contract always holds enough Concur tokens to fulfil reward payouts during staking, deposit or withdrawal operations. The contract’s internal helper safeConcurTransfer reads the token balance but never verifies that the amount to be transferred is actually available; when the balance is zero or lower than the requested reward, the function simply executes a transfer of zero tokens without reverting or emitting an error. As a result, any user action that triggers a reward distribution after the MasterChef’s token reserve has been exhausted will silently credit the user with no Concur tokens, even though the protocol’s business logic promises a reward. This mismatch between expected and actual behavior can be observed from the user’s perspective as a missing or zero‑value reward: a staker may see that their transaction succeeded, their balance on the UI updates to reflect the deposited amount, yet the reward balance remains unchanged or is reduced unexpectedly, leading to confusion and the perception that the protocol is not paying out. The flaw becomes exploitable when an attacker, or even regular high‑volume activity, drains the token reserve—by triggering many deposits, withdrawals, or reward claims—so that the contract’s balance falls below the amount needed for subsequent payouts. Subsequent legitimate users will then receive no tokens, effectively losing yield without any on‑chain indication that an error occurred. The impact is a loss of expected earnings for users, erosion of trust in the protocol’s incentive mechanism, and potential financial damage if large numbers of participants are affected. The condition under which the issue manifests is simply a zero or insufficient token balance in the MasterChef contract at the time reward distribution is attempted. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a unit test demonstrated that after depleting the contract’s token balance, safeConcurTransfer emitted no error and transferred nothing. The difficulty in noticing this bug stems from the fact that the transaction does not revert; it appears successful and therefore does not raise an exception that would alert developers or users. To remediate the issue, the safeConcurTransfer routine should enforce a pre‑condition that the contract’s Concur balance is greater than zero (or at least greater than or equal to the amount to be transferred) and revert with a clear error message when the condition is not met. This change restores the invariant that rewards are only dispensed when the contract actually possesses sufficient tokens, preserving the economic guarantees of the protocol and aligning the on‑chain execution with user expectations of receiving a reward.

title: Owner can lock tokens in `MasterChef`
description:
[MasterChef.sol#L82-L84](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/MasterChef.sol#L82-L84)  

Owner can remove a depositor. Since only depositors can deposit and withdraw, the owner may add a contract to the whitelist, let users deposit in the contract and remove the depositor from the whitelist. Depositor’s reward cannot be withdrawn then. And takes a share of Concur tokens that will not be distributed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the access‑control logic of the MasterChef contract, where withdrawal of deposited tokens and accrued rewards is gated by an onlyDepositor modifier that checks a whitelist maintained by the contract owner. Because the owner retains the ability to add or remove addresses from this whitelist, a malicious or compromised owner can deliberately remove a legitimate depositor after users have already deposited funds. Once an address is removed, the onlyDepositor check fails, preventing the affected account from calling the withdraw function. As a result, the deposited principal remains locked inside the contract and any pending Concur token rewards are never distributed, effectively stealing a share of the protocol's token emissions. The issue occurs whenever the owner exercises the removeDepositor function after deposits have been made, and it impacts every user who relied on the whitelist entry to retrieve their assets. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s permission model, where the relationship between the whitelist and the withdraw path was examined. The problem may be hard to notice because the whitelist appears to be a simple administrative list and the withdraw function itself contains no obvious restriction on the caller besides the modifier, leading reviewers to assume that whitelisted entries are static or benign. To remediate the defect, the contract should either eliminate the onlyDepositor check from the withdraw function, replace it with a per‑account deposit record that allows any address that has a positive balance to withdraw, or make the depositor list immutable or governed by a multi‑signature process to prevent unilateral owner interference. In generic terms, this is an access‑control misconfiguration that enables a denial‑of‑service style attack on fund retrieval, breaking the business expectation that users can always withdraw their deposits and earn rewards, and instead causing user balances to appear unchanged while rewards become inaccessible.

title: Rewards get diluted because `totalAllocPoint` can only increase.
description:
[MasterChef.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/MasterChef.sol)  

There is no functionality for removing pools/setting pool’s allocPoints. Therefore `totalAllocPoint` only increases and rewards for pool decreases.
poc:
Scenario:

1. Owner adds new pool (first pool) for staking with points = 900 (totalAllocPoint=900).
2. 1 week passes.
3. First pool staking period ends (or for other reasons that pool is not meaningfully anymore).
4. Owner adds new pool (second pool) for staking with points = 100 (totalAllocPoint=1000).
5. 1 block later Alice stake 10 tokens there (at the same time).
6. 1 week passes.
7. After some time Alice claims rewards. But she is eligible only for 10% of the rewards. 90% goes to unused pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the MasterChef contract tracks reward distribution across staking pools. The contract maintains a global variable called totalAllocPoint, which represents the sum of allocation points assigned to every pool. Allocation points determine each pool's share of the overall reward emission. Because the contract does not provide any mechanism to remove a pool or to decrease a pool's allocation points after it has been created, totalAllocPoint can only increase over the lifetime of the contract. When a new pool is added, its allocation points are added to totalAllocPoint, and the relative share of every existing pool is automatically reduced. This design flaw creates a reward‑dilution effect: users who stake in an older pool continue to receive rewards proportional to the new, larger totalAllocPoint, meaning they receive a smaller fraction of the total rewards than they originally expected. In practice, an owner can add a new pool with a small number of allocation points after an existing pool becomes inactive; the inactive pool’s allocation points remain counted in totalAllocPoint, causing the active pool’s reward share to shrink dramatically. For example, if the first pool is created with 900 points (totalAllocPoint = 900) and later a second pool with 100 points is added (totalAllocPoint = 1000), a user staking in the first pool will only be entitled to 10 % of the rewards while 90 % is effectively allocated to the second pool, which may never be used. From a user’s perspective this appears as a sudden drop in expected yields – the UI may still show that the contract is emitting the same total amount of reward tokens, but the individual pool’s reward balance becomes far lower, leading to “funds disappear” or “my rewards are missing” symptoms. The issue was identified during an audit by analyzing the accounting logic of the contract and observing that the totalAllocPoint variable is immutable upwards, which violates the fundamental assumption that allocation points should reflect only active pools. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an error; the total reward emission remains correct, yet the distribution is skewed, making it hard to notice without drilling into per‑pool accounting. To remediate the issue, the contract should include functionality for the owner or governance to either remove a pool or adjust its allocation points, thereby allowing totalAllocPoint to be decreased when a pool is retired. Such a change would restore the intended proportional reward calculation and prevent long‑term dilution of existing stakers’ earnings.

title: Deactivate function can be bypassed
description: onlyClient can deactivate a token even after deadline is passed and transfer all token balance to itself.
poc:
1. Navigate to contract [Shelter.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/Shelter.sol)
2. Observe that token can only be deactivated if activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD > block.timestamp. We will bypass this
3. onlyClient activates a token X using the activate function
