4. Assume Grace period is crossed such that activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD < block.timestamp
5. Now if onlyClient calls deactivate function, it fails with “too late”
6. But onlyClient can bypass this by calling activate function again on token X which will reset the timestamp to latest in activated[_token] and hence onlyClient can now call deactivate function to disable the token and retrieve all funds present in the contract to his own address
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the token‑sheltering contract that allows a privileged client to bypass the intended grace‑period deadline for deactivating a token and withdraw the entire token balance to its own address. The contract records the timestamp of the last activation of a token in a mapping called activated and only permits deactivation while activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD is greater than the current block timestamp. However, the activate function can be called repeatedly by the same client; each call overwrites the stored timestamp with the current block time. As a result, after the original grace period has elapsed, the client can simply invoke activate again, which resets the activation timestamp, thereby extending the window during which deactivate will succeed. The client then calls deactivate and triggers the transfer of all tokens that were held for other users back to itself, effectively rugging the protocol. The impact is that any user who deposited tokens into the shelter expects their assets to be secured for the duration of the grace period, but instead sees their balance disappear, receiving no refunds or withdrawals. This condition occurs only when the caller possesses the onlyClient role, which is assumed to be trustworthy, and when the contract does not enforce a one‑time activation check. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Code4rena team, which derived a proof‑of‑concept that steps through activation, waiting for the grace period to expire, re‑activating to reset the timestamp, and finally deactivating to extract the funds. The flaw can be hard to notice because the deactivate function correctly validates the deadline against the stored timestamp, giving the appearance of a sound time‑based restriction, while the ability to overwrite that timestamp is hidden in the activate function’s lack of guard against repeated calls. Conceptually, the fix is to make activation a one‑time operation per token, for example by requiring that activated[_token] be zero before allowing a new activation, or by storing an immutable activation flag that prevents the timestamp from being reset after the first activation. By doing so, the contract would preserve the intended accounting invariant that funds remain locked until the grace period ends, preventing the client from re‑setting the deadline and extracting other users’ deposits.

title: Users Will Lose Concur Rewards If The Shelter Mechanism Is Enacted On A Pool
description:
The shelter mechanism aims to protect the protocol’s users by draining funds into a separate contract in the event of an emergency. However, while users are able to reclaim their funds through the `Shelter.sol` contract, they will still have a deposited balance from the perspective of `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol`.

However, if the shelter mechanism is enacted before users are able to claim their Concur rewards, any accrued tokens will be lost and the `MasterChef.sol` contract will continue to allocate tokens to the sheltered pool which will be forever locked within this contract.

There is currently no way to remove sheltered pools from the `MasterChef.sol` contract, hence any balance lost in the contract cannot be recovered due to a lack of a sweep mechanism which can be called by the contract owner.
poc:
[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol)  

[MasterChef.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/MasterChef.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the interaction between the emergency shelter mechanism and the reward distribution logic of the protocol. When an administrator triggers the shelter on a pool, funds are transferred to a separate Shelter.sol contract to protect user deposits. While users can later withdraw their original principal through the shelter, the protocol’s reward accounting—implemented in MasterChef.sol—continues to calculate and allocate Concur token rewards to the now‑sheltered pool. Because ConvexStakingWrapper.sol still registers the pool as having a deposited balance, the MasterChef contract believes the pool is active and keeps minting rewards based on its internal accounting. However, the shelter contract provides no interface to claim or sweep these newly minted tokens, and there is no function for the owner to remove a sheltered pool from the MasterChef’s poolInfo list. As a result, any rewards that accrue after the shelter is enacted become permanently locked inside the MasterChef contract, effectively disappearing from the users’ perspective. This loss occurs only when the shelter is activated before users have harvested their pending Concur rewards; if users had already harvested, the already‑claimed tokens would be safe. The impact is a loss of yield for every depositor of the affected pool: users see their deposited balance unchanged, but the expected reward balance remains zero, leading to a mismatch between the protocol’s accounting assumptions and the actual funds users can retrieve. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the emergency flow and noticed that the reward distribution did not account for pools being moved to the shelter. It is subtle because the shelter appears to safeguard principal, so the missing rewards may not be immediately obvious—especially when the UI only shows the principal amount and not the hidden reward accrual. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that any pool transferred to the shelter is also removed from the MasterChef’s reward distribution list, preferably after calling massUpdatePools to settle pending rewards. Additionally, the pid calculation should be decoupled from the length of the poolInfo array to avoid gaps, and a sweep or emergency withdrawal function should be added to allow the owner to retrieve or re‑allocate unclaimed rewards from a sheltered pool. By aligning the emergency protection mechanism with the reward accounting, the protocol can prevent permanent reward loss and preserve both principal and earned yield for users.

title: Rogue pool in Shelter
description:
[Shelter.sol#L38-L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/72b5216bfeaa7c52983060ebfc56e72e0aa8e3b0/contracts/Shelter.sol#L38-L42)  

Shelter contract can steal user tokens.
poc:
Shelter `client` can call `activate` on an already activated token, this will reset its start time, so if the client activate a token when it `GRACE_PERIOD` is almost finished, it will reset this time.  
This will prevent the user to call `withdraw` because the condition `activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD < block.timestamp` but will allow the client to call `deactivate` and receive all funds from the users because it will satisfy the condition `activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD > block.timestamp`.

Steps:

* client `activate` tokenA.
* Users deposit tokenA using `donate`.
* client `activate` tokenA again until they has enough tokens.
* More users use `donate`.
* client deactivate tokenA and receive all tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the Shelter contract that allows a privileged client to repeatedly invoke the activate function on a token that has already been activated. Each call overwrites the stored activation timestamp, effectively resetting the start of the grace period. Because withdrawal is only permitted after the expression activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD is less than the current block timestamp, an attacker can keep extending the grace period by re‑activating the token just before it would expire. This prevents honest users from calling withdraw, while the same condition in the deactivate function (activated[_token] + GRACE_PERIOD > block.timestamp) remains true, enabling the attacker to call deactivate and drain all tokens that were deposited through the donate function. The issue manifests when a malicious admin repeatedly activates a token after users have deposited, then deactivates to collect the funds. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful deposit but later the user would see no ability to claim the funds and the balance would appear unchanged or disappear after the attacker’s deactivation. The root cause is the lack of a guard against multiple activations and an asymmetric time check that treats activation and deactivation differently, breaking the intended accounting model where funds are locked for a fixed grace period before becoming withdrawable. The bug was uncovered during an audit when the warden demonstrated a concrete exploit sequence: activate token, users donate, activate again many times, more users donate, then deactivate to capture all tokens. It is hard to notice because the contract’s interface does not explicitly forbid re‑activation, and the timestamp update appears benign. To remediate, the contract should enforce a single activation per token, reject subsequent activate calls, allow deactivation only after the grace period has elapsed, and ensure that both withdraw and deactivate functions use consistent time‑based conditions. By correcting the state‑transition logic, the protocol can preserve user deposits and uphold the promised escrow behaviour.

title: `MasterChef.updatePool
description:
The `updatePool` function intends to calculate the accumulated Concur rewards by tracking the number of blocks passed since the last update to correctly determine how many Concur tokens to distribute to each share. The reward distribution has a start and end block which dictates the timeframe by which rewards will be distributed to the underlying pool.

If a pool has not recently updated itself and has reached the `block.number >= endBlock` statement in `updatePool`, then any rewards that it would normally be entitled to prior to reaching `endBlock` will not be attributed to the pool. Therefore, once rewards are no longer being distributed, pools who had not recently called `updatePool` before reaching `endBlock` are at a disadvantage as compared to more active pools.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑accrual logic of the MasterChef contract’s updatePool function. The function is responsible for calculating how many Concur tokens each share in a liquidity pool should receive by counting the number of blocks that have passed since the pool’s lastRewardBlock. When the current block number reaches or exceeds the predefined endBlock, the function immediately returns after setting lastRewardBlock to the current block, without first calculating the pending rewards for the interval between the previous lastRewardBlock and the endBlock. This early exit condition (block.number >= endBlock) therefore truncates the reward accounting for any pool that has not been updated shortly before the end of the reward period. The root cause is a logical oversight: the contract assumes that no further rewards need to be accrued after the endBlock, but it fails to account for the last portion of rewards that should be credited up to the endBlock itself. An attacker or simply an inactive participant can exploit this by allowing a pool to become "stale" – i.e., not calling updatePool for a prolonged period – and then the contract will silently skip the reward calculation for the final blocks. Consequently, depositors in that pool receive fewer Concur tokens than the protocol’s economic model promises, effectively losing yield. The impact manifests as missing or reduced reward balances; from a user’s perspective, a harvest transaction yields zero or unexpectedly low tokens, contradicting the expectation that rewards continue to accumulate until the endBlock. This issue occurs only when a pool’s lastRewardBlock is earlier than endBlock and no updatePool call is made before the block number crosses the endBlock threshold. All participants who rely on the contract’s automatic distribution – typically passive LP providers – are affected, as their financial incentives are diminished. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the early‑return path was identified as bypassing the reward calculation. It can be difficult to notice because the function still updates lastRewardBlock, giving the impression that state has progressed correctly, while the critical accConcurPerShare variable remains unchanged for the final reward interval. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the multiplier and pending rewards up to endBlock before returning, ensuring that pool.accConcurPerShare is increased by the exact amount of rewards earned between the previous lastRewardBlock and endBlock, and then set lastRewardBlock to endBlock. This adjustment aligns the implementation with the intended reward distribution schedule and prevents stale pools from being disadvantaged.

title: [ConcurRewardPool] Possible reentrancy when claiming rewards
description:
[ConcurRewardPool.sol#L34](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/ConcurRewardPool.sol#L34)  

Since the reward tokens are transferred before the balances are set to 0, it is possible to perform a reentrancy attack if the reward token has some kind of call back functionality e.g. ERC777. pBTC is an ERC777 token that is currently available on Convex. A similar attack occurred with [imBTC on uniswap v1](https://zengo.com/imbtc-defi-hack-explained/).
poc:
* Preparation

    1. Assume that pBTC is used as extra rewards for this victim convex pool.
    2. A malicious user interacts with Concur through a smart contract. He follows the standard flow and has some rewards to be claimed.
    3. The malicious user interacts with this smart contract to register a bad `tokensToSend()` callback function through the ERC-1820 contract.
    4. In this `tokensToSend()` function, he calls `ConcurRewardPool.claimRewards()` n-1 more times to drain contract.
* Attack

    1. When he calls `ConcurRewardPool.claimRewards()` for the first time, the pBTC reward tokens are transferred.
    2. You can see from the [pBTC contract](https://etherscan.io/address/0x5228a22e72ccc52d415ecfd199f99d0665e7733b#code) on line 871 that `_callTokensToSend(from, from, recipient, amount, "", "");` is called inside the `transfer()` function.
    3. If you trace to the `_callTokensToSend` function definition to line 1147, you will notice that it calls `IERC777Sender(implementer).tokensToSend(operator, from, to, amount, userData, operatorData);` on line 1159.
    4. Since the malicious user already registered a bad `tokensToSend()` function, this function will be called thus draining majority of the pBTC rewards available on the `ConcurRewardPool` contract.

You can also find a walkthrough replicating a similar attack [here](https://medium.com/amber-group/preventing-re-entrancy-attacks-lessons-from-history-c2d96480fac3).
bug_full: The ConcurRewardPool contract contains a reentrancy vulnerability in its claimRewards function. The function transfers reward tokens to the caller before resetting the caller's reward balance to zero. Because the transfer is performed using the ERC20 transfer interface, it can invoke external logic if the token implements the ERC777 standard, which includes a tokensToSend hook defined in ERC1820. An attacker can register a malicious ERC777 sender contract that implements tokensToSend and, during the token transfer, this hook is called. Inside the malicious tokensToSend implementation the attacker can recursively call claimRewards again before the original call has cleared the balance. Since the balance is still non‑zero, each re‑entrant call can withdraw the same amount of rewards, allowing the attacker to drain most or all of the reward pool. The issue occurs only when a reward token that supports ERC777 callbacks (for example pBTC) is used, but the bug is present in the pool logic regardless of token type. Users who try to claim rewards may see their expected payout reduced to zero or notice that the pool's reward balance suddenly drops, while the attacker ends up receiving the stolen tokens. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order of operations and tested the claimRewards path with an ERC777 token that triggers the callback. It is difficult to notice because standard ERC20 tokens do not execute callbacks, so normal testing with typical tokens will not reveal the reentrancy. The flaw belongs to the class of reentrancy bugs caused by making an external call (the token transfer) before updating internal state (the reward balance), violating the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. To remediate, the contract should first set the claimant's reward balance to zero (or use a pull‑based accounting model) and then transfer the tokens, and additionally protect the function with a nonReentrant guard to block recursive entry. This fix restores the expected accounting behavior: users claim their earned rewards once, the pool balance reflects the actual remaining rewards, and no malicious token can trigger additional calls during the transfer. The vulnerability compromises the reward distribution mechanism, potentially causing loss of earned incentives for honest participants and undermining confidence in the protocol's fairness.

title: If The Staking Token Exists In Both `StakingRewards.sol` And `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` Then It Will Be Possible To Continue Claiming Concur Rewards After The Shelter Has Been Activated
description:
Staking tokens are used to deposit into the `StakingRewards.sol` and `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` contracts. Once deposited, the user is entitled to Concur rewards in proportion to their staked balance and the underlying pool’s `allocPoint` in the `MasterChef.sol` contract.

The `Shelter.sol` mechanism allows the owner of the `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` to react to emergency events and protect depositor’s assets. The staking tokens can be withdrawn after the grace period has passed. However, these staking tokens can be deposited into the `StakingRewards.sol` contract to continue receiving Concur rewards not only for `StakingRewards.sol` but also for their `ConvexStakingWrapper.sol` deposited balance which has not been wiped. As a result, users are able to effectively claim double the amount of Concur rewards they should be receiving.
poc:
[MasterChef.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/MasterChef.sol)  

[StakingRewards.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/StakingRewards.sol)  

[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/shelter-client/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an accounting flaw that allows a user’s staking tokens to be counted twice for reward distribution when the emergency shelter mechanism of the ConvexStakingWrapper contract is activated. When the contract owner triggers the shelter, the wrapper’s internal state blocks withdrawals for a grace period but does not reset the user’s staked balance in the MasterChef contract that tracks reward allocations. Because the same ERC‑20 staking token can still be deposited into the separate StakingRewards contract, the protocol continues to calculate Concur rewards for the user’s balance in both the StakingRewards contract and the unchanged balance recorded in the MasterChef contract for the wrapper. An attacker can therefore deposit the same tokens into StakingRewards after shelter activation and claim rewards from both sources, effectively receiving double the amount of Concur rewards that the economic model expects. This double counting does not affect the principal amount locked in the wrapper, but it inflates the total reward payout, reducing the protocol’s overall reward pool and potentially harming other participants. The issue is only observable when the shelter is used and when the StakingRewards contract holds a sufficient reward balance to make the extra claim noticeable; otherwise the excess reward may appear as a subtle discrepancy in accounting reports. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the wardens examined the shelter’s interaction with MasterChef and identified that the user’s balance was never cleared, allowing further reward extraction. The problem is difficult to spot because normal operation shows correct reward accrual, and the double reward only emerges under the specific emergency flow, which many test suites do not exercise. To remediate, the protocol should either prevent the same staking token from being deposited into both contracts simultaneously, or explicitly zero‑out the user’s balance in the MasterChef contract when shelter is invoked, ensuring that no rewards can be claimed from the wrapper after an emergency. This change restores the intended one‑way reward accounting and eliminates the possibility of receiving more Concur rewards than entitled.

title: `ConvexStakingWrapper` deposits and withdraws will frequently be disabled if a token that doesn’t allow zero value transfers will be added as a reward one
description:
```solidity
If deposits and withdraws are done frequently enough, the reward update operation they invoke will deal mostly with the case when there is nothing to add yet, i.e. `reward.remaining` match the reward token balance.

If reward token doesn’t allow for zero value transfers, the reward update function will fail on an empty incremental reward transfer, which is now done unconditionally, reverting the caller deposit/withdrawal functionality
```
poc:
When ConvexStakingWrapper isn’t paused, every deposit and withdraw update current rewards via `_checkpoint` function before proceeding:

[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L233](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L233)  

[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L260](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L260)  

`_checkpoint` calls `_calcRewardIntegral` for each of the reward tokens of the pid:

[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L220](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L220)  

`_calcRewardIntegral` updates the incremental reward for the token, running the logic even if reward is zero, which is frequently the case:

[ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L182](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur/blob/main/contracts/ConvexStakingWrapper.sol#L182)  

If the reward token doesn’t allow zero value transfers, this transfer will fail, reverting the corresponding deposit or withdraw.
bug_full: The ConvexStakingWrapper contract updates reward balances on every deposit or withdraw by invoking an internal checkpoint routine. During this routine the contract calculates an incremental reward amount (d_reward) for each reward token and then unconditionally calls the ERC‑20 transfer function to move d_reward tokens to a separate claim contract. For standard ERC‑20 tokens a transfer of zero tokens is a no‑op, but some reward tokens deliberately revert when the amount is zero. Because the code does not first verify that d_reward is greater than zero, a zero‑value transfer triggers a revert, causing the whole deposit or withdraw transaction to fail. This failure manifests as deposits and withdrawals being frequently disabled whenever the reward token being added does not support zero‑value transfers, even though the underlying accounting shows no new reward to distribute. The root cause is the unconditional transfer statement in the reward‑update logic, which assumes all ERC‑20 implementations tolerate zero transfers. The vulnerability is exploitable simply by interacting with the wrapper in the normal usage pattern: a user who makes a deposit that results in no pending reward will have the transaction reverted, receiving no confirmation and no token balance change, effectively locking them out of the staking pool. The impact is that legitimate users cannot add or remove liquidity, their expected balances appear unchanged, and the protocol may lose confidence because the staking interface appears broken. The condition under which this occurs is frequent deposits/withdrawals when the incremental reward for a given token is zero and the token’s transfer function reverts on a zero amount. All participants who rely on the wrapper – stakers, liquidity providers, and the broader protocol that aggregates rewards – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the _checkpoint and _calcRewardIntegral functions and noted the unconditional IERC20.transfer call. It can be hard to detect because most ERC‑20 tokens silently accept zero‑value transfers, so standard unit tests may not surface the problem unless a non‑standard token is used. To remediate, the contract should guard the transfer with a condition that checks d_reward > 0 before calling transfer, or alternatively redesign the reward accounting to store claimable amounts and only execute transfers when a positive amount is available. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards are only distributed when there is something to distribute, preventing unnecessary reverts and ensuring that deposits and withdrawals function as users expect.

title: Approve race condition in FETH
description:
```solidity
[FETH.sol#L212](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-foundation/blob/4d8c8931baffae31c7506872bf1100e1598f2754/contracts/FETH.sol#L212)  

Front running attack in approve.
```
poc:
The contract of the `FETH` does not have any protection against the well-known “Multiple Withdrawal Attack” attack on the Approve/TransferFrom methods of the ERC20 standard.

Although this attack poses a limited risk in specific situations, it is worth mentioning to consider it for possible future operations.

There are solutions to mitigate this front running such as, to first reduce the spender’s allowance to 0 and set the desired value afterwards; another solution could the one that Open Zeppelin offers, where the non-standard decreaseAllowance and increaseAllowance functions have been added to mitigate the well-known issues involving setting allowances.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a classic ERC20 allowance race condition that manifests in the FETH token contract’s approve function. Because the contract does not enforce any checks when an allowance is changed, an attacker who observes a transaction that calls approve can front‑run that transaction, transfer the spender’s current allowance before it is reduced, and then allow the new allowance to be set, effectively enabling a double withdrawal. The root cause is the lack of a safe allowance‑update pattern – the contract permits a direct call to approve without first setting the allowance to zero or using increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance helpers. Exploitation requires a malicious actor to monitor pending approve transactions, submit a TransferFrom call that consumes the existing allowance in the same block, and then let the original approve transaction proceed, resulting in the spender gaining more tokens than intended. The impact is the unauthorized loss of token balances for any user who grants an allowance to a third party, potentially causing funds to disappear from the user’s wallet. This condition can occur whenever a token holder updates an allowance to a non‑zero value while the spender is potentially malicious or compromised, and it is especially risky in environments with high transaction mempool visibility. The affected parties are token holders, the Foundation protocol that relies on the FETH token, and any external contracts that may be authorized via approve. The issue was identified during a formal security audit that examined standard ERC20 functions and looked for known patterns such as the “multiple withdrawal attack”. Because the behavior only diverges from expectations when a malicious spender acts in the narrow time window between allowance changes, it can be difficult to notice during normal operation – balances may appear correct until a front‑run transaction triggers an unexpected transfer. To remediate, the contract should adopt the recommended allowance‑change pattern: either require the allowance to be set to zero before a new value is written, or provide non‑standard increaseAllowance and decreaseAllowance functions that adjust the allowance atomically, thereby eliminating the race window. This aligns with best practices for ERC20 tokens and prevents the front‑running scenario that currently allows an attacker to steal funds after a user attempts to grant permission, violating the token’s accounting assumptions that a given allowance corresponds to a single, bounded transfer.

title: `StakingRewards` reward rate can be dragged out and diluted
poc:
Imagine the current rewardRate is `1000 rewards / rewardsDuration`.  
20% of the `rewardsDuration` passed, i.e., `now = lastUpdateTime + 20% * rewardsDuration`.  
A malicious actor notifies the contract with a reward of `0`: `notifyRewardAmount(0)`.  
Then the new `rewardRate = (reward + leftover) / rewardsDuration = (0 + 800) / rewardsDuration = 800 / rewardsDuration`.  
The `rewardRate` just dropped by 20%.  
This can be repeated infinitely.  
After another 20% of reward time passed, they trigger `notifyRewardAmount(0)` to reduce it by another 20% again:  
`rewardRate = (0 + 640) / rewardsDuration = 640 / rewardsDuration`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the StakingRewards contract recalculates the reward distribution when the notifyRewardAmount function is called. The function accepts a new reward amount, extends the current reward period by adding the configured rewardsDuration to the current block timestamp, and then recomputes the rewardRate by dividing the sum of the newly supplied reward and any leftover rewards by the full rewardsDuration. Because the implementation does not enforce that the resulting rewardRate must be equal to or greater than the previous rate, an attacker with permission to invoke notifyRewardAmount can deliberately supply a reward value of zero. When this call is made after a portion of the original reward period has elapsed, the leftover value is smaller than the initial allocation, causing the newly calculated rewardRate to be lower than before. By repeating this operation after each successive interval, the attacker can continuously shrink the rewardRate, effectively dragging the reward distribution out indefinitely while keeping the periodFinish time moving forward. The impact is a gradual dilution of the expected yield for every participant that has staked tokens: users who expect a certain return see their accrued rewards grow more slowly, and in the worst case the reward may become negligible, resulting in a loss of yield that was originally promised by the protocol. This situation occurs whenever the contract grants an admin (or any privileged account) the ability to call notifyRewardAmount without a safeguard that prevents the rewardRate from decreasing. Stakeholders affected include all token holders who have deposited into the staking pool, as well as the protocol’s reputation for delivering promised returns. The issue was identified during a code audit where the logic of notifyRewardAmount was examined and a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated that calling the function with a zero reward after 20 % of the original period had elapsed reduced the rewardRate by exactly 20 %. Repeating the call further reduced the rate, confirming that the mechanism can be abused indefinitely. The bug is subtle because the contract continues to emit rewards and the UI may still show an active reward period, making the reduction of the reward rate easy to miss; users only notice that the amount of tokens they receive over time is lower than expected. To mitigate the problem, the contract should guarantee that rewardRate never decreases: either by keeping periodFinish unchanged and only increasing rewardRate when new rewards are added, by adding a require statement that the new rate is not lower than the existing one, or by redesigning the reward accounting so that additional rewards are added on top of the existing schedule without resetting the timeline. Limiting the notifyRewardAmount function to a trusted, non‑malicious entity or adding multi‑signature controls would also reduce the attack surface. In essence, the flaw belongs to the class of reward‑schedule manipulation bugs where improper recalculation of distribution parameters allows an adversary to dilute or extend payouts, breaching the economic assumptions of the staking protocol.

title: execute in VoteProxy should be payable
description:
```solidity
`execute` will revert when `msg.value > 0`
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a governance proxy contract that provides an `execute` function intended to forward arbitrary calls, optionally with ether, to a target address. The function accepts a `_value` argument and uses low‑level `call{value: _value}` to transfer the supplied amount, but it lacks the `payable` mutability specifier. Because Solidity rejects any transaction that supplies non‑zero ether to a non‑payable function, any attempt to invoke `execute` with `msg.value > 0` will cause the whole call to revert before the internal forwarding logic runs. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended behavior (acting as a payable proxy) and the function’s declaration, which does not permit receiving ether. Exploitation does not require sophisticated tooling; a user simply calls `execute` with a non‑zero value, either intentionally to forward funds or inadvertently by sending ether along with the transaction. When this occurs, the transaction reverts, the forwarded call never executes, and any expected state changes or fund transfers are aborted. From a functional perspective, this means that proposals or administrative actions that rely on moving ether through the proxy cannot succeed, leading to a broken governance flow. Users observing the UI may see that their transaction fails with a generic revert message, that no funds are transferred, or that a proposal that should have executed remains pending. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noticed the absence of the `payable` keyword despite the presence of a value‑forwarding call. The bug can be subtle because the function compiles without warnings and the call pattern appears correct; only when a non‑zero ether amount is supplied does the revert surface. To remediate, the function should be marked as `payable`, allowing it to accept ether and forward it as intended. Conceptually, the fix aligns the function’s signature with its purpose as a value‑forwarding proxy, restoring the expected business logic that funds can be moved through the governance contract. This class of problem falls under "missing payable modifier" or "incorrect function mutability", a common source of runtime reverts that break financial flows in smart contracts.

title: EIP-712 signatures can be re-used in private sales
description:
```solidity
[NFTMarketPrivateSale.sol#L123-L174](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-foundation/blob/main/contracts/mixins/NFTMarketPrivateSale.sol#L123-L174)  

Within a NFTMarketPrivateSale contract, buyers are allowed to purchase a seller’s NFT. This is done through a seller providing a buyer a EIP-712 signature. The buyer can then call `#buyFromPrivateSaleFor` providing the v, r, and s values of the signature as well as any additional details to generate the message hash. If the signature is valid, then the NFT is transferred to the buyer.

The problem with the code is that EIP-712 signatures can be re-used within a small range of time assuming that the original seller takes back ownership of the NFT. This is because the NFTMarketPrivateSale#buyFromPrivateSaleFor method has no checks to determine if the EIP-712 signature has been used before.
```
poc:
Consider the following example:

  1. Joe the NFT owner sells a NFT to the malicious buyer Rachel via a private sale.
  2. Rachel through this private sale obtains the EIP-712 signature and uses it to purchase a NFT.
  3. Joe the NFT owner purchases back the NFT within two days of the original sale to Rachel.
  4. Joe the NFT owner puts the NFT back on sale.
  5. Rachel, who has the original EIP-712 signature, can re-purchase the NFT by calling `#buyFromPrivateSaleFor` again with the same parameters they provided in the original private sale purchase in step 1.

The `#buyFromPrivateSaleFor` [function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-foundation/blob/main/contracts/mixins/NFTMarketPrivateSale.sol#L123) runs several validation checks before transferring the NFT over to the buyer. The validations are as follows:

  1. L#132 - The signature has expired.
  2. L#135 - The deadline is beyond 48 hours from now.
  3. L#143 - The amount argument is greater than msg.value.
  4. L#149 - The msg.value is greater than the amount set.
  5. L#171 - This checks that the EIP-712 signature comes from the NFT seller.

As you can see, there are no checks that the EIP-712 signature has been used before. If the original NFT seller purchases back the NFT, then they are susceptible to having the original buyer taking back the NFT. This can be problematic if the NFT has risen in value, as the original buyer can utilize the same purchase amount from the first transaction in this malicious transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay weakness in the private‑sale flow of an NFT marketplace that relies on EIP‑712 signatures to authorize a single purchase. The contract accepts a seller‑signed message containing the sale terms (NFT contract, token ID, buyer address, price, deadline, etc.) and, after verifying the signature, transfers the NFT to the caller. Because the implementation does not record whether a particular signed offer has already been consumed, the same signature can be presented again as long as it remains within the permitted time window (the contract enforces a maximum deadline of 48 hours and an expiration check). The root cause is the absence of a nonce, replay‑guard, or any mapping that marks a signature as spent. Consequently, if the original seller re‑acquires the NFT after the first sale—e.g., by buying it back within the two‑day window—and lists it again, the original buyer can reuse the previously obtained signature to purchase the NFT a second time, paying the same amount as the first transaction. This attack is possible whenever the signature has not expired, the deadline constraint is satisfied, and the contract’s other validation checks (price versus msg.value, signature provenance) all pass, which they do because the signature itself is still valid. The impact is that the buyer can repeatedly reclaim the same NFT for the original price, potentially profiting from price appreciation or draining the seller’s ability to resell the asset. Sellers, buyers, and the overall protocol lose trust because funds can disappear from the seller’s balance without a clear on‑chain indication that a replay occurred. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the private‑sale mixin and noted the missing usage‑tracking logic. It can be hard to notice because the signature verification succeeds and the contract emits the usual transfer events, giving the impression that each sale is a fresh, independent transaction. The proper mitigation is to introduce a replay‑prevention mechanism, such as a per‑offer nonce incorporated into the signed payload or a mapping that records a boolean flag indicating that a given set of sale parameters has already been claimed. This ensures that once a signature has been consumed, any subsequent attempt to call the purchase function with the same signature will revert, eliminating the ability to replay the transaction. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “signature replay” or “re‑use of off‑chain authorizations” vulnerabilities, where off‑chain signed data is not sufficiently invalidated after first use, breaking the assumed one‑time nature of the authorization and violating the marketplace’s accounting guarantees.

title: `SendValueWithFallbackWithdraw`: `withdrawFor` function may fail to withdraw ether recorded in `pendingWithdrawals`
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in a marketplace contract that uses an internal function to send Ether to various participants (treasury, creators, sellers, bidders). The function attempts to transfer the specified amount with a bounded gas stipend using a low‑level call. If the call fails – for example because the recipient is a contract that does not implement a payable fallback, exceeds the supplied gas limit, or contains logic that reverts – the contract records the amount in a mapping called pendingWithdrawals and emits a WithdrawPending event. Users can later retrieve these funds through withdraw or withdrawFor, which read the amount from pendingWithdrawals, reset the entry to zero, and then invoke a helper that forwards the Ether to the same address. However, withdrawFor does not provide an alternative destination; it always calls sendValue on the originally recorded address. When that address is a contract that cannot accept Ether, the sendValue call reverts, the transaction rolls back, and the pending withdrawal entry remains unchanged. Because the contract offers no mechanism to redirect the funds to a different, payable address, the Ether becomes effectively locked in the contract for the affected user. This issue manifests when a user’s withdrawal attempt fails silently, showing a transaction revert or a pending‑withdrawal event, while the balance displayed by the marketplace still attributes the amount to the user. The problem was uncovered during a code audit that examined the error‑handling path of the fallback withdrawal logic. It is difficult to notice because the primary withdraw function appears to work for normal EOAs, and the failure only occurs for specific contract recipients, which may be rare in production. The impact is a loss of accessibility to funds – users may see their escrowed Ether disappear from their wallet and receive no refund, violating the marketplace’s accounting assumptions that every recorded balance can be reclaimed. The issue belongs to the class of “withdrawal‑to‑non‑payable‑address” bugs, where a contract’s fallback withdraw mechanism does not account for recipients that reject Ether, leading to trapped assets. A proper fix is to introduce a withdrawal path that allows the contract owner or the user to specify an alternative payable address (for example, a withdrawTo function) or to migrate the locked Ether to a token representation that can be claimed later. Such a change restores the invariant that every pending balance can be withdrawn, eliminates the stuck‑funds scenario, and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations of being able to reclaim their funds.

title: adminAccountMigration
description: The `adminAccountMigration()` function is called by the operator role to update all sellers’ auctions. The `auction.seller` account is updated to the new address, however, the protocol fails to update `buyPrice.seller`. As a result, the protocol is put in a deadlock situation where the new address cannot cancel the auction and withdraw their NFT without the compromised account first cancelling the buy price and vice-versa. This is only recoverable if the new account is migrated back to the compromised account and then `cancelBuyPrice()` is called before migrating back.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an administrative account migration routine that is intended to transfer ownership of all seller‑related data for an NFT when the operator role invokes the adminAccountMigration() function. The routine correctly updates the seller field stored within the auction structure, but it neglects to update the seller reference held by any active buy‑price offer (buyPrice). Because the buy‑price contract still points to the original (compromised) address, the new owner is unable to perform critical actions such as cancelling the auction or withdrawing the NFT, while the old address cannot cancel the buy price without first regaining control of the auction. This mismatch creates a deadlock where each side depends on the other to complete a state‑change, effectively locking the asset in a limbo state. The issue is discovered during a manual security audit that examined state transitions after administrative actions. It is subtle because the two data structures (auction and buyPrice) are updated in separate parts of the code, and the test suite only exercised auctions without an accompanying buy‑price, allowing the inconsistency to go unnoticed. Exploitation does not require a malicious actor beyond the legitimate use of the admin migration feature; simply invoking the function while a buy‑price is active triggers the deadlock. The impact is that the NFT becomes non‑transferable, the new seller cannot cancel the auction or retrieve the token, and the old seller cannot clear the buy‑price without regaining control, leading to potential loss of marketability and user funds if the situation persists. The condition occurs only when the migration is performed on an NFT that simultaneously has an active auction reserve price and a set buy‑price. Affected parties include sellers, bidders, and the overall protocol, as the locked asset reduces liquidity and may erode trust. Recovery is possible only by reversing the migration: moving the NFT back to the original address, calling cancelBuyPrice() to clear the stale offer, and then re‑migrating if needed. This workaround is cumbersome, requires manual verification, and is not scalable. The recommended fix is to either invalidate any active buy‑price before performing the migration or to extend the migration logic to update both the auction.seller and buyPrice.seller fields atomically, thereby preserving consistency across related contracts. By ensuring that all ownership references are synchronized, the protocol avoids the deadlock, maintains expected behavior (the new owner can cancel or withdraw), and upholds the business rule that an NFT should never be in a state where it cannot be sold or reclaimed. The bug falls under the class of state‑inconsistency or cross‑contract reference mismatch, where divergent storage updates lead to asset lockup and break accounting assumptions about ownership.

title: Escrowed NFT can be stolen by anyone if no active `buyPrice` or auction exists for it
description:
If a NFT happens to be in escrow with neither buyPrice, nor auction being initialised for it, there is a way to obtain it for free by any actor via `makeOffer`, `acceptOffer` combination.

I.e. a malicious user can track the FNDNFTMarket contract and obtain any NFT from it for which there are no buyPrice or auction structures initialised. For example, if a NFT is mistakenly sent to the contract, an attacker can immediately steal it.

This will happen as NFT is being guarded by buyPrice and auction structures only. The severity here is medium as normal usage of the system imply that either one of them is initialised (NFT was sent to escrow as a part of `setBuyPrice` or `createReserveAuction`, and so one of the structures is present), so this seems to leave only mistakenly sent assets exposed.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the market contract protects NFTs that are held in escrow. The contract assumes that every escrowed token is associated with either a buy‑price structure or an active reserve auction, and relies on those structures to authorize the transfer of the token to a buyer. When a token is transferred to the market contract without initializing a buy price or creating an auction— for example, because the sender mistakenly sent the NFT directly to the contract— the internal guard that checks the seller’s authorization is never triggered. Consequently, an attacker can call the public functions makeOffer and acceptOffer with a minimal offer amount. The offer is recorded, and when acceptOffer is invoked the contract’s internal _acceptOffer routine calls _transferFromEscrow. Because none of the escrow‑manager overrides (buy‑price, auction, or offer) are present for that token, the call falls through to the core transfer implementation, which simply moves the token from the contract to the caller. This results in the NFT leaving the market contract without any legitimate sale or auction, effectively allowing any actor to obtain the token for free. From a user perspective the symptom is that an NFT that was thought to be safely escrowed suddenly disappears from the owner’s wallet or appears as if it was never listed, while the attacker receives the NFT after paying only gas and a negligible offer. The impact is the loss of ownership of the NFT; the original creator may also lose future royalty revenue. The issue is hard to notice because the UI typically shows only listed items, so a token without a price or auction does not appear in the marketplace view, giving a false impression that it is locked or burned. The root cause is the missing validation that an escrowed token must be tied to at least one escrow manager before a transfer is permitted. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit checks that prevent makeOffer/acceptOffer from succeeding when no buy‑price or auction record exists, or to enforce that the internal authorizeSeller parameter is forced to address(0) only after a legitimate escrow manager confirms ownership. The implemented fix changes the internal _transferFromEscrow routine to require that authorizeSeller is address(0) before allowing a transfer, causing the transaction to revert for tokens that are not properly escrowed, thereby closing the loophole that allowed free acquisition of unallocated NFTs.

title: Upgradable escrow contract
description:
Upgradable escrow contract poses great risk to user who approved their NFT to the contract. Most popular token / NFT exchange do not require user to approve their asset to admin upgradable contract.

This also increases user gas usage because they would have to revoke approval when they are done with the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the design of an upgradeable escrow contract that users must approve their NFTs for before interacting with a marketplace. Because the contract is proxy‑based and can be upgraded by an admin, the escrow logic is not fixed at deployment. This flexibility introduces a trust dependency: the admin can modify the escrow code after users have granted approval, potentially altering the transfer rules so that NFTs can be withdrawn without receiving the agreed Ether payment, or even be transferred to the admin’s address for zero value. The root cause is the combination of a mutable contract implementation with an open‑ended approval mechanism, which gives the contract owner the ability to change asset‑handling behavior after the user’s consent. An attacker who obtains the admin’s upgrade rights, or a malicious admin themselves, could deploy a new implementation that simply calls transferFrom on the approved token IDs without checking payment, thereby stealing the NFTs. The impact is the loss of users’ NFTs and erosion of confidence in the platform; users may also incur extra gas costs because they must later revoke the NFT approval to protect themselves after the transaction, a step that is not required in non‑upgradeable designs. The issue manifests whenever a user approves an NFT to the escrow contract and the contract is later upgraded, which can happen at any point before the trade finalizes. All participants who hold NFTs and interact with the marketplace are affected, including casual traders and the protocol itself, because the escrow is a critical escrow‑and‑settlement component. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the upgradeability pattern and approval flows, noting that most reputable NFT exchanges avoid requiring users to approve assets to a contract that can be altered. The problem can be subtle because the approval transaction appears innocuous and the upgradeability is not visible to the end user, making it easy to overlook that future code changes could invalidate the original trust assumptions. To remediate, the escrow functionality should be isolated into an immutable contract with a minimal, well‑audited interface that does not rely on upgradeable logic, and approvals should be limited to the exact token IDs required for a single transaction, or replaced with a pull‑based transfer model (e.g., safeTransferFrom) that does not require prior approval. This architectural change removes the admin’s ability to retroactively change transfer rules, aligning the contract’s behavior with the users’ expectations that an approved NFT will only be transferred under the originally agreed payment terms.

title: Royalties can be distribution unfairly among `creatorRecipients` for NFT contracts with non-standard `getRoyalties`
poc:
Given:

  * `NFT-Token1` `Royalties`:

    * Address0 = 10,000 (1%)
    * Address1 = 10,000 (1%)
    * Address2 = 100,000 (10%)
    * Address3 = 880,000 (88%)
  * Alice owns the `NFT-Token1`
  * Alice `setBuyPrice()` and listed `NFT-Token1` for `10 ETH`;
  * Bob `buy()` with `10 ETH`:
  * `foundationFee` = `0.5 ETH`
  * `creatorFee` = `1 ETH`
  * `ownerRev` = `8.5 ETH`

Since `creatorShares[address2]` > `BASIS_POINTS` (10,000), all the `creatorFee` will be sent to the first address: `Address0`, which is expected to receive only `1%` of the royalties.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s assumption that the getRoyalties() function of an NFT collection always returns royalty shares expressed in basis points (BPS, where 10,000 equals 100%). In reality, getRoyalties() is not a standardized interface and some implementations use a higher precision, such as 1e6 to represent 100%. The contract contains a check that treats any share value greater than BASIS_POINTS (10,000) as an error condition: if a creatorShare entry exceeds this threshold, the loop aborts and the contract redirects the entire creator fee to the first address in the creatorRecipients array, ignoring all other recipients. This logic was introduced to guard against malformed values, but because it is based on a fixed BPS ceiling, it misclassifies legitimate higher‑precision values as abusive. When a royalty share is reported in the larger unit, the condition creatorShares[i] > BASIS_POINTS becomes true, the maxCreatorIndex is forced to zero, and the royalty distribution collapses to a single recipient. An attacker can exploit this by deploying an NFT contract that reports royalty percentages in the non‑standard unit, thereby ensuring that all royalty payments from secondary sales are funneled to a chosen address (usually the first entry). The impact is a systematic under‑payment of rightful creators: some creators receive a fraction of what they expect, while others receive nothing at all, effectively causing funds to disappear from their balances. This flaw manifests whenever a sale triggers the royalty payout path and the royalty data supplied by the NFT contract exceeds the 10,000 BPS limit, which can occur with any collection that follows the higher‑precision convention. The parties affected include creators listed as royalty recipients, buyers who assume correct royalty distribution, and the marketplace protocol that relies on accurate accounting for trust and compliance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s handling of getRoyalties() against various real‑world NFT implementations and observed the erroneous behaviour with a test case where one share was set to 100,000 (representing 10% in a 1e6 scale). Because the contract silently redirects the fee without emitting a warning, the problem can be hard to notice from the UI; users may see the expected royalty percentages displayed but observe that their payouts are zero or dramatically lower after a sale. To remediate, the contract should stop assuming a fixed BPS scale and instead calculate the total of all creatorShares dynamically, using that total to proportionally distribute the creator fee. By summing the shares and handling the case where totalShares is zero, the contract can fairly allocate royalties regardless of the precision used by the NFT’s getRoyalties() implementation, eliminating the conditional that forces maxCreatorIndex to zero.

title: Inappropriate support of EIP-2981
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect implementation of the EIP‑2981 royalty standard in the marketplace contract. Instead of forwarding the actual sale price of an NFT to the royaltyInfo function, the code passes a constant value equal to the maximum basis‑points representation (10,000). Because the royalty amount is calculated as (salePrice * royaltyBPS) / 10,000, using a fixed sale price inflates the denominator for low‑value royalties. Consequently, any royalty share that is configured to be less than one basis point (0.01 % of the sale price) is rounded down to zero, so the intended recipient receives no payout at all. In addition, the logic enforces a hard‑coded minimum of 10 % total royalty cut; if an NFT’s royalty configuration specifies a total rate lower than 10 %, the contract artificially scales the payout up to the 10 % threshold, overpaying the seller or marketplace. This behaviour can be triggered whenever an NFT implements the EIP‑2981 interface and either (a) its per‑recipient royalty fraction is below one basis point, or (b) its total royalty percentage is set below ten percent. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the royalty handling flow and noticed the constant sale‑price argument. It is subtle because the contract still returns a non‑zero royalty address, giving the impression that royalties are being honored, yet the actual transferred amount may be missing or inflated, a discrepancy that can easily go unnoticed without precise accounting. The impact is twofold: creators or artists expecting tiny royalty payments may receive nothing, violating the economic expectations of the platform, while buyers may unknowingly overpay royalties when the contract forces a 10 % minimum, breaking the intended revenue model. To remediate the problem, the contract should pass the true `_salePrice` received in the transaction to the royaltyInfo call, ensuring accurate proportional calculation, and should adjust the capping logic to enforce a maximum of 10 % while allowing lower configured rates to pass through unchanged. This correction aligns the implementation with the EIP‑2981 specification, restores correct royalty accounting, and prevents both under‑payment and unintended over‑payment of royalties.

title: There is no Support For The Trading of Cryptopunks
description: Cryptopunks are at the core of the NFT ecosystem. As one of the first NFTs, it embodies the culture of NFT marketplaces. By not supporting the trading of cryptopunks, Foundation is at a severe disadvantage when compared to other marketplaces. Cryptopunks have their own internal marketplace which allows users to trade their NFTs to other users. As such, cryptopunks does not adhere to the `ERC721` standard, it will always fail when the protocol attempts to trade them.
poc: Here is an example [implementation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-nftx/blob/main/nftx-protocol-v2/contracts/solidity/NFTXStakingZap.sol#L417-L424) of what it might look like to integrate cryptopunks into the Foundation protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability identified in the Foundation NFT marketplace is a functional incompatibility with CryptoPunks, a historically significant NFT collection that does not conform to the ERC‑721 standard. The core of the issue is that the marketplace’s trading logic assumes every NFT implements the standard ERC‑721 interface, specifically functions such as transferFrom and safeTransferFrom. CryptoPunks, however, use a custom internal marketplace and expose a proprietary transfer mechanism that lacks these standard methods. When a user attempts to list or trade a CryptoPunk on Foundation, the contract invokes the expected ERC‑721 transfer call, which inevitably fails because the CryptoPunk contract does not provide the required interface. This failure manifests as a reverted transaction, often without a clear error message, leaving the user unable to complete the trade. The impact is primarily a loss of expected functionality: users who own CryptoPunks cannot sell or transfer them through Foundation, contrary to the marketplace’s advertised capability to handle NFTs. From a business perspective, this breaks the assumption that any NFT can be traded on the platform, leading to a poor user experience, potential loss of revenue, and a competitive disadvantage against marketplaces that support CryptoPunks via wrappers or custom integrations. The issue was discovered during an audit that examined the contract’s handling of external NFT standards and observed that attempts to invoke standard ERC‑721 functions on CryptoPunk contracts always revert. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the UI may indicate that a listing was created, yet the backend transaction fails silently, giving users the impression that the operation succeeded. To remediate, the recommended approach is to introduce a wrapper contract that abstracts CryptoPunk’s custom transfer logic behind a standard ERC‑721 interface, allowing the marketplace to interact with the wrapper as if it were a regular ERC‑721 token. This wrapper would handle the necessary approvals and call the CryptoPunk contract’s proprietary functions internally, shielding users from the incompatibility. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “non‑standard token integration failures,” where a platform’s reliance on a de‑facto standard prevents it from supporting assets that deviate from that standard, resulting in trade failures, user confusion, and a breach of expected marketplace functionality.

title: Exchange does not split royalty revenue correctly
description:
According to the `README.md`:
If royalty information was not defined when the NFT was originally deployed, it may be added using the Royalty Registry which will be respected by our market contract.

The actual exchange code only respects the Royalty Registry or other royalty information if the number of recipients is less than or equal to four.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the market contract’s handling of royalty payouts for NFTs that have more than four royalty recipients registered in the Royalty Registry. The contract deliberately limits the number of recipients it processes by capping the maximum index to a constant (MAX_ROYALTY_RECIPIENTS_INDEX), which is currently set to three (allowing four recipients total). When an NFT’s royalty data contains five or more addresses, the loop that distributes the creator fee only iterates over the first four entries, silently discarding the remaining shares. As a result, the calculated share for each of the processed recipients is based on the original totalShares value, but the total amount actually sent out (totalDistributed) is less than the full royalty amount owed. This discrepancy causes the creator to receive less funds than stipulated in the royalty agreement, effectively making a portion of the royalty revenue disappear. The issue can be exploited by any party that lists an NFT with an oversized royalty array; the market contract will accept the offer, compute the royalty fee, but will only transfer a truncated portion, leaving the rest unclaimed. The impact is primarily on creators who expect their full royalty distribution, as well as on buyers and secondary sellers who may be unaware that the royalty obligations are not being fulfilled. The bug manifests only when the marketplace processes a sale involving an NFT whose royalty registry reports more than four recipients – a condition that is not obvious from the user interface and is only hinted at in the README documentation. It was identified during a manual code audit that examined the payout loop and compared it against the documented royalty handling policy. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it merely limits the payout silently, making it hard for users to notice that part of the royalty is missing. The correct mitigation strategy is to retrieve the royalty information at the time an offer is created, cache it for later use, and explicitly reject any NFT whose royalty recipient array exceeds the allowed maximum, or to require creators to route royalties through a dedicated split contract that can handle an arbitrary number of beneficiaries in a gas‑efficient manner. By enforcing a clear limit or providing a documented fallback mechanism, the marketplace can ensure that royalty obligations are either fully satisfied or transparently declined, preserving the expected financial outcomes for all participants.

title: `buyFromPrivateSaleFor
description: The `buyFromPrivateSaleFor()` function allows sellers to make private sales to users. If insufficient `ETH` is provided to the function call, the protocol will attempt to withdraw the amount difference from the user’s unlocked balance. However, if the same user has an open offer on the same NFT, then these funds will remain locked until expiration. As a result, the user cannot make use of these locked funds even though they may be needed for a successful sale.
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the private‑sale purchase routine of the marketplace contract. The function that executes a private sale, `buyFromPrivateSaleFor()`, is designed to allow a seller to offer an NFT directly to a specific buyer. When the buyer does not send enough Ether to cover the agreed price, the contract falls back to pulling the shortfall from the buyer’s unlocked balance. The flaw occurs when the same buyer already has an open offer on the very same NFT. In that situation part of the buyer’s balance is locked inside the existing offer until the offer expires. Because the private‑sale logic does not check for or release those locked funds, the contract attempts to draw the required amount from the unlocked portion only, leaving the locked portion untouched. As a result the transaction cannot satisfy the price requirement and the private sale fails, while the buyer’s funds remain stuck in the locked state. This creates an inconsistent user experience where a buyer appears to have sufficient total holdings, yet is unable to complete the purchase because a portion of those holdings is unavailable.

The root cause is an oversight in the accounting flow: the private‑sale path reuses the same balance‑withdrawal mechanism employed for normal offers but neglects to cancel or adjust any pre‑existing offer that would otherwise free the needed funds. Consequently the contract’s internal state diverges from the user’s expectation that all owned funds can be used for a purchase. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that compared the behaviour of the public offer functions with the private‑sale function and identified the mismatch.

Exploitation does not require malicious intent; it can be triggered simply by a user who has placed an offer on an NFT and later receives a private‑sale invitation for that same token. The user attempts to accept the private sale with insufficient Ether, assuming the contract will automatically draw the missing amount from their total balance. The contract instead rejects the trade, and the previously locked offer funds remain confined until the offer’s expiration, effectively locking the buyer out of the transaction. In a worst‑case scenario an attacker could deliberately create a private‑sale invitation for a buyer who already has a pending offer, causing a denial‑of‑service condition where the buyer cannot purchase the NFT despite having enough overall assets.

The impact is limited to the affected buyer and the specific NFT involved, but it undermines the reliability of the marketplace’s financial logic. Users may see their transaction revert with a “insufficient ETH” error even though their wallet shows a sufficient balance, leading to confusion, missed purchasing opportunities, and potential loss of trust in the platform. Because the funds are merely locked and not transferred, there is no direct loss of Ether, but the inability to access those funds creates a functional denial of service.

The bug manifests only under the condition that a buyer has an active, unexpired offer on the same token and then participates in a private sale where the Ether sent is less than the sale price. If no prior offer exists, the function behaves as intended. The problem is subtle because the same withdrawal logic works correctly for regular sales, so the edge case is not obvious without testing the exact sequence of actions.

To remediate the issue, the private‑sale function should explicitly cancel any existing buyer offer on the targeted NFT before attempting to withdraw the shortfall. By invoking a `_cancelBuyersOffer()` (or equivalent) when insufficient Ether is supplied, the contract guarantees that the buyer’s locked balance is released, making the total funds available for the private purchase. This aligns the accounting model with the user’s expectation that all owned assets can be used for a sale and eliminates the locked‑fund dead‑lock.

In abstract terms, this is a classic case of improper handling of locked or escrowed balances when multiple transaction pathways share the same asset pool. The bug violates the fundamental accounting invariant that the sum of locked and unlocked balances must equal the user’s total holdings, and that any operation requiring funds should first reconcile locked portions. The symptom from a user’s perspective is a failed private‑sale transaction accompanied by an error message about insufficient ETH, even though their wallet balance appears adequate, and the confusing observation that their funds remain frozen in an offer they can no longer act upon.

title: `_getCreatorPaymentInfo
description: The `_getCreatorPaymentInfo()` function is utilised by `_distributeFunds()` whenever an NFT sale is made. The function uses `try` and `catch` statements to handle bad API endpoints. As such, a revert in this function would lead to NFTs that are locked in the contract. Some API endpoints receive an array of recipient addresses which are iterated over. If for whatever reason the function reverts inside of a `try` statement, the revert is actually not handled and it will not fall through to the empty `catch` statement.
poc: The end result is that valid and honest NFT contracts may revert if the call runs out of gas due to an unbounded `_recipients` array. `try` statements are only able to handle external calls.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal helper function that gathers payment information for a creator when an NFT is sold. This function iterates over an array of royalty recipients and wraps the iteration in a try‑catch construct that is intended to protect the contract from failing API endpoints. However, the try statement only catches failures that arise from external calls; reverts generated by internal logic, such as a loop that runs out of gas, are not intercepted. When the recipient array is large enough to exceed the block gas limit, the loop triggers a revert inside the try block. Because the empty catch block never executes for this type of error, the revert propagates back to the caller, causing the surrounding distribution routine to abort. As a result, the NFT remains locked in escrow and the sale cannot be completed, leaving buyers without the purchased token and creators without their expected royalties. The issue manifests whenever the contract processes a sale involving an unbounded list of royalty recipients, which may happen with legitimate contracts that have many collaborators or with a malicious API that deliberately returns an oversized array. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the contract’s defensive coding patterns and identified that the try‑catch was being misapplied. It is difficult to notice because the presence of a try‑catch gives the impression of proper error handling, and the loop length appears to be constrained elsewhere in the code, masking the fact that this particular helper function lacks an explicit bound. The bug belongs to the class of improper exception handling combined with unbounded iteration, which can lead to out‑of‑gas reverts and fund‑locking. To remediate the issue, the contract should either enforce a hard cap on the number of royalty recipients within this helper function, move the potentially failing logic to an external call that can genuinely be caught, or redesign the payment distribution to avoid loops over untrusted data altogether. By ensuring that any revert is either caught and handled or prevented by pre‑validation of input sizes, the contract can guarantee that NFTs are not unintentionally trapped and that users receive the assets and payouts they expect.

title: Primary seller can avoid paying the primary fee
description: A primary seller can circumvent the 15% fee and pay 5% as a secondary seller.
poc:
Both of these conditions can be easily circumvented by the primary seller.

1. He could transfer the NFT to a different wallet and sell it from there to break the first condition.
2. He can make a private sale to himself for 1$ (paying the 15% fee on a dust amount) and then do a public auction with the real price.

With any of these 2 methods, the primary seller can circumvent the 15% fee and pay 5% as a secondary seller which makes the primary seller fee optional to pay.
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a primary seller—typically the original creator or minter of an NFT—to evade the platform's intended 15% primary sale fee and instead be charged only the 5% secondary fee. The root cause lies in the fee calculation logic, which bases the fee level solely on the address that initiates the sale, without verifying the provenance of the token or ensuring that the seller has not transferred ownership before the fee is assessed. Because the contract does not enforce that the seller of a primary sale be the original creator, a seller can manipulate the sale flow in two main ways. First, the seller can transfer the NFT to a different wallet under their control and list it from that address, causing the contract to treat the transaction as a secondary sale and apply the lower fee. Second, the seller can execute a private “dust” sale to themselves for a negligible amount (e.g., $1), thereby paying the 15% fee on an insignificant price, and subsequently initiate a public auction from the same or a different address at the true market price, which will again be classified as a secondary sale and only incur the 5% fee. This exploit can be performed without any special privileges and does not require modifying the contract code. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the marketplace, as the platform foregoes the higher primary fee that funds development and maintenance. Creators, collectors, and the protocol itself are affected: creators may unintentionally receive less revenue than anticipated, while the protocol’s economic model assumes that primary sales generate a larger fee share. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the fee‑assessment conditions and testing alternative sale paths. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction logs show a normal fee deduction, albeit the lower rate, and there is no explicit error or warning. From a user perspective, a seller who expects to pay a 15% fee sees only a 5% deduction, leading to confusion when the platform’s fee summary does not match the advertised terms. The bug belongs to the class of “fee‑bypass” or “provenance‑verification” vulnerabilities, where accounting assumptions about who should be charged are violated. To remediate, the fee logic should be tied to the token's provenance, enforcing that the original creator or the address that first received the NFT from the creator must be subject to the primary fee, regardless of any intermediate transfers. Additionally, the contract could prohibit private dust sales that serve only to trigger the primary fee on a negligible amount, or it could record the intended sale type at minting and enforce it during subsequent transfers and listings. Implementing these checks would close the loophole that permits primary sellers to avoid the intended fee structure.

title: Missing receiver validation in `withdrawFrom`
description:
The `FETH.withdrawFrom` function does not validate its `to` parameter.  
Funds can be lost if `to` is the zero address.
Similar issues have been judged as medium recently, see [Sandclock M-15](https://code4rena.com/reports/2022-01-sandclock/) / [Github issue](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-sandclock-findings/issues/183#issuecomment-1024626171).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a withdrawal routine that allows a caller to specify an arbitrary destination address for the transferred assets. The function does not verify that the supplied address is a legitimate recipient; specifically, it accepts the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) and the contract’s own address as valid targets. This omission creates a scenario where funds can be sent to an address that is either unrecoverable (the zero address) or locked inside the contract itself, effectively removing the assets from the user’s control. The root cause is the absence of a validation check on the `to` parameter before the transfer is executed. An attacker or a careless user can exploit the flaw simply by invoking the withdrawal function with `to` set to the zero address, either directly or through a malicious contract that tricks a victim into approving a transfer on their behalf. When the function attempts to transfer Ether (or an equivalent token) to the zero address, the transfer succeeds according to the EVM semantics but the funds are burned, leading to an irreversible loss. The impact is that any user who initiates a withdrawal expecting the assets to arrive in their wallet may see their balance decrease while receiving nothing, breaking the fundamental accounting assumption that withdrawals always result in a positive receipt. This condition manifests whenever the withdrawal function is called without an explicit safeguard against invalid recipients, which is typical in many smart‑contract wallets and token wrappers that expose flexible withdraw interfaces. The affected parties include ordinary users of the contract, third‑party applications that integrate the withdrawal feature, and the protocol itself because the lost funds reduce its total capital. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the contract’s public entry points for missing input checks.
