Down‑stream processing logic iterates over the array and uses the first occurrence of each token to compute balances. Consequently, the system will continue to reference the zero‑amount entry and ignore the later, correct entry, effectively causing the user’s funds to disappear from accounting. The impact is a loss of token value for any participant who relies on the recorded balance, as withdrawals or further operations will be based on an incorrect, zero balance. This condition can only arise when a zero‑amount entry is allowed to be inserted; in the current deployment the only caller of the store function is NestedFactory, which obtains the amount from a safeTransfer and then passes the delta of reserve balances. The existing operators (ZeroExOperator and FlatOperator) deliberately revert if the amount bought is zero, meaning that under normal operation a zero entry cannot be produced. However, the contract does not enforce a non‑zero amount nor a duplicate‑token guard at the storage level, so a future operator or a malicious ERC‑20 token that silently burns the entire transfer could trigger the scenario. The issue is subtle because the array may contain duplicate entries that are not readily visible, and because the zero‑amount case is masked by the operator checks, auditors might overlook it during functional testing. The appropriate remediation is to add validation in the store function that rejects a zero amount and checks whether the token is already present, updating the existing record instead of inserting a new one. By enforcing these constraints, the protocol preserves accurate accounting, prevents fund loss, and aligns with the intended business logic that each token should have a single, up‑to‑date balance entry.

title: `NestedFactory`: User can utilise accidentally sent ETH funds via `processOutputOrders`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NestedFactory contract’s handling of plain Ether (ETH) that is accidentally transferred to the contract. The contract’s receive() function is payable without any validation of the sender, which means any address can send ETH directly to the contract. Later, the function processOutputOrders(), which is intended to process orders whose funds originate from the internal reserve, does not inspect msg.value at all. Moreover, the helper function transferInputTokens() contains a branch that treats ETH as a token address and, when the input token is ETH, simply checks that the contract’s balance is sufficient before wrapping the Ether into WETH. Because this branch does not verify that the ETH being wrapped came from the expected reserve source, an attacker who has managed to send ETH to the contract (or who discovers that a user mistakenly sent ETH) can create an output order that specifies ETH as the token and requests an amount equal to the contract’s entire ETH balance. When processOutputOrders() is invoked, the contract will wrap the accidentally sent ETH into WETH and transfer it to the caller, effectively allowing the attacker to drain the stray Ether. The impact is that funds disappear from the contract without any legitimate business reason, violating the accounting assumptions that only reserve‑backed assets should be usable. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing balance: users expecting their funds to remain safe see their Ether vanish, or a refund that should be received is instead zero. This issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined the flow of ETH through receive(), processOutputOrders() and transferInputTokens(), noting that no sender restriction or reserve‑origin check existed. It can be hard to notice because the contract accepts ETH silently and does not emit events indicating that the Ether is being wrapped or transferred out, so the loss may go unnoticed until a significant amount is missing. The recommended remediation is to restrict the receive() function so that only the WETH contract (the authorized source of wrapped Ether) can send ETH, mirroring the pattern used in the FeeSplitter contract, and to add an explicit check that the _fromReserve flag is false when the input token is ETH, thereby preventing the accidental ETH balance from being used in output orders. By enforcing these constraints the contract will no longer allow arbitrary parties to exploit accidentally sent Ether, preserving the intended invariant that only reserve‑backed assets are consumable.

title: Wrong logic around `areOperatorsImported`
description:
[OperatorResolver.sol#L42-L43](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-nested/blob/fe6f9ef7783c3c84798c8ab5fc58085a55cebcfc/contracts/OperatorResolver.sol#L42-L43)  

The logic related to the `areOperatorsImported` method is incorrect and can cause an operator not to be updated because the owner thinks it is already updated, and a vulnerable or defective one can be used.
poc:
The `operators` mapping is made up of a key `bytes32 name` and a value made up of two values: `implementation` and `selector`, both of which identify the contract and function to be called when an operator is invoked.

The `areOperatorsImported` method tries to check if the operators to check already exist, however, the check is not done correctly, since && is used instead of ||.

If the operator with name `A` and value `{implementation=0x27f8d03b3a2196956ed754badc28d73be8830a6e,selector="performSwapVulnerable"}` exists, and the owner try to check if the operator with name `A` and value `{implementation=0x27f8d03b3a2196956ed754badc28d73be8830a6e,selector="performSwapFixed"}` exists, that function will return `true`, and the owner may decide not to import it , producing unexpected errors. Because operators manage the tokens, this error can produce a token lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the operator management logic of the Nested protocol, specifically in the `areOperatorsImported` function. This function is intended to verify whether an operator entry – identified by a name, a contract implementation address, and a function selector – already exists in the system before allowing a new operator to be imported. The implementation mistakenly uses a logical AND (`&&`) to compare the stored implementation address and selector with the values supplied for the import. As a result, when an operator with the same name and the same implementation address but a different selector (for example, a fixed version of a function) is checked, the condition incorrectly evaluates to true, leading the caller to believe that the operator is already present. Consequently, the owner may skip the import of the corrected operator, leaving the vulnerable version active. This flaw originates from a simple logical error in the conditional expression, which fails to detect a mismatch in the selector field. An attacker or an unwitting user can exploit the bug by relying on the protocol’s assumption that the operator has been updated, while in reality the old, potentially malicious or defective selector remains in place. The impact is that token transfers or swaps routed through the operator may invoke the vulnerable code path, causing token loss or denial of expected functionality. The bug manifests whenever an upgrade attempt targets an existing operator name with a new selector while keeping the implementation address unchanged – a scenario common during bug‑fix releases. All participants that rely on operator‑managed token movements – token holders, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol may silently execute the outdated, unsafe function. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, and its subtle nature makes it hard to notice: the UI shows the operator as present, balances appear unchanged, and no error is emitted, so users see no immediate symptom. However, the underlying accounting assumption that the latest selector is in effect is violated, breaking the protocol’s safety guarantees. To remediate the problem, the conditional should be rewritten to use a logical OR (`||`) so that a mismatch in either the implementation address or the selector correctly signals that the operator is not yet imported, thereby forcing the import of the intended fixed version. In broader terms, this is a classic example of incorrect conditional logic leading to flawed state validation, which can cause business‑logic failures such as "refund calculation error" or "funds disappear" when the wrong code path is executed.

title: Manipulations of `setFee`
description:
[BribeVault.sol#L104-L113](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L104-L113)  
[BribeVault.sol#L164](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L164)  
[BribeVault.sol#L213](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L213)  
[BribeVault.sol#L256](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L256)  

If we consider that the fee variable is meaningfully applied, there will still be several problems with this:

  1. Admin can setFee up to 100%. This is bad for users, fees should have a reasonable upper limit, e.g. 30% to prevent potential griefing.
  2. Tokens are transferred in a separate function called transferBribes, which means that depositBribe txs have already settled. setFee can happen anytime, so an admin can change fees for already made deposits. I think this is again bad for users, as you need extra trust on an admin to not exploit this, and smart contracts should aim for as little external trust as possible.
  3. Even if a fee would be applied in depositBribe, function setFee could frontrun user deposits. Consider using a timelock, so that users have time to react and adjust.

We will likely set an upper bound as recommended, to ease user concerns. The admin being the Redacted multisig should also instill much trust and address most concerns.

The warden identified a potential admin privilege that would allow to set the fee to 100%.

I agree with the finding and severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted administrative fee mechanism in the BribeVault contract. The contract stores a fee parameter that is intended to be deducted from user‑deposited bribes, but the only restriction on this fee is that it is a uint256 value set by the admin via the setFee function. Because the setter does not enforce an upper bound, the admin can configure the fee to be as high as 100 % of the deposited amount. The fee is applied in a separate function (transferBribes) that runs after deposits have already been recorded, which means the fee value can be altered at any time, even after a user’s deposit has been accepted but before the transfer occurs. Consequently, an admin can retroactively increase the fee for previously made deposits, effectively confiscating users’ funds without prior notice. Moreover, because the fee can be changed in a single transaction, an attacker with admin privileges can front‑run pending deposit transactions, setting the fee to a maximal value just before a user’s deposit is processed, causing the user to receive no payout or to lose the entire deposited amount. The impact on users is loss of expected returns, potential disappearance of the full deposit, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s fee model. This situation arises whenever the contract is deployed with an admin that has unrestricted authority over setFee, and there is no timelock or upper limit to constrain fee adjustments. The affected parties include any user who deposits tokens into the BribeVault, the protocol’s reputation, and any downstream contracts that rely on the bribe payouts. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the privilege model and fee logic, noting that the lack of constraints on fee values constitutes an economic attack surface. The problem can be difficult to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the fee is changed, and the fee is applied in a separate function, so a user may not directly observe the fee value at the time of deposit. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable maximum fee (for example 30 %), introduce a timelock that delays fee changes to give users a window to react, and consider moving fee calculation into the same transaction as the deposit to prevent retroactive manipulation. By treating the fee as an immutable economic parameter or at least limiting its mutability, the contract can align with the principle of minimal trusted authority and protect user funds from arbitrary confiscation.

title: DEPOSITOR_ROLE can be granted by the deployer of `BribeVault` and transfer briber’s approved ERC20 tokens to `bribeVault` by specifying any `bribeIdentifier` and `rewardIdentifier`
poc: [BribeVault.sol#L164-L205](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L164-L205)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization flaw in the BribeVault contract that allows any address holding the DEPOSITOR_ROLE to initiate a token transfer from an arbitrary briber’s wallet. The depositBribeERC20 function of BribeVault accepts a briber address as a parameter and then calls IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(briber, address(this), amount). Because the contract only checks that the caller has the DEPOSITOR_ROLE and does not validate that the briber address matches the caller or any other on‑chain state, a malicious depositor contract can supply any user address that has previously granted an allowance to the BribeVault token contract. The root cause is that the permission check is performed solely on the caller’s role, while the source of the funds (the briber argument) is trusted implicitly without any additional verification. An attacker who obtains the DEPOSITOR_ROLE—either by being the deployer or by being granted the role by the admin—can craft calls that move approved ERC20 tokens from unsuspecting users to the vault, effectively stealing funds. The exploit can be carried out as soon as the malicious contract is granted the role and the targeted user has approved the BribeVault to spend their tokens; no further conditions are required. The parties affected are token holders who interact with the bribe system, the protocol that relies on honest bribe deposits, and any third‑party integrators that assume deposits are only performed by legitimate bribe contracts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of token approvals and role‑based access controls. It is difficult to notice because the function signature appears benign and the role check seems appropriate; the dangerous combination of a mutable role and an unchecked briber parameter is subtle. The bug belongs to the class of “insecure external caller authorization” or “unrestricted parameter trust” where a privileged role can act on behalf of arbitrary users. From a user’s perspective, a wallet that has approved the BribeVault may see its token balance drop unexpectedly after a proposal is submitted, even though the user never initiated a bribe. The expectation that a bribe transaction moves only the caller’s funds is violated; in reality the funds can disappear or be redirected without consent, breaking the accounting assumptions of the bribe system. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that the source of the transferred tokens is the caller (msg.sender) or a verified contract that can only move its own approved funds, and that the DEPOSITOR_ROLE is either removed or tightly scoped to known, audited contracts. A safer design would transfer tokens into the BribeVault from the caller first, then record the deposit, eliminating the need for an external briber parameter, or at minimum require that the briber address equals msg.sender. Additionally, limiting or auditing the granting of DEPOSITOR_ROLE reduces the attack surface.

title: `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` of `BribeVault` can steal tokens from users’ wallets
bug_full: The BribeVault contract contains an authorization flaw that enables the holder of the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to exfiltrate tokens from any address that has granted the contract an ERC‑20 allowance. The root cause is the combination of two design choices: (1) the admin role is allowed to call grantDepositorRole, which arbitrarily assigns the DEPOSITOR_ROLE to any address, including the admin itself; and (2) the depositBribeERC20 function trusts a caller‑supplied briber address and performs a safeTransferFrom from that address without ensuring that the caller is the same as the token source. Because safeTransferFrom pulls tokens from the briber’s allowance to the contract, a malicious admin can first grant themselves the DEPOSITOR_ROLE, then invoke depositBribeERC20 with a victim’s address as the briber argument. This causes the contract to withdraw the approved amount from the victim’s wallet into the vault. Immediately afterwards the admin can call emergencyWithdrawERC20, which lacks any additional access checks, to transfer the stolen tokens out of the vault to an address of their choosing. The attack can be carried out whenever a user has previously approved BribeVault for a token, which is often done with an unlimited allowance. The impact is direct theft of the approved token balance, leaving the victim with a zero or reduced balance without any user‑initiated transaction. Users experience the symptom of their token balance disappearing after merely approving the contract, contrary to the expectation that approval alone does not move funds. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit that examined role management and token transfer logic, and it is subtle because the deposit function appears benign and the emergency withdrawal is intended for legitimate rescue scenarios, masking the malicious path. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the token source in depositBribeERC20 is always msg.sender, remove the ability of the admin to grant DEPOSITOR_ROLE arbitrarily, add proper access controls to emergencyWithdrawERC20 (e.g., multi‑signature or time‑lock), and consider using a dedicated contract such as TokemakBribe that isolates user allowances from admin control. This class of bug falls under improper access control and allowance hijacking, where privileged roles can misuse user‑granted allowances to siphon funds, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that deposited bribes remain within the contract for the intended purpose.

title: Send ether with call instead of transfer
description: Use call instead of transfer to send ether. And return value must be checked if sending ether is successful or not. Sending ether with the transfer is no longer recommended.
poc: [RewardDistributor.sol#L181](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L181)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s use of the built‑in “transfer” function to forward Ether to external accounts. Transfer enforces a fixed 2300‑gas stipend for the recipient’s fallback execution and automatically reverts on failure, but recent protocol changes (such as EIP‑1884) and the prevalence of smart‑contract wallets that require more than 2300 gas can cause legitimate transfers to fail. Because the contract relies on transfer without any fallback handling, a malicious or even benign recipient contract that consumes more gas will trigger a revert, causing the Ether to remain locked in the sending contract and preventing the intended payout. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who deploys a contract with a fallback function that deliberately exceeds the stipend, causing every subsequent transfer to fail and effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition that halts the distribution logic. The impact is that users expecting a refund or reward receive nothing, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol may be unable to continue normal operation, potentially leading to loss of trust and frozen funds. The condition occurs whenever the contract attempts to send Ether to an address that is a contract with a fallback or receive function requiring more than the stipend, or when network upgrades raise the gas cost of opcodes used in the fallback. Both end‑users and the protocol itself are affected because payouts disappear and the accounting assumptions—“Ether sent will always be received”—are violated. The issue was identified during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which flagged the use of transfer as outdated and risky. It can be hard to notice because transfer appears to be a safe, high‑level abstraction, and developers may assume the 2300‑gas stipend is sufficient for all contracts, overlooking modern wallet implementations. The recommended mitigation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas, captures the boolean success flag, and explicitly reverts on failure, e.g., `(bool success, ) = payable(recipient).call{value: amount}(""); require(success, "Failed to send Ether");`. This approach aligns with current best practices, ensures that the contract actively checks delivery, and prevents silent reverts that would otherwise lock funds.

title: Wrong slippage check
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the addLiquidity function calculates a slippage guard for Curve pool deposits. The function first calls calc_token_amount to obtain the expected number of LP tokens for a given pair of assets and then reduces this value by a fixed‑percentage slippage amount before passing it as the minimum acceptable amount to the pool. According to Curve documentation, calc_token_amount already returns the exact number of LP tokens that the pool will mint for the supplied amounts, taking the current pool state and the inherent price impact (i.e., slippage) into account. By subtracting an additional percentage, the contract creates a minimum amount that is artificially low and does not reflect any real protection against price manipulation. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the Curve oracle semantics: the developer assumed calc_token_amount provides a pre‑slippage estimate, when in fact it already incorporates the pool’s price curve. Consequently, an attacker who can front‑run the transaction can first modify the pool balance (for example, by swapping a large amount of one asset) so that calc_token_amount returns a reduced LP token amount. Because the contract then subtracts further slippage, the resulting minAmount can become extremely small, allowing the maliciously altered transaction to succeed and mint far fewer LP tokens than the user expects. From the user’s perspective the UI would show a normal deposit request, but after execution the user may receive far fewer LP tokens, or even zero, contrary to the expectation of receiving a proportional share of the pool. This loss of value can occur whenever the pool is imbalanced or when a sandwich attack is possible; it does not require a direct front‑run if the pool is already heavily skewed, as the calculation would already return a low amount that the extra slippage subtraction fails to detect. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑checked the contract logic against Curve’s official documentation. It can be difficult to spot because the code appears to implement a defensive slippage check, yet the check is logically redundant and, in practice, nullifies the intended protection. The impact is a medium‑severity value extraction risk: liquidity providers can lose a portion of their deposited assets, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fair token minting are violated. To remediate, the slippage guard should be removed from on‑chain calculations. Instead, the expected minimum LP token amount should be calculated off‑chain using an accurate price source (e.g., a Chainlink feed) or supplied as a parameter, and the contract should enforce that the pool returns at least this external minimum. This approach restores a meaningful slippage check and prevents the contract from mistakenly accepting arbitrarily low token amounts.

title: `SafeERC20.sol` is imported but not used in the `transferBribes`
description: In BribeVault.sol the transferBribes() function uses token.transfer() instead of token.safeTransfer. Tokens that don’t correctly implement the latest EIP20 spec, like USDT, will be unusable in the protocol as they revert the transaction because of the missing return value. The fact that the SafeERC20.sol library is imported at the top of the BribeVault.sol implies that safeTransfer should be being used but may have been forgotten.
poc: [BribeVault.sol#L296](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L296)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the BribeVault contract moves ERC‑20 tokens when distributing bribes. The function that should transfer tokens calls the standard token.transfer() method directly, even though the contract imports OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library. SafeERC20’s safeTransfer() wrapper adds a check for the return value of the ERC‑20 call and gracefully handles tokens that do not follow the latest EIP‑20 specification – for example, USDT, which does not return a boolean and instead reverts when the caller does not handle the missing return data. Because the contract uses plain transfer(), any token that diverges from the spec will cause the transaction to revert, preventing the bribe from being sent and effectively making that token unusable in the protocol. This problem was discovered during an audit when the source code was examined and the mismatch between the imported library and the actual call pattern was noticed. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without errors and most well‑behaved tokens (e.g., DAI, USDC) return a boolean as expected, so the issue only surfaces with non‑standard tokens. When an attacker or a regular user attempts to invoke transferBribes() with a non‑compliant token, the call fails at the token.transfer() step, the whole transaction reverts, and the user sees no change in balances – the expected refund or bribe amount is not received, leading to a perception that the protocol “lost” funds or is broken. The impact is limited to users and the protocol that rely on those specific tokens; it does not affect tokens that are fully compliant, but it does break the business logic that assumes any ERC‑20 token can be transferred as a bribe. The flaw occurs whenever transferBribes() is called with a token that does not return a boolean – typically during bribe distribution or withdrawal. To remediate, the contract should replace direct token.transfer() calls with SafeERC20.safeTransfer(), which internally checks the call result and supports tokens that omit the return value, ensuring the transfer either succeeds or fails in a controlled manner without unexpected reverts. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “unsafe ERC‑20 transfer” bugs, where the caller assumes compliance with the ERC‑20 standard without verifying the return data, leading to incompatible token handling, loss of functionality, and broken accounting in the protocol.

title: Changing `bribeVault` in `RewardDistributor.sol` will Lock Current ETH Rewards
description:
[RewardDistributor.sol#L178-#L182](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L178-#L182)  
[RewardDistributor.sol#L65-#L73](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L65-#L73)

Claiming of the ETH native currency requires `token` to be set to `bribeVault`. If the `bribeVault` is modified in `setBribeVault()` then users who have ETH rewards will now be considered to have `ERC20(bribeVault)` tokens. Since `bribeVault` is not an ERC20 token the `transfer()` call will fail and the users will not be able to claim their funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RewardDistributor contract’s handling of ETH rewards through the configurable bribeVault address. The contract treats the variable token as an ERC20 token and invokes its transfer() function when a user claims rewards. For native ETH rewards, the token field is deliberately set to the address of the bribeVault, which the contract expects to behave like an ERC20 token that proxies the ETH payout. However, the bribeVault is not an ERC20 contract; it is merely a holder of native ETH. If the contract owner calls setBribeVault() and changes the bribeVault to a different address after users have accrued ETH rewards, the internal token reference is updated to point to a non‑ERC20 contract. Subsequent claim() calls attempt to execute ERC20.transfer() on this address, causing the call to revert because the contract does not implement the ERC20 interface. As a result, users who are entitled to ETH rewards are unable to claim them and the funds remain locked in the contract. The issue manifests only after the bribeVault address is altered while the contract still holds a positive ETH balance, making it easy to miss during routine testing that focuses on token rewards. This bug is a classic example of improper handling of native currency via an ERC20 abstraction combined with an insecure mutable configuration. It violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each reward type can be reclaimed through a standard transfer call, breaking the expectation that a claim will always succeed. From the user’s perspective, the UI may still display a claim button and show a pending reward amount, but the transaction fails silently or reverts, leaving the displayed balance unchanged and the user receives zero ETH. The root cause is the mutable bribeVault variable that does not enforce immutability or a zero‑balance precondition before being changed. To remediate, the bribeVault should be made immutable at deployment, or the contract must enforce that no ETH balance remains (balanceOf(address(this)) == 0) before allowing any change, or alternatively use a sentinel address such as address(0) or 0xeeeeeeee to represent native ETH in a way that does not rely on ERC20 semantics. These measures would prevent the lock‑up of ETH rewards and restore confidence that users can reliably retrieve their entitled funds.

title: Admin Privilege - Owner can rug via `ThecosomataETH.withdraw`
description:
Due to the generalized nature of `withdraw` the function is a clear rug-vector, allowing the `owner` to steal all funds.

Ideally, you should add some validation logic to limit the tokens or the amounts that the owner can withdraw.

Additionally, it’s important that you disclose the level of admin privilege and the risk it can cause to your users and depositors.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an unrestricted withdrawal routine that allows the contract owner – which in this deployment is a multisignature wallet that also funds the contract – to call a generic `withdraw` function and move any ERC‑20 token held by the contract to an arbitrary address. The root cause is the absence of any validation that distinguishes between tokens that should be recoverable (e.g., accidental stray tokens) and tokens that constitute user deposits or protocol‑owned assets such as BTRFLY and WETH. Because the function contains no protected‑token list, no amount limits, and relies solely on the `onlyOwner` modifier, the owner can invoke it at any time and sweep the entire balance of any token stored in the contract. An attacker with access to the owner’s signing keys, or a malicious internal participant, could therefore execute a rug pull by transferring all deposited funds out of the vault. From the user’s perspective, a depositor expects that after supplying BTRFLY or ETH their balance will be used by the protocol’s keepers to provide liquidity, but instead the balance may suddenly become zero with no refund or error message, indicating that the funds have vanished. The issue was identified during a security audit where the auditor examined the access control of the `withdraw` method and noted that it is a classic “admin‑rug” pattern often seen in vault contracts that lack protected‑token checks. The problem can be difficult to notice because the function is described as a utility for cleaning up stray tokens, a legitimate need in many contracts, and the presence of an owner role is common practice, leading developers to assume it is safe. To mitigate the risk, the contract should enforce a whitelist or protected‑token list that excludes core assets from being withdrawn, impose amount caps for recoverable tokens, and consider moving the withdraw role to a separate, tightly scoped role rather than the full owner authority. By structurally preventing the owner from moving user‑funds, the contract aligns with the expected business logic that deposits remain locked until processed by the protocol’s keepers, thereby eliminating the rug‑vector inherent in the current implementation.

title: Improper control over the versions of distributions’ metadata may lead to repeated claims of rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the BribeVault contract allows its DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to call updateRewardsMetadata() on the RewardDistributor. Each call overwrites the reward metadata and increments a per‑reward updateCount, which is also used as a version identifier to reset the internal claimed‑tracker for that distribution. Because the function does not verify the current version before applying the new metadata, an admin can submit two identical updateRewardsMetadata transactions—often inadvertently when the first transaction stalls due to network congestion and a second transaction with the same calldata is sent using the same nonce. When the first transaction is finally mined, the updateCount is incremented, the claimed‑tracker is reset, and any user who was eligible can claim the reward. If a user (e.g., Alice) claims after the first update and then the second identical update is mined in a later block, the claimed‑tracker is again reset to zero, permitting Alice to claim the same reward a second time. The impact is a double payout of the same reward, resulting in an unintended loss of funds for the protocol and a breach of the accounting assumptions that each reward may be claimed only once per distribution version. This issue surfaces primarily under congested network conditions where transaction re‑submission is common, and it affects any participant who can claim rewards as well as the protocol’s overall security posture because an admin with the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can arbitrarily reset reward eligibility, either accidentally or maliciously, to grant or deny claims at will. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the admin‑only metadata update and the reward‑claim logic, noting that the updateCount is used solely as a monotonically increasing counter without any guard against replaying the same version. The problem is subtle because the contract emits a normal RewardMetadataUpdated event and the metadata values appear unchanged, making the double‑claim scenario easy to miss in routine testing. The recommended mitigation is to require callers to provide the expected previous updateCount (or a similar version number) and to enforce that the stored updateCount matches this expected value before applying any changes, thereby preventing identical updates from resetting the claim state. In broader terms, this is an instance of improper version control or state‑reset vulnerability, where uncontrolled state changes enable replay of a claim‑reset operation and lead to double spending of allocated rewards.

title: Distributions must not match actual bribes
description:
The `BribeVault.transferBribes` transfers tokens for distribution.  
All parameters (`amounts`, `distributions`) are blindly accepted by the function and never verified to match the actual bribes that were deposited for the `distributions[i].rewardIdentifier`.

The `distributions[i].token` must not match the `distributions[i].rewardIdentifier`’s token (included in the reward identifier hash), and the `amounts[i]` (and fees) must not match the `bribes[bribeIdentifier].amount`.

The admin can submit arbitrary values and create distributions that don’t reflect the bribe the distribution is actually for. It’s easy to under-or overreport amounts for a bribe, take amounts from a different bribe, or steal all amounts from users by using 100% fees, distribute the same bribe over and over, etc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BribeVault contract’s transferBribes function, which is responsible for moving deposited bribe tokens to the recipients defined by a list of Distribution structs. The function accepts three external arrays—distributions, amounts and fees—directly from the caller without any on‑chain verification that these values correspond to the bribe that was previously recorded for each reward identifier. Because the contract never checks that the token address embedded in each Distribution matches the token encoded in the rewardIdentifier, and it never ensures that amount plus fees equals the amount stored in the bribes mapping, an administrator (or any entity that can submit a transaction from the protocol multisig) can submit arbitrary values. This permits the admin to under‑report or over‑report the amount to be paid, to assign a different token than the one originally bribe‑d, to charge excessive fees (up to 100 %), or to repeatedly distribute the same bribe by resetting the stored amount incorrectly. Exploitation proceeds by the admin crafting a call to transferBribes with mismatched parameters, causing the contract to debit the bribe pool according to the supplied numbers rather than the actual deposited amounts. As a result, users who deposited bribes may receive no reward, receive a smaller amount than expected, or see their entire balance disappear. The protocol’s accounting assumptions—that the on‑chain math for bribes distribution matches the off‑chain pledged amounts—are violated, breaking trust in the system. This flaw manifests whenever the admin invokes transferBribes, which is the only function permitted to move bribe funds, and therefore the risk is limited to the admin’s permissions but is severe because the admin controls a multisig that could be compromised or act maliciously. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the code paths for bribe distribution and noted the absence of any validation logic. It is difficult to notice from a user perspective because the UI typically displays the intended distribution amounts, and the contract does not emit explicit errors when the supplied data diverges from the stored bribe amounts, making the discrepancy invisible on‑chain until funds are missing. The recommended mitigation is to introduce explicit checks inside transferBribes: verify that each distribution’s token matches the token specified in its rewardIdentifier, confirm that amount + fee equals the bribe amount recorded for the corresponding bribeIdentifier, and clear the stored bribe amount after a successful payout. By tying the on‑chain transfer logic to the recorded bribe state, the protocol removes the need to trust the admin’s input and prevents arbitrary manipulation of reward payouts.

title: Depositor can spend funds of another Depositor
description:
1. One depositor can spend funds of another depositor
2. Depositor can deposit in expired proposal
3. rewardIdentifier and bribeIdentifier can point to different rounds/tokens
poc:
One depositor can spend funds of another depositor:

1. Malicious depositor can call depositBribeERC20 at BribeVault.sol#L164 with briber as User B (Malicious user can generate bribeIdentifier with his own proposal)
2. Assume this User B has approved amount x to this contract
3. BribeVault.sol#L187 (IERC20(token).safeTransferFrom(briber, address(this), amount);) will transfer this amount x to the contract due to call at step 1. All this happen without User B knowledge

Expired Proposal:

1. Malicious depositor can generate bribeIdentifier of an expired proposal (proposalDeadlines[proposal] < block.timestamp) using generateBribeVaultIdentifier at TokemakBribe.sol#L166
2. Malicious depositor can then simply call depositBribeERC20 at BribeVault.sol#L164
3. Since there is no deadline check and this function blindly trusts bribeIdentifier, user deposit will be success even though the associated proposal already expired

RewardIdentifier and bribeIdentifier can point to different rounds/tokens:

1. Similar to expired proposal, depositor can generate bribeIdentifier and RewardIdentifier with different tokens and rounds.
2. Depositor now calls depositBribeERC20 at BribeVault.sol#L164 with the generated bribeIdentifier and RewardIdentifier
3. rewardToBribes[rewardIdentifier].push(bribeIdentifier); will update reward for round x and bribeIdentifier will point to round y which is incorrect
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BribeVault contract’s depositBribeERC20 function, which is callable by any address that holds the DEPOSITOR_ROLE. The function accepts a bribeIdentifier that encodes a target proposal and token, but it performs no validation that the caller is authorised to act on behalf of the proposal’s owner, nor does it check whether the proposal has already expired. As a result, a malicious depositor can craft a bribeIdentifier that references another user’s active or expired proposal, call depositBribeERC20, and trigger an IERC20.safeTransferFrom that pulls the approved token amount from the unsuspecting user (the “briber”) into the vault. Because the contract trusts the supplied identifier blindly, the transfer succeeds without the briber’s consent or any deadline verification. In addition, the function allows a depositor to submit mismatched rewardIdentifier and bribeIdentifier values, causing the internal rewardToBribes mapping to link a bribe to a different round or token than the reward that is supposed to be paid. This breaks the accounting logic of the protocol: rewards may be credited to the wrong round, and the total token balances recorded for a round become inconsistent. The issue is triggered whenever a contract or externally owned account with DEPOSITOR_ROLE calls depositBribeERC20 with crafted identifiers; it does not require any special blockchain state beyond a user having previously approved the BribeVault to transfer tokens on their behalf. The affected parties are all users who have approved token allowances to the BribeVault, the protocol’s bribe‑reward accounting mechanisms, and any downstream contracts that rely on the integrity of those mappings. It was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected role assignments and the logic of the deposit functions, noticing the lack of checks on the identifiers and the open DEPOSITOR_ROLE privilege. The flaw is subtle because the function appears to be an internal utility for legitimate bribe contracts, and the absence of explicit require statements makes the problem easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict depositBribeERC20 to be invoked only by the designated TokemakBribe contract, enforce that the briber address matches the caller or is explicitly authorized, verify that the referenced proposal has not passed its deadline, and ensure that rewardIdentifier and bribeIdentifier refer to the same round and token before updating the reward‑to‑bribe mapping. By tightening the access control and adding identifier validation, the protocol can prevent unauthorized token transfers, protect users from silent fund loss, and maintain correct accounting of rewards and bribes.

title: Users Can Frontrun Calls to `updateRewardsMetadata`
description:
The `updateRewardsMetadata()` function is called by the `BribeVault` contract by the admin role. The function will take a list of distributions which are used to update the associated reward metadata. It is expected that the merkle root will be updated to correctly identify which claimers have already claimed tokens.

`reward.updateCount` is incremented to reset the claimed tracker, allowing users that may have previously claimed, to claim their updated reward. However, there is potential for mis-use if users frontrun calls to `updateRewardsMetadata()` and claim their reward after the new merkle root has been calculated and updated by the admin role. This may allow the claimer to double claim their rewards or lead to a loss in rewards if the reward metadata completely replaces the previous list of claimers.
poc:
[RewardDistributor.sol#L97-L119](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L97-L119)  
[RewardDistributor.sol#L127-L209](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L127-L209)
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from a race condition that allows a user to front‑run the administrative update of reward metadata in a merkle‑proof based reward distribution system. The contract stores a merkle root that encodes which addresses have already claimed a reward for a given distribution. When the admin calls updateRewardsMetadata() the contract increments reward.updateCount, which effectively resets the internal claimed‑tracker and replaces the stored merkle root with a new one that reflects a refreshed list of eligible claimers. Because the contract does not enforce a claim‑freeze period or otherwise prevent claims from being processed between the moment the new merkle root is written and the moment the system is ready to enforce the new state, an attacker can observe the pending admin transaction, wait until the new root is on‑chain, and then submit a claim transaction that uses a proof generated from the previous snapshot. The claim succeeds because the updateCount change clears the record of previous claims, and the new merkle root still validates the attacker’s proof. This enables a double‑claim of the same reward allocation, or, if the new metadata completely replaces the previous list, it can cause legitimate claimers to lose their entitlement because the contract now believes they have already been satisfied. The issue manifests when the admin role is able to change merkle proofs at any time without a timelock or a “blank” placeholder root, and when users are free to call claim immediately after the update. From a user perspective the symptoms are confusing: a user may see their reward balance disappear from the pool after a successful claim, or may notice that the same reward can be claimed twice, or that a later claim returns zero even though the user was previously eligible. The impact is a potential loss of funds for the protocol and for honest participants, as well as the possibility for a malicious actor to drain the reward pool by repeatedly exploiting the timing window. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running and state‑transition race conditions common in systems that rely on off‑chain generated proofs and on‑chain root updates without proper synchronization. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between updateRewardsMetadata() and the claim logic and noted that reward.updateCount is incremented without any protective delay. The problem is subtle because the claim function behaves normally and does not emit an explicit error; the double‑claim appears as a legitimate transaction, making it hard to detect without explicit accounting checks. A proper mitigation is to enforce a claim‑freeze interval whenever the merkle root is updated, to replace the root with a temporary empty placeholder while processing pending claims, or to adopt a single‑proof‑per‑distribution model that prevents a new proof from being generated while an older one is still valid. Additional safeguards such as submitting the new root through a private transaction relay (e.g., Flashbots) or using a snapshot‑based verification that rejects any claim made after the root change can also close the timing window and restore the integrity of the reward distribution logic.

title: Reentrancy in `depositBribeERC20` function
description:
[BribeVault.sol#L164-L205](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L164-L205)

```solidity
depositBribeERC20``` function in ``BriveVault``` is reentrant in line 187, where an address supplied by the caller is called.

A bad actor that has `DEPOSITOR_ROLE` and is a contract can execute a folowing attack:

1. Create a dummy token contract, reentrant in the transferFrom() function. All tokens are approved to the `BriveVault` and the attacker contract has unlimited tokens. Reentrancy aims back to a function in the attacker contract, which calls `depositBribeERC20` again.
2. The first call by the contract must use a novel `bribeIdentifier`. `token` is set to a dummy contract and `amount` to `uint(-2)`.
3. All checks pass, `transferFrom` is called, which calls attacker contract, which can call `depositBribeERC20` again, this time will transfer 1 wei of a valuable token, using the same `bribeIdentifier`. All checks pass as the previous token hasn’t been registered yet. Then, a valid transfer happens. After that, the amount is set to 1 wei and the token is saved. Event is emitted and the function returns value. Then, attacker function returns and dummy token returns. The operation is to increment amount in storage by the transfer value, which increases `b.amount` to the maximum integer. The token is nonzero, so the if statement is passed.

Thus, an attacker can grant any amount of tokens from `BriveVault` to a certain bribe, stealing all the funds once the bribe will be withdrawn.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the `depositBribeERC20` function of the BribeVault contract. The function performs an external call to the ERC‑20 token's `transferFrom` method before it updates the internal bookkeeping that tracks the amount of tokens associated with a given bribe identifier. Because the contract does not employ a re‑entrancy guard or follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, a malicious token contract can re‑enter `depositBribeERC20` during the `transferFrom` call. An attacker that holds the `DEPOSITOR_ROLE` can deploy a dummy ERC‑20 token whose `transferFrom` implementation calls back into the same `depositBribeERC20` function with the same `bribeIdentifier`. In the first call the attacker supplies a huge or special value (e.g., `uint256(-2)`) that passes the function's validation checks. When the token’s `transferFrom` triggers the re‑entrancy, the attacker makes a second deposit with a tiny legitimate amount (1 wei) of a valuable token. Because the internal `b.amount` storage variable has not yet been updated from the first call, the second call adds the 1 wei to the previously stored (malicious) amount, causing the stored amount to overflow to the maximum `uint256` value. The contract then records the token address as non‑zero, passes the final conditional check, emits an event and returns. Subsequent withdrawal of the bribe will therefore release the entire balance of the valuable token to the attacker, effectively stealing all funds allocated to that bribe. This flaw can be exploited any time a contract with the depositor role invokes `depositBribeERC20` using a token that the attacker controls, and it occurs because the contract trusts the token contract not to execute arbitrary code during `transferFrom`. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the code was examined for external calls that could lead to re‑entrancy. It can be hard to notice because token transfers are usually considered safe and the contract does not explicitly restrict the token address, allowing a malicious token to be injected unnoticed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a bribe that should contain a small amount of tokens suddenly appears to contain an enormous balance, or that after a legitimate withdrawal the vault’s funds are missing, contrary to the expectation that only the deposited amount can be withdrawn. The vulnerability belongs to the class of re‑entrancy bugs caused by improper ordering of state changes and external calls. To remediate the issue the contract should first record the token address and update the amount storage variables before invoking `transferFrom`, enforce a one‑time association between a bribe identifier and a token, and add a `nonReentrant` modifier (or otherwise use a re‑entrancy lock) to prevent recursive calls. Applying the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and restricting which tokens can be used mitigates the risk of the vault’s funds being drained by a malicious depositor.

title: transferBribes could transfer before proposal deadline + Input validation
description: It seems that Admin can call transferBribes even when proposals belonging to this rewardIdentifier have not expired. Also due to lack of input validation, token in distributions[i].rewardIdentifier might differ from distributions[i].token and also amount is not validated
poc:
transferBribes could transfer before proposal deadline:

1. Observe the transferBribes function at [BribeVault.sol#L256](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L256)
2. This is directly distributing the rewards for a rewardIdentifier even though proposal (bribeIdentifier) linked to this rewardToBribes[rewardIdentifier] might not have expired. This means users are still depositing and Admin transferred reward early

Input Validation:

1. Observe the transferBribes function at [BribeVault.sol#L256](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L256)
2. amounts object is directly passed by Admin and there is no verification to see that sum amount of all proposals under rewardToBribes[rewardIdentifier] is equal to amount provided by admin in argument
3. distributions[i].token is directly passed by Admin and there is no verification to see that token under distributions[i].rewardIdentifier is equal to the one provided by admin in argument
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BribeVault contract’s transferBribes function, which is intended to distribute reward tokens to users after a proposal’s voting period has ended. The function lacks two essential safety checks. First, it does not verify that the proposal linked to the supplied reward identifier (or bribe identifier) has actually expired, allowing the contract’s admin to execute a transfer before the official deadline. Second, the function performs no input validation on the data supplied by the admin: the token address associated with each distribution entry is not cross‑checked against the token tied to the reward identifier, and the total amount declared by the admin is not compared to the sum of the individual amounts in the distribution array. As a result, an admin (or any party that gains admin permission) can prematurely move reward funds, possibly before users have finished depositing or voting, and can mis‑allocate rewards by specifying an incorrect token or by providing a mismatched total amount. The exploit scenario is straightforward: the admin calls transferBribes with a valid reward identifier while the corresponding proposal is still active, and supplies an arbitrary distribution list. Because the contract does not enforce the deadline or validate the amounts and token mapping, the transaction succeeds, causing the contract to emit transfer events that appear legitimate while the underlying accounting is broken. Users may observe that their expected bribe reward is missing, that they receive zero tokens, or that they receive a different token than anticipated. From a business‑logic perspective this violates the core assumption that rewards are only distributed after a proposal’s outcome is final, undermining fairness and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the source code, where the absence of deadline checks and input assertions was highlighted. It is subtle because the function’s external behavior – emitting Transfer events – looks normal, and no revert or error is produced, making it difficult to detect without inspecting the code. The appropriate remediation is to enforce that the proposal’s deadline has passed before allowing any transfer, to verify that each distribution entry’s token matches the token associated with its reward identifier, and to ensure that the sum of the individual distribution amounts equals the total amount supplied by the caller. These checks move the validation logic on‑chain, eliminating reliance on off‑chain trust and providing clear, enforceable guarantees to users.

title: Fees can be any amount
description:
In `transferBribes`, the fees are user input, rather than calculation using `fee` (state var).  
Currently, `fee` is unused: [BribeVault.sol#L23](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L23).  

Therefore the fees amounts might be wrong.

I don’t believe M-14 mentions validation of fees, as such will mark this finding as unique.
 
Ultimately the function trusts the Admin input instead of using the storage variable, giving less security guarantees as to the fairness of the Distribution of the Bribes.
 
Because this is contingent on a malicious admin, I believe medium severity to be appropriate.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic flaw in the function responsible for distributing bribes, where the amount taken as a fee is supplied directly by the caller instead of being derived from the immutable fee parameter stored in contract state. The state variable that should define the fee percentage or amount is never referenced, leaving it effectively unused. Because the function trusts an externally supplied fee value—typically provided by an admin—the fee can be set to any arbitrary number, including values that exceed the total bribe amount or that completely drain the remaining tokens. This flaw originates from the mismatch between intended business logic (a fixed, validated fee) and the actual implementation (unrestricted user‑provided fee). An attacker who controls the admin role can invoke the bribe‑distribution routine with a malicious fee, causing the contract to deduct an excessive portion of the bribe before allocating the remainder to participants. The immediate impact is an unfair redistribution where legitimate participants receive less than expected, potentially resulting in a total loss of funds for the intended recipients. The condition for exploitation is straightforward: the adversary must have the authority to call the function and supply the fee argument, which is typical for an admin or privileged account. All users who rely on the bribe‑distribution mechanism are affected, as they may receive no payout or a dramatically reduced amount, contrary to the protocol’s advertised fairness guarantees. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public state variables with the actual code paths and noticed that the fee variable was never used, exposing a gap in validation. Because the function does not perform any sanity checks on the fee argument, the problem can be subtle to detect through normal testing unless edge cases with extreme fee values are explored. To remediate the vulnerability, the fee calculation should be hard‑coded to reference the immutable fee state variable, and the function should enforce bounds (e.g., fee ≤ maximum allowed percentage) and reject any fee that would cause under‑allocation. By aligning the implementation with the intended fee policy and adding proper validation, the contract can restore the expected economic behavior where participants receive a proportional share of the bribe after a predictable, limited fee is deducted. This class of bug falls under "unchecked user‑controlled parameters" that violate economic invariants, leading to scenarios where "funds disappear" or "reward calculation error" is observed from the user’s perspective, as users may see their expected refunds reduced to zero or unexpectedly low amounts.

title: `DEPOSITOR_ROLE` can manipulate `b.amount` value
description:
[BribeVault.sol#L187](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/BribeVault.sol#L187)  

Malicious `DEPOSITOR_ROLE` can doing self transfer and manipulate `b.amount`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BribeVault contract’s deposit routine, where a caller that possesses the DEPOSITOR_ROLE can invoke a token transfer that updates the internal bookkeeping variable b.amount without actually moving any assets. The root cause is the lack of validation that the destination address (the briber) is distinct from the vault itself. By supplying a token such as WETH, whose transferFrom implementation treats a self‑transfer (source and destination equal to the vault) as a regular transfer that does not require an allowance, a malicious depositor can craft a call where the vault transfers tokens to itself. Because the token contract does not adjust balances in this scenario—the source and destination are the same—the vault’s external token balance remains unchanged, yet the BribeVault logic adds the transferred amount to b.amount based on the value reported by the successful call. An attacker can therefore inflate the recorded bribe amount at zero cost. This manipulation can be exploited repeatedly, allowing the attacker to claim a larger share of any reward distribution that depends on the recorded bribe totals, effectively siphoning value from honest participants. The impact ranges from inaccurate accounting, misleading UI displays where the vault shows a higher total of bribes than the actual token balance, to potential economic loss for users who receive inflated rewards at the expense of the protocol’s integrity. The issue manifests whenever a DEPOSITOR_ROLE user supplies the address of a token that permits self‑transfer without allowance checks and sets the briber argument to the vault’s own address. It affects any participant relying on the vault’s accounting, including token holders, reward claimants, and the protocol governance that assumes correct bribe accounting. The flaw was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when the team examined the deposit logic and identified that the contract does not guard against self‑transfer scenarios. The problem is subtle because the external token transfer emits a success event and the contract’s internal state update proceeds without any apparent error, making the phantom increase in b.amount easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the briber (or any recipient) address is not the same as the vault contract, thereby rejecting self‑transfer calls, and optionally verify that the token balance of the vault decreases by the expected amount before updating the internal accounting. By introducing this check, the vault would only record genuine inflows, preserving the integrity of its accounting and preventing malicious inflation of bribe amounts.

title: ThecosomataETH: Oracle price can be better secured
description:
[ThecosomataETH.sol#L94-L110](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/ThecosomataETH.sol#L94-L110)  

The `ThecosomataETH` contract adds ETH and BTRFLY tokens as liquidity into the [ETH-BTRFLY curve crypto pool](https://etherscan.io/address/0xf43b15ab692fde1f9c24a9fce700adcc809d5391). The `calculateAmountRequiredForLP()` function relies on the `price_oracle` value returned by the pool to calculate the ETH and BTRFLY amounts to be added as liquidity. It is therefore important to ensure that `price_oracle` is accurate.

At the time of writing, the pool has about $5M in liquidity, which is comparable to that of the [liquidity provided on UniswapV3](https://info.uniswap.org/#/pools/0xdf9ab3c649005ebfdf682d2302ca1f673e0d37a2). Flash loan attacks are therefore possible, but ineffective (explained further later).

In the [curve v2 whitepaper](https://curve.fi/files/crypto-pools-paper.pdf), the price oracle mechanism is explained briefly in the “Algorithm for repegging” section. It is reproduced below for convenience.

Internally, we have a price oracle given by an exponential moving average (EMA) applied in N-dimensional price space. Suppose that the last reported price is `pLast`, and the update happened `t` seconds ago while the half-time of the EMA is `T1/2`. Then the oracle price `p_new` is given as:
    
    α = 2^(− t / T1/2);
    p_new = pLast * (1 - α) + α * p_old // p_old = current price_oracle
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the Curve crypto pool’s internal price oracle when calculating the amount of ETH and BTRFLY tokens required to add liquidity. The function `calculateAmountRequiredForLP()` takes the EMA‑based `price_oracle` value as the sole source of market price, but the contract does not enforce any freshness or volatility constraints on that oracle. Because the EMA smooths price changes over time, the reported price can become stale if the pool has not been updated recently, and it can be temporarily distorted during periods of high volatility or after a flash‑loan‑induced price swing. An attacker who can move a large amount of capital into the pool (for example via a flash loan) can cause the pool’s price to shift, and before the EMA converges back to the true market price the contract will read the manipulated `price_oracle`. It will then compute token amounts based on this incorrect price, leading the liquidity provider to deposit an unfavourable ratio of ETH to BTRFLY. The immediate impact is a mis‑allocation of capital: the provider may receive fewer LP tokens than expected, see part of their contribution effectively lost, or experience a sudden drop in the value of the LP position. In the worst case, repeated exploitation could erode the pool’s capital and reduce the protocol’s overall liquidity. The issue manifests whenever the pool’s price update interval exceeds a reasonable threshold (e.g., more than an hour) or when market volatility pushes the EMA‑derived price away from the instantaneous market price. All participants who rely on the contract to add liquidity – individual users, the protocol’s treasury, and downstream contracts – are affected. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the price‑oracle handling code and compared it against Curve’s white‑paper description of the EMA algorithm, noting the absence of any on‑chain checks for price staleness or volatility. It can be hard to detect in normal operation because the oracle still returns a numeric value, so there is no explicit error, and the loss may appear as a small discrepancy in received LP tokens rather than an outright failure. To remediate the issue, the contract should verify that the oracle price has been refreshed within a bounded time window and that the deviation between the last recorded price and the current EMA price stays within a defined tolerance (for example, 5%). Alternatively, an external, tamper‑resistant price feed could be used to replace the internal EMA oracle, providing a more reliable source of market data. From a user’s perspective, they expect to add liquidity at a fair market rate and receive a proportional amount of LP tokens; instead they might see their balance after the transaction be lower than anticipated, or in extreme cases receive no LP tokens at all, indicating that the calculated token amounts were based on stale or manipulated price data.

title: When transferring tokens native on SKALE to Ethereum with `TokenManagerERC20.exitToMainERC20`
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the TokenManagerERC20 contract that handles exiting ERC20 tokens from a SKALE sidechain back to Ethereum. When a user invokes exitToMainERC20, the function forwards the request to an internal _exit routine with the chain identifier set to MAINNET_HASH. The implementation does not contain a guard that blocks exits of tokens that are native to the sidechain (i.e., tokens that were minted directly on the SKALE chain rather than cloned from an existing Ethereum token). As a consequence, a user can supply a native sidechain token address and a main‑net contract address, causing the bridge logic to treat the token as a main‑chain token, invoke the auxiliary _receiveERC20 helper and encode the transfer message with the type TRANSFER_ERC20_AND_TOKEN_INFO or TRANSFER_ERC20_AND_TOTAL_SUPPLY. The DepositBoxERC20 contract on Ethereum, however, is designed to accept only messages of type TRANSFER_ERC20. When it receives the mismatched message, the message decoder in Messages.sol reverts, aborting the transfer on the main‑net side. At this point the sidechain TokenManagerERC20 has already taken the tokens from the user (by transferring them to its own balance and possibly burning them), while the main‑net contract refuses to credit the corresponding address. The net effect is that the user's tokens become frozen on the sidechain and never appear on Ethereum, effectively causing a loss of funds. This situation occurs only when the token is native to the sidechain and the caller deliberately sets the target chain to the main network; it does not affect regular cloned tokens that follow the intended bridge flow. The flaw was uncovered during a formal code audit that spotted the missing require(chainHash != MAINNET_HASH) check and the mismatch between the message types generated by TokenManagerERC20 and those accepted by DepositBoxERC20. The problem is subtle because the exitToMainERC20 function appears to succeed from the caller’s perspective – it does not revert on the sidechain – and the failure happens on a remote contract, making the loss hidden until the user inspects the main‑net balance. The correct remediation is to enforce a chain‑hash validation that prevents native sidechain tokens from being routed to the Ethereum mainnet, or alternatively to extend the DepositBoxERC20 to understand the additional message types. In abstract terms, the bug is a cross‑chain message‑type mismatch combined with insufficient input validation, leading to a token‑freeze scenario where the accounting assumptions of the bridge are violated: tokens deducted on one chain are not credited on the other.

title: S2S Transfer from the origin schain to another schain with automatic deploy disabled can cause funds to be frozen
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns cross‑chain token transfers on the SKALE bridge when the destination schain has automatic contract deployment disabled. When a user initiates a S2S transfer of a token that is native to the origin schain, the TokenManagerERC20 contract on the source chain calls the internal function _exit, which eventually calls _receiveERC20. If the token is an ERC20 that is not yet registered on the target schain, the bridge logic attempts to create (clone) a corresponding ERC20 contract on the destination chain during message processing in postMessage → _sendERC20. This creation is gated by the boolean automaticDeploy; when automaticDeploy is false, the code executes require(automaticDeploy, "Automatic deploy is disabled"), causing the inbound transaction to revert. Because the revert happens only on the destination side, the source‑side transaction appears to have succeeded – the amount is deducted from the user's balance and locked in the bridge contract – but the counterpart contract is never deployed and the inbound message is not completed. Consequently the locked tokens remain permanently frozen in the bridge contract on the origin schain. The root cause is an unchecked assumption that the destination schain will always be able to automatically deploy the ERC20 clone, together with a missing pre‑flight check on the automaticDeploy flag before allowing the outbound transfer. An attacker or a malicious admin could exploit the issue by disabling automaticDeploy on the target schain immediately before or during a user's transfer, causing the user's funds to become inaccessible without any indication on the source chain. The impact is that token holders lose access to their assets, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent (the total supply on the source chain is reduced while the destination chain shows no increase), and trust in the bridge erodes. The condition under which this occurs is narrow: the transferred token must be native to the origin chain, the token must not already have a deployed clone on the destination chain, and automaticDeploy must be false at the moment the inbound message is processed. This scenario was discovered during a static and functional audit of the bridge’s TokenManagerERC20 contract, where the control flow revealed the require statement without a corresponding safeguard on the outbound side. The issue can be hard to notice because the user's transaction receipt on the source chain does not contain an error, and no funds are moved on the destination chain, leading users to think the transfer succeeded while their balance on the target chain remains zero. To remediate, the bridge should cache the automaticDeploy status for each schain and reject outbound transfers when the flag is disabled, optionally requiring manual mapping of the token beforehand. Adding a timelock (e.g., 24 hours) before an admin can disable automaticDeploy would also mitigate race‑condition attacks. In broader terms, this is a class of cross‑chain deployment dependency bug where a downstream contract creation failure leads to asset lock, violating the expected invariant that a transferred amount appears on the target chain after a successful source‑side transaction.

title: Rewards can be lost
description: Reward can be lost if bribeVault calls the updateRewardsMetadata on same rewardIdentifier again before user can claim his reward (since merkleRoot and proof will get updated).
poc:
1. bribeVault calls the updateRewardsMetadata at [RewardDistributor.sol#L97](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-redacted-cartel/blob/main/contracts/RewardDistributor.sol#L97) using rewardIdentifier X  
2. Assume _distributions[i].proof contains merkle proof for User A  
3. User A fails to call claim function  
4. bribeVault again calls the updateRewardsMetadata at RewardDistributor.sol#L97 using rewardIdentifier X updating _distributions[i].proof which might not contain merkle proof of User A now. So User A loses his rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the ability of the bribeVault contract to invoke the updateRewardsMetadata function multiple times for the same rewardIdentifier while a reward distribution is still active. The function overwrites the stored merkleRoot and the associated proof data that users rely on to prove eligibility for their rewards. Because the merkle tree is recomputed and the proof for a particular user (for example, User A) is replaced when the metadata is updated, the original proof becomes invalid. Consequently, if a user has not yet called the claim function before the second update occurs, the contract will reject the claim or return zero, effectively causing the user’s allocated reward to disappear. This occurs whenever an admin or privileged account calls updateRewardsMetadata before all claimers have submitted their claims, either unintentionally due to a mistaken re‑initialisation of the merkle root or maliciously to deny payouts. The impact is a loss of expected funds for legitimate participants, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and erosion of trust in the reward distribution mechanism. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between bribeVault’s admin functions and the merkle‑proof‑based claim workflow; the auditors noted that the contract does not enforce a "claim‑finished" condition before allowing metadata to be altered. Detecting this problem in production can be difficult because the front‑end may still display that a reward is allocated, yet the claim transaction silently fails, leaving users confused by a zero‑balance result without obvious error messages. The flaw belongs to the class of mutable‑state‑or‑overwrites bugs in merkle‑proof‑based reward systems, where the integrity of the proof set is assumed to be immutable for the duration of the claim period. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict updateRewardsMetadata so that it can only be called after all entitled addresses have claimed, or it should make the merkleRoot immutable once a distribution is active, possibly by introducing a separate finalisation step or by storing claim state per user and refusing to replace proofs that would invalidate pending claims. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is that they see a reward allocated to their address but, when attempting to claim, they receive no tokens or encounter a revert, contrary to the expectation that the system will honor the announced payout. This mismatch between displayed rewards and actual claimability violates the protocol’s financial logic and can result in unrecoverable loss of funds for affected participants.

title: Transactions can be replayed when a connectedChain is removed and then reconnected
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the contract tracks message processing for connected sidechains. Each sidechain is represented by a struct that stores an incomingMessageCounter and an outgoingMessageCounter, which are used together with a cryptographic signature to guarantee that a given cross‑chain message can be processed only once. When a sidechain is removed via the removeConnectedChain function, the entire struct entry is deleted, including the counters, and when the same sidechain is later added again with _addConnectedChain the counters are re‑initialised to zero. Because the anti‑replay logic relies solely on the current counter values, resetting them to zero erases the historical record of which messages have already been processed. An attacker who controls the sidechain removal and reconnection (or who can trigger it through a governance or admin action) can therefore re‑submit a previously signed message that was valid before the removal. The contract will see the message as new because the counters have been reset, and the signature will still be valid, allowing the same operation to be executed repeatedly. This replay can lead to double‑spending, duplicate state changes, or unauthorized fund transfers, effectively causing funds to disappear or be transferred multiple times. The issue manifests only when a connected chain is disconnected and then reconnected while retaining the same validator set, which means the same signing keys are still accepted. Users of the affected protocol experience symptoms such as seeing the same transaction appear in logs multiple times, receiving duplicate events, or observing unexpected reductions in their balances after a single action. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of sidechain connections and identified that the counter reset logic undermines the replay protection mechanism. It is subtle because the delete operation appears benign and the contract otherwise behaves correctly when normal add/remove operations are performed; only when an attacker intentionally cycles the connection does the flaw become exploitable. To remediate the issue, the contract should preserve the monotonic counters across disconnections instead of deleting them, or at a minimum mark the connection as inactive without resetting the counters.
