bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw function of the LidoVault contract. When the vault is active (started but not yet ended) and a slashing event occurs in the underlying Lido liquid staking protocol, the stETH/ETH exchange ratio drops. The contract calculates the amount a user can withdraw based on the current ratio rather than the ratio that existed at the moment the user deposited. As a result, a user who withdraws after the slash receives less than their original deposit, while users who withdraw later, after the ratio has partially recovered, can receive more than their original deposit. This mis‑alignment breaks the intended accounting rule that each participant should receive either exactly their initial contribution or, in the case of a loss, share that loss proportionally. The bug can be exploited by timing withdrawals: an attacker can wait for a slash, withdraw a small portion to lock in a reduced amount, and then let the protocol recover, causing subsequent withdrawers to over‑receive at the attacker’s expense. The impact is a redistribution of funds that may leave later participants with inflated balances and earlier participants with a shortfall, effectively causing a loss of funds for some users and a gain for others. The condition occurs only while the vault is open and the underlying Lido pool experiences a slash; it does not affect closed vaults. The affected parties are any depositor who uses the vault during an active slash period, including regular users and protocol participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s withdrawal logic, where the auditor noticed that the pre‑condition users should receive exactly their initial amount was not enforced after a slash. The problem is subtle because the contract still allows withdrawals and the numbers appear plausible; only a careful comparison of pre‑slash and post‑slash balances reveals the discrepancy. To fix the issue, the withdrawal calculation should be anchored to the user’s original deposit amount and the stETH/ETH ratio at the time of deposit, or the contract should lock the ratio for the duration of the vault and apply it consistently, ensuring that losses are shared proportionally and no user can receive more than their entitled share. This class of bug is an accounting mismatch caused by using a mutable external price feed (the stETH/ETH ratio) for internal accounting without snapshotting, leading to withdrawal over‑payment after slashing recovery and violating the protocol’s financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective, a participant may see their balance drop unexpectedly after a slash and later notice that other users receive larger refunds than expected, contradicting the expectation that each user gets back exactly what they put in or a proportional loss.

title: Attacker will DoS LidoVault up to 36 days which
description:
upfront premium and variable depositors in return get all the yield produxed by the However, the protocol does not account for the fact that Lido may be DoSed for up to 36 days if it enters bunker mode. Assuming the return is 4% a year, users are losing approximately 4 * 36 / 365 == 0.4 %, which goes against the intended returns of the protocol.
Additionally, an attacker may forcefully trigger this by transferring only up to 100 wei of steth, which will make the protocol request an withdrawal and be on hold for 36 days.
The protocol should allow users to withdraw by swapping or similar, taking a much lower amount such as 0.12%, described here.
In LidoVault:712, anyone may transfer just 100 wei of steth and DoS the protocol, Internal pre-conditions None.
External pre-conditions
Lido enters bunker mode, which is in scope as it happens when a mass slashing event happens, which is in scope
The Lido Liquid Staking protocol can experience slashing incidents (such as this https://blog.lido.fi/post-mortem-launchnodes-slashing-incident/).
These incidents will decrease income from deposits to the Lido Liquid Staking protocol and could decrease the stETH balance. The contract must be operational after it
Attack Path
1. Vault has already requested all withdrawals, but they have not yet been claimed, so funds are in the protocol but it does not hold stEth anymore.
2. Attacker transfers 100 wei of steth, triggering the request of this 100 steth.
3. All funds are DoSed for 36 days.
36 days DoS, which means the protocol can not get the expected interest rate calculated.
poc: Look at the function LidoVault::vaultEndedWithdraw() for confirmation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the LidoVault contract that can be triggered by sending a trivial amount of stETH (as little as 100 wei) while the underlying Lido protocol is in bunker mode. Bunker mode is entered after a mass slashing event and causes withdrawal requests to be held for up to 36 days. The vault’s withdrawal logic does not check that the amount being requested is above a meaningful threshold; any non‑zero transfer causes the contract to issue a withdrawal request to Lido. Because the request is subject to the 36‑day delay, all capital that the vault is trying to manage becomes locked, preventing the vault from collecting the expected 4 % annual yield. From a user perspective, deposits appear to be stuck; balances shown in the UI remain unchanged and expected rewards are not credited, leading to a shortfall of roughly 0.4 % of the principal after 36 days. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s withdrawal function, where the auditor observed that the function vaultEndedWithdraw can be called with a minimal stETH amount and that the contract does not enforce a minimum request size. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly under normal conditions; only when Lido is in bunker mode does the delay become visible, making the bug easy to miss in routine testing. The root cause is the lack of a safeguard against tiny withdrawal triggers and the absence of an alternative exit path when the primary withdrawal mechanism is stalled. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum withdrawal request that reflects the expected claimable amount, and it should provide a fallback withdrawal method (for example, a direct token swap) that can be used when the standard request is pending for an extended period. This class of bug falls under ‘withdrawal‑request denial‑of‑service due to insufficient input validation’ and violates the protocol’s economic assumptions that deposited funds remain liquid enough to generate the advertised yield.

title: Stakers lose their commission
description:
Once a staker unstakes or gets removed, they permanently lose access to all their accrued commissions.
This is a problem as it can either happen mistakenly or if the staker gets removed by an admin or slashed. However even in that case, they should still be able to claim their previously accrued rewards since they did not act negatively during that period.
has the onlyStaker modifier, making it only callable by stakers.
Internal pre-conditions
None
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
Issue path in this case
• Staker stakes and accrues commissions over a few epochs
• Now either the staker unstakes or gets removed forcibly by the admin
• The staker has now lost access to all previously accrued rewards
Loss of unclaimed rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a reward‑claiming logic error that permanently blocks former stakers from retrieving commissions they have already earned. The contract uses an onlyStaker modifier on the function that distributes accrued commissions, meaning the function can be called only while the caller is actively listed as a staker. When a user voluntarily unstakes or is forcibly removed by an admin, their staker status is cleared before any pending rewards are withdrawn. Because the claim function is gated by the onlyStaker check, the user no longer satisfies the pre‑condition and therefore cannot invoke the reward payout. As a result, all previously accumulated commissions become inaccessible, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. This situation can be triggered during normal unstaking, accidental removal, or a malicious admin action, and it affects every participant who has earned commissions but later loses staker status. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s access control and reward flow, where the auditor noticed that the onlyStaker guard is applied to the reward‑distribution path without any fallback for former stakers. The bug is subtle because the function works correctly for active stakers, so no error is emitted; the loss only becomes apparent after the user attempts to claim rewards post‑unstake and receives nothing. The impact is a loss of unclaimed rewards, breaking the economic assumption that earned commissions remain claimable regardless of staking status, and it can erode trust in the protocol. To remediate, the claim function should be decoupled from the staker status – either by removing the onlyStaker modifier, allowing any address to invoke the claim, or by introducing a separate withdrawal mechanism that tracks pending commissions for former stakers and permits them to withdraw after unstaking. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that earned rewards are always withdrawable, regardless of the user’s current staking position.

title: Attacker can fill merkle tree in
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by a bounded Merkle tree that records every L2‑to‑L1 withdrawal message. The protocol allocates a single Merkle tree with a hard‑coded maximum of 2**32‑1 leaf entries and does not provide any mechanism to handle the situation when this limit is reached. When the leaf counter reaches the limit, the internal function that appends a new leaf reverts with a MerkleTreeFull error, which propagates back to the L2CrossDomainMessenger._sendMessage call and aborts the withdrawal transaction. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly invoking the cross‑domain messenger’s sendMessage function, batching many withdrawals (for example 200 per transaction) and automating the calls until the tree is completely filled. Because there are no pre‑conditions or access controls on the sendMessage function, any address can trigger the overflow, and the attacker only needs to spend gas to fill the tree. Once the tree is full, every subsequent withdrawal attempt fails with a revert, meaning users who try to move funds from L2 to L1 receive no funds, see a transaction revert, and may be told that the withdrawal “failed” without a clear reason. The impact is a permanent lock‑up of all L2‑to‑L1 funds, effectively bricking the rollup’s exit path and undermining user confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the Merkle tree implementation and noticed the hard limit without any rollover or emergency handling. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the tree will not be full under typical usage, and the error only appears after an extreme number of withdrawals, which may be mistaken for a transient failure. The bug belongs to the class of resource‑exhaustion or bounded‑data‑structure DoS vulnerabilities, where a fixed‑size container is allowed to be filled by untrusted callers. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that a withdrawal request results in a corresponding L1 transfer, but in the attacked state the user sees a transaction that reverts, receives no L1 funds, and may see a generic “MerkleTreeFull” error. To remediate the issue, the contract should not treat a full tree as a fatal condition; instead it could rotate to a new tree, increase the capacity, or provide an alternative withdrawal path when the limit is reached, ensuring that the protocol can continue to process exits even after the original tree is saturated.

title: Malicious sequencer can DoS proposal execution by inflating the amount of proposals to be pruned Found by HaxSecurity, underdog
bug_full: A governance contract contains a pruning routine that is executed every time a proposal is finalized. The routine iterates from the index of the first undeleted proposal (undeletedProposalStart) up to the ID of the proposal being executed, deleting the stored data for each intermediate proposal. Because the contract allows any address that holds the sequencer role to call createProposal without any rate‑limit or maximum‑proposal check, a malicious sequencer can submit a large number of dummy proposals in rapid succession. Each call to createProposal increments a global counter (currentProposalID) and stores a new entry, but never removes old entries. When a legitimate proposal is later executed, the pruning loop must walk through every proposal ID that was created since the last execution. If the counter has been inflated to thousands or millions, the loop consumes more gas than the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. From a user’s perspective the execution transaction fails with an out‑of‑gas error, the UI reports that the proposal cannot be executed, and governance parameters remain unchanged. The issue is a classic denial‑of‑service caused by an unbounded linear iteration over a data structure that can be arbitrarily grown by an attacker. It occurs only when the attacker possesses the sequencer role, which is obtainable by staking or delegation, and when the contract does not enforce any cooldown or maximum number of proposals. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the governance flow and noticed that the pruning logic lacked safeguards. The bug is subtle because the loop works correctly under normal conditions with a modest number of proposals, making the gas exhaustion only appear after the attacker deliberately inflates the proposal count. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a limit on the number of active proposals, introduce a time‑based cooldown between successive createProposal calls, or redesign the pruning mechanism to avoid iterating over every proposal (for example by using a batch‑prune approach or by storing a bitmap of deleted proposals). Restricting proposal creation to a trusted set of actors or adding rate‑limiting checks would also mitigate the risk and restore reliable governance execution.

title: In the revertBatch function, in
description:
An unchecked batch reversion will cause challenge invalidation for any committed batch, leading to batch rollback issues for challengers, as the isChallenged flag will reset unexpectedly. In the revertBatch function, the inChallenge state is set to false even if the batch that was challenged is not part of the reverted batch set. This causes ongoing challenges to be incorrectly invalidated:

```solidity
function revertBatch(bytes calldata _batchHeader, uint256 _count) external onlyOwner {
    // .... REDACTED FOR BREVITY ...
    if (!challenges[_batchIndex].finished) {
        batchChallengeReward[challenges[_batchIndex].challenger] += challenges[_batchIndex].challengeDeposit;
        inChallenge = false;
    }
    // .... REDACTED FOR BREVITY ...
}
```

In the above code, `if (!challenges[_batchIndex].finished)` will hold true for challenges that don't exist. If there are no challenges for a specific `_batchIndex`, then `challenges[_batchIndex].finished` will be false which in turn makes the if condition true. This will cause `inChallenge` to be set to false even when there are ongoing challenges.

Lets assume the following batches were committed to L1 Rollup:

Batch 123  
Batch 124  
Batch 125  
Batch 126

Challenger calls `challengeState` on batch 123. This sets `isChallenged` storage variable to true.

Batch 123 (challenged)  
Batch 124  
Batch 125  
Batch 126  
isChallenged = true

While the challenge is ongoing, the owner calls `revertBatch` on Batch 125 to revert both Batch 125 and Batch 126.

Batch 123 (challenged)  
Batch 124  
Batch 125 (reverted)  
Batch 126 (reverted)  
isChallenged = true

Due to the bug in the `revertBatch` function, `isChallenged` is set to false even though the challenged batch wasn’t in the reverted batches.

Batch 123 (challenged)  
Batch 124  
isChallenged = false

This will lead to issues when the protocol is paused. Due to the following check in the `setPause` function, the challenge will not be deleted while the protocol is paused:

```solidity
function setPause(bool _status) external onlyOwner {
    // .... REDACTED FOR BREVITY ...
    // inChallenge is set to false due to the bug in revertBatch
    if (inChallenge) {
        batchChallengeReward[challenges[batchChallenged].challenger] += challenges[batchChallenged].challengeDeposit;
        delete challenges[batchChallenged];
        inChallenge = false;
    }
    // .... REDACTED FOR BREVITY ...
}
```

During the protocol pause, the prover will not be able to verify the proof and if the pause period is larger than the proof window, prover will lose the challenge and gets slashed.

Internal pre-conditions
1. Owner calls `revertBatch` on batch n, reverting the nth batch.
2. Challenger monitors the mempool and initiates a challenge on the n-1 batch.
3. Due to the bug in `revertBatch`, the `inChallenge` flag is reset to false, even though batch n-1 is under challenge.
4. Owner calls `setPause` and the protocol is paused longer than the challenge window.

External pre-conditions
None.

Attack Path
1. The owner calls `revertBatch` on batch n, reverting batch n.
2. A challenger monitors the mempool and calls `challengeBatch` on batch n-1.
3. The `revertBatch` function incorrectly resets the `inChallenge` flag to false despite batch n-1 being under challenge.
4. The protocol is paused, preventing the challenge from being deleted.
5. The prover cannot prove the batch in time due to the paused protocol.
6. The prover gets slashed, even though the batch is valid. If the protocol is paused when there's an ongoing challenge (albeit `inChallenge` is set to false due to the vulnerability explained above), the protocol slashes the batch submitter for failing to prove the batch in the challenge window, even though the batch is valid. The challenger may incorrectly receive the challenge reward + slash reward despite no actual issue in the batch.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batch reversion routine of a roll‑up contract where a global boolean that signals an active challenge (often called inChallenge or isChallenged) is cleared without confirming that the reverted batch actually participates in the ongoing dispute. The root cause is an unchecked condition that reads the finished flag of a challenge struct at an arbitrary index; when no challenge exists for that index the struct fields default to zero, making finished evaluate to false. Consequently the conditional branch that resets the challenge flag executes even for non‑existent challenges. An attacker – typically the contract owner – can invoke revertBatch on any batch while a challenger has an open dispute on a different batch. The function will mistakenly set the global challenge flag to false, leading the protocol to believe that no challenge is active. When the owner subsequently pauses the contract, the pause logic checks the same flag and skips the deletion of the legitimate challenge. Because the protocol is paused, the prover cannot submit the required proof within the challenge window, causing the batch submitter to be slashed despite having submitted a correct batch, while the challenger may still receive the challenge reward. The impact includes loss of funds for honest batch submitters, unintended reward distribution to challengers, and a breach of the protocol’s security guarantees that rely on accurate challenge state tracking. This bug manifests only when a revertBatch call occurs during an active challenge and is followed by a pause that exceeds the challenge window; it therefore affects batch submitters, challengers, and the overall integrity of the roll‑up system. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined state transitions of the challenge lifecycle and noticed that the inChallenge flag could be cleared by unrelated batch reverts. It is hard to detect because the flag is a single boolean and typical unit tests may not exercise the specific sequence of revert, challenge, and pause. The proper remediation is to verify that a challenge actually exists for the batch being reverted before resetting the flag, for example by using a helper function that checks the challenge mapping and only clears inChallenge when the challenged batch is part of the reverted set, and by deleting the challenge entry appropriately. This class of bug is an unchecked state mutation that leads to false positives in challenge detection, violating accounting assumptions that a challenge flag accurately reflects active disputes. From a user perspective, a challenger may see their challenge disappear and still receive a reward even though no fault existed, while a batch submitter may see their batch slashed and funds disappear, contradicting the expectation that a valid batch should not be penalised.

title: Rollup.sol cannot split batches
description:
The maximum amount of calldata that can be passed to an L2 transaction is too large to fit in a single blob. Because Rollup.sol does not allow splitting batches, L2 blocks are capped by their calldata size. This is not properly accounted for in the L2 gas prices, and leads to an attack where blocks can be inexpensively stuffed, blocking all L2 transactions on the chain. Batches are expected to commit to many blocks. We can expect up to 100 blocks per chunk (MaxBlocksPerChunk in node/types/chunk.go), and 45 chunks per batch (maxChunks in Gov.sol). This means that a batch can commit to 4500 blocks. However, Rollup.sol has the surprising quirk that a full batch must fit into a single blob. For that reason, the batch is not just limited based on blocks, but also by calldata. We can see this logic in miner/pipeline.go#L260-266, where the block size is being tracked, and we skip all transactions that push it past0 over the limit for the blob. In the event that a user submits a single transaction with enough calldata to fill a whole blob, this transaction will end the block, and the entire batch will consist of the single block with one transaction. This has two important implications: First, the gas cost of stuffing an entire block is loosely the price of sending 128kb of calldata. For a transaction with no execution or value, we can calculate the L2 gas cost as intrinsicgas + calldata + l1DataFee. If we assume an l1BaseFee of 30 gwei, an l1BlobBaseFee of 1, and the scalar and l2BaseFee values from the config file, we get:
• intrinsicgas = 21_000 gas = 21 gwei
• calldata = 1024 * 128 * (4 + 16) / 2 = 1,310,720 gas = 1,310 gwei (assumes half non-zero bytes to avoid compression)
• l1DataFee = (1024 * 128 * 1 * 0.4) + (230 * 30) = 59,328 gwei
• total cost = 21 + 1,310 + 59,328 = 60,659 gwei ≈ 0.06 ETH

Second, and more importantly, block stuffing is usually protected by EIP1559 style gas pricing, where the base fee increases dramatically if sequential blocks are full. However, this block stuffing attack has the strange quirk that only 1.3 million gas (out of 30 million gas limit) will be used, which will actually lower the base fee over time.

Internal Preconditions
None

External Preconditions
None

Attack Path
1. Submit a large number of transactions on L2 that use 128kb of calldata.
2. Each time one is picked up (which should be each block), it costs only 1.3 million gas, but seals the block with no other L2 transactions. L2 blocks will be stuffed and most activity on L2 will be blocked. This can cause major and unpredictable issues, such as oracles getting out of date, liquidations not occurring on time, and users being unable to take other important actions.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a design limitation in the rollup contract that forces an entire batch of L2 blocks to be stored in a single calldata blob. Because the maximum blob size is fixed, the contract does not provide a mechanism to split a batch across multiple blobs. As a result the batch size is bounded not only by the number of blocks it can contain (up to 4 500 blocks according to the protocol parameters) but also by the total calldata volume of the batch. When a user submits a transaction whose calldata alone occupies the full 128 KB blob, the rollup logic treats the transaction as the sole block of the batch and immediately seals the block. This behaviour can be abused by repeatedly sending large‑calldata transactions that contain almost no execution logic or value transfer. Each such transaction consumes roughly 1.3 million gas, far below the 30 million gas block limit, yet it fills the blob and prevents any other transactions from being included in the same block. Because the gas consumption is low, the EIP‑1559 base fee does not rise as it would for a genuinely full block; instead the base fee may even drift downward, further reducing the cost of the attack. The practical impact is a denial‑of‑service condition on the L2 chain: users see their transactions remain pending indefinitely, balances appear unchanged, and the UI shows no new blocks or activity. Oracles may become stale, liquidations can be delayed, and any time‑sensitive protocol action is blocked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the rollup’s batch‑handling code, where the auditor observed that the pipeline tracks blob size and skips transactions that would exceed the limit, but never attempts to split a batch. The problem is subtle because the low gas cost makes the attack cheap and the base‑fee dynamics hide the congestion, making it easy to overlook during routine testing. The correct mitigation is to redesign the batch architecture so that a batch may be divided across multiple blobs when its calldata exceeds the single‑blob limit, and to adjust gas pricing or block‑formation rules to account for calldata size, thereby preventing a single large‑calldata transaction from monopolising block space.

title: Possible wrong accounting in
description:
Possible wrong accounting in L1Staking.sol during some slashing occasions. Stakers are permitted to commit batches in the rollup contract and these batches can be challenged by challengers. If the challenge is successful, the challenger gets part of the staker's ETH and the staker is removed; the owner also takes the rest. If it wasn't successful, the prover takes all the challengeDeposit. According to proofWindow, which is the time a challenged batch has to go without being proven for it to be successfully challenged, can be set to as high as 604800 seconds (7 days), and withdrawalLockBlocks default value is also 7 days (No relation between the two was done and owner can change proofWindow value in rollup contract). For this vulnerability we'll assume proofWindow is set to 7 days.

The issue stems from a staker being able to commit a wrong batch and still being able to withdraw from the staking contract without that batch being finalized or proven. Let's cite this example with proofWindow being set to 7 days:
• Alice, a staker, commits a wrong batch and immediately goes ahead to withdraw her ETH from the staking contract. Her 7 days period countdown starts.
• Bob, a challenger, sees that wrong batch and challenges it. Since it's a wrong batch, there's no proof for it, so a 7-day countdown starts. But remember the withdraw function's 7-day countdown started first, so when it elapses, Alice quickly withdraws her ETH.
• Then when Bob calls proveState(), Alice is supposedly slashed, but it's useless as she's already left the system.
• Then the contract is updated as though Alice's ETH is still in the contract:

```solidity
uint256 reward = (valueSum * rewardPercentage) / 100;
slashRemaining += valueSum - reward;
_transfer(rollupContract, reward);
```

So a current staker's ETH is the one being sent to the rollup contract and being assigned to the owner via `slashRemaining`. So there's less ETH than the contract is accounting for, which is already an issue. This will be detrimental when all the ETH is being withdrawn by stakers and the owner, the last person's transaction will revert because that ETH is not in the contract.

Incorrect contract accounting.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that arises when a staker is allowed to withdraw their stake while a batch they submitted is still under challenge. In L1Staking.sol a staker can commit a batch and then call withdraw, which starts a withdrawal lock period (default 7 days). Independently, a challenger can dispute the batch, triggering a proofWindow that also lasts up to 7 days before the challenge can be resolved. Because the contract does not enforce any relationship between the withdrawal lock and the proofWindow, the staker can complete the withdrawal before the challenge is resolved. When the challenger later calls proveState, the contract treats the staker as still having the original stake, calculates a slash amount, transfers a reward to the rollup contract and records the remaining amount in slashRemaining, even though the staker’s ETH has already left the contract. This double‑counting inflates the contract’s internal balance, so later withdrawals by honest participants or the owner may revert due to insufficient actual ether. The bug occurs whenever proofWindow is set to a value that does not exceed the withdrawal lock, which the owner can change arbitrarily, and when a malicious staker submits an invalid batch and immediately withdraws. Affected parties include all stakers, challengers, the protocol owner and any user attempting to withdraw funds after the inconsistency has accumulated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the staking contract’s state‑transition logic, where the interaction between batch challenges and withdrawal timing was examined. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert at the moment of the double‑count; the mismatch only surfaces after many withdrawals have been processed, leading to unexpected reverts or missing funds. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of race‑condition accounting errors where a withdrawal is permitted before a pending penalty is applied, often described as a “withdraw‑before‑slash” or “double‑spend accounting” flaw. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a staker who submitted a bad batch can still retrieve their full deposit, while later users see their balance become zero or experience failed withdrawals despite the contract reporting sufficient funds. The proper fix is to prevent withdrawals while any of the staker’s batches remain unfinalized or unproven and to enforce that the withdrawal lock period is strictly greater than the proofWindow, ensuring that the stake is either slashed or locked before it can be withdrawn. Additionally, the accounting updates should deduct the stake at the moment a withdrawal is initiated or when a challenge is resolved, eliminating the possibility of counting ether that is no longer present in the contract.

title: The 255th staker in L1Staking.s
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the bitmap‑to‑address conversion used when slashing stakers. L1Staking stores up to 255 stakers in a fixed‑size array and represents their presence with a bitmap where each bit corresponds to a staker index plus one. The helper function that extracts addresses from the bitmap iterates with a loop condition i < 255, therefore it never checks the 255th bit (i.e. the bit representing the staker stored at index 254). When the 255th staker is the only participant in a challenge, the bitmap contains only that highest bit. The conversion routine builds an array of length one but fills it with address(0) because the loop never matches the bit. Consequently, the slash() routine receives address(0) instead of the real staker address. The code that removes a slashed staker treats address(0) as a normal address, adds it to the delete list and updates internal bookkeeping, but the actual 255th staker remains in the active set. This allows the 255th staker to avoid being removed after a successful challenge while the challenger still receives the slashing reward. Over time the protocol’s staking pool can be drained because slashed funds are deducted from the contract balance but the offending staker is never expelled, breaking the business assumption that a slashed participant is always removed. The bug manifests only when the contract reaches its maximum capacity of 255 stakers and the highest‑indexed staker is involved in a challenge, a situation that typical tests with fewer participants do not cover. It was discovered during a systematic audit that registered exactly 255 stakers and observed that the slashing function returned a zero address. The issue is subtle because the off‑by‑one condition does not raise a runtime error; it merely produces an unexpected zero address that silently bypasses the removal logic. To fix the problem the bitmap extraction loop must include the 255th bit, for example by changing the loop condition to i <= 255 or by redesigning the bitmap handling so that the highest bit is correctly mapped to the last array entry. This ensures that any staker, including the 255th, is properly identified and removed when slashed, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing inadvertent loss of funds.

title: Batches committed during an
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the batch finalization logic of a roll‑up protocol where batches are committed, challenged and then finalized. A batch is normally given a fixed finalization period (finalizationPeriodSeconds) after which anyone may call finalizeBatch(). When a challenger initiates a challenge, the contract extends the finalization timestamps of all *unfinalized* batches except the one being challenged by adding the proofWindow (the duration of the challenge). This extension is intended to compensate for the time during which those batches cannot be challenged. However, the code that creates a new batch during an active challenge does not apply the same compensation. The new batch receives a finalization timestamp equal to block.timestamp + finalizationPeriodSeconds, ignoring the fact that a challenge is already in progress. Because proofWindow (2 days) is longer than finalizationPeriodSeconds (1 day), a batch committed shortly after a challenge starts becomes eligible for finalization before the ongoing challenge finishes. The protocol permits finalizing a batch only after its parent batch is finalized, but an attacker can back‑run two finalizeBatch() calls – first for the challenged parent batch (once the defender wins) and immediately afterwards for the newly committed child batch. Since the child batch’s challenge window never opened, no challenger can ever dispute it. Consequently, an invalid batch can be permanently accepted, breaking the accounting guarantees of the L2, potentially allowing a malicious sequencer to submit fraudulent state transitions and, in the worst case, brick the entire system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between challengeState() and the batch commitment routine. It is subtle because the normal flow of extending timestamps appears correct; the edge case only manifests when a batch is created while inChallenge is true, a scenario that is not covered by the existing tests. The proper mitigation is to adjust the finalization timestamp of a newly committed batch to also include the remaining challenge time, i.e., add proofWindow minus the elapsed time of the current challenge when inChallenge is true. This ensures that every batch, regardless of when it is committed, respects the full challenge window and cannot be finalized before it is safely challengeable.

title: Malicious challenger can brick f
description:
A malicious challenger can brick the delay for the finalization of batches. This is possible due to the uncapped extension of the finalization period for all unfinalized batches within the challengeState function. The challengeState function extends the finalizeTimestamp by doing an addition with the proofWindow variable (2 days) for each index (all unfinalized batches) except the challenged one, with not a single check or safeguard:
```solidity
for (uint256 i = lastFinalizedBatchIndex + 1; i <= lastCommittedBatchIndex; i++) {
    if (i != batchIndex) {
        batchDataStore[i].finalizeTimestamp += proofWindow;
    }
}
```
The permissionless proveState function allows anyone including challengers to provide a ZK-proof and immediate resolution of a challenge, setting inChallenge to false:
```solidity
// Mark challenge as finished
challenges[_batchIndex].finished = true;
inChallenge = false;
```
Attack details:
• An attack window of 15 minutes (could be longer)
  – 15 minutes = ~ 75 Ethereum blocks (12 seconds per block)
  – Challenge-prove cycle (due to inChallenge flag) => 2 blocks per cycle => 37 batches
  – Each cycle extends the finalization period for all other batches by proofWindow = 2 days (37 cycles * 2 days per cycle) means that each batch would incur an additional extension of ~74 days!
• Attackers capital: 37 ETH => while risking 1 ETH!
  – Or maybe not, because the malicious challenger could get his deposit back whenever admin pauses the contract see Rollup::L444
  – claimReward function doesn't have a whenNotPaused modifier meaning that the owner has no ability to freeze attackers funds see Rollup::L543
This combination allows an attacker to:
1. Pre-generate ZK proofs for multiple batches (32 unfinalized batch)
2. Call challengeState function - Initiate a challenge on a batch
3. Call proveState function - Immediately prove the batch in the next block
• Repeat steps 2-3 multiple times
Result: Each cycle extends the finalization period for all other batches by proofWindow (2 days), finalizeTimestamp accumulates a significant delay due to repetitive extension.
• Massive delay for unfinalized batches (uncapped delay) - Huge impact on L2 - Short-term: loss of time and money
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded extension of the finalization deadline for L2 batches caused by the challengeState function. When a challenger initiates a challenge on a specific batch, the function iterates over every unfinalized batch and adds the proofWindow (two days) to each batch’s finalizeTimestamp, except for the challenged batch. Because the loop contains no guardrails—no cap on the total added time, no check that a batch actually needs an extension, and no per‑address cooldown—the timestamp can be increased repeatedly. The exploit is enabled by the permission‑less proveState function, which allows any actor, including the challenger, to submit a zero‑knowledge proof and immediately mark the challenge as finished, resetting the inChallenge flag in a single block. An attacker can therefore repeat the following steps many times: pre‑compute valid ZK proofs for a set of unfinalized batches, call challengeState to start a challenge on one batch, call proveState in the next block to resolve it instantly, and repeat. Each cycle adds two days to every other pending batch; with roughly 37 cycles possible within a 15‑minute window, the cumulative delay can exceed 70 days for each batch. From a user’s point of view the system appears to “brick”: withdrawals and state updates that should finalize within hours remain pending for weeks, the UI shows batches stuck in an unfinalized state, and users receive no confirmation that their funds are moving. The impact is a severe degradation of L2 throughput, loss of confidence in the roll‑up, and potential economic loss for participants who rely on timely finality. The issue occurs whenever the contract is active (not paused) because claimReward lacks a whenNotPaused guard, allowing the attacker to keep the deposit available. It was discovered during a manual audit of the roll‑up’s challenge logic, where the auditor noticed that the loop blindly increments timestamps without limits. The bug is hard to spot because each individual extension looks legitimate—protocol rules permit a two‑day proof window—yet the aggregate effect is hidden until many cycles are executed. To remediate, the design should enforce a maximum total extension per batch, introduce a cooldown period for repeated challenges from the same address, limit the loop to only batches that truly require an extension, add pause protection to reward‑related functions, and consider restricting the prover role to trusted entities. These mitigations would prevent a malicious challenger from artificially inflating finalization times and protect the protocol’s expected accounting and user experience.

title: A batch can be unintentionally
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the challengeState function of a roll‑up contract that allows a challenger to submit a deposit and specify a batch by its numeric index only. The function checks that the index refers to an existing, unfinalized batch and that the challenge window is still open, but it never verifies that the batch data stored at that index matches the batch the challenger intends to dispute. Because the contract relies on the L1 ordering of transactions that create batches, a reorganization of the underlying Ethereum chain can change which batch occupies a given index after the challenger has decided which index to challenge. In a typical scenario, two conflicting batches are submitted to the same index: an incorrect batch first, followed by a correct batch that reverts because the slot is already occupied. If an L1 reorg flips the order of these two submissions, the correct batch becomes the one stored at the index at the moment the challengeState transaction is mined. The challenger, believing they are targeting the incorrect batch, ends up challenging the correct batch. The protocol then proves the challenge invalid and slashes the challenger’s deposit, resulting in a loss of funds for the challenger. This issue manifests only when an L1 reorg occurs and when multiple batches compete for the same index, conditions that are rare but possible in a decentralized environment. The affected parties are challengers who expect to recover a bond by proving an invalid batch, as well as the protocol’s economic security because honest challengers may be discouraged from participating. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of challengeState with other functions such as revertBatch, which correctly validate the batch hash before proceeding. The problem is subtle because the contract’s public checks (index existence, challenge window) all pass, making the incorrect challenge appear legitimate from the UI perspective; users see no error messages, only the unexpected loss of their stake. To remediate, the function should load the batch header supplied by the challenger, compute the batch hash, and assert that the stored hash at the given index matches this value, mirroring the verification performed in revertBatch. By binding the challenge to a specific batch hash rather than just an index, the contract prevents a reorg from silently swapping the challenged batch and protects challengers from unintended loss.

title: Delegators can lose their re-wards when a delegator has removed a del-egatee and claims all of his rewards before delegating again to a previous removed delegatee. Found by 0xStalin
bug_full: A delegator can lose earned rewards due to the interaction of two logical bugs in the reward‑claiming and delegation workflow. The first bug appears in the function that claims all pending rewards for a delegator. The contract stores the set of delegatees in an EnumerableSet and iterates over it with a for‑loop that uses the current length of the set as its upper bound. When a delegatee has been undelegated, the claim routine removes that delegatee from the set during the same iteration. Because the set shrinks, the loop counter eventually reaches the new, smaller length and the loop terminates early, leaving the remaining delegatees unprocessed and their rewards unclaimed. The second bug occurs when a delegator later re‑delegates to a delegatee that was previously undelegated. The delegation logic records a new unclaimedStart epoch equal to the effective epoch of the new delegation without checking whether the delegatee still has pending rewards from earlier epochs. The internal _claim function requires the claimed epoch to be greater than or equal to unclaimedStart, so any rewards earned before the effective epoch become permanently inaccessible. The attack path is: (1) the delegator undelegates one or more delegatees, (2) calls claimAll, which skips rewards for some delegatees because the set shrinks, (3) claims the undelegation, (4) re‑delegates to a previously removed delegatee, which resets the accounting window and discards the unclaimed rewards that were missed in step 2. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful claim transaction but the token balance increases by less than the expected amount; later the user sees zero reward for a delegatee that should still have pending rewards. The impact is a loss of funds that become stuck in the distribution contract, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all earned rewards are claimable. The issue was discovered by the auditor 0xStalin through manual code inspection and a reproducible proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated missing rewards after the described sequence. The bug is hard to notice because the loop does not revert or emit an error; it simply stops iterating, so developers may assume all delegatees were processed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of mutable‑collection‑iteration bugs (modifying a data structure while iterating over it) combined with improper state reset that leads to accounting loss. To fix the first bug the contract should snapshot the delegatee list into a fixed‑size array before iterating, or avoid removing entries during the loop. To fix the second bug the delegation routine must check for any pending rewards for the delegatee before overwriting unclaimedStart, either by claiming those rewards or by reverting the transaction. Both fixes restore the guarantee that a delegator’s rewards are fully claimable and that re‑delegation does not erase previously earned amounts.

title: A borrower can not repay to a USDC black-
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the repayment logic that moves the loan token directly from the borrower to the lender using safeTransferFrom. When the loan token is USDC, which supports a blacklist feature, any lender address that has been added to the USDC blacklist will reject incoming transfers. Because the contract does not anticipate or handle this external restriction, the repayment transaction reverts, leaving the borrower unable to complete the repayment, unable to retrieve the ERC‑1155 collateral, and preventing the protocol’s default‑auction mechanism from operating correctly. The loan status is set to Repaid before the token transfer is attempted, so even if the transfer fails the contract may record an inconsistent state. This failure only manifests after a lender has been blacklisted by the USDC contract after the loan was originated; it affects any borrower who tries to repay a loan whose lender is on the blacklist, as well as the protocol because collateral can become permanently locked or be seized improperly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the repayment flow, where the auditor observed that the contract assumes a token transfer will always succeed and does not check for token‑level restrictions such as blacklisting. The bug is subtle because the blacklist is an external state that is not visible from within the loan contract, and it only triggers under the specific condition of a blacklisted lender, which may not be covered by standard tests. From the user’s perspective the repayment transaction fails with a revert, the UI may incorrectly show a successful repayment, the borrower receives no USDC back, and the collateral remains locked, leading to confusion and potential loss of assets. The proper mitigation is to redesign the repayment process to a push‑pull model: the borrower should transfer the loan token to the PredictDotLoan contract, which then credits the lender’s balance, and the lender can later withdraw the funds. This removes the dependency on a direct transfer to a possibly blacklisted address and ensures that repayment can always be recorded even if the token contract rejects the transfer. In generic terms the flaw belongs to the class of external token transfer failures caused by blacklist or other token‑level restrictions and violates the accounting assumption that a token transfer will always succeed when invoked.

title: Collateral can already be seized even when
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the lending contract decides whether a market outcome is available for collateral seizure. The function that guards the seizure, _isQuestionPriceAvailable, returns true when either the UMA oracle reports an answer or the NegRisk market is marked as determined. Because the check treats a raw oracle answer as sufficient, it does not consider the second verification step performed by the negRiskAdapterOperator, who can flag or overwrite the oracle result after it has been posted. Consequently, if the UMA oracle returns a value that is later flagged by the operator, the contract still believes the price is available and permits the lender to claim the borrower’s collateral even though the final market state has not been settled. An attacker can exploit this by creating a loan on a market that resolves quickly, waiting for the oracle to publish an answer, and then invoking the seizure function before the operator finalises the outcome. The impact is a loss of collateral for the borrower, breaking the invariant that collateral may only be taken after a definitive market result. This condition occurs whenever the oracle answer is flagged or changed and the market remains undetermined, a scenario that can be hard to notice because the contract’s public view appears to indicate that a price is available. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the two‑step verification process. It belongs to the class of premature state validation bugs where a contract proceeds on incomplete oracle finality, effectively creating a race condition between oracle reporting and market determination. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the market as pending while the lender’s transaction already drains the collateral, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual behaviour. The recommended remediation is to base the seizure permission solely on the _isNegRiskMarketDetermined flag, ensuring that collateral can only be taken after both the UMA oracle and the negRiskAdapterOperator have agreed on a final outcome.

title: Refinancing and auction take less fee than ex-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic miscalculation in the way the protocol fee is derived during loan refinancing and auction operations. In the normal loan creation path the fee is calculated on the full amount transferred from the lender, using the formula fee = (loanAmount * feeBps) / 10_000, and the fee is taken out of the transferred amount. In the refinance and auction code the same fee basis points are applied to the outstanding debt – the principal plus accrued interest – and the fee is computed as fee = (debt * feeBps) / 10_000. Because the debt already includes interest that will later be paid back to the lender, applying the fee to the debt rather than to the amount that actually moves out of the lender’s wallet results in a smaller fee being collected. For example, with a 2 % fee a lender who fulfills a 1,000 USDC loan receives 980 USDC and the protocol correctly receives 20 USDC. If the same loan is later auctioned with a debt of 980 USDC, the protocol only receives 19.6 USDC, losing 0.4 USDC (2 % of the fee). This under‑collection occurs every time a refinance or auction is executed while a protocol fee is configured, meaning the protocol consistently earns less revenue than its economic model expects. The impact is a systematic loss of fee revenue that can exceed 1 % of total loan volume, directly harming the protocol’s profitability and potentially reducing funds available for future incentives. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows the correct fee at loan creation, and the difference during later actions is only a fraction of a percent, making it easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑handling functions, where the auditor compared the fee calculation in _acceptOffer with the logic used in refinance and auction and noticed the mismatch. The issue belongs to the class of “incorrect fee calculation” or “under‑collection arithmetic bug”. To fix the problem the fee should be calculated on the debt using an adjusted denominator that accounts for the fee being taken out, for instance fee = (debt * feeBps) / (10_000 - feeBps), or the original loan amount should be used consistently across all pathways. Correcting the formula restores the intended fee amount, aligns protocol revenue with specifications, and eliminates the discrepancy that caused the protocol to earn less than expected.

title: Using wrong format of questionId for
bug_full: The PredictDotLoan contract is intended to block loan operations once a binary question or a multi‑outcome market has been resolved. The contract determines the resolution status by calling _isNegRiskMarketDetermined with a questionId that originates from the UmaCtfAdapter. However, the format of the identifier produced by UmaCtfAdapter (a keccak256 hash of ancillary data) differs from the format generated by the NegRiskOperator (a concatenation of a 248‑bit marketId and an 8‑bit index). The contract treats these two identifiers as interchangeable and passes the UmaCtfAdapter identifier directly to the NegRiskAdapter. Because NegRiskIdLib.getMarketId simply masks the lower 8 bits of the supplied identifier, the call to NEG_RISK_ADAPTER.getDetermined looks up a mapping entry that was never populated. Consequently the function always reports that the market is not determined, even when the underlying multi‑outcome market has already resolved. This logical mismatch allows an attacker to open loan proposals against positions that are known to be worthless, or to provide collateral for a resolved outcome, effectively seizing funds that should be unavailable. From a user perspective the loan system appears to accept collateral and issue loans for markets that have already settled, leading to situations where a borrower receives a loan for a position that will never pay out, or a lender loses the collateral without compensation. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s interaction with the NegRiskAdapter, where the auditor noticed that the questionId conversion logic did not align with the adapter’s specification. The bug is subtle because both adapters use a bytes32 identifier, so a simple type check does not reveal the mismatch, and the contract’s internal assertion only checks a boolean flag that is always false. The root cause is a missing indirection step: the contract should retrieve the correct NegRisk questionId from a public mapping that links the UmaCtfAdapter requestId to the NegRiskOperator questionId before querying the market state. Fixing the issue requires adding such a mapping and using the mapped identifier in _isNegRiskMarketDetermined, thereby ensuring that resolved multi‑outcome markets are correctly detected and loan operations are blocked. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of identifier‑format mismatches that lead to incorrect state queries, breaking business logic that assumes a market is unresolved when it is actually settled, and causing potential loss of funds.

bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect EIP-712 type hash for the Proposal struct in the PredictDotLoan contract. The struct defines questionId as bytes32, but the hard-coded type string used in hashProposal encodes questionId as uint256. Because EIP-712 requires the type definition to match the actual data layout, the keccak256 hash of the encoded struct differs from the hash that was signed off-chain. As a result, the _hashTypedDataV4 digest that the contract computes does not correspond to the signer’s digest, causing signature verification to fail for otherwise valid proposals. This mismatch also violates the protocol’s stated EIP-712 compatibility, breaking the assumption that atomic types are used directly and not transformed. The bug can be triggered whenever a user or a relayer submits a signed proposal via acceptLoanOfferAndFillOrder, _refinance, or matchProposals, because those functions call _assertValidSignature which relies on hashProposal. An attacker could exploit the situation by submitting malformed proposals that appear to have valid signatures but are rejected, effectively causing a denial-of-service for legitimate borrowers or lenders, and potentially preventing the execution of loan offers, which may leave funds idle. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a transaction was signed but the contract reverts with a signature-invalid error, or that a loan request never appears in the market despite a successful off-chain signing step. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s EIP-712 implementation, where the type string was compared against the struct definition and the inconsistency was observed. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the function runs, but the mismatch only manifests during signature verification, making it easy to miss in functional testing. The correct fix is to update the type string in hashProposal so that questionId is declared as bytes32, matching the struct, and to ensure that all other fields in the type definition reflect the exact order and types of the Proposal struct. After correcting the type hash, the generated digest will align with the signer’s digest, restoring proper signature validation and compliance with EIP-712.

title: settleUpnl function can be DOSed by other

settleUpnl function can be DOSed. Users will not be able to close their positions, which could lead to a loss to the users due to the inability to close their positions. from incurring further losses due to unfavorable market conditions. However, since PartyA is unable to close its losing position, PartyA continues to incur more losses and might eventually be liquidated. Furthermore, trading is a time-sensitive activity. Thus, any blockage or delay would eventually lead to a loss of assets.
• Other PartyBs/hedgers can front-run the transaction and increment their own nonce to block the settleUpnl transaction from executing.

External pre-conditions
Attack Path
Assume the following scenario:
• PartyA has open positions with PartyB_1 and PartyB_2
• PartyA has one (1) losing position with PartyB_1 (PartyA loses, PartyB_1 wins)
• PartyA has one (1) winning position with Party_2 (PartyA wins, PartyB_2 loses)
• PartyA has zero or low allocated balance
PartyA wants to close its losing position to stop its account from incurring further losses due to unfavorable market conditions.
However, the close position transaction cannot go through due to an insufficient allocated balance on PartyA's account. This is a similar scenario described in the Symm IO v0.8.4 documentation.
In order for PartyB_1 to close PartyA's position, it first has to execute the settleUpnl function to settle PartyA's unrealized profit so that PartyA's allocated balance will be "refilled" with more funds. Once there are sufficient funds in PartyA's allocated balance, PartyB_1 can proceed to fulfill PartyA's closing request.
The only option to increase the PartyA's allocated balance is to close the PartyA's winning position with PartyB_2.
When the settleUpnl function is executed, it will verify the signature provided by Muon via the verifySettlement function below. Line 20 below shows that the encoded data in the signature includes the nonce of the PartyBs of the positions/quotes where the PnL is to be settled. In this case, PartyB_2's nonce will be included in the signature.
Assume that the time when PartyB_1 fetches the signature is T0. At T0, PartyB_2's nonce is 890. Thus, the signature is signed against encoded data where PartyB_2's nonce is 890.
At T1, PartyB_1 executes the settleUpnl function along with the signature.
However, PartyB_2 could front-run the transaction and perform certain actions (e.g., open/close position, charge funding rate) that will increment its own nonce to 891. bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the settleUpnl function of the protocol. The function settles unrealized profit and loss (UPnL) for a party A by verifying a Muon signature that includes, among other fields, the current nonce of each counter‑party (PartyB) involved in the settlement. Because the nonce is read from storage at the moment the signature is verified, an adversarial PartyB can change its nonce after the signature has been obtained but before the settleUpnl transaction is executed. By performing a transaction that increments its own nonce (for example by opening or closing a position or charging a funding rate) the attacker creates a mismatch between the nonce embedded in the signed data and the nonce stored at verification time. The require statement that checks the signature then fails and the whole transaction reverts. As a result the settlement cannot be completed, the allocated balance of PartyA is not refilled, and PartyA is unable to close a losing position. The user experience is that a trader attempts to close a position, the transaction is submitted, but it repeatedly reverts with an invalid signature or generic revert, leaving the position open and the account balance unchanged. The expectation that the position can be closed and the loss limited is violated; instead the loss may continue and the account can be liquidated. The condition occurs only when the settlement relies on a nonce that can be modified by a counter‑party after the off‑chain signature is produced. It is triggered in time‑sensitive trading where the signer (PartyB1) fetches the signature at time T0, but another counter‑party (PartyB2) front‑runs and updates its nonce before the transaction is mined at T1. The attack surface is the public nature of the nonce and the lack of a mechanism to lock or snapshot the nonce value for the duration of the settlement. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LibMuonSettlement.verifySettlement logic, where the loop that builds the nonces array was identified as dependent on mutable storage. Detecting the problem is difficult because the revert looks identical to a normal signature‑expiration or malformed‑data error, and the front‑running transaction can be arbitrarily timed, making the failure appear intermittent. The class of bug is a race condition on mutable state used in off‑chain signed messages, often referred to as a nonce‑replay or front‑runable signature vulnerability. To remediate, the protocol should either (i) include the nonce values inside the signed payload that is generated on‑chain at the moment of settlement, (ii) lock the relevant nonces for the duration of the settlement, or (iii) redesign the settlement verification to avoid reliance on mutable per‑party nonces, for example by using a monotonically increasing global version or by requiring the counter‑party to provide a fresh on‑chain commitment before the signature is accepted. These changes would prevent an attacker from altering the nonce after the signature is produced and thus eliminate the denial-of-service vector.

bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the settleUpnl function of the Settlement facet. The function is intended to allow a PartyB to settle the unrealized profit and loss (UPnL) of a specific PartyA position, but it lacks the notPartyB access‑control modifier that would restrict calls to only authorized PartyB addresses. Instead the code checks only that the caller has a non‑empty entry in the partyBOpenPositions mapping, which can remain true for a PartyB that has been removed from the system but still has residual open positions. Consequently any address that satisfies this length check, including a malicious or unauthorized PartyB, can invoke settleUpnl and force settlement of another PartyB’s or a user’s positions. An attacker can exploit this by calling settleUpnl at a moment when the market is highly volatile and the victim’s positions are temporarily underwater; the premature settlement forces the victim to realize the loss immediately instead of waiting for a possible price recovery. The impact is that victims may lose assets they would otherwise have retained, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent, and core functionality such as fair PnL settlement is broken. The bug manifests when a PartyB that is no longer authorized still has a residual position entry, or when the contract is called during volatile price swings. Affected parties include the victim PartyB, any users whose positions are settled without consent, and the overall protocol which relies on correct settlement logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that reviewed the function’s modifiers and noticed the missing notPartyB guard. It is hard to notice because the length check appears to validate the caller, and residual entries are not obvious in normal operation. The appropriate remediation is to add the notPartyB modifier (or an equivalent explicit authorization check) to the settleUpnl function so that only currently authorized PartyB addresses can trigger settlement, and to ensure that removed PartyBs cannot retain residual position entries that pass the length test. This class of bug is a missing access‑control or privilege‑escalation vulnerability that leads to unauthorized state changes and financial loss.

It was discovered during a security audit when the auditor noticed that settleUpnl increments nonces even when the settlement payload is empty, a condition that is not protected by any cooldown or minimum‑PnL guard. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of nonce‑manipulation or state‑tampering vulnerabilities that break replay‑protected signature schemes. When the protocol enters emergency mode, PartyB can call emergencyClosePosition to liquidate an open position of PartyA. The function first checks that PartyA has a non‑negative available balance for liquidation by calling LibAccount.partyAAvailableBalanceForLiquidation. This check uses the current allocated balance of PartyA, which does not include any unrealized profit that could be settled at the moment of closure. If PartyA’s allocated balance is zero or otherwise too low to cover a loss on the position, the require statement fails and the transaction reverts. As a result the position remains open, the loss cannot be realized, and the protocol is unable to protect funds during an emergency. The root cause is the missing call to settleUpnl (or an equivalent accounting step) before the balance verification, leaving the contract with an edge‑case where a losing position cannot be closed because the counter‑party appears insolvent even though the protocol could settle the profit/loss first. Both PartyA and PartyB, as well as any liquidity providers relying on the emergency close mechanism, are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the emergencyClosePosition logic and identified the missing settlement step. The recommended fix is to invoke the settleUpnl routine (or otherwise settle PartyA’s unrealized PnL) inside emergencyClosePosition before performing the solvency check, ensuring that PartyA’s balance reflects the latest PnL and allowing the emergency close to proceed.

title: Inconsistent in the liquidation fee leads to un-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the liquidation fee calculation that arises when a position is closed using the force‑close mechanism. The root cause is that the forceClosePosition function transfers the entire balance of the liquidated party’s reserve vault into the party’s allocated balance before the liquidation logic runs. This extra amount inflates the partyBAvailableBalance used by the LibLiquidation.liquidatePartyB routine, making the computed availableBalance less negative than it would be in a normal liquidation. Because the liquidation fee (remainingLf and liquidatorShare) is derived from the negative availableBalance, the liquidator who triggers the force‑close (PartyA) receives a larger share of the fee than a regular liquidator who calls the standard LiquidationFacet.liquidatePartyB function. The exploit can be carried out by any actor who has permission to invoke forceClosePosition on an underwater account that holds reserve‑vault funds. When successful, the attacker walks away with a higher liquidation reward while other liquidators receive a reduced payout. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that normal liquidators see their expected fee drop unexpectedly, or that the protocol appears to reward certain participants unfairly, potentially leading to fewer participants willing to liquidate bad positions. The issue occurs only when the liquidated account has a non‑zero reserve vault and the force‑close path is used; in standard liquidations the reserve vault is ignored, so the fee calculation differs. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation workflow, where the auditor traced the balance adjustments and compared the fee formulas between the two code paths. It can be hard to notice because the liquidation fee logic itself looks correct in isolation, and the discrepancy only appears after the reserve‑vault transfer step. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic inconsistencies where privileged functions manipulate internal balances in a way that changes downstream financial calculations. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that both liquidation paths use the same set of funds when computing the liquidator’s share – either by excluding reserve‑vault funds from the force‑close calculation or by including them in the normal liquidation path, thereby restoring fee parity and preserving the incentive structure required for healthy liquidation activity.

title: _calculateMaxBorrowCollateral
description:
```solidity
When calculating the amount to repay, _calculateMaxBorrowCollateral incorrectly applies unutilizedLeveragePercentage when calculating netRepayLimit. The result is that if the borrowBalance ever exceeds liquidationThreshold*(1-unutilizedLeveragePercentage) then all attempts to repay will revert. This is nearly identical to the valid issue In MorphoLeverageStrategyExtension.sol:L1124 the borrow limit is reduced by unutilized LeveragePercentage which will cause L1134 to underflow and revert.
Internal pre-conditions
unutilizedLeveragePercentage must be a nonzero value. For context this is nonzero for every existing leveraged token currently deployed by Index Coop.
External pre-conditions
The underlying collateral value decreases rapidly in price pushing the set towards liquidation
Attack Path
1. The price of the underlying collateral decreases rapidly causing liquidationThreshold to drop
2. borrowBalance exceeds liquidationThreshold*(1-unutilizedLeveragPercentage)
3. Calls to MorphoLeverageStrategyExtension#ripcord will revert due to underflow
4. Set token is liquidated
Set token suffers losses due to liquidation fee. For most Morpho markets this is at least 5%. Due to the leveraged nature of the set the loss will be multiplicative. This means a 3x leverage token will lose 15% NAV (5% * 3), 5x leverage will lose 25% NAV (5% * 5), etc.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that determines the maximum amount of collateral that can be borrowed when a leveraged set token is being deleveraged. The calculation mistakenly multiplies the net repayment limit by the unutilizedLeveragePercentage, a parameter that is always non‑zero for the Index Coop leveraged tokens. Because the formula reduces the allowable borrow limit, a situation can arise where the current borrow balance exceeds the adjusted threshold defined as liquidationThreshold × (1 - unutilizedLeveragePercentage). When this condition is met, any subsequent call that tries to repay part of the debt triggers an arithmetic underflow, causing the transaction to revert. The underflow is not a generic overflow bug but a logical error that only manifests when the collateral price falls sharply, driving the liquidationThreshold lower while the borrow balance remains high. In practice, an attacker does not need to interact directly with the contract; a rapid price drop of the underlying asset is sufficient to push the system into the vulnerable state. Once the repayment function reverts, the protocol cannot reduce leverage, the set token becomes under‑collateralised and the built‑in ripcord mechanism fails, leading to an automatic liquidation of the set token. Liquidation incurs a fee (typically at least 5 % of the position) which, because the token is leveraged, is multiplied by the leverage factor – a 3× token loses roughly 15 % of its net asset value, a 5× token loses about 25 %, and so on. Users experience this as failed repayment transactions, unexpected zero‑return values, and a sudden drop in their token balance or NAV. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit of the MorphoLeverageStrategyExtension contract, where the auditor noticed that the same mis‑application of unutilizedLeveragePercentage caused an underflow in a related function. The bug is subtle because the revert only occurs under specific market stress, making it easy to mistake for a normal contract failure. To remediate the problem, the calculation of the maximum borrow collateral should be performed without scaling by unutilizedLeveragePercentage when the contract is in a deleveraging path, ensuring that the net repayment limit never falls below the actual borrow balance and preventing the underflow condition.

title: Division precision loss in createD
description:
The createDistribution function in the contract contains a potential vulnerability
related to precision loss during division calculations, which could lead to incorrect
distribution of rewards. This occurs because the distribution logic divides _amount by
The createDistribution function calculates amountPerEpoch by dividing realAmountToDistribute by the number of epochs. In cases where _amount is large, this division may lead
to precision loss because Solidity's integer division discards the fractional component,
potentially causing small discrepancies in each epoch's reward distribution. These
inaccuracies accumulate over multiple epochs, leading to an overall loss in reward
accuracy. The vulnerability is found in this segment of the createDistribution function:
rder/contracts/GammaRewarder.sol#L108-L147
```solidity
function createDistribution(
    address _hypervisor,
    address _rewardToken,
    uint256 _amount,
    uint64 _startBlockNum,
    uint64 _endBlockNum
) external nonReentrant {
    // Other requirements and checks
    uint256 fee = _amount * protocolFee / BASE_9;
    uint256 realAmountToDistribute = _amount - fee;
    uint256 amountPerEpoch = realAmountToDistribute / ((_endBlockNum - _startBlockNum) / blocksPerEpoch);
    // Further processing
}
```
In this code, amountPerEpoch is calculated by dividing realAmountToDistribute by the
number of epochs (which is derived from block range). The result may have a fractional
part, but Solidity’s integer division will truncate it, leading to precision loss.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
While this vulnerability does not entirely prevent the function’s operation, it introduces
inaccuracies in reward distribution that may lead to small amounts being unrewarded
over time. This could be noticeable with large distributions or over long durations, where
cumulative precision loss can result in rewards lower than anticipated.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes the per‑epoch reward amount in the createDistribution function. The code calculates amountPerEpoch by dividing the net amount to be distributed (realAmountToDistribute) by the number of epochs derived from the block range. Because Solidity only supports integer arithmetic, any fractional component of the division is discarded. When the total amount to distribute is large or the epoch count creates a small per‑epoch share, the truncation removes a non‑zero remainder on each iteration. Over many epochs these tiny truncations accumulate, resulting in a total reward that is lower than the amount that should have been paid out. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the expected reward balance is smaller than anticipated, sometimes even zero for very small allocations, leading to a perception that “my rewards are missing” or “the protocol is not paying me”. The issue is triggered whenever a caller creates a distribution with a sizable _amount and a block range that yields multiple epochs, i.e., when (_endBlockNum‑_startBlockNum)/blocksPerEpoch is greater than one and does not divide the net amount evenly. All participants who rely on the distribution – token holders, liquidity providers, or any role that expects a proportional reward – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the protocol (that the sum of per‑epoch rewards equals the total net amount) are violated. The problem was identified during a manual audit and confirmed with a Hardhat test that deliberately used a very large token amount and a modest number of epochs, showing that amountPerEpoch was consistently lower than the mathematically correct value. The bug can be hard to notice in production because the loss per epoch may be only a few wei, which is invisible in normal UI displays, but the discrepancy becomes measurable after many epochs or with high‑value distributions. To remediate the issue, the calculation should retain higher precision, for example by scaling the numerator with a 10**18 factor before division and then scaling back, or by explicitly handling the remainder and spreading it across epochs so that the sum of all per‑epoch payouts matches the intended total. This approach eliminates the truncation error and restores the protocol’s guarantee that every token allocated for rewards is actually distributed.

description:
Per the contest README:
The codebase expected to comply with the following EIPs
• Strictly compliant:
– EIP-4907 (rental standard for ERC721)
Per the EIP-4907 standard:
The supportsInterface method MUST return true when called with 0xad092b5c
However the interface IERC4907, inherited by EwmNftController, does not adhere to this
requirement. Because the EwmNftController is a rental NFT that is expected to follow the
EIP-4907 standard, this in turn breaks the rental NFT's compliance.
If a contract is in contest Scope, then all its parent contracts are included by
default.
The interfaceId of an interface/contract type is determined by XOR-ing all of their
function selectors together. The 0xad092b5c is the magic value that is the interfaceId of
IERC4907 defined in the standard:
