https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4907
However, the current function signature/selector of setUser is as follow:
```solidity
function setUser(uint256 tokenId, address user) external;
```
ontracts/interfaces/IERC4907.sol#L15
Which is different from the 4907 standard, having an extra expires parameter:
```solidity
function setUser(uint256 tokenId, address user, uint64 expires) external;
```
causing the interfaceId to become different. Then it is impossible for supportInterface
to return true for the interface ID 0xad092b5c.
ontracts/EwmNftController.sol#L211-L213
Internal pre-conditions
None
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
N/A
Non-compliance with the ERC-4907 standard which the protocol expects strictly.
Smart contract integration issues may also arise for contracts interacting with the NFT
and expecting strict interface support, given that the NFT holders are meant to be EWM
Light Client runners, which can be expected to be smart contract users, as opposed to
regular app users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a non‑compliant implementation of the ERC‑4907 rental standard in the EwmNftController contract. The ERC‑4907 specification requires the contract to expose a setUser function that accepts three parameters – tokenId, user address, and an expires timestamp – and to report support for the interface identifier 0xad092b5c via supportsInterface. In the current code the inherited IERC4907 interface defines setUser with only two parameters (tokenId and user), omitting the expires argument. Because the interface identifier is calculated by XOR‑ing the selectors of all declared functions, the missing parameter changes the selector of setUser, which in turn changes the overall interfaceId. Consequently, supportsInterface cannot return true for the required 0xad092b5c value, breaking strict compliance with ERC‑4907. This mismatch is not caught by the compiler; it only becomes apparent when another contract or off‑chain tool queries the interface support, making the issue subtle and easy to overlook. The practical impact is that any system that relies on the rental NFT behaving according to ERC‑4907 – for example, rental marketplaces, light‑client runners, or other smart contracts that check for interface support before interacting – will see the interface check fail and may reject the NFT, refuse to set rental periods, or misinterpret the absence of an expiry field. From a user perspective the symptom is that a rental NFT cannot be assigned a time‑limited user; attempts to set a user may succeed but the expiry is never recorded, leading to unexpected perpetual access or, conversely, the contract refusing to accept the NFT because it does not advertise ERC‑4907 compliance. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that compared the contract’s declared interface against the EIP‑4907 reference and observed a mismatched interfaceId (0x96745459 instead of 0xad092b5c). The bug is hard to notice because the contract compiles and the function signatures appear plausible, yet the subtle change in the function selector silently breaks the interface fingerprint. To remediate, the setUser function must be updated to include the expires parameter (uint64 expires) matching the official ERC‑4907 definition, and the contract’s supportsInterface implementation should be verified to return true for the correct interfaceId. Aligning the interface restores compliance, ensures that rental periods are correctly enforced, and prevents integration failures with other contracts that expect strict ERC‑4907 support.

title: Improper Limit Enforcement Al-
bug_full: The contract promises a maximum of ten NFTs per address when operating in integer allowance mode. The implementation checks the requested quantity only for each individual allocation call, not the cumulative total owned by the address. As a result, an attacker can call the allocation function repeatedly, each time requesting up to ten NFTs, and accumulate more than ten NFTs overall. The root cause is that the limit condition uses the parameter nftQuantity instead of the sum of previously allocated NFTs, and the state variable tracking total NFTs per address is not consulted when enforcing the cap. Exploitation requires the admin to enable integer allowance, after which any whitelisted address can repeatedly invoke the allocation function. The impact is an unfair distribution where a single participant can acquire a disproportionate share of the limited NFT supply, potentially exhausting the pool and preventing legitimate participants from receiving any NFTs. The issue appears only when the integer allowance flag is true; otherwise the check is irrelevant. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract's README documentation with the source code logic. The bug is subtle because the require statement appears to enforce the limit, leading reviewers to assume the constraint is effective, while the cumulative accounting is missing. The proper fix is to enforce the limit against the total number of NFTs already allocated to the address, either by checking a dedicated mapping or by updating the existing total allocation variable before each new allocation, and to ensure that any release or stake‑withdrawal function also updates this total so the cap remains accurate. In user‑facing terms, a user expecting to receive at most ten NFTs may see their balance exceed ten, while other users see zero NFTs available. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper cumulative limit enforcement, where per‑account caps are validated only per‑transaction rather than across the lifetime of the account.

title: User to sell the last supply will
description:
BancorExchangeProvider::_getScaledAmountOut() decreases the amount out when the
token in is the supply token by the exit contribution, that is, scaledAmountOut=(scaledAmountOut*(MAX_WEIGHT-exchange.exitContribution))/MAX_WEIGHT;.
Whenever the last supply of the token is withdrawn, it will get all the reserve and store it
in scaledAmountOut, and then apply the exit contribution, leaving these funds forever
stuck, as there is 0 supply to redeem it.
In BancorExchangeProvider:345, the exchange contribution is applied regardless of there
being supply left to redeem it.
Internal pre-conditions
1. All supply must be withdrawn from the exchange.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Users call Broker::swapIn(), that calls GoodDollarExchangeProvider::swapIn(),
which is the exchange contract that holds the token and reserve balances, selling
supply tokens until the supply becomes 0.
The last exit contribution will be forever stuck. This amount is unbounded and may be
very significant.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the exchange logic that calculates the amount of reserve tokens returned when a user sells the last remaining supply tokens of a pool. The function that scales the output amount applies an exit contribution factor regardless of whether any supply tokens remain after the trade. When the final supply token is withdrawn, the contract first computes the full reserve amount that should be returned, then multiplies it by (MAX_WEIGHT‑exitContribution)/MAX_WEIGHT. Because the supply is now zero, there is no token left that can be redeemed for the reduced amount, so the portion taken by the exit contribution becomes permanently locked in the contract. This occurs only when a user repeatedly calls the swapIn entry point until the pool’s token supply reaches zero; the last trade triggers the faulty scaling. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the expected refund is smaller than it should be and the missing funds never reappear, effectively disappearing from the system. The impact is that any amount taken by the exit contribution—potentially a large, unbounded sum—becomes unrecoverable, undermining the economic guarantees of the protocol and risking user confidence. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when a test case exercised a swap that drained the token supply to zero and observed that the contract still attempted to apply the exit contribution, leading to a revert on subsequent swaps and confirming that the previous trade had locked funds. The bug is subtle because it only manifests at the extreme edge case of zero supply, a scenario that may not be exercised in normal operation, making it easy to overlook during routine testing. Conceptually, the fix is to treat the zero‑supply condition as a special case and skip the exit‑contribution deduction, or to redesign the accounting so that any contribution is only taken when a positive supply remains to be redeemed. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the exit fee should be charged on actual token transfers, not on a state where no tokens exist to justify the fee.

title: GoodDollarExchangeProvider::
description:
GoodDollarExchangeProvider::mintFromExpansion() mints supply tokens while keeping
the current price constant. To achieve this, a certain formula is used, but in the process it
scales the reserveRatioScalar*exchange.reserveRatio to 1e8 precision (the precision of exchange.reserveRatio) down from 1e18.
However, the calculation of the new amount of tokens to mint is based on the full ratio
with 1e18, which will mint more tokens than it should and change the price, breaking the
readme.
est() due to using mul and then div, as mul divides by 1e18 unnecessarily in this case.
it calculates the ratio using the formula and then scales it down, changing the price.
In GoodDollarExchangeProvider:147, newRatio is calculated with full 1e18 precision and
used to calculate the amount of tokens to mint, but exchanges[exchangeId].reserveRatio
is stored with the downscaled value, newRatio/1e10, causing an error and price change.
This happens because the price is reserve/(supply*reserveRatio). As supply is increased
by a calculation that uses the full precision newRatio, but reserveRatio is stored with less
precision (1e8), the price will change due to this call.
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. GoodDollarExchangeProvider::mintFromExpansion() is called and a rounding error
happens in the calculation of newRatio.
The current price is modified due to the expansion which goes against the readme:
What properties/invariants do you want to hold even if breaking them has a
low/unknown impact?
Bancor formula invariant. Price = Reserve / Supply * reserveRatio
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mintFromExpansion function of the GoodDollarExchangeProvider contract. The function is intended to expand the token supply while keeping the market price constant by using a Bancor‑style invariant where price equals reserve divided by the product of supply and reserveRatio. To preserve the invariant the code computes a new reserve ratio (newRatio) with 1e18 precision, then stores the reserveRatio in the exchange struct with only 1e8 precision (scaled down by a factor of 1e10). When the new amount of tokens to mint is calculated, the full‑precision newRatio is used together with the down‑scaled reserveRatio, causing the minted amount to be larger than required. This mismatch creates a rounding error that silently changes the price after each expansion. The error can be triggered whenever the expansion controller calls mintFromExpansion, which has no external pre‑conditions, so any authorized caller can cause the price drift. The impact is that the token price no longer remains constant as promised in the README; holders see their token value diluted, the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken, and an attacker could repeatedly invoke the function to mint excess tokens at an unchanged reserve, effectively extracting value. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a slightly lower price after an expansion, or a balance that appears unchanged while the total supply has grown, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The bug belongs to the class of precision‑mismatch or rounding‑error vulnerabilities that violate financial invariants. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the calculation of newRatio used 1e18 precision while the stored reserveRatio was only 1e8, and that the subsequent multiplication and division sequence introduced an unnecessary division by 1e18. The issue is hard to notice because the price deviation can be small and only becomes apparent after multiple expansions. The correct fix is to align the precision of the ratio used in the minting calculation with the stored reserveRatio, for example by dividing newRatio by 1e10 before applying it, thereby eliminating the rounding error and preserving the price invariant.

title: Malicious user may frontrun Goo
description:
GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromReserveBalance() or
GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromInterest() transfer funds to the reserve and
mint $G to the distribution helper. However,
GoodDollarExchangeProvider::mintFromInterest() mints 0 tokens whenever the supply is
0. An attacker can buy all $G from the exchange to trigger this.
In GoodDollarExpansionController::142 and GoodDollarExpansionController::161, amountMinted is not checked for a null value.
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Attacker calls Bancor::swapIn() or Bancor::swapOut(), buying all $G in the
exchange, making PoolExchange.tokenSupply null.
2. GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromReserveBalance() or GoodDollarExpansionController::mintUBIFromInterest() is called, adding reserve asset funds
without minting $G.
Funds are added to the reserve without the corresponding amount of $G being minted.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the minting workflow of the GoodDollar protocol where two controller functions, mintUBIFromReserveBalance and mintUBIFromInterest, forward the amount returned by GoodDollarExchangeProvider.mintFromInterest to the GoodDollar token contract without verifying that the returned amount is non‑zero. The exchange provider calculates the amount to mint based on the current tokenSupply of the pool; when the pool tokenSupply is zero, the calculation yields zero and the function returns zero. An attacker can exploit this by first draining the entire $G supply from the Bancor exchange using swapIn or swapOut, which reduces the pool tokenSupply to zero. After the supply is exhausted, the attacker triggers one of the controller mint functions. The controller then transfers reserve assets into the protocol’s reserve but mints zero $G tokens for the distribution helper. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – reserve funds are moved and an InterestUBIMinted event is emitted – yet no new tokens are created, effectively allowing the attacker to add value to the reserve without compensating token holders. This breaks the accounting invariant that every unit of reserve added must be matched by an equivalent amount of newly minted $G, leading to dilution of existing holders and a mismatch between reserve balance and token supply. The issue occurs whenever the pool tokenSupply is zero, which can be induced at any time by a malicious participant buying all available $G. It affects the protocol’s economic model, the distribution helper, and any user expecting to receive newly minted tokens in exchange for contributed reserve assets. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow and noticed the missing zero‑check after the call to mintFromInterest. Because the functions do not revert on a zero return, the problem is subtle and may be missed if only error messages are inspected. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit require that the amount returned from mintFromInterest (or mintFromExpansion) is greater than zero and to revert otherwise, thereby preserving the invariant that reserve contributions always result in token minting.

title: TradingLimits::update() incor-
description:
TradingLimits::update() divides the traded funds by the decimals of the token, int256 _deltaFlowUnits = _deltaFlow / int256((10 ** uint256(decimals)));. In a token with 18 decimals,
for example, swapping 1.999...e18 tokens will lead to a _deltaFlowUnits of just 1, taking a
major error. This can be exploited to swap up to twice the trading limit, if tokens are
swapped 2 by 2 and the state is updated only by 1 each time. Overall, even without
malicious intent, the limits will always be bypassed due to the rounding.
In TradingLimits:135, it only rounds up whenever deltaFlowUnits becomes 0, but the
error is just as big if it becomes 1 from 2, effectively not providing enough protection.
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User calls Broker::swapIn/Out() with amounts in and out that produce rounding
errors (almost always).
The trading limits may be severely bypassed with malicious intent (by double the
amount) or by a smaller but still significant amount organically.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error in the function that updates trading limits. The contract computes the change in flow units by dividing the raw token amount by 10**decimals, using integer division. Because Solidity discards the fractional part, a swap of 1.999…e18 tokens (for an 18‑decimal token) yields a deltaFlowUnits value of only 1 instead of the expected 2. This truncation systematically under‑counts the amount of tokens that have been traded. The under‑count allows a user to perform two swaps of roughly the same size while the internal accounting records only one unit of flow, effectively letting the trader exceed the configured trading limit by up to a factor of two. The bug can be triggered simply by calling the public swap functions (Broker::swapIn or Broker::swapOut) with amounts that are not exact multiples of the token’s decimal factor – a condition that occurs in almost every realistic trade. The impact is that the protocol’s risk‑management layer, which relies on accurate flow accounting to enforce per‑user or per‑period caps, is bypassed. Consequently, a malicious actor could trade far more than allowed, potentially draining liquidity or causing market manipulation, while honest users see no protection from excessive exposure. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Mento‑Good$ integration, where the auditor noticed that the update routine only rounds up when the computed deltaFlowUnits equals zero, but does not compensate when the division rounds down to one. The problem is subtle because the loss of a fractional unit looks negligible in isolation, yet it accumulates across multiple swaps and defeats the intended accounting guarantees. To remediate the bug, the calculation should be changed to a ceiling division – for example, subtracting one before division and adding one afterwards – so that any non‑zero remainder is rounded up, ensuring that the recorded flow never under‑estimates the actual token movement. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of integer‑division rounding errors that break financial invariants in smart contracts. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that a trade was successful while the protocol silently allows more volume than advertised, leading to unexpected balance changes or missing enforcement of limits.

title: _getReserveRatioScalar() will give a lesser value than expected Found by 0x73696d616f, 0xc0ffEE, Ollam, Robert, onthehunt
description:
numberOfExpansions = (block.timestamp - config.lastExpansion) / config.expansionFrequency
The calculation divides it by the expansionFrequency, but this will cause significant
rounding issues.
If the expansionFrequency is 1 day (as specified in the docs), time may pass without
anybody calling the function and the following scenario will be present.
Let's say 30 hours since last expansion and someone decides then to call it, it will be
rounded due to the division to be 1 day, producing a smaller value than the hours that've
passed.
The root cause is the potential of rounding down numberOfExpansions, which will give a
significantly smaller value, depending on how big will be remainder of the division. (6 for
30 hours, 3 for 27 hours, etc)
Internal pre-conditions
mintUBIFromExpansion() need to be callable.
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. Alice calls mintUBIFromExpansion() to create an expansion
2. 30 hours pass and nobody calls the function, Bob sees that he can call mintUBIFromExpansion()
3. Due to the rounding down of the calculation, it will a value equivalent of 24 hours
passing.
The protocol will expand slower than intended, thus less $G will be minted, which will
become significant overtime.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error in the calculation of the number of expansion periods that have elapsed since the last token supply expansion. The contract computes numberOfExpansions as (block.timestamp - config.lastExpansion) / config.expansionFrequency using integer division. Because Solidity discards the remainder, any partial day that has passed is rounded down to the nearest whole day. When the expansionFrequency is set to one day, a delay of 30 hours results in the division yielding 1 instead of the expected 1.25, effectively treating only 24 hours as having elapsed. This under‑counts the elapsed time, causing the _getReserveRatioScalar() function to return a smaller scalar, and consequently mintUBIFromExpansion() mints fewer $G tokens than the protocol’s economic model specifies. The bug can be triggered whenever there is a gap between calls to the expansion function that exceeds the configured frequency. An attacker or any participant can simply wait longer before invoking mintUBIFromExpansion(), causing the protocol to expand slower than intended. The impact is a systematic reduction of newly minted tokens, which over time leads to lower inflation, reduced rewards for users, and a deviation from the promised monetary policy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Mento‑Good$ integration, where the auditor observed the integer division and recognized the rounding‑down effect. Because the contract does not emit an explicit warning and the token supply change is gradual, the problem may remain unnoticed until the supply curve diverges noticeably from expectations. The fix is to avoid truncating division; for example, compute the number of expansions using ceiling division, add a check for remainder, or store timestamps in a way that accounts for partial periods. Replacing the division with ((block.timestamp - config.lastExpansion) + config.expansionFrequency - 1) / config.expansionFrequency or using a fixed‑point representation eliminates the rounding error. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “integer division rounding down” or “time‑based accounting truncation” errors that break economic assumptions, causing users to receive fewer minted tokens than they anticipate.

title: Incorrect closing fee calcula-
description:
According to the Avantis documentation (doc), the closing fee should be based on the adjusted position size:
AdjustedPositionSize=TotalPositionSize+AccruedPnL-AccumulatedMarginFee
The documentation provides a clear example:
if a trader puts up $100 of collateral at a 30x leverage, then the total position size would be $3,000. After deducting the opening fee (and assuming no change in the price of the underlying asset), the leveraged position size with an accumulated margin fee on the position of $10 is $(3000-10)=$2990. Hence, the closing fee is 2990*0.08%=$2.392.
However, during closing fee calculation, the AccumulatedMarginFee (rollover fee) is not deducted as expected.
In the TradingCallbacks contract, where AdjustedPositionSize is calculated during position closing, the AccumulatedMarginFee is not accounted for and does not reduce the position size (here and here).
This leads to users paying higher closing fees than they should.
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User closes their position.
2. Closing fees are overinflated.
• Incorrect closing fee calculations result in users losing funds.
• Documentation discrepancy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect closing‑fee calculation in the Avantis trading contracts. According to the official documentation the fee must be computed on the adjusted position size, which is defined as total position size plus accrued PnL minus the accumulated margin (rollover) fee. The implementation in the TradingCallbacks contract calculates the adjusted size but fails to subtract the accumulated margin fee, so the fee is applied to a larger amount than intended. This omission occurs whenever a trader closes a position that carries a non‑zero accumulated margin fee. As a result the closing fee is systematically higher than the 0.08 % rate described in the docs, causing users to lose a small but measurable amount of funds on each close. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that a $100 collateral at 30× leverage will incur a closing fee of roughly $2.39, but the contract may charge $2.40 or more, leading to a balance that is lower than expected and a missing refund. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract code, where the formula used for AdjustedPositionSize was compared against the documented specification. Because the discrepancy is only a few cents per trade, it can be difficult to notice without a detailed review of the fee calculation logic. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a financial formula omits a required term, breaking the invariant that fees are proportional to the true exposure after accounting for accrued costs. To remediate the problem the contract should be updated so that the accumulated margin fee is deducted from the position size before the fee percentage is applied, thereby aligning the on‑chain calculation with the documented model and preventing users from being overcharged.

title: Incorrect data is passed to the TradingStorage.withinExposureLimit s() function. The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by Afriaudit, eeyore
description:
When TradingStorage.withinExposureLimits() is called from the TradingCallbacks contract, the check is performed using an inaccurate OpenInterest value.
The value passed is derived from positionSizeUSDC and leverage, where positionSizeUSDC has not yet been reduced by the open fee.
If the open fee will be deducted from positionSizeUSDC, the actual OpenInterest used to update the OI storage values would be lower than the value used in the TradingStorage.withinExposureLimits() check.
This discrepancy leads to valid trades that would fit within the OI limits being rejected, resulting in potential loss of funds due to fees paid for operations such as initiating a market open trade (msg.value) and missing fees for the protocol.
TradingStorage.withinExposureLimits() uses an OpenInterest value that has not been reduced by the potential open fee, causing the rejection of valid Open market or limit orders that would otherwise fit within OI limits after fee deduction.
The incorrect behavior can be observed here and here.
Internal pre-conditions
1. The OI limits are nearly reached.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. A user creates a pending Open market order (not isPnl), calculating the OI limits to fit the largest possible OI trade.
2. The open fee is not correctly deducted when TradingStorage.withinExposureLimits() is used, causing the user pending market order to be rejected.
3. The user collateral is returned, but the fee is retained by the protocol, based on the assumption that an attempt was made.
• Time-sensitive function is not executed correctly.
• Loss of user funds due to fees.
• Loss of fees for protocol and referrer.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inaccurate OpenInterest (OI) value being supplied to the TradingStorage.withinExposureLimits() function when a pending open market or limit order is evaluated. The contract calculates OI using positionSizeUSDC multiplied by leverage, but it does so before subtracting the open fee that will later be taken from the position size. Consequently, the OI used for the exposure‑limit check is higher than the OI that will actually be recorded after fee deduction. When the protocol’s OI limits are close to being reached, this over‑estimation causes the check to fail for trades that would otherwise be permissible after the fee is applied. The user’s order is therefore rejected, the collateral is returned, but the open fee is retained by the protocol under the assumption that an attempt was made. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a loss of the fee without receiving the expected trade execution, often appearing as “order rejected despite having enough margin” or “funds disappear after a failed open trade”. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Afriaudit, eeyore) that compared the OI calculation used in the check with the OI value stored after fee deduction and observed the mismatch. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s logic for fee deduction and OI accounting are separated, and the failure manifests only when OI limits are nearly exhausted, a condition that may not be exercised in routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a financial invariant is violated due to inconsistent state updates. To remediate the problem the contract should pre‑calculate the open fee, subtract it from positionSizeUSDC, and then use the reduced amount together with leverage to compute the OpenInterest passed to withinExposureLimits(). This ensures that the exposure check reflects the true post‑fee OI and prevents valid trades from being incorrectly rejected, protecting users from unexpected fee loss and preserving the protocol’s intended fee accounting.

title: The trader might get liquidated
description:
In certain cases, the trader could get liquidated when attempting to close their position, resulting in a portion of their collateral being seized.
A trader's position will be liquidated if their PnL loss exceeds 85% of the collateral. When the trader closes the position, several fees are incurred, such as closing fees, margin fees, and limit close fees (only if the user has set take-profit or stop-loss limits).
When a trader’s position is liquidated or closed, the following check in getTradeValuePure determines the action based on the position's value.
```solidity
if (value <= (int(collateral) * int(100 - liqThreshold)) / 100) {
    value = lossProtectedPnl - pnl;
    lossProtectedPnl = fees - int(collateral) + value;
}
```
This check ensures that if the position is liquidated, the user receives nothing (if there is no loss rebate). If the position is closed, they receive the remaining value after accounting for PnL and fees.
However, the above check calculates value as int value = int(collateral) + lossProtectedPnl - fees, where fees represent the total fees:
total fees = closing fee + margin fee + limit close fee (if the trader opts for TP or SL)
The trader should be liquidated when their position loss exceeds 85% of the collateral.
Suppose the trader closes their position with a loss of x% of the collateral and the total fees incurred for closing the position is y.
This issue occurs when:
y > 85% of collateral - x% of collateral
• In PairInfos.sol:671 the check for liquidation compares the position's remaining value (collateral minus PnL and total fees) to the liquidation threshold (85% of collateral). However, this threshold does not include the effect of these fees, effectively lowering the trader's actual position value relative to the threshold.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. If a user closes their position with a loss of 84% of the collateral and the total fees amount to 2% of the collateral, then the position’s value is calculated as follows:
value = collateral - pnl - total fees
value = collateral - 84% of collateral - 2% of collateral = 14% of collateral
2. Since the position value is less than 15% of the collateral, the condition is met and code block mentioned above would be executed, causing the trade to be liquidated. Their collateral is seized, and they receive no remaining value.
Trader gets liquidated if he tries to close his position loosing a part of his collateral value
bug_full: The contract contains an accounting flaw in the liquidation logic that can cause a trader to be liquidated when they are merely closing a losing position. The code determines liquidation by checking whether the position value, calculated as collateral minus profit‑and‑loss (PnL) and minus the total fees charged on close, falls below a fixed percentage of the original collateral (85%). However, the comparison threshold is derived from the raw collateral amount and does not incorporate the fees that are deducted from the trader’s balance. As a result, the effective value of the position after fees can be lower than the threshold even when the loss itself is within the allowed range. An attacker – or any trader – can trigger this situation by closing a position that has a loss just under the 85 % limit while the sum of closing fee, margin fee and any limit‑close fee pushes the net value below the threshold. For example, with a loss of 84 % of the collateral and total fees of 2 % of the collateral, the net value becomes 14 % of the collateral, which is below the 15 % threshold (100 %‑85 %). The contract then executes the liquidation branch, seizing the remaining collateral and returning nothing to the user. This leads to an unexpected loss of funds: the trader sees no payout, their balance may drop to zero, and the UI may simply report that the position was closed without explaining that a liquidation occurred. The issue affects any user who attempts to close a position near the liquidation boundary, especially those who have enabled take‑profit or stop‑loss limits that add an extra fee. It was discovered during a manual audit of PairInfos.sol where the liquidation condition was examined and found to ignore fee impact. The bug is subtle because the fee amounts are small and the liquidation only happens on close, making it easy to assume the loss alone triggered the event. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect financial threshold calculation” or “off‑by‑fee liquidation” bugs, where accounting assumptions about collateral, loss, and fees are inconsistent. To remediate, the liquidation check should be rewritten to compare the net position value (collateral ‑ PnL ‑ fees) against the liquidation threshold that also accounts for fees, or the threshold itself should be adjusted to include the fee component, ensuring that only genuine losses exceeding the defined percentage cause liquidation.

title: PriceAggregator uses the same
description:
The fulfill function in PriceAggregator.sol function uses the same heartbeat (chainlinkValidityPeriod) to check the freshness of the price for all the price feeds. The problem with this is different price feeds have different heartbeats. Since they use the same heartbeat the heartbeat needs to be slowest of all of them or else the staleness check will fail most of the time. The issue is that if we use slowest heartbeat of all the feeds as chainlinkValidityPeriod it would allow the consumption of potentially very stale data.
In PriceAggregator.sol:126 and PriceAggregator.sol:158 same heartbeat value chainlinkValidityPeriod is used to check the freshness of all price feeds.
Internal pre-conditions
No pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
No external pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. Lets take BTC-USD feed and EUR-USD feed as examples.
2. On Base BTC-USD chainlink feed's heartbeat is 20 minutes and EUR-USD feed's heartbeat is 24 hours.
3. So If price is not changed beyond deviation threshold they will only be updated after heartbeat period is passed.
4. If we use 20 minutes as heartbeat period to check freshness of prices staleness check will fail for EUR-USD will fail most of the times because its heartbeat is 24 hours it doesn't get updated every 20 mins.
5. If we use 24 hours as heartbeat we might consume stale BTC-USD price because the actual heartbeat of that price feed is 20 mins and chainlink sets it heartbeat to 20 mins because BTC is volatile.
6. So two different heartbeat periods should be used for validating these two price feeds.
1. Stale prices will be confirmed or
2. Price staleness check will fail most of the times.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price aggregation contract that validates the freshness of each Chainlink price feed using a single global timeout value, referred to as chainlinkValidityPeriod. This design assumes that all feeds update at the same rate, but in practice different assets have distinct heartbeat intervals – for example the BTC‑USD feed may update every twenty minutes while the EUR‑USD feed may only update once every twenty‑four hours. Because the contract applies the same timeout to both feeds, two contradictory problems arise. If the timeout is set to the shortest interval (twenty minutes), the staleness check for the slower EUR‑USD feed will fail most of the time, causing the contract to reject otherwise valid price data and potentially halt operations that depend on that asset. Conversely, if the timeout is set to the longest interval (twenty‑four hours), the contract may accept BTC‑USD prices that are up to twenty‑four hours old, even though the feed normally provides fresh data every twenty minutes. This means the protocol can consume significantly stale price information for volatile assets, leading to inaccurate pricing, incorrect liquidation triggers, and financial loss for users. The issue is triggered whenever a price feed does not change beyond the deviation threshold within its heartbeat, because the contract will not request a new update and will rely on the stale cached value. All participants that depend on the aggregator – traders, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected, as they may receive outdated prices without any visible warning. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented heartbeat of each feed with the single validity period used in the contract’s fulfill function. It is subtle because the contract appears to work correctly for assets with the shortest heartbeat, masking the problem for other assets until a stale‑price scenario is observed. To remediate, the contract should store and enforce a separate heartbeat or validity period for each price feed, ensuring that the freshness check matches the specific update frequency of that feed. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees that prices reflect recent market conditions and prevents the protocol from acting on outdated data.

title: status of referral code is al-
description:
In updateReferral function in Referral.sol is setting the status of the referral code to true irrespective of the passed value. But when false is passed it should change the status of the referral code to false.
In updateReferral function in Referral.sol:200 is setting the status of the referral code always to true irrespective of the passed boolean value.
Internal pre-conditions
None
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
1. Handler first set the status of Referral code ALICE to private by calling updateReferral(ALICE,true).
2. Now after some time handler needs to set the status of the code from private to normal for some reason.
3. Now handler calls updateReferral(ALICE,false) but status of the code will not be set to public because updateReferral is always setting the status of code to true irrespective of the value passed.
Referral code statuses cannot be set to public from private.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the referral management function that updates the privacy status of a referral code. The function is intended to accept a boolean flag indicating whether the code should be private (true) or public (false) and store that flag in a mapping. However, the implementation unconditionally writes the value true to the mapping, ignoring the caller‑provided boolean. This occurs because the assignment uses a literal true instead of the parameter, so any call to the function—whether it passes true or false—results in the code being marked private. An attacker or legitimate handler can exploit this by calling the function with false in an attempt to make a previously private referral code public; the call succeeds but the status remains private, effectively locking the code in a private state. The impact is that referral codes cannot be reverted to public, preventing users from receiving referral rewards, breaking expected business logic, and potentially causing loss of revenue for the protocol. The condition arises whenever the updateReferral function is invoked, which is typically restricted to governance or a designated handler, but the bug defeats the intended flexibility of the API. All parties that rely on the ability to toggle referral visibility—such as marketers, users expecting to claim a referral bonus, and the protocol’s accounting system—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that inspected the function body and noticed the hard‑coded true assignment. Because the function still emits an event indicating the requested status, the bug can be subtle and may not be immediately obvious from transaction logs, making it hard to detect without reviewing the source. The proper fix is to assign the supplied boolean parameter to the status mapping instead of a constant, thereby respecting the caller’s intent and restoring the ability to change a code from private to public. Conceptually, this is a classic case of an input‑validation or state‑update bug where the contract ignores user‑provided data, leading to incorrect state persistence and violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions about referral availability.

title: Stop loss orders cannot be liqui-
description:
Due to a check that requires the liquidation price to be greater than the Stop Loss price (in the case of a buy) in the executeLimitOrder function of the Trading.sol contract, the operator cannot liquidate an order if the stop loss is higher than the liquidation price, even when the trade is liquidatable due to sudden price moves or gaps. This check should only apply to guaranteed Stop Loss (SL) orders. Currently, however, it is also applied to non-guaranteed orders, making them unliquidatable in these cases.
Incorrect check in Trading.sol:522
```solidity
require(t.sl == 0 || (t.buy ? liqPrice > t.sl : liqPrice < t.sl), "HAS_SL");
```
This check should only be done for pairs with guaranteed stop loss.
Internal pre-conditions
Gap down or gap up or sudden price move
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. Trader open XYZ long at 500.
2. Set his stop loss to 450 and his liquidation price is 400.
3. XYZ is a commodity which got opened at a gap down price the later day at 395.
4. The traders position is now liquidatable because current price of XYZ is less than the liquidation price of 400. But it cannot be liquidated by the operator because of the above mentioned check and it can only be closed using a stop-loss limit close.
Positions can’t be liquidated even if they are in the liquidation stage.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect validation check in the executeLimitOrder function of the Trading.sol contract that prevents the operator from liquidating a position when the stop‑loss price is higher (for a buy) or lower (for a sell) than the calculated liquidation price. The check require(t.sl == 0 || (t.buy ? liqPrice > t.sl : liqPrice < t.sl), "HAS_SL"); is applied to every order, but the business rule it enforces – that the liquidation price must be on the correct side of a guaranteed stop‑loss – is only valid for pairs that support guaranteed stop‑loss protection. For regular (non‑guaranteed) stop‑loss orders the condition is irrelevant and, when it fails, the contract reverts with the HAS_SL error, making the position effectively unliquidatable. The root cause is a misplaced conditional that mixes two independent concepts: liquidation eligibility and stop‑loss guarantee. An attacker (or any trader) can exploit this by opening a leveraged long position, setting a normal stop‑loss below the liquidation price, and then waiting for a sudden market gap that pushes the market price below the liquidation threshold. Because the stop‑loss price is still higher than the liquidation price, the require statement fails and the operator’s liquidation routine cannot close the position. The impact is that liquidatable positions remain open, exposing the protocol to increased loss exposure, preventing margin recovery for the trader, and potentially causing funds to be locked indefinitely. The condition occurs only under extreme price movements such as gaps or rapid drops where the liquidation price is crossed while the stop‑loss remains on the opposite side. Users who rely on automatic liquidation see their positions stay open, their margin may be consumed, and they may observe that the UI shows the position as “liquidatable” but the backend refuses to execute the liquidation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Trading.sol contract where the logic of the HAS_SL check was examined and found to be applied universally rather than conditionally for guaranteed‑SL pairs. It can be hard to notice because the require statement only triggers in rare market scenarios, and normal operation (where liquidation price and stop‑loss are on the same side) passes silently. The proper fix is to move the stop‑loss comparison behind a check that the trading pair supports guaranteed stop‑loss protection, or to remove the condition entirely for non‑guaranteed pairs, ensuring that liquidation logic is evaluated independently of stop‑loss settings. In generic terms this is a business‑logic validation bug where an invariant is enforced in an inappropriate context, leading to a denial‑of‑service style failure for liquidations. From the user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected inability to close a losing position automatically; the UI may indicate that the position is eligible for liquidation, yet the transaction reverts with “HAS_SL”, resulting in funds appearing to disappear or become stuck.

title: No slippage protection in the c
description:
When users call the closeTradeMarket() function, a new Close pending market order is created. This pending market order can only be finalized by the Operator role. Since this action may be delayed, users can be negatively impacted by market conditions.
This would be acceptable if the user action was fully within their control, such as when they control transaction gas usage.
However, as users do not control when this pending action will be completed and are unable to cancel it, they are exposed to potential fund loss.
Combining this with the fact that the protocol supports a guaranteed stop loss price, which is not respected in the case of market orders, users may experience greater losses than expected if the execution is delayed.
No slippage protection in the closeTradeMarket() function flow; the slippageP and wantedPrice parameters of the PendingMarketOrder struct are set to 0. (here)
Even if set, these parameters are not used within the TradingCallbacks.closeTradeMarketCallback() function. (here)
Internal pre-conditions
1. User has an open position in one of the guaranteed stop loss markets.
2. User sets the stop loss at 10% below the position open price.
External pre-conditions
1. There are external negative market conditions, and the user expects these to worsen over time.
2. The current loss is only 5% and is still above the guaranteed stop loss.
3. User calls closeTradeMarket(), expecting the trade to close soon.
Attack Path
1. User calls closeTradeMarket() while facing a 5% loss, expecting the trade to close shortly.
2. The Operator call is delayed, and by the time it is executed, the market has declined further, resulting in a 12% loss.
3. The guaranteed stop loss at 10% is not respected, causing the user to lose an additional 2% beyond the expected stop loss.
• User experiences a loss of funds beyond his control, which cannot be seen as user mistake.
bug_full: When a trader calls the closeTradeMarket function the contract creates a pending market order that can only be finalized by an address that holds the Operator role. The pending order stores slippage parameters (slippageP and wantedPrice) as zero and the callback that actually executes the market close never reads these fields nor checks the trader’s guaranteed stop‑loss price. Because the order remains pending until the Operator manually triggers it, the execution may be delayed arbitrarily. If the market moves unfavourably during this delay, the order is settled at the new market price, which can be far beyond the stop‑loss threshold that the trader expected to be respected. In the described scenario a trader with a 10 % guaranteed stop loss initiates a market close while the position is only 5 % underwater. The Operator’s delayed execution occurs after the price has fallen to a 12 % loss, so the stop loss is ignored and the trader suffers an additional 2 % loss. The vulnerability stems from the lack of slippage protection and the omission of stop‑loss enforcement in the market‑close callback, combined with the inability of the user to cancel the pending order. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful close request, yet the funds received are lower than expected or even appear to disappear, violating the business logic that a guaranteed stop loss should cap losses. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock through a crafted test that simulated price drops and delayed operator execution. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about pending execution or slippage limits, and the pending order fields are set to zero by design. To remediate, the protocol should either enforce the guaranteed stop‑loss price when processing market closes or introduce explicit slippage protection that limits how far the execution price may deviate from the trader’s request, and ideally provide a mechanism for the trader to cancel a pending market close before it is executed.

title: User collateral value may be
description:
If the Governor switches the system to useBackupOnly, a malicious user can exploit this condition by performing a Trading.updateMargin() DEPOSIT action, effectively increasing their collateral without transferring the necessary USDC.
This occurs because Trading.updateMargin() is a user-triggered action that calls PriceAggregator.fulfill(). In useBackupOnly mode, the price sent to TradingCallbacks.updateMarginCallback() will always be 0. Although updateMarginCallback() verifies if price!=0, it does not revert if the price is 0. As a result, the entire if block is skipped, including the users required USDC transfer.
Furthermore, the system updates the users open trade data with the new DEPOSIT amount, artificially increasing initialPosToken without any USDC backing.
Consequently, the system data becomes corrupted, making it impossible to exit useBackupOnly, liquidate the user position accurately, or distribute fees correctly, leading to potential protocol losses.
Prematurely updating the user trade (here) and failing to revert when price=0 (here) in useBackupOnly mode (here) enables collateral increases without any USDC deposit (here).
Internal pre-conditions
1. The system is set to useBackupOnly state.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. The user calls updateMargin() to deposit collateral.
2. The users trade data is updated based on the deposit amount, with initialPosToken and leverage adjusted to reflect the original open interest.
3. In useBackupOnly mode, the UPDATE_MARGIN order type bypasses the if/else block in fulfill(), setting price=0 for updateMarginCallback().
4. Within updateMarginCallback(), the if block is skipped due to price=0.
5. The transaction completes without transferring USDC from the user to the Vault Manager.
• Direct funds loss if useBackupOnly is lifted.
• Data corruption in storage.
• Incorrect fee accounting upon position liquidation.
• Potential protocol loss if the position is force-closed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a collateral inflation bug that appears when the protocol is switched to the backup‑only pricing mode. In this mode the PriceAggregator always returns a price of zero to the TradingCallbacks.updateMarginCallback function. The callback checks that the price is not zero but, instead of reverting, simply skips the if‑block that contains the USDC transfer from the caller to the Vault Manager. Because the updateMargin() function updates the user’s open‑trade record before the price check, the trade’s initialPosToken and leverage are increased based on the declared deposit amount even though no USDC has actually been moved. A malicious user can therefore call Trading.updateMargin() with the DEPOSIT action, trigger the zero‑price path, and inflate their collateral by the requested amount while their USDC balance remains unchanged. This corrupts the protocol’s accounting state, makes it impossible to correctly liquidate the position or calculate fees, and can cause direct loss of funds when the backup mode is later disabled. The issue only manifests when the governor has enabled useBackupOnly; no external conditions are required. It was discovered during an audit by reproducing the scenario in a test that showed the initialPosToken value doubling without any USDC transfer. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, the UI reports a higher collateral amount, and the user’s wallet still shows the same USDC balance, so the discrepancy is hidden in internal storage. The root cause is the missing revert on a zero price and the premature update of trade data before validating the price. The class of bug is an invariant‑violation caused by insufficient input validation, leading to state inconsistency and economic loss. The recommended fix is to revert the transaction when the price supplied to updateMarginCallback is zero, or to prevent updateMargin calls while the system is in backup‑only mode, ensuring that collateral can only increase after a successful USDC transfer.

title: Incorrect calculations in the
description:
An incorrect divisor is used in the deviation calculation when the Chainlink backup price is less than the Pyth price. This can result in unintended reverts even when the price is within the allowed deviation.
The issue stems from using bkPrice as the divisor in the if(bkPrice<price) case (here), whereas the correct divisor should be price. This causes the deviation to be calculated from bkPrice instead of from the intended price.
Internal pre-conditions
1. The pair in addition to Pyth is using a Chainlink backup feed.
2. The backup maxDeviation is set to 2% (or any other valid value).
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. A transaction is executed for a pair that is using the Chainlink backup feed.
2. The Chainlink reported price is approximately -2% from the Pyth price.
3. The transaction is incorrectly reverted in a situation where it should be accepted.
• Reverting time-sensitive function.
• Loss of fees, as the system may subsequently decide to cancelPendingMarketOrder(). In case it was a market order.
poc:
Consider a simple calculation with a BTC price of 50,000 and a 2% backup deviation.
This deviation allows an acceptable range of 49,000 to 51,000.
Currently, if Pyth reports a price of 50,000 and the Chainlink backup feed is 49,000, this should be within the acceptable deviation, and the transaction should proceed.
However, due to the incorrect divisor, the transaction is reverted as follows:
(50000 - 49000) * 100 / 49000 > 2%
(50000 * 10**10 - 49000 * 10**10) * 100 * 10**10 / (49000 * 10**10) = 20408163265 > 2%
Using the correct price divisor would yield the intended 2%:
(50000 * 10**10 - 49000 * 10**10) * 100 * 10**10 / (50000 * 10**10) = 20000000000
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mathematical miscalculation in the price deviation check that is used when a Chainlink backup oracle is consulted alongside a primary Pyth price feed. The contract compares the backup price (bkPrice) to the primary price (price) and, if the backup price is lower, it calculates the percentage deviation by dividing the price difference by bkPrice instead of by the primary price. This incorrect divisor inflates the computed deviation, causing the contract to treat a price that is actually within the allowed tolerance as out‑of‑range. The root cause is a simple logic error: the divisor should be the reference price (price) but the code mistakenly re‑uses the backup price when bkPrice < price. An attacker can trigger the bug by submitting a transaction that relies on the backup feed, for example a market order whose execution price is derived from the backup price. If the backup price is roughly two percent lower than the primary price – a scenario that is perfectly acceptable under the configured maxDeviation – the contract will still revert the transaction because the inflated deviation exceeds the threshold. The impact is that legitimate trades are blocked, users see unexpected revert messages, and the protocol may lose accrued fees or be forced to cancel pending market orders, effectively reducing liquidity and user confidence. The condition occurs only for pairs that have a Chainlink backup feed and a non‑zero maxDeviation setting; it does not affect pairs without a backup feed. All participants who submit orders through the affected pair – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their transactions may be rejected without any visible price anomaly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the deviation logic and noticed the divisor mismatch; reproducing the scenario with a simple numeric example (e.g., Pyth price 50,000 and Chainlink price 49,000 with a 2 % tolerance) confirmed that the contract incorrectly reverts. The bug is subtle because the price values themselves appear correct and the deviation threshold is respected when calculated properly; only the internal arithmetic is wrong, making it easy to miss during functional testing. To remediate, the deviation calculation should consistently use the primary price as the divisor regardless of the relative ordering of the two feeds, ensuring that the percentage difference reflects the intended tolerance. Conceptually, this is a class of “incorrect denominator” or “division‑by‑wrong‑value” bugs that lead to false‑positive validation failures, breaking business logic that assumes a price within the allowed deviation will be accepted. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a transaction failure or a “revert” error even though the quoted price looks correct, leading to confusion such as “my order was rejected even though the price is within 2 %”. The expectation that a price within the configured deviation will be processed is violated, resulting in lost fees, delayed order execution, and potential loss of confidence in the protocol’s reliability.

title: Incorrect depositCap check in T
description:
The depositCap check in the _deposit function of the Tranche contract uses an assets amount that includes a fee. However, this fee is transferred out of the vault, meaning it does not contribute to the actual asset amount in the vault and thus should not impact the depositCap.
In the line require(totalAssets()+assets<depositCap,"DEPOSIT_CAP_BREACHED");, the function checks assets without accounting for the deduction of getDepositFeesTotal(assets). As a result, the depositCap check is inflated by the fee amount, potentially causing deposits to be rejected incorrectly when the vault is close to the cap. The check should use assets-fee to accurately reflect the true impact on the vault balance. (here)
Internal pre-conditions
1. The vault is close to reaching its depositCap.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. A user attempts to deposit when the vault is close to its depositCap.
2. Due to the fee being included in the assets amount, the cap check fails, rejecting the deposit unnecessarily.
The current implementation may cause users to be incorrectly prevented from depositing due to an inflated assets value. This issue is more prominent when the vault balance is near the depositCap, as it could block further deposits prematurely.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect deposit cap verification in the Tranche contract’s _deposit function. The contract enforces a maximum total asset amount (depositCap) by checking require(totalAssets()+assets<depositCap,"DEPOSIT_CAP_BREACHED");. However, the variable assets includes the full amount a user intends to deposit before the protocol fee is deducted. The fee is immediately transferred out of the vault via getDepositFeesTotal(assets) and therefore does not increase the vault’s actual balance. Because the fee is counted as part of assets in the cap check, the condition is artificially inflated; the contract treats the fee as if it were additional assets contributing to the cap. This mis‑accounting occurs when the vault’s current balance is close to the configured depositCap. An attacker or any user attempting to deposit a small amount that would keep the net balance under the cap can be rejected because totalAssets()+assets exceeds the limit once the fee is added, even though the net increase (assets‑fee) would be acceptable. The impact is that legitimate deposits are needlessly blocked, leading to a poor user experience where users see the DEPOSIT_CAP_BREACHED error despite there being sufficient space in the vault. No funds are stolen; the transaction simply reverts, but the protocol’s liquidity intake is reduced and users may lose confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee calculation was performed after the cap check, contradicting the intended accounting model. It can be hard to notice because the error only manifests when the vault is near its cap, a state that may not be exercised in routine tests. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or invariant‑violation errors where fees or other deductions are not accounted for in resource‑limit checks. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a deposit failure with a message that the cap is breached, while the expectation was that the deposit should succeed because the vault still has free capacity. To remediate, the cap verification should use the net amount that actually remains in the vault after fees, i.e., require(totalAssets()+assets‑getDepositFeesTotal(assets)<depositCap,…), ensuring that only the true increase to vault assets is considered. This aligns the contract’s business logic with its accounting assumptions and prevents premature deposit rejections.

title: The closing fee is not factored
description:
Based on Avantis documentation (docs) and general logic, the closing fee should be included in the liquidation price calculation, just as the rollover fee is. The documentation specifies:  
CollateralHealthRatio=(NetCollateral+PnL-accumulatedmarginfee-closingfee)/NetCollateral  
Omitting the closing fee deduction results in the getTradeLiquidationPrice() function calculating a liquidation price that is higher than it should be.  
The standard closing fee is not deducted in the getTradeLiquidationPricePure() function (here). This discrepancy with the documentation creates potential for inaccurate liquidation price ranges.  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
This is a straightforward calculation error.  
• Incorrect distribution between PnL and standard fees.  
• The tranches reserves and OI will be affected by the trade that should be already liquidated.
bug_full: An error in the liquidation price calculation causes the protocol to omit the standard closing fee when determining the price at which a leveraged position will be liquidated. According to the documented CollateralHealthRatio formula, the closing fee must be subtracted from the net collateral together with accumulated margin fees and profit‑and‑loss. The implementation of getTradeLiquidationPricePure, however, only deducts the accumulated margin fee and ignores the closing fee, resulting in a liquidation price that is systematically higher than the correct value. This mis‑calculation can occur for any trade, regardless of pre‑conditions, because the function is invoked whenever the system needs to assess liquidation risk. When the liquidation price is inflated, a position may appear sufficiently collateralised while in reality it is closer to insolvency. Consequently, the protocol may delay or skip liquidation, allowing the trader’s loss to grow and potentially exhausting the tranche reserves and distorting open interest metrics. From a user perspective the UI may display a liquidation price that does not match the fee schedule shown in the documentation, leading to expectations of a lower liquidation threshold that are not met; users may see their positions liquidated later than anticipated or, conversely, may suffer larger losses because the system fails to protect the pool. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditor compared the on‑chain calculation with the documented formula and identified the missing subtraction. Because the discrepancy is purely arithmetic, it does not raise obvious runtime errors and can be hard to notice without a side‑by‑side formula check. The appropriate remediation is to modify the liquidation price logic to include the closing fee in the numerator of the CollateralHealthRatio, ensuring that the fee is deducted before the price is derived. This aligns the implementation with the documented accounting model, restores accurate liquidation thresholds, and prevents unintended exposure of tranche reserves and open interest to excess risk.

title: Wrong skew impact spread will
description:
Wrong skew impact spread will be returned in case when there is already a short position and a trader opens a long position i.e the first long position on the same pair.  
antis-contracts/src/PairInfos.sol#L346 The function incorrectly returns 0 when openInterestUSDCLong is zero for a trading pair.  
Internal pre-conditions  
Na  
External pre-conditions  
Initially a short position must be opened on a trading pair and then the first long position should be opened.  
Attack Path  
1. Suppose there is initially some short positions opened on a trading pair i.e openInterestUSDCShort not equal to zero.  
2. Now a trader opens a long position on this trading pair which is currently short skewed. Now as the pair is short skewed currently therefore better price should be offered to the current trader i.e getSkewImpactSpread function should return negative value as the trader is trying to balance the long/short position ratio but currently 0 is returned which is incorrect.  
3. If this scenario had been reversed i.e there had been initially long position and then a short position was opened then the getskewImpactSpread function would have worked completely fine by not returning 0 instead returning a negative value.  
The long traders are not offered better prices for reducing the short skew thus there is no incentive for the traders to balance the trading pair.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the getSkewImpactSpread function that calculates a price incentive (spread) intended to reward traders who help rebalance a market’s long/short exposure. The function contains an early guard that returns zero whenever the long open interest (openInterestUSDCLong) is zero. This guard is meant to avoid division‑by‑zero errors, but it also prevents the spread calculation in a legitimate edge case: when a trading pair already has short positions (openInterestUSDCShort > 0) and a trader attempts to open the first long position. In that situation the market is short‑skewed, so the correct economic behaviour is to return a negative spread, giving the long trader a better price as an incentive to reduce the skew. Because the function returns 0, the trader receives a neutral price instead of the expected discount. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the PairInfos contract, where the auditor noticed that the conditional `if(openInterestUSDCLong == 0) return 0;` short‑circuits the calculation for the first‑long scenario. The issue is subtle because most normal trading activity involves both sides having non‑zero open interest, so the function behaves correctly in the majority of cases and the faulty path is only exercised in a specific market state. Exploitation does not require malicious code; any user opening a long position under the described conditions will experience the incorrect pricing. The impact is economic rather than a direct loss of funds: traders expecting a price improvement see none, which can discourage them from providing the balancing long side, leading to persistent short‑skewed exposure, higher slippage for future trades, and potential imbalance of risk for the protocol. The problem affects all participants who trade the affected pair, especially those who rely on the protocol’s advertised incentive mechanism. It occurs whenever the pair has existing short positions, no long positions, and a trader opens a long order while the order is not a profit‑and‑loss (Pnl) based order. To remediate, the early return for a zero long open interest should be removed or replaced with logic that still computes the spread based on the short side alone, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This class of bug is an edge‑case conditional guard error that leads to incorrect incentive calculation, violating the business rule that traders who reduce market skew should receive a better price. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing discount: a trader opens a long on a short‑skewed market and sees the same execution price as a neutral market, contrary to the expectation of a lower price.

title: If a trader of market order or
poc: None
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol releases USDC collateral when a trade is closed. The contract calls the ERC20 transfer function on the USDC token to send the reserved amount back to the trader. USDC implements a blacklist feature that causes any transfer to a blacklisted address to revert. Because the protocol does not check the blacklist status before attempting the transfer, a trader whose address is blacklisted for USDC cannot receive the funds. When the close‑order function reaches the internal _sendUSDCToTrader call, the transfer reverts, the whole order‑closing transaction is rolled back, and the reserved USDC remains locked in the vault forever. This situation can be triggered for both market and limit orders as soon as the trader’s address appears on the USDC blacklist, which may happen after the order is opened. From a user’s perspective the order appears to be still open, the UI may show the position as active, but the trader sees no funds returned and the collateral balance stays unchanged, effectively disappearing from the trader’s usable balance. The impact is that the affected trader loses access to their collateral, and the protocol’s capital pool may become partially immobilised, reducing liquidity and potentially harming other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Avantis v1.5 cross‑asset leverage contracts, where the auditor noticed that the transfer to the trader is performed without any fallback or claim mechanism. It is subtle because the failure only occurs at the moment of closing, and there is no explicit error message indicating a blacklist problem; the transaction simply reverts. The bug belongs to the class of “transfer‑revert due to recipient restrictions” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that collateral can always be returned to the trader on order settlement. To remediate, the contract should decouple the accounting of owed USDC from the immediate transfer. Instead of calling transfer directly, the contract should record the amount owed to each trader and provide a separate claim function that allows the trader (or an authorized party) to withdraw the funds later, possibly using a safe‑transfer pattern with try/catch to handle blacklisted recipients. This change ensures that even if a transfer would revert, the protocol’s state remains consistent and the funds are not permanently locked.

title: The slippage percent is not up-
poc: None
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing state update for the slippage percentage when a trader attempts to modify an existing open limit order through the Trading.updateOpenLimitOrder() function. The external function receives a _slippageP argument and forwards an OpenLimitOrder struct containing this value to TradingStorage.updateOpenLimitOrder(), which is expected to persist the new slippage percentage in storage. However, the internal implementation only copies fields such as positionSize, buy, leverage, tp, sl, price and block, and omits the assignment of o.slippageP = _o.slippageP. Consequently, the contract continues to use the previously stored slippage value, typically the default or an older user‑specified value. This discrepancy arises from a simple coding oversight: the slippage field is not written to storage, breaking the intended business logic that traders rely on to control price tolerance for limit order execution. Exploitation is straightforward: a trader believes they have tightened or relaxed slippage limits, but the contract ignores the change, allowing the order to be filled at a price outside the trader’s expectations. In worst‑case scenarios, the order may be executed with a much tighter slippage (e.g., zero), causing the transaction to revert or be front‑run, or with a looser slippage, resulting in execution at an unfavorable price and potential loss of funds. The impact is felt by any user who updates slippage on open limit orders, as the UI may display the new percentage while the on‑chain logic still applies the old one, leading to confusion, unexpected zero refunds, or orders filling at prices that appear to “slip” beyond the user’s tolerance. The issue manifests whenever the updateOpenLimitOrder() function is called; there are no explicit pre‑conditions, and the contract does not emit an event indicating the failure, making the bug silent and hard to notice without a code review. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the security researcher Sherlock, who compared the external interface with the storage contract and observed the missing assignment. Because the contract does not revert or emit an error, users receive no immediate feedback, and the discrepancy can remain unnoticed until a trade executes with unexpected slippage. The recommended remediation is to add the missing line o.slippageP = _o.slippageP; in the storage update function so that the slippage percentage is correctly persisted. This aligns the implementation with the intended contract semantics, restores the guarantee that traders can control price tolerance, and prevents silent mismatches between UI expectations and on‑chain behavior.

title: In the Tranche.sol, there is no
poc: None
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection in the tranche contract that governs deposit, withdraw, mint and redeem operations. The contract charges a balancing fee that is calculated on‑chain from the dynamic reserve ratio, which itself is derived from the current token balances of the junior and senior tranches. Because the fee calculation uses mutable state, an attacker who can modify the tranche balances immediately before a victim’s transaction can push the reserve ratio beyond the configured thresholds, causing the getBalancingFee function to return a non‑zero balancingFee where the user expected none. In practice this means a user may submit a deposit expecting to receive a certain number of shares with zero fee, but after a front‑running transaction the contract applies the balancing fee, reducing the minted shares and effectively taking extra value from the user. The same effect can occur on withdrawals, where the user receives fewer assets than anticipated. The impact is financial loss for ordinary users and liquidity providers, who may end up with fewer shares or assets than they intended. The issue manifests only when other participants can change the tranche balances between the moment the user estimates the fee and the moment the transaction is mined, a condition that is common in permissionless environments with pending mempool transactions. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑calculation logic and noticed the absence of any check that the fee remains within an acceptable slippage range. The problem is hard to notice because the fee function returns zero under normal conditions, so developers may assume the fee is static, overlooking that the underlying ratio can be manipulated. Conceptually, this is a class of “missing slippage check” or “price manipulation via mutable fee basis” bugs, where a contract relies on on‑chain state that can be altered by adversaries without re‑validating the user’s expectations. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected fee deductions, fewer shares minted, or reduced withdrawal amounts, contrary to the expectation of receiving the full amount they supplied. To remediate, the contract should capture the expected fee before the state‑changing operation, allow the caller to specify a maximum acceptable slippage, and revert the transaction if the actual fee after state changes exceeds that tolerance. This ensures that front‑running or balance‑shifting attacks cannot silently impose extra fees.

title: Inconsistency referrerRebate
poc: None
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent fee allocation logic for the referrer rebate that occurs between the opening and closing of a leveraged trade. When a trade is opened, the contract calculates a variable called feeAfterRebate without including the referrerRebate amount; the vault allocation is then derived from this feeAfterRebate and the referrer rebate is subtracted only at the point of transfer to the vault. Conversely, when the same trade is closed, feeAfterRebate is calculated to already contain the referrerRebate, and the vault allocation is computed after explicitly subtracting the rebate from feeAfterRebate. This mismatch means that the same logical fee component is treated differently in two complementary phases of the same transaction lifecycle. The root cause is the divergent handling of the referrerRebate flag in the two functions that compute fees for opening and closing orders, leading to two distinct formulas for vaultAllocation, governance fees and developer fees. An attacker or a malicious user could exploit this by opening a position with a referrer, then closing it to trigger the inconsistent calculation, potentially causing the protocol to allocate more funds to the vault or governance than intended, or to under‑pay the referrer. The impact is a distortion of the economic accounting of the protocol: referrers may receive less rebate than expected, the vault may receive an incorrect amount of fees, and overall protocol revenue accounting becomes unreliable.
