The condition under which this occurs is any trade that includes a referrer rebate; trades without a referrer are unaffected. Affected parties include the referrer (who may lose expected earnings), the vault (which may receive an inaccurate fee amount), governance token holders (who may see altered fee distribution), and end‑users who rely on correct fee calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TradingStorage and TradingCallbacks contracts, where the auditor noticed that the same variable feeAfterRebate was used with opposite inclusion semantics. Because the contract still compiles and executes without reverting, the bug can be subtle and may only be observed through mismatched accounting reports or unexpected rebate amounts in the UI. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a referrer sees a lower or zero rebate after closing a trade, or that the vault’s fee balance appears higher than expected. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or fee‑allocation inconsistencies, where the same logical component is treated differently across code paths, violating the protocol’s financial invariants. To remediate, the fee calculation should be unified so that feeAfterRebate either always includes or always excludes the referrerRebate, and the subsequent vault, governance and developer fee formulas should be derived from the same base amount in both opening and closing functions. This ensures consistent fee distribution, preserves the intended economic incentives, and restores confidence in the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: The VeTranche.getTotalLockP
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the reward accounting logic caused by an incorrect scaling of the aggregate lock points. The contract stores a cumulative value representing the total amount of lock points contributed by all participants, but the public getter returns this value divided by a fixed precision constant. As a result the reported total is smaller than the actual total, and subsequent reward calculations that rely on the getter use the reduced figure. When the protocol distributes rewards, it multiplies the reward pool by a large precision factor and then divides by the undersized total lock points. This produces a per‑share reward that is slightly higher than it should be. Each user’s pending reward is then calculated using this inflated per‑share value, which leads to a sum of individual rewards that exceeds the amount of tokens actually available for distribution. The impact is that the protocol may attempt to allocate more tokens than it holds, causing reward claims to fail, balances to appear reduced, or the contract to run out of funds. The issue manifests whenever the lock‑point totals are large enough for the division by the precision constant to truncate significant digits, which is typical in high‑value staking or leverage scenarios. All participants who are eligible for rewards are affected because the accounting error is global. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the VeTranche contract by the auditor, who noticed that the getter performed an unexpected division and traced the arithmetic through the reward distribution functions. It can be hard to notice because the returned value still looks plausible and the discrepancy may be only a few units, yet it accumulates across many users and large reward pools. The proper fix is to return the raw total lock points without dividing by the precision constant, and to adjust any downstream calculations to use the correct scaling factor consistently. Conceptually, this is a classic arithmetic precision or scaling bug where an intermediate value is incorrectly normalized, breaking the invariant that total allocated rewards must never exceed the reward pool. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or partially missing rewards, unexpected zero balances after a claim, or transaction reverts due to insufficient contract balance. The contract’s business logic assumes that the sum of all individual rewards equals the total rewards distributed; the precision error violates this accounting assumption and can lead to fund shortfalls.

title: Fees is not sent to the operator
bug_full: The contract implements an openTrade function that accepts a payable fee (msg.value) intended for the operator. The fee is forwarded to the operator only in the branch that handles market orders (type MARKET or MARKET_PNL). When a trader opens a limit order of type reversal or momentum (any type that is not MARKET or MARKET_PNL), the function follows the first branch of the conditional and stores the limit order without executing the payable call that transfers the fee to the operator. As a result, the operator does not receive the execution fee even though the trader has sent ether with the transaction. This discrepancy originates from the conditional logic that omits the fee‑transfer statement for non‑market order types. An attacker can exploit the bug by repeatedly opening limit orders of the affected types, thereby consuming the protocol’s fee revenue without compensating the operator. The impact is primarily economic: the operator loses expected fee income and may eventually be unable to fund external services such as the Pyth price‑feed updates that are paid for in the executeLimitOrder function. The issue manifests every time openTrade is called with a limit‑order type; no revert occurs, so the transaction succeeds and the trader sees the order placed, while the operator’s balance remains unchanged. Users of the protocol are affected indirectly because the operator’s revenue model is broken, which could jeopardize the long‑term sustainability of the service. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee handling paths for market and limit orders and noticed the missing payable call in the limit‑order branch. Because the function does not emit a specific event for fee transfer, the omission is subtle and may go unnoticed in normal testing or UI monitoring – the trader’s UI shows the order placed and the fee appears to be deducted, but the operator’s account does not reflect the receipt. The correct remediation is to move the payable call that forwards msg.value to the operator outside of the conditional, or to duplicate it in the limit‑order branch, ensuring that every order type, including reversal and momentum limit orders, pays the operator the execution fee as intended. This aligns the contract’s behavior with its economic assumptions and restores the expected fee flow.

title: User fund loss and incorrect
description: The Trading.closeTradeMarket() function allows for partial position closing. However, when partial closing occurs, an issue within the TradingCallbacks._unregisterTrade() function leads to user fund losses and incorrect fee calculations. When the condition if(_trade.initialPosToken==_collateral||(_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken)) evaluates to true solely due to the second part (_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken), the position is closed as if the entire remaining collateral was requested for withdrawal (_collateral=_trade.initialPosToken;). This condition causes direct user fund losses, as the total fees were already deducted from the users collateral during pairInfos.getTradeValue() calculations and reflected in the withdrawal amount usdcSentToTrader. When the condition (_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken) is met, the user is penalized again with his remaining collateral. In addition to this double penalization, the funds are locked in the Vault Manager, and reflect the remaining _trade.initialPosToken when calculating fees for closing the position. The broken condition in if(_trade.initialPosToken==_collateral||(_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken)) causes direct user fund losses and incorrect fee accounting when (_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken) is met. (here) Internal pre-conditions None. External pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. A user performs a partial close on OpenTrade. 2. The if/else block in the (_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken) check matches, with _collateral less than _trade.initialPosToken. 3. User is penalized. 4. The _collateral used in fee calculations in pairInfos.getTradeValue() was incorrect. • Direct user fund losses. • Fees calculated based on an incorrect _collateral value are undercalculated.
poc: Add the following to MarketTrade.t.sol and call forgetest-vv--match-testtest_PocPartialClose: function test_PocPartialClose() public { vm.startPrank(traders[0]); usdc.transfer(traders[2], usdc.balanceOf(traders[0])); uint amount = 10000e6; usdc.mint(traders[0], amount); usdc.approve(address(tradingStorage), amount); uint id1 = _placeMarketLong(traders[0], amount / 2, btcPairIndex, 50000); uint id2 = _placeMarketLong(traders[0], amount / 2, btcPairIndex, 50000); vm.stopPrank(); _executeMarketLong(traders[0], amount / 2, btcPairIndex, 50000, id1); _executeMarketLong(traders[0], amount / 2, btcPairIndex, 50000, id2); vm.startPrank(traders[0]); uint pnlRewardsBefore = vaultManager.pnlRewards(); uint totalRewardsBefore = vaultManager.totalRewards(); vm.warp(100000); ITradingStorage.Trade memory _trade = tradingStorage.openTrades(traders[0], btcPairIndex, 0); _setChainlinkBTC(50000); uint closed1 = _placeMarketClose(btcPairIndex, _trade.initialPosToken, 0, 50000); ,→ uint closed2 = _placeMarketClose(btcPairIndex, 4900000000, 1, 50000); vm.stopPrank(); _executeMarketClose(btcPairIndex, _trade.initialPosToken, 0, 50000, closed1); uint pnlRewardsAfter1 = vaultManager.pnlRewards() - pnlRewardsBefore; uint totalRewardsAfter1 = vaultManager.totalRewards() - totalRewardsBefore; uint userBalanceAfter1 = usdc.balanceOf(traders[0]); _executeMarketClose(btcPairIndex, _trade.initialPosToken, 0, 50000, closed2); uint pnlRewardsAfter2 = vaultManager.pnlRewards() - pnlRewardsBefore; uint totalRewardsAfter2 = vaultManager.totalRewards() - totalRewardsBefore; uint userBalanceAfter2 = usdc.balanceOf(traders[0]); assert(tradingStorage.openTrades(traders[0], btcPairIndex, 0).leverage == 0); assert(tradingStorage.openTrades(traders[0], btcPairIndex, 1).leverage == 0); console2.log("User loss:", userBalanceAfter1 - (userBalanceAfter2 - userBalanceAfter1)); ,→ console2.log("Pnl reward loss:", pnlRewardsAfter1 - (pnlRewardsAfter2 - pnlRewardsAfter1)); ,→ console2.log("Reward loss:", totalRewardsAfter1 - (totalRewardsAfter2 - totalRewardsAfter1)); ,→ } Console output: Logs: User loss: 39313147 Pnl reward loss: 287140 Reward loss: 319770 The log shows a direct loss of approximately $40 for the user when closing the position partially, compared to closing it fully, highlighting the edge case error.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the logic that determines whether a trade is being fully closed or only partially closed when a user invokes Trading.closeTradeMarket() with a partial amount. Inside TradingCallbacks._unregisterTrade() the contract checks the condition if(_trade.initialPosToken==_collateral||(_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken)). The second part of this expression can become true when the sum of the remaining collateral (_collateral) and the fees already deducted (totalFees) reaches or exceeds the original position size (_trade.initialPosToken). When this happens the code treats the operation as a full closure, overwriting _collateral with the full initial position value and proceeding to unregister the trade. Because totalFees have already been subtracted from the user’s collateral during the pairInfos.getTradeValue() calculation, the user is effectively charged twice: once through the fee deduction and again through the erroneous full‑close logic that withdraws the remaining collateral as if no fees had been taken. The result is a direct loss of funds for the trader, an under‑calculation of fees in the vault manager, and locked assets that remain reflected as the original position size for subsequent fee calculations. The bug manifests only when a partial close is performed and the collateral left after the first fee deduction is just enough to satisfy the (_collateral+totalFees>=_trade.initialPosToken) check. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the remaining collateral after a partial close – is not met; the balance may drop to zero or to an unexpectedly low amount, and the UI shows a missing refund. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Sherlock, who created a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated a loss of roughly $40 when closing a position partially versus fully. The problem is subtle because the condition appears to allow both exact‑match and “greater‑or‑equal” scenarios, and the second clause is mistakenly interpreted as a full‑close trigger even though fees have already been accounted for. To remediate the flaw the second clause should be removed, leaving only the equality check to detect a true full closure. The partial‑close path must retain the original collateral value and only register the remaining portion without resetting _collateral to the initial position size. This change restores correct fee accounting, prevents double penalisation, and ensures that users receive the correct amount after a partial close.

title: Incorrect Spread Percentage
description: In the fulfill function of the PriceAggregator contract, the spread percentage (spreadP) for orders of type MARKET_OPEN_PNL is incorrectly derived. Instead of fetching the spread for PnL-based orders, the function defaults to using the spread percentage for regular orders. PriceAggregator.sol#L185 The issue lies in the fulfill function where spreadP is set using pairsStorage.pairSpreadP(r.pairIndex,false), regardless of the OrderType. When OrderType.MARKET_OPEN_PNL is used, the PnL-based spread should instead be retrieved with pairsStorage.pairSpreadP(r.pairIndex, true). if (answers.length > 0) { ICallbacks.AggregatorAnswer memory a = ICallbacks.AggregatorAnswer( orderId, _median(answers), pairsStorage.pairSpreadP(r.pairIndex, false) // Issue: Not distinguishing between PnL-based orders ,→ ); Internal pre-conditions External pre-conditions Attack Path improper spread percentage usage for pnl Order type
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect spread percentage applied to orders of type MARKET_OPEN_PNL in the PriceAggregator contract. The fulfill function always calls pairsStorage.pairSpreadP(r.pairIndex,false) which retrieves the spread configured for regular orders, regardless of the order type. For PnL‑based market orders the contract is supposed to use the PnL‑specific spread, obtained with pairsStorage.pairSpreadP(r.pairIndex,true). Because the function does not check the OrderType before selecting the spread flag, the pricing logic uses the wrong spread value. An attacker or any user submitting a MARKET_OPEN_PNL order can therefore receive a price that is calculated with an inappropriate spread, leading to unexpected slippage, reduced profit, or higher cost than the protocol’s business rules intend. The impact is primarily on traders who rely on the PnL spread for accurate execution; they may see their balances decrease more than expected, refunds become zero, or profit calculations become inaccurate, which in turn can affect the protocol’s accounting and liquidity pool health. The bug manifests only when the fulfill function processes a MARKET_OPEN_PNL order; all other order types continue to use the correct spread. It was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the spread flag argument was hard‑coded to false. The issue is subtle because the spread is an internal parameter not displayed in the UI, so users only observe a price that is slightly off, making the problem hard to detect without inspecting the contract code. To fix the issue the fulfill function must be updated to inspect the OrderType and pass true for PnL‑based orders, ensuring the correct spread percentage is used. This class of bug falls under business‑logic errors where a function selects an incorrect configuration parameter based on context, violating the intended accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: Loss protection inconsistency
description: In skewed market, users can have loss protection of 10%-20%. Based on the provided docs, the loss protection should work as follows: Example 2 (Directional Trader): If the net PnL of the above trader is -20%, then technically the trader should have lost $2,000 (20% $10K). However, with loss protection, the trader only loses $2000 * (1-20%) = $1,600. This is the magic of loss protection ! However, the current implementation works slightly different. function getTradeValuePure( uint collateral, int percentProfit, uint rolloverFee, uint closingFee, uint lossProtection ) public view returns (uint, int, uint) { int pnl = (int(collateral) * percentProfit) / int(_PRECISION) / 100; int lossProtectedPnl = pnl; if (pnl < 0) { lossProtectedPnl = (pnl * int(lossProtection)) / 100; } int fees = int(rolloverFee) + int(closingFee); int value = int(collateral) + lossProtectedPnl - fees; if (value <= (int(collateral) * int(100 - liqThreshold)) / 100) { value = lossProtectedPnl - pnl; lossProtectedPnl = fees - int(collateral) + value; } return (value > 0 ? uint(value) : 0, lossProtectedPnl, uint(fees)); } We can see that if the value is less than 15% of the collateral, the value paid out to the user is the delta of the lossProtectedPnl-pnl. Consider the following situation: 1. User has opened a $10k position with loss protection of 10%. 2. Position's current pnl is -95%. This would make the lossProtectedPnl equal to 85.5%. For simplicity we ignore the margin/ rollover fees. 3. This would cause us to enter the if-statement. Then the value assigned to the position would be -$8550-(-9500)=$950. 4. According to the example above, the position's value should've been $10000-0.9*(9500)=$1450. Instead it is just $950, resulting in $450 extra loss to the user. This is an extra loss of $450, or the user receiving ~35% less than supposed to. Wrong calculation of position's value Affected Code PairInfos.sol#L671 Loss of funds
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the loss‑protection accounting logic of the trading contract, where the payout calculation deviates from the documented formula when a position’s net value falls below the liquidation threshold (approximately 15 % of the initial collateral). The root cause is a conditional branch in the getTradeValuePure function that overwrites the computed position value with the difference between the loss‑protected PnL and the raw PnL (lossProtectedPnl‑pnl) instead of applying the intended loss‑protection factor after fees and liquidation checks. This branch is triggered only when the intermediate value (collateral plus loss‑protected PnL minus fees) is less than or equal to collateral × (100‑liqThreshold)/100, i.e., when the position is deeply underwater. An attacker or a market move can exploit this by opening a leveraged trade with a non‑zero loss‑protection percentage, allowing the price to move against the trader until the PnL reaches a large negative value (for example –95 %). At that point the faulty branch activates and the contract returns a payout that is the raw loss amount minus the protected portion, resulting in an extra loss (e.g., a $10 000 position with 10 % protection should return $1 450 but only returns $950, a $450 shortfall). The impact is that users receive less than the guaranteed protected amount, effectively losing additional funds and experiencing unexpected zero or near‑zero balances after closing a trade. This occurs only under extreme loss conditions, so it may be hard to notice during normal operation; the UI simply shows a lower final balance without indicating a calculation error. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who identified the mismatch between the documented loss‑protection example and the actual contract behavior by testing edge‑case PnL values. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect conditional logic leading to mis‑applied financial guarantees, a type of accounting or rounding bug that violates the business rule that loss protection should cap losses to a defined percentage. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a discrepancy between the expected refund (or remaining collateral) and the actual amount received, such as “I expected a $1 450 refund but got only $950” or “my position closed with almost no funds left despite having loss protection”. To remediate, the contract should be refactored so that loss protection is applied after all fee and liquidation checks, the erroneous branch should be removed or corrected, and the payout formula must guarantee that the protected loss never exceeds the configured percentage, thereby aligning on‑chain behavior with the documented guarantee.

title: Wrong handling of wallet open
description: Wrong handling of wallet open interest will cause issues Not properly handling wallet open interest per each pair. Each wallet can have a certain amount of max interest (the code below is a check in TradingStorage::withinExposureLimits() that must hold true when opening a trade): walletOI(_trader) + _leveragedPos <= pairsStored.maxWalletOI(_pairIndex); The issue is that we are checking the total wallet open interest of a trader against the max wallet open interest for a particular pair. Let's take a look at PairStorage::maxWalletOI(): function maxWalletOI(uint _pairIndex) external view override returns (uint) { return (storageT.maxOpenInterest() * pairs[_pairIndex].values.maxWalletOI) / 100; ,→ } As seen, we calculate the max open interest for a wallet based on the pair index provided. For the walletOI function used in the check above, we can clearly see that there is no pair index input, thus we can see that the return value of the function is not based on the pair of the trade. Let's also take a look at TradingStorage::_updateOpenInterestUSDC() where the wallet open interest for a trader gets updated: _walletOI[_trader] = _open ? _walletOI[_trader] + _leveragedPosUSDC : _walletOI[_trader] - _leveragedPosUSDC; ,→ As seen, it gets updated the same way regarding of the pair index. From the docs, I could not deduct whether the intentions were for each pair to have its own max wallet OI or for there to be a max wallet OI across all pairs. Either way, the current implementation is wrong as it is a mixture of the 2. Internal pre-conditions External pre-conditions Attack Path 1. There are 2 pairs, each with a maximum open interest of 100 2. Bob creates a trade on one of the pairs with a position size of 100 3. His wallet open interest gets updated to 100 4. He tries to create another trade on the other pair with a position size of 100 5. This reverts as he already has 100 wallet open interest which is also the maximum wallet open interest for the other pair (despite him having 0 open trades on the other pair) Unexpected reverts
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the protocol tracks and limits a trader’s wallet open interest (OI) across multiple trading pairs. The contract enforces a per‑pair maximum wallet OI by checking the sum of a trader’s total wallet OI (walletOI) plus the leveraged position size against the maximum allowed OI for the specific pair (maxWalletOI). However, the walletOI function does not accept a pair identifier, and the internal mapping that stores OI is updated globally regardless of which pair the trade belongs to. Consequently, the total OI of a trader is compared against a limit that is intended to apply only to a single pair. This mismatch means that once a trader reaches the maximum OI on one pair, any subsequent attempt to open a position on a different pair will be rejected, even though the trader has no exposure on that second pair. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the exposure‑limit logic, where the auditor noticed that the function signatures and the update routine were inconsistent with the intended per‑pair accounting. The issue is subtle because the contract will simply revert with a generic “exceeds exposure limits” error, offering no indication that the problem stems from an accounting mismatch rather than a malicious block. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should succeed will fail with an unexpected revert, leading the user to believe that the protocol is rejecting their trade arbitrarily or that their funds are being frozen. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style limitation: legitimate traders cannot diversify across pairs once they hit the per‑pair cap, reducing liquidity and potentially discouraging usage. The bug belongs to the class of logical accounting errors where global state is incorrectly used to enforce a local constraint. To remediate, the code should be refactored to either track OI per pair (by storing a mapping of trader → pair → OI and passing the pair index to the walletOI query) or to compare the aggregate wallet OI against a single global maximum, but not a mixture of both. Aligning the data structures and the limit checks with the intended business rule will prevent the erroneous reverts and restore the expected multi‑pair trading behavior.

title: Precision loss in VaultManager#g
description: On deposits and withdrawals, a balancing fee may or may not be charged, depending on the current reserve ratio in tranches: 1. Tranche#deposit -> ERC4626#previewDeposit -> Tranche#_deposit -> getDepositFeesTotal -> balancingFee; Tranche#withdraw -> ERC4626#previewWithdraw -> Tranche#_withdraw -> getWithdrawalFeesRaw -> balancingFee 2. Tranche#balancingFee -> VaultManager#getBalancingFee VaultManager.sol#L415-L429 As we can see, instead of bps, getDynamicReserveRatio returns percents. Therefore, if the actual reserve ratio is 6299 bps, it would return 62. in getBalancingFee: if ((getDynamicReserveRatio(tranche, isDeposit, assets) * 100) > balancingDeltaThreshold) { ,→ 62*100 < 6250 => getBalancingFee returns 0 instead of 500, despite the actual reserve ratio being outside of the target range so instead of paying the balancingFee because actual ratio is above 6250 (value from initializer), users will not. Similarly, when the ratio is between 3751 and 3799 bps, getDynamicReserveRatio would return 37, and balancingFee return a fee of 500, even though the current reserve ratio is within the target range. Percentage precision instead of bps in getDynamicReserveRatio. Internal pre-conditions getDynamicReserveRatio is in 3750-3799 or 6750-6799 bps range External pre-conditions Deposit or withdrawal into a Tranche. Deposits and withdrawals pay [do not pay] the balancingFee they shouldn't [should].
poc: Case 1: juniorTranche has 62_999e6 USDC seniorTranche has 37_101e6 USDC Alice wants to withdraw 100e6 from seniorTranche ratio = 62999e6 * 100 / 100_000e6 = 62 62*100 = 6200 6200 < 6250 balancingFee is not charged (but it should be) Case 2: seniorTranche has 62_001e6 USDC juniorTranche has 38_099e6 USDC Alice wants to withdraw 100e6 from juniorTranche ratio = 37_999e6 * 100 / 100_000e6 = 37 37*100 = 3700 3700 < 3750 balancingFee is charged (but it should not be)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss arithmetic error in the fee calculation path of the VaultManager contract. When a user deposits into or withdraws from a tranche, the system is supposed to apply a balancing fee if the tranche’s reserve ratio falls outside a predefined target window. The ratio is obtained from the function getDynamicReserveRatio, which is intended to return the value in basis points (bps). However, the function actually returns a plain percentage (e.g., 62 for 62%). The fee logic in getBalancingFee then multiplies this return value by 100, assuming it is already expressed in bps. As a result, the effective comparison against the balancingDeltaThreshold is off by a factor of 100. Consequently, when the true reserve ratio is 62.99 % (6299 bps), getDynamicReserveRatio yields 62, the multiplication produces 6200, which is below the 6250 bps threshold, and the balancing fee is incorrectly omitted. Conversely, when the ratio is 37.99 % (3799 bps), the function returns 37, the multiplication yields 3700, which is below the lower threshold of 3750 bps, causing a fee to be charged even though the ratio is inside the acceptable range. The root cause is a unit mismatch: the contract mixes percentages and basis points without proper conversion. An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by timing deposits or withdrawals near the threshold boundaries to avoid fees that should be paid, or to incur fees that should not be charged, thereby gaining an economic advantage or suffering unexpected loss. The impact includes inaccurate fee collection, which can erode protocol revenue, create unfair cost distribution among tranche participants, and potentially destabilize the intended risk‑adjusted returns. The bug manifests only when the reserve ratio is close to the threshold values (approximately 37.5‑38 % or 62.5‑63 %). Users of the affected tranches—both junior and senior investors—are the parties who may see their balances change unexpectedly: a user may expect a fee to be deducted but receives the full amount, or may see a fee deducted when they believed the tranche was within the safe range. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Avantis v1.5 cross‑asset leverage contracts, where the auditor traced the fee calculation flow from ERC4626 preview functions through Tranche internal methods to VaultManager#getBalancingFee and observed the mismatched scaling. The problem is subtle because the returned numbers are still plausible percentages, and the fee amounts are relatively small, making the discrepancy easy to overlook in routine testing. To remediate, getDynamicReserveRatio should be corrected to return values in basis points, and the subsequent multiplication by 100 in getBalancingFee should be removed, ensuring that the comparison against balancingDeltaThreshold uses consistent units. This class of bug falls under arithmetic precision or unit‑conversion errors, commonly seen when mixing percent and bps representations. From a user‑interface perspective, a user might notice that a withdrawal that should have incurred a fee arrives with the full amount, or that a withdrawal that should have been fee‑free shows a small deduction, violating the expectation that fees are applied only when the tranche is out of balance. The miscalculation violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees reflect reserve‑ratio deviations, potentially leading to revenue leakage or unfair cost allocation.

title: Fee distribution will be DOS'd
description: Whenever the vaultManager distributes fees it attempts to call _distributeCollectedFeeShares. VaultManager.sol#L642-L652 function _distributeCollectedFeeShares(address _tranche) internal { ITranche(_tranche).maxRedeem(address(this)), address(this), address(this) ); if (assets > 0) { _distributeVeRewards(IVeTranche(ITranche(_tranche).veTranche()), assets); } } We see above that it will always attempt to redeem from the tranche. Tranche.sol#L288-L305 function _withdraw( address caller, address receiver, address owner, uint256 assets, uint256 shares ) internal virtual override { uint256 fee = getWithdrawalFeesRaw(assets); super._withdraw(caller, receiver, owner, assets, shares); if (fee > 0) { SafeERC20.safeTransfer(ERC20(asset()), address(vaultManager), fee); vaultManager.allocateRewards(fee, false); emit FeeTransferredToVM(fee, false); } require(utilizationRatio() < withdrawThreshold, "UTILIZATION_RATIO_MAX"); <- ,→ } The problem here is that L304 reverts when utilizationRatio() < withdrawThreshold, hence all distributions will fail. VaultManager:L643 always redeems shares even if maxRedeem = 0 Internal pre-conditions utilizationRatio >= withdrawThreshold External pre-conditions None Attack Path 1. Fees are ready to be distributed 2. utilizationRatio >= withdrawThreshold for one of the tranches 3. Fee distributions will always revert Fee distribution will be DOS'd
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution routine of the VaultManager contract. When the manager attempts to distribute collected fees it unconditionally calls the internal function _distributeCollectedFeeShares, which in turn invokes the tranche contract’s redeem operation via ITranche(_tranche).maxRedeem(address(this)). The code does not verify whether the returned maxRedeem amount is zero before proceeding. Consequently, the tranche’s _withdraw logic is executed even when there are no shares to redeem. Inside the tranche’s _withdraw function a safety check require(utilizationRatio() < withdrawThreshold, "UTILIZATION_RATIO_MAX") is performed after the fee transfer. The VaultManager expects the internal pre‑condition utilizationRatio ≥ withdrawThreshold before calling redeem, but the tranche requires the opposite condition (utilizationRatio < withdrawThreshold). When the pre‑condition is not satisfied – which is the case for any tranche whose utilization ratio is at or above the configured threshold – the require statement fails and the transaction reverts. Because the VaultManager always attempts the redeem step, the entire fee distribution transaction aborts, leaving the collected fees locked in the contract and never transferred to the intended recipients. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for fee distribution: any user or automated process that triggers fee distribution while the utilization ratio condition holds will see the transaction revert, receive no rewards, and observe a zero balance change in the UI despite fees having been accrued. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Avantis v1.5 cross‑asset leverage contracts when the auditor noticed that the redeem call was made without checking the maxRedeem return value and that the tranche’s withdraw function contains a contradictory utilization‑ratio guard. The bug can be hard to spot because the revert only occurs under specific utilization‑ratio states, which may not be exercised in normal test scenarios. To remediate, the VaultManager should first query maxRedeem and skip the redeem step when it is zero, or otherwise ensure that the utilization‑ratio condition matches the tranche’s expectation before invoking the withdraw logic. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an unchecked external call combined with mismatched invariant assumptions, leading to a failure mode where funds appear to disappear from the fee distribution pipeline and users receive no expected payouts.

title: Guaranteed SL, forced trade du-
description: The following exploit hinges on 3 factors: 1. Stop losses are guaranteed to execute even if the current price is below the SL price 2. Trades over a certain amount CANNOT be closed before a certain amount of time Trading.sol#L512-L522 if (_orderType == ITradingStorage.LimitOrder.LIQ) { uint liqPrice = pairInfos.getTradeLiquidationPrice( t.trader, t.pairIndex, t.index, t.openPrice, t.buy, t.initialPosToken, t.leverage ); require(t.sl == 0 || (t.buy ? liqPrice > t.sl : liqPrice < t.sl), "HAS_SL"); <- will revert because sl price is better than liquidation price ,→ } We see above that liquidation cannot be called unless the liquidation price is worse than the sl price. This means that as long as we have a stop loss open we can never be liquidated under that price. This means that we must execute as a stop loss limit to liquidate a position with a valid stop loss. Trading.sol#L523-L525 }else{ require(block.timestamp - t.timestamp >= pairsStored.openCloseThreshold(t.pairIndex, t.initialPosToken.mul(t.leverage)), "EARLY_CLOSE"); ,→ ,→ } This leads us to the next point. Stop losses cannot be triggered until at least a certain amount of time has passed for the largest position sizes, this is 15 minutes. This give us 15 free minutes in which we cannot be liquidated. TradingCallbacks.sol#L454-L463 _trade.positionSizeUSDC -= isPnl : storageT.handleDevGovFees( _trade.trader, _trade.pairIndex, _trade.positionSizeUSDC.mul(_trade.leverage), true, true, _trade.buy ); PairStorage.sol#L608-L618 function getPnlBasedFee(uint pairIndex, uint collateral, int percentProfit) external view override returns(uint) { ,→ if(percentProfit < 0) return 0; // No Fee charged for losses uint i = 0; for(i; i < fees[pairIndex].pnlFees.numTiers; i++){ if(uint(percentProfit) < fees[pairIndex].pnlFees.tierP[i]) break; } uint pnl = collateral*uint(percentProfit)/ _PRECISION/ 100; return fees[pairIndex].pnlFees.feesP[i] * pnl/ _PRECISION / 100; } We see for pnl trades that the open fee is 0 and that exit fees are applied only on the profit made on the trade. Together these three small issues lead to a large problem. A trade can place two opposing trades, one long and one short. Each trade has a stop loss with tolerance just small enough for the stop loss to be valid. For 15 minutes neither of these trades can be liquidated or closed. During this time however, the underlying asset will move either up or down even by a small amount. After 15 minutes, one trade will be liquidated for virtually no loss and the other can be closed for a profit. Reporting as HIGH since currently pairIndex 34 (ORDI) and 35 (STX) are hardcoded to behave in this manner and can be exploited from the moment this upgrade goes into effect. 1. Trading.sol:L522 guarantees that stop losses must be used instead of liquidation for all crypto pairs (including ORDI and STX) 2. Trading.sol:L524 guarantees that stop losses cannot be executed for 15 minutes after the order is place 3. PairStorage.sol:L574 enforces open close timer for pairIndex 34 (ORDI) and 35 (STX) 4. TradingCallbacks.sol:L455 charges no open fee Internal pre-conditions None External pre-conditions Target asset price is different by any amount in 15 minutes Attack Path 1. Open a long and short PNL market order with extremely tight stop loss with max leverage 2. Wait 15 minutes 3. Allows one order to trigger stop loss with minute loss 4. Close the other order for guaranteed profit All funds can be drained from LPs

bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a combination of two contract rules that together create an exploitable window for profit extraction. First, the trading logic forces a stop‑loss (SL) order to be executed instead of a liquidation whenever the SL price is more favorable than the liquidation price, as enforced by the require statement that checks `t.sl` against `liqPrice`. Second, the contract imposes a forced‑trade duration (`openCloseThreshold`) that blocks any SL or early close for large positions for a fixed period – fifteen minutes for the affected pairs. Because the SL cannot be triggered during this lock‑out, a trader can open two opposing leveraged positions (one long, one short) on the same asset with very tight stop‑losses that sit just inside the liquidation boundary. After the fifteen‑minute window expires, the losing side can be liquidated at a negligible loss while the winning side can be closed for a guaranteed profit, since the fee model charges no opening fee and only takes a fee on profit. The impact is that liquidity providers lose funds, the protocol’s risk assumptions are broken, and users may see unexpected profit or loss patterns that contradict the intended protective behavior of stop‑losses. The issue manifests only for pairs that have the forced‑trade duration hard‑coded (e.g., ORDI and STX) and may be hard to notice because the stop‑loss appears to work correctly after the lock‑out, while the hidden fifteen‑minute protection window is not visible in the UI. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a unit test that opened delta‑neutral trades and observed a net gain after the lock‑out period. To remediate, the contract should decouple guaranteed SL execution from liquidation logic, remove or adjust the forced‑trade duration for pairs that support stop‑losses, allow SLs to be triggered during the lock‑out, and revise the fee model to ensure that opening a position incurs a cost that offsets potential arbitrage. This class of bug can be described as an asymmetric liquidation protection or forced‑trade duration combined with guaranteed stop‑loss flaw that enables profit extraction through timing manipulation.

title: VaultManager accounting is off
description: Whenever a user has to receive funds for their payout, the VaultManager only makes sure to hold enough funds to cover for the currently accrued borrowing fees. function _sendUSDCToTrader(address _trader, uint _amount) internal { // For the extereme case of totalRewards exceeding vault Manager balance int256 balanceAvailable = int(storageT.usdc().balanceOf(address(this))) - int(totalRewards); ,→ if (int(_amount) > balanceAvailable) { // take difference (losses) from vaults uint256 difference = uint(int(_amount) - int(balanceAvailable)); uint256 seniorUSDC = (getSeniorLossMultiplier() * difference * (100 - getReserveRatio(0)))/100 / 100; ,→ seniorUSDC = (seniorUSDC > difference) ? difference : seniorUSDC; uint256 juniorUSDC = difference - seniorUSDC; junior.withdrawAsVaultManager(juniorUSDC); senior.withdrawAsVaultManager(seniorUSDC); } require(storageT.usdc().transfer(_trader, _amount)); emit USDCSentToTrader(_trader, _amount); } This means that in case the contract holds other funds, it will first use them, instead of the tranche funds. Such funds that might be within the contract are: • Traders' collateral • Liquidators' execution fees. Using either of these funds will result in unfair results for the liquidity providers. Consider the following scenarios: Scenario 1 1. There are only 2 traders, both with $1000 position size, one of them is +100% pnl and the other one is -100% pnl. Borrowing fees and pnl fees accrued currently within the contract are currently 0. (for simplicity, we'll ignore borrowing fees) 2. The positive pnl trader closes their position first. Since there are enough funds within the VaultManager (due to the other trader's collateral), the funds are simply transferred to the trader. None of the tranche's share values are impacted, although they should be (as pnlrewards are 0). 3. When the negative pnl position is closed, the user has nothing to receive, but the Va hold any funds and there's nothing to actually back up these pnl rewards. Scenario 2 1. There are only 2 traders, both with $1000 position size, both are at +100% pnl. Borrowing fees and pnl fees accrued currently within the contract are currently 0. (for simplicity, we'll ignore borrowing fees) 2. One of them closes their position. Since there are enough funds within the contract, the position will be instantly paid out and no funds will be taken from any of the tranches and therefore their share value will not be decreased (although they should). 3. After some time the the other trader closes their position too (assuming at same pnl). Now, since the contract will not hold any funds, it will take all of the payout from the tranche's ($2000). This would mean that the funds will be taken based on the tranche ratios at the closure of the 2nd position, when instead they $1000 should've been taken based on the ratio at the closure of first position and only the other $1000 at the closure of the 2nd position. unfairly overvalued tranche shares, which would be -EV action. Any LPs aware of the following issue, can withdraw in steps 2 and 3 to avoid a loss. Wrong accounting Affected Code VaultManager.sol#L607 Tranche share values will often be significantly off and not correspond to their true value. Tranche payouts will happen based at wrong ratios, which are not the ones at the time a position was closed. Possibly, there would be no funds to cover for accrued pnlfees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the VaultManager contract’s payout routine, which determines how USDC is transferred to a trader when a position is closed. The function checks only that the contract’s USDC balance minus the total rewards is sufficient to cover the borrowing fees, and if the requested amount is less than or equal to that balance it uses the contract’s existing USDC pool. This pool may contain funds that do not belong to the senior or junior tranches, such as other traders’ collateral or liquidators’ execution fees. Consequently, when a trader receives a payout, the contract may draw the funds from these external sources instead of proportionally reducing the tranche balances at the moment of the payout. The root cause is the lack of a global accounting mechanism that tracks all inbound and outbound cash flows and ties each payout to the tranche share values that were valid at the time of the position closure. Exploitation occurs when multiple traders close profitable positions sequentially: the first payout is satisfied from collateral or fees, leaving tranche share values unchanged, while the second payout must be taken from the tranches, but the contract applies the current tranche ratios rather than the ratios that should have been applied after the first payout. This leads to inaccurate tranche accounting, over‑valued LP shares, and potentially insufficient funds to cover accrued PnL fees. The impact is primarily on liquidity providers who may see their tranche token value remain artificially high after payouts, or later discover that the vault cannot honour all rewards because earlier payouts were funded from unrelated assets. The issue manifests whenever the vault holds non‑tranche USDC (collateral, execution fees) and traders close positions that require payouts larger than the accrued borrowing fees. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the _sendUSDCToTrader logic and identified that the balanceAvailable calculation ignores the source of funds. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balance appears sufficient, so no revert occurs, yet the internal accounting of tranche shares diverges from the economic reality. To remediate, the contract should implement a unified accounting layer that records all collateral deposits, execution fees, and tranche balances, and ensures that each payout reduces the appropriate tranche share values based on the ratios that were in effect at the exact time of the payout, rather than after subsequent transactions. This would prevent the vault from unintentionally using unrelated funds and would keep tranche valuations accurate, preserving fairness for LPs and ensuring that all accrued fees can be covered.

title: Liquidation might occur in- stantly after withdrawing max possible margin Found by jokr
description: An incorrect position health check after withdrawing margin could lead to the position becoming liquidatable immediately after the withdrawal. The trader can withdraw margin up to an amount such that the effective position, after accounting for PnL, should be greater than 20% of the collateral. This ensures the position still has a 5% buffer to avoid reaching the liquidation state after withdrawing the maximum possible margin. require((int(_trade.initialPosToken) + pnl) > (int(_trade.initialPosToken) * int(100 - _WITHDRAW_THRESHOLD_P)) / 100, "W_T_B"); ,→ However, this check fails in cases where the trader has loss protection. Since the PnL used in the above check is the loss-protected PnL, the trader is able to withdraw more margin than intended based on the loss protection. But because the PnL used in the liquidation check does not consider loss protection, if the trader withdraws the maximum possible margin, their position will enter a liquidatable state immediately after the withdrawal. • In TradingCallbacks:85 margin withdrawal health check uses lossProtectedPnl, inflating position value and allowing excessive collateral than intended withdrawal while appearing healthy but actually not based on the liquidation price Internal pre-conditions 1. Trader should have pnl protection External pre-conditions 1. Trader should withdraw margin from open trade Attack Path The trader opens a long position with the following parameters: Collateral = 250 USDC Leverage = 4x LevPositionToken = 1000 Loss protection rebate = 20% The price then drops by 9%, reducing the price to 910 USDC. profitP = -9% * 4 = -36% pnl = -36% of 250 = -90 USDC net position value = 250 - 90 = 160 So the position remains in a healthy state. Next, the trader tries to withdraw 150 USDC from the margin. newCollateral = 100 USDC newLeverage = 10x profitP = -9% * 10 = -90% pnl = -90% of 100 = -90 USDC lossProtectedPnl = -72 USDC (20% loss protection rebate applied) net position value = initialPosToken - lossProtectedPnl = 28 In this case, the health check passes since 28 is greater than 20% newCollateral. The withdrawal is successful. However, on checking if the account is liquidatable: profitP = -90% pnl = -90% of 100 = -90 USDC net position value = 100 - 90 = 10 The position is now liquidated immediately because the net position value is less than 15% of the collateral. The health check does not work as intended in cases with loss protection, leading to traders potentially being liquidated after withdrawing margin.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect health‑check performed when a trader withdraws margin from an open leveraged position that is protected by a loss‑protection rebate. The contract calculates the post‑withdrawal health using the loss‑protected PnL value, which artificially inflates the apparent equity of the position. Because the liquidation logic later uses the raw PnL (which does not include the protection rebate), the two checks become inconsistent. A trader can therefore request the maximum allowable margin withdrawal, pass the health check, and have the transaction succeed, only to find that the position becomes immediately liquidatable once the liquidation routine evaluates the raw PnL. This occurs only when the trader has an active loss‑protection setting and the withdrawal amount pushes the collateral low enough that the raw equity falls below the required liquidation buffer (for example, below 15 % of the remaining collateral). The impact is that the trader’s position is closed unexpectedly, resulting in a loss of the remaining collateral and any potential profit, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective. From the UI the user sees a successful withdrawal, a healthy position indicator, and then a sudden liquidation event where the balance drops to zero or a very small amount, contradicting the expectation that the position should remain open after the withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the health‑check formula with the liquidation formula and identified the mismatch caused by the use of lossProtectedPnl instead of raw pnl. It is hard to notice because the on‑chain health check returns true, so no warning is emitted, and the UI does not display any error until the liquidation step executes. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑inconsistency or margin‑withdrawal validation errors, where different parts of the contract use divergent definitions of equity. To remediate the problem the health‑check should be rewritten to use the same PnL metric as the liquidation check (i.e., the raw, unprotected PnL) or otherwise ensure that both checks apply the loss‑protection rebate consistently, thereby preserving the intended 5 % safety buffer after any withdrawal.

title: Frontrunning of `setPerTokenWalletCap` edge case
description:
The `setPerTokenWalletCap()` function in WhitelistPeriodManager.sol [contains a comment](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L196-L200) stating:
    
    Special care must be taken when calling this function
    There are no checks for _perTokenWalletCap (since it's onlyOwner), but it's essential that it should be >= max lp provided by an lp.
    Checking this on chain will probably require implementing a bbst, which needs more bandwidth
    Call the view function getMaxCommunityLpPositon() separately before changing this value

Even if the manual step of calling the `getMaxCommunityLpPositon()` function is properly performed, it is possible for a user to add liquidity to increase the `maxLp` value in between when the `getMaxCommunityLpPositon()` function is called and when the `setPerTokenWalletCap()` function is called. Because this process is manual, this doesn’t need to be bot frontrunning in the same block as when the `setPerTokenWalletCap()` function is called, but can be cause by poor timing of an innocent unknowing user adding liquidity to the protocol. If this condition occurs, the liquidity provider will have provided more liquidity than the perTokenWalletCap limit, breaking the assumptions for this variable and leading to some denial of service conditions.

This edge situation can impact the `setTotalCap()` function and the “perTokenTotalCap[_token]” state variable as well, but the “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value would have to be reduced before the “perTokenTotalCap[_token]” value is reduced. The impact to `setTotalCap()` follows the same execution path but adds the additional step of calling the `setTotalCap()` function at the end of the process.
poc:
1. Owner [calls `getMaxCommunityLpPositon(_token)` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L245-L255) to identify maxLp value to confirm new perTokenWalletCap value is below maxLp value
2. An innocent user adds liquidity to their position without the knowledge that the owner is going to reduce the “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value soon
3. Owner [calls `setPerTokenWalletCap()` function ](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L202-L208)to reduce “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value
4. The innocent user has more liquidity than the new “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value. This means that the user can be in a situation where if they remove x amount of liquidity and attempt to add x liquidity back to their position, the innocent user will be unable to do so. Other functions that rely on the assumption that the largest user deposit is below the “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value may break due to incorrect assumptions

This edge situation can impact the `setTotalCap()` function and the “perTokenTotalCap[_token]” state variable as well, but the “perTokenWalletCap[_token]” value would have to be reduced before the “perTokenTotalCap[_token]” value is reduced. The impact to `setTotalCap()` follows the same execution path but adds the additional step of calling the `setTotalCap()` function at the end of the process.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition caused by the contract’s reliance on an off‑chain view call to enforce the per‑token wallet cap invariant. The function that sets the per‑token wallet cap (setPerTokenWalletCap) is protected only by an onlyOwner modifier and contains no on‑chain check that the new cap is greater than or equal to the largest liquidity position (maxLp) already held by any provider. The intended workflow, described in a comment, asks the owner to first call a view function (getMaxCommunityLpPositon) to obtain the current maximum liquidity and then manually set the cap to a value not lower than that number. Because this check is performed off‑chain, an innocent liquidity provider can add liquidity after the owner has read maxLp but before the owner submits the transaction that lowers the cap. When this timing overlap occurs, the provider’s new deposit becomes larger than the newly set per‑token wallet cap. The contract assumes that all individual deposits are bounded by the cap; once the invariant is broken, functions that rely on it (such as setTotalCap and any logic that validates deposits against the cap) may revert or behave incorrectly. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after adding liquidity, attempts to withdraw or to re‑add the same amount fail, often with a revert message indicating the cap limit, and the user’s balance appears stuck. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected liquidity providers and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, potentially leading to locked funds and erratic total‑cap calculations. The issue manifests only under specific timing conditions and is hard to notice because the owner‑only function does not emit warnings and the contract otherwise operates normally. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed the comment warning about the need for an external check and reasoned that the absence of an on‑chain validation could be abused. To remediate, the contract should enforce the invariant atomically by adding a require that the new per‑token wallet cap is less than or equal to the current maximum community liquidity (require(_perTokenWalletCap <= getMaxCommunityLpPositon(_token), "ERR_PWC_GT_MCLP")); this programmatic check prevents the race condition at the cost of additional gas consumption. The vulnerability belongs to the class of off‑chain validation and race‑condition bugs that violate business‑logic invariants.

In `deposit` function it is possible to push to `nftIdsStaked` of anyone, an attacker can deposit too many nfts to another user, and when the user will try to withdraw an nft at the end of the list, they will iterate on the list and revert because of gas limit.

[HP-25: C4 Audit Fixes, Dynamic Fee Changes bcnmy/hyphen-contract#42](https://github.com/bcnmy/hyphen-contract/pull/42)

A valid concern, but I think it should be of medium severity because the victim can still withdraw NFTs one by one until reaching the necessary index because it breaks inside the loop: [LiquidityFarming.sol#L234-L235](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityFarming.sol#L234-L235).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by unbounded growth of a per‑user array that stores staked NFT identifiers. In the contract’s deposit routine, an attacker can add an arbitrary number of NFT IDs to the victim’s nftIdsStaked array because the function does not verify that the caller is the owner of the NFTs being recorded. This unchecked push operation allows the attacker to inflate the array size far beyond normal usage. When the legitimate user later calls the withdraw function, the contract iterates over the entire nftIdsStaked list to locate the NFT at a specific index. If the list has become very large, the iteration consumes more gas than the block gas limit permits, causing the transaction to revert with an out‑of‑gas error. The user therefore cannot retrieve the requested NFT; from the UI perspective the withdrawal attempt simply fails, often with a generic “transaction reverted” or “out of gas” message, leaving the user’s assets seemingly stuck. The impact is that the affected user is denied access to their staked NFTs, which may represent significant value, while the attacker incurs no cost beyond the gas used to inflate the array. The condition occurs whenever any address can invoke the deposit function on behalf of another address, a scenario that the original design assumed to be benign. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LiquidityFarming contract, where the auditor observed that the withdrawal loop does not have a bounded iteration count or a gas‑efficient lookup mechanism. It can be difficult to notice because the contract behaves correctly under normal load; only when the array size is artificially inflated does the gas exhaustion manifest, which may be interpreted as a generic performance problem rather than a security flaw. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded array iteration leading to gas limit denial‑of‑service” defects, commonly found in contracts that store per‑user collections in dynamic arrays and later iterate over them without safeguards. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a maximum length for the nftIdsStaked array per user, or replace the array with a mapping that enables constant‑time lookup and removal. Alternatively, the withdrawal logic could be restructured to allow direct removal by NFT identifier without looping, or a pull‑based design could be employed that does not require iterating over the full collection. These changes would prevent an attacker from abusing the deposit function to create a gas‑exhaustion scenario and ensure that legitimate users can always withdraw their NFTs in a predictable, gas‑efficient manner.

title: Sending tokens close to the maximum will fail and user will lose tokens
description:
[LiquidityPool.sol#L171](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L171)  
[LiquidityPool.sol#L273](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L273)  

When a user calls the deposit function the reward amount is calculated and an event is emited with amount+reward as the transfer amount. The function checks amount is smaller than the max amount.

An executor then listens to this event and calls sendFundsToUser with rewards + amount as the amount parameter. This function checks amount+reward is smaller than max amount.

This is a problem because the amount transferred may be in the limit but amount + reward could pass the limit and the executor won’t be able to send the transaction. The user will lose the funds. Both checks should be made with the reward or without the reward but the checks should be the same for this not to happen.

Step by step :  
Max transfer is set to 50 for token A  
Bob transfers 49 tokens, this will pass since 49<50. The reward is calculated in 2 tokens.  
The executor then calls sendFundsToUser with 52. This transaction will revert and user will lose their tokens.  

This value of amount includes rewards but the previous check didn’t include rewards: [LiquidityPool.sol#L273](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L273).
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an inconsistent application of a maximum transfer limit in the LiquidityPool contract. When a user calls the deposit function, the contract validates that the raw deposit amount is strictly less than a configured maximum (for example, 50 tokens). After the deposit, a reward is calculated and added to the user’s balance, and an event is emitted containing the sum of the deposited amount and the reward. An external executor listens for this event and attempts to transfer the combined total (deposit plus reward) to the user by invoking sendFundsToUser. This second function also checks that the transferred amount does not exceed the same maximum, but it applies the check to the total (deposit + reward) rather than to the originally deposited amount. If the reward pushes the total over the limit, the second check fails, the transaction reverts, and the user’s tokens remain locked in the contract. From the user’s perspective, the deposit appears to succeed, but the subsequent transfer never arrives; the user may see a reduction or disappearance of their balance without any explicit error message. The root cause is a logical flaw where two related functions enforce different accounting rules: the first validates only the raw amount, while the second validates the amount including the reward. This mismatch can be exploited unintentionally by any user whose deposit is close enough to the maximum that the added reward exceeds the cap, causing the executor to be unable to complete the transfer. The impact is the loss of deposited tokens for affected users, as the contract does not provide a recovery path for the reverted transaction. The issue was identified during a formal audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditors noticed that the max‑transfer check was not applied uniformly across the deposit and reward‑distribution flow. It is hard to detect in normal testing because the deposit transaction itself succeeds, and only the later executor call fails, which may be observed only as a missing credit in the user’s wallet. To remediate the problem, the same limit check should be performed on the same value in both functions – either by adding the reward to the amount before the first check or by checking only the raw amount in the second function. An alternative mitigation is to raise the maximum limit to accommodate the largest possible reward, but the preferred fix is to align the validation logic so that the contract never attempts a transfer that exceeds the configured cap, thereby preventing accidental loss of funds and preserving the intended accounting invariants of the liquidity pool.

title: Incentive Pool can be drained without rebalancing the pool
description:
[LiquidityPool.sol#L149-L173](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L149-L173)  
[LiquidityPool.sol#L263-L277](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L263-L277)  

`depositErc20` allows an attacker to specify the destination chain to be the same as the source chain and the receiver account to be the same as the caller account. This enables an attacker to drain the incentive pool without rebalancing the pool back to the equilibrium state.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the cross‑chain deposit function of the liquidity pool contract, where the `depositErc20` method does not verify that the destination chain identifier (`toChainId`) differs from the source chain, nor does it enforce that the receiver address is distinct from the caller (`msg.sender`). Because of this missing validation, an attacker can initiate a deposit on a given chain and set the destination chain to be the same chain, while also setting the receiver to be the caller themselves. When the pool is in a deficit state—meaning the current on‑chain liquidity is lower than the amount that was originally provided—a sizable incentive pool accumulates as a reward for rebalancing actions. The contract’s internal accounting credits the entire incentive pool to the caller when such a self‑referencing deposit is processed, without executing the intended rebalancing that would normally restore equilibrium. Consequently, the attacker can repeatedly borrow the liquidity shortfall, invoke the flawed deposit, and extract the full incentive amount (up to roughly ten percent of the total pool value) after a small fee is deducted. The pool remains in the same deficit condition, the incentive pool is drained, and the attacker pockets the reward each time. This issue appears when the pool is heavily imbalanced after large transfers and the attacker possesses sufficient collateral to cover the borrowed amount. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit through manual review of the `depositErc20` and `sendFundsToUser` logic, noting the absence of checks on chain identifiers and receiver address. The flaw is subtle because the function otherwise behaves correctly for legitimate cross‑chain deposits, and the UI does not surface any error, making the drain of the incentive pool easy to miss. To remediate, the contract should enforce that `toChainId` cannot equal the source chain and that `receiver` is not the caller, thereby preventing self‑targeted deposits that bypass the rebalancing mechanism. This class of bug is an input‑validation bypass leading to unauthorized reward extraction, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that incentives are only awarded when a genuine cross‑chain liquidity shift occurs. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms include a sudden disappearance of the incentive pool, zero rewards received after a deposit, and balances that remain unchanged despite a successful transaction, contrary to the expectation that a deposit would trigger a reward distribution.

title: Improper Upper Bound Definition on the Fee
description: The **equilibriumFee** and **maxFee** does not have any upper or lower bounds. Values that are too large will lead to reversions in several critical functions or the LP user will lost all funds when paying the fee.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the absence of any upper or lower bound checks on the fee parameters that govern the pricing of liquidity pool operations. Specifically, the contract allows the owner to call a fee‑changing function and set the equilibrium fee and the maximum fee to any non‑zero uint256 value. Because the code only verifies that the values are not zero, there is no safeguard against excessively large numbers. When an attacker—or a malicious owner—sets these fee variables to an extreme value, subsequent calculations that incorporate the fee can overflow, cause arithmetic errors, or produce a fee that exceeds the total amount being transferred. In practice, this means that any user attempting to withdraw, swap, or otherwise interact with the pool may be charged a fee larger than the entire transaction amount, leading to a revert of the operation or the complete loss of the user’s funds after the fee is deducted. The impact is most acute for liquidity providers and token holders who rely on the pool to receive predictable returns; they may observe that their balances become zero, that withdrawals fail with out‑of‑gas or revert errors, or that the pool appears to be empty despite having deposited assets. The condition under which the bug manifests is any invocation of the fee‑change function with unchecked large values, which can happen at any time because the contract does not enforce a maximum fee threshold. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that inspected the fee management logic and noted the lack of constraints beyond a non‑zero requirement. This omission can be hard to detect because the function superficially appears to validate inputs, yet the validation is insufficient to guarantee safe economic behavior. To remediate the issue, the contract should define sensible upper and lower limits for both equilibriumFee and maxFee—such as a maximum of a few basis points relative to the transaction amount—and enforce those limits with require statements. Additionally, the contract could implement sanity checks that compare the fee against the amount being transferred, ensuring the fee never exceeds a predetermined percentage of the transaction value. By constraining the fee range, the protocol preserves its accounting assumptions, maintains user expectations that a fee will be a small, predictable deduction, and prevents scenarios where funds disappear or refunds are unexpectedly zero.

title: Call to non-existing contracts returns success
description:
[LiquidityFarming.sol#L140](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityFarming.sol#L140)  
[LiquidityFarming.sol#L145](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityFarming.sol#L145)  
[LiquidityFarming.sol#L187](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityFarming.sol#L187)  

Low level calls (call, delegate call and static call) return success if the called contract doesn’t exist (not deployed or destructed).

This makes a user be able to send his funds to non-existing addresses.

`LiquidityFarming`  
`reclaimTokens` - if the owner calls by accident with a non-existing address he’ll lose the funds.  
`_sendRewardsForNft` - if the `withdraw` or `extractRewards` will be called with a `to` non-existing address, the funds will be lost. That’s because of the call to `_sendRewardsForNft` which contains a low level call to the `to` address.  

`sendFundsToUser` - if an executor calls by accident with a non-existing address the funds will be lost.  
`transfer` - if the `transfer` function will be called (by the LiquidityProvidors contract of course) with a non existing address as a receiver, the funds will be lost.  

This can be seen here <https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/main/audits/tob/audit.pdf> (report #9) and here <https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/develop/control-structures.html#error-handling-assert-require-revert-and-exceptions>

[HP-25: C4 Audit Fixes, Dynamic Fee Changes bcnmy/hyphen-contract#42](https://github.com/bcnmy/hyphen-contract/pull/42)

I am hesitating if this should be with the severity of Medium or Low but leaving in favor of wardens this time. I believe checking against empty addresses is not enough, low-level calls return true even for non-empty but not valid addresses. It would be better to use interfaces if possible.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of unchecked low‑level calls (call, delegatecall and staticcall) that report success even when the target address does not contain deployed contract code. In the LiquidityFarming contract several public and internal functions—reclaimTokens, _sendRewardsForNft (used by withdraw and extractRewards), sendFundsToUser and transfer—forward funds to an address supplied by a caller using a low‑level call. Because the code does not verify that the destination address hosts a contract or that the call actually performed the intended token or ether transfer, the call returns true regardless of whether the address is empty, an externally owned account, or a contract that has self‑destructed. Consequently, a user or an executor can inadvertently—or a malicious actor can deliberately—cause funds to be sent to an address that cannot receive or process them, resulting in permanent loss of those assets. The issue is triggered whenever a function accepts an arbitrary address and then performs a low‑level call without additional checks such as checking the code size of the target or using a typed interface that would revert on failure. The affected parties are the users of the liquidity farming protocol, liquidity providers, and any entity that relies on the contract’s reward distribution or token reclamation mechanisms. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noted that the Solidity specification states low‑level calls return true for non‑existent contracts and that the same flaw was identified in other well‑known contracts (e.g., Uniswap v3). The flaw can be hard to notice because the transaction receipt shows a successful call and no revert, giving the impression that the transfer succeeded, while in reality the funds have been sent to an address that cannot retrieve them. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that expected rewards or reclaimed tokens never appear in their wallet, balances remain unchanged, or a transaction that should have transferred tokens simply results in a zero balance change, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The root cause is the misuse of low‑level calls without proper validation of the recipient, which bypasses Solidity’s built‑in safety checks provided by high‑level interface calls. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace low‑level calls with calls to explicit interfaces (e.g., IERC20.transfer) that automatically revert on failure, or explicitly check that the target address contains contract code (using extcodesize) before performing the call, and handle the false‑positive success return appropriately. By ensuring that a failed transfer results in a revert, the protocol can guarantee that funds are either correctly transferred or the operation is rolled back, preserving user assets and aligning with the intended business logic of reward distribution and token reclamation.

title: `LiquidityProviders`: Setting new liquidity pool will break contract
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L171](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/db8a1fdddd02e8cc209a4c73ffbb3de210e4a81a/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L171)  

Owners can change the `liquidityPool` variable any time with the `setLiquidityPool` function.  
If a liquidity pool was already set and users added liquidity with `addTokenLiquidity`, the tokens are directly transferred to the liquidity pool and not kept in the `LiquidityProviders` contract.  
Changing the `liquidityPool` to a different contract will make it impossible for the users to withdraw their liquidity using `removeLiquidity` because the tokens are still in the old `liquidityPool` and cannot be retrieved.  

All users will lose their funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the contract allowing the owner to change the address of the external liquidity pool at any time through the setLiquidityPool function. When users contribute assets via the addTokenLiquidity function, those assets are transferred directly to the currently configured liquidity pool contract, not held within the LiquidityProviders contract itself. If the owner subsequently modifies the liquidityPool variable to point to a different contract, the removeLiquidity function will attempt to retrieve the tokens from the new pool address, while the actual tokens remain locked in the original pool that is no longer referenced. As a result, liquidity providers are unable to withdraw their contributions; from the user’s perspective the withdraw operation returns no tokens, balances appear unchanged, and the expected refund is missing. This breakdown occurs whenever a liquidity pool has already received deposits and the owner changes the pool address before all users have withdrawn. The affected parties include any user who has added liquidity, the protocol that relies on correct accounting of deposited assets, and any downstream contracts that assume liquidity can be reclaimed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state‑changing functions and identified that the liquidityPool reference is mutable without any migration safeguards. It is difficult to notice because the contract functions correctly when the pool address is stable; only after an owner‑initiated change does the withdrawal logic silently fail, leaving funds seemingly stuck. The root cause is the lack of an immutable or safely upgradable reference to the external pool and the absence of a migration mechanism that would either move the deposited assets to the new pool or allow users to retrieve them from the old pool. Conceptually, this is a mutable external‑dependency bug that violates the accounting invariant that tokens deposited to a pool can always be reclaimed by the same pool. To remediate the problem, the contract should either set the liquidityPool address only once, enforce a timelocked or multisig governance process for any change, and provide an explicit migration procedure that either transfers the existing liquidity to the new pool or permits users to withdraw from the previous pool before the address is overwritten. Implementing these safeguards restores the guarantee that deposited funds remain withdrawable and prevents accidental or malicious loss of user assets.

title: `LiquidityProviders`: Setting new LP token will break contract
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L116](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/db8a1fdddd02e8cc209a4c73ffbb3de210e4a81a/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L116)  

Owners can change the `lpToken` variable at any time with the `setLpToken` function.
