If an LP token was already set and users added liquidity with `addTokenLiquidity` and were minted a `lpToken` NFT, changing the `lpToken` to a different contract will make it impossible for the users to withdraw their liquidity using `removeLiquidity`.  

All users will lose their funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LiquidityProviders contract where the address of the LP token is stored in a mutable state variable called `lpToken`. The contract owner can invoke the public `setLpToken` function to replace this address at any time. The root cause is the lack of immutability or access control restrictions on the LP token reference after the contract has begun accepting liquidity. When a user deposits tokens through `addTokenLiquidity`, the contract mints an NFT that represents the user’s share of the pool, and the NFT is linked to the current `lpToken` contract. The withdrawal function `removeLiquidity` assumes that the same `lpToken` contract is still valid to verify ownership and burn the NFT. If the owner changes `lpToken` to a different contract after liquidity has been added, the withdrawal logic will attempt to interact with the new LP token contract, which does not recognize the previously minted NFTs. As a result, legitimate users are unable to burn their NFTs and retrieve the underlying assets, effectively locking the funds in the pool. This situation can be triggered at any moment after liquidity provision, simply by the owner calling `setLpToken` with a new address, and it affects all participants who have deposited liquidity, regardless of their role. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined state‑changing functions and identified that the LP token reference could be altered without any migration safeguards. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings or revert when the token address changes, and the UI may continue to display a normal balance while the withdrawal button silently fails, leading users to believe their funds are still accessible. The impact is a breach of the fundamental accounting assumption that the LP token contract is stable; users expect that the NFT they receive can always be redeemed for their share, but the contract can violate that promise, causing "funds disappear" or "liquidity stuck" symptoms. To remediate, the contract should either make the LP token address immutable after initial deployment or enforce a controlled migration process that includes a grace period, event emission, and a mechanism for users to withdraw from the old token before the switch. In essence, this is an instance of a mutable external contract reference bug that enables a denial‑of‑service style lock‑up of deposited assets.

title: Unsupported tokens cannot be withdrawn
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L273](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/db8a1fdddd02e8cc209a4c73ffbb3de210e4a81a/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L273)  

Supported tokens can be turned off again by calling `TokenManager.removeSupportedToken`.  
Users won’t be able to withdraw their liquidity anymore because of [this check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/db8a1fdddd02e8cc209a4c73ffbb3de210e4a81a/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L352) in `removeLiquidity`.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from a state‑dependent restriction placed on the liquidity withdrawal function of the Hyphen LiquidityProviders contract. The contract maintains a list of supported ERC‑20 tokens, and the function that removes a token from this list – TokenManager.removeSupportedToken – does not update the withdrawal logic accordingly. Specifically, the removeLiquidity routine contains a check that aborts the transaction if the token for which the caller is attempting to withdraw liquidity is no longer marked as supported. Consequently, once a token is removed, any liquidity provider who previously deposited that token can no longer execute a withdrawal, even though their deposited balance is still recorded in the contract. The root cause is the tight coupling between the token support flag and the withdrawal permission, without a fallback path that allows users to reclaim assets that become unsupported. An attacker or governance participant could trigger the token removal deliberately or inadvertently, causing legitimate users to be unable to retrieve their funds. The impact is that funds appear to be locked: a user’s UI will still display a positive balance for the deposited token, but the withdraw button will either be disabled or the transaction will revert with a generic “unsupported token” error. This situation can occur at any time after a token has been added to the supported list and later removed, affecting all liquidity providers for that token, regardless of their role or stake size. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s withdrawal flow, where the auditor noted that the removal of a token does not emit any mechanism to permit pending withdrawals. It may be hard to notice in normal operation because the contract continues to accept deposits for supported tokens, and the problematic branch is only exercised when a token is actively removed – a scenario that might not be covered by standard unit tests. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent access control” or “withdrawal gating” errors, where a change in contract state unintentionally revokes a user’s right to recover assets. The recommended remediation is to decouple the withdrawal permission from the supported‑token flag, for example by allowing withdrawals for any token that has a non‑zero balance irrespective of its support status, or by providing a dedicated emergency withdrawal path for unsupported tokens. This ensures that users can always reclaim their deposits, preserving the accounting invariants of the protocol and aligning with the expectation that a deposit can be withdrawn unless the contract is explicitly halted or funds are burned. From the user’s perspective, the symptom is a sudden inability to withdraw – the UI shows a balance but the transaction fails or returns zero, counter to the expectation that the deposited amount should be withdrawable at any time.

title: A `pauser` can brick the contracts
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the interplay between the pause mechanism and the ability of the designated pauser to permanently relinquish its authority. In this contract the pauser role is granted through a mutable address variable and the function renouncePauser() allows the current pauser to set that address to zero after emitting a PauserChanged event. The pause() function can be invoked by the pauser, and the counterpart unpause() function is protected by the onlyPauser modifier, meaning that only the current pauser can resume operation. Because there is no guard that prevents the pauser from renouncing its role while the contract is in the paused state, a malicious or compromised pauser can call pause() and immediately follow it with renouncePauser(). Once the pauser address is cleared, the contract remains in a paused state with no entity capable of satisfying the onlyPauser requirement for unpause(). Consequently, all functions that are guarded by whenNotPaused or similar modifiers become permanently unavailable, and no participant—including the contract owner—can restore normal operation. From a user's perspective this manifests as an inability to perform any action that would normally succeed, such as deposits, withdrawals, or token swaps; the user interface may display generic "contract paused" messages or simply revert transactions, leading to the perception that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is frozen. The impact is that any assets held by the contract become effectively locked, violating the core business logic that users should be able to retrieve or move their funds. This issue was discovered during a formal audit when the security team examined the Pausable.sol implementation and identified the missing restriction on renouncePauser(). It can be difficult to spot because renouncing a role is often considered a harmless administrative action, and the pause state itself may be assumed to be reversible by the owner. To remediate the problem, the contract should either disallow renouncing the pauser while the contract is paused, remove the renouncePauser() function entirely, or redesign the unpause authority to include a fallback role such as the contract owner. Additionally, any function that changes the pauser should be restricted to a trusted role (e.g., onlyOwner) to prevent a compromised pauser from taking unilateral control. By ensuring that there is always at least one authorized account capable of unpausing the contract, the protocol can avoid the scenario where funds become permanently inaccessible.

title: Incompatibility With Rebasing/Deflationary/Inflationary token
description: The scope contracts do not appear to support rebasing/deflationary/inflationary tokens whose balance changes during transfers or over time. The necessary checks include at least verifying the amount of tokens transferred to contracts before and after the actual transfer to infer any fees/interest.
poc: [TokenManager.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/token/TokenManager.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the assumption that an ERC‑20 token transfer will move exactly the amount specified by the caller. The examined contracts, particularly the token vault and manager components, do not verify the token balance before and after a transfer. This omission makes the contracts incompatible with rebasing, deflationary, or inflationary tokens – token types whose total supply or individual balances may change during a transfer because of built‑in fees, interest accruals, or periodic rebase adjustments. When a user deposits a fee‑on‑transfer token, the contract records the intended deposit amount but the actual amount received is lower, as part of the transfer is taken as a fee or redistributed by the token's logic. The contract therefore believes it holds more tokens than it actually does, leading to accounting errors in later operations such as withdrawal, payout or reward distribution. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a malicious token that deducts a large hidden fee on each transfer, causing the contract to under‑deliver on user expectations – for example a user initiates a withdrawal expecting a full refund but receives zero or a reduced amount because the vault’s internal accounting was based on the inflated pre‑transfer value. The impact is that users may lose funds, see balances disappear from the UI, receive empty refunds, or experience failed transactions while the protocol’s financial invariants are broken. This condition manifests whenever the protocol accepts arbitrary ERC‑20 tokens without explicitly checking for fee‑on‑transfer or rebasing behaviour, which is common in generic token vault designs. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the token manager’s transfer flow and noticed the lack of balance verification after a token transfer. The problem is subtle because the token contract itself does not revert; the transfer succeeds and the UI may still show a successful deposit, making the discrepancy hard to notice without explicit balance assertions. To remediate, the contract should capture the token balance of the vault before invoking the token’s transfer function, execute the transfer, then read the balance again to compute the actual amount received, and adjust internal accounting accordingly. Alternatively, the protocol could whitelist only standard ERC‑20 tokens that guarantee fee‑free transfers, or implement explicit support for fee‑on‑transfer tokens by adding logic to handle the deducted portion. In any case, the fix must ensure that the amount credited to the vault matches the amount truly transferred, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s financial model and preventing funds from unintentionally disappearing.

title: Owners have absolute control over protocol
description:
[LiquidityFarming.sol#L174-L192](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityFarming.sol#L174-L192)  

Owners have full control over the protocol.
poc:
Owners have full control over:
  * executors who perform token transfers on behalf of the destination chain
  * reclaiming / withdrawing any tokens (including reward tokens) held by farming contract
  * total upgradeability
  * instant parameters change (no timelock)
  * 1 step owner change (gold standard is 2-step owner change)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑privileged ownership model that gives a single address (the contract owner) unrestricted authority over the LiquidityFarming protocol. Because the owner can unilaterally appoint executors, withdraw any token held by the farming contract (including reward tokens), upgrade the contract implementation, and modify critical protocol parameters without any timelock or multi‑step governance, the root cause is the absence of decentralized control mechanisms such as role‑based access, delayed governance, or a two‑step ownership transfer. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting voluntarily, can exploit this by instantly replacing the executor that moves tokens across chains, siphoning or freezing user deposits, changing reward rates to zero, or pushing a malicious upgrade that redirects funds. The impact is a loss of user funds, disappearance of expected rewards, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that token balances remain invariant under normal operation. This scenario manifests whenever the contract is live and users have deposited assets expecting a neutral, trust‑less bridge; it can be triggered at any time because the owner’s actions are immediate and do not require community approval. All participants—depositors, reward claimants, and the broader ecosystem that relies on the bridge—are affected because they may see their balances become zero, receive no refunds, or observe unexpected changes in reward calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the access control patterns of the contract and identified that critical functions were protected only by an `onlyOwner` modifier without any safeguards. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and works as intended under normal conditions, making the centralization risk easy to overlook unless the governance model is examined. To remediate, the protocol should replace single‑owner control with a decentralized executor set, introduce a timelock for parameter updates, adopt a two‑step ownership transfer process, and consider upgradeability patterns that require community voting, thereby aligning the contract with standard decentralized governance practices. This class of bug falls under “centralized privileged access” and “owner‑only governance” vulnerabilities, where the business logic assumes trust‑less operation but the implementation grants absolute power to a single party, violating users’ expectations of a secure, permissionless system.

title: Compromise check will prevent
description:
A missing compromise check in verifiedProfileIdForAddress will cause unauthorized access for affected contracts as compromised addresses can bypass security measures and perform malicious actions. (e.g: Attacker can steal user's private key, so address is compromised)
In EthosProfile.sol, the verifiedProfileIdForAddress function is missing a check to ensure _address is not compromised, allowing compromised addresses to interact with network/blob/979e352d7bcdba3d0665f11c0320041ce28d1b89/ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/EthosProfile.sol#L568-L574
The verifiedProfileIdForAddress function used in many contracts.
a3d0665f11c0320041ce28d1b89/ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/EthosAttestation
cdba3d0665f11c0320041ce28d1b89/ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/EthosDiscuss
52d7bcdba3d0665f11c0320041ce28d1b89/ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/EthosDiscussion.sol#L158-L160 ...
In this project, there are many issues about this compromised address. In almost contracts, it doesn't check msg.sender is compromised address. Address is already unregistered from profile by deleteAddressAtIndex function, but it is still used in many functions.
Internal pre-conditions
User needs to call deleteAddressAtIndex to set isAddressCompromised to be true for the target address.
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. Attack steal user's private key.
2. User detected it is compromised and calls deleteAddressAtIndex for marking isAddressCompromised as true for the target address.
3. Attacker can calls addReview in EthorsReview contract by compromised address. (private key is stolen so attacker can do this operation) It calls ethosProfile.verifiedProfileIdForAddress(msg.sender); msg.sender is compromised but it doesn't revert.
The protocol suffers a potential security breach as compromised addresses can bypass verification and execute unauthorized actions in dependent contracts, potentially leading to manipulation of contract functionality. The attacker gains access to otherwise restricted operations without proper authorization.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass caused by a missing compromise check in the verifiedProfileIdForAddress function of the EthosProfile contract. The function is intended to return a profile identifier for a given address, but it does not verify whether the address has been marked as compromised. When a user detects that their private key has been stolen, they can call deleteAddressAtIndex, which sets an internal flag isAddressCompromised to true for that address. The contract’s design assumes that other contracts will respect this flag, yet many dependent contracts (such as EthosAttestation, EthosDiscuss, and EthosReview) call verifiedProfileIdForAddress without performing an additional check. As a result, a malicious actor who possesses the stolen private key can continue to invoke functions like addReview, because the verification call succeeds and does not revert, even though the address is flagged as compromised. This flaw allows unauthorized actions, manipulation of contract state, and potential abuse of protocol features that were meant to be restricted to legitimate users. The issue manifests when a compromised address is used after the user has marked it as compromised; the user expects the address to be blocked, but the contract silently accepts it, leading to symptoms such as unexpected reviews being posted, state changes occurring from a supposedly disabled account, and a general loss of trust in the protocol’s security guarantees. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of address compromise handling and identified that the verifiedProfileIdForAddress function lacks any internal guard against compromised addresses. The bug is hard to notice because the function returns a valid profile identifier and does not emit an error, so normal operation appears unchanged from the perspective of external callers. Conceptually, the fix requires enforcing the compromise check inside the function or applying a dedicated modifier (e.g., checkIfCompromised) that invokes the internal checkIsAddressCompromised routine and reverts when the flag is true. By ensuring that any call to verifiedProfileIdForAddress validates the address status, the protocol can prevent compromised keys from bypassing security controls and restore the intended protection model.

title: Hardcoded gas for bridge trans-
description:
Code sets static hardcoded gas for all the bridge messages but the issue is that commands GET_INCENTIVES and GET_FEES consumes dynamic amount of gas based on unclaimed epochs and total epochs so leading to stuck messages, i.e. needing manual intervention to deliver the message.
Commands GET_INCENTIVES and GET_FEES are used to collect fee and incentives from IncentiveVotingReward and FeesVotingReward in the leaf chains for users. The amount of gas required for those transactions in the leaf chains depends on the unclaimed epochs of the user and total snapshot counts as code loops through all the unclaimed epochs and also perform a binary search inside all the snapshots. Also user can specify multiple tokens (up to 5) in those commands so the gas consumption may be differ based on number of tokens user specifies. In the current configurations, code uses 440K and 220K gas for those commands:
```solidity
if (_command == Commands.GET_INCENTIVES) return 440_000;
if (_command == Commands.GET_FEES) return 220_000;
```
These hardcoded gas amounts won't be enough to perform transactions on the leaf chain if users didn't claimed their rewards for some times.
Users need to pay for additional gas in a separate transaction in order to deliver their message to the destination chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a static, hard‑coded gas stipend that the bridge contract uses for all outbound messages, regardless of the actual execution cost of the target command. Specifically, the contract returns a fixed 440,000 gas for the GET_INCENTIVES command and 220,000 gas for the GET_FEES command. These commands are responsible for pulling incentive and fee rewards from leaf‑chain contracts. The amount of gas required by these functions is not constant: it depends on how many reward epochs a user has left unclaimed, the total number of snapshot entries that must be examined, and the number of token types (up to five) the user requests in a single call. The implementation iterates over every unclaimed epoch and performs a binary search over the snapshot array, causing gas consumption to grow with the size of the user’s reward history and with the token count. Because the bridge always supplies the same gas limit, a user who has not claimed rewards for several epochs, or who requests multiple tokens, can exceed the supplied stipend. When this happens the transaction reverts with an out‑of‑gas error on the leaf chain, leaving the bridge message in a “stuck” state. The message cannot be automatically delivered; it requires a manual follow‑up transaction that supplies additional gas to complete the operation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a claim transaction appears to succeed on the source chain but no funds are received on the destination chain, often accompanied by a generic “out‑of‑gas” revert or a silent failure where the UI shows the request as pending forever. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for reward collection: users are unable to retrieve earned incentives or fees until they intervene, and the protocol’s accounting may appear inconsistent because expected balances remain unchanged. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the bridge’s message‑routing logic and identified that the gas limits were hard‑coded without accounting for the dynamic nature of the reward‑distribution functions. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because most users claim rewards regularly, keeping the number of unclaimed epochs low, so the fixed gas amount is sufficient for the majority of cases. The root cause is the mismatch between a static gas stipend and a function whose execution cost varies with data size, a classic example of an under‑estimation of gas requirements. To remediate the problem the contract should either compute the required gas at runtime, allow the caller to specify a higher gas limit, or provide a mechanism for the user to pay additional gas when needed. In conceptual terms, the fix replaces the fixed‑gas model with a flexible, data‑aware gas provisioning strategy, ensuring that bridge messages can always complete regardless of how many epochs or tokens are involved.

title: XERC20 does not work on Super-
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between the XERC20 contract implementation used by the Velodrome protocol and the current Superchain ERC20 bridge specification. The contract defines internal functions __crosschainMint and __crosschainBurn and emits events named CrosschainMinted and CrosschainBurnt, while the Superchain spec expects externally callable functions crosschainMint and crosschainBurn and events named CrosschainMint and CrosschainBurn. Because the contract was compiled against an older version of the Superchain interface, the bridge contract that orchestrates cross‑chain token transfers cannot locate the expected functions nor recognise the emitted events. As a result, when a user attempts to move XVELO tokens to the Superchain, the bridge call succeeds at the transaction level but the mint or burn operation is never triggered, and the corresponding event is not captured. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction yet the token balance on the destination chain remains unchanged, leading to the impression that funds have disappeared or that a refund was not received. The issue occurs whenever the XERC20 contract is deployed on Superchain in its current form, i.e., any time the bridge interacts with the contract under the updated specification. Token holders, the Velodrome protocol, and any integrators relying on cross‑chain functionality are affected because their assets cannot be transferred across chains, breaking the intended accounting guarantees of the system. The problem was identified during a manual audit by Sherlock, who compared the contract’s interface definitions and emitted events against the latest Superchain documentation. The discrepancy is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the functions perform the correct internal logic; the failure only manifests at runtime when external contracts expect different signatures. To remediate the issue, the XERC20 contract should be refactored to implement the current ICrosschainERC20 interface: rename the internal functions to crosschainMint and crosschainBurn, adjust the access modifier to match the bridge’s expectations, and emit the standard CrosschainMint and CrosschainBurn events. Verifying the finality of the Superchain ERC20 token standard before redeployment will ensure that future spec changes are incorporated and that cross‑chain token transfers function as intended.

title: Upgradability of Token Bridge
description:
The TokenBridge address will change when migrating from Hyperlane to Superchain. As a result, external integrators might not be able to bridge XVELO.
It is announced that Velodrome will migrate from Hyperlane to Superchain in the future.
However, the TokenBridge is immutable and not upgradable. As a result, to facilitate the migration from Hyperlane to Superchain, a new TokenBridge contract with the new Superchain's logic has to be deployed, which will inevitably lead to a new bridge address.
As a result, external protocols that integrate with the TokenBridge and hardcode the bridge address OR the external protocol itself is immutable will encounter issues when the bridge address changes.
External integrators might not be able to bridge XVELO if the TokenBridge address changes due to migration to the Superchain bridge and the older Hyperplane's token bridge has been decommissioned.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the TokenBridge contract being immutable and therefore not upgradable. When Velodrome migrates its cross‑chain messaging layer from Hyperlane to Superchain, a new bridge implementation with different logic must be deployed at a new address. Because the original bridge address is hard‑coded in many external integrators or in contracts that themselves are immutable, those integrations continue to point to the old, decommissioned bridge. The root cause is the reliance on a fixed contract address for core bridging functionality, which violates the expectation that the bridge will remain reachable across protocol upgrades. An attacker does not directly gain control of funds, but the situation can be exploited to cause a denial‑of‑service: users attempting to bridge XVELO send tokens to the stale address, where the transfer either reverts or is silently ignored, resulting in lost or stuck assets. The impact is that users may see their balances unchanged or become zero after a bridge attempt, refunds may not be issued, and the overall token flow across chains is broken. This condition occurs precisely at the moment of the protocol migration, i.e., when the Hyperlane bridge is retired and the Superchain bridge is launched. All parties that rely on the bridge—end‑users, dApps, liquidity providers, and other protocols—are affected because their contracts cannot dynamically discover the new address. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the upgrade path of the bridge and identified that the address is hard‑coded and immutable. It can be hard to notice because the bridge continues to exist on‑chain, but its internal logic no longer processes messages, leading to silent failures that only surface when a bridging transaction is attempted. To remediate, the bridge should be designed as an upgradable proxy or include a registry that can be updated to point to the new implementation without changing the external address. At a minimum, documentation must clearly state that the bridge address will change during migration so integrators can update their references. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an address‑immutability or upgradeability flaw, where business logic assumes a static contract address while the underlying protocol evolves, breaking accounting assumptions and causing funds to disappear or become inaccessible.

title: Restored addresses will not be
description:
When an address is restored after being deleted due to being compromised, it remains marked as compromised in the isAddressCompromised mapping. This prevents the address from taking any actions on behalf of the profile, even though it should be able to.
When an address is compromised, it can be deleted by calling EthosProfile::deleteAddressAtIndex(), which marks the address as compromised in the isAddressCompromised mapping.
```solidity
function deleteAddressAtIndex(uint256 addressIndex) external whenNotPaused {
    isAddressCompromised[addressStr] = true;
}
```
The purpose of the isAddressCompromised mapping is to ensure that no address marked as compromised and deleted can take any action on behalf of the profile. If a previously deleted address is no longer compromised, it can be restored when an address associated with the same profile as the deleted address calls EthosProfile::registerAddress() and provides that address.
However, the address is not unmarked in isAddressCompromised, meaning that restored addresses will still be unable to take any actions on behalf of the profile as they remain flagged as compromised.
Attack Path
1. AddressA calls EthosProfile::registerAddress() to register AddressB.
2. AddressB is compromised.
3. AddressA calls EthosProfile::deleteAddressAtIndex() to delete AddressB and mark it as compromised in isAddressCompromised.
4. AddressB is no longer compromised.
5. AddressA calls EthosProfile::registerAddress() to restore AddressB.
6. AddressB remains marked as compromised in isAddressCompromised and cannot act on behalf of the profile, even though it should be able to.
A previously deleted address will not be able to take any action on behalf of the profile when restored, as it remains marked as compromised.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the address‑management subsystem of the EthosProfile contract. When a compromised address is removed, the contract’s deleteAddressAtIndex function records the address as compromised in the isAddressCompromised mapping. The contract later allows a previously removed address to be re‑added by calling registerAddress, but the restoration logic never clears the compromised flag. As a result, a restored address remains permanently marked as compromised and is blocked from executing any function on behalf of the profile. The root cause is that the state variable that tracks compromised status is only ever set to true and never reset, even when the same address is later considered safe. An attacker can exploit this by first compromising a legitimate address, forcing its deletion, and then allowing the owner to restore the address (or the owner may do it unintentionally). After restoration the address appears in the profile’s address list, but any transaction sent from it will be rejected by the contract’s access checks, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service for the rightful owner. The impact is that users lose the ability to act with a previously trusted address, which may prevent them from managing their profile, withdrawing funds, or performing any privileged operation, potentially leading to lost or frozen assets. This condition occurs whenever an address transitions from compromised to non‑compromised and is subsequently re‑registered without an explicit step to clear the compromised flag. All profile owners and any parties that rely on address‑based permissions are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of address registration and deletion. It can be hard to notice because the UI may show the address as successfully registered, yet calls from that address silently fail, giving no obvious error message. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent access‑control errors where a revocation flag is not properly reset. To fix the problem the contract should either clear the isAddressCompromised entry when an address is restored, or maintain a separate historical mapping for removed addresses and keep the compromised flag independent of the restoration process. This ensures that a restored address regains its full permissions and that the contract’s accounting of compromised status accurately reflects the current security state.

title: Corruptible Upgradability Pat-
description:
The EthosContracts (EthosProfile, EthosReview, ...) are UUPSUpgradeable. However, the current implementation has multiple issues regarding upgradability.
Following is the inheritance chain of the EthosContracts.
The Ethos contracts are meant to be upgradeable. However, it inherits contracts that are not upgrade-safe.
Also, AccessControl inherits the non-upgradeable version Pausable and AccessControlEnumerable from Openzeppelin's library, when it should use the upgradeable version from openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable lib.
https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/upgradeable
There is also another issue that in all EthosContract, the constructor does not have initializers disabled for the implementation contract. This is also a best practice for proxy contracts.
```solidity
constructor() {
    _disableInitializers();
}
```
kages/contracts/contracts/utils/AccessControl.sol#L15
kages/contracts/contracts/utils/SignatureControl.sol#L11
Internal pre-conditions
If admin performs an upgrade and wants to add another storage slot in AccessControl or SignatureControl contract, the storage slot would mess up.
External pre-conditions
N/A
Attack Path
N/A
Storage of vault contracts might be corrupted during upgrading.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe upgradeability pattern in the Ethos contracts that are built as UUPSUpgradeable proxies but inherit from non‑upgradeable OpenZeppelin contracts such as Pausable and AccessControlEnumerable. Because those base contracts store state variables in a fixed layout, the proxy’s storage slots become misaligned when the implementation is upgraded and new variables are added to the AccessControl or SignatureControl contracts. The root cause is the mismatch between the storage layout expected by the upgradeable proxy and the layout defined by the non‑upgradeable parent contracts, combined with the fact that the implementation contracts contain a constructor that does not call _disableInitializers(). This omission leaves the implementation contract initializable, meaning an attacker could call an initializer on the implementation after deployment and gain privileged roles. The exploit scenario proceeds as follows: an admin triggers a contract upgrade, the new implementation adds a storage variable to AccessControl or SignatureControl, but because the parent contracts were not designed for upgradeability the new variable overwrites an existing slot, corrupting role assignments or pausable state. Simultaneously, because the implementation contract’s constructor does not disable initializers, a malicious actor can directly invoke the initializer on the implementation contract, thereby acquiring the admin role or other privileged permissions. The impact includes loss of access control integrity, the possibility of pausing the contract unexpectedly, and in the worst case the theft or freezing of user funds stored in vault contracts that rely on the corrupted storage. The issue manifests whenever an upgrade adds storage to the affected contracts or when an attacker gains the ability to call the implementation’s initializer; it affects all users, reviewers, and any entity holding assets in the Ethos system. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the inheritance chain against OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable guidelines and noted the missing _disableInitializers() call. It is hard to notice because the contract continues to function after an upgrade, but subtle misbehaviour such as incorrect role checks or zero‑value returns may only appear under specific upgrade scenarios. To remediate, the contracts should replace the non‑upgradeable OpenZeppelin modules with their upgradeable counterparts (e.g., PausableUpgradeable, AccessControlEnumerableUpgradeable), introduce storage gaps in AccessControl and SignatureControl to allow future variable additions without colliding, and add a constructor that calls _disableInitializers() in every implementation contract. These steps restore a safe storage layout, prevent the implementation contract from being initialized, and align the code with the upgradeable contract best practices, thereby protecting the protocol’s business logic and users’ funds from corruption or unauthorized control.

title: AmirX.defiToStablecoinSwap()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swap logic that handles a two‑step conversion from a decentralized finance (DeFi) token such as USDC to a protocol‑defined stablecoin (XYZ) and then to another stablecoin variant. The contract first validates the amount of the origin stablecoin (ss.oAmount) that will be burned by calling _verifyStablecoinSwap, which checks that burning this amount will not push the total supply of the origin token below its configured minimum (minSupply). After this check the function performs an external aggregation swap via _defiSwap, which can return a different amount of the origin token than the one originally supplied. The code then recomputes ss.oAmount based on the wallet’s balance change but does not re‑run the min‑supply validation. Consequently, if the external swap yields a larger amount of the origin stablecoin, the contract may burn more tokens than allowed, causing the total supply of the origin XYZ token to fall below its minSupply threshold. This breaks the accounting invariant that the protocol enforces for each stablecoin, potentially leading to supply inconsistencies, unexpected token shortages, or failed future minting operations. From a user’s perspective the swap may appear to succeed while the protocol’s internal accounting is corrupted; users might see their balance reduced unexpectedly or receive fewer minted tokens than expected, effectively losing value. The flaw occurs only when the origin token is an XYZ stablecoin and the swap path includes an external defi swap before the internal stablecoin conversion, i.e., in defiToStablecoinSwap and the generic swap function when directional is true. It affects any user invoking these functions, the protocol’s stablecoin supply guarantees, and any downstream contracts that rely on the minSupply constraint. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the order of checks and state updates. It is subtle because the initial validation passes, the external call is trusted, and the contract does not re‑validate after the external call, making the problem invisible in normal testing unless the external swap is manipulated to return a higher amount. The recommended remediation is to move the _verifyStablecoinSwap call to after the external _defiSwap execution and after ss.oAmount has been recomputed, ensuring that the final burn amount is always checked against the minSupply rule. This change restores the intended safety check and prevents the protocol from unintentionally violating its supply limits.

title: Changing the bridging modules
description:
Changing the module state parameter of RootMessageBridge and LeafMessageBridge contracts can cause the delivery of in-flight messages to always revert.
The RootMessageBridge and LeafMessageBridge contracts have the ability to change the module parameter via setModule functions.
63a33b963e3bdf76a1c871e6a6ecd7c5403d/superchain-contracts-private/src/bridge/CrossChainRegistry.sol#L45-L50
63a33b963e3bdf76a1c871e6a6ecd7c5403d/superchain-contracts-private/src/bridge/LeafMessageBridge.sol#L25-L29
During the module change, in case there exists a message which got transmitted from the root chain but haven't arrived on leaf chain then that in-flight message cannot be delivered on leaf chain. Delivery of that message will revert because all leaf chain operations validate that they are being called by latest leaf module.
c871e6a6ecd7c5403d/superchain-contracts-private/src/gauges/LeafGauge.sol#L192
Hence delivery of that in-flight message will revert on leaf chain.
Scenario:
1. A cross chain operation gets initiated via RootMessageBridge.sendMessage.
2. Owner of RootMessageBridge and LeafMessageBridge contracts changes the modules on both root and leaf chains.
3. The message from step 1 arrives to leaf chain but gets reverted.
This scenario can occur in real life when Velodrome decides to upgrade their currently active bridge modules.
Atomicity of cross-chain messages will get broken when a module upgrade is in progress.
The messages will get executed on root chain but will fail on leaf chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ability of the RootMessageBridge and LeafMessageBridge contracts to change their module address through public setModule functions. When the owner upgrades the module on either the root or leaf chain while a cross‑chain message is still in flight, the leaf‑side validation that the caller must be the current module fails. Consequently, the delivery transaction on the leaf chain reverts, even though the corresponding sendMessage call on the root chain has already been executed. This race condition breaks the atomicity guarantee of cross‑chain operations: the source chain state changes are committed, but the destination chain state remains unchanged, leading to inconsistent accounting and potentially locked or lost funds. The issue manifests only when there are pending messages, for example when leaf‑chain buffers (such as XERC20 limits) delay processing. From a user’s perspective the source‑chain transaction appears successful, yet the expected balance update on the destination chain never occurs, creating the impression that the bridge “lost” the funds. The problem was discovered during a security audit of the bridge contracts, where the logical flow of module validation was examined. It is difficult to notice because normal messages succeed; only those caught in the upgrade window revert, producing silent failures without explicit alerts on the source side. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that no in‑flight messages exist before a module change, for instance by pausing the bridge or introducing a message‑pause mechanism that blocks new messages and safely drains or migrates pending ones during upgrades. In broader terms, this is a class of cross‑chain bridge state‑inconsistency bugs caused by non‑atomic upgrades of critical contract components, violating the fundamental business assumption that a cross‑chain operation either completes fully on both chains or not at all.

title: Token bridges process messages
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token bridge component that forwards cross‑chain messages to the XVELO minting function. The bridge accepts any message that arrives from the Hyperlane mailbox and originates from the bridge contract itself, but it does not verify that the originating chain identifier (_origin) belongs to a set of chains that the protocol administrator has explicitly approved. Because the contract lacks this chain‑whitelist check, messages sent from chains that have been deregistered or were never registered are still processed. An attacker who can inject a malicious message on an unsupported chain – for example by exploiting a bug on one of the many Hyperlane‑supported networks or by somehow reproducing the bridge’s address on another chain – can cause the bridge to call the mint function with arbitrary recipient and amount values. This results in unauthorized creation of XVELO tokens, inflating the supply and potentially devaluing legitimate holders’ balances. The issue manifests when the admin calls deregisterChain to remove a chain; the bridge continues to accept messages from that chain, so users may notice unexpected token balances appearing in their wallets or, conversely, see the token’s value drop due to supply inflation. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the handle function’s access controls and observed that the only checks performed were msg.sender == mailbox and _sender == address(this), with no validation of the origin chain. The flaw can be subtle because the bridge’s external behavior – minting tokens – appears normal, and the missing chain check does not generate an explicit error, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the bridge should maintain a collection of approved chain identifiers and reject any message whose _origin is not present in that collection, typically by adding a require or revert statement such as "if (!_chainids.contains(_origin)) revert UnsupportedChain();" before invoking the mint operation. This change restores the intended business logic that only messages from trusted, registered chains can trigger token minting, thereby preserving accounting integrity and protecting users from unauthorized token creation.

title: An attacker may DoS user Fluid
description:
FluidLocker::claim() connects to the fluid pool and then calls EPProgramManager::batchUpdateUserUnits() to verify the signature and update user points.  
However, any attacker may frontrun this call and call directly EPProgramManager::batchUpdateUserUnits(), spending the signature (nonce) and making the claim transaction revert.  
As the Fluid balances only increase whenever the user connects to the pool, the user balance will be 0.  
An attacker will profit from this because a large tax amount may be coming from a user instantly unlocking or a program being stopped, which transfer immediately funds to the stakers by calling FLUID.distributeToPool(address(this),TAX_DISTRIBUTION_POOL,amount);.  
As the user wanted to stake, they needed Fluid balance to do so, but as the attacker DoSed their claim transaction, they will not have balance to stake and will completely miss these large instant funds. Even if users had already staked before, this claim transaction could be increasing their points (by increasing their program points, they could get more Fluid and stake more Fluid to get more staker points), so an attacker profits from not allowing the user to do so just before the tax is distributed.  
EP_PROGRAM_MANAGER::updateUserUnits() may be called directly allowing attackers to DoS FluidLocker::claim().  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
1. Attacker spots that a user is unlocking or a program is coming to an end and a large sum of tax is coming.  
2. Attacker frontruns users that are going to increase their Fluid balance in the Locker by calling FluidLocker::claim() so that the Locker connects to the program pool and receives the corresponding Fluid tokens.  
3. Due to the FluidLocker::claim() call reverting, users will have less Fluid in the Locker and will stake less funds, getting less points, which means the attacker will get a bigger share of the funds.  
Attacker profits from having a bigger share of the TAX distributions and users lose this share.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service (DoS) that allows an attacker to block a user’s FluidLocker.claim() call and prevent the user from receiving newly minted Fluid tokens. The root cause is that FluidLocker.claim() internally calls EPProgramManager.updateUserUnits() with a user‑provided signature and nonce, but the same updateUserUnits() function can be invoked directly by any external account. An attacker can observe that a user is about to unlock a position or that a program is about to end, which will trigger a large tax distribution to the pool, and then front‑run the user’s transaction by calling EPProgramManager.updateUserUnits() first, consuming the signature nonce. When the legitimate user’s claim transaction executes, the signature has already been spent, causing the call to revert. Because the Fluid balance only increases when the locker successfully connects to the program pool, the user’s balance remains zero and the claim fails. From the user’s perspective the UI shows no Fluid received, staking opportunities disappear, and expected rewards are missing, even though the transaction appears to have been submitted. The impact is that the user loses the chance to stake the newly received Fluid and therefore receives a smaller share of the tax distribution, while the attacker, by preventing the user’s claim, captures a larger portion of the distributed funds. This condition can occur at any time when a claim is attempted; there are no explicit internal or external pre‑conditions required. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between FluidLocker.claim() and EPProgramManager.updateUserUnits(). It is hard to notice because the failure manifests as a silent revert with no obvious error message, and the user only observes that their balance does not increase. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of signature‑replay and front‑running race conditions that lead to a denial‑of‑service. The recommended mitigation is to separate the pool‑connection logic from the claim operation, for example by providing a dedicated method that only the locker can call to connect to the pool, and to protect updateUserUnits() so that it cannot be invoked directly with a user’s signature by an arbitrary attacker. This would prevent the attacker from consuming the nonce and ensure that a legitimate claim can always update the user’s units and receive the expected Fluid tokens.

title: FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPe
description:
FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage() is calculated as:  
```solidity
function _getUnlockingPercentage(uint128 unlockPeriod) internal pure returns (uint256 unlockingPercentageBP) {
    unlockingPercentageBP = (
        _PERCENT_TO_BP
        * (
            ((80 * _SCALER) / Math.sqrt(540 * _SCALER)) *
            (Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod * _SCALER) / _SCALER)
            + 20 * _SCALER
        )
    ) / _SCALER;
}
```
As can be seen, it divides before multiplying, leading to precision loss.  
The loss is always ((80*1e18)/Math.sqrt(540*24*3600*1e18))=1712139.4821, so the 0.4821 component is discarded. This corresponds to 0.4821*sqrt(540*24*3600*1e18)*100/1e18=0.00032929935 BPS.  
As this loss is present in every calculation and it will make a 1 BPS different in many instances, it is significant. For example, if the maximum duration is picked, instead of 10000 BPS, it will actually be 9999BPS and 1 BPS goes to the TAX pool. If the user unlocks for example 1e5 USD, this is a 10 USD loss. As it will happen frequently, the loss will accumulate.  
In FluidLocker::388, it divides before multiplying.  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
1. User calls unlock with vesting period, but due to the precision loss it rounds down and 1 BPS more goes to the tax distribution pool.  
User suffers a 1 BPS loss of funds. For example, 1e5 USD will yield a 10 USD loss.
poc: Presented in the summary.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision loss in the function that computes the unlocking percentage for the FluidLocker contract. The formula multiplies a constant by a term that includes a square‑root of the unlock period, but it performs a division before the final multiplication. Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the intermediate division truncates any fractional part, discarding roughly 0.4821 of a scaled unit. This truncation translates to a loss of about 0.00033 basis points per calculation, which accumulates to a full basis point (1 BPS) when the maximum unlock period is used. As a result, users who call the unlock function receive slightly less than the expected amount; the missing 1 BPS is automatically redirected to the protocol’s tax distribution pool. The impact is a systematic reduction of user payouts – for example, unlocking a position worth 100 000 USD yields a shortfall of roughly 10 USD. The issue occurs on every unlock call, regardless of the chosen vesting period, because the same arithmetic order is used each time. It affects all participants of the FluidLocker system, reducing their expected returns and inflating the tax pool. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the internal calculation logic and identified the division‑before‑multiplication pattern as a source of rounding error. The problem is subtle because the per‑transaction loss is tiny and may be perceived as normal variance, making it hard to notice without precise accounting. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “integer division truncation” or “precision loss due to operation ordering” bugs, which violate the business assumption that the unlocking percentage should sum to exactly 10 000 BPS (100 %). From the user’s perspective the UI shows a slightly lower unlocked amount than expected, leading to confusion when the balance appears reduced by a small amount. The correct mitigation is to reorder the arithmetic so that multiplication occurs before division, eliminating the truncation and ensuring the unlocking percentage is calculated with full precision. This change prevents the inadvertent transfer of 1 BPS to the tax pool and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended financial model.

title: Token bridging with Hyperlane
description:
Token bridging through Hyperlane doesn't allow the user to specify the gas limit for message delivery on the destination chain leading to stuck messages, i.e. needing manual intervention to deliver the message.  
There is also no refund mechanism for sending msg.value that is higher than the Hyperlane fee as default hooks for Hyperlane don't refund.  
TokenBridge.sendToken(...) function calls Mailbox.dispatch(...) function with default parameters, i.e. doesn't allow specifying additional gas for message delivery. The default gasLimit is 50k and this might not be sufficient to execute the handle function on the destination chain and bridge the tokens. The only option the user has is paying for additional gas through InterchainGasPaymaster.payForGas(...) function call. This is not ideal as user needs to monitor the delivery of his message and in case it can't be delivered send another transaction to pay for the additional gas.  
Aside from this, Hyperlane's default hook doesn't allow any gas refunds. If the msg.value is higher than needed it's not going to be refunded.  
Users sending msg.value higher than needed are not getting refunded and they might need to pay for additional gas in a separate transaction in order to deliver their message to the destination chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑limit and fee‑refund deficiency in the Hyperlane token‑bridging flow. When a user calls TokenBridge.sendToken, the contract forwards the request to Mailbox.dispatch with the default parameters, which set a fixed gas limit of 50 000 for the message execution on the destination chain. If the handle function that finalises the token transfer on the destination requires more gas, the dispatched message cannot be executed and remains stuck in the Hyperlane inbox. From the user’s perspective the source‑chain transaction appears successful, but the tokens never appear on the target chain and the user receives no error, making the problem easy to miss. In addition, the default Hyperlane hook does not implement any refund logic; any msg.value sent that exceeds the quoted dispatch fee is retained by the bridge contract. Consequently a user who over‑pays the fee loses the excess ETH unless they manually intervene. The issue manifests whenever a bridge operation is performed with a destination payload that needs more than the 50 k gas limit or when the caller includes a higher msg.value than required. It affects all participants who rely on the bridge – token holders, the protocol’s liquidity providers, and any downstream applications that assume successful cross‑chain delivery. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the TokenBridge contract where the dispatch call was examined and the lack of a configurable gas parameter and refund hook were noted. The bug is subtle because the transaction receipt on the source chain shows success, and there is no on‑chain revert to signal the failure. To remediate, the bridge should use the overload of Mailbox.dispatch that accepts StandardHookMetadata, allowing the caller to specify an appropriate gas limit, and it should query Mailbox.quoteDispatch to determine the exact fee and return any surplus msg.value to the sender. This change would align the implementation with the expected business logic that a user pays exactly for the gas needed and receives their tokens on the destination chain without manual follow‑up.

title: Hyperlane fee is always under-
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the Hyperlane fee that is taken from a user when calling the cross‑chain messaging function RootMessageBridge.sendMessage(...). The contract determines the fee by invoking Mailbox.quoteDispatch with only the destination chain identifier and the recipient address, which returns a fee based on the default gas limit of 50 000 units. However, the RootHLMessageModule that actually performs the dispatch enforces a much higher gas limit (for example 2 000 000) through the defaultHookMetadata supplied to Mailbox.dispatch. Because the fee extraction step does not incorporate this additional gas limit, the amount deducted from the sender is always insufficient to cover the real cost of the dispatch call. When the dispatch is executed, the contract attempts to forward the message with the higher gas limit but the attached fee is too low, causing the call to revert due to an out‑of‑gas or insufficient‑fee error. This mismatch creates a permanent denial‑of‑service condition: any user trying to send a message through RootMessageBridge.sendMessage will consistently fail, and the fee that was taken cannot be refunded because the contract does not have a recovery path. The impact is that cross‑chain communication is halted, users see their transactions marked as successful on the source chain but receive no message on the destination chain, and any funds that were intended to be transferred remain locked or are effectively lost. The bug affects all participants of the protocol that rely on the bridge, including token holders, liquidity providers, and any automated system that depends on cross‑chain messaging. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor compared the fee returned by Mailbox.quoteDispatch with and without the metadata that specifies a larger gas limit, observing that the quoted fee never increased despite the higher gas requirement. The issue is subtle because the fee appears reasonable and the contract does not emit a clear error indicating insufficient payment, making it easy to overlook during routine testing that only uses the default gas limit. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of fee‑quotation mismatches where the cost estimation does not reflect the actual execution parameters, breaking the accounting invariant that the fee paid must be at least the gas cost incurred. The recommended remediation is to compute the fee using the same overload of Mailbox.quoteDispatch that accepts the defaultHookMetadata, ensuring that the quoted fee incorporates the exact gas limit that will be used in the subsequent dispatch call. By aligning the fee extraction with the dispatch parameters, the bridge can correctly charge users, prevent permanent DoS, and restore reliable cross‑chain messaging.

title: Signer can avoid restrictions and
bug_full: The issue is a re‑entrancy flaw in the multi‑signature contract’s transaction validation logic that allows a signer to bypass the intended restrictions on owner list and threshold changes. The contract records a snapshot of the current owners, threshold and fallback handler before executing a delegatecall, storing these values in temporary variables. After the delegatecall finishes, a post‑execution check compares the current state with the stored snapshot to ensure that the delegatecall did not modify critical governance parameters. However, the checkTransaction function can be entered again from within the delegatecall, causing the snapshot variables to be overwritten with the new, malicious state. Because the post‑execution verification uses the overwritten snapshot, it incorrectly concludes that no unauthorized change occurred. An attacker can exploit this by first submitting a transaction that changes the owners array and lowers the threshold to one, then, inside the same delegatecall, re‑enter checkTransaction and submit a second transaction that updates the snapshot variables to reflect the attacker’s new ownership configuration. When the outer call finishes, both the inner and outer post‑execution checks compare against the attacker‑controlled snapshot and therefore succeed, leaving the contract with a single owner and a threshold of one. This gives the attacker full control over the multi‑sig, allowing them to approve and execute any future transaction, potentially draining funds or altering protocol parameters. The vulnerability manifests only when a delegatecall is allowed and the validation routine does not protect against re‑entrancy; it is difficult to notice because the snapshot appears consistent after execution, masking the underlying state change. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic of checkTransaction and identified that the temporary variables are not protected against being overwritten by a nested call. To remediate, the contract should either make the validation function non‑re‑entrant, store the snapshot in immutable storage for the duration of the call, or explicitly revert if the snapshot variables have already been set and differ from the current state, thereby preventing an attacker from overwriting the recorded owners and threshold. The bug belongs to the class of re‑entrancy‑based state‑corruption vulnerabilities where post‑execution invariants are bypassed by nested calls that manipulate the data used for verification. From a user’s perspective, the UI may still show the original owners list, but after the exploit the contract will only recognize the attacker as the sole owner, causing legitimate owners to lose the ability to approve transactions and potentially seeing their funds become inaccessible or drained.

title: A malicious user may unlock in multiple times
description:
The missing check in FluidLocker::_instantUnlock() for stakers in the tax pool allows users to unlock their funds without paying any tax instantly. This happens because whenever there are 0 stakers in the tax pool, the flow rate is set to 0 and it does not revert, so the user can loop unlocking until funds are withdrawn.

In FluidLocker::_instantUnlock() there is a missing check for 0 stakers in the tax pool.
Internal pre-conditions
1. There are 0 stakers in the tax pool.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User loops FluidLocker::unlock() with a null unlocking period and instantly withdraws their funds.
The user is able to unlock their funds without paying any tax.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the instant unlock routine of a fluid‑locking contract that allows a user to bypass the tax mechanism when the tax pool contains no active stakers. The contract calculates a flow rate based on the amount of staked units in the tax pool; when that count drops to zero the flow rate is set to zero. Because the unlock function does not check for this zero‑staker condition, it proceeds without reverting, meaning the caller can invoke unlock with a zero unlocking period repeatedly. Each call instantly withdraws the caller’s locked balance without any tax deduction. This can be exploited by a malicious participant who first empties the tax pool (or waits until it is naturally empty) and then loops the unlock operation, draining the locker’s assets while the protocol records no tax revenue. The impact is a loss of expected tax fees and potential depletion of funds that were meant to be locked, undermining the economic model of the system. The issue manifests only when the tax pool has zero units, a state that may be rare and therefore easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test case repeatedly called unlock with a zero period and observed that the user’s balance increased far beyond the expected taxed amount. The bug is subtle because the function otherwise works correctly when the pool has participants, so the missing guard does not raise an obvious error. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify that the tax pool contains a positive amount of staked units before allowing an instant unlock, and revert the transaction if the pool is empty, thereby enforcing the tax collection logic under all conditions. This class of flaw belongs to the broader category of unchecked state‑dependent logic errors that allow fee‑exemption bypasses, violating the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Attacker will prevent lenders
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the absence of a validation that a lend order is active before additional funds can be added. The contract’s addFunds function permits any caller that is either the order owner or an authorized loan contract to increase the availableAmount of a lend order without checking whether the order has been marked inactive. Because cancelOffer sets the order’s isActive flag to false and then calls the factory’s deleteOrder, an attacker can repeatedly add a tiny amount of funds to a cancelled (inactive) order, invoke cancelOffer again, and thereby decrement the factory’s activeOrdersCount. By alternating addFunds and cancelOffer the attacker can drive activeOrdersCount to zero. When the count reaches zero, subsequent calls to deleteOrder attempt to decrement the counter below zero, triggering an arithmetic underflow and causing the transaction to revert. This revert propagates to higher‑level functions such as matchOffersV3 and acceptLendingOffer, preventing legitimate lenders from cancelling their orders, withdrawing funds, or having their non‑perpetual lend orders fully matched. The impact is that funds become stuck, lenders cannot retrieve their capital, and the matching engine is effectively halted, breaking the core lending functionality of the protocol. The condition occurs only when at least one non‑perpetual lend order exists and an attacker can create and cancel their own orders to manipulate the activeOrdersCount. It affects all participants who rely on the ability to cancel or match lend orders, including lenders, borrowers, and any aggregator users invoking matchOffersV3. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined state transitions around order lifecycle management and identified that addFunds lacked an isActive guard. It is subtle because the addFunds call succeeds and appears harmless, yet it changes the internal accounting in a way that enables the underflow later. The bug belongs to the class of missing state‑validation or improper lifecycle checks, leading to arithmetic underflow and denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective, a lender may see that their order cannot be cancelled, receives no refund, or that the matching function suddenly reverts with an arithmetic error, even though the UI shows the order as existing. The expected behavior is that a cancelled order cannot receive further funds and that activeOrdersCount never drops below zero. To fix the issue, the contract should enforce that addFunds can only be called while the order is active, and cancelOffer should require the order to be active before proceeding, thereby preserving the integrity of the activeOrdersCount counter and preventing the underflow scenario.

title: An attacker can wipe the order-
description:
A malicious actor can wipe the complete buy order orderbook in buyOrderFactory.sol.
The attack - excluding gas costs - does not bear any financial burden the attacker. As a result of the exploit, the orderbook will be temporarily inaccessible in the factory, leading to a DoS state in buy order matching, and in closing and selling existing positions.
The function sellNFT(uint receiptID) lacks reentrancy protection.

Internal pre-conditions
N/A
External pre-conditions
N/A
Attack Path
1. Attacker calls createBuyOrder(address _token, address wantedToken, uint _amount, uint ratio) with exploit contract supplied in parameter wantedToken
2. Attacker calls sellNFT(uint receiptID) which triggers the exploit sequence
3. Exploit contract will reenter sellNFT multiple times, triggering a cascade of buy order deletions
The orderbook in buyOrderFactory.sol will be inaccessible. The function getActiveBuyOrders(uint offset, uint limit) is used by off-chain services to gather buy order data - this data will be temporarily blocked. Deleting existing buy orders (deleteBuyOrder()) and selling NFTs (sellNFT(uint receiptID)) will also be temporarily blocked until the issue is resolved manually. Issue can be resolved manually by:
• Opening dummy buy orders with very little collateral
• Closing/selling positions on existing ”legit” orders
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw located in the function that sells an NFT within the buy‑order factory contract. The function does not use any reentrancy guard, allowing a malicious contract to call back into the same sell function before the original execution finishes. When an attacker supplies a malicious contract as the wanted token during order creation, the attacker can trigger the sellNFT function, which then re‑enters itself through the fallback of the malicious contract. Each re‑entry invokes the internal routine that deletes a buy order, and because the guard is missing the contract repeatedly deletes orders until the entire orderbook is emptied. This results in a temporary denial‑of‑service: off‑chain services that query active buy orders receive no data, users are unable to match new buy orders, and existing positions cannot be closed or sold. The impact is not a direct loss of funds – the attacker does not pay any gas‑free cost – but the protocol’s core matching logic becomes unavailable, breaking user expectations that their orders remain listed and that they can close positions on demand. The issue manifests whenever sellNFT is called on a buy order that was created with a malicious token address, and it can be reproduced by deploying an exploit contract that re‑enters sellNFT via its fallback. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sellNFT implementation and noticed the absence of a reentrancy modifier. Because the symptom is a silent disappearance of orders rather than an explicit revert, it can be hard to notice without monitoring the orderbook state. The proper mitigation is to apply a reentrancy protection mechanism, such as the OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard, to the sellNFT function so that any subsequent call is blocked until the first execution completes. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of reentrancy‑induced state‑corruption vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions by allowing an attacker to manipulate internal data structures during execution. From a user’s perspective the UI will suddenly show zero active buy orders, the expected list of orders is empty, and attempts to close or sell a position will fail or be blocked, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence in the protocol.

title: Lender may loose part of the interest when converting to perpetual offer after loan extension
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that can cause a lender to lose interest that was accrued before a loan is extended when the lender later changes the lend order to a perpetual mode. The root cause lies in the interaction between the extendLoan() function and the payDebt() function. When a borrower calls extendLoan(), the contract adds the newly accrued interest to the interestToClaim field only if the lend order is not marked as perpetual. If the lender subsequently switches the same lend order to perpetual without first claiming the accumulated interest, the next call to payDebt() treats the offer as perpetual, approves the principal amount, adds the funds to the perpetual lend contract and sets the debtClaimed flag to true. At this point the contract does not transfer the previously recorded interestToClaim to the lender, effectively discarding it. The impact is that the lender receives only the principal repayment and any interest generated after the conversion, while the interest earned before the conversion is permanently locked in the contract. This loss can be significant depending on the loan size, duration and APR. The issue occurs under the specific conditions that (1) the loan was originally created with a non‑perpetual lend order, (2) the borrower later extends the loan, and (3) the lender changes the lend order to perpetual before claiming the accrued interest. The affected parties are lenders who rely on the perpetual option to automatically collect interest and borrowers who may assume that their lenders will receive the full accrued amount. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the DebitaV3Loan.sol contract, where the auditor observed that the interest accounting path diverges for perpetual versus non‑perpetual offers and that the claimDebt() function becomes unreachable for previously accrued interest after a conversion. The bug is subtle because the user interface does not warn the lender that interest will be lost, and the expectation that a perpetual offer continuously accumulates interest is violated. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after extending a loan and switching to perpetual, the lender’s interest balance remains unchanged or drops to zero, even though they expected to receive the earned amount. The contract’s business logic assumes that all interest can be claimed later, but the state transition to perpetual breaks this assumption. A conceptual fix is to separate the interest claiming mechanism from the perpetual conversion, for example by introducing a dedicated claimInterest function that can be called before or after the conversion, or by ensuring that any pending interest is transferred to the lender before the debtClaimed flag is set. This would preserve the lender’s right to the previously accrued interest and align the contract’s behavior with user expectations.

title: Mixed Token Price Will Be Inaccurate Due to Decimal Miscalculation in MixOracle
bug_full: The MixOracle contract provides a getThePrice function that returns the USD price of a token based on a Uniswap pair and an external Pyth price feed. The function reads the decimals of the target token (token0) and the attached token (token1) but mistakenly uses the decimals of token1 when scaling the computed amount of attached token. As a result, when token0 and token1 have different decimal precision—such as DAI (18 decimals) paired with USDC (6 decimals)—the final price is multiplied or divided by 10^(difference) (for example 10^12), inflating or deflating the reported price. This arithmetic error causes downstream contracts that rely on the oracle to execute trades at wildly incorrect rates. The bug is triggered whenever an admin registers a token pair with mismatched decimals and a caller invokes getThePrice while the contract is not paused and the price feed is available. Users who trade through protocols that consume this oracle may receive far fewer tokens than expected or lose funds because the protocol believes the price is higher than it actually is. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the audit team, and it is subtle because the function returns a non‑zero price and the deviation may only become apparent when large decimal differences exist. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unit‑conversion or decimal‑scaling bugs, where the wrong token precision is applied to a formula. To remediate, the division should use the decimals of token0 (the token whose price is being reported) instead of token1, ensuring that the amount of attached token is correctly normalized. After the fix, the price calculation aligns with the intended accounting model and prevents the accidental creation of exchange rates that are off by orders of magnitude.

title: Precision loss leads to locked incentives in DebitaIncentives contract
description:
When a lender or borrower calls DebitaIncentives::claimIncentives() to claim a share of the incentives for a specific token pair they interacted with during an epoch, their share is calculated as a percentage. This percentage is determined based on the amount they lent or borrowed through the protocol during that epoch, relative to the total amount lent and borrowed by all users in the same period.
The percentage is rounded to two decimal places, which means up to 0.0099% of the incentives may remain unclaimed for each lender or borrower. Consider the following simple scenario:
1. Six lenders each lent 5e18 over a 14-day period for a specific token pair
2. That token pair is incentivized with 1000e18
3. The total amount lent equals 6 * 5e18 = 30e18
After each lender calls DebitaIncentives::claimIncentives(), there will still be 4e17 locked in the contract permanently. This means the incentivizer loses 0.04% of their incentives and every lender lost 4e17 / 6.
In DebitaIncentives.sol, there is no mechanism for incentivizers to withdraw unclaimed incentives that cannot be claimed due to precision loss.
Internal pre-conditions
1. Incentivizers need to call DebitaIncentives::incentivizePair() to incentivize specific token pairs.
2. Users need to interact with one of these incentivized pairs by borrowing or lending them.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
