Because the vault allows deposits and withdrawals to occur in the same transaction without any time‑based restriction, an attacker can obtain a large amount of the principal asset via a flash loan, deposit it into the vault, immediately open a position, and then close the position and repay the flash loan within the same block. By doing so the attacker inflates the total supply of shares at the moment interest is calculated, effectively capturing almost the entire interest that would otherwise be distributed among honest depositors. This attack works only when the vault does not enforce a deposit/withdraw window or a lock‑up period, allowing the share count to be manipulated atomically. The impact is that legitimate users see their expected interest dramatically reduced, sometimes to near zero, while the attacker walks away with a large, almost interest‑free profit. From a user’s perspective the UI may show normal balances but the interest column remains empty or shows a much smaller amount than anticipated, violating the business logic that interest should be shared fairly among all participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interest‑distribution formula and identified that the share calculation does not account for flash‑loan‑driven, instantaneous deposits. It is hard to notice because normal operation shows correct interest accrual; only an attacker with a flash‑loan source can trigger the abnormal state. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a deposit/withdraw window or a time‑lock that prevents a user from depositing and withdrawing in the same block, or to use a snapshot mechanism that fixes the share base at the start of an interest period, thereby preventing share manipulation. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “share dilution” or “flash‑loan‑driven interest siphon” vulnerabilities, where the accounting assumptions about static share totals are broken by rapid, atomic capital movements, leading to loss of funds for honest participants.

title: LendingPool::setBorrowingRate
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑synchronisation defect in the lending pool where a call to setBorrowingRateConfig updates the stored borrowing‑rate parameters but fails to invoke the internal functions that recalculate the reserve's current borrowing rate. The root cause is the omission of updateState and updateInterestRates calls after the configuration values are written, meaning the contract’s accounting variables are not refreshed to reflect the new rates. An attacker or any external actor can exploit this by triggering a rate change and then relying on the fact that the contract will continue to apply the previous borrowing rate until the next state‑changing operation such as a deposit, withdrawal or borrow occurs. Because those operations may not happen for an extended or indefinite period, the protocol effectively loses the expected interest revenue; borrowers continue to be charged the lower, outdated rate while the protocol’s revenue model assumes a higher rate. This condition occurs whenever the governance or admin invokes setBorrowingRateConfig, which is intended to adjust rates based on utilisation, but the missing calls cause the new configuration to remain dormant. All participants that depend on accurate interest calculations – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected because the financial accounting diverges from the announced policy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LendingPool contract where the control flow was examined and the absence of state‑updating calls was noted. It can be hard to notice because the UI may display the new configuration values, giving the impression that the rates have changed, while the on‑chain calculations still use the old values, leading to subtle revenue leakage rather than an outright functional failure. The bug belongs to the class of delayed‑effect configuration bugs where changes to protocol parameters are not propagated to dependent state variables. To remediate, the setBorrowingRateConfig routine should invoke updateState before writing the new parameters and call updateInterestRates after the write, ensuring that the reserve’s currentBorrowingRate is recomputed immediately and that the protocol regains control over when the new rate becomes effective.

title: The reserve fee is calculated incorrectly
description:
The reserve fee is calculated incorrectly leading to loss of fees for the reserve. The actual minted shares will represent a lower value than the set reserveFeeRate represents.
In ReserveLogic._mintToTreasury the calculation of shares uses reserveToETokenExchangeRate(reserve) to calculate the shares represented by the set reserveFeeRate
s/contracts/libraries/logic/ReserveLogic.sol#L217-L246
The issue is that minting of shares will increase the total supply of eTokens and therefore lead to the shares minted actually representing a lower value of underlying that was intended.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
Lets consider the following values and use them in the _mintToTreasury function:
currentDebt = 2000e18 previousDebt = 1000e18 totalDebtAccrued = currentDebt.sub(previousDebt) = 2000e18-1000e18=1000e18 reserveValueAccrued = totalDebtAccrued.mul(feeRate).div(Constants.PERCENT_100) = (1000e18*1500)/10000=150e18
totalLiquidity = 10000e18 totalETokens = 5000e18 exchangeRate = reserveToETokenExchangeRate(reserve) = (5000e18*1e18)/10000e18=0.5e18 feeInEToken = reserveValueAccrued.mul(exchangeRate).div(Precision.FACTOR1E18) = (150e18*0.5e18)/1e18=75e18
This means that the treasury will get minted 75e18 shares which are meant to represent 150e18 of the underlying. This is however flawed because after minting, the totalETokens now become 5000e18+75e18=5075e18 after the minted shares are added.
If the treasury shares are claimed, the exchange rate would be:
totalLiquidity.mul(Precision.FACTOR1E18).div(totalETokens) = (10000e18*1e18)/5075e18 and the value of underlying would therefore be:
underlyingTokenAmount = reserve.eTokenToReserveExchangeRate().mul(eTokenAmount).div(Precision.FACTOR1E18) = (((10000e18*1e18)/5075e18)*75e18)/1e18=147.78e18
This value is lower that the intended 150e18
The protocol loses some of the reserve fees every time an operation is done. This figure will progressively compound over time as more transactions are done.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in theway the protocol calculates the reserve fee when minting treasury shares in the ReserveLogic._mintToTreasury function. The contract determines the number of eToken shares to mint by multiplying the accrued reserve value by the current reserve‑to‑eToken exchange rate, which is derived from the total eToken supply before the new shares are added. Because minting new shares increases the total supply, the pre‑mint exchange rate under‑estimates the dilution effect, causing the minted shares to represent a smaller amount of underlying assets than the fee rate intends. In practice, when a debt accrual triggers a fee of, for example, 150e18 units of the underlying asset, the contract mints only 75e18 eToken shares based on a 0.5 exchange rate. After minting, the total eToken supply rises, the exchange rate falls, and the treasury can redeem those shares for roughly 147.8e18 underlying units instead of the expected 150e18. This systematic shortfall means the protocol loses a portion of the reserve fees on every operation that invokes the fee‑minting logic, and the loss compounds over time as more transactions occur. The issue is triggered whenever the _mintToTreasury function is called, typically after a change in debt or a user‑initiated operation that generates fees. It affects the protocol’s treasury, token holders who rely on accurate fee distribution, and any user expecting the advertised fee rate to be honored. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the fee‑minting routine and identified that the exchange rate used does not account for the dilution caused by the newly minted shares. The problem is subtle because the numerical discrepancy per transaction is small and may appear as normal rounding variance, making it hard to detect without a detailed accounting analysis. Conceptually, the fix is to compute the number of shares to mint based on the post‑mint total supply or to adjust the formula so that the minted shares correspond exactly to the intended underlying fee amount, as suggested by the corrected expression reserveValueAccrued * totalETokens / (totalLiquidity ‑ reserveValueAccrued). From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that the treasury receives fewer tokens than expected, leading to lower fee accruals displayed in dashboards, and users may notice that their refunds or fee rewards are slightly short of the advertised amounts. This class of bug can be described as an “accounting dilution error” or “incorrect share minting calculation” that violates the protocol’s financial invariants and erodes revenue over time.

title: Users may lose funds when they deposit/wrap
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch in how share amounts are calculated between the stUSR token and its wrapped counterpart wstUSR. In the stUSR contract, the internal conversion function adds a constant offset of 1000 shares to the total share count when a user deposits a tiny amount of USR, a design choice intended to mitigate inflation attacks. However, the wstUSR contract derives the amount of wstUSR tokens to mint by calling the stUSR previewDeposit function and then dividing the result by the same constant offset (ST_USR_SHARES_OFFSET). When an attacker first empties the stUSR pool, deposits a single wei of USR (receiving 1000 shares because of the offset), and subsequently donates a massive amount of USR to inflate the price of a single share to one whole USR, the share price becomes artificially high. Under these conditions, a legitimate user who later tries to wrap a normal amount of USR (for example 500 × 10^18) will have the contract compute the required stUSR shares correctly, but the subsequent division by the offset rounds the result down to zero. Consequently the user receives no wstUSR tokens while the underlying USR has been transferred to the wrapper contract, effectively losing the deposited funds. This attack can be carried out by any malicious participant who can control the majority of shares after the pool has been emptied, and it exploits the fact that the offset is applied inconsistently: it is added during share minting in stUSR but subtracted during share-to-wstUSR conversion, leading to a rounding error that nullifies the minted amount. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful wrap transaction, but the balance of wstUSR would remain unchanged, contradicting the expectation that the deposited USR is represented by an equivalent amount of wrapped tokens. The issue is difficult to spot because the division by a constant may appear harmless and the zero result can be mistaken for a normal outcome when wrapping very small amounts. The root cause is a flawed accounting assumption that the same offset can be used on both sides of the conversion without adjusting for the changed share price. To remediate the problem the wstUSR contract should align its share precision with stUSR, either by removing the division by the offset or by applying a consistent scaling factor that mirrors the stUSR conversion logic, thereby ensuring that the amount of wrapped tokens accurately reflects the underlying USR value even after share price manipulation.

title: In OracleLess.createOrder() fee-
description:
The max value of feeBips should be <=10000. But this validation is missing in createOrder(). All such orders where feeBips is > 10000 will revert in execute() method. A malicious user can create 100s of such orders which never execute even if the price conditions are met. It can use USDC as tokenIn and blacklist itself so that _cancelOrder() also reverts. As _cancelOrder() tries to transfer tokenIn to user. If the receiver is blacklisted user then transfer will fail. This was the malicious user can create 1 wei orders will can neither execute nor cancellable.
ntracts/automatedTrigger/OracleLess.sol#L38C5-L67C6

Missing feeBips input validation in createOrder()

Internal pre-conditions  

External pre-conditions  

Attack Path  
Such orders will exist in the pendingOrderIds which can not be deleted from the queue. These orders can increase the queue size until the max gas usage limit is reached. Which will DoS all other orders.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an input‑validation flaw in the order creation function of the OracleLess contract. The function accepts a parameter called feeBips, which represents the fee expressed in basis points and should never exceed 10000 (the equivalent of a 100 % fee). Because the contract does not enforce this upper bound when an order is created, a user can submit an order with feeBips greater than 10000. The order is stored in the pendingOrderIds queue, but later when the execute() routine attempts to apply the fee it encounters an invalid value and reverts, meaning the order can never be fulfilled even if the market price condition is satisfied. In addition, the cancel routine (_cancelOrder) tries to transfer the tokenIn back to the order creator; if the creator is blacklisted, the transfer also fails and the cancellation reverts. Consequently, a malicious actor can flood the system with many such malformed orders – for example, orders that request only 1 wei of tokenIn – that remain permanently stuck in the queue. Over time the pending order list grows until the block gas limit is reached, effectively denying service to all legitimate orders. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents other users’ trades from being processed and may lock the tokenIn amounts inside the contract, causing users to see balances that never change and orders that never disappear. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that noted the missing feeBips check. It is hard to notice because the createOrder function appears to accept any fee value and the failure only manifests later during execution or cancellation, which may be observed only after many orders have been queued. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked input parameters that lead to stuck state and queue‑bloat. To remediate, the contract should enforce a require statement that feeBips is less than or equal to 10000 at the point of order creation, thereby preventing malformed orders from entering the system and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: A malicious attacker can create
description:
When a user creates an order in the OracleLess contract, he can add a malicious token contract that reverts when tokens are transferred from the OracleLess contract. This order can't be canceled by admin. A malicious attacker can create this kind of order as many as he can to grieve the protocol.  
At OracleLess.sol#L38, there is no restrictions for tokenIn. Any contract that implements IERC20 can be tokenIn.

Internal pre-conditions  
N/A

External pre-conditions  
N/A

Attack Path  
• Alice creates a malicious token contract that reverts if token is transferred from the OracleLess contract.  
• Alice creates orders by using fake token contract.  
• This order can't be cancelable as it reverts at L160.
```solidity
function _cancelOrder(Order memory order) internal returns (bool) {
    //refund tokenIn amountIn to recipient
    order.tokenIn.safeTransfer(order.recipient, order.amountIn);
```

• A malicious attacker can grieve the protocol by making a lot of uncancelable orders.  
• All users of the protocol waste significant gas whenever they fill or cancel orders.
bug_full: The OracleLess contract allows a user to specify any ERC20 token as the input token when creating an order. Because the contract does not enforce a whitelist or any validation on the token address, an attacker can deploy a malicious token contract that deliberately reverts any transfer initiated by the OracleLess contract. When the attacker creates an order using this token, the order appears normal on‑chain, but any attempt to cancel the order triggers the internal _cancelOrder function, which calls safeTransfer to refund the tokenIn amount to the recipient. The malicious token’s transfer function reverts, causing the entire cancellation transaction to revert. As a result the order becomes uncancelable. The same revert can also occur during order execution, forcing users who try to fill the order to spend gas only to see the transaction fail. This behaviour effectively enables a griefing or denial‑of‑service attack: the attacker can flood the order book with many such malicious orders, preventing legitimate participants from cancelling or filling them and causing unnecessary gas consumption for every interaction. The impact is a degradation of protocol usability, potential loss of liquidity, and increased operational costs for users, although the attacker does not directly steal funds. The vulnerability stems from the missing restriction on tokenIn, i.e., the contract trusts that any address implementing the IERC20 interface will behave correctly, which is not guaranteed. It was discovered during a manual audit review of the order creation and cancellation logic, where the lack of token validation was noted and a proof‑of‑concept token that reverts on transfer was considered. The issue can be subtle because the contract compiles and works with standard tokens, and the failure only manifests at runtime when a malicious token is used, making it hard to detect through static analysis alone. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a token whitelist or registry that only permits vetted ERC20 contracts, or it should add defensive coding such as try/catch around token transfers and explicit checks that the token does not revert on standard operations. By ensuring only approved tokens can be used, the protocol restores the ability to cancel and fill orders reliably and prevents attackers from creating uncancelable orders that waste gas and block legitimate activity.

title: authorProfileId can avoid being
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent enforcement of the 24‑hour lock that should be applied to staking and withdrawal actions for a participant whose profile has been accused of misconduct. According to the protocol documentation, once a whistleblower files an accusation, the accused authorProfileId must be prevented from withdrawing any previously staked funds for a period of 24 hours, after which a slashing mechanism can confiscate a portion of those funds. In the current implementation the unvouch function allows the author of a vouch to withdraw the full balance at any time, provided the caller is the address that originally created the vouch. The function checks only that the caller matches the stored authorAddress and that the vouch exists, but it never checks whether the authorProfileId is under a lock or whether actions for that profile have been paused. Because the lock is tied to the profile identifier rather than the address, and because the contract does not query the lock status before processing the withdrawal, an accused participant can simply call unvouch and retrieve the funds before the slashing logic has a chance to execute. This can be exploited by the accused themselves (or a colluding party with access to the author’s address) to empty the vouch balance immediately after an accusation, effectively avoiding any penalty. The impact is that the protocol’s economic deterrent against false claims or unethical behavior is neutralised, leading to potential loss of funds for honest participants, erosion of trust in the slashing mechanism, and an unfair advantage for malicious actors. The issue manifests whenever an accusation is recorded – the expected 24‑hour lock is not enforced, so withdrawals remain possible. All participants who rely on the slashing guarantee, including whistleblowers and token holders, are affected because the system can no longer guarantee that misbehaving profiles will be penalised. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented behaviour with the actual Solidity code and identified the missing lock check as a discrepancy. It may be hard to notice because the unvouch function appears to work correctly in isolation and the lock is not referenced anywhere in the function body, so routine testing that does not simulate an accusation will not reveal the problem. To remediate the issue the contract should retrieve the authorProfileId associated with the caller, verify that actions for that profile are not paused (i.e., the 24‑hour lock is not active), and reject the unvouch call if the lock is in place. This can be achieved by adding a require statement that checks a mapping of locked profiles or by integrating the existing pauseActions mechanism, ensuring that withdrawals respect the intended lock period and that slashing can be applied as designed.

title: Missing slippage protection on
description:
The ReputationMarket contract provides preview functions (simulateBuy() and simulateSell()) to estimate outcomes before actual transactions (buyVotes() and sellVotes()). While buyVotes() includes slippage protection against price changes between simulation and execution, sellVotes() lacks this safeguard. While Base L2's private mempool prevents traditional frontrunning, users are still exposed to two risks:  
1. Market volatility between simulation and execution could result in receiving fewer funds than expected  
2. The sequencer prioritizes transactions with higher fees (ref), allowing users paying higher fees to execute trades first, potentially leading to unfavorable price movements for pending transactions with lower fees.  
sellVotes() is missing slippage protection.

Internal pre-conditions  

External pre-conditions  

Attack Path  
1. User calls simulateSell() to preview expected returns  
2. Market experiences high sell volume, causing price decline  
3. User submits sellVotes() transaction with outdated price expectations  
4. Due to missing slippage protection, transaction executes at significantly lower price than simulated, resulting in unexpected losses

Loss of assets for the affected users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection mechanism in the sell path of the ReputationMarket contract. The contract offers preview functions simulateBuy() and simulateSell() that let users estimate the amount they will receive before committing a transaction. While the buy side (buyVotes()) checks that the execution price has not moved beyond a user‑specified tolerance, the sell side (sellVotes()) does not perform any such verification. The root cause is the absence of a price‑stability guard in the sell execution path, meaning the contract trusts the price at the moment of execution even if the market has moved since the simulation. An attacker, or simply market volatility, can cause the price to drop between the time a user runs simulateSell() and the time the sellVotes() transaction is mined. Because the sequencer on Base L2 orders transactions by fee, a higher‑fee transaction can be placed ahead of the victim’s pending sell, further pushing the price down. When the victim’s sellVotes() finally executes, it uses the stale price from the simulation, resulting in the user receiving fewer tokens or ETH than expected. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful sell but the balance after the transaction is lower than the previewed amount, or the user may see a “0” or unexpectedly small refund. The impact is a loss of assets for any participant who relies on the simulation for budgeting, especially during periods of high volatility or when competing transactions pay higher fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the buy and sell paths and noted the asymmetry in slippage checks. It can be hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds and the contract does not emit an explicit error; only the post‑transaction balance reveals the discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of “stale price execution” or “missing slippage guard” vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that the quoted price at execution matches the quoted price at simulation. The recommended remediation is to add a slippage control to sellVotes() that reverts the transaction if the actual received amount falls below a user‑defined threshold, mirroring the protection already present in buyVotes().

title: Separate calculation of fees in
description:
The separate calculation of fees in applyFees using multiple calls to calcFee causes a higher total fee percentage than expected. This leads to users being overcharged because each fee is calculated independently, rather than as a proportion of the total deposit. As a result, the total effective fee exceeds the intended basis points when multiple fees are applied.  
/main/ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/EthosVouch.sol#L936

In the applyFees function of the EthosVouch contract, the protocol fee, donation fee, and vouchers pool fee are calculated independently using the calcFee function. This results in compounding effects where the combined fees are higher than intended.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. applyFees is called with amount and configured basis points for protocol, donation, and vouchers pool fees.  
2. Each fee (protocol, donation, and vouchers pool) is calculated using calcFee, which computes the fee based on the provided basis points independently of other fees.

External pre-conditions  
1. A user initiates an operation that triggers applyFees, such as buying or selling votes, where multiple fees are involved.  
2. The basis points for each fee (entryProtocolFeeBasisPoints, entryDonationFeeBasisPoints, entryVouchersPoolFeeBasisPoints) are configured with non-zero values.

Attack Path  
1. The user makes a transaction that triggers applyFees (e.g., buying votes).  
2. The protocol calculates multiple fees (protocol, donation, vouchers pool) using calcFee independently.  
3. Due to separate fee calculations, the total effective fee percentage exceeds the sum of the intended basis points, leading to user overcharging.

Affected users are overcharged due to inflated fees. For example: • If entryProtocolFeeBasisPoints = 2000 (20%) and entryDonationFeeBasisPoints = 2500 (25%), the total fee is expected to be 4500 basis points (45%). However, due to independent calculations, the effective fee becomes approximately 5789 basis points (57.89%), as shown in the testFee example.  
The protocol’s reputation and user trust may suffer due to higher-than-expected charges.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑charging bug that arises from the way the contract computes several fees – protocol fee, donation fee and vouchers‑pool fee – separately inside the applyFees routine. Each fee is derived by calling a generic calcFee function with the original deposit amount and its own basis‑point parameter. Because the calculations are performed independently, the percentages are applied to the full amount rather than to the amount that remains after the previous fee, which creates a compounding effect. When a user initiates an operation that triggers applyFees, such as buying or selling votes, and the contract is configured with non‑zero basis points for more than one fee, the sum of the individually calculated fees exceeds the intended total fee. For example, with a 20 % protocol fee and a 25 % donation fee the contract should deduct 45 % of the deposit, but the independent calculations result in roughly 57.9 % being taken. This leads to users receiving less net value than expected, seeing balances drop more than advertised, and potentially losing trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester reproduced the fee logic with a small script and observed the inflated total fee. It is hard to notice because each fee component appears correct in isolation and the UI may still display the configured percentages, masking the higher aggregate deduction. The bug belongs to the class of percentage‑compounding or double‑counting errors where multiple proportional charges are summed incorrectly. To remediate, the contract should first compute the combined fee using the sum of all basis points in a single arithmetic step and then distribute the resulting amount proportionally to the individual recipients, ensuring that the total effective fee matches the advertised sum of basis points.

title: Incorrect Freshness Logic Vali-
description:
The PythOracle contract incorrectly validates the freshness of price data using the getPriceUnsafe() function. The current logic ensures that prices are always considered stale, which results in valid orders failing to execute.  
main/oku-custom-order-types/contracts/oracle/External/PythOracle.sol#L28-L31 is incorrect. The condition ensures that the price is always considered stale, regardless of whether the price is recent or valid. The comparison fails to verify if the price.publishTime is newer than the defined threshold.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. The noOlderThan parameter is set during the function call, defining the allowed freshness window for price data.  
2. A valid price.publishTime is provided by the oracle, but due to incorrect logic, it fails validation.

External pre-conditions  
1. The price feed from the Pyth Oracle contains a valid and fresh publishTime that is newer than block.timestamp - noOlderThan.  
2. No tampering or delays in oracle updates occur externally.

Attack Path  
1. Alice places a stop-limit order for a token pair using the PythOracle as the price feed.  
2. The oracle updates its price feed, providing a fresh price with a publishTime newer than block.timestamp - noOlderThan.  
3. When checkInRange() is called, the require condition in PythOracle.sol:29 evaluates the price as stale, despite it being valid.  
4. The order fails to execute as the system misinterprets the freshness of the price data.

The protocol and its users face the following consequences:

User Losses:  
• Orders fail to execute at the right price, leading to missed opportunities for profit or failure to exit losing positions.  
• This affects users placing stop-loss or take-profit orders reliant on timely price updates.

Protocol Reputation:  
• Continuous failures in executing valid orders due to perceived stale data undermine user trust in the system.
poc:
Example Scenario  
1. Alice places a stop-limit order to sell Token A for Token B if the price of Token A falls below 50.  
2. The oracle updates its price feed with a publishTime of block.timestamp - 5 seconds.  
3. The noOlderThan parameter is set to 30 seconds.

Execution: The condition in PythOracle.sol:29 evaluates:  
```solidity
require(price.publishTime < block.timestamp - noOlderThan, "Stale Price");
```

• With price.publishTime = block.timestamp - 5, the condition becomes: block.timestamp - 5 < block.timestamp - 30  
• This condition is always false, causing the price to be deemed stale.

Result:  
• Alice's stop-limit order does not execute, resulting in financial losses as she misses the opportunity to sell her tokens before the price drops further.
bug_full: An incorrect freshness validation in the PythOracle contract causes every price update to be treated as stale, preventing legitimate orders from executing. The contract’s getPriceUnsafe() function checks the oracle’s publishTime against a freshness threshold using a less‑than comparison (price.publishTime < block.timestamp - noOlderThan). Because the condition is reversed, even when the oracle reports a recent publishTime that is newer than the allowed window, the check evaluates to false and the require statement throws a \"Stale Price\" error. The root cause is a simple logical inequality bug: the contract should verify that the publishTime is greater than or equal to the threshold, not less than it. An attacker does not need to manipulate the oracle; the vulnerability is triggered automatically whenever a user submits a stop‑limit, take‑profit or any order that relies on the Pyth price feed. In the described attack path, Alice places a stop‑limit order, the oracle updates the price with a publishTime only five seconds old, the contract’s check incorrectly flags the price as stale, and the order is rejected. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that the order failed or that the price is stale, and the expected trade never occurs, leading to missed profit or an inability to close a losing position. The impact is limited to missed executions and potential financial loss for users who depend on timely price data, and it can erode confidence in the protocol if many orders repeatedly fail. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the test suite demonstrated that a valid publishTime was incorrectly classified as stale. It can be hard to notice because the require message \"Stale Price\" appears only when the condition is triggered, and developers may assume the inequality is correct without reviewing the logical direction. The bug belongs to the class of time‑based freshness validation errors, often referred to as reversed inequality or off‑by‑one logic bugs, which break accounting assumptions that a price must be recent to be used. The correct fix is to change the require to require(price.publishTime >= block.timestamp - noOlderThan, \"Stale Price\"); so that only truly outdated prices are rejected. After the fix, orders that meet the freshness window will execute as intended, restoring expected behavior and protecting user funds.

title: Order will be executed with wrong
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract determines the direction of a bracket order at the moment the order is created. The direction flag is set by comparing the current exchange rate with the user‑specified take‑profit price, and this flag is never recomputed when the order is later executed. If the market price moves beyond the take‑profit level before the transaction that triggers execution is mined, both the take‑profit and the stop‑price end up on the same side of the current price. In that situation the order becomes immediately executable, but the execution logic treats it as a stop order because the stored direction still indicates the original market orientation. Consequently the contract applies the stop‑slippage parameter instead of the take‑profit slippage. Because stop‑slippage is typically larger (for example 15 % versus a 5 % take‑profit slippage), the user suffers a higher loss than expected. The bug is triggered only when the price moves past the take‑profit threshold between order creation and execution, which can happen naturally in volatile markets or be induced by an attacker who manipulates the price feed. From the user’s perspective the order appears to have been placed with a modest profit target, yet when it is filled the user receives little or no profit and may see a larger-than‑expected deduction from their balance, effectively “money disappears” or “refund calculation error”. The issue is subtle because the direction flag is stored internally and not exposed in the UI, so the order looks valid while the underlying accounting assumptions are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order‑creation logic and the execution path. To remediate the flaw the contract should either recompute the direction at execution time or allow the user to explicitly specify the intended direction, ensuring that the correct slippage parameter is always applied and that take‑profit and stop thresholds remain on opposite sides of the price as intended.

title: User can brick the Bracket con-
bug_full: The vulnerability allows an attacker to permanently disable the swapping functionality of the Bracket contract suite by exploiting the way token allowances are managed. The root cause is the use of an outdated OpenZeppelin SafeERC20.safeApprove implementation, which only permits an approval when the new allowance is zero or the current allowance is zero. Because the performUpkeep function accepts arbitrary transaction data from the caller, an attacker can craft a swap that deliberately approves only amountIn‑1 tokens instead of the full amountIn recorded in the order. After the malicious swap, the target contract consumes amountIn‑1 tokens, leaving a residual allowance of exactly one wei. When the contract later attempts to approve the same token for a new swap, safeApprove sees a non‑zero existing allowance and a non‑zero new value, causing the require statement to revert. This revert blocks every subsequent call to execute for that token, effectively bricking the contract and locking all user funds that rely on that token. The issue manifests when an order is ready for execution and the attacker calls performUpkeep with crafted txData; the contract’s internal accounting updates succeed, but the approval step fails on the next attempt. From a user’s perspective, swap transactions start failing with generic “approval failed” or “transaction reverted” messages, balances remain unchanged, and no refunds are received, giving the impression that funds have disappeared. The bug belongs to the class of allowance‑manipulation or approval‑locking vulnerabilities, where a leftover non‑zero allowance prevents future approvals. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between performUpkeep, execute, and safeApprove. The problem is subtle because the failure occurs only after a specific sequence of calls, making it hard to reproduce without the crafted txData. To remediate, the contract should upgrade to a recent OpenZeppelin version that provides a forceApprove (or safeIncreaseAllowance) pattern, or explicitly reset the allowance to zero before setting a new value, thereby eliminating the non‑zero‑to‑non‑zero restriction and preventing the bricking scenario.

title: Improper `tokenGasPrice` design can overcharge user for the gas cost by a huge margin
poc:
Given:

* `baseGas` = 21000
* `tokenGasPrice` for WBTC = `1 wei`
* `transferFeeAmount` = 0
* 1 WBTC = 20,000 MATIC
* Alice send `0.1 WBTC` to Bob’s address on Polygon
* `Executor` calls `sendFundsToUser()` with `tokenGasPrice` = `1` on Polygon, `totalGasUsed` = `42000` and the gas price is `30G wei`, `Executor` paid `0.00126 MATIC` for gas.

```solidity
uint256 gasFee = 42000 * 1;
...
amountToTransfer = 10000000 - (0 + 42000);
```

3. Bob received 0.09958 WBTC, and paid `0.00042 WBTC` for the gas, the gas fee was overcharged by 6666 times.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract calculates a per‑transaction gas fee in token units using the variable tokenGasPrice. tokenGasPrice is stored as a plain uint256 representing the amount of the token’s smallest unit (wei) that should be charged for one unit of gas, but the calculation does not take the token’s decimal precision into account. When a token with fewer than 18 decimals (for example WBTC with 8 decimals or USDC with 6 decimals) is transferred, a tokenGasPrice value of "1" actually represents a full smallest token unit, which can be worth many orders of magnitude more than the real gas cost on the underlying blockchain. The contract computes gasFee = totalGasUsed * tokenGasPrice and then deducts this fee directly from the amount the user should receive (amountToTransfer = amount - (transferFeeAmount + gasFee)). Because the tokenGasPrice is not scaled by 1e18 or a token‑specific factor, the resulting gasFee can be hundreds or thousands of times larger than the actual gas expense. In the publicly disclosed proof‑of‑concept, an executor sending 0.1 WBTC on Polygon with tokenGasPrice set to 1 wei per gas overcharged the recipient by roughly 6,666 ×, leaving the user with only 0.09958 WBTC instead of the expected 0.1 WBTC. This overcharge occurs every time sendFundsToUser() is called for a low‑decimal token while tokenGasPrice is configured without proper scaling. The affected parties are token holders using the liquidity pool, the protocol that expects to charge fair fees, and any executor that relies on the calculated gasFee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the fee logic and noted the mismatch between token precision and fee arithmetic. It is subtle because the contract emits no explicit warning; the user simply observes a smaller received amount or an unexpected loss of token balance, which may be mistaken for normal rounding or network fees. To remediate, tokenGasPrice should be stored with 18‑decimal precision and the fee calculation should include a division by 1e18 (gasFee = totalGasUsed * tokenGasPrice / 1e18), or alternatively a token‑specific scaling factor should be applied. This ensures that the token fee aligns with the actual gas cost and prevents inadvertent or malicious overcharging, preserving the expected economic behavior of the protocol.

title: `LiquidityFarming.sol` Unbounded for loops can potentially freeze users’ funds in edge cases
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an unbounded iteration in the LiquidityFarming contract’s reward accounting routine. Specifically, the function getUpdatedAccTokenPerShare walks backwards through the rewardRateLog array with a while‑true loop that only terminates when it reaches the first entry. Each call to setRewardPerSecond appends a new element to this log, so when the reward per second value is updated frequently while liquidity providers remain inactive, the log can grow arbitrarily large. When a user finally invokes withdraw, the contract calls _sendRewardsForNft, which triggers updatePool and subsequently getUpdatedAccTokenPerShare. At that point the loop must iterate over every stored entry, and the cumulative gas required can exceed the block gas limit. The transaction then runs out of gas and reverts, preventing the withdrawal from completing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a pending withdrawal, but the transaction fails and the user receives no tokens; balances appear unchanged and funds seem to be “frozen”. The root cause is the reliance on a data‑driven loop without any explicit bound, turning a bookkeeping operation into a potential denial‑of‑service vector. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined control‑flow and gas consumption patterns. It is subtle because the loop appears to have a clear exit condition, yet the exit depends on the size of a mutable on‑chain array, a fact that only manifests under edge‑case usage patterns. The impact is medium severity: assets are not directly stolen, but users may be unable to claim their rewards or principal, harming protocol availability and user confidence. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded for‑loop or gas‑exhaustion vulnerabilities that can lead to contract lock‑up. A conceptual fix is to eliminate the ever‑growing rewardRateLog and store only the current reward‑per‑second value, updating the pool once per change. Alternatively, the loop could be capped or the log pruned periodically. By simplifying the accounting to a constant‑time operation, the contract avoids the gas‑limit breach and restores reliable withdrawal functionality.

title: `WhitelistPeriodManager`: Improper state handling of exclusion removals
description:
[WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L178-L184](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L178-L184)  
[WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L115-L125](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L115-L125)  

The `totalLiquidity` and `totalLiquidityByLp` mappings are not updated when an address is removed from the `isExcludedAddress` mapping. While this affects the enforcement of the cap limits and the `getMaxCommunityLpPositon()` function, the worst impact this has is that the address cannot have liquidity removed / transferred due to subtraction overflow.

In particular, users can be prevented from withdrawing their staked LP tokens from the liquidity farming contract should it become non-excluded.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the WhitelistPeriodManager contract, where the internal accounting of liquidity is decoupled from the management of exclusion status for addresses. Specifically, the contract maintains two mappings—totalLiquidity and totalLiquidityByLp—that track the amount of liquidity each address contributes. When an address is marked as excluded via the isExcludedAddress mapping, the contract does not adjust these liquidity mappings. The root cause is the omission of any state‑update logic in the function that removes an address from the exclusion list; consequently, the liquidity accounting for that address remains unchanged (often zero) after the exclusion flag is cleared. This mismatch becomes exploitable when a user who has previously deposited liquidity while the address was excluded later attempts to withdraw after the owner revokes the exclusion. During the withdrawal, the contract attempts to subtract the user’s balance from totalLiquidityByLp, but because the mapping entry is still zero, the subtraction underflows, triggering a panic (error code 0x11) and reverting the transaction. The immediate impact is that the user’s staked LP tokens become non‑withdrawable, effectively bricking the funds in the farming contract. The issue affects liquidity providers who expect to retrieve their tokens, as well as the protocol’s overall reliability and reputation. It was discovered during a security audit when a test case reproduced the underflow error after toggling the exclusion status. The problem is subtle because exclusion removal is an infrequent operation, and the faulty state is only revealed during a later withdrawal, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate the bug, the contract should either forbid the removal of an exclusion status entirely—ensuring that once an address is excluded it remains so—or it must correctly update the totalLiquidity and totalLiquidityByLp mappings whenever an address’s exclusion flag changes, keeping the accounting consistent with the permission state. This class of bug can be described as improper handling of state transitions for permissioned addresses that leads to arithmetic underflow and loss of withdrawability, violating the fundamental business logic that users should always be able to reclaim their deposited assets.

title: `WhitelistPeriodManager`: Improper state handling of exclusion additions
description:
[WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L178-L184](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L178-L184)  
[WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L83-L99](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/WhitelistPeriodManager.sol#L83-L99)  

The `totalLiquidity` and `totalLiquidityByLp` mappings are not updated when an address is added to the `isExcludedAddress` mapping. This affects the enforcement of the cap limits and the `getMaxCommunityLpPositon()` function, which implicitly assumes that whitelisted addresses will have 0 liquidity, for addresses with non-zero liquidity at the time of addition to the whitelist.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the WhitelistPeriodManager contract’s handling of address exclusion. The contract maintains two mappings – totalLiquidity, which records the aggregate amount of liquidity for each token, and totalLiquidityByLp, which records the per‑address liquidity for each token. When an address is marked as excluded via the isExcludedAddress mapping, the contract does not adjust these liquidity mappings to reflect the removal of the address’s contribution. Consequently, the system continues to count the excluded address’s liquidity when enforcing per‑token caps and when calculating the maximum community liquidity position through getMaxCommunityLpPositon(). This mismatch leads to several adverse effects. First, the function getMaxCommunityLpPositon() returns the full token cap instead of zero for an excluded address that still holds liquidity, violating the assumption that excluded accounts have zero balance. Second, other participants who are not excluded are blocked from adding liquidity because the cap appears fully consumed by the excluded address’s stale balance, causing transactions to revert with ERR__LIQUIDITY_EXCEEDS_PTTC. The issue is triggered whenever an address that already owns LP tokens is added to the exclusion list without first withdrawing its liquidity. Users are affected: a whitelisted (excluded) liquidity provider sees their existing liquidity ignored, while regular users experience failed liquidity provision attempts and see zero available community capacity despite the pool appearing empty. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that simulated exclusion of a provider holding liquidity and observed the deviant behaviour. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the contract’s external interface does not expose the internal liquidity totals, and the returned max community position value appears plausible at a glance. To remediate, the contract should enforce that an address can only be excluded if its LP token balance is zero, or it should actively decrement totalLiquidity and totalLiquidityByLp for that address when exclusion occurs, thereby preserving correct cap accounting. This class of bug is an improper state update or accounting error in access‑control‑driven whitelist logic, where business rules assume a zero‑balance state that the contract fails to enforce, leading to funds effectively disappearing from the perspective of legitimate users and breaking the expected accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: wrong condition checking in price calculation
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L180-L186](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L180-L186)  

The `getTokenPriceInLPShares` function calculates the token price in LP shares, but it checks a wrong condition - if supposed to return `BASE_DIVISOR` if the total reserve is zero, not if the total shares minted is zero. This might leads to a case where the price is calculated incorrectly, or a division by zero is happening.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑calculation routine that converts a base token amount into LP‑share units. The function is intended to return a constant divisor when the pool has no liquidity, but it checks the wrong variable: it returns the constant when the total number of LP shares minted is zero instead of when the total reserve of the base token is zero. Consequently two distinct error cases arise. First, when the pool’s token reserve is zero while some shares have already been minted, the function proceeds to divide the share count by a zero reserve, triggering a division‑by‑zero exception that reverts the transaction. Second, when the reserve is non‑zero but no shares exist, the function incorrectly returns the constant divisor, producing an inaccurate price that deviates from the contract’s economic specification. The bug is a classic case of an incorrect conditional guard leading to wrong arithmetic and a potential runtime error. It can be exploited by external callers that invoke the public view function directly or indirectly through other contract functions such as removeLiquidity and claimFee, which rely on the price calculation for accounting. An attacker could cause a transaction that calls removeLiquidity to revert, effectively preventing a liquidity provider from withdrawing their assets, or could cause fee calculations to be based on a malformed price, resulting in under‑ or over‑payment of fees. The impact is primarily on protocol accounting integrity: users may see their expected refund amount reduced to zero, balances appear unchanged, or fees appear incorrectly calculated, undermining trust in the protocol’s financial logic. The condition fails only in edge cases—when the pool is empty or when a new pool is initialized with zero shares—making it easy to overlook during manual testing because typical usage always involves a non‑zero reserve. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that reviewed contract invariants and discovered a mismatch between the specification (price should be BASE_DIVISOR only when the reserve is empty) and the implemented guard. Fixing the bug requires swapping the condition to examine the reserve amount instead of the share supply, ensuring that the function returns BASE_DIVISOR only when the reserve is zero and otherwise performs a safe division of totalSharesMinted by totalReserve. This adjustment restores correct price calculation, prevents division‑by‑zero reverts, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended economic model.

title: Possible frontrun on deposits on `LiquidityPool`
description:
Rewards are given to a user for depositing either ERC20 tokens or their native token into the LiquidityPool. This reward is used to incentivize users to deposit funds into the liquidity pool when the pool is not in an equilibrium state.

For regular users, this liquidity pool state fluctuates based on the frequency and amount of deposits made to the liquidity pool. If a malicious user can control the state of the liquidity pool before a victim deposits tokens into the liquidity pool, they can gain double rewards.

To gain these double rewards, a malicious user can watch the mempool for transactions that will receive a reward when the deposit occurs. When a malicious user sees that victim deposit, the malicious user can attach a higher fee to their transaction and initiate a deposit. This will allow the malicious user’s transaction to front-run before the victim’s transaction.

Once the malicious user’s deposit is complete, the liquidity pool state will be in a near equilibrium state. Then, the victim’s deposit will occur which causes the liquidity pool state to no longer be in equilibrium.

Finally, the malicious user will make a final deposit gaining yet another reward for bringing the liquidity pool state back to equilibrium.

To sum up, a malicious user can create a sandwich attack where they deposit their own tokens before and after a victim’s transaction. This will allow the malicious user to double dip and gain rewards twice due to victim’s deposit.
poc:
Let’s look at the depositNative function which is the simpler of the two deposit functions.

The key component in the depositNative function is the getRewardAmount which can be found [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L255). The getRewardAmount calculates how much available vs supplied liquidity exists in the liquidity pool. [Here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/main/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L175-L188) there are no time-weighted checks to calculate the available vs. supplied liquidity. With a lack of checks for time-weight and that there are no frontrun checks against deposits, it’s trivial to front-run deposits and control the liquidity of the liquidity such that the reward amount can be double-dipped.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running sandwich attack on the LiquidityPool reward mechanism. The pool distributes a reward each time a user deposits ERC‑20 tokens or the native token, and the reward amount is calculated solely from the instantaneous ratio of available versus supplied liquidity. Because the reward function does not incorporate any time‑weighted averaging, block‑level state snapshot, or checks that prevent multiple deposits from manipulating the same liquidity imbalance, an attacker can observe a victim’s pending deposit in the mempool, submit a higher‑fee deposit that executes first, and then submit a second deposit after the victim’s transaction. By depositing before the victim, the attacker pushes the pool toward equilibrium and collects the first reward. The victim’s deposit then moves the pool away from equilibrium, generating a second reward that the attacker captures with their follow‑up deposit. This double‑dip yields extra reward tokens for the attacker while the victim receives a smaller or no reward than expected. The impact is economic: honest users lose part of the incentive they anticipated, the reward distribution becomes unfair, and the protocol’s intended equilibrium‑restoring incentives are subverted. The issue occurs whenever rewards are computed based only on the current liquidity state without protection against ordering attacks, which is the case for both native and token deposit functions. All participants who rely on the reward, including regular users and liquidity providers, are affected because they may see lower returns or unexpected zero rewards. The problem was uncovered through a manual audit that identified the lack of time‑weighted checks and the absence of any front‑run mitigation in the getRewardAmount logic. Because the reward appears legitimate on‑chain and the loss is only a fraction of a deposit, the flaw can be difficult to notice without tracing transaction ordering. The recommended remediation is to redesign the reward calculation to use a block‑level snapshot or a time‑weighted average of liquidity, to record the pool state at specific timestamps and ensure that a single reward is granted per equilibrium shift, or to adopt an auction‑style distribution that smooths rewards across users, thereby eliminating the incentive for an attacker to manipulate state through sandwich deposits. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent reward front‑running” vulnerabilities, where mutable contract state is used directly to compute economic benefits without ordering safeguards, allowing an adversary to profit by reordering transactions.

title: `sharesToTokenAmount`: Division by zero
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L192](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/db8a1fdddd02e8cc209a4c73ffbb3de210e4a81a/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L192)  

The public `sharesToTokenAmount` function does not check if the denominator `totalSharesMinted[_tokenAddress]` is zero.  
Neither do the callers of this function. The function will revert.  
Calling functions like `getFeeAccumulatedOnNft` and `sharesToTokenAmount` from another contract should never revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the public sharesToTokenAmount function, which converts a holder's share balance into an equivalent token amount by dividing the share quantity by the total number of shares minted for a given token address. The function does not verify whether totalSharesMinted[_tokenAddress] is zero before performing the division. When the protocol has not yet minted any shares for a particular token—such as immediately after deployment or after a complete withdrawal of liquidity—the denominator is zero, causing a division‑by‑zero exception that triggers a revert. This flaw is not mitigated by any of the caller functions, including getFeeAccumulatedOnNft, which forward the call without checking the return value. Consequently, any external contract or off‑chain client that invokes sharesToTokenAmount expecting a numeric result may experience an unexpected transaction failure. From a user's perspective, this manifests as a transaction that simply reverts with no token amount returned, leading to confusing UI messages like "operation failed" or "no balance displayed" despite the user holding shares. The impact stretches beyond the immediate caller; any downstream logic that relies on this conversion—fee calculations, reward distributions, or withdrawal processes—may be halted, potentially freezing funds or preventing legitimate withdrawals. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the lack of a zero‑check was flagged as a runtime error risk. Detecting this problem can be difficult because the function behaves correctly once shares are minted, making the bug invisible under normal operation until the edge case of zero shares is exercised. To remediate, the function should include a guard that returns zero when totalSharesMinted for the token address equals zero, thereby preserving graceful degradation and allowing callers to handle the zero‑balance scenario without a revert. This fix aligns the contract with standard defensive programming practices for arithmetic operations and ensures that the business logic—converting shares to token amounts—remains sound even when no shares exist, preventing unexpected fund‑withdrawal failures and preserving protocol reliability.

title: Liquidity providers unable to remove liquidity when the pool is in deficit state
description:
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L388](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L388)  
[LiquidityProviders.sol#L392](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityProviders.sol#L392)  

LP token holders can not redeem their tokens when the pool is in the deficit state, i.e. `currentLiquidity << providedLiquidity`. This is due to that LP shares are computed based on `providedLiquidity` and the actual available pool balance is based on `currentLiquidity`.
poc:
When a high valued withdrawal happens in the liquidity pool of the destination chain, the current liquidity will be reduced when the executor calls `sendFundsToUser`  
[LiquidityPool.sol#L285](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-biconomy/blob/04751283f85c9fc94fb644ff2b489ec339cd9ffc/contracts/hyphen/LiquidityPool.sol#L285)  

and the pool contract balance will also be reduced by the same amount. The pool reached a deficit state with provided liquidity much bigger than current liquidity.

The LP shares are computed based on the value of `totalReserve` that is roughly equivalent to `totalLiquidity + LpFees`. In a deficit state, `totalReserve` could be much bigger than the available pool balance (up to 90% since max fee is 10%). If the LP token holder wants to redeem his shares,
    
```solidity
_decreaseCurrentLiquidity(_tokenAddress, _amount);
```

will underflow and revert and
    
```solidity
_transferFromLiquidityPool(_tokenAddress, _msgSender(), amountToWithdraw);
```

will revert because there is not enough balance.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability of liquidity providers (LPs) to redeem their LP tokens when a Hyphen liquidity pool enters a deficit condition. The contract records two separate values: `providedLiquidity`, which reflects the amount of liquidity that LPs have deposited, and `currentLiquidity`, which represents the actual balance that remains in the pool after withdrawals and bridging operations. LP shares are calculated using the `providedLiquidity` (or the derived `totalReserve` variable), while the withdrawal function checks the `currentLiquidity` balance before transferring assets. When a large withdrawal on the destination chain reduces `currentLiquidity` significantly, the two figures diverge and `providedLiquidity` may remain much larger than the available pool balance. In this state, the internal call `_decreaseCurrentLiquidity` attempts to subtract the withdrawal amount from `currentLiquidity`. Because the pool no longer holds enough tokens, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts, preventing the LP from receiving any funds. From a user’s perspective, an LP who initiates a redemption expects to receive a proportional amount of the pool’s assets, but instead the transaction fails and the LP tokens remain locked, creating a situation where funds appear to “disappear” or become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the LP redemption path and simulated a scenario where a high‑value withdrawal caused the pool’s liquidity to drop below the recorded provisioned amount. The bug is subtle because the contract logic does not visibly restrict redemption; the failure only surfaces under the specific condition where `currentLiquidity` is substantially lower than `providedLiquidity`. The impact is medium severity: LPs cannot withdraw during a deficit, which may erode confidence in the protocol and freeze capital until the pool is rebalanced, either by external incentives or additional deposits. The root cause is the decoupling of the accounting of deposited liquidity from the actual pool balance without a corresponding safeguard during redemption. To remediate the issue, the protocol should align the share calculation with the real, current balance, introduce a guard that disallows redemption when `currentLiquidity` is insufficient, allow partial withdrawals proportional to the available balance, or redesign the accounting model so that `providedLiquidity` tracks only the amount that can be safely reclaimed. Such changes would restore the expected behavior that LPs can always redeem a fair share of the pool’s assets, preserving the accounting invariants and preventing funds from becoming locked.

title: Malicious User can Poison
description:
The missing check for blacklisted accounts when creating orders allows users to specify a blacklisted account as the recipient of an easily executable order to freeze execution of the orderbook. This will also prevent the order from being canceled by the admin, since the cancelOrder function attempts to send tokens to the order.recipient, which is blacklisted. This can be used to fill up the arrays which contain pendingOrders, which will eventually DOS the protocol when the maxPendingOrders is reached.
The protocol expects to use tokens with blacklists, and allows users to specify the recipient address where tokens will be sent without properly validation if transferring tokens is possible to the recipient address.
Bracket.sol:procureTokens uniquely uses msg.sender to take the tokens from:
337c5cfdbd6/oku-custom-order-types/contracts/automatedTrigger/Bracket.sol#L362
C1-L368C15
This allows a non-blacklisted address to create and pay for an order for a blacklisted account. This then becomes uncancelable due to the Bracket.sol:_cancelOrder function attempting to return these tokens to the order.recipient:
337c5cfdbd6/oku-custom-order-types/contracts/automatedTrigger/Bracket.sol#L510
C1-L511C77
Internal pre-conditions
1. A token with a blacklist is added to the protocol.
External pre-conditions
1. The token must have a blacklist.
Attack Path
1. The attacker calls createOrder in Bracket.sol with the recipient field set to a blacklisted address for a token pair added to the protocol as cheaply as possible.
2. The attacker repeats this until the pendingOrderIds array is full of uncancelable orders.
This will cause a DOS to the protocol when the pendingOrderIds reaches maxPendingOrders:
337c5cfdbd6/oku-custom-order-types/contracts/automatedTrigger/Bracket.sol#L462
C1-L465C11
This will also cause the ArrayMutation:removeFromArray to explode in gas costs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the recipient address when creating an order for a token that implements a blacklist. Because the contract does not check whether the specified recipient is blacklisted, a malicious user can supply a blacklisted address as the order recipient. The order creation succeeds, but later when the protocol or an admin attempts to cancel the order, the cancel function tries to transfer the locked tokens back to the blacklisted recipient. The token’s blacklist logic rejects the transfer, causing the cancel transaction to revert. As a result the order remains in the pendingOrders array and cannot be removed. By repeatedly creating such orders the attacker can fill the pendingOrders array up to the configured maxPendingOrders limit, effectively denying service to all legitimate users. The denial‑of‑service manifests as the orderbook stopping, new orders being rejected, and gas costs for array mutation exploding. The issue occurs only when a token with a blacklist feature is registered in the protocol and the createOrder function is called with a blacklisted recipient. All participants that rely on the orderbook – users placing trades, the protocol admin trying to manage orders, and any downstream contracts – are affected because their funds become locked and the protocol becomes unavailable. The flaw was discovered during an audit when a test case created an order with a known blacklisted address and the subsequent adminCancelOrder call reverted with the token’s “Blacklistable: account is blacklisted” error. The problem is subtle because order creation appears successful and the failure only surfaces on cancellation, making it easy to overlook during normal operation. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the recipient address is not blacklisted for any token that supports blacklisting before accepting the order, and should handle cancellation in a way that does not rely on transferring tokens to a blacklisted address, such as reverting the creation or redirecting the refund to a safe address.

title: Create order can be DOSed as
description:
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
Assume that:
• maxPendingOrders is set to 25, which is similar to the value configured in the test script
• minOrderSize is set to 10 USD, which is similar to the value configured in the test script
Bob (malicious user) can spend 250 USD to create 25 orders, which will cause the number of pending orders to reach the maxPendingOrders (25) limit. For each of the orders Bob created, he intentionally configured the order in a way that it will always never be in range. For instance, setting the takeProfit, stopPrice, and/or stopLimitPrice to uint256.max - 1. In this case, no one can fill his orders.
The protocol admin can attempt to delete Bob's order by calling adminCancelOrder function to remove Bob's order from the pendingOrderIds to reduce the size. When Bob's order is canceled, the 10 USD worth of assets will be refunded back to Bob.
The issue is that this protocol is intended to be deployed on Optimism as per the Contest’s README where the gas fee is extremely cheap. Thus, Bob can simply use the refunded 10 USD worth of assets and create a new order again.
Thus, whenever the admin cancels Bob's order, he can always re-create a new one again. As a result, whenever innocent users attempt to create an order, it will always revert with a "Max Order Count Reached" error.
ntracts/automatedTrigger/Bracket.sol#L444
File: Bracket.sol
444:
function _createOrder(
..SNIP..
462:
require(
    pendingOrderIds.length < MASTER.maxPendingOrders(),
    "Max Order Count Reached"
);
ntracts/automatedTrigger/StopLimit.sol#L300
File: StopLimit.sol
300:
function _createOrder(
..SNIP..
320:
require(
    pendingOrderIds.length < MASTER.maxPendingOrders(),
    "Max Order Count Reached"
);
Medium. DOS and broken functionality. This DOS can be repeated infinitely, and the cost of attack is low.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that arises when the contract enforces a hard limit on the number of pending orders (maxPendingOrders) without imposing any economic cost or validation on the orders themselves. An attacker can spend a small amount of capital—equal to the minimum order size—to create the maximum allowed number of orders, each deliberately configured with parameters (such as takeProfit, stopPrice or stopLimitPrice set to uint256.max‑1) that make the order impossible to be matched by any market price. Because the contract only checks that the pending order count is below the configured limit before accepting a new order, these unfillable orders are accepted and occupy all available slots. When the protocol admin later cancels one of the attacker’s orders, the contract refunds the full order value to the attacker, who can then immediately recreate another unfillable order, repeating the cycle indefinitely. This loop keeps the pending order count at the maximum, causing any legitimate user who attempts to create a new order to hit the require statement that enforces pendingOrderIds.length < maxPendingOrders and receive the error “Max Order Count Reached”. From the user’s perspective the UI will show no available slots for new orders, transactions revert unexpectedly, and funds that should be usable for trading appear to be locked out. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the order‑creation logic and identified that the only gating condition is a simple length check, with no fee, no order‑validity verification, and no protection against rapid re‑creation after cancellation. The problem is hard to notice because the orders appear syntactically correct and the contract behaves as coded; however, the business logic that assumes pending orders will eventually be filled is violated, breaking the accounting assumption that pending slots represent actionable trades. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a cost for order creation or cancellation (e.g., a non‑refundable fee), enforce that newly created orders are within a realistic price range, limit the frequency of order re‑creation after a cancellation, or increase the maxPendingOrders threshold combined with anti‑spam measures such as rate‑limiting or stake‑based ordering. These changes would make it economically infeasible for an attacker to repeatedly fill the order pool with unfillable orders and restore normal functionality for honest users.

title: StopLimit order cannot be filled
description:
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
Assume that the MASTER.checkMinOrderSize is 100 USD. Assume that the current USDC price is 1.1 USD per USDC.
Bob creates a StopLimit order with order.tokenIn = USDC, order.amountIn = 100e6 (100 USDC), and order.stopLimitPrice = 100 USD. During the order creation, the MASTER.checkMinOrderSize function will be executed and the total USD value is 110 USD (100 USDC * 1.1 USD). Thus, the check will pass as it is over the minimum size of 100 USD.
ntracts/automatedTrigger/AutomationMaster.sol#L144
File: AutomationMaster.sol
142:

Medium. Loss of core functionality under certain conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the minimum order size validation that prevents a StopLimit order from ever being executed once market conditions change. When a user creates a StopLimit order, the contract checks that the USD value of the supplied token amount exceeds a configured threshold (for example 100 USD). This check uses the token price at the moment of order creation, so an order of 100 USDC is accepted when the price is 1.1 USD per USDC because the calculated value is 110 USD, which satisfies the requirement. Later, when the price of USDC falls to 0.9 USD, the StopLimit order becomes eligible for execution. The automation contract calls performUpkeep, which attempts to fill the order by creating a new Bracket order that carries the same token amount. The Bracket contract repeats the same minimum‑size verification using the current price (0.9 USD), resulting in a calculated value of only 90 USD. Because this is below the minimum threshold, the internal check reverts the transaction, causing the whole fill operation to fail. Consequently, the user’s StopLimit order remains unfilled, the funds stay locked in the contract, and the expected trade never occurs. The issue manifests only when the token price moves enough to make the original USD value drop below the minimum after the order has been created, which is a realistic market scenario. It affects any participant who relies on StopLimit orders for automated trading, potentially leading to loss of expected execution and locked capital. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the execution flow from the StopLimit contract into the Bracket contract and noticed the duplicated size check. It can be hard to spot because the initial validation succeeds, giving a false sense of safety, and the failure only appears later under specific price movements. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent business‑logic validation” where the same rule is applied at different stages with differing state, causing functional regressions. From a user perspective the UI would show the order as “ready to execute” but after the price trigger the transaction reverts, leaving the user with a message like “order not in range” or simply no fill, and the balance of the token appears unchanged despite the expectation of a trade. To remediate, the contract should either skip the minimum‑size check when the Bracket order is created as part of a StopLimit fill, or redesign the validation to reference the original order’s USD value rather than the current market price, ensuring that an order that passed the initial check can still be executed later.

title: cancelOrder order can be DOSed
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded linear scan over the contract's pendingOrderIds array inside the internal _cancelOrder routine. The function iterates from index zero to the length of the array looking for a matching order identifier, then removes the entry and attempts to refund the tokenIn amount to the order recipient. Because the array can grow without a hard limit, an attacker can create a very large number of orders – in the reported proof‑of‑concept 20,800 orders were sufficient – and deliberately cause the token transfer to revert. When a legitimate user or the protocol admin later calls cancelOrder, the loop must traverse the entire oversized array, consuming more gas than the block gas limit or making the transaction extremely expensive (hundreds of millions of gas, roughly $150 at current rates). The result is a denial‑of‑service condition: the cancel operation fails or becomes prohibitively costly, preventing any further cancellation of pending orders. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a failed cancel, no refund is received, and the order remains stuck in a pending state, contrary to the expectation that a cancel request would instantly release the deposited tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that measured gas consumption before and after the attack. It is hard to notice because the array grows gradually and normal cancellations appear cheap; only after the array reaches a large size does the gas cost explode, which may be overlooked in routine testing. The root cause is the reliance on a linear search over a mutable array for order lookup, a classic example of a gas‑exhaustion denial‑of‑service bug. To remediate, the contract should avoid iterating over an unbounded list. A common fix is to store orders in a mapping keyed by orderId, or to maintain a separate index that allows O(1) removal, or to impose a strict cap on the number of pending orders and provide a batch‑clear mechanism. By eliminating the need to scan the entire array, the protocol restores the ability for users and admins to cancel orders reliably and prevents the ransomware‑style exploitation where an attacker forces the protocol to pay excessive gas fees.

title: Malicious users can createOrder
description:
Malicious users can createOrder with 0 amount and can cause DOS / block users to fillOrder, cancelOrder
Malicious users will create huge numbers of orders with 0 amountIn.
Now if anyone wants to fillOrder or cancelOrder they can not do it because:
