• Due to the block gas limit, there is a clear limitation in the amount of operation that can be handled in an Array.
• ArrayMutation::removeFromArray is called on fillOrder, cancelOrder functions.
• Now because the malicious users have created a huge amount of orders with 0 amount,
• When normal users go to fillOrder or cancelOrder they simply run out of gas while iterating a huge array of pendingOrderIds.
• This makes them and every one impossible to do any further action on fillOrder, cancelOrder
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises because the contract’s createOrder function does not enforce a minimum input amount. An attacker can call createOrder with amountIn set to zero, which the contract accepts and stores as a normal order. Each zero‑amount order is added to the pendingOrderIds array, which is later traversed by the fillOrder and cancelOrder functions using a linear iteration and the ArrayMutation::removeFromArray helper. Because the array can grow without bound, a malicious user can flood the contract with a huge number of zero‑amount orders. When a legitimate user later attempts to fill or cancel an order, the function must iterate over the entire pendingOrderIds array; the gas required to process the massive list exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. From the user’s perspective, attempts to fill or cancel orders simply fail with an out‑of‑gas error, the UI may show “transaction failed” or “insufficient gas”, and the expected outcome of a successful trade never occurs. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who observed that the createOrder function lacks any validation on amountIn and that the order‑management functions rely on unbounded array iteration. The problem is hard to notice because zero‑amount orders appear syntactically valid and the out‑of‑gas failure looks like a generic blockchain limitation rather than a logical flaw. The impact is that normal participants are unable to execute trades or cancel their orders, effectively freezing the market and undermining confidence in the protocol. The affected parties include all users who rely on the order‑matching functionality, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s overall reliability. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a positive amountIn check (for example require(amountIn > 0) or a call to a minimum‑order‑size validator) and consider redesigning order storage to avoid linear scans over an ever‑growing array, such as using mappings, pagination, or bounded data structures. By preventing zero‑amount orders and limiting the size of data structures that must be iterated, the denial‑of‑service vector is eliminated and the protocol’s business logic—matching deposits with withdrawals—remains sound.

title: Attacker can revoke any user
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized revocation flaw in the market stakeholder management logic. The contract provides a function that allows a lender or other stakeholder to be removed from a market via a delegated revocation call. The implementation does not verify that the caller is the market owner or an authorized attestor before forwarding the revocation request to the external attestation service. Because the access control check is missing, any address can invoke the public revoke entry point and supply arbitrary parameters, causing the contract to generate a revocation identifier and instruct the attestation contract to revoke the target stakeholder. This can be exploited by an attacker who simply calls the revoke function with the address of any participant and the identifier of any market. The attestation contract will accept the request and mark the supplied stakeholder as revoked, effectively removing their rights to lend, borrow, or receive rewards in that market. The impact is that the targeted user loses all permissions in the affected market, potentially rendering the market unusable if critical participants are removed, and may lead to loss of access to deposited funds or inability to claim accrued interest. The condition for exploitation is that the market’s attestation mechanism is enabled, which is the normal operating mode, and no additional signatures or approvals are required beyond the parameters passed by the attacker. All users of the market, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself, are affected because the revocation can be performed arbitrarily. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the delegation path and noticed the absence of any require statements checking msg.sender or role permissions before calling the external revocation function. Because the function appears to be internal and the call chain is indirect, the missing check can be easy to overlook, especially when the surrounding code performs other verification steps that give a false sense of safety. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict access control, ensuring that only the market owner, a designated admin, or a holder of a valid attestation signature can invoke the revocation flow, and it should validate that the supplied stakeholder address matches the intended target. Adding a require statement that checks the caller’s role or that the attestation signature originates from an authorized entity will close the attack vector. This class of bug is commonly known as an unauthorized function call or missing access control that leads to privilege escalation and denial‑of‑service for legitimate participants.

title: Not updating state before mak-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw caused by updating the loan repayment state after an external call to a user‑controlled repayment listener. The contract follows a pattern where it first transfers or escrows the repayment funds and then invokes ILoanRepaymentListener.repayLoanCallback with a fixed gas stipend. Only after this callback returns does the contract update the internal mappings that record the total repaid principal, interest and the timestamp of the last repayment. Because the external call is executed before the contract’s internal state reflects the repayment, a malicious listener can re‑enter the TellerV2 contract during the callback and call lenderCloseLoan, which is allowed when the loan is in default. By doing so the attacker can seize the borrower’s collateral even though the borrower has just made a repayment. The attack works only when the loan’s defaultTimestamp has passed (the loan is considered defaulted) and the borrower initiates a repayment. Under these conditions the borrower expects the repayment amount to be credited and the collateral to remain untouched, but the re‑entrancy allows the lender to capture both the repayment amount and the collateral, effectively causing the borrower to lose all remaining assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state changes and external calls in the _repayLoan and _sendOrEscrowFunds functions. It is hard to notice because the external call is wrapped in a try/catch block and limited to 80000 gas, which suppresses errors and gives the impression that the call is safe. Moreover, the contract does not use a re‑entrancy guard or the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, so the unsafe ordering can be overlooked. This bug belongs to the class of re‑entrancy vulnerabilities where effects (state updates) are performed after interactions (external calls). From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after a repayment the borrower’s balance shows the repayment amount deducted, yet the collateral is also taken, resulting in an unexpected zero or reduced balance. The business logic that repayment should only affect the loan’s accounting is violated, breaking the accounting invariants of the protocol. The recommended remediation is to move all state updates that record the repayment before the external callback, or to employ a re‑entrancy guard and follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, ensuring that no external call can manipulate the contract’s state before it is safely recorded.

title: Repayer can brick lending func-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsigned integer underflow in the accounting of outstanding principal tokens within a lending pool. The contract calculates the amount of principal still owed by subtracting the total amount repaid from the total amount originally lent (totalPrincipalTokensLended - totalPrincipalTokensRepaid). Because the subtraction is performed without any safety check, an attacker can trigger a situation where the repaid amount exceeds the amount originally lent. The repayment function allows the caller to specify any amount greater than the minimum required, so a borrower can deliberately over‑repay a loan. When the over‑repayment occurs, totalPrincipalTokensRepaid becomes larger than totalPrincipalTokensLended, causing the subtraction to underflow to a very large uint256 value. This underflow is detected by the EVM and makes the subsequent call to getTotalPrincipalTokensOutstandingInActiveLoans revert, which is executed before every new lending operation. As a result, the lending functionality becomes permanently blocked – new loans cannot be created and the pool cannot accept further deposits, effectively “bricking” the protocol’s core feature. The impact is that borrowers are unable to obtain new credit, lenders cannot place new funds, and the protocol’s business logic that assumes repayments never exceed the principal is violated. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the repayment flow and noticed that the contract does not cap the repayment amount nor guard the subtraction. It is hard to notice because the underflow only manifests after a specific sequence of actions (borrow, then over‑repay) and does not appear in normal operation where repayments match the outstanding principal. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a transaction failure when trying to borrow after the over‑repayment, or a loan that appears to be stuck with no outstanding balance despite having repaid more than borrowed. The expected behavior is that the pool continues to lend after repayments, but the reality is that the pool reverts and funds become inaccessible for new lending. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow vulnerabilities caused by unchecked subtraction in financial accounting code. The recommended mitigation is to enforce that the repayment amount cannot exceed the outstanding principal, or to clamp the result of the subtraction to zero (e.g., return 0 when totalPrincipalTokensRepaid > totalPrincipalTokensLended) and to use safe arithmetic checks such as require statements or Solidity’s built‑in overflow protection.

title: Bracket and StopLimit contracts
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the order creation logic of the Bracket and StopLimit contracts, where the address that should receive the refunded token (order.recipient) is not validated and can be set to the zero address. When an admin attempts to cancel an order, the contract calls safeTransfer to send the tokenIn amount back to the recorded recipient. For USDT, the ERC20 implementation explicitly rejects transfers to address(0) by requiring the recipient to be non‑zero, causing the cancellation transaction to revert. Because the cancellation reverts, the admin cannot remove the order from the pendingOrderIds array. An attacker can repeatedly create orders with recipient set to address(0) and tokenIn equal to USDT, filling the pending order list until it reaches the maximum size defined in AutomationMaster. Once the limit is reached, the only available action for the admin is to increase the maxPendingOrders value, which can be done repeatedly until the array becomes so large that iterating over it exceeds the block gas limit, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service condition for the Bracket and StopLimit contracts. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept orders normally, but later legitimate users see that new orders cannot be placed because the system is stuck, and no refunds are returned for the blocked orders. The impact is a loss of ability to cancel orders, locked funds for the affected orders, and a potential complete halt of order processing for the affected contracts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the cancellation path and identified the missing recipient validation. It is hard to notice because zero address is a technically valid value in Solidity and many contracts do not explicitly guard against it; the failure only surfaces when the cancel function interacts with a token that enforces a non‑zero recipient check. The proper remediation is to enforce that order.recipient is never address(0) at order creation, or to add a special‑case handling in the cancellation routine that avoids calling safeTransfer when the recipient is zero, thereby ensuring that orders remain cancellable and the pending order array can be managed within the intended gas limits.

title: The totalPrincipalTokensRep aid and totalInterestCollected may not be updated even when funds are already transferred Source: Found by KupiaSec
poc: none
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan repayment accounting path of the Lender Commitment Group. When the contract is paused, the internal callback that records the repaid principal and interest is protected by a pause modifier, causing it to revert. The caller invokes this callback inside a try/catch block and deliberately ignores any revert. As a result, the external transfer of repayment funds succeeds, but the state variables that track totalPrincipalTokensRepaid and totalInterestCollected are never updated. Because the exchange rate for lenders is derived from these cumulative totals, the stale values cause the rate to be calculated on a lower denominator, effectively diluting the value of existing shares. The bug can be triggered by any borrower who repays a loan while the protocol is paused; the transaction will appear successful from the borrower’s perspective, but the protocol’s accounting will be out of sync. Shareholders may later notice that their token balances are worth less than expected or that the protocol reports an incorrect exchange rate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the pause modifiers and the surrounding try/catch logic. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert, so standard testing that only checks for successful execution will not reveal the missing accounting update. The proper fix is to allow the repayment callback to execute even when the contract is paused, or to move the pause protection to the outer function while ensuring that accounting updates are performed regardless of the pause state. In general, this is a class of state‑update‑omission after silent failure bugs, where a silent catch hides a revert that prevents critical state changes, leading to inconsistent on‑chain accounting and potential financial loss.

title: EMI calculation is flawed
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) repayment amount in the loan contract. The code uses a Math.min operation to cap the amount owed for a payment cycle, assuming that the owed amount should never exceed the predefined paymentCycleAmount plus accrued interest. This assumption is wrong for EMI loans because the amount due after multiple cycles should grow proportionally with time (paymentCycleAmount * owedTime / paymentCycleDuration). By taking the minimum, the contract often selects the smaller value – the fixed paymentCycleAmount plus interest – instead of the larger, ratio‑wise amount that reflects the elapsed periods. The root cause is a logical error in the financial formula: the min function is applied where a direct proportional calculation is required. An attacker, typically the borrower, can exploit this by waiting for several payment cycles before calling the repayment function. The contract will compute a lower owed amount, accept a smaller payment, and record the loan as partially repaid, leaving the lender with less principal and interest than the schedule dictates. The impact is a systematic under‑payment that reduces revenue for lenders, distorts accounting, and can eventually lead to protocol insolvency if many borrowers exploit the flaw. The condition for the bug to manifest is any EMI‑type repayment that occurs after more than one payment cycle and when the contract is not in the final payment cycle. All participants in the lending protocol are affected: borrowers can pay less than required, while lenders and the protocol lose expected funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed the min usage while reviewing the V2Calculations.sol file. It is hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, no revert occurs, and the UI may simply display the lower amount as the amount due, giving the impression that the contract is functioning correctly. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after two months a borrower sees a repayment amount of 10.84 units instead of the expected 17.68 units, and the lender observes that the loan balance does not decrease as anticipated. This bug belongs to the class of financial‑logic errors where an inappropriate bounding operation (min) truncates a formula, leading to under‑payment or rounding issues. To remediate, the min should be removed and the owed amount should be calculated solely as ((_bid.terms.paymentCycleAmount * owedTime) / _paymentCycleDuration), optionally adding the correct interest component afterwards. This restores the intended linear accumulation of EMI payments and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business rules of amortized loans.

title: ERC20.approve Used Instead of
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s use of the standard ERC20.approve function to grant the TELLER_V2 contract permission to transfer the loan principal. The code calls principalToken.approve(address(TELLER_V2), _principalAmount) without any safety wrapper or return‑value handling. While the ERC20 specification states that approve should return a boolean, several widely deployed tokens such as USDT and USDC on Ethereum Mainnet, Polygon, Arbitrum and Base deviate from the standard and do not return a value. When the contract invokes approve on these non‑standard tokens, the call reverts because the expected return data is missing. This root‑cause – an assumption that all ERC20 tokens behave identically – leads to a denial‑of‑service failure: any loan bid that tries to use USDT, USDC or similar stablecoins cannot be accepted, causing the acceptFundsForAcceptBid function to abort before any funds are transferred. From a user’s perspective the borrower initiates a loan, the UI may indicate that the “BorrowerAcceptedFunds” event was emitted, yet the transaction fails and no principal is disbursed, leaving the borrower with an unchanged balance and the lender with no loan issued. The impact is that the protocol becomes unusable for a large class of mainstream tokens, effectively blocking access to stablecoin liquidity and breaking the intended lending workflow. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token interaction patterns and identified that the contract uses a plain approve call instead of a safeApprove utility that can handle tokens with non‑standard return behavior. Because the failure occurs at the token‑approval step, it can be subtle: the transaction simply reverts without a clear error message, making it hard for developers or users to pinpoint the cause. The bug belongs to the broader class of ERC20 non‑compliant token handling errors, where contracts assume strict adherence to the ERC20 interface. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct approve call with a safeApprove pattern (for example, using OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library) that checks for both boolean returns and the absence of return data, and include proper error handling to prevent the entire loan acceptance flow from failing when interacting with non‑standard tokens.

title: Users can lower the interest rate by dividing a loan into multiple smaller loans Source: The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by KupiaSec
poc: none
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑rate manipulation bug in the loan‑interest calculation logic. The function that returns the minimum APR adds a term that is proportional to the pool utilization ratio, and the utilization ratio is computed by adding the amount being borrowed (activeLoansAmountDelta) directly to the current outstanding principal. Because the calculation uses the end value of the delta instead of an average or midpoint, a borrower can artificially lower the utilization ratio by requesting the same total amount in several smaller increments. By splitting a $10,000 loan into ten $1,000 loans, the borrower experiences APRs that start at 2.4 % and rise to 6 %, with an average of about 4.2 %, instead of the 6 % that would be applied if the loan were taken in a single request. The root cause is the use of the full delta in the utilization formula, which makes the APR a decreasing function of the number of sub‑loans. The exploit can be carried out by any user who can issue multiple loan requests before the protocol updates the pool state, and it requires no special permissions. The impact is a loss of expected interest revenue for the protocol and for other lenders, creating an unfair advantage for the attacker while the protocol appears to function correctly for each individual loan. The condition for the bug to manifest is a non‑zero pool total estimated value and a positive interest‑rate range; the calculation is performed on‑chain each time a loan is taken, so the manipulation is invisible to external observers unless the aggregate borrowing pattern is examined. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by KupiaSec and reported by Sherlock. It is hard to notice because each loan’s APR matches the formula and therefore looks legitimate; only the cumulative effect reveals the discrepancy. To fix the problem the utilization ratio should be calculated using a middle value of the delta (for example, (activeLoansAmountDelta + 1)/2) or by basing the APR on the total borrowed amount after all sub‑loans are accounted for, thereby preventing the rate from being reduced by loan splitting. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of economic‑logic manipulation where on‑chain formulas depend on mutable input in a way that can be gamed by partitioning actions. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a borrower receives a lower interest rate than expected, while lenders see their returns shrink, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that interest scales linearly with utilization.

title: Tokens that revert of zero value
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s liquidation routine that invokes ERC20 safeTransferFrom calls with a calculated amount that can become zero. Some ERC20 implementations revert when the transfer amount is zero, even though the call is syntactically correct. Because the code does not verify that the amount to transfer is non‑zero before invoking safeTransferFrom, a liquidation where the computed amountDue minus tokensToGiveToSender equals zero triggers a revert. The revert aborts the transaction before the internal accounting variables tokenDifferenceFromLiquidations and totalPrincipalTokensRepaid are updated. As a result, the protocol’s accounting state diverges from reality: the share balance of the liquidated position remains unchanged while the internal share accounting assumes a successful settlement at a zero price, effectively inflating the reported share value. This condition can be reproduced when rounding or liquidation logic produces a zero net token transfer, for example when tokensToGiveToSender equals the full amountDue. Users attempting to liquidate experience a transaction failure with no token movement, yet the protocol may later display an incorrect higher share balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the liquidation flow and identified missing zero‑value checks. It is subtle because zero‑value transfers are often assumed to be no‑ops, but the heterogeneous behavior of ERC20 tokens makes this assumption unsafe. The recommended mitigation is to guard each safeTransferFrom with a condition that the amount is greater than zero, or to restructure the liquidation logic so that zero‑value transfers are simply omitted. By ensuring that only positive amounts are transferred, the contract avoids unexpected reverts and maintains correct accounting, preserving the expected invariant that liquidations either fully settle or leave the state unchanged without hidden inflation of share values.

title: Users may not withdraw their funds
description:
Malicious users can manipulate the tranche share's price. They can burn more strategy tokens than expected. This will cause other users cannot withdraw their funds.
In IdleCDOEpochVariant:requestWithdraw, users can request withdraw their funds. The withdraw underlying token amount will be calculated according to the current tranche share's price.
In function requestWithdraw(), we will burn the related strategy share according to the underlying token amount. The problem is that when we increase tranche share's price via donation, we can burn more strategy tokens than expected. This will cause left users cannot withdraw funds because the strategy share is not enough.
For example:
1. Empty market.
2. Alice deposits 2000 DAI.
3. Bob deposits 2000 DAI.
4. Pass one epoch.
5. Alice donates 3000 DAI.
6. Alice requests withdraw her tranche share(2000*1e18).
7. Alice will get back 3500 DAI. The left strategy share is around 500*1e18.
8. Bob can only get back around 500 DAI.
```solidity
function requestWithdraw(uint256 _amount, address _tranche) external returns (uint256) {
    ...
    uint256 _underlyings = _amount * _tranchePrice(_tranche) / ONE_TRANCHE_TOKEN;
    ...
    creditVault.requestWithdraw(_underlyings, msg.sender, netInterest);
}
```
```solidity
function requestWithdraw(uint256 _amount, address _user, uint256 _netInterest) external {
    _onlyIdleCDO();
    _burn(msg.sender, _amount - _netInterest);
    _mint(_user, _amount);
    withdrawsRequests[_user] += _amount;
    pendingWithdraws += _amount;
    lastWithdrawRequest[_user] = epochNumber;
}
```
Internal Pre-conditions
N/A
External Pre-conditions
Empty market
Attack Path
1. Empty market.
2. Alice deposits 2000 DAI.
3. Bob deposits 2000 DAI.
4. Pass one epoch.
5. Alice donates 3000 DAI.
6. Alice requests withdraw her tranche share(2000*1e18).
7. Alice will get back 3500 DAI. The left strategy share is around 500*1e18.
8. Bob can only get back around 500 DAI.
In this attack vector, the attacker cannot earn some profits. But we still take this as one grief attack. Because of this grief attack, the Bob fails to withdraw his expected underlying token.
Users may fail to request withdraw, will lose their funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a withdrawal denial caused by the ability of a malicious participant to manipulate the price of a tranche share through a donation, which leads the contract to burn more strategy tokens than correspond to the underlying amount being withdrawn. The root cause lies in the requestWithdraw function that computes the amount of underlying tokens to return by multiplying the requested tranche amount by the current tranche price, and then calls the credit vault to burn the equivalent number of strategy tokens. When a donor inflates the tranche price by sending extra underlying tokens directly to the epoch contract, the price rises, so the same tranche amount translates into a larger underlying amount. The subsequent burn operation therefore consumes a larger portion of the strategy token balance than intended, leaving an insufficient pool for subsequent withdraw requests. An attacker can exploit this by first creating a market with only their own deposits, advancing an epoch, donating a large amount of underlying tokens to raise the tranche price, and then withdrawing their own tranche share. The attacker receives a higher payout, while the remaining strategy token balance is depleted, causing other users who later request withdrawal to receive only a fraction of their expected funds or nothing at all. This situation manifests to honest users as a failed withdrawal: they submit a request for the full amount they deposited, but the contract returns a much smaller amount, sometimes zero, and their wallet balance appears unexpectedly reduced. The issue occurs only when the market is initially empty or has low liquidity, an epoch has passed, and the contract permits direct donations that affect the tranche price. It affects all participants of the Idle CDO protocol who rely on the credit vault to redeem their underlying assets, effectively locking or reducing access to their funds. The problem was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that simulated the described steps and observed the imbalance of strategy tokens after the attacker’s withdrawal. The bug is subtle because the donation operation is a legitimate feature and the price increase is not obviously malicious; only after a second user attempts to withdraw does the shortage become apparent. To remediate the issue, the protocol should decouple the withdrawal calculation from a mutable tranche price, enforce that donations cannot alter the price used for withdrawals, or implement a snapshot of the price at deposit time and use it for redemption. Additionally, the contract could restrict direct donations, add checks that the total strategy token balance remains sufficient for all outstanding tranche shares, or redesign the burn/mint logic to preserve the invariant that the sum of minted shares equals the underlying assets held. Fixing the logic will prevent a grief attack that otherwise causes users to lose access to their deposited funds.

title: A user can avoid paying fees in
description:
Due to precision loss in the fees calculation a user will be able to avoid fees by splitting their withdraw into multiple smaller amounts
```solidity
function requestWithdraw(uint256 _amount, address _tranche) external returns (uint256) {
    ...
    uint256 _underlyings = _amount * _tranchePrice(_tranche) / ONE_TRANCHE_TOKEN;
    ...
    uint256 interest = _calcInterestWithdrawRequest(_underlyings) * _trancheAprRatio(_tranche) / FULL_ALLOC;
    uint256 fees = interest * fee / FULL_ALLOC;
    uint256 netInterest = interest - fees;
    ...
}
```
In the requestWithdraw function above we can see that the user will specify the amount of funds they are withdrawing. After that their portion of the interest is computed based on the specified amount. Then the fees are taken as a percentage of this amount.
However the issue is that if a user specifies a small enough amount that will gain interest, then the fees from that interest will be rounded down to 0. By splitting their withdraw into multiple smaller amounts they will be able to avoid paying the fees. When we look into the contest readMe we can see that tokens with 6 decimals will be supported:
Standard ERC20 tokens + USDT with no less than 6 decimals and no more than 18 decimals. Rebasing tokens, fee-on-transfer tokens, and tokens with multiple entry points are NOT supported. And also the contract will be deployed on Optimism and other L2s which has extremely low transaction fees. This attack will cause even bigger loss for the protocol with tokens that have 6 decimals and have a huge value.
Internal Pre-conditions
1. The contract is deployed on an L2(eg. Optimism which is allowed by the readMe)
2. The contract will use tokens with less than 8 decimals(eg. wbtc). In the readMe it is specified that standard tokens with 6 to 18 decimals will be supported.
External Pre-conditions
N/A
Attack Path
Consider the following scenario: The attacker wants to withdraw 0.01WBTC which is equal to 1e6 (around 1000$ of value). Expected fee is (10%*4%*1e6) = 4e3WBTC=4$ The interest that the attacker will gain is 4% and the fee is 10% In order for the attack to be profitable the 10% of the gained interest shall be rounded down to 0 here: racts/IdleCDOEpochVariant.sol#L519 which means that the interest for a single transaction shall be less than 9 wei so that the fees will round down to 0. In order for the interest to be 9 wei the total withdrawn amount shall be 225 wei for a transaction.(which is 0.225).Placingthisinalooptheattackerwillrunitmultipletimeswhichwillcostlessthan1 in total on optimism as transaction fees are extremely small(even negligible). As a result the fee will go to the attacker leading to a loss of the whole fee of the withdraw for the protocol.
On L2 the attack will be very cheap and will be profitable for the attacker, especially for big amounts. Loss of protocol fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss or rounding error in the fee calculation of the withdraw routine. The contract computes the interest earned on a withdrawal, then derives the protocol fee as a percentage of that interest using integer arithmetic: fees = interest * feeRate / FULL_ALLOC. Because Solidity performs floor division on unsigned integers, when the interest amount is small enough the product interest * feeRate is less than FULL_ALLOC, causing the division to truncate to zero. Consequently, for withdrawals that are sufficiently tiny – which is especially likely for tokens with only six to eight decimals – the fee field becomes zero even though a non‑zero fee is defined by the protocol. An attacker can exploit this by splitting a larger desired withdrawal into many small sub‑withdrawals, each of which yields an interest amount below the rounding threshold. Each transaction therefore incurs no fee, while the attacker still receives the full net interest. On Layer‑2 networks such as Optimism, where transaction costs are negligible, the attacker can repeat the operation many times at a very low gas cost, effectively siphoning the protocol’s fee revenue. The impact is a loss of expected fee income for the protocol and a breach of the accounting assumptions that fees are always deducted from earned interest. The bug manifests only when the withdrawn amount is small enough that the computed fee rounds down to zero; for typical withdrawal sizes the fee appears correct, making the issue easy to miss in standard testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the requestWithdraw function, where the auditor observed the integer division and reasoned about the rounding behavior for low‑decimal tokens. The problem is hard to notice because most test vectors use realistic withdrawal amounts, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a fee of zero is applied. To remediate, the contract should either use a higher‑precision fixed‑point library, enforce a minimum withdrawal amount that guarantees a non‑zero fee, aggregate multiple withdrawals within a buffer period, or redesign the fee logic to avoid floor division on small values. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the expected interest but no fee deduction, leading to a discrepancy between the expected fee and the actual amount received, effectively “money disappears” from the protocol’s balance while the user receives more than intended.

title: Interest will be lost if funds are
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes interest when a user withdraws from the junior (BB) tranche. The withdrawal routine first calculates the interest owed to the withdrawing user by multiplying the accrued interest by the tranche‑specific APR ratio. For the junior tranche this ratio is defined as zero because the junior tranche is configured with a 0 % APR. Consequently the formula yields zero interest for the junior portion of the withdrawal. While the user’s personal interest component is still added to the withdrawal amount, the contract fails to add the corresponding interest that should be attributed to the senior (AA) tranche for the extra epoch during which the funds remain lent. The net effect is that the senior tranche’s expected yield is under‑reported and effectively lost, because the funds borrowed during that epoch generate interest that is never credited to the senior vault. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever a depositor first places assets into the junior vault and later initiates a withdrawal from that same tranche. No explicit pre‑conditions are required; the bug manifests as soon as the withdrawal path is executed. The impact is a reduction of the senior tranche’s earnings, observable to users as a lower-than‑expected return or a missing portion of the accrued interest. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the interest paid to borrowers against the interest accounted for in each tranche, revealing a discrepancy when the BB tranche was withdrawn. Because the contract still records a correct interest amount for the withdrawing user, the loss is subtle and may go unnoticed unless the total interest distribution is examined. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where per‑tranche interest ratios are applied incorrectly, leading to an incomplete aggregation of total interest. To remediate, the contract should first compute the total interest generated for the epoch, allocate the user‑specific portion to the withdrawing principal, and then add the remaining interest to a dedicated expected‑epoch‑interest pool that is later distributed to the senior tranche. This ensures that all interest earned by the protocol is accounted for, preserving the intended yield for senior investors.

title: Missing staleness check in PythOracle can lead to forced liquidations and theft of funds from borrowers. Found by 0xRiO, 0xc0ffEE, 0xpetern, bbl4de, c3phas, d4y1ight, eeyore, fuzzysquirrel, miaowu, silver_eth, vahdrak1, zanderbyte, zxriptor
description:
The Pyth integration contract uses the getPriceUnsafe() function to retrieve the latest reported price from a specified price feed.
However, Pyth does not have sponsored price feeds on the Sonic chain, that will guaranty the proper data freshness. As such, this function depends on users or the Mach protocol to update the price data with fresh values.
As a result, the prices retrieved using getPriceUnsafe() can be significantly outdated, even with the protocol best efforts to maintain price freshness due to its keeper/bot outages.
The documentation for getPriceUnsafe() incorrectly suggests that it will revert with a StalePrice error when the price is outdated. In reality, this function returns a price with its associated timestamp, regardless of how old the timestamp is, as long as the price was updated at some point in the past.
This issue becomes critical if the prices used by the protocol are not updated for extended periods, during which significant price changes could occur for assets being borrowed or used as collateral in the project.
The Pyth integration contract does not perform a staleness check, and did not switch to fallback oracle in such situation. It only verifies that the price is > 0 (here), which is insufficient.
Although Compound V2 does not enforce staleness checks in its Chainlink oracle integration, the situation differs because Chainlink prices cannot be updated directly by anyone. Even stale prices from Chainlink are deemed acceptable under these circumstances, especially to avoid blocking liquidations.
In contrast, Pyth allows anyone to update the price feed (via updatePriceFeeds() function), in situation where the new price adheres to the rule that it must be newer than the previous price and is a valid Pyth price component for given price feed.
This introduces a vulnerability where price updates can be manipulated to extract value from users.
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
• Pyth prices have not been updated for an extended period.
Attack Path
An attacker can construct a transaction that updates the price feed with a desired value reported at a timestamp between the last update and the current time. This enables the attacker to inflate the price of borrowed assets and deflate the price of collateral assets, leading to forced liquidations.
The reported prices can originate from any valid price component with timestamp within the allowed timeframe. As observed in real-world scenarios, asset prices can rise by 10% in one day and fall by 20% on another day (e.g., FTM).
Consider a three-day timeframe during which Pyth prices for two supported assets are not updated:
1. Day 1: Asset A and Asset B prices are accurately reported.
2. Day 2: Both assets experience a 10% price increase, but the prices are not updated in Pyth. Although exploitation is possible at this stage, the attacker may wait another day.
3. Day 3: Both assets experience a 20% price drop.
The attacker can then update:
• The borrow asset price to the inflated value from Day 2 (+10%).
• The collateral asset price to the deflated value from Day 3 (-20%, or ~-10% from Day 1).
This manipulation allows the attacker to extract maximum liquidable value from users, profiting from the actual prices of the assets.
This attack would not be possible with fresh price updates, as the user shortfall would not fall below 1 in the given scenario of volatile prices.
• Direct loss of funds from forced liquidation of users, in situations where accurate price updates would prevent shortfalls from falling below 1.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the integration of the Pyth price oracle in the Mach Finance protocol, where the contract calls the getPriceUnsafe() function to obtain the latest price of an asset. Although the function name and documentation imply that it will reject stale data, the implementation merely returns the most recent price together with its timestamp, regardless of how old that timestamp is, as long as the price is greater than zero. Because Sonic does not provide sponsored price feeds that guarantee freshness, the protocol relies on external actors—either users or the Mach keeper bot—to push fresh price updates. When the keeper is offline or users fail to update the feed for an extended period, the stored price can become significantly outdated. The contract does not perform any staleness verification nor does it fall back to an alternative oracle, so it continues to use the stale price for critical calculations such as collateral valuation and liquidation thresholds. An attacker can exploit this gap by submitting a price update that is technically newer than the last recorded timestamp but deliberately chosen to be advantageous: inflating the reported price of a borrowed asset while deflating the price of the collateral asset. By doing so within the allowed timestamp window, the attacker can artificially lower the health factor of borrowers, triggering forced liquidations that would not occur with up‑to‑date market data. From the user’s perspective, a borrower may see their position liquidated despite having sufficient collateral under current market conditions, resulting in an unexpected loss of funds or a sudden drop of their balance to zero. The impact is a direct theft of value from borrowers and a loss of confidence in the protocol’s risk management. This issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the oracle integration, where the auditors noted the mismatch between the documented behavior of getPriceUnsafe() and its actual code, and observed that no staleness guard existed. The problem is subtle because the returned price appears valid (non‑zero) and the contract’s liquidation logic does not raise any alarms, making the bug easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a staleness check on the timestamp returned by getPriceUnsafe(), reject prices older than a defined freshness threshold, and optionally switch to a trusted fallback oracle such as API3 when the primary feed is stale. Additionally, deploying a reliable off‑chain bot with redundancy to keep the Pyth feed continuously updated would reduce the window for manipulation. Restricting who can call updatePriceFeeds() or adding stricter validation on the allowed timestamp range could further mitigate the risk of malicious price injection.

title: Determining how many votes to
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑inefficient algorithm used to determine how many votes a user can purchase in the reputation market. The contract receives a msg.value together with a minimum and maximum number of votes the user wishes to buy, then calls an internal pricing function to compute the total cost for the maximum amount. If the total cost exceeds the supplied ether, the code enters a while loop that decrements the vote count one by one, recomputes the cost on each iteration, and stops when the cost fits within the sent value. This linear search creates an O(n) gas consumption pattern where n is the difference between the maximum affordable votes and the actual affordable votes. The root cause is the absence of a more efficient search method such as binary search or a direct formula, causing the contract to execute thousands of expensive price‑calculation calls. An attacker or any user attempting to buy a large quantity of votes—especially when slippage limits force the contract to adjust the amount—can trigger many loop iterations. In the worst‑case scenario described, buying 100 000 votes with a 10 % slippage tolerance may require around 9 000 iterations, which exceeds the Base block gas limit and results in an out‑of‑gas (OOG) revert. Even when the transaction fits within the block, the gas cost can reach roughly 0.03 ETH (about $100 at current rates), making the operation prohibitively expensive. The impact is that legitimate users cannot complete large vote purchases, experience failed transactions, or pay excessive gas fees, effectively denying service and eroding confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where a proof‑of‑concept test measured gas usage and demonstrated that the loop consumes approximately 33 k gas per iteration, quickly scaling to the block limit. Because the problem manifests only for large purchase amounts, it may be overlooked during normal testing with small values, making it hard to notice. To remediate, the contract should replace the decrement‑by‑one loop with a binary search or a direct calculation that determines the maximum affordable vote count in logarithmic time, thereby reducing gas consumption dramatically and preventing OOG failures. This class of bug falls under inefficient algorithmic design leading to excessive gas usage, a common issue in smart contracts that perform iterative searches over monetary calculations.

title: Incorrect rounding in the
description:
When buying and selling, the cost is calculated using rounding based on isPositive.
However, the rounding should be based on isBuy, not isPositive.
The _calcCost() function calculates cost by rounding based on isPositive.
If isPositive is false (indicating that DISTRUST votes are being traded), the calculation is rounded up.
Consider the following scenario:
1. A user buys 2 DISTRUST votes.
2. A user sells a DISTRUST vote.
3. A user sells another DISTRUST vote.
During the buying process, rounding up occurs once, but when selling, rounding up occurs twice—at steps 2 and 3. As a result, marketFunds will be decremented by a dust amount.
If marketFunds was originally 0 (with the market created by the admin at a 0 creation cost), then step 3 becomes impossible.
In fact, isPositive is never related to the rounding direction.
```solidity
function _calcCost(
    Market memory market,
    bool isPositive,
    bool isBuy,
    uint256 amount
) private pure returns (uint256 cost) {
    ...
    int256 costRatio = LMSR.getCost(
        market.votes[TRUST],
        market.votes[DISTRUST],
        voteDelta[0],
        voteDelta[1],
        market.liquidityParameter
    );
    uint256 positiveCostRatio = costRatio > 0 ? uint256(costRatio) : uint256(costRatio * -1);
    // multiply cost ratio by base price to get cost; divide by 1e18 to apply ratio
    cost = positiveCostRatio.mulDiv(
        market.basePrice,
        1e18,
        isPositive ? Math.Rounding.Floor : Math.Rounding.Ceil
    );
}
```
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
The last vote might not be sold.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect rounding decision in the cost calculation routine of a prediction‑market style contract that trades TRUST and DISTRUST votes. The routine determines whether to round the computed cost down (floor) or up (ceil) based on a boolean flag named isPositive, which indicates the sign of the raw cost ratio. However, the rounding direction should depend on the trade direction – whether the operation is a buy or a sell – represented by the isBuy flag. Because the contract uses isPositive instead of !isBuy, a sell transaction (where isBuy is false) may be rounded up when it should be rounded down, and vice‑versa for a buy. This mismatch causes a small “dust” amount to be subtracted from the market’s internal fund balance each time a sell is executed after a buy, eventually depleting marketFunds or making a subsequent sell impossible when the balance reaches zero. The bug manifests when a user first purchases DISTRUST votes (triggering a single rounding up) and then sells DISTRUST votes twice; the second sell incurs an extra rounding up, reducing marketFunds by an unintended amount. From a user perspective the market may reject a sell, appear to have no funds, or simply return zero proceeds, contradicting the expectation that selling a vote yields a proportional refund. The impact is a loss of accounting integrity: funds disappear from the market, users cannot liquidate positions, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken. The condition occurs whenever the contract processes a trade and the rounding flag is derived from isPositive rather than the trade direction, which is true for all buy and sell paths. The affected parties are any participants who trade votes, the market contract itself, and any downstream protocols that rely on accurate market fund accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the _calcCost function’s rounding logic and compared it against the intended economic model. It is hard to notice because the rounding error is tiny (dust) and only accumulates after specific sequences of buys and sells, making it unlikely to surface in casual testing. Conceptually, the fix is to base the rounding choice on the trade direction: use !isBuy to select floor for sells and ceil for buys, thereby aligning the rounding with the intended sign of the cost change. This class of bug belongs to rounding‑direction errors in financial calculations, where an incorrect rounding mode leads to subtle accounting drift and potential fund loss. Correcting the rounding logic restores the invariant that marketFunds reflect the exact sum of trade proceeds and prevents unexpected zero balances or failed sell operations.

title: Very large sends from AvailBridge will break
description:
When sending tokens, up to uint256.max can be sent by AvailBridge, however lib.rs can only receive amounts up to uint128.max. Any values over uint128.max will cause the AVAIL side of the bridge to panic and deposit will be permanently lost.
lib.rs#L394-L399
```rust
T::Currency::transfer(
    &Self::account_id(),
    &destination_account_id,
    amount.as_u128().saturated_into(),
    ExistenceRequirement::AllowDeath,
)?;
```
When receiving a token transfer, lib.rs attempts to convert the amount from uint256 to uint128 via as_u128(). When amount is more than uint128.max this will panic and prevent processing of the transaction. Since the bridge doesn't have any way handle failed transactions, the deposit will be permanently lost.
Large deposits will break the receiving end of the bridge and cause loss of funds
bug_full: During token bridging, the AvailBridge contract can emit a transfer amount encoded as a uint256 value. The receiving library (lib.rs) assumes the amount fits into a uint128 and converts the value with as_u128(). When the transferred amount exceeds the maximum value representable by uint128 (2^128‑1), the conversion triggers a runtime panic. Because the bridge does not have a fallback or retry mechanism, the transaction is aborted on the AVAIL side and the deposited tokens become unrecoverable. The vulnerability therefore manifests whenever a user or an automated process attempts to bridge a very large token amount, intentionally or accidentally. The impact is a permanent loss of funds: the sender sees the transaction succeed on the source chain, but the destination balance remains unchanged or shows zero, violating the expectation that the bridge will deliver the same amount. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the bridge code, where the size mismatch between the uint256 send path and the uint128 receive path was observed. It can be hard to notice because normal usage rarely reaches the uint128 ceiling, so the bug only appears with extreme values. The proper mitigation is to enforce a maximum amount check on the sending side, reverting any transfer larger than uint128.max, or to redesign the receiving logic to handle uint256 amounts safely. This class of bug belongs to integer‑size mismatch and unchecked conversion errors, which break accounting assumptions and can cause funds to disappear without any on‑chain indication other than a failed transaction on the destination chain.

title: M-04 | Rightful Disputer Might Lose Bonds
description: Currently, there is no mechanism that checks whether there is already an ongoing dispute or not while submitting a price. Asserter can submit a new price after an initial incorrect submission without waiting a dispute to resolve in 48-96 hours. This would cause disputer to lose their bonds since the settlement will fail at [this line](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-1/blob/50373325e4ad7bb98382b5b4adce241a1ac1e770/packages/protocol/src/market/modules/UMASettlementModule.sol#L156) as the assertionIds won't match.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked price submission path that allows a new price to be posted while a previous dispute is still pending. The root cause is the absence of a state guard that verifies whether an active dispute exists before accepting a new assertion. An attacker acting as the asserter can submit a second price immediately after the first incorrect price, without waiting the 48‑96 hour dispute window. Because the settlement logic later expects the original assertion identifier, the mismatch causes the settlement transaction to revert, and the party that posted the bond (the disputer) cannot retrieve the locked funds. This results in the disputer losing the bond even though the dispute was never resolved. The issue manifests whenever a price is submitted while a dispute is open; it affects any participant who stakes a bond to challenge a price, as well as the overall protocol integrity because bond‑based incentives are broken. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the settlement module where the code path for price submission was examined and no check for an ongoing dispute was found. It can be hard to notice because the contract still accepts the new price and does not emit an explicit error, so normal operation appears to succeed until the later settlement step fails. To remediate, the contract should enforce a single‑active‑dispute rule, rejecting any new price submission while a dispute is unresolved, and optionally clearing or resetting the dispute state before allowing a new assertion. This class of bug is a missing‑state‑validation or re‑entrancy‑like flaw where the protocol’s lifecycle management is incomplete, leading to financial loss and a breach of the expected accounting invariant that bonds are returned after a dispute is settled.

title: M-05 | Decreasing LP May Require Collateral
description: Whenever a position is modified in position.updateValidLp, the required collateral for that position is calculated and compared the current available collateral. The collateral is calculated by using two values - debitEth and creditEth (debit is taken from the user and credit is given to them). When removing a small amount of liquidity, it's possible that the decrease in creditEth is larger than the decrease in debitEth, which would lead to increased collateral requirements. Since additionalCollateral is 0 when decreasing a position, the transaction will revert with InsufficientCollateral().
bug_full: The vulnerability is a collateral‑calculation flaw that appears when a liquidity provider tries to reduce the amount of liquidity (LP) they have supplied. The contract computes the required collateral for a position using two internal values, debitEth (the amount taken from the user) and creditEth (the amount returned to the user). The logic assumes that decreasing a position will either keep the collateral requirement the same or lower it. However, when a small amount of liquidity is removed, the reduction in creditEth can be larger than the reduction in debitEth. This imbalance causes the required collateral to increase even though the user is withdrawing liquidity. Because the function that processes a decrease sets the additionalCollateral parameter to zero, the transaction cannot provide the extra collateral that is now needed and the call reverts with an InsufficientCollateral() error. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the position.updateValidLp routine, where the auditor noticed that the collateral check does not handle the case where creditEth drops faster than debitEth. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal “remove liquidity” button, but after confirming the transaction the wallet reports a revert and the user’s balance appears unchanged, leading to confusion and the impression that funds are stuck. The impact is that liquidity providers may be unable to partially withdraw their stake in certain edge cases, effectively locking part of their capital and preventing rebalancing or emergency exits. The problem is subtle because most withdrawals do not trigger the condition, so the bug can remain hidden until a specific small‑withdrawal scenario is exercised. To remediate the issue the contract should either allow the caller to supply extra collateral when decreasing a position or adjust the collateral formula so that required collateral never rises when LP is reduced. In broader terms this is a class of accounting‑logic error where a decrease in a position unintentionally raises the security margin, violating the protocol’s expectation that withdrawing assets reduces risk exposure.

title: M-06 | Using LP For More Efficient Trades
description: Instead of opening a long position in the TradeModule to gain exposure vGas, traders can use the LiquidityModule for a more efficient strategy. By adding liquidity with a lower tick set to their desired entry price, traders can effectively create a limit order. When the price reaches this minimum tick, the LP position converts fully vGas, which can then be closed and transitioned into a Trade position. Since LP positions have reduced collateral requirements (no swap fees nor price impact on entry), this approach allows for the same vGas position with less collateral.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-1/pull/6/files
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the LiquidityModule allowing a trader to add liquidity at a specific low tick that effectively acts as a limit order. When the market price reaches this tick, the liquidity‑provider (LP) position is automatically converted into a full vGas exposure and then closed into a Trade position. Because LP positions are exempt from swap fees and do not suffer price‑impact‑related collateral requirements, the protocol treats them as having a lower collateral burden than a normal trade. Consequently, a user can obtain the same vGas exposure with substantially less collateral than the protocol’s risk model expects. This behavior can be exploited by deliberately opening an LP position at the desired entry price, waiting for the price to hit the tick, and then triggering the automatic conversion, thereby bypassing the intended collateral checks. The impact is that under‑collateralised trade positions may be created, increasing the risk of liquidation or loss for the protocol and its liquidity providers. The issue manifests whenever a trader uses the LiquidityModule to create a limit‑order‑style LP and the price reaches the predefined tick; it does not depend on any special permissions, so any participant can take advantage. The affected parties include regular users who expect the protocol to enforce proper collateralisation, the protocol itself which may suffer unexpected debt, and any liquidity providers whose pool composition could be altered by sudden large position closures. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the LiquidityModule and the TradeModule and noticed that the internal function _closeLiquidityPosition performs a transition rather than a full closure, leaving the collateral accounting unchanged. Because the conversion happens automatically and the UI shows a normal trade closure, the problem can be hard to notice; users may see a successful trade without realizing that the underlying collateral was insufficient. To remediate, the protocol should either prevent LP positions from being converted into trade positions or ensure that, upon conversion, the full collateral requirements of a trade are applied and the LP position is fully closed. In practice this means adjusting _closeLiquidityPosition to enforce a complete liquidation of the LP stake before opening a new trade, and adding slippage and low‑liquidity safeguards so that the conversion cannot be abused. The bug belongs to the class of “collateral bypass via state transition” vulnerabilities, where one contract’s relaxed accounting is inherited by another contract that assumes stricter guarantees, leading to under‑collateralised exposure and potential financial loss.

title: M-07 | Dangerous Price Used For Resolution Callback
description: If settlement.settlementPriceD18 in assertionResolvedCallback() is outside the acceptable price range for the given epoch, the new price for the epoch will be capped to either min or max with function setSettlementPriceInRange. However, resolutionCallback() is still called with the original settlement.settlementPriceD18 and not the newly set price of the epoch. Whenever the settlement price is outside the acceptable range, the callback will receive an incorrect price. The protocol team plans to create new epochs with that price which will lead to an epoch starting with prices outside the valid range.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑validation logic error in the settlement module. When a settlement price reported by an external oracle falls outside the predefined acceptable range for a given epoch, the contract calls setSettlementPriceInRange which clamps the price to the minimum or maximum allowed value and stores the clamped value in the epoch’s settlementPriceD18 field. However, the subsequent call to assertionResolvedCallback (and the downstream resolutionCallback) is still supplied with the original, uncapped settlement.settlementPriceD18 instead of the clamped epoch.settlementPriceD18. As a result, any consumer of the callback receives a price that is mathematically invalid for the epoch. The protocol then uses this incorrect price to initialise the next epoch, causing the new epoch to start with a price that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions. This can lead to mis‑priced trades, incorrect collateral valuations, and potentially loss of funds for users who rely on the price for liquidation or settlement. The bug manifests only when the oracle price is out of bounds; under normal in‑range prices the flow works as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the data flow from the settlement function to the callback and noticed that the price argument was never rewritten after the clamping step. The issue is subtle because the contract does enforce a range check and updates the stored epoch price, so a superficial test that only inspects the stored value would not reveal the mismatch. To remediate, the code should pass the clamped epoch.settlementPriceD18 to assertionResolvedCallback (and consequently to resolutionCallback) so that all downstream logic operates on a price that respects the defined bounds. This aligns the observable price with the protocol’s internal state and prevents epochs from being seeded with out‑of‑range values, preserving the integrity of price‑dependent calculations.

title: M-01 | Position With Zero Collateral
description: When a position is operating with small amounts, the required collateral for the position can be calculated to be zero due to rounding when calculating value of debt. Consequently, a user can modify their position to a size within a couple thousand wei and have to provide zero collateral. All their prior deposited collateral would be returned, and their position would have no backing. In the original review, this issue was not possible since the minimum requiredCollateral was always at least 2 wei.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-fuzzing/commit/defacd8f629985c2c446dd481b5a078be7990f68
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑induced collateral bypass that allows a position to be opened or modified with an effectively zero collateral requirement. The root cause lies in the integer arithmetic used to compute the value of the debt for very small position sizes; the division rounds down and can produce a requiredCollateral value of zero. Because the contract no longer enforces a hard floor of at least two wei, the system believes no collateral is needed and consequently returns any previously deposited collateral to the user while leaving the position open and unbacked. An attacker can create a position, then adjust its size to a few thousand wei, trigger the zero‑collateral calculation, and withdraw all collateral. From the user’s point of view the UI will show that the required collateral is 0 and that the full balance is returned, which contradicts the expectation that a position must always be backed by some amount of funds. The impact is that the protocol can end up with an under‑collateralized position that may be liquidated by anyone, leading to potential loss of funds and a break in the accounting guarantees of the vault. This condition occurs only when the position size is extremely small, a scenario that is easy to miss because the amounts involved appear negligible and the rounding error is not obvious in normal testing. The issue was discovered through targeted fuzzing that exercised edge‑case sizes and revealed that the minimum collateral check could be bypassed. Because the bug manifests only at the lower bound of numeric precision, it can remain hidden unless specific low‑value cases are examined. The proper remediation is to enforce a non‑zero minimum collateral requirement (for example, at least one wei or a protocol‑defined floor) and to use rounding‑up arithmetic when calculating required collateral, ensuring that the debt valuation never yields a zero requirement regardless of position size. This change restores the invariant that every open position must be backed by some collateral, preserving the protocol’s risk model and preventing funds from disappearing due to rounding errors.

title: M-02 | Inaccessible onlyOwner Functions
description: Since the Vault contract will be executing the onlyOwner createEpoch() function, it will be set as the owner of the foil system. The ConfigurationModule.updateMarket() function can be called by the Foil owner to update the market parameters. However, this function is never called in the Vault contract. This means the market can never be updated once the ownership is transferred to the contract. There is also no call to transferOwnership in Vault, so you can't just use a new vault as the owner.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccessible privileged function bug caused by ownership mis‑routing between two contracts. When the Vault contract executes the onlyOwner createEpoch() function, it becomes the owner of the Foil system. The Foil system’s ConfigurationModule contains an onlyOwner updateMarket() function that is intended to let the owner adjust market parameters such as fees, caps or pricing formulas. However, the Vault contract never calls updateMarket() and also does not expose any mechanism to transfer ownership away from itself. As a result, once ownership is transferred to the Vault, the market parameters become permanently immutable because the only entity with the required rights cannot reach the function and cannot delegate its rights to another contract. This situation can be exploited by simply relying on the fact that the owner is stuck: any governance process that expects to modify market settings will silently fail, leaving the protocol operating with stale or incorrect parameters. The impact includes potential economic loss for users, as market rates may no longer reflect current conditions, leading to over‑ or under‑charging, and it undermines the protocol’s ability to respond to emergencies or upgrades. The condition occurs whenever the Vault is deployed and createEpoch() is called, which is the normal initialization flow; no additional trigger is required. All participants—users, market makers, and the protocol itself—are affected because they cannot rely on the advertised ability to update market settings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the ownership flow with the set of onlyOwner functions and noticed that updateMarket() was never invoked and that there was no transferOwnership call in the Vault. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and runs without errors; the missing calls are not obvious from the code alone and only become apparent when attempting to perform an administrative update. To remediate, the Vault should be extended to call updateMarket() whenever a market change is required and should include a transferOwnership call (or an equivalent proxy pattern) that allows the owner role to be reassigned to a new contract or to a multisig, thereby restoring the ability to manage the Foil system. Conceptually, the fix restores the link between the privileged owner role and the functions that require it, preventing the permanent lock‑out of critical configuration logic.

title: M-03 | DoS Via Deposit Before First Epoch
description: Deposits before the first epoch are possible, with a minimum deposit amount of 1e3. Any pending deposits before the first epoch are utilized to establish the initial liquidity position within the _createNewLiquidityPosition function. This function deducts a dust amount of 1e4 from the deposited collateral amounts. If a user intentionally deposits an amount between 1e3 and 1e4 before the first epoch, and there are no other deposits, the initialization will fail due to underflow at [this line](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-1/blob/5b3416a28dfaa24ba3844e10081e55425d0a286a/packages/protocol/src/vault/Vault.sol#L341).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a user makes a deposit before the protocol’s first epoch with an amount that is larger than the documented minimum (1e3) but smaller than the internal dust constant (1e4). The contract’s initialization routine creates the first liquidity position by calling a function that subtracts a fixed dust amount from the total deposited collateral. Because the subtraction is performed without a safety check, a deposit that falls between the two thresholds triggers an unsigned integer underflow, causing the transaction to revert. This underflow prevents the creation of the initial liquidity position, effectively locking the protocol from ever becoming operational. The impact is that no liquidity can be added, users see their deposit transaction fail silently or revert, and the protocol remains unusable until a larger deposit is made or the bug is patched. The condition only manifests during the very first epoch when the initial position is being set up; later epochs use a different path that does not perform the dust deduction. The affected parties are any depositor who interacts with the contract before the first epoch and the protocol itself, which loses the ability to start trading or earn fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the initialization logic and identified the mismatch between the public minimum deposit requirement and the internal dust subtraction. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error message for the underflow; the transaction simply fails, which may be interpreted as a generic network or gas issue. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction submission but the on‑chain state remains unchanged, leading to confusion such as “my balance stayed the same after I deposited”. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow errors caused by inconsistent validation of input ranges versus internal constants. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum deposit that is at least equal to the dust amount, or remove the dust subtraction entirely, or add explicit checks that prevent the underflow before performing the subtraction. Any of these approaches would align the public deposit constraints with the internal accounting logic and eliminate the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: M-04 | DoS Via Frontrunning Pool Creation
description: After the implementation of the Vault, epoch settlements and the creation of the new epoch happens at the same transaction via callbacks. Because of this atomic behavior, failure of the pool creation for the next epoch will DoS the settlement of the previous epoch. An attacker can precompute the virtual token addresses and create the Uniswap pool with these addresses as creating pools is permissionless in the Uniswap. This will cause Epoch.createValid function to revert while calling IUniswapV3Factory.createPool due to require(getPool[token0][token1][fee] == address(0)) check in the [factory.](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/d8b1c635c275d2a9450bd6a78f3fa2484fef73eb/contracts/UniswapV3Factory.sol#L45) The attack can cause complete blocking of the epoch settlements and creations. However, attackers must keep frontrunning and create new pools every time someone tries to settleAssertion in the optimistic oracle.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that arises when the vault contract tries to settle the current epoch and, in the same atomic transaction, creates the Uniswap V3 pool required for the next epoch. The contract calls the factory’s createPool function without first confirming whether a pool for the given token pair and fee already exists. Uniswap V3’s factory enforces a require statement that the pool address must be zero before a new pool can be created. If an attacker pre‑computes the deterministic pool address and front‑runs the settlement transaction by creating the pool beforehand, the require check fails, the createPool call reverts, and consequently the epoch’s settlement logic also reverts. This makes the whole settlement step impossible, effectively blocking the progression of epochs. The impact is that users who expect their rewards or withdrawals to be processed see their transactions fail, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol cannot advance to the next trading period, potentially locking funds indefinitely. The condition occurs only when settlement and pool creation are bundled together and when an adversary can observe pending transactions and submit a competing transaction that creates the pool first. All participants of the vault – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol’s accounting and reward distribution are halted. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the callback flow and noticed that the factory’s createPool function is called without a prior existence check, making it vulnerable to front‑running. It is hard to notice because the revert originates from an external contract (the Uniswap factory) and appears as a generic settlement failure rather than a clear indication of a pool‑creation conflict. To remediate, the contract should query the factory’s getPool method before attempting to create a new pool, handle the case where the pool already exists (including checking whether it has been initialized and setting the appropriate starting price), or redesign the workflow so that pool creation is performed off‑chain or in a separate transaction that cannot be front‑run. Using a private RPC endpoint for settlement calls can also reduce the chance of an attacker observing and front‑running the transaction. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of front‑running‑induced DoS vulnerabilities caused by unchecked external contract calls that assume a unique resource does not already exist.

title: M-05 | Gas Griefing Of Epoch Creation
description: When a new epoch is created, block.timestamp is used as the salt for generating two virtual tokens. In _createVirtualToken, a loop probes for an available salt if a collision occurs. However, the salt increments by 1 on each iteration, making it highly predictable and susceptible to front-running. An attacker can exploit this predictability to deliberately create collisions. During testing, each iteration of the loop was found to cost approximately 600k gas, making it feasible for an attacker to force the epoch creation process to fail due to an Out-of-Gas error.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deterministic and predictable salt generation mechanism used when a new epoch is created. The contract takes block.timestamp as the initial salt for two virtual token deployments and, if a collision occurs, it enters a loop that increments the salt by one on each iteration until an unused value is found. Because the increment is linear and the initial value is publicly known, an attacker can front‑run the epoch‑creation transaction, deliberately cause a salt collision, and force the loop to iterate many times. Each iteration consumes roughly 600 000 gas, so an attacker can drive the total gas consumption beyond the block gas limit or the caller’s gas stipend, causing the epoch‑creation call to run out of gas and revert. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users cannot create new epochs, potentially halting protocol progress and leaving funds inaccessible until the issue is resolved. The problem occurs only during the epoch‑creation function, which relies on block.timestamp and a simple ++ counter for collision resolution. It affects any participant who attempts to start a new epoch, including token holders and protocol operators. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester observed that the collision‑resolution loop consumed a large amount of gas per iteration, making it feasible to trigger an out‑of‑gas failure.
