The bug is subtle because the loop appears harmless at first glance and collisions are rare in normal operation, so developers may not notice the excessive gas cost without detailed profiling. To remediate, the salt should be derived from a cryptographically unpredictable source, such as a hash of multiple block variables (e.g., keccak256(blockhash, block.timestamp, msg.sender)) or by using a deployment scheme like CREATE3 that ties the address to the deployer and a unique salt without predictable increments. This change eliminates the ability for an attacker to pre‑compute the next salt value and prevents the gas‑griefing attack, restoring reliable epoch creation and preserving protocol availability.

title: M-06 | Positions With 0 Collateral
description: When a position is operating with small amounts, the required collateral for the position can be calculated to be zero due to rounding when calculating value of debt. Consequently, a user can modify their position to a size within a couple thousand wei and have to provide zero collateral. All their prior deposited collateral would be returned, and their position would have no backing. In the original review, this issue was not possible since the minimum requiredCollateral was always at least 2 wei.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑induced collateral calculation error that can allow a trading position to be created or modified with a required collateral amount of zero wei. The contract computes the value of the debt for a position in wei and then derives the minimum collateral needed to back that debt. When the position size is extremely small – on the order of a few thousand wei – the integer division or rounding performed by the calculation truncates the debt value to zero, which in turn makes the required collateral zero. Because the protocol automatically returns any excess collateral to the user, the user’s previously deposited collateral is refunded while the position remains open but unbacked. This situation can be triggered by a user deliberately shrinking a position to a size that falls below the rounding threshold, or by an attacker opening a tiny position and then withdrawing all collateral. The impact is that the protocol holds a position with no economic backing, exposing it to immediate liquidation or loss of funds, and effectively allowing the user to extract collateral without providing any security. The bug manifests only when the position’s debt value is small enough for the rounding logic to produce zero, which is why it may go unnoticed during normal operation where positions are larger. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case arithmetic and noticed that the minimum requiredCollateral constant, previously set to at least 2 wei, could be bypassed by the rounding behavior. The issue is hard to spot because the contract appears to enforce collateral requirements for typical positions, and the zero‑collateral case only occurs in a narrow numeric range that is rarely exercised in standard tests. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of rounding or underflow errors in financial calculations, where integer arithmetic leads to a loss of precision and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every debt must be fully collateralised. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a position with a non‑zero size but a collateral field of zero, and the user may see their previously locked funds returned unexpectedly, creating a false sense of profit. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a non‑zero minimum collateral amount (for example, at least 2 wei) and should use safe arithmetic that prevents rounding down to zero, such as rounding up or adding a small epsilon before division. This ensures that every active position always retains a positive collateral backing, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: M-07 | Fee Collector Can Hoard Fees
description: M-01 of the previous audit was not addressed. Fee collectors can create under-collateralized positions and collateralize them using depositCollateral. Currently, there are no restrictions preventing a fee collector from creating an oversized liquidity position, which can monopolize all available liquidity and hoard fees, preventing other fee collectors from benefiting.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic monopolisation flaw in the fee‑collector module of the vault contract. Because the contract does not enforce any upper bound on the amount of liquidity a fee collector may open, nor does it verify that the collateral posted against a position is sufficient relative to its size, a malicious or greedy fee collector can create an extremely large liquidity position that is under‑collateralised. By doing so the collector can absorb virtually all of the available liquidity and consequently capture the majority, or even the entirety, of the fees generated by the pool. This behaviour violates the protocol’s intended accounting model where fees are supposed to be distributed proportionally among all active fee collectors. The exploit is carried out by calling the function that creates a liquidity position (often combined with depositCollateral) with parameters that specify a size far exceeding the normal operational range, while providing only minimal collateral. Since there are no checks limiting the position size or enforcing a minimum collateral‑to‑liquidity ratio, the transaction succeeds and the oversized position begins to earn fees at the expense of other collectors. From the perspective of other fee collectors the symptom is that their fee balance remains unchanged or drops to zero despite normal pool activity; they expect to receive a share of the fees but receive none, leading to apparent loss of earnings. The issue was identified during a follow‑up audit where a previously reported problem (M‑01) had not been remedied, indicating that the missing constraints were overlooked. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the fee collector’s address may appear legitimate and the fee distribution simply looks skewed rather than outright broken. The flaw belongs to the class of resource‑monopolisation or economic denial‑of‑service bugs, where the lack of caps allows a single actor to hoard a shared revenue stream. To remediate the issue the contract should impose sensible limits on the maximum size of a liquidity position that any fee collector can open, enforce a minimum collateralisation ratio, and optionally require that new positions respect the proportion of total available liquidity. These controls would restore fair fee distribution, prevent fee hoarding, and align the contract’s behaviour with its intended economic model.

title: M-08 | Decreasing LP May Require Collateral
description: The [M-05'](https://www.notion.so/M-05-1348bda5828c81c086e6d49037558a91?pvs=21)s recommendation to let the user specify an amount of collateral to be added when decreasing a liquidity position has not been implemented which leaves the problem unsolved.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-fuzzing/pull/7
bug_full: The vulnerabilityconcerns the process of decreasing a liquidity provider (LP) position in a vault contract where the protocol expects the user to supply additional collateral to keep the position adequately backed. The root cause is that a previously identified recommendation (M‑05') to allow users to specify an amount of collateral when shrinking their position was never implemented, leaving the contract without a mechanism to accept extra collateral at that moment. As a result, when a user attempts to decrease their LP while the position still carries obligations—such as outstanding debt, pending rewards, or a minimum collateralisation ratio—the contract may reject the operation or allow it to proceed in an under‑collateralised state. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by initiating a decrease that triggers a collateral shortfall; the contract either reverts the transaction, causing the user to receive no tokens back, or silently accepts the decrease, leading to a state where the protocol’s accounting is inconsistent and the user’s funds become effectively locked or lost. The impact includes users being unable to withdraw their liquidity, balances appearing as zero or unchanged, and the protocol potentially exposing itself to liquidation risk if many positions become under‑collateralised. This condition occurs specifically when the LP reduction is performed without sufficient collateral and the contract lacks a path for the user to add the required amount. All liquidity providers who try to shrink their positions under these circumstances are affected, as are the protocol’s overall health and any downstream contracts that rely on correct accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the missing implementation of the collateral‑addition step was noted as a gap between the specification and the actual code. It can be hard to notice because the UI may allow the user to submit a decrease request, but the transaction either fails silently or results in a zero‑balance outcome, giving the impression that funds have disappeared. To remediate, the contract should be updated to accept an explicit collateral amount as part of the decrease function, enforce the required collateral ratio before allowing the operation, and provide clear error messages when the supplied collateral is insufficient. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a reduction in exposure must be matched by an appropriate increase in backing, thereby preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.

title: M-09 | vEth Credited When Closing A Position
description: When closing a position, the vEthToZero is calculated as initialSize * tradeRatio and should be equal to the signedTradedVEth. However, Solidity division truncates the result. Because of this, tradeRatio will be slightly off - both when rounded down or up - therefore vEthToZero as well. Even though vEthFromZero should be roughly equal to targetSize * tradeRatio, the value assigned to it (for targetSize = 0) will be non-zero - positive or negative depending on the rounding. After that the absolute value of vEthFromZero will be assigned to vEthAmount. In result, closed positions end up having positive vEthAmount, which is especially bad for long positions. This ultimately leads to an undercollateralized market, preventing the last user from settling.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-fuzzing/commit/c6d9b52b12a46e0a52f31ef28ecf343980b9ec01
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs when a position is closed and its target size becomes zero. The contract calculates a trade ratio using integer division, which truncates any fractional part. Because of this truncation the computed tradeRatio is slightly off, and the derived values vEthToZero (initialSize * tradeRatio) and vEthFromZero (targetSize * tradeRatio) are also inaccurate. When targetSize is zero the contract still assigns vEthFromZero a non‑zero value – positive or negative depending on whether the division rounded down or up. The absolute value of this mis‑computed vEthFromZero is then stored in vEthAmount, resulting in a closed position that appears to have a positive vEth balance. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that closing a fully settled position yields no residual vEth, yet the UI may show an unexpected credit or the market may become under‑collateralised, preventing later users from settling. The issue was discovered by the Guardian audit team through fuzz‑testing of the vault contract. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is small and only manifests when a position size reaches exactly zero, so normal operation may not reveal the error. The impact is that long positions can end up with a spurious positive vEth amount, which reduces the total collateral backing the market and can block settlement for the final participant, effectively creating an under‑collateralised market state. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic rounding or truncation bugs in smart contracts, where integer division leads to incorrect accounting. To remediate the problem the contract should explicitly set vEthAmount to zero whenever the position size is zero, or use a rounding‑safe calculation method that guarantees vEthFromZero is zero in that case. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that a closed position carries no residual vEth, preserving market collateralisation and preventing unexpected user balances.

title: M-10 | resolutionCallback Fails On Small Amounts
description: Function _createEpochAndPosition passing is critical to the Vault's flow, since if the resolutionCallback fails the Vault's functionality is stopped. If the Vault has more collateral than the current minimum collateral, the Vault attempts to _createNewLiquidityPosition. The issue is that even with enough collateral to meet the minimum threshold, is it not guaranteed that the liquidity to-be minted from the calculated amount0 and amount1 is greater than 0 due to Uniswap rounding down on small amounts, which would trigger a revert in UniswapV3Pool.mint: require(amount > 0); Ultimately, the Vault will attempt to mint which will revert, causing the callback to fail and the mints/epoch creation will not occur.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the vault’s epoch‑creation flow where the internal function that prepares a new liquidity position calls Uniswap V3’s mint routine. The contract first checks that the total collateral supplied by a user exceeds a configured minimum threshold and, based on that amount, computes the two token quantities (amount0 and amount1) that should be supplied to the Uniswap pool. Because Uniswap V3 rounds down any fractional token amount, a situation can arise where, despite the collateral being above the minimum, one of the computed amounts is rounded to zero when the supplied amount is very small. The UniswapV3Pool.mint function contains a guard require(amount > 0) that reverts the transaction if either token amount is zero. When this revert occurs inside the resolutionCallback, the callback fails, the mint operation is aborted and the epoch creation does not complete. From a user’s perspective the deposit transaction appears to fail silently or with a generic “require amount > 0” error, the expected new position never appears, and the user’s funds remain locked in the transaction revert, giving the impression that the vault stopped working. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the vault’s logic only validates the collateral amount but does not guarantee that the derived token amounts will be non‑zero after Uniswap’s rounding. The bug is hard to notice because the contract’s own checks pass, and the failure only surfaces when the external Uniswap call is executed, which may only happen for edge‑case deposits that are just above the minimum. The impact is medium severity: it does not allow an attacker to steal funds, but it can halt the vault’s core functionality, preventing users from creating new epochs or providing liquidity, effectively freezing the protocol’s revenue stream. The class of bug is a rounding‑to‑zero error in cross‑contract calls that rely on external libraries enforcing non‑zero inputs. To remediate, the vault should enforce a higher minimum collateral that guarantees a non‑zero mint amount, or it should add an explicit check after the amount calculations to ensure both amount0 and amount1 are greater than zero before invoking Uniswap’s mint function. This preventive measure aligns the contract’s assumptions with Uniswap’s requirements and restores reliable epoch creation.

title: M-11 | Cleared borrowedVEth
description: When a long position is being modified, its borrowedVEth is set to the absolute value of vEthFromZero. In some cases, it's possible to have a small amount of vGasAmount with 0 vEthFromZero due to the traded vETH matching the vEthToZero, primarily when operating with small position sizes and trade prices. This leads to a long position that does not have a loaned amount. This leaves the Foil contract with less available collateral than it should have and in result, the last user will not be able to exit.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-fuzzing/blob/22f09a942e332c3e37c724943ce8f1635cc35e2f/packages/protocol/test/fuzzing/FoundryPlayground.sol#L42
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the Foil protocol that allows a long position to be recorded with a borrowedVEth value of zero. The contract determines borrowedVEth by taking the absolute value of vEthFromZero when a position is modified. In edge cases where the trade size is very small and the amount of vETH being bought exactly matches the amount being sold (vEthFromZero equals vEthToZero), vEthFromZero becomes zero while a non‑zero vGasAmount may still be present. Because the code does not verify that vEthFromZero is positive, the borrowedVEth field is set to zero, effectively clearing the loan amount for that position. This creates a mismatch between the protocol’s internal accounting of collateral and the actual collateral that should be locked, leaving the Foil contract with less available collateral than required. When the last user attempts to exit the vault, the contract cannot provide sufficient collateral and the exit transaction fails or returns no funds, causing the user’s balance to appear unchanged. The issue is triggered during the modification of a long position, specifically when small position sizes and certain trade prices cause vEthFromZero to be zero. Any participant who opens or modifies a position under these conditions can unintentionally reduce the pool’s collateral, potentially locking funds for subsequent users. The flaw was discovered through fuzz testing performed by the Guardian audit team, where generated inputs exposed the zero‑borrowedVEth scenario. It is difficult to notice because the condition only occurs with atypically small trades, and other parts of the contract do not explicitly check for a zero borrowed amount, so the state may appear normal until an exit is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of “zero‑loan‑amount” or “cleared borrowed amount” accounting bugs that break the invariant that every leveraged position must have a positive loan. From a user perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal or position close returns nothing, contrary to the expectation that the protocol will release the user’s funds. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that any opened or modified long position has a positive borrowedVEth, for example by adding a require statement that borrowedVEth > 0 before the position is accepted. This restores the invariant that collateral accounting matches the loaned amount and prevents users from being unable to exit the vault.

title: M-01 | Fee Collector Can Horde Fees
description: Fee collectors can create under-collateralized positions and collateralize them using depositCollateral. Currently, there are no restrictions preventing a fee collector from creating an oversized liquidity position, which can monopolize all available liquidity and hoard fees, preventing other fee collectors from benefiting.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the fee‑collector role in a liquidity‑providing protocol. The contract allows a fee collector to open a liquidity position and later add collateral through a depositCollateral function, but it does not enforce any upper bound on the size of the position relative to the amount of collateral supplied. Because there is no validation that the position is adequately collateralised, an attacker can create an extremely large, under‑collateralised liquidity position that consumes the majority of the pool’s available liquidity. Once the oversized position is in place, the fee‑distribution logic awards the bulk of the protocol’s fees to that single position, effectively hoarding the fees and preventing other legitimate fee collectors from earning any meaningful reward. This situation arises whenever a fee collector initiates a new position; there are no time‑based or size‑based checks that would stop a malicious actor from repeatedly opening oversized positions. The affected parties are the fee‑collector community, token holders who rely on fair fee distribution, and the protocol itself, which may lose its incentive‑alignment guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the economic assumptions of the fee‑distribution mechanism and identified the missing size constraints as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because the contract continues to function – fees are still collected and the UI shows normal activity – but the distribution becomes heavily skewed, leading users to see their expected fee earnings drop to near zero while a single address appears to receive an outsized share. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden disappearance of expected rewards, a UI that shows a single collector receiving all fees, and a mismatch between the anticipated fair share and the actual payout. The root cause is the absence of a cap on liquidity position size and the lack of a proportional collateral requirement, which together constitute an economic‑logic vulnerability often classified as a “fee‑hoarding” or “resource‑monopolisation” bug. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce limits on the maximum liquidity that any single fee collector can provide, require collateral to be proportional to the liquidity contributed, and possibly introduce per‑collector caps or tiered fee‑distribution rules to ensure a fair and decentralized allocation of fees.

title: M-02 | _checkOnERC721Received Bool Is Not Checked
description: While creating a position in the liquidity or trading modules, _checkOnERC721Received function is called and then the position NFT is minted. However, _checkOnERC721Received does not revert on failure but only returns false. Return value is not checked and positions can be minted to contracts that can't hold NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing verification of the boolean result returned by the internal helper _checkOnERC721Received, which is invoked when a new position NFT is minted in the liquidity and trading modules. The helper attempts to call the ERC721Receiver interface on the target address and returns false if the call fails, but the calling code does not examine this return value and proceeds to mint the NFT regardless. As a result, the contract can assign ownership of a newly created position NFT to any address, including contracts that do not implement the ERC721Receiver callback. When such a contract receives the token, the ERC721 standard does not enforce a revert, so the token becomes effectively locked: the owning contract cannot invoke safeTransferFrom, cannot approve the token, and the protocol’s accounting assumes the position is held by a valid holder. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a minimal contract that lacks the ERC721Receiver implementation, then invoking the position‑creation function; the protocol will mint the NFT to the attacker‑controlled address, after which the attacker (or any user) will be unable to retrieve or transfer the position, leading to loss of access to the underlying liquidity or trading rights and potentially locking associated funds. The issue manifests whenever a user creates a position, which is a routine operation in normal protocol usage, and therefore affects all participants who rely on the NFT to represent their stake. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the minting flow and noticed that the boolean result of _checkOnERC721Received was ignored. Because the transaction does not revert, the UI may report a successful position creation, making the bug subtle and hard to detect until a user attempts to move or withdraw the NFT and finds it stuck. To remediate, the contract should explicitly check the return value of _checkOnERC721Received and revert if it is false, or replace the custom minting logic with OpenZeppelin’s _safeMint pattern that automatically enforces the receiver check. This change restores the invariant that every minted NFT is owned by an address capable of handling ERC721 tokens, preventing silent loss of position ownership and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: M-03 | Incorrect deltaCollateral Check When Negative
description: Users provide deltaCollateralLimit when modifying their trade positions. While a positive deltaCollateralLimit indicates the maximum amount a user wants to provide to the protocol, a negative deltaCollateralLimit represents the minimum collateral amount a user wishes to receive from the protocol when decreasing or closing a position. However, the negative case in _checkDeltaCollateralLimit is incorrect and behaves oppositely. It reverts when deltaCollateralLimit < 0 && deltaCollateral < deltaCollateralLimit. The user-provided value functions as a maximum limit instead of a minimum limit, resulting in the user receiving less than intended all the time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect validation of a user‑provided deltaCollateralLimit when the limit is negative. In the protocol, a positive deltaCollateralLimit represents the maximum amount of collateral a trader is willing to add, while a negative deltaCollateralLimit is intended to specify the minimum amount of collateral the trader expects to receive when reducing or closing a position. The contract’s internal function _checkDeltaCollateralLimit contains a conditional that is reversed for the negative case: it reverts when deltaCollateralLimit < 0 && deltaCollateral < deltaCollateralLimit. Because the comparison uses a less‑than operator, the negative limit is treated as an upper bound rather than a lower bound. Consequently, the contract may either reject legitimate withdrawals or, more commonly, allow the trade to proceed while returning less collateral than the trader requested. This mis‑behaviour occurs whenever a user supplies a negative deltaCollateralLimit, i.e., when they are trying to enforce a minimum collateral receipt. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of collateral adjustments and identified that the condition does not match the intended business rule. It can be hard to notice because the code path is only exercised for negative limits, which many users may never use, and the symptom – receiving a smaller amount of collateral than expected – may be attributed to market movements rather than a contract bug. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful position close, but the returned balance is lower than the minimum the user set, leading to confusion such as “I expected to get at least X tokens but got less”. The impact is a breach of accounting assumptions: the protocol fails to guarantee a minimum payout, potentially causing financial loss for traders who rely on that guarantee. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect limit checks or inverted comparison errors, where a minimum constraint is mistakenly implemented as a maximum constraint. To remediate, the comparison should be changed to deltaCollateral > deltaCollateralLimit for the negative case, thereby enforcing that the actual collateral returned is not below the user‑specified minimum. Proper unit tests covering both positive and negative deltaCollateralLimit scenarios should be added to prevent regression.

title: M-12 | Resetting Does Not Refund Tokens
description: When a user calls withdrawRequestRedeem(), if their balance after is less than minimumCollateral then resetTransaction() will set their pending amount to zero. However, totalPendingWithdrawals will only be decremented by the amount of shares the user passes in. This will lead to totalPendingWithdrawals being larger than the actual amount that is intended to be withdrawn. A malicious user could continuously call requestRedeem() in conjunction with withdrawRequestRedeem in order to inflate totalPendingWithdrawals to be larger than collateralFromPreviousEpoch plus totalPendingDeposits. This will cause a DoS via underflow when _reconcilePendingTransactions() is called. Additionally, when a user calls withdrawRequestDeposit(), totalPendingDeposits is only decremented by assets. This will lead to the user’s remaining tokens to be donated to other users of the protocol.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/foil-2/compare/rd2-remediations...POC_DOS_MIN_COLLAT?expand=1#diff-4fe03eaa0c5a23c3854772730dd5ca9a0a7de11d8d7e4394a623f6cf2b5496e5
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the vault contract when a user attempts to withdraw a redemption request that leaves their remaining balance below the protocol‑defined minimum collateral. The function withdrawRequestRedeem resets the user’s pending amount to zero, but the global counter totalPendingWithdrawals is reduced only by the number of shares the caller supplied, not by the full value of the user’s residual balance. Consequently the global counter can become larger than the actual amount that is still owed to users. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly issuing requestRedeem followed by withdrawRequestRedeem, each time forcing the contract to record a smaller decrement than the true reduction. Over many iterations totalPendingWithdrawals can be inflated beyond the sum of collateralFromPreviousEpoch and totalPendingDeposits. When the internal reconciliation routine _reconcilePendingTransactions later attempts to subtract the inflated total, an unsigned integer underflow occurs, causing a denial‑of‑service condition that halts further processing of withdrawals. A second, related flaw appears in withdrawRequestDeposit: the function only subtracts the deposited asset amount from totalPendingDeposits, leaving any leftover tokens in the user’s balance unaccounted for. Those leftover tokens are effectively transferred to other participants without an explicit transfer event, meaning the original user sees their tokens disappear while other users receive an unexpected credit. From a user’s point of view the symptoms are a missing refund (the UI shows a zero or unchanged balance after a withdrawal) and, in the worst case, the entire vault may become unusable because the reconciliation step reverts. The issue is triggered only when the post‑withdrawal balance falls below the minimum collateral threshold, a condition that can be deliberately engineered by an attacker. It affects all participants of the vault because the global counters drive the accounting for every epoch, so any distortion can corrupt the protocol’s financial state. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between resetTransaction, totalPendingWithdrawals and totalPendingDeposits and identified that the counters were not being fully reconciled. The problem is subtle because the mismatched counters are internal variables that are not directly exposed to users, making the discrepancy hard to notice without deep inspection of the contract’s state changes. To remediate the issue the contract should either decrement totalPendingWithdrawals by the full residual amount or explicitly refund the remainder to the caller before invoking resetTransaction, and similarly adjust totalPendingDeposits to reflect the exact amount removed, ensuring that global accounting always mirrors the actual token balances held by users.

title: M-03 | Release Stuck On Zero Address Beneficiary
description: In the releaseOnEid function there is no validation that the beneficiary address is not the zero address. Therefore a layerzero message can be sent with the beneficiary set as the zero address. The execution of this message will perpetually fail as all attempts to execute the executeMessage function will revert as the Solady ERC721 library does not support mints or transfers to the zero address. Therefore the Shadow NFTs and base collection NFT will remain locked on all chains with this message stuck in perpetuity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the beneficiary address in the releaseOnEid function, which allows a LayerZero cross‑chain message to specify the zero address as the recipient of a Shadow NFT. The root cause is that the function does not check whether the beneficiary is the zero address before invoking the executeMessage routine. When the zero address is passed, the Solady ERC721 library, which underlies both the Shadow NFT and the base collection NFT, rejects any mint or transfer to address(0) and reverts the transaction. An attacker or a faulty client can therefore craft a message with beneficiary set to 0x0, causing every subsequent attempt to process that message to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style lock‑up: the NFTs remain permanently locked on every chain involved, the message stays in the LayerZero queue, and users never receive the expected token. This condition occurs whenever releaseOnEid is called with an unchecked beneficiary, which can happen during normal operation or through a malicious request. All participants who rely on the cross‑chain release – token holders, the protocol’s users, and the overall ecosystem – are affected because their assets become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the message handling logic and identified the absence of a zero‑address guard. It can be hard to notice because typical test cases use valid addresses, and the failure only manifests when a zero address is supplied, which may not be exercised in standard unit tests. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked input or zero‑address validation errors that lead to permanent asset lock‑up. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a pending release, the transaction may revert with a generic error, and the expected NFT never appears in the wallet, creating confusion and loss of confidence. To remediate, the releaseOnEid function should explicitly require that the beneficiary is not the zero address before proceeding with the cross‑chain execution, thereby preventing the mint/transfer revert and ensuring that the release flow can complete as intended.

title: M-04 | Insufficient Gas
description:
Inside releaseOnEid getSendOptions is used to calculate the amount of gas needed for the _lzReceive call. However due to rigid nature of the math and vast possible routes that the call could go, it would often result in an revert. Not only that but the math currently lacks the GAS_RESERVE, which is taken before that call is executed, resulting in the total gas allocated to be 30k + (20k * NFT count) Lets look into an example call: Total gas for 5 NFTs gets to be - 80k - 50k + 20k * 5 -> 130k
1. The call goes as usual executeMessage -> _executeMessage, but then we enter the else for _updateLockState
2. _updateLockState would in tern perform a couple of checks and call _clearDelegationsAndReleaseTokens if we are on the native chain
3. _clearDelegationsAndReleaseTokens would execute transferFrom for every NFT
4. This is followed by _clearDelegations which would call DELEGATE_REGISTRY.delegateERC721 again for every NFT Both transferFrom and delegateERC721 access storage, be it warm or cold, costing huge amounts of gas.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient-gas calculation in the releaseOnEid workflow of the NFT contract. The function builds a gas stipend for the internal _lzReceive call by using a fixed formula that multiplies a base amount (30k gas) by the number of NFTs and adds a per-NFT component (20k gas). The formula does not include a safety buffer (GAS_RESERVE) and assumes that each NFT will consume exactly the same amount of gas when transferFrom and delegateERC721 are executed. In reality those calls touch storage both warm and cold, and the actual gas cost grows with the number of NFTs and with the state of the storage, often exceeding the estimated 30k + 20k * count. When a user attempts to release several NFTs, for example five, the contract allocates only about 130k gas, but the combined cost of five transferFrom operations and five delegate calls can easily surpass this limit, causing an out-of-gas revert. The revert aborts the whole transaction, leaving the NFTs locked and the user’s balance unchanged, which appears to the user as a failed release or 'nothing happened' after clicking the release button. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the execution path of releaseOnEid and observed that the gas stipend calculation is rigid and lacks a reserve. It is hard to notice because small numbers of NFTs succeed, giving a false impression that the function works, while larger batches silently fail. The bug belongs to the class of 'insufficient gas stipend' or 'gas-estimation under-allocation' bugs, where a contract incorrectly predicts the gas needed for a downstream call and therefore reverts. The impact is a denial-of-service for users trying to withdraw multiple NFTs and a potential loss of confidence in the protocol, although no funds are directly stolen. The correct fix is to redesign the gas calculation to use a dynamic estimate that accounts for the worst-case storage access cost, include a reasonable GAS_RESERVE margin, or avoid relying on a fixed stipend altogether by letting the caller provide sufficient gas or by splitting large releases into smaller batches.

title: M-05 | Enforced Options Not Applied On releaseOnEid
description: In the releaseOnEid function the options provided to the _lzSend call are not combined with the apps enforced options using the combineOptions function. As a result the enforced options for the send message type are not applied.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the releaseOnEid function of the contract that forwards cross‑chain messages via the internal _lzSend call. The function accepts a set of user‑provided messaging options, but it fails to merge those options with the protocol‑enforced options by calling the combineOptions helper. As a result, the mandatory options that the LayerZero endpoint requires for a send‑type message – such as gas limits, payment enforcement, or reliability flags – are never attached to the outbound packet. The root cause is a missing combineOptions invocation, which means the caller’s raw options are passed directly to _lzSend, effectively overriding any safety defaults that the contract intended to enforce. An attacker who can influence the options argument (for example by calling releaseOnEid through a malicious contract) can supply a crafted option set that disables gas budgeting or removes verification flags, allowing the message to be sent with insufficient resources or without required security checks. This can be exploited to cause the cross‑chain transfer to fail silently, to trigger a denial‑of‑service on the destination chain, or in worst cases to manipulate the message payload because the enforced integrity checks are bypassed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction appears to succeed on the source chain but the expected asset (NFT, token, or state update) never appears on the destination chain, or the user receives an empty or zero‑value response. The issue occurs every time releaseOnEid is invoked, i.e., whenever a user attempts to release a token on a remote chain, and only when the caller can control the options parameter. All participants that rely on the contract’s cross‑chain functionality – token holders, marketplace operators, and the broader protocol – are affected because the reliability and accounting guarantees of the messaging layer are compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the flow of options through the LayerZero integration and noticed that the combineOptions step was omitted. It is hard to notice because the function still compiles and the transaction does not revert; the missing options are invisible in the transaction receipt, and the failure only manifests as missing assets on the remote chain. To remediate the issue the releaseOnEid implementation should invoke combineOptions with the contract’s enforced options and the caller‑provided options before passing the result to _lzSend, thereby guaranteeing that all mandatory messaging parameters are present regardless of user input. This class of bug is a typical “option enforcement bypass” where user‑controlled configuration overrides required security settings, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential loss of funds.

title: M-06 | Different Gas Limits May Lead To DOS
description: Different chains have different gas limits. Due to the fact that a user can send as many tokens as they have using releaseOnEid, it may be possible that the tx has enough gas limit on the source chain, but not enough gas Limit to execute on destination chain. For example ETH Mainnet gas limit is 30M, however Avalanche C-chain is 15M, half the gas limit. This can lead to permanently stuck NFT's when the execution of the _lzReceive will exceed the max block gas limit and any retry attempts will fail. This issue may be more prevalent on chains with an even lower gas limit such as some chains have as low as 8M gas limit. This small of a gas limit can be reached with about 57 tokens being sent.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain denial‑of‑service condition caused by mismatched block gas limits between the source and destination blockchains when a user bridges a large batch of NFTs using the releaseOnEid function. The root cause is that the bridging contract assumes the destination chain can execute the _lzReceive handler with the same gas budget that was available on the source chain. Because each blockchain enforces its own maximum block gas limit (for example 30 million on Ethereum mainnet versus 15 million on Avalanche C‑chain, and as low as 8 million on some other networks), a transaction that includes many NFTs may exceed the destination’s gas ceiling. When this happens the _lzReceive call runs out of gas, the message cannot be processed, and any automatic retry attempts also fail because the gas requirement remains above the block limit. The impact is that the NFTs become permanently stuck on the bridge: the user sees a successful transaction on the source chain, but the corresponding NFTs never appear on the destination chain, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show no error, leading the user to believe the assets are lost. This condition occurs whenever a user attempts to bridge more than a few dozen NFTs in a single transaction on a chain with a low gas limit; the report notes that about 57 tokens are enough to hit an 8 million‑gas limit. All parties that rely on the bridge – individual token holders, the protocol’s cross‑chain marketplace, and any downstream applications – are affected because the bridge can no longer deliver assets and may appear unreliable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared gas limits across supported chains and identified that the contract does not perform any gas‑limit checks before batching transfers. It is hard to notice because the source‑chain transaction succeeds and emits events, while the failure occurs silently on the destination chain, leaving no obvious revert or error message. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a conservative batch size (for example 10‑20 NFTs per transaction) or dynamically calculate the maximum safe batch based on the destination chain’s gas limit, possibly splitting larger batches into multiple transactions or providing a fallback mechanism that retries with reduced payload size. This class of bug falls under “gas‑limit mismatch leading to cross‑chain denial‑of‑service” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a bridged asset will be delivered atomically after the source transaction confirms.

title: M-07 | Callback Gas Is Never Specified
description: The _updateOwnership function concludes with a callback to the shadow NFT via _shadow.executeCallback(guid);. While this callback is included in the gas cost, it adds only a negligible increase of 20k gas: uint128 baseGasCost = withCallback _BASE_OWNERSHIP_UPDATE_COST_WITH_CALLBACK // 100k _BASE_OWNERSHIP_UPDATE_COST; // 80k This small gas amount is insufficient to cover any callback, especially a more complex one. Additionally, the callback has no predefined gas limit, which means it could unintentionally consume more gas than expected, causing the function to revert with an OOG error.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing gas limit on a callback that is executed at the end of the ownership‑update routine. When the internal function that changes NFT ownership finishes, it invokes a shadow contract through a call like _shadow.executeCallback(guid). The surrounding code adds a small constant (approximately twenty thousand gas) to the estimated cost, assuming that the callback will be trivial. However, the callback itself is not constrained by any explicit gas stipend, and the base gas allocation is far below what a non‑trivial callback may require. Consequently, if the shadow contract’s callback contains any appreciable logic – for example, additional state writes, external calls, or loops – it can consume more gas than the tiny buffer, causing the whole _updateOwnership transaction to run out of gas and revert. This failure can happen whenever ownership is transferred, minted, or otherwise updated, because every such operation triggers the callback. From a user perspective the symptoms are confusing: a transaction may appear to have been submitted successfully, the UI may show a “transfer” button that seems to work, yet the ownership record does not change, or the transaction receipt reports an out‑of‑gas error after the fact. The protocol’s guarantee that ownership updates are atomic is broken, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate transfers cannot be completed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined gas accounting and noticed that the callback gas was never bounded. It is hard to notice because the extra gas cost is small and the callback is external, so developers may assume it will always fit within the added buffer. The root cause is the reliance on an implicit gas assumption rather than an explicit limit, which violates the principle that any external call should be supplied with a known gas amount. To remediate, the contract should accept a gas limit as a parameter or enforce a safe maximum when invoking the callback, ensuring that the called code cannot unexpectedly exhaust the caller’s gas and cause a revert. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked callback gas limit or an under‑estimated external call gas cost, and it can lead to funds appearing to disappear, ownership updates failing silently, and overall loss of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: M-08 | releaseOnEid In NFTShadow May Lead To DOS
description: The releaseOnEid function in NFTShadow assumes that we are only releasing to non native chains. This can be observed by the send calculations below function getSendOptions(uint256[] calldata tokenIds) public pure returns (bytes memory) {uint128 totalGasRequired = _BASE_OWNERSHIP_UPDATE_COST + (_INCREMENTAL_OWNERSHIP_UPDATE_COST * uint128(tokenIds.length)); returnOptionsBuilder.newOptions().addExecutorLzReceiveOption(totalGasRequired, 0);} The function assumes that we are always doing an ownership update but does not account for the fact that if we release to chain that includes the native collection that we will instead use delegations which are more expensive. This may result in a DOS due to not enough gas being sent to the destination chain to execute the message. However the tx can be retried after failure.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the releaseOnEid function of the NFTShadow contract. The function builds a set of LayerZero send options based on a fixed gas estimate that only covers the base ownership‑update cost and an incremental cost per token ID. It implicitly assumes that the destination chain never hosts the native collection, therefore the transfer will always be performed via a simple ownership update. When the destination chain does include the native collection, the contract uses a delegation mechanism that requires additional gas for each delegation step. Because the gas estimate does not include this extra cost, the message sent to the destination chain may run out of gas, causing the cross‑chain release to fail. The failure manifests as a reverted transaction or a silent drop of the message, leaving the NFT locked in the shadow contract and preventing the user from receiving the asset on the target chain. This situation creates a denial‑of‑service condition: an attacker (or even an honest user) can trigger the release to a native‑chain destination and cause the operation to consistently fail, effectively freezing the NFT until the transaction is manually retried with higher gas or the contract logic is corrected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the gas calculation logic with the actual execution path for native‑chain releases. It is subtle because the function name and the surrounding code suggest that the gas estimate is generic, and the extra delegation cost is only incurred for a subset of chains, making the problem easy to miss in testing that only covers non‑native destinations. The root cause is an incorrect assumption about the execution path and a hard‑coded gas formula that does not account for delegation overhead. To remediate, the contract should detect whether the target Eid includes the native collection and, if so, add the delegation gas cost to the send options, or redesign the shadow to delegate gas estimation to a central beacon that knows the exact cost per chain. By ensuring that sufficient gas is always supplied, the release operation will succeed, preserving the expected business logic that an NFT can be moved across chains without being locked or lost.

title: M-09 | Same Address Controlled By Multiple Parties
description: The releaseOnEid function transfers the delegation rights to the beneficiary address on the origin chain. This means that the owner of the beneficiary address must be the same on both the origin and destination chain. If this is not the case one party is able to steal potential delegated airdrops, or the other party is unable to claim. In the case of multisig accounts across different chains, it is viable that contract addresses are not the same across different chains despite trading across EVM compatible chains.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an unsafe assumption that a single Ethereum address is owned by the same entity on every EVM‑compatible chain. The releaseOnEid function of the Beacon contract automatically transfers delegation rights for Shadow tokens to the beneficiary address on the origin chain at the moment the function is called. This transfer is performed without confirming that the caller controls the beneficiary address on the origin chain, only that the address exists on the destination chain. When the same address is controlled by different parties on different chains – a situation that can occur with multisig contracts that have distinct deployments per chain – the party that controls the address on the destination chain can receive the delegated airdrop rights even though they do not own the address on the origin chain. Consequently the legitimate owner on the origin chain loses the right to claim the airdrop, and the malicious party may steal the delegated tokens. The flaw is triggered whenever releaseOnEid is executed and the cross‑chain ownership of the beneficiary address diverges. Users experience the symptom of a missing or zero balance after they expected a delegated airdrop, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The issue was identified during a manual audit by the Guardian team, and it is subtle because the address string looks identical on both chains, masking the underlying ownership mismatch. To remediate, delegation rights should not be granted immediately; instead the contract should wait for the releaseOnEid lifecycle to complete on the origin chain and then synchronize the ownership state using the triggerOwnershipUpdate function. This approach allows users who control the address only on the destination chain to pre‑delegate their rights to an address they control on all chains, preventing accidental or malicious delegation on the origin chain. The bug belongs to the class of cross‑chain ownership assumption errors, where business logic incorrectly treats an address as a universal identifier for authority, violating accounting assumptions that token rights are tied to a single, consistent owner.

title: M-10 | Read Response Censoring
description: Because the _lzReceive function invokes the executeMessage function in a try/catch and specifically leaves behind 50,000 gas units to complete the outer function execution it is possible for a malicious actor to intentionally censor an lzRead response by executing the lzReceive function with a minimal amount of gas. This way the inner executeMessage function is not forwarded enough gas to complete execution and fails. As a result the message is added to the payloadHashes mapping in the Beacon contract. Both normal layerzero messages and layerzero read responses can be censored this way. But specifically layerzero read requests are not allowed to be retried in the Beacon contract so they are effectively censored. To pull off this attack a malicious actor can simply observe that the last required DVN has submitted their verification and then call the commitVerification and lzReceive functions on the receive library and EndpointV2 contracts accordingly.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑censorship flaw in the _lzReceive function of the receive library and EndpointV2 contracts. _lzReceive forwards the incoming LayerZero payload to an internal executeMessage call inside a try/catch block and deliberately reserves only 50,000 gas units for the outer function after the catch. Because the inner executeMessage requires more gas to complete, a malicious actor can invoke lzReceive with a minimal gas stipend, causing the inner call to run out of gas and revert. The catch block swallows the error, the outer function still returns, and the message identifier is stored in the Beacon contract's payloadHashes mapping. For normal messages this may be observable, but for LayerZero read responses the Beacon contract does not provide a retry mechanism, so the censored response is permanently lost. The attack can be carried out by watching for the moment when the last required DVN verification is submitted, then calling commitVerification followed by lzReceive with insufficient gas. From a user perspective a read request appears to be processed on‑chain but the UI receives no data, leading to empty results or a missing refund, contrary to the expectation that the request will return the requested information. The issue is hard to detect because the outer transaction does not revert and the failure is hidden inside the try/catch, making the contract state look normal while the payload is effectively dropped. The root cause is the combination of a fixed low gas reservation after a try/catch and the lack of a retry path for read responses. To remediate, the contract should validate at the beginning of _lzReceive that enough gas is available to safely execute the inner logic and any callbacks, and revert if the gas left is below a safe threshold. This prevents an attacker from deliberately starving the inner call and censoring messages, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: M-11 | Insufficient Return Data Length Options
description: In the triggerMetadataRead and triggerOwnershipUpdate functions there is no enforcement of the expected returndata length for the read request. The expected returndata length must be speciﬁed so that the executor can be adequately compensated for executing the lzReceive function once the message has been veriﬁed. If users call the triggerMetadataRead and triggerOwnershipUpdate functions with extra options including the correct return data size then the executor will not execute the lzReceive function upon DVN veriﬁcation and users will have to manually execute the message through the endpoint. Furthermore the return data size cannot be enforced at the enforced options level since it varies based upon the query being made.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of the expected return‑data length in the functions that trigger cross‑chain metadata reads and ownership updates. When a caller invokes these functions without specifying the correct size of the data that will be returned, the executor that processes the LayerZero message cannot determine how much gas to allocate for the lzReceive callback after the decentralized verification network (DVN) confirms the message. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum return‑data size, an attacker or careless user can supply options that omit or underestimate the required length. In that situation the executor will skip the automatic execution of lzReceive, leaving the message unprocessed until someone manually calls the endpoint to complete the operation. From a user’s perspective the expected metadata (for example a tokenURI) or ownership change never appears, the UI shows a missing or empty value, and the user may be forced to perform extra steps or lose the ability to retrieve the data altogether. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition for cross‑chain reads: users cannot rely on the contract to deliver metadata or ownership updates automatically, which breaks the business logic that assumes timely propagation of state across chains. The flaw occurs whenever the trigger functions are called with custom options that do not include a correct expected return‑data length, which is possible because the contract does not enforce this parameter and the required size varies depending on the specific query. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the option handling logic and noticed that the getReadOptions helper was only used in a downstream contract, leaving the Beacon contract without a safeguard. The problem is subtle because the contract still compiles and works for correctly‑sized calls, so the missing check does not raise an immediate error and may only be observed when a call fails to return data. The proper fix is to centralise the construction of read options at the Beacon level, enforce that every trigger includes a correctly calculated expected return‑data length, and expose only the safe wrapper through the collection contract. By guaranteeing that the executor always knows the required data size, the lzReceive callback will be executed automatically after DVN verification, restoring the intended cross‑chain flow and preventing users from having to manually intervene.

title: M-12 | Burned Tokens Minted Arbitrarily
description: The NFTShadow contract makes incorrect assumptions about access control on minting. On an unlocked chain, after a token is burned, it remains unlocked. While unlocked it is possible for any user to to re mint(), updateOwnership() and steal delegations on other chains. In the comments "Only the Beacon contract can mint tokens, enforced by _beforeTokenTransfer". However the condition is actually as follows: if (msg.sender = BEACON_CONTRACT_ADDRESS) if (tokenIsLocked(tokenId)) revert CallerNotBeacon(); // if not beacon and locked} // if you are beacon, or unlocked
bug_full: The NFTShadow contract contains an access‑control flaw that permits arbitrary minting of tokens that have previously been burned. The contract’s internal comment claims that only the Beacon contract may mint tokens and that this restriction is enforced in the _beforeTokenTransfer hook. In reality the implemented condition only reverts when the caller is not the Beacon address and the token is locked; when the token is unlocked the check passes for any caller. After a token is burned the contract fails to mark the token as locked, leaving it in an unlocked state. Because the lock flag is false, any user can invoke the public mint function with the burned token identifier, and subsequently call updateOwnership on other chains to claim delegation rights that originally belonged to the legitimate owner. This bug can be exploited by an attacker who watches for burn events, then immediately re‑mintes the same token ID and updates the cross‑chain ownership record, effectively stealing the delegation. The impact is the creation of unauthorized NFTs and the loss of delegation or control over assets that were thought to be destroyed. The vulnerability manifests only after a burn transaction when the token remains unlocked; it does not require any special privileges beyond being able to call the contract’s public functions. All participants in the ecosystem – token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the stolen delegation may be used to authorize actions on other chains. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s comments with its actual logic and identified the mismatch in the access‑control condition. It is easy to miss because the comment suggests proper restriction and the unlocked flag is a subtle state that is not visible in typical UI displays. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the Beacon address can call mint regardless of the token’s lock state, and it should ensure that burned tokens are permanently locked or marked as non‑mintable, preventing any further re‑creation of the same identifier.

title: M-13 | Collateral Of Epoch Ahead Can Be Stolen
description: When updating share price after an epoch, if no collateral was received, the share price is set to 1e18. This creates a significant issue as depositors can redeem their entire collateral even though no collateral was received after closing the liquidity position. Effectively, this allows depositors to withdraw funds that belong to the next epoch's depositors, who have already transferred their collateral into the contract.
bug_full: During the epoch transition the contract updates a variable called sharePrice that represents the amount of collateral each share is worth. The implementation contains a conditional that, when the amount of collateral received for the just‑finished epoch is zero, forces sharePrice to be set to the fixed‑point constant 1e18 (representing a 1:1 ratio). This default value is correct when collateral is present, but it becomes incorrect when no collateral was actually transferred. Because redemption logic multiplies the number of shares held by the stored sharePrice, a sharePrice of 1e18 makes the contract believe that each share is still fully backed, even though the vault holds no assets for that epoch. An attacker who holds shares from the previous epoch can therefore call the redeem function after a zero‑collateral epoch and receive the full amount of collateral that has already been deposited for the next epoch. The bug is triggered only when an epoch ends with zero collateral and there are already deposits for the following epoch, which makes the condition relatively rare and easy to overlook during testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal request returns far more tokens than were originally supplied, or that later depositors find their balances reduced to zero without any explicit penalty. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the share‑price update routine, where the logic for handling a zero‑collateral case was found to be missing. It is hard to notice because the default value of 1e18 looks like a neutral “no‑change” setting and the contract does not emit a warning when the collateral amount is zero. The proper fix is to avoid assigning a non‑zero sharePrice when no collateral is received; the sharePrice for the affected epoch should be set to zero (or left unchanged) and the next epoch’s sharePrice must be recomputed based on the actual collateral that arrives. By ensuring that the redemption calculation reflects the true amount of assets in the vault, the protocol prevents users from withdrawing funds that belong to future depositors and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: M-01 | Insufficient Gas Estimated
description: In the requestClaim function the checks.numNFTs and checks.numCollectors values are used to compute the gas that should be provided to the lzReceive function on the L2. However the checks.numCollectors value only includes the number of collector claims that need to be veriﬁed on the L1, which does not include claims where the collector is the claimer. These claims will still have to be iterated over in the lzReceive function though, and thus should be accounted for in the gas estimation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient gas estimation in the cross‑chain claim flow. In the requestClaim function the contract calculates the amount of gas to forward to the lzReceive function on L2 by multiplying the number of NFTs and the number of collectors stored in the checks struct. The checks.numCollectors field only counts collector claims that must be verified on L1; it deliberately excludes claims where the collector is also the claimer. However, the lzReceive implementation on L2 still iterates over every collector entry, including those where the collector equals the claimer, to update internal accounting. Because these extra iterations are not reflected in the gas estimate, the forwarded gas may be lower than required, causing the lzReceive call to run out of gas. When this occurs the transaction reverts on L2, the claim is not recorded, and the user receives no tokens or refund, appearing as a silent failure in the UI. The bug manifests whenever a user submits a claim that involves at least one collector‑as‑claimer situation, which is common in many claim scenarios. It affects any participant attempting to claim NFTs through the cross‑chain bridge, as well as the protocol itself because failed claims can lock funds and degrade user trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic used for gas estimation with the actual loop bounds in lzReceive, revealing a mismatch. Because the failure is an out‑of‑gas revert rather than an explicit error, it can be hard to notice; the transaction simply fails without a clear reason, and the front‑end may only show a generic “claim failed” message. This class of bug belongs to gas‑estimation or out‑of‑gas vulnerabilities, where the contract under‑estimates the resources needed for a dynamic loop. The correct mitigation is to base the gas estimate on the length of the configuration array (configs.length), which accurately reflects the number of iterations performed in lzReceive, or to add a safety margin. By aligning the gas calculation with the actual loop count, the contract will provide sufficient gas, preventing out‑of‑gas reverts and ensuring that claims are processed correctly.

title: M-02 | Incompatible Types
description: A VestingConfig object contains uint256 streamId but the VestingConfigStorage contains uint8 streamId. Consequently, some user configurations will be unclaimable when the uint256 type is cast to uint8 within _saveClaimParameters, as it will revert with error Overflow().
bug_full: The contract defines a VestingConfig struct that stores a stream identifier as a uint256, but the persistent storage mapping VestingConfigStorage stores the same identifier as a uint8. When the internal function _saveClaimParameters copies the value from the struct to storage, Solidity performs an implicit down‑cast from uint256 to uint8. If the original streamId exceeds the maximum value that fits in 8 bits (255), the cast triggers the custom Overflow() error and the transaction reverts. As a result, any vesting configuration that uses a streamId larger than 255 becomes permanently unclaimable: the user can call the claim function, but the transaction fails before the claim logic updates balances, leaving the allocated tokens locked in the contract. The bug appears only when a user or the protocol creates a stream with an identifier that does not fit into a uint8, which can happen in systems that generate sequential IDs using a uint256 counter. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the data types used in the struct and the storage layout and noticed the mismatch. Because the revert occurs inside an internal helper function, the failure may be observed only as a generic transaction reverted message without a clear indication that the overflow is the cause, making it hard for users to understand why their funds are not claimable. The vulnerability belongs to the class of type‑mismatch or integer‑truncation bugs, where a larger integer type is silently down‑cast to a smaller one without proper validation. The impact is that legitimate token holders may lose access to their vested assets, effectively causing a loss of funds for the affected users, while the protocol’s reputation suffers because claimed balances do not match expectations. To remediate the issue, the contract should keep the streamId type consistent across all layers (e.g., store it as uint256 everywhere) or add explicit range checks before casting, reverting with a clear error message if the value does not fit. Documentation should also state the maximum allowed streamId if a smaller type is intentionally used.

title: M-03 | Sanctions Can Be Avoided
description: Currently checkClaims only validates sanctions against the claimer: if (isSanctioned(claimer)) return (claimNonce, false); However, there's is no validation that the actual owner of the NFT is not sanctioned in the case that the claimer is a delegate.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing sanctions validation on the true owner of an NFT when a claim is performed through a delegated address. The contract’s checkClaims routine only calls isSanctioned on the address that initiates the claim (the claimer) and returns false if that address is sanctioned. It never inspects the ownership record of the token that is being claimed. Consequently, if the token owner is listed on a sanctions list but authorises a non‑sanctioned delegate to submit the claim, the contract treats the transaction as legitimate and transfers the reward to the delegate, effectively allowing the sanctioned owner to receive value indirectly. This flaw arises from an incomplete authorization check: the business rule that “no sanctioned participant may receive claim proceeds” is enforced only for the caller, not for the token holder. Exploitation requires a sanctioned NFT holder to grant claim rights to an unrestricted address, which then calls the claim function; the contract sees a clean caller and skips the sanction barrier, resulting in the transfer of funds that should have been blocked. The impact includes potential violation of regulatory compliance, exposure of the protocol to legal risk, and the possibility that malicious actors could funnel assets to prohibited parties while appearing to comply with the contract’s checks. The condition under which the bug manifests is any scenario where the claim function is invoked by a delegate on behalf of an owner who is on a sanctions list. Users may notice that a claim succeeds even though the underlying NFT is owned by a blacklisted address, leading to unexpected fund flows or refunds that appear to come from a legitimate source. The issue is subtle because the contract emits no explicit warning about the owner’s status, and the only logged check is for the caller, making the bypass easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate, the contract should perform an isSanctioned check on both the caller and the current owner of the token before approving any claim, or the documentation must clearly state that only the caller’s sanction status is enforced, so that callers understand the limitation.

title: M-14 | Tick Modulus Hardcoded For Fee Tier
description: _calculateTickBounds() uses modulus 200 in order to set the target tick value to the closest acceptable tick range. However, Foil is compatible with multiple fee tiers, but the value 200 is not. For instance, the 0.3% fee tier uses a tick spacing of 60, which is not a divisor of 200. This will cause a revert when attempting to create the epoch.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded modulus value (200) used in the internal function _calculateTickBounds to snap a target tick to the nearest allowed tick range. The contract is designed to work with multiple fee tiers, each of which defines its own tick spacing (for example the 0.3 % tier uses a spacing of 60). Because 200 is not a multiple of 60, the modulus operation can produce a tick that does not align with the pool’s allowed tick grid. When the contract later attempts to create an epoch with this mis‑aligned tick, the pool’s validation logic reverts the transaction. This manifests as a revert during epoch creation, preventing users from opening new positions or claiming rewards. It occurs whenever a pool with a fee tier whose spacing does not divide 200 is used, i.e., any tier other than those with spacing 200, 100, 50, etc. The affected parties are liquidity providers and protocol operators who rely on the vault to open epochs; funds may remain locked because the epoch never materialises. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the tick‑calculation routine and compared it against the fee‑tier configuration. Because the revert only happens under specific fee‑tier configurations, it can be easy to miss in generic testing that only covers the default tier. The bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded configuration errors where a constant is assumed to be universal but is actually tier‑specific. From a user’s point of view the UI shows a transaction failure or an empty response when “Create Epoch” is pressed, and the expected new epoch does not appear, leading to confusion and wasted gas. To fix the problem the contract should retrieve the tick spacing from the pool’s fee tier (or pass it as a parameter) and use that value in the modulus operation instead of the literal 200. This ensures the calculated tick always aligns with the pool’s allowed grid, eliminating the unexpected revert and restoring the expected behaviour of epoch creation.

title: M-01 | ShadowFactory Cannot Deploy NFTs
description: ShadowFactory is used to create shadow NFTs. It implements Ownable and has onlyOwner on deployAndRegister to prevent anyone but the owner from using this function. However, the issue is that this owner is never initialized, meaning that after deployment, the owner would be address 0 and no one would be able to call deployAndRegister.
bug_full: The vulnerability in the ShadowFactory contract is an uninitialized ownership variable that results from the contract inheriting an Ownable pattern but never invoking the internal owner‑initialization routine. Because the constructor does not call _initializeOwner (or an equivalent setup function), the owner field remains the zero address after deployment. The onlyOwner modifier on the deployAndRegister function therefore rejects every call, as no external account can match the zero address. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the contract cannot be used to create shadow NFTs, users attempting to mint receive no token, and the expected business logic of registering and issuing NFTs is broken. The issue manifests immediately after the contract is deployed, before any interaction, and affects any party that relies on the factory to generate NFTs, including end users, the protocol’s revenue model, and developers expecting the function to be callable by the contract owner. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the constructor and ownership initialization flow, noting that the inherited Ownable contract requires explicit initialization. The problem can be subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the owner variable defaults to zero, which may not be obvious without testing the access‑controlled function. To remediate, the contract should initialize the owner in its constructor by invoking _initializeOwner, or provide a dedicated initialization function that also calls the guard _guardInitializeOwner to prevent re‑initialization. Conceptually, this is a classic initialization bug where critical state is left at its default value, leading to inaccessible functionality and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that minted NFTs will be delivered to users.

title: M-02 | There Is No Function For triggerMetadataRead
description: MetadataReadRenderer has a function to update the metadata for NFTs on different chains. Where the main function - triggerMetadataRead must be called by the NFTShadow contract to invoke the change, as it gets the baseCollectionAddress from IBeacon(beacon).shadowToBase(msg.sender). Meaning that msg.sender must be NFTShadow. However the NFTShadow lacks a method which invokes triggerMetadataRead.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing entry point in the NFTShadow contract that should forward calls to the MetadataReadRenderer contract’s triggerMetadataRead function. MetadataReadRenderer is designed to refresh on‑chain NFT metadata across multiple chains, but it only accepts calls when the caller (msg.sender) is the NFTShadow contract, as it derives the base collection address from the beacon via shadowToBase(msg.sender). Because NFTShadow does not expose any public or external function that invokes triggerMetadataRead, there is no legitimate way for the protocol or its owner to initiate a metadata refresh. The root cause is a design omission: the contract author assumed the existence of a trigger function without implementing the corresponding accessor in NFTShadow. Exploitation is not a classic attack vector; instead, the bug prevents the intended functionality. Any party that expects the metadata to be updated – for example, a user who purchases an NFT on a secondary chain and expects the artwork or attributes to reflect a later change – will see stale or missing information. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a blank image, an unchanged description, or a zero‑value attribute when a change was announced on the primary chain. The issue manifests whenever the protocol attempts to call triggerMetadataRead, which will silently fail because the call never originates from NFTShadow. All token holders, the protocol’s governance, and any downstream applications that rely on up‑to‑date metadata are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the interface of MetadataReadRenderer with the functions actually implemented in NFTShadow, revealing the absence of a forwarding method. Because the contracts compile and no transaction reverts, the bug can remain unnoticed until a metadata update is required and the UI shows no change. To remediate, the NFTShadow contract should be extended with an onlyOwner external function that calls the renderer’s triggerMetadataRead, ensuring that the authorized party can initiate metadata refreshes.
