This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that metadata updates must be possible after deployment, restoring the contract’s ability to keep NFT information consistent across chains.

title: M-01 | Incorrect Bump Calculation
description:
The criteria for a bump is described as:
That the total reserves in the system (inclusive of debt), when placed across the anchor position
(with no reserves the floor), is enough to buy back the entire circulating supply.
However, in the _canBump function the capacity is calculated with the activeX96 as the upper to the
Anchor range.
This is however flawed because the activeX96 may not reside within the new Anchor range. Instead
the anchorTick may be selected such that the activeX96 is actually within the Discovery range.
This would not be an issue if the Discovery and Anchor ranges were guaranteed to have the same
concentration of reserves.
However it is possible that the Discovery range liquidity is actually lower than the Anchor range
liquidity, in which case assuming that the reserves were evenly spread out across this range would
underestimate the capacity of the protocol and errantly indicate that a bump would not be possible
when in fact it can be.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect bump‑eligibility calculation in the protocol’s liquidity management logic. The contract determines whether a "bump" – a reallocation of reserves that should allow the total reserves (including debt) to repurchase the entire circulating supply – is possible by computing a capacity value. The root cause is that the _canBump function uses the current activeX96 price as the upper bound of the new Anchor range, assuming that this price always lies inside the Anchor range after the tick is moved. In reality the new anchorTick can be chosen so that activeX96 falls outside the Anchor range but remains inside the Discovery range. The function also implicitly assumes that reserves are uniformly distributed across the Anchor and Discovery ranges. When the Discovery range holds less liquidity than the Anchor range, this uniform‑distribution assumption leads to an under‑estimation of the protocol’s true capacity. Consequently the function may return false, indicating that a bump is not possible, even though sufficient reserves exist. An attacker or a malicious governance action could deliberately set the anchorTick and liquidity distribution to trigger this mis‑calculation, preventing a legitimate bump. The impact is that the protocol may fail to execute a bump that would otherwise protect liquidity providers or maintain price stability, effectively freezing part of the capital and reducing expected returns. The bug manifests only when the new anchorTick places activeX96 outside the Anchor range while the Discovery range has a different concentration of liquidity – a condition that is not obvious from the code and therefore easy to miss during testing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted the logical inconsistency between the range definitions and the capacity formula. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a bump transaction that should succeed is rejected, leading to unexpected “no bump” messages, unchanged balances, and potentially lower yields. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of range‑based liquidity accounting errors, where assumptions about uniform reserve distribution cause incorrect financial decisions. To remediate, the bump logic should be executed only after the new anchorTick and the actual liquidities of both Anchor and Discovery ranges have been finalized, and the capacity calculation must use the real liquidity values of each range rather than a proxy based on activeX96. Additionally, the bump routine should be prohibited from altering the liquidity of either range during its execution, ensuring that the decision is based on a stable snapshot of the system state.

title: M-05 | WETH Rewards Stolen From Owner
description: The ExitVault will distribute GMX and WETH rewards to stakers based on the sbfGMX and fGLP provided. If owner also transfers sbfGMX and fGLP tokens to vault during deployment, these will also earn WETH rewards. The issue relies on how the protocol calculates the accumulated rewards per share, as it does not include the sbfGMX and fsGLP tokens in the vault using gmxSide and glpSide. There are two major impacts here: • External users can steal owner's WETH rewards generated by sbfGMX and fGLP tokens in vault • Owner is DoS'ed from depositing or claiming, as the pendingWeth calculation leads to more WETH than the contract's balance.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/eGMX-1/pull/4/files
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the ExitVault reward logic. The contract distributes GMX and WETH rewards to stakers based on the amount of sbfGMX and fGLP tokens that are considered for vesting. During deployment the contract owner also transfers sbfGMX and fGLP tokens into the vault, but the internal calculation of accumulated rewards per share only uses the gmxSide and glpSide variables, which track only a subset of the deposited assets. Because the owner‑supplied sbfGMX and fGLP are omitted from the per‑share denominator, the reward‑per‑share value becomes artificially high. An external attacker who stakes any amount can call the claim function and receive a share of the WETH rewards that actually belong to the owner’s tokens. The owner therefore loses WETH that should have been allocated to their own position, and the pendingWeth value can exceed the contract’s actual WETH balance, causing subsequent deposit or claim calls to revert and effectively denying service to the owner. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution code where the relationship between deposited token balances and the variables used in the reward calculation was examined. It is subtle because the contract appears to distribute rewards correctly for ordinary users; the problem only manifests when the owner also contributes the same token types that are excluded from the accounting, a scenario that is not obvious from the UI. The bug belongs to the class of “reward‑share miscalculation” or “incorrect accounting of stake assets”, which violates the fundamental business assumption that rewards are proportional to the actual amount of assets held in the vault. From a user perspective the symptoms are that the owner sees WETH rewards disappear or become zero despite having supplied tokens, while other users receive unexpectedly large WETH payouts. To remediate the issue the reward‑per‑share computation must be updated to include all sbfGMX and fGLP tokens held by the vault, or the owner should deposit those tokens during initialization so that they are correctly reflected in the gmxSide and glpSide variables. Ensuring that the accounting variables accurately represent the total stake eliminates the possibility of reward theft and prevents the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: M-06 | Protocol Will Be DoS'd When Private Mode True
description: GMX's reward tracker has the ability to set inPrivateClaimingMode to true. When this happens claiming will revert as the action is no longer enabled. If this happens any function that interacts with the _updateVester will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the GMX reward tracker caused by the boolean flag inPrivateClaimingMode. When this flag is set to true, the contract disables the public claim functionality; any attempt to claim rewards triggers a revert because the claim action is no longer enabled. Moreover, the internal function _updateVester, which is invoked by several other protocol operations, also reverts when the flag is active. The root cause is that the private‑claiming mode is implemented without isolating its effect to only the intended claim path, so other functions that rely on vesting updates inherit the same revert behaviour. An attacker or a privileged account that can toggle the flag can therefore lock the reward‑claiming mechanism and cause any transaction that touches the vesting logic to fail. This can be exploited simply by setting inPrivateClaimingMode to true, after which users who try to claim their accrued rewards receive a transaction failure and see no change in their token balance. The impact is that users are unable to receive expected rewards, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol may be unable to process vesting updates, effectively freezing reward distribution for the duration of the flag being true. The condition occurs whenever the flag is true, regardless of who initiates the claim or vesting update. Affected parties include token holders, reward claimants, and any component of the protocol that depends on vesting state updates. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the private‑claiming mode and the vesting update logic, noting that the revert path was not guarded. It can be hard to notice because the flag is intended for a legitimate private mode, and the UI may simply hide the claim button without clearly indicating that underlying transactions will revert, leading users to think the contract is malfunctioning. To remediate, the contract should either separate the private‑claiming mode from the vesting update path, add explicit checks before calling _updateVester when the flag is true, or provide an administrative mechanism to disable the flag promptly. At a minimum, the risk of funds being temporarily inaccessible should be documented so that users understand the possibility of a denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: M-07 | Unfair Reward Distribution On Donation Update
description: The donationPart can be updated with the increaseDonation function. This update will probably lead to an unfair distribution of rewards: • Current donationPart is 10% • Alice & Bob are the only stakers and deposit the same amt of funds • y amt of rewards are accumulated • Bob claims his part of the rewards and receives y/2*0.1% of the accumulated rewards • One block later the donation amt is increased to 20% • Alice claims her part of the rewards and receives y/2*0.2% of the accumulated rewards Now one staker received double the rewards for depositing the same amount of funds over the same period of time. Both should receive 10% of the accumulated rewards up to the point of changing the donationPart and 20% after that.
bug_full: The contract allows the protocol owner to change the donation share (donationPart) through the increaseDonation function. Rewards that have been accumulated for stakers are calculated at the moment a user claims, using the current donationPart value rather than the value that was in effect when each portion of the reward was earned. As a result, if the donationPart is increased after some rewards have accrued but before all stakers have claimed, a user who claims after the change receives a larger percentage of the total accumulated rewards than a user who claimed before the change, even though both deposited the same amount for the same time period. In the described scenario, Bob claimed his reward while the donationPart was 10 % and received y/2 * 0.1 % of the total rewards. One block later the donationPart was raised to 20 % and Alice claimed her reward, receiving y/2 * 0.2 % of the same reward pool. Consequently Alice obtained twice the share that she should have received for the period before the change. The vulnerability stems from the reward‑distribution logic not snapshotting the donation share at the time each reward is generated, and from using a single mutable factor for the whole pool. It can be exploited by timing a claim after a donationPart increase, allowing a staker to capture a larger slice of rewards that were earned under the previous, lower share. The impact is an unfair redistribution of funds: the protocol loses the excess amount paid to the later claimant, stakers receive inconsistent returns, and the accounting assumptions that each staker gets a proportional share of rewards based on their stake and the active donation rate are violated. The issue appears only when the donationPart is modified while rewards are still pending, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of reward calculation and the update of donationPart. Because the contract still reports that rewards were correctly claimed, the discrepancy is not obvious from the UI – a user sees a normal claim transaction but may notice that another user received a higher payout for the same stake. To remediate, the reward logic should employ an accumulator (e.g., a per‑share reward index) that records the cumulative reward per token at each donationPart change, and each user’s pending reward should be calculated based on the difference between the current accumulator and the user’s last recorded checkpoint. The protocol and owner share should be removed from the _updateVester function and handled separately, ensuring that historical reward portions are always allocated using the donationPart that was active when they were generated.

title: M-08 | Centralization Issues
description: The ExitVaultEntryPoint contract grants the admin extensive control, posing significant centralization risks. Specifically, the rescueFunds function allows the admin to withdraw arbitrary tokens from any vault under the contract's management, including user-deposited assets and accrued rewards such as GMX and WETH. This enables the admin to transfer user funds without consent. Additionally, the admin has the authority to upgrade the implementation of the ExitVault contract via the UpgradeableBeacon. While intended for enhancements and bug fixes, this upgradability feature allows the admin to deploy malicious implementations that could manipulate user balances or drain assets across all existing vaults. Together, these privileges place excessive trust in a single admin, increasing the risk of unauthorized fund withdrawals and malicious activities that could compromise the entire protocol and its users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an excessive centralization risk caused by the admin role in the ExitVaultEntryPoint contract. The admin is granted unrestricted authority to call a rescueFunds function that can transfer any ERC20 token from any vault managed by the contract, including tokens that users have deposited and reward tokens such as GMX and WETH. In addition, the admin can change the implementation address of the ExitVault contract through an UpgradeableBeacon, meaning the admin can replace the logic of all existing vaults with a new contract. Because there are no additional access checks, time locks, or multi‑party approval, the root cause is a design flaw that places too much trust in a single privileged address. An attacker who compromises the admin key, or a malicious admin acting voluntarily, can exploit the rescueFunds function by invoking it with the address of a user vault and the token identifier of the user’s deposit, causing the contract to transfer the full token balance to the admin’s address. Likewise, the admin can deploy a malicious implementation that rewrites balance accounting, disables withdrawals, or includes a hidden drain function, and then upgrade the beacon so that every existing vault instantly runs the malicious code. The impact is that user deposits and accrued rewards may disappear, balances shown in the UI drop to zero, users receive no refunds, and the entire protocol’s asset pool can be emptied. The condition for exploitation is simply that the admin role is active; no special state or user interaction is required. All users of the protocol, as well as the protocol’s reputation and liquidity, are affected. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the access control model and upgrade mechanisms. Because the rescueFunds function appears to be a legitimate emergency tool and upgradeability is a common pattern, the risk can be easy to overlook, especially if the code does not emit clear warnings or if the admin address is assumed to be trustworthy. To remediate, the rescueFunds function should be limited to non‑user tokens, include explicit checks that prevent withdrawal of assets belonging to users, and possibly require a multi‑signature or governance vote. The upgrade path should be protected by a decentralized governance process, such as a DAO or multi‑sig wallet, that requires consensus before changing the beacon implementation. Reducing the admin’s unilateral power mitigates the centralization risk and aligns the contract with the expectation that user funds are safe and cannot be taken without community approval.

title: M-01 | No Way Of Canceling Stuck Order
description: For a variety of reasons keepers may not execute an order in a timely manner or at times may never execute an order. This includes not canceling an order. When this happens Umami has no functionality to cancel such an order themselves which means that the order along with any collateral provided will be stuck. This also impacts the rebalance period as there is intended to be no pending orders when the rebalance period is closed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing cancellation path for pending orders created through the GMX integration in the PositionManager contract. When a keeper fails to execute an order—because of network congestion, gas price spikes, or simply being offline—the order remains open on GMX and the collateral that was supplied to back the order stays locked forever. The contract never calls GMX's cancelOrder function, so there is no mechanism for the keeper or any authorized party to withdraw the locked funds. This situation can arise during normal operation when an order is expected to be filled within a certain time window, or during the rebalance period when the protocol assumes that no orders are pending at the end of the cycle. Because the contract does not emit any event indicating that an order is stuck, users and auditors may not notice the problem until funds are effectively lost. The impact is that users see their order listed as open, but after the expected execution window their token balance does not change and they receive no refund, violating the expectation that an order will either be filled or cancellable. The protocol’s rebalance logic also breaks, as it relies on a clean state with no pending orders, potentially causing the rebalance period to stall or produce incorrect accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PositionManager source code, where the absence of a call to GMX's cancelOrder function was identified as a logical omission. This class of bug can be described as an order‑lifecycle management omission, where the contract implements order creation and execution but neglects the cancellation step required for robust integration with external exchanges. To remediate, the contract should expose a function that allows an authorized keeper to invoke GMX's cancelOrder for any pending order, include proper access control, emit an event on successful cancellation, and update internal state to reflect the released collateral. Implementing this fix restores the expected behavior that users can either have their order filled or retrieve their collateral, and it re‑establishes the invariant that no pending orders exist when a rebalance period closes.

title: M-01 | deployVault Calls Can Be Front-run
description: The ExitVaultEntryPoint.deployVault function is designed to deploy a new vault contract using the CREATE2 opcode, mint an ERC721 token representing ownership of the vault and initialize the newly deployed vault with specific parameters. However, the function accepts a _counter parameter provided by the caller, which must match the current proxiesCounter stored in the contract. When a user attempts to deploy a vault by calling deployVault with a specific _counter, an attacker or even a legitimate user could submit their own deployVault transaction with the same _counter before the original one is mined. If this transaction is processed first, it increments the proxiesCounter and successfully deploys a vault. Consequently, when the original user's transaction is executed, the _counter no longer matches the updated proxiesCounter, causing the transaction to revert with an InvalidCounter error. This results in wasted approvals, as users must perform multiple approvals before calling deployVault.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deployVault function of the ExitVaultEntryPoint contract, which uses a caller‑supplied _counter that must equal the contract’s internal proxiesCounter before a new vault can be created with CREATE2. Because the check is performed after the transaction is mined, an attacker (or any other user) can submit a transaction with the same _counter value before the legitimate user’s transaction is included. The attacker’s transaction is processed first, increments proxiesCounter and successfully deploys a vault. When the original transaction later executes, the _counter no longer matches the updated proxiesCounter, causing the call to revert with an InvalidCounter error. This front‑running scenario leads to wasted ERC20 approvals and failed vault deployments, effectively denying service to the intended user. The issue is caused by relying on a mutable, externally supplied counter for a deterministic deployment address, rather than deriving the salt from immutable data such as the caller’s address and a nonce. It is discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the counter check and the CREATE2 deployment pattern. The problem can be hard to notice because the revert only occurs after the transaction is mined, and the user may not realize that their approvals were consumed without any visible outcome. To remediate, the contract should stop enforcing the equality between proxiesCounter and the supplied counter. Instead, it should compute a unique salt using keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_counter, msg.sender)) and store this salt in the vaults mapping. The tokenId to be minted can then be derived from the salt, ensuring that each deployment is deterministic and cannot be pre‑empted by another transaction with the same counter. This change removes the race condition, restores expected behavior where a user’s vault is created and the corresponding ERC721 token is minted, and prevents loss of approvals and gas due to front‑running.

title: M-02 | Precision Loss May Not Allow All Users To Claim
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding error in the reward‑distribution logic of the ExitVault contract that can cause the contract to attempt to transfer a few wei more GMX tokens than it actually holds. The root cause lies in the use of integer division when calculating pending rewards and reward debts based on an accumulated‑per‑share value. Because Solidity truncates fractional parts, the accumulated per‑share multiplication and the time‑based vesting formula can produce a value that is off by one or a few wei. When a user calls the claim function, the contract computes a pending reward, adds it to the already claimed amount, and then calls the GMX token’s transfer function with this computed amount. If the rounding error makes the computed amount slightly larger than the contract’s current GMX balance, the external token contract reverts with an error such as “transfer amount exceeds balance by 1 wei”. This revert prevents the claim from completing, leaving the user with no reward despite the contract’s accounting indicating that a reward is due. The impact is that legitimate users may be unable to claim their full entitlement, effectively losing access to a small portion of their rewards, and the protocol’s accounting appears inconsistent because the internal accounting shows a positive pending reward while the external transfer fails. The condition occurs only when the cumulative rounding error reaches the point where the computed payout exceeds the actual token balance, which typically happens after many small claims or when the contract’s balance is low. The affected parties are token holders who are entitled to vesting rewards, the protocol that promises those rewards, and any downstream applications that display claim status. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed occasional revert messages during test claims and traced them back to the reward‑debt and pending‑reward formulas. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the discrepancy is usually a single wei, which does not affect large transfers and may only surface under edge‑case timing or after many incremental claims. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “rounding‑error token transfer” vulnerabilities, where arithmetic precision loss leads to an over‑estimation of payable amounts. To remediate, the contract should verify the available token balance before initiating a transfer and cap the transfer amount to the lesser of the calculated reward and the actual balance, or redesign the accounting to use a rounding‑down approach that guarantees the payout never exceeds the contract’s holdings. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a pending reward, but after pressing the claim button the transaction reverts and the user receives nothing, contrary to the expectation that the reward will be transferred. This mismatch between expected and actual behavior constitutes a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees and can erode trust in the reward mechanism.

title: M-03 | Users Should Ensure They Hold Only esGMX Before Deploying A Vault To Optimize Gains
description: To deploy an ExitVault contract the user must perform a full account transfer. This process transfers all tokens and stakes associated with the user's GMX protocol account into the vault, including any staked GMX, esGMX, and other tokens. For instance, if a user has staked 1000 GMX tokens and has earned 100 esGMX tokens that they wish to convert through the vault, initiating the vault deployment and performing the account transfer moves all these assets into the vault. Once the vault holds the staked GMX and the esGMX tokens, it can immediately use the staked GMX to unlock the esGMX without needing additional participants. This renders the collaborative aspect of the vault pointless, as the vault no longer requires contributions from other users to maximize its vesting capacity. Moreover, the user's staked GMX and other tokens are now locked within the vault and the user loses direct operational control over them. They cannot claim rewards, adjust their staking positions, or interact with their tokens outside the vault. To regain access and control, the user would need to exit the vault by performing another full account transfer, which can only be done after a year due to the vesting period. This situation may lead vault creators to inadvertently lock up their staked tokens and lose flexibility in managing their assets, contrary to their intentions. It also negates the primary purpose of the vault system, which is to pool resources from multiple users to collectively unlock esGMX tokens, maximizing gains through collaboration. By having sufficient GMX within the vault to unlock the esGMX independently, the need for other users to participate is eliminated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical asset‑transfer flaw in the ExitVault deployment flow. When a user calls the vault deployment, the contract executes a full account transfer that automatically moves every token and stake associated with the user’s GMX protocol account – including staked GMX, esGMX, and any other staked assets – into the newly created vault. Because the vault now holds both the staked GMX and the esGMX, it can immediately satisfy the unlocking condition for esGMX without requiring contributions from other participants. This defeats the intended collaborative design of the vault, which is supposed to pool GMX from multiple users to collectively unlock esGMX and increase vesting efficiency. The root cause is that the transfer function does not filter or restrict the types of assets being moved; it treats the account transfer as an all‑or‑nothing operation. An attacker does not need to exploit code execution; any user who follows the normal deployment steps can unintentionally trigger the condition. The exploitation scenario is straightforward: a user who still holds staked GMX initiates the vault deployment, the contract pulls the staked GMX into the vault, the vault instantly unlocks the user’s esGMX, and the user’s original GMX stake becomes locked inside the vault for the full vesting period (typically one year). From the user’s perspective the symptoms are that after deployment the user can no longer see or interact with their staked GMX, cannot claim rewards, and any attempt to withdraw the assets fails until the vesting timer expires. The impact is loss of flexibility, potential reduction of overall protocol efficiency because the pooling incentive disappears, and the risk that the user’s assets remain inaccessible for a long period. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ExitVault.initialize logic, where the auditor noticed that the account transfer does not enforce any pre‑condition on the composition of the transferred balance. Because the behavior matches the expected flow of a normal deployment, it can be hard to notice unless the auditor checks the post‑deployment asset composition. The recommended mitigation is to document the requirement that users must hold only esGMX before deploying, and to add a require statement that checks the vault’s total GMX and GLP balance against the staked esGMX balance, rejecting deployments where the vault already possesses enough GMX to unlock the esGMX on its own. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a whitelist or filter on transferred assets, or to require that the vault start with zero GMX, thereby preserving the collaborative unlocking mechanism.

title: M-04 | ExitVaultEntryPoint Centralizes Governance Power Instead Of Delegating To ExitVault Owners
description: In the current design of the ExitVaultEntryPoint and ExitVault contracts, the governance power associated with the staked GMX tokens is centralized within the ExitVaultEntryPoint contract’s treasury rather than being held by the individual ExitVault owners. When users deposit their GMX tokens into an ExitVault, the tokens are staked under the contract's address, and the resulting voting power accumulates to the ExitVaultEntryPoint’s treasury. This setup means that all the governance rights derived from these staked tokens are controlled by the ExitVaultEntryPoint’s treasury rather than the actual owners of the tokens. Consequently, the vault owners are deprived of their ability to participate in governance decisions proportionally to their stake.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a governance centralization flaw in the ExitVaultEntryPoint and ExitVault design. When a user deposits GMX tokens into an ExitVault, the contract stakes those tokens under its own address and automatically attributes the resulting voting power to the ExitVaultEntryPoint treasury instead of to the individual vault owners. This occurs because the staking implementation does not delegate or assign governance rights per depositor; it treats the contract as a single token holder. An attacker or any entity that controls the EntryPoint treasury can therefore cast votes on behalf of all deposited tokens, influencing protocol proposals without the consent of the actual token owners. The impact is that vault participants lose the ability to participate proportionally in governance, undermining the expected democratic control of the protocol and potentially allowing malicious or self‑serving proposals to pass. The issue manifests whenever a user locks GMX in an ExitVault, which is a normal operation from the user’s perspective, making the problem hard to notice because the token balance appears correctly staked and no explicit error is shown. The audit discovered the flaw by reviewing the flow of token ownership and governance delegation logic. From a user’s point of view the UI may display a correct token balance but the user receives no voting power, cannot vote on proposals, and may see their influence disappear. This violates the business assumption that staking through a vault should preserve each depositor’s voting rights. To remediate, the contract should be modified so that governance power is either delegated to each ExitVault owner or otherwise made claimable by them, ensuring that voting rights remain proportional to each participant’s stake rather than being concentrated in a single treasury address.

title: Gas costs will likely result in any fees sent to the Splitter being economically unviable to recover.
description: Collection owners will likely lose money by claiming fees unless the fees from a single NFT sale outweighs the cost of claiming it (not guaranteed).
poc:
Consider a new `Collection` with a `RoyaltyVault` and `Splitter` set and a nonzero mint fee.

When calling `mintToken`, the `_handlePayment` function is called <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-joyn/blob/c9297ccd925ebb2c44dbc6eaa3effd8db5d2368a/core-contracts/contracts/CoreCollection.sol#L161-L163>

This will transfer the minting fee to the `RoyaltyVault` contract.

On each transfer of an NFT within the collection (for instance in the `_mint` call which occurs directly after calling `_handlePayment`), the `Collection` contract will call `sendToSplitter` on the `RoyaltyVault`:

This function will forward the collection owners’ portion of the minting on to the `Splitter` contract but another important thing to note is that we call `Splitter.incrementWindow`.

This results in the fees newly deposited into the `Splitter` contract being held in a separate “window” to the fees from previous or later mints and need to be claimed separately. Remember that this process happens on every NFT sale so the only funds which will be held in this window will be the minting fees for this particular mint.

From this we can see that the `claim` function will only claim the fraction of the fees which are owed to the caller from a single NFT mint.

Note that we can attempt to claim from multiple windows in a single transaction using `claimForAllWindow` but as the name suggests it performs an unbounded loop trying to claim all previous windows (even ones which have already been claimed!) and it is likely that with a new window for every NFT sold this function will exceed the gas limit (consider an 10k token collection resulting in trying to do 10k SSTOREs at 20k gas each.), leaving us to claim each window individually with `claim`.

We’re then forced to claim the royalties from each NFT sold one by one, having to send huge numbers of calls to `claim` incurring the base transaction cost many times over and performing many ERC20 transfers when we could have just performed one.

Compound on this that this needs to be repeated by everyone included in the split, multiplying the costs of claiming.

Medium risk as it’s gas inefficiency to the point of significant value leakage where collection owners will lose a large fraction of their royalties.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the economic viability of claiming royalty fees in a split‑payment architecture that uses a per‑mint "window" mechanism. Each time an NFT is minted, the collection contract forwards the mint fee to a RoyaltyVault, which immediately calls a Splitter contract and invokes `incrementWindow`. The Splitter stores the newly received amount in a distinct accounting window that must be claimed separately from earlier windows. Consequently, every minted token creates a fresh window, and the only way to retrieve the fees is to call `claim` for each window individually or invoke `claimForAllWindow`, which iterates over all windows without bounds. In practice, a collection with thousands of tokens generates thousands of windows, and the claim transaction must perform a separate SSTORE for each window (approximately 20 000 gas per storage write). The unbounded loop in `claimForAllWindow` quickly exceeds block gas limits, forcing callers to submit a separate claim transaction for each window. This design results in a situation where the total gas cost required to retrieve the accumulated royalties can be greater than the royalties themselves, effectively causing funds to disappear from the perspective of the collection owners and royalty recipients. The issue manifests only when a collection has multiple mints; the more tokens sold, the more windows are created, and the greater the cumulative gas burden. It was discovered during a security audit that measured gas usage for the claim pathways and identified an unbounded iteration that scales linearly with the number of windows. The problem is subtle because the contract functions as intended – fees are correctly deposited and can be claimed – yet the economic model is broken, and users may not notice the excessive gas until they attempt to claim. The impact is a loss of expected royalty income, as owners may forgo claiming due to prohibitive transaction costs, leading to a mismatch between the business logic (royalties should be claimable) and the actual outcome (royalties become uneconomical to retrieve). To remediate, the window mechanism should be removed or redesigned so that royalty distribution is performed asynchronously or batched, allowing a single claim transaction to retrieve all pending fees without an unbounded loop. Shifting the cost of splitting to the royalty stakeholders rather than the NFT holder, or providing a pull‑payment model where the Splitter aggregates fees and permits a single, gas‑efficient withdrawal, would align the contract’s behavior with its intended financial semantics.

title: CoreCollection’s token transfer can be disabled
description:
When royaltyAsset is an ERC20 that doesn’t allow zero amount transfers, the following griefing attack is possible, entirely disabling CoreCollection token transfer by precision degradation as both reward distribution and vault balance can be manipulated.

Suppose splitterProxy is set, all addresses and fees are configured correctly, system is in normal operating state.

POC:

Bob the attacker setup a bot which every time it observes positive royaltyVault balance:

  1. runs `sendToSplitter()`, distributing the whole current royaltyAsset balance of the vault to splitter and platform, so vault balance becomes zero
  2. sends `1 wei` of royaltyAsset to the royaltyVault balance
  3. each next CoreCollection token transfer will calculate `platformShare = (balanceOfVault * platformFee) / 10000`, which will be 0 as platformFee is supposed to be less than 100%, and then there will be an attempt to transfer it to `platformFeeRecipient`

If royaltyAsset reverts on zero amount transfers, the whole operation will fail as the success of `IERC20(royaltyAsset).transfer(platformFeeRecipient, platformShare)` is required for each CoreCollection token transfer, which invokes `sendToSplitter()` in `_beforeTokenTransfer()` as vault balance is positive in (3).

Notice, that Bob needn’t to front run the transfer, it is enough to empty the balance in a lazy way, so cumulative gas cost of the attack can be kept moderate.

Setting severity to medium as on one hand, the attack is easy to setup and completely blocks token transfers, making the system inoperable, and it looks like system has to be redeployed on such type of attack with some manual management of user funds, which means additional operational costs and reputational damage. On the another, it is limited to the zero amount reverting royaltyAsset case or the case when platformFee is set to 100%.

That is, as an another corner case, if platformFee is set to 100%, `platformShare` will be `1 wei` and `splitterShare` be zero in (3), so this attack be valid for any royaltyAsset as it is required in Splitter’s `incrementWindow` that `splitterShare` be positive.
poc:
As royaltyAsset can be an arbitrary ERC20 it can be reverting on zero value transfers:

`_beforeTokenTransfer` runs `IRoyaltyVault(royaltyVault).sendToSplitter()` whenever royaltyVault is set and have positive balance:

`sendToSplitter()` leaves vault balance as exactly zero as `splitterShare = balanceOfVault - platformShare`, i.e. no dust is left behind:

This way the balance opens up for the tiny amount manipulation.

One require that can fail the whole operation is `platformShare` transfer:

Another is positive `royaltyAmount` = `splitterShare` requirement:
bug_full: The vulnerability is a griefing attack that can completely block token transfers in the CoreCollection contract. The root cause lies in the transfer logic that tightly couples token movement with an on‑the‑spot royalty fee split. Every time a CoreCollection token is transferred, the contract calls the royalty vault’s sendToSplitter() function in the _beforeTokenTransfer() hook. This function attempts to move the entire royalty balance to a splitter contract and then forwards the platform’s share to a fee recipient. The amount sent to the platform is calculated as platformShare = (vaultBalance × platformFee) / 10000. When an attacker controls a bot that repeatedly empties the vault by calling sendToSplitter() and then deposits a single wei of the royalty asset, the subsequent transfer computes a platformShare of zero (because the fee is less than 100 %). The contract still tries to execute IERC20(royaltyAsset).transfer(platformFeeRecipient, 0). Some ERC20 tokens, however, revert when asked to transfer a zero amount. Because the transfer of the platform share is a required step, the revert aborts the whole token transfer, and the _beforeTokenTransfer() hook is invoked again on every later transfer, keeping the operation stuck. The attack does not require front‑running; the attacker merely keeps the vault balance at the minimal non‑zero value, ensuring low gas costs. The impact is that all token holders are unable to move their tokens, effectively rendering the protocol inoperable until the contract is redeployed or manual fund management is performed, causing operational overhead and reputational damage. The issue surfaces only when the royalty asset is an ERC20 that rejects zero‑value transfers or when the platform fee is configured to 100 %, which makes the platformShare equal to one wei and the splitter share zero, reproducing the same failure. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑splitting flow and identified that the contract assumes zero‑value transfers never revert. The problem is subtle because zero‑amount transfers are rarely exercised in normal operation, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the fee‑splitting mechanism should be decoupled from the core transfer: the contract should attempt to send fees but, if a transfer fails or the amount is below a sensible threshold, it should record the pending amount and proceed with the token transfer. Introducing a minimum royalty amount guard before invoking sendToSplitter() or allowing the fee distribution to be performed later eliminates the need for a successful zero‑value transfer and blocks the griefing vector. In user terms, a holder trying to send a token experiences a transaction revert with no change in balances, contrary to the expectation that the token should move while fees are deducted silently. This violation of the accounting assumption that fee processing cannot prevent token movement classifies the bug as a fee‑splitting precision degradation or zero‑transfer denial of service vulnerability.

title: Ineffective Handling of FoT or Rebasing Tokens
description:
Certain ERC20 tokens may change user’s balances over time (positively or negatively) or charge a fee when a transfer is called (FoT tokens). The accounting of these tokens is not handled by `RoyaltyVault.sol` or `Splitter.sol` and may result in tokens being stuck in `Splitter` or overstating the balance of a user

Thus, for FoT tokens if all users tried to claim from the Splitter there would be insufficient funds and the last user could not withdraw their tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inaccurate accounting model used by the RoyaltyVault and Splitter contracts when handling ERC‑20 tokens that modify the amount actually received by the contract. Tokens that charge a transfer fee ( fee‑on‑transfer, or FoT) or that rebalance their total supply (rebasing tokens) can cause the number of tokens that arrive in the Splitter to differ from the amount that the Vault reports it sent. The Vault assumes the transfer succeeds and forwards a fixed share amount, then tells the Splitter to split exactly that share via the incrementWindow function. Because the token contract may deduct a fee or adjust balances after the transfer, the Splitter receives fewer tokens than expected, yet it still records the original share amount as available for distribution. Consequently, early claimers can withdraw their full entitled amount, while the final claimant may receive nothing because the contract’s internal ledger overstates the pool balance. The problem also manifests when a rebasing token reduces its balance while held in the Splitter, leading to the same shortfall; an upward rebase is not reflected in the protocol’s accounting, causing a potential over‑allocation of rewards. This flaw is triggered whenever the protocol processes a royalty payment in a token that is not a plain fixed‑supply ERC‑20, i.e., any token that implements transfer fees or supply rebasing. All users who rely on royalty claims are affected, as the protocol may either over‑pay some users or leave others with an empty balance, breaking the expectation that each participant receives the exact proportional share of the royalty pool. The issue was uncovered during a code audit that highlighted the mismatch between the transfer’s return value (which only indicates success, not the net amount) and the actual token balance change. It is difficult to spot because the transfer call returns true, and standard balance checks are not performed, allowing the discrepancy to remain hidden until a claim is made. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid the use of fee‑on‑transfer and rebasing tokens altogether, clearly documenting the restriction, or implement pre‑ and post‑transfer balance snapshots to verify the exact amount received and adjust the Splitter’s accounting accordingly. Introducing such balance verification, however, creates a re‑entrancy surface, so a ReentrancyGuard must protect the function that moves tokens to the Splitter. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect token accounting for non‑standard ERC‑20 variants” and leads to mis‑allocation of funds, potential loss of royalties for some users, and the risk of tokens becoming permanently stuck in the Splitter contract.

title: CoreCollection: Starting index is pseudo-randomly generated, allowing for gameable NFT launches
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the launch contract computes the "starting index" that determines which token identifier corresponds to each NFT at mint time. Instead of relying on a source of true randomness, the contract uses the current block number combined with a deterministic keccak256 hash to derive an index. Because block numbers increase predictably and can be known in advance, an attacker can calculate the exact starting indexes for the next several thousand blocks. This predictability enables a malicious user to pre‑scrape the collection’s metadata (the base URI is set at deployment) and identify which token IDs correspond to rare or valuable attributes. Armed with that knowledge, the attacker can front‑run or selectively mint the rare NFTs, effectively gaming the launch. The issue manifests whenever the contract is initialized for a new series of NFTs and the starting index is derived from block.number, which is a publicly known state variable. Users who are not aware of the deterministic calculation may expect a fair, random distribution of rarity, but instead see rare items disappear or be allocated to a few early participants. The impact is a breach of the fairness guarantee promised by the launch design, leading to a loss of trust and potential economic disadvantage for regular participants. The flaw was identified during a security audit that compared the implementation against best‑practice guidelines for NFT launches, noting that block.number is not an entropy source. Because the output looks random at first glance, the issue can be hard to notice without deeper analysis of the entropy source. To remediate, the contract should replace the block.number‑based seed with a cryptographically secure randomness source, such as a commit‑reveal scheme, a Verifiable Random Function (VRF), or at minimum a hash that mixes unpredictable data like the previous blockhash, miner address, and the caller’s address. This change reduces the ability of any single participant to predict the resulting index, restoring the intended fairness of the NFT distribution.

title: Differing percentage denominators causes confusion and potentially brick claims
description:
There is a `PERCENTAGE_SCALE = 10e5` defined, but the actual denominator used is `10000`. This is aggravated by the following factors:

  1. Split contracts are created by collection owners, not the factory owner. Hence, there is a likelihood for someone to mistakenly use `PERCENTAGE_SCALE` instead of `10000`.
  2. The merkle root for split distribution can only be set once, and a collection’s split and royalty vault can’t be changed once created.

Thus, if an incorrect denominator is used, the calculated claimable amount could exceed the actual available funds in the contract, causing claims to fail and funds to be permanently locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatched scaling factor used for calculating percentage‑based splits and royalties. The contract defines a constant named PERCENTAGE_SCALE with a value of 10e5 (one million) but the arithmetic that distributes funds expects a denominator of 10 000 (basis points). This inconsistency originates from the fact that split contracts are deployed by collection owners rather than by a single trusted factory, so a creator can inadvertently apply the wrong constant when configuring the split percentages. Because the merkle root that determines the distribution is immutable after deployment and the split and royalty vaults cannot be altered, an incorrect denominator results in a claimable amount that may be larger than the actual ether or token balance held by the contract. When a claimant attempts to withdraw the overstated amount, the transfer reverts due to insufficient balance, leaving the funds locked in the contract with no further way to adjust the distribution. The impact is that users who are supposed to receive a share of the revenue see their claim transactions fail, often receiving a “transfer failed” or “insufficient balance” error, while the total pool of funds remains unrecoverable because the contract logic does not permit retroactive correction of the percentages. This condition occurs only when a split contract is instantiated with the wrong denominator, which is a subtle mistake that can be easily overlooked during deployment because both constants are numeric literals and the code does not emit warnings or checks for consistency. The issue was identified during a formal audit that compared the declared constant with the actual divisor used in the payout calculation. It is hard to notice in regular testing because the contract may appear to work correctly for small percentages, while larger values expose the overflow of the claimable amount. To remediate, the unused PERCENTAGE_SCALE constant should be removed or its value changed to match the expected 10 000 denominator, and all calculations should consistently reference a single, well‑documented scaling factor. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of financial‑logic errors caused by inconsistent units or scaling factors, which violate the accounting assumption that the sum of allocated percentages never exceeds 100 % of the available balance.

title: Add a timelock to `setPlatformFee`
description:
It is a good practice to give time for users to react and adjust to critical changes. A timelock provides more guarantees and reduces the level of trust required, thus decreasing risk for users. It also indicates that the project is legitimate.

Here, no timelock capabilities seem to be used

I believe this impacts multiple users enough to make them want to react / be notified ahead of time.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted, immediate change to the platform fee via the setPlatformFee function. Because the contract does not enforce any timelock or notice period, the privileged account (typically the owner or governance role) can modify the fee in a single transaction and the new rate becomes effective for all subsequent interactions without any delay. The root cause is the absence of a delay mechanism (such as a timelock contract or scheduled proposal) that would otherwise give users a window to react, withdraw, or adjust their behavior before the fee change takes effect. An attacker who compromises the privileged key, or a malicious administrator, can exploit this by raising the fee abruptly, causing users to incur higher costs on every transaction or withdrawal performed after the change. The impact is financial loss or over‑charging for any user of the protocol because the fee applied to their operations may suddenly increase, often without any on‑chain warning or off‑chain announcement. This situation occurs whenever the privileged role invokes setPlatformFee, which the contract accepts and applies instantly. All participants who rely on the platform’s fee schedule—traders, lenders, liquidity providers, and any entity that pays the fee—are affected. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined governance‑related functions and noted that best practice recommends a timelock for critical parameter updates to reduce trust requirements and signal legitimacy. The vulnerability can be hard to notice because the fee change does not emit a distinct warning or enforce a delay, so users may only observe the higher cost when they submit a transaction and see an unexpectedly large deduction. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a timelock pattern for setPlatformFee: changes should be proposed, stored, and only become executable after a predefined waiting period (e.g., 24–72 hours), with clear event emission announcing the upcoming fee adjustment. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of “governance parameter change without delay” bugs, ensuring that the platform’s accounting assumptions remain transparent and that users are not surprised by sudden fee hikes.

title: DoS: Attacker May Front-Run `createSplit`
description:
A `merkleRoot` may only be used once in `createSplit()` since it is used as `salt` to the deployment of a `SplitProxy`.

The result is an attacker may front-run any `createSplit()` transaction in the mem pool and create another `createSplit()` transaction with a higher gas price that uses the same `merkleRoot` but changes the other fields such as the `_collectionContract` or `_splitAsset()`. The original transaction will revert and the user will not be able to send any more transaction with this `merkleRoot`.

The user would therefore have to generate a new merkle tree with different address, different allocations or a different order of leaves in the tree to create a new merkle root. However, the attack is repeateable and there is no guarantee this new merkle root will be successfully added to a split without the attacker front-running the transaction again.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service that stems from the way the contract creates a SplitProxy. The function createSplit uses a user‑supplied merkleRoot as the sole salt for the deterministic deployment of the proxy, effectively tying the resulting contract address to that merkleRoot. Because the salt is predictable and publicly visible in the transaction calldata, any observer can copy the same merkleRoot, construct a competing createSplit transaction with a higher gas price, and submit it to the mempool before the original transaction is mined. The attacker’s transaction will win the race, deploy a SplitProxy at the expected address, and then revert the legitimate user’s transaction because the address is already taken. From the user’s point of view the createSplit call simply fails, the expected split contract is never created, and the user receives no confirmation or funds. The impact is that the user is forced to generate a new merkle tree with a different root, but the attacker can repeat the front‑run on every new root, effectively preventing the protocol’s split functionality from being used. This condition occurs whenever a user attempts to create a split and the attacker can observe the pending transaction and out‑bid it on gas. It affects any participant who relies on the split mechanism to distribute assets, and it undermines the business logic that each merkleRoot should correspond to a unique, immutable split contract. The issue was discovered during a static audit that noted the deterministic use of merkleRoot as a salt and recognised that this opens a classic front‑running attack vector. The problem is subtle because the failure appears as a normal revert without indicating malicious interference. The recommended mitigation is to avoid using an externally supplied value as the sole salt; either remove the salt altogether when the address does not need to be known in advance, or bind the salt to the caller’s address (e.g., keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, merkleRoot))) so that only the legitimate initiator can claim the address. By making the salt unpredictable to third parties, the front‑running opportunity disappears and the split creation process regains its intended reliability.

title: Fixed Amount of Gas Sent in Call May Be Insufficient
description: The function `attemptETHTransfer()` makes a call with a fixed amount of gas, 30,000. If the receiver is a contract this may be insufficient to process the `receive()` function. As a result the user would be unable to receive funds from this function.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using a hard‑coded gas stipend of 30,000 when sending ether via a low‑level call inside the function that extracts funds from the contract. The root cause is the assumption that 30,000 gas is enough for any receiver, including a contract that implements a receive or fallback function. In reality, the amount of gas required to execute a contract's inbound logic can vary depending on the code executed, the state of the blockchain, and future changes to opcode pricing. If the recipient contract needs more than the supplied gas, the call will run out of gas, the transfer will fail, and the function will return false without reverting. An attacker can deliberately deploy a contract with a receive function that consumes more than 30,000 gas (for example by emitting events, writing to storage, or performing complex calculations) and then request a withdrawal. The withdrawal transaction will appear successful on‑chain, but the user's balance will not increase because the ether was never transferred. This creates a denial‑of‑service scenario where funds become locked in the contract, especially if the vulnerable function is the sole mechanism for extracting ether. The impact is that legitimate users may attempt to withdraw funds and receive nothing, leading to lost or inaccessible assets. The problem manifests whenever the contract attempts to send ETH to an address that is itself a contract, and it becomes more likely after network upgrades that modify gas costs, potentially turning a previously sufficient stipend into an insufficient one. The affected parties include any user who tries to withdraw ether, the protocol that relies on the ability to move funds out of the contract, and any downstream integrations that expect successful refunds or payouts. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the source code and identified the fixed gas limit. It can be difficult to notice because the call does not throw; it simply returns false, so the transaction may be recorded as successful while the expected balance change does not occur, leading to confusing UI symptoms such as a “withdrawal completed” message with unchanged wallet balance. To remediate the problem, the contract should remove the explicit gas limit and allow the call to forward all available gas, while simultaneously protecting against re‑entrancy by employing a re‑entrancy guard and following the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. This change ensures that the receiver can execute any reasonable amount of code and that the contract’s state is updated before the external call, eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector and restoring reliable fund extraction.

title: `RoyaltyVault.sol` is Not Equipped to Handle On-Chain Royalties From Secondary Sales
description:
The Joyn documentation mentions that Joyn royalty vaults should be equipped to handle revenue generated on a collection’s primary and secondary sales. Currently, `CoreCollection.sol` allows the collection owner to receive a fee on each token mint, however, there is no existing implementation which allows the owner of a collection to receive fees on secondary sales.

After discussion with the Joyn team, it appears that this will be gathered from Opensea which does not have an on-chain royalty mechanism. As such, each collection will need to be added manually on Opensea, introducing further centralisation risk. It is also possible for users to avoid paying the secondary fee by using other marketplaces such as Foundation.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing on‑chain royalty enforcement mechanism for secondary sales in the Joyn protocol. While the CoreCollection contract correctly forwards a fee to the collection owner on each primary mint, the system does not contain any logic that automatically collects royalties when a token is resold on a secondary marketplace. The root cause is the absence of an ERC‑2981 compatible implementation, combined with a reliance on external platforms such as OpenSea to manually register royalty information. Because OpenSea does not provide an on‑chain royalty enforcement hook, royalty data must be entered off‑chain, which introduces a centralisation point and a manual step that can be omitted or altered. An attacker or a seller can exploit this gap simply by executing a secondary sale on a marketplace that does not respect the off‑chain royalty configuration, for example Foundation or any other platform that does not query OpenSea’s royalty database. In such a scenario the contract does not trigger any fee transfer, the collection owner receives no royalty, and the protocol’s revenue model is bypassed. The impact is a loss of expected royalty income for the collection owner and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s ability to enforce its economic rules. The condition under which the issue manifests is any secondary transaction that is settled on a marketplace without an on‑chain royalty check, which is the default state for most existing NFT marketplaces. The affected parties include collection owners who expect to be compensated for secondary trades, the Joyn protocol that advertises royalty collection on both primary and secondary sales, and users who may believe that royalties are automatically deducted. The problem was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, supplemented by a discussion with the Joyn development team who confirmed the reliance on OpenSea’s off‑chain system. The issue is subtle because the contract functions correctly for primary sales, giving the false impression that royalties are fully supported, while the missing secondary logic is hidden from the UI and only becomes apparent when a resale yields an unexpected zero royalty payout. To remediate the flaw, the contract should be extended with an ERC‑2981 compliant royalty interface that enforces royalty payment on every token transfer, or alternatively integrate a trusted on‑chain royalty escrow that can be triggered by any marketplace. This would eliminate the need for manual off‑chain configuration, reduce centralisation risk, and align the protocol’s on‑chain accounting with its advertised royalty policy, ensuring that users receive the expected royalty deductions and that collection owners are fairly compensated for secondary market activity.

title: createProject can be frontrun
description: This is dangerous in scam senario because the malicious user can frontrun and become the owner of the collection. As owner, one can withdraw `paymentToken`. (note that _collections.isForSale can be change by frontrunner)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the public function createProject, which allows any external address to invoke it without any form of authentication or pre‑approval. Because the contract does not restrict who may call createProject, a malicious actor can observe a legitimate user's pending transaction, submit the same call with their own parameters (or the same parameters) in a separate transaction with a higher gas price, and therefore be mined first. This front‑running attack results in the attacker being recorded as the owner of the newly created collection. As the owner, the attacker gains the permission to withdraw the paymentToken associated with that collection, effectively stealing funds that were intended for the legitimate project creator. The issue also extends to the _collections.isForSale flag, which can be altered by the frontrunner before the original transaction is processed, further compromising the sale logic. The problem occurs whenever createProject is called in an environment where transactions are publicly visible and miners can prioritize higher‑fee submissions, which is the default behavior of most EVM‑compatible blockchains. All users who rely on the contract to securely register projects and collections are affected, as they may lose ownership rights and associated token balances. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of access control and the potential for race conditions inherent in public transaction ordering. It can be difficult to notice because the contract will still execute successfully from the perspective of the blockchain, but the business logic—ownership assignment—does not match the expectation of the original caller, leading to silent loss of funds. To remediate, the contract should enforce an allow‑list or whitelist for authorized project creators, and/or require the caller to provide a signed message proving that the address they intend to act as matches msg.sender, using a cryptographic signature verification (e.g., OpenZeppelin's ECDSA). This moves the vulnerability from an unauthorized access and front‑running class of bug to a properly authenticated operation, restoring the intended invariant that only the intended creator can become the owner of a collection and withdraw its payment tokens. From a user’s point of view, the symptom is that after creating a project they see the collection listed under another address, receive no payment token, or notice that their balance has been reduced to zero despite having performed the creation step. The expectation that they would become the owner and retain control over the collection is violated, breaking the accounting guarantees of the platform.

title: Anyone can deploy a new `FraxSwapPair` with a Low fee incurring losses to the protocol
description: When `LiquidityManager::moveLiquidity` function is called then either a new `FraxSwapPair` is created with a fee of `1%` or if a pair already exists then the liquidity is transferred to that `FraxSwapPair` but the issue is that any user can deploy this `FraxSwapPair` with fee as low as `0.01%` which can only be changed back by the owner of the `FraxSwapFactory` and if left unchecked will result in loss of fee for the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the LiquidityManager.moveLiquidity routine, which is responsible for either creating a new FraxSwapPair with a default fee of 1 % or, if the pair already exists, moving existing liquidity into it. The contract does not restrict who can trigger the creation of a new pair, nor does it enforce a minimum fee at the point of creation. Consequently, any external address can call the factory’s createPair function with an arbitrarily low fee value – as low as 0.01 % – before moveLiquidity is executed. The root cause is the lack of access control and validation on the fee parameter during pair deployment. An attacker can exploit this by first deploying a FraxSwapPair with the minimal fee, supplying the required initial liquidity, and then allowing the protocol’s moveLiquidity call to route swaps through this low‑fee pool. Because the fee applied to each swap is dramatically reduced, the protocol receives far less fee revenue than expected. For a single 1 ether swap, the difference between a 1 % fee and a 0.01 % fee translates to a loss of roughly 0.039 ether worth of AI tokens; the loss scales with transaction size and is multiplied by the three swaps performed during moveLiquidity. The impact is a systematic erosion of fee income for the protocol, affecting token holders, liquidity providers, and any party that relies on the fee model for economic security. This condition occurs whenever moveLiquidity is called and the corresponding FraxSwapPair does not already exist, allowing any user to pre‑emptively create the pair with a custom fee. The affected parties include the protocol itself, its governance (owner of the FraxSwapFactory who can later reset the fee), and end‑users who may notice unusually high output amounts from swaps but are unaware that the protocol is losing fees. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that a malicious user could set the fee to 0.01 % and then execute swaps that bypass the intended fee collection. The problem is subtle because the fee parameter is a small numeric value that is not prominently displayed in user interfaces, making the discrepancy easy to overlook. To remediate, the factory should enforce that only the owner or an authorized role can set the fee, or it should enforce a minimum fee threshold at pair creation. Alternatively, moveLiquidity could be redesigned to reference a pre‑approved pair with a fixed fee, eliminating the need for on‑the‑fly pair creation. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “unauthorized parameter manipulation during contract deployment” and results in fee‑drain due to a lowered swap fee.

title: Attacker can DOS liquidity migration in LiquidityManager.sol
description:
The LiquidityManager’s liquidity migration function, `moveLiquidity()` is susceptible to a DOS attack that any malicious attacker can perform. 

The reason for this is that `moveLiquidity()` relies on the raw ERC20 balance of the currency token held by the contract to determine the amount of agent token liquidity to add. In particular, the function calculates the currency token balance via:

```solidity
uint256 currencyAmount = currencyToken.balanceOf(address(this));
uint256 liquidityAmount = (currencyAmount * 1e18) / price;
```

This design assumes that the only currency tokens held by the LiquidityManager are those coming from the controlled bootstrap pool. However, an attacker can directly transfer extra currency tokens (e.g., IQ tokens) into the LiquidityManager.

This “injection” increases the raw balance reported by `balanceOf(address(this))`, causing the computed `liquidityAmount` — which represents the amount of agent tokens required for migration — to be artificially inflated.

When the LiquidityManager then attempts to transfer agent tokens to add liquidity (via a subsequent call to `addLiquidityToFraxswap()`), the computed amount exceeds the actual agent token balance held by the contract. This results in a failure (an `ERC20InsufficientBalance` revert) during the migration process, effectively causing a denial-of-service (DoS) that blocks liquidity migration and disrupts normal protocol operations.

**Impact:**

  * Protocol Disruption: The migration process is a core functionality for moving liquidity from the bootstrap pool to the Fraxswap pair. 
  * User Harm: Disrupted liquidity migration can result in poor market pricing or loss of confidence, potentially causing users to incur losses when trading or exiting positions.
  * Denial-of-Service (DoS): An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to prevent liquidity migration, indirectly impacting the protocol’s ability to function as intended.

Impact: High

Likelihood: Medium as it requires an attacker to spend funds. How well-funded he must be depends on the exact amount of tokens that will be used in a real environment and how willing he is to cause damage to the protocol and its users (a competitor or someone else with malicious intent).
bug_full: The LiquidityManager contract contains a denial‑of‑service (DoS) weakness that stems from the way it determines the amount of agent tokens to add when migrating liquidity. The function moveLiquidity() reads the raw ERC20 balance of the currency token held by the contract and uses a simple division by the current price to compute a liquidityAmount. This calculation assumes that the only currency tokens in the contract are those that originated from the controlled bootstrap pool. An attacker can break this assumption by directly transferring additional currency tokens into the LiquidityManager. Because the balanceOf query returns the inflated total, the computed liquidityAmount becomes larger than the actual amount of agent tokens that the contract possesses. When the manager later calls addLiquidityToFraxswap() and attempts to transfer the calculated liquidityAmount of agent tokens, the transfer reverts with an ERC20InsufficientBalance error. The revert aborts the whole migration, preventing the bootstrap pool from moving its liquidity to the Fraxswap pair. The issue is triggered only when an adversary is able to inject enough extra currency tokens to make the required agent token amount exceed the contract’s real balance, which typically requires spending a non‑trivial amount of tokens. The affected parties are the protocol itself, which loses the ability to migrate liquidity, and its users, who may see missing or delayed liquidity, abnormal price quotes, or empty balances when trying to trade or withdraw. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the moveLiquidity() implementation and verified the arithmetic relationship between currency reserves and agent token requirements. It is easy to miss because the balance check appears correct at a glance and the contract does not validate that the currency balance originates from the expected source. The bug belongs to the class of “balance‑origin injection” or “incorrect trust of raw token balances”, where a contract trusts a raw on‑chain balance without filtering out unsolicited deposits, leading to mis‑calculated accounting values. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a migration transaction reverts, the UI may report that liquidity migration failed, prices may appear frozen, or the user may see that no new liquidity is added despite a successful request. The root cause can be mitigated by separating the accounting of legitimate currency reserves from arbitrary token deposits, for example by tracking the amount of currency tokens received from the bootstrap pool in a dedicated state variable, or by requiring that the contract only uses tokens that it has explicitly approved or minted for the migration. In conceptual terms the fix is to avoid using balanceOf(address(this)) as the sole source of truth for the amount of currency tokens that should be paired with agent tokens, and to add validation that the computed liquidityAmount does not exceed the actual agent token balance before attempting the transfer.

title: Ineffective proposal threshold validation allows setting arbitrary high values
description:
The `setProposalThresholdPercentage` function in TokenGovernor checks the wrong variable when trying to enforce the maximum 10% threshold limit. Instead of validating the new incoming value, it checks the current stored value, making the protection completely ineffective.

This means anyone can propose and pass a governance proposal that sets the threshold to any value (even 100% or higher), which could effectively break the governance system by making it impossible for token holders to create new proposals.

The impact is severe because:

  * It could lock out all governance participation if set too high
  * It breaks the intended maximum 10% threshold protection
  * It could require another governance proposal to fix, which might be impossible if the threshold is set too high
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ineffective validation of the proposal threshold in the governance contract. The function that updates the proposal threshold percentage is intended to enforce a maximum of 10 % of total token supply, but it mistakenly checks the currently stored threshold value instead of the new input value supplied by a governance proposal. Because the check compares the old value, any proposal that tries to set a higher threshold passes the guard as long as the existing threshold is below the limit. An attacker can therefore create a successful governance proposal that sets the threshold to an arbitrarily high percentage, for example 90 % or even 100 %. Once the threshold is raised, subsequent proposals require an impractically large share of tokens to be created, effectively freezing the governance process. Token holders and any participants who rely on the ability to submit proposals will see proposals being rejected or simply unavailable, contrary to the expectation that a low threshold allows easy proposal creation. The issue was discovered during a code audit that highlighted the logical error in the validation condition. It is hard to notice because the require statement looks syntactically correct and the contract compiles without warnings, masking the fact that the wrong variable is used. The bug belongs to the class of improper input validation where state is checked instead of the new parameter, leading to privilege escalation and denial‑of‑service of the governance mechanism. To remediate, the function should compare the incoming _proposalThresholdPercentage against the maximum allowed value (e.g., 1000 representing 10 %) before updating storage, ensuring that only values within the intended range are accepted. This change restores the intended governance economics and prevents the protocol from being locked out of future proposals.

title: User can earn rewards by frontrunning the new rewards accumulation in Ron staking without actually delegating his tokens
description: [LiquidProxy.sol#L39](https://github.com/OwlOfMoistness/liquid_ron/blob/b9b462cb1f8554796b78ad81a935dbce19cce0c5/src/LiquidProxy.sol#L39)
