bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing‑based reward manipulation that allows a participant to capture staking rewards without actually providing a lasting delegation of tokens. The root cause lies in the contract’s reward accounting logic, which updates the reward pool based on the total amount of tokens recorded at the moment a new reward period is calculated, but does not enforce any lock‑up or fee on tokens that are deposited immediately before that calculation. Because newly deposited tokens are instantly included in the reward share, an attacker can monitor the schedule of reward updates, deposit a modest amount of tokens just before the reward distribution, and then withdraw the same amount after the rewards have been allocated. In this short window the attacker receives a proportional share of the newly minted or distributed rewards even though the tokens were never staked for the intended duration. The impact is that honest delegators see their expected reward share reduced, the reward pool can be drained over time, and the economic incentives of the protocol are undermined. The condition for exploitation is the ability to deposit and withdraw within a single reward period, which is possible because the contract lacks a deposit‑locking mechanism, a time‑based restriction, or a fee that would offset the expected reward for a short‑term deposit. Any user of the staking interface can perform this front‑running, but it is especially attractive to opportunistic actors who can automate the timing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through logical analysis of the reward distribution flow; it is subtle because the contract appears to credit rewards correctly and the UI shows normal balances, making the loss of reward value difficult to attribute directly to a bug. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a lock‑up period for new deposits comparable to the one used by the Ron staking contract, apply a deposit fee that approximates one day’s expected reward, restrict deposits to predefined windows relative to reward issuance, or require an operator to finalize deposits after a reward update. These measures would prevent a user from earning rewards on tokens that are not held for the full reward interval, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees and protecting honest participants from unfair loss of rewards.

title: Operators are unable to perform any actions due to incorrect modifier implementation
description: [LiquidRon.sol#L91](https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-01-liquid-ron/blob/e4b0b7c256bb2fe73b4a9c945415c3dcc935b61d/src/LiquidRon.sol#L91)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect implementation of an access‑control modifier that is intended to restrict certain functions to the contract owner or to addresses that have been granted operator status. The modifier checks that the caller is the owner and that the caller is not an operator, and it reverts when both conditions are true. Because the logical operator is an AND instead of an OR, the condition is satisfied for every address that is not the owner, regardless of whether the address is listed as an operator. As a result, any call originating from a legitimate operator triggers the revert, effectively preventing operators from executing any function that uses the onlyOperator modifier. This bug was discovered during a manual audit when the tester attempted to call the harvest function after adding an address as an operator and observed an unexpected ErrInvalidOperator revert. The issue is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the modifier name suggests correct behaviour, making it easy to overlook during a quick review. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for operator roles: operators cannot perform expected actions such as harvesting rewards, updating parameters, or any other privileged operation, which may halt protocol functionality that relies on delegated operator actions. Users interacting through an operator interface will see transactions fail with a revert, balances remain unchanged, and expected state transitions (for example, reward distribution) do not occur, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The condition occurs whenever a function guarded by onlyOperator is called by any address other than the contract owner, which includes all legitimate operators. The affected parties are the protocol’s operators, any downstream contracts or users that depend on operator‑initiated actions, and the overall system reliability. To remediate, the modifier should be rewritten so that it reverts only when the caller is neither the owner nor an authorized operator, typically by using a logical OR (||) in the condition: if (msg.sender != owner() && !operator[msg.sender]) revert ErrInvalidOperator();. This change restores the intended access control, allowing operators to execute their functions while still protecting against unauthorized callers. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control logic errors where the condition that determines permission is inverted or mis‑combined, leading to unintended restriction rather than unauthorized access. It violates the business assumption that operators have delegated authority to act on behalf of the owner, breaking the accounting of who may trigger state changes and causing functional outages without directly exposing funds to theft.

title: ERC-20 allowance bypass: spender can force sender to pay extra fees beyond approved amount
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance bypass in an ERC‑20 token that charges a transaction fee. In the transferFrom function the contract first deducts a fee from the sender’s balance via an internal call, and only afterwards invokes the standard ERC‑20 transfer logic which checks that the amount is within the spender’s allowance. Because the fee amount is not included in the allowance verification, a spender can trigger a transfer of the full approved amount while the fee is taken from the owner’s balance as an extra, unauthorised deduction. This occurs whenever the fee rate is greater than zero and a spender uses transferFrom on an approved allowance. The root cause is the missing check that amount + fee does not exceed the remaining allowance, i.e., the contract assumes the fee is covered by the allowance but never validates it. An attacker (or any approved spender) can simply call transferFrom with the exact allowance value; the contract will deduct the fee from the owner’s balance, causing the owner to lose more tokens than they consented to. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, the allowance value displayed in wallets remains unchanged, but the balance drops by the amount plus the fee, leading to unexpected zero or reduced balances. This violates the ERC‑20 specification which requires that a spender may not transfer more than the approved amount, and it breaks the accounting assumptions of the token economy. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by testing a scenario where a 100‑token allowance with a 10 % fee resulted in an 110‑token balance reduction. The bug is subtle because the fee deduction is performed in a separate internal function and does not emit an event that clearly ties it to the allowance check, making it easy to miss in manual reviews. The proper fix is to incorporate the fee into the allowance verification, either by requiring the allowance to cover amount + fee, by deducting the fee from the allowance itself, or by moving the fee deduction to a point after the allowance has been validated. In general this class of bug is known as an allowance accounting error where additional token transfers (fees, taxes, or burns) are not accounted for in the allowance logic.

title: Approve operation is not overridden to call `transferSanity`, thus its allowed to approve blacklisted accounts, which breaks protocol invariant
description:
In the readme invariant docs it is specified, as requirement for approval operations, the following conditions:

  * Owner not being blacklisted
  * Spender not being blacklisted

[Reference](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1VUANWsOjzKbkMDn5pB2gseK2wlYgw0r8/view).

_Note: to view the provided image, please see the original submission[here](https://code4rena.com/evaluate/2025-01-next-generation/submissions/S-542)._

However, this invariant is broken by the protocol’s implementation, as there is no logic to enforce that. The `approve()` function is not overridden and `transferSanity()` is not called for the operation.
poc:
To confirm we can refer to `Token.sol`:

The `approve()` function is not overridden.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an approval operation that does not enforce the protocol’s blacklisting invariant. The contract’s design documentation specifies that both the token owner and the spender must be free of blacklist status before an allowance can be granted. However, the implementation of the approve function is inherited from the standard ERC20 base and is not overridden to invoke the internal transferSanity check that validates blacklist conditions. As a result, the contract permits a token holder to set an allowance for any address, including those that have been marked as blacklisted. The root cause is the omission of a safeguard in the approve pathway; the transferSanity routine, which contains the logic to reject blacklisted participants, is only called by transfer‑related functions and not by approve. An attacker controlling a blacklisted address can therefore be approved as a spender by any token holder, either inadvertently or through a malicious UI that encourages approval. Once approved, the blacklisted spender can invoke transferFrom to move tokens from the approver’s balance, effectively bypassing the intended restriction. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: funds that should be protected from blacklisted actors become transferable, leading to potential loss of user balances and erosion of trust in the token’s compliance mechanisms. This condition manifests whenever a user calls approve without the contract checking blacklist status, which is any time the standard ERC20 approve function is used. All token holders are affected because any of them can unintentionally grant permission to a prohibited address, and the protocol itself loses its guarantee that blacklisted entities cannot spend tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented invariants with the actual code and noticed that approve was not overridden. It can be hard to notice because the approve function behaves normally from a UI perspective – the transaction succeeds, emits the expected Approval event, and does not revert – giving a false sense of security while silently violating the blacklist rule. From the user’s point of view, the symptom may appear as an unexpected loss of tokens after approving a spender that the user believed was blocked; the user expects the approval to be rejected but receives no error, and later observes that the approved blacklisted address has transferred funds, resulting in a balance that drops to zero or an unexplained deficit. The bug belongs to the class of invariant‑violation or access‑control bypass bugs where a critical business rule is not enforced in all code paths. To remediate, the approve function should be overridden to call transferSanity (or an equivalent blacklist‑checking routine) before updating the allowance, ensuring that both the owner and the spender are validated against the blacklist. This change restores the protocol’s guarantee that blacklisted accounts cannot be granted spending rights, aligning the implementation with the documented invariant and preventing unauthorized token movement.

title: M-01 | Working With Stale State Can Cause DoS
description:
When a user wants to update delegate rights on the base chain or mint an NFT on the shadow chain
they call lzread. However in lzread we use EVMCallComputeV1 with the current timestamp.
Meanwhile in lzmap we rely on a reading state that could potentially be outdated. This is because
the state is based on the timestamp set in EVMCallComputeV1, and by the time _executeMessage is
called, that state may no longer be accurate.
Example: (lzread from Shadow chain to Shadow chain or Base chain)
For now Shadow chain to Shadow chain example it taken. ApeChain is Shadow chain 1 and Arbitrum
is Shadow chain 2. Initially, an NFT is locked on the Arbitrum but unlocked and owned by User A on
ApeChain, with lzRead delegating rights to User A. At timestamp x, someone calls lzRead from
Arbitrum, and while the owner on ApeChain has changed to User B, the Arbitrum chain lists
staleOwner as User A at timestamp x.
At a later timestamp y, another lzRead call occurs from Arbitrum, and now the owner on ApeChain is
User C, the Arbitrum chain lists staleOwner as User A at timestamp x. When processing these
updates, ownership is transferred from User A to User B for the ﬁrst call because User A was owner
and from User A to User C ownership transfer for the second call will not work because Current
owner will be User B. This causes DOS.
bug_full: An attacker can cause a denial-of-service condition by exploiting a stale-state race in the cross-chain read routine. The contract uses a function that records the current block timestamp when it builds a compute request (EVMCallComputeV1) and later reads ownership information from a mapping (lzmap) that was populated with the owner value captured at that timestamp. Because the mapping is not refreshed before the message execution step (_executeMessage), the stored owner may no longer reflect the actual owner on the source chain when the ownership update is applied. When a user calls the cross-chain read (lzRead) to delegate rights or mint an NFT, the contract attempts to transfer ownership from the staleOwner to the new owner. If the real owner has already changed, the transfer from the staleOwner fails, leaving the NFT in an inconsistent state and preventing further updates. This situation appears to the user as a successful transaction that does not change the displayed owner, or as a transfer that silently does nothing, effectively locking the asset. The bug occurs only when ownership changes on the source chain between the timestamp captured for the compute request and the execution of the message on the destination chain, a scenario that is common in multi-chain environments where messages are delayed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of state between lzread, EVMCallComputeV1, and _updateOwnership and noticed that the contract relied on a previously stored owner instead of querying the current owner. Because the failure does not revert the transaction, it can be hard to notice without explicit state checks. The vulnerability belongs to the class of stale-state or race-condition bugs that break accounting assumptions, allowing an attacker to deliberately trigger the condition and cause a denial of service for NFT owners and delegators. The recommended mitigation is to avoid reading the staleOwner from lzmap and instead obtain the previous owner directly within the _updateOwnership routine, ensuring that the ownership transfer logic always works with up-to-date state.

title: M-02 | Delegation Is Broken For Punks
description:
Try
IExclusiveDelegateResolver(EXCLUSIVE_DELEGATE_RESOLVER_ADDRESS).exclusiveOwnerByRights(shadowCollectionAddress, tokenId, SHADOW_TOKEN_RIGHTS
The logic attempts to ﬁnd the owner via the exclusive delegate resolver, However we are using the
punk adapter address (shadowCollectionAddress) instead of the punk721 address to ﬁnd the owner.
This will result in delegated wallets not being able to mint a shadow nft.
The functionality of the contract should allow non locked nft to mint shadow NFT’s using the
delegation functionality, however since we query the wrong address in the delegate resolver, it is not
possible to retrieve the delegated user via the beacon contract.
Given that users usually hold punks in cold wallets and use delegations to the hot wallet, this will
limit the functionality of shadow nfts as they cannot be minted to delegated wallet addresses of the
punk holders.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a delegation logic error that prevents users from minting shadow NFTs when they rely on delegated ownership of CryptoPunks. The contract attempts to resolve the exclusive owner of a Punk by calling the exclusive delegate resolver with three parameters: the shadow collection address, the token identifier, and the rights flag. However, instead of passing the address of the CryptoPunks ERC‑721 contract, it mistakenly passes the address of the Punk adapter (the shadow collection address). Because the resolver expects the original ERC‑721 contract to locate delegated wallets, the call returns an empty or zero address, meaning the system cannot recognise the delegated owner. This flaw occurs whenever a user holds a Punk in a cold wallet and delegates authority to a hot wallet for the purpose of minting a shadow NFT. From the user’s perspective the mint transaction appears to succeed – no revert or explicit error – but no shadow token is created, leaving the user with an unchanged balance and no visible NFT. The impact is that delegated wallets are effectively blocked from using the shadow‑minting feature, limiting the utility of the protocol for a large class of Punk holders who rely on delegation for convenience or security. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the delegation flow and identified the mismatched address argument. It can be hard to notice because the function call does not fail outright; it simply returns an unexpected owner value, which downstream logic treats as “no owner” and therefore skips the minting step. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of incorrect contract address usage in cross‑contract calls, leading to broken access‑control checks. To remediate, the contract should be updated to use the correct CryptoPunks ERC‑721 contract address when querying the exclusive delegate resolver, ensuring that delegated owners are correctly resolved and shadow NFTs can be minted as intended. This fix restores the expected behaviour where a user delegates a Punk to a hot wallet, initiates a shadow‑mint, and receives the new NFT, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that ownership rights are transferable via delegation.

title: M-03 | Deployment Scripts Conﬁguration Issues
description:
1. Incorrect Send Library Conﬁguration:
• The ChainConﬁgurator contract currently sets ChainConﬁg.sendLibrary for Ethereum to
0xD231084BfB234C107D3eE2b22F97F3346fDAF705
• This is the sendUln301 library meant for LayerZero EndpointV1
2. Maximum Message Size:
• The ConﬁgureBeacons contract run script sets ExecutorConﬁg.maxMessageSize to 1_000_000
• This is signiﬁcantly higher than the default executor conﬁguration of 10_000 bytes
3. Send Library Conﬁguration:
• The ConﬁgureBeacons contract run script only sets LayerZero send libraries when they differ from
defaults
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deployment‑time configuration error that causes the contract suite to use an incompatible LayerZero send library and an oversized executor message size, while also relying on implicit defaults for library addresses. The root cause is that the ChainConﬁgurator script assigns the sendLibrary address 0xD231084BfB234C107D3eE2b22F97F3346fDAF705, which corresponds to the older SendUln301 implementation designed for LayerZero EndpointV1. The deployed system, however, runs against EndpointV2, which expects the newer SendUln302 library at 0x21F33EcF7F65D61f77e554B4B4380829908cD076. In addition, the ConfigureBeacons script sets ExecutorConﬁg.maxMessageSize to 1_000_000 bytes, far above the standard 10_000‑byte limit, and it only overwrites LayerZero library addresses when they differ from defaults, leaving implicit values unchecked. This misconfiguration can be exploited when a cross‑chain message is sent: the executor will accept an oversized payload that the underlying LayerZero endpoint cannot process, leading to message drops, out‑of‑gas reverts, or silent failures. Because the send library does not match the endpoint version, the payload encoding may be incorrect, causing the remote chain to reject the message entirely. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing NFTs after a cross‑chain mint, transactions that appear to succeed but never result in a token, or error messages such as “message failed” or “no response received”. The impact is loss of expected functionality, potential locking of funds that were meant to be transferred across chains, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s reliability. The issue manifests only after deployment, making it hard to notice during normal unit testing because the contracts compile and deploy without error; the failure appears only when the cross‑chain flow is exercised in production. The audit team discovered the problem by reviewing the deployment scripts and comparing the configured library addresses against the LayerZero documentation. To remediate, the deployment scripts should explicitly set the sendLibrary to the correct SendUln302 address, reset ExecutorConﬁg.maxMessageSize to the default 10_000 bytes, and always write explicit library addresses even when they match defaults, thereby eliminating reliance on implicit configuration and ensuring compatibility with the intended LayerZero endpoint version.

title: M-04 | NFT Owner Can Cause exclusiveOwnerByRights() Call To Revert
description:
unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights() gets called by an LayerZeroV2 DVN off chain to read the new
owner of a NFT from a remote chain. Based on certain conditions the function will make a internal
call wrapped in a try catch block to the exclusive delegate resolver with the aim to return the address
to which the owner of the NFT have delegated and return it as the new owner instead.
IExclusiveDelegateResolver(EXCLUSIVE_DELEGATE_RESOLVER_ADDRESS).exclusiveOwnerByRights
() can loop over all outgoingDelegations of a particular owner of an NFT while it loads all in memory,
and performs checks in a loop. An owner on a remote chain could create/have thousands of active
delegations via IDelegateRegistry with different delegation type than ERC721.
When the off chain read request is processed
IExclusiveDelegateResolver(EXCLUSIVE_DELEGATE_RESOLVER_ADDRESS).exclusiveOwnerByRights
() inside unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights() will loop for a very long time and will consume a lot of
gas. Off chain calls do not consume gas but they still simulate the consumption of gas in order to
revert if such off chain call loops for ever or is too computationally expensive like reaching the block
gas limit or some other limit set by the node.
Seems like the owner of the NFT will not be able to make unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights() to
revert, which would be considered a critical issue since it will block future read requests from being
executed, because Layer Zero sets a 300M gas limit on such off chain view calls and second
because the inner call is wrapped in a try catch block. 63/64 part of the gas would be forwarded to
the internal call and the rest 1/64 would be suﬃcient to ﬁnish the rest of the function.
The impact of this would be that the read request will retrieve the actual owner of the NFT instead of
the delegated address and that the off chain services will more time to process the request since it
might be more computationally intensive. This could harm the owner of the NFT or the systems that
integrate and base their protocol logic on the result of the read request.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a view function that resolves the effective owner of an NFT across chains. The function unlockedExclusiveOwnerByRights invokes an internal call to exclusiveOwnerByRights on a delegate resolver contract. That resolver iterates over every outgoing delegation recorded for the NFT owner, loading the full list into memory and performing checks inside a loop. Because the iteration has no bounds or pagination, an owner who creates a very large number of delegations – for example thousands of entries of a non‑ERC721 delegation type – can cause the loop to consume an excessive amount of gas. LayerZero’s off‑chain view calls simulate gas consumption and enforce a hard limit of roughly 300 million gas. When the internal call exhausts the available gas, the call reverts; however the revert is caught by a try‑catch block, allowing the outer function to continue and ultimately return the raw NFT owner address instead of the delegated address. From a user perspective the read request may return the original owner when a delegated address was expected, or the off‑chain service may take unusually long to respond or even fail, effectively blocking future read requests that rely on the delegated owner information. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the delegation resolution logic and identified the unbounded loop as a potential denial‑of‑service vector. It is hard to notice because view functions are typically assumed to be inexpensive, and the large gas limit masks the problem until an extreme number of delegations is present. The root cause is the lack of limits on the number of delegations processed in a single call, combined with the fact that the internal call forwards almost all gas (63/64) leaving insufficient gas for the surrounding logic. To remediate, the resolver should enforce a maximum number of delegations processed per call, introduce pagination or off‑chain indexing, or otherwise cap gas consumption. Informing integrators and users about the possibility of a blocked read request is also recommended.

title: Lack of deadline check in forwarded request
description: Without a deadline parameter, each `ForwardRequest` is potentially valid indefinitely. This means that once a request is signed, it can be executed at any point in the future, provided that the nonce has not yet been used. If a request remains valid forever without a deadline, allowing it to be executed much later than the signer might have intended. This can lead to situations where the execution context (e.g., market conditions, contract states) has drastically changed from when the request was originally signed. Signers have no mechanism to limit the time window during which their request is valid, reducing their control over their own transactions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing expiration check on a signed ForwardRequest that is forwarded through a generic forwarding contract. Because the request structure does not contain a deadline field, a signature that authorises a specific operation (for example a token transfer) remains valid indefinitely as long as the associated nonce has not been consumed. The root cause is the contract’s execute function accepting any request that passes signature verification without verifying a timestamp or block number against a maximum allowed time. An attacker, or any party that obtains the signed request, can simply wait until market conditions change – such as a token price moving dramatically, a liquidity pool shifting, or a contract state being altered – and then submit the request for execution. The exploit is demonstrated by increasing the blockchain time by six months in a test and still successfully forwarding a transfer, proving that the request can be replayed far after its creation. The impact is that the original signer loses control over when their transaction is performed; they may unintentionally cause a transfer when the value of the assets has changed, leading to financial loss, unexpected balance reductions, or a breach of business logic that assumed a limited time window. This issue affects any user who signs a forward request, the forwarder contract itself, and downstream protocols that rely on timely execution of delegated actions. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors added a test that artificially advanced the blockchain timestamp and observed that the forwarder still executed the signed request. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction appears fully authorized – the signature is valid and the nonce is fresh – so there is no obvious on‑chain indicator that the request is stale. To remediate, the request format should be extended with a deadline (or expiration timestamp) and the execute function must enforce that the current block timestamp is less than or equal to this deadline before processing the request. This change restores the signer’s ability to bound the execution window and prevents indefinite replay. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after signing a forward request they may later see a token balance change unexpectedly, for example “my balance went to zero” or “the transfer happened months later when I thought the request was expired”. The discrepancy between the expectation (the operation should happen soon or not at all after a reasonable period) and reality (the operation can be executed at any future time) violates the accounting assumptions of the protocol and can lead to funds disappearing or being moved under unfavorable conditions.

title: M-01 | Mismatching Baseline Values
description:
After the updates, the blv is calculated based on the upper ﬂoor tick in the MarketMaking,
CreditFacility, and LoopFacility contracts. However, in the BPOOL contract, it is still calculated using
the lower ﬂoor tick.
The BaselineInit.launch function uses the baseline value from the BPOOL contract when calculating
capacity, which creates a discrepancy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatched baseline value calculation across contracts. After recent updates, the baseline value (blv) is derived from the upper floor tick in three core contracts (MarketMaking, CreditFacility, LoopFacility). However, the BPOOL contract still derives the baseline from the lower floor tick. The BaselineInit.launch routine reads the baseline from BPOOL to compute the pool's capacity. Because the two sources use different tick directions, the capacity is calculated with an inconsistent baseline. This inconsistency can be exploited by submitting trades or credit requests that rely on the reported capacity; an attacker can cause the system to think there is more (or less) available liquidity than actually exists, leading to over‑allocation of funds, unexpected reverts, or loss of collateral. The impact is that users may see their deposits locked, receive zero refunds, or experience failed transactions because the contract believes capacity is exhausted when it is not, or vice‑versa. The condition occurs whenever the BaselineInit.launch function is called after the contract upgrades that changed the tick direction, i.e., any deployment that mixes the new upper‑floor logic with the old BPOOL logic. All participants that interact with the pool—liquidity providers, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting invariant that capacity equals baseline × some factor is broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the baseline calculation across contracts and noticed the divergent tick reference. It is subtle because the contracts expose the same public function name (getBaselineValue) and the returned number appears plausible; only a cross‑contract consistency check reveals the mismatch. The proper fix is to align the BPOOL implementation with the other contracts by updating its getBaselineValue function to use the upper floor tick, or alternatively to refactor BaselineInit to fetch the baseline from a single source. This resolves the accounting inconsistency, restores correct capacity computation, and prevents scenarios where funds disappear or refunds are missing due to a wrong baseline.

title: M-02 | updateTicks Should Use Previous Liquidity
description:
In the _updateTicks function of the MarketMaking policy there is logic to alter the upper tick of the
anchor position based upon the liquidity of the Discovery position relative to the Anchor position
liquidity.
This is done to ideally prevent bAsset supply being minted in excess of the Discovery position
liquidity in the range above the price in the Anchor position.
This reduces the magnitude of an arbitrage opportunity that would arise from selling through the
Discovery range into the Anchor range and beneﬁtting from the increased liquidity due to a higher
leverage of the Anchor.
However in such an arbitrage scenario, the liquidity that the Anchor position should be compared
against is the liquidity of the previous Discovery position rather than the liquidity of the current
Discovery position.
This is because the old Discovery position is the one which is sold through to reach the new Anchor
range and thus trigger the rebalance and therefore is the liquidity which the Arbitrage economics are
based upon.
As a result the Anchor range upper tick handling should consider the liquidity of the old Discovery
position rather than the current result of the _getThresholdLiquidity function, which will be the new
Discovery position liquidity.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market‑making policy's _updateTicks routine, which adjusts the upper tick of the anchor position based on the liquidity of the discovery position. The intended logic is to prevent the minting of bAsset supply that exceeds the discovery position's liquidity when the price moves into the anchor range, thereby limiting arbitrage profit from selling through the discovery range into a higher‑leverage anchor range. However, the routine compares the current discovery liquidity (the liquidity that will exist after the rebalance) instead of the liquidity of the previous discovery position, which is the actual amount being sold through to reach the new anchor range. Because the arbitrage economics are derived from the old discovery liquidity, using the new liquidity underestimates the amount of liquidity available for arbitrage, allowing a trader to sell a larger volume through the discovery range, mint excess bAssets, and capture a larger price swing. This can lead to unintended inflation of the bAsset supply, distortion of the protocol's accounting, and potential loss of value for other participants. The issue manifests when a rebalance is triggered by price movement that pushes the market into the anchor range; at that moment the _updateTicks function calculates the upper tick using _getThresholdLiquidity, which returns the liquidity of the new discovery position. An attacker can exploit the mismatch by executing a rapid arbitrage trade that sells through the discovery range before the tick is updated, thereby extracting profit from the mis‑priced anchor range while the protocol still believes the liquidity protection is sufficient. The affected parties include liquidity providers, borrowers, and any user relying on the protocol's guarantee that bAsset supply will not exceed the discovery liquidity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the market‑making contract, where the logical flow of liquidity comparison was examined and found to reference the wrong state variable. The problem is subtle because the contract still updates the tick, but the protection window is narrower than intended, making the bug easy to miss in functional testing that does not simulate the exact arbitrage sequence. From a user perspective the symptom may appear as an unexpected increase in bAsset balances or accounting numbers that do not match the expected liquidity limits. To remediate, the _updateTicks logic should compare the predicted anchor liquidity against the minimum of the newly calculated threshold liquidity and the liquidity of the previous discovery position, ensuring that the most conservative liquidity figure is used to bound the upper tick. This change restores the intended economic safeguard, preventing excess bAsset minting and reducing arbitrage profit opportunities.

title: M-03 | DISCOVERY_LENGTH Hardcoded For 1% Fee Pools
description:
The DISCOVERY_LENGTH variable in the MarketMaking contract is intended to represent 30 tick
spacings, as indicated by the comment.
However, its current implementation as 30 x 200 only aligns with 1% fee pools. This means the
calculation will be incorrect if applied to pools with different fee tiers.
bug_full: The MarketMaking contract contains a constant named DISCOVERY_LENGTH that is meant to represent a window of thirty tick spacings, as documented by an inline comment. In practice the value is hard‑coded as 30 × 200, which corresponds to the tick spacing used by Uniswap‑style pools that charge a 1 % fee. Tick spacing, however, varies with the fee tier of a pool – for example a 0.3 % fee pool typically uses a spacing of 100. Because the contract never queries the actual tick spacing from the BPOOLv1 contract, the discovery window is calculated incorrectly whenever the market maker is deployed on a pool with a fee tier other than 1 %. The mismatch causes the market maker to look for price ticks that do not exist in the target pool, resulting in missed order placements, zero trade execution, and an apparent loss of liquidity from the user’s perspective. From a user’s point of view the interface may show that a liquidity provision was submitted but no fills occur, balances remain unchanged, and the user may suspect that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is malfunctioning. The bug was uncovered during a manual audit of the MarketMaking source code, where the auditor noted the discrepancy between the comment and the hard‑coded multiplication. It can be difficult to spot because the contract behaves correctly on the default 1 % fee pools that were likely used in initial testing, masking the problem for other fee tiers. The root cause is the use of a static constant instead of dynamically obtaining the tick spacing from the pool contract, violating the accounting assumption that the discovery length is proportional to the actual tick spacing of the pool. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the tick spacing from the BPOOLv1 instance for each pool it interacts with, or make DISCOVERY_LENGTH configurable per pool, thereby aligning the discovery window with the true market parameters and restoring correct order discovery across all fee tiers.

title: M-08 | Position Fee Not Factored Into Margin
description: During liquidation, when _isMaintenanceMarginSafe is called, pending borrow fees are included in the required Maintenance Margin (MM). However, the position fee is not factored into the MM calculation. Since this position fee depends on the position value, it can sometimes be substantial. In such cases, _isMaintenanceMarginSafe might return true, even when the collateral is insufficient to cover the position fee. Despite this, the liquidation proceeds due to shouldCollateralSufficient = false in _dispatchPositionFee, leading to unpaid fees. This results in lost fee revenue for LPs and veMUX holders.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a margin‑checking omission that allows a liquidation to be approved even when the trader’s collateral is insufficient to cover the full cost of the position fee. During the liquidation flow the contract calls _isMaintenanceMarginSafe to verify that the required maintenance margin (MM) is satisfied. This function correctly adds pending borrow fees to the MM requirement, but it neglects to include the liquidation position fee, which is calculated as a percentage of the position value and can become sizable for large positions. Because the position fee is omitted, _isMaintenanceMarginSafe may return true, signalling that the account is safe, while in reality the collateral cannot pay the fee. The subsequent call to _dispatchPositionFee sets shouldCollateralSufficient to false, yet the liquidation proceeds, leaving the position fee unpaid. From a user perspective the liquidation appears to happen normally, but the expected fee payout is missing; balances that should have increased with fee revenue remain unchanged, creating the impression that “funds disappear” or that “refunds are missing”. The issue surfaces only when a liquidation is triggered for a position with a high fee component, making it hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the liquidation event, not the internal fee accounting discrepancy. The root cause is the failure to treat the position fee as part of the collateral sufficiency check, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all costs must be covered by the margin. This bug was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who observed that fee revenue for liquidity providers and veMUX holders could be lost. The impact is financial: fee revenue that should be distributed to LPs and token holders is not collected, reducing overall protocol earnings. To remediate, the maintenance‑margin verification logic should be updated so that the liquidation position fee is added to the required margin calculation, ensuring that _isMaintenanceMarginSafe only returns true when the collateral can cover both borrow fees and the position fee, thereby preventing unpaid fees and preserving expected revenue flows.

title: M-09 | Empty Collateral Can Be Activated
description:
Market._realizeProfit() calls CollateralPool.realizeProfit which charges a given amount of the pool's collateral token from the LPs in order for the trader to be paid. After that, the charged collateral token is added towards the activeCollaterals of that trader. This is done regardless of the charged amount. Because CollateralPool.realizeProfit converts from USD to the collateral token and divides multiple times, it's possible to have positive PnL in USD, but the result in collateral token to be 0. When this happens, LPs won't be charged and the trader won't profit, but the collateral token of the pool will still be added to their activeCollaterals. This will result in users having tokens with 0 balance in their activeCollaterals, which:
• Increases unnecessarily their collateral tokens count, making it harder to add new tokens.
• Can block the fulfilment of a close order which withdraws USD because withdrawUsd goes over each active collateral and tries to withdraw from it by passing the needed amount to _withdrawFromAccount. Inside that internal function there is a require assertion that will revert the transaction if the amount is 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the market contract’s profit realization flow. When a trader closes a position with a positive profit expressed in USD, Market._realizeProfit invokes CollateralPool.realizeProfit to convert that USD amount into the pool’s collateral token. The conversion routine performs several division operations, which can truncate the result to zero when the profit is small relative to the token’s price or when rounding occurs. Despite the conversion yielding a zero token amount, the implementation unconditionally adds the collateral token identifier to the trader’s activeCollaterals list. Consequently, the trader’s activeCollaterals may contain entries for tokens that have a balance of zero. From a user perspective this appears as an extra token listed in the UI with no amount, which is confusing because the user expects to see only tokens that hold value. The problem becomes critical when a later close order attempts to withdraw USD. The withdrawUsd routine iterates over each active collateral and calls an internal _withdrawFromAccount function, which contains a require statement that reverts if the withdrawal amount is zero. When the iteration reaches a zero‑balance token entry, the require fails and the whole transaction reverts, preventing the user from completing the withdrawal or adding new collateral tokens because the activeCollaterals count is artificially inflated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of profit realization and the handling of active collateral bookkeeping. It is subtle because the zero‑balance token entry does not immediately cause a loss of funds; the symptom only surfaces when a withdrawal is attempted, making it easy to overlook during testing. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state is updated without validating the underlying value, leading to inconsistent bookkeeping and potential denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the contract should conditionally add the collateral token to activeCollaterals only when the converted collateral amount is greater than zero, ensuring that only tokens with a positive balance are tracked and that subsequent withdrawal logic will not encounter a zero‑amount revert.

title: M-10 | donateLiquidity Should Update Market Borrowing
description: Whenever a pool's liquidity changes, the updateMarketBorrowing function must be called to snapshot cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd. This ensures the borrowing costs are accurately tracked and distributed across the pool participants. Currently, the donateLiquidity function does not perform this update. While this omission may not pose a risk when fees are donated through the fee distributor—since borrowing is updated during add/remove liquidity steps—donateLiquidity can also be called directly by external parties. This could lead to an inconsistency in cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd, particularly if significant liquidity is donated without triggering the borrowing update, impacting the fair distribution of borrowing costs.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the donateLiquidity function not invoking the market‑level accounting routine that snapshots the cumulative borrowing metric (cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd) whenever the pool’s liquidity changes. In this protocol the updateMarketBorrowing routine is responsible for recording the current borrowing cost state so that subsequent fee distribution and cost allocation reflect the true amount of liquidity that has been supplied. Because donateLiquidity can be called directly by any external address, bypassing the fee‑distributor path that already performs the update, the cumulative borrowing snapshot remains stale when a large amount of liquidity is donated. This stale snapshot leads to an inconsistency between the actual liquidity present in the pool and the borrowing cost that participants are charged. As a result, borrowers may be under‑charged or over‑charged, and the fair distribution of borrowing fees across liquidity providers becomes inaccurate. The issue is observable when a user donates a significant amount of liquidity and then notices that their borrowing fee share is unexpectedly low or that the protocol reports a borrowing cost that does not match the expected value based on the pool’s size. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the market‑level functions, where the auditor noted that the donateLiquidity entry point lacked the required call to updateMarketBorrowing, unlike the addLiquidity and removeLiquidity paths. The problem is subtle because the fee‑distributor flow does perform the update, so normal usage may not expose the inconsistency, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the issue, the donateLiquidity implementation should be amended to invoke updateMarketBorrowing before adjusting the pool’s liquidity balance, ensuring that the borrowing cost snapshot is always in sync with the current liquidity state. This change restores the accounting invariant that borrowing costs are proportional to the actual liquidity supplied, preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees and preventing unfair fee allocation.

title: M-11 | Broker Should Be Paid For Cancelling Orders
description: Brokers have the ability to cancel stale position and withdrawal orders and the gas fees incurred for these cancellations are refunded to the user who created the order. This design leaves brokers unreimbursed for the gas costs of performing the cancellations. A malicious actor can exploit this by creating multiple orders with unrealistic limit prices, ensuring that the orders never get filled and eventually go stale. The broker would then be forced to expend gas to cancel these orders repeatedly, incurring significant costs without compensation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the order‑cancellation mechanism of a perpetual trading protocol. When a broker cancels a stale position or withdrawal order, the gas that was spent to perform the cancellation is automatically refunded to the user who originally created the order. The broker, who is the entity executing the cancellation, receives no compensation for the gas it consumes. This design misaligns incentives because the broker is expected to keep the order book clean, but the cost of doing so is borne entirely by the broker. An attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a large number of orders with limit prices that are deliberately unrealistic, ensuring that the orders never become fillable and will eventually become stale. As each stale order must be cancelled by the broker, the attacker forces the broker to repeatedly execute cancellation transactions, each of which incurs gas that is refunded to the attacker’s address rather than to the broker. Over time the broker’s balance can be drained by the accumulated unreimbursed gas costs. The impact is financial loss for the broker, which may lead to reduced service quality, delayed cancellations, or even abandonment of the broker role, thereby harming the overall health of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the protocol’s logic triggers a cancellation of an order that has not been filled within its timeout window. It affects any party that acts as a broker – typically a contract or off‑chain service responsible for order management – and indirectly affects users who rely on timely order cancellation. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting of gas refunds in the cancellation path. It can be hard to notice because refunding gas to the order creator is a common pattern, and the extra cost to the broker is not obvious from a superficial review of the code. The bug belongs to the class of incentive‑misalignment or accounting errors where the party performing an operation is not reimbursed for its execution cost. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as the broker suddenly stopping cancellations, orders remaining stale in the UI, or the broker’s balance decreasing without an obvious reason. The expected behavior is that the broker should be compensated for the gas it spends, but the reality is that the gas is refunded to the order creator, creating a loss. To remediate the issue the contract should be changed so that a portion of the gas used for cancellation is deducted from the refunded amount and transferred to the broker, or the protocol should allow the broker to claim the full gas cost directly. This aligns incentives, prevents malicious actors from draining broker funds, and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the system.

title: M-12 | Borrowing State Not Updated Before Config Change
description:
Borrowing params such as baseApy can be changed by admin in FacetManagement.setConfig. However, when borrowing params are changed, it affects the interest accrued by users since the last update time. For example, if baseApy was increased, users will be unfairly charged the higher rate since the last update. Consider this scenario:
T0 (last updated timestamp):
• baseApy = 1%
T5:
• Admin updates baseApy to 2%
T10:
• Trader closes position, borrowing rate is based on baseApy 2%, when it should have been 1% from T0 - T5 and 2% from T5-T10
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that borrowing parameters such as the base annual percentage yield (baseApy) can be modified by an admin through the FacetManagement.setConfig function without first updating the market’s borrowing state. The market stores the timestamp of the last interest accrual and the accumulated interest up to that point. When the admin raises the baseApy, the contract continues to calculate interest for the period that has already elapsed using the new higher rate because the stored borrowing state has not been refreshed. Consequently, a trader who opened a position when the baseApy was 1% and later closed it after the admin increased the rate to 2% will be charged interest as if the 2% rate applied retroactively from the previous update time. This results in an over‑charge: the user expects to have been billed 1% for the first interval and 2% only after the change, but the contract applies 2% for the entire duration. The bug manifests whenever an admin changes borrowing configuration parameters without invoking pool.updateMarketBorrowing beforehand. It primarily affects borrowers who close positions after a config change, leading to unexpected loss of funds, reduced balances, or even a zeroed‑out position after settlement. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal closing transaction but the net proceeds are lower than anticipated, creating confusion and a perception that the protocol is unfair or possibly malicious. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between configuration updates and interest accrual logic. It is subtle because the interest calculation is internal and only becomes visible at settlement, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The root cause is a missing state‑synchronisation step: the borrowing market’s accrued interest is not snapshot before the rate change. To remediate, the contract should call pool.updateMarketBorrowing (or an equivalent state‑refresh function) before any borrowing parameter is altered, ensuring that interest accrued up to the change is locked in at the old rate and that subsequent accrual uses the new rate. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where interest rates apply only prospectively, preserving fairness and preventing unintended fund loss.

title: M-13 | Gaming Capped Pnl By Increasing Position
description: Traders’ PnL is capped based on _adlMaxPnlRate, and the capped PnL is used when realizing profits. uint256 maxPnlRate = _adlMaxPnlRate(marketId); uint256 maxPnlUsd = (size * entryPrice) / 1e18; maxPnlUsd = (maxPnlUsd * maxPnlRate) / 1e18; The capped PnL is calculated as above, with maxPnlUsd being directly influenced by the average entry price and the position size. When a trader’s PnL is higher than the capped PnL, the trader can intentionally increase their position at the current price just before closing it, then immediately close the position. This will result higher profit for the trader without any additional risk since both the size and entryPrice are momentarily inflated by the trader, causing maxPnlUsd to be higher.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/mux-2/pull/1
bug_full: The vulnerability is a profit‑capping bypass that allows a trader to obtain more profit than the contract’s intended maximum PnL limit. The contract calculates a capped profit (maxPnlUsd) by multiplying the position size and the average entry price, then applying a market‑specific rate (_adlMaxPnlRate). Because the calculation uses the current size and entry price, a trader who already has a profitable position can artificially inflate both values immediately before closing. By calling the function that increases the position at the prevailing market price, the trader raises the average entry price and the total size, which in turn raises the derived maxPnlUsd. The contract then settles the position using this inflated cap, so the trader receives a profit that exceeds the genuine earned amount without taking additional risk. This exploit can be performed whenever the protocol permits an immediate position increase followed by an immediate close, i.e., there is no grace period or lock‑up after a size change. Any trader with a positive unrealized PnL can trigger the attack, but malicious actors benefit most, while the protocol and other participants lose funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Guardian, who noticed that the cap calculation depends on mutable state that can be changed after profit accrual. It is hard to detect because the transaction sequence looks like a normal trade – the trader simply adds to the position and then closes it, and the profit appears legitimate on‑chain. From a user perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly large profit or a sudden increase in the withdrawn amount, while the protocol’s reserves shrink unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑manipulation profit‑capping bypass” where accounting assumptions are violated by altering the variables used in the profit formula. To remediate, the contract should either compute the capped profit based on immutable entry data captured at the moment the position is opened, or enforce a delay (grace period) after any position increase before allowing a close, thereby re‑introducing risk for the trader and preventing instantaneous profit inflation.

title: M-14 | Imprecise PnL In realizeProfit
description: Market._realizeProfit accepts a poolPnlUsd amount that should be realized as a profit in the collateral pool. The same poolPnlUsd is being returned from the function as deliveredPoolPnlUsd and will later be saved in the corresponding ClosePositionResult/LiquidatePositionResult struct. However, when Market_.realizeProfit() calls CollateralPool.realizeProfit, the pool recalculates the wad amount of collateral for tokens with different decimal tokens. This will cause a discrepancy between the real USD value realized as profit and the value assigned to deliveredPoolPnlUsd for tokens with less than 18 decimals. This can cause some close orders with isWithdrawProfit = true to revert because the deliveredPoolPnlUsd will be added towards the withdrawUsd that the order book will try to withdraw from the user's collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an imprecise profit calculation that occurs when the market contract finalizes a position and tries to transfer the realized profit to the user. The market function receives a USD amount (poolPnlUsd) that represents the profit to be credited, and it expects the same amount to be returned from the collateral pool as deliveredPoolPnlUsd. However, the collateral pool recalculates the profit in token units using the token's native decimal precision before converting it back to a USD wad. For tokens whose decimals are lower than the standard 18, this conversion introduces rounding or truncation errors, so the USD value that the pool reports back does not exactly match the original poolPnlUsd. When a close or liquidation order is executed with the flag isWithdrawProfit set to true, the order book attempts to withdraw the exact deliveredPoolPnlUsd from the user’s collateral. Because the delivered amount may be slightly smaller than the expected profit, the withdrawal fails and the transaction reverts. The impact is that traders see their expected profit disappear or the close order fail, leading to a mismatch between the protocol’s accounting and the user’s balance. The bug manifests only for collateral tokens with fewer than 18 decimals and only when profit withdrawal is requested, making it easy to miss during normal testing where 18‑decimal tokens are used. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended USD profit with the value stored in the result struct. The issue is hard to notice because the discrepancy may be a few wei and only surfaces under specific token configurations. To fix the problem the contract should recompute the actual USD profit based on the collateral amount returned by the pool and assign that recomputed value to deliveredPoolPnlUsd, ensuring the accounting stays consistent regardless of token decimals. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of arithmetic precision and unit‑conversion errors that break financial invariants in DeFi contracts, causing profit calculations to be off and withdrawals to revert.

title: M-15 | Wrong Pause Check For Liquidations
description: OrderBook.liquidate() liquidates a user by closing their position for a given market and potentially withdrawing their collateral if their MM is above their margin balance. This allows the Broker to keep the market in a healthy state. Currently, OrderBook.liquidate() will execute the whenNotPaused modifier and revert if LiquidityOrder is paused. LiquidityOrder has nothing to do with liquidate even though their names are similar. In result, if the market has the liquidity orders paused to manage some type of risk, the broker won't be able to liquidate position accounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misplaced pause check in the liquidation routine of a perpetual market contract. The function that liquidates under‑collateralised positions, OrderBook.liquidate(), is protected by the generic whenNotPaused modifier, which reads the pause flag from the LiquidityOrder contract. LiquidityOrder is unrelated to liquidation logic; its pause state is only meant to control the submission of new liquidity orders. Because the modifier checks the wrong contract, any time the LiquidityOrder contract is paused – for example to mitigate risk or during maintenance – the liquidate function will revert and refuse to close positions. This happens even though the market itself is still active and should be able to liquidate risky accounts. The root cause is a naming collision and an incorrect reference in the access‑control layer, causing the liquidation path to be unintentionally gated. An attacker or even a legitimate admin could pause LiquidityOrder, intentionally or accidentally, and thereby block the broker from liquidating accounts that have fallen below the required maintenance margin. As a result, positions that should be closed remain open, the market can become under‑collateralised, and other participants may suffer losses because the protocol cannot recover the required collateral. The issue manifests when the LiquidityOrder pause flag is set while the market remains enabled; users see no liquidation events, their positions stay open, and the protocol’s health metrics may deteriorate. The affected parties include any trader whose position should be liquidated, the broker that manages the market, and ultimately the protocol’s liquidity providers. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended liquidation guard (_marketDisableTrade in FacetClose.liquidatePosition) with the actual modifier applied, revealing the mismatch. It is subtle because the whenNotPaused modifier is a common pattern and the pause flag lives in a contract with a similar name, so tests that only verify normal operation may miss the scenario where LiquidityOrder is paused. To remediate, the whenNotPaused modifier should be removed from OrderBook.liquidate() and the existing market‑disable check should be relied upon to prevent liquidation when the market is deliberately disabled. This aligns the access control with the business rule that only the market’s trading state, not the liquidity order state, should gate liquidation, restoring the protocol’s ability to enforce margin requirements and protect funds.

title: M-16 | WithdrawUsd May Try To Withdraw 0
description: FacetPositionAccount.withdrawUsd calculates the amount of payingCollateral to withdraw from the user's account by calling _withdrawFromAccount. It's possible for payingCollateral to result in 0 because of rounding if the user has small amount of collateral (may happen naturally by realizing negative PnL). If this happens, the whole transaction will revert since _withdrawFromAccount fails if the amount to be withdrawn is 0. In result, the user won't be able to use withdrawUsd.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawUsd function of the FacetPositionAccount contract. The function attempts to compute the amount of payingCollateral that can be withdrawn for a user by invoking an internal routine called _withdrawFromAccount. Because the calculation uses integer arithmetic with rounding, a user who holds only a small amount of collateral – for example after realizing a negative profit‑and‑loss – may end up with a computed payingCollateral value of zero. The internal _withdrawFromAccount routine contains a guard that reverts the transaction when the withdrawal amount is zero. Consequently, when the rounding produces a zero amount, the entire withdrawUsd call fails and the transaction is reverted. This situation occurs only under the condition that the user’s withdrawable collateral is so small that it rounds down to zero; it does not affect users with larger balances. The impact is that affected users cannot execute a withdrawUsd operation, effectively locking their funds in the contract even though the UI may indicate that a withdrawal was requested. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts, they see no funds transferred, and the balance displayed in the UI may still show the original collateral, leading to confusion such as “I tried to withdraw but got nothing”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of withdrawUsd and identified that the zero‑amount guard could be triggered by rounding. It can be hard to notice because the failure only manifests for edge‑case balances and the revert message does not explicitly mention a zero amount, making it appear as an unexplained transaction failure. The bug belongs to the class of zero‑amount withdrawal or rounding‑induced accounting errors, where a mathematical edge case violates the business assumption that a withdrawal request always yields a positive amount. To remediate the problem the contract should check the computed payingCollateral before calling _withdrawFromAccount and simply skip the withdrawal step when the amount is zero, rather than allowing the internal function to revert. This change aligns the implementation with the intended logic that a zero‑withdrawal is a no‑op, preserving user experience and preventing unnecessary transaction failures.

title: M-17 | Brokers Can Be Gas Griefed
description: Users place orders in the order book and pay a gas fee to compensate the broker that fulfils their orders. Users can also cancel their orders after a given time passes. When they do that, they will be refunded the whole gas amount they paid to compensate the broker. This can be used to place multiple always reverting orders. For example, withdrawal orders with slippage over 100%, liquidity orders that exceed the liquidity cap, or just normal orders that happen to revert. The broker will try executing them, which means it will pay gas for execution for the reverting transaction. The user can then cancel all their orders and get their funds back, resulting in lost funds for the broker.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑griefing flaw that allows a user to cause a broker to lose the gas it spends on executing orders without providing any compensation. The root cause is the refund mechanism that returns the full amount of gas the user originally paid when an order is cancelled, regardless of whether the broker has already incurred execution costs. Because the contract does not differentiate between gas that should be returned to the user and gas that should be retained by the broker, a malicious user can submit orders that are guaranteed to revert – for example, withdrawal orders with slippage over 100 %, liquidity orders that exceed the pool’s cap, or any order that deliberately fails. The broker, following the protocol, attempts to fulfil each order and therefore pays the transaction gas. After the execution attempt, the user is allowed to cancel the order after a timeout and receives a full refund of the original gas payment. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful refund and no loss, while the broker’s balance is reduced by the gas that was spent on the failing execution. This situation can be repeatedly exploited: the attacker creates many always‑reverting orders, the broker repeatedly pays gas, and the attacker cancels each order to reclaim the full gas fee, resulting in a net loss of ether for the broker. The impact is financial loss for brokers and potentially for the protocol if broker incentives become unsustainable, leading to reduced liquidity or service denial. The issue manifests whenever the contract permits order cancellation after execution attempts and refunds the entire gas amount without accounting for the gas already consumed. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the order‑cancellation and refund logic. The flaw is subtle because the refund appears fair to users and does not raise an immediate error, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should split the paid gas into two portions: one part that is returned to the user upon cancellation and a second part that is retained by the broker as compensation for any execution effort, or otherwise enforce that refunds are only issued for unused gas. This change aligns the accounting with the intended business logic that brokers should be reimbursed for the actual cost they incur, preventing the possibility of gas‑griefing attacks.

title: M-01 | ClosePosition Only Updates The Current Market’s Borrowing Fee
description: When a position is closed, the contract updates only the borrowing fees for the currently closed market before verifying maintenance margin safety. This means that the margin check is performed without considering the borrowing fees pending to be paid in other still open markets. As a result, once all borrowing fees eventually get updated for those other markets, the position may fall below the required maintenance margin and become liquidatable. This could allow users to close a position on one market and leave the account appearing safe at the time of closure, despite actually being unsafe once all borrowing fees are updated. Moreover, it also allows users to close a position that could be in a liquidated state but appears safe because the borrowing fees were not applied in the other markets.
bug_full: When a trader closes a position on a perpetual market that supports multiple underlying markets, the contract’s closePosition routine updates the borrowing fee only for the market that is being closed. After this partial update the function performs a maintenance‑margin safety check, but it does so while ignoring any borrowing fees that are still pending in the other markets where the trader may still hold open positions. Because those fees are not accounted for, the margin check can incorrectly report that the account is safe. Later, when the protocol’s periodic fee‑updating mechanism finally applies the outstanding borrowing fees for the remaining markets, the trader’s total collateral may fall below the required maintenance margin. At that point the position becomes liquidatable even though the trader believed the account was already safe at the moment of closure. This discrepancy allows a user to close a position that is already in a liquidatable state, or to close a safe‑looking position and later suffer an unexpected liquidation once the hidden fees are applied. The impact is that funds can be taken from the user’s account without any visible warning, the protocol may incur unnecessary liquidation losses, and the overall risk model is broken because the accounting assumptions about margin safety no longer hold. The issue appears only after the delayed fee update, making it hard to notice during normal testing; the UI typically shows a healthy margin ratio at the time of closure, so users receive no error or warning. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete state update before safety check” vulnerabilities, where a contract validates a condition on a stale view of the system. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who observed that the maintenance‑margin verification does not invoke the global fee‑updating routine. To remediate the problem the contract should invoke the function that updates borrowing fees for all markets (for example _updateBorrowingForAllMarkets) before performing the margin safety check, ensuring that the true, up‑to‑date collateral value is used. In practice this means that after a closePosition call the user’s account balance will reflect all accrued fees, the UI will correctly indicate whether the account is safe, and unexpected liquidations caused by hidden fees will be prevented.

title: M-18 | MAX_COLLATERALS_PER_POSITION_ACCOUNT Can Be Bypassed
description: When closing a position, collaterals are added to the user's account, without validation. If a user only partially closes their account, they will then have all of these collaterals as active. When going to deposit collateral, the validation inside of _depositToAccount() will see that the collateral is already active and not revert even though the user is using more collateral assets than allowed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the enforcement of the maximum number of distinct collateral assets that may be associated with a single position account, defined by the constant MAX_COLLATERALS_PER_POSITION_ACCOUNT. When a trader closes a position, the contract automatically transfers any collateral that was locked for that position back into the trader’s account. However, the logic that performs this transfer does not verify whether adding those collaterals would cause the total number of active collaterals for the account to exceed the configured limit. Consequently, if a trader only partially closes a position – leaving the position open but retrieving some collateral – the newly added collaterals become active without any check. Later, when the trader attempts to deposit additional collateral, the internal _depositToAccount() routine only checks whether the specific collateral token is already marked as active; it does not count the total number of active collaterals. Because the previously transferred collaterals are already marked active, the deposit function does not revert, allowing the trader to add more collateral types than the protocol intends to permit. An attacker can exploit this by opening a position with several collateral types, performing a partial close to import those collaterals into the account, and then depositing further collateral assets, effectively bypassing the MAX_COLLATERALS_PER_POSITION_ACCOUNT restriction. The impact is that the protocol’s risk parameters, which assume a bounded set of collaterals per position, can be violated, potentially leading to inaccurate margin calculations, over‑collateralisation, or other accounting inconsistencies. This condition occurs only when a position is not fully closed and the user subsequently interacts with the deposit function. All users of the perpetuals contract who manage multiple collateral assets are affected, as the bug allows them to exceed the intended limit silently. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted the missing validation step in the close‑position flow. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows a successful close operation and no error on deposit, masking the fact that the internal collateral count has grown beyond the limit. To remediate, the contract should enforce the MAX_COLLATERALS_PER_POSITION_ACCOUNT constraint on every state‑changing operation that can modify the set of active collaterals, including partial closes, and should recompute the total active collateral count before allowing any new deposit. This aligns the implementation with the business rule that a position may only hold a bounded number of distinct collateral assets, preventing the described limit‑bypass scenario.

title: M-19 | Inaccurate aumUsd When Removing Liquidity
description: When removing liquidity from the collateral pool, a check is performed to ensure that the remaining asset value is sufficient to cover the reservedUsd amount. This check is implemented using require(reservedUsd = aumUsd). This aumUsd value being compared to reservedUsd is calculated by subtracting the value of the removed asset from the pool’s previous aumUsd value: aumUsd = removedValue. However, after this calculation, a portion of the removedValue is deposited back into the pool during _distributeFee. Normally, this deposited amount increases the pool’s aumUsd. However, this increase is not accounted for, making the aumUsd value used in the require(reservedUsd = aumUsd) statement inaccurate. As a result, liquidity removal may fail incorrectly with an InsufficientLiquidity error, even though the actual aumUsd is sufficient to cover reservedUsd.
bug_full: When a liquidity provider attempts to withdraw assets from the collateral pool, the contract performs a safety check that compares the amount of USD value that remains in the pool (aumUsd) with the amount that has been reserved for open positions (reservedUsd). The check is implemented as require(reservedUsd == aumUsd). The aumUsd used in this comparison is derived by taking the pool's previous aumUsd value and subtracting the USD value of the assets that are being removed. After the subtraction, the contract calls an internal function _distributeFee that returns a portion of the removed value back to the pool as a fee. This returned fee normally increases the pool's total USD value, but the increase is not added back to the aumUsd variable before the require statement is evaluated. As a consequence the aumUsd value used in the comparison is lower than the actual pool value after fee redistribution. The mismatch can cause the require to fail, triggering an InsufficientLiquidity error even though the pool still holds enough USD to satisfy the reservedUsd amount. The bug appears only during liquidity removal operations that involve fee redistribution, making it hard to notice because the error surface is a generic insufficient‑liquidity revert rather than an explicit accounting mismatch. Users experience a situation where they expect their withdrawal to succeed, see their transaction revert with an InsufficientLiquidity message, and may see no change in their displayed balance, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting flow of aumUsd and fee distribution. To fix the problem the fee amount that is re‑added to the pool must be included in the aumUsd calculation before the reservedUsd comparison, or the check must be rewritten to compare against the correctly updated pool value. This correction restores the invariant that the pool’s total USD value always covers the reserved amount, preventing false reverts and ensuring that liquidity providers can withdraw their funds as expected.

title: M-20 | Signature Replay In MuxPriceProvider Contract
description: The getOraclePrice function in the MuxPriceProvider requires oracleData.sequence to be greater than the sequence of the contract. It doesn’t specifically require it to be the next sequence, nor does it require it to be greater than the sequence of the last accepted oracle data. When a valid signature sequence is beyond the contract’s sequence, this signature can be used repeatedly by the broker until the sequences match. For example, if the current contract sequence is 4 and oracle data with a sequence of 10 is used, the contract sequence will be updated to 5. Another oracle data with a sequence of 8 would still be considered valid.
