Assuming this is expected behavior, any broker can repeatedly call the getOraclePrice function, increment the contract's sequence to 10, and render the oracle data with a sequence of 8 invalid.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature replay issue in the MuxPriceProvider contract's getOraclePrice function. The function checks that the incoming oracleData.sequence is greater than the contract's stored sequence, but it does not require the sequence to be exactly the next integer nor to be greater than the last accepted sequence. Consequently, an attacker or any broker can submit a signed oracle payload with a high sequence number, causing the contract to advance its internal sequence only by one step per call. Because the contract still accepts any later sequence that is merely greater than the current value, the same signed payload can be replayed multiple times until the contract's sequence catches up to the payload's sequence. This allows the attacker to repeatedly influence the price returned by getOraclePrice, potentially causing stale or manipulated price data to be used in downstream calculations such as margin calls or liquidations. The impact is that market participants may receive incorrect pricing, leading to unexpected liquidations, loss of collateral, or unfair advantage for the broker who replays the signature. The condition occurs whenever the oracle data is supplied with a sequence number that is not the immediate successor of the stored sequence, which is allowed by the current check. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the contract's oracle handling logic, where the sequence validation rule was examined and found to be insufficient. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract still updates its sequence and appears to accept newer data, masking the fact that older signatures remain valid until the sequence catches up. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the incoming sequence equals the stored sequence plus one, or alternatively update the stored sequence to the exact value of the accepted oracle data, thereby preventing replay of older signatures. Adding proper access control to the getOraclePrice function can also mitigate abuse if unordered data is intentional. This class of bug falls under replay attacks caused by weak monotonicity checks on signed messages, breaking the assumption that each oracle update is unique and cannot be reused. From a user perspective, a trader may see the price feed jump unexpectedly, receive a price that does not reflect the latest market, or experience a liquidation that seems unjustified because the price used was derived from a replayed older signature. The expectation that each new oracle update provides a fresh, non‑reusable price is violated, leading to potential financial loss.

title: M-21 | ADL Is Triggered Per Pool
description: When fillADLOrder is called, it validates that the position is viable for an auto deleverage. This is accomplished in isDeleverageAllowed function when it checks if any of the pools that the user has their position in is above the trigger PnL threshold. The issue is that a user could have a position, in its entirety, not exceed the trigger threshold, but has exceeded the threshold in a singular pool. This will cause the entire position to be auto deleverage, even if their position has negative PnL.
bug_full: When the fillADLOrder function is invoked, the contract attempts to verify that a trader's position qualifies for an automatic deleverage (ADL) by calling the isDeleverageAllowed routine. The routine currently inspects each liquidity pool that the trader participates in and triggers ADL if any single pool reports a profit‑and‑loss (PnL) value that exceeds a predefined threshold. The flaw arises because the check is performed per‑pool rather than on the aggregate PnL of the entire multi‑pool position. Consequently, a trader may hold a composite position whose overall PnL is negative or below the trigger level, yet if one of the constituent pools shows a PnL above the threshold, the contract will deem the whole position eligible for ADL and will automatically unwind it. This mis‑alignment with the intended business rule—ADL should only occur when the whole position is sufficiently profitable—creates a scenario where users lose positions prematurely, experience unexpected loss of capital, and see their balances drop to zero without any apparent reason. The issue manifests specifically during the execution of fillADLOrder when the isDeleverageAllowed function evaluates the per‑pool condition, and it affects any user who maintains exposure across multiple pools. It was uncovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the logical condition used an OR across pools instead of an aggregate AND/threshold comparison. The problem can be difficult to spot because the contract’s code appears to perform a sensible safety check, and the UI typically displays only the net PnL, hiding the fact that an individual pool crossed the limit. To remediate the vulnerability, the validation logic should be revised to compute the total PnL across all pools for the position and compare that sum against the ADL trigger threshold, ensuring that ADL is only executed when the overall position meets the profitability requirement. This class of bug falls under business‑logic validation errors where per‑component thresholds are incorrectly applied to a whole‑entity decision, leading to unintended fund disappearance and violation of the protocol’s risk management assumptions.

title: M-22 | Broker Can Abuse oracleSigner Signatures
description: The MuxPriceProvider contract does not include oracleData.oracleId in the message that is signed and verified. The signed message is built as: bytes32 message = ECDSAUpgradeable.toEthSignedMessageHash(keccak256(abi.encodePacked( Block.chainid, address(this), oracleData.sequence, oracleData.price, oracleData.timestamp))); Because the oracleId is not part of the signed data, a malicious broker can exploit this by taking a valid signature intended for one asset and using it to update the price of another asset. By calling the setPrices function with a different oracleId but supplying the same oracleData and signature, they can manipulate the price feeds of other assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature replay flaw in the price oracle integration where the signed message that the oracleSigner produces does not contain the identifier of the asset (oracleId). Because the verification routine only hashes the chain id, contract address, sequence number, price and timestamp, any signature that is valid for one asset can be presented to the setPrices function together with a different oracleId and the same oracleData, and the contract will accept it as authentic. This happens because the root cause is the omission of the oracleId from the signed payload, which means the cryptographic binding between a signature and a specific asset is missing. An attacker, typically a malicious broker that has access to a legitimate signature for a given asset, can exploit the flaw by reusing that signature to update the price of another asset under their control. The exploitation flow is: (1) obtain a valid signature for asset A from the trusted oracleSigner, (2) call setPrices with a different oracleId that points to asset B while supplying the unchanged oracleData and the signature, (3) the contract verifies the signature against the incomplete message, which succeeds, and (4) the price of asset B is overwritten with the price intended for asset A. The impact is that price feeds can be arbitrarily manipulated, leading to incorrect pricing, unintended liquidations, loss of collateral, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting. This condition can occur whenever a broker submits price updates and the contract does not enforce asset‑specific signing, which is typical during normal operation of the price update mechanism. All participants who rely on the oracle – traders, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the manipulated price can cause trades to execute at wrong rates or trigger margin calls. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the composition of the signed message and identified the missing oracleId field. It is hard to notice because the signature verification passes, no error is thrown, and the price change may appear legitimate on‑chain, making the bug subtle and only observable through unexpected price movements. The proper remediation is to include the oracleId in the data that is hashed and signed, thereby ensuring each signature is uniquely tied to a specific asset and cannot be replayed across different assets. Conceptually, this is a classic case of insufficient binding in signed messages, a class of bugs that break the integrity of off‑chain data authentication and violate the business logic that each asset’s price must be independently verified.

title: M-23 | Zero Balance Active Collaterals
description: The _depositToAccount function checks the raw amount is not zero, converts raw amount to wad amounts, and then adds collateral to the active collaterals. However, if the collateral's decimal value is higher than 18, wad amount can be zero while the raw amount is not zero. Since the balances are tracked as wad in the protocol, this collateral will still be added to active collaterals even though the wad balance is zero. Similarly, there will be some precision loss when withdrawing collaterals if the decimal value of the collateral is higher than 18.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol records collateral balances using a fixed‑point representation called wad, which has 18 decimal places. When a user deposits a token whose native decimal precision is greater than 18, the contract first checks that the raw amount supplied is non‑zero, then converts that raw amount to a wad value by truncating any excess precision. If the raw amount is small enough, the conversion can produce a wad value of zero even though the raw amount is positive. Because the contract only validates the raw amount, it proceeds to add the token to the list of active collaterals despite the resulting wad balance being zero. Consequently, the protocol’s accounting layer believes the user holds collateral that, in reality, has no value in the wad accounting system. This discrepancy can also appear during withdrawals: when converting a wad balance back to the token’s native units, the extra decimal places are discarded, causing a loss of precision that may leave a tiny remainder that cannot be withdrawn. The impact is that users may see a token listed as active in their portfolio while the on‑chain balance is effectively zero, leading to confusion, potential liquidation logic errors, and situations where a user cannot retrieve the small amount they deposited because it was rounded away. The issue manifests whenever a deposit or withdrawal involves a token with more than 18 decimals and the amount is below the threshold that survives the wad conversion. It affects any participant who interacts with such high‑precision assets, the protocol’s risk engine, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate collateral accounting. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the _depositToAccount function, where the auditor noticed that the zero‑check was performed only on the raw amount and not on the derived wad amount. Because the active‑collateral list is populated based on the raw‑amount check, the bug can remain hidden: the UI may display the token as present, but the balance shown in the protocol’s accounting view is zero, which is not an obvious error. To remediate, the contract should also verify that the wad amount is non‑zero before marking a collateral as active, and it should implement a safer conversion strategy for tokens with >18 decimals, such as storing the raw amount alongside the wad amount or using a higher‑precision arithmetic library to avoid rounding to zero. This change restores consistency between the user‑visible balances and the protocol’s internal accounting, preventing phantom collateral entries and ensuring that withdrawals correctly return the deposited amount.

title: M-02 | Inconsistent Borrowing Fee Calculation
description: The current borrowing fee implementation can lead to situations where certain users end up paying proportionally more in borrowing fees than others, depending on how frequently their position or market is updated. The protocol defines _updateMarketBorrowing as a function that accumulates a per USD “borrow cost” (i.e. cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd) every time a funding interval elapses. However, the actual “charging” of that borrowing fee to a trader’s position happens only in _updateAndDispatchBorrowingFee or _updateAccountBorrowingFee calls. Practically speaking, a position pays the difference between the current market’s cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd and the position’s stored entryBorrowing whenever the code calls _updateAccountBorrowingFee. In an idealized continuous interest model, it should not matter how many times you pay your borrowing fee, because the net owed over a specific time interval is the same. However, the code’s logic effectively runs each time _updateAccountBorrowingFee is triggered for a position. Because the fee is calculated as: feeUsd = positionValue * (cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd[i] - pool.entryBorrowing) / 1e18 and immediately removed from the user’s collateral, if your position is “touched” or updated more frequently, you might (depending on how the position’s size or price changes between updates) accumulate fees in multiple smaller increments, each pulled from your collateral. Meanwhile, a position that is only “touched” at the very end of a long interval might remain unaffected until a single large settlement occurs. If Trader A’s position has _updateAccountBorrowingFee called multiple times over an interval, then Trader A is “paying down” incrementally. If that triggers more “positionValue” recalculations at times when the position might be large or at unfavorable spot prices, Trader A can end up paying more total borrowing fees across many increments. Trader B, who never triggers a fee update until the end of a long period, might in some scenarios come out behind or ahead, depending on how the position size or price environment changed. If the size is smaller or the price is favorable near the time of the eventual update, B may pay less over that same time interval.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/mux-2/pull/4
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent borrowing fee calculation in the perpetual market contract. The protocol accumulates a per‑USD borrow cost (cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd) each funding interval, but the fee is only deducted from a trader’s position when _updateAccountBorrowingFee (or the related dispatch function) is executed. The deduction formula multiplies the current position value by the difference between the market’s cumulative borrowing index and the position’s stored entryBorrowing. Because this deduction runs every time the update function is called, a trader whose position is touched many times during the interval pays the fee in several smaller installments. If the position value changes between those calls – for example because the market price moves or the position size is adjusted – each installment is calculated on a potentially larger or less favorable value, causing the sum of all installments to be higher than the fee that would be owed under a continuous‑interest model. Conversely, a trader whose position is not touched until the end of the interval settles the entire fee in one large payment, which may be lower if the position value has decreased or the price moved favorably. The root cause is the coupling of fee accrual with position‑update events rather than with time, breaking the assumption that fee accrual is time‑based and independent of user actions. An attacker does not need to exploit code; the vulnerability is triggered simply by normal usage patterns: frequent trades, re‑balances, or any operation that calls the fee‑update routine. The impact is economic – affected users can lose additional collateral, see their balances shrink unexpectedly, or even become liquidated earlier because the protocol has taken more fees than intended. The issue appears only after a series of updates, making it hard to notice in isolated tests, and the discrepancy may be small enough to be dismissed as normal fee variance. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the theoretical continuous fee model with the contract’s discrete update logic. To fix the problem, the fee calculation should be decoupled from position‑update frequency; the contract should record the cumulative borrowing index at the last settlement and charge the total difference only once per funding interval, or use a time‑weighted accrual that yields the same total regardless of how many times the update function is called. This class of bug belongs to "inconsistent accounting due to event‑driven fee settlement" and violates the protocol’s financial invariants that borrowing costs must be proportional solely to time and not to user‑triggered actions. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a series of trades the UI shows a larger‑than‑expected fee deduction, sometimes reducing the collateral to zero or causing a missed refund, whereas the user expected a stable fee based on the elapsed time.

title: M-02 | Inconsistent Borrowing Fee Calculation
description:
Typically, in a continuous or properly time-based interest model, two traders borrowing the same amount of capital over the same timespan should pay the same interest, irrespective of how many times that interest is “settled.” The logic here is subtly different because the fee for each update depends on:
• The position’s value at that update moment (positionValue = pool.size * price / 1e18).
• The difference between cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd[i] and the stored entryBorrowing from the last time the fee was applied.
If your position value or the feePerUsd differs across multiple, intermediate calls, you can pay more or less than a user who sees only a single large update. Therefore, frequent updaters might end up paying more overall borrowing fees if the position’s size or mark price remains large each time an incremental fee is triggered and infrequent updaters could manage to pay less in total, if the price or position size shrinks by the time they do a final update. This difference becomes especially pronounced if the protocol or the broker calls _updateAccountBorrowingFee for some positions more often than others. On the other hand, the protocol ties borrowing fees to the current market price rather than a fixed entry price. Consequently, short positions that are winning (as the price went down) see their borrowing fees shrink and long positions in profit see the opposite effect, facing higher charges if their position is marked up repeatedly.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/mux-2/pull/4
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent borrowing fee calculation in the perpetual trading contract. The fee is computed each time _updateAccountBorrowingFee is called, using the current position value (pool size * price / 1e18) and the difference between cumulatedBorrowingPerUsd and the stored entryBorrowing. Because the fee depends on the market price and on the number of times the function is invoked, two traders who borrow the same amount for the same total duration can end up paying different total fees. A trader whose position is updated many times while the price stays high will accrue a larger fee than a trader who waits and performs a single update after the price has moved favorably. The root cause is that the fee accrual is not time‑based but event‑based and is tied to the instantaneous market price rather than a fixed reference. An attacker or a protocol component that calls the update function more frequently for certain accounts can deliberately increase those accounts’ borrowing costs, effectively extracting value from them. The impact is that users may see unexpectedly high borrowing fees, see their net profit reduced, or even receive a net loss when the protocol should have been neutral. The condition occurs whenever the protocol or a broker invokes _updateAccountBorrowingFee at uneven intervals, especially when the position size or price remains large across many calls. All borrowers, including retail users and institutional traders, are affected because the accounting mismatch can erode their capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared fee outcomes for identical positions under different update patterns. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a warning; the fee appears as a normal deduction from the account balance, and the discrepancy only becomes visible when the same trade is executed with different timing. The bug belongs to the class of inconsistent state‑dependent fee accrual or event‑driven interest calculation bugs, where the accounting logic violates the expectation that interest should be proportional only to time and not to the number of internal state updates. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal trade execution but later display a larger‑than‑expected fee, or a user expecting a refund of borrowing costs may receive zero or a reduced amount. To remediate the problem the contract should be refactored to a continuous, time‑based fee model that accrues interest proportionally per second or per block, using a fixed or averaged notional amount, so that the total fee depends solely on the elapsed time and the borrowed amount, independent of how many times the fee‑updating function is called.

title: M-03 | setPrices Function Does Not Accurately Retrieve The Asset Prices
description: The protocol’s current configuration for the oracle-driven pricing mechanism allows the price expiration to be set anywhere between 30 seconds and up to 24 hours which. As a result, when a broker performs a multicall that begins with calling setPrices to load price data and then proceeds to fill position orders, liquidity orders etc. the entirety of these operations may rely on prices that belong to different timestamps from the range: [block.timestamp - 24 hours, block.timestamp]. Traders can use multiple collateral tokens to maintain their positions. Let’s imagine that a trader holds a position backed by USDC, WETH and WBTC and the oracleIds for these assets have an expiration time of 24 hours and are using Chainlink Price Feeds with a heartbeat of 86400 seconds. When the broker calls setPrices the price received for USDC could be from second 86399, for WETH 40000 and for WBTC 1. Therefore, this could result in positions that might be incorrectly assessed as safe or unsafe leading to unfair liquidations, missed opportunities for profitable trades…
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract function that loads oracle prices, commonly called setPrices, which permits a price expiration window ranging from thirty seconds up to twenty‑four hours. Because the function does not enforce that all fetched prices share a recent, common timestamp, a single multicall can retrieve a mixture of fresh and stale price data for different assets. For example, when a broker invokes setPrices and then immediately executes position fills, liquidation checks, or liquidity orders, the price for USDC might be taken from a timestamp just before the 24‑hour limit while the price for WETH could be from a much more recent block. This discrepancy arises from the underlying Chainlink price feeds being configured with a heartbeat of 86400 seconds, allowing the oracle to return a value that is up to a day old. An attacker can deliberately order calls so that stale prices are used to assess a trader’s collateral, causing the protocol to deem a safe position as under‑collateralised and trigger an unfair liquidation, or conversely to miss a profitable arbitrage opportunity. The impact is that traders may lose funds, see unexpected liquidations, or be unable to execute trades that should be viable, undermining confidence in the platform. The issue manifests only when the price expiration is set near its maximum and when multiple assets with different feed timestamps are processed in the same transaction batch. All participants who rely on accurate margin calculations – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the price‑age check was missing and that the wide expiration range could be abused. Because the displayed prices appear numerically correct, the problem is subtle and may not be evident from the UI; users typically see a normal price feed but experience sudden liquidation or loss of expected profit. This class of bug is a stale‑data or oracle‑freshness validation error, where the system fails to enforce a consistent, recent price snapshot before performing critical accounting. To remediate, the protocol should either integrate a high‑frequency oracle with a short heartbeat (such as Pyth), enforce a strict maximum age for any price used in margin calculations, or require that all asset prices be fetched within the same block and validated against a common timestamp before any state‑changing operation is performed. By ensuring that price data is fresh and synchronized, the protocol can prevent incorrect safety assessments and protect user funds.

title: M-04 | Avoid Using _strictStableIds
description: The PricingManager’s pricing logic for stable assets includes a mechanism to use a hardcoded reference value of 1 USD unless there is a major depeg. While intended to maintain stability, this approach causes the protocol to rely on an artificially normalized value rather than accurate market data. This can cause positions backed by these stable assets to appear safer or riskier than they actually are, leading to incorrect margin calculations, mispriced positions, unexpected liquidations or unearned profits. Essentially, traders and LPs might face unfair conditions due to the system forcibly ignoring genuine price signals and relying instead on an arbitrary stable reference price.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a price‑normalisation mechanism that forces the on‑chain price of a stable asset to a hard‑coded value of 1 USD whenever the system does not detect a major de‑peg event. This design choice replaces the real market price supplied by the oracle with an artificial constant, causing the protocol’s risk engine to calculate margins, collateral requirements and liquidation thresholds on the basis of an inaccurate price. The root cause is the use of a static reference price in the PricingManager instead of always relying on the latest oracle data, and the de‑peg detection logic being too lax to trigger when the stablecoin drifts modestly from its peg. An attacker or a market participant can exploit the situation by trading or providing liquidity with a stable asset whose market price has deviated from 1 USD but is still treated as exactly 1 USD by the contract. Because the protocol believes the asset is perfectly stable, positions may appear over‑collateralised while they are actually under‑collateralised, leading to unexpected liquidations, unearned profits, or loss of funds for honest traders. The impact is financial loss for users, distorted pricing for LPs, and increased systemic risk for the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the stable asset’s price moves away from the peg but the de‑peg guard does not fire – for example during gradual de‑peg, market stress, or oracle latency. All participants who trade or provide liquidity against the affected stable asset are affected, including retail traders, professional market makers and the protocol itself. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the pricing logic, where the hard‑coded price was identified as a logical inconsistency that could not be observed from the UI because the displayed price remains 1 USD, masking the underlying mis‑pricing. The problem is hard to notice because the contract surface appears to maintain stability, yet internal calculations diverge from reality, leading to silent margin mis‑calculations. To remediate, the hard‑coded price override should be removed; instead the contract should always use the latest oracle price and implement a dynamic safeguard that activates only when a genuine de‑peg is detected, such as pausing trading, tightening collateral ratios, or invoking emergency price feeds. This aligns the protocol with its intended accounting assumptions that collateral value reflects true market value, preventing money from disappearing, refunds from being mis‑calculated, or positions being liquidated unfairly.

title: M-05 | Lack Of A Grace Period For Configuration Changes
description: The contract’s use of setConfig calls to modify critical parameters, such as MCP_ADL_MAX_PNL_RATE and other parameters, can impose immediate and drastic changes to the trading environment without providing users any time to adjust their positions. Sudden alterations to margin requirements, liquidation thresholds or other essential settings can leave traders caught off guard and result in unexpected position losses and forced liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an immediate‑activation design for on‑chain configuration changes. The contract exposes a setConfig function that can modify critical parameters such as the maximumprofit‑and‑loss rate, margin requirements, liquidation thresholds and other risk‑related settings. Because the new values become effective in the same transaction, there is no grace period or buffer that gives market participants time to react. The root cause is the lack of a delayed activation mechanism; the contract treats configuration updates as instantaneous state changes without any pending state or notification system. An attacker or any privileged account that can call setConfig can therefore raise margin requirements or tighten liquidation thresholds at any moment, causing open positions that were previously safe to become under‑collateralised. When the new parameters take effect, the protocol’s liquidation engine may immediately trigger forced liquidations, wiping out trader balances, reducing collateral to zero, or leaving users with unexpected losses. This impact is felt by any trader holding positions at the time of the change, as well as by the protocol’s overall health because sudden liquidations can cascade and reduce liquidity. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of setConfig that alters a risk‑sensitive parameter; no additional checks, timelocks or alerts are performed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the governance and configuration pathways and noted that no time‑delay or event‑based warning exists. It can be hard to notice because configuration changes may be infrequent and the contract does not emit a distinct “pending change” event, so users see only the final state after the transaction. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a position that was previously safe suddenly shows a liquidation flag, the UI displays a zero or dramatically reduced balance, and the trader receives no warning that margin requirements have changed. The bug belongs to the class of “instant configuration change without grace period” or “missing timelock for critical parameter updates”. To remediate, the contract should introduce a pending state for any critical parameter change, enforce a predefined buffer period (for example 24 hours) before the new value becomes active, emit an event announcing the pending change, and optionally provide an on‑chain alert mechanism so that traders can rebalance, add collateral or close positions before the change takes effect.

title: M-06 | Add And RemoveLiquidity Orders Are Missing Slippage Checks
description: When a Liquidity Order is placed there is no way for the caller to specify a minimum acceptable output amount. In typical AMM or liquidity pool scenarios, a user will include a minAmountOut parameter to protect themselves from adverse price movements or sandwich attacks that may occur between the placement of the order and the fulfilment. Without this parameter, the liquidity providers are subject to price changes and certain actions that can occur between the placement of their order and the fulfilment and therefore the liquidity provider could receive far fewer tokens (in the case of removing liquidity) or far fewer shares (in the case of adding liquidity) than they would expect under stable conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection on add‑and‑remove liquidity orders. When a user creates a liquidity order the contract does not require a minimum acceptable output amount, often expressed as a minAmountOut parameter in automated market maker designs. The root cause is that the LiquidityOrderParams struct lacks this field and the execution logic does not compare the actual amount of tokens or shares received against any user‑specified threshold. An attacker can exploit the gap by performing price‑impacting trades or sandwich attacks between the moment the order is placed and the moment it is fulfilled. Because the contract does not revert or enforce a lower bound, the liquidity provider may receive far fewer tokens when removing liquidity or far fewer LP shares when adding liquidity than they anticipated under stable market conditions. The impact is a reduction of the provider’s effective capital, which appears to the user as a successful transaction that delivers an unexpectedly small balance increase or even a near‑zero receipt of shares. This situation occurs whenever an order remains pending in the pool and any external transaction can shift the pool’s price, which is common in volatile or heavily traded environments. The affected parties are liquidity providers, any user who relies on the protocol’s accounting to receive a predictable amount of assets, and the protocol itself because the accounting assumptions about fair value are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted the absence of a slippage check in the order‑handling code. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the on‑chain logs show normal execution, while the user‑facing UI merely reports success; the discrepancy only becomes visible when the user inspects the resulting token balance or LP share count. Conceptually the fix is to introduce a minAmountOut field to the order parameters and to enforce that the actual output meets or exceeds this threshold before completing the transfer, thereby restoring the standard slippage‑protection pattern used in AMM contracts. This class of bug is a missing price‑validation or slippage‑check vulnerability, which breaks the business logic that a liquidity operation should deliver at least the amount promised by the user under normal market conditions. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that “succeeds” but leaves the wallet with far fewer tokens than expected, contradicting the expectation that adding liquidity yields a proportional share of the pool and that removing liquidity returns the original contribution. The failure mode can be described as funds disappearing or refunds being lower than anticipated due to unchecked price movement.

title: M-07 | No Post-Deposit Safety Check In depositCollateral Function
description: The depositCollateral function allows users to add collateral to an existing position but fails to verify whether the position is then sufficiently collateralized or safe from liquidation immediately afterward. A user might deposit too little collateral, resulting in a position that still remains under collateralized and can be liquidated right away.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a collateral‑deposit routine that permits a user to add funds to an existing leveraged position but does not perform a verification step after the deposit to ensure that the position satisfies the required margin ratio. Because the function lacks a post‑deposit safety check, a user can submit an amount that is insufficient to bring the position back into a safe zone, yet the transaction still succeeds. Consequently the position remains under‑collateralized and becomes immediately eligible for liquidation by anyone monitoring the protocol. This flaw originates from a missing invariant check: the contract assumes that any deposit will automatically satisfy the margin requirement, an assumption that is not enforced by code. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker can watch for a pending deposit, allow it to complete with a small amount, and then trigger a liquidation, capturing the remaining collateral or earning a liquidation reward. The impact is loss of user funds, unexpected liquidation of positions that the user believed were secured, and erosion of confidence in the protocol’s risk management. The condition occurs whenever depositCollateral is called on a position that is already close to the liquidation threshold and the supplied collateral does not cover the shortfall. All participants who hold leveraged positions are potentially affected, especially those who rely on the UI to indicate that a deposit will make their position safe. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business logic – “deposit must result in a safe position” – with the actual implementation, revealing the missing safety assertion. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error or warning, the problem can be hard to notice; users only see the downstream symptom of an immediate liquidation, which may be attributed to market volatility rather than a code defect. The proper remediation is to insert a check after the collateral transfer that recomputes the position’s health factor and reverts the transaction if the required margin is still not met. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of bugs known as “missing post‑condition validation” or “insufficient collateral verification”, ensuring that business rules around margin safety are enforced at runtime. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit, but the account balance can drop to zero shortly after, contradicting the expectation that the deposit protects the position. The failure mode therefore manifests as funds disappearing, liquidation events occurring despite a recent deposit, and accounting records that no longer reflect the intended safety guarantees.

title: M-24 | Profit Can Only Be Realized With The Pool’s Collateral Token
description: The CollateralPool contract calculates its overall assets under management by summing balances of its primary collateral token and any additional tokens that arrive via fees, trader losses or rebalance operations. Although traders can open positions based on this total multi-token value, the code that settles profit only checks the availability of the main collateral, see CollateralPool.realizeProfit function below. When traders attempt to realize profits, if there is insufficient balance of the primary collateral, even though other tokens in the pool collectively exceed the required amount, the function realizeProfit will revert, blocking some traders from closing and profiting from their positions due to the following require check: require(wad = _liquidityBalances[token], InsufficientLiquidity(wad, _liquidityBalances[token])); The expected approach would be for rebalancers to convert these other tokens into the main collateral token, but there is no guarantee that this can be done quickly as it requires that the pool1’s foreign token is held by any of the other pools. Therefore a significant time gap might occur before rebalancing is performed. Furthermore, even if the protocol attempts to swap these foreign tokens for the main collateral on, for example through Uniswap, the pool would have to pay a high fee of around 5%, causing the CollateralPool to lose a portion of its AUM with each of those swaps.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the profit settlement logic of the CollateralPool contract. The pool tracks its total assets by adding the balance of the main collateral token with any secondary tokens that arrive from fees, trader losses or rebalancing. However, when a trader calls the realizeProfit function the contract validates only the balance of the primary collateral token. The require statement compares the requested profit amount (wad) with the stored balance of that single token and reverts if the primary token is insufficient, even though the combined value of all tokens in the pool may be enough to cover the payout. This mismatch occurs because the code does not automatically convert or consider other supported collateral tokens during profit realization, and it relies on an external rebalancing process that may be delayed or costly. An attacker or even a regular trader can trigger the failure by opening a position that generates profit while the pool’s primary token balance is low but other tokens are plentiful. When the trader attempts to claim the profit, the transaction reverts with an InsufficientLiquidity error, the user receives no funds, and the position remains open. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style blockage of profit withdrawals, loss of expected earnings for traders, and potential erosion of the protocol’s total assets under management if the pool is forced to swap foreign tokens at high fees to satisfy the primary‑token check. The issue manifests whenever the pool holds a mix of tokens and the main collateral is temporarily depleted, a situation that can arise during normal fee collection or after large trader losses. All traders, liquidity providers and the protocol itself are affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions – that profit can always be paid from the total pool value – are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the asset accounting view with the settlement code and noticed the single‑token require. It can be hard to spot because the pool’s overall balance appears healthy, masking the underlying token‑specific shortfall. The recommended remediation is to modify realizeProfit so that profit can be settled using any supported collateral token held by the pool, or to automatically convert secondary tokens into the primary token before the require check, thereby aligning the settlement logic with the multi‑token asset accounting model.

title: M-05 | ERC-777 Reentrancy In reinvest
description: When the bounty is sent to the given bountyTo address with an ERC-777 token the receiver can re-enter the system. At this point, the fee growth values of the position were already reset, but the position had not received the liquidity yet. Therefore the collateral value of the position is smaller than it is in reality. This could lead to the system seeing the position as liquidatable or underwater when the caller reenters the system. Therefore a malicious actor can potentially abuse this state to either: • Liquidate the position to steal from its owner • Call restructureBadDebt to reduce the debt of the position and steal from the lenders (could be abused by the owner of the position)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that appears when the contract distributes a bounty using an ERC‑777 token during the reinvest operation. ERC‑777 tokens invoke a user‑controlled hook (tokensReceived) on the recipient before the transfer completes, allowing the recipient contract to call back into the vulnerable contract. In the affected flow the contract first resets the fee‑growth accounting for a position, then attempts to transfer the bounty, and finally credits the newly minted liquidity to the position. Because the bounty transfer occurs before the liquidity credit, a malicious recipient can re‑enter the contract while the fee‑growth values have already been cleared but the position’s collateral has not yet been increased. This creates a temporary state where the recorded collateral is lower than the true value, causing the protocol’s liquidation checks to believe the position is under‑collateralised. An attacker can exploit this window to trigger a liquidation of the victim’s position and seize the collateral, or, if the attacker is the position owner, call the restructureBadDebt function to artificially reduce the debt owed to lenders and extract value from the lending pool. The impact is loss of user funds, incorrect liquidation of otherwise healthy positions, and potential theft from lenders. The bug manifests only when the bounty token implements ERC‑777 callbacks; with standard ERC‑20 tokens the re‑entrancy does not occur. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state changes and external calls, and it can be hard to notice because ERC‑777 hooks are less common and the incorrect ordering of fee‑reset versus liquidity addition is subtle. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected liquidation notices, sudden disappearance of collateral, or a debt balance that appears reduced without any legitimate action. The issue belongs to the class of “checks‑effects‑interactions” violations where an external call is made before all internal state updates are finalized. The recommended remediation is to move the bounty transfer to the end of the function, after all position state (fee growth, liquidity, collateral) has been updated, or to replace the ERC‑777 token with a non‑re‑entrant transfer mechanism, thereby eliminating the re‑entrancy window.

title: M-06 | Frontrun Restructure Bad Debt
description: When restructureBadDebt is called, the exchangeRate will immediately decrease due to the reduction in _totalBalance without a proportional reduction in pool token supply. A user can frontrun the restructuring to redeem before the exchange rate drop to avoid the penalty. The LP exploiting this receives yield without risk while increasing the risk of all the other LP as the bad debt is socialized among all other LPs. Furthermore, the LP taking advantage of the stepwise jump in the exchange rate can then mint the same amount of PoolTokens for a fraction of the price.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the pool’s debt‑restructuring routine, specifically the function that updates the exchange rate when bad debt is socialized. When restructureBadDebt is invoked, the contract reduces the internal _totalBalance to reflect the newly accounted bad debt but does not simultaneously reduce the total supply of pool tokens. Because the exchange rate is calculated as the ratio of total balance to token supply, this imbalance causes the exchange rate to drop abruptly. An attacker can observe the pending transaction, submit a redeem call that executes before the exchange rate adjustment takes effect, and therefore withdraw pool tokens at the pre‑drop rate, receiving more underlying assets than the new rate would allow. After the exchange rate has fallen, the same attacker can mint new pool tokens at the reduced price, effectively acquiring the same amount of tokens for a fraction of the previous cost. This front‑running sequence lets the attacker capture yield without bearing the associated risk, while the remaining liquidity providers absorb the bad debt through a lower per‑token value. The issue manifests only when a bad‑debt restructuring transaction is pending and the pool’s accounting does not enforce a proportional token‑supply update. It affects all LPs who rely on the exchange rate to represent the true value of their shares; users may notice that their redemption yields are unexpectedly high just before a restructuring, and later see their token value decline sharply, leading to a perceived loss of funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting logic of the debt‑socialization pathway and identified the missing token‑supply adjustment as a classic front‑runable state‑change bug. It can be hard to notice because the exchange rate change is instantaneous and the pool’s UI may not display the intermediate rate, making the profit opportunity invisible to casual observers. To remediate, the protocol should decouple redemption from the immediate exchange‑rate shift, for example by introducing a two‑step deposit/redeem process that locks the rate for a block or by updating both total balance and token supply atomically, ensuring that the exchange rate cannot be manipulated by ordering of transactions. In essence, the bug is a race‑condition in the accounting of a shared pool where a state variable (exchange rate) is derived from two interdependent values that are not updated together, allowing an adversary to exploit the timing of state transitions to extract value at the expense of other participants.

title: M-01 | Funds Trapped On Ethereum
description: The MultiHopComposerV1 contract uses an interface which returns a boolean value for the approve function, however USDT on Ethereum does not return a boolean from the approve function. This results in a revert upon approval which will cause the compose message to be un-executable, thereby trapping the USDT in the MultiHopComposerV1 contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the ERC20 interface used by the MultiHopComposerV1 contract and the actual behaviour of the USDT token on Ethereum. The contract imports an interface that defines the approve function as returning a boolean value, following the standard ERC20 specification. However, USDT on Ethereum implements approve as a non‑returning function; it does not emit a boolean result. When MultiHopComposerV1 invokes approve through the mismatched interface, the Solidity runtime expects a return value and attempts to decode it. Because no data is returned, the call reverts. This revert aborts the compose operation, leaving the USDT that was transferred into the MultiHopComposerV1 contract permanently locked because the subsequent logic that would normally release or forward the funds never executes. The issue can be exploited simply by initiating a compose transaction that includes USDT; the transaction will revert at the approval step, but the contract may have already received the tokens before the revert, depending on the internal ordering, resulting in the tokens being trapped. The impact is that users who try to move USDT through the multi‑hop pathway lose access to their funds, seeing their balances drop to zero in the contract while the UI may still indicate a pending or successful request. The condition occurs only on Ethereum mainnet where USDT follows the non‑standard approve signature; on chains where USDT conforms to the standard ERC20 interface the bug does not manifest. All participants who interact with the compose function—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the trapped assets reduce available liquidity and break accounting assumptions that funds will be forwarded after approval. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s imported IERC20 definition with the actual ABI of USDT, revealing the incompatibility. It is easy to miss because the approve call compiles without error and many developers assume all ERC20 tokens follow the same interface; the revert only appears at runtime, often hidden behind higher‑level transaction handling. To remediate, the contract should import an interface that matches USDT’s approve signature, i.e., an IERC20 variant that declares approve without a return value, or use a low‑level call that ignores the return data. This change aligns the contract with the token’s actual behaviour, preventing the revert and ensuring that funds are not unintentionally locked. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of interface mismatch or non‑standard token implementation errors, where a contract assumes a standard ABI that the token does not provide, leading to failed calls and loss of asset accessibility.

title: M-01 | Arbitrary NFTLP Code Can Be Used
description: The ImpermaxFactory contract allows for the creation of lending pools with a completely arbitrary NFTLP address. Consequently, a malicious user may create a lending pool with a malicious tokenized position which could lead to loss of user data and assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ImpermaxFactory contract, which permits the creation of lending pools by supplying an arbitrary address for the NFTLP (tokenized position) contract. Because the factory does not verify that the provided NFTLP address originates from the official tokenized‑position factory, an attacker can pass a malicious contract that pretends to be a legitimate NFTLP. When users later interact with a pool that was instantiated with such a malicious NFTLP, the malicious contract can execute arbitrary code during deposit, withdrawal or reward distribution, potentially stealing deposited assets, corrupting accounting data, or preventing users from retrieving their positions. The flaw originates from a missing validation step: the factory trusts any address supplied by the caller, assuming it implements the expected interface, but it never checks the contract’s provenance or source code. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious actor calls the factory’s pool‑creation function, provides a crafted NFTLP address that contains back‑doors, and then advertises the pool to unsuspecting users. Users, expecting to deposit collateral and receive a tokenized representation of their loan, may see their balances become zero, receive no rewards, or find that withdrawals revert without returning funds. The issue manifests whenever the factory’s create‑pool functions are invoked with an unverified NFTLP address; it does not require any special blockchain state beyond the attacker’s control of the malicious contract. All participants who deposit into the compromised pool—individual users, liquidity providers, and the broader protocol—are at risk of asset loss and data inconsistency. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the factory’s input validation logic and noted the absence of any source‑verification or whitelist checks. Because the address field looks like any other contract address, the bug can be difficult to spot in normal operation until funds disappear or accounting mismatches are observed. To remediate, the factory should enforce that any NFTLP address supplied to its functions has been deployed by the authorized tokenized‑position factory contracts, for example by checking the creator’s address, using an interface‑registry, or maintaining a whitelist of approved NFTLP implementations. This ensures that only vetted tokenized‑position contracts can be used, preserving the integrity of user deposits and the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: M-02 | Interest Lost On Low Decimal Tokens
description: In the accrueInterest function, the interest calculation interestFactor.mul(_totalBorrows).div(1e18) can round down to zero for low-decimal tokens (such as USDC), particularly when the borrow rate or total borrows are low. Specifically, when the product of interestFactor and _totalBorrows is less than 1e18, the division results in zero. This leads to a loss of interest for lenders, as the interestAccumulated is zero. Furthermore, this can cause a discrepancy between totalBorrows and accountBorrows, since accountBorrows does not experience the same precision loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding error that occurs in the interest accrual routine of a lending market when the underlying asset has a low number of decimal places, such as USDC which uses six decimals. The contract computes the accrued interest by multiplying a factor representing the per‑block borrow rate (interestFactor) with the total amount borrowed (_totalBorrows) and then dividing the product by 1e18, which is the scaling constant for 18‑decimal fixed‑point arithmetic. Because Solidity performs integer division, if the product of interestFactor and _totalBorrows is smaller than the scaling constant, the division truncates the result to zero. This situation is common when either the borrow rate is very small or the total borrowed amount is modest, which is typical for low‑decimal tokens. As a result, the variable that records accumulated interest (interestAccumulated) remains zero, meaning lenders receive no interest for that accrual period. Moreover, the per‑account borrow tracking (accountBorrows) does not suffer the same truncation, creating a mismatch between the protocol‑wide totalBorrows and the sum of individual accountBorrows. From a user perspective, a lender expects their balance to grow after an interest accrual but observes no change, effectively losing the interest that should have been earned. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mathematical operations in the accrueInterest function and identified the edge case where the multiplication result falls below the 1e18 divisor. The issue can be hard to notice because the overall pool balances may still look reasonable, while only the incremental interest amounts are silently dropped, especially when dealing with small loan sizes. The impact is financial: lenders lose accrued interest, the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, and over time the discrepancy could lead to under‑collateralisation or reduced trust in the platform. The problem belongs to the broader class of fixed‑point precision errors that arise when using a single scaling factor for assets with differing decimal granularity. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a higher‑precision representation for rates (for example, scaling by 1e27 or using a library that supports variable‑precision arithmetic) so that the product of rate and principal never falls below the divisor, ensuring that interest calculations round up or at least do not truncate to zero. In summary, the bug is a rounding‑to‑zero error in interest computation for low‑decimal tokens, leading to lost lender earnings and accounting inconsistencies, and it should be fixed by increasing the precision of rate values or by redesigning the arithmetic to avoid integer division truncation.

title: M-03 | Borrow Rate Gaming
description: The currentBorrowBalance and trackBorrow functions accrue interest and therefore update the totalBorrows which would influence the utilizationRate and therefore the borrowRate. However, they do not have the _update modifier and therefore do not update the borrowRate. Therefore the system potentially deals with a stale borrowRate and the lenders receive less yield than they should. Furthermore, the system allows for interest gaming, since calling sync() every second will provide a different debt accumulated than calling sync() once over the same timespans. For example, with a decreasing _kinkBorrowRate every sync the borrow rates will also decrease and cause less to be repaid over the borrow’s lifetime, which in turn is less yield for lenders.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑borrow‑rate bug that arises because the functions responsible for accruing interest – the routine that calculates the current borrow balance and the helper that tracks borrow activity – update the total amount of borrows but do not trigger the protocol’s internal rate‑update mechanism. In this system the borrow rate is derived from the utilization rate, which itself depends on the total borrows. The missing _update modifier means that after totalBorrows changes, the borrowRate variable is left unchanged until another function that does include the modifier is called. As a result the protocol can operate with an outdated (typically lower) borrow rate. This stale rate can be exploited by repeatedly calling the sync function (or any function that forces interest accrual) at short intervals. Because the protocol’s kink‑borrow‑rate curve is decreasing, each successive sync with a lower utilization produces a slightly lower borrow rate. By chaining many rapid sync calls an attacker can reduce the effective interest cost on a loan, causing the borrower to repay less over the loan’s lifetime while lenders receive less yield than expected. The impact is a loss of expected interest income for lenders and a distortion of the protocol’s economic model; users may notice that their supplied assets earn less than advertised, or that a borrow appears to cost less than the published rate. The condition for the bug to manifest is any scenario where totalBorrows changes (e.g., a new loan, repayment, or interest accrual) without a subsequent borrow‑rate recomputation, which is common in normal operation of the contract. All participants – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that link utilization to rate are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s state‑changing functions with the documented rate‑update flow. It is hard to notice because the contract still reports a borrow rate value that looks plausible, and the UI may not display the intermediate stale state; only after many sync calls does the cumulative discrepancy become evident. The proper remediation is to ensure that every function that mutates totalBorrows also invokes the rate‑update logic, typically by adding the _update modifier to currentBorrowBalance and trackBorrow. Additionally, the protocol should consider limiting the frequency of sync calls or normalising the interest calculation so that varying sync intervals cannot produce different total costs for the same elapsed time. This aligns the implementation with the intended economic model and prevents interest‑gaming attacks.

title: M-04 | Interest Not Accumulated Before Admin Changes
description: Interest should always be accrued before updating parameters that will impact the outcome of the next update to fairly calculate the accumulated interest. The _setAdjustSpeed function in the BSetter contract for example can update the adjustSpeed variable that will influence the borrowRate, but it does not accrue interest before updating this variable. Therefore the next time the borrowRate is updated it applies the updated adjustSpeed value on the whole timeElapsed since the last update while in reality a part of the timeElapsed should be calculated with the old adjustSpeed value to fairly update the borrowRate.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing interest accrual step when an administrator modifies protocol parameters that influence interest calculations. In the BSetter contract the function that updates the adjustSpeed variable, which directly feeds into the borrowRate formula, does not first call the internal accrueInterest routine. Because interest is not recorded for the portion of time that elapsed before the parameter change, the subsequent borrowRate update applies the new adjustSpeed value to the entire elapsed interval instead of splitting the interval between the old and new values. This mis‑calculation leads to an inaccurate borrowRate and consequently an incorrect amount of interest credited to borrowers. The flaw can be exploited by an attacker or a malicious admin who deliberately changes adjustSpeed right before a large time interval passes, causing the protocol to credit less interest than it should, effectively stealing accrued earnings from users. The impact is that users see lower returns than expected, balances may appear stagnant or even decrease relative to the promised rate, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fair interest distribution are violated. The condition for the bug to manifest is any administrative update to a variable that participates in interest computation without a preceding interest accrual; it affects all borrowers whose positions span the update window, regardless of their individual actions. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the ordering of state‑changing functions and identified that the _setAdjustSpeed function omitted the required accrueInterest call. Because the symptom is a subtle deviation in accrued interest rather than an outright failure, it can be hard to notice without detailed accounting checks or comparison against expected rates. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a pattern where any state change that influences interest formulas first triggers the interest accrual mechanism, ensuring that the historical period is accounted for with the previous parameters before the new ones take effect. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an "interest accrual ordering" or "state‑update sequencing" flaw, where the logical order of operations breaks the financial invariants of the system. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected balance remaining unchanged after an admin action, or the displayed reward may be lower than advertised, leading to confusion when the protocol promises a certain APY but delivers less because the calculation ignored the old adjustSpeed for part of the period.

title: Lack of slippage protection allows exploitation of Pendle trades
description:
** The [`Pendle_Module`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol) is designed to interact with the Pendle protocol. [Pendle](https://pendle.finance/) is a permissionless yield-trading protocol that enables users to execute various yield-management strategies. It utilizes a complex system of different token types—`PT`, `YT`, and `SY`—to facilitate trading across different components of yield.

Within Pendle, users can deposit assets to receive these tokens and subsequently swap between them. The `Pendle_Module` facet implements these functionalities.

The issue, however, is that slippage protection is completely absent, as the slippage parameters are hardcoded to `0` in multiple functions:
* [`Pendle_Module::pendle_deposit`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L35-L74), [L69](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L69):
  ```solidity
  router.addLiquiditySingleToken(
      address(this),
      address(market),
      0, // @audit `minLpOut` hardcoded to 0
      approxParams,
      input,
      limitOrderData
  );
  ```
* [`Pendle_Module::pendle_withdraw`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L76-L107), [L86](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L86):
  ```solidity
  IPRouter.TokenOutput memory output = IPRouter.TokenOutput({
      tokenOut: ast,
      minTokenOut: 0, // @audit `minTokenOut` hardcoded to 0
      tokenRedeemSy: ast,
      pendleSwap: address(0),
      swapData: swapData
  });
  ```
* [`Pendle_Module::pendle_swap`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L109-L188), [L140](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L140), [L150](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L150) and [L170](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L170):
  ```solidity
  IPRouter.TokenOutput memory output = IPRouter.TokenOutput({
      tokenOut: ast,
      minTokenOut: 0, // @audit `minTokenOut` hardcoded to 0
      tokenRedeemSy: ast,
      pendleSwap: address(0),
      swapData: swapData
  });
  ```
  ```solidity
  router.swapExactTokenForPt(
      address(this),
      market,
      0, // @audit `minPtOut` hardcoded to 0
      approxParams,
      input,
      limitOrderData
  );
  ```
  ```solidity
  router.swapExactTokenForYt(
      address(this),
      market,
      0, // @audit `minYtOut` hardcoded to 0
      approxParams,
      input,
      limitOrderData
  );
  ```
* [`Pendle_Module::pendle_claim`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L190-L200), [L197](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L197):
  ```solidity
  IPSY(sy).redeem(
      address(this),
      IERC20(sy).balanceOf(address(this)),
      IPSY(sy).getTokensOut()[0],
      0, // @audit `minTokenOut` is hardcoded to 0
      false
  );
  ```
* [`Pendle_Module::pendle_exit`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L202-L227), [L216](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/modules/Pendle.sol#L216):
  ```solidity
  router.exitPostExpToToken(
      address(this),
      market,
      amount,
      amountLp,
      IPRouter.TokenOutput({
          tokenOut: asset,
          minTokenOut: 0, // @audit `minTokenOut` hardcoded to 0
          tokenRedeemSy: asset,
          pendleSwap: address(0),
          swapData: IPSwapAggregator.SwapData({
              swapType: IPSwapAggregator.SwapType.NONE,
              extRouter: address(0),
              extCalldata: "",
              needScale: false
          })
      })
  );
  ```
Since all these functions allow transactions with zero slippage protection, they may be exploited by MEV bots causing value loss for the stakers in D2.

** The absence of slippage protection exposes the protocol to front-running and price manipulation. Attackers can take advantage of these hardcoded zero values to extract value from trades at the expense of D2’s stakers, leading to potential financial losses.
bug_full: The Pendle_Module contract interacts with the Pendle yield‑trading protocol but it does not enforce any slippage protection on its core liquidity and swap functions. In each of the deposit, withdraw, swap, claim and exit calls the parameters that define the minimum acceptable amount of output tokens (minLpOut, minTokenOut, minPtOut, minYtOut) are hard‑coded to zero. This design choice removes the safety check that would normally revert a transaction when the market price moves unfavourably between the time a user signs a transaction and the moment it is executed. Because the contract will accept any amount of output, a malicious actor – typically an MEV bot – can front‑run the user’s transaction, manipulate the price on the underlying Pendle market, and cause the user’s trade to execute at a dramatically worse rate. From the user’s perspective the expected receipt of LP tokens, PT, YT or underlying assets is reduced or may even be zero, leading to missing balances, lower yields, or a complete loss of the deposited value. The vulnerability is triggered whenever the contract is called in a volatile market environment where price slippage can be exploited, which is a common condition for decentralized finance protocols. All stakers and liquidity providers that rely on the module to manage their positions are affected because the module’s lack of protection can drain their accrued value without any warning. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the function signatures and noticed the hard‑coded zero values, a subtle mistake that can be easily overlooked because zero is a syntactically valid value and does not raise compiler warnings. The problem is hard to notice in normal operation because successful trades still occur; only when an attacker deliberately creates adverse price movement does the loss become apparent. To remediate the issue the contract should expose a configurable minimum‑out parameter for each operation, validate that the actual amount received meets or exceeds this threshold, and revert the transaction otherwise. Adding slippage checks restores the expected economic guarantees of the protocol, aligns on‑chain behaviour with user expectations, and prevents front‑running attacks that would otherwise cause funds to disappear or yields to be unexpectedly reduced.

title: Unsafe token transfers in `VaultV3` can lead to state inconsistencies
bug_full: The vulnerability in VaultV3 is an unchecked ERC-20 token transfer in both the custodyFunds and returnFunds functions. The contract updates internal state variables (custodied, custodiedAmount, epoch end) before verifying that the external token transfer succeeded, and it does not inspect the boolean return value of the transfer calls. This pattern violates the Checks-Effects-Interactions principle and creates a situation where a transfer that fails – for example because the token is paused, the allowance is insufficient, the token implements a blacklist, or the token returns false instead of reverting – leaves the vault’s bookkeeping in an inconsistent state. An attacker or even a benign network condition can cause the transfer to return false while the transaction continues, resulting in the vault remaining marked as custodied, epoch timestamps being set, and asset balances being recorded as moved even though no tokens actually left the contract. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – the trader receiving the assets or the vault receiving a repayment – does not happen; the UI may show a successful operation, but the user’s balance remains unchanged and the vault becomes stuck, preventing further deposits or withdrawals until manual governance intervention. The issue was identified during a security audit by Cyfrin, and it is difficult to notice because the ERC-20 transfer does not revert and the contract does not emit an error, so the failure is silent. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls and missing return-value validation, which breaks accounting assumptions that transferred amounts equal recorded amounts. The recommended remediation is to employ OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library (safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom) or explicitly check the boolean result of each transfer, and to reorder the logic so that state changes occur only after a successful transfer, thereby restoring consistency between on-chain state and actual token balances.

title: Incorrect `chainid` prevents correct Strategy deployment on Berachain
description:
** The Strategy contract includes a special configuration specifying which facets should be used for different chains. However, the `chainid` assigned to Berachain is incorrect, as seen in [`Strategy::constructor`](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/Strategy.sol#L25-L337), [L216](https://github.com/d2sd2s/d2-contracts/blob/c2fc257605ebc725525028a5c17f30c74202010b/contracts/Strategy.sol#L216):
```solidity
} else if (block.chainid == 80000) { // @audit Berachain id is 80094
```
According to the [official documentation](https://docs.berachain.com/developers/network-configurations), the correct `chainid` for Berachain is `80094`, not `80000`.

** Facets intended for deployment on Berachain will not be correctly initialized until a new Strategy contract is deployed with the corrected `chainid`. This prevents the expected functionality from being executed on Berachain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded network identifier error in the Strategy contract that selects which facet implementations to initialise based on the blockchain's chain ID. The source code contains a conditional branch that checks for block.chainid == 80000 and labels it as the Berachain configuration, while the official Berachain chain ID is 80094. This mismatch is the root cause: a static numeric constant was entered incorrectly during development. When the contract is deployed on the actual Berachain network (chain ID 80094), the condition evaluating block.chainid == 80000 evaluates to false, causing the execution path for Berachain to be skipped. As a result, the facets that should be instantiated for Berachain are never initialised, and the Strategy contract remains in a default or incomplete state. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the bug manifests automatically whenever a user or protocol attempts to deploy or interact with the Strategy on Berachain. The impact is functional: users expecting the strategy to manage assets, generate yields, or perform protocol‑specific actions on Berachain will find that those functions are unavailable, may receive no returns, or see their balances remain unchanged. From the user’s point of view the UI may show the strategy as available but any transaction to engage it either does nothing or reverts silently, leading to confusion such as “my funds are not moving” or “the strategy returns zero”. The issue occurs only under the condition that the contract is compiled and deployed on a chain whose chain ID is 80094; on other supported chains the correct branch is taken and the bug is not observable. The affected parties include the protocol developers who intended to support Berachain, any users who allocate capital to the strategy on that network, and any downstream contracts that rely on the strategy’s facet initialisation. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the hard‑coded chain ID against the official Berachain documentation. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without error, the incorrect constant does not trigger a runtime exception, and tests may have been run only on other networks where the condition is true. The bug belongs to the class of configuration‑driven logic errors, specifically hard‑coded environment identifiers that are wrong. To remediate, the constant should be updated to the correct chain ID (80094) or, preferably, the contract should use a configurable mapping or external registry to resolve chain‑specific facet sets, eliminating the need for magic numbers. Correcting the identifier ensures that the Berachain‑specific facets are instantiated, restoring the intended functionality and preventing users from experiencing missing returns or non‑functional strategy deployments.

title: Incorrect interface for `ExchangeRouter::updateOrder` prevents order updates in GMX V2
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an ABI mismatch between the GMX_Module contract and the external GMX V2 ExchangeRouter. The module’s gmxv2_update function invokes ExchangeRouter.updateOrder with five arguments (key, sizeDeltaUsd, acceptablePrice, triggerPrice, minOutputAmount). However, the actual router implementation expects seven arguments, adding validFromTime and autoCancel to the signature. Because the interface declared in the module does not include these two parameters, the generated calldata does not match the router’s function selector, causing every call to revert due to missing arguments. This mismatch makes the gmxv2_update entry point permanently non‑functional; any attempt to modify an existing order will fail at runtime, even though the code compiles without errors. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to be submitted but immediately reverts, leaving the executor’s balance unchanged and the order unchanged.
