The root cause is an unchecked external call to a token contract, a classic example of a false‑positive state signaling bug. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) can trigger a transferFrom that fails—by providing insufficient allowance, insufficient balance, or by using a token that deliberately returns false—yet the protocol will still emit the event, potentially granting access to minted NFTs, releasing funds, or updating accounting as if payment succeeded. The impact includes loss of accounting integrity, unintended asset distribution, and potential financial loss for the protocol if it assumes it has received tokens that were never transferred. The condition occurs whenever the contract executes the unchecked transferFrom, which is true for the two identified functions. Users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because they may believe a payment was made when it was not, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as a UI displaying "Payment successful" while the token balance remains unchanged, or an NFT appearing in the user's wallet without the corresponding token deduction. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that highlighted the missing require statement. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert, no error is thrown, and the emitted event matches expected successful behavior, making the failure invisible to casual observation. To remediate, the contract should enforce that transferFrom returns true—either by wrapping the call in a require statement, using OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 library, or otherwise reverting on a false return—ensuring that events are only emitted after a confirmed token transfer. This aligns the on‑chain state with the protocol's logical expectations and prevents the false emission of events that mislead downstream consumers.

title: Anyone can get swaps for free given certain conditions in `swap`.
description:
[LibSwap.swap](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Libraries/LibSwap.sol#L29-L48)  
[GenericSwapFacet.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Facets/GenericSwapFacet.sol)

Remaining or unaccounted ERC20 balance could be freely taken through `swapTokensGenerics` and `swap`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the swap logic used by the Li.Fi protocol in the LibSwap.swap routine. The function determines whether it needs to pull the input token from the caller by checking if the contract's own balance of the sending asset is less than the declared fromAmount. Because the contract assumes it never holds a residual balance of the source token, the condition uses a strict "less than" comparison. When the contract already contains a positive balance of the sending ERC20 token – for example after a previous operation that left leftover funds – an attacker can submit a swap request with a fromAmount that is just below that existing balance. In this scenario the first if‑statement is skipped, meaning no tokens are transferred from the user to the contract. The swap then proceeds using the contract's internal balance as the source, and the external call to the DEX executes normally. After the external call the routine measures the increase in the contract’s balance of the receiving token by subtracting the pre‑swap balance from the post‑swap balance. The calculated increase is then transferred to the caller without any verification that an equivalent amount of the source token was actually supplied. Consequently the attacker walks away with the newly received tokens while having contributed nothing, effectively receiving a free swap. This flaw can be triggered whenever the contract holds any amount of the input ERC20 token and the attacker sets the fromAmount just under that amount, making the exploit repeatable until the latent balance is exhausted. Users, developers, and the protocol are all affected: honest users may see unexpected drains of leftover token balances, the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, and an attacker can acquire assets without paying. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the balance‑based guard was insufficient and that the profit calculation relied solely on the receiving‑asset delta. The bug is subtle because the code appears to protect against under‑funding, yet the implicit invariant that the contract never holds source tokens is not enforced, allowing the condition to be silently bypassed. To remediate the problem, the contract should always ensure that the source amount is deducted from the caller (or from the contract’s balance) before invoking the external swap, or it should compute the net flow of both assets and only transfer the net gain after confirming that the caller supplied the required input. Additionally, the contract should either enforce a zero balance invariant for source tokens or use safe accounting patterns that do not rely on the contract’s internal balances to determine whether funds have been supplied. This would close the accounting gap and prevent free swaps from being executed.

title: LibSwap: Excess funds from swaps are not returned
description:
[LibSwap.sol#L29-L58](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Libraries/LibSwap.sol#L29-L58)  

It is probable for `_swapData.fromAmount` to be greater than the actual amount used (eg. when swapping for an exact output, or when performing another swap after swapping with an exact input). However, these funds aren’t returned back to the user and are left in the lifi contract.
poc:
[AnyswapFacet.test.ts#L153-L194](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/test/facets/AnyswapFacet.test.ts#L153-L194)  

The test referenced above swaps for MATIC for 1000 USDT exactly. Logging the matic amounts before and after the swap and bridge call, one will find 18.01 MATIC is unused and left in the contract when it should be returned to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LibSwap library used by the Li.Fi contract suite. When a swap operation is invoked, the caller supplies a _swapData.fromAmount that represents the maximum amount of the source token the contract is allowed to spend. In cases where the swap is performed for an exact output amount, or when a subsequent swap is chained after an exact‑input swap, the actual amount of source token consumed can be lower than the supplied fromAmount. The library does not recalculate the unused portion nor transfer it back to the caller; instead, the surplus remains trapped in the Li.Fi contract’s balance. This occurs because the implementation never records the contract's pre‑swap balance of the source asset, never computes the delta after the external call, and lacks a refund step. An attacker does not gain access to other users’ funds; the bug only causes the user who initiates the swap to lose the excess tokens that the contract keeps. The impact is a loss of funds for the user: after a swap that should return, for example, 0.0 MATIC, the user may notice that a small amount (e.g., 18.01 MATIC in a test case) is missing from their wallet and appears as a balance increase in the Li.Fi contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction, but the expected refund is absent, leading to confusion and potentially panic. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where a test swapping exactly 1000 USDT for MATIC logged the before‑and‑after balances and identified the leftover MATIC. The bug is subtle because the contract can still complete the swap successfully, and the retained funds are not directly visible in transaction logs, making it easy to overlook. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of accounting or refund bugs where external calls are not symmetrically balanced with internal state updates. To remediate, the contract should capture its own balance of the source asset before invoking the external swap, compute the actual amount spent after the call, ensure that the spent amount does not exceed the declared fromAmount, and explicitly transfer any surplus back to the transaction initiator. Implementing such a refund mechanism restores the expected invariant that the caller’s token balance after a swap equals the original balance minus the exact amount used plus any returned excess, thereby aligning the protocol’s financial logic with user expectations.

title: `msg.value` is Sent Multiple times When Performing a Swap
description:
[LibSwap.sol#L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Libraries/LibSwap.sol#L42)  
[Swapper.sol#L12-L23](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Facets/Swapper.sol#L12-L23)  

`msg.value` is attached multiple times to external swap calls in `LibSwap.swap()`.

If `Swapper._executeSwaps()` is called with the native token as the `swapData.fromAssetId` more than once and `msg.value > 0` then more value will be transferred out of the contract than is received since `msg.value` will be transferred out `_swapData.length` times.

The impact is that the contract can have all the native token balance drained by an attacker who has makes repeated swap calls from the native token into any other ERC20 token. Each time the original `msg.value` of the sender will be swapped out of the contract. This attack essentially gives the attacker `_swapData.length * msg.value` worth of native tokens (swapped into another ERC20) when they should only get `msg.value`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the LI.Fi Swapper contract forwards the native cryptocurrency (msg.value) to external swap contracts. In the internal function _executeSwaps, the contract iterates over an array of SwapData structures and calls LibSwap.swap for each element. LibSwap.swap performs a low‑level call to the target DEX, attaching msg.value as the value field of the call. Because msg.value represents the total amount of native token supplied by the caller, and the loop does not adjust or consume this amount, the same full value is attached to every external call. Consequently, if the caller includes the native token as the source asset in more than one element of the swap array, the contract will forward the original msg.value multiple times – once for each iteration. This leads to the contract transferring out a multiple of the received ether while only receiving the original amount, effectively draining the contract's native token balance. An attacker can exploit this by constructing a swap request that contains several consecutive swaps where fromAssetId equals the native token and by providing a non‑zero msg.value. Each swap will pull the same ether amount from the contract, allowing the attacker to obtain _swapData.length × msg.value worth of ether (converted into the chosen ERC20 tokens). The impact is that users see their sent ether disappear from the contract, balances become zero, and the protocol loses native funds that should have been retained or refunded. The issue manifests only when msg.value > 0 and the swap list contains more than one native‑token entry; under normal single‑swap usage the bug is not observable. All participants who rely on the contract for safe swapping – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumption that the contract holds exactly the amount of native token sent by the caller is violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the swap library, where the repeated use of msg.value inside a loop was identified as a logical flaw. It is subtle because the code appears to forward value correctly for a single swap, and the whitelist checks do not flag the misuse. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the native token appears at most once in the swap array, or it should track the remaining native balance and forward only the portion that has not yet been sent. Alternatively, the implementation could reject any swap request that includes multiple native‑token sources, or it could calculate and forward the precise amount required per swap. After the fix, any leftover native funds are swept back to the user, ensuring that the contract never retains more ether than intended. This class of bug is commonly referred to as improper handling of msg.value in iterative external calls, leading to double‑spending or fund leakage.

title: cBridge integration fails to send native tokens
description:
[CBridgeFacet.sol#L150-L156](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Facets/CBridgeFacet.sol#L150-L156)  

The external `sendNative()` call fails to include sending the native tokens together with it.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the integration of the Li.Fi contract with the CBridge protocol when attempting to transfer native blockchain tokens (e.g., ETH). The contract invokes the external function sendNative on the CBridge interface without forwarding the Ether value and without declaring the interface function as payable. Consequently, the call executes without actually sending any native tokens to the bridge, while the Li.Fi contract retains the sent value. This mismatch triggers a revert from the bridge contract, typically with the message "Amount mismatch", because the bridge receives a zero amount while the caller expects the specified amount to be transferred. The root cause is a missing value parameter in the low‑level call and an incorrect function signature that does not include the payable modifier, leading to a logical error in the handling of native token transfers. An attacker or a malicious user can exploit this behavior by repeatedly invoking the bridge function with native tokens, causing the transaction to revert each time, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents legitimate users from bridging their funds. The impact is that any user who tries to bridge native tokens via the startBridgeTokensViaCBridge function experiences a failed transaction, receives no token transfer, and may be left uncertain why their funds appear to be locked. This issue manifests only when the token address is the zero address (indicating a native token) and a non‑zero amount is supplied; ERC‑20 token bridging remains unaffected. Users of the Li.Fi platform, the protocol developers, and any downstream services relying on successful native token bridges are affected because the core bridging functionality is broken. The problem was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated the revert behavior when the transaction included a value of one wei. The issue is subtle because the Solidity compiler does not flag the missing payable keyword, and the revert message does not directly point to the missing value transfer, making it easy to overlook during manual reviews. To remediate the flaw, the sendNative call must be updated to forward the exact amount of native tokens using the Solidity syntax ICBridge(bridge).sendNative{value: _cBridgeData.amount}(…) and the corresponding ICBridge interface definition must be marked payable. This change ensures that the bridge receives the intended funds, aligns the on‑chain accounting with business expectations (the user expects their native tokens to be transferred to the destination chain), and restores the correct operational flow of the protocol.

title: DexManagerFacet: batchRemoveDex
poc:
Add the following lines below [L44 of](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-Li.finance/blob/main/test/facets/AnyswapFacet.test.ts#L44) `[AnyswapFacet.test.ts](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/test/facets/AnyswapFacet.test.ts#L44)`

```solidity
await dexMgr.addDex(ANYSWAP_ROUTER)
await dexMgr.batchRemoveDex([ANYSWAP_ROUTER, UNISWAP_ADDRESS])
// UNISWAP_ADDRESS remains as approved dex when it should have been removed
console.log(await dexMgr.approvedDexs())
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batchRemoveDex function of the DexManagerFacet contract, where an internal for‑loop uses a return statement after successfully locating a matching DEX to remove. This return exits the entire external function instead of only terminating the inner loop, so only the first DEX found in the supplied array is actually removed. The root cause is an incorrect control‑flow choice: the developer intended to break out of the inner loop after calling the private _removeDex helper, but mistakenly used return, causing premature termination. An attacker or any caller can exploit this by providing multiple DEX addresses to batchRemoveDex while assuming all of them will be deregistered. Because the function stops after the first match, any subsequent DEXes remain in the approvedDexs list, allowing swaps to be routed through those contracts even though the caller believed they had been disabled. This leads to a deviation from the protocol’s intended accounting and security model: unauthorized DEXes may process trades, potentially introducing malicious behavior, fee leakage, or loss of funds for users who trust the approved list. The bug manifests only when batchRemoveDex is invoked with more than one DEX address and at least one of them is already approved; under those conditions the function returns early. The affected parties include the protocol governance (who expects to manage the whitelist), developers integrating the contract, and end‑users who rely on the whitelist to avoid rogue swap partners. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit and confirmed with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed the second DEX remained approved after the call. It is hard to notice because the function does not emit any event on removal, so external observers see no indication of failure, and the transaction does not revert. To remediate, the return should be replaced with a break so the loop continues to process the remaining DEX entries, and appropriate events should be emitted for both addition and removal of DEXes to provide transparent state changes. Conceptually, this is an instance of improper loop termination leading to incomplete batch processing, a class of bugs that can cause stale or unintended entries to persist in access‑control lists.

title: `CoreCollection.setRoyaltyVault` doesn’t check `royaltyVault.royaltyAsset` against `payableToken`, resulting in potential permanent lock of `payableTokens` in royaltyVault
description: Each CoreProxy is allowed to be associated with a RoyaltyVault, the latter which would be responsible for collecting minting fees and distributing to beneficiaries. Potential mismatch between token used in CoreProxy and RoyaltyVault might result in minting tokens being permanently stuck in RoyaltyVault.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the CoreCollection contract’s setRoyaltyVault function, which assigns a RoyaltyVault to a CoreProxy without verifying that the token used for minting fees (payableToken) matches the token that the RoyaltyVault is programmed to handle (royaltyAsset). Because the contract does not perform any compatibility check, a CoreProxy can be paired with a RoyaltyVault that expects a different ERC‑20 token. When a user pays minting fees, the _handlePayment routine transfers the payableToken directly to the assigned RoyaltyVault. Inside the RoyaltyVault, all outgoing transfers are hard‑coded to use the royaltyAsset token; any other token received cannot be transferred out because the transfer calls reference royaltyAsset, not the token that was actually deposited. Consequently, the minting fees become permanently locked in the vault. This condition manifests to the user as a missing or zero balance after a successful mint operation – the user expects the fee to be recorded and possibly later redistributed, but the funds simply disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The issue is discovered during a security audit that inspected the logic of vault assignment and observed the absence of a require statement linking payableToken to royaltyAsset. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the vault receives the tokens and later internal transfers fail silently, making the loss appear as a normal accounting discrepancy. The impact is limited to the funds sent as minting fees, potentially ranging from a few tokens to large amounts, depending on the price of the payable token. It affects any user who initiates a mint, as well as the protocol’s revenue model and any beneficiaries expecting royalty distributions. The vulnerability can be mitigated by adding a validation step in setRoyaltyVault that enforces payableToken == royaltyVault.royaltyAsset(), ensuring that only compatible vaults can be assigned. A broader remediation includes making the vault pairing immutable after a successful compatibility check or providing a mechanism to re‑assign a vault if a mismatch is detected, thereby preventing permanent lock of funds. This class of bug is a token‑type mismatch leading to irrevocable asset loss, commonly referred to as a “royalty vault token incompatibility” or “asset lock due to mismatched token handling”.

title: `AnyswapFacet` can be exploited to approve arbitrary tokens.
description:
[AnyswapFacet.sol#L35-L53](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/main/src/Facets/AnyswapFacet.sol#L35-L53)  

In `AnyswapFacet.sol` we parse arbitrary data in `_anyswapData` allowing an attacker to drain funds (ERC20 or native tokens) from the LiFi contract.

Functions effected:

* `AnyswapFacet.startBridgeTokensViaAnyswap()`
* `AnyswapFacet.swapAndStartBridgeTokensViaAnyswap()`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AnyswapFacet contract, which processes an externally supplied structure called `_anyswapData`. The contract calls `IAnyswapToken(_anyswapData.token).underlying()` twice – once to obtain the token that will be transferred into the contract for the bridge, and a second time just before calling the Anyswap router to forward the funds. Because the contract does not validate that the two calls return the same address, an attacker can supply a malicious token contract whose `underlying()` function returns different token addresses on each invocation. In the first call the malicious contract pretends to be a legitimate token and makes the balance‑check logic succeed, allowing the contract to pull the attacker‑controlled ERC20 into its own balance. In the second call it returns the address of a token that the contract already holds (or native ETH), which the attacker then approves for the router or transfers directly to an attacker‑controlled router address. The router, being under the attacker’s control, can then move the approved tokens or native assets out of the LiFi contract. This double‑fetch of the underlying token enables an arbitrary‑token approval or transfer, effectively draining any assets that happen to be held by the contract at the time of the call. The issue is triggered whenever a user initiates a bridge via `startBridgeTokensViaAnyswap` or `swapAndStartBridgeTokensViaAnyswap` with crafted `_anyswapData`. The affected parties are the protocol (LiFi) and its users because funds that were meant to be bridged can disappear, leaving the user with a failed bridging transaction and an empty balance. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined how external data is parsed in the facet and identified the lack of whitelist checks and the repeated call to `underlying()`. It is difficult to spot because the `underlying()` function is expected to be a pure view that always returns the same address, and the balance verification logic appears correct on the surface. To remediate, the contract should whitelist only known Anyswap token contracts and router addresses, call `underlying()` once and store the result, and avoid using mutable external data to determine which token to approve. By restricting the token and router set and eliminating the double‑fetch, the protocol restores its accounting guarantees and prevents an attacker from gaining arbitrary approval over any token held by the contract. From a user’s viewpoint, a transaction that should have resulted in a successful bridge instead leaves their balance unchanged or shows that the contract’s balance has dropped, contradicting the expectation that the bridge will transfer the specified amount to the destination chain.

title: Improper Transfer Restrictions on Non-Bridged Tokens Due to Boolean Bridged Token Tracking, Allowing a DoS Attack Vector
description:
**Root Cause** The `Titn.sol` contract incorrectly tracks bridged token holders using a boolean flag (`isBridgedTokenHolder`). Once an address receives _any_ bridged tokens (via cross-chain bridging), it is permanently marked as a “bridged token holder,” subjecting **all** tokens held by that address (including non-bridged ones) to transfer restrictions. This flawed design allows malicious actors to disrupt legitimate users by sending them a trivial amount of bridged tokens, thereby locking their entire TITN balance from being transferred freely.

**Impact**
  * **Loss of User Control**: Users holding both bridged and non-bridged tokens cannot transfer _any_ tokens unless sending them to the LayerZero endpoint or `transferAllowedContract`.
  * **Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attack Vector**: An attacker can send 1 wei of bridged TITN to any address, permanently locking their TITN tokens (even those obtained through non-bridged means).
  * **Protocol Functionality Breakdown**: The intended economic model (allowing free transfer of non-bridged tokens) is violated, undermining user trust and utility.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect accounting mechanism that marks an address as a bridged‑token holder using a single boolean flag. When an address ever receives a token that originated from a cross‑chain bridge, the flag is set to true and never cleared. Because the contract applies transfer restrictions based on this flag, every token held by the flagged address – including tokens that were never bridged – becomes subject to the same restrictive rules. Consequently, a malicious actor can send a trivial amount (for example, 1 wei) of a bridged token to any user, causing the flag to be set and permanently preventing the user from transferring any of their regular tokens unless the destination is a whitelisted bridge endpoint or a designated transfer‑allowed contract. This flaw is discovered during a security audit that examined the token’s transfer logic and identified that the boolean state is not scoped per token type. The issue is subtle because the contract still reports the correct balance and the user interface shows the expected amount, yet attempts to move the tokens fail with a generic revert, making the problem hard to spot without inspecting the internal flag logic. The impact is a loss of user control over their assets and a denial‑of‑service vector that can be weaponized at scale, effectively freezing funds for any affected address. Affected parties include all token holders who might receive even a minimal amount of bridged tokens, the protocol’s economic model that assumes non‑bridged tokens are freely transferable, and any downstream applications that rely on unrestricted token movement. To remediate, the contract should track bridged‑token status per token type or per balance rather than using a global boolean, and it should allow the flag to be cleared when no bridged tokens remain, thereby restoring normal transfer rights for non‑bridged holdings. This change would align the implementation with the intended business logic that only bridged tokens are subject to special transfer rules, preventing accidental or malicious locking of unrelated assets.

title: M-06 | Missing Execute Order Function
description: During submitOffchainDelayedOrderWithTracking, a keeperFee is deducted from the position margin: _updatePositionMargin(messageSender, position, sizeDelta, ﬁllPrice, -int(keeperDeposit)); This fee is reserved for the caller of executeOffchainDelayedOrder that will settle the delayed order. However, according to the PerpsV2MarketDelayedExecution.sol contract: If this is called by the account holder the keeperFee is refunded into margin, otherwise it sent to the msg.sender. For the ETH Perp market, this keeper fee ranges from 1.05 to 100 sUSD. The LeveragedToken is the account holder in this case, but it does not contain any function to execute the delayed order, missing out on the fee refunds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing execution entry point for delayed orders in the LeveragedToken contract that holds positions on the ETH perpetual market. When a user submits an off‑chain delayed order, the market contract deducts a keeper fee from the position margin and reserves it for the entity that later calls executeOffchainDelayedOrder. The protocol’s fee logic states that if the caller of the execution function is the same account that owns the position, the fee is refunded back into the margin; otherwise the fee is transferred to the caller as a reward. In the current deployment the LeveragedToken contract is recorded as the account holder, but it does not expose any public function that can invoke executeOffchainDelayedOrder. Consequently the fee that was taken from the margin can never be reclaimed by the LeveragedToken and is instead paid out to any external keeper that happens to execute the order. This results in an unexpected reduction of the position’s margin, effectively causing a small but real loss of funds (typically between 1.05 and 100 sUSD per order) for users of the LeveragedToken. The issue appears whenever a delayed order is created via submitOffchainDelayedOrderWithTracking, which is a normal workflow for off‑chain price feeds. Users see their margin shrink without receiving the expected refund, leading to confusion when the UI shows a lower available balance after an order is settled. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the interaction between PerpsV2MarketDelayedExecution.sol and the LeveragedToken implementation, where the auditor noticed that the contract lacked a method to trigger the delayed order execution and therefore could not benefit from the fee‑refund mechanism. Because the fee amount is modest relative to typical position sizes, the discrepancy can be easy to overlook, especially if the UI does not surface detailed fee breakdowns. To remediate the issue, the LeveragedToken should be extended with a public function that forwards a call to executeOffchainDelayedOrder on the market contract, allowing the contract itself to act as the executor and receive the keeper fee refund, or alternatively the protocol could be modified to automatically credit the fee back to the position owner when no explicit executor is present. This class of bug falls under missing function or incomplete interface design, where a required action is not exposed, leading to unintended economic loss and violation of the expected accounting invariant that fees paid by the position owner are either refunded or correctly accounted for.

title: M-07 | Depositing Minimum Amount Leads To Position Closure
description:
When a user deposits the MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT into an empty LT a position will be created and most likely closed right after. This punishes the user with paying for order fees twice without any beneﬁt:
• User deposits the MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT (100 sUSD) into an empty LT
• The _validateMintAmount check is executed and it passes as the given amount is not less than the MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT of 100 sUSD
• The given amount of 100 sUSD is deposited as margin
• The _canRebalance check is executed and it passes as the remainingMargin (100 sUSD) in the position is not less than the MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE (100 sUSD) it is equal and the position is heavily under leveraged as it has no size yet
• Therefore _rebalance will be executed and a delayed order to open a position in perps v2 is created
• The delayed order is executed:
• To open the position order fees and price impact must be paid and therefore the position's remainingMargin is probably < 100 sUSD now
• This will trigger the rebalancer:
• The _canRebalance check is executed and it will pass as the remainingMargin after paying for order fees is less than the MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE now while the notional value of the position is > 0
• Therefore _rebalance will be executed and a delayed order to close the position in perps v2 is created
• The delayed order is executed:
• The position is closed and more order fees are paid
bug_full: A user who deposits exactly the protocol‑defined MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT (100 sUSD) into an empty liquidity token (LT) can trigger a sequence of automated rebalancing actions that open a position and then immediately close it, causing the user to pay order fees twice without receiving any trading exposure. The root cause is that the minimum amount required to mint a new position is set equal to the minimum margin balance that the rebalancer uses to decide whether a position is sufficiently collateralised. When the deposit equals this threshold, the _validateMintAmount check passes and the margin is recorded, but the subsequent _canRebalance check also passes because the remaining margin is not less than the minimum margin balance (it is exactly equal). The rebalancer therefore creates a delayed order to open a perpetual position. As the order executes, the protocol deducts opening fees and price‑impact costs, reducing the remaining margin below the minimum margin balance while the position already has a non‑zero notional value. This condition satisfies the second _canRebalance check, causing the rebalancer to generate a delayed order to close the position. The closing order again incurs fees, so the user ends up paying fees for both opening and closing while the net position size returns to zero. From the user’s perspective the expectation is to lock 100 sUSD as margin and obtain a leveraged exposure, but the UI may briefly show a position that disappears instantly, and the user’s balance is reduced by two sets of fees, effectively “money disappears” after a single deposit. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the mint‑and‑rebalance flow, where the logical relationship between MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT and MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE was examined. It is hard to notice because the contract does not explicitly reject the deposit and the rapid open‑close sequence can happen within a single block, leaving little trace in transaction logs beyond fee deductions. The vulnerability belongs to the class of economic‑logic bugs where threshold values are misaligned, leading to unintended rebalancing loops and fee‑drain attacks. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a MINIMUM_MINT_AMOUNT that is strictly greater than the MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE, or adjust the rebalance logic to require a safety buffer after fee deduction before allowing a position to be opened, thereby preventing an immediate close and double‑fee scenario.

title: M-08 | Order Fees Do Not Include Rebalance Costs
description: In the _orderFee function the order fee computed does not include the fees to cover Perps V2 keeper fee to execute an order or the rebalance gas cost (if a rebalance is not triggered during the action) This is a one time hard cost that will be applied to every rebalance that occurs and is not speciﬁcally remunerated by the depositors/withdrawers who are triggering the rebalance.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the fee charged for executing an order in a perpetual futures protocol. The fee that the contract reports to the user is derived from a function that only accounts for the protocol’s standard order fee, but it omits two mandatory costs: the keeper fee paid to the off‑chain service that actually triggers the order execution, and the gas expense required to perform a rebalance when the order does not itself cause a rebalance. The root cause is a missing addition of these hard, one‑time costs in the fee‑computation logic, which means the protocol assumes that the fee collected from the depositor or withdrawer fully covers the operational expense of the transaction. Because the omitted costs are incurred on every rebalance, the protocol systematically under‑charges users. An attacker or any participant who triggers a rebalance can exploit this by repeatedly initiating rebalances without paying the hidden costs, causing the protocol’s treasury to be depleted over time. The impact is a gradual erosion of the protocol’s funds, potentially leading to insufficient liquidity to cover future positions or to a need for emergency fund injections. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where an order is processed and a rebalance is required but not directly triggered by the order; the fee shown to the user will be lower than the actual cost incurred. All users who interact with the order‑execution endpoint, as well as the protocol’s governance and liquidity providers, are affected because the missing fee is effectively subsidised by the system rather than the actor causing the expense. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑calculation routine, where the auditor noted that the function comment mentioned keeper and rebalance costs but the implementation did not add them. The problem can be hard to notice because the fee appears to be correctly calculated from the perspective of the contract’s state variables, and the missing costs are external (keeper payments and gas) that are not directly visible on‑chain. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that the fee displayed in the UI is lower than expected when they compare it to the actual transaction receipt, and the protocol’s balance may shrink without an obvious cause. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or business‑logic errors where required operational expenses are not accounted for in the pricing model. To remediate, the fee‑computation should be extended to include the keeper fee and the estimated gas cost of a rebalance, or the protocol should require the actor who triggers the rebalance to pay these costs explicitly, ensuring that the economic model remains balanced.

title: M-09 | Decaying Redemption Fee Can Be Bypassed
description: The decayingRedemptionFee function decays the user's fee as time passes. However, the if-else statement's conditions are checked in wrong order. The code tries to set percentPassed if mintedTimestamp[user] = 0 only if percentPassed = 1e18. But if mintedTimestamp[user] = 0, the value of percentPassed will be much higher than 1e18. This can be combined with the decayingRedemptionFeeMinBaseAmount (which is currently set to 5e18) to avoid paying fees. When a user wants to exit the system, instead of redeeming and paying a decaying fee, they can transfer 5e18 of their tokens as many times as they want to a brand new account. This will result in them having all of the tokens in that new account and the mintedTimestamp = 0 = percentPassed = 1e18 and no fees being paid.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee‑decay routine that determines how much a user must pay when redeeming tokens. The contract is supposed to reduce the redemption fee over time, using a variable that represents the percentage of time elapsed (percentPassed) and a timestamp that records when the user first minted tokens (mintedTimestamp). In the current implementation the if‑else chain checks the percentPassed condition before verifying whether mintedTimestamp is zero. When a user’s mintedTimestamp is zero – which is the case for a brand‑new address that has never minted – the code incorrectly assumes percentPassed equals the maximum value (1e18). In reality percentPassed can be far larger than 1e18, causing the subsequent branch that should apply a minimum base fee (decayingRedemptionFeeMinBaseAmount, set to 5e18) to be skipped. As a result, an attacker can transfer exactly the minimum base amount of tokens to a freshly created account, reset mintedTimestamp to zero, and trigger the fee calculation path that returns a zero fee. By repeating this transfer to multiple new accounts, the attacker can withdraw the entire token balance without ever paying the intended redemption fee. The bug manifests only when the contract evaluates the fee for an address with a zero mintedTimestamp and when the transferred amount meets or exceeds the configured minimum base amount. It primarily affects the protocol’s revenue model because the fee that should be collected is completely avoided, while the protocol’s token holders and fee pool lose expected income. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the condition order did not correctly handle the zero‑timestamp case. It can be hard to spot because normal redemption flows (where mintedTimestamp is non‑zero) appear to work as intended, and the fee‑bypass only occurs when deliberately creating fresh accounts – a scenario that may not be covered by standard unit tests. To remediate the problem the conditional logic must be reordered so that the mintedTimestamp == 0 case is evaluated first, and only then should the percentPassed comparison be applied. This ensures that the minimum base fee is always enforced for new accounts, restoring the intended fee decay behavior and preventing fee‑free exits.

title: M-10 | Incorrect Calculation Of currentSize
description: In _validateMintAmount, we should avoid using currentSize = long_ + short_ because maxMarketValue returns the maximum allowable value for each side of the market. Let's say the maxMarketSize for each side of the market is 1000, meaning we can open 1000 in long and 1000 in short using the market, which is possible. However, if we do the same using LeveragedToken, it causes a DoS.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the market’s current size during the mint‑validation step of a leveraged token contract. The function _validateMintAmount derives currentSize by adding the requested long and short token amounts (currentSize = long_ + short_), assuming that the market’s maximum capacity is a single combined limit. In reality the market enforces separate maximum values for each side – a long side and a short side – and the maxMarketValue function returns the allowable amount for each side independently. By summing both sides, the contract over‑estimates the occupied capacity, causing the validation logic to think the market is full when it is not. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever a user attempts to mint either a long or a short position, especially when the market is near its per‑side limits. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit the bug by submitting a mint request that appears to exceed the combined limit, causing the transaction to revert. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate minting operations are blocked, users receive no tokens, and funds may become temporarily locked because the contract refuses further deposits. The issue is most visible to users as failed mint transactions, unexpected “insufficient market capacity” errors, or a market that appears to be permanently closed despite available per‑side capacity. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the LeveragedToken contract where the auditor noticed that the currentSize computation did not respect the per‑side constraints. It is subtle because the contract still respects the individual max values, so the error only manifests under edge conditions when both sides are close to their limits, making it easy to miss in routine testing. Conceptually, the fix is to compute currentSize based on the side being minted: if the request is for a long position, use only the long amount; otherwise use only the short amount. This aligns the validation with the market’s accounting model and prevents the artificial capacity ceiling that leads to a DoS. The class of bug is an accounting or state‑validation error where aggregate metrics are derived from independent limits without proper segregation, violating the business logic that each side of the market should be tracked separately.

title: M-11 | Insuﬃcient OdosRouter Calldata Validation
description: ZapSwap._validateOdosSwapAllData() tries to validate the whole amount of received sUSDC tokens is being spent by calling swapCompact. [OdosRouter.swapCompact()](https://github.com/odos-xyz/odos-router-v2/blob/21f4124510aa5c1045f9b3eb1ac2cdcacf235ddd/contracts/OdosRouterV2.sol#L121) supports two main formats for each token - input and output. Each of these tokens may be speciﬁed directly in the calldata or loading them by the odos router storage. The code in ZapSwap.validateOdosSwapAllData adjust the amountLengthPosition accordingly depending on which format is used for the input token. However, it assumes the output token will always use the second format where there is no token address in the calldata. This will result in a failed validation. One of the tokens' bytes will be checked instead of checking the byte showing whether there is input amount speciﬁed. This will either result in allowing not all tokens to be spent or reverting if that token byte is not 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ZapSwap contract’s internal function that validates the calldata passed to the OdosRouter’s swapCompact method. The function assumes that the output token description will always follow the compact format where the token address is omitted from the calldata and only an amount flag is present. In reality, swapCompact supports two encoding styles for each token – a full format that includes the token address and a compact format that omits it. Because the validator only adjusts its parsing logic for the input token’s format, it misinterprets the bytes that belong to the output token when the latter is supplied in the full format. Consequently the validator reads a token‑identifier byte instead of the byte that signals whether an input amount is specified. This mismatch can cause two distinct outcomes: the contract may accept a swap where not all of the received sUSDC tokens are actually spent, leaving a residual balance that can be siphoned off, or the transaction may revert if the mis‑read byte is non‑zero, effectively denying legitimate swaps. The flaw is triggered whenever a caller crafts a swapCompact calldata where the output token uses the full format – a scenario that is valid according to the router’s specification but was not anticipated by the ZapSwap validation logic. Users are affected because they expect their deposited sUSDC to be completely exchanged; instead they may see part of their funds remain locked in the contract or experience unexpected reverts with no clear error message. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the parsing of calldata fields and identified the hard‑coded assumption about the output token layout. It is subtle because the common deployment pattern uses the compact format for outputs, so the validator appears to work correctly in most tests, hiding the edge case. To remediate the problem the validator must detect the encoding format of both input and output tokens independently, adjust the amountLengthPosition for each case, and verify the correct amount‑presence byte. In broader terms this is a calldata‑validation bug where an implementation makes an unsafe assumption about external contract interfaces, leading to incorrect accounting and potential fund loss or denial‑of‑service.

title: M-12 | Tokens Are Tradable When The LT Is Liquidatable
description:
• The docs state out that LTs are supposed to be used in third-party DeFi protocols and they are transferable.
• The mintFor function checks that the LT's position is not liquidatable and active, to make sure that a user does not enter the system and likely loses their invested funds right after.
The _update function executed during transfers when users acquire LTs on third-party protocols does not perform these checks. Therefore users could end up acquiring worthless LTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing liquidity tokens (LTs) to be transferred or acquired through the contract’s internal _update function even when the underlying position represented by the token is already liquidatable or inactive. The protocol documentation states that LTs are intended to be used in third‑party DeFi applications and should be freely transferable, but they must only represent active, non‑liquidatable positions. The mintFor function correctly checks that a newly minted LT is tied to a position that is both active and not liquidatable, preventing users from entering the system with a doomed position. However, the _update function, which is invoked during token transfers initiated by external protocols, does not repeat these safety checks. As a result, a user can acquire an LT that corresponds to a position that can be liquidated immediately, effectively receiving a worthless token. An attacker could create a position that becomes liquidatable, then trigger a transfer through a third‑party protocol so that an unsuspecting recipient receives the LT. The recipient sees a normal token balance in their wallet, but any attempt to redeem or trade the token yields no value because the underlying collateral has already been flagged for liquidation. This discrepancy may go unnoticed because the UI shows a positive token balance and the transfer transaction succeeds, while the business rule that a token must represent a viable position is silently violated. The impact includes loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential downstream effects on integrated DeFi services that assume transferred LTs are safe. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic of mintFor with that of _update and identified the missing liquidatable/active checks. The bug belongs to the class of missing state validation on token transfer functions, a common source of accounting inconsistencies where business invariants are not enforced on all code paths. To remediate, the _update function should include the same checks as mintFor—reverting the transaction if the LT’s underlying position is liquidatable or no longer active—thereby ensuring that only valid, redeemable tokens can be transferred or acquired.

title: M-13 | Only Current Mint Amount Validated
description: In the _validateMintAmount function only the current amount being minted, represented as the mintAmount is validated against the max market size and value validations. However several smaller mints could take place where each of the individual mint amounts remain below the max market validations, while the summation of the mints are above the max market validations. All of these mints may occur before a rebalance is triggered. Additionally, price action can also create an imbalance scenario that will need an increase in position size (additional size delta), which is not contemplated by _validateMintAmount. Finally, order fees could be charged incorrectly, as the outstanding size delta plus the new mint amount, could be a position decrease (i.e. minting when price moves up in a long LT).
bug_full: The contract contains a validation flaw in the function that checks how many tokens can be minted for a market. The logic only looks at the amount being minted in the current transaction (mintAmount) and compares it to the market’s maximum size limits. It does not take into account the amount that is already pending in the system, known as the outstanding rebalance sizeDelta. Because of this, an attacker or any user can submit a series of small mint calls, each of which passes the individual check, and the sum of those calls can push the total market exposure above the defined maximum before a rebalance is triggered. In addition, the same oversight ignores the effect of price movements on the required position size. When the market price moves, the protocol may need to increase the position size (a positive sizeDelta). The current check does not consider this scenario, so a price rise in a long position could cause the contract to mint additional tokens when it should actually be decreasing the position, leading to incorrect fee calculations and potentially charging users the wrong amount. From a user’s point of view the symptoms are subtle: a trader may notice that their position size is larger than expected, that fees are higher or lower than the quoted amount, or that a refund or settlement comes back as zero because the contract believes the position has been over‑minted. The impact is that the protocol can become over‑leveraged, exposing it to market risk, and users may lose funds or receive incorrect fee charges. The issue manifests whenever multiple mint transactions occur in quick succession before a rebalance, or when price volatility creates a need for a size adjustment that the validation logic does not handle. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the validation routine and compared it against the intended accounting model. The bug is hard to spot because each individual transaction appears legitimate; only the aggregate state violates the business rule. To remediate the problem the contract should validate the sum of the outstanding sizeDelta and the new mintAmount against the market’s maximum limits, and it should also incorporate price‑driven size adjustments into the same check. In other words, the validation must be performed on the total pending exposure rather than on a single transaction amount, turning the issue from a “single‑mint amount check” into a “cumulative exposure enforcement” bug that aligns with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: M-14 | LeveragedTokens Pay Disproportionately Higher Streaming Fees
description: Within the LeveragedToken contract, the getStreamingFee(remainingMargin) function is named and documented as if it calculated the streaming fee based on the “remaining margin”. However, rather than passing the contract’s remainingMargin to the _getStreamingFee call, the code calls it with the position’s notionalValue: uint256 streamingFee = _getStreamingFee(transientState.notionalValue); As a result, the leveraged token charges streaming fees on the full leveraged exposure instead of the LeveragedToken position’s margin. A 10x LeveragedToken thus would pay 5 times higher streaming fees than a 2x one that has the same actual collateral. This is at odds with the function’s parameter naming convention, which implies that the fee should be assessed against the margin balance rather than the entire notional.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee calculation logic of a leveraged token contract. The public function is named and documented to compute a streaming fee based on the remaining margin of a position, yet the implementation forwards the position's notional value to the internal fee routine. Because the notional value represents the total leveraged exposure rather than the actual collateral, the contract charges fees on the full leveraged amount. Consequently, a token with ten‑times leverage incurs roughly five times the streaming fee of a two‑times token that holds the same amount of collateral. This discrepancy arises from a mismatch between the parameter name (remainingMargin) and the argument supplied (notionalValue), a classic case of a mis‑parameterized accounting formula. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; the bug is triggered automatically whenever the contract settles streaming fees, which occurs on each fee accrual interval. All token holders are affected because they see their balances erode faster than the protocol’s fee schedule promises. From a user’s perspective the token value drops unexpectedly, the displayed fee amount appears higher than anticipated, and the collateral may be depleted prematurely, leading to lower returns or even liquidation. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit where the auditor compared the function signature with the actual call and noticed the inconsistency. It can be hard to spot because the fee calculation itself is mathematically correct; only the input variable is wrong, so the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error. The proper remediation is to replace the argument with the actual remaining margin, ensuring the streaming fee is proportional to the collateral rather than the leveraged exposure. In broader terms this is a mis‑aligned financial calculation bug where a fee is applied to the wrong base amount, violating the intended accounting model of the protocol and breaking the expectation that fees scale with user‑provided margin.

title: M-15 | Streaming Fee Starts Too Late
description: The streaming fee is 2%/year of the LT position notional value and starts to accrue when the ﬁrst redemption happens. If users decide to not redeem for a while after the LT is deployed the protocol may lose signiﬁcant revenue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the streaming‑fee mechanism of the long‑term (LT) position contract. The protocol is designed to charge a 2 % per‑year fee on the notional value of an LT position, but the implementation only begins to accrue this fee when the first redemption transaction is executed. Consequently, if a user deposits an LT position and then holds it without ever redeeming, the fee never starts to accumulate, allowing the user to keep the position fee‑free for an indefinite period. The root cause is that the fee‑accrual trigger is tied to a redemption event rather than to the initial deposit or any subsequent rebalance, which is the moment when the economic exposure actually begins. An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by simply never calling the redeem function, thereby avoiding the intended streaming fee entirely. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol because the fee that should have been collected over time is never realized, potentially undermining the economic model and reducing funds available for protocol maintenance or token holders. This condition occurs whenever an LT position is created and the holder chooses not to redeem for a prolonged time; it does not affect users who redeem normally, as they will see the fee applied at redemption. The affected parties include the protocol itself, its token holders, and any stakeholders relying on the fee revenue stream. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑calculation flow and identified that the fee start timestamp was incorrectly set. It can be hard to notice because the fee appears correct after a redemption, masking the fact that earlier periods generated no fee. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a zero streaming‑fee amount and the balance remains unchanged, leading the user to believe they are not being charged. In reality the protocol is losing expected income. The recommended remediation is to initialize fee accrual at the moment of the first deposit or any rebalance operation, ensuring that the fee starts counting from the moment the position becomes active, and to adjust the accounting logic accordingly. This aligns the implementation with the intended economic model and prevents revenue leakage.

title: M-01 | Last User Cannot Fully Redeem If LT Position Is Still Open
description: In the LeveragedToken contract, when a user calls redeemFor to withdraw all the remaining margin, Synthetix will revert because removing that margin, IPerpsV2MarketConsolidated(marketAddress).transferMargin(-int256(amount)), would cause the position to be liquidatable. Synthetix enforces that a margin withdrawal can not put the account under the liquidation threshold. The last user would be unable to fully close out his position in a single transaction. He would have to do multiple smaller partial redemptions to avoid the liquidation check. First, the user would have to call redeemFor (possibly multiple times) until the LeveragedToken’s margin would fall below MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE so a delayed close position order would be created. Then, wait for the execution of the delayed order that closes the position. And ﬁnally call redeemFor with the remaining amount of leveraged tokens. All these steps, trusting that no other user would front-run his ﬁnal redeemFor call reopening the LeveragedToken’s position.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the LeveragedToken contract when a user attempts to redeem all remaining leveraged tokens in a single call to redeemFor. The function tries to withdraw the full margin by invoking IPerpsV2MarketConsolidated(marketAddress).transferMargin(-int256(amount)). Synthetix enforces a rule that a margin withdrawal may not reduce the account’s collateral below the liquidation threshold. Because the last user’s redemption would leave the position under‑collateralised, the transferMargin call reverts, preventing the full close‑out. As a result, the user is forced to perform several smaller partial redemptions that keep the margin above the threshold, wait for a delayed close‑position order to be created once the LeveragedToken’s margin falls below MINIMUM_MARGIN_BALANCE, and finally execute another redeemFor after the delayed order has closed the position. This multi‑step process relies on the assumption that no other participant will front‑run the final redemption and reopen the position, exposing the user to potential loss or stuck funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s redemption logic, where the auditor observed that the liquidation check in Synthetix blocks a full margin withdrawal. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens in the edge case where the caller is the last holder of the token and attempts a full withdrawal; normal partial redemptions succeed. The impact is that a legitimate user may be unable to retrieve the full value of their investment in one transaction, leading to unexpected zero or reduced balances, extra gas costs, and exposure to front‑running attacks. The affected parties are token holders, especially the final exiting user, and the protocol itself, which may appear unreliable. To remediate, the contract should detect when the caller is redeeming the entire remaining supply and, instead of performing a margin withdrawal that triggers the liquidation check, directly submit a close‑off‑chain delayed order with tracking (submitCloseOffchainDelayedOrderWithTracking) to safely close the position without violating Synthetix’s collateral rules. This change aligns the redemption flow with the business logic that a full exit should close the position atomically, eliminating the need for manual partial withdrawals and reducing the attack surface.

title: M-02 | Redeemer Avoids Paying The Streaming Fee
description:
Within the LeveragedToken’s redeemFor ﬂow, the contract calculates:
• baseWithdrawn = (leveragedTokenAmount * exchangeRate) - decayingRedemptionFee - slippage.
• Then it calls _withdrawMargin(baseWithdrawn + streamingFee).
• Lastly, it charges the streaming fee (_chargeStreamingFee(streamingFee)) out of the contract’s Synthetix margin.
However, the user’s baseWithdrawn portion is based on an exchange rate computed before the streaming fee is removed from margin and consequently the user does not pay his pro-rata share of that streaming fee. All holders end up paying the streaming fee out of the leftover margin collectively, while the redeemer takes out margin as if no fee had been deducted. By computing baseWithdrawn from the pre-fee exchangeRate, the user is granted a higher share. The streaming fee is then subtracted from the contract’s margin but not from the user’s ﬁnal redemption proceeds.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/snx-leveraged-tokens-1/commit/fbeddc0dc032495e7186d330c0a4a5f614b32a35
bug_full: During the redemption flow of a leveraged token the contract first computes a base withdrawal amount using the current exchange rate, then adds the accumulated streaming fee to the amount that will be withdrawn from the margin pool, and finally charges the streaming fee from the contract’s margin balance. Because the exchange rate is calculated before the streaming fee is removed, the base withdrawal amount does not reflect the user’s proportional share of that fee. The user therefore receives a larger portion of the margin than they are entitled to, while the streaming fee is deducted from the remaining margin and is effectively paid by the other token holders. This accounting mismatch occurs every time a holder calls the redeem function while a non‑zero streaming fee is pending. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the redeemFor implementation, where the sequence of calculations was traced and it became clear that the fee is subtracted after the user’s withdrawal rather than being allocated proportionally. The issue is subtle because the contract’s total margin does decrease by the fee amount, so the overall pool balance appears correct, but individual redemption receipts are inflated and other participants see a reduced share of the pool. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected redemption amount, yet the actual amount received is higher than it should be, and other users may notice that their balances shrink unexpectedly after a redemption. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑misallocation or pro‑rata accounting bugs, where a fee is charged from a shared pool but not deducted from the participant who triggers the fee. An attacker can repeatedly redeem large amounts, effectively shifting the streaming fee cost onto the remaining holders and draining the collective margin over time. To remediate the problem the contract should recalculate the exchange rate after accounting for the streaming fee, or directly reduce the user’s base withdrawal by their proportional share of the fee (for example, based on their percentage of total supply). Implementing a regular, explicit fee‑charging function that updates the exchange rate before any redemption would also prevent the misallocation.

title: M-03 | Decaying Redemption Fee Manipulation
description: In the leveraged token system a decaying redemption fee is applied to users who have recently deposited. Throughout the codebase the decaying redemption fee is assigned to start off at a 1% fee and decay to 0% over the course of 5 minutes. The minimum deposit for a user which will reset the timer for the decaying redemption fee is set to 5 USD in the Config contract as the DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT value. With these conﬁgured parameters it can be signiﬁcantly proﬁtable for one vault depositor to do a small deposit on behalf of another depositor who is about to redeem and cause them to experience a signiﬁcant decay fee. The malicious vault depositor in this case (and the rest of LeveragedToken holders) would gain from the signiﬁcant fee paid by the victim depositor in this case. On networks without a public mempool speciﬁcally frontrunning a user’s withdrawal transaction is not reliably possible so this attack may operate based upon key indicators that a user is about to withdraw such as Discord messages or market volatility. Furthermore, if the DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT is conﬁgured too high, then a depositor could simply deposit DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT - 1 wei multiple times to avoid the decaying redemption fee while still depositing a large amount. This could occur in a single transaction with a multicall or for-loop contract call around the mintFor function.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the decaying redemption fee mechanism used in a leveraged token vault. The protocol applies a fee that starts at 1 % for a user who has recently deposited and linearly decays to 0 % over a five‑minute window. The timer that controls this decay is reset whenever a deposit equal to or larger than the constant DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT (configured as 5 USD) is made. Because the fee reset is triggered solely by the amount of a single deposit, an attacker can manipulate the fee by making a tiny deposit on behalf of a victim just before the victim initiates a redemption. The attacker’s deposit restarts the decay timer, causing the victim’s redemption to be charged the full 1 % fee even though the victim expected the fee to have already decayed to near zero. The fee is collected by the vault and ultimately benefits all token holders, including the attacker, who can profit from the additional fee revenue. A second, related abuse arises when the minimum‑deposit threshold is set too high. An attacker can split a large intended deposit into many sub‑deposits each smaller than DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT (for example, DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT − 1 wei). By batching these sub‑deposits in a single transaction using a multicall or a loop around the mint function, the attacker avoids triggering the fee‑reset logic while still supplying a large amount of capital, thereby sidestepping the intended fee decay protection. The impact is that honest users who try to redeem shortly after a legitimate deposit may receive less than expected – the protocol deducts a higher redemption fee than anticipated, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective. This breach of accounting assumptions undermines trust in the fee model and can lead to systematic loss of value for depositors. The issue manifests only when a redemption occurs within the decay window after a qualifying deposit, or when an attacker deliberately fragments deposits to stay below the threshold. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the fee‑reset logic and its interaction with deposit size checks. The bug is subtle because the fee appears as a normal protocol charge; there is no explicit on‑chain flag indicating that the fee was artificially inflated by a third‑party deposit, making it hard for users to notice until they compare expected versus actual redemption amounts. To remediate, the protocol should redesign the fee‑reset condition so that it cannot be triggered by deposits on behalf of other users, enforce per‑address or per‑session timers, and reject or aggregate sub‑threshold deposits that collectively exceed the minimum amount. Additionally, the configuration parameters DECAYING_REDEMPTION_MIN_BASE_AMOUNT, decayingRedemptionFeeStart and decayingRedemptionFeeDuration should be calibrated to avoid incentives for both front‑running deposits and split‑deposit attacks, ensuring that the fee decay behaves as intended without being exploitable.

title: M-04 | Leverage Mismatch Because Different Price Sources
description: Within the LeveragedToken’s redeemFor method, the redemption amount is reduced by a “decaying redemption fee” plus a slippage deduction (intended to represent expected order fees and price impact). Ordinarily, these fees stay in the contract or go to other token holders. However, if the user redeeming is the last, meaning he redeems the entire totalSupply, there are no other holders to beneﬁt from these leftover fees and the contract itself can no longer distribute them. That portion of sUSD remains stuck in the PerpsV2 protocol as unused margin. The ﬁnal user is penalized, losing this fraction of their redeemable amount for no net beneﬁt to the system. On the other hand, this also happens if the LeveragedToken currently has no position as it dropped below 100 sUSD and the rebalancer closed it. In that case it is not fair to remove this slippage amount from the user and distributing it among the other users.
bug_full: Within the LeveragedToken contract the redeemFor function applies a decaying redemption fee and an additional slippage deduction to the amount returned to the caller. These deductions are intended to be redistributed to remaining token holders or retained by the protocol as compensation for order fees and price impact. The logic, however, does not check whether any holders will remain after the redemption. When a user redeems the entire totalSupply – i.e., they are the last holder – the contract still subtracts the fee and slippage, but there are no other accounts to receive the collected amount. Consequently the deducted portion stays locked in the PerpsV2 contract as unused margin, effectively burning the user’s sUSD. A similar situation occurs when the leveraged token’s underlying position has been closed because the collateral fell below the minimum threshold (≈100 sUSD). In that state the contract still removes the slippage amount even though there is no active position to justify the charge. The vulnerability therefore manifests as a mismatch between the fee‑charging mechanism and the actual distribution context. An attacker or an unwary user can trigger the condition by being the sole redeemer or by waiting until the position is closed, and will receive less than the expected redemption amount, seeing a shortfall in their wallet or a zero balance after the transaction. The impact is a loss of funds for the user and a distortion of the protocol’s accounting, because the protocol retains fees that were never meant to be burned. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the redemption flow, where the fee‑distribution assumptions were examined. It is subtle because the fee deduction appears normal for typical redemptions, and only becomes apparent in the edge case of a full‑supply redemption, which may not be exercised frequently in testing. The proper remediation is to add a guard that skips the decaying redemption fee and the slippage deduction whenever the amount being redeemed equals the totalSupply, and also when the token holds no active position (balance below the minimum). This ensures that users receive the full value of their holdings and that the protocol’s fee accounting remains consistent.

title: M-01 | Reward Distributor Is Not Future-Proof
description: We have one reward distributor per collateral as speciﬁed with this: globalMarginConﬁg.supported[runtime.collateralAddress].rewardDistributor and a PerpRewardDistributor instances can be linked to only one pool as we can see from their _poolId variable. During liquidation, nonUsd collaterals are distributed only to that pool distributor is connected with. Although currently pool creation is done by governance only, this will create problems when the pool creation became permissionless. After creating pools became permissionless, when a pool owner choose to back a BFP-Market instance that they don't own, they won't be able to get something from liquidations (at least nonUsd collaterals). This will either disincentivize pool creators to back a BFP-Market instance that they don't own (which is against SNX's vision), or a pool owner that is not aware of this situation will back these markets and LP's will lose funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the reward distribution mechanism is architected for non‑USD collateral liquidations. Each collateral type is associated with a single reward distributor instance that is hard‑wired to a single pool identifier via an internal _poolId variable. Consequently, when a liquidation occurs, the rewards for that collateral are sent only to the pool that is linked to the distributor, regardless of which pool actually supplied liquidity to the market where the liquidation happened. This design works while pool creation is restricted to governance, because the only pools that can back a market are those owned by the same entity that created the pool. However, once pool creation becomes permissionless, a pool owner may choose to back a BFP‑Market instance that they do not own. In that scenario the liquidation rewards for non‑USD collateral are still routed to the distributor tied to the original pool, leaving the backing pool with no reward. From a user’s perspective the expected liquidation reward never arrives; LP balances appear unchanged or even reduced relative to the amount of collateral they supplied, creating the impression that “funds disappear” or that “my reward is missing”. The impact is economic loss for liquidity providers and a disincentive for third‑party pool creators, which contradicts the protocol’s goal of encouraging open market participation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward distribution logic and identified the single‑pool binding as a structural flaw. It can be hard to notice because the system behaves correctly for markets owned by the pool creator, so the missing rewards only surface in cross‑ownership scenarios that may be rare during early testing. To remediate the problem the reward distributor should be refactored to support multiple pool identifiers, aggregating collateral from all pools that back a market and allocating rewards proportionally. The distribution routine must iterate over every registered pool, calculate each pool’s share of the liquidated collateral, and transfer the appropriate reward amount. Care must be taken to avoid introducing new attack vectors such as reward hijacking or double counting when implementing the multi‑pool logic. By making the reward distribution future‑proof, the protocol can safely allow permissionless pool creation without risking loss of liquidation rewards.

title: M-02 | Risk Free Trades Via Pay Debt
description: An order can be committed that would attempt to merge with another account upon settlement but would then revert due to not meeting the Initial Margin Requirements. That same order could then be "enabled" by paying down some debt in the account which would allow for the ﬁnal merged account to meet IMR. A trader could use this to create a risk-free trade whereby if the actual price moved enough from the Pyth price at the beginning of the settlement window, the trader could enable the trade and then immediately sell for a proﬁt.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/synthetix-pocs/pull/9
bug_full: The vulnerability is a margin‑enforcement bypass that allows a trader to create an order which would normally be rejected because the merged account does not satisfy the Initial Margin Requirements (IMR) at the time of settlement, and then later satisfy those requirements by calling the payDebt function before the order is finally settled. The root cause is that the contract does not prevent a payDebt call while a pending order exists, and the IMR check is performed only at settlement rather than at order creation. An attacker can therefore commit a trade, watch the external price feed (Pyth) during the settlement window, and when the price moves sufficiently in a favorable direction, they can reduce the account’s debt just enough to bring the merged account into compliance with IMR. At that point the previously failing order becomes valid, can be settled, and the trader can immediately sell the acquired position for a profit that appears risk‑free because the trader only enables the trade after the price move. This impacts any user who can create orders and call payDebt, effectively allowing profit extraction without exposing the trader to market risk and undermining the economic integrity of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team when they examined the interaction between order commitment, account merging, and the payDebt function and noticed that the margin check could be satisfied retroactively. The bug is subtle because the order appears to be rejected only at settlement, and there is no explicit warning that paying debt can change the outcome of a pending order, making it easy to overlook in normal testing.
