To remediate, the contract should either enforce IMR at the moment an order is created, or explicitly block calls to payDebt while there is a pending order that would otherwise fail the margin check, thereby preventing a trader from retroactively enabling a trade after a favorable price movement. This class of issue can be described as a margin‑requirement bypass or state‑manipulation vulnerability that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that margin must be satisfied before a trade is considered executable, leading to unexpected profit or loss scenarios such as "funds disappear" or "unexpected profit without risk" from the user’s perspective.

title: M-03 | Orders Can Be Censored By Front-running
description: Any one can control whether or not their order is settled by front-running keeper bots. A user may commit an Order A that has a very tight price limit in block 0. To prevent Order A from settling, in the same block 0, through a different account, they could also commit an Order B that would move the market slightly so that the slippage guard would prevent settlement of Order A. In the next block 1 they could pay higher gas on a call to settleOrder for Order B which would "disable" Order A. The keeper would notice that Order A was outside of price tolerance and during the next block would call cancelOrder. In anticipation of this, the user could, through yet another account, create an order to move the market back so that Order A could not be canceled. Back and forth they dance, until the user decides to let the order be canceled or settled. This ability to censor trades at-will would give the user an opportunity to perform risk-free trades. Proﬁt on a large risk-free trade could easily cover the gas for the multiple orders needed to manipulate the order's settleability.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/snx-bfp-1/blob/devtooligan-pocs/markets/bfp-market/test/integration/modules/guardian/poc/realizePnlTest.test.ts#L222-L366
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running based order‑censorship flaw that allows an attacker to control whether a pending order can be settled by deliberately manipulating the market price within the same block. The root cause lies in the contract’s settlement logic, which checks a slippage guard against the current market price and permits any address to invoke the settleOrder function. By submitting a second order that moves the price just enough to push the original order outside the allowed tolerance, the attacker can cause the settlement check to fail. In the following block the attacker can trigger a cancelOrder call, effectively censoring the original order. This can be repeated with additional accounts to swing the price back and forth, creating a back‑and‑forth dance that lets the attacker decide when the order is finally cancelled or settled. The impact is that a malicious actor can prevent legitimate trades from executing, enabling risk‑free arbitrage or profit that can easily cover the gas costs of the multiple manipulative orders. The condition occurs when an order with a tight price limit is pending and the protocol allows unrestricted calls to settleOrder in the same block as other market‑moving orders. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because market integrity and fair order execution are compromised. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept script demonstrating the manipulation across two blocks. It is hard to notice because the price movements appear legitimate and the failure manifests only as an unexpected cancellation or non‑settlement of an order, which may be attributed to normal market volatility. To remediate, the settlement function should be restricted to trusted keeper contracts, and the execution order of pending settlements should be randomized or otherwise protected against deterministic front‑running, thereby removing the ability for arbitrary actors to influence the settleability of an order.

title: M-04 | Liquidation Fees Not Covered By non-sUSD Collateral
description: When a liquidation is ﬂagged, the liquidator is paid out in sUSD regardless of the collateral type. liquidateCollateral() will decrement the amount of collateral and send the amount to the distributor. After, withdrawMarketUsd() is called, sending the liquidator sUSD. This will lower the credit capacity. Credit capacity is primarily affected through withdrawals and deposits, which will essentially cancel out over time (although it is expected for there to be more deposits than withdrawals). However, the negative impact on credit capacity from liquidation rewards will not be balanced out in the long run. This will cause accrual of negative credit capacity. Once the credit capacity decreases to a large enough state, withdrawMarketCollateral() will revert since it veriﬁes that the credit capacity plus the deposited collateral must be greater than 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of liquidation rewards in a market that supports multiple collateral types. When a position is flagged for liquidation, the protocol’s liquidateCollateral function removes the seized collateral and forwards it to a distribution pool, but the subsequent withdrawMarketUsd call always pays the liquidator in sUSD, regardless of which asset was actually liquidated. This creates a mismatch: the protocol’s credit capacity metric, which tracks the net amount of sUSD that can be withdrawn, is reduced by the sUSD reward, while the collateral side of the balance sheet is unchanged because the seized non‑sUSD assets are not accounted for as a reduction in credit capacity. Over time, repeated liquidations that involve non‑sUSD collateral cause the credit capacity to drift negative because withdrawals and deposits normally offset each other, but the sUSD rewards are a one‑way drain. When the credit capacity becomes sufficiently negative, the withdrawMarketCollateral function reverts, as it checks that credit capacity plus the amount of deposited collateral remains positive. From a user’s perspective this manifests as an inability to withdraw their collateral – the UI may show a “withdraw failed” error or simply no funds being returned, even though the user’s balance appears unchanged. The impact is that legitimate users can have their funds frozen, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about solvency are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation flow and the credit‑capacity invariant. It is subtle because the credit capacity variable is not directly exposed to users, and the protocol’s normal deposit/withdraw patterns mask the gradual erosion caused by the sUSD‑only rewards. The root cause is the design decision to reward liquidators in a single stablecoin irrespective of the underlying collateral, leading to an accounting imbalance. The recommended remediation is to pay the liquidator in the same asset that was seized and to deduct the reward from the distribution amount, thereby keeping the credit‑capacity invariant intact and preventing negative capacity accumulation.

title: M-05 | Negative New Margin Is Not Recognized
description: When an order is impacted positively or negatively the price impact is applied to the rest of the existing position when computing the newMarginUsd. Because the newMarginUsd cannot go below 0, this behavior can potentially allow traders to erase losses from their position. In the case of lower minimum margin conﬁgurations, the effect from the new entry price based on the ﬁll price could create a situation which zeroes out sUSD collateral and then should create a new debtUSD amount but it does not because the newMarginUSD is not allowed to be negative in this case.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/synthetix-pocs/pull/6/files
bug_full: The vulnerability is a margin‑clamping error in the settlement routine of the perpetual trading module. When an order is executed the contract calculates a new margin value (newMarginUsd) by applying the price impact of the order to the remaining portion of the trader’s position. The implementation forces newMarginUsd to be at least zero; if the arithmetic would produce a negative value, the result is silently clamped to zero. Because a negative margin represents a debt that should be recorded as debtUSD, the clamp prevents the protocol from creating the corresponding debt entry. As a result a trader can submit an order whose price impact pushes the margin below zero, causing the on‑chain accounting to show zero sUSD collateral while the underlying position still carries a loss. The UI therefore displays a healthy, fully collateralised position with a zero balance, while the protocol’s internal accounting omits the expected debt. This situation is more likely when the system is configured with a low minimum margin requirement, because the smaller safety buffer allows the price impact to drive the margin to zero more easily. The bug can be exploited by deliberately crafting orders that generate a large adverse price impact, erasing losses and avoiding liquidation or fee penalties. The impact is that the protocol may become under‑collateralised, allowing malicious traders to walk away with positions that should be insolvent, potentially leading to loss of funds for other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the margin‑update logic and noticed that the function marginUsdForNextMarginUsd is never allowed to be negative and that debtCorrection is not applied when the clamp occurs. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply records a zero margin, which can look normal in transaction logs and UI dashboards. To remediate the issue the contract should either reject orders that would produce a negative margin (or a margin smaller than the required fees) or refactor the settlement so that the profit‑and‑loss of the entire new position is realised against the current market price and the resulting debt is correctly recorded. In either case the accounting must allow a negative margin to be represented as debtUSD rather than being silently forced to zero, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the system.

title: M-06 | Account Can Be Made Liquidatable By Cancelling
description: An account can be put into a liquidatable state when they are canceled. This would cause the immediate loss to a user of all funds that they could have instead withdrawn through modifyColatteral. This is made possible by the lack of a check for isLiquidatable at the end of the cancelOrder function. As mentioned in ﬁnding M-03, an order’s cancel-ability can be controlled by manipulating the skew. In addition to the fee for cancellation, the liquidation fees provide an added incentive to cancel the order which could even cover the costs of the skew manipulation.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/snx-bfp-1/blob/devtooligan-pocs/markets/bfp-market/test/integration/modules/guardian/poc/realizePnlTest.test.ts#L422-L546
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing liquidation safety check in the function that cancels an open order. When a user calls cancelOrder the contract updates the position but does not verify whether the resulting collateral ratio falls below the required threshold. Because the cancelability of an order can be manipulated by altering the market skew, an attacker can create a situation where the order appears cancellable, trigger the cancellation and leave the account under‑collateralised. The contract then marks the account as liquidatable and a liquidation can be executed immediately, causing the user to lose the funds that could otherwise have been withdrawn through a modifyCollateral call. This loss is experienced by the user as a sudden disappearance of their balance or a zero‑balance UI after a seemingly harmless cancel action. The issue occurs only when the cancelOrder path is taken and the new position, including any cancellation fees, would breach the collateral requirement, but because there is no isLiquidatable check at the end of the function the breach is not detected. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that linked the cancel‑ability control described in finding M‑03 with the lack of a post‑cancel liquidation guard. It is hard to notice because the cancel function does not revert or emit an error; the account simply becomes eligible for liquidation later, and the cancellation fee may mask the underlying risk. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of “post‑operation collateral validation missing” or “liquidation‑triggering state transition without guard”. To remediate the issue the protocol should add logic in the trade validation routine (for example in validateTrade) that reverts any operation – including order cancellation – if the resulting position, after accounting for fees, would make the account liquidatable. Additionally, an explicit isLiquidatable check after cancelOrder would prevent the unintended state transition and preserve the user’s expectation that cancelling an order does not cause an immediate loss of funds.

title: M-07 | Debt With Zero Collateral Is Unliquidateable
description: An account that has debt but no collateral and no position cannot be liquidated. This is due to a check within the liquidateMarginOnly function which reverts with CannotLiquidateMargin in the case there is no collateral. This would effectively lock the loss in the system and never recognize it which would mean credit capacity would be overstated since the total debtUSD is added back to the ﬁnal calculation. The severity is reduced due to the diﬃculty since we were unable to ﬁnd a way to put an account in this state with any signiﬁcant debt value. Currently the only identiﬁed means to achieve such a state is due to rounding error when splitting a position, such that a position can be left with 0 collateral and a few wei of debt. However, depending on how M-07 is resolved, this may become more likely and impactful in the future.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unliquidatable debt condition that occurs when an account holds a non‑zero debt balance but has no collateral and no open position. The contract’s liquidateMarginOnly function contains a guard that checks the collateral amount and deliberately reverts with the error CannotLiquidateMargin if the collateral is zero. Because the liquidation path is blocked, the outstanding debt cannot be seized or repaid through the normal liquidation mechanism. This creates a locked loss that remains on the ledger indefinitely. The system’s accounting routine later adds the total debtUSD back into the calculation of available credit capacity, so the presence of an unliquidated debt artificially inflates the protocol’s perceived borrowing power. The condition can be triggered only in edge cases where rounding errors during position splitting leave a residual debt of a few wei while the collateral amount rounds down to zero. Under normal operation the contract never creates such a state, which makes the issue difficult to observe; the debt is so small that balances appear correct and the revert message is rarely encountered. From a user perspective the symptoms are that an account that should be liquidated remains unchanged, the user may see a tiny debt amount that never disappears, and the protocol may report higher credit capacity than actually available. The bug belongs to the class of liquidation bypass or accounting inconsistency bugs, where business logic assumes that any debtful account can be forced into liquidation. It violates the fundamental assumption that collateralized debt can always be reclaimed, breaking the accounting invariant that total debt is offset by seized collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the liquidateMarginOnly logic was examined and edge‑case tests were performed with minimal debt values. Because the condition relies on rare rounding artifacts, it may go unnoticed in routine testing and in production monitoring. To remediate the problem the constraint that forbids liquidation of zero‑collateral accounts should be removed or the liquidation logic should be extended to handle debt‑only accounts, ensuring that any outstanding debt can be settled and that credit capacity calculations reflect the true risk exposure.

title: M-08 | Missing Staleness Check For Chainlink Oracles
description: When the price is fetched in functions like ﬂagPosition, the function will query Chainlink for the said price by calling the latestRoundData function. At this point, the price as well as the updatedAt are returned. The issue, however, is that the freshness of the price is not conﬁrmed, which can lead to stale prices being used to determine if a price is liquidatable or not. This can result in a position being wrongly liquidated using this function, and can lead to inaccurate proﬁt/losses when closing a position.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing staleness validation when the contract retrieves price data from a Chainlink oracle. The contract calls the oracle’s latestRoundData function to obtain the current price and the timestamp (updatedAt), but it never checks whether the returned price is recent enough for the current block. The root cause is the absence of a freshness guard – no comparison between block.timestamp and the oracle’s updatedAt, and no configurable maximum staleness interval. An attacker or even a benign user can exploit this by triggering a function such as flagPosition after the oracle feed has stopped updating, causing the contract to use an outdated price. Because liquidation logic and profit‑loss calculations rely on that price, a stale value can incorrectly mark a healthy position as under‑collateralised, leading to an unwarranted liquidation, or can produce an inaccurate P/L when a position is closed. The impact is that users may lose collateral or see their balances reduced unexpectedly, while the protocol may record incorrect accounting data, undermining trust in the system. This condition occurs whenever the oracle feed experiences a delay, outage, or simply when the contract is called after the last update exceeds the intended freshness window. All participants who hold positions – traders, liquidators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the core risk‑management logic depends on timely price information. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation path and noted the lack of any timestamp comparison before using the price. It can be hard to notice because the contract still receives a price value that appears syntactically correct, and the UI may not surface the age of the data, so users see a liquidation event without an obvious market move. To remediate, the contract should enforce a staleness check by comparing the oracle’s updatedAt with the current block timestamp and rejecting or reverting the operation if the difference exceeds a predefined threshold (for example, a few minutes). This pattern belongs to the broader class of oracle freshness or stale‑data bugs, where smart contracts assume external data is always current without verification, leading to accounting errors, unexpected liquidations, and potential loss of funds.

title: M-09 | Pending Fees Altered By setMarketConﬁguration
description: When the setMarketConﬁguration function is called, the admin can change the utilizationBreakpointPercent, lowUtilizationSlopePercent, and highUtilizationSlopePercent. Once these values are adjusted, all pending utilization fees will be updated according to the new slope, rather than the slope that was initially set when the fees were accruing. This adjustment will result in a sudden increase in fees owed by users, potentially putting them in a liquidatable state due to the past utilization incorrectly increasing based on the new slope.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a function that allows the contract administrator to modify three market configuration parameters: utilizationBreakpointPercent, lowUtilizationSlopePercent and highUtilizationSlopePercent. These parameters define the slope of utilization fees that are accrued on user positions. The contract calculates pending utilization fees on demand by reading the current values of these slopes instead of storing the rates that were in effect when the fees began to accrue. Consequently, when the administrator calls setMarketConfiguration and changes any of the slope values, the pending fee amount for every open position is recomputed using the new slopes. This retroactive recalculation can cause a sudden and significant increase in the fee balance owed by users. Users who expected their debt to grow at the original rate suddenly see a larger amount due, which may push their collateralisation ratio below the required threshold and trigger liquidation. The issue manifests only after a configuration change, making it difficult to notice because the UI typically shows the same utilization level while the underlying fee calculation has silently changed. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, where the logical flow of fee accrual and configuration updates was examined. It belongs to the class of bugs where mutable global parameters affect retroactive accounting, often referred to as fee‑manipulation or accounting‑inconsistency vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a debt that jumps unexpectedly, a liquidation that occurs without any new activity, or a balance that appears to disappear. The expected behaviour is that fees accrue at the rate that was set when the position opened; the actual behaviour after the admin change violates this expectation. To remediate the issue the contract should either snapshot the fee‑rate parameters at the moment fees start accruing, or prevent the setMarketConfiguration function from altering the calculation of already pending fees, or explicitly recompute pending fees in a way that preserves the original slope for each position. Implementing one of these fixes restores the accounting integrity and prevents users from being unfairly penalised by later configuration changes.

title: M-10 | DoS To Keeper Transactions
description: Market's atomic actions that are not executed with a delay (modifyCollateral and payDebt) can be used to DOS keepers' liquidation calls. Benign keeper who possibly simulated the transaction before executing it and saw that it is executable will see that their orders reverted because a user front-ran the keeper execution. Which in turn keeper will lose gas. Attack Vector: When someone sees a liquidation call for themselves (or ﬂagging), they can front-run this call and either modifyCollateral or payDebt just enough that liquidation call will revert. Although it’s not a problem system-wise considering the trader will be above liquidation threshold in the end, it is an effective way to DOS keepers' liquidation attempts. In the end, user can stay at the liquidation threshold as long as they want and this can lead to fund loss for liquidators for their every liquidation attempt.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that affects keeper contracts that submit liquidation transactions on a market where users can adjust their collateral or repay debt in the same atomic step. The root cause is that the market’s core functions (modifyCollateral and payDebt) are executed without any temporal separation or protection against transaction reordering, allowing an attacker to front‑run a pending liquidation call and change the account’s state just enough to make the liquidation revert. An attacker monitors the mempool for a keeper’s liquidation transaction, then submits a modifyCollateral or payDebt transaction that executes first, moving the user’s position marginally above the liquidation threshold. When the keeper’s transaction finally executes, the protocol’s liquidation check fails, the transaction reverts, and the keeper loses the gas spent. This can be repeated indefinitely, keeping the user at the liquidation threshold and preventing any successful liquidation. The impact is that keepers (or third‑party liquidators) experience repeated gas loss and are unable to capture the under‑collateralised position, which may lead to financial loss for the liquidators and a slowdown of the protocol’s risk‑mitigation mechanism. The condition occurs whenever a liquidation is attempted on a position that is exactly at the threshold and the protocol permits immediate collateral adjustments or debt repayments in the same block. Both keepers and users with borderline positions are affected: keepers lose execution funds, while users can remain at risk without being liquidated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of market actions and identified that the atomic calls could be manipulated by a front‑runner. It is hard to notice because the reverted transaction looks like a normal failure and the simulation that keepers perform before execution shows a successful liquidation, masking the fact that the state can be altered in the interim. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a delay or commit‑reveal scheme for collateral modifications and debt repayments, enforce that liquidation checks are performed after a block has passed, or require keepers to submit liquidation calls via private transaction relays (e.g., Flashbots) that prevent front‑running. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of front‑run‑induced DoS where state‑changing actions can be reordered to invalidate dependent transactions, breaking the expected accounting invariant that a position above the liquidation threshold can be liquidated immediately.

title: M-11 | Value Extraction Via Trustless Keepers
description:
Orders may be executed by any actor as soon as they are ready which allows for several potential value extraction or grieﬁng mechanisms. For example:
1. An attacker creates two accounts
2. The attacker watches the mempool and when they see that a trader will be positively impacted for an order that is going to be committed, the attacker creates two orders with these two accounts in order to sandwich trader. All 3 orders are committed in the same block.
3. When all 3 orders are ready, the attacker can sandwich the trader with their two orders and settle all 3 of these orders by calling the settleOrder function.
4. The attacker gets positively impacted by their two orders via negatively impacting user who was expecting positive impact
Although the limit price of the order will limit how much can be stolen, users are not likely to set their priceLimit ahead of the market price to lock in any positive impact.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a value‑extraction scenario that stems from the protocol’s trustless keeper design, where any actor is allowed to call the order‑settlement routine as soon as an order meets its execution criteria. Because the system does not restrict who may settle ready orders, a malicious participant can monitor the mempool, create two complementary orders with separate accounts, and wait for a third order placed by an honest trader to become executable in the same block. When all three orders are ready, the attacker invokes the settlement function, causing the three trades to be executed together. By positioning their two orders on either side of the victim’s order, the attacker creates a sandwich that captures the positive price impact that the victim expected, while simultaneously pushing the market price against the victim. The root cause is the lack of access control and insufficient price‑limit enforcement on the settlement path, which allows an attacker to profit from the price movement that should have benefited the user. This can be exploited whenever the market price moves within the 12‑second window before an order becomes executable and the attacker can submit their own orders fast enough to be included in the same block. The impact is that the victim’s order may receive a reduced or even negative impact, effectively losing the profit they anticipated; in extreme cases the user’s balance may appear lower after settlement, and the protocol’s overall market fairness is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the open settlement model enables front‑running‑style sandwich attacks without any on‑chain penalty. The problem is subtle because the settlement transaction looks legitimate – all three orders are settled together and the attacker’s profit is recorded as a normal trade, so there is no obvious error flag or revert. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should either move to a centralized or semi‑centralized keeper system that can be punished for malicious behavior, or, if the trustless model is retained, enforce stricter price‑limit rules that require users to set limits that capture the full expected positive impact, and introduce mechanisms such as keeper bonds, slashing, or explicit authorization checks on the settlement function. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of front‑running or sandwich attacks enabled by unrestricted order execution permissions, and it violates the business assumption that a user’s positive price impact is protected once an order is ready to be settled.

title: M-12 | Unexpected Liquidations Caused By Block.basefee
description: To ensure that liquidators are adequately compensated for liquidating unhealthy positions, the liquidation fee is partially based on block.basefee. This differs from most liquidation functionality that does not base the fee on network activity. The issue here is that users may get liquidated due to factors beyond their position's actual health. A seemingly healthy position could become unhealthy simply because of an increase in network activity. The block.basefee can increase by as much as 12.5% from one block to another. This could potentially incentivize attackers to manipulate block.basefee, or it could occur naturally as the network experiences spikes in activity. All of this would be unexpected for users and could result in a loss of collateral for those affected.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the liquidation fee calculation that incorporates the block.basefee, a network‑level parameter that can fluctuate dramatically with changes in transaction demand. Because the fee is partially derived from block.basefee, a position that appears healthy according to its collateralisation ratio can become effectively under‑collateralised when the basefee spikes, causing the protocol to deem it liquidatable. This coupling of an economic incentive (the liquidation fee) to a volatile on‑chain metric creates a situation where external factors unrelated to the user’s risk profile can trigger liquidation. An attacker could deliberately raise the basefee by flooding the mempool with high‑gas transactions, or a natural surge in network activity could produce a similar effect, increasing the fee component by up to roughly twelve and a half percent from one block to the next. When the liquidation check runs, the inflated fee reduces the effective health of the position, the protocol initiates liquidation, and the user loses a portion of their collateral unexpectedly. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal collateral ratio, yet the transaction reverts with a liquidation event, leading to the symptom “my position was liquidated even though my collateral looks sufficient” or “my balance dropped to zero after a gas price jump”. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation logic and noticed the unconventional dependence on block.basefee. It can be hard to notice because most liquidation designs rely solely on health metrics, so developers and users do not anticipate that network congestion can affect liquidation eligibility. The bug belongs to the class of economic‑logic coupling errors where a volatile external variable is used in a safety‑critical calculation. To remediate, the protocol should decouple the fee from block.basefee, for example by adopting a flat liquidation fee or by clearly documenting that network activity may influence liquidation status, thereby aligning the incentive model with user expectations and preventing unintended collateral loss.

title: M-13 | payDebt Affects Utilization Without Update
description: In the payDebt function when the caller provides sUSD to repay an account’s debt the creditCapacity of the market will be immediately incremented by the amountToBurn. As a result the utilization of the market will decrease, as the delegatedCollateralValueUsd which relies on the creditCapacity will increase. The utilization of the market will also be affected by the updateDebtAndCollateral function call for sUSD collateral repayments from the account. However the utilization rate is not recomputed in the payDebt function so this utilization change is not reﬂected in the resulting utilization charged over any period where payDebt occurs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale utilization calculation in the payDebt function of the market contract. When a user repays debt with sUSD, the function immediately increases the market's credit capacity, which should lower the utilization ratio because the amount of available collateral rises. However the function never recomputes the utilization metric after the credit capacity change. Consequently the on‑chain utilization value that is used to charge interest or fees remains at its pre‑repayment level for the remainder of the period in which the repayment occurs. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a borrower calls payDebt, either directly or via a delegated collateral repayment, and it persists until another operation that updates utilization is executed. The impact is that the protocol may continue to charge higher utilization‑based fees on a position that has actually reduced its risk exposure, leading to over‑charging of borrowers and distorted market statistics. From a user perspective the borrower sees that the debt was repaid but the displayed utilization or fee accrual does not drop, resulting in unexpected fee deductions or a balance that appears unchanged. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the market’s accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that depositMarketUsd is called to adjust credit capacity but the subsequent call to recompute utilization was missing. The bug is subtle because the state change (credit capacity) is visible, yet the derived metric (utilization) is not automatically refreshed, making the inconsistency easy to overlook in testing that only checks final balances. The class of bug is a state‑inconsistency or stale‑derived‑value error, where a dependent variable is not updated after its base variable changes. To remediate, the contract should invoke the utilization‑recalculation routine after any operation that modifies credit capacity, such as at the end of payDebt, ensuring that the market’s utilization accurately reflects the new collateral amount before any fees are applied. This fix restores the intended business logic that utilization decreases when debt is repaid, preserving correct fee calculations and market health.

title: M-14 | BFP Market Liquidations May Liquidate LPs
description:
During the ﬂagging of a position in the BFP market, the non-sUSD collateral of the ﬂagged account is removed from the market deposited collaterals and credited to the LPs through a reward distributor. However this action will remove the LPs collateral value from the totalDebt and re-allocate it to the distributor rewards which do not contribute to a V3 account’s health. Consider the following scenario:
• A BFP position holds 2 wETH, valued at $5,000 each
• The position has a $7,000 loss and is liquidatable
• Before the liquidation totalDebt = reportedDebt - marketDepositedCollateral = $3,000 - $10,000 = -$7,000
• After the liquidation totalDebt = 0 - 0 = 0, but the LPs have received $10,000 through the reward distributor
This reallocation of debt to the distributor may cause some v3 positions to unexpectedly become immediately unhealthy as they no longer are credited with the negative debt of the BFP position that was liquidated. This may cause loss of assets for those V3 accounts as they are liquidated even though they received collateral from the liquidation that would have made position healthy. Their debt and collateral would then be socialized amongst the other v3 positions, however these positions would not receive the BFP collateral rewards that would have gone to the liquidated account through the distributor this way. Unexpected liquidations in V3 could be triggered by the wiping of a position’s debt upon ﬂagging as well. This is most likely to occur when the liquidated BFP position holds little or no collateral and is supported by position proﬁt.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the BFP market handles collateral when a position is flagged for liquidation. When a BFP position is liquidated, the protocol removes the non‑sUSD collateral that was deposited in the market and immediately credits it to liquidity providers through a reward distributor. This removal also subtracts the corresponding amount from the marketDepositedCollateral field, which is used in the calculation of totalDebt for V3 accounts. Because the negative debt that the BFP position contributed to the overall health of V3 positions is transferred to the reward distributor – a component that does not participate in V3 health calculations – the totalDebt for those V3 accounts is artificially set to zero. As a result, V3 positions that previously relied on the negative debt of the liquidated BFP position to stay healthy can suddenly appear under‑collateralised and be liquidated despite having just received collateral from the same liquidation event. The impact is that delegators of V3 pools may lose assets, see their balances drop to zero, or experience unexpected liquidations, while the LPs receive the redistributed collateral as rewards. This scenario occurs most often when the liquidated BFP position holds little or no collateral and its loss is primarily represented by a negative debt figure. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the liquidation flow, where the logical relationship between marketDepositedCollateral, totalDebt, and V3 health metrics was examined. It can be hard to notice because the totalDebt variable appears to reset to zero, which seems benign, yet the health check that depends on that value silently fails. To remediate the problem, the distribution of market‑deposited collateral should be decoupled from the immediate health calculation – for example by locking the collateral and streaming it to the reward distributor over time, or by requiring an explicit exchange for sUSD before it can be claimed – thereby preserving the negative debt contribution until the V3 health state is safely updated. In essence, the bug is a mis‑allocation of debt that breaks accounting assumptions about how collateral and debt interact, leading to funds disappearing from user positions and rewards being unfairly allocated.

title: M-15 | Inadequate Estimated Liquidation Costs
description: In the getLiquidationKeeperFee function the resulting estimated keeper fee is restricted to the maxKeeperFeeUsd. However when estimating the initial margin and maintenance margin values necessary for a position the estimated keeper fee may apply to multiple liquidatePosition transactions. Therefore a single maxKeeperFeeUsd is insuﬃcient to cover these multiple transactions. As a result, positions which would require multiple liquidatePosition calls are not required to hold the estimated keeper fee for each transaction. It is unlikely that positions large enough to require multiple liquidatePosition calls would not be able to cover the keeper fees due to increased maintenance margin requirements. However out of an abundance of caution, the estimated keeper fees should allow multiple liquidate position calls to be accounted for.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑estimation of the keeper fee required to execute liquidation of a margin position. The contract calculates an estimated keeper fee for a liquidation and then caps this estimate with a global constant maxKeeperFeeUsd. When a position is large enough that the liquidation process must be performed over several iterations – i.e., multiple calls to liquidatePosition – the same capped value is applied to each iteration, but the cap is not multiplied by the number of iterations. Consequently the total fee that the position is required to hold may be lower than the sum of fees needed for all iterations. The root cause is the use of a single maxKeeperFeeUsd limit without scaling it by the iteration count when estimating initial‑margin (IM) and maintenance‑margin (MM) requirements. An attacker or a user can trigger a liquidation that needs more than one iteration; because the contract believes the fee reserve is sufficient, the liquidation call may run out of gas or revert when the keeper fee cannot be paid. The impact is that a position that should be liquidated may remain partially liquidated, leaving the user with an unexpected loss of collateral, or the protocol may be unable to recover the under‑collateralised position, potentially exposing funds to loss. The condition occurs only for positions whose size or market volatility forces the liquidation logic to split the process into multiple steps; for small positions the single‑fee cap is adequate. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the liquidation fee estimation logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee calculation used MathUtil.min(liquidationFeeInUsd * iterations, globalConfig.maxKeeperFeeUsd) instead of multiplying the max fee by the iteration count. The bug is subtle because the contract still enforces a fee ceiling, so most normal liquidations succeed and the problem is not visible in routine tests. To fix the issue, the fee estimation should multiply the global maximum keeper fee by the number of expected iterations, ensuring that the total estimated fee covers all calls required for a multi‑step liquidation. This change aligns the accounting model with the business rule that each liquidation step must be paid for, preventing situations where users see liquidation failed or balance becomes zero despite having apparently sufficient fee reserves.

title: M-16 | Attacker Profits From Block Stuffing Orders
description:
Because orders only have about 5 blocks to have their order be settled before they become stale an attacker could congest the network so that attempts to call settleOrder fail due to all the gas for that block being used.
If an attacker were to stuff the blocks with their own transactions so that settleOrder will fail for 60 seconds, the attacker would then be able to cancel all of the pending orders and collect the cancelation reward for each one.
The lower the block.baseFee is and the more pending orders there are the more profitable this attack becomes.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a design choice that limits the time window for an order to be settled to roughly five blocks before the order is considered stale. Because the contract relies on the ability to call a settlement function within this short period, an attacker can deliberately congest the blockchain by flooding it with a high volume of their own transactions, a technique often referred to as block stuffing. When the network is saturated, the gas limit for the block is fully consumed, causing legitimate calls to the settlement routine to run out of gas and revert. As a result, pending orders cannot be settled within the allowed timeframe and automatically become eligible for cancellation. The protocol rewards the caller who cancels a stale order, so the attacker, after ensuring settlement failures for about sixty seconds, proceeds to cancel each pending order and collect the cancellation reward. This profit mechanism is amplified when the base fee of the block is low, because the cost of the attacker’s own transactions is reduced, and when many orders are pending, increasing the total reward pool. From a user perspective, an expected trade or position update never materialises; the UI may show a pending order that later disappears without execution, leaving the user without the anticipated outcome and potentially missing a market opportunity. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the order lifecycle and the assumptions about block availability. It can be hard to notice because the failure manifests as normal network congestion, and the contract does not emit a distinct error indicating that settlement was blocked by an external attacker rather than ordinary gas limits. The root cause is the combination of a short settlement window and a reward structure that incentivises cancellation without verifying that the failure was due to malicious congestion. To mitigate the problem, the protocol should either extend the settlement period, implement a back‑off or retry mechanism that does not rely on a single block window, or redesign the cancellation reward so that it does not create a direct profit incentive for attackers who can artificially induce settlement failures. In broader terms, this is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) vulnerability coupled with an economic incentive flaw that allows an adversary to profit from intentionally blocking legitimate contract operations.

title: M-17 | Setting SkewScale Disrupts Markets
description:
Setting the skewSkale with setMarketConfigurationById will cause unexpected results the next time recomputeFunding is called. The logic in recomputeFunding expects that the skew has not changed since the last time it was called which is respected in the current codebase.
However, it is also assumed that the skewScale has not been changed and therefore setting it in between will result in inaccurate funding numbers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑dependency flaw in the market funding logic. When the market configuration function setMarketConfigurationById is used to modify the parameter known as skewScale, the next call to recomputeFunding produces incorrect funding numbers. The root cause is that recomputeFunding is written with the implicit assumption that both the market skew and the skewScale remain unchanged between successive invocations. While the code enforces the unchanged skew, it does not enforce or account for a change in skewScale. Consequently, if an administrator or any caller updates skewScale between funding periods without first invoking recomputeFunding, the funding algorithm will use a stale skew value together with a new skewScale, breaking the mathematical relationship that determines funding rates. An attacker who can call setMarketConfigurationById could deliberately alter skewScale after a funding round, causing the subsequent funding distribution to be either inflated or deflated. This can be exploited to siphon excess funding, deprive honest participants of their expected rewards, or create market imbalances that affect price stability. The impact is that traders, liquidity providers, or any users relying on the funding mechanism may receive payouts that do not reflect the true market state; balances may appear lower or higher than expected, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are violated. The condition for the bug to manifest is any sequence where setMarketConfigurationById is executed after a funding period and before the next recomputeFunding, without an intervening recomputeFunding call. The affected parties are the market contract itself, its participants, and any downstream systems that assume correct funding calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the documentation of recomputeFunding mentions an invariant about unchanged skew but makes no mention of skewScale, leading to a logical inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the funding numbers may still look plausible; there is no explicit revert or error, so the discrepancy can go unnoticed until users compare expected versus actual payouts. To remediate, the simplest conceptual fix is to invoke recomputeFunding at the beginning of setMarketConfigurationById, ensuring that the funding state is refreshed before any configuration change. A more robust solution would be to redesign recomputeFunding so that it does not rely on the skewScale remaining constant, or to add explicit checks that prevent skewScale updates without a prior recomputeFunding. This class of bug falls under invariant‑violation or state‑dependent calculation errors, where a function assumes hidden state immutability that the surrounding system can violate. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a mismatch between expected funding (e.g., “I should receive a reward based on my position”) and the actual amount received (e.g., “my balance stayed the same or dropped unexpectedly”). The expectation that funding reflects the current market skew is broken, leading to potential loss of funds or unfair advantage.

title: M-18 | Utilization Fees Are Not Accurate To Liquidity Updates
description:
The utilization fees in the BFP market are dependent on the amount of credit capacity delegated to the market by the V3 core system, however the utilization rate does not update when the amount of backing liquidity changes.
For instance, a delegator can undelegate from a vault which provides credit capacity to the BFP market and increase the utilization ratio. However this utilization update is not reflected in the utilization rate until a recomputeUtilization is triggered on the BFP side.
Therefore the utilization fees that are charged can be misrepresentative of the actual amount of liquidity utilized during these periods before a utilization recompilation is triggered.
A malicious LP could abuse this by minting sUSD directly before a utilization update in the BFP market, this way increasing the utilization ratio and forcing the the utilization fees for all traders to be higher over the next period. The LP may then backrun the utilization update and burn their sUSD that was minted.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a stale utilization fee calculation in the BFP market that does not automatically reflect changes in the amount of credit capacity delegated by the V3 core system. The root cause is that the contract relies on an explicit recomputeUtilization call to update the utilization rate, and no callback or automatic trigger is executed when liquidity is added or removed. Consequently, when a delegator undelegates from a vault, the backing liquidity decreases, the true utilization ratio rises, but the on‑chain utilization variable remains unchanged until a manual recompute is performed. An attacker can exploit this timing gap by minting sUSD just before the utilization update, artificially inflating the apparent utilization ratio and causing the protocol to charge higher utilization fees to all traders during the interim period. After the higher fees have been collected, the attacker can back‑run the recomputeUtilization transaction, burn the freshly minted sUSD, and keep the excess fees as profit. The impact is that traders are overcharged for borrowing, receiving fees that are higher than the economic reality, which erodes trust and can lead to financial loss for users while benefitting a malicious liquidity provider. This condition occurs whenever credit capacity changes without an immediate utilization recompute, which can happen frequently in markets that allow dynamic delegation. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Guardian, who noted the logical flaw that the fee‑related state is not kept in sync with liquidity updates. The bug is hard to notice because the UI may display the nominal utilization rate, and the fee calculation appears to work, yet the underlying metric used for fee computation is outdated, leading to a discrepancy that only becomes visible after the manual recompute. The problem belongs to the class of state‑synchronization or stale‑data bugs, where a financial parameter is derived from an outdated variable, violating the accounting assumption that fees should be proportional to actual utilization. From a user’s perspective, a trader may expect to pay a certain fee based on current market usage but instead sees an unexpectedly high charge, or may notice that their balance is reduced more than anticipated without a clear explanation. To remediate the issue, the protocol should implement automatic callbacks or hooks that update the utilization rate immediately upon any change in credit capacity, or otherwise restrict the mintUsd function so that liquidity providers cannot profit from timing the utilization recompute. Ensuring that the utilization fee calculation always reflects the current liquidity state will restore correct fee accounting and prevent malicious fee inflation.

title: M-19 | Debt Is Not Reflected In CreditCapacity Until Repaid
description:
In the payDebt function users may pay their existing debt with sUSD from outside of the BFP market system. This sUSD is deposited for the market with the depositMarketUsd function on the Synthetix V3 core system.
The depositMarketUsd function will increase the creditCapacity of the market by the repaid amount.
This net increase in the market’s creditCapacity counts towards the minimumCredit validation for the market, however it is not added until the trader repays their debt.
Regardless of when the trader pays their debt the LPs receive the value lost by the trader as a delta reduction in their debt. This debt reduction may not be fully utilizable by the LPs until the trader’s debt is repaid as the minimumCredit validation would fail because the debt has not been added to the market’s creditCapacity.
Trader’s can therefore unjustly lock a portion of the LPs rightful gains until their debt is repaid.
Notice that this will only occur when a market’s creditCapacity is close to the minimumCredit and will not always have a noticeable locking effect on the LPs gains.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a credit‑capacity accounting mismatch that occurs in the payDebt workflow of the BFP market. When a trader repays outstanding debt using sUSD that is deposited through the core Synthetix V3 depositMarketUsd function, the deposit instantly increases the market’s creditCapacity. However, the protocol’s minimumCredit validation, which governs whether liquidity providers (LPs) can mint new positions, does not consider the reduction of the trader’s debt until the repayment transaction is fully processed. As a result, the market’s creditCapacity appears higher, but the corresponding debt reduction is not reflected in the minimumCredit check, causing the validation to fail. This timing gap means that LPs experience a delta reduction in their own debt that they cannot immediately utilise; their ability to mint additional liquidity or claim realized gains is effectively locked until the trader’s debt is officially cleared. The impact is most noticeable when the market’s creditCapacity is close to the required minimumCredit threshold, at which point LPs may see their expected gains disappear or their minting transactions rejected despite the market having received additional collateral. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the market’s accounting logic, where the relationship between depositMarketUsd, creditCapacity, and minimumCredit was examined. It can be hard to notice because the locking effect only manifests under specific boundary conditions and does not always produce an obvious error; the protocol continues to operate, but LPs receive less than expected. From a user perspective, an LP might observe that after a trader pays back debt, the UI still shows insufficient credit to mint, or that their accrued rewards remain stagnant, contrary to the expectation that the repayment should unlock additional capacity. The root cause is the delayed inclusion of debt repayment in the creditCapacity calculation used for minimumCredit validation. To remediate the issue, the protocol should offset the timing mismatch by adjusting the minimumCredit requirement to subtract any outstanding debt that has not yet been accounted for, allowing LPs to utilise the realized debt reduction immediately. This conceptual fix aligns the accounting of creditCapacity with the actual debt state, preventing unjust locking of LP gains and preserving the intended economic incentives of the market.

title: M-20 | Liquidation Prevented By Zero Vault Delegation
description:
When a PerpRewardDistributor is deployed it is assigned a list of poolCollateralTypes which it distributes rewards to. In the liquidateCollateral function, the BFP market distributes liquidated collateral to each poolCollateralType in the backing pool according to the value of collateral in each corresponding vault.
However if one of the vaults holds zero collateral then the distributeRewards call will attempt to distribute 0 rewards to 0 vault shares. This action reverts in the RewardDistribution.distribute function, where the totalSharesD18 value is validated to be nonzero.
As a result liquidation flagging or liquidation by margin only where the account holds the collateral token which would be distributed to the empty vault will be DoS'd.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/synthetix-pocs/pull/8
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs during the liquidation of collateral when the reward distribution logic attempts to allocate rewards to a vault that holds zero collateral. The root cause is that the PerpRewardDistributor’s liquidateCollateral function iterates over a list of poolCollateralTypes and calls RewardDistribution.distribute for each vault. The distribute function validates that the totalSharesD18 value – representing the amount of vault shares that should receive rewards – is non‑zero. When a vault’s collateral balance is zero, the calculated reward amount is also zero, leading to a call with totalSharesD18 equal to zero. This triggers a revert in the distribute function, aborting the entire liquidation transaction. An attacker or any user can exploit this by triggering liquidation on an account that holds the collateral type associated with the empty vault. Because the liquidation transaction reverts, the under‑collateralised position remains un‑liquidated, leaving the protocol exposed to further loss and effectively blocking the liquidation mechanism for that collateral. The impact is a denial of service on the liquidation pathway: users expecting their positions to be liquidated see the transaction fail, their collateral remains locked, and the protocol may accumulate unsafe debt. The condition occurs only when at least one vault in the backing pool has a zero collateral balance at the moment liquidation is attempted. All users who rely on the liquidation process – especially those holding the affected collateral – are affected, as are the protocol’s risk management and overall solvency. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the reward distribution and liquidation code paths, where the auditors observed that the reward distribution contract enforces a non‑zero share check and that this check could be hit by a zero‑balance vault. It is hard to notice because normal operation rarely involves empty vaults, and the revert only manifests during liquidation, a less frequently exercised path. To remediate, the liquidation logic should include a guard that skips any vault for which the reward amount or the vault’s share balance is zero, thereby avoiding the call that would revert. Conceptually, this is a “zero‑share reward distribution” bug, a subclass of arithmetic‑or‑state‑validation errors where a function assumes a positive divisor or share count. From a user’s perspective, a liquidation transaction that should reduce debt and return collateral instead fails with no visible reward, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and possibly showing an error like “execution reverted”. The expectation that liquidation will succeed is violated, resulting in a situation where funds appear to disappear from the protocol’s risk engine while the user sees no change to their position. The fix restores the intended business logic that liquidation proceeds even when some reward destinations are empty, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants.

title: Transfer Amount enforcer for ERC20 and Native transfers increase spend limit without checking actual transfers
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑tracking flaw in the Transfer Amount enforcer used for ERC20 and native token delegations. The enforcer records the amount a delegate has spent by incrementing a spent counter in its beforeHook, i.e. before the actual token transfer is executed. When a delegation is executed with the EXECTYPE_TRY mode, a failing token transfer does not revert the whole call; execution continues, but the spent counter has already been increased. Consequently a malicious delegate can repeatedly invoke transfers that are deliberately made to fail (for example by halting the token contract) and each attempt will consume part of the delegator’s predefined spending limit even though no tokens move. The impact is that the delegator’s allowance can be exhausted without any token movement, leading to a situation where subsequent legitimate transfers are rejected because the allowance appears spent, while the delegator’s balances remain unchanged. This occurs only when the enforcer is used together with the try execution type and the beforeHook performs the accounting. The affected parties are delegators who rely on the enforcer to enforce spend limits, their delegates, and any users of the protocol that assume allowances reflect actual token transfers. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised both successful and failing transfer scenarios and observed that the spentMap value grew even when the token transfer reverted silently. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an error on failed transfers in try mode, and the allowance consumption appears correct from a contract‑state perspective, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The flaw belongs to the class of accounting or state‑tracking bugs where state is updated before an external call without verifying the call’s success. From a user’s point of view the UI may show that the allowance is depleted while the token balance has not changed, leading to confusion such as “my funds disappeared” or “my transfer limit is zero even though I didn’t send anything”. To remediate the issue the spend accounting should be moved to an afterHook that compares the pre‑execution and post‑execution balances and only increments the spent counter when the transfer actually succeeds, or the enforcer should be restricted to the default execution mode where failed calls revert and the allowance is not incorrectly updated.

title: Gas griefing via duplicate entries in `Allowed` class of enforcers
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑griefing issue that stems from the way the AllowedMethodsEnforcer and AllowedTargetsEnforcer contracts process the list of permitted method selectors or target addresses supplied in a delegation. These contracts read the raw bytes supplied as terms, split them into fixed‑size entries and then perform a linear search over the resulting array to check whether a requested call matches an allowed entry. Because the contracts never enforce that the entries are unique or sorted, an attacker who can control the terms data can deliberately insert a large number of duplicate selectors or addresses. The duplicate entries do not change the logical permission – the same method is still allowed – but they inflate the length of the array, causing the linear search loop to iterate many more times. Each additional iteration consumes gas, so a delegation that contains hundreds of identical entries can increase gas consumption by several hundred thousand units, as demonstrated by a test where 100 duplicate method signatures raised gas usage from roughly 50 k to 155 k. This inflated cost is paid by the delegator or the end‑user who triggers the delegation, effectively making the operation expensive or even causing it to run out of gas, which constitutes a denial‑of‑service style attack. The problem appears only when the enforcer’s beforeHook is executed, i.e., whenever a delegation with a caveat that references these enforcers is redeemed. Users of the framework, protocol developers and anyone relying on the delegation mechanism are affected because they may see unexpectedly high gas fees, transactions that revert due to out‑of‑gas, or a sudden drop in available funds after a seemingly normal operation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case creating terms with many duplicate entries and observed the gas spike. It is hard to notice because the functional outcome – the method is still allowed – remains correct, and the duplicate data does not raise any explicit error. To remediate the problem, the contract should validate the uniqueness of each entry, for example by requiring the list to be strictly increasing (which implicitly forbids duplicates) or by sorting the array and performing a binary search, or by using a mapping for constant‑time look‑ups. Enforcing uniqueness eliminates the ability to inflate the array size and therefore prevents the gas‑griefing attack, restoring the expected low‑cost behavior of delegations.

title: M-01 | NoToken Cap May Be Exceeded During Minting
description:
The mint function enforces the yesNoTokenCap, but it only checks the supply of Yes tokens.
This creates a potential issue where the supply of No tokens can exceed the cap if there is an
imbalance between the total supply of Yes and No tokens.
This imbalance can occur because Yes tokens can be burned (since YesNoToken is an
ERC20Burnable contract).
For example:
• yesNoTokenCap = 100
• Initial supply: Yes = 90, No = 90
• A user burns 10 Yes tokens, reducing the Yes supply to 80.
• The same user mints 20 Yes tokens, bringing the Yes supply back to 100.
• The final supply becomes: Yes = 100, No = 110, exceeding the cap.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect cap enforcement in a dual‑token minting contract where a single maximum supply (yesNoTokenCap) is intended to limit the combined amount of Yes and No tokens. The root cause is that the mint function validates the cap only against the current Yes token supply, ignoring the No token balance. Because the Yes token is burnable, a user can reduce the Yes supply below the cap, then mint additional Yes tokens up to the cap while the No token supply remains unchanged. This sequence results in a total token supply that exceeds the intended maximum. An attacker can exploit this by first burning a portion of Yes tokens, thereby creating headroom, and then calling the mint function to restore Yes tokens to the cap; the No tokens, which were never reduced, cause the overall supply to surpass the cap. The impact is inflation of the No token side, breaking the economic assumptions of a fixed‑supply market, potentially allowing extra No tokens to be transferred or sold, diluting value for holders and undermining trust in the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the contract permits burning of Yes tokens and the mint logic checks only the Yes supply during each mint operation. All token holders and the protocol itself are affected because the total supply no longer matches the documented limit, leading to accounting mismatches and possible regulatory concerns. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the cap check referenced only the Yes token variable and did not consider the No token balance. It can be hard to notice because user interfaces often display the Yes supply at the cap, giving the impression that the limit is respected, while the hidden No supply silently exceeds the cap. To remediate, the mint function should enforce the cap on the aggregate supply of both token types, or maintain separate caps for each, ensuring that any minting operation validates that the sum of Yes and No tokens does not surpass yesNoTokenCap. From a user perspective, the symptom is that after minting, the expected total token count is higher than advertised; users may see their Yes balance reach the maximum while the overall market shows more tokens than should exist, leading to confusion such as “my refund is zero” or “my balance is unexpectedly high”. This class of bug falls under improper supply constraint enforcement and can be described as a cap‑validation flaw that allows token inflation through asymmetric burn‑mint cycles.

title: M-02 | Council Members Cannot Set Challenge Period
description:
Inside TruthMarketManagerV2, several functions are available to manage the market's configuration
that can be called by the oracle council, such as setYesNoTokenCap, setEndOfTrading,
setFirstChallengePeriod, and setSecondChallengePeriod.
While setYesNoTokenCap and setEndOfTrading are currently available in the OracleCouncilV2
contract, setFirstChallengePeriod and setSecondChallengePeriod are not implemented, preventing
council members from configuring those market settings.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing administrative functions that prevent members of the Oracle Council from configuring the challenge periods of a market. In the TruthMarketManagerV2 contract the market owner can normally adjust parameters such as the token cap, the end of trading, and two distinct challenge windows – the first and second challenge periods. While the token‑cap and trading‑end setters are exposed through the OracleCouncilV2 contract, the setters for the first and second challenge periods are absent from that contract. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended interface of the council and the actual implementation: the OracleCouncilV2 contract does not implement or forward setFirstChallengePeriod and setSecondChallengePeriod calls to the market manager. As a result, when a council member attempts to invoke these functions, the transaction either reverts due to an undefined selector or silently does nothing because the function does not exist. This can be exploited indirectly: without a configurable challenge window the market may default to a zero‑length period or remain at an insecure preset, allowing disputes to be bypassed and outcomes to be finalized without any opportunity for participants to challenge them. The impact is that users expecting a reasonable time to contest market results receive none, potentially leading to incorrect settlements, loss of funds, or manipulation of the market outcome. The condition occurs whenever the governance process reaches the stage where the council should set the challenge periods – typically after market creation but before trading ends. All council members, market participants, and the broader protocol are affected because the economic guarantees of the market rely on those challenge periods being enforceable. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s public interface, where the auditor compared the functions listed in the specification with those actually present in OracleCouncilV2. It is easy to miss because the contract still compiles and the missing functions do not generate immediate errors; only a functional test or a UI that attempts to call the setters would reveal the problem. To remediate, the OracleCouncilV2 contract should be extended to include setFirstChallengePeriod and setSecondChallengePeriod functions that enforce the council’s access control and forward the new period values to TruthMarketManagerV2, with appropriate validation of the input values. This aligns the implementation with the intended governance model and restores the ability for participants to rely on a proper challenge window, preventing the market from finalising without dispute opportunities.

title: M-03 | Possible DOS In _getTotalOpenDisputes
description:
The _getTotalOpenDisputes function is used by the addOracleCouncilMember and
removeOracleCouncilMember functions in the OracleCouncil contract.
This function calculates the total open disputes by looping through all active markets and checking
if each market is in the DisputeRaised status and has any open disputes. The issue is that
_activeMarkets does not have a cap, meaning it could grow indefinitely.
As a result, the gas costs for calling _getTotalOpenDisputes can become excessively high,
potentially exceeding the block gas limit and causing the transaction to fail.
This could effectively lock the addOracleCouncilMember and removeOracleCouncilMember
functions, preventing them from being executed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an unbounded iteration in the private helper function that counts open disputes. The function walks through the contract's internal list of active markets and checks each market's status, adding to a counter when a market is in a disputed state. Because the list of active markets (_activeMarkets) has no maximum size, it can grow without limit as the protocol creates new markets. When the list becomes large, the gas required to iterate over every entry can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction that calls the helper to run out of gas and revert. This helper is invoked by the public functions that add or remove members of the oracle council, so any call to change council membership may fail with an out‑of‑gas error. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts, the UI shows a generic out‑of‑gas or “transaction failed” message, and the expected change – a new council member being added or an existing one being removed – never happens. The impact is that the governance mechanism for updating the oracle council can be effectively locked, preventing protocol upgrades or dispute resolution adjustments that rely on council composition. The issue appears only when the number of active markets reaches a size where the gas cost of the loop exceeds the block limit; in normal operation with few markets the functions work as intended, making the problem easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the gas profile of the council‑management functions and noted the lack of a cap on the market array. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded‑loop or gas‑limit DoS vulnerabilities, where a contract’s logic iterates over a dynamic data structure without safeguards. To remediate the issue the contract should either enforce a maximum length on the active‑market list, prune markets that are finalized, or redesign the dispute‑counting logic to avoid full iteration – for example by maintaining a separate counter that is updated when disputes are opened or closed, or by using a mapping that can be queried in constant time. Such a fix restores the ability of users to add or remove council members without risking transaction failure, aligning the contract’s behavior with the expectation that governance actions are always executable.

title: M-04 | Owner Cannot Trigger disputeMarket
description:
Many operations inside TruthMarketManagerV2 that change the market state can be manually
triggered by the owner. This is needed in cases where markets are paused, as only the owner can
initiate market state transitions, including disputeMarket.
However, disputeMarket uses the onlyOracleCouncil modifier, which restricts the function to being
called only by the oracle council. This is despite the function logic including a check allowing the
owner to trigger disputeMarket when markets are paused.
As a result, disputeMarket cannot be manually called by the owner when markets are paused.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control mismatch in the TruthMarketManagerV2 contract that prevents the contract owner from invoking the disputeMarket function when a market is paused. The function’s internal logic contains a condition that permits the owner to trigger a dispute during a paused state, but the function is protected by the onlyOracleCouncil modifier, which restricts calls exclusively to members of the oracle council. Because Solidity modifiers are evaluated before the function body, the owner’s call is rejected by the modifier even though the body would otherwise allow it. This discrepancy occurs only when the market is in a paused state; under normal operation the oracle council can still call disputeMarket, but the owner loses the ability to resolve disputes during pauses. As a result, markets can become permanently stuck in a paused state, preventing the resolution of disputes, the distribution of payouts, or the release of locked funds. Users experience symptoms such as missing refunds, balances that never change, or markets that appear frozen in the UI. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s access modifiers with its internal permission checks. It can be hard to notice because the source code shows an explicit owner check inside the function, giving the impression that the owner has authority, while the surrounding modifier silently overrides that permission. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect access control” or “modifier‑logic inconsistency” vulnerabilities, where the declared access rights do not match the intended business logic. To remediate, the contract should replace the onlyOracleCouncil modifier with a combined onlyOracleCouncilAndOwner modifier (or adjust the existing modifier) so that both the oracle council and the owner are authorized to call disputeMarket when required, thereby aligning the access control with the intended dispute resolution flow.

title: M-05 | Inefficient Distribution In StakingRewards
description:
If stake is not called in the same block of notifyRewardAmount, depending on delay, a portion of
rewards will remain unused inside the contract.
For example, at time X rewards are transferred into the contract. Then some time Y has passed
before the first user stakes. However, the reward period will end at X + rewardsDuration not X + Y +
rewardsDuration.
Therefore, the rewards for Y * rewardRate will remain un-distributed till the next cycle. If a new
reward cycle is never started (e.g. final cycle), then any undistributed amount will remain inside the
contract.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/truth-markets-1/pull/2/files
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inefficient reward distribution flaw in a staking rewards contract. The contract records the start of a reward period when the owner calls notifyRewardAmount and immediately computes a periodFinish timestamp based on the configured rewardsDuration. If no user stakes in the same block, or if there is a delay before the first stake, the elapsed time between the reward funding (time X) and the first stake (time Y) is not accounted for in the reward allocation. As a result, the amount equal to Y multiplied by the rewardRate remains un‑distributed and stays locked inside the contract until the next reward cycle is started. When the final reward cycle ends without a subsequent notifyRewardAmount call, any leftover tokens are permanently trapped in the contract.
