The root cause is the assumption that staking activity begins at the moment rewards are transferred, while the contract’s accounting logic ties the reward period to the notification timestamp regardless of actual deposits. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger the condition simply by waiting before staking, causing the contract to consume part of the reward window without any participants earning rewards. The impact is that stakers receive less than the advertised return, the protocol’s APR appears inflated, and users may see their earned balance remain unchanged or receive zero rewards despite having a stake. From a user perspective the UI may show a reward rate but the earned amount stays at zero, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the timing relationship between notifyRewardAmount and the first stake. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the tokens simply sit idle, making the problem appear as a normal state. To remediate, the contract should defer setting periodFinish until the first stake occurs when total deposits are zero, or otherwise recalculate the rewardRate based on the actual start of staking activity, ensuring that the full reward amount is available for distribution over the intended duration.

title: M-06 | Invalid Outcome Voting In voteForDispute
description:
Council members can cast votes referencing an invalid _winningPosition, one not recognized by the
market. If enough votes align on this invalid outcome, the dispute remains unresolvable.
Consequently, it remains open indefinitely, blocking certain system actions (e.g., adding or removing
council members) which require all disputes to be closed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the dispute voting mechanism of the market contract, specifically the function that records a council member’s vote for a winning position (voteForDispute). The function accepts a parameter representing the alleged winning position (_winningPosition) but does not verify that this value corresponds to a valid outcome defined by the market. Because the market defines a finite set of possible positions – enumerated from 1 up to the value returned by ITruthMarket(_market).positionCount() – any integer outside this range is technically invalid. The missing validation allows a council member, either maliciously or inadvertently, to submit a vote that references a non‑existent outcome. If a sufficient number of council members cast votes for the same invalid outcome, the dispute resolution logic interprets the aligned votes as a consensus and marks the dispute as unresolved rather than closed. Consequently, the dispute remains in an open state indefinitely. This state blocks any protocol actions that require all disputes to be settled, such as adding or removing council members, updating governance parameters, or performing upgrades that depend on a clean dispute ledger. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a dispute that never resolves, and attempts to change council composition fail with generic errors like “cannot add council member, an open dispute exists.” Users expect the dispute to close after voting, but instead the system appears stuck, effectively freezing governance functions and potentially locking funds that depend on dispute resolution. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the voteForDispute entry point and noticed the absence of a range check on the _winningPosition argument. It is subtle because the function compiles and runs without reverting, and the problem only manifests after a coordinated set of votes, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation failures where unchecked enum or index values lead to inconsistent contract state. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict validation of the _winningPosition argument, reverting any call where the supplied value is less than 1 or greater than the market’s positionCount. This ensures that only legitimate outcomes can be voted on, preventing the dispute from entering an unresolvable state and restoring the expected governance flow.

title: M-07 | OracleBonds Address Change Mishandles Funds
description:
The setOracleBonds function in the TruthMarketManager contract allows the owner to change the
oracleBonds address. The problem is that the oracleBonds address is hardcoded into markets when
they are created.
If the address is updated in the TruthMarketManager contract, active markets not yet finalized will
send and account for resolve, dispute, and escalate bonds to the new address.
However, when issuing them back, the old address in the market contract will be used, which will not
have the funds or have them accounted for, leading to users losing those funds.
Furthermore, any unclaimed dispute bonds will also be unclaimable because the OracleCouncil
contract will fetch the new address from the TruthMarketManager contract, while these dispute
bonds are stored in and accounted for in the old contract.
bug_full: The vulnerabilityoriginates from the ability of the contract owner to call setOracleBonds on the TruthMarketManager contract and replace the address of the OracleBonds contract after markets have already been created. When a market is instantiated, the address of the OracleBonds contract is stored directly in the market’s state and is later used as the destination for returning resolve, dispute and escalation bonds. Because the stored address is immutable for that market, changing the OracleBonds address in the manager does not automatically update the reference inside each active market. Consequently, if the owner updates the address while there are still markets that have not been finalized, any bond that is supposed to be returned to a user is sent to the new OracleBonds contract, while the market contract still attempts to pull the funds from the old address. The old contract either holds no balance or does not account for the incoming funds, so the user receives nothing and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent. The same mismatch also affects unclaimed dispute bonds: the OracleCouncil reads the current OracleBonds address from the manager, which now points to the new contract, but the disputed bonds are still recorded in the old contract, making them permanently unclaimable. This issue manifests only when the address change occurs before all active markets are settled, which is a subtle condition that can be overlooked during routine upgrades. Users experience symptoms such as receiving a zero refund for a bond they expected back, seeing their balance unchanged after a dispute resolution, or finding that previously claimable dispute rewards are missing. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of market contracts and the handling of external contract references. It is difficult to notice because the address change function appears harmless and does not emit explicit warnings about pending markets, allowing the loss of funds to occur silently. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or reference‑mismatch vulnerabilities, where mutable configuration data is changed without synchronising dependent contracts. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid changing the OracleBonds address while any market remains open, or implement a migration routine that safely transfers existing bond balances and updates all market references before the address is altered. Additionally, any pending dispute bonds must be manually reclaimed or migrated to ensure users can still claim their rewards. In short, the root cause is the hard‑coded OracleBonds address in each market combined with an unrestricted address‑update function, leading to lost or unclaimable funds when the address is changed prematurely.

title: M-08 | Lacking Incentives For The Escalator
description:
Currently, if the escalator is correct, the reward is sent to either the resolver or the disputor. This
assumes that the escalator is also the resolver or disputor.
However, considering that the escalator requires a larger bond, it’s possible that the resolver or
disputor does not have the required bond, and another party could step in and become the escalator.
This third party should be able to receive the reward independently for a correct escalation.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward distribution logic for a dispute escalation mechanism. When a participant correctly escalates a dispute, the contract currently sends the reward only to the party that acted as the resolver or the disputor, based on the assumption that the escalator is also one of those roles. In practice, the escalator must post a larger bond than a normal resolver or disputor, which means a third‑party actor who is not the resolver or disputor may be the only entity capable of performing a correct escalation. Because the reward is not allocated to this third‑party escalator, the escalator receives no compensation for its correct action. The root cause is a missing incentive clause in the reward‑splitting logic: the contract does not recognise the escalator as a distinct beneficiary when the escalation succeeds. An attacker or rational participant can exploit this by refusing to act as an escalator, knowing that no reward will be granted, thereby preventing legitimate escalations and potentially allowing incorrect dispute outcomes to persist. The impact is a reduction in the economic incentive for participants to provide the higher bond required for escalation, which can lead to stalled dispute resolution, loss of confidence in the protocol, and possible financial loss for users whose disputes remain unresolved. This condition occurs whenever a dispute is escalated and the escalator is not also the resolver or disputor, i.e., when a separate party with the required bond steps in. All users of the dispute system, including token holders and market participants, are affected because the correctness of dispute outcomes may be compromised. The issue was identified during a systematic security audit that examined the reward flow and noticed that the escalator address was never referenced in the reward calculation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still transfers a reward, just to the wrong party, and the UI may not display any error, making the problem appear as a silent loss of incentive. To fix the issue, the reward logic should be amended to recognise a successful escalation as a distinct event and split the reward between the resolver/disputor and the escalator, or allocate the full reward to the escalator when it is a separate entity. This aligns the economic model with the intended security guarantees, ensuring that participants who provide the higher bond are properly compensated and that the escalation mechanism remains functional.

title: M-09 | Disputer Cannot Re-Dispute After Reset
description:
When a market is reset following multiple active disputes, a user whose dispute is still considered
“open” cannot reclaim their bond because the system only allows bond retrieval after the market is
finalized.
As a result, that user remains in a state with an unclaimed (open) dispute bond, which prevents them
from initiating a new dispute on a subsequent outcome proposal. This essentially locks them out of
further participation in the dispute process for that market.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of dispute bonds when a market undergoes a reset while one or more disputes remain open. In the affected system a bond that a participant posts to initiate a dispute is designed to be refundable only after the market reaches a finalized state. When the market is reset – a state that clears previous outcomes and prepares for a new round – the contract does not provide a path for users to retrieve or reuse the bond associated with an open dispute. Consequently the participant’s bond stays locked in an “open” status, the contract treats it as still tied to a dispute that can never be resolved because the market is no longer in the original dispute lifecycle. This situation prevents the user from reclaiming the locked funds and also blocks the user from creating a new dispute on any subsequent outcome proposal, effectively excluding them from further participation in the market’s dispute process. The root cause is a logical flaw in the state transition logic: the reset transition does not reset or release dispute‑related accounting, and the bond‑withdrawal function checks only for a finalized market flag. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the issue manifests automatically for any participant who has an active dispute at the moment the market is reset, which may happen due to governance actions, oracle failures, or timed market cycles. The impact is a loss of liquidity for the affected user, potential erosion of trust in the dispute mechanism, and a reduction in the overall robustness of the market because participants cannot reliably re‑engage after a reset. The condition occurs whenever a market moves from an “active dispute” state directly to a “reset” state without first finalizing the dispute. All users who have posted bonds for disputes are affected, as are the protocol designers who rely on the assumption that bonds are always recoverable after a dispute concludes. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the market lifecycle functions, where the auditor observed that the bond‑withdrawal path was gated by a finalization flag that never becomes true after a reset. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the transaction simply leaves the bond in storage and later calls to dispute again fail with generic “cannot dispute” messages, giving the impression of a generic contract bug rather than a systematic accounting flaw. To remediate, the contract should either (a) automatically release or migrate any open dispute bonds when a market reset occurs, or (b) allow users to explicitly claim their bond after a reset, treating the reset as a termination of the dispute. This change restores the expected behavior that a participant’s funds are either returned or made reusable, aligning the implementation with the business logic that bonds are a temporary security deposit, not a permanent lock. The bug belongs to the class of state‑transition accounting errors where resources are not correctly reconciled during lifecycle changes, similar to “resource leakage after contract upgrade” or “funds stuck after state reset”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a market reset the UI shows the dispute still listed, the user’s balance appears unchanged, and attempts to start a new dispute result in a silent failure or a generic error, leading the user to see “my bond is missing” or “I cannot dispute again”. The expectation that the bond will be returned or that a new dispute can be opened is violated, causing confusion and potential financial loss.

title: M-10 | DoS In Dispute Process USDC Is Paused
description:
The market’s dispute and escalation mechanisms rely on the ability to deposit bonds in USDC. If
USDC—being a pausable token—is paused, no new bonds can be deposited, effectively blocking any
new disputes or escalations.
An attacker can exploit this by proposing a resolution in their favor just before USDC becomes
paused; if the pause period extends past the challenge window, the outcome remains uncontested,
leading to unjust financial gains for the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the market’s dispute and escalation workflow that stems from the use of a pausable stable‑coin (USDC) as the sole payment token for bond deposits. Because the contract requires a USDC transfer to lock a bond before a dispute can be opened or a challenge can be raised, the logic assumes that the token is always transferable. When the USDC contract is paused—either by its owner or through an emergency pause—any call to transfer or transferFrom reverts, causing the bond‑deposit function to fail. As a result, no new disputes can be initiated and existing disputes cannot be challenged during the pause. An attacker can exploit this timing window by submitting a resolution that favours them just before the pause is triggered; the subsequent pause blocks any challenger from posting the required bond, so the resolution remains unchallenged and the attacker receives the disputed funds. The impact is that the protocol’s dispute resolution mechanism is effectively disabled, preventing honest participants from defending their positions and allowing a malicious party to capture funds that would otherwise be contested. This condition occurs whenever the USDC token enters a paused state, which can be temporary or indefinite, and it affects any user who relies on the dispute process, including market makers, traders, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the dispute flow, where the auditor noted that the bond‑deposit call does not check for token pausability and therefore lacks a fallback path. The problem is subtle because the pause does not generate an explicit error in the market contract; it simply propagates the revert from the token, making the failure appear as a generic ‘transfer failed’ without indicating a systemic denial-of-service. To remediate, the contract should detect when the payment token is paused and either extend the dispute and challenge windows until transfers are possible again, or allow an alternative escrow mechanism that does not depend on a single pausable token. In broader terms, this is a class of DoS vulnerability caused by reliance on external token contracts that can be halted, breaking critical protocol invariants such as the ability to post collateral. From a user’s perspective, the UI would show that a dispute cannot be created or a challenge cannot be submitted, often displaying an empty or zero‑balance error, while the user expects their bond to be locked and the dispute to proceed. The mismatch between expected functionality (bond deposited, dispute opened) and reality (transaction reverts, dispute blocked) leads to loss of confidence and potential financial loss.

title: M-11 | Risk Of Re-org Attack
description:
In the case of a block re-org event, disputors may unknowingly have submitted disputes for what
they believe to be the correct result, leading to slashing and the loss of their disputor bonds.
For example, consider the following scenario:
(1) Alice proposes an incorrect resolution.
(2) Bob disputes Alice’s resolution.
(3) A block re-org occurs and Alice’s proposal is replaced with a correct resolution.
(4) Bob’s dispute is invalid and will be punished.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑organization‑sensitive dispute validation flaw. The contract allows a participant to open a dispute without recording the exact state (such as the block number, hash, or result snapshot) that the dispute refers to. Because the contract later re‑evaluates the dispute against the current on‑chain result, a block re‑org that replaces the disputed result with a different one can turn an apparently valid dispute into an invalid one. When this happens the protocol’s slashing logic punishes the disputor by confiscating their bonded stake. The root cause is the reliance on mutable on‑chain state rather than an immutable reference to the disputed position. An attacker, or even natural network conditions, can trigger a re‑org after a dispute is submitted but before the dispute is finalized, causing the disputor’s bond to be slashed despite having acted on the information displayed at the time of submission. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, the UI shows the dispute was accepted, and the user expects the bond to be returned if the dispute is later resolved in their favor. Instead the bond disappears, leading to confusion and loss of funds. The impact includes financial loss for any disputor, reduced confidence in the dispute mechanism, and potential centralisation if participants avoid disputing due to fear of accidental slashing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the dispute workflow and identified that the openDispute function does not capture the exact position being disputed. It can be hard to notice because block re‑orgs are relatively rare and the contract otherwise behaves as intended, so the slashing only occurs in specific edge‑case scenarios. The bug belongs to the class of state‑dependent validation errors where logic depends on mutable blockchain state without anchoring to an immutable snapshot. To remediate, the protocol should require the caller to pass the precise position they wish to dispute (for example, the block number, hash, or result identifier) to the openDispute function, store this reference, and compare the dispute against that immutable snapshot rather than the current state. This change ensures that even if a re‑org occurs, the dispute is evaluated against the original result the user saw, preventing unintended slashing.

title: M-12 | USDC Blacklisted Users Can Freeze Market
description:
If the market is disputed or escalated, it could transfer bonds back to the disputor and escalator if
they are not punished. However, since the paymentToken is USDC, which has a blacklist feature, it is
possible for the disputor or escalator is blacklisted when the market attempts to return the bonds.
This would cause the market state transitions to fail. The same issue could occur when attempting to
send rewards to the resolver or disputor if the reward token also has a blacklist feature.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the market contract’s reliance on a direct (push) transfer of USDC bonds and rewards during dispute resolution and escalation phases. USDC implements a blacklist feature that can prevent transfers to or from addresses flagged as prohibited. When a market enters a disputed or escalated state, the contract attempts to return the bonded USDC to the disputor or escalator and to pay rewards to the resolver. If any of these recipients have been blacklisted, the token transfer reverts, causing the state‑transition function to fail. As a result, the market becomes stuck in its current state, bonds remain locked, and expected rewards are never delivered. This failure occurs only under the specific condition that a blacklisted address participates in the resolution flow, which is why it may remain hidden during normal testing where all participants are unblocked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token handling logic and identified the push‑style transfer pattern as incompatible with tokens that can reject transfers. From a user’s perspective, the contract appears to freeze: a participant who expects to receive their bond back sees no change in balance, the UI may show the market as “disputed” indefinitely, and reward claims return empty or revert. The problem belongs to the broader class of “push‑transfer” bugs where external token restrictions (such as blacklists, pausable flags, or transfer hooks) can break a contract’s state machine. To mitigate the risk, the contract should adopt a pull‑over‑push design, allowing each participant to withdraw their own bonds and rewards after the dispute resolves, or it should verify that the recipient is not blacklisted before attempting a transfer, or replace USDC with a token that does not enforce blacklist restrictions. Implementing these changes restores the expected accounting flow, ensures that funds are not unintentionally frozen, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: M-13 | Market DOS From Direct Reset Or Resolve
description:
A market can be resolved or reset by the owner directly from the TruthMarketManager contract. One
instance where this will be used is, if a market is paused, only the owner can call the reset or resolve
market functions instead of following the general flow through either the OracleCouncil contract or
the Escalation contract.
The issue is that when called directly, the dispute or escalation processes are not fully completed as
they would be in the general flow. In the dispute case, for instance, one issue would be the
marketLastClosedDispute not being updated, meaning the isResolverPunished and
isDisputorPunished flags remain unset, defaulting to false.
Consequently, when the market either resets or finalizes, it will attempt to send funds to the
disputer’s address fetching the address from the unset marketLastClosedDispute. Since this
address is not set, it would return the zero address, leading to a revert and locking up the market.
Furthermore, the marketClosedForDisputes is also not set to true as done in the general flow,
meaning unclaimed disputes for the market will remain locked.
Similarly, in the escalation case, if called directly for either reset or resolve, the lack of updates to
marketToEscalatedDispute will leave multiple variables such as punishment outcomes empty.
This will also cause incorrect outcomes, as the punishment outcomes will all default to false and
possibly other issues.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/truth-markets-2/blob/3564c644d4a874d187adfbe6d748156bd0abcfdd/test/Guardian/poc_direct_resolve.t.sol#L347
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a privileged function in the market manager contract thatallows the contract owner to reset or resolve a market directly, bypassing the normal dispute and escalation workflow that is normally mediated by the OracleCouncil or Escalation contracts. Because the direct path does not execute the full dispute or escalation logic, several critical state variables remain unchanged. In the dispute scenario the marketLastClosedDispute field is never updated, so the flags that indicate whether the resolver or the disputor has been punished stay at their default false value. When the market is later finalized the contract attempts to transfer the disputor’s reward using the address stored in marketLastClosedDispute; because this address is still zero, the transfer call reverts, causing the market to become permanently locked and user funds to remain inaccessible. Additionally, the marketClosedForDisputes flag is never set, meaning that any pending disputes stay in an unresolved state. In the escalation path the marketToEscalatedDispute mapping is not populated, leaving punishment outcome variables empty and defaulting to false, which can produce incorrect or missing penalty assignments. The issue manifests whenever the owner invokes resetMarket or resolveMarket on a paused market, a situation that may arise during emergency maintenance or manual intervention. All participants who have placed stakes, submitted disputes, or are awaiting payouts are affected because their expected refunds or rewards are never delivered; from a user’s perspective the UI may show the market as closed but the balance shown for the user remains unchanged or appears as zero, and attempts to claim rewards fail with a transaction revert. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by the Guardian team, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test that triggers the direct call and observes the revert. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit a specific error indicating a missing address; instead the transaction simply fails, making it easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate the issue the contract should either forbid direct owner resets/resolves on markets that have active disputes or escalations, or it must replicate the full dispute and escalation finalisation steps within the privileged functions so that all relevant state variables (marketLastClosedDispute, punishment flags, marketClosedForDisputes, marketToEscalatedDispute, etc.) are correctly populated before any fund transfers occur. This ensures that reward distribution proceeds to the correct address and that the market can be safely closed without locking user funds.

title: Native token prizes cannot be funded due to missing `receive()` function
description:
SpinGame supports multiple prize types, including ERC721, ERC20, and native tokens, where native tokens are represented as `prize.tokenAddress = address(0)`.

To ensure that prizes can be successfully claimed, the protocol team is responsible for maintaining a sufficient token balance in the contract by transferring the necessary assets to the Spin contract.

However, there is an issue specifically with native token prizes: the Spin contract does not have a `receive()` or `fallback()` function, and none of its functions are `payable`. This means there is no way for the team to fund the contract with native tokens using a standard transfer, preventing users from successfully claiming native token prizes.

Native token prizes cannot be claimed because there is no mechanism to deposit native tokens into the contract. The only way to provide a native token balance would involve esoteric workarounds, such as self-destructing a contract that sends funds to the Spin contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing native‑token reception mechanism in the SpinGame contract. The contract is designed to award prizes that can be ERC721, ERC20, or native Ether, with native prizes identified by a token address of zero. However, the contract does not implement a receive() or fallback() function, and none of its external functions are marked payable. Because of this omission, the contract cannot accept Ether sent via a plain transfer or a low‑level call with value. The root cause is the absence of a payable entry point that would allow the protocol team to fund the contract with native tokens. As a result, when the team attempts to deposit Ether to back a native‑token prize, the transaction reverts or returns false, leaving the contract balance at zero. Users who see a native‑token prize in the UI expect to claim a certain amount of Ether, but the claim transaction either fails silently or returns no funds, creating a mismatch between expectation and reality. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for native‑token prizes: the prize cannot be funded, users cannot receive the advertised Ether, and the protocol’s incentive model is broken. This condition occurs whenever a native‑token prize is created or when the contract is expected to hold Ether for future claims. All participants—prize claimants, the protocol operators, and any downstream applications that rely on the prize distribution—are affected because the promised reward cannot be delivered. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors added a test that attempted to send Ether to the contract using a low‑level call; the call returned false, confirming that no payable fallback existed. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract functions correctly for ERC20 and ERC721 prizes, so the missing Ether handling may be overlooked if only token‑based prizes are exercised. To remediate, the contract should include a receive() external payable function (or a payable fallback) that simply accepts incoming Ether, allowing the team to fund the contract with native tokens and enabling users to claim their Ether prizes as intended. This change restores the contract’s ability to hold and dispense native tokens, aligning the implementation with the business logic that prizes must be claimable regardless of token type.

title: Unauthorized reallocation in `NudgeCampaign::handleReallocation` and reward disruption vulnerability in `NudgeCampaign::invalidateParticipations`
description:
The `NudgeCampaign::handleReallocation` function allows any attacker to manipulate reward allocations through flash loans or repeated calls with real fund Li.Fi’s executor. This can lead to reward depletion and disruption of legitimate user rewards even after invalidating the attacker

The vulnerability stems from two main issues:

1. **Insufficient Caller Validation**: While the function checks for `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE`, this role is assigned to Li.Fi’s executor which can be called by anyone, effectively bypassing intended access controls.
2. **Reward Accounting Flaw**: The system fails to properly reset claimable amounts when participations are invalidated, allowing attackers to:

   * Claim all allocations through flash loans
   * Perform repeated reallocations via Li.Fi’s executor
   * Cause permanent reduction of available rewards through multiple invalidations

The `invalidateParticipations` function only subtracts from `pendingRewards` but doesn’t return the fees to the claimable pool, creating a growing discrepancy in reward accounting.

This vulnerability allows attackers to:

* Maliciously allocate campaign rewards through flash loans
* Perform denial-of-service attacks on legitimate users’ rewards
* Permanently reduce available rewards through repeated invalidations
* Disrupt the intended economic model of the campaign system

The attack could be executed at minimal cost and would be difficult to detect until rewards are significantly depleted.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NudgeCampaign contract where the function handleReallocation can be invoked by any address because the only check performed is for the SWAP_CALLER_ROLE, which is granted to the Li.Fi executor contract. The executor contract is publicly callable, so an attacker can trigger handleReallocation through a flash‑loan or a series of cheap calls. When handleReallocation is executed, the contract updates internal reward allocations without resetting the claimable amounts that belong to participants. At the same time, the invalidateParticipations function subtracts the invalidated amount from pendingRewards but does not add the corresponding fees back to the pool of claimable rewards. This combination creates a reward accounting flaw: an attacker can repeatedly reallocate rewards, claim the newly allocated amounts, and then invalidate the same participations, permanently shrinking the total claimable reward balance. The attack can be carried out with minimal gas cost, as demonstrated by a test that performed 157 iterations and reduced the claimable reward from the initial funding to a fraction of its original value. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop to zero or a much lower amount in the displayed reward balance, failed reward claims, or a situation where legitimate participants receive no payout even though they fulfilled the campaign requirements. The issue occurs whenever an external caller can reach the Li.Fi executor, which is effectively any address, and when the campaign’s invalidateParticipations logic is used after a reallocation. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by executing a series of calls on a mainnet fork and observing the depletion of rewards. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit error events when the claimable pool shrinks, and the normal flow of reward distribution appears to work for honest participants until the pool is exhausted. The bug belongs to the class of improper access control combined with flawed accounting of token balances, similar to reward‑drain or escrow‑mismanagement bugs. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce strict access control on handleReallocation, restrict the SWAP_CALLER_ROLE to trusted contracts only, and modify invalidateParticipations so that any reduction of pendingRewards is mirrored by an equivalent increase in the claimable pool or by preventing double counting of rewards. Proper event emission and balance checks would also help detect abnormal depletion early.

title: Anyone can DOS `handleReallocation` over and over
description:
Li.Fi’s Executor contract is granted `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE`. The function `handleReallocation` is used inside the protocol to notify about user’s reallocation and can only be called by address that has `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE`. The intention of the protocol is to use the executor’s functions so that executor swaps assets and then calls `handleReallocation` inside `NudgeCampaign` / `NudgePointsCampaign` contract.

However, the Executor contract that has `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE` can be used by anyone (its functions do not have access control restrictions which is expected), anyone can call function `swapAndExecute`. This means that **any user** can call the `swapAndExecute` function and instruct the `Executor` to call **arbitrary functions** on other contracts.

As a result, an attacker can use the `Executor` to call `renounceRole` on the `NudgeCampaignFactory` contract, causing the `Executor` to lose its `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE`. This leads to DOS of every next `handleReallocation` call from Executor. Admin has to `grantRole` again to Executor contract, but user can repeat the process of `renouncingRole` using Executor.

Executor function that can be called is [here](https://github.com/lifinance/contracts/blob/b8c966aad30407b3f579723847057729549fd353/src/Periphery/Executor.sol#L105-L126).
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Executor contract, which is granted the SWAP_CALLER_ROLE required to call handleReallocation in NudgeCampaign and NudgePointsCampaign, exposes a function swapAndExecute that can be called by any address because it lacks its own access control. An attacker can invoke swapAndExecute with a crafted SwapData payload that calls renounceRole on the NudgeCampaignFactory, causing the Executor to lose its SWAP_CALLER_ROLE. Once the role is removed, every subsequent call to handleReallocation from the Executor reverts, effectively denying the protocol the ability to process user reallocations, distribute rewards, or update campaign state. This denial-of-service can be triggered at any time by any user, and the attacker can repeat the renounceRole call after the admin re-grants the role, keeping the system perpetually blocked. The impact is that campaigns become stuck, users see no reward distribution, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that reallocations will always be processed are broken. The issue occurs whenever swapAndExecute is used to forward arbitrary calls, which the protocol expects only the executor itself to perform, but the lack of restriction allows external actors to misuse it. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the role-based access control flow and identified that the Executor’s external interface does not enforce any caller restrictions. The bug is hard to notice because the Executor contract is intended to be a trusted internal component, and the renounceRole call does not emit obvious error messages; the failure only appears as a silent revert of handleReallocation calls. The class of bug is an unrestricted proxy function that enables arbitrary external calls, leading to role revocation and a DOS condition. To fix the issue, the swapAndExecute function should enforce that only authorized callers (e.g., the protocol’s core contracts) can invoke it, or it should validate that the target of the forwarded call is a whitelisted contract, thereby preventing an attacker from calling renounceRole on the factory. In user-facing terms, a participant expecting their reallocation to be recorded or their reward to be credited will instead see no change, possibly a zero balance, and the campaign will appear frozen.

title: All reallocate cross-chain token and rewards will be lost for the users using the account abstraction wallet
description:
Users with account abstraction wallets have a different address across same wallet on chains, so if user using an account abstraction wallet initiate reallocate cross-chain token, the `toToken` will be sent to wrong address and lost permanently.

With 6.4 million users and 100+ billion assets, there is very high risk that safe wallet users will try to initiate cross-chain reallocations and suffering a loss.

In addition, there are other impacts, the user cannot claim rewards on the destination chain and the rewards for that user end up being locked forever in the `NugeCampaign.sol` contract because no one can’t rescue the reward token even with `rescueTokens()` and `withdrawRewards()` functions.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Nudge’s cross‑chain reallocation function handles the recipient address for users that employ account‑abstraction wallets. When a user initiates a reallocation from one chain to another, the contract receives a single userAddress parameter that is taken from the source chain (for example the Ethereum mainnet address). The implementation then forwards the swapped tokens to that address on the destination chain using an internal _transfer call. Because account‑abstraction wallets generate a distinct contract address on each blockchain, the source‑chain address does not correspond to a valid recipient on the target chain. Consequently the transferred amount is sent to an address that the user does not control, resulting in a permanent loss of the reallocated tokens. The same mismatch also affects the reward‑claiming flow: the participation record stores the source‑chain address, and the claimRewards function checks that msg.sender equals this stored address. On the destination chain the user’s AA wallet has a different address, so the check fails and the reward tokens remain locked in the NudgeCampaign contract. Neither the rescueTokens nor the withdrawRewards functions can retrieve these locked rewards because they are gated by the same address verification. The issue is triggered whenever an AA‑wallet holder performs a cross‑chain reallocation through the Nudge UI or SDK, which does not provide a field to specify the destination address. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the expected balance on the destination chain remains unchanged or becomes zero, and attempts to claim rewards are rejected with an unauthorized‑caller error. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that examined the handleReallocation and claimRewards logic together with the LiFi SDK integration. It is difficult to notice because the UI does not expose the address mismatch and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the loss. This class of bug can be described as an address‑mismatch cross‑chain transfer combined with an authorization check that assumes a single immutable user address across chains. To remediate the issue the protocol should either require the user to supply the correct destination‑chain address, implement a mapping from a universal identifier to the appropriate per‑chain address, or redesign the reward‑claim logic to allow proof of ownership across chains. Such changes would prevent funds from being sent to an uncontrolled address and would enable users to claim or rescue their rewards safely.

title: Not verifying that transaction initiator is the actual participator allows malicious user to allocate full reward as Uniswap V2 pool
description:
To participate in campaign, user has to call swap provider (Li.Fi) `Executor::swapAndExecute` function. This function performs swap required to get campaign `target` tokens and calls `NudgeCampaign::handleReallocation`. `NudgeCampaign` will receive and forward `target` tokens to `userAddress` and update user participation details accordingly. `handleReallocation` is only callable by `SWAP_CALLER_ROLE` which is given to `Executor` to make sure user swaps tokens before being able to participate.

However, user can encode `NudgeCampaign::handleReallocation` calldata inside `Executor::swapAndExecute` and set arbitrary `userAddress` that doesn’t have to be the same as the swap initiator address. This allows user to “gift” allocation to anyone. Protocol backend will track `userAddress` `target` tokens balance and invalidate participation if the balance drops participation amount, so this should not be an issue.

Yet, this becomes problematic if there is an existing Uniswap V2 pool in which one of the tokens is `target` token. This is highly probable, since `target` tokens must have a DEX pool in order to be “bought” via swap provider. Malicious user could take advantage of this and create smart contract that would initiate a flash swap, borrow substantial amount of `target` tokens, and encode a swap call on `Executor::swapAndExecute` such that it forwards all tokens to the `NudgeCampaign` calling `handleReallocation` with `userAddress` of the Uniswap pool. `NudgeCampaign` would register valid participation because `handleReallocation` was called from `Executor` and monitoring system wouldn’t invalidate participation since pool has more than enough tokens to pass the balance checks. Flash swap would be successful because `NudgeCampaign` would send all tokens back to pool in the same transaction.

Attacker would have to buy tokens to cover Uniswap’s 0.3% fee. This is the only cost for the attacker. Fee can be calculated using unallocated amount and PPQ (rewards factor):

    (UnallocatedRewards * PPQ_DENOMINATOR / REWARD_PPQ) * 0.3%

It’s important to note here that funds can be recovered if protocol invalidates malicious participation manually. If this doesn’t happen, funds will stay locked in `NudgeCampaign`. More importantly, other users won’t be able to participate so whole campaign would be in Denial of Service and with good chance that nobody would even notice it, most likely being marked as success, while campaign admin basically burned rewards for no buying volume in return which is the reason campaign is created for.

Additionally, the exploit wouldn’t work with any other lending protocol because of different flash loan implementation details. Here, for flash loan to be successful pool will verify that funds are returned by checking pool balance at the end, while other protocols usually pull the borrowed funds from the borrower which in this case wouldn’t be possible since `NudgeCampaign` returns funds for attacker who is borrower.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper authorization check in the campaign participation flow that allows an attacker to allocate the entire reward pool to an arbitrary address, such as a Uniswap V2 liquidity pool, without being the actual participant. The root cause is that NudgeCampaign.handleReallocation, which records a user’s contribution and transfers the target tokens, is only protected by a role (SWAP_CALLER_ROLE) granted to the Executor contract. It does not verify that the userAddress supplied in the call matches the transaction initiator or the address that performed the token swap. Because the Executor.swapAndExecute function forwards arbitrary calldata to the campaign, a malicious actor can craft a call that sets userAddress to any contract address. When the target token already has a Uniswap V2 pair, the attacker can initiate a flash swap, borrow a large amount of the target token, and embed a call to Executor.swapAndExecute that forwards the borrowed tokens to NudgeCampaign.handleReallocation with the pool’s address as userAddress. The campaign registers a valid participation because the call originates from the authorized Executor, and the pool’s balance check passes since the flash‑swap contract returns the tokens to the pool within the same transaction. The attacker only needs to cover the 0.3 % Uniswap fee, after which the full unallocated reward amount is recorded as belonging to the pool, effectively draining the reward pool. From a user’s perspective the campaign appears to have a participant with a large token balance, but no real user receives any reward; the reward balance becomes zero and subsequent participants are unable to join, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the access control logic of handleReallocation and noticing that the participant address is not tied to msg.sender. It is hard to notice because the participation entry looks legitimate, the balance checks succeed, and no explicit error is emitted. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑authorization and accounting inconsistencies, where the system trusts externally supplied identifiers without verification. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the userAddress argument equals the address that initiated the swap (e.g., msg.sender or tx.origin), or restrict handleReallocation to be callable only by the participant’s own address. Alternatively, the campaign could derive the participant address internally rather than accepting it as a parameter, and add explicit checks that the transferred amount matches the recorded contribution before allocating rewards.

title: Supply function doesn’t account for market maxDeposit when providing assets to it
description: Some vaults that the Silo vault deposits into have their own supply caps (do not confuse with `config[market].cap`), which may prevent `_supplyERC4626` from fully depositing user-provided assets. If these caps are not accounted for, the deposit function may revert instead of distributing assets across multiple vaults.
bug_full: The Silo vault contains a supply routine that forwards user assets to a list of ERC4626 markets (vaults). The routine calculates how many tokens to send to each market based solely on a global configuration value (config[market].cap) and the internal balance of that market. It does not take into account the market's own remaining deposit capacity, exposed through the ERC4626 maxDeposit view. As a result, when a user attempts to deposit an amount that exceeds the remaining capacity of the first market in the queue, the routine tries to deposit the full amount into that market. The market’s deposit function then reverts because the amount is larger than its maxDeposit. The try/catch block only catches a revert that occurs after the call, but the logic still subtracts the full amount from the user‑provided assets only on success, leaving the remainder untouched. Because the routine expects the entire user amount to be supplied before exiting, the overall deposit operation fails even though the combined free space across all markets would have been sufficient. This mismatch between per‑market capacity and the global cap creates a classic capacity‑handling bug: the contract assumes a single cap is enough to represent available space, ignoring individual market limits. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker can submit a deposit that is larger than the first market’s remaining capacity, causing legitimate users’ deposits to revert and effectively denying service to the deposit function. The impact is that users see their transaction revert, their UI shows no balance change, and they lose gas fees, leading to a poor user experience and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The condition occurs whenever multiple markets have independent supply caps and the deposit amount is larger than the first market’s free space but smaller than the sum of all free spaces. Affected parties include any user trying to deposit through the Silo vault, liquidity providers relying on the vault’s aggregation logic, and the protocol itself because the deposit path becomes unreliable. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the supply logic and testing edge cases where market caps differ. It can be hard to notice because the overall system appears to have enough capacity; only the ordering of markets and the lack of per‑market checks cause the failure. The proper fix is to incorporate each market’s maxDeposit (or remaining capacity) into the allocation calculation, splitting the user’s assets across markets in a way that never exceeds any individual market’s limit, and to ensure the routine only returns success after all assets have been allocated or to gracefully handle partial allocations without reverting the whole transaction. This class of bug is generally referred to as an improper capacity check or allocation overflow, which violates the business assumption that the sum of individual caps equals the total available deposit space, leading to unexpected “funds disappear” or “deposit fails” symptoms from the user’s perspective.

title: SiloVault will incorrectly accrue rewards during user transfer/transferFrom actions due to unsynced totalSupply
description:
SiloVault’s totalSupply() [accrueFees](https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-03-silo-finance/blob/0409be5b85d7aabfbbe10de1de1890d4b862d2d5/silo-vaults/contracts/SiloVault.sol#L944) from interests (delta totalAssets). Such fee accrual is updated through _accrueFee() which mints an additional share to the fee reciever.

We see that when claiming rewards directly through `claimRewards()` the accrued extra share is updated first before _claimRewards().

The vulnerability is when `_claimRewards()` is invoked atomically through hooks (_update), the `_accrueFee()` will be missed in the user’s transfer/transferFrom call. In this case, an incorrect totalSupply() will be used for fee accrual, leading to incorrect fee accrual.

Impacts: incorrect and inconsistent reward accrual due to unsynced `totalSupply()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑accrual logic of the SiloVault contract. The vault calculates protocol fees as newly minted shares based on the change in total assets (delta totalAssets) and records this through the internal function _accrueFee, which also increases the contract's totalSupply. When a user calls claimRewards directly, the contract first executes _accrueFee, updates totalSupply, and only then distributes the rewards, so the accounting stays consistent. However, during a token transfer or transferFrom, the contract’s internal _update hook invokes _claimRewards before any state changes and crucially omits a call to _accrueFee. Because totalSupply has not been refreshed to reflect the latest fee accrual, the reward calculation uses a stale supply value. This mismatch leads to an incorrect amount of reward shares being minted for the fee recipient and, consequently, an inaccurate reward allocation for the transferring user. The bug manifests only when rewards are claimed atomically as part of a transfer operation; normal deposit or withdraw flows are safe because they call _accrueFee first. From a user’s perspective, a transfer that should include a proportional reward may result in a lower-than‑expected reward, a zero reward, or in rare cases an inflated reward, breaking the expectation that “my rewards are correctly calculated on every action”. The impact is inconsistent and potentially unfair reward distribution, which can erode trust in the protocol’s accounting and cause financial loss for participants who receive fewer shares than they are entitled to. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the claimRewards path with the transfer path and noticed that the fee‑accrual step was missing in the latter. Because the token balances themselves appear correct, the problem is subtle and may go unnoticed unless reward claim amounts are inspected or compared across different transaction types. The root cause is a synchronization flaw: the contract fails to keep the totalSupply variable in sync with fee accrual before reward distribution in certain code paths. To remediate, the transfer/transferFrom logic should be amended to invoke _accrueFee (or an equivalent totalSupply update) before calling _claimRewards, ensuring that reward calculations always use the latest supply figure. This aligns the transfer flow with the deposit/withdraw flow and restores consistent accounting across all user actions.

title: SiloVault.sol :: Markets with assets that revert on zero approvals cannot be removed.
description: To remove a market from the vault, the supply `cap` must be set to 0. However, when this happens, the market’s allowance to use tokens from the vault is also reset to 0. The issue arises because some tokens revert when attempting to approve a 0 value, preventing these markets from being removed from the vault.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way SiloVault removes a market. To delete a market the contract first forces the market’s supply cap to zero. The internal setCap routine then calls forceApprove on the underlying ERC‑20 asset with an approval amount of zero, intending to clear the market’s allowance. This logic assumes that calling approve(0) always succeeds, which is true for most tokens but false for a class of tokens that deliberately revert when the approval amount is zero (for example certain BNB‑derived tokens). When such a token is used, the forceApprove call reverts, the transaction aborts, and the cap cannot be set to zero. Because the cap never reaches zero, the removableAt flag is never cleared and the market remains permanently locked in the vault’s withdraw queue. The protocol enforces a maximum queue length, so a permanently locked market prevents the addition of new markets, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for future upgrades. The impact is that administrators cannot remove misbehaving or deprecated markets, users may see a market listed as “removal pending” forever, and the system may run out of queue slots, blocking legitimate new markets. The issue is discovered during a Code4rena audit when testing market removal with tokens known to revert on zero approvals. It is hard to notice because the majority of ERC‑20 tokens accept a zero approval, so standard test suites may not trigger the failure. The root cause is an unsafe assumption about ERC‑20 approve semantics and the limited scope of OpenZeppelin’s forceApprove helper, which only handles tokens that reject non‑zero approvals when a previous allowance exists, not tokens that reject zero approvals outright. To remediate, the contract should avoid resetting the allowance to zero, for example by using increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance patterns, by skipping the approve call when the new cap is zero, or by employing a token‑agnostic accounting mechanism that does not rely on ERC‑20 approvals. In user‑facing terms, a user attempting to remove a market will see the removal transaction fail, the market will stay listed, and attempts to add new markets may be rejected with “withdraw queue full”. The protocol’s business logic that assumes markets can always be removed is violated, breaking the intended lifecycle management of assets.

title: Lack of slippage and deadline protection in deposit
description:
1. When users [deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-03-silo-finance/blob/main/silo-vaults/contracts/SiloVault.sol#L569) funds, those assets are allocated to one or more underlying ERC4626 markets according to the supply queue.
2. When withdrawing or redeeming, assets are pulled from the underlying markets according to the withdraw queue and shares burned.

None of these actions allow the user to specify any acceptable slippage or deadline.

  * The vault interacts with multiple ERC4626 vaults. Share price in these underlying vaults can change between transaction submission and execution.
  * During deposit, the protocol might need to distribute assets across multiple markets based on their caps. This multi-step process could expose users to price changes.
  * During withdrawals or redemptions, the protocol attempts to pull assets from markets in a specific order. If a market has insufficient liquidity, the next market is tried, which might have different share pricing.
  * The [_accrueFee()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-03-silo-finance/blob/main/silo-vaults/contracts/SiloVault.sol#L942) function is called during both deposit and withdrawal, which can change the conversion rate between shares and assets.

Additionally, there’s a risk of transactions getting stuck in the mempool during periods of network congestion and hence deadline protection is needed.

User may recieve less than expected shares or assets due to unfavourable price movement or execution delays.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage and deadline controls in the deposit, withdraw and redeem functions of a vault that forwards user funds to several underlying ERC4626 markets. When a user calls deposit, the contract distributes the assets across a supply queue of markets, each of which may have a different share price that can change between the moment the transaction is signed and the moment it is mined. The same situation applies to withdrawals, where assets are pulled from a withdraw queue and the conversion rate between shares and assets may be altered by the internal _accrueFee() call that runs on every deposit and withdrawal. Because the external interface does not accept parameters such as minShares, minAssets or a transaction deadline, a user cannot protect themselves against adverse price movement, front‑running, or execution delays caused by network congestion. An attacker or a volatile market can therefore cause the vault to allocate assets at a less favorable price, resulting in the user receiving fewer shares on deposit or fewer assets on withdrawal than expected. The impact is that users see a shortfall – for example, they expect to receive 100 shares but only receive 95, or a withdrawal that should return 10 ETH returns only 9.5 ETH – without any explicit error, making the problem hard to notice from the UI. The issue manifests whenever the underlying markets have variable share prices, when fee accrual changes conversion rates, or when transactions are delayed in the mempool during periods of high congestion. All depositors and withdrawers of the protocol are affected, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about one‑to‑one value preservation are violated. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the flow of assets through the supply and withdraw queues and noted the absence of any slippage or deadline checks. Because the contract silently accepts the transaction and only later returns a reduced amount, the bug can go unnoticed until users compare expected versus actual balances. The recommended remediation is to add user‑controlled slippage limits – for example, a minShares argument on deposit and a minAssets argument on withdraw/redeem – and to enforce a deadline (e.g., block.timestamp must be less than a user‑provided expiry) so that the transaction reverts if execution is delayed beyond the acceptable window. This brings the contract in line with standard practices for interacting with external price‑sensitive vaults and prevents value loss due to price drift or front‑running.

title: Incorrect reward distribution due to feeShares minting order
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect reward distribution caused by the order in which fee shares are minted and rewards are claimed. When a user calls claimRewards, the contract first updates the total assets and accrues the protocol fee, which calculates the number of fee shares that should be minted for the fee recipient. However, the internal _update function that is triggered by the mint operation calls _claimRewards before the new fee shares are actually added to totalSupply. As a result, the reward calculation is performed while the fee recipient still holds zero shares for the current period, so the entire reward is allocated to the existing shareholders. The fee recipient receives the newly minted shares but receives no reward for the interest that generated those shares, while the other shareholders receive a larger than fair portion of the reward. This occurs every time claimRewards is executed while there is a pending fee to be minted, i.e., when totalInterest is positive and the fee rate is non‑zero. The affected parties are the fee recipient (often the protocol treasury) and any investors who rely on the advertised proportional reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call flow from claimRewards through _accrueFee, _mint and the overridden _update function, noticing that _claimRewards is invoked twice and that the second invocation finds no rewards left for the newly minted fee shares. The bug is subtle because the overall reward numbers appear correct for the main shareholders and the protocol’s total assets still increase, making the discrepancy easy to miss in surface‑level testing. The impact is a systematic over‑allocation of rewards to existing shareholders and an under‑allocation to the fee recipient, which can erode the protocol’s fee revenue and break the intended accounting model. To fix the issue, the reward distribution logic must be adjusted so that fee shares minted in the same transaction are accounted for when rewards are calculated. This can be achieved by moving the reward claim after the fee shares are minted, by adding a flag that tells _claimRewards to include the freshly minted shares, or by recalculating the reward portion based on the updated totalSupply before the distribution occurs. The correction restores the intended proportional reward split and ensures that the fee recipient receives its fair share of the accrued interest.

title: Deflation attack
description:
The flow of assets between SiloVault and its markets favour the markets (per standard ERC4626 specifications). This means that SiloVault can lose assets compared to its total supply of shares. This deflates the share price. At low total asset levels, this can be exploited to deflate the share price until the shares per asset is close to overflowing.

This can be exploited to either simply brick the vault, or such that the attacker is the guaranteed sole holder and recipient of the incentive rewards.
poc:
The shares minted is calculated as `_assets.mulDiv(_newTotalSupply + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), _newTotalAssets + 1, _rounding)`, where the [total assets](https://github.com/code-423n4/2025-03-silo-finance/blob/0409be5b85d7aabfbbe10de1de1890d4b862d2d5/silo-vaults/contracts/SiloVault.sol#L647-L652) is based on the redeemable value of all market shares held by SiloVault.

For example, the first depositor deposits 1 wei into SiloVault, which deposits this into a market, and mints `10 ** _decimalsOffset()` shares. The market, however, is likely to round this away and not return any share to SiloVault. On the next deposit into SiloVault, `totalAssets` is zero, but `10 ** _decimalsOffset()` shares were minted. Again depositing 1 wei mints `2 * 10 ** _decimalsOffset()`, without increasing `totalAssets`. Each repetition doubles the total supply.

The same would, of course, happen if `totalAssets` on deposit did increase to `1` but due to the market updating its price, this later became `0`.

Suppose SiloVault were to instead mint shares according to the increase in `totalAssets`. Then no shares would be minted in the above example. Suppose then instead 10 wei are deposited into SiloVault, which deposits this into a market, in return, for 8 market shares (let’s say the market’s price is 1.13 assets/share). This is redeemable for 9 asset tokens, so SiloVault mints `9 * 10 ** _decimalsOffset()` shares. Now, redeeming `8 * 10 ** _decimalsOffset()` shares from SiloVault makes SiloVault withdraw 8 asset tokens from the market. Withdrawing 8 asset tokens burns not 7.08 but all 8 market shares, and SiloVault is now, just as above, left with zero totalAssets but a total supply of `1 * 10 ** _decimalsOffset()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deflation attack on a vault that follows the ERC4626 standard. The vault calculates the number of shares to mint on each deposit using a formula that incorporates the total supply of shares and the total assets reported by the markets in which the vault holds positions. Because the markets round the redeemable value of their shares downwards, the reported total assets can become zero or drop sharply even though the vault’s share supply continues to increase. When a user deposits a tiny amount, the vault may mint a large number of shares based on the previous total supply plus a decimal offset while the total assets remain unchanged. Repeating this process causes the share supply to grow exponentially while the underlying asset balance stays at or near zero. This mismatch deflates the share‑price (shares per asset) and can eventually push the share‑price calculation close to an overflow condition. An attacker can exploit the situation by repeatedly making minimal deposits, inflating the share supply, and then becoming the sole holder of the vault’s incentive rewards because the protocol distributes rewards per share. From a user’s perspective the vault appears to accept deposits and show an increasing share balance, but later redemption attempts return no assets, leaving the user with a balance of shares that are effectively worthless. The issue occurs only when the vault’s total assets are low enough for rounding to reduce the reported value to zero, which can happen after a market price update or when the market’s internal accounting discards fractional shares. All participants in the vault – depositors, reward recipients, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariants of ERC4626 are broken, leading to potential loss of funds and a bricked vault. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the minting logic and identified that the share calculation does not guard against a zero‑asset scenario and that the rounding behaviour of the markets can be abused. The problem is subtle because the vault’s external interface still reports successful deposits and share minting, masking the fact that the underlying asset pool is not growing. To remediate the issue the vault should mint shares based on the actual increase in total assets rather than on the previous total supply plus an offset, and it should enforce a minimum asset increase or use a rounding‑safe formula that prevents the total‑asset value from being rounded to zero. In short, the bug is a class of accounting deflation where share supply outpaces asset growth due to rounding errors, causing share‑price collapse, potential overflow, and loss of incentive rewards.

title: Stale prices can cause inaccurate validation of funding ticks in `funding_tick`
description:
The function `assets.funding_tick()` updates the funding index for all active synthetic assets. This helps ensure that long and short positions are economically balanced over time. The function can be called only by the operator and takes as an input the parameter `funding_ticks` which is a list of `FundingTick` structs, each specifying an `asset_id` and its new `funding_index`. The number of `funding_ticks` provided matches the number of active synthetic assets and each active asset receives a funding tick update. For every funding tick in `funding_ticks`, the function `assets.

`_process_funding_tick()` is executed with the new funding tick for the asset and the storage read `max_funding_rate` where downstream the function `funding.validate_funding_rate()` is executed. This function validates that the change in the old and new funding index doesn’t violate the `max_funding_rate`, however, the function relies on the price of the synthetic asset fetched through `get_synthetic_price()`. 

However, `get_synthetic_price()` retrieves the asset price from `self.synthetic_timely_data` but does not check if the price is up to date. This can result in the use of stale prices, which can cause incorrect validation of the funding rate. As a result, invalid funding rate changes might incorrectly pass validation, or valid funding rate updates could be wrongly rejected. The more severe case is invalid funding rate changes passing validation since the funding tick directly affects the collateral balance of positions and can lead to erroneously updated balances - modification to the collateral balance based on the funding index happens in `positions.

`_update_synthetic_balance_and_funding()` and the funding index is also considered in health validations that use `positions.get_collateral_provisional_balance()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑price bug in the funding tick update mechanism of a perpetual synthetic asset protocol. The function that updates funding indexes for all active synthetic assets receives a list of new funding ticks and validates each tick against a maximum funding rate. The validation routine calls a price oracle helper that reads the synthetic price from a storage mapping called synthetic_timely_data, but it never checks whether the stored price is recent. Because the price may be outdated, the validation can use a stale price to decide whether the change in funding index respects the max funding rate. This happens whenever the price feed has not been refreshed before the operator calls the funding_tick function, for example after a delay in the oracle update or when the operator deliberately triggers the update before the price is refreshed. An attacker who can influence the timing of price updates, or who can submit a malicious funding index while the price is stale, can cause the validation to incorrectly accept a funding rate change that should be rejected. The accepted funding tick is then applied to positions, altering the synthetic balance and funding component of each position’s collateral. As a result, users may see unexpected funding payments, collateral balances that are higher or lower than they should be, or health checks that incorrectly report a safe position, potentially allowing liquidation avoidance or causing unintended loss of funds. The issue affects every holder of long or short positions on the affected synthetic assets, as well as the protocol’s risk model and the operator who is allowed to call the function. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers examined the funding_tick logic and noticed that the price retrieval function does not enforce a freshness constraint. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the protocol appears to operate normally, but the underlying accounting invariant is broken, and the discrepancy may only surface later when users observe abnormal funding amounts or unexpected balance changes. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a timestamp check on the price data, reject stale prices, or fetch the price directly from a trusted oracle that guarantees freshness before performing the max‑funding‑rate validation. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of time‑dependency or stale‑data vulnerabilities where economic calculations rely on up‑to‑date external data but fail to verify its recency, leading to incorrect accounting and potential fund loss.

title: Streaming enforcers increase token spending even without actual token transfer
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑depletion bug in the streaming enforcers that manage ERC20 and native token streams. Both ERC20StreamingEnforcer and NativeTokenStreamingEnforcer increase the recorded spent amount in their before‑hook function before the actual token transfer is executed. When a delegation is executed with the `EXECTYPE_TRY` mode, a failed transfer does not cause a revert; the call continues and the allowance entry has already been marked as spent. An attacker who controls a delegate can repeatedly invoke the streaming delegation with deliberately failing transfers – for example by using a token that is paused or by sending insufficient gas – causing the allowance counter to be reduced by the requested amount each time while no tokens leave the sender’s balance. Over many iterations the streaming allowance can be drained completely, leaving legitimate users unable to redeem further streaming payments. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on streaming delegations: users see their allowance exhausted and receive no funds even though their token balances remain unchanged. The bug occurs only when the streaming enforcer is used together with the TRY execution type; with the default execution type the transaction would revert on failure and the spent amount would not be updated. The affected parties are delegators who grant streaming permissions, delegates who attempt to redeem those permissions, and any protocol relying on the streaming enforcer for rate‑limited payments. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which reproduced the problem with a test that forces the token transfer to fail while observing that the stored spent amount still increased. The problem is subtle because the allowance bookkeeping appears correct at a glance – the contract emits an event indicating increased spent amount – yet the external token balance does not reflect any transfer, making the discrepancy easy to miss in normal operation. The bug belongs to the class of “state update before external call” violations of the check‑effects‑interactions pattern, where internal accounting is modified prior to confirming that the external operation succeeded. To remediate, the enforcer should only update the spent field after verifying that the token transfer succeeded, or it should restrict delegations to the `EXECTYPE_DEFAULT` mode so that failed transfers automatically revert and prevent allowance consumption. Alternatively, the contract could roll back the spent increment when a transfer fails. Fixing the issue restores the invariant that the sum of spent amount and remaining allowance always matches the amount that has actually been transferred, preventing unintended denial‑of‑service and ensuring that users receive the expected streaming payments.

title: Inconsistency in API and swap payloads in DelegationMetaSwapAdapter can potentially lead to unauthorized transfers
bug_full: The DelegationMetaSwapAdapter contract implements a swapByDelegation function that receives two separate payloads: apiData, which declares the token to be swapped (tokenFrom) and the amount, and swapData, which is passed to an underlying MetaSwap contract and also contains a tokenFrom field. The function validates the delegations, token allowances and aggregator identifiers, but it never checks that the token address (or amount) encoded in apiData matches the token address (or amount) encoded in swapData. Because swapData is an opaque byte array, a caller can craft a mismatch where apiData advertises a small, authorized transfer of TokenA while swapData actually instructs the MetaSwap contract to pull a larger amount of TokenB from the adapter’s reserves. The adapter then executes the swap using the token information from swapData, effectively transferring TokenB without any explicit delegation permitting that token. This inconsistency can be exploited by an attacker who creates a delegation that limits a small amount of TokenA, then submits malicious apiData that claims to use TokenA but embeds swapData that references TokenB. When the MetaSwap contract processes the swap, it moves TokenB from the adapter’s balance to the caller, draining funds that were never authorized. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a swap of TokenA for TokenC, yet the user’s TokenB balance drops unexpectedly while the expected refund of TokenC arrives, leading to the perception that “funds disappeared” or “the swap gave me nothing”. The vulnerability appears only when the adapter’s swapByDelegation function is called with non‑empty delegations and allowed tokens, conditions that are typical for legitimate swaps, making it easy to miss during testing because the mismatch resides in the encoded swapData rather than in explicit Solidity variables. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing validation comment.
