By supplying arbitrary amounts of RA and CT, the attacker sets a skewed initial reserve ratio (for example 10 RA : 1 CT instead of the intended 10 RA : 10 CT). Once this artificial ratio is recorded, every subsequent deposit made by the vault uses the attacker‑controlled ratio to compute how much of each token to add. Consequently, the vault deposits liquidity at a price that is far from market value, causing the pool’s constant‑product invariant to be distorted. When the protocol later liquidates the pool or users redeem their LV tokens, the reserves contain far fewer RA tokens than expected. In the reported scenario the pool’s RA reserve drops from 1 000 000 to roughly 300 000, a loss of about 70 % of the original liquidity. LP tokens issued to users therefore represent a much smaller share of the pool, and each LV token redeems only about 0.3 RA instead of the intended 1 RA, leading to a substantial devaluation for all LV holders. The attack can be carried out by anyone who can front‑run the vault’s first liquidity addition, which is possible because the vault does not enforce any access control or slippage protection on the initial deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual code review of the vault library, where the ratio‑fetching logic and the fallback to a default value were identified as insufficient when the pool is empty. It is hard to notice because the transaction that adds liquidity appears to succeed and the on‑chain ratio matches the attacker‑chosen values; the UI may still display the expected token amounts, while the underlying accounting is silently corrupted. The bug belongs to the class of “first‑liquidity‑initialisation” or “pool‑creation front‑run” vulnerabilities, where the lack of a trusted initializer allows price manipulation before the protocol takes control. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that only the vault (or a designated configuration contract) can perform the first addLiquidity call, enforce a fixed initial reserve ratio that cannot be overridden, and add explicit slippage or minimum‑amount checks that reject deposits when the observed pool price deviates from the expected default. Additionally, the contract could reject any external addLiquidity calls while the pool is empty, or require a time‑locked initialization step that prevents front‑running. Implementing these controls would restore the intended economic relationship between RA and CT and protect LV token holders from unexpected devaluation.

title: Withdrawing all lv before expiry
description:
VaultLib:redeemEarly() redeems users' liquidity vault positions, lv for Ra, before expiry.
After expiry, it is not possible to deposit into the vault or redeem early.
Whenever all users redeem early, when it gets to the expiry date, VaultLib::_liquidatedLp() is called to remove the lp position from the AMM into Ra and Ct (redeem from the PSM into more Ra and Pa) and split among all lv holders.
However, as the total supply of lv is 0 due to users having redeemed all their positions via VaultLib::redeemEarly(), when it gets to VaultPoolLib::reserve(), it reverts due to a division by 0 error, never allowing the Vault::_liquidatedLp() call to go through.
As the Ds has expired, it is also not possible to deposit into it to increase the lv supply, so all funds are forever stuck.
In MathHelper:134, the ratePerLv reverts due to division by 0. It should calculate the rate after the return guard that checks if the totalLvIssued==0.

Internal pre-conditions
1. All users must redeem early.

External pre-conditions
None.

Attack Path
1. All users redeem early via Vault::redeemEarlyLv().
2. The Ds expires and there is no lv tokens, making all funds stuck.
All funds are stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero arithmetic error that occurs in the liquidity‑separation routine of the vault contract. When all users redeem their liquidity‑vault (lv) tokens early, the total supply of lv becomes zero. After the vault’s expiry the system attempts to liquidate the remaining AMM position by calling VaultPoolLib::reserve, which internally invokes MathHelper.separateLiquidity to compute a rate per lv (ratePerLv). The implementation calculates ratePerLv before checking whether totalLvIssued or totalLvWithdrawn is zero, so with totalLvIssued equal to zero the division (totalAmount * 1e18) / totalLvIssued reverts. Because the vault is already expired, no further deposits can create new lv tokens, and the liquidation step never completes. As a result the contract reverts on every attempt to finalize liquidation, leaving all underlying assets permanently locked in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s post‑expiry logic, where the auditor observed that the guard for zero‑lv supply was placed after the division operation. The bug is hard to notice because the division is only executed in a rarely‑reached code path that runs after expiry and only when the total lv supply is zero, a state that may not be exercised in normal testing. Users experience the symptom of being unable to withdraw any funds after the expiry; the UI may show a zero balance or a transaction that reverts with a generic arithmetic error, contrary to the expectation that their deposited assets would be returned or that the vault would automatically distribute the remaining value. The class of bug is an unchecked arithmetic operation leading to a division‑by‑zero, a common pattern in financial smart contracts where guard conditions are placed after the calculation. The correct mitigation is to move the zero‑supply guard before the division, returning a safe default (e.g., ratePerLv = 0 and attributing the whole amount to the AMM) when totalLvIssued or totalLvWithdrawn is zero. This prevents the revert and allows the liquidation routine to complete, ensuring that funds are correctly distributed to the remaining participants.

title: Rebasing tokens are not supported
description:
The readme states that rebasing tokens are supported
Rebasing tokens are supported with exchange rate mechanism
However, only non rebasing tokens such as the wrapped version wsteth are supposed. If stETH is used, it will accrue value in the Psm and Vault (technically they are the same contract) which will be left untracked as Ra and Pa deposits are tracked in state variables.
The code does not handle rebasing tokens even though the readme says it does. The exchange rate mechanism only supports non rebasing tokens such as wsteth.

Internal pre-conditions
None.

External pre-conditions
None.

Attack Path
Admin creates steth pairs using it as Ra or Pa, whose value will grow in the protocol but left untracked as the quantites are tracked with state variables.
Stuck yield accruel in the Vault/Psm contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the protocol's token handling logic assumes that the assets used as redemption asset (Ra) or profit asset (Pa) are non‑rebasing ERC‑20 tokens. The documentation states that rebasing tokens are supported via an exchange‑rate mechanism, but the implementation only records static balances (dsBalance, ctBalance, paBalance) and never updates them when the underlying token’s total supply changes due to rebasing. When a rebasing token such as stETH is configured as Ra or Pa, the token automatically accrues value inside the Vault/Psm contract. Because the contract does not query the current token balance or adjust the stored accounting variables, the extra value remains invisible to the protocol’s accounting layer. An admin can create a pair that uses a rebasing token, causing the protocol to believe that the deposited amount is unchanged while the actual token balance grows. This leads to “stuck yield” – the protocol cannot correctly redeem or distribute the accrued tokens, and users may see zero or reduced payouts despite the contract holding more assets. The issue manifests whenever the admin sets a rebasing token as Ra or Pa, and it is not prevented by any on‑chain checks. The affected parties are the protocol itself, its users who expect correct redemption values, and any liquidity providers who rely on accurate accounting. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the readme versus the source code, where the mismatch between the claimed support for rebasing tokens and the actual balance‑tracking implementation was observed. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit errors; the token balance simply diverges from the recorded state, making the discrepancy hard to notice without explicit balance queries. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid rebasing tokens from being used as Ra or Pa, or extend the accounting logic to query the token’s current balance (or its exchange rate) on each operation and synchronize the stored variables accordingly. This would bring the implementation in line with the documented exchange‑rate mechanism and prevent hidden yield accumulation.

title: Providing liquidity to the AMM
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑discrepancy bug that occurs when a contract supplies liquidity to an automated market maker (AMM) without verifying the exact token amounts that the AMM actually consumes. The root cause is that the internal __addLiquidityToAmmUnchecked function calls the router’s addLiquidity method and supplies a target amount for each token, but it never checks the returned actual amounts (actual0 and actual1) that the AMM accepted. Because the AMM’s constant‑product formula and integer division can cause a 1‑2 wei deviation between the requested amount and the amount finally locked, the contract ends up holding a tiny surplus of each token after the transaction. This surplus is not returned to the user and is not accounted for in the protocol’s accounting, so the tokens become effectively locked inside the contract. The issue can be exploited simply by repeatedly providing liquidity; each call may leave a microscopic amount of tokens stranded, and over many operations these residues accumulate, reducing the overall efficiency of the protocol and causing a gradual erosion of user funds. The problem manifests whenever a user or the protocol adds liquidity to the RA:CT pair, i.e., during any call to __addLiquidityToAmmUnchecked, which is the normal path for liquidity provision. All participants who rely on the contract to correctly handle their deposits – individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the hidden loss contradicts the expectation that the exact supplied amounts are either fully used by the AMM or returned. The discrepancy was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended token amounts with the values returned by the router call; the auditor noticed that the contract never examined the returned actual0 and actual1 fields, leading to the realization that rounding errors could remain unhandled. The bug is subtle because the differences are extremely small (often just a few wei) and therefore do not cause immediate, obvious failures; they only become apparent after many transactions or when inspecting low‑level balances. To remediate the issue, the contract should capture the actual amounts returned by addLiquidity, compare them with the requested amounts, and either revert the transaction or implement a safe fallback that returns the surplus to the user or records it for later redistribution. In conceptual terms, the fix is to enforce a post‑condition that the AMM’s consumed amounts match the supplied amounts, eliminating unchecked rounding errors and ensuring that no tokens are unintentionally trapped. This class of bug falls under unchecked external call return values leading to token lock‑up, a common pattern in DeFi contracts that interact with AMMs where precise accounting is required. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after adding liquidity the user’s wallet shows a slightly lower balance than expected, or the UI displays a missing fraction of tokens with no corresponding LP token reward, violating the expectation that all supplied tokens are either used or returned. The discrepancy violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that total token supply remains conserved across liquidity operations, thereby breaking the invariant that user deposits are fully accounted for.

title: `PaladinRewardReserve.sol` may have potential bugs if it uses new tokens as rewards
description: `PaladinRewardReserve.sol` may have potential bugs if it uses new tokens as rewards.
poc:
Currently, `PaladinRewardReserve.sol` has following behaviors:

  * `mapping(address => bool) public approvedSpenders` does not store the info regarding which token it targets
  * `setNewSpender`, `updateSpenderAllowance`, `removeSpender` and `transferToken` functions can set `token` arbitrarily

Hence, some corner cases may happen as follows:

  * Use TokenA at PaladinRewardReserve.sol and do operations.
  * Start TokenB as rewards at PaladinRewardReserve.sol.
  * All the information stored in `approvedSpenders` was intended for TokenA. So it is possible that following corner cases happen:

    * `setNewSpender` function cannot set new token
    * If userA is already added in `approvedSpenders` for TokenA, it can call `updateSpenderAllowance`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution contract where spender authorisation is recorded in a simple mapping that links an address to a boolean flag, without any association to the specific token that the spender is allowed to manage. Because the contract’s public functions – setNewSpender, updateSpenderAllowance, removeSpender and transferToken – accept an arbitrary token address as a parameter, the same approval flag is applied to every token that may be used as a reward. This design flaw originates from the omission of a token dimension in the approvedSpenders data structure, causing the permission logic to be token‑agnostic. An attacker or a legit spender that has been approved for TokenA can, after the contract switches the reward token to TokenB, invoke updateSpenderAllowance or transferToken for TokenB because the contract believes the spender is already approved. Conversely, the contract may reject the addition of a new spender for TokenB because the existing boolean entry (intended for TokenA) already indicates approval, preventing legitimate onboarding. The impact is a breach of the intended accounting model: funds intended for one token can be wrongfully transferred, rewards may be stolen, or legitimate reward distribution may become impossible, resulting in users receiving no rewards, balances appearing as zero, or funds becoming locked. The issue surfaces only when the reward token is changed after spenders have been registered, a scenario that is not covered by standard single‑token tests, making it difficult to detect during routine audits. It was discovered through manual code review that highlighted the mismatch between the function signatures (which include a token argument) and the underlying storage (which does not). To remediate, the contract should either be hard‑coded to a single reward token – removing the token argument from spender‑management functions and fixing the token at deployment – or the approval mapping should be extended to a two‑dimensional structure (e.g., mapping(address => mapping(address => bool))) that records approvals per spender per token, and the require checks must be updated accordingly to reference the correct token‑specific flag. By aligning the data model with the business logic that each token has its own set of authorized spenders, the contract restores correct accounting, prevents unauthorized fund movement, and ensures that reward distribution behaves as users expect.

title: Updating the state
description: In the Emergency withdraw function userCurrentBonusRatio and durationRatio aren’t update which will user clime funds with the wrong ratio.
poc: [HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1338](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1338)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the emergency withdrawal routine of a staking‑type token contract. When a user invokes the emergencyWithdraw function, the contract transfers the user's principal but fails to reset two accounting variables that track the user’s accrued bonus and the duration‑based reward multiplier (often called userCurrentBonusRatio and durationRatio). Because these variables retain their previous values, the contract’s later reward‑claim logic—executed after the protocol exits the emergency state—will calculate the user’s reward using stale ratios. This mismatch can cause the user to receive an amount that does not correspond to the actual time and bonus they have earned. The root cause is a missing state‑reset operation in the emergencyWithdraw implementation. The flaw can be exploited by a malicious participant who triggers an emergency withdrawal for themselves (or any user) and then, once the protocol is restored to normal operation, calls the claim function to pull rewards that are multiplied by the outdated bonus or duration factors. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s accounting: users may obtain more tokens than they are entitled to, or conversely, legitimate users may receive less if the stale ratios are lower than the correct values. The issue manifests only after two conditions are met: (1) an emergency withdrawal has been performed, leaving the internal ratios unchanged, and (2) the contract is taken out of the emergency state, re‑enabling the claim function. Until the protocol exits emergency, the bug is silent because the claim path is blocked, making it hard to notice during routine testing. The affected parties include all token holders who rely on the correct calculation of rewards, the protocol’s overall tokenomics, and any downstream services that assume accurate balance reporting. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that reviewed state transitions in the emergency handling logic. To remediate the problem, the emergencyWithdraw function should explicitly set the user’s bonus and duration ratios to zero (or otherwise invalidate them) before completing the withdrawal, ensuring that subsequent reward calculations start from a clean state. This correction restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents reward manipulation after an emergency period.

title: Add a timelock to `PaladinRewardReserve` functions
description: The owner of PaladinRewardReserve can approve and transfer any amount of tokens with no limits on any account. This is not good for investors. To give more trust to users: these functions should be put behind a timelock.
poc:
[PaladinRewardReserve.sol#L28](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/PaladinRewardReserve.sol#L28)  

[PaladinRewardReserve.sol#L52](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/PaladinRewardReserve.sol#L52)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PaladinRewardReserve contract where the privileged owner (initially a multisig) is able to call approve and transfer functions for any ERC20 token without any amount limits or timing restrictions. This unrestricted authority originates from the lack of a governance‑controlled timelock or any additional checks that would normally enforce a delay or community approval before moving funds. An attacker who gains control of the owner address, or a malicious decision taken by the multisig, can instantly approve a spender for an arbitrary token balance and then transfer the full amount to an arbitrary address. From the user's perspective, this manifests as a sudden disappearance of funds that were expected to be held securely in the reserve; investors may see their balances drop to zero or notice that expected reward payouts never arrive. The issue is triggered whenever the owner executes the approve or transfer functions, which currently have no guardrails, and it affects all token holders who rely on the reserve for rewards or safety. It was identified during a formal audit where the auditors noted the absence of a timelock mechanism that is standard in many DAO‑controlled vaults. The problem can be difficult to spot because the functions themselves appear standard and the contract compiles without errors, yet the governance model silently trusts a single party with unrestricted power. To remediate, the contract should be modified to place approve and transfer calls behind a timelock governed by the Paladin DAO, ideally requiring multi‑signature approval and a predefined delay before execution, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected trust model and preventing immediate, unapproved fund movements.

title: Function `cooldown
description:
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L228-L235](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L228-L235)  

Function cooldown() is not protected when protocol is in emergency mode.  
Its behavior is not consistent with the other major functions defined.
poc: Contract Name : HolyPaladinToken.sol Function cooldown()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a state‑changing function that is intended to be disabled when the protocol enters its emergency mode, but the function lacks the protective check that other critical functions have. During an emergency, the contract sets a global flag that should block all operations capable of altering token balances, cooldown periods, or any timing‑dependent state. Because the cooldown() function does not verify this flag, it can still be invoked while the system is supposedly paused. The root cause is a missing guard clause – typically a require(!emergency) or a revert with an EmergencyBlock error – that was added to the rest of the contract but omitted here, likely due to an oversight during development or code refactoring. An attacker, or any user, can call cooldown() while the emergency flag is true, resetting or shortening the cooldown timer that the protocol relies on to limit withdrawals, stake releases, or other privileged actions. By manipulating the cooldown timer, the attacker can bypass the intended safety window, potentially withdrawing funds or performing actions that should be prohibited during the emergency shutdown. The impact is that the emergency mechanism does not provide a complete freeze, exposing user funds to premature access, creating an unfair advantage for those who discover the flaw, and undermining the protocol’s guarantee of safety during critical incidents. The issue manifests only when the contract is in emergency mode; under normal operation the function behaves as expected, which makes it easy to miss during standard testing. The flaw was discovered by auditors during a code review that compared the implementation of cooldown() against other privileged functions and noticed the inconsistent handling of the emergency flag. Because the function may appear harmless and does not directly move funds, the bug can be overlooked until an emergency is triggered. To remediate the issue, the function should include the same emergency check used by the rest of the contract, for example: if (emergency) revert EmergencyBlock(); thereby ensuring that no state changes can occur while the protocol is paused. This correction restores the intended invariant that all mutable actions are blocked during emergencies, preserving the protocol’s security guarantees and preventing scenarios where users see their expected cooldown period ignored, leading to unexpected fund withdrawals or missing expected delays.

title: `UserLock` information can be found during emergency mode
description:
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L446-L468](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L446-L468)  

When the contract is in blocked state (emergency mode), the protocol wants to return an empty UserLock info, on calling the function getUserLock. However, there is another way, by which the users can find the same information.

The below function is not protected when in emergency mode, and users can use this alternatively. Line#466 function getUserPastLock(address user, uint256 blockNumber)
poc:
Contract Name : HolyPaladinToken.sol  
Functions getUserLock and getUserPastLock
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the exposure of user lock information when the HolyPaladinToken contract is placed in emergency (blocked) mode. In normal operation, the public view function getUserLock is designed to return an empty lock structure while the protocol is in emergency, thereby hiding users' staking positions. However, the auxiliary view function getUserPastLock(address user, uint256 blockNumber) lacks any check for the emergency flag and remains callable. As a result, any caller can query a specific block number and retrieve the exact lock details (amount, start time, unlock schedule) that should be concealed during the emergency state. The root cause is an omitted access control condition on getUserPastLock; the developer assumed that only getUserLock needed protection, overlooking that both functions expose the same underlying storage. An attacker can simply invoke getUserPastLock with a recent block number and read the lock data, which may reveal the amount of tokens a user has locked, the vesting schedule, and the remaining time until unlock. This information leakage compromises user privacy and can be leveraged for market manipulation, front‑running, or targeted attacks, as adversaries gain insight into participants' financial commitments while the protocol is supposed to be in a safe, paused state. The issue manifests only when the contract is switched to emergency mode, and it affects all users whose lock information is stored, as well as the protocol itself because the disclosed data undermines the intended confidentiality of the emergency pause. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which examined the contract's state‑dependent logic and identified that getUserPastLock was not guarded. The flaw can be difficult to notice because both functions are view‑only and appear harmless, and testing often focuses on the primary function (getUserLock) without checking alternative read paths. To remediate the problem, the contract should include an emergency‑mode guard in getUserPastLock that mirrors the behavior of getUserLock – either reverting with an EmergencyBlock error or returning an empty Lock struct – and optionally restrict the call to privileged addresses (admin or owner) if the information must be accessible for internal purposes. This change restores the intended privacy guarantees and aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented emergency protocol.

title: Emergency mode enable/disable issue
description: Enabling emergency mode should be one way process that sets contract(s) in emergency mode. It should be not possible to revert that process, otherwise it puts owner of the contract(s) in very privileged position. Owner can trigger emergency mode, perform emergency withdrawal operations without any restrictions and then disable emergency mode.
poc: [HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1425](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/9c26ec8556298fb1dc3cf71f471aadad3a5c74a0/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1425)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the emergency‑mode control flow of the HolyPaladinToken contract. The contract exposes a function called triggerEmergencyWithdraw that accepts a Boolean parameter named trigger, which determines whether the internal emergency flag is set to true (emergency mode enabled) or false (emergency mode disabled). Because this parameter is unrestricted for the contract owner, the owner can arbitrarily turn emergency mode on, execute any logic that is permitted only while the flag is true—most notably an emergency withdrawal that bypasses normal access controls—and immediately turn the flag back off by calling the same function with trigger set to false. The root cause is the design of the emergency switch as a reversible, one‑step operation rather than a one‑way transition; the contract does not enforce immutability of the emergency state once it has been entered. An attacker who controls the admin role can therefore exploit the contract by enabling emergency mode, draining or reallocating user funds without further restriction, and then disabling emergency mode to hide the abuse and restore the contract to a normal‑looking state. The impact is a loss of user assets and a breach of trust: users expect that emergency mode is a protective fail‑safe that can only be entered to safeguard their balances, not a mechanism that the owner can toggle at will. This issue manifests whenever the admin (in the audited version a single‑signer owner) calls triggerEmergencyWithdraw, which is possible during any normal transaction; the problem is amplified if the admin is a single key rather than a multisig, because there is no collective oversight. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the presence of a reversible emergency flag placed the owner in an excessively privileged position, contrary to the intended design of a one‑way emergency shutdown. Detection is non‑trivial because the function signature appears legitimate and the emergency flag is commonly used in many contracts; the reversible nature is subtle and may be missed if the reviewer does not trace the state transition logic or consider post‑withdrawal actions. To remediate, the boolean trigger parameter should be eliminated, and the emergency flag should be set to true unconditionally when the function is executed, without providing any path to reset it to false within the same function. Control over disabling emergency mode, if required, should be moved to a separate governance process with robust multi‑signature approval, ensuring that no single actor can both enable emergency mode and later revert it after exploiting the privileged state. In practice, this transforms the emergency mechanism from a mutable toggle into a one‑way safeguard that aligns with the expectation that users can exit the system safely during an incident, while preventing the owner from abusing the same path to siphon funds and then hide the event.

title: Users with large `cooldown`s can grief other users
description: If an account has a large cooldown, that account can grief other accounts that are waiting for their own cooldowns, by sending small amounts to them.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the token contract updates a user’s cooldown period on every incoming transfer. When a transfer is executed, the contract computes a new cooldown for the receiver by taking a weighted average of the sender’s current cooldown and the receiver’s existing cooldown, where the weights are the transferred amount and the receiver’s existing balance. Because the calculation does not impose any cap on how much the sender’s cooldown can influence the result, an attacker who has accumulated a very large cooldown can send an arbitrarily small amount of tokens to a victim and cause the victim’s cooldown to jump close to the attacker’s value. This means that a user who is waiting for their own cooldown to finish – for example before they can unstake or claim rewards – can be forced to wait much longer than expected simply because another user transferred a tiny amount to their address. The issue manifests as a denial‑of‑service style grief attack: the victim’s balance appears unchanged, the UI shows the correct token amount, but any operation that checks the cooldown (such as a withdrawal or unstake) fails with a “cooldown not finished” error. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that they attempt to withdraw after the expected waiting period and receive nothing, or see the transaction reverted, even though their token balance is sufficient. The root cause is the lack of a safeguard limiting the impact of a sender’s cooldown on the receiver’s cooldown, combined with the fact that the contract applies this logic to every external transfer, not only to self‑transfers. The bug was discovered during a static analysis audit of the _beforeTokenTransfer hook, where the code was examined and the mathematically unbounded influence of the sender’s cooldown was identified. It can be hard to notice because the transferred amount may be negligible, making the operation look normal, while the hidden state (cooldown) changes dramatically. This type of flaw belongs to the class of economic denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities where an attacker can inflate time‑locked state variables of other participants. The impact is not a loss of funds but a disruption of protocol functionality: users cannot access their staked assets when expected, which harms user experience and can affect the protocol’s availability. A proper mitigation is to restrict the cooldown update so that a single transfer can increase the receiver’s cooldown by at most one step, or to require the transferred amount to be proportional to the receiver’s balance (a financial safeguard), thereby preventing a small transfer from having a disproportionate effect. Alternatively, the contract could ignore cooldown updates on inbound transfers from accounts with a cooldown exceeding a certain threshold, or only apply the update on self‑transfers. Implementing such a check restores the intended business logic that cooldowns reflect a user’s own staking activity, not the state of arbitrary third parties.

title: Users Can Bypass Emergency Restrictions on `updateUserRewardState
description:
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1338-L1378](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/main/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1338-L1378)  
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L876-L906](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/main/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L876-L906)

The `emergencyWithdraw()` function intends to withdraw their tokens regardless if they are locked up for any duration. This emergency must be triggered by the owner of the contract by calling `triggerEmergencyWithdraw()`. A number of functions will revert when the protocol is in an emergency state, including all stake, lock, unlock and kick actions and the updating of a user’s rewards. However, a user could bypass the restriction on `_updateUserRewards()` by transferring a small amount of unlocked tokens to their account. `_beforeTokenTransfer()` will call `_updateUserRewards()` on the `from` and `to` accounts. As a result, users can continue to accrue rewards while the protocol is in an emergency state and it makes sense for users to delay their emergency withdraw as they will be able to claim a higher proportion of the allocated rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an unintended interaction between the contract's emergency‑withdraw mechanism and its reward‑updating logic. When the owner calls `triggerEmergencyWithdraw()`, a global boolean `emergency` is set to true and the protocol is expected to freeze all reward accruals; functions that stake, lock, unlock, kick, or otherwise modify a user’s reward state deliberately revert during this period. However, the internal hook `_beforeTokenTransfer()` is programmed to invoke `_updateUserRewards()` for both the sender and the receiver of every token transfer. Because the hook does not check the `emergency` flag, a user can initiate a trivial token transfer – for example, moving a small amount of unlocked tokens to their own address – and thereby trigger `_updateUserRewards()` even while the contract is in emergency mode. This bypass allows the user’s reward balance to keep increasing, contrary to the protocol’s design that rewards should be frozen until the emergency is resolved. The impact is that a malicious or opportunistic holder can accrue additional rewards during the emergency window, potentially claim a larger share of the reward pool when they finally execute `emergencyWithdraw()`. The effect is a distortion of the tokenomics and an unfair advantage over honest participants, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions about reward stagnation are violated. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as the normal expectation that "my rewards stop growing during an emergency" is broken; instead, users may notice that their reward balance continues to rise despite the emergency flag being active, and the protocol may later distribute more rewards than intended. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s state‑transition functions, where the auditor noticed that the reward‑update call in `_beforeTokenTransfer()` lacked any guard against the emergency state. Because the transfer hook is a low‑level internal function, the problem can be easily overlooked, especially when only larger or explicit staking actions are examined. To remediate the issue, the contract should either prevent `_beforeTokenTransfer()` from calling `_updateUserRewards()` when `emergency` is true, or make `_updateUserRewards()` itself early‑return when the protocol is in emergency mode. Either approach restores the intended invariant that reward accrual is paused during emergencies, aligning the contract behavior with its documented security posture.

title: Increasing the Lock Amount on an Expired Lock Will Cause Users to Miss Out on Rewards
description:
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L284-L294](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/main/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L284-L294)  
[HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1137-L1233](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-paladin/blob/main/contracts/HolyPaladinToken.sol#L1137-L1233)

Paladin protocol allows users to increase the amount or duration of their lock while it is stil active. Increasing the amount of an active lock should only increase the total locked amount and it shouldn’t make any changes to the associated bonus ratios as the duration remains unchanged.

However, if a user increases the lock amount on an expired lock, a new lock will be created with the duration of the previous lock and the provided non-zero amount. Because the `action != LockAction.INCREASE_AMOUNT` check later on in the function does not hold true, `userCurrentBonusRatio` will contain the last updated value from the previous lock. As a result, the user will not receive any rewards for their active lock and they will need to increase the duration of the lock to fix lock’s bonus ratio.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward‑calculation logic of the Paladin protocol’s token lock mechanism. When a user creates a lock, the contract records a bonus ratio that determines how many rewards the lock will earn over its remaining duration. The protocol permits users to increase either the amount or the duration of an active (non‑expired) lock without affecting the bonus ratio for a duration change, or without recalculating it for an amount change. The flaw appears when a user attempts to increase the locked amount after the original lock has already expired. In that scenario the contract creates a new lock using the expired lock’s original duration and the newly supplied amount, but it fails to reset or recompute the bonus ratio because the condition that checks for a pure amount increase (`action != LockAction.INCREASE_AMOUNT`) evaluates to false. Consequently, the new lock inherits the last bonus ratio that was associated with the expired lock, which is effectively zero for rewards. Users therefore receive no rewards for the newly funded lock even though they expect the same or higher reward accrual, and the only way to restore the reward flow is to also increase the lock’s duration, which updates the bonus ratio. This bug manifests only when the lock is expired at the time of the amount increase; it does not affect normal extensions of active locks. The impact is that users lose expected token rewards, see their balance remain unchanged after performing an increase, and may become confused or think the protocol is malfunctioning or malicious. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the HolyPaladinToken contract, where the audit team traced the state transition logic and identified that the bonus ratio was not being refreshed for the specific edge case of amount‑only increases on expired locks. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a warning or error; the transaction succeeds, but the reward accounting silently yields zero, which may be attributed to normal variations in reward distribution by an inexperienced observer. The bug belongs to a class of state‑inconsistency or accounting‑logic errors where derived values (bonus ratios) are not updated after a state change that should trigger a recalculation. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid amount increases on expired locks or explicitly recompute the bonus ratio whenever a new lock is instantiated from an expired one, ensuring that the reward formula reflects the current lock parameters. In user‑facing terms, a participant who adds more tokens to an old lock expects a higher or at least unchanged reward, but instead receives nothing, leading to a mismatch between expectation (“my lock should earn rewards”) and reality (the reward balance stays at zero).

title: Precision loss in boostPrice in V
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the boostPrice view function of the V3AMO contract, which belongs to the class of fixed‑point arithmetic rounding errors. The function computes the price of the BOOST token relative to a stablecoin using integer arithmetic. When the stablecoin price is only modestly higher than the BOOST price (for example 20 % higher) the execution follows the branch where sqrtPriceX96 is greater than or equal to the Q96 constant. In that branch the code divides the expression (sqrtPriceX96**2 / Q96**2) before applying it as a denominator. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the ratio that should be a fractional value (e.g., 0.8) is rounded down to 1. Consequently the final price is calculated as 10**(boostDecimals‑usdDecimals+PRICE_DECIMALS) / 1, which corresponds to a reported price of 1 (scaled) instead of the expected 0.8. This mis‑reported price propagates to downstream logic, most notably the public unfarmBuyBurn() function, which checks that the newly computed boost price stays within a predefined upper bound. The inflated price causes the check newBoostPrice > boostUpperPriceBuy to fail, triggering a revert with PriceNotInRange. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts, they receive no tokens, and the UI may show an unexpected “price out of range” error or a missing balance update. The bug is triggered only under the specific condition that boost is cheaper than the stablecoin and the pool’s sqrtPriceX96 is at least Q96, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the function still returns a plausible integer value. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the researcher Sherlock, who reproduced the problem by initializing the pool with a sqrtPriceX96 value 10 % above 2**96 and observing that boostPrice returned 1,000,000 (the scaled representation of 1) instead of the expected 800,000. The root cause is the order of operations that forces a division before a multiplication, leading to loss of fractional precision. To fix the problem the calculation should be rearranged to perform multiplication first or, preferably, use a high‑precision arithmetic library such as FullMath.mulDiv to compute (boostDecimals‑usdDecimals+PRICE_DECIMALS) * Q96**2 / sqrtPriceX96**2 without intermediate truncation. Adding explicit rounding or checking for denominator values less than one can also mitigate the error. By correcting the arithmetic, the reported boost price will reflect the true market ratio, allowing unfarmBuyBurn calls to succeed and preserving the intended economic behavior of the protocol.

title: The V3AMO._mintAndSellBoost(
description:
The protocol mints BOOST tokens and sells them for USD using the _mintAndSellBoost() function for V3 DEXes. Since Velodrome, Aerodrome, Fenix, Thena and Ramses are parts of the V3 DEXes, they should be compatible. However, the _mintAndSellBoost() function does not work with the DEXes due to incorrect function parameters. In the _mintAndSellBoost() function, it mints BOOST tokens and swaps them for USD tokens.
```solidity
(int256 amount0, int256 amount1) = IV3Pool(pool).swap(
    address(this),
    boost < usd,
    int256(boostAmount), // Amount of BOOST tokens being swapped
    targetSqrtPriceX96, // The target square root price

```
However, the swap() function of Velodrome, Aerodrome, Fenix, Thena and Ramses has different parameters.
```solidity
function swap(
    address recipient,
    bool zeroToOne,
    int256 amountRequired,
    uint160 limitSqrtPrice,
    bytes calldata data
) external override returns (int256 amount0, int256 amount1) {
```
As a result, the _mintAndSellBoost() function does not work with Velodrome, Aerodrome, Fenix, Thena and Ramses due to incorrect function parameters. Internal pre-conditions For convenience, let's assume that the USD token is USDC from this point forward. price back down to peg. External pre-conditions • The BOOST-USDC price diverges from peg and BOOST is trading above $1 in Velodrome. Attack Path It reverts. The mintAndSellBoost(), mintSellFarm() functions will be permanently DoSed for OST and sell them for USDC to bring the price back down to peg.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the _mintAndSellBoost function that is intended to mint BOOST tokens and immediately swap them for USDC on V3‑style DEXes. The implementation assumes that every V3 pool exposes a swap(address,bool,int256,uint160,int256) signature, and therefore calls IV3Pool(pool).swap with parameters (address(this), boost < usd, int256(boostAmount), targetSqrtPriceX96, minUsdAmountOut, deadline). In reality the deployed DEX contracts – Velodrome, Aerodrome, Fenix, Thena and Ramses – implement a different swap interface: swap(address recipient,bool zeroToOne,int256 amountRequired,uint160 limitSqrtPrice,bytes calldata data) returns (int256 amount0,int256 amount1). Because the call supplies six arguments of mismatched types, the external call reverts at runtime. The root cause is an incorrect external contract interface assumption, a classic ABI mismatch bug. When the protocol price diverges and the system tries to correct the BOOST‑USDC peg by invoking mintAndSellBoost, the transaction fails, leaving the newly minted BOOST tokens un‑sold and the price correction mechanism disabled. From a user perspective the transaction appears to succeed up to the point of the swap, then reverts with no USDC received; users may see a “swap failed” error or simply receive zero USDC after expecting a refund. The impact includes a denial‑of‑service condition for the price‑stabilisation path, potential loss of confidence, and economic damage because the protocol cannot bring BOOST back to its $1 peg. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected V3 pool interface with the actual code of the supported DEXes. It is hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not check external contract signatures, and the mismatch only manifests when the function is executed on‑chain. The appropriate remediation is to replace the generic IV3Pool call with the correct interface for each DEX, passing the required five arguments in the order and types defined by the pool contract, and to handle the returned amounts accordingly. This fixes the ABI mismatch and restores the ability of the protocol to mint BOOST and sell it for USDC, re‑enabling the peg‑maintenance mechanism.

title: Boost can be sold under peg de-
poc: Not required according to the terms
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑peg enforcement flaw in the AMO contracts that handle mint‑and‑sell of the BOOST token. The code attempts to prevent selling BOOST below the 1:1 peg with USDC by adjusting a minimum USD output variable, but it only checks the current conversion rate and does not verify that the pool price after the trade remains at or above the peg. Consequently, when the pool is initially imbalanced (e.g., 90 BOOST and 110 USDC) a call to _mintAndSellBoost with 20 BOOST will succeed, leaving the pool with 110 BOOST and 90 USDC. The first portion of the sale occurs while the price is still above the peg, but the remaining BOOST is sold after the pool has crossed the 1:1 balance point, meaning those BOOST tokens are exchanged for less than one USDC each. An additional check that compares the reported USD amount out with the change in the USDC balance is ineffective because, in the absence of transfer fees, the two values are always equal, so the revert never triggers. The root cause is the missing invariant that the post‑trade price must stay ≥ peg; the contract only enforces a pre‑trade minimum output, not a post‑trade price constraint. An attacker or any user can trigger the function repeatedly, causing the protocol to sell BOOST at a price below the intended peg, which results in a loss equal to the area under the price curve below the peg. In the numeric example the protocol loses roughly 1.0 USDC, about 5 % of the value moved in the transaction, and larger de‑pegs would amplify the loss. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as a discrepancy between the expected 1 USDC per BOOST and the actual amount received; users may see their USDC balance decrease more than anticipated or notice that after a series of sales the pool’s price is no longer 1:1, violating the business logic that BOOST should never be sold at a discount. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s readme‑stated invariant and the corresponding Solidity checks. It is subtle because the code contains explicit ‘peg‑protection’ comments and a revert that appears to guard the invariant, yet both checks are logically insufficient, making the problem easy to overlook. The proper fix is to enforce that the pool’s sqrt price after the sale remains at or above the 1:1 level, for example by calculating the resulting reserves and reverting if the post‑trade price would fall below the peg, or by using a fee‑adjusted minimum‑output formula that accounts for price impact. This would restore the intended invariant that BOOST cannot be sold for less than its peg value, preventing fund loss and preserving protocol accounting integrity.

title: V2AMO and V3AMO: USDT Ap-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the ERC‑20 interface used by the V2AMO and V3AMO contracts and the actual behaviour of the USDT token contract. Both AMO contracts import OpenZeppelin's IERC20Upgradeable interface, which defines the approve(address spender,uint256 amount) function as returning a boolean value that indicates success. USDT, however, implements approve as a non‑standard function that does not return any value. When the AMO contracts call IERC20Upgradeable(usd).approve(pool, amount) inside the internal functions _addLiquidity() and _unfarmBuyBurn(), the Solidity runtime expects a boolean to be returned. Because USDT returns no data, the call triggers a low‑level revert, causing the whole transaction to fail. The root cause is therefore an assumption in the contract code that all ERC‑20 tokens conform to the standard return‑value convention, which is violated by USDT’s legacy implementation. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply supplying USDT as the USD token is sufficient to cause the failure. The impact is that any attempt to add liquidity to the BOOST‑USD pool or to unwind a position using USDT will revert, leaving the user’s transaction unexecuted and the funds untouched. From a user’s perspective the UI will report a failed transaction, often with a generic “revert” message, while the user expected the liquidity to be added and possibly to receive BOOST tokens. The protocol’s accounting logic assumes that the approve call succeeds, so the failure breaks the expected flow of depositing, farming, and withdrawing USDT, effectively resulting in a denial‑of‑service for that stablecoin. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the AMO contracts, where the auditor noticed that the approve calls were not wrapped in a safety check and that USDT’s source code does not return a bool. The problem can be subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the revert only occurs at runtime when interacting with USDT, making it easy to miss in basic testing that only uses standard ERC‑20 tokens. To remediate the issue the contracts should replace direct approve calls with a safe approval pattern, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeApprove, which handles tokens that do not return a boolean by checking the call’s success flag and the returned data length. Alternatively, a wrapper contract could be deployed for USDT that implements a compliant approve function, or the AMO logic could be refactored to avoid relying on approve altogether. By using a safe approval method the contracts will no longer revert when dealing with USDT, restoring the intended liquidity‑adding and unfarming functionality and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Contracts of the codebase will
description: Contracts of the codebase isn't strictly compliant with the ERC-1504. This breaks the readme. As per readme: Is the codebase expected to comply with any EIPs? Can there be/are there any deviations from the specification? Strictly compliant: ERC-1504: Upgradable Smart Contract But the contracts of the codebase uses openzepplin upgradable contracts as base contract which are not compliant with ERC-1504. As per ERC-1504, the upgradable contract should consists of have handler contract, data contract and optionally the upgrader contract. But the contracts of the codebase are not compliant with ERC-1504 because they has no data contract and has data inside the handler contract. Internal pre-conditions External pre-conditions Attack Path Break the readme.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the smart‑contract system does not follow the ERC‑1504 upgradable contract pattern. ERC‑1504 requires a three‑component architecture: a handler contract that contains only logic, a separate data contract that stores all state variables, and optionally an upgrader contract that mediates upgrades. In the audited codebase the developers built the contracts on top of OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable proxy pattern, which stores state variables directly in the handler (logic) contract and does not provide a distinct data contract. This architectural deviation is the root cause: the design assumes that the proxy’s storage layout will remain compatible across upgrades, but ERC‑1504 explicitly forbids mixing logic and data in the same contract because it makes upgrade safety checks impossible. An attacker could exploit this mismatch by triggering an upgrade that changes the storage layout, causing variables to be overwritten, corrupted, or lost. Because the system lacks a dedicated data contract, there is no automated verification that new implementations preserve the exact storage slots, so a malicious or even accidental upgrade could silently erase user balances, break permission checks, or cause the contract to behave inconsistently. The impact is that funds held by the protocol, user balances, or governance state may become inaccessible or incorrectly modified, leading to loss of assets or a breach of trust. The issue manifests whenever an upgrade transaction is executed, which in practice occurs during normal governance or maintenance cycles. All participants who interact with the contract—users depositing tokens, lenders, borrowers, or governance voters—are potentially affected because their stored data resides in a contract that is not protected by the ERC‑1504 safety guarantees. The problem was discovered during a manual compliance audit that compared the deployed contracts against the ERC‑1504 specification listed in the project’s README. It is easy to miss because the contracts compile and function correctly under normal operation; the non‑compliance is a structural property that does not raise compiler warnings. To remediate, the codebase should be refactored to separate logic and storage according to ERC‑1504: introduce a dedicated data contract that holds all state variables, keep the handler contract free of storage, and optionally add an upgrader contract that enforces storage‑layout compatibility before any upgrade. This redesign restores the intended safety checks of ERC‑1504 and prevents accidental or malicious state corruption during upgrades.

title: MasterAMO should not use the
description: MasterAMO is a utils contract that intended to be inherited by V2AMO, V3AMO contracts, therefore. it's initializer function should not use the initializer modifier, instead, it should use onlyInitializing modifier. In the MasterAMO.sol:104 contract, the initialize function uses the initializer modifier. This is incorrect for a contract like MasterAMO, which is meant to be inherited by other contracts, such as V2AMO and V3AMO. In this inheritance model, the V2AMO contract also has its own initialize function, which includes the initializer modifier and calls the initialize function of MasterAMO. The problem here is that both the parent contract MasterAMO and the child contracts V2AMO, V3AMO are using the initializer modifier, which limits initialization to only one call. According to the OpenZeppelin documentation, the onlyInitializing modifier should be used to allow initialization in both the parent and child contracts. The onlyInitializing modifier ensures that when the initialize function is called, any contracts in its inheritance chain can still complete their own initialization. https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/proxy#Initializable-initializer-- A modifier that defines a protected initializer function that can be invoked at most once. In its scope, onlyInitializing functions can be used to initialize parent contracts. Internal pre-conditions External pre-conditions Attack Path In this scenario, no direct attack or monetary loss is likely. However, the vulnerability causes a significant operational issue, preventing inheriting contracts from completing initialization. This could lead to a failure in the deployment of critical protocol components, affecting the overall system functionality.
poc: A simple POC in Remix.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper use of the OpenZeppelin Initializable pattern in the MasterAMO utility contract. MasterAMO is designed to be a base contract that other AMO implementations (V2AMO, V3AMO) inherit from, and its initialize function is marked with the initializer modifier. The initializer modifier can be executed only once across the entire inheritance chain, which means that when a child contract also defines an initialize function with the initializer modifier and calls the parent’s initialize, the second call is blocked. As a result the child contract’s own initialization logic never runs, causing the deployment transaction to revert or leave the contract in an uninitialized state. This occurs whenever MasterAMO is inherited and the child contract also uses the initializer modifier, which is the typical pattern for upgradeable contracts. The root cause is the misuse of the initializer modifier in a contract that is intended to be part of an inheritance hierarchy; the correct modifier for a parent contract in such a hierarchy is onlyInitializing, which permits parent initialization while still allowing child contracts to run their own initializer. From a user’s point of view the symptom is a failed deployment or a contract that appears on‑chain but cannot perform any AMO functions, leading to missing balances, zero‑output operations, or a UI that shows the AMO component as unavailable. No direct monetary loss is observed because the contract never becomes operational, but the protocol’s critical components cannot be launched, effectively halting the peg‑maintenance mechanism and reducing overall system functionality. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s inheritance structure against OpenZeppelin’s documentation. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles and the modifier does not raise a warning; the failure only manifests at runtime when the child contract attempts to initialize. The bug belongs to the class of upgradeable‑contract initialization flaws where parent and child contracts both use a single‑call initializer, violating the expected initialization flow. To remediate, the initialize function in MasterAMO should be changed from initializer to onlyInitializing, allowing the parent’s initialization to execute while still permitting each child contract to run its own initializer safely.

title: Redemption fees can be manipulated dur-
description: During Recovery mode, the borrowing fees are waived (not charged) when opening a den, this can be taken advantage by a malicious borrower to manipulate the redemption fees. All he can do is to open a den with large debt during recovery mode with no borrowing fees and this will directly affect the redemption rate because redemption rate computation depend on total borrowed amount of the system and collateral being redeemed. The lower the collateral being redeemed compared to total debt of the system, the lower the redemption fees that will be charge for that collateral. Look at the function below in line 507, total debt supply can be inflated in which will lower the redemption rate at the end. This is true specially if the collateral being drawn or redeemed is much smaller compared to total debt of the system. File: DenManager.sol 498: function _updateBaseRateFromRedemption( 499: uint256 _collateralDrawn, 500: uint256 _price, 501: uint256 _totalDebtSupply 502: ) internal returns (uint256) { 503: uint256 decayedBaseRate = _calcDecayedBaseRate(); 504: 505: /* Convert the drawn collateral back to debt at face value rate (1 debt:1 USD), in order to get 506: * the fraction of total supply that was redeemed at face value. */ 507: uint256 redeemedDebtFraction = (_collateralDrawn * _price) / the redemption rate at the end 508: 509: uint256 newBaseRate = decayedBaseRate + (redeemedDebtFraction / BETA); 510: newBaseRate = BeraborrowMath._min(newBaseRate, DECIMAL_PRECISION); // cap baseRate at a maximum of 100% 511: 512: // Update the baseRate state variable 513: baseRate = newBaseRate; 514: emit BaseRateUpdated(newBaseRate); 515: 516: _updateLastFeeOpTime(); 517: 518: return newBaseRate; 519: } 520: The root cause is allowing malicious actor an opportunity to manipulate redemption rate through inflating the total debt of the system through opening a den with large debt. There should be somehow way to discourage them for doing this and the solution will be applying borrowing fees during Recovery mode period. Internal Pre-conditions The system is in recovery mode. External Pre-conditions Attack Path This can be the scenario. 1. An attacker has a remaining open Den in the protocol. Let's call it Den A with 1e18 debt. 2. The protocol enters into Recovery Mode. 3. The attacker knowing the vulnerability, open another Den with very large debt of 1e20. Let's call it Den B 4. Since the total debt of the system increases significantly, this will affect redemption fee rate for redeeming Den A and becomes lower. 5. Attacker take advantage of the situation and redeemed Den A with lower redemption fee. 6. Attacker closes Den B as if nothing happened and system back into original state. Manipulation of redemption fees to lower it. Loss of funds for the protocol
bug_full: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the redemption fee calculation that becomes possible when the protocol is in recovery mode. In recovery mode the contract waives borrowing fees for newly opened positions (Dens). Because the redemption fee is derived from the ratio of the amount of collateral being redeemed to the total outstanding debt of the system, an attacker can artificially inflate the total debt by opening a very large Den with no borrowing cost. The inflated debt reduces the fraction of debt that is considered redeemed, which in turn lowers the redemption fee applied to any subsequent redemption of collateral from other positions. An attacker who already has a small Den can trigger recovery mode, open a huge debt position, then redeem the collateral of the small Den and pay a much smaller fee than would be expected. After the redemption the attacker can close the large debt position, leaving the protocol with reduced fee revenue and effectively a loss of funds. The issue occurs only while the system flag recoveryMode is true and borrowing fees are disabled; it relies on the fact that the redemption rate calculation uses the current total debt supply without excluding newly created debt that has not yet incurred fees. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by observing that the _updateBaseRateFromRedemption function computes redeemedDebtFraction based on _totalDebtSupply, which can be increased arbitrarily by opening a Den. The problem is subtle because the fee reduction is not obvious from the UI – users see the usual redemption transaction succeed but receive less fee charged, which may appear as a normal variation. From a user perspective the symptom is that a redemption that should cost, for example, 5 % of the withdrawn collateral may only charge 0.5 % or even less, leading to an unexpected surplus of funds for the redeemer and a shortfall for the protocol. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of economic manipulation through state‑inflation where fee or interest calculations depend on mutable global aggregates. The recommended mitigation is to re‑introduce a borrowing fee even during recovery mode, preferably a reduced fee that still discourages the creation of massive debt solely for fee manipulation, or to adjust the redemption fee formula so that it excludes debt that has not yet been subject to borrowing fees. Implementing such a guard restores the intended accounting invariant that the redemption fee reflects the true proportion of debt being retired, thereby preventing the protocol from losing revenue.

title: Anyone can avoid receiving bad debt dis-
description: The protocol implements redistribution of a liquidated Den's bad debt during its liquidation. This bad debt will be shared to the remaining dens of the Den Manager. However, any user can prevent receiving bad debt if they will close their dens right before liquidation. This could result race condition and every one want to close their dens. If there is only 1 den remained open, he will receive all bad debts which will further increase his debt. This can have a devastating impact because either he will be forced to pay that debt to recover the collateral or be liquidated. There is no preventive measure applied by the protocol in this kind of situation. The current protocol design somehow allows it to happen. Closing of den can be freely executed anytime the user want in which can't be help during this kind of situation. Internal Pre-conditions 1. Den with large bad debt is being liquidated. External Pre-conditions Attack Path This can be the scenario. 1. There are 3 remaining dens in the den manager. Den A, B and C. 2. Den A and B each hold the same amount of collateral and debt and in healthy state while C is in near liquidation risk. 3. Suddenly, collateral price drops and Den C accumulated bad debt. 4. Den B owner knew about vulnerability and immediately closed his den right before liquidation. 5. At this point, only 1 den remaining which is Den A, in which it receives all bad debt distribution from Den C liquidation. This can impact the remaining Dens that will unfairly receive the bad debt. This will increase their debt and forced to pay for it to recover their collateral or avoid liquidation.
poc: See attack path
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition in the liquidation and debt‑redistribution logic of the protocol that manages multiple dens. When a den accumulates bad debt and is liquidated, the protocol is designed to spread that bad debt across all still‑open dens managed by the same Den Manager. The root cause is that the contract allows any user to close (withdraw) their den at any moment without a lock‑up or protection period, even when a liquidation event is imminent. Because the closing operation removes the den from the pool before the bad‑debt distribution step, the closed den is excluded from receiving any portion of the bad debt. An attacker can monitor market conditions, detect that a particular den is about to be liquidated due to a price drop, and close his own den a few seconds before the liquidation transaction is executed. After the attacker’s den is closed, the remaining open dens – possibly only one – receive the entire bad‑debt amount that originated from the liquidated den. This results in a sudden and disproportionate increase in the debt of the surviving den(s). The impact is that the affected den owner sees his debt balance jump, may be forced to repay a much larger amount to recover collateral, or may be liquidated himself because the newly added debt pushes the position below the required collateralisation ratio. The condition occurs only during a liquidation trigger, i.e., when collateral prices fall sharply and a den becomes under‑collateralised. All den owners are potentially affected because the fairness of debt sharing is broken; the protocol’s economic assumptions that bad debt is evenly distributed among participants no longer hold. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of calls in the liquidation routine and identified that the close‑den function has no guard against being called in the same block as a liquidation. It is hard to notice because closing a den is a normal user action and the protocol does not emit any warning when a den is closed just before a liquidation, making the problem appear only as an unexpected debt spike after the fact. To remediate the issue the protocol should introduce a protection window that prevents a den from being closed for a short period after a liquidation is announced, or it should ensure that closed dens are still accounted for in the bad‑debt redistribution calculation. In other words, the debt‑sharing mechanism must be made atomic with respect to den closure, guaranteeing that every den that existed at the moment of liquidation receives its fair share of the bad debt. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a price drop and a liquidation, a user may notice that his den’s debt balance has increased dramatically while another user’s den has been closed and received no bad debt, leading to confusion and potential loss of collateral.

title: Wrong slippage check in LSPRouter::
bug_full: The vulnerability is a slippage‑protection logic error in the LSPRouter contract’s withdraw function. The function accepts a parameter named minSharesWithdrawn and then asserts that the number of shares returned by the underlying LSP vault is greater than or equal to this value. This check only guarantees that the user receives at least a minimum number of shares, but it does not prevent the vault from burning more shares than the user anticipated. Because the share‑to‑asset ratio in the LSP can decrease under certain conditions—such as when the liquid stability pool offsets more debt than collateral or when the price of the underlying collateral changes between the user’s transaction submission and execution—the number of shares required to represent a given asset amount may rise. In that situation the contract may deduct a larger amount of shares than the user expected while still satisfying the condition shares ≥ minSharesWithdrawn. Consequently a user can experience unexpected slippage, seeing their share balance drop dramatically or even become zero after a withdrawal, despite having set a protective minimum. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the router’s withdrawal path, where the asymmetry between the withdraw and redeem functions was noted: redeem correctly checks a maximum shares limit, whereas withdraw does not. The bug is subtle because the require statement uses a comparison that appears to protect the user, yet it only guards against receiving too few shares, not against receiving too many. Exploitation does not require a malicious actor; any user executing a withdrawal when the LSP ratio is unfavorable can suffer the loss. The impact is a potential loss of funds for any participant who withdraws assets, especially during periods of high volatility or large liquidation events. The contract currently offers no way for callers to specify an upper bound on shares, so users cannot defend themselves against this slippage. The recommended remediation is to replace the minimum‑shares check with a maximum‑shares check (e.g., require(shares <= params.maxSharesWithdrawn,…)) and to expose a corresponding parameter, thereby restoring symmetric protection for both withdraw and redeem operations. This change aligns the function with the intended business logic that users should never be forced to burn more shares than they are willing to accept.

title: Setting peripheryFlashLoanFee does not
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of flash‑loan fees in the DebtToken contract. When a flash‑loan is requested, DebtToken invokes an internal helper _flashFee which queries the per‑contract fee by calling getPeripheryFlashLoanFee on the BeraborrowCore contract. The core of the problem is that getPeripheryFlashLoanFee determines the fee based on the caller (msg.sender) being equal to a specific address (nect). Because the call originates from DebtToken, the msg.sender seen by BeraborrowCore is the BeraborrowCore contract itself, not the MetaBeraborrowCore contract where per‑periphery fees are configured. Consequently the conditional check fails and the function falls back to returning the global DEFAULT_FLASH_LOAN_FEE, ignoring any fee that a periphery contract may have set. This mismatch makes it impossible for a periphery contract to receive a reduced or increased flash‑loan fee; users of that periphery will always be charged the default rate. The issue can be exploited by a malicious or simply unaware periphery contract that expects a lower fee – it will still be charged the default, leading to higher costs than anticipated. From a user perspective the UI may display a normal flash‑loan request, but the actual fee deducted is larger than expected, potentially causing failed arbitrage or profit erosion. The bug manifests whenever flash‑loan fee retrieval is performed through DebtToken, i.e., any flash‑loan initiated via the standard path. It affects all users of the protocol who rely on per‑periphery fee customization, as well as the protocol itself because the economic model assumes that periphery contracts can adjust fees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the tester attempted to set a custom fee for a periphery address and observed that the returned fee remained at the default value. The problem is subtle because the fee calculation code appears syntactically correct and the default fee is a valid number, so no exception is thrown and the discrepancy may only be noticed by comparing expected versus actual fee amounts. To remediate the issue the getPeripheryFlashLoanFee function should be modified to recognise calls that are proxied through BeraborrowCore, for example by passing the original caller as a parameter or by checking against both the core address and the MetaBeraborrowCore address. Alternatively, DebtToken could call MetaBeraborrowCore directly when querying the fee. In either case the logic must ensure that the periphery‑specific fee is correctly returned, restoring the intended ability to increase or decrease flash‑loan fees on a per‑contract basis.

title: InternalizeDonations will never work for
description:
If any tokens are donated to the InfraredCollateralVault, owner can call internalizeDonations and create a linear vesting for the newly donated funds. The exact donated amount is calculated in the following line:
```solidity
uint donatedAmount = IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) - getBalanceOfWithFutureEmissions(token);
```
require(donatedAmount >= amount, "CollVault: insufficient balance"); It subtracts the virtual balance from the actual token balance and treats it as donation. The problem when this asset is the main asset, is that usually the token balance would be 0, while the virtual accounting would be high. This is because all deposited assets get staked directly in the Infrared Vault. This would make the line above revert due to underflow and if any funds are sent as donation, they'd simply remain stuck. Same issue exists also in receiveDonations Logic issue Loss of funds/ Stuck funds, Broken functionality Affected Code edCollateralVault.sol#L237
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the donation internalization routine of the InfraredCollateralVault. The function attempts to determine the amount of newly donated tokens by subtracting a virtual accounting balance (the amount that will be emitted in the future) from the contract's actual token balance. When the primary asset of the vault is used, the contract normally holds zero physical tokens because all deposits are immediately staked in an external Infrared Vault, while the virtual balance remains high due to pending emissions. Consequently, the subtraction yields a negative value, causing the require check to fail and the transaction to revert. This logical error means that any tokens sent as a donation are never recognized as such and become permanently locked in the contract with no vesting schedule created. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the internalizeDonations logic and identified that the accounting model mixes on‑chain balances with off‑chain emission forecasts, leading to an underflow condition. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s balanceOf call returns zero, which appears normal, while the hidden virtual balance is not visible in standard explorers. The impact is that the donation feature is effectively broken: donors see their tokens disappear, the protocol cannot accept external contributions, and the locked funds are unrecoverable without a contract upgrade. The bug violates the fundamental business assumption that any positive token balance should be treated as a donation and vested linearly. To remediate, the contract should either avoid subtracting the virtual balance when calculating donations or adjust the logic to treat any non‑zero token balance as a donation, ensuring that the require statement never reverts under normal operating conditions.

title: InfraredCollateralVault::rebalance()
description: InfraredCollateralVault::rebalance() decreases a currency balance for the asset(). However, the decrease in the sent currency is not capped to the current unlocked balance, allowing balance allocated to future emissions to be used. An attacker can force this by withdrawing some funds in the currency sent used to rebalance, before the admin rebalances, in order to make the rebalance send too many sent currency and DoS the protocol. In InfraredCollateralVault:180, rebalance(), there is no cap in the sent currency to rebalance. Internal Pre-conditions None. External Pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1.
