Attacker frontruns admin rebalance with withdraw() call in the token that is going to be rebalanced by an admin. 2. The rebalance call withdraws too many token, leading to an underflow when calculating the unlocked balance in totalAssets(), 1, 2, 3 DoSing the protocol. All protocol functions are DoSed due to the underflow above.
poc: See above.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the rebalance routine of the InfraredCollateralVault contract. The function is intended to move a specified amount of a given currency from the vault’s unlocked balance to a target allocation, but it fails to enforce a ceiling that limits the withdrawal to the actual unlocked amount currently available. Because the amount to be sent is not capped, an attacker can manipulate the vault’s state by withdrawing part of the same currency immediately before an admin‑initiated rebalance. By front‑running the admin’s transaction with a withdraw call, the attacker reduces the unlocked balance below the amount the rebalance will attempt to transfer. When rebalance then tries to deduct the uncapped amount, the internal accounting calculation for the unlocked balance underflows, causing totalAssets to produce an incorrect (typically very large) value or to revert. This arithmetic underflow propagates to every function that relies on totalAssets, effectively rendering the entire protocol inoperable – users see transactions fail, balances appear unchanged, and the UI may show zero or missing values. The issue occurs only when a rebalance is scheduled and an external withdrawal of the same token happens shortly before it, a scenario that is realistic in a permissioned admin workflow. The affected parties include any user attempting to interact with the vault (deposit, withdraw, borrow) and the protocol itself, which can be denied service. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the pre‑conditions of rebalance and identified the missing check on the unlocked balance. It is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the underflow happens; the failure manifests as generic revert messages or silent transaction failures, making it easy to overlook during testing. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or balance‑capping errors where a transfer amount is not validated against the source’s available funds. To remediate, the rebalance implementation should first compute the current unlocked balance and ensure that the amount to be moved does not exceed this value, reverting or adjusting the amount if necessary. This simple guard restores the invariant that totalAssets always reflects a non‑negative, accurate accounting of the vault’s holdings, preventing the denial‑of‑service condition and aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations that a rebalance will never pull more tokens than are actually free to move.

title: Non EIP712 compliance in Liquidation
description: LiquidationManager::batchLiquidateDensWithPermit() is not EIP712 compliant as it does not hash the _denArray to include in the structHash, as per the EIP: The dynamic values bytes and string are encoded as a keccak256 hash of their contents. In LiquidationManager:599, _denArray is not hashed. Internal Pre-conditions None. External Pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. Call LiquidationManager::batchLiquidateDensWithPermit(). Non EIP712 compliance.
poc: Code
bug_full: An EIP‑712 compliance issue exists in the batch liquidation function that accepts a permit. The function builds a typed‑data struct hash but omits the required keccak256 hash of the dynamic array that contains the identifiers of the positions to be liquidated. According to the EIP‑712 specification, any dynamic type such as bytes or string must be represented by the hash of its contents before being included in the struct hash. Because the contract inserts the raw array directly, the resulting struct hash does not reflect the actual data that will be processed. This mismatch allows a signer to produce a signature that appears to authorize one set of positions while the contract will verify the signature against a different hash, effectively letting an attacker submit a permit that signs a benign array and then replace it with a malicious array during execution. The exploit can be carried out by calling batchLiquidateDensWithPermit with a crafted permit and a manipulated _denArray; the contract will accept the signature as valid even though the signed data does not match the liquidation request. The impact is that unauthorized liquidations can be performed, potentially draining user collateral or causing unintended loss of funds. The vulnerability manifests whenever the batch liquidation with permit is used, regardless of the caller, because the verification step is always based on the incomplete struct hash. All participants who rely on the permit mechanism – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected, as the integrity of the authorization process is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against the EIP‑712 reference algorithm and noticed that the dynamic array was never hashed. Because the function still compiles and the signature verification does not throw, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed when unexpected liquidations occur or when signatures appear to be valid for different data. To remediate, the contract should compute keccak256(_denArray) (or the appropriate encoding for an array of identifiers) and include that hash in the structHash before calling the EIP‑712 domain separator and recovering the signer. This brings the implementation in line with the specification and ensures that the signed permit accurately reflects the exact set of positions being liquidated, restoring the intended security guarantees.

title: Missing slippage control for certain router
description: Router actions such as CollVaultRouter::redeemCollateralVault() only check slippage when the CollVault asset is unwrapped. However, the amount of collateral to redeem depends on the price of the collateral, which means the amount of collateral redeemed may vary a lot and the user has no control over it. Router actions such as CollVaultRouter::redeemCollateralVault() do not validate the amount of collateral redeemed if it is not unwrapped. Internal Pre-conditions None. External Pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. User calls CollVaultRouter::redeemCollateralVault() without unwrapping and loses significant collateral due to a price drop in the meantime. Loss of funds.
poc: CollVaultRouter::redeemCollateralVault() DenManager::_removeCollateralFromDen()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage control in the CollVaultRouter when redeeming collateral without unwrapping the underlying asset. The router function calculates the amount of collateral to return based on the current market price of the collateral token, but it does not enforce any minimum‑receive constraint or slippage tolerance when the asset remains wrapped. Because the price can change between the moment the transaction is submitted and the moment it is executed, a user who calls redeemCollateralVault expecting a certain amount of collateral may receive significantly less, or even near‑zero, if the price drops in the interim. The root cause is the absence of a price‑based validation step for non‑unwrapped redemption paths; the code only checks slippage for the unwrapping branch. An attacker or a volatile market can therefore trigger the loss by causing a price dip, after which the router hands out a smaller collateral amount without warning. The impact is a direct loss of user funds: the user’s balance appears to shrink, the UI may show a successful redemption but the received collateral amount is far below expectations, effectively making the funds disappear. This condition occurs whenever a user redeems collateral through the router without specifying a slippage limit and the underlying price is volatile. All participants who rely on the CollVaultRouter – individual borrowers, lenders, and the protocol’s accounting system – are affected because the accounting assumptions that the redeemed amount matches the quoted value are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the slippage checks across different execution paths and noticed that the non‑unwrapped path lacked any price validation. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply returns a lower amount, which may be attributed to normal market movement unless the discrepancy is large. To remediate, the router should enforce a slippage tolerance for any redemption that depends on a price feed, rejecting the transaction if the actual amount falls below the user‑specified minimum. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that users receive at least the amount they were quoted, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unexpected fund loss.

title: BoycoVault::totalAssets() uses asset.
description: BoycoVault::totalAssets() calls super.totalAssets();, which is the ERC4626 function, that simply does return $._asset.balanceOf(address(this));. As such, it's possible to do donation the case. /// @dev Virtual accounting to avoid donations, asset valued denomination, returned in WAD BoycoVault:186 does not use virtual accounting. Internal Pre-conditions None. External Pre-conditions None. Attack Path Simple donation attack due to not using virtual accounting, that is, attacker mints 1 share and before a user deposits assets, the attacker donates assets and inflates the share price, making the vulnerable user loss all or part of its deposit due to rounding down. Loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the vault reports its total assets. The totalAssets() view function simply returns the raw token balance of the vault contract by calling the ERC4626 implementation, which reads the underlying asset balance with balanceOf(address(this)). Because the function does not incorporate any virtual accounting layer, an attacker can increase the reported total assets without correspondingly increasing the total share supply. The attack proceeds by minting a minimal amount of shares (for example one share) and then sending additional tokens directly to the vault address as a donation. This extra token transfer inflates the vault's asset balance while the share count remains unchanged, causing the share‑to‑asset conversion rate to rise. When a legitimate user later deposits assets, the vault calculates the number of shares to mint based on the inflated conversion rate, rounding down the result. Consequently the user receives fewer shares than their deposited value warrants, effectively losing part or all of their deposit when they later withdraw. The impact is a loss of funds for honest participants and a distortion of the accounting model that the protocol relies on for fair share pricing. The issue manifests whenever the vault allows direct token transfers (donations) without updating its internal accounting, which is typical for ERC4626‑compatible vaults that do not protect against unsolicited asset deposits. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the implementation of totalAssets() and noted the absence of virtual accounting logic that many other vaults employ to guard against donation attacks. The problem can be hard to notice because the vault’s balance simply grows, which may be interpreted as legitimate earnings, while the share price subtly shifts, leading to rounding errors that only become apparent when users experience unexpected share allocations or reduced withdrawals. To remediate the issue the vault should adopt a virtual accounting scheme that tracks an internal “virtual total assets” value separate from the raw token balance, updating it only when shares are minted or burned, or alternatively reject direct token transfers and enforce that all asset inflows go through the deposit function. This change restores the invariant that total assets and total shares move together, preventing an attacker from inflating the share price and protecting users from inadvertent loss of funds.

title: Double Performance Fee on Donations
description: When a token without an oracle is donated, it's treated as a donation without fees. Later, when an oracle is mapped to the token, internalizing the donation incorrectly applies the performance fee a second time, reducing the escrowed funds twice. edCollateralVault.sol#L109 edCollateralVault.sol#L244 Duplicate Fee Logic: Fees are applied during both donation and internalization. Internal Pre-conditions External Pre-conditions Attack Path without oracle harvested without an oracle mapped. Map Oracle: Oracle is assigned Internalize Donation: Protocol processes the donation again. Apply Fee Twice: Performance fees are deducted both during donation and internalization. double fee applied reducing harvest
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double application of the performance fee on token donations when the token initially has no price oracle attached. The contract treats a donation of an oracle‑less token as fee‑free, but later, when an oracle is mapped to that token, the internalization routine re‑processes the same donation and deducts the performance fee again. This occurs because the fee‑calculation logic is executed both at the point of donation and again during the internalization step without a guard that checks whether a fee has already been taken or whether the token lacked an oracle at the time of the first deposit. An attacker or a malicious donor can exploit the flow by first donating a token that has no oracle, then triggering the oracle mapping (or waiting for the protocol to map it) which causes the contract to apply the performance fee a second time, effectively reducing the escrowed amount by roughly twice the intended fee percentage. The impact is that donors receive less than the amount they expected to be held in escrow, leading to apparent loss of funds, inaccurate accounting, and potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s fee model. The issue manifests only when a token without an oracle is donated and later an oracle is associated with that token before the donation is internalized. Users who contribute such tokens, as well as the protocol that relies on correct fee accounting, are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the donation and internalization pathways and identified that the same fee‑deduction code was invoked in both places. Because the initial donation appears fee‑free, the subsequent reduction can be mistaken for market volatility or other unrelated losses, making it hard to spot without a detailed code review. To remediate, the contract should either skip fee calculation for tokens that lack an oracle at the time of donation and ensure that internalization does not reapply the fee, or implement a flag that records whether the fee has already been taken for a given donation. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “duplicate fee” or “double‑charging” logic errors where financial deductions are unintentionally applied more than once, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and causing users to see their balances shrink unexpectedly.

title: During Recovery Mode Liquidation, the
description: During liquidation in recovery mode, protocol implements separate tracking of Total Collateral Ratio (TCR) (see line 350 and 526 below) which is incorrectly calculated because the entireSystemColl value has a missing subtraction of collateral gas compensation that lead to inaccuracy of computation. This will inflate the value of TCR and affects both liquidateDens and batchLiquidateDens File: LiquidationManager.sol 337: entireSystemColl -= totals.totalCollToSendToSP * ~ continue 350: uint256 TCR = here is inflated ,→ ,→ ~ continue 364: entireSystemColl -= 365: (singleLiquidation.collToSendToSP + compensation ,→ ,→ 366: denManagerValues.price; File: LiquidationManager.sol 503: entireSystemColl -= totals.totalCollToSendToSP * ~ continue 526: uint256 TCR = here is inflated ,→ ,→ ~continue 541: entireSystemColl -= 542: (singleLiquidation.collToSendToSP + compensation ,→ ,→ 543: denManagerValues.price; entireSystemColl is supposed to track the total system collateral during liquidations. While it correctly deducts the collateral sent to the Stability Pool and the surplus collateral amount, it fails to account for the collateral gas compensation. The collateral gas compensation is necessary to deduct so the system can compute the real value of TCR. Remember that collateral gas compensation is being sent as reward for liquidators, snect gauge and validator pool, in which being deducted from actual system collateral. If we don't deduct it, the TCR is inflated, that will affect the liquidation of dens, like for example, that a den should be liquidated but due to inflated TCR, it will become higher than CCR, therefore no liquidation. The root cause can be trace in a situation where the system's TCR falls below the Critical Collateralization Ratio (CCR), triggering recovery mode in which proper liquidation will apply. The bug arises here because the TCR is inflated as collateral gas compensation is not deducted from the system's collateral. The issue is present in both liquidateDens and batchLiquidateDens Internal Pre-conditions External Pre-conditions Attack Path See POC section for vulnerability path. TCR is artificially inflated, it means calculated TCR during liquidation is higher than actual. It means that Dens higher than actual TCR will be wrongly liquidated. Another case is that liquidation should happen but won't because the TCR is inflated in which it becomes higher than CCR. Therefore no liquidation happened.
bug_full: During recovery mode the protocol calculates a Total Collateral Ratio (TCR) that determines whether a borrower (referred to as a "Den") is eligible for liquidation. The contract keeps a variable that represents the total system collateral, called entireSystemColl, and updates it each time a liquidation occurs. The vulnerability stems from the fact that the code subtracts the collateral that is sent to the Stability Pool and any surplus collateral, but it forgets to subtract the collateral that is paid out as gas compensation to liquidators, the gauge and the validator pool. Because this gas compensation is effectively removed from the system’s real collateral, the omission causes the computed TCR to be higher than the true value. An inflated TCR can make the protocol believe that the overall collateralisation is safe when it is actually below the Critical Collateralisation Ratio (CCR). Consequently, a Den that is under‑collateralised may not be liquidated, or a Den that is sufficiently collateralised may be liquidated incorrectly. The bug appears in both the liquidateDens and batchLiquidateDens paths, where entireSystemColl is adjusted without accounting for the gas compensation amount. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test compared the TCR emitted by an event with the value returned by the getter function and observed a consistent discrepancy of several thousand units. The problem is subtle because the TCR still looks plausible and the missing amount is relatively small compared to the total collateral, making it easy to overlook in routine monitoring. The impact is that borrowers may retain positions that should have been closed, potentially leading to larger systemic losses, while liquidators receive rewards that are not reflected in the protocol’s safety metrics. To remediate the issue the entireSystemColl update must also subtract the gas compensation amount, ensuring that the TCR reflects the true collateral available after all payouts. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that TCR accurately represents the ratio of remaining collateral to debt, thereby re‑enabling correct liquidation decisions in recovery mode.

title: Incorrect debt calculation for BrimeDen
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect debt calculation that affects the BrimeDen special borrower within the DenManager contract. When the protocol computes the Individual Collateral Ratio (ICR) for any borrower, it calls getCurrentICR which in turn invokes getDenCollAndDebt. This function delegates to getEntireDebtAndColl, a routine that adds accrued interest to the stored debt by multiplying the debt with a current interest index and dividing by the borrower’s activeInterestIndex. The root cause is that getEntireDebtAndColl does not verify whether the caller is the BrimeDen address, which by design does not accrue interest. Consequently, BrimeDen’s debt is artificially inflated each time the interest index is non‑zero, while its collateral remains unchanged. Because ICR is calculated as collateral divided by debt, the inflated debt lowers the ICR value over time. The liquidation logic in LiquidationManager checks the ICR against a maximum allowed value and a minimum collateral ratio; when the mis‑computed ICR falls below these thresholds, the contract may trigger a liquidation of BrimeDen’s position even though the borrower should be exempt from interest and therefore safe. From a user’s perspective this manifests as an unexpected liquidation event: the user sees their collateral being taken, balances dropping to zero, or a “liquidation” notification despite having sufficient collateral. The impact is loss of funds for honest BrimeDen participants and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that interest‑bearing dens are the only ones that can become under‑collateralised. The issue occurs only when BrimeDen holds debt and the global interest index is greater than zero, which is a condition that can persist for long periods, making the bug hard to notice because the ICR degradation is gradual and may be attributed to market price movements rather than a contract bug. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the codebase, where the auditor observed that the interest accrual step lacked a check for the BrimeDen exemption. To remediate the problem, the getEntireDebtAndColl function should include a condition that skips the interest multiplication when the borrower address equals the BrimeDen address, ensuring that BrimeDen’s debt remains unchanged and its ICR reflects the true health of the position. This class of bug falls under incorrect financial state computation due to missing special‑case handling, which can lead to false liquidation triggers and erosion of user trust.

title: InfraredCollateralVault is incompatible
description:
InfraredCollateralVault always scales the totalAssets() result up to 18 decimals. I believe this is fixing the problem with totalAssets() accounting, it introduces another problem when doing shares conversion.
InfraredCollateralVault overrides the ERC4626 totalAssets() implementation to include reward tokens value and scale the result to 18 decimals. This makes huge inconsistency between the first minted shares and all subsequently minted shares.
Taking a look into the _convertToShares() method of inherited OZ ERC4626 implementation:
```solidity
function _convertToShares(uint256 assets, Math.Rounding rounding) internal view virtual returns (uint256) {
    return assets.mulDiv(totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, rounding);
}
```
and we have for _decimalsOffset():
```solidity
function _decimalsOffset() internal view override virtual returns (uint8) {
    return 18 - assetDecimals();
}
```
Initially, totalAssets() and totalSupply() would be 0 as no assets have been deposited and donation is not possible. So, lets say that the first depositor want to add 100e6 (asset is with 6 decimals, decimalsOffset is 12) of the underlying assets, which would result in (100e6 * (0+1e12))/1 = 100e18 shares. This minting is correct and shares are correctly scaled up to 18 decimals because of the decimalsOffset.
Next depositor also want to deposit 100e6 assets. Going through the formula for shares but totalAssets() return is scaled to 18 decimals. Shares for the second mint are ~ 10000e24/100e18 = 100e6 which is significantly lower than the initially minted 100e18 shares.
lob/main/blockend/src/core/vaults/InfraredCollateralVault.sol#L134C1-L159C6
Internal Pre-conditions
Vault asset with < 18 decimals
External Pre-conditions
N/A
Attack Path
After initial mint, all subsequent minting will result in significantly lower amount of shares for the same amount of deposit (1e12 times lower for 6 decimals asset). Taking the example from the Root Cause section - second depositor would be able to claim 100e6/(100e18 + 100e6) of 200e6 (actual deposited balance) which is 0.
This bricks the whole vault as all depositors except the first one would lose their funds. There are or normal user. In both cases the issue persists and the vault cant function normally.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The InfraredCollateralVault contract overrides the ERC4626 totalAssets() function to add the value of reward tokens and then forces the returned amount to 18 decimal places regardless of the underlying asset's native precision. ERC4626’s internal share‑to‑asset conversion assumes that totalAssets is expressed in the same number of decimals as the underlying token, while the contract only applies a decimal offset to the totalSupply side of the formula. As a result, the first depositor receives a correct amount of shares because both totalSupply and totalAssets are zero at that moment and the conversion uses the decimal offset to scale the minted shares up to 18 decimals. After the initial mint, totalAssets is reported in 18‑decimal units, inflating the denominator of the share calculation. When a second user deposits the same amount of the underlying token (for example 100 × 10⁶ units of a 6‑decimal asset), the conversion formula now divides by a much larger totalAssets value, producing a share amount that is roughly 10¹² times smaller than the first user’s shares. Consequently, the second and subsequent depositors receive an almost negligible share balance, which translates into a withdrawal entitlement that is effectively zero. From a user’s perspective the vault appears to accept deposits but later shows no balance or returns a tiny amount on withdrawal, violating the expectation that deposited funds are safely stored and proportionally represented by shares. The bug manifests only for assets whose decimals are less than 18, because the decimal offset is non‑zero and the forced 18‑decimal scaling of totalAssets creates the mismatch. It was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s accounting logic, where the auditor traced the _convertToShares internal function and observed the inconsistent scaling. The issue is subtle because the first deposit behaves correctly, masking the problem until multiple deposits occur. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “decimal‑mismatch accounting bugs” in tokenized vaults, where inconsistent precision handling leads to incorrect share issuance and potential loss of user funds. To remediate, the contract should either avoid scaling totalAssets to 18 decimals or apply the same decimal offset to the totalAssets side of the conversion, ensuring that both numerator and denominator are expressed in the same unit before performing the division. Properly aligning the precision eliminates the disproportionate share minting and restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between deposited assets and issued shares.

title: CollVaultRouter::redeemToOne will lead
poc: N/A
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the CollVaultRouter function redeemToOne, which is intended to redeem a user’s shares from a collateral vault, convert all reward tokens into a single target token and deliver the result to the caller. The flaw appears when the collateral vault also receives iBGT rewards that are automatically staked into a separate iBGTVault. The staking operation mints iBGTVault shares, which the vault records as an additional reward token. When a user redeems directly from the collateral vault, the internal withdrawal routine recognises these iBGTVault shares, redeems them and forwards the underlying reward tokens to the user. In contrast, redeemToOne builds the list of tokens to be swapped by querying only the collateral vault’s own rewarded token set. Consequently, any extra reward token that originates from the iBGTVault – for example a token C that is not part of the collateral vault’s reward list – is omitted from the swap array. The router therefore receives the iBGTVault shares, but because they are not included in the token list they are never swapped or transferred to the user, leaving token C permanently locked inside the router contract.

The root cause is the mismatch between the reward token sets of the collateral vault and the iBGTVault and the assumption that the former is a superset of the latter. The router’s logic does not account for the possibility that the iBGTVault may emit additional reward tokens, nor does it verify that the amount of each received token is non‑zero before proceeding with the swap. This oversight allows reward tokens to become stranded.

An attacker can exploit the stuck tokens by invoking the router’s depositFromAny function, which accepts an arbitrary DEX calldata payload and an input token amount supplied by the caller. Because the router may already hold the stranded token C, the attacker can inflate the declared input amount by the amount of the locked token, causing the router to use the previously trapped funds as part of the swap without providing any additional capital. The attacker thereby extracts value that should have been returned to legitimate redeemers.

The impact is a loss of funds for users who rely on redeemToOne: they receive fewer reward tokens than expected, the target token amount is lower than anticipated, and in the worst case the missing token is permanently lost unless an admin rescues it via claimLockedTokens. The issue manifests only when the collateral vault accrues iBGT rewards that are auto‑compounded into iBGTVault shares and when the iBGTVault distributes reward tokens not present in the collateral vault’s reward list. All participants who use the router’s redeemToOne – regular users, liquidity providers and the protocol itself – are affected.

The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the reward harvesting and redemption flows. It is subtle because the router’s external behaviour appears normal: the transaction succeeds, the user receives the expected target token for the known rewards, and no explicit error is thrown. The missing token is silently omitted, making the loss difficult to detect without tracing internal token balances.

To remediate the issue, the router should construct the token array using the union (or at least the intersection) of the reward token sets from both the collateral vault and the iBGTVault, ensuring that every token received by the router is either swapped or transferred to the caller. Additionally, the contract should validate that the amount of each token to be processed is non‑zero and reject or handle unexpected tokens gracefully. By aligning the reward token enumeration with the actual tokens held after redemption, the router will no longer leave funds stranded, and the depositFromAny pathway will not be able to misuse hidden balances.

title: Users can redeem more CollateralToken
description:
Users can redeem more CollateralToken by splitting a single debtAmount into multiple smaller debtAmount.
The _updateBaseRateFromRedemption function increases the baseRate proportionally to collateralDrawn:
sol#L498-L513
In DenManager.sol#L692, collateralFee is calculated by the increased baseRate.
sol#L687-L692
Internal Pre-conditions
External Pre-conditions
Attack Path
Users can redeem more CollateralToken by splitting a single debtAmount into multiple smaller debtAmount.
bug_full: The contract allows a user to redeem collateral against a debt position through the redeemCollateral function. The function calls an internal routine that updates a global baseRate proportionally to the amount of collateral drawn in that specific call. Because the baseRate is increased on every individual redemption, the fee that is later calculated from the baseRate is also recomputed for each call. When a user splits a single large debt redemption into many smaller debtAmount values and invokes redeemCollateral repeatedly, the baseRate is raised multiple times instead of once. This repeated increase reduces the effective redemption fee that is taken from the user and consequently lets the user receive a larger amount of CollateralToken than would be possible with a single redemption of the same total debt. The vulnerability manifests when there is no lower bound on the _debtAmount parameter, allowing arbitrarily small redemption requests, and when the protocol does not aggregate the fee impact across multiple calls. An auditor discovered the issue by comparing the collateral received from a single redemption of 0.5e18 debt with the total collateral received after ten successive redemptions of 0.05e18 each; the latter yielded approximately 11 % more collateral for the same total debt, while the fee receiver collected less. The problem is subtle because each individual redemption appears to charge a correct fee, but the cumulative effect deviates from the intended accounting model, making it hard to spot without systematic testing. The impact is a loss of protocol assets: users can extract excess collateral, reducing the fee pool and potentially destabilising the collateralisation ratios. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑manipulation or accounting‑state‑mutation vulnerabilities where state variables are updated per operation without proper aggregation. To remediate, the contract should either enforce a minimum redemption amount, compute the baseRate update based on the total debt redeemed in a transaction, or redesign the fee calculation so that repeated small redemptions cannot artificially lower the fee. This would restore the intended one‑to‑one relationship between debt repaid and collateral withdrawn and protect the protocol’s economic invariants.

title: Vault.settle(account=coordinator) will lose
bug_full: Vault.settle() is intended to convert a portion of accumulated profit into profitShares for the protocol's coordinator. The function calls an internal helper _credit() that writes the newly minted profitShares to the coordinator’s account storage. However, the in‑memory execution context (context.local.shares) is never updated when the settlement target address is the same as the coordinator. After the loop finishes, the private function _saveContext() persists context.local back to the coordinator’s storage slot, overwriting the value that _credit() just stored. As a result, any profitShares that were supposed to be credited are replaced by the stale value that was present before settlement, often zero. This bug can be triggered by any user who calls settle() and deliberately passes the coordinator address as the settlement account. The attacker does not need special permissions; the contract’s public settle() interface allows the account parameter to be chosen arbitrarily. When profitShares are positive, the coordinator’s balance is reduced by exactly that amount, effectively stealing the profit. From the coordinator’s perspective the expected outcome – a positive increase in share balance – is replaced by a missing or zero increase, which may appear as “funds disappeared” or “my profit share did not arrive”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that _credit() writes to storage but the subsequent _saveContext() call unconditionally stores context.local.shares for the supplied account, without considering that the account may be the same as the coordinator. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an event after the overwrite and the intermediate storage write succeeds, so the loss is silent and can be missed in normal testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs where a temporary in‑memory state is not kept in sync with persistent storage, leading to overwriting of freshly written values. The recommended fix is to make _credit() aware of the special case where the credited address equals the current context.account (the coordinator) and update context.local.shares directly, or to skip the final overwrite for that address. Aligning the in‑memory and on‑chain representations ensures that profitShares are correctly added to the coordinator’s balance and prevents accidental loss of funds.

title: Some accounts using Intents to trade might
description:
When user trades using signed intents, pending order is created using the price specified by the user. Upon settlement, there is some pnl realized due to difference of intent price and market price. The issue is that this difference is added to account only when checking margin to add pending order, but when protection (liquidation) is validated, collateral doesn't include pending intent's pnl from the difference of intent and market price. As such, user can be unfairly liquidated if price moves against him but he has enough collateral (with pnl from pending intent orders). If there is a loss from intent price difference, then this loss is not added when checking liquidation either, thus liquidation will revert as if account is healthy.
When protection is validated, only account's collateral is checked in InvariantLib.sol#L127 and InvariantLib.sol#L92
Internal Pre-conditions
• User account is close to liquidation
• Position is opened or closed via Intent with intent price far enough from the latest oracle price (far enough - meaning the difference in price can make account safe)
• Price moves against the user
External Pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
Happens by itself (unfair user liquidation) or can be crafted by the user (avoid liquidation).
• Margin ratio is 0.5%, maintenence ratio is 0.3%
• Trading fee is 0.1%
• User has collateral = 350 and settled position of long = 1000 at the latest oracle price of 100 (account margin ratio is 350 / (1000 * 100) = 0.35%, very close to liquidation, but still healthy)
• User signs intent to partially close position of the size 500 at the price of 101.
• The intent is sent on-chain and user now has pending position of long = 500. His additional profit from the intent price is 500 * (101 - 100) = 500.
• Liquidator commits unrequested price of 99.9
• User's collateral is now 350 + 1000 * (99.9 - 100) = 250, however since the intent is guaranteed to be executed at the price of 101, his additional profit from the intent makes the expected margin ratio for liquidation reason = (250 + 500) / (1000 * 100) = 0.75%, so account should be safe.
• However, liquidator immediately liquidates user account, because this additional profit from the intent is ignored.
• Besides liquidation fee, upon settlement, user pays fees to close the position from instead of 750.
• User was unfairly liquidated (as his account was healthy) and user has lost 50 / 750 = 6.7% of his funds.
• User can be unfairly and unexpectedly liquidated and lose 1%+ of his funds (because this happens only to users with low collateral and the pnl from intent price difference will mostly be small enough, the user loss relative to collateral will be above 1%).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the liquidation health check of a perpetual trading protocol that uses signed intents to create pending orders. When a user creates a pending intent, the protocol records the intended execution price and calculates the profit or loss that will be realized once the intent settles. However, the margin‑ratio validation that determines whether an account can be liquidated only considers the current collateral and the already settled position, ignoring the unrealized profit or loss from any pending intents. As a result, if the market price moves against the user after the intent is signed, the user’s collateral may appear insufficient for liquidation even though the pending intent would generate enough profit to keep the account healthy. This discrepancy allows a liquidator to trigger a liquidation on an account that is actually solvent according to the user’s expected final state. The impact is that users with low collateral and pending intents can be unfairly liquidated, losing a portion of their funds (often more than one percent of their collateral) and paying liquidation fees despite having a margin ratio that would be safe after the intent is settled. The issue occurs when an account is close to the maintenance margin, a pending intent is signed at a price that deviates significantly from the current oracle price, and the oracle price subsequently moves unfavorably. It affects any trader who relies on intents for partial position closures or openings, as well as the protocol’s overall fairness and trustworthiness. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the margin‑ratio logic in InvariantLib.sol with the intent settlement flow and identified that the pending‑intent PnL is never added to the collateral during liquidation checks. The problem is subtle because the pending intent is stored separately and only used during settlement, so the liquidation routine appears to work correctly for accounts without pending intents, making the bug easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the protocol should incorporate the sum of price adjustments from all pending intents into the effective collateral when evaluating liquidation eligibility, and it should adjust the position size to reflect pending intent reductions or additions. This change aligns the liquidation health check with the accounting assumptions used for settlement, preventing users from being liquidated when their eventual margin ratio would be above the maintenance threshold. The issue belongs to the class of margin‑calculation and accounting consistency bugs, where different parts of the system use divergent views of an account’s equity, leading to incorrect enforcement of safety checks and unintended fund loss.

title: Liquidations are temporarily blocked if
description:
A new feature in v2.4 is guaranteed position change via Intents: since the price is provided in Intent itself, it doesn't need corresponding epoch oracle price to be valid. This makes it possible to close positions even when position opening in still pending (if all orders are from Intents), as such pending negative (pending position closure) is allowed to be greater than latest position size for intent orders:
```solidity
if (
    context.pendingLocal.invalidation != 0 &&
    //
    pending orders are partially invalidatable
    context.pendingLocal.neg().gt(context.latestPositionLocal.magnitude()) // total pending close is greater than latest position
) revert IMarket.MarketOverCloseError();
```
The issue is that liquidation order is always a ”normal” order (invalidation == 1), thus this condition is always enforced for liquidations. However, if pending negative is already greater than latest position magnitude, it's impossible to create liquidation order which will satisfy this condition (order can only increase pending negative and can't influence latest position). In such situations liquidations will temporarily be impossible until some pending order becomes commited and the condition can be satisfied.
Incorrect validation for protected orders in case pendingLocal.neg > latestPosition.magnitude():
al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/InvariantLib.sol#L118-L122
Notice, that there is a special handling for the case of crossing zero (when pending order closes long and opens short or vice versa): in such case liquidation order must be empty (since crossing zero is prohibited for non-empty non-intent orders). But there is no such handling for the case of large pending position closure.
Internal pre-conditions
• User has more pending close than latest position at the last commited oracle price (for example, user fully closes long position, then opens long again, then closes again).
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User has some position open (for example, long = 10)
2. User uses Intent to fully close position
3. Shortly after that (order to close still pending) user uses Intent to open position again (for example, long = 10).
4. Then immediately user uses Intent again to partially close position of size = 1
5. Shortly after that (all user orders are still pending) the price sharply drops and user becomes liquidatable.
6. At this time, user's latest position = 10, pending positive (open) = 10, pending negative (close) = 11.
7. All liquidations will revert, because regardless of liquidation order size, pending negative will remain greater than latest position (10).
8. Once pending order to close is settled, liquidation is possible again, but might be too late as user might already accumulate bad debt.
Result: User can not be liquidated in time and is liquidated much later, when his position is already in bad debt, which is a funds loss for all market users or a risk of a bank run as the last to withdraw won't have enough funds in the market to pay out.
All liquidation attempts revert although the user should be liquidatable, thus liquidation happens later than it should, potentially creating bad debt and loss of funds for all market users.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a validation rule in the market’s invariant library that rejects any order whose pending negative amount (the total size of pending close orders) exceeds the magnitude of the latest committed position. This rule was introduced to protect against crossing‑zero scenarios, but it is applied indiscriminately to all order types, including liquidation orders, which always have an invalidation flag of one. When a user creates a series of Intent orders that leave the pending negative amount larger than the current position – for example by fully closing a position, immediately opening a new one, and then adding another close Intent before any of the pending orders are settled – the contract’s check `pendingLocal.neg().gt(context.latestPositionLocal.magnitude())` triggers and reverts with `MarketOverCloseError`. Because a liquidation order cannot reduce the pending negative amount (it can only increase it) and cannot modify the latest position, the condition can never be satisfied, causing every liquidation attempt to revert while the user’s position is technically under‑collateralized. The impact is that liquidation is delayed until one of the pending orders is finally committed, at which point the user may already have accrued bad debt. This creates a systemic risk: other market participants may lose funds, and the protocol could face a liquidity shortfall resembling a bank run. The issue appears only when all of a user’s orders are still pending and the pending negative exceeds the latest position magnitude, a state that is hard to observe in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a security audit of the new Intent feature in version 2.4, where the invariant checks were examined for correctness. The bug violates the core accounting assumption that a liquidatable position can always be closed by a liquidation order. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts with an over‑close error despite the account being under‑collateralized, no liquidation event, and potentially a sudden loss of equity later when the pending orders finally settle. The recommended remediation is to add a special case for liquidation orders similar to the crossing‑zero handling: when the pending negative amount is greater than the latest position, the liquidation order should be allowed to be empty, or the validation should be relaxed for liquidation orders so that they are not blocked by the over‑close check.

title: Users can pay off statements by just us-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the conversion of a native asset amount to a cent representation that is used to settle statements. The contract rounds the division result half up, meaning it adds half of the divisor before dividing. This introduces a possible deviation of up to 0.5 cents from the true value. When a user makes a payment, the amount in native units is first converted to cents using this rounding rule and then the resulting cent value is applied to the outstanding statement balance. Because the rounding can inflate the reported cent amount by one whole cent while the user actually transferred only half a cent, an attacker can repeatedly submit payments of 0.5‑cent worth of the asset and have each payment credited as one full cent. By iterating this process enough times, the attacker can fully satisfy a statement that originally required a much larger amount, effectively paying only 50 % of the true debt. The impact is that the protocol loses the equivalent of half of every statement’s value, allowing malicious users to drain funds from the treasury without providing the full value. The condition under which this occurs is any statement settlement that relies on the getAssetAmountCents conversion, which is used by multiple payment entry points including makePaymentFromUserAccountForStatement, makePaymentFromCollateralForStatement and similar functions. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit when a test case repeatedly called the payment function with a value equal to one half of a cent and observed that the statement balance was reduced by a full cent each time. The issue is subtle because the rounding operation is a common practice to avoid fractional cents, yet the half‑up approach unintentionally creates a systematic over‑credit. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a statement is marked as paid while the user’s wallet balance has only decreased by a negligible amount, leading to confusion when the expected refund or remaining balance does not match the displayed status. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or rounding bugs where monetary values are incorrectly rounded, causing accounting mismatches and loss of funds. To remediate the problem the conversion should use floor division (round‑down) or a precise fixed‑point arithmetic that does not add the half‑divisor, ensuring that the cent amount never exceeds the true value of the transferred asset. Additionally, the contract could include sanity checks that compare the native amount with the derived cent amount to prevent over‑crediting. Implementing these changes would align the on‑chain accounting with the intended business logic that a payment of X native units must correspond to at most X converted cents, thereby protecting the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: min/maxAnswer check is not done in for
description:
Not validating for min/max answer on chainlink feeds can cause loss of funds for the credit issuer
When reading from Chainlink feeds validation is not done for min/max answers even though such oracles are used.
Eg: ETH/USD chainlink feed in optimism has min and max value set
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Huge crash in price of tokens should occur
Attack Path
1. Price of token A drops below the minAnswer set on the feed (eg: 100 is the minAnswer and the token price goes to 1)
2. A statement is published with amount == 100
3. Attacker pays the statement balance by transferring 1 token A (incorrectly priced at 100 instead of 1) and the statement is settled
4. Loss for the credit issuer since they only receive 1 value compared to 100
Loss of funds for the credit issuer
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing sanity check on the minimum and maximum answer values that are defined by a Chainlink price feed. When the contract reads a price from an external oracle it trusts the raw value without verifying that the value lies within the feed’s configured bounds (minAnswer and maxAnswer). This omission creates a logical flaw: if the market price of the underlying token drops below the feed’s minAnswer (or rises above maxAnswer), the contract will still accept the out‑of‑range price and use it to settle financial statements. An attacker can trigger the condition by waiting for a large price crash, for example when the feed’s minAnswer is set to 100 but the token price falls to 1. The attacker then publishes a statement that claims an amount equal to the minAnswer (100) and pays the settlement using only the actual market amount (1 token). Because the contract does not validate the price range, it settles the statement as if 100 tokens were transferred, while only receiving the 1 token that the attacker sent. The credit issuer, which relies on the contract to receive the full amount, suffers a loss equal to the difference between the expected and actual payment. The bug manifests only under extreme price movements and is hard to notice because the oracle still returns a numeric value and the contract’s logic appears to function normally for typical price ranges. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s interaction with Chainlink feeds, where the absence of a min/max check was identified as a missing pre‑condition. To remediate, the contract should explicitly read the feed’s minAnswer and maxAnswer and reject any settlement where the reported price is outside these limits, reverting the transaction or refusing the statement. This class of bug falls under “oracle sanity‑check omission” or “unchecked external data bounds”, which can lead to economic loss, incorrect accounting, and user‑visible symptoms such as payments being accepted but the protocol receiving far fewer tokens than expected, balances unexpectedly decreasing, or refunds appearing to be zero. Proper validation restores the intended business logic that payments must match the declared amount and protects the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Incorrect initializer modifier in Vesting
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect use of the OpenZeppelin initializer pattern in a contract hierarchy. The parent Vesting contract defines its internal setup function __vesting_init with the initializer modifier, while the child SymmVesting contract also defines an external initialize function that uses the same initializer modifier. The initializer modifier records that a particular version of initialization has already been performed and blocks any subsequent calls to functions marked with initializer. Because both parent and child use the same modifier, only the first call succeeds; the second call reverts, leaving the contract partially or completely uninitialized. This situation occurs during deployment when the child contract’s initialize function is invoked. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the Initializable contract’s inheritance rules: parent initialization functions should be marked onlyInitializing so they can be called from a child initializer without triggering the version‑check flag. As a result, the Vesting contract may never execute its internal calls to __AccessControlEnumerable_init, __Pausable_init, and __ReentrancyGuard_init, meaning role‑based access control, pause functionality, and re‑entrancy protection remain unset. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to deploy successfully but critical state variables such as the admin address remain zero, vesting schedules never become active, and any attempt to claim or withdraw tokens results in no balance change or a revert. The impact is effectively a denial‑of‑service: protocol components that rely on the vesting logic cannot be used, funds may be locked indefinitely, and the overall system functionality is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract code against OpenZeppelin’s recommended patterns. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without errors and the failure only manifests at runtime when the initializer is called, which may be overlooked if deployment scripts do not check for revert messages. The proper fix is to replace the initializer modifier on the parent __vesting_init function with onlyInitializing, allowing the child’s initializer to invoke it safely while preserving the versioning guarantees. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of inheritance‑related initialization bugs where multiple contracts in a hierarchy misuse upgradeable‑contract guards, leading to incomplete setup and broken business logic such as missing refunds, zero balances, or stalled vesting periods.

title: Readding the reward token causes user to receive excess rewards
description:
New users who deposit during the time when the reward token is not added do not get their userRewardPerTokenPaid updated for this token, so it remains 0. When the token is re-added, however, perTokenStored for this token is not 0 because it retains the previous state. This leads to a situation where users who joined in the meantime when the reward token was not added, can receive all the previous rewards of the token when new rewards are notified, effectively taking them away from other users.
acts/staking/SymmStaking.sol#L319-L328 Here you can see that when removing a reward token, the token is only removed from the rewardTokens list without resetting the other state. That means if the token is added again, it takes over the previous state. The problem is that if perTokenStored for the reward token is not 0 when it is removed, it will also not be 0 when the token is re-added. If new users make a deposit while the token is not added, they do not get userRewardPerTokenPaid updated for this token because the token is no longer in the rewardTokens list. Normally userRewardPerTokenPaid is always updated before a deposit through _updateRewardsState to ensure that a user does not receive rewards that existed before the deposit for the deposited amount:
acts/staking/SymmStaking.sol#L406-L418
Internal Pre-conditions
1. There must be a token that is re-added by an authorized address
2. There must be users who start staking during the time when the token is removed and has not yet been re-added
External Pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
1. A new reward token is added
2. User1 deposits
3. Rewards for the token are notified
4. One week passes, and User1 claims his rewards
5. The reward token is removed
6. User2 deposits
7. The reward token is added again
8. Rewards for the token are notified
9. One week passes, and User2 claims his rewards, but he received too many because he also received rewards from the time when the token was first added
10. User2 can no longer claim because there are not enough rewards left in the contract.
It is very likely that the staking contract will no longer function properly if a reward token is re-added, as some users would receive too many rewards, while others would no longer be able to claim anything due to the lack of rewards. For the users who have too few rewards available, they will also not be able to claim any other reward tokens, as the entire claimRewards function would be reverted.
poc:
The POC can be added to the file token/tests/symmStaking.behavior.ts and run with npx hardhat test --grep "readding token":
```solidity
it("readding token", async () => {
    //Reward token is added for the first time
    await symmStaking.connect(admin).configureRewardToken(await usdcToken.getAddress(), true)
    
    //User1 stakes 100 SYMM
    await stakingToken.connect(user1).approve(await symmStaking.getAddress(), e("100"))
    await symmStaking.connect(user1).deposit(e("100"), user1.address)
    
    //604.8 USDC are notified as rewards
    await usdcToken.approve(await symmStaking.getAddress(), 604800*1000)
    await symmStaking.notifyRewardAmount([await usdcToken.getAddress()], [604800*1000])
    
    time.increaseTo(await time.latest() + 2*30*24*60*60) //Wait 2 months
    await symmStaking.connect(user1).claimRewards() //User1 claims his rewards
    await symmStaking.connect(admin).configureRewardToken(await usdcToken.getAddress(), false) //The reward token gets removed
    
    time.increaseTo(await time.latest() + 24*60*60) //Wait 1 day
    //User2 stakes 100 SYMM
    await stakingToken.connect(user2).approve(await symmStaking.getAddress(), e("100"))
    await symmStaking.connect(user2).deposit(e("100"), user2.address)
    
    time.increaseTo(await time.latest() + 24*60*60) //Wait 3 months
    await symmStaking.connect(admin).configureRewardToken(await usdcToken.getAddress(), true) //Reward token is added for the second time
    
    //1209.6 USDC are notified as rewards
    await usdcToken.approve(await symmStaking.getAddress(), 604800*1000*2)
    await symmStaking.notifyRewardAmount([await usdcToken.getAddress()], [604800*1000*2])
    
    time.increaseTo(await time.latest() + 2*7*24*60*60) //Wait 2 weeks
    //Shows that user2 gets all pending rewards and there is nothing left for user1
    console.log("symmStaking pendingRewards before: ", await symmStaking.pendingRewards(await usdcToken.getAddress()))
    await symmStaking.connect(user2).claimRewards()
    console.log("symmStaking pendingRewards after: ", await symmStaking.pendingRewards(await usdcToken.getAddress()))
})
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution logic error that occurs when a reward token is removed from the staking contract and later added again. The contract keeps the previous per‑token reward accumulator (perTokenStored) and does not reset the user‑specific reward checkpoint (userRewardPerTokenPaid) for accounts that deposited while the token was absent. Because the checkpoint stays at zero for those new users, the next time rewards are notified the contract calculates their pending reward based on the stale accumulator, effectively granting them the entire reward balance that was earned before they even staked. This situation can be triggered whenever an authorized address removes a reward token, a new user stakes during the removal period, and the token is subsequently re‑added without clearing the stored state. The impact is that the later depositor receives excess rewards, draining the pool and leaving earlier stakers with little or no claimable amount; the claimRewards function may even revert because the contract no longer holds enough tokens to satisfy the inflated claim. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a staker who expects a modest reward sees an unexpectedly large payout, while other participants see their balances stay at zero or their claim transaction fail. The bug is hard to notice because normal operation (adding a token once and never removing it) works correctly; only the edge case of token lifecycle changes reveals the flaw. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included a targeted test case reproducing the removal‑re‑addition sequence. Conceptually, the contract fails to treat the reward token as a distinct accounting period; it mixes old accounting state with new deposits, violating the invariant that a user’s pending reward should only reflect rewards accrued after their last checkpoint update. The proper fix is to reset or re‑initialize all per‑token accounting variables when a token is removed, or to prohibit re‑adding a token without a fresh initialization, and to ensure that userRewardPerTokenPaid is updated for all accounts whenever the token list changes. This restores the accounting separation between different reward periods and prevents users from receiving rewards that were generated before they participated.

title: Worker-Induced Denial-of-Service in Deployment Requests
description:
Primary Root Cause:
The root cause is the contract’s design, which permits only one active deployment request per project and lacks a timeout or cancellation function to reset a stalled request when the assigned worker does not complete the process.
Impact:
The project owner cannot progress the deployment, effectively halting the project lifecycle. Funds or NFT-based agent creation fees become unusable as the deployment never completes.
Mitigation:
Implement a timeout mechanism that allows the deployment owner to cancel and reset a stalled deployment request if no proof is submitted within a defined period (e.g., 7 days).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition that arises from the contract’s design allowing only a single active deployment request per project and providing no mechanism to timeout or cancel that request. When a worker is assigned to a deployment, the contract expects the worker to submit a proof of completion; however, if the worker never submits the proof, the request remains permanently pending. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum waiting period nor expose a function for the project owner to abort the request, the owner is unable to initiate a new deployment, and any fees paid for the deployment or for minting an NFT-based agent remain locked in the contract indefinitely. This situation can be triggered at any time a deployment request is created and the assigned worker becomes unresponsive, either accidentally or maliciously. The impact is that the project lifecycle is halted, the owner cannot progress, and the locked funds become effectively unrecoverable, violating the expectation that a deployment either completes or can be cancelled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state-machine governing deployment requests and noted the absence of a timeout or cancellation path. Because the contract simply stays in a "waiting for proof" state without emitting error events, the problem may be hard to notice from the UI, where users only see that nothing happens after submitting a request. The bug belongs to the class of “stuck state” or “resource-locking” denial-of-service vulnerabilities, where a single mutable request blocks further operations. To remediate, the contract should introduce a configurable timeout after which the owner can cancel the pending request and reclaim any locked fees, and optionally allow the owner to replace the worker or submit a cancellation transaction before the timeout expires, and ensure that appropriate events are emitted when a request is cancelled or times out.

title: Non whitelisted user can also create agent
description:
Non whitelisted user can also create agent by calling createAgentWithNFT instead of createAgentWithWhitelistUsers affecting the motive of protocol to only allow whitelisted user to create agent
createAgentWithWhitelistUsers function is designed by protocol with motive to only allow a particular amount of whitelisted users to create agent but this motive can be bypassed by anyone by calling createAgentWithNFT function instead.
Internal Pre-conditions
NA
External Pre-conditions
NA
Attack Path
1. Non whitelisted user can call createAgentWithNFT function instead of createAgentWithWhitelistUsers function and can create agent breaking the whitelist check
Non whitelisted user can also create agent breaking the motive of protocol to only allow whitelisted users to create agent.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass that allows any address, even if it is not part of the protocol’s approved whitelist, to create a new agent by invoking the createAgentWithNFT function. The protocol was designed with a dedicated createAgentWithWhitelistUsers function that checks a stored whitelist before permitting agent creation, thereby restricting the number of participants that can join the system. However, the alternative entry point createAgentWithNFT does not perform the same whitelist verification, so a malicious or simply uninformed user can call this function directly and bypass the intended restriction. This occurs whenever the contract is live and the createAgentWithNFT function is callable, which is typically the case after deployment because no modifier or guard limits its access. An attacker can exploit the flaw by sending a transaction that calls createAgentWithNFT with the required parameters (for example, an NFT identifier) and the contract will register a new agent under the caller’s address without consulting the whitelist. The impact is that the protocol’s economic model, which may rely on a limited set of vetted agents for fairness, security, or fee distribution, is undermined; unauthorized agents can appear, potentially diluting rewards, increasing competition, or violating regulatory assumptions. Users of the platform may notice unexpected agents listed in the UI, see their own expected exclusivity disappear, or observe that the system no longer enforces the promised “whitelisted‑only” rule. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the two agent‑creation functions and observed the missing access‑control check in the NFT‑based path. Because both functions share similar signatures, the omission can be subtle and may not be caught by automated tools that only look for missing modifiers on the primary function. The bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization check” or “inconsistent access control” vulnerabilities, where one code path enforces a policy while another equivalent path does not. To remediate, the contract should enforce the same whitelist verification in createAgentWithNFT, or alternatively introduce a pausability guard that allows the admin to disable the function during the whitelist‑only period, ensuring that only approved users can create agents. This conceptual fix restores the intended business logic that only whitelisted participants may instantiate agents, aligning the contract’s behavior with its public specifications and protecting the protocol’s economic integrity.

title: Bad check in Vesting.sol::_resetVesting
description:
The _resetVestingPlans check makes it impossible to increase a user's locked tokens if the increase does not push the new amount above the total unlocked tokens. This is problematic as it will prevent users from adding additional liquidity to the SymmVesting.sol after a certain number of their lp tokens have been unlocked.
In Vesting.sol:231, the check will cause a revert when a user tries to add additional liquidity
Internal Pre-conditions
The user must already have some vested lp tokens
External Pre-conditions
NIL
Attack Path
NIL
Users are unable to add additional liquidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical validation error in the internal function that resets vesting plans. The contract checks that the new amount supplied to the reset operation is not smaller than the amount of tokens that have already been unlocked, and if it is, the transaction reverts with an error. Because the function is used when a user tries to add additional liquidity, the check unintentionally blocks the operation after any portion of the vesting schedule has become unlocked. The root cause is that the condition compares the supplied amount with the unlocked token balance instead of the total locked balance, so when a user attempts to increase the locked amount by providing the remaining locked tokens, the supplied amount is lower than the unlocked amount and the require statement fails. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any honest user who has a partially unlocked vesting position will experience a revert when calling the addLiquidity method. The impact is that users are unable to add more liquidity to the protocol after a certain amount of their vested tokens have unlocked, effectively freezing the ability to increase their stake and potentially reducing overall protocol liquidity. This occurs only when the user already holds some vested tokens and at least a portion of those tokens has become unlocked; users with fully locked or fully unlocked positions are not affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that simulates unlocking over time and then attempts a second liquidity addition, which reverts with the custom error. The bug is subtle because the revert message does not clearly indicate that the problem is a mistaken comparison, and the contract otherwise functions correctly for initial liquidity provision, making the failure mode easy to miss in casual testing. To fix the issue, the validation should be changed to ensure the new amount is not less than the already unlocked amount only when it would cause an inconsistency, or the check should be removed entirely as recommended, allowing the reset to accept any amount that does not attempt to reduce the already unlocked balance. In broader terms, this is a class of accounting‑logic bugs where a contract enforces an incorrect invariant on token balances, leading to unexpected denial of service for legitimate users and breaking the business rule that users should be able to increase their locked stake at any time.

title: Malicious User can dilute staking Rewards
description:
The SymmStaking contract allows anyone to add new rewards using the notifyRewardAmount function. However, if new rewards are continuously added while existing rewards are still active, the total rewards get spread over a longer period. A malicious actor can exploit this by repeatedly adding tiny amounts, effectively delaying stakers from receiving their full rewards.
• notifyRewardAmount function can be called by anyone, with any reward amount.
• Each time it's called, the reward rate is recalculated as:
– amount / state.duration (if the previous reward period has ended).
– (amount + leftover) / state.duration (if the previous reward period is still ongoing).
The issue arises when an attacker keeps adding tiny amounts (e.g., 1 wei) repeatedly. While the total rewards (amount + leftover) barely change, the duration (state.duration)
Example:
1. Alice is the only staker, and 100 USDC is added as a reward.
2. Halfway through, Alice has earned 50 USDC.
3. A malicious user then adds just 1 wei USDC as a new reward.
4. This recalculates the reward rate, cutting it in half:
• From 100e6 / 1 week → 50e6 / 1 week.
5. The attacker can repeat this process multiple times, continuously lowering the rate.
This DoS-like attack prevents stakers from claiming their rewards in a reasonable timeframe.
Internal Pre-conditions
None.
External Pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Users stakes in SymmStaking.
2. A new reward is notified via notifyRewardAmount for the stakers.
3. A malicious user calls notifyRewardAmount multiple times with dust values to dilute the reward rate.
4. User get rewards slower than what they were supposed to get.
Time to gain the intended reward can be arbitrarily increased by malicious users.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s reward‑notification mechanism, which permits any address to invoke the notifyRewardAmount function and supply an arbitrary amount of reward tokens. Each invocation recomputes the per‑second reward rate by dividing the total pending reward (new amount plus any leftover from the previous period) by the configured reward duration. When the previous reward period has not yet finished, this recalculation effectively spreads the combined reward over the same duration, lowering the rate. A malicious actor can exploit this by repeatedly calling the function with negligible (dust) amounts, such as 1 wei, while a reward period is active. Because the total reward changes only marginally but the denominator (duration) stays constant, the reward rate is continuously halved or otherwise reduced, causing the accrual of rewards for legitimate stakers to slow dramatically. From a user’s perspective, a staker who expects to earn a certain amount of USDC each week may see their earned balance increase only marginally or appear to stall, even though the contract still reports that rewards are being distributed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition: stakers can be forced to wait an arbitrarily long time to receive the full amount they are entitled to, effectively diluting the economic incentive of the protocol. This issue manifests whenever the reward period is ongoing and the contract does not restrict who may add rewards or enforce a minimum addition size. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑rate calculation logic and identified that the function lacks access control and input validation. The problem can be subtle because the UI may continue to show the total reward amount as unchanged, while the underlying rate is silently reduced, making the slowdown hard to detect without inspecting on‑chain state. To remediate, the contract should restrict the caller of notifyRewardAmount to a trusted role (e.g., owner or governance), or enforce a minimum reward amount that meaningfully increases the total reward pool, thereby preventing an attacker from diluting the rate with dust values. This class of bug falls under “unrestricted reward injection leading to rate manipulation” and violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that reward distribution proceeds at a predictable rate once a period starts.

title: Double spending attack in the Vesting
description:
The function resetVestingPlans() is called by an administrator account and resets vesting plans for a list of users, with the corresponding amount provided as input. The function calls _resetVestingPlans(), where it checks whether the given amount is greater than or equal to the claimed amount for the user. After that, it calls resetAmount() from LibVestingPlan. In this function, the state is updated, the new amount is recorded, and claimedAmount is set to 0.
The issue here is that this can lead to double spending. Even though the user executing the request is trusted, they cannot know whether another transaction has been executed before theirs, in which the user whose vesting plan is being reset has withdrawn their locked amount by paying a penalty fee. If this happens, the user will be able to claim the same amount again after the reset, which would harm other users who might not be able to claim their rewards.
acts/vesting/Vesting.sol#L222-L237
Internal Pre-conditions
None
External Pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
1. Trusted user sends a transaction for executes resetVestingPlans()
2. Regular user subject of this reset sends a transaction that is executed before the first one and claim their locked tokens as they pay a penalty
3. After the reset the user is able to claim the tokens up to amount again
Loss of funds for the protocol and for the users
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition style double‑spending flaw in the vesting contract’s resetVestingPlans workflow. An administrator can invoke resetVestingPlans to overwrite a user’s vesting plan with a new amount, after the internal _resetVestingPlans routine checks that the supplied amount is at least the user’s already‑claimed amount and then calls LibVestingPlan.resetAmount, which records the new amount and resets the claimedAmount field to zero. Because the reset operation is not atomic with respect to a user’s claim transaction, a regular user can submit a claim (paying a penalty fee) that is mined before the admin’s reset transaction. When the reset finally executes, the contract believes the user has not claimed any tokens (claimedAmount has been cleared) and therefore allows the user to claim the full amount again. From the user’s point of view the UI may show that after a reset their vesting balance is restored to the original amount, even though they already withdrew the tokens earlier; the user expects the reset to reflect the current state, but instead they can withdraw the same tokens a second time, effectively creating extra tokens out of thin air.
