The impact is a loss of protocol funds and a reduction of rewards available to other participants, because the same tokens are paid twice. The issue occurs whenever an admin resets vesting plans for a list of users without first ensuring that no pending claim transaction can be mined before the reset, and it affects any user with a vesting schedule as well as the overall protocol treasury. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of resetVestingPlans and identified that the contract does not enforce any ordering or locking between claim and reset operations, making the bug subtle and easy to miss because the reset function appears to be called only by a trusted account. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a user’s claimedAmount is zero before allowing a reset, or introduce a re‑entrancy‑style lock, a nonce, or a two‑step reset that first disables claims, then updates the amount, thereby guaranteeing that a claim cannot be executed between the check and the state change. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent reset” or “race‑condition double spend” vulnerabilities where a privileged state change does not account for concurrent user actions, violating the accounting assumption that each token can be withdrawn only once per vesting period.

title: createCommonProjectIDAndDeployment
description:
createCommonProjectIDAndDeploymentRequest() is called by createAgent(), in which the user pays fees to create an agent. The index is supposed to protect the user from overwritting a requestId with the same requestId but different serverURL. However, it is hardcoded to 0.
In BlueprintCore:373, index is 0.
Internal Pre-conditions
None.
External Pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User creates an agent for a certain projectId, base64Proposal, server url.
2. User creates an agent (at the same block) with the same projectId, base64Proposal but different server url.
3. First request is overwritten.
First request is overwritten and one of them will not be finalized as submitProofOfDeployment() and submitDeploymentRequest() can only be called once as only one of them will go through.
poc: See above.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that registers a new deployment request for an agent. The contract is supposed to keep a separate index for each user so that two requests that share the same project identifier cannot overwrite each other when they contain different server URLs. In the current implementation the index variable is hard‑coded to zero, meaning every call to the registration function writes to the same slot in the mapping. As a result, if a user (or an attacker) submits two createAgent transactions in the same block with identical projectId and proposal data but different serverUrl, the second call overwrites the first request. The overwritten request can no longer be finalized because the subsequent functions that complete the deployment – submitProofOfDeployment and submitDeploymentRequest – are designed to be called only once per request identifier. From the user’s perspective the fees paid for the first request appear to be lost: the UI shows the request as created, but later attempts to submit proof fail silently or revert, leaving the user with no deployment and no refund. The issue is triggered only when two creation calls collide on the same request identifier, which is possible because the index does not advance per user mapping. It affects any participant that relies on the agent creation flow, potentially causing financial loss and inconsistent protocol state. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of request indexing and identified the hard‑coded zero as a logical error. Because the contract does not emit an explicit warning when an overwrite occurs, the problem can be hard to notice until the deployment step fails. The proper fix is to replace the constant index with a per‑user counter that increments each time a new request is stored, or to generate a unique request identifier using a nonce, block number, or cryptographic hash, ensuring that each request occupies a distinct storage slot and cannot be unintentionally overwritten.

title: Signatures missing some parameters being signed
description:
createAgentWithSigWithNFT() for example signs projectId, base64RecParam, serverURL. However, it does not sign privateWorkerAddress or tokenId. This is an issue because although Base has a private mempool, the protocol integrates with Biconomy, which leverages ERC4337 and has a mempool for bundlers. Hence, the signatures will be available in the mempool and anyone can fetch them and submit it directly to base with other malicious tokenId or privateWorkerAddress.
Thus, users can be forced to create agents with token ids they didn't intend to use or use invalid worker addresses, DoSing them. Workers have incentive to do this as they can censor other workers this way from using other workers and only they will be able to make the deployments, censoring other workers. The protocol intends to benefit workers from their work, so they have incentive to do so.
crestal-network/blob/main/crestal-omni-contracts/src/BlueprintCore.sol#L491), the token address used can be another one that has a bigger cost and users end up paying more.
In createAgentWithSigWithNFT() and similar, tokenAddress, tokenId, privateWorkerAddress are not signed.
Internal Pre-conditions
None.
External Pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. User sends signature to be used on createAgentWithSigWithNFT() or createAgentWithTokenWithSig() to the offchain protocol, which forwards it to Biconomy, adding the user operation to the mempool.
2. Attacker picks up the signature from the eip4337 mempool and submits the onchain transaction with other malicious inputs.
Worker censors other workers, DoSes users, makes them pay fees without getting services and ultimately forces users to use the attacker worker's services, who gets illegitimate fees. Or, attacker steals tokens from users by specifying a different token address. Or, another token id ownership is used.
poc:
Here is how the biconomy bundler works (which is the same as the typical bundler):
Aggregating userOps in an alternative mempool to normal Ethereum Transactions
Attacker can become a bundler and listen to the same mempool and perform the attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a partial signing flaw in the functions that allow a user to create an agent with an off‑chain signature, such as createAgentWithSigWithNFT and createAgentWithTokenWithSig. The contract verifies a signature that only covers a subset of the input parameters – typically projectId, a base64‑encoded request parameter and the serverURL – while omitting critical fields like privateWorkerAddress, tokenAddress and tokenId. Because the signature does not bind these mutable values, an attacker who can observe the signed user operation in the public EIP‑4337 mempool (used by Biconomy and other bundlers) can replay the same signature together with altered values for the unsigned fields. The contract’s verification logic accepts the transaction as valid, since it only checks the signed subset, allowing the attacker to substitute a different worker address, a higher‑cost token address or an arbitrary tokenId. This can force users to deploy agents with workers they did not authorize, effectively denying service or censoring competing workers, and can cause users to pay unexpected fees or lose tokens when the token address is swapped for one with a larger cost. The issue manifests whenever a user relies on the signed agent‑creation flow and the transaction is relayed through a public mempool; no explicit pre‑conditions are required. Affected parties include end‑users who expect their chosen worker and token parameters to be honoured, the workers who may be unfairly censored, and the protocol itself which loses trust in its economic model. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature verification code and noticed that several mutable parameters were not included in the signed payload. It can be hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed and the contract emits no error, while the UI may simply display an agent with unexpected attributes, leading users to think the service behaved incorrectly rather than being compromised. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient signing” or “parameter tampering after signature” vulnerabilities, where a valid signature does not protect all user‑controlled data. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a created agent that points to a different worker address, a token cost higher than anticipated, or a token transfer that never occurs despite a successful transaction. To remediate the issue the contract should include every mutable argument – privateWorkerAddress, tokenAddress and tokenId – in the signed message hash, enforce that on‑chain values match the signed values, and preferably adopt a full EIP‑712 typed‑data scheme so that any alteration of the parameters invalidates the signature.

title: Signature Replay attack possible on updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig
description:
The lack of replay protection in the updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig function will cause a significant loss of funds for users as a malicious actor will replay a signed transaction to repeatedly transfer funds from the deployment owner to the fee collection wallet. The protocol didn't have the functionality to refund these funds to the respective users if this issue occurs. So anyway user is gonna lose their fund.
In BlueprintCore.sol at the updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig function, the function verifies a signature using getRequestDeploymentDigest but does not include a nonce, timestamp, or chain ID in the signed message. This allows a valid signature to be reused indefinitely, triggering multiple calls to updateWorkerDeploymentConfigCommon and its payWithERC20 payment logic.
```solidity
function updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig(
    address tokenAddress,
    bytes32 projectId,
    bytes32 requestID,
    string memory updatedBase64Config,
    bytes memory signature
) public {
    bytes32 digest = getRequestDeploymentDigest(projectId, updatedBase64Config, "app.crestal.network");
    address signerAddr = getSignerAddress(digest, signature);
    updateWorkerDeploymentConfigCommon(tokenAddress, signerAddr, projectId, requestID, updatedBase64Config);
}
```
Internal Pre-conditions
1. The updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig function remains public and unchanged in the deployed contract.
2. A user (deployment owner) has approved the BlueprintCore.sol contract to spend their ERC-20 tokens via approve on the token contract.
3. The user has signed a valid message (with projectId, updatedBase64Config, “app.crestal.network”) and submitted it to update a deployment configuration for a requestID with status not equal to Init or Issued.
4. The paymentOpCostMp[tokenAddress][UPDATE_AGENT_OP] returns a non-zero cost.
External Pre-conditions
1. The Base blockchain allows transaction replay if the signature remains valid, which
2. The ERC-20 token contract at tokenAddress supports safeTransferFrom and doesn’t prevent replay.
Attack Path
1. A user (deployment owner) signs a message to update a deployment configuration (projectId, requestID, updatedBase64Config) and submits it via updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig, paying $token to feeCollectionWalletAddress via payWithERC20.
2. The transaction succeeds, updating the configuration and emitting UpdateDeploymentConfig, with the signature recorded on-chain.
3. A malicious actor captures the signature and replays the transaction by calling updateWorkerDeploymentConfigWithSig with the same parameters (tokenAddress, projectId, requestID, updatedBase64Config, signature).
4. Each replay re-executes updateWorkerDeploymentConfigCommon, transferring another $token from the user to feeCollectionWalletAddress (if funds/allowance remain) and resetting status to Pickup if it was GeneratedProof, repeatable until the user’s funds are drained or allowance is revoked.
The user suffers an approximate loss of $token per replay. If replayed indefinitely (e.g., 20 times), the loss could reach 20x more, potentially draining 100% of approved funds. The attacker gains no direct funds but indirectly benefits feeCollectionWalletAddress, incurring only gas costs per replay. The protocol didn't have the functionality to refund this token to the respective users if this issue occurs. So anyway user is gonna lose their fund.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay attack in the function that updates a worker deployment configuration with a signed message. The function verifies a signature that is generated over the project identifier, the new base64 configuration and a static domain string, but it does not embed any nonce, timestamp, block number or chain identifier. Because the signed digest is static, an attacker who obtains a valid signature can call the same function repeatedly with the identical parameters. Each call triggers the internal payment routine that transfers a fixed amount of ERC‑20 tokens from the deployment owner's approved allowance to the protocol's fee‑collection wallet. The contract does not keep any record of previously processed signatures, so the same signature can be replayed until the owner's allowance is exhausted or the owner revokes approval. From a user's perspective the UI shows the deployment configuration being updated successfully, but the token balance of the owner decreases unexpectedly, often to zero, while no additional error is reported. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the deployment owner; the protocol does not provide a refund mechanism, so the drained tokens are effectively permanent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the signature verification logic and noticed the absence of replay protection fields. It is hard to notice because each replay transaction is syntactically valid, emits the same event, and the fee transfer looks like a normal operation, so monitoring tools may not flag it as abnormal. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of missing nonce or signature replay vulnerabilities, where a signed authorisation can be reused without a unique identifier. The proper fix is to include a per‑user nonce (or a timestamp, block number, or chain ID) in the signed message, store the highest used nonce, and reject any call that presents an already‑used nonce, thereby ensuring each signature can be processed only once. Adding such replay protection restores the intended accounting guarantees that a single signed request results in a single fee transfer.

title: Lack of access control in setWorker
description:
The lack of access control in the setWorkerPublicKey function will cause a significant loss of funds for users as a malicious actor will register a fake Worker public key to intercept and disrupt deployment payments.
In BlueprintCore.sol at the setWorkerPublicKey function, the function is declared as public without any restrictions, allowing any address to register or update a public key in the workersPublicKey mapping and add themselves to the workerAddressesMp list.
```solidity
function setWorkerPublicKey(bytes calldata publicKey) public {
    if (workersPublicKey[msg.sender].length == 0) {
        workerAddressesMp[WORKER_ADDRESS_KEY].push(msg.sender);
    }
    workersPublicKey[msg.sender] = publicKey;
}
```
Internal Pre-conditions
1. The setWorkerPublicKey function remains public and unchanged in the deployed contract.
2. Users rely on the workerAddressesMp list or getWorkerPublicKey to select Workers for private deployments (via createProjectIDAndPrivateDeploymentRequest or createAgent).
3. The createAgentWithToken function is callable, requiring payment (via payWithERC20) for agent creation linked to a Worker.
External Pre-conditions
1. The Base blockchain (per the README) allows any address to send transactions to the contract, which is standard behavior for public networks.
Attack Path
1. A malicious actor calls setWorkerPublicKey with a fake public key, registering their address in workersPublicKey and adding it to workerAddressesMp["worker_address_key"].
2. A user queries getWorkerAddresses or getWorkerPublicKey and selects the malicious actor’s address as the privateWorkerAddress for a deployment.
3. The user pays in ERC-20 tokens to create an agent, encrypting base64Proposal with the malicious Worker’s public key and triggering a deployment request.
4. The malicious actor receives the deployment request (status set to Pickup) but does not deploy the agent, either keeping the encrypted data or ignoring the request, causing the deployment to fail.
• The user suffers the loss of there ERC-20 tokens. The attacker gains no direct funds but may extract value from the encrypted base64Proposal (sensitive data), incurring only gas costs.
• Also, the transfered token will go to feeCollectionWalletAddress and protocol didn't have a functionality to refund this token to the respective users if this issue occurs. So anyway user is gonna lose their fund.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized access control flaw in the function that allows a worker to register or update its public key. Because the function is declared as public and lacks any modifier restricting callers, any address can call setWorkerPublicKey and insert its own entry into the workersPublicKey mapping and the workerAddressesMp list. The contract’s business logic assumes that the addresses returned by getWorkerAddresses or getWorkerPublicKey correspond to legitimate workers that will reliably perform private deployments. When a malicious actor registers a fake public key, a user who queries the list may select the attacker’s address as the privateWorkerAddress, pay ERC‑20 tokens to create an agent, and encrypt the deployment proposal with the attacker’s key. The attacker receives the encrypted proposal and can simply ignore the request, causing the deployment to remain in a 'Pickup' state and the user’s tokens to be transferred to the fee collection wallet with no refund mechanism. The impact is loss of the user’s payment and potential exposure of sensitive proposal data, while the attacker gains no direct token reward but may profit from the leaked information. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed with the current version of setWorkerPublicKey and when users rely on the worker list for private deployments, which is the normal operating condition of the protocol. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the worker registration flow and identified that the function lacked any access restriction. The flaw can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when an unknown address is added, and the list of workers may appear to grow normally, masking the presence of a malicious entry. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of authorization bypass or improper access control vulnerabilities, where a privileged operation is exposed to any caller. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist of registered workers, controlled by the contract owner, and apply a modifier that checks the caller against this list before allowing a public key to be set. This restores the intended invariant that only vetted workers can receive deployment payments, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that payments are made to trustworthy agents.

title: booster#buy fails to apply discount
description:
[Booster.sol#L92-L95](https://github.com/Buffer-Finance/Buffer-Protocol-v2_5/blob/84b6060b4447b2550de595202e8820c7f515988b/contracts/core/Booster.sol#L92-L95)
```solidity
    uint256 price = couponPrice - discount;
    require(token.balanceOf(user) >= price, "Not enough balance");

    token.safeTransferFrom(user, address(this), couponPrice); // @> transfers couponPrice rather than price
```
When buying boosts the contract mistakenly transfers couponPrice rather than price which is reduced by discount. Additionally the event also emits this incorrect value.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect token transfer amount in the boost purchase function. The contract calculates a discounted price as couponPrice minus discount and stores it in a local variable called price, but when it collects payment it calls safeTransferFrom with couponPrice instead of price. As a result the user is charged the full coupon price even though a discount was advertised. The same mistake is reflected in the emitted event, which logs the undiscounted amount. The root cause is a simple logic error: the variable used for the transfer and the event was not updated after the discount calculation. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any user who purchases a boost with a non‑zero discount will unintentionally overpay. The impact is that users lose tokens equal to the discount amount, the protocol’s accounting shows a higher inflow than expected, and the UI may display a discounted price while the on‑chain state reflects a full payment. The bug manifests only when a discount is applied, i.e., when the discount value is greater than zero. It affects all participants who rely on the boost purchase function, including regular users and the protocol’s revenue model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the purchase logic and compared the calculated price with the amount transferred. Because the transfer succeeds and no revert occurs, the problem can be hard to notice unless the developer checks the event data or compares token balances before and after the call. To fix the issue the contract should transfer the variable price, which already incorporates the discount, and the event should emit price as well. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect value used in external call or payment amount mismatch where the amount sent does not match the amount intended by the business logic, leading to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective.

title: Transferred options can only be closed early by previous owner
description:
[BufferRouter.sol#L197-L205](https://github.com/Buffer-Finance/Buffer-Protocol-v2_5/blob/84b6060b4447b2550de595202e8820c7f515988b/contracts/core/BufferRouter.sol#L197-L205)
```solidity
    (address signer, ) = getAccountMapping(queuedTrade.user);

    bool isUserSignValid = Validator.verifyCloseAnytime(
        optionsContract.assetPair(),
        closeParam.userSignInfo.timestamp,
        params.optionId,
        closeParam.userSignInfo.signature,
        signer
    );
```
Options are minted as NFTs allowing options to be transferred to other users. This allows users to potentially sell/transfer their options to other user. This cause 2 issues:
1) The previous owner can close the option early to cause damage to the new owner
2) The new owner cannot close their option early by themselves
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns theearly‑close mechanism of option NFTs that can be transferred between users. When an option is minted it is represented as an ERC‑721 token and the contract stores a mapping from the original user address to a signer that is later used to validate a closeAnytime request. The closeAnytime function calls getAccountMapping with the address recorded at the time the option was created (queuedTrade.user) and verifies the supplied signature against that signer. If the option NFT is transferred to a new owner, the ownership record in the ERC‑721 registry is updated, but the internal mapping that supplies the signer is not. Consequently the contract still accepts a signature from the previous owner as valid, allowing that former holder to close the option early. The new owner, who now holds the NFT, cannot provide a valid signature because the contract does not recognise them as the signer, so they are unable to close the option themselves. This logic flaw can be exploited by a seller who transfers an option and then immediately submits a signed closeAnytime transaction, causing the option to be settled in the seller’s favour and depriving the buyer of any remaining value. The impact is a loss of the buyer’s premium or payoff, effectively making the transferred option worthless to the new holder. The bug manifests only after a transfer event; before any transfer the closeAnytime function works as intended. Users who purchase options expect to retain full control, including the ability to close early, but instead see their position disappear without any action on their part. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between NFT transfer logic and the closeAnytime verification routine. It is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an obvious error – it simply processes the closure as if it were authorized, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate the issue the contract should either disallow transferring option NFTs altogether or adjust the closeAnytime implementation to derive the signer from the current owner of the NFT (for example by calling ERC721.ownerOf) and verify the signature against that address. This would align the access control with the actual ownership semantics and prevent a previous owner from unilaterally closing a transferred option.

title: _fetchTWAP incorrectly assumes that blb is always token0 leading to bad pricing if it isn't
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle price inversion bug in the staking contract. The contract calls Uniswap V3 pool.observe and directly uses the returned tick to compute a TWAP price assuming that the BLB token is always token0. Uniswap V3 sorts the two tokens by address, so depending on the address ordering BLB may be token1. When BLB is token1 the price returned by the pool is the inverse of the true BLB/quote price. Because the code does not detect this situation, it uses the inverted price for vesting calculations and user‑facing pricing. An attacker or any user can trigger a transaction that reads the wrong price, causing the protocol to overcharge users for deposits or to vest tokens at a rate that is far cheaper than intended, effectively draining treasury value. The bug manifests only when the pool was created with BLB as token1, which occurs when the stable asset address is numerically lower than the BLB address. Users experience unexpectedly high fees, rewards that are much lower than expected, or balances that appear to shrink after a vesting operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the _fetchTWAP function where the token ordering assumption was identified as missing. It is hard to notice because the price value itself looks plausible and the contract does not emit any warning; the inversion only becomes apparent when comparing expected versus actual amounts. The correct mitigation is to record the token order at pool initialization and, when fetching the TWAP, invert the price if BLB is token1 before using it in any accounting logic. This aligns the oracle output with the protocol’s business logic that treats BLB as the base asset, restoring accurate pricing and preventing overcharging or under‑vesting.

title: It is impossible to complete any vest unless all vests are mature
bug_full: The contract implements a batch vesting function that iterates over a list of vest indexes supplied by the caller. The code mistakenly caches the length of the global `vests` array instead of the length of the caller‑provided `_vestIndexes` array. As a result, the loop runs for `vests.length` iterations and accesses `_vestIndexes[i]` for each index. When the caller owns fewer vest entries than the total number of vests in the system, the loop attempts to read beyond the end of `_vestIndexes`, triggering an out‑of‑bounds error and causing the transaction to revert. Because the function first checks that the caller’s vesting array length is at least the cached length, the only way for the check to pass is when the caller’s vesting entries are exactly as many as the global vest count. Consequently, a user who wants to claim a single mature vest cannot do so unless every other vest owned by that user is also mature; otherwise the call fails and none of the funds are released. From the user’s perspective the expected behaviour – receiving the vested amount for a specific schedule – is replaced by a transaction revert and the user’s balance remains unchanged, which may appear as “my funds disappeared” or “the vesting function does nothing”. The impact is that legitimate token holders can have their vested tokens locked indefinitely until all of their vest schedules mature simultaneously, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions about independent vest releases. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the length checks with the actual array being iterated over. It is subtle because the length comparison itself looks plausible and only fails when the caller’s vest count is smaller than the global count, a condition that may not be exercised in simple test cases. The proper fix is to use `_vestIndexes.length` for the loop bound and for the length validation, ensuring that the function only iterates over the indexes actually supplied by the caller. Additional defensive checks, such as verifying that each index is within the bounds of the `vests` array, would further harden the function against similar mistakes. In summary, the vulnerability is a classic array‑length mismatch leading to an out‑of‑bounds read, which forces users to vest all schedules at once and can effectively lock funds.

title: Rewards will be permanently lost for ibToken with no deposits
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the reward‑distribution logic of the staking contract. When the contract attempts to update reward data for a particular ibToken, it first calls rewardPerToken which returns the previously stored reward per token value if the total supply of that ibToken is zero. The calling code then unconditionally writes rewardPerTokenStored[_ibToken] = rewardPerToken(_ibToken) and advances lastUpdateTime[_ibToken] to the current block timestamp, even though no ibTokens are deposited. Because the supply is zero, the reward‑per‑token calculation for the elapsed time yields no new reward, but the timestamp is still moved forward. Consequently any reward that would have accrued during the period with zero deposits is permanently discarded. The problem is compounded by the fact that rewards start accruing at the moment an ibToken is registered, before any user can deposit, guaranteeing a loss of reward tokens for every newly added ibToken until the first deposit occurs. This bug manifests when a user later deposits ibTokens and expects to receive rewards for the entire time the contract has been active; instead the user receives less than expected, and the protocol loses the unclaimed reward amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward accounting functions, where the conditional guard for zero totalSupply was found to be insufficient. It is hard to notice because the UI may still display a non‑zero reward rate, and the missing rewards only become apparent when users claim or when the protocol’s accounting reports lower than expected payouts. The affected parties are liquidity providers who stake ibTokens, the protocol that promises a certain APY, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward accounting. To remediate, the contract should refrain from updating lastUpdateTime and rewardPerTokenStored when totalSupply[_ibToken] is zero, i.e., only advance the timestamp after the first deposit or guard the update with a check that the supply is positive. This ensures that reward accrual starts only when there are actual staked tokens, preventing permanent loss of rewards and aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of rewarding only active participants.

title: _convertMatchOrders will fail to function properly for lenders if any borrower has canceled a matched order
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the matching logic of a lending pool contract that pairs lenders with borrowers through a per‑lender array of MatchOrder structs. When a borrower invokes the killBorrowerMatch function to cancel a matched order, the contract zeroes out the lCollateral, bCollateral and borrower fields but deliberately keeps the empty struct in the lender's matches array to preserve ordering. Later, the internal _convertMatchOrders routine iterates over this array in a last‑in‑first‑out (FILO) fashion, calculating how much collateral can be removed from each match. The loop contains a guard that breaks execution when the calculated amountToRemove equals zero, which occurs whenever the stored match has zero collateral. Because the zeroed entry remains in the array, the conversion loop encounters it, triggers the break, and stops processing any earlier matches that still hold valid collateral. Consequently, deposits made before the cancelled order become impossible to match or convert, effectively locking those funds. A malicious borrower can deliberately cancel a match, creating the zero‑collateral sentinel that halts the conversion process for the associated lender and any other borrowers whose orders depend on that lender’s liquidity. From the user’s perspective, a lender may see that their balance does not change after a conversion attempt, no MatchOrderConverted events are emitted, and the UI shows funds as still pending or “stuck”. Borrowers may notice that their own orders are cancelled while other borrowers cannot be matched, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the matching routine, where an auditor flagged the comment “@audit matching loop breaks when collateral in match is 0”. It is difficult to spot because the zeroed struct appears syntactically valid and the break condition seems reasonable for normal operation, yet it fails to account for sentinel entries left by cancellations. The root cause is a logic error: the algorithm does not properly handle empty or cancelled matches and treats a zero removal amount as a termination signal instead of skipping the entry. This class of bug falls under improper handling of sentinel values in data structures, leading to premature loop termination. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style attack that can lock liquidity, require borrowers to manually cancel and resubmit orders, and degrade the protocol’s reliability. Affected parties include lenders with pending matches, borrowers whose orders are matched through the same pool, and the overall protocol governance. The vulnerability manifests whenever a borrower cancels a match before the pool processes the lender’s conversion. To remediate, the contract should detect empty matches, remove them from the array (e.g., by popping) and continue the iteration rather than breaking, ensuring that valid earlier matches are still processed and funds remain accessible.

title: In the event of a partial match inside _convertMatchOrders, borrower funds will be over-allocated
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error that occurs during the partial‑match handling of loan orders in the matching loop. When a lender’s funds are applied to a borrower’s order, the code correctly removes the match entry if the lender’s funds exactly equal the lender collateral (full fill). However, in the partial‑fill branch the implementation only reduces the lender collateral field (lCollateral) while leaving the borrower collateral field (bCollateral) unchanged. Because the borrower’s collateral is not decremented, the same borrower funds can be accounted for a second time in subsequent matches, effectively over‑allocating the borrower’s position. This double‑allocation creates a shortfall in the contract’s accounting: the contract believes it has transferred more borrower collateral than it actually holds, leading to a deficit that can only be patched by external donations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the matching algorithm, where the auditor noticed that the borrower side of the state update was missing in the partial‑fill case. It can be hard to notice because the full‑fill path behaves correctly and the contract may still appear to function for simple cases; the discrepancy only surfaces when orders are partially filled multiple times, which may be rare in normal testing. An attacker could exploit this by deliberately submitting partial matches that trigger the faulty branch, causing the contract to think it has allocated more borrower collateral than it actually did, and then withdrawing the excess funds before the shortfall is noticed. The impact is that funds can disappear from the protocol’s balance sheet, borrowers may receive less collateral than expected, and the protocol’s financial integrity is compromised. The bug manifests to users as missing or reduced borrower collateral after a partial match, or as a situation where the contract’s total collateral accounting does not match the sum of individual positions. The affected parties include borrowers, lenders, and any protocol participants relying on accurate collateral accounting. The root cause is a missing state update for the borrower collateral variable in the partial‑fill branch, violating the invariant that total allocated collateral must equal the sum of lender and borrower allocations. To remediate, the partial‑fill logic should decrement both the lender collateral and the borrower collateral by the amount of funds transferred, restoring the accounting balance and preventing over‑allocation. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a “partial update” or “incomplete state mutation” bug, where only a subset of related variables are updated, leading to inconsistent internal state and potential fund loss.

title: Using address rather than bytes32 for destinationAddress in wstUsdcBridge#bridgeWstUsdc causes incompatibility with chains that utilize 32 byte addresses
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the bridgeWstUsdc function in the wstUsdcBridge contract, which accepts a destination address parameter typed as address (20‑byte EVM format) while the LayerZero cross‑chain messaging protocol expects a 32‑byte identifier (bytes32) for destination chains that do not use the standard Ethereum address size. This type mismatch is the root cause of an incompatibility that only manifests when a user attempts to bridge wstUSDC to a chain that represents accounts with 32‑byte identifiers, such as non‑EVM or custom LayerZero endpoints. Because the function stores the destination address in a 20‑byte slot, the higher‑order bytes required by the target chain are silently dropped, leading to an incorrect or truncated address being transmitted. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by initiating a bridge transaction to a supported chain; the contract will emit a bridging receipt that appears successful, but the underlying LayerZero message will contain an invalid address, causing the remote bridge to either reject the transfer or route the funds to an unintended address. The impact is that users may see their tokens disappear from the source chain while receiving nothing on the destination chain, balances may become zero, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about successful cross‑chain delivery are violated. This condition occurs only under the specific circumstance where the destination chain uses a 32‑byte address format; on standard EVM chains the function behaves as expected, which makes the bug hard to notice during normal testing. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the function signature against LayerZero’s specification and identified the mismatch. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction hash, but the expected refund or received balance on the target chain remains unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. To remediate the problem the destinationAddress parameter should be changed from address to bytes32, and all encoding/decoding logic must be updated to correctly handle the larger identifier, ensuring that the LayerZero message carries the full 32‑byte address and that the bridge’s accounting logic validates successful delivery before confirming the transaction.

title: Fees will be lost in the event that a user withdraws from MarketFundingPool and there isn't enough reserves to cover fees
bug_full: The contract implements a fee‑harvesting routine in the private function _reevaluateGainsOnPool. Each time the function is called it measures the increase of the pool’s total value since the last evaluation (valueHighPoint), computes a proportional fee (gains * feePortion / 256) and then limits the fee amount to the amount of collateral that is currently held in the contract, as reported by reserves(). The intention of the min‑operation is to avoid trying to transfer more tokens than the contract actually possesses. However, after the fee amount is capped, the function still updates valueHighPoint by adding the full gains value, as if the full fee had been collected. When a user subsequently withdraws from the MarketFundingPool and the contract’s reserves are lower than the fee that should be taken, the capped fee is taken (or possibly zero) and the remaining “missing” fee is silently discarded because valueHighPoint has already been increased. This creates a situation where accrued fees are effectively lost and can never be reclaimed. The bug manifests only when the pool experiences a withdrawal that reduces the on‑chain collateral below the amount of fees that were expected to be collected at the next evaluation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the protocol’s accounting shows that fees have been charged, but the actual token balance does not reflect the expected revenue – the user may see lower returns or notice that the pool’s fee‑share is smaller than advertised. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the fee‑evaluation logic; it is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error, it merely updates an internal accounting variable incorrectly, making the loss of fees appear as a normal state transition. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting after conditional fee capping” bugs, where a conditional reduction of a payable amount is not reflected in the corresponding accounting state. To remediate the problem the contract should adjust valueHighPoint based on the actual fee that was transferred, or defer the update of valueHighPoint until sufficient reserves are available, ensuring that any uncaptured fee remains recorded and can be collected later. Properly fixing the logic restores the invariant that total fees accrued equals the sum of fees actually transferred, preventing silent revenue loss and preserving the economic guarantees of the MarketFundingPool.

title: ParentFundingPool#removeCollateral fails to update valueHighPoint resulting in lost fees
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the collateral withdrawal routine of a funding pool contract. When a user calls the function that removes collateral, the contract correctly burns the user's shares and transfers the underlying token, but it neglects to adjust an internal accounting variable known as valueHighPoint. valueHighPoint represents a high‑water mark used to calculate protocol fees on subsequent gains. Because the variable is left unchanged after collateral is taken out, it remains artificially high. As a result, the fee calculation logic, which compares new gains against this high‑water mark, determines that no additional fees have been generated, even though the pool’s value may have increased. This flaw originates from the omission of a proportional reduction of valueHighPoint in the removeCollateral implementation. An attacker or any participant can exploit the bug simply by invoking removeCollateral with any non‑zero share amount; the contract will silently keep the high‑water mark inflated, causing future fee accruals to be skipped. The impact is that the protocol collects less revenue than intended, effectively allowing users to withdraw collateral while the pool continues to earn gains that are never taxed. The condition under which it occurs is any execution of the withdrawal path while the contract is not paused. All participants who rely on fee distribution—typically the protocol treasury and possibly other stakeholders—are affected because the missing fees reduce the overall revenue pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state updates performed after collateral removal and identified that valueHighPoint was never decreased. It can be hard to notice because the withdrawal itself succeeds and the user receives the expected collateral, so the symptom is invisible from a UI perspective; only the fee accounting deviates from the expected model, leading to a subtle loss of revenue over time. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency errors where a high‑water‑mark or checkpoint is not updated after a state‑changing operation. From a user’s point of view the contract behaves normally—balances are transferred and events are emitted—but the protocol’s expected fee revenue disappears, violating the business rule that fees should be collected on every positive gain. To remediate the issue, the contract should recalculate valueHighPoint after collateral is removed, reducing it proportionally to the amount of collateral withdrawn, thereby restoring the correct fee baseline for future gain calculations.

title: PT donation attack will DOS spell deposit permanently
description:
```solidity
(uint256 ptAmount, , ) = IPendleRouter(_pendleRouter).swapExactTokenForPt(
    address(this),
    market,
    minPtOut,
    params,
    input,
    limitOrder
);

if (ptAmount != IERC20Upgradeable(pt).balanceOf(address(this))) revert Errors.SWAP_FAILED(pt);
```
After swapping from debt token to PT, the contract makes an exact check against the balance of the contract to ensure the swap executed as expected. The issue with this is that even if it is a single wei over, the contract will revert. This makes it trivial to permanently DOS opening positions via the contract by donating a small amount of PT to the contract.
bug_full: The contract that opens a Pendle position swaps a debt token for principal tokens (PT) using the router and then validates the swap by comparing the amount returned from the router (ptAmount) with the PT balance of the contract. The validation uses a strict inequality check (ptAmount != balance) and reverts if the two values differ. The root cause is that the check assumes the contract holds exactly the amount received from the swap, ignoring any PT that may already be present in the contract. An attacker can exploit this by sending a tiny amount of PT (even a single wei) to the contract before the swap is executed. When the router returns ptAmount that matches the newly swapped amount, the contract’s balance will be larger by the donated PT, causing the != condition to evaluate to true and triggering a revert. The revert aborts the whole position‑opening transaction, effectively denying service to any user trying to deposit through the contract. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with a “SWAP_FAILED” error, the expected position is not created, and no funds are transferred, even though the user supplied the correct input. This denial‑of‑service can be made permanent because the donated PT remains in the contract, continuously breaking the equality check for all future calls. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the swap logic, where the equality comparison stood out as unusually strict. It is hard to notice because a balance mismatch of a single wei is rare in normal operation and the revert message does not indicate a malicious PT donation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect post‑condition validation” or “over‑strict state checks” that can be abused to create a permanent denial of service. The proper fix is to replace the != comparison with a check that only ensures the contract received at least the expected amount, for example using a greater‑than-or‑equal comparison (ptAmount <= balance) or verifying that the balance is not less than ptAmount. This change allows the contract to tolerate any pre‑existing PT balance and prevents the DOS vector while preserving the intended accounting guarantees.

title: stUSDC#deposit compares current tby price with potentially stale pool price which can lead to small yield loss for pool
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the depositTby function of the stUSDC token, which calculates the amount of stUSDC to mint by multiplying the deposited TBY amount with the current exchange rate obtained from the associated BloomPool. The pool’s exchange rate is only refreshed when the poke function is called, and poke is deliberately throttled to at most once every 24 hours. Consequently, if the pool has not been poked for several hours – for example, a 12‑hour window – the rate returned by getRate is stale and does not reflect the yield that has accumulated during that period. When a user deposits TBY during this interval, the contract uses the outdated high rate, causing the deposited TBY to be valued slightly higher than its true worth in the pool. This over‑valuation results in the user receiving more stUSDC than should be minted, effectively siphoning a small amount of the pool’s accrued yield. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who monitors the pool’s poke schedule, waits until a significant amount of yield has built up without a recent poke, and then performs a deposit to mint stUSDC at the inflated rate, thereby extracting the unaccounted yield. The impact is a gradual erosion of the pool’s profitability and a mismatch between the accounting of deposited assets and the actual pool balance, which may go unnoticed by users because the discrepancy is modest and only manifests after extended periods without a poke. The bug affects all participants of the protocol – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – because any deposit performed under stale‑rate conditions reduces the pool’s overall yield. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the poke timing restriction and the deposit logic, revealing that the rate used for minting does not compensate for pending yield. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning or error when the rate is stale, and the UI typically shows only the resulting stUSDC balance, which may appear correct from the user’s perspective. To remediate the issue, the rate calculation should be adjusted to subtract the yield that has accrued since the last successful poke, or the contract should allow more frequent or on‑demand rate updates, ensuring that the exchange rate used for minting always reflects the current pool state. This class of bug falls under stale‑price or oracle‑delay vulnerabilities, where a contract relies on a value that is not refreshed in real time, leading to inaccurate financial calculations and potential loss of funds.

title: Airdrop supply methodology has been changed leading to excess token emissions
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the airdrop contract accounts for token supply when the emission schedule is calculated. In the original VELO MerkleClaim implementation tokens are minted only when a user successfully claims, so the contract’s balance does not contain any unclaimed tokens. The PegAirdrop fork, however, pre‑funds the contract with the full airdrop allocation and distributes those tokens from its balance as users claim. The EmissionScheduler contract determines the amount to emit each epoch by taking the difference between the reported peg supply and the ve supply and applying a fixed percentage. Because the peg supply value includes the tokens that are still locked inside the PegAirdrop contract, the scheduler counts those unclaimed tokens as if they were already in circulation. This double‑counting causes the calculated epoch emission to be larger than intended, leading to excess token minting until the claim period ends. The issue is a classic accounting mismatch where reserved tokens are mistakenly treated as circulating supply. It can be exploited indirectly: the protocol will emit more tokens than the economic model predicts, diluting existing holders, inflating the total supply, and potentially allowing governance to recover the surplus later. The problem manifests only when the airdrop contract holds a non‑zero balance of unclaimed tokens and the emission function runs each epoch, which is the normal operating condition for the protocol. All token holders, the governance team, and users expecting a fixed emission schedule are affected because the token economics are altered without any explicit on‑chain warning. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two MerkleClaim implementations and traced the supply values used by the emission logic. It is hard to notice because the emission numbers may appear reasonable at a glance; the excess supply is hidden in the aggregate peg supply figure and only becomes apparent when the total supply diverges from the expected model. To remediate the issue the PegAirdrop balance should be excluded from the peg supply used in the emission calculation, or the contract should adopt an on‑demand minting approach similar to the original VELO implementation, ensuring that only truly circulating tokens are considered when determining new emissions. This correction restores the integrity of the accounting model and prevents unintended inflation of the token supply.

title: Curve gauge rewards can be griefed
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the Hyperstable contract’s expectation of how the Curve gauge’s claimRewards function behaves and the actual logic implemented in the gauge. The Hyperstable contract exposes a claimFees function that is guarded by a lock modifier and a require statement allowing only the team address to invoke it. Inside this function the contract calls ICurveGauge(staking).claimRewards(address(this), msg.sender). The developers assumed that passing the team address as the second argument would cause the gauge to transfer the accrued reward tokens directly to the team. However, the Curve gauge’s claim_rewards implementation treats a zero‑address receiver as a special case: if the _receiver argument equals ZERO_ADDRESS, the function uses the default reward receiver, which is the gauge contract itself. When the Hyperstable contract calls claimRewards with address(this) as the _addr parameter, it is effectively asking the gauge to claim rewards on behalf of the gauge contract. Because the second argument (msg.sender) is non‑zero, the gauge asserts that _addr must equal msg.sender; this assertion fails, causing the call to revert. As a result, the rewards are never transferred to the team and remain locked inside the gauge contract. In practice, an attacker (or even an honest team member) can trigger the permissionless path by calling the gauge’s claim_rewards directly with the _receiver set to ZERO_ADDRESS, causing the rewards to be sent to the gauge contract itself where they become permanently unrecoverable. The issue manifests whenever claimFees is executed or when any actor invokes the gauge’s claim function with a zero‑address receiver while the rewards are still pending. The affected parties are the protocol’s team, which loses access to the fees it is supposed to collect, and indirectly the users who rely on those fees for the protocol’s economic model. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Hyperstable governance contracts by inspecting the call flow to the external Curve gauge and comparing it with the gauge’s source code. It is subtle because the claimFees function appears to enforce a strict access control, yet the external call’s semantics are not obvious, making the loss of funds easy to overlook during testing. The root cause is a logical assumption that the external contract will honor the supplied receiver address, ignoring the gauge’s default‑receiver fallback. To remediate, the protocol should route LP staking through a dedicated proxy contract that explicitly forwards rewards to the team address, ensuring that the gauge’s default‑receiver path is never exercised and that rewards cannot be inadvertently sent to the gauge itself. This class of bug falls under “incorrect handling of external contract callbacks” and “reward‑distribution logic mismatch”, where assumptions about third‑party contract behavior lead to permanent loss of assets.

title: `AdaptiveIRM#_curve` multiples instead of dividing leading to "V" shaped curve instead of expected "L" shaped curve
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mathematical implementation error in the Adaptive Interest Rate Model (AdaptiveIRM) curve function. The original design from Morpho uses a division operation to compute a coefficient that shapes the interest rate curve as an L‑shaped function, meaning the rate rises as utilization approaches the target level. In the forked Hyperstable version the division (WAD.wDivToZero(ConstantsLib.CURVE_STEEPNESS)) was mistakenly replaced with a multiplication (INT_WAD.sMulWad(CURVE_STEEPNESS)). Because of this substitution the coefficient is calculated incorrectly when the utilization error (err) is negative, causing the curve to slope downward as utilization moves toward the target from the left. The result is a V‑shaped interest rate curve where rates unintentionally decrease as utilization rises toward the target, contrary to the intended economic incentives. This bug occurs whenever the utilization is below the target, i.e., when err < 0, and the contract computes the coefficient using the erroneous multiplication. It affects all participants that rely on the interest rate calculation: borrowers see lower than expected borrowing costs, lenders receive lower returns, and the protocol’s risk management assumptions are violated because the rate no longer penalizes high utilization. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the forked implementation line‑by‑line with the reference Morpho contract and identified the mismatched arithmetic operation. The problem is subtle because the function still returns a non‑negative rate, so the contract does not revert, and the curve still appears monotonic, making the deviation hard to notice without inspecting the shape of the curve. From a user perspective the UI may display unusually low interest rates when the pool is lightly utilized, leading to expectations of normal rates being broken; users may wonder why their expected higher returns are missing. The economic impact is a mispricing of capital that can be exploited: an attacker could keep utilization below the target to obtain artificially low borrowing rates while still earning lending rewards, potentially draining the pool over time. The correct remediation is to restore the original division operation, i.e., replace the multiplication with a division so that the coefficient is computed as 1 − 1/C when err < 0, thereby re‑establishing the intended L‑shaped curve and aligning incentives with the protocol’s design.

title: `AdaptiveIRM` has been integrated incorrectly and will not work as expected
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect integration of the Adaptive Interest Rate Model (AdaptiveIRM) into the Morpho market logic. The contract calculates the average borrow rate using a cached value that reflects the previous period’s rate instead of the current, dynamically‑computed rate. This stale rate is then used when the system accrues interest for borrowers and suppliers, as well as when it updates vault‑specific interest indexes. Because the cached rate does not incorporate the most recent market conditions, the amount of interest added to total borrow assets and total supply assets can be either higher or lower than it should be. An attacker or an ordinary user can trigger the bug simply by performing a normal operation such as depositing collateral or borrowing assets; the contract will first accrue position debt based on the outdated rate and only afterwards update the interest rate, meaning the accrued interest is calculated with the wrong figure. The impact is a mis‑allocation of funds: borrowers may be charged more interest than warranted, while lenders may receive less accrued interest, leading to balances that appear lower than expected, missing refunds, or supply shares that do not match the underlying assets. This effect becomes visible when users check their balances after a transaction and see that the supplied amount has not grown as anticipated or that the debt has increased unexpectedly. The issue is triggered whenever the market’s _accrueInterest function is called after a non‑zero elapsed time and the AdaptiveIRM integration follows the pattern of using the previous average rate before state changes, which is the case for most vault‑related operations such as PositionManager.deposit. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Morpho integration flow with the reference AdaptiveIRM implementation and identified that the average rate calculation was performed before the market state was updated, contrary to the intended trapezoidal approximation. Because the discrepancy is often small on a per‑block basis, it can be difficult to notice without a detailed accounting comparison, especially in a live system where many transactions occur. To remediate the problem, the contract should stop caching the interest rate for a vault and instead compute it on‑the‑fly from the IRM each time interest needs to be accrued, updating only the endRateAt and lastUpdate fields as prescribed by AdaptiveIRM.updateInterestRateAtTarget. This change ensures that the interest charged reflects the current market conditions, restoring the expected accounting invariants and preventing users from experiencing unexpected loss of funds or incorrect interest accrual. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “stale‑state interest calculation” bugs, where a protocol relies on outdated financial parameters to perform monetary updates, violating the core business logic that interest must be computed from the most recent rate.

title: In the event of yield loss, yield will be double counted leading to excess fees
bug_full: The vulnerability is a performance‑fee over‑charging bug that occurs when the contract calculates fees based solely on the difference between the current USD‑per‑share value and the value recorded in the previous update. Because the code does not keep a high‑water mark, a temporary drop in the share price resets the reference point. When the price later climbs back above the lowered reference but still below the original peak, the contract treats the entire climb as new yield and charges the performance fee again. This results in the same yield being counted twice, effectively extracting excess fees from token holders. The root cause is the lack of a persistent high‑water tracker; the fee logic uses lastUsdPerShare which is overwritten even on downward movements, so subsequent upward movements are incorrectly considered fresh profit. An attacker or even normal market volatility can trigger the condition by causing the share price to fall and rise repeatedly, for example a price path 1.0 → 1.1 (fee taken on 0.1) → 1.05 → 1.1 (fee taken again on the 0.05 increase, which includes part of the original 0.1 gain). Users see their balances grow less than expected, or notice that the protocol’s fee deductions are higher than the advertised 10 % performance fee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the StUsdc.sol fee‑distribution function, where the auditor noticed that the else if (newUsdPerShare < lastUsdPerShare) branch only updates the share price without adjusting any fee‑related state, allowing the next upward move to be treated as new profit. Because each individual fee calculation looks correct, the problem is subtle and may only become apparent after several price oscillations. To remediate, the contract should store a high‑water mark (the maximum USD‑per‑share observed) and compute fees only on the amount that exceeds this mark, or otherwise ensure that fees are charged only on net positive gains that have not been previously taxed. This change aligns the fee mechanism with the intended business logic that users pay fees only on genuine, untaxed yield, preserving the accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: SUP rewards for depositing TBYs can be gamed by depositing TBYs that are close to expiration
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑minting logic of the stUSDC contract when a user deposits a tokenized bond (TBY) via the depositTby function. The contract calculates the amount of stUSDC to mint by multiplying the current exchange rate of the TBY with the deposited amount and a scaling factor, and then it awards rewards based solely on this amountMinted value. Because the exchange rate is higher for TBYs that are close to their expiration date, a depositor can obtain a large number of stUSDC shares while the underlying yield that the TBY will generate after maturity is minimal. The root cause is the absence of any weighting for the remaining time until the TBY’s maturity; the reward formula treats all non‑redeemable TBYs as equal regardless of how soon they will become redeemable. An attacker can therefore acquire TBYs that are about to expire, deposit them, receive a disproportionate amount of reward tokens, and later withdraw the underlying assets, leaving the protocol with inflated TVL but little real value. This situation occurs whenever a TBY passes the isTbyRedeemable check (i.e., it is not yet redeemable) but is close to the redemption deadline. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward calculation code, where the logic appeared to reward deposits proportionally to the minted amount without considering the bond’s remaining lifespan. The bug is subtle because the emitted event and the user‑visible reward amount look correct; only a deeper analysis of the bond’s time‑to‑maturity reveals the mismatch. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after depositing a near‑expiry TBY the UI shows a large increase in stUSDC balance and reward tokens, yet the expected future yield or redemption value is far lower than anticipated, effectively causing “money to disappear” from the protocol’s perspective. The class of bug can be described as a reward‑calculation or accounting mismatch where incentives are not aligned with the economic value of the deposited asset. To remediate the issue the reward algorithm should be adjusted to factor in the remaining time until maturity, for example by scaling rewards proportionally to the length of time left or by capping rewards for TBYs that are close to expiration, thereby ensuring that rewards reflect the true value contributed to the protocol’s TVL.

title: `PositionManager#liquidatePosition` fails to update vaultDebt and vaultCollateral
bug_full: The PositionManager contract contains a logic error in the liquidatePosition function. When a liquidation is performed the function correctly reduces the individual debt snapshot and collateral shares of the target account, but it fails to adjust the aggregate vault debt snapshot (_vaultDebtSnapshot) and the total vault collateral (vaultCollateral). Because these global accounting variables remain unchanged, the protocol continues to treat the vault as if the repaid debt and withdrawn collateral still exist. This creates phantom debt and collateral that distort the inputs to the interest rate strategy, causing interest rates to be calculated on stale, inflated values. An attacker who can trigger liquidations through the authorized liquidationManager can repeatedly invoke liquidatePosition, causing the vault’s reported debt to stay high while the actual debt is lower, which may lead to artificially low interest rates for borrowers or artificially high rates for lenders, and can also cause healthy positions to be mistakenly considered under‑collateralized and liquidated. The bug manifests only in internal state variables; there is no direct UI indication, making it hard to notice until interest rates appear inconsistent or unexpected liquidations occur. The issue was discovered by the development team during an audit of the contract code. To remediate, the function must update both _vaultDebtSnapshot and vaultCollateral after adjusting the target’s balances, ensuring that the vault’s total debt and collateral accurately reflect the liquidation. This class of bug is an accounting state‑inconsistency error where aggregate metrics are not kept in sync with per‑account changes, violating the protocol’s financial invariants and potentially leading to loss of funds through mis‑priced liquidations.

title: Duplicate `_tokenNameSuffix` and `_tokenSymbolSuffix` will incorrectly update current Market
description:
[PrePOMarketFactory.sol#L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/main/contracts/core/PrePOMarketFactory.sol#L42)  

Impacted Function: `createMarket`.

1. Owner calls createMarket with _tokenNameSuffix S1 and _tokenSymbolSuffix S2 which creates a new market M1 with _deployedMarkets[_salt] pointing to M1. Here salt can be S which is computed using _tokenNameSuffix and _tokenSymbolSuffix
2. This market is now being used
3. After some time owner again mistakenly calls createMarket with _tokenNameSuffix S1 and _tokenSymbolSuffix S2
4. Instead of returning error mentioning that this name and symbol already exists, new market gets created. The problem here is that salt which is computed using _tokenNameSuffix and _tokenSymbolSuffix will again come as S (as in step 1) which means _deployedMarkets[_salt] will now get updated to M2. This means reference to M1 is gone
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the market factory contract that creates new markets using a deterministic salt derived from the token name suffix and token symbol suffix supplied by the caller. Because the factory does not enforce uniqueness of these suffixes, an owner can invoke the createMarket function multiple times with the same _tokenNameSuffix and _tokenSymbolSuffix. When this happens, the same salt value is recomputed, leading to the same mapping key in the internal _deployedMarkets table. The second call overwrites the entry that previously pointed to the original market (M1) with the address of the newly created market (M2). Consequently, the reference to M1 is lost and any external code or users that rely on the factory’s mapping to locate the original market will now be redirected to M2 or will be unable to locate M1 at all. This is a classic identifier‑collision or mapping‑overwrite bug caused by the absence of a check that the salt is unused before inserting a new market. Exploitation is straightforward: the contract owner (or any privileged caller) simply repeats a market creation with duplicate suffixes, causing the factory to silently replace the stored address. The impact is that the original market becomes inaccessible through the factory, potentially locking user deposits, breaking ongoing trades, and violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each market is uniquely identifiable by its name and symbol. The issue manifests only when the same suffix pair is reused, which may happen unintentionally during deployment or maliciously by an insider. It affects all participants that interact with the overwritten market, including traders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that query the factory for the market address. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the createMarket logic and noticed the lack of a uniqueness guard. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the contract does not emit an error; instead it silently creates a new market, giving the impression that the operation succeeded as intended. The recommended mitigation is to add a require statement that checks _deployedMarkets[_salt] is zero before creating a new market, thereby preventing accidental or intentional overwrites. In broader terms, this belongs to the class of bugs where deterministic identifiers are reused without proper existence checks, leading to state corruption and loss of reference to previously deployed contracts.

title: Market expiry behaviour differs in implementation and documentation
description:
[prePO Docs: Expiry](https://docs.prepo.io/concepts/markets#expiry)  
[PrePOMarket.sol#L145-L156](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/main/contracts/core/PrePOMarket.sol#L145-L156)  

The docs say that “If a market has not settled by its expiry date, it will automatically settle at the lower bound of its Valuation Range.”

However, in the implementation, the expiry date is entirely ignored. The default settlement after expiry is a 1:1 ratio of long and short token for 1 collateral token.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a discrepancy between the documented behaviour of market expiry settlement and the actual implementation in the PrePO market contract. According to the official documentation, if a market has not been settled by its expiry date, the system should automatically settle at the lower bound of the market's valuation range. In practice, however, the contract’s settlement routine completely ignores the expiry timestamp and proceeds with a default 1:1 redemption ratio between long and short tokens for each unit of collateral, regardless of the valuation range. The root cause is a missing conditional check for the _expiryTime variable; the code only evaluates whether a final long price has been set, and never enforces the lower‑bound rule after the expiry moment. This can be exploited by participants who rely on the documented lower‑bound settlement to calculate expected returns. If they wait until after expiry, they will receive a different payout than anticipated, potentially receiving a higher or lower amount than the lower bound would dictate. The impact is primarily financial: users may experience unexpected token balances, see their long positions redeemed at a rate that does not match the promised lower‑bound price, and consequently lose confidence in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only when a market reaches its expiry without being settled beforehand, affecting all holders of long or short positions as well as the protocol’s overall accounting integrity. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain logic with the written specifications, a mismatch that can be subtle because the contract still settles without error, masking the logical deviation. The problem is hard to notice because the settlement function executes successfully and does not revert, leading auditors to assume correct behaviour unless they explicitly verify the expiry handling. To remediate, the contract should be updated to include an explicit expiry check that, when the current block timestamp exceeds the stored expiry time, calculates the settlement using the lower bound of the valuation range (for example, by deriving the short price as MAX_PRICE minus the floor long price and applying the appropriate formula). Alternatively, if the designers intend the 1:1 behavior, the documentation must be revised to accurately reflect the real settlement logic. This class of bug—documentation‑implementation mismatch—violates core business logic concerning price discovery and settlement guarantees, resulting in user‑facing symptoms such as “my long tokens were redeemed for a full collateral amount instead of the expected reduced amount” or “the market settled with a different ratio than described”, thereby undermining trust in the protocol’s reliability.

title: `getSharesForAmount` returns wrong value when `totalAssets == 0`
description:
The [`getSharesForAmount`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/f63584133a0329781609e3f14c3004c1ca293e71/contracts/core/Collateral.sol#L328) function returns `0` if `totalAssets == 0`.

However, if **`totalSupply == 0`** , the actual shares that are minted in a [`deposit` are `_amount`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/f63584133a0329781609e3f14c3004c1ca293e71/contracts/core/Collateral.sol#L83) even if `totalAssets == 0`.

Contracts / frontends that use this function to estimate their deposit when `totalSupply == 0` will return a wrong value.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the accounting routine that converts a token amount into share units for a vault-like contract. The public view function getSharesForAmount is intended to return the number of shares that would be minted for a given deposit amount. However, when the vault has no assets (totalAssets == 0) the function unconditionally returns 0, ignoring the case where the total supply of shares is also zero. In the deposit implementation the developers correctly special‑case an empty vault: if totalSupply() == 0 the function mints exactly the deposit amount as shares. Because getSharesForAmount does not replicate this logic, any external code – such as front‑ends, SDKs, or other contracts – that calls the view function to estimate a deposit will receive a misleading result of zero shares during the first deposit. This mismatch occurs only when the vault is brand new, i.e., both totalAssets and totalSupply are zero, a state that may be visited rarely and therefore can be hard to notice during routine testing. The impact is primarily user‑experience and accounting: a user expecting a one‑to‑one share allocation sees a UI that reports "0 shares" or a missing refund, which can discourage participation, cause incorrect UI calculations, or lead to downstream contracts making erroneous assumptions about share values. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the deposit logic with the share‑estimation function and identified the missing zero‑supply guard. It belongs to the class of initial‑state accounting bugs where division‑by‑zero or fallback return values are not handled consistently. To remediate, the getSharesForAmount function should include a check for totalSupply() == 0 and return the input amount, matching the deposit path, or otherwise compute shares based on a correct mathematical model that accounts for the empty‑vault scenario. By aligning the view function with the deposit logic, the contract will respect the intended invariant that the first depositor receives shares equal to the amount supplied, thereby restoring correct accounting and user expectations.

title: SingleStrategyController doesn’t verify that new strategy uses the same base token
description:
When migrating from one strategy to another, the controller pulls out the funds of the old strategy and deposits them into the new one. But, it doesn’t verify that both strategies use the same base token. If the new one uses a different base token, it won’t “know” about the tokens it received on migration. It won’t be able to deposit and transfer them. Effectively they would be lost.

The migration is done by the owner. So the owner must make a mistake and migrate to the wrong strategy by accident.
