Conceptually, the fix is to eliminate the state inconsistency by ensuring that reward distribution and reserve reading are performed atomically or in the required sequence, thereby preventing the revert and restoring reliable reward accounting.

title: M-2 Rates can be updated for a deactivated farming
description: There is no check that the incentive maker can't set non-zero rates for a deactivated pool. AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L198-L202
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation that allows an incentive maker to set non‑zero M‑2 reward rates for a farming pool that has already been deactivated. The root cause is that the function responsible for updating the rates does not check the pool's active flag before applying the new values, so the contract treats a closed pool as if it were still operational. An attacker who controls the incentive‑making role can call the update function after the pool has been marked inactive and assign arbitrary positive rates. Because the pool is supposed to stop distributing rewards once deactivated, the contract may continue to allocate tokens based on the newly set rates, leading to unintended token transfers, accounting mismatches, and potential loss of treasury funds. This situation occurs only when the pool state is deactivated but the rate‑update function is still accessible; it affects the protocol’s treasury, token holders, and any users who expect the farm to be closed. The issue was discovered during a MixBytes audit when the auditors examined the rate‑update logic and noticed the absence of a state check. It can be hard to notice because the user interface typically shows the pool as closed, no explicit error is thrown, and the abnormal reward distribution may only become apparent after several blocks when balances diverge from expectations. To remediate, the contract should enforce a requirement that if a pool is deactivated, only zero rates may be set, or better, prohibit any rate changes after deactivation entirely. This class of bug falls under improper state validation and business‑logic violation, where the contract’s accounting assumptions (no rewards after deactivation) are broken. From a user’s perspective, they may see a pool listed as closed yet still observe reward events, or they may notice that their expected refund or reward is missing while the protocol’s balance shrinks, contradicting the expectation that no further rewards will be issued after deactivation.

title: M-3 Initialization of the virtualPool should be made earlier
description: virtualPool is currently initialized after using it in the check. AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L398
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a use‑before‑initialisation error in a farming contract where the internal data structure representing the virtual liquidity pool (virtualPool) is accessed in a validation check before the variable is assigned a proper value. The root cause is the ordering of statements inside the function: the code performs a condition that reads virtualPool, but the assignment that creates or points virtualPool occurs later in the same execution path. Because Solidity initializes storage references to the zero address (or a default empty struct) before they are explicitly set, the check operates on an uninitialised or zero value. An attacker can trigger the function when virtualPool is still zero, causing the validation to either always succeed or always fail depending on the logic, which may allow unauthorized actions such as claiming rewards, bypassing fee calculations, or depositing into a pool that does not exist. The impact is that users may see their expected rewards disappear, deposits be rejected silently, or the protocol’s accounting become inconsistent, potentially leading to loss of funds or a state where the contract cannot correctly track virtual liquidity. This condition occurs each time the function is called before virtualPool has been set, which is typically on the first invocation after deployment or after a state reset. All participants that interact with the farming mechanism – liquidity providers, reward claimers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the core accounting relies on a correctly initialised virtualPool. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the control flow and noticed that the variable was read before being written. It is hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not emit a warning for this pattern, and the default zero value may appear to be a legitimate address in simple tests, masking the logical flaw. To remediate, the virtualPool should be initialised at the very beginning of the function (or in the contract constructor) before any checks that depend on it, ensuring that all subsequent logic works with a valid, fully‑initialised pool object. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper initialization or order‑of‑operations errors, which violate the business assumption that the pool exists and is correctly configured before any accounting or permission checks are performed. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that a transaction that should grant a reward instead returns zero, or that a deposit appears to succeed but the balance never updates, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds.

title: M-4 Admin can drain all rewards from all incentives
description: AlgebraEternalFarming.decreaseRewardsAmount() sends rewards to the address of admin: AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L172. It creates the danger of a rugpull and reduces the trust in the incentive system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an admin‑controlled backdoor that allows the contract owner to withdraw the entire pool of reward tokens from every farming incentive. The root cause lies in the decreaseRewardsAmount function, which unconditionally transfers the specified reward amount to the admin address without validating that the caller is the incentive’s registered reward source or that the withdrawal respects any accounting limits. Because the function is exposed to the admin and lacks granular access control, the admin can invoke it at any time and repeatedly request the full remaining balance, effectively draining all rewards. Exploitation is straightforward: the admin calls decreaseRewardsAmount with the total reward amount for a given incentive, the contract sends those tokens to the admin, and the same can be repeated for each incentive, leaving no rewards for participants. The impact is a loss of expected earnings for users who have staked tokens, resulting in balances that appear empty or unchanged despite active farming, and a breach of trust in the incentive mechanism. This condition occurs whenever the admin decides to execute the function, which can be after deployment and at any later block. All participants in the farming protocol—liquidity providers, token holders, and any downstream applications—are affected because the promised reward distribution is nullified. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑adjustment logic and noticed the direct transfer to the admin address. It can be hard to notice because the function may be documented as a legitimate administrative tool for adjusting rewards, and the transfer to the admin is not flagged as suspicious by standard static analysis. To remediate, the reward‑refund logic should be redesigned so that only the address registered for a specific incentive can receive refunds, and any reduction of rewards must be accounted for against the incentive’s own balance rather than sent to the admin. Implementing stricter access controls, multi‑signature governance, or removing the direct admin transfer altogether will close the backdoor and restore confidence in the reward accounting system.

title: M-1 Ownership renouncement will grant a role to zero address
description: After the ownership renouncement, the owner will be zero address, and it will be granted with DEFAULTADMINROLE AlgebraFactory.sol#L165.
bug_full: The vulnerability isan improper role assignment that occurs when the contract owner renounces ownership. After the renounceOwnership call the internal owner variable becomes the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000). The contract logic that automatically grants the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE uses the current owner value without checking whether it is a non‑zero address, so the zero address is added as an admin. This happens because the code assumes the owner will always be a valid account and does not include a guard such as require(owner != address(0)) before calling the AccessControl grant function. An attacker cannot directly claim the role, but the effect is that the privileged admin role is assigned to an address that no one controls. Consequently, any function protected by onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) becomes inaccessible, effectively freezing upgrade mechanisms, emergency withdrawals, or any other admin‑only operation. Users experience symptoms such as “admin functions return nothing”, “upgrade transaction reverts”, or “no one can perform a rescue”. The issue manifests only after the ownership renouncement transaction is mined; before that the admin role is correctly held by the owner. All parties that rely on the admin role – the protocol maintainers, auditors, and ultimately the end‑users whose funds depend on admin actions – are affected because the contract can no longer be managed. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of renounceOwnership followed by a role grant was examined. It is easy to miss because the AccessControl library does not reject the zero address, so the grant succeeds silently and the contract state appears consistent, yet the role is effectively dead. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit check that the address used for granting DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is not the zero address, or to redesign the flow so that the admin role is transferred to a trusted multisig before ownership is renounced, thereby preserving the ability to execute privileged functions.

title: M-2 A broken hook can block user funds
description: For closing position, a user should call the burn function which uses hooks to external contract AlgebraPool.sol#L137. If a hook were broken, then users would not be able to get the deposited funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is alock‑up condition caused by a broken external hook that is invoked when a user attempts to close a position by calling the burn function. The burn routine relies on a hook call to an external contract (AlgebraPool) to perform final accounting and fund transfer. If the hooked contract reverts, runs out of gas, or otherwise fails, the burn transaction cannot complete and the user’s deposited assets remain trapped in the protocol. This occurs because the core contract does not protect the external call with a try/catch mechanism nor provide an alternative withdrawal path, assuming the hook will always succeed. An attacker could deploy a malicious hook that deliberately reverts on every invocation, or a legitimate hook could contain a bug that triggers a revert under certain inputs, effectively preventing any user from executing the burn function. The impact is that users who try to close their positions receive no funds; the UI may show a successful transaction but the balance stays unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between the core contract and its external hooks. It is hard to notice because the failure manifests only when the external contract misbehaves, which may be rare in normal operation, and there is no visible error message indicating that the hook is the source of the problem. To remediate, the protocol should implement an emergency exit or fallback withdrawal mechanism that can be triggered when the hook fails, such as using Solidity's try/catch to handle hook failures and allowing users to withdraw directly from the core contract, or providing an admin‑controlled escape hatch that bypasses the hook entirely. This class of bug falls under external‑call dependency and fund‑locking vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes external components are always operational, violating the accounting invariant that deposited funds must be recoverable on position closure.

title: M-3 Active pool plugin can be modified without updating pluginConfig
description: AlgebraPool.sol#L402 An issue has been found in the setPlugin function. Pool administrators can alter the plugin of an active pool. However, there is a discrepancy as the pluginConfig of the newly-introduced plugin might differ from its predecessor. This could lead to invoking unimplemented hooks that were previously operational in the old plugin. Furthermore, if the former plugin employed dynamic fees set beforehand, and the succeeding plugin operates with static fees or vice versa, the pool fee parameter stays in an inconsistent state resulting in incorrect fee withdrawals. Additionally, when associating a plugin to an active pool, certain pre-initialization logic might be imperative, particularly when establishing the new plugin configuration, initializing internal local variables, and designating the new fee. This vulnerability is classified as medium as linking a new plugin to the pool could temporarily block specific pool functionality and unintentionally trigger inappropriate fee actions, persisting until the correct plugin initialization is carried out.
bug_full: An active Algebra pool allows its administrator to replace the attached plugin through the setPlugin function. The function only updates the address of the new plugin but does not refresh the stored pluginConfig or invoke any initialization hook of the new contract. Because the old plugin may have exposed a set of hooks, fee parameters and internal state that differ from those required by the new plugin, the pool can end up calling functions that are not implemented in the replacement, or it can retain fee settings that were appropriate for the previous plugin. For example, if the previous plugin used a dynamic fee that was set by the pool, and the new plugin expects a static fee, the pool’s fee variable remains in an inconsistent state and fee withdrawals are calculated incorrectly. The mismatch can also prevent required pre‑initialisation steps such as setting local variables inside the plugin, leading to temporary loss of functionality (e.g., swaps or deposits failing) or unintended fee transfers. The issue manifests only when an administrator calls setPlugin on a pool that is already active; normal users see no explicit warning, but they may notice that expected rewards are missing, that fees are zero or excessively high, or that certain actions revert. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of plugins and identified that setPlugin does not propagate the new configuration. It is hard to notice because the UI continues to display a functioning pool while the internal accounting is silently broken. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent configuration after dynamic module replacement” and violates the accounting assumption that the pool’s fee parameters always reflect the active plugin’s logic. The proper mitigation is to extend setPlugin so that it calls an initialization hook on the new plugin, updates the stored pluginConfig, and synchronises the fee variables with the expectations of the new module before the pool resumes normal operation.

title: M-4 Admin can set non-zero pluginConfig in pool with zero plugin
description: AlgebraPool.sol#L431 The Administrator can set a non-zero value for pluginConfig while setting the plugin to zero. Such a configuration can potentially trigger reverts in pool functions. This issue is classified as medium, as the combination of a non-zero pluginConfig with a zero plugin can disrupt certain functionalities of the pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the pool configuration where the contract allows the Administrator to set a non-zero plugin configuration value while simultaneously disabling the plugin by setting its address to zero. The root cause is the absence of a validation check that ties the pluginConfig parameter to the presence of a plugin contract; the setter function only updates the two fields independently. An attacker or even a benign admin can trigger this state by calling the configuration function with plugin equal to address(0) and pluginConfig set to any non-zero value. When the pool later executes functions that assume a valid plugin when pluginConfig is non-zero, internal calls to the missing plugin contract revert, causing the whole transaction to fail. From a user perspective this appears as deposits, withdrawals or other pool actions reverting with no obvious error message, leaving the user with the impression that the operation "did nothing" or that "funds disappear". The impact is a denial-of-service condition for any operation that depends on the plugin, potentially freezing user funds until the configuration is corrected. The issue manifests only after the admin changes the configuration; it does not affect pools that never modify the plugin settings. It was discovered during a manual audit of the AlgebraPool contract where the setPlugin function was examined and the missing conditional check was identified. The bug is subtle because a zero address is commonly interpreted as "no plugin", so a non-zero configuration may be overlooked, yet the code later reads pluginConfig without guarding against a missing plugin. The appropriate remediation is to enforce that when the plugin address is zero, the pluginConfig must also be zero, typically by adding a require statement that rejects mismatched settings. This aligns the configuration with the intended business logic that a pool without a plugin should not hold any plugin-specific configuration, thereby preventing unexpected reverts and preserving the expected user experience of successful deposits and withdrawals.

title: M-1 Manipulation of volatility through zero-amount swaps
description:
Swaps executed with a zero amount are currently factored into the volatility oracle. This vulnerability allows an attacker to artiﬁcially manipulate the volatility index, which in turn affects the dynamic fee calculations to their advantage.
The issue has been categorized with a MEDIUM severity level. This is because the attacker can manipulate the fee only under speciﬁc conditions and within a predeﬁned range.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the inclusion of zero‑amount swap operations in the calculation of the protocol’s volatility oracle. The oracle aggregates recent swap data to produce a volatility index that is subsequently used by the dynamic fee module to adjust transaction fees. Because the implementation does not filter out swaps where the transferred amount is zero, an attacker can submit a large number of such no‑value swaps, which nevertheless are counted as price‑changing events. This artificial activity inflates or deflates the volatility index depending on how the oracle aggregates data, and the altered index feeds directly into the fee formula. As a result, the attacker can cause the fee to move outside its normal range – typically lowering it to a level that makes a subsequent profitable trade cheaper, or raising it to penalise other users. The exploit is only possible when the fee calculation relies on the volatile index and when the contract accepts zero‑amount swaps, which are otherwise harmless from a token‑transfer perspective. Users may notice that their expected fee, which should reflect market activity, is unexpectedly low or unusually high, and that the protocol’s accounting appears inconsistent even though no real trades have occurred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data flow into the volatility oracle and identified that the input validation step omitted a check for a non‑zero amount. Because zero‑amount swaps generate events that look like normal trades, the manipulation can be hard to detect without explicit monitoring of swap amounts. The proper mitigation is to exclude any swap where the transferred amount is zero from the volatility calculation, or to require a minimum amount before the swap is recorded for oracle updates. This change restores the integrity of the volatility index, ensures that dynamic fees reflect genuine market movements, and prevents attackers from gaining an economic advantage through artificial volatility manipulation.

title: M-2 Missing ﬂags validation in new pluginConfig
description:
There is no validation of ﬂags in new pluginConfig set with AlgebraPool.setPluginConfig(). This can lead to the invocation of hooks that will constantly revert. E.g. BEFOREFLASHFLAG, AFTERFLASHFLAG, AFTERSWAPFLAG (without currently connected incentive) can be switched on.
This issue has a MEDIUM severity since it can partially or fully stop the pool until pluginConfig is corrected.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of the flag fields when a new plugin configuration is supplied to AlgebraPool via the setPluginConfig function. The root cause is that the function accepts any combination of flag bits without checking whether the corresponding hook callbacks are actually implemented by the attached plugin or whether the required incentive contracts are connected. As a result, an actor with permission to call setPluginConfig can enable flags such as BEFOREFLASHFLAG, AFTERFLASHFLAG or AFTERSWAPFLAG even when no incentive contract is linked. When the pool later processes a flash loan, a swap or any operation that would trigger the enabled hook, the callback code immediately reverts because the hook has no valid implementation. This behaviour can be exploited by submitting a malicious or simply mis‑configured pluginConfig, causing the pool to enter a state where core operations constantly revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: liquidity providers, traders and any user trying to interact with the pool will see their transactions fail, balances remain unchanged and the pool appears to be out of service. The condition occurs whenever a privileged caller updates the pluginConfig with unsupported flags; it does not require any special on‑chain conditions beyond the flag setting. The affected parties include all users of the pool, the protocol governance that relies on the pool’s availability, and any external contracts that depend on successful flash loans or swaps. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the AlgebraPool plugin architecture, where the lack of flag validation was noted as a logical oversight. It can be hard to notice because the pool may function correctly until a transaction reaches a code path that invokes the mis‑configured hook, at which point the transaction simply reverts without a clear diagnostic message. The recommended remediation is to move all interaction with pluginConfig into the plugin contract itself and to enforce that any modification checks the current plugin version and validates that each flag corresponds to a hook that the plugin actually implements and that any required incentive contracts are set. This fixes the missing input‑validation class of bug and prevents accidental or malicious activation of reverting hooks. From a user perspective, attempts to perform a flash loan or a swap result in a transaction that reverts instantly, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and creating the impression that the pool “does nothing” or “returns zero” when in fact the pool has been disabled by an invalid configuration.

title: M-3 Plugin timestamps data can be overwritten by a call to the
description:
There is an issue at the line AlgebraBasePluginV1.sol#L67.
Plugin timestamps data can be overwritten by a call to the prepayTimepointsStorageSlots function in cases when the plugin was conﬁgured from AlgebraPool by a call to setPluginConfig (and setPlugin) and the initialize function inside plugin wasn't called. An attacker can wait for some swaps and data in the timepoints array to overwrite the existing timestamps. But due to uninitialized ticks in the ﬁrst timepoint, users won't be able to perform many swaps from AlgebraPool because the plugin will operate with null initial data.
This issue has been assigned a MEDIUM severity level because an attacker is able to overwrite data only for a few timepoints.
bug_full: The issue is a storage‑overwrite vulnerability in the AlgebraBasePluginV1 contract where the timestamps stored in the plugin’s timepoints array can be overwritten by calling the prepayTimepointsStorageSlots function. The root cause is that when the plugin is attached to an AlgebraPool via setPluginConfig and setPlugin, the plugin’s initialize function is not automatically executed, leaving the storage slots that hold the first timepoint’s tick and timestamp uninitialized. Because prepayTimepointsStorageSlots is callable without restriction, an attacker can wait for a few swaps to generate entries in the timepoints array and then invoke the function to write arbitrary data into the same storage slots, effectively replacing the original timestamps with null or attacker‑controlled values. This manipulation causes the plugin to operate with a null initial data point, breaking the calculation of time‑weighted average prices and preventing many subsequent swaps from succeeding. From a user’s perspective the pool may appear to stop trading, price data may show zero or become missing, and swaps may revert or produce no output, even though the contract still holds funds. The vulnerability is discovered during a MixBytes audit by analysing the plugin initialization flow and spotting that the initialize function can be omitted. It is hard to notice because the overwrite only affects a few early timepoints and the symptoms resemble normal price‑feed latency or temporary swap failures. The impact is functional rather than direct theft: users lose the ability to trade, the protocol’s price oracle becomes unreliable, and overall confidence in the pool may be reduced. The recommended mitigation is to enforce proper initialization of the plugin and to restrict calls to prepayTimepointsStorageSlots to the plugin factory manager or another trusted authority, thereby preventing arbitrary overwrites of the timestamp storage.

title: M-1 Incorrect usage of the parameter
description: There are not enough checks on the amount of liquidity that can be removed from the limit order in the decreaseLimitOrder function. liquidity can be greater than the available liquidity on the limit order and in this case tx will revert. LimitOrderManager.sol#L162
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that reduces the amount of liquidity attached to a limit order. The contract accepts a user‑supplied parameter representing the liquidity to be removed, but it does not verify that this value is less than or equal to the liquidity that is actually still available on the order. Because the check is missing, a caller can pass a number that exceeds the remaining liquidity. When this happens the internal accounting attempts to subtract more liquidity than exists, causing the transaction to revert. The root cause is an unchecked parameter that is used directly in a state‑changing operation without a guard against over‑draw. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the revert simply by calling the decrease function with an excessively large amount, which may be done unintentionally or deliberately to block further operations on the order. The impact is that legitimate users attempting to adjust their positions receive a failed transaction, lose the gas spent on the call, and may be unable to free or reallocate their funds if the contract does not provide an alternative path. This situation can effectively act as a denial‑of‑service on the affected limit order, especially in a high‑frequency environment where many participants rely on the ability to decrease liquidity. The condition occurs whenever decreaseLimitOrder is invoked with a liquidity argument greater than the cached value representing the order’s current liquidity (cache.liquidityLast). All liquidity providers and any protocol component that interacts with limit orders are potentially affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions—namely that liquidity can only be reduced up to the amount present—are violated. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit performed by MixBytes, which identified the missing validation as a logical flaw. Because the transaction simply reverts, the problem may be hard to notice in normal operation; users might attribute the failure to network congestion or other unrelated errors rather than a contract bug. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a ceiling on the requested reduction, for example by capping the input to the current cached liquidity or by explicitly reverting with a clear error message when the supplied amount exceeds the available liquidity. This change restores the invariant that liquidity cannot become negative and prevents unexpected reverts, ensuring that users can reliably decrease their positions without risking loss of gas or denial of service.

title: M-2 The operator address is not reset after the position token transfer
description: A NFT position owner can set token operator to use permit functionality - LimitOrderManager.sol#L275. The operator address is used at the line LimitOrderManager.sol#L270. The getApproved function is used in a ERC721 standard to get an address of the entity which is allowed to make transfers. The user may give a permit to desired operator, then sell/transfer the NFT token. A new owner may not know about the given permit - the token operator is still able to make transfers and burn/collect a limit order position on behalf of the new token owner.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a persistent operator permission that is not cleared when an ERC721‑based position token is transferred to a new owner. In this contract the owner of a position NFT can grant a separate address the right to act on the token through a permit function. The address is stored in a custom mapping that is consulted when the contract performs actions such as transferring, burning or collecting a limit order position. Because the contract overrides the standard ERC721 approval mechanism but does not reset the custom operator entry during the internal _transfer routine, the previously approved operator remains authorized after the token changes hands. An attacker who was previously given permission can therefore invoke functions that rely on the stored operator, moving or destroying the token even though the new holder never granted such rights. This can be exploited by a malicious operator who monitors token transfers, waits for a transfer event, and then immediately calls the contract’s transfer or burn functions, causing the new owner to lose control of the position and any funds locked in the associated limit order. The impact is unauthorized transfer or destruction of assets, loss of user funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees because the protocol assumes that only the current token owner or an explicitly approved address may act on a position. The issue manifests whenever a position token is transferred using the standard ERC721 transfer functions without an additional step that clears the custom operator mapping. All token holders are affected, as any transfer may leave a hidden permission dangling. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s behaviour against the ERC721 specification and noticed that the custom operator field is never reset. It is subtle because the standard ERC721 approval is automatically cleared on transfer, leading reviewers to assume that all permission‑related state is handled, while the custom mapping is overlooked. To remediate the issue the contract should override the internal _transfer function (or the safeTransferFrom hooks) and explicitly clear the stored operator entry for the transferred tokenId, ensuring that only the new owner can later grant permissions. This aligns the contract with the expected ERC721 permission model and prevents unauthorized post‑transfer actions.

title: M-3 An inverted price is used for overﬂow validation during the creation of new limit
description:
In function core.LimitOrderManagement.addOrRemoveLimitOrder the price used to evaluate whether the parameter amountToBuy is prone to overﬂow or does not appear to be inverted: LimitOrderManagement.sol#L46-L48
```solidity
uint256 amountToBuy = (tick > currentTick)
? FullMath.mulDivRoundingUp(_amountToSell, Constants.Q144, priceX144)
: FullMath.mulDivRoundingUp(_amountToSell, priceX144, Constants.Q144);
```
Price is represented as the ratio token1/token0. In the speciﬁed expression, if tick is greater than currentTick, then the new limit order position will sell token0 in exchange for token1. Accordingly, to calculate the amountToBuy, _amountToSell, it should be multiplied by priceX144 instead of being divided.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic mis‑use of the price ratio during the creation of a new limit order in the addOrRemoveLimitOrder function. The contract stores the price as token1/token0 (priceX144) and decides how to compute the amount of token1 that can be bought (amountToBuy) based on whether the requested tick is above the current market tick. When tick > currentTick the logic should multiply the amount of token0 being sold by the price (i.e., amountToBuy = _amountToSell * priceX144 / Q144). Instead the code divides by priceX144 (amountToBuy = _amountToSell * Q144 / priceX144). This inversion means the contract uses the wrong formula for both the actual amount calculation and the overflow validation that guards the multiplication. The root cause is a copy‑and‑paste or logical error that treats the price as if it were token0/token1 in this branch. An attacker can exploit the bug by submitting a limit order with tick > currentTick, causing the contract to compute a dramatically inflated amountToBuy value. Because the overflow check is performed on the incorrectly inflated value, it may either falsely trigger a revert or, if the value stays within uint256 limits, allow the order to be recorded with a mis‑priced amount. The practical impact is that users placing such orders receive far fewer token1 than expected, see their balances reduced without receiving the correct value, or experience unexpected overflow reverts. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful order placement but the received token amount is near zero, or the transaction may fail with an overflow error even though the input amounts look reasonable. The bug occurs only when the tick parameter is greater than the current tick, i.e., when the order is intended to sell token0 for token1. It affects any participant who creates limit orders under these conditions, including regular traders and potentially malicious actors who can profit from the mis‑pricing. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the arithmetic expressions in the limit order management module and identified that the price variable was used in the wrong orientation. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles and the overflow guard appears to be present, yet the logical direction of the price is reversed, leading to subtle accounting errors that only manifest under specific market conditions. To remediate, the expression must be inverted: when tick > currentTick the calculation should be FullMath.mulDivRoundingUp(_amountToSell, priceX144, Constants.Q144) instead of using Constants.Q144 as the numerator. This correction restores the proper price orientation, ensures accurate amount calculations, and re‑enables correct overflow validation. The bug belongs to the class of price‑inversion or arithmetic‑direction errors that break financial invariants and can cause funds to disappear or orders to be mis‑priced.

title: Content Spoofing via Parameters
description:
Content spoofing, also known as content injection, arbitrary text injection, or virtual defacement, is an attack targeting a user through a vulnerability in a web application. This occurs when the application improperly handles user-supplied data, allowing an attacker to inject content, typically via a parameter value, which is then reflected back to the user. This results in the user seeing a modified page under the trusted domain's context. Often, this type of attack is combined with social engineering tactics, exploiting both a code-based vulnerability and the user's trust.
The impact of a content spoofing attack varies based on context. If user-supplied information is reflected in a way that is correctly escaped and clearly visually marked, such as in error messages, it may be harmless. However, if the input is not clearly visually distinguished from the legitimate content, it can be used in social engineering attacks. Moreover, if the input is not correctly escaped, it may contain active components, enabling attacks similar to Cross-site Scripting (XSS).
In the specific case of allyourbase.virtual.tech, parameters url, w and q can be modified to reflect the frontend changes/defacements directly in the response. The parameters can be used initially to self-deface the website as the application allows the user to change the values on the fly while the components are loading.
poc:
Using a proxy intercept the request when browsing to allyourbase.virtual.tech. The following GET request will be available:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=48&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech
// Other headers not shown.
From the request above, you can see that parameter url, w and q are having predictable values that can be modified in the request and overalls are parsed by the frontend. Similarly as the content spoofing vulnerability from above we are able to modify the parameter with different values and the following error messages appear:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2F../../../&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ffoo.png&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
The requested resource isn't a valid image.
For parameters q and w:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=48&q=7500 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech
Response:
”q” parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=4800&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech
Response:
”w” parameter (width) of 4800 is not allowed
It is clear that application response changes according to the url, q and w values which are allowed to be modified on the fly. In this way, when content is loading, it is possible to execute a defacement by changing the values of the images loading: We modify the tails image for heads on the fly (which will be processed by the application) in this example:

Figure 1: Response (rendered):
Figure 2: Original
bug_full: The vulnerability is a content spoofing (also known as content injection or virtual defacement) flaw in the image‑optimization endpoint of allyourbase.virtual.tech. The endpoint accepts three query parameters – url, w and q – which are used directly by the frontend to locate and resize images. Because the application does not properly validate or sanitize these parameters, an attacker can supply arbitrary values that are reflected back in the generated HTML or image request. When a user loads a page, the malicious values are processed by the image service, causing the page to display altered or malformed images, error messages such as “Unable to optimize image” or “The requested resource isn’t a valid image”, and in extreme cases a completely defaced visual layout. The root cause is the lack of strict whitelisting and type checking for user‑controlled parameters, allowing path traversal, out‑of‑range dimensions and non‑numeric quality values to be accepted. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker intercepts a legitimate request with a proxy, modifies the url, w or q values to point to unintended resources or to extreme numeric values, and forwards the request. The backend responds with either a rendered image that contains attacker‑chosen content or a 400 error that reveals internal validation messages, both of which are displayed to the end‑user under the trusted domain. The impact is primarily visual – users may see a page that looks different from the intended design, potentially leading to social‑engineering attacks, loss of trust, or phishing attempts that exploit the perceived legitimacy of the domain. The issue manifests whenever the image component loads, i.e., during normal navigation or when dynamic content is rendered, and affects any visitor of the site, including regular users and the protocol’s reputation. It was discovered through manual testing with a proxy that revealed the parameters could be altered and that the server returned predictable error messages. The flaw can be hard to notice because the altered content may appear as a normal image loading failure or a subtle visual change, which users might attribute to a temporary glitch rather than a security breach. To remediate, the application should enforce strict validation: only allow URLs that resolve to known static assets, constrain width and quality to the documented numeric ranges, and escape any reflected values before they are inserted into the response. In addition, the endpoint should reject any path traversal attempts and ensure that error messages do not expose internal validation logic. By treating the parameters as untrusted input and applying a whitelist‑based approach, the content spoofing risk can be eliminated.

title: First mint could be frontrun to break L1 `totalSupply` calculation
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the migration logic of the AMKT token that can cause the L1 totalSupply to be reduced to zero. During the migration, the contract is designed to mint the L1 totalSupply on L2 and then lock the full amount in the L2 bridge. To keep the locked amount out of the L1 totalSupply, the mint function deliberately skips the first mint by checking a boolean flag MIGRATED; the flag is set to true after the first call and subsequent calls perform a normal mint. The root cause is the assumption that the first mint will always be the team’s withdrawal of the entire migrated supply. Because the flag is automatically flipped on the first mint, any user who can trigger a mint before the team does will cause the flag to be set, after which the contract will ignore the intended first mint. An attacker can exploit this by burning their L1 tokens, claiming the equivalent L2 tokens, and immediately initiating a withdrawal back to L1 during the seven‑day waiting period. Their withdrawal transaction will be queued minutes after the large team withdrawal, and if the team does not trigger their withdrawal instantly, the attacker’s withdrawal will be processed first. When the team’s withdrawal finally executes, the contract sees MIGRATED already true, skips the mint, and sends the ~30 000 AMKT tokens to address(0), permanently removing them from circulation. The impact is a loss of the migrated supply, a mismatch between expected and actual balances, and a totalSupply that no longer reflects the true token amount, effectively making the funds disappear. The issue occurs only when there is a window between the L2 deployment and the team’s first withdrawal, i.e., during the seven‑day bridge finalisation period, and it can be triggered by any L1 user with sufficient tokens. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration flow and identified that the automatic MIGRATED flag could be set by an external actor. The bug is hard to notice because the contract silently skips the first mint without emitting an error, and the loss is only observable when the delayed withdrawal finally executes, at which point the tokens have already been burned. The vulnerability belongs to the class of initialization‑flag race conditions and token supply accounting bugs. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful withdrawal request but the resulting balance would be zero, contrary to the expectation of receiving the migrated tokens. To remediate the issue the flag should be controlled manually by the team or the migration should use a dedicated burner contract instead of relying on an automatically toggled flag, ensuring that no external mint can be processed before the intended first mint and preserving the correct totalSupply calculation.

title: Improper Error Handling in Parameters
description:
Improper error handling can introduce numerous security issues for a website. The most common issue arises when detailed internal error messages, such as stack traces, database dumps, and error codes, are displayed to users (potential attackers). These messages reveal implementation details and vulnerabilities in the site. Additionally, such messages can be disturbing for regular users.
Web applications often generate error conditions during normal operation, such as out-of-memory errors, null pointer exceptions, system call failures, database unavailability, and network timeouts. These errors must be managed according to a well-designed scheme that provides meaningful error messages to users, diagnostic information to site maintainers, and no useful information to attackers.
Even when error messages lack detail, inconsistencies in these messages can still reveal critical information about a site's inner workings and the data it contains. For example, an error message stating ”file not found” when a user attempts to access a non-existent file, and ”access denied” when trying to access a restricted file, can inadvertently disclose the existence of hidden files or the site's directory structure. This inconsistency allows users to infer the presence or absence of files they should not be aware of.
In the specific case of allyourbase.virtual.tech, the application does not gracefully handle the errors displayed when the user supplies values for the given parameters, as described in the PoC below.
poc:
Using a proxy intercept the request when browsing to allyourbase.virtual.tech. The following GET request will be available: GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=48&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech // Other headers not shown. From the request above, you can see that parameter url, w and q are having predictable values that can be modified in the request and overalls are parsed by the frontend. Similarly as the content spoofing vulnerability from above we are able to modify the parameter with different values and the following error messages appear: Request: GET /_next/image?url=%2F../../../&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2 Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech Response: HTTP/2 400 Bad Request Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image Request: GET /_next/image?url=%2Ffoo.png&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2 Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech Response: HTTP/2 400 Bad Request The requested resource isn’t a valid image. For parameters q and w: Request: GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=48&q=7500 HTTP/2 Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech Response: “q” parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100 Request: GET /_next/image?url=%2Ficons%2Fclassic.png&w=4800&q=75 HTTP/2 Host: allyourbase.virtual.tech Response: ”w” parameter (width) of 4800 is not allowed
bug_full: An image‑optimization endpoint exposed by the web application accepts three query parameters – url, w and q – that control the source path, the desired width and the compression quality of the returned image. The server validates each parameter and, when a validation rule fails, returns a 400 Bad Request response that contains the exact reason for the failure. For example, providing a non‑numeric quality value yields the message 'q parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100', while requesting a width outside the allowed range produces 'w parameter (width) of 4800 is not allowed'. Supplying a path that traverses directories results in 'Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image', whereas requesting a file that exists but is not a valid image returns 'The requested resource isn’t a valid image'. These messages disclose internal validation constraints, the existence or non‑existence of files, and the internal processing flow. An attacker can deliberately craft malformed requests, observe the differing error texts, and infer the presence of hidden files, the allowed numeric ranges, and the logic used to locate and process images. This information leakage can be leveraged to enumerate the server’s directory structure, plan path‑traversal attacks, or craft content‑spoofing payloads. The vulnerability manifests whenever the endpoint returns raw validation errors directly to the client instead of a generic error message. It was discovered during manual security testing by intercepting HTTP requests with a proxy and modifying the query parameters to trigger the various error responses. The issue is subtle because the responses are still HTTP 400 codes, which may be interpreted as normal client‑side errors, yet the textual content provides an attacker with valuable reconnaissance data. The impact is primarily informational – it does not directly lead to loss of funds or code execution – but it weakens the security posture by violating the principle of not exposing internal implementation details. To remediate, the application should replace all detailed validation messages with a uniform, user‑friendly error such as 'Invalid image request', log the specific reasons internally for debugging, and ensure that error responses do not differ based on the existence of files or the exact validation rule that failed. Consistent error handling eliminates the side‑channel that leaks internal state and aligns the system with secure coding best practices.

title: Owner can steal all funds locked in bridge by changing `REMOTE_TOKEN` value
poc:
In order to steal the funds locked in the contract, the owner would perform the following:

1) Deploy a new ERC20 token on L2, and mint themselves a quantity equal to the number of AMKT tokens locked in the bridge.

2) Deposit all these tokens into the L2 bridge, with a target of the legitimate L1 contract.

3) Wait for the 7 day waiting period so that withdrawals are permitted on L1.

4) Change the `REMOTE_TOKEN` on the L1 contract to match their newly deployed contract on L2.

5) Withdraw the tokens on L1, which will be permitted because of the matching `REMOTE_TOKEN`.

6) Change the `REMOTE_TOKEN` back to the original, and deposit the newly minted tokens back into the bridge.

7) This will convert them into the legitimate L2 AMKT tokens, which will be immediately withdrawn from the bridge, leaving the L2 bridge contract empty, so all the users with funds on L1 will be rugged.

Note that, while funds cannot be stolen by changing the `BRIDGE` value, the owner can perform a similar attack to brick in progress withdrawals, so this value should be secured as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a privileged configuration change in the upgraded BridgedIndexToken contract. The contract exposes a setBridge function that can be called by the owner at any time to overwrite the REMOTE_TOKEN and BRIDGE addresses. These two addresses are used by the Optimism bridge to verify that minted tokens on L1 correspond to the remote token deposited on L2, and by the token contract to restrict mint and burn calls to the authorized bridge contract. Because the function lacks any initialization guard, the owner can replace REMOTE_TOKEN with an address of a token they control after a user has deposited assets, wait for the normal 7‑day withdrawal period, and then invoke the bridge’s withdrawal logic. The bridge will see the matching REMOTE_TOKEN value, allow the minting of the attacker’s token on L1, and transfer the full amount of locked funds to the attacker. The attacker can then restore the original REMOTE_TOKEN address, deposit the newly minted tokens back into the bridge, and convert them into the legitimate L2 token, which is immediately withdrawn, leaving the L2 bridge empty and causing all honest users to lose their balances. The attack does not require changing the BRIDGE address, although that variable could be abused to block pending withdrawals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s upgrade path, where the unrestricted setter was identified as a logical flaw that contradicts the accounting assumption that the remote token identity is immutable after deployment. The problem is hard to notice because the setBridge function appears to be a normal initialization routine, emits no special events when called, and the UI shows normal deposit and withdrawal steps; users only observe that their L1 balance becomes zero after a withdrawal. The impact is a complete loss of funds locked in the bridge for any user who relies on the contract, effectively a rug pull by the owner. The vulnerability belongs to the class of mutable configuration or privileged parameter bugs that allow an authorized party to bypass critical access checks. The recommended mitigation is to make setBridge callable only once, enforce that both addresses are initially zero, and reject any further changes, or to remove owner control entirely, thereby locking the remote token and bridge addresses after initial deployment.

title: Insufficient input validation
description:
The DKIMRecoverySigValidator contract uses the AccInfo struct that has fields which values are not validated. Here are the fields that are problematic:
- secondaryKey can be the zero address, which can result in a loss of access to the AmbireAccount wallet
- waitUntilAcceptAdded is a time value and can be too big, resulting in inability to add DKIM keys
- waitUntilAcceptRemoved is a time value and can be too big, resulting in inability to remove DKIM keys
- onlyOneSigTimelock is a time value and can be too big, resulting in forever locked recovery
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient input validation flaw in the DKIMRecoverySigValidator contract where the AccInfo struct fields are accepted without any sanity checks. Specifically, the secondaryKey field can be set to the zero address, which removes any valid authority to control the associated AmbireAccount wallet. In addition, three time‑related fields – waitUntilAcceptAdded, waitUntilAcceptRemoved and onlyOneSigTimelock – are stored without upper‑bound validation. If an attacker or a careless user supplies an excessively large timestamp, the contract will interpret the value as a far‑future deadline, effectively preventing the addition or removal of DKIM keys and locking the recovery mechanism indefinitely. The root cause is the lack of require statements or other validation logic when these struct members are written, allowing arbitrary values to be persisted. Exploitation can occur during any transaction that updates the AccInfo struct, such as setting up a recovery configuration or managing DKIM keys. By passing address(0) for secondaryKey, the contract loses a valid signing authority, and by passing a maximum uint256 timestamp for the time fields, the contract enforces a deadline that will never be reached. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users expect to be able to add or remove DKIM keys and to recover their wallet, but they may find that the UI shows no response, that key addition transactions never become effective, or that recovery attempts are permanently blocked. From the user’s perspective the wallet may appear to be frozen, balances may seem inaccessible, and expected recovery actions return nothing. This condition occurs whenever the contract processes external input for the AccInfo struct without validation, which was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the unchecked parameters. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error at the time of input; the problem only manifests later when time‑based checks fail or when a zero address is used for authorization, making the failure mode appear as a silent loss of functionality rather than an explicit bug. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of unchecked input or parameter validation bugs that can lead to denial‑of‑service or loss of control. To remediate, the contract should enforce that secondaryKey is never the zero address and that each time‑related field is bounded by a reasonable maximum (for example, a few weeks or months from the current block timestamp). Adding explicit require statements or using a library that validates timestamps will prevent the contract from entering an unrecoverable state and restore the expected behavior of key management and wallet recovery.

title: `proposedOwner` not reset on transfer, allowing ownership to be seized back
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a stale authorization slot left behind when a contract that extends OpenZeppelin OwnableUpgradeable implements a two‑step ownership transfer via a proposedOwner variable. The contract provides functions to propose a new owner, to accept that proposal (takeOwnership), and also inherits the standard renounceOwnership and transferOwnership functions from OwnableUpgradeable. Those inherited functions change the _owner storage but never clear the proposedOwner storage slot. Consequently, any address that was previously stored as a proposed owner remains authorized to call takeOwnership even after the current owner has renounced ownership or transferred it to another address. The root cause is the missing reset of the proposedOwner variable in the direct ownership‑changing paths, creating a backdoor where ownership can be reclaimed later. An attacker (or the original owner) can exploit this by first proposing their own address as the new owner, then renouncing or transferring ownership to a third party or to the zero address, and finally invoking takeOwnership from the still‑proposed address to regain control. This leads to a situation where the contract appears to have no owner (owner address is zero) while a hidden slot still grants ownership rights, violating the expectation that renouncing ownership is final. The impact includes unauthorized takeover of privileged functions, potential alteration of contract state, upgrade of logic, or draining of funds, affecting token holders, protocol participants, and any party relying on the contract’s governance model. The issue manifests only when the contract inherits OwnableUpgradeable and uses its renounceOwnership or transferOwnership functions without additional cleanup; it is discovered during a security audit that reviews the ownership flow and notices that proposedOwner is never reset. The bug is hard to notice because standard events show a normal ownership transfer or renunciation, and the UI may display a zero address as the owner, giving a false sense of safety. The appropriate remediation is to either explicitly set proposedOwner to address(0) inside renounceOwnership and transferOwnership, or to replace the custom implementation with OpenZeppelin’s Ownable2StepUpgradeable, which handles the cleanup automatically. This class of vulnerability is a state‑variable residue or stale authorization bug, where leftover privileged data enables a backdoor that contradicts business logic assuming that ownership relinquishment is irreversible.

title: If bounty is created without all underlying tokens, accounting will be permanently thrown off
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a bounty is created and the contract updates the nominal values for underlying tokens. Each token has a stored nominal amount that represents the amount of that token per unit of the vault share, and a global multiplier (lastKnownMultiplier) that is applied to all tokens during rebalancing. After a rebalance the multiplier is reset to the scalar value of 1, and the nominal for every token must be recomputed to reflect the accrued fees. The implementation calls invokeSetNominal with an array that may contain only a subset of the underlying tokens. For any token that is omitted, the function skips the update, leaving its old nominal unchanged while the multiplier is reset globally. Because the vault calculates a token's virtual units as nominal * multiplier * totalSupply, the unchanged nominal combined with the reset multiplier makes the contract believe the vault holds more of that token than it actually does. This stale state is permanent: the vault will continue to project inflated balances for the omitted token, preventing correct withdrawals and breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The bug is triggered during bounty creation or any operation that invokes invokeSetNominal with an incomplete token list, which is a normal part of the protocol’s rebalancing flow. All users who hold or interact with the affected vault are impacted, as they may see balances that appear correct in the UI but are actually higher than the real holdings, leading to failed withdrawals, missing refunds, or funds that become permanently locked. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the rebalancing logic and noticed that the multiplier reset is applied globally without ensuring every token’s nominal is updated. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the mismatch only surfaces when a user attempts to move assets and the vault refuses due to insufficient real balance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of partial‑state‑update or accounting‑drift bugs, where related state variables are not kept in sync after a global change. To remediate, the invokeSetNominal function must be enforced to receive a complete list of all underlying tokens, or the contract must redesign the multiplier handling so that each token’s nominal is adjusted individually even when its amount does not change. Properly synchronizing nominal values with the multiplier reset will restore accurate accounting, allow withdrawals, and prevent permanent balance distortion.

title: Authority address can (maliciously or accidentally) steal user funds from the vault
description:
Rather than using an oracle, the system relies on an `authority` address (stored on the `HashStore.sol` contract) to set the `nominals` for each asset in the vault. These nominal values are used in rebalancing the pools.

The assumption is that these values that are set reflect a rebalancing of assets that maintains approximately equal value to the current value of the vault (perhaps with some small discount to incentivize the rebalancer).

However, there are no checks to ensure this is the case.

In a reasonable case, the `authority` address may perform a simple miscalculation that leads to a rebalancer profiting greatly from their action, draining value from the vault.

In a more malicious case, the `authority` could set all the `nominals` values to 0 and immediately rebalance the pool themselves. The result would be that they would be sent all assets in the vault, leaving it empty.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the design choice of trusting a single authority address to provide the nominal values for each asset that drive the vault’s rebalancing logic. Because the contract that stores these values (HashStore.sol) does not enforce any sanity checks or compare the supplied nominals against an external price source, the system assumes that the authority will always submit values that keep the total value of the pool roughly constant. This assumption is the root cause: there is no invariant guaranteeing that the sum of the new nominal values matches the pre‑rebalance vault value within an acceptable margin. An attacker who controls, compromises, or simply mis‑uses the authority address can therefore submit arbitrary nominal values. By setting the nominals to values that dramatically undervalue the assets – for example, zero for every asset – the rebalancing function will calculate that the pool holds no value and will transfer the entire balance to the caller (the rebalancer). In a less extreme scenario, a mis‑calculation by the authority can still create a large discrepancy, allowing the rebalancer to extract a disproportionate amount of assets while the vault’s reported value appears unchanged. The exploit is triggered when the rebalancing transaction reads the malicious nominals and executes the transfer logic; no additional permissions are required beyond the authority’s ability to write the nominals and the rebalancer’s ability to call the rebalance function. The impact is the complete or partial draining of user funds from the vault, leaving depositors with zero or reduced balances. From a user’s perspective the UI would show their deposited amount disappearing, or a “balance: 0” message after a rebalance they did not initiate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of validation on the authority‑provided data. It can be hard to notice because the nominal values are stored off‑chain and may look plausible at a glance; the contract does not emit warnings or revert on extreme values. To remediate, the protocol should replace the single‑authority model with a decentralized oracle or at least add a validation step that checks the new pool value against the previous value and enforces a tolerance threshold. Additional safeguards such as multi‑signature control over the authority address, time‑locked updates, or on‑chain price feeds would further reduce the risk of accidental or malicious fund loss. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked external input leading to invariant violation in financial rebalancing logic, where the lack of proper price verification enables fund‑stealing attacks.

title: Allowing multiple bounties to be live at once creates race condition
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that arises when the contract allows more than one bounty to be active at the same time. The authority can register a bounty by calling setHash which writes a boolean flag into the isValidHash mapping. Because the mapping can hold many keys, there is no enforcement that only a single bounty hash is considered valid. When two bounties are live, the permission‑less function that resolves a bounty can be invoked for either bounty in any order. The order of calls changes the final state of the protocol: executing bounty A first and then bounty B produces a different set of balances or rebalancing actions than executing bounty B first and then bounty A. This violates the intended business logic that the team should deterministically dictate how the system moves to a rebalanced state after a bounty is announced. The condition can be triggered whenever the authority creates a new bounty before the previous one has been fully resolved, which is possible because the deadline field only limits the lifetime but does not prevent overlap. From a user’s point of view the symptom may be that after submitting a claim the protocol ends in an unexpected configuration, funds appear to be missing from a pool, or the rebalancing does not happen as advertised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑management logic of HashStore.sol. It is hard to notice because the mapping appears to correctly record validity, yet the contract never checks that only one hash is active, so the bug does not manifest as an outright revert but as subtle state divergence. The proper fix is to replace the mapping with a single variable that stores the current bounty hash, and to require that any function processing a bounty first verifies that the supplied hash matches the stored bountyHash, rejecting any call that references an outdated or concurrent bounty. This eliminates the possibility of overlapping bounties and removes the race condition, restoring deterministic behavior.

title: Vault should have two step ownership transfer
description:
While many of the contracts in the system inherit `ProposableOwnable.sol` for their ownership, `Vault.sol` simply tracks an `owner` in storage and has a one step `setOwner()` function.

Because the vault is (a) one of the only non-upgradeable contracts in the system and (b) has some very important `onlyOwner` functionality, it seems especially important that transfers of ownership should be handled with care.
bug_full: The vulnerability is the presence of a single‑step ownership transfer function in the Vault contract. The contract stores an owner address in storage and exposes a public setOwner() function that can be called by the current owner to immediately replace the owner with any address. Because the Vault is a non‑upgradeable contract that holds critical assets and protects them with onlyOwner modifiers, the lack of a two‑step hand‑over mechanism creates a risk that ownership can be changed without the new owner explicitly accepting the role. The root cause is that the Vault does not inherit the ProposableOwnable pattern used by the rest of the system and therefore does not require a proposal and acceptance step, nor does it emit a confirmation event or enforce a delay. An attacker who obtains the private key of the current owner, or who tricks the owner into calling setOwner with a malicious address, can instantly transfer ownership to themselves. Once the attacker becomes the owner they can invoke any onlyOwner function, such as withdrawing funds, changing critical parameters, or freezing the contract, leading to potential loss of user funds and loss of trust in the protocol. This condition can be triggered at any time the owner executes setOwner; there is no safeguard, timelock, or confirmation step to prevent accidental or malicious transfers. The issue affects the protocol’s security guarantees, the users who rely on the vault to safeguard their deposits, and any stakeholders expecting proper governance over the contract. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Vault implementation with other contracts that inherit ProposableOwnable.sol and noted the deviation. The problem is subtle because the function name setOwner appears normal and the contract compiles without warnings, so developers may not notice the missing acceptance step until an ownership hijack occurs. From a user’s perspective the UI may still show the vault as operational, but after the takeover withdrawals may fail or funds may disappear without warning, violating the expectation that only a trusted owner can manage the vault. The recommended remediation is to replace the single‑step setOwner with a two‑step ownership transfer pattern, such as inheriting ProposableOwnable.sol or OpenZeppelin’s Ownable2Step.sol, which requires the new owner to call acceptOwnership after a proposal, emits appropriate events, and optionally includes a timelock to further harden the process.

title: Inflation will be overapplied if there is a time period when `totalSupply() == 0`
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol applies inflation when any action triggers the tryInflation() function. The function first reads the current total supply of the index token and then computes the inflation amount based on the fee accrued since the last recorded timestamp. A conditional block checks if the calculated inflation value is greater than zero before updating two critical storage variables – lastKnownMultiplier and lastKnownTimestamp – and before minting new tokens. When the total supply is zero, the inflation formula inevitably yields zero, causing the if (inflation > 0) guard to skip the entire block. Consequently, the multiplier and timestamp are never refreshed during the period of zero supply. If the supply later becomes non‑zero, the protocol will use the stale multiplier and timestamp to compute inflation on the new, larger supply, effectively applying the accumulated multiplier change all at once. This results in an over‑application of the intended inflation rate, minting more tokens than should be created, diluting existing holders and breaking the accounting assumptions of gradual fee accrual. The issue manifests only after a prolonged interval where totalSupply() == 0, such as when the protocol is paused or all tokens are withdrawn for a day or more. Users may notice an unexpected large increase in their token balance after re‑depositing funds, contradicting the expectation that inflation should be a small, continuous fee. The bug is subtle because a zero‑supply state is uncommon and the faulty logic does not produce an immediate error; the problem only becomes visible later when the inflated mint occurs. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of tryInflation() and identified that state updates were tied to the mint condition. To remediate, the storage updates should be decoupled from the minting check: the contract must always record the new multiplier and timestamp whenever new fees have accrued, regardless of whether the inflation amount is zero, and only conditionally mint tokens when inflation > 0. This change restores correct accounting, prevents sudden token over‑minting, and aligns the protocol’s behavior with its economic design.

title: System implicitly relies on off chain oracle
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an implicit trust relationship between the AMKT vault contract and an off‑chain oracle operated by the Alongside team. The vault’s rebalancing logic, which determines how assets are allocated, is calculated off‑chain and the result is only represented on‑chain as a hash stored in a HashStore contract. Because the contract merely records a bytes32 hash together with a boolean flag set by a privileged authority, there is no on‑chain verification of the correctness, freshness, or authenticity of the underlying calculation. The root cause is the absence of a verifiable on‑chain data source; the system relies on an external process that cannot be audited, replayed, or challenged by users or third parties. An attacker who can compromise the off‑chain computation environment, intercept the data transmission, or collude with the authority can submit a manipulated hash that the contract will accept as valid. Once accepted, the vault will execute rebalancing based on the falsified numbers, leading to incorrect asset distribution. The impact may include users receiving less than expected when withdrawing, balances appearing to shrink or become zero, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting. The condition occurs whenever the team uploads a new hash, typically after each rebalance cycle, and there is no additional on‑chain check. All participants who rely on the vault – depositors, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the financial state of the vault can be altered without transparent evidence. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the reliance on an off‑chain oracle as a non‑verifiable component. Because the contract does not expose the underlying data, the problem can be hard to notice; users only see the final outcome (e.g., unexpected balance changes) and have no way to trace the calculation back to a trusted source. Conceptually, the fix is to introduce an on‑chain oracle or verification mechanism that either computes the rebalancing parameters directly on‑chain or validates the off‑chain result against a consensus‑based data feed, thereby eliminating the single point of trust. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “off‑chain oracle trust issue” or “oracle integrity violation,” where business logic assumes correct external data without cryptographic proof. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the expected refund or asset allocation and the actual amount received, often manifesting as missing funds or zero balances after a rebalance, contrary to the user’s expectation of a correct and transparent calculation.

title: Invalid signature execution is possible if address(0) has non-zero privileges
description:
The problem is similar to this issue from a previous audit. The code in
SignatureValidator::recoverAddrImpl will return address(0) if it receives a
valid Schnorr signature but not one that is for the given hash (transactions
hash). Now the result will be checked like this:
```solidity
signerKey = SignatureValidator.recoverAddrImpl(hash, signature, true);
require(privileges[signerKey] != bytes32(0), 'INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGE');
```
Meaning signerKey will be address(0) and now if the value for
privileges[address(0)] is non-zero, then anyone will be able to execute any
transaction for this wallet, for example stealing all funds.
Also, it is possible to get recoverAddrImpl to return address(0) if you
provide a signature with SignatureMode == Multisig and then the signatures
inside it to be of type SignatureMode == Spoof. Since allowSpoofing
argument will be false, then we will get to the return address(0); code in
the end of the method.
A third way to get recoverAddrImpl to return address(0) is if you use
SignatureMode == Multisig and just provide an empty array of signatures -
then it will return the default value of address signer which is address(0).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an invalid‑signature execution path that allows any caller to be treated as the authorized signer when the signature verification routine returns the zero address. The root cause lies in the recoverAddrImpl function of the SignatureValidator contract. This function can return address(0) not only when the supplied Schnorr signature is malformed, but also when a multisig signature is supplied with inner signatures marked as spoof, or when an empty signature array is provided. The contract subsequently reads the signerKey returned by recoverAddrImpl and checks privileges[signerKey] != bytes32(0). Because the check does not explicitly exclude address(0), a non‑zero entry in the privileges mapping for the zero address will satisfy the condition. If such an entry exists—whether set accidentally during deployment or by a later upgrade—any attacker can craft a signature that forces recoverAddrImpl to return address(0) and then pass the privilege test, gaining the ability to execute arbitrary transactions on behalf of the wallet. This can be exploited to transfer all funds out of the wallet, approve malicious contracts, or otherwise violate the intended access control. The impact is a loss of funds and a breach of trust in the protocol, affecting all users of the affected wallet contract. The issue manifests only when the zero‑address privilege entry is non‑zero; otherwise the check fails and the transaction reverts. Because address(0) is commonly used as a sentinel value, developers may assume it can never be a valid signer, making the bug easy to overlook during code review. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the logic to a previously reported issue.
