The bug manifests only during the execution of the rollover function and only when the old loan has an affiliate distinct from the new loan’s affiliate; in all other cases the fee distribution appears correct, making the issue subtle and easy to overlook. From a user perspective the affiliate may see a zero payout after a rollover, even though the loan generated interest, leading to confusion such as “my affiliate balance is empty” or “I expected a refund but got nothing”. The problem was identified during a manual security audit performed by Renascence, which noted that the fee calculation does not differentiate between repayment and rollover fees. Because the contract does not expose detailed fee breakdowns in the UI, the misallocation can remain hidden until an affiliate audits their earnings. The recommended remediation is to separate repayment fees from rollover fees, introduce distinct parameters for each, and split repayment fees between the protocol and the original affiliate while allocating rollover fees to the new affiliate. This requires refactoring the fee calculation logic in the OriginationController and related contracts so that each fee type is routed to the appropriate party, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing affiliates from losing revenue during loan renewals.

title: Borrowers can use RepaymentController.forceRepay() to temporarily prevent lenders from claiming collateral
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service that lets a borrower temporarily block a lender from claiming collateral after a loan has passed its due date. The claim() function in the loan core contract first verifies that the loan is active and then checks that the stored note receipt amount for the loan is zero. This check is intended to ensure that no outstanding note balance exists before the lender can seize the collateral. However, the note receipt amount is a mutable value that can be altered by the borrower through the RepaymentController.forceRepay() function, which creates a note receipt with a non‑zero amount even as small as one wei. Because the blockchain processes transactions in the order they are included in a block, a borrower can front‑run a lender’s claim transaction, invoke forceRepay() to set the note receipt amount to a non‑zero value, and cause the subsequent claim() call to revert due to the zero‑amount check. The lender then receives a revert error, sees no collateral transferred, and must first call redeemNote() to withdraw the newly created note before attempting another claim. From the user’s perspective the lender expects the collateral to be transferred after the loan matures, but instead the transaction fails and the balance appears unchanged, creating confusion and potential financial loss. The impact is that the borrower can extend the loan indefinitely for the cost of gas, effectively preventing the lender from recovering the pledged assets and undermining the protocol’s liquidation guarantees. This issue occurs only when the loan is overdue, the lender initiates a claim, and the borrower has the ability to execute a repayment transaction in the same block. It affects all participants relying on the automatic collateral claim mechanism, including lenders, borrowers, and the overall protocol’s trust model. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state checks in claim() and identified that the note receipt validation could be manipulated by an external call. The problem is subtle because the zero‑amount requirement appears logical and the revert path is rarely exercised in normal operation, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the zero‑amount check should be removed or relocated after the note receipt has been cleared, or the claim logic should be restructured to prevent state changes by other actors between the check and the execution, ensuring that a borrower cannot create a blocking note receipt right before a claim. In broader terms, this is a class of front‑running state‑dependency bugs where a contract’s pre‑condition can be altered by a competing transaction, leading to a temporary denial of service and violation of the expected accounting flow of collateral seizure.

title: Missing signingCounterparty in loanHash can lead to the signature being used with the wrong address
description:
loanHash is used in recoverTokenSignature and recoverItemsSignature to determine the external signer for a signature specifying only a collateral address and ID.
```solidity
bytes32 loanHash = keccak256(
    abi.encode(
        OriginationLibrary._TOKEN_ID_TYPEHASH,
        loanTerms.interestRate,
        loanTerms.durationSecs,
        loanTerms.collateralAddress,
        loanTerms.deadline,
        loanTerms.payableCurrency,
        loanTerms.principal,
        loanTerms.collateralId,
        loanTerms.affiliateCode,
        sigProperties.nonce,
        sigProperties.maxUses,
        uint8(side)
    )
);
```
However, it doesn't include the address of the signingCounterparty. Depending on the side, this could be the lender or the borrower address. This makes it possible for the recently disclosed ERC1271 bug to occur, where if a signer's smart wallet's isValidSignature() follows the reference implementation in ERC-1271, their signature can be used with the wrong address as the signingCounterparty. Consider the following example:
• Bob wants to be a lender with his smart wallet - he signs a signature with his EOA, which will return true when passed to his smart wallet's isValidSignature().
• Alice calls initializeLoan() with his signature but with his EOA as the lender address.
• isSelfOrApproved() in _validateCounterparties() passes since signer is Bob's EOA.
An important note is that the signature can't be replayed in this case, so the only impact is that it can be used with the wrong address.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the loan contract builds the hash that is signed by a counter‑party. When a loan is created the contract computes a loanHash that includes loan terms such as interest rate, duration, collateral address and ID, but it deliberately omits the address of the party that actually produced the signature – the signingCounterparty, which can be either the lender or the borrower depending on the side of the transaction. Because the signer’s address is not part of the signed message, the signature can be verified against a different address without changing the hash. This omission creates a domain‑separation flaw that can be abused together with the recently disclosed ERC‑1271 bug, where a smart‑wallet implementation of isValidSignature may return true for any supplied address if the reference logic is followed. In practice an attacker can supply a signature generated by a smart‑wallet (for example Bob’s wallet) and then present that signature to the loan initialization function while claiming a different counter‑party address (for example Alice’s address). The internal check _validateCounterparties() only verifies that the recovered signer matches the address supplied in the transaction, which succeeds because the signature itself is still valid for the original signer’s contract. Consequently the loan is recorded with the wrong lender or borrower address. The impact is that the loan’s accounting is corrupted – the protocol believes that a different party is involved, which could lead to funds being transferred to an unintended address or to a mismatch between on‑chain state and off‑chain expectations. The bug does not allow replay attacks because the nonce and maxUses fields prevent the same signature from being reused, so the damage is limited to a single loan creation. The condition for exploitation is that the loan initialization path uses recoverTokenSignature or recoverItemsSignature, that the loanHash is built without the signingCounterparty, and that the counter‑party’s wallet follows the vulnerable ERC‑1271 reference implementation. All users who rely on the signature to bind a specific address to a loan – lenders, borrowers and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the loan contract by the Renascence team, who noticed that the signed data omitted the signer’s address. It is hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed, the signature verification passes, and the UI shows the expected addresses, while the underlying binding is wrong. The proper mitigation is to include the signingCounterparty in the data that is hashed before signing, thereby ensuring that any change in the counter‑party address changes the hash and invalidates the signature. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a missing signer binding or domain‑separation omission, which can lead to signature misuse and accounting errors such as “funds disappear” or “wrong party receives the loan”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a loan may be created with an unexpected lender or borrower, causing confusion when the expected counterpart does not receive the funds or when the recorded balance does not match the user’s expectation.

title: New lenders are unfairly charged for interestFee when rolling over an loan
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect fee allocation during a loan rollover. When a borrower calls rolloverLoan and the new lender is different from the previous lender, the contract's rolloverAmounts function adds the interestFee to amounts.amountFromLender unconditionally. This causes the new lender to pay the interest that belongs to the old loan, increasing the amount the borrower must provide and reducing the net proceeds for the new lender. The root cause is the lack of a check that compares the address of the current lender with the address of the old lender before applying the interestFee. An attacker can exploit this by arranging a rollover with a third‑party lender, causing the third party to overpay the interest fee. The impact is economic: the new lender receives less than expected, borrowers may need to supply extra funds, and the protocol's accounting assumptions about fee distribution are violated. The condition occurs only when borrowerFee, lenderFee, or interestFee are non‑zero and the old and new lender differ, which is a common scenario for loan refinancing. Users experience the symptom of a higher required deposit or a lower received amount after rollover, contrary to the expectation that a rollover should cost the same as initializing a fresh loan. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee handling in rolloverAmounts with the logic used in RepaymentController._prepareRepay, where the interest fee is correctly deducted from the amount sent to the lender. Because the fee is added to a variable that is later used to calculate the amount transferred to the new lender, the misallocation can be subtle and may not trigger obvious test failures unless the specific case of different lenders is exercised. The recommended remediation is to conditionally add the interestFee only when the new lender is the same as the old lender, and to subtract the interestFee from the repayment to the old lender when the lenders differ. This aligns the fee distribution with the intended business logic that interest fees belong to the loan being repaid, not to a newly originated loan.

title: The borrowers callbackData is not included in signatures
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unauthenticated mutable parameter in the loan initialization flow. When a loan is created, the caller (typically the lender) provides a BorrowerData structure that may contain a non‑empty callbackData field. The contract verifies a signature that covers the loan terms, the borrower address, and other static parameters, but it deliberately omits the callbackData from the signed hash. Consequently, if the neededSide is Side.BORROW – meaning the borrower is the counter‑party and the caller is the lender – the lender can supply arbitrary callbackData or even an empty byte array without invalidating the signature. The borrower’s executeOperation function is then invoked with this attacker‑controlled data. Because the callback may dictate token transfers, state changes, or external calls, the borrower may experience a different outcome than intended, ranging from a missed repayment to a complete loss of assets. The issue is triggered only during the initializeLoan transaction when borrowerData.callbackData.length > 0 and the signature verification step does not include that field. All parties that rely on the correctness of the callback – the borrower, the lender, and any downstream users of the protocol – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the signature composition, where the absence of callbackData in the signed message was noted. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, no revert occurs, and the on‑chain data does not reveal that the callback was altered; the UI may show that the loan was created but the expected operation does not happen, leading to confusion. The bug belongs to the class of “missing data in signed authorization” or “unauthenticated mutable parameter” vulnerabilities, where a critical input is excluded from the cryptographic commitment, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the borrower’s callback will execute exactly as agreed. To remediate, the signature generation function should be extended to hash the callbackData together with the other signed fields, ensuring that any change to the callback would invalidate the signature and be detectable by the counter‑party. This change restores the integrity of the loan agreement and prevents a lender from silently modifying the borrower’s post‑initialization behavior.

title: migrateV3Loan() will revert for lenders that are approved or use ERC-1271
description:
migrateV3Loan() checks that externalSigner, the address retrieved from the signature, is the same as the lender address:
```solidity
function migrateV3Loan(
    uint256 oldLoanId,
    LoanLibrary.LoanTerms calldata newTerms,
    address lender,
    Signature calldata sig,
    SigProperties calldata sigProperties,
    LoanLibrary.Predicate[] calldata itemPredicates
) external override whenNotPaused whenBorrowerReset {
»
    if (externalSigner != lender) revert OCM_SideMismatch(externalSigner);
```
However, checking that externalSigner is the lender address will revert for lenders that:
1. Are smart wallet addresses that validate signatures through ERC-1271.
2. Approve other addresses to create offers on their behalf using approve()
As such, borrowers cannot migrate their V3 loans using loan offers in V4 if the lender is either of the above.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migrateV3Loan function of the loan origination contract, where the implementation validates that the address recovered from the lender's signature (externalSigner) is exactly equal to the lender address supplied as a parameter. This equality check is performed with a simple comparison and causes the transaction to revert when the two addresses differ. The root cause is that the validation logic does not account for two legitimate ways a lender can authorize a migration: (1) the lender may be a smart‑wallet contract that validates signatures via the ERC‑1271 standard, in which case the recovered signer is the contract itself and the externalSigner address will not match the EO‑address stored as lender; (2) the lender may have previously approved another address to act on its behalf using the standard approve() mechanism, meaning the signature can legitimately be produced by an approved operator rather than the lender directly. Because the function only checks for strict equality, any migration attempt involving either of these patterns triggers the OCM_SideMismatch revert, preventing borrowers from migrating existing V3 loans to the newer V4 version. From an exploitation perspective the issue is not a malicious attack but a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate lenders and borrowers are unable to complete a migration, effectively locking the loan in its original version. The impact is that funds tied to the loan remain inaccessible for refinancing or other protocol features, and the protocol’s promised upgrade path is broken for a subset of users, namely those using contract wallets or delegated operators. The condition occurs whenever migrateV3Loan is called with a lender that is a contract wallet implementing ERC‑1271 or when the lender has granted approval to another address. Both borrowers and lenders are affected, as borrowers cannot trigger the migration and lenders see their loan offers become unusable. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined signature handling and noticed the simplistic equality check. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to correctly recover a signer and compare it, which works for regular externally owned accounts; only when testing with contract wallets or delegated signatures does the problem surface. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct equality check with a more permissive validation that accepts either the lender itself, an address approved by the lender, or a contract‑wallet signature verified via ERC‑1271. The recommended fix introduces a helper isSelfOrApproved and leverages OriginationLibrary.isApprovedForContract to perform this broader check, and also updates nonce consumption to use the actual externalSigner rather than the lender address. By aligning the signature verification with the protocol’s approval model, the migration flow can succeed for all legitimate lender configurations, restoring the intended upgrade path and preventing accidental fund lock‑up.

title: Stale feeSnapshot is used when rolling over a loan
description:
When rolling over a loan, instead of fetching the most recent fees through FeeController.getOriginationFeeAmounts() the function assigns the new loan fees by reusing data.feeSnapshot that was taken when the previous loan was created. This means that even if the protocol's default, interest and principal fees were updated, the new loan created by rollover() would still use old fee values.
```solidity
function rollover(
    uint256 oldLoanId,
    address oldLender,
    address borrower,
    address lender,
    LoanLibrary.LoanTerms calldata terms,
    uint256 _settledAmount,
    uint256 _amountToOldLender,
    uint256 _amountToLender,
    uint256 _amountToBorrower,
    uint256 _interestAmount
) external override whenNotPaused onlyRole(ORIGINATOR_ROLE) nonReentrant returns
(uint256 newLoanId) {
>
    LoanLibrary.LoanData storage data = loans[oldLoanId];
    loans[newLoanId] = LoanLibrary.LoanData({
        state: LoanLibrary.LoanState.Active,
        startDate: uint64(block.timestamp),
        lastAccrualTimestamp: uint64(block.timestamp),
        terms: terms,
>
        feeSnapshot: data.feeSnapshot,
        balance: terms.principal,
        interestAmountPaid: 0
    });
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale fee snapshot that is reused when a loan is rolled over to a new term. When the rollover function creates a new LoanData structure it copies the feeSnapshot field from the previous loan instead of querying the FeeController for the current origination fee amounts. The root cause is a design oversight: the feeSnapshot is stored as part of the loan state and the rollover logic assumes it is still valid, ignoring the possibility that the protocol’s default, interest, or principal fees may have been changed after the original loan was created. An attacker or any user can exploit this by initiating a rollover after a fee change; the new loan will be charged with the old fee values. If the protocol increased fees, the borrower benefits from a lower-than‑expected charge, reducing protocol revenue. Conversely, if fees were reduced, the borrower may be overcharged, violating the expected business logic that fees reflect the current rates. The impact is financial mis‑alignment: users may see refunds that are too small or fees that are higher than advertised, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions break because the fee calculation no longer matches the on‑chain fee policy. This condition occurs every time the rollover() external function is called while the contract is not paused and the caller has the ORIGINATOR_ROLE, because the code unconditionally assigns feeSnapshot: data.feeSnapshot. The affected parties are borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself, as any rollovers performed after a fee update will inherit stale values. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer compared the rollover implementation with the intended fee‑fetching pattern and noticed that the feeSnapshot was never refreshed. It can be hard to notice because the feeSnapshot field is present and appears to be set, giving the impression that fee data is being handled correctly, while the UI may continue to display the old fee numbers without warning. The recommended fix is to replace the stale assignment with a fresh call to FeeController.getOriginationFeeAmounts() using the new principal amount, and to store that fresh snapshot in the new loan’s feeSnapshot field. This aligns the loan creation logic with the current fee policy and restores correct accounting, preventing users from receiving unexpected zero refunds or paying incorrect fees, and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s revenue model.

title: Low-level transfer via `call
poc: Please find the documentation [here](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/develop/control-structures.html#error-handling-assert-require-revert-and-exceptions).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of a low‑level `call` within the TimelockController contract to execute scheduled operations. The `_call()` internal function forwards the supplied `value` and `data` to an arbitrary `target` address and only checks the boolean `success` flag returned by the low‑level call. Solidity’s specification states that `call` returns true even when the called address does not contain contract code; the EVM treats a call to a non‑existent account as successful because no revert is raised. Consequently, the TimelockController assumes the underlying transaction has been executed correctly simply because `success` is true, while in reality the target may be an empty address or a contract that does not implement the expected function. This results in a silent failure: the scheduled action—such as a token transfer, contract upgrade, or any state‑changing call—does not take place, yet the timelock emits a `CallExecuted` event and the protocol proceeds as if the operation succeeded. The issue manifests whenever the timelock processes a queued operation, i.e., after the required delay has elapsed and the `_call()` function is invoked. It affects all participants that rely on the timelock for governance, token holders, and any downstream contracts that expect the scheduled action to have been performed. The problem was discovered during a security audit that cross‑referenced the Solidity documentation on low‑level calls and identified that the contract does not verify the existence of the target contract before invoking it. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; blockchain explorers and UI dashboards will show a successful execution event, while the expected state change (for example, a balance update or contract upgrade) is missing, leading users to see “nothing happened” after the delay. To remediate, the contract should explicitly check that the `target` address contains code—using `extcodesize` or `address.code.length`—or employ higher‑level interface calls that automatically revert if the target contract does not exist. This additional verification ensures that a failure to execute the intended logic is caught and reported, preventing silent no‑ops and preserving the integrity of the timelock’s governance guarantees.

title: Arbitrary code can be run with Controller as msg.sender
description:
A malicious user can call Controller’s operate with ActionType.QTokenPermit, providing a precooked contract address as qToken, that will be called by Controller contract with IQToken(_qToken).permit(), which implementation can be arbitrary as long as IQToken interface and permit signature is implemented.

The Controller is asset bearing contract and it will be msg.sender in this arbitrary permit() function called, which is a setup that better be avoided.
poc:
When the Controller’s operate with a QTokenPermit action, it parses the arguments with Actions library and then calls internal _qTokenPermit:

[Controller.sol#L91-L92](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/Controller.sol#L91-L92)  

_qTokenPermit calls the IQToken(_qToken) address provided without performing any additional checks:

[Controller.sol#L497-L516](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/Controller.sol#L497-L516)  

This way, contrary to the approach used in other actions, qToken isn’t checked to be properly created address and is used right away, while the requirement that the address provided should implement IQToken interface and have permit function with a given signature can be easily met with a precooked contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked delegation of control in the Controller contract’s QTokenPermit action. When a caller invokes Controller.operate with ActionType.QTokenPermit, the contract extracts a qToken address from the supplied arguments and immediately executes IQToken(_qToken).permit() without validating that the address is a legitimate QToken instance. This lack of verification allows a malicious user to supply a crafted contract that conforms to the IQToken interface and implements the permit function with arbitrary logic. Because the Controller contract is the msg.sender inside the called permit() function and holds assets, the malicious permit implementation can execute code that manipulates the Controller’s state, transfer tokens, or perform other unauthorized operations. The exploit is triggered whenever the operate function is called with a QTokenPermit action, which can be done by any external account that can submit actions to the Controller. The affected parties include the protocol’s funds, any users who rely on the Controller to manage assets safely, and the overall integrity of the system. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the code paths of Controller.operate and noticing that the qToken address is used without any provenance checks, unlike other actions that verify the token through an OptionsFactory. The problem is subtle because the permit selector is a standard part of many token contracts, so the call appears legitimate and may not raise alarms during normal testing. In practice, a user may see their balances unchanged while the contract silently executes malicious logic, or they may observe unexpected loss of assets without any explicit error messages. The root cause is a missing whitelist or factory‑based verification step that should ensure the supplied address implements a trusted QToken contract. To remediate, the Controller should validate the qToken address against the IOptionsFactory.isQToken method, restrict the action to known QToken contracts, or remove the QTokenPermit action entirely if it is not required for UI convenience. By enforcing proper validation, the protocol can prevent arbitrary code execution and preserve the expected accounting guarantees of the Controller.

title: Spreads can be minted with a deactivated oracle
description:
When deactivateOracle() is called for an oracle in OracleRegistry it is still available for option spreads minting.

This way a user can continue to mint new options within spreads that rely on an oracle that was deactivated. As economic output of spreads is close to vanilla options, so all users who already posses an option linked to a deactivated oracle can surpass this deactivation, being able to mint new options linked to it as a part of option spreads.
poc:
Oracle active state is checked with isOracleActive() during option creation in validateOptionParameters() and during option minting in _mintOptionsPosition().

It isn’t checked during spreads creation:

[FundsCalculator.sol#L91-L117](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/libraries/FundsCalculator.sol#L91-L117)  

In other words besides vanilla option minting and creation all spectrum of operations is available for the deactivated oracle assets, including spreads minting, which economically is reasonably close to vanilla minting.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the creation of option spreads in a protocol that relies on external price oracles. When an oracle is deactivated through the deactivateOracle() function in the OracleRegistry, the protocol is expected to block any further financial operations that depend on that oracle, effectively moving existing positions to a read‑only or “close‑only” state. While the vanilla option creation and minting paths correctly enforce this restriction by invoking isOracleActive() inside validateOptionParameters() and _mintOptionsPosition(), the spread‑minting path does not perform the same check. Specifically, the FundsCalculator.sol library calculates the required funds for a spread without verifying the oracle’s active flag, allowing the createSpread or related minting functions to succeed even when the oracle is marked inactive. The root cause is a missing guard clause in the spread creation logic, an oversight that permits the protocol to treat a deactivated oracle as still valid for new option issuance. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by first ensuring an oracle is deactivated—either by waiting for an admin action or triggering it themselves—and then submitting a transaction that creates a spread referencing the same oracle. Because the contract never validates the oracle’s status, the new options within the spread are minted based on stale or potentially manipulated price data. The immediate impact is a violation of the protocol’s risk model: users expect that deactivated oracles cannot be used to open new positions, so the ability to mint additional options undermines the intended safety barrier, potentially leading to mispriced contracts, unintended exposure to price swings, and financial loss for both the protocol’s treasury and participants who rely on correct oracle behavior. This issue becomes noticeable only when a user attempts to create a spread after an oracle shutdown and observes that the transaction succeeds, contrary to the expectation set by the behavior of vanilla options. The bug is subtle because the code paths for vanilla options and spreads are separate; developers may assume that the same validation applies globally, and standard test suites often focus on the primary option flow, leaving the spread path unchecked. Discovery originated from a manual code audit that compared the validation steps across the two pathways and identified the missing isOracleActive() call. To remediate, the spread creation and minting functions should incorporate the same active‑oracle verification as vanilla options, either by reusing validateOptionParameters() or by adding an explicit require(isOracleActive(oracleId), ...) guard before any financial calculation or state change. This change restores the intended contract semantics, ensuring that once an oracle is deactivated, no new financial instrument—whether a single option or a composite spread—can be minted against it, thereby preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees and protecting user funds.

title: Admin of the upgradeable proxy contract of `Controller.sol` can rug users
description:
[Controller.sol#L22-L34](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/a06418c9cc847395f3699bdf684a9ac066651ed7/quant-protocol/contracts/Controller.sol#L22-L34)  

Use of Upgradeable Proxy Contract Structure allows the logic of the contract to be arbitrarily changed.

This allows the proxy admin to perform malicious actions e.g., taking funds from users’ wallets up to the allowance limit.

This action can be performed by the malicious/compromised proxy admin without any restriction.

Considering that the purpose of this particular contract is for accounting of the Collateral and LongShortTokens, we believe the users’ allowances should not be hold by this upgradeable contract.
poc:
Given:

  * collateral: `USDC`
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of an upgradeable proxy pattern for the Controller contract, which is responsible for accounting of collateral and LongShortTokens. The proxy’s admin role retains the unrestricted ability to replace the underlying implementation contract at any time. Because the proxy holds user allowances – the permission for the contract to transfer user‑owned collateral such as USDC – a malicious or compromised admin can upgrade the logic to a contract that calls transferFrom on those allowances and drain the permitted amount of tokens from users’ wallets. This class of issue is commonly known as an admin‑controlled upgradeability backdoor, where the centralization of upgrade rights defeats the expected trust model of the protocol. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (typically the proxy admin, which may be a governance-controlled address) deploys a malicious implementation that, upon upgrade, iterates over stored allowances and invokes the token’s transferFrom function, thereby moving funds up to each user’s approved limit. The impact is the loss of user collateral, erosion of trust, and a violation of the protocol’s accounting invariants that assume collateral is safely locked. The condition for the attack to materialize is the existence of a compromised admin key or a hostile governance decision that approves a malicious upgrade; until such a governance compromise occurs, assets are not directly at risk, which is why the finding was downgraded to medium severity. The flaw was identified during a formal audit that highlighted the mismatch between the contract’s purpose (secure accounting) and the architectural choice of storing allowances in an upgradeable proxy. It can be difficult to notice because upgradeable proxies are a standard design pattern, and the admin role is often assumed to be benign, masking the underlying power to alter business logic arbitrarily. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that their approved collateral remains locked and inaccessible to the protocol, yet after a malicious upgrade the user may observe that their USDC allowance has been consumed, their balance reduced to zero, or withdrawal attempts failing despite having sufficient allowance. To remediate, the protocol should eliminate the upgradeable proxy for the component that stores allowances, either by deploying a non‑upgradeable CollateralToken contract or by renouncing the admin role and employing immutable logic, thereby aligning the contract’s architecture with the security expectations of collateral protection.

title: Pool Credit Line May Not Able to Start When _borrowAsset is Non ERC20 Compliant Tokens
description:
`IERC20(_borrowAsset).transfer(_to, _fee);`

If the USDT token is supported as _borrowAsset, the unsafe version of .transfer(_to, _fee) may revert as there is no return value in the USDT token contract’s transfer() implementation (but the IERC20 interface expects a return value).

Function start() will break when _borrowAsset is USDT or Non ERC20 Compliant Tokens. USDT is one of the most borrowed Asset in DEFI. This may cause losing a lot of potential users.
poc: [LenderPool.sol#L327](https://github.com/sublime-finance/sublime-v1/blob/46536a6d25df4264c1b217bd3232af30355dcb95/contracts/PooledCreditLine/LenderPool.sol#L327)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s use of the standard IERC20 interface to invoke the function transfer on the borrowed asset token. The code calls IERC20(_borrowAsset).transfer(_to, _fee) assuming that the token adheres to the ERC‑20 specification that requires the transfer function to return a boolean value indicating success. Certain widely used stablecoins, most notably USDT, implement a non‑standard transfer that does not return any value. When the Solidity compiler generates the call, it expects a return value and attempts to decode it; the absence of data causes the call to revert. Consequently, the start() function of the pooled credit line, which relies on this transfer to move the fee to a designated address, will fail whenever the selected borrow asset is a non‑ERC20‑compliant token. An attacker does not need to craft a special exploit – simply selecting USDT (or any similar token) as the borrow asset triggers the failure automatically. The impact is that the credit line cannot be initiated, preventing users from borrowing, repaying, or accessing any functionality that depends on a successful start. This condition manifests only when the pool creator chooses a non‑standard token, making the bug hard to detect during normal testing with compliant ERC‑20 tokens. The affected parties include borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself, as the inability to start a credit line translates into lost revenue and a degraded user experience. The issue was uncovered during a manual source‑code audit that flagged the direct use of transfer without safety checks. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the transfer works with most tokens, so developers may assume the code is safe. To remediate, the call should be replaced with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer, which internally handles missing return values and reverts only when the token explicitly fails, thereby restoring compatibility with non‑standard tokens. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of ERC‑20 interface compliance errors, where an implementation assumes strict adherence to the standard and therefore breaks when confronted with a deviating token. From a user’s perspective, attempting to start a credit line results in an unexpected transaction revert, no fee is transferred, and the UI may indicate that the operation failed without a clear reason, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have vanished or the protocol is unsafe.

title: Lack of access control allow anyone to `withdrawInterest
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing access‑control check on the public withdrawInterest function of the LenderPool contract. The function allows any external caller to specify an arbitrary lender address and credit‑line identifier, and then executes the internal _withdrawInterest routine which calculates the accrued interest for that lender and transfers the amount to the supplied address. Because the function does not verify that msg.sender is the same as the _lender parameter, an attacker can invoke withdrawInterest on behalf of any participant. This can be exploited by calling withdrawInterest for a victim lender at an arbitrary moment, causing the system to immediately transfer the currently accrued interest to the victim’s address and, more critically, to reset the lender’s internal interest‑share bookkeeping (sharesHeld is reduced by the withdrawn amount). As a result, the lender loses the opportunity to continue compounding that interest, effectively leaking future value. The impact is a business‑logic violation: users expect their interest to accrue until they deliberately withdraw it, but the contract permits anyone to trigger the withdrawal, leading to premature interest extraction and reduced returns. The issue manifests whenever withdrawInterest is called, regardless of the caller’s identity, and it affects all lenders participating in the pooled credit line. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit when reviewers noted the absence of a require(msg.sender == _lender) guard that is present in similar withdrawal functions. The problem may be hard to notice because the transferred funds are still sent to the correct lender address, so there is no direct loss of assets; however, the subtle erosion of expected earnings can be observed as a sudden drop in projected returns or a zero balance where accrued interest should appear. The appropriate remediation is to enforce proper access control, typically by adding a require statement that ensures only the designated lender (or an authorized operator) can invoke the withdrawal, or by employing role‑based permissions. This aligns the contract’s behaviour with the intended accounting model where interest is only withdrawn at the lender’s discretion, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s financial logic.

title: No use of upgradeable SafeERC20 contract in `Controller.sol`
description: Controller.sol makes use of Open Zeppelins `ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable.sol` in the file but does not use an upgradeable version of SafeERC20.sol
poc: [Controller.sol#L5](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/Controller.sol#L5)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the Controller contract being built as an upgradeable contract (it inherits OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable) while it imports and uses the regular, non‑upgradeable version of SafeERC20. In an upgradeable deployment the contract lives behind a proxy and its logic contract must only rely on upgrade‑compatible components, i.e., contracts that are compiled without constructors and that reserve storage gaps for future extensions. The standard SafeERC20 library is written for non‑proxy deployments and does not include the Initializable pattern or storage gap that the upgradeable variant provides. Consequently, when the Controller is deployed behind a proxy, the library may interact with the token contracts in an unexpected context, potentially causing token transfer calls to fail silently, revert, or behave inconsistently across upgrades. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who triggers a token transfer through the Controller after an upgrade; because the library’s internal assumptions about the contract’s storage layout are violated, the transfer may succeed without proper checks or may be blocked, leading to funds being locked or unintentionally transferred to an attacker‑controlled address. The impact is that users of the protocol may see their expected refunds, withdrawals, or other token movements disappear or be reduced to zero, contradicting the protocol’s accounting rules. The issue only manifests when the Controller is used as an upgradeable proxy; in a simple deployment the code compiles and appears to work, making the problem hard to notice during regular testing. It was discovered during a third‑party audit when reviewers inspected the import statements and identified the inconsistency between upgradeable and non‑upgradeable components. To remediate the problem the Controller should replace the import of SafeERC20 with SafeERC20Upgradeable and adjust any usage to the upgradeable library’s API, ensuring that all linked libraries share the same upgradeable lifecycle and that storage gaps are respected. This change restores the intended safety guarantees of token transfers, aligns the contract with best practices for proxy‑based systems, and prevents the subtle accounting failures that could otherwise cause funds to disappear or refunds to be missing.

title: `COLLATERAL_MINTER_ROLE` can be granted by the deployer of `QuantConfig` and mint arbitrary amount of tokens
poc:
[CollateralToken.sol#L101-L117](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/options/CollateralToken.sol#L101-L117)  
[CollateralToken.sol#L138-L160](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/options/CollateralToken.sol#L138-L160)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑privileged access control on the CollateralToken contract that allows any address holding the COLLATERAL_MINTER_ROLE to call mintCollateralToken and create an arbitrary amount of collateral tokens for any recipient. This arises because the contract checks only that the caller possesses the COLLATERAL_MINTER_ROLE, which can be granted by the deployer of the QuantConfig contract, and the role can later be reassigned or renounced, meaning the privilege may persist or be transferred unintentionally. An attacker who obtains the private key of the deployer or any account that currently holds the role can invoke the mint function with a chosen token identifier and a large amount, causing unlimited token minting. The exploit proceeds by submitting a transaction that passes the role check, emitting the CollateralTokenMinted event, and executing the internal _mint routine, thereby inflating the total supply of the collateral token without any economic restriction. The impact is a potential devaluation of all existing collateral holdings, disruption of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, and the ability for a malicious actor to rug users by flooding the market with newly created tokens, which can lead to loss of confidence and financial loss for token holders, borrowers, and any other participants that rely on the collateral token’s scarcity. This condition manifests whenever the COLLATERAL_MINTER_ROLE is assigned and has not been permanently renounced, which is typical after deployment when the role is used for administrative purposes. The affected parties include regular users who expect the token balance to reflect genuine collateral, the protocol that assumes a fixed or controlled supply for its risk calculations, and any external integrations that display token statistics. The issue was identified during a systematic audit of role‑based permissions, where the auditors noted that the mint function lacked any quantitative limit or secondary guard, and that the role could be reassigned, creating a centralization risk. The problem may be hard to notice because the role name appears legitimate and the presence of a mint function is standard for ERC‑1155 tokens, leading reviewers to assume that proper governance is in place. To remediate, the COLLATERAL_MINTER_ROLE should be eliminated, minting rights should be confined to a single trusted contract (the Controller) or the contract owner, and any existing minter roles should be renounced and removed. This aligns the contract with the principle of least privilege, eliminates unnecessary centralization, and restores confidence that collateral token supply cannot be arbitrarily expanded.

title: Usage of deprecated Chainlink functions
description: The Chainlink functions `latestAnswer()` and `getAnswer()` are deprecated. Instead, use the [`latestRoundData()`](https://docs.chain.link/docs/price-feeds-api-reference/#latestrounddata) and [`getRoundData()`](https://docs.chain.link/docs/price-feeds-api-reference/#getrounddata) functions.
poc:
[ChainlinkOracleManager.sol#L120](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/pricing/oracle/ChainlinkOracleManager.sol#L120)  

[ChainlinkFixedTimeOracleManager.sol#L81](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/pricing/oracle/ChainlinkFixedTimeOracleManager.sol#L81)  

[ChainlinkFixedTimeOracleManager.sol#L84](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/pricing/oracle/ChainlinkFixedTimeOracleManager.sol#L84)  

Go to <https://etherscan.io/address/0x5f4eC3Df9cbd43714FE2740f5E3616155c5b8419#code> and search for `latestAnswer()` or `getAnswer()`. You’ll find the deprecation notice.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the contract’s reliance on deprecated Chainlink pricing oracle functions, specifically `latestAnswer()` and `getAnswer()`. These functions were part of an older version of the Chainlink AggregatorV3Interface and have been superseded by `latestRoundData()` and `getRoundData()`, which provide a richer data structure including round ID, answer, startedAt, updatedAt, and answeredInRound. The root cause is that the developer imported and called the outdated functions without updating the interface to the current version, which means the contract is tied to an API that Chainlink may discontinue or modify the semantics of. When the contract invokes `latestAnswer()` or `getAnswer()` to fetch a price, it receives only a single value and loses the additional safety checks that the newer functions provide, such as verifying that the round is complete and that the data is recent. If Chainlink deprecates or removes these functions, or changes their return behavior, the contract could start receiving stale, zero, or otherwise incorrect price data. An attacker could exploit this by feeding manipulated data through the oracle (for example, by causing a round to be incomplete) and the contract would have no way to detect the anomaly, leading it to calculate trades, collateralizations, or liquidations based on wrong prices. The impact may manifest as users seeing unexpected zero balances, trades failing, or liquidations occurring at unfair prices, effectively causing financial loss for traders and the protocol. The issue appears whenever a price lookup is performed – typically during minting, redeeming, or liquidation flows – and it affects all participants who rely on the oracle for accurate pricing. It was discovered during a manual code audit that flagged the presence of the deprecated function calls. The problem can be subtle because the functions still compile and return values on many networks, so the contract appears to work in testing, but the hidden risk emerges when the upstream oracle provider disables the old endpoints. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to use `latestRoundData()` (or `getRoundData()` when a specific round is needed) and incorporate the full tuple validation, checking that the answer is non‑zero, the timestamp is recent, and the round is marked as answered. This aligns the contract with the current Chainlink best practices, restores proper accounting guarantees, and eliminates the risk of silent price feed failures. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of "use of outdated external dependencies" that can break business logic assumptions and lead to incorrect financial calculations.

title: `ConfigTimeLockController` will put `QuantConfig` in a stalemate
description:
The QuantConfig contract has these important setters, setProtocolAddress(), setProtocolUint256, setProtocolBoolean() and setProtocolRole(). This contract is subjected to a timelock before all such processes above are executed. But, the issue arises in the fact that in configTimeLockController, the state variable minimum delay can be set to an arbitrary value, up to type(uint256).max(cannot assume what value will be set) and could potentially render the QuantConfig contract unusable. All the previous values and addresses would not be able to be changed because of a very high delay being set:

[ConfigTimelockController.sol#L28](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/efe4a3c1af8d77c5dfb5ba110c3507e67a061bdd/quant-protocol/contracts/timelock/ConfigTimelockController.sol#L28)  

I discussed with one of the devs about the use of this specific mapping:

[QuantConfig.sol#L27](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/efe4a3c1af8d77c5dfb5ba110c3507e67a061bdd/quant-protocol/contracts/QuantConfig.sol#L27)  

After discussions with one of the devs(#0xca11.eth), it was understood that these values are for the rollaOrderFee which is a part of their limit order protocol contract(outside of the scope of the contest) but given the argument above, its configuration will be severely impacted (old percentage fees won’t be able to be changed). Rolla limit order protocol depends on this configuration setting within QuantConfig.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the interaction between the ConfigTimeLockController contract and the QuantConfig contract. ConfigTimeLockController stores a mutable variable called minimumDelay, which determines the waiting period that must elapse before any of QuantConfig’s privileged setter functions (such as setProtocolAddress, setProtocolUint256, setProtocolBoolean, and setProtocolRole) can be executed. Because the contract allows the minimumDelay to be set to any uint256 value, an administrator (or any entity with the appropriate role) can increase this delay to an extremely large number, potentially up to type(uint256).max. When such a high delay is applied, every future configuration change in QuantConfig becomes effectively unreachable – the required waiting time exceeds any practical horizon, creating a stalemate where the contract’s parameters cannot be updated. This situation is especially damaging for the Rolla limit‑order protocol, which relies on QuantConfig to store fee percentages and other critical parameters; after the delay is inflated, existing fee values (for example the rollaOrderFee) cannot be altered, breaking the protocol’s ability to adjust its economics or respond to market conditions. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit when reviewers examined the timelock’s delay‑setting logic and noted that there was no upper bound on the value that could be written. It can be hard to spot because the delay variable appears to be a normal configuration knob, and the contract does not emit any warning when an unreasonable value is set. Exploitation follows a simple flow: an attacker with setter privileges calls the function that updates minimumDelay, provides a massive value, and then any subsequent attempts by legitimate operators to call QuantConfig’s setters are forced to wait for the absurdly long delay, which in practice never expires. From a user’s perspective, the protocol may appear to function normally at first, but later any attempt to change fees or other settings results in no visible effect, leading to confusion and the perception that the contract is “stuck” or “unresponsive”. The impact is a loss of governance flexibility, potential business logic violations (fees cannot be updated to reflect market changes), and the risk that the protocol becomes unusable if essential parameters need adjustment. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce a maximum allowable delay, for example by defining a constant MAXIMUM_DELAY and adding a require statement that rejects any proposed minimumDelay greater than this cap. Alternatively, the timelock could be removed or its mutable delay field made immutable after deployment, thereby preventing the possibility of setting an unbounded delay. The recommended fix, applied by the Rolla project, was to introduce such a cap and eventually remove both the ConfigTimeLockController and QuantConfig contracts from the protocol, eliminating the attack surface entirely.

title: QTokens with the same symbol will lead to mistakes
description:
The [`README.md`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/efe4a3c1af8d77c5dfb5ba110c3507e67a061bdd/README.md?plain=1#L70) states:

Bob can then trade the QToken with Alice for a premium. The method for doing that is beyond the scope of the protocol but can be done via any smart contract trading platform e.g. 0x.

It is therefore important that tokens be easily identifiable so that trading on DEXes is not error-prone.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way QTokens generate their on‑chain symbol string. The contract builds the symbol by concatenating a fixed prefix, the underlying asset identifier, a formatted day, a month symbol, a two‑digit representation of the year (obtained by taking the modulo‑100 of the full year), the strike price and an option type marker. Because the year component is reduced to only the last two decimal digits, different options that expire in different calendar years can end up sharing the exact same symbol. For example, a token minted for 2023 and another minted for 2123 would both contain "23" in the year field and therefore be indistinguishable by their symbol. This lack of uniqueness violates the basic accounting assumption that a token’s symbol should uniquely identify its economic parameters. When users interact with decentralized exchanges or other trading platforms, they typically rely on the token symbol to select the correct asset. If two distinct QTokens carry identical symbols, a trader may unintentionally send or receive the wrong token, leading to misplaced premiums, failed settlements, or outright loss of value. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a trade appears to succeed but the received asset has an unexpected or zero balance, or the expected premium is missing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the protocol’s README and the token‑symbol construction function, where the documentation emphasized the need for easily identifiable tokens while the implementation deliberately truncated the year. The problem is subtle because the symbol still looks well‑formed and the truncation only manifests across year boundaries, a condition that may not be exercised in normal testing. The appropriate remediation is to include the full four‑digit year in the symbol (or otherwise guarantee global uniqueness) so that each QToken can be reliably differentiated on any marketplace. By ensuring that the symbol encodes all relevant temporal information, the protocol restores the invariant that a token’s identifier uniquely maps to its underlying option contract, eliminating the risk of accidental trades and protecting users from inadvertent fund loss.

title: `OperateProxy.callFunction
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OperateProxy contract's callFunction method, which forwards an arbitrary calldata to a user‑specified address using a low‑level call(). The function only checks that the target address is not the zero address; it does not verify that the target is a deployed contract. In Ethereum, a call to an address that has no contract code (i.e., an externally‑owned account or an address where a contract has self‑destructed) succeeds with the boolean success flag set to true and returns empty data. Consequently, any business logic that interprets a true return value as proof that the called function executed correctly can be deceived. For example, the controller may rely on OperateProxy to execute token.transferFrom() on an ERC‑20 token. If the supplied token address points to a non‑contract, the low‑level call will report success even though no transfer occurred, breaking the protocol’s accounting and potentially allowing an attacker to lock or steal funds. The root cause is the missing contract‑code validation before performing the external call. An attacker can exploit the bug by supplying a non‑contract address (an EOA or a destroyed contract) as the callee when the protocol expects a token transfer or any other state‑changing operation. The low‑level call will return true, the calling function will assume the operation succeeded, and the protocol will record a debit or a state transition that never actually moved assets. This can lead to funds disappearing from user balances, withdrawals appearing successful while no tokens are transferred, and overall accounting inconsistencies that may be leveraged for theft or denial‑of‑service attacks. The issue manifests whenever the Controller invokes its internal _call helper, which proxies calls through OperateProxy, and the supplied address is not a contract. Users of the Quant protocol, liquidity providers, and any party relying on the correctness of token transfers are affected. The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the OperateProxy implementation and noting the absence of an isContract guard, a pattern reminiscent of the qBridge exploit from January 2022. The problem is hard to notice because the low‑level call does not revert; the transaction is recorded as successful and emits a FunctionCallExecuted event, giving a false sense of correctness. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit contract‑code check (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s Address.isContract) before executing the call and to revert if the target is not a contract. This fix aligns the behavior with standard safe‑call utilities and prevents false‑positive success outcomes. In broader terms, the bug is an instance of an unchecked external call to an arbitrary address without contract verification, a class of vulnerabilities that can cause logical accounting errors and unintended fund loss. From a user’s perspective, a withdrawal may appear to have succeeded, the UI shows a completed status, yet the token balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, contradicting the expectation that a token transfer was performed.

title: Under certain conditions, direct theft of funds is possible during liquidation
description:
The absence of the notDuringAuction modifier in the AccountV1.deposit() function allows a scenario where a malicious actor can take advantage of the liquidation process. Specifically, a liquidator can bid for assets with a stale share amount that does not consider newly deposited collateral. This results in the liquidator acquiring additional assets for free.

Contrary to withdrawing assets, depositing new collateral into an Account during liquidation is possible because of a missing notDuringAuction modifier.
```solidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic race condition that allows a liquidator to acquire collateral without paying for it when a user deposits new assets while a liquidation auction is in progress. The root cause is the missing notDuringAuction guard on the deposit function, which permits deposits during an active auction. The auction logic calculates each asset's share based on a snapshot taken before the deposit; if the newly deposited asset has a share value of zero – for example because its USD value falls below the protocol‑defined minimum – the stored share remains zero even though the actual balance has increased. A malicious liquidator can monitor the deposit event, then submit a bid that references the stale share data, specifying an amount of the newly deposited asset that the auction believes is worth nothing. The bid price calculation therefore ignores the added collateral, and the liquidator receives the newly deposited tokens for free. This results in direct theft of funds: the account owner loses the deposited collateral, the liquidator gains assets without cost, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken. The issue manifests only while a liquidation auction is active and a deposit occurs; under normal operation the deposit function works as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the AccountV1.deposit function and the liquidation flow, noting that the notDuringAuction modifier was present on other state‑changing functions but omitted here. The bug is hard to notice because the deposit function appears harmless in isolation and typical unit tests do not simulate concurrent deposits and auctions. To remediate, the deposit function should be protected by the notDuringAuction modifier or the auction share calculation should be refreshed after any deposit, ensuring that new collateral cannot be exploited with stale share values. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or race‑condition bugs that enable economic theft by exploiting outdated pricing data during a time‑sensitive operation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after depositing collateral during a liquidation the balance may drop to zero or be lower than expected, and the user receives no compensation for the missing assets, contrary to the expectation that deposited funds remain safe until the auction concludes.

title: Zero account value renders liquidations impossible
description:
The liquidation process fails to handle edge cases where collateral values drop below a specified minimum (minUSDValue). This leads to a division by zero error during the assetShares calculation, rendering liquidations impossible and bad debt remaining unresolved.

When triggering a liquidation, the function computes the assetShares by calculating the relative value of each asset in relation to the totalValue of the Account.
```solidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error that occurs during the liquidation routine when the summed USD value of all collateral assets for an account becomes zero. The protocol enforces a per‑creditor minimum USD value (minUsdValue). In Registry.getValuesInUsd the function iterates over each asset and, if an asset’s computed USD value is below the minimum, it overwrites the value with zero. When every asset of an account falls below the threshold, the array passed to Liquidator._getAssetShares contains only zeros, so totalValue computed as the sum of assetValues is zero. The subsequent calculation of assetShares divides each assetValue by totalValue, causing a revert due to division by zero. Because the liquidation call reverts, the protocol cannot liquidate the under‑collateralised position, leaving the debt un‑resolved and effectively locking the borrower’s funds while the lender’s claim remains unpaid. The issue appears only in edge cases where collateral prices drop sharply or the minUsdValue parameter is set too high, which may not be covered by typical test suites, making it hard to notice. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation logic and the handling of low‑value assets. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with a revert, the expected liquidation event never occurs, and the borrower sees no reduction of debt while the lender sees no recovery of collateral. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑error vulnerabilities caused by insufficient validation of aggregate values. To remediate, the contract should either prevent totalValue from being zero before performing the division, for example by returning early with a safe fallback, or by adjusting the minUsdValue logic so that at least one asset retains a non‑zero value, and by adding explicit checks and tests for the zero‑total scenario.

title: UniswapV3AssetModule exposure can be manipulated by withdrawing zero amounts
description:
Exposure limits for Uniswap V3 positions can be bypassed. The exposure limits are a defense mechanism against price manipulation attacks and so bypassing them would allow an attacker to deposit large amounts of inflated assets to then steal other assets.

The AbstractDerivedAssetModule keeps track of the exposure of each asset.
```solidity
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniswapV3AssetModule, which is responsible for tracking the exposure of each creditor to individual Uniswap V3 positions. The module stores a mapping from an asset identifier to the amount of liquidity that backs the position (assetToLiquidity) and a separate struct that records the last known exposure in token units and USD value. Exposure limits are enforced by checking these records before allowing new deposits, with the intention of preventing a creditor from accumulating a position large enough to manipulate market prices. The flaw occurs when a creditor invokes the withdrawal functions (processDirectWithdrawal or processIndirectWithdrawal) with an amount of zero. The withdrawal logic unconditionally deletes the entry in assetToLiquidity for the supplied assetId before any exposure values are examined, and then conditionally repeats the deletion only if the recorded exposure has dropped to zero. Because a zero‑amount withdrawal does not modify the exposure fields, the condition is never true, yet the initial unconditional delete has already removed the liquidity record. Consequently, the off‑chain valuation routine that reads assetToLiquidity sees a zero liquidity value and assumes the creditor no longer holds any exposure to that asset. The exposure limits therefore treat the creditor as if they were unexposed, allowing them to deposit arbitrarily large amounts of the same asset in subsequent transactions. An attacker can repeatedly call zero‑amount withdrawals to clear the internal liquidity mapping without actually withdrawing any tokens, effectively bypassing the protective exposure checks. The impact is that the attacker can inflate their position, manipulate the price of the underlying pool, and potentially extract value from other participants or the protocol. This issue manifests whenever the withdrawal functions are called with a zero amount, which is a valid input according to the public interface. All creditors are affected because the bug resides in the shared module, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about exposure continuity are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the asset module’s state‑management code, where the unconditional delete statement stood out as inconsistent with the conditional check that follows. The bug is subtle because a zero‑amount withdrawal does not produce any on‑chain token transfer, making it appear harmless, and the mapping deletion does not emit an event, so observers may not notice the state change. To remediate the issue, the module should only delete the assetToLiquidity entry after confirming that the creditor’s exposure has truly reached zero, and it should reject zero‑amount withdrawals or treat them as no‑ops that leave the liquidity mapping untouched. In broader terms, this is a state‑inconsistency bug where the bookkeeping of asset exposure can be desynchronized from the actual holdings, allowing a breach of the intended accounting invariants and leading to potential fund loss or market manipulation.

title: Calling batchProcessDeposit() before batchProcessWithdrawal() allows bypassing exposure limits
description:
Exposure limits for Uniswap V3 positions can be bypassed. The exposure limits are a defense mechanism against price manipulation attacks and so bypassing them would allow an attacker to deposit large amounts of inflated assets to then steal other assets. When a user deposits assets through UniswapV3AssetModule.processDirectDeposit(), it first makes a call to UniswapV3AssetModule._addAsset()
```solidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the way exposure limits are enforced for Uniswap V3 positions when a creditor is switched. The contract stores the liquidity of each position in a mapping called assetToLiquidity. When a direct withdrawal is processed, the entry for the withdrawn asset is deleted, which forces later value queries to read the current on‑chain liquidity instead of the previously recorded amount. In the account opening and flash‑action flows the code calls batchProcessDeposit for the new creditor, then batchProcessWithdrawal for the old creditor, and finally batchProcessDeposit again for the new creditor. Because the withdrawal is executed after the first deposit, the stored liquidity entry is removed before the second deposit is evaluated. An attacker can therefore deposit a small position that passes the exposure check, switch the creditor, add a large amount of liquidity, and the system will calculate the account value using the new, inflated liquidity while the exposure control still believes the old, low‑risk amount. This bypasses the risk‑control mechanism that is intended to prevent price‑manipulation attacks and limits on how much exposure a creditor may hold. From a user’s point of view the account appears to have a modest risk profile after the first deposit, but after the creditor switch the reported value jumps and the protocol allows far larger positions than intended, effectively letting the attacker take on excessive risk and potentially steal assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Arcadia V2 codebase (Renascence audit) by tracing the sequence of calls in AccountV1.openMarginAccount and AccountV1.flashActionByCreditor. It is subtle because the same batchProcessDeposit function is invoked twice and the deletion of the mapping entry is not obvious, making the exposure check appear to work correctly on the surface. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent accounting errors where mutable on‑chain state is used for risk calculations after a prior state‑clearing operation. To remediate, the withdrawal should be performed before any new deposit when switching creditors, or the exposure calculation should be based on the stored liquidity that is not cleared until after the new deposit is validated. Alternatively, the contract could avoid deleting the mapping entry until the new creditor’s exposure has been fully assessed, ensuring that the risk limits cannot be circumvented.

title: UniswapV3AssetModule calculates underlying asset amounts irrespective of amount parameter
description:
Exposure of creditors in UniswapV3AssetModule can be manipulated to the upside. This results in a DoS attack where further deposits are blocked by maxing out the exposure of a Creditor.

The UniswapV3AssetModule._getUnderlyingAssetsAmounts() function calculates the amounts of underlying tokens for a Uniswap V3 position.
```solidity
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniswapV3AssetModule function that determines how many underlying tokens correspond to a given Uniswap V3 position. The routine receives an explicit amount parameter that is supposed to represent the portion of the position a creditor wishes to expose. However, the implementation ignores this amount and always computes the full token amounts based on the total liquidity of the position. Consequently, a creditor can request a zero or very small amount and the contract will still treat the exposure as if the entire position were being used. This mis‑calculation inflates the perceived exposure of the creditor, allowing the exposure limit of the protocol to be reached artificially. When the limit is reached, the protocol rejects any further deposits for that creditor, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for other users who might want to add liquidity. The issue manifests whenever the internal helper _getUnderlyingAssetsAmounts is invoked, which happens during deposit, withdrawal, and risk‑assessment flows. Any participant that can trigger this helper – typically a creditor interacting with the module – can exploit the flaw by supplying a manipulated amount value, causing the system to record an exaggerated exposure. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are that deposits suddenly fail, balances appear unchanged or zero, and the UI may report that the maximum exposure has been reached even though the user has not supplied that much capital. The bug is subtle because the function still returns a correctly sized array, and the downstream logic assumes the returned amounts are proportional to the supplied amount, so the discrepancy is not obvious without inspecting the arithmetic. The root cause is the absence of a scaling factor that ties the underlying token amounts to the requested amount, i.e., the amount argument is never used in the calculation. To remediate the issue the function should multiply the derived token quantities by the ratio of the requested amount to the total position liquidity, or otherwise enforce that a zero amount yields zero underlying amounts. By aligning the calculation with the amount parameter, the protocol’s exposure accounting will reflect the true risk, preventing artificial maxing of exposure and restoring normal deposit functionality.

title: Contract lacks graceful retirement feature
description:
Commonly in lending platforms, when a certain token or lending pool has been deemed to be too risky or have been hacked, it is retired. This means that all deposits and borrows from the pool are stopped, however the pool is still kept in the system for users to withdraw and repay their loans. This is a common feature in lending platforms and is a good way to deleverage the system from risky assets while preventing users from being locked out of their funds. This has happened multiple times in Aave, with some other examples below:
GHST borrowing disabled on polygon
agEUR borrowing disabled on polygon
UST disabled on Venus protocol on BSC
SXP disabled on Venus protocol on BSC
TRXOld disabled on Venus protocol on BSC
The main idea being that protocols often delist tokens, and they do that by disabling deposits and borrows, but still allowing users to withdraw and repay their loans. The issue is that this functionality does not exist in this protocol. In the current protocol, each operation of borrow, deposit, repay and withdraw are controlled by the variables repayPaused, withdrawPaused, borrowPaused, depositPaused. These are defined and controlled in the LendingPoolGuardian.sol contract. However, there is an auto-unlock feature which can trigger after a cooldown period.
```solidity
function unpause() external override afterCoolDownOf(30 days) {
    emit PauseFlagsUpdated(
        repayPaused = false,
        withdrawPaused = false,
        borrowPaused = false,
        depositPaused = false,
        liquidationPaused = false
    );
}
```
Thus while the protocol can pause a pool to only allow withdrawals and repays they can only do so for a period of 30 days. After that, the pool is automatically unpaused and users can deposit and borrow from the pool again. The only other way to suspend deposits is by manipulating the lock variable in the Tranche contracts. However, that will also prevent withdrawals. So there is no way for the protocol to selectively disable only deposits and borrows for a pool for a long period of time. This issue can be ignored if it is a design decision by the team, however, it is being flagged here since it is a common feature in other lending protocols.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the inability of the lending protocol to keep a pool in a withdraw‑and‑repay‑only state for an extended period. In many lending platforms a token that becomes risky or is compromised is “retired”: deposits and new borrows are permanently disabled while existing users are still allowed to withdraw their collateral and repay outstanding loans. In the examined contract the pause mechanism is implemented with four boolean flags (repayPaused, withdrawPaused, borrowPaused, depositPaused) that can be toggled by the LendingPoolGuardian. However, the contract also contains an automatic unpause function that can be called after a fixed cooldown of thirty days, which resets all flags to false and re‑enables deposits and borrowing. Because of this design, the protocol can only temporarily suspend deposits and borrows; after the cooldown the pool automatically becomes fully active again. There is no separate “retire” flag that can permanently disable only deposits and borrows while still permitting withdrawals and repayments. The root cause is the coupling of the pause logic with a time‑based auto‑unpause and the absence of a dedicated retirement state. An attacker or a malicious governance action could exploit this by forcing the pool to remain open for borrowing after a token has been identified as unsafe, potentially exposing users to further loss, or by relying on the automatic re‑enablement to re‑introduce risky assets without proper risk assessment. The impact is that users who have deposited or borrowed a now‑risky asset may be unable to safely exit the position, leading to possible fund loss, liquidation cascades, or loss of confidence in the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the protocol attempts to retire a pool – i.e., after a security incident, a token delisting, or a risk assessment that warrants disabling new activity.
