All depositors, borrowers, and the protocol itself are affected because the safety guarantees that rely on a controlled retirement are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s functionality with industry‑standard retirement mechanisms used by platforms such as Aave and Venus. It can be hard to notice because the pause flags appear to work correctly for the first thirty days, and the automatic unpause is hidden behind a time‑based modifier, so reviewers may assume the pool remains in a safe state indefinitely. To remediate, the contract should introduce a dedicated retirement flag in the pool guardian that disables only deposits and borrows and cannot be cleared automatically after a cooldown; the flag should require an explicit governance action to re‑enable the functions, thereby allowing the protocol to keep a pool in a withdraw‑only mode for as long as needed. This change aligns the contract with the common class of “graceful retirement” bugs where a system lacks a persistent safe‑mode for decommissioning risky assets, violating the expected business logic that users can always retrieve their funds and repay loans when a pool is retired.

title: Tranche share ratios can be manipulated by donating via liquidations
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑ratio manipulation flaw that allows an attacker to increase the reported total assets of a tranche vault without minting any additional share tokens, thereby distorting the conversion rate between deposited tokens and issued shares. The root cause lies in the way the contract tracks assets: instead of deriving the total asset amount from the ERC20 balance, it stores the value in a mutable variable that can be increased by the liquidation mechanism. When a liquidation occurs, any surplus tokens are credited to the owner of the liquidated account via the realisedLiquidityOf mapping. Because the tranche can become the owner of such an account through a simple transfer, the surplus is added directly to the tranche’s asset accounting while the totalShares counter remains unchanged. An attacker can exploit this by first depositing a minimal amount (for example one wei) to obtain a single share, then creating a near‑liquidatable borrowing account, transferring ownership of that account to the tranche, and finally triggering liquidation. The surplus – often on the order of 1e18 tokens – is then recorded as additional assets, so the tranche’s totalAssets become the original deposit plus the surplus while totalShares stay at one wei. When a legitimate user later deposits tokens, the vault’s share‑calculation formula (deposit amount divided by totalAssets) yields a dramatically lower share amount due to the inflated asset denominator, causing the user to receive far fewer shares than expected, effectively losing part of the deposited value. This effect is most pronounced when the tranche starts with a very low share supply, but it can also be pre‑seeded by predicting future tranche addresses and funding them with surplus before they are deployed, ensuring the manipulation is baked in from the outset. The impact is that honest depositors may see their balances remain unchanged or receive an unexpectedly small number of share tokens, leading to funds that appear to disappear and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Arcadia protocol when the auditor examined the solmate ERC4626 implementation and noticed that the liquidation code could credit tokens to any account owner, including a tranche, without adjusting share counts. The flaw is subtle because the totalAssets variable is updated internally and does not reflect the external token balance, making the manipulation hard to detect through simple balance checks. To remediate the problem, the protocol should ensure that the share supply is never zero by minting a large number of “ghost” shares to a neutral address or by burning an initial batch of shares, as done in OpenZeppelin’s latest ERC4626 implementation and Yieldbox. Alternatively, the liquidation routine could be changed to pay surplus directly to the original account owner rather than storing it in realisedLiquidityOf, or the contract could forbid tranches from becoming owners of liquidatable accounts. These measures restore the invariant that totalAssets and totalShares grow together, preventing the rounding‑error exploitation and preserving the expected deposit‑to‑share conversion for users.

title: Liquidators can earn extra yield by flash depositing into tranches
description: The liquidationPenalty part of the liquidation incentives is dealt out to the tranches as extra yield according to their weights via the _syncLiquidationFeeToLiquidityProviders function. This increases the amount corresponding to each tranch share. The issue is that liquidators can snipe this extra yield at no extra cost via flash deposits. During liquidations, only the juinor-most tranche is locked, while other tranches are open and can be deposited into. The liquidationPenalty is given at an instant of time, thus users can theoretically deposit a very large amount to these tranche pools, collect the yield, and then withdraw it all out and pay off the flash loan. However, the liquidators themselves can do this at no cost. So when a liquidator sees a profitable liquidation position, they can flash deposit into the tranches in the very same transaction, carry out the liquidation, and collect the termination fee, a large part of the liquidation penalty, and any discounts on the collateral price. This is a very profitable attack, and can be carried out by any liquidator. This affects all the unlocked tranches, i.e. all except the junior-most tranche. This attack requires no frontrunning, so can be executed on all chains, irrespective of the visibility of transactions. Yield from liquidations can be denied to liquidity providers at no extra cost for the attacker.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic exploit that allows a liquidator to capture the liquidation penalty that is distributed as extra yield to tranche holders without any cost to the liquidator. The root cause lies in the way the protocol’s _syncLiquidationFeeToLiquidityProviders function immediately credits each unlocked tranche with additional share value proportional to its weight when a liquidation occurs. Because the junior‑most tranche is locked during liquidation while all other tranches remain open, the contract does not prevent deposits or withdrawals to those open tranches within the same transaction or block. A liquidator can therefore initiate a flash loan, deposit a large amount into any unlocked tranche, trigger the liquidation, receive the newly minted yield that represents the liquidation penalty, and then withdraw the same amount to repay the flash loan, all atomically. This sequence can be performed without any frontrunning and on any chain, meaning the attack is universally applicable. The impact is that liquidity providers of the unlocked tranches receive less yield than expected; the extra yield that should have been shared among them is siphoned by the attacker, effectively reducing their returns and violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that liquidation penalties are distributed fairly. The issue manifests when a liquidation is processed, the junior tranche is locked, and other tranches are still open for interaction. From a user’s perspective, a liquidity provider may notice that after a liquidation their tranche balance does not increase as anticipated, or that overall yield appears lower than before, while a liquidator observes an unexpected profit. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation incentive logic and identified that the sync function updates tranche share values instantly without any re‑entrancy or timing guard. The problem is subtle because the extra yield looks like a normal distribution and there is no explicit error or revert, making it hard to detect without detailed analysis of the state changes. To remediate the issue, the protocol should forbid deposits and withdrawals to a tranche in the same transaction or block, or otherwise delay the crediting of liquidation penalties until after a safe period, ensuring that the extra yield cannot be captured by a flash‑deposit attack.

title: Pending interests not processed when updating treasury weight
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the treasury weight update function, which changes the interest weight assigned to the protocol treasury but does not trigger the interest‑processing routine that should be executed before the change takes effect. The function setTreasuryWeights modifies the global totalInterestWeight by subtracting the old treasury weight and adding the new one, yet it lacks the processInterests modifier that forces pending interest calculations to be settled first. Because pending interests are left unprocessed, the next call to processInterests applies the new weight retroactively from the previous interest calculation point instead of from the exact moment the weight was altered. This timing mismatch can cause interest to be allocated incorrectly: some accrued interest may be attributed to the wrong weight, leading to under‑payment or over‑payment of treasury rewards. The issue manifests when the contract owner updates treasury weights without first processing pending interests, a scenario that can easily be missed during routine operation because the protocol continues to accrue interest and appears functional, while the internal accounting diverges from the intended distribution model. The impact is primarily on the protocol’s accounting integrity and on any participants who rely on accurate interest payouts, such as token holders or liquidity providers; they may receive less (or more) than expected, and the treasury’s balance may drift from its intended target. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined state‑changing functions and identified the missing modifier. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy only becomes apparent when comparing expected versus actual interest allocations after a weight change, which may require detailed ledger analysis. To remediate the issue, the setTreasuryWeights function should be protected with the processInterests modifier or explicitly invoke the interest‑processing routine before adjusting the weight, ensuring that all pending interest is settled under the old weight and that subsequent calculations use the new weight from a clean state. This correction restores the invariant that interest distribution follows the most recent weight configuration and prevents accounting drift that could otherwise erode trust in the protocol’s financial logic.

title: Supporting fee-on-transfer tokens can lead to bad debt
description:
The protocol claims it can support fee-on-transfer (FOT) tokens if necessary. According to the pre-audit questionlist:
- If enabled, the collateral and liquidation factors
- (haircut on the value) will be adjusted to accommodate for the value loss due to fee
The issue is that changing the liquidation and collateral factors will not be enough to resolve the issue. This can be explained by a simple example.
Say Token A is a FOT token, with a 1% fee.
1. Alice deposits 100,000 tokens of token A.
2. Contract receives 99,000 tokens, but credits Alice's account with the full 100,000 tokens
3. Alice now withdraws 99,000 tokens
4. Alice receives 89,100 tokens after fees. Contract has 0 tokens, since it paid out all its holdings, but contract still thinks that it holds (100,000 - 99,000)=1,000 tokens.
5. Alice can now take out a loan against those 1,000 tokens which the contract thinks it holds. This is entirely bad debt.
With deposits and successive withdrawals, FOT tokens can be used to create bad debt positions at very minimal costs. Since this directly affects the health of the system, this is a problem.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatch when the protocol accepts fee‑on‑transfer (FOT) tokens. The contract records the amount that the user intended to deposit, but it does not verify how many tokens actually arrived after the transfer fee is deducted. Consequently the internal balance for the user is inflated. When the user later withdraws, the contract sends out the tokens it actually holds, which are fewer than the recorded balance, and the internal accounting is not updated to reflect the loss. The leftover “phantom” balance can then be used as collateral for new loans, allowing the borrower to obtain credit against tokens that no longer exist in the contract. This creates bad‑debt positions with little or no cost to the attacker. The problem appears whenever the protocol is configured to support FOT tokens and relies on pre‑transfer accounting instead of post‑transfer balance checks. It affects any user who deposits a fee‑on‑transfer token, the lending pool that assumes the collateral is present, and ultimately the whole protocol’s solvency. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that simulated a 1 % fee token: a deposit of 100 000 tokens was credited in full, a withdrawal of 99 000 tokens left the contract empty, yet the system still believed the user owned 1 000 tokens, which could be borrowed against. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external view shows the correct token balance (zero) while the internal ledger still reports a positive amount, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol must adopt post‑transfer accounting – i.e., read the actual token balance after each transfer and adjust the internal ledger accordingly – or simply refuse to accept fee‑on‑transfer tokens. Properly accounting for transfer fees eliminates the phantom collateral and prevents the creation of under‑collateralized loans.

title: ETH withdrawn is sent to msg.sender instead of the to address
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An ETH withdrawal function in the AccountSpot contract sends the withdrawn ether to msg.sender instead of the address supplied in the to parameter. The function iterates over a list of assets and, when the asset address is zero (indicating native ETH), it executes payable(msg.sender).call{value: amount}(''). The NatSpec comment and the function signature both state that the to address is the recipient, so callers naturally provide a destination address different from their own. Because the implementation ignores to and always uses msg.sender, the contract violates its own specification. This mismatch can be exploited by any caller who passes a to address that they do not control; the contract will transfer the ether to the caller instead, effectively allowing the caller to divert funds that were intended for another party. The bug manifests whenever a non‑zero ETH amount is withdrawn, i.e., when assetAddresses[i] == address(0) and assetAmounts[i] > 0. Users see a successful transaction but the intended recipient receives no funds, while the caller’s wallet is credited. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the NatSpec documentation with the actual transfer logic. It is easy to miss because the surrounding code correctly handles ERC‑20 and ERC‑721 assets, and the transfer line uses a common pattern (payable(...).call) that looks correct in isolation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect recipient address handling or misdirected fund transfer bugs, where the contract uses the wrong variable to determine the destination of a value transfer. To remediate, the transfer should use payable(to) instead of payable(msg.sender), or the function should explicitly require that to == msg.sender if the design intends to restrict withdrawals to the caller. Correcting the recipient logic restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents accidental or malicious loss of ether.

title: First Tranche depositor can withdraw all the previously earned interest
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw that allows the very first participant who holds 100 % of a tranche’s shares to withdraw not only their original principal but also any interest that has already been accrued for that tranche. The root cause lies in the way the _syncInterestsToLiquidityProviders function adds the incoming interest amount to the tranche’s totalAssets before the share‑to‑asset conversion is performed. Because the first depositor owns all of the tranche shares, the previewRedeemAndSync calculation treats the entire totalAssets value – which now includes the newly synced interest – as redeemable against those shares. When the depositor calls redeem, the contract burns their shares and transfers the full assets amount, effectively extracting the interest that should belong to the protocol or future investors. This can be exploited simply by being the initial liquidity provider, waiting for the first interest sync event, and then calling redeem; no special permissions or external calls are required. The impact is a loss of accrued interest revenue for the protocol, a reduction of the treasury balance, and a breach of the intended risk‑return profile for later participants. The condition for exploitation is that a single address controls the entire share supply of a tranche at the moment interest is synchronized, which is typical for the first deposit. All users of the tranche, the protocol’s treasury, and any subsequent investors are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that interest accrues to the pool and is shared proportionally – are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the interest‑sync and redemption flow, where the auditor noticed that the totalAssets value used for redemption already contained the freshly synced interest, yet no mechanism prevented a full‑share holder from claiming it. The bug is subtle because the code appears to correctly allocate interest to each tranche, but it fails to separate protocol‑owned interest from user‑owned share value, making the problem easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should either exclude newly synced interest from the redeemable amount for the tranche that generated it, allocate interest to a distinct pool that is not claimable via share burning, or enforce that a holder cannot redeem more than their principal contribution. In essence, the fix requires a proper accounting separation between principal, user‑share value, and protocol‑owned interest to prevent a single holder from draining all accrued earnings.

title: Borrower pays interest on their debt while liquidation is running
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of continued interest accrual on a borrower’s debt while a liquidation auction is active. When a liquidation is started, the contract mints additional debt to cover initiation and termination rewards as well as a liquidation penalty, but it does not suspend the interest‑processing modifier that runs on most state‑changing functions. As a result, the _syncInterests call inside the processInterests modifier keeps updating the borrower’s accrued interest even though the position is already being liquidated. This happens because the startLiquidation function is guarded only by whenLiquidationNotPaused and processInterests, and there is no separate flag that disables interest calculation for the duration of the auction. An attacker or any user can trigger liquidation on a vulnerable account; once the auction begins, the borrower’s debt balance continues to grow at the normal interest rate for up to the maximum auction length of four hours. The extra interest is added on top of the already‑minted liquidation incentives, inflating the total debt and reducing the amount of collateral that can be recovered. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a higher debt figure after liquidation, a smaller net payout of collateral, and an unexpected interest charge that was not disclosed in the protocol’s documentation. Borrowers expect that, as in other systems such as MakerDAO, interest stops the moment liquidation starts, but the reality is that interest keeps accruing, violating the accounting assumption that a liquidated position is a closed financial state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the interaction between the startLiquidation function and the processInterests modifier was examined. It can be hard to notice because interest accrual is a background operation that does not emit explicit events, and the UI typically shows only the auction status and collateral transfer, not the incremental interest. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency bugs where a financial invariant is broken during a critical operation. To remediate, the protocol should pause or skip interest synchronization while a liquidation auction is in progress, for example by adding a liquidation‑in‑progress flag checked by the processInterests modifier or by removing the modifier from liquidation‑related functions. This would align the behavior with expected business logic, prevent borrowers from paying unnecessary interest, and preserve the integrity of the liquidation accounting model.

title: If address is a smart contract that can't handle ERC721 tokens they will be stuck after a whitelisted mint
description:
The mintPublic method has a check that allows only EOAs to call it
```solidity
if (tx.origin != msg.sender) revert ContractsNotAllowed();
```
but it is missing in the whitelisted mint methods (mintArcanaList, mintAspirantList, mintAllianceList). This means that if the address that is whitelisted is a contract and it calls those functions but it can't handle ERC721 tokens correctly, they will be stuck. This problem is usually handled by using _safeMint instead of _mint but all mint functionality in ArcanaPrime uses _mint.
This can result in a user losing his newly minted tokens forever, which is a potential values loss. It requires the user to be using a smart contract that does not handle ERC721 properly, so it is Medium severity.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from three whitelisted mint functions that use the low‑level ERC721 _mint operation instead of the safety‑checked _safeMint. In the public mint function the contract deliberately blocks calls from other contracts by comparing tx.origin with msg.sender, but this protection is absent in the whitelist mint paths (mintArcanaList, mintAspirantList, mintAllianceList). As a result, a whitelisted address that is itself a smart contract can invoke these functions. If that contract does not implement the ERC721Receiver interface (onERC721Received) the ERC721 token is transferred to an address that cannot acknowledge receipt. Because _mint does not perform the receiver check, the transaction succeeds and the token appears to be minted, yet the receiving contract is unable to invoke any ERC721 transfer functions. From the user’s perspective the newly minted NFT may show up in a wallet explorer but any attempt to transfer, sell or otherwise move it will fail, often with a generic “transfer to non‑ERC721Receiver implementer” error or simply no visible balance change. The impact is a loss of access to the minted asset – the token is effectively locked forever unless the contract is upgraded or a rescue mechanism is added. This scenario occurs only when a contract, rather than an externally owned account, is whitelisted and calls one of the three mint functions, and the contract lacks proper ERC721 handling logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the access control logic of the public mint with the whitelist mint implementations and noted the missing safe‑mint call. It can be hard to notice because the mint transaction does not revert and the token appears to be created, so developers may assume normal operation until a transfer attempt fails. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe token minting or transfer patterns where the receiver contract is not validated, leading to token lock‑up. The recommended remediation is to replace the internal _mint calls with _safeMint in all whitelist mint functions, optionally re‑introducing the tx.origin check, and to protect the new code with a nonReentrant modifier to mitigate the reentrancy risk introduced by the safe‑mint callback.

title: Starknet tokens deposited with use_withdraw_auto can never be withdrawn
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain bridge logic error that makes tokens deposited with the use_withdraw_auto flag permanently non‑withdrawable. When a user deposits assets on Starknet, the deposit function still accepts a request header that contains the auto‑withdraw flag. On the Ethereum side, the withdrawTokens function reads the first uint256 of the serialized request as a header and calls Protocol.canUseWithdrawAuto. Because the flag is set, the function executes revert NotSupportedYetError(). The comment in the code indicates that automatic withdrawal was disabled after a previous audit, but the disabling was only applied to the L1 withdrawal path; the L2 deposit interface was never updated. Consequently, any request that includes the flag passes the deposit stage, appears successful on Starknet, but later fails on L1 with a revert, leaving the user's NFT or native token locked on Starknet with no mechanism to unlock or retrieve it. The impact is that users lose access to their assets; from a UI perspective the deposited token disappears from the L1 balance while the L2 side still holds the locked NFT, leading to a mismatch where the user expects a refund or withdrawal but receives nothing. The bug occurs whenever use_withdraw_auto is set to true, either intentionally or by mistake, and it is hard to notice because the deposit transaction does not emit an error and the failure only manifests during the withdrawal attempt. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case constructing a request with the auto‑withdraw flag and observing the expected revert. This class of bug can be described as inconsistent feature flag handling across a bridge, where a disabled feature is still accepted on one side, resulting in an unrecoverable locked state. The recommended remediation is to reject deposits that contain the auto‑withdraw flag, either by reverting the deposit transaction or by removing the flag from the user interface, thereby ensuring that only supported withdrawal paths are used.

title: Tokens irrecoverable by owner on L1 if not an `ERC721` receiver
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the bridge's withdrawTokens function uses IERC721.safeTransferFrom to move tokens from the escrow to the caller's L1 address. safeTransferFrom requires the recipient to implement the ERC721TokenReceiver interface; if the recipient is a contract that does not implement this interface, the call reverts and the token remains locked in the escrow. This situation can be triggered whenever a user configures their L1 withdrawal address to be a smart contract that is not ERC721‑compatible and then attempts to withdraw an ERC721 token that was previously bridged from L2. The root cause is the assumption that all possible recipients are ERC721‑receivers and the lack of a fallback path such as using transferFrom or a custom handling for non‑receiver contracts. An attacker does not need to be involved; the issue is self‑inflicted by the user’s choice of address, but it effectively makes the token unrecoverable because the transaction reverts and the escrow mapping is not cleared. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction fails, no tokens appear in their wallet, and the bridge UI may show the request as pending or completed while the balance on L1 stays at zero. The impact is loss of access to the bridged asset, potential financial loss, and erosion of trust in the bridge protocol. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the token‑withdrawal path and noticed the use of safeTransferFrom without checking whether the destination contract implements the required interface. It can be hard to notice because typical test suites use externally owned accounts as recipients, which always succeed, masking the failure mode for contract recipients. The issue belongs to the class of “receiver‑interface enforcement” bugs where safe token transfer functions revert when the recipient does not conform to the expected callback interface, leading to permanent asset lock. The recommended remediation is to replace the safeTransferFrom call with a non‑safe transfer such as IERC721.transferFrom, or to add logic that detects non‑receiver contracts and either uses a different transfer method or requires the recipient to implement ERC721TokenReceiver before allowing the withdrawal.

title: There is No `msg.value` check in `depositTokens`, causing potential token stuck
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a cross‑chain bridge function thataccepts ether (msg.value) without any validation of the amount supplied. The depositTokens routine forwards the caller‑provided ether to the Starknet messaging contract, assuming that the value covers the L2 transaction fee. Because the code does not enforce a minimum fee, does not calculate the exact fee required, and does not refund any surplus, a user can submit a transaction with an arbitrarily low amount (as little as one wei) or with an excessive amount. When the fee is too low, the L2 message may be recorded on L1 but the sequencer on Starknet will reject or delay processing, causing the deposited NFT to remain locked on the bridge for an extended period (potentially up to five days until a cancellation window opens). When the fee is higher than necessary, the extra ether stays in the bridge contract with no mechanism to return it, resulting in a direct loss of funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Forge test that called depositTokens with a value of one wei; the transaction succeeded, emitted the expected LogMessageToL2 event, yet the fee field in the event showed the insufficient amount. The problem is subtle because the call does not revert and the event suggests success, so users may not notice that their cross‑chain transfer will never complete. The root cause is the absence of any fee‑estimation logic or validation check on msg.value, which violates the business assumption that the bridge will always forward enough ether to cover L2 execution costs. From a user’s perspective the bridge appears to accept the deposit, but the NFT never arrives on L2 and the user’s balance on the source chain shows the token as still owned, while the ether sent is either insufficient for processing or permanently retained. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked payable parameters leading to under‑payment or over‑payment bugs. To remediate, the contract should query the current L2 fee schedule, enforce a minimum fee (e.g., the documented 20 000 wei plus any dynamic component), reject transactions that do not meet this threshold, and optionally return any excess ether to the sender. Implementing a public fee‑estimation function would also allow users to calculate the correct amount before calling depositTokens, restoring confidence that their assets will be transferred and that they will not lose ether unnecessarily.

title: Potential Blockage of User Withdrawals When Bridge is Disabled in `withdrawTokens`
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style restriction that blocks user withdrawals when the bridge contract is in a disabled state. The root cause is an unconditional check of the global _enabled flag at the beginning of the withdrawTokens function, which reverts with BridgeNotEnabledError if the flag is false. Because the same flag is used to gate deposit‑related operations, the contract unintentionally applies the disabled condition to withdrawals as well. An attacker or even a legitimate administrator can trigger the condition by disabling the bridge for maintenance, upgrades, or any other reason, after which any user who attempts to call withdrawTokens will receive a revert, see no token transfer, and observe that their on‑chain balance remains unchanged. From the user’s perspective the UI may display an error message, the transaction fails, and the expected refund or token transfer never arrives, leading to confusion and frustration. The impact is that users’ assets become effectively locked on the contract for the duration of the disabled state, undermining trust in the bridge and exposing the protocol to operational risk if the disabled period is prolonged. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined state‑gate checks across the contract’s public functions. It can be hard to notice because the same enabled flag is a reasonable safeguard for deposit flows, and developers may assume that withdrawals are inherently safe when the bridge is paused. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of over‑restrictive access‑control checks that cause denial‑of‑service for legitimate users. The correct mitigation is to decouple the enabled check from withdrawal logic, allowing withdrawals to proceed regardless of the bridge’s enabled state, or to introduce a separate flag that only governs deposit‑related actions. This adjustment restores the expected behavior where users can always reclaim their tokens, even when the bridge is temporarily disabled for non‑withdrawal operations.

title: Starknet bridge contract does not check if the collection supports IERC721Metadata interface, so the ones that do not implement it will not be able to bridge NFTs
bug_full: The Starknet NFT bridge contract assumes that every ERC‑721 collection implements the optional IERC721Metadata interface and calls the metadata functions name(), symbol(), and tokenURI() directly without first verifying support via ERC165. Because the metadata extension is optional under the ERC‑721 standard, a collection that complies with ERC‑721 but does not provide these functions will cause the external calls to revert, and the whole bridging transaction fails. This missing interface check is a classic unchecked‑optional‑interface bug that breaks the bridge’s business logic that any ERC‑721 token should be transferable across chains. The vulnerability is triggered when a user attempts to bridge an NFT from Starknet to Ethereum using the erc721_metadata function; the contract creates an IERC721Dispatcher instance and immediately invokes name() and symbol() on the target collection. If the collection lacks the IERC721Metadata implementation, the call throws, the transaction reverts, and the NFT never leaves the source chain. From the user’s perspective the bridge transaction appears to fail with a generic revert error, the UI may show “bridge failed” or “no response”, and the expected outcome – the NFT appearing on Ethereum – does not happen, leaving the user confused and potentially thinking their funds are lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Starknet bridge code with the Ethereum bridge, which correctly checks ERC165 support before calling metadata functions. The bug is hard to notice because most popular NFT contracts implement the metadata interface, so the bridge works for the majority of cases; only less common or deliberately minimal ERC‑721 contracts exhibit the failure. The impact is limited to collections that omit metadata, but it effectively denies service for those assets and can be abused to create a denial‑of‑service condition for any collection that does not implement the optional interface. To remediate, the bridge should perform an ERC165 interface‑support query for IERC721Metadata before invoking any metadata functions, and handle the case where the interface is absent by either returning empty strings or skipping metadata retrieval, thereby preserving the core bridging functionality. This aligns with the ERC‑721 specification that treats metadata as optional and restores the protocol’s guarantee that any compliant ERC‑721 token can be bridged regardless of optional extensions.

title: Reentrancy attack to make an NFT unbridgeable
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the NFT bridge’s escrow withdrawal routine that allows a malicious contract to corrupt the escrow bookkeeping and render an NFT permanently unbridgeable. The root cause is that the _withdrawFromEscrow function calls safeTransferFrom to move the token from the bridge to the recipient before it clears the _escrow mapping. safeTransferFrom triggers the recipient’s onERC721Received callback, giving the malicious contract control to call depositTokens while the original withdrawal is still in progress. During this re‑entered call the contract re‑escrows the same token under its own address, and when the original withdrawal finally resumes it overwrites the escrow entry with address(0). As a result the bridge believes the token is not escrowed on L1. When the honest user later tries to bridge the token back to L1, the bridge checks the escrow flag, finds it false, and attempts to mint the token again. Because the token already exists on L1 and is owned by the bridge, the mint operation reverts, leaving the token stuck on L2 with no way to move it back to its native chain. The attack can be carried out on both L1‑native and L2‑native NFTs whenever the withdrawal destination is a contract that implements onERC721Received and can invoke the bridge’s deposit function. The affected parties are honest users who receive the NFT on the destination chain, the bridge protocol itself, and any downstream applications that rely on the ability to move NFTs across chains. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge contracts when the reviewer noticed that the escrow state was updated after an external call. It is hard to notice because the transaction completes without error and the escrow mapping appears cleared, yet the logical invariant that an escrowed token must be marked as such is broken only when a re‑entrancy occurs. To remediate, the contract should either place the escrow state update before any external call, employ a reentrancy guard on both depositTokens and withdrawTokens, or replace safeTransferFrom with a non‑callback transfer method such as transferFrom. Conceptually the fix restores the atomicity of the escrow state change, ensuring that no external code can observe an intermediate inconsistent state.

title: ETH item purchases can be DOSed
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ETH purchase path of the marketplace where the function that processes NFT purchases with native Ether obtains the current spot price from an on‑chain price source and then checks whether the deviation between that spot price and a previously stored time‑weighted average price (TWAP) exceeds a configured percentage. If the deviation is larger than the allowed threshold the function reverts the transaction. Because the contract relies directly on the spot price without any additional safeguards, an attacker who can influence the price feed – for example by providing liquidity to the underlying pool, submitting manipulated oracle data, or otherwise causing a temporary price spike – can push the deviation beyond the limit. When this happens any subsequent call to buy an item with ETH will hit the deviation check and revert, meaning the buyer’s transaction fails, no NFT is transferred, and the Ether is automatically refunded. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome (receiving the purchased NFT) is replaced by a silent failure or a revert error, which appears as “purchase failed” or “no NFT received” even though the user supplied sufficient funds. The issue manifests whenever the spot price is volatile or can be deliberately skewed, i.e., under conditions where the price oracle is not protected against short‑term manipulation. The affected parties include ordinary buyers, the marketplace protocol (which loses revenue and reputation), and any downstream services that rely on successful sales. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the price validation logic and identified that the deviation check could be triggered by external price manipulation. It is difficult to notice because the deviation guard is intended to protect against abnormal price movements, so a revert may be interpreted as a normal safety mechanism rather than an exploitable denial‑of‑service vector. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “price oracle manipulation leading to availability denial” and violates the business assumption that price feeds are trustworthy for short‑term decisions. The recommended remediation is to avoid using the volatile spot price for purchase validation; instead the contract should rely on the TWAP directly, or incorporate additional safeguards such as price smoothing, minimum time windows, or fallback mechanisms that prevent a single price spike from aborting all purchases. By decoupling the purchase logic from manipulable short‑term price data, the marketplace can ensure that legitimate buyers are not blocked and that the protocol’s economic flow remains intact.

title: M-1 Centralization risks
description:
The project exhibits a centralized structure, primarily under the control of the owner, who possesses the ability to withdraw the project's liquidity in a single transaction. Additionally, other components within the project possess excessive control, posing further risks to users' funds. Notably:
• Strategies can mint arbitrary amounts of the aETH tokens.
• Tokens deposited in strategies may not be returned.
• RewardOracle features a centralized design, increasing the risk of inaccurate reporting.
• The aETH token may have multiple managers, implying that entities other than the CorePrimary contract might have minting rights.
This issue is rated as medium since there are multiple centralized points of vulnerability within the project, each of which requires precise management and security measures.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a systemic centralization risk that stems from privileged control over several core components of the protocol. The contract owner holds a single‑transaction authority to withdraw the entire liquidity pool, meaning that at any moment the owner can move all funds out of the system without requiring consensus from other participants. In addition, the strategy contracts are granted the ability to mint arbitrary amounts of the aETH token, and there is no guarantee that tokens deposited into these strategies will be returned to users. The RewardOracle, which supplies reward data to the protocol, is also designed with a centralized decision point, allowing a single entity to influence the reported rewards. Moreover, the aETH token can be managed by multiple addresses beyond the CorePrimary contract, giving several parties minting rights. These design choices create a class of bugs known as privileged‑authority or centralization flaws, where a small set of actors can unilaterally affect token supply, fund availability, and reward calculations. Exploitation occurs when a privileged actor (the owner, a strategy manager, or a token manager) exercises their rights: they may mint excessive aETH to inflate supply, withhold or misallocate deposited tokens, or withdraw the whole liquidity pool in one transaction. The impact is that users may see their balances remain unchanged after a withdrawal request, receive zero or incorrect rewards, or find that their deposited assets are permanently locked or disappear from the system. This situation manifests whenever a user interacts with the protocol—depositing, withdrawing, or claiming rewards—under the assumption that the system is decentralized and that funds are safely managed. The affected parties include ordinary users who trust the protocol with their assets, as well as any downstream contracts that rely on the integrity of the aETH supply and reward data. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the concentration of privileged functions and the lack of multi‑party governance. It can be difficult to notice because the contract may appear to function correctly under normal conditions; only when a privileged actor decides to misuse their powers does the problem become evident, and the symptoms (missing funds, zero rewards) may be attributed to normal market risk rather than a design flaw. To remediate the risk, the recommended mitigation is to replace single‑owner control with multisignature governance for all addresses that have withdrawal, minting, or reward‑oracle authority, thereby distributing decision‑making and reducing the chance of unilateral fund extraction. In essence, the bug violates fundamental accounting assumptions of invariant token supply and guaranteed fund return, and it belongs to the broader category of centralization and privileged‑minting vulnerabilities that can lead to fund loss, reward manipulation, and loss of user trust.

title: M-2 The supplyReward() function doesn't check the balance increase
description: There is no verification that the specified reward amounts exist in the current implementation of reward delivery. RewardOracle.sol#L240 In this way, there is a risk of an uncontrolled increase in the overall supply.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution routine, specifically the supplyReward() function, which allocates token rewards without verifying that the contract actually holds the claimed amount. In the current implementation the function simply records a reward amount and updates internal accounting, but it never checks that the contract's token balance has increased by at least that amount. This missing verification creates a logical flaw: an attacker or a malicious caller can invoke supplyReward() with an arbitrary large reward value, causing the contract to record a higher total supply than the underlying token balance supports. The root cause is the absence of a balance‑increase guard or a delta check between the contract's token holdings and the sum of rewards reported. Exploitation is straightforward: a user calls supplyReward() with a reward value that exceeds the contract's actual token reserves; the contract accepts the request, updates its internal supply counter, and may later allow the caller to claim or withdraw the overstated reward. Because the function does not emit an explicit error or revert when the balance is insufficient, the transaction succeeds silently, making the inflation invisible at the UI level. The impact is an uncontrolled increase in the overall token supply, which can dilute existing holders, break economic assumptions of the protocol, and potentially enable a runaway minting attack that drains the token’s value. The issue manifests whenever supplyReward() is executed, especially in environments where the contract’s balance can be manipulated or is low. All participants who rely on the token’s fixed supply—investors, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts—are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the reward delivery logic, where the auditor noted the lack of a balance check after the reward amount was recorded. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit a warning; the only symptom may be an unexpected increase in total supply visible on‑chain or a mismatch between reported rewards and actual token holdings. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal reward claim, but the underlying token balance may be lower than expected, leading to “missing funds” or “reward amount seems too high”. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the difference between the contract’s token balance and the cumulative rewards does not exceed a predefined tolerance, typically by asserting that balanceBefore + newlyMinted >= rewardAmount or by using a safe‑mint function that caps total supply. This change restores the invariant that rewards are always backed by real tokens, preventing inflation and preserving protocol integrity.

title: M-3 Race condition in the submitEpochReward() start epoch ID
description: The submitEpochReward() function is designed to report the reward amount over the interval of one or several epochs. The arguments of this function are the end epoch ID and the reward amount. The start epoch ID is calculated onchain. Due to a potential race condition in the offchain oracle mechanics, there's a possibility that the start epoch ID will be miscalculated. This could lead to reporting extra rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition affecting the submitEpochReward function, which is responsible for reporting reward amounts for a range of epochs. The function receives the end epoch identifier and the reward amount, while the start epoch identifier is derived on‑chain from the contract’s internal state. Because the start epoch is calculated based on data that may be updated by an off‑chain oracle, a timing gap can occur: if the oracle submits a reward report before the contract has recorded the previous submission, the on‑chain calculation will use stale information and produce an incorrect start epoch ID. This mismatch allows a malicious or compromised oracle to claim rewards for a longer interval than actually earned, effectively inflating the reported reward amount. Exploitation consists of submitting a reward transaction with a deliberately mismatched start epoch, causing the contract to allocate extra tokens or ether to the reward pool. The impact is an over‑payment of rewards that can drain protocol funds, distort accounting, and undermine trust in the reward distribution mechanism. The condition appears when multiple reward submissions are made in rapid succession or when the off‑chain oracle does not synchronize its view of the latest epoch state before constructing the transaction. Users may notice unusually high reward balances, unexpected reductions in the protocol’s treasury, or reward calculations that do not match the expected epoch range. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the oracle interaction pattern and noticed that the start epoch is derived implicitly rather than being supplied explicitly, creating a window for race conditions. Because the contract does not verify the start epoch against the caller’s intent, the bug can remain hidden until a discrepancy in total rewards is observed. The recommended mitigation is to make the start epoch an explicit function argument, compare it with the on‑chain derived value, and revert the transaction if the two differ. This change eliminates the reliance on a timing‑sensitive off‑chain calculation and restores deterministic reward accounting.

title: Insufficient Observations for TWAP Calculation
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Ascendant contract configures the Uniswap V3 pool when it is first created. The contract explicitly sets the observation cardinality – the number of price and liquidity snapshots stored by the pool – to a fixed value of 100. These observations are later used to compute a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) over a configurable look‑back window that the protocol allows to range from five to thirty minutes. Because the number of stored observations is static, a look‑back period close to the upper bound may require more than one hundred samples to produce an accurate average, especially when the pool experiences high trading volume or rapid price swings. The root cause is therefore a mismatch between the maximum allowed look‑back duration and the limited number of historical data points the pool retains. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by creating a short‑term price distortion within the window that is not sufficiently covered by the stored observations. By doing so, the attacker can manipulate the TWAP that the contract relies on for slippage checks, causing the contract to accept a price that is artificially favorable to the attacker. The impact of such manipulation is that honest users may receive a worse exchange rate than expected, see a larger slippage than advertised, or even lose funds if the contract executes a trade at a price that deviates significantly from the true market price. This situation occurs only when the pool is active enough that the last hundred observations span less than the configured look‑back period, which is common for popular token pairs or during periods of high volatility. The parties affected include any trader interacting with the Ascendant contract, liquidity providers whose pool balances may be altered by unfair trades, and the protocol itself, which could suffer economic loss or reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s initialization logic, where the auditor noted the hard‑coded observation cardinality and compared it against the configurable TWAP window. The problem is subtle because the contract will still return a price and the UI may display a reasonable quote; however, the underlying average may be skewed, making the bug hard to detect without deep inspection of the pool’s observation history. To remediate the issue, the contract should increase the observation cardinality to a value that comfortably covers the maximum look‑back period – for example, 150 to 200 observations – or dynamically adjust the cardinality based on the chosen look‑back duration. By ensuring enough historical data points, the TWAP calculation becomes reliable, slippage checks reflect true market conditions, and users receive the rates they expect, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting and economic assumptions.

title: sqrtPX96 can be manipulated to inflate or deflate pool launch price
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an initialization-price manipulation in the function that creates a Uniswap V3 pool for the dragonX-ascendant pair. The contract computes the sqrtPX96 value, which encodes the pool's initial price, by calling the Quoter contract's quoteExactInput function to obtain a simulated swap amount (dragonXAmount) and then applying a deterministic formula. Because the Quoter contract returns a value that is derived from a simulated trade rather than a trusted on-chain price source, an attacker can influence the returned amount by supplying a crafted path or by manipulating the state of the tokens involved in the simulation. By inflating or deflating dragonXAmount, the attacker can cause the sqrtPX96 calculation to produce a price that is arbitrarily higher or lower than the market rate. This manipulated price is used as the pool's launch price, so the pool is effectively launched with a price that the attacker controls. The impact is that liquidity providers who add capital at launch receive a severely skewed token ratio, leading to loss of value, arbitrage opportunities for the attacker, and potential draining of funds from the pool. The condition occurs only during the pool-creation transaction, specifically when _createUniswapV3Pool is executed; any subsequent swaps are unaffected unless the pool is re-initialized. The affected parties include the protocol's users, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on the pool's price for accounting or incentive calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the price-initialisation logic and identified the reliance on a simulated-swap oracle as a weak trust assumption. It can be hard to notice because the pool appears to be created successfully and the price variable is a large integer that does not immediately reveal that it is out of range; only when users observe abnormal token balances or extreme price quotes does the problem become apparent. The bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation or price-initialisation vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts a value that can be forged or influenced by an adversary. From a user's perspective the symptoms are a launch price that is far from market expectations, liquidity providers receiving far fewer tokens than expected, or one side of the pool showing a near-zero balance. The correct mitigation is to replace the simulated-swap quote with a reliable price source, such as a time-weighted average price (TWAP) obtained from a trusted oracle library, or to compute the initial sqrtPX96 from on-chain market data that cannot be manipulated by the caller.

title: transfer(...) function in _issuePayout(...) can be replaced by a direct call
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal _issuePayout function of the vault implementation. When the asset being repaid is WETH, the contract first calls IWETH9.withdraw to convert the wrapped token into native ETH and then sends the resulting ETH to the borrower using payable(borrower).transfer(newAmount). The .transfer method forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback function. This gas limit is insufficient for any non‑trivial logic, such as logging events, interacting with other contracts, or performing arithmetic, and it may become even more restrictive as the EVM gas cost schedule evolves. Consequently, if the borrower is a contract that requires more than 2300 gas in its receive or fallback function, the transfer will revert, causing the payout to fail. The failure manifests to the user as a missing or zero payout, a transaction that reverts, or a loan that appears to be repaid while the borrower’s balance remains unchanged. The issue is a classic example of a gas‑stipend or unsafe ETH transfer bug, where the use of .transfer (or .send) imposes a hard gas cap that can break business logic. It is discovered during a manual audit that traced the payout flow and noted the reliance on .transfer after a WETH withdrawal. The problem can be hard to notice because the code appears to correctly move funds, and the 2300‑gas limit is a hidden constraint that only surfaces when the recipient contract has a non‑empty fallback. The impact is a potential denial‑of‑service for borrowers, loss of expected payouts, and a break in the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a successful repayment always results in the borrower receiving the full amount. The bug affects any borrower contract, the vault protocol, and ultimately the users who rely on timely payouts. The recommended mitigation is to replace the .transfer call with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (e.g., (bool success, ) = borrower.call{value:newAmount}(''); require(success, ...)), and to ensure that the surrounding storage updates are performed after the external call as described in the related storage‑parameter issue. By removing the gas stipend restriction, the payout can succeed regardless of the complexity of the borrower’s fallback logic, restoring the intended financial flow.

title: The risk of bad debt is transferred to the non-redeeming shareholders and not the redeeming holders
description:
Right before a successful epochProcess(), the total assets A equals to
A = y0 + s(t - tlast) = B +
sum_{s∈U1} a(s, t)
+ sum_{(s,tl)∈U2} a(s, tl)
All the parameter values in the below table are considered as just before calling the processEpoch() endpoint unless stated otherwise.
• A | totalAssets() |
• y0 | yIntercept |
• s | slope |
• tlast | last timestamp used to update y0 or s |
• t | block.timestamp |
• B | ERC20(asset()).balanceOf(PublicVault), underlying balance of the public vault |
• U1 | The set of active liens/stacks owned by the PublicVault, this can be non-empty due to how long the lien durations can be |
• U2 | The set of liquidated liens/stacks and their corresponding liquidation timestamp (tl) which are owned by the current epoch's WithdrawProxy Wecurr. These liens belong to the current epoch, but their auction ends in the next epoch duration. |
• a(s, t) | total amount owned by the stack s up to the timestamp t.
• S | totalSupply().
• SW | number of shares associated with the current epoch's WithdrawProxy ,currentWithdrawProxy.totalSupply() |
• E | currentWithdrawProxy.getExpected().
• wr | withdrawReserve this is the value after calling epochProcess().
• y0' | yIntercept after calling epochProcess().
• tp | last after calling epochProcess().
• A' | totalAssets after calling epochProcess().
• Wn | the current epoch's WithdrawProxy before calling epochProcess().
• Wn+1 | the current epoch's WithdrawProxy after calling epochProcess().
Also assume that claim() was already called on the previous epoch's WithdrawProxy if needed.
After the call to epochProcess() (in the same block), we would have roughly (not considering the division errors)
A' = y0' + s(t - tp)
A' = (1 - SW/S)A + sum_{s∈U1} (a(s, t) - a(s, tp))
wr = (SW/S) B + sum_{s∈U1} a(s, tp)
A = A' + wr + (SW/S) sum_{(s,tl)∈U2} a(s, tl)
and so:
ΔA = wr + (SW/S)E
To be able to call processEpoch() again we need to make sure wr tokens have been transferred to Wn either from the public vault's assets B or from Wn+1 assets. Note that at this point wr equals to
wr = SW/S B + SW/S sum_{s∈U1} a(s, tp)
The SW/S B is an actual asset and can be transferred to Wn right away. The SW/S sum_{s∈U1} a(s, tp) portion is a percentage of the amount owed by active liens at the time the processEpoch() was called. Depending on whether these liens get paid fully or not we would have:
• If they get fully paid there are no risks for the future shareholders to bare.
• If these liens are not fully paid since we have transferred SW/S sum_{s∈U1} a(s, tp) from the actual asset balance to Wn the redeeming shareholder would not take the risk of these liens getting liquidated for less than their value.
But these risks are transferred to the upcoming shareholders or the shareholders who have not redeemed their positions yet.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that causes the risk of unpaid liens, often called bad debt, to be shifted from shareholders who redeem their positions in the current epoch to those who keep their shares for later epochs. The root cause lies in the way the withdraw reserve (wr) is calculated during the epochProcess function. The formula adds a component proportional to the total share supply (SW/S) multiplied by the balance of the public vault (B) – which is a genuine liquid asset – and also adds a second component that represents a share of the amount owed by active liens at the moment the epoch is processed (SW/S * sum of a(s,tp)). This second component is treated as if it were fully available cash and is transferred to the new WithdrawProxy before the underlying liens have been settled. If any of those liens are later liquidated for less than their recorded value, the shortfall is not absorbed by the redeeming shareholders who already received their withdraw tokens; instead it is borne by the shareholders who have not yet redeemed, effectively transferring bad debt to future holders. An attacker could trigger epochProcess when a large number of liens are under‑collateralized, causing the withdraw reserve to contain a sizable contingent liability. When later shareholders attempt to redeem, they may receive less than expected, see their balances unexpectedly reduced, or receive a zero refund, even though the protocol UI shows that sufficient assets were transferred to the withdraw pool. The issue occurs on every call to processEpoch that occurs while there are active, unsettled liens, and it affects any token holder who holds shares across epochs, as well as the overall financial integrity of the protocol. The problem was discovered during a detailed audit of the epoch accounting equations, where the mismatch between actual liquid assets and the claimed withdraw reserve became apparent. It is hard to notice because the withdraw reserve appears to be fully funded, masking the hidden liability tied to active liens. To remediate, the accounting should be changed so that the withdraw reserve only includes the truly liquid portion (SW/S * B) and the lien‑related portion is either retained in the public vault until the liens are settled or accounted for as a contingent liability rather than being transferred to the withdraw proxy. This adjustment ensures that the risk of bad debt remains with the parties responsible for the liens and does not unfairly burden future shareholders, aligning the protocol’s financial logic with its stated guarantees.

title: validateOrder(...) does not check the consideration amount against its token balance
description:
When a lien position gets liquidated the CollateralToken creates a full restricted Seaport auction with itself as both the offerer and the zone. This will cause Seaport to do a callback to the CollateralToken's validateOrder(...) endpoint at the end of order fulfilment/matching. In this endpoint we have:
```solidity
uint256 payment = zoneParameters.consideration[0].amount;
```
This payment amount is not validated.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the validateOrder function that Seaport calls after matching a liquidation auction created by the CollateralToken contract. When a lien position is liquidated, the CollateralToken builds a fully restricted Seaport auction where it acts as both the offerer and the zone. During the finalisation step Seaport invokes the contract's validateOrder endpoint and the code extracts the first consideration amount with the line `uint256 payment = zoneParameters.consideration[0].amount;`. The function never checks whether the CollateralToken actually holds enough of the specified ERC‑20 token to satisfy that payment, nor does it derive the correct amount based on the auction’s start/end timestamps using the AmountDeriver utilities. As a result, an attacker who can influence the zoneParameters can supply an arbitrarily large consideration amount. Because the contract does not verify its token balance, Seaport will treat the order as valid and may proceed with the transfer of the collateral to the buyer even though the contract does not possess the required funds. This can lead to a situation where the buyer receives the collateral for free, the protocol loses value, or the transfer reverts and locks assets in an inconsistent state. The issue manifests only during the liquidation flow when the CollateralToken creates the restricted auction and validateOrder is executed. It affects all participants of the protocol – lenders, borrowers and token holders – because it undermines the accounting guarantees that the amount paid must be covered by the contract’s balance. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the liquidation path and noticed the missing balance verification. It is subtle because the function appears to read a payment amount, which gives the impression that the amount is being used, yet no explicit safeguard is present, making the problem easy to overlook in testing where the contract usually holds sufficient tokens. To remediate, the validateOrder logic should first query the ERC‑20 balance of the CollateralToken for the token specified in the consideration and ensure it is at least the payment amount. Additionally, the contract should inherit from the AmountDeriver module and call the internal `_locateCurrentAmount` routine to compute the correct amount based on the auction’s time‑based schedule, then compare that derived amount with the payment value before approving the order. This change restores the invariant that every considered payment is fully backed by the contract’s token holdings, preventing free‑minting of collateral and preserving protocol accounting integrity.

title: If the auction window is 0, the borrower can keep the lien amount and also take back its collater- alised NFT token
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the auction configuration of the Astaria lending protocol that allows a borrower to liquidate a lien and then reclaim the underlying NFT while still retaining the borrowed funds. The root cause is that the contract permits an authorized entity to set the auctionWindow parameter to zero, which results in the auction start and end timestamps being identical (tauction_s = tauction_e). The Seaport auction validation routine does not enforce that the timestamps are a valid interval, so the created auction cannot be fulfilled by any external participant because Seaport requires tauction_s ≤ tnow < tauction_e. Nevertheless, the CollateralToken’s liquidatorNFTClaim function does not check the auction’s validity before transferring the NFT back to the caller. An attacker can therefore follow a sequence: (1) set auctionWindow to zero via a fileBatch call, (2) open a lien by collateralising an NFT, (3) wait until the lien becomes liquidatable, (4) trigger liquidation which creates an unfulfillable auction, and (5) immediately invoke liquidatorNFTClaim to retrieve the NFT. Because the auction never matches, the protocol does not deduct the lien amount from the borrower, so the borrower ends up with both the original loan amount and the reclaimed NFT. From a user perspective the borrower sees their ETH balance unchanged and the NFT still owned by them after a liquidation event, which contradicts the expected outcome where the collateral should be transferred to the liquidator and the borrower should lose the NFT. The impact is a loss of collateral for the vault and lenders, effectively allowing borrowers to steal assets while keeping the loan, compromising the economic security of the protocol. This issue was uncovered during a security audit by constructing a test scenario that deliberately set the auction window to zero and observed the unexpected retention of both funds and NFT. The flaw is subtle because the auction creation appears successful and no error is emitted, while the claim function silently succeeds, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a non‑zero lower bound on auctionWindow, validate that tauction_s < tauction_e before creating an auction, and ensure that liquidatorNFTClaim can only be called when the auction has a valid, fulfillable time window, thereby preventing borrowers from reclaiming collateral under an invalid auction.

title: A malicious collateralized NFT token can block liquidation and also epoch processing for public vaults
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the assumption that an ERC721 token will always accept an approval request during the liquidation of a collateralized NFT lien. When a lien is liquidated, the CollateralToken contract calls the standard ERC721 approve function to grant the Seaport conduit permission to transfer the underlying NFT. If the NFT contract is malicious or compromised and deliberately reverts the approve call, the liquidation process aborts. Because the protocol only allows epoch processing for a public vault when all open liens have been either paid or successfully liquidated, a single reverted approval leaves the lien marked as open. Consequently, the epoch cannot be closed, the public vault’s state check fails, and any further operations that depend on epoch finalisation are blocked. From a user perspective this manifests as a vault that appears frozen: attempts to process the epoch or withdraw funds revert with an InvalidVaultState error, and the expected liquidation of an expired position never occurs, effectively locking the collateral and any associated funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation flow and noted that the approve call is made without any try/catch or validation of the token’s behaviour. It is difficult to notice because the revert happens deep inside an external contract call, and the immediate symptom (a failed liquidation) only surfaces later when the epoch processing check triggers. The root cause is a lack of defensive programming around external ERC721 interactions and an implicit trust in token compliance. To remediate, the protocol should either validate that the NFT contract conforms to the ERC721 standard and does not revert on approve before accepting it as collateral, move the approval step to the lien‑creation phase where a revert would prevent the lien from being recorded, or wrap the approve call in a try/catch and handle failures gracefully, possibly by marking the lien as unliquidatable and allowing alternative resolution paths. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of external call reentrancy‑or‑failure‑handling flaws where a malicious token can disrupt protocol state transitions, leading to dead‑locked vaults and loss of expected fund flow.

title: Storage parameters are updated after a few callback sites to external addresses in the commitToLien(...) flow
description:
In the commitToLien(...) flow the following storage parameters are updated after some of the external call back sites when payout is issued or a lien is transferred from a private vault to its owner:
• collateralStateHash in LienToken: One can potentially re-enter to take another lien using the same collateral, but this is not possible since the collateral NFT token is already transferred to the CollateralToken (unless one is dealing with some esoteric NFT token). The createLien(...) requires this parameter to be 0., and that's why a potential re-entrancy can bypass this requirement. | Read re-entrancy: Yes
• slope in PublicVault: - | Read re-entrancy: Yes
• liensOpenForEpoch in PublicVault: If flash liens are allowed one can re-enter and process the epoch before finishing the commitToLien(...). And so the processed epoch would have open liens even though we would want to make sure this could not happen | Read re-entrancy: Yes
The re-entrancies can happen if the vault asset performs a call back to the receiver when transferring tokens (during issuance of payouts). And if one is dealing with WETH, the native token amount is transfer(...) to the borrower. Note in the case of Native tokens if the following recommendation from the below issue is considered the current issue could be of higher risk:
• 'transfer(...) function in _issuePayout(...) can be replaced by a direct call'
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy caused by updating critical storage variables only after the contract makes external calls during the commitToLien flow. In commitToLien the contract first issues a payout by transferring tokens (for example ERC20 or WETH) to the borrower. The transfer invokes the receiver’s fallback or token contract code, which can call back into the same vault contract before the function finishes. Because the contract postpones updates to collateralStateHash in the lien token, the slope value in the public vault, and the liensOpenForEpoch counter until after the external call, a malicious receiver can re‑enter commitToLien and create a second lien on the same collateral, or process the epoch a second time. This bypasses the check that collateralStateHash must be zero for a new lien and allows the attacker to obtain multiple liens on a single NFT or to keep the epoch marked as having open liens when it should be closed. The impact is that funds can be locked incorrectly, extra liens can be minted without proper accounting, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are violated, potentially leading to loss of collateral value or incorrect fee distribution. The issue manifests when the vault’s asset is an ERC20 token that performs a callback on transfer (for example WETH’s transfer function) or any token that executes code on receipt. Users may notice that after a successful payout their collateral appears to be liened again, or that the epoch still reports open liens despite having been processed. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that identified that storage writes occur after external calls. It is hard to spot because the code appears to follow a logical order, and the external call is assumed to be safe, while the re‑entrancy window is subtle. The proper mitigation is to reorder the logic so that all state changes – setting collateralStateHash, updating the vault’s slope, and incrementing or resetting liensOpenForEpoch – are performed before any external call, and to use the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern or re‑entrancy guards. By moving the state updates ahead of the payout transfer and adding the lien before issuing the payout, the contract eliminates the re‑entrancy window and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: UNI_V3Validator fetches spot prices that may lead to price manipulation attacks
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a validator component that determines the value of a Uniswap V3 liquidity‑position by reading the pool’s current sqrt price directly from the pool’s slot0 storage field. The validator calls LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity, which ultimately computes the amount of token1 as liquidity multiplied by the difference between the upper and lower sqrt price bounds. When the current price (slot0.poolSQ96) falls inside the position’s tick range, the lower bound used in the calculation becomes the live spot price. Because the spot price is taken directly from the pool without any external verification, an attacker who can temporarily move the pool price – for example by using a flash loan to perform a large swap – can cause the validator to over‑estimate the value of the LP token. In a typical attack scenario the attacker supplies a small amount of liquidity within a narrow price range, then uses a flash loan to push the pool price to the upper bound of that range. The validator reads the manipulated spot price, calculates a much larger token1 amount, and the protocol’s lending logic believes the collateral is worth far more than it truly is. The attacker can then borrow an amount equal to the inflated valuation, restore the pool price, repay the flash loan and walk away with the excess funds. This flaw manifests whenever the validator is used to assess collateral or to enforce borrowing limits, i.e., when the protocol relies on the spot price from slot0 as a trustworthy market reference. The affected parties include the protocol’s vault, lenders, and any users whose deposits are used as collateral, because the protocol may lend out more assets than it actually holds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the validator’s source code, where the direct use of slot0 was identified as a price‑oracle‑free dependency. It can be difficult to notice because the slot0 value is a legitimate on‑chain variable that normally reflects the market price, and the calculation itself follows the official Uniswap V3 library, giving a false sense of correctness. From a user’s perspective the system appears to accept a normal LP position as collateral, but the user may later see that the borrowed amount exceeds the real value of the deposited LP, leading to unexpected loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of “oracle manipulation via on‑chain state exposure” or “price‑manipulation through direct pool state usage”. To remediate the problem the validator should obtain price data from a trusted, tamper‑resistant oracle rather than reading slot0, and the codebase should clearly document the risk of using raw pool state for valuation. By decoupling the valuation from the mutable pool price, the protocol can prevent attackers from inflating collateral values and protect the integrity of its lending logic.

title: Users pay protocol fee for interests they do not get
description:
