The recommended remediation is to replace the direct admin with a timelocked governance contract, enforce that core address can be set only once, introduce immutable constants for reasonable bounds on maxListingDuration and minDonationBps, and add validation checks in the setter functions. By moving admin privileges to a multi‑sig or DAO and by hard‑coding safe limits, the protocol can prevent a single party from unilaterally stealing assets or breaking the economic model.

title: M-1 Facade allows any unauthorized Executor
description:
SwapFacade allows to choose any SwapExecutor address, even not authored by the team. Fees are charged on SwapExecutor. So, it is rational to fork SwapExecutor with zero fees and choose it as an executor for swaps.
• SwapFacade.sol#L87
Some other possible scenarios:
• users can choose out date executors
• users can choose executors with bugs
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SwapFacade contract, which exposes a public parameter that lets callers specify an arbitrary address to act as the SwapExecutor for a token swap. Because the contract does not enforce any whitelist or ownership check on the supplied executor, any user can pass a malicious or freshly‑deployed executor contract that implements the expected interface but deviates from the intended business logic. The root cause is the absence of access control on the executor selection, allowing the facade to delegate fee collection and swap execution to an untrusted contract. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a custom SwapExecutor that either omits the fee calculation, returns zero fees, or contains malicious code that redirects swapped assets to the attacker’s address. When a victim initiates a swap and selects the attacker‑controlled executor—either intentionally or because the UI does not restrict the choice—the facade forwards the call, the swap proceeds, and the protocol’s fee revenue is bypassed or the funds are misdirected. The impact includes loss of expected fee income for the protocol, potential theft of user funds if the rogue executor contains a backdoor, and overall erosion of trust because users may receive a swap that appears successful but yields no fee or results in missing tokens. This condition occurs every time the swap function is called with a user‑supplied executor address, which is allowed for any caller without restriction. The affected parties are the protocol operators who rely on fees for sustainability, and the end‑users who expect their swaps to be executed safely and with the advertised fee structure. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the lack of validation on the executor address parameter. It can be difficult to notice because the function signature looks normal and the parameter is simply an address, so developers may assume that any address implementing the required interface is safe. To remediate, the facade should maintain a curated list of approved executor contracts, enforce that only addresses from this list can be used, and optionally move fee calculation from the executor to the facade itself so that fee logic cannot be bypassed. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents malicious actors from inserting zero‑fee or harmful executors into the swap flow.

title: M-2 Anyone can withdraw funds left on SwapExecutor
description:
Funds left on the SwapExecutor can be withdrawn by anyone who speciﬁes a transfer call in the swaps.
There are multiple reasons why funds may be left on the SwapExecutor:
1. A user may not set the tokenRatio to 100% in a swap.
```solidity
uint256 poolSwapAmount = (balanceToSwap * swap.tokenRatio) / _ONE;
```
sum (tokenRatio) > _ONE - is not risky, revert happens
sum (tokenRatio) < _ONE - is risky, as some tokens are left not swapped and can be taken by anyone.
2. The SwapExecutor may run arbitrary calls to protocols that reward it with additional tokens. The SwapFacade only checks the tokenToTransfer, and a user may forget to transfer other tokens from the SwapExecutor immediately.
3. If a user transfers tokens to the SwapExecutor ﬁrst and then runs the SwapFacade.swap() function in a separate transaction.
• SwapExecutor.sol#L58
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted withdrawal path in the SwapExecutor component of the protocol. When a swap is executed, the contract calculates the amount to exchange using a tokenRatio parameter that is expected to represent the full proportion of the input balance. If the tokenRatio is set below the maximum denominator (i.e., less than 100%), a portion of the original tokens remains locked inside the executor because the arithmetic only swaps the specified fraction. Additionally, the executor is capable of performing arbitrary external calls that may reward it with extra tokens; the surrounding SwapFacade only validates a single tokenToTransfer field and does not automatically sweep any other assets that arrive. Because the executor does not enforce any access control on the function that transfers out residual balances, any address can craft a transfer call in a subsequent transaction and move those leftover tokens to an arbitrary account. This flaw can be triggered when a user deliberately or inadvertently supplies a tokenRatio below the full amount, when the executor receives unexpected tokens from external protocol interactions, or when a user separates the token deposit and the swap execution into two distinct transactions, leaving a window where the executor holds assets. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a swap the expected refund or remaining balance is missing, often appearing as a zero balance or a loss of funds without any explicit error. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as assets that should have been either swapped or returned to the user can be taken by anyone. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the tokenRatio handling and the lack of restrictions on the executor’s transfer function. It is subtle because the leftover amounts may be small or appear only after complex interactions, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should restrict swap execution to a whitelist of trusted manager contracts, enforce that the sum of all tokenRatio values used in a swap equals the full denominator (ensuring no residual tokens), and add a sweep mechanism that either automatically transfers any remaining assets to the intended recipient or blocks external withdrawals unless authorized. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that all swapped assets are accounted for and prevents arbitrary parties from draining leftover balances.

title: M-3 ETH value above limited value can be lost
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a contract that forwards Ether to a target address after optionally limiting the amount that can be sent. When a caller supplies an Ether value that exceeds a predefined limit, the contract truncates the forwarded amount to the limit and then executes a low‑level call with the reduced value. The excess Ether remains in the contract’s balance because the code does not forward it, nor does it provide a mechanism to return it to the original sender. As a result, any user who initiates a transaction with more Ether than the limit will see part of their funds become locked in the contract, effectively disappearing from their perspective. This situation can be reproduced whenever the supplied Ether is greater than the limit, which may happen unintentionally due to user error or deliberately by an attacker who crafts a transaction that includes a large Ether amount to increase the amount that becomes trapped. The trapped Ether can later be withdrawn by anyone who discovers the contract’s internal accounting, meaning that the loss is not limited to the original sender. The impact is a partial loss of user funds and a potential avenue for malicious actors to siphon the accumulated excess Ether. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the Ether handling logic and noticed that the contract caps the value without handling the remainder. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert and appears successful, so users receive no explicit error or warning, making the loss easy to overlook. To remediate the problem, the contract should either reject transactions that exceed the limit, return the surplus Ether to the sender, or redesign the limit mechanism so that no Ether can be unintentionally retained. In broader terms, this is an instance of an unchecked value‑capping bug that violates the expectation that all supplied Ether is either used or returned, breaking the accounting invariants of the protocol and leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds for users.

title: M-4 A swap with permit can be blocked if a frontrunner swaps using copied permit
description:
Facade does not check that msg.sender is the owner of a permit.
So, a frontrunner can use permits of other users available from mempool, so that their transactions would revert (as permit are used by the frontrunner).
• SwapFacade.sol#L58-L64
A user will receive revert and will have to build new calldata, without permit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ownership verification on ERC20 permit data used by the swap facade. When a user submits a swap transaction that includes a signed permit, the contract forwards the permit to the token contract without checking that the caller (msg.sender) is the same address that created the signature. Because the permit only proves that the token holder signed an approval, any external account can reuse the same permit data. An attacker monitoring the mempool can copy the permit from a victim’s pending transaction and submit a front‑running transaction that consumes the permit first. The token contract then records the allowance for the attacker, leaving no remaining allowance for the original user. When the victim’s transaction is mined, the permit is no longer valid, causing the swap to revert with an allowance‑related error. From the user’s perspective the swap fails, they receive no tokens, and they must rebuild the calldata without the permit, incurring additional gas costs. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style attack that can repeatedly block users who rely on permits for gas‑less approvals, potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The issue occurs only when a permit is supplied and the transaction is visible in the mempool before being mined; it does not affect swaps that do not use permits. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, which noted that the contract does not decode the permit to extract the signer and compare it with msg.sender. The problem is subtle because the permit signature itself is valid and the contract does not emit an explicit warning that the caller is unauthorized, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should decode the permit, obtain the owner address embedded in the signed data, and require that this address equals msg.sender before forwarding the permit. This pattern is used by 1inch’s SafeERC20 implementation and prevents any third party from reusing a permit that does not belong to them. The bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization check on off‑chain signatures” and violates the business assumption that a permit is bound to the transaction sender, breaking the expected flow where a user’s approval is consumed only by their own transaction.

title: M-5 Unprotected access to makeCheckpoint() in SwapGuardV2
description:
SwapGuardV2 functions are planned to be used as separate calls in a set of swaps. However, if during the swaps process a hacker manages to get a callback to their own contract (for example, if the victim operates with ERC-777 tokens), the hacker can call public accessible function makeCheckpoint() to modify the SwapGuardV2 state so that the ensureCheckpoint() function at the victim's end would not work correctly.
SwapGuardV2.sol#L20
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unprotected public function named makeCheckpoint in the SwapGuardV2 contract. This function records the current token balances as a checkpoint that later ensureCheckpoint uses to verify that no unexpected balance changes occurred during a series of swaps. Because makeCheckpoint has no access control, any external address can invoke it at any time. The root cause is the missing restriction on who may call the checkpoint‑recording routine, which was intended to be used only internally as part of the swap flow. Exploitation becomes possible when the swap process involves a token that can trigger a callback to an attacker‑controlled contract, such as an ERC‑777 token that invokes a tokensReceived hook. During that callback the attacker can call the public makeCheckpoint, causing the contract to store a manipulated snapshot of balances that reflects the attacker’s desired state. When the swap finishes, ensureCheckpoint compares the post‑swap balances against the attacker‑controlled checkpoint, mistakenly concluding that the balances are unchanged. As a result, the protocol’s accounting check is bypassed and the attacker can move tokens out of the pool without detection. The impact is that users may see their expected refunds or swapped tokens disappear, balances may become zero, or swaps may complete while the protocol silently loses funds. The issue occurs only when a re‑entrancy‑capable token is used and the contract relies on separate calls to makeCheckpoint and ensureCheckpoint instead of a single atomic operation. All participants in the swap – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the guard that should protect their assets can be subverted. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of SwapGuardV2 and identified that makeCheckpoint is publicly exposed. It is hard to notice because the function appears benign and is normally called as part of legitimate swap logic; the problem only surfaces under a specific re‑entrancy scenario, which may not be exercised in standard testing. To remediate, the checkpoint routine should be made internal or protected by an appropriate access modifier, or the design should be changed to a single function that records balances in memory, invokes the user‑provided callback, and then validates the balances before any state changes are persisted. This eliminates the window where an attacker can tamper with the stored checkpoint and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: `NonCustodialPSM` can become insolvent as CPI index rises
description:
[NonCustodialPSM.sol#L236-L248](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-volt/blob/main/contracts/peg/NonCustodialPSM.sol#L236-L248)  

NonCustodialPSM mints and redeems VOLT to a chosen stablecoin at the current market rate minus a fixed fee. It is assumed that the difference to be covered with pcvDeposit funds. That assumption is similar to one used in FEI protocol, but there no rate growth takes place as FEI to USD rate supposed to be stable, while VOLT to USD rate will rise over time.

VOLT market rate is tied to the off-chain published CPI index. The growth of this index can easily surpass the yield of the pcvDeposit used, so its interest cannot be guaranteed to be always greater than CPI index advancement. The contract can end up in the situation when no redeem be possible, i.e. NonCustodialPSM can become insolvent.

For example, let’s say the stablecoin is USDC, and now investors are worried about inflation and buy/mint 100m VOLT for 100m USDC. Fast forward 1 year, and investors were generally right, as due to rise of the oil prices happening simultaneously with logistics issues the CPI index growth end up being 30% APR for the year.

Then, inflation fears abated and, say, stocks become stronger, and investors want their funds now to put them there and sell/redeem 100m VOLT expecting 125m USDC in return (for simplicity say 5m USDC goes to mint and redeem fees combined). USDC deposit strategy used in pcvDeposit yielded 10% APR for the year. The contract cannot redeem all the funds due as it is 125 - 100 * 1.1 = 15m USDC short.

Putting severity to high as the contract serves requests sequentially and the last investors’ funds are lost this way, i.e. in the example above all the users, who came in to redeem when contract has 15m USDC in obligations and no funds, will lose their entire deposits.
poc:
Continuing the example, current low risk USDC deposit rates are circa 2.5 lower than US CPI:

AAVE: <https://classic.aave.com/#/markets>

Compound: <https://compound.finance/markets/USDC>

US CPI: <https://www.bls.gov/cpi/>

NonCustodialPSM.redeem uses current oracle price to determine what amount of stablecoins to be paid for 1 VOLT:

NonCustodialPSM.mint does the same:

For example, FEI protocol use a wide range of pcvDeposits, whose yields vary depending on the underlying strategy:

But there are no PCV deposits whose returns are linked to CPI of any country, so mismatch (basis) risk exists, which has to be addressed.
bug_full:
The vulnerability concerns the economic model of the NonCustodialPSM contract, which mints and redeems the VOLT token against a chosen stablecoin (e.g., USDC) at the prevailing market rate minus a fixed fee. The contract assumes that any shortfall between the amount of stablecoin owed to redeemers and the amount received from minting can be covered by earnings generated by a pcvDeposit holding the stablecoin. This assumption is valid only when the exchange rate of VOLT to the stablecoin remains stable, as was the case for the FEI protocol. However, VOLT’s market rate is explicitly tied to the off‑chain Consumer Price Index (CPI), which can increase over time. When CPI growth outpaces the yield earned by the pcvDeposit, the contract’s liability to redeemers can exceed the assets it controls, creating a situation where the contract cannot fulfill redemption requests – in other words, it becomes insolvent. 

An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by minting VOLT when the CPI is low, thereby depositing relatively cheap stablecoins. After a period during which CPI rises substantially, the same user or a different user can request redemption, expecting to receive a larger amount of stablecoins corresponding to the higher VOLT price. Because the pcvDeposit’s yield is typically far lower than the CPI increase (e.g., 10 % yield versus a 30 % CPI rise), the contract ends up short of the required stablecoins. The redemption function calculates the payout using the current oracle price and attempts to withdraw the necessary amount from the pcvDeposit; when insufficient, the call fails or, depending on implementation, the contract may simply transfer whatever balance remains, leaving the redeemer with an incomplete payout. 

The impact is that users who attempt to redeem after a CPI surge may receive less than the contractual amount or, in the worst case, nothing at all, effectively losing their entire deposited funds. This risk manifests whenever the contract processes redemption requests sequentially and the cumulative obligations exceed the liquid assets held. The affected parties include all token holders interacting with the NonCustodialPSM, the protocol governance that relies on the contract for stablecoin liquidity, and any downstream applications that assume reliable redemption. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the economic assumptions of the contract, rather than a code flaw, highlighting a logical mismatch between the CPI‑linked price feed and the static yield of the pcvDeposit. 

Because the contract does not enforce any sanity check on the relationship between CPI growth and pcvDeposit earnings, the problem can be subtle and may not be apparent during normal operation, especially when CPI is relatively stable. From a user’s perspective, the symptom appears as an unexpected shortfall: a user attempts to redeem 100 m VOLT expecting roughly 125 m USDC (including fees) but receives only the 100 m USDC originally deposited, or receives nothing, contradicting the expectation that the contract will always honor the quoted price. 

To mitigate the issue, the design should incorporate a dedicated stability fund that can be topped up from separate sources (e.g., governance‑controlled reserves) and that also receives mint‑ and redeem‑fee revenue. Redemption should be limited to the proportion of funds that are actually available in the combined pcvDeposit and stability fund, making any deficit visible to users before they execute the transaction. This allows users to decide whether to accept a reduced payout now or to wait for the stability fund to be replenished. In addition, mechanisms such as dynamic fee adjustments, periodic rebalancing of the pcvDeposit strategy, or linking deposit yields to inflation‑indexed assets could reduce the basis‑risk exposure. These conceptual fixes address the root cause—the mismatch between CPI‑driven liability growth and static yield—rather than merely patching a line of code.

title: Reentrancy at _requestLoan allows requesting a loan without supplying collateral
description: `_requestLoan` makes an external call to the collateral contract before updating the NFTPair contract state.
poc:
Assume the NFT contract has an [afterTokenTransfer hook](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/token/erc721#ERC721-_afterTokenTransfer-address-address-uint256-) which calls back to the malicious borrower. POC in short: borrower will call `requestLoan` with `skim==false`, then during the hook will reenter `requestLoan` with `skim==true`, then call `removeCollateral` to get his collateral back, then the first `requestLoan` will resume and initiate the loan, although the collateral is not in the contract any more.

POC in long: the borrower will do the following:

  * Call [`requestLoan`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L205:#L227) with skim==false.
  * `requestLoan` [will call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L218) `collateral.transferFrom()`.
  * The collateral will be transferred to the NFTPair. Afterwards, the ERC721 contract will execute the `afterTokenTransfer` hook, and hand control back to Malbo (malicious borrower).
  * Malbo will call `requestLoan` again with `skim==true`.
  * As the first request’s details have not been updated yet, the tokenId status is still LOAN_INITIAL, and the [require statement of the loan status](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L214) will pass.
  * The NFT has already been transferred to the contract, so the [require statement of token ownership](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L216) will pass.
  * `requestLoan` (the second) will continue and set the loan details and status.
  * After it finishes, still within the `afterTokenTransfer` hook, Malbo will call [`removeCollateral`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L247:#L268). His call will succeed as the loan is in status requested. So the collateral will get sent back to Malbo.
  * Now the `afterTokenTransfer` hook finishes.
  * The original `requestLoan` will resume operation at the [point](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-abranft/blob/main/contracts/NFTPair.sol#L220:#L224) where all the loan details will be updated.
  * Therefore, the contract will mark the loan is valid, although the collateral is not in the contract anymore. A lender might then lend funds against the loan without Malbo needing to pay back.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the loan‑request workflow of the NFTPair contract. The function that grants a loan, _requestLoan, performs an external call to the collateral token contract (via transferFrom) before it updates the internal loan state that records the collateral's ownership and the loan status. Because the external call can trigger a callback – for example the ERC‑721 afterTokenTransfer hook – a malicious borrower can re‑enter _requestLoan while the first invocation is still pending. During this re‑entrancy the attacker calls _requestLoan a second time with different parameters, then invokes removeCollateral to pull the NFT back out of the contract before the first call finishes. At that point the contract still believes the collateral is locked, updates the loan record, and marks the loan as valid, even though the NFT has been withdrawn. Consequently a lender can fund a loan that is effectively unsecured, allowing the borrower to receive funds without providing any collateral. The issue occurs only when the collateral token implements a hook that can call back into the NFTPair contract, and when the borrower initiates the loan request with skim set to false followed by a re‑entered request with skim set to true. It was discovered during a formal audit that examined the call ordering and identified that the checks‑effects‑interaction pattern was violated. The flaw can be hard to notice because the external call is a standard token transfer and the contract’s state appears consistent from a superficial read; the re‑entrancy only manifests when the token contract’s hook is maliciously crafted. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions – collateral is assumed to be locked for the duration of a loan – leading to potential loss of funds for lenders and erosion of trust in the protocol. To remediate, the external call should be moved after all state changes, or a re‑entrancy guard modifier should be applied, thereby enforcing the checks‑effects‑interaction pattern and ensuring that collateral cannot be withdrawn before the loan status is finalized. This class of bug is a classic re‑entrancy vulnerability where state updates are performed after external calls, violating the invariant that assets remain locked for the duration of an operation. From a user’s perspective, a lender may see a loan being approved and funded while the NFT that was supposed to back it is no longer in the contract, resulting in an unexpected zero balance of collateral and a loan that should not exist.

title: M-4 A swap with permit can be blocked if a frontrunner swaps using copied permit
description:
Facade does not check that msg.sender is the owner of a permit.
So, a frontrunner can use permits of other users available from mempool, so that their transactions would
revert (as permit are used by the frontrunner).
• SwapFacade.sol#L58-L64
A user will receive revert and will have to build new calldata, without permit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ownership verification for ERC20 permits used in a swap façade. When a user supplies a signed permit to approve token transfer, the façade forwards the permit to the token contract without checking that the caller of the swap function is the same address that created the permit. The root cause is an oversight in the input validation logic: the contract trusts the permit data but does not extract the permit's owner field and compare it to msg.sender. An attacker monitoring the mempool can copy a pending transaction that contains a valid permit, submit a front‑running transaction that consumes the same permit, and cause the original user’s transaction to revert because the permit has already been used. This exploit can be carried out whenever a user includes a permit in a swap call, which is a common pattern for gas‑optimized approvals. The affected parties are the end‑users who rely on permits for seamless swaps and the protocol that promises friction‑less trading; they experience failed swaps, unexpected reverts, and additional gas costs because they must rebuild the calldata without the permit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the swap façade source code, where the auditor noted that the function handling permits does not perform any ownership check. It can be hard to notice because the transaction simply reverts with a generic error, offering no clear indication that the permit was front‑run rather than malformed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style disruption: users cannot complete their intended swap on the first attempt, leading to a poor user experience and potential loss of confidence, although no direct theft of funds occurs. To remediate, the contract should decode the permit, extract the owner address, and assert that msg.sender matches this owner before forwarding the permit to the token contract. This pattern is used by established aggregators such as 1inch, where the SafeERC20 library includes an explicit ownership check. Implementing this check restores the intended security property that only the permit issuer can authorize a transfer on its behalf, preventing front‑runners from hijacking permits and blocking legitimate swaps.

title: M-5 Unprotected access to makeCheckpoint() in SwapGuardV2
description:
SwapGuardV2 functions are planned to be used as separate calls in a set of swaps. However, if during the
swaps process a hacker manages to get a callback to their own contract (for example, if the victim
operates with ERC-777 tokens), the hacker can call public accessible function makeCheckpoint() to
modify the SwapGuardV2 state so that the ensureCheckpoint() function at the victim's end would not
work correctly.
SwapGuardV2.sol#L20
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unprotected public function named makeCheckpoint in the SwapGuardV2 contract. Because the function has no access control, any external address can invoke it at any time. SwapGuardV2 is intended to be used as a helper that records token balances before a series of swaps, then later verifies that the balances have not been altered by calling ensureCheckpoint. The design assumes that only the contract itself will call makeCheckpoint, but the public visibility breaks this assumption. If a swap involves a token that can trigger a callback – for example an ERC‑777 token that executes a user‑provided hook during transfer – an attacker can cause their contract to be called in the middle of the swap process. During that callback the attacker can invoke makeCheckpoint and deliberately modify the stored checkpoint data. When the protocol later calls ensureCheckpoint, the verification will compare the current balances against the attacker‑controlled checkpoint, causing the check to succeed even though the real balances have been changed. This allows the attacker to bypass the guard, potentially moving tokens out of the victim’s account or causing the protocol to accept an invalid state. The impact is that users performing swaps may see their expected balances unchanged while the protocol believes the swap was safe, leading to loss of funds or accounting inconsistencies. The issue occurs only when a malicious token can invoke external code during a transfer, but any token that provides a similar callback mechanism could be exploited. The affected parties are the end‑users who rely on the swap service, the protocol that assumes the guard is trustworthy, and any role that manages token balances. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, where the public visibility of makeCheckpoint stood out as a deviation from the intended internal‑only usage. It can be hard to notice because the function does not perform any token movement itself and appears harmless in isolation; the problem only manifests when combined with a re‑entrancy‑capable token. To remediate, the contract should either make makeCheckpoint internal or protect it with proper access control, and preferably redesign the guard so that a single function records balances in memory, invokes the user‑provided callback, and then checks the balances before any state is persisted. This eliminates the window where an attacker can tamper with the checkpoint and restores the intended safety guarantees of the swap process.

title: M-6 Incorrect hardcoded address
description:
During the deployment of SwapExecutorArbitrum two addresses are hardcoded:
• uniswapV3Factory as 0x1F98431c8aD98523631AE4a59f267346ea31F984
• sushiV3Factory as 0xbACEB8eC6b9355Dfc0269C18bac9d6E2Bdc29C4F
SwapExecutorArbitrum.sol#L12
However, the sushiV3Factory address is incorrect as there is no such smart contract deployed on
Arbitrum:
• 0xbACEB8...Bdc29C4F
The correct address is:
• 0x1af415...3D82231e
Sushi Docs:
• https://dev.sushi.com/docs/Products/V3 AMM/Core/Deployment Addresses
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect hard‑coded deployment address for the SushiSwap V3 factory in the SwapExecutorArbitrum contract. The source code embeds the constant 0xbACEB8eC6b9355Dfc0269C18bac9d6E2Bdc29C4F as sushiV3Factory, but on the Arbitrum network no contract exists at that location. The contract assumes the address points to a valid factory and uses it to create or interact with Sushi V3 pools when executing a swap. Because the address is wrong, any call that routes through the Sushi V3 factory reverts or becomes a no‑op, causing the swap execution to fail silently or to revert after the user has already transferred tokens to the executor. From a user's perspective the transaction may appear successful in the UI, but the expected output – a received token amount or a refund – is missing, leading to a perception that funds have disappeared or that a refund was not received. The issue occurs only when the executor attempts to use the Sushi V3 path; operations that rely on the Uniswap V3 factory continue to work. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the hard‑coded addresses against the official Sushi documentation for Arbitrum. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles without error and the incorrect address does not raise a compile‑time warning; the failure only manifests at runtime when the specific function is called. This class of bug belongs to misconfiguration or hard‑coded address errors, where a contract references a non‑existent external contract, breaking business logic that assumes the external component is available. The impact is a loss of functionality and potential user frustration, as swaps intended to go through Sushi V3 cannot be completed and users may need to resend transactions or abandon the operation. The recommended remediation is to replace the hard‑coded address with the correct Sushi V3 factory address for Arbitrum (0x1af415a1EbA07a4986a52B6f2e7dE7003D82231e) or to set the variable to address(0) and guard the code path so that Sushi V3 is not used when the address is unset.

title: M-1 Facade allows any unauthorized Executor
description:
SwapFacade allows to choose any SwapExecutor address, even not authored by the team. Fees are
charged on SwapExecutor. So, it is rational to fork SwapExecutor with zero fees and choose it as an
executor for swaps.
• SwapFacade.sol#L87
Some other possible scenarios:
• users can choose out of date executors
• users can choose executors with bugs
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SwapFacade contract, which accepts an arbitrary address as the SwapExecutor for each swap operation. Because the contract does not enforce any whitelist or ownership check on the executor address, any user can supply a malicious or unintended executor contract. The root cause is the absence of access control that ties the executor to a trusted list maintained by the protocol team. An attacker can deploy a custom SwapExecutor that overrides the fee logic, for example by setting the fee to zero, and then pass the address of this contract to SwapFacade when initiating a swap. When the facade forwards the call, the custom executor processes the swap without charging the protocol’s expected fee, resulting in lost revenue. Additionally, users may unintentionally select outdated executors that contain known bugs, or executors that behave incorrectly, leading to failed swaps, unexpected token balances, or other undesirable outcomes. The issue manifests whenever a swap is performed through the facade’s function that takes an executor address as a parameter; under these conditions the protocol cannot guarantee that the executor adheres to the intended fee schedule or functional correctness. The affected parties include the protocol (which loses fee income), token holders who rely on accurate fee calculations, and any third‑party integrators that assume swaps are executed by vetted contracts. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s external interfaces and noted the lack of validation on the executor argument. Because the contract simply forwards the address without checks, the problem can be subtle and may not be evident from normal usage or UI feedback, especially if the malicious executor mimics the interface of a legitimate one. To remediate the issue, the facade should maintain an explicit list of authorized executor contracts and enforce that only addresses on this list can be used. Fee collection should also be performed directly in the facade or verified against the executor’s fee configuration, ensuring that the protocol’s economic model cannot be bypassed. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked external contract reference or missing whitelist validation, which can lead to fee bypass, functional regression, or broader security implications when untrusted code is executed in the context of a privileged contract.

title: M-2 Anyone can withdraw funds left on SwapExecutor
description:
Funds left on the SwapExecutor can be withdrawn by anyone who specifies a transfer call in the swaps.
There are multiple reasons why funds may be left on the SwapExecutor:
1. A user may not set the tokenRatio to 100% in a swap.
```solidity
uint256 poolSwapAmount = (balanceToSwap * swap.tokenRatio) / _ONE;
```
sum (tokenRatio) > _ONE - is not risky, revert happens
sum (tokenRatio) < _ONE - is risky, as some tokens
are left not swapped and can be taken by anyone.
2. The SwapExecutor may run arbitrary calls to protocols that reward it with additional tokens. The
SwapFacade only checks the tokenToTransfer, and a user may forget to transfer other tokens
from the SwapExecutor immediately.
3. If a user transfers tokens to the SwapExecutor first and then runs the SwapFacade.swap()
function in a separate transaction.
• SwapExecutor.sol#L58
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted withdrawal path that allows any address to extract tokens that remain on the SwapExecutor contract after a swap operation. The root cause is that the swap logic does not enforce that the sum of tokenRatio values used in a multi‑step swap equals the full scaling factor (ONE), so when the combined tokenRatio is lower than ONE a portion of the input tokens is never swapped and stays locked in the executor. In addition, the SwapExecutor can execute arbitrary external calls that may credit it with extra tokens, and the surrounding SwapFacade only validates the primary tokenToTransfer, ignoring any secondary tokens that may be received. Because there is no access control on the function that moves tokens out of the executor, an attacker can simply craft a swap that leaves residual balances and then invoke a transfer to move those tokens to an address of their choice. The issue manifests when a user either sets a tokenRatio below 100%, performs swaps that involve external protocol calls that reward the executor, or splits the token transfer and swap into separate transactions, leaving the executor with a non‑zero balance. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a swap the expected amount is not received, balances appear unchanged or suddenly zero, and an unexpected withdrawal can be observed from the executor contract. The impact is a loss of funds for token holders and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as the protocol assumes that all supplied assets are either swapped or returned to the user. The problem was identified during a manual audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of token handling was examined and the missing validation of tokenRatio sums and missing withdrawal restrictions were noted. The flaw can be hard to detect because leftover balances may be small, the contract does not emit explicit events for residual tokens, and the code only checks for tokenRatio exceeding ONE (which triggers a revert) but not for it being below ONE. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that the total tokenRatio across all swap steps exactly equals ONE, restrict execution of swaps and any token‑moving functions to a whitelist of trusted manager contracts (as done in CowProtocol), and add a final sweep that automatically transfers any remaining tokens back to the initiator or a designated vault. Additionally, the SwapFacade should verify that no unexpected token balances remain after each external call, and the executor should disallow arbitrary withdrawals by non‑authorized parties, thereby restoring the intended accounting invariants and protecting user funds.

title: M-3 ETH value above limited value can be lost
bug_full: SwapExecutor contains a logic branch that capsthe amount of ETH forwarded to a target contract. When the caller supplies an ETH value that exceeds the configured valueLimit, the code replaces the supplied value with valueLimit before performing a low-level call. The excess amount (original value minus valueLimit) is never forwarded and remains in the SwapExecutor balance. Because the contract does not provide a dedicated mechanism to return or account for this leftover ETH, the funds become effectively locked. Any external address can later invoke the contract’s withdrawal routine and extract the accumulated excess, meaning that the contract can be used as a sink for unintended ETH. The vulnerability is triggered whenever a transaction sends more ETH than the limit, which can happen in normal user operations (e.g., a user expects to swap 5 ETH but the limit is 2 ETH). From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the swap succeeded, yet the received amount is lower than expected and the user’s wallet shows a missing portion of ETH with no refund. The root cause is an accounting mismatch: the contract assumes that capping the value is sufficient, but it fails to handle the surplus, violating the business rule that all sent funds must either be used in the swap or returned to the sender. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the SwapExecutor source code, where the conditional truncation of the value was noted without accompanying logic to reclaim the remainder. Because the excess ETH is silently retained, the problem can be hard to notice unless the auditor checks the contract’s balance after multiple over-limit calls. To remediate, the design should either reject transactions that exceed the limit, forward the full amount and enforce the limit elsewhere, or explicitly refund the surplus to the caller, ensuring that no ETH can be unintentionally trapped.

title: M-4 A swap with permit can be blocked if a frontrunner swaps using copied permit
description:
Facade does not check that msg.sender is the owner of a permit.
So, a frontrunner can use permits of other users available from mempool, so that their transactions would
revert (as permit are used by the frontrunner).
• SwapFacade.sol#L58-L64
A user will receive revert and will have to build new calldata, without permit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ownership verification for token permits used in a swap facade. A permit is an off‑chain signature that authorises a contract to transfer a user’s tokens without a prior approval transaction. In the current implementation the facade accepts a permit supplied in the calldata but never checks that the caller (msg.sender) is the address that created the signature. Because of this omission a malicious actor monitoring the mempool can copy the permit from a victim’s pending transaction and submit a front‑running transaction that consumes the same permit. When the victim’s transaction is later mined, the permit has already been used or is considered invalid, causing the swap call to revert. The exploit occurs whenever a user includes a permit in a swap request; the attacker only needs to see the permit data in the pending transaction and act before it is mined. The impact is that legitimate users experience failed swaps, lose the gas spent on the reverted transaction, and must rebuild the calldata without the permit or wait for a new block. No funds are stolen directly, but the denial‑of‑service effect can erode confidence in the protocol and increase transaction costs for users. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, which noted that the contract does not compare the permit’s signer with msg.sender. It can be hard to notice because the permit data looks like any other parameter and the contract does not emit a specific error indicating a mismatched owner; developers may assume that the permit’s signature implicitly ties it to the caller. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization checks” or “signature replay without sender validation”. To remediate, the facade should decode the permit, extract the address that signed it, and enforce that this address equals msg.sender before proceeding with the swap. This pattern is demonstrated in the SafeERC20 library used by 1inch, where the permit handling includes an explicit owner check. Implementing such a check restores the intended security model where only the permit owner can authorize token transfers, preventing front‑runners from hijacking or blocking legitimate swaps.

title: M-5 Unprotected access to makeCheckpoint() in SwapGuardV2
description:
SwapGuardV2 functions are planned to be used as separate calls in a set of swaps. However, if during the
swaps process a hacker manages to get a callback to their own contract (for example, if the victim
operates with ERC-777 tokens), the hacker can call public accessible function makeCheckpoint() to
modify the SwapGuardV2 state so that the ensureCheckpoint() function at the victim's end would not
work correctly.
SwapGuardV2.sol#L20
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unprotected public function named makeCheckpoint in the SwapGuardV2 contract that can be invoked by any external address. The contract was designed to use SwapGuardV2 as a series of separate calls during a multi‑step token swap, where makeCheckpoint records the current token balances and ensureCheckpoint later verifies that those balances have not changed unexpectedly. Because makeCheckpoint is public, an attacker who can trigger a callback during the swap—such as when the protocol interacts with ERC‑777 tokens that invoke a hook on the recipient—can call makeCheckpoint from their malicious contract before the original swap finishes. This call overwrites the stored checkpoint state, causing ensureCheckpoint to compare against a falsified baseline. As a result, the protocol fails to detect that token balances have been altered, allowing the attacker to siphon funds or cause the swap to complete with an incorrect accounting outcome. The issue manifests when a user initiates a swap that involves a token capable of reentrancy, and the attacker’s contract receives the callback. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful swap while the received token amount is lower than expected, or the balance may appear to drop to zero, violating the expectation that a swap either completes fully or reverts. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external function exposure combined with reentrancy, where internal state intended for internal bookkeeping is exposed to arbitrary callers. It was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which examined the contract’s call flow and identified that makeCheckpoint lacked any access control. The problem can be hard to notice because the function appears harmless and is not directly involved in token transfers, so typical testing may not trigger the reentrancy scenario. The recommended remediation is to redesign the guard so that the checkpointing and user callback are performed within a single internal function that records balances in memory, executes the callback, and then validates the balances, or to restrict makeCheckpoint to internal or onlyOwner visibility, thereby eliminating the external manipulation vector.

title: M-1 Facade allows any unauthorized Executor
description:
SwapFacade allows to choose any SwapExecutor address, even not authored by the team. Fees are
charged on SwapExecutor. So, it is rational to fork SwapExecutor with zero fees and choose it as an
executor for swaps.
• SwapFacade.sol#L87
Some other possible scenarios:
• users can choose out of date executors
• users can choose executors with bugs
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SwapFacade contract, which accepts an arbitrary address as the SwapExecutor for each swap operation. Because the facade does not enforce any whitelist or access‑control check on the executor, any external contract – including ones deployed by third parties – can be supplied as the executor. The fee mechanism is implemented inside the executor contract, so when a user selects a custom executor that omits or modifies the fee logic, the protocol’s expected fee revenue is bypassed. This design flaw allows an attacker to fork the official executor, set the fee to zero, or introduce buggy or malicious behavior, and then have users unknowingly route swaps through that contract. Exploitation occurs when a user calls the swap function and provides the address of a malicious or outdated executor; the facade forwards the call without validation, the executor performs the token exchange, and either no fee is collected or the swap may fail or produce incorrect output. The impact includes loss of fee income for the protocol, potential user loss if the executor behaves incorrectly, and erosion of trust because users cannot be sure that the swap will be executed by a vetted component. The condition for the bug to manifest is any swap transaction that includes an executor parameter – which the current interface permits – and the affected parties are the protocol (fee revenue), its users (possible incorrect swap results or loss of funds), and any role that relies on the integrity of the swapping service. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s external calls and noted the absence of a permitted‑executor list. It can be hard to notice because the function signature appears normal and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when an unknown executor is used. The recommended remediation is to introduce a maintained list of authorized executors on the SwapFacade and to move fee collection to the facade itself, ensuring that only vetted executors can be called and that the protocol always receives its fee regardless of the executor’s internal implementation. This class of bug is a whitelist‑bypass or unchecked external contract reference, which violates the business assumption that only approved components will handle fee logic and token accounting, leading to scenarios where "funds disappear" from the protocol’s fee pool or users receive unexpected zero balances or failed swaps.

title: M-2 Anyone can withdraw funds left on SwapExecutor
description:
Funds left on the SwapExecutor can be withdrawn by anyone who specifies a transfer call in the swaps.
There are multiple reasons why funds may be left on the SwapExecutor:
1. A user may not set the tokenRatio to 100% in a swap.
```solidity
uint256 poolSwapAmount = (balanceToSwap * swap.tokenRatio) / _ONE;
```
sum (tokenRatio) > _ONE - is not risky, revert happens
sum (tokenRatio) < _ONE - is risky, as some tokens
are left not swapped and can be taken by anyone.
2. The SwapExecutor may run arbitrary calls to protocols that reward it with additional tokens. The
SwapFacade only checks the tokenToTransfer, and a user may forget to transfer other tokens
from the SwapExecutor immediately.
3. If a user transfers tokens to the SwapExecutor first and then runs the SwapFacade.swap()
function in a separate transaction.
• SwapExecutor.sol#L58
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of token balances inside the SwapExecutor component of the protocol. When a swap is executed, the contract calculates the amount to be swapped using a tokenRatio parameter. If the sum of all tokenRatio values for a given swap is less than 100 % (the constant _ONE), a portion of the input tokens remains unswapped and stays in the SwapExecutor. The contract does not enforce that the total tokenRatio equals 100 %, nor does it restrict who can invoke a transfer call on the residual balance. Consequently, any user can craft a swap that includes a call to transfer the leftover tokens to an address of their choosing. Additionally, the SwapExecutor can receive arbitrary tokens from external protocol calls (for example, reward tokens) and the SwapFacade only checks a single tokenToTransfer field, allowing other tokens to remain in the executor unchecked. If a user sends tokens to the SwapExecutor in one transaction and calls the swap function in a later transaction, the same residual balance issue can arise. An attacker can therefore exploit these accounting gaps by submitting a swap that deliberately leaves tokens behind and then withdrawing them, effectively stealing funds that belong to honest users or the protocol. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome is that all supplied tokens are either swapped or returned; instead the UI may show a successful swap while the contract still holds a hidden amount, and the attacker can later move those tokens out, resulting in missing balances or unexpected zero refunds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of tokenRatio aggregation and the lack of access control on transfer calls were identified as risky. The problem is subtle because the leftover amounts can be small and are not directly visible in standard transaction logs, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that the sum of tokenRatio values for any swap equals 100 % before execution, and it should restrict transfer operations on the SwapExecutor to a whitelist of trusted manager contracts, similar to the approach used in CowProtocol. A final sweep of any residual tokens should be limited to the intended recipient, and comprehensive accounting checks should be added to ensure no unexpected token balances remain after a swap.

title: M-3 ETH value above limited value can be lost
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a logic block that caps the amount of native ether forwarded to a downstream contract when the supplied value exceeds a predefined limit. The code checks if the supplied ether amount is greater than a configurable threshold and, if so, replaces the amount with the threshold before invoking the target contract via a low‑level call. The excess ether – the difference between the original amount and the threshold – is never transferred and remains locked in the executor contract. Because the contract does not provide any mechanism to return or correctly account for this surplus, the trapped ether becomes effectively lost to the original sender. Moreover, the contract’s withdrawal function does not restrict who can claim these excess funds, allowing any address to withdraw the accumulated surplus. This can be exploited by a malicious actor who deliberately sends a transaction with an ether value higher than the limit, causing the surplus to be retained in the contract and later withdrawn by the attacker. The impact is a reduction of user funds: a user expects the full amount of ether they supplied to be forwarded or used in a swap, but only the limited portion is actually processed, resulting in a shortfall that appears as missing balance or a zero‑refund situation. The issue manifests whenever the executor is called with an ether amount that exceeds the configured limit, which may happen in edge cases such as large swaps, rounding errors, or maliciously crafted inputs. All participants who interact with the executor – including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes that the full supplied amount is either forwarded or correctly accounted for. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the value handling logic and identified that the excess ether is neither forwarded nor accounted for, and that the withdrawal path lacks proper access control. The problem can be subtle because the transaction may succeed without reverting, giving the impression that the operation completed normally, while the hidden loss only becomes visible when users check their balances or when the surplus accumulates. To remediate the issue, the contract should either reject transactions that exceed the limit, forward the full amount, or implement a safe accounting mechanism that either refunds the surplus to the sender or securely stores it with restricted access. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “value capping with unhandled remainder” or “improper fund forwarding” vulnerabilities, where a capped transfer leads to trapped assets and potential unauthorized extraction.

title: PreimageOracle.loadPrecompilePreimagePart an outOfGas error in the precompile will overwrite cor- rect preimageParts
description:
Alexis Williams from Coinbase initially identified this issue in the loadPrecompilePreimagePart function during the engagement with Spearbit. The function calls any _precompile passed as a parameter for a given _input.

```solidity
function loadPrecompilePreimagePart(
    uint256 _partOffset,
    address _precompile,
    bytes calldata _input
) external
```

The _partOffset variable defines which 32 bytes of the precompile returned result will be stored in a preimageParts mapping. The key for the mapping is based on a keccak hash, including the _precompile address and _input parameter. The function is public and can be called multiple times. A call with the same parameters should produce again the same key and state updates.

If the precompile call reverts, the returned error would be stored in the preimageParts mapping instead. The transaction itself would be successful (see the related test).

An attacker could call loadPrecompilePreimagePart with less gas to produce an outOfGas error in the precompile. The 63/64 gas rule applies for staticcall and precompiles even when all the available gas() passed as parameter.

```solidity
// Call the precompile to get the result.
res := staticcall(
    gas(), // forward all gas
    _precompile,
    add(20, ptr), // input ptr
    _input.length,
    0x0, // Unused as we don't copy anything
    0x00 // don't copy anything
)
```

The loadPrecompilePreimagePart function can have enough gas left to update preimageParts mapping with the outOfGas error. This means a successful preimage result can be overwritten with the outOfGas error for some _partOffset in the preimageParts mapping. Given that the correct preimageParts mapping is needed to reproduce the VM.step in a FaultDisputeGame.step it can lead to an incorrect outcome.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑gas (OOG) overwrite bug in a function that loads a precompile result into a mapping of preimage parts. The function forwards all available gas to a staticcall of an arbitrary precompile and then stores the 32‑byte slice identified by a part offset into a mapping whose key is derived from the precompile address and the input data. Because the code does not check the success flag returned by staticcall, a precompile that reverts due to OOG still allows the surrounding function to continue execution and write a value into the mapping. When the precompile runs out of gas, the EVM returns a failure flag but also provides an error code that the caller mistakenly records as the preimage part. Consequently a previously correct preimage entry can be silently overwritten with an error value. This can be triggered by an attacker who calls the function with deliberately low gas, causing the precompile to hit the 63/64 gas rule and revert, while the caller still has enough gas left to update storage. The bug manifests only when the function is called multiple times with the same parameters; the second call with insufficient gas replaces the correct slice, leading to a corrupted preimage that later steps of a FaultDisputeGame use to reconstruct VM execution. From a user perspective the dispute may resolve incorrectly, showing unexpected zero or wrong values, and funds that should be returned in a successful dispute may be lost or withheld. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the test suite showed that a transaction succeeded even though the precompile reverted, and the mapping contained the error code. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no explicit error is emitted, and the corrupted state only becomes apparent later in the dispute logic. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call failures that corrupt on‑chain state. The proper fix is to verify the staticcall return value and revert the whole transaction if the precompile fails, or to avoid writing to the preimageParts mapping when the call was unsuccessful, thereby preserving the integrity of the preimage data required for correct dispute outcomes.

title: Invalid Ancestor Lookup Leading to Out-of-Bounds Array Access
description: When finding an ancestor via the _findTraceAncestor function, the code allows specifying the global flag, which limits the ancestor search to the split depth. When _global is set to false the function uses the _pos.traceAncestorBounded(SPLIT_DEPTH) method. This method violates an invariant assumption: "It is guaranteed that such a claim exists." In scenarios when SPLIT_DEPTH + 1 = MAX_DEPTH. The code will not be able to find a right-side node, causing the code to loop until reaching the root node. The root node, containing type(uint32).max as its parentIndex, results in an out-of-bounds array access. This issue specifically arises when the last game step is a defend action.
bug_full: When the dispute game searches for an ancestor node using the internal _findTraceAncestor function, it can be instructed to limit the search to the split depth by passing the _global flag as false. In that mode the function calls traceAncestorBounded with SPLIT_DEPTH as the bound. The implementation assumes that a claim exists at that depth – an invariant that a parent node will always be found. If the contract is configured so that SPLIT_DEPTH + 1 equals MAX_DEPTH, the bounded search reaches the right‑most leaf of the binary dispute tree and cannot locate a right‑side ancestor. The loop then continues until it reaches the root node, whose parentIndex field is set to type(uint32).max as a sentinel value. Because the code later uses this parentIndex to index into the internal array of nodes without checking the sentinel, the array access is performed with an index of 2^32‑1, which is outside the bounds of the array. The out‑of‑bounds access triggers a Solidity panic and causes the transaction to revert. The bug manifests specifically when the final step of a game is a defend action, because that is the point at which the bounded ancestor lookup is performed. Users who attempt to defend the last claim see their transaction revert with an “array out‑of‑bounds” error and any ether sent as a bond is returned to the caller by the revert, but the game state remains incomplete, potentially locking further progress. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, which exercised the contract with a test case that created a game where MAX_DEPTH was set to 2 and SPLIT_DEPTH to 1, reproducing the out‑of‑bounds panic. The problem is subtle because the invariant that a parent always exists is true for most depth configurations, so the faulty path is not exercised in normal operation and may be missed by casual testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked index errors caused by incorrect assumptions about data structure invariants. To remediate, the contract should enforce that MAX_DEPTH is strictly greater than SPLIT_DEPTH + 1 at deployment, and it should validate that any computed parent index is within the bounds of the node array before using it. Adding explicit checks or redesigning the ancestor lookup to handle the sentinel value safely would prevent the out‑of‑bounds access and ensure that the game can progress even when the split depth reaches the maximum depth.

title: An attacker with more available funds can counter an honest rootClaim defender
description:
An attacker (challenger) with more funds available than an honest rootClaim defender can win the Game with the status CHALLENGER.WINS even if the rootClaim provided by the honest defender is correct. The attacker only needs to win one subgame that goes uncountered to counter the rootClaim.

This can be achieved by opening so many subGames with different incorrect claims at the same gameTree level until the honest defender runs out of funds. The attacker would open new games at the same level (tree depth) instead of continuing to play the existing subgames closer to the leaves.

Once the honest defender has no funds left, one subgame win by the attacker due to opponent timeout is enough to counter the correct rootClaim.

We want to point out, that these are the technical mechanisms by which the honest defender would loss the rootSubGame.

From a game-theoretical perspective such an attack would cost a lot of money, since all opened subgames with incorrect claims if countered by the honest defender would result in a loss for the attacker.

The attacker could theoretically win the entire TVL available on the L2 and might be willing to lose a lot of subgames. On the other hand, anyone can support the honest defender team because it is free money to win and should incentivise to provide the required liquidity. The other parties owning the TVL on the L2 have an incentive as well to protect it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic denial‑of‑service condition in the dispute‑resolution game where a challenger who controls more liquid assets than the honest defender can force a CHALLENGER.WINS outcome even when the root claim submitted by the defender is mathematically correct. The root cause is that the game allows the challenger to open an arbitrary number of parallel subgames at the same tree depth, each containing an incorrect claim. Because each subgame requires the defender to post a bond or provide liquidity to counter the claim, the defender’s total required capital grows with the number of subgames. An attacker can deliberately flood the game with many incorrect subgames, exhausting the defender’s available funds. When the defender runs out of liquidity, any remaining subgame that the attacker wins by timeout (the defender cannot respond) is sufficient to counter the original root claim, causing the protocol to mark the root claim as invalid. This can be exploited by a well‑funded attacker who is willing to lose many individual subgames; the cost is high but may be justified if the attacker can capture the entire TVL locked on the layer‑2 chain. The impact is that honest participants who rely on the dispute mechanism to protect their assets may see their correct claims rejected, leading to loss of funds, erosion of trust, and potential draining of protocol TVL. The condition occurs whenever the game logic does not limit the number of concurrent subgames or does not enforce sufficient bonding requirements for challengers, and when the defender’s liquidity is not guaranteed. All parties that depend on the dispute game – honest claimants, protocol users, and TVL providers – are affected because the protocol’s safety guarantees are undermined. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the game‑theoretic flow and identified that the attacker’s ability to open many subgames could out‑spend the defender. It is hard to notice because each individual subgame appears to be a normal dispute and the attacker may lose many of them, making the overall attack look like normal loss rather than a coordinated exploit. To remediate, the protocol should make participation for honest defenders as frictionless as possible, provide clear documentation and tooling, and introduce economic safeguards such as limits on concurrent subgames, scaling bonds with the number of opened subgames, or automatic liquidity provisioning for defenders. Conceptually, the fix is to prevent a single actor from draining the defender’s capital by restricting how many parallel challenges can be launched and ensuring that the defender always has enough bonded funds to respond, thereby preserving the intended accounting invariants of the dispute game. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a correct claim being rejected, balances appearing to drop to zero, or refunds not being returned despite the user’s expectation of a successful dispute resolution.

title: challengeRootL2Block can be abused to block honest gamer from receiving the bond.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the dispute resolution contract where the function challengeRootL2Block can be invoked after an honest challenger has already submitted a valid challenge. The contract stores the address of the caller in a variable (l2BlockNumberChallenger) and sets a flag (l2BlockNumberChallenged). When the root claim subgame is settled, the bond distribution logic checks this flag first and, if true, unconditionally awards the bond to the stored challenger address, regardless of any prior valid challenge. This behavior originates from a design decision that treats a root‑level block number challenge as a higher‑priority counter, but the implementation does not verify whether the root claim has already been countered by another participant. An attacker can therefore submit a malicious claim with an incorrect L2 block number, wait for an honest participant to challenge it, and then immediately call challengeRootL2Block. Because the flag is set to true, the bond payout logic will always select the attacker’s address, effectively blocking the honest challenger from receiving the bond they are entitled to. The exploit can be carried out by any user who can observe the pending challenge transaction and react within the same block or before the root claim is resolved. The impact is that honest gamers lose the security bond that should compensate them for correctly disputing an invalid claim, leading to financial loss and erosion of trust in the dispute game mechanism. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DisputeGame contract where the bond distribution branch was examined and the unconditional priority rule was noted. It can be hard to notice because the code path is only exercised for root claims and the flag manipulation appears innocuous; typical test cases may not include a scenario where a challenger and a block‑number challenger act in succession. The bug belongs to the class of priority override or unconditional reward redirection vulnerabilities, where a later action can overwrite earlier entitlement without proper checks. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after successfully challenging a claim, the user’s wallet receives no bond payout and the balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the bond should be transferred to the challenger. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that only one party can be designated as the bond recipient for a given root claim, for example by checking whether the claim has already been countered before allowing challengeRootL2Block to set the flag, or by merging the two challenge mechanisms into a single, mutually exclusive decision. Alternatively, the bond distribution logic could prioritize the first valid counter rather than the special block‑number challenger, or require explicit consent from the original challenger before overriding the payout. Implementing these checks restores the intended accounting guarantees that a correct challenge yields a bond reward.

title: Subscriptions Tokens Distinguish Functionality Is Broken
description: The function _processNativePayment() will be called only in case the sub.erc20TokensValid is false, and this condition will only be met if the input _erc20Token address is set to address(0). Therefore, the user could add a different token other than ERC20, such as an address of a malicious contract or any other standard. This could lead to unexpected behavior.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the subscription contract decides which payment routine to invoke. The internal flag sub.erc20TokensValid is set to false only when the supplied token address equals the zero address, and the contract assumes that any non‑zero address represents a valid ERC‑20 token. Consequently, there is no explicit verification that the address actually implements the ERC‑20 interface. When a subscriber registers a subscription with an address that is not zero but also not a genuine ERC‑20 contract—such as a malicious contract or a contract adhering to a different standard—the contract will still call the ERC‑20 payment handler. This mismatch can cause the payment function to interact with an unexpected contract, leading to reverts, loss of funds, or execution of attacker‑controlled code. The impact is that users may see their subscription payment fail silently, receive no tokens, or have funds locked in a contract that does not honor the expected transfer semantics. The issue manifests whenever a subscription is created with a token address that is not zero but is also not a compliant ERC‑20 token, a condition that can be triggered by an attacker supplying a crafted address. All participants who rely on the subscription service—subscribers, the protocol, and the dApp owner—are affected because the business logic that guarantees correct payment processing is broken. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit that employed fuzzing to register a subscription with a deliberately invalid token address, observing that the contract reverted instead of safely rejecting the input. The problem is subtle because the code path works correctly for legitimate ERC‑20 tokens, making the missing validation easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce explicit token validation, for example by maintaining a whitelist of approved ERC‑20 token addresses that the dApp is willing to accept, or by using interface detection mechanisms such as ERC‑165 where applicable, and by falling back to the native payment handler only when the token address is explicitly recognised as unsupported. This ensures that only verified ERC‑20 tokens trigger the ERC‑20 payment routine, preventing malicious or incompatible contracts from being processed as payments and preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the subscription system.

title: It's not possible to execute a rewards migration of a BatonFarm
description: The BatonFarm contract which is an external dependency of the Nft contract (a BatonFarm is deployed in seedYieldFarm) has a migration mechanism to move the unearned rewards to a new contract. This functionality is currently blocked, because it depends on a call from the BatonFarm owner (the Nft contract in this case) to the initiateMigration method of BatonFarm. Since such a call is not possible as there is no code for it, migrations are currently impossible in the system. This means that if there are rewards left in a BatonFarm contract deployed by some Nft contract, they will be stuck there forever.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the rewards migration mechanism of the BatonFarm contract cannot be executed because the contract that owns BatonFarm (the NFT contract) does not contain any code that calls BatonFarm.initiateMigration. The migration function is intended to transfer any unearned reward balance from an existing BatonFarm instance to a newly deployed contract, but because the required external call is missing, the function is effectively dead. As a result, whenever a BatonFarm instance holds leftover rewards at the time a migration is planned, those tokens remain locked in the original contract forever. This situation can be triggered whenever the system attempts to upgrade or replace a BatonFarm deployment, which is a normal operational scenario for the platform. The affected parties are the users who have earned rewards through the NFT‑linked farm, as well as the protocol that expects to be able to reallocate unclaimed rewards during upgrades. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the seedYieldFarm integration, where the auditor noted that the migration flow described in the documentation had no corresponding call in the NFT contract code. Because the failure is silent – no revert or error is emitted – it can be hard to notice; the UI may simply show that a migration transaction succeeded while the reward balance stays unchanged. The impact is a loss of economic value: users may never receive the pending rewards, effectively causing funds to disappear from the perspective of the user. The bug belongs to the class of “inaccessible state due to missing external call” or “dead code path preventing asset migration”. To remediate, the NFT contract (or another privileged admin) should be extended with a function that invokes BatonFarm.initiateMigration, or the BatonFarm contract should expose a public migration entry that can be called directly by an authorized address. This change restores the intended accounting flow, allowing unearned rewards to be transferred to the new farm contract and preventing permanent lock‑up.

title: Possible front-running griefing attack on NFT creations
description: The create method in BatonLaunchpad calls the cloneDeterministically method from LibClone that uses the create2 opcode. The create method also has a salt parameter that is passed to the cloneDeterministically call. A malicious actor can front-run every call to create and use the same salt argument. This will result in reverts of all user transactions, as there is already a contract at the address that create2 tries to deploy to.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running griefing flaw in the NFT creation flow of the BatonLaunchpad contract. The contract’s create function delegates to LibClone.cloneDeterministically, which uses the CREATE2 opcode together with a user‑supplied salt to deploy a minimal proxy for each new NFT. Because the salt is supplied directly by the caller and does not incorporate any unique identifier such as the caller’s address, an attacker can observe a pending create transaction, submit their own transaction with the identical salt, and cause the CREATE2 deployment to succeed first. CREATE2 guarantees that a contract address is deterministic based on the deploying address, the salt and the init‑code; once a contract exists at that address, any subsequent CREATE2 with the same parameters reverts with an address‑already‑in‑use error. Consequently, every legitimate user transaction that later tries to create an NFT with the same salt will revert, preventing the NFT from being minted and causing the user to lose the gas spent on the failed transaction.
