Because the reward pool is transferred to the contract before the claim function is called, any address that submits a deposit transaction immediately before invoking claim will be treated as if it had been staking for the same number of blocks as earlier participants. An attacker can therefore submit a deposit transaction in the same block (or just before the claim transaction) and then call claim, receiving a reward that is mathematically identical to that earned by users who have been staking for many blocks. The impact is that legitimate stakers receive a reduced share of the reward pool, potentially receiving zero net gain, while the front‑runner extracts the full reward and can immediately withdraw the underlying collateral. This situation erodes the economic incentive to stake, as users observe that their long‑term deposits are not rewarded proportionally to time, leading to loss of confidence in the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any period when the reward distribution is triggered after the contract holds a reward balance and before it enforces a time‑weighted accounting of each depositor’s share. All participants who rely on the staking contract – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the reward pool is depleted unfairly. The issue was discovered during a unit‑test audit where two accounts (Bob and Alice) deposited at different block heights; the test showed that Alice, who deposited only moments before the claim, received exactly the same amount of reward as Bob, who had been staking for 100 blocks. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external interface does not expose the duration of each stake, making the reward calculation appear correct at a glance; only a detailed inspection of the reward‑allocation logic reveals the missing time factor. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a time‑weighted reward allocation algorithm, such as accruing rewards per block per staked token and tracking each user’s accumulated share over time, ensuring that rewards are proportional to both the amount staked and the length of the staking period. In user‑facing terms, a staker who expects to earn a higher return for locking assets for many days may instead see the same small reward as a user who deposited a fraction of a second before claiming, or may notice that their balance after claim is unchanged while another user walks away with the full reward. This violates the core business logic that staking rewards compensate users for the risk of locking capital over time, effectively allowing “funds disappear” from honest participants and “reward calculation error” for the protocol.

title: Lender contract can be drained by re-entrancy in `refinance` (collateral)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the lender contract’s refinance logic that can be exploited when the collateral token supports a callback on transfer, such as ERC777 or any custom ERC20 that overrides _afterTokenTransfer. In the refinance function, when a borrower requests a lower amount of collateral than currently locked, the contract first transfers the excess collateral back to the borrower using IERC20.transfer and only afterwards updates the loan’s internal state. Because the transfer call invokes the token’s hook, the attacker’s contract can execute its tokensReceived callback while the lender’s state is still reflecting the old, higher collateral amount. Inside this callback the attacker calls lender.refinance again, causing the contract to repeat the transfer of excess collateral before the state is corrected. By looping this re‑entered call until the lender’s collateral balance is exhausted, the attacker drains all tokens from the pool. The bug occurs only with tokens that allow re‑entrant calls on transfer and only when the refinance path reduces collateral; normal transfers of standard ERC20 tokens are not affected. From a user’s perspective the borrower sees the expected reduction in collateral but the pool’s balance unexpectedly becomes zero, and the attacker ends up with a large amount of the collateral token and any loan tokens held by the pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the refinance implementation and identified the missing Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. It is hard to notice because the transfer appears legitimate and the token’s callback is not obvious from the lender’s code. The flaw violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the contract’s internal state always reflects the actual token balances after an external call. The recommended mitigation is to follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: update the loan’s collateral amount before performing any external token transfer, and protect the function with a nonReentrant modifier or otherwise block re‑entrancy. Using tokens without transfer hooks or explicitly disallowing such tokens can also eliminate the attack surface.

title: Some ERC20 tokens would revert on zero value fee transfers.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the repayment logic of a generic ERC20‑based lending pool that does not verify the amount of protocol fee before invoking a token transfer. When the internal _calculateInterest routine returns a protocolInterest value of zero, the contract still executes IERC20(loanToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, feeReceiver, protocolInterest). While most ERC20 tokens silently accept a zero‑value transfer, some implementations – notably the LEND token – deliberately revert on such calls. Because the protocol permits any ERC20 token to be used as collateral, a borrower can trigger a repayment transaction that attempts to move a zero‑valued fee, causing the entire repay function to revert. This can be reproduced by configuring loan parameters (rate, time, debt) so that the computed interest and consequently the fee become zero, a situation that is not prevented by the pool’s parameter validation which only caps the upper bound of the interest rate. The exploit does not require malicious code; it merely exploits the arithmetic edge case where the fee calculation yields zero. When the revert occurs, the borrower sees a transaction failure, the loan remains outstanding, and the expected fee transfer never happens, effectively locking the repayment path and potentially causing a denial‑of‑service for that loan. Users, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the loan cannot be closed, funds may remain tied up, and the protocol’s reliability is questioned. The issue was uncovered through fuzz‑testing that generated zero‑fee scenarios and observed the failing assertion. It is subtle because zero‑value transfers are usually considered a no‑op, so developers may not anticipate a revert, especially when supporting arbitrary tokens. The proper mitigation is to treat zero‑fee transfers as a no‑op by adding a conditional check (if protocolInterest > 0) before calling transferFrom, or by using a safe transfer wrapper that gracefully handles zero amounts. This change aligns the contract with the expected business logic that fees are optional and should not cause a repayment to fail when they are zero.

title: Rounding error leads to borrowing loans without paying interest
description:
There is a rounding error when calculating the interest and fees in the Lender::_calculateInterest() if the loan token (debt) has too small decimals. As a result, a borrower (or attacker) can borrow loans without paying interest.

The _calculateInterest() calculates the interest (lenderInterest) and fees (protocolInterest) that a borrower has to pay for their loan. However, the formulas for calculating the interest and fees do not support the case that the loan token (debt) has too small decimals, leading to a rounding error.
```solidity
    function _calculateInterest(
        Loan memory l
    ) internal view returns (uint256 interest, uint256 fees) {
        uint256 timeElapsed = block.timestamp - l.startTimestamp;
        interest = (l.interestRate * l.debt * timeElapsed) / 10000 / 365 days;
        fees = (lenderFee * interest) / 10000;
        interest -= fees;
    }
```
interest (lenderInterest): https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-07-beedle/blob/658e046bda8b010a5b82d2d85e824f3823602d27/src/Lender.sol#L724  
fees (protocolInterest): https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-07-beedle/blob/658e046bda8b010a5b82d2d85e824f3823602d27/src/Lender.sol#L725

Proof of Concept  
Consider the GUSD (Gemini dollar) token, which has 2 decimals.  
l.debt: 100 GUSD  
l.interestRate: 100 (1%) per year  
timeElapsed: 86400 seconds (1 day)  
lenderFee: 100 (1%)
```solidity
interest = (l.interestRate * l.debt * timeElapsed) / 10000 / 365 days
		 = (100 * (100 * 1e2) * 86400) / 10000 / 31536000
		 = 8640 / 31536
		 = 0 (rounding down; since Solidity has no fixed-point numbers)

fees = (lenderFee * interest) / 10000
     = (100 * 0) / 10000
     = 0
```

As you can see, the resulting interest and fees will become 0 due to the rounding down since Solidity has no fixed-point numbers. Consequently, a borrower does not need to pay the lender interest or protocol interest.

As explained in the Proof of Concept section, a borrower does not need to pay the lender interest or protocol interest if the loan token (debt) has too small decimals (e.g., GUSD (Gemini dollar) has 2 decimals).

An attacker can leverage this vulnerability by borrowing a lot of short-term loan positions with a small debt. In this way, the attacker can borrow a bigger debt without paying interest.
poc:
Consider the GUSD (Gemini dollar) token, which has 2 decimals.  
l.debt: 100 GUSD  
l.interestRate: 100 (1%) per year  
timeElapsed: 86400 seconds (1 day)  
lenderFee: 100 (1%)
```solidity
interest = (l.interestRate * l.debt * timeElapsed) / 10000 / 365 days
		 = (100 * (100 * 1e2) * 86400) / 10000 / 31536000
		 = 8640 / 31536
		 = 0 (rounding down; since Solidity has no fixed-point numbers)

fees = (lenderFee * interest) / 10000
     = (100 * 0) / 10000
     = 0
```

As you can see, the resulting interest and fees will become 0 due to the rounding down since Solidity has no fixed-point numbers. Consequently, a borrower does not need to pay the lender interest or protocol interest.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the interest and fee calculation performed by the internal _calculateInterest function of the lending contract. The function multiplies the annual interest rate, the outstanding debt and the elapsed time, then divides by a fixed‑point factor (10000) and by the number of seconds in a year. Because Solidity does not support fractional numbers, the division truncates any fractional part. When the loan token has a very small number of decimals – for example a stablecoin with only two decimal places such as GUSD – the product of rate, debt and time can be smaller than the divisor, causing the whole expression to evaluate to zero. Consequently both the lender interest and the protocol fee become zero for that loan period. This occurs whenever a borrower opens a short‑term loan (e.g., one day) with a token whose decimal precision is below a threshold, and the contract does not enforce a minimum decimal requirement when the pool is created. An attacker can exploit the bug by repeatedly opening many small‑debt, short‑duration loans in a low‑decimal token, effectively borrowing large amounts of capital without ever paying interest or fees. The impact is that the protocol loses expected revenue, lenders receive no compensation, and the overall economic model is broken – users may see their loan balances unchanged while the protocol’s accounting shows no accrued interest. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the interest formula and tested it with tokens of different decimal settings. It is hard to notice because the UI typically displays the loan amount correctly and may not highlight that the accrued interest is zero; the zero value can be mistaken for a normal state, especially for short loan periods where interest is expected to be small. The root cause is the lack of fixed‑point handling and the absence of a validation step for token decimal precision. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum number of decimals for any loan token (for example three or more) when a pool is configured, or it should rewrite the interest formula using a higher‑precision arithmetic library or scaling factor that prevents truncation to zero. By ensuring that the intermediate multiplication result is large enough relative to the divisor, the calculation will produce a non‑zero interest amount even for low‑decimal tokens, preserving the intended economic incentives and preventing interest‑free borrowing.

title: Setting borrower fees to 0 permits the borrow functionality to be completely DoS
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition that arises when the protocol’s borrower fee parameter is set to zero. The borrow function calculates a fee as (debt * borrowerFee) / 10000 and transfers that amount to the fee receiver. When borrowerFee equals zero the computed fee is zero, so no tokens are taken from the borrower and no revenue is generated for the protocol. The repay function derives lender interest and protocol interest from the elapsed time; if the loan is repaid in the same block the elapsed time is zero, causing both interest and the derived fees to be zero as well. Because the protocol does not enforce a minimum fee, an attacker can front-run a legitimate borrow request, borrow the entire available balance of the pool, and immediately repay the loan in the same transaction without paying any fee. The pool is left empty for the original borrower, whose transaction reverts due to insufficient liquidity. The attacker can then back-run a repayment of his own loan, again paying zero fees, and the pool remains drained. This sequence blocks all subsequent borrow operations until new liquidity is supplied, effectively denying the core borrowing feature of the protocol. The issue is triggered only when the borrowerFee variable is allowed to be zero and when an adversary can control transaction ordering (e.g., via front-running). Users experience failed borrow attempts, see no funds transferred, and may observe the available borrow amount reported as zero in the UI. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation logic and identified that a zero fee removes the economic cost of borrowing, enabling a cheap DoS attack. The bug belongs to the class of “fee-waiver denial-of-service” or “zero-fee exploitation” where business logic assumes a non-zero fee to protect against resource exhaustion. The difficulty in spotting the issue stems from the fact that setting fees to zero is a legitimate configuration for promotional periods, and the code otherwise functions correctly. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a non-zero minimum borrower fee, or modify the interest calculation to always produce a positive fee even when borrowerFee is zero or when timeElapsed is zero, thereby making the attack economically unviable.

title: The lack of a WETH-Profits Token pair upon calling sellProfits can expose it to malicious pool creation
description:
Some tokens do not have Uniswap V3 pools with WETH, which allows a bad actor to frontrun the transaction and create a pool with an offset liquidity ratio and subsequently steal the funds.

When calling sellProfits the function calls exactInputSingle on the Uniswap V3 SwapRouter with a token pair of WETH and the profits token address from calldata. In the case of a token pair between the two not existing the call will revert. This absence of such a pool can be used maliciously by a bad actor to frontrun the call and create a pool with an offset price so they can extract the tokens.

The tokens will be mostly lost due to the bad exchange rate. This will occur very rarely due to most tokens already having Uniswap v3 pairs with WETH, hence the medium severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an absence‑of‑pair issue in the sellProfits function. The function attempts to swap a profit token for WETH by calling Uniswap V3's exactInputSingle with the token pair (WETH, profitToken). If the Uniswap V3 pool for that pair does not already exist, the call reverts. A malicious actor can observe the pending transaction, front‑run it and create a new pool with a deliberately skewed price before the contract’s call is executed. Because the contract does not verify the pool’s existence or price, the swap proceeds against the attacker‑controlled pool, delivering far fewer WETH than expected or even zero, effectively stealing the profit tokens. The impact is loss of funds for the user or the protocol; from the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction that either fails silently or returns an unexpectedly low amount of WETH, making it appear as if the funds vanished. The condition occurs only for profit tokens that lack an established WETH pool, which is rare but possible for newer or less liquid assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the swap logic and identified that no fallback or price validation is performed. It is hard to notice because the revert message does not indicate a missing pool, and the contract assumes the existence of a market‑price pool. The bug belongs to the class of “missing liquidity‑pair assumptions” or “price‑oracle‑free swap” vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts an external DEX to provide a correct price without checking that the pool is trustworthy. To remediate, the contract should avoid relying on a single direct pair; instead it can use a multihop swap path that first converts the profit token into a highly liquid stablecoin such as USDC before converting to WETH, or it should explicitly check that a pool exists and that its price is within acceptable bounds before executing the swap. Implementing these safeguards restores the expected behavior where a user who initiates sellProfits receives a fair amount of WETH and prevents an attacker from creating a malicious pool to siphon funds.

title: Undelegations from pool cannot be paused
description:
Accounts that are granted the OPERATOR or DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE role are entitled to pause multiple features of the SonicStaking contract. According to the documentation this should include, among others,  
undelegation of assets.  
However, while the undelegate function correctly implements this security mechanism to check whether undelegations are paused (by reading the undelegatePaused state variable flag), the undelegateFromPool function does not. This means that users can still undelegate assets from the pool even after an operator or admin intended to pause all types of undelegations.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing pause enforcement in the function that allows users to undelegate assets directly from the staking pool. The contract defines a global pause flag (undelegatePaused) that is consulted by the standard undelegate function to prevent any undelegation when an operator or admin activates the emergency stop. However, the alternative entry point undelegateFromPool does not read this flag, so it proceeds with the withdrawal logic even while the pause is active. This inconsistency originates from an incomplete access‑control implementation: the pause check was copied to one function but omitted from the other, creating a gap in the contract’s security model. An attacker or any user can exploit the flaw by calling undelegateFromPool during a period when the protocol intends to freeze all undelegations, thereby extracting staked assets while the rest of the system believes withdrawals are disabled. The impact is that the intended safeguard against sudden mass exits or malicious draining of the pool is ineffective, potentially leading to unexpected loss of funds for the protocol, reduced confidence for delegators, and a breach of the contract’s documented behavior. The issue manifests only when the admin invokes the pause mechanism; under normal operation the bug is invisible, which makes it hard to notice because the primary undelegate function behaves correctly and the UI may still show a disabled state, giving a false sense of security. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the implementations of the two undelegation pathways and identified the missing require statement. To remediate, the undelegateFromPool function should be updated to include the same pause verification as the undelegate function, ensuring that any call to withdraw from the pool respects the global undelegatePaused flag. Conceptually, this is a classic case of inconsistent enforcement of an emergency‑stop (circuit‑breaker) pattern, where one entry point bypasses the intended guard. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that they can still trigger an undelegation and receive funds even though the contract documentation and UI indicate that undelegations are paused, leading to confusion when expected refunds are received unexpectedly or when the pool balance appears to shrink without an authorized action.

title: Unhandled error in emergency clawback execution may prevent accounting lost funds after slashing
description:
The operatorExecuteClawBack function of the SonicStaking contract is intended for an operator to withdraw assets to the pool. It's intended to be the only way to reduce the rate. An operator can acknowledge that the amount withdrawn may be less than what's owed (setting emergency to true), having lost these funds in slashing events of the SFC contract.  
To execute the actual withdrawal of funds from the SFC contract, the operatorExecuteClawBack function calls SFC::withdraw, indicating the validator's ID from which it intends to withdraw. However, this validator may be fully slashed. If so, the call to SFC::withdraw will revert with a StakeIsFullySlashed error. This error is unhandled in the operatorExecuteClawBack function, and therefore will pop-up the revert too, preventing the clawback execution. This means that neither totalPool nor pendingClawBackAmount will be updated, thus failing to account for the lost funds in the fully slashed validator. At this point the SonicStaking contract will have lost assets, but would not be able to realize the losses and reduce the rate accordingly.  
The only alternative left would be to wait until the validator's slashing refund ratio is updated in the SFC contract, which may allow avoiding the StakeIsFullySlashed error and withdrawing funds from the validator again.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unhandled revert in the emergency clawback path of the SonicStaking contract. When an operator calls operatorExecuteClawBack with the emergency flag set, the function attempts to withdraw the validator’s stake from the SFC contract by invoking SFC.withdraw. If the targeted validator has been fully slashed, SFC.withdraw reverts with the StakeIsFullySlashed error. Because operatorExecuteClawBack does not catch this exception, the revert propagates and aborts the whole transaction. As a result, the contract’s accounting variables – totalPool and pendingClawBackAmount – are never updated to reflect the loss of assets belonging to the fully slashed validator. The pool therefore retains an inflated view of its holdings, the rate that determines token value is not reduced, and users may continue to see a higher token price while the underlying assets have actually disappeared. This situation occurs only under the specific condition that a validator is fully slashed and an emergency clawback is attempted; under normal withdrawals the call succeeds and the state is updated correctly. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the error‑handling logic of the clawback function. It can be hard to notice because the transaction simply reverts, leaving no on‑chain evidence that the accounting update was skipped, and the edge case is rarely exercised in typical test scenarios. The impact is primarily financial: pool participants may lose value because the protocol cannot account for the missing funds, leading to inaccurate reward calculations and potentially lower payouts in the future. To fix the issue, the contract should explicitly handle the StakeIsFullySlashed error – for example by catching the revert, treating the withdrawal amount as zero, and still updating the accounting to record the loss, or by checking the validator’s slashingRefundRatio before attempting the withdraw and only proceeding when a non‑zero refund is available. Adding symmetry to the withdraw function to clean up the withdrawId would also improve robustness. In summary, the bug is a classic case of missing error handling for an external call that can fail under certain state conditions, causing accounting inconsistencies and financial loss for users.

title: Malicious Stakers can grief Keepers
poc: I have implemented a [PoC](https://github.com/sseefried/codearena-backd-2022-04/blob/4d3c3ba7a0139bea01a0bdee9e84a7921572a9fd/backd/tests/top_up_action/sseefried_test_staker_grief.py) in a fork of the contest repo. The attacker’s contract can be found [here](https://github.com/sseefried/codearena-backd-2022-04/blob/4d3c3ba7a0139bea01a0bdee9e84a7921572a9fd/backd/contracts/AliceAttacker.sol).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) scenario that allows a malicious staker to prevent a keeper from successfully executing a top‑up action and receiving its reward. The root cause lies in the contract’s reliance on an external call to the payer address during the cleanup phase of the `execute` function. When the keeper calls `execute`, the code checks whether the staker’s position should be removed and, if so, invokes `gasBank.withdrawUnused(payer)`. This call transfers ether to the address stored in `payer`. If the payer address is a contract that implements a `receive()` function which deliberately reverts, the transfer fails and the entire `execute` transaction reverts. Because the revert happens after the keeper has already consumed gas, the keeper forfeits the gas spent and never receives the expected reward for performing the top‑up. The impact is that keepers can be forced to waste gas without compensation, effectively griefing them and reducing network reliability. The condition under which this occurs is when a staker’s top‑up position is cleared (`vars.removePosition` is true) and the payer address has been replaced or set to a malicious contract capable of rejecting ether transfers. The affected parties are the keepers who submit the transaction, the protocol that relies on their incentives, and indirectly any users who depend on timely top‑ups. The issue was discovered during a security audit through manual code review and a proof‑of‑concept test that deployed a contract to the payer address with a reverting `receive()` function. Because the failure occurs only in a specific branch of the execution path, it may be missed by casual testing that does not simulate a malicious payer, making it relatively subtle. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts after a keeper calls `execute`, resulting in the keeper receiving no reward and losing gas, even though the top‑up was intended to succeed. This violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that the gas bank can always withdraw unused funds from the payer without error. Conceptually, the fix is to make the withdrawal from the payer address non‑reverting, for example by using a pull‑payment pattern, by checking the return status of the transfer and handling failures gracefully, or by ensuring the payer is always an EOA or a contract that cannot reject ether. By decoupling the reward logic from a potentially malicious external call, the protocol can guarantee that keepers are either compensated or the transaction is aborted before they incur irreversible gas costs.

title: When an attacker lends to a loan, the attacker can trigger DoS that any lenders can not buyout it
description:
[NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L205-L208](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/main/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L205-L208)  
[NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L215-L218](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/main/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L215-L218)

If an attacker (lender) lends to a loan, the attacker can always revert transactions when any lenders try to buyout, making anyone can not buyout the loan of the attacker.
poc:
1. A victim calls `lend()`, trying to buyout the loan of the attacker.
2. In `lend()`, it always call `ERC20(loanAssetContractAddress).safeTransfer` to send `accumulatedInterest + previousLoanAmount` to `currentLoanOwner` (attacker).
3. If the `transfer` of `loanAssetContractAddress` is ERC777, it will call `_callTokensReceived` that the attacker can manipulate and always revert it.
4. Because `NFTLoanFacilitator` uses `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` to check return value, the transaction of the victim will also be reverted. It makes anyone can not buyout the loan of the attacker.

In `_callTokensReceived`, the attacker just wants to revert the buyout transaction, but keep `repayAndCloseLoan` successful. The attacker can call `loanInfoStruct(uint256 loanId)` in `_callTokensReceived` to check if the value of `loanInfo` is changed or not to decide to revert it.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan‑facilitating contract when a lender attempts to buy out an existing loan using the `lend()` function. The contract unconditionally calls `ERC20(loanAssetContractAddress).safeTransfer` to send the sum of the accumulated interest and the principal to the current loan owner. If the loan asset token implements the ERC777 standard, the transfer triggers the `_callTokensReceived` hook on the token contract. Because the attacker controls the token contract, they can program the hook to always revert the transfer. The `safeTransfer` helper checks the return value and propagates the revert, causing the entire `lend()` transaction – the buyout attempt – to fail. Consequently, any user trying to buy out the loan of an attacker-controlled lender is blocked, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition. The root cause is the assumption that token transfers behave like pure ERC20 transfers and the lack of safeguards against ERC777 callbacks that can maliciously revert. The attack can be carried out by a lender who supplies an ERC777 token as the loan asset and then manipulates the token’s `tokensReceived` callback to reject transfers only when a buyout is attempted, while allowing normal repayments to proceed. The impact is that legitimate lenders cannot purchase the loan, borrowers may be prevented from repaying, and the protocol’s collateral seizure mechanism can be forced into a default state, undermining trust in the system. This condition occurs whenever the loan asset is an ERC777 token, the attacker is the current loan owner, and a third party calls `lend()` to buy out the loan. All participants – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the normal economic flow is disrupted. The issue was discovered during an audit that exercised the contract with tokens implementing ERC777 hooks, revealing that the `safeTransfer` call does not protect against malicious callbacks. It is difficult to notice because most ERC20 tokens lack callback logic, so developers often assume transfers are side‑effect‑free. To remediate, the contract should avoid transferring the loan asset directly in `lend()`. Instead, it can record redemption rights in a mapping and provide a separate `redeem` function that pulls tokens from the contract, or it can explicitly block ERC777 tokens. By decoupling the transfer from the buyout logic and preventing callback‑induced reverts, the protocol can restore reliable loan buyout and repayment functionality.

title: Protocol doesn’t handle fee on transfer tokens
description:
[NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L155-L160](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/e8015d7c4b295af131f017e646ba1b99c8f608f0/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L155-L160)  

Since the borrower is able to specify any asset token, it is possible that loans will be created with tokens that support fee on transfer. If a fee on transfer asset token is chosen, the protocol will contain a point of failure on the original `lend()` call.

It is my belief that this is a medium severity vulnerability due to its ability to impact core protocol functionality.
poc:
For the first lender to call `lend()`, if the transfer fee % of the asset token is larger than the origination fee %, the second transfer will fail in the following code:

```solidity
ERC20(loanAssetContractAddress).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
uint256 facilitatorTake = amount * originationFeeRate / SCALAR;
ERC20(loanAssetContractAddress).safeTransfer(
    IERC721(borrowTicketContract).ownerOf(loanId),
    amount - facilitatorTake
);
```

Example:

* `originationFee = 2%` Max fee is 5% per comments
* `feeOnTransfer = 3%`
* `amount = 100 tokens`
* Lender transfers `amount`
* `NFTLoanFacilitator` receives `97`.
* `facilitatorTake = 2`
* `NFTLoanFacilitator` attempts to send `100 - 2` to borrower, but only has `97`.
* Execution reverts.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the NFTLoanFacilitator contract handles loan assets that charge a fee on each ERC‑20 transfer. The protocol assumes that the full amount transferred by the lender is available for subsequent operations, but fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a percentage of the transferred value before the recipient’s balance is updated. Consequently, the facilitator calculates the origination fee based on the nominal amount supplied by the lender, while the actual balance that arrives after the transfer fee is smaller. When the contract then attempts to forward the loan amount minus its own fee to the borrower, it may try to send more tokens than it actually holds, causing the second transfer to revert. This failure can happen whenever a borrower selects a token that implements a transfer fee and the fee percentage exceeds the protocol’s origination fee or any safety margin. The impact is that the loan cannot be fulfilled, the lender’s transaction reverts, and the protocol may lose potential origination revenue. Users affected include lenders, who see their transaction fail; borrowers, who receive no funds or a reduced amount; and the protocol itself, which cannot service loans with such assets and may leak facilitator balances if edge‑case transfers succeed partially. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the lend() function and identified that the contract does not account for the net amount received after a fee‑on‑transfer deduction. It can be hard to notice because the ERC‑20 interface does not expose the fee, and the contract’s balance checks are performed after the transfer, making the discrepancy invisible until the second transfer is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches for fee‑on‑transfer tokens, where on‑chain logic assumes a one‑to‑one transfer of value. From a user’s perspective, a lender expects their tokens to be fully available for the loan, but the borrower may observe that the promised loan amount never arrives or arrives reduced, and the UI may show a transaction revert without a clear error message. To remediate, the contract should calculate the origination fee based on the actual amount received (i.e., after deducting any transfer fee) or enforce that only fee‑free tokens can be used, or require lenders to supply enough extra tokens to cover the maximum possible transfer fee. The recommended fix is to base fee calculations on the net received amount or to validate that the token does not implement a transfer fee before allowing it to be used in a loan.

title: Missing type hash when hashing sub-struct breaks EIP-712 compliance
bug_full: The vulnerability is a non‑compliant EIP‑712 implementation in the SeaportProxy contract where the hashing of nested struct arrays omits the required type hash for each array element. According to the EIP‑712 specification, the encodeType function must collect and concatenate the definitions of all referenced struct types, sorted alphabetically, and the encodeData function must prepend the struct's type hash before encoding the field values. In the current code the functions hashOfferItem and hashConsiderationItem call abi.encode with only the raw field values, leaving out the OFFER_ITEM_TYPE_HASH and CONSIDERATION_ITEM_TYPE_HASH. As a result, the resulting struct hash for the Cancel type does not match the hash that a correctly‑formed EIP‑712 signature expects. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who crafts a Cancel payload that produces the same keccak256 digest as a legitimate user‑signed message, allowing unauthorized cancellation of orders or manipulation of order state. The impact is that users may see a cancellation appear to succeed while the underlying order remains unchanged, or conversely an attacker may cancel a victim’s order without consent, potentially leading to loss of assets or locked funds. The bug manifests whenever the Cancel struct is hashed for signature verification, i.e., during the order cancellation flow, and affects any participant that relies on the cancel functionality – including regular users, the protocol’s order book, and any downstream applications. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s EIP‑712 compliance, where the auditor compared the implementation against the specification and noticed the missing type hash. Because the contract still produces a 32‑byte hash, the problem is subtle and may not be evident from UI feedback; signatures appear to be accepted, yet the underlying data does not correspond to the intended order, making the bug hard to notice without a deep inspection of the hashing logic. To remediate, the contract should define explicit type hashes for the OfferItem and ConsiderationItem structs, include those hashes as the first argument in abi.encode when hashing each array element, and construct the Cancel type hash by concatenating the definitions of Cancel, OfferItem and ConsiderationItem in alphabetical order. This change restores full EIP‑712 compliance, ensures that signatures are bound to the exact data structure, and prevents unauthorized order cancellations.

title: Lack of validator penalties enables risk-free economic censorship and liveness attacks
description:
Following is the current economic security / consensus safety model:
• Genesis validator set is picked by social trust.
• There is a cap on total no. of active validators participating in consensus at any given point in time.
• To become a validator, a deposit of arguably high stake needs to be made on execution layer such that it is greater than minimum balance of current validator set.
• There are no penalties, slashing, reputation score in current state. Also, any cometbft evidences are not considered.
• Rewards are accrued and distributed outside of the consensus layer.
Several points to note:
• Deposit barrier can easily be bypassed by pooling the required amount from multiple parties.
• There is no way to differentiate between an honest validator and validator who is acting maliciously, so even the offchain rewards distribution would be on basis of current active validator set for a given epoch or some derivative of that.
There are several issues with this approach:
• Allows voting on multiple proposal without any risk.
• Validator can propose block for any additional rewards (via fee recepient on block.coinbase) when its turn (which is deterministic due to cometbft weighted round-robin) and refrain from participating in any other activities.
• There is no inactivity leak so even any honest validator who is offline or has lost access to keys would not be kicked out of network unless someone else deposits more stake.
• There are potential spam and grieving vectors on all direct entry points to network such as filling up deposit queue, sending spam proposals, withdrawing and creating new validator from same stake, etc. which are zero-cost & risk-free activites.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing accountability layer for validators: the protocol does not impose any slashing, inactivity penalties, reputation scores, or evidence handling for misbehaviour. Because the validator set is chosen solely on the amount of stake deposited, an attacker can bypass the intended high‑stake barrier by pooling funds from many parties and obtain validator rights without risk. Once in the set, the malicious validator can propose blocks that contain extra reward payments to itself, or simply refuse to include certain transactions, achieving economic censorship. Since there is no inactivity leak, a validator that goes offline or loses its keys remains in the active set indefinitely unless another participant deposits more stake, allowing a liveness attack where the network stalls or block production slows without any automatic removal. The design also permits spam actions such as filling the deposit queue, submitting empty or malicious proposals, and repeatedly withdrawing and re‑registering with the same stake, all at zero cost. From a user perspective this may appear as transactions never being confirmed, unusually long block times, or validators receiving no rewards despite being active, while the protocol’s economic incentives appear broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the consensus safety model and identified that the lack of penalties makes it impossible to differentiate honest from malicious validators, undermining the core assumptions of stake‑based security. The problem is hard to notice because the network continues to operate superficially; the absence of explicit failures masks the underlying loss of liveness and censorship capability. To remediate, the protocol should integrate slashing logic for double‑signing or censorship, enforce inactivity penalties that automatically remove idle validators, embed reward and penalty calculations directly into the consensus layer, and process evidence through the underlying consensus engine. Adding a reputation or penalty score and preventing stake pooling from circumventing the deposit barrier would restore the economic security guarantees and align validator incentives with honest behaviour.

title: validatorUpdates ignores the effects of ProcessBlock leading to wrong voting power for validators temporarily
description:
Here is the current order of state processing in Transition function:
• Transition
– ProcessSlots (validatorUpdates and IncreaseBalance/DecreaseBalance happens correctly).
  * processSlot (for each slot until target).
    · If epoch boundary: processEpoch.
– ProcessBlock (IncreaseBalance/DecreaseBalance happens correctly, validatorUpdates are ignored and not sent to cometbft till next epoch).
  * processBlockHeader.
  * processExecutionPayload.
  * processWithdrawals (can decrease balance).
  * processRandaoReveal.
  * processOperations (can increase balance).
This breaks the various invariants and specs, major ones being voting power does not reflect the underlying stake and can be temporarily undermined or inflated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑ordering defect in the beacon‑chain transition logic that causes validator voting power to diverge from the actual stake for a short period after a block is processed. The root cause is that the transition function applies balance changes (increase or decrease) during the ProcessBlock step, but the corresponding validatorUpdates that should adjust voting power are only emitted during the ProcessSlots step, which runs at epoch boundaries. Consequently, any balance modification that occurs inside a block – such as rewards, penalties, or withdrawals – is reflected in the validator’s stored balance but is not communicated to the underlying consensus engine (CometBFT) until the next epoch. An attacker or honest validator can therefore exploit the timing gap: by triggering a balance increase in a block, the validator’s stake rises while its voting power remains at the old lower value, or vice‑versa, creating a temporary over‑ or under‑representation in the consensus set. The impact is a temporary violation of the protocol’s invariant that voting power must equal stake, which can lead to inaccurate proposer selection, potential manipulation of block finality, and a brief window where a validator may wield more influence than warranted or lose influence unexpectedly. This condition occurs whenever a block contains operations that modify validator balances and the chain is not at an epoch transition. All validators, delegators, and any users relying on correct voting power calculations are affected because the consensus state is inconsistent with the accounting state. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit of the state‑transition ordering, where the auditors observed that validatorUpdates were omitted after ProcessBlock. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy disappears at the next epoch, and most monitoring tools only check voting power at epoch boundaries, missing the transient mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of delayed state propagation or consensus‑state synchronization errors, where updates to one part of the system are not promptly reflected in another. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as a validator showing a higher or lower voting power than expected, unexpected missed block proposals, or irregular proposer rotation, even though the on‑chain stake balance is correct. The recommended remediation is to emit validatorUpdates to CometBFT immediately after the ProcessBlock step, or to reorder the transition logic so that voting power adjustments are applied in the same block where balance changes occur, thereby preserving the invariant that voting power always mirrors stake.

title: Arrays hashed wrong when tokenizing breaks EIP-712
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the tokenization function builds the EIP‑712 message hash for signature verification. The function is supposed to allow an admin to mint a batch of tokens for a list of receivers with corresponding amounts, and it verifies a signed message that encodes the chain identifier, a signer counter, the receiver addresses array, the amounts array, and a database identifier. Instead of encoding the arrays according to the EIP‑712 specification, the implementation concatenates the raw arrays using abi.encodePacked and hashes the result directly. EIP‑712 requires each element of an array to be hashed individually and then the collection of those hashes to be encoded, because the encoding of an array is defined as the keccak256 hash of the concatenated encodeData of its contents. By skipping this per‑element hashing step, the digest that the contract expects does not match the digest that a legitimate signer would have produced. Consequently, a signature that appears valid for one set of receivers and amounts can be replayed or forged for a different set, allowing an attacker to either mint tokens to unintended addresses or cause the minting transaction to fail despite a correct signature. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users may receive no tokens when they expect a mint, or they may receive tokens they did not request, leading to supply inflation or loss of trust. The flaw manifests whenever the admin calls the tokenize function with non‑empty arrays, i.e., under normal operational conditions for batch minting. All participants that rely on the correctness of the minting process – the protocol itself, token holders, and downstream applications – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s hashing logic against the EIP‑712 standard. It is subtle because the signature verification still succeeds from a cryptographic standpoint; the mismatch is semantic, so developers may not notice the discrepancy without a deep inspection of the encoding rules. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the direct abi.encodePacked of the arrays with helper functions that hash each array element individually (e.g., hashing each address and each amount) and then encode the resulting list of hashes using abi.encode, as prescribed by EIP‑712. This change restores the intended binding between the signed message and the exact list of receivers and amounts, preventing unauthorized token creation and ensuring that the minting outcome matches user expectations.

title: Slippage During Transfer Fee Swap
description:
If Berabot contains at least 0.02% of the totalSupply then a swap can be made during transfer(). Such swaps can be vulnerable to sandwich attacks which can cause the feeRecipient to receive way less WBERA than the normal market price for the swapped tokens.
This is possible in 2 scenarios:
• Every fee-whitelisted address can perform the sandwich attack since they will not trigger an internal swap themselves when they increase the balance of the pool.
• If the Berabot balance is larger than 0.04%+ or 0.4%+ then again the front-running swap will be executed as normal but the second swap will cause the feeRecipient to get far fewer native tokens than expected.
Token feeRecipient fee value can be extracted by an attacker.
bug_full: During a token transfer the contract checks if its own token balance exceeds a small fraction of the total supply (approximately 0.02%). If the condition is met, the transfer function automatically swaps the accumulated tokens for the native blockchain token (WBERA) and sends the resulting amount to the feeRecipient. Because the swap is executed inside the same transaction as the user‑initiated transfer, an attacker can place a front‑running transaction that changes the pool price just before the internal swap and a back‑running transaction that restores the price afterwards. This sandwich pattern creates extreme slippage: the attacker buys the token just before the contract’s swap, inflating the price, and sells immediately after, driving the price down. As a result the feeRecipient receives far fewer native tokens than the market price would dictate. The vulnerability is triggered only when the contract’s token balance crosses the defined thresholds (0.02% for the first swap, and above roughly 0.04% or 0.4% for a second swap), and it can be exploited by any address that is fee‑whitelisted because such addresses do not cause an internal swap when they increase the pool balance, allowing them to front‑run without self‑interference. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a transfer the expected fee payout is dramatically reduced or appears to be zero, even though the transaction succeeds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the transfer logic and identified the implicit swap as a potential vector for price manipulation. The problem is subtle because the swap is hidden inside a standard transfer call, making the slippage invisible to casual observers and to tools that only track explicit swap functions. The bug belongs to the class of “price‑impact / front‑running vulnerabilities in internal token swaps” and violates the accounting assumption that fees are transferred at fair market value. To remediate, the design should separate the fee‑swap from the transfer routine and enforce a minimum amount‑out parameter, or otherwise protect the swap from being front‑run, ensuring that the feeRecipient receives at least the expected value.

title: Users Can Always Grief the Protocol
description:
Users can reduce the amount of fees that go to the protocol by always specifying a referral address that is not able to claim these fees. Such addresses could be address(0xdead), etc.
Protocol fees will be reduced and the reduced amount will not be accessible anymore.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked referral address mechanism that allows any caller to specify an arbitrary address to receive protocol fees. Because the contract does not verify that the referral address is capable of claiming or receiving those fees, a user can deliberately provide an address that is permanently unspendable, such as the zero address, a known burn address (e.g., 0xdead...), or any contract that does not implement the required claim function. The root cause is the absence of validation logic that ensures the referral address is active, non‑zero, and has performed a qualifying action (such as staking) before being eligible for fee allocation. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a transaction that includes a malicious referral address; the protocol’s fee distribution routine will transfer the calculated fee portion to the supplied address, where it becomes irretrievable. Consequently, the protocol’s revenue pool is reduced, leading to lower fee accrual for legitimate stakeholders, distortion of tokenomics, and potential loss of trust. This condition occurs whenever a function that accepts a referral parameter is called, which is typically any user‑initiated operation that generates fees. All participants who rely on protocol fee income—stakers, token holders, and the protocol treasury—are affected because the expected fee share is silently burned. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the lack of input sanitisation for referral addresses. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the fee loss is reflected only in reduced protocol balances, which may appear as normal variance in fee statistics. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a referral address is non‑zero, not blacklisted, and has a verifiable interaction with the protocol (e.g., a positive stake or prior claim) before allocating fees. If the address fails these checks, the fee should be redirected to the protocol’s own treasury or a default safe address, ensuring that no fees are sent to an address that cannot claim them. This class of bug falls under improper input validation and economic grief attacks, where malicious actors can deliberately drain protocol revenue without breaking functionality.

title: Not Being Able To Manage Configurations Appropriately Allows Users to Avoid Fees
description:
The isAmmPair variable is used to track the AMMs in order for the Berabot token to know when to apply fees on transfers from and to such pools. The uniswap V2 WBERA/BerabotToken pool is the one being set in the constructor but there are no other functions that can add other pools to the isAmmPair.
Users can decide to avoid this pool and use another WBERA/BerabotToken pool for their swaps to not pay fees to the protocol.
On a separate note:
• Addresses can be added to the fee whitelist (_feesWhitelisted) but cannot be removed.
• _isMaxWalletExcluded can’t be updated outside of the constructor.
• Trading can be turned on but not stopped (isTradingOpen) and limitMaxWallet can be turned off but not on after that.
• In BerabotRouter, addRouterV2() and addRouterV3() once the configurations are set they cannot be changed. If they are set incorrectly the contract might need to be upgraded in order to change the configs.
Users can avoid paying fees by using different pools.
Once set many configurations cannot be changed without needing an upgrade or redeploy. If the token contract is already widely used redeploying might not be possible.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the immutable configuration of the Berabot token contract, specifically the way it tracks automated market maker (AMM) pools for fee assessment. A mapping called isAmmPair is populated only in the constructor with the address of the official Uniswap V2 WBERA/BerabotToken pool and there is no public or owner‑only function that can add or remove entries later. Because the fee‑charging logic checks this mapping to decide whether a transfer should be taxed, any swap that occurs through a pool not listed in isAmmPair will bypass the fee mechanism entirely. An attacker or any user can therefore create a second liquidity pool for the same token pair on another DEX, or even on the same DEX with a different address, and perform swaps through that pool without incurring the protocol’s intended fees. The contract also contains several other immutable settings: fee‑whitelisted addresses can be added but never removed, the _isMaxWalletExcluded flag cannot be changed after construction, the trading flag (isTradingOpen) can be turned on but never turned off, and the limitMaxWallet toggle can be disabled once but never re‑enabled. In the router contract, the addresses for V2 and V3 routers are set once via addRouterV2() and addRouterV3() and cannot be altered, meaning a mis‑configuration would require a full contract upgrade. These design choices mean that once the token is deployed, the protocol cannot react to emerging threats, correct accidental mis‑settings, or enforce policy changes without redeploying, which may be impossible for a widely used token. Exploitation is straightforward: a user deploys an alternative pool, routes swaps through it, and the transfer function does not recognise the pool as an AMM pair, so the fee calculation branch is skipped. The impact is a loss of expected fee revenue for the protocol, distortion of tokenomics, and an unfair advantage for users who discover the loophole. From the end‑user perspective, a transaction that should have deducted a fee appears to transfer the full amount, leading to confusion when other users report fee deductions. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the contract’s state‑changing functions and noticed the absence of any setter for isAmmPair and other configuration variables. Because the fee logic works correctly for the hard‑coded pool, the problem can be subtle and may only be revealed when a user intentionally tests an alternative pool. To remediate, the contract should expose owner‑only (or governance‑controlled) functions that allow adding and removing AMM pair addresses, updating fee‑whitelist entries, toggling trading and max‑wallet restrictions, and changing router addresses. Making these parameters mutable restores the ability to enforce fee policy, correct configuration errors, and adapt to future protocol upgrades, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of charging fees on all relevant swaps.

title: Berachain Users Cannot Use Flashloans from Uni V2 WBERA/BerabotToken Pool
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy‑blocking interaction between the token’s automatic fee‑swap logic and Uniswap V2 flash‑loan mechanism. The token contract executes swapBack() during any normal transfer when its internal balance exceeds a threshold and neither the sender nor the receiver is whitelisted. Because swapBack() itself performs a swap on the same Uniswap V2 pair, a flash‑loan that transfers the borrowed tokens triggers swapBack() while the pair’s swap function is still under the lock modifier. The Uniswap V2 lock prevents the nested swap call, causing the whole transaction to revert. As a result, users cannot obtain flash loans of the token from the WBERA/BerabotToken pool; attempts to do so simply fail with a revert and no tokens are received. The issue occurs only when the token’s fee‑swap conditions are satisfied, which is typical during normal transfers of flash‑loaned tokens that are not whitelisted. The affected parties are borrowers, arbitrage bots, and any protocol that relies on flash loans from this pool, effectively removing a key liquidity feature. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the transfer() function and its interaction with Uniswap V2’s lock‑based reentrancy protection. It is subtle because the token’s swapBack() call is legitimate in ordinary transfers, so the failure only appears when a flash‑loan transaction also tries to invoke a swap on the same pair, a scenario that is not obvious from the token code alone. The bug belongs to the class of ‘unintended reentrancy lock conflict’ or ‘flash‑loan blocking due to internal swap triggers’. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that a flash‑loan request returns an error or that the transaction reverts, and the expected profit from arbitrage never materialises. The impact is a loss of functionality rather than direct loss of funds, but it can prevent profitable strategies and may lead users to think the protocol is broken. The fix is to decouple the automatic fee‑swap from external transfers that occur inside a locked swap, for example by disabling swapBack() when the call originates from a Uniswap V2 pair, adding a re‑entrancy guard that recognises the lock, or moving the fee conversion to a separate, explicitly‑called function that cannot be triggered during a flash‑loan swap.

title: BerabotRouter Cannot Make Swaps with V3 Pools with Fee Different than 500
bug_full: The BerabotRouter contract contains a logic error in its uniswapV3SwapCallback implementation. The callback attempts to verify that the caller is a legitimate Uniswap V3 pool by recomputing the pool address, but it does so with a hard‑coded fee value of 500 basis points. This hard‑coding means that when a user initiates a swap through a V3 pool that uses any other fee tier (for example 3000 or 10000), the calculated address will not match the actual pool address, causing the isValid flag to remain false and the transaction to revert with V3InvalidCaller. The root cause is the static fee parameter in the internal _calculateV3PoolAddress call, which ignores the fee tier supplied by the pool. An attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger the failure simply by selecting a pool with a non‑500 fee, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where swaps cannot be completed. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails silently or returns a generic revert, the UI may show “transaction reverted” or “swap failed” and the expected token balance does not change, giving the impression that funds have disappeared even though they remain in the contract. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the callback logic and noticed the hard‑coded fee. It is hard to notice because the code compiles and works for the most common 0.05% fee tier, so tests that only cover that tier pass. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter hard‑coding” or “pool address miscalculation” bugs that break business logic assumptions about fee‑dependent pool identification. To remediate, the router should accept the fee tier as an input or retrieve it from the pool, and compute the pool address using the actual fee value, mirroring the approach used by the official Uniswap V3 router. This change restores the ability to swap through any whitelisted V3 pool regardless of its fee tier, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations and protocol specifications.

title: Broker's Publish, Broadcast & Shutdown are unrealiable for delivery guarantees and prone to various race panics
description:
Publish/Broadcast and shutdown (due to <- ctx.done() in start) can happen concurrently, this
results in non-deterministic and unsound behavior resulting in following scenarios:
• Return ctx.Canceled or ctx.DeadlineExceeded error.
• Msg delivered to some subscribers but not to others.
• panic: closing already closed channel when ctx cancels/timeout from multiple places.
• panic: send on closed channel when broadcast is trying to iterate and shutdown has already closed
some.
Here, only returning error is desirable and rest are unwanted side-effects can cause severe damage. These effects
are observed when node operations deviate from the happy path.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a concurrency race condition in the broker component that handles Publish, Broadcast and Shutdown operations. The root cause is the absence of proper synchronization when multiple goroutines access the shared subscriber map and the underlying channels. When a context cancellation (ctx.done) triggers a shutdown while another goroutine is still executing a Publish or Broadcast, the shutdown routine may close channels that the publishing routine is still iterating over or trying to send messages through. This leads to nondeterministic outcomes such as returning ctx.Canceled or ctx.DeadlineExceeded errors, partial delivery where some subscribers receive a message while others do not, and runtime panics caused by closing an already‑closed channel or sending on a closed channel. The issue can be exploited by forcing a timeout or cancellation during a publish operation, causing the broker to panic and potentially halt the node, which results in a denial‑of‑service condition and breaks the protocol’s delivery guarantees. The impact is that users expecting reliable notifications or transaction confirmations may see missing messages, error messages, or a completely unresponsive node, which can translate into financial loss if the missing messages represent fund transfers or state updates. The race manifests only under specific timing conditions, such as high load, network latency, or maliciously induced context cancellations, making it hard to reproduce in standard testing. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit when the auditors exercised concurrent shutdown and publish paths and observed the described panics and inconsistent delivery. The bug is difficult to notice because the failures are intermittent and may only appear as occasional error returns or occasional panics, which can be dismissed as transient issues. To remediate, the shared subscriber map must be protected by a mutex or another synchronization primitive, and the shutdown logic must be made idempotent so that channels are closed exactly once. Publish and Broadcast functions should check the channel state before sending and handle closed‑channel errors gracefully, returning a clear error instead of panicking. In broader terms, this is a classic unsafe channel‑close race that violates the expected atomicity and reliability of message delivery in a concurrent system, leading to broken business logic where messages disappear or are delivered inconsistently, contrary to user expectations of reliable notification delivery.

title: max_tx_bytes default 1MB can be exceeded in PrepareProposal()
description:
In CometBFT ABCI++, the proposed transactions from PrepareProposal() in total byte size cannot exceed req.max_tx_bytes. In one of the configs testing/networks/80084/config.toml#L368 (80084 is for the bArtio testnet), the max_tx_bytes seems to be set to 1048576 (1MB) which is the default for CometBFT.
However, both the BeaconBlock and the BlobSidecars can exceed this limit individually.
• Maximum BeaconBlock size - constrained by the ExecutionPayload gas limit (15 million average, 30 million max). An ExecutionPayload filled with 0's can be up to a maximum block of 7,500,000 bytes. So with headers and stuff, it's around 7.5 MB.
• Maximum Sidecars size - 128KB per blob and MAX_BLOBS_PER_BLOCK is 6, so (128KB * 6) + negligible header size = 768 KB.
If the size of the BeaconBlock and Sidecars together exceed req.max_tx_bytes, then the proposal will not be accepted. In the current state, all honest validators using the current codebase will never prune transactions and thus if a proposed BeaconBlock plus BlobSidecars exceeds req.max_tx_bytes (1MB) in size the proposal will be rejected. Presumably, other honest proposers will try to craft the same proposed block or similar, potentially halting the chain entirely with all of the proposals being rejected.
This 1MB limit isn't super hard to hit. If a proposal has MAX_BLOBS_PER_BLOCK (6), then that is automatically ~768KB of 1MB used. Then the BeaconBlock would only have to exceed 280KB to hit this limit. This could easily happen.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the default configuration of CometBFT ABCI++ where the PrepareProposal() function enforces a maximum total transaction byte size (req.max_tx_bytes) of 1 MB. In the bArtio testnet configuration the limit is left at the default 1 048 576 bytes, but the protocol allows a BeaconBlock whose execution payload can be up to roughly 7.5 MB and up to six BlobSidecars whose combined size can reach about 768 KB. When a proposer includes the maximum number of sidecars, the sidecars alone consume roughly three‑quarters of the allowed budget, leaving only about 280 KB for the BeaconBlock. Because a realistic BeaconBlock can easily exceed this remaining space, the combined size of the BeaconBlock and BlobSidecars can surpass the 1 MB threshold. When this happens the PrepareProposal() call rejects the proposal, causing the validator to refuse the block. Since honest validators do not prune transactions, every proposer that assembles a block exceeding the limit will have its proposal rejected, leading to a situation where no new blocks are accepted and the chain stalls. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the blockchain stops progressing, users see no new blocks, validators receive error messages about proposal rejection, and funds that depend on block finalisation remain locked. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the configuration files and the PrepareProposal() size check, noting that the default limit does not account for the maximum possible payload sizes. It is hard to notice because the limit is a configuration parameter rather than a code defect, and it only manifests when the block reaches a size that is uncommon in normal operation but possible under the protocol’s specifications. To remediate the problem the configuration should be changed to a much larger max_tx_bytes value—such as 100 MB—so that the combined size of a BeaconBlock and the maximum number of BlobSidecars can never exceed the limit. Alternatively, the proposer logic could be updated to prune or split transactions when the limit is approached. In any case, the fix restores the expected business logic that a valid proposal should always be accepted when it respects the protocol’s gas limits, preventing the chain from halting due to an oversized proposal.

title: Race condition results in mismatch between BeaconBlock.StateRoot and BlobSidecar
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that can cause the state root stored in the block header to diverge from the state root recorded in each associated sidecar. When a validator builds a block, two concurrent operations are launched: one that computes the block’s state root and writes it into the block header, and another that constructs sidecar objects that copy the current state root from the block header into their own header field. Because the two goroutines run in parallel, the sidecar may read the state root before the computation finishes, resulting in a sidecar that contains an outdated or zero value while the block header later receives the correct root. This mismatch violates the protocol’s invariant that every sidecar must reference the exact state root of the block it belongs to. An attacker or a faulty validator can trigger the condition simply by proposing a block as usual; no special input is required. If the mismatch is detected by the consensus client, the block is considered malformed and will be rejected, causing the proposer to lose the expected block reward and potentially be slashed for proposing an invalid block. The issue is hard to notice because the two operations are intended to run in parallel for performance, and the resulting state root values may appear correct in logs when the race does not manifest, leading to intermittent failures that are difficult to reproduce. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the concurrency model of the block‑building pipeline. To remediate the problem, the two steps must be serialized so that the state root is computed and stored before any sidecar reads it, or a placeholder value must be written into the sidecar and later replaced after the state root is known. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of concurrency‑related state inconsistency, where shared mutable data is accessed without proper synchronization, breaking accounting assumptions that the block header and its auxiliary data remain consistent.

title: Broker broadcasts sequentially can potentially timeout upstream block building / verification
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the broker component delivers messages to its subscribed clients. The broadcast function iterates over the subscription list and performs a blocking send to each client channel, waiting either for the client to accept the message or for a one‑second timeout to fire. Because the loop processes subscribers sequentially, a single slow or unresponsive subscriber – for example one whose channel buffer is full, one that is deliberately not reading, or one that is blocked by an upstream context – can hold up the entire broadcast for the full timeout period before the function proceeds to the next subscriber. This design creates a hidden bottleneck that can cascade into the surrounding protocol stack. When the broker is used to propagate consensus‑layer (CL) or execution‑layer (EL) events, the delay may cause the downstream block‑building or verification steps to miss their expected time windows, leading to out‑of‑sync services, non‑deterministic state transitions, and partially committed states. The issue is most likely to surface under stress conditions such as a network partition, reconnection after a failure, an initial sync phase where many events are emitted, or when the number of subscribers grows large enough that the linear broadcast cost scales non‑linearly. The affected parties include validators, any off‑chain services that rely on timely broker notifications, and ultimately end‑users whose transactions may be delayed or dropped because the protocol cannot reach consensus in time. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the broker’s concurrency model and noted that the single‑threaded broadcast could become a single point of failure. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the timeout is relatively short and most subscribers behave correctly; only under pathological conditions does the delay become observable as missing updates or stalled block production. To remediate the issue, the broadcast should be made concurrent: each client send should be dispatched in its own lightweight execution context (e.g., a goroutine) with an independent timeout, ensuring that a misbehaving subscriber cannot block the whole system. Alternative mitigations include using non‑blocking sends with a default case, increasing channel buffer sizes, or implementing back‑pressure handling, but the core fix is to decouple subscriber delivery from the main broadcast loop so that the protocol’s timing guarantees remain intact.

title: rpc.Client race condition in header http.Header field
description:
The rpc.Client.header field is an http.Header from the go library. This is a wrapper over a map, and it is not concurrency-safe. In the current usage, there is a race condition in the following spots:
• rpc.Start() is an infinite loop that will update the header with the rpc.header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token).
• rpc.CallRaw() will read the rpc.header value in a separate go routine. This could result in undefined behavior that could cause invalid data or panic.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic concurrency race condition affecting the rpc.Client.header field, which is an instance of Go's http.Header type. http.Header is implemented as a map[string][]string and, like all Go maps, it is not safe for simultaneous reads and writes from multiple goroutines. In this client implementation, an infinite loop inside rpc.Start continuously updates the Authorization entry of the shared header with rpc.header.Set("Authorization","Bearer "+token). At the same time, rpc.CallRaw runs in a separate goroutine and reads the same header to attach it to outgoing RPC requests. Because there is no synchronization primitive protecting the header, the two goroutines can access the map concurrently, leading to a data race. The race can manifest as corrupted header data (e.g., a partially written token) or as a runtime panic caused by the Go runtime detecting a concurrent map read/write. From a user's perspective this appears as intermittent RPC failures, unexpected error messages, or the client process crashing with a panic stack trace, which contradicts the expectation that the client will reliably forward requests. The issue occurs whenever the client is started and used in a multi‑goroutine environment, which is the normal operating mode for most blockchain nodes and services that rely on asynchronous RPC calls. All users of the client library—including developers, protocol operators, and end‑users whose transactions depend on the RPC layer—are potentially affected because a panic or malformed Authorization header can halt communication with the blockchain, leading to denial‑of‑service conditions or missed transaction submissions. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that included static code review and race‑condition analysis; it may be hard to notice in production because the race does not always trigger and may only surface under specific timing conditions or high request volume. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of unsafe shared mutable state in concurrent programs. The recommended remediation is to serialize access to the header by protecting all reads and writes with a sync.RWMutex (or by copying the header for each request), thereby eliminating the race and ensuring that the Authorization value is always consistent when used. In summary, the client currently violates the concurrency safety guarantees of Go's map type, leading to possible data corruption or panics that break the expected reliable RPC communication.

title: Frontrunners can corrupt the initialization of the TimeLock and BerachainGovernance contracts
description: The deployment process implemented in DeployGovernance.s.sol begins with two transactions (see DeployGovernance.s.sol#L39-L44) that deploy the corresponding implementation and proxy contracts for BerachainGovernance and TimeLock. However, the initialization of the proxies' state is not done in those deployment transactions. Instead, it's done afterwards, in two individual transactions that call the contracts' initialize function (see DeployGovernance.s.sol#L49 and DeployGovernance.s.sol#L63). This means that, after the deployment transactions and before the initialization transactions, the proxies are temporarily left in an uninitialized state. Then, anyone can frontrun the initialization transactions and initialize the proxies of TimeLock and BerachainGovernance with malicious parameters to corrupt the deployment process.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition that affects the initialization of upgradeable proxy contracts used for the TimeLock and BerachainGovernance components. The deployment script DeployGovernance.s.sol first creates the implementation contracts and their TransparentUpgradeableProxy instances in two separate transactions, but deliberately postpones the call to the initialize function to later transactions. During the interval between the proxy deployment and the subsequent initialize call, the proxy’s storage variables—including the admin address, delay period, and other critical governance parameters—remain unset.
