Because the handler is executed without signature validation, the attacker can trigger fund transfers, token approvals, or other privileged actions that the handler would normally perform only on behalf of the account owner. The impact is the potential loss or unauthorized use of the account’s assets, violation of the account’s accounting assumptions, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s security model. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access restrictions of external functions and noted that fallback() was the sole function without a onlyEntrypoint or similar guard. The problem can be subtle because fallback handlers are often trusted modules supplied by the user, so developers may assume they are safe; the missing authorization is not obvious from the UI, which still shows normal balances until an unauthorized call drains funds. To remediate, the fallback function should enforce an authorization check such as onlyEntrypoint() or a whitelist of allowed callers, and/or each handler should validate msg.sender or include its own access control. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unrestricted fallback or unauthorized delegate call, where a generic entry point can be abused to bypass authentication and execute privileged logic.

title: Modules other than validators cannot be installed in enable mode
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the Module Enable Mode feature that is intended to allow any type of module – validators, hooks, executors or fallback handlers – to be installed during the validation phase of a UserOperation. In the current implementation the address of the module to be installed is extracted from the nonce and then the same address is passed to the validator interface and its validateUserOp function. This design assumes that the module being installed implements the IValidator interface, which is only true for validator modules. Consequently, when a non‑validator module such as a hook or executor is supplied, the contract attempts to call validateUserOp on a contract that does not provide that function. The call either reverts or returns an unexpected value, causing the validation step to fail. The root cause is a mismatch between the documented behaviour (any module type can be installed) and the code logic that treats every module as a validator. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit this by crafting a UserOperation that claims to enable a non‑validator module; the system will mis‑interpret the module as a validator, leading to a failed validation and a transaction that never reaches the execution phase. The impact is that legitimate users who rely on the documentation to install hooks or executors via enable mode will see their operations revert, their prefunded ether may be consumed without any state change, and the protocol’s promised flexibility is broken. This situation occurs whenever enable mode is used with a module that lacks a validateUserOp implementation – essentially any module that is not a validator. The affected parties are end‑users attempting to configure their smart‑account modules, developers building on the Biconomy SDK, and the protocol itself because the discrepancy can lead to denial‑of‑service conditions and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the official documentation with the source code and verified the behaviour by testing module installations of different types. It can be hard to notice because enable mode is a relatively new feature and most test suites focus on validator modules; the failure only manifests at runtime when a non‑validator module is used. To remediate the problem the code should either restrict enable mode to validator modules only, matching the actual validation flow, or redesign the installation path so that the module address is not used as a validator during validation – for example by separating the installation logic from the validation call or by providing a generic installer that does not require a validateUserOp function. In practice the fix would involve adding a type check before invoking validateUserOp, updating the documentation to reflect the restriction, and ensuring that fallback mechanisms exist for installing non‑validator modules via batching rather than enable mode. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that appears to succeed in the UI (the user signs a request to install a hook) but the on‑chain operation reverts or completes without the hook being active, leaving the user with no change in behaviour and possibly with prefunded funds that are not returned.

title: Missing call type validation in _installFallbackHandler
description: When installing a fallback handler, there is no check that the call type is either CALLTYPE_STATIC or CALLTYPE_SINGLE. This will result in a successful installation including completion of the initialization steps. However, when the fallback is called nothing will happen when the selector for the fallback handler is passed. Additionally, the fallback does not revert in this case. This could have a serious effect on an integrator depending on the fallback and it may not be caught immediately due to lack of reverting.
bug_full: The contract permits an integrator to register a fallback handler through the internal function _installFallbackHandler, which stores the handler address together with a call type that determines how the fallback will be invoked. The implementation fails to verify that the supplied call type matches one of the two supported constants CALLTYPE_STATIC or CALLTYPE_SINGLE. Consequently, an attacker or a careless developer can provide an arbitrary call type value, causing the handler to be recorded with an unsupported type. The installation routine completes without error, so the registration appears successful. When the fallback entry point is later triggered, the dispatcher checks the stored call type, finds a value that does not match either supported branch, and simply falls through without executing any logic and without reverting. From the user’s perspective a transaction that is supposed to be handled by the fallback returns silently, often with an empty return data payload, giving the impression that the call succeeded. Integrators that rely on the fallback for critical operations such as token transfers, meta‑transactions, or permission checks may experience silent failures, lost funds, or state inconsistencies because the expected side‑effects never occur. This is a classic case of missing input validation leading to an unsupported execution path, which is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an error and the transaction receipt shows a successful status. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the fallback installation logic and noticed the absence of a require statement for the call type. Exploitation can be performed by calling _installFallbackHandler (or any public wrapper that eventually reaches it) with a calltype value that is neither CALLTYPE_STATIC nor CALLTYPE_SINGLE, then invoking the fallback selector; the call will complete with no state change and no revert, effectively disabling the fallback. The impact is medium risk because it does not directly allow theft of funds, but it can cause functional failures that may lead to loss of user assets or denial of service for contracts that depend on the fallback. The vulnerability affects any user or contract that interacts with the fallback mechanism, including developers integrating the library, end‑users sending transactions that rely on the fallback, and the protocol that expects the fallback to enforce business rules. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit validation check in _installFallbackHandler that requires the calltype to be either CALLTYPE_SINGLE or CALLTYPE_STATIC, and to modify the fallback dispatcher to revert with a clear error when an unsupported call type is encountered. This restores the invariant that only known call types are accepted and ensures that unexpected values cause a visible failure rather than silent no‑ops.

title: Cannot install fallback handler for empty calldata
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the interaction between Solidity's receive/fallback dispatch rules and the contract's internal module‑handler design. The contract inherits a receive() function from a base contract, which means that any call with empty calldata – such as a plain native‑token transfer – will always trigger the receive() function and never reach the fallback function. The contract’s logic, however, assumes that an empty calldata call should be routed to a fallback handler identified by the selector bytes4(0). This assumption is encoded in the _isModuleInstalled helper, which defaults an empty additionalContext to the zero selector and expects a corresponding handler to be invoked. Because the receive() function pre‑empts the fallback, the zero‑selector handler is never called, causing any installed module that relies on that selector to be effectively dead. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or honest user sends a transaction with no data, expecting the module to process the call (for example, to accept ether or execute custom logic). Instead, the receive() function executes (or, if absent, the fallback is still bypassed for the zero selector), resulting in the intended handler being ignored. The impact is that funds sent with empty calldata may be rejected, silently dropped, or processed by a default receive() that does not perform the expected accounting, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as “my ETH transfer failed”, “no module executed”, or “balance did not increase”. This condition occurs whenever the contract is called without calldata – a common pattern for native‑token deposits – and only affects callers that rely on the zero‑selector fallback handler, i.e., users, integrators, and any protocol component that expects module‑based processing of empty calls. The issue was discovered during a security review that compared the contract’s documented expectations with Solidity’s language semantics, revealing a mismatch that is easy to miss because empty‑calldata calls are indistinguishable from normal ether transfers and the receive() function silently masks the problem. The bug belongs to the class of “fallback handler bypass due to receive function precedence”, where business logic assumes a fallback will run but language rules prevent it. To remediate, the contract should either remove the receive() function entirely or augment the fallback to explicitly detect msg.data.length == 0, check for an installed handler for the zero selector, and invoke it if present; otherwise it should behave like a standard receive() that accepts ether. This change aligns the implementation with the intended module‑handler model and restores correct processing of empty‑calldata transactions.

title: `requiredImprovementRate` can not work as expected when `previousInterestRate` less than 10 due to precision loss
poc:
1. Alice `createLoan()` with `maxPerAnumInterest` = 10, received `loanId` = 1
2. Bob `lend()` with `interestRate` = 9 for `loanId` = 1
3. Charlie `lend()` with `interestRate` = 9 (and all the same other terms with Bob) and buys out `loanId` = 1

Charlie is expected to provide at least 10% better terms, but actually bought out Bob with the same terms.
bug_full: The contract enforces a minimum improvement when a new lender buys out an existing loan by checking that at least one loan term (principal increase, duration increase, or interest rate reduction) improves by the percentage defined in the `requiredImprovementRate` variable. The check is performed with pure integer arithmetic: `previousInterestRate * requiredImprovementRate / SCALAR`. Because Solidity rounds division toward zero, the expression can evaluate to zero when the product is smaller than `SCALAR`. This situation occurs when the existing loan’s annual interest rate (`previousInterestRate`) is low – for example, any rate below 10 when `requiredImprovementRate` is set to 100 (representing a 100 % improvement). In that case the calculated improvement amount becomes zero, and the condition `previousInterestRate - (previousInterestRate * requiredImprovementRate / SCALAR) >= interestRate` is satisfied even if the new `interestRate` is identical to the old one. Consequently, a buyer can refinance or buy out a loan without delivering any better terms, violating the protocol’s economic guarantee that a refinance must be strictly better for the borrower. The bug is a classic precision‑loss or rounding‑error vulnerability that stems from using integer division for percentage calculations. It is exploitable by submitting a loan offer with the same interest rate as the incumbent loan when the incumbent rate is sufficiently small; the contract’s require statement will mistakenly accept the offer. The impact is that borrowers may believe they are receiving a more favorable rate, but in reality the rate remains unchanged, potentially leading to higher cumulative costs if the attacker further manipulates other terms. The issue manifests only under the specific condition of a low original interest rate combined with a high required improvement percentage, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the surrounding checks for principal and duration appear correct. The vulnerability was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case (Alice creates a loan with a 10 % max rate, Bob lends at 9 %, and Charlie attempts to buy out at the same 9 % rate) demonstrated that the required improvement constraint was not enforced. From the user’s perspective, the UI would show the same interest rate after a refinance, contradicting the expectation that the rate should drop, and the borrower may feel misled or notice that the “better terms” message is inaccurate. To remediate the issue, the contract should avoid truncating division by using a rounding‑up division function such as OpenZeppelin’s `Math.ceilDiv`, or by rearranging the arithmetic to compute the required decrement before division, ensuring that any non‑zero improvement requirement yields a non‑zero reduction even for small rates. This change restores the intended business logic that a refinance must improve at least one loan parameter and prevents the inadvertent acceptance of unchanged or worsening terms.

title: Borrowers lose funds if they call `repayAndCloseLoan` instead of `closeLoan`
description:
[NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L241](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/e8015d7c4b295af131f017e646ba1b99c8f608f0/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L241)  

The `repayAndCloseLoan` function does not revert if there has not been a lender for a loan (matched with `lend`). Users should use `closeLoan` in this case but the contract should disallow calling `repayAndCloseLoan` because users can lose funds.

It performs a `ERC20(loan.loanAssetContractAddress).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, lender, interest + loan.loanAmount)` call where `interest` will be a high value accumulated from timestamp 0 and the `loan.loanAmount` is the initially desired min loan amount `minLoanAmount` set in `createLoan`. The user will lose these funds if they ever approved the contract (for example, for another loan).
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the loan repayment pathway of the NFT‑backed lending contract. When a borrower invokes the repayAndCloseLoan function, the code assumes that a lender has already been matched to the loan and blindly executes an ERC20 safeTransferFrom that moves interest plus the original loanAmount from the borrower to the recorded lender. However, the function lacks a guard verifying that a lender actually exists. In the current implementation the NFT‑owner lookup (ownerOf) is performed through Solmate’s ERC721 wrapper, which does not revert when the token has no owner; instead it returns the zero address. Consequently, if a borrower calls repayAndCloseLoan on a loan that has never been matched (i.e., no lender and loan.lastAccumulatedTimestamp remains zero), the contract still attempts the transfer. The calculated interest starts from timestamp 0, producing an astronomically high value, and the loanAmount is the minimum loan amount defined at creation. Because the borrower has previously approved the facilitator to spend the specified ERC20 token, the transfer proceeds and the tokens are sent to the zero address (or an uninitialized lender), effectively burning them. From the user’s perspective the transaction completes successfully, but the borrower’s balance drops by the full loan amount plus an unexpectedly large interest, leading to a loss of funds that they did not anticipate. The issue manifests only when the borrower mistakenly uses repayAndCloseLoan instead of the intended closeLoan function for an unmatched loan, a scenario that can be hard to detect because the UI does not clearly differentiate the two pathways and the contract does not emit an explicit error. The bug was identified during a security audit that inspected the repayment logic and noticed the missing lender check, and it was further confirmed by the observation that Solmate’s ownerOf implementation diverges from the ERC721 specification by not reverting on a missing owner. To remediate, the contract should enforce a condition such as require(loan.lastAccumulatedTimestamp > 0, "loan was never matched by a lender; use closeLoan") or verify that the lender address is non‑zero before performing the token transfer. This change restores the intended business logic that borrowers can only repay when a loan has been funded, preventing accidental token burns and protecting users from unintended fund loss.

title: Might not get desired min loan amount if `_originationFeeRate` changes
description:
[NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L309](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/e8015d7c4b295af131f017e646ba1b99c8f608f0/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L309)  

Admins can update the origination fee by calling `updateOriginationFeeRate`. Note that a borrower does not receive their `minLoanAmount` set in `createLoan`, they only receive `(1 - originationFee) * minLoanAmount`, see [`lend`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backed/blob/e8015d7c4b295af131f017e646ba1b99c8f608f0/contracts/NFTLoanFacilitator.sol#L159). Therefore, they need to precalculate the `minLoanAmount` using the **current** origination fee to arrive at the post-fee amount that they actually receive. If admins then increase the fee, the borrower receives fewer funds than required to cover their rent and might become homeless.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the NFTLoanFacilitator contract defines and applies the origination fee for loans. When a borrower creates a loan they specify a `minLoanAmount`, which the protocol documentation presents as the minimum amount the borrower expects to receive. Internally, however, the contract applies the current global `originationFeeRate` at the time the loan is funded, delivering only `(1 - originationFeeRate) * minLoanAmount` to the borrower. Because the fee rate is stored globally and not captured in the loan’s state, an administrator can later call `updateOriginationFeeRate` and increase the fee. When this occurs, any loan that has already been created but not yet funded will be processed using the new, higher fee, causing the borrower to receive fewer funds than the amount they calculated based on the earlier fee. This discrepancy can be severe: a borrower who relied on the originally advertised minimum loan to cover a rent payment may end up with insufficient funds, potentially leading to loss of housing. The issue manifests only when the fee is changed after loan creation and before loan funding, affecting any borrower who does not manually recalculate the expected post‑fee amount with the updated rate. It was identified during a security audit that examined the loan creation and funding flow. The problem is subtle because the UI and contract parameters expose the pre‑fee `minLoanAmount`, leading users to assume that this is the net amount they will receive, while the underlying accounting logic subtracts a fee that can vary over time. From a user perspective the symptom is receiving less ether than expected – for example, a borrower sees a loan of 10 ETH listed but only receives 9.5 ETH after funding, resulting in an unexpected shortfall. This violates the business assumption that a loan’s minimum amount guarantees sufficient liquidity for the borrower’s intended purpose. To remediate the flaw, the contract should either store the `originationFeeRate` within each loan’s data at the moment of creation, ensuring the fee applied during funding is the one the borrower accounted for, or redefine `minLoanAmount` to represent the post‑fee amount that the borrower will actually receive. Both approaches align the displayed loan amount with the real funds transferred and prevent administrators from retroactively altering the effective fee for pending loans.

title: `mintBorrowTicketTo` can be a contract with no `onERC721Received` method, which may cause the BorrowTicket NFT to be frozen and put users’ funds at risk
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the BorrowTicket NFT is minted during loan creation. The contract calls the standard ERC721 `_mint` function to assign the newly created BorrowTicket to the address supplied in the `mintBorrowTicketTo` parameter. Because `_mint` does not perform a safety check on the recipient, it allows the token to be transferred to any address, including a contract that does not implement the `onERC721Received` callback defined by the ERC721Receiver interface. When such a contract receives the token, the transfer succeeds silently; however, the contract cannot handle ERC721 callbacks, resulting in the BorrowTicket becoming permanently locked inside the recipient contract. The loan logic later relies on the BorrowTicket to redeem the user’s collateral and release the borrowed funds. If the NFT is trapped, the protocol is unable to verify ownership or transfer the ticket back, and the borrower cannot repay the loan or reclaim the underlying assets. This situation effectively freezes the user’s funds and may cause permanent loss of liquidity for both the borrower and the lender. The issue manifests whenever a borrower’s address is a smart contract that lacks the ERC721Receiver implementation, a condition that is not checked during the `createLoan()` execution. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, the loan is listed as created, but later attempts to withdraw or repay result in no action, missing balances, or error messages indicating that the loan cannot be closed. The problem was identified during a security audit by observing the use of `_mint` instead of `_safeMint` and recognizing the associated risk of NFT lockup, a known class of bug often referred to as an "unsafe ERC721 mint/transfer". The bug is subtle because the blockchain records no revert, and the UI may simply show the loan as active without indicating the underlying token is inaccessible. To remediate, the mint function should be changed to use `_safeMint`, which triggers the ERC721Receiver check and reverts the transaction if the recipient cannot correctly handle the token. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce that the recipient is an EOA or a contract that implements ERC721Holder, ensuring the BorrowTicket remains accessible and preserving the integrity of the loan lifecycle.

title: No way to collect uniswap fees
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing fee‑collection mechanism for the initial Uniswap V3 liquidity position that the Bridge contract creates when the minting stage is closed. After the admin calls Bridge::closeMint, the contract invokes NonfungiblePositionManager.mint to open a new LP position and stores the tokenId, liquidity amount and tick bounds. However, the contract never calls NonfungiblePositionManager.collect for that tokenId, so any trading fees that accrue in the pool remain locked inside the Uniswap position and cannot be transferred to the protocol. The root cause is a design oversight: the Bridge contract assumes that providing liquidity is sufficient and does not implement the required call to retrieve fees, nor does it expose any interface for doing so. An attacker does not gain direct control over the funds, but the protocol is unable to harvest the fees that are expected to fund its operations or be distributed to token holders. This results in a business‑logic failure where revenue that should be recorded and possibly shared with users never materialises, breaking accounting assumptions about fee income. The issue manifests after the mint stage ends, i.e., immediately after Bridge::_mintInitialPosition executes; from that point onward, any trade activity in the pool generates fees that are invisible to the protocol. Users and stakeholders may notice that the pool shows liquidity but reports zero fee earnings, contradicting the expectation that the protocol will earn a share of trading fees. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Bridge contract’s lifecycle functions, where the absence of a collect call was identified as a logical gap. It can be hard to notice because the LP position appears normal and the Uniswap pool functions correctly; only a deeper inspection of fee‑withdrawal logic reveals the omission. To remediate, the Bridge contract should implement a function that invokes NonfungiblePositionManager.collect for the stored tokenId, restrict the call to an authorized role (e.g., the admin or a designated fee‑collector), and update the protocol’s accounting to include the retrieved fees. This change restores the intended revenue flow and aligns the contract’s behaviour with its economic model.

title: Centralization issues
description: The Hybrid NFT protocol uses OpenZeppelin AccessManager to guard sensitive calls withing the contracts. These include: Token::mint, Token::setTrusted, NFT::mint, NFT::burn, Referral::generateReferrerId, Bridge::closeMint, Bridge::enableBridge, Bridge::pullGenesisShare. Were the admin account in control of AccessManager to be compromised all the above calls would be available to an attacker which would cause great harm to the project.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk caused by a single privileged account that controls the OpenZeppelin AccessManager used by the Hybrid NFT protocol. This admin account is the sole authority that can invoke a set of high‑value functions such as token minting, setting trusted addresses, NFT minting and burning, referral identifier generation, bridge closure, bridge activation and the withdrawal of the Genesis share. The root cause is the design choice to grant all these sensitive operations to one address without any additional governance or delay mechanisms. If an attacker gains control of the admin key—through phishing, key leakage, or a compromised wallet—they can execute any of the protected calls. Exploitation would involve the attacker calling the mint function to create arbitrary NFTs or tokens, calling burn to destroy legitimate user assets, altering trusted contracts to redirect funds, generating referral IDs to siphon rewards, closing the minting phase to freeze legitimate activity, enabling the bridge to move assets out of the intended ecosystem, or pulling the Genesis share which holds a substantial portion of the protocol’s capital. The impact includes unauthorized creation of assets, loss of user balances, disruption of the referral economy, potential theft of locked capital, and overall loss of trust in the protocol. This condition can occur at any time the admin key is exposed; there is no time‑based safeguard or multi‑party approval to mitigate it. All participants—token holders, NFT owners, referrers, and bridge users—are affected because the attacker can manipulate the core accounting rules that the protocol relies on. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined role‑based access controls and noted the absence of decentralised governance or timelocks. Because the privileged functions are correctly guarded, the contract behaves normally under regular operation, making the risk hard to notice until a malicious transaction is observed (e.g., unexpected NFTs appearing, balances dropping to zero, or sudden bridge activation). The recommended remediation is to replace the single admin with a multi‑signature wallet, DAO‑based governance, or at least a timelock that gives users a window to react to privileged changes. Conceptually, the fix removes the single point of failure by requiring multiple independent approvals before any sensitive call can be executed, thereby aligning the contract’s control model with the expected decentralized security guarantees of a public NFT platform.

title: User can lose the right to claim tokens when calling claim
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token claim routine of the contract. When a contributor calls the claim function, the contract first records that the user has claimed by setting a flag, then attempts to transfer the entitled BIO_TOKEN amount using an internal helper called _safeClaimTransfer. This helper checks the contract’s current token balance and, if the requested amount exceeds the balance, it silently transfers only the available balance (which may be zero) instead of reverting. Because the claim function marks the user as having claimed before verifying that the transfer succeeded, a situation can arise where the contract’s BIO_TOKEN balance has been drained – for example by the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE exercising an emergency withdrawal – and the subsequent claim transaction will emit a Claim event with non‑zero expected amounts, but the actual token transfer will be zero. The user’s hasClaimed flag is set, preventing any future claim, so the contributor loses the right to receive their tokens. In addition, the code creates a vesting schedule for VBIO_TOKEN based on the same expected amount even though the contract transferred zero VBIO_TOKEN to the vesting contract. Consequently the vesting contract records a schedule that cannot be fulfilled because the underlying token balance is insufficient. The issue occurs whenever the contract balance is lower than the amount calculated by getExpectedClaimAmount at the moment of claim, which can happen after an admin withdrawal, rounding errors, or any other reduction of the token pool. Affected parties include all contributors who have a non‑zero contribution and expect to receive BIO_TOKEN or VBIO_TOKEN, as well as the vesting contract that relies on those tokens. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the claim flow and the safe transfer helper, noticing that the transfer logic does not enforce a failure when the balance is insufficient and that the claim state is updated before the transfer. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert, events indicate a successful claim, and the UI may show a successful claim, yet the user’s token balance remains unchanged and the vesting schedule is under‑funded, making the loss of funds hard to detect. To remediate, the contract should either remove the _safeClaimTransfer helper or modify it to revert when the contract balance is lower than the required amount, and the claim function should only set the hasClaimed flag after a successful transfer. Additionally, the protocol should prevent the admin from withdrawing tokens that are needed for pending claims, or at least enforce that withdrawals cannot reduce the balance below the total outstanding claim amount. This class of bug is an “insufficient balance handling leading to claim state inconsistency” where a user’s right to claim is lost while the contract silently transfers zero tokens, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the token sale and vesting system.

title: Referrer can steal commission from another referrer
bug_full: The contract implements a referral system for NFT minting where each mint costs 0.1 ETH and the designated referrer receives a fixed 25 % commission (0.025 ETH) per minted token. The vulnerability stems from the logic that binds a user to the first referrer they ever interact with and never allows this association to be changed. This binding is performed in ReferralMap::trySetReferrerForUser by checking whether a stored referrer identifier already exists for the user; if it does, the function returns false and the referrer remains unchanged. Because the commission is calculated per mint based solely on the stored referrer, an attacker who can front‑run a legitimate user’s transaction can mint a single NFT for that user using the attacker’s own referral code. After this initial mint, the user’s subsequent mints – even if they explicitly specify a different referrer – will still route the 0.025 ETH commission to the attacker’s address. The exploit requires the attacker to submit a transaction that calls mintWithReferer with the target user and the attacker’s referral code before the user’s intended transaction is mined. If the user later mints five or more NFTs, the attacker profits because the commission earned (0.025 ETH × number of mints) exceeds the 0.1 ETH the attacker spent on the initial front‑run mint, resulting in a net gain (e.g., 0.15 ETH profit for five subsequent mints). From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they selected a particular referrer, yet the referral rewards appear missing or zero, violating the expectation that the chosen referrer receives the commission. The issue was discovered during an audit when a test case demonstrated that a malicious referrer could “steal” the commission by front‑running the user’s transaction. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit warning when a referrer change is ignored, and the accounting logic assumes the first‑referrer binding is acceptable, making the loss of commission hard to notice without detailed event analysis. Conceptually, this is a classic case of immutable referral binding combined with per‑mint commission calculation, leading to a revenue‑diversion attack. The recommended mitigation is to redesign the referral accounting so that commissions are tracked per purchase rather than per user, or to allow explicit referrer updates with proper consent, thereby preventing a single early transaction from permanently hijacking future commission flows.

title: Attacker can spam function deposit() to always increase price
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auction contract’s deposit() routine, which records user demand by incrementing a counter named prevRoundDeposits each time the function is called. The root cause is that the contract increments this demand counter unconditionally, regardless of the amount actually deposited. Because the function permits a deposit of as little as one wei, an attacker can repeatedly invoke deposit() with a negligible amount while still causing prevRoundDeposits to grow. The price‑setting logic of the auction reads prevRoundDeposits to adjust the ticket price for the current round, assuming that a higher counter reflects genuine market demand. By artificially inflating the counter, the attacker creates the illusion of strong demand, causing the price algorithm to raise the ticket price for subsequent honest participants. This manipulation can occur at any time the contract is live, as there is no minimum‑deposit check or validation that the deposited amount meets the current ticket price. The impact is economic: legitimate users see the price climb unexpectedly, may be forced to pay more for a ticket, or may be priced out entirely, undermining the fairness and revenue model of the auction. The protocol’s participants, token holders, and any downstream contracts that rely on the auction price are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the deposit() implementation, where the auditor noted the unconditional increment of prevRoundDeposits. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to simply record a deposit, and the price increase may be mistakenly attributed to genuine market activity rather than a malicious spam attack. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the ticket price rising rapidly even though only tiny deposits are being made, leading to confusion such as “the price keeps going up for no reason” or “my deposit didn’t buy a ticket but the price is higher now”. This class of bug falls under economic manipulation of demand counters or price‑oracle distortion, where a state variable used for pricing is updated without proper validation of the underlying economic value. To remediate, the contract should only increase prevRoundDeposits when a deposit meets or exceeds the current ticket price, or alternatively base demand on the total value deposited rather than the number of calls, and enforce a sensible minimum deposit that aligns with the pricing logic.

title: Incorrect variable used in function setupNewRound()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect variable reference in the function that initializes a new auction round. The contract uses a state variable numberOfTickets to decide whether the price should be adjusted, but this variable is reset to zero at the end of the previous round by selectWinner(). Consequently the condition that compares prevRoundDeposits with numberOfTickets always evaluates as if numberOfTickets is zero. This means the price calculation logic never sees the actual amount of tickets sold in the previous round, leading to a price that may stay at zero or not increase when it should. An operator who calls setupNewRound can therefore start a round with an unintended price, potentially allowing participants to acquire tickets for free or at a price that does not reflect market demand. The impact is that the auction's economic model is broken: users expect the price to reflect the previous round's ticket volume, but they receive a price that is too low or unchanged, causing loss of revenue for the seller and unfair advantage for buyers. The bug manifests whenever a round ends and selectWinner() resets numberOfTickets, which is the normal flow of the protocol. It affects all participants, the operator, and the seller because the contract’s accounting assumptions about ticket counts are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that noted the comment numberOfTickets is always reset to 0 and verified that the variable is never updated after round finalization. Because the price calculation uses the stale variable, the problem can be subtle: the UI may still display a round as started, but the price shown to users is unexpectedly zero, leading to confusion without obvious error messages. The fix is to replace the reference to numberOfTickets with a variable that retains the ticket count from the previous round, such as prevRoundTicketsAmount, which is not cleared by selectWinner(). This change restores the intended price‑adjustment logic and aligns the contract’s state with its business rules.

title: startLottery() sets status for the non-existing round
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that initiates a lottery round. The contract stores lottery rounds in a mapping indexed from zero up to roundCounter‑1, meaning the highest valid index is roundCounter minus one. The variable roundCounter is incremented after a round is created, so its current value points to the next, not‑yet‑created round. When startLottery() is called, it writes the flag lotteryStarted = true into rounds[roundCounter] instead of the active round. Because the mapping entry does not exist, the write creates a default struct with the flag set, while the real current round (roundCounter‑1) never receives the started flag. Consequently the contract believes a round is active when the internal state of the actual round remains inactive. This mismatch can be triggered whenever the seller calls startLottery() after a round has been created but before roundCounter is adjusted. An honest participant may observe that the lottery never accepts entries, that tickets cannot be purchased, or that refunds are never processed, leading to funds being locked or participants receiving no outcome. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the auction base contract by checking state transitions and noticing that the index used did not correspond to an existing round. It is subtle because the mapping automatically creates a new entry on write, so no revert occurs and the contract appears to have executed successfully, making the bug easy to miss in testing. The proper fix is to reference the existing round by using roundCounter‑1 (or storing the current round identifier in a separate variable) before setting the lotteryStarted flag, ensuring the state change applies to the correct round. This class of bug is an off‑by‑one indexing error that violates the business assumption that a round must be explicitly marked as started before participants can interact with it, breaking the accounting of round lifecycle and potentially causing loss of user trust.

title: Unbounded loop can prevent seller from withdrawing funds
bug_full: In LotteryV2 the contract selects a winner based on how close a buyer's random number is to the seller's random number. When a buyer wins, the VRF callback executes claimNumber which marks the participant as a winner, pushes the address into winnerAddresses and emits a WinnerSelected event. Later the sellerWithdraw function iterates over winnerAddresses, sums each winner's deposit, deducts the protocol tax and transfers the total to the seller. The vulnerability arises because claimNumber can be invoked by any external account any number of times and there is no guard preventing the same participant from being added to winnerAddresses repeatedly. Each call appends the same address again, causing the array to grow without bound. An attacker can repeatedly call claimNumber for a known winner, inflating the array until the gas required to iterate over it exceeds the block gas limit. When the seller later attempts to call sellerWithdraw, the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, effectively locking the seller's funds and preventing the protocol tax from being collected. This condition occurs after a lottery round has a winner and before the seller has successfully withdrawn. The affected parties are the seller, who cannot receive the payout, and indirectly the participants who rely on the lottery to function. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the claimNumber logic and noticed the lack of a duplicate‑winner check. It can be hard to notice because the contract still works correctly for a small number of winners; only when the array becomes very large does the out‑of‑gas failure appear, which may be attributed to normal gas limits rather than a malicious exploit. To remediate, the contract should verify that a participant has not already been recorded as a winner before pushing the address into winnerAddresses, for example by checking the winners mapping, or by clearing the array after a successful withdrawal, or by using a more gas‑efficient data structure that does not require unbounded iteration. This fixes the root cause by preventing unbounded growth of the winner list and ensures that the seller can always withdraw the expected funds.

title: The swap mechanism does not have a deadline parameter
description:
Swap mechanisms should implement a transaction deadline mechanism, due to the following attack vector:
1. Alice wants to execute a swap, sets slippage to 10% and sends a transaction to the mempool, but with a very low gas fee
2. Miners/validators see the transaction but the fee is not attractive, so the transaction is stale and pending for a long time
3. After a week (let's say) the average gas fees drop low enough for the miners/validators to execute the transaction but the price of the assets has changed drastically
4. Now the value Alice receives is much lower and possibly close to the max slippage she set.
The effects are even worse when there is no slippage as it is the current case in the protocol.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: Swap functions that omit a deadline parameter are vulnerable to stale‑transaction attacks. The contract allows a user to submit a swap with a slippage tolerance, but because the function does not record an expiry time, the transaction can remain pending in the mempool for an arbitrarily long period. If miners or validators delay execution until gas prices drop, the market price of the traded assets may have moved significantly. When the transaction finally executes, the on‑chain price oracle returns the current price, which can be far outside the user’s original expectation. The user therefore receives an amount that is close to the maximum slippage they allowed, or even worse when the protocol forces zero slippage. From the user’s perspective the swap appears to have completed successfully, yet the received token amount is dramatically lower than expected, often looking like a “funds disappear” or “refund missing” symptom. The root cause is the absence of a time‑bound validation check – a missing deadline field that should be compared against block.timestamp and cause a revert if the transaction is older than a reasonable window. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the swap workflow and noted that no deadline argument is passed to the internal _swap method. Because the contract does not emit any warning when a transaction is executed after a long delay, the problem can be hard to notice unless the auditor inspects the code path or observes abnormal price outcomes in testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing expiration” or “time‑dependency” bugs, where business logic assumes that a price quote remains valid for the duration of the transaction. Exploitation steps are: (1) attacker or a low‑fee user submits a swap with a reasonable slippage; (2) the transaction is left pending because the fee is too low; (3) market conditions change; (4) a miner eventually includes the transaction when gas is cheap; (5) the contract executes the swap at the new price, delivering far fewer tokens; (6) the user’s balance is reduced accordingly. The impact is financial loss for any user who relies on the quoted price, and it undermines trust in the protocol’s pricing guarantees. The recommended mitigation is to add a deadline timestamp parameter to the swap function (e.g., SwapFacility::_swap) and to revert the transaction if block.timestamp exceeds the supplied deadline, thereby enforcing a maximum age for price quotes.

title: Missing price feed validation and usage of a deprecated method can lead to 0 price
description:
The _getTokenPrices method in SwapFacility makes use of the latestAnswer method from Chainlink price feeds. The problem is that the NatSpec of latestAnswer says this:
```solidity
@dev #[deprecated] Use latestRoundData instead. This does not error if no answer has been reached, it will simply return 0. Either wait to point to an already answered Aggregator or use the recommended latestRoundData instead which includes better verification information.
```
So currently it is possible that latestAnswer returns 0 and the code operates with zero price, leading to miscalculations in the rate of underlyingToken to billyToken which will lead to a loss of funds.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the price returned by a Chainlink price feed in the SwapFacility contract. The contract calls the deprecated latestAnswer function, which according to Chainlink documentation returns 0 when the aggregator has not yet produced a round. Because the code does not check for a zero value, a zero price can be used in the calculation that converts underlyingToken to billyToken. When this occurs the swap rate becomes zero, causing the contract to credit the user with no tokens or to debit the user without providing the expected amount, effectively resulting in loss of funds. This situation can happen whenever the price feed is newly deployed, paused, or otherwise has not reported a valid answer, and it is not limited to any particular user role; any participant invoking the swap may be affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the NatSpec of latestAnswer and noted the lack of a guard against a zero return. Because the contract proceeds silently with the zero price, the symptom from a user’s perspective is that a transaction appears successful but the received token balance is unchanged or zero, which can be hard to notice without inspecting on‑chain events or the price feed state. The bug belongs to the class of "unchecked external data" or "missing input validation" vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts a value that may be invalid. To remediate, the contract should replace latestAnswer with the recommended latestRoundData call, and additionally assert that the returned price is greater than zero before using it in any arithmetic. This change ensures that the contract only operates with verified, non‑zero prices and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Centralization attack vectors are present
description: The owner of SwapFacility can change the pool variable any time, meaning it can be set to address(0) for example, breaking the protocol's swap functionality. Another such issue is that the setSpreadPrice method does not do any input validation, meaning the spreadPrice can be set to a huge number that is bigger than the token prices, which will make the spread subtraction revert the swap transactions every time.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization weakness that allows the contract owner to modify critical protocol parameters after deployment. Specifically, the owner can call a function that changes the address of the liquidity pool used for swaps, and can set this address to the zero address or any arbitrary contract. Because the swap logic reads the pool address at execution time, setting it to an invalid address disables the core swapping functionality, causing every swap call to fail or revert. In addition, the function that sets the spread price does not enforce any bounds or sanity checks, so the owner can assign an excessively large spread value that exceeds the actual token prices. When the swap routine attempts to subtract this spread from the quoted amount, the subtraction underflows or triggers a require condition, causing the transaction to revert consistently. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the access control and input validation of administrative functions. It may be hard to notice because the functions appear to work correctly under normal settings, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the pool address is changed to an unusable value. The impact is that users attempting to trade will see their transactions revert, receive no tokens, and may lose gas fees, effectively making the protocol unusable. This condition occurs whenever the owner deliberately or accidentally changes the pool address or sets an extreme spread price, and it affects all participants who rely on the swap feature, including traders and liquidity providers. The root cause is the lack of proper access restrictions (the function is callable at any time) and missing validation on the spread parameter. To remediate, the pool address should be immutable after initial configuration or limited to a one‑time set, and the spread price setter should enforce an upper bound that reflects realistic market spreads, together with appropriate role‑based access control. The bug belongs to the class of “centralized admin parameter manipulation” and “unchecked input leading to arithmetic revert” vulnerabilities, which break business logic assumptions that the pool is always valid and that spreads remain within reasonable limits.

title: Tokens with a fee-on-transfer mechanism will break the protocol
description:
The ERC20 logic in BloomPool is incompatible with tokens that have a fee-on-transfer mechanism. Such tokens for example is PAXG, while USDT has a built-in fee-on-transfer mechanism that is currently switched off. One example of this BloomPool::depositBorrower where the following code:
```solidity
UNDERLYING_TOKEN.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
```
This will work incorrectly if the token has a fee-on-transfer mechanism - the contract will cache amount as its expected added balance, but it will actually add amount - fee balance. This will result in a revert in the last person to withdraw tokens out of the contract. Same thing applies for other transferFrom calls that transfer tokens into the protocol, for example in SwapFacility::_swap.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An incompatibility exists between the protocol’s ERC20 handling logic and tokens that charge a fee on each transfer (fee‑on‑transfer or taxed tokens). Thecontract assumes that the amount passed to safeTransferFrom will be the exact amount that arrives in its balance, and it records this amount as the newly added balance. When a token deducts a fee during transfer, the contract’s balance increases by amount‑fee, but the internal accounting still records the full amount. Consequently the protocol believes it holds more tokens than it actually does. This discrepancy is not detected at deposit time; it only surfaces later when another user attempts to withdraw or when the contract tries to settle a loan, at which point the contract attempts to transfer more tokens than are available and the transaction reverts. The bug can be triggered by depositing any fee‑on‑transfer token such as 'PAXG' or a 'USDT' instance with fees enabled, and also applies to 'ERC777' tokens that can invoke callbacks during transfer. The impact is that users who deposit such tokens may see their deposit appear successful, but later withdrawals fail, effectively locking their funds and breaking the borrowing/lending flow. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the BloomPool contract by examining the depositBorrower function and noticing that the code does not verify the actual received amount. It is subtle because the transfer call itself does not revert and the contract’s balance check is performed only later, making the problem easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should record the token balance before the transfer, perform the transfer, then compute the difference between the post‑transfer and pre‑transfer balances and use that delta as the true added amount. This approach must be protected with a non‑reentrant guard to prevent re‑entrancy attacks possible with ERC777 tokens. Alternatively, the protocol can explicitly reject tokens that implement a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism and document this limitation. From a user’s perspective, a depositor expects the full amount to be credited and later to be able to withdraw the same amount, but instead receives a transaction revert or a zero balance when trying to withdraw, leading to confusion and potential loss of access to funds. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that token transfers are fee‑free and that the amount sent equals the amount received.

title: getTxOutputValue() doesn't sum up all the values
description: To calculate the bridged amount code calls getTxOutputValue() to find the transferred amount to the onramp address. That function only took the first value of the target address in outputVector list. The issue is that the same address may repeat multiple times in the outputVector and the code should sum all of them to calculate the total amount transferred to the target address.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that determines how much Bitcoin has been transferred to the on‑ramp address during a bridge transaction. The code assumes that the target address appears only once in the list of transaction outputs (outputVector) and therefore returns the value of the first matching entry. In reality a Bitcoin transaction can contain several outputs that pay the same address, for example when a user splits the payment or when change is sent back to the same script. Because the function stops after the first match, it ignores any additional outputs that also belong to the on‑ramp address. This logical flaw leads to an under‑count of the total transferred amount. An attacker or a regular user can craft a transaction with multiple outputs to the on‑ramp address; the bridge will only recognise the first output and will calculate a smaller bridged amount than was actually sent. Consequently the user may see fewer tokens minted, refunds may be missing, or the protocol may flag the transaction as insufficiently funded, causing funds to become locked. The issue appears only when duplicate entries for the target address exist, which is not covered by typical test cases that use a single‑output transaction, making the bug easy to overlook. It was discovered during a manual audit of the on‑ramp contract where the reviewer noticed that the loop returns immediately upon finding a match instead of aggregating all matching values. The problem belongs to the class of accounting or aggregation bugs where a summation over a collection is incorrectly implemented. To remediate the issue the function should iterate over the entire outputVector, sum every value whose scriptPubKeyHash matches the on‑ramp address, and return the accumulated total, thereby ensuring that the reported transferred amount reflects the true amount locked on the Bitcoin side.

title: BTC transactions can have multiple inputs and outputs
description: BTC txs can have multiple inputs and outputs and the relayer chooses the receiver and onramp contract based on the BTC transaction after users make the BTC transactions. The issue is that it's not clear which input address would be chosen as a token receiver and which output address is going to be chosen as an onramp contract. Funds may go to a different receiver address or the relayer may use the wrong onramp contract. If the relayer handles only specific BTC txs users should be informed about relayer limitations.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the way the relayer interprets Bitcoin transactions that contain more than one input or output. Because a Bitcoin transaction can aggregate funds from several addresses and send them to several destinations, the relayer must decide which address corresponds to the user’s on‑chain deposit and which address corresponds to the on‑ramp contract that will mint the corresponding ERC‑20 tokens. The current implementation does not define a deterministic rule for this mapping; it simply picks the first input or output it encounters. As a result, when a user sends a transaction with multiple inputs or outputs, the relayer may associate the wrong input address with the user’s identity or may forward the funds to an unintended on‑ramp contract. An attacker controlling the relayer, or even a benign relayer that processes only a subset of transaction patterns, could cause user deposits to be credited to a different address, leaving the original sender with no minted tokens. The impact is loss of funds or tokens, mismatched balances, and a breach of the trust model of the on‑ramp service. The issue manifests whenever a user’s Bitcoin deposit is not a simple one‑input, one‑output transaction – for example when using coin‑join, change outputs, or when the wallet automatically aggregates UTXOs. Users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting between Bitcoin deposits and minted tokens becomes inconsistent. The problem was discovered during a manual security review of the on‑ramp’s relayer logic, where the code was observed to select addresses without explicit validation. Because the mis‑selection does not generate an on‑chain error, it can be difficult to notice until users report missing tokens or unexpected balances. The correct mitigation is to enforce an unambiguous mapping rule, such as requiring deposits to use a single‑input, single‑output transaction, or to embed a unique identifier (e.g., a payment‑reference script) that the relayer can reliably parse, and to reject any transaction that does not meet the defined pattern. In addition, the relayer should explicitly verify that the chosen input address matches the sender’s declared address and that the output address matches the registered on‑ramp contract before forwarding funds. This eliminates ambiguity, prevents funds from being sent to the wrong recipient, and restores confidence in the deposit‑to‑mint flow.

title: selectWinners() incorrectly pops eligibleParticipants
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the winner‑selection routine of a lottery‑style contract. When the number of requested tickets exceeds the available supply, the function iterates over the list of eligible participants, marks a subset as winners, and then attempts to remove the winners from the original array by shifting the remaining entries and repeatedly calling pop(). The core problem is that the loop which performs the pop operations uses the live value of eligibleParticipants.length as its termination condition while the array length is being reduced on each pop. Because the length shrinks during iteration, the loop exits early, leaving some entries un‑popped and consequently discarding legitimate participants or failing to record winners correctly. This logical error stems from mutating the array while simultaneously relying on its length for loop bounds, a classic off‑by‑one/iteration‑state bug. An attacker or a malicious participant could exploit the flaw by crafting a scenario where demand greatly exceeds supply, causing the contract to mis‑manage the participant list; winners may be omitted, tickets may disappear, and the accounting of remaining participants becomes inconsistent. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s fairness guarantees: users may see their expected ticket allocation vanish, balances may show zero tickets despite having entered, and the overall lottery may award fewer winners than intended, undermining trust. The condition triggers only during the selectWinners execution when the eligibleParticipants array is non‑empty and the number of tickets to allocate is less than the array size. All participants who entered the lottery are potentially affected because the bug can silently drop entries without emitting an error. The issue was identified during a manual security audit by CD Security, which noted that the pop loop’s stopping condition does not account for the decreasing length, making the bug subtle and easy to miss in testing because the contract does not revert or throw; it simply produces an incorrect final state. To remediate, the implementation should capture the original array length before entering the pop loop (e.g., store uint256 originalLength = eligibleParticipants.length) and iterate against that fixed value, or alternatively rebuild the array without in‑place shifting, ensuring that removal logic does not depend on a mutating length. This correction restores proper accounting, guarantees that all non‑winners remain in the list, and preserves the intended ticket distribution logic.

title: Users can exploit the system by depositing 1 wei
bug_full: An attacker can obtain a free dice roll by calling deposit() with any positive amount, even as low as 1 wei. The function checks only that amount > 0 and that the caller has not already won in a previous lottery version. When the caller's rolledNumbers entry is zero, the contract automatically requests randomness and emits a RandomRequested event, effectively granting a roll without charging the required rollPrice. Because the contract does not require the rollPrice for this first roll, the attacker can deposit a negligible amount, receive the random number, and if the number is favorable they can later deposit the full rollPrice to claim the winning mint, or simply withdraw their tiny deposit if the roll is not winning. This behavior violates the economic assumptions of the lottery, giving an unfair advantage to users who exploit the free‑roll path and potentially reducing the expected revenue for the protocol. The issue occurs only for participants who have never rolled before (rolledNumbers == 0) and who invoke deposit(). It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the comment @audit Free roll. The bug is subtle because the deposit function appears to be a normal funding entry point, and the free‑roll side effect is hidden behind a conditional that does not reference the rollPrice. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the amount sent is at least equal to the rollPrice for every roll, or separate the free‑roll logic from the deposit path and explicitly charge the price. Fixing the check restores the intended fairness, ensures that each dice roll costs the advertised amount, and prevents attackers from obtaining a zero‑cost chance to win.

title: User can join multiple times to increase chances of winning
bug_full: The contract implements a lottery where users join by calling a payable deposit function. When a user sends ether for the first time, the function records the address in a participants array and tracks the deposited amount. Later, when the seller starts the lottery, the contract iterates over the participants array and copies any address whose total deposit meets a minimum threshold into an eligibleParticipants array. The vulnerability arises because the deposit logic only checks whether the stored deposit balance is zero before adding the address to participants. If a user withdraws their deposit before the lottery begins, the withdraw function resets the stored balance to zero but does not remove the address from the participants array. The user can then call deposit again, causing the same address to be pushed a second time into participants. Because the eligibility check iterates over the entire participants list, the duplicate entry is also copied into eligibleParticipants, giving the attacker multiple entries in the pool from which the winner is drawn. The winner‑selection routine prevents a single address from being awarded more than once, but the duplicated entries increase the probability that the attacker’s address is chosen, effectively skewing the odds in their favour. This flaw is triggered only while the lottery is inactive, i.e., when the whenLotteryNotActive modifier permits both deposit and withdraw calls. All participants are affected because the inflated chance reduces the expected payout for honest users and undermines the fairness guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that added a test case reproducing the duplicate entries; the problem is subtle because the participants array still contains the correct address, and a UI that merely shows the number of unique participants may not reveal the duplication. To remediate, the contract should either forbid withdrawals until the lottery has ended, enforce a check that prevents pushing an address that already exists in participants, or replace the array with a set that guarantees uniqueness. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “duplicate entry” or “inadequate participant deduplication” vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to manipulate selection weight by re‑entering the same identity multiple times.

title: Race condition for bridged BTC
description: To bridge BTC users need to transfer their funds to the onramp address (scriptPubKeyHash) and then the relayer would call proveBtcTransfer() and the target onramp would transfer the bridged token to the user. The issue is that multiple users may have transferred their BTC to that address at the same time and the onramp may not have enough tokens to handle all those orders so some of the users would lose their funds.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition in the BTC‑to‑token bridge onramp logic. When a user sends Bitcoin to the onramp’s scriptPubKeyHash, an off‑chain relayer later calls proveBtcTransfer() which triggers the onramp contract to mint or transfer the corresponding bridged token to the user. The contract does not enforce a per‑request accounting check or a sequential processing order, so if several users deposit BTC to the same address in a short time window, the relayer may invoke proveBtcTransfer() for each deposit before the onramp’s token balance is updated. Because the onramp contract holds a finite pool of bridged tokens, it can run out of tokens while still processing later proofs. As a result, some users’ BTC deposits are considered proven, but the contract cannot deliver the promised tokens, effectively causing the users to lose their funds. The root cause is the lack of a queue or atomic balance reservation for each incoming BTC transfer, leading to concurrent execution paths that oversubscribe the token reserve. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; it can happen naturally under high traffic or be amplified by an attacker who deliberately floods the onramp address with many small deposits, forcing the relayer to process many proofs in rapid succession. The impact is that users receive no bridged token (their on‑chain balance remains unchanged) despite having sent BTC, which violates the bridge’s fundamental accounting invariant that every deposited BTC must be matched by an equal amount of bridged tokens. The condition occurs whenever multiple proveBtcTransfer() calls are made before the onramp’s token pool is replenished, i.e., during peak usage or when the relayer’s off‑chain logic does not serialize requests. The affected parties are bridge users, the protocol’s token holders, and any downstream applications that rely on the bridged token supply. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the onramp’s state‑transition flow and noticed that the contract does not reserve tokens per request. It is hard to notice in unit tests because the race only manifests under concurrent calls, which are not typically simulated in single‑threaded test environments. To remediate, the bridge should introduce a deterministic queue for the relayer so that each BTC proof is handled one at a time, or it should redesign the flow to avoid direct BTC deposits to the onramp address. A safer design is to have the relayer collect BTC in its own address, verify the total amount, and then credit the onramp’s token pool in a single, atomic operation before fulfilling individual user claims. Additionally, the contract should check that sufficient bridged tokens are available before completing each transfer and revert the proof if the balance is insufficient, thereby preserving the invariant that no user can lose funds due to oversubscription.

title: Gas Price can change, making sigFees calculation insufficient
description:
When a user asks for a redemption, the validators submit signatures which eventually transfer out the bitcoin ordinal. To compensate the validator's gas fees, the user is required to pay for them.
```solidity
uint256 sigFees = BTC_SIG_GAS_USAGE * tx.gasprice * uint256(multisig.activeCommitteeSize);
```
This sigFees is meant to cover the gas cost of the validators, which is incurred by them when they post a multisig signature. The issue is that this function uses tx.gasPrice. This is a user controlled argument, and heavily depends on the network traffic.
Say Alice wants to redeem her ordinal. She calls redeem during a time of low network traffic, so she sets her tx.gasPrice as 0.1 gwei. When the validators are required to submit the signatures, the gas price might have shot up due to higher network traffic. The validators are then forced to use a higher gas price, say 0.2 gwei to get their transaction through.
Since only 0.1 gwei priced gas fees were set aside, the validator will simply refuse to do the transaction.
This is not Alice's fault, since she probably did the transaction with a wallet that guesses the optimum gas price to set for the current block. If Alice wants to make sure her redemption goes through, she needs to manually set her tx.gasPrice higher, anticipating future higher network usage. However, this causes her to waste gas, since she is now bidding at a much higher gas price for the current transaction, which doesn't need it.
In addition, it is possible to avoid paying fees by setting zero gas prices.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑payment of validator gas fees caused by using the transaction field tx.gasprice to compute the amount of ether that a redeemer must lock for validator signatures. The contract multiplies a constant gas usage estimate by tx.gasprice and the size of the active validator committee to obtain a fee (sigFees). Because tx.gasprice is supplied by the user and reflects the gas price at the moment the redemption transaction is mined, it can be significantly lower than the gas price that validators will need when they later submit their multisig signatures. If network congestion rises after the user’s redemption call, validators must increase their own gas price to have their signature transaction included. The pre‑locked sigFees, however, remain based on the earlier lower price, leaving validators under‑compensated. As a result validators may refuse to sign, causing the redemption to stall or fail, effectively a denial‑of‑service for the user. In the extreme case a user could deliberately set tx.gasprice to zero, causing the contract to allocate no fee at all and allowing the validator to be forced to pay the full cost, which may be rejected or lead to a situation where the user avoids paying any fee. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation logic and identified the reliance on a mutable, user‑controlled variable. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to charge a fee that matches the estimated gas usage, yet the dynamic nature of gas price is not obvious from a static view. The impact includes failed redemptions, loss of confidence in the protocol, potential economic loss for validators, and a vector for fee‑evading attacks. The bug belongs to the class of “dynamic fee miscalculation” or “gas price dependent fee under‑allocation”. To fix the problem the contract should decouple fee calculation from tx.gasprice; for example, allow the redeemer to specify a maximum fee amount, use an on‑chain price oracle, or calculate the exact gas used after the validator transaction and reimburse any surplus, ensuring validators are always fully compensated regardless of future gas price fluctuations.

title: Malicious recipient can gas grief the relayer
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑grief denial‑of‑service vector that arises when the on‑ramp contract pushes an ETH gratuity to the swap recipient using a low‑level call after transferring wrapped BTC. The contract does not impose any gas stipend or fallback handling and immediately requires the call to succeed. A malicious recipient can implement a receive() function that deliberately consumes all available gas and then reverts, causing the call to fail. Because the on‑ramp contract checks the return value with require(sent, "Could not transfer ETH"), the entire executeSwap transaction reverts, wasting the relayer's gas while the token transfer is also rolled back. This situation can be triggered with arbitrarily small BTC amounts, limited only by the dustThreshold, allowing an attacker to repeat the attack many times and exhaust the relayer's resources, potentially leading to a protocol‑wide denial of service. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of funds and the handling of external calls. It is hard to notice because sending ETH via call is a common pattern and the failure manifests only when the recipient is malicious; normal users see successful swaps and therefore do not expect a failure mode. The impact is that users do not receive their swapped tokens or ETH, the relayer incurs unnecessary gas costs, and the protocol’s availability can be degraded. The affected parties include the relayer operator, any user attempting a swap, and the overall protocol that relies on the on‑ramp for liquidity. The root cause is the push‑based payment model combined with an unchecked external call and the absence of a minimum transfer amount or gas‑limit protection. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the direct ETH transfer with a pull‑based mechanism where recipients claim their gratuity in a separate transaction, or at minimum use a low‑level send with a fixed gas stipend and handle failure gracefully without reverting the whole swap.

title: MJR-1 Potential safeApprove blocking
description:
At several places, e.g. Investment.sol#L182 contract perform safeApprove before uniswap's function call, however in case if uniswap doesn't use full provided allowance that can lead to blocking next safeApprove call because safeApprove requires zero allowance.
Another lines with same issue:
Market.sol#L248
Buyback.sol#L125
ProfitSplitter.sol#L195
ProfitSplitter.sol#L204
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L116
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L124
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L125
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L151
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L152
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L181
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic allowance‑reset issue that appears when the contract uses a safeApprove helper to set a new ERC20 allowance for Uniswap calls. SafeApprove follows the OpenZeppelin pattern that requires the current allowance to be zero before a non‑zero amount can be approved. In the audited code the contract first grants a large allowance to the Uniswap router, then calls a Uniswap function that may consume only part of that allowance. Because the remaining allowance is non‑zero, the next invocation of safeApprove attempts to set a new allowance without first resetting the old value to zero. The safeApprove call reverts, which blocks the subsequent logic that depends on the allowance being updated. This can happen repeatedly whenever a Uniswap swap does not use the full approved amount, causing a cascade of failed transactions. The impact is that users attempting to invest, buy back tokens, claim profits or interact with the market maker may see their transactions revert with an “ERC20: approve from non‑zero to non‑zero allowance” error, effectively freezing their ability to move funds through the affected functions. From a user perspective the UI may show “transaction failed” or “insufficient allowance” even though the user still holds the tokens, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s interaction with Uniswap, where the auditor noticed repeated safeApprove calls after partial swaps. It is hard to notice because the failure only occurs after a specific usage pattern (partial consumption of allowance) and the revert message is generic, not directly pointing to a business‑logic problem. The bug belongs to the broader class of allowance‑reset or race‑condition vulnerabilities in ERC20 token approvals.
