The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to execute a flash loan, deposit, or withdrawal see their transaction revert, receive no tokens, and may observe that their balances appear unchanged or that a loan was not provided. In the worst case, funds can become temporarily locked in the contract because the expected approval never materializes, breaking accounting assumptions that a transfer will occur after approval. The issue manifests whenever the contract attempts to set an allowance without first clearing the previous one, which occurs in the flash‑loan contract at lines where it directly calls `IERC20(...).approve(address(LP_VAULT), amounts[0])` and similar statements. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s approval pattern against the behaviour of known non‑standard tokens. It is subtle because most tokens follow the original ERC‑20 behaviour, so the code looks correct on the surface and passes typical unit tests that use standard‑compliant tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “non‑standard ERC‑20 approval” or “missing zero‑reset before approve” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should either reset the allowance to zero before each new approval or, preferably, use OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20` library which provides `safeIncreaseAllowance`/`safeDecreaseAllowance` and handles the zero‑reset pattern internally. Another safe approach is to avoid using `approve()` altogether for token transfers and instead rely on `safeTransferFrom` where the spender’s allowance is set off‑chain by the token holder. By adopting these patterns the contract will work correctly with both standard and non‑standard ERC‑20 tokens, preserving expected user experience—users will see their balances updated as expected, refunds will be received, and flash‑loan operations will succeed without unexpected reverts.

title: Bypassing K epochs cooldown limit of NextBid
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a bidding mechanism where the highest‑rent bid becomes the active TopBid. To prevent last‑minute bid sniping, the protocol requires that any new bid first become a NextBid and remain in that state for at least K epochs before it is allowed to replace the current TopBid. The intended flow is: a bid is submitted, it is stored as NextBid, the system records the epoch at which the NextBid may become eligible, and only after the current TopBid’s deposit is exhausted for K full epochs can the NextBid be promoted. In the implementation, when the rent owed by the current TopBid exceeds its deposit, the contract transitions from a “depleted” state (State D) to a “ready‑to‑replace” state (State B). During this transition the code calculates a new start epoch for the incoming bid using an unchecked arithmetic expression and immediately overwrites the TopBid with the NextBid, without verifying that the current blockchain epoch is at least K epochs after the originally scheduled activation time. Because there is no explicit check such as `currentEpoch >= nextBid.epoch + K`, an attacker can submit a NextBid just moments before the existing TopBid expires, and the contract will promote the attacker’s bid after only a single epoch (or even a single second) instead of the required K‑epoch cooling period. This bypass allows the attacker to seize the TopBid position far earlier than honest participants expect. From a user perspective, a participant who has waited the full K‑epoch period to become TopBid may see their bid unexpectedly displaced after only a few seconds, resulting in loss of expected rent revenue and a perception that the system is unfair or manipulable. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined state transitions and identified the missing cooldown verification in the State D→State B path. It is subtle because the same cooldown check exists in other state transitions, leading reviewers to assume it is universally enforced. The impact is medium: it does not directly steal funds, but it undermines the economic guarantees of the auction, enables bid‑sniping, and could erode trust in the protocol. The issue manifests when a TopBid is about to run out of deposit and an attacker submits a higher‑rent bid as NextBid in the same block or shortly thereafter. The affected parties are all bidders, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream users relying on the fairness of the auction. To remediate, the contract should enforce the K‑epoch waiting period for every transition that promotes a NextBid to TopBid, including the State D→State B case, by adding a condition that checks `currentEpoch >= nextBid.startEpoch + K` before overwriting the TopBid. Alternatively, the design could introduce an explicit intermediate state (e.g., State C) that records the required cooldown and prevents premature promotion. Implementing this check restores the intended economic barrier against last‑second sniping and aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented auction rules.

title: BunniZone does not verify amAMM manager properly
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BunniZone contract that validates which entity may fulfil a rebalance order. The contract queries the am‑AMM hook for the current top bid and then permits the fulfiller if it is either whitelisted or matches the manager recorded in that top bid. However, the validation logic never checks whether the am‑AMM feature is currently enabled for the pool, either through a pool‑specific override or a global override. Consequently, if an administrator disables the am‑AMM manager, the contract will still accept the previously recorded manager as a valid fulfiller because it only inspects the stored manager address. In addition, the contract does not verify that the manager associated with a rebalance order corresponds to the manager that was active when the order was created. When an order is created near the end of an epoch and the pool switches to a new manager in the next epoch, the old manager can still satisfy the order and claim the rebalance rewards that rightfully belong to the new manager. An attacker or a malicious manager can therefore trigger a rebalance order after the am‑AMM has been disabled or after a manager change, and still receive the associated fees or token swaps. From a user perspective this may appear as a missing or reduced reward, or as unexpected token movements that do not match the expected accounting for the current epoch. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the order‑fulfilment path and identified the missing call to the am‑AMM enable‑check function (getAmAmmEnabled) as well as the lack of epoch‑aware manager verification. The bug is subtle because the contract does perform a manager equality check, which gives the impression that only the authorised manager can act, yet the enable‑flag is hidden behind a separate hook and the epoch logic is not obvious from the surface code. To remediate the problem the contract should first query the am‑AMM hook to confirm that the feature is enabled for the given pool (using getAmAmmEnabled) before allowing any manager‑based fulfilment, and it should also store the manager that was active at order creation and compare it against the fulfiller at execution time, rejecting fulfilments that originate from a manager that was not active when the order was issued. This correction restores the intended business logic that only currently authorised managers may execute rebalance orders and that rewards are allocated to the correct epoch’s manager, preventing unauthorized fund movement and preserving protocol accounting integrity.

title: Incorrect use of "memory-safe" assembly blocks in HookletLib.sol
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An incorrect use of Solidity's "memory-safe" assembly modifier is present in the HookletLib.sol functions callHooklet and staticcallHooklet. The functions attempt to bubble up a revert by copying the returned error data to memory location 0 and then calling revert(0, returndatasize()). Under the memory‑safe rules, even when the assembly block reverts, the code must not write to memory below the free‑memory pointer (the value stored at 0x40). Writing to address 0 can overwrite Solidity's internal bookkeeping data, and when the revert data exceeds 64 bytes the compiler may allocate additional memory that collides with this illegal write. The root cause is the assumption that the temporary memory slot at 0 is always safe for small revert payloads, which contradicts the specification that memory‑safe blocks must respect the free‑memory pointer regardless of control flow. An attacker or a malformed hooklet can trigger a revert with a long error message, causing the assembly to write beyond the allowed region, potentially corrupting the stack or causing the transaction to behave unpredictably, such as returning an empty revert reason or silently failing. The impact is that callers of the hooklet may not receive the original error message, making debugging difficult, and in worst‑case scenarios the corrupted memory could lead to incorrect state updates or loss of funds if subsequent logic relies on the overwritten data. The bug manifests whenever a hooklet call reverts and the revert data size is larger than the small constant assumed by the developer, which can happen during normal operation if a downstream contract uses require with a long string. All users of contracts that rely on HookletLib.sol are affected because the library is a shared component. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑checked the assembly code against Solidity's documentation on memory‑safe blocks. It is hard to notice because the revert still propagates and the transaction appears to fail normally; only the missing or truncated revert reason reveals the problem. The recommended fix is to allocate fresh memory using the free‑memory pointer (e.g., let fmp := mload(0x40)) before copying the return data, and then revert using that pointer, ensuring the write stays within the allowed region. This aligns the code with the generic class of bugs known as “memory‑safe assembly misuse” or “unsafe memory writes in revert handling”, which break the contract’s accounting of error data and can lead to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds.

title: DoS on pool by minting shares without increasing balance
description: When a deposit is made to a pool using rehypothecation, a portion of the tokens are sent to the vault. However, it is not checked if the deposit to the vault increases the balance on the pool. This allows the first depositor to mint shares without increasing the balance of the pool, rendering the pool unusable, as future swaps or deposits will revert because the balance of both tokens is zero. Another way of exploiting this vulnerability would be leaving just one token with a balance in the pool, allowing the following deposits to add liquidity only to one side of the pool.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a liquidity pool allows a depositor to mint pool shares without the underlying token balances of the pool being increased. The root cause is the absence of a verification step after a deposit that uses rehypothecation: the contract sends a portion of the deposited tokens to an external vault but does not check that the vault transfer actually results in a higher balance for the pool’s internal accounting. Because of this missing check, the first depositor can receive shares while the pool’s recorded reserves for both tokens remain at zero. Subsequent operations such as swaps, additional deposits, or withdrawals rely on non‑zero reserves; when the reserves are zero the arithmetic in the pricing formulas fails and the calls revert, rendering the pool unusable. An attacker can also exploit the same flaw by depositing only one of the two required tokens, leaving the pool with a single‑sided balance; later deposits will only be able to add liquidity to that side, breaking the invariant that both sides must have positive liquidity. The impact is that the pool becomes permanently locked, liquidity providers cannot add or remove funds, and users attempting to trade receive transaction reverts, effectively losing access to their capital. This condition occurs immediately after the first successful deposit that does not update the pool balances, and it affects every participant that interacts with the pool thereafter, including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol that relies on the pool for fee generation. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the deposit flow and noticed that the contract did not assert a balance increase after the vault transfer. It can be hard to notice because the deposit transaction itself appears successful and the minted share amount is returned, giving the impression that the pool is correctly funded, while the internal reserves stay at zero. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the pool’s token balances increase by at least the amount deposited, and it should require a minimum non‑zero deposit for the initial liquidity provision. Adding explicit checks after the vault transfer and rejecting deposits that would leave either token balance at zero will prevent the share‑minting‑without‑funding attack and restore the expected accounting guarantees of the pool.

title: DoS in cancelNextBid() due to insufficient topBid deposit
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the function that allows a manager of a pending bid to cancel that bid. The contract only checks whether the current top bid’s deposit divided by its rent is lower than a protocol constant K. If this inequality holds, the function reverts with a specific error, preventing any cancellation of the next bid. The root cause is that the validation logic considers only the top bid’s financial health and ignores the combined ability of the top and next bids to cover the required K epochs. An attacker who holds the top position can deliberately keep their deposit just below the threshold (for example deposit 22 when rent is 1 and K is 24) so that the inequality is always true. Because the contract does not require the sum of the top‑bid and next‑bid deposit‑to‑rent ratios to meet K, the next‑bid manager is permanently blocked from invoking the cancel operation. This results in the next bidder’s funds being locked in the contract, the user interface showing no refund, and the expectation that a bid can be cancelled being violated. The issue manifests whenever a top‑bidder with a low deposit remains active and a subsequent bidder attempts to cancel; it affects any participant who relies on the ability to withdraw their pending bid, effectively freezing their capital. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit of the bidding logic, where the specification in the protocol paper required Dtop/Rtop + Dnext/Rnext ≥ K for cancellation, but the implementation only enforced Dtop/Rtop ≥ K. The bug can be subtle because the revert only occurs under a specific numeric relationship, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the cancellation routine should be extended to either (i) allow the next bid to proceed when the combined deposit‑to‑rent ratio satisfies the K requirement, or (ii) enforce that the top bid maintains enough deposit to meet K on its own, thereby restoring the intended safety check and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: BunniQuoter may not provide accurate quotes
description: BunniQuoter provides quote functions for swaps, deposits, and withdrawals, allowing users to simulate these operations and get expected results without actually executing the transactions. However, these quote functions do not perform calls to the hooklet functions, with the exception of hookletBeforeSwapView. This means that the quotes may not accurately reflect the actual results of the operations if the hooklet functions were to affect the results. For example, a pool with KYC requirements may implement a hookletBeforeDeposit function that reverts if the depositor is not in a whitelist. In this case, an unauthorized user calling the quoteDeposit function should receive (0, 0, 0) no matter the input values they provide.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the quoting module of the Bunni protocol, which offers view‑only functions that simulate swaps, deposits and withdrawals. These quote functions are intended to return the amounts a user would receive if the operation were executed, but they omit calls to the contract's hooklet callbacks, except for the hookletBeforeSwapView. Hooklets are external hooks that can enforce additional logic such as KYC checks, fee adjustments or state‑changing validations. Because the quote functions do not invoke view‑compatible versions of these hooks, the simulated results ignore any restrictions or side‑effects that the hooks would impose during a real transaction. Consequently, a user may receive a quote indicating a non‑zero output while the actual call would revert or return zero due to a hooklet condition. For example, a pool that requires a whitelist may implement hookletBeforeDeposit that reverts for non‑whitelisted addresses; the quoteDeposit function would still return positive numbers, misleading the caller. The impact is that users are given false expectations about the outcome of their operations, potentially leading them to attempt transactions that fail, waste gas, or result in zero token transfers. This mis‑representation can erode trust in the protocol and may cause financial loss if users act on inaccurate quotes. The issue manifests whenever any hooklet that influences the result is present and the corresponding view version is not called by the quoting logic. It affects all participants who rely on the quote functions – regular users, integrators, and front‑ends that display expected returns. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the quoting code against the hooklet interface and noted the missing calls. It is subtle because the quote functions compile and return plausible numbers, and the discrepancy only appears when a hooklet’s condition is triggered, which may not be obvious during casual testing. To remediate, the contract should expose view‑only variants of every hooklet function and invoke them inside each quote function, ensuring that the simulated outcome respects the same validation and calculation logic as the live execution. This aligns the quoting mechanism with the protocol’s business rules and prevents users from being misled about potential returns.

title: Referrer rewards can be arbitraged by sandwich attacks
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a design flaw in the token contract’s referral accounting logic. When a token transfer occurs, the contract automatically moves the referral score associated with the sender’s referrer to the recipient’s referrer if the two referrers differ. This score is used later by the distributeReferralRewards function to calculate how much reward each referrer receives. Because the score transfer happens instantly and is based solely on the amount transferred, a malicious referrer can manipulate the score by performing a large purchase of tokens immediately before the admin triggers a reward distribution, then claim the inflated reward, and finally sell the purchased tokens in the same block. The attack relies on front‑running the reward distribution transaction and exploiting the fact that the score update does not use a snapshot or time‑based vesting, allowing the referrer’s score to be temporarily inflated. The impact is that the attacker can claim rewards that far exceed their legitimate entitlement, draining the reward pool and reducing the amount available to honest participants. This situation occurs whenever the admin calls the reward distribution routine while a referrer is able to submit token transfers in the same block, which is feasible in a public mempool where transactions can be reordered. The affected parties include the protocol’s reward treasury, other token holders who expect fair referral payouts, and any users relying on the integrity of the referral program. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between token transfers and referral score updates. It can be difficult to notice because the contract’s arithmetic appears correct on a per‑transaction basis; the problem only manifests when the timing of transfers and reward distribution is considered, a nuance that is not obvious from static analysis alone. To remediate the flaw, the referral reward mechanism should be decoupled from immediate token transfers, for example by releasing rewards gradually over time, using a snapshot of scores taken before the distribution, or preventing score changes within the same block as a reward payout. Such changes would eliminate the ability to inflate a referrer’s score through rapid buy‑sell cycles and restore the intended economic guarantees of the referral system.

title: Using AAVE vaults for rehypothecation might lead to an underestimation of the value of the reserve
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the implementation of the previewRedeem function in AAVE vault contracts that are used for rehypothecation in a pool. According to the ERC‑4626 (EIP‑4626) specification, a preview function must ignore withdrawal limits such as those returned by maxWithdraw and must behave as if any amount of shares could be redeemed. The AAVE vault, however, incorporates a check for the vault’s paused state and for the amount of liquidity that can actually be withdrawn from the AAVE pool. It computes a maximum withdrawable amount and then returns the minimum of the converted asset value and this limit. When the vault is paused or when all assets are borrowed, the maximum withdrawable amount becomes zero, causing previewRedeem to return zero regardless of the actual underlying balance. This deviation leads to an underestimation of the reserve’s value, which propagates to critical protocol calculations: the number of shares minted for new deposits, the amounts used in token swaps, and the amounts users receive on withdrawals. From a user’s perspective, deposits may yield fewer shares than expected, swap rates can appear unusually unfavorable, and withdrawals may return less than the user believes they are entitled to, sometimes even showing a zero balance in the UI when the vault is paused. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the ERC‑4626 specification and identified the mismatch in the previewRedeem logic. It is difficult to notice because the function is read‑only and only returns an unexpected zero in edge cases, which may be attributed to normal market conditions rather than a bug. The vulnerability belongs to the class of specification‑non‑compliant accounting view functions, where a contract’s accounting logic does not faithfully represent the true asset holdings. To remediate, the previewRedeem implementation should be altered to ignore withdrawal limits and pause checks, returning the full converted asset value for any share amount, or a proxy contract should be introduced that calls the convertToAssets function directly, thereby aligning the behavior with the ERC‑4626 requirements and preventing reserve undervaluation.

title: Incorrect rounding in computeSwap()
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect rounding behavior in the computeSwap routine of the liquidity distribution libraries used by the protocol. The function determines a rounded tick by inverting a cumulative amount and then uses that tick to calculate swapLiquidity, which represents the amount of liquidity available for a trade. The root cause is that the inverse‑cumulative‑amount helper rounds down when the price (sqrtPrice) is extremely close to a tick boundary, even though the specification and comments require rounding up to the next tick. The conditional logic checks that the price difference exceeds a small threshold before applying a tick‑spacing increment; when the difference is equal to or below the threshold the code leaves the tick unchanged, effectively keeping the tick on the left side of the boundary. As a result, computeSwap may return a swapLiquidity value of zero despite there being a non‑zero amount of liquidity in the adjacent rounded tick. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the bug by submitting a swap request whose price lies within the narrow margin where the rounding condition fails. The exploit consists of crafting a trade that pushes the sqrtPrice just below the rounding threshold, causing the contract to believe no liquidity exists and therefore compute an amount‑in of zero and an amount‑out of zero. From the user’s perspective the swap appears to execute but yields no tokens, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show a successful transaction with a zero output, violating the expectation that a trade with available liquidity should transfer value. The impact includes loss of expected revenue for traders, potential denial‑of‑service for liquidity providers who cannot be accessed, and accounting inconsistencies across all liquidity distribution functions that rely on the UniformDistribution and GeometricDistribution libraries. The issue manifests only when the price is extremely close to a rounded tick, a situation that is rare and therefore easy to miss during casual testing; it may only be discovered through precise mathematical fuzzing or formal audit of the rounding logic. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error – it simply returns zero liquidity, which can be interpreted as a normal “no‑trade” outcome. The recommended remediation is to adjust the rounding logic so that any case where sqrtPrice is equal to or greater than sqrtPriceAtTick triggers an upward rounding to the next tick, ensuring that swapLiquidity never incorrectly collapses to zero when liquidity exists. Conceptually, this is a classic rounding‑down error in a financial calculation that violates the invariant that available liquidity must be reflected in swap amounts, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: depositIncentive and incentivizeRecurPool do not verify if the incentiveToken exists
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of the incentive token address in functions that accept an external token to be transferred as a reward incentive. The contract calls a safeTransferFrom routine from the solady library, but the underlying implementation treats the absence of return data as a successful transfer. Consequently, when an attacker supplies an address that does not contain contract code – for example an externally owned account or a placeholder address that will later host a token contract – the call returns true even though no token transfer occurs. This flaw arises because the code does not check the code size of the supplied token address before attempting the transfer, and the library version used does not perform such a check. An attacker can exploit the issue by front‑running the creation of a predictable token address (such as a Bunni LP token), submitting a fake incentive token address, and causing the contract to record that incentives were deposited while in reality no tokens were moved. The impact is that reward accounting becomes inaccurate: users may see a pool advertised with a certain incentive amount but receive zero or reduced rewards, balances may appear unchanged, and the protocol’s incentive mechanism loses credibility. The condition occurs whenever the incentive token is expected to be a newly deployed contract or any token whose existence is not guaranteed at the time of the call. Affected parties include token holders, stakers, protocol participants, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct incentive distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the token transfer logic and noticed the lack of a contract‑code verification step. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert; the library reports success even though no token movement happened, so the failure is silent. To remediate, the contract should verify that the incentive token address contains contract code (for example by checking extcodesize) or upgrade to the latest solady version that includes this verification. Additionally, the contract could enforce that the token adheres to the ERC‑20 interface and revert on any failed transfer, ensuring that the recorded incentive amount truly reflects transferred tokens. From a user perspective the UI may show a newly created reward pool with a non‑zero incentive amount, yet later the user’s reward balance remains zero, contradicting the expectation that a deposit of tokens has been made. This discrepancy violates the business logic that incentives must be funded before they can be distributed, leading to potential loss of trust and financial misallocation.

title: DOS Attack in joinRushPool
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition in the joinRushPool function of a staking pool contract. The root cause is that the function only checks the remaining capacity of the pool at the moment of execution and does not reserve or lock that capacity for the caller. An attacker can observe a pending joinRushPool transaction from a legitimate user, then front‑run the transaction by calling joinRushPool themselves and filling the pool up to its stake cap. Because the pool is now full, the victim’s transaction encounters the capacity check, evaluates to zero stake amount, and reverts. After the victim’s transaction fails, the attacker immediately back‑runs by calling exitRushPool to withdraw the stake they just added, restoring the pool’s free capacity for the next attack cycle. This sandwich pattern can be repeated indefinitely, allowing the attacker to consistently block other users from joining the pool while only paying gas for the two extra transactions. The impact is that honest users are unable to stake, their transactions revert, and they lose only the gas spent; the pool’s intended functionality is effectively crippled. The condition occurs whenever there is a race between multiple joinRushPool calls and the contract does not enforce a minimum staking period or a delay on unstaking, making it possible to fill and empty the pool within the same block. The affected parties include any user trying to join the pool, the protocol’s overall liquidity and trustworthiness, and potentially token holders who rely on the pool’s staking incentives. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the pool’s capacity logic and identified that the capacity check is not atomic with respect to stake reservation. It can be hard to notice because the failure only manifests under specific front‑running scenarios that may not appear in standard unit tests. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running‑induced DoS or capacity‑exhaustion vulnerabilities, where a contract’s accounting assumptions (that capacity will remain available after a check) are violated. From a user’s perspective, attempts to join the pool result in a transaction revert with no stake being recorded, often described as “my stake failed, I got nothing, and my gas was spent”. To remediate, the contract should introduce a minimum stake duration or an unstaking delay, preventing an attacker from withdrawing immediately after front‑running, thereby ensuring that capacity once allocated cannot be instantly reclaimed and protecting honest users from being blocked.

title: Rewards are permanently locked when totalSupply = 0 in RecurPools
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the reward calculation of RecurPools that permanently locks incentive tokens when the pool has no staked balance. The function that updates the per‑token reward returns the previously stored reward value unchanged if totalSupply equals zero, but the surrounding logic always advances the lastUpdateTime after the call. Consequently, during any interval where rewardRate is positive, totalSupply is zero, and time elapses between the previous update and the period finish, the contract marks the interval as processed without actually crediting any stakers. Because the stored reward amount is never increased and there is no rescue mechanism, the allocated rewards become unrecoverable for both future stakers and the incentive depositor. The bug manifests when all users withdraw their stakes before a reward period ends, or when the pool starts with no participants and rewards are funded in advance. From a user’s perspective, stakers see no accrued rewards despite the pool being funded, and incentive providers notice that their deposited tokens disappear from the contract balance without any event indicating a transfer. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑per‑token helper and observed the mismatch between rewardPerTokenStored handling and lastUpdateTime mutation. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error or revert; the state simply advances, giving the illusion that rewards have been accounted for. The flaw belongs to the class of “reward accounting lock” bugs where state updates are performed out of order, violating the assumption that rewards are only considered distributed when there is a non‑zero supply. To remediate, the contract should either skip updating lastUpdateTime when totalSupply is zero or provide a path for the incentive provider to reclaim undistributed rewards after the period, ensuring that rewards accumulate correctly for future participants and that no funds are permanently locked.

title: Incorrect tick rounding in TWAP calculation
description:
```solidity
function _queryTwap(
    PoolKey memory poolKey,
    uint32 twapSecondsAgoStart,
    uint32 twapSecondsAgoEnd
)
    internal
    returns (int24 arithmeticMeanTick)
    int56 tickCumulativesDelta = tickCumulatives[1] - tickCumulatives[0];
    return int24(tickCumulativesDelta / int56(uint56(windowSize))); // @audit rounding towards zero if tickCumulativesDelta < 0
```
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect rounding behavior in the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) calculation used by the pool contract. The function computes the arithmetic mean tick by dividing the difference of two tick cumulative values (tickCumulativesDelta) by the window size. In Solidity, integer division truncates toward zero, so when tickCumulativesDelta is negative and not an exact multiple of the window size, the result is rounded up (toward zero) instead of being rounded down (toward negative infinity). This off‑by‑one rounding produces a tick that is one unit higher (less negative) than the mathematically correct value. The bug can be triggered whenever the price movement over the observation window is downward enough to make tickCumulativesDelta negative and the division leaves a remainder. Users who rely on the TWAP for price quotes, such as traders executing swaps or liquidity providers whose positions are re‑balanced based on the oracle, may receive a slightly worse price than expected, effectively losing a fraction of a tick per trade. Because the deviation is only one tick, it may not be obvious in normal operation and can be missed during casual testing; it only appears in edge cases with negative cumulative changes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the arithmetic expression and identified the use of plain division without handling the sign of the dividend. The bug belongs to the class of integer rounding errors where signed division does not follow floor semantics required by financial calculations. To fix the problem, the contract should explicitly round toward negative infinity when the dividend is negative and a remainder exists, for example by decrementing the result by one in that case. After the correction, the TWAP will always reflect the true arithmetic mean tick, preserving the protocol’s accounting assumptions and preventing users from receiving unexpectedly unfavorable rates.

title: LiqFacet::removeLiq temporarily disabled when vault is paused
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity removal routine of the LiqFacet contract. When a user calls the function that withdraws liquidity, the implementation iterates over every vault that belongs to the same closure and attempts to withdraw the proportional share from each vault. The code assumes that every vault is always operational and does not verify whether a vault is in a paused state before invoking its withdraw method. If any vault in the closure has been paused – for example by an admin or governance action – the withdraw call on that vault fails (typically by reverting). Because the loop does not catch this failure, the entire transaction reverts and the user receives no tokens, even though other vaults in the same closure might still contain withdrawable balances. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for liquidity providers: they cannot retrieve their deposited assets as long as at least one vault remains paused. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s control‑flow logic, where the auditor noticed that the pause flag of a vault is never consulted in the removal path. It can be hard to spot because the function works correctly under normal conditions and only exhibits the problem when a vault is deliberately paused, a state that may be rare in routine testing. The impact is that users expecting a refund of their liquidity see the transaction fail or receive zero tokens, breaking the business assumption that liquidity can always be withdrawn on demand. The affected parties include any liquidity provider who added funds to a paused vault, the protocol that relies on smooth liquidity flows, and potentially token holders who depend on accurate accounting. To remediate, the removal logic should check the paused status of each vault and either skip paused vaults or handle them separately, ensuring that withdrawals from active vaults can still be processed. This change restores the intended behavior that users receive the portion of their liquidity that is still available, while preserving the pause mechanism for security or upgrade purposes.

title: Fee-on-transfer token compatibility Issue in protocol Burve::mint
description:
The Burve::mint function interacts with the uniswapV3MintCallback, which transfers token0 and token1 to the Uniswap pool. However, fee-on-transfer tokens (tokens that deduct a percentage as a fee on each transfer) are not properly accounted for in this implementation.
When using fee-on-transfer tokens, the amount received by the pool will be less than the expected amount, causing the minting process to fail due to an arithmetic underflow.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the minting routine of the Burve protocol, specifically the Burve::mint function that calls the Uniswap V3 mint callback to transfer token0 and token1 into a Uniswap pool. The implementation assumes that the amount of each token sent to the pool will be received in full, but it does not account for fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens, which deduct a percentage of the transferred amount as a fee. Because the callback transfers a fixed amount while the pool actually receives a smaller amount, the subsequent arithmetic that checks the received balances can underflow, causing the mint transaction to revert. This flaw originates from a missing verification step that compares the pre‑transfer and post‑transfer balances, leading to an unchecked subtraction based on an optimistic expectation. An attacker or any user supplying a fee‑on‑transfer token can trigger the condition simply by providing the token as either token0 or token1; the pool receives less than required, the contract’s internal accounting sees a deficit, and the minting process fails. The impact is that legitimate liquidity providers are unable to create new positions, potentially locking funds that were already approved for transfer, and the protocol may experience denial‑of‑service conditions for the affected token pairs. The issue appears only when a token with a transfer fee is used, which makes it easy to miss during standard testing that employs fee‑free ERC20 tokens. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected transfer amounts with the actual balances after the callback. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction that appears to be submitted, but later the transaction reverts with an “underflow” error, leaving the user with no minted liquidity and possibly with approved tokens still held by the contract. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect token accounting for fee‑on‑transfer tokens” and violates the protocol’s assumption that token transfers are lossless, breaking the accounting invariants that guarantee correct liquidity minting. The recommended remediation is to adopt a safe‑transfer pattern that records the token balance before the callback, performs the transfer, then checks the actual amount received and adjusts the required amounts accordingly, or to explicitly reject tokens that charge a fee on transfer.

title: Missing selectors from SimplexFacet for diamond cuts
description:
Several functions from SimplexFacet are missing from the diamond cuts:
- withdrawFees
- setName
- getName
Since these functions are not included in the selector list, they cannot be called through the diamond contract, effectively making them inaccessible.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing function selectors for three external functions in the SimplexFacet when the facet is added to the diamond via a FacetCut. In the diamond pattern, the contract routes calls based on a mapping from function selector to facet address that is built from the selector list supplied in each cut. Because the selectors for withdrawFees, setName and getName were omitted from the array, the diamond never registers these selectors. As a result, any call sent to the diamond with one of those selectors is not forwarded to SimplexFacet; the call falls back to the diamond’s fallback function and effectively does nothing. This makes the functions inaccessible to anyone, including the contract owner who would normally call withdrawFees to collect accumulated protocol fees, or users who rely on getName to read the contract’s identifier, or governance processes that need setName to update metadata. The issue appears at deployment or during an upgrade when the facet cut is executed; it does not cause a compilation error and therefore can be easily missed during testing. The impact is a functional outage: fees that should be withdrawable remain locked in the contract, the contract name cannot be read or changed, and any UI that expects these calls will show missing data or disabled actions. The bug is a classic case of incomplete facet registration, a selector omission error that violates the assumption that every external function of a facet is reachable through the diamond. It was discovered during a manual audit of the diamond cut configuration, where the auditor compared the list of functions defined in SimplexFacet with the selectors supplied to the cut and found a mismatch. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and the missing selectors do not generate runtime errors until a call is attempted; the fallback simply returns no data, which may be interpreted as a normal empty response. To remediate, the facet cut should be updated to include the missing selectors, expanding the selector array to contain the selectors for withdrawFees, setName and getName, and the cut should be re‑executed or the contract upgraded accordingly. Ensuring that the selector list matches the full public interface of each facet restores the intended business logic, allowing fee withdrawal, name management and proper read‑only access.

title: Missing supportsInterface Selector from DiamondLoupeFacet
description: The SimplexDiamond contract is intended to support multiple interfaces, including IERC165, IDiamondCut, IDiamondLoupe, and IERC173. While SimplexDiamond correctly adds these interfaces to ds.supportedInterfaces, it fails to include the supportsInterface function from DiamondLoupeFacet as a selector. This omission prevents the contract from properly supporting interfaces, making it incompatible with standard interface detection mechanisms.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incomplete facet registration in a Diamond proxy contract that implements the ERC‑165 based Diamond standard. The SimplexDiamond contract correctly records that it supports several interface identifiers – IERC165, IDiamondCut, IDiamondLoupe and IERC173 – in its internal supportedInterfaces mapping. However, when the DiamondLoupeFacet is added to the diamond, the selector for the supportsInterface function itself is omitted from the list of function selectors supplied to the diamond cut. Because ERC‑165 relies on the supportsInterface(bytes4) function to answer queries about which interfaces a contract implements, the absence of this selector means that external callers invoking supportsInterface on the diamond will receive a default false response for the IDiamondLoupe interface even though the facet’s logic is present. This mismatch prevents standard interface detection tools, other contracts, and off‑chain services from recognizing that the diamond implements the loupe functions, leading to incompatibility with any component that expects ERC‑165 compliance. The bug can be exploited indirectly: an attacker or a benign integrator that first checks supportsInterface(IDiamondLoupe) will conclude that the contract does not implement the loupe, and therefore may avoid calling facetAddress, facets, or other loupe queries, causing functionality that depends on those calls to be unavailable. In practice the impact is a broken user experience – for example a UI that lists available facets will appear empty, or a DeFi protocol that relies on the loupe to discover facet addresses will fail to route calls, potentially resulting in missed opportunities or halted operations. The condition occurs whenever the diamond is queried via ERC‑165 for the IDiamondLoupe interface, which is a common pattern for contract introspection. All participants that interact with the diamond – developers, auditors, integrators, and end‑users – are affected because the contract appears non‑compliant despite containing the correct code. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the facet registration logic, where the auditor compared the expected selector array size with the actual array and noticed that the supportsInterface selector was not included. The problem is subtle because the facet’s functions are otherwise reachable via direct calls, so normal testing that does not perform an ERC‑165 check may not reveal the discrepancy. To remediate the issue, the DiamondLoupeFacet’s supportsInterface selector must be added to the facet cut array, increasing the selector count accordingly, so that the diamond’s ERC‑165 response correctly reports support for IDiamondLoupe. This aligns the contract’s declared interfaces with its actual capabilities and restores compatibility with standard interface detection mechanisms.

title: EnsureClosure would not add a vertex's closure if added in future
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ensureClosure function that is invoked for each vertex when liquidity is added through addLiq(). The function iterates over the vertices that belong to a closure identifier and, for each vertex, checks whether the closure already contains the neighbor and whether the homSet mapping for that neighbor and closure is already populated. If both conditions are true, the code executes a return statement, which exits the entire ensureClosure call immediately. This logic works correctly when all vertices of the closure are already registered, but it fails when a new vertex is introduced after the initial deployment. In that scenario, the first two vertices satisfy the early‑return condition because their homSet entries are already set, causing the function to return before processing the third, newly added vertex. Consequently, the homSet and homs structures for the new vertex remain unset, meaning the protocol cannot correctly reference that vertex during swaps or further liquidity operations. From a user’s perspective, adding liquidity that includes the new token appears to succeed, yet subsequent swaps involving that token either return zero or revert, and the token balance may appear unchanged or missing in the pool UI. The impact is a partial loss of functionality: liquidity providers cannot trade the newly added token, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about complete closure state are violated. The bug is triggered only when a closure identifier contains a mix of already‑registered vertices and vertices that are added later, i.e., when the addLiq() loop encounters a vertex whose closure entry is missing while earlier vertices have already set the homSet flag. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of ensureClosure and identified that the return statement prevents the loop from continuing to the remaining vertices. It is subtle because the guard appears to protect against duplicate work, yet it unintentionally blocks legitimate updates. The recommended remediation is to replace the return with a continue (or restructure the logic) so that the function skips only the already‑processed neighbor but still iterates over the remaining vertices, ensuring that every vertex in the closure receives its required state initialization. This change restores the intended invariant that all vertices referenced by a closure are fully registered, eliminating the scenario where funds become inaccessible or swaps fail due to missing closure data.

title: FeeLib calculations can revert
description:
The FeeLib library is based on the Uniswap's V3 PositionValue library.
However, it is not taken into account that the fee calculations expect overflows and underflows. This is not an issue in the original library, as it uses a solc version lower than 0.8.0, which does not revert to overflow/underflow. But in the Burve implementation, this will cause the transaction to revert.
The issue can be reproduced by running the test_QueryValue_V3_NoFees test on a fork of the Berachain network:
```bash
forge test --mt test_QueryValue_V3_NoFees --fork-url https://rpc.berachain.com/
// --fork-block-number 2073480
```
As a result, all the query functions in Burve.sol might revert unexpectedly.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a fee‑calculation library that was copied from Uniswap V3 PositionValue and integrated into the Burve protocol. The library performs arithmetic operations that were originally written for a Solidity compiler version older than 0.8.0, where overflow and underflow silently wrapped around. In Solidity 0.8 and later, the same operations automatically trigger a revert when the result exceeds the type limits. Because the Burve implementation compiles with a newer compiler, any fee calculation that would have overflowed or underflowed now causes the whole transaction to revert. This issue is discovered during a security audit when the test_QueryValue_V3_NoFees test was executed against a fork of the Berachain network and consistently reverted. The root cause is the mismatch between the expected unchecked arithmetic behavior and the compiler’s built‑in safety checks. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug by providing inputs that lead to an overflow or underflow in the fee formula, causing the query functions in Burve.sol to revert unexpectedly. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on all fee‑related query calls: users attempting to read fee information see transaction failures, UI components may display empty or zero values, and the protocol cannot correctly report or distribute fees. The problem occurs whenever the fee calculation is invoked, especially in edge cases such as zero‑fee scenarios that still trigger the arithmetic path. Affected parties include any contract or off‑chain service that relies on these query functions, as well as end‑users who expect to see accurate fee data or to receive fee payouts. The bug is subtle because the library compiles without warnings and the overflow condition may only appear with specific input ranges, making it easy to miss during manual testing. To remediate, the library should be adapted to use unchecked blocks for the arithmetic that intentionally allows wrap‑around, or it should employ explicit safe‑math functions that handle overflow and underflow without reverting. Conceptually, the fix restores the original unchecked behavior while preserving the intended fee logic, eliminating unexpected reverts and restoring reliable fee queries.

title: setAdjustor selector not included from SimplexFacet
description: The SimplexFacet contract is missing the setAdjustor selector from the simplexSelectors array. This means that the setAdjustor function cannot be called.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an omission in the registration of the setAdjustor function within the selector array that the SimplexFacet exposes to the Diamond proxy. In a Diamond architecture, each facet declares an array of function selectors that the proxy uses to route external calls. The audit found that the simplexSelectors array is allocated with length nine and only nine selectors are assigned, while the setAdjustor selector is never added. As a result, any call to setAdjustor is not recognized by the proxy and is either forwarded to the fallback function or rejected, making the function effectively unusable. The root cause is a simple off‑by‑one error in the array size and a missing assignment statement, which does not trigger a compilation error and therefore can remain unnoticed during development. Exploitation is straightforward: an authorized user or contract attempting to update the adjustor – for example to change fee calculation parameters – will observe that the transaction does not modify the state, returns no error, or reverts with an unknown selector error. From a user perspective the UI may show a button to change the adjustor, but after submission the balance or fee rate remains unchanged, leading to confusion such as “my fees are still the old amount” or “the adjustor update did nothing”. The impact is that the protocol cannot adjust a critical economic parameter after deployment, which may lock the system into an undesired fee schedule, prevent emergency adjustments, and potentially cause funds to be collected under an incorrect rate. This limitation affects protocol administrators, liquidity providers, and any user relying on the ability to modify the adjustor. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the expected list of facet functions against the actual selector array. Because the missing selector does not produce a compile‑time warning and the function is not called in the test suite, the bug can be hard to notice without explicit inspection of the selector registration logic. The recommended remediation is to increase the selector array size to ten and add SimplexFacet.setAdjustor.selector at the appropriate index, ensuring that the function is properly exposed through the Diamond proxy. Conceptually, the fix is to guarantee that every external function intended to be callable via the proxy is included in the facet’s selector list, thereby preserving the contract’s intended business logic and accounting assumptions.

title: No slippage protection
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing slippage protection mechanism in the share‑minting logic of the Burve contract when users provide liquidity to the Island pool and Uniswap V3 pools. The contract calculates the number of shares to mint by reading the current sqrtRatioX96 from the pool’s slot0 and converting the supplied liquidity into token amounts before calling island.getMintAmounts. Because sqrtRatioX96 reflects the instantaneous price of the pool, any change in price between the moment a user signs a transaction and the moment it is mined will directly affect the computed share amount. The root cause is the reliance on a volatile on‑chain price variable without enforcing a minimum acceptable share output or locking the price at the time of the quote. An attacker or a market movement can therefore front‑run the transaction, manipulate the price, or simply wait for natural volatility, causing the user to receive fewer shares than expected. From the user’s perspective the UI may display an estimate such as “you will receive 100 shares”, but after execution the wallet shows a lower balance, sometimes even zero, leading to confusion and the perception of lost funds. The impact is a reduction in the user’s effective ownership of the liquidity position, potential accounting inconsistencies for the protocol, and a breach of the business assumption that the amount of shares minted is deterministic based on the supplied liquidity. The issue manifests whenever a liquidity‑adding transaction is processed while the pool price is not static, which is common in volatile markets. It was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the absence of a minSharesOut or slippage‑tolerance parameter in the mint and burn functions. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; it simply mints a lower number of shares, which may be interpreted as a normal outcome. The recommended remediation is to introduce a minimum‑shares‑out argument (or equivalent slippage protection) that reverts the transaction if the computed shares fall below the user‑specified threshold, or to snapshot the price at the time of the quote and use that immutable value for the calculation. This change restores the guarantee that users receive at least the amount of shares they expect, aligning the contract’s behavior with typical financial expectations and preventing value erosion due to price volatility.

title: Lack of slippage protection in buy and sell functions
description: The buy and sell functions in the BondingCurve contract currently lack slippage protection mechanisms. These functions are integral to the contract's operation as they facilitate the purchase and sale of tokens based on a bonding curve model, which acts similarly to an Automated Market Maker (AMM). The absence of slippage protection can lead to users receiving fewer tokens or less Ether than expected due to price fluctuations between the time a transaction is initiated and when it is executed. This can result in a poor user experience and potential financial loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the buy and sell functions of a bonding‑curve based token contract. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum amount of tokens to be received when buying, nor a minimum amount of Ether to be received when selling, a user can submit a transaction that is executed at a price that has moved unfavorably between the moment the transaction is signed and the moment it is mined. The root cause is the absence of parameters such as minTokens or minEthers and the lack of corresponding require checks that compare the actual output of the bonding‑curve formula with the user‑specified expectations. An attacker, or simply natural market volatility, can cause the price to shift, resulting in the transaction completing but delivering fewer tokens or less Ether than the user anticipated. This can be exploited by front‑runners who observe a pending transaction, execute a trade that moves the curve price, and then let the original transaction settle at the new, worse rate. The impact is financial loss for any participant who relies on the contract’s quoted price without a safety margin: users may see their token balance increase by a smaller amount than expected, or their Ether balance decrease after a sell, sometimes appearing as if the funds have disappeared. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the bonding curve price is not static during transaction execution, which is typical in decentralized environments where block times allow price movement. All users of the contract, including traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, are affected because the economic model assumes accurate price execution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public interface with standard AMM best practices and noted the lack of slippage checks. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it succeeds, but the outcome is sub‑optimal, which may be interpreted as normal market risk rather than a contract flaw. To remediate, the contract should be extended with explicit minimum‑output parameters for both buying and selling, and view functions should be provided so callers can compute the expected output before submitting a transaction. The functions should then enforce that the actual output meets or exceeds the caller‑specified minimum, causing the transaction to revert if the price has moved beyond the acceptable range. This aligns the contract with the generic class of slippage‑protection bugs common in AMM implementations and restores user confidence that the contract will not silently deliver less value than promised.

title: Hardcoding gas costs should be avoided
description: The modifier markCost in SimpleAdministrator has some hard coded gas cost values like for example 21000 (the base cost of an EVM transaction). We have seen previous EVM forks changing the gas cost of some key things, for example the SSTORE opcode. This can happen again and in this case the hardcoded values in markCost might not be correct anymore which will lead to wrong accounting for incurred gas costs. Also if the project is deployed on a different EVM-compatible chain, the gas costs there might be different.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of hard‑coded gas cost constants inside the markCost modifier of the SimpleAdministrator contract. Instead of querying the EVM for the current gas price of operations such as the base transaction cost (21000) or the cost of SSTORE, the code stores fixed numeric values. This design assumes that the gas schedule will never change, which is false because Ethereum and other EVM‑compatible chains periodically adjust opcode costs during network upgrades. When a fork modifies the cost of an opcode, the hard‑coded numbers become inaccurate, causing the contract’s internal accounting of gas consumption to be wrong. An attacker or any user can trigger a function that relies on the markCost modifier; the contract will record a lower (or higher) gas usage than actually incurred. If the recorded cost is lower than the real cost, the contract may believe it has sufficient gas allowance and proceed, only to run out of gas and revert, potentially leaving a transaction partially executed or causing a denial‑of‑service condition. Conversely, if the recorded cost is higher, users may be over‑charged for gas, receiving less net value than expected. The issue manifests whenever the contract is executed on a network where the gas schedule differs from the hard‑coded assumptions – for example after an Ethereum hard fork that changes SSTORE pricing, or when the contract is deployed on a side‑chain with a distinct gas model. All participants who interact with the contract – end‑users paying fees, the protocol’s accounting system, and administrators relying on accurate gas metrics – are affected because the financial accounting and fee calculations become unreliable. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the presence of static numeric gas values and recognized the risk of future schedule changes. It is subtle because the contract will function correctly under the current schedule, so the bug does not produce immediate failures and may only surface after a network upgrade or on a different chain, making it hard to detect through ordinary testing. The recommended remediation is to replace the constants with configurable parameters that are set during contract initialization and can be updated via dedicated setter functions, allowing the protocol to adapt the expected gas costs whenever the underlying EVM changes. This approach restores accurate gas accounting, prevents unexpected transaction reverts, and ensures that users receive the fee treatment they anticipate, aligning the contract’s behavior with the evolving gas economics of the platform.

title: transferERC20ToTreasury won't work as intended if assetToken is a multiple-address token
description: Some ERC20 tokens on the blockchain are deployed behind a proxy, so they have at least 2 entry points (the proxy and the implementation) for their functionality. Example is Synthetix’s ProxyERC20 contract from where you can interact with sUSD, sBTC etc). If such a token was used as the assetToken token in an InvestmentPool, then the admin will be able to rug all depositors with the transferERC20ToTreasury method, even though it has the following check require(tokenAddress != _assetTokenAddress, "IP: Asset transfer"); Since the tokens have multiple addresses the admin can give another address and pass those checks.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the transferERC20ToTreasury function of the InvestmentPool contract. The function attempts to prevent the pool’s own asset token from being moved to the treasury by checking that the address supplied to the transfer call is not equal to the stored _assetTokenAddress. This check assumes that a single contract address uniquely identifies the token. However, many ERC20 tokens are deployed behind a proxy pattern, where the proxy contract and the implementation contract each have distinct addresses but together represent the same logical token (for example Synthetix’s ProxyERC20). Because the check only compares raw addresses, an administrator can supply the implementation contract’s address instead of the proxy address, satisfy the require statement, and invoke the transfer. The pool then moves the deposited tokens to the treasury, effectively allowing the admin to rug all depositors. The flaw occurs whenever the asset token used in the pool is a proxy‑based token with multiple entry points. Users who have deposited expect their balances to remain locked in the pool; instead they may see their token balance drop to zero or receive no refund when attempting to withdraw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the address comparison and recognized the proxy token pattern. It is subtle because a simple address inequality appears to enforce a safety rule, yet the underlying token identity is not verified, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should not rely on address equality alone. A robust approach is to record the pool’s token balance before the transfer, execute the transfer, and then assert that the balance of the intended asset token has not decreased, or otherwise ensure that the transferred amount is zero for the asset token. This prevents any token, regardless of how many contract addresses it uses, from being unintentionally moved to the treasury and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the InvestmentPool.

title: Front-running risk in key admin actions
description: The methods forceTransfer, whitelistAccount and freezeAccount from InvestmentPoolCore and Whitelist can be monitored for transactions and front-ran. Imagine the following scenario: 1. Bob holds some InvestmentPool ERC20 tokens 2. For some reason, a holder of the TOKEN_FREEZE_ROLE decides Bob is malicious and his balance should be frozen, so he calls Whitelist::freezeAccount 3. Bob was expecting that and was already monitoring the mempool, so he front-runs the transaction with a transfer transaction to another address he controls 4. Now his address is frozen, but he can still move/redeem/swap his tokens since the new address is not frozen The same logic applies for the whitelistAccount and forceTransfer functionalities.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a transaction‑ordering (front‑running) weakness affecting privileged admin functions that modify account status, such as freezing an account, adding an address to a whitelist, or forcibly transferring tokens on behalf of a user. The root cause is that these functions are exposed as regular external calls that can be observed in the public mempool and are executed without any protection against being reordered by other participants. An attacker who monitors pending transactions can see an admin transaction that intends to freeze a target address and, before that transaction is mined, submit a transfer from the target address to a different address they control. Because the freeze only takes effect on the original address after the admin transaction is confirmed, the attacker’s pre‑emptive transfer succeeds, allowing the tokens to leave the account that is about to be frozen. The same pattern applies to whitelist and force‑transfer operations: a user can move assets away before the whitelist change or forced transfer is applied. This results in the intended security measure – freezing or restricting an address – being bypassed, so the protocol’s risk‑management logic is broken. The impact is that malicious actors can retain control over funds that should be locked, potentially leading to loss of compliance, financial loss for the protocol, and erosion of trust among users. The issue manifests when an account with a privileged role (e.g., TOKEN_FREEZE_ROLE) initiates a state‑changing admin call while the targeted address is actively monitoring the mempool and can submit a competing transaction in the same block or earlier. All token holders who rely on the freeze or whitelist mechanisms are affected, as the protocol can no longer guarantee that a frozen address is truly unable to move its tokens. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of admin functions and identified that no anti‑front‑running measures were present. It can be hard to notice because the freeze transaction itself succeeds and the contract state appears correct after mining; the problem only becomes visible when a previously frozen address is observed to have transferred tokens shortly before being frozen, which may look like normal user behavior. To remediate, the admin actions should be executed in a way that removes them from the public mempool, such as using a private transaction relay, a commit‑reveal scheme, or a timelocked governance proposal that gives the protocol time to react before the state change is applied. Alternatively, the contract could enforce a pending‑freeze flag that blocks outgoing transfers from the target address within the same block as the freeze request, or redesign the logic so that freezing is performed by an internal call that cannot be front‑run. In essence, the fix requires eliminating the ability for external actors to reorder privileged state changes, thereby restoring the intended guarantee that frozen or whitelisted accounts cannot be manipulated after the admin decision.

title: An important flow of admin actions is not enforced, just documented
description: The NatSpec of InvestmentPoolCore::setInflowOutflowPool contains the following comment: /// @notice call batchSettlement (id) beforehand, otherwise it will rug the old pool tokenholders This can easily be forgotten or missed when executing a call to the method. This way of ensuring proper flow of operations is used is error-prone.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a missing on‑chain enforcement of a required administrative workflow in the InvestmentPoolCore contract. The function that updates the inflow/outflow pool, setInflowOutflowPool, is documented in its NatSpec comment to be called only after batchSettlement(id) has been executed, otherwise the operation will “rug” the holders of the previous pool token. However, the contract does not contain any state variable, modifier, or require statement that checks whether batchSettlement was performed before the update. Consequently, the prerequisite exists only as a comment that can be easily overlooked by the admin or any automated script that invokes the function. When an administrator calls setInflowOutflowPool without first invoking batchSettlement, the protocol skips the settlement step that redistributes or locks the assets of the old pool, causing those assets to become inaccessible to the original token holders. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a sudden loss of balance: token holders may see their holdings drop to zero or notice that expected refunds or payouts are missing after a pool change. The impact is a direct financial loss for the token holders of the old pool, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that assets are always settled before a pool transition—are violated. The issue occurs only under the condition that the admin executes the update function without the preceding settlement call; it is not triggered by regular user interactions. It was discovered during a manual security review that compared the NatSpec documentation with the actual contract logic and identified the absence of any enforcement mechanism. Because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error, the problem can remain hidden until a pool transition is performed and users notice missing funds, making it hard to detect through automated testing alone. The recommended remediation is to introduce a persistent flag or storage variable that records whether batchSettlement has been called for a given pool identifier and to add a require statement in setInflowOutflowPool that checks this flag, thereby guaranteeing the correct order of operations and preventing accidental or malicious rug pulls of old pool token holders.

title: Single-step ownership transfer can be dangerous
description: Single-step ownership transfer means that if a wrong address was passed when transferring ownership or admin rights it can mean that role is lost forever. This can be detrimental in the context of InvestmentPoolCore, where if transferAdminRole method was called with a wrong newAdmin address, then the InvestmentPoolCore contract will be bricked, since it relies heavily on admin-only methods.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: Single-step ownership transfer is a design flaw where the contract immediately assigns admin or owner rights to the address supplied in a single function call. The root cause is the lack of a confirmation step; the contract trusts the caller to provide a correct destination address and does not retain any fallback control. If the caller mistakenly provides an incorrect address—such as a zero address, an address without a private key, or an address controlled by an attacker—the new admin role is set to that address instantly. Because the contract relies on admin‑only functions for critical operations (e.g., managing investment pools, updating parameters, withdrawing funds), the loss of a valid admin makes those functions permanently inaccessible. An attacker who receives the admin role can execute privileged actions, while a wrong but inert address effectively bricks the contract, leaving user funds locked and the protocol unable to perform essential governance or maintenance tasks. This condition occurs whenever the transferAdminRole (or similar) function is called with an unintended address, which may happen during deployment, upgrade, or routine admin handover. The issue was identified during a manual security review that examined role‑changing functions and noted the absence of a pending‑owner mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may succeed without reverting, and the contract does not emit a warning; only after attempts to call admin functions fail does the problem become apparent. The appropriate mitigation is to adopt a two‑step ownership transfer pattern, where the current admin designates a pending admin and the new admin must explicitly claim the role, preserving the original admin’s control until the claim is made. This pattern prevents accidental loss of privileges and provides a safety window to correct address mistakes, thereby protecting the protocol’s ability to manage funds and maintain its business logic.

title: Incorrect key usage in transfer delay feature causes global sell swap restriction
description: The transferDelayEnabled function is designed to enforce a delay between consecutive token transfers to prevent rapid trading and potential market manipulation. This feature is particularly relevant during the initial trading period, where it enforces a 10-block delay between sell transactions to automated market maker (AMM) pairs. However, there is an issue in the implementation of this feature within the _transfer function. The key used to track the last transfer timestamp in the _holderLastTransferTimestamp mapping is msg.sender, which is typically the address of the Uniswap router during swaps. This results in the transfer delay being applied globally to all users, rather than individually. Consequently, during the first 20 minutes of trading, only one sell swap can be performed every ten blocks across the entire user base, severely restricting trading activity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the transfer‑delay anti‑bot feature that causes the delay to be enforced globally instead of per individual holder. The contract stores the timestamp of the last transfer in a mapping keyed by msg.sender, which during a sell to an automated market maker (AMM) pair is the address of the router contract rather than the actual token holder. Because the router address is the same for every user, the contract records a single last‑transfer timestamp for the whole ecosystem. When the transferDelayEnabled flag is active – typically during the first 20 minutes of trading – the _transfer function checks this timestamp and rejects any sell that occurs within ten blocks of the previous sell, regardless of which user initiates it. As a result, only one sell swap can be executed across all participants every ten blocks, dramatically restricting market activity. Users experience failed or reverted sell transactions, see no change in their balances after attempting to sell, and may assume the token is frozen or malicious. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition for traders, loss of liquidity, and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue occurs only when the transfer‑delay feature is enabled and the destination address is an AMM pair; normal transfers between user wallets are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noted that the delay logic behaved unexpectedly during early trading.
