In the standard LayerZero design the amount of native cryptocurrency supplied with a send call (msg.value) must match the nativeFee field returned by the endpoint, and any surplus is automatically refunded to the refundAddress supplied by the caller. The adapter relaxes this rule and permits msg.value to be equal to or greater than the required nativeFee. When a user already holds enough wrapped Bitcorn tokens to cover the transfer amount, the contract accepts the call with an excess native fee but does not forward the surplus to the refundAddress. Instead the extra amount remains locked in the adapter’s balance, effectively stealing the over‑paid funds. The bug is triggered only when the user’s wrapped token balance is sufficient and the caller deliberately or inadvertently includes more native currency than the quoted fee. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, yet the wallet shows a reduction of native tokens with no corresponding refund; the UI may display a successful send while the user’s balance is lower than expected or a zero‑value refund is received. The impact is a loss of native assets that cannot be recovered automatically, breaking the accounting assumption that fees are exact and any overpayment is returned. The issue was discovered during a security audit by constructing a proof‑of‑concept test that called send with fee.nativeFee plus an arbitrary overshoot and then asserting that the adapter’s balance did not increase; the assertion failed, confirming that the surplus was retained. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an event indicating a retained surplus, and the excess may be small enough to escape casual inspection. Conceptually this is a fee‑refund mis‑implementation, a class of bugs where a contract fails to enforce strict fee equality or to return over‑paid amounts, violating the expected economic model of the protocol. To remediate, the contract should either revert to the original strict equality check (msg.value must equal nativeFee) or explicitly calculate the refund and transfer the surplus back to the refundAddress, thereby restoring the standard LayerZero behaviour and preventing unintended fund loss.

title: Inconsistent pause enforcement in WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter
description:
The _credit function in the WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter.sol contract lacks the whenNotPaused modifier, allowing token credits even when the contract is paused.
This enables users to receive tokens through cross-chain transfers during a pause, undermining the effectiveness of the emergency pause mechanism. It also creates an inconsistent state, with some operations blocked while others continue after an emergency pause.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent enforcement of the emergency pause mechanism in the WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter contract. The internal _credit function, which is responsible for crediting tokens to a recipient after a cross‑chain transfer, does not include the whenNotPaused modifier. Because of this omission, the function can be called even when the contract’s pause flag is set, allowing token credits to be processed while other operations that respect the pause are blocked. The root cause is a missing access‑control check in the crediting path, which was likely an oversight during development. An attacker or any user can exploit this by initiating a cross‑chain transfer while the contract is paused; the transfer will be accepted, the _credit function will execute, and the recipient will receive the transferred amount despite the pause. This undermines the intended safety guarantee of the pause, creates an inconsistent state where some actions are halted while others continue, and may lead to unexpected token inflows that users cannot anticipate. The issue manifests when the contract owner or governance triggers an emergency pause to stop activity, yet users still see their balances increase after a transfer, contradicting the expectation that no token movements should occur. It affects all participants of the protocol, including token holders, relayers, and the overall system’s accounting logic, because the accounting assumptions that a paused state freezes all token movements are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the contract’s modifiers and identified that _credit lacked the pause guard. It can be hard to notice because the pause flag is typically checked in public entry points, and internal functions may be assumed to inherit the same protection, leading to a false sense of security. The recommended remediation is to add the whenNotPaused modifier to the _credit function so that every token credit operation respects the pause state, restoring consistent behavior across all token flows. Conceptually, this is a classic case of incomplete access‑control enforcement, where a critical state‑changing operation is not guarded by the same security checks as other functions, resulting in a partial bypass of the emergency stop mechanism.

title: Minting users may not be able to swap back to their original collateral token, having to rely on alternative collateral tokens
description:
The architecture revolves around multiple SwapFacility type contracts being able to mint BitcornOFT. These different swap facilities will accept a variety of wrapped BTC tokens.
This allows users that may have swapped their hypothetical wrapped aBTC tokens for BitcornOFT, to swap their debt for the entirety of the bBTC token Vault. This means that all users that may have swapped their bBTC for BitcornOFT, would not be able to swap back to bBTC, and would have to swap to aBTC. This includes the fee recipient of the bBTC Swap Facility, there would not be any bBTC collateral to back their fees, and instead it would be the aBTC and any other SwapFacility contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the design choice that BitcornOFT, an omnichain token minted by several independent SwapFacility contracts, is completely fungible and carries no information about the specific facility from which each unit was issued. Each SwapFacility accepts a distinct wrapped BTC collateral (for example aBTC or bBTC) and mints BitcornOFT against the deposited collateral, storing the underlying asset in its own vault. Because the minted tokens are indistinguishable, any holder can present BitcornOFT to any SwapFacility and receive the collateral that the facility currently holds, regardless of the original source of the debt. This creates a situation where a user who originally swapped aBTC for BitcornOFT may later be forced to redeem the same tokens for bBTC, or may be unable to obtain aBTC at all if the bBTC‑backed facility drains the aBTC vault. The root cause is the absence of per‑token metadata that ties each BitcornOFT unit to its backing facility, combined with the protocol’s assumption that fungibility across facilities does not affect collateral accounting. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit this by depositing a small amount of a high‑value collateral in one facility, then using a large amount of BitcornOFT to swap out of another facility, thereby emptying the first vault. The proof‑of‑concept test demonstrates that after a user mints debt from a simpleSwapFacility backed by wBTC, another user can mint BitcornOFT from a different facility and swap it back for wBTC, leaving the original vault with zero balance while the debt remains outstanding. The impact is that original depositors may lose access to their expected collateral, incur extra costs to obtain it from external markets, or suffer a reduction in the effective value of their holdings because the overall value floor of BitcornOFT is determined by the weakest collateral in the system. This risk materialises whenever multiple collateral types are active and one of them becomes de‑pegged or is exploited; the protocol’s accounting assumes that all collateral remains fully backed, which is no longer true once a vault is emptied. Users experience symptoms such as receiving a different token than anticipated, seeing their balance of the original wrapped BTC token remain unchanged while their BitcornOFT cannot be redeemed for it, or observing a sudden drop in the market price of BitcornOFT that reflects the devaluation of a single collateral type. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a targeted test case designed to clear a vault by swapping debt from another facility. It can be hard to notice because the token’s fungibility is an intended feature, and the problem only surfaces under specific cross‑facility interactions that are not exercised in normal operation. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should either embed facility‑specific metadata in each minted token so that redemption is restricted to the original vault, or enforce strict controls such as pausing facilities, equal‑weight collateral thresholds, or limiting cross‑facility swaps. These measures would preserve the accounting guarantees and prevent a scenario where a single compromised collateral token drags down the value of all BitcornOFT holders.

title: Arbitrary contract call within `UniV3LpVault._swap` with controllable `swapPath`
description:
[UniV3LpVault.sol#L621](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-dualityfocus/blob/main/contracts/vault_and_oracles/UniV3LpVault.sol#L621)  
[UniV3LpVault.sol#L379](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-dualityfocus/blob/main/contracts/vault_and_oracles/UniV3LpVault.sol#L379)  
[UniV3LpVault.sol#L520](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-dualityfocus/blob/main/contracts/vault_and_oracles/UniV3LpVault.sol#L520)  
[UniV3LpVault.sol#L521](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-dualityfocus/blob/main/contracts/vault_and_oracles/UniV3LpVault.sol#L521)  

`UniV3LpVault._swap` utilizes `swapRouter.exactInput` to perform swaps between two tokens. During swaps, `transfer` function of each token along the path will be called to propagate the assets.

Since anyone can create a uniswap pair of arbitrary assets, it is possible to include intermediate hop with malicious tokens within the path. Thus `UniV3LpVault._swap` effectively grants users the ability to perform arbitrary contract calls during the swap process if `swapPath` is not validated properly.

Usage of invalidated `swapPath` can be found in `UniV3LpVault.flashFocusCall` and `UniV3LpVault.repayDebt`.
poc:
The security of `Comptroller` and `UniV3LpVault` relies on validating all used tokens thoroughly. This is done by a whitelist mechanism where admin decides a predefined set of usable tokens, and users can only perform actions within the allowed range. This whitelist approach eliminates most of the attack surface regarding directly passing in malicious tokens as arguments.

Apart from passing malicious tokens directly, there are a few other potential weaknesses, the most obvious one is leveraging flash loans for collaterals. However, due to the adoption of AAVE LendingPool, the external validation within flash loan pool blocks this approach.

Unfortunately, a more obscure path exists. Looking at the swapping mechanism, it is not hard to realize it is backed by uniswapV3. An interesting characteristic of uniswap pools is that anyone can create pools for any token pairs, thus if we don’t fully validate each and every pool we are using, chances are there will be malicious entries hidden within them.

This is partially the case which we see here, the user gets to supply a path, where the source and target are validated against benign tokens, the intermediate ones are not. An example of utilizing path for arbitrary function call is illustrated below

1. Create malicious token tokenM
2. Create pools tokenS<->tokenM and tokenM<->tokenT where tokenS and tokenT are benign tokens
3. Supply path (tokenS, tokenM, tokenT) for swapping

In the above case, when transferring tokenM while doing swap, we have full control over code executed and can insert arbitrary contract calls within.

Noticeably, while gaining arbitrary contract calls sounds dangerous, it does not necessarily mean the contract is exploitable. It still depends on the scenario in which an arbitrary call happens.

In the case of duality, the two locations where arbitrary `swapPath` can be provided is in `flashFocusCall` and `repayDebt`, both in which holds a local lock over `UniV3LpVault`. No global are applied to `Comptroller` or `Ctokens` while performing swaps.

```solidity
function flashFocusCall(FlashFocusParams calldata params) external override {
    ...
    {
        ...
        if (!tokenOfPool && params.swapPath.length > 0) amountIn0 = _swap(params.swapPath, params.amount);
        ...
    }
    ...
}

function flashFocus(FlashFocusParams calldata params)
    external
    override
    nonReentrant(true)
    isAuthorizedForToken(params.tokenId)
    avoidsShortfall
{
    ...
    flashLoan.LENDING_POOL().flashLoan(
        receiverAddress,
        assets,
        amounts,
        modes,
        onBehalfOf,
        newParams,
        referralCode
    );
}

function repayDebt(RepayDebtParams calldata params)
    external
    override
    nonReentrant(true)
    isAuthorizedForToken(params.tokenId)
    avoidsShortfall
    returns (uint256 amountReturned)
{
    ...
    {
        ...
        if (amountOutFrom0 == 0 && params.swapPath0.length > 0) amountOutFrom0 = _swap(params.swapPath0, amount0);
        if (amountOutFrom1 == 0 && params.swapPath1.length > 0) amountOutFrom1 = _swap(params.swapPath1, amount1);
        ...
    }
    ...
}
```

The lack of global locks here had us doubting whether an attack is possible. While we spent a considerable amount of time and failed to come up with any possible attack vectors, the complexity of the system held us back from concluding that an attack is impossible.

Thus we report this finding here in hope of inspiring developers either to prove the attack impossible or mitigate the attack surface.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniV3LpVault contract where the internal function _swap forwards a user‑supplied swapPath to Uniswap V3's exactInput router. The router iterates over each hop in the path and invokes the ERC‑20 transfer function of the intermediate token contracts. The vault only checks that the first and last tokens of the path belong to a trusted whitelist, while any intermediate token is left unchecked. Because anyone can create a Uniswap V3 pool for an arbitrary token pair, an attacker can introduce a malicious token as an intermediate hop, craft a path such as (benignTokenA, maliciousToken, benignTokenB), and cause the vault to execute the malicious token's transfer implementation during the swap. The malicious contract can contain arbitrary logic – for example, it may call back into the vault, alter internal balances, or initiate further external calls – effectively granting the attacker an uncontrolled contract call inside the vault’s execution context. This situation can be triggered through two public entry points, flashFocusCall and repayDebt, both of which accept a swapPath parameter and do not enforce a global reentrancy lock. When a user initiates a flash‑loan‑backed operation and supplies a crafted path, the router’s transfer call on the malicious token is executed, allowing the attacker’s code to run. From a user perspective the swap may appear to succeed while the vault’s token balances shrink unexpectedly, or a user may receive zero tokens after a swap, leading to the perception that funds have mysteriously disappeared. The issue was identified during a manual audit by observing that only the endpoints of the path were validated while the router’s transfer callbacks were not, revealing a classic "untrusted token transfer callback" class of bug where unvalidated external code can be invoked through token transfers. The flaw is subtle because the transfer calls are part of the normal swap flow and a malicious token can mimic a well‑behaved ERC‑20 contract, making the unexpected behaviour hard to spot without deeper inspection of the token’s code. To remediate, the contract should enforce validation of the entire swapPath against a predefined whitelist of allowed token addresses, introduce a global reentrancy guard for all functions that perform swaps, and consider using a router interface that does not rely on external token callbacks or that restricts callbacks to known safe contracts. By ensuring that every hop in the swap is trusted, the protocol eliminates the ability for an attacker to inject arbitrary logic via token transfers, restoring the expected accounting guarantees and protecting user funds.

title: SwapFacility.swapExactCollateralForDebt() calls by unvigilant users may be owner frontrunnable for value capture via fees
description: A malicious owner that has access to the setters setSwapInFeeRate() or setSwapOutFeeRate(), may frontrun calls to SwapFacility.swapExactCollateralForDebt() or SwapFacility.swapExactCollateralForDebtAndLzSend() or swapDebtForExactCollateral() done by unvigilant users without appropriate debtOutMin or debtOutMax set, allowing for up to 100% value capture of the collateral in the most ideal scenario, which would require a setting of 0 on debtOutMin, and the owner to frontrun the user by changing setSwapInFeeRate() to effectively 100% or MAX_BPS. Since most users would likely utilize an owner provided UI for contract interaction, the UI could be trivially set to send such parameters, and the biggest challenge would be to achieve the frontrun.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a swap facility where the contract owner can arbitrarily adjust the fee rates used by the functions that exchange collateral for debt (swapExactCollateralForDebt, swapExactCollateralForDebtAndLzSend, and swapDebtForExactCollateral). The root cause is that the owner is granted unrestricted access to setter functions setSwapInFeeRate and setSwapOutFeeRate, and there is no timelock or upper bound limiting how large those fees can become. When a user initiates a swap without explicitly providing safe bounds for the amount of debt they expect to receive (debtOutMin or debtOutMax), the contract will accept whatever output the fee calculation produces. Because many users interact through a UI supplied by the same owner, the UI often defaults these bounds to zero, leaving the transaction vulnerable. An attacker who controls the owner role can monitor the mempool, detect a pending swap transaction, and immediately call setSwapInFeeRate (or setSwapOutFeeRate) to set the fee to the maximum basis‑points value (effectively 100%). The pending user transaction then executes with the inflated fee, causing the contract to deduct the full amount of collateral as a fee and return little or no debt to the user. The impact is a potential total loss of the user’s collateral – the user sees their balance drop to zero, receives no debt tokens, and the UI may simply show a successful transaction with a zero‑output amount. This scenario occurs only when the user does not set protective min/max parameters and when the owner can change fee rates without delay. All participants who rely on the swap facility – regular users, liquidity providers, and the broader protocol – are affected because the loss of collateral undermines the accounting assumptions of the system. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined permissioned functions and their interaction with user‑controlled parameters. It can be difficult to notice because the fee change is a legitimate state change from the contract’s perspective, and the UI may not surface the fee value or the fact that the owner can modify it instantly. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable upper bound on fee rates (well below 100 %), require users to specify non‑zero debtOutMin/debtOutMax values, and introduce a timelock or multi‑signature delay on any owner‑only fee‑setting functions. These measures would make front‑running the fee change impractical and protect unvigilant users from losing their collateral.

title: Weighted average prices are unable to handle currency and tranche tokens with varying decimals
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect weighted‑average price calculation used when deposit or redeem orders are decreased in a liquidity pool that supports two different token types: a currency token and a tranche token. The function that computes the price assumes that the two amount arguments – the currency amount and the tranche token amount – share the same decimal precision, and therefore adds them directly. When the two tokens have different numbers of decimals, the addition mixes values that are scaled differently, causing the resulting price stored in state.depositPrice or state.redeemPrice to be mis‑scaled. In practice the price is often recorded as 1.0, which makes the contract treat the currency payout and the tranche token payout as equivalent even though they represent different values after accounting for decimals. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by submitting a decrease order that triggers the faulty price update; the contract will then credit the user with an amount that does not reflect the true market value of the assets, leading to either an inadvertent loss of funds for the protocol or an unintended gain for the attacker. The impact is that previewDeposit() and previewMint() from the ERC4626 interface return inaccurate token amounts, users see balances that do not match their expectations, and the accounting invariants of the pool are broken. The bug manifests only when the pool processes a decrease‑invest or decrease‑redeem order and the two involved tokens have mismatched decimal places; it does not appear when both tokens share the same precision. All participants who interact with the pool – depositors, redeemers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the internal accounting can diverge from the external view, potentially causing fund misallocation or loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which identified the logical flaw in the price‑calculation routine. It is hard to notice because the price value may appear reasonable (e.g., exactly 1.0) and the UI may still display expected numbers, while the underlying state is silently corrupted. The proper fix is to normalize both token amounts to a common decimal base before performing the weighted average, for example by scaling each amount to 18 decimals or by using the token’s decimals() metadata, and then recompute the price using these normalized values. This ensures that the price reflects the true ratio of currency to tranche tokens regardless of their individual decimal configurations, restoring correct ERC4626 preview behavior and preserving the pool’s accounting integrity.

title: Centrifuge only partially supports fee-on-transfer tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incomplete support for fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) ERC20 tokens in the Centrifuge multi‑chain liquidity protocol. During a deposit, the contract correctly measures the actual amount received by comparing the escrow balance before and after the transfer, which captures any token transfer fee. However, when a user redeems their investment, the protocol first moves the tokens from the pool contract to an intermediate user escrow contract and only afterwards processes the redemption after the Centrifuge chain finalises the exit intent. The accounting logic in the user escrow contract records the full amount that the protocol intends to pay out (currencyPayout) without subtracting the fee that is automatically deducted when the tokens are transferred from the pool escrow to the user escrow. Consequently, the fee is effectively taken from the pool of funds that will be distributed to the remaining withdrawers, meaning the last users to claim their redemption receive less than the amount recorded on‑chain. This mismatch can cause users to see a lower balance than expected, experience “missing” or “partial” refunds, or even see their withdrawal amount drop to zero in extreme cases. The issue is triggered only when a token that charges a transfer fee is used and the redemption path involves the two‑step transfer described above. It was discovered during a security audit that compared the intended payout values with the actual token balances after redemption, revealing that the protocol’s accounting assumptions – namely that the transferred amount equals the recorded payout – do not hold for FoT tokens. The bug is subtle because the deposit side correctly handles fees, so the failure only appears during redemption, making it easy to miss in functional testing. The impact is financial: investors receive less than their entitled share, the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, and the overall trust in the system may be eroded. To remediate, the accounting in the user escrow contract must be adjusted to deduct the expected transfer fee from the payout amount, or the protocol should reject FoT tokens altogether, thereby avoiding the complexity of handling tokens with non‑standard transfer behaviour.

title: Frozen and non-member accounts can always redeem tranche tokens
description: The RestrictionManager contract implements a simple restricted token standard (ERC-1404) for which accounts can be frozen and added/removed from a member list. This member list restricts who can be the recipient of token transfers. For example, deposit requests are entirely restricted to this member set as it is not possible to request or process a deposit unless the account is a valid member of the protocol. This is not true when requesting to redeem tranche tokens. The _processIncreaseRedeemRequest() function calls authTransferFrom() which does not detect any transfer restrictions as outlined by the ERC-1404 token standard. Therefore, frozen and non-member accounts are able to redeem tranche tokens even when restricted. This is not compliant with regulatory authorities as it is no longer possible to blacklist users where necessary.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an authorization bypass in the token redemption path of the protocol. The RestrictionManager contract implements ERC‑1404 style transfer restrictions, maintaining a frozen flag and a whitelist of members. The contract correctly blocks transfers to non‑members and from frozen accounts when tokens are moved via the normal transfer functions, because those functions call detectTransferRestriction before executing the transfer. However, the internal function _processIncreaseRedeemRequest, which is used when a user redeems tranche tokens, invokes authTransferFrom instead of the standard transfer routine. authTransferFrom does not perform the ERC‑1404 restriction check, so the protocol does not verify whether the sender or the recipient is frozen or outside the member list. As a result, an address that has been frozen by the protocol or that has never been added to the member list can still call the redeem function and receive tranche tokens. This bypass allows blacklisted users to obtain value from the protocol, violating regulatory requirements that mandate the ability to block certain participants. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the token flow, where the auditor noticed that the redemption path does not call detectTransferRestriction. The bug is subtle because the same contract correctly enforces restrictions on deposits and normal transfers, leading reviewers to assume that all token movements are protected. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker whose address is frozen or not whitelisted submits a redeem request; the contract processes the request, calls authTransferFrom, and the transfer succeeds, delivering tranche tokens to the attacker. The impact is that prohibited users can extract value, potentially causing regulatory non‑compliance, loss of trust, and financial loss if the protocol is forced to reverse the unauthorized redemptions. The condition occurs whenever the redemption function is used; it does not depend on the amount or other state variables. Affected parties include any user of the protocol, the protocol operators, and regulators who rely on the blacklist mechanism. The fix is to ensure that the redemption path respects the ERC‑1404 restriction interface, either by replacing authTransferFrom with a function that calls detectTransferRestriction for both the sender and the recipient, or by inserting an explicit call to detectTransferRestriction before the transfer is executed. This change restores the intended blacklist behavior and aligns the contract with regulatory expectations.

title: Tranche token deployments can be overwritten in PoolManager
description: It is important to note that the Centrifuge chain has complete autonomy over adding new tranche details, but anyone is able to deploy tranches as it adheres to the details stored in undeployedTranches. However, there is no check when adding new tranche details that poolId and trancheId does not already belong to a deployed tranche. Therefore, if for whatever reason a new tranche is deployed, it will overwrite the existing pools[poolId].tranches[trancheId].token and completely break the redemption of the former tranche token. It is also possible to deploy liquidity pools under this new tranche token for which the state might not be recoverable by upgrading the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked overwrite of a tranche token address in the PoolManager contract. When a new tranche is added through the addTranche function the code does not verify that the storage slot pools[poolId].tranches[trancheId].token is still empty. Because the contract allows any caller to invoke addTranche and because there is no guard that poolId and trancheId refer to an already deployed tranche, an attacker can submit a second deployment with the same identifiers. The second call replaces the original token address with the address of a newly deployed token contract. From that point onward the redemption logic, which relies on the stored token address, points to the attacker‑controlled contract. Users who hold the original tranche tokens see their balances unchanged in the UI but attempts to redeem return zero tokens or revert, effectively making the funds inaccessible. The problem is triggered whenever addTranche is called with a poolId/trancheId pair that already has a non‑zero token address, which can happen at any time because the function lacks access control and the check for an existing token. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the tranche management flow, where the absence of a token‑zero check was noted as a logical flaw. It is difficult to notice because the UI may still list the tranche, giving the impression that everything is normal, while the underlying accounting is broken. The bug belongs to the class of state‑overwrite vulnerabilities that break business logic assumptions about immutable asset identifiers. To remediate, the addTranche implementation should enforce that pools[poolId].tranches[trancheId].token equals address(0) before assigning a new token, and ideally restrict the function to an authorized role so that only the protocol can introduce new tranches. This prevents accidental or malicious replacement of tranche tokens and preserves the ability of users to redeem their holdings.

title: Anyone can front-run and deny deposit requests in requestDepositWithPermit
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑run and denial‑of‑service issue in the requestDepositWithPermit workflow of a liquidity pool contract. The function is intended to combine a permit call with a deposit request so that a user can approve token transfer and deposit in a single transaction. However, the internal _withPermit helper accepts arbitrary owner and spender addresses supplied by the caller, and it does not enforce that the owner is the transaction sender. An attacker can observe a pending legitimate deposit request, then submit a competing transaction that calls permit with the same owner and spender but specifies a very small allowance value. Because the permit succeeds (or silently fails while the allowance check passes for a tiny amount), the subsequent deposit call finds that the owner’s token allowance is insufficient for the intended deposit amount and reverts with the LiquidityPool/permit-failure error. When the pool uses WETH as its currency, the situation worsens: the WETH contract’s fallback function is payable and simply forwards any received ether to its internal deposit() function without reverting on zero value. The requestDepositWithPermit call can therefore invoke the fallback with an empty msg.value, causing deposit() to execute with no funds and return to the original function without performing a strict allowance verification. The net effect is that a malicious actor can front‑run a legitimate user’s request, cause the permit to be recorded for an insufficient amount, and force the deposit to revert, effectively denying all deposit requests for the affected token. This issue manifests whenever requestDepositWithPermit is used, especially with ERC20 tokens that implement the EIP‑2612 permit interface and when WETH is used as the pool’s base currency. The affected parties are any users attempting to add liquidity, the liquidity pool’s accounting logic, and ultimately the protocol’s reputation because deposits appear to fail silently. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the permit handling logic and the interaction with the WETH fallback, noting that the owner parameter is not constrained and that the fallback does not revert on zero value, making the problem easy to miss in normal testing. The bug is hard to notice because the permit call may succeed or fail without obvious on‑chain signals, and the fallback’s silent execution does not emit an error, so the transaction appears to have processed normally while actually denying the deposit. To remediate, the contract should restrict the owner argument to msg.sender, ensuring that only the token holder can authorize a permit for their own deposit. Additionally, the allowance check inside _withPermit should be applied in both the try and catch branches and should require that the allowance covers the full intended deposit amount, preventing an attacker from supplying a minimal allowance. A further safeguard is to make the WETH fallback revert when called with zero value or to add an explicit allowance verification after the permit call before proceeding with the deposit. Implementing these changes restores the intended business logic that a user’s deposit either succeeds with the approved amount or fails due to their own insufficient allowance, eliminating the front‑run denial vector.

title: Inconsistent native fee validation leading to transaction failures
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inconsistent validation of the native fee supplied to the WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter contract. Two separate functions perform contradictory checks: the internal _payNative function requires the caller to provide at least the calculated native fee (msg.value < _nativeFee triggers a revert), while the public send function demands that the supplied value match the fee exactly (msg.value != feeWithExtraAmount.nativeFee triggers a revert). Because the LayerZero endpoint automatically refunds any excess native fee that is forwarded to the refund address, the equality check in send is unnecessary and can cause legitimate transactions to fail when a user overpays. The root cause is a mismatch in the contract’s input validation logic, where one component enforces a lower‑bound condition and another enforces an equality condition for the same parameter. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract directly; a normal user who includes a small surplus of ether – for example, to cover gas fluctuations – will see the transaction revert with the NotEnoughNative error even though the supplied amount is sufficient. This leads to a denial‑of‑service‑like impact: users experience failed cross‑chain transfers, see error messages suggesting insufficient funds, and may lose confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the send function is called with msg.value greater than the required native fee, which can happen during routine usage where callers add a safety margin. All participants that rely on the adapter – end‑users, dApp developers, and the broader protocol – are affected because their transactions may be unexpectedly rejected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, where a test case deliberately overpaid the fee and observed a revert despite the refund mechanism being present. The bug is subtle because overpayment is not a common test scenario and the revert message (NotEnoughNative) misleadingly points to an insufficient‑funds problem rather than a validation mismatch. To remediate, the redundant equality check should be removed or aligned with the >= check used in _payNative, allowing the contract to accept any amount equal to or greater than the required native fee and rely on the LayerZero endpoint to refund the surplus. This brings the validation logic into a single, consistent class of input‑validation bugs where mismatched conditions cause false negatives, restores expected behavior (users can send a higher amount without failure), and eliminates unnecessary transaction reverts that could otherwise erode user trust.

title: Inaccessible pause mechanism in WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter
description:
The WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter.sol contract inherits ERC20PausableUpgradeable but fails to implement the pause() and unpause() functions. Due to the absence of these functions, pausing the protocol during emergencies is not possible. Additionally, the whenNotPaused modifier, added to the impossible function to restrict transfers after a pause, will become ineffective and unnecessary.  
```solidity
contract WrappedBitcornNativeOFTAdapter is
ERC20PausableUpgradeable,
// ...other inheritances
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inaccessible pause mechanism in a token adapter contract that inherits the ERC20PausableUpgradeable module. Although the contract includes the whenNotPaused modifier on a function that should be blocked when the contract is paused, the contract does not expose any external pause() or unpause() functions. Consequently, the inherited _pause and _unpause internal hooks can never be triggered by an authorized party. The root cause is the omission of public pause control functions after inheriting a pausable base, which leaves the pause state permanently false. An attacker or any malicious actor cannot directly exploit the missing functions, but the real risk is that the protocol loses the ability to halt token transfers during emergencies such as a discovered vulnerability, a market crash, or a coordinated attack. When a critical event occurs, the administrators are unable to call pause, so transfers continue unchecked, potentially leading to loss of funds, market manipulation, or violation of the intended security model. The issue manifests when the contract is deployed and used in production; any UI that presents a pause button will appear non‑functional, and users may observe that transfers still succeed even after an attempted pause. The affected parties include token holders, the protocol’s governance or admin roles, and any downstream contracts that rely on the pause flag for safety checks. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the inheritance hierarchy and noted the absence of required external functions. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the inherited pausable logic is present, giving a false impression that pausing is available. To remediate, the contract should implement external pause and unpause functions guarded by appropriate access control (for example, a requiresAuth modifier) that invoke the internal _pause and _unpause hooks, thereby restoring the intended emergency stop capability. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of “missing access control for pausable contracts” and ensures that the whenNotPaused modifier actually enforces transfer restrictions when the contract is paused, matching user expectations that a paused token cannot be transferred.

title: Unbounded schnorrData in opPoke
description:
Invalid optimistic pokes should always be challengeable and it is important that the opChallenge call challenging a previous schnorrData submitted through opPoke does not revert and the gas cost do not exceed the block gas limit. Otherwise, the invalid optimistic poke data will automatically be finalized after the challenge period.  
The opChallenge function must copy the schnorrData to memory and hash it to compare it against the committed Schnorr hash. The schnorrData submitted via opPoke is not bounded in size as its feedIds array length can be arbitrary. A malicious feed can create an optimistic poke with a very large feedIds array that would cost more to challenge than the challenge reward, making it economically unprofitable for keepers to challenge it. In the worst case, challenging it might even exceed the block gas limit making it impossible to challenge even given enough incentive. (Note that opPoke might cost more gas than the opChallenge for large schnorrData as the former hashes schnorrData.feedIds twice, making the block gas limit attack vector potentially impossible to execute. We still recommend restricting the size.)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded input size in the optimistic poke mechanism of the contract, specifically the schnorrData.feedIds array that is accepted by the opPoke function and later copied and hashed by opChallenge. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum length for feedIds, a malicious actor can construct an opPoke transaction that includes an arbitrarily large list of feed identifiers. When a keeper later attempts to challenge the optimistic poke using opChallenge, the function must copy the entire feedIds array into memory and compute its hash. The gas cost of this operation grows linearly with the number of identifiers, and for a sufficiently large array the gas required can exceed the block gas limit or become higher than the economic reward offered for a successful challenge. Consequently, keepers are economically disincentivized to submit a challenge, and the protocol may automatically finalize the invalid optimistic poke after the challenge period expires. This breaks the core security assumption that every optimistic poke can be disputed, allowing malformed or malicious data to be accepted as final. The issue manifests only when the feedIds array is unusually large; normal‑size pokes behave correctly, which makes the problem easy to miss during functional testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data flow between opPoke and opChallenge and noted the lack of a size check on the feedIds array. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a feed may appear to have been updated with incorrect or nonsensical values, or that a transaction that should have been rejected silently succeeds, leading to potential loss of trust or financial loss if downstream logic relies on the feed data. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded input leading to gas exhaustion” and “economic denial‑of‑service via oversized calldata”. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that schnorrData.feedIds.length equals the expected number of feeds (the variable bar) before accepting the poke, rejecting any transaction that exceeds this bound. Additional defensive measures could include limiting the amount of data copied in opChallenge, using incremental hashing, or capping the gas consumption of the challenge routine. By ensuring the feedIds array is bounded, the challenge operation remains affordable, preserving the incentive for keepers to dispute invalid pokes and maintaining the protocol’s integrity.

title: marketData handling in getSwapData and verifyQuote misaligned
bug_full: The vulnerability is a validation mismatch between two internal functions that prepare and check swap information. The function that gathers swap data, referred to as getSwapData, treats marketData as a legitimate source of parameters and will continue processing a task when marketData is present. In contrast, the subsequent verification routine, verifyQuote, only looks for limitOrderData or dcaData and completely ignores marketData. This discrepancy means that when a user submits a task that includes marketData, the data passes the first stage without any sanity checks, but it never reaches the second stage where quotes are validated. The root cause is an inconsistent conditional expression that selects different fields from the task object in each function. An attacker or a careless user could craft a marketData payload that bypasses the quote validation step, causing the protocol to execute a swap based on unchecked or malformed parameters. The impact may appear as a swap that returns an unexpected amount, a transaction that succeeds but yields zero tokens, or accounting entries that do not reflect the intended trade, effectively leading to funds disappearing or being allocated incorrectly. The issue manifests only when a task contains marketData; tasks that rely on limit orders or DCA remain unaffected. Anyone who can submit marketData – typically end‑users or bots interacting with the contract – is potentially exposed, and the protocol’s overall accounting integrity is at risk. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer noticed that the two functions did not share the same data‑selection logic. Because the code paths look similar, the missing branch can be easy to overlook, especially if tests only cover limitOrderData and dcaData scenarios. To remediate, the code should be made consistent: either remove marketData handling from getSwapData if it is not part of the intended feature set, or extend verifyQuote to include the same marketData validation performed in getSwapData. This aligns input validation across the workflow and eliminates the chance that unchecked marketData reaches the execution layer. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of input validation inconsistencies where different components of a workflow apply divergent rules, leading to unchecked data flowing into critical logic. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be a market order that appears to be accepted by the UI, but later results in no tokens received, a zero balance, or a failed refund, contradicting the expectation that the protocol will honor the quoted price.

title: The requestRedeem mistakenly burns from the receiver
description:
The requestRedeem burns from the receiver address instead of the owner, which means that one can just freely burn from any address which then triggers a redeem for that address.  
Chateau indicated validation on the server side prevents this from being exploitable.  
Medium severity as low likelihood of materializing but meaningful impact if it does materialize.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the redeem workflow where the contract burns tokens from the address supplied as the receiver instead of the address that actually owns the tokens. The root cause is that the burn function is called with the receiver parameter rather than the caller (msg.sender), allowing the contract to deduct balance from an arbitrary account. An attacker who can invoke the requestRedeem function can specify any target address as the receiver, causing the contract to reduce that address's token balance and then trigger a redeem operation for the same address. Because the burn is performed on the victim’s balance, the victim may see their token balance unexpectedly drop to zero or a partial amount, and any expected refund or redemption payout may be missing. The impact is loss of funds for the affected address and a breach of the accounting guarantees that tokens can only be burned by their owner. The bug manifests whenever requestRedeem is called with a receiver that is not the caller, which can happen in any client that forwards user‑controlled parameters to the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the mismatch between the intended owner‑only burn and the actual implementation was identified. It can be hard to notice because the front‑end or server side may still enforce correct behaviour, masking the problem in normal usage, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the wrong address is burned. The recommended mitigation is to enforce the burn on the contract side by using the caller’s address (msg.sender) as the source of the burn, and to add explicit checks that the receiver matches the sender or that only authorized parties can specify a different receiver. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unauthorized asset manipulation caused by incorrect authority checks in token burning functions, violating the fundamental business logic that only token owners may destroy their own holdings.

title: Incorrect decimals for the vault token
description:
The current implementation returns as decimals the asset's decimals:  
function decimals()  
public  
view  
virtual  
override(IERC20Metadata, ERC20)  
returns (uint8)  
{  
return _underlyingDecimals + _decimalsOffset();  
}  
The decimalsOffset is 0. While this can be a way of defining the vault token's decimals, we can see from the _convertToShares and _convertToAssets functions that the intention was actually to have 18 decimals.  
If the asset will have different decimals than 18, the calculations will result in returning erroneous amounts of shares/assets.  
For example, if the asset used will be USDC which has 6 decimals, for converting 1 asset to shares, it will generate 1e12 shares instead of 1 share.  
Imagine a user wants to convert 1 USDC = 1e6 to 1 share == 1e6:  
1e6 * 1e12 / 1e18 * 1e18 = 1e18 which means 1e12 after transformation.  
Furthermore, we see that a division before multiplication is performed in the _convertToShares which should always be avoided to avoid rounding issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the vault token reporting the same number of decimal places as the underlying asset instead of the standard 18 decimals that the vault logic assumes. The contract’s decimals function simply returns the underlying token’s decimals plus an offset that is always zero, so for assets such as USDC (which uses 6 decimals) the vault token also reports 6 decimals. The conversion routines that translate between assets and vault shares are written under the assumption that the vault token has 18 decimals; they multiply or divide by 10**18 to normalise values. When the reported decimals are lower, the arithmetic produces values that are off by several orders of magnitude. For example, depositing 1 USDC (1 × 10⁶ units) is converted to shares using a formula that effectively multiplies by 10¹², resulting in a share balance of 1 × 10¹² instead of the expected 1 share. This mismatch also introduces rounding problems because the code performs a division before a multiplication, which can truncate fractional parts before they are scaled back up. The impact is that users see inflated or deflated share balances, receive incorrect amounts on withdrawal, and any external contract that relies on the vault’s decimals for accounting will calculate wrong payouts, potentially leading to loss of funds or over‑payment. The bug manifests whenever the vault is instantiated with an underlying token whose decimals differ from 18, which includes many stablecoins and ERC‑20 tokens. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors compared the decimals returned by the contract with the expected 18‑decimal standard and traced the conversion formulas. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and basic deposits appear to succeed; only the numerical values are wrong, which may only be revealed by inspecting large‑scale deposits or by external accounting checks. The proper fix is to decouple the vault’s displayed decimals from the underlying token by introducing a fixed offset (18 − underlyingDecimals) stored at construction time and using this offset in all conversion calculations, or alternatively to hard‑code the vault token to always report 18 decimals. Multiplication should be performed before division to avoid rounding loss. By correcting the decimal handling, the vault will honour the intended 1‑to‑1 relationship between deposited assets and minted shares regardless of the underlying token’s precision, restoring accurate accounting and user expectations.

title: Unprotected event emission functions
description: In the contract we can see two functions that just emit DepositClaimable/RedeemClaimable events with parameters received from the call. By doing this, anyone can just emit fraudulent events or can DoS the off-chain infrastructure by emitting a very big number of events or mislead anyone reading the events.
bug_full: The contract contains two public functions whose sole purpose is to emit DepositClaimable and RedeemClaimable events with arguments supplied by the caller. Because these functions have no access control, any external address can invoke them and cause the contract to broadcast events that do not correspond to any actual on‑chain state change. The root cause is the absence of authentication or validation before emitting the events, turning the event emission into an unrestricted external interface. An attacker can exploit this by calling the functions with arbitrary parameters, for example large token amounts or fabricated claim identifiers, thereby flooding the blockchain logs with fraudulent events. Off‑chain services that rely on these events for accounting, user notifications, or claim processing will interpret the spurious data as legitimate, leading to incorrect UI displays (such as users seeing claimable balances that do not exist), potential denial‑of‑service when the event volume overwhelms indexing pipelines, and overall loss of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The vulnerability manifests whenever an untrusted party can send a transaction to the contract, which is always possible because the functions are public and lack modifiers. All participants that consume the events – front‑end applications, analytics dashboards, custodial services, and auditors – are affected because they may act on false information. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged functions that only emit events without any state mutation or permission checks. Because the contract does not modify balances, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple unit tests that focus on value transfers; only a review of the event‑emitting surface reveals the flaw. To remediate, the event‑emitting functions should either be removed if they are not required for legitimate off‑chain workflows, or protected with appropriate access control (e.g., only the contract owner or a designated oracle may emit them) and input validation to ensure that emitted data reflects real on‑chain actions. This class of bug falls under unrestricted event emission or missing access control, which violates the assumption that events are trustworthy representations of state changes and can break accounting invariants, cause user‑visible anomalies such as “my claimable balance is huge but I cannot withdraw”, and degrade the reliability of any system that parses the event stream.

title: ClaggBaseAdapter._handleIncentive() withdraws the wrong token from the incentive vault
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the incentive handling routine of the ClaggBaseAdapter contract. When the private function _handleIncentive attempts to move incentive tokens from the external IncentiveVault to the users who have deposited, it calls withdrawTokens with three arguments: the pool identifier, a token address, and the amount to withdraw. The token argument that is supplied is the pool's primary token rather than the specific incentive token that the vault holds for that pool. Because the IncentiveVault expects the incentive token address, the call fails – the vault either does not hold the requested token or rejects the request due to a mismatched token type – and the Solidity try/catch block captures the exception and returns a zero value. Consequently, every execution of _handleIncentive results in a silent revert of the incentive withdrawal, causing the function to report that no incentive was distributed. From a user perspective, a depositor who expects to receive reward tokens after a deposit sees either a transaction that completes without any reward or a transaction that reverts and returns zero incentive, leading to confusion and the perception that the protocol is not paying out promised rewards. The issue is a classic case of an incorrect parameter being passed to an external contract, a logic error that stems from confusing the pool's token with the incentive token. It was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the token variable used in the withdrawTokens call does not correspond to the incentive token defined for the pool. The bug can be hard to notice because the surrounding try/catch hides the revert, making the failure appear as a normal zero‑return path rather than an error. The impact is limited to the loss of incentive distribution – user funds remain safe, but the promised rewards are never delivered, and the protocol may suffer a denial‑of‑service condition if incentive distribution is a prerequisite for further actions. To remediate the issue, the contract should pass the correct incentive token address (poolIncentive.token) to the IncentiveVault’s withdrawTokens function, ensuring that the vault can locate and transfer the appropriate reward tokens. This change restores the intended accounting logic, aligns the contract’s behavior with business expectations, and prevents silent failures that break the reward mechanism.

title: Consider restricting users' gas sponsorship usage
description: In the GaslessPaymaster contract, accounts that are registered in the claveRegistry will receive free gas sponsorships on userLimit number of transactions. Each of these sponsored transactions can have arbitrary gasLimit and maxFeePerGas values, so users can potentially spend a large amount of the paymaster's ETH in each of their sponsored transactions. With enough unreasonably expensive transactions, the paymaster's balance could be depleted quickly, which would ruin the experience for honest users.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a gas‑sponsorship contract that grants registered accounts a fixed number of free transactions (userLimit) without imposing any limits on the gas parameters of each transaction. Because the contract only tracks the count of sponsored calls and does not cap the gasLimit or the maxFeePerGas supplied by the caller, a malicious or careless user can craft a transaction with an excessively high gas limit and a very large max fee per gas. When such a transaction is processed, the paymaster must front the full gas cost from its own ETH balance. By repeatedly submitting a small number of these inflated transactions, the attacker can quickly exhaust the paymaster’s ETH reserve. This economic denial‑of‑service occurs whenever a registered user initiates a sponsored call; the condition is triggered as soon as the gas parameters exceed the amount of ETH the paymaster can afford. The affected parties include the paymaster contract owner, any honest users who rely on the gasless service, and the broader protocol that may lose usability. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the resource‑allocation logic and noticed the absence of per‑transaction caps. It can be hard to detect because normal usage with reasonable gas values appears to work correctly, while only extreme values cause the balance to drain, a scenario often omitted from test suites. The impact is that the paymaster’s balance may be depleted, leading to failed gas‑sponsored transactions, users receiving no service, or UI messages indicating out‑of‑gas or unavailable paymaster. From a user’s perspective the expectation that a transaction will be free is violated; instead the transaction may revert or the user may see their balance unexpectedly reduced to zero. The bug belongs to the class of economic DoS or unbounded resource allocation flaws, where a contract allocates a valuable resource (ETH) based solely on a count metric rather than on the actual cost. To remediate, the contract should allocate sponsorship based on a budget of ETH rather than a fixed number of calls, enforce sensible upper bounds on gasLimit and maxFeePerGas, or implement a per‑user gas‑budget that is decremented by the actual gas cost of each transaction. Such constraints would prevent a single user from draining the paymaster with a few expensive calls and preserve service for honest participants.

title: Native ETH cannot be used as the incentive token
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the assumption that every incentive token is an ERC20 contract. In ClaggBaseAdapter.setIncentive the function unconditionally calls IERC20(token).safeApprove before invoking IIncentiveVault.storeTokens. When the caller supplies the native ETH sentinel as the token, the safeApprove call attempts to interact with a non‑contract address, causing the transaction to revert or silently skip the approval step. Moreover, storeTokens and withdrawTokens in IncentiveVault are written to handle only ERC20 transfers; they do not accept a value field for native ETH nor adjust their accounting for ETH balances. As a result, the protocol cannot accept, store, or withdraw native ETH as an incentive token. This bug can be exploited by simply trying to set ETH as the incentive token; the transaction will fail or the incentive will never be recorded, leading users to receive no reward, see their expected balance remain zero, or experience missing refunds. The impact is a broken incentive mechanism that may cause users to lose confidence, miss out on promised rewards, and potentially lock ETH if it is sent to a function that does not handle it. The condition occurs whenever setIncentive is called with token equal to the system ETH address, and it affects any participant who expects ETH incentives, including end users and the protocol’s reward logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected token handling paths and noticed the lack of a native‑ETH branch. It is easy to miss because the code compiles and the ERC20 interface is widely used, so developers may assume the same pattern works for ETH. The proper fix is to add a conditional branch that detects the native ETH sentinel, skips the ERC20 approval, and passes the ETH amount as msg.value to storeTokens, and to refactor storeTokens and withdrawTokens to correctly handle ETH transfers and balance accounting. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect token type handling” where a contract treats native cryptocurrency as an ERC20 token, violating the accounting assumptions of the incentive system.

title: SyncSwap._swapFrom() does not encode native ETH correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in how native ETH is identified across the SyncSwap ecosystem. In the Swapper contract, the native token is represented by ZkSync’s special system contract address (ETH_TOKEN_SYSTEM_CONTRACT). The code checks this address to decide whether to forward value to the router and then encodes the same address directly into the SwapPath and SwapStep structures that are passed to SYNC_ROUTER.swap(). However, the router implementation expects native ETH to be denoted by the zero address (address(0)) and the pools themselves treat ETH as wrapped ETH (WETH). Because the Swapper forwards the system‑contract address instead of address(0) or WETH, the router receives an unexpected token identifier. When the router attempts to resolve the token pair, it cannot match the supplied address to any known pool token, causing the swap to revert. This mismatch is triggered whenever _swapFrom is invoked with _from equal to ETH_TOKEN_SYSTEM_CONTRACT – a situation that occurs during incentive‑token handling and reward‑compounding logic. The impact is that any pool configured to use native ETH as an incentive or reward token becomes non‑functional: swaps revert, users see no reward distribution, and balances remain unchanged. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails with a generic revert, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed the divergent address constants and the resulting failure path. It is hard to spot because both addresses are syntactically valid and the code compiles without warnings; the problem only manifests at runtime when the router validates token addresses. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of native‑asset misrepresentation errors, where different components of a system use incompatible identifiers for the same underlying asset. To remediate the problem the Swapper should normalize the input token by wrapping native ETH into WETH (or by using address(0) consistently) before constructing the swap path, mirroring the handling used in other adapters such as ClaggSyncAdapter._addLiquidity. Aligning the token representation eliminates the revert, restores correct incentive distribution, and ensures that the protocol’s accounting assumptions about ETH balances remain valid.

title: ClaggSyncAdapter._removeLiquidity() incorrectly withdraws ETH when token is WETH
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity‑removal function of the ClaggSyncAdapter contract. When a caller requests to withdraw liquidity from a SyncSwap pool whose underlying token is Wrapped Ether (WETH), the adapter builds the call data for syncRouter.burnLiquiditySingle() with a withdrawMode value of 1. WithdrawMode 1 is defined to return assets as native ETH, regardless of whether the requested token is ETH or WETH. Consequently, the function attempts to pull ETH from the pool even though the caller expects WETH. After the router returns ETH, the adapter later calls _transferToCaller() with the original token identifier (WETH) and the amount that was supposed to be withdrawn. Because the contract never received any WETH, the internal balance for WETH is zero and the transfer reverts, causing the whole transaction to fail. The root cause is an incorrect conditional that treats the WETH case the same as native ETH and selects the wrong withdrawal mode. Exploitation is straightforward: a user (or an attacker) invokes the withdraw() entry point on a pool that uses WETH, and the transaction will always revert, preventing the user from receiving their tokens. The impact is that liquidity providers cannot retrieve their WETH, effectively locking their funds in the contract and breaking the expected accounting invariant that a liquidity removal returns the same token that was deposited. This condition occurs only when the token address supplied to _removeLiquidity() is not the system ETH token but is the address of the WETH contract. The affected parties are any users of the affected SyncSwap pool, the protocol’s liquidity‑provider base, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful withdrawals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the adapter’s withdrawal logic, where the auditor noticed that the same withdrawMode value was used for both ETH and WETH paths. The bug can be hard to notice because the code appears to encode the correct token address, and the withdrawMode constant is a numeric flag that does not convey its semantic meaning at a glance. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a successful transaction submission, but the wallet will receive no WETH and may display an error or a zero balance after the call, contradicting the expectation that “my WETH should be returned”. This is a classic case of asset‑type mismatch caused by an incorrect parameter selection, a class of bugs often referred to as “wrong token withdrawal” or “mode‑selection error”. To remediate the issue the adapter should use withdrawMode 2 (which returns assets as WETH) when the token is not the native ETH system contract, ensuring that the token type withdrawn matches the token type requested. A conceptual fix is to differentiate the ETH and WETH paths explicitly and encode the appropriate mode flag, thereby restoring the invariant that liquidity removal returns the same asset that was originally supplied.

title: ClaggSyncAdapter._addLiquidity() wrongly calls approve() instead of safeApprove()
description:
In ClaggSyncAdapter._addLiquidity(), approve() is called instead of safeApprove() when depositing token as liquidity:
```solidity
IERC20(token).approve(address(syncRouter), amount);
liquidity = syncRouter.addLiquidity2(
    pool,
    inputs,
    abi.encode(address(this)),
    0,
    address(0),
    new bytes(0),
    address(0)
);
```
However, safeApprove() should be called instead as token could be a token that does not comply with the ERC20 specification.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity‑deposit routine of the ClaggSyncAdapter contract. When the internal function _addLiquidity attempts to grant the external syncRouter contract permission to transfer a user‑supplied token, it invokes the standard ERC20 approve method directly (IERC20(token).approve(address(syncRouter), amount)). This call does not verify the return value or handle tokens that deviate from the ERC20 specification, such as those that do not return a boolean or that silently reject the allowance change. The root cause is the use of a raw approve call instead of the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 safeApprove wrapper, which performs a low‑level call and checks that the operation succeeded, reverting on failure. An attacker or a careless user could supply a non‑standard token that either returns an unexpected value or fails to set the allowance while still reporting success. In that scenario the syncRouter believes it has permission to pull the tokens, proceeds with the addLiquidity2 call, and records a liquidity position, but the actual token transfer never occurs. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, yet the expected liquidity is not credited and the user’s balance may appear unchanged or become zero after the operation. The impact includes loss of funds, stuck or phantom liquidity, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants because the contract’s internal state no longer matches the real token balances. This condition manifests only when a token that does not fully comply with ERC20 is used; with well‑behaved tokens the bug remains invisible, making it hard to detect during normal testing. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that inspected the contract’s token‑handling logic. To remediate the problem the contract should replace the direct approve call with SafeERC20.safeApprove, ensuring that any failure to set the allowance aborts the transaction and prevents inconsistent state. Conceptually, the fix upgrades the allowance granting step to a verified operation, aligning it with the safe‑token handling pattern used throughout secure Solidity codebases.

title: Incentives May Become Locked in the System After Switching Incentive Tokens
description:
The setIncentive function allows the owner to configure and update protocol incentives for a specific pool. It offers two scenarios:
• If the previous incentive round has ended, the entire configuration can be updated.
• If the previous round is still active, additional incentives can only be added.
However, the protocol currently uses only the elapsed time as a criterion to determine if a round has ended, instead of also verifying whether there are any remaining unclaimed incentives in the vault.
If the current block.timestamp exceeds the round's expiry and some incentives remain unprocessed, these unclaimed tokens will become locked in the IncentivesVault when the owner changes the configuration into another token. This issue arises because the action does not compound before updating the incentive token.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the incentive configuration function that allows the contract owner to set or update the reward token for a liquidity pool. The function decides whether a full re‑configuration is permitted based solely on the current block.timestamp compared with the stored round expiry. It does not verify whether any reward tokens remain unclaimed in the IncentivesVault. When the timestamp indicates that the round has ended but some incentive tokens are still pending, the owner can call setIncentive with a new token address. Because the function does not invoke the compound routine before changing the token, the remaining unclaimed tokens stay in the vault under the old token identifier and become permanently inaccessible. This creates a locked‑funds condition: participants who expected to claim rewards after the round see their pending balance become zero, and the protocol loses the ability to distribute those tokens. The issue appears only when a round is considered finished by time yet still holds unclaimed incentives, and the owner performs a token switch during that window. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑transition logic of setIncentive and noticed the missing check for residual vault balance. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error and the UI may simply show no pending rewards, leading users to think there were no rewards rather than that they were locked. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑locking vulnerabilities where improper cleanup of residual balances leads to loss of assets. To remediate, the function should call the compound routine (or otherwise settle all outstanding incentives) before updating the incentive token, ensuring that any remaining rewards are either distributed or returned to the vault under the new configuration.

title: ClaggSyncAdapter LP staking cannot be disabled without bricking the vault
description: In ClaggSyncAdapter, SyncSwap liquidity can be automatically staked in a contract if this one has been previously configured by the owner. In order to switch staking contracts the owner can call migrate on the adapter, effectively migrating the assets to the new staking contract. However, the current migration function does not allow for disabling staking (setting an empty address as staking contract). As a result, staking cannot be disabled without effectively locking the liquidity by changing the configuration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the ClaggSyncAdapter contract does not permit the owner to disable the automatic staking of SyncSwap liquidity by migrating to a zero‑address staking contract. The migration function enforces a non‑zero staking address, so when the owner attempts to clear the staking configuration the call reverts. Consequently the liquidity that has been deposited into the adapter becomes permanently locked in the vault because there is no path to withdraw or re‑assign the assets without a valid staking contract. This situation arises whenever the protocol governance wishes to stop staking, for example after a migration plan is aborted or when the staking pool is deprecated. The affected parties are the contract owner, the protocol that relies on the adapter, and any liquidity providers whose funds are held in the vault; they may see their balances remain unchanged while the UI reports that staking is still active, leading to confusion and potential loss of access to their assets. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the migrate function’s parameter validation. It is subtle because the contract otherwise appears to support migration correctly, and the UI may not expose a “disable staking” button, so the lock‑up condition can remain unnoticed until an attempt to disable staking fails. The root cause is a missing code path that allows a staking address of address(0) or a dedicated disable function, combined with a hard‑coded require that the new staking address is not zero. To remediate, the contract should either accept address(0) as a valid target during migration, or provide an explicit disableStaking function that safely withdraws or re‑routes the LP tokens before clearing the staking configuration, ensuring that funds can be recovered and the vault remains operable.

title: Disallow changing cloud guardian during recovery
description: An account can change its cloud guardian address by calling the updateGuardian() function on the CloudRecoveryModule. The comments of this function state that "Recovery must not be in progress for the account", but this is currently not enforced.
bug_full: The issue resides in the CloudRecoveryModule function that allows an account to change its cloud guardian address. The function documentation states that a recovery must not be in progress for the account, yet the implementation does not enforce this rule. As a result, an account that has already initiated a recovery can call the updateGuardian method and replace the guardian address while the recovery process is still pending. The root cause is the missing check for an active recovery state (isRecovering) before permitting the guardian update. An attacker who can trigger the updateGuardian call after a recovery has started can redirect the recovery flow to an address of their choosing. This can be exploited by first starting a recovery, then swapping the guardian to a malicious contract or wallet; when the recovery completes, the assets intended for the original guardian are transferred to the new address, effectively stealing the funds. The impact includes loss of funds for the affected user, breach of trust in the recovery mechanism, and potential reputational damage to the protocol. The vulnerability manifests only when a recovery is in progress for a given account; accounts without an active recovery are not affected. It was discovered during a manual audit where the comment and intended behavior were compared against the actual code, revealing the missing guard clause. The problem is subtle because the function appears to perform a simple update and the comment suggests the correct behavior, so developers may assume the check exists. From a user perspective, the expected outcome is that a recovery will deliver assets to the originally designated guardian, but after the guardian is changed the user may see no funds arriving, balances unexpectedly drop to zero, or refunds disappear. This violates the business logic that recovery should be immutable once started, breaking accounting assumptions about asset flow. The recommended fix is to add an explicit revert when isRecovering(msg.sender) returns true, thereby preventing any guardian change while a recovery is active and preserving the integrity of the recovery process.

title: Use OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20
description: Some ERC20 tokens may not follow the entire ERC20 speciﬁcation. For example, transfer() and transferFrom() are expected to return true and revert on any failure, but USDT doesn't return any value. OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library handles these cases.
