bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract calling ERC20 token functions transfer() and transferFrom() directly and assuming they follow the full ERC20 specification, namely that they return a boolean value indicating success and revert on failure. Some widely used tokens, such as USDT, deviate from the spec by not returning any value. When the contract does not check the return data, it may interpret a missing return as a successful call, even though the token transfer could have silently failed. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who deploys a malicious token that deliberately returns no value or returns false without reverting; the vulnerable contract will believe the transfer succeeded and may continue execution based on the false premise that it holds the transferred assets. Consequently, users may see a UI message indicating a successful deposit or withdrawal while their token balance remains unchanged, leading to accounting inconsistencies, potential loss of funds, or denial‑of‑service conditions where the protocol cannot progress because expected tokens were never received. The issue appears whenever the contract interacts with non‑standard ERC20 tokens and is discovered during manual audit review of token handling code. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, so developers may assume normal operation. The proper mitigation is to replace raw calls with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, using safeTransfer() and safeTransferFrom(), which internally verify the call success, handle missing return data, and revert on any failure, thereby restoring the intended safety guarantees of token transfers. This class of bug is commonly referred to as unchecked ERC20 return values or non‑standard token handling, and it violates the business logic that a successful transfer should result in the recipient’s balance increasing as expected.

title: Malicious module/hook may not be removed
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the removal mechanism for privileged extensions (modules and hooks) in a contract that uses a ModuleManager and a HookManager. When a module is removed, the manager invokes the module’s disable() function via a low‑level call, deliberately ignoring any revert so that the outer transaction can continue even if the module misbehaves. The HookManager, however, calls IHook(hook).disable() with a regular external call. Because a normal call propagates a revert, a malicious hook can cause the removal transaction to fail by reverting inside its disable() implementation. Moreover, even if the HookManager were changed to use a low‑level call, the call currently forwards 63/64 of the remaining gas and does not cap the amount of returned data. A crafted hook or module can deliberately consume all forwarded gas or return a huge payload, triggering out‑of‑gas or excessive memory‑expansion costs. This “gas‑griefing” technique can block the removal of the extension entirely. The root cause is the inconsistent use of call semantics and the lack of explicit gas limits or data‑size safeguards when disabling extensions. An attacker can exploit the flaw by deploying a malicious module or hook whose disable() function either reverts (for hooks) or exhausts gas/returns massive data (for modules). When the protocol owner attempts to deregister the extension, the transaction either reverts or runs out of gas, leaving the malicious code permanently attached to the system. The impact is that privileged code that may contain backdoors, fee‑stealing logic, or other harmful behavior cannot be removed, potentially compromising the protocol’s security, causing loss of user funds, or violating the expected upgradeability guarantees. The issue manifests only during administrative removal operations; normal user interactions appear unaffected until a removal is attempted, at which point the admin may see transaction failures or unexpected out‑of‑gas errors. The affected parties include the protocol administrators who cannot cleanly deregister extensions, and indirectly all users whose assets are managed by the protocol. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that noted a TODO comment indicating the need for a low‑level call and that the existing implementation differed between modules and hooks. It can be hard to notice because the removal function may appear to work in simple cases, while a malicious implementation only triggers the failure under specific gas or data conditions. To remediate, the HookManager’s _removeHook() should be rewritten to use a low‑level call that discards the success flag, mirroring the module removal logic. Additionally, both removal paths should employ an explicit gas stipend (for example, 30 000 gas) and limit the size of returned data, using a safe‑call library such as ExcessivelySafeCall or inline assembly to prevent gas‑griefing attacks. By ensuring that disable() cannot revert the outer transaction and cannot exhaust gas, the protocol regains reliable ability to deregister malicious extensions, preserving upgradeability and protecting user funds.

title: Minters can mint double the max allowance in an interval
description:
Callers can mint more tokens than maxAllowance in an interval. Let's say interval is 1 hour and maxAllowance is 60 cbBTC. At t = 0, caller's allowance is 60 cbBTC. Consider this scenario (more scenarios can be crafted):
• At t = 0, caller mints 60 cbBTC, their allowance drops to 0.
• At t = 0.5 hour, amountToReplenish is 30 cbBTC, so the new allowance becomes 30 cbBTC. Caller mints 30 cbBTC.
• Just before the 1 hour intervals ﬁnishes, amountToReplenish becomes 30 cbBTC and the caller can mint another 30 cbBTC. So with maxAllowance = 60 cbBTC, caller can mint 120 cbBTC in the same interval. A similar issue happens when a minter doesn't use his allowance in an interval. This allows the minter to mint double the max allowance in the next interval.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑replenishment flaw that permits a minter to mint more tokens than the configured maxAllowance within a single rate‑limiting interval. The contract tracks a per‑caller allowance that is intended to be capped at maxAllowance and to replenish linearly over a fixed interval (for example one hour). The root cause is that the replenishment calculation is performed based solely on elapsed time since the last update, without enforcing that a full interval has passed before the allowance can be increased again. Consequently, after a caller exhausts their allowance early in the interval, a partial replenishment occurs before the interval ends, allowing the caller to mint additional tokens. By repeating this pattern, the caller can mint up to twice the intended maximum in the same interval, and a similar effect can be observed in the following interval if the allowance was not fully used. An attacker who is authorized to call the mint function can therefore inflate the token supply by repeatedly minting up to double the allowed amount, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol and potentially devaluing the token for all holders. The issue manifests when the interval parameter is greater than zero, maxAllowance is non‑zero, and the caller performs mint operations at times that allow partial replenishment before the interval expires. It affects any minter that has been configured with a non‑zero allowance, and consequently any users or downstream contracts that rely on the token’s capped supply. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by observing that after a mint at time t the allowance returned to zero, but a subsequent call to the internal replenish function restored a positive allowance before the interval elapsed, enabling a second mint of the same size. The problem is subtle because the allowance value appears correct at each checkpoint, and the UI may simply show “allowance: 0” followed by “allowance: 30” without indicating that the total minted amount exceeds the limit. To remediate, the contract should enforce that allowance can only be replenished after the previous update is at least one full interval ago, or it should reset the allowance to zero on initialization and only increase it in discrete steps that never exceed maxAllowance. In essence, the minting logic must be changed to guarantee that the cumulative amount minted in any interval never exceeds the configured cap, thereby preserving the intended token supply constraints.

title: Every RateLimit.configureCaller call grants instant allowance to callers which leads to instant token minting
description:
The RateLimit.configureCaller function sets the allowances map value for caller to amount. This gives the caller an instant allowance of amount amount. After the configureCaller call the caller can instantly mint amount amount of tokens without any delay. Consider the following scenario:
• At time t1, a caller is granted an allowance of 1000 tokens per interval.
• At time t1 the caller mints 1000 tokens.
• After that the caller can only mint 1000 tokens in every interval.
• At time t2 the caller's allowance is changed to 800 tokens per interval.
• At time t2 the caller can mint 800 tokens instantly without any interval delay. This ability of callers to utilize their new allowance instantly could be unintended and can lead to tokens getting minted faster than expected.
bug_full: An instant‑allowance bug exists in the rate‑limiting contract. The function that configures a caller’s allowance writes the new amount directly into the allowances mapping without taking the caller’s current usage or the interval timer into account. Because the contract checks only the stored allowance when a mint request is processed, a caller can immediately mint up to the newly configured amount as soon as configureCaller is executed. In practice this means that after a caller has already exhausted its quota for the current interval, a privileged entity can lower or raise the allowance and the caller can still mint the full new amount before the interval expires. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the token minting logic. It is subtle because the allowance change looks benign and typical unit tests verify that the allowance value is updated, but they do not verify that the minting window is reset. The impact is that tokens can be minted faster than the intended per‑interval cap, inflating the supply and breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol. Users expecting a fixed minting rate may see their token balances increase unexpectedly, while the protocol may suffer from uncontrolled inflation. The bug can be reproduced by configuring a caller with a certain allowance, letting the caller mint the full amount, then calling configureCaller again with a different allowance and observing that the caller can immediately mint the new amount without waiting for the next interval. To remediate the issue the contract should either reset the caller’s used‑quota to zero only when a new interval starts, or initialize the allowance entry to zero before applying the new limit, and enforce that allowance changes affect only future intervals. Proper accounting of minted amounts versus allowed quota per interval is required to prevent instant token creation.

title: CloudRecoveryModule never increments the recovery nonce
description: When the startRecovery() function is called on a recovery module, it is intended that the account's recovery nonce is incremented. However, this is currently missing from the CloudRecoveryModule. As a consequence, anyone can replay an account's cloud recovery. This could temporarily disable additional recovery attempts, and if the private key for the original recovery's newOwner has been lost, would lock the account.
bug_full: The CloudRecoveryModule contains a logical omission in its startRecovery() routine: after validating that the supplied recovery nonce matches the stored value, the contract never increments the recoveryNonces mapping for the recovering address. The intended design is that each successful recovery consumes a unique nonce, preventing the same recovery data from being reused. Because the nonce is never updated, the same nonce remains valid indefinitely. An attacker who can observe or guess a valid recovery payload can replay the startRecovery call any number of times, causing the guardian’s signature to be accepted repeatedly. This replay can temporarily block further legitimate recovery attempts, and if the attacker supplies a newOwner address whose private key is unavailable, the original account owner may become permanently locked out. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user initiates a cloud‑based recovery, i.e., when startRecovery() is invoked on an account that has been initialized and is not already in a recovery state. All accounts that rely on the CloudRecoveryModule for key recovery are affected, including regular users, custodial services, and any protocol component that assumes a one‑time recovery flow. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which identified that the state‑changing line that should increment recoveryNonces was missing. Because the function still passes the nonce check, automated tests that only verify a single successful recovery may not reveal the problem, making it easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful recovery, but subsequent attempts to recover the same account either succeed unexpectedly or fail because the account appears to be in a perpetual recovery state, leading to confusion such as “my account keeps resetting ownership” or “I cannot recover my funds after the first attempt”. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑nonce failures where a nonce intended to provide freshness is not updated, breaking the accounting invariant that each recovery consumes a unique identifier. To remediate, the contract should update the recoveryNonces mapping (e.g., recoveryNonces[recoveringAddress]++) after all checks pass and before storing the new recovery state, thereby ensuring that any subsequent call with the same nonce is rejected and that the recovery process remains single‑use as designed.

title: If Optimism Wallet has expensive receive() function, their payments can be bypassed
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked external call when the contract attempts to send the calculated Optimism fee using a low‑level SafeCall.send. Because the return value of the call is ignored, a failure of the receive() function on the Optimism wallet – either a revert or an out‑of‑gas condition – does not stop the execution of disburseFees. After the failed send the function proceeds to bridge the entire remaining ETH balance to the L1 wallet via the L2StandardBridge. As a result the fees that should have been transferred to Optimism are silently omitted and the full contract balance is moved to L1. This payment bypass occurs only when the call to the Optimism address fails, which can happen if Optimism deploys a contract at that address that deliberately reverts in its receive() function or that consumes an unusually large amount of gas, exhausting the gas stipend left for the bridge call. The impact is that the protocol’s revenue share intended for Optimism is lost or mis‑routed, potentially causing missing refunds for users or incorrect accounting on the Optimism side while the L1 side receives more ETH than expected. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that flagged the SafeCall.send usage without a success check, similar to a known vault count bug. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the contract appears to succeed and the bridge event is emitted, while the Optimism side simply receives zero funds, which may only be observed by comparing expected versus actual balances. The affected parties include the protocol’s fee‑distribution mechanism, Optimism’s revenue share, and any users relying on correct fee allocation. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked low‑level call failures that lead to payment bypass or fund misallocation. To remediate, the contract should capture the boolean result of the send, store the fee amount in a dedicated variable when the call fails, and exclude that amount from the subsequent bridge transfer. A separate withdrawal function for the stored Optimism holdings allows the intended recipient to claim the fees later without risking a denial‑of‑service on the main disbursement path.

title: Optimism can be overpaid by up to 70% if disburseFees() is called regularly
description:
The agreement between Optimism and Coinbase is that Optimism will earn a portion of the fees equal to:
max(netRevenue * 0.15, grossRevenue * 0.025)
It is not clear from the documentation what time period these calculations should be performed over, but presumably we are looking to reflect this formula over the long term. Allowing disburseFees() to be called daily perturbs the formula in such a way that increases Optimism's payout. To understand why, let's look at the two possible scenarios when calculating the long term payout:
1) netRevenue * 0.15 > grossRevenue * 0.025
2) netRevenue * 0.15 < grossRevenue * 0.025
In the first case, all of the netRevenue will be paid out to the Optimism wallet as its withdrawn from the vaults. However, any time that disburseFees() is called when L1_FEE_VAULT has a balance over 2 ether and the other vaults have a balance under 2 ether, the gross revenue payout will be higher on that day, and therefore an additional payout will happen of 2.5% of these L1 vault fees. In the second case, at least 2.5% of all the revenue will be paid out. However, any days where L1_FEE_VAULT was not withdrawn and another vault was, we will be paying out the balance as net revenue, and will be paying 15% instead. In both cases, Optimism earns a surplus of fees compared to the same calculation performed on an annual basis.
Proof of Concept
Starting with Scenario 1, imagine each of the three vaults earns 10 ether per month. This would result in annual calculations of:
• netRevenue = 240 ether
• grossRevenue = 360 ether
• optimism payout = 240 ether * 0.15 = 36 ether
However, the total 360 ether could be distributed in 180 separate distributions, assuming the vaults reach 2 ether on different days. In this case, we would have:
• 120 days where 2 ether was withdrawn from a net revenue vault, resulting in 120 * 2 * 0.15 = 36 ether
• 60 days where 2 ether was withdrawn from the L1 fee vault, resulting in 60 * 2 * 0.025 = 3 ether
This results in an extra 3 ether (+8.3%) of fees being sent to Optimism.
Looking at Scenario 2. Imagine that the L1 vault earns 30 ether per month, and the others earn 2.5 ether each. This would result in annual calculations of:
• netRevenue = 60 ether
• grossRevenue = 360 + 60 = 420 ether
• optimism payout = 420 ether * 0.025 = 10.5 ether
However, we can again assume that these could be distributed over 210 separate withdrawals:
• 180 days where 2 ether was withdrawn from the L1 fee vault, resulting in 180 * 2 * 0.025 = 9 ether
• 30 days where 2 ether was withdrawn from the other vaults, resulting in 30 * 2 * 0.15 = 9 ether
This result in an extra 7.5 ether (+71.4%) of fees being sent to Optimism.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the fee‑disbursement mechanism that allows the Optimism party to receive a larger share of fees than the contract’s intended formula specifies. The contract is supposed to pay Optimism the greater of 15 % of net revenue or 2.5 % of gross revenue, calculated over a long‑term period such as a month or a year. However, the implementation applies this formula each time the disburseFees() function is invoked and only when a vault balance exceeds a 2 ether threshold. Because the three fee vaults (L1 fee vault and two other vaults) reach the threshold on different days, calling disburseFees() daily causes many small withdrawals to be classified alternately as net‑revenue or gross‑revenue payouts. In the net‑revenue case the contract pays 15 % of the withdrawn amount, while in the gross‑revenue case it pays 2.5 % of the L1 vault amount. By splitting the total annual revenue into many 2‑ether slices, the contract ends up paying Optimism on each slice, which mathematically adds up to an excess of up to 70 % compared with a single annual calculation. The root cause is the use of per‑withdrawal calculations combined with a minimum‑balance trigger, rather than aggregating revenue over the intended accounting period. An attacker – or any actor with permission to trigger disburseFees() – can exploit this by ensuring the function is called as often as possible, ideally every day, so that the vaults repeatedly cross the 2‑ether threshold and the contract repeatedly applies the payout formula. The impact is that Optimism receives more fees than contractually agreed, reducing the revenue share that should belong to Coinbase and potentially to the protocol’s users. This overpayment occurs whenever the vault balances are uneven and the disbursement interval is short, i.e., when disburseFees() is called frequently. The parties affected are Optimism (who benefits), Coinbase (who loses expected revenue), and indirectly the users who may see higher fees or reduced incentives. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the theoretical annual payout with the sum of payouts generated by daily disbursements, revealing a systematic surplus. It is hard to notice because the total fees transferred still appear reasonable and the discrepancy only becomes evident when aggregating many small payouts over time. To remediate, the contract should compute Optimism’s share based on cumulative net and gross revenue over a longer interval, store historical revenue totals and apply the max‑formula once per period, or increase the disbursement interval so that the minimum‑balance condition is less likely to be triggered by a single vault. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect cumulative accounting due to per‑transaction fee calculation”, where the business logic of revenue sharing is violated, leading to money disappearing from Coinbase’s expected share and being sent to Optimism.

title: verifyingSigner has no authority over paymaster-related gas limits
description:
In ERC4337 v0.7, the gas limits used for calling the paymaster functions validatePaymasterUserOp() and postOp() are now included in the userOp.paymasterAndData bytes, as detailed in PR 363.
In the new version of the VerifyingPaymaster, these gas limit values are not inspected or included in the hash signed by the verifyingSigner. This means that the userOp sender has the ability to modify these gas limits after the verifyingSigner signature is generated, without affecting the validity of the signature.
This may be a concern in scenarios where allowAnyBundler == true. For example, if the userOp sender decreases the postOp() gas limit to be much lower than the verifyingSigner initially expected, they could potentially cause the entire userOp to fail and leave the VerifyingPaymaster liable for the gas fees. At the very least, it seems that the verifyingSigner would have stronger guarantees if they knew their signature was agreeing to specific paymaster gas limits.
Note that in the previous version of the VerifyingPaymaster, the verifyingSigner always had full authority over the gas limits used in the paymaster calls, since the gas limit was simply the verificationGasLimit and the contributed hash found in VerifyingPaymaster.sol#L239 that was signed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature‑scope mismatch in the VerifyingPaymaster implementation for ERC‑4337 version 0.7. The paymaster’s verifyingSigner signs a hash that includes the user operation data but deliberately omits the two gas limit fields – the validation gas limit used by validatePaymasterUserOp() and the post‑operation gas limit used by postOp() – which are now supplied by the sender inside the paymasterAndData byte array. Because these limits are not part of the signed message, a malicious user operation sender can alter them after the signature has been produced without invalidating the signature. This can be done by decreasing the postOp gas limit to a value far lower than the signer expected, causing the paymaster’s postOp call to run out of gas and revert, which forces the paymaster to cover the gas cost of the failed operation. The issue is most acute when the paymaster is configured with allowAnyBundler == true, allowing any bundler to forward the manipulated user operation. The impact is that the paymaster may lose funds to gas fees that were not authorized by the signer, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol and potentially leading to unexpected balance reductions for the paymaster contract. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can appear as a transaction that suddenly fails with an out‑of‑gas error while the paymaster’s balance drops, or as a refund that never arrives because the postOp execution never completes. The flaw was discovered during a security audit of the VerifyingPaymaster code when the auditor compared the hash generation in version 0.7 with the previous version, noticing that the new gas limit fields were no longer incorporated into the signed payload. The problem is subtle because the gas limits are technically part of the user operation data, yet they are not visible in the signature verification step, making the mismatch easy to overlook during code review. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete signed data” or “mutable parameter tampering” vulnerabilities, where a contract signs a subset of the inputs but later relies on additional mutable inputs for critical logic. To remediate, the getHash function should be extended to include both the paymaster validation gas limit and the postOp gas limit, and the signature verification should be performed against this expanded hash, ensuring that any change to those limits would invalidate the signature and prevent unauthorized gas‑limit manipulation.

title: Unsupported fee-on-transfer tokens
description:
The implementation of Transfers.sol should be token agnostic and cater to most atypical token types. In most cases, two token transfers are made, firstly to the contract and secondly to the intent recipient. This causes a fee to be charged twice when it is really only necessary to make a single transfer from the payer to the merchant.
In the case where the input token is swapped to the recipient currency, the maxAmountWillingToPay argument is not adjusted to account for the fee charged in the first transfer. This leads to cases where the signed transfer intent may revert, this can happen when:
• Uniswap executes a swap where amountInMax is greater than the available amount to swap.
• Prior to swap execution, the input token is sent to the universal router contract in its entirety, which will fail because maxAmountWillingToPay includes the deducted fee.
Additionally, the swapTokens() function will potentially return incorrect informative swapped amounts as payerBalanceBefore makes use of maxAmountWillingToPay.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s assumption that all ERC20 tokens behave identically during transfers. The implementation performs two sequential transfers: first it moves the payer’s tokens to the contract, then it forwards the same amount to the intended merchant. For fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens, each transfer automatically deducts a percentage as a fee, so the contract unintentionally charges the fee twice. Because the contract does not adjust the maxAmountWillingToPay parameter to reflect the first fee deduction, the amount available for the subsequent swap may be lower than the signed intent. When the router attempts to execute a swap, the amountInMax supplied by the user can exceed the actual token balance after the first fee, causing the swap to revert. This situation can also produce misleading swap result data, as the function reports the pre‑swap balance based on the original maxAmountWillingToPay rather than the reduced balance after fees. The impact is that legitimate transactions may fail unexpectedly, users may see their balances reduced to zero or receive no refund, and the protocol may report incorrect swapped amounts, breaking accounting assumptions. The issue manifests only when a user pays with a token that implements a transfer fee, and it is triggered during the transfer‑to‑contract and subsequent swap steps. It was discovered during a security audit that examined token‑agnostic transfer logic and identified that the code does not handle atypical token behaviours. The bug is subtle because fee‑on‑transfer tokens appear to work correctly in simple transfers, and the double‑fee effect only becomes visible when the contract chains multiple transfers together. To remediate, the contract should either detect FoT tokens and adjust the transferred amount to account for the fee, or explicitly reject such tokens by reverting the transaction when a fee‑on‑transfer token is used, thereby preserving the intended economic flow and preventing double‑charging and swap reverts.

title: Transfer intents cannot be invalidated
description:
Operators earn fees by being facilitators of trades between payers and merchants. Protocol operators are a permissionless role in which coinbase is one of these. Transfer intents are signed by payers and when processed, the processedTransferIntents is set.
If an operator is at any time intentionally malicious and causes a transfer intent to revert, then it is the responsibility of the payer to sign a new transfer intent with an honest operator instead. If this same user does not wait for the previous intent to expire and uses the same ID, then they are prone to an attack where two intents are executed instead of one.
It is important that payers have the ability to invalidate previously signed transfer intents before signing and executing new ones. The operator can forcibly revert a transfer once a signed transaction is in the mempool in the following ways:
• Front-running a transfer by unregistering the operator account, causing operatorIsRegistered() to fail.
• If the transfer sends native funds, the operator can revert on the native call() method.
• Some tokens also have callbacks, which the operator could revert on when fees are sent to their address.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability to invalidate previously signed transfer intents in a permissionless operator model where operators act as facilitators of trades between payers and merchants. A transfer intent is a signed message from a payer that, when processed, records the intent identifier in a mapping called processedTransferIntents. The current implementation stores the intent identifier only against the operator address, which means the same identifier can be reused by the same payer if the operator deliberately causes the original transaction to revert. A malicious operator can achieve this by front‑running the transaction and unregistering its own account, causing the operatorIsRegistered check to fail, or by reverting the native call that transfers funds, or by exploiting token callbacks that revert when fees are sent. When the original intent reverts, the payer is expected to sign a new intent with a different operator, but if the payer reuses the same identifier before the previous intent expires, the contract will accept and execute the second intent as if it were fresh. This results in two executions of the same intent, effectively moving funds twice and causing a loss of value for the payer or the merchant. The impact includes double spending, unexpected balance reductions, and potential denial of service for users who cannot reliably complete a single payment. The issue manifests only when an operator acts maliciously and the payer does not wait for the prior intent to become invalid, a scenario that may be hard to detect because the UI typically reports a successful transaction without indicating that a previous attempt was reverted. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑or‑re‑use vulnerabilities where signed messages lack proper invalidation or single‑use enforcement. To remediate, the processedTransferIntents mapping should associate payer addresses with intent identifiers, ensuring each identifier is consumed only once per payer, and a dedicated function should allow payers to explicitly mark an intent as invalid before signing a new one. Additionally, any operator‑controlled revert paths should be wrapped in try/catch logic so that fees are returned to the payer if the operator cannot receive them, eliminating the incentive for an operator to force a revert and reuse an intent identifier.

title: Any refunded ETH is stuck in the StaticAttester contract
description: Based on the functionality of the EAS, if the total sent ETH during an attestation isn't fully spent, it is refunded back to the attester or to the msg.sender in cases of attestation delegation. However, the StaticAttester.sol contract lacks a method to extract any refunded ETH. Although it is mentioned that current usages will not involve payments, this is not enforced in the StaticAttester contract, and valid attestations can still be created for payable SchemaResolvers.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a situation where the StaticAttester contract can receive Ether refunds from the Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS) but provides no mechanism to retrieve that Ether. In the EAS workflow, when an attestation is submitted with a payable SchemaResolver, any excess ETH that is not consumed by the resolver is automatically sent back to the caller (the attester or the delegating msg.sender). Because StaticAttester does not enforce that the call is made with zero value, an attacker or a careless user can trigger a payable resolver, causing the EAS to send a refund to the StaticAttester contract. The contract lacks a withdraw function and does not expose any admin‑only method to transfer the accumulated balance, so the refunded Ether becomes permanently locked inside the contract. This can be exploited by deliberately invoking an attestation that uses a payable resolver and sending a small amount of ETH; the EAS will return the unused portion to StaticAttester, and the attacker (or any user) will have no way to extract those funds. The impact is that Ether sent to the contract disappears from the user's perspective – the user expects a refund or a zero‑balance after the operation, but the contract balance increases silently. The issue manifests only when a payable SchemaResolver is used or when a caller mistakenly includes value with the attestation; in normal usage with non‑payable resolvers the problem does not appear, which makes it easy to overlook during testing. The affected parties are the attesters, delegators, and any protocol component that relies on StaticAttester for attestations, because their funds may become unrecoverable. The bug was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s handling of payable functions and noticed the absence of any withdrawal logic. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit events or provide UI feedback about incoming Ether, and the source code does not contain any payable modifiers, giving a false sense of safety. The proper remediation is to either add an admin‑only withdraw function that transfers the contract’s Ether balance to a trusted address, or to explicitly require that all attestation calls to StaticAttester are made with msg.value == 0, thereby preventing interaction with payable resolvers and eliminating the possibility of refunds being sent to the contract. This class of bug falls under stuck funds due to missing withdrawal path or unintended payable fallback without extraction mechanism, which violates the accounting assumption that all Ether sent to a contract can be reclaimed or accounted for.

title: Attacker can make restricted calls from any wallet
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass that occurs when the spend() function is invoked with a transfer amount of zero. In the normal flow, spend() first calls an internal helper _useSpendPermission() which checks that the supplied SpendPermission object has been approved via isApproved(). However, _useSpendPermission() contains an early‑return clause that exits immediately if the value argument equals zero, and the approval check is placed after this clause. As a result, when value is zero the contract skips the isApproved() verification entirely and proceeds to call _transferFrom() with a zero amount. Although a zero ERC20 transfer does not move any tokens, the _transferFrom() implementation still performs an external call to the recipient address (or to the token contract for ERC20) and, for ERC721 tokens that follow the older transfer(address,uint256) signature such as CryptoKitties, the call can trigger a legitimate token transfer even when the amount parameter is zero. Consequently, an attacker can craft a SpendPermission that references a wallet they do not control, set the value to zero, and invoke spend() from any address. The contract will then execute the fallback function of an arbitrary contract or, in the special case of an ERC721 with a transfer function that does not require a non‑zero amount, transfer ownership of the NFT to the attacker. The impact is that the permission model of the wallet is broken: unauthorized parties can cause the wallet to interact with external contracts, potentially stealing NFTs or executing unwanted logic. This condition manifests only when the spend amount is zero, which is a legitimate edge case for many legitimate operations, making the bug easy to overlook during code review. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included unit tests exercising zero‑value spend calls; the test demonstrated that the fallback of a mock recipient contract was invoked with the wallet address as the caller, confirming the bypass. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because zero‑value transfers are often considered harmless and may not emit events or change balances, so developers may not notice the unauthorized external call. The proper fix is to move the isApproved() check before the early‑return, ensuring that permission validation occurs regardless of the transfer amount. This aligns the function with the broader class of “authorization bypass on zero‑value paths” bugs, where a guard is unintentionally skipped for a special input value, violating the intended security invariant that only approved spend permissions may trigger any external interaction from the wallet.

title: Accidentally sent ETH can be stuck in protocol resolver contract
description: The protocol currently does not intend to support ETH transfers to resolvers. However, the attest and revoke functions of SchemaResolverUpgradeable.sol have the payable specifier which allows ETH transfers to underlying resolvers via these functions. Impact: Accidentally sent ETH can be stuck in resolver contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unintended ability to lock ether in a resolver contract because the public functions that manage schema attestations and revocations are marked payable. The root cause is that the attest and revoke functions in the resolver implementation were declared with the payable modifier even though the protocol’s design does not require or expect any ether to be transferred to resolver contracts. When a caller includes a non‑zero msg.value while invoking either function, the ether is transferred to the resolver address. Because the resolver contract contains no logic to forward, withdraw, or otherwise handle received ether, the funds become permanently inaccessible – they are effectively stuck. This can be exploited unintentionally: a user who mistakenly sends ether together with an attest or revoke transaction will see the ether disappear from their wallet while the resolver’s balance increases, but there is no way for the user or the protocol to retrieve it. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that resolver contracts hold no ether, potentially eroding trust. The condition under which the issue occurs is any call to attest or revoke with a positive ether value; it does not depend on any special role or permission, so any participant can trigger it. The affected parties are users who interact with the schema functions, the protocol operators who may be blamed for lost funds, and any downstream contracts that assume a zero ether balance for resolvers. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined function signatures and noticed the payable specifier without accompanying withdrawal mechanisms. The issue is subtle because the functions are primarily used for data operations, so developers may not anticipate that sending ether is possible, and user interfaces typically do not display a value field for these calls, making accidental transfers easy to overlook. To remediate, the payable modifier should be removed or the function should explicitly revert when msg.value is greater than zero, and a withdrawal path should be added if receiving ether is ever intended. In generic terms, this is a classic ether‑locking bug caused by an unnecessary payable function that violates the contract’s intended financial model, leading to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective while the contract’s balance silently grows.

title: Valid CB NonUS attestations will fail veriﬁcation
description: SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION is set to 1 which implies that this is a valid schema version. However, verifyNonUsAttestation() reverts with UnsupportedSchemaVersion if the attestation has version <= SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION, which reverts even for valid attestations with version == 1. The inequality operator should be < not <= because version == SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION should be valid based on inferring from the name. Only attestations for older versions of schema, i.e. 0 for now, should revert for being unsupported. Thus, valid CB NonUS attestations with version == 1 will revert functions using the onlyNonUsAttestation modifier leading to failure of all such protocol verification functionality.
bug_full: The contract defines a constant SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION with the value 1, indicating that schema version 1 is the minimum version that the system should accept for Coinbase Non‑US attestations. The verification routine verifyNonUsAttestation() checks the version field of an incoming attestation and deliberately reverts with an UnsupportedSchemaVersion error when the supplied version is less than or equal to the supported constant (version <= SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION). Because the comparison includes equality, a perfectly valid attestation whose version field equals 1 is incorrectly treated as unsupported and causes the transaction to revert. The root cause is a logical error in the conditional operator: the intended rule is that only older schema versions (e.g., version 0) should be rejected, which requires a strict less‑than check (version < SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION). This bug can be exploited simply by submitting a legitimate attestation with version 1; the contract will reject it, causing any function guarded by the onlyNonUsAttestation modifier to fail. The impact is that all protocol functionality that relies on successful verification of Non‑US attestations—such as user onboarding, compliance checks, or fund transfers that depend on a verified attestation—will be blocked. From a user’s perspective, transactions that should succeed will revert with an obscure UnsupportedSchemaVersion error, leading to confusion, apparent loss of funds (because the transaction does not complete), and an inability to progress through the protocol. The condition manifests whenever the contract processes a Non‑US attestation, i.e., during any call that passes through verifyNonUsAttestation or the onlyNonUsAttestation modifier. The affected parties include end‑users submitting attestations, the protocol operators who rely on the verification step, and any downstream contracts that expect a successful attestation check. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the verification logic and compared the constant’s semantic meaning with the actual comparison used in code. It can be hard to notice because the revert message does not clearly indicate that the version is actually supported; developers may assume the check is correct based on the constant name. To remediate, the conditional should be changed to a strict less‑than comparison (version < SUPPORTED_VERIFIED_BY_CB_VERSION), thereby allowing version 1 attestations while still rejecting older, unsupported versions. This correction aligns the implementation with the intended schema‑version policy and restores normal verification flow, preventing unnecessary transaction reverts and ensuring that compliant users can successfully interact with the protocol.

title: Incorrect UPGRADER_ROLE allows unauthorized proxy upgrades leading to protocol hijacking
description: UPGRADER_ROLE is used to enforce role-based access control to allow the UUPS proxy to upgrade its implementation via _authorizeUpgrade(). However, the value of UPGRADER_ROLE in AttestationIndexer is incorrectly set to cbattestations.staticattester.upgrader instead of cbattestations.attestationindexer.upgrader. This appears to be a copy-paste typographical error. cbattestations.staticattester.upgrader is also used for the UPGRADER_ROLE of StaticAttester proxy. An untrusted or compromised or malicious StaticAttester upgrader can now not only arbitrarily change the StaticAttester implementation but also arbitrarily change the AttestationIndexer implementation, which arguably could have a greater/broader negative impact leading to hijacking the core protocol functionality of indexing. Also, if AccessControlUpgradeable.DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE correctly assigns cbattestations.attestationindexer.upgrader role to any address for authorizing upgrades of AttestationIndexer, that address will not be able to upgrade AttestationIndexer.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect assignment of the UPGRADER_ROLE constant in the AttestationIndexer contract, which governs who may invoke the UUPS proxy’s _authorizeUpgrade function. Instead of referencing the dedicated upgrader identifier for the AttestationIndexer (cbattestations.attestationindexer.upgrader), the contract mistakenly reuses the identifier belonging to the StaticAttester (cbattestations.staticattester.upgrader). This copy‑paste mistake creates a single role that controls upgrades for two distinct proxies. Because the role is checked only against the stored constant, any address that holds the StaticAttester upgrader role can also call the upgrade routine of the AttestationIndexer, even though it was never intended to have that authority. An attacker who compromises or is granted the StaticAttester upgrader role can therefore deploy a malicious implementation of the AttestationIndexer, hijacking the core indexing logic of the protocol. The impact is that the protocol’s attestation indexing may be corrupted, leading to missing or falsified attestations, which in turn can cause downstream contracts to behave incorrectly, potentially blocking fund releases or misrouting rewards. The condition under which this occurs is at deployment time when the AccessControlUpgradeable roles are initialized; the bug is latent because the role identifiers are opaque bytes32 values that look similar, making the mistake easy to overlook during code review. The affected parties include protocol operators who rely on correct indexing, developers integrating the indexer, and end‑users whose transactions depend on valid attestations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared role constants across contracts and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice in runtime because the proxy will accept any upgrade request that passes the _authorizeUpgrade check, and the check passes for the wrong role without emitting any warning. Conceptually, the fix is to assign the correct, contract‑specific upgrader identifier to the AttestationIndexer’s UPGRADER_ROLE and to ensure that the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE only grants upgrade rights to the intended address. This separates the upgrade authority of the two proxies, restoring the intended role‑based access control and preventing unauthorized implementation changes that could cause the protocol’s accounting assumptions to break, such as users expecting their attestations to be recorded but seeing them disappear or become invalid.

title: Incorrect INDEXER_ROLE value may prevent indexer access
description: INDEXER_ROLE is used to enforce role-based access control to the index() function. However, the value of INDEXER_ROLE is incorrectly set to cbattestations.staticattester.indexer instead of cbattestations.attestationindexer.indexer. This appears to be a copy-paste typographical error. If AccessControlUpgradeable.DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE correctly assigns cbattestations.attestationindexer.indexer role to addresses which are authorized to access the indexer, they will be denied access. The dynamic role assignment will also need to intentionally use the incorrect cbattestations.staticattester.indexer role during assignments which will be confusing and error-prone or this contract will require upgrading to fix this error.
bug_full: The contract uses AccessControlUpgradeable to restrict the index() function to callers that hold the INDEXER_ROLE. The constant that represents this role is defined incorrectly: it points to the role identifier of the static attester contract (cbattestations.staticattester.indexer) instead of the intended attestation indexer contract (cbattestations.attestationindexer.indexer). Because role identifiers are hashed values, the mismatch means that any address that has been granted the correct attestation indexer role by the admin will not match the required role check, and the call to index() will revert with an access‑control error. Conversely, if an address is mistakenly granted the static attester role, it will be able to call index(), which is not intended. The bug originates from a copy‑paste typo when assigning the constant value. An attacker who can obtain the static attester role (for example by being added to the admin's role list) could gain unauthorized access to the indexing function, potentially manipulating or disrupting the indexing process. Legitimate indexers, on the other hand, will be blocked from performing their duties, causing the protocol’s indexing pipeline to stall, leading to missing data, delayed rewards, or even loss of funds that depend on successful indexing. The condition occurs at runtime whenever the index() function is invoked; the check fails if the caller does not hold the mismatched role. The affected parties are the protocol operators who rely on the indexer, the indexer addresses themselves, and any users whose transactions depend on up‑to‑date indexing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s role definitions, where the auditor noticed that the role constant referenced the wrong library. Because the failure manifests only as an access‑control revert, it may be overlooked if tests only cover successful paths and do not attempt calls from a correctly authorized indexer. The proper remediation is to replace the constant with the correct attestation indexer role identifier, and to ensure that role assignments use the corrected identifier throughout the contract and any upgrade scripts. This type of bug belongs to the class of misconfigured access‑control constants, where a typo in a role hash leads to unintended permission checks. From a user’s perspective, an authorized indexer would see transactions failing with ‘access denied’ or ‘missing permission’, while the protocol would appear to have no indexing activity, contradicting the expectation that indexing proceeds automatically. The bug violates the business logic that only designated indexers may modify the indexing state, breaking the accounting assumptions of the system.

title: _pendingltv[asset] will be set to 0 if 2 consecutive calls to setreservefreeze(asset, true) are executed Submitted by r0bert, also found by StErMi, krikolkk, zigtur, lukaprini, Chad0 and 99Crits
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the setReserveFreeze function of the Aave reserve configuration. When an authorized admin calls setReserveFreeze with freeze set to true, the function saves the current loan‑to‑value (LTV) of the asset in a temporary mapping _pendingLtv and then forces the on‑chain LTV to zero. The implementation does not check whether the asset is already frozen. If a second authorized admin calls setReserveFreeze with freeze true while the asset is still frozen, the function reads the already‑zero LTV from the configuration and overwrites the previously stored pending value with zero. Consequently, when an admin later calls setReserveFreeze with freeze false, the contract restores the LTV from the pending mapping, which now contains zero instead of the original value. The result is that the asset remains with an LTV of zero even though it is reported as unfrozen, preventing users from using the asset as collateral for borrowing. The bug is triggered only when two consecutive freeze calls are made by accounts that satisfy the onlyRiskOrPoolOrEmergencyAdmins modifier, which includes risk admins, pool admins and emergency admins. In practice this can happen because multiple administrators may act independently during periods of high price volatility. From a user’s point of view the protocol UI shows the asset as available for deposit and earning interest, but attempts to borrow against it fail with messages such as “collateral not allowed” or “asset cannot be used as collateral”. Users therefore experience a mismatch between expectation (“asset is unfrozen, I should be able to borrow”) and reality (borrow fails, collateral value appears to be zero). The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the state‑transition logic of the reserve configuration. It is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the LTV is incorrectly restored, and the UI does not highlight that the LTV is zero after unfreeze, making the problem easy to miss until borrowing attempts fail. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent bugs where a temporary storage variable is unintentionally overwritten, leading to incorrect restoration of protocol parameters. The recommended fix is to add a guard that stores the pending LTV only when the current LTV is non‑zero, or to check whether a pending value has already been recorded before overwriting it. Restoring the original LTV on unfreeze will align the on‑chain configuration with the expected business logic that an unfrozen asset can be used as collateral for borrowing purposes.

title: Stepwise jump vulnerability in affiliate fee splits configuration Submitted by 0xTheBlackPanther
description:
There is a stepwise jump vulnerability within the LoanCore affiliate fee split configuration. The setAffiliateSplits function, callable by an admin role, allows for modifications to the affiliate fee splits without a gradual adjustment or notification to users. This could lead to abrupt changes in protocol fees and potentially impact users relying on the existing fee structure.
The stepwise jump vulnerability in the affiliate fee split configuration could have the following impacts:
1. Sudden changes in protocol fees: Admins have the authority to modify affiliate fee splits, leading to sudden changes in protocol fees. Users initiating loans may experience unexpected variations in fees without prior notification.
2. User discontent: Abrupt modifications to affiliate fee splits may result in user dissatisfaction, especially affiliates who rely on predictable earnings. Lack of transparency and communication can erode trust and confidence in the lending platform.
3. Operational disruption: sudden changes in protocol fees could disrupt the operations of users, such as lenders and borrowers, who have established their financial strategies based on the existing fee structure. This may lead to financial losses and operational challenges.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an abrupt configuration change, often called a stepwise jump, in the affiliate fee split parameters of the loan core contract. The root cause is that the setAffiliateSplits function, which is restricted to an admin role, allows the fee split percentages to be overwritten in a single transaction without any enforced delay, gradual transition, or notification mechanism. Because the contract does not impose a time‑lock, rate‑limit, or event‑driven warning, an admin (or a compromised admin key) can instantly increase the protocol’s share of fees and decrease the affiliate’s share. An attacker can exploit this by calling setAffiliateSplits with a new split that favours the protocol, causing all subsequent loan creations to charge higher fees for borrowers and to credit lower or zero payouts to affiliates. The impact is that users who rely on a predictable fee structure see unexpected higher costs, affiliates experience sudden drops in earnings (sometimes to zero), and the overall trust in the platform erodes. This situation occurs whenever the admin executes the function; there is no condition that forces a notice period or a phased rollout, so the change takes effect immediately for any loan taken after the transaction. The affected parties include borrowers who pay the loan fee, lenders who may receive reduced returns, affiliates who earn a portion of the fee, and the protocol itself because reputation damage can lead to reduced usage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s governance functions, where the lack of a transition or notification pattern stood out as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the current fee amount; users may not see a history of fee changes, and the contract does not emit a distinct warning event before the change. To remediate, the contract should enforce a gradual transition mechanism such as a time‑locked update or a phased schedule, emit clear events, and optionally require a governance vote or user‑defined split preferences. Providing advance notice through on‑chain or off‑chain notifications would align the implementation with the expectation that fee structures change predictably rather than abruptly, thereby preventing sudden fee spikes and protecting affiliate earnings.

title: Exploiting the exclusion of principal fee from old principal when reroll is called Submitted by Lanrebayode77, also found by jesjupyter, glcanvas and Nyksx
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission that occurs when the RepaymentController contract settles an existing loan through the rolloverLoan option. In the normal repayment flow the contract calculates a fee on the principal amount (principalFee) and subtracts it from the amount that will be transferred to the previous lender. The calculation is performed in _prepareRepay() as: principalFee = (paymentToPrincipal * data.feeSnapshot.lenderPrincipalFee) / Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR and amountToLender = amountFromBorrower - interestFee - principalFee. However, the helper function _calculateRolloverAmounts, which is used exclusively for the rollover path, only computes the interest fee and completely skips the deduction of principalFee. As a result, when the old lender is the same address as the new lender, the protocol transfers the full principal amount plus interest minus only the interest fee, leaving the principal fee unpaid to the protocol. This omission can be exploited by a borrower who triggers a rollover with a lender that signs the transaction. The lender then receives an extra amount equal to the principal fee that should have been collected by the protocol. For example, with a 1,000,000 USDC loan at 10 % interest and a 1 % principal fee, the protocol should collect 20,000 USDC in fees (10,000 interest fee + 10,000 principal fee). Because the rollover path does not deduct the principal fee, the lender ends up receiving 1,089,890 USDC instead of the correct 1,080,000 USDC, effectively stealing 10,000 USDC from the protocol. The bug manifests only when the rolloverLoan option is used and the old lender equals the new lender, i.e., when the same party continues to fund the loan after settlement. It affects borrowers, lenders, and the protocol’s fee pool, causing a loss of revenue and breaking the accounting assumptions that fees are always collected on both interest and principal. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the repayment logic, where the auditor noticed a comment asking “What about Principal fee???”. It is hard to notice because the overall repayment amounts appear plausible and the missing fee is a relatively small percentage of the total, making balance mismatches easy to overlook in routine testing. The proper fix is to mirror the fee deduction performed in _prepareRepay(): compute the principal fee using the same snapshot and subtract it from amountToLender when the rollover amounts are calculated. This ensures that the protocol receives its entitled fees and that the accounting invariants hold across all repayment paths.

title: lender may incur losses on a loan if the borrower repays it quickly, considering the lender- principlefee Submitted by jesjupyter
description:
There is no minimum time limit for a borrower to repay the debt. If he calls repayFull not soon after the loan is signed, this may incur a loss of fund of the lender. The lender has to pay the following fees:
```solidity
Principal * (LENDER_ORIGINATION_FEE + LENDER_PRINCIPAL_FEE) / Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR;
```
And the lender will receive the following:
```solidity
interest * (Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR - lenderInterestFee) / Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR;
```
However, the interest here isn't fixed. It is calculated using the following formula in InterestCalculator::getProratedInterestAmount:
```solidity
Principal * timeSinceLastPayment * interestRate / (Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR * Constants.SECONDS_IN_YEAR);
```
If the borrower calls repayFull not soon after the loan is signed, timeSinceLastPayment would be quite small, and the interest they receive may not be able to cover the fees they paid for the loan. Thus, this may incur a loss of fund of the lender. The uncertainty of income and principal losses hinders the motivation and information for lenders to participate in lending.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the lending contract does not enforce any minimum loan duration before a borrower can call repayFull. The contract charges the lender an origination fee and a principal fee that are calculated as a fixed percentage of the principal at loan creation. At the same time the interest that the lender receives is computed prorated to the elapsed time since the last payment using the formula Principal * timeSinceLastPayment * interestRate / (Constants.BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR * Constants.SECONDS_IN_YEAR). Because timeSinceLastPayment can be arbitrarily small, a borrower who repays the loan immediately generates almost zero interest. The lender still pays the full origination and principal fees, so the net amount received may be lower than the fees paid, resulting in a loss of funds for the lender. This situation can be triggered by any borrower who calls repayFull shortly after the loan is signed, because the contract contains no check that enforces a minimum repayment period or a minimum interest floor. The affected parties are the lenders who provide capital to the protocol, as well as the overall lending pool which relies on predictable returns to attract capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee and interest calculation logic, where the relationship between the fixed fees and the time‑dependent interest was examined. The problem is subtle because the repayment transaction appears successful and the interest calculation itself is mathematically correct; however the economic outcome is unfavorable and may not be obvious from the UI, which simply shows that the loan was repaid. Users may notice that after a repayment their balance is reduced by the amount of fees they paid, while the expected interest reward is missing or negligible. This violates the business assumption that lenders earn at least enough interest to cover the fees associated with providing a loan. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a minimum loan term, introduce a minimum interest amount that must be paid regardless of elapsed time, or adjust the fee structure so that fees are proportional to the actual time the capital was deployed. Implementing any of these mitigations would prevent a borrower from causing a lender loss by repaying the loan too quickly.

title: Refinanceloan() places old lender on at unfair disadvantage Submitted by kodyvim, also found by Nyksx
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a permissionless refinance function that allows any address to roll over an existing loan without obtaining explicit consent from the original lender. The contract stores loan data, including the principal, interest rate, and the address of the lender who originally funded the loan. When refinanceLoan() is called, the function retrieves the loan data, validates the new terms, and immediately creates a new loan tied to the caller (msg.sender) while preserving the same NFT collateral. Because there is no check that the old lender approves the refinance, a third party can invoke the function as soon as the loan becomes eligible (approximately two days after creation) and replace the original lender with themselves. An attacker can monitor the market value of the NFT collateral; if the collateral’s market price exceeds the outstanding balance plus accrued interest, the attacker can front‑run the refinance transaction, create a new loan with more favorable terms, and later claim the collateral when the borrower defaults. This exploitation results in the original lender losing expected interest revenue and potentially losing the right to claim the collateral altogether. The issue manifests when a loan is freshly created and the refinance window opens, and it is triggered by any external account that can submit a transaction before the original lender reacts. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of an approval step for the old lender in the refinance workflow. It can be difficult to notice because the UI may simply show a new loan ID and the original loan disappearing, without an explicit error or warning, leading users to assume the refinance was a normal protocol operation. The bug belongs to the class of “unauthorized state transition” or “consent‑missing financial operation” vulnerabilities, where critical financial rights are transferred without holder approval. From a user perspective, a lender may see their loan disappear, their expected interest never materialize, and the NFT collateral being transferred to another party, contradicting the expectation that only the original lender can claim the collateral after a default. To remediate, the protocol should require explicit approval from the current lender before allowing a refinance, enforce a lock‑up period that prevents third‑party refinancing, or redesign the refinance mechanism to preserve the original lender’s rights, thereby aligning the contract behavior with the intended business logic of lender‑borrower agreements.

title: Rewards will be locked if user transfer directly to pool without using deposit function
description:
[LPFarming.sol#L190](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-jpegd/blob/e72861a9ccb707ced9015166fbded5c97c6991b6/contracts/farming/LPFarming.sol#L190)  

Reward will be locked in the farming, when user execute a direct transfer with lpToken to farm without using deposit.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the farming contract calculates the total amount of LP tokens that participate in a reward pool. Instead of maintaining an internal counter that reflects only those tokens deposited through the official deposit() function, the contract queries the ERC‑20 token’s balanceOf(address(this)) to obtain the pool’s LP supply. When an external actor sends LP tokens directly to the contract address via a plain ERC‑20 transfer, those tokens are added to the contract’s balance but are never recorded in the internal accounting structures. As a result, the reward distribution algorithm believes that the pool contains more LP tokens than actually belong to legitimate depositors. During an epoch, the reward per share is computed by dividing the total reward amount by this inflated token count. Consequently, honest users receive a smaller share of the reward, and the excess portion remains locked in the contract because the contract assumes the extra LP tokens will be withdrawn later, which never happens. The issue manifests whenever a user (malicious or accidental) transfers LP tokens directly to the farming contract address before or during an active reward epoch. Affected parties include LP token holders who deposit via the proper interface, the protocol’s overall reward accounting, and any funds that become permanently inaccessible. The bug was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that performed a direct transfer of LP tokens to the farm address and observed that a portion of the allocated rewards stayed unrecoverable after the epoch ended. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract’s external balance appears normal and no explicit farming‑related events are emitted for the direct transfer, masking the mismatch between on‑chain token balance and internal state. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a dedicated state variable (e.g., totalLPSupply) that is incremented and decremented only within deposit() and withdraw() calls, and this variable should be used for all reward calculations instead of the token’s balanceOf. This change restores the integrity of the reward accounting, ensuring that only tokens that have been properly deposited influence reward distribution and preventing permanent locking of reward tokens.

title: Oracle data feed is insufficiently validated.
description: Price can be stale and can lead to wrong `answer` return value.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from insufficient validation of the on‑chain price oracle data used by the contract to compute the USD value of collateral. The contract calls the oracle’s latestRoundData (or latestAnswer) and directly accepts the returned price (answer) after a single check that the value is positive. It fails to verify that the round is fresh – there is no comparison between the round identifier and the latest answered round – and it does not ensure that the round is complete, i.e., that the timestamp is non‑zero and that the data is not stale. Because Chainlink aggregators can return outdated or incomplete data when a round is still being answered or when the feed experiences a pause, the contract may accept a price that is significantly lower or higher than the current market value. An attacker who can control or influence the oracle (for example by feeding stale data during a network delay) can trigger the contract to use this incorrect price when calculating collateral requirements, liquidation thresholds, or redemption values. The immediate impact is a mis‑pricing of collateral: users may be allowed to borrow more than they should, or conversely, legitimate borrowers may be liquidated prematurely. From the user’s perspective this may appear as an unexpected loss of funds, a zero or missing refund, or a transaction that reverts with an obscure "invalid_oracle_answer" error despite the oracle appearing functional. The bug manifests only when the oracle’s latest round is either stale or incomplete, which can happen intermittently during feed updates or network congestion, making it difficult to reproduce consistently. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that identified the lack of round‑freshness checks in the _collateralPriceUsd function. The problem is subtle because a positive answer alone seems sufficient, yet without validating timeliness the contract’s accounting assumptions are violated. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the answered round is at least as recent as the round identifier, verify that the timestamp is non‑zero (indicating a completed round), and reject any price that is older than an acceptable freshness window. This aligns with the standard pattern for secure oracle consumption and prevents the contract from acting on stale or incomplete price data, thereby preserving the economic integrity of the protocol.

title: Wrong calculation for `yVault` price per share if decimals != 18
description:
The [yVault.getPricePerFullShare()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-jpegd/blob/main/contracts/vaults/yVault/yVault.sol#L196) function calculates the price per share by multiplying with `1e18` token decimals with the assumption that the underlying token always has 18 decimals. `yVault` has the same amount of decimals as it’s underlying token see ([yVault.decimals()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-jpegd/blob/main/contracts/vaults/yVault/yVault.sol#L70))

But tokens don’t always have `1e18` decimals (e.g. USDC).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the yVault contract’s getPricePerFullShare() function, which calculates the price per share by multiplying the underlying token balance by a hard‑coded 1e18 factor, under the assumption that the underlying ERC‑20 token always uses 18 decimal places. In reality, many tokens, such as USDC, use a different number of decimals (e.g., 6). Because yVault.decimals() simply mirrors the underlying token’s decimals, the price‑per‑share calculation becomes mismatched when the token does not have 18 decimals. This mismatch leads to an incorrect price value: the function returns a number that is off by a factor of 10^(18‑tokenDecimals). When users deposit tokens, the vault uses this price to mint yVault shares. With a distorted price, the vault either mints too many or too few shares relative to the actual deposited amount. Consequently, a user who expects to receive a proportional amount of shares may receive an inflated share balance, while a later withdrawal will return less underlying token than anticipated, effectively causing funds to disappear or refunds to be missing. The bug manifests whenever the underlying token’s decimal count differs from 18, which includes a large class of stablecoins and other assets. It affects any participant who deposits or withdraws from the vault – individual users, protocols that rely on the vault’s accounting, and the overall fund safety. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit by Code4rena, where a test that set the underlying token’s decimals to 6 caused the getPricePerFullShare() call to return 2 × 10^18 instead of the expected 2 × 10^6, leading to a failed assertion. The problem can be subtle because the erroneous price value is a large integer that may not be displayed directly to users, and the vault’s internal accounting may still appear to work in a superficial sense, hiding the mis‑allocation of value. To remediate the flaw, the price calculation should be made decimal‑aware: instead of a fixed 1e18 multiplier, the contract must scale the balance by 10^tokenDecimals, using the token’s decimals() value or a safe math library that respects the token’s precision. This adjustment restores correct share minting and withdrawal ratios, aligning on‑chain accounting with users’ expectations that the amount of shares received equals the deposited value divided by the true price per share.

title: `_swapUniswapV2` may use an improper `path` which can cause a loss of the majority of the rewardTokens
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the token swap routine used by the StrategyPUSDConvex contract when converting harvested reward tokens into WETH before finally swapping to USDC. The routine builds a Uniswap V2 swap path that is hard‑coded to a two‑element array consisting of the reward token address followed by the WETH address. This static path assumes that the most liquid pool for the reward token is the rewardToken/WETH pair, but in practice the reward token may have deeper liquidity in a different pool, such as rewardToken/USDC. Because the contract never checks the available liquidity or price impact on the selected pool, it may execute a trade through a thin or poorly funded pool, receiving only a dust amount of WETH. The root cause is the lack of a dynamic routing mechanism and the absence of any guard that verifies that the output amount is reasonable compared to market rates. An attacker does not need to directly interact with the contract to exploit this flaw; instead, the economic conditions of the market can be manipulated—by adding or removing liquidity from the rewardToken/WETH pool, or by deliberately inflating the price impact—so that the contract’s forced path yields a dramatically reduced return. When the harvest function is called, each reward token is swapped using this fixed path; if the path is suboptimal, the majority of the reward value is lost, leading to a lower overall USDC balance that is eventually deposited back into the vault. The impact is primarily financial: users who have deposited assets into the vault expect their reward tokens to be efficiently converted into USDC, but they may see their expected returns shrink or disappear, with balances reducing to near zero after harvest. This condition occurs whenever a reward token’s primary liquidity pool is not the rewardToken/WETH pair, which can happen for newly listed tokens, tokens with preferential stable‑coin pools, or when market dynamics shift. The affected parties are the protocol’s investors, the strategy contract, and any downstream vault that relies on accurate accounting of harvested rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the hard‑coded path and compared it against on‑chain liquidity data, revealing that the chosen route is not universally optimal. Because the swap transaction does not revert on low output (the minimum‑out parameter is set to zero), the problem can remain invisible to users—they receive a successful transaction receipt but see an unexpectedly low balance, a symptom that can be mistaken for a contract bug or a scam. To remediate, the contract should allow an administrator or governance process to specify custom swap paths for each reward token, or dynamically compute the optimal route by querying Uniswap’s router for the best price across multiple hops. Adding a reasonable minimum‑out check based on external price feeds would also prevent dust‑level swaps and ensure that the economic expectations of users align with the actual protocol behavior.

title: The noContract modifier does not work as expected.
description:
[yVault.sol#L61](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-jpegd/blob/59e288c27e1ff1b47505fea2e5434a7577d85576/contracts/vaults/yVault/yVault.sol#L61)  
[yVaultLPFarming.sol#L54](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-jpegd/blob/59e288c27e1ff1b47505fea2e5434a7577d85576/contracts/farming/yVaultLPFarming.sol#L54)
