The issue occurs whenever transaction inclusion is not immediate, which is common on congested networks, making the bug highly likely in practice. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit and independently reported by Om Parikh, who noticed that the EMA behaved erratically under simulated delay conditions. The problem is subtle because the EMA values still appear as plausible numbers; the error only becomes evident when a price spike coincides with a delayed block, producing a large deviation that may be attributed to market volatility. To remediate, the contract should replace block.timestamp with the keeper‑provided _submitTimestamp for both the time‑difference calculation and the update of the stored lastTimestamp, ensuring that the EMA always reflects the intended observation interval. This class of bug falls under “incorrect time source for time‑weighted calculations”, a common source of accounting errors in on‑chain financial contracts.

title: The stale price feed update in the _isLoanLiquidatable can cause loss of funds to the lender Submitted by Udsen, also found by Tripathi
description:
In the hyperlend-p2p/LendingP2P contract the _isLoanLiquidatable function is implemented to check whether a particular loan is liquidatable. The _isLoanLiquidatable function is called during the liquidation of a loan via the LendingP2P.liquidateLoan() transaction (triggered by the liquidator).  
Now let's imagine the following scenario:  
1. The block.timestamp < _loan.startTimestamp + _loan.duration and the _loan.liquidation.isLiquidatable is true. Hence the loan enters the if (_loan.liquidation.isLiquidatable) block.  
2. require(MAX_ORACLE_PRICE_AGE > block.timestamp - assetPriceUpdatedAt, "stale asset oracle") check fails since the asset price is stale.  
3. Hence cannot execute the LendingP2P.liquidateLoan transaction (since it reverts) even though the loan is undercollateralized ((loanValueUsd > (collateralValueUsd * _loan.liquidation.liquidationThreshold / 10000)).  
4. Due to the stale asset price the loan cannot be liquidated and the collateral asset price further declines such that the loanValueUsd > collateralValueUsd itself. Then the asset price feed is updated and require statement evaluates to true thus allowing liquidation to proceed.  
5. But now the loanValueUsd > collateralValueUsd and as a result _loan.borrower can immediately execute the liquidateLoan transaction and liquidate his own loan since the borrower will have more value in loan.asset than he is losing on loan.collateral due to liquidation. And the borrower will get the liquidator bonus fee as well.  
6. Due to this the lender will have to incur bad debt and bear the loss due to stale price feed update. Hence the lender is losing funds in this scenario.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑price‑oracle logic flaw in the loan liquidation flow of the Hyperlend P2P contract. The function that determines whether a loan can be liquidated, _isLoanLiquidatable, first checks a flag that marks the loan as liquidatable based on the current collateral and loan values. It then validates that the asset price feed is recent by requiring MAX_ORACLE_PRICE_AGE to be greater than the time elapsed since the last price update. When the asset price feed becomes stale, this require statement reverts with the message "stale asset oracle" and prevents the liquidateLoan transaction from executing, even though the loan is already under‑collateralised. Because the contract does not fall back to an alternative price source or use the last known price, the liquidation eligibility check and the actual liquidation execution become inconsistent. After the stale price condition clears (for example when the oracle is updated), the loan may have become even more under‑collateralised, causing loanValueUsd to exceed collateralValueUsd. At this point the borrower, who is also the loan owner, can call liquidateLoan on his own loan, receive the collateral asset plus the liquidator bonus, and effectively profit because the amount of collateral he receives is worth more than the debt he repays. The lender, who supplied the loan asset, suffers a bad‑debt loss because the protocol transfers collateral to the borrower instead of covering the debt. This issue occurs only when the asset price feed is stale while the loan is already flagged as liquidatable, a condition that can be reproduced in testing by artificially aging the oracle. The parties affected are the lenders (who lose funds), borrowers (who can gain an unintended profit), and the protocol itself (which loses trust and may incur financial loss). The bug was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a dedicated test that manipulates the oracle timestamps. It is hard to notice because the contract correctly emits a revert for a stale oracle, which appears to be a protective measure, yet it masks the underlying accounting mismatch that later enables self‑liquidation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle‑freshness and liquidation‑eligibility mismatches, where a contract’s safety checks depend on a single external data source without a fallback. From a user’s perspective the borrower sees a successful liquidation of his own loan and receives extra collateral value, while the lender sees his balance shrink and the loan status change to liquidated with a loss. The expected behaviour is that an under‑collateralised loan should be liquidated by an external liquidator, protecting the lender’s capital, not allowing the borrower to profit. To remediate the issue the contract should either implement a fallback oracle, avoid reverting on stale data by using the last known price, or redesign the liquidation eligibility logic so that the same price data is used for both the flag and the actual liquidation execution, thereby preventing a borrower from exploiting a price‑feed timing window.

title: Yield source does not correctly calculate share conversions
description:
The aTokens’ value is pegged to the value of the corresponding supplied asset at a 1:1 ratio and can be safely stored, transferred or traded. All yield collected by the aTokens’ reserves are distributed to aToken holders directly by continuously increasing their wallet balance.

<https://docs.aave.com/developers/tokens/atoken>
poc:
File: contracts/AaveV3YieldSource.sol   #X
    
    352     /**
    353      * @notice Calculates the number of shares that should be minted or burnt when a user deposit or withdraw.
    354      * @param _tokens Amount of asset tokens
    355      * @return Number of shares.
    356      */
    357     function _tokenToShares(uint256 _tokens) internal view returns (uint256) {
    358       uint256 _supply = totalSupply();
    359   
    360       // shares = (tokens * totalShares) / yieldSourceATokenTotalSupply
    361       return _supply == 0 ? _tokens : _tokens.mul(_supply).div(aToken.balanceOf(address(this)));
    362     }
    363   
    364     /**
    365      * @notice Calculates the number of asset tokens a user has in the yield source.
    366      * @param _shares Amount of shares
    367      * @return Number of asset tokens.
    368      */
    369     function _sharesToToken(uint256 _shares) internal view returns (uint256) {
    370       uint256 _supply = totalSupply();
    371   
    372       // tokens = (shares * yieldSourceATokenTotalSupply) / totalShares
    373       return _supply == 0 ? _shares : _shares.mul(aToken.balanceOf(address(this))).div(_supply);
    374     }

[AaveV3YieldSource.sol#L352-L374](https://github.com/pooltogether/aave-v3-yield-source/blob/e63d1b0e396a5bce89f093630c282ca1c6627e44/contracts/AaveV3YieldSource.sol#L352-L374)  

The above code is used for both `supplyTokenTo()` and `redeemToken()` and does not return one for one. Consider the following chain of events:

  1. There are no deposits yet
  2. Alice deposits one wBTC, getting back a AaveV3YieldSource share, while the yield source gets the aToken
  3. Some time later a total of one extra wBTC worth of aToken is generated as yield and is in the `balanceOf(this)`
  4. Alice attempts to withdraw her one share but gets zero wBTC, because `(tokens{1} * totalSupply(){1}) / aToken.balanceOf(this){2}` is zero
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the AaveV3YieldSource contract converts deposited asset tokens to internal shares and back again. The contract implements a conversion function that calculates shares as (tokens × totalSupply) ÷ aToken.balanceOf(this) and the reverse conversion as (shares × aToken.balanceOf(this)) ÷ totalSupply. This formulation assumes that the balance of the underlying aToken remains constant after a deposit. In reality the aToken balance grows as interest accrues, because aTokens continuously increase their wallet balance to reflect earned yield. When the aToken balance rises, the denominator in the token‑to‑share formula becomes larger, causing the contract to mint fewer shares than the number of tokens supplied. Conversely, the share‑to‑token formula then divides a larger aToken balance by the (now lower) totalSupply, which can reduce the amount of underlying tokens returned on withdrawal. In the edge case where a single user (for example Alice) is the only depositor and the yield source accrues a full token of interest, the conversion yields a zero‑token withdrawal: Alice deposits 1 wBTC, receives 1 share, the aToken balance later grows to 2 wBTC, and when she redeems her single share the formula computes (1 share × 2 wBTC) ÷ 1 share = 2 wBTC, but due to integer division ordering the contract actually evaluates (1 wBTC × 1 share) ÷ 2 wBTC = 0, resulting in her receiving no tokens. The impact is a loss of user funds: the user expects a 1:1 redemption but receives less, potentially zero, effectively leaking value from the protocol. The issue manifests only when the yield source’s aToken balance diverges from the initial deposit amount, which is typical after any interest accrual, but becomes most visible when the pool has a single participant or when the token uses unconventional decimals that exacerbate the rounding error. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the conversion logic and constructing a concrete scenario that highlighted the mismatch between expected one‑to‑one share behavior and actual math. The problem is subtle because the conversion functions appear to be standard proportional calculations; the error is hidden behind integer division and the assumption that the aToken balance is static, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should eliminate the conversion entirely and enforce a strict one‑share‑equals‑one‑token invariant, or use a separate accounting variable that tracks accrued interest without affecting the share conversion ratio. In practice this means minting shares equal to the exact token amount deposited and redeeming shares at the same amount, while distributing interest through a different mechanism, ensuring that users always receive at least the amount they deposited and that balances displayed in the UI match on‑chain expectations.

title: `xERC4626.sol` Some users may not be able to withdraw until `rewardsCycleEnd` the due to underflow in `beforeWithdraw
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the xERC4626 contract’s withdrawal accounting. The contract maintains a cached variable called storedTotalAssets that reflects the amount of assets that are currently considered withdrawable, excluding any rewards that are still locked in the ongoing rewards cycle. In the beforeWithdraw hook the implementation blindly subtracts the withdrawal amount from storedTotalAssets (storedTotalAssets -= amount). When a user attempts to withdraw an amount that includes a portion of the unlocked rewards before the rewardsCycleEnd timestamp, the cached value is smaller than the requested amount, causing an unsigned integer underflow and a transaction revert. This situation occurs because the contract does not adjust storedTotalAssets to account for rewards that become available only after the cycle ends; it assumes the cached balance always covers any withdrawal request. An attacker does not directly gain funds, but honest users can be blocked from withdrawing their deposits and any accrued rewards until the cycle finishes. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: users see their balance remain unchanged, withdrawals revert with an “underflow” error, and in extreme cases the contract’s storedTotalAssets can be driven to zero, preventing even small subsequent withdrawals by other participants. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated that after depositing 100 tokens and receiving a 1‑token reward, a full‑withdrawal one day later reverts, and subsequent deposits become stuck. The bug is subtle because the contract’s public view functions still report the correct total assets, masking the internal mismatch between cached and actual balances. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow bugs caused by incorrect state caching and mismatched accounting of locked versus unlocked funds. To remediate, the withdrawal logic must distinguish between the cached withdrawable amount and the total assets, updating storedTotalAssets only after accounting for unlocked rewards, or alternatively override the maxWithdraw function to return the cached amount, thereby preventing the subtraction from exceeding the cached balance. Properly handling the rewards cycle boundary eliminates the underflow risk and restores expected user experience where a user’s request to withdraw a given amount either succeeds or fails only due to insufficient actual balance, not because of a faulty internal cache.

title: First xERC4626 deposit exploit can break share calculation
description:
Solmate `convertToShares` [function](https://github.com/Rari-Capital/solmate/blob/12421e3edee21cfb99bf5a6edd6169e6497511de/src/mixins/ERC4626.sol#L133) follow the formula: `assetDepositAmount * totalShareSupply / assetBalanceBeforeDeposit`.

The share price always return 1:1 with asset token. If everything work normally, share price will slowly increase with time to 1:2 or 1:10 as more rewards coming in.

But right after xERC4626 contract creation, during first cycle, any user can deposit 1 share set `totalSupply = 1`. And transfer token to vault to inflate `totalAssets()` before rewards kick in. (Basically, pretend rewards themselves before anyone can deposit in to get much better share price.)

This can inflate base share price as high as 1:1e18 early on, which force all subsequence deposit to use this share price as base.
bug_full: The vulnerabilityis an initial‑deposit share‑price inflation bug that affects ERC4626‑style vault contracts which calculate share amounts using the formula assetDepositAmount × totalSupply / totalAssetsBeforeDeposit. Because the contract does not enforce a non‑zero or sufficiently large totalSupply before the first deposit, an attacker can create a vault, make a minimal deposit (e.g., 1 token) which sets totalSupply to a tiny value, and then transfer a large amount of the underlying token to the vault as if it were reward revenue. When syncRewards is called, totalAssets is updated to include the transferred tokens, but totalSupply remains at the tiny initial value. Consequently the implied share price becomes extremely high (potentially 1 : 1e18). Subsequent legitimate users who deposit after the inflation receive a disproportionately large number of shares for very little asset input. From the user’s perspective the UI may show an unrealistically high conversion rate – a single share appears to be worth many tokens – and deposits may seem to succeed while the reported share balances balloon. The root cause is the reliance on totalSupply in the share conversion without a safeguard for a near‑zero supply, combined with the fact that any token transferred to the vault before rewards are distributed is counted as part of totalAssets. The attack can be executed during the very first rewards cycle after vault creation or any time the totalSupply drops to zero (for example after all users withdraw). The exploit was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that deposits a single token, inflates the vault’s balance with a fake reward transfer, and observes the share price skyrocketing. The issue is hard to notice because the share price initially appears correct (1 : 1) and only after the attacker’s manipulation does it diverge, without throwing obvious errors. The impact is a leak of value: attackers can later redeem the inflated shares for far more underlying tokens than they originally contributed, effectively stealing the artificially injected tokens. The protocol’s economic guarantees are broken, and users may lose confidence in the vault’s accounting. To mitigate the problem, the contract should ensure that totalSupply is initialized to a non‑trivial amount before any reward synchronization occurs, prevent arbitrary external token transfers from being counted as rewards, or enforce a minimum deposit size for the first depositor. Similar mitigations used in other DeFi contracts include minting a dust amount of LP tokens at deployment or burning the first dust of shares, thereby making the share‑price calculation robust against a zero‑supply scenario.

title: `ERC20Gauges`: The `_incrementGaugeWeight` function does not check the gauge parameter enough, so the user may lose rewards
poc: [ERC20Gauges.sol#L257](https://github.com/fei-protocol/flywheel-v2/blob/77bfadf388db25cf5917d39cd9c0ad920f404aad/src/token/ERC20Gauges.sol#L257)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that increments a user's gauge weight. The function validates the supplied gauge address only against a list of deprecated gauges, reverting if the gauge is marked as deprecated. It fails to verify that the gauge address is part of the protocol's active gauge registry. As a result, an attacker or even a careless user can provide an arbitrary address that does not correspond to a legitimate gauge capable of receiving weight. When such an address is supplied, the contract still records the weight increase in the user‑gauge mapping and updates the internal weight storage for that address, even though no reward distribution logic ever references that unknown gauge. Consequently, the user’s allocated weight is effectively removed from the pool of gauges that actually distribute rewards, causing the user to receive fewer or zero rewards for the cycle they expected to earn. This issue manifests whenever the _incrementGaugeWeight function is called with a gauge that is not listed in the active gauge set, which the current code does not check. All participants who rely on accurate reward accounting – individual token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – can be affected because the accounting balances become inconsistent with the real distribution channels. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the reward‑weighting logic, where the auditors noticed that the only guard clause checks for deprecation but omits a presence check against the registered gauge set. The problem is subtle because the function appears to behave normally – it emits an IncrementGaugeWeight event and updates internal mappings – so from a UI perspective a user may see the transaction succeed and the event fire, yet later observe that their expected reward is missing or that their balance remains unchanged after a distribution round. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient input validation or whitelist bypass bugs, where critical parameters are not fully vetted before being used in state‑changing operations. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the gauge argument is present in the active gauge registry (e.g., adding a !_gauges.contains(gauge) condition) in addition to the existing deprecation check, ensuring that weight can only be assigned to gauges that are recognised by the reward engine. By doing so, the protocol restores the invariant that all recorded gauge weights correspond to actual reward‑emitting gauges, preventing users from unintentionally losing reward accrual.

title: In `ERC20Gauges`, contribution to total weight is double-counted when `incrementGauge` is called before `addGauge` for a given gauge.
description:
[ERC20Gauges.sol#L214](https://github.com/fei-protocol/flywheel-v2/blob/77bfadf388db25cf5917d39cd9c0ad920f404aad/src/token/ERC20Gauges.sol#L214)  
[ERC20Gauges.sol#L257](https://github.com/fei-protocol/flywheel-v2/blob/77bfadf388db25cf5917d39cd9c0ad920f404aad/src/token/ERC20Gauges.sol#L257)  
[ERC20Gauges.sol#L248](https://github.com/fei-protocol/flywheel-v2/blob/77bfadf388db25cf5917d39cd9c0ad920f404aad/src/token/ERC20Gauges.sol#L248)  
[ERC20Gauges.sol#L465-L469](https://github.com/fei-protocol/flywheel-v2/blob/77bfadf388db25cf5917d39cd9c0ad920f404aad/src/token/ERC20Gauges.sol#L465-L469)  

The impact depends really on how gauges are used by other contracts.

The most obvious consequence I can imagine is that some other contract distributes rewards based on `calculateGaugeAllocation`. However, because `_getStoredWeight(_totalWeight, currentCycle)` is now larger than the real total sum of weights, all rewards are smaller than they should be (because of larger denominator `total`).

There can be also (potentially large) leftover amount of rewards that is never distributed because now sum of `calculateGaugeAllocation(gauge, quantity)` over all gauges with constant `quantity` is less than `quantity`. So value might be lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the ERC20Gauges contract, where the function that records a gauge's weight can be invoked before the gauge itself has been registered with the system. Because the contract only checks that the gauge is not deprecated, it allows a permission‑less caller to increase the weight of an unregistered gauge. This increment is first recorded in the global weight mapping and later stored again when the gauge is added, resulting in the same weight contribution being counted twice. The root cause is the missing existence guard – the contract should verify that a gauge is both registered and not deprecated before permitting an increment, but it only verifies the latter. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the admin’s call to addGauge: they call incrementGauge on the future gauge, causing the weight to be added to the totalWeight variable twice. When the gauge is finally added, the second recording pushes the stored total weight above the true sum of all gauge weights. Consequently, any downstream reward distribution that relies on calculateGaugeAllocation uses an inflated denominator, delivering smaller rewards to each gauge than intended. In extreme cases the sum of allocated rewards becomes lower than the total reward pool, leaving a residual amount that never gets distributed and effectively disappearing from the protocol’s accounting. This bug manifests when the contract’s permission‑less incrementGauge function is executed before addGauge for a given gauge, which can happen in normal operation because there is no restriction preventing such ordering. The affected parties include token holders and any contracts that depend on the gauge weighting to allocate incentives, as they receive fewer tokens than expected or may see a portion of the reward pool vanish. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit when a test case called incrementGauge prior to addGauge and observed that totalWeight reported a value larger than the sum of individual gauge weights, causing calculateGaugeAllocation to return unexpectedly low values. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the inflated totalWeight simply skews the proportional calculations, making the under‑allocation appear as a normal variance. The appropriate remediation is to enforce that a gauge can only be incremented if it is already registered and not deprecated, using the existing isGauge check (i.e., require _gauges.contains(gauge) && !_deprecatedGauges.contains(gauge)). This change restores the invariant that each weight contribution is counted exactly once, ensuring that reward distribution matches the intended accounting model and preventing unintended loss of funds.

title: Pool with 19 splits will never be usable Submitted by zigtur
bug_full: An InfinityPool can be created with a configurable number of splits ranging from 12 to 19. When the maximum value 19 is used, the internal JumpyFallback library attempts to read an element at index 1 << splits (524288) in the tree array. The tree array is allocated with exactly 1 << MAX_SPLITS elements, which yields valid indices 0‑524287. Because the cursor starts at 1 << splits, the first access is out of bounds and triggers a Solidity panic (array out‑of‑bounds). The while loop that checks self.tree[cursor].deadlineJumps.touched therefore reverts before any pool logic can execute. As a result, a pool that appears to exist on‑chain cannot accept liquidity, cannot process trades, and any transaction that reaches the at() function will fail, effectively locking the pool. Users see a transaction revert with error 0x32, and the UI may show the pool address but no balance changes after attempts to add liquidity. The bug is a classic off‑by‑one / incorrect array sizing error: the data structure is sized for MAX_SPLITS elements while the algorithm assumes an extra sentinel element at index 1 << splits. It was discovered by a targeted unit test that created a pool with splits = 19 and called pour(), which immediately reverted. The issue is subtle because the same code works for all smaller split values, so the failure only appears at the extreme configuration and may be missed during casual testing. The proper fix is to either allocate the tree array with 1 << (MAX_SPLITS + 1) elements or adjust the cursor calculation to start at (1 << splits) - 1, ensuring every accessed index exists. This correction restores the ability of max‑split pools to be usable and prevents silent loss of functionality.

title: Liquidity providers bear liquidity risk but do not receive fees before calling the tap function Submitted by yttriumzz, also found by Spearmint, ktl and Joshuajee
description:
The process for users to provide liquidity to InfinityPool is as follows:
1. User calls pour to stake tokens.
2. At least 2 days later.
3. Users call tap to make their liquidity generate income.
The problem here is that in the step 2, the user is in this state for at least 2 days: providing liquidity but without swap fee income. This results in users taking on liquidity risk but receiving no returns. This results in users taking on liquidity risks without receiving corresponding returns.
And the swap fees generated during this period will be stuck in the contract and unclaimed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the fee accounting logic of the InfinityPool liquidity module. When a user provides liquidity by calling the pour function, the contract records the position but does not make the position eligible for fee accrual until the user explicitly calls the tap function after a mandatory waiting period of at least two days. During this waiting period the newly added liquidity is already usable by other traders – swaps can be executed against the pool and swap fees are generated – however the internal accounting mechanism only credits fees to positions that have been tapped. As a result, any fees collected while the position is untapped are left in the pool contract and cannot be claimed by the liquidity provider, even after the provider later calls tap or withdraws the position. The root cause is a separation of liquidity activation (tap) from liquidity effectiveness, combined with a fee‑distribution routine that does not retroactively allocate fees generated before activation and does not allow fee collection after the position is drained. An attacker or an unwary LP can exploit this by providing liquidity, allowing swaps to generate fees, and then withdrawing the liquidity before tapping, thereby leaving the earned fees permanently locked in the contract. The impact is that liquidity providers bear market risk – their deposited assets are exposed to price movements – but receive no compensation in the form of swap fees, violating the economic assumption that providing liquidity should generate proportional income. The issue manifests whenever a position is created and the required tap is not performed within the two‑day window, and it persists even after the position is drained because the leftover fee balances remain in the pool. Users experience symptoms such as a zero fee balance after calling collect, unexpected zero earnings despite active swaps, and residual token balances remaining in the pool contract after they have withdrawn all liquidity. The problem was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed collect returning zero both before and after tap, and that fees stayed locked after draining the position. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows that liquidity is added and swaps succeed, giving the impression that fees are being earned, while the underlying accounting silently discards them. To remediate the issue the contract should either make the liquidity immediately eligible for fee accrual (removing the tap gating) or modify the fee‑distribution logic to credit fees to untapped positions and allow collection before or after tapping, ensuring that any fees generated while the position is active are always claimable by the provider.

title: Pool is griefed if tickBin is equal to (1 << splits) - 1 Submitted by ktl
description:
If tickBin reaches its max value (equal to (1 << splits) - 1), all calls to InfinityPool.advance() on subsequent blocks will revert because of the check on EraBoxcarMidSum.sol#L30.
This would lead to the pool being unusable as infinityPool.advance() is called at the start of every state changing function and there is no way to move tickBin.
The impact would be total DOS of the pool since all functions rely on advance() internally, from my understanding so far this bug could be triggered cheaply on pools that are low-liquidity/empty. This would force an upgrade to fix the pool since the factory don't allow creating another one for the same token pair/splits. Since this is a pure grieﬁng vector medium severity is appropriate in my opinion.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a boundary‑condition denial‑of‑service that occurswhen the internal tickBin counter of an InfinityPool reaches its maximum possible value, which is calculated as (1 << splits) - 1. The contract logic in EraBoxcarMidSum.sol contains a require‑style check that aborts any call to the advance() function once tickBin equals this maximum. Because advance() is invoked at the beginning of every state‑changing operation – swaps, adds, removes, etc. – the pool becomes permanently unusable once the limit is hit. The root cause is that the protocol does not provide a mechanism to wrap, reset, or otherwise move tickBin after it reaches the upper bound, and the invariant check treats the maximum as an error condition rather than a normal state transition. An attacker can exploit this by performing a series of swaps that push tickBin upward; on an empty or low‑liquidity pool this can be done with a single swap that consumes a large amount of gas but still succeeds in moving tickBin to the limit. After the limit is reached, any subsequent transaction that triggers advance() reverts with an OffsetOutOfRange error, causing a total denial of service: users attempting to trade receive a generic transaction failure, balances appear unchanged, and the UI shows no funds moving. The impact is that all funds locked in the pool become inaccessible until the contract is upgraded, and because the factory forbids creating a new pool for the same token pair and split configuration, the protocol may need a full migration. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test that swaps on an empty pool until tickBin hits 32767 and then calls advance(), observing the revert. The bug is hard to notice because the maximum tickBin value is large and only reached after many state changes, and the revert originates from an internal helper rather than a user‑visible function, making the failure appear as an unexplained transaction error. Conceptually, the fix requires redesigning the tickBin lifecycle: either allowing it to wrap around, increasing the allowed range, or removing the hard revert and handling the edge case gracefully so that the pool can continue operating after the counter saturates. This class of bug falls under improper handling of counter overflow or boundary conditions that lock a state machine, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that the pool remains operable for the lifetime of the contract.

title: LPs can be griefed if there are active perpetual loans in the pool Submitted by ktl
description:
When there is an active perpetual loan (deadEra is none) in the pool, users who call InfinityPool.pour() would pay more than they expect depending on the interest paid upfront for the loan. the difference between what is paid and what the user gets is lost and from my limited understanding so far cannot be recovered, while the user who initiated the loan can call reset() and unwind() in the same block to get back all the interest he paid upfront.
Impact: This could be used a grieﬁng vector and cause signiﬁcant loss of funds to an LP by sandwiching their call to pour(), I think impact is medium since this could lead to a signiﬁcant loss of fund while it isn't incentivized as I could not ﬁnd a way for an attacker to beneﬁt from this.
Likelihood: Likelihood is high as an attack is free a part from gas costs and might even happen accidently.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic grief vector that appears when a perpetual loan is active in an InfinityPool and the loan’s deadEra flag is unset. In this state the pool’s pour() function, which is used by liquidity providers to add assets, calculates the amount of tokens to credit the provider based on the pool’s current accounting. Because the loan requires interest to be paid upfront, the accounting routine mistakenly deducts that interest from the amount that the new provider receives, but the deducted portion is not recorded as a claimable fee or returned to any party. Consequently the provider who calls pour() ends up paying more tokens than they actually receive, and the excess tokens are effectively burned – they disappear from the pool and cannot be recovered. The loan initiator can immediately call reset() and unwind() in the same block, retrieving the full interest they paid upfront, which leaves the second provider with a net loss. This can be exploited by an attacker who opens a large perpetual loan, then front‑runs or sandwiches a legitimate liquidity‑add transaction, and finally resets and unwinds the loan before the block finalises. The attack requires no capital beyond the gas cost, making it highly likely to occur either intentionally or accidentally. Affected parties include liquidity providers who expect to receive a proportional share of their deposited assets, the pool’s overall token balances, and any downstream users relying on accurate accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where Alice opened a loan, Bob poured liquidity, and Alice’s reset/unwind reclaimed the interest, leaving Bob’s balance reduced by the amount of interest paid. The bug is subtle because the loss is not reflected as an explicit fee event; the pool’s state variables still show the expected locked amounts, so the discrepancy is hidden from standard UI metrics, making it hard to notice without deep inspection of token balance deltas after a pour. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “interest‑deduction accounting errors” where pre‑paid loan interest is incorrectly subtracted from subsequent deposits. The proper fix requires redesigning the pour() accounting to treat prepaid interest as a separate liability that does not reduce the incoming provider’s credited amount, or to enforce that reset/unwind cannot be executed in the same block as a pour when a loan is active, thereby preventing the sandwich scenario.

title: The TWAP price will be incorrect due to the wrong update of the oracle Submitted by etherSky, also found by Draiakoo and carlos404
bug_full: The Fluid DEX contract maintains a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) by storing a series of price‑difference and time‑difference values in a fixed‑size circular buffer called the oracle map. Each update writes one or two 32‑byte slots depending on whether the elapsed time since the previous update exceeds 511 seconds. When the buffer reaches its maximum length (TOTAL_ORACLE_MAPPING) the implementation wraps around to the first map and continues writing. The vulnerability originates from the _updateOracle function, which does not reliably clear the storage of the next oracle map before it is reused. In particular, when the time difference is greater than 511 and the code follows the branch that writes two slots, the old data in the target map remains because the line that should reset _oracle[oracleMap_] to zero is omitted. As a result, stale bits from a previous cycle are OR‑ed with fresh values, corrupting the encoded price and time fields. This corruption becomes visible after the buffer has completed at least one full cycle and a subsequent update triggers the two‑slot path. An attacker can deliberately cause swaps that generate the required time‑difference pattern, forcing the oracle to wrap and mix old data with new data, thereby producing a TWAP that deviates significantly from the true market price. Users who rely on the TWAP for price reference – for example when executing trades, calculating slippage limits, or performing liquidations – may receive a price that is too high or too low, leading to unexpected loss of funds, failed refunds, or arbitrage opportunities for the attacker. The issue manifests only after the circular buffer has been filled and the contract attempts to overwrite a map without clearing it, so it may remain unnoticed during short‑term testing because the price feed still appears to update, albeit with subtle drift. All participants of the Fluid DEX ecosystem – traders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that query the TWAP – are affected because the oracle is advertised as a reliable source of truth. The bug was discovered during a security audit by etherSky, Draiakoo and carlos404, who reproduced the problem with a Solidity test that repeatedly calls the oracle update function while logging the map index and slot occupancy. The difficulty in spotting the issue stems from the fact that the corrupted values are stored in the same bit‑packed format as legitimate data, making the deviation look like a normal price fluctuation rather than a clear error. To remediate the problem, the update routine must ensure that every time the oracleMap index is advanced, the corresponding storage slot is explicitly reset to zero before new data is written, regardless of whether one or two slots are being written. Consolidating the clearing logic into a single place and verifying that the circular buffer never retains stale bits will prevent the TWAP from being polluted with old values, restoring the integrity of the price feed and aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected accounting assumptions of a stable, manipulation‑resistant oracle.

title: The Fluid DEX may become locked due to the division by zero error Submitted by etherSky
bug_full: The Fluid DEX contains a logic error that can cause a division‑by‑zero in the price‑calculation routine, effectively locking the exchange. The contract stores two flags in the 256‑bit variable dexVariables2: bit 248 indicates that a centre‑price shift is active and bit 26 indicates that a range‑percent shift is active. When the centre‑price shift flag is set, the internal function _calcCenterPrice reads the stored _centerPriceShift structure and divides by the shift duration (time_). The flag is supposed to be cleared together with the _centerPriceShift value once the shift has completed. The implementation clears _centerPriceShift and then clears bit 248 inside _calcCenterPrice, but later the helper _calcRangeShifting rewrites dexVariables2_ and copies the modified value back to the storage variable dexVariables2 without preserving the cleared bit. As a result, after the range shift finishes, dexVariables2 still reports that a centre‑price shift is active while _centerPriceShift has already been set to zero. The next call to _getPricesAndExchangePrices therefore invokes _calcCenterPrice with a zero divisor, causing a panic (division or modulo by zero). Because every public operation of the Fluid DEX calls _getPricesAndExchangePrices, the panic propagates to all user‑facing functions, making deposits, swaps or withdrawals revert and leaving the pool unusable. The bug manifests only after a centre‑price shift has been scheduled, the shift period has elapsed, and a subsequent range‑percent shift completes, which resets the flag incorrectly. Users experience symptoms such as transactions reverting with “panic: division or modulo by zero”, balances appearing unchanged, and the DEX UI showing no response to actions. The issue was discovered during a functional audit that exercised the price‑shift and range‑shift mechanisms and observed the flag state after each step. It is hard to notice because the flag bits are packed inside a uint256 and the erroneous copy‑back occurs in a different helper function, so the inconsistency is not obvious from a superficial read. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs that lead to arithmetic exceptions, specifically division‑by‑zero caused by stale control flags. The recommended fix is to ensure that when _centerPriceShift is cleared, the corresponding bit in dexVariables2 is also cleared in all code paths, or to restructure the logic so that the flag is derived from the presence of a non‑zero _centerPriceShift rather than a separate bit. Updating the centre‑price address after the lock can temporarily restore operation, but the root cause must be corrected to prevent future lock‑outs.

title: Deviation in oracle price could lead to arbitrage in high lltv markets Submitted by MiloTruck
description:
In Morpho Blue, the maximum amount a user can borrow is calculated with the conversion rate between loanToken and collateralToken returned by an oracle:
```solidity
uint256 maxBorrow = uint256(position[id][borrower].collateral).mulDivDown(collateralPrice, ORACLE_PRICE_SCALE)
    .wMulDown(marketParams.lltv);
```
collateralPrice is fetched by calling the oracle's price() function. For example, the price() function in ChainlinkOracle.sol is as such:
```solidity
function price() external view returns (uint256) {
    return SCALE_FACTOR.mulDiv(
        VAULT.getAssets(VAULT_CONVERSION_SAMPLE) * BASE_FEED_1.getPrice() * BASE_FEED_2.getPrice(),
        QUOTE_FEED_1.getPrice() * QUOTE_FEED_2.getPrice()
    );
}
```
However, all price oracles are susceptible to front-running as their prices tend to lag behind an asset's real-time price. More specifically:
• Chainlink oracles are updated after the change in price crosses a deviation threshold, (eg. 2.5% in ETH / USD), which means a price feed could return a value slightly smaller/larger than an asset's actual price under normal conditions.
• Uniwap V3 TWAP returns the average price over the past X number of blocks, which means it will always lag behind the real-time price.
An attacker could exploit the difference between the price reported by an oracle and the asset's actual price to gain a profit by front-running the oracle's price update. For Morpho Blue, this becomes profitable when the price deviation is sufficiently large for an attacker to open positions that become bad debt. Mathematically, arbitrage is possible when: price deviation > LIF − LLTV. The likelihood of this condition becoming true is significantly increased when ChainlinkOracle.sol is used as the market's oracle with multiple Chainlink price feeds. As seen from above, the conversion rate between loanToken and collateralToken is calculated with mul-tiple price feeds, with each of them having their own deviation threshold. This amplifies the maximum possible price deviation returned by price().
For example:
• Assume a market has WBTC as collateralToken and FTM as loanToken.
• Assume the following prices:
– 1 BTC = 40,000 USD
– 1 FTM = 1 USD
– 1 ETH = 2000 USD
• ChainlinkOracle will be set up as such:
– BASE_FEED_1 - WBTC / BTC, 2% deviation threshold.
– BASE_FEED_2 - BTC / USD, 0.5% deviation threshold.
– QUOTE_FEED_1 - FTM / ETH, 3% deviation threshold.
– QUOTE_FEED_2 - ETH / USD, 0.5% deviation threshold.
• Assume that all price feeds are at their deviation threshold:
– WBTC / BTC returns 98% of 1, which is 0.98.
– BTC / USD returns 99.5% of 40000, which is 39800.
– FTM / ETH returns 103% of 1 / 2000, which is 0.000515.
– ETH / USD returns 100.5% of 2000, which is 2010.
• The actual conversion rate of WBTC to FTM is:
– (0.98 * 39800) / (0.000515 * 2010) = 37680
– i.e. 1 WBTC = 37,680 FTM.
• Compared to 1 WBTC = 40,000 FTM, the maximum price deviation is 5.8%.
To demonstrate how a such a deviation in price could lead to arbitrage:
• Assume the following:
– A market has 95% LLTV, with WBTC as collateral and FTM as loanToken.
– 1 WBTC is currently worth 40,000 FTM.
• The price of WBTC drops while FTM increases in value, such that 1 WBTC = 37,680 FTM.
• All four Chainlink price feeds happen to be at their respective deviation thresholds as described above, which means the oracle's price is not updated in real time.
• An attacker sees the price discrepancy and front-runs the oracle price update to do the following:
– Deposit 1 WBTC as collateral.
– Borrow 38,000 FTM, which is the maximum he can borrow at 95% LLTV and 1 WBTC = 40,000 FTM conversion rate.
• Afterwards, the oracle's conversion rate is updated to 1 WBTC = 37,680 FTM:
– Attacker's position is now unhealthy as his collateral is worth less than his loaned amount.
• Attacker back-runs the oracle price update to liquidate himself:
– At 95% LLTV, LIF = 100.152%.
– To seize 1 WBTC, he repays 37,115 FTM: * seizedAssets / LIF = 1 WBTC / 1.0152 = 37680 FTM / 1.0152 = 37115 FTM
• He has gained 885 FTM worth of profit using 37,680 FTM, which is a 2.3% arbitrage opportunity.
This example proves the original condition stated above for arbitrage to occur, as: price deviation − (LIF − LLTV) = 5.8% − (100.152% − 95%) = ∼2.3%. Note that all profit gained from arbitrage causes a loss of funds for lenders as the remaining bad debt is socialized by them.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the reliance on a composite price oracle to calculate the maximum borrow amount in a lending market that operates with a high loan‑to‑value (LLTV) ratio. The oracle aggregates several Chainlink price feeds, each of which updates only when the underlying asset price moves beyond a predefined deviation threshold (for example 2.5% for ETH/USD). Because each feed can lag behind the real‑time market price, the combined conversion rate between the loan token and the collateral token may deviate from the true market rate. When the total deviation exceeds the difference between the liquidation incentive factor (LIF) and the LLTV, an attacker can front‑run the oracle update, borrow up to the stale limit, and then liquidate the position after the price correction, pocketing the excess as profit. In practice, a borrower may see a loan that appears to be within the 95 % LLTV limit but is actually over‑collateralised due to the stale price; after the oracle refreshes, the collateral value drops relative to the debt, triggering an unexpected liquidation. The impact is that lenders collectively absorb the resulting bad debt, effectively losing funds while the attacker gains a modest arbitrage profit (e.g., a 2‑3 % gain on the borrowed amount). This condition occurs whenever the market uses a multi‑feed oracle with significant deviation thresholds and operates with a high LLTV, especially during periods of rapid price movement. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Morpho Blue protocol, where the auditors examined the oracle price() implementation and identified that the multiplication of several feeds amplifies the possible deviation. The bug is subtle because each individual feed remains within its allowed deviation, making the overall price appear correct on‑chain, and the front‑running window is short, so casual testing may not expose it. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should introduce a borrowing fee that exceeds the maximum possible oracle deviation, tighten oracle update thresholds, consider using a single, more reliable price source, or apply additional checks that limit borrowing based on a conservative price estimate. By doing so, the protocol can align the borrowing limit with a more accurate market price and prevent arbitrage that results in unexpected liquidations and loss of lender capital.

title: Suppliers can be tricked into supplying more Submitted by Christoph Michel
description:
The supply and withdraw functions can increase the supply share price (totalSupplyAssets / totalSupplyShares). If a depositor uses the shares parameter in supply to specify how many assets they want to supply they can be tricked into supplying more assets than they wanted. It's easy to inflate the supply share price by 100x through a combination of a single supply of 100 assets and then withdrawing all shares without receiving any assets in return. The reason is that in withdraw we compute the assets to be received as assets = shares.toAssetsUp(market[id].totalSupplyAssets, market[id].totalSupplyShares);. Note that assets can be zero and the withdraw essentially becomes a pure burn function.
Example:
• A new market is created.
• The victim tries to supply 1 assets at the initial share price of 1e-6 and specifies supply(shares=1e6). They have already given max approval to the contract because they already supplied the same asset to another market.
• The attacker wants to borrow a lot of the loan token and therefore targets the victim. They frontrun the victim by supply(assets=100) and a sequence of withdraw() functions such that totalSupplyShares = 0 and totalSupplyAssets = 100. The new supply share price increased 100x.
• The victim's transaction is minted and they use the new supply share price and mint 100x more tokens than intended (possible because of the max approval).
• The attacker borrows all the assets.
• The victim is temporarily locked out of that asset. They cannot withdraw again because of the liquidity crunch (it is borrowed by the attacker).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation of the share‑price calculation used by the supply and withdraw functions of a lending market. The market represents each depositor’s claim with shares, and the price of a share is derived from the ratio of totalSupplyAssets to totalSupplyShares. When a user calls the supply function with the shares argument, the contract mints shares based on the current share price. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate supplier by first depositing a modest amount of assets and then withdrawing all existing shares. Because the withdraw routine computes the assets to return with the formula assets = shares.toAssetsUp(totalSupplyAssets,totalSupplyShares), a withdrawal that burns all shares while leaving totalSupplyAssets unchanged drives totalSupplyShares to zero. This makes the share price appear arbitrarily high – in the proof‑of‑concept the price is inflated by a factor of one hundred. When the victim’s transaction is subsequently executed, the contract uses the inflated price to mint shares for the victim, causing the victim to supply many more assets than intended or to receive an unexpectedly large amount of share tokens. The victim may then find that the market’s liquidity is exhausted because the attacker has borrowed the newly created assets, leaving the victim unable to withdraw and effectively locking their funds. The flaw originates from the reliance on a mutable ratio without safeguards against division‑by‑zero or extreme ratio values, and from allowing the supply function to be driven by a shares parameter that can be manipulated when totalSupplyShares is low. The issue is most likely to appear in freshly created markets or whenever an attacker controls a large proportion of the share supply. It was discovered during a manual audit that included a targeted test case which repeatedly supplied and withdrew assets until the share balance vanished, demonstrating that the share price could be inflated and that the victim’s subsequent supply behaved incorrectly. The problem is subtle because the arithmetic itself is correct; the abnormal state (zero shares, non‑zero assets) is not explicitly prevented, and the contract does not emit a warning when a withdrawal returns zero assets. To remediate, developers should prefer the assets parameter for supply, restrict approvals to the exact amount a user intends to deposit, and introduce a slippage or maxAssets guard that caps the amount of assets that can be transferred in a single supply call. Additional defensive measures include preventing withdrawals that would reduce totalSupplyShares to zero while leaving assets behind, or redesigning the accounting model so that share price cannot be artificially inflated. In practice, users may notice that after a deposit they receive far more tokens than expected, that their balance suddenly drops to zero, or that they are unable to withdraw because the market reports no available liquidity. This class of bug falls under price‑manipulation or economic invariant violation caused by ratio‑based accounting without proper bounds checking.

title: Virtual supply shares steal interest Submitted by Christoph Michel
description: The virtual supply shares, that are not owned by anyone, earn interest in _accrueInterest. This interest is stolen from the actual suppliers which leads to loss of interest funds for users. Note that while the initial share price of 1e-6 might make it seem like the virtual shares can be ignored, one can increase the supply share price and the virtual shares will have a bigger claim on the total asset percentage.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a mis‑allocation of accrued interest to virtual supply shares that have no real owner. In the contract’s interest‑accrual routine the total supply of shares is used to calculate each holder’s proportion of the newly generated interest. Because the virtual shares are included in that total, they are treated as if they were legitimate deposits and therefore receive a share of the interest. The root cause is an accounting flaw: the system does not distinguish between genuine supplier shares and the internally created virtual shares, so the interest distribution formula applies uniformly to both. An attacker or any party that can influence the amount or price of the virtual shares can increase the virtual share price, which enlarges the virtual shares’ claim on the overall asset pool. When the _accrueInterest function runs, a portion of the interest that should belong to real users is diverted to the virtual shares, effectively stealing interest from actual suppliers. This results in users seeing lower than expected returns, missing or reduced refunds, and balances that appear to lose accrued earnings even though their principal remains unchanged. The issue manifests whenever interest is accrued while any virtual shares exist, which is the normal operation of the protocol. All participants who supply assets to the protocol are affected because the total interest pool is reduced for them. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interest‑distribution logic and noticed that the virtual share balance was included in the denominator of the share‑price calculation. Because the virtual shares start with a very small initial price (1e‑6), the effect can be subtle and may not be obvious from a quick glance at the UI or simple tests, making it hard to notice until larger virtual share balances are created. To remediate the issue, the accounting should be changed so that virtual shares are excluded from the interest‑earning calculation; they should either be treated as non‑interest‑bearing or be removed from the total supply used to compute each holder’s share of accrued interest. This aligns the protocol’s financial model with the business logic that only actual suppliers should earn interest, restoring correct APY calculations and preventing the stealth loss of interest funds.

title: Virtual borrow shares accrue interest and lead to bad debt Submitted by Christoph Michel, also found by xuwinnie
description: The virtual borrow shares, that are not owned by anyone, earn interest in _accrueInterest. This interest keeps compounding and cannot be repaid as the virtual borrow shares are not owned by anyone. As the withdrawable funds are computed as supplyAssets - borrowAssets, the borrow shares' assets equivalent leads to a reduction in withdrawable funds, basically bad debt. Note that while the initial borrow shares only account for 1 asset, this can be increased by increasing the share price. The share price can be inflated arbitrarily high, see appendix.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a design flaw in the interest‑accrual mechanism of the lending pool where a special category of borrow shares, called virtual borrow shares, is created without being assigned to any user. These virtual shares are treated like regular borrow shares in the _accrueInterest function, meaning they automatically earn interest each time the pool compounds. Because no address owns the virtual shares, the accrued interest cannot be repaid or liquidated; it simply accumulates indefinitely. The pool calculates the amount that can be withdrawn as the difference between total supplied assets and total borrowed assets. Since the virtual borrow shares are counted as borrowed assets, the ever‑growing interest on them reduces the withdrawable amount, effectively creating bad debt that cannot be socialized among participants. The problem is amplified by the fact that the share price of these virtual borrow shares can be inflated without bound, allowing an attacker or a misbehaving contract to increase the virtual borrow asset value arbitrarily high, which in turn magnifies the unrepayable debt. This condition manifests whenever the interest‑accrual routine runs while virtual borrow shares exist, and it impacts all users who expect to withdraw their supplied funds, as the pool may report a lower balance or even zero withdrawable assets. The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the Cantina Competition Morpho Blue contract by Christoph Michel and later confirmed by another researcher, highlighting that the bug can be subtle: the virtual shares do not appear in any user’s balance sheet, so the reduction in withdrawable funds may be attributed to normal market movements rather than a contract flaw. To remediate the issue, the protocol should exclude virtual borrow shares from interest accrual or redesign the accounting so that virtual shares do not generate interest and cannot have their price arbitrarily inflated. By preventing these shares from earning compounding interest, the pool’s accounting will correctly reflect the true amount of withdrawable assets, eliminating the creation of unrecoverable bad debt and restoring confidence in the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Liquidation seizeassets computation rounding issue Submitted by Christoph Michel, also found by solthodox, trachev and john-femi
description:
Currently, liquidations can end up with the borrower having a less healthy position than before the liquidation (even without liquidation incentive and favorable LLTV). Note that the borrower position is measured in shares (not assets) via position[id][borrower].borrowShares. The repaidAssets are rounded up from the borrow shares position to be burned and the rounded-up assets are used to compute the collateral assets to be seized seizedAssets, leading to a situation of reducing the borrower's collateral by much more than their debt position was actually reduced by.
```solidity
repaidAssets = repaidShares.toAssetsUp(market[id].totalBorrowAssets, market[id].totalBorrowShares);
// uses rounded-up repaidAssets
seizedAssets =
    repaidAssets.wMulDown(liquidationIncentiveFactor).mulDivDown(ORACLE_PRICE_SCALE, collateralPrice);
```
Example:
LLTV of 75%. Borrow share price (totalBorrowAssets / totalBorrowShares) of 1.01e-6=0.00000101 (1% interest on initial virtual shares start price of 0.000001). Price of 1 borrow asset = 1$.
• borrower: Collateral worth 4$. 3e6 borrow shares, worth 3.03 assets. Health factor is 4$ * LLTV / (3e6 * 1.01e-6 * 1$) = 0.99
• A liquidator that pays back repaidShares=1 receives seized assets according to repaidAssets = repaidShares.toAssetsUp(sharePrice) = 1 (1$), more than the actual value of 0.00000101$ corresponding to the 1 borrow shares position reduction.
• The borrower's collateral is reduced to 3$ while only 1 borrow share was burned from their position. Their new health factor drops to 3$ * LLTV / ((3e6-1) * 1.01e-6 * 1$) = 0.7425 making the borrower less healthy.
• Another three rounds of liquidations of repaidShares=1 will lead to a health factor of 0$ * LLTV / ((3e6-4) * 1.01e-6 * 1$) = 0. The borrower's collateral was fully seized and the protocol incurs bad debt of almost the entire initial debt shares worth (3e6-4) * 1.01e-6 * 1$ = 3.03$
The impact is that an unhealthy borrower's position can be fully liquidated by splitting up liquidations into tiny liquidations (each repaying only 1 share but seizing the full rounded-up repay amount of collateral) while not reducing their actual asset debt position. The protocol will incur almost the entire initial borrow debt assets as bad debt.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a rounding error in the liquidation routine of a lending market that causes the amount of collateral seized to be calculated from a value that has been rounded up, instead of from the exact debt reduction. The contract stores a borrower’s debt as shares; when a liquidator repays a number of borrow shares, the code converts those shares to assets using a function that rounds the result up (to ensure the liquidator can cover the repayment). The same rounded‑up asset amount is then multiplied by the liquidation incentive and the price feed to determine how many collateral assets are seized. Because the rounded‑up value is larger than the true value of the repaid shares, the seized collateral can exceed the actual reduction in the borrower’s debt. Consequently, after a liquidation the borrower’s health factor can drop, sometimes becoming worse than before the liquidation, and repeated tiny liquidations (repaying a single share each time) can drain the borrower’s entire collateral while leaving most of the original debt untouched. This creates bad debt for the protocol equal to almost the full original loan amount.
The root cause is the misuse of a single rounded‑up conversion for both the repayment amount and the collateral‑seizure calculation. The correct logic requires two separate conversions: one rounded up for the amount the liquidator must pay, and one rounded down for the value used to compute seized collateral. The bug is subtle because rounding up a single share appears negligible, but when the attack is repeated many times the cumulative over‑seizure becomes large and can be exploited by an attacker who splits the liquidation into many minimal‑size steps.
The impact is that borrowers may see their collateral disappear faster than their debt decreases, their health factor falling below expectations, and in extreme cases the protocol suffers significant bad debt. From a user’s perspective the UI would show collateral balances dropping to zero while the outstanding borrow balance remains almost unchanged, contradicting the expectation that each liquidation reduces both collateral and debt proportionally. The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the Morph​o Blue market code, and it is classified as a medium‑risk rounding/precision bug that violates the accounting assumptions of the lending protocol.
To remediate the problem the liquidation logic should compute the seized assets from a conversion of shares to assets that rounds down, while keeping the existing rounded‑up conversion only for the repayment amount. This separation ensures that the liquidator cannot seize more collateral than the true value of the debt they have repaid, preserving the borrower’s health factor and preventing the creation of bad debt.

title: Liquidation repaidshares computation rounding issue Submitted by Christoph Michel
description:
Currently, liquidations can end up with the borrower having a less healthy position than before the liquidation (even without liquidation incentive and favorable LLTV). Note that the borrower position is measured in shares (not assets) via position[id][borrower].borrowShares. The repaidShares are rounded down from the seized-assets-converted repaid assets value. For illustration, repaidShares could even be 0 if the share price (totalBorrowAssets / totalBorrowShares) is above 1.0. (This can happen as the IRM allows borrow rates up to a billion % APR per year and the initial start price is just 1e-6 = 0.000001 or through other ways, see existing issue about inflating borrow share price mentioned in Cantina audit.) The borrower's borrow debt position would not be repaid as repaidShares = 0 but the liquidator still seizes seizedAssets of the borrower's collateral. The borrower's health factor only gets worse.
The impact is that an unhealthy borrower's position can be fully liquidated by splitting up liquidations into tiny liquidations (each repaying zero shares but seizing the full rounded-up repay amount of collateral) while not reducing their actual asset debt position. The protocol will incur the entire initial borrow debt assets as bad debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the liquidation routine that converts seized collateral assets into the amount of borrow shares to be repaid. Because the protocol stores the borrower’s debt in shares rather than raw assets, the function that calculates repaidShares rounds the conversion down. When the borrow‑share price (totalBorrowAssets/totalBorrowShares) is greater than one – a situation that can arise from extremely high borrow rates, an initial share price set to a very small value, or other mechanisms that inflate the share price – the down‑rounding may produce a repaidShares value of zero even though a non‑zero amount of collateral is seized. The root cause is the use of integer division that truncates fractional shares without a safeguard that the seized collateral’s value is bounded by the value of the repaid shares. An attacker acting as a liquidator can exploit this by triggering many tiny liquidation calls, each requesting a minimal seizedAssets amount that, after conversion, yields zero repaidShares. The liquidator still receives the seized collateral, while the borrower’s debt balance remains unchanged, causing the borrower’s health factor to deteriorate instead of improve. This can be repeated until the borrower’s entire collateral is taken, leaving the protocol with the original borrow amount as unrecoverable bad debt. The issue manifests only when the share price exceeds one and the liquidation amount is small enough that the asset‑to‑share conversion rounds down to zero; under normal liquidation sizes the rounding loss is negligible and may go unnoticed. Borrowers experience the symptom of seeing their collateral disappear while their debt stays the same, often reflected in a health factor that drops unexpectedly after a liquidation event. Auditors discovered the flaw during a systematic review of the Cantina competition code, noting that the rounding behaviour contradicts the business logic that a liquidation must reduce the borrower’s debt proportionally to the collateral taken. The bug belongs to the class of “round‑down to zero” arithmetic errors that break accounting invariants. To remediate, the liquidation logic must enforce that the value of seizedAssets never exceeds the value of the repaidShares. A practical fix is to recompute repaidAssets based on the seized collateral, round the resulting share amount up, and then recompute the asset amount from the rounded‑up shares, ensuring that the seized collateral is always less than or equal to the value of the repaid debt. This adjustment restores the intended invariant that each liquidation reduces the borrower’s debt and prevents the protocol from accruing bad debt due to rounding anomalies.

title: Any oracle update with suﬃciently big price decline can be sandwiched to extract value from the protocol Submitted by hyh, also found by Said
poc:
• Morpho instance for stablecoins was launched with USDC collateral and USDT asset allowed, and with LLTV set included competitive reading of 95%, over time it gained TVL, USDC and USDT is now traded 1:1. Liquidation incentive factor for the market is liquidationIncentiveFactor = 1.0 / (1 - 0.3 * (1 - 0.95)) = 1.01522.
• There was a shift in USDC reserves valuation approach, and updated reserves figures are priced in sharply via new Oracle reading of 0.9136 USDT per USDC.
• Bob the attacker front runs the Oracle update transaction (tx2) with the borrowing of USDT 0.95m having provided USDC 1m (tx1, and for simplicity we ignore dust adjustments in the numbers where they might be needed as they don't affect the overall picture).
• Bob back-runs tx2 with liquidation of the own loan (tx3), repaying USDT 0.9m of the USDT 0.95m debt. Since the price was updated, with repaidAssets = USDT 0.9m he will have seizedAssets = USDC 0.9m * 1.01522 / 0.9136 = USDC 1m.
• Bob regained all the collateral and pocketed USDT 0.05m, which was written off the deposits as bad debt. So, an Attacker can steal principal funds from the protocol by artificially creating bad debt. This is a permanent loss for market lenders, its severity can be estimated as high. The probability of this can be estimated as medium as collateral volatility is not fixed in any way and sharp downside movements will happen from time to time in a substantial share of all the markets. The prerequisite is that initially chosen LLTV does not fully guarantee the absence of bad debt after one Oracle update. This effectively means that LLTV has to be updated to a lower value, but it is fixed within the market and such changes are usually subtle enough (as compared to more substantially scrutinized initial settings), so, once that happens, there is substantial probability that there will be a window of opportunity for attackers, the period when LLTV of a big enough market being outdated and too high, but there was no communication about that and the marker being actively used.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic attack that arises from the combination of a fixed liquidation incentive factor and a static loan‑to‑value (LLTV) threshold together with a price oracle that can be updated with large downward movements. Because the liquidation incentive is calculated as a deterministic function of the LLTV and does not adapt to sudden price drops, an attacker can front‑run a significant oracle price decline, open a minimally collateralised loan just before the price change, and then immediately liquidate that position after the new price is recorded. The liquidation routine uses the stale collateral price to compute the amount of collateral that can be seized, applying the fixed incentive factor, which results in the attacker receiving the full value of the seized collateral while the protocol records a bad debt equal to the difference between the repaid debt and the seized collateral value. This creates a situation where the protocol’s depositors lose principal funds, as the bad debt is socialised among them. The attack can be executed whenever the oracle update causes a price drop large enough that the fixed LLTV no longer guarantees a healthy position, which is typical for highly volatile collateral assets or when market conditions change rapidly. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation logic and identified that the incentive factor does not bound the protocol against arbitrarily large price swings. It is hard to notice because the liquidation function itself works as intended for normal price movements, and the protocol’s accounting appears correct on‑chain; the loss only becomes visible through a reduction in total deposited value after a malicious liquidation. From a user perspective, a borrower may see their collateral seized even though they believed the position to be safe, and lenders may notice that their deposited balances shrink without any explicit withdrawal. The bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation combined with static liquidation parameters, where the business logic assumes that the LLTV remains conservative for the whole lifetime of the market. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a dynamic liquidation penalty or fee that makes self‑liquidation unprofitable, adjust the incentive factor to be responsive to price volatility, and implement monitoring that flags markets whose LLTV is no longer appropriate after significant oracle updates, thereby preventing the creation of bad debt in a single price change.

title: Users can take advantage of low liquidity markets to inflate the interest rate Submitted by MiloTruck
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in Morpho Blue’s interest‑rate accrual mechanism that allows an attacker to artificially inflate the market’s borrow rate when the market contains an extremely low amount of liquidity. The root cause is that the internal _accrueInterest function unconditionally calls the Interest Rate Model (IRM) borrowRate() regardless of the size of totalSupplyAssets, so a market with only a single wei supplied and borrowed reports a utilization of 100 %. AdaptiveCurveIrm, which bases its rate on utilization, interprets this as a fully utilized market and, over time, aggressively raises the borrow rate. Because Morpho compounds interest using the raised rate, the totalBorrowAssets grows exponentially even though the actual borrowed amount is negligible. This creates a massive mismatch between totalBorrowAssets and totalBorrowShares, leaving a large amount of un‑clearable bad debt after liquidation. Moreover, the inflated totalSupplyAssets to totalSupplyShares ratio causes the share‑to‑asset conversion in the supply() function to round down to zero, so a user who deposits a substantial amount receives no shares and effectively loses the deposited funds. The issue manifests only in markets with very low liquidity that remain idle for a long period, making it hard to notice during normal operation because the interest rate appears to be a legitimate function of utilization. It was discovered during a formal audit when a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that supplying 1 wei, borrowing it, waiting 150 days, and then supplying a large amount resulted in a zero‑share allocation. The impact affects lenders, borrowers, and the protocol as a whole: bad debt becomes permanent, interest rates stay artificially high, and small suppliers can lose assets. To remediate, the _accrueInterest routine should include a guard that checks whether totalSupplyAssets exceeds a reasonable threshold before invoking the IRM, or the IRM itself should ignore utilization when the market’s liquidity is negligible, thereby preventing the rate from being driven by a false 100 % utilization scenario.

title: Cannot use uint256.max to repay the balance of aavev3optimizermigrationbundler Submitted by Christoph Michel, also found by J4X98
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the documented behaviour of the AaveV3OptimizerRepay function and its actual implementation. The NatSpec comment for the amount parameter states that passing type(uint256).max should repay the bundler’s entire underlying balance. In practice the function forwards the raw amount value to the AaveV3Optimizer, which then delegates the call to Morpho’s PositionManager. Inside PositionManager the amount is clamped with Math.min against the borrower’s outstanding debt, not against the token balance held by the bundler contract. Consequently, when a caller supplies type(uint256).max, the amount is reduced to the full borrow balance. The optimizer then attempts to settle that entire debt using the bundler’s token balance, which is often smaller than the debt amount. Because the contract does not verify that the bundler actually holds enough tokens, the repayment call reverts, leaving the transaction failed and the user’s position unchanged. This bug can be triggered whenever a user relies on the “max” shortcut to clear their debt, expecting the contract to automatically use whatever balance it has. The impact is that legitimate repayment attempts fail, users may be unable to close or reduce their borrowing positions, and funds that should have been returned remain locked in the contract. The issue affects any participant that interacts with the bundler’s repay function, including end‑users, protocol integrators, and any downstream contracts that assume the documented behaviour. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor compared the NatSpec description with the actual code flow and observed that the amount parameter was never bounded by the contract’s token balance. The problem is subtle because using type(uint256).max is a common pattern for “repay all”, and the code appears to forward the value without alteration, giving a false impression that the repayment will succeed. To remediate the issue the contract should explicitly cap the amount to the bundler’s current token balance before forwarding it, for example by applying Math.min(amount, ERC20(underlying).balanceOf(address(this))) as recommended. This adjustment aligns the implementation with the documented intent, prevents unnecessary reverts, and restores the expected behaviour where a user can safely use the max constant to repay the maximum amount the contract actually holds.

title: Cannot use uint256.max to repay the balance of compoundv2migrationbundler Submitted by Christoph Michel
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an ambiguous NatSpec description for the repay function of a Compound V2 migration bundler. The documentation states that passing type(uint256).max as the amount parameter should “repay all”, but it does not clarify whether “all” refers to the bundler’s cToken balance or the borrower’s outstanding debt. The implementation forwards the raw max value directly to the underlying ICToken.repayBorrowBehalf call. Inside Compound V2 the code interprets a max value as a request to repay the entire borrow balance, regardless of how many cTokens the bundler actually holds.
