This creates a timing‑dependent discrepancy: a user who redeems their shares before the curator calls withdrawPerformanceFee receives a larger amount of underlying tokens than a user who redeems after the fee has been taken, even though both users deposited the same amount at the same time. The impact is that later withdrawers effectively lose part of their principal, seeing a lower redemption amount or a sudden reduction in their balance, which can be perceived as “funds disappearing” or an “unfair refund”. The condition under which the bug manifests is after market redemption when the accrued interest has been calculated and the performance fee is ready to be claimed, but before the curator actually withdraws it. All participants who hold shares – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting inconsistency breaks the fundamental guarantee that each share corresponds to a proportional claim on the vault’s assets. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit where test cases demonstrated that two users with identical deposits received different redemption amounts solely due to withdrawal order. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the totalAssets view still returns a plausible number and the share price appears correct until a withdrawal is performed; only by comparing withdrawals at different times does the discrepancy become evident. The proper fix is to exclude the performance fee from the totalAssets calculation, treating the fee as a separate claim and ensuring that totalAssets reflects only the assets owed to share‑holders. This aligns the contract with ERC‑4626 expectations, restores fair share valuation, and prevents users from receiving fewer tokens than expected when withdrawing after fee collection.

title: Redeem fee is incorrectly factored into bad debt mapping due to incorrect logic Submitted by 0xJoos, also found by BengalCatBalu
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the TermMaxVault contract records bad debt when a user redeems an order that carries a non‑zero redeem fee. During the redeem flow the market contract calculates a fee amount (feeAmt) and subtracts it from the amount of debt tokens that are transferred back to the vault (debtTokenAmt). The reduced amount is returned to the OrderManager as totalRedeem. Because the OrderManager compares totalRedeem with the original ftReserve and finds totalRedeem < ftReserve, it records the difference in the _badDebtMapping. The logic does not distinguish between a shortfall caused by market slippage and the shortfall caused by the protocol fee, so the fee amount is mistakenly classified as bad debt. As a result the bad‑debt counter for the collateral token becomes inflated. When the protocol later settles bad debt through dealBadDebt, the inflated bad‑debt figure is used to compute the proportion of collateral that is transferred to the recipient, diluting the payout. Users therefore receive less collateral than they expect, and the protocol’s accounting of outstanding debt versus collateral becomes inaccurate. The issue only manifests when a redeem fee ratio is configured for the market and the redeem operation returns less than the full ftReserve, which is the normal case when fees are charged. It affects all participants that interact with the vault – curators, lenders and anyone calling redeemOrder – because the protocol may appear to have higher bad debt than actually exists, potentially eroding trust and causing financial loss. The bug was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that sets a high redeemFeeRatio and observes an unexpected increase in the bad‑debt mapping after a redeem. The problem is subtle because fee collection is a legitimate operation and the shortfall is recorded without any explicit comment, making it easy to overlook during code review. To remediate, the contract should separate fee handling from bad‑debt accounting, for example by subtracting the fee amount before comparing totalRedeem with ftReserve or by adding a guard that prevents fee‑derived shortfalls from being added to the bad‑debt mapping. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that bad debt only reflects genuine market shortfalls, not protocol fees, and ensures that collateral payouts remain proportional to the true amount of bad debt.

title: Collateral transfers to msg.sender instead of receiver in TermMaxMarket::redeem Submitted by BengalCatBalu
description:
Impact Explanation:
The biggest impact of this error is if the funds sent to the caller get stuck on the contract. That is, a special smart contract will call this function, specifying a certain EOA as the recipient, but the collateral will be sent to the address of the smart contract.
If the smart contract does not have a mechanism to withdraw tokens, they will just be stuck on the smart contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect destination address when the TermMaxMarket contract processes a redeem request. Instead of sending the collateral to the address supplied by the caller as the intended recipient, the contract uses msg.sender as the transfer target. Because msg.sender is the address that invoked the function, when a smart contract calls redeem on behalf of an external user, the collateral is transferred to the calling contract rather than to the user‑specified address. This logic error arises from a misplaced use of the global variable msg.sender instead of the explicit receiver parameter. An attacker or any contract can trigger the function, causing the protocol to move tokens to a contract that may not implement a withdrawal mechanism. The tokens become locked in the contract with no way for the original user to retrieve them, effectively making the collateral disappear from the user's perspective. The issue manifests only when the redeem function is invoked through an intermediate contract; direct calls from an externally owned account still receive the correct collateral. Users expect that after redeeming they will receive their collateral at the address they provided, but they instead see a zero balance while the contract's balance increases. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the TermMaxMarket contract by Spearbit, and it can be subtle because the transfer succeeds and no revert is emitted, so the transaction appears normal. To remediate, the contract should replace the use of msg.sender with the explicit receiver argument, add validation that the receiver is not the calling contract unless intended, and optionally provide a rescue function that allows the contract owner or the intended recipient to withdraw tokens that were mistakenly sent to the contract. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect address handling or misdirected fund transfers, which violates the accounting assumption that collateral is always returned to the original owner.

title: Incorrect proxy implementation by declaring initial values in storage Submitted by giraffe0x, also found by Saaj and waﬄemakr
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect initialization pattern in an upgradeable vesting contract that declares storage variables with inline default values instead of setting them in the contract’s initializer. The contract defines a dead address and a vesting duration as immutable‑looking state variables, but because the contract is intended to be used behind a proxy, those inline assignments are only written to the implementation contract’s storage, not to the proxy’s storage. When the proxy delegates calls to the implementation, the proxy’s storage slots for those variables remain at their type defaults – address(0) for the dead address and 0 for the uint256 duration. The zero duration collapses the intended three‑month vesting period to an instantaneous schedule. As a result, the penalty calculation, which checks whether the current time exceeds startTime + duration, always evaluates the condition as true, returning a 0 % penalty regardless of how early a withdrawal occurs. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to allow early withdrawals without any fee, contradicting the expectation that a penalty would be applied during the vesting window. This can be exploited by any participant who can trigger the withdrawal function: they can retrieve their vested tokens immediately and keep the full amount, effectively bypassing the economic incentive model of the protocol. The impact is a loss of intended revenue or deterrent for early exits, potentially draining funds that were supposed to be locked for three months. The issue manifests only when the contract is accessed through a proxy, which is the normal deployment mode for upgradeable contracts, making it easy to miss during testing that targets the implementation directly. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the initializer code with the storage declarations and noted the mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of “uninitialized proxy storage” or “incorrect initializer pattern” vulnerabilities, where default values are not propagated to the proxy’s state. To remediate, the contract should remove inline initializers and explicitly assign both the dead address and the vesting duration inside the initialize function, ensuring the proxy’s storage reflects the intended configuration. This aligns the contract’s business logic with its accounting assumptions and prevents the zero‑duration edge case that leads to penalty calculation errors and unintended fund release.

title: Transferring tokens to feedistributor after calling checkpointtoken may cause incorrect distribution Submitted by osmanozdemir1
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing and ordering flaw in the reward distribution flow of a staking emissions system. The StakingEmissions contract calls the fee distributor’s checkpoint functions before it transfers the newly minted weekly emission tokens to the fee distributor. The fee distributor’s internal _checkpointToken routine calculates the amount to distribute based on the contract’s current token balance, stores this balance as the last checkpointed balance, and then updates the timestamp. Because the token transfer occurs after the checkpoint, the balance used for the calculation does not include the freshly transferred tokens. The checkpoint function is throttled to once per 24 hours, so the stale balance persists for an entire day. As a result, users who claim rewards within the first 24 hours after an emission receive a smaller share than they are entitled to, while users who claim later receive a larger share. If the distribution call happens late in an epoch (for example between the 6th and 7th day), part of the transferred amount is recorded in the next epoch’s checkpoint, causing rewards to be shifted across epochs and creating unfair allocation. The impact is economic: stakers see inconsistent reward amounts, some may receive zero or reduced tokens, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional distribution are violated. The issue affects any participant who locks tokens and expects a fair, epoch‑aligned reward, as well as the protocol’s reputation for honest accounting. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the checkpoint routine reads the contract balance before the transfer and that the checkpoint cannot be called again for 24 hours. The bug is subtle because the contract still distributes tokens, but the amounts differ only when examined across claim times, making it hard to spot without detailed testing. The correct mitigation is to reverse the order: transfer the emission tokens to the fee distributor first, then invoke the checkpoint functions, or redesign the checkpoint to use the expected incoming amount or allow multiple checkpoints per epoch. This class of bug is a state‑inconsistency or race‑condition caused by an improper sequence of state‑changing calls, leading to an accounting mismatch and unfair reward distribution.

title: zerolend.votingpowerof() doesn't check ownershipchange block of the token, makes ﬂash nft protection redundant Submitted by osmanozdemir1, also found by Chinmay Farkya, tnch, waﬄemakr, 3agle and karanctf
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ownership‑change block check in the votingPowerOf function of the ZeroLocker protocol. The contract records the block number at which an NFT representing a locked token is transferred in a mapping called ownershipChange. This information is used by the balanceOfNFT view function to return zero voting power when the function is called in the same block as a transfer, providing flash‑NFT protection that prevents a user from buying an NFT and voting immediately. However, votingPowerOf iterates over all NFTs owned by an address and sums the result of the internal _balanceOfNFT call without consulting ownershipChange. Consequently, after a transfer, the votingPowerOf function still counts the transferred NFT’s balance in the same block, allowing an attacker to acquire an NFT and cast votes or claim rewards before the protocol’s intended protection takes effect. The impact is a potential governance manipulation where a malicious actor can temporarily inflate voting power, sway proposals, or capture reward allocations that should be unavailable during the same block. This condition occurs whenever an NFT is transferred and the votingPowerOf view is queried in the same block, which can be triggered by a single transaction or a series of rapid calls. All token holders, the protocol’s governance mechanism, and any reward distribution logic that relies on votingPowerOf are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions about when voting rights become active are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementations of balanceOfNFT and votingPowerOf and noticed the absence of the block‑number guard in the latter. It is subtle because the contract already contains a flash‑NFT protection mechanism in one function, leading reviewers to assume the same protection applies globally. The bug belongs to the class of logical race‑condition or state‑inconsistency errors where a security check is omitted in a code path that is otherwise protected. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a zero balance for the NFT after a transfer (as intended by balanceOfNFT) but the vote still succeeds, contradicting the expectation that the NFT cannot be used for voting in that block. To remediate, the votingPowerOf function should incorporate the same ownershipChange block comparison as balanceOfNFT, skipping any NFT whose ownershipChange equals the current block number before adding its balance to the total voting power. This restores the intended flash‑NFT protection and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its documented governance rules.

title: NFTs can be transferred to zero address and fees can be claimed for these tokenids Submitted by Chinmay Farkya, also found by osmanozdemir1 and Naveen Kumar J - 1nc0gn170
description: The comment in _transferFrom says that it does not allow transferring to the zero address. This gives a false impression because this is not true. Any tokenID can in fact be transferred to zero address because the transferFrom flow does not check for it anywhere. The _to parameter can be address(0) and the transfer will happen along with all the state updates (i.e. now address(0) will be the owner of this tokenID and it will be in the list of tokenIDs for ownerToNFTokenIdList[address(0)]). This is similar to burning an NFT position (via merge/ withdraw) because the associated voting power will not be accessible to the previous owner, and the deposited asset can never be withdrawn by the actual owner of the tokenID, after this transfer happens. But there are some differences. There will be no checkpoint for this kind of burn until the lock expires, the voting power i.e. bias and slope values will keep getting considered in global point history calculations, only after that the slopechanges might get applied. The total "supply" value becomes wrong and is not reduced like it should be in case of a burn. This causes wrong accounting external voting contracts (e.g. wrong quorum calculations). This can never be corrected even after the lock expires. Fees can still be claimed via the feedistributor because it doesn't check if the ownerOf(tokenID) is not address(0) and because there has been no ending checkpoint (like the one in withdraw →_burn flow setting a new checkpoint with zero values). So even though the claimed fees will go to address(0), claim can be called by anyone until the lock expires or the maxepoch has passed. The underlying assets will be stuck forever in the zerolocker contract. And the voting power of these tokenIDs held by the zero address can be used by anyone because votingPowerOf / _balanceOfNFT etc... functions do not check if the owner of tokenID is address(0), and non-zero checkpoint exists based on which these tokenIDs will have a substantial voting power until the lock expires. Because of so many different impacts, this is a critical severity issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability allows any NFT managed by the contract to be transferred to the zero address even though a comment in the internal _transferFrom function states that such a transfer is prohibited. The root cause is that the public transferFrom (and related internal) flow does not contain a require(to != address(0)) check, so the zero address is accepted as a valid recipient. When a token is transferred to address(0) the contract updates its internal ownership mappings, placing the token ID in the list of tokens owned by address(0). This effectively burns the token from the perspective of the original owner, but the contract does not emit a burn event nor adjust the total supply counter, nor create a checkpoint with zero voting power. Consequently the voting power associated with the locked token continues to be counted in global point history calculations, inflating the apparent supply and breaking quorum calculations in external voting contracts. In addition, the fee distributor contract does not verify that ownerOf(tokenId) is non‑zero before allowing fee claims, so anyone can call claimFees for a token that now belongs to address(0). The claimed fees are sent to address(0) and are therefore irretrievably lost, while the claim function can be called repeatedly until the lock expires or the maximum epoch is reached. From a user’s point of view the NFT disappears from their wallet, the protocol shows a higher total supply than expected, and governance votes may be counted incorrectly. The issue is hard to notice because the contract’s comment gives a false impression of safety, the zero address is a valid Solidity address, and no explicit burn event is emitted, so the transfer appears to succeed silently. The bug belongs to the class of missing zero‑address validation or improper burn handling, which can lead to phantom ownership, accounting errors, and unclaimed fee leakage. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the comment with the actual code path and observed that transferring to address(0) succeeded without a revert. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a require(to != address(0)) check in all transfer functions, treat a transfer to zero as a proper burn by updating the total supply and emitting a Burn event, and the fee distributor should reject claims for tokens whose owner is the zero address. Proper checkpointing with zero values should also be added so that voting power is removed immediately.

title: Voting power miscalculation in balanceofnftat function Submitted by elhaj
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance‑related function that returns the voting power of a locked‑token NFT at an arbitrary timestamp. The routine computes a bias value by subtracting the product of a slope and the difference between the requested time and the last checkpoint timestamp. Because the arithmetic uses signed integers but does not verify that the supplied timestamp is not earlier than the checkpoint, a negative time delta is multiplied by a positive slope, turning the subtraction into an addition. Consequently, when a caller queries a time that precedes the user’s most recent lock (for example a snapshot taken before the user locked tokens), the function erroneously inflates the bias instead of returning zero. This miscalculation allows a participant who locked tokens after a governance snapshot to appear as if they possessed voting power at the snapshot, effectively granting them influence they never earned. The bug also lacks any protection against flash‑loan style attacks; an attacker can pass the current block timestamp as the query parameter, obtain a temporarily inflated balance, and then revert the loan, thereby manipulating a vote without a lasting stake. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case showed that a later‑staking user received a higher voting power than a user who locked earlier, and the bias value grew instead of decaying. It is subtle because the same formula works correctly for forward‑looking timestamps, so the error only manifests for past queries, which are common in snapshot‑based voting. The impact is that governance decisions may be swayed by artificially created voting power, undermining the protocol’s consensus and potentially leading to malicious parameter changes or fund misallocation. The problem occurs whenever balanceOfNFTAt (or its internal helper) is called with a timestamp earlier than the user’s last checkpoint or when the caller can manipulate the timestamp via a flash loan. All token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself are affected because the voting tally can be distorted. To remediate, the implementation must enforce that the queried timestamp is not earlier than the stored checkpoint, returning zero or clamping the bias to a non‑negative value when it would otherwise become negative. Additionally, the function should reject calls that use the current block timestamp in a context where flash‑loan manipulation is possible, or it should rely on immutable block numbers for snapshots. In short, the bug is a classic “negative‑delta bias increase” arithmetic error that violates the accounting assumption that voting power can only decrease over time, and it must be fixed by adding proper time‑order checks and flash‑loan safeguards.

title: initiallastpoint mismanagement compromises epoch accuracy and snapshot governance Submitted by elhaj
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismanagement of a temporary struct used for epoch extrapolation in the ZeroLocker governance contract. The contract stores voting power checkpoints in a Point struct that records bias, slope, timestamp and block number. During each checkpoint the code creates a variable called initialLastPoint by assigning the current lastPoint struct: Point memory initialLastPoint = lastPoint. Because of Solidity's handling of memory structs, this assignment does not produce an independent copy; instead both variables refer to the same memory location. Consequently any later modification of lastPoint also changes initialLastPoint. The logic that follows expects initialLastPoint to remain unchanged so that the time difference (tI‑initialLastPoint.ts) reflects the elapsed time since the previous checkpoint. In practice the shared reference makes that difference always zero, because tI is set to the same timestamp stored in initialLastPoint. As a result the calculation of lastPoint.blk, which uses the time delta multiplied by a block‑per‑second slope, always yields the original block number of the first checkpoint. All subsequent epochs therefore reference the same block number, breaking the contract’s ability to compute accurate voting power at arbitrary block heights. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who triggers a checkpoint after locking tokens and then queries balanceOfAtNFT for a past block; the contract will return an incorrect (often zero or stale) voting power, allowing the attacker to manipulate governance outcomes, hide voting power, or cause proposals to be accepted or rejected incorrectly. The impact is a loss of integrity in snapshot‑based voting, potentially allowing malicious actors to sway decisions without proper token weight, and it may also cause users to see their voting power disappear from the UI, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The issue manifests whenever the _checkpoint function runs, i.e., on any token lock, unlock or balance change, and it affects every participant who relies on historical voting power queries. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the memory handling of structs and verified the behavior with a Forge test that showed both structs changing together. The bug is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the shared reference is not obvious without inspecting the memory semantics, making it easy to miss during testing. The proper fix is to ensure that initialLastPoint is a true copy of lastPoint, for example by creating a new struct in memory and copying each field explicitly or by using a storage reference that is read‑only, thereby preserving the original timestamp and block number for correct extrapolation. In generic terms this is a memory aliasing bug that leads to incorrect state derivation in time‑based snapshot calculations, breaking the accounting assumptions that voting power should evolve linearly over time.

title: Allowing merge of expired locks may prevent reward claiming and break some invariants Submitted by elhaj, also found by 0xTheBlackPanther, Naveen Kumar J - 1nc0gn170, bin2chen, ethan and 0xarno
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the merge function of the ZeroLocker contract, which combines the locked balances of two NFT‑based locks. The function updates the end timestamp of the destination lock to the later of the two timestamps, but it does not verify whether either lock has already expired. When an expired lock (whose end time is in the past) is merged with a still‑active lock, the expired lock is effectively re‑activated by adopting the newer end time. This re‑activation creates a period in the protocol’s accounting where the total voting power (veSupply) is zero because no active locks existed during the interval between the original expiration and the merge. The FeeDistributor contract calculates rewards based on the user’s share of veSupply for each epoch; when it encounters an epoch with veSupply equal to zero, the division by zero triggers a revert, preventing the claim function from completing. Consequently, users who merge an expired lock cannot claim any of the rewards that accrued before the merge, and those rewards become permanently unclaimable. The bug also allows a user to construct a lock whose total duration exceeds the protocol‑defined maximum by merging two maximum‑duration locks, although this does not increase voting power. The issue manifests only when a merge involves at least one expired tokenId and the protocol’s veSupply has dropped to zero during the gap, conditions that are not obvious from the UI because the merged token appears active and the user expects to receive the accumulated rewards. It was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately created an expired lock, waited for veSupply to become zero, and then performed a merge before attempting a claim. The problem is hard to notice because the merge transaction succeeds and the lock’s end time is updated, masking the underlying accounting inconsistency. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit check that both tokenIds being merged have end timestamps greater than the current block timestamp, rejecting any attempt to merge expired locks. This restores the invariant that only active locks participate in reward distribution and prevents division‑by‑zero reverts and unintended lock‑duration extensions.

title: _burn() approved users cannot execute normally Submitted by bin2chen, also found by 8olidity, AuditorPraise, cccz, osmanozdemir1, ravikiranweb3, Chinmay Farkya, jovi.eth, atarpara, saucecri, elhaj, Naveen Kumar J - 1nc0gn170, Ch301, pauleth, 0x175, waﬄemakr and 0xarno
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal _burn function of the ZeroLocker contract, which is intended to allow any address that is either the token owner or an approved operator to destroy a token as part of withdraw or merge operations. The function begins with a correct check using _isApprovedOrOwner, so on the surface it appears that approved users should be able to call _burn. However, the implementation then calls two internal helpers that each perform their own ownership verification. First, it invokes _approve(address(0), _tokenId) to clear the token approval. This helper internally requires that msg.sender be the owner or be approved for all, and it does not consider the explicit per‑token approval stored in idToApprovals. Consequently, even if an address has been granted permission through approve(user, tokenId), the call to _approve fails, preventing the approval from being cleared. Second, the function calls _removeTokenFrom(msg.sender, _tokenId). Inside this helper an assert checks that the supplied _from address matches the recorded owner of the token (idToOwner[_tokenId] == _from). Because msg.sender is the approved operator rather than the true owner, the assertion fails and the token removal is aborted. The combined effect is that any approved operator, despite passing the initial _isApprovedOrOwner check, cannot successfully execute _burn, and therefore cannot perform withdraw() or merge() that rely on burning the token. This bug manifests when a token owner grants permission to another user via approve() or setApprovalForAll() and that user attempts to trigger a withdrawal or merge; the transaction reverts with either the generic "caller is not owner nor approved" error from the initial require or an internal assertion failure from _removeTokenFrom. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a failed transaction, no funds being returned, or a balance that remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation that an approved operator can act on the token. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s logic, and it can be difficult to notice because the superficial approval check appears correct, masking the deeper ownership checks hidden in the helper calls. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper handling of delegated authority, where internal functions re‑enforce ownership constraints instead of respecting approved operators. To remediate, the contract should replace the call to _approve with a direct clearance function that does not re‑check ownership (e.g., _clearApproval(owner, tokenId)) and should pass the actual token owner to _removeTokenFrom rather than msg.sender. This ensures that approved operators can successfully clear approvals and remove the token, restoring the intended functionality of withdraw and merge operations without breaking the contract’s accounting logic.

title: Inequitable reward distribution in zlrewardscontroller due to dynamic available rewards adjustment Submitted by elhaj
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward controller that allocates emission tokens to a set of liquidity pools based on each pool's allocation points. The contract calculates a raw reward amount for the whole update interval using the global rewards‑per‑second rate and the elapsed time. When the total raw reward exceeds the amount of tokens actually deposited in the contract, the code reduces the raw reward to the current available balance before distributing it to each pool. Because the available balance is recomputed after every pool update, the amount that later pools see is smaller than the amount that should be allocated to them according to their share of the total allocation points. This creates a compounding shortfall: the first pool receives its full proportional slice, the second pool receives a reduced slice because the available balance has already been decreased, and subsequent pools receive progressively less, leaving a remainder of undistributed tokens in the contract. The root cause is the use of a mutable available‑rewards variable inside the per‑pool reward calculation instead of treating the total reward pool as a constant for the duration of the mass update. The flaw can be exploited by arranging pool order, adding many low‑allocation pools, or simply by waiting for a period where the contract’s deposited rewards are insufficient for the elapsed time, causing later participants to earn far less than expected. Affected parties include liquidity providers staking in any pool that is processed after another pool in the same update cycle, as well as the protocol itself because the accounting assumptions of fair, proportional distribution are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the function that returns the remaining rewards is called inside the loop that updates each pool, causing the balance to shrink with each iteration. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the total amount of tokens transferred out of the contract matches the available balance, but the distribution ratios are wrong, making the bug easy to miss in normal testing. From a user perspective the symptom is that a user who expects a certain amount of reward after a claim may receive a smaller amount or even zero, while the UI still shows that rewards are being generated. The protocol’s business logic that rewards are allocated proportionally to allocation points is violated, leading to unfair earnings and leftover tokens that never get claimed. The recommended mitigation is to keep the available‑rewards value constant for the whole mass‑update operation, compute each pool’s share based on that constant, and only update the accounted‑rewards counter after all pools have been processed, thereby preserving the intended proportional distribution.

title: Possible underﬂow of uint128
description: Possible underﬂow of uint128
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer underflow that occurs when a signed 128‑bit value is directly cast to an unsigned 128‑bit type without first ensuring the value is non‑negative. In the contract, the calculation of a bias term (pt.bias - pt.slope * dt) and a similar user‑specific bias (oldUserPoint.bias - dt * oldUserPoint.slope) are performed using signed arithmetic, but the result is immediately converted to uint128 via int128 casting. If the subtraction yields a negative number, the cast wraps the value to a very large unsigned integer, effectively inflating the stored veSupply or user balance. This happens whenever the time delta (dt) grows large enough that the slope component exceeds the bias, which is a normal condition in many voting‑escrow or reward‑distribution schemes. The underflow is hard to notice because the contract may still compile and run, and the inflated numbers can pass superficial checks; however, downstream accounting that assumes the supply is bounded can produce incorrect rewards, zero payouts, or even allow an attacker to claim more tokens than entitled. From a user perspective the UI may display a massive total supply while individual balances appear unchanged or become zero, leading to confusion such as “my reward claim returns 0” or “my balance disappeared”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected type conversions and identified the missing max‑zero guard before casting. It belongs to the broader class of signed‑to‑unsigned conversion bugs that cause underflow/overflow. To remediate, the code should compare the signed result with zero and clamp it to a non‑negative value before casting, for example by using Math.maxInt((bias - slope * dt),0) and then converting the clamped result to uint128. This ensures that only valid, non‑negative values are stored, preserving the intended accounting logic and preventing supply inflation or balance loss.

title: vestedzerolend whitelist logic is incorrectly implemented Submitted by StErMi, also found by tnch
bug_full: The contract implements a whitelist access control inside the _afterTokenTransfer hook, which is executed after every mint, burn or transfer. The intended rule is that when whitelist enforcement is enabled, both the sender (from) and the receiver (to) must be members of the whitelist, otherwise the operation should be rejected. However, the actual implementation uses a logical OR (whitelist[from] || whitelist[to]) instead of an AND. As a result, a transfer is allowed if either the sender or the receiver is whitelisted. This flaw permits a whitelisted address to send tokens to an arbitrary non‑whitelisted address, and also allows a non‑whitelisted address to receive tokens from a whitelisted sender. The root cause is an incorrect boolean condition in the access‑control check. An attacker can exploit the bug by simply initiating a transfer from a whitelisted account to any target address, bypassing the intended restriction without needing any special privileges or re‑entrancy tricks. The impact is that tokens can flow to addresses that the protocol intended to block, breaking compliance, potentially exposing funds to unauthorized parties, and undermining trust in the whitelist mechanism. The vulnerability manifests whenever the whitelist feature is enabled and a transfer involves at least one whitelisted participant; it does not depend on the amount transferred or other state variables. All token holders, the protocol governance, and any external users who rely on the whitelist for security or regulatory reasons are affected because they may see tokens appear in accounts that should have been blocked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token contract, where the reviewer noticed that the require statement used an OR operator. It can be hard to notice because the transfer still succeeds and no explicit error is emitted, so normal usage may not reveal the missing restriction. The correct fix is to replace the OR with an AND, ensuring that both parties are required to be whitelisted before the transfer is allowed. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of improper access‑control checks where the logical condition does not reflect the intended policy, leading to unauthorized state changes. From a user’s perspective, a user who expects that only whitelisted recipients can receive tokens may see their tokens arrive at a non‑whitelisted address, or a non‑whitelisted user may unexpectedly receive tokens, violating the expectation that "only whitelisted accounts can interact". The failure mode is effectively a whitelist bypass that allows money to move to prohibited accounts, breaking accounting assumptions that the whitelist enforces a closed set of participants.

title: Zerolend contract will mint 100B tokens each time is deployed on a new chain Submitted by StErMi
description: The current implementation of the ZeroLend token is minting 100B tokens each time it is deployed on a new chain. Moreover, the owner of the contract is allowed to mint additional amounts of such token by calling the mint function in those chains. The ZeroLend tokens should be minted only once, or at least only in the main chain where such a contract is deployed. When deployed on the other chains it should not be possible to mint tokens but just transfer them.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an uncontrolled token minting mechanism that triggers a massive supply creation each time the ZeroLend token contract is deployed on a new blockchain. The contract’s constructor automatically mints a fixed amount of 100 billion tokens without verifying whether the deployment target is the intended main network. In addition, the contract exposes a public mint function that can be called by the contract owner on any chain, allowing further arbitrary token creation after deployment. The root cause is the absence of any chain‑specific guard or access restriction that ties the initial supply to a single, authoritative environment. Because the mint function is unrestricted for the owner, an attacker who gains control of the owner role—or the legitimate owner acting unintentionally—can inflate the token supply on any fork, side‑chain, or testnet where the contract is instantiated. Exploitation is straightforward: once the contract is deployed on a secondary chain, the constructor immediately creates 100 B tokens, and the owner can subsequently invoke mint to create additional tokens at will. This results in a supply explosion that dilutes the token’s economic model, potentially rendering the token worthless on those chains and confusing users who expect a stable, limited supply. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected balances that are orders of magnitude larger than anticipated, or conversely a token that appears to have no value because the market is flooded with newly minted units. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the token’s initialization logic and owner privileges, and it may be hard to notice in normal operation because the contract still complies with ERC‑20 standards and the inflated supply does not immediately break functional calls. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted minting” or “unconditional initial supply” vulnerabilities, where token economics are broken by missing checks on deployment context and owner permissions. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the initial mint only occurs on the designated mainnet, for example by checking a known chain identifier or by passing an explicit initial‑mint amount that can be set to zero on other networks. Moreover, the mint function should be either removed, restricted to a governance process, or limited to a role that cannot be exercised on non‑mainnet deployments, thereby preventing accidental or malicious inflation across chains.

title: streamedvesting denies bonus when the lock is for 4 years and bonuspool has not enough to cover it Submitted by StErMi, also found by XDZIBECX, osmanozdemir1, erictee, nethoxa, tnch, pauleth, bLnk and Naveen Kumar J - 1nc0gn170
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the 4‑year staking path of the StreamedVesting contract. When a user calls stakeTo4Year, the function calculates a 20 % bonus based on the amount that will be locked and then checks whether the dedicated bonus pool holds at least that exact bonus amount. If the pool balance is lower than the calculated bonus, the code simply skips the transfer and proceeds to create a four‑year lock with the original amount only. Consequently, the user receives no bonus even though the pool contains some tokens that could have been used to provide a partial reward. The root cause is a binary balance check (balance >= bonusAmount) without a fallback to a proportional payout; the logic treats any shortfall as a total failure rather than a partial one. An attacker or any party that drains or reduces the bonus pool can trigger this condition, causing honest participants to lock their tokens for the full duration while receiving zero extra tokens. The impact is financial: users expect a 20 % increase on their vested amount, see the UI indicating a bonus, but end up with the same amount after four years, effectively losing the anticipated reward. This situation occurs whenever the bonus pool is under‑funded but not empty, which may happen after large bonus withdrawals, mis‑management, or a malicious depletion of the pool. All users who wish to stake for four years are affected, and the protocol’s credibility suffers because the promised incentive is not honored. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s accounting logic with the intended business rule of “always grant the maximum possible bonus up to the pool’s balance”. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it silently creates the lock, making the problem easy to miss unless the actual received amount is inspected after the lock is created. To remediate, the function should compute the payable bonus as the minimum of the calculated bonus and the current pool balance, transfer that amount, and add it to the lock amount. This ensures that users receive whatever bonus is available, preserving the incentive structure even when the pool is partially depleted. The fix aligns the implementation with the intended accounting rule that a user should receive the full bonus if possible, or a proportional partial bonus if the pool cannot cover the full amount, thereby preventing silent loss of expected rewards.

title: _newrewards does not take endrewardtime into account, which may lead to incorrect allocation of rewards Submitted by cccz, also found by bin2chen and Ch301
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the reward‑distribution routine of the contract. The function that calculates new rewards (_newRewards) uses the current block timestamp to determine the elapsed time since the last pool update, but it does not cap this timestamp with the emission end time (endRewardTime). endRewardTime is only refreshed when a configurable update cadence has elapsed, so it can remain stale after the scheduled reward emission period. When _updatePool limits the timestamp to endRewardTime but _newRewards continues to use block.timestamp, the contract may allocate more tokens than the remaining reward balance permits. This can be exploited by triggering a reward deposit shortly before the stale endRewardTime expires, then allowing a pool update after the true emission period; the pool will claim rewards based on a longer duration than actually allowed, inflating the reward share for that pool. The impact is an over‑allocation of rewards, which distorts accounting, creates unexpected token inflation, and can drain the contract’s reward pool, harming other liquidity providers and the protocol’s economic model. The bug manifests only when the time since the last endRewardTime update is less than the update cadence, and a pool update occurs after the real emission end. Users may notice that their balances increase more than expected or that the total distributed rewards exceed the amount deposited. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑emission logic, where the mismatch between the timestamp handling in _updatePool and _newRewards was observed. It is subtle because the contract still reports a plausible endRewardTime and the UI may not show the over‑distribution directly. The proper fix is to compute the duration in _newRewards using the minimum of endRewardTime and block.timestamp, mirroring the logic already applied in _updatePool, thereby ensuring rewards stop accruing once the emission period ends. This class of bug belongs to time‑window miscalculations in token‑distribution contracts, where stale state leads to arithmetic overrun and incorrect accounting.

title: addpool doesn't always call _massupdatepools, which can lead to incorrect reward allocation Submitted by cccz
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the function that adds a new liquidity pool does not trigger a mass update of all existing pools before the global allocation weight is increased. As a result the pending reward calculation for already‑existing pools is performed with the new total allocation weight, causing the previously earned rewards to be retroactively reduced. This happens because the internal routine that updates emissions only calls the mass‑update routine when the reward schedule has already ended; during the normal reward period the routine is skipped. An attacker who has the privileged role that can call addPool can introduce a new pool at any time before the end of the reward schedule, causing the earlier pool’s reward per share to be recomputed with a larger denominator. Users who have staked in the original pool will see their pending reward balance drop, receiving fewer tokens than the protocol’s accounting originally promised. The impact is a systematic under‑allocation of rewards, which can lead to loss of expected earnings for liquidity providers and may erode trust in the incentive mechanism. The issue manifests when the contract’s addPool function is invoked while rewards are still being emitted; the UI may show a lower pending reward amount or a sudden drop after a new pool appears. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order of state updates in the reward‑distribution logic. The bug is subtle because the contract still distributes rewards, but the amount is silently reduced, making the discrepancy easy to miss without a precise accounting check. The proper fix is to ensure that a mass update of all pools is performed before the total allocation point is modified, or to restructure the reward‑calculation routine so that pending rewards are always computed using the allocation point value that was in effect during the elapsed time. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where each pool’s share of rewards is fixed for the period that has already passed.

title: supply in the zerolocker.sol is incorrectly increased during merge_type actions Submitted by osmanozdemir1, also found by m4rio, Chinmay Farkya, jovi.eth, Sujith Somraaj, 0x175, Naveen Kumar J - 1nc0gn170, bLnk, Ch301, ethan, elhaj, waﬄemakr, 3agle and 0xarno
bug_full: The ZeroLocker contract keeps a public variable called supply that is intended to represent the total amount of the underlying token locked in all positions. The contract allows users to create locks, add to existing locks, extend lock time, and merge two separate lock NFTs into one. The merge operation is implemented as a special deposit type (MERGE_TYPE) that moves the amount from the source lock to the destination lock without transferring any underlying tokens, because the tokens are already held by the contract. However, the internal function _depositFor unconditionally adds the deposited amount to the supply variable before checking the deposit type. As a result, when a merge is performed the supply counter is increased by the amount of the source lock even though no new tokens have entered the contract. This creates a mismatch between the logical total supply and the actual token balance held by the contract. The bug can be exploited by repeatedly merging many locks, causing the reported supply to grow arbitrarily while the real token balance stays unchanged. The condition for the bug is any call to merge where the source and destination NFTs are owned or approved by the caller. The affected parties include protocol users who rely on the supply figure for TVL calculations, external dashboards, and any downstream contracts that might read the supply for accounting or incentive purposes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a unit test that showed the supply value jumping from 2 × amount to 3 × amount after a single merge, while the token balance remained at 2 × amount. Because the current code does not use the supply variable in core financial calculations, the problem may appear harmless at first glance, making it easy to overlook. Nevertheless, the broken invariant violates the fundamental accounting assumption that supply equals the sum of locked tokens, leading to inflated TVL reports and potential integration failures if future contracts depend on this metric. The proper fix is to conditionally update the supply only for deposit types that actually transfer tokens, i.e., to guard the supply increment with a check that the deposit type is not MERGE_TYPE, or to move the supply update out of the generic deposit routine and handle it explicitly for each deposit scenario. This aligns the on‑chain accounting with the real token holdings and restores the integrity of the supply invariant.

title: streamedvesting.claimvestearlywithpenalty() charges much more penalties than required Submitted by osmanozdemir1, also found by giraffe0x, StErMi, jovi.eth, elhaj and Chinmay Farkya
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the early‑withdrawal function of the StreamedVesting contract. The function claimVestEarlyWithPenalty is intended to let a user retrieve the entire vesting amount before the 90‑day schedule finishes, while charging a penalty only on the portion that has not yet vested. Instead, the implementation calculates the pending amount as vest.amount‑vest.claimed and then applies the penalty percentage to this whole pending amount. Because vest.claimed does not include the portion that is already claimable without penalty, the penalty is mistakenly applied to tokens that should be released free of charge. As a result, when a user who has already accrued, for example, two months of vesting calls claimVestEarlyWithPenalty directly, the contract deducts the penalty from the full original vest amount rather than from the remaining unvested tokens. This produces a much higher penalty, causing the user to receive far fewer tokens than expected – often only the unvested portion after a large penalty, while the vested portion that should be free is also taxed. The bug can be triggered by any holder of a vesting schedule who calls the early‑claim function before any partial claim has been made. It occurs whenever the contract is not paused and the caller is the vest owner. The impact is a systematic loss of funds for users, breaking the economic assumptions of the vesting model and leading to unfair token depletion. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test compared the token delta of a user who first called claimVest and then claimVestEarlyWithPenalty with a user who called only claimVestEarlyWithPenalty; the latter consistently received a smaller amount. The problem is subtle because the contract still transfers tokens, so a casual observer may not notice that the penalty amount is inflated; the UI simply shows a lower received balance without indicating an error. To remediate, the function must first compute the amount that is already claimable without penalty (using the same logic as claimVest) and apply the penalty only to the remaining unvested tokens, or alternatively invoke claimVest internally before applying the penalty. This adjustment restores the intended accounting logic, ensures that users receive the correct free portion of their vest, and prevents excessive, unintended token loss.

title: Certain cost models may be exploited with callback tokens
description: At the moment, the Set's sell() function first makes an external call in order to transfer the refund to receiver_ and only afterwards calls the cost mode's update() function. Under a specific configuration where the asset has receive-callbacks (e.g., an ERC777 token) and the cost model used by a Set's market is stateful (ie. actually makes use of update() function calls) this might be vulnerable to reentrancy: Upon receiving the tokens, the receiver_ might exploit the fact that the cost model has not been updated yet by calling back into the Set.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the Set contract's sell() function that arises from the ordering of operations. The function first performs an external call to transfer a refund token to the receiver address and only afterwards invokes the cost model's update() routine, which may modify internal accounting state. When the refunded asset implements a receive‑callback mechanism such as the ERC777 token standard, the receiver contract can execute code during the token transfer. If the market associated with the Set uses a stateful cost model that relies on the update() call to adjust pricing or balances, the callback can re‑enter the Set contract before the cost model has been updated. By re‑entering, the attacker can invoke sell() or other market functions while the contract is still in an inconsistent state, potentially causing the cost model to be applied multiple times or with stale data. This can lead to incorrect refund calculations, inflated payouts, or complete loss of funds for honest users. The issue manifests only when two conditions are met: the asset being sold supports receive callbacks, and the selected cost model performs state‑changing logic in its update() function. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no refund, seeing their balance unexpectedly drop to zero, or observing refunds that do not match the expected amount. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which identified the unsafe call order as a logical flaw that is easy to miss because most ERC20 tokens lack callbacks, making the reentrancy vector non‑obvious. To mitigate the risk, the contract should call the cost model's update() before any external token transfer, thereby ensuring that the contract’s internal state is fully consistent before untrusted code is executed. Additional defenses include avoiding assets with callback hooks, using stateless cost models, or applying a reentrancy guard around the sell() logic. Implementing these changes restores the intended business logic that a user’s refund is calculated correctly and that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.

title: First deposit price inflation vulnerability exists
bug_full: The vulnerability is a first‑deposit price inflation bug that allows an attacker to manipulate the share price of a Set token by performing a tiny initial deposit, sending a large blind transfer of assets to the Set contract, and then making another tiny deposit. The protocol’s internal accounting records a variable called assetsExcess, which is later added to accounting.assetBalance. Because assetsExcess is incorporated into the total asset balance, the large off‑chain donation is treated as part of the pool’s collateral, inflating the reported price per share. When a user later calls the router’s convertToShares (or uses the router’s deposit function with a minSharesReceived parameter derived from convertToShares), the calculation uses the inflated price, causing the user to receive fewer shares than expected for the amount of assets supplied. Conversely, during redemption the inflated price means each share is worth less than the underlying assets, so the user receives fewer assets than anticipated. The attack scenario proceeds as follows: (1) an attacker deposits a negligible amount of assets (e.g., 1 wei) to establish a baseline share price; (2) the attacker performs a blind transfer of a large amount of the underlying token directly to the Set contract, bypassing the router’s slippage checks; (3) the attacker deposits another tiny amount, which triggers the internal accounting to recognize the previous donation as part of the pool, thereby raising the share price; (4) subsequent honest users who deposit or redeem based on the now‑inflated price suffer loss of value because the conversion formulas are based on a manipulated price. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a mismatch between expected and actual balances: a user may deposit a certain amount of WETH and later receive fewer WETH after redemption, or see their share balance unchanged while the underlying asset balance drops unexpectedly. The issue is hard to notice because the manipulation only becomes apparent after a sequence of deposits and redemptions, and the router’s slippage protection only guards against front‑running of the router call itself, not against external donations that affect the on‑chain price oracle used by convertToShares. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which observed that assetsExcess was added to accounting.assetBalance, negating the intended protection of internal accounting. The root cause is the improper inclusion of external asset donations in the accounting of total collateral, leading to a price‑inflation class of bug often referred to as “share price manipulation via deposit front‑run”. To remediate the issue, the protocol should stop adding assetsExcess to accounting.assetBalance, ensuring that only assets deposited through the router are counted for price calculations, and should reinforce price oracle logic to ignore unsolicited transfers. This conceptual fix restores the integrity of share pricing, prevents fund loss, and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its intended economic model.

title: Malicious owner or manager may DoS the Set
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an inefficient read of the inactivity periods array in the contract that tracks pause/unpause events. Each pause adds an entry to an internal periods array. When the contract later calculates a user’s matured balance it copies the whole InactivityData struct into memory (InactivityData memory inactivityData_ = inactivityData;) and then performs a binary search on the copied array. Because the copy operation expands the entire array into memory, the gas cost grows linearly with the number of pause/unpause cycles. A malicious owner or manager can deliberately invoke pause and unpause thousands of times, inflating the array to tens of thousands of entries. When a legitimate user later calls claim or balanceOfMatured, the function attempts to load the massive array, exhausting the block gas limit or causing the transaction to run out of gas, effectively preventing claims and locking user funds. The issue appears only after the array has grown large; normal operation with a few pauses works fine, which makes the problem easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered by an audit that added a stress test looping 45000 pause/unpause calls and observed a dramatic gas increase when claiming. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded array copy or storage‑to‑memory copy DoS vulnerabilities, where a contract copies an unbounded data structure into memory before processing it. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a claim transaction reverts or consumes all gas, leaving the expected refund or balance at zero even though the user has deposited funds. The business logic assumes that the pause history is only a small helper for accounting, but the implementation violates that assumption by treating the history as arbitrarily large. The proper fix is to avoid copying the array into memory; the function should work directly with the storage reference (e.g. InactivityData storage inactivityData_ = inactivityData;) or redesign the accounting to use incremental counters or limit the size of the periods array. By keeping the data in storage the binary search can be performed without the costly copy, restoring the ability for users to claim their funds.

title: Create public Token Integration Checklist
description: At first glance Sets appear to be able to deal with any form of ERC20 tokens, but that might not be true in practice. There exist some tokens that use extension standards or generally don't follow a standard specification which could potentially cause issues when used as an asset for a Set. Furthermore there's no way for a Set to check whether the chosen token is compatible automatically, a manual review of each new asset is required.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the Set contract assuming that any ERC20 token supplied as an asset fully complies with the standard ERC20 interface. In practice, many tokens implement extensions, omit expected return values, charge fees on transfer, or revert on approve, which deviates from the canonical specification. Because the Set contract does not perform any runtime compatibility verification, a token that does not exhibit the required behaviours can be added to a Set without any automated safeguard. When the Set later attempts to transfer, mint, redeem, or calculate balances for that token, the call may silently fail, revert, or produce an incorrect accounting result. This can manifest as users receiving zero refunds, balances appearing unchanged, or assets becoming permanently locked. The issue occurs whenever a Set owner creates a new Set with a non‑standard token without manually reviewing the token’s code or behaviour. Affected parties include Set owners, token holders, and the protocol itself, as the Set may become unusable or expose users to unexpected loss of funds. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the token handling logic and noted the absence of automated compatibility checks. The bug is hard to notice because the contract compiles and interacts with the token using the standard ABI, so static analysis does not flag any error; the failure only surfaces at runtime with specific tokens. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should provide a public Token Integration Checklist that enumerates the required ERC20 behaviours—such as returning boolean values on transfer/approve, not charging transfer fees, and adhering to expected revert semantics—and enforce these checks either programmatically or through a pre‑deployment verification step. By ensuring that only tokens meeting the checklist are accepted, the protocol can avoid accounting breaks, missing refunds, and situations where funds appear to disappear.

title: When a purchase occurs, other markets do not maintain the same utilization
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that appears after a purchase is executed in a multi‑market lending protocol. The contract is supposed to keep the utilization ratio – the proportion of borrowed assets to total collateral – identical across all markets that did not experience a purchase. This invariant breaks because the purchase flow does not invoke the fee‑dripping routine (dripSupplierFees) that is normally called during deposits and withdrawals. As a result, the purchase fee pool for the market where the trade occurs accumulates new fees that are immediately added to the totalCollateralAvailable calculation, even though no time has elapsed for those fees to be dripped. Consequently, the total collateral is overstated for markets that did not receive the purchase, causing their reported utilization to drop compared with the expected value. The root cause is the missing call to dripSupplierFees() in the purchase path, which leads to an incorrect formula: (previous fees + new fees) × dripRate is applied instead of only (previous fees) × dripRate. An attacker can exploit this by triggering a purchase in one market to artificially lower utilization in other markets, potentially influencing interest rates, borrowing limits, or liquidation thresholds in those untouched markets. The impact includes mispricing of assets, unfair borrowing conditions, and possible loss of collateral if the protocol’s risk parameters rely on accurate utilization metrics. The condition occurs whenever a purchase is performed and the fee‑dripping step is omitted; it is observable during testing when utilization values differ across markets after a purchase. All participants – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol’s accounting no longer reflects the true state of collateral. The issue was discovered during an invariant test that recorded utilization before and after a purchase and found that markets without a purchase reported lower utilization than expected. It is subtle because the discrepancy is numeric and may not produce an outright failure, making it easy to miss in manual reviews. The correct fix is to invoke dripSupplierFees() as part of the purchase execution, ensuring that only fees that have had time to accrue are considered for drippage, thereby preserving the utilization invariant across all markets. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of fee‑drip or accounting‑state‑synchronisation errors, where state updates are applied inconsistently across related components, leading to divergent financial metrics and broken business logic.

title: Calls to Set.previewRedeem() will revert if a market of the set is frozen
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that causes the view function Set.previewRedeem() to revert when any market belonging to the Set is in a frozen state. The root cause lies in the delay calculation performed in DelayLib.sol, where the contract returns now_ - startTime_ - inactiveDurationAfterStartTime_. When a market is marked as FROZEN, the inactiveDurationAfterStartTime_ value can become larger than the elapsed time (now_ - startTime_), resulting in a subtraction that underflows. Solidity 0.8’s built‑in overflow checks detect this condition and automatically revert with a FAIL error, even though previewRedeem is a read‑only function. An attacker or any user can exploit this by simply invoking previewRedeem after the market has been frozen; the call will revert and the subsequent redemption flow cannot be completed. The impact is that users who expect to see their redemption amount or to receive a refund are instead presented with an error, effectively locking their funds and breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol. This occurs only after the market transitions to the frozen state and a subsequent block timestamp advances, as demonstrated by the test that mocks MarketState.FROZEN and then warps time forward. All participants who rely on redemption – token holders, liquidity providers, and buyers – are affected because the protocol’s UI will show a missing or zero refund, contrary to the expectation that redemption should succeed. The issue was discovered during a formal audit using Forge tests that simulated the frozen market condition and observed the arithmetic overflow error. It is hard to notice because view functions are generally assumed not to revert, so developers may overlook the need for safe arithmetic in delay calculations. To fix the problem, the contract should adjust the inactive period data when a market becomes frozen (or when it exits the frozen state) so that the subtraction never underflows; this can be achieved by resetting inactiveDurationAfterStartTime_ to zero, capping it to the elapsed time, or adding explicit underflow guards before performing the subtraction. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “time‑based arithmetic underflow” errors that break business logic for delayed operations, leading to failed refunds and disrupted redemption flows.

title: Set.updateMarketState(MarketState.TRIGGERED) call could revert under specific conditions
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs when a Set attempts to transition its market state to TRIGGERED while a shortfall exists and the Set is approved by the backstop. In this scenario the Set calls backstop.claim with the shortfall amount. The backstop.claim function retrieves the current token balance of the backstop and then performs a safeTransfer of the lesser of the balance and the requested amount. If the backstop holds zero tokens, the calculated transfer amount becomes zero. Certain ERC20 implementations revert on zero‑value transfers, causing the safeTransfer call to revert. Because the revert happens inside the claim call, the surrounding Set.updateMarketState logic never reaches the point where it updates the market state to TRIGGERED. This means the protocol cannot progress to the liquidation or settlement phase, leaving collateral calculations unchanged and potentially freezing user funds. The issue is triggered only under the specific combination of a shortfall, an approved Set, and a backstop with a zero asset balance, making it easy to miss during normal testing where the backstop usually holds assets. It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the possibility of a zero‑balance transfer. From a user perspective the UI may show that a market never reaches the expected triggered state, that collateral appears unchanged, or that a liquidation event never occurs despite a shortfall, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The bug belongs to the class of transfer‑revert bugs caused by missing pre‑conditions before token transfers. To fix the issue the claim function should include an explicit check that the backstop balance is greater than zero before attempting the transfer, or it should handle the zero‑balance case gracefully, for example by skipping the transfer or using a token that does not revert on zero transfers. This ensures that the Set can successfully update its market state and that the protocol’s accounting and liquidation logic remain sound.

title: Interface inconsistencies
description:
The following inconsistencies have been found around interfaces:
• ISet's definition of the claim() function returns a uint256 while the actual implementation returns uint128
• ISet's definition of the redemptions() function has different returns values than the actual Redemption struct: There's no delay variable and the shares variable has a different data type.
• IPToken defines an external function called inactiveTransitionTime() which is not implemented in the actual PToken contract.
• The interfaces folder contains the interfaces of IDripDecayModel and ICostModel despite the fact that cozy-models-v2 is a dependency of the repository and could make use of the original interfaces without duplication.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of mismatched interface definitions and implementations across several contracts. The ISet interface declares claim() returning uint256, but the concrete Set contract implements claim() returning uint128. This type mismatch means that callers compiled against the interface will interpret the returned value as a 256‑bit integer, while the actual runtime value is only 128 bits. If the caller assumes the full 256‑bit range, the truncated value can be silently cast, potentially leading to under‑payment or over‑payment depending on how the value is used. Similarly, the redemptions() function in ISet is defined to return a struct that includes a delay field and shares of a certain type, but the implementation’s Redemption struct omits the delay field and uses a different data type for shares. Code that reads the delay or expects the original share type will receive malformed data, causing logic errors such as incorrect vesting periods or mis‑calculated share amounts. In addition, the IPToken interface declares an external function inactiveTransitionTime() that is not present in the PToken implementation, so any external contract that calls this function through the interface will encounter a missing‑function error, leading to transaction reverts or the contract becoming unusable for certain lifecycle transitions. Finally, the repository contains duplicated copies of the IDripDecayModel and ICostModel interfaces even though the same definitions exist in the external cozy‑models‑v2 package. This duplication creates a maintenance risk: when the upstream interfaces change, the local copies may not be updated, resulting in subtle incompatibilities that are hard to detect at compile time because the contracts may still compile against the stale local version. The overall impact is that developers and users interacting with these contracts may experience unexpected return values, failed calls, or incorrect accounting, which can manifest as refunds that are zero, balances that appear wrong, or transactions that revert without clear reason. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared interface files with their corresponding implementation contracts and identified mismatches in function signatures and missing implementations. Because Solidity’s compiler only checks that a contract implements the functions it inherits, and because the contracts do not explicitly inherit the interfaces, these inconsistencies can slip through testing and only become apparent at runtime when a caller relies on the interface definition. The bug belongs to the class of interface contract mismatches and ABI incompatibility errors. To remediate, each contract should inherit the declared interface so the compiler enforces matching return types and function presence, and duplicated interface files should be removed in favor of importing the canonical definitions from the external library. This ensures that callers receive data in the expected format, that all declared functions exist, and that future updates to shared interfaces propagate automatically, eliminating the risk of silent data truncation, failed calls, or accounting errors.

title: Set owner unable to update configuration when insolvent
description:
Set owner may only update the configuration in a manner that does not cause the utilization of any market to rise to and over 100%. This would create insolvent markets, meaning a market would not have enough collateral to cover its claims when triggered.
But the insolvency of markets can naturally occur from the fact that Sets may choose to use leverage, i.e., use the same collateral to cover multiple markets. In that case, a Set owner would now be unable to apply any changes to the configuration until enough new collateral has been supplied to ensure the solvency of all markets.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic deadlock that prevents the designated Set owner from modifying any configuration parameters once the utilization of any market reaches or exceeds the 100 percent threshold. The root cause is an overly strict safety check that ties the ability to update settings to the condition that no market may become insolvent. Because the protocol permits leveraged positions – where the same collateral backs multiple markets – an attacker or even a legitimate user can push a market’s utilization to the full limit, causing the check to fail. When this happens the contract rejects every configuration change, including actions that would normally add fresh collateral or adjust risk parameters, effectively locking the owner out of any remedial operation. An exploit scenario consists of a malicious participant deliberately over‑leveraging a market until its utilization hits 100 percent; the subsequent transaction that attempts to update the configuration is reverted by the guard clause, leaving the market insolvent and unable to accept new collateral. The impact is that the protocol may become unable to restore solvency, user balances can appear frozen, withdrawals may fail, and the expected ability of the owner to intervene is lost. This condition occurs only in the extreme case where utilization is at the maximum, but because leveraged strategies can naturally drive utilization to that point, it can arise during normal operation as well. The parties affected include the Set owner, any governance participants who rely on configuration updates, and end‑users whose funds are tied to the affected markets. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the logic governing configuration changes and noticed that the guard clause does not distinguish between temporary over‑utilization and a permanent deadlock. It is hard to notice because the check appears to be a protective measure rather than a functional restriction, and no explicit error is emitted – transactions simply revert with a generic message. To remediate, the business logic should be relaxed to allow configuration updates even when a market is at or above full utilization, possibly by introducing an emergency path that permits adding collateral or adjusting parameters without violating the utilization guard, or by separating the solvency check from the configuration‑update permission.
