In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “over‑restrictive state‑dependent access control” where a safety condition unintentionally blocks essential administrative functions, leading to frozen funds and broken accounting assumptions.

title: _maxRedemptionRequest() reverts when set is insolvent
description:
The maximum amount that can be redeemed by a supplier is calculated as follows:
```solidity
totalCollateralAvailable_ - _getMaxAssetsRequiredToBackMarkets()
```
Redemptions are not possible when a set is insolvent, in that case totalCollateralAvailable_ will be smaller than the value returned by _getMaxAssetsRequiredToBackMarkets() causing the subtraction to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a view function that calculates the maximum amount a supplier may redeem from a liquidity set. The function computes the value by subtracting the amount of assets required to back all active markets from the total collateral currently available. When the set becomes insolvent, the total collateral is lower than the required backing amount, causing the subtraction to underflow. In Solidity versions that enforce arithmetic safety, this underflow triggers an automatic revert, so the view function throws instead of returning a numeric result. The root cause is the lack of a guard condition that checks for insolvency before performing the subtraction. An attacker or any external caller can exploit this behavior by forcing the protocol into a state where collateral is insufficient, for example by draining assets or by creating market positions that consume more backing than the pool holds. Once the condition is met, any call to the maximum redemption query reverts, which can break front‑end components that rely on the value, prevent legitimate users from estimating how much they can withdraw, and potentially lead to a denial‑of‑service scenario where the protocol appears unresponsive. The impact is felt by suppliers who expect to see a positive redemption limit, by the UI that may display an error or blank field, and by any downstream contracts that call the view function as part of their logic. The issue occurs only when the protocol’s collateral balance falls below the required backing threshold; under normal solvency the function works as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic expressions used in the redemption calculation. Because view functions are generally assumed to be safe and non‑reverting, developers may overlook the need for explicit safety checks, making the bug subtle and easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the function should first verify that total collateral is at least as large as the required backing amount and, if not, return a safe default such as zero or use a saturating subtraction that caps the result at zero. This change aligns the implementation with the business rule that a supplier cannot redeem more than the available collateral and restores predictable behavior for users and integrators.

title: A well financed attacker could prevent any other users from minting synthetic tokens
description:
[AlchemistV2.sol#L676-L683](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/main/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L676-L683)  
[AlchemistV2.sol#L704](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/main/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L704)  
[Limiters.sol#L84](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/main/contracts-full/libraries/Limiters.sol#L84)  

In the `AlchemistV2` contract, users can deposit collateral to then borrow/mint the synthetic tokens offered by the protocol. The protocol also defines a minting limit that specifies how many synthetic tokens can be minted in a given time period. This exists to prevent unbounded minting of synthetic tokens.

Every time a user calls `mint`, the internal `_mint` method decreases the current mint limit. This works as intended. However, there is nothing stopping an attacker from immediately burning their synthetic tokens by calling `burn` and then calling `mint` again. This is possible because the debt position is updated during the `burn` phase, which lets the user then mint again against the same deposited collateral.

In most cases this probably wouldn’t be a problem if the mint limit is sufficiently high. However, it is currently possible for a well financed attacker to grief the contract by repeatedly minting and burning synthetic tokens to keep the contract pegged at the mint limit. This will prevent any normal users from minting any synthetic tokens, and hence prevents the protocol from performing as it should.
poc: An attacker can repeatedly call `mint` followed by `burn` after depositing some collateral with `deposit`. If this is appropriately sized and timed, it can cause the `mint` call to fail for another user due to the check [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/main/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1068) that is called during `mint` [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/main/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1192).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition on the synthetic‑token issuance mechanism of the AlchemistV2 protocol. The contract enforces a time‑based minting limit – a quota that specifies how many synthetic tokens can be created in a given period. Each successful call to the mint function reduces the remaining quota, which is the intended behaviour. However, the protocol does not restore that quota when a user subsequently burns the same amount of synthetic tokens. Because the debt position is cleared during the burn step, the same collateral can be reused to mint again without any penalty, and the internal limiter is never incremented. An attacker with sufficient capital (or a flash‑loan source) can repeatedly execute the sequence: deposit collateral, mint the maximum amount allowed by the current quota, immediately burn the minted tokens, and repeat this loop many times within the same period. Each iteration consumes the minting quota permanently, eventually exhausting the limit. When the quota is fully consumed, any subsequent legitimate user who attempts to mint synthetic tokens encounters a failure – the transaction reverts with a “mint limit exceeded” error, or the user receives no tokens despite providing collateral. From the user’s point of view the UI shows an unexpected zero‑mint, or an error message, contradicting the expectation that depositing collateral will result in token issuance. The attack does not directly steal funds; rather it blocks the core functionality of the protocol, undermining its utility and potentially eroding trust. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the interaction between the mint and burn pathways was examined and it was observed that the limiter is only decremented, never incremented. The bug is subtle because normal operation (single mint followed by burn) appears to work correctly; the problem only manifests under repeated rapid cycles, which are not part of typical user behaviour and therefore can be missed in standard testing. To remediate the issue, the limiter logic should be made symmetric: when a burn reduces a user’s debt, the corresponding amount should be added back to the minting quota, or an alternative mechanism such as a small fee on mint/burn actions should be introduced to discourage gratuitous cycling. Adding an increase function to the Limiters library and invoking it during the burn process would restore the quota and prevent the quota‑exhaustion attack. Other mitigations include imposing a minimum waiting period between mint and burn for the same account, capping the number of cycles per block, or raising the overall mint limit via governance if a griefing event occurs. Overall, the vulnerability is a classic quota‑exhaustion or rate‑limiter bypass that leads to a denial of service on synthetic‑token minting.

title: `BaseRewardPool4626` is not IERC4626 compliant
description:
[BaseRewardPool4626.sol](https://github.com/aurafinance/convex-platform/blob/9cae5eb5a77e73bbc1378ef213740c1889e2e8a3/contracts/contracts/BaseRewardPool4626.sol)  

BaseRewardPool4626 is not IERC4626 compliant.  
This makes the BaseRewardPool4626 contract irrelevant as it is for now since projects won’t be able to integrate with BaseRewardPool4626 using the [eip-4626](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626) standard.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the BaseRewardPool4626 contract failing to conform to the IERC4626 (EIP‑4626) tokenized vault interface. In principle the contract is intended to act as a vault that users can deposit assets into and withdraw shares from, but it does not implement the set of external view functions (such as totalAssets, convertToShares, convertToAssets, maxDeposit, maxWithdraw, etc.) and the corresponding events (Deposit, Withdraw) required by the standard. This mismatch is the root cause: the contract’s source code was written without referencing the ERC‑4626 specification, so required function signatures, return types, and event emissions are missing or incorrectly named. When an external protocol or a user‑facing front‑end attempts to interact with the pool using the standard ERC‑4626 methods – for example calling deposit(uint256 assets, address receiver) – the call will either revert with an "undefined function" error or silently do nothing because the expected function does not exist. This can be exploited indirectly: a developer who assumes the pool behaves like a compliant vault may write integration code that calls the standard functions, leading to transaction failures, lost user experience, and potentially stranded funds if the calling code does not handle the error gracefully. The impact is primarily functional rather than financial: projects cannot compose the BaseRewardPool4626 with other ERC‑4626‑compatible contracts, users cannot rely on standard UI components that expect the vault interface, and the protocol loses the ability to attract integrations that depend on standardization. The issue surfaces whenever any contract or off‑chain tool queries the ERC‑4626 interface – i.e., during deposits, withdrawals, balance checks, or when reading maxDeposit limits – and finds that the required functions are absent. Affected parties include smart‑contract developers integrating the pool, end‑users attempting to deposit or withdraw through standard wallets or dashboards, and the protocol itself, which may suffer reduced composability and credibility. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, where auditors compared the contract’s ABI against the ERC‑4626 specification and noted the missing compliance. Because the contract does compile and can be called directly via its own custom methods, the non‑compliance may not be obvious during casual testing, making it easy to miss until a standard integration is attempted. To remediate the issue, the contract should either be removed entirely (saving deployment gas) or updated to implement all required ERC‑4626 functions and emit the proper Deposit and Withdraw events, thereby achieving full IERC4626 compliance. In broader terms, this is a classic case of interface non‑conformance: a contract claims to provide vault functionality but does not expose the standardized API, breaking user expectations that "deposit should work" and causing functional failures that manifest as "transaction reverts with unknown function" or "no tokens received after deposit". By aligning the implementation with the ERC‑4626 spec, the protocol restores composability, ensures that user‑facing interfaces behave as advertised, and upholds the accounting assumptions inherent to tokenized vaults.

title: `CrvDepositorWrapper.sol` relies on oracle that isn’t frequently updated
description:
[CrvDepositorWrapper.sol#L56-L65](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/CrvDepositorWrapper.sol#L56-L65)  

Unpredictable slippage, sandwich vulnerability or frequent failed transactions
poc:
CrvDepostiorWrapper uses the TWAP provided by the 20/80 WETH/BAL. The issue is that this pool has only handled ~15 transactions per day in the last 30 days, which means that the oracle frequently goes more than an hour without updating. Each time a state changing operation is called, the following code in the balancer pool takes a snapshot of the pool state BEFORE any operation changes it:

[OracleWeightedPool.sol#L156-L161](https://github.com/balancer-labs/balancer-v2-monorepo/blob/80e1a5db7439069e2cb53e228bce0a8a51f5b23e/pkg/pool-weighted/contracts/oracle/OracleWeightedPool.sol#L156-L161)  

This could result in the price of the oracle frequently not reflecting the true value of the assets due to infrequency of update. Now also consider that the pool has a trading fee of 2%. Combine an inaccurate oracle with a high fee pool and trades can exhibit high levels of “slippage”. To account for this outputBps in AuraStakingProxy needs to be set relatively low or risks frequent failed transactions when calling distribute due to slippage conditions not being met. The lower outputBps is set the more vulnerable distribute becomes to sandwich attacks.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CrvDepositorWrapper contract which derives the price of a 20/80 WETH/BAL liquidity pool from the pool’s time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle. Because the underlying Balancer pool processes only about fifteen trades per day, the TWAP can remain unchanged for periods exceeding an hour, meaning the oracle frequently returns a stale price that does not reflect the current market value of the underlying assets. The contract captures a snapshot of the pool state before any state‑changing operation, so each call to the wrapper uses this potentially outdated price to compute the expected amount of LP tokens to be minted or redeemed. This stale pricing combined with the pool’s 2 % trading fee creates a situation where the calculated output may be far from the actual amount a user would receive, causing unpredictable slippage. When the contract enforces a low outputBps parameter to avoid frequent transaction reverts, it inadvertently lowers the tolerance for price variance and makes the distribute function highly susceptible to sandwich attacks: an attacker can observe a pending transaction, execute a trade that moves the pool price before the victim’s transaction is mined, and then profit from the victim receiving a worse rate or from the victim’s transaction failing. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms include receiving zero or significantly reduced token amounts, transactions reverting unexpectedly, or a sudden inability to claim rewards despite sufficient balances. The issue affects any participant interacting with the AuraStakingProxy through the CrvDepositorWrapper, including token holders, liquidity providers, and downstream protocols that rely on the wrapper’s price feed. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors noted the low update frequency of the Balancer TWAP and its impact on slippage and sandwich risk. The flaw is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the oracle is stale; it merely produces an out‑of‑range price that only manifests as occasional failed transactions or reduced payouts, making it hard to detect during normal operation. The recommended remediation is to replace the infrequently updated Balancer TWAP with a real‑time price source such as a Chainlink oracle for both BAL and ETH, or to implement a more aggressive keeper system that validates a minimum output before execution. By using a continuously refreshed oracle, the contract can maintain accurate pricing, reduce slippage variance, and mitigate the opportunity for sandwich attacks, thereby aligning the actual user experience with the expected economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Improperly Skewed Governance Mechanism
description:
[AuraLocker.sol#L594-L609](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L594-L609)  
[AuraLocker.sol#L611-L618](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L611-L618)  

File | Lines | Type  
---|---|---  
AuraLocker.sol | [L594-L609](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L594-L609), [L611-L618](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L611-L618) | Governance Susceptibility
poc:
Issue is deducible by inspecting the relevant lines referenced in the issue and making note of the calculations within the `getPastVotes` individual voting power function as well as the `getPastTotalSupply` cumulative voting power function.

This is intended behaviour. There is no incentive for users not to delegate their votes. And even if there were, not delegating is the equivalent to having voting power but not voting. Therefore this is not a relevant issue.

I’m going to leave this one in play and downgrade the severity. The warden’s report is accurate; however, if the required percentages of voting cannot be met, the DAO would simply have to go on a campaign to get people to delegate their votes. This would be annoying but not critically destructive. That said, medium severity makes sense because a bad actor could potentially gather voting power and intentionally disrupt things by not delegating it. I’d recommend implementing the fix suggested by the warden.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the governance accounting logic of the AuraLocker contract, specifically in the way the contract calculates both individual voting power (via the getPastVotes function) and the aggregate voting power of the DAO (via the getPastTotalSupply function). The contract mistakenly treats the total token supply as the total voting supply, without filtering for tokens that have actually been delegated to the governance system. Because delegation is optional, token holders who choose not to delegate retain voting power on paper but are excluded from the actual voting tally, causing the recorded total voting supply to be skewed. This mismatch occurs whenever a token holder either delegates or revokes delegation, yet the contract fails to update the checkpointed total supply to reflect only the delegated balances. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately withholding delegation of a large token balance, thereby artificially reducing the reported total voting supply. With a lower denominator in quorum calculations, the attacker can either make it easier to meet the required voting percentage for malicious proposals, or conversely prevent legitimate proposals from reaching quorum if the contract expects a higher total supply. The impact is a corrupted governance process: proposals may be approved or rejected under incorrect assumptions, quorum thresholds become unreliable, and the DAO’s decision‑making integrity is compromised. The issue becomes visible to users when a proposal appears to have sufficient affirmative votes according to the UI, yet the transaction reverts because the internal quorum check fails, or vice‑versa where a proposal with evident support cannot pass. All DAO participants, token holders, and any downstream protocol that relies on governance decisions are affected because the governance outcomes may no longer reflect the true will of the community. The flaw was discovered through a code review that examined the arithmetic in the getPastVotes and getPastTotalSupply functions, noticing that the total supply was derived from token balances rather than from the sum of delegated voting power. The problem is subtle because the contract still returns non‑zero values for individual votes, and the UI may display vote counts that seem plausible, making the discrepancy easy to overlook during casual testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should track a separate total delegated voting supply that updates on every delegation or undelegation event, and the getPastTotalSupply function should return this adjusted value. By aligning the total voting supply with the actual delegated balances, quorum calculations will correctly reflect the proportion of votes needed, restoring the intended security guarantees of the governance mechanism.

title: `AuraLocker` kick reward only takes last locked amount into consideration, instead of whole balance
description:
The issue occurs in AuraLocker, when expired locks are processed via kicking, and if all the user locks have expired.  
In this scenario, to calculate the kick reward, `_processExpiredLocks` multiplies the last locked amount by the number of epochs between the last lock’s unlock time and the current epoch.  
A comment in this section mentions `"wont have the exact reward rate that you would get if looped through"`. However, there’s no reason not to multiply _user’s whole locked balance_ by the number of epochs since the _last lock’s_ unlock time, _instead of only the last locked amount_.  
While this will still not be as accurate as looping through, this will give a more accurate kick reward result, which is still bounded by the full amount that would have been calculated if we had looped through.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the kick‑reward calculation of the AuraLocker contract. When a user's lock positions have all expired, the contract allows anyone to "kick" the expired locks and collect a reward that is meant to compensate for the time the locks remained unused. The current implementation determines this reward by taking only the amount of the last lock in the user's array of locks, multiplies it by a per‑epoch reward rate, and divides by a denominator. Consequently, the reward is proportional solely to the last lock’s balance, while the total locked balance – the sum of all expired lock amounts – is ignored. The root cause is an intentional gas‑optimisation that skips iterating over the full list of locks; the developers inserted a comment acknowledging that the calculation is an approximation, yet they never adjusted the formula to incorporate the user's overall locked amount. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by triggering the kick function on accounts that have multiple expired locks, thereby receiving a reward that is systematically lower than what the protocol’s economics imply. From the user’s perspective, the expectation is that the kick reward reflects the entire locked stake over the elapsed epochs; instead, users see a smaller reward, often perceived as a missing or partial refund. This economic discrepancy becomes evident when users with large or multiple expired locks repeatedly notice that their kick rewards are consistently below the amount they would receive if the contract summed all lock amounts before applying the reward rate. The issue manifests only when the condition "all locks have expired" is true and the kick‑reward branch (_checkDelay > 0_) is executed; it does not affect cases where at least one lock is still active, because those paths use a different, more accurate calculation. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the low‑gas shortcut against the reference implementation that loops through each lock, and flagged the inconsistency. Because the code intentionally sacrifices precision for gas savings, the under‑payment may go unnoticed in routine testing, especially when the reward differential per epoch is modest. The impact is an economic loss for the protocol: incentives for third‑party actors to clean up expired locks are weakened, leading to stale locks persisting longer and users receiving less compensation than warranted. To remediate, the reward should be computed using the total locked balance (the variable `locked`) multiplied by the same reward rate, rather than using only the last lock’s amount. This change retains the low‑gas advantage while aligning the reward with the protocol’s intended accounting rules, thereby restoring correct incentives and preventing systematic fund loss.

title: Users can grief reward distribution
description: Users can grief reward distributions by spending dust.
poc:
If a reward is targeted for an epoch in the past, a user can front-run the txn in the mempool and call `addRewardToEpoch()` with a dust amount at an epoch after the one in question. This will cause the transaction in the mempool to revert
    
    File: contracts/ExtraRewardsDistributor.sol   #1
    
    require(len == 0 || rewardEpochs[_token][len - 1] < _epoch, "Cannot backdate to this epoch");

[ExtraRewardsDistributor.sol#L74](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/ExtraRewardsDistributor.sol#L74)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a denial‑of‑service (grief) vector in the reward distribution mechanism of the Aura protocol's ExtraRewardsDistributor contract. The contract enforces a strict monotonic ordering of reward epochs, rejecting any attempt to add a reward for an epoch that is earlier than the most recent epoch recorded for a given token. This check is implemented through a require statement that ensures the new epoch identifier is greater than the last stored epoch. The root cause lies in the reliance on this ordering constraint without accounting for transaction ordering within the mempool. An attacker can exploit the situation by front‑running a legitimate transaction that intends to add a reward for a past epoch. By submitting a separate transaction that adds a minimal (dust) reward for a later epoch before the original transaction is mined, the attacker causes the contract's epoch list to contain a newer epoch. Consequently, when the pending legitimate transaction is finally processed, the require condition fails because the contract now sees a later epoch already recorded, leading to a revert of the reward addition. The impact is that users who were expecting to receive rewards for the targeted past epoch experience a failed claim and receive no tokens, effectively losing their expected payout. This grief attack does not steal funds; it merely prevents the distribution of rewards, which can be perceived as a service denial. The vulnerability manifests only when an attacker can observe the pending transaction (e.g., via the public mempool) and has the ability to submit a competing transaction with a higher epoch identifier, even with an arbitrarily small reward amount (dust). All users, reward claimants, and the protocol’s incentive mechanisms are affected because the reliability of reward distribution is compromised. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the epoch backdating protection logic and identified that the simple greater‑than check can be subverted by transaction ordering. It may be hard to notice in standard testing because the failure only occurs under specific front‑running conditions that are not typically simulated. To remediate the issue, the contract should allow rewards to be added for earlier epochs even when later epochs already exist, or it should maintain per‑epoch mappings that are independent of order, thereby eliminating the reliance on a single monotonic list. Conceptually, the fix involves relaxing the backdating restriction or redesigning the data structure to support out‑of‑order epoch inserts, ensuring that a dust transaction cannot invalidate a legitimate reward addition. This addresses the business‑logic violation where the system incorrectly assumes that later rewards cannot be added before earlier ones, which breaks the accounting invariants of the reward distribution scheme.

title: Rewards distribution can be delayed/never distributed on `AuraLocker.sol#L848`
description: Rewards distribution can be delayed/never distributed on [AuraLocker.sol#L848](https://github.com/aurafinance/aura-contracts-lite/blob/main/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L848)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the rewards distribution logic of the AuraLocker contract. When new rewards are queued, the contract checks whether the amount of newly added tokens exceeds 120 % of the tokens already distributed during the current reward period. If this condition is not met, a new reward period is not started and the pending rewards remain locked. Because the threshold is based on a relative increase rather than an absolute minimum, an attacker or even a benign user can submit a reward amount that is too small to satisfy the 120 % rule. In that case the contract never advances to the next distribution window, causing the previously accrued rewards to stay unclaimed indefinitely. This means that users who have locked tokens expect to receive periodic reward payouts, but instead see their reward balance remain at zero, experience missing refunds, or notice that the UI displays "no rewards available" despite having participated in the lock. The flaw is a classic example of a denial‑of‑service or logic‑flaw bug where a protective condition meant to prevent spam unintentionally blocks legitimate reward flow. It manifests whenever the queued reward amount is less than the required 120 % increase, which can happen frequently in low‑volume periods or when an attacker deliberately supplies a minimal reward amount to stall the system. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the contract’s reward queueing function, where the auditor observed that the period‑advancement guard could be satisfied only by a large token addition, leaving the contract in a state where rewards are never distributed. The problem may be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or throw an error; it simply stays silent, and the UI does not provide a clear indication that the distribution mechanism is stalled. To remediate, the reward‑queueing logic should be adjusted to either remove the relative‑increase requirement, replace it with an absolute‑minimum threshold, or add a fallback path that forces period advancement after a reasonable timeout. By ensuring that a new reward period can be started regardless of the exact size of the queued amount, the contract will maintain its intended accounting guarantees and users will receive the rewards they expect.

title: Lido adapter incorrectly calculates the price of the underlying token
description:
The Lido adapter incorrectly calculates the price of WETH in terms of WstETH.

The function returns the price of WstETH in terms of stETH. The underlying token which we desire is WETH. Since stETH does not have the same value as WETH the output price incorrect.

The impact is severe as all the balance calculations require the price of the yield token converted to underlying. The incorrect price may over or understate the harvestable amount which is a core calculation in the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Lido adapter used by the protocol to derive the price of the underlying asset for the wstETH token. The adapter’s price() function calls IWstETH(token).getStETHByWstETH() which converts wstETH to stETH and returns that amount, effectively reporting the price of wstETH in terms of stETH. However, the protocol treats the underlying asset as WETH, which is not equivalently valued to stETH before the Ethereum merge and the activation of withdrawals (Shanghai). Because the conversion from stETH to ETH is omitted, the reported price is systematically inaccurate: it may be higher or lower than the true market rate of WETH. This mis‑pricing propagates to every calculation that relies on the price of the yield token, such as balance updates, harvestable amount determination, and collateral valuation. When the protocol’s accounting code uses the faulty price to compute how much ETH can be harvested or withdrawn, it can either under‑credit users, leaving them with less value than expected, or over‑credit the protocol, effectively leaking value to the contract. The flaw manifests whenever the price() view is invoked, which occurs during deposits, withdrawals, and the periodic harvest routine. All participants—depositors, yield token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because their financial outcomes depend on correct accounting. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewer traced the price source and noted that the function never performed the required stETH‑to‑ETH conversion. It is subtle because the raw stETH value looks plausible and the UI may display normal balances, making the discrepancy hard to spot without deep inspection of the conversion logic. To remediate, the price() implementation must be extended to include the additional conversion step from stETH to ETH, for example by querying the same Curve pool that the unwrap() function uses, or by deferring to a future direct redemption mechanism once withdrawals are enabled. This adjustment restores the proper like‑kind collateral model where wstETH is valued against its true underlying WETH, eliminating the potential for discounted asset accrual and aligning on‑chain accounting with user expectations.

title: If `totalShares` for a token falls to zero while there is `pendingCredit` the contract will become stuck
description:
[AlchemistV2.sol#L1290-L1300](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/de65c34c7b6e4e94662bf508e214dcbf327984f4/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1290-L1300)  
[AlchemistV2.sol#L1268](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/de65c34c7b6e4e94662bf508e214dcbf327984f4/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1268)  
[AlchemistV2.sol#L1532](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/de65c34c7b6e4e94662bf508e214dcbf327984f4/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1532)  
[AlchemistV2.sol#L899](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/de65c34c7b6e4e94662bf508e214dcbf327984f4/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L899)  
[AlchemistV2.sol#L1625](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-alchemix/blob/de65c34c7b6e4e94662bf508e214dcbf327984f4/contracts-full/AlchemistV2.sol#L1625)  

It is possible for the contract to become stuck and unable to perform any actions if the `totalShares` of a yield token fall to zero while there is some `pendingCredit` still to be paid.

It will then be impossible to call deposit or withdraw functions, mints, burns, repay, liquidate, donate or harvest due to division by zero reverts in:
  * `_distributeCredit()`
  * `_distributeUnlockedCredit()`
  * `_calculateUnrealizedDebt()`
  * `_convertSharesToYieldTokens()`
  * `donate()`

Furthermore, any `pendingCredit` amount of tokens are still in the contract will become permanently stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by a division‑by‑zero error that occurs when the accounting variable representing the total number of shares for a yield token (totalShares) becomes zero while there is still a non‑zero amount of pending credit awaiting distribution. The contract assumes that totalShares is always positive when calculating ratios for credit distribution, share conversion, and unrealized debt; this assumption is violated when the last user withdraws all of their shares after a harvest has generated pending credit. At that point, internal functions such as _distributeCredit, _distributeUnlockedCredit, _calculateUnrealizedDebt, _convertSharesToYieldTokens and donate attempt to divide a numerator by totalShares, which is now zero, causing the transaction to revert with a division‑by‑zero exception. As a result, the contract can no longer accept deposits, process withdrawals, mint or burn tokens, repay loans, liquidate positions, accept donations, or harvest rewards. Any pending credit that was accumulated before totalShares reached zero remains locked in the contract forever, effectively freezing those rewards and preventing future users from interacting with the protocol. This state can be triggered when a user fully withdraws their position after a keeper has harvested rewards, leaving pendingCredit > 0 but totalShares = 0. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the AlchemistV2 contract, where the auditor traced the share‑to‑token conversion logic and identified the unchecked division. Because the condition only arises in an edge case where the last share is removed, it may be difficult to notice in normal operation, especially when the protocol has many active users and the totalShares rarely reaches zero. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that totalShares never becomes zero while pending credit exists—for example by requiring the final user to retain at least one minimal share, by automatically burning a small amount of shares on the first deposit, or by transferring any remaining pending credit to the withdrawing user and resetting the accounting variables when the last share is withdrawn. Such fixes restore the invariant that totalShares > 0 whenever credit distribution calculations are performed, eliminating the division‑by‑zero revert and preventing the protocol from becoming permanently locked.

title: Debt can be repaid with a depegged underlyingToken, which can be exploited by arbitrageurs and drives the market price of alToken to match the worst depegged underlyingToken
poc:
Given:
  * alUSD is trading at $1
  * minimumCollateralization: 4/3
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way AlchemistV2 normalizes the amount of an underlying token when a borrower repays debt. The internal function _normalizeUnderlyingTokensToDebt simply multiplies the supplied amount by a static conversionFactor that reflects token decimals, implicitly assuming a 1:1 price relationship between the underlying token and the synthetic alToken debt representation. Because this conversion does not reference any on‑chain price oracle or market data, the repayment calculation ignores the actual market price of the underlying asset. When an underlying token depegs – that is, its market value diverges from the assumed parity – an attacker can exploit the discrepancy. By minting alTokens (which represent a claim on the underlying collateral) and selling them on the open market for the depegged underlying token, the attacker obtains a larger amount of the cheap underlying token than the nominal debt value would suggest. The attacker then calls repay() with the depegged token; the contract records a full debt reduction based on the static conversion factor, even though the underlying token supplied is worth less in market terms. Consequently, the protocol’s accounting is skewed: the debt is considered repaid while the protocol has effectively been under‑collateralized, and the market price of alToken is driven downward to reflect the lower‑value underlying token. This issue manifests only when the repayment token’s market price deviates from the assumed 1:1 peg, which may happen during a depeg event or prolonged market stress. Users who hold alTokens experience a reduction in the token’s purchasing power – they expect their alTokens to retain a stable value but instead observe a drop in price or a loss of buying power. The flaw was identified during a manual audit of the repay() implementation, where the fixed conversionFactor was noted as a potential source of price mismatch; however, because the code follows a common pattern of using token decimals for scaling, the problem is not readily apparent without scrutinizing economic assumptions. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “price‑oracle‑independent debt normalization” bugs, where on‑chain accounting assumes static parity instead of dynamic market pricing, leading to accounting inconsistencies and exploitable arbitrage. To remediate, the protocol should replace the static conversionFactor with a market‑driven price feed when converting repayment amounts to debt units, or otherwise restrict repayments to assets that maintain a reliable peg, and update the repay() logic to burn the corresponding alTokens based on the actual market exchange rate. Such a change would align the recorded debt reduction with the true economic value transferred, preventing arbitrageurs from profiting by exploiting depegged assets and preserving the intended value of alTokens for legitimate users.

title: Donation attack using paymentToken affects intended protocol behavior
bug_full: Thevulnerability is an economic logic flaw that allows an attacker to manipulate the market‑cap check of a bonding‑curve token sale by directly transferring the payment token to the contract. The contract’s isMarketCapReached function determines whether the required market cap has been reached by calling paymentToken.balanceOf(address(this)) and comparing it to a fixed threshold. Because this check relies on the external token balance rather than on an internal accounting of tokens sold through the buyTokens function, an adversary can donate exactly the threshold amount of payment token to the contract without purchasing any agent tokens. Once the balance condition is satisfied, the next call to buyTokens with a minimal amount triggers the automatic creation of a liquidity‑pool (LP) position, even though the bonding curve has not progressed as intended. This early LP creation inflates the amount of agent tokens allocated to the pool, resulting in a devalued pool price and an inflated contribution amount that is transferred to the attacker if they are the sole buyer. The impact is that the protocol’s intended token distribution and price discovery mechanisms are subverted: the LP price is lower than expected, the remaining token supply for future buyers is reduced, and the attacker can capture the entire inflated contributor distribution for a small investment. The condition occurs whenever automaticLPCreation is enabled, the market‑cap flag is true, and no additional safeguards prevent LP creation based on external token balances. All participants who rely on the bonding‑curve economics—such as token purchasers, liquidity providers, and the protocol governance—are affected because the economic guarantees of the sale are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the market‑cap oracle logic and noticed that the balance check could be satisfied by arbitrary token transfers. It is hard to notice because the balanceOf call appears legitimate and there is no explicit restriction on the source of the tokens, making the check look like a standard threshold verification. To remediate, the contract should track the amount of payment token received through its own buyTokens logic and use that internal counter for the market‑cap condition, or otherwise require that LP creation be gated by a permissioned function or additional verification that the tokens were acquired via the sale process. This change eliminates the ability to inflate the market‑cap flag with external donations and restores the intended bonding‑curve behavior, preventing the attacker from creating an LP prematurely and capturing inflated rewards.

title: Donation attack using agentToken shifts the bonding curve
description:
The buyTokens and sellTokens (subsequently calculateSellReturn) methods of the Agent contract rely on the actual balance of agentToken in the contract using balanceOf to determine the current buy/sell price according to the bonding curve. However, the actual balance and therefore the price calculation can be manipulated by donating agentToken to the contract.

Impact Explanation:  
Medium: The bonding curve is shifted, i.e. buy prices as well as sell prices become lower than expected and intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑oracle manipulation flaw that arises because the Agent contract calculates token buy and sell amounts directly from the on‑chain balance of the agentToken using the ERC20 balanceOf function. The bonding curve logic assumes that the contract’s token balance reflects only tokens that have been purchased through the buyTokens function, but any external transfer of agentToken into the contract – for example a direct donation – changes the reported balance without a corresponding update to the internal accounting. As a result the curve’s state is shifted: the denominator in the price formula becomes larger, causing both buy prices and sell returns to be lower than the economic model intends. An attacker can exploit this by sending a modest amount of agentToken to the contract before legitimate users interact, thereby reducing the amount of new tokens a buyer receives for a given payment and decreasing the amount a seller receives when redeeming tokens. The impact is that users may receive fewer tokens than expected when buying, or obtain a reduced payout when selling, effectively losing value. This condition occurs whenever the contract’s balance can be altered by external token transfers, which is possible because the contract does not restrict incoming token transfers nor does it maintain a separate internal ledger for the token supply used in the curve calculations. All participants that interact with the contract after the manipulation are affected, including regular users and the protocol’s liquidity pool. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the price‑calculation functions and noticed the reliance on balanceOf instead of a trusted internal counter. The flaw can be subtle because the contract still appears to hold the correct total token supply, and the price deviation may only be noticeable when users observe unexpectedly low returns. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain its own accounting variable that tracks the amount of agentToken minted or burned through the bonding curve, and use that internal value for price calculations, thereby isolating the curve from arbitrary external token deposits. This class of bug falls under price‑oracle manipulation via uncontrolled token balance reads, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the on‑chain balance equals the protocol‑controlled supply.

title: Incompatible Token Standard Handling in ERC20 Operations
description:
In the Agent contract, ERC20 operations such as transfer, transferFrom, and approve rely on the assumption that the underlying token strictly adheres to the ERC20 standard, specifically by returning a boolean value. The contract uses the IERC20Metadata interface, which declares these functions with a returns (bool) signature. However, several widely-used tokens — most notably USDT (Tether) — deviate from the ERC20 standard by not returning a value or by reverting on failure silently, making them incompatible with this implementation.  
Consequently, any interaction with such tokens (e.g., fee claiming, liquidity provisioning via createLPPosition, or any approve operation) would result in a revert. This prevents the creation of an Agent with such tokens and blocks further functionality, limiting interoperability and creating unnecessary friction for users attempting to use popular non-compliant tokens.

Impact Explanation:  
High, because this issue completely blocks the functionality of the contract with non-standard tokens like USDT. Users will be unable to create agents, stake, or claim fees using such tokens, leading to failed interactions and degraded protocol usability. This limitation could also impact protocol adoption if users cannot use tokens they expect to work seamlessly.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s assumption that every ERC20 token strictly follows the original ERC20 specification by returning a boolean value from transfer, transferFrom and approve calls. The Agent contract imports IERC20Metadata, which declares these functions with a returns(bool) signature, and then calls them directly. However, several widely‑used tokens, most notably USDT, deviate from the spec: they either omit the return value or silently revert on failure. When the contract invokes such a non‑standard token, the Solidity runtime expects a 32‑byte boolean in the returned data; the absence of this data causes the low‑level call to fail and the whole transaction to revert. Consequently, any operation that relies on token transfers – fee claiming, liquidity provisioning via createLPPosition, approvals, or even the initial creation of an Agent – will be blocked when the supplied token is non‑compliant. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who simply supplies a non‑standard token to cause a denial‑of‑service, preventing users from creating agents, staking, or claiming fees. The impact is high for affected users because they see transaction failures, UI messages such as “failed to create agent” or “operation reverted”, and their balances remain unchanged despite expecting a transfer or approval. The issue manifests only when the contract interacts with tokens that do not return a boolean, so standard ERC20 tokens work as intended while popular tokens like USDT break the workflow. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s interface against the ERC20 standard and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the failure only appears at runtime with specific tokens, leading developers to misinterpret the revert as a generic bug. To remediate, the contract should stop relying on the boolean return and instead use OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which wraps token calls with low‑level checks that handle missing return data and silent failures. Alternatively, refactoring the interface to IERC20 (without a bool return) and employing safeTransfer, safeTransferFrom and safeApprove functions would normalize behavior across both compliant and non‑compliant tokens, restoring interoperability and preventing the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: Mispricing at Bonding Curve Terminal Due to Incorrect Price Approximation
description:
In the Agent contract, the bonding curve implements a price function that asymptotically approaches infinity as token supply is depleted. Mathematically:  
P(x) = (a / (D − x − o + 1)) · P0  
Where:  
• x is the number of tokens sold (or the complement of current balance).  
• a = CURVE_NUMERATOR.  
• D = CURVE_DENOMINATOR.  
• o = CURVE_OFFSET.  
• P_0 = initialPrice.  
As x → D, the denominator of the curve approaches zero, and the price diverges toward infinity. However, in the current Solidity implementation, calculatePrice(0) — which represents the case where all tokens are sold (i.e., currentBalance == 0) — returns a capped value such as initialPrice * 1000.  
This approximation introduces significant inaccuracies during high-end curve interactions, especially for large buy operations nearing full supply depletion. While this is meant as a safety fallback to avoid division-by-zero, it results in the following issue:  
• The price at full supply (P(D - 1)) should be:  
P(D − 1) = (35,190,005,730 / (-32 + 1)) · P0 = 35,190,005,699 · P0  
• But the contract may return:  
P(0) = 1000 · P0.  
This results in a mispriced endPrice during calculateAveragePrice() calls for buys close to terminal supply, severely undervaluing tokens and breaking the intended convex price dynamics of the bonding curve.  
Given that the average price formula for buys is:  
Pavg = Pstart + 3 · Pend  
If P_end is incorrectly capped, the resulting P_avg is significantly lower than expected, allowing users to purchase tokens below their intended cost. The issue is amplified due to the buy-weighted averaging favoring endPrice.  
Exploitation Scenario:  
1. A buyer targets a moment when the remaining token supply is minimal.  
2. tokenAmount pushes endBalance = 0.  
3. calculatePrice(0) returns initialPrice * 1000 rather than the mathematically correct terminal value (~$35B).  
4. averagePrice is vastly under-calculated.  
5. The buyer receives tokens at a deep discount.  
6. If LP creation hasn't occurred yet (or is delayed), the user can resell those tokens through the curve or other mechanisms, profiting from the mispricing.  
Mitigations and Friction Points:  
• The buyToken function checks:  
```solidity
scaledTokensSoldPercentage + scaledNewTokensPercentage < CURVE_DENOMINATOR * PRECISION;
```  
This may not be a sufficient boundary, as it incorrectly uses CURVE_DENOMINATOR instead of 1 * PRECISION, failing to prevent x → D edge conditions.  
• The isMarketCapReached() function typically finalizes the curve by triggering LP creation before this scenario manifests, acting as a strong preventative layer.  
• Additionally, the sellPenalty mechanism discourages arbitrage unless the market deviates by 10% or more, providing an additional disincentive in many practical cases.

Impact Explanation:  
High, because if a user manages to purchase tokens at the terminal end of the bonding curve and receives them at a mispriced average (far below intended value), it could result in extractable economic value and undermine the curve’s integrity. This breaks the expected cost gradient of the curve and could be exploited to drain protocol value under precise timing or adversarial automation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mispricing error that occurs at the terminal point of a bonding‑curve token sale when the remaining supply approaches zero. The contract’s price function is designed to grow without bound as the denominator (D‑x‑o+1) shrinks, but the Solidity implementation substitutes a hard‑coded fallback in calculatePrice(0) that returns initialPrice * 1000 instead of the mathematically correct asymptotic value. This approximation is introduced to avoid a division‑by‑zero exception, yet it caps the price far below what the curve dictates, causing the average‑price calculation for large buys that empty the curve to be severely understated. An attacker can trigger the condition by submitting a purchase that drives the token balance to zero, causing calculatePrice to return the low fallback, which in turn makes the average price (computed as Pstart + 3 * Pend) dramatically lower than intended. The attacker then receives a large amount of tokens for a fraction of their true cost and can resell them, extracting economic value from the protocol. The issue manifests only when a transaction pushes the supply to the extreme edge; normal trades do not expose the bug because the boundary check uses CURVE_DENOMINATOR instead of a proper precision limit, allowing the edge case to slip through. Affected parties include token buyers, the protocol’s economic model, and any stakeholder relying on the convex price dynamics of the curve. The bug was uncovered during a manual audit of the bonding‑curve mathematics, where the auditor observed that calculatePrice returned a constant multiplier for a zero balance rather than a value that grows as the denominator approaches zero. The problem is subtle because the fallback prevents a runtime error, so the contract appears functional for most operations, and the extreme discount only appears when the supply is almost exhausted—a scenario that may not be covered by routine tests. This belongs to the class of price‑oracle approximation errors caused by incorrect handling of edge‑case division‑by‑zero, leading to an artificial price cap. To remediate, the contract should either simulate the final step of the curve by using x = CURVE_DENOMINATOR‑1 or pre‑compute and return the correct terminal multiplier, thereby ensuring that calculatePrice reflects the intended asymptotic price. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal price for small purchases but suddenly display a dramatically lower price when the remaining supply is tiny, violating the expectation that the price should increase sharply. Users may see tokens being credited at a near‑zero cost, experience confusion, and suspect a scam, while the protocol suffers a loss of value because funds effectively disappear when sold far below market price.

title: Anyone can cause DoS of the distributeTokens method
description:
The distributeTokens method of the Agent contract transfers each share of the agent token distribution to the corresponding contributor using ERC-20 transfers in a for-loop. Since the maximum number of contributors (length of the contributors storage array) is unbounded, the for-loop might exceed the block gas limit due to the costly transfers.

Impact Explanation:  
High: DoS of the distributeTokens method once the for-loop of agent token transfers exceeds the block gas limit if the contributors array is too large. Consequently, the main use case of the protocol will be dysfunctional and agent tokens become stuck in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token distribution routine that iterates over an unbounded list of contributors and performs an ERC‑20 transfer for each entry inside a single transaction. Because the length of the contributors storage array is not limited, an attacker or any participant can increase the array size until the cumulative gas required for all transfer calls exceeds the block gas limit. When the distributeTokens method is invoked under these conditions the transaction runs out of gas, reverts, and the distribution process is halted. As a result the contract’s internal balance of agent tokens remains locked and no contributor receives their expected share, breaking the core accounting assumption that every holder will be automatically credited after a distribution event. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the for‑loop logic and recognized that the gas consumption grows linearly with the number of contributors, a classic unbounded‑loop‑gas‑exhaustion denial‑of‑service pattern. It can be hard to notice because the function works correctly with a modest number of participants, so normal testing does not reveal the failure until the array grows beyond realistic limits. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a distribution has been executed, yet the displayed token balance stays unchanged and the user receives nothing, contrary to the expectation of an automatic refund or reward. The impact is high for the protocol because the primary use case—automated token sharing—becomes non‑functional, effectively freezing the allocated tokens. The flaw affects all token holders, contributors, and any downstream services that rely on the distribution completing. The recommended mitigation is to replace the push‑style transfer with a pull‑style claim mechanism, allowing each contributor to withdraw their share individually, or to introduce batching or off‑chain settlement techniques that keep the on‑chain work within safe gas limits. This redesign eliminates the unbounded loop, restores predictable gas usage, and ensures that funds can be claimed even when the contributor set is large.

title: Incorrect calculation of interests when taking fee
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the interest fee that is taken from a user’s position. The contract’s internal function that collects the fee first reads the user’s outstanding interest and then calls a helper that returns the user’s collateral. The helper computes collateral as the user’s token balance minus the same outstanding interest value. Because the same interest amount is subtracted twice – once explicitly in the fee‑collection logic and once implicitly inside the collateral helper – the resulting interest that is actually charged can be lower than it should be, or, when the interest exceeds the balance, the subtraction in the helper can underflow. This mis‑calculation occurs whenever the fee‑collection routine is invoked, which in the current code happens only during withdraw or liquidate operations. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the fee collection while the contract’s balance is sufficient to cover the full interest, but the double subtraction causes the contract to treat only a fraction of the interest as payable. Consequently the protocol receives less fee revenue than intended, and the user may be able to withdraw more assets than the economic model permits. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the expected fee is missing or appears unusually low – for example a user with a 15 USD balance and 10 USD accrued interest sees only 5 USD deducted as fee, even though the full 10 USD should have been taken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑collection path, where the auditor noticed that the collateral helper already accounts for interest and that the subsequent conditional cap on interest re‑applies the same subtraction. The bug is subtle because the code appears to guard against over‑charging by capping interest to collateral, yet the collateral value itself is already reduced by the interest, making the guard ineffective. The class of bug is a double‑counting / incorrect accounting error in financial smart contracts, where a value is subtracted twice, leading to under‑payment of fees or potential underflow. To fix the problem the fee‑collection routine should obtain the raw token balance directly, without subtracting interest, and then cap the interest to that raw balance. After correcting the calculation, the fee should be transferred to the designated recipient and the interest state reset. Optionally, exposing the fee‑collection function publicly would allow anyone to trigger fee collection promptly, preventing timing‑related loss of fees.

title: If a rewards schedule's start time is set as 0, reward interests do not get accumulated
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect early‑exit condition in the reward‑calculation routine of the WrappedVault contract. When a rewards interval is created with a start timestamp of zero, the internal function _calculateRewardsPerToken checks if (rewardsInterval_.start == 0) and therefore skips the accumulation of reward interest for the whole interval. The contract assumes that a start value of zero means no active schedule, but the protocol allows an immediate‑start schedule where start can legitimately be zero. As a result, any user who deposits tokens while such a schedule is active sees no increase in their reward balance; the vault retains the allocated reward tokens and the user’s balance remains unchanged. The bug manifests whenever the setRewardsInterval or extendRewardsInterval functions are called with a start argument of 0, and the condition is evaluated during deposit, claim or any operation that triggers reward‑per‑token updates. It affects all participants of the incentive program, breaking the economic model that promises accrued rewards, and may lead to loss of trust because funds appear to disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case where the start time was set to zero; the test showed that after the rewards period elapsed the user’s reward token balance stayed at zero while the vault still held the undistributed amount. The problem is subtle because zero is a common sentinel value in many contracts, so developers may not expect it to be a valid start time, and the early‑return hides the bug from normal execution paths. The correct fix is to replace the start‑zero check with a check of the reward rate (or another indicator of an active schedule) so that reward accumulation proceeds whenever the rate is non‑zero, even if the start timestamp is zero. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards should accrue from the moment the interval begins, regardless of whether the start value is zero or a future timestamp.

title: The rewardsAdded calculation in extendRewardsInterval is incorrect
description:
The rewardsAdded calculation in extendRewardsInterval is incorrect. The rewardsAdded and the new rate are calculated as below in extendRewardsInterval:

```solidity
uint256 remainingRewards = rewardsInterval.rate * (rewardsInterval.end - newStart);
uint256 rate = (rewardsAdded - frontendFeeTaken - protocolFeeTaken + remainingRewards) / (newEnd - newStart);
rewardsAdded = (rate - rewardsInterval.rate) * (newEnd - newStart) + frontendFeeTaken + protocolFeeTaken;
```

we have:

ar = rold(te,0 −ts,1)  
rnew = floor(a0 + ar −f / (te,1 −ts,1))  

and so a1 should have been calculated as:  

a0 ≥ a1 = rnew(te,1 −ts,1) −ar + f  
or  
a1 = rnew(te,1 −ts,1) −rold(te,0 −ts,1) + f  

but the current implementation incorrectly calculates a1 as:  

a1,incorrect = (rnew −rold)(te,1 −ts,1) + f  

which assumes that te,1 and te,0 are equal. The effect would be that the vault pulls less funds from the owner of the vault which would not match the newly set rate. The discrepancy is the following:  

a1 − a1,incorrect = rold(te,1 −te,0) = rold∆te  

| parameter | description |
|----------|-------------|
| rold | rewardsInterval.rate |
| rnew | rate |
| ar | remainingRewards |
| a0 | rewardsAdded before update |
| a1 | rewardsAdded after update |
| f | frontendFeeTaken + protocolFeeTaken |
| ts,0 | rewardsInterval.start before update |
| ts,1 | newStart |
| te,0 | rewardsInterval.end |
| te,1 | newEnd |
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect arithmetic calculation performed when a rewards interval is extended in the extendRewardsInterval function. The contract attempts to compute the additional rewards (rewardsAdded) and the new reward rate based on the old rate, the remaining rewards, and the fees taken by the frontend and the protocol. However, the implemented formula assumes that the old interval end time and the new interval end time are identical, effectively omitting the term that accounts for the time difference between the old end (te,0) and the new end (te,1). As a result, the computed rewardsAdded value is smaller than it should be by an amount equal to the old rate multiplied by the time delta (rold × (te,1 − te,0)). This mis‑calculation causes the vault to pull fewer funds from the owner than required to match the newly set rate, leading to a shortfall in the total rewards that should be distributed and a mismatch between the expected and actual fee amounts. The bug manifests only when the caller extends the interval with a new end time that differs from the previous end, a condition that is common in dynamic reward programs. Users and protocol participants notice the issue as missing or reduced rewards, zero or unexpectedly low balances after an extension, and frontend fees that are lower than advertised. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting equations with the on‑chain implementation and identified the missing time‑difference term. It is hard to spot because the numerical discrepancy may be small for short extensions and can be masked by rounding, making the contract appear to work correctly in many test cases. To remediate the issue, the rewardsAdded calculation should be rewritten to explicitly subtract the previously accounted remaining rewards and then add the taken fees, using the correct duration of the new interval: rewardsAdded = rate * (newEnd − newStart) − remainingRewards + frontendFeeTaken + protocolFeeTaken. This adjustment restores the accounting invariants, ensures that the vault extracts the proper amount of funds, and aligns the actual reward distribution with the protocol’s business logic.

title: Inflation of zero totalBorrowShares to disable borrowing is possible
description:
• When totalBorrowShares equals zero, an attacker can exploit the rounding by borrowing SHARES_OFFSET - 1 shares.
– Initially, totalBorrowShares = 0 and totalBorrowAssets = 0.
– The borrow amount (borrowAssets) is calculated as:
borrowAssets = (borrowShares * totalBorrowAssets) / (totalBorrowShares + SHARES_OFFSET)
= (SHARES_OFFSET - 1) * 1 / SHARES_OFFSET = 0
– The attacker receives SHARES_OFFSET borrowShares and 0 borrowAssets, causing totalBorrowShares to increase by SHARES_OFFSET - 1.
– Repeating this process in a loop, the attacker exponentially inflates totalBorrowShares by borrowing totalBorrowShares + SHARES_OFFSET -1 of shares each time, while keeping totalBorrowAssets at 0.
• The attacker continues until totalBorrowShares reaches type(uint128).max. No collateral is required since the attacker hasn't borrowed any assets.
• At this point, genuine users are unable to borrow even a minimal amount because borrowing 1 wei results in an overflow: borrowShares minted > type(uint).max.
• Additionally, since repaying debts on behalf of others is allowed, the attacker can reset totalBorrowShares to zero when the market is in use to execute the attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding flaw in the borrowing logic of a lending market that allows an attacker to inflate the internal counter of total borrowed shares while keeping the total borrowed assets at zero. The root cause is the use of a virtual‑share calculation that adds a constant offset (SHARES_OFFSET) to the denominator when converting requested shares to assets. When totalBorrowShares is initially zero, the formula (borrowShares * totalBorrowAssets) / (totalBorrowShares + SHARES_OFFSET) evaluates to zero for any borrowShares that is less than SHARES_OFFSET, meaning the borrower receives no assets even though shares are minted. By requesting exactly SHARES_OFFSET‑1 shares, the attacker can mint SHARES_OFFSET shares, increase totalBorrowShares by SHARES_OFFSET‑1, and still receive zero assets. Repeating this step in a loop causes totalBorrowShares to grow exponentially while totalBorrowAssets remains zero. Once totalBorrowShares approaches the maximum value of a uint128, any attempt by a legitimate user to borrow even a single wei of assets would require minting more shares than the type can hold, triggering an arithmetic overflow and causing the transaction to revert. Because the protocol permits repaying on behalf of others, the attacker can also reset totalBorrowShares to zero after the market is in use, allowing the attack to be re‑executed at will. The impact is that honest borrowers are unable to obtain any funds; the UI may show a successful borrow transaction but the user’s balance does not change, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The attack does not require collateral because the borrowed asset amount is zero, so the attacker’s position appears legitimate while effectively locking the market. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the tester crafted a loop that repeatedly called the borrow function with zero assets and observed the unchecked growth of totalBorrowShares. It is hard to notice because the borrow operation appears to succeed, no tokens are transferred, and the internal share counter is not exposed to end‑users. The recommended mitigation is to stop using the virtual‑share rounding scheme and instead compute assets directly from shares (or vice‑versa) with proper rounding direction, and to enforce a minimum asset amount when only shares are supplied to the borrow endpoint. Adding a lower‑bound check such as require(assets > minimumBorrow) ensures that a borrow request that would result in zero assets is rejected, preventing the share inflation path. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “share‑to‑asset rounding and overflow” vulnerabilities that break the accounting invariants of a lending protocol, allowing an attacker to disable borrowing for all users without moving any funds.

title: Inconsistency between precision factors / dimensional analysis
description:
The precision/dimensional analysis for rewardsRate and dahliaRate are matching:
10^18[I]
[T][L]
and in this case where [I] = [L] simplifies to:
10^18
[T]
The discrepancy arises when one looks at the code in VaultMarketHub.allocateOffer(...) (VaultMarketHub.sol#L232-L234):
offer.incentivesRatesRequested[i] > WrappedVault(offer.targetVault).previewRateAfterDeposit(offer.incentivesRequested[i], fillAmount)
In this comparison both sides should have the same precision/dimension. According to the NatSpec for incentivesRatesRequested (VaultMarketHub.sol#L23-L24) we have:
/// @custom:field incentivesRatesRequested The desired incentives per input token per second to fill the offer, measured in
/// wei of incentives per wei of deposited assets per second, scaled up by 1e18 to avoid precision loss
or in other words:
[incentivesRatesRequested] = 10^18 · (10^18/10^dI)[I] / [T](10^18/10^dL)[L] = 10^18+dL−dI[I] / [T][L]
In the finding the notation [·] represents the precision ( prec = 10^x ) or dimension of a quantity.
parameter description
I reward
L DEPOSIT_ASSET or loan token of the corresponding Dahlia market.
T timestamp in seconds
dX X.decimals()
And so as soon as the reward and deposit token do not have the same decimals the precision of WrappedVault(offer.targetVault).previewRateAfterDeposit(...) and offer.incentivesRatesRequested[I] would not match.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision and dimensional mismatch between the incentives rate supplied by a market maker and the rate calculated by the vault when an offer is allocated. The contract expects the value offer.incentivesRatesRequested[i] to be expressed as wei of incentives per wei of deposited assets per second, scaled up by 1e18, and it compares this value directly with the result of WrappedVault.previewRateAfterDeposit. However, previewRateAfterDeposit returns a rate that is also scaled by 1e18 but does not incorporate the difference in decimal places between the reward token (I) and the deposit asset (L). When the two tokens have different decimals, the two sides of the comparison are off by a factor of 10^(dL‑dI). This root‑cause stems from an incomplete dimensional analysis: the NatSpec documentation describes the expected dimension as 10^18·(10^18/10^dI)[I]/[T](10^18/10^dL)[L], but the implementation omits the 10^(dL‑dI) adjustment. An attacker or a careless user can craft an offer with mismatched token decimals that passes the comparison with an unintended rate, causing the protocol to either under‑pay or over‑pay incentives. The impact is economic: liquidity providers may receive fewer rewards than promised, or the protocol may dispense excess incentives, draining treasury funds. The bug manifests only when the reward token and the deposit token do not share the same decimal precision; in markets where both tokens have identical decimals the mismatch is invisible. It was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑checked the NatSpec comments with the actual code paths and noticed the missing scaling factor. The issue is subtle because both numbers are large 10^18‑scaled integers, making the discrepancy hard to spot without explicit unit analysis or tests covering heterogeneous token decimals. To remediate, the previewRateAfterDeposit function should be modified to apply the additional scaling factor of 10^(dL‑dI) (or equivalently, the comparison should normalize both sides to a common precision) before the > check. This aligns the dimensions, restores the intended business logic that incentives are paid exactly per second per deposited asset, and prevents unintended loss or gain of funds.

title: minDepositAmount check in deposit() doesn't include the user's locked balance
description:
The deposit() function ensures that the amount currently being deposited is not less than minDepositAmount:
```solidity
function deposit(uint256 amount) external nonReentrant {
    if (amount < minDepositAmount) {
        revert MinimumDepositNotMet();
}
```
However, this check does not include the amount of DEGEN tokens currently locked by the user. If a user currently holds some LDEGEN and wants to lock more, the new amount of tokens to deposit has to be more than minDepositAmount. For example:
• minDepositAmount is 10,000 DEGEN.
• User calls deposit() with 10,000 DEGEN.
• After a period of time, the user wants to increase his locked DEGEN amount to 15,000.
• He calls deposit() with amount = 5000e18 to increase his locked amount:
– The check shown above reverts as amount < minDepositAmount.
As shown above, the user is forced to deposit more than minDepositAmount of DEGEN again, even though his current LDEGEN balance is above the minimum deposit.
bug_full: The contract’s deposit() function enforces a minimum deposit amount by checking only the value supplied in the transaction, i.e. it verifies that the incoming amount is greater than or equal to minDepositAmount and reverts otherwise. The logical flaw is that this verification ignores any DEGEN tokens the caller already has locked in the protocol (the LDEGEN balance). As a result, a user who already satisfies the minimum requirement cannot increase their locked balance with a small additional amount because the check still compares the new amount alone against the threshold. This situation occurs whenever a user who has previously deposited at least minDepositAmount attempts to top‑up with a value smaller than the threshold, for example depositing an extra 5 000 DEGEN after already holding 10 000 DEGEN. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with a “MinimumDepositNotMet” error, the UI may display a generic revert message, and the user sees no change in their locked balance despite having sufficient total holdings. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service‑like condition: legitimate participants are prevented from incrementally adding to their stake, which can lead to loss of expected rewards, reduced participation, or frustration that may drive users away from the protocol. The issue was identified during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the condition does not incorporate the caller’s existing balance. It can be hard to spot because the initial deposit works correctly and the error only appears on subsequent deposits, making the failure mode appear intermittent. The vulnerability belongs to the class of business‑logic errors where input validation does not consider the full state, leading to incorrect enforcement of protocol rules. To remediate the problem the deposit() check should be rewritten to compare the sum of the caller’s current locked balance and the new amount against minDepositAmount, thereby ensuring that the total locked amount always satisfies the minimum requirement. This conceptual fix restores the intended accounting invariant and prevents users from being blocked when adding small amounts to an already sufficient balance.

title: Unnecessary payable functions may lead to permanently locked funds
description: The payable modifier on withdraw and claimInterest enables callers to pass nonzero msg.value which is not used by the function implementation. There is no functionality anywhere to withdraw these funds so they will be stuck permanently.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of functions that are marked payable but do not contain any logic that utilizes or returns the ether sent with the call. Because the functions simply perform a withdrawal or interest claim without handling msg.value, any non‑zero ether transferred to them is accepted by the EVM and then becomes part of the contract's balance with no code path to retrieve it. This situation arises when the developer adds the payable modifier out of habit or copies a template without removing it. An attacker or any user can unintentionally or deliberately send ether together with a call to withdraw or claimInterest. The transaction will succeed, the contract will accept the ether, but the function will ignore it, so the sent amount is permanently locked inside the contract because no other function provides a way to transfer those funds out. The impact is that users may lose ether they thought they were sending as a fee or mistakenly, leading to a reduction of available liquidity and potentially breaking the economic model of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a caller includes a non‑zero value in the call data; it does not depend on any particular state of the contract.
