All participants—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the locked ether reduces the total assets under management. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected function modifiers and noticed that payable was present on functions that never read msg.value nor forward it. Because the functions appear to work correctly from a functional standpoint, the hidden loss of ether can be hard to notice unless the contract's balance is audited or compared against expected totals. The bug belongs to the class of “unintended payable” or “ether‑locking” vulnerabilities, where a contract unintentionally accepts ether without a withdrawal path. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction, but the user’s wallet will show a reduction in balance and no corresponding credit or reward, leading to confusion such as user expects refund but receives 0. The correct mitigation is to remove the payable modifier from any function that does not need to receive ether, or alternatively add explicit checks that reject non‑zero msg.value and emit a revert with a clear error message. By ensuring that only intended functions can receive ether, the contract prevents accidental fund lock‑up and preserves the integrity of its accounting.

title: Vault tokens lose fungibility after a user claims interest
description:
As explained in the finding "WrappedVault share transfers results in stuck funds":
Only the wrappedVault is allowed to lend and withdraw assets to/from the Dahlia lending contract. Users can interact with wrappedVault through its deposit and withdraw functions.
When a user deposits assets into wrappedVault, they are minted shares of wrappedVault as expected. Internally, wrappedVault calls dahlia.lend and assigns the Dahlia shares to the receiver (the depositor) instead of keeping them for itself. This ensures that individual accounting for claimInterest works correctly for each depositor.
All the interest accrued is claimed for the depositor by the vault whenever the user calls the vault.claim function. This, in turn, calls dahlia.claimInterest for the depositor. The dahlia.claimInterest function decreases the lendShares equivalent to the interest accrued and sends it to the depositor. However, the problem is that the wrappedVault balance equivalent to the claimed interest is never burned.
This means that wrappedVault.balanceOf(depositor) is no longer the same as wrappedVault.balanceOfDahlia(depositor). The last wrappedVault balance equivalent to the claimed interest can never be withdrawn or burned.
As a result, each wrappedVault share balance for a user is worth a different amount, and wrappedVault shares are no longer fungible.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a loss of fungibility in the wrapper vault token after a depositor calls the claim function to receive accrued interest. The wrapper vault is the only entity permitted to lend assets to the underlying lending contract and to withdraw them. When a user deposits assets, the wrapper vault mints an equivalent amount of wrapper shares and forwards the underlying lending shares directly to the depositor so that each depositor’s interest can be tracked individually. Interest accrues in the underlying contract and is claimed by the wrapper vault on behalf of the depositor by calling the underlying claimInterest function. That function correctly reduces the amount of underlying lend shares belonging to the depositor and transfers the interest amount to the depositor, but the wrapper vault does not burn the wrapper shares that correspond to the transferred interest. Consequently the wrapper vault’s balanceOf for the depositor no longer matches the amount of underlying shares that the depositor actually controls. The visible token balance remains unchanged while the economic value of each share diverges, meaning that two users holding the same number of wrapper tokens may be entitled to different amounts of withdrawable assets. The issue manifests whenever a user successfully claims interest; it does not affect users who have never claimed. All depositors are potentially impacted because any claim creates a mismatch for that account, and the mismatch persists for the lifetime of the token. The problem was discovered during an integration test that compared the wrapper token balances of two users after one of them claimed interest and observed that the maxWithdraw value for the claimant was lower despite identical token balances. The bug is subtle because the standard ERC‑20 balance view shows the same number for both users, so a UI that only displays token balances would not reveal the discrepancy; only functions that compute withdrawable amounts expose the loss of value. The root cause is the missing accounting step that should reduce the wrapper token supply in proportion to the interest that has been transferred out of the wrapper. To remediate, the contract must burn or otherwise deduct the wrapper shares that correspond to the claimed interest, ensuring that wrapper token balances always reflect the underlying share holdings and that each token remains fungible. This class of bug falls under token accounting inconsistency leading to loss of fungibility and violates the business assumption that each share represents an equal claim on the vault’s assets.

title: Protocol and Reserves shares calculation is incorrect
description:
The protocol and reserves are being underpaid by a small amount each time. In the equation, totalLendAssets is increased by the full interestEarnedAssets, which is incorrect. This results in a slightly lower rate than what the protocol and reserves deserve, as the protocolFee and reserveFee are included in the interestEarnedAssets.
It's analogous to adding a depositor's assets to totalLendAssets before calculating shares using totalLendShares and totalLendAssets ratio.
Additionally, since virtual shares are not being accounted for, Dahlia underpays protocols and reserves by a multiple of 10^6.
bug_full: The issue is an incorrect fee‑share calculation performed when the Dahlia market accrues interest. Instead of basing the protocol and reserve fee share conversion on the pre‑interest total lend assets, the implementation adds the full amount of interestEarnedAssets to totalLendAssets before applying the shares‑to‑assets ratio. Because the interest that includes the protocolFeeRate and reserveFeeRate is counted twice – once as new assets and again as part of the fee base – the resulting fee shares are slightly smaller than they should be. The root cause is the misuse of the accounting invariant that totalLendShares / totalLendAssets must represent the value of a share; by inflating totalLendAssets with interest before the conversion, the denominator becomes larger, producing a lower share count for the same fee assets. This mis‑calculation also ignores virtual shares, which amplifies the under‑payment by up to a factor of 10⁶. An attacker does not gain direct control over funds, but any user who triggers interest accrual causes the protocol and reserve to receive fewer fee shares than entitled, slowly draining expected revenue from the protocol over many accrual cycles. The bug manifests whenever interest is accrued and both protocolFeeRate and reserveFeeRate are non‑zero, which is the normal operating condition for the market. Affected parties include the protocol itself, the reserve pool, and indirectly lenders who rely on accurate fee distribution for correct APY calculations. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when a test compared the buggy calcFeeSharesFromInterest function against a mathematically derived fixed version; the test showed a measurable deviation from the expected 1 ether fee asset at a 10 % fee rate. Because the discrepancy is small per accrual, it can be hard to notice in routine operation and only becomes evident through precise accounting checks or over long periods. From a user perspective the symptoms are subtle: the UI may show slightly lower protocol fee balances, reserves may appear to receive zero or negligible fees, and the overall yield may be marginally lower than advertised, leading to confusion when expected returns do not match observed values. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors, specifically an incorrect fee‑share conversion formula that fails to respect the invariant between assets and shares and omits virtual share considerations. To remediate, the fee share calculation should be rewritten to exclude interestEarnedAssets from the totalLendAssets denominator and to incorporate virtual shares, as demonstrated by the fixedCalcFeeSharesFromInterest formula. The executeMarketAccrueInterest function should be updated to first subtract protocol and reserve fee assets from totalLendAssets, then convert those assets to shares using the corrected ratio, and finally re‑add the assets and shares to the protocol and reserve positions. This change restores the intended fee distribution without altering the overall interest accrual logic.

title: The AxelarBridgedGovernor contract cannot support non-zero value cross-chain calls
description: The AxelarBridgedGovernor contract lacks receive & fallback functions due to which there is no easy way to send ETH to AxelarBridgedGovernor contract. Moreover the execute function is not payable. Combination of the above two behaviours results in AxelarBridgedGovernor's inability to support Calls with non-zero Call.value.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the AxelarBridgedGovernor contract being unable to accept Ether or any non‑zero value when it is called from another chain through Axelar. The contract does not implement a receive() or fallback() function, and its main execute() entry point is not marked payable. Because of this, any cross‑chain call that includes a value field – for example a governance proposal that is supposed to forward ETH to a target contract – will be rejected by the EVM. The root cause is a missing payable entry point combined with the expectation that the Axelar bridge will forward the supplied value to the destination contract. An attacker or honest user who attempts to send ETH via the bridge will see the transaction revert, resulting in a failed governance action or a denial‑of‑service condition where proposals that rely on moving funds cannot be executed. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a proposal was submitted, but the expected ETH transfer never occurs, leaving balances unchanged or appearing as zero. The issue affects all participants of the protocol that rely on cross‑chain value transfers, including token holders, governance participants, and any downstream contracts that expect to receive funds. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s external interface and noted the absence of payable functions despite the cross‑chain design. The problem can be subtle because the contract compiles and works for calls without value, so tests that only cover zero‑value paths may miss the failure. To remediate, the contract should implement a receive() external payable {} (or a fallback() external payable {}) and the execute() function should be marked payable, or the logic should be refactored to handle incoming value through a dedicated internal accounting mechanism. This change restores the ability to forward ETH across chains, aligns the implementation with the intended business logic of moving funds, and prevents the situation where funds disappear or governance actions become ineffective due to a missing value transfer capability.

title: BridgedGovernor.lzReceive can be executed with different msg.value than intended
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the cross‑chain message handler of the BridgedGovernor contract. The lzReceive function is declared payable and is invoked by the LayerZero endpoint after a message has been verified, but the implementation does not validate the address of the caller that forwards the call (the executor) nor does it ensure that the ether attached to the call (msg.value) matches the amount that the originating chain intended to spend. Because the endpoint’s lzReceive entry point is publicly callable, a malicious actor can observe a legitimate message being relayed, front‑run the expected executor, and invoke BridgedGovernor.lzReceive with a different msg.value. The function decodes the message into a list of external calls and executes them without checking that the supplied ether covers the expected execution cost. Consequently, the external calls may be executed with insufficient funds or with altered semantics, leading to a state update that diverges from the sender’s intention and potentially causing loss of tokens that were meant to pay for executor options on the source chain. This flaw manifests whenever a cross‑chain governance action is relayed through the endpoint, i.e., any time a message passes through lzReceive after verification. All participants that rely on the correct execution of these governance calls – token holders, the protocol’s governance process, and any contracts that receive the calls – are affected because the outcome of a vote or proposal may be silently altered. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of an executor address check and the reliance on msg.value without an explicit verification step. It can be difficult to detect in testing because the function still succeeds and emits no error, yet the resulting state may be subtly wrong, such as a proposal being marked as executed with different parameters or funds being drained from the contract. The recommended mitigation is to embed the expected ether amount inside the encoded message on the source chain, decode it inside lzReceive, and compare it against the actual msg.value, rejecting the call if they differ. Additionally, the contract should verify that the caller matches the intended executor address, ensuring that only the authorized relayer can trigger the execution. By enforcing these checks, the protocol restores the guarantee that cross‑chain messages are executed with the exact economic parameters they were created with, preserving token balances and governance integrity.

title: commonFunds can be burned by anyone
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted fee‑draining path in the Drips protocol that allows any address to trigger the requestUpdateOwner() function, which in turn initiates a Gelato callback that charges a fee. The protocol is designed to first deduct the fee from a user’s deposited funds and, only when those are insufficient, to fall back on a shared pool called commonFunds. Because the requestUpdateOwner() entry point is not limited to trusted callers, a malicious actor can repeatedly invoke it without providing any user funds, causing the fallback logic to draw the fee from commonFunds each time. Over many calls the entire commonFunds balance can be exhausted, effectively “burning” the pool. This occurs whenever the function is called and the caller’s userFunds balance is zero; the contract checks that commonFunds() is at least the required amount, but there is no guard on the number of calls or on who may invoke them. The impact is that the shared pool, which is intended to cover occasional fee shortfalls, becomes empty, leading to future ownership‑update requests failing with a “Not enough funds” error and potentially halting the protocol’s ability to process repo ownership changes. Users see symptoms such as failed ownership updates, unexpected zero balances in the common pool, or refunds that never arrive because the fee cannot be covered. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑payment logic and noticed the lack of access control on the callback trigger. It is hard to notice because the fallback to commonFunds is a legitimate feature, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the pool is being drained by unauthorized calls. To remediate, the protocol should restrict requestUpdateOwner() to a trusted identity, such as a whitelist of authorized contracts or owners, or add a rate‑limiting mechanism that prevents repeated fee extraction. Additionally, the fee‑charging logic could be hardened by requiring explicit approval before drawing from commonFunds, or by separating the fee pool into a non‑spendable reserve. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external call leading to unauthorized fund depletion” and violates the accounting assumption that commonFunds are only used as a safety net, not as a freely spendable resource.

title: State proof dependencies enable denial of service attacks
description:
The Prover contract's L2 world state proofs depend on previously proven L1 states. Due to the contract only storing the latest proven state for each chain, a malicious actor can invalidate in-progress L2 proofs by rapidly submitting newer L1 state proofs, effectively denying service to other provers. The Prover contract uses a hierarchical proof system where:
1. L2 world state proofs depend on proven L1 states via provenStates[settlementChainId].
2. Intent proofs depend on proven L2 states.
3. Only the latest proven state is stored for each chain in provenStates.
This creates an opportunity for a malicious actor to disrupt proving by:
1. Waiting for multiple unproven L1 blocks to accumulate.
2. Detecting when someone starts creating an L2 proof targeting a specific L1 block.
3. Quickly submitting a proof for a newer L1 block before the L2 proof completes.
4. Causing the L2 proof to fail when submitted since its target L1 state is no longer the latest.
Impact: If executed correctly this vulnerability could allow malicious actors to temporarily block L2 state proofs and consequently intent proofs. A legitimate prover could be unaware of the reasons for their proofs not succeeding. In a worst case scenario, the intent rewards could be returned to the intent creator once the expiry time is reached.
Likelihood: The likelihood of exploitation is low and depends on several factors:
• Speed of L2 proof generation vs L1 block time.
• Number of accumulated unproven L1 blocks available.
• Predictability of when L2 proofs will be submitted.
Currently, L2 proof generation (1-2 seconds) is faster than L1 block time (~12 seconds), making exploitation harder but still possible by accumulating multiple unproven blocks.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition arising from the way the Prover contract records world‑state proofs. The contract keeps only the most recent proven state for each settlement chain, and higher‑level proofs (L2 world state and intent proofs) are required to reference that latest L1 state. Because the contract discards any older proven states, an attacker who can observe when a prover begins constructing an L2 proof can submit a proof for a newer L1 block before the L2 proof is finalized. When the L2 proof is later submitted, its dependency on the now‑out‑of‑date L1 state is no longer satisfied, causing the proof to revert. This attack vector exists whenever multiple unproven L1 blocks accumulate and the attacker can react faster than the prover’s proof generation time. The impact is that legitimate provers experience unexplained proof rejections, their intents remain unclaimed, and reward payouts may be delayed or, in the worst case, returned to the intent creator after the expiry period. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an intent stuck in a pending state, a reward balance that never increases, or a refund that never arrives, contrary to the expectation that a submitted proof will be accepted and the reward paid out. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the hierarchical proof flow and noticed that only the latest state is stored, creating a single point of failure. It is difficult to notice because the contract simply reports a generic proof failure without indicating that the underlying L1 state has been superseded. The root cause is the design decision to store a single latest state instead of a history, combined with the implicit assumption that once an L1 state is proven it will remain the reference for any dependent proofs. To remediate, the contract should maintain a history of proven states (e.g., mapping chain‑id and block‑number to proofs), allow L2 proofs to target any previously proven L1 state, and ensure that once an intent is proven its claimant cannot be overwritten. These changes break the attack chain by preventing newer L1 proofs from invalidating in‑progress L2 proofs and by preserving the integrity of intent claims.

title: Missing enforcement of openDeadline check breaks ERC-7683 requirement and user expectations
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing enforcement of the openDeadline field defined by ERC‑7683 for gasless cross‑chain intent orders. ERC‑7683 requires that each order contain a timestamp, openDeadline, which specifies the latest block time at which a filler may call the openFor() function on behalf of the user. In the examined contract the openFor() implementation does not compare block.timestamp with the stored openDeadline, so the require statement that should reject calls after the deadline is absent. As a result a filler can invoke openFor() at any moment, even long after the user‑specified deadline, and the order will be opened and subsequently resolved. This can be exploited by an attacker or any filler who monitors pending orders, waits until market conditions change, and then opens the order past its intended window, thereby executing a time‑sensitive intent such as a cross‑chain arbitrage that was meant to be invalid after the deadline. The impact is that users who rely on the deadline to protect themselves from volatile market movements may see their intents executed at an undesired time, leading to lost profit, unexpected slippage, or exposure to adverse price movements. The bug manifests whenever an order includes a non‑zero openDeadline; there is no conditional guard preventing late opening, so the issue is present for all such orders. Users, protocol operators, and any party relying on the ERC‑7683 guarantee are affected because the contract no longer enforces the intended temporal constraint. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the specification of ERC‑7683 with the actual code and noticed the absence of a deadline check in openFor(). It can be hard to notice because the function otherwise behaves correctly, and no revert is emitted; the contract simply accepts the call, making the failure subtle unless one inspects the timing logic. To remediate, the openFor() function should include a defensive check such as require(block.timestamp <= order.openDeadline, "open deadline passed") before proceeding with the opening logic, thereby restoring compliance with ERC‑7683 and aligning contract behavior with user expectations that an order cannot be opened after the deadline. This class of bug is a missing temporal validation, commonly seen in contracts that expose time‑bound actions without enforcing the corresponding constraints, and it violates the business logic that intents are only valid within a predefined window.

title: Missing enforcement of fillDeadline check breaks ERC-7683 requirement and may lead to loss of filler rewards
description:
ERC-7683 specifies requirements for cross-chain intent orders on behalf of a user, which are filled via fill() function. One of the requirements is the enforcement of fillDeadline, which is the timestamp by which the order must be filled by the filler on the destination chain. This is part of all the ERC-7683 structs and allows users to specify time-sensitive intents:
* @param fillDeadline The timestamp by which the order must be filled on the destination chain
However, fillDeadline check is not enforced against block.timestamp in Eco7683DestinationSettler.fill(), which allows fillers to accidentally fill such intents at any time even beyond the fillDeadline specified. But such fillers cannot withdraw their rewards because this check is enforced during withdrawRewards() within IntentVault.constructor() when rewards for expired intents are refunded to intent creator.

Impact Explanation:
High, because this missing check breaks ERC-7683 requirement and may lead to loss of filler rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing time‑based validation in the Eco7683DestinationSettler.fill() function. ERC‑7683 requires that each cross‑chain intent order include a fillDeadline timestamp and that the contract enforce block.timestamp <= fillDeadline before allowing a filler to complete the order. In the current implementation the fillDeadline check is omitted, so a filler can call fill() after the deadline has passed. The fill call itself succeeds, but later when withdrawRewards() is executed the contract treats the intent as expired and refunds the reward to the intent creator instead of paying the filler. As a result the filler receives no reward even though the fill transaction was successful. This breaks the ERC‑7683 specification, undermines the incentive model, and may cause filler participants to lose expected earnings, reducing confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever an order’s fillDeadline has elapsed; any filler that submits a fill after that moment will be unable to claim the reward. The bug was discovered during a security audit that verified compliance with ERC‑7683 requirements and noticed that the deadline condition was not checked in fill(). It can be hard to notice because the fill transaction does not revert and appears to work, while the missing reward is only observed later during reward withdrawal, leading to a silent loss of funds. The root cause is a missing conditional check – a classic example of a time‑based validation omission that violates business logic assumptions about reward accounting. From a user’s perspective the filler sees a successful fill transaction, expects a reward to be credited, but the balance remains unchanged or the reward amount is zero, contrary to the expectation that a filled intent yields a payout. The proper remediation is to add a defensive check such as require(block.timestamp <= order.fillDeadline) in the fill() function and ensure that reward distribution logic aligns with the deadline enforcement, thereby restoring compliance with ERC‑7683 and protecting filler rewards.

title: ERC-7683 intents can never be filled because of incorrectly encoded originData
description:
Eco adds ERC-7683 compliant wrappers to allow ERC-7683 aware fillers to inter-operate with the protocol. These wrappers are implemented in Eco7683OriginSettler.sol on the origin/source chains and Eco7683DestinationSettler.sol on the destination chains. Eco7683OriginSettler implements open(), openFor(), resolve() and resolveFor() functions and Eco7683DestinationSettler implements fill() function per ERC-7683.
However, while resolving an OnchainCrossChainOrder to a ResolvedCrossChainOrder in resolve() and resolveFor(), onchainCrosschainOrderData.route.calls[j] is encoded instead of onchainCrosschainOrderData for FillInstruction.originData that is expected to be "The data generated on the origin chain needed by the destinationSettler to process the fill." Eco7683DestinationSettler.fill() attempts to decode this as OnchainCrosschainOrderData, which will be incorrect.

Impact Explanation:
Medium, because fillers cannot use the ERC-7683 wrappers and instead have to rely on Eco's native intent logic.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an encoding mismatch in the ERC‑7683 wrapper contracts used by the Eco protocol. When an on‑chain cross‑chain order is resolved on the source chain, the Eco7683OriginSettler contract should place the complete onchainCrosschainOrderData structure into the FillInstruction.originData field, which the destination contract expects to decode in order to execute a fill. Instead, the implementation mistakenly encodes only onchainCrosschainOrderData.route.calls[j] – a sub‑field that represents a single call – and stores that in originData. The destination contract Eco7683DestinationSettler.fill() then attempts to decode the supplied originData as the full OnchainCrosschainOrderData struct. Because the data layout does not match, the decoding fails, causing the fill operation to abort silently. This bug prevents any ERC‑7683‑aware filler from successfully completing an intent using the wrapper, forcing participants to fall back to Eco’s native intent logic. The issue occurs whenever resolve() or resolveFor() is invoked on the origin side, which is the normal path for creating a ResolvedCrossChainOrder. All users, developers, and third‑party services that rely on the ERC‑7683 wrappers are affected because their expected cross‑chain fill never happens; from a UI perspective a user may see a “fill” button that appears to submit but the transaction reverts or does nothing, leaving the intended transfer unexecuted. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the data written to originData did not correspond to the struct definition used by the destination contract. The mismatch is subtle because the transaction does not necessarily throw an explicit error; it simply fails to decode, which can be mistaken for a benign no‑op. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect data encoding/decoding” or “cross‑chain message format mismatch” vulnerabilities, where the sender and receiver disagree on the binary layout of a payload. To remediate, the resolve() and resolveFor() functions must be updated to serialize the entire onchainCrosschainOrderData struct into FillInstruction.originData, ensuring that the destination contract can correctly deserialize it and process the fill. Proper unit tests that verify successful decoding on the destination side should be added to prevent regression.

title: Intents can be published multiple times due to default claim state
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the IntentSource contract determines whether an intent has already been published. The publishIntent() function checks the claim status of the intent hash against the enum value ClaimStatus.Initiated, which is represented by the integer 0. In Solidity, all storage variables are automatically initialised to zero, so a mapping entry that has never been written to also returns a status of 0. Because the contract treats the zero value as both "uninitialized" and "initiated", the condition that should reject duplicate intents never triggers for a brand‑new intent. Consequently, a user can call publishIntent() multiple times with the same intent data before the intent is claimed or refunded, and each call will be accepted, emitting duplicate IntentCreated events and potentially allocating funding more than once. From a user’s perspective this may appear as the intent being created twice, leading to confusion when monitoring events or when trying to track funding; the UI might show two creation logs for the same intent hash, and a filler that relies on a single creation event could allocate resources twice. The impact is classified as low to medium because no direct loss of funds is guaranteed – the protocol does not automatically steal assets – but operational integrity is compromised. Duplicate funding can cause unnecessary expense for users and may break accounting assumptions that each intent corresponds to a single funding transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of intents and noticed that the status check relied on a value that is also the default for unmapped keys. It is subtle because the code appears to guard against re‑publishing, yet the guard is ineffective due to the overlapping enum value. The proper fix is to introduce an explicit Uninitialized state as the zero value in the ClaimStatus enum and shift Initiated to a non‑zero value. The publishIntent() function should then verify that the stored status equals Uninitialized before proceeding, and explicitly set the status to Initiated after successful creation. This change separates the concept of “never seen before” from “already started”, ensuring that duplicate publishing attempts are rejected and that the intent lifecycle is correctly tracked.

title: Missing nonce tracking in EIP-7683 integration allows for duplicate intent openings
description:
The Eco7683OriginSettler contract is designed to integrate with the EIP-7683 standard, which includes nonce functionality to prevent replay attacks. However, the implementation is stateless and does not track nonces. The nonce parameter from EIP-7683 is only used as salt in the Route struct, and IntentSource allows publishing the same intent multiple times. This means a valid signature can be reused to open the same intent repeatedly, allowing a malicious relayer to obtain a valid user signature and use it to call openFor() multiple times, transferring additional tokens from the user's account if they have granted sufficient allowance to the vault.

Impact Explanation:
The impact is medium. While users can eventually recover excess transferred tokens as the intent creator, this vulnerability creates significant usability issues in the protocol. Any excess token transfers would require manual recovery by the user, creating friction and potential confusion about intent status and token balances. This behavior also represents a meaningful deviation from EIP-7683's security model, which relies on nonce tracking to prevent replay attacks.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing nonce tracking mechanism in a contract that implements the EIP‑7683 cross‑chain intent standard. EIP‑7683 defines a nonce that must be incremented for each intent so that a signed intent cannot be replayed. In the affected contract the nonce value is only used as a salt when constructing a routing structure and is never stored or compared against a per‑user counter. Because the contract is stateless with respect to nonces, the same signed intent can be submitted to the openFor function repeatedly. An attacker who obtains a legitimate user signature – for example a relayer that forwards the user’s intent – can call openFor multiple times with the identical parameters. Each call triggers a token transfer from the user’s allowance to the vault, so the attacker can drain additional tokens beyond the amount the user originally intended. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that an intent was created once, but the token balance of the user decreases unexpectedly, or the intent appears to be “already executed” while the user still sees a pending status. The issue occurs whenever the contract receives a signed intent and the user has granted sufficient allowance; there is no condition that blocks repeated submissions. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against the EIP‑7683 specification and noticed that the nonce field was never persisted. It is hard to notice because the nonce appears to be used in the code, but its role is only as a salt, so the contract compiles and runs without obvious errors, and no explicit replay‑prevention check is present. The impact is medium: users can eventually recover the excess tokens by manually withdrawing them as the intent creator, but the process adds friction, creates confusion about the state of the intent, and violates the security guarantees of the standard. To remediate, the contract should maintain a mapping of the last used nonce for each user and reject any intent whose nonce does not match the expected next value, or alternatively prevent publishing the same intent more than once at the source level, thereby restoring the intended replay‑protection semantics of EIP‑7683.

title: Fund intent allows creation with invalid or incorrect route parameters
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from two functions that accept pre‑computed data without verifying the underlying parameters. The fundIntent function receives a routeHash that is assumed to represent a valid routing configuration, yet it never checks that the hash corresponds to actual route fields such as source chain, destination, or token identifiers. Consequently an attacker can supply an arbitrary or malformed routeHash, causing the contract to create an intent that points to a non‑existent or incorrect route. The publishIntent function suffers from a similar omission: when the caller requests funding (the fund flag) the contract does not confirm that the intent’s declared source chain matches the current blockchain’s chain identifier. This allows intents to be funded on a chain that is different from the one they are supposed to originate from. Exploitation is straightforward – a malicious actor can call fundIntent with a fabricated routeHash, then call publishIntent with fund set to true on any chain, causing the contract to lock the supplied ether or tokens in an intent vault that is tied to an invalid route. The locked funds become unrecoverable because the reward calculation and claim logic rely on the original route data; when solvers attempt to fill the intent they find that the route does not exist or the source chain mismatch prevents the claim, so the reward is never released. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a transaction appears successful, the vault balance shows the deposited amount, but later the user receives no reward and the balance remains permanently stuck. The impact is high because legitimate participants may lose access to their funds, the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, and the overall trust in the system is eroded. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted missing validation checks. It is hard to notice because the contract only stores hashes, so a superficial test that only checks that a hash is present will not reveal the inconsistency, and the UI may display a funded intent without indicating the underlying route problem. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient input validation and hash‑trust vulnerabilities, where the contract trusts externally supplied hashes instead of recomputing and verifying them. The proper remediation is to recompute the routeHash from the full route structure inside fundIntent, verify that intent.route.source equals block.chainid, and add the same source‑chain check in publishIntent before allowing any funding operation, reverting the transaction if the checks fail.

title: Swap execution can completely fail in some cases when tokens like BNB are involved
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batch‑swap routine that processes a series of token swaps ending in a wrapped native token (WNATIVE) which is later unwrapped and bridged. The routine wraps each individual router call in a try‑catch block so that if a single swap fails the contract can reset the token allowance, refund the user and continue with the remaining swaps. The catch block uses OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeDecreaseAllowance, which internally calls forceApprove(0) followed by approve(newAmount). Some ERC20 implementations, notably BNB on Ethereum, deliberately revert when approve(0) is called. Because the safeDecreaseAllowance call is placed inside the catch block, the revert triggered by approve(0) bubbles out of the catch, causing the entire swapExactInputMultiple transaction to revert. Consequently, the intended fallback – decreasing allowance and returning the input tokens – never executes. This defect can be triggered simply by including a token that does not support a zero‑allowance approval in the batch, leading to a denial‑of‑service where the whole batch swap fails even though only one leg is problematic. From a user perspective the transaction appears to have failed with a generic "Router error" event, the user receives no tokens, and the gas spent is lost; the expected behaviour of receiving a refund of the input amount does not occur. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the error‑handling logic of the batch swap function and identified that the catch block itself could revert. It is subtle because the try‑catch construct normally protects against router failures, so developers may assume the fallback always succeeds. The bug belongs to the class of improper error handling where a recovery routine can itself revert, breaking the contract’s resilience. To remediate, the allowance‑reset operation should be protected with its own try‑catch, or the contract should explicitly document that tokens which reject approve(0) are unsupported, preventing them from being used in batch swaps. By ensuring the catch block cannot fail, the contract can reliably refund users and maintain the intended flow of batch swaps.

title: Bridge refunds could be lost if URBurner is not deployed at the same address on all supported chains
description:
ERCBurner uses relay protocol for bridging ETH from one chain to another. There is no validation of the bridgeData in swapExactInputMultiple() or relayBridge() functions: the data is passed as it is supplied by the user. Utmost care is needed to handle bridge refunds in case bridge operation fails.
According to the relay protocol docs, in some cases {notably, when the refundTo and recipient addresses are both unspecified in bridgeData}, in case of the bridge operation failing ⇒the refund will be sent to the caller address on the destination chain.
For this protocol's case, this might happen:
• URBurner is deployed at address X on Ethereum Mainnet.
• User bridges ETH to Arbitrum.
• The bridge operation fails.
• There was no refundTo address specified and no recipient address specified, so the refund will go to the caller on destination chain: which means address X on Arbitrum.
• But this address would not be the URBurner if URBurner is not deployed at the same address on all chains.
This means the refunded ETH will not be recoverable and will lead to loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of bridge refunds in a cross‑chain ETH relay protocol used by the ERCBurner contract. The contract forwards user‑supplied bridgeData to the relay without any validation, and the relay documentation states that when both the refundTo and recipient fields are omitted, a failed bridge operation will automatically send the refund to the caller address on the destination chain. In the typical deployment the URBurner contract resides at a fixed address on the source chain (for example Ethereum Mainnet). If the same contract is not deployed at the identical address on the destination chain (such as Arbitrum), the automatic refund will be directed to an address that does not correspond to the URBurner instance. Consequently the refunded ETH is sent to an address that is not controlled by the protocol, making the funds unrecoverable. This issue arises only when a bridge transaction fails and the bridgeData lacks explicit refund instructions, which is a realistic scenario because the contract does not enforce the presence of those fields. Users who initiate a bridge expect that, if the bridge cannot be completed, their ETH will be returned to the protocol’s refund handler; instead they see no refund and the protocol’s balance on the destination chain remains unchanged. The loss is subtle because the relay does not emit a specific error event for the silent refund, so the disappearance of funds can go unnoticed during normal monitoring. The root cause is a combination of missing input validation (no check that refundTo or recipient are set) and an implicit assumption that the contract address is identical across all supported chains, which is not guaranteed by standard deployment processes. The bug belongs to the class of cross‑chain address‑mismatch and default‑fallback refund errors, where a contract relies on platform‑provided fallback behavior without explicitly specifying the destination of funds. It was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which examined the relayBridge and swapExactInputMultiple functions and compared the documented refund logic with the actual implementation. To remediate the issue, the protocol should either ensure that the URBurner contract is deployed at the same address on every target chain, or, more robustly, modify the bridgeData to always include a valid refundTo address that points to the URBurner instance on the destination chain. Adding validation logic that rejects bridge calls lacking explicit refund destinations would also prevent accidental loss. By guaranteeing that refunds are sent to a controlled address, the protocol can track failed bridges, rescue the funds, and redistribute them to the original users, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees and user expectations.

title: 3.1.1.1 Anyone with access to the machine hardware can tamper with keystore or configuration files
description:
Anyone with access to the machine hardware can tamper with the L1 keystore or configuration files related to Batch Poster.
From the gramine docs, allowed-files "are allowed to be created or opened in the enclave unconditionally. In other words, allowed files, directories and devices can be opened for reading/writing and can be created if they do not exist already. Allowed files are not cryptographically hashed and are thus not protected." This has an associated warning that: "It is insecure to allow files containing code or critical information; developers must not allow files blindly! Instead, use trusted or encrypted files."
However, 
nitro-espresso.manifest 
has 
sgx.allowed_files = ["file:/home/user/.arbitrum", "file:/home/user/kzg10-aztec20-srs-1048584.bin", "file:/config", "file:/l1keystore"]. 
The l1keystore will include the signing keys among others and the config may include critical configuration parameters that affect the liveness and security of the system.
Impact: High, because anyone with access to the machine hardware can tamper with the keystore or configuration to affect liveness and security guarantees of the Batch Poster.
Likelihood: Low, because access to machine hardware is presumably guarded with the highest level of OpSec best practices.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the Batch Poster component is configured to run inside a Gramine enclave. The manifest lists several host‑side paths in the sgx.allowed_files array, including the L1 keystore directory and a configuration directory. Files that appear in allowed_files are granted unconditional read/write access from within the enclave and are not cryptographically hashed or otherwise protected. Consequently, any actor who can reach the underlying machine – for example by having physical access, root privileges, or the ability to compromise the host operating system – can modify the keystore files that contain the signing keys or alter configuration parameters that control the poster’s behaviour. This tampering can be performed silently because the enclave does not verify the integrity of these files at runtime, making the attack difficult to detect through normal enclave logs or monitoring. An attacker could replace the signing key with one under their control, causing the Batch Poster to sign fraudulent batches, or they could corrupt configuration values to stop batch posting altogether, leading to loss of liveness and potentially exposing funds to theft or lock‑up. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as missing or delayed batches, failed transaction confirmations, or unexpected zero balances after a batch should have been posted. The issue was identified during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted the discrepancy between Gramine’s documentation – which warns against allowing critical files – and the actual manifest configuration. The problem belongs to the class of insecure file‑handling or trust‑boundary violations where secret material is stored in plaintext on an untrusted host. To remediate, critical files should be stored encrypted or sealed, loaded via trusted channels, and the allowed_files list should be limited to non‑sensitive resources. Employing SGX sealing, remote attestation, or a secure key management service would restore the intended confidentiality and integrity guarantees of the Batch Poster.

title: 3.2.2.1 Pending transaction positions not properly tracked when messages are skipped
description:
The current integration with the Espresso network lacks proper transaction validation in the EspressoFinalityNode, allowing potential malicious transactions to be processed until they are eventually rejected by the L1 sequencing contract. While this does not compromise the final ordering or validity of transactions (due to TEE verification on L1), it creates unnecessary overhead for nodes processing these unvalidated transactions.
The EspressoFinalityNode.createBlock() function processes transactions from the Espresso network without validating their authenticity or origin. The only validation performed is checking if transactions can be properly deserialized:
```solidity
for _, tx := range arbTxns.Transactions {
    var out types.Transaction
    // signature from the data poster is the first 65 bytes of a transaction
    tx = tx[65:]
    if err := out.UnmarshalBinary(tx); err != nil {
        log.Warn("malformed tx found")
        continue
    }
    txes = append(txes, &out)
}
```
This means that any actor can submit transactions to the Espresso network, which will be processed by nodes until they are ultimately rejected at the L1 sequencing contract level where TEE proofs are properly verified.
Impact: The impact is medium. While the final sequencing security is maintained through L1 TEE verification, the lack of transaction validation means:
1. Node operators cannot distinguish between valid and invalid transactions before L1 confirmation.
2. Nodes waste resources processing potentially invalid transactions.
3. Network bandwidth is consumed by transactions that will eventually be rejected.
Likelihood: The likelihood is medium. The current design makes it straightforward for anyone to submit transactions to the network. However, an actual attack requires preparation and various conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of two closely related flaws in the EspressoFinalityNode component that aggregates transactions from the Espresso network before they are sealed on L1. First, the node tracks pending transaction positions using an array (pendingTxnsPos) and a counter that assumes every slot in the array corresponds to a transaction that has been processed. When a message at a given position is nil or cannot be deserialized, the loop that extracts the transaction slices the data, logs a warning and continues, but the bookkeeping logic still increments the submitted‑position counter. As a result the node marks positions that were never actually processed as submitted, leading to an internal state where the pending‑transaction list and the submitted‑position list diverge. From a user perspective this manifests as a node reporting that a transaction has been included while the UI shows no change in balance or receipt, creating confusion about whether the transaction succeeded. The second flaw is the absence of any authenticity or origin verification for the transactions received from the Espresso network. The only check performed is a binary deserialization step; the node does not verify the TEE proof or signature that proves the transaction is legitimate. Consequently any actor can inject malformed or malicious transactions into the network. These transactions are accepted, deserialized (or rejected with a warning) and then forwarded to the L1 sequencing contract where the true verification occurs. Until that point the node expends CPU cycles, memory and network bandwidth processing data that will inevitably be rejected. The impact is classified as medium because the final ordering and validity of transactions remain guaranteed by the L1 TEE verification, but the inefficiency can degrade node performance, increase operational costs and obscure the true health of the mempool. The issue occurs whenever a nil message appears in the incoming batch or when an attacker submits arbitrary data to the Espresso network; under those conditions the node’s bookkeeping logic mis‑records the submission status and the lack of validation allows the malicious payload to be processed. Node operators, protocol participants and any users relying on timely confirmation are affected because they may see inflated processed‑transaction counters, experience unnecessary latency, or waste resources. The flaw was discovered during a security audit of the createBlock function, where the auditor observed that the pendingTxnsPos array was updated based on the loop index rather than on successful processing, and that the transaction validation step consisted only of a deserialization check. The bug is subtle because the system still reaches a correct final state on L1, so no outright failure or revert is observed; only internal metrics and logs reveal the discrepancy, making it easy to overlook in routine operation. To remediate the issue, the node should incorporate full TEE proof verification at the Espresso network layer, rejecting any transaction that fails the proof before it is added to the pending list, and the bookkeeping logic must be revised to only advance the submitted‑position counter after a transaction has been successfully processed, explicitly handling nil or malformed messages by skipping both processing and position advancement. This aligns the implementation with the expected invariant that each recorded position corresponds to a genuinely processed transaction, restoring accurate accounting and preventing wasteful processing of invalid data.

title: Inconsistent interest charged due to integer truncation
description:
In Eggs.getInterestFeeInEggs, we compute the interest fee with the following logic:
```solidity
uint256 interest = ((3900 * numberOfDays) / 365) + 100;
```
Using numberOfDays = 1 as an example, we can compare the output of this logic using integers versus real numbers:
• Integers: 3900 * 1 / 365 = 10 (0.01%).
• Real numbers: 3.9% * 1 / 365 ~= 0.0106849315%.
Here we can see that the output using integers is rounded down by nearly 7%. Since Solidity arithmetic uses integers, this becomes a problem. This can be intentionally exploited by borrowing for shorter durations and repeatedly extending the loan instead of creating a full duration loan. We can see how this creates a variance in the interest paid for one 365 day loans versus 365 one day loans:
• 3900 * 365 / 365 = 3900 (3.9%).
• (3900 * 1 / 365) * 365 = 3650 (3.65%).
bug_full: The contract calculates an interest fee in Eggs.getInterestFeeInEggs by multiplying a fixed rate (3900) by the number of days and dividing by 365, then adding a constant. Because Solidity only supports integer arithmetic, the division truncates any fractional part. For a one‑day loan the integer calculation yields 10 (0.01 %) while the mathematically correct value is about 0.01068 %, a loss of roughly 7 % of the intended fee. When the same loan is split into many one‑day extensions, the truncation error compounds: a 365‑day loan is charged 3900 (3.9 %) but 365 consecutive one‑day loans are charged only 3650 (3.65 %). An attacker can therefore borrow for short periods, repeatedly extend the loan, and pay less interest than the protocol’s pricing model assumes. The impact is a systematic under‑collection of fees, reducing revenue and potentially allowing malicious borrowers to drain the protocol’s profitability. The bug appears only when the interest calculation is performed; users see a lower interest amount displayed in the UI, may notice that their repayment amount is smaller than expected, or that the protocol’s accounting does not match the advertised rate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain integer result with a high‑precision floating‑point reference. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy per day is small and the contract does not emit warnings; only aggregated over many extensions does the loss become significant. The proper fix is to perform the calculation with a high‑precision denominator (e.g., 1e18) and to use a safe mulDiv routine that preserves fractional precision and avoids overflow. By scaling the rate and the constant to 18‑decimal fixed‑point, the contract can compute the exact interest fee and enforce the intended economic model.

title: Users can bypass the borrow expiry restriction by calling leverage() instead
description:
The leverage() function acts as a function that combines both buy() and borrow(). The borrow() function restricts user from taking loans for a period of more than a year:
```solidity
require(
    numberOfDays < 366,
    "Max borrow/extension must be 365 days or less"
);
```
However, leverage() lacks this kind of check, effectively allowing users to bypass it.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent validation in the leverage() entry point that permits borrowers to specify a loan term longer than the protocol‑defined maximum of 365 days. The contract’s borrow() function contains a require statement that enforces numberOfDays < 366, but leverage() internally combines buy() and borrow() without reproducing this check. As a result, an attacker can call leverage() with a numberOfDays value of 366 or more, obtaining a loan that extends beyond the intended expiry period. This bypass undermines the accounting assumption that all loans are bounded by one year, potentially leading to inaccurate interest calculations, extended exposure for lenders, and a mismatch between expected repayment schedules and actual contract behavior. The issue manifests when a user invokes leverage() with an oversized term; the transaction succeeds and the loan is recorded with the supplied duration, while the UI may still display a normal borrow flow, causing users to believe the loan will be subject to the usual one‑year limit. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the code paths of borrow() and leverage() and noted the missing require clause. Because the function name suggests it performs the same checks as borrow(), developers and auditors may overlook the omission, making the bug subtle. To remediate, the same require(numberOfDays < 366, 'Max borrow/extension must be 365 days or less') should be added to leverage() before the borrowing logic is executed, ensuring consistent enforcement of the loan‑duration policy across all entry points.

title: Floored rounding can cause DoS
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract converts between two token types using integer division that always rounds down (floor rounding). When a user converts an amount of token A to token B, the contract computes the output as (input * backing) / totalSupply, discarding any fractional part. The same floor rounding is applied when converting back, using a formula that also truncates fractions. Because the rounding is always performed in the same direction, a small amount of value is systematically lost on each round‑trip. In a simple example, converting 100 units of token A yields 333 units of token B, and converting those 333 units back yields only 99 units of token A, leaving one unit permanently missing. This loss becomes critical when the last remaining participant attempts to close their position: the protocol may no longer hold enough of the second token to satisfy the mathematically computed payout, causing the transaction to revert and effectively denying service to that user. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conversion logic and identified the floor‑rounding bias. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is often a single unit, which may appear as normal rounding noise in typical usage, but it accumulates and can render the system insolvent in edge cases. The impact includes users receiving fewer tokens than expected (e.g., “I expected to get my 100 eggs back but only got 99”), potential loss of funds that become unrecoverable, and a denial‑of‑service condition where withdrawals fail. The affected parties are any token holder interacting with the conversion functions and the protocol itself, which relies on accurate accounting to remain solvent. To remediate, the contract should round in favor of the protocol: when calculating an amount that the protocol must receive, it should round up (ceil), and when calculating an amount that a user receives, it should round down (floor). This can be achieved by adding (denominator‑1) to the numerator for ceiling operations or by providing separate helper functions for each rounding direction and using the appropriate one in each conversion path. By ensuring that rounding bias does not systematically erode token balances, the protocol preserves its accounting invariants and prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Rogue Key Attacks Against BLS Aggregate Signature Veriﬁcation
description: The approach taken in this implementation is secure if either (1) the aggregated messages are unique, or (2) veriﬁcation keys are checked to have a proof of knowledge of the secret signing key. Otherwise, the scheme would be susceptible to "rogue key attacks".
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rogue‑key attack on the verification of aggregated BLS signatures. It occurs when the contract aggregates signatures from multiple signers without ensuring that each public key is bound to a secret key through a proof of knowledge, and when the messages being signed are not guaranteed to be distinct. Because the verification step only checks the aggregate pairing equation, an attacker can generate a malicious public key that cancels out the contributions of honest signers, allowing the attacker to forge an aggregate signature that appears valid even though they never possessed the required private keys. Exploitation consists of the attacker registering a rogue public key, submitting a signature that includes this key together with legitimate signatures from other participants, and then having the contract accept the aggregate as authentic. The impact is that the contract may execute privileged actions – such as transferring funds, approving proposals, or updating state – based on a signature that was never truly authorized, leading to unauthorized asset movement or protocol state corruption. The condition under which this flaw manifests is any call to the aggregate verification routine where (1) the signed messages are not unique per signer, or (2) the contract does not perform a proof‑of‑knowledge check on each public key. All users, delegators, and the protocol itself are affected because the security guarantees of the signature scheme are broken, potentially resulting in loss of funds or loss of trust in the system. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the cryptographic assumptions of the BLS aggregation implementation. It can be hard to notice because the verification function returns true, so the transaction proceeds without error, and the UI may simply display a successful operation, masking the underlying forgery. To remediate, the contract should either require each participant to provide a proof of knowledge of the corresponding secret key (for example by using a pairing‑based proof or a signature of knowledge) or switch to a BLS variant that is provably secure against rogue keys, such as BLS Multi‑Signatures or the constructions described in the IRTF BLS documentation. In essence, the fix is to bind every public key to its secret counterpart before aggregation, thereby restoring the intended security properties of the signature scheme.

title: Signatures Validated to be On-Curve
description: For all veriﬁcation methods, verify, aggregate_verify, and multi_sig_verify, if the signature is not checked to be on-curve (or in the appropriate large prime-order) subgroup of the elliptic curve then various "low-order" attacks can be used to leak information about the secret key.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation that an ECDSA‑like signature lies on the expected elliptic curve subgroup. In the contract's verification routines – including single‑signature verify, aggregate verification and multi‑signature verification – the code accepts any point presented as a signature without confirming that it belongs to the prime‑order subgroup of BN254. Because the curve contains low‑order points, an attacker can craft signatures that are not on‑curve or belong to a small subgroup. When such malformed signatures are processed, the verification equation leaks linear relations involving the signer's secret scalar, allowing an adversary to recover bits of the private key through repeated queries. The attack can be carried out by submitting specially crafted transactions that contain low‑order signatures; each successful verification reveals information that, after enough samples, can be combined to reconstruct the secret key. Once the private key is known, the attacker can forge arbitrary signatures and drain funds or perform unauthorized actions on behalf of the compromised account. The flaw manifests whenever a user submits a signature to the contract, regardless of whether the signature is otherwise syntactically correct, because the on‑curve check is omitted. All participants who rely on the contract for authentication – token holders, liquidity providers, or any role that signs messages – are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the cryptographic primitives and noticed the absence of a subgroup membership test. It is subtle because the contract still returns true for many malformed signatures, so normal testing that only checks for acceptance or rejection may not reveal the leakage. The proper mitigation is to add an inexpensive on‑curve or subgroup check before any arithmetic involving the signature point, ensuring that only points in the correct large prime‑order subgroup are processed. This aligns the implementation with standard elliptic‑curve security assumptions and prevents low‑order attacks that could otherwise compromise secret keys and lead to loss of funds.

title: Unsafe Token Transfer
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract moves ERC‑20 tokens to the protocol fee recipient. The code calls the standard IERC20.transfer function and assumes that the call will return a boolean indicating success, as defined by the ERC‑20 specification. In practice many popular tokens, such as USDT, deviate from the spec by either not returning any value or by returning a value that does not follow the expected convention. Because the contract does not check the return data and does not use a wrapper that validates the call, a transfer can silently fail while the transaction continues to execute. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the fee‑collection path with a non‑compliant token; the transfer call will not revert, the contract will record that the fee was sent, but the tokens will remain locked in the contract or be lost. This mismatch between the expected accounting (fee deducted from the user and credited to the fee recipient) and the actual state (fee never leaves the contract) can lead to revenue loss for the protocol, incorrect balance reporting, and potential downstream logic errors that rely on the fee having been paid. The issue appears whenever the protocol processes a swap, deposit, or any operation that charges a fee in a token that does not strictly implement ERC‑20. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a fee was taken, yet the fee recipient’s balance stays at zero, creating confusion and the impression that funds have disappeared. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error event is emitted; only a careful inspection of token balances would reveal the discrepancy. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined token transfer patterns and identified the reliance on the raw transfer call without safety checks. To remediate the issue the contract should replace direct calls to IERC20.transfer with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer (or an equivalent safe‑transfer wrapper) which correctly handles tokens that omit return values and reverts on failure, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of guaranteed fee collection.

title: Software Execution Timing Side Channel of Secret Signing Key
description: The group scalar multiplication that makes up the core cryptographic operation of BLS signature is implemented using the arkworks library which currently does not support constant-time elliptic curve / ﬁeld arithmetic. Fine-grained timing of this operation can lead to leakage of the bits of the singing key.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fine‑grained timing side‑channel that arises from the implementation of the group scalar multiplication used in BLS signature generation. The core operation relies on the arkworks library, which does not provide constant‑time elliptic‑curve or field arithmetic. Because the execution time of the scalar multiplication varies with the secret scalar (the signing key), an attacker who can trigger the signature routine and accurately measure how long it takes can recover individual bits of the private key. This leakage occurs whenever the Espresso system exposes an interface that allows untrusted users to request a signature or otherwise cause the scalar multiplication to run, and the attacker can observe the elapsed time, for example over a network or via local timing hooks. The impact is the gradual exposure of the signing key, which can eventually enable the attacker to forge valid signatures, impersonate the signer, or manipulate protocol state that depends on the authenticity of BLS signatures. From a user’s point of view the service may appear to respond with variable latency; a legitimate user expects a quick, consistent response, but an attacker notices that certain inputs cause longer or shorter processing times. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the cryptographic primitives for constant‑time guarantees. It is difficult to notice because the timing differences are subtle, require high‑resolution measurement, and do not manifest as functional bugs such as incorrect signatures. The bug belongs to the class of side‑channel vulnerabilities where non‑constant‑time arithmetic leaks secret data. To remediate the problem the implementation should be replaced with a constant‑time group scalar multiplication routine, or the system should be redesigned to prevent untrusted parties from measuring execution time, for example by adding noise, batching, or moving the operation to a trusted enclave. In short, the flaw violates the fundamental security assumption that private keys remain confidential regardless of how the cryptographic algorithm is executed, and it can be mitigated by adopting constant‑time cryptographic libraries or by eliminating the timing channel altogether.

title: Incorrect Parameter Ordering in Curve Evaluation
description:
In the EulerSwap swap logic, the call to CurveLib.f is made with an incorrect ordering of parameters during the evaluation of the post-swap state. The function f() is defined to compute a new reserve value based on the curve. However, the EulerSwap contract incorrectly inverts the order of px and py in some branches of its logic:
- yNew = CurveLib.f(xNew, py, px, y0, x0, cx);
+ yNew = CurveLib.f(xNew, px, py, x0, y0, cx);
This misordering distorts the price weight applied in the curve’s internal calculations, leading to incorrect reserve updates and swap results that violate the intended AMM curve. Specifically, this causes inconsistencies in the swap symmetry: when executing an exact-out swap followed by an exact-in reversal using the same token pair and path, the system fails to return to the original state — demonstrating loss or unintended gain.
This error was clearly observed in simulated outputs. For instance, under the following parameter set:
priceX = 1
priceY = 2
x0 = 1000
y0 = 1000
cX = 0.8
cY = 0.8
reserve0 = 1000
reserve1 = 1000
amount = 500
asset0IsInput = False
exactIn = False
The uncorrected logic produced:
Starting reserves: (1000, 1000)
New Reserve: (500.00, 2200.00)
Output: 1200.00
Attempting to reverse this swap using exact input 1200 with exactIn = True should have brought the reserves back to (1000,1000). Instead, the incorrect computation yielded:
New Reserve: (106.11, 2200.00)
Output: 893.89
This asymmetry stems from misaligned price parameters in the curve formula. After correcting the line the outputs aligned as expected. The output of the exact-out leg becomes:
New Reserve: (500.00, 1300.50)
Output: 300.50
and the exact-in reversal with amount = 300 restores the reserves to:
New Reserve: (500.00, 1300.00)
Output: 500.00
This confirms that the pricing logic and reserve transitions now obey the intended curve dynamics and yield symmetry across swap paths.
Visual validation using the provided plot script (see below) further illustrates the discrepancy. The invalid version of the logic plots a destination point far outside the feasible curve region:
Whereas the corrected computation yields a valid, curve-consistent transition:
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect ordering of theprice parameters when the EulerSwap contract invokes the curve evaluation routine provided by CurveLib. The function f() expects the arguments (newX, priceX, priceY, oldX, oldY, curveConstant) in that exact sequence, but in several execution branches the contract passes (newX, priceY, priceX, oldY, oldX, curveConstant), effectively swapping the two price tokens. This mismatch changes the weight applied to each side of the constant‑product‑like curve, causing the computed new reserve values to deviate from the mathematically intended curve. The bug becomes visible when a user performs an exact‑out swap (specifying the desired output amount) and then immediately attempts to reverse the trade with an exact‑in swap (specifying the amount received). Under correct logic the reserves should return to their original state, preserving symmetry, but because the price arguments are inverted the second trade yields a different reserve configuration, resulting in a net loss or unintended gain. The impact is that traders may receive less output than advertised, liquidity pools can become imbalanced, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about invariant preservation are violated. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately crafts a swap‑then‑reverse sequence to extract value from the pool, or by any user who unintentionally suffers reduced returns. The condition under which the flaw manifests is when the swap direction follows the y‑based flow (asset0IsInput false) and the contract selects the branch that uses the inverted parameter order; in other paths the error is hidden, making it hard to notice during casual testing. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included simulation of reserve trajectories and visual plotting of the curve; the plotted points fell outside the feasible region, prompting a deeper inspection that revealed the swapped arguments. Because the function signature contains many parameters of the same type, the mistake does not raise a compiler warning and can easily slip past code review, especially when developers rely on copy‑and‑paste patterns. To remediate the problem, every call to CurveLib.f (and its inverse) must be audited to confirm that priceX and priceY are supplied in the correct order, and wrapper functions should be introduced to encapsulate the curve call with a clear, self‑documenting interface. Adding comprehensive unit tests that verify swap symmetry for both exact‑in and exact‑out scenarios, as well as automated invariant checks, will reduce the risk of re‑introducing the bug. In user‑facing terms, a trader may notice that after swapping token A for token B and then swapping back, their token balances do not match the original amounts, or that the quoted price seems unusually unfavorable, indicating that the underlying reserve calculation is flawed.

title: Net repayments can be counted across multiple solverOps
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract determines whether a solver operation (solverOp) has a reconciled balance. The reconciliation check requires that the total repayments recorded for a solver are at least equal to its total borrows and that the solver has prepaid enough ETH to cover its maximum gas liability, either through an approved bonded token or through excess repayment. The implementation adds the net repayment amount to a global counter and compares it against each solver's gas liability. When the flag multipleSuccessfulSolvers is true, the same net repayment value can be applied independently to every active solverOp because the contract does not track how much of the repayment each solver actually consumes. Consequently, a single 1 ETH excess repayment left by one solver can be counted ten times if ten solverOps are present, causing the _isBalanceReconciled function to return true for all of them even though the total excess is sufficient for only one. This logical flaw allows the contract to falsely assume that each solver has enough gas coverage, leading to a shortfall that only becomes visible during the final settlement step, where the bundler is forced to cover the missing gas cost. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that expected refunds or gas reimbursements disappear; the UI may show a zero or reduced balance after a batch of solverOps despite the contract reporting successful reconciliation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the accounting logic for solver operations and identified that the repayment accounting is not isolated per solver. It is hard to notice because the reconciliation function returns a boolean that appears correct on a per‑solver basis, masking the aggregate deficit until settlement. The bug belongs to the class of accounting double‑counting errors, where shared resources are incorrectly reused across independent entities. To remediate the problem the contract should deduct the portion of net repayment allocated to a solver from the global pool before evaluating the next solver, ensuring that each repayment is only counted once. This change restores the invariant that total repayments must cover total gas liabilities across all solverOps, preventing unexpected loss of funds and preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: moveOut() can be exploited using reentrancy for tokens with callbacks
description:
TokenFlow.moveOut() calculates the amount of tokens transferred to the payer by taking the difference between the payer's balance before and after the transfer:
```solidity
function moveOut(address token, uint128 amount) external requireScope(INTERNAL_SCOPE) {
    uint balanceBefore = token.balanceOf(payer);
    token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, payer, amount);
    uint received = token.balanceOf(payer) - balanceBefore;
    TransientNetflows.add(token, int256(uint256(received)));
}
```
However, while this pattern works for fee-on-transfer tokens, it can be exploited through reentrancy if token.transferFrom() gives external callbacks to other addresses.
