To fix the issue, the timestamp condition should be expanded to require the current time to be after the auction start and before the end plus reveal window, i.e., block.timestamp >= listing.start && block.timestamp <= (listing.end + BLIND_BID_REVEAL_WINDOW). This restores the intended ability for makers to cancel blind auctions before they begin, aligning the contract behavior with its business logic and preventing unintended fund lock‑up.

title: Buyer can grief attack seller in english and blind auction
description: After the English auction or Blind auction ends, if there are any bidders, the auction cannot be cancelled by the seller and anyone can call settleAuction() to send the NFT to the bidder to send the tokens to the seller. When the NFT is sent, the bidder's callback function will be called, which gives the bidder the opportunity to grief the seller by refusing to receive the NFT. This means a malicious bidder can "extort" the seller. Consider that the bidder is a contract that refuses to receive NFTs by default. Only by sending 1 ETH to the contract will the key variables of the contract be changed so that it can receive NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a grief or denial‑of‑service attack that arises in the settlement phase of both English and blind auctions when the contract assumes that the transfer of the auctioned NFT to the winning bidder will always succeed. After the auction ends and at least one bid exists, any caller can invoke settleAuction, which first attempts to send the NFT to the highest bidder using the ERC721 safeTransfer mechanism. The safeTransfer triggers the bidder's onERC721Received callback. If the bidder is a contract that deliberately reverts or refuses to accept the NFT—commonly by implementing onERC721Received to revert unless a specific condition such as receiving 1 ETH is met—the NFT transfer fails and the entire settleAuction transaction reverts. Because the payment to the seller is sent only after the NFT transfer, the seller never receives the funds and the auction remains in an incomplete state. This allows a malicious bidder to extort the seller by demanding a payment (for example 1 ETH) to change the contract’s internal flag so that it will accept the NFT, effectively holding the seller’s proceeds hostage. The issue occurs only when the winner is a contract capable of rejecting ERC721 tokens; it is not visible when normal externally owned accounts win, making it easy to miss during testing. The impact is that the seller’s expected revenue is blocked, the auction cannot be finalized, and funds may become permanently locked unless the seller manually intervenes or the contract is upgraded. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of settlement and identified the unchecked external call to the bidder’s callback. To remediate, the settlement logic should be restructured to separate payment and token transfer, for example by first sending the payment to the seller and then attempting the NFT transfer inside a try/catch block. If the NFT transfer fails, the token should remain escrowed and a public claim function should be provided so the bidder can retrieve the NFT later, eliminating the ability to block the seller’s payment. This class of bug is a classic unchecked‑external‑call or token‑transfer‑failure denial‑of‑service, violating the business assumption that auction settlement is atomic and that the seller will always receive the proceeds once the auction ends.

title: Immediately expired bid will replace good bid
description: For listings of type BUY_IT_NOW_WITH_BIDS, the bidder bids with an expiryTimestamp, and when the bid expires, the bid will not be accepted. Since the protocol does not limit the minimum valid time, a bidder can offer a higher bid with a 1-second valid time, which will replace the current best bid and expire immediately, which may prevent the seller from accepting a good bid.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the bid handling logic of a marketplace contract that supports listings of type BUY_IT_NOW_WITH_BIDS. In this design each bid is submitted together with an expiryTimestamp that determines how long the bid remains valid. The contract accepts a new bid if its amount is higher than the current best bid, but it does not enforce any lower bound on how far in the future the expiryTimestamp must be. Consequently an attacker can place a bid that is higher than any existing bid while setting the expiryTimestamp to only a few seconds (or even one second) after the current block timestamp. Because the contract immediately treats the higher amount as the new best bid, it overwrites the previously good bid even though the new bid will become expired almost instantly. When the seller later attempts to accept a bid, the contract checks only that the selected bid is not expired at the moment of acceptance. Since the attacker‑submitted bid expires before the seller can act, the contract rejects it and, depending on the implementation, may prevent the seller from accepting the earlier, still‑valid bid because the contract only allows acceptance of the current best bid. This results in a situation where a seller sees a higher bid displayed in the UI, expects to be able to accept it, but receives an error or simply cannot complete the sale, effectively losing a legitimate offer. The root cause is the missing validation that expiryTimestamp must be greater than a minimum duration relative to block.timestamp, allowing bids with arbitrarily short lifetimes to dominate the ordering. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the bid replacement and acceptance flow and identified that the expiry check is performed only at acceptance time, not at bid insertion time. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the highest amount without highlighting that the bid will expire in a few seconds, leading users to assume the bid is usable. The impact is primarily on sellers who may miss out on good offers, but it also undermines the economic fairness of the protocol and could be abused to manipulate market prices. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum bid lifetime, for example by requiring expiryTimestamp >= block.timestamp + MIN_BID_DURATION, and should ensure that bid replacement logic only considers bids that satisfy this constraint. This change restores the intended business rule that a higher bid must remain valid for a reasonable period before it can replace an existing bid, preventing immediate expiry attacks and preserving the integrity of the auction process.

title: Operator admin key can mint (and thus withdraw) arbitrary funds
description: There is no validity check or way to challenge a bad deposit (showing it doesn't exist). Rather the process of challenging (as described in the design document supplied by the client) has no step which would check the existence of the receipts. Hence if the admin signs off on a deposit, then it is considered valid and they can steal funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked privileged minting flaw that allows the operator admin key to create and withdraw arbitrary funds by approving deposits that never actually occurred. The root cause is the absence of any validity check or challenge step that confirms the existence of a deposit receipt before the admin signs it off; the design document describes a challenge process but omits a verification of whether the receipt is real. An attacker who controls the admin key can simply fabricate a receipt, mark it as valid, and the contract will treat the fabricated deposit as genuine, minting the corresponding amount of tokens which can then be transferred out of the rollup. This can be exploited at any time the admin processes a deposit, effectively letting the admin steal funds from the protocol. The impact is that users may see their expected balances increase after a deposit, only to have the funds disappear later, resulting in zero or negative balances, missing refunds, and overall loss of trust in the system. All participants of the rollup – depositors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the total supply can be inflated without any real backing, breaking the fundamental accounting assumption that total minted tokens equal the sum of verified deposits. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the implementation against the design specification and noticed that the challenge routine never checks receipt existence, making the flaw subtle and easy to overlook since no explicit mint function is present; the minting happens implicitly through the deposit approval flow. Because the problem resides in a high‑level business logic step rather than a low‑level arithmetic error, it may not be obvious from simple unit tests or UI observations until funds actually disappear. The recommended remediation is to enforce a receipt existence verification either in the Rollman contract or on the deposit contract side, and to ensure that the admin cannot sign off on a deposit without a provable proof of its existence, possibly by adding a Merkle proof or a challenge period that requires external validation before minting occurs. In generic terms this is a privileged‑mint or unchecked‑state‑transition bug that violates the protocol’s accounting guarantees and allows an insider to create money out of thin air, leading to user balances being reduced to zero or unexpected negative values.

title: Deprecate DisperseBlob endpoint still in use
description: The current implementation includes the DisperseBlob endpoint, which is marked for deprecation according to the API documentation. The documentation states: This endpoint will be deprecated in future releases. All production traffic should prefer the DisperseBlobAuthenticated endpoint.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of continued use of a legacy API endpoint, DisperseBlob, that the official documentation marks for future deprecation. The root cause is that the contract’s client code and the Disperser implementation still invoke the unauthenticated DisperseBlob function instead of the newer DisperseBlobAuthenticated variant. Because the old endpoint does not enforce authentication, an attacker who can reach the endpoint may be able to trigger dispersal operations without proper permission checks, potentially causing unauthorized fund transfers or denial‑of‑service conditions. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary crafts a call to the public DisperseBlob endpoint, which the contract accepts because it lacks the authentication guard present in the replacement endpoint. When production traffic relies on the deprecated call, the system may silently accept malformed or malicious requests, leading to funds being sent to unintended recipients, refunds failing, or balances appearing to disappear from user interfaces. The issue manifests whenever any user or automated process invokes the DisperseBlob endpoint in a live environment; it does not require special privileges beyond network access to the API. All participants that depend on the dispersal service – including end‑users expecting correct payouts, the protocol that assumes authenticated dispersal, and developers maintaining the contract – are affected. The problem was identified during a security audit that cross‑checked the code against the published API specification and noticed a mismatch between the implemented calls and the deprecation notice. Because the endpoint still functions, the flaw can be easy to miss during functional testing, especially if test suites only verify successful dispersal without checking authentication. To remediate, the codebase should be updated to replace every invocation of DisperseBlob with DisperseBlobAuthenticated, and the Disperser implementation should be extended to support the authenticated flow. Migration should be performed before the deprecated endpoint is removed from the service to avoid runtime failures and to restore the intended security guarantees of authenticated dispersal.

title: Insecure handling of admin signing key
description: The current implementation exposes the admin signing key in an insecure manner, potentially compromising the entire system's security. This key is critical for authenticating administrative actions and should be handled with utmost care. The signing key is passed as a command-line argument or environment variable, making it visible in process lists, logs, and command history.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of exposing the administrative signing key in an insecure manner by passing it as a command‑line argument or environment variable. This practice makes the secret visible in operating‑system process listings, shell history, and any logs that capture the start‑up command line, allowing anyone with read access to the host or to log files to retrieve the key. The root cause is the lack of a dedicated secret‑management mechanism; the code treats the signing key as ordinary input data rather than a protected credential. An attacker who can inspect the process table, read environment variables, or view historical command logs can extract the key and then impersonate the admin. With the stolen key the attacker can sign arbitrary administrative messages, trigger privileged actions such as rollup state updates, configuration changes, or fund transfers, effectively taking control of the entire system. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, unauthorized protocol state changes, and a breach of trust in the platform’s governance. The issue manifests whenever the service is launched with the key supplied on the command line or via an environment variable, which is common in development or containerised deployments that expose process details. All participants that rely on the admin’s authority – the protocol itself, its users, and any custodial entities – are at risk. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined how secrets are handled and noted that the key appears in clear text in the start‑up script. Because the exposure is indirect, it may be missed by developers who assume that environment variables are safe or who do not routinely inspect process listings on production hosts. To remediate, the signing key should never be passed in clear text; instead a secure key‑management solution such as a hardware security module, a vault service, or encrypted storage should be used, with decryption performed only in memory at the moment of signing. This aligns the implementation with best practices for credential protection and prevents accidental leakage through logs or command histories. In user‑facing terms, the bug can cause unexpected admin actions, unauthorized fund movements, or protocol state changes that appear to come from the legitimate administrator, violating the expectation that only the trusted admin can perform such operations. The class of bug is insecure secret handling, specifically leakage of high‑privilege cryptographic material through process arguments and environment variables, which breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that only the holder of the private key can authorize privileged actions.

title: Implement pyth confidence interval check
description: Currently, the system uses price data from Pyth without explicitly checking if the price falls within the provided confidence interval. This could lead to using potentially unreliable price data in volatile market conditions or during unusual events. Impact: • Risk of using inaccurate or unreliable price data. • Potential for financial loss or system instability during high market volatility. • Missed opportunity to implement protective measures for users during uncertain market conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the contract accepting price data from the Pyth oracle without verifying that the reported price lies inside the confidence interval that Pyth supplies alongside each price. The root cause is the absence of a sanity‑check that compares the price to the lower and upper bounds of the confidence interval, and the lack of any policy for handling intervals that are unusually wide. An attacker or natural market turbulence can cause Pyth to emit a price together with a very large confidence interval, signalling that the price is uncertain. Because the contract does not inspect this interval, it may use the nominal price even when the true market price could be far outside the reported value. An exploit can be carried out by triggering a situation where the oracle reports a price with a wide interval (for example by feeding the oracle with stale data or by exploiting a temporary feed disruption). The contract then proceeds with calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, or trade settlement based on the unreliable price. As a result users may see unexpected liquidations, trades executing at unfavorable rates, or balances that appear to shrink without an obvious on‑chain event. The impact is financial loss for users and potential instability of the protocol during periods of high volatility or unusual market events. The condition under which the bug manifests is when the confidence interval is either larger than a predefined safety margin or when the actual price falls outside the interval, both of which are common during rapid price swings or oracle outages. All participants that rely on the price – lenders, borrowers, traders and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the oracle integration code and noted the missing interval validation. It is hard to notice because the contract logs only the price value; the confidence interval is not emitted in events nor displayed in the UI, so the contract appears to work correctly until a bad price leads to an adverse outcome. The proper mitigation is to add a check that the price is bounded by the lower and upper confidence limits, to reject or flag prices when the interval exceeds a configurable width, and to define a fallback behaviour such as using a conservative price, pausing sensitive operations, or reverting the transaction. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of oracle data validation failures, where insufficient sanity checks allow untrusted or uncertain data to drive critical financial logic, breaking the accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on.

title: Inability to unstake after cooldown period removal
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a time‑lock logic error that prevents a user from unstaking assets after the protocol’s cooldown duration has been reduced or removed. When a participant initiates a cooldown by calling the contract’s cooldown function, the contract records an absolute timestamp representing the moment when the cooldown will finish. This timestamp is calculated once using the current cooldown duration and then stored permanently for that user. If the governance or owner later changes the global cooldown duration – for example setting it to zero in an emergency to allow immediate withdrawals – the stored timestamp is not recomputed. Consequently, the user’s recorded cooldown end time remains in the future, even though the protocol now permits instant unstaking. The root cause is the use of a fixed end‑time field instead of a relative start‑time that can be combined with the current duration at the moment of withdrawal.

An attacker does not need to act maliciously; the issue is triggered simply by a legitimate administrative action that shortens or eliminates the cooldown period. After the admin calls the function that updates the global cooldown duration, any account that had previously started a cooldown will find that calls to unstake or redeem revert with an “InvalidCooldown” error or an ERC4626 redemption limit error. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a “unstake” button that appears to work, but the transaction fails and the user’s balance remains locked, leading to the symptom “my funds are still stuck even though the protocol says withdrawals are now instant.”

The impact is that funds become effectively inaccessible for those users, breaking the expectation that a zero‑duration cooldown means immediate liquidity. In emergency scenarios where rapid withdrawals are required to protect solvency, the protocol may be unable to free all user assets, potentially causing loss of confidence or even a cascade of withdrawals from users who can still withdraw. The bug affects any holder who has started a cooldown before the duration change – typically regular users, but also could affect large delegators or institutional participants.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors simulated a scenario in which the owner reduced the cooldown to zero after a user had already called cooldownShares. The test showed that the user’s subsequent unstake call reverted, confirming the logical flaw. The problem can be hard to notice in production because the contract behaves correctly for users who have not started a cooldown; only the subset of users who have already entered the cooldown experience the failure, and the failure manifests as a generic revert rather than an obvious “cooldown still active” message.

The appropriate fix is to store the cooldown start time rather than the absolute end time. By recording when the cooldown began, the contract can compute the effective end time at the moment of unstake by adding the current global cooldown duration. This makes the logic automatically respect any later changes to the duration, allowing immediate withdrawals when the duration is set to zero. The fix also requires clearing the stored start time after a successful unstake to avoid reuse. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of “static time‑lock mis‑management” where a contract caches a deadline that should be derived dynamically, leading to stale state and locked funds.

From a user‑experience standpoint, the bug causes the UI to show a successful “unstake” request but the transaction reverts, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and possibly displaying an error like “InvalidCooldown” or “redeem more than max.” Users expect their assets to be returned instantly after the protocol announces a zero‑day cooldown, but reality is that their assets remain trapped until they manually wait for the originally recorded deadline or the contract is upgraded. The vulnerability violates the core accounting assumption that the cooldown period is a mutable policy parameter, not a fixed per‑user constant.

In summary, the contract stores a fixed cooldown end timestamp, which does not adapt when the global cooldown duration is altered. This leads to a situation where users who initiated a cooldown cannot withdraw even when the protocol intends to allow immediate withdrawals, effectively locking their funds. The recommended remediation is to store the cooldown start time and compute the end time on‑demand, thereby aligning user withdrawals with the current policy and eliminating the stale‑deadline bug.

title: FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE blacklist can be bypassed using approvals
bug_full: The vulnerability is a blacklist bypass in the StakedlvlUSD contract that implements the EIP‑4626 vault interface. The contract assigns a special role called FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE to addresses that are supposed to be prevented from withdrawing their slvlUSD shares for lvlUSD. The intended protection is enforced in the internal _withdraw function, which checks that the caller and the receiver do not hold the restricted role and reverts if they do. However, the function does not verify the role of the owner argument that can be supplied to the public withdraw() and redeem() entry points. Because EIP‑4626 allows a caller to withdraw on behalf of an owner after the owner has granted an ERC20 allowance, a blacklisted address can first call approve() to give another address permission to transfer its shares. The approved address then invokes redeem() or withdraw() with the blacklisted address specified as the owner and itself as the receiver. The _withdraw check only sees that the caller (the approved address) and the receiver (the same address) lack the restricted role, so the transaction succeeds and the blacklisted shares are transferred out. This bypass occurs whenever the contract relies on the role check to enforce a compliance or risk‑management freeze, and when the standard EIP‑4626 allowance mechanism is used. The impact is that users who are supposed to be frozen can still extract their funds, undermining the protocol’s ability to enforce sanctions, potentially leading to regulatory breaches or loss of trust. From a user perspective the symptom is that a blacklisted account can still withdraw and see its balance drop to zero, contrary to the expectation that the withdrawal should be blocked. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the role verification omitted the owner parameter. It can be hard to spot because the public interface follows the standard EIP‑4626 pattern and most tests exercise only direct withdrawals by the caller, not third‑party withdrawals on behalf of an owner. The proper fix is to extend the role check in _withdraw to also reject transactions where the owner holds FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE, thereby aligning the enforcement with the intended blacklist semantics. Conceptually, this is a privilege‑escalation bug caused by incomplete access‑control validation in a delegated withdrawal function, a class of flaw where role checks do not cover all actors involved in a state‑changing operation.

title: _checkMinShares() does not account for shares in the silo
description:
In StakedlvlUSD, _checkMinShares() ensures that the total supply of slvlUSD is either 0, or not less than MIN_SHARES:
```solidity
function _checkMinShares() internal view {
    uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
    if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES)
        revert MinSharesViolation();
}
```

When users initiate a withdrawal using cooldownAssets()/cooldownShares(), instead of being burned, their shares are transferred into slvlUSDSilo and temporarily held there.

However, since _checkMinShares() only checks that totalSupply() is not less than MIN_SHARES, shares in the silo are not considered burned. Most notably, the following call to _checkMinShares() in _escrow() does not check anything as _escrow() transfers slvlUSD, so the total supply of slvlUSD does not change:
```solidity
super._transfer(_owner, receiver, shares);
_checkMinShares();
```

This allows users to initiate withdrawals using cooldownAssets()/cooldownShares() that subsequently cannot be executed using unstake(). For example:
• Assume that:
  – MIN_SHARES = 1e18.
  – Alice has 0.5e18 shares, while Bob has 1e18 shares.
  – totalSupply = 1.5e18.
• Bob calls cooldownShares() to withdraw 1e18 shares. _checkMinShares() in _escrow() passes as totalSupply remains at 1.5e18.
• When Bob calls unstake(), _checkMinShares() reverts as burning his 1e18 shares reduces totalSupply to 0.5e18, which is below MIN_SHARES.

Note that even if users pay special care not to go below MIN_SHARES when initiating withdrawals, other users could still cause their withdrawal to become un-executable:
• Assume that:
  – Bob has 1e18 shares.
  – totalSupply = 1e18.
• Bob calls cooldownShares() to withdraw 1e18 shares, which should reduce totalSupply to 0.
• Alice calls deposit(), which mints 0.5e18 shares:
  – totalSupply = 1e18 + 0.5e18 = 1.5e18
• When Bob calls unstake(), _checkMinShares() reverts as burning his 1e18 shares ends up reducing totalSupply to 0.5e18.

In such scenarios, the user's shares become stuck in the silo as unstake() can never be called to withdraw their shares, causing a loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the token contract that enforces a minimum total share supply. The internal function that validates the minimum share threshold only examines the global totalSupply value, but it ignores shares that have been moved to a temporary holding contract (the silo) when a user initiates a cooldown withdrawal. During a cooldownAssets or cooldownShares call the contract transfers the user’s shares to the silo instead of burning them, so the totalSupply reported by the token remains unchanged. Because the minimum‑share check does not subtract the silo balance, the check passes even though the effective circulating supply has dropped below the required MIN_SHARES. When the user later attempts to complete the withdrawal with unstake, the contract tries to burn the shares, which reduces the totalSupply below the threshold and triggers a revert. This revert prevents the unstake operation from succeeding, leaving the user’s shares locked inside the silo with no way to retrieve the underlying assets. The issue manifests when a holder with a small share balance (or a balance that becomes small after other deposits) uses the cooldown mechanism; the affected parties are any token holder who relies on the withdrawal flow, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken. The bug was uncovered during a security audit that inspected the interaction between the _checkMinShares guard and the escrow transfer logic. It is hard to notice because the totalSupply variable appears consistent after the transfer, giving a false impression that the invariant holds, and the failure only surfaces later during the burn step. Conceptually, the contract violates a business rule that the circulating share supply must never fall below a minimum, leading to a situation where funds appear to disappear from the user’s perspective. From a user interface standpoint, a user may see a withdrawal transaction revert, their share balance remain unchanged, and no tokens are received, creating the impression that their funds are stuck. The recommended remediation is to adjust the minimum‑share check to treat siloed shares as already burned by subtracting the silo’s balance from totalSupply before performing the comparison, thereby restoring the intended accounting invariant.

title: Shares cannot be redistributed from users blacklisted during the cooldown period
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑locking defect in the StakedlvlUSD contract that occurs when a staker initiates a 7‑day cooldown and is subsequently placed on the denylist with FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE. During cooldown the contract moves the user’s shares to an internal escrow (the silo) via an internal _escrow call. The blacklist role blocks the silo.withdraw function, causing any later call to unstake to revert because the escrow cannot transfer the shares back to the caller. The admin‑only function redistributeLockedAmount is intended to reallocate shares from blacklisted accounts, but it determines the amount to move by reading balanceOf on the external address only. Since the user’s shares are held inside the silo, balanceOf returns zero and the function burns nothing, leaving the shares permanently trapped in the escrow. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an admin who adds a user to the denylist while the cooldown is still active, or unintentionally if the denylist logic is applied without checking the cooldown state. The impact is that the affected staker receives no assets when attempting to unstake, sees no change in their on‑chain balance, and effectively loses access to the underlying lvlUSD value of the locked shares. From the protocol’s perspective, a portion of the total slvlUSD supply becomes non‑circulating, reducing liquidity and potentially undermining confidence in the token’s accounting guarantees. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the cooldown escrow and the blacklist enforcement logic; it is subtle because the external balance appears zero, so the admin may assume there is nothing to redistribute. The issue belongs to the class of escrow‑locking or blacklist‑interaction bugs where privileged roles prevent the normal release path of assets that have been moved to an internal holding contract. Users experience a mismatch between expectation (the ability to retrieve their stake after the cooldown) and reality (the transaction reverts and no funds are returned). To remediate, the redistribution routine should also consider shares stored in the escrow, either by burning them from the silo or by allowing the escrow to release them despite the blacklist, thereby ensuring that blacklisted accounts cannot permanently lock protocol assets.

title: Cooldown period can be bypassed as users gain yield during the withdrawal process
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a withdrawal cooldown mechanism that can be effectively bypassed because the amount of underlying assets returned is calculated at the moment of unstake rather than being locked at the time the cooldown is initiated. When a user initiates a cooldown, the contract records the number of shares to be withdrawn and a timestamp after which unstake is allowed. However, the contract does not snapshot the share‑to‑asset conversion rate at that moment. Consequently, if rewards are added to the staking pool during the cooldown period, the share price rises and the user receives a larger amount of assets than would have been entitled at the start of the cooldown. Conversely, if the share price falls, the user can front‑run an admin‑initiated loss‑socialisation (freeze) and withdraw before the loss is applied, thereby avoiding negative exposure. The exploit works by depositing, immediately calling the cooldown function, waiting for the cooldown timer to expire, then waiting for a reward distribution or for the admin to trigger a loss, and finally calling unstake. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal that should have yielded the original balance now includes extra rewards, or that the protocol appears to allow “instant” profit without waiting the full cooldown. The impact is that the protocol’s economic model is broken: it cannot rely on a cooldown to give the system time to unwind off‑chain positions, and it may suffer liquidity drain if many participants use the bypass. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of cooldown and unstake functions and observed that the redemption amount is taken from previewRedeem at the time of unstake. The bug is subtle because the contract does enforce the time lock, so a superficial test that only checks the timestamp passes, while the financial effect is hidden. The proper fix is to lock the expected asset amount at the moment the cooldown is started and to enforce that the withdrawal amount cannot exceed this locked value, effectively using the minimum of the snapshot and the current share price. This change prevents users from gaining extra yield during the cooldown and restores the intended risk‑mitigation properties of the cooldown period.

title: Proof Submission Delay Attack
description:
The shared document mentions that there is a finite "challenge time window" in which fraud proofs must be submitted after proposals have been finalized on the L1 chain. A malicious actor could exploit this time constraint to cause delays and potentially allow fraudulent transitions to be finalized.

1. The attacker monitors the network for new proposals.
2. When a fraudulent proposal is detected, instead of immediately submitting a fraud proof, the attacker intentionally waits until near the end of the challenge time window.
3. The attacker then submits the fraud proof at the last possible moment.
4. This last-minute submission could potentially cause network congestion or overwhelm the system's ability to process the proof in time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing‑based attack on the fraud‑proof challenge window of a rollup protocol. After a proposal is finalized on the L1 chain, the protocol opens a finite period – the challenge time window – during which any participant may submit a fraud proof that demonstrates the proposal is invalid. The root cause is that the protocol treats this window as a static deadline without providing incentives for early submission or mechanisms to handle a sudden surge of proofs near the deadline. Because the system does not dynamically adjust processing capacity or extend the window when proofs arrive at the last moment, an attacker can deliberately wait until the end of the window, submit a proof just before the deadline, and overload the proof‑verification pipeline. This can cause the proof to be processed too slowly, allowing the fraudulent transition to be finalized before the proof is accepted. The impact is that an invalid state may become part of the canonical chain, potentially resulting in loss of user funds, incorrect balances, or a breach of the protocol’s security guarantees. The attack occurs whenever a proposal is vulnerable to fraud and the protocol enforces a fixed challenge period; it is especially effective under high network load or when the verification infrastructure is limited. All users who rely on the rollup’s correctness – depositors, withdrawers, and any contracts interacting with the rollup – are affected because they may see their expected balances unchanged, withdrawals stuck, or funds disappearing without an obvious on‑chain error. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which identified that the challenge window’s design permits strategic delay without penalty. It is hard to notice because the delayed proof looks like a legitimate late submission and does not raise an explicit alarm; the failure only becomes apparent when the system cannot keep up with the verification load. To remediate the problem, the protocol should introduce a graduated reward scheme that gives higher payouts for earlier fraud‑proof submissions, dynamically extend the challenge window when a proof arrives close to the deadline, and increase the processing capacity or queue management for last‑minute proofs. These changes would discourage intentional delay, ensure timely verification, and preserve the integrity of the rollup’s state transition logic, aligning the system’s behavior with the expectation that fraudulent proposals are rejected promptly and users receive correct balances.

title: getFreezableAmount does not account for already frozen assets
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that reports how many assets may be frozen, commonly called getFreezableAmount. The function calculates the allowed freeze amount as a fixed percentage of the contract's total assets, but it only considers the balance held by the staking contract itself. When assets are frozen, they are transferred out of the staking contract to a separate Freezer contract, which reduces the staking contract's balance. Because the calculation does not add the already‑frozen assets back into the total, each subsequent call to getFreezableAmount uses a smaller base value. As a result, after the first freeze the reported freezable amount shrinks dramatically, preventing further freezes even though the protocol’s policy may still permit a larger overall percentage. This mis‑calculation can be observed in two typical scenarios: a single large freeze where the frozen amount exceeds the newly reported freezable amount, and multiple smaller freezes where the second call reports zero freezable assets despite only a fraction of the intended percentage being frozen. The root cause is the omission of the Freezer contract’s balance from the total‑assets computation, turning a simple percentage check into a progressively decreasing limit. An attacker or any entity with the freezer role can trigger the first freeze successfully, but subsequent attempts will revert because the contract believes no more assets are eligible for freezing. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a successful freeze the UI still shows a high freeze percentage policy, yet further freeze actions fail or result in zero assets being frozen, leading to confusion and a perception that funds are disappearing or that the protocol is not honoring its own rules. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, where a test case demonstrated that the actual freezable amount after the first freeze was lower than the expected amount based on the original percentage. The bug is subtle because the function name and return type suggest a straightforward percentage of total assets, and the contract’s balance does change after a freeze, but the impact on the calculation is not obvious without inspecting the source. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state changes are not fully accounted for in derived metrics, leading to incorrect financial limits. To remediate the problem the getFreezableAmount function should be rewritten to include both the staking contract’s current balance and the balance held by the Freezer contract when computing the total assets, thereby ensuring the percentage is applied to the true aggregate of assets under management. This conceptual fix restores the ability of the protocol to freeze the intended proportion of assets and aligns the on‑chain accounting with the governance‑defined emergency controls.

title: No slippage protection in mintlvlUSD in case of matching decimals
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mintlvlUSD function of the LevelBaseReserveManager contract.The function builds a mint order that includes a minimum lvlUSDAmount parameter intended to protect the collateral provider from excessive slippage. The code scales the collateral amount up or down depending on whether the collateral token has fewer or more decimals than the lvlUSD token. However, when the two tokens have the same number of decimals, the conditional branches do not assign any value to the minimum amount, leaving it at the default value of zero. This edge‑case omission is the root cause. Because the minimum amount is zero, the protocol accepts any amount of minted lvlUSD, even if the actual amount is far below the expected value. An attacker or a market condition that reduces the minting rate can therefore cause the receiver to obtain far fewer lvlUSD tokens than the collateral value would suggest, effectively losing value. The exploit can be triggered simply by supplying a collateral token whose decimals match the lvlUSD token (for example, an 18‑decimal stablecoin) and allowing the mint transaction to proceed; no additional code is required. The impact is a loss of funds for the user who provides collateral, as the UI will still indicate a successful mint while the user may receive a negligible or zero amount of lvlUSD, violating the expectation that the minimum amount protects against loss. The issue appears only when collateralDecimals equals lvlUsdDecimals, a situation that is common because lvlUSD itself uses 18 decimals and many stablecoins also use 18 decimals. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the slippage protection logic. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles and the variable is initialized to zero, which is a valid uint256 value, so tests that only cover the less‑than and greater‑than branches pass. The vulnerability belongs to the class of edge‑case arithmetic bugs where an equality condition is omitted, resulting in a missing slippage guard. To remediate, the function should explicitly handle the equality case and set the minimum lvlUSDAmount to the unscaled collateral amount, thereby restoring the intended protection. After the fix, users will see the expected minimum amount reflected in the transaction and will be prevented from receiving an unexpectedly low amount of minted tokens.

title: Grieﬁng attack possible by frontrunning the callDiamondWithEIP2612Signature function call
description:
The callDiamondWithEIP2612Signature function performs two distinct actions:
1. Calls ERC20.permit to submit the signature provided by msg.sender, ensuring the contract has sufficient allowance to pull funds from the user.
2. Pull the funds from msg.sender to execute diamondCalldata on a specific diamond.
However, there is a potential frontrunning attack where an attacker can ensure that the ERC20.permit call fails, causing the entire transaction to revert.
1. A user signs a permit and sends a callDiamondWithEIP2612Signature transaction to the network.
2. An attacker frontruns this transaction and sends their own transaction to directly call the ERC20.permit function, using the permit information copied from the user's transaction:
• The attacker's transaction succeeds, setting the allowance and marking the permit signature as used.
3. When the user's transaction is eventually included, it fails:
• The ERC20.permit call made by the Permit2Proxy fails because the signature has already been used. This causes the entire transaction to fail.
While the attacker cannot profit from this attack, they can prevent users from successfully executing callDiamondWithEIP2612Signature.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service on the callDiamondWithEIP2612Signature function. The function first calls ERC20.permit with a user‑provided EIP‑2612 signature to grant the contract allowance, then immediately pulls the tokens and forwards a calldata payload to a diamond contract. Because an EIP‑2612 permit can be used only once, an attacker who observes the pending transaction can copy the signature and submit a separate transaction that calls the token’s permit function before the victim’s transaction is mined. The attacker’s transaction consumes the signature and sets the allowance, so when the victim’s transaction executes the internal permit call it reverts with "invalid signature". The contract does not catch this failure and therefore reverts the whole operation, preventing the token transfer and the diamond call from occurring. The impact is that users see their intended action fail – they receive no tokens, the diamond call does not happen, and no funds are moved – effectively a denial‑of‑service. This can happen any time a user relies on a single transaction that both submits a permit and performs a token pull, and the network allows another transaction to be mined first. The affected parties are the end‑users who sign permits, the protocol that expects the diamond call to succeed, and any downstream contracts that depend on the transferred funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by reproducing the scenario with a test that front‑runs the permit call and expects a revert. It is subtle because the revert message originates from the token contract and may be interpreted as a user error rather than a protocol flaw, and there is no explicit event indicating that the transaction was blocked by a front‑runner. The bug belongs to the class of “permit‑reuse front‑run” or “single‑transaction allowance acquisition” vulnerabilities, where state‑changing authorization is assumed to be atomic but is actually separable. To remediate, the contract should either verify that sufficient allowance already exists before calling permit, or wrap the permit call in a try/catch (or Solidity’s try) and continue execution if the call fails but the allowance is already sufficient. Alternatively, splitting the permit and the token pull into separate transactions or using a different authorization mechanism would eliminate the attack surface.

title: LevelMinting contract can be used as a premeditated attack in case a stablecoin depegs to drain the contract
description:
In addition to the arbitrage finding (see the issue "Stablecoins residing on LevelMinting contract can be arbitraged if instant redemption is enabled"), swapping a de-pegged stablecoin can be done via an alternative way. This way enables us to deposit an x amount of a de-pegged stable and:
1. Receive a non de-pegged asset.
2. Receive an value amount that is higher than the deposited value.
When calling initiateRedeem(), we specify which collateral we want to redeem, which is then stored.
1. This is not the case when initiating a deposit, the collateral type is not stored while receiving lvlUSD.
2. Next to that, it's possible to call the initiateRedeem() to start the cooldown period without having any collateral deposited.
Since stable collateral and lvlUSD are swapped 1:1, this enables the following planned attack in case a depeg occurs:
1. Alice calls initiateRedeem() for all collateral types (must specify the amount to withdraw).
2. USDT depegs after e.g. 6 months to $0.50 for simplicity.
3. Alice swaps 100 UDSC to 200 USDT on Uniswap and calls LevelMinting.deposit(), receiving 200 lvlUSD.
4. Alice then immediately calls LevelMinting.completeRedeem(address USDC) where she receives 200 USDC.
5. Protocol ends up with 200USDT at 0.50(100 loss).
bug_full: The LevelMinting contract contains a logical flaw that allows a user to initiate a redemption request without first locking any lvlUSD collateral and without the contract recording the type of collateral that will be redeemed. Because the contract treats stablecoin collateral and lvlUSD as a 1:1 interchangeable asset, an attacker can exploit a de‑peg event of a stablecoin to extract value from the protocol. The attack proceeds as follows: the attacker calls initiateRedeem for each supported collateral type, specifying the amount to withdraw, even though no collateral has been deposited and the contract does not store the collateral type. When a stablecoin such as USDT loses its peg (for example dropping to $0.50), the attacker swaps a de‑pegged stablecoin (USDC) for the non‑de‑pegged counterpart (USDT) on an external DEX, then deposits the obtained USDT into LevelMinting, receiving lvlUSD at a 1:1 rate that does not reflect the reduced market price. Immediately after, the attacker calls completeRedeem for the original collateral type (USDC) and receives the full amount of USDC, effectively converting de‑valued USDT into full‑value USDC. The protocol is left holding the de‑pegged USDT at half its nominal value, resulting in a net loss of funds. This vulnerability is triggered only when a stablecoin de‑pegs and when the contract’s cooldown period can be started without any prior deposit, conditions that are not obvious during normal operation. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s redemption logic and identified that the collateral type is not stored on deposit and that redemption can be initiated without locked lvlUSD. The issue is subtle because the 1:1 swap appears correct under normal peg conditions, making the loss invisible until a de‑peg occurs. To remediate, the contract should record the deposited asset type and enforce that redemption can only be performed against collateral that the user has previously locked, or alternatively use an oracle‑based price feed to calculate lvlUSD value based on the current market price of each stablecoin. Additionally, the existing bug that permits redemption without locking lvlUSD must be fixed. By aligning the redemption path with the actual collateral and incorporating price awareness, the protocol can prevent the described drain of assets and restore confidence that user deposits are protected against peg failures.

title: Any token account owned by delegate can be used
description: Different delegate_token_account can be used here as long as the mint is expected and the delegate is the owner of the account. One can change ownership of their token account to set the delegate and use this account with Lingo's program. This ends up with fees being collected in multiple different token accounts (liquidity fragmentation).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an insufficient validation of the token account used by a delegate when claiming fees in Lingo's transfer‑hook program. The contract only checks that the supplied token account holds the expected mint and that the delegate is listed as the owner of that account. It does not enforce that the account is the delegate’s associated token account, which is the single account the protocol assumes will receive all fee payments. Because of this missing check, an attacker or a malicious liquidity provider can create arbitrary token accounts, set themselves as the delegate, and submit those accounts to the fee‑claim instruction. The program will accept any such account, causing fee amounts to be deposited into many different token accounts instead of the single, expected one. This fragmentation of liquidity makes accounting difficult, can hide fee diversion, and may lead to users seeing their fee balance split across several accounts or appearing to be missing from the primary account. The issue is triggered whenever the fee‑claim back instruction is executed with a token account that satisfies the minimal mint‑and‑delegate check; no additional constraints are applied. All participants that rely on a single fee‑receiving account – including liquidity providers, token holders, and the protocol’s accounting layer – are affected because the protocol’s invariant that fees are consolidated in one place is broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the program’s expectations with its actual validation logic. It is subtle because the Solana runtime permits many token accounts for the same mint, and the UI typically shows only the primary associated account, so the extra accounts may go unnoticed. To remediate the issue, the program should enforce the use of the delegate’s associated token account, or otherwise verify that the supplied token account matches a pre‑registered fee destination, thereby preventing arbitrary accounts from receiving fees and preserving the intended accounting model.

title: Deposit and redeem functions can be DOSed by exploiting the replay prevention mechanism
description:
This issue affects both minting and redemption, as both use the same _deduplicateOrder function to prevent replay.
The _deduplicateOrder function relies on the order.benefactor and order.nonce values to prevent replaying of orders. The order.benefactor and order.nonce can be set to an arbitrary value when the mint function is executed.
Assuming that Alice executes a mint() TX with lvlusd_amount, order.benefactor and order.nonce set to 1000e18, Bob and 999, respectively. A malicious user could front-run Alice's TX and submit a similar TX with lvlusd_amount, order.benefactor and order.nonce set to 1 wei, Bob and 999.
Thus, when Alice's TX is executed, it will revert as the nonce has already been "used".
Malicious users could keep repeating this attack to DOS Alice. The cost of attack might be low if this can be executed on an L2 EVM environment where front-running is possible (sidenote: front-running might not be possible on some L2 chains).
The impact will be greater when used for DOS redemptions while the cooldown period is enabled since users will need to wait another 7 days to withdraw.
bug_full: The contract implements a replay‑prevention routine called _deduplicateOrder that stores a combination of order.benefactor and order.nonce to ensure that the same order cannot be processed twice. Because the mint and redeem functions allow the caller to set both the benefactor address and the nonce arbitrarily, an attacker can submit a transaction that uses the same nonce as a pending legitimate user transaction but with a different (typically minimal) amount. When the attacker’s transaction is mined first, the contract records the nonce as already used. The subsequent legitimate transaction then hits the _deduplicateOrder check, finds the nonce already consumed, and reverts. This behaviour effectively creates a denial‑of‑service vector: any user who tries to deposit (mint) or withdraw (redeem) can be blocked by a front‑runner who repeatedly front‑runs with the same nonce. The problem is amplified for redemption when a cooldown period is active, because a reverted redemption forces the user to wait the full cooldown (seven days) before trying again, potentially locking funds for an extended time. The vulnerability stems from the fact that the replay‑prevention logic was retained after the contract’s signature verification was removed, leaving a stale deduplication mechanism that no longer has a cryptographic binding to the order data. It is discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of mint and redeem and noticed that the order fields are not validated against any signature, making them manipulable. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract simply reverts with no explicit error message, appearing as a normal transaction failure rather than an attack. To remediate, the deduplication logic and its associated nonces should be removed entirely, or the nonce should be tied to a signed message that cannot be forged. In practice the recommended fix is to delete the _deduplicateOrder function and clear any stored cooldown entries when a redemption succeeds, thereby eliminating the replay check that enables the DOS condition. This class of bug is a replay‑based denial‑of‑service arising from improperly scoped anti‑replay state that can be abused by front‑running, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as “my deposit transaction keeps reverting” or “I cannot withdraw my funds and the UI shows a pending cooldown”.

title: Removing assets from _supportedAssets bricks pending redemptions in LevelMinting
description:
In LevelMinting, the _transferToBeneficiary() function checks if the asset to be transferred is in the _supportedAssets set:
if (!_supportedAssets.contains(asset)) revert UnsupportedAsset();
_transferToBeneficiary() is used to transfer collateral assets to users upon withdrawal. As such, once a collateral asset is removed from supportedAssets, it cannot be withdrawn by users anymore as this check would fail.
This is problematic as:
• All pending redemptions with that asset as collateral cannot be completed.
• If the protocol still owns some of that collateral asset, it cannot be withdrawn forever.
This makes it such that an asset cannot be removed from supportedAssets unless the protocol's balance for that asset is zero.
bug_full: During a withdrawal, the contract calls _transferToBeneficiary which first verifies that the collateral token is present in the _supportedAssets set. The check is performed with if (!_supportedAssets.contains(asset)) revert UnsupportedAsset(). When an admin removes a token from _supportedAssets, the verification starts to reject that token even if there are pending redemption requests that were created while the token was still supported, or even if the protocol itself still holds a balance of that token. Consequently users cannot receive their collateral and the protocol cannot retrieve its own holdings, effectively locking the assets forever. The bug originates from conflating the notion of “currently supported for new deposits” with “eligible for redemption of existing positions”. Because the same set is used for both purposes, removing an asset changes the contract’s view of what can be transferred, breaking the accounting invariant that every deposited asset must remain redeemable until the balance is zero. An attacker who has the admin role can trigger the condition simply by calling the asset‑removal function while there are outstanding redemptions, causing user funds to disappear from the user’s perspective – the UI will show a pending withdrawal that never resolves and the user’s balance will remain unchanged. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the LevelMinting contract where the flow of assets was traced. It is subtle because the revert message “UnsupportedAsset” only appears when a withdrawal is attempted, which may be interpreted as a user error rather than a protocol‑level lock. The impact is medium‑risk: funds are not stolen but become inaccessible, leading to loss of confidence and potential regulatory concerns. The proper fix is to separate the set that governs which assets can be newly deposited from the set that tracks assets that are still redeemable, or to forbid removal of an asset until the contract’s balance for that token is zero. This aligns the contract’s state machine with the business rule that collateral must remain withdrawable for the lifetime of any position.

title: Missing setter for cooldownDuration in LevelMinting
description:
In the LevelMinting contract, cooldownDuration is set to 7 days in the constructor. However, the contract does not have a function to update the value of cooldownDuration.
Therefore, the protocol admin will not be able to update the withdrawal period that users need to go through or disable it. This is problematic as users the protocol's withdrawal period cannot be adjusted to match the withdrawal period of vaults in LevelReserveManager. Additionally, redeem() can never be called.
bug_full: The LevelMinting contract defines a state variable called cooldownDuration that determines the mandatory waiting period a user must observe before being able to call the redeem function and withdraw their minted assets. This variable is hard‑coded to seven days in the constructor and, due to a design oversight, the contract does not expose any external or internal function that can modify its value after deployment. The root cause is the absence of a permissioned setter, which means the protocol administrator cannot adjust the withdrawal period to align with the withdrawal windows of the associated LevelReserveManager vaults, nor can they disable the cooldown entirely. Because the redeem logic checks that the elapsed time since minting is greater than or equal to cooldownDuration, the inability to set cooldownDuration to zero or a shorter interval makes the redeem call permanently unavailable when the protocol’s business rules require a different timing. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a “Redeem” button that either does nothing or reverts, leading to the symptom that users receive no funds and their balances appear frozen. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: users cannot retrieve their assets, the protocol’s promised liquidity feature is broken, and trust in the system may erode. This condition manifests immediately after deployment and persists for the lifetime of the contract unless the code is upgraded. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public interface with its intended functional specifications. It can be hard to notice because the variable is correctly initialized and the contract compiles without warnings, giving the false impression that the cooldown can be managed later. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of immutable‑parameter design flaws where critical protocol parameters are set once and cannot be updated, violating the principle of configurability for on‑chain governance. The recommended remediation is to add a permissioned function, guarded by an admin role, that allows the authorized party to update cooldownDuration to a new value or to zero, thereby restoring the ability to call redeem under the correct conditions and aligning the contract’s accounting assumptions with the broader protocol logic.

title: Stablecoins residing on LevelMinting contract can be arbitraged if instant redemption is enabled
description:
The LevelMinting supports multiple collateral assets (e.g., USDC, USDT, DAI).
It is possible that the LevelMinting contract will hold some USDC, USDT, and DAI at the same time. One lvlUSD can always be redeemed for exactly one USDC, USDT, or DAI (1:1 ratio). If the cooldown is disabled, it is possible for users to deposit and redeem within a single transaction. As a result, if the price of a stablecoin deviates from one dollar, MEV/arbitrager can take advantage of the LevelMinting contract to swap lower-value collateral with higher-value collateral (deposit + redeem). Unlike a swap in typical pools (e.g., Uniswap Pool), performing such a swap in LevelMinting contract does not incur any fee for the arbitrager.
In the end, the LevelMinting contract will left with a stablecoin of lower value as a higher-value one will be redeemed by MEV/arbitrager. If there is one of the stablecoins depeg (e.g., events similar to terraUSD crash), the impact will be greater, and it is possible that all the stablecoin residing on the LevelMinting contract will be swapped to the worthless stablecoin within a short period of time.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LevelMinting contract’s instant redemption feature, which allows a user to deposit a collateral stablecoin and redeem the corresponding lvlUSD for another collateral token within the same transaction. The contract treats all supported stablecoins (USDC, USDT, DAI) as having an exact 1:1 value with lvlUSD, ignoring any market price deviation or depeg risk. Because there is no cooldown, no fee, and no price oracle check, an attacker can exploit temporary price differences by depositing a lower‑valued stablecoin and immediately redeeming lvlUSD for a higher‑valued one. This creates a fee‑less swap that can be repeated by MEV bots or arbitrageurs, draining the contract of its higher‑value assets and leaving it holding only the lower‑value or even worthless stablecoin. The issue manifests when the instant redemption flag is enabled and at least one of the stablecoins deviates from the dollar peg, which is common during market stress or depeg events. Users may notice that after a transaction their expected refund or balance is smaller than anticipated, or that the protocol’s pool appears to have lost value, effectively “funds disappear”. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the redemption logic and identified the lack of price validation and the ability to combine deposit and redemption in a single block. It is subtle because stablecoins are normally assumed to be interchangeable, so the contract’s behavior looks correct on the surface, and no explicit error is emitted. To remediate, the instant redemption option should be disabled or guarded by a cooldown, a price oracle should be consulted to enforce proportional redemption based on real‑time market rates, and a modest fee or slippage protection should be added to prevent fee‑less arbitrage. In essence, the bug is a classic “price‑oracle‑free 1:1 peg assumption” that enables fee‑less cross‑stablecoin swaps, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each lvlUSD is backed by an equal‑value stablecoin and exposing the system to value loss.

title: Deposit and redeem functions can be DOSed by exceeding the deposit and redemption cap
description:
There is a maximum number of stablecoins that can be minted per block. In the current design, it is possible that the cooldown for redemptions is turned off. In this case, users can immediately execute the redeem() to withdraw assets.
Assuming that the deposit cap and redemption cap are both set to 10000. In an L2 environment where the gas fee is cheap, malicious users can DOS the deposit and redemption by atomically depositing and redeeming 10000 within a single transaction every block, thus resulting in the cap to be reached. As such, innocent users attempting to deposit or redeem will revert.
bug_full: The contract enforces a per‑block limit on the amount of stablecoins that can be minted through the deposit() function and a similar limit on the amount that can be withdrawn through the redeem() function. The design also allows the redemption cooldown to be disabled, meaning a user can call redeem() immediately after a deposit. Because the caps are applied per block and not per address, a malicious actor can submit a single transaction that first deposits the maximum allowed amount (for example 10,000 tokens) and then immediately redeems the same amount within the same block. This atomic sequence consumes both the deposit cap and the redemption cap for that block. As a result, any subsequent honest user who attempts to deposit or redeem in the same block will hit the exhausted cap and their transaction will revert, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service (DoS) on the core liquidity functions. The issue is most exploitable in low‑cost L2 environments where gas is cheap and users can submit many transactions per block. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the cap logic and the optional cooldown flag. The problem can be hard to notice because the caps appear to protect the system from runaway minting, yet they do not prevent a single actor from saturating the limits. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “deposit failed” or “redeem failed” error with no obvious reason, and the user’s balance remains unchanged even though they expected a successful mint or withdrawal. The business logic that assumes each block will have available capacity for legitimate users is violated, breaking the accounting invariant that total minted tokens should reflect genuine deposits. To mitigate the issue the contract should introduce additional throttling mechanisms such as per‑address rate limits, a mandatory non‑zero cooldown period, or a small fee on deposits and withdrawals that makes it economically unattractive to repeatedly hit the caps. These changes would prevent an attacker from repeatedly exhausting the per‑block limits and restore normal operation for honest participants.

title: No-mix staking wallets are not fully handled in the codebase
description:
In the Lombard codebase, there are two types of staking wallets - the regular staking wallet and the no-mix staking wallet. The problem is that the no-mix staking wallets are not handled in numerous parts of the codebase. In all of these instances, it only checks that the public key is the regular staking wallet. If it is the no-mix staking wallet, it will return an error.
1. validateStakingInputs: This function is called in Babylon deposit and Lombard unstake, which means that it would actually be impossible to deposit to Babylon or withdraw funds from the no-mix staking wallet.
2. validateStakingOutputs: This function is called in Lombard transfer, meaning it would be impossible to transfer funds from the deposit wallet to the no-mix staking wallet from regular UTXOs. Notably, it is still possible via the change UTXO.
3. validateStakerKey: This function is called in Babylon early unbond and timelock withdraw, which means it would be impossible to perform an early unbonding request or withdraw from Babylon to the no-mix staking wallet. In the current implementation, as elaborated earlier, funds can still enter the no-mix staking wallet via the change UTXO, so it is possible for funds to become stuck there.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the Lombard codebase distinguishes two staking wallet types – a regular staking wallet and a no‑mix staking wallet – but the validation logic throughout the contract suite only recognises the regular type. Functions such as validateStakingInputs, validateStakingOutputs and validateStakerKey perform a public‑key check against the regular staking wallet and reject any transaction that references a no‑mix wallet, returning an error instead of handling it. As a result, legitimate operations like depositing to Babylon, withdrawing from a no‑mix wallet, transferring funds from a deposit wallet to a no‑mix wallet, or performing early unbond or timelock withdrawals cannot be completed. The root cause is incomplete input validation: the code does not include the no‑mix wallet in its allowed set, so the execution path aborts whenever that wallet appears. Exploitation is straightforward – a user who attempts any of the aforementioned actions with a no‑mix wallet will see the transaction revert, while the protocol still permits funds to reach the no‑mix wallet via a change UTXO. Consequently, assets can become trapped: they are visible on‑chain in the no‑mix wallet but cannot be moved out because every subsequent operation that would normally release or transfer them fails the validation check. This asset‑locking effect is observable from the user’s perspective as a successful deposit followed by an inability to withdraw, a balance that appears to stay at zero, or error messages indicating an invalid staking wallet. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which traced the validation calls across the codebase and noted the missing handling of the no‑mix wallet. The problem is subtle because the change‑UTXO path still allows funds to enter the wallet, giving the impression that the operation succeeded, while later steps silently fail, making the lock hard to detect without deep code inspection. To remediate, the validation routines should be extended to recognise and correctly process no‑mix staking wallets, or the contract should unify the handling of both wallet types so that all staking‑related functions treat them equivalently. This would prevent funds from becoming irretrievable and restore the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Not all staking key enabled status are checked
description: The staking key enabled status is not checked in multiple places. The approver service checks that the staking key is enabled before accepting it, as in the event of a key compromise. This allows the Lombard team to disable such a compromised key via Cubist, which will automatically prevent the approver service from approving such keys. The problem arises due to the fact that the approver does not sufficiently check that the key is enabled in numerous places.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of inconsistent validation of a staking key's enabled status across the contract code. The business logic requires that a staking key be marked as enabled before it can be used to approve staking operations, especially after a key compromise where the protocol team disables the key via an external management tool. However, several functions that handle key approval do not perform this enabled‑status check, allowing a disabled (and potentially compromised) key to be accepted in those specific execution paths. The root cause is a missing guard clause or modifier in multiple places, leading to a situation where the contract assumes a key is valid based on incomplete information. An attacker who possesses a compromised key can submit a transaction that reaches one of the unchecked functions, causing the system to treat the key as active and approve actions such as staking, reward distribution, or fund transfers. This can result in unauthorized movement of assets, loss of staked balances, or disruption of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only when the code path that lacks the check is exercised; normal operations that go through the correctly guarded functions appear safe, making the bug hard to detect during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended security model with the actual implementation and identified several locations where the enabled flag was not verified. From a user perspective the symptoms may include approvals succeeding despite the key being shown as disabled, unexpected zero balances after a transaction, or rewards not being credited. The vulnerability belongs to the class of insufficient input validation or missing authorization checks, where a critical state variable is not consistently enforced. To remediate, the enabled status should be verified in every function that processes staking key approvals, ideally by centralising the check in a reusable modifier or internal routine, ensuring that no execution path can bypass the validation. This will align the implementation with the intended security policy and prevent compromised keys from being used inadvertently.

title: Missing validation that ensures unspent BTC is fully sent back as change in Lombard transfer signing strategy
description: The Lombard transfer signing strategy is used to transfer BTC from the Cubist deposit wallets to the Cubist staking hot wallets. validateLombardTransferRequest() ensures that the transfer request is valid before approving it. However, there is no validation that ensures that the BTC miner fee is reasonable and that the remaining unspent BTC is sent back as change to one of Lombard's staking addresses. This could lead to a situation where the UTXO outputs only spend a fraction of the input BTC, with the remaining BTC going to the miner.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the Lombard transfer signing strategy that fails to guarantee that any unspent Bitcoin from a transaction is returned to a designated change address after deducting a reasonable miner fee. The root cause is that the function responsible for checking a transfer request does not compare the total value of the UTXO inputs with the sum of the declared outputs plus an acceptable fee, nor does it enforce the presence of a change output. Because of this omission, an attacker or a careless operator can craft a request where the outputs consume only a small portion of the input value, allowing the remainder to be unintentionally or maliciously treated as an excessive miner fee. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious actor submits a Lombard transfer that specifies a low output amount, omits a change output, and relies on the unchecked logic to let the Bitcoin network treat the difference as a fee, effectively stealing the unspent BTC. The impact is loss of funds from the Cubist deposit wallets, reduction of user balances, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting because users may see their deposited BTC disappear or be reduced far more than expected. The condition under which this occurs is any execution of the Lombard transfer signing strategy that does not include a change output or does not enforce a fee ceiling, which is typical when moving BTC from deposit wallets to staking hot wallets. All parties that rely on the correctness of the transfer – depositors, the staking infrastructure, and the overall protocol – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, which noted the absence of a sanity check on the relationship between inputs, outputs, and fees. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction remains valid on the Bitcoin network; the only symptom is an unexpectedly high fee or a missing change amount, which may not be highlighted in UI components that simply display the intended transfer amount. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a certain amount of BTC was sent to the staking address, yet the user’s balance drops by a larger amount, or the staking wallet receives less than expected, leading to confusion and potential panic. This class of bug falls under insufficient output validation and change‑output omission, a common accounting flaw in cryptocurrency transaction construction. To remediate, the contract should sum all input UTXO values, compute the expected change after subtracting a reasonable miner fee, enforce that the change is sent to a known Lombard staking address, and reject any request where the fee exceeds a predefined threshold or where the change output is missing. Implementing these checks restores the invariant that total inputs equal total outputs plus fee, preserving funds and aligning with the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: Integer overflow will lock all rewards in `AuraLocker`
description:
[AuraLocker.sol#L176-L177](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L176-L177)
