[AuraLocker.sol#L802-L814](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L802-L814)  
[AuraLocker.sol#L864](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/AuraLocker.sol#L864)  

There is a potential overflow in the rewards calculations which would lead to `updateReward()` always reverting.

The impact of this overflow is that all reward tokens will be permanently locked in the contract. User’s will be unable to call any of the functions which have the `updateReward()` modifier, that is:

  * `lock()`
  * `getReward()`
  * `_processExpiredLocks()`
  * `_notifyRewardAmount()`

As a result the contract will need to call `shutdown()` and the users will only be able to receive their staked tokens via `emergencyWithdraw()`, which does not transfer the users the reward tokens.

Note that if one reward token overflows this will cause a revert on all reward tokens due to the loop over reward tokens.

This issue will always be present if the staked token is one with a low number of decimal places such as USDC or USDT which have 6 decimal places. This is because the `totalSupply` will be limited in size by the decimal places of the `stakingToken`.
poc:
The overflow may occur due to the base of values in `_rewardPerToken()`.
    
```solidity
    function _rewardPerToken(address _rewardsToken) internal view returns (uint256) {
        if (lockedSupply == 0) {
            return rewardData[_rewardsToken].rewardPerTokenStored;
        }
        return
            uint256(rewardData[_rewardsToken].rewardPerTokenStored).add(
                _lastTimeRewardApplicable(rewardData[_rewardsToken].periodFinish)
                    .sub(rewardData[_rewardsToken].lastUpdateTime)
                    .mul(rewardData[_rewardsToken].rewardRate)
                    .mul(1e18)
                    .div(lockedSupply)
            );
    }
```

The return value of `_rewardPerToken()` is in terms of
    
    (now - lastUpdateTime) * rewardRate * 10**18 / totalSupply

Here `(now - lastUpdateTime)` has a maximum value of `rewardDuration = 6 * 10**5`.

Now `rewardRate` is the `_reward.div(rewardsDuration)` as seen in `_notifyRewardAmount()` on line #864. Note that `rewardDuration` is a constant 604,800.

`rewardDuration = 6 * 10**5`

Thus, if we have a rewards such as AURA or WETH (or most ERC20 tokens) which have units 10**18 we can transfer 1 WETH to the reward distributor which calls `_notifyRewardAmount()` and sets the reward rate to,

`rewardRate = 10**18 / (6 * 10**5) ~= 10**12`

Finally, if this attack is run either by the first depositor they may `lock()` a single token which would set `totalSupply = 1`.

Therefore our equation in terms of units will become,
    
    (now - lastUpdateTime) * rewardRate * 10**18 / totalSupply => 10**5 * 10**12 * 10**18 / 1 = 10**35

In since `rewardPerTokenStored` is a `uint96` it has a maximum value of `2**96 ~= 7.9 * 10**28`. Hence there will be an overflow in `newRewardPerToken.to96()`. Since we are unable to add more total supply due to `lock()` reverting there will be no way to circumvent this revert except to `shutdown()`.
    
```solidity
                uint256 newRewardPerToken = _rewardPerToken(token);
                rewardData[token].rewardPerTokenStored = newRewardPerToken.to96();
```

Note this attack is described when we have a low `totalSupply`. However it is also possible to apply this attack on a larger `totalSupply` when there are reward tokens which have decimal places larger than 18 or tokens which such as SHIB which have small token value and so many of the tokens can be bought for cheap.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the reward accounting logic of the AuraLocker contract. The contract stores the cumulative reward per token in a variable that is typed as a 96‑bit unsigned integer. When the system calculates a new reward‑per‑token value, it multiplies the elapsed time, the configured reward rate and a 1e18 scaling factor, then divides by the amount of tokens currently locked (totalSupply). If totalSupply is very small – for example a single USDC or USDT unit with six decimals – the division produces a huge intermediate result. Because the result is added to the existing 96‑bit value, the sum can exceed the maximum of 2^96‑1 (≈7.9×10^28). When this happens the conversion to the 96‑bit storage slot overflows and the transaction reverts inside the updateReward() modifier. This revert propagates to every external function that is protected by updateReward, namely lock(), getReward(), the internal lock‑expiration processing, and the reward‑notification routine. Consequently, users are unable to lock additional tokens, claim any accrued rewards, or process expired locks; the only remaining option is to invoke emergencyWithdraw(), which returns only the staked principal and leaves all reward tokens permanently locked in the contract.

The overflow occurs only under a specific set of conditions: the staking token must have a low decimal precision, causing totalSupply to be bounded by a small integer; the reward token uses the typical 18‑decimal representation; and the reward rate is large enough that (now‑lastUpdateTime) × rewardRate × 1e18 exceeds the 96‑bit ceiling when divided by the tiny totalSupply. An attacker can trigger the condition by being the first depositor, locking a single token, and then supplying a reward amount that results in a high rewardRate. The audit identified the flaw by tracing the arithmetic in _rewardPerToken() and noticing that rewardPerTokenStored is a uint96 while the intermediate product can reach 10^35, far beyond the storage limit. The bug is difficult to observe in everyday usage because it requires extreme parameter values that are not normally exercised, and the overflow manifests as a generic revert without an explicit error message.

The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the reward distribution mechanism and permanent loss of reward tokens for all participants. Users expecting to receive rewards find their transactions failing and their balances unchanged, leading to a situation where “my rewards never arrive” or “the lock function keeps reverting”. The class of bug is a reward accounting overflow, a subset of integer overflow vulnerabilities that break financial invariants. To remediate the issue the contract should store rewardPerToken and rewardRate using a larger integer type such as uint256 or uint224, or enforce a strict upper bound on rewardRate (for example rewardRate < 1e17) before accepting new rewards. By ensuring the intermediate calculation cannot exceed the storage capacity, the overflow and the resulting lock‑out of rewards can be prevented.

title: `ConvexMasterChef`: `safeRewardTransfer` can cause loss of funds
description:
Same as <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-02-concur-findings/issues/244>

All calculations are rounded down, since a lack of tokens in the contracts cannot be rounding errors’ fault. So the function is redundant.  
On the other hand, if the contract is undersupplied with cvx tokens, this will cause depositors to be sent less tokens than needed (or none). This is especially unsafe because the tokens that were lacking are not resembled in accountings at all. Thus a depositor may invoke the safeRewardTransfer and not receive tokens they were supposed to.
poc: [ConvexMasterChef.sol#L299-L306](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/convex-platform/contracts/contracts/ConvexMasterChef.sol#L299-L306)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution routine of the ConvexMasterChef contract, specifically the safeRewardTransfer function that is used to send CVX reward tokens to depositors. The function assumes that the contract always holds enough CVX tokens to cover the calculated reward amount, but it does not enforce this assumption. Instead, it checks the available token balance and, if the balance is lower than the amount owed, it silently truncates the transfer to the remaining balance without reverting or emitting an explicit error. This design choice eliminates rounding errors by rounding down all calculations, yet it creates a hidden shortfall when the contract is undersupplied. As a result, a user who invokes safeRewardTransfer may receive fewer tokens than the protocol promises, or even receive nothing, while the accounting records still reflect the full reward entitlement. The impact is a loss of funds for any users claiming rewards during a period when the contract’s CVX balance is insufficient, breaking the core business logic that rewards must be fully delivered. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s reward token reserve is depleted, for example due to mis‑allocation, accidental token transfer out of the contract, or an imbalance between reward accrual and actual token funding. The issue affects all participants who rely on the contract to distribute their rewards, undermining trust in the protocol’s fairness and potentially leading to user complaints such as "my balance shows a reward but I got nothing" or "my expected refund is zero". The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reward accounting with the transfer logic and noted that the function does not revert on insufficient balance, making the failure silent and easy to miss because no error event is emitted and the UI may still display the theoretical reward amount. This class of bug can be described as a silent‑failure token transfer due to unchecked balance constraints, which violates the accounting invariant that total rewards owed must equal total rewards paid. To remediate, the contract should replace safeRewardTransfer with a standard safeTransfer that reverts when the source balance is insufficient, or it should add explicit checks and revert on shortfall, together with proper accounting updates and events that alert users to any discrepancy. Ensuring the contract is always funded before reward distribution, or implementing a fallback mechanism that records the deficit for later settlement, would also close the vulnerability and restore the expected guarantee that users receive the full amount of rewards they are entitled to.

title: DDOS in `BalLiquidityProvider`
description: DDOS to liquidity providers in BalLiquidityProvider.
poc:
* bal is equal to the contract’s balance of the asset: [BalLiquidityProvider.sol#L56](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/BalLiquidityProvider.sol#L56)
  * bal is required to be equal to the input parameter _request.maxAmountsIn[i]: [BalLiquidityProvider.sol#L57](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/contracts/BalLiquidityProvider.sol#L57)

An attacker can front-run liquidity providers by sending 1 Wei of the asset to make the balance not equal to the input. This can be repeated and be used to impede the liquidity provider from using the function which will always revert since bal != _request.maxAmountsIn[i]
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BalLiquidityProvider contract, where a function that adds liquidity requires the contract's token balance (bal) to be exactly equal to an input parameter _request.maxAmountsIn[i]. This strict equality creates a denial‑of‑service condition because any external actor can alter the contract's balance by sending a trivial amount of the token (for example, 1 wei) before the liquidity‑provider transaction is executed. When the attacker performs this front‑run, the on‑chain balance becomes slightly larger than the value supplied in the request, causing the require statement to fail and the transaction to revert. As a result, legitimate liquidity providers are unable to submit their deposits, the pool does not receive new liquidity, and expected fees or market‑making functions are blocked. The issue surfaces whenever the add‑liquidity function is called and the contract balance is expected to match the caller‑provided maximum amount; it can be triggered repeatedly with negligible cost to the attacker. The parties impacted include liquidity providers who see their transactions revert with a balance mismatch error, the protocol that loses fresh capital and potentially suffers reduced trading volume, and end‑users who may experience higher slippage or missing market depth. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewer noticed the equality check between an externally mutable balance and an input variable, recognizing that the balance can be altered by anyone. It is difficult to notice because the discrepancy may involve only a single wei, which does not appear in most UI dashboards, and the revert message may be generic. This flaw belongs to the broader class of bugs that rely on exact equality with external state, enabling front‑running or other actors to break invariants. To remediate, the contract should either remove the equality requirement entirely or replace it with a non‑strict check such as bal >= _request.maxAmountsIn[i], and should rely on internal accounting rather than the raw token balance to enforce limits. By doing so, the contract no longer depends on an immutable balance value that can be manipulated, thereby eliminating the DoS vector and restoring the expected behavior where users can provide liquidity without unexpected reverts.

title: `ConvexMasterChef`’s deposit and withdraw can be reentered drawing all reward funds from the contract if reward token allows for transfer flow control
description:
Reward token accounting update in deposit() and withdraw() happens after reward transfer. If reward token allows for the control of transfer call flow or can be upgraded to allow it in the future (i.e. have or can introduce the _beforetokentransfer, _afterTokenTransfer type of hooks; or, say, can be upgraded to ERC777), the current implementation makes it possible to drain all the reward token funds of the contract by directly reentering deposit() or withdraw() with tiny _amount.

Setting the severity to medium as this is conditional to transfer flow control assumption, but the impact is the full loss of contract reward token holdings.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution logic of the ConvexMasterChef contract, specifically within its deposit() and withdraw() functions. Both functions calculate a user's pending reward amount and then immediately transfer that reward token to the caller through an external call (safeRewardTransfer) before any internal accounting variables such as user.amount or user.rewardDebt are updated. This ordering creates a classic reentrancy window: if the reward token being transferred implements transfer‑flow control hooks—such as the _beforeTokenTransfer or _afterTokenTransfer callbacks introduced by ERC777 or a custom token that can be upgraded to include such hooks—an attacker can craft a malicious token that invokes the contract’s deposit() or withdraw() again during the reward transfer. Because the contract’s state has not yet been reconciled for the initial call, each re‑entry sees the same pre‑transfer accounting and believes the caller is still entitled to the full pending reward. By repeatedly re‑entering with a minimal _amount, the attacker can drain the entire balance of the reward token held by the contract. The issue manifests only when the reward token supports or can be upgraded to support callback hooks that allow code execution on transfer, which is why it is classified as conditional and assigned a medium severity. From a user perspective, the symptom is that the protocol’s reward pool becomes empty, causing legitimate stakers to receive no rewards or to see their expected balances disappear. The problem is subtle because standard ERC20 tokens do not provide such callbacks, so typical testing may not reveal the reentrancy path; the audit uncovered the flaw by analyzing the order of external calls relative to state mutations. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) and, more fundamentally, move all internal accounting updates—including user.amount, user.rewardDebt, and pool.accCvxPerShare—ahead of any external token transfer. Alternatively, a pull‑payment pattern where users claim rewards after the contract’s state is fully settled would eliminate the reentrancy window. Implementing these changes restores the invariant that reward balances are only transferred after the contract’s internal accounting accurately reflects the user's new position, thereby protecting the protocol’s reward assets from being siphoned by a token with malicious transfer hooks.

title: `AuraBalRewardPool` charges a penalty to all users in the pool if the `AuraLocker` has been shut down
description: Users are charged the penalty due to admin actions, and they have no way to avoid it
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the AuraBalRewardPool contract’s reward claiming logic, where every user who attempts to claim their accrued AuraBAL rewards faces a mandatory 20 % penalty when the associated AuraLocker contract has been shut down. The root cause is a design flaw in the getReward(bool _lock) function: it offers only two mutually exclusive paths – locking the reward via auraLocker.lock(...) or receiving the reward after a hard‑coded penalty calculation. The AuraLocker’s internal _lock function contains a require(!isShutdown) guard, causing any call to lock to revert once the locker is marked as shut down. Because the getReward function does not check the locker’s shutdown status before deciding which path to execute, a user who chooses the lock option experiences a revert, and the only remaining viable option is the else branch that deducts a penalty of reward × 2/10. This means that, under the condition that the AuraLocker has been shut down (a state change that can be triggered by admin governance), all participants are forced to accept the penalty, losing a fifth of their entitled reward. The impact is a direct loss of funds for users: they receive only 80 % of the expected reward, while the deducted amount is accumulated in a pendingPenalty pool that is not returned to the affected users. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a successful claim but the received balance is smaller than anticipated, or the balance may even become zero if the reward itself was small, leading to confusion and a perception that the protocol is unfair or malicious. The issue was discovered during a formal code audit (Code4rena) that examined the reward distribution flow and identified the unconditional penalty application when the locker is unavailable. It is hard to notice because the penalty logic appears legitimate under normal operation – the locker is expected to be active for the short two‑week reward window, so the shutdown case is rarely exercised. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of “involuntary penalty enforcement due to unavailable fallback path” and violates the business assumption that users can either lock their reward or claim it without a punitive charge. To remediate, the contract should first verify that the locker is operational before offering the lock option, and if the locker is shut down it should either allow a penalty‑free claim or expose an explicit opt‑out mechanism, thereby restoring the intended economic guarantees of the reward pool.

title: `CrvDepositor.sol` Wrong implementation of the 2-week buffer for lock
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CrvDepositor contract’s logic that governs when a user’s token lock may be extended. The contract is supposed to enforce a two‑week buffer before allowing another increase of the lock duration, but the implementation mistakenly treats a time value that is stored in seconds as if it were expressed in weeks. Specifically, the code computes `unlockInWeeks` by truncating the target unlock timestamp to the nearest week boundary, then subtracts the previously stored `unlockTime` (which remains a raw Unix timestamp) and compares the result to the constant `2`. Because the subtraction yields a value measured in seconds, the condition `> 2` effectively checks for a two‑second gap rather than a two‑week gap. Consequently, the contract permits the lock to be extended as soon as a new week starts, violating the intended two‑week waiting period. This bug was identified during a static audit of the source code, where the mismatched units became apparent. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or any participant can call the internal function that triggers a lock extension each week, thereby maintaining an always‑maximized lock length without respecting the designed buffer. The impact includes distortion of protocol economics, as the system assumes a minimum two‑week interval to calculate voting power, reward accrual, and overall tokenomics; bypassing this interval can lead to inflated boost rewards, unfair advantage over honest participants, and potential downstream accounting errors. The issue manifests subtly: users see their lock being extended more frequently than expected, but there is no immediate error message or revert, making it hard to notice without reviewing the contract’s timing logic. From a user perspective, the symptom is that the lock appears to be extended every week, contrary to the expectation that a two‑week waiting period would be enforced, leading to confusion about why their lock behaves differently. The affected parties are any token holder interacting with the CrvDepositor, as well as the protocol itself, which relies on the lock timing for correct distribution of rewards and governance weight. To remediate, the contract should store and compare lock timestamps consistently in the same unit—either convert the stored `unlockTime` to weeks or keep both values in seconds. Renaming the variable to reflect its unit (e.g., `unlockTimeInWeeks`) and adjusting the calculation to compare week counts rather than raw seconds restores the intended two‑week buffer, ensuring the protocol’s business logic and accounting assumptions remain intact.

title: `massUpdatePools`
description:
[ConvexMasterChef.sol#L178-L183](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/convex-platform/contracts/contracts/ConvexMasterChef.sol#L178-L183)  

massUpdatePools() is a public function and it calls the updatePool() function for the length of poolInfo. Hence, it is an unbounded loop, depending on the length of poolInfo.  
If poolInfo.length is big enough, block gas limit may be hit.
poc: <https://consensys.github.io/smart-contract-best-practices/attacks/denial-of-service/#dos-with-block-gas-limit>
bug_full: The contract exposes a public function called massUpdatePools that iterates over the entire poolInfo array and invokes updatePool for each entry. Because the loop size is directly tied to the length of poolInfo, there is no intrinsic bound on how many iterations can be performed in a single transaction. When an administrator or any external actor adds a large number of pools, calling massUpdatePools will require more gas than the block gas limit permits, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This denial‑of‑service condition means that the accounting information for the pools is not refreshed, so pending rewards are not tallied and users may observe that their expected earnings remain unchanged or disappear entirely. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a zero or stale balance, while the protocol’s internal bookkeeping assumes rewards should have been distributed. The vulnerability stems from a classic unbounded‑loop pattern, where a mutable array is traversed without a cap, and the function is publicly callable rather than restricted to a trusted role. It was uncovered during a manual audit that flagged the loop as a potential gas‑limit issue, a known class of DoS attacks. The problem can be subtle because it only manifests when the pool count grows beyond a threshold; with a modest number of pools the function appears to work correctly, making the risk easy to overlook. The proper mitigation is to impose a maximum number of pool updates per call, split the work into batches, or restrict the function to privileged callers and enforce a sensible upper bound on the poolInfo length. By ensuring that the gas consumption of massUpdatePools stays within block limits, the protocol can continue to update rewards reliably and avoid accounting gaps that could lead to lost earnings for participants.

title: `ConvexMasterChef`: When using `add`
poc: [ConvexMasterChef.sol#L96-L138](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/4989a2077546a5394e3650bf3c224669a0f7e690/convex-platform/contracts/contracts/ConvexMasterChef.sol#L96-L138)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward allocation logic of a master‑chef style staking contract where each pool’s share of the total reward is derived from the global variable totalAllocPoint. When a new liquidity pool is added (or an existing pool’s allocation points are changed) the contract offers an optional _withUpdate flag that, if set to false, skips the call to massUpdatePools() before modifying totalAllocPoint. Because massUpdatePools() is responsible for bringing every pool’s accumulated reward per share (accCvxPerShare) up‑to‑date based on the current totalAllocPoint, omitting this step causes the pending reward for all previously‑added pools to be calculated against a stale totalAllocPoint value. The root cause is therefore a missing state‑synchronisation step: the contract updates a critical accounting variable without first reconciling the dependent reward state. An attacker who controls the contract owner can exploit this by adding a pool with _withUpdate set to false and choosing an allocation point that artificially inflates or deflates totalAllocPoint. Existing pools will continue to accrue rewards based on the outdated totalAllocPoint, resulting in an incorrect distribution where some users receive fewer tokens than entitled, while the owner’s new pool may capture a larger share of the emission schedule. This mis‑allocation manifests to users as missing or unexpectedly low rewards – for example, a staker who expects a proportionate amount of CVX per block may see their balance remain unchanged or grow far slower after a new pool is added. The condition under which the defect occurs is every time the admin invokes add() or set() with the _withUpdate parameter set to false. All participants who have deposited LP tokens in any pool prior to that call are affected, as their pending reward calculations become inaccurate. The issue was uncovered during a manual code audit that compared the function to a reference implementation and noticed that the optional flag allowed the contract to be left in an inconsistent state. It can be hard to detect in normal operation because reward balances appear correct until a pool addition occurs without updating, at which point the discrepancy is only observable through a detailed inspection of pending reward values. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the _withUpdate flag and enforce a mandatory call to massUpdatePools() before any change to totalAllocPoint, ensuring that reward accounting is always synchronized. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of allocation‑point synchronization bugs where a global accounting variable is modified without updating dependent derived values, leading to reward calculation errors and potential loss of earned tokens.

title: Duplicate LP token could lead to incorrect reward distribution
description:
[ConvexMasterChef.sol#L96](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-aura/blob/main/convex-platform/contracts/contracts/ConvexMasterChef.sol#L96)  

It was observed that add function is not checking for duplicate lpToken which allows 2 or more pools to have exact same lpToken. This can cause issue with reward distribution

In case of duplicate lpToken, lpSupply will become incorrect (ConvexMasterChef.sol#L160), hence rewards will be calculated incorrectly
poc:
1. Owner call add function and uses lpToken as A
  2. Owner again call add function and mistakenly provides lpToken as A
  3. Now 2 pools will be created with lpToken as A
  4. This becomes a problem while reward calculation or updatePool function which uses pool.lpToken.balanceOf(address(this)). Since both pool have same lpToken so lpSupply will be calculated as same which is wrong. Since lpSupply defines the rewardRate so this directly impact reward calculation
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing the creation of multiple liquidity pools that reference the exact same LP (liquidity provider) token. The root cause is the missing validation in the contract's add function, which does not verify whether the supplied lpToken address has already been registered for an existing pool. When a duplicate lpToken is added, two distinct pool records end up pointing to the same token contract. During reward calculation, the system aggregates the LP token balance of each pool by calling pool.lpToken.balanceOf(address(this)). Because both pools reference the identical token, the same token balance is counted twice, inflating the reported lpSupply value. The reward distribution logic then divides the total reward amount by this inflated lpSupply, resulting in a lower per‑share reward for all participants in the affected pools. In practice, users who expect a certain amount of reward for their deposited liquidity may receive less than anticipated, or in edge cases the distribution may become uneven, effectively stealing value from honest participants. The issue manifests whenever an authorized account (typically the contract owner or a multi‑signature controller) calls the add function more than once with the same lpToken address; it does not require any special conditions beyond the duplicate registration. All users who stake the duplicated LP token may be harmed, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that each pool tracks a unique token supply—are violated. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the pool‑registration logic and identified the absence of a duplicate‑check mechanism. Because the symptom is subtle—both pools appear legitimate and the UI may simply list two entries with the same token name—users may not notice that their rewards are being diluted, making the bug hard to detect without deep inspection of the reward calculations. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain a global registry of LP token addresses that have already been added and reject any attempt to add a token that already exists in the registry, causing the add function to revert on duplicate submissions. This change restores the invariant that each LP token is uniquely associated with a single pool, ensuring correct lpSupply values and accurate reward distribution. The class of bug falls under "duplicate asset registration leading to accounting drift" and is a typical example of an unchecked input causing logical errors in financial calculations.

title: Proxy does not support payable functions in its implementation
description:
The UpgradeableProxy.fallback function that forwards the calls to the implementation con-  
tract is not defined as payable. If the implementation contract defines any functions that require ETH to  
be sent, they will be inaccessible as the UpgradeableProxy.fallback will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing payable modifier on the fallback function of an upgradeable proxy contract. The proxy’s fallback is responsible for delegating any call that does not match a defined function signature to the implementation contract, but because the fallback is not declared payable, any call that includes a non‑zero ether value is automatically rejected and the transaction reverts. This occurs when the implementation contract defines functions that are intended to receive ether – for example deposit, mint, or any payable operation – and a user or another contract invokes those functions through the proxy while sending ether. The root cause is the proxy’s fallback signature being defined as `fallback() external` instead of `fallback() external payable`, which violates the Solidity rule that a non‑payable function cannot receive value. An attacker or an unwitting user can exploit this by attempting to send ether to the proxy expecting the implementation’s payable logic to execute; the proxy will reject the value, causing the call to fail and any ether sent to be reverted. The impact is that legitimate users are unable to perform ether‑based actions through the proxy, leading to a loss of expected functionality, potential locking of funds if the caller does not handle the revert correctly, and a break in the protocol’s economic model that assumes deposits or payments can be made via the proxy. The issue manifests only when a payable function is called through the proxy with a value attached; calls without value work as intended. All participants that interact with the proxy – end‑users, integrators, and the protocol itself – are affected because they cannot successfully execute ether‑receiving operations. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the proxy’s source code, where the fallback definition was examined and found to lack the payable keyword. It can be hard to notice because the proxy may appear to work for read‑only or non‑payable functions, and the failure only surfaces when value is sent, which may not be exercised in basic unit tests. To remediate, the fallback function should be marked payable (e.g., `fallback() external payable { … }`) or a separate `receive()` function should be added to explicitly accept ether, ensuring that value‑bearing calls are correctly forwarded to the implementation. This class of bug – a non‑payable fallback in a proxy pattern – violates the expected accounting logic where ether sent to a contract should be accepted and processed, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as “transaction failed” or “no balance change” when attempting to deposit funds, contrary to the expectation that the deposit would succeed.

title: StakingContract.setRewardsDuration can be DoS'd
description:
The  
StakingRewards.setRewardsDuration  
function  
can  
only  
be  
called  
after  
periodFinish. However,  
anyone  
can  
call  
VestedRewardsDistribution.distribute  
which  
calls  
StakingReward.notifyRewardAmount and sets a new periodFinish. It's unlikely that the rewardDuration  
can ever be changed as long as the DssVest is still active.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract's setRewardsDuration function, which is intended to be callable only after the current rewards period has finished (periodFinish). The contract relies on an external VestedRewardsDistribution contract that can be invoked by any address through its distribute function. This distribute function internally calls StakingRewards.notifyRewardAmount, which updates the periodFinish timestamp to a new value, effectively resetting the rewards period. Because the condition for setRewardsDuration is that the current block timestamp must be greater than periodFinish, an attacker who can repeatedly trigger distribute can keep extending periodFinish indefinitely, preventing the owner or governance from ever calling setRewardsDuration. The root cause is the lack of access control on the distribute function combined with the fact that notifyRewardAmount unconditionally overwrites periodFinish. Exploitation consists of an attacker (or any user) calling distribute at regular intervals, causing the staking contract to think a rewards period is still active. As a result, the rewards duration cannot be changed, which may lock the protocol into an undesired reward schedule, reduce flexibility, and in extreme cases cause a denial‑of‑service where future reward adjustments are impossible. This situation occurs after the DssVest vesting schedule has been activated, because the vesting contract continuously calls distribute as part of its vesting logic. All participants who rely on the ability to adjust reward parameters – typically the protocol’s governance, token holders, and liquidity providers – are affected because they may be unable to respond to market changes or correct mis‑configured reward rates. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the staking module when the reviewer noticed that setRewardsDuration checks only periodFinish but does not consider that periodFinish can be repeatedly refreshed by an external call. The problem can be subtle because the contract still distributes rewards correctly; only the inability to change the duration is observable, which may only be noticed when an attempt to call setRewardsDuration reverts. To remediate, the contract should either restrict who can call distribute/notifyRewardAmount, or modify setRewardsDuration to first pause reward notifications, accrue any pending rewards, compute the leftover amount, and then safely update rewardDuration and rewardRate before re‑enabling distribution. Alternatively, adding a separate access‑controlled function to change the duration without depending on periodFinish would eliminate the lockout. In user‑facing terms, a participant may see that the reward rate remains unchanged even after a governance proposal to extend the rewards period, leading to expectations of higher returns being unmet. The bug belongs to the class of “parameter lockout via external state mutation” or “unrestricted external call causing denial‑of‑service of admin functions.”

title: Depositors might be unable to withdraw desired asset
description:
The PSM3 allows deposits of three assets. It allows anyone to swap between these three  
assets. A depositor may not expect to always be immediately able to withdraw the asset they deposited  
(or an asset of their choice) as the contract's balance might have been depleted by a swap.  
A malicious user can deliberately DoS withdrawals by sandwiching the withdrawal, swapping out the with-  
drawal asset, and later swapping it back in. As there are no fees only cheap L2 gas costs are to be paid.  
They could even leave 1 wei in the contract balance to burn a rounded-up user's share balance each time  
for maximum impact.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a withdrawal denial condition in a multi‑asset peg stability module (PSM) that permits deposits of three different tokens and allows unrestricted swaps among them. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum reserve of each asset, the total balance of a given token can be reduced to zero by a series‑of swaps performed by an attacker. An attacker can execute a sandwich attack: they observe a pending withdrawal request, perform a swap that removes the requested asset from the contract, let the withdrawal execute (which then receives either zero or a rounded‑up amount that is burned), and later swap the asset back in to restore the balance. On L2 networks the attack costs only cheap gas and no protocol fees, so it can be repeated many times. The result is that honest depositors who expect to receive the same asset they deposited, or any asset of equivalent value, may receive nothing or a truncated amount, effectively losing their funds. The issue manifests when the contract’s internal accounting assumes that the pool always holds enough of each token to satisfy withdrawals, an assumption that is violated by the attacker’s swaps. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined edge‑case withdrawal logic and noticed that the contract does not check for sufficient asset reserves before processing a withdrawal. Because the failure appears only under specific timing and balance conditions, it can be difficult to detect in routine testing where swaps are not deliberately crafted to deplete a reserve. The bug belongs to the class of “asset‑reserve depletion” or “withdrawal denial” vulnerabilities, where a protocol’s accounting model is decoupled from the actual token balances. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal transaction but the received amount is zero or unexpectedly small, contradicting the expectation that the deposited amount will be returned. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a minimum reserve for each supported asset, or implement a withdrawal function that automatically selects the most liquid asset and converts the requested value, thereby guaranteeing that a user can always withdraw an amount equal to their share. Alternatively, the protocol could add a fee or a slippage guard on swaps to prevent an attacker from draining a reserve without cost.

title: Out-of-sync DSRAuthOracle's pot data leads to conversion factor jumps
description:
The DSRAuthOracle uses the cached pot data to extrapolate the conversion rate (chi) in functions like getConversionRate. This cached pot data is updated through a cross-chain message, at least once whenever the dsr is updated on ETH. The extrapolated conversion rates can become out of sync with the actual pot.chi() and when new pot data is set in DSRAuthOracle the conversion rate will experience sudden jumps (both up and down are possible). It can become out of sync if wrong pot data is submitted or pot data updates are not received in chronological order. It also happens naturally as there is a time delay between updating the pot on ETH and the message being received on the L2 through DSRAuthOracle.setPotData. Imagine the following timeline and states:
1. Both ETH's pot and L2's DSRAuthOracle's pot state is in sync and set as (rho_0, dsr_0, chi_0).
2. At time rho_1 on ETH: pot.drip() is called and a new DSR is filed via pot.file(dsr). This updates the state to (rho_1, dsr_1, chi_1).
3. Immediately, at time rho_1 on ETH, a cross-chain message is sent to L2 to update the state on the L2's oracle.
4. At time tau, the message is relayed on the L2 and DSRAuthOracle.setPotData() also updates its state to (rho_1, dsr_1, chi_1). The conversion factor is now extrapolated with the new state.
On L2, the conversion factors were computed as:
• Before the update (t < tau): chi_0 * dsr_0^(now - rho_0).
• After the update (t >= tau): chi_1 * dsr_1^(now - rho_1).
During the time period [rho_1, tau] the pot data is out of sync and at the time of update tau the conversion factor on the L2 jumps. The difference (after - before) can be computed as:
chi_1 * (dsr_1^(tau - rho_1) - dsr_0^(tau - rho_1))
The new conversion factor increases when dsr_1 > dsr_0 (decreases when dsr_1 < dsr_0) and the cross-chain update delay tau - rho_1 amplifies this difference.
As the conversion rate can be used for pricing assets like L2 sDAI (see PSM3 contract), the price jumps can be sandwiched and profited from. The profit per $ investment is the growth in chi which can be computed as (dsr_1^(tau - rho_1) / dsr_0^(tau - rho_1)) - 1.
See the proof of concept below that compute the profit per $. Essentially, it is always profitable because there are no swap fees, the profit (and therefore the LPs' loss) is just bounded by the number of sDAI tokens in the PSM3.
poc:
The following script computes the profit percentage per $ spent by swapping into sDAI in the PSM3 before the new pot data is set, and then swapping back out of sDAI.
Some example values for profit / $ spent:
• DSR APR: 5% →10%, delay = 1 day: 0.0138%
• DSR APR: 5% →10%, delay = 7 days: 0.0968%
• DSR APR: 5% →15%, delay = 1 days: 0.0277%
• DSR APR: 5% →15%, delay = 7 days: 0.1937%
Assuming similar TVL as the ETH PSM is achieved and estimating 100M$ of sDAI in the PSM3 an attacker can steal 10,000$ in the first example, 193,700$ in the second example.
def get_chi(oldChi, dsr, seconds_elapsed):
    return oldChi * dsr ** seconds_elapsed
def get_apr(dsr):
    return (dsr - 1) * 31536000
chi_0 = 1.5
dsr_old = 1.0000000016 # 5% APR
dsr_new = 1 + (dsr_old % 1.0) * 2 # 10% APR
print(f"DSR_old APR: {get_apr(dsr_old) * 100:.2f}%")
print(f"DSR_new APR: {get_apr(dsr_new) * 100:.2f}%")
# t_rho1 = rho_1 - rho_0
t_rho1 = 90 * 24 * 60 * 60 # DSR changes after 90 days (this value is irrelevant for profit)
# t_tau = tau - rho_1
t_tau = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 # syncing takes this time
# chi on L2 before update runs for t_rho1 + t_tau seconds
chi_unsynced = get_chi(chi_0, dsr_old, t_rho1 + t_tau)
# chi on ETH runs with old dsr until dsr updates after t_0 seconds
chi_1 = get_chi(chi_0, dsr_old, t_rho1)
# then runs with new dsr t_tau seconds
chi_synced = get_chi(chi_1, dsr_new, t_tau)
print(f"chi_unsynced = {chi_unsynced:.6f}")
print(f"chi_synced = {chi_synced:.6f}")
chi_growth_percentage = (chi_synced - chi_unsynced) / chi_unsynced
print(f"chi growth = {chi_growth_percentage * 100:.4f}%")
# Note that the chi growth (jump percentage) is the profit that can be made.
# Verify
# 1. swap USD to sDAI on PSM3
usd_investment = 1_000_000
sDai_bought = usd_investment / chi_unsynced
# 2. setPotData runs on L2, synching chi
usd_received = sDai_bought * chi_synced
profit = usd_received - usd_investment
print(f"Profit per $: {profit / usd_investment * 100:.4f}%")
# Direct way to compute profit
# profit = (dsr_1^(tau - rho_1) / dsr_0^(tau - rho_1)) - 1
profit = (dsr_new ** t_tau / dsr_old ** t_tau) - 1
print(f"Profit per $: {profit * 100:.4f}%")
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the DSRAuthOracle on the layer‑2 chain stores a cached snapshot of the MakerDAO DSR pot state and uses it to extrapolate the conversion factor (chi) that determines the price of sDAI tokens. The oracle updates this cached pot data only when it receives a cross‑chain message that conveys the new pot parameters after a DSR change on Ethereum. Because the message must travel across chains, there is an inherent time lag between the moment the DSR is modified on Ethereum and the moment the L2 oracle incorporates the new pot data. During this lag the oracle continues to extrapolate chi using the old pot parameters, while the true pot on Ethereum has already started accruing interest at the new rate. Consequently the conversion factor that users see on L2 diverges from the actual value, and when the delayed message finally arrives the oracle overwrites its cached state, causing a sudden jump in the reported chi value. The jump can be upward or downward depending on whether the new DSR is higher or lower than the previous one, and the magnitude of the jump grows with the length of the cross‑chain delay. This behavior violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the conversion rate should evolve smoothly and predictably; instead it creates a discontinuity that can be exploited by traders who sandwich the update, buying sDAI before the jump and selling after, thereby extracting profit equal to the relative change in chi. The impact is felt by any user interacting with the L2 sDAI market, especially liquidity providers in the PSM3 contract, who may see their token value shift unexpectedly and suffer losses when arbitrageurs capture the price discrepancy. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle’s update mechanism and simulated DSR changes, revealing that the extrapolation logic does not enforce chronological ordering of pot updates and that out‑of‑order or delayed messages produce the described jumps. The problem is subtle because the oracle’s interface appears to return a single numeric conversion rate, making the underlying stale data invisible to casual observers; only a careful analysis of the timing between DSR updates and cross‑chain messages exposes the inconsistency. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should either ensure that DSR updates are propagated to all chains atomically, or replace the abrupt overwrite with a smoothing function that gradually aligns the cached chi with the target value, thereby eliminating sharp jumps. Reducing sDAI liquidity in the affected market around DSR changes is another mitigation that limits the amount of value that can be captured by an attacker. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑staleness and timing‑dependency vulnerabilities, where reliance on delayed external data leads to incorrect financial calculations and exploitable price volatility.

title: addLiquidityCurve rateLimit miscalculation for Curve pool N > 2 enables partial limit bypass
bug_full: The vulnerability is a miscalculation in the rate‑limit adjustment performed by the addLiquidityCurve function when a Curve pool contains more than two tokens and the supplied depositAmounts are not evenly distributed. The function attempts to reduce the swap‑rate limit by an amount that reflects the internal swap required to rebalance the pool, but it computes this reduction by dividing the total absolute difference between the intended deposits and the post‑swap balances (totalSwapped) by the number of tokens (depositAmounts.length). Because totalSwapped already represents twice the sum of tokens that would be sold in the internal swap, dividing by the token count underestimates the true swap volume for pools with three or more assets. The root cause is the incorrect averaging formula – the code should divide totalSwapped by two, not by the token count, before applying the 1e18 scaling factor. An attacker controlling the relayer can craft a depositAmounts array such as [150,30,60] for a three‑token pool, causing the internal Curve logic to perform swaps equivalent to selling 70 units of token0 and receiving 50 and 20 units of the other tokens. The contract, however, only reduces the LIMIT_CURVE_SWAP by roughly one‑third of the required amount, leaving a larger unused portion of the rate limit. By repeatedly submitting such uneven deposits, the attacker can bypass the intended partial limit, add more liquidity or execute larger swaps than the protocol intended to allow. This can lead to excessive liquidity injection, distortion of pool balances, and potential economic loss for the protocol or its users. The issue manifests only when addLiquidityCurve is called with unequal deposit amounts in a pool with N>2 tokens; in two‑token pools the division by length coincidentally yields the correct factor. The affected parties are relayers and any users relying on the rate‑limit mechanism to protect against oversized operations. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the rate‑limit helper logic and noticed that the averageSwap calculation did not match the expected swap accounting for multi‑token pools. It is subtle because the code appears to compute an average and the division by length looks plausible, making the bug easy to miss without concrete multi‑token test cases. To remediate, the contract should replace the averageSwap computation with an effectiveSwap calculation that divides totalSwapped by two (and then by 1e18) before invoking triggerRateLimitDecrease. This aligns the rate‑limit reduction with the actual amount of tokens that would be swapped, restoring the intended protection. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may be that a liquidity addition succeeds with a larger amount than expected and the UI does not warn about rate‑limit exhaustion, giving the impression that the protocol is allowing unlimited deposits when, in fact, the limit enforcement is flawed.

title: maxSlippage is insufficient swap protection for unbalanced Curve Pools
description:
Currently the Curve swap function utilizes a maxSlippage protection. This value is set by the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to a percentage (i.e. 0.98e18 or 1.02e18). It is then used as a check against the RELAYER during the swap to ensure the RELAYER specifies an acceptable minAmount parameter when doing the swap. It always specifies that the minAmount parameter must be amountIn * rates[inputIndex] / rates[outputIndex] * maxSlippage so with 1:1 priced tokens and max slippage set to 98% the minAmount would have to be 98 or greater when amountIn = 100. If all the same conditions existed, but max slippage was 102%, the minAmount would have to be 102.
Essentially maxSlippage provides a floor to ensure that the RELAYER is not making trades that incur more slippage than is acceptable.
Curve uses slippage to punish/reward making the Pool less/more healthy. So a trade that significantly moves the pool away from equilibrium will incur more slippage than one that does not substantively affect the equilibrium. If the pool is already imbalanced between the tokens, then trades that move it towards equilibrium will be rewards. This is done to encourage arbitragers to keep the stable pools in balance.
This graph helps us visualize how slippage works:
• Point (5,5) represents a balanced pool, trading around that point would incur little slippage in either direction.
• Point (~2,~9), The Green Dot, represents an out of balance pool with too much of asset X.
• Point (~9,~2), The Red Dot, represents an out of balance pool with too much of asset Y.
• Trading from equilibrium to either dot will incur slippage such that the amountOut will be less than the amountIn.
• Trading from either dot will incur slippage such that amountOut will be greater than the amountIn.
• We assume the red shaded area represents invalid trades for the spark-controller (based on maxSlippage) if the trade moves from any point on the curve near equilibrium to any point further from equilibrium.
It is likely that the Spark system will be a large participant in the pools the spark-controller is interacting with, which means that it is reasonable to consider the pools to be a relatively "low liquidity" environment, relative to the potential size of the trades. This will be bounded some by the Spark RateLimit contract, but moving the market with swaps should be considered likely for the spark-controller swaps.
Pairing sDAI and other Maker/Sky stable coins with stable coins in the Curve Stable Pools will have impact on the price peg of the Maker/Sky stable coins and thus, it should be desirable that the spark-controller system ideally improves the health of the Curve pools or at least does not harm it.
It should also be desirable, as partially expressed by the maxSlippage, that the swaps done by the RELAYER should benefit or at least not harm the spark-controller system (i.e. do not execute trades that cost the system "too much").
With this background in place, we can evaluate the efficacy of the maxSlippage protection with a couple of scenarios.
For ease of description, we will make a couple of assumptions:
• maxSlippage is 0.98e18 unless otherwise stated.
• The store_price function returns a 1:1 price pairing for the assets unless otherwise noted (so the only deviation from 1:1 pricing is due to Curve pool slippage).
• the pool is in equilibrium at the point (5,5).
• We are ignoring Curve fees for this analysis (so the only deviation from 1:1 pricing is due to Curve pool slippage).
Scenario 1: Imbalanced pool:
In this scenario, we assume that regular market forces have pushed the Pool into an imbalanced state, lets assume that current balance between (x,y) is skewed towards asset Y into the red zone past the green dot. Any trade that moves the balance towards equilibrium will be rewarded. Because our current pool balance is in the red zone, any RELAYER swap from asset Y to asset X will be blocked by maxSlippage because it would be more than a 2% discount. However, almost any RELAYER swap from asset X to asset Y will be accepted by the Controller since it would have a slippage above -2%.
If the RELAYER swaps enough asset Y to asset X to move the pool back into equilibrium, then it would be rewarded a bonus in amountOut. However, if the RELAYER trades even more of asset Y for asset X, such that the pool starts to be imbalanced in the other direction, the spark-controller will allow this too. Assuming a swap that leaves the pool containing more asset X than asset Y, the swap would still have slippage such that the amountOut is greater than the amountIn, but this second amountOut would be less than the first, balancing trade's amountOut because the Curve pool would reward it up to the equilibrium point, but then start punishing it for the portion of the trade that moves beyond that. The RELAYER's swap could entirely flip the pool with a trade that does not violate the maxSlippage protection effectively it would have an end state that is the reverse of the initial state. Visually we could say this trade moved all the way from the Green dot to the Red dot (or visa versa).
If the Curve pool is filling up with Asset X, it is likely that Asset X is loosing its value relative to Asset Y and because this swap changes the balance of the pool such that it ends up with more Asset Y, the spark-controller will accumulate Asset X, thus putting itself at risk of "holding the bag". Though if the price of Y is too high in Curve compared to other markets, the RELAYER may see an arbitrage opportunity.
Even setting aside this sort of more extreme market situation, allowing the RELAYER to move the market from one Dot to another is not the most efficient, profitable trade. The spark-controller is missing out on the slippage reward it would have received by moving the market from an imbalanced state to a balanced one. This lost profit is roughly amountIn * (percent market is imbalance + 100e18 - maxSlippage).
Scenario 2: De-pegging asset + Other pool whale.
This scenario shares some similar aspects to the first scenario, but includes a 3rd party actor who is also a large liquidity provider. In this scenario, we can assume there is a major de-peg event that is just starting.
The pool is still relatively in equilibrium. Seeing a trade from the RELAYER, the 3rd party calls remove_liquidity_one_coin to pull all their liquidity out in the form of asset X. Assuming they are large enough, this could swing the pool to be imbalanced with too much asset Y. This 3rd party would lose a quantity of asset X tokens due to slippage on this removal. If the reduction in quantity is less than the predicted reduction in value for asset X during a black swan de-peg and/or less than the cost of pulling out asset Y, the actor might choose to accept this loss. Further, arbitraging the pool back to equilibrium after the RELAYER's swap could help off set some of these costs. The RELAYER's trade could then swing the pool from a state where it had too much asset Y to one where it had too much asset X. The 3rd party could then use the received asset X to arbitrage the pool back to equilibrium, swapping their soon to be worth less asset X for asset Y. Lets outline the steps here:
1. The X/Y pool is at a 1:1 ratio.
2. A third-party liquidity provider decides to `remove_liquidity_one_coin` due to market conditions, removing X, which is not yet reflected in the Curve pool.
- Removing only one coin in large amounts will change the price and result in extra fees compared to removing both coins equally (the standard removal function).
3. The pool now contains more Y than X, meaning X has a higher price. (removing X here would be similar to buying X with Y).
4. The relayer wants to sell X or Y and is front-run by step 3.
- If selling Y for X, the relayer's swap would be blocked because of the `maxSlippage` constraint, so only possible to sell X.
- Selling X for Y, if the price after the trade returns to 1:1, the relayer would have made more money than without the front-running.
- However, if the relayer pushes the price in the other direction, the overall trade would still satisfy the `maxSlippage` constraint but with even less money returned for the swap.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the reliance on a static maxSlippage parameter as the sole protection against unfavorable swaps in Curve stable pools. The contract calculates a minimum acceptable output amount by multiplying the input amount by the on‑chain price rates and by the maxSlippage factor (for example 0.98 for a 2 % tolerance) and enforces that the relayer must supply at least this amount. This check assumes that the pool price is close to its equilibrium, but Curve pools deliberately adjust the price based on the current token balances: trades that move the pool toward equilibrium receive a positive slippage (output greater than input) while trades that move it away incur a negative slippage (output less than input). When the pool is already imbalanced, a trade that restores balance can produce an output that is higher than the input even though the maxSlippage check still passes, because the formula only enforces a lower bound on the output. Consequently a relayer can submit a swap that pushes the pool from one extreme imbalance to the opposite extreme while still satisfying the maxSlippage condition. The contract therefore fails to prevent swaps that degrade the health of the pool, allow the system to “hold the bag” of a de‑valued asset, and miss out on the slippage reward that would have been earned by moving the pool back toward equilibrium. The issue manifests when the pool is low‑liquidity relative to the size of the relayer’s trade, or when a third‑party large liquidity removal creates a sudden imbalance. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected loss of value: a user may see a trade that should have yielded a profit or at least a neutral outcome instead receiving a lower amount, or the protocol may accumulate excess of a depreciating token without realizing it. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the spark‑controller’s interaction with Curve, where the auditor observed that the maxSlippage check does not consider the direction of price movement and therefore does not guarantee that the swap improves pool health. The bug is subtle because the minAmount calculation appears mathematically correct and passes basic unit tests, yet it does not capture the economic invariant that the pool’s balance should move toward equilibrium. To remediate, the contract should incorporate an on‑chain assessment of the pool’s token reserves before and after the swap, rejecting trades that increase the imbalance or that move the price away from the target peg, and optionally enforce a dynamic slippage ceiling that accounts for the current pool state. In summary, the flaw is a classic insufficient slippage protection where a static tolerance is used in a context where price is state‑dependent, leading to potential fund loss, sub‑optimal earnings, and exposure to market manipulation.

title: Incorrect slippage protection in addLiquidityCurve and removeLiquidityCurve due to missing virtual price conversion
description:
The addLiquidityCurve and removeLiquidityCurve functions contain incorrect slippage protection checks that compare LP token amounts directly with token values without accounting for the LP token's virtual price. In addLiquidityCurve, the function checks:
require(
    minLpAmount >= valueDeposited * maxSlippage / 1e18,
    "MainnetController/min-amount-not-met"
);
This is incorrect because minLpAmount represents LP tokens (shares of the pool), while valueDeposited represents the total value of the tokens that should be deposited into Curve. These values cannot be directly compared without converting the LP tokens to their underlying value using Curve's get_virtual_price() function. Similarly, in removeLiquidityCurve, the function checks:
require(
    valueMinWithdrawn >= lpBurnAmount * maxSlippage / 1e18,
    "MainnetController/min-amount-not-met"
);
Here, valueMinWithdrawn represents token values, while lpBurnAmount represents LP tokens. Again, these cannot be directly compared without accounting for the virtual price.
Impact: These errors currently have the following impact assuming the virtual price only increases starting from 1e18.
1. For addLiquidityCurve: The check is too strict. It will reject transactions with acceptable slippage levels because it's comparing LP tokens directly with token values. This is because after multiplying minLpAmount by the virtual price (which is > 1e18), the left side of the comparison would be greater, therefore making the check harder to satisfy than intended.
2. For removeLiquidityCurve: The check is too soft. It will allow transactions with excessive slippage to pass because it's comparing token values with LP tokens. This allows a lower valueMinWithdrawn to pass than should be permitted.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect slippage protection mechanism in the addLiquidityCurve and removeLiquidityCurve functions of a Curve‑based liquidity manager. The root cause is a unit mismatch: the code compares LP‑token amounts (shares of the pool) directly with token value amounts without converting the LP tokens to their underlying value using the pool’s virtual price obtained from get_virtual_price(). In addLiquidityCurve the contract checks that the minimum LP amount is greater than or equal to the deposited value multiplied by the slippage tolerance, but minLpAmount is expressed in LP shares while valueDeposited is expressed in token value, so the comparison is meaningless unless the LP amount is multiplied by the virtual price. In removeLiquidityCurve the reverse mistake occurs: the contract checks that the minimum token value to be withdrawn is greater than or equal to the LP amount to be burned multiplied by the slippage tolerance, again mixing units. Because the virtual price normally grows above 1e18, the add‑liquidity check becomes overly strict and rejects legitimate deposits that would satisfy the intended slippage bound, while the remove‑liquidity check becomes too permissive and allows withdrawals with far higher slippage than users expect. An attacker can exploit the permissive remove check by submitting a removal transaction with a low valueMinWithdrawn parameter, causing the contract to burn LP tokens but return far fewer underlying tokens than the user anticipated, effectively stealing value from liquidity providers. Conversely, honest users may experience failed add‑liquidity transactions, seeing error messages such as “min‑amount‑not‑met” even though the slippage is within acceptable limits, leading to frustration and loss of opportunity to provide liquidity. The issue manifests whenever the pool’s virtual price exceeds its initial 1e18 baseline, which is the normal state after the pool accrues fees or gains value. All participants who add or remove liquidity – individual users, protocol operators, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate slippage checks – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the require statements mixed different economic units without conversion. The bug is subtle because the require messages are generic and the arithmetic appears plausible; only a careful unit analysis reveals the mismatch, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the slippage checks must be rewritten to convert LP token amounts to their value equivalents using the virtual price before comparison, ensuring that both sides of the inequality are expressed in the same unit. This class of bug falls under “incorrect unit handling in financial calculations” or “slippage protection mis‑implementation”, which can cause funds to disappear, refunds to be lower than expected, or legitimate transactions to be rejected, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations of fair value exchange.

title: Malicious user can frontrunning buyMemecoin funtion minting less tokens for the user
description:
The buyMemecoin can be frontrun by a malicious user, leaving only 1 wei of ETH to buy. The next user would be paying more gas fees to execute the ﬁnalization of the launch transaction than receive tokens in value. Example: targetETH = 100 ETH, left ETH to buy: 20 ETH
1. A malicious user sent a value of 19.999...999 ETH, resulting in a remaining targetETH - collectedETH = 1 wei.
2. The next user who intends to purchase 5 ETH in tokens will only buy 1 wei in tokens, and pay the gas to ﬁnalize the launch.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the buyMemecoin function calculates the amount of tokens to mint based on the remaining ETH needed to reach a predefined launch target. Because the contract only checks the difference between the target amount and the ETH already collected, a malicious actor can front‑run a legitimate purchase by sending a transaction that consumes almost all of the required ETH, leaving only a single wei of ETH remaining. When a regular user later submits a transaction with a larger ETH value, the contract allocates tokens only for the tiny remaining wei, so the user receives essentially no tokens while still paying the gas required to finalize the launch. This is a front‑running or miner‑extractable‑value (MEV) issue caused by the lack of a minimum token amount check and by the assumption that the remaining ETH will always be sufficient for the requested purchase. An attacker can exploit the vulnerability by observing pending buyMemecoin calls, then submitting a transaction with a value just below the target, thereby starving subsequent buyers of meaningful token allocations. The impact is that users lose the gas spent on the transaction without receiving proportional tokens, effectively a denial‑of‑service on token acquisition and a financial loss. The condition occurs whenever the contract is in its launch phase and uses a simple subtraction (targetETH‑collectedETH) to determine the purchasable amount without enforcing a lower bound. All participants who intend to buy tokens are affected, especially those who rely on the function to receive a proportional amount of tokens for their ETH contribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the launch logic and identified that the remaining ETH could be reduced to a negligible amount, allowing a front‑runner to manipulate the outcome. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful, but the user ends up with a near‑zero token balance, which may be missed if the UI does not display the exact token amount. The recommended fix is to enforce a minimum token purchase threshold (for example, a minAmountTokens parameter) or to reject purchases that would result in an unreasonably small token allocation, and to consider adding slippage protection. This class of bug belongs to economic manipulation vulnerabilities where contract accounting assumes sufficient remaining liquidity and does not guard against depletion by malicious actors. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction, yet the token balance after the call is zero or almost zero and the gas cost exceeds the value received, violating the expectation that sending ETH yields a proportional token amount. The failure mode is that funds appear to disappear into gas costs while the intended token purchase silently fails.

title: Creating tiers with same nftId but different isFungible
bug_full: The contract allows the creation of multiple reward tiers that reference the same NFT identifier (nftId) without enforcing that the fungibility flag (isFungible) stays consistent. When a new tier is added the code checks whether the NFT already exists by looking up an address stored in existingNFTAddr, but it does not compare the isFungible value of the previously stored tier with the one supplied for the new tier. As a result an attacker can define two tiers that share the same nftId – one marked as fungible (ERC‑1155) and the other as non‑fungible (ERC‑721). This mismatch breaks the assumptions built into the tier‑ordering logic, such as the expectation that a non‑fungible tier cannot be followed by a fungible tier and that ID ranges do not overlap. Because the contract believes the NFT is the same, it may incorrectly allocate token IDs, allow overlapping lowerId/upperId ranges, or treat a fungible balance as a unique token. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can be confusing: a user may receive no token, receive a token of the wrong type, or see their balance disappear after a tier transition. The issue is triggered only when the contract creator adds more than one tier and re‑uses an nftId with a different isFungible flag; normal operation with unique nftIds is unaffected. The vulnerability was discovered during a systematic audit that supplied a test case with two tier parameters sharing nftId = 1 but differing in isFungible, which passed the existence check and exposed the logical inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows only the NFT name and does not expose the fungibility flag, so developers may assume the same nftId always refers to the same token standard. To remediate, the contract must validate that whenever an nftId is reused the isFungible flag matches the original tier, and it should also enforce ordering rules that prevent a fungible tier from following a non‑fungible tier and prevent overlapping ID ranges. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents funds or token ownership from being mis‑assigned.

title: Incorrect ordering tiers in MEME404
bug_full: The MEME404 contract allows a series of tier definitions to be supplied by the caller when creating a new meme collection. Each tier is supposed to be unique and ordered so that later tiers have higher NFT identifiers and non‑overlapping token ID ranges. The implementation only validates the tier that immediately precedes the current one, checking that the previous tier’s nftId is lower and that its amountThreshold is smaller. Because the check does not compare the new tier against all earlier entries, an attacker can submit a tier list where a later entry repeats the same nftId, lowerId and upperId as an earlier entry. This duplicate tier passes the validation logic because the immediate predecessor is different, and the contract therefore records two identical tier specifications for the same NFT. The root cause is an insufficient ordering and uniqueness check that relies on a single‑step comparison instead of a global ordering constraint. An exploit consists of constructing a TierCreateParam array that contains duplicate tier objects – for example, tier 0 and tier 2 both reference nftId 1 with lowerId 10 and upperId 20 – and submitting it to the createMeme function. When the contract processes the array, it accepts the duplicate and stores both entries, leading to overlapping token ID ranges and ambiguous accounting for that NFT. The impact is that the protocol’s business logic, which assumes each tier maps to a distinct range of token IDs and a distinct amount threshold, is broken. Users may see unexpected behaviour such as minting the same token ID twice, refunds being calculated incorrectly, or the UI showing duplicate tier entries where only one should exist. Funds that are meant to be allocated to a specific tier may be split or lost because the contract cannot reliably determine which tier should receive a payment. The issue manifests whenever a creator supplies tier parameters without a strict global ordering check – essentially any call to createMeme that includes more than one tier. All participants who rely on the tier ordering – creators, collectors, and the protocol’s accounting layer – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the tier validation loop and identified that only the previous element was inspected. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings for duplicate IDs, the problem can be hard to notice in normal operation; the contract will appear to accept the input without reverting, and the duplicate may only surface later when token IDs clash. The proper fix is to enforce a total ordering across the entire tier list, for example by requiring that each new tier’s nftId be greater than the maximum nftId seen so far and that its lowerId be greater than the previous tier’s upperId, and by checking that no two tiers share the same nftId‑lowerId‑upperId combination. This ensures uniqueness and prevents overlapping ranges, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Inability to use NFT Marketplaces
description: Users should be aware of the risks involved when selling their NFTs through an NFT marketplace. Potential losses could occur after creating an order in the marketplace. For instance, if users send different NFTs of MEME404 to the marketplace, it could result in changes to the marketplace tier through the burning/minting process. This could lead to the loss of their NFT.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the marketplace contract allows a seller to create an order for an NFT, but during the order creation the contract may invoke a burn/mint routine that changes the NFT's tier. Because the marketplace does not verify that the NFT being transferred remains the same after the internal burn or mint operation, the original token can be permanently removed or replaced, resulting in the seller losing ownership of the NFT. This occurs because the marketplace trusts external tier‑adjustment logic that can be triggered by arbitrary token IDs and fails to enforce a post‑transfer ownership check. An attacker or even the marketplace itself can exploit this by submitting an order that includes a token from a collection that implements tier‑changing logic; when the order is accepted the contract calls the collection's burn function, which destroys the token, and then mints a new token of a different tier that is not owned by the seller. The seller sees the order appear as created, but later the NFT balance in their wallet is zero or the token ID no longer exists, effectively losing the asset. The impact is loss of the NFT and any associated value, potentially affecting any user who attempts to sell through the marketplace, as well as the reputation of the platform. The condition occurs whenever a marketplace order is created for an NFT whose contract includes a burn‑or‑mint side effect, especially collections that change tier on transfer. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the marketplace's order‑creation flow, where the auditor noticed that the contract does not enforce a post‑transfer ownership check. The bug is subtle because the marketplace UI shows the order as successfully placed and does not display any error, so users may assume the sale will proceed normally. The class of bug is an unsafe external call leading to unintended state changes and insufficient validation of token continuity. To mitigate, the marketplace should either prohibit orders for tokens that implement tier‑changing logic, or it should perform a post‑transfer verification that the same token ID is still owned by the seller before finalizing the order, and clearly document the risk to users. Providing explicit warnings in the UI and documentation about potential loss when selling NFTs that may be burned or reminted is also recommended.

title: The token balance of the ERC4626Router will return wrong balances for vaults with fees
bug_full: The ERC4626Router implements a helper function called _tokenBalance that is intended to report the total amount of a given token that the router controls. The function first reads the raw ERC20 balance of the router and then, if a vault is registered for that token, adds the result of vault.convertToAssets(vault.balanceOf(address(this))). The vulnerability arises because convertToAssets, as defined by the ERC4626 specification, returns the gross amount of assets that correspond to a share balance without taking any withdrawal fees into account. When a vault charges a fee on redeem or withdraw, the actual amount of assets that can be extracted from the vault is lower than the value returned by convertToAssets. Consequently, _tokenBalance over‑states the router’s holdings.
