This mis‑calculation can be exploited by any component that relies on the reported balance for accounting, slippage checks, or permission decisions. An attacker could trigger operations that assume the router is solvent, causing the protocol to attempt withdrawals that exceed the net assets, potentially leading to failed transactions, loss of expected funds, or inconsistent state. The issue manifests whenever a vault with fee‑on‑withdraw logic is associated with a token in the router; it does not depend on any particular user action and affects all users, the router contract, and any downstream contracts that query the balance. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the ERC4626 specification with the implementation and noticing that the view function does not respect fee semantics. It is subtle because the function is read‑only and returns a plausible‑looking number, making the discrepancy easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate the problem, the router should replace the call to convertToAssets with previewRedeem (or previewWithdraw), which the ERC4626 standard requires to return the maximum amount of assets that would be received after fees in the same transaction. Using previewRedeem ensures the reported balance never exceeds the amount that can actually be redeemed, restoring correct accounting and preventing over‑optimistic balance displays that could mislead users who expect to withdraw the full amount shown in the UI.

title: Missing slippage checks on deposits and withdrawals could result in sandwich attacks
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the absence of slippage validation on ERC4626 deposit and withdrawal operations performed by a router contract that manages token vaults. The ERC4626 standard does not mandate slippage checks, and the router implementation relies on the underlying vault’s _deposit and redeem functions without enforcing a minimum‑out amount. When the router’s admin calls setVaultForToken to replace the vault associated with a token, the contract first redeems all of its shares from the current (old) vault and then deposits the resulting token balance into the newly assigned vault. Because neither the redemption nor the deposit includes a check that the amount of assets received matches the expected value, an attacker who can observe the pending transaction can execute a sandwich attack: they lower the share price of the old vault just before the redemption, causing the router to receive fewer underlying tokens, and then raise the share price of the new vault before the deposit, causing the router to receive even fewer vault shares for the same token amount. The attacker profits from the price manipulation while the router – and consequently any users whose balances are held by the router – end up with a reduced amount of assets or shares. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a vault change the expected token balance or share balance is lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as a sudden loss or a zero balance when a deposit was thought to be successful. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the router’s logic and noted that the ERC4626 functions were called without any slippage guard. It can be hard to notice because the transaction itself succeeds and emits no error, yet the economic outcome is unfavorable. The problem is most relevant on networks such as Arbitrum and Base where the lack of a public mempool reduces the frequency of front‑running but does not eliminate accidental MEV. The appropriate mitigation is to add explicit slippage checks – for example, requiring that the amount of assets received from a redeem call is at least a user‑specified minimum and that the number of shares minted on deposit meets a minimum threshold – for every interaction with a vault, thereby preventing price‑manipulation attacks and preserving the expected accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: Reentrant tokens should not be allowed by governance
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that arises when the protocol transfers tokens that support ERC777‑style callbacks in the middle of a loan‑related function instead of following the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The root cause is that the contract performs a token transfer before all internal state variables have been safely updated, and the existing reentrancy guard in LoanManager only protects the single contract, not the whole call chain that includes Pool, PoolManager, LoanManager and the Loan contract. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a malicious token that invokes a callback during the transfer, re‑entering the same or a related function with altered parameters. For example, during OTLoan.makePayment the contract updates the loan state, then calls the token transfer, and afterwards LoanManager.claim reads the loan’s principal again. By re‑entering makePayment with a different principal amount while the callback is executing, the attacker can cause the claim logic to read an inconsistent principal value, resulting in an incorrect calculation of loan impairment. This can leave unrealized losses in the pool or cause the pool’s reported assets to be higher than the actual cash on hand because the pool receives interest and principal before LoanManager’s principalOut variable is decreased. The impact is a breach of accounting invariants: borrowers may appear to have repaid less than they actually sent, lenders may see inflated pool balances, and the protocol’s financial guarantees can be undermined. The issue occurs only when governance allows tokens with transfer callbacks to be listed as funds or collateral assets, and when loan functions embed transfers before final state updates. All participants that rely on accurate loan balances – borrowers, lenders, pool participants and the protocol’s governance – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing checks‑effects‑interactions discipline and the limited scope of the reentrancy guard. It is hard to notice because the reentrancy only manifests with callback‑enabled tokens, which are less common than standard ERC20 tokens, and the resulting accounting errors are subtle, often appearing as a small discrepancy in impairment values rather than an outright loss of funds. To remediate, the protocol should prohibit tokens that implement transfer callbacks from being used as collateral or pool assets, and redesign the affected functions so that token transfers occur after all state changes have been finalized, complemented by a comprehensive reentrancy lock that spans the entire call chain. This aligns the implementation with the standard reentrancy‑safe pattern and restores the integrity of loan repayment and pool accounting logic.

title: MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintUniswapV3() updates reserves incorrectly
bug_full: The contract updates its internal accounting of token reserves using a calculated expected amount rather than the actual amount that was transferred to the Uniswap V3 pool. In the mintUniswapV3 function the code computes amount0UniswapV3 and amount1UniswapV3 from the stored reserves and then subtracts those values from the reserve variables. However, the Uniswap V3 position manager may mint fewer tokens than requested because of price differences or slippage, and it returns the real amounts (amount0 and amount1) that were deposited. Because the contract continues to subtract the expected amounts, the reserve variables end up reflecting a larger reduction than what really happened on‑chain. When the next step (mintMarginalV1) reads the reserves it believes there are still tokens available, while the contract’s actual token balances are lower. This mismatch can cause the protocol to attempt to use tokens that are not present, leading to failed liquidity provision, missing refunds, or users receiving zero or reduced payouts. The bug appears only when the Uniswap mint returns less than the target ratio, a situation that is common in volatile markets. It is hard to notice because the reserve variables are updated without any explicit check against the returned amounts, so the UI may still show a successful deposit while the underlying accounting is inconsistent. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the expected reserve deduction with the values returned by the Uniswap call. It belongs to the class of accounting‑state mismatch bugs where on‑chain state is updated based on assumptions rather than concrete return data. To remediate, the contract should subtract the actual amount0 and amount1 returned by the mint call, or otherwise reconcile the reserve variables with the real token transfers, ensuring that the internal accounting always mirrors the true token balances.

title: Active LP may not be able to provide more liquidity
description: lpDeposit() is called by LP to deposit initial principal, deposit more principal, or adjust their riskPercentage. However, due to the highlighted require check, an active LP won't be able to deposit more principal if the number of active LPs reach lpLimit. This action by LP doesn't increase the number of active LPs, hence should be allowed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical restriction in the liquidity‑provider deposit routine that prevents an already‑active liquidity provider (LP) from adding more principal or adjusting their risk percentage once the contract’s maximum number of active LPs (lpLimit) has been reached. The root cause is a require statement that checks activeLpAddresses.length < lpLimit for every call to lpDeposit(), regardless of whether the call would actually increase the count of active LPs. Because the check is unconditional, an LP who is already registered is treated the same as a new LP, and when the limit is hit the transaction reverts even though the operation does not add a new address to the active list. An attacker could fill the lpLimit with dummy or low‑value LP entries, effectively locking out legitimate LPs from increasing their stakes, which constitutes a denial‑of‑service style attack on the liquidity‑adding functionality. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a “deposit failed” or “cannot add liquidity” error despite the user having sufficient balance and the protocol having room for more capital; the user expects to be able to top‑up their position but receives no funds added and may see no change in their recorded balance. The impact includes loss of expected earnings for LPs, reduced overall liquidity for the protocol, and potential erosion of trust because participants cannot adjust risk exposure as advertised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of lpDeposit() and identified that the limit check is applied without considering the action’s effect on the active‑LP count. It can be hard to notice because the function works correctly for new LPs and only fails for existing LPs under a specific state (when the limit is already reached), a condition that may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. To remediate, the contract should apply the lpLimit check only when the transaction would add a new LP address to the active list; calls that merely increase an existing LP’s principal or modify risk parameters should bypass the length check. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the limit governs the number of distinct LP participants, not the total amount of liquidity they can provide.

title: User can self-refer to avoid LP fees partially
description:
User can self-refer to counter LP fees with referral fees. This will cause direct loss to LP depositors.
Impact Explanation:
LP depositors will get lower than expected fees.
poc:
1. Let's say if referralFeeBps is 50% of feeBps.
2. User call purchaseTickets function and set himself as referrer.
3. Assume X amount of fees was deducted as feeBps then X/2 would be refunded back to User as referralFee.
```solidity
uint256 lpFeeAmount = allFeeAmount - referralFeeAmount;
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑distribution flaw that allows a user to refer themselves when purchasing tickets, causing a portion of the liquidity‑provider (LP) fee to be refunded back to the same user as a referral reward. The root cause is the contract’s calculation order: the total fee (allFeeAmount) is split into a referral fee and an LP fee by subtracting the referral amount directly from the total, without first allocating the LP fee. Because the referral fee is expressed as a basis‑point fraction of the overall fee (for example 50 % of feeBps), a malicious caller can set the referrer address to their own address in the purchaseTickets function. The contract then refunds half of the fee that would have gone to LPs, effectively offsetting the LP fee. This can be exploited by calling purchaseTickets with the caller’s address as the referrer, causing the contract to compute lpFeeAmount = allFeeAmount - referralFeeAmount, where referralFeeAmount is derived from the same allFeeAmount. The impact is that LP depositors receive lower than expected fee earnings, reducing the incentive for providing liquidity and potentially draining the LP pool over time. The issue manifests when the referral fee percentage is non‑zero and the contract does not enforce a check that the referrer differs from the transaction sender. Users may notice that after paying a fee they receive an unexpected refund, while the protocol’s accounting shows a shortfall in LP fee accrual. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑splitting logic and identified that the referral fee is deducted before the LP fee, creating a self‑referral loophole. It can be hard to notice because the referral mechanism appears legitimate and the refund is credited to the same user, making the loss invisible to external observers. To remediate, the referral fee should be calculated after the LP fee has been deducted, or the contract should enforce that the referrer address cannot be the caller, or cap the referral fee to a safe maximum. Conceptually, the fix restores the intended accounting invariant that LP fees are fully collected before any referral rewards are distributed, thereby preventing users from artificially reducing the fee owed to liquidity providers.

title: LP deposit can be DoS
description:
Attacker can DOS LP deposit functionality by risking a very low amount as shown below.
Impact Explanation:
High, since Protocol will lose anymore LP deposit and LP stake will remain 0.
poc:
1. Attacker creates 100 address (current lpLimit) and calls lpDeposit from each giving 0.1 eth (minLpDeposit). He sets 1% as risk percentage for all.
2. Overall investment by attacker is 0.1eth*100 = 10 eth.
3. In next lottery run, LP are staked since attacker set 1% risk for all 100 LP address so total LP staked would be 10eth* 1% = 0.1 eth.
4. Before the next lottery run, Attacker immediately request to withdraw each LP which sets risk percentage of each to 0.
5. In the next lottery run, LP stakes are updated to 0 (Attacker might incur loss if User wins over LP but loss is limited to <0.1 eth).
6. Now no new LP can deposit as LP limit is reached and LP stakes will be 0 for all future lottery. This will remain case till Attacker calls withdraw.
7. At current rate ~315 USD is all required by Attacker to risk this attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the liquidity‑provider (LP) deposit mechanism of the contract. The root cause lies in the way the contract tracks LP participation: it limits the number of LP addresses (lpLimit) but does not enforce a minimum effective stake or risk percentage before an address is counted toward that limit. An attacker can exploit this by creating the maximum number of LP accounts, each depositing the minimum allowed amount (0.1 ETH) and setting an extremely low risk percentage (e.g., 1%). After the deposits are recorded, the attacker immediately withdraws each LP, which resets the risk percentage of every entry to zero. Because the contract updates the total staked LP amount based on the risk percentages, the combined stake collapses to zero while the lpLimit remains fully occupied. Subsequent users are then unable to add new LPs because the limit is considered reached, even though no actual liquidity is available. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the LP pool is full but the displayed LP stake is zero, leading to confusion and the inability to provide liquidity or earn rewards. The impact is high for the protocol: new liquidity cannot be added, the lottery or other mechanisms that depend on LP stake receive no backing, and the protocol’s revenue model is effectively halted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge cases around LP registration and withdrawal logic. It is difficult to notice because the attacker’s deposits are tiny and appear legitimate, and the contract does not emit a clear warning when the total stake drops to zero while the address limit is saturated. To remediate, the contract should either prevent LP entries with a zero effective stake, enforce a minimum risk percentage greater than zero, allow the admin to deactivate or purge LP slots that have zero stake, or redesign the limit logic to count only active, staked LPs rather than all registered addresses. Implementing such checks restores the ability for honest participants to add liquidity and prevents a single actor from locking the LP pool with negligible funds.

title: lpFeesTotal is not reset to 0
description:
LP fees is not reset after distribution. This causes User/LP to get more funds than expected.
Impact Explanation:
1. If not corrected, duplicate lpFeesTotal can be claimed by User pool in all future cycles until lpPoolTotal = 0.
2. Even when LP actually deposits, the first cycle will give more fees to LP.
3. User wont be able to claim winning as protocol will lack funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the fee distribution logic of the contract. When the function that distributes accumulated LP fees is executed, the code correctly resets the lpFeesTotal variable after distributing fees to liquidity providers in the normal case where lpPoolTotal is greater than zero. However, in the edge case where lpPoolTotal equals zero – meaning no liquidity providers are currently staked – the contract adds the pending lpFeesTotal to the userPoolTotal but fails to reset lpFeesTotal to zero before returning. This omission leaves the accumulated fee amount in storage, allowing it to be added again in subsequent cycles. The root cause is a missing state‑reset statement in the conditional branch that handles an empty LP pool. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by triggering a distribution cycle with no LPs staked, causing the same fee amount to be transferred to the user pool while the lpFeesTotal variable retains its previous value. In later cycles, even if LPs re‑enter the pool, the stale lpFeesTotal will be added again, resulting in duplicate fee claims. The impact includes liquidity providers receiving more fees than the protocol intended, users being unable to claim their rightful winnings because the protocol’s funds are depleted, and overall accounting inconsistencies that can erode trust in the system. The bug manifests only when lpPoolTotal is zero at the moment of fee distribution, a condition that may be infrequent and therefore easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the reset statement was present in the main path but absent in the early‑return path. Because the contract’s state appears correct in the common case, the issue can be subtle and may only be revealed by specific scenario testing or by observing unexpected fee balances. The recommended remediation is to set lpFeesTotal to zero in the branch that handles an empty LP pool, ensuring that the fee accumulator is cleared regardless of the pool composition. This change restores proper accounting, prevents double‑counting of fees, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that each fee should be distributed exactly once.

title: Zero token ID and shares in free functions of MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the liquidity receiver contract that causes the token identifier for a Uniswap V3 position and the share amount for a Marginal V1 position to be overwritten with zero before the contract attempts to transfer them to the caller. The root cause is the premature assignment of zero to the fields of a temporary storage struct (info.tokenId and info.shares) and the subsequent use of those cleared values in the transfer and event emission statements. When a user invokes the freeUniswapV3 function, the contract first sets info.tokenId to zero, stores the modified struct, and later calls the non‑fungible position manager to transfer the NFT using the now‑zero tokenId. Because the tokenId is zero, the transfer call does nothing and the NFT remains locked inside the contract. The emitted FreeUniswapV3 event also records a tokenId of zero, which can mislead observers. A similar pattern occurs in freeMarginalV1: the share amount is reset to zero before the internal pay routine is called, resulting in a transfer of zero shares and an event that reports zero shares. The impact is that liquidity providers who expect to retrieve their NFT or their share tokens receive nothing; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful call but the balance of the NFT or shares remains unchanged, effectively causing a loss of funds. This condition occurs every time the free functions are executed, regardless of the caller, and affects any participant who has deposited liquidity into the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the code compiles and the events fire, making the bug subtle and easy to miss because no explicit revert or error is produced. The bug violates basic accounting assumptions that a free operation should return the exact assets that were previously held, and it breaks the contract’s business logic that the free functions are meant to unwind positions safely. To remediate the problem, the contract should cache the original tokenId and share values in local variables before clearing the struct, or reorder the operations so that the transfer and event emission occur before the fields are reset. This change ensures that the correct identifiers are used for the transfer and that events accurately reflect the assets being released, restoring the intended functionality and preventing silent asset loss.

title: ETH Dust in createAndInitializePool
description:
The createAndInitializePool function is marked as payable, but it doesn't handle any potential dust ETH that might be sent along with the transaction. This could lead to ETH being trapped in the contract or potentially stolen by an attacker.
```solidity
function createAndInitializePool(
    CreateAndInitializeParams calldata params
)
external
payable
checkDeadline(params.deadline)
returns (
    address pool,
    address receiver,
    uint256 shares,
    uint256 amount0,
    uint256 amount1
)
{
    // ... function implementation ...
}
```
1. ETH sent to this function could become trapped in the contract.
2. An attacker could potentially extract any dust ETH left in the contract.
3. Users might lose small amounts of ETH unintentionally.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unhandled payable function that allows ether sent with the createAndInitializePool call to become unintentionally retained in the contract, commonly referred to as dust ETH. The root cause is that the function is declared payable but contains no logic to forward, use, or refund the incoming msg.value, so any non‑zero ether attached to the transaction is added to the contract’s balance without being accounted for in the pool initialization logic. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately sending a small amount of ether together with a call to createAndInitializePool and later invoking the existing refundETH routine (or any other withdrawal path) to extract the trapped dust, effectively stealing the ether that was meant to be ignored. The impact is that legitimate users who accidentally include a tiny amount of ether—perhaps due to wallet rounding, gas estimation errors, or misunderstanding of the payable flag—will see that amount disappear from their wallet with no corresponding token allocation, leading to a loss of funds that may appear as a mysterious reduction in balance. This condition occurs whenever the transaction includes a non‑zero msg.value, which is not validated or cleared by the function, and it affects any participant interacting with the pool creation interface, including end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the contract’s accounting no longer matches the expected state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the payable modifier was present without any handling of the ether, a pattern that can be easy to miss because the function’s primary purpose is pool creation and the ether amount is often negligible, so developers may not notice the silent balance increase. The bug belongs to the class of “unhandled payable” or “ether dust retention” vulnerabilities, where contract logic violates the business assumption that payable functions either use or return all received ether. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful pool creation while the wallet balance drops and no refund or token appears, contradicting the expectation that sending ether either contributes to the pool or is returned. To remediate, the function should either be made non‑payable, enforce msg.value == 0, or explicitly refund any leftover ether at the end of execution by calling the existing refundETH helper, thereby aligning the contract’s state with the intended accounting model and preventing accidental or malicious extraction of dust ether.

title: Lack of slippage protection in liquidity provision
description:
The current implementation of mintUniswapV3 and mintMarginalV1 functions sets the minimum amount parameters (amount0Min and amount1Min) to zero. This lack of slippage protection could potentially expose the contract to sandwich attacks during liquidity provision.
In both mintUniswapV3 and mintMarginalV1 functions:
```solidity
amount0Min: 0,
amount1Min: 0, // TODO: issue for slippage?
```
The worst-case scenario would result in less liquidity in Uniswap v3 and Marginal v1 pools, with excess funds being swept to the treasuryAddress.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the functions that mint liquidity for Uniswap V3 and Marginal V1 pools. Both functions hard‑code the minimum amount parameters amount0Min and amount1Min to zero, which means the contract accepts any amount of token0 or token1 that the pool returns during the mint operation. The root cause is the absence of a user‑controlled bound on the acceptable execution price, a design decision that leaves the transaction open to price manipulation. An attacker can observe a pending liquidity‑addition transaction, submit a preceding trade that moves the pool price, and then let the victim’s transaction execute at the altered price. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum received amount, the victim may receive fewer pool shares than expected while the attacker captures the price difference. The excess tokens that would have been allocated to the liquidity provider are instead transferred to the treasury address, effectively draining funds from the user. This scenario can occur whenever a user calls mintUniswapV3 or mintMarginalV1 without specifying slippage limits, which is the default behavior of the current implementation. All participants who provide liquidity are potentially affected, as the bug does not depend on any privileged role. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the parameter values passed to the Uniswap V3 and Marginal V1 pool contracts and noted the TODO comment indicating a missing slippage check. Because the transaction still succeeds and the pool state appears valid, the problem can be hard to notice; users may only observe that the amount of liquidity tokens received is lower than expected or that the treasury balance has increased unexpectedly. From a user‑experience perspective, a provider expects to receive a certain amount of LP tokens or a proportional share of the pool, but instead receives fewer tokens and sees no refund, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. Conceptually, the fix is to introduce a slippage protection mechanism: the caller should be able to specify a minimum acceptable amount for each token, and the contract should revert if the actual amounts fall below these thresholds. This aligns the implementation with standard accounting assumptions that the amount of assets contributed equals the amount of liquidity minted, preventing sandwich attacks and ensuring that funds are not silently redirected to the treasury.

title: RebalanceParams.callback can steal accrued fees of liquidity NFTs during rebalance
description:
During the rebalancing process the liquidity NFTs are transferred to the RebalanceParams.callback address.
In case the CallbackParams of a user's managed position are empty (a scenario when the user just want rebalancing without gauge deposits) then it would be possible for RebalanceParams.callback address to claim the accrued fees of that NFT at the moment when it receives the NFT for rebalancing. Essentially stealing the accrued fees of the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper authorization flaw that allows a malicious callback contract to appropriate the accrued fees attached to a liquidity NFT during the rebalancing process. When a user initiates a rebalance, the protocol transfers the user’s liquidity NFT to the address specified in RebalanceParams.callback. If the user’s CallbackParams are empty – a situation that occurs when the user only wants a rebalance and does not provide any gauge deposit – the callback contract receives the NFT without any additional checks on fee ownership. Because the contract does not validate that the accrued fees belong to the original position owner, the callback can immediately invoke the fee‑claim function on the NFT and transfer the fees to itself. This can be exploited by deploying a malicious contract as the callback address, triggering a rebalance, receiving the NFT, and calling claimFees before the NFT is returned to the user. The impact is that the user’s expected fee payout disappears; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful rebalance but the fee balance becomes zero or the expected refund is missing. The issue manifests only under the specific condition of an empty CallbackParams during a rebalance, making it easy to overlook in normal operation where callbacks usually include gauge logic. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of NFT ownership and fee accounting, and it is hard to notice because the fee‑claim function is normally allowed for the NFT holder, and the temporary transfer of ownership is a legitimate part of the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control checks during token transfer, effectively allowing fee theft. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that accrued fees can only be claimed by the original position owner or that the callback address is prohibited from invoking fee‑claim while holding the NFT, similar to existing liquidity checks that validate fee entitlement. Implementing a validation step that locks fee claims during the rebalance or that verifies the caller’s rights before allowing fee extraction will close the attack vector and restore confidence that fees cannot be stolen during rebalancing.

title: LpWrapper deposits and withdraws will be bricked if Velodrome gauge is killed.
description:
Within the LpWrapper contract, all withdraws make a withdraw and deposit back in Core.sol.
The problem is that in case the corresponding Velodrome gauge is killed, it will not allow for any new deposits to happen. This would lead to all funds within the LpWrapper forever stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LpWrapper contract, which implements a withdraw routine that first calls the Core contract to withdraw liquidity from a Velodrome gauge and then immediately attempts to deposit the withdrawn amount back into the same gauge. This design assumes that the gauge will always accept new deposits. However, if the gauge is killed – a state that can be triggered by the gauge’s governance or an admin – the deposit operation is rejected. Because the withdraw function does not contain any fallback logic or an emergency path, the failure of the deposit step leaves the caller’s funds locked inside the LpWrapper contract with no way to retrieve them. The root cause is a missing guard against the gauge‑killed condition and the absence of an alternative withdrawal mechanism. Exploitation does not require a malicious actor; simply killing the gauge makes any subsequent withdraw call ineffective, effectively bricking the funds. The impact is that liquidity providers who have deposited LP tokens through the LpWrapper will see their balances remain unchanged while the UI may show a pending withdrawal or a zero payout, leading to a loss of access to their assets. This situation occurs only after the gauge has been killed and a user attempts to withdraw; under normal operation the contract behaves as expected, which makes the issue easy to overlook during testing. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between LpWrapper and Core.sol and noticed that the withdraw flow does not handle a failed deposit. It is hard to notice because the failure path is rarely exercised and the contract does not emit explicit error messages when the deposit reverts. To remediate the issue, the contract should include an emergency withdraw function that bypasses the re‑deposit step, or it should check the gauge’s status before attempting to deposit and revert with a clear error if the gauge is killed. Conceptually, the fix introduces a safe exit path that restores user funds even when the external gauge is disabled, aligning the implementation with the expected business logic that users can always retrieve their deposited assets.

title: Usage of a TWAP price instead of the exact current sqrtPriceX96 will lead to wrong calculation of token amounts within the position
description: When depositing in the LpWrapper getAmountsForLiquidity is called in order to calculate the the exact token0 and token1 amounts within the position. The problem is that the sqrtPriceX96 used is not the current one, but rather the TWAP value returned from the oracle. This would lead to inaccurate token amounts calculated and users depositing less than expected and at a different ratio than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the LP wrapper contract using a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) value instead of the current pool price when it calculates the token amounts required for a liquidity position. The function that determines the exact token0 and token1 quantities calls getAmountsForLiquidity with a sqrtPriceX96 that is sourced from the oracle’s TWAP rather than the slot0.sqrtPriceX96 that reflects the live market price. Because the TWAP can lag behind rapid price movements, the computed amounts can be lower or higher than the true amounts needed for the intended price ratio. When a user initiates a deposit, they expect the contract to allocate token0 and token1 in the exact proportion dictated by the current price; however, the stale price causes the contract to mint a position with an unexpected token ratio. From the user’s perspective the UI may display the intended deposit amounts, but after the transaction the actual balances show fewer tokens received or a different composition, leading to the perception that funds have disappeared or that the refund is missing. The issue is a classic case of using outdated oracle data for accounting, a class of bugs where price staleness breaks financial invariants. It occurs whenever the deposit path invokes getAmountsForLiquidity, i.e., on every new liquidity addition through the wrapper. All liquidity providers and the protocol’s accounting layer are affected because the mis‑calculated amounts corrupt the internal bookkeeping of token reserves. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the price source used in the wrapper against the pool’s slot0 value and identified the mismatch. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the deviation may be small and only becomes apparent after a series of deposits, especially when market volatility is high. To remediate the issue the contract should retrieve the current sqrtPriceX96 directly from the pool’s slot0 storage and use that value for all amount calculations, ensuring that token allocations match the real‑time market price and preserving the intended ratio of assets in each position.

title: When depositing a position into a gauge, accrued fees are sent to Core.sol
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misdirected fee transfer that occurs when a user deposits an NFT position into a gauge contract. The deposit function internally calls the NonfungiblePositionManager.collect method with the recipient set to msg.sender. In the context ofthe gauge, msg.sender is the Core.sol contract itself, not the external user who initiated the deposit. Consequently, any fees that have accrued on the position prior to the deposit are transferred to the gauge contract instead of the position owner. This logic error arises from assuming that the caller of the deposit function is the fee beneficiary, ignoring the fact that the call is proxied through the gauge. An attacker or any subsequent user can later invoke a skim or similar function on the gauge to extract those fees, effectively stealing them from the original depositor. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful deposit, but the expected refund or fee payout never arrives; balances may appear unchanged or zero, leading to confusion. The issue is hard to notice because the deposit transaction does not revert and the fee movement is silent, making the loss only observable when another party claims the fees. The root cause is a flawed accounting assumption that the contract’s msg.sender equals the position owner. To remediate, the collect call should direct the accrued fees to the actual NFT owner (retrieved via nft.ownerOf(tokenId)) rather than to msg.sender, ensuring that fee distribution respects ownership. This class of bug falls under incorrect fund routing or misdirected transfer logic, which violates the protocol’s financial guarantees and can result in users losing accrued rewards.

title: Denial of service attack on LpWrapper's deposit and withdraw functions
description:
The Core contract allows any address to be set as the CallbackParams.counter address of a managed position. The LpWrapper also has its own CallbackParams.counter set in its managed position.
Combination of the above stated mechanisms can be used to DoS the deposit and withdraw functions of LpWrapper.
Scenario:
• An attacker brings an NFT with insignificant (but >0) liquidity and deposits it in Core.
• Attacker updates the gauge and counter addresses of his position such that:
  – gauge returns a malicious rewardToken which returns a huge uint256 value as Core contract balance.
  – counter is set to the Counter contract which is used by an LpWrapper instance.
• Attacker performs an emptyRebalance of his position. Here the value state of LpWrapper's Counter becomes uint256.max.
• Now no more rewards can be counted in LpWrapper's Counter as the Counter.add call will always reverts due to overflow.
• As on every LpWrapper's deposit and withdraw call the flow goes like this LpWrapper.deposit() → Core.withdraw() → VeloAmmModule.beforeRebalance() → Counter.add().
• All deposit and withdraw transactions will revert. Resulting in DoS of LpWrapper.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the LpWrapper contract that arises from the way the wrapper interacts with a Counter contract during deposit and withdraw operations. The Core contract permits any address to be stored as the CallbackParams.counter for a managed position, and the LpWrapper itself also stores a Counter address in its position. Because the counter address can be chosen or changed by the position owner, an attacker can point it to the generic Counter contract that simply adds the reported reward amount to an internal uint256 balance. By depositing an NFT that carries a non‑zero but negligible amount of liquidity, then updating the gauge to return a malicious reward token whose reported balance is an extremely large uint256 value, the attacker can cause the Counter’s internal balance to be set to uint256.max after calling emptyRebalance. Once the Counter balance equals the maximum value, any subsequent call to Counter.add will overflow and revert. Every LpWrapper.deposit or LpWrapper.withdraw internally calls Core.withdraw, which triggers VeloAmmModule.beforeRebalance and finally Counter.add; therefore each of those external calls now reverts, effectively blocking all further deposits and withdrawals. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that attempts to add liquidity or withdraw funds fail with a generic revert message, and users may see their balances appear unchanged or “nothing happens” despite confirming the transaction. The impact is a complete denial of service for the LpWrapper component: liquidity providers cannot add new positions nor retrieve existing ones, which can freeze funds and erode confidence in the protocol. The issue occurs only when the attacker can control both the gauge’s reward token address and the counter address of a managed position, and when the reward token reports a balance large enough to push the Counter to its maximum value. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flexibility of the CallbackParams fields and the arithmetic in the Counter contract. The bug is subtle because the overflow only manifests after the Counter reaches its maximum, a state that normal testing rarely reaches, and because the Counter contract itself performs no on‑chain accounting that would otherwise raise suspicion. To remediate the problem the protocol should either eliminate the use of the external Counter contract—tracking rewards off‑chain instead—or prohibit changing the Counter address from an arbitrary user, and enforce safe arithmetic checks or caps on the values that can be added to the Counter. By removing the mutable counter reference or adding overflow protection, the deposit and withdraw flows can resume normal operation without the risk of being permanently blocked.

title: Unsafe max deadline provided
description:
A maximum deadline is provided for execution of multiple NonfungiblePositionManager functions: increaseLiquidity, decreaseLiquidity and mint:
```solidity
deadline: type(uint256).max,
```
Note also that the following format provided in VeloDeployFactory._mint is also effectively a max deadline because it marks the deadline as the current timestamp at the time of execution, which effectively causes the deadline check to validate that block.timestamp <= block.timestamp, which is always true:
```solidity
deadline: block.timestamp,
```
Use of a maximum deadline is unsafe as it may result in the transaction to sit in the mempool for a very long time, until the conditions in which we're modifying our liquidity position have become undesirable, potentially even as a result of an MEV builder processing the transactions alongside some other actions to intentionally cause a loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using an effectively unlimited deadline when calling liquidity‑management functions of the NonfungiblePositionManager contract, such as increaseLiquidity, decreaseLiquidity and mint. The code supplies deadline values of type(uint256).max or block.timestamp, both of which cause the internal deadline check (require(block.timestamp <= deadline)) to always succeed. This happens because the maximum uint256 value is far beyond any realistic block timestamp, and setting the deadline to the current block timestamp creates a condition where the check compares the same value (block.timestamp <= block.timestamp), which is trivially true. As a result, the transaction is allowed to remain in the mempool indefinitely without being forced to execute within a bounded time window. An attacker or an MEV builder can therefore delay the execution until market conditions have shifted unfavourably for the liquidity provider, or can reorder the transaction with other profitable actions, potentially causing a loss of funds, unexpected slippage, or a failed liquidity operation. The issue manifests when a user expects their liquidity addition or removal to happen promptly and at the quoted price, but the transaction may be executed much later, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual outcomes – for example, the user may see their position value drop, receive a smaller amount of tokens than anticipated, or even end up with a zero balance after the operation. The problem is subtle because the deadline parameter appears to be correctly passed and the contract does not revert; the logic simply never enforces a time limit, making the bug easy to overlook during functional testing. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the parameter handling of deadline fields across the factory and manager contracts. To remediate, the contract should require callers to provide a realistic deadline (e.g., now + reasonable buffer) and enforce an upper bound on the deadline value, rejecting max‑uint or identical‑timestamp values. This change restores the intended protection against stale or front‑run transactions and aligns the contract behaviour with the business logic that liquidity actions must be executed within a predictable time frame.

title: Lack of consideration of time in ensureNoMEV leads to unexpected reverts
description:
VeloOracle.ensureNoMEV works by looking back at a given amount of observations and reverting if the tick delta between observations exceeds a maxAllowedDelta. The observations are retrieved from the given CLPool where they are written any time an in-range liquidity position is modified, or a swap occurs, updating the most recent observation if it was within 15 seconds. This logic is used to ensure that the price of the pool has not recently changed beyond a certain amount.
The problem with ensureNoMEV's logic here is that it implicitly assumes that the observations that are being considered are recent, however if there have not been any swaps or in-range liquidity modifications recently, then there will not be recent observations. Instead, we may be looking further back in time than intended.
Consider for example a circumstance where there's a large swap that exceeds the maxAllowedDelta, then there is no activity for a while. Even though the price has not recently changed, the function will revert since it's looking at the most recent observations, regardless of when they actually occurred.
The result of this is that rebalances can be DoS'd until sufficient observations are written such that ensureNoMEV no longer reverts. This can lead to extended periods of time in which the position is out of range and thus not earning liquidity fees.
bug_full: VeloOracle.ensureNoMEV is intended to protect against miner‑extracted value (MEV) by examining a fixed number of recent price observations from a CLPool and reverting if the tick delta between any two observations exceeds a configured maxAllowedDelta. The function assumes that the observations it inspects are temporally recent, but it does not verify the timestamps of those observations. When a pool experiences a large swap that triggers a tick delta larger than maxAllowedDelta, the function will revert as expected. However, if after that event there is a period with no swaps or in‑range liquidity modifications, the pool stops writing new observations. Because ensureNoMEV still looks back the same number of entries, it ends up comparing the last stored observation, which may be arbitrarily old, against the current state. The stale observation can still show a delta that exceeds the limit, causing the function to revert even though the price has been stable for many seconds. This mismatch between observation count and elapsed time creates a denial‑of‑service condition: any attempt to rebalance the position will revert until enough new observations are generated to push the stale entry out of the look‑back window. From a user perspective the rebalance transaction fails, the UI may report that the position is out of range, and liquidity providers see a sudden drop in accrued fees because the position cannot be re‑balanced into the optimal range. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the rebalancing logic, where the auditor noticed that the revert condition did not consider the age of the observations. It can be hard to notice because the revert appears to be triggered by a price change, which is the intended behavior, yet it occurs even when the price is unchanged. The root cause is the lack of a time‑based guard in the ensureNoMEV check. To remediate, the logic should incorporate a timestamp check, for example by requiring that no observation exceeding maxAllowedDelta has been recorded within a configurable time window (e.g., x seconds). Alternatively, the function could fall back to a safe path when the most recent observation is older than the allowed freshness threshold. Fixing the issue restores the intended accounting guarantees, prevents unnecessary reverts, and eliminates the possibility of a DoS attack that stalls fee generation for liquidity providers.

title: Unexpected ETH transfer DoS
bug_full: The issue is an unexpected ETH transfer denial of service in contracts that call the NonfungiblePositionManager.refundETH function. refundETH is designed to send any ETH held by the NonfungiblePositionManager back to the caller using TransferHelper.safeTransferETH(msg.sender, address(this).balance). However, the caller contracts – VeloDepositWithdrawModule (used in deposit) and VeloDeployFactory (used in createStrategy) – do not implement a receive() external payable or fallback() external payable function. According to Solidity semantics, when a contract receives Ether without a payable fallback, the transfer reverts. Consequently, if the NonfungiblePositionManager ever accumulates a non‑zero ETH balance, any subsequent call to deposit or createStrategy will trigger refundETH, the transfer will fail, and the whole transaction will revert. This can happen unintentionally when the manager receives ETH through a self‑destruct of another contract, a SENDALL call, or any payable function that does not immediately refund the balance. An attacker can deliberately front‑run a legitimate deposit or strategy creation, force ETH into the manager (for example by deploying a contract that self‑destructs and sends its balance to the manager), and cause the pending transaction to revert, effectively denying service to honest users. The impact is that users attempting to add liquidity or launch a strategy see their transactions fail, receive no confirmation, and their intended funds remain unprocessed; from a protocol perspective, the liquidity onboarding flow is blocked and the system may appear unreliable. The condition occurs only when the manager’s balance is greater than zero, which may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing, especially if the test suite never forces ETH into the manager. The bug belongs to the class of “missing payable fallback/receive function leading to forced Ether transfer revert” and manifests as a denial‑of‑service vector rather than a direct theft of funds. It was discovered during a manual audit of the VeloDepositWithdrawModule and VeloDeployFactory code paths that invoke refundETH. The symptom from a user’s point of view is a transaction that reverts with no obvious reason, often described as “deposit failed” or “strategy creation reverted”, while the UI may show that the operation did not complete and no funds were moved. To remediate, the caller contracts should implement a payable receive or fallback function that can accept Ether, and optionally include logic to forward any received ETH to a designated treasury or to safely burn it, ensuring that refundETH never triggers a revert due to an unhandled transfer.

title: Inﬂation Attack
description: Impact Explanation: Impact is High since Attacker can perform this attack to cause loss of victim funds.
bug_full: An inflation attack arises from the way the contract calculates shares on the very first mint. The function that converts deposited assets to shares treats the situation where totalShares is less than a constant LOCKED_SHARES as an “initial deposit”. In that branch it subtracts LOCKED_SHARES from the computed share amount, assuming that the caller has already contributed at least that many locked shares. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum asset amount that matches the locked share count, an attacker can deposit LOCKED_SHARES+1 assets. The formula then yields shares equal to the asset amount, and after subtracting LOCKED_SHARES the attacker receives exactly one share while having supplied a huge amount of assets. Consequently the internal accounting now values one share as LOCKED_SHARES+1 assets. Any subsequent user who deposits after this inflated state receives fewer shares than expected, effectively losing part of their contribution to the attacker. The vulnerability is triggered only on the first mint when totalSupply is zero; after the initial share price has been inflated, normal deposits continue to use the distorted price. Users notice the problem as a sudden drop in the number of shares they receive for a given deposit, or as missing refunds when they try to withdraw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the edge case of the initial deposit logic. It is difficult to spot because the conversion function works correctly for typical deposits and the subtraction of LOCKED_SHARES appears to protect the protocol, masking the fact that an oversized initial deposit can manipulate the share price. To remediate, the contract should either mint the locked shares to an irrecoverable address at deployment, enforce that the first deposit exactly matches the locked share amount, or prevent any subtraction of locked shares on the initial mint. In general, the bug belongs to the class of “initialization‑state arithmetic manipulation” where assumptions about a zero‑state balance are violated, leading to inflation of token value and loss of funds for later participants.

title: Deposits into risky ticks will have funds lost upon insolvency
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing users to deposit liquidity into price ticks (nodes) that are already close to insolvency, which can later cause the deposited funds to become unrecoverable. A node stores two key values: "shares", representing the total claim tokens issued to depositors, and "value", representing the realized profit‑and‑loss of the node. The contract determines insolvency with the internal function _isInsolvent, which returns true only when node.shares is non‑zero and node.value * FIXED_POINT_SCALE is less than node.shares. Because FIXED_POINT_SCALE is 1e18, this condition is satisfied only after the node has lost more than 99.9999999999999999% of its value. Consequently, the contract permits deposits while the node is still technically solvent but already extremely under‑collateralised. When a new liquidation occurs after such a deposit, the node’s value can drop just enough to satisfy the insolvency condition, triggering a garbage‑collection routine that zeroes node.value. At that point all previously minted shares, including those of the recent depositor, become worthless because the redemption formula divides by node.value, which is now zero. An attacker can exploit this by forcing a liquidation at a price just below the borrowed amount after a user has deposited, causing the node to cross the insolvency threshold and locking the user’s funds. From the user’s perspective the deposit transaction appears successful, but later attempts to withdraw or redeem show a zero balance or a failure to receive any funds, effectively “money disappears”. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by constructing a test case that reproduces the scenario: a first loan is liquidated at a minimal price, a second user deposits a large amount of shares, a second loan is liquidated at a price only slightly below the borrowed amount, and the node is then marked insolvent, zeroing its value. The bug is hard to notice because the node still reports a non‑zero share balance and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the health of a tick deteriorates; only the internal zeroing reveals the problem after the fact. The root cause is an insufficient health check before minting new shares and an overly permissive insolvency definition that only triggers at an extreme loss threshold. To remediate, the protocol should block deposits into nodes that are deemed unhealthy, for example by requiring node.value to remain above a configurable fraction (e.g., 50%) of node.shares, or by tightening the insolvency condition and performing a pre‑deposit sanity check. This would prevent the creation of new shares in a node that is on the brink of collapse and protect users from having their funds stuck or lost.

title: First depositor can be frontrun to lose funds from inﬂated shares
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw that allows an attacker to front‑run the first deposit into a newly created price‑tick and cause the depositor to receive zero or near‑zero shares, effectively losing the deposited funds. The root cause lies in the way the contract calculates the deposit price: it adds half of the pending interest to the node's current value and divides by the total number of shares. When the pending interest is artificially inflated while the share count for the target tick is kept extremely low (for example, a single wei of shares), the computed price can become larger than the amount being deposited. Because the number of minted shares is calculated as amount * FIXED_POINT_SCALE / price, a price that exceeds amount * FIXED_POINT_SCALE results in shares < 1, which are truncated to zero by the integer conversion. An attacker can achieve the inflated pending interest by using interest‑free flash loans to borrow large amounts across many ticks, thereby routing a large amount of accrued interest into the target tick before the victim’s deposit is processed. The attack sequence is: (1) attacker deposits a minimal amount (e.g., 1 wei) into the target tick to create a node with almost no shares; (2) attacker opens flash loans on many adjacent ticks, causing the protocol’s interest‑allocation mechanism to accumulate a substantial pending interest that is credited to the target tick; (3) the victim submits a normal‑sized deposit to the same tick; (4) due to the inflated price, the victim receives zero shares; (5) the victim later redeems the “deposit” and receives nothing, losing the original ETH. A second variant exploits an unsafe casting in the interest‑rate model combined with a low tickExponential value, causing the pending interest to be assigned to the lowest tick and again resulting in a price that mints zero shares. The impact is a loss of the victim’s deposited funds, typically ranging from a few percent up to around 17 % of the deposit under default pool parameters, and potentially higher with larger APRs or longer loan durations. The flaw manifests only when a tick is freshly initialized with a negligible share balance and when an attacker can manipulate pending interest before the first legitimate deposit. It primarily affects users who are the first to deposit into a new tick, but the economic loss can be transferred to the protocol’s liquidity pool as a whole. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the share‑minting formula and identified that the price calculation could be driven arbitrarily high by external interest flows, a scenario that is not covered by standard unit tests. The bug is subtle because the contract’s state appears normal—no revert occurs, and the deposit transaction succeeds—yet the user receives no shares, which may be missed without explicit checks on the minted share amount. To remediate, the contract should enforce a slippage or max‑price parameter that reverts if the computed price exceeds a reasonable bound, and it should include a sanity check that prevents minting zero shares. Additionally, the interest‑rate model must be corrected to avoid unsafe casting to a smaller integer type, ensuring that pending interest cannot be disproportionately allocated to a tick with an almost empty share balance. This class of bug falls under “price manipulation leading to zero‑share minting” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every deposit yields a positive share proportionate to the contributed value.

title: Gas forwarding mechanism may cause liquidity restoration failure
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from Ethereum’s default gas‑forwarding rule, which forwards only 63/64 of the remaining gas to an external call. In the liquidation routine, the contract invokes a callback on the source pool via a try‑catch block. Because the call receives only a fraction of the gas, the callback can deliberately consume a large amount of gas – more than 63 times the gas that remains for the rest of the liquidate() function – and then revert. The surrounding try‑catch silently swallows the revert, allowing the outer transaction to be reported as successful while the internal state changes performed after the callback (deleting liquidation records, emitting events, restoring liquidity nodes, and transferring collateral) are never executed. This mismatch means that the pool’s liquidity nodes are not restored and the liquidated collateral becomes permanently locked in the contract. The issue appears only when the source contract’s onCollateralLiquidated function is gas‑intensive, which can happen when the pool must restore many nodes, perform garbage collection, handle pending redemptions, or execute a token transfer. From a user’s perspective the transaction receipt shows success and events are emitted, yet the expected liquidity restoration does not occur and funds remain inaccessible, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that liquidation always frees up collateral. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow and gas semantics of the try‑catch pattern. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is logged; only the missing state updates reveal the problem. The recommended mitigation is to remove the try‑catch so that any revert in the callback propagates and aborts the whole liquidation, or alternatively to forward all remaining gas or redesign the callback mechanism to avoid reliance on the 63/64 stipend. By ensuring that a failed callback aborts the liquidation, the protocol can guarantee that liquidity nodes are either correctly restored or the transaction is rolled back, preserving the integrity of user balances.

title: Overﬂow is possible should the node's available liquidity + pending interest exceed type(uint128).max
description: The subtraction and addition of a node's available liquidity when it's used and restored are wrapped in unchecked blocks. Because the restoration may include pending interest, it's possible for the addition to overﬂow, cause the available liquidity to be smaller than expected. It's highly unlikely to happen as it requires the token's supply to be at least type(uint128).max, given the permissionless nature of pool creations, and that any token of 18 decimals can be used, it can be exploited.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow that can occur when a node’s available liquidity and its pending interest are summed inside an unchecked block. The contract subtracts the amount used from the node’s available balance and then adds any pending interest to the node’s pending field without any overflow protection. If the sum of node.available and node.pending reaches or exceeds type(uint128).max (2^128‑1), the addition wraps around, causing the stored available liquidity to become smaller than it should be. This mis‑calculation can be triggered when a token with 18 decimals is used to create a pool whose total supply is close to the uint128 maximum, a scenario that is theoretically possible because pool creation is permissionless. An attacker could deliberately supply a massive amount of tokens, invoke deposit() or use() functions, and cause the overflow, resulting in the protocol believing that less liquidity is available than actually exists. Consequently, users may see their balances reduced unexpectedly, refunds may be zero, or withdrawals may succeed with insufficient backing, effectively allowing funds to disappear or be drained. The issue manifests only under extreme supply conditions, making it hard to notice during normal testing, and it was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the unchecked arithmetic. To remediate, the contract should perform a pre‑check that the addition of available liquidity and pending interest does not exceed the uint128 ceiling before executing the unchecked block, or replace the unchecked arithmetic with safe math operations that revert on overflow. This correction restores the accounting guarantees of the protocol and prevents the scenario where the available liquidity is incorrectly wrapped, preserving user expectations that deposited funds remain fully accounted for.

title: Centralization risks
description:
Admin can allow new collateral wrappers using setCollateralWrapper function. This could bring centralization risk
1. Lets say Admin wants to prohibit auction of collateral X with token id Y.
2. Admin creates a malicious bundle and allows it using setCollateralWrapper function.
3. This malicious bundle always return collateral X with token id Y on calling enumerate function. Also on calling unwrap it does nothing.
4. Now Admin creates a NFT using this malicious bundle and calls liquidate function.
5. enumerate function is called which sets underlyingCollateralToken as X and underlyingCollateralTokenIds as Y.
```solidity
if (_collateralWrappers[collateralToken]) {
    /* Get underlying collateral token and underlying collateral token IDs */
    (underlyingCollateralToken, underlyingCollateralTokenIds) = ICollateralWrapper(collateralToken).enumerate(
        collateralTokenId,
        collateralWrapperContext
    );
}
```
6. This means Auction will get started on token id Y of X even though contract does not have this token.
7. Bidding will start and bidder fund will be locked.
8. Claim will fail since contract does not have the NFT.
9. So, bidder fund is stuck and if token id Y actually need to be placed for auction then it will fail since an auction is already in place.
Another way
1. Admin simply approves a malicious wrapper.
2. Admin mints himself a new bundle token with NFT X,Y,Z without actually passing these NFT.
3. Admin borrows and provide the bundle token from step2.
4. Borrow passes and Admin gets extra.
Another Instance: if Bot only calls withdrawCollateral on ExternalCollateralLiquidator.sol and liquidateCollateral is never called, this will mean collateral will be taken without paying any proceeds.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an admin‑controlled function that can register arbitrary collateral wrapper contracts. Because the protocol trusts the wrapper to correctly report the underlying collateral token and token IDs through its enumerate method and to transfer the assets back on unwrap, a malicious wrapper can mislead the liquidation logic. An attacker with admin rights (or a compromised admin) can add a wrapper that always returns a specific NFT identifier even though the protocol does not actually hold that NFT. When a liquidation is triggered, the contract calls enumerate, receives the fabricated token address and ID, and proceeds to start an auction for that non‑existent asset. Bidders place funds, the auction locks their capital, and when the claim phase is reached the contract cannot transfer the NFT because it never owned it, causing the claim to fail and the bidder funds to remain stuck. The same mechanism also allows the admin to mint a bundle token that claims to contain NFTs without supplying the underlying assets, then borrow against the bundle and obtain extra funds. Additionally, the ExternalCollateralLiquidator can be instructed to withdraw collateral without ever invoking the liquidateCollateral function, meaning collateral can be taken without any proceeds being paid to the protocol. The root cause is the lack of validation of wrapper behavior and the concentration of power in a single admin address, which creates a centralization risk and opens a path for asset misrepresentation and fund lock‑up. The issue may be hard to notice because the wrapper interface is generic; the protocol only sees a successful call to enumerate and assumes the returned data is truthful, so the problem only surfaces during liquidation when an auction cannot be settled. To remediate, the admin role should be hardened, for example by requiring multi‑signature approval, limiting who can add wrappers, and adding runtime checks that the contract actually owns the reported NFT before starting an auction. The protocol should also verify that unwrap correctly transfers the underlying asset and reject wrappers that do not conform to expected behavior. By reducing the trust placed in a single privileged account and enforcing asset ownership checks, the risk of funds being locked or stolen can be mitigated.

title: Zero duration will fail all repayment attempt
bug_full: A borrower can request a loan with a duration value of zero. The contract stores this duration in the loan receipt and later uses it as the divisor in a repayment‑interest calculation performed with Math.mulDiv. Because the divisor is zero, the call triggers a divide‑by‑zero revert, causing the repay() function to fail. As a result the borrower is unable to settle the debt even if they try to repay in the same block, and the protocol’s liquidation logic treats the loan as defaulted and initiates liquidation. The root cause is the absence of input validation on the duration parameter in the borrow function, allowing an edge‑case value that violates the arithmetic assumption that duration is strictly positive. The bug is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the repayment formula and noticed the direct use of loanReceipt.duration without a guard. It can be hard to notice because zero is a valid uint256 value and the borrow path may appear to work; the failure only surfaces later during repayment, a code path that may receive less testing. The impact is that borrowers lose the ability to close their positions, potentially suffer liquidation losses, and lenders may receive reduced recovery because the loan is forced into liquidation prematurely. Users experience a transaction revert with a generic error, see no funds returned, and may observe their loan balance remain unchanged while the protocol marks the loan as liquidatable. The issue belongs to the class of arithmetic‑validation bugs where unchecked user‑controlled parameters are used as divisors, leading to runtime exceptions and business‑logic violations. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a non‑zero duration at loan creation, for example by adding require(duration > 0, "Invalid duration") in the borrow function, and optionally adding a defensive check before any division that uses the duration field.

title: `BkdLocker#depositFees`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way BkdLocker distributes reward tokens when the function depositFees is called. The contract adds newly deposited reward tokens directly to a feeIntegral that is calculated as the amount divided by the current totalLockedBoosted value, and the feeBalance is increased by the same amount. Because the feeIntegral is updated immediately and the reward allocation for each locker is based on the totalLockedBoosted snapshot taken after the deposit, a user who can increase their locked balance shortly before or during the fee deposit can capture a disproportionate share of the newly added rewards. The root cause is that rewards are emitted instantly without any vesting schedule or protective delay, and the contract relies on a withdrawal delay that can be configured to zero by the admin. An attacker can monitor pending fees, front‑run the depositFees transaction by submitting a lock transaction that adds a large amount of tokens to the pool, then immediately call claimFees and withdraw the locked tokens before any delay expires. In the described proof‑of‑concept, the attacker locks an amount equal to half of the existing pool, causing the feeIntegral to be computed on a doubled denominator, and then claims half of the newly deposited 1,000 reward tokens, stealing 500 reward tokens that rightfully belong to existing users. The impact is a loss of yield for honest participants and a direct transfer of value to the front‑runner, effectively stealing a large portion of the newly added rewards. The attack is feasible whenever the withdrawal delay is short or zero and when an adversary can front‑run transactions, which is common in MEV‑rich environments. Users affected are token holders who lock their governance tokens expecting a proportional reward; they may notice that after a fee deposit their expected reward is missing, that their balance shows no increase, or that the reward they receive is far smaller than anticipated. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the accounting logic of fee distribution and identified that the instantaneous feeIntegral update combined with a mutable withdrawal delay creates an exploitable timing window. The flaw is subtle because on‑chain state appears consistent – the feeIntegral and feeBalance correctly reflect the deposited amount – yet the allocation to individual lockers is skewed by the attacker’s temporary increase in share. To remediate the problem, the protocol should migrate to a rewardRate‑based gradual release model with linear vesting, as used by Synthetix’s StakingRewards contract, or enforce a non‑zero minimum withdrawal delay, or postpone the feeIntegral update until after a lock‑period window, thereby preventing an attacker from front‑running and immediately harvesting the rewards.

title: DoS on KeeperGauge due to division by zero
description:
In the **_calcTotalClaimable()** function it should be validated that perPeriodTotalFees[i] != 0 since otherwise it would generate a DoS in **claimableRewards()** and **claimRewards()**.  
This would be possible since if **advanceEpoch()** or **kill()** is executed by the InflationManager address, the epoch will go up without perPeriodTotalFees[newIndexEpoch] is 0.  
The negative of this is that every time the **InflationManager** executes these two methods (**kill() and advanceEpoch()**) DoS is generated until you run **reportFees()**.  
Another possible case is that **kill()** or **advanceEpoch()** are executed 2 times in a row and there is no way of a perPeriodTotalFees[epoch-1] updating its value, therefore it would be an irreversible DoS.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error that manifests in the reward‑distribution routine of the KeeperGauge contract. In the internal function that aggregates a beneficiary's claimable fees, the code performs a scaled division of the recorded fees by the total fees for the current epoch (perPeriodTotalFees[i]). If perPeriodTotalFees[i] equals zero, the division triggers a Solidity revert, causing the public view function claimableRewards() and the state‑changing function claimRewards() to fail. This condition can arise when the InflationManager contract calls advanceEpoch() or kill() and moves the protocol to a new epoch without having recorded any fees for that period. A second consecutive call to either of these methods can leave an epoch without an associated perPeriodTotalFees entry, and because the beneficiary’s nextEpochToClaim pointer includes the empty epoch, the division by zero persists until reportFees() is called to populate the missing total. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users attempting to claim accrued rewards receive a transaction revert and see no funds transferred, effectively locking their earned fees. The issue is observable from a user perspective as repeated claim attempts that suddenly revert or as a sudden disappearance of expected reward balances after an epoch transition, contradicting the expectation that rewards accrue continuously. The root cause is the lack of input validation or fallback logic for the case where the total fee amount for an epoch is zero, a scenario that is rare and therefore easy to overlook during testing. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑error DoS vulnerabilities, where unchecked mathematical operations cause contract execution to abort, breaking business logic that assumes positive denominators in accounting formulas. To remediate, the contract should explicitly check for a zero perPeriodTotalFees value and either skip the division, treat the claimable amount as zero for that epoch, or emit a safe default, ensuring that reward claims remain functional even when an epoch has no fees. This adjustment restores the intended invariant that users can always query and withdraw whatever fees have been recorded, preserving protocol honesty and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.

title: The first AMM Staker will have control over how the shares are calculated.
description: The first staker can take control of how the subsequent shares are going to be distributed by simply staking 1wei amount of the token and frontrunning future stakers. The reasons of this are related on how the variables are updated and with the amounts that the Gauge allows users to stake (anything but zero). The origin of this vulnerability relies on the evaluation of the `totalStaked` variable on its inception.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unfair share‑calculation flaw that gives the very first staker of the AMM gauge control over how reward shares are allocated to all subsequent participants. The contract computes each user’s reward share by integrating a global "staked integral" that depends on the variable totalStaked. When totalStaked is zero, the first iteration of the points‑allocation loop is skipped, and the global integral remains at its default value. As a result, the first depositor – even with a trivial amount such as 1 wei – can front‑run later users, stake again before their transactions are mined, and receive a disproportionately large amount of shares.
