The root cause is the contract’s failure to handle the transition from a zero to a non‑zero totalStaked state: the share‑calculation logic assumes totalStaked is already positive and does not correctly initialise the integral or adjust the per‑user share denominator. This condition is triggered only when the pool is empty and the first stake occurs. An attacker can exploit it by making a minimal initial deposit, then repeatedly front‑running larger deposits from honest users, each time increasing their own share count while the honest users receive far fewer shares than warranted by their contribution. The impact is a systematic over‑rewarding of the first depositor, effectively siphoning reward tokens that should belong to later stakers; in the demonstrated proof‑of‑concept the attacker earned roughly 100 % more shares than a comparable honest participant. Users perceive the problem as missing or reduced rewards: a participant expecting a fair proportion of the accrued inflation finds their balance stagnating or their reward claim yielding far less than anticipated, while the first staker sees an unexpectedly high payout. The issue was uncovered during a security audit through controlled testing that simulated front‑running scenarios and inspected the evolution of totalStaked, global integral and per‑user shares. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the rewards appear to accrue normally, and only a detailed state comparison reveals the share imbalance. To remediate, the share‑calculation routine must be rewritten to correctly initialise the global integral when totalStaked transitions from zero, or to enforce a non‑zero minimum initial stake, or to perform a dummy seed deposit by the deployer so that the first real user cannot gain an advantage. In essence, the protocol needs a robust guard against zero‑state share calculations to preserve the intended fairness of reward distribution.

title: THE first AMM Staker may not receive according rewards because of poor checkpoints
description: The first staker within the `AmmGauge` may not get the rewards if the pool is not checkpointed right after he stakes and before he wants to claim the rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the AMM gauge contract updates its accounting variables when the pool is empty. When the very first participant stakes tokens, the contract does not perform a pool checkpoint immediately after the stake, nor does it correctly handle the zero‑state in the checkpoint routine. As a result, the per‑user share and the cumulative staked integral are calculated with a stale or zero denominator, causing the first staker’s reward share to be severely underestimated. If the protocol later receives additional stakes or inflates rewards without an explicit call to _poolCheckpoint() between the first stake and the reward claim, the first user’s claimable balance will be far lower than expected, while later participants receive the correct amounts. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the first depositor sees a very small reward (for example 6.6 tokens instead of roughly 115 tokens) even though they have staked the same amount and for the same duration as the others. The impact is a loss of expected rewards for that single participant, which can be perceived as the protocol “stealing” or mishandling funds. This edge case occurs only when the pool has not been checkpointed after the initial deposit and before subsequent deposits or reward claims, making it easy to miss in normal operation because subsequent users are unaffected and the discrepancy appears only for the first address. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit where a test harness reproduced the staking sequence and compared reward calculations with and without an intermediate checkpoint, revealing a dramatic divergence for the first staker. Detecting the problem in production is difficult because the contract does not emit a warning, and the accounting inconsistency is hidden behind normal reward‑claim functions. The appropriate remediation is to adjust the checkpoint logic to correctly handle a zero‑total‑staked state, ensuring that a checkpoint is triggered after the first stake or that the reward formula safely addresses the empty‑pool case. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “reward‑distribution arithmetic errors caused by improper initialization and missing state updates”, which violate the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each staker receives a proportionate share of accrued inflation.

title: Amount distributed can be inaccurate when updating weights
description:
When updating pool inflation rates, other pools see their `currentRate` being modified without having `poolCheckpoint` called, which leads to false computations.

This will lead to either users losing a part of their claims, but can also lead to too many tokens could be distributed, preventing some users from claiming due to the `totalAvailableToNow` requirement in `Minter`.
poc:
Imagine you have 2 AMM pools A and B, both with an `ammPoolWeight` of 100, where `poolCheckpoint` has not been called for a moment. Then, imagine calling [`executeAmmTokenWeight`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backd/blob/c856714a50437cb33240a5964b63687c9876275b/backd/contracts/tokenomics/InflationManager.sol#L318) to reduce the weight of A to 0.

Only A is checkpointed [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backd/blob/c856714a50437cb33240a5964b63687c9876275b/backd/contracts/tokenomics/InflationManager.sol#L591), so when B will be checkpointed it will call `getAmmRateForToken`, which will see a pool weight of 100 and a total weight of 100 over the whole period since the last checkpoint of B, which is false, therefore it will distribute too many tokens. This is critical has the minter expects an exact or lower than expected distribution due to the requirement of `totalAvailableToNow`.

In the opposite direction, when increasing weights, it will lead to less tokens being distributed in some pools than planned, leading to a loss for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inaccurate distribution of inflation tokens when the weight of a single AMM pool is changed without synchronously updating the accounting state of the other pools. In the InflationManager contract, the function that retrieves the per‑token rate (getAmmRateForToken) calculates the rate based on the global totalAmmTokenWeight and the individual pool weight. When an admin calls executeAmmTokenWeight to modify the weight of pool A, only pool A is explicitly checkpointed – its internal accounting (last update timestamp, accrued points) is refreshed. The other pools, for example pool B, retain their previous checkpoint data. Because the total weight has changed but pool B’s checkpoint has not been executed, the next time pool B is queried it will use a stale total weight value while still assuming its old pool weight, producing a mismatched rate. This leads to two opposite failure modes: if a weight is decreased, pool B will appear to have a higher relative weight than it actually does, causing the contract to allocate more tokens to B than the protocol intends; if a weight is increased, pool B will be allocated fewer tokens than owed. From a user’s point of view, a staker may notice that the expected inflation reward is either missing or lower than advertised, or that a claim transaction reverts because the minter reports that the totalAvailableToNow amount is insufficient – effectively the user receives nothing or receives an unexpectedly small amount while the protocol may have over‑minted tokens for other pools. The impact is a loss of claimable tokens for some users and a potential over‑distribution that can break the invariant that total minted tokens never exceed the scheduled supply, a situation similar to the historic Sushi MasterChef massUpdatePools bug. The issue manifests whenever the governance or an admin changes a pool’s weight via executeAmmTokenWeight without invoking poolCheckpoint on every LpStakerVault, KeeperGauge, or AmmGauge. The affected parties are all token holders who stake in the impacted pools, the protocol’s inflation accounting, and any external integrators relying on accurate reward calculations. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors constructed a proof‑of‑concept with two pools of equal weight, reduced one pool’s weight to zero, and observed that the untouched pool received an inflated reward due to the stale checkpoint. The bug is hard to notice because the token distribution discrepancy can be subtle and only becomes apparent under specific weight‑change scenarios; normal operation without weight adjustments shows correct behavior. To remediate, the contract should enforce a mass checkpoint (or equivalent state‑sync) of all pools whenever the global weight configuration changes, ensuring that each pool’s accrued points are updated before the new total weight is used for rate calculations. Conceptually, this is a state‑synchronisation bug where stale accounting data leads to an incorrect formula for reward allocation, violating the business logic that each staker receives a proportionate share of the inflation supply based on the current weights.

title: High borrowRate values in the new fixed rate IRM could lead to user funds stuck in Morpho Blue markets
description:
The FixedRateIrm allows anyone to set a custom fixed arbitrary borrowRate for a specified market. The current implementation of setBorrowRate reverts only if the specified newBorrowRate value is equal to zero or if the market has been already configured with a non-zero borrow rate. This means that an arbitrary value between 1 and type(uint256).max is accepted as a valid borrowRate for a market. While a very low borrow rate has the only consequence that borrowers will pay a tiny interest (and suppliers will earn a very tiny amount for the money lent), a high value of borrowRate will make the Morpho Blue operations for such market to always revert when the _accrueInterest function is executed. The _accrueInterest can revert when one of the following operations is executed:
• wTaylorCompounded could revert for overflow.
• market[id].totalBorrowAssets.wMulDown could overflow.
• interest.toUint128() could revert if interest > type(uint128.max).
• Adding interest to totalBorrowAssets and totalSupplyAssets could revert if interest is big enough to make the sum overflow.
Such internal function is always called when one of the following functions is executed:
• accrueInterest
• setFee
• supply
• withdraw
• borrow
• repay
• withdrawCollateral
• liquidate
The only function that does not call _accrueInterest is supplyCollateral. Let's assume that IIrm(marketParams.irm).borrowRate(marketParams, market[id]) returns a borrowRate that makes _accrueInterest revert. User funds will be stuck forever in the Morpho Blue market in these cases:
• If a borrower provides collateral by executing supplyCollateral. This function never calls _accrueInterest and can't revert. The problem in this case is that the borrower won't be able to withdraw his collateral because withdrawCollateral will always revert.
• Any funds supplied to the contract at market creation or, in general, when elapsed == 0. After that suppliers and borrowers have provided loan/collateral tokens, those tokens will not be able to be withdrawn or borrowed because those transactions will revert when _accrueInterest is executed.
Note that MetaMorpho Vaults and Bundlers that interact with these reverting markets will also be influenced by these side effects.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the FixedRateIrm component of Morpho Blue, which permits any caller to set an arbitrary fixed borrowRate for a market without enforcing upper limits. The setBorrowRate function only rejects a zero value or a second attempt to change an already‑configured non‑zero rate, meaning that a borrowRate anywhere between one and the maximum uint256 value is accepted. When an excessively high borrowRate is stored, the internal _accrueInterest routine, which is invoked by most user‑facing actions such as accrueInterest, setFee, supply, withdraw, borrow, repay, withdrawCollateral and liquidate, performs arithmetic that can overflow. Specific overflow points include the compounded interest calculation, multiplication of total borrow assets, conversion of interest to a uint128, and addition of interest to total borrow or supply balances. If any of these operations overflow, the transaction reverts, effectively freezing the market. Consequently, users who have supplied assets, borrowed, or provided collateral find that subsequent calls to withdraw, repay, or withdrawCollateral always revert, leaving their tokens permanently locked in the contract. The issue manifests when a market is created with a high borrowRate or when a borrower later sets such a rate via setBorrowRate. It affects all participants of the affected market, including regular lenders, borrowers, collateral providers, as well as higher‑level constructs like MetaMorpho vaults and bundlers that interact with the market. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the parameter validation of FixedRateIrm. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because typical borrowRate values are modest and do not trigger overflow; only extreme values cause the failure, which may be overlooked if tests do not cover boundary conditions. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or parameter validation errors that break accounting invariants, leading to a denial‑of‑service where funds become unrecoverable. To remediate, the contract should enforce sensible lower and upper bounds on the borrowRate input, ensuring that the resulting interest calculations cannot overflow the underlying numeric types, and the documentation should clearly warn users about the potential for market lock‑up when extreme rates are set.

title: avgBorrowRate is miscalculated as zero when newBorrowRate equals to borrowRateAfterJump
description: The SpeedJumpIrm calculates the interest rate based on SpeedFactor and JumpFactor. According to the document, at any time t, the level of the rate is given by the formula: r(t) = r(last(t)) ∗jump(t) ∗speed(t) For Morpho blue to calculate the interests during two interactions of IRM, the SpeedJumpIrm calculated the avgBorrowRate as uint256((int256(newBorrowRate) - int256(borrowRateAfterJump)).wDivDown(linearVariation)). borrowRateAfterJump is the interests rate applied by the JumpFactor and the newBorrowRate is the end interest rates applied by both SpeedFactor and JumpFactor. In the SpeedJumpIrm implementation, two variables are calculated as follow: • SpeedJumpIrm.sol#L134-L139 int256 linearVariation = speed * int256(elapsed); uint256 variationMultiplier = MathLib.wExp(linearVariation); // newBorrowRate = prevBorrowRate * jumpMultiplier * variationMultiplier. uint256 borrowRateAfterJump = marketIrm[id].prevBorrowRate.wMulDown(jumpMultiplier); uint256 newBorrowRate = borrowRateAfterJump.wMulDown(variationMultiplier); // ... uint256 avgBorrowRate; if (linearVariation == 0) avgBorrowRate = borrowRateAfterJump; // Safe "unchecked" cast to uint256 because linearVariation < 0 <=> newBorrowRate <= borrowRateAfterJump. else avgBorrowRate = uint256((int256(newBorrowRate) - int256(borrowRateAfterJump)).wDivDown(linearVariation)); Since the speed variable depends on the err of the current utilization rate and the target utilization rate, it can be really small results in linearVariation very small or zero. Thus, in the implementation, it returns avgBorrowRate as borrowRateAfterJump when linearVariation is zero. However, there's an edge case when linearVariation is small but not zero. In this case, borrowRateAfterJump.wMulDown(variationMultiplier); equals borrowRateAfterJump because of rounding down. Resulting in the wrong avgBorrowRate at SpeedJumpIrm.sol#L149 since linearVariation = 0
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the average borrow rate (avgBorrowRate) inside the SpeedJumpIrm module, which is responsible for applying both a JumpFactor and a SpeedFactor to the base interest rate. The contract computes a linear variation as speed multiplied by the elapsed time and then derives a variation multiplier via an exponential function. The new borrow rate is obtained by multiplying the rate after the jump (borrowRateAfterJump) with this variation multiplier. When the speed variable is extremely small, the exponential multiplication rounds down to the original borrowRateAfterJump, making newBorrowRate equal to borrowRateAfterJump. The code contains a special case that returns borrowRateAfterJump directly only when linearVariation is exactly zero. However, when linearVariation is merely very small but non‑zero, the subtraction newBorrowRate‑borrowRateAfterJump yields zero because of the rounding, and the subsequent division by a tiny linearVariation produces an avgBorrowRate of zero. This mis‑calculation occurs because the implementation assumes that a non‑zero linearVariation guarantees a non‑zero difference between the two rates, which is not true under rounding. An attacker can deliberately drive the utilization rate close to the target so that the speed factor becomes minuscule, trigger a transaction that causes a tiny elapsed interval, and cause the contract to record an avgBorrowRate of zero. As a result, borrowers are charged no interest for the period, effectively receiving a free loan, while lenders and the protocol lose expected revenue and may become under‑collateralised. The issue manifests only in edge‑case scenarios where the speed is near zero but not exactly zero, making it hard to detect in standard testing because typical test vectors use larger utilization changes. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the average rate could collapse to zero for small linearVariation values. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error and approximation‑error vulnerabilities in financial formulas, where integer division and fixed‑point arithmetic hide subtle loss of precision. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see that the interest accrued on their loan is unexpectedly zero, while a lender may observe that their expected yield disappears without any explicit error message. To remediate the issue, the contract should employ a safer approximation for avgBorrowRate when linearVariation is below a defined threshold, such as using the borrowRateAfterJump directly or applying a higher‑precision arithmetic routine, thereby avoiding the division of a zero numerator by a tiny denominator and ensuring that interest calculations remain consistent with the protocol’s economic model.

title: Non-whitelisted users can mint vault shares with permissioned tokens through the bundler
description: In PR 233, GeneralAdapter1.erc20WrapperDepositFor() was modified such that wrapped tokens are minted to the initiator() instead of any receiver address: ```solidity function erc20WrapperDepositFor(address wrapper, uint256 amount) external onlyBundler3 { IERC20 underlying = ERC20Wrapper(wrapper).underlying(); if (amount == type(uint256).max) amount = underlying.balanceOf(address(this)); require(amount != 0, ErrorsLib.ZeroAmount()); SafeERC20.forceApprove(underlying, wrapper, type(uint256).max); require(ERC20Wrapper(wrapper).depositFor(initiator(), amount), ErrorsLib.DepositFailed()); SafeERC20.forceApprove(underlying, wrapper, 0); } ``` This change was made to prevent users who are not whitelisted by a permissioned token from minting vault shares through the bundler. Using verUSDC as an example, a non-whitelisted user could previously do the following: • Send USDC to GeneralAdapter1. • Call erc20WrapperDepositFor() to wrap USDC →verUSDC, with receiver as GeneralAdapter1. • Call morphoSupply() to deposit verUSDC, with onBehalf as himself. However, by directly minting permissioned tokens to the adapter, it is still possible for a non-whitelisted user to mint vault shares. More specifically, a non-whitelisted user can: • Directly call verUSDC.depositFor() with account as GeneralAdapter1, which mints verUSDC to GeneralAdapter1. • Call morphoSupply() to deposit verUSDC, with onBehalf as himself. This attack is possible as depositFor() only checks if account is whitelisted; there is no restriction on the caller. As a result, attackers will still be able to use the bundler to bypass any form of whitelist in permissioned tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a permissioned ERC20 token that restricts minting to a whitelist of approved accounts. An adapter called GeneralAdapter1 includes a bundler function erc20WrapperDepositFor that was altered to mint wrapped tokens directly to the transaction initiator, aiming to stop non‑whitelisted users from receiving vault shares. However, the underlying wrapper contract’s depositFor method only validates that the target account (the address that will receive the minted tokens) is whitelisted; it does not verify the caller of the function. Consequently, a malicious actor who is not on the whitelist can call depositFor with the adapter address as the recipient, causing the permissioned token (for example verUSDC) to be minted to the adapter despite the caller’s lack of permission. The attacker can then invoke morphoSupply, specifying themselves as the onBehalf argument, and deposit the newly minted tokens into the vault, thereby obtaining vault shares that should have been inaccessible. This bypass occurs whenever the token is permissioned, the wrapper’s depositFor lacks caller restrictions, and the bundler does not enforce a whitelist check on the initiator. The affected parties include the protocol’s vault, legitimate token holders who rely on the whitelist for fair participation, and any user expecting that non‑whitelisted addresses cannot acquire shares. The issue was discovered during a security audit of PR 233 when the auditor noticed that the bundler’s whitelist enforcement could be circumvented via a direct call to the wrapper contract. The bug is subtle because the bundler function appears to enforce the whitelist, masking the fact that the underlying wrapper contract can be invoked independently, making the flaw easy to overlook in code reviews. From a user’s perspective, a non‑whitelisted participant can unexpectedly see vault shares appear in their account after using the bundler, contradicting the expectation that the transaction would be rejected. This results in unauthorized participation, potential dilution of share value, and a breach of the protocol’s access‑control guarantees. To remediate the issue, the adapter should be refactored so that any function that mints or withdraws permissioned tokens verifies that the initiator is itself whitelisted before proceeding. Alternatively, the permissioned token’s wrapper could be modified to require that the caller is also whitelisted, or the deposit functions such as morphoSupply and erc4626Mint could include explicit whitelist checks on the caller. Moving the wrapper‑related functions to a dedicated adapter that enforces these checks would close the bypass vector and restore the intended security model.

title: Funds can be redirected to the idle market by reaching the MetaMorpho supply cap using a flash loan
description: The public allocator allows the users to move the funds in the MM permissionless. However, to prevent undesired states in the MM portfolio, FlowCaps are configured, placing limitations on users' capabilities. One feature of the publicAllocator is to permit users to revert to flow caps in case the portfolio management is suboptimal. Reversing the publicAllocator action does not equate to reversing MM portfolio management, as the portfolios of MM may undergo changes between two publicAllocator actions. Consider the following configuration of MM and the public allocator: in the ETH MM vault, there are two markets in the supply queue: stEth and the idle market. The withdrawal queue consists of three markets: the idle market, stEth market, and the rEth market. The allocator is configured to encourage funds to be transferred out from the idle market. supplyQueue index market current assets Cap stETH market 1,000,000 5,000,000 idle market (unlimited) withdrawalQueue index market current assets Cap idle market (unlimited) stETH market 1,000,000 5,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 5,000,000 publicAllocator market maxIn maxOut idle market 10,000,000 stETH market 1,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 The malicious users can move funds into the idle market and place the MM in an undesired state with the following steps: 1. Flashloan and calls metaMorph.deposit with 5,000,000 assets. This fills up the first market (stETH market) and an extra 1,000,000 goes to the idle market. The users get 5,000,000 worth of MM shares in this step. • States: supplyQueue index market current assets Cap stETH market 5,000,000 5,000,000 idle market 1,000,000 (unlimited) withdrawalQueue index market current assets Cap idle market 1,000,000 (unlimited) stETH market 5,000,000 5,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 5,000,000 publicAllocator market maxIn maxOut idle market 10,000,000 stETH market 1,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 2. Let PublicAllocator withdraw assets from the idle market by calling publicAllocator.reallocateTo, with the the idle market as the only withdrawal and the rETH market as the supplying market: • States: supplyQueue index market current assets Cap stETH market 5,000,000 5,000,000 idle market (unlimited) withdrawalQueue index market current assets Cap idle market (unlimited) stETH market 5,000,000 5,000,000 rETH market 2,000,000 5,000,000 publicAllocator market maxIn maxOut idle market 1,000,000 9,000,000 stETH market 1,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 3. Withdraw all the MM shares that the exploiter got in the first step. The MM would try to pull 5,000,000 worth of assets. Since there are no assets in the idle markets, MM pulls assets from the second markets in the withdrawal queue. MM pulls 5,000,000 asses from the stETH market. • States: supplyQueue index market current assets Cap stETH market 5,000,000 idle market (unlimited) withdrawalQueue index market current assets Cap idle market (unlimited) stETH market 5,000,000 rETH market 2,000,000 5,000,000 publicAllocator market maxIn maxOut idle market 1,000,000 9,000,000 stETH market 1,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 4. Let publicAllocator reverse the previous cap flow and move funds out of the idle market. • States: supplyQueue index market current assets Cap stETH market 5,000,000 idle market 1,000,000 (unlimited) withdrawalQueue index market current assets Cap idle market (unlimited) stETH market 5,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 5,000,000 publicAllocator market maxIn maxOut idle market 10,000,000 stETH market 1,000,000 rETH market 1,000,000 In the above example, the flowCaps remain the same after funds are moved to the idle market. Thus, the exploit still works even with a lower non-zero flowCaps limit. For instance, assume the maxOut of the idle market is 500,000, the exploit steps would be: 1. Deposit 4,500,000 in the first step, letting MM deposit 500,000 into the idle market. 2. Have the public allocator move 500,000 from the idle market to the rEth market. 3. Withdraw all shares from MM. At this point, 500,000 assets still exist in the stETH market. 4. Reverse the cap flow and move funds from rETH to the idle market. 5. Repeat steps 1 to 4.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a flow‑cap manipulation flaw in the MetaMorpho public allocator that allows an attacker to redirect assets into an idle market and then withdraw them, effectively bypassing the intended portfolio allocation limits. The root cause lies in the design of the publicAllocator’s reallocateTo function, which permits a reversal of the configured flow caps (maxIn and maxOut) without enforcing that the total assets moved respect those caps after the operation. Because the idle market is configured with an unlimited supply cap and a non‑zero maxOut, an attacker can use a flash‑loan to deposit a large amount, causing the excess to overflow into the idle market. The publicAllocator can then withdraw the overflow from the idle market and supply it to another market (for example rETH) while still keeping the original caps unchanged. When the attacker later withdraws their MetaMorpho shares, the vault’s withdrawal queue pulls assets from the original high‑yield market (stETH) rather than the idle market, leaving the idle market empty and the protocol’s asset distribution in an unintended state. The attacker can then reverse the cap flow again, moving assets back into the idle market and repeat the cycle, effectively siphoning yield‑generating assets without being blocked by the flow caps. This exploit can be triggered whenever the publicAllocator is permissionless, the idle market has a non‑zero maxOut, and the flow caps are not locked after a reallocation. All depositors and token holders of the affected MetaMorpho vault are at risk because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that assets remain within the configured supply and withdrawal queues – are violated. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as a sudden drop in expected yield, withdrawals returning less than anticipated, or balances showing unexpected zeros in the primary market while the idle market holds unexplained funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, where the logical interaction between the publicAllocator and the flow‑cap mechanism was examined. It is hard to notice because the idle market’s unlimited cap masks the abnormal asset flow, and the reallocation actions are permissionless and do not emit obvious alerts. To remediate the problem the protocol should prevent the publicAllocator from reversing cap flow – i.e., disallow increasing maxIn when withdrawing from a market and disallow increasing maxOut when supplying to a market – or set maxIn and maxOut to zero for markets that should not be reallocated. Additional safeguards such as proportional fees on reallocation or stricter invariant checks on total assets per market can also mitigate the attack surface, though each mitigation carries trade‑offs for flexibility and efficiency.

title: Routers can access components from other routers as well as other tokens
description: Currently routers can access components from other routers. This means if one router contains a bug or a vulnerability it could access all funds of all routers in all nodes. This is especially important if other parties would be allowed to create routers in the future. Note: the code currently assumes components are not shared between routers, as keen be seen in _getTotalAssets() of QuoterV1. Via execute() routers can also access: • Tokens from escrow(), which already belong to controllers. • The asset token from node.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that router contracts are allowed to interact with components that belong to other routers without any ownership verification. The codebase assumes that each component (such as ERC4626 or ERC7540 vaults) is exclusively bound to a single router, an assumption that is reflected in functions like _getTotalAssets() in QuoterV1. However, the execute() function accepts an arbitrary target address and forwards calls and value transfers without checking whether the caller router actually owns the target component. As a result, a router that contains a bug or is deliberately malicious can invoke functions on components that are registered to different routers, read or modify their state, and move tokens that are held in escrow or the node’s asset token. This cross‑router access can be triggered whenever multiple routers are deployed, especially if the protocol later permits third‑party creation of routers. An attacker could deploy a rogue router, call execute() with the address of a victim router’s vault, and trigger withdrawals or state changes that drain the victim’s funds. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or assets that seemingly disappear after a transaction that should have succeeded. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the assumptions around component isolation and identified that the router‑to‑component mapping is missing and that execute() lacks a component‑ownership guard. The problem is subtle because the generic execute() interface is common in upgradeable contracts and the lack of explicit checks does not raise immediate red flags in normal operation. The impact is that any router that can be compromised or maliciously created could potentially access and transfer funds from all other routers in the system, compromising user deposits, escrowed tokens, and the overall financial integrity of the protocol. To remediate the issue, routers should be isolated so that each can only call functions on components that are explicitly assigned to it. This can be achieved by introducing a TypeOfVault enumeration, storing a router‑to‑component relationship in the Node contract, and enforcing ownership checks inside execute() (e.g., verifying that the target component’s TypeOfVault matches the caller’s registered TypeOfVault). Additional consistency checks should be added when adding or removing components, and the QuoterV1 contract should maintain a mapping from component address to its vault type. By restricting execute() to operate only on owned components and by keeping the component registry consistent across the system, the protocol can prevent unauthorized cross‑router fund access and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Inflation attack to steal first deposits
description: The updateTotalAssets() function, callable by the owner or rebalancer, can be exploited to perform an inflation attack against initial depositors. This vulnerability exists because the function updates the contract's total assets and stores it in the cacheTotalAssets variable. A malicious node owner can front-run the first deposit through these steps: • Deposit 1 asset and mint 1 share. • Transfer assets directly to the node. • Call updateTotalAssets() to update the cacheTotalAssets. Consequently, when the first legitimate depositor calls deposit(), they receive 0 shares because the share price has been artificially inflated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation attack that allows the contract owner or a privileged rebalancer to manipulate the reported total assets before the first legitimate deposit, causing the share price to be artificially inflated and resulting in new depositors receiving zero shares. The root cause lies in the updateTotalAssets() function, which can be called by the owner to overwrite the cached total assets (cacheTotalAssets) after assets have been transferred directly to the contract without minting corresponding shares. Because the share price is calculated as total assets divided by total shares, inflating total assets while keeping the share count unchanged makes the price appear higher than it should be. An attacker can front‑run the first deposit by depositing a minimal amount (e.g., 1 asset for 1 share), then transferring a large amount of assets directly to the node contract and invoking updateTotalAssets(). When a genuine user later calls deposit(), the contract believes the share price is extremely high, so the user’s large deposit is converted into zero new shares. The impact is that early users lose their expected ownership tokens, effectively stealing their funds, and the protocol’s accounting logic is broken, undermining trust. This condition only occurs when the owner can call updateTotalAssets() before any substantial amount of shares exist, i.e., during the initial deposit phase, and when the owner can move assets into the contract outside of the deposit flow. The affected parties are the users who attempt to deposit after the manipulation, the protocol’s reputation, and any stakeholders relying on correct share accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a front‑run test case reproducing the attack scenario. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may not revert and the UI may show a successful deposit, yet the user’s balance of shares remains unchanged, appearing as a silent loss. Conceptually, the fix is to prevent arbitrary updates of the total‑asset cache by privileged accounts, enforce a minimum initial deposit that makes price manipulation infeasible, or compute share price directly from the contract’s actual token balance rather than a mutable cache, following the OpenZeppelin ERC4626 pattern that restricts such state changes. By ensuring that total assets cannot be inflated without a proportional increase in shares, the protocol restores correct accounting and prevents funds from disappearing during the first deposit.

title: _getInvestmentSize() doesn't retrieve the asset balance correctly
description: The function _getInvestmentSize() in ERC4626Router doesn't retrieve the asset balance correctly. This means investments can't be done effectively. The balanceOf() value is in shares and needs to be converted to assets, similar to QuoterV1::_getErc4626Assets().
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal helper _getInvestmentSize() of the ERC4626Router contract. The function attempts to determine the amount of underlying assets that are currently held by the router by calling balanceOf() on the ERC4626 component. In the ERC4626 standard, balanceOf() returns the number of vault shares owned by an address, not the quantity of the underlying asset. Because the code treats the returned share count as if it were an asset amount, the router computes an investment size that is either too high or too low depending on the current share‑to‑asset conversion rate. This mis‑calculation originates from a conceptual misunderstanding of the ERC4626 accounting model: the router does not apply the required convertToAssets() conversion that translates shares into the actual asset value, a step that is performed correctly in the QuoterV1::_getErc4626Assets() helper. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this flaw by initiating an investment or withdrawal that relies on the erroneous size. For example, a user may be told that the router holds 1000 tokens, while in reality the share balance only represents 200 tokens; the router will then attempt to allocate or withdraw 1000 tokens, causing the transaction to revert or, if the router proceeds, to over‑draw assets from the vault, potentially draining funds or leaving the user with a zero balance. The impact is that investments become ineffective: users may receive no assets, see their balances unexpectedly drop to zero, or experience failed transactions because the router’s internal accounting does not match the vault’s reality. The issue manifests whenever _getInvestmentSize() is called, which occurs during any investment, redemption, or balance‑query operation that involves an ERC4626 component. All participants that interact with the router – investors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the router’s view of its holdings is inaccurate. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the router’s source code, where the auditor noticed that the function used balanceOf() directly without conversion, a pattern that contradicts the ERC4626 specification and the existing QuoterV1 implementation. The problem can be subtle because the contract may still compile and appear to work on testnets with a 1:1 share‑to‑asset ratio, making the bug easy to miss until the vault’s share price diverges from parity. To remediate the issue, the router should replace the raw balanceOf() call with a conversion to assets using IERC4626(component).convertToAssets(IERC20(component).balanceOf(address(this))) or reuse the proven logic from QuoterV1::_getErc4626Assets(). This change ensures that the router’s internal accounting reflects the true amount of underlying tokens, restoring correct investment sizing, preventing unexpected zero balances, and aligning the contract with ERC4626 accounting rules.

title: Missing slippage control for ERC4626 deposits and withdrawals in the underlying vaults
description: The functions liquidate(), fulfillRedeemRequest() and invest() in ERC4626Router have validation for depositing and withdrawing from the underlying vault, but this validation does not protect against slippage. A sandwich attack could manipulate share values in the vault, causing it to return fewer assets than expected while still passing the current validation. Note: there is also no slippage protection on node functions, but there is no good way to implement this within the ERC4646 standard. Note: there is also no slippage protection on the ERC7540Router but there is no good way to implement this due the asynchronous nature and the ERC7540 standard.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the ERC4626Router functions that interact with underlying vaults, namely liquidate(), invest() and fulfillRedeemRequest(). The code validates that a deposit or withdrawal call succeeds, but it does not compare the amount of assets or shares that were expected before the call with the amount actually received after the call. Because the router relies only on a basic success check, an attacker can execute a sandwich attack: by front‑running a user’s deposit or withdrawal, the attacker temporarily shifts the vault’s share‑price (the ratio of assets per share). When the router subsequently calls the vault, the vault returns fewer assets (or more shares) than the user’s calculation anticipated, yet the router’s validation still passes because the call did not revert. This manipulation leads to users receiving less token value than they expected, effectively stealing the price difference. The issue manifests whenever any of the three functions are invoked without a slippage limit, especially in volatile markets or when the underlying vault has low liquidity. All users of the router, the protocol that depends on accurate accounting, and liquidity providers are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumption that assets equal shares at a known rate is violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that noted the absence of a comparison between expected and actual amounts, a pattern commonly used for slippage protection in DeFi routers. It is hard to notice because the transaction receipts show success and balances are updated, but the net economic value transferred to the user is lower than anticipated; no explicit error is emitted. The recommended mitigation is to add a slippage parameter to each function, compute the minimum acceptable assets (or maximum acceptable shares) based on the price at the start of the transaction, and revert if the actual amount falls outside this bound. This aligns the router with the standard slippage‑control pattern and prevents price‑manipulation attacks. In user‑facing terms, a user may see a transaction marked as successful while the received token amount is unexpectedly small or even zero, causing confusion and a mismatch between expected and actual balances. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑slippage‑control or price‑manipulation‑via‑sandwich‑attack vulnerabilities that break financial guarantees in token‑swap or vault‑interaction contracts.

title: In _getSwingFactor(): reserveImpact >= targetReserveRatio not handled correctly
description: The situation of reserveImpact >= targetReserveRatio is not handled correctly in function _getSwingFactor(). The return of 0 results in a 100% bonus, which is not as intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reserve‑impact calculation used to determine the deposit bonus (often called a swing factor). In the function that computes the swing factor, the code checks whether the signed reserve impact is negative, then whether the unsigned reserve impact is greater than or equal to the target reserve ratio. If that second condition is true, the function returns a literal zero. Downstream logic interprets the returned swing factor as a multiplier that is applied to the user’s deposit amount to calculate how many protocol shares are minted. Because a zero swing factor is treated as “no reduction”, the arithmetic that applies the factor ends up granting the depositor a 100 % bonus – effectively minting double the expected shares. The root cause is an incorrect edge‑case handling: the contract assumes that a zero value means “no bonus”, while the surrounding formula actually treats zero as “full bonus”. This mismatch is triggered whenever the current reserve impact meets or exceeds the target reserve ratio, i.e., when the protocol’s cash reserves are already at or above the desired level. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug simply by depositing when the reserve impact condition holds; the contract will mint an excessive amount of shares, diluting existing holders and potentially draining the protocol’s reserve pool. The impact is a loss of economic value for the protocol and its participants, as the protocol may issue more shares than it can back with assets, breaking the accounting invariant that each share represents a proportional claim on the reserve. The issue was discovered during a manual audit (Spearbit) that examined the mathematical relationship between reserve impact and the swing factor. It is subtle because the function returns a value that is technically valid (zero) and does not revert, so normal testing that only checks for reverts or obvious arithmetic errors may miss it. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal deposit transaction, but the user would receive an unexpectedly large number of shares, or conversely other users would see their share value shrink as the pool becomes over‑issued. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect edge‑case handling in financial formulas” or “bonus calculation overflow due to zero‑factor misinterpretation”. To remediate, the contract should return a neutral factor (e.g., 1 × 10^18 in fixed‑point representation) when reserveImpact >= targetReserveRatio, or adjust the downstream formula to treat a zero swing factor as “no bonus” rather than “full bonus”. In practice the fix involves changing the conditional branch to compute a proper swing factor for the high‑reserve scenario, ensuring that the deposit bonus never exceeds the intended maximum and that the accounting relationship between shares and reserves remains sound.

title: Unfair pricing of metamorpho share when it is used as collateral in morpho market
description: MetaMorpho uses MorphoChainlinkOracleV2.sol for fair pricing of the vault's share. However, in the case of vault which supports lostAssets (i.e no share price decrease feature), if lostAssets > 0 and bad debt is not repaid externally, the oracle would give the inflated price. As per discussion with morpho team in this comment: For a vault with 50% of bad debt, it is highly more likely that it will experience bad debt, sooner or later. When it will happen, users will not be able to get anything out of their shares. Is it sound to price shares at $0.5, not sure. But in this case, lenders lending against these shares already lost, so it's not even very useful to care about the price. It is still important that shares are priced closest to the actual redeemable price since that would allow borrowers to be liquidated and lenders having fair chance to participate in bank-run for remaining 50%. Morpho Labs believes that it's not a good idea to lend against a vault that has significant lost assets, so pricing the vault in such situation should not be cared of. Though this true that lending will pause against such vault when offchain consensus is reached that debt hole is large enough, but the majority of impact is from the capital already at stake and not then newly anticipated incoming assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inaccurate share price calculation for MetaMorpho vaults that allow lost assets. The contract relies on MorphoChainlinkOracleV2 to fetch a price that assumes the vault’s share value equals the total assets divided by total shares. When the vault records lostAssets – for example because a portion of the collateral has become unrecoverable and the vault does not implement a mechanism to decrease the share price – the oracle continues to report the pre‑loss price. If bad debt accumulates and is not repaid off‑chain, the oracle therefore returns an inflated price that can be up to 50 % higher than the actual redeemable value of a share. An attacker (or any borrower) can then supply these over‑priced shares as collateral in the Morpho market, borrow against them, and avoid liquidation while the underlying vault is effectively insolvent. The impact is that lenders who provide capital against the vault receive less than expected, potentially losing their entire stake, and the protocol’s liquidation engine may fail to trigger because the collateral is deemed sufficient by the faulty price. The condition occurs only for vaults that support the lostAssets flag and that have a non‑zero lostAssets balance combined with outstanding bad debt that is not cleared externally. Users experience symptoms such as being unable to redeem their shares for the expected amount, seeing their balance drop to zero after a liquidation attempt, or observing that borrow limits remain unusually high despite the vault’s deteriorating health. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors compared the oracle’s price output with the actual asset balance of a vault that had recorded lost assets, noticing a mismatch that persisted even after the vault’s net asset value had fallen. The bug is subtle because the price function is called only when computing borrow limits and liquidation thresholds, so the discrepancy does not appear in regular view functions, making it easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate, the oracle should incorporate an off‑chain risk assessment for vaults with lost assets, apply a tolerance or step‑down function that reduces the reported price proportionally to the amount of unrecoverable assets, and include circuit‑breaker logic that temporarily disables price updates and borrowing/ liquidation actions until a fair price is re‑established on‑chain. In essence, the flaw belongs to the class of “oracle price inflation when underlying asset accounting does not reflect losses”, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that collateral value equals the redeemable value of the underlying shares.

title: Liquidators can make suppliers inadvertently deposit assets to unhealthy MetaMorpho vaults
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting model of MetaMorpho vaults that integrate Morpho markets. The vault exposes a state variable called lostAssets that is intended to record the amount of assets missing due to realized bad debt or forced market removal. By design the vault’s totalAssets function does not decrease when assets disappear; instead the protocol expects lostAssets to be increased whenever a liquidation results in a position with zero collateral and positive debt, i.e., when bad debt is realized. However, Morpho’s liquidation routine permits a liquidator to leave a tiny amount of collateral – often a single dust unit – while the borrower’s debt is fully repaid. In that situation the position does not trigger a bad‑debt event, so the MetaMorpho vault never updates lostAssets. Consequently totalAssets remains unchanged and lostAssets stays at zero even though the vault has effectively lost the collateral that was taken by the liquidator. This discrepancy creates a false sense of health: users and automated contracts that query lostAssets see a clean vault and may decide to supply assets, while the underlying asset balance has been reduced. A malicious liquidator can exploit this by first acquiring shares of the vault, then performing a liquidation that leaves dust collateral, then bundling legitimate‑looking supply transactions from unsuspecting suppliers (which pass the lostAssets==0 check), and finally redeeming the shares to withdraw the newly supplied assets. The suppliers end up holding shares that cannot be redeemed because the vault’s real asset pool has been drained, effectively losing their deposited funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that after an “almost total” liquidation the vault’s totalAssets did not change and lostAssets remained zero despite the collateral balance being reduced to a single unit. The problem is hard to notice because the public health indicators (totalAssets and lostAssets) both appear normal, and the loss only manifests when a user attempts to withdraw or when the share price diverges from the underlying asset balance. The root cause is the narrow definition of lostAssets that only tracks realized bad debt and the allowance for dust collateral in Morpho liquidations, which together prevent the vault from reflecting any reduction in actual assets. To mitigate the risk the protocol should either expand the accounting of lostAssets to include any reduction of collateral, adjust totalAssets to represent net assets, prevent liquidations that leave dust, or provide clearer documentation and tooling so suppliers can assess the true health of the vault before depositing. In essence, the bug is a mis‑accounting class flaw where the on‑chain health metrics do not capture all loss scenarios, enabling an attacker to drain assets while the vault appears healthy.

title: _enforceLiquidationQueue() checks shares in the wrong location
description: Function _enforceLiquidationQueue() checks the amount shares in the router contract. However the shares are located in the node. This disables the entire liquidationsQueue mechanism.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that enforces the liquidation queue. Instead of reading the amount of shares held by the node contract, the code queries the balance of the candidate token on the router contract itself (address(this)). Because the actual share holdings are stored in the node, the balance returned from the router is typically zero or otherwise incorrect, causing the liquidation logic to believe that there are no shares to liquidate. This logical misreference disables the entire liquidation queue mechanism: under‑collateralised positions are never flagged, liquidation proposals are never executed, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about collateral coverage are violated. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who opens a position that would normally be liquidated; the faulty check prevents the system from detecting the shortfall, allowing the attacker to keep the position open indefinitely and potentially extract value from other participants. The impact is a loss of protocol safety, possible erosion of funds, and a mismatch between user expectations (liquidation should occur) and reality (nothing happens). The bug manifests whenever the liquidation enforcement routine runs, which is typically during periodic maintenance or when a user initiates a liquidation. All participants who rely on the liquidation mechanism – lenders, borrowers, and token holders – are affected because the protocol can become under‑collateralised without any visible warning. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting flow with the actual contract calls and noticed that the balance query targeted the wrong contract address. It is hard to notice because the function does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns a false‑negative result, making the failure silent in logs and UI. The appropriate remediation is to query the share balance from the node contract (using the node’s address) instead of the router, thereby restoring the correct accounting path and re‑enabling the liquidation queue. This class of bug falls under incorrect contract address references, a common source of accounting errors in decentralized finance systems where assets are split across multiple contracts.

title: Component asset could be different than node asset
description: Functions ERC4626Router::_deposit() and ERC7540Router::_requestDeposit() rely on the component to retrieve the asset address. It is never checked this asset is the same as the node asset. There could be a difference due to a mistake or the component could be malicious and return a wrong asset on purpose.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑address mismatch in the router contracts that mediate deposits to vaults. The deposit functions obtain the ERC‑20 token address from a supplied component contract and then forward the user’s funds to the vault based on that address. No verification is performed that the component’s reported asset is identical to the asset that the node (the vault owner) expects. Because the component can be either incorrectly configured or deliberately malicious, it may return a different token address. When this occurs the router will transfer the user’s tokens to a vault that holds a different asset, or it may attempt to transfer the wrong token altogether. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed – no revert is emitted – but the expected token balance does not increase, or the user’s funds are locked in an unexpected contract. The impact is loss or misallocation of user funds, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol and potentially allowing an attacker to siphon assets. The condition arises whenever a deposit is performed through the affected router without an explicit check that component.asset() equals node.asset(). It affects any participant who uses the router to deposit, including regular users and integrators that rely on the router’s correctness. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the code paths of ERC4626Router._deposit and ERC7540Router._requestDeposit and noted the absence of an asset equality assertion. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the UI may simply show a successful deposit, while the underlying token balance remains unchanged. The proper mitigation is to replace the component‑derived asset address with the node’s canonical asset address when constructing the deposit call, and to add an explicit validation step when registering a component that its asset matches the node’s asset. This aligns the router’s behavior with the intended business logic that deposits must be made in the exact token defined by the node, preventing fund misdirection and preserving accounting integrity.

title: MigratorZap's v2InventoryToXNFT() allows for NFT stealing as a result of operational mis- take
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MigratorZap contract function v2InventoryToXNFT, which lets a caller provide an arbitrary vault identifier (vaultIdV2) together with an arbitrary ERC‑20 token address (vTokenV2). The function assumes that the supplied token address corresponds to the vault’s underlying token, but it never validates this relationship. After transferring the caller’s share tokens to the contract, the function invokes v2Inventory.withdraw(vaultIdV2, shares). This call moves the underlying vault tokens into the MigratorZap contract, but the subsequent balance check reads the balance of the user‑supplied vTokenV2 address only. If vTokenV2 does not match the actual token that was withdrawn (i.e., nftxVaultFactory.vault(vaultIdV2) returns a different address), the balance query returns zero while the real tokens remain trapped in the contract’s balance. Because the code does not contain a zero‑balance assertion or any other revert condition, the transaction completes successfully, leaving the withdrawn assets silently held by the contract. An attacker can then submit a second, back‑running call to v2InventoryToXNFT using the correct token address for the same vaultIdV2. In that call the contract sees a positive balance of the correct token and can transfer it out, effectively stealing the assets that were unintentionally left behind. The flaw is a classic mismatch‑between‑input‑validation and state‑change bug, where the contract trusts external input to identify a token without cross‑checking it against the vault registry. It can be exploited whenever a user (or a malicious actor) supplies a wrong token address together with a valid vault identifier, and then quickly follows up with a correctly‑addressed call before the contract’s balance is cleared. The impact is loss of user funds: users who mistakenly specify the wrong token address see their tokens disappear, and an attacker can extract those tokens, resulting in a “funds disappear” symptom where the user’s balance on the UI shows zero or unchanged while the contract holds the assets. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, and it is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error event is emitted, making the loss hard to detect without inspecting internal balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce that vTokenV2 equals the token returned by nftxVaultFactory.vault(vaultIdV2) before proceeding, or it should compute the token balance delta before and after the withdraw call and require the delta to be positive, thereby guaranteeing that the expected token was actually transferred. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that the amount withdrawn from the vault matches the token balance the contract later manipulates, preventing the stealthy theft vector.

title: MarketplaceUniversalRouterZap's swap1155() and _mint1155() allow for mistreating NFT type and freezing the tokens on the contract balance
bug_full: The vulnerability is a token‑type mismatch in the MarketplaceUniversalRouterZap contract where the functions swap1155() and _mint1155() assume that the target vault follows the ERC‑1155 standard. The root cause is the absence of any check on the vault’s actual token type; the code calls the ERC‑1155 interface on a vault that may be an ERC‑721 implementation. When a user supplies multiple NFTs that are compatible with both ERC‑1155 and ERC‑721, the contract transfers the tokens to itself, approves the vault, and then invokes the vault’s swap function. Because the vault interprets each token ID as a single ERC‑721 asset, it only processes one unit per ID, leaving any additional units (or extra IDs) locked in the MarketplaceUniversalRouterZap balance. This can be exploited simply by a user (for example Bob) providing three ERC‑1155‑compatible NFTs to a vault that is actually ERC‑721; the swap will succeed for only one NFT while the other two remain permanently frozen in the contract. The impact is a loss of assets for the user and an operational error for the protocol, as the tokens become unrecoverable without contract modification. The condition occurs whenever swap1155() or _mint1155() is called with a vault that is not ERC‑1155, which can happen with NFTs that support both standards. The affected parties are the end‑users who expect their NFTs to be swapped or minted and the protocol that holds the frozen tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, referencing a similar type‑confusion problem in the core protocol. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful, yet the user’s balance is reduced and the contract holds the missing tokens, leading to silent asset loss. The recommended fix is to add an explicit vault‑type verification (e.g., calling is1155() and reverting with WrongVaultType if the check fails) before performing any ERC‑1155 operations, thereby preventing the mismatch and ensuring that only compatible vaults are used. This class of bug is a token‑standard type confusion that violates the accounting assumption that the amount supplied matches the token’s transfer semantics, resulting in funds disappearing from the user’s perspective while remaining locked in the contract.

title: Potential loss of user funds due to optimistic peer assumption
description:
The _lzSend internal function in OmniXMultisender bridges gas from the source chain to the destination chain by passing in the native airdrop value using the options parameter of LayerZero.
Since the contract is used only for native airdrop, an empty message is passed in, and the receiver is considered the peer contract on the destination chain (or), if not conﬁgured, will use the sender address (assuming the factory is deployed to the same address using CREATE2 assumptions).
This deviates from the usual OApp functionality, where sending a message to a chain where the peer is not conﬁgured is not allowed. Refer here.
Due to this, if a user bridges gas tokens to a chain where an Omni X multi-sender is not present, the funds would be temporarily locked until the team deploys to that new chain. If the team cannot access the same address / deploy to the same address, the users' funds are permanently lost.
The severity of the issue should be MEDIUM as it has a HIGH impact but has a LOW likelihood as most users will interact directly through the front-end application where misconﬁguration is highly unlikely.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an optimistic peer assumption in the OmniXMultisender contract that bridges native gas tokens across chains using LayerZero. The internal _lzSend function builds the destination address by reading a peers mapping; if the mapping entry for the target chain identifier is zero, the code falls back to using the address of the current contract derived from a CREATE2 deployment assumption instead of rejecting the operation. This fallback deviates from the standard OApp behaviour where sending a message to an unconfigured remote endpoint is prohibited. The root cause is the lack of a validation check that the remote peer contract actually exists on the destination chain. When a user initiates a bridge to a chain where the OmniXMultisender has not been deployed at the expected address, the contract still forwards the native token payload to the assumed address. Because no contract resides at that address, the funds become locked on the source chain or are sent to an address that cannot be recovered. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, the front‑end reports a completed bridge, but the expected balance on the destination chain remains unchanged or becomes zero, leading to the perception that the funds have vanished. The impact is a potential permanent loss of user funds, which is high in severity, although the likelihood is low because most users interact through the official UI where the unsupported‑chain path is unlikely to be chosen. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which identified the fallback logic as a logical flaw rather than a coding error. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; only after checking the destination balance does the problem become apparent. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of misconfiguration or trust‑assumption vulnerabilities where a contract implicitly trusts a derived address instead of verifying its existence. To remediate, the contract should revert when the peers mapping does not contain a valid remote address and should enforce that bridges are only allowed to known, whitelisted destination chain identifiers, thereby eliminating the optimistic assumption and preventing funds from being sent to non‑existent contracts.

title: Uniswap V3 pool cardinality should not be hardcoded to 60 in MemeFactory._createUniswapPair()
description:
In MemeFactory._createUniswapPair(), whenever a new Uniswap V3 pool is created, increaseObservationCardinalityNext() is called with a hardcoded value of 60:
```solidity
// Increase observation cardinality
IUniswapV3(pool).increaseObservationCardinalityNext(60);
```
However, this leads to two issues:
1. A cardinality of 60 is too small.
2. Cardinality should not be hardcoded to the same value across different chains.
Calling increaseObservationCardinalityNext() increases the cardinality of the pool, which is the maximum number of observations that can be stored. Considering that an observation is stored at most once per block, the cardinality of the pool must be large enough to cover the desired TWAP window when observe() is called (ie. should be at least twapWindowSeconds / secondsPerBlock).
Regarding (1), Base produces a block every 2 seconds. Assuming an observation is stored every block, setting cardinality = 60 limits the oldest observation to 2 * 60 = 120 seconds ago, which is extremely short and susceptible to manipulation.
Regarding (2), the cardinality should be set depending on the block time of each chain. Since BuyBackBurner uses an observation window of 1800 seconds (BuyBackBurner.sol#L57-L58), the minimum cardinality for Base and Celo should be:
• Base - 1800 / 2 = 900.
• Celo - 1800 / 5 = 360.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the MemeFactory contract when it creates a new Uniswap V3 pool. The factory calls the Uniswap V3 pool’s increaseObservationCardinalityNext function with a hard‑coded value of 60. Observation cardinality defines the maximum number of price observations the pool can retain, and each observation is stored at most once per block. Because the cardinality is fixed at 60, the pool can only keep data for roughly two minutes on a chain that produces a block every two seconds (Base) and even less on slower chains. The protocol’s BuyBackBurner component expects a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) window of 1800 seconds, so the pool must retain at least 1800 seconds / secondsPerBlock observations (900 on Base, 360 on Celo). By limiting the history to 60 observations, the TWAP calculation can be manipulated within a very short window, allowing an attacker to push a price up or down and trigger trades based on a falsified average. This issue is subtle because the pool still functions and returns a price; however, the price may be inaccurate, leading users to receive fewer tokens, experience unexpected slippage, or see their refunds disappear. The problem occurs every time MemeFactory._createUniswapPair is executed on any supported chain, affecting all users who rely on the protocol’s price oracle, token holders, and the overall economic security of the system. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that compared the hard‑coded value with the required observation window. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the only symptom is an unusually volatile or manipulable price feed. The correct mitigation is to replace the constant with a dynamic calculation that derives the needed cardinality from the configured TWAP window and the chain’s block time, for example by introducing a virtual _observationCardinalityNext function overridden in each chain‑specific implementation (MemeBase, MemeCelo) and passing its result to increaseObservationCardinalityNext. This ensures the pool stores enough observations to produce a reliable TWAP and prevents price manipulation attacks.

title: sendDeposits user-favoured rounding in surcharge allows certain Omni X NFT owners to siphon collected fees or oversends
description:
Within sendDeposits, the application of the Omni X surcharge is applied in a fashion that attempts to round in favour of the user in all cases. In general, this is bad practice and can lead to exploits of contracts, and contracts should generally aim to always round in their favour.
The rounding is done incorrectly, in that it is adding a proportional value dependend on the input, rather than just a constant of 1 to the end value.
It is further exacerbated by the fact that Omni X NFT owners with 5 or more NFTs are intended to get a 100% discount of the surcharge. This incorrect calculation and rounding yields their input value as being interprreted 0.01% higher than the actual passed msg.value. Meaning that these Omni X NFT owners can actually dip into an accrued OmniXMultisender balance, either from collected fees or other usere's oversends, for their own sendDeposits usage.
In the case there is $100 in value in the contract, a user could hypothetically do a sendDeposits with $1M to extract this value, however, in practice LayerZero enforces certain maximums for these values, so the attack is limited by this.
bug_full: sendDeposits contains a rounding error in the calculation of the Omni X surcharge. The code adds a proportional value based on the input amount and then adds a constant of 1 to the multiplier, which makes the final nativeAmount slightly larger than the amount that should be charged. For owners of five or more Omni X NFTs the contract is supposed to waive the surcharge completely, but because the rounding is performed in the user’s favour the computed amount is interpreted as about 0.01 % higher than the actual msg.value. As a result the discounted user can withdraw a fraction of the contract’s accumulated fee balance or other users’ oversends when they call sendDeposits. The bug is triggered only when a discounted NFT holder invokes sendDeposits; the exploit can be amplified by sending a very large value, limited only by the maximum amount allowed by the underlying LayerZero bridge. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept the deposit, but the protocol’s internal accounting credits the caller with more value than they supplied, effectively siphoning funds that belong to the protocol or other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, where the rounding logic was examined and identified as user‑favoured rather than contract‑favoured. Such errors are hard to notice because the discrepancy is tiny (one hundredth of a percent) and does not manifest as an outright failure; the UI shows a successful deposit while the contract balance silently shrinks. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “rounding‑bias” or “integer‑division rounding” bugs that break accounting assumptions and allow an attacker to extract value. The recommended fix is to remove the “+ 1” addition to the multiplier and to perform the surcharge calculation so that any remainder is rounded down, ensuring that the contract always receives at least the intended amount. By correcting the rounding direction the protocol will no longer permit discounted users to over‑claim fees, preserving the integrity of the fee pool and preventing fund loss.

title: Refund unused gas fees to user
description:
The functions sendDeposits and sendMessages are both payable and allow the user to overpay more than the required amount to complete the bridging action. Both functions interact with the Layerzero's send() method.
Layerzero send() method refunds any unused gas fees to the users.
But in the OmniXMultisender, the refund address is passed in as address(this) instead of the user address, as it runs in the loop for multiple destinations to avoid calculating the exact fees each time. This will result in suﬃcient gas savings for users. However, at the end of the loop, the ﬁnal user should receive any unused funds instead of locking them in the OmniXMultisender contract.
Per the contract design, only fee tokens must be locked inside the OmniXMultisender, but mixing unused refunds will lead to incorrect on-chain accounting.
The severity of the issue should be MEDIUM as it has a HIGH impact but has a LOW likelihood as most of the time, the off-chain estimates will be accurate, but in some cases, it could change between the on-chain execution and off-chain estimation.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the OmniXMultisender contract forwards the refund address to LayerZero's send() function. Both the sendDeposits and sendMessages functions are payable and allow a caller to provide more native token than strictly required for the bridging operation. LayerZero is designed to return any unused gas fees to the address supplied as the refund destination. In this implementation the contract passes its own address (address(this)) as the refund destination for every iteration of the multi‑destination loop. Consequently, when a user overpays – for example because the off‑chain fee estimator is slightly inaccurate – the surplus is credited to the OmniXMultisender contract instead of being sent back to the original caller. The contract’s design expects only fee tokens to be retained, so the unexpected accumulation of native tokens distorts on‑chain accounting and effectively locks the excess funds. The issue can be triggered whenever the actual gas consumption differs from the estimate, which may happen sporadically due to network conditions or state changes between estimation and execution. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a bridging transaction the wallet balance is reduced by more than the visible fee, and the expected refund of “unused gas” never arrives, leading to a perception of missing funds. The problem is subtle because the contract’s balance simply grows, which may be interpreted as normal fee collection rather than an error, making it hard to detect without detailed accounting checks. The root cause is the misuse of a generic refund address in a looped context, ignoring the need to forward the surplus to the original sender after the final iteration. To remediate, the contract should either track the excess amount per user and transfer it back after the loop completes, or directly supply the caller’s address as the refund destination for the final LayerZero call, ensuring that any unused gas fees are returned to the rightful owner and accounting remains consistent.

title: Increase in calldata cost due to EIP-7623 affects L1 <> L2 transactions
description:
As part of the Pectra upgrade, EIP-7623 increases the cost of calldata for transactions. More specifically, the total gas used per transaction is now the maximum between the execution gas and the following:  
10 * (zero_bytes_in_calldata + nonzero_bytes_in_calldata * 4)  
However, Optimism's L1 and L2 contracts have not been updated to account for this change. Calldata cost is used in two contracts:  
1. In CrossDomainMessenger, baseGas() calculates the amount of gas needed for relayMessage() to complete execution on the destination chain. This ensures messages sent through CrossDomainMessenger can be replayed and will never be stuck:  
```solidity
// Calldata overhead
+ (uint64(_message.length) * MIN_GAS_CALLDATA_OVERHEAD)
```
2. In OptimismPortal2, minimumGasLimit() calculates the minimum gas limit for an L1 -> L2 transaction. This ensures the gas cost of deposit transactions scale with calldata size:  
```solidity
function minimumGasLimit(uint64 _byteCount) public pure returns (uint64) {
    return _byteCount * 16 + 21000;
}
```
(1) does not affect L2 → L1 transactions as:  
• EIP-7623 does not impact the inner workings of the EVM. It only impacts the whole transaction gas cost, and not the inner VM gas cost (named execution_gas_used in the EIP).  
• For L2 → L1 transactions, relayMessage() is a sub-call from OptimismPortal2, so its calldata cost will remain at 4/16 gas per zero/non-zero calldata byte.  
As such, the gas cost calculated with baseGas() will still be correct. However, L1 → L2 transactions are impacted by (1) as relayMessage() is called directly by the node.
