The issue manifests only when the `inflationRecipient` variable is non‑zero, i.e., after the protocol has elected to direct a portion of newly minted tokens to a specific address. Under those conditions, any user calling the affected view functions receives inconsistent numbers. The problem is subtle because view functions do not modify state; they are often used only for UI display or off‑chain analytics, making the mismatch easy to overlook during manual testing. The inconsistency violates the fundamental business assumption that all reward‑related read‑only calls reflect the same pending amount, breaking accounting transparency.

The vulnerability was identified during a Code4rena audit through careful inspection of the reward accounting logic. Fixing the issue requires harmonising the reward calculation across all view functions, specifically by adding the missing `if (inflationRecipient == address(0))` guard to `claimableRewards()` (and any other functions that omit the inflation adjustment). Ensuring that every read‑only query uses the same formula restores user confidence, aligns the UI with on‑chain reality, and eliminates the risk of future misuse stemming from misleading reward displays.

title: StakerVault.unstake
description: StakerVault.unstake(), StakerVault.unstakeFor() would revert with a uint underflow error of StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked, StakerVault._poolTotalStaked.
poc:
Currently it saves totalStaked for strategies and non-strategies separately.

uint underflow error could occur in these cases.

Scenario 1.

  1. Address A(non-strategy) stakes some amount x and it will be added to StakerVault_poolTotalStaked.
  2. This address A is approved as a strategy by StakerVault.inflationManager.
  3. Address A tries to unstake amount x, it will be deducted from StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked because this address is a strategy already.

Even if it would succeed for this strategy but it will revert for other strategies because StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked is less than correct staked amount for strategies.

Scenario 2. There is a transfer between strategy and non-strategy using StakerVault.transfer(), StakerVault.transferFrom() functions. In this case, StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked and StakerVault._poolTotalStaked must be changed accordingly but there is no such logic.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the StakerVault contract’s accounting of staked tokens across two distinct pools: one tracking the total amount staked by strategy contracts (strategiesTotalStaked) and another tracking the total amount staked by non‑strategy addresses (_poolTotalStaked). The root cause is that the contract does not update these counters when an address that previously held a non‑strategy balance is later approved as a strategy, nor does it adjust the counters when tokens are transferred between a strategy and a non‑strategy address. Consequently, the internal totals can become inconsistent, with strategiesTotalStaked being lower than the actual amount that should be attributed to strategies. When a user then attempts to unstake or call unstakeFor, the contract attempts to decrement strategiesTotalStaked by the requested amount. Because the counter is already too low, the subtraction underflows, triggering a Solidity runtime error and causing the transaction to revert. This underflow can also be triggered during transfers that cross the strategy boundary, as the transfer and transferFrom functions lack the necessary logic to rebalance the two totals. The impact is that users’ funds become permanently locked in the vault: the revert prevents any tokens from being returned, so from the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction finishes with no tokens received, often described as a “refund missing” or “balance becomes zero”. The issue manifests under specific conditions – namely when a non‑strategy address is promoted to a strategy without moving its existing balance, or when a transfer occurs between a strategy and a non‑strategy address – and it can be exacerbated by a front‑running attacker who times a malicious addStrategy call to force the counters out of sync. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors traced the underflow path and identified that the contract’s invariant (the sum of strategiesTotalStaked and _poolTotalStaked should equal the total staked supply) is violated. The problem is subtle because the revert only occurs when the counters are mismatched, a state that may be rare in normal operation, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate the issue, the contract must reconcile the two totals whenever a strategy is added (by moving the address’s existing balance from the pool total to the strategy total) and must adjust the counters inside both transfer and transferFrom when tokens move across the strategy boundary. Implementing these changes restores the accounting invariant, eliminates the underflow risk, and prevents funds from becoming irretrievably stuck.

title: FALLBACK_ACTIONID policies can be used directly
bug_full: The vulnerability is a policy‑bypass flaw in the smart‑session validator where the fallback action identifier can be invoked directly by a user. The system defines a special FALLBACK_ACTIONID that is derived from the constant address(1) and the selector 0x00000001; this identifier is meant to be consulted only when the requested target and selector have no explicit policy attached. The checkSingle7579Exec function builds the action identifier from the caller‑supplied target and selector and then looks up the corresponding policy, but it only blocks self‑calls to the execute function. Because there is no explicit prohibition against using address(1) as a target, an attacker can deliberately set target == address(1) and targetSig == 0x00000001, causing the generated actionId to match the FALLBACK_ACTIONID. As a result, the validator applies the fallback policies directly, bypassing the intended fallback logic. This may allow the caller to trigger policies that were not meant to be exposed, such as invoking the ecRecover pre‑compile at address(1) or any other privileged operation encoded in the fallback policy. The flaw occurs whenever a user crafts a user operation with those exact values, which is possible because the function does not validate the target against the fallback flag. Users are affected because they may see unexpected behavior: a transaction that appears to succeed but executes unintended code, leading to missing refunds, zero balances, or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the policy‑lookup flow and noticed that the fallback constants are publicly known and not guarded. It is subtle because address(1) is a syntactically valid address and the selector is a simple constant, so typical testing may not exercise this path. The impact ranges from unauthorized calls to privileged pre‑compiles to potential fund loss if the fallback policy grants excessive permissions. To remediate, the validator should explicitly reject any use of the FALLBACK_ACTIONID outside the internal fallback mechanism, for example by adding a check that reverts when target == address(1) before computing the action identifier, or by redesigning the policy lookup to ensure fallback policies are only consulted when no explicit policy exists. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that fallback policies are a safety net, not a direct entry point for users.

title: Batch executions array can be empty
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an edge‑case where the batch of 7579 executions supplied to the SmartSession validation routine can be empty, allowing the validateUserOp function to return success without any action policy being evaluated. The root cause is that the internal helper checkBatch7579Exec iterates over the decoded executions array but never asserts that the array length is greater than zero; consequently the minPolicies parameter, which normally forces at least one policy check, is never applied when the length is zero. An attacker can craft a UserOperation whose callData decodes to an empty batch and submit it to the account’s execute() entry point. Because the loop body is never entered, no call to checkSingle7579Exec occurs and the accumulated ValidationData remains empty, so the operation passes the policy validation step. The immediate impact is a deviation from the intended security model: the protocol assumes that every user operation is subject to at least one policy check, and downstream logic may rely on that assumption for access control or accounting. While the empty batch itself results only in a no‑op execution that still consumes gas, the bypass could be combined with other logic errors to permit actions that should have been blocked. The condition occurs whenever the calldata supplied to the account can be decoded into an empty executions array, which is technically allowed by the current decoder implementation. All users of the SmartSession, as well as the protocol that trusts its policy enforcement, are affected because they may believe that their transactions have been vetted when in fact no policies were applied. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the validation flow, where the auditor noticed that the fallback policy mechanism does not guarantee a policy check if the batch is empty. It is subtle because the function does not revert and the transaction appears successful, making it easy to miss during testing unless the empty‑batch case is explicitly exercised. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑empty executions array, for example by adding a require statement that executions.length > 0 before entering the loop, or by validating that the intersected ValidationData contains at least one policy result after the loop. This class of bug falls under input‑validation omissions where an empty collection bypasses mandatory checks, leading to unexpected no‑op behavior and potential security policy violations. From a user’s perspective the transaction may succeed, gas is spent, but no state change occurs – the user expects a policy‑checked action but receives nothing, which contradicts the business logic that every operation must be authorized by at least one policy.

title: Uninstalling the fallback submodule of SmartSession will break the whole validation process
description:
The SmartSession can behave as a multi-type module where it is serving as the "validator" for a smart account and also serve as a fallback handler for supportsNestedTypedDataSign() callbacks.
Since ERC7739 usage would require the smart account to have a fallback to expose a "supportsNested-TypedDataSign" view function, the same SmartSession module can be used as a fallback handler for this method by installing it on the smart account.
The problem here is that the way it is implemented right now breaks compatibility with some smart wallet providers like Biconomy.
For Biconomy's nexus smart account, it can be seen in ModuleManager.sol#L346 that whenever any component(validator/fallback handler etc...) is removed from the account, onUninstall is called on the module address.
It is expected to be the job of the module to distinguish what part of the multi-type module is being uninstalled.
But SmartSession lacks logic to specifically uninstall the fallback submodule when the smart account would want to remove it as a fallback handler and continue using it as a validator. When SmartSessionBase::onUninstall() is called, it completely wipes out the session storage.
A smart account trying to uninstall only the fallback handler part of the SmartSession module breaks the entire session and validation operations thereafter.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a module‑uninstall logic flaw in the SmartSession contract that is used simultaneously as a validator and as a fallback handler for ERC7739 nested typed‑data signing. When a smart account that relies on SmartSession removes only the fallback handler part, the ModuleManager calls the onUninstall function of the SmartSession module. The current implementation of onUninstall does not differentiate which sub‑module is being removed; instead it indiscriminately clears the entire session storage that holds the validator state. As a result, the validator data is erased even though the validator functionality is intended to remain active. This can be exploited by any wallet provider or user that supports uninstalling fallback handlers – for example Biconomy’s Nexus smart account – by simply uninstalling the fallback handler while keeping the validator. After the uninstall, subsequent validation calls fail because the required session information no longer exists, causing transaction reverts, “validation failed” errors, or complete inability to execute actions that depend on the validator. The impact is that the smart account appears to be broken: users expect the fallback to be removable without affecting their ability to sign or validate transactions, but instead they see missing balances, zero‑return values from validation functions, or generic errors. The condition under which this occurs is when the account invokes the uninstall routine for the fallback submodule while the SmartSession contract is still registered as the validator. The affected parties are owners of smart accounts that use SmartSession as both validator and fallback, especially those integrating ERC7739 support. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between ModuleManager’s onUninstall hook and SmartSession’s onUninstall implementation, revealing that the storage wipe is unconditional. The bug is subtle because uninstall operations are infrequent and the failure manifests as a generic validation error rather than an obvious storage corruption, making it hard to trace back to the uninstall call. To remediate, the fallback handler should be extracted into an independent optional submodule, or the onUninstall logic should be enhanced to detect which role is being removed and only clear the corresponding storage, preserving validator state. This aligns the contract with the principle of separation of concerns and prevents accidental loss of validation data when only the fallback is intended to be removed.

title: _enablePolicies() does not install ERC7739Content
description:
In the validateUserOp() function, the _enablePolicies() logic allows an account to atomically install policies during validation. Part of the data that's provided to the installation logic is enableData.sessionToEnable.erc7739Policies.allowedERC7739Content, which is an array of type names that are allowed to be used during an ERC-7739 compliant isValidSignature() call.
Despite this data being provided to _enablePolicies(), there is currently no logic to use it. As a result, accounts that install policies through _enablePolicies() will have incorrectly installed permissions, and future calls to isValidSignature() will fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the policy‑installation routine used during user‑operation validation. The function that enables policies receives a data structure that includes an array of type names (allowedERC7739Content) which should be recorded as part of the ERC‑7739 policy configuration. However, the implementation never stores or applies this array, so the resulting account state lacks the intended content permissions. Consequently, when the contract later calls isValidSignature() in an ERC‑7739‑compliant manner, the call checks against a missing or empty whitelist and rejects signatures that would otherwise be valid. This mismatch between the user’s expectation (that the policy was installed with the supplied content types) and the actual contract state leads to denial‑of‑service behaviour: transactions that depend on a successful isValidSignature() revert, users see “signature verification failed” errors, and funds may become temporarily inaccessible. The bug appears only when an account installs policies through the atomic _enablePolicies() path; accounts that rely on pre‑installed policies are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit of the smart‑session core where the auditor noticed that the enableData.sessionToEnable.erc7739Policies.allowedERC7739Content field was never read. The issue is subtle because the function otherwise succeeds and emits no error, making it easy to assume the policy was correctly configured. The proper fix is to extend _enablePolicies() so that it records the allowedERC7739Content array in the account’s policy storage and ensures that isValidSignature() consults this stored whitelist during verification. In generic terms, the bug is a missing‑state‑initialisation or incomplete configuration handling that leads to a policy‑enforcement bypass or failure. Users experience unexpected zero‑return values from signature checks, “refund” or “operation” calls that silently fail, and a discrepancy between the UI that shows the policy as enabled and the blockchain that does not enforce the intended content types.

title: onUninstall() has unbounded gas costs
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded gas consumption in the onUninstall() function of a SmartSession ERC‑7579 module. The function loops over every enabled session stored for the caller and for each session calls removeSession, which itself iterates over all action policies attached to that session and deletes several mappings. Because there is no cap on the number of sessions, actions or policies that an account can register, the total amount of work performed by onUninstall() grows linearly with that data. When the accumulated storage deletions exceed the block gas limit, the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, meaning the uninstall operation cannot be completed. This can be triggered simply by calling uninstall on an account that has accumulated a large number of sessions, which may happen over normal usage or after an attacker deliberately inflates the session count. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the account holder is unable to remove the SmartSession module, and if the uninstall call is wrapped in a try‑catch the partial cleanup may leave stale permissions that cause unexpected behavior when the module is re‑installed. Users observe that their attempt to uninstall results in a failed transaction with an out‑of‑gas error, and the UI may show the module still listed as active even though some state may have been partially cleared. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s lifecycle functions, where the lack of a bound on the loop length was noted. It is hard to notice because the function works correctly for small numbers of sessions and only fails when the data set grows large, a condition that may not be exercised in typical test cases. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration leading to gas exhaustion” and violates the protocol’s expectation that module removal is always possible. A proper fix is to enforce a reasonable upper limit on the number of sessions, actions or policies that can be attached to an account, or to redesign onUninstall to use a pull‑based cleanup or batch processing that guarantees execution within the block gas limit. Alternatively, the contract could reject uninstall attempts that would exceed a predefined gas budget, or require the caller to manually clear sessions in smaller batches.

title: requirePolicyType() missing revert logic
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal helper function that validates a policy contract during installation. The function queries the candidate contract with supportsInterface to check whether it implements the expected interface for the selected policy type (USER_OP, ACTION, or ERC1271). Although the boolean result of this query is stored in a local variable, the code never uses it to enforce a requirement; the only revert path is the default branch for an unknown policy type. Consequently, when supportsInterface returns false – meaning the contract does not implement the required callback – the installation proceeds as if the policy were valid. This logical omission allows any arbitrary address, including a contract that lacks the required functions, to be registered as a policy. An attacker could therefore register a malicious or incomplete policy that bypasses intended checks, leading to situations where user operations are not validated, actions are not filtered, or signature verification is skipped. From a user’s perspective the protocol appears to accept the policy, but later calls to the policy may silently fail or return default values, causing refunds to be missing, transactions to be approved without proper scrutiny, or funds to be transferred without the expected safeguards. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s security guarantees: the accounting assumptions that each policy enforces a specific rule are violated, potentially resulting in unauthorized asset movement or loss. The flaw manifests whenever a policy is installed – a routine operation performed by administrators or automated scripts – and is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and no error event is emitted; the system simply records the policy address and continues execution. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the policy‑installation routine and identified that the supportsInterface flag was never checked. To remediate, the function should explicitly revert when supportsInterface is false, ensuring that only contracts adhering to the declared interface can be installed. This aligns the implementation with the intended contract‑type enforcement and restores the protocol’s defensive posture against malformed or malicious policies.

title: Aggregators in ValidationData break core logic
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the SmartSession library interprets the packed ValidationData structure defined by ERC‑4337. ValidationData contains three fields: an aggregator address, a validAfter timestamp and a validUntil timestamp. The specification reserves address(0) to indicate that the account validated its own signature and address(1) to indicate a failed validation; any other address represents a signature‑aggregator contract. In the SmartSession code the logic that checks the aggregator assumes only the two reserved values. Functions such as isFailed read only the least‑significant bit of the packed value and treat a bit value of 1 as a failure flag. Consequently, if a real aggregator address happens to have its least‑significant bit set to 1, the function incorrectly reports a signature failure. The intersect routine also treats a mismatch of aggregator bits as address(1) and later the setSig function uses an XOR between the stored ValidationData and a boolean sigFailed flag. Because XOR flips the same bit, an error signaled by the aggregator mismatch can be cancelled out by the XOR operation, turning a failing validation into a seemingly successful one. This flaw can be triggered whenever a full aggregator address is passed through the SmartSession flow – for example when a user operation is signed by an external aggregator contract. Under those conditions the protocol may accept a UserOp that should have been rejected, allowing an attacker to execute operations without a valid signature. The impact is that unauthorized transactions may be processed, potentially leading to loss of funds or state corruption for any account that relies on the SmartSession validation path. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SmartSession core logic, where the auditor noticed that bitwise checks only examined a single bit and that the XOR‑based error propagation could neutralise a failure flag. The problem is subtle because the code works correctly for the common cases (address(0) and address(1)) and the incorrect behaviour only appears with specific aggregator addresses, making it hard to reproduce with standard tests. To remediate the issue the code should explicitly validate that the aggregator field is either address(0) or address(1) before any further processing, and the setSig function should be rewritten to use a clear boolean flag instead of XOR, eliminating the possibility of error cancellation. In broader terms this is a classic case of improper handling of packed bit‑fields and ambiguous use of bitwise operators, leading to logical inconsistencies in signature validation and breaking the intended security guarantees of the ERC‑4337 account abstraction model.

title: Default Provider’s endSequenceNumber Can Lead to Permanent DoS and Sequence Collisions with New Providers
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract relies on a single default entropy provider whose hash‑chain is limited by an endSequenceNumber. The contract checks that the provider’s current sequenceNumber is less than endSequenceNumber and reverts with OutOfRandomness when the limit is reached. Because the RiskItV1_1 contract never rotates the provider, the sequenceNumber eventually equals the endSequenceNumber, causing every subsequent request for randomness to revert. This creates a permanent denial‑of‑service for new game spins: users submit a spin, the transaction fails, and no random number is returned. If the system later switches to a different provider without resetting the sequenceNumber to a value higher than any previously used number, the contract will reuse a sequenceNumber that may already exist in the games mapping. Since the games mapping is keyed only by the raw sequenceNumber, a reused number from a new provider collides with an existing entry, causing the contract to revert with GameAlreadyResolved. The impact is that players cannot start new games and may be unable to resolve existing ones, effectively locking funds that depend on a successful spin. The condition occurs when the default provider’s hash chain is exhausted or when a provider change is performed without proper sequence offset. The affected parties are all users of the RiskItV1_1 protocol, the protocol’s operator, and any downstream contracts that rely on the randomness service. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the providerInfo lifecycle and the keying scheme of the games storage. It is subtle because the sequenceNumber appears to be a simple monotonically increasing counter, and the code does not explicitly enforce uniqueness across providers, making the collision scenario easy to overlook. To remediate, the provider should be rotated or its hash chain extended before reaching endSequenceNumber, and the games mapping should use a composite key that includes both the provider address and the sequenceNumber (for example, keccak256(provider, sequenceNumber)). This prevents out‑of‑randomness reverts and eliminates the risk of sequence collisions when providers are swapped.

title: Registration Manipulation in Referral System allows points inflation
description:
The registerPlayer function is vulnerable to exploitation through automated smart contract interactions. There are no restrictions preventing contract-based registrations, which allows attackers to manipulate the referral system and artificially inflate points. The attack leverages the following weaknesses:
1. Automated Multi-Account Registration – The attacker can programmatically generate new addresses, whether EOAs or contract-deployed proxies, to repeatedly register under a referral.
2. Gas-Optimized Exploitation – By using CREATE2, an attacker can deploy self-destructing contracts that perform the registration and then remove traces to minimize costs.
3. Unrestricted Referral Usage – Since there is no limit on how many times a referral can be used, an attacker can continuously earn points by creating new fake accounts.
4. Blacklist Dependency – While the contract implements a blacklist system, it requires active monitoring and manual intervention, which is inefficient and reactive rather than preventive.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted registration mechanism in a referral‑based reward contract that permits automated smart‑contract accounts to create unlimited player profiles and claim referral points. Because the registerPlayer function does not differentiate between externally owned accounts and contract accounts, and because there is no limit on how many times a single referrer can be used, an attacker can programmatically generate new addresses (using CREATE2 or self‑destructing proxy contracts), register each address with the attacker’s address as the referrer, and receive the referral reward for every registration. The root cause is the absence of any anti‑automation or uniqueness checks and the reliance on a manually maintained blacklist that only reacts after abuse has been observed. Exploitation proceeds by deploying a cheap contract that calls registerPlayer, optionally self‑destructing to erase its code, repeating the process many times, and observing the attacker’s point balance increase linearly with each fake referral. The impact is inflation of reward points, which can be exchanged for in‑game items or monetary value, thereby draining the incentive pool and breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol. The condition under which this occurs is any open registration period where the function is callable by any address without proof of human origin. Users may notice that a single account suddenly holds a very high point total while other legitimate players see little or no points, contradicting the expectation that points are earned through genuine referrals. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor wrote a test that repeatedly called registerPlayer from newly created contracts and observed the point total climb to 1000 points. The problem is hard to detect because the contract does not emit explicit events for each referral and the blacklist only flags known malicious addresses after the fact, allowing the attacker to stay under the radar. To remediate, the contract should enforce registration through a backend‑signed authorization or a captcha‑like proof of humanity, limit the number of referrals that a single referrer can earn, restrict calls to EOAs or verified identities, and incorporate rate‑limiting or gas‑price checks to deter mass automated registrations. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of referral‑system abuse where unrestricted account creation enables points inflation, violating the intended accounting model of one‑referral‑one‑reward.

title: Missing User-Provided Random Number Leading to Potential Bias
description:
The contract calls entropy.requestWithCallback, but instead of supplying a user-generated random number as required by the Entropy protocol, it uses a predefined variable named choice. This choice-based approach does not contribute any actual entropy to the final random number and deviates from the intended commit-reveal mechanism. The Entropy protocol follows an optimized commit-reveal scheme where the final randomness is derived from the combination of the provider’s pre-committed random number and a user-provided random input (xU). By failing to provide xU, the contract makes the final randomness entirely dependent on the provider, allowing potential manipulation.
The risk of this approach is that a malicious or compromised provider could selectively withhold their reveals or rotate their commitments to bias the outcome in their favor. Since the final random number is computed as r = hash(xi, xU), excluding xU removes the user's ability to influence the result, weakening the protocol’s fairness guarantees. Additionally, providers who can observe transactions in the mempool may strategically adjust their commitments based on anticipated outcomes, further exacerbating the problem.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing user‑provided random input in a contract that relies on the Entropy protocol for unbiased randomness. The contract invokes entropy.requestWithCallback but supplies a fixed variable called choice instead of the required user‑generated random number (often denoted xU). This design flaw removes the user’s contribution to the commit‑reveal scheme, causing the final random value to be computed solely from the provider’s pre‑committed secret. Because the user input is omitted, the provider can fully control or bias the outcome by selectively revealing or rotating its commitment after observing pending transactions. The issue manifests whenever the contract calls the Entropy service, regardless of the surrounding business logic, and was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s call pattern against the Entropy specification. It is difficult to notice because the contract compiles and executes without errors, and the bias may only become apparent through statistical analysis of outcomes or when a provider consistently wins. The impact is a loss of fairness: users expect a random, unpredictable result (for example, a game payout or allocation) but may receive deterministic or manipulable results, potentially leading to financial loss, reduced trust, and protocol abuse. The affected parties include any user interacting with the contract, the protocol operators who rely on unbiased randomness, and any downstream applications that depend on the random output. To remediate, the contract should generate a truly unpredictable on‑chain value or accept a securely supplied user random number and pass it as the xU argument to entropy.requestWithCallback. Additionally, monitoring and blacklisting of providers that exhibit suspicious reveal patterns can mitigate the risk of manipulation. By restoring the user contribution, the system regains the security guarantee that at least one party (user or provider) remains honest, preserving the intended fairness of the randomness service.

title: Inconsistent Pausing Mechanism Leading to Potential Fund Loss
description:
The entropyCallback function is currently restricted by the whenNotPaused modifier, meaning it cannot execute if the contract is paused between a spin request and the callback. Since the user already pays the entropy fee upfront, a pause occurring before the callback execution will cause the function to revert, effectively resulting in a loss of funds without completing the action.
Although the contract includes a recovery mechanism through the refundGame function, which allows the admin to issue refunds, this solution relies on manual intervention and does not guarantee timely compensation. There is also a consideration that refundGame could be callable by the original game creator, but this functionality would need to be reassessed for security implications before being implemented.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent pausing mechanism that can cause users to lose the entropy fee they pay when interacting with the contract. The root cause is the use of the whenNotPaused modifier on the entropyCallback function, which is executed after a user has already transferred the fee. Because the contract can be paused by an admin at any time, a pause that occurs after the fee payment but before the callback is processed forces the callback to revert. When the callback reverts, the fee remains locked in the contract and the intended game action is not completed, resulting in a denial‑of‑service style loss of funds. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who gains control of the pause mechanism or by a malicious admin who deliberately pauses the contract after a user’s request, causing the callback to fail and the user’s fee to be unrecoverable without manual intervention. The impact is that users receive no game result, see no change in their balance, and may see the fee disappear from their wallet, violating the expectation that paying the fee guarantees a game round. The condition under which this occurs is any time the contract is paused between the spin request and the execution of entropyCallback. All users who pay the fee are affected, as well as the protocol’s reputation because funds can be lost without an automated refund path. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the pause control and post‑payment callbacks. It is hard to notice because pause mechanisms are typically assumed to protect the contract, not to interfere with functions that have already received payment, and the manual refundGame function masks the problem by providing a fallback that is not automatically triggered. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent execution blocking” where a contract’s emergency stop can be invoked after a financial commitment, breaking the accounting invariant that every fee paid must be either consumed by the intended action or returned. From the user’s point of view the UI shows a successful transaction receipt for the fee, but the game never resolves and the displayed balance may appear unchanged or the fee may be missing, leading to confusion and loss of trust. To fix the issue the whenNotPaused guard should be removed from entropyCallback or replaced with logic that allows the callback to be queued and executed once the contract is unpaused. Additionally, an automatic refund mechanism should be integrated so that if the callback cannot be performed within a reasonable time frame the contract returns the fee without requiring manual admin action, thereby restoring the expected economic flow and preserving protocol integrity.

title: Re-Entrancy Vulnerability potentially Leading to Contract Deadlock and Permanent Insolvency
description:
The refundGame function is vulnerable to a re-entrancy attack, which can be exploited to manipulate totalOnLine and cause an underflow. This happens because payable(game.player).call{value: refundAmount} is executed before updating critical state variables, allowing an attacker to re-enter the contract and invoke functions that modify totalOnLine in an unintended way.
Since refundGame also uses unchecked arithmetic on totalOnLine, an attacker can reduce this value below expected limits, leading to contract insolvency and a permanent deadlock. When totalOnLine becomes an enormous value due to underflow, it triggers integrity checks that will always fail, preventing any further gameplay or withdrawals. This creates a situation where no admin action, including removeLiquidity, can resolve the issue, effectively bricking the contract forever.
The proof-of-concept (PoC) showcases the worst-case scenario by modifying ethReferralAmount directly, demonstrating how the issue can be artificially induced to illustrate the contract's failure state.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the function that processes player refunds. The function sends ether to the player using a low‑level call before it updates the contract’s accounting variable that tracks the total amount currently on‑line. Because the external call can invoke the contract’s fallback function, an attacker can re‑enter the contract and trigger another refund before the original state change occurs. This re‑entrancy allows the attacker to manipulate the totalOnLine variable while the contract is still using unchecked arithmetic, causing an underflow that wraps the value to a very large number. When totalOnLine wraps, subsequent integrity checks that compare the on‑line amount with available liquidity always fail, so any new game request or withdrawal reverts. As a result the contract becomes effectively deadlocked: no player can receive a refund, no admin can withdraw liquidity or call removeLiquidity, and the protocol is permanently insolvent. The issue appears only after a refund is processed; normal gameplay works until the underflow occurs, making it hard to notice during routine testing because the contract still functions until the specific re‑entrancy path is exercised. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept where the attacker’s fallback called redeemReferral, causing the re‑entrancy and underflow. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing refund, a balance that suddenly shows zero or an unexpectedly huge on‑line total, and transactions that always revert despite sufficient ether being deposited. The bug belongs to the class of re‑entrancy combined with unchecked arithmetic leading to underflow and permanent lock‑out. To fix the issue the refund function must be protected with a re‑entrancy guard and the arithmetic on totalOnLine must be performed with safe checks or using Solidity’s built‑in overflow/underflow protection. Additionally, a fallback upgrade mechanism should be considered so that an admin can migrate the contract if an integrity failure occurs.

title: Unrestricted Gameplay and Deposits Without Registration
description:
The contract allows players to request spins and deposit funds without first registering. This creates a fundamental inconsistency, as the system assumes that only registered players who meet the age requirement should be able to participate. Without enforcing a registration check:
• Players can bypass the registration process and interact with the game directly, ignoring potential restrictions such as the age requirement.
• Since only registered players are expected to meet the isOldEnough condition, allowing unregistered users to play means that age restrictions are effectively unenforced.
• The system may rely on player data stored during registration for tracking purposes. If unregistered users are allowed to play, this could result in incorrect tracking of rewards, losses, or other metrics.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control flaw that permits any address to deposit funds and request game spins without first completing the contract’s registration routine. The contract’s business logic assumes that only registered players, who have passed an age verification check, are allowed to interact with the gameplay functions. Because the code does not perform a mapping lookup to confirm that msg.sender is registered, the isOldEnough condition is never evaluated for unregistered callers. An attacker can simply call the deposit or spin functions directly, bypassing the registration step and therefore the age restriction. This can be exploited by sending a transaction that calls the gameplay entry point with no prior registration, allowing under‑age or otherwise unauthorized participants to play and potentially win rewards. The impact includes violation of regulatory or policy requirements, loss of confidence in the platform’s compliance, and incorrect accounting because the system tracks rewards, losses and player statistics based on data stored at registration. When unregistered users play, their activity is not linked to a proper player record, leading to misattributed balances, missing reward entries, and potentially inaccurate aggregate metrics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended flow (register → verify age → play) with the actual contract code, revealing the missing require statement. It may be hard to notice in a live UI because the front‑end can still present a registration form, yet the back‑end does not enforce it, allowing users to bypass it via direct contract calls. To remediate, the contract should enforce a registration check (for example, require(registered[msg.sender]) ) before any deposit or spin logic, thereby re‑instating the age verification and ensuring that all gameplay actions are tied to a verified player record. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an authentication or authorization bypass, where critical business rules are not enforced at the contract level, leading to unexpected behavior such as users receiving gameplay services without meeting eligibility criteria and the platform’s accounting assumptions being broken.

title: Incorrect Liquidity Check in requestToken Could Lead to Insolvency
description: The contract's requestToken function currently checks liquidity using the condition totalOnLine + betAmount * _multiplier, but it does not properly account for the entropyFee, which is used as the value for the callback. This creates a misleading assessment of available liquidity since entropyFee will be spent in the next transaction and should not be considered part of the contract’s solvency. As a result, the protocol might allow bets that exceed the actual available balance, leading to situations where user payouts cannot be fulfilled. If this happens, the contract may become insolvent, breaking the invariant that the contract balance should always be equal to or greater than totalOnLine. In edge cases, this could result in unintended reverts or discrepancies in fund distribution, disrupting the protocol’s integrity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect liquidity verification in the requestToken function that leads to a systematic over‑estimation of the contract’s available funds. The root cause is that the check adds the pending bet amount multiplied by the multiplier to the total amount currently on‑line, but it ignores the entropyFee that will be deducted in the subsequent callback transaction. Because entropyFee is treated as if it were still part of the contract’s balance, the condition may evaluate to true even when the real balance after paying the fee would be insufficient to cover all outstanding liabilities. An attacker or any user can exploit this by placing a bet that appears to be within the allowed limits; the contract will accept the bet, record the liability, and later attempt to pay out a winning claim with a balance that is actually lower than required. When the payout is executed, the contract either reverts or silently fails to transfer the full amount, resulting in missing or zero payouts, unexpected transaction failures, and balances that appear unchanged despite a win. The impact is a breach of the fundamental invariant that the contract’s ether balance must always be greater than or equal to the sum of all on‑line obligations, potentially rendering the protocol insolvent and causing user funds to become unrecoverable. This condition occurs whenever requestToken is called with a bet that, after accounting for entropyFee, would exceed the true liquid assets of the contract. All participants who place bets – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol may be unable to honor its promised rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the accounting logic of the requestToken function and identified that the entropyFee was omitted from the solvency equation. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balance variable still shows a positive value, and the fee is only deducted later, making the over‑allocation hard to notice without tracing the full execution flow. The appropriate remediation is to adjust the liquidity check so that the comparison is made against the contract’s balance minus the pending entropyFee, ensuring that only truly available funds are considered when approving new bets. In generic terms, this is an accounting or liquidity‑miscalculation bug where a reserved fee is mistakenly counted as free capital, violating the business logic that guarantees sufficient reserves for all user payouts.

title: Incorrect Accounting in forceWithdraw Leading to Liquidity Miscalculation
description:
The forceWithdraw function does not correctly update tokenTotalOnLine or totalOnLine after executing a forced withdrawal. This leads to inaccurate tracking of funds, as the withdrawn amount remains counted as part of the available liquidity even though it has already been transferred out of the contract.
By failing to decrement tokenTotalOnLine and totalOnLine, the protocol incorrectly assumes that more funds are available than actually exist. This can lead to protocol insolvency, where winnings or withdrawals that should be covered by on-chain liquidity may be approved when the contract does not actually hold sufficient funds. Since the system still considers withdrawn amounts as “active” liquidity, future payout calculations will rely on incorrect values, potentially resulting in failed transactions or unintended insolvency.
bug_full: An accounting inconsistency in the contract's forced withdrawal routine causes the internal liquidity counters to remain unchanged after a user's funds are transferred out. The vulnerability originates from the forceWithdraw function not decrementing the variables that track total token liquidity (tokenTotalOnLine) and overall on-chain liquidity (totalOnLine). Because these counters still include the amount that has already been sent to the caller, the protocol believes it has more available funds than it actually does. An attacker or any user can trigger a forced withdrawal, receive the tokens, and the contract's bookkeeping will still report the withdrawn amount as part of the active pool. Subsequent operations that rely on these counters—such as payout calculations, reward distribution, or eligibility checks—will use inflated numbers, potentially approving payouts that the contract cannot cover. In practice this may manifest as users receiving a "withdrawal successful" message while later attempts to claim winnings fail, or the contract reverting due to insufficient balance despite appearing solvent in its UI. The issue appears only after a forced withdrawal has been executed; normal deposits and regular withdrawals correctly update the counters, so the bug can be missed during routine testing that does not exercise the forceWithdraw path. It was discovered during a systematic audit that compared on-chain balances with the contract's internal accounting variables. The problem is subtle because the external state (the token balance) does decrease correctly, so visual inspection of token transfers shows no anomaly, while the internal accounting remains out of sync. The proper remediation is to modify the forceWithdraw implementation so that it explicitly subtracts the withdrawn amount from both tokenTotalOnLine and totalOnLine, ensuring that the contract's view of available liquidity matches the actual token holdings. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of "state-variable mis-update" or "accounting mismatch" where a function fails to keep invariant bookkeeping variables consistent after a state-changing operation. By fixing the decrement, the protocol restores the invariant that totalOnLine always equals the sum of tokens currently held, preventing over-allocation of funds and protecting users from unexpected loss of payouts.

title: IPOrders with upfront points program rewards cannot be ﬁlled
description: When ﬁlling IP orders with an upfront reward style (RecipeOrderbook.sol#L476), the reward token is assumed to be an ERC20 token; everywhere else in the codebase, a check is done to see if token is actually a points program. Skipping this check means orders that attempt to award points upfront will fail to be ﬁlled (since Points contracts do not implement ERC20 logic and have a reverting fallback function).
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the order‑filling routine for IP orders that use an upfront reward style. The routine assumes that the reward token implements the ERC20 interface and directly invokes ERC20‑specific logic (such as transferFrom) without first verifying whether the token is actually a points‑program contract. Throughout the rest of the codebase a check is performed to detect points‑program tokens, but this particular path (RecipeOrderbook.sol line 476) skips that validation. Points‑program contracts do not expose ERC20 functions and typically contain a fallback function that reverts any unexpected call. Consequently, when an order that promises points as an upfront reward is processed, the contract attempts an ERC20 call on a non‑ERC20 token, triggering a revert. The root cause is a missing type‑validation step, leading to an interface‑assumption bug where the contract treats heterogeneous token standards as homogeneous. Exploitation is straightforward: any user who creates or fills an order with a points‑program reward will experience a transaction revert, meaning the order cannot be filled and the expected points are never credited. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with a generic “execution reverted” error, no points appear in their balance, and the order remains unfilled, contrary to the expectation that the reward would be received instantly. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition for legitimate use of points rewards, loss of gas fees for the caller, and a breach of the protocol’s business logic that assumes rewards are always delivered. This issue manifests only when the reward token is a points program and the fill function is invoked; standard ERC20 rewards work correctly because the required interface is present. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared token handling across the codebase and identified the missing check as a logical flaw. The bug can be hard to notice because most code paths correctly handle token type detection, and tests may only cover ERC20 scenarios, leaving the points‑program path untested. To remediate, the fill routine should incorporate the same token‑type detection used elsewhere, branching to a points‑program‑specific handling routine or explicitly rejecting upfront points rewards with a clear error message. In broader terms, the flaw belongs to the class of interface‑assumption vulnerabilities where a contract assumes a particular token standard without verifying it, leading to unexpected reverts when interacting with contracts that follow a different interface.

title: The previewed deposit rate is inaccurate and inconvenient
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the previewRateAfterDeposit function of the ERC4626i contract, which is intended to give liquidity providers (LPs) an estimate of the reward rate they will receive after depositing a certain amount of tokens into a campaign. The function currently calculates the preview rate by multiplying the campaign's stored rate by the deposit amount and dividing by a fixed-point constant (WAD). This simplistic formula ignores the dilution effect caused by the issuance of new shares and the existing total supply of shares, meaning the returned value cannot be interpreted as the true post‑deposit reward rate for the whole deposit. As a result, an LP who relies on this preview to guarantee a specific return‑on‑capital may be misled: the UI may display a favorable rate, but after the deposit the actual rate is lower because the calculation did not account for the increased share pool. The issue occurs whenever the previewRateAfterDeposit function is called, typically during order‑book interactions where an LP specifies a desired reward rate per token or per share. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s implementation with its usage in the VaultOrderbook contract and identified a mismatch between the expected economic semantics and the actual arithmetic. The problem is subtle because the function returns a numeric value that looks plausible and the contract does not emit any warning, making it easy for users to assume the preview is accurate. The impact is primarily financial: LPs may allocate capital based on an inaccurate expectation, leading to lower yields, potential loss of confidence in the protocol, and mis‑aligned incentives. To remediate the issue, the preview calculation should be rewritten to first determine the number of shares that would be minted for the given deposit (using the existing previewDeposit logic), then compute the new overall share supply (totalSupply plus the new shares), and finally derive the effective reward rate by proportionally scaling the campaign’s rate according to the new share distribution. The corrected formula must also incorporate the correct token precision constant to avoid rounding errors. By aligning the preview with the actual post‑deposit accounting, LPs can reliably assess expected returns, preserving the protocol’s economic integrity.

title: Non-forfeitable wallets can be Forfeited
description: The WeirollWallet contract includes an immutable ﬁeld (WeirollWallet.sol#L86) meant to determine whether the forfeit() function can be called or not. However, this ﬁeld is not checked in the forfeit() function and an associated event, WalletNotForfeitable, is never emitted. As a consequence, non-forfeitable wallets can be forfeited.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing enforcement of an immutable flag that designates a wallet as non‑forfeitable. The WeirollWallet contract stores a boolean value at deployment that is intended to indicate whether the public forfeit() function may be invoked. However, the forfeit() implementation never reads this flag, nor does it emit the WalletNotForfeitable event that would signal an illegal call. As a result, any actor with permission to call forfeit() – typically the orderbook contract – can trigger forfeiture on wallets that were explicitly created to be immune to such action. Exploitation consists of calling forfeit() on a protected wallet, causing the contract to set its internal forfeited state to true and potentially lock or destroy the assets held therein. The impact is that users who rely on the non‑forfeitable guarantee may lose access to their funds, see their balances become zero, or be unable to withdraw, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that certain wallets are safe from forced liquidation. This condition occurs whenever the forfeit() function is reachable, which is usually during normal orderbook operations, but the missing check makes the protection ineffective for all wallet instances regardless of the immutable flag value. All users of wallets that were deployed with the non‑forfeitable setting are affected, as are the protocol operators who may be held liable for unexpected fund loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s state variables with its functional logic and noted that the immutable flag was never consulted. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors, the flag is immutable and appears to be set correctly, and the forfeit() function otherwise behaves as expected for forfeitable wallets, masking the logical omission. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control or state‑validation errors where a required condition is omitted, leading to unintended state transitions. To remediate, the forfeit() function should explicitly check the immutable flag via an isForfeitable() view, revert with the WalletNotForfeitable error when the flag is false, and emit the appropriate event, thereby restoring the intended protection and preventing accidental or malicious forfeiture of protected wallets.

title: Rate check can be subverted in VaultOrderbook.allocateOrder() due to unbounded cam- paign id list length
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the rate‑verification logic of VaultOrderbook.allocateOrder(). The function iterates over a list of campaign identifiers supplied by the caller and, for each identifier, queries ERC4626i.previewRateAfterDeposit to obtain a provisional reward rate, which is then summed into a token‑to‑rate mapping. The protocol’s ERC4626i contract limits each liquidity provider to a maximum of five active campaigns per token, but allocateOrder() does not enforce this same bound on the length of the campaignIds array. Consequently, an attacker can submit an arbitrarily long array containing many campaign IDs – possibly repeating the same campaign or using several campaigns per token – and artificially inflate the summed rate so that the “desired reward rate” check appears satisfied. This subversion can occur whenever a user creates an order that relies on the rate check, i.e., during normal order allocation. The impact is that the vault may allocate more reward tokens than it can actually deliver, breaking the accounting assumption that the summed preview rates represent achievable rewards. From a user’s perspective the LP expects to receive a certain amount of reward tokens after depositing base tokens, but the protocol may later dispense less or run out of rewards, leading to missing balances or zero‑reward outcomes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s documented campaign limit with the implementation of allocateOrder(). It is subtle because the loop looks innocuous and the additive assignment bug that also exists in the function can mask the problem, making the flaw easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce the same maximum‑of‑five‑campaigns rule on the campaignIds array – either by rejecting arrays longer than five entries or by cross‑checking each token’s campaign count against the ERC4626i limit – and ensure that the rate calculation reflects only permissible campaigns. This correction restores the integrity of the reward‑rate verification and prevents the possibility of reward‑rate inflation that could lead to fund loss or unfair advantage.

title: Fees can be sent to the zero address
description: If the protocolFee is set to a non-zero amount and an IP order is created without setting protocolFeeRecipient, the fees will be sent to the zero address.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑distribution flaw where protocol fees are unintentionally transferred to the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000). This occurs because the contract stores a protocolFeeRecipient address that is never validated or initialized when a non‑zero protocolFee is configured. When an order is created without explicitly providing a protocolFeeRecipient, the stored recipient defaults to the zero address, and the fee transfer logic sends the specified amount to that address. As a result, the fee amount is effectively burned and cannot be recovered, leading to a loss of expected revenue for the protocol and a mismatch between user expectations and actual outcomes. The issue manifests only when two conditions are met simultaneously: (1) the protocolFee variable holds a value greater than zero, and (2) the order‑creation function is called without setting a non‑zero protocolFeeRecipient. Users who pay a fee expect the amount to be credited to the protocol’s treasury or designated fee collector, but instead they observe no increase in the treasury balance, sometimes seeing their own balance unchanged after the transaction. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing assignment and lack of a non‑zero check for the recipient address. It can be hard to notice because a transfer to the zero address does not revert; the transaction succeeds, giving a false impression that the fee was processed correctly. To remediate, the contract should enforce that protocolFeeRecipient is set to a valid, non‑zero address whenever protocolFee is non‑zero, preferably by initializing the recipient in the constructor and adding a require statement that rejects zero‑address recipients during fee configuration or order creation. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that protocol fees are collected and accounted for, preventing silent fund loss and preserving the economic assumptions of the protocol.

title: Reentrancy issues in forfeit and claim could lead to drain funds
description: The forfeit and claim functions in the contract are vulnerable to reentrancy attacks if a reward token has hooks (such as those that implement the ERC777 standard). The reentrancy occurs because the functions perform external calls via safeTransfer before clearing the state by deleting the weirollWalletToLockedRewardParams mapping. This allows an attacker to reenter the function and drain funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw affecting the forfeit and claim functions of the contract. When a reward token implements callback hooks such as those defined by the ERC777 standard, the contract performs an external token transfer using safeTransfer before it clears the internal bookkeeping that records the locked reward amounts. Because the state update – deleting the mapping that ties a wallet to its locked reward parameters – occurs after the external call, a malicious token can invoke a fallback function during the transfer and call back into the same forfeit or claim function. This re‑entry happens while the contract still believes the rewards are unclaimed, allowing the attacker to repeat the transfer logic and drain the tokens that were supposed to be released to legitimate users. The impact is that an attacker can repeatedly claim or forfeit rewards, causing the contract’s balance of the affected token to be reduced to zero while honest users receive no tokens or see their balances unexpectedly drop to zero. The issue manifests only when the reward token is capable of executing code on receipt, which is why standard ERC20 tokens are not affected but ERC777‑compatible tokens are. It was discovered during a targeted audit that included a mock re‑entrant ERC20 token designed to trigger a fallback on transfer, demonstrating that the contract’s logic does not follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The problem is subtle because the external call appears to be a harmless safeTransfer, and the state mutation is later, making the re‑entrancy vector easy to overlook in code reviews. To remediate, the contract should update all internal accounting – for example, zeroing out the amounts array or deleting the mapping – before any external token transfer, and it should also employ a reentrancy guard to block recursive calls. This aligns the implementation with established best practices for preventing reentrancy and restores the expected behavior that users receive their full reward and that the contract’s accounting remains consistent after each claim or forfeit.

title: Use of Foundry's ffi cheatcode should be avoided if possible
description: constructCreate2Salt() uses foundry's ffi cheatcode to create a salt for deterministic deployment of the contracts based on the version of the contracts. Use of ffi is considered dangerous as documented here It is generally advised to use this cheat code as a last resort, and to not enable it by default, as anyone who can change the tests of a project will be able to execute arbitrary commands on devices that run the tests.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the use of Foundry's ffi cheatcode inside the helper function constructCreate2Salt() to generate a deterministic CREATE2 salt based on the contract version. The ffi cheatcode allows the test environment to execute arbitrary shell commands on the host machine. Because the cheatcode is enabled by default in the test suite, any actor who can modify the test files – for example a malicious contributor, a compromised CI runner, or an attacker who gains write access to the repository – can inject a command that will be executed when the tests are run. This creates an attack surface that is unrelated to the on‑chain logic of the contracts but can compromise the development or continuous‑integration infrastructure. An exploit would involve adding a malicious command (e.g., curl … | sh, or rm -rf …) to the constructCreate2Salt() implementation or to any test that calls it. When the test suite is executed with ffi enabled, the command runs with the privileges of the test runner, potentially stealing private keys, exfiltrating source code, or corrupting the build environment. The impact is therefore a breach of the developer’s environment, loss of confidential data, and possible insertion of back‑doors into the compiled contracts, which can later affect users of the protocol. The condition for the bug to manifest is the presence of ffi enabled in the Foundry configuration and the ability to edit the test source; it does not affect the contracts when deployed on‑chain, but it undermines the trustworthiness of the development pipeline. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the test suite, where the use of vm.ffi was flagged as a high‑risk cheatcode. It is hard to notice because the command execution happens silently during test runs and does not affect contract behavior, so developers may not see any abnormal output. The recommended remediation is to remove the ffi call and instead read the version information from a file using vm.readFile() and parse it with vm.parseJson(), which keeps all operations inside the sandboxed VM and eliminates the possibility of arbitrary host‑side command execution. In generic terms, this is an unsafe external command execution vulnerability in the test harness, a class of bug where test code can run uncontrolled system commands, violating the principle that test environments should be deterministic and isolated. From a user perspective, the symptom might be unexpected changes to the developer’s machine after running tests, such as new files, altered environment variables, or network traffic, while the contract UI still shows normal behavior. Users expect the test suite to be safe and deterministic, but the reality is that a malicious test could cause their local or CI environment to be compromised.

title: UX on stream cancel might hinder or deter sender from canceling or recipient from with- drawing
description: When the sender cancels a stream the SablierV2Lockup does a callback to the sender's onLockupStreamCancled() if it is a contract. A try/catch makes sure any revert would not block the cancel but a deliberate gas bomb by the recipient could cause the user to be prompted with a high gas cost: if (recipient.code.length > 0) { try ISablierV2Recipient(recipient).onLockupStreamCanceled({ streamId: streamId, sender: sender, senderAmount: senderAmount, recipientAmount: recipientAmount }) { } catch { } } The sender can just lower the transaction's gas limit. The callback will then run out of gas, the transaction will continue and the stream will be canceled. However when a less sophisticated user is prompted with the high gas cost they may not realize it and will be unable to predict if the cancel will even still work with the lower gas limit. If the user actually sends the transaction they might end up paying a high amount of ETH (or equivalent on other chains) on gas fees to get the stream canceled while a lot less would have suﬃced. Theoretically the predicted gas cost might even be so high the transaction never gets included in a block due to the high gas limit. The same issue is present on the withdraw() where the sender might try to hinder a recipient from with- drawing an un-cancelable stream.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded gas consumption issue that appears when a SablierV2Lockup stream is cancelled or when a recipient withdraws from an uncancelable stream. The contract performs an external callback to the recipient (or to the sender if the sender is a contract) via the onLockupStreamCanceled or onLockupStreamWithdrawn functions. Because the callback is invoked with the full remaining gas and no explicit gas stipend, a malicious recipient can deliberately write a callback that consumes a large amount of gas – effectively a gas bomb. The try/catch wrapper prevents the callback’s revert from aborting the cancel or withdraw, but it does not limit the gas that must be supplied for the transaction to succeed. Consequently, a user who initiates a cancel or a withdraw is presented with a very high gas estimate. A less‑experienced user may not understand why the estimate is so large, may attempt to send the transaction with the default gas limit and end up paying an excessive fee, or may set a lower gas limit that causes the callback to run out of gas – the transaction still succeeds because the error is caught, but the user still pays for the wasted gas. In extreme cases the required gas limit may exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to never be included, which effectively locks the stream indefinitely. The impact is primarily on the sender who wishes to cancel a stream and on the recipient who wishes to withdraw: both can be forced to overpay or be prevented from completing the intended action, breaking the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of cancel and withdraw functions and noticed the lack of a gas cap on the external callbacks. It is hard to notice because the try/catch hides the failure of the callback, making the contract appear to work correctly while silently inflating gas costs. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded external call” or “gas‑limit denial‑of‑service” vulnerabilities, where a contract’s logic relies on an external contract that can arbitrarily increase gas consumption. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal cancel button but then display a gas fee that is orders of magnitude higher than expected, leading to confusion (“I expected a cheap cancel but I’m being charged a lot”). The expected behavior – a cheap cancellation or withdrawal – is violated, and the accounting assumption that a stream can always be closed or withdrawn with reasonable gas costs no longer holds. The recommended mitigation is to impose a configurable gas stipend or a percentage‑of‑remaining‑gas limit on the callbacks, or to redesign the protocol to avoid mandatory external calls during cancel or withdraw, thereby preventing a malicious recipient from inflating gas usage and improving the overall user experience.

title: Potential use of malicious Lockup contract when creating an airstream from the factory
description: createMerkleLL() and createMerkleLT() take an address for the LockupLinear and LockupTranched contracts to be used when the streams are claimed. In the constructor of both SablierV2MerkleLL and SablierV2MerkleLT it also max approves these contracts in order to allow it to use the funds held by the them during the claim process. The provided address can be any contract as long as it supports the required functions not to attract any suspicion in the front-end. This can be abused by a team member of the project designated to creating the SablierMerkleLL or SablierMerkleLT even if the team applies separation of duty between them and the person sending the funds to the newly created contract. The provided contract can be a custom one deployed by the malicious team member and allow them to withdraw the funds from the Merkle lockup contract to their own address. This could also be an issue when users provide the wrong contract address accidentally. For instance providing the address for the LockupLinear when creating a MerkleLockupLT or possibly even an older contract that doesn't take the same parameter types when creating a stream.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Merkle lockup factory functions createMerkleLL() and createMerkleLT() accept an arbitrary address for the underlying lockup contract (LockupLinear or LockupTranched) and automatically grant it an unlimited token allowance. Because the factory does not verify that the supplied address belongs to a trusted implementation, a malicious actor who can supply the address – for example a team member responsible for deploying the Merkle contracts or a user who mistakenly provides a wrong address – can cause the factory to approve a contract that contains malicious logic. The malicious lockup contract can then intercept the claim process and transfer the streamed tokens to an attacker‑controlled address. The bug can be exploited during the creation of a Merkle stream: the attacker deploys a contract that implements the required functions but also includes a back‑door that calls transfer on the token held by the Merkle contract. When the factory creates the stream it calls maxApprove on the supplied address, giving the back‑door contract permission to move any amount of tokens. Later, when a legitimate user tries to claim their stream, the malicious contract executes its back‑door and drains the funds, leaving the user with a zero balance or a missing refund. The impact is loss of user funds, broken accounting, and loss of trust in the protocol. The issue occurs whenever the factory is used to create a MerkleLockupLL or MerkleLockupLT stream and the caller supplies a non‑whitelisted lockup address, either intentionally or by mistake. All participants – token holders, the protocol, and the project team – are affected because the funds that should be locked for a vesting schedule can disappear. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s constructor and the approval logic, noting that the address parameter is not constrained to a known safe implementation. The flaw is subtle because the front‑end shows no warning; the contract simply calls external functions, so the malicious behavior is hidden from users who only see that their claim transaction succeeds but receives no tokens. To remediate, the factory should maintain a whitelist of approved LockupLinear and LockupTranched contract addresses, enforce that the supplied address matches the expected interface and parameter types, and avoid granting unlimited allowances to arbitrary contracts. By restricting the set of permissible lockup contracts, the protocol can ensure that only vetted code can receive the approval and handle token transfers, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Merkle tree and proof depth not checked
description: When claiming an airstream the Merkle proof is checked against the Merkle root, but the length of the proof is not checked against the expected depth of the Merkle tree. function _checkClaim(uint256 index, bytes32 leaf, bytes32[] calldata merkleProof) internal view { if (_claimedBitMap.get(index)) { revert Errors.SablierV2MerkleLockup_StreamClaimed(index); } if (!MerkleProof.verify(merkleProof, MERKLE_ROOT, leaf)) { revert Errors.SablierV2MerkleLockup_InvalidProof(); } } The way this can be exploited is if a malicious member of team deploying the MerkleLockup makes one of the leaves of the Merkle tree a root hash of another tree (which can hold their own list of addresses, amounts and indexes even outside of expected index range). This would however be visible by anyone that actually validates the Merkle tree of course as one of the leaves is not the hash of the address, amount and index, it would just be the precomputed root hash of a subtree.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation of the Merkle proof length against the expected depth of the Merkle tree used in the claim function of a MerkleLockup contract. The claim routine only checks that the supplied proof correctly reconstructs the stored Merkle root for a given leaf, but it never verifies that the number of elements in the proof matches the height of the tree that was originally generated. Because of this omission, an attacker who can influence the leaf data – for example a malicious team member who deploys the contract – can replace a legitimate leaf with the root hash of a completely different Merkle tree that contains its own set of address‑amount‑index tuples, possibly outside the range that the original contract intended to support. When the attacker submits a proof that corresponds to this hidden subtree, the MerkleProof.verify call succeeds, the contract believes the claim is valid, and the attacker can withdraw funds that were never meant to be claimable.
