The impact is the unauthorized transfer of tokens from the lockup pool to the attacker, effectively causing a loss of funds for legitimate users. The issue manifests whenever a claim is processed, because the contract does not enforce any relationship between the proof length and the stored tree depth, nor does it ensure that the leaf is the hash of the expected (address, amount, index) tuple. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the claim logic and noticed the absence of a depth check. The bug can be subtle because the Merkle verification still passes, so a casual test that only checks for a true/false result will not reveal the problem; only a deeper inspection of the leaf contents or a comparison with the original tree would expose the inconsistency. To remediate the flaw, the contract should store the original tree depth at deployment and, during each claim, compare the length of the supplied merkleProof array with this depth, rejecting any proof that is longer or shorter. Additionally, the contract could enforce that the leaf is computed as keccak256(abi.encodePacked(address, amount, index)) to guarantee that only legitimate entries can be claimed. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees, ensuring that each claim corresponds to a unique, pre‑registered entry and that no extra or hidden sub‑trees can be used to siphon funds.

title: Use safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom instead of transfer and transferFrom
description: Tokens that do not comply with the ERC20 specification could return false from the transfer function call to indicate the transfer fails, while the calling contract would not notice the failure if the return value is not checked. Checking the return value is a requirement, as written in the EIP-20 specification: Callers MUST handle false from returns (bool success). Callers MUST NOT assume that false is never returned! Some tokens do not return a bool (e.g. USDT, BNB, OMG) on ERC20 methods. This will make the call break, making impossible to use these tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from calling ERC20 transfer or transferFrom functions without verifying the boolean return value that indicates success. According to the ERC20 (EIP‑20) specification, callers must handle a false return because some tokens deliberately return false to signal a failed transfer, and others (such as USDT, BNB, OMG) do not return any value at all, causing the call to revert or silently succeed without moving tokens. This unchecked call pattern creates a situation where a contract assumes the transfer succeeded, updates internal accounting, and emits events, while the external token balance remains unchanged. An attacker or a misbehaving token can exploit this by returning false or by having a non‑standard implementation, causing the calling contract to believe funds were transferred when they were not. The impact is that users may see a successful transaction in the UI, receive a confirmation, but their deposited or withdrawn balance stays the same, effectively losing access to the intended funds. The issue manifests whenever the contract interacts with any ERC20 token that does not strictly follow the specification, which includes many popular stablecoins and legacy tokens. All users of the affected contract, including depositors, withdrawers, and any downstream protocol that relies on accurate token accounting, are potentially affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of return‑value checks and the presence of direct transfer calls. Because the transaction does not revert, the failure is hard to notice without explicit balance checks or event analysis, leading to silent financial loss. The proper mitigation is to replace raw transfer and transferFrom calls with safe wrappers such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 or Solmate’s SafeTransferLib, which enforce a revert on false returns and handle tokens that omit the return value. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call failures and non‑compliant ERC20 interactions, where the contract’s business logic assumes successful token movement without verification. From a user perspective the symptom is a “deposit succeeded” message while the on‑chain token balance remains zero, or a “withdrawal completed” notice with no funds received. The expectation that a transfer will always move tokens is violated, breaking accounting invariants and potentially allowing funds to disappear from the protocol’s perspective. Implementing safe transfer utilities restores the guarantee that a failed token operation aborts the whole transaction, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting.

title: Clawback not possible in case of erroneously conﬁgured MerkleLockup and no expiration
description: If for any reason the conﬁguration of the MerkleLockup is wrong (like a bad Merkle root hash) the funds can not be recovered until the expiration date has been met. In the case that no expiration has been set, the funds cannot be recovered as clawback() is only allowed after expiration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a configuration‑dependent lockup bug in a MerkleLockup contract. The contract stores funds that can be released either by a valid Merkle proof or by a clawback function that is only callable after a predefined expiration timestamp. If the Merkle root stored in the contract is incorrect, no Merkle proof will ever satisfy the verification logic, making the normal claim path impossible. Because the contract also requires an expiration timestamp to be set before the clawback function can be executed, a deployment that omits the expiration or sets it to zero leaves the clawback permanently disabled. Consequently the locked assets remain in the contract forever, effectively disappearing from the perspective of users and the protocol. This situation occurs when the contract is deployed with a bad Merkle root and without a proper expiration value. It affects any participant who expects to receive a payout, as well as the protocol that relies on the lockup for escrow or vesting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the claim and clawback mechanisms and identified that the two recovery paths are mutually exclusive when the configuration is wrong. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and the functions are reachable, but the failure manifests only as a silent claim rejection and an unavailable clawback, which may not be obvious from the UI. The root cause is the lack of a fallback recovery path for mis‑configured lockups. To remediate, the contract should permit clawback before the first successful claim or within a short grace period when the Merkle root does not correspond to any valid leaf, or provide an admin‑only override that can reset the configuration or force a withdrawal. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “irrecoverable funds due to improper state validation” and violates the basic accounting assumption that locked funds must always be recoverable by either the intended recipient or an authorized fallback mechanism.

title: Claim indexes can appear multiple times in the Merkle tree possibly leading to stuck funds
description: MerkleLockup uses a Merkle tree to distribute airstream funds The leaves contain the combination of the recipient address, the amount and an index. The index is used keep track of which leaf of the Merkle tree has already been claimed. There is no check that the same index isn't used in multiple leaves during creation of the MerkleLockup contract, as this would be unfeasible to validate this on-chain. This means that if this happens to be the case, one address/leaf will be unclaimable when the other instance has been claimed already. When the aggregate amount of all the amounts in the leaves is sent to the contract the part of those funds cannot be claimed and therefor stuck in the contract until expiration or forever in case the expiration is set to 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the MerkleLockup contract records which Merkle leaves have already been claimed. Each leaf encodes a recipient address, an amount and an index, and the contract marks an index as claimed after a successful withdrawal. Because the contract does not enforce that the index value is unique across all leaves, it is possible to construct a Merkle tree where the same index appears in two different leaves. When a user claims the first leaf, the contract records the index as used; any subsequent claim that presents a different leaf but the same index will be rejected as already claimed. This makes the second leaf permanently unclaimable, causing the funds associated with that leaf to remain locked in the contract until the expiration time is reached, or forever if the expiration is set to zero. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors noticed that the on‑chain verification logic only checks the index bitmap and never validates that the index is unique in the off‑chain Merkle data. The problem is subtle because the UI typically shows a successful claim for one address while the other address receives a generic “already claimed” error, giving no indication that the root cause is a duplicate index rather than a malicious contract. The impact is that affected recipients lose access to their allocated tokens, the protocol may hold unrecoverable balances, and the overall fairness of the airdrop distribution is broken. The bug belongs to the class of “duplicate identifier” or “non‑unique claim key” flaws, where a unique claim identifier is assumed but not enforced. Exploitation requires only that the attacker (or a malicious airdrop creator) include duplicate indexes in the Merkle tree; no special on‑chain privileges are needed. To remediate, the contract should derive the claim identifier from the Merkle proof path itself, or otherwise enforce that each index can appear only once, for example by using the inclusion‑proof algorithm from Eigenlayer’s Merkle library which ties the index to the proof structure. This change guarantees that each leaf has a distinct claim key and prevents funds from becoming permanently stuck.

title: Calls to untrusted contracts on Blast are incentivized to steal gas from users
description: On Blast every contract can claim the gas fees payed by the users executing their code. When calling out to untrusted contracts (e.g. callbacks to receiver and sender, but also the transferFrom calls on the underlying tokens) could be used by the owners of those contracts to inﬂate gas usage and steal gas from Sablier's users. The callback function onLockupStreamWithdrawn could be used by a scam project to create an airstream with the sole intent to steal gas whenever a user withdraws, either in small increments or with maximum gas usage (gas bombs). This also applies to any novel token that does the same on token transfers which is used in the withdraw() and cancel() functions. The onLockupStreamCanceled could be used by a recipient as incentivized grieﬁng attack if the stream gets canceled.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑rebate abuse that arises because the Blast execution environment reimburses the contract that pays the gas for any gas that was consumed during the transaction. Sablier’s withdraw() and cancel() functions invoke external callbacks such as onLockupStreamWithdrawn and onLockupStreamCanceled, and they also rely on token transfer hooks that may execute code in untrusted token contracts. When a user initiates a withdrawal or a cancellation, the protocol forwards control to these external contracts without limiting the amount of gas they can consume. A malicious contract can deliberately inflate its gas consumption – for example by running long loops, performing heavy computations, or deploying a so‑called gas bomb – and because Blast credits the gas usage back to the contract that initiated the call, the extra gas is effectively stolen from the user who paid for the transaction. The attacker therefore receives a gas rebate that the user never sees, while the user experiences higher than expected transaction costs or even out‑of‑gas reverts. This issue is discovered during a security audit that examined Blast’s gas‑rebate model and identified that Sablier’s design trusts callbacks from arbitrary contracts. The problem is subtle because the transaction still appears to succeed and the extra gas usage is not reflected in the user‑visible fee; only the gas‑rebate accounting is affected, making it hard to notice without deep analysis of the underlying platform. The impact is that users may lose gas refunds, see unexpectedly high gas fees, or have their withdrawals fail due to gas exhaustion, effectively reducing the economic benefit of the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of “untrusted callback gas‑steal” or “gas rebate exploitation” where external calls are not sandboxed. To remediate, the contract should either cap the gas forwarded to untrusted callbacks, use staticcall with a fixed stipend, avoid invoking external hooks on Blast, or implement a whitelist of trusted contracts. By limiting or eliminating the ability of a malicious callee to consume arbitrary gas, the protocol can prevent the attacker from profiting from the Blast rebate mechanism and restore the expected gas economics for honest users.

title: createMerkleLT() can revert causing loss of funds when used for counterfactual deployment
description: When creating a Merkle lockup from the factory CREATE2 is used to ensure a deterministic address. If the the combined percentages of the tranches do not add up to 100% the createMerkleLT() reverts as creating such a Merkle lockup would create streams that do not fully stream the allotted amount to the recipient. uint256 totalDuration; for (uint256 i = 0; i < tranchesWithPercentages.length; ++i) { uint64 percentage = tranchesWithPercentages[i].unlockPercentage.unwrap(); totalPercentage = totalPercentage + percentage; } if (totalPercentage != uUNIT) { revert Errors.SablierV2MerkleLockupFactory_TotalPercentageNotOneHundred(totalPercentage); } bytes32 salt = keccak256( abi.encodePacked( // ... abi.encode(tranchesWithPercentages) ) ); merkleLT = new SablierV2MerkleLT{ salt: salt }(baseParams, lockupTranched, tranchesWithPercentages); If however this is used for a counterfactual deployment where funds are sent to the contract's off chain computed address, the funds will be lost if the percentages do not add up to 100%. Changing the percent- age so they do add up to 100% would also change the salt used for the CREATE2 which in turn leads to a different address for the contract. As no contract can thus be deployed on the precomputed address, the funds cannot be retrieved. The team indicated however this isn't a typical use case and funds are sent after the contract is created. The same issue exists in the constructor of SablierV2MerkleLockup where the name is required to be less than 32 bytes. In this case however the impact is limited as merely calling createMerkleLT() again with the (same) name capped to 32 bytes does create the contract at the pre-computed address (provided the off chain compute code also capped the name to 32bytes).
bug_full: The vulnerability originatesfrom the createMerkleLT function in the Merkle lockup factory, which uses CREATE2 to deploy a contract at a deterministic address. Before the contract is created, the function checks that the sum of the unlock percentages of all tranches equals exactly 100 percent (the constant uUNIT). If the percentages do not add up, the function reverts with an error and the contract is never deployed. In a counter‑factual deployment workflow, users often compute the address off‑chain, send funds to that address, and then rely on the factory to create the contract at the pre‑computed address. Because the deployment reverts, the address remains empty of code while still holding the transferred funds. Moreover, changing any tranche percentage changes the salt used for CREATE2, which in turn changes the deterministic address; therefore the contract cannot be redeployed at the original address and the funds become permanently inaccessible. A similar, but less severe, issue exists in the Merkle lockup constructor where the lockup name must be shorter than 32 bytes; an oversized name also causes a revert that prevents deployment at the expected address. The root cause is the placement of strict validation checks before the CREATE2 deployment, causing a revert that leaves a pre‑funded address without contract code. Exploitation does not require an attacker; an honest user who mis‑calculates tranche percentages or provides an overly long name can unintentionally lock their assets. The impact is that the user’s balance appears to disappear – the UI may show the address with a non‑zero balance but no contract logic to release the funds, leading to a loss of the locked amount. This condition occurs only when the counter‑factual pattern is used and the validation fails; in normal workflows where funds are sent after successful deployment, the issue is not triggered. The affected parties are anyone who relies on deterministic addresses for Merkle lockups, including token holders, protocol developers, and auditors. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that the revert prevents the CREATE2 deployment and consequently makes pre‑funded addresses unrecoverable. The bug is hard to notice because the address computation succeeds and the funds can be transferred without any immediate error, yet the later deployment step fails silently, leaving the funds stuck. To remediate, the factory should avoid reverting on validation failures when using CREATE2; instead it could deploy the contract regardless and allow a clawback mechanism to retrieve the funds, or it could provide a view function that predicts the address only after the same checks have passed, ensuring that users never send funds to an address that cannot be created. Conceptually, the issue belongs to the class of deterministic‑address deployment bugs where pre‑deployment validation interferes with the ability to occupy a pre‑computed address, resulting in permanent fund loss.

title: Create2 salt based on tx.origin alone
description:
When deploying a proxy from the PRBProxyRegistry contract the tx.origin is used together with an incremental nonce (tracked per tx.origin) to form the salt for the CREATE2 when deploying the PRBProxy contract. However, this means the proxy address is determined solely by the gas payer of the transaction (and its relative position in a sequence of deploying proxies). It does not depend on the state of the proxy created in any way, not even the owner. The assumption is that in most cases the owner is the tx.origin and in these cases, no one can front-run the transaction to hijack the proxy address. The Auditor's Handbook for PRBProxy mentions the following about Account Abstraction: We are aware of a potential “feature clash” with Account Abstraction (if and when it gets implemented in Ethereum). This seems to refer to the Account Abstraction efforts that require a change in the Ethereum protocol (like EIP2938 and EIP3074). However, there are other situations where the choice of using (only) tx.origin heavily impacts the deployment process:
• EIP-2771 AA using meta-transactions
• EIP-4337 AA using UserOperations
• Multisigs where the last signer is the tx.origin and as such the predicted proxy address may or may not be correct.
Some major problems present themselves in a relayer/gasMaster type scenario.
• Scenario 1 Imagine when the relayer is asked to predict a proxy address for a user (Alice). The relayer uses nonce = 1 to predict the proxy address and request Alice to sign some type of meta-transaction (e.g. for refunding gas in a gasless transaction, but this could include an interaction with a third party contract). Then Alice delays her signature and a second user (Bob) asks the relayer to predict their proxy (using nonce = 2). The relayer does so and asks Bob to sign a second meta-transaction. Now Bob may be assured the predicted address is his based on the assumption the relayer will send them out in the order they were predicted. However, if the sequence of Alice's and Bob's signatures are sent out in reverse order they end up with each other's predicted proxy address as the SablierV2ProxyTarget uses the nonce in the order they are included in the block. This is obviously an implementation issue of the relayer but it points to the design flaw of not including the owner in the salt of the CREATE2.
• Scenario 2 Imagine the same scenario but Alice never signs the transactions and the relayer is correctly implemented. The relayer is now in a state where they can't proceed because there is no way to deploy Bob's proxy without first deploying Alice's proxy. They can't honestly deploy Alice's without reputation damage as they would have to deploy her proxy designating themselves or a dead address as owner which looks like they maliciously provided Alice with the wrong address.
• Scenario 3 Imagine Bob having requested the deployment of a proxy to a relayer. Firstly Bob has to trust the relayer to present the correct address (there is no way Bob can validate the given address). Bob then may sign a message to the relayer to initiate the gasless deployment. The malicious relayer however decides to use the deployAndExecuteFor() to deploy the proxy but in an altered state (e.g. plugins installed, envoy permission sets, ERC20/NFT token allowances set, basically anything they want relating to interactions with third party contracts). The address of this proxy would be identical to one deployed using the simple deployFor() function and hence Bob will accept this address without realizing the altered state of the proxy. Note that this issue is similar to the issues surrounding transferOwnership(), but even if they are resolved the deployAndExecuteFor() would still allow a relayer to maliciously deploy a proxy on behalf of a user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deterministic address generation flaw in the PRBProxyRegistry contract when it creates a PRBProxy via CREATE2. The contract builds the salt from tx.origin together with an incremental nonce that is tracked per tx.origin. Because the salt does not incorporate any information about the intended proxy owner, the resulting proxy address is a function only of the transaction sender and the order in which proxies are created. This design assumption works only when the owner is exactly the tx.origin, but it breaks for any scenario that involves meta‑transactions, account abstraction (EIP‑2771, EIP‑4337), multisig owners, or relayer‑based gas‑master services. An attacker or a poorly implemented relayer can manipulate the order of signatures or the deployment sequence, causing two users to receive each other’s predicted addresses, or forcing a relayer to deploy a proxy with an unexpected owner or with malicious state (plugins, permissions, allowances) while the address matches the user’s expectation. From the user’s point of view the proxy appears at the correct address, but the contract may have a different owner or altered configuration, leading to situations where a user receives no funds, refunds are missing, or interactions with the proxy fail because the proxy is controlled by an attacker. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the CREATE2 salt construction and modeled realistic relayer workflows. It is hard to notice because the address itself matches the prediction, so UI checks that only compare addresses will not detect the mismatch in internal state. The impact ranges from loss of funds, inability to deploy a required proxy, reputational damage for relayers, and potential front‑running attacks that hijack the address space. The vulnerability belongs to the class of deterministic‑address‑generation bugs where the salt does not bind the deployment to the intended beneficiary. The recommended mitigation is to include the owner address in the salt (and, for deployAndExecuteFor, also the target contract address and calldata), to track nonces per owner rather than per tx.origin, and to expose a view function that lets users independently compute and verify the expected proxy address. This change removes the reliance on tx.origin, prevents address collisions across different users, and restores the integrity of the proxy’s state, making the system compatible with account‑abstraction mechanisms and safe for relayer‑mediated deployments.

title: Token allowances stay in effect on proxy ownership transfer
description: The proxy contract acts as a smart contract wallet for it's owner and it is a reasonable scenario that the proxy will at some point have (infinite) approvals set for other contracts on some (ERC20) tokens. When the ownership of a proxy for some reason is transferred to another entity (person or contracts as part of a protocol) the existing approvals stay in effect as they are based on the proxy's address. In such a scenario the new owner (if a person) is unaware of the existing approvals and this would allow the old owner to use those approvals to potentially steal the tokens via the approved contracts. Note that this is also true for approval on the permit2 contract although they have an expiration and in the case of AllowanceTransfer are reset on each new approval.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the persistence of ERC20 token allowances that are granted by a proxy contract acting as a smart‑contract wallet. When the proxy’s ownership is transferred to a new entity, the allowances that were previously set for third‑party contracts remain attached to the proxy’s address because approvals are recorded against the address, not against the owner. Consequently, the former owner, or any party that can still trigger the approved contracts, retains the ability to invoke transferFrom on the proxy’s token balances. This situation arises whenever a proxy that has granted infinite or long‑lived approvals is handed over without explicitly revoking those approvals. The root cause is the mismatch between the proxy’s internal access‑control (owner variable) and the external token contracts’ allowance model, which does not automatically clear allowances on ownership change. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling the previously approved contract (for example a staking or liquidity contract) to move tokens from the proxy to an address they control, effectively stealing funds that the new owner expects to be under their exclusive control. The impact is a loss of token assets, breach of trust in the protocol, and potential reputational damage, especially when the new owner is unaware that the proxy still holds active approvals. From the user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected balance reductions, missing refunds, or tokens disappearing after a wallet hand‑over, even though the UI shows no direct transaction from the new owner. The issue is difficult to notice because allowances are stored on the token contracts and are not displayed in typical wallet interfaces, and because the proxy’s ownership change does not emit any warning about lingering approvals. The problem belongs to the class of “allowance persistence” or “stale approval” bugs, where external contracts continue to have authority over an address after the internal ownership semantics have changed. To remediate the issue the proxy should either automatically revoke all token allowances during an ownership transfer, enforce a pattern where approvals are only granted to contracts that are themselves owned by the proxy, or avoid using the proxy as a wallet that holds tokens with open approvals. In any case, the design must align the external allowance model with the internal ownership model so that a change of owner also revokes or requires explicit re‑approval of any delegated spending rights.

title: Time dependent data in NFT metadata
description: The SablierV2NFTDescriptor contract creates an SVG image and embeds it in the image property of the JSON metadata returned by the tokenURI() function. However, the generated image contains time dependent data of the stream including the status, streamed amount, and progress as a percentage. Although this information is up to date every time the tokenURI() function is called, marketplace platforms such as OpenSea cache this information as explained here (Although this is OS specific, most marketplaces will have similar caching optimizations in place) image: This is the URL to the image of the item. Can be just about any type of image (including SVGs, which will be cached into PNGs by OpenSea), and can be IPFS URLs or paths. We recommend using a 350 x 350 image. | image_data: Raw SVG image data, if you want to generate images on the fly (not recommended). Only use this if you're not including the image parameter. Not only does OpenSea cache the image as a rasterized version but the complete metadata is cached as there is no way of knowing when the metadata has changed (except when ERC4906 events are used). To refresh the metadata the user needs to manually request to refresh the metadata for the NFT. Their API does allow for refreshing specific tokens programmatically but this is for obvious reasons heavily rate limited. This means that whenever the image is displayed on a marketplace the time dependent data in the image will not be up to date and potential buyers will be misinformed about the status of the stream.
bug_full: An NFT minted by the SablierV2NFTDescriptor contract includes a tokenURI function that returns a JSON object whose image field contains an SVG generated on‑the‑fly. The SVG embeds the current status of the underlying payment stream, the amount already streamed and a percentage progress value. Because the SVG is built at the moment tokenURI is called, the data is technically up‑to‑date. However, most NFT marketplaces (for example OpenSea) cache both the metadata JSON and the rendered image. The cache is refreshed only when an ERC‑4906 MetadataUpdate event is emitted or when a user manually requests a metadata refresh, which is rate‑limited and rarely performed. Consequently, when the marketplace displays the NFT, the cached image may show an old status – for instance a completed stream when the stream is still active, or a zero streamed amount when funds have already been transferred. From the buyer’s perspective the UI shows a misleading picture: the user expects to see the current progress of the stream but receives a stale image, leading to potential overpayment, underpayment, or loss of trust. The vulnerability is discovered during a security audit that examined the tokenURI implementation and the interaction with marketplace caching policies. It is hard to notice because a wallet that reads the tokenURI directly will display correct data, while the same token shown on a marketplace will appear outdated, creating a discrepancy that is not obvious without comparing both sources. The root cause is the inclusion of time‑dependent data in a field that is assumed to be immutable by external platforms. The issue belongs to the class of dynamic metadata caching bugs, where mutable on‑chain information is presented through a static metadata endpoint that external services cache. To remediate, the contract should avoid embedding mutable values in the image field, either by removing them, adding a generation timestamp, moving the dynamic content to an animation_url, or by emitting ERC‑4906 events whenever the stream state changes so that marketplaces can invalidate their cache. This aligns the on‑chain reality with the off‑chain presentation and prevents users from being misinformed about the stream’s status.

title: Plugin or target with selfdestruct
description: Until the 'Cancun' upgrade scheduled for later this year, whenever a delegatecall is made to a target contract or plugin that would do a SELFDESTRUCT the proxy would be destroyed at the end of the transaction and all ETH in the proxy would be sent to the address designated in the SELFDESTRUCT call. This would obviously be problematic but would also mean that the current owner of the proxy could not create a new proxy as the registry's proxies mapping for the user still points to the destroyed proxy address. After the upgrade, the selfdestruct opcode will not destroy the proxy contract but still send the ETH to the designated address. Although target and plugin contracts are gated by the plugins and permissions access control mechanisms it is still possible for an owner to unsuspectedly call a contract that selfdestructs.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of delegatecall to external target or plugin contracts that contain the SELFDESTRUCT opcode. Because delegatecall executes the callee’s code in the context of the calling proxy, a SELFDESTRUCT executed by the callee destroys the proxy itself, not the callee, and transfers any ether held by the proxy to the address supplied in the SELFDESTRUCT instruction. This behaviour is present on Ethereum networks that have not yet applied the Cancun hard‑fork, where the opcode still removes the calling contract. An attacker – or even an honest owner who unintentionally invokes a contract that self‑destructs – can trigger the destruction of the proxy, causing the proxy’s address to become unusable and the ether stored in it to be sent to an arbitrary destination. From the user’s perspective the proxy disappears from the UI, balances read as zero, and attempts to create a new proxy fail because the registry still points to the now‑dead address. The impact includes loss of control over the proxy, permanent loss of any funds it held, and disruption of the protocol’s accounting because the registry mapping is left pointing at a non‑existent contract. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the delegatecall pathways and recognised that the SELFDESTRUCT opcode is not filtered by the existing permission system. It is hard to notice because SELFDESTRUCT is rarely used, and the delegatecall abstraction hides the fact that the callee’s self‑destruct will affect the caller. The root cause is the combination of (1) unchecked delegatecall to arbitrary contracts and (2) reliance on pre‑Cancun semantics where SELFDESTRUCT removes the calling contract. The recommended mitigation is to avoid delegatecall to untrusted code, to employ staticcall where possible, to implement a whitelist of audited target contracts at proxy creation, and to ensure that after the Cancun upgrade the proxy’s code is protected against self‑destruct side‑effects. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “delegatecall‑induced self‑destruct” vulnerabilities that break contract invariants and cause unintended ether drainage.

title: Permission and plugins not reset on proxy ownership transfer
description: When a plugin is installed the mapping between function selectors and plugin contract is stored in the plugins mapping of the proxy. Similarly, the permissions mapping holds the target contracts envoys are allowed to call. mapping(bytes4 method => IPRBProxyPlugin plugin) public plugins; mapping(address envoy => mapping(address target => bool permission)) public permissions; On ownership transfer of the proxy, these mappings are not reset, meaning any plugins installed or envoy permissions stay in effect. As these are mapping there is no easy way for the new owner to detect or list installed plugins and envoy permissions. As such in a scenario where ownership of a proxy is effectively transferred to another person (i.e. not to another account of the same person) this would allow the previous owner to maliciously install a plugin or set themselves as envoy to a malicious target contract before the transfer and potentially steal funds or cancel streams.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a privilege‑persistence flaw in a proxy contract that manages plugins and envoy permissions. When a plugin is installed, the proxy stores a selector‑to‑plugin mapping, and when an envoy is granted permission, the proxy stores a target‑address allowance mapping. Both mappings are kept in simple Solidity mappings that are not enumerable and, crucially, the contract does not clear them when the proxy’s ownership is transferred. The root cause is the absence of any reset or cleanup logic in the ownership‑transfer function, meaning that the state associated with the previous owner remains intact after the transfer. An attacker who is the outgoing owner can exploit this by installing a malicious plugin or by granting themselves envoy permission to a target contract just before handing over ownership. Because the new owner inherits a proxy that still contains the old mappings, the attacker can later invoke the plugin’s code or use the lingering envoy permission to interact with the target contract, potentially stealing funds, cancelling active streams, or otherwise subverting the intended business logic. The impact is a loss of assets and a breach of trust: users expect that after ownership changes the proxy is a clean slate, but instead hidden logic can continue to execute on their behalf, leading to unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or terminated streams. The issue manifests only when ownership is transferred to a different party; if the same person retains control, the problem is not observable. It affects any user or protocol that relies on the proxy for secure fund management, including stream‑based payment systems and any contract that delegates calls through plugins. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the proxy’s state‑management functions and noticed that the mappings were never touched on transfer. Because the mappings cannot be listed from the outside, the new owner may never realize that hidden plugins or permissions exist, making the bug subtle and hard to detect without source‑code review. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit ownership transfer altogether, or explicitly reset the plugins and permissions mappings during the transfer. An alternative design is to store permissions in a separate registry keyed by the owner address, ensuring that a change of owner automatically yields a fresh permission set. This class of bug falls under “access‑control persistence after ownership change” and is a form of privilege escalation that violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only the current owner can influence proxy behaviour. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that a stream is still active, but the funds disappear or the expected refund never arrives because the hidden plugin silently redirects or blocks the operation, contrary to the user’s expectation that the new owner has full and exclusive control over the proxy’s behavior.

title: Plugins and permissions storage variables are unprotected
description:
The installed plugins and the permissions given to the envoys are stored in mappings defined in the PRBProxyStorage contract which is inherited by he proxy and as such they are stored in the proxy. Any target or plugin contract is supposed to inherit the same PRBProxyStorage contract to avoid storage slot collision. abstract contract PRBProxyStorage is IPRBProxyStorage { address public override owner; uint256 public override minGasReserve; mapping(bytes4 method => IPRBProxyPlugin plugin) public plugins; mapping(address envoy => mapping(address target => bool permission)) public permissions; This however can lead to accidental or malicious manipulation of the mappings which represent important access control features of the proxy. Some examples of possible scenarios are:
• A faulty target or plugin contract accidently overwriting these storages slots.
• A malicious target or plugin contract assigning the attacker as envoy for other malicious contracts.
• A malicious envoy using faulty target contracts to try and manipulate the mappings to gain unauthorized control.
This problem also applies to the owner and minGasReserve storage variables, but they have additional impact which is addressed in other findings.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the proxy contract stores the mappings that hold installed plugins and envoy permissions directly in its own storage layout, inherited from the abstract PRBProxyStorage contract. Because any target or plugin contract is expected to inherit the same storage definition, a malicious or even a faulty contract that is called via delegatecall can write to the same storage slots, overwriting the plugins mapping, the permissions mapping, the owner address or the minimum gas reserve. When such a contract deliberately assigns the attacker’s address as an authorized envoy, or clears existing permissions, it gains the ability to invoke arbitrary calls through the proxy, effectively bypassing the intended access‑control checks. This can be exploited by deploying a crafted plugin that implements the same storage layout and then invoking a function that writes to the mappings, or by using a target contract that unintentionally writes to those slots during normal execution. The impact is that unauthorized parties may obtain control over the proxy, execute transactions on behalf of legitimate users, and potentially drain funds or alter contract state. The issue manifests whenever the proxy interacts with external contracts that share the PRBProxyStorage layout, especially after upgrades or when new plugins are added, and it affects all users of the proxy, the protocol that relies on its security guarantees, and any funds managed through the proxy. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined storage inheritance patterns and identified that no protective mechanism (such as isolated EIP‑1967 slots or registry‑based storage) is in place, making the collision subtle and easy to miss because the mappings are not directly visible in the proxy’s interface. From a user’s perspective the proxy may suddenly reject calls that were previously authorized, or appear to execute actions without the expected permission checks, leading to confusion and potential loss of assets. The bug belongs to the class of storage‑collision and unprotected‑state‑variable vulnerabilities, where shared storage layouts enable unintended state manipulation. To remediate the issue the mappings and critical variables should be moved out of the proxy’s storage, for example into a dedicated registry keyed by the proxy address, or stored in a custom namespace using EIP‑1967 slots, and the permissions should be reset on ownership transfer to ensure that stale authorizations cannot be abused.

title: Deployment front running protection not effective
description: Deployment of a proxy is protected from frontrunning by salting the CREATE2 with the tx.origin of the deployer. function _deploy(address owner) internal returns (IPRBProxy proxy) { bytes32 seed = nextSeeds[tx.origin]; // Prevent front-running the salt by hashing the concatenation of "tx.origin" and the user-provided seed. bytes32 salt = keccak256(abi.encode(tx.origin, seed)); // Deploy the proxy with CREATE2. transientProxyOwner = owner; proxy = new PRBProxy{ salt: salt }(); delete transientProxyOwner; // Set the proxy for the owner. proxies[owner] = proxy; } While this does protect users from having their proxy address sniped from the mempool (which would cause a revert with CREATE), it does not protect against other opportunities for a frontrunning attacker to cause deployment to revert. This is due to the noProxy() modifier, which will revert if the owner already has a proxy deployed: modifier noProxy(address owner) { IPRBProxy proxy = proxies[owner]; if (address(proxy) != address(0)) { revert PRBProxyRegistry_OwnerHasProxy(owner, proxy); } _; } However, an attacker can force a proxy on another user at any time using deployFor() or transferOwnership() to the victim before their transaction is processed. In the least impactful case this will just mean the victim will have to burn the proxy (for which there is no function, so would involve transferring the proxy to a random address) and deploy the proxy again. In the worst case, the user may not notice the revert (or upon noticing the revert, checks for a proxy they own via the public proxies mapping in the registry and determine that it must have worked, since they have one). Unbeknownst to the victim, the attacker could have installed a malicious plugin or given themselves permission to execute on a (malicious) target contract during their frontrunning. Neither of these changes are easily detectable (because they are stored as mappings), but would put the proxy in extreme danger.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the proxy registry’s front‑running mitigation strategy, which only salts the CREATE2 deployment with the caller’s tx.origin. This approach prevents an attacker from pre‑computing the proxy address and causing a CREATE failure, but it does not stop a malicious actor from front‑running a legitimate deployment and forcing the registry to revert. The root cause is the combination of a noProxy modifier that checks whether the target owner already has a proxy registered and the public functions deployFor() and transferOwnership() that allow any address to assign a proxy to an arbitrary owner. An attacker can submit a transaction that calls deployFor(victim) or transferOwnership(victim, maliciousProxy) just before the victim’s deployment transaction reaches the mempool. Because the registry sees that the victim already has a proxy, the victim’s transaction hits the noProxy revert and never creates the intended proxy. From the user’s perspective the deployment transaction simply fails or appears to succeed while the proxy mapping already contains an address, leading to confusion such as “my proxy was not created” or “my balance is unchanged”. In the least severe scenario the victim must discard the unwanted proxy (the contract lacks a burn function, so the only option is to transfer it to a random address) and attempt deployment again, incurring extra gas costs and potential downtime. In the worst case the attacker may have attached a malicious plugin or granted themselves execution rights on the newly forced proxy, which is not readily visible because the permissions are stored in internal mappings. This can expose the victim’s funds to theft or unauthorized actions, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a user‑owned proxy is under the user’s exclusive control. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the registry’s ownership logic, where the interaction between the salt generation and the noProxy check was examined. It is hard to notice because the revert does not emit a distinctive error beyond the generic OwnerHasProxy message, and the malicious state changes are hidden in mappings that are not displayed in typical front‑ends. To remediate the problem the registry should make ownership transfers and proxy deployments a two‑step process where the new owner must explicitly accept the assignment before the proxies mapping is updated, or, as a stronger alternative, make proxy ownership immutable after deployment, thereby eliminating the attack surface that allows an adversary to pre‑emptively claim a victim’s proxy address.

title: refundableAmountOf will return a value when isCancelable is false
description: The refundableAmountOf() function is an external view function that returns the amount of tokens that can be refunded to the sender of the transaction. It specifically checks that, if the stream is either depleted or canceled, it will return 0. Otherwise, it will return the amount deposited minus the streamed amount. if (!_streams[streamId].isDepleted && !_streams[streamId].wasCanceled) { refundableAmount = _streams[streamId].amounts.deposited - _calculateStreamedAmount(streamId); } However, there is no check whether the stream is cancelable. In the case that stream.isCancelable = false, the amount that is refundable is actually zero, and it would be more accurate to return this value. This can be particularly dangerous when interacting with other areas in DeFi, where, for example, a lending protocol might use this return value to determine the amount that the stream could be liquidated for, which in fact it cannot be liquidated at all.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a view function that reports the amount of tokens that can be refunded from a streaming payment. The function checks only whether the stream is depleted or has been cancelled before returning the deposited amount minus the amount already streamed. It omits a crucial check of the stream's cancelability flag. Consequently, when a stream is active (not depleted and not cancelled) but is marked as non‑cancelable, the function still returns a positive refundable amount even though the protocol logic forbids any refund. This mismatch occurs because the underlying business rule – that a non‑cancelable stream should have zero refundable value – is not enforced in the code. An external caller, such as a lending or liquidation contract, may read the returned value and assume that the stream can be liquidated or cancelled for that amount. When the caller attempts the operation, the transaction will revert or simply fail, leaving the caller with an inaccurate expectation and potentially causing financial loss or stalled workflows. Users experience the symptom of seeing a non‑zero refundable balance in the UI, attempting to cancel or liquidate, and receiving no funds or a failed transaction, which contradicts their expectation of receiving a refund. The issue is discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that compared the contract’s documented accounting rules with its implementation. It is hard to notice because the function is read‑only and does not emit errors; the returned number looks legitimate, and typical testing may not cover the edge case where isCancelable is false. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state‑dependent return value” or “missing condition check” vulnerabilities, where a function returns a value that is mathematically correct for a subset of states but violates higher‑level business logic for other states. To remediate, the function should also verify that the stream is marked as cancelable before calculating a refundable amount, ensuring that the returned value aligns with the protocol’s accounting assumptions and prevents downstream contracts from acting on a false premise.

title: Protocol fees can be skirted because of default 0 value
description:
Sablier's protocol fees are tracked in the Comptroller contract on a per-asset basis, stored in the following mapping:
```solidity
mapping(IERC20 asset => UD60x18 fee) public override protocolFees;
```
When a new stream is created, the protocol fees are pulled by accessing this mapping through the public getter function:
```solidity
UD60x18 protocolFee = comptroller.protocolFees(params.asset);
```
As a result, any assets without a fee set will default to a value of zero. Given the BUSL license and noDelegateCall checks, it appears there is a strong effort being made to avoid using the protocol's code and logic without following the expected behavior and paying fees. However, this issue can be abused to stream any asset with no fees by wrapping it in another contract that allows 1-for-1 deposits and withdrawals of the underlying token, and streaming this contract's token instead. In an extreme case, it would even be possible for someone to spin up a FreeSablier.sol contract, which takes in any asset, creates a proxy, starts a stream with the proxy's token, and distributes everything back to the users.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Sablier’s Comptroller contract stores protocol fees for each supported asset. Fees are kept in a public mapping that returns a UD60x18 value, and the getter simply reads the entry for the requested token. Because Solidity mappings return the default value for keys that have never been written, any asset that has not been explicitly assigned a fee will return zero. The contract does not enforce a non‑zero fee nor provide a fallback fee, so the protocol assumes a zero‑fee is a legitimate configuration. An attacker can exploit this by wrapping an arbitrary token in a thin proxy contract that mints a new ERC‑20 representing the underlying asset on a 1‑for‑1 basis. The attacker then creates a Sablier stream using the proxy’s token as the asset. Since the proxy token has never had a fee set in the Comptroller, the protocol fee lookup returns zero and no fee is deducted from the stream. In an extreme scenario the attacker could deploy a generic “FreeSablier” contract that automatically creates such proxies for any incoming token, starts streams with them, and distributes the full amount back to users, effectively providing fee‑free streaming. This bypass undermines the economic model of the protocol, causing loss of expected revenue and potentially allowing malicious actors to offer “free” streaming services that appear legitimate. The issue manifests whenever a stream is created for an asset without a configured fee, which can happen unintentionally for newly added tokens or deliberately via wrapper contracts. Users see streams that appear to work normally but incur no fee, contrary to the expectation that the protocol always takes a small percentage. Because a zero value is a natural default for unmapped keys, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple tests that only verify fee collection for known assets. The flaw was identified during a manual audit of the fee‑retrieval logic. To remediate, the contract should enforce a default fee fallback (for example returning a predefined defaultFee when the stored fee is zero) or require that a non‑zero fee be explicitly set for every asset before it can be used in a stream. Additionally, the protocol could reject streams that involve tokens whose fee entry is zero, or add validation that the asset is a known, fee‑configured token. Implementing such safeguards would close the fee‑skipping vector and restore the intended fee collection behavior.

title: Withdraw by the sender when the NFT is in a Deﬁcontract may lead to lost funds
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an authorization flaw in the withdraw function of a token‑streaming protocol that uses an NFT to represent each stream. The contract permits the original sender of the stream to invoke withdraw() on behalf of the current NFT holder, because the isAuthorizedForStream modifier explicitly allows the caller if it is the stream sender. This design was introduced to handle cases where the designated recipient cannot call withdraw themselves. However, when the NFT is transferred to a smart contract – for example a vault, pool, or any other DeFi contract – that contract may not be programmed to receive or correctly account for the incoming ERC20 tokens. If the sender calls withdraw() while the NFT is owned by such a contract, the protocol will transfer the streamed tokens directly to the contract’s address. The contract may then lock the tokens, discard them, or redistribute them across its participants, effectively causing the funds to disappear from the intended recipient’s balance. The issue manifests only when the NFT holder is a contract that lacks a fallback or explicit handling for token transfers; with regular externally owned accounts the withdrawal behaves as expected, making the bug easy to miss during standard testing. The impact is a loss or misallocation of streamed assets, affecting the stream sender, the intended recipient, and any users of the contract that temporarily holds the NFT. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the authorization logic of the withdraw function. The problem is subtle because the withdraw call succeeds and emits no error, so observers may assume the transfer succeeded even though the receiving contract cannot use the funds. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should require the recipient to explicitly accept the stream before any tokens can be withdrawn. This can be achieved by adding an accept() function or by requiring the recipient to call withdraw with a zero amount as a proof of capability. If the recipient never accepts, the sender should be allowed to cancel the stream without fees and recreate it for an address that can correctly call withdraw. This change eliminates the need for the sender to force withdrawals on behalf of a contract that cannot handle them, thereby preventing accidental or malicious loss of funds.

title: Protocol and Broker are overpaid in the event of a canceled stream
description:
When the stream is created, both the broker fee and the protocol fee are immediately paid in full. This means that when a stream is canceled, both fees have been paid in full by the sender. This does not seem ideal for any situation in which the stream is canceled early, but there are two situations where it is particularly harmful:  
1) If the stream is canceled before the start time (for example, if parameters were set incorrectly), so no actions were taken at all.  
2) The Sablier team mentioned potential functionality where a periphery contract would change the parameters of a stream by canceling and restarting a new stream. In this case, the sender would have to pay the protocol fees in full each time a change was made.  
Additionally, it is worth considering that the protocol fee is calculated on the total amount of the stream (including the broker fee). Therefore, it seems that front-ends/brokers would be better served by creating a second transaction for their broker fee, generating the same result but at less cost to the sender or more revenue for the broker.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑payment of both broker and protocol fees when a linear payment stream is cancelled before it has fully executed. The contract design takes the entire broker fee and the full protocol fee from the sender at the moment the stream is created, regardless of how much of the stream will actually be delivered. Because the fees are paid upfront as a lump sum, cancelling the stream – especially before the start time or after a short period – does not trigger any refund of those fees. This problem is amplified in two concrete scenarios. First, if the sender discovers an error in the stream parameters and cancels before any tokens are transferred, the sender still loses the full fee amount even though no service was rendered. Second, the Sablier team has discussed a periphery contract that would modify a stream by cancelling the existing one and creating a new one with updated parameters; each cancellation forces the sender to pay the full protocol fee again, leading to repeated unnecessary fee extraction. The root cause is the fee‑collection logic that treats fees as immutable, upfront costs calculated on the total stream amount (which already includes the broker fee). Consequently, the protocol fee is effectively charged on top of the broker fee, inflating the total cost. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal fee deduction at creation, but after cancellation the user receives the remaining streamed tokens while the deducted fees disappear, creating a symptom of “funds disappear” or “refund missing”. The impact is financial loss for senders, inflated revenue for the protocol and brokers, and a distortion of the intended economic model where fees should be proportional to the actual streamed value. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined fee handling and cancellation paths. It can be hard to notice because the fee transfer occurs in a single transaction that appears legitimate, and there is no explicit refund mechanism visible in the contract code. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or economic mis‑allocation vulnerabilities, where fees are not correctly prorated to the amount of service actually delivered. To remediate, the fee‑payment mechanism should be changed to a gradual, linear release that mirrors the stream’s schedule, either by incorporating the fees into the same stream with identical parameters or by creating a separate linear fee stream that starts at the same time as the main payment stream. This ensures that only the portion of fees corresponding to the elapsed streaming period is actually paid, and any cancellation will automatically refund the unearned portion of the fees.

title: Reentrancy risk in _cancel() for interacting protocols
description:
The _cancel() function is used to end a stream, sending the total streamed amount to the recipient and the remaining funds back to the sender. It also implements the onStreamCanceled() callback function for protocols that interact with Sablier. The basic ﬂow of the function is as follows:  
• Calculate the funds to send to each party  
• Send recipient funds to the recipient  
• Send sender funds back to the sender  
• If the function is being called by the sender, notify the recipient with a callback  
• Otherwise, notify the sender with a callback  
For any tokens that implement callbacks themselves (for example, ERC777s), this creates a reentrancy risk, because control ﬂow is being passed to the sender before the recipient is sent the callback to update state.  
As a simple example, let's imagine an interacting protocol that holds Sablier NFTs as collateral in publicly investable vaults:  
• A new stream is posted as collateral on this protocol, and valued according to its total maturity value  
• The protocol's vault adjusts its internal "assets" calculations to account for this increased value  
• When the stream is canceled, the remaining streamed funds are sent to the protocol  
• Then the sender receives their funds, but because the token implements a callback in the transfer method, control ﬂow is passed to the sender  
• The sender is then able to enter into the protocol at a time when the value of the assets has changed, but the accounting hasn't yet been updated  
• As a result, they may be able to liquidate a position, short the vault, or perform any other action that beneﬁts from the protocol's incorrect accounting  
• Only after the sender takes this action is the callback called and the protocol's accounting is updated
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy risk in the internal _cancel() routine that terminates a streaming payment. The function first computes how much each party should receive, then transfers the recipient’s portion, then transfers the sender’s portion, and finally invokes a protocol‑specific callback (onStreamCanceled) depending on who initiated the call. When the streamed token implements a transfer hook – for example ERC777’s tokensReceived callback – the external call to transfer the sender’s funds hands control back to the sender contract before the callback that updates the accounting of the interacting protocol is executed. This ordering violates the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: state that reflects the new asset balance of the protocol is not updated until after the sender has regained execution control, allowing the sender to re‑enter the protocol while its internal “assets” accounting still reflects the pre‑cancellation value. An attacker can therefore cancel a stream, receive the sender‑side funds, trigger the token’s callback, and in that same transaction call functions of the protocol (such as liquidation or shorting) that rely on the stale asset valuation. The result is that the protocol may release collateral, liquidate positions, or otherwise transfer value based on an incorrect balance, effectively allowing the attacker to extract value that should remain locked. The issue manifests only when the token used in the stream supports callbacks; with standard ERC20 tokens the problem does not appear, which makes it easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Sablier contract suite (file cantina_sablier_mar2023) by the Spearbit team, who noted that the alternating sequence of external calls creates a window for re‑entrancy. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: after cancelling a stream the sender receives their refund, the recipient may receive nothing, and the protocol’s vault may show unchanged asset totals while the attacker’s position is unexpectedly liquidated or profit is realized. The bug violates the core business assumption that the protocol’s accounting is always consistent with the actual token balances after a cancellation. The recommended mitigation is to batch each party’s fund transfer together with its corresponding callback, or otherwise reorder the logic so that the state update occurs before any external call, thereby eliminating the re‑entrancy window. Applying the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern or a non‑reentrant guard would also close the vulnerability.

title: isTransferable() will succeed and return false for non-existent streams
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the view function isTransferable does not check that the stream identifier refers to an existing stream. All other public view functions use a notNull modifier that reverts when the stream does not exist. The missing modifier means that a call with a non‑existent stream returns the default value false instead of reverting, contradicting the NatSpec comment that states the function should revert. The root cause is that the developer omitted the notNull guard when implementing isTransferable, allowing the function to read from an uninitialized storage slot. An attacker or any caller can query an arbitrary streamId that has never been created; the contract will silently return false. This can be exploited in off‑chain logic that assumes a false result means the stream exists but is not transferable, leading to incorrect business decisions such as skipping necessary checks, misreporting stream status, or allowing a user to think a stream is non‑transferable when it actually does not exist. The impact is primarily informational: users, front‑ends, or other contracts may make decisions based on the returned boolean, potentially causing loss of expected functionality, denial of service, or misallocation of funds if downstream logic proceeds under the wrong assumption. The condition occurs whenever isTransferable is called with a streamId that has never been created or has been deleted. All participants that rely on the function – token holders, dApp users, integrators, and other contracts – are affected because they receive misleading data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by checking that each view function respects the notNull modifier as described in the NatSpec documentation. It is subtle because the function does not revert, so no transaction failure is observed; instead it returns a plausible boolean, making the bug easy to miss during testing that only checks for reverts. The proper fix is to add the notNull modifier to the function signature, ensuring that any call with an invalid streamId reverts, aligning the implementation with its documented behavior. This aligns the function with the class of bugs known as missing input validation or unchecked existence checks, which can cause silent logical errors. From a user perspective, a UI that displays “transferable: false” for a stream that never existed may mislead users into thinking a stream is locked, while in reality the stream does not exist, potentially causing confusion or abandoned actions. The expectation that the function will revert on invalid ids is violated, leading to a discrepancy between documented and actual behavior.

title: New protocol fee applies retroactively on debt before fee change
description:
The _withdraw() function applies the protocol fee on the withdrawn amount regardless of whether the debt was accumulated before or after the fee change.
As such, users may be reluctant to use the protocol since:
- The admin can potentially steal 10% from all users at any time
- Even if the admin is not malicious, users can not have conﬁdence in the fee that will be applied up front.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a retroactive protocol fee applied during withdrawal. The contract’s withdraw function reads the current global protocol fee and deducts it from the amount being withdrawn, regardless of whether the underlying debt was generated before or after the fee was changed. Because the fee value is not captured when the stream is created, an admin can increase the fee at any time and the higher fee will be applied to all existing streams when users later call withdraw. This means that a user who deposited when the fee was zero may see a portion of the expected payout disappear after the admin raises the fee, violating the expectation that fees are fixed at stream creation. The issue can be exploited by an admin or any entity with permission to call setProtocolFee; they can raise the fee shortly before a large withdrawal, effectively stealing the fee percentage from users’ accrued balances. The impact is monetary loss for stream participants, loss of confidence in the protocol’s fee model, and potential regulatory concerns. The bug manifests only when the fee is changed after a stream is created but before the stream is withdrawn; streams created after the change are unaffected because they use the new fee at creation. Users experience symptoms such as receiving less USDC than anticipated, sometimes seeing the withdrawal amount reduced to zero when the fee exceeds the withdrawable amount. The problem was discovered during a security audit that added a test case demonstrating that after a fee update the withdraw call transfers the amount minus the new fee, even for debt accrued before the update. The issue is subtle because the contract does not expose the fee used for a particular stream, making it hard for users to predict the cost. The proper mitigation is to store the fee that is in effect at the moment the stream is created as part of the stream’s immutable parameters and to use that stored fee for all subsequent accounting, ensuring that fee changes only affect future streams.

title: Sender can steal deposits from depositors/recipient via refund
description:
Anyone can create a ﬂow and anyone can deposit in to the ﬂow which is used in the case of grants where multiple contributors fund the project as a recipient. The sender is speciﬁed by the creator of the stream and can be the creator, ﬁrst depositor or any other actor.
A sender can also refund the balance of a stream that exceeds the debt accumulated. As such the funds from other depositors can be stolen by the sender if they exceed the current totalDebt.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑refund flaw in a streaming (flow) contract that allows the designated sender to withdraw more funds than the debt owed to the recipient, effectively stealing deposits contributed by other participants. The root cause lies in the refund logic, which calculates the refundable amount as the total stream balance minus the accumulated debt without distinguishing which portion of the balance belongs to the sender versus other depositors. Because the contract does not track per‑depositor contributions, any actor that can act as the sender – including the creator, the first depositor, or an arbitrary address – can invoke the refund function with an amount that exceeds the current totalDebt. By doing so, the sender can transfer the entire remaining balance to themselves, leaving the recipient with insufficient funds and causing subsequent withdraw calls to revert with an overdraw error. This can be exploited in a multi‑depositor scenario: an attacker creates or joins a grant stream, other users deposit tokens, and the attacker then calls refund with the full balance. The contract transfers the requested amount to the attacker, after which the recipient’s withdraw attempts fail because the balance is zero. The impact is the loss of contributed funds for depositors, a breach of trust in the protocol’s accounting, and potential financial damage to users who expect their contributions to be safely held until the recipient claims them. The issue manifests whenever a stream has more than one depositor and the sender exercises the refund function; it does not require any special permissions beyond being recognized as the sender. It was discovered during a security audit by adding a targeted test case that demonstrated the sender’s ability to refund the exact amount deposited by another user, resulting in the attacker’s balance increasing and the recipient’s withdraw failing. The bug can be hard to notice because the refund feature is intended to allow the sender to reclaim excess unallocated funds, and in single‑depositor streams the behavior appears correct; only when multiple parties contribute does the accounting discrepancy become evident. To remediate, the contract should either make streams non‑refundable or restrict refunds to the sender’s own contributions, ensuring that the refundable amount never exceeds the sender’s deposited balance. Conceptually, the fix requires proper accounting of each depositor’s share and preventing unauthorized extraction of other users’ funds, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that contributions are protected until legitimately claimed by the recipient.

title: Refunds processed for incorrect direction
bug_full: The contract implements a refund mechanism that is intended to return funds to the original counterparty when a timelock expires for an incoming transaction. An incoming transaction is identified by a flag (incoming) and the contract pulls the tokens from the counterparty using a transferFrom call. The refund logic, however, checks the opposite condition: it only executes a transfer back to the counterparty when the transaction is marked as outgoing (!incoming). As a result, when a legitimate incoming transaction reaches its timelock and the counterparty requests a refund, the contract does not release the locked tokens; instead, it releases tokens only for outgoing transactions that were never meant to be refunded. This inversion of the direction check is the root cause of the vulnerability. An attacker who knows that the refund function is gated by the wrong flag can trigger a refund on an outgoing transaction and cause the contract to transfer tokens to the counterparty even though no funds were ever deposited for that path, effectively allowing unauthorized withdrawals. Conversely, a legitimate counterparty whose incoming transaction is refunded will receive nothing, leading to a loss of funds that appear to disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue manifests whenever the timelock expires and the refund function is called, affecting any user or counterparty that relies on the refund guarantee. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conditional logic of the refund routine. Because the condition is a single boolean inversion, it can easily slip past basic unit tests that only verify successful refunds for one direction, making the bug hard to notice without explicit coverage of both incoming and outgoing cases. To remediate the problem, the refund condition must be corrected so that the transfer back to the counterparty is executed when the transaction is marked as incoming (incoming == true) rather than when it is outgoing. This aligns the refund flow with the intended business logic that funds pulled from a counterparty should be returned to that same counterparty upon timeout, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from being locked or improperly released.

title: HTLCERC20Settle event emits hashlock instead of preimage
description:
In ForwarderHashedTimelockERC20.sol, the settle function completes a transaction once it receives the preimage from the lightning network. This function also triggers the HTLCERC20Settle event along with the transaction.
The HTLCERC20Settle event is defined as follows:
```solidity
event HTLCERC20Settle(bytes32 indexed preimage, address tokenContract, uint256 amount);
```
When processing outgoing transactions with the settle function, the contract generates the HTLCERC20Settle event, which logs the hashlock value instead of the preimage that unlocks the transaction. In contrast, incoming transactions correctly log the preimage, leading to an inconsistency in the contract's event-logging mechanism.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an event‑logging inconsistency in the HTLCERC20 settlement function of the ForwarderHashedTimelockERC20 contract. When an outgoing hashed timelock transfer is settled, the contract emits the HTLCERC20Settle event with the hashlock value (the commitment hash) instead of the actual preimage that unlocks the transfer. The root cause is a mistaken argument passed to the event during the else branch of the settle function: the code uses the stored hashlock variable rather than the _preimage parameter supplied by the caller. Because the incoming‑direction branch correctly emits the preimage, the discrepancy is only visible for outbound settlements. An attacker or any off‑chain observer who relies on the event to prove that a preimage was revealed cannot obtain the correct data from the blockchain logs; they see a hashlock that does not change, which may be interpreted as a missing or failed settlement. The impact is primarily informational: users, auditors, or monitoring services see an event that suggests the preimage was never disclosed, leading to confusion, potential disputes, and reduced trust in the protocol’s accounting. The bug manifests whenever the settle function is called for an outgoing transaction, i.e., when the contract transfers tokens to the counter‑party after verifying the preimage. It affects all participants who depend on event data for reconciliation, including liquidity providers, bridge operators, and external analytics tools. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s event definitions and the settle implementation, where the emitted arguments were compared against the specification. Because the contract still transfers the correct amount of tokens, the problem does not cause a loss of funds and may be overlooked if only balance changes are inspected. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect event emission or data‑integrity bugs, where the contract records the wrong value in an emitted log, breaking the contract’s observable state. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a settlement transaction with a missing preimage field or a hashlock that remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the preimage should be displayed after settlement. To remediate the issue the settle function should emit the _preimage argument in both branches, ensuring that the HTLCERC20Settle event always carries the actual preimage. This change restores consistency, enables reliable off‑chain verification, and aligns the contract’s observable behavior with its intended business logic of revealing the secret that unlocks the transfer.

title: EVM channel task may terminate early
description:
Currently, the codebase has two main components that interact together: the plugin and EVM channel. The plugin provides the RPC endpoints and send notifications to the EVM channel to execute the underlying logic. These two components are two independent tasks. However, the EVM channel task can terminate early due to multiple return in the task code.
