When this occurs, the plugin component will still handle RPC requests, but there will be no EVM channel task to execute the logic. The plugin will always timeout in this condition. The impacted notification logics in evm_channel are:
• TokenSettleHTLC and TokenForwardHTLC: when the gas oracle fails.
• GetBalance: when one of the balance retrieval fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unexpected early termination of the EVM channel background task that is responsible for processing blockchain‑related notifications. The plugin component, which exposes RPC endpoints to users, runs as a separate asynchronous task and assumes that the EVM channel task is always alive to execute the underlying logic. In the current implementation the EVM channel code contains several unconditional return statements that exit the task loop when certain error conditions occur, such as a failed gas‑price oracle query or an inability to retrieve an on‑chain balance. When one of those returns is hit, the task ends permanently; the plugin continues to accept RPC calls but has no worker to fulfil them, so every request eventually times out. This situation manifests for the notification flows TokenSettleHTLC and TokenForwardHTLC (both of which rely on a successful gas‑oracle lookup) and for GetBalance (which depends on a successful balance query). From a user’s point of view the UI will show operations “stuck”, “settlement failed”, or “balance query returned nothing”, while the user expects a successful settlement or a valid balance. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: HTLC settlements cannot be completed, token forwards are aborted, and balance information becomes unavailable, potentially leaving funds locked in contracts until the service is manually restarted. The bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the plugin and the EVM channel and noticed that the channel task could exit without being respawned. It is hard to notice because the plugin does not crash and no explicit error is logged; only the prolonged RPC timeout reveals the problem. Conceptually the issue belongs to the class of “task‑lifecycle management” or “worker‑termination” bugs where error handling aborts a long‑running service instead of allowing it to continue or be restarted. The proper fix is to replace the premature return statements with control‑flow that keeps the task alive (e.g., using continue to skip the failed iteration) and to add supervisory logic in the main program that detects a terminated channel task and automatically restarts it, ensuring that the plugin always has a functional backend worker.

title: Concurrent RPC requests disrupt execution due to broadcast channel misuse
description:
When a RPC request is received by the lightning node, it is forwarded to a plugin thread which creates a notification sent to the EVM channel through the broadcast channel. A response notification is sent through the same broadcast channel. The following workflow graph shows the expected behaviour.
However, a broadcast channel works by distributing to all subscribers the message sent. Then, when notification_receiver.recv() is called to receive the response from the EVM channel, it may receive a message from a new RPC request that has just arrived. The recv docs indicate:
Receives the next value for this receiver.
Each [Receiver] handle will receive a clone of all values sent after it has subscribed.
First, the plugin receives an RPC request and sends a notification for the EVM channel to process the request. The following graph shows this first step.
But, during the processing of this first RPC request, a new RPC request is received. A new plugin thread is created and sends a message through the broadcast channel. The issue is that this message will be received by the thread of the first RPC request. It will either fail decoding it or decode incorrect value depending on the endpoint. The following graph shows this issue through a red arrow.
Then, the response from the first request will be sent and received by the second thread. It will make both RPC call fail.
poc:
On a local running node, execute the two following commands in parallel in a short timeframe.
Note: ethbalance endpoint is chosen as it makes multiple requests to the Ethereum RPC node so it will take longer to process.
**Execute ethbalance first:** lightning-cli --regtest ethbalance
**Once the first command started, execute the following ASAP:** lightning-cli --regtest ethgas
Both commands fail because:
• ethbalance plugin thread receives the ethgas request.
• ethgas plugin thread receives the ethbalance response.
{
"code": 1,
"message": "No response received on balance request"
}
{
"code": 1,
"message": "Impossible to request gas"
}
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition caused by the misuse of a broadcast channel that delivers notifications from RPC requests to all subscribed plugin threads in a Lightning node. When an RPC request arrives, the node forwards it to a plugin thread which publishes a request notification on the broadcast channel and later expects a response notification on the same channel. Because the broadcast channel clones every message for every subscriber, a second RPC request that arrives while the first request is still being processed can publish its own notification, which is then received by the first plugin thread. The first thread therefore reads a message that belongs to the second request, fails to decode it or decodes an incorrect value, and subsequently the response intended for the first request is consumed by the second thread. This interleaving of messages leads to both RPC calls failing, producing error messages such as "No response received on balance request" or "Impossible to request gas". The issue occurs only when multiple RPC calls are executed concurrently, especially for endpoints that take longer to complete (for example ethbalance). It affects any user or service that relies on the node’s RPC interface, including wallet front‑ends and automated scripts, because they receive missing or incorrect data, which may appear as a balance that suddenly becomes zero or a gas estimate that cannot be retrieved. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by reproducing the failure with two parallel lightning‑cli commands; the nondeterministic nature of the bug makes it hard to notice, as occasional failures can be mistaken for network glitches. The root cause is the lack of a correlation mechanism between request and response messages; the broadcast channel provides no way for a thread to filter out messages that do not belong to its own request. To fix the issue, the notification protocol should embed a unique incremental index or request identifier in each request and require the corresponding response to carry the same identifier, allowing each plugin thread to ignore unrelated messages. Alternatively, a per‑request private channel or a point‑to‑point (mpsc) channel could be used instead of a broadcast channel. This class of bug is generally known as a message‑interleaving race condition or channel hijacking, where concurrent operations corrupt each other's communication streams, violating the expected accounting logic that each request receives exactly one matching response.

title: Plugin approves the EVM contract to pull funds
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unintended ERC20 token allowance that is granted by the TokenForwardHTLC contract (the bridge plugin) to the HTLC contract during a successful Lightning‑to‑EVM transfer. The bridge workflow expects the forward contract to only lock tokens that are explicitly transferred by the user, but the code calls IERC20(_tokenContract).approve(address(this), _amount) as part of the route execution, thereby authorising the HTLC contract to pull the approved amount from the plugin wallet at any later time. This approval is created without any additional checks on the caller of the subsequent settle function, so a malicious actor can craft a route transaction where the counterparty address is set to the plugin wallet, causing the HTLC contract to invoke transferFrom and move the approved tokens to an attacker‑controlled address. The root cause is the misuse of the ERC20 approve mechanism in a context where the forward contract should act only as a passive forwarder, not as a token holder with spending rights. Exploitation is possible whenever the bridge processes a forward transaction; after the approval is in place, any external party that can call the HTLC contract’s route or settle functions can trigger a transferFrom against the plugin’s balance. The impact is the unauthorized draining of funds from the plugin wallet, leading to loss of user assets and a breach of the bridge’s accounting guarantees – users expect their tokens to be transferred only to the intended counterparty, not to be withdrawn by a third party. The condition occurs under normal bridge operation, i.e., after a successful bridging event, and affects any user whose funds are managed by the plugin wallet, as well as the overall protocol’s reputation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge contracts, where the auditor noticed an approve call that was not aligned with the documented flow and recognized that the allowance could be abused. The problem is subtle because the approve call does not revert or emit an obvious warning; it merely creates a silent permission that can be exercised later, making it easy to overlook in functional testing. To remediate, the approval step should be removed entirely, ensuring that the forward contract never grants spending rights to the HTLC contract, and the token transfer logic should rely solely on safeTransferFrom from the user’s address without prior allowance. This correction restores the intended trust model where only the designated counterparty can receive funds, preserving the bridge’s financial integrity and preventing unauthorized token withdrawals.

title: it’s possible to initialize contract BkdLocker for multiple times by sending startBoost=0 and each time different values for other parameters
bug_full:
The vulnerability originates from the initialization routine of the BkdLocker contract, which is intended to be executed only once to set permanent configuration parameters such as startBoost, maxBoost, increasePeriod and withdrawDelay. The routine assumes that a zero value for the startBoost field can be used as an indicator that the contract has not yet been initialized, because it checks `currentUInts256[_START_BOOST] == 0` before proceeding. However, startBoost is a legitimate input that may be set to zero by design, and the contract does not enforce a non‑zero constraint. Consequently, a malicious actor with governance privileges can invoke `initialize` with `startBoost = 0`, causing the check to succeed while still writing arbitrary values to the other configuration slots. Because the flag the contract uses to detect prior initialization is the same storage slot that can be deliberately set to zero, the contract can be re‑initialized multiple times, each time overwriting the boost‑related parameters.

When the parameters are overwritten, the functions that compute user boost (`computeNewBoost`) and the unlock delay (`prepareUnlock`) operate on the newly injected values. These functions are used to determine how rewards are allocated and when users may withdraw their locked tokens. By repeatedly re‑initializing the contract with different `maxBoost`, `increasePeriod` or `withdrawDelay` values, governance can alter the reward‑distribution math in favor of selected accounts, reduce the effective yield for other participants, or create an unfair advantage for themselves. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior—receiving a boost proportional to their locked amount and a predictable withdrawal schedule—no longer holds; users may see their rewards drop unexpectedly, their withdrawal becomes delayed, or they receive nothing at all despite having locked tokens. The symptom on the front‑end could appear as a sudden loss of pending reward balance or a zero‑value boost field where a positive value was anticipated.

The flaw was uncovered during a third‑party audit that examined the contract’s initialization logic and identified that the sole guard (`require(currentUInts256[_START_BOOST] == 0)`) can be bypassed by providing a zero startBoost. The issue is subtle because the check does not raise an exception when the parameter is zero, making the re‑initialization path appear legitimate under the contract’s own rules. Detecting the problem in production would require monitoring the configuration values for unexpected changes, which may not be obvious without explicit logging.

To remediate the issue, the contract should separate the initialization flag from any user‑controlled parameter. A dedicated boolean variable (e.g., `bool initialized`) that is set to true after the first successful call would provide an unambiguous indicator that the contract has already been configured. Alternatively, the contract could enforce `startBoost > 0` as a precondition, ensuring that the guard cannot be satisfied with a deliberately chosen zero value. Any approach that guarantees immutability of the configuration after the first successful initialization would restore the intended security guarantees and prevent governance from arbitrarily altering reward calculations.

In summary, the bug belongs to the class of "re‑initialization or mutable‑configuration vulnerabilities" where an initialization check relies on a mutable value that can be set to its sentinel state, allowing privileged actors to overwrite essential protocol parameters. The attack vector is limited to accounts with governance rights, but its impact can cascade to all token holders by distorting reward distribution, reducing yields, and breaking the economic assumptions of the locker system.

title: `call`
description:
This is a classic Code4rena issue:

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-meebits-findings/issues/2>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-tally-findings/issues/20>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-openleverage-findings/issues/75>
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on Solidity’s built‑in transfer() function to forward Ether to a caller during a claim or withdrawal operation. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas, which is sufficient for a simple external account but insufficient for many smart contracts whose fallback or receive functions perform additional logic, such as logging events, updating storage, or calling other contracts. Because the contract does not anticipate this limitation, the call can revert when the recipient is a contract that requires more gas, causing the entire claim transaction to fail. This failure manifests as a user‑facing symptom where a legitimate claim appears to succeed on‑chain but the user receives no funds, or the transaction reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving the user’s balance unchanged. The root cause is the use of transfer() instead of a low‑level call() that forwards all available gas and returns a success flag, combined with a lack of proper checks‑effects‑interactions (CEI) ordering and missing re‑entrancy protection on the comptroller state. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who deploys a malicious contract with a fallback that deliberately consumes more than 2300 gas, then initiates a claim on behalf of a victim. When the vulnerable contract attempts to transfer the reward, the fallback reverts, causing the claim to fail and potentially locking the reward in the contract if the code does not handle the failure gracefully. The impact is that funds intended for users may become inaccessible, breaking the economic guarantees of the protocol and eroding trust. The bug appears under the condition that the recipient of the Ether is a contract with a non‑trivial fallback, which is common in composable DeFi ecosystems where users often interact through proxy or wrapper contracts. It affects any participant who tries to claim rewards, as well as the protocol itself because locked funds reduce liquidity and can cause cascading failures in downstream contracts that expect those rewards to be distributed. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit, referencing several prior public findings where similar transfer‑related failures caused severe disruptions in Compound forks. It is hard to notice because the failure only occurs when the recipient is a contract; simple EOAs work fine, so tests that only use external accounts may pass. Moreover, the revert may be silent if the calling code does not check the return value of transfer(), leading to hidden loss of funds. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer() with a low‑level call() that forwards all gas, checks the returned success flag, and reverts only if the call fails. The implementation must follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern to update internal state before making the external call, and a global re‑entrancy lock (e.g., a mutex) should be added to the comptroller to prevent re‑entrancy attacks similar to those observed in Rari. By doing so, the protocol ensures that rewards are reliably delivered even to contract wallets, preserving the intended accounting logic and user expectations that a successful claim results in a positive balance change.

title: `COMP` Distributions Can Be Manipulated And Duplicated Across Any Number Of Accounts
description:
[Comptroller.sol#L240-L242](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L240-L242)  
[Comptroller.sol#L260-L262](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L260-L262)  
[Comptroller.sol#L469-L472](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L469-L472)  
[Comptroller.sol#L496-L499](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L496-L499)  
[Comptroller.sol#L1139-L1155](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L1139-L1155)  
[Comptroller.sol#L1222-L1243](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/Comptroller.sol#L1222-L1243)  

The `updateCompSupplyIndex()` and `distributeSupplierComp()` functions are used by Compound to track distributions owed to users for supplying funds to the protocol. Bunker protocol is a fork of compound with NFT integration, however, part of the original functionality appears to have been mistakenly commented out. As a result, whenever users enter or exit the protocol, `COMP` distributions will not be correctly calculated for suppliers. At first glance, its possible that this was intended, however, there is nothing stated in the docs that seems to indicate such. Additionally, the `COMP` distribution functionality has not been commented out for borrowers. Therefore, tokens will still be distributed for borrowers.

Both the `updateCompSupplyIndex()` and `updateCompBorrowIndex()` functions operate on the same `compSpeeds` value which dictates how many tokens are distributed on each block. Therefore, you cannot directly disable the functionality of supplier distributions without altering how distributions are calculated for borrowers. Because of this, suppliers can manipulate their yield by supplying tokens, calling `updateCompSupplyIndex()` and `distributeSupplierComp()`, removing their tokens and repeating the same process on other accounts. This completely breaks all yield distributions and there is currently no way to upgrade the contracts to alter the contract’s behaviour. Tokens can be claimed by redepositing in a previously “checkpointed” account, calling `claimComp()` and removing tokens before re-supplying on another account.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the COMP reward distribution mechanism of the Bunker protocol’s Comptroller contract. The contract inherits Compound’s reward logic, which relies on two separate index update functions – updateCompSupplyIndex() for suppliers and updateCompBorrowIndex() for borrowers – as well as distribution helpers such as distributeSupplierComp(). In the Bunker fork, the code that correctly updates and checkpoints supply‑side rewards has been mistakenly commented out, yet the public functions that read the shared compSpeeds variable remain callable. Because the same compSpeeds value governs both supply and borrow distributions, disabling the supply side without also disabling the borrow side is impossible. Consequently, a malicious supplier can manipulate the reward calculation by performing the following steps: (1) supply assets to the protocol, (2) manually invoke updateCompSupplyIndex() and distributeSupplierComp() to create a checkpoint and accrue COMP tokens, (3) claim the accrued COMP via claimComp(), (4) withdraw the supplied assets, and (5) repeat the process on a fresh address or a previously checkpointed account. By iterating this cycle, the attacker can generate arbitrarily many COMP tokens without providing additional economic activity, effectively duplicating rewards across any number of accounts. The impact is a dilution of the COMP token supply, loss of fairness for legitimate borrowers and suppliers, and potential erosion of confidence in the protocol’s incentive model. This flaw manifests whenever a user interacts with the supply functions – deposit, withdraw, or any other call that triggers the update functions – and it requires no special permissions because the functions are public. The affected parties include all token suppliers, borrowers who rely on a fair reward distribution, and any downstream participants who hold COMP. The issue was uncovered during a source‑code audit that compared Bunker’s implementation with Compound’s reference logic and identified the missing supply‑side update code. It is subtle because the UI does not display supply‑side rewards (the documentation suggests COMP distribution may be disabled), yet the underlying contract still permits reward accrual, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the protocol should either completely disable the supply reward pathway by commenting out or removing all calls to updateCompSupplyIndex() and distributeSupplierComp() and ensuring compSpeeds for suppliers is set to zero, or fully restore the intended logic by uncommenting the missing code, separating supply and borrow speed variables, and adding safeguards that prevent the same supply index from being claimed multiple times. Either approach restores the contract’s accounting invariants and prevents arbitrary reward inflation.

title: Strategy in StakerVault.sol can steal more rewards even though it’s designed strategies shouldn’t get rewards.
description:
Strategy in StakerVault.sol can steal more rewards even though it’s designed strategies shouldn’t get rewards.

Also there will be a problem with a rewarding system in LpGauge.sol so that some normal users wouldn’t get rewards properly.
poc:
1. Strategy A staked amount x and x will be added to StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked.

contracts\StakerVault.sol#L312

2. Strategy A transferred the amount x to non-strategy B and StakerVault.strategiesTotalStaked, StakerVault._poolTotalStaked won’t be updated. contracts\StakerVault.sol#L111

3. After some time for the larger LpGauge.poolStakedIntegral, B claims rewards using the LpGauge.claimRewards() function. contracts\tokenomics\LpGauge.sol#L52

Inside LpGauge.userCheckPoint(), it’s designed not to calculate LpGauge.perUserShare for strategy, but it will pass this condition because B is not a strategy. contracts\tokenomics\LpGauge.sol#L90

Furthermore, when calculate rewards, LpGauge.poolStakedIntegral will be calculated larger than a normal user stakes same amount. It’s because StakerVault._poolTotalStaked wasn’t updated when A transfers x amount to B so LpGauge.poolTotalStaked is less than correct value. contracts\tokenomics\LpGauge.sol#L113-L117

Finally B can get more rewards than he should and the reward system will pay more rewards than it’s designed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the accounting and access‑control logic of the StakerVault contract, which together with the LpGauge reward contract allows a contract classified as a “strategy” to indirectly acquire staking rewards that are intended solely for regular users. A strategy is expected to hold staked tokens without being eligible for reward distribution, and the protocol keeps two separate aggregates: strategiesTotalStaked, which tracks the amount owned by strategies, and _poolTotalStaked, which tracks the amount owned by regular participants. The code fails to adjust these aggregates when a strategy transfers tokens to a non‑strategy address. Specifically, the transfer() and transferFrom() functions do not check the source and destination types, nor do they update the two totals when the transfer crosses the strategy‑non‑strategy boundary. Consequently, the protocol’s reward calculation in LpGauge, which relies on the ratio of a user’s stake to the reported pool total, sees an inflated per‑user share for the non‑strategy recipient. The attacker’s flow is: (1) a user deposits tokens through a strategy, causing the amount to be counted in strategiesTotalStaked; (2) the strategy moves the same amount to a normal address via a plain token transfer; (3) because the internal pool total remains unchanged, the normal address’s stake appears larger relative to the pool, and the LpGauge checkpoint treats it as a regular user, allowing the address to claim rewards that exceed its legitimate entitlement. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the protocol pays out more reward tokens than should exist, while the “lost” yield manifests as a reduction in the overall reward pool for honest participants. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through a proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the mis‑accounting of strategiesTotalStaked after a cross‑type transfer. The bug is subtle because ordinary transfers between two regular users correctly update the pool totals, so the anomaly only appears when a strategy is involved, making it easy to overlook in manual testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should either forbid any token movement between strategy and non‑strategy accounts (by adding a require that the sender and receiver share the same strategy flag) or, more comprehensively, modify the transfer logic to adjust strategiesTotalStaked and _poolTotalStaked whenever a cross‑type transfer occurs, and ensure addStrategy correctly re‑classifies the balances. Both approaches restore the invariant that the sum of strategy and non‑strategy stakes always equals the reported pool total, thereby preventing unintended reward capture and preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Fees from delisted pool still in reward handler will become stuck after delisting
description: Unclaimed fees from pool will be stuck.
poc:
When delisting a pool the pool’s reference is removed from address provider:

Burning fees calls a dynamic list of all pools which no longer contains the delisted pool:

Since the list no longer contains the pool those fees will not be processed and will remain stuck in the contract
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the reward handling contract processes and distributes accumulated fees for liquidity pools. When a pool is removed from the system—typically through a delisting operation—the address of that pool is erased from the central address provider, which maintains the list of active pools. A separate function, often called burnFees or similar, iterates over the current list of pools to allocate each pool’s share of the accumulated fees. Because the delisted pool’s address is no longer present in the list at the time burnFees is invoked, the iteration skips the pool entirely, leaving its portion of fees locked inside the reward handler contract. This flaw is a classic case of a state‑dependency bug where a later operation assumes that all relevant entities remain in a dynamic collection, but a prior state change (delisting) invalidates that assumption. An attacker or simply a negligent maintainer could exploit the issue by deliberately delisting a pool without first invoking the fee‑burning routine, causing the unclaimed fees to become unreachable. The practical impact is that the liquidity providers of the removed pool lose their expected yield; the fees that should have been credited to them disappear from the system’s accounting, effectively reducing the total funds available for distribution. This situation manifests only when the delisting transaction precedes the fee‑distribution call; if burnFees is called before the pool is removed, the problem does not arise. The affected parties include pool participants, the protocol’s revenue model, and any stakeholders relying on accurate fee accounting. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the warden demonstrated the sequence of calls that leads to the loss of yield. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings or revert when fees remain unclaimed, the bug can be difficult to notice during normal operation; balances appear correct for active pools, while the hidden fees silently accumulate for the removed pool. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should enforce a proper ordering of operations—specifically, it must invoke the fee‑burning routine before removing a pool from the address provider. Alternatively, the fee‑distribution function could be redesigned to reference a persistent registry of pools that includes delisted entries until their fees are fully settled, or it could accept an explicit list of pools to settle before deletion. The core fix is to ensure that no pool can be omitted from the fee‑allocation loop while still having a non‑zero fee balance, thereby preserving the accounting invariant that total fees are always distributed or explicitly burned. In summary, the bug constitutes a “post‑delisting fee lock” where rewards become unrecoverable because the system’s dynamic pool list no longer contains the target, causing a mismatch between expected and actual fund flows and violating the protocol’s guarantee of proportional yield distribution.

title: `CNft.sol` - revert inside `safeTransferFrom` will break composability & standard behaviour
description:
[CNft.sol#L204](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/CNft.sol#L204)  

The function safeTransferFrom is a standard interface in ERC1155, and its expected to succeed if all the parameters are valid, and revert on error, which is not the case here so its a deviation.

Refer to the EIP-1155 safeTransferFrom rules:

> MUST revert if _to is the zero address.  
> MUST revert if balance of holder for token _id is lower than the _value sent to the recipient.  
> MUST revert on any other error.  

There is no loss of assets, but the assets or tokens and CNft contract can be unusable by other protocols, and likelihood & impact of this issue is high.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the implementation of the ERC1155 `safeTransferFrom` function within the CNft contract. According to the ERC1155 specification, `safeTransferFrom` must succeed when all parameters are valid and must revert only on genuine errors such as a zero‑address recipient, insufficient holder balance, or other protocol‑level failures. In this contract, the function contains a hardcoded `revert("CNFT: Use safeBatchTransferFrom instead")` at line 204, causing the method to abort even when the transfer parameters are correct. This deviation from the standard breaks the contract’s composability, because any external caller—whether a marketplace, wallet, or another protocol—that relies on the standard `safeTransferFrom` interface will encounter an unexpected revert and be unable to move a token using the single‑transfer path. The root cause is a deliberate but misguided design decision to discourage the use of `safeTransferFrom` by forcing callers to invoke `safeBatchTransferFrom` with a single‑element array instead. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft any special input; simply invoking `safeTransferFrom` will trigger the revert, causing the transaction to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style issue for token holders and integrators: users see their transfer attempts fail with an unclear error, balances appear unchanged, and the token becomes effectively unusable through standard ERC1155 workflows. This condition occurs every time the `safeTransferFrom` entry point is called, affecting all token holders, marketplaces, and any third‑party contracts that expect ERC1155 compliance. The issue was uncovered during a manual code audit that examined the contract’s adherence to the ERC1155 interface and identified the non‑standard revert statement. It can be hard to notice because the revert message is generic and may be overlooked when testing basic transfer scenarios, especially if developers assume batch transfers will cover all use cases. To remediate, the contract should either implement `safeTransferFrom` according to the ERC1155 specification—performing the necessary balance checks and invoking the recipient’s `onERC1155Received` hook—or internally delegate to `safeBatchTransferFrom` while preserving the original function signature and expected behaviour. By aligning the implementation with the standard, the contract regains compatibility with existing tooling, prevents unexpected transaction failures, and restores confidence that token transfers will behave as users anticipate.

title: Chainlink pricer is using a deprecated API
description: According to Chainlink’s documentation, the latestAnswer function is deprecated. This function might suddenly stop working if Chainlink stop supporting deprecated APIs. And the old API can return stale data.
poc: [PriceOracleImplementation.sol#L29-L30](https://github.com/bunkerfinance/bunker-protocol/blob/752126094691e7457d08fc62a6a5006df59bd2fe/contracts/PriceOracleImplementation.sol#L29-L30)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on Chainlink’s latestAnswer function, which the Chainlink documentation marks as deprecated. Because the function is no longer guaranteed to be supported, the oracle may abruptly stop returning values or may continue to return values that are no longer refreshed. The root cause is the use of an outdated API without any validation of the data’s freshness or completeness. An attacker, or simply the natural evolution of the Chainlink service, can cause the contract to receive a stale price or a zero value, which the contract then uses for critical calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, and fee assessment. When the price feed returns an out‑of‑date or missing price, the protocol may underestimate the value of deposited assets, triggering premature liquidations, mispriced trades, or denial of service when the function reverts. This situation occurs whenever Chainlink decides to discontinue the deprecated endpoint or when the feed has not been updated for a period longer than the contract expects. All participants who interact with the pricing logic — borrowers, lenders, and any user whose balances depend on accurate market data — are affected because the protocol’s business rules assume that the price is current and reliable. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that identified the call to latestAnswer instead of the recommended latestRoundData and noted the lack of any freshness checks. It may be hard to notice because the function continues to return a numeric value, so tests that only check for a non‑zero return will pass, while the underlying data may be arbitrarily old. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the deprecated call with latestRoundData, verify that the returned round is complete, compare its timestamp against a reasonable freshness window, and revert with clear error messages if the data is stale. By enforcing these checks, the protocol restores its guarantee that pricing information reflects the latest market state, preventing inadvertent loss of funds and maintaining the intended economic guarantees of the system.

title: Incorrect rounding in _convertToShares for withdrawal-based actions leads to 1 dead share for users
description:
The _convertToShares function currently does floor rounding in all cases. This works correctly for any deposit actions. In the case of withdrawals, it ends up rounding down the shares needed to withdraw for a set amount of equity. Thereby, this leads to instances where if users attempt to withdraw all equity they have that requires more than 1 share, such as in the case of 50 shares representing the user's entire equity, they will have 1 share remaining. The final effect is different depending on a combination of decimal and price differential between the associated collateral and debt tokens for a Leveraged Token.  
In the ETH2x Long case, the collateral asset is ETH represented with 18 decimals, while the debt asset is USDC represented with 6. If there's a lone user in the LT and withdraws all their equity, they will succeed in withdrawing it and repaying all debt. Following this, all equity is withdrawn, but the user will remain with 1 dead share. Even if more equity enters, this dead share is unusable in this case, and can't be withdrawn.  
In the ETH2x Short case, the collateral is USDC and ETH is the debt. Since ETH as the debt has more precision, it leads to a case where requesting all equity, results in 1 leftover share, with fractional equity and debt being represented in that share. A secondary withdrawal action is required with 1 share to completely remove a user's position. This case doesn't lead to dead shares, but requires 2 withdrawal actions.  
Other than the dead share that can't be withdrawn or leftover share requiring 2 withdrawals, the effect this can have on Leveraged Tokens in the first case is an artificial overinflation of the total supply (as these shares will permanently keep it increased even though there's no equity backing it) that can't be removed. This results in an increased dilution to current Leveraged Token holders proportional to the amount of unique accounts that have attempted a complete withdrawal and have 1 dead share remaining, to the benefit of future deposits. This effect should generally not be significant enough in non-inflation attacked tokens, however, this effect can be greatly amplified if a token has been inflated.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a rounding mistake in the internal share conversion routine used by leveraged token contracts. The function that translates a user’s equity amount into token shares always applies floor rounding, regardless of whether the operation is a deposit or a withdrawal. For deposits this behaviour is acceptable, but when a user attempts to withdraw their entire equity the floor operation truncates the exact number of shares required, leaving a fractional remainder that is rounded down. Consequently the contract records that the user still owns one share even though the corresponding equity and debt have already been settled. In practice this manifests as a “dead share” that cannot be redeemed in a single transaction; the user must perform an additional withdrawal of exactly one share to clear the position, or the share remains permanently stranded. The problem is amplified in tokens where the collateral and debt assets have different decimal precisions, such as an ETH‑based long token (ETH collateral 18 decimals, USDC debt 6 decimals) or a short token (USDC collateral, ETH debt). In the long case the dead share is truly unusable, inflating the total supply of shares without any backing equity, which dilutes existing holders because the share count is higher while the asset pool is unchanged. In the short case the leftover share forces a second withdrawal step but does not create dead supply. The issue appears only when a user fully exits a position and the required share count exceeds an integer boundary by less than one share, a scenario that is rare and therefore easy to miss during routine testing. It was uncovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, who noted the mismatch between rounding direction and the financial semantics of withdrawals. From a user perspective the symptoms are confusing: after a successful withdrawal the UI may still display a non‑zero token balance, or the user may see that their balance cannot be reduced to zero despite having no remaining equity, leading to “funds disappear” or “share stuck” messages. The bug violates the core accounting invariant that total shares should always correspond to the total underlying equity and debt, breaking the expected one‑to‑one relationship. To remediate the issue the conversion routine should use ceiling rounding for withdrawal actions, ensuring that the calculated share amount is never less than the exact amount needed to settle the user’s equity. Adjusting the rounding mode and updating all callers to pass the correct action context restores the invariant, eliminates dead shares, and prevents artificial supply inflation.

title: Re-entrancy risk with ERC777 tokens in multiple functions
bug_full: The contract provides two public entry points – deposit and depositWithPermit – that allow a user to transfer ERC20 tokens into a vault and receive minted shares. The implementation assumes that the transferred token follows the ERC20 standard, which does not invoke any callbacks during a transfer. However, ERC777 tokens introduce a tokensReceived hook that is executed by the token contract after the transfer but before the caller’s execution resumes. Because the deposit functions perform external calls (such as safeApprove, vault.enter, and the permit call) before they finalize internal accounting and before any re‑entrancy protection is applied, a malicious ERC777 token can trigger its hook to call back into the same deposit function (or another state‑changing function) while the contract’s state is still partially updated. This ordering creates a classic re‑entrancy window. An attacker who controls an ERC777 token can craft the hook to re‑enter deposit, cause the contract to mint additional shares, and bypass the share‑lock period that is supposed to restrict when newly minted shares become transferable. The attacker may also repeat the process through depositWithPermit, using the permit call as an additional entry point. The vulnerability manifests only when the contract is not paused, the token is listed as supported, and the token implements the ERC777 hooks – conditions that are true for several tokens in the supported list. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour is that a deposit results in a single share allocation that is locked for a defined period; under attack the user may see their balance unchanged while the attacker extracts value, or the protocol may show an unexpected increase in total shares, effectively “money disappears” from the vault. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s external calls against the ERC777 specification and noticed the lack of a non‑reentrant guard or a checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. Because ERC777 hooks are rarely used, the problem can be easy to miss in testing that only covers standard ERC20 transfers. To remediate the flaw the contract should enforce a re‑entrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or restructure the code so that all state changes occur before any external token call, and optionally restrict deposits to tokens that do not implement ERC777 callbacks. This would close the re‑entrancy window, preserve the intended share‑lock semantics, and protect user funds from being siphoned through malicious token hooks.

title: Missing checks in the bulkDeposit and bulkWithdraw functions
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing safety checks in the bulkDeposit (and bulkWithdraw) entry points of a multi‑asset vault contract. The function that allows accounts with the on‑ramp role to deposit ERC20 tokens does not verify two conditions that are enforced elsewhere: whether the contract is currently paused and whether the token being deposited is listed as a supported asset. Because the pause flag is intended to stop public deposits, the absence of this guard means that even when the contract owner has paused the system, a privileged caller can still push tokens into the vault. Likewise, the lack of an isSupported validation permits any ERC20 contract – including malicious or non‑standard tokens – to be accepted. An attacker who controls an on‑ramp address could therefore deposit an unsupported token while the system is paused, causing the vault’s accounting to record a balance for a token that the protocol does not recognise or cannot later process. This can lead to funds becoming unrecoverable, withdrawals failing, or the contract entering an inconsistent state where internal accounting assumes a token is supported while external logic rejects it. The issue manifests only when the bulkDeposit (or bulkWithdraw) path is used, which is typically hidden behind role‑based access control, making it easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation of bulkDeposit with other deposit functions and noted the missing require statements. The problem is subtle because the function emits a successful event and returns share tokens, giving the impression that the operation succeeded, while downstream logic may later reject the asset. To remediate, the contract should add a pause check (e.g., require(!paused, ...) ) and an asset support check (e.g., require(isSupported(depositAsset), ...) ) to the bulkDeposit and bulkWithdraw functions, or explicitly document and enforce a different security model for privileged deposits. By restoring these guards the protocol regains its intended invariant that only approved assets can be stored and that pausing truly halts all deposit activity, preventing accidental loss of funds or exploitation of unsupported token behaviour.

bug_full: The vulnerability consists of minting share tokens for an asset that does not exist because the contract uses solmate's SafeTransferLib to move ERC20 tokens without first verifying that the supplied token address is a deployed contract. The root cause is the missing contract‑address check in SafeTransferLib, which contrasts with OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 that performs such validation. When a caller invokes the enter function and passes the zero address or any address without contract code as the asset parameter, the safeTransferFrom call silently succeeds (it performs a low‑level call that returns true even though no code is executed). Consequently the function proceeds to mint the requested amount of shares and emits events as if a real token transfer occurred. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a non‑existent token address, causing the protocol to record shares that are backed by no actual assets. The immediate impact is an accounting discrepancy: the vault’s totalShares counter increases while the underlying asset balance remains unchanged, leading to inflated share supply and potential dilution of legitimate holders. If later a contract is deployed at the same address, the previously minted shares could be claimed against real tokens, opening a route for fund extraction. The issue manifests whenever the enter (or bulkDeposit) function is called with an arbitrary address that is not a contract, which may happen unintentionally due to user error or malicious input. All participants who rely on the share token – users, auditors, and the protocol itself – are affected because the share accounting no longer reflects true asset holdings. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined token transfer handling and observed that transactions with the zero address did not revert. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert and emits normal events, making the discrepancy visible only through deeper state inspection or mismatched balances. To remediate, the contract should replace solmate's SafeTransferLib with a library that validates the token address, such as OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20, or add an explicit require statement checking that the asset address contains contract code before attempting the transfer. This change restores the invariant that each minted share corresponds to a real token deposit, preserving accounting integrity and preventing the creation of phantom shares.

title: Hardcoded deadline in the DEX interaction
description:
In the DexSwapperUManager.sol contract, specifically in the swapWithUniswapV3 function, the deadline parameter for the IUniswapV3Router.ExactInputParams struct is set to block.timestamp. This means that the deadline for the trade is set to the current block timestamp, which could lead to issues if the trade execution is delayed due to network congestion or other factors.  
Hardcoding the deadline in this manner can result in failed transactions if the deadline is exceeded before the trade is executed. This can cause users to lose their funds or incur additional transaction fees when attempting to resubmit the trade.  
```solidity
IUniswapV3Router.ExactInputParams memory params = IUniswapV3Router.ExactInputParams({
    path: packedPath,
    recipient: boringVault,
    deadline: block.timestamp,
    amountIn: amountIn,
    amountOutMinimum: amountOutMinimum
});
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded deadline value in a Uniswap V3 swap call. In the swapWithUniswapV3 function the deadline field of the ExactInputParams struct is set to block.timestamp, which represents the current block time. The deadline parameter is intended to define a future point in time after which the trade must be rejected; using the current timestamp therefore creates a zero‑length window for execution. The root cause is a logical mistake in the contract’s time‑bound logic: the developer assumed that the current block timestamp would be sufficient, but failed to account for any latency between transaction submission and block inclusion. An attacker or even normal network congestion can cause the transaction to be mined in a later block, at which point block.timestamp will be greater than the hard‑coded deadline and the router will revert the swap. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful token exchange – does not occur; instead the transaction fails, the user receives no output tokens, and may be forced to resubmit the trade, incurring additional gas costs. In some implementations the contract may have already transferred the input tokens to the router before the revert, leaving the user’s funds temporarily locked or requiring a manual recovery step. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, where the code was examined for proper parameter handling. It is subtle because the deadline field is syntactically correct and block.timestamp is a legitimate value, so a quick visual scan may not reveal the problem. The bug belongs to the class of time‑bound logic errors or deadline misconfiguration, similar to using an expired timestamp for a payment deadline. To remediate the issue the contract should accept a deadline argument supplied by the caller, or compute a future deadline such as block.timestamp + bufferTime, allowing enough time for the transaction to be mined. This change restores the intended safety guarantee that the swap will either succeed within the allotted window or fail cleanly without unexpected fund loss, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations and standard DEX interaction patterns.

title: Protect external facing LeverageManager functions from reentrancy
description:
A number of the external functions in LeverageManager, namely deposit, withdraw, rebalance, and createNewLeverageToken read and change state, while doing external calls to user-specifiable contracts. This could result in exploits by temporarily affecting the contract's state through one of these functions initial calls and then re-entering into another to take advantage of this modified state.  
Some attacks have been considered with deposit and withdraw as the entrypoints, but utilizing reentrancy on them would likely not benefit an attacker. Others utilizing rebalance may allow a Leveraged Token to be put into a temporarily invalid state, where isStateAfterRebalanceValid would normally not pass, however, a reentrance would allow this invalid state to be utilized for minting shares at a discounted rate. Following the minting, the middle execution of rebalance can be cleaned up and it reset to a valid state to allow the transaction to confirm without reverting.
bug_full: The LeverageManager contract exposes several external functions—deposit, withdraw, rebalance and createNewLeverageToken—that both modify internal state and perform external calls to contracts supplied by the caller. Because these functions lack a reentrancy guard, an attacker can craft a malicious callee that re‑enters the LeverageManager during the external call, thereby observing a temporarily altered state before the original execution finishes. The root cause is the classic checks‑effects‑interactions pattern being violated: state changes are performed after an external call, or the external call occurs before the contract has locked its state. In practice an attacker can invoke rebalance, trigger a call to a malicious contract, and during that callback re‑enter a minting path while the internal accounting variables are in an inconsistent, “invalid” state that would normally be rejected by the isStateAfterRebalanceValid check. By minting shares at a discounted rate while the contract believes the leveraged token is still in a pre‑rebalance condition, the attacker can acquire more value than entitled, later allowing the rebalance to complete and the contract to return to a valid state without reverting. The impact includes unauthorized creation of leveraged token shares, dilution of existing holders, and potential loss of value for honest participants. The vulnerability manifests whenever any of the listed functions is called with a user‑controlled contract that can execute a callback, i.e., when the external call is not protected by a nonReentrant modifier or similar lock. All users of the leveraged token, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity, are affected because the exploit can change the token’s supply and pricing logic. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of state changes and external calls. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear to perform legitimate operations and the external calls are expected to be to trusted contracts; the reentrancy window is subtle and only visible when a malicious contract deliberately re‑enters. To remediate, the contract should apply a reentrancy guard such as the nonReentrant modifier to every external state‑changing entry point, or restructure the code to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, ensuring that all state updates occur before any external call and that a lock is held during the entire execution. This will prevent an attacker from exploiting the temporary invalid state and protect the accounting invariants of the leveraged token system.

title: UniswapV3DecoderAndSanitizer allows strategies to drain the vault through providing malicious positions on UniV3
description:
The UniswapV3DecoderAndSanitizer supports two methods for providing liquidity. The first is through mint, where the provided tokens are checked. The second is through increaseLiquidity, where it verifies that the owner of the position is the boringVault. However, this validation is not sufficient to prevent malicious strategies from draining the boringVault  
• For increaseLiquidity, since the increaseLiquidity function only verifies that the owner of the current position is the boringVault, an exploiter can send a malicious UniswapV3 position to the boringVault and trigger increaseLiquidity to have the boringVault provide liquidity to the malicious position, thereby enabling the exploiter to profit.  
For example, let's assume the base token of the Vault is USDT. The exploiter can first create a fake token, FAKE, and establish a FAKE-USDT market on UniswapV3. By sending a dust position of FAKE-USDT to the boringVault, the UniswapV3DecoderAndSanitizer would consider it a valid position and proceed to provide liquidity to the FAKE-USDT market. The exploiter can then profit by buying all USDT on the FAKE-USDT market.  
• For mint, since the UniswapV3DecoderAndSanitizer only checks the tokens of the market. The malicious strategy can provide liquidity at a malicious tick. Providing liquidity at a malicious tick is similar to selling tokens at a really bad price. It creates a arbitrage space for the exploiter to further take profit by selling tokens on the market.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniswapV3DecoderAndSanitizer component that is used by the boringVault to add liquidity to Uniswap V3 pools. The contract provides two entry points – a mint function that checks only that the supplied token pair matches the expected market, and an increaseLiquidity function that merely verifies that the owner of the existing position is the vault. Because the validation stops at these superficial checks, an attacker can craft a malicious Uniswap V3 position and submit it to the vault. In the increaseLiquidity path the attacker creates a fake token, pairs it with the vault’s base token (for example USDT), and sends a tiny “dust” position to the vault. The decoder sees that the position is owned by the vault and therefore calls Uniswap to increase liquidity, effectively allocating the vault’s USDT to a pool that the attacker controls. The attacker can then trade against that pool, buying all USDT at a favorable price and draining the vault’s funds. In the mint path the attacker can supply a legitimate token pair but choose a malicious tick or fee tier, causing the vault to provide liquidity at an extreme price. This creates an arbitrage window where the attacker can sell the base token at a heavily discounted rate, again extracting value from the vault. The issue occurs whenever a strategy interacts with the decoder to provide liquidity without additional constraints on the pool parameters. It affects the vault itself, its users, and any token holders whose assets are managed by the vault because the vault may lose a substantial portion of its capital. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, where the logical assumption that ownership verification is sufficient was challenged. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit obvious errors; from a user interface perspective the vault appears to have successfully added liquidity, while the underlying accounting shows a sudden reduction in the base token balance. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient input validation and trust‑boundary violations, specifically allowing untrusted external positions to be injected into a financial primitive. To remediate, the decoder should enforce strict validation of the pool’s fee tier, tick range, and token addresses, and should only accept positions that originate from a whitelist of known, vetted pools. Additional checks could include confirming that the position’s price range aligns with the vault’s risk parameters and that the caller is an authorized strategy. By tightening these constraints the vault can prevent malicious positions from being used to siphon funds, preserving the expected accounting behavior where users receive liquidity tokens that correspond to legitimate market conditions.

title: The slippage protection in the MicroManager does not account for the harvested rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the slippage protection logic of the MicroManager used by the BoringVault. The contract records the balance of the output token before a managed trade, executes the trade via manager.manageVaultWithMerkleVerification, then measures the balance change and converts that delta into an equivalent input‑token value using a price router. The check only verifies that this quoted value is not lower than the expected amount after applying the allowed slippage tolerance. Because the calculation only considers the token balance delta that results directly from the swap, it ignores any additional tokens that may be credited to the vault after the swap completes, such as harvested rewards. When a strategy or an attacker initiates a trade that simply transfers tokens out of the vault and then immediately calls a reward‑claim function (for example Pendle Finance’s redeemDueInterestAndRewards), the vault’s token balance increases due to the newly claimed rewards. This increase inflates the quoted token‑in value, causing the slippage condition to appear satisfied even though the net outflow of user‑owned assets exceeds the permitted limit. An attacker can therefore withdraw the intended swap amount and also capture the newly claimed rewards, effectively stealing funds that should belong to the vault’s users. The issue manifests whenever the vault holds assets that generate claimable rewards and the reward‑claim function is callable by arbitrary addresses within the same transaction as a managed trade. It was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the slippage check does not account for balance changes unrelated to the swap path. The bug is subtle because the slippage logic looks correct at first glance; the extra reward credit occurs after the balance delta is measured, so the protection appears to work while silently allowing extra value to be extracted. To remediate, the slippage verification should be extended to include any token balance increase that occurs during the managed call, or the contract should sanitize the entire swap path and prevent the caller from influencing reward claims within the same transaction. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce that reward‑claiming functions are executed in separate transactions or that the slippage check is performed after all balance modifications, ensuring that harvested rewards are not mistakenly counted as legitimate swap proceeds. This class of bug falls under improper accounting of token inflows during slippage checks, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual token values and resulting in potential loss of user funds.

title: Malicious strategies can bypass slippage protection to drain the BoringVault with Reentrancy attacks
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a vault contract that allows external strategy contracts to manage token swaps on its behalf. The contract attempts to protect users from excessive slippage by recording the token balance of the vault before a swap, executing the swap through a manager call, measuring the balance change afterwards, and reverting if the quoted value of the received token is lower than the expected amount after applying the allowed slippage tolerance. However, the manager call is an external interaction that does not employ any re‑entrancy guard. Because the balance check is performed after the external call, a malicious strategy can re‑enter the vault during the swap execution and modify the vault’s token balance before the delta is calculated. By depositing tokens that it controls (or by moving tokens into the vault) during this re‑entrancy window, the attacker inflates the observed balance increase, causing the slippage verification to succeed even though the actual swap transferred all tokens to the attacker. The attacker then withdraws the newly minted vault shares, effectively draining the vault. This flaw occurs whenever a strategy is executed via the manager’s manageVaultWithMerkleVerification function, which makes external calls without a non‑reentrant modifier. All participants who deposit into the vault – including regular users and the protocol itself – are at risk because the vault’s accounting assumptions are violated; the protocol expects that the token balance can only change as a result of the swap, not through concurrent re‑entrancy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing re‑entrancy protection despite the presence of a slippage check. It is difficult to notice in standard testing because the slippage logic appears correct in isolation, and the exploit only manifests when a malicious contract deliberately re‑enters during the external call. To remediate, the contract should enforce a protocol‑wide re‑entrancy lock around the entire manageVault operation or, alternatively, snapshot the vault balance before any external interaction and perform the slippage verification using that immutable snapshot. Applying the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern or adding a nonReentrant modifier will prevent the balance manipulation and restore the intended safety guarantees of the slippage protection.

title: Inconsistency in minimum value out for native deposits via receive function
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the handling of native token deposits through the contract's receive() fallback. The receive() function forwards the call to the internal deposit() routine with a hard‑coded minimum‑out parameter of zero. In the ERC20 deposit path the caller must supply a minMint value that protects against slippage; the native path lacks this safeguard. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum amount of minted shares, a user who sends ether may receive fewer shares than expected, or even zero shares, if the share price moves unfavourably between the moment the transaction is signed and when it is mined. This can happen especially in volatile markets where the price of the underlying asset changes rapidly. The root cause is the omission of a slippage check for native deposits and the use of a fixed zero value instead of propagating a user‑provided bound. An attacker does not need to interact directly; any user sending ether through the receive() function is exposed. The impact is a potential loss of value for users, as they may be minted an amount of shares that does not meet their expectations, leading to perceived “funds disappearing” or “refund calculation error”. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the two deposit entry points and noted the missing min‑out validation. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds and the contract does not revert; the only symptom is an unexpected share balance after the deposit. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent input validation / missing slippage protection” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the receive() function should be removed or modified to require a user‑specified minimum output, aligning its behaviour with the ERC20 deposit flow. This restores the guarantee that users receive at least the amount of shares they anticipate, preserving accounting integrity and protecting against market volatility.

title: Rewards will be lost if a gauge is killed before ﬁrst period ﬁnishes
bug_full: A reward‑distribution bug exists in the gauge‑termination logic of the protocol. When a new gauge is created, rewards for the current period are allocated, but because votes are only counted for the next period, the first period has a poolTotalVotesPerPeriod value of zero. The internal function that calculates claimable rewards multiplies the total reward for the period by the pool’s vote weight and then divides by the total votes. With zero votes the numerator becomes zero and the function returns zero claimable amount. The killGauge routine iterates over undistributed periods and only marks a period as distributed when the additional claimable amount is greater than zero. Consequently, if the gauge is killed before the first period ends, the loop sees a zero claimable amount, leaves the period undistributed and does not set the distributed flag. Later, the stuckEmissionsRecovery mechanism, which is supposed to reclaim undistributed rewards, checks the distributed flag and therefore cannot recover the funds, leaving the rewards permanently locked. This situation can be triggered by any actor with permission to kill a gauge – for example an admin or a malicious governance proposal – who terminates the gauge early. The impact is that protocol‑allocated reward tokens disappear from the system: users who expected a refund or pending reward see no increase in their balance, dashboards may still show an allocated amount but the withdrawal function returns zero, and the overall incentive model is broken because the accounting assumption that every period will eventually be distributed is violated. The bug is subtle because the calculations return zero silently; there is no revert or explicit error, so the loss is not obvious during normal testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the killGauge function and the reward‑claim calculation, where the interaction between vote timing and period finalisation was examined. The issue belongs to the class of “zero‑vote period reward lock” bugs, where a reward distribution routine assumes a non‑zero denominator and fails to handle the edge case where no participants have voted yet. To remediate the problem the recovery function should be extended to allow reclamation of rewards for periods that have a positive totalRewardPerPeriod but zero voting weight, or the termination logic should be changed to force distribution of any remaining rewards regardless of vote count. Either approach restores the intended accounting flow, ensuring that rewards are either claimable by participants or recoverable by the protocol when a gauge is removed before any votes are recorded.

title: ERC1967Factory: Unsafe memory pointer allocation
description:
In the ERC1967Factory contract the _initCode function is responsible for allocating memory and for writing the deployment bytecode for proxies to memory. In an effort to save gas the function does not adjust the memory pointer to indicate that the section of memory storing the bytecode is now in use.
Not only is this not memory safe, creating a pointer to memory that may be reallocated/used by other parts of the code can lead to bugs if a developer attempts to inherit from and use the ERC1967Factory contract and subsequently implicitly allocates some memory.
Standalone the ERC1967Factory contract seems to be correct, however, this issue is still relevant because there's no indication to potential users of the Solady library that the ERC1967Factory.sol:ERC1967Factory contract is not intended for 3rd party use. The ﬁle sits under the library's src/utils/ folder along with other libraries intended for use by library consumers & does not have any comments directly indicating that it's not for consumption by library users.
Beyond being unsafe the _initCode function also violates Solidity's conventions. Typically bytes memory pointers in Solidity are expected to point to a word of memory storing the length of the data directly followed by the data itself. The memory pointer created by the _initCode directly points to a static piece of data, offset by 19 bytes and not having any length.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC1967Factory contract's internal _initCode function, which builds the creation bytecode for proxy contracts. Instead of advancing Solidity's free‑memory pointer after writing the bytecode, the function leaves the pointer unchanged and returns a raw memory address that points directly to a static slice of data offset by 19 bytes, without a preceding length word. This breaks Solidity's memory layout conventions where a bytes memory variable must start with a 32‑byte length field followed by the data. Because the free‑memory pointer is not updated, the region of memory that holds the init code is considered free by the runtime and may be overwritten by any subsequent allocation performed by the same transaction or by a contract that inherits from ERC1967Factory. When a developer extends the factory or calls _initCode from another contract, the implicit memory allocation performed later can corrupt the stored bytecode, leading to deployment of a proxy with malformed or truncated init code. From a user's perspective this may appear as a proxy that fails to initialize, returns no code, or behaves unexpectedly after deployment, effectively causing funds to become inaccessible or the contract to revert on calls. The issue is subtle because the factory works correctly in isolation; the memory corruption only manifests when the contract is used as a library component, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests. The root cause is the unsafe handling of memory pointers and the violation of Solidity's expected bytes memory format. The impact is limited to contracts that rely on ERC1967Factory for proxy creation, potentially affecting any third‑party developer who inherits from it, as well as end‑users whose assets are managed by the resulting proxies. The problem was identified during a security audit of the Solady library, where the auditors noted the lack of documentation indicating that the factory is intended only for standalone deployment and observed the non‑standard memory pointer returned by _initCode. To remediate, the contract should either be clearly marked as a standalone component and isolated from library consumers, or, if it is meant for third‑party use, the _initCode function must update the free‑memory pointer to reserve the written bytecode and return a properly formatted bytes memory value that includes the length prefix. Additionally, documentation should be added to warn developers about the memory safety considerations, and the file should be relocated to a folder that signals its special status.

title: AccessHub missing functionality
description:
In the current codebase, many functions are decorated with the onlyGovernance modifier, indicating they are intended to be called by the AccessHub contract. However, the AccessHub contract does not implement the necessary external calls to invoke these functions. To address this, the following functions should have corresponding implementations within the AccessHub contract:
1. Voter.createArbitraryGauge.
2. Voter.setMainTickSpacing.
3. Voter.stuckEmissionsRecovery.
4. LauncherPlugin.label.
5. XShadow.migrateOperator.
6. XShadow.rescueTrappedTokens.
7. XShadow.operatorRedeem.
8. XShadow.unpause.
9. XShadow.pause.
10. PairFactory.setSkimEnabled.
11. PairFactory.setFeeSplit.
12. PairFactory.setFeeSplitWhenNoGauge.
13. PairFactory.setTreasury.
14. PairFactory.setFee.
15. RamsesV3Factory.setFeeProtocol.
16. RamsesV3Factory.setFeeCollector.
17. x33.transferOperator.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of privileged functions that are protected by an onlyGovernance modifier, which is intended to restrict calls to the central AccessHub contract. In the deployed code the AccessHub contract does not contain external wrappers that forward calls to these privileged functions, meaning that no entity, including the designated governance address, can invoke them. The root cause is a mismatch between the access control design and the actual implementation: the contract author declared the onlyGovernance restriction but omitted the corresponding external entry points in AccessHub. As a result, any attempt to perform governance actions such as creating arbitrary gauges, adjusting tick spacing, recovering stuck emissions, labeling plugins, migrating or rescuing operators, pausing or unpausing contracts, changing fee parameters, or transferring operator rights will silently fail because the call cannot reach the target function. An attacker cannot directly exploit the onlyGovernance functions because they are still protected, but the absence of a legitimate call path creates a governance dead‑lock: the protocol cannot be upgraded, fees cannot be adjusted, emergency pause cannot be triggered, and trapped tokens cannot be rescued. This situation may lead to funds becoming effectively inaccessible, fee structures remaining stale, and the system being unable to respond to emergencies, which undermines the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a governance transaction is submitted through the AccessHub interface; the transaction reverts or does nothing, leaving users with expectations of a successful operation (for example, a user expects a pause but sees no change in contract state, or expects a token rescue but the balance stays unchanged). The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the list of onlyGovernance‑protected functions with the public methods exposed by AccessHub and found a large gap. Because the functions are internal and the AccessHub simply lacks the forwarding code, the defect can be hard to notice without a systematic review of access control mappings. The recommended remediation is to add external functions in AccessHub that call each of the privileged methods, preserving the onlyGovernance check, or to redesign the access control so that the intended caller is correctly wired. Implementing these wrappers restores the ability of governance to manage the protocol, ensures that emergency controls work as expected, and prevents funds from becoming permanently locked due to missing administrative pathways.

title: ERC20: Memory unsafe assembly is not future proof
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in an ERC20 library function that builds an EIP‑712 domain separator using inline assembly marked as memory‑safe. The routine first caches the current free‑memory pointer, then invokes a view function that returns the token name, and finally writes several 32‑byte words to the previously cached pointer before hashing the data. Because the name‑returning function also reads and writes to the free‑memory area, the cached pointer may no longer point to unused memory when the assembly stores the domain data. This overlap can corrupt the temporary buffer that holds the token name, causing the subsequent keccak256 calculation to use altered input. The root cause is the incorrect assumption that the free‑memory pointer remains stable across a call to a memory‑using function, combined with an assembly annotation that falsely guarantees safety. Exploitation becomes possible when the Solidity compiler or optimizer decides to inline the domain‑separator routine together with the name function, as may happen in newer compiler versions or with aggressive optimization flags. In such a scenario the overwritten memory leads to an incorrect domain separator hash, which breaks the integrity of EIP‑712 signatures: contracts that verify signed messages may reject legitimate signatures or accept forged ones if the domain separator is mismatched. Users attempting to sign or verify off‑chain messages may see unexpected failures, such as “signature verification failed” or “invalid domain”. The issue primarily affects developers and protocols that rely on the library’s DOMAIN_SEPARATOR for meta‑transactions, permit signatures, or any functionality that depends on correct EIP‑712 domain data.
