It was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the assembly blocks as memory‑safe despite the presence of a preceding call that manipulates memory. The problem is subtle because the immediate result of the name call is consumed directly by the hash function, so typical unit tests that only check the returned hash may pass, masking the underlying memory corruption. To remediate, the free‑memory pointer should be re‑loaded after the name function returns, or the assembly should avoid using a cached pointer altogether, ensuring that any memory writes occur on a region that is guaranteed to be free. In broader terms, the bug exemplifies a class of unsafe inline‑assembly patterns where developers assume memory safety without accounting for compiler‑generated memory usage, leading to potential data corruption and signature verification failures.

title: ECDSA: Empty signature can result in valid recovered address
description:
```solidity
The ECDSA.recover(bytes32, bytes memory) and ECDSA.tryRecover(bytes32, bytes memory) functions each take a hash and bytes signature argument carrying the components of an ECDSA
signature r || s || v and attempt to recover the signer's Ethereum address via the EVM's ecrecover
precompile. The only difference between the two is that recover will revert if no valid signer could be
recovered and tryRecover fails silently, returning the zero-address.
The ecrecover precompile takes 4 words (128 bytes) as input: hash || bytes31(0) || v || r || s. To
save gas on memory expansion costs, Solady's ECDSA library temporarily overwrites the memory region
0x00-0x80 (including the free memory pointer at [0x40:0x60) and the default null pointer at [0x60:0x80))
for the precompile's input. To save gas the functions ﬁrst optimistically copies the 65 bytes of the signature
from memory and then validate its length. This means that if the signature is <65 bytes long it may copy
out-of-bound data, the length check is meant to still invalidate such signatures.
There is however an edge case that is unaccounted for: uninitialized bytes memory objects. These point
to 0x60 giving them a length of zero thanks to the default null pointer. If such a signature is validated
the recover functions will copy the data at [0x80:0xc1] which may have other variables allocated. The
optimistic copy will overwrite the null pointer at 0x60 temporarily changing the implicit length to the word
at 0xa0. This can allow a non-zero address to be recovered from an empty signature.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an edge‑case in Solady’s ECDSA utility where an empty, uninitialized bytes memory variable can be interpreted as a valid signature and cause the ecrecover precompile to return a non‑zero address. The root cause is the library’s optimisation that temporarily overwrites the memory region 0x00‑0x80, including the free‑memory pointer and the default null pointer at 0x60, and then copies the first 65 bytes of the supplied signature before checking its length. When the signature argument is an empty bytes object, its internal pointer is 0x60 and its length field is zero. The optimistic copy reads from memory locations 0x80‑0xc1, which may contain other variables, and overwrites the null pointer’s length word at 0x60 with the word found at 0xa0. If that word equals 65, the library believes the signature has the required length and passes the data to ecrecover, which can then recover an address from the inadvertently copied r, s and v values. An attacker can exploit this by providing an empty signature, arranging for suitable data to reside at the overwritten memory slots (for example by placing a struct with r, s, v values in memory), and ensuring the length word is 65. The recovered address may be controlled by the attacker or any address that ecrecover can produce, allowing the contract to accept a forged signature and potentially authorize unauthorized actions such as token transfers or privileged function calls. This issue manifests only when the vulnerable ECDSA functions are used with the described memory optimisation and when the signature argument is not explicitly allocated (e.g., bytes memory sig; without new bytes(0)). It affects any contract that relies on ECDSA.recover or tryRecover for authentication, exposing users’ funds and breaking the protocol’s trust model. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which produced a Forge test that demonstrates a non‑zero address being recovered from an empty signature. The bug is subtle because the function appears to revert on invalid signatures, yet the length check is bypassed by the memory overwrite, making it hard to notice in normal testing. The recommended mitigation is to validate the signature length before performing the optimistic copy, or to avoid overwriting the null pointer region altogether, thereby ensuring that an empty signature cannot be misinterpreted as valid. In abstract terms, this is a memory‑corruption edge case that leads to incorrect signature verification, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that a signature must be present and correctly formatted before an address can be recovered.

title: The info function in the AgreementStaking will run out of gas
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded read of role member lists in the info() view function of the AgreementStaking contract. The function assembles a Metadata struct that includes the full list of lenders and borrowers by calling _getRoleMembers for each role and also iterates over the collaterals set. Because the number of lenders, borrowers, and collaterals can grow without a hard limit, the amount of gas required to execute the function grows linearly with the size of these collections. When the collections become large enough, the call exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert. The function is invoked by ThresholdsVerifier.verifyThresholds, which means that a malicious or simply large set of participants can cause the verification step to fail, effectively denying service to any operation that depends on the verification. The impact is a denial-of-service on protocol logic that relies on the verification, potentially halting loan creation, staking, or other core actions. The issue appears only when the view function is called on-chain (e.g., from another contract) because off-chain calls do not have a gas limit, but the protocol uses it on-chain, making the problem exploitable. Any user, lender, borrower, or protocol component that triggers verification may experience failed transactions and see no error message other than a generic out-of-gas revert. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the info() implementation and identified the unbounded loops over role members. It is hard to notice because the function is marked view and appears harmless, and the gas cost only becomes problematic after the collections have grown, which may take time. The root cause is the lack of pagination or selective retrieval; the function tries to return the entire state in a single call, violating the assumption that view functions can return arbitrarily large data without gas constraints. The recommended fix is to separate the data retrieval: provide a lightweight function that returns only the scalar metadata needed for verification, and expose a separate off-chain or paginated function for the full list of lenders, borrowers, and collaterals. This reduces on-chain gas consumption and prevents the verification step from being DoS-ed. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of unbounded iteration in view functions leading to out-of-gas reverts and breaks the accounting assumption that the contract can always supply the full participant list on-chain.

title: Missing slippage check on curve's remove liquidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage check in the helper that builds a Curve remove_liquidity call. The function constructs calldata by hard‑coding the minAmounts array to all zeros, meaning the contract does not enforce any lower bound on the amount of each underlying token that must be received when liquidity is withdrawn. The root cause is the developer’s decision to ignore slippage parameters and to encode a static zero array instead of passing user‑controlled minimum amounts. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running or sandwiching the transaction: after the user’s transaction is submitted but before it is mined, a malicious actor can perform swaps or other actions that change the pool’s token ratios, especially draining a specific token that is becoming scarce. Because the contract accepts any ratio, the removal may return far fewer tokens than expected, potentially zero for the depleted token, leading to significant financial loss. The impact is that liquidity providers using this contract receive less value than anticipated, their balances may show unexpected zeros or dramatically reduced amounts, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional token distribution are violated. The issue manifests whenever the _constructNCoinsDecreasePosition helper is used to call remove_liquidity, which is the default path for all pool sizes (2, 3, or 4 coins). It is discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which flagged the hard‑coded zero minAmounts as a logical flaw. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply completes with a different output, so users may only see a discrepancy between expected and actual token amounts. To remediate, the contract should accept minAmounts as an input parameter, enforce a slippage tolerance, and verify that the amounts received meet the specified minimums before finalizing the withdrawal. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a missing slippage protection or unchecked output amount vulnerability, and it breaks the business logic that liquidity removal should return a proportional share of the pool’s assets.

title: Missing executor/clipperExchange check could result in malicious command
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of external address parameters that are used as executors or exchange contracts in two public functions. Both functions accept an addresssupplied by the caller – one called executor in the generic swap routine and another called clipperExchange in a specialized swap-to routine – and later embed these addresses into command structures that are executed to move funds. Because the contract does not check whether the supplied address belongs to a trusted or whitelisted contract, an attacker can provide a malicious contract address that implements the expected interface but contains code to redirect or siphon tokens. This flaw arises from the absence of an access‑control or whitelist check on user‑controlled address arguments, a classic case of unchecked external address injection leading to arbitrary command execution. An exploit can be carried out by a malicious actor calling the vulnerable function with a crafted executor or exchange address that, when invoked, transfers the input amount or any subsequent funds to an address under the attacker’s control. The impact is the potential loss of user funds, disruption of the protocol’s accounting, and erosion of trust in the platform, as any participant invoking the function may unintentionally trigger a transfer to a malicious contract. The condition for exploitation is simply the presence of a caller willing to supply a rogue address; no special privileges or timing constraints are required. All users who interact with the swap or clipperSwapTo functions are affected because the contract does not enforce any role‑based restriction on who can provide these parameters. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the function signatures and noted the lack of any require statement or mapping lookup that would restrict the executor or exchange to known entities. The problem can be subtle because the functions otherwise behave correctly with legitimate addresses, making the missing check easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should maintain a whitelist mapping of approved executor and exchange contracts and enforce a require check that the supplied address is present in the whitelist before constructing and returning the command array. Alternatively, the design could be changed to use internal, immutable contract references instead of user‑supplied addresses, thereby eliminating the attack surface. In practice, users may observe that after initiating a swap they receive no tokens, see their balance drop to zero, or notice that funds have been transferred to an unexpected address, which contradicts the expectation that the protocol safely routes assets to the intended recipient. This vulnerability belongs to the broader class of trust‑boundary violations where external contract addresses are accepted without verification, enabling arbitrary command injection and fund misdirection.

title: The Risk Operator can improperly trigger liquidation
bug_full: The contract defines two external functions, close and liquidate, each guarded by different role modifiers. The liquidate function is intended to be called only by a designated liquidation operator, but the contract does not enforce any additional on-chain validation of the account being liquidated. Because the risk operator also possesses the onlyLiquidator permission (or can be granted it), it can invoke liquidate on any address, including accounts that are not under-collateralized. The root cause is the absence of a check that the target account meets the protocol’s liquidation criteria before the function executes, combined with an overly permissive access control that allows a risk-management role to act as a liquidator. An attacker who controls the risk operator role can therefore trigger a liquidation transaction against a healthy user, causing the protocol to seize collateral, transfer assets, or otherwise modify balances in a way that the user did not expect. The impact is that users may lose funds or see their balances reduced without a legitimate default, breaking the economic guarantees of the system. This can happen at any time the risk operator decides to call liquidate, because the function is callable whenever the contract state is OPENED or SUSPENDED. All participants—depositors, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected, as the unauthorized liquidation can erode trust and lead to financial loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended separation of duties between risk and liquidation roles and noticed that no on-chain eligibility test is performed. Because the contract does not emit explicit error messages or revert when a non-eligible account is passed, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed through unexpected balance changes or missing refunds. To remediate, the contract should include a verification step that checks the account’s health factor, collateralization ratio, or any other liquidation trigger condition before proceeding, and the access control should be tightened so that only the authorized liquidator role can invoke the function, or the risk operator should be prevented from calling liquidate altogether. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of improper access control combined with missing business-logic validation, leading to unauthorized liquidation and potential loss of user funds.

title: Lenders will lose everything if they get removed
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a design flaw where the permission that grants a lender the ability to retrieve deposited capital and earned rewards is directly tied to the LENDER_ROLE access control. The Agreement Factory contract, which holds administrative privileges, can arbitrarily revoke the LENDER_ROLE from any address without any additional checks or safeguards. When a lender’s role is removed, the smart contract’s withdraw and claim functions are protected by the onlyRole(LENDER_ROLE) modifier, so the revoked address can no longer invoke them. As a result, the lender loses practical access to both the principal amount they deposited and any accrued rewards, effectively rendering those funds permanently inaccessible from the user’s perspective. This situation can be triggered at any time the factory decides to remove the role, including maliciously by an insider or unintentionally through a governance mistake. The impact is that lenders may see their UI balance drop to zero, receive transaction reverts when attempting to withdraw, or experience missing reward payouts, contradicting the expectation that they can always retrieve their own assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined role management and fund‑withdrawal pathways. It is subtle because the contract does not contain an explicit “freeze funds” flag; the loss of access is implicit in the role revocation, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control‑coupled‑fund‑ownership errors, where revoking a permission unintentionally locks user assets. To remediate, the contract should decouple ownership of funds from role‑based function gating, allowing an address to withdraw or claim even after its role is removed, or introduce a dedicated blacklist mechanism that explicitly controls whether a lender’s funds are frozen while preserving a separate recovery path. Such a redesign restores the invariant that users retain the ability to retrieve their own capital unless a clearly defined freeze condition is met, thereby aligning contract behavior with typical financial expectations and reducing the risk of total loss for lenders.

title: DoS with block gas limit
description:
```solidity
MultiRewards.updateReward is responsible for reward accounting logic and is executed at the start of critical functions: stake, withdraw, getReward, and notifyRewardAmount. The modiﬁer loops over every reward token, checkpointing reward emissions. The problem with this logic is that rewardTokens is an array that can grow in size to an undeﬁned capacity without the ability to reduce the size of the array. As a result, the gas costs required to execute this logic can also grow to an undeﬁned capacity. If the gas costs ever exceed the block gas limit, the critical functions executing this logic will be permanently blocked. Since this modiﬁer is used on every function responsible for removing staking and reward tokens from the contract, this would result in all staking and reward tokens being permanently locked in the contract.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an unbounded loop over a dynamic array that stores reward token addresses. The contract’s updateReward modifier iterates over every element of the rewardTokens array each time a user calls stake, withdraw, getReward or notifyRewardAmount. Because the array can grow without any upper limit and there is no function to shrink it, the amount of gas required to complete the loop can increase indefinitely. When the cumulative gas needed to process the loop exceeds the block gas limit, the modifier reverts with an out‑of‑gas error and the protected functions become permanently unusable. This means that any user attempting to stake more tokens, withdraw their stake, claim accrued rewards or add new reward tokens will see their transaction fail, often with a generic out‑of‑gas or “execution reverted” message. From the user’s perspective the expected behaviour – receiving a receipt of a successful stake or a refund of their tokens – is replaced by a silent failure where the transaction never confirms and the UI may show “transaction failed” or simply no change in balances. The impact is that all staked assets and pending rewards become locked in the contract, effectively freezing user funds. The condition occurs only after the rewardTokens array has grown large enough that the gas cost of the loop surpasses the block limit; it does not require any malicious transaction beyond the natural addition of reward tokens, although an attacker could deliberately add many tokens to accelerate the condition. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting logic, where the auditor noted that the array length was not bounded and that the modifier performed a full scan on each call. Because the failure manifests as a generic out‑of‑gas error, it can be hard to attribute to this specific loop without inspecting the source code, especially in production where users only see failed transactions. The issue belongs to the class of unbounded iteration or gas‑limit DoS vulnerabilities, where a data structure can grow arbitrarily and later cause critical functions to exceed the block gas limit. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum size for the rewardTokens array, reject additions beyond that limit, and ideally provide a way to remove or replace tokens so the loop size can be kept under control. Alternative designs could replace the per‑call iteration with a more scalable accounting scheme, such as storing cumulative reward rates per token or using a mapping that does not require full enumeration. Fixing the bug restores the expected behaviour where users can stake, withdraw and claim rewards without hitting the block gas ceiling, thereby protecting the protocol’s funds and maintaining trust in its operation.

title: MED - Not using safeTransfer may cause sweep to fail for some tokens
description:
```solidity
ModeStaking uses IERC20 from forge-std:
import {IERC20} from "forge-std/interfaces/IERC20.sol";
The interface is:
function transfer(address to, uint256 amount) external returns (bool);
This will fail for tokens that do not return a boolean (e.g. USDT).
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the standard ERC‑20 transfer function that is defined to return a boolean value indicating success. ModeStaking imports IERC20 from forge‑std and calls transfer(address,uint256) directly. While most tokens follow the specification and return true or false, a number of widely used tokens – most notably USDT – deviate from the standard and do not return any value. When the Solidity compiler attempts to decode a missing return value as a bool, the call reverts. Consequently, any sweep or withdrawal operation that uses this raw transfer call will fail for those non‑standard tokens. The root cause is the absence of a safety wrapper that validates the call outcome and tolerates tokens with non‑standard return data. An attacker or even an honest user could deposit a token that does not return a bool, and later when the contract’s sweep function is invoked, the transaction will revert, preventing the token from being moved out of the contract. This effectively locks the funds, leading to a loss of recoverable assets for token holders and for the protocol that expects to be able to reclaim or redistribute those tokens. The issue manifests only when the sweep logic is executed for a token whose transfer implementation does not conform to the ERC‑20 return‑value requirement; for standard‑compliant tokens the function behaves as expected. The problem was identified during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted the direct use of IERC20.transfer without any safety checks. Because the failure only appears with a subset of tokens, it can be difficult to detect through typical unit tests that use only well‑behaved ERC‑20 contracts. The recommended remediation is to replace direct calls to transfer with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer (or an equivalent wrapper) which performs a low‑level call, checks that the call succeeded, and gracefully handles tokens that omit a return value. By using a safe transfer abstraction, the contract will correctly revert only when the token truly fails, and will allow sweep operations to succeed for both standard and non‑standard ERC‑20 tokens, preserving the ability to move funds and maintaining the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: _baseURI Is Not Being Overriden for Any of the Protocol NFTs
description: An added advantage of representing positions as NFTs is that users can sell their NFTs to exit their positions before expiry. All NFT marketplaces call the tokenURI(uint256) method to retrieve the metadata associated with each NFT. Since the protocol is not overriding function tokenURI(uint256 tokenId) returns (string memory) or function _baseURI() returns (string memory), the NFT marketplace will be forced to display a default image, which isn't ideal.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing metadata exposure for the protocol's position NFTs. The contract inherits the standard ERC721 implementation but does not provide an override for either tokenURI(uint256) or the internal _baseURI() function. Because the base implementation returns an empty string, any NFT marketplace or wallet that queries tokenURI receives no URI and therefore falls back to a generic placeholder image or an empty metadata field. This situation arises whenever a user or a third‑party platform requests the tokenURI of a minted position NFT, which is the normal flow for displaying NFT details on marketplaces such as OpenSea. The root cause is a simple omission in the contract code: the developer assumed that the default behaviour would be sufficient, but the ERC721 base contract requires an explicit URI to be supplied for each token. Exploitation does not involve a direct financial attack; instead, the impact is primarily on user experience and market perception. Users expect to see a visual representation and descriptive metadata that confirms the underlying financial position; instead they see a blank image or missing description, which can lead to confusion, reduced trust, and potentially lower secondary‑market liquidity because buyers cannot verify the asset at a glance. The issue affects all holders of the protocol's NFTs, the protocol itself (as the perceived transparency of its positions is diminished), and any marketplace that relies on tokenURI for rendering. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s public interface, where the auditor noted that the tokenURI function was never overridden. The problem can be subtle because a generic placeholder may still render, giving the impression that the NFT is functional, while the underlying metadata is absent. To remediate, the contract should override _baseURI() (or tokenURI) to return a valid HTTP(S) URL that points to a JSON metadata file for each token, or embed an on‑chain SVG that conveys at least a static label such as "Collar Position". This change restores the expected behaviour of displaying correct metadata, aligns with the protocol’s promise of transparent position representation, and prevents user confusion or loss of confidence in the NFT marketplace listings.

title: withdrawRevenue() transfers USDB back to itself
description: withdrawRevenue() transfers USDB back to itself, thus making this function unnecessary since the funds are already in the contract. The intention here is to withdraw it to owner's address or a specified address as mentioned in comments.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the withdrawRevenue function sends USDB tokens to the contract's own address instead of an external recipient. This occurs because the implementation uses address(this) as the destination in the token transfer call. As a result, when the function is executed, the transfer succeeds but the token balance of the contract does not change, leaving the revenue locked inside the contract. The issue can be triggered by any caller (typically the owner) who expects to move accumulated USDB to their wallet; the contract will appear to have performed the withdrawal, but the funds remain inaccessible. This breaks the business logic that revenue should be claimable by the owner, violates accounting assumptions that a withdrawn amount reduces the contract balance, and may cause users to believe payouts have been made when they have not. The condition is present whenever withdrawRevenue is called; no special inputs are required. The affected parties are the contract owner and any stakeholders relying on the revenue distribution. The problem was identified during a manual code review that compared the comment describing the intended behavior with the actual transfer target. Because the transaction does not revert and emits no error, the bug can be subtle and may only be noticed when the owner checks the contract balance after a withdrawal and sees no change. The proper fix is to replace the recipient address with the owner's address or to add a parameter that specifies a valid external receiver, and then transfer the USDB tokens to that address.

title: riskPoolBalance is not used
description: For each winner picking, a portion of the funds is taken to account for risk balance. This balance is never used again, and the only way to retrieve is for the owner to include it in the merkle tree which is not the intended use for the risk pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting logic error where a portion of the funds that should be paid to a winner is diverted into a variable representing a risk pool balance, but that balance is never referenced again in the contract logic. The root cause is that the contract deducts a risk amount during each winner‑picking operation without implementing any subsequent mechanism to consume, redistribute, or return those funds. An attacker or any user can exploit this by simply triggering winner selection, causing the contract to lock away a slice of the total pool that will never be part of any future payout. The impact is that legitimate participants receive a smaller payout than expected, and the locked amount effectively disappears from the user’s perspective, leading to missing refunds or zero balances where funds should appear. This condition occurs every time the winner‑selection function is called, under normal operating conditions of the protocol. All users who rely on the contract to receive their full winnings are affected, while the contract owner retains the only possible path to retrieve the stranded funds by manually inserting the risk pool amount into a Merkle tree—a method that was not intended for this purpose and may be abused. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared state variable usage against the intended financial flow, noticing that the riskPoolBalance variable is written to but never read. Because the contract does not emit explicit events or revert when the risk pool is populated, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed as an unexpected shortfall in payouts, making it hard to notice without thorough state‑tracking. To remediate, the risk pool feature should either be fully implemented—providing a clear purpose such as covering slashing, insurance, or future rewards—or removed entirely to prevent dead‑money accumulation. In generic terms, this is a dead‑funds or unused‑balance bug, where money is sent to a storage slot that is never utilized, violating the accounting assumptions of the protocol and breaking the expectation that all deposited funds will eventually be distributed to participants.

title: Loss of precision possible due to rewardRate rounding
description:
In MultiRewards.notifyRewardAmount, we compute the rewardRate given the amount of reward tokens to distribute divided by the rewardsDuration, e.g.:
```solidity
rewardData[_rewardsToken].rewardRate = reward.div(
    rewardData[_rewardsToken].rewardsDuration
);
```
Since we're using integer math, when we divide, we round the result down to the nearest integer. In most circumstances, this is not a concern and results in only dust amounts of rewards to be left in the contract after they've been distributed. However, in some edge cases this can result in a much more significant loss. For example, consider a circumstance where we use a low decimal _rewardsToken, e.g. GUSD (2 decimals), and a high rewardsDuration, e.g. 4 years (126,227,808 seconds). Any reward amount less than 1,262,278 GUSD would result in the rewardRate being rounded down to 0, permanently locking all the transferred GUSD. We can also round down to non-zero amounts in less extreme circumstances which still result in some amount of tokens never being claimable. For example, with the same preconditions as above, a reward amount of 2,524,555 GUSD would give us: 252455500 / 126227808 = 1.999999081 which rounds down to a rewardRate of 1, resulting in about 50% of the GUSD being lost.
bug_full: The contract calculates a per‑second reward rate by dividing the total amount of reward tokens that have been transferred into the contract by the configured rewardsDuration. Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the division truncates any fractional part, effectively rounding the result down. When the reward token has few decimal places (for example a stablecoin with only two decimals) and the rewardsDuration is very long (several years), the numerator can be smaller than the denominator after accounting for the token’s precision. In such cases the integer division yields a rewardRate of zero, meaning that the contract’s internal accounting never registers any claimable reward. Even when the division produces a non‑zero integer, the truncation can discard a large fraction of the intended reward, leaving a substantial amount of tokens permanently locked in the contract because the rewardRate is too low to ever distribute the full balance. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who supplies a modest reward amount together with an excessively long duration, or it can arise unintentionally when the protocol’s parameters are chosen without considering the token’s decimal precision. The impact is that users who are supposed to receive rewards see no increase in their balances, the protocol’s advertised APR becomes inaccurate, and the locked tokens are effectively lost forever. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noticed that the division does not account for precision loss. It is easy to miss because a small amount of “dust” is normally expected, yet the same mechanism can cause a much larger loss under edge‑case parameters. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum ratio between the reward amount and the rewardsDuration, reject tokens with very low decimal counts for long durations, or compute the rewardRate using a higher‑precision representation (for example by scaling the numerator before division or by using a library that supports fixed‑point arithmetic with rounding up). By ensuring that the rewardRate cannot be rounded down to zero or an excessively low value, the protocol guarantees that all transferred reward tokens remain claimable and that users receive the rewards they expect.

title: Insuﬃcient validation of amount provided to notifyRewardAmount
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the MultiRewards contract validates the amount of reward tokens supplied through the notifyRewardAmount function. The contract checks that the current token balance is at least the product of the configured rewardRate and the rewardsDuration, which ensures that the contract holds enough tokens to cover future emissions. However, this check ignores any rewards that have already been emitted but not yet claimed by users. Because rewards are only transferred to users when they explicitly call getReward, a portion of the contract’s token balance may already be earmarked for pending claims. When an attacker or a careless caller invokes notifyRewardAmount with a large rewardAmount while the contract still holds unclaimed rewards, the balance‑based validation still passes, even though the total obligations (future emissions plus pending claims) exceed the actual token balance. Consequently, the invariant that the contract always has sufficient tokens to satisfy all rewards is broken. Under these conditions later users may call getReward and receive zero tokens, even though the UI indicates that rewards are available. The impact is a loss of expected earnings for participants and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees; funds appear to be locked in the contract but are effectively unavailable to claimants. The issue is most likely to arise when the contract is used directly, bypassing the MultiRewardsFactory which normally transfers exactly the rewardAmount together with the notifyRewardAmount call. Because the balance check looks correct on the surface, the problem can be subtle and may only be discovered through careful audit of the reward accounting logic. To remediate the flaw, the contract should verify that the transferred amount covers both future emissions and any outstanding unclaimed rewards, for example by using safeTransferFrom inside notifyRewardAmount to pull the exact amount needed, or by augmenting the validation formula to include pending rewards. This ensures that the contract never promises more rewards than it can actually dispense, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the system.

title: Upgradable contracts used for immutable deployment
description: Upgradable contracts are used but no Proxy contract found. Upgradable contracts are designed to be used with Proxy contracts due to the intricacies of delegatecall and storage slot clashing concerns. The repository doesn't contain any proxy contract indicating that the contracts will be deployed in an immutable way.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from deploying contracts that were written for an upgradeable pattern without actually using a proxy. The source code inherits from upgradeable base contracts such as OwnableUpgradable and contains an initializer function that is meant to replace a constructor when the contract is deployed behind a proxy. Because no proxy contract is present, the contract is deployed as an immutable implementation and the initializer is never executed automatically. Consequently, any external account can invoke the initializer after deployment, which typically grants privileged rights (for example, setting the contract owner). This situation allows an attacker to take ownership of the contract, call admin‑only functions, change critical parameters, or withdraw funds. The impact is a loss of control for the legitimate deployer and potential theft of user assets. The issue appears only when the contract is deployed directly, i.e., without a proxy, and the initializer is left public or protected only by the upgradeable‑specific initializer modifier. Users may notice that the contract behaves as if it has no owner or that ownership can be claimed by anyone, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s inheritance hierarchy with the deployment artefacts and noticed the absence of a proxy. It can be hard to spot because the code compiles without errors and the upgradeable libraries are imported correctly, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, the developer should either replace the upgradeable base contracts with their non‑upgradeable equivalents (e.g., Ownable instead of OwnableUpgradable), move any initialization logic into a proper constructor, and remove the initializer function, or alternatively introduce a correctly configured proxy that ensures the initializer runs exactly once at deployment. This fixes the root cause by aligning the contract’s design pattern with its deployment model, thereby preventing unauthorized ownership takeover and preserving the intended security guarantees.

title: multiWithdrawals which has first leg consuming all forwarded gas, will be bricked with high probability
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑exhaustion problem that occurs during a multiWithdrawal operation that attempts to pull assets from up to five vaults in a single transaction. The contract iterates over the list of vaults and for each entry calls an external function to perform the actual withdrawal. Because of the EIP‑150 rule that forwards only 63/64 of the caller’s remaining gas to a sub‑call, the first withdrawal consumes roughly 63/64 of the total gas supplied to the CoreStateRegistry function. The second call then receives 63/64 of the already tiny remainder, the third call receives 63/64 of that, and so on. After a few iterations the remaining gas is effectively zero, leaving insufficient gas for the internal _processAck routine that finalises the transaction. When this routine runs out of gas the whole transaction reverts, meaning the user’s withdrawal does not complete and the assets remain locked in the vaults. The root cause is the use of an internal loop that forwards almost all available gas to each withdrawal call without reserving gas for the post‑processing logic. An attacker can exploit the situation by providing a malicious payload – for example a swap operation that deliberately consumes a large amount of gas in the first vault – ensuring that the subsequent calls run out of gas and cause the transaction to fail. The impact is that users attempting a multi‑withdrawal see the transaction revert, receive no tokens, and their balances appear unchanged; the protocol’s guarantee of atomic multi‑vault withdrawals is broken and funds become effectively bricked until the user retries with a smaller batch or the contract is patched. The issue manifests only when the withdrawal involves multiple vaults and the first vault’s logic is gas‑heavy; single‑vault withdrawals work as expected. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the gas forwarding semantics of the loop. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction may succeed for simple cases and the out‑of‑gas error is reported at the end of the call stack, making it appear as a generic failure rather than a systematic gas‑drain problem. The appropriate mitigation is to move the iteration over vaults into an external call or explicitly limit the gas forwarded to each sub‑call, thereby preserving enough gas for the final acknowledgement step. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of cascading gas‑exhaustion vulnerabilities caused by repeated 63/64 gas forwarding, which can unintentionally brick complex multi‑step operations. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a pending withdrawal that later fails with an out‑of‑gas revert, the expected tokens never arrive, and the balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that a multi‑withdrawal should deliver all requested assets in one atomic action.

title: ERC5115Form::withdraw/deposit strict checks can cause stETH (and other rebasing tokens) to revert
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from strict equality checks on token balances during cross‑chain deposits and withdrawals in the ERC5115Form contract. When a rebasing token such as stETH is transferred, the internal share‑to‑amount conversion can produce a rounding discrepancy of up to two wei, meaning the balance of the destination address after the transfer may differ from the intended amount by a tiny amount. The deposit routine pulls tokens from the sender, increases allowance, and then calls a helper that validates the received shares against the exact amount supplied. Because the amount recorded after the transfer can be off by a few wei, the validation fails and the transaction reverts. Similarly, the withdrawal function compares the post‑transfer balance to the pre‑transfer balance with a strict "!= assets" test and also checks a slippage condition that assumes an exact match. If the balance difference is not precisely equal to the requested assets, the contract triggers a generic revert error. This issue was discovered during a security audit that referenced a known rounding problem in Lido’s stETH implementation (Lido‑DAO issue 442). The bug is subtle because the discrepancy is only a couple of wei, which is invisible to users and does not appear in UI balances; the only symptom is a failed transaction with a generic error message, leading users to believe their deposit or withdrawal “didn’t work” or that the contract is malicious. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users cannot deposit or withdraw rebasing tokens, potentially locking funds in the vault and eroding confidence in the protocol. The problem occurs whenever the contract handles rebasing tokens that do not guarantee a one‑to‑one correspondence between shares and underlying assets, and only when the strict equality checks are used. Affected parties include any user attempting to deposit or withdraw such tokens, the vault’s accounting logic, and any downstream protocol that relies on successful cross‑chain transfers. Because the failure manifests as a generic revert, it can be hard to diagnose without inspecting the balance differences. The recommended mitigation is to replace exact equality with a tolerance window (for example, an EPSILON of 10 wei) when comparing balances, and to compute the actual received amount after the transfer rather than assuming the requested amount. This approach aligns the contract’s logic with the inherent rounding behavior of rebasing tokens and prevents unnecessary reverts, restoring expected functionality and preserving user funds.

title: DeBridgeValidator::validateTxData missing destination chain equals liquidity destination chain check
description: In the case of a cross-chain deposit, an arbitrary message is sent through the AMB alongside liquidity and to the same chain. This is checked in some of the IBridgeValidator implementations but not all, and could cause lost funds if there is a user mistake setting these destination chains to be different.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation check in the cross‑chain deposit path of the DeBridgeValidator (and SocketValidator) contract. When a user initiates a deposit that involves sending liquidity to a destination chain, the validator is supposed to ensure that the destination chain identifier used for the AMB message (dstChainId) matches the chain identifier where the liquidity will be allocated (liqDstChainId). Because the code does not perform this equality check in all implementations, a transaction can be crafted where these two identifiers differ. The contract will then forward the AMB message to one chain while the liquidity is expected on another chain. As a result, the message reaches a chain that has no corresponding liquidity pool, and the funds become locked or effectively disappear. This condition occurs only in the deposit branch of the validateTxData function, i.e., when args_.deposit is true. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared multiple IBridgeValidator implementations and noticed the missing condition in DeBridgeValidator.sol. The bug is subtle because the transaction may still emit events and appear successful, so users see no immediate error, yet the expected token balance on the target chain never arrives. The impact is loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariant that each cross‑chain transfer must have a matching liquidity provision. The affected parties are any user who performs a cross‑chain deposit and any protocol component that relies on the validator to enforce correct routing. To remediate, the validator should add an explicit require that dstChainId equals liqDstChainId in the deposit case, reverting with an error if they differ. This restores the intended business logic that the destination of the message and the destination of the liquidity are identical, preventing funds from being sent to a chain without liquidity and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: DeBridgeValidator::validateTxData wrong destination chain for Debridge/DLN order rescuer
description: When liquidity is bridged via DLN, an order is created on destination chain. If the order is never taken or if it needs to be cancelled for other reasons, a superform controlled address (role CORE_STATE_REGISTRY_RESCUER_ROLE) is set to be able to cancel the order. In DeBridgeValidator::validateTxData it is enforced for the order orderAuthorityAddressDst to be the CORE_STATE_REGISTRY_RESCUER_ROLE but on the wrong chain (see DeBridgeValidator.sol#L58). Indeed in the case of withdrawals, dstChainId, which is the chain on which the ack must be received, can be different from liqDstChainId which is the chain on which the order is created. In that case funds may end up unavailable since nobody has the authority to cancel the order on the destination chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect authority verification in the DeBridgeValidator contract when handling liquidity that is bridged via the Decentralized Liquidity Network (DLN). The validator checks that the address designated as the order authority on the destination chain (orderAuthorityAddressDst) matches the address assigned to the CORE_STATE_REGISTRY_RESCUER_ROLE, but it performs this check against the dstChainId – the chain where the acknowledgement is expected – instead of the liqDstChainId – the chain where the order is actually created. This mismatch occurs in withdrawal scenarios where the acknowledgement chain differs from the order creation chain. Because the rescuer role is looked up on the wrong chain, no address on the true destination chain possesses the required authority to cancel the order. Consequently, if an order is never taken or needs to be cancelled, the authorized rescuer cannot perform the cancellation, leaving the bridged funds locked and unavailable to the user. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the cross‑chain order lifecycle and identified that the validator’s chain‑ID parameter was mis‑used. It is subtle because most normal transfers use the same chain identifier for both acknowledgement and order creation, so the bug only manifests in specific withdrawal flows. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a pending withdrawal that never resolves, balances may appear unchanged, or refunds may be missing despite the protocol indicating that a rescuer can cancel the order. The impact is a medium‑risk loss of funds availability, not necessarily a total loss, but users cannot retrieve their assets until the bug is fixed. The proper fix is to replace the use of dstChainId with liqDstChainId when querying the CORE_STATE_REGISTRY_RESCUER_ROLE, ensuring that the authority check is performed on the chain where the order actually resides, thereby restoring the ability for the rescuer to cancel orders and release locked liquidity.

title: No smart contract dev framework used
description: Frameworks like Foundry lets you write unit tests, do fork testing and write deployment scripts based on which chain you're deploying on (Blast testnet vs mainnet here for example). Some bugs reported in this report would have been caught through unit and fork testing.
bug_full: The issue identified is a process‑level vulnerability arising from the complete absence of a smart‑contract development framework such as Foundry, Hardhat or Truffle. Because no unit tests, integration tests or fork‑based simulations were written, the codebase lacks automated verification of its business logic, arithmetic correctness, access‑control enforcement and deployment parameters. The root cause is a development workflow that relies solely on manual compilation and ad‑hoc testing, which fails to expose edge‑case behaviours that only appear under realistic chain conditions (for example when interacting with the Blast mainnet versus its testnet). An attacker can exploit this gap by invoking functions that were never exercised in a test suite, such as a mis‑calculated fee, an unchecked token transfer, or a missing re‑entrancy guard. Since the contract has not been proven to handle these scenarios, the attacker may trigger a state transition that drains funds, creates an inconsistent accounting balance, or blocks legitimate users from receiving expected refunds. The impact can range from minor accounting errors to total loss of user assets, depending on which hidden bug is triggered. The vulnerability manifests when the contract is deployed to a live network without prior fork testing that mirrors the target environment; it is therefore most likely to be observed after a real transaction fails, a user reports receiving zero tokens, or a balance unexpectedly becomes negative. All participants who interact with the contract – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the missing tests undermine confidence that the contract behaves as advertised. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit, where the auditor noted the lack of any test directory, no CI configuration and no deployment scripts, concluding that many of the logical flaws reported elsewhere could have been caught earlier. This type of omission is hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and may even pass basic functional checks, yet hidden bugs remain dormant until a specific on‑chain state triggers them. To remediate, the development team should adopt a proven framework like Foundry, create comprehensive unit tests for each public function, write fork‑based integration tests that simulate mainnet conditions, and maintain deployment scripts that enforce correct network parameters. By doing so, the contract’s business logic will be continuously validated, reducing the risk of undiscovered vulnerabilities that could lead to fund loss or broken protocol invariants.

title: Cooling Period Reset on Multiple Requests
description: If a user makes multiple withdrawal requests within the COOLING_PERIOD window, the withdrawal eligibility date keeps getting pushed back, causing indefinite delays. For example, with COOLING_PERIOD set to 7 days: The user requests withdrawal X1, which is eligible for claiming at T1. 6 days later, they request another withdrawal X2. Now, the eligibility time for both X1 and X2 resets to T1 + 6 days. This setup prevents X1 from being claimed at T1 as intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑lock logic error in the withdrawal flow where the eligibility timestamp for a pending withdrawal is overwritten each time the same user submits a new withdrawal request while the original cooling period is still active. The root cause is that the contract stores a single global or per‑user next‑claim time and updates it on every request, rather than preserving the original claim time for each individual request. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by repeatedly calling the withdrawal function before the cooling period expires, which pushes the claim date further into the future and can delay the ability to claim indefinitely. This results in funds appearing to be locked: the user expects to be able to claim after the configured COOLING_PERIOD (for example seven days), but after a second request the claim button remains disabled and the balance stays unchanged, creating the impression that the funds have disappeared or are stuck. The issue manifests only when multiple withdrawal requests are made within the cooling window; a single request behaves as intended. It affects any participant who tries to withdraw more than once during the period, reducing liquidity availability and potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the withdrawal scheduling logic, where the auditor observed that the eligibility date was recomputed on each call instead of being fixed at the first request. Because the contract does not emit explicit errors and the UI simply shows a pending state, the bug can be hard to notice until users experience repeated delays. The appropriate fix is to treat each withdrawal request as an independent entity with its own immutable eligibility timestamp, or to only set the timestamp on the first request and ignore subsequent ones, thereby preventing the cooling period from being reset. This class of bug falls under state‑mutation and time‑lock mismanagement, where mutable timestamps lead to unintended denial‑of‑service of funds, violating the business assumption that a withdrawal becomes claimable after a fixed waiting period.

title: DebtManager.manualAllocation vault.totalIdle can be lower than vault.minimum_total_idle()
description: In case the vault.totalIdle() is smaller the vault.minimum_total_idle() there should be a continue. The totalIdle can be lower than the minimum.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the manual allocation routine of the DebtManager contract, where the logic that decides whether to skip a rebalancing step does not correctly guard against a situation in which the vault’s idle liquidity falls below the protocol‑defined safety threshold (minimum_total_idle). The code only skips the allocation when two conditions are simultaneously true: the position’s recorded debt exceeds the strategy’s current debt *and* the vault’s totalIdle is less than or equal to the minimum_total_idle. Consequently, if the vault’s idle balance is already below the minimum but the position’s debt is not greater than the current debt, the guard is bypassed and the contract proceeds to allocate additional debt. This logical oversight allows the system to allocate more funds than are safely available, breaking the accounting invariant that idle funds must never drop below the configured minimum. An attacker or a careless user could trigger the allocation path (for example by submitting a deposit or by calling a function that forces a manual allocation) and cause the vault to over‑commit its liquidity. The immediate impact is that subsequent withdrawal requests may fail or return zero, user balances can appear reduced, and in extreme cases the protocol could become insolvent because the accounting model assumes a buffer that no longer exists. The issue manifests only when the vault is already under‑collateralized and a manual allocation is attempted while the position’s debt does not exceed the strategy’s current debt. It was discovered during a manual audit of the DebtManager’s allocation loop, where the auditor noticed that the condition does not cover the case of low idle liquidity independent of the debt comparison. The bug is subtle because the guard appears to check the safety threshold, yet the conjunction with the debt comparison hides the failure mode, making it easy to miss during testing that focuses on typical debt‑increase scenarios. To remediate the problem, the allocation loop should unconditionally skip any operation that would execute while vault.totalIdle() is below vault.minimum_total_idle(), regardless of the debt relationship. In practice this means adding a separate early‑continue check for totalIdle < minimum_total_idle or restructuring the condition so that the safety threshold is evaluated first. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that the vault must retain a minimum idle buffer to guarantee user withdrawals and preserve protocol solvency.

title: Newly added lender without an aprOracle entry would block
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing entry in the APR oracle mapping for a newly added lender in the DebtManager workflow. When the DebtManager sorts lenders it calls the AprOracle.getExpectedApr function, which looks up the oracle address for the given strategy. If the mapping does not contain an address, the lookup returns the zero address and the subsequent call to IOracle(oracle).aprAfterDebtChange reverts because the contract at address 0 does not implement the expected interface. This revert propagates back to the sorting routine, causing the entire operation to fail. The root cause is the lack of a validation step that ensures every lender added to the DebtManager has a corresponding APR oracle entry. An attacker or a careless admin could add a lender without first registering an oracle, which would block any subsequent calls that depend on APR calculations. The impact is that the protocol’s core accounting logic is halted: users attempting to borrow, repay, or view updated rates encounter transaction failures, balances appear unchanged, and the UI may display generic error messages such as “sorting failed” or “operation reverted”. The condition under which this occurs is any execution path that triggers getExpectedApr after a lender has been added without an oracle entry, typically during the periodic rebalancing or when new credit lines are opened. All participants—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself—are affected because funds cannot be moved and the system’s financial state cannot be updated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the AprOracle contract where a comment explicitly warned that the function will revert if an oracle is not set. It can be hard to notice because the addition of a lender succeeds, and the failure only manifests later when the sorting algorithm invokes the oracle, making the bug appear as an intermittent or unrelated transaction revert. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “missing dependency validation” errors, where a contract assumes the existence of a required component without enforcing it. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that suddenly fails with no obvious reason, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. To remediate, the protocol should enforce the presence of an APR oracle before a lender is registered in the DebtManager, either by adding a require check in the lender‑addition function, providing a default oracle, or handling the missing‑oracle case gracefully within getExpectedApr so that the sorting algorithm can continue without reverting.

title: Routes with applyPermit() can be forced to revert through front-running
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the router's applyPermit() helper, which unconditionally forwards a user‑provided ERC20 permit signature to OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safePermit() function. SafeERC20 verifies that the token's nonce for the owner has increased by exactly one after calling permit(); if the nonce has not changed, the call reverts with the message "SafeERC20: permit did not succeed". Because the router does not first check whether the caller already has sufficient allowance, an attacker can front‑run the user’s transaction and submit a permit() call with the identical signature before the router executes safePermit(). When the router later attempts to apply the same signature, the token’s nonce has already been incremented, causing the nonce check to fail and the entire processRoute() call to revert. This denial‑of‑service style flaw can affect any user who relies on applyPermit() to approve token transfers, leading to unexpected transaction failures, loss of gas, and broken expectations for external integrations that assume a successful swap. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that examined the interaction between the router and the SafeERC20 library. It is subtle because the revert only occurs under a specific front‑running scenario; normal operation shows no error, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The root cause is the lack of a pre‑condition check for existing allowance and the reliance on a one‑time permit signature without protecting against replay by a malicious actor. To remediate, the router should first query the caller’s allowance for the router contract and only invoke safePermit() when the allowance is insufficient, thereby ensuring that a previously used permit does not trigger a revert. Conceptually, this fixes the bug by treating the permit as a fallback mechanism rather than the sole means of granting allowance, eliminating the front‑run exploit vector and restoring reliable execution of routes that include applyPermit().

title: wrapNative() wrongly transfers all native tokens out when unwrapping
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the wrapNative() routine that is responsible for converting wrapped native tokens back into native currency. After the contract withdraws the requested amount from the wrapped token, it attempts to forward the native tokens to the destination address using a low‑level call. Instead of sending exactly the amount that was unwrapped (amountIn), the implementation uses address(this).balance as the transfer value. Consequently, if the router contract holds any native balance unrelated to the current unwrapping operation – for example, residual ETH from previous swaps, fees, or other temporary holdings – the entire balance is drained to the caller’s address. The root cause is a logical error: the code references the contract’s total native balance rather than the specific amount that should be transferred. An attacker can trigger the function with a small amountIn while the contract already contains a larger native balance, causing the contract to unintentionally forward all its funds. The impact is a loss of native tokens for the protocol or any user that relied on the router to retain its balance, effectively emptying the contract’s treasury. This condition occurs whenever wrapNative() is called while the contract’s balance is non‑zero, which may happen in normal operation when the router processes multiple swaps in a single transaction or retains fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of native token handling and identified the mismatch between the intended transfer amount and the actual value used. Because the function still succeeds and the call returns true, the bug can be subtle and may not surface in tests that start with a zero balance. To remediate, the transfer should be limited to amountIn, i.e., payable(to).call{value: amountIn}(''), ensuring only the unwrapped tokens are sent and any other native balance remains untouched. This class of bug falls under improper handling of contract balances and incorrect value calculations during token unwrapping, violating the accounting assumption that the contract’s balance after a withdrawal equals the amount withdrawn. From a user’s perspective, the expected outcome – receiving exactly the amount they unwrapped – is replaced by an unexpected receipt of the entire contract balance, or conversely, the contract’s funds disappear, leading to missing balances and potential loss of funds.

title: wrapNative() wrongly transfers all native tokens out when unwrapping
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the wrapNative() routine that is responsible for converting wrapped native tokens back into native currency. The function performs an unwrapping step by calling IWETH(tokenIn).withdraw(amountIn) and then attempts to forward the resulting native tokens to a destination address using a low‑level call. However, instead of sending exactly the amount that was unwrapped (amountIn), the code mistakenly uses address(this).balance as the transfer value. This means that any native ether held by the contract at the time of the call – whether it originates from previous swaps, fees, or accidental deposits – will be sent to the recipient together with the intended amount. The root cause is a logic error: the contract assumes its balance equals the amount just withdrawn, which is only true when the contract holds no other ether. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can trigger a wrapNative() operation when the router contract already contains a non‑zero ether balance, causing the entire balance to be drained to the attacker‑controlled address. The impact is a loss of funds for the protocol and any users whose assets were temporarily held by the router, effectively breaking the accounting guarantees of the swap route. The issue manifests whenever wrapNative() is called in a context where the contract’s ether balance is not empty – for example, during multi‑hop swaps that temporarily hold native tokens. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the token flow logic and identified the misuse of address(this).balance. The bug can be subtle because in simple test cases the contract balance does equal amountIn, so the transfer appears correct, masking the problem until more complex routing scenarios are exercised. To remediate, the transfer should be limited to the exact amount that was unwrapped (amountIn) rather than the whole contract balance, ensuring that only the intended funds are moved and the router’s residual ether remains intact. This class of bug falls under improper handling of contract balances and incorrect value calculations during token transfers, leading to unintended fund leakage and violation of the protocol’s financial invariants. From a user’s perspective, a participant may notice that after a swap their expected refund is either missing or that the router’s balance suddenly drops to zero, contradicting the expectation that only the swapped amount is transferred.

title: swapCurve() is incompatible with input tokens where approve() has no return value
description:
In the swapCurve() function, approval for the input token to Curve's pool is granted by calling the token's approve() function directly.
```solidity
IERC20(tokenIn).approve(pool, amountIn);
```
This is not compatible with ERC-20 tokens where the approve() function does not return a bool, most notably USDT. approve() in the IERC20 interface expects a bool to be returned. However, since USDT's approve() function does not return a bool, the function will revert when attempting to decode its return value.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swapCurve() routine that attempts to grant the Curve pool permission to transfer the input token by invoking the token’s approve() function directly through the standard IERC20 interface. The IERC20 definition expects approve() to return a boolean indicating success, and the Solidity compiler therefore tries to decode a bool from the call’s return data. Certain popular ERC‑20 implementations, most notably USDT, deviate from the standard by implementing approve() without any return value. When swapCurve() calls approve() on such a token, the runtime attempts to read a bool that does not exist, causing a decoding error and an automatic revert of the entire transaction. The root cause is a mismatch between the assumed ERC‑20 interface and the actual behaviour of non‑standard tokens, a classic case of ERC‑20 compatibility incompatibility. An attacker could exploit this by supplying a token that deliberately omits the return value, causing every swap that relies on swapCurve() to fail and effectively denying service to users who hold that token. Even without a malicious token, any legitimate user trying to swap a token like USDT will experience a failed transaction: the UI will report that the swap did not go through, no output tokens are received, and the user only loses the gas spent. The issue manifests whenever swapCurve() is invoked with a token whose approve() does not return a bool, which includes a handful of widely used stablecoins. The affected parties are end‑users attempting to trade those tokens, the protocol that cannot provide the advertised swap functionality, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful allowance grants. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s allowance logic against the ERC‑20 specification and identified the unsafe direct call. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without warnings and the failure only appears at runtime when the token’s approve() is called. To remediate the issue, the contract should stop using the raw approve() call and instead employ OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, for example safeIncreaseAllowance() or safeApprove(), which correctly handles tokens that do not return a boolean and will revert only on genuine failure. This change aligns the contract with the broader class of “non‑standard ERC‑20 token handling” bugs, ensuring that allowance granting works for all tokens and that swaps no longer silently revert, preserving user expectations that a successful swap yields the expected output tokens.

title: Use .call() instead of .transfer() to transfer native tokens in swapCurve()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token swap routine that sends native blockchain currency (for example ETH) to the recipient using the Solidity .transfer() method. .transfer() imposes a hard‑coded 2300‑gas stipend on the callee, which is sufficient only for very simple fallback logic. When the destination address is a contract that performs any non‑trivial work on receipt – such as logging an event, updating storage, or interacting with other contracts – the limited gas may be exhausted, causing the .transfer() call to revert. The root cause is the choice of a fixed‑gas transfer primitive instead of a flexible one that forwards all available gas. An attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger the failure simply by swapping into a token that is paid out as native currency and specifying a contract address that requires more than 2300 gas to accept the funds. The exploit scenario is straightforward: the swapCurve() function calculates the amountOut, attempts to send it with payable(to).transfer(amountOut); if the recipient’s fallback consumes more gas, the transfer reverts, the entire swap transaction reverts, and the user receives no output token despite having approved the input. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction hash but the expected balance increase never appears, or the swap appears to have completed while the funds are effectively locked in the contract. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any participant using contract wallets, potentially leading to loss of confidence, missed arbitrage opportunities, and reduced liquidity because swaps to native tokens become unreliable. The issue manifests whenever the output token is the native currency and the recipient is a contract, which includes many common use‑cases such as DeFi vaults, smart wallets, or escrow contracts. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token‑out handling logic and recognized the outdated use of .transfer() in a modern EVM environment where gas costs evolve. The problem can be subtle because a successful transfer to an externally owned account (EOA) masks the bug, and only contracts with complex receive logic exhibit the failure, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. The recommended remediation is to replace .transfer() with a low‑level .call{value: amountOut}('') pattern, which forwards all remaining gas and returns a boolean indicating success, allowing the contract to handle failures gracefully. This change aligns the code with current best practices for sending native tokens and eliminates the fixed‑gas limitation that underpins the vulnerability. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “inadequate gas stipend for external calls” or “unsafe native token transfer pattern”, which can cause unexpected reverts, loss of funds, or broken business logic when the receiving contract’s fallback exceeds the stipend.

title: swapCurve() is incompatible with input tokens where approve() has no return value
description:
In the swapCurve() function, approval for the input token to Curve's pool is granted by calling the token's approve() function directly.
```solidity
IERC20(tokenIn).approve(pool, amountIn);
```
This is not compatible with ERC-20 tokens where the approve() function does not return a bool, most notably USDT. approve() in the IERC20 interface expects a bool to be returned. However, since USDT's approve() function does not return a bool, the function will revert when attempting to decode its return value.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swapCurve() function of the contract, where the code attempts to grant an allowance to the Curve pool by invoking the ERC‑20 token's approve() method directly through the IERC20 interface. The IERC20 definition expects approve() to return a boolean value indicating success, and the Solidity compiler therefore tries to decode a bool from the call’s return data. However, a number of popular tokens, most notably USDT, implement approve() without returning any value. When swapCurve() is called with such a token, the runtime attempts to decode a non‑existent bool, causing the call to revert. The root cause is a mismatch between the assumed ERC‑20 interface and the actual implementation of certain tokens, a classic case of non‑standard token behavior breaking contract logic. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the mere presence of a non‑standard token is sufficient to trigger a denial‑of‑service condition. When a user initiates a swap that involves an affected token, the transaction reverts before any token transfer occurs, meaning the user pays gas fees while receiving no output tokens. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the swap was submitted but then fails silently or displays an error, leaving the user confused because the expected token balance does not change. The protocol’s liquidity pool may also be impacted because swaps involving the problematic token cannot be executed, reducing overall utility. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s token handling code against the ERC‑20 specification and identified the direct approve() call as unsafe for tokens that deviate from the standard. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the problem only manifests at runtime with specific tokens, which may not be covered by unit tests that use only compliant ERC‑20 mocks. The recommended remediation is to replace the raw approve() call with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 functions such as safeIncreaseAllowance() or safeApprove(), which internally handle missing return values and revert only on genuine failures. By using these wrappers, the contract becomes tolerant to both standard and non‑standard ERC‑20 implementations, restoring the expected behavior where a user’s allowance is correctly set and the swap proceeds or fails only for legitimate reasons, thereby preventing unexpected reverts and preserving user funds and protocol functionality.

title: RefundAddress forwarded to LayerZero endpoint is incorrect
description: The sendMessageUsingNative function from the LayerZeroAdapter.sol contract is used by the Bridge.sol contract to send a message using LayerZero. This function, in turn, calls the _sendMessage function, which again calls _lzSend to call the LayerZero endpoint with the right parameters. The sendMessageUsingNative function accepts msg.value equal to / greater than the fee quoted by LayerZero to cover LayerZero's messaging costs. It forwards them to the endpoint contract, from which any unused value is refunded to the refundAddress specified. However, these refunds don't work as expected as the refund address is always specified as the Bridge.sol contract, which is the msg.sender in the context of the LayerZeroAdapter.sol contract. Thus, any refunds received from LayerZero's endpoint are locked indefinitely in the Bridge.sol contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration of the refund destination when the Bridge contract uses the LayerZeroAdapter to forward a native token payment to the LayerZero endpoint. The sendMessageUsingNative function accepts msg.value that should cover the quoted LayerZero fee and forwards any excess value to the endpoint, which is supposed to return the unused amount to a refund address.
