The impact is limited in the current deployment because no other contracts read the _cumulativeRewards store and the off‑chain calculator does not depend on it, but the bug violates the business rule that reward snapshots must be tied to the period’s final block. The issue appears only when the owner calls increaseClaimableByBatch with a non‑zero endBlock; if the function were called without an endBlock, the bug would be invisible. Users may notice that their reward balance appears lower or higher than expected after a batch claim, or that a historical reward chart shows gaps. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function signature with its implementation and identified the use of block.number. It is hard to notice because the stored value is not currently used elsewhere, so no failing transaction is observed. The proper fix is to extend _incrementCumulativeRewards to accept the endBlock parameter and store that value instead of block.number, and to add validation that the supplied block is in the past. This aligns the on‑chain cumulative reward record with the intended accounting period and restores consistency with off‑chain calculations.

title: Swapper can lose all thusdAmount if Price Feed is down
description:
The swap function is meant to allow purchasing of collateral as a way to automate autocompounding of collateral into more THUSD. To allow the swap, getSwapCollateralAmount will query the Chainlink Price Feed for the Collateral / USD pair and use that value to compute the price. In the case in which the call fails, getSwapCollateralAmount will return 0, which means that msg.sender will pay the thusdAmount but receives no collateral in return, as seen in BAMM.sol#L234:
```solidity
if(collateral2usdPrice == 0) return (0, 0); // chainlink is down
```
The slippage check would prevent this from happening, but a distracted buyer (or an automated strategy) may just use 0, causing the transaction to go through.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swap function that automates thepurchase of collateral using a Chainlink price feed. The function calls getSwapCollateralAmount, which queries the Collateral/USD price. If the price feed call fails or returns zero, the helper returns (0,0). The swap then proceeds, charging the caller the specified thusdAmount while the calculated collateral amount is zero, so the caller receives no collateral. The slippage check is intended to block such a scenario, but a caller can set the slippage limit to zero or an automated strategy may ignore it, allowing the transaction to succeed. This bug occurs only when the external price oracle is unavailable or returns a zero value, which can happen during network outages or feed de‑registration. Any user invoking the swap during this condition loses THUSD without receiving any asset, effectively making funds disappear. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the conditional if(collateral2usdPrice == 0) return (0,0); and noted that the contract does not revert on a zero price. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the UI reports success, yet the user's collateral balance remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation that a swap yields collateral. This is an instance of an oracle‑failure handling bug, where unchecked external data leads to a zero‑value calculation and economic loss. To remediate, the contract should revert when the price feed is down or fallback to a safe price, and it should enforce a non‑zero collateral amount before accepting payment. Proper validation prevents the scenario where a user pays THUSD and receives nothing, preserving the accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: Inability to change thusd2UsdPriceAggregator can lead to DOS or negative side effects
description:
CL Price feeds are maintained, meaning that they could be deprecated. Due to the check, the extra feed cannot be removed, and thus in case of deprecation, the BAMM contract will stop working. Price Feeds could start reverting for following reasons:
• Logical Flaw
• Paused by the Owner (Chainlink Admin)
Price Feeds may also not be deprecated, hence they will return old prices. It would be best to allow to edit the PriceFeed as to allow the BAMM rebalancing to work. More speciﬁcally, because the feed would be only to handle the peg for THUSD vs USD, it may be best to assume the price is 1 dollar (which creates opportunities for arbitrage), when the Feed Reverts.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an immutable reference to a THUSD/USD price aggregator that cannot be replaced or overridden once the contract is deployed. The root cause is a design decision that hard‑codes the address of a Chainlink price feed and does not provide any administrative function to update it, nor does it include a fallback mechanism for when the feed becomes unavailable. When the external price feed is deprecated, paused by its owner, or begins to revert calls because of a logical flaw, the BAMM contract attempts to read the price during its rebalancing routine and receives a revert or an outdated value. Because the contract cannot handle the revert, the rebalancing transaction itself reverts, effectively halting the protocol’s core functionality. This denial‑of‑service condition can be triggered simply by the feed operator pausing the feed or by the feed being phased out, which are realistic operational events. The impact is that users see no rebalancing activity, their expected profit or redemption values remain unchanged, and in extreme cases funds may become locked because the contract cannot execute the necessary swaps. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s reliance on external oracles and noted the absence of any setter or try‑catch logic around the price query. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the feed usually returns a valid price, so the contract behaves correctly until the feed status changes. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of immutable external dependency failures and missing fallback handling. To remediate, the contract should expose a secure admin function that allows the price feed address to be updated, and it should catch oracle reverts and substitute a safe default price (for example, a hard‑coded 1 USD value for a stable‑coin peg) so that rebalancing can continue or fail gracefully. From the user’s perspective the UI would show no change in balances after a rebalance attempt, transactions would revert with generic errors, and users might receive zero profit or see their redemption amount stay at the previous level, contrary to the expectation that the protocol continuously adjusts positions. The failure violates the business logic that assumes a reliable, up‑to‑date price feed for accounting and arbitrage protection, leading to a situation where money appears to disappear or become inaccessible when the oracle stops working.

title: TELLOR_DIGITS will be incorrect for newer feeds
description:
The implementation will work only for the ETH / USD Feed (exclusively if Liquity's current Feed is used) but will not work for a BTC / USD Feed as new feeds have 18 decimals of precision. Proof of concept: By checking the following links, we can see how the Liquity Feed has been normalized on purpose by Tellor. So, newer feeds will instead have 18 decimals of precision:
• Etherscan address 0xD9157453E2668B2fc45b7A803D3FEF3642430cC0:
– See the implicated code here.
• Etherscan address 0xd3b9a1dcabd16c482785fd4265cb4580b84cded7:
– See the implicated code here.
Here one can see that the adjustment is done exclusively for ETH / USD query. Another Tellor oracle, for example for tBTC, will not be using the same decimals.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of decimal precision for price feeds obtained from the Tellor oracle. The contract assumes that the ETH/USD feed is normalized to a specific number of decimals (the implementation contains a hard‑coded adjustment that only applies to the ETH/USD query). Newer feeds, such as BTC/USD, are provided with 18 decimals of precision and are not subject to the same adjustment. As a result, when the contract reads a BTC/USD price, it interprets the value using the wrong scaling factor, leading to an incorrect price calculation. This mis‑scaled price can cause the contract’s business logic – for example, collateral‑to‑debt ratios, liquidation thresholds, or fee calculations – to be evaluated against a wrong number. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected liquidation, zero or unusually low refunds, or balances that seem to disappear because the protocol believes the asset value is far lower or higher than it actually is. The issue occurs whenever the contract queries a non‑ETH feed that provides 18‑decimal precision while still applying the ETH‑specific scaling logic. It primarily affects any participant that relies on accurate price data from Tellor, including borrowers, lenders, and any automated agents that trigger actions based on price thresholds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor observed that the decimal adjustment code was gated by a check for the ETH/USD query identifier and did not generalise to other identifiers. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a price is mis‑scaled, the problem can remain hidden until a threshold is crossed and an unexpected state transition occurs. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect numeric scaling” or “decimal handling” vulnerabilities, where hard‑coded assumptions about external data formats break when the data format changes. To remediate the issue the contract should retrieve the decimal count from the Tellor feed metadata or apply a uniform scaling approach that does not depend on the asset type, ensuring that every price is normalised to the same precision before it is used in calculations. This change would restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent users from experiencing unexplained balance changes or premature liquidations.

title: redemptionQueueTotal not decreased during _decreaseRedemptionAmount could lead to overes- timation of availableForInvestment
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the investment manager contract. A state variable that records the total amount of tokens waiting in the redemption queue – redemptionQueueTotal – is used by the availableForInvestment view to calculate how many new tokens can still be invested in a deal. When an investor’s token balance falls below the amount they originally queued for redemption, the internal function _decreaseRedemptionAmount reduces the individual redemption request’s amount, but it fails to adjust the global redemptionQueueTotal for queued redemptions. As a result, the view function continues to add an outdated, larger queue total to the investable emission, producing an inflated availableForInvestment figure. This over‑estimation can mislead automated keepers or front‑end interfaces into submitting a reviewOffer transaction with an acceptedAmount that exceeds the true remaining capacity. The transaction then reverts, causing unexpected failures and potentially leaving investors unable to place legitimate investments until the discrepancy is resolved. The bug manifests only when a queued redemption is partially decreased – for example, after a token transfer that reduces the investor’s balance – and only for the queued phase of the request. Users see a higher “available for investment” number in the UI, attempt to invest, and receive a transaction error or see their funds appear to disappear. The issue was identified during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted the missing state update. It is subtle because the view function itself appears correct and the missing update occurs in a rarely exercised branch, making it easy to overlook during testing. The proper remediation is to decrement redemptionQueueTotal by the exact amount by which the queued redemption request is reduced, ensuring that the global queue total always reflects the sum of all active queued redemption amounts. Conceptually, any accounting variable that aggregates per‑user values must be kept in sync whenever any individual component changes, otherwise downstream calculations that rely on the aggregate become unreliable and can break business logic such as investment caps and fund availability.

title: burnDealTokens can brick queued redemptions processing
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency that occurs when an account with a pending redemption is stripped of tokens through the privileged burnDealTokens function. The DEAL_ADMIN role can invoke a burn operation on any holder, which directly reduces the holder’s token balance without adjusting the amount that the redemption queue expects the holder to supply later. When the redemption processor later attempts to transfer the queued amount, it checks the holder’s current balance and fails because the balance is now insufficient. This failure aborts the redemption step, leaving the entire redemption queue stuck; subsequent redemptions cannot be processed even for users whose balances were not directly burned. The issue arises because the burn function does not call the internal routine that decreases pending redemption amounts before destroying tokens. It was discovered during an audit that the managedTransfer call in the redemption logic contains a comment noting a possible transfer failure when the investor’s balance is insufficient, and that the burn path does not invoke the safeguard used in principal payout callbacks. Exploitation is straightforward: any entity with the DEAL_ADMIN role can burn tokens from a user who has an outstanding redemption request, causing that request to fail and the queue to halt. The impact is that users may see their redemption attempts revert, balances appear unchanged or zero, and funds that should be released remain locked in the contract. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a redemption button that does nothing, or a transaction that succeeds but results in no token transfer, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The problem is hard to notice because the burn operation itself succeeds and only manifests later when the redemption queue is processed, which may be delayed. The correct mitigation is to adjust pending redemption amounts before burning, for example by iterating over each burn target, computing the holder’s current balance, and decreasing the queued redemption amount accordingly, as suggested in the recommended code change. This aligns the contract’s accounting state with the actual token supply and prevents the redemption queue from becoming permanently blocked, preserving the expected business logic that a redemption request should either succeed or be rejected, but never leave the system in a deadlocked state.

title: Partial redemptions will fail if max holders is reached and deal manager's dealToken balance is zero
poc:
• Preconditions: DEAL_MAX_HOLDERS = 2
1. Alice and Bob are two holders which initially sign into the deal by providing 1M$ each. DealManager holds zero tokens.
• Scenario 1: redemptionBudget = 0
2. Alice wants out of the deal by 500k$, and thus submits a redemption request.
3. Bob submits an offer for 500k$ expecting to "buy" the deal tokens from Alice.
4. When the deal admin calls reviewOffer for the full amount, it reverts, because Alice's deal tokens are first transferred to DealManager, thus attempting to add DealManager address as an additional holder.
• Scenario 2: redemptionBudget = 500k
5. Alice wants out of the deal by 500k$, and thus submits a redemption request.
6. When deal admin calls reviewRedemptionRequest, the call fails because the deal tokens must be transferred to DealManager.
bug_full: During a partial redemption the contract first moves the redeemed deal tokens from the investor to the DealManager contract using a managedTransfer, and only afterwards transfers the same amount from the DealManager to the final redeemer. The Deal token tracks holders by adding any address whose balance changes from zero to a positive value, enforcing a global DEAL_MAX_HOLDERS limit. The original holder‑update logic does not treat the DealManager as a special case, so when the DealManager’s balance is initially zero it is counted as a new holder. If the maximum number of holders has already been reached, the addition of the DealManager triggers the MaxHoldersExceeded revert before the second transfer can occur. Consequently, a redemption request that should succeed is rejected, leaving the investor’s funds locked and the user sees a transaction revert with a MaxHoldersExceeded error. The bug appears only when the holder limit is tight (e.g., two holders) and the DealManager holds no tokens at the start of the operation, which makes it easy to miss during testing because the manager’s balance returns to zero after the internal transfer. The issue was discovered by the Spearbit audit team through code inspection and a proof‑of‑concept that created two holders, set DEAL_MAX_HOLDERS to 2, and attempted a partial redemption, causing the revert. This is a class of accounting bugs where temporary internal transfers inflate the holder count and violate business logic that assumes the manager is not a regular holder. The impact is that users cannot redeem their positions when the holder cap is reached, potentially breaking liquidity guarantees and damaging trust in the protocol. The recommended fix is to modify the _afterBalanceUpdate routine to ignore the manager address when updating holder status, thereby preventing the temporary holder from being counted toward the maximum and allowing redemptions to proceed as intended.

title: Incorrect PayoutManager.payoutDustThreshold implementation leads to more tokens getting burned than expected
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑implemented dust‑threshold function in the PayoutManager contract. The function is supposed to return the smallest amount of the deal token that should be considered payable – defined as 0.01 token – but the code multiplies 0.01 by 1e4, which evaluates to 100 times larger than intended, effectively returning a threshold of one whole token. The root cause is an incorrect scaling factor in the arithmetic expression that calculates the dust amount based on the token’s decimal precision. When the contract later calls _principalPayoutDistribution, any investor balance that is below the returned threshold is classified as dust and is automatically burned instead of being transferred. Because the threshold is one token rather than one‑hundredth of a token, balances that would normally be paid out as small residual amounts (for example 0.5 or 0.2 tokens) are treated as dust and disappear from the user’s account. This can be exploited simply by triggering a payout when an investor’s remaining balance is small; the contract will burn those tokens without any further checks, leading to a loss of user funds. The impact is that investors receive less than expected, often seeing a zero balance after a payout even though they were entitled to a fractional remainder. The condition under which this occurs is any payout execution where the investor’s residual balance is less than one token. All participants who hold the deal token – individual investors, the protocol’s accounting system, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate balance reporting – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended dust amount (0.01 token) with the actual return value of the function. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is hidden in a small constant; user interfaces typically display balances rounded to whole tokens, so a missing fractional amount may not raise an immediate alarm. The bug violates the business logic that small leftover amounts should be returned to users, not destroyed, breaking accounting assumptions about token conservation. To fix the problem, the calculation should be changed to return exactly 10**(decimals‑2), which corresponds to 0.01 token, removing the erroneous multiplier. Conceptually, the fix restores the intended dust threshold so that only amounts truly smaller than one‑hundredth of a token are burned, preserving user funds and maintaining correct token supply dynamics.

title: Redemption requests can be reviewed more than once
description:
The InvestmentManager._reviewRedemptionRequest function currently lacks protection against reviewing a redemption request more than once. Due to this a single redemption request can be reviewed multiple times by the DEAL_ADMIN, leading to unintended scenarios and accounting issues.
Consider a redemption request of 100 tokens which got accepted, 50 tokens were redeemed from redemption budget and 50 tokens were queued. For this request, the DEAL_ADMIN can perform any of these operations:
• Call the _reviewRedemptionRequest again with acceptedAmount as 0 and delete the queued request of 50 tokens.
• If liquidity is present then call the _reviewRedemptionRequest with acceptedAmount as 100, in this case 100 tokens will be redeemed instantly.
• If liquidity is not present then call the _reviewRedemptionRequest with acceptedAmount as 100, in this case 100 tokens will be queued in redemption queue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an idempotency flaw in the redemption review logic of the InvestmentManager contract. The internal function that processes a redemption request does not record that the request has already been reviewed, so the DEAL_ADMIN role can invoke the function repeatedly on the same request. Because the function updates the redeemed amount and the queued amount each time it is called, a single request can be accepted, partially redeemed, and then re‑reviewed with a different acceptedAmount value. This allows the admin to either redeem additional tokens that were already accounted for, delete a queued portion, or re‑queue the full amount, effectively creating or destroying token balances. The root cause is the absence of a state flag or a check that reverts when a request is already in a processed or queued state. An attacker with the DEAL_ADMIN role can exploit this by calling the review function multiple times after the initial acceptance, choosing acceptedAmount=0 to delete a queued portion, or acceptedAmount equal to the original request size to cause a second redemption or a second queue entry. The impact includes accounting inconsistencies, potential over‑redemption of tokens, loss of liquidity, and a mismatch between investor expectations and actual token balances. The issue manifests when a redemption request has been partially or fully processed but remains stored without a processed marker; under those conditions the admin can trigger the flaw. All investors who submit redemption requests are affected because their balances may be altered unexpectedly, and the protocol’s overall token accounting can become unreliable. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of redemption requests and noticed that the function lacks a guard against repeated reviews. It can be hard to notice because each call appears successful and the UI may still show the request as pending, hiding the double‑processing from users. The correct mitigation is to introduce a status field (e.g., Reviewed or Processed) and to revert any attempt to review a request that is already in a queued or completed state, thereby enforcing single‑use semantics for each redemption request.

title: Incorrect EIP712 typehash
description:
The TYPE_HASH used for EIP712 signing for the order that is signed by the users is incorrect.
According with EIP-712's speciﬁcations, the structs are encoded as follows:
If the struct type references other struct types (and these in turn reference even more struct types), then the set of referenced struct types is collected, sorted by name and appended to the encoding. An example encoding is
Transaction(Person from,Person to,Asset tx)
Asset(address token,uint256 amount)
Person(address wallet,string name)
```solidity
bytes internal constant V3_DUTCH_ORDER_TYPE = abi.encodePacked(
    "V3DutchOrder(",
    "OrderInfo info,",
    "address cosigner,",
    "uint256 startingBaseFee,",
    "V3DutchInput baseInput,",
    "V3DutchOutput[] baseOutputs)"
);
bytes internal constant V3_DUTCH_INPUT_TYPE = abi.encodePacked(
    "V3DutchInput(",
    "address token,",
    "uint256 startAmount,",
    "NonlinearDutchDecay curve,",
    "uint256 maxAmount,",
    "uint256 adjustmentPerGweiBaseFee)"
);
bytes internal constant V3_DUTCH_OUTPUT_TYPE = abi.encodePacked(
    "V3DutchOutput(",
    "address token,",
    "uint256 startAmount,",
    "NonlinearDutchDecay curve,",
    "address recipient,",
    "uint256 minAmount,",
    "uint256 adjustmentPerGweiBaseFee)"
);
bytes internal constant NON_LINEAR_DECAY_TYPE =
    abi.encodePacked(
        "NonlinearDutchDecay(",
        "uint256 relativeBlocks,",
        "int256[] relativeAmounts)"
    );
```
As we can see above, the order should be deﬁned as:
```solidity
abi.encodePacked(V3_DUTCH_ORDER_TYPE, NON_LINEAR_DECAY_TYPE, OrderInfoLib.ORDER_INFO_TYPE, V3_DUTCH_INPUT_TYPE, V3_DUTCH_OUTPUT_TYPE);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect EIP‑712 typehash used when signing Dutch auction orders. EIP‑712 requires that the full definition of a struct, including any nested structs, be concatenated in alphabetical order of the struct names before hashing. The contract builds the typehash by encoding only the top‑level order struct and a subset of its component structs, but it does not sort the referenced struct types nor include them in the exact order prescribed by the specification. As a result the hash that the contract expects does not match the hash that off‑chain signers generate. When a user signs an order they assume the signature will be verified against the exact fields they approved, such as token addresses, start amounts and decay curves. Because the contract checks a mismatched typehash, the signature may be considered valid for a different logical layout, allowing the contract to accept an order that differs from the one the user signed. This can lead to unexpected token transfers, missing refunds, or execution of orders with altered parameters, effectively causing funds to disappear or be sent to unintended recipients. The issue manifests whenever a user creates and signs a V3DutchOrder; the contract will either reject the order despite a valid signature (causing user panic) or, worse, accept a malformed order that violates the business logic of the auction. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who compared the on‑chain typehash construction with the EIP‑712 reference implementation and noticed the missing alphabetical sorting of struct definitions. The problem is subtle because the signature appears cryptographically correct, so developers may not notice the mismatch without inspecting the typehash generation code. To remediate, the contract must recompute the typehash by concatenating all referenced struct definitions in alphabetical order, exactly as the EIP‑712 spec dictates, and then use that hash for signature verification. This change restores the intended binding between the signed data and the on‑chain execution, preventing accidental or malicious order manipulation and ensuring that users receive the outcomes they expect when they sign an order.

title: Incorrect use of L1 block.number on Arbitrum
description:
According to Arbitrum's documentation, block.number returns the approximate L1 block number at which the sequencer received the transaction instead of the current L2 block number.
Compared to the L1 block time, which is 12 seconds, the L2 block time on Arbitrum is only about 0.25 seconds. Since orders on Arbitrum usually decay within a few seconds (less than 8 seconds at the time of writing), it would be necessary to calculate blockDelta based on L2 block numbers to allow the orders to decay as expected and enable more ﬂexible conﬁgurations of the decay curve.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the global variable block.number to compute the decay of orders on Arbitrum. On Arbitrum, block.number does not represent the current L2 block height; instead it returns an approximation of the L1 block number at which the sequencer received the transaction. Because L1 blocks are produced roughly every 12 seconds while L2 blocks are produced about every 0.25 seconds, the value returned by block.number advances far more slowly than the actual L2 chain progresses. The contract assumes that each increment of block.number corresponds to a 0.25‑second step, and therefore calculates a blockDelta that is used to determine when an order should decay. In practice the calculated delta is off by a factor of about 48, causing orders that are supposed to become invalid after a few seconds to remain active for many seconds or even indefinitely. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who submits transactions that rely on the decay window; by submitting them within the unintended extended window the attacker can capture trades that should have been unavailable, potentially extracting value or causing the protocol’s accounting to diverge from its intended economic model. The impact is that users may see their orders stay open longer than expected, leading to unexpected executions, loss of expected refunds, or funds being locked in stale orders. The issue manifests only when the contract is deployed on Arbitrum and uses block.number for time‑sensitive logic; on other EVM chains the variable behaves as usual, so the bug can be hard to notice during testing on local environments that do not emulate Arbitrum’s semantics. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s decay formula with Arbitrum’s documentation, revealing the semantic mismatch. Because the contract appears to function correctly on testnets that do not replicate the L1‑L2 block number relationship, the bug may remain hidden until live deployment. The correct mitigation is to replace block.number with ArbSys(100).arbBlockNumber(), which returns the actual L2 block number, thereby aligning the decay calculation with the true progression of the Arbitrum chain. Conceptually, the fix is to use a source of time that reflects the L2 environment for any logic that depends on block progression, ensuring that order expiration, fee accrual, or other time‑based mechanisms behave as intended.

title: Incorrect fee calculation in withdraw and redeem functions
description:
The calculations in previewRedeem() and previewWithdraw() use different mathematical approaches that result in inconsistent fee application:
1. In previewRedeem(), the contract:
   • Calculates fee shares directly: feeShares = _feeOnRaw(shares, feeRateBps).
   • Subtracts the fee from shares: netShares = shares - feeShares.
   • Returns assets corresponding to remaining shares: return super.previewRedeem(netShares).
2. In previewWithdraw(), the contract:
   • Calculates shares needed without fee: sharesWithoutFee = super.previewWithdraw(assets).
   • Calculates fee on those shares: feeShares = _feeOnRaw(sharesWithoutFee, feeRateBps).
   • Returns total shares needed: return sharesWithoutFee + feeShares.
The current implementation of previewWithdraw() uses the formula `shares = toShares(assets) * (1 + f)` However, the mathematically equivalent formula to previewRedeem() should be: `shares = toShares(assets / (1 - f))`

Impact Explanation:
The impact is medium. Users may receive more or fewer assets than expected when withdrawing from the vault. This discrepancy becomes more pronounced as the fee rate increases, potentially affecting users' financial positions and a loss in revenue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent fee calculation between the previewRedeem and previewWithdraw functions of an ERC4626‑style vault. The root cause is that the two preview functions apply the fee using different mathematical formulas: previewRedeem subtracts a fee calculated on the raw share amount and then converts the net shares to assets, while previewWithdraw first determines the share amount required for the requested assets and then adds a fee on that share amount using a linear multiplier (1+f). This multiplier is not mathematically equivalent to the division‑by‑(1‑f) approach used in previewRedeem, causing the vault to either over‑charge or under‑charge fees depending on the fee rate. An attacker or ordinary user can exploit the discrepancy by calling withdraw with a specific asset amount and receiving fewer assets than expected, or by being required to provide more shares than necessary, effectively losing value. The impact is medium because users may receive more or fewer assets than they anticipate, especially as the fee basis points increase, which can erode user balances and reduce protocol revenue. The issue manifests whenever the fee rate is non‑zero and a user initiates a withdrawal or redemption; it affects all participants who interact with the vault, including regular token holders and the protocol treasury that receives the mis‑calculated fee shares. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the outputs of previewRedeem and previewWithdraw for identical inputs and identified a mismatch in the resulting fee amounts. It is hard to notice because both functions appear to work in isolation and typical unit tests may only verify one path, allowing the subtle arithmetic inconsistency to remain hidden. To remediate the problem the fee logic should be unified using a single, mathematically correct helper that computes the fee on the total amount (feeOnTotal) and on the raw amount (feeOnRaw), and both preview functions should be rewritten to use these helpers so that the fee is applied consistently. The corrected previewWithdraw should calculate the fee on the total assets and then request shares for assets plus fee, while previewRedeem should compute the fee on the asset amount and subtract it from the returned assets. Consolidating the internal withdrawal logic into a single function that mints the proper fee shares to the treasury also ensures accounting integrity. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal transaction may return less cash than shown on the UI, or the UI may indicate that more vault shares are needed to receive a given amount, contradicting the user’s expectation of a straightforward 1‑to‑1 conversion after fees. This deviation from expected behavior violates the vault’s accounting assumptions and can lead to user confusion and financial loss.

title: Incorrect asset calculation in maxWithdraw() function
description:
There are two issues with the maxWithdraw() implementation:
1. The withdraw() function calls super.maxWithdraw(owner) (which refers to ERC4626Upgradeable's implementation) instead of calling the overridden maxWithdraw() from WrappedDollarVault. This means the fee calculation in WrappedDollarVault's maxWithdraw() is bypassed.
2. The fee calculation in maxWithdraw() doesn't align with the fee calculation in previewWithdraw(), which leads to inconsistent behavior.

Impact Explanation:
The impact is medium. The incorrect calculation in maxWithdraw() can lead to a poor user experience where withdrawal transactions fail unexpectedly. It could also potentially lead to users being unable to withdraw their full entitled assets if the function underestimates the maximum amount. This creates confusion and may reduce trust in the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect asset calculation in the maxWithdraw function of the WrappedDollarVault contract. Two related defects cause the problem. First, the public withdraw function forwards the call to super.withdraw, which internally invokes the ERC4626Upgradeable implementation of maxWithdraw instead of the overridden version defined in WrappedDollarVault. Because the overridden maxWithdraw contains the fee deduction logic, bypassing it means the fee is not accounted for when the contract determines how many assets a user may withdraw. Second, the fee calculation performed inside the overridden maxWithdraw does not match the fee logic used in previewWithdraw, resulting in a mismatch between the amount shown to the user and the amount that can actually be withdrawn. The root cause is a misuse of inheritance combined with inconsistent fee formulas, leading to an under‑estimation of the maximum withdrawable assets. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by calling withdraw with an amount that appears to be within the displayed limit; the transaction will revert because the internal maxWithdraw reports a lower value, or the user will receive less than expected after fees are applied. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a failed withdrawal transaction, a zero or unchanged balance after the attempt, and a discrepancy between the amount shown in the UI and the amount actually transferred. The issue occurs whenever the contract is not paused and the feeRateBps parameter is set, because the overridden maxWithdraw returns zero only when paused. All token holders of the WrappedDollarVault are affected, as the bug reduces confidence in the protocol’s accounting and can lead to loss of liquidity if users are unable to retrieve their full entitlement. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, and it can be hard to notice because the function signatures are identical and the fee logic is hidden behind internal calls, making the mismatch invisible to superficial testing. To remediate the issue the withdraw function should either call the contract’s own maxWithdraw implementation or simply use super.withdraw, ensuring the fee logic is applied consistently. Additionally, maxWithdraw should be re‑implemented so that its fee calculation mirrors the previewWithdraw formula, returning the gross withdrawable assets minus the correctly computed fee. This aligns the contract’s accounting with user expectations and restores reliable withdrawal behavior.

title: Incorrect fee share calculation in harvest function
description:
In the current implementation of the harvest() function, fee shares are calculated as a percentage of the existing token supply:
```solidity
uint256 currentSupply = totalSupply();
sharesMinted = currentSupply.mulDiv($.feeRateBps, BPS_DIVIDER, Math.Rounding.Floor);
```
This approach doesn't properly calculate the correct proportion of fee shares to mint. When new shares are minted, the total supply increases, but the fee calculation doesn't account for these new shares in the total. For a fee rate of f, the correct proportion of new shares relative to the post-mint total supply should be f/(1-f) of the total. The current implementation simply mints f of the pre-mint total, which results in less than f of the post-mint total being fee shares. This means the protocol is earning fewer fees than intended according to the fee rate.

Impact Explanation:
The impact is medium. The treasury receives fewer fee shares than it should based on the intended fee rate. This effectively reduces the protocol's fee income and benefits existing token holders at the expense of the treasury. The magnitude of this issue increases with higher fee rates.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee‑share calculation inside the harvest() function of a token vault. The code determines the number of fee shares to mint by multiplying the current total supply by the fee rate expressed in basis points and dividing by the BPS divisor. This computes a fraction f of the pre‑mint supply, but the correct economic model requires that the fee shares represent f/(1‑f) of the total supply after the new shares are minted. Because the calculation ignores the shares that are about to be created, the minted fee amount is smaller than the intended proportion, causing the treasury to receive fewer fee shares than the protocol’s fee rate promises. The bug originates from using the pre‑mint totalSupply as the denominator and not adjusting for the increase in supply caused by the minting operation. It can be exploited indirectly: any entity with the harvest role can trigger the function and the protocol will consistently under‑collect fees, which benefits existing token holders at the expense of the treasury. The impact is economic rather than a direct loss of user funds; the treasury’s fee income is reduced, and the discrepancy grows with higher fee rates. The condition occurs each time harvest() is called after the required time interval, and it affects the protocol’s treasury, token holders, and any user who expects a certain fee return. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑distribution logic and compared the expected post‑mint proportion with the actual minted amount. It is hard to notice because the total supply does increase as expected, so balances appear correct, but the proportion allocated to the treasury is subtly off, making the shortfall visible only when comparing against the fee rate specification. The proper fix is to compute the fee shares using the formula sharesMinted = currentSupply * feeRateBps / (BPS_DIVIDER - feeRateBps) with appropriate rounding, thereby ensuring the minted fee shares constitute the correct f/(1‑f) share of the post‑mint total. This class of bug falls under incorrect proportional minting or fee‑calculation errors, where a formula fails to account for state changes caused by the operation itself, leading to accounting mismatches and reduced revenue.

title: Active redirection can be removed when the DistributionModule contract is paused
description: The DistributionModule.removeRedirectedOffChainDistribution function is missing whenNotPaused modifier. Due to this an active redirection can be removed by an account when the DistributionModule contract is paused. Pausing of contract is only intended to be triggered in critical scenarios (exploit, upgrades, active bug, etc...) and performing any user operation in paused state can lead to unintended outcomes. One scenario could be when the redirection admin address gets compromised. Pausing the contract would not prevent the compromised redirection admin from removing the redirections.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control omission in the DistributionModule contract: the function that removes an active off‑chain distribution redirection does not include the whenNotPaused guard that is applied to all other user‑facing operations. Because the contract can be placed into a paused state only during emergencies such as a detected exploit, an upgrade, or a critical bug, the expectation is that no state‑changing actions are possible while paused. However, the missing modifier allows any caller that satisfies the redirection‑admin check to invoke removeRedirectedOffChainDistribution even when the contract is paused. The root cause is the absence of the pause‑state validation in the function’s signature, which defeats the intended safety barrier. An attacker who compromises the redirection‑admin address can exploit this by calling the function during a pause, thereby deleting the stored activeRedirectedOffChainDistribution entry for a target account. This removal can cause the protocol’s accounting to lose the association between a user and its off‑chain distribution destination, leading to funds being sent to an unintended address or simply not being distributed at all. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a previously set redirection disappears: a user who expects their rewards to be forwarded to a designated off‑chain address sees no reward, or the reward is sent to the original address, effectively resulting in “funds disappear” or “refund missing”. The impact is medium‑risk because it does not directly steal funds, but it breaks the business logic of the distribution system, can cause loss of trust, and may require manual remediation. The issue manifests only when the contract is paused and the redirection admin is compromised; in normal operation the function works as intended, which makes the bug easy to overlook during testing because pause‑related paths are rarely exercised. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which identified the missing whenNotPaused modifier by reviewing the contract’s pause handling. To remediate, the function should be protected with the whenNotPaused modifier (or an equivalent pause‑state check) so that removal of redirections is prohibited while the contract is paused, restoring the guarantee that no state changes occur during emergency pauses. This aligns the function with the broader contract design and prevents accidental or malicious redirection removal during critical periods.

title: Claim reward function reverts after distribution period ends
description:
A vulnerability in the reward distribution mechanism allows the first user to claim their reward after the distribution period ends, but subsequent claims by other users result in a function revert due to an underflow error. This issue effectively locks out other users from claiming their rewards once the distribution period has concluded.
The vulnerability occurs in the _rewardPerToken() function, which is used to calculate the reward per token. The function attempts to calculate the time elapsed since the last update, but when the current time exceeds the period finish time and a claim has already been made, it results in an underflow.
The issue manifests as follows:
1. The distribution period ends.
2. The first user successfully claims their reward.
3. This updates the lastUpdateTime to a value greater than periodFinish.
4. When subsequent users try to claim, the calculation Math.min(block.timestamp, $.periodFinish) - $.lastUpdateTime results in an underflow, causing the function to revert.
This behavior effectively prevents all but one user from claiming their rewards after the distribution period has ended.
Impact: The impact of this vulnerability is high. It can result in users being unable to claim their rightfully earned rewards, potentially leading to significant financial losses for affected users. Although users can reclaim their rewards in subsequent reward periods.
Likelihood: The likelihood of this issue occurring is high. It will consistently happen in any scenario where multiple users attempt to claim rewards after the distribution period has ended. If rewards are continuously emitted without any gaps, this issue might not be encountered.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution contract’s accounting routine that calculates the reward per token when a user calls the claimReward function. The contract stores the timestamp of the last update (lastUpdateTime) and the moment when the distribution period is supposed to finish (periodFinish). After the period ends, the first user who successfully claims a reward causes lastUpdateTime to be set to a value that is greater than periodFinish. Subsequent calls compute the elapsed time as Math.min(block.timestamp, periodFinish) minus lastUpdateTime. Because lastUpdateTime is now larger than the capped timestamp, the subtraction underflows, producing a very large unsigned integer that triggers a revert in the arithmetic library. As a result, later users see their claim transaction fail, their balances remain unchanged, and they receive no reward even though they are entitled to it. The bug manifests only after the distribution window has closed and when more than one participant attempts to claim, making it easy to miss during basic testing where only a single claim is exercised. It was discovered during a formal audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the first claim succeeded and the second reverted. The issue is a classic example of an underflow caused by improper handling of time boundaries in accounting logic, effectively locking out users from their earned rewards. From a user perspective the UI shows a “claim” button that appears to work for the first address but then returns an error or transaction revert for everyone else, contradicting the expectation that all eligible participants can collect their share after the period ends. The impact is high because users may lose access to funds that were already earned, although the rewards can be reclaimed in a later distribution round if the contract is reset. To remediate, the reward‑per‑token calculation must guard against the case where lastUpdateTime is greater than or equal to the period end, for example by only computing elapsed time when lastUpdateTime is less than the minimum of the current block timestamp and periodFinish, or by clamping lastUpdateTime to periodFinish before the subtraction. This change eliminates the underflow and restores the ability for every eligible user to claim their reward regardless of when the claim is made.

title: PAR mechanism mistakenly transfers USD0 tokens to AirdropDistribution contract instead of treasury
description:
The USD0++ token's Parity Arbitrage Right (PAR) mechanism contains a mistake in its implementation. When activated, excess USD0 tokens are incorrectly sent to the AirdropDistribution contract instead of the intended DAO treasury, potentially making funds inaccessible.
The USD0++ token includes a PAR mechanism designed to stabilize its price relative to USD0 when it falls below parity on the open market. This mechanism can be activated when more USD0++ tokens exist on the market than USD0 tokens and the price ratio of USD0:USD0++ is below 1. When triggered, the mechanism unwraps USD0++ for USD0 and exchanges it on the market to support the USD0++ price. Any excess USD0 received from this operation is supposed to be sent to the DAO's treasury.
However, the current implementation incorrectly forwards this excess amount to the AirdropDistribution contract. This contract is not designed to hold tokens and lacks methods for transferring them out, potentially leading to locked funds.
Impact: The impact of this vulnerability can potentially be significant, as funds are effectively locked in the AirdropDistribution contract. Yet, as the contract is upgradeable the impact can be lowered to medium.
Further, addressing this in an emergency upgrade carries its own risks and complications.
Likelihood: The likelihood of this issue occurring is high when the PAR mechanism is activated. The PAR mechanism itself is, however, not intended to be used frequently lowering the likelihood of the vulnerability occurring to medium.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misrouted fund transfer in the PAR (Parity Arbitrage Right) mechanism of the USD0++ token. When the mechanism is triggered because the market price of USD0++ falls below parity and there is an excess of USD0 tokens after unwrapping, the contract is supposed to send the surplus USD0 to the DAO treasury. However, the implementation mistakenly calls safeTransfer with the address of the AirdropDistribution contract. Because the AirdropDistribution contract does not implement any function to move received tokens out, the surplus USD0 becomes permanently locked. The root cause is an incorrect hard‑coded reference (or registry lookup) that resolves to the airdrop contract instead of the treasury contract. An attacker does not need to do anything special; the bug is exercised automatically whenever the PAR mechanism is activated. The exploit flow is: 1) market conditions cause PAR activation, 2) the contract unwraps USD0++ into USD0, 3) the excess USD0 amount is calculated, 4) the contract transfers that amount to the airdrop contract, 5) the airdrop contract has no withdrawal path, so the tokens are stuck. From a user’s point of view the expected outcome – the treasury receiving funds to support the token price – does not happen; the treasury balance stays unchanged and the airdrop contract’s balance increases invisibly, leading to funds disappear or refund missing symptoms. The impact is that any amount of USD0 meant for the treasury becomes inaccessible, potentially reducing the protocol’s ability to stabilize the token price and harming token holders. The issue occurs every time the PAR mechanism is triggered, which is likely when the price is below parity, making the likelihood medium to high. The bug was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the triggerPARMechanismCurvepool function and noticing the wrong destination address. It is hard to notice because the transfer succeeds on‑chain and no revert is emitted; only a post‑mortem of balances reveals the misdirection. The class of bug is a wrong‑address fund transfer or locked‑funds due to incorrect recipient which violates the accounting assumption that surplus assets are always routed to the treasury. The recommended fix is to replace the address argument in the safeTransfer call with the registry lookup for the treasury contract, ensuring excess USD0 is sent to the correct destination, and optionally adding a safeguard that checks the recipient implements a withdrawal interface.

title: Incorrect total staked amount calculation leads to inaccurate reward distribution
description:
The UsualSP contract incorrectly uses the total minted supply of UsualS tokens instead of the actual staked amount in its reward calculations. This leads to inaccurate reward distributions, particularly when users claim their original allocations or unstake their liquid allocations.
In the RewardAccrualBase contract, the _rewardPerToken() calculation uses totalSupply() to determine the amount of tokens staked. However, totalSupply() returns the entire minted supply of UsualS tokens in circulation, not just the amount staked in the contract. This discrepancy causes the contract to assume that all minted UsualS tokens are always staked, which is not the case when users claim their original allocation or unstake their liquid allocation.
As a result, the reward distribution becomes inaccurate, potentially leading to users receiving fewer rewards than they should, as rewards are diluted across a larger perceived supply than what is actually staked.
Impact: The impact of this vulnerability is medium to high. Users are not at risk of losing their staked funds, however they receive fewer rewards than they should based on their actual staked amounts. This undermines the entire reward mechanism of the platform and can lead to indirect financial losses for users who stake their tokens.
Likelihood: The likelihood of this issue occurring is high. It affects all reward calculations and becomes more pronounced as the difference between the total minted supply and the actually staked amount increases over time due to users unstaking or claiming original allocations.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect reward accounting bug caused by the contract using the total minted supply of the reward token as the denominator for reward‑per‑token calculations instead of the actual amount of tokens that are currently staked in the contract. The root cause is that the RewardAccrualBase logic calls totalSupply() on the token contract, which returns the entire circulating supply, while the protocol’s business logic assumes that only tokens held by the staking contract represent the active stake. When users claim their original allocation or unstake their liquid allocation, the token balance of the staking contract drops, but the reward calculation continues to treat the full minted supply as if it were still staked. An attacker or any user can therefore trigger a scenario where the perceived stake is larger than the real stake, diluting the reward pool across phantom tokens. In practice, a user who is the sole staker may receive only a fraction of the entitled reward because the contract believes that additional tokens are also contributing to the pool. The impact is that honest participants receive fewer rewards than they are mathematically owed, violating the platform’s promised yield and leading to indirect financial loss. This condition occurs whenever the total minted supply diverges from the actual staked balance – for example after users have withdrawn, claimed allocations, or when new tokens are minted without being staked. All participants who rely on the reward distribution – stakers, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s incentive model – are affected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors simulated a single‑staker scenario and observed that the reward claim was only half of the expected amount, despite the contract holding the full reward pool. The bug is subtle because the contract’s public view functions report a non‑zero totalSupply, which appears correct at a glance, and the discrepancy only surfaces in the reward‑per‑token formula, making it easy to miss without precise accounting tests. To remediate, the contract should replace the use of totalSupply() with a function that returns the actual token balance held by the staking contract (e.g., totalStaked()), or maintain an internal accounting variable that tracks the net staked amount. This change aligns the reward calculation with the true economic state, restores correct proportional distribution, and prevents reward dilution caused by token minting or unstaking events. The class of bug can be described as a “misused total supply metric in reward accounting,” a common mistake in staking or yield‑farm contracts where on‑chain accounting of staked balances is conflated with token supply metrics. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after staking and later claiming rewards, the user sees a smaller token balance than expected – the UI may show “reward claimed: 0.5 USUAL” when the user anticipated the full amount, leading to confusion and perceived loss of earnings.

title: Inconsistent withdrawal fee calculation between redeem and withdraw functions
description:
The UsualX contract implements withdrawal fees inconsistently between the redeem() and withdraw() functions. This discrepancy allows users to extract more assets than intended when using the withdraw() function repeatedly, effectively reducing the withdrawal fee.
The previewRedeem() and previewWithdraw() functions, which are used by redeem() and withdraw() respectively, calculate the withdrawal fee using different approaches:
1. previewRedeem() calculates assets as: assets = convertToAssets(shares) * (1 - feeRate)
2. previewWithdraw() calculates shares as: shares = convertToShares(assets * (1 + feeRate))
However, the correct approach should be: shares = convertToShares(assets / (1 - feeRate))
This inconsistency leads to:
• redeem() correctly deducting 5% fee (for a 5% fee rate).
• withdraw() allowing users to initially withdraw 95% of assets, but leaving a small amount of shares that can be further withdrawn.
By repeatedly calling withdraw(), users can extract more assets than intended, resulting in an effective fee of approximately 4.762% instead of the intended 5%. The corrected formula's derivation can be seen as follows:
assets = convertToAssets(shares) · 0.95
=⇒ assets / 0.95 = convertToAssets(shares)
=⇒ convertToShares(assets / 0.95) = shares
=⇒ convertToShares(assets + assets · 0.05 / 0.95) = shares
=⇒ convertToShares(assets + assets · 0.05 / (1 - 0.05)) = shares
Impact: The impact is moderate. Users can exploit this discrepancy to pay less in withdrawal fees than intended, potentially leading to a loss of revenue for the protocol or other stakeholders who were meant to benefit from these fees.
Likelihood: The likelihood of this issue occurring is high. While deliberate exploitation by sophisticated users or automated systems is possible, especially for large withdrawals, this discrepancy will also affect regular users unknowingly. Any user who chooses to withdraw using the withdraw() function instead of redeem() will inadvertently benefit from the lower effective fee rate, regardless of their awareness of the underlying issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent withdrawal fee calculation between the redeem and withdraw entry points of the UsualX contract. The contract is supposed to charge a fixed percentage fee on every withdrawal, but the previewRedeem function computes the net assets by multiplying the converted assets by (1‑feeRate) while previewWithdraw computes the required shares by converting assets multiplied by (1+feeRate). The correct relationship is shares = convertToShares(assets / (1‑feeRate)). Because previewWithdraw uses the wrong formula, a user who calls withdraw can initially receive 95 % of the underlying assets (for a 5 % fee) and still retain a small amount of shares. By calling withdraw repeatedly the user can repeatedly extract the remaining shares, ending up with an effective fee of about 4.762 % instead of the intended 5 %. This discrepancy can be exploited by any participant who prefers the withdraw interface, allowing them to pay a lower fee and thereby reducing the protocol’s revenue. The issue manifests whenever a user invokes withdraw or any function that relies on previewWithdraw, such as maxWithdraw or withdraw, and it is observable as a higher net asset payout and leftover share balance after each call. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the outputs of previewRedeem and previewWithdraw for identical inputs and noticed a systematic offset. It is subtle because both functions appear to work and the fee is still deducted, so casual testing may not reveal the small residual share amount. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑calculation inconsistencies and accounting bugs where two complementary functions use mismatched formulas, breaking the invariant that total assets before and after fee deduction should be equal. From a user perspective the UI may show that a withdrawal of 100 tokens should result in 95 tokens received, yet the wallet balance after the transaction shows a slightly higher amount and a non‑zero share balance, contradicting the expectation that the share balance becomes zero. The contract should be fixed by aligning previewWithdraw with the correct formula, i.e., calculating the fee on the requested assets, adding it to the assets, and then converting the total to shares, ensuring both redeem and withdraw charge the same fee.

title: User receives excess rewards for allocation after distribution start
description:
The UsualSP contract incorrectly calculates rewards for users who receive allocations after the reward distribution has started. This results in users receiving rewards as if they had been staking since the beginning of the distribution period, even if they were allocated tokens much later.
The issue stems from the _earned() function in the RewardAccrualBase contract. When calculating rewards, it uses the difference between the current rewardPerTokenStored and the user's lastRewardPerTokenUsed. For a newly allocated user, lastRewardPerTokenUsed is zero, causing the calculation to assume the user has been staking since the start of the distribution.
The allocate() function in UsualSP does not update the user's reward state when allocating new tokens. This means that when a user claims rewards after receiving a late allocation, they receive rewards for the entire period since the start of distribution, rather than just for the time since their allocation.
This issue also arises in the case that the allocation increases for users which have previously staked.
Impact: The impact is high as it results in an unfair distribution of rewards. Users receiving late allocations are overpaid at the expense of users who have been staking since the beginning of the distribution period.
Likelihood: The likelihood is low to medium and depends on the intended functionality and frequency of late allocations. This issue only arises when users receive their first allocation after the distribution has started and have not previously staked.
bug_full: The contract implements a reward distribution that is intended to accrue proportionally to the amount of tokens a user has been allocated and the time those tokens have been locked. The vulnerability originates from the reward‑calculation routine that determines a user’s earned amount by multiplying the user’s balance with the difference between the globally stored rewardPerToken value and a per‑account snapshot called lastRewardPerTokenUsed. When a user receives their first allocation after the distribution period has already begun, the snapshot for that account is still zero because the allocate() function never updates the reward state for the new holder. Consequently, the calculation treats the user as if they had been holding the allocation since the very start of the distribution, awarding rewards for the entire elapsed period instead of only for the time after the allocation. This flaw can be triggered whenever the contract’s allocate() method is called for a fresh recipient or when an existing recipient’s allocation is increased after the start timestamp. An attacker or a legitimate user who is allocated tokens late can simply claim rewards and receive an amount that far exceeds the intended share, effectively draining excess tokens from the reward pool. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a newly allocated address receives a large token balance or reward payout even though it has not been staking for any meaningful duration; the UI may show a “reward claimed” event with a surprisingly high amount, or a balance that jumps from zero to a large value. The impact is an unfair redistribution of rewards that harms early stakers, reduces the overall incentive pool, and may compromise the economic model of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the RewardAccrualBase and UsualSP contracts when the auditor noticed that the lastRewardPerTokenUsed variable was never initialized for newly allocated accounts and that allocate() did not invoke the internal _updateReward() hook. Because the bug manifests only under the specific condition of a late allocation, it can be easy to miss in routine testing that focuses on the happy path of allocations made before distribution start. To remediate the problem the contract should either update each recipient’s reward snapshot before changing their allocation, or forbid any allocation changes after the distribution start, and the _earned() function should guard against a zero snapshot by treating it as no accrued reward. These changes ensure that rewards are calculated only for the period during which a user actually holds an allocation, restoring fairness and preserving the intended token economics.

title: Gamma is never scaled in USUAL token distribution formula
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent scaling error in the USUAL token distribution routine. The contract is supposed to increase the amount of tokens minted when more than 24 hours have elapsed since the previous distribution by applying a factor called gamma. Gamma is calculated from the time difference (timePassed) between the current block timestamp and the stored lastOnChainDistributionTimestamp. However, the function distributeUsualToBuckets updates lastOnChainDistributionTimestamp to block.timestamp before calling the internal routine that computes gamma. Because the timestamp has already been overwritten, the expression timePassed = block.timestamp - lastOnChainDistributionTimestamp always evaluates to zero, causing gamma to remain equal to its base value. Consequently, the derived variables mt and kappa are computed with an unscaled gamma, resulting in a lower than intended USUAL token reward (under‑distribution). The bug manifests only when the distribution is invoked after the required 24‑hour interval; the call succeeds, but the reward amount does not reflect the elapsed time. Users and token holders are affected because they expect a larger reward after a longer waiting period, but they receive the same baseline amount, effectively losing potential earnings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which noted that the timestamp update precedes the calculation, a subtle ordering mistake that does not trigger a revert or obvious error, making it easy to overlook. The problem belongs to the class of “state‑update‑order” bugs where a contract writes a state variable before using its previous value in a dependent calculation, breaking business logic that relies on time‑based scaling. From a user‑interface perspective, a participant might see their balance increase by the usual amount even though the protocol documentation promises a higher payout after a day, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. To remediate, the contract should compute the distribution (including gamma, mt, and kappa) using the stored timestamp from the previous distribution, and only after the calculation should it update lastOnChainDistributionTimestamp to the current block timestamp. This restores the intended time‑based scaling and aligns the actual token distribution with the protocol’s economic model.

title: Multiple Mech Marketplace proxies using the same implementation have the same domain separators
description: Currently in MechMarketplace, the immutable variable domainSeparator is set in the constructor. This causes all the proxies using this implementation to have the same domainSeparator which would allow signature replays across multiple mech marketplace proxies on the same chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that every MechMarketplace proxy contract on the same blockchain shares the same EIP‑712 domain separator because the implementation contract stores the domainSeparator as an immutable variable that is set once in its constructor. When a proxy is deployed it delegates calls to this implementation, so the immutable value is read from the implementation’s storage rather than being generated per‑proxy. The root cause is the misuse of an immutable variable for a value that must be unique to each contract instance, typically derived from the contract address or chain ID. Because the domain separator is identical across proxies, a signature that is valid for one marketplace proxy can be replayed on any other proxy that uses the same implementation. An attacker can therefore copy a signed order, listing, or purchase from one marketplace and submit it to another marketplace where the same domain separator makes the signature appear authentic. This enables cross‑proxy replay attacks that may allow unauthorized asset transfers, fee bypasses, or execution of actions the user never intended on a different marketplace. The issue manifests when multiple proxies are initialized from the same implementation; it is observable only through internal calls such as getDomainSeparator, which return the same value for distinct proxies. Users typically do not see the domain separator, so the problem is hard to notice until a replayed transaction succeeds unexpectedly, for example when a user sees a purchase appear on a marketplace they never interacted with. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that added a test checking that two freshly deployed proxies have different domain separators; the test failed, revealing the shared value. To remediate, the domain separator should be computed during the proxy’s initialization routine (e.g., in an initialize function) using the proxy’s address, and the implementation’s constructor should no longer set it. Additionally, the proxy’s initializer should be protected against being called more than once. This change ensures each marketplace proxy has a unique domain separator, restoring the intended cryptographic isolation and preventing signature replay across proxies.

title: deliverMarketplaceWithSignatures can be frontrun
description:
When a requester signs requests to be delivered by a priority mech through deliverMarketplaceWithSignatures, the request/signature and its verification process does not bind the request to a specific mech. Assume a mech M1 has in possession a request of a requester and its corresponding signature, then it performs a very resource intensive task to deliver the delivery data for the requester. When M1 calls the deliverMarketplaceWithSignatures endpoint of the marketplace while its transaction is in the mempool (public mempools), any other mech M2 can frontrun this transaction to deliver the computed data and in returns:
• Increase its karma for M2.
• Steal the payment from M1.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the marketplace function that accepts off‑chain signed delivery requests, called deliverMarketplaceWithSignatures. The function verifies a signature that authenticates the request data and the requester address, but the identifier that is hashed and signed (the requestId) does not incorporate the address of the priority mech that is expected to fulfil the request. Because the requestId is independent of the mech, any mech that obtains the signed request can submit a transaction that satisfies the same signature. When the priority mech M1 creates a request, performs an expensive computation and places its transaction in the public mempool, a competing mech M2 can observe the pending transaction, copy the request data and signature, and broadcast its own transaction that calls deliverMarketplaceWithSignatures before M1’s transaction is mined. The contract treats the second transaction as a valid fulfilment, awards the payment and karma to M2, and marks the request as completed. When M1’s transaction later reaches the block, the contract rejects it with a SignatureNotValidated error because the request has already been satisfied. The impact is that the priority mech loses the payment it expected, the requester may receive the delivery from an unintended source, and the marketplace’s incentive model is subverted. This flaw occurs whenever a signed request is submitted without binding the mech address into the request hash, which is typical for any off‑chain signature scheme that only signs request parameters. The affected parties are the priority mech operators, requesters who rely on a specific mech, and the overall protocol because the economic guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case reproducing a front‑run scenario: the test creates multiple signed requests, performs a costly computation, then lets a non‑priority mech deliver the data first, causing the priority mech’s call to revert. The problem is subtle because the signature verification itself succeeds – the contract correctly validates the signer – yet the business rule that the designated mech must be the only one able to fulfil the request is not enforced. This makes the bug easy to miss in code reviews that focus on cryptographic correctness but overlook the binding of authorisation context. To remediate, the request identifier should be derived from a hash that includes the priority mech’s address (or another unique identifier) together with the requester, data payload, and payment terms, ensuring that the signature is only valid for that specific mech. This change turns the vulnerability into a proper authorization check, preventing any other participant from replaying or front‑running the signed request.

title: Use safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom
description:
In BalanceTrackerFixedPriceNative and BalanceTrackerFixedPriceToken, the IToken interface has been used that defines transfer and transferFrom functions to return a bool.
1. Not all tokens conform to this interface when transferring amounts.
2. The returned bool value has not been checked.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on a custom token interface that mirrors the ERC20 standard by declaring transfer and transferFrom functions with a boolean return value, but the implementation never checks that boolean. Because the code assumes a successful transfer whenever the call does not revert, it fails to detect tokens that either return false on failure or that do not return any value at all, which is common for legacy or non‑standard ERC20 contracts. When a token transfer silently fails, the contract proceeds as if the funds were moved, updating internal accounting structures such as balances or order states based on the assumed transfer. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by supplying a token that deliberately returns false or by triggering a condition (e.g., insufficient allowance, paused token) that causes the transfer to fail without reverting. The contract will then record a sale or a balance change that never actually happened, leading to a mismatch between on‑chain token balances and the contract’s internal ledger. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a missing refund, a purchase that appears successful but the token balance remains unchanged, or a zero‑amount receipt where a positive amount was expected. The impact is that funds may become effectively locked or disappear from the protocol’s perspective, breaking accounting guarantees and potentially allowing the protocol to claim more assets than it actually holds. This issue occurs whenever the contract interacts with any ERC20 token that does not strictly adhere to the expected return‑value semantics, which includes many popular tokens and any custom token deployed by third parties. The affected parties are token holders, buyers, and the protocol itself, because the internal state can become inconsistent, leading to loss of trust and possible financial loss. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s token interface against the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library and noted the absence of return‑value checks. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the EVM reports success, and only the internal accounting appears wrong, which may only be revealed through discrepancy audits or user complaints. The recommended remediation is to replace direct calls to transfer and transferFrom with the safe wrappers provided by OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which handle missing return values and revert on failure, thereby ensuring that any unsuccessful token movement aborts the whole operation and keeps the contract’s state consistent. In broader terms, this is a classic example of unchecked external call results, a class of bugs where a contract assumes success of an external call without verifying its outcome, leading to silent failures and accounting errors.

title: Request to mech marketplace can be frontrun by the mech operators to change deliveryRate and paymentType
description:
When calling the request endpoints of the mech marketplace, the requester only provides the priorityMechServiceId. Then the deliveryRate and paymentType are fetches from the corresponding priorityMech. This mech's operator can frontrun the requests call and:
• Create a new mech for the same service id but with a different mech factory / payment type.
• Change the max delivery rate of the mech.
And thus force the requester to use potentially unwanted settings for its request.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the mech marketplace request flow. When a user (the requester) calls the request endpoint they only supply a priorityMechServiceId. The contract then looks up the currently registered priority mech for that service id and automatically copies the mech’s deliveryRate and paymentType into the request.
