Because the lookup is performed after the transaction is included but before the request parameters are fixed, a malicious mech operator can observe the pending request transaction in the mempool, submit a competing transaction that either registers a new mech for the same service id with a different factory or payment type, or updates the max deliveryRate of the existing priority mech. If the operator’s transaction is mined first, the request will read the altered values and the requester will be forced to accept a deliveryRate that may be higher than expected or a payment type that routes funds to an address controlled by the operator. This can lead to users paying more than intended, sending funds to an unintended payment contract, or receiving services under unfavorable economic terms. The issue manifests whenever the marketplace relies on a single on‑chain lookup of mech parameters without requiring the requester to explicitly specify them, and when the underlying mech registry permits updates that are not atomic with the request creation. It affects any participant that uses the marketplace to request services, including end‑users and downstream protocols that assume the quoted rate and payment method are immutable. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the request flow, where the auditor noted that the priority mech data is fetched after the request transaction is broadcast, creating a window for transaction‑ordering attacks. The problem is subtle because the UI may display the expected rate and payment type before the transaction is mined, giving the impression that the request is safe, while the actual on‑chain values can change in the same block. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or oracle‑manipulation vulnerabilities where external actors can influence contract state between the time a user submits a transaction and the time the contract reads that state. To remediate, the request function should require the caller to pass the desired deliveryRate and paymentType explicitly, and the contract should verify that these values match the current mech configuration or reject the request if they differ. Alternatively, the marketplace could lock the mech parameters at the moment the request transaction is submitted, for example by using a commit‑reveal scheme or by making the mech registry immutable for the duration of the request. By binding the economic terms to the user’s transaction, the attack surface for front‑running is eliminated and users receive the rates they expect.

title: Make sure requesters provide the payment type and also the max delivery rate to the request endpoints
description: Currently when a request is create by a requester the deliveryRate and paymentType are fetched from the corresponding priorityMech of a service id. Just before this transaction get published those values could change and potentially cause harm to the requester. For example if the request was for a token mech and the requester had approved the token balance tracker infinite approval for the token, just before the call the mech operator could change the max delivery rate to the token balance of the user and thus pull out all the requester's fund upon delivery of the request.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) race condition in the request creation flow of the service. When a requester creates a request, the contract reads the deliveryRate and paymentType from the priority mechanism (priorityMech) associated with the service identifier. These values are used to calculate how much the requester must pay and which token is accepted. Because the contract does not lock or snapshot these parameters, they can be altered by the mech operator after the request is signed but before the transaction is mined. If the requester has granted an unlimited token allowance to the balance tracker, a malicious operator can lower the max delivery rate to the requester’s entire token balance just before the delivery transaction is executed. The request then proceeds with the altered rate, causing the contract to transfer the full approved amount from the requester’s wallet to the operator. From the user’s perspective the request appears to have been accepted, but the user receives no service and their token balance drops to zero, which contradicts the expectation that only the quoted delivery rate would be deducted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state reads and writes. It is difficult to notice because the contract logs the originally quoted rate, yet the actual transfer uses the later‑changed rate, and the discrepancy may only be visible after the funds have disappeared. The impact is a potential loss of all funds approved for the request, affecting any requester who relies on the quoted delivery rate and payment type. The bug belongs to the class of economic‑logic flaws where external mutable parameters are trusted without verification at execution time. To remediate, the protocol should require the requester to submit the expected payment type and a maximum delivery rate together with the request, and the contract must assert that the on‑chain values from the priorityMech match the requester‑provided values (requesterPaymentType == mechPaymentType and requesterMaxDeliveryRate >= mechMaxDeliveryRate). This eliminates the race window and ensures that the contract cannot be forced to accept a lower rate after the request is signed, preserving the economic guarantees of the service.

title: Setting a balance tracker for a payment type which already has a balance tracker can cause issues
description:
Setting a balance tracker for a payment type which already has a balance tracker can cause the following issue:
• If some requesters have unused credit for the old balance tracker of that payment type after the switch to the new balance tracker, they would not be able to use their unused credits (unless those parameters are also migrated to the new balance tracker).
• The mechs who have already performed some of the requests using the payment type in question when trying to deliver to the marketplace upon balance tracker accounting callback, after the deliver call they might not be able to withdraw their credits because the new balance tracker might not have enough underlying assets. Or if the delivery to the marketplace is with signatures, the requesters might have not approved the new balance tracker to pull tokens (or it might not have native tokens or NFT subscriptions, ...).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing the marketplace owner to replace the address that tracks balances for a given payment type without first migrating the existing credit state. The root cause is that the mapping linking a payment type to its balance‑tracker contract is overwritten without any guard or migration logic. When the old tracker still holds credit allocations for requesters or for service providers (mechs), those allocations remain attached to the previous contract address. After the replacement, the system continues to reference the new tracker for accounting callbacks, but the new contract does not contain the previously allocated tokens, nor does it have the necessary approvals to pull them from requesters. Consequently, requesters with unused credit cannot spend it, and mechs that have already delivered services may be unable to withdraw the earned credits because the new tracker lacks sufficient underlying assets or the required token allowances. The issue manifests whenever the marketplace owner calls the function that sets or updates the balance‑tracker for a payment type that already has a non‑zero tracker address. It affects all participants that rely on the payment type – requesters, service providers, and ultimately the protocol’s economic guarantees. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the payment‑type configuration logic, where the absence of a check for an existing tracker and the lack of state migration were noted. The bug can be hard to notice because the UI may still show that the payment type is active, yet users experience silent failures such as “no credit available” or “withdrawal failed” without obvious error messages. The impact is a partial loss of usable funds: requesters see their remaining credit disappear, and mechs may be unable to claim earned rewards, which can lead to reduced trust in the marketplace and potential financial loss. To remediate, the contract should either forbid overwriting a non‑zero balance‑tracker address or require explicit migration of all outstanding credit balances and token approvals to the new tracker before the switch. This can be enforced by adding a guard that reverts if the mapping already points to a non‑zero address, or by implementing a migration routine that transfers credit state and updates allowances atomically.

title: GovNFTFactory/GovNFTTImelockFactory.govNFTs() will fail if registry values grow.
description: The factory getter for deployed NFT's returns the array of deployed addresses. These contracts are expected to deploy many GovNFT's and this getter will begin to fail on gas limitations when returning an array of 100-200 values or more. The registry values are internal so there is no other available accessor to iterate these values after that point. Without this available integrators will need to catalogue creation events to access this information.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the factory contract that stores the addresses of every deployed GovNFT contract in an internal dynamic array and exposes a public getter named govNFTs() which returns the entire array. Because the function attempts to return an unbounded list of addresses, the amount of calldata that must be generated grows linearly with the number of deployed NFTs. When the registry contains roughly one hundred to two hundred entries, the gas required to copy the full array into memory and encode it for the external call exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This situation occurs only after a sufficient number of GovNFT contracts have been created; before that threshold the getter works as expected. The root cause is the lack of pagination or bounded access patterns for a potentially large on‑chain collection, a classic case of an out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service on data‑availability functions. An attacker does not need to perform any malicious action; simply deploying many GovNFT contracts is enough to trigger the failure, effectively preventing any external integrator, UI, or analytics tool from retrieving the full list of NFT addresses. The impact is that users and third‑party services see an empty or incomplete list, may assume that no NFTs exist, or experience UI errors such as “failed to load NFTs” or “balance shows zero”. Protocol participants who rely on the factory’s getter for enumeration (for example, governance dashboards, indexers, or other contracts that need to interact with each GovNFT) are unable to discover or interact with the existing contracts without manually parsing historical events. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors attempted to call the getter after deploying a large number of NFTs and observed a consistent out‑of‑gas revert. Because the failure manifests only after the array reaches a certain size, it can be hard to notice in early testing or on testnets with few deployments. The recommended remediation is to replace the single unbounded getter with bounded accessors, such as a function that returns a single address by index or a function that returns a slice of the array given start and end indices, combined with a length query. This pagination approach limits the gas cost of each call, restores reliable data retrieval, and aligns the contract with common design patterns for enumerable collections. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of “unbounded array return causing out‑of‑gas errors”, which violates the expectation that a read‑only view function can always be called without side effects, and it breaks the accounting assumption that all deployed NFTs can be enumerated on‑chain.

title: Split ﬁnalization succeeds with non-existent split proposals
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the GovNFTTimelock.finalizeSplit function, which is intended to create a new split only after a timelock period has elapsed for a previously committed split proposal. The implementation checks that block.timestamp is greater than splitProposal.timestamp plus the timelock, but it does not verify that a splitProposal actually exists for the given address. When no proposal has been recorded, the default struct has a timestamp value of zero. Because block.timestamp is always greater than zero plus the timelock, the timelock check passes and the function proceeds as if a valid proposal were present. Consequently, the function executes the split logic, updates the _parentLock storage and emits a MetadataUpdate event, yet no new split is created. This mismatch between expected and actual behavior can be observed by users who see an event indicating a split operation but notice that their split balance remains unchanged or that no new split token appears. The root cause is the missing existence guard for the split proposal, allowing an attacker or any user to call finalizeSplit on an address that never submitted a split, thereby wasting gas and potentially causing unintended side‑effects in the contract’s accounting state. The issue was discovered during an audit when a test called finalizeSplit after skipping the timelock delay and observed that execution succeeded without any split data. It is hard to notice because the function does not revert and appears to perform its work, yet the observable outcome (no new split) contradicts the emitted event. The impact includes unnecessary gas consumption for the caller, possible corruption of internal bookkeeping, and a breach of the protocol’s business logic that assumes a split only occurs after a valid proposal. The vulnerability manifests whenever finalizeSplit is invoked for an address with no pending proposal, after the timelock condition is satisfied (or in a test environment where block.timestamp is zero). All participants—users, auditors, and protocol engineers—are affected because the contract’s state may become inconsistent. To remediate, the function should explicitly revert when splitProposal.timestamp is zero, ensuring that a proposal must exist before the timelock check is evaluated. Additionally, GovNFT._split should revert when the parameters list is empty, preventing execution of split logic with insufficient data. Implementing these checks restores the intended invariant that a split can only be finalized after a genuine proposal has been recorded and the timelock has elapsed, thereby aligning contract behavior with user expectations and preserving accounting integrity.

title: Current frontrun protection of GovNFTTimelock works only under limited conditions
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the timelock‑based front‑run protection on the governance‑NFT lock only prevents manipulation when the NFT is in a specific committed state; if the owner commits a split before the NFT is listed, the split can be executed during the timelock delay, allowing the owner to drain part of the vault before a buyer’s purchase is settled. This occurs because the contract only checks that a split has not been performed after a transfer is initiated, but it does not enforce a freeze of split‑related functionality during the commit period. An attacker (the NFT holder) can call the split function, wait for the timelock delay, and then list the NFT on a marketplace. A buyer, seeing the full vault balance, submits a purchase transaction; the attacker’s earlier split reduces the vault balance, so the buyer receives a smaller amount than expected. From the buyer’s perspective the transaction succeeds, the NFT is transferred, but the token balance in the associated vault is lower than advertised, leading to a loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that simulated a realistic marketplace flow and observed that the assert checking the buyer’s expected vault value failed. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a timelock, yet the timelock does not cover split operations, making the front‑run possible without any explicit re‑entrancy or visibility of the split to the buyer. The class of bug is an incomplete state‑transition guard: functionality that should be frozen during a pending transfer is not, allowing value‑draining actions before the transfer finalises. To remediate, the contract should require the NFT owner to enter a “frozen” or “committed” state before any transfer can be executed, during which split and any other mutable operations are disabled until the timelock expires. This can be implemented by overriding the internal update hook to check the frozen flag and by adding explicit freeze/unfreeze functions that block split, burn, or mint actions while the lock is active. Such a change would ensure that a buyer always receives the full vault amount that was visible at listing time, eliminating the possibility of a front‑run split.

title: verifier signatures can be replayed
bug_full: In the ZyfiPaymaster flow a user sends ERC20 tokens to Zyfi and Zyfi pays the transaction gas on the user's behalf. To prove that Zyfi approves the exchange, the contract calls _isValidSignature with a hash that includes the sender address, the destination address, the token, the amount, the expiration time, the maxFeePerGas and the gasLimit. Because the hash does not contain a unique per‑transaction element such as a nonce, the same signature can be presented repeatedly as long as the caller, the target contract and the gas parameters remain identical. An attacker who obtains a valid verifier signature for one approved payment can replay that signature in subsequent transactions that meet the same criteria, causing the paymaster to fund additional gas without a fresh approval from Zyfi. This replay can happen whenever the same user invokes the same contract with the same gas settings, which is a common pattern for recurring operations. The impact is that sponsors who rely on the verifier to limit ETH spending may see their funds drained or allocated to unintended calls, breaking the accounting assumptions of the ERC20SponsorPaymaster. From a user perspective the token balance appears to be deducted once while the gas cost is charged multiple times, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature verification logic and noticed the absence of a nonce or transaction identifier in the signed message. Because the contract still executes successfully with a replayed signature, the problem can be subtle and may not surface until sponsors observe unexplained ETH consumption. The vulnerability belongs to the class of replay attacks caused by insufficient binding of a signature to a unique transaction context. The recommended mitigation is to bind a nonce or the transaction's own nonce to the signed hash, and to reject any signature that has already been used, thereby ensuring each verifier approval can be consumed only once.

title: Temporary failed L1 to L2 token transfers might lock tokens in L1 if replayed after migrating to native USDC
description: The current system uses a well-known token bridging mechanism, locking tokens on one chain and minting them on the other. The L2OpUSDCBridgeAdapter contract is assigned the minter role within the bridged USDC contract. This role is intended to be revoked as part of the migration process as described in bridged_USDC_standard.md: Additionally, the partner is expected to remove all configured minters prior to (or concurrently with) transferring the roles to Circle. Although unlikely, messages to Optimism L2 chains might fail due to business logic issues (pausing of the bridged USDC contract for instance) or an out-of-gas exception on L2 (as described in replaying-messages). In the current system, this could cause calls to USDC.mint to revert. If messages are not replayed before migrating the bridged USDC contract to native USDC, any call to USDC.mint will revert since the bridged USDC minting permission was revoked for the L2OpUSDCBridgeAdapter contract. This will result in user funds being locked inside the L1OpUSDCBridgeAdapter contract in L1. Impact: High since users funds will be locked in L1. Likelihood: Low since it is less likely that messages will have to be replayed and will be replayed only after the migration.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the USDC bridge handles temporary failures of L1‑to‑L2 transfer messages when the system is upgraded to a native USDC implementation. The bridge adapter on L2 holds the minter role for the bridged USDC contract on L2. During the migration to native USDC the minter role is deliberately revoked from the adapter and transferred to Circle. If a message that was supposed to mint USDC on L2 fails – for example because the bridged contract is paused, a business‑logic check reverts, or an out‑of‑gas error occurs – the bridge records the failure but does not immediately retry the mint. Later, after the migration has completed, the bridge may attempt to replay the failed message. At that point the adapter no longer has permission to call USDC.mint, so the call reverts. Because the mint cannot be performed, the amount that was locked on L1 remains stuck in the L1 bridge contract and cannot be withdrawn by the user. From a user’s perspective the deposit transaction on L1 appears successful, but when they try to claim the tokens on L2 they receive nothing, or after the migration they find that their balance on L2 is zero while the L1 contract still holds the locked amount. The impact is severe because the funds are effectively frozen; the likelihood is low because it requires a combination of a temporary failure and a replay after migration, but the condition can be triggered intentionally by pausing the contract or causing an out‑of‑gas situation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration flow and identified that the bridge does not handle the Upgraded state correctly. It is hard to notice because the failure only manifests after the upgrade, not during normal operation, and the UI may not surface any error until the user attempts to retrieve the funds. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑upgrade message replay failures” where permission changes invalidate previously queued actions. The correct mitigation is to redesign the messaging status to distinguish between Active, Paused and Upgraded states, to wrap the mint call in a try‑catch when the system is Upgraded, and to fallback to a secondary message that re‑routes the mint request back to L1 for processing. This ensures that even if the original mint cannot be performed, the funds can still be released rather than being permanently locked.

title: BurnAmount sent from L2 to L1 may not be accurate as it does not account for pending failing messages
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the L2 bridge adapter function that initiates migration of bridged USDC to its native counterpart. When the migration is started, the contract captures the current total supply of the L2 USDC token and forwards this value as the amount to be burned on L1. This approach assumes that the total supply fully represents the amount of USDC that is locked on L1. However, the L2 messenger may still hold pending cross‑chain messages that have not yet been processed or have failed. Those pending messages, when eventually executed, will invoke the receiveMessage function and mint additional bridged USDC tokens on L2. Because the burn amount is calculated before these pending messages are resolved, the value sent to L1 does not include the tokens that will be minted later. Consequently, after migration the L2 side may retain extra USDC that was never burned on L1, violating Circle’s Bridged USDC standard which requires the burn amount to exactly match the circulating supply of bridged tokens. An attacker or any user could deliberately create a failing cross‑chain transfer that remains pending in the messenger, then trigger the migration, resulting in a lower burn amount and leaving surplus tokens on L2 that can be transferred or used, effectively inflating the supply. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected balance before migration, but after migration the bridge’s balance may contain unexpected tokens, leading to confusion such as “my balance did not change” or “extra tokens appeared”. The issue is subtle because the totalSupply variable appears correct at the moment of the call, and the discrepancy only becomes visible after the pending messages are finally processed. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of message handling and the assumptions made by the migration function. To remediate, the contract should either wait until the messenger queue is empty before calculating the burn amount, or record any amounts that are minted after the migration trigger and include them in a subsequent burn call, ensuring that the final burned amount equals the true locked supply. This adjustment restores compliance with the Bridged USDC standard and prevents unintended inflation of the token supply.

title: USDC sent may be permanently locked/burnt in/by the Adapter if the _to address is blacklisted in the destination chain
description:
The current USDC contract implements a blacklist through the notBlacklisted(address) modifier which only allows transferring/minting USDC from/to addresses that are not blacklisted:
```solidity
/**
* @dev Throws if argument account is blacklisted.
* @param _account The address to check.
*/
modifier notBlacklisted(address _account) {
    require(
        !_isBlacklisted(_account),
        "Blacklistable: account is blacklisted"
    );
    _;
}
```
If the _to address set in the sendMessage() call is a blacklisted address in the USDC contract of the destination chain the transfer/minting will revert and the message will be permanently stuck in a failed state. Let's imagine the following scenario:  
1. Alice has 10000 USDC in Optimism and wants to bridge them to Bob in the Ethereum mainnet.  
2. Alice checks if Bob is blacklisted in the Ethereum mainnet. Bob is not.  
3. Alice calls L2OpUSDCBridgeAdapter.sendMessage(BOB, 10000e6, 2000000).  
4. As per the Optimism docs: Transactions sent from L2 to L1 take approximately 7 days to get from OP Mainnet to Ethereum"  
5. Before these 7 days have passed, Bob is blacklisted in the USDC Ethereum Mainnet contract.  
6. When the relayMessage() function is called it reverts/fails as Bob was blacklisted in Ethereum mainnet.  
7. Alice's tokens were already burnt in the L2OpUSDCBridgeAdapter without any possible way to recover them.  
Note, that this issue is more likely to occur in L2 ⇒ L1 than L1 ⇒ L2 operations, as the transactions sent from L1 to L2 take approximately 1-3 minutes to get from Ethereum to the L2, while transactions sent from L2 to L1 can take around 7 days.  
Impact: High as USDC may be permanently locked/burnt in/by the Adapter contracts. Likelihood: Medium as an account might not be blacklisted when the bridge transaction is initiated, but it could be blacklisted by the time the transaction is finalized.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a black‑list‑induced permanent lock of USDC when a cross‑chain bridge adapter attempts to mint or transfer tokens to an address that becomes blacklisted on the destination chain. The USDC contract on each chain protects transfers with a notBlacklisted modifier that reverts if the target address is listed. The adapter burns the sender’s tokens on the source chain before the message is relayed, and then calls the USDC contract on the destination chain to mint the same amount to the _to address. Because the adapter does not verify that the destination address remains un‑blacklisted after the relay delay, a situation can arise where the _to address is added to the blacklist between the time the bridge transaction is initiated and the time the relayMessage function executes. When this happens the mint call reverts, the message remains in a failed state and the tokens that were already burnt on the source chain cannot be recovered. This is effectively a loss of funds for the user and a permanent lock of USDC inside the adapter contract. The issue is most likely to appear in L2‑to‑L1 bridges where finalisation can take several days, giving an attacker or a governance action enough time to blacklist the recipient. Users who initiate a bridge see their balance on the source chain decrease and receive a transaction receipt indicating success, but the destination balance stays at zero and no explicit error is shown to the user. The root cause is the lack of proper error handling for external calls that may revert due to dynamic contract state such as blacklisting, and the premature burning of tokens without a fallback path. The bug belongs to the class of improper handling of external call failures and missing validation of recipient eligibility, which can lead to irreversible token loss. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the bridge adapter’s sendMessage implementation and the USDC blacklist logic. The problem is hard to notice because the bridge transaction appears successful on the originating chain and the failure only manifests later, often after the user has already assumed the transfer completed. To remediate, the adapter should attempt the mint or transfer inside a try/catch block, and if the call fails, it must not burn the source tokens but instead keep them in an internal escrow mapping that can be reclaimed by an authorized party. Additionally, the contract should expose an owner‑only function to withdraw or re‑process stuck funds, and it should optionally check the blacklist status of the destination address before burning tokens. Implementing these safeguards restores the expected behavior that a user’s USDC either arrives at the recipient or remains recoverable, eliminating the risk of permanent fund loss.

title: boughtShares is wrongly initialized
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract creates an initial allocation of shares for the card owner when an IPO card is minted, but the amount allocated to the initial owner is stored only in the per‑address share balance and never added to the global boughtShares counter that tracks how many shares have been purchased from the market. Because the boughtShares mapping does not reflect the initial owner’s shares, the accounting of total circulating shares becomes inconsistent: the actual number of shares in circulation equals initialOwnerShares plus boughtShares, while the contract’s sell logic checks only the boughtShares value. When the initial owner later sells their shares, the boughtShares counter is not increased, so the remaining buyers appear to own more shares than the contract believes were bought. The sell function contains a require statement that enforces boughtShares[id] >= amount, causing any attempt by later buyers to sell their shares to revert with the message "Total shares cannot be less than initial owner shares". This results in a permanent lock of the last batch of shares, effectively causing a loss of funds for those buyers because they cannot redeem their holdings. The issue manifests whenever an IPO card is created with a non‑zero initialOwnerShares value and at least one other participant purchases shares before the initial owner sells theirs. It affects all users who buy shares after the card is launched, the protocol’s liquidity, and the overall trustworthiness of the share‑trading mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by inspecting the share accounting logic and reproducing the scenario with a test that creates a card, buys shares, sells the initial owner’s shares, and then attempts to sell the buyer’s shares, which fails. The problem is subtle because the initial allocation appears correctly in the balance view, so a casual inspection may not reveal that the global boughtShares counter is out of sync. To remediate the issue, the contract should record the initial owner’s shares in the boughtShares mapping at the time of card creation, ensuring that the total purchased share count includes the initial allocation. This aligns the accounting invariant that total shares in circulation equals boughtShares, preventing the sell‑restriction check from erroneously blocking legitimate sell operations and preserving users’ ability to retrieve their funds.

title: Revert if supply is less than premint parameter
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic underflow in the getTokensNeededToAddEthValue function. The function assumes that the current token supply is always greater than or equal to the curve's premint parameter and directly computes ud(supply - p). When the market is initialized with a premint value that is lower than the curve's premint, the subtraction yields a negative unsigned result, which in Solidity 0.8+ triggers a revert. This situation can occur during the spawning of a new project, where the initial supply equals the Market Parameters premint, but the curve's premint may be set higher for pricing reasons. When a user later attempts to mint additional tokens to meet the funding goal, the contract calls getTokensNeededToAddEthValue with the current total supply. Because the supply is smaller than the curve premint, the call reverts, causing the entire mint transaction to fail. From the user’s perspective the transaction is rejected, no tokens are received, and any ETH sent is refunded only after the revert, leaving the user with a failed contribution and lost gas. The impact is effectively a denial‑of‑service: the funding round cannot reach its goal, contributors cannot acquire tokens, and the protocol may appear broken or untrustworthy. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Market Parameters premint with the curve’s premint and identified the unchecked subtraction. It is subtle because the contract’s comments suggest the premint values may differ, yet the implementation does not guard against the resulting negative value. The issue belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic operations leading to underflow/revert errors. To remediate, the subtraction should be protected by a conditional that treats a negative result as zero (e.g., supply > p ? supply - p : 0) before converting to a fixed‑point type, ensuring the function returns a sensible token amount instead of reverting. This change restores the intended business logic where the protocol can calculate the required tokens even when the current supply is below the curve’s premint, allowing funding rounds to complete as expected.

title: Presale buyers can block other whitelisted buyers from purchases
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During the presale stage Cardex uses a nonce‑based off‑chain signature to authorize each whitelisted buyer. The signer creates a signature that includes the buyer address, card id, amount and a sequential nonce (preSaleNonce). The contract checks that the supplied signature matches the stored preSaleSigner and then increments preSaleNonce only after the purchase succeeds. Because the nonce is not advanced when a signed message is never used, any buyer who holds a signature for nonce N can prevent all later buyers (with signatures for N+1, N+2, …) from ever succeeding. If Alice receives a signature for nonce 1 and never calls buyPreSaleShares, the contract’s nonce remains 1; Bob’s signature for nonce 2 and Charlie’s for nonce 3 will be rejected as “Invalid Signature”. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the entire whitelist: legitimate participants expect to be able to buy during the one‑day presale, but they see their transactions revert with an invalid‑signature error and their balances remain unchanged. The issue stems from the business logic that couples a globally shared nonce with individual buyer authorizations and only updates it on successful execution, violating the assumption that the nonce will always progress regardless of who holds the signature. It was discovered during a manual audit of the presale function where the flow of nonce handling was examined. The problem is subtle because the signature itself is cryptographically correct; the failure only appears when the contract’s nonce is out of sync with the signed message, which may be attributed to a user mistake rather than a contract bug. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “nonce starvation” or “queue‑blocking” attacks, where an attacker can block progress by withholding a transaction. The impact is a loss of fairness, possible reduction of funds raised, and a poor user experience, as whitelisted buyers cannot acquire shares even though they possess valid signatures. To remediate, the contract should decouple the nonce from a single global counter or allow the nonce to be advanced independently of a successful purchase, for example by using per‑buyer nonces, a time‑based fallback that skips stalled nonces, or by requiring the signer to issue fresh signatures on demand. Implementing such a change restores the intended first‑come‑first‑served behavior and prevents a single participant from griefing the entire presale queue.

title: No slippage attached to buys and sells
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract exposes two public entry points, buyShares and sellShares, that allow users to purchase or redeem fractional ownership tokens without any built‑in slippage protection. The functions simply check that the operation is allowed in the current trade stage and then forward the request to internal logic that calculates the price based on the contract’s current state. Because the price is derived at execution time, any other buy or sell transaction that is mined earlier in the same block can shift the price before a pending transaction is processed. Consequently, a user who submits a buyShares transaction may end up paying a higher price than expected if other buys are executed first, while a user who submits a sellShares transaction may receive a lower amount of ether than anticipated if earlier sells depress the price. This situation creates an unfair trading condition that can cause financial loss, especially for users who cannot specify a minimum acceptable price when selling. The vulnerability manifests whenever multiple participants interact with the contract within a short time window, such as during a public sale or a volatile market period, because the contract does not enforce a price ceiling for purchases or a price floor for sales. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function signatures and noted the absence of any slippage‑related parameters or checks. The issue can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the quoted price at the moment the transaction is signed, but the actual execution price may differ after the block is sealed, leading users to see unexpected reductions in their token balances or ether refunds. From a security perspective, this is a classic “missing slippage protection” bug that appears in many automated market maker or token‑sale contracts. The recommended mitigation is to allow callers to provide a slippage tolerance – for example, a maximum price they are willing to pay when buying and a minimum price they will accept when selling – and to revert the transaction if the on‑chain price moves outside that range. Implementing such checks restores the economic guarantees expected by users, aligns the contract’s behavior with standard trading logic, and prevents price manipulation through transaction ordering.

title: Missing check in the `updateValset` function
description:
[Gravity.sol#L276-L358](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L276-L358)  
The `updateValset` function don’t check that the sum of the powers of the new validators in the new valset is greater than the threshold, which can lead to unwanted behavior.
There are 2 main problems that can occur in that situation:
1. The sum of the new validators’ powers will be lower than the `state_powerThreshold`
2. The sum of the new validators’ power will overflow and become lower than the `state_powerThreshold`
The second case is less dangerous, because it won’t stuck the system in every case (only in specific cases where every sum of validators’ power is less than the threshold). The first case is very dangerous though. It can lead to the system becoming stuck and to all of the tokens on the cudos chain to become locked for users, because the validators won’t have enough power to approve any operation - whether it is transferring tokens or updating the valset.
poc:
For the first case, consider the current validators set containing 100 validators with each ones power being equal to 10, and the threshold is 900 (91+ validators are needed for approvement). Now the `updateValset` function is being called with 100 validators with each ones power being equal to 1. This will lead to a state where no matter how much validators have signed a message, the sum of the powers won’t pass the threshold and the action won’t be able to be executed. This will cause all the tokens in the cudos blockchain become locked, and will DoS all the actions of the gravity contract - including updating the valset.
For the second case, consider the new validators set will have 128 validators, each validator’s power is equal to `2**249` and `_powerThreshold = 2**256 - 1`. In this case the system will be stuck too, because every sum of validators’ power won’t pass the threshold.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the `updateValset` function which allows a new validator set to be accepted without verifying that the aggregate voting power of the proposed validators exceeds the protocol's predefined power threshold. Because the function lacks this essential summation check, an attacker who can influence the validator set update can submit a set whose total power is either deliberately low or, in extreme cases, so large that an unsigned integer overflow occurs, causing the computed sum to wrap around to a value below the threshold. When the combined validator power is below the required threshold, the contract’s quorum‑based permission checks will never succeed, regardless of how many validators sign a message. Consequently, operations that depend on validator approval—such as token transfers, cross‑chain bridges, and subsequent validator set updates—are permanently blocked. From a user’s perspective this manifests as transactions that appear to be submitted but never execute, balances that appear stuck, and UI elements indicating pending or failed operations without explicit error messages. The issue affects all participants of the Cudos chain: token holders cannot move their assets, validators are unable to perform their duties, and the overall protocol becomes effectively deadlocked. The flaw was discovered during a professional audit by Code4rena, where the missing power‑threshold validation was observed in the source code and demonstrated with concrete proof‑of‑concept scenarios. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or throw an exception; it simply fails the internal quorum condition, making the failure appear as a generic “no‑op”. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of insufficient quorum validation and integer‑overflow induced logic errors. To remediate the issue, the `updateValset` implementation should explicitly compute the total power of the incoming validator set and assert that it is greater than the stored `state_powerThreshold` before applying the update. Incorporating the existing power‑normalization logic from the Gravity module ensures that the sum of powers always represents 100 % of the voting weight, thereby guaranteeing that the threshold condition can be met under normal operation and preventing both low‑power and overflow scenarios from causing a denial‑of‑service.

title: Admin drains all ERC based user funds using `withdrawERC20`
description:
[Gravity.sol#L632-L638](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L632-L638)  
[Gravity.sol#L595-L609](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L595-L609)
Ability for admin to drain all ERC20 funds stored in contract at will, meaning all ERC20 based Cudos tokens (and any other ERC20 tokens stored in the contract) could be extracted by anyone with admin role and later sold, leaving users funds bridged on Cudos Cosmos chain with no ERC20 representation stored across the bridge - similar in impact as the wormhole hack.
This issue ought to fall within the limits the team allocated on assessing the governance role setups, since it describes a full-fledged security risk regarding users’ funds. Crucially, this function is not in the [original Gravity Bridge contract for Gravity.sol](https://github.com/Gravity-Bridge/Gravity-Bridge/blob/f65d9da692c1af76f8188bd17b55dea58c1d8723/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol).
Furthermore, the function has not been commented and does not appear in the documentation, suggesting that it has perhaps not yet been reasoned through by the development team and it’s critical this is flagged in the security audit.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unprotected admin‑only function called withdrawERC20 that enables any address holding the admin role to transfer the entire ERC20 token balance held by the bridge contract to its own wallet. The root cause is a design flaw: the function calculates the token balance of the contract with balanceOf(address(this)) and then calls safeTransfer to the caller without any further restriction, time‑lock, multi‑signature approval, or intention to burn the tokens. Because the function is present in the deployed Gravity bridge code but absent from the original Gravity‑Bridge reference implementation and lacks documentation, its purpose was never reviewed, allowing a privileged admin to misuse it. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker with the admin role invokes withdrawERC20, passing the address of any ERC20 token stored in the contract—most notably the bridged Cudos token or any other token accidentally deposited. The contract then empties its balance and sends all funds to the attacker’s address. This can be performed at any time while the contract holds tokens, and no further conditions are required. The impact is severe for users who have locked assets on the bridge: the ERC20 representation of their bridged tokens disappears, leaving the Cosmos‑side balance with no counterpart on Ethereum. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a zero balance or missing tokens, and attempts to withdraw or trade will fail, effectively causing funds to vanish. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit, where the auditors compared the source to the upstream contract and noted the undocumented function. It is hard to notice because the code appears as a benign administrative utility and the admin role is typically trusted, so the dangerous transfer of the full balance is not obvious at a glance. To remediate, the function should be removed entirely or altered to burn the tokens (sending them to the zero address) rather than transferring them to an admin, and access control should be tightened, possibly requiring multi‑signature governance or a time‑locked proposal. This class of bug falls under “privileged asset withdrawal” where an authorized party can drain contract holdings without proper safeguards, violating the accounting assumption that contract‑held tokens are escrowed for users and not freely withdrawable by administrators.

title: The `Gravity.sol` should have pause/unpause functionality
description:
In case a hack is occuring or an exploit is discovered, the team (or validators in this case) should be able to pause functionality until the necessary changes are made to the system. Additionally, the gravity.sol contract should be manged by proxy so that upgrades can be made by the validators.
Because an attack would probably span a number of blocks, a method for pausing the contract would be able to interrupt any such attack if discovered.
To use a thorchain example again, the team behind thorchain noticed an attack was going to occur well before the system transferred funds to the hacker. However, they were not able to shut the system down fast enough. (According to the incidence report [here](https://github.com/HalbornSecurity/PublicReports/blob/master/Incident%20Reports/Thorchain_Incident_Analysis_July_23_2021.pdf)).
poc: [Gravity.sol#L175](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/main/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L175)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of an emergency stop (pause/unpause) mechanism and the lack of a proxy‑based upgrade path in the Gravity.sol contract that governs cross‑chain transfers. Because the contract does not expose a callable function that validators can use to halt state‑changing operations, there is no way to interrupt a malicious sequence of calls once an exploit is detected. The root cause is the design decision to omit a circuit‑breaker pattern and to deploy the contract as a monolithic implementation without an upgradeable proxy, which leaves the code immutable after deployment. An attacker who discovers a flaw can repeatedly invoke the vulnerable functions over many blocks, draining or misrouting assets before the community can react. The exploit would typically start with a malicious actor submitting crafted messages that trigger unintended token releases; because the contract continues to process these messages uninterrupted, the protocol may transfer funds to the attacker or to an address under the attacker’s control. The impact includes loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the bridge, and potential disruption of the entire cross‑chain ecosystem. This situation manifests when a security incident is identified during live operation, but the validators lack a fast‑acting tool to stop further execution. The affected parties are the bridge users who expect their assets to remain secured, the validators responsible for governance, and any downstream protocols that rely on the bridge’s integrity. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit by Code4rena, which highlighted the missing pause functionality as a gap in defensive controls. It can be hard to notice in routine testing because normal operation does not require the contract to be paused, and the lack of an upgrade mechanism is only apparent when a bug needs fixing after deployment. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to include a standardized pause/unpause function guarded by a validator‑only role, and the whole contract should be deployed behind a transparent or UUPS proxy so that future security patches can be applied without redeploying a new bridge. This would align the implementation with common best practices for high‑value smart contracts, ensuring that, in the event of a discovered exploit, the system can be quickly halted and corrected, preventing funds from disappearing or refunds from failing.

title: Protocol doesn’t handle fee on transfer tokens
description:
[Gravity.sol#L600](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/main/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L600)  
Since the `_tokenContract` can be any token, it is possible that loans will be created with tokens that support fee on transfer. If a fee on transfer asset token is chosen, other user’s funds might be drained.
poc:
1. Assume transfer fee to be 5% and `Gravity.sol` has 200 token.
2. Alice sendToCosmos 100 token. Now, `Gravity.sol` has 295 token.
3. Alice calls the send-to-eth method to withdraw 100 token.
4. `Gravity.sol` ends up having 195 token.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s assumption that a token transfer will deliver exactly the amount specified in the call to sendToCosmos. Because the contract accepts an arbitrary ERC‑20 token address, it can be instructed to work with a fee‑on‑transfer token – a token that deducts a portion of the transferred amount as a burn or transfer fee. When a user calls sendToCosmos, the contract records the requested _amount but does not verify the actual number of tokens that arrived in its balance after the safeTransferFrom call. Consequently, the contract’s internal accounting records a higher amount than it truly received. Later, when the same user (or another party) withdraws the recorded amount, the contract attempts to send out tokens that it never possessed, leaving the fee that was taken on the original transfer trapped inside the contract. This discrepancy can be exploited repeatedly: an attacker can choose a fee‑on‑transfer token, deposit a known amount, and then withdraw the same nominal amount, causing the contract to retain the deducted fees while the attacker extracts the full claimed amount. The impact is a gradual draining of funds from the contract, as each fee‑on‑transfer operation leaves undistributed tokens that can be siphoned by malicious users, potentially affecting all token holders that rely on the contract for bridging or loan services. The condition under which this occurs is any execution of sendToCosmos with a token that implements a transfer fee, which is possible because the contract does not restrict the token type to a known fee‑free asset. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that considered token diversity and the business logic of fee handling; it is subtle because the contract’s balance after the transfer still appears to increase, masking the fact that the increase is smaller than expected. From a user perspective, a depositor expects that the amount they sent will be fully credited and later returned; instead they may see their balance reduced by the fee while the contract retains the leftover, resulting in “funds disappear” or “refund is missing” symptoms. The bug belongs to the class of accounting / balance‑verification flaws in token‑handling contracts, specifically the failure to reconcile actual received token amounts with expected amounts when interacting with fee‑on‑transfer tokens. The recommended mitigation is to capture the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer, compute the real received amount, and emit that value and use it for subsequent accounting, or to restrict accepted tokens to those known not to charge transfer fees. By doing so, the contract’s internal state accurately reflects the true token holdings, preventing the inadvertent locking of fee amounts and protecting user funds.

title: Calls inside loops that may address DoS
description:
Calls to external contracts inside a loop are dangerous (especially if the loop index can be user-controlled) because it could lead to DoS if one of the calls reverts or execution runs out of gas. [Reference](https://swcregistry.io/docs/SWC-113)
[Gravity.sol#L453-L456](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L453-L456)  
[Gravity.sol#L568-L573](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L568-L573)  
[Gravity.sol#L579-L581](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-cudos/blob/de39cf3cd1f1e1cf211819b06d4acf6a043acda0/solidity/contracts/Gravity.sol#L579-L581)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of invoking external contracts inside a for‑loop where the loop bound can be influenced by a caller. When the contract iterates over a list of token addresses and calls each token's transfer function, a malicious or non‑standard ERC‑20 implementation can deliberately revert, run out of gas, or otherwise fail. Because Solidity treats a revert inside a loop as a failure of the whole transaction, the failure of a single external call aborts the entire processing of the loop. This creates a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition: an attacker can supply a token address that always reverts, causing the orchestrator contract to stop processing any further tokens, preventing legitimate users from receiving expected transfers or refunds. The impact is that funds may appear to be locked or disappear from the user’s perspective; a user initiates a multi‑token withdrawal expecting each token balance to be transferred, but receives nothing because the transaction reverts partway through. The issue manifests whenever the function that performs batch transfers is called with a list that includes a malicious token, which can be supplied by an adversary or inadvertently included by a user. It primarily affects token holders, the protocol that relies on batch processing for efficiency, and any downstream services that assume all transfers will succeed. The problem was identified during a security audit by Code4rena, where reviewers flagged the pattern of external calls inside loops as a known anti‑pattern (SWC‑113). The flaw is subtle because loops are a common way to handle arrays, and the external calls appear benign; the risk only becomes evident under adversarial conditions where a token contract behaves unexpectedly. To remediate, the contract should avoid making state‑changing external calls inside unbounded loops, employ a pull‑based pattern where recipients claim their own tokens, use try/catch or low‑level call with explicit handling of failure, or limit the size of the batch and process failed calls separately. By redesigning the logic to tolerate individual call failures, the protocol can preserve overall execution and prevent a single malicious token from halting the entire operation, thereby protecting user balances and maintaining the intended business logic of batch transfers.

title: Non-Cudos Erc20 funds sent through `sendToCosmos`
description:
No checks for non-Cudos tokens mean that non-Cudos ERC20 tokens will be lost to the contract, with the user not having any chance of retrieving them.
However, the admin can retrieve them through withdrawERC20.
Impact is that users lose their funds, but admins gain them.
The mistakes could be mitigated on the contract, by checking against a list of supported tokens, so that users don’t get the bad experience of losing funds and CUDOS doesn’t have to manually refund users
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the bridge contract that forwards ERC20 tokens from Ethereum to the Cudos blockchain through the sendToCosmos function. The function accepts an arbitrary token contract address and transfers the specified amount from the caller into the bridge without verifying that the token is part of the approved Cudos token list. Because there is no whitelist or any other validation, any ERC20 token – including those not supported by the Cudos ecosystem – can be deposited. Once deposited, the contract emits an event and records the transfer, but the subsequent logic that mints the synthetic representation on the target chain only handles tokens that are officially supported. Consequently, non‑Cudos tokens remain locked in the bridge contract with no automated pathway for their release. The only mechanism that can move those funds is the admin‑only withdrawERC20 function, which allows an administrator to extract the entire balance of any token held by the contract. From a user’s perspective, the experience is that a transfer appears to succeed (the transaction is confirmed and an event is emitted) but the expected synthetic assets never appear on the Cudos side, effectively resulting in a loss of the original tokens. The impact is a financial loss for ordinary users who inadvertently send unsupported tokens, while the protocol administrators retain the ability to reclaim the assets, creating an asymmetry where user funds are at risk and the protocol’s economic assumptions about token custody are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token handling logic and noted the absence of a validation step before the safeTransferFrom call. It is subtle because the function signature and event name suggest a successful cross‑chain operation, making it easy to assume that any token transferred will be processed correctly. The root cause is the missing whitelist check, which enables a class of "unsupported token deposit" bugs common in cross‑chain bridge contracts. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain a list of supported token addresses and enforce a require statement that the provided token address exists in that list before accepting the transfer. Additionally, the bridge could reject unsupported tokens at the UI level and provide clear feedback to users, preventing accidental deposits. By aligning the contract’s token acceptance logic with the protocol’s supported asset set, the discrepancy between user expectations (receiving a synthetic token) and reality (tokens being locked) is eliminated, preserving trust and ensuring that funds are either properly bridged or rejected before they become unrecoverable.

title: Donating without transferring contribution
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a proportional contribution accounting scheme that ties a contributor's seed token balance to a separate contribution value. When a token holder transfers a portion of their seed tokens, the contract calculates the amount of contribution to move using the formula transferContribution = values[i] * contributions[ids[i]][from] / balanceOf(from, ids[i]). Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, any fractional part of the division is truncated. If the product values[i] * contributions[ids[i]][from] is smaller than the sender's total token balance, the division yields zero, meaning no contribution is transferred even though tokens have moved. An attacker can exploit this by first sending a batch of seed tokens to a victim without any associated contribution, inflating the victim's token balance while leaving their contribution unchanged. When the victim later transfers a subset of those tokens, the proportional calculation now produces a smaller contribution transfer than expected, effectively stealing a portion of the victim’s contribution value. This bug manifests only after a market reaches the FUNDED state, where token transfers become unrestricted and the proportional transfer logic is activated. Users see their token balance increase but their contribution balance remain the same, leading to confusion when subsequent transfers result in less contribution than anticipated. The issue was uncovered during a security audit through a crafted test that performed a large batch transfer followed by a normal transfer, revealing that the received contribution was lower than the mathematically expected amount. The problem is subtle because the token balance change is visible, yet the contribution accounting discrepancy is hidden until a later transfer, making it hard to detect from the UI. To remediate, the transfer logic should ensure that a non‑zero contribution is always moved when the sender holds a non‑zero contribution, for example by rounding up the division, using a higher‑precision representation, or explicitly handling the zero‑result case and transferring at least a minimal contribution amount. This correction restores the invariant that contribution value remains proportional to token ownership, preserving accounting integrity and preventing loss of contribution rights.

title: burn() function doesn't have slippage control
description:
Currently there is no mechanism for user to specify accepted price on selling tokens.
Therefore following scenario is possible:
1. User submits transaction to sell
2. Price goes down As a result, user receives less collateral for sell than expects. And there is no mechanism to set expected amount.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the token burn function that is used to sell tokens for collateral. The function does not provide any mechanism for the caller to specify a minimum acceptable amount of collateral (slippage protection). Because the contract calculates the sell price at the moment of execution, an attacker or market movement can cause the price to drop between the time the transaction is submitted and the time it is mined. When this happens the contract will still execute the burn, returning the lower net amount to the user without any check that the received collateral meets the user’s expectation. This results in a situation where a user initiates a sell expecting a certain amount of collateral, but receives less, potentially even a negligible amount, while the transaction still succeeds. The issue is triggered whenever the sell price is volatile or can be manipulated, such as during periods of low liquidity or when a front‑runner can submit a price‑affecting transaction just before the victim’s burn call. The affected parties are token holders who rely on the burn function to exchange their tokens for value, as well as the protocol which may lose trust if users consistently receive less than anticipated. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the absence of a slippage guard in the sell path. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply yields a lower output, which may be interpreted as normal market variation rather than a contract flaw. From a user‑interface perspective the symptom is a missing or unexpectedly small balance increase after a sell, contrary to the user’s expectation of receiving a specific amount. The bug belongs to the class of “price‑slippage” or “missing output validation” vulnerabilities, where the contract fails to enforce that the actual output is at least as high as the user’s quoted or expected amount. To remediate the issue the contract should be extended to accept a minOutputAmount parameter and enforce a require statement that the net collateral is greater than or equal to this threshold, causing the transaction to revert if the market moves unfavorably. This aligns the on‑chain execution with the off‑chain expectation and restores confidence that users will not lose value due to price manipulation or sudden market shifts.

title: Inconsistency in message library between rust and solidity implementations
description:
Message data is passed between Ethereum and Centrifuge through the gateway contract. Incoming messages are dispatched when quorum has been reached. The first byte indicates the intended action to be executed on a target manager contract. Each manager contract implements a handle() function which decodes this data according to the message ID. There are some inconsistencies in the formatting of data that is passed from Centrifuge chain to Ethereum.
The inconsistencies apply to the following messages (as per latest commit):
• There is an extra 32 bytes that is expected from Centrifuge but not used in:
– TransferAssets.
– TransferTrancheTokens.
• UpdateTrancheHook is missing a 16 byte tranchId parameter.
• UpdateCentrifugeGasPrice should pass two parameters, a uint128 and uint64 when only a uint64 is being provided.
• DisputeMessageRecovery is missing the adapter address.
• RecoverTokens should decode the amount parameter to a uint128 instead.
• Two types of addresses are used: a 20 byte address and a 32 bytes address, while the Solidity toAddress() uses a 32 byte address.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a systematic mismatch between the binary message format used on the Centrifuge chain (implemented in Rust) and the Solidity decoder used by the Ethereum gateway contract. When a message is sent from Centrifuge to Ethereum, the first byte selects an action such as TransferAssets, TransferTrancheTokens, UpdateTrancheHook, UpdateCentrifugeGasPrice, DisputeMessageRecovery or RecoverTokens. Each manager contract then decodes the remaining payload according to a hard‑coded layout. Because the Rust library and the Solidity library were not kept in sync, several fields are either shifted, omitted, or encoded with the wrong size. For example, TransferAssets and TransferTrancheTokens include an extra 32‑byte segment that the Solidity decoder never reads, UpdateTrancheHook is missing a 16‑byte trancheId, UpdateCentrifugeGasPrice supplies only a uint64 where a uint128 followed by a uint64 is expected, DisputeMessageRecovery lacks the adapter address, RecoverTokens interprets the amount as a uint256 instead of the required uint128, and address values are sometimes treated as 20‑byte values and other times as 32‑byte values. The root cause is a divergence in the specification of the message schema between the two codebases, likely introduced by independent updates without a shared source of truth. The mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who crafts a message that, when decoded incorrectly, causes the contract to read a different value than intended – for instance, moving assets to an unintended address, applying an incorrect gas price, or failing to recover tokens. Even without malicious intent, honest messages may be misinterpreted, leading to failed asset transfers, zero balances appearing where funds should be, or tranche token operations silently doing nothing. The impact is medium risk because it can result in loss of user funds, disruption of pool operations, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s cross‑chain accounting. The condition occurs whenever the gateway contract receives a message that relies on the affected encoding rules, i.e., after a quorum is reached on the Centrifuge side and the message is dispatched to the target manager contract. All participants that depend on correct cross‑chain asset movement – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that compared the Rust message definitions with the Solidity decoding logic and identified the inconsistencies. It is hard to notice because the gateway contract does not revert on a malformed payload; instead, it simply reads the wrong offsets, leading to silent logical errors that may only surface as missing transfers or unexpected zero balances in the UI. To remediate, the message library must be unified: the Rust and Solidity implementations should share a single canonical schema, address formats must be standardized to either 20‑byte or 32‑byte consistently, and each decoder must be updated to match the exact field order, size, and type (e.g., uint128 for amounts, uint64 for timestamps). The PoolManager contract’s handling of TransferAssets and TransferTrancheTokens should be corrected to read the proper offsets, and all other message handlers must be revised to include the missing parameters and correct type casts. By aligning the encoding and decoding logic, the protocol will restore reliable cross‑chain accounting and prevent funds from disappearing or being sent to wrong destinations.

title: Frozen users may transfer tranche tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing transfer restriction check in the PoolManager contract that allows a user whose account has been frozen to move tranche tokens despite the protocol’s freeze policy. The freeze mechanism is enforced when a user interacts with the CentrifugeRouter because the router invokes a hook that consults the restriction manager before any token movement. However, the PoolManager’s transferTrancheTokens function directly burns the sender’s shares and forwards the request to the underlying pool without calling tranche.checkTransferRestriction. As a result, a frozen account can call PoolManager.transferTrancheTokens and have its tokens burned and subsequently transferred to any recipient, even if the recipient is also frozen or not a registered member. This bypass occurs whenever a frozen user invokes the PoolManager function directly, which is a legitimate entry point for token transfers. The impact is that the protocol’s security guarantee that frozen accounts cannot move assets is violated, enabling unauthorized asset migration and potentially allowing malicious actors to circumvent compliance rules. Additionally, because the recipient may be frozen or non‑member, the final cross‑chain transfer can fail after the sender’s shares have already been burned, leading to loss of tokens for the sender and unnecessary gas consumption. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit through functional testing of frozen‑account behavior. It is subtle because the router path works correctly, so developers may assume all transfer routes are protected, overlooking the direct PoolManager call. The bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control or business‑rule enforcement where validation is performed in one code path but omitted in another. From a user’s perspective a frozen account may unexpectedly see its balance drop to zero after a transfer attempt, while the intended recipient receives nothing, contradicting the expectation that a frozen account cannot send tokens. The recommended remediation is to invoke tranche.checkTransferRestriction inside PoolManager.transferTrancheTokens before burning the sender’s shares, ensuring that both sender and recipient are verified as unfrozen and valid members, thereby restoring the intended freeze semantics and preventing token loss and gas waste.

title: 10% maximum pre-mint check can be bypassed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss bug in the pre‑mint validation logic of a market creation contract. When a market is created the LinearCurve.checkParameters function decodes the curve parameters, computes the total token supply that corresponds to the supplied collateral (fundingGoalInTokens) and then verifies that the pre‑mint amount p does not exceed ten percent of that supply. The check is implemented as ((100 * p) / fundingGoalInTokens) > 10, which uses integer division. Because Solidity discards the fractional part, a configuration where the true percentage is slightly above ten percent (for example 10.9 %) can be rounded down to ten percent, causing the condition to evaluate to false and the transaction to pass. This rounding error allows an attacker to supply curve parameters that produce a supply value just low enough for the division to truncate, thereby minting more than the intended ten percent of tokens – in the reported proof‑of‑concept the pre‑mint amount becomes eleven percent. The bug is triggered during the market creation flow, specifically when checkParameters is called, and it affects any user who relies on the pre‑mint cap, the market’s token economics, and the overall protocol because the extra tokens dilute other participants and break the accounting assumptions that the pre‑mint is bounded. The issue was discovered by writing a unit test that printed the collateral collected and the result of supplyAtCollateral, revealing that the market entered the FUNDED state while the pre‑mint exceeded the limit. It is hard to notice because the on‑chain check appears to enforce the ten‑percent rule, and the UI typically displays the configured percentage, not the actual minted amount, so users see no obvious error. The correct mitigation is to avoid the loss of precision by either scaling the numerator and denominator with a larger factor (e.g., using 10000 instead of 100) or, more robustly, by rearranging the inequality to compare products directly: 100 * p > 10 * fundingGoalInTokens. This eliminates the division and ensures that any amount above ten percent is rejected, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Iterating over unbounded array can run out of gas
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic array that stores a user’s stake positions in the StakingPool contract. When a user calls the unstake function, the contract executes a for‑loop that walks through the entire userIssueIndexs array, checking each stored index to determine whether it falls within the requested range and whether the associated issue is still marked as staking. Because the loop does not prune entries that have already been unstaked, the array can grow indefinitely as the user interacts with the protocol over a long period. The root cause is the lack of a bounded termination condition or a mechanism to remove or compact stale entries, which makes the gas consumption of the loop directly proportional to the total number of historical positions. An attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger the vulnerability simply by accumulating a large number of stake positions; once the array length exceeds the amount of gas that can be supplied in a single transaction, the unstake call will run out of gas and revert. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition for the StakingPool: users are unable to withdraw their funds, the contract appears frozen, and the protocol’s promised liquidity guarantees are broken. The issue manifests when the unstake function is invoked after the user’s position array has become large, which can happen after many staking/unstaking cycles or after a malicious actor deliberately creates many tiny positions for a target address. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with an “out of gas” error, no tokens are transferred, and the on‑chain balance of the user remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the unstake operation will release the locked amount. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the unstake logic and identified the for‑loop over userIssueIndexs without any size limitation. It can be hard to notice because the function works correctly for small arrays, and the gas limit error only appears after the array grows beyond a threshold, which may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration leading to gas exhaustion” and is a common source of DoS in smart contracts that manage per‑user collections. To remediate, the contract should either remove entries from the array once they are unstaked (e.g., by popping or swapping with the last element), maintain a separate counter of active positions, or redesign the data structure to allow constant‑time access without iterating over the entire history. Any of these approaches will bound the gas cost of the unstake operation and restore the ability of users to retrieve their funds safely.

title: whenNotPaused should not be used while redeem
description: Pausing functionality is a great feature in times of emergency. But you should be careful about which functionalities you want to pause and which not. The redeem function should be free of any Pausing constraints, otherwise if owner decides to never unpause the contract then user funds will get stuck in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inappropriate coupling between the contract’s pause mechanism and the user‑facing redeem function. The contract implements a Pausable pattern that allows the owner to halt certain operations by setting a paused flag, and the redeem function is protected by the whenNotPaused modifier. Because of this design, when the contract is in a paused state the redeem call reverts, preventing any user from withdrawing their deposited assets.
