The root cause is a logical error: the developer assumed that pausing should apply to all state‑changing functions, but failed to consider that redeem is an essential exit point for users and must remain available even during emergencies. An attacker—or more realistically, a malicious or negligent owner—can invoke pause and then never call unpause, effectively freezing all user funds inside the contract. Exploitation is straightforward: the owner triggers pause, the contract records the paused flag, and any subsequent redeem attempts are blocked, causing transactions to fail with a pause‑related error. The impact is that users see no change in their balances, receive no tokens or underlying assets, and may be unable to recover their capital as long as the contract remains paused. This condition occurs whenever the paused flag is true, which can happen at any time after deployment and persists until the owner explicitly unpauses. All token holders, investors, and any party relying on the redeem functionality are affected, as the protocol’s promised liquidity guarantee is broken. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between modifiers and public functions. It can be hard to notice because pause mechanisms are generally viewed as safety features, and developers may not test the scenario where the contract stays paused for an extended period. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a redeem button that either does nothing or throws an error, leading to confusion when “my balance stays the same after I try to redeem” or “I get a transaction that fails with a pause error”. The business logic that users can always retrieve their funds is violated, turning the contract into a money‑locking trap. The recommended remediation is to decouple the pause guard from redeem, either by removing the whenNotPaused modifier from the redeem function or by implementing a separate emergency unpause path that guarantees users can always exit the contract, thereby preserving the intended accounting invariants and preventing funds from disappearing due to a permanently paused state.

title: Registered modules have access to critical functions
description: Registered modules have access to several critical functions, such as addModule / removeModule, r1AddOwner / k1AddOwner, r1RemoveOwner / k1RemoveOwner / resetOwners, r1AddValidator / k1AddValidator, and r1RemoveValidator / k1RemoveValidator through onlySelfOrModule modifier. This excessive access could allow a maliciously registered module to hijack the wallet by changing its owner or validator.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates fromthe design of the module registration system, where any contract that has been added to the wallet’s list of approved modules is granted permission to invoke a set of privileged management functions through the onlySelfOrModule access control modifier. These privileged functions include the ability to add or remove other modules, to add or remove owners, to reset the entire owner set, and to add or remove validators. Because the onlySelfOrModule modifier treats a registered module as equivalent to the wallet itself, a malicious module can call these functions and replace the legitimate owners or validators with addresses under the attacker’s control. The root cause is an overly permissive access rule that does not differentiate between the wallet’s internal logic and external modules, effectively delegating critical governance operations to any module that may be registered. An attacker can exploit this by first registering a malicious contract as a module – a step that may be allowed by the protocol’s onboarding process – and then invoking the owner‑management functions to change the owner address to one they control, or to replace the validator set, thereby gaining the ability to approve transactions, withdraw funds, or block legitimate users. The impact is a potential full takeover of the wallet: the original user loses control, funds can be drained, and the security guarantees of the wallet are nullified. This scenario occurs whenever a module is added without additional restrictions on its authority, meaning any future module, even one added innocently, could be swapped for a malicious version through an upgrade or a compromised deployment. The affected parties are the wallet owners, any users relying on the wallet’s security, and the broader protocol that assumes only the wallet itself can perform governance actions. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access control modifiers applied to management functions and identified that the onlySelfOrModule modifier does not enforce a strict self‑only policy. The problem can be subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the functions behave correctly when called by the wallet itself, making the excessive privilege easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate, the privileged functions should be restricted to onlySelf, removing module access, or a separate, more granular permission scheme should be introduced that explicitly limits which modules, if any, may call governance‑level functions. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model where only the wallet’s core logic can modify owners or validators, preserving the integrity of the ownership and validation mechanisms and preventing a malicious module from hijacking the contract.

title: removeHook should attempt to remove the context if it exists.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the execution‑hook management of a contract that uses a runExecutionHooks modifier. The modifier registers a list of execution hooks, calls each hook’s preExecutionHook, stores the returned data as a context, and after the main function finishes it iterates again to call each hook’s postExecutionHook and finally deletes the stored context. The problem occurs when a hook is removed during the execution of a function that is protected by the same modifier. The removeHook function deletes the hook’s address from the linked list but does not clear the context that was previously stored for that hook. Because the post‑execution loop checks the linked list to decide which hooks to invoke, the removed hook is no longer visited, so its stale context remains in storage. If the same hook is later re‑added, the contract will retrieve the old context and may invoke the postExecutionHook with data that no longer corresponds to the current transaction. This can lead to unexpected behavior such as incorrect accounting, wrong state updates, or failed refunds, because the contract assumes the context reflects the most recent pre‑execution call. The issue manifests only when a hook is removed inside a function that is itself wrapped by runExecutionHooks, which is a relatively rare but plausible scenario in upgradeable or modular systems. Users, developers, and auditors are affected because the contract may appear to work correctly while silently retaining outdated data, making debugging difficult. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that traced the control flow of the modifier and noticed that the context deletion step is tied to the hook list rather than the hook’s lifecycle. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit events when the context is left behind, and the stale data does not immediately cause a revert; instead it corrupts later logic in subtle ways. The correct mitigation is to modify removeHook so that it also deletes any stored context associated with the removed hook, ensuring that no leftover data can be reused after re‑registration. Conceptually, this is a state‑cleanup bug where resources allocated for a component are not released when the component is deregistered, violating the invariant that each registered hook has a fresh, valid context for each execution cycle.

title: Transaction fees can be underestimated due to early return
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑estimation of transaction gas fees caused by an early return in the contract’s transaction validation routine. The IAccount.validateTransaction function is supposed to be executed both for real execution and for gas‑fee estimation, preserving all computational steps so that the estimated gas matches the actual consumption. In the ClaveImplementation.validateTransaction implementation, the code checks if the supplied signature length equals 65 bytes and, when this condition is true, immediately returns a magic value without performing any further checks such as signature decoding, validation hooks, or the core validator call. This shortcut is intended to identify estimation calls, but it mistakenly treats any transaction with a 65‑byte signature as an estimation, skipping a large portion of the validation logic. Because the skipped logic consumes a non‑trivial amount of gas, the fee estimation returned to the user is lower than the gas that will actually be required when the transaction is executed on‑chain. An attacker can craft a transaction with a deliberately short (65‑byte) signature, causing the fee estimator to report a cheap transaction. When the same transaction is submitted for execution, the full validation path runs, consuming more gas than was supplied, which leads to an out‑of‑gas revert. The user sees a transaction that appears to have sufficient funds, but the call fails and the user loses the gas spent on the failed attempt. This situation can also be abused to create a denial‑of‑service vector, where many transactions are submitted with the short signature, causing repeated out‑of‑gas failures and draining users’ gas budgets. The issue manifests only during calls that are meant to estimate gas – typically eth_estimateGas or similar RPC methods – and only when the signature length matches the hard‑coded 65‑byte check. All participants that rely on accurate fee estimation – end‑users, dApp front‑ends, and the protocol’s fee‑budgeting logic – are affected because they receive misleading fee information. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the validation flow, where the early‑return branch was identified as bypassing the expected validation steps. It is hard to notice because the estimation call succeeds quickly and returns a plausible fee, while the failure only appears later during execution, making the discrepancy easy to miss in testing. The recommended remediation is to follow the IAccount specification by avoiding early returns for estimation calls. Instead, the contract should perform a dummy verification that mimics the full validation cost, for example by padding an invalid signature to the expected length and running the signature verification logic without actually rejecting it. Validation hooks should also be executed during estimation so that their gas cost is accounted for. By ensuring that the estimation path mirrors the execution path, the reported gas fee will accurately reflect the true cost, preventing users from under‑paying and avoiding unexpected transaction failures.

title: sessionCounter check not enforced when removing SessionKeyValidator
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the removal process of a SessionKeyValidator module in a smart‑contract system. The contract provides a disable function that is supposed to enforce a sessionCounter check – it requires that the number of active session keys for the caller (sessionCounter[msg.sender]) is zero before the validator can be uninstalled. This check is critical because if a validator is removed while session keys remain active, those keys could be reused after the module is re‑installed, breaking the intended security model that assumes no lingering sessions. The disable function correctly includes a require statement, so when sessionCounter is non‑zero the call reverts with the message "Revoke all keys first". However, the internal _removeModule routine invokes disable via an excessivelySafeCall and deliberately discards the boolean success flag returned by the low‑level call. Because the success value is never examined, the surrounding transaction proceeds to emit a RemoveModule event and treats the removal as successful even though the disable call reverted. Consequently, the module is considered removed while the sessionCounter check was never enforced, leaving active session keys in the system. An attacker who can keep a session key alive (for example by not revoking it) can later reinstall the same validator module and use the stale key to perform privileged actions that should have been impossible. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: the contract believes no active sessions exist after removal, but in reality they do, allowing unauthorized operations that may lead to loss of assets or manipulation of protocol state. This condition occurs whenever a caller attempts to uninstall the validator while any session keys remain, and the transaction does not explicitly check the success of the disable call. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the module removal flow and noticed that the return value of the low‑level call was ignored, effectively silencing the revert. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no error is emitted, making it appear that the validator was cleanly removed. To remediate, the contract should either propagate the revert from disable by checking the success flag and reverting if false, or redesign the flow so that the sessionCounter check is performed before the module is unlinked (for example in an init function). Ensuring that the removal routine validates the outcome of the disable call restores the guarantee that no active session keys survive module removal, aligning the implementation with its security model.

title: SessionKeyValidator module cannot be removed properly
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the removal process of the SessionKeyValidator module in a modular smart‑contract system. When a module is deregistered, the core contract executes a private _removeModule function that first deletes the module from the linked list of registered modules and only afterwards performs a low‑level call to the module’s disable function. The disable function is designed to clean up the module by revoking all active session keys and by calling two restricted management functions – removeModuleValidator and removeHook – which can only be invoked by the module itself or by other registered modules. Because the module has already been removed from the registry at the time disable is called, these restricted calls fail silently; the low‑level call does not revert and its success flag is ignored. Consequently, the validator and hook remain registered inside the validator manager and hook manager, and any session keys that were not manually revoked before uninstall remain active. From a user’s perspective the UI or event logs indicate that the SessionKeyValidator has been removed, yet the contract’s internal accounting still permits the stale validator to be invoked, leading to unexpected behavior such as refunds not being processed, balances appearing unchanged, or unauthorized actions being accepted. The root cause is an ordering flaw: the contract calls disable after deregistering the module instead of before, and it does not enforce that the disable call succeeds. This bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the module lifecycle logic. It is difficult to notice because there is no revert or explicit error; the silent failure leaves the system in an inconsistent state that only manifests when a user expects the module to be fully deactivated, for example when trying to revoke all keys or when reinstalling the module later and finding that old sessions are still valid. The impact is medium severity: while funds are not directly stolen by the bug itself, the lingering validator can be abused to perform actions with previously issued session keys, potentially compromising user assets or protocol integrity. The issue belongs to the class of “improper cleanup after deregistration” or “order‑of‑operations bug in module lifecycle”. To remediate, the disable call should be moved before the module is removed from the registry, or the contract should verify that the disable call succeeded and revert otherwise, ensuring that all keys are revoked and that the validator and hook are properly deregistered before the module disappears from the list.

title: validateFeeLimit does not properly limit the transaction fee
poc: No poc.
bug_full: validateFeeLimit is intended to enforce a maximum fee that a session‑key holder mayspend on a transaction. The function is called after signature verification and should compare the product of maxFeePerGas and gasLimit against a per‑period feeLimit stored in the session state. However, the implementation checks the fee only when transaction.paymaster is non‑zero, i.e., when a paymaster is present, and skips the check when paymaster is zero. Because most session‑key transactions are expected to be paid directly by the caller (paymaster == 0), the fee limit is effectively disabled. An attacker controlling a session key can therefore submit a transaction with arbitrarily large maxFeePerGas or gasLimit, causing the contract to accept fees far beyond the allocated budget. The impact is that the session’s fee allowance can be exhausted or drained, leading to unexpected loss of funds for the account that delegated the session key. The bug manifests during the validationHook execution of SessionKeyValidator, specifically after the ECDSA signature recovery step. It is discovered during a security audit that examined the validation flow and noticed the inverted condition in validateFeeLimit. The issue is subtle because the function is separated from the main validation to avoid gas‑estimation failures, so the missing check does not raise an obvious revert; instead, it silently permits higher fees. The correct behavior is to perform the fee‑limit check when no paymaster is used (paymaster == 0) and to skip it only when a paymaster explicitly covers the fee. Fixing the condition restores the intended accounting invariant that the session’s fee budget cannot be exceeded. From a user’s perspective, a wallet expecting a bounded fee may see the transaction succeed while the balance drops more than anticipated, or a refund may be missing because the fee limit was never enforced. This class of bug is a logic error in fee‑limit enforcement, often categorized as an incorrect conditional check or authorization bypass via inverted flag.

title: Broken initial call functionality
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from missing payable modifiers on two critical functions that are responsible for initializing a newly deployed account with an optional ether transfer. The factory contract’s deployAccount function creates a new account contract and then performs a low‑level call to the account’s initialize function, passing an initializer payload. Because deployAccount is not marked payable, the transaction cannot carry ether, and any value sent with the call is rejected by the EVM. Inside deployAccount the call is explicitly made with a value of 0, regardless of any msg.value that might have been supplied. Likewise, the initialize function in the account implementation is not payable, and when it processes the initCall structure it forwards the value field only after casting it to a 128‑bit integer, but the value it receives is always zero because the external call supplied no ether. As a result, the “initial call” feature – intended to allow the deployer to fund the account and optionally execute a first transaction in a single step – works only partially: the code path executes, but no ether is transferred. An attacker or honest user who expects the account to be funded at creation will see the transaction succeed while the account balance remains empty, leading to a mismatch between expectation (funded account) and reality (zero balance). This can be exploited by submitting a deployment transaction with a non‑zero msg.value; the transaction will either revert because the function is non‑payable, or it will succeed but the ether will be trapped in the factory contract and never reach the new account. Consequently, users may lose funds or be forced to perform a second transaction to fund the account, breaking the intended user experience and potentially causing accounting inconsistencies in protocols that rely on the initial funding to be atomic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initialization flow and noticed that the payable keyword was absent and that the call assembly used a hard‑coded zero value. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without warnings and the call succeeds, yet the financial effect is invisible unless the deployer checks the account balance after deployment. To remediate, both deployAccount and initialize should be declared payable, and the assembly call should forward msg.value (or the value specified in the initCall) instead of a constant zero. This change restores the atomic funding and execution semantics originally intended, ensuring that the account receives the ether supplied by the caller and that the business logic of “deploy‑and‑fund‑in‑one‑step” is correctly enforced.

title: User can bypass deployment restrictions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deployAccount function of the factory contract. The function is designed to let users create a new smart‑account proxy and then initialise it by forwarding a user‑supplied calldata block (the initializer) to the freshly deployed contract via a low‑level call. The contract assumes that the initializer will only invoke the proxy’s initialise() routine, which contains a check that only the authorised factory deployer may set the initialK1Owner field. Because the initializer is not validated, an attacker can craft calldata that calls any function on the proxy, including a second initialise call through a malicious clone of the factory. By doing so the attacker can bypass the “thisDeployer == factory.deployer()” check and set the initialK1Owner to an address of their choosing. The exploit works whenever a user supplies arbitrary initializer data, i.e., during any normal account creation request. The impact is that the ownership of the newly created account can be hijacked, allowing the attacker to control the account, withdraw funds, or perform actions on behalf of the legitimate user. From the user’s perspective the account appears to be created successfully, but later attempts to use the account fail because the owner is not the expected address, or funds sent to the account become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of user‑controlled calldata and identified that the low‑level call does not enforce a specific function selector. The bug is subtle because the deployment transaction itself does not revert and the proxy’s initialise function still executes, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. The proper mitigation is to restrict the initializer to the known initialise selector, either by hard‑coding the selector in the factory, by validating the calldata length and selector before the low‑level call, or by using a safe wrapper that only forwards the intended initialise call. In generic terms this is an unchecked external call injection vulnerability that allows arbitrary function execution during contract deployment, breaking the intended access‑control model and compromising account ownership.

title: Use of constant authenticator data in WebAuthn Protocol
description:
The PasskeyValidator contract's _validateSignature function is responsible for verifying signatures derived from the WebAuthn protocol. This verification process constructs a message hash that includes the transaction hash, specific WebAuthn protocol strings, and a constant AUTHENTICATOR_DATA:
```solidity
clientData = bytes.concat(
    bytes(ClIENT_DATA_PREFIX),
    challengeBase64,
    bytes(IOS_ClIENT_DATA_SUFFIX)
);
bytes32 message = _createMessage(AUTHENTICATOR_DATA, clientData);
```
The AUTHENTICATOR_DATA is defined as a constant with a hardcoded counter value of zero:
```solidity
// hash of 'https://getclave.io' +
// (BE, BS, UP, UV) flags set + unincremented sign counter
bytes constant AUTHENTICATOR_DATA =
    hex'175faf8504c2cdd7c01778a8b0efd4874ecb3aefd7ebb7079a941f7be8897d411d0000000';
```
The authData is composed of the following fields, concatenated in the order presented:
1. rpIdHash (32 bytes): SHA-256 hash of the Relying Party Identifier (RP ID).
2. flags (1 byte): Bit flags indicating user presence, user verification, and the inclusion of additional data.
3. signCount (4 bytes): Signature counter to prevent replay attacks.
4. attestedCredentialData (variable length, optional): Includes credential information; present during registration.
5. extensions (variable length, optional): Contains extension data; included if extensions are used.
By using a constant AUTHENTICATOR_DATA with a static counter, the contract fails to account for the dynamic nature of the authenticator's counter. Authenticators (such as secure enclaves or TPMs) increment this counter with each signing operation. Consequently, the signatures produced by authenticators will include a counter value that does not match the static value expected by the contract.
This mismatch causes all signature verifications to fail, effectively leading to a denial of service (DoS) for any user account operations that rely on signature validation through the PasskeyValidator. Users are then forced to rely on alternative validators or key owners, undermining the security and usability of the system.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PasskeyValidator contract where the internal function that validates WebAuthn signatures builds the signed message using a hard‑coded AUTHENTICATOR_DATA constant. This constant contains a fixed signature counter set to zero, even though the WebAuthn specification requires the authenticator to embed an ever‑increasing signCount value with each signing operation. Because the contract never updates this counter, the message hash it computes does not match the hash produced by a genuine authenticator, whose counter will be non‑zero after the first use. As a result, every signature verification performed by _validateSignature fails, causing any transaction that relies on a passkey‑based signature to be rejected. From a user’s perspective the operation simply reverts or returns an “invalid signature” error, leaving balances unchanged and giving the impression that the contract is unresponsive. Users expect their passkey to authenticate actions, but instead they receive no confirmation and are forced to fall back to alternative validators, effectively a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue occurs each time the contract attempts to verify a WebAuthn signature, i.e., for any account operation that depends on the PasskeyValidator. All participants who rely on passkey authentication – end‑users, the protocol’s access‑control logic, and any funds guarded by this validator – are affected. The flaw was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature verification flow and noticed the static AUTHENTICATOR_DATA definition. It is subtle because the contract does not emit a distinct event for the mismatch; it merely reports a generic signature failure, making it easy to mistake for a user error or a malformed request. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of authentication‑data misuse where mutable fields (such as replay counters) are treated as immutable, breaking the cryptographic guarantees of the protocol. To remediate, the contract should accept the authenticatorData supplied by the client, extract the dynamic signCount, and incorporate it into the message hash, or otherwise compute the expected authenticatorData at runtime instead of relying on a constant value. This change restores proper replay protection and allows legitimate signatures to be verified, eliminating the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: SessionKeyValidator is not working on ZkSync mainnet
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded environment check that causes the SessionKeyValidator contract to revert on ZkSync mainnet (chainId 324). The locate function in the TimestampAsserterLocator component contains an explicit revert when the chain identifier equals 324, assuming that a TimestampAsserter contract is not deployed on that network. This defensive check was introduced during audit but never updated when the TimestampAsserter was later deployed on mainnet. Because the revert is unconditional for the specific chain, any call that triggers the locate routine – which is required for validating session keys – fails, breaking the entire session‑key workflow on the live network. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply invoking any function that relies on session‑key validation will cause the transaction to revert with the message “Timestamp asserter is not deployed on ZKsync mainnet yet”. The impact is that users and integrators cannot use session keys for gas‑less or delegated actions on ZkSync mainnet, leading to failed transactions, missing expected functionality, and potentially locked user experience where a UI reports “operation failed” or “no response”. The issue manifests only on the mainnet deployment; testnets or other chains where the condition is false operate correctly, making the bug easy to miss during local testing. It was discovered during a security review that inspected the locate function and noted the explicit revert for chainId 324. The problem is subtle because the revert message suggests a missing deployment rather than a bug, and developers may assume the check is harmless until they attempt to use session keys on mainnet. Conceptually, the fix is to replace the hard‑coded revert with the correct mainnet address of the TimestampAsserter, or to make the locator retrieve the address from a configurable source rather than a static chain‑id check. This class of bug – hard‑coded network assumptions that cause functionality to be disabled in production – violates the contract’s business logic that session keys should be universally available, breaking accounting assumptions that delegated actions will be processed. From a user perspective, the UI may show “transaction reverted” or “session key validation failed”, whereas the expectation is that the operation proceeds transparently using the session key. The remedy is to update the TimestampAsserterLocator with the proper mainnet address or to remove the chain‑specific revert entirely, ensuring that session‑key validation works across all supported networks.

title: M-2 Stake is locked for the contract owner in _createPool()
description:
The _createPool() method is called from the createPoolInitial() and createPool() methods which are marked with the onlyOwner modifier.
Thus,
```solidity
info.staker = msg.sender;
info.stakedAmount = staking.lockStake(msg.sender);
```
at PoolFactory.sol#L509 uses the owner's address to lock the stake, while it's a manager who is supposed to be staking tokens according to the whitepaper:
2.1 Borrower Whitelisting & Credit Evaluation
<…>
To become whitelisted, the institution must first complete a due diligence, KYC and AML procedure, agree to the Clearpool Terms & Conditions, and stake an amount of CPOOL tokens before a pool can be launched.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect assignment of the staker address during pool creation. In the internal _createPool function, which is invoked only through the public createPoolInitial and createPool functions protected by the onlyOwner modifier, the code sets info.staker to msg.sender and then locks the stake of that same address. Because only the contract owner can call these functions, the owner’s address is recorded as the staker and the owner’s CPOOL tokens are locked, even though the protocol’s whitepaper specifies that a whitelisted manager (the institution that has passed KYC/AML) must provide the stake before a pool can be launched. The root cause is the use of msg.sender without passing the intended manager address, combined with the restrictive onlyOwner access control that prevents the correct party from being used. An attacker who controls the owner account, or a malicious owner, can trigger pool creation and unintentionally (or deliberately) lock their own tokens, preventing the designated manager from staking the required amount. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition where the pool cannot be launched because the required stake is missing, and it also leads to unexpected loss of tokens from the owner’s balance, appearing to users as a sudden reduction to zero or missing funds after a pool creation transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract implementation with the business requirements described in the whitepaper. It is subtle because the function is internal and the incorrect address is not obvious without tracing the call flow, and tests may not cover the scenario where a manager, rather than the owner, should be the staker. To remediate, the contract should accept the manager’s address as a parameter (or retrieve it from a whitelist mapping) and assign that address to info.staker before calling the staking lock function, ensuring that the correct party’s tokens are locked and that the business rule of manager‑provided stake is enforced. This change restores alignment with the intended accounting model, prevents accidental token locking of the owner, and eliminates the potential for a pool launch failure caused by the wrong stakeholder being recorded.

title: M-3 The pool borrower must not be permitted to participate in the auction
description:
In setWhitelistedBidder there aren't any checks for bidder (Auction.sol#L179).
But in whitepaper:
3.3 Auction
<…>
Bidders can be individuals or institutions but must be whitelisted. Whitelisting is achieved through providing KYC information and by declaring the UBO of the bid. The pool borrower is not permitted to participate in the auction.
It requires excluding the manager of the pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent restriction that allows the pool borrower, typically the manager of a lending pool, to be added to the list of approved bidders for the auction that liquidates collateral. The whitepaper explicitly states that bidders must be whitelisted through KYC and that the pool borrower is not permitted to participate, but the smart‑contract function setWhitelistedBidder does not enforce this rule. The root cause is a missing access‑control check in the whitelisting routine, which simply records any address supplied by the caller without verifying that the address is not the borrower or a related manager. An attacker who controls the manager role can call setWhitelistedBidder with its own address or with an address it controls, thereby becoming a legitimate bidder. Once whitelisted, the borrower can submit bids during the auction, potentially winning the collateral at a price that is favorable to the borrower and detrimental to the lenders. This can lead to a situation where lenders receive less repayment than expected, or where the borrower extracts value from the auction that should have been distributed to the pool participants. The issue manifests whenever the manager invokes the whitelisting function, which is allowed by the contract’s design, and it may go unnoticed because the function appears to perform a benign administrative task and does not emit any warning about prohibited participants. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract implementation against the protocol’s specification. To remediate the flaw, the contract should include a check in setWhitelistedBidder that rejects the borrower’s address (and optionally any address derived from the manager) before adding it to the whitelist, or the protocol documentation should be updated to reflect the actual behaviour if the exclusion is intentional. By enforcing the exclusion, the auction’s economic assumptions—namely that only independent third‑party bidders compete—are restored, preventing the borrower from manipulating the outcome and protecting the integrity of the pool’s collateral liquidation process.

title: Compounding shares will overtime get less rewards than non compounding shares
description: keepPortion and sellPortion are based on the total number of shares of each type. However, compoundShareRate is expected to increase due to accumulating rewards. This means that, for compounding shares, the same liquidity minted compared to non compounding shares will lead to less shares, when depositing. Thus, over time, assuming equal deposits of compounding and non compounding shares, the total supply of non compounding shares is expected to grow more than compounding shares.
bug_full: The issue originates from the way the protocol calculates the portions of liquidity that are kept and sold for each share class. Both keepPortion and sellPortion are derived from the total number of shares of a given type, while the reward‑generating asset is the underlying liquidity that those shares represent. Because compoundShareRate is expected to rise as rewards accumulate, the same amount of newly minted liquidity that would create a certain number of non‑compounding shares creates fewer compounding shares when the calculation is based on share count. Over time, assuming users deposit comparable amounts of compounding and non‑compounding shares, the total supply of non‑compounding shares expands faster than the supply of compounding shares. This creates a gradual dilution of compounding shares: each compounding share represents a smaller fraction of the total reward‑producing liquidity, so holders receive fewer rewards than they anticipate. The vulnerability is subtle because the contract appears to mint shares correctly on each deposit, and short‑term balances look normal; the discrepancy only becomes evident after multiple reward cycles when the reward per compounding share falls below that of non‑compounding shares. It affects any user who opts for compounding shares, the protocol’s economic model, and any stakeholder relying on the promised higher yield from compounding. The flaw was identified during a systematic audit of the share‑minting and reward‑distribution logic, where the auditor noticed that the share‑to‑liquidity ratio diverged over time. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the UI typically shows the share balance increasing, while the underlying reward rate is hidden, leading users to assume their earnings are on track. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute keepPortion and sellPortion based on the total liquidity attributable to each share class rather than on the raw share count, ensuring that the reward‑generating base is proportionally allocated and that compounding shares retain their intended advantage.

title: M-1 Risks of non-complete initialization
description:
PoolFactory.initialize() is far from being the final initialization.
It sets only:
• cpool
• staking
• poolBeacon
• interestRateModel
• auction
But many of crucial parameters remain not set and require calling a separate function for every parameter.
• treasury - if not set, a reserve token can be transferred to a zero address on pool.processAuctionStart(), pool.close()
• reserveFactor - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• insuranceFactor - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• warningUtilization - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• provisionalDefaultUtilization - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• warningGracePeriod - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• maxInactivePeriod - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• periodToStartAuction - if not set, a pool will work wrong
• rewardPerSecond - if not set, cPool token rewards will be set zero, that is ok
It is not so bad that these parameters are not set during the factory initialization. The problem is that Factory allows createPool() if some of these parameters are not set.
• PoolFactory.sol#L181-201
This can lead to a situation where a human error causes one of these variables to be undefined, resulting in a new pool being created with incorrect parameters in the PoolFactory contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete initialization pattern in the pool factory. The initialize function only assigns a subset of the configuration variables (cpool, staking, poolBeacon, interestRateModel, auction) while leaving many critical parameters such as treasury, reserveFactor, insuranceFactor, warningUtilization, provisionalDefaultUtilization, warningGracePeriod, maxInactivePeriod, periodToStartAuction and rewardPerSecond unset. Because the factory's createPool routine does not enforce that these variables have been initialized, an attacker or a careless operator can trigger the creation of a new pool with one or more zero‑valued parameters. When treasury is zero, the pool's processAuctionStart or close functions may attempt to transfer the reserve token to address(0), effectively burning user funds. Missing reserveFactor, insuranceFactor, warningUtilization and related utilization thresholds cause the pool's accounting logic to produce incorrect interest calculations, premature or delayed auction triggers, and may violate the protocol's risk assumptions. The rewardPerSecond being zero simply disables token rewards but does not cause a loss of funds. The bug manifests only after a pool is created; there is no immediate revert, making it hard to notice during normal deployment testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the factory's initialization flow and the createPool guard conditions. The impact is that users depositing into an improperly initialized pool may see their balances unchanged, receive no rewards, or have their tokens unintentionally sent to the zero address, breaking the economic guarantees of the protocol. The affected parties include depositors, liquidity providers, and the overall protocol because a mis‑configured pool can undermine confidence and cause financial loss. The issue belongs to the class of partial initialization or missing parameter validation bugs, where critical state variables are left at their default zero value and later used in sensitive calculations or transfers. To remediate, the factory should either move all required parameter assignments into the initialize function or add explicit require checks in the internal _createPool routine that reject pool creation unless every essential parameter is non‑zero. This ensures that the pool cannot be instantiated with undefined configuration and prevents the described loss of funds and accounting errors.

title: Atomic fees delivery susceptible to funds lockout
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑collection routine that attempts to transfer both the base token and the quote token fees to the DAO treasury and the host in a single atomic operation. The function collectFees is restricted to be called only by the host, and it invokes an internal helper _collectFees for each token. Inside _collectFees the contract calculates the DAO share and the host share, then calls _transferToken for each destination. Because the two transfers are performed sequentially without any error handling, a failure of either transfer – for example when the DAO treasury address or the host address is blacklisted, when the token contract is malicious and deliberately reverts on transfer, or when the token does not conform to the ERC‑20 standard – causes the entire transaction to revert. When a revert occurs the fee balances (_baseFeeBalance and _quoteFeeBalance) are left at a sentinel value of 1, meaning the accumulated fees remain locked inside the contract and are never delivered. This situation can be triggered deliberately by a hostile host that wants to prevent the DAO from receiving its guaranteed fees, or unintentionally by a compromised DAO that points its treasury to an invalid address. From a user’s perspective the DAO may see that no fees have been credited after a collectFees call, while the UI might still indicate that the operation succeeded, leading to confusion and the impression that “funds disappear”. The impact is primarily economic: the protocol loses expected revenue, the DAO’s treasury does not grow, and the host may also be deprived of its share, potentially undermining the incentive model. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) by analysing the atomic fee delivery pattern and recognizing that a single revert blocks the whole process. It is hard to notice because the function does not emit a distinct error for each transfer and the contract state after a failure does not clearly signal that fees are stuck. The recommended remediation is to decouple the fee collection per token, maintain separate counters for delivered fees, and allow the caller to specify which token to collect. Additionally, the contract should handle transfer failures gracefully – for example by using a pull‑based claim pattern, try/catch blocks, or by permitting partial delivery – so that a failure affecting one token or one recipient does not prevent the other fees from being transferred. This transforms the bug from an “atomic transfer lockout” class into a more robust, fault‑tolerant fee distribution mechanism.

title: DAO fees potentially unavailable due to overly strict access control
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overly restrictive access control on the fee‑collection routine of the market contract. The collectFees function contains a require that only the market host (msg.sender == _host()) may execute it. Because the function is responsible for transferring both the host’s share of the accumulated fees and the portion that belongs to the DAO treasury, limiting its execution to a single address creates a single point of failure. If the host’s private key is lost, the host address is transferred, or the host becomes unresponsive, no external actor can trigger the fee distribution. Consequently the accumulated base‑token and quote‑token fees remain locked in the contract, and the DAO never receives its entitled revenue. The issue was identified during a manual security review that examined the contract’s permission checks. It is subtle because the function appears to be a harmless internal accounting routine, and the restriction does not raise an immediate error; the contract simply retains the balances. Exploitation does not require malicious code – the mere inability of the authorized address to call the function is sufficient to lock the funds. The impact is financial: DAO participants see their expected fee payouts disappear, the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, and the overall trust in the system may be eroded. The problem manifests whenever the host cannot or does not call collectFees, for example after a key compromise, a wallet migration, or a deliberate refusal to execute the function. Affected parties include the DAO treasury, token holders who rely on fee distributions, and any users expecting the market to forward fees to the designated addresses. To remediate, the access control should be relaxed so that any external account can invoke collectFees, or a fallback mechanism such as a timelocked admin or a pull‑payment pattern should be introduced to ensure that fee distribution can occur even if the original host is unavailable. Removing the host‑only restriction aligns the contract with the intended business logic that fees are automatically forwarded to fixed recipient addresses, eliminating the risk of permanently locked funds.

title: Group claim clashing condition
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batch claim mechanism of the order book contract, where a single transaction can attempt to claim multiple orders on behalf of users. The function iterates over an array of order identifiers and invokes a private _claim routine for each entry. However, the implementation does not verify whether an individual order has already been fulfilled, cancelled, or otherwise rendered unclaimable before calling _claim. The _claim routine contains a require statement that aborts the whole transaction if the order’s open amount is zero, which is the case for already claimed or cancelled orders. Because the outer claim function does not catch or skip these failures, a revert in any single iteration propagates to the top‑level call, causing the entire batch to revert. This creates a race‑condition style clash: when two independent actors (for example, two bots or a bot and the order owner) submit overlapping order lists, the first successful claim marks the order as fulfilled, and any subsequent batch that still includes that order will hit the require check and revert. From a user perspective the transaction appears to have failed with a generic revert message, no assets are transferred, and the caller still pays the full gas cost despite receiving no bounty or token amount. The impact is primarily economic – operators lose gas and potential bounty revenue, and the protocol’s reliability is reduced because legitimate batch claims can be blocked by harmless timing overlaps. The issue manifests only when batch claiming is used; single‑order claims that are correctly sequenced do not exhibit the problem. It affects any third‑party operator that relies on the batch claim feature, as well as the end users whose orders are being claimed, and indirectly the protocol’s fee model. The flaw was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of the claim functions and identified the missing idempotency check. It can be difficult to notice in routine testing because the revert only occurs under specific concurrency conditions that may not be reproduced in a single‑threaded test environment. To remediate the issue, the contract should incorporate a pre‑check that skips orders whose open amount is zero, or redesign _claim to return a status code instead of reverting, allowing the outer loop to continue processing remaining orders. Alternatively, the batch function could be split into independent calls or wrapped in a try/catch construct so that a failure on one order does not invalidate the entire batch. In essence, the bug is a classic example of an atomic batch operation lacking proper handling of already‑processed items, leading to a denial‑of‑service style loss of gas and missed rewards.

title: Order owner isn't zeroed after burning
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug that occurs when an order‑related NFT is burned. The contract’s internal burn routine records the transfer of the token to the zero address via the onBurn() hook, but it fails to clear the stored owner field of the token. Consequently the ERC‑721 ownerOf() function continues to return the previous owner even though the token has been marked as burned. This mismatch allows callers to invoke approve() and safeTransferFrom() on a token that no longer represents a live order. An attacker can therefore “resurrect” a burned NFT by transferring it to another address, list it on a secondary marketplace and receive payment, even though the underlying order has zero open amount and any attempt to cancel or claim the order will revert. The issue manifests after an order is cancelled (which triggers the burn) and persists until the owner field is manually overwritten, which never happens in normal flow. Users, order makers, and any party relying on the token’s ownership information are affected because they may see a token that appears to be owned and transferable while it carries no economic value. The bug was uncovered during a manual security review that compared the onBurn event with the result of ownerOf() after a cancellation. It is subtle because the ERC‑721 transfer event shows a move to address(0), which many developers interpret as sufficient proof of token destruction, while the contract’s internal accounting still reports a valid owner. The root cause is the omission of a line that sets the token’s owner to address(0) inside the internal _burnToken() function. To fix the issue, the burn routine must explicitly zero the owner storage slot after invoking onBurn(), ensuring that ownerOf() returns the zero address and that subsequent ERC‑721 calls revert as expected. This class of bug falls under “incomplete token burn” or “ownership not cleared after token destruction”, which can lead to unexpected token resurrection, loss of trust in the protocol’s accounting, and potential financial loss for users who acquire seemingly valid but valueless NFTs.

title: Lack of two-step role transfer
description: The contracts lack two-step role transfer. Both the ownership of the MarketFactory as well as the change of market's host are implemented as single-step functions. The basic validation whether the address is not a zero address for a market is performed, however the case when the address receiving the role is inaccessible is not covered properly. Taking into account the handOverHost can be invoked without any supervision, by anyone who created the market it is possible to make a typo unintentionally or intentionally if the attacker wants simply to brick fees collection as currently the host affects collectFees in OrderBook (described as a separate issue). The ownership transfer in theory should be less error-prone as it should be done by DAO with great care, however still two-step role transfer should be preferable.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing two‑step role transfer mechanism for privileged roles such as the MarketFactory owner and the market host. The contracts currently allow a single‑step handOverHost call that immediately assigns the host role to a new address after only checking that the address is not the zero address. No additional verification is performed to ensure that the recipient can actually accept the role or that the transfer is intentional. Because the function can be invoked by any account that created the market, a typo in the target address or a malicious actor can deliberately assign the host role to an inaccessible or zero address. When the host role is held by an address that cannot execute the collectFees function in the OrderBook, fee collection stops, leaving users without expected fee payouts and potentially bricking the market’s revenue stream. The same single‑step pattern is used for ownership transfer of the MarketFactory, which, although typically performed by a DAO, is still vulnerable to accidental mis‑assignment because there is no claim step that forces the new owner to accept the role. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined role‑changing functions and noted the lack of a confirmation step. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert on an inaccessible recipient; the transaction succeeds, but downstream fee collection silently fails, producing a symptom where users see no fees being transferred despite successful trades. The impact is that fee revenue may disappear, market participants may receive zero refunds, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fee accrual are violated. The problem occurs whenever a role transfer is executed, especially when the caller makes a mistake or an attacker exploits the unrestricted handOverHost function. A proper fix is to replace the single‑step transfer with a two‑step pattern: the current role holder designates a pending recipient, and the recipient must explicitly claim the role, ensuring that the address is capable of receiving it and that the transfer was intentional. This change aligns the contract with the standard “push‑then‑pull” role transfer design and prevents accidental or malicious bricking of fee collection and ownership control.

title: M-1 WalletUpgradable initialization is risky
description: The current initialization of an upgradable wallet includes multiple steps, where a wallet proxy is owned by some external admin. The admin has to transfer proxy ownership directly to the wallet to ﬁnalize the initialization.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the initialization process of an upgradable wallet that relies on a proxy contract. In the current design the proxy is initially owned by an external administrator and the wallet’s constructor performs several setup steps, after which the admin must manually transfer ownership of the proxy to the wallet contract to complete the initialization. This hand‑off creates a window of risk because the external admin retains full control over the proxy until the transfer occurs. If the admin never performs the transfer, or if the transfer is performed to an address controlled by an attacker, the attacker can invoke the upgrade mechanism of the proxy and replace the wallet logic with a malicious implementation. Consequently the attacker could redirect withdrawals, freeze the wallet, or otherwise compromise the funds held by the wallet. The issue manifests whenever a new wallet is deployed through the existing factory but the factory does not enforce the final ownership transfer; it depends on an off‑chain step that may be omitted or tampered with. Users of the wallet, the wallet owners, and any protocol that relies on the wallet’s security are affected because they may lose control over their assets without any visible warning. The problem was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the multi‑step initialization and the reliance on an external admin for the final ownership change. It is easy to miss because the ownership transfer is a separate transaction that does not appear in the constructor code, and the proxy’s admin role is not visibly linked to the wallet’s address in the source. To remediate the issue the wallet should be instantiated using a factory pattern that automatically sets the proxy’s admin to the wallet itself, eliminating the need for a manual hand‑off. Alternatively, the contract can adopt the UUPSUpgradeable pattern with a properly restricted _authorizeUpgrade function that only allows upgrades when called by the wallet contract itself (onlySelfCall), ensuring that no external party can hijack the upgrade path. By guaranteeing that the proxy is owned by the wallet from the moment of deployment, the risk of unauthorized upgrades and fund loss is removed.

title: Minipool owner can create unliquidatable loan, imposing bad debt on main lending pool
description:
In the scenario where minipool owner is not the same entity as the main pool admin, and the minipool has some borrowing capacity from the main lending pool (available flow), the minipool owner can create an unliquidatable loan, forcing bad debt upon the main lending pool. Note that initially main lending pool owner and minipools owner should be the same entity. The risk reported here would be impactful with decentralization of minipool ownership in the future.
To achieve this, the minipool owner can simply deactivate the reserve associated with the collateral of his loan. This is possible due to a flawed _checkNoLiquidity for deactivating reserves:
• MiniPoolConfigurator.sol#L481-L490:
```solidity
function _checkNoLiquidity(address asset, IMiniPool pool) internal view {
    DataTypes.MiniPoolReserveData memory reserveData = pool.getReserveData(asset);
    uint256 availableLiquidity = IERC20Detailed(asset).balanceOf(reserveData.aTokenAddress); // <<<
    require(
        availableLiquidity == 0 && reserveData.currentLiquidityRate == 0,
        Errors.LPC_RESERVE_LIQUIDITY_NOT_0
    );
}
```
Scenario: Let's examine the concrete way of creating an unliquidatable loan:
• Parameters:
Parameter
Value
Collateral
aWETH
Debt
aUSDC
Available flow
500k aUSDC
aUSDC Liquidity
aWETH LTV
1.2
• Steps:
– Alice the minipool owner deposits 600k$ of WETH into the minipool and borrows 500k USDC, using all available flow.
– Alice flashloans all of WETH out of erc6909 market, enabling the deactivation of reserve because _checkNoLiquidity allows it.
bug_full: The vulnerability allows the owner of a MiniPool to create a loan that cannot be liquidated, thereby imposing unrecoverable bad debt on the main lending pool. The root cause lies in the internal function that checks whether a reserve can be deactivated. The function reads the token balance of the aToken contract using IERC20Detailed.balanceOf, which returns zero because aTokens do not hold a balance at their own address. However, the actual amount of liquidity backing the reserve is stored in the scaled total supply of the aToken (via IERC6909.scaledTotalSupply). Because the check only verifies that the balance is zero and that the current liquidity rate is zero, it incorrectly assumes the reserve is empty even when there is still liquidity backing outstanding loans. An attacker who controls a MiniPool but is not the main pool admin can exploit this by first depositing collateral, borrowing the full available flow, and then flash‑loaning the collateral out of the market. With the collateral removed, the attacker calls the reserve‑deactivation routine; the flawed check passes, the reserve is marked inactive, and the loan becomes unliquidatable because the protocol can no longer access the collateral to cover the debt. The impact is that the main lending pool records a loss equal to the borrowed amount, lenders’ capital is reduced, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken. This situation occurs only when MiniPool ownership is decentralized from the main pool admin and the MiniPool has borrowing capacity. The affected parties include the main pool’s liquidity providers, borrowers who rely on liquidation mechanisms, and the overall protocol reputation. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the MiniPoolConfigurator contract, where the logical flaw in _checkNoLiquidity was identified. It is hard to notice because the balance‑of query legitimately returns zero in normal operation, leading developers to believe the reserve is empty, while the hidden scaled supply still holds value. To remediate, the check should query the scaled total supply (or another reliable metric) instead of the token balance, and it should also ensure that no outstanding debt exists before allowing deactivation. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect liquidity verification” or “reserve deactivation without proper collateral accounting”, which can cause funds to disappear from the pool and break the expected refund or liquidation flow.

title: getCurrentInterestRates() does not calculate the interests correctly
description:
The current borrow rate in getCurrentInterestRates() is calculated as:
```solidity
// borrow rate
uint256 currentVariableBorrowRate = transferFunction(getControllerError(getNormalizedError(utilizationRate)));
```
This does not take into the consideration the following storage update for _errI which is used in getControllerError:
```solidity
_errI += int256(_ki).rayMulInt(err * int256(block.timestamp - _lastTimestamp));
if (_errI < _maxErrIAmp) _errI = _maxErrIAmp; // Limit _errI negative accumulation.
```
The NatSpec for getCurrentInterestRates() mentions:
```solidity
/**
* @notice The view version of `calculateInterestRates()`.
* @dev Returns the current interest rates without modifying state.
...
*/
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the view function getCurrentInterestRates(), which is intended to return the current borrow rate without modifying contract state. Instead of using the up‑to‑date controller error value, the function calculates the borrow rate by calling transferFunction(getControllerError(getNormalizedError(utilizationRate))) and completely ignores the storage variable _errI and its time‑dependent update logic. The contract maintains an accumulated error term _errI that is adjusted each block by the expression _errI += int256(_ki).rayMulInt(err * int256(block.timestamp - _lastTimestamp)) and then clamped by _maxErrIAmp to limit negative accumulation. This term is later incorporated into the full interest‑rate calculation performed by calculateInterestRates(), but the view version does not include it, resulting in a stale or underestimated borrow rate. The root cause is a missing reference to the current value of _errI and its update when deriving the currentVariableBorrowRate. An attacker or any user can call getCurrentInterestRates() to obtain a rate that appears lower than the actual rate that will be applied when a loan is opened or when interest is accrued. This discrepancy can be exploited to misprice loans, allowing borrowers to believe they will pay less interest while the protocol later charges a higher rate, potentially leading to under‑collateralized positions, unexpected debt growth, or loss of funds for lenders. The issue manifests whenever utilization changes and _errI is updated between blocks, because the view function still returns a rate based on the old error state. All participants that rely on the displayed rate – borrowers, lenders, front‑end interfaces, and protocol governance – are affected, as the UI may show a borrow rate that does not match the actual accounting performed on‑chain. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation of calculateInterestRates() with its view counterpart and noticed that the storage update for _errI was omitted. Because the function is read‑only, the bug does not cause immediate transaction failures and can be hard to notice without a detailed code review or specific tests that validate the consistency of interest calculations over time. To remediate, the view function must incorporate the current _errI value and the same clamping logic used in calculateInterestRates(), effectively sharing the interest‑rate derivation code between the two functions. Refactoring the common logic into a utility function and ensuring that getAvailableLiquidity() for mini pools also follows the same formula will restore accounting integrity and prevent users from seeing misleading rates. In summary, the contract suffers from an interest‑rate miscalculation bug where a critical state variable is omitted from a view calculation, leading to inaccurate borrow‑rate information, potential financial loss, and violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: variableBorrowIndex is only updated in _updateIndexes of the mini pool if currentLiquidityRate is non-zero
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the update of the variable borrow index in a mini‑pool implementation. The contract updates the index only inside a block that first checks whether the current liquidity rate is non‑zero. Inside that block a second check for non‑zero scaled variable debt is performed, and the index is updated only when both conditions are true. Because the second check is nested, the index update is skipped whenever the outer condition fails, even if there is outstanding variable debt. Rounding errors or a configuration where the reserve factor and the protocol’s reserve factor sum to 100 % can cause the current liquidity rate to be reported as zero while scaledVariableDebt remains non‑zero. In that situation the borrow index becomes stale and interest accrual is no longer calculated correctly. An attacker or a careless user could trigger the zero‑rate condition, for example by adjusting reserve factors or by exploiting rounding edge cases, and then perform borrow or repayment actions while the index is frozen. The impact is that borrowers may repay less than they owe or withdraw more than they should, while lenders receive less interest than entitled, breaking the accounting invariants of the protocol. This condition occurs only when the outer liquidity‑rate check evaluates to false, which can be hard to notice because a zero rate is a legitimate value in many normal scenarios and the contract does not emit any warning when the inner debt‑related update is bypassed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control‑flow of the index‑updating function and identified the nested if as a logical flaw. It is difficult to detect in automated testing because the state appears consistent until a specific combination of reserve factors and rounding produces the edge case. The proper fix is to decouple the two checks so that the index update for scaled variable debt runs independently of the liquidity‑rate condition, ensuring that the borrow index is always refreshed whenever there is variable debt. Conceptually this belongs to the class of conditional‑logic bugs where an essential state update is unintentionally gated by an unrelated condition, leading to stale accounting data and potential financial loss. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that after borrowing or repaying, the displayed balance does not change, or that a refund or interest amount is unexpectedly zero, contrary to the expectation that the protocol always reflects accrued interest.

title: Mini pool reserves for unique tokens can be reinitialised
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the initialization routine of a mini‑pool reserve that stores accounting data for unique tokens. The contract allows the same unique token to be added to the ATokenERC6909 registry multiple times, each time with a different incremental identifier. The init function in MiniPoolReserveLogic only checks that the supplied asset matches the underlying asset of the aToken, but it does not verify whether the reserve storage slot has already been populated. Consequently, when a caller invokes init with a previously used token identifier, the function overwrites the existing reserve fields: the liquidityIndex and variableBorrowIndex are reset to the ray constant, the aTokenID and variableDebtTokenID are replaced with the new identifiers, and the interestRateStrategyAddress is swapped out. This re‑initialisation erases all previously recorded user balances, accrued interest, and debt positions, effectively causing accounting data to disappear. From a user perspective the symptoms are striking – balances that previously showed a positive amount become zero, expected interest accrual stops, and withdrawals may fail because the protocol no longer recognises the user’s position. The issue is triggered whenever a unique token is added more than once, which can happen unintentionally during deployment or maliciously if an attacker can call the init function with a crafted token ID. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of reserve creation and identified the missing guard against duplicate initialization. It is difficult to notice because the function appears to perform a legitimate setup and emits no warning; the only check is a require that validates the asset, which passes even on re‑initialisation. The class of bug is an improper initialization guard, a common pattern where state variables can be overwritten without protection, leading to loss of state and potential fund mis‑allocation. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a one‑reserve‑per‑unique‑token rule, for example by storing a flag or checking that aTokenID is zero before allowing init, or by redesigning the reserve mapping so that adding a token with a new ID does not collide with an existing reserve. Additionally, the init function should revert with a clear error if a reserve is already initialized, preventing accidental or malicious overwrites and preserving the integrity of user accounting and interest calculations.

title: Pi interest rate model is manipulatable due to current balances used
bug_full: The Pi protocol calculates its variable borrow and liquidity rates using a PID‑based interest rate model that derives the utilisation factor from the instantaneous values of availableLiquidity and totalVariableDebt. The model updates an internal error accumulator (_errI) only once per block, based on the error between the current utilisation and a target curve. Because _errI is not refreshed for each state‑changing operation, an attacker can influence the direction of the rate within a single block by performing a sequence of actions that alter the utilisation but do not trigger another _errI update. For example, a borrower can flash‑loan assets, deposit them into the pool, immediately withdraw them and then take a loan; the deposit raises availableLiquidity, the withdrawal lowers it, and the subsequent borrow changes totalVariableDebt, yet _errI remains based on the utilisation measured before these operations. Similarly, a lender can borrow to increase totalVariableDebt (raising the error term) and then repay the same amount in the same block, leaving _errI unchanged while the utilisation appears lower. This manipulation lets the attacker steer the calculated borrow rate downwards (or the liquidity rate upwards) to obtain more favourable interest terms than the protocol intends. The impact is that borrowers may obtain artificially low rates, lenders may receive inflated returns, and the overall economic model of the protocol can be distorted, potentially leading to loss of value for honest participants. The issue manifests only when multiple state‑changing actions occur within the same block without an intermediate _errI update, a situation that is common with flash‑loan attacks or rapid borrow‑repay cycles. It was discovered during a manual audit of the BasePiReserveRateStrategy contract, where the auditor noted that the PID controller uses only the current balances and that the error accumulator is updated a single time per block, creating a timing window for manipulation. The bug is subtle because the on‑chain events still emit plausible utilisation and rate values, making the manipulation hard to detect from external monitoring. To remediate, the contract should base the PID update on the previous block’s balances (a snapshot) or recompute _errI for each balance‑changing operation, ensuring that the error term reflects every change in utilisation. This change eliminates the stale‑state window and restores the intended invariant that interest rates respond continuously and fairly to actual pool dynamics, preventing rate‑direction attacks and preserving the protocol’s economic integrity.

title: setFlowLimit does not change the indices and interest rates
description: Changing the flow limit of a reserve in for a mini pool affects its virtual available liquidity and thus one should updates the interest rates and the indices for that reserve in the mini pool. Moreover setting the flow limit to a non-zero value or resetting it to 0 can trigger calculation the minimum liquidity rate calculation and this adds another reason as to why calling setFlowLimit should trigger updating the interest rates and indices.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that adjusts the flow limit of a reserve within a mini‑pool. When the flow limit is increased, decreased, or reset to zero, the contract changes the virtual available liquidity of that reserve, which should in turn cause the protocol to recompute the interest rates and the accounting indices that track accrued interest. However, the implementation of setFlowLimit does not invoke any update routine for these rates or indices. As a result, the stored interest rates and indices remain based on the previous liquidity state, while the virtual liquidity used for subsequent calculations reflects the new limit. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who changes the flow limit to a non‑zero value or back to zero, thereby creating a window where the protocol reports stale, overly optimistic or pessimistic rates to users. Users interacting with the pool after such a change may receive interest that is higher or lower than the protocol’s economic model intends, leading to potential loss of expected earnings or, in extreme cases, to a situation where the pool appears to have sufficient liquidity while it actually does not, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The issue manifests only when setFlowLimit is called; normal deposit or withdrawal operations continue to work, making the bug subtle and easy to miss during functional testing because the function’s name suggests a simple configuration change rather than a financial state transition. The problem was identified during a formal security audit that examined the flow‑limit management logic and noticed that the interest‑rate update hook was absent. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that any modification of the flow limit triggers the same internal routine that updates the reserve’s indices and recalculates the interest rates, keeping the virtual liquidity and the accounting state consistent. This aligns the implementation with the protocol’s business logic that assumes liquidity changes are always reflected in the interest‑rate model, preventing users from seeing unexpected zero refunds, missing accruals, or other accounting anomalies.

title: Rounding directions
description:
• GenericLogic.sol#L236-L242, MiniPoolGenericLogic.sol#L202-L209: Make sure all operations round-up when calculating totalDebtInETH.
• AToken.sol#L184-L185: Best to round-up amountScaled.
• ValidationLogic.sol#L205-L212, MiniPoolValidationLogic.sol#L208-L214: It would be best to round up the vars.amountOfCollateralNeededETH or instead check:
```solidity
vars.userBorrowBalanceETH + validateParams.amountInETH <= (vars.userCollateralBalanceETH).percentMul(vars.currentLtv)
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑direction flaw in the core accounting logic of the lending protocol. When the contract computes the total debt expressed in ETH, the amount of scaled tokens, or the amount of collateral required for a borrow, it performs arithmetic that rounds down instead of rounding up. This systematic under‑approximation means that the protocol records a slightly smaller debt or a slightly smaller collateral requirement than the true value. The root cause is the use of integer division or multiplication without applying a ceiling operation in functions located in GenericLogic.sol, MiniPoolGenericLogic.sol, AToken.sol, ValidationLogic.sol and MiniPoolValidationLogic.sol. Because the protocol enforces borrowing limits based on a loan‑to‑value (LTV) ratio, the under‑rounded values allow a borrower to appear to stay within the allowed LTV while actually exceeding it. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a borrow request that is just above the real limit; the contract’s check will incorrectly approve the request, granting extra ETH or tokens. The impact is that the protocol may lend more than it is collateralised for, opening the door to under‑collateralised positions that can be liquidated at a loss to the pool, ultimately causing funds to disappear from lenders. The condition occurs whenever a user initiates a borrow or when the system updates a user’s debt or collateral balance, especially when the amounts are not exact multiples of the scaling factor. All participants who rely on the protocol’s safety guarantees – lenders, borrowers, and the overall ecosystem – are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noticed that the rounding direction did not match the intended safety margin.
