oracle.getUSDPrice(wbtc) returns the error "token not supported"
```
As the result, it is impossible to add Curve pools with WBTC. But, Conic mentions pools with WBTC in tests:
ConicTest.sol#L39
...
address internal constant REN_BTC = 0x9305...895B;
address internal constant BBTC = 0x071c...8F4b;
...
Also, there are many Curve pools with WBTC, some of them supported by Convex as well.
BTC is a reserved denomination with the address: 0xbBbBBBBbbBBBbbbBbbBbbbbBBbBbbbbBbBbbBBbB
• Denominations.sol#L7
So WBTC price feed can be received only by:
WBTC = 0x514910771AF9Ca656af840dff83E8264EcF986CA
BTC = 0xbBbBBBBbbBBBbbbBbbBbbbbBBbBbbbbBbBbbBBbB
wbtcbtc = _feedRegistry.getFeed(WBTC, BTC)
It will be WBTC/BTC price; then it must be adjusted to BTC/USD price:
BTC = 0xbBbBBBBbbBBBbbbBbbBbbbbBBbBbbbbBbBbbBBbB
USD = address(840)
btcusd = _feedRegistry.getFeed(WBTC, BTC)
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ChainlinkOracle implementation used by the Conic Finance protocol, where the function that retrieves a token’s USD price rejects the Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC) token with the explicit error message "token not supported". This occurs because the oracle’s internal support check only recognises a limited set of denomination pairs – specifically the native BTC address and a handful of pre‑registered tokens – and does not include the WBTC contract address. Consequently, when the contract calls oracle.getUSDPrice(wbtc) the isTokenSupported routine returns false, causing _getPrice to abort without providing a price feed. An attacker or any user attempting to interact with Curve pools that contain WBTC will experience a failed transaction or a UI that simply hides the WBTC option, leading to the perception that the pool cannot be added. The impact is functional rather than directly financial: liquidity providers cannot deposit WBTC, the protocol cannot expose WBTC‑based pools despite test code referencing them, and any downstream logic that assumes a price will be available may behave incorrectly or revert. The issue manifests whenever a call is made to fetch the USD price for WBTC, i.e., during pool creation, deposit, or any price‑dependent calculation involving that token. It affects end‑users who expect to add WBTC pools, developers who rely on the oracle for pricing, and the protocol’s overall market coverage. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit when the auditors noticed that the test suite referenced WBTC pools while the live oracle returned an unsupported‑token error. Because the failure is signalled only by an error string rather than a silent revert, it can be easy to miss in automated testing, especially if the UI simply disables the option without a clear explanation. To remediate, the oracle should be extended to recognise WBTC as a supported token, either by adding a direct WBTC/USD feed or by composing the price from the existing WBTC/BTC feed together with the BTC/USD feed, and the support‑check logic should be updated accordingly. This class of bug – missing token support in a price oracle – is common in DeFi contracts that rely on external feeds and can lead to broken business logic, such as “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” when the expected price cannot be retrieved.

title: M-7 Reentrancy in GovernanceProxy._executeChange()
bug_full: An reentrancy vulnerability exists in the GovernanceProxy contract's internal function that processes a batch of arbitrary calls defined in a governance change. The function iterates over the list of calls and invokes each target contract before it updates the change's status to Executed. Because the state change (marking the change as completed) occurs after the external calls, a malicious callee that implements a callback mechanism (for example an ERC-777 token with a hook) can re-enter the same executeChange function while the original change is still marked as pending. This re-entrancy allows the attacker to trigger the same batch of calls repeatedly within a single transaction or across multiple transactions, effectively bypassing the intended one-time execution guarantee. The root cause is a violation of the Check-Effect-Interaction pattern: the contract performs external calls before completing its internal state update. Exploitation requires the attacker to be able to include a malicious contract address in the change.calls array; once the malicious contract is called, its fallback or hook can invoke GovernanceProxy.executeChange again, causing the loop to restart or the function to be called again before _endChange runs. The impact includes unintended multiple executions of governance actions, which can lead to double spending, repeated token transfers, or manipulation of protocol parameters, potentially draining funds or corrupting protocol state. The issue manifests when a governance proposal containing a call to a contract with re-entrancy capabilities is executed; users may see a proposal reported as executed while the underlying state changes occur multiple times or not at all, leading to missing refunds, zero balances, or unexpected token movements. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the ordering of state updates and external calls. Because the re-entrancy occurs only when a specially crafted callee is used, it can be difficult to notice in normal operation where calls are to trusted contracts. The recommended mitigation is to move the internal state transition (_endChange) before any external calls, thereby adhering to the Check-Effect-Interaction pattern and preventing re-entrancy. More generally, any contract that processes a batch of external calls must update its internal bookkeeping before invoking untrusted code to avoid similar re-entrancy bugs.

title: M-8 GovernanceProxy DOS via updateDelay()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the GovernanceProxy contract that stems from the way the contract computes the execution delay for governance actions. The contract stores a per‑function delay in a mapping called delays and uses a helper _computeDelay to retrieve the current delay based on the function selector extracted from the calldata. When the admin calls updateDelay(targetFunction, newDelay), the helper recognises the updateDelay selector, extracts the selector of the function whose delay is being changed from the calldata, and then returns delays[selector]. This design creates a feedback loop: if the admin mistakenly sets a very large delay (for example a value that approaches the maximum uint64) for an important governance function, the delay for that function becomes huge. Because the contract enforces that any subsequent call to updateDelay for the same function must wait for the currently stored delay, the admin would have to wait for the previously set super‑large delay before being able to lower it again. In practice this means that the affected governance function becomes effectively unusable for an extremely long period, blocking proposals, parameter changes, or emergency actions that rely on that function. The impact is a functional lock‑out of the protocol’s governance mechanisms, which can prevent the community or the admin from reacting to market events, fixing bugs, or performing upgrades, thereby endangering user funds and the overall health of the system. The condition occurs only when an admin with the appropriate role invokes updateDelay with an excessively large value; it does not require any malicious external actor, but a simple mistake can render the protocol inert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the governance code where the special‑case handling of the updateDelay selector was examined and the self‑referential delay logic was identified as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the delay mapping appears to work correctly for normal values, and the special case is hidden behind a selector comparison that looks innocuous. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that governance proposals that previously executed within minutes now appear to be stuck, the UI shows “pending” or “queued” forever, and expected actions such as parameter updates or emergency pauses never happen, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The bug belongs to the class of “self‑referential configuration” or “delay‑parameter lock” vulnerabilities where a configuration change can unintentionally set a guard that prevents future changes. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a reasonable upper bound on any delay value, separate the delay used for updateDelay itself from the delay being set for other functions, or allow an emergency override that can bypass the stored delay for governance updates. By capping the maximum delay or adding a safeguard, the protocol ensures that a single mis‑configuration cannot permanently block governance operations.

title: M-9 GovernanceProxy pending change cannot expire
description:
One can imagine a situation where a pending change is created, locked by a delay, but over time becomes irrelevant and no one executes it. Or, for instance, over time it becomes evident that the requested change reverts upon attempted execution, and it's forgotten.
This could result in lingering transactions accumulating in pendingChanges, which might not only become irrelevant in the future but even detrimental (e.g., setting outdated thresholds for certain contracts). Any such change could be executed by any user in any order, leading to adverse effects.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance proxy’s handling of pending changes: once a change is submitted it is stored with a mandatory delay before it can be executed, but the contract does not enforce any expiration or cleanup of that pending entry. The root cause is the absence of a time‑based invalidation rule; the pendingChanges data structure can retain entries indefinitely. An attacker, or any arbitrary user, can later invoke the execution function after the delay has passed, even if the proposal has become obsolete, was never intended to be executed, or would now revert due to changed contract state. Exploitation proceeds by first creating a malicious or outdated proposal, allowing the required delay to elapse, and then calling the execution path at any later moment; because the contract never checks whether the proposal is still relevant, the call succeeds and can overwrite critical parameters such as thresholds, fee rates, or access controls. The impact is that protocol governance loses its intended safety window: outdated thresholds may be set, security parameters can be weakened, and funds may become exposed to unintended risk. This situation occurs whenever a pending change is left unattended—either because the proposer forgets to execute it, the proposal is later found to be invalid, or the governance UI does not surface stale entries. All participants who rely on the governance process—token holders, protocol users, and developers—are affected because the integrity of parameter updates is compromised. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of governance proposals and noticed that the pendingChanges mapping is never pruned nor bounded by a maximum age. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about stale entries and the front‑end may hide them, leading to a false sense of security that only fresh proposals exist. To remediate, the contract should record an expiration timestamp for each pending change and reject execution after that point, automatically remove expired entries, and optionally require re‑submission of proposals that have aged beyond a reasonable window. This aligns the implementation with the expected governance model where proposals either get executed promptly or become void, preserving the protocol’s accounting assumptions and preventing money or configuration from disappearing due to forgotten pending changes.

title: diamondCut() allows re-execution of old updates
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upgrade mechanism of a diamond proxy contract, specifically the diamondCut() function in the LibDiamond library. The function validates an upgrade request by checking that a signed version identifier exists in the acceptanceTimes mapping and that a required delay has elapsed. However, the implementation never records that a particular signed upgrade has already been applied, nor does it impose an expiration on the signature. As a result, once an upgrade is executed, the same signed payload remains valid indefinitely. If the contract owner later rolls back the change—replacing a facet or function with its previous implementation—the original signed upgrade can be submitted again because the acceptanceTimes entry is still non‑zero and the delay condition is satisfied. A malicious owner can therefore re‑execute the old version immediately after a rollback, re‑introducing any bugs, backdoors, or undesirable logic that were previously fixed. This replay of an old upgrade undermines the intended governance flow, allowing the contract to revert to a vulnerable state at will. The issue is triggered only when an upgrade is performed, subsequently rolled back, and the owner retains the ability to call diamondCut again; it does not require any external attacker beyond the privileged caller. Users of the protocol are affected because the contract’s business logic may change unexpectedly, leading to symptoms such as previously resolved errors resurfacing, transactions failing, or funds becoming exposed to known exploits. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the upgrade path and noticed that the acceptanceTimes mapping is never cleared and that there is no nonce or one‑time flag to prevent replay. The bug is subtle because the function appears to enforce a delay and signature verification, giving a false sense of security, while the missing idempotency check is easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the contract should either assign a limited validity period to each signed upgrade, store a record of executed upgrade hashes and reject duplicates, or introduce a nonce/sequence number that must be incremented for each new upgrade, thereby ensuring that each signed payload can be used only once. This class of flaw is commonly referred to as an upgrade replay vulnerability, where governance actions can be replayed after they have been superseded, breaking accounting assumptions and the expected immutable progression of contract code.

title: Not always safeApprove(..., 0)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistent handling of ERC20 allowance updates within the Connext protocol contracts. Certain functions, such as _reconcileProcessPortal in BaseConnextFacet and _swapAssetOut in AssetLogic, first call SafeERC20.safeApprove with a zero amount before increasing the allowance, while other functions like xcall in BridgeFacet, _backLoan in PortalFacet, _swapAsset in AssetLogic, and execute in Executor directly call SafeERC20.safeIncreaseAllowance without resetting the allowance to zero. This discrepancy matters for non‑standard tokens such as USDT, which enforce a rule that an allowance must be set to zero before it can be changed to a new non‑zero value. When a previous allowance remains (for example after a partial repayment where the backUnbacked call does not consume the entire allowance), a subsequent safeIncreaseAllowance call will revert because the token rejects the change unless the allowance is first cleared. The root cause is the reliance on the ERC20 standard’s allowance‑increase pattern without accounting for tokens that deviate from the standard. An attacker does not need to exploit this directly; the issue is a functional bug that can cause legitimate user transactions to fail. If a user initiates a bridge, swap, or loan repayment involving USDT, the contract may attempt to increase the allowance, encounter the zero‑first requirement, and revert the whole transaction. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the operation “failed” or “reverted”, the expected funds are not transferred, and balances appear unchanged or even temporarily locked in the contract. The impact is medium‑risk: funds are not stolen, but operations can be blocked, leading to a loss of liquidity, delayed repayments, and a degraded user experience. The condition occurs only when a non‑zero allowance already exists for the spender and the token enforces the zero‑first rule; it does not affect standard ERC20 tokens that allow direct allowance increases. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared allowance handling across different contract entry points and identified the missing zero‑approval step for USDT‑like tokens. It can be hard to notice because most testing uses standard tokens where the pattern works, masking the problem until a token with the stricter rule is used. The recommended remediation is to standardize allowance updates across all functions by always resetting the allowance to zero before setting a new value, either by calling safeApprove(...,0) followed by safeIncreaseAllowance, or by using a safeApprove with the exact desired amount. This aligns the code with the most restrictive token implementations and prevents unexpected reverts, ensuring that user expectations (e.g., “my bridge should succeed and my USDT should be transferred”) match reality.

title: _slippageTol does not adjust for decimal differences
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes the minimum amount of output tokens (minReceived) that a user must obtain when performing a swap. The code multiplies the input amount by the user‑provided slippage tolerance and divides by a fixed denominator, but it never adjusts the result for the difference in decimal precision between the input token (assetIn) and the output token (assetOut). Because ERC‑20 tokens can have anywhere from 6 to 18 decimals, the raw arithmetic can produce a value that is many orders of magnitude smaller or larger than the true expected amount. For example, swapping a 6‑decimal token for an 18‑decimal token makes minReceived ten‑to‑the‑12th smaller than it should be, while swapping the opposite direction makes it ten‑to‑the‑12th larger. This mis‑scaling means that a user who sets a reasonable slippage tolerance may either always trigger the slippage check (causing the cross‑chain transfer to get stuck) or receive far less than expected, opening the transaction to sandwich attacks where a malicious actor front‑runs the swap and extracts value. The issue is discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) and is subtle because the UI shows the slippage percentage correctly, yet the underlying calculation silently mis‑computes the threshold. Users experience symptoms such as receiving zero or a dramatically reduced amount of the output token, or seeing their transaction revert with a slippage error even though the market price is within the quoted tolerance. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the slippage tolerance should bound the price impact, not amplify it due to token precision mismatches. To remediate, the minReceived value must be scaled by the appropriate token precision multiplier (10^(decimals difference)) before being used in the swap logic, ensuring that the slippage check reflects the true value of the trade regardless of token decimal configuration.

title: Canonical assets should be keyed on the hash of domain and id
description:
A canonical asset is a tuple of a (domain, id) pair. TokenRegistry’s owner has the power to register new tokens in the system (See TokenRegistry.ensureLocalToken() and TokenRegistry.enrollCustom()). A canonical asset is registered using the hash of its domain and id (See TokenRegistry._setCanonicalToRepresentation()). Connext uses only the id of a canonical asset to uniquely identify. Here are a few references:
• swapStorages
• canonicalToAdopted
It is an issue if TokenRegistry registers two canonical assets with the same id. If this id fetches the incorrect canonical asset an unintended one might be transferred to the destination chain, of the transfers may revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Connext's TokenRegistry stores canonical assets. A canonical asset is defined by a pair (domain, id) but the registry creates a mapping that uses only the id as the key. Because the owner can register arbitrary assets, it is possible to register two distinct assets that share the same id but belong to different domains. When Connext later resolves a canonical asset it looks up the mapping by id alone, ignoring the domain, and therefore may retrieve the wrong asset. If a user initiates a cross‑chain transfer expecting asset A (domain X, id 123) but another asset B (domain Y, same id 123) has been registered, the system will fetch B and attempt to move it to the destination chain. The user will either receive an unexpected token, experience a failed transfer that reverts, or see their balance reduced without receiving the intended asset. This situation can occur whenever the registry owner registers a new token and the protocol relies on the id‑only lookup, which is the default behaviour of functions such as ensureLocalToken and enrollCustom. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the asset registration flow and identified that the canonicalToAdopted mapping and related storage structures do not incorporate the domain component. The bug is subtle because id collisions are not obvious in normal operation and the protocol does not emit explicit warnings when the wrong asset is selected. It violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each canonical asset is uniquely identifiable, breaking the guarantee that a user’s cross‑chain swap will deliver the exact token they sent. The recommended remediation is to change the mapping key to the keccak256 hash of the concatenated domain and id, ensuring that each (domain, id) pair maps to a unique entry and preventing accidental or malicious collisions. After the fix, the protocol will correctly resolve the intended canonical asset, and users will receive the expected token or a clear error if the asset is not registered.

title: Missing checks for Chainlink oracle
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the ConnextPriceOracle contract validates price data obtained from a Chainlink oracle. The getTokenPrice function iterates through a list of price sources and, for the Chainlink source, delegates to getPriceFromChainlink. This helper checks that the reported answer is non‑zero, that the round identifier is not older than the expected round, and that the update timestamp is not zero. However, it does not verify that the timestamp is recent nor that the reported price respects the oracle’s configured minAnswer and maxAnswer limits. Because of this omission, a stale round – one whose updateAt value is old but still non‑zero – can be accepted, and a price that sits exactly on the minimum or maximum bound can also be returned. An attacker who can influence the Chainlink aggregator (for example by feeding a delayed round or by pushing the price to the extreme bounds) can cause getTokenPrice to return a price that is either outdated or outside the intended safe range. The contract then uses this price in downstream calculations such as token swaps, bridging, or fee assessments. Consequently, a user who expects to receive a certain amount of tokens may receive less, may be over‑charged, or may see their balance reduced unexpectedly. The impact is therefore a potential loss of funds for end‑users and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the Chainlink oracle reports a valid round that is older than an acceptable freshness window or when the price reaches the oracle’s minAnswer or maxAnswer thresholds. All participants that rely on Connext’s price feed – including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the oracle validation logic and noticed the absence of a freshness check and bounds enforcement. It can be difficult to spot in testing because the returned price may still look plausible and the contract does not revert; the only symptom is a subtle deviation in transferred amounts. To remediate the issue, the contract should compare block.timestamp with updateAt and reject prices that are older than a defined tolerance, and it should also enforce that the answer lies strictly between the oracle’s minAnswer and maxAnswer values. Adding off‑chain monitoring for price excursions can further reduce risk. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an oracle freshness or bounds validation flaw, where insufficient checks allow stale or out‑of‑range data to influence financial logic.

title: Fee-On-Transfer tokens are not explicitly denied in swap()
description: The swap() function is used extensively within the Connext protocol, primarily when swapping between local and adopted assets. When a swap is performed, the function will check the actual amount transferred. However, this is not consistent with other swap functions which check that the amount transferred is equal to dx. As a result, overwriting dx with tokenFrom.balanceOf(address(this)).sub(beforeBalance) allows for fee-on-transfer tokens to work as intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swap() routine that the Connext protocol uses to exchange local and adopted assets. The function determines the amount of input tokens that actually arrived by reading the contract’s token balance after the transfer and subtracting the balance recorded before the transfer. This value is then written over the variable dx, which originally represents the amount the caller intended to swap. Because the code does not verify that the observed balance change equals the declared input amount, fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens – tokens that deduct a fee on each transfer – can be processed without being rejected. The root cause is the missing require(dx == tokenFrom.balanceOf(address(this)).sub(beforeBalance)) check that other swap implementations enforce. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a FoT token with a known transfer fee; the contract will accept the reduced amount as the full input, leading to a mismatch between the expected and actual token flow. Consequently, the protocol may credit the user with fewer output tokens than anticipated, or it may record an inaccurate accounting state that can be leveraged to drain liquidity or cause slippage attacks. The issue manifests whenever swap() is called with a token that charges a transfer fee, which is not explicitly prohibited by the contract. Users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting assumptions that “dx tokens were received in full” are violated, resulting in unexpected zero or reduced balances, missing refunds, or failed swaps from the user’s perspective. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared swap() with other swap functions and noticed the inconsistency. It is subtle because the function still completes successfully and the fee is silently taken by the token contract, making the discrepancy hard to spot without detailed balance tracing. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the transferred amount matches the declared dx before overwriting it, and to reject any token that does not satisfy this equality, thereby preventing fee‑on‑transfer tokens from being used in swaps and restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Same params.SlippageTol is used in two different swaps
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using a single slippage‑tolerance parameter for two distinct swap operations that occur during a Connext cross‑chain transfer. When a user initiates a transfer, the bridge first swaps the adopted token for the local (Nomad) token on the source chain and later swaps the local token back to the adopted token on the destination chain. Both swaps receive the same value from _args.params.slippageTol, even though the optimal tolerance for each direction is different. The root cause is a design decision in BridgeFacet where the same struct field is forwarded to AssetLogic.swapToLocalAssetIfNeeded and AssetLogic.swapFromLocalAssetIfNeeded without any per‑direction adjustment. An attacker, typically an MEV searcher, can exploit this by creating a price imbalance between the adopted and Nomad assets. If the price on one chain deviates such that the required tolerance for that leg exceeds the single user‑provided value, the swap will either execute at a worse rate or revert, causing the user’s funds to be partially lost, to arrive in a reduced amount, or to become stuck in a pending state. The impact is economic: users may receive less than the expected amount, see their balances unchanged after a transaction, or experience a transfer that never finalises, effectively “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. This condition manifests when the market price of the Nomad asset is not exactly 1:1 with the adopted asset, for example when 1 Nomad equals 1.01 adopted on both chains, requiring a tolerance of 1.01 for the first swap and 0.98 for the second. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) by analysing the bridge’s swap logic and noticing the reuse of the same slippage field. It is hard to notice because under normal market conditions the single tolerance often suffices, and the UI only shows a single slippage input, so users do not see the mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of economic‑parameter‑reuse vulnerabilities where a single user‑controlled value is incorrectly applied to multiple independent financial operations. To remediate, the protocol should expose two independent slippage‑tolerance inputs—one for the source‑to‑local swap and another for the local‑to‑destination swap—or compute a safe combined tolerance internally. This change would align the bridge’s behaviour with the expected accounting logic that each swap must respect its own price risk, preventing MEV exploitation and reducing the chance of stuck or under‑filled transfers.

title: xcall() may erroneously overwrite prior calls to bumpTransfer()
description: The bumpTransfer() function allows users to increment the relayer fee on any given transferId without checking if the unique transfer identifier exists. As a result, a subsequent call to xcall() will overwrite the s.relayerFees mapping, leading to lost funds.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic flaw in the way it manages relayer fees for cross‑chain transfers. The function that allows a user to increase the relayer fee, bumpTransfer(), does not verify that the supplied transfer identifier already exists in the system. Consequently, an attacker can invoke bumpTransfer() with an arbitrary, non‑existent transferId and write a value into the s.relayerFees mapping. Later, when the legitimate owner of that transfer calls xcall() with the same identifier, xcall() overwrites the previously stored fee entry instead of adding to it. Because xcall() replaces the mapping entry rather than incrementing it, the fee that was previously set – possibly a non‑zero amount intended for the relayer – is lost. This loss manifests to the user as a missing or zero relayer fee, meaning the relayer may not receive compensation and the transfer could be delayed or fail. The vulnerability is triggered only when bumpTransfer() is called before the transfer is created, which is allowed because the function lacks a check for the existence of the transferId. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the fee‑adjustment logic. It can be difficult to notice because the contract permits a zero fee in xcall(), so a simple non‑zero check on s.relayerFees would not catch the problem. The bug belongs to the class of state‑overwrite vulnerabilities where a mapping entry is unintentionally replaced, breaking accounting assumptions about cumulative fee calculations. To remediate, the contract should either verify that the transferId is already present before allowing a fee bump, mirroring the check used in PromiseRouter.bumpCallbackFee(), or modify xcall() so that it adds the new fee to the existing value instead of overwriting it. Either approach restores the invariant that relayer fees are cumulative and prevents accidental loss of funds.

title: _handleExecuteLiquidity doesn’t consistently check for receiveLocalOverrides
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity execution routine of the bridge contract, specifically the internal function that decides which asset to return to the user. The function first evaluates whether the caller has requested a local asset (receiveLocal) but it omits the secondary flag receiveLocalOverrides that can be set to force a local payout even when receiveLocal is false. Later in the same function the code does check both flags, creating an inconsistency. Because the early eligibility test does not consider receiveLocalOverrides, the execution path may incorrectly treat a transfer that has the override flag enabled as if no override were present. When the router’s balance of the local token is insufficient and the Aave pool is configured, the contract enters a branch that swaps the amount into the adopted asset and pays the user that asset. Consequently, a user who explicitly opted to receive the local token (by setting receiveLocalOverrides) can be sent the adopted token instead. This mismatch violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a user’s asset preference is always respected, leading to unexpected token types appearing in the user’s wallet, potential slippage, or loss of value if the adopted asset is less desirable. The issue manifests only when receiveLocal is false, receiveLocalOverrides is true, the router’s local balance is lower than the amount to swap, and the Aave pool address is non‑zero. It was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which noticed the divergent conditional checks. The bug is subtle because the later check does appear to enforce the override, but the earlier branch can already have committed to the wrong asset, making the problem easy to miss in standard unit tests that do not cover the specific combination of flags and low router balance. The appropriate remediation is to incorporate receiveLocalOverrides into the initial eligibility condition, ensuring that any transfer with the override flag set bypasses the Aave‑portal path or is handled consistently throughout the function. In broader terms, this is a logic‑flaw class of bug where optional override flags are not uniformly applied, leading to a breach of business logic that guarantees users receive the asset they requested. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful bridge transaction but the received token type differs from the one selected, or the balance of the expected token remains unchanged while an unexpected token appears, creating confusion and potential financial loss.

title: Router signatures can be replayed when executing messages on the destination domain
description: Connext bridge supports near-instant transfers by allowing users to pay a small fee to routers for providing them with liquidity. Gelato relayers are tasked with taking in bids from liquidity providers who sign a message consisting of the transferId and path length. The path length variable only guarantees that the message they signed will only be valid if _args.routers.length - 1 routers are also selected. However, it does not prevent Gelato relayers from re-using the same signature multiple times. As a result, routers may unintentionally provide more liquidity than expected.
bug_full: The issue is a replayable router signature flaw in the Connext bridge liquidity routing mechanism. When a Gelato relayer receives a bid from a liquidity provider (router), the provider signs a message that contains the transferId and the expected path length. The contract checks that the number of routers in the path matches the signed length, but it does not record whether the signed message has already been used for that transferId. Because there is no nonce, timestamp, or boolean flag tied to the transferId, a malicious or careless relayer can submit the same signed message multiple times on the destination domain. Each submission passes the signature verification and the path‑length check, causing the router to be credited for providing liquidity more than once for a single transfer. This can lead to routers unintentionally providing extra liquidity and receiving multiple fee payments, effectively draining protocol funds or inflating router earnings. The vulnerability is discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that examined the message‑validation logic and noticed the absence of a replay‑prevention mechanism. It is hard to notice because the signature itself is valid and the path‑length condition is satisfied, so the contract state appears consistent while the economic accounting is off. The impact is primarily on liquidity providers who may be over‑paid or under‑paid depending on how the relayer reuses signatures, and on the protocol’s overall financial integrity because fees may be paid out without corresponding service. The flaw manifests whenever Gelato relayers execute messages on the destination domain and rely solely on the path‑length check without tracking usage. To remediate, the contract should ensure that each router’s signed message can be used only once per transferId, for example by storing a boolean mapping of used signatures or by incorporating a unique nonce or timestamp into the signed payload. This change would align the implementation with the intended accounting model where each liquidity provision is paid exactly once, preventing replay attacks and preserving the expected economic behavior of the bridge.

title: Message can be delivered out of order
description: Messages can be delivered out of order on the spoke. Anyone can call the permissionless proveAndProcess to process the messages in any order they want. A malicious user can force the spoke to process messages in a way that is beneficial to them (e.g., front-run).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an out-of-order message processing flaw in the cross-chain messaging layer of Connext. The system receives messages on a spoke and a public function proveAndProcess can be called by any address to validate and execute those messages. Because the function does not enforce a strict sequential ordering, a caller can supply the messages in an arbitrary order. The root cause is the lack of a monotonic sequence check or a replay-protected ordering mechanism, allowing the internal message queue to be reordered at will. An attacker can therefore submit a crafted transaction that processes a later message before an earlier one, effectively front-running legitimate users. Exploitation proceeds by observing pending messages, then invoking proveAndProcess with a reordered set so that the attacker’s operation is applied first, potentially capturing funds, altering state, or causing a user-initiated transfer to fail. The impact is that users may see expected cross-chain transfers not executed, balances unexpectedly unchanged, or funds diverted to the attacker. The condition occurs whenever messages are pending on the spoke and the permissionless proveAndProcess function is invoked; there is no built-in safeguard that checks that the next expected sequence number matches the supplied message. All participants of the protocol – senders, receivers, and relayers – are affected because the ordering guarantee that underpins the accounting model is broken. The issue was discovered during a security review that examined the message handling logic and identified that the ordering invariant was not enforced. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a message is processed out of order, the problem can remain hidden until a user experiences a missing transfer or an unexpected state change. The bug belongs to the class of ordering or race-condition vulnerabilities where the lack of deterministic sequencing allows malicious reordering. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that messages are processed strictly according to their monotonic sequence identifier, reject any attempt to process a message with a lower or non-sequential identifier, or redesign the interface to make ordering immutable. Alternatively, the documentation should clearly state that messages may be processed out of order and that users must implement their own safeguards, such as waiting for finality or using signed commitments that include ordering information. From a user perspective the symptom is a transfer that never arrives, a balance that remains zero when a refund is expected, or a transaction that appears to have been front-run. The expectation that a cross-chain message will be applied in the order it was sent is violated, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential loss of funds.

title: Extra checks in _verifySender() of GnosisBase
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the hub connector's internal verification function only checks that msg.sender equals the AMB address and that the messageSender returned by the AMB matches the expected mirror connector, but it does not verify that the source chain identifier reported by the AMB matches the predefined MIRROR_DOMAIN. Because the bridge may later support multiple source chains, an attacker who can deploy a contract at the same address as the AMB on a different chain can cause the hub connector to accept a forged root, making it believe the message originated from the legitimate mirror domain. This enables the attacker to craft a payload root and associated Merkle proofs that are accepted by the L1 hub connector, resulting in unauthorized asset transfers or arbitrary function calls on L1. The impact is that funds can be moved out of user accounts without consent, balances may appear to drop to zero, and the accounting guarantees of the bridge are broken. The condition for exploitation is that the bridge is expanded to handle more than one source chain and that the attacker has control over a contract at the mirrorConnector address on a chain that is not the MIRROR_DOMAIN. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that compared the implementation against the bridge documentation, which explicitly mentions checking messageSourceChainId. The issue is subtle because the existing checks appear to validate the sender, so a reviewer may overlook the missing domain verification. The proper mitigation is to extend _verifySender to also compare the AMB's messageSourceChainId with the expected MIRROR_DOMAIN, typically by adding an extra parameter and a require statement. This class of bug falls under insufficient authentication across domain boundaries, allowing cross‑chain replay or spoofing attacks.

title: Absence of Minimum delayBlocks
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a lower bound check on the configurable fraud‑protection delay parameter. The contract stores a value representing the number of blocks that must elapse before a disputed operation can be finalized, and the owner can update this value through a public function that only checks that the new value differs from the current one. Because there is no requirement that the new delay be greater than or equal to a minimum safe threshold, the owner (or an attacker who gains ownership) can set the delay to zero or an arbitrarily small number. This collapses the intended time‑window that protects users from front‑running or fraudulent state changes. The flaw originates from missing validation logic in the setter routine, which assumes that any non‑identical value is acceptable. An exploit is straightforward: the malicious party calls the setter with a zero argument, the contract records the new delay, and subsequent operations that rely on the delay no longer wait for any block confirmations. As a result, a user who expects a delayed settlement, such as a refund or a cross‑chain transfer, may see the transaction execute immediately, allowing the attacker to race the user’s request and capture the funds. The impact is a breach of the economic guarantees of the protocol: funds can be stolen, refunds can be denied, and the overall trust model is undermined. The condition occurs whenever the owner updates the delay parameter, which can happen at any time because the function lacks a minimum‑delay guard. All participants who rely on the delay—traders, liquidity providers, and any user awaiting a settlement—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the contract’s governance functions and identified that the setter does not enforce a sensible lower bound. It can be hard to notice because the function compiles and runs without error, and the contract may appear to work correctly when the delay is set to a reasonable value; only when the delay is deliberately reduced does the protection disappear. To remediate, the contract should introduce a constant or configurable `minDelay` and add a requirement that any new delay be greater than or equal to this minimum. This ensures that the fraud‑protection window cannot be eliminated, preserving the intended security guarantees. The bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or unchecked parameter constraints, which can lead to logic bypasses and economic loss. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior—receiving a delayed refund or seeing a settlement after a waiting period—does not occur; instead the operation completes instantly, often resulting in a zero balance or missing funds, contrary to the user’s expectation of a protected transaction.

title: Add extra 0 checks in verifyAggregateRoot() and proveMessageRoot()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of zero values in the functionsthat confirm aggregate and message Merkle roots. Both verifyAggregateRoot and proveMessageRoot accept a bytes32 root parameter and only check whether the root has already been marked as proven. Because there is no explicit require that the supplied root is non‑zero, a caller can pass the special value 0x0. In the current logic a zero root is treated as a normal identifier; if it has not been recorded as proven the function will proceed with the remaining verification steps, which may succeed trivially or be bypassed, and then mark the zero root as proven. This allows an attacker to submit a fabricated proof that references a zero root, effectively bypassing the intended cryptographic guarantee that the root corresponds to a valid state snapshot. The impact is that the protocol can accept invalid state transitions, potentially causing funds to be released, locked, or accounted for incorrectly. The issue manifests whenever a cross‑chain message or aggregate state is being proven; under the condition that the caller supplies a zero root, the contract will skip proper validation and may mark the proof as valid. Users of the bridge, including liquidity providers and end‑users performing cross‑chain transfers, are affected because the system’s accounting assumptions are violated and balances may be altered without a legitimate state change. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that noted the absence of a zero‑check in the verification functions. It can be hard to notice because the functions otherwise appear to perform extensive checks, and a zero value may not raise an obvious error in testing unless edge‑case inputs are tried. The class of bug is an input‑validation omission, specifically a missing guard against a sentinel value that should be rejected. To remediate, the contract should explicitly require that the supplied aggregateRoot and messageRoot are not equal to bytes32(0) before any other logic, thereby preventing the zero‑root edge case from being accepted. This change restores the intended invariant that only genuine, non‑zero Merkle roots can be proven, preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity.

title: diamondCut() allows re-execution of old updates
description:
Once diamondCut() is executed, ds.acceptanceTimes[keccak256(abi.encode(_diamondCut, _init, _calldata))] is not reset to zero. This means the contract owner can rerun the old updates again without any delay by executing diamondCut() function.
Assume the following:
diamondCut() function is executed to update the facet selector with version_2 A bug is found in version_2 and it is rolled back Owner can still execute diamondCut() function which will again update the facet selector to version 2 since ds.acceptanceTimes[keccak256(abi.encode(_diamondCut, _init, _calldata))] is still valid
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the diamondCut upgrade function of a Diamond‑Standard proxy contract. The function records a timestamp in a mapping called ds.acceptanceTimes keyed by the hash of the upgrade parameters (_diamondCut, _init, _calldata) to enforce a timelock before the upgrade can be executed. After the first successful call, the stored timestamp is never cleared. Consequently, any subsequent call that supplies exactly the same parameters will find a non‑zero timestamp that is already less than or equal to the current block time, causing the timelock check (require(time != 0 && time <= block.timestamp)) to pass instantly. This allows the contract owner (or any entity with the diamondCut permission) to re‑execute the same facet update without waiting for the intended delay, effectively bypassing the upgrade safety mechanism. The issue can be exploited by rolling back a previously patched version that contained a bug, or by repeatedly invoking a malicious upgrade that was thought to be time‑locked, thereby re‑introducing vulnerabilities or unexpected behavior after a fix has been applied. The impact is that the protocol’s upgrade governance assumptions are broken: users expect that once an upgrade is applied, a delay must elapse before the same upgrade can be reapplied, but the contract permits immediate re‑execution, potentially leading to funds being at risk, contract state being altered unexpectedly, or the protocol appearing to be unstable. The condition occurs whenever the same upgrade payload is submitted more than once after the initial execution; it does not depend on external state beyond the stored timestamp. The affected party is primarily the contract owner or any privileged role that can call diamondCut, but the downstream effect harms all protocol participants because the upgrade may re‑introduce a vulnerable version. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the upgrade logic and noticed that ds.acceptanceTimes was never reset after use. It is subtle because the mapping entry is not visible in normal operation and tests often cover only a single execution path, making the repeated‑call scenario easy to miss. To remediate, the implementation should clear or delete the acceptanceTimes entry for the given hash after the upgrade is performed, ensuring that a subsequent identical call will require a fresh timelock entry or will be rejected. This aligns the contract with the intended upgrade delay semantics and prevents the owner from bypassing the safety window.

title: User may not be able to override slippage on destination
description:
If BridgeFacet.execute() is executed before BridgeFacet.forceUpdateSlippage(), user won't be able to update slippage on the destination chain. In this case, the slippage specified on the source chain is used. Due to different conditions on these chains, a user may want to specify different slippage values.
This can result in user loss, as a slippage higher than necessary will result the swap trade being sandwiched.
bug_full: The issue is a slippage‑override flaw in the cross‑chain bridge implementation. When a user initiates a transfer through BridgeFacet.execute, the contract reads the slippage value that was supplied on the source chain and applies it to the destination swap. The intended mechanism to change the destination slippage – calling BridgeFacet.forceUpdateSlippage before execute – is ineffective if the calls are made in the wrong order. Consequently, the destination slippage parameter supplied by the user is ignored and the source‑chain slippage is used instead. This happens because the contract stores a single slippage field that is populated during the source‑side call and is not refreshed when forceUpdateSlippage is invoked after execute, leading to a logic error where the destination value never overwrites the stored value. An attacker or a market participant can exploit this by submitting a transaction that executes before the user’s forceUpdateSlippage, causing the bridge to use a higher slippage than the user expected. The higher slippage widens the price range for the destination swap, making it vulnerable to sandwich attacks or other price‑impact manipulations. Users may notice that the trade they expected to execute at a tight price instead executes at a much worse rate, sometimes receiving little or no output tokens, or seeing their balance reduced unexpectedly after the bridge call. The problem manifests only when the user relies on being able to set a distinct destination slippage – a common scenario when the source and destination chains have different liquidity conditions. It affects any participant who uses the bridge, potentially leading to financial loss and undermining trust in the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the ordering of state‑changing functions and identified that the slippage field is not correctly re‑initialized for the destination side. The bug is subtle because the user interface typically shows a field for destination slippage, giving the impression that the value will be respected, yet the contract silently discards it. To remediate, the bridge should accept two independent slippage arguments – one for the source and one for the destination – and encode both values in the TransferInfo structure passed to the internal xcall function. The xcall signature should be extended to include separate _sourceSlippage and _destinationSlippage parameters, and the contract logic must ensure that the destination slippage is applied when performing the swap on the target chain. This change restores the intended business logic that each chain can have its own risk tolerance for price movement, preventing unnecessary exposure to sandwich attacks and aligning contract behavior with user expectations.

title: Do not rely on token balance to determine when cap is reached
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Connext Diamond determines whether the per‑token custody cap has been reached. The contract computes the custodied amount by reading the ERC‑20 token balance of the contract (balanceOf) and adding the amount that is about to be deposited. If this sum exceeds a stored cap, the transaction is reverted with a cap‑reached error. Because the balance is taken directly from the token contract, any external transfer of tokens to the Connext address – even one that bypasses the protocol’s internal accounting functions – artificially inflates the reported custodied amount. An attacker can therefore send a large amount of tokens directly to the contract, causing the balance‑based check to think the cap is already full. Subsequent legitimate users who try to add liquidity will see their transactions revert with the cap‑reached error, receiving no tokens and often receiving no clear indication why their operation failed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on liquidity provision and potentially a loss of confidence in the protocol, as users cannot add assets even though the internal accounting may still have capacity. This condition occurs whenever the cap for a token is greater than zero and the contract’s balance, plus the incoming amount, exceeds that cap – a situation that can be triggered simply by an out‑of‑band token transfer. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the cap‑enforcement logic and noticed that the contract relied on an external source of truth (the token balance) rather than an internal ledger. It is hard to notice because token balances normally change only through the protocol’s own functions, so an unexpected increase may be attributed to normal activity. The bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches where on‑chain balances are used as authoritative state for business rules, allowing external token injection to corrupt logic. To remediate, the protocol should maintain its own custodied‑amount variable that is updated exclusively by the AssetLogic.handleIncomingAsset and handleOutgoingAsset functions, ensuring that every token movement is recorded in the internal ledger and that the cap check uses this internal value instead of the raw ERC‑20 balance. By forcing all token transfers to go through controlled pathways, the contract eliminates the possibility of an attacker inflating the balance and falsely triggering the cap limit.

title: Router recipient can be configured more than once
description: The comments from the setRouterRecipient function mentioned that the router should only be able to set the recipient once. Otherwise, no problem is solved. However, based on the current implementation, it is possible for the router to set its recipient more than once.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a router contract that allows its designated recipient address to be changed multiple times through the setRouterRecipient function. The source code includes a comment stating that the recipient should be set only once, but the implementation lacks any guard that prevents a second call with a different address. The root cause is the absence of a check for an existing non‑zero recipient entry in the routerPermissionInfo mapping before overwriting it. An attacker who controls the router owner role can invoke setRouterRecipient repeatedly, each time supplying a new address. By doing so the attacker can redirect future payouts, refunds or any funds that the router forwards to the newly chosen recipient. This exploitation is possible whenever the router owner calls the function after the initial recipient has already been recorded; there is no time‑based restriction or additional access control beyond the existing onlyRouterOwner modifier. Users of the protocol who expect their funds to be sent to the originally configured recipient may instead see the balance transferred to an unexpected address, resulting in missing refunds, zero balances on the intended recipient, or outright loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract comments with the actual code logic. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly on the first call, and the comment alone may give a false sense of safety; without explicit tests for a second call the bug remains hidden. To remediate the problem the function should first read the current recipient from storage, revert if it is already non‑zero, and also revert if the new address equals the existing one. Emitting an event after a successful set helps with transparency. This class of bug is an improper state‑transition guard, where a mutable configuration that should be immutable is left mutable, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a recipient address is fixed after deployment. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful recipient update, but later the expected payout never arrives, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The fix restores the intended invariant that the recipient can be set only once, preventing malicious redirection of funds.

title: The set of tokens in an internal swap pool cannot be updated
description:
Once a swap is initialized by the owner or an admin (indexed by the key parameter) the _pooledTokens or the set of tokens used in this stable swap pool cannot be updated.
Now the s.swapStorages[_key] pools are used in other facets for assets that have the hash of their canonical token id and canonical domain equal to _key, for example when we need to swap between a local and adopted asset or when a user provides liquidity or interact with other external endpoints of StableSwapFacet.
If the submitted set of tokens to this pool _pooledTokens beside the local and adopted token corresponding to _key include some other bad/malicious tokens, users' funds can be at risk in the pool in question. If this happens, we need to pause the protocol, push an update, and initializeSwap again.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an immutable token‑set configuration in a stable‑swap pool. After the pool is created by the owner or an admin through the initializeSwap function, the list of pooled tokens (_pooledTokens) cannot be changed. This design choice means that the contract trusts the initial token list forever and provides no mechanism to remove or replace a token later. The root cause is the absence of any administrative or governance function that can update the token whitelist, combined with the fact that the same storage slot (s.swapStorages[_key]) is referenced by other facets for operations such as local‑to‑adopted asset swaps, liquidity provision, and external endpoint interactions. An attacker who can influence the initialization—by compromising an admin key, submitting a malicious transaction, or exploiting a governance flaw—could include a malicious ERC‑20 token in the _pooledTokens array. Once the pool is live, users will see the expected local and adopted tokens in the UI, but the hidden malicious token will also be part of the pool’s accounting. When users add liquidity or perform swaps, the contract may accept the malicious token or route funds through it, allowing the attacker to drain or lock the assets. The impact is that user funds can disappear or become unrecoverable, the protocol may need to be paused, and a full re‑initialization of the swap pool is required to restore safety. This condition occurs whenever a swap pool is initialized for a given domain key and later used for any operation that references the pooled token set. All participants—liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the invariant that only legitimate tokens are in the pool is broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle of swap pools and noted that the token list is never mutable. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically displays only the primary local and adopted tokens, masking the presence of any extra token in the internal storage. The bug belongs to the class of immutable configuration or whitelist‑bypass vulnerabilities, where a critical list is set once and never validated again. From a user’s perspective, they expect to swap between two known assets and to see their deposited balance reflected correctly; instead they may observe that their balance becomes zero after a swap or that a “refund” never arrives, indicating that funds have been siphoned through the hidden token. To remediate, the contract should include a controlled update mechanism for the token list, such as a governance‑approved function that can add, remove, or replace tokens, and it should enforce strict validation of token addresses against a trusted registry at every operation. Additionally, documentation should clearly describe how the token list is chosen during initialization, and a whitelist of approved tokens should be enforced to prevent accidental or malicious inclusion of harmful assets.

title: An incorrect decimal supplied to initializeSwap for a token cannot be corrected
description: Once a swap is initialized by the owner or an admin (indexed by the key parameter) the decimal precisions per tokens, and therefore tokenPrecisionMultipliers cannot be changed. If the supplied decimals also include a wrong value, it would cause incorrect calculation when a swap is being made and currently there is no update mechanism for tokenPrecisionMultipliers nor a mechanism for removing the swapStorages[_key].
bug_full: The vulnerability is an immutable configuration error in the swap initialization routine. When the contract owner or an authorized admin calls the function that creates a new internal swap pool, the decimal precision for each token is supplied and stored in a multiplier used for all subsequent amount calculations. Because the contract does not provide any function to modify the stored tokenPrecisionMultipliers and also lacks a mechanism to delete or replace the swap storage entry, an incorrect decimal value entered at deployment becomes permanent. This root cause stems from the design choice to treat the decimal parameter as immutable without a safeguard or correction path. An attacker or even a well‑meaning admin who mistakenly provides, for example, 6 decimals for a token that actually uses 18 will cause every swap to apply a multiplier that is off by a factor of 10^12. As a result, users may receive far fewer tokens than expected, see their balances reduced to near zero, or experience refunds that are missing. The impact is a systematic mis‑calculation of swap amounts that can lead to loss of funds, broken accounting, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a swap pool is created with an incorrect decimal precision; it persists for the lifetime of that pool because there is no update or removal function. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the initialization logic and noted the absence of any administrative correction path. The bug is hard to notice because the UI may display the intended token amounts while the underlying arithmetic silently applies the wrong multiplier, making the discrepancy appear only after several swaps or when users compare expected versus actual received amounts. To remediate, the contract should include a restricted, role‑based endpoint that allows the owner or a designated governance role to update the tokenPrecisionMultipliers for an existing pool, and optionally a function to delete or re‑initialize a swap storage entry so that a mistaken configuration can be corrected without redeploying the whole contract. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an immutable configuration or parameter‑initialization flaw that leads to arithmetic errors and violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Presence of delegate not enforced
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step for the delegate address when a cross‑chain transfer is initiated via the internal _xcall function. In the contract design, a delegate is intended to act as a privileged actor that can adjust slippage limits and re‑execute a transfer that becomes stuck on the destination chain. However, the code that creates the transfer does not enforce that a non‑zero delegate address is supplied, nor does it document the consequences of omitting it. Because the delegate field may be left empty, the subsequent functions that rely on the delegate – such as forceUpdateSlippage, which is guarded by onlyDelegate, and execute, which checks that the caller is either an approved relayer or the delegate – can behave incorrectly. If the delegate is the zero address, the onlyDelegate modifier will reject any legitimate caller, and the execute function will fall back to requiring an approved relayer. In deployments where no relayer is approved or the relayer set is compromised, the transfer may become permanently stuck, effectively locking the user's funds on the destination chain. This situation can be triggered whenever a user or an automated system calls _xcall without providing a delegate, which may happen unintentionally due to UI defaults or programmatic oversight. The impact is that tokens may disappear from the user's perspective: the user expects the cross‑chain transfer to complete and the destination balance to increase, but instead the balance remains unchanged and the funds are inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of delegated recovery mechanisms and noticed that the delegate presence check was absent in the entry point. It is subtle because the contract still compiles and functions for normal cases, and the missing check does not produce an immediate error; the problem only manifests when a transfer needs recovery. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a valid delegate address is supplied in _xcall, either by adding a require statement that the delegate is non‑zero or by documenting that a missing delegate disables recovery and must be avoided. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that every cross‑chain transfer must have an accountable party capable of adjusting parameters and finalising the transfer, thereby preventing funds from becoming irretrievable.

title: Relayer could lose funds
description:
The xReceive function on the receiver side can contain unreliable code which Relayer is unaware of. In the future, more relayers will participate in completing the transaction.
Consider the following scenario:
1. Say that Relayer A executes the xReceive function on receiver side.
2. In the xReceive function, a call to withdraw function in a foreign contract is made where Relayer A is holding some balance.
3. If this foreign contract is checking tx.origin (say deposit/withdrawal were done via third party), then Relayer A's funds will be withdrawn without his permission (since tx.origin will be the Relayer).
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the xReceive callback executed by a relayer may contain arbitrary external calls to contracts that perform authentication based on tx.origin. Because the relayer initiates the transaction, tx.origin resolves to the relayer’s address. If a malicious or poorly designed receiver contract invokes a withdraw function on a foreign contract that uses tx.origin to authorize withdrawals, the foreign contract will treat the relayer as the authorized party and transfer the relayer’s balance to an attacker‑controlled address. This can happen whenever a relayer processes a cross‑chain message and the receiver’s xReceive implementation includes such a call. The impact is a potential loss of the relayer’s funds, which may be significant if the relayer holds a large balance for fee collection or collateral. The issue was discovered during a security review of the Connext/Nxtp bridge code, where the auditor noted that the xReceive function is not sandboxed and that the protocol does not enforce the use of a dedicated, empty wallet for relayers. The problem is subtle because the transaction appears to succeed from the protocol’s perspective; the relayer receives no error, yet its balance is drained silently. The bug belongs to the class of “tx.origin authentication misuse” and “unsafe external call in callback” vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes that the caller cannot be tricked into authorising transfers. From a user’s point of view, a relayer may notice that after processing a message its wallet balance drops to zero or that expected fee earnings are missing, without any on‑chain revert. The protocol’s accounting assumes that relayers retain their funds after completing a transaction, which this flaw violates. The recommended mitigation is to require relayers to use a fresh, empty wallet address that never holds assets, or to redesign xReceive so that it does not perform external calls that rely on tx.origin, and to replace tx.origin checks with explicit msg.sender based authorisation. By isolating the relayer’s address from any privileged operations, the risk of unauthorised withdrawals is eliminated.

title: _domainSeparatorV4() not updated after name/symbol change
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the public DOMAIN_SEPARATOR view and the internal cached domain separator used by the EIP‑712 implementation. The BridgeToken contract permits the owner to change the token's name and symbol through a setDetails function, but it does not clear or recompute the cached _CACHED_DOMAIN_SEPARATOR that is stored by the EIP712 base contract. The public DOMAIN_SEPARATOR() function recomputes the separator on‑the‑fly using the current token name, while the internal _domainSeparatorV4() function first checks whether the cached values are still valid (same contract address and chain id) and, if so, returns the stale _CACHED_DOMAIN_SEPARATOR. Because the cache is not invalidated when the name changes, any call to permit() – which internally calls _hashTypedDataV4() and therefore _domainSeparatorV4() – continues to use the old domain separator. This discrepancy allows a signature that was valid under the previous name to remain valid after the name has been altered, effectively enabling a replay of a permit approval. An attacker who obtained a signed permit before the name change can submit the same signature after the change and still have the contract accept it, granting them allowance to transfer tokens without the owner's consent. From the user’s perspective the token UI shows the new name, yet approvals that were thought to be tied to the old name still work, leading to unexpected allowance changes, possible loss of funds, or failed expectations such as “my new token name should invalidate old permits”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation of DOMAIN_SEPARATOR() with the internal caching logic of EIP712 and noticed that the cache is never refreshed on metadata updates. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit any warning and the UI does not display domain separator values, so the bug manifests only when a permit is used after a name change. The proper remediation is to make the cached domain separator consistent with the public view: either update the cache whenever the name or symbol changes, or stop using a cached value altogether and compute the separator each time, ensuring that both DOMAIN_SEPARATOR() and _domainSeparatorV4() return the same, up‑to‑date value. This aligns the contract with the EIP‑712 specification and prevents replay of stale permit signatures, preserving the intended security guarantees of gas‑less approvals.

title: TypedMemView.sameType does not use the correct right shift value to compare two bytes29s
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a helper routine that checks whether two packed values of type bytes29 share the same type identifier. The routine performs an XOR of the two inputs and then right‑shifts the result by a fixed number of bytes before comparing the outcome with zero. Because a bytes29 value is stored in a 256‑bit slot with right‑hand zero padding, the five‑byte type flag occupies the most significant bits of the word, while the lower three bytes are always zero. The implementation mistakenly shifts only 24 bytes (2 × 12) instead of the required 27 bytes (2 × 12 + 3) to reach the type flag. Consequently the comparison also includes three padding bytes that are always zero, meaning the function may report that two values have the same type even when their actual type flags differ, or it may reject values that actually share the same flag. This logical error can be exploited whenever the routine is used as a gatekeeper for type‑based access control, message routing, or validation of user‑supplied data. An attacker could craft a bytes29 payload whose type flag differs from the expected one but whose lower padded bits happen to make the shifted XOR equal to zero, thereby bypassing the check and causing the contract to treat the payload as a legitimate type. The impact ranges from unauthorized function execution to misrouting of funds or data, potentially leading to loss of assets or protocol state corruption. The bug manifests only when the sameType function is invoked; in the current codebase it is not called, which makes the issue easy to overlook during testing. However, future extensions that reuse the library may inadvertently rely on this routine, exposing the protocol to the described risk. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the bit‑layout of the TypedMemView library and identified an inconsistency between the documented packing scheme and the shift constant used in the code. The difficulty in spotting the flaw stems from the fact that the function returns a boolean and does not emit events, so a failed type check may not be obvious without deep inspection of the bitwise logic. To remediate the issue the shift constant must be adjusted to account for the three‑byte right padding, for example by shifting 27 bytes (8 × 27 bits) or by masking the type flag directly before comparison. Adding a comment that references the original library source and explains the padding rationale will help prevent regressions. In user‑facing terms, a transaction that should be rejected because of a mismatched type may be accepted, leading to unexpected behavior such as funds being transferred to the wrong channel or a message being processed under an incorrect protocol version. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect bit‑masking due to padding assumptions” and violates the protocol’s fundamental accounting assumption that type identifiers uniquely determine how data should be handled.

title: Incorrect formula for the scaled amplification coefficient in NatSpec comments
description:
In the context above, the scaled amplification coefficient a is described by the formula An(n - 1) where A is the actual amplification coefficient in the stable swap invariant equation for n tokens.
* @param a the amplification coefficient * n * (n - 1) ...
The actual adjusted/scaled amplification coefficient would need to be Ann-1 and not An(n - 1), otherwise, most of the calculations done when swapping between 2 tokens in a pool with more than 2 tokens would be wrong. For the special case of n = 2, those values are actually equal 22-1 = 2 = 2 * 1. So for swaps or pools that involve only 2 tokens, the issue in the comment is not so critical. But if the number of tokens are more than 2, then we need to make sure we calculate and feed the right parameter to AppStorage.swapStorages.{initial, future}A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a documentation‑level error in the NatSpec comment that describes how the amplification coefficient should be scaled for multi‑token stable‑swap pools. The comment states that the scaled coefficient is calculated as A*n*(n-1) (written as An(n‑1)), but the mathematically correct scaling is A multiplied by n to the power of (n‑1), i.e., A*n^(n‑1). This discrepancy does not affect two‑token pools because A*2*(2‑1) equals A*2^(2‑1), but for any pool with more than two tokens the formula in the comment yields a value that is too small. Developers who rely on the NatSpec description to compute the parameter passed to the swap storage (initialA or futureA) will feed an incorrectly scaled amplification coefficient, causing the invariant calculations used during swaps to be wrong. As a result, token exchange rates can be mis‑priced, leading to users receiving less than expected, potential arbitrage opportunities for attackers, and overall erosion of the pool’s accounting integrity. The issue manifests only when the contract is initialized or when a swap function is called with a manually supplied scaled coefficient for pools containing three or more tokens.
