It was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the comment against the mathematical definition of the stable‑swap invariant. Because NatSpec comments are not compiled and the error is silent for the common two‑token case, it can easily go unnoticed in testing. To remediate, the comment must be corrected to reflect the exponentiation (A * n ** (n‑1)) and any code paths that accept an amplification coefficient as input must ensure the value is pre‑scaled using the n^(n‑1) factor before being stored in the swap storage structures. This aligns the implementation with the intended economic model and prevents miscalculations that could cause funds to disappear or refunds to be calculated incorrectly.

title: RootManager.propagate does not operate in a fail-safe manner
description:
A bridge failure on one of the supported chains will cause the entire messaging network to break down.
When the RootManager.propagate function is called, it will loop through the hub connector of all six chains (Arbitrum, Gnosis, Multichain, Optimism, Polygon, ZKSync) and attempt to send over the latest aggregated root by making a function call to the respective chain's AMB contract. There is a tight dependency between the chain's AMB and hub connector.
The problem is that if one of the function calls to the chain's AMB contract reverts (e.g. one of the bridges is paused), the entire RootManager.propagate function will revert, and the messaging network will stop working until someone figure out the problem and manually removes the problematic hub connector.
As Connext grows, the number of chains supported will increase, and the risk of this issue occurring will also increase.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a lack of fail‑safe error handling in the RootManager.propagate function of the messaging bridge. The function iterates over the hub connectors for all supported chains and forwards the latest aggregated root to each chain’s AMB contract. Because each external call is made without a try‑catch or low‑level call guard, a single revert – for example when a bridge on one chain is paused or otherwise fails – causes the entire propagate transaction to revert. This aborts the propagation of the root to every other chain, effectively halting the whole cross‑chain messaging network until an operator manually removes the problematic connector. The root cause is an implicit assumption that third‑party bridge contracts will always succeed, leading to a single point of failure in a multi‑chain loop. An attacker or a misbehaving bridge can trigger the revert deliberately, creating a denial‑of‑service condition where users see their cross‑chain messages remain pending, UI balances do not update, and expected refunds or state synchronisations never occur. The impact is an availability outage: the protocol cannot relay messages, users cannot complete cross‑chain operations, and funds may become temporarily inaccessible though not directly stolen. The issue manifests only when propagate is invoked while at least one AMB contract reverts, making it hard to notice during normal operation when all bridges are healthy. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of the propagate routine. Because the failure is silent – the function simply reverts without emitting a specific error – operators may not immediately understand why the network stopped. The bug belongs to the class of improper error handling in multi‑contract orchestration, where a loop over external calls does not isolate failures. To remediate, the propagate logic should catch individual call failures (using try‑catch or low‑level address.call) and continue processing the remaining connectors, optionally logging the failed chain and allowing later retry. This change removes the single point of failure and restores the protocol’s resilience as the number of supported chains grows.

title: Arborist once whitelisted cannot be removed
description: Arborist has the power to write over the Merkle root. In case Arborist starts misbehaving (compromised or security issue) then there is no way to remove this Arborist from the whitelist.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an irreversible whitelisting mechanism for the Arborist role. The contract allows the owner to add an address to the Arborist whitelist through a function that checks for a zero address and for the address already being listed, then stores a boolean status. However, the logic prevents changing the stored status from true back to false because the function reverts if the address is already marked as an Arborist. As a result, once an address is granted Arborist privileges it cannot be removed, even if the address becomes compromised or behaves maliciously. The Arborist role has the authority to overwrite the Merkle root that underpins claim verification, so a malicious Arborist can replace the root with a value that validates fraudulent proofs. This can be exploited by an attacker who either gains the Arborist role initially or is added by a careless owner; after the role is granted, the attacker can submit a transaction that writes a crafted Merkle root, causing subsequent claim checks to succeed for arbitrary recipients. The impact includes potential unauthorized withdrawals, loss of user funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees because the Merkle tree no longer reflects the true state of deposits. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls the whitelist function to add an Arborist; any later attempt to revoke the privilege silently fails due to the revert condition, leaving the contract in a permanently vulnerable state. All participants that rely on the integrity of the Merkle root – users submitting claims, the protocol’s settlement logic, and any external auditors – are affected because the security assumption that only trusted Arborists can modify the root is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual security review where the auditor noted that the setArborist function lacks a path for removal and that the existingArborist check blocks status toggling. It can be hard to notice because the UI may only expose an “add Arborist” button and not indicate that removal is impossible, leading developers to assume normal revocation semantics. To remediate, the whitelist function should be rewritten to allow the owner to set the status flag to either true or false, removing the alreadyArborist revert and adding explicit checks that prevent accidental overwriting while permitting revocation. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “immutable privilege escalation” or “non‑revocable access control” flaws, where a role with critical permissions cannot be rescinded, violating the principle of least privilege and opening a backdoor for fund theft.

title: WatcherManager is not set correctly
description:
The setWatcherManager function missed to actually update the watcherManager, instead it is just emitting an event mentioning that Watcher Manager is updated when it is not.
This could become a problem once new modules are added/revised in WatcherManager contract and WatcherClient wants to use this upgraded WatcherManager. WatcherClient will be forced to use the outdated WatcherManager contract code.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical state‑update flaw in the administrative function that is supposed to replace the address of the WatcherManager contract. The setWatcherManager function emits a WatcherManagerChanged event but never assigns the new address to the internal watcherManager storage variable. Because the assignment is missing, the contract continues to reference the original WatcherManager instance even though the logs suggest a successful upgrade. This occurs whenever the contract owner calls setWatcherManager expecting to point the system to a newer or patched WatcherManager implementation. The root cause is an omitted state‑write statement, likely introduced by a copy‑paste or oversight during development. Exploitation does not require external interaction; the impact is functional rather than immediate loss of ether. Any module that relies on the watcherManager, such as WatcherClient, will interact with outdated logic, which may contain known bugs, missing features, or security weaknesses. Users may notice that actions performed by the watcher (for example, cross‑chain message verification or timeout handling) behave incorrectly or do not reflect recent upgrades, leading to failed refunds, missed events, or stalled transfers. The issue is hard to detect because the emitted event gives the impression that the upgrade succeeded, and there is no on‑chain check confirming the storage change. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the function body against its intended behavior. To remediate, the function must include a proper assignment of the new address to the watcherManager variable before emitting the event, and optionally guard against re‑setting the same address. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper state mutation or upgradeability misconfiguration, where contract state is not aligned with emitted logs, breaking the contract’s business logic that assumes the manager can be swapped safely.

title: Check __GAPs
description:
All __GAPs have the same size, while the different contracts have a different number of storage variables. If the __GAP size isn't logical it is more difficult to maintain the code.
Note: set to a risk rating of medium because the probably of something going wrong with future upgrades is low to medium, and the impact of mistakes would be medium to high.

```solidity
LPToken.sol:
uint256[49] private __GAP; // should probably be 50

OwnerPausableUpgradeable.sol: uint256[49] private __GAP; // should probably be 50

StableSwap.sol:
uint256[49] private __GAP; // should probably be 48

Merkle.sol:
uint256[49] private __GAP; // should probably be 48

ProposedOwnable.sol:
uint256[49] private __GAP; // should probably be 47
```
bug_full: The issue is a mis‑configured storage gap, commonly named __GAP, that is used in upgradeable Solidity contracts to preserve storage layout across future implementations. In the examined code base every contract declares a fixed‑size uint256[49] array for __GAP, regardless of how many state variables each contract actually defines. Because the number of real storage slots differs between contracts, a uniform gap size can leave insufficient free slots in some contracts while leaving excess unused slots in others. The root cause is an assumption that a single gap size is universally safe, ignoring the variable‑specific storage layout of each contract. When an upgrade adds new state variables, the compiler will place them in the first available slots after the existing variables. If the previously allocated __GAP is too small, the new variables may overwrite slots that belong to a parent contract or to other inherited contracts, causing a storage collision. An attacker or a careless developer could exploit this by deploying an upgraded implementation that unintentionally (or maliciously) writes to overwritten slots, leading to corrupted balances, altered access controls, or loss of funds. The impact can range from subtle accounting errors—such as a user receiving a zero refund or a token balance appearing to disappear—to severe protocol failures where critical parameters are overwritten, potentially freezing funds or allowing unauthorized withdrawals. The vulnerability manifests during any upgrade that introduces new storage variables without first adjusting the __GAP size to accommodate the existing layout. All contract users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the integrity of stored data cannot be guaranteed after an upgrade. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the declared __GAP sizes against the actual number of storage variables in each contract. It is hard to notice because the contracts compile and run correctly before the upgrade; the problem only becomes visible when a new implementation is deployed and the corrupted storage leads to unexpected runtime behavior. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as missing tokens, zero payouts, or functions that silently fail without reverting. The bug belongs to the class of upgradeable‑contract storage‑layout mismatches, often referred to as “storage gap misconfiguration”. To remediate, each contract should calculate the required gap size based on its current storage layout and the expected number of new variables in future upgrades, adjusting the __GAP array length accordingly, or relocate the gap to a dedicated base contract that can be individually sized. Proper testing of upgrade scenarios with tools that simulate storage layout (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s storage‑gap checker) should be performed to ensure no slot collisions occur.

title: Merkle-tree-related contracts vulnerable to cross-chain-replay attacks
description:
Bank is a token vesting, airdrop and payroll tool. It uses merkle trees to massively scale token distributions with integrated vesting (time locks). The idea of this tool is that it allows DAOs to vest pre-sale participants, and future allocations of tokens (such as DAO treasury allocations) far into the future. These are important contracts since they need longevity and will secure large allocations of tokens.

Since these trees are long-lived, they need to be able to handle forks correctly. If someone generates an exchange address for their drops, that address may only be valid for that chain (e.g. exchange supports BTC but not BSV), and any funds sent to the unsupported chain are lost.
poc:
There are no EIP-712 protections in the encoding:
    
    File: contracts/MerkleDropFactory.sol   #1
    
    94           bytes32 leaf = keccak256(abi.encode(destination, value));

    File: contracts/MerkleVesting.sol   #2
    
    109           bytes32 leaf = keccak256(abi.encode(destination, totalCoins, startTime, endTime, lockPeriodEndTime));

and anyone can trigger a withdrawal:
    
    File: contracts/MerkleDropFactory.sol   #3
    
    82       /// @dev Anyone may call this function for anyone else, funds go to destination regardless, it's just a question of
    83       /// @dev who provides the proof and pays the gas, msg.sender is not used in this function
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Merkle‑based token distribution contracts used by the Bank system for vesting, airdrops and payroll. These contracts compute a leaf hash for each allocation by directly encoding the destination address and associated numeric parameters with keccak256(abi.encode(...)). Because the leaf is not wrapped in an EIP‑712 domain separator, the resulting hash is identical on every EVM‑compatible chain that deploys the same bytecode. The withdrawal function is deliberately public – anyone can submit a valid Merkle proof and trigger the token transfer, and the call does not inspect the caller (msg.sender) for any additional authorization. Consequently, an attacker can reuse a proof that was generated for a legitimate recipient on one chain (for example, an exchange address that only exists on Bitcoin or an L2) and replay it on another chain where the same contract is deployed. When the replay is executed, the contract transfers the allocated tokens to the same address on the unintended chain. If that address is not supported on the target chain, the funds become unrecoverable, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s balance. This cross‑chain replay can be carried out at any time after the Merkle root is published, and the attacker only needs to provide the proof and pay the gas. Users who expect a refund or vesting payout may see their balance remain unchanged while the protocol’s total token holdings shrink, violating the accounting assumption that each leaf can be redeemed exactly once on the intended chain. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that flagged the absence of EIP‑712 signing in the leaf construction and noted the public withdrawal interface. Because the code looks normal – a simple keccak256 over ABI‑encoded parameters – the problem is not obvious without examining the replay‑attack surface. To remediate, the contracts should incorporate a signed EIP‑712 message that includes the domain (chain ID, contract address) and the recipient data, or alternatively require an EIP‑2612 permit that authorizes the transfer on a per‑chain basis. This would bind each proof to a specific chain context, preventing the same proof from being accepted elsewhere and ensuring that only the intended beneficiary can claim the tokens on the correct network.

title: PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory’s withdraw can become frozen on zero reward token transfers
description:
Reward tokens that do not allow for zero amount transfers can prevent user pool exit.

Now it is required that all reward amounts be successfully transferred to a receipt owner and the reward token amount isn’t checked in the process.

If withdraw was called at the moment when some reward amount is zero (because either zero time passed or zero slope is set), the withdraw() will revert.

Say once such reward token is there (say with no malicious intent, as it’s just a specifics of some valid tokens), user cannot withdraw immediately after deposit as no rewards accrued yet and this token transfer will revert the whole call even if it is one of the many.

As withdraw() the only way for a user to exit pool, her funds will be frozen within.

If slope is set to zero for such a token, either maliciously or mistakenly, the withdrawals are impossible for all the users.

As this is user fund freeze case with external assumptions, setting the severity to medium.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw function of the PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory contract, where it iterates over all configured reward tokens and attempts to transfer the calculated reward amount to the recipient without first verifying that the amount is non‑zero. Certain ERC20 tokens reject transfers of a zero token amount and revert the whole transaction. Consequently, when a user initiates a withdrawal at a moment when the accrued reward for any token is zero—such as immediately after deposit before any time has passed, or when the reward rate (slope) for that token has been set to zero—the transfer call for that token reverts, causing the entire withdraw call to fail. Because withdraw is the sole mechanism for a participant to exit a pool and retrieve the deposited assets, the failure effectively freezes the user's funds inside the pool. This condition can be triggered unintentionally by legitimate tokens that simply do not support zero‑value transfers, or deliberately by an attacker who configures a pool with a token that has a zero reward rate, making withdrawals impossible for all participants. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a transaction that reverts with little explanation, leaving the deposited balance unchanged and giving the impression that the funds have disappeared or are stuck. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case reward scenarios and observed the revert behavior. It is difficult to spot because most ERC20 implementations accept zero transfers, masking the problem until a non‑conforming token is introduced. The flaw belongs to the class of improper handling of external token contracts and missing input validation, where the contract assumes that all token transfers will succeed regardless of amount. To remediate, the withdraw logic should explicitly check that the reward amount is greater than zero before attempting the transfer, or otherwise gracefully skip the transfer for zero amounts while still allowing the overall withdrawal to proceed. This adjustment restores the correct accounting semantics, prevents user funds from being frozen, and aligns the contract’s behavior with expected business logic that a user can always exit a pool and receive their original deposit.

title: ERC20 tokens with different decimals than 18 leads to loss of funds
description: Contract `PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory` calculates rewards by using hardcoded value of decimals `18` (1e18) for ERC20 tokens. This leads to wrong rewards calculations and effectively loss of funds for all pools that will be using ERC20 tokens with different decimals than `18`. Example of such a token is USDC that has 6 decimals only.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-factorydao/blob/db415804c06143d8af6880bc4cda7222e5463c0e/contracts/PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory.sol#L169>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-factorydao/blob/db415804c06143d8af6880bc4cda7222e5463c0e/contracts/PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory.sol#L282>
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the PermissionlessBasicPoolFactory contract assuming that every ERC20 token used for reward calculations has exactly 18 decimals and therefore hard‑coding the scaling factor 1e18. This assumption is baked into the reward‑distribution logic, so when a token with a different decimal precision—such as USDC, which uses only 6 decimals—is added to a pool, the contract applies an incorrect multiplier. The root cause is the lack of a dynamic query to the token’s decimals() function and the absence of any validation that the token conforms to the 18‑decimal expectation. Under the condition that a non‑18‑decimal token is supplied to a pool, the contract computes rewards based on the wrong magnitude, effectively delivering far fewer reward tokens than the protocol’s economic model promises. From a user’s perspective the symptoms appear as missing or dramatically reduced payouts: a participant may see a balance that remains unchanged after a claim, receive a fraction of the expected amount, or observe the UI indicating a reward amount that is orders of magnitude lower than anticipated. The impact is a systematic under‑payment that translates into a loss of value for liquidity providers, stakers, or any address that relies on the reward mechanism, while the protocol’s incentive alignment is broken because the accounting assumptions (that rewards scale with 1e18) no longer hold. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors inspected the reward‑calculation code paths and identified the hard‑coded decimal constant. It may be difficult to notice in testing because most popular ERC20 tokens use 18 decimals, causing the bug to manifest only with a limited set of assets, often not covered by default test suites. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the actual decimals of each reward token at runtime and adjust the scaling factor accordingly, or, if the design deliberately wants to limit supported tokens, enforce a require statement during pool creation that checks token.decimals() == 18. This change restores correct proportional reward distribution and aligns the contract’s accounting logic with the diverse decimal configurations of real‑world ERC20 tokens.

title: Owner of a pool may prevent any taxes being withdrawn
description: It is possible for the owner of a pool to prevent any taxes being withdrawn by the `globalBeneficiary`. The impact is the taxed tokens will be permanently locked in the contract and `withdrawTaxes()` will not be callable for that `poolId`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the tax‑withdrawal mechanism of a liquidity pool contract. The contract stores a separate tax amount for each reward token associated with a pool and provides a `withdrawTaxes(uint poolId)` function that iterates over all reward tokens, transfers the stored tax to a designated `globalBeneficiary`, and then requires that every transfer succeeded. The root cause is that the function aggregates the success flag with a boolean AND and later asserts it with a `require`. If any of the token transfers revert, the cumulative flag becomes false and the `require` reverts the whole transaction, causing the state changes—including the clearing of the tax balances—to be rolled back. Because the pool owner can specify the list of reward token addresses at pool creation, a malicious owner can inject a contract that deliberately reverts when the `transfer` call targets the `globalBeneficiary`. When the malicious token is present, any attempt by the tax beneficiary to call `withdrawTaxes` for that pool results in a transaction revert, leaving the taxed tokens permanently locked in the contract. This situation can arise whenever the pool’s reward token list contains at least one token that misbehaves on transfer to the beneficiary, which is under the control of the pool owner. The affected parties include the protocol’s revenue collector (the globalBeneficiary) and, indirectly, token holders whose rewards are partially diverted as taxes, because those tax portions become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during an audit by constructing a proof‑of‑concept malicious ERC‑20 token that reverts on transfers to the beneficiary, then invoking `withdrawTaxes` and observing the revert. It may be hard to notice in normal operation because a single failed token transfer simply produces a generic "Token transfer failed" error, which could be mistaken for a temporary token pause or network issue rather than a deliberate sabotage. The flaw represents a class of bugs where batch operations abort entirely on the first failure, preventing partial progress and causing locked assets. To remediate, the withdrawal logic should be refactored so that each reward token is handled independently, for example by passing a specific `rewardIndex` to the function, or by wrapping each individual `transfer` in a `try‑catch` block. In the catch branch the contract should either restore the tax amount for the failed token or skip it while still allowing successful transfers to proceed, thereby ensuring that honest tax amounts can still be collected even if a malicious token is present. This approach restores the intended accounting behavior—taxes are withdrawn when possible and remain claimable—while preventing a single token from locking the entire tax pool.

title: DoS: Attacker may significantly increase the cost of `withdrawExcessRewards`
description:
An attacker may cause a DoS attack on `withdrawExcessRewards()` by creating a excessive number of `receipts` with minimal value. Each of these receipts will need to be withdrawn before the owner can call `withdrawExcessRewards()`.

The impact is the owner would have to pay an unbounded amount of gas to `withdraw()` all the accounts and receive their excess funds.
poc:
`withdrawExcessRewards()` has the requirement that `totalDepositsWei` for the pool is zero before the owner may call this function as seen on line 245.
    
    require(pool.totalDepositsWei == 0, 'Cannot withdraw until all deposits are withdrawn');

`pool.totalDepositsWei` is added to each time a user calls `deposit()`. It is increased by the amount the user deposits. There are no restrictions on the amount that may be deposited as a result a user may add 1 wei (or the smallest unit on any currency) which has negligible value.

The owner can force withdraw these accounts by calling `withdraw()` so long as `block.timestamp > pool.endTime`. They would be required to do this for each account that was created.

This could be a significant amount of gas costs, especially if the gas price has increased since the attacker originally made the deposits.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the withdrawExcessRewards function of the pool contract. The root cause lies in the contract’s accounting rule that the pool owner may only call withdrawExcessRewards after the aggregate totalDepositsWei field has been reduced to zero. Because the contract allows any address to create a deposit receipt with an arbitrarily small amount – even a single wei – an attacker can submit a very large number of such minimal‑value receipts. Each receipt creates an entry that must be individually cleared by the owner via the withdraw function before the pool’s total deposit balance reaches zero. The exploitation flow is straightforward: the attacker repeatedly calls deposit with the smallest possible amount, generating thousands or millions of receipts; the contract’s state variable totalDepositsWei remains non‑zero until each receipt is withdrawn; when the owner later attempts to claim the excess rewards, the require‑statement blocks the call, forcing the owner to iterate over every tiny receipt and pay gas for each withdraw operation. The impact is that the pool owner faces an unbounded gas cost to process all those withdrawals, potentially rendering the withdrawExcessRewards action economically infeasible, effectively freezing the protocol’s reward distribution. This condition occurs only after the auction end time, when the owner is permitted to call withdrawExcessRewards, but any outstanding deposits – no matter how small – block the call. All participants, including pool users who rely on timely reward distribution and the protocol’s treasury, are affected because the owner may be unable to release excess funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit when the requirement pool.totalDepositsWei == 0 was examined and it became clear that there were no minimum‑deposit constraints, allowing a malicious party to flood the contract with negligible deposits. The problem is hard to notice because the individual deposits appear harmless and the contract behaves correctly for normal usage; only when the number of receipts grows large does the gas consumption become evident. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration over untrusted user‑generated data” leading to a DoS via excessive gas consumption. From a user’s perspective the owner may see transactions revert with the error “Cannot withdraw until all deposits are withdrawn,” experience unexpectedly high gas fees, or be unable to claim rewards that were promised. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a configurable minimum deposit amount per receipt or to introduce alternative withdrawal criteria – such as a time lock after the auction ends or a threshold percentage of deposits withdrawn – so that the owner is not forced to iterate over an unbounded list of trivial entries before accessing excess rewards.

title: Centralisation Risk: Owner may abuse the tax rate to claim 99.9% of pools
description:
It is possible for the owner to increase the tax rate to 99.9% in `setGlobalTax()`.

The impact of this is that any future pools will be required to pay 99.9% of their rewards in tax to the `globalBeneficiary`.

It is possible for the `globalBeneficiary` to modify this and front-run any transactions in the mem-pool which call `addPool()`. These transactions will succeed and create pools with the 99.9% tax rate.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralisation risk that stems from an unbounded tax parameter in the contract. A privileged address, referred to as the globalBeneficiary, can call the function setGlobalTax and set the tax rate to any value below the hard coded cap of 1000, which corresponds to 100 %. Because the contract does not enforce a reasonable upper limit, the owner is able to increase the tax to 99.9 % (newTaxPerCapita = 999). When this extreme tax is in place, any pool that is subsequently created or that continues to accrue rewards will have to remit 99.9 % of its earned rewards to the globalBeneficiary, leaving participants with only a fraction of the expected return. The exploit can be performed simply by the owner submitting a transaction that changes the tax right before a user’s addPool transaction is mined, or by the globalBeneficiary front‑running the addPool transaction from the mem‑pool and setting the tax to the maximum allowed value. This results in users observing that their pool balances increase only marginally, rewards appear to disappear, or the APR shown in the UI drops to near zero, contradicting the expectation of a normal yield. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the lack of an upper bound on the tax variable was noted as a logical flaw. It can be difficult to notice in normal operation because the tax is a mutable parameter that may initially be set to a reasonable figure, and only when an extreme value is applied does the abnormal behavior become apparent. The impact affects every participant that stakes into a pool – their funds are effectively siphoned to the globalBeneficiary, undermining trust in the protocol’s economic model. To remediate, the contract should enforce a sensible ceiling on the tax rate (for example 5 %), move tax‑setting authority to a multi‑sig or governance process, or include timelocks and community oversight to prevent unilateral abuse. In broader terms, this is an example of an unchecked privileged configuration that can be abused to seize a disproportionate share of economic rewards, violating the intended accounting assumptions of fair fee distribution.

title: MerkleResistor: zero coinsPerSecond will brick tranche initialization and withdrawals
poc: We assume vesting time chosen is the maximum (`tree.maxEndTime`) so that `totalCoins = maxTotalPayments`. These examples showcase some possibilities for which the calculated `coinsPerSecond` can be zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the calculation of the per‑second vesting rate, referred to as `coinsPerSecond`. In certain configurations the arithmetic expression that derives this rate can evaluate to zero because it uses integer division without guaranteeing a minimum non‑zero result. When `coinsPerSecond` is zero, the contract later computes the tranche start time using the formula `uint startTime = block.timestamp + vestingTime - (totalCoins / coinsPerSecond);`. This division by zero triggers a runtime revert, preventing the tranche from being initialized and consequently blocking any subsequent withdrawal of vested tokens. The bug appears when the vesting period is set to its maximum allowed value, the total amount of tokens to be paid out is at its upper bound, and the upfront percentage (`pctUpFront`) is chosen such that the numerator of the `coinsPerSecond` calculation becomes insufficient to produce a value greater than zero after integer truncation. Under these circumstances the protocol appears functional but silently locks user funds: a participant who has deposited tokens expects to see a growing balance and eventually claim their vested reward, yet the UI shows no progress, withdrawals return nothing, and the contract state remains stuck. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined edge‑case parameter combinations; it is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error message for a zero rate, and the division‑by‑zero only manifests when a later function accesses the zero value. The impact is medium‑severity: funds remain inaccessible for the affected tranche, undermining the economic guarantees of the vesting mechanism, though the locked tokens are not exposed to external theft. To remediate the problem, the design should ensure that `coinsPerSecond` can never be zero. A common mitigation is to multiply the intermediate result by a large constant (`PRECISION`) before the division and then scale it back down during withdrawals, thereby preserving fractional precision and avoiding truncation to zero. Additionally, a defensive check that validates `coinsPerSecond` is non‑zero before proceeding with start‑time computation would prevent the contract from entering an unrecoverable state. By applying these adjustments, the protocol restores predictable vesting behaviour, aligns with the intended accounting logic, and guarantees that users can eventually receive the rewards they anticipate.

title: Verification should be leafed based and not address based
description: Contracts should clarify what is the intended behavior for Merkle trees with multiple leafs with the same address.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way a Merkle‑based vesting contract records whether a claim has already been processed. The contract stores a boolean flag keyed by the beneficiary address, so when a Merkle tree contains multiple leaves that map to the same address – for example, different vesting schedules or parameters for the same user – the contract treats them as a single claim. This design flaw arises from an implicit assumption that each address appears only once in the tree, which is not enforced nor documented. An attacker or even a legitimate user can exploit this by submitting a claim for a leaf that grants a lower amount or less favorable vesting terms, thereby marking the address as "claimed" and preventing any subsequent leaf – even if it offers a higher allocation – from being redeemed. The impact is that funds intended for the user may be partially or completely unavailable, leading to a discrepancy between the expected and actual token balance after a claim. The issue manifests whenever the Merkle root is generated with duplicate addresses, a situation that can occur inadvertently during tree construction or be deliberately crafted by a malicious tree builder. Both end‑users and the protocol are affected: users may receive no tokens or a smaller amount than advertised, while the protocol’s accounting logic is violated because the total allocated amount no longer matches the sum of unclaimed leaves. The problem was identified during a security audit that highlighted ambiguous documentation and the lack of a clear claim‑tracking policy for multi‑leaf addresses. It is subtle because the contract’s public interface appears to work correctly for a single‑leaf scenario, and the claim transaction does not revert – it simply succeeds with an unexpected (often zero) token transfer, which can be mistaken for a normal outcome. To remediate the issue, the contract should track claims per leaf identifier (e.g., the leaf hash or an index) rather than per address, or it should explicitly reject Merkle trees that contain duplicate addresses. Additionally, the intended behavior must be documented clearly for developers building the Merkle tree, stating whether only one claim per address is allowed or each leaf is independent. By adopting a leaf‑based claim map or by providing unambiguous comments, the contract can guarantee that every leaf, even when addressed to the same user, can be claimed according to its own vesting parameters, preserving the intended distribution of funds.

title: MJR-1 Unstable gauge version check
description: ShashFactory contract have gauge version check based on call probes defined at StashFactory.sol#L51-L61, that approach is very dangerous in case of new version added to curve. E.g if curve will add new version of gauge that have rewardedtoken() or rewardtokens(uint256) and with different behavior, then version checker will wrongly classify version and allow to create stash with invalid version. That can lead to broken logic.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the ShashFactory contract determines the version of a Curve gauge before creating a stash. Instead of using a static whitelist or an explicit version identifier, the contract performs a series of low‑level call probes that inspect the presence of functions such as rewardedToken() or rewardTokens(uint256) on the gauge contract. This dynamic probing works for the current set of ~40 known gauges, but it assumes that every future gauge will expose the same set of functions with identical semantics. If Curve later deploys a new gauge version that either adds, removes, or changes the behaviour of these functions, the probe logic can mis‑classify the gauge’s version. Consequently, ShashFactory may accept a gauge that it believes to be compatible while the underlying contract follows a different reward‑distribution logic. An attacker or an unwitting developer could therefore create a stash linked to an incompatible gauge, causing the reward‑calculation code in Convex to operate on unexpected data. From a user’s perspective this may manifest as missing or zero rewards, balances that appear to be frozen, or refunds that never arrive despite successful deposits. The impact is primarily logical: accounting invariants break, reward distribution becomes incorrect, and funds may become effectively unrecoverable because the protocol can no longer reconcile the stash state with the gauge’s actual state. The issue appears only when a new gauge version is introduced; under the existing gauge set the checks pass, making the bug hard to notice during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the version‑checking code and identified the reliance on function‑presence probes as a brittle pattern. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the probe‑based detection with a deterministic whitelist of known gauge addresses or explicit version identifiers supplied by Curve, ensuring that only vetted gauges can be used. This eliminates the risk of mis‑classification and restores confidence that reward calculations align with the intended gauge logic. The flaw belongs to the class of “dynamic interface probing” bugs, where contracts infer contract type from optional functions, leading to unsafe assumptions when interfaces evolve.

title: MJR-2 Wrong logic in withdrawAll
description: At the moment withdrawAll counts balance as: balanceOfPool(_gauge) (VoterProxy.sol#L92) Correct logic should be: balanceOfPool(gauge).add(IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this))). The withdrawAll method is used by shutdownSystem so potentially some tokens could remain in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the withdrawAll function of the protocol’s proxy contract. Instead of calculating the total amount of tokens that can be withdrawn as the sum of the gauge’s pooled balance and any tokens that are already held by the proxy contract, the implementation only queries balanceOfPool(_gauge). Consequently, when the system is shut down via shutdownSystem, any token balance that resides directly in the proxy contract is ignored and remains locked. The root cause is a missing addition of IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) to the withdrawal amount, which violates the expected accounting invariant that the contract’s total token holdings equal the sum of the gauge balance and the contract’s own balance. An attacker does not gain direct access to the omitted tokens, but the bug can be exploited by a malicious operator who triggers shutdown and then claims that all assets have been withdrawn while a portion stays trapped, effectively reducing the available liquidity for users. The impact is that users may see a zero balance or receive no refund after a shutdown, yet the tokens are still present in the contract, leading to apparent loss of funds, broken accounting, and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The condition under which the issue manifests is any execution of withdrawAll during or after a shutdown, where the proxy contract holds a non‑zero token balance outside the gauge. All participants that rely on the shutdown process – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol cannot correctly report or return the full amount of assets. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the withdrawal logic and identified the mismatch between the intended formula and the actual code. Because the symptom is that funds simply do not leave the contract, it can be hard to notice without inspecting the internal token balances, especially if the UI only shows a successful shutdown message. The recommended fix is to modify withdrawAll so that it computes the withdrawable amount as balanceOfPool(gauge) plus the token balance held by the contract, thereby restoring the correct accounting and ensuring that all assets are transferred out during shutdown. This type of bug belongs to the class of withdrawal or accounting miscalculations where the contract fails to aggregate all sources of token holdings before performing a transfer, leading to funds appearing to disappear or refunds being zero when they are actually still locked in the contract.

title: MJR-3 Zero gauge could be added via addPool
description: In addPool defined at Booster.sol#L160 there is no check for _gauge variable. For example during this call booster.addPool(threeCrvSwap, "0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000", 0) Gauge will be found because get_gauges returns array like [address1, address2, 0x0, 0x0, ...]. Intruder can call some errors in Booster logic. It's major because at the moment StashFactory call address(0x0).call.value(0)(data) (StashFactory.sol#L53) and due to specific of EVM there is true.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the function that registers a new liquidity pool in the Booster contract. When a caller invokes the pool‑addition routine, the supplied gauge address is stored without any validation that it is a non‑zero, contract‑type address. Because the internal helper that enumerates existing gauges returns a fixed‑size array that may contain empty slots, a caller can deliberately pass the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) as the gauge parameter. The Booster contract then records this zero gauge and later invokes the StashFactory to create a stash for the pool. The StashFactory performs a low‑level call to the gauge address using address(0).call.value(0)(data). In the Ethereum Virtual Machine a call to the zero address with zero value does not revert; it simply returns true. Consequently, the Booster logic interprets the call as a successful stash creation even though no real contract was interacted with. An attacker who can add a pool with a zero gauge can therefore trigger erroneous execution paths, bypass the intended accounting of rewards, and potentially cause funds to be mis‑routed, locked, or lost. The impact is considered major because the protocol’s reward distribution and stash management rely on the assumption that every gauge is a valid contract that will execute the expected logic. The bug manifests whenever the addPool function is called with a gauge argument that is zero, which can happen either accidentally or maliciously because there is no explicit check. All participants that rely on correct reward accounting – including liquidity providers, the protocol’s treasury, and any downstream contracts – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the Booster contract’s input validation and noticed the absence of a non‑zero gauge requirement. It is subtle because the zero‑address call succeeds silently, providing no error signal, and the surrounding code does not emit an event or revert, making the problem easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the gauge address supplied to addPool is non‑zero and points to a contract that implements the expected interface. Additionally, the StashFactory should verify the success of the low‑level call by checking that the target address contains code, or by using a higher‑level interface that reverts on failure. By adding these checks, the protocol can prevent the creation of invalid stashes and preserve the integrity of reward calculations, ensuring that users receive the expected refunds and that balances do not unexpectedly become zero.

title: MJR-1 Error while calculating the value
description: The getPricePerFullShare() function for a yDAI token contract returns the value multiplied by a factor of 1e18. But it doesn't divided by 1e18: CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L90 CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L155 CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L182
bug_full: The vulnerability is a scaling error in the price‑per‑share calculation of a yDAI token wrapper. The function that should return the price per full share multiplies the raw share value by the fixed‑point factor 1e18 but fails to divide the result by the same factor before returning it. As a result the reported price is inflated by exactly 1e18 times the correct value. This mistake originates from an incorrect handling of the token’s 18‑decimal precision, a common pitfall when mixing integer arithmetic with fixed‑point scaling. Any contract that relies on this function – for example the flash‑loan borrower implementation that calls getPricePerFullShare at several points – will receive a massively overstated share price and will therefore compute token amounts that are off by the same factor. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit the bug by triggering a transaction that uses the erroneous price to request or repay assets, causing the protocol to transfer far more tokens than intended or to believe a repayment has been satisfied when it has not. The impact includes potential loss of funds, incorrect accounting, and failure of flash‑loan repayment logic, which may leave user balances empty or cause the protocol to become under‑collateralised. The condition occurs every time the price‑per‑share getter is invoked, which in the audited code happens in the CoverFlashBorrower contract at the indicated lines. All participants that interact with the yDAI wrapper – borrowers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bug corrupts the fundamental accounting invariant that one share equals a fixed amount of underlying assets. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between the multiplication and the missing division. The bug can be subtle because the returned number is still a valid uint256 and may be used in subsequent calculations that also apply a 1e18 scaling, thereby masking the error until a concrete mismatch in token balances appears. To remediate the problem the getter should either divide the multiplied value by 1e18 before returning it or, alternatively, avoid the unnecessary multiplication altogether and keep the value in its native fixed‑point representation. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of decimal‑scaling or unit‑conversion bugs that break financial invariants and lead to erroneous token transfers, refund failures, or balance disappearances.

title: MJR-2 Wrongly used safeApprove
description: At the line CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L351 contract call safeApprove method, however that method fails if account have remaining allowed tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect use of the safeApprove function from the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library. The contract calls safeApprove(recipient, amount) without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. SafeERC20’s safeApprove internally checks that the current allowance for the spender is either zero or that the new allowance is zero; if the allowance is non‑zero and the new value is non‑zero, the call reverts. Consequently, when the contract or a user has previously granted a non‑zero allowance to the same token contract, any subsequent attempt to increase or change that allowance fails, causing the transaction to revert, which can be exploited by an attacker who can pre‑set a non‑zero allowance (for example by calling approve directly) and then trigger a function that relies on safeApprove to set a new allowance, causing the function to fail and potentially locking funds or preventing a flash‑loan operation that depends on the approval. The impact is that legitimate users may see their transactions revert with no obvious error, balances may appear unchanged, and flash‑loan borrowers may be unable to execute the loan, effectively “funds disappear” from the perspective of the user because the intended operation does not happen. The condition occurs whenever the contract executes the approval line (CoverFlashBorrower.sol line 351) and the token already has a non‑zero allowance for the recipient. The affected parties are token holders, borrowers, and any protocol component that relies on dynamic approvals, such as the flash‑loan module. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noted the unsafe pattern. It is hard to notice because the revert message from SafeERC20 is generic (“ERC20: approve from non‑zero to non‑zero allowance”) and may be swallowed by higher‑level error handling, making the failure appear as a silent “nothing happened”. The proper fix is to follow the standard two‑step allowance change: first call safeApprove(recipient, 0) to clear the existing allowance, then call safeApprove(recipient, newAmount) to set the desired value, or use safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance where appropriate. This aligns with the ERC20 allowance change best practice and prevents the revert. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect ERC20 allowance reset” or “unsafe approve pattern” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes it can overwrite an existing allowance without resetting it first, violating the token’s accounting assumptions and breaking expected business logic of token transfers.

title: MJR-1 It is possible to carry out attacks to manipulate pools within one
description: In contracts CoverRouter.sol and Rollover.sol, any user can exchange tokens with a contract. Any user can add and remove liquidity. An attacker can take a flash loan and perform multiple liquidity manipulations within a single transaction. These manipulations can lead to a loss of funds for other users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan‑driven liquidity manipulation bug present in the CoverRouter and Rollover contracts. The contracts allow any address to add liquidity, remove liquidity and perform token swaps without any per‑transaction or per‑block restrictions. Because the contracts do not keep track of the origin of a swap or enforce a delay between successive liquidity operations, an attacker can obtain a large amount of capital through a flash loan, inject that capital into a pool, execute a series of swaps or liquidity additions/removals within the same transaction, and then withdraw the manipulated assets before the transaction is settled. The root cause is the absence of a protection mechanism that ties a user’s actions to a specific block (for example, a mapping that records the last block in which the address performed a swap) and the lack of any flash‑loan detection or reentrancy‑style guard. Exploitation proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker borrows a flash loan; (2) the attacker adds a large amount of liquidity to a pool, artificially inflating the pool’s balance; (3) the attacker performs one or more swaps that shift the pool’s price curve in the attacker’s favor; (4) the attacker removes the previously added liquidity, capturing the price distortion as profit; (5) the transaction completes, leaving the pool with an altered token ratio that harms other users who later trade or withdraw. The impact is a direct loss of funds for honest liquidity providers and traders, as the pool may dispense fewer tokens than expected, causing refunds to be zero or balances to be unexpectedly reduced. The issue manifests whenever a user can call the addLiquidity, removeLiquidity or swap functions in rapid succession within a single block, which is permitted by the current contract logic. All participants who rely on the pool’s pricing – including regular users, other liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the contracts lack any safeguard against same‑transaction token manipulation. Because the manipulation happens entirely inside one atomic transaction, the abnormal state is not observable on‑chain until after the damage is done, making it hard to detect through ordinary monitoring. To remediate the problem, the contracts should record the block number of the last swap or liquidity operation for each origin address and reject further operations from the same address within the same block, as illustrated by the sample mapping _lastSwapBlock and the _preventSameTxOrigin check. Additional mitigations may include limiting the amount of liquidity that can be added or removed per block, integrating flash‑loan detection, or employing a more comprehensive reentrancy guard. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “same‑transaction price manipulation” or “flash‑loan liquidity attack” vulnerabilities, where unchecked rapid state changes enable an attacker to profit at the expense of other participants.

title: MJR-2 Possibility to steal tokens from the contract balance
description: Method addCoverAndCreatePools defined at CoverRouter.sol#L128 accepts _protocol and collateral addresses as arguments, then call addCover that makes approve for protocol an unlimited amount of collateral tokens and call _protocol.addCover. There are no checks of protocol and collateral validity, so an attacker can pass malicious protocol and get unlimited approval of collateral tokens: if (token.allowance(address(this), spender) < _amount) { token.approve(spender, uint256(-1)); } According to the contract logic in an optimistic flow a contract shouldn't have any tokens in balance, but this invariant not fully checked, e.g. if _protocol.addCover at Rollover.sol#L75 fails and returns false, then the transaction will be executed successfully, but the user's funds will be left on the CoverRouter balance.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the addCoverAndCreatePools function, which accepts arbitrary protocol and collateral token addresses and then calls an internal addCover routine thatunconditionally grants the supplied protocol an unlimited allowance of the collateral token using token.approve(spender, uint256(-1)). Because the function does not validate that the protocol address corresponds to a trusted contract, an attacker can supply a malicious protocol contract that, once approved, can invoke transferFrom to move any amount of the collateral tokens held by the CoverRouter. Additionally, the contract assumes an optimistic flow in which the router’s token balance should remain zero after a successful call, but it does not enforce this invariant nor does it check the boolean return value of _protocol.addCover. If the external addCover call fails and returns false, the transaction does not revert, leaving the user’s deposited tokens stranded in the router’s balance. The root cause is a combination of missing address validation, the use of an unlimited token approval pattern, and inadequate error handling that fails to enforce the zero‑balance invariant. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling addCoverAndCreatePools with a malicious protocol address, causing the router to approve unlimited tokens to the attacker’s contract, which can then drain the router’s balance. The impact includes complete loss of user‑deposited collateral, funds becoming irretrievable, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue manifests when a user initiates a cover addition; the transaction appears successful, but the user’s tokens disappear or remain locked in the router, contradicting the expectation that the tokens are transferred to a newly created pool. This bug was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which noted the unchecked external address and the unsafe approve call. It can be difficult to notice because the approve pattern is common and the transaction does not revert on failure, giving a false sense of success. To remediate, the contract should stop using unlimited approvals, instead approving only the exact amount required, implement strict validation or whitelisting of protocol addresses, and enforce that addCover returns true, reverting otherwise, thereby preserving the zero‑balance invariant and preventing token theft.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect check of timeWindow
description: At the line ClaimConfig.sol#L50 there is incorrect check of _newTimeWindow.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an incorrect validation of the claim time window in thecontract that governs claim periods. The contract is supposed to enforce a minimum duration of three days for any new claim window that can be set by privileged callers. However, the implemented check compares the supplied _newTimeWindow against the threshold using an inappropriate condition, allowing values that are shorter than the intended three‑day minimum to pass. This logical error originates from a faulty comparison operator or missing boundary condition in the require statement. An attacker who can invoke the function that updates the claim window can therefore set an arbitrarily short window, even zero, which collapses the intended claim period. By shortening the window, the attacker can either prevent legitimate users from submitting claims within the expected timeframe or, if the claim logic permits immediate execution, claim the funds before others have a chance. The impact is that users expecting a three‑day claim period may see their refunds or payouts disappear, balances remain unchanged, or the UI shows a claim window that never actually allows a claim. The bug manifests whenever the function that updates the time window is called, which may be during normal protocol governance or administrative actions. It affects all participants who rely on the claim mechanism, including token holders, claimants, and the protocol itself, because the accounting assumptions about a minimum claim period are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors identified that the require statement did not correctly enforce the intended lower bound. Because the check looks syntactically correct, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple testing unless edge‑case windows are exercised. To remediate, the contract should enforce the condition require(_newTimeWindow >= 3 days, "CC: window too short"); ensuring that any new time window is at least three days long, thereby restoring the intended claim period and preventing premature or impossible claim scenarios.

title: MJR-2 Lack of claim validation
description: At lines: ClaimManagement.sol#L112 ClaimManagement.sol#L145 ClaimManagement.sol#L176 the claim is taken by coverPool, nonce, _index, however caller may send incorrect indexes to the method. At the line ClaimManagement.sol#L114 even the flow with invalid claim will pass the require condition and go to claim.state = ClaimState.Validated; resetCoverPoolClaimFee(coverPool); this is unexpected behavior and potentially can lead to the contract misfunctioning.
bug_full: The contract's claim management function accepts three parameters: coverPool, nonce, and an index that selects a claim from an internal array. The code does not verify that the supplied index is within the bounds of the stored claim list. Consequently, a caller can pass an out‑of‑range index, causing the function to read uninitialized storage or a different claim. The require statement that checks other conditions does not include an index bounds check, so the transaction proceeds and the claim state is set to Validated and the cover‑pool claim fee is reset even though the claim data is invalid. This bug belongs to the class of unchecked array‑index vulnerabilities and improper input validation. An attacker can exploit it by submitting a transaction with a deliberately wrong index, causing the contract to mark a non‑existent or unrelated claim as validated, potentially resetting fees, mis‑accounting, or allowing the attacker to claim rewards they are not entitled to. The impact includes incorrect accounting, loss of fee revenue for the protocol, and possible denial of service if the state machine becomes inconsistent. The issue manifests whenever the claim function is called with any index that is not less than the length of the claim array for the given coverPool and nonce. All participants that rely on correct claim processing – policy holders, claim submitters, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol may think a claim has been settled when it has not. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the missing bounds check. Because the function still passes its internal require, the bug can be subtle and may not produce an obvious revert; instead the contract state silently diverges from expected accounting, making it hard to notice without explicit testing of edge cases. The proper fix is to add an explicit require that the index is smaller than the length of the claim array (e.g., require(index < coverPoolClaims[coverPool][_nonce].length, 'bad indexes')), ensuring that only existing claims can be processed. This restores the invariant that a claim can only be validated if it actually exists, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Overly restrictive API rate limiting
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overly restrictive API rate‑limiting configuration applied at the contract gateway. The limiter is set to allow only 100 requests per 15‑minute window per IP address. This restriction is applied globally to all endpoints, so any IP that aggregates traffic from multiple users—such as corporate NAT, VPNs, or mobile carriers—can quickly exceed the quota. The root cause is a mis‑chosen parameter (max = 100) that does not reflect realistic usage patterns. An attacker does not need to craft malicious payloads; simply sending a modest number of legitimate calls from a shared IP will cause the limiter to reject further calls with HTTP 429 responses. The impact is a self‑imposed denial‑of‑service: legitimate users experience failed transactions, UI elements show no response, balances may appear unchanged because calls are dropped, and the application may appear broken. The condition occurs whenever the request volume from a single IP exceeds the configured threshold within the 15‑minute window, which can happen during normal peak usage or when many users are behind the same gateway. All participants that rely on the contract—end users, dApp front‑ends, and integrators—are affected because they cannot interact with the contract until the window resets. The issue was discovered during a functional audit that examined usage patterns and compared them against the hard‑coded limiter values. Because the failure manifests as intermittent HTTP errors rather than a contract revert, it can be difficult to notice without systematic monitoring of request logs. The bug belongs to the class of rate‑limiting misconfigurations that unintentionally block legitimate traffic, a form of self‑inflicted denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the limiter should be re‑parameterised to a higher ceiling (for example 500‑1000 requests per 10‑minute window) and, preferably, applied per endpoint or per user identifier rather than globally per IP. Adding adaptive limits, burst allowances, or whitelisting trusted internal IPs can also mitigate the problem while preserving protection against abusive traffic.

title: Potential for cross-chain token replay attacks
bug_full: The issue is a cross‑chain replay vulnerability arising from the way JWT authentication tokens are validated in the middleware. The token payload contains a chain identifier and a service name, and the code checks that these fields match the expected values before allowing the request to proceed. However, the validation relies on a single shared secret that is used to sign tokens for all chain deployments. When the same secret is reused across multiple chains or when the architecture is extended to support several chains simultaneously, an attacker who obtains a legitimate token issued for one chain can present the same token to a different chain endpoint. Because the signature verification succeeds and the chain identifier check may be bypassed if the target chain does not enforce strict isolation, the token is accepted as authentic on the wrong chain. This enables the attacker to replay authenticated actions, such as invoking privileged functions, transferring assets, or impersonating a user, on a chain where they were not originally authorized. The impact includes unauthorized access to contract functions, potential loss of funds, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s access control model. The vulnerability manifests only in environments where multiple chains share the same authentication backend or where the deployment configuration changes to include additional chains without rotating the JWT secret. Users may notice that actions they never performed appear on a different chain, or that their account seems to be accessed without their intent, leading to confusion and possible fund disappearance. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the authentication middleware and identified that the secret management strategy did not account for chain isolation. It can be difficult to spot because the token validation logic appears correct at a glance, and the chain identifier check is present, giving a false sense of security. To remediate, each chain and each service should use a distinct secret, and the token should incorporate a chain‑specific nonce or timestamp that is invalidated when the user switches chains. Additionally, implementing a blacklist for tokens that have been used on a different chain can prevent replay. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of authentication replay attacks where credential reuse across isolated domains enables unauthorized actions.

title: MJR-1 Excess reserve amount
description: At lines CCapableErc20.sol#L250-L252 contract increases internalCash and totalReserves values, but it's so strange that internalCash increased by totalFee and totalReserves increased by reservesFee so we totally increased assets amount by reservesFee + totalFee however user paid only totalFee . It seems there are some uncollateralized reservesFee . May be there totalFee paid by user should be splitted to internalCash and totalReserves ?
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting error in the CCapableErc20 contract where two state variables, internalCash and totalReserves, are updated incorrectly when a user pays a fee. Specifically, the contract adds the full amount of totalFee to internalCash and also adds the full amount of reservesFee to totalReserves. Because reservesFee is derived from the same user‑paid totalFee, the net effect is that the protocol’s recorded assets increase by the sum of totalFee and reservesFee, even though the user only transferred totalFee. This creates an uncollateralized reserve amount – the protocol appears to hold more reserves than it actually received. The root cause is a misplaced accounting rule: the fee should be split between cash and reserves, not added to both independently. An attacker could exploit this discrepancy by triggering fee‑related operations repeatedly, causing the protocol’s reserve balance to inflate artificially and potentially allowing withdrawal of funds that were never deposited. The impact includes inflated reserve metrics, broken accounting invariants, and a risk that legitimate users’ withdrawals could be denied or that the protocol could become under‑collateralized, leading to loss of funds. The condition occurs whenever the fee‑processing function at lines 250‑252 is executed, typically during flash‑loan repayments or other fee‑bearing actions. All participants that rely on the protocol’s reserve accounting – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the internal accounting no longer reflects reality. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between fee inflow and reserve growth. It is subtle because the contract still records a positive cash flow, so the bug does not produce an outright revert or obvious error; instead, it silently skews the accounting numbers, making it hard to detect without detailed balance tracing. To remediate, the fee handling logic should be revised so that the incoming totalFee is partitioned appropriately: a portion should increase internalCash while the complementary portion should be recorded as reserves, ensuring that the sum of internalCash and totalReserves grows exactly by totalFee, not by totalFee plus reservesFee. This correction restores the invariant that total assets equal the sum of cash and reserves, eliminating the uncollateralized reserve surplus and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: A Buyer Can Use Two Different Referral Codes for the Same Trade
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a buyer to supply one referral code when initiating a purchase and have a different referral code applied when the trade proceeds to fee distribution, resulting in the buyer receiving a larger discount than intended and the referral owner receiving a larger fee. The root cause is the absence of validation on the referral code argument in the commitBuy function; the code is stored directly and later, during _distributeProceeds, the contract queries the ReferralRegistry for any existing code attached to the buyer. If a stored code exists and differs from the one supplied, the stored code overwrites the original variable. Because the discount calculation uses the initially supplied code while the fee payout uses the overwritten code, a single trade can be associated with two distinct referral codes. Exploitation follows a simple flow: the attacker registers a referral code with a 100 % buyer discount (buyerRatio) and another code with a 100 % referrer fee (ownerRatio). The attacker then calls commitBuy with the discount‑heavy code, receives the maximum discount on the purchase, and after trade completion the _distributeProceeds function pays the maximum fee to the owner of the second code. This yields extra referral fees beyond the protocol’s accounting rules. The issue manifests whenever a buyer already has a referral code recorded in the ReferralRegistry and supplies a different code in the purchase call. Affected parties include the buyer (who gains an unintended discount), the referral code owner (who receives excess fees), and potentially the seller, because if a related M‑02 issue is fixed the mismatched code handling can be leveraged to cause a permanent denial‑of‑service in _distributeProceeds, preventing sellers from claiming their tokens. The problem was discovered during a security audit (Shiedify) by noticing that the referral code variable is reassigned without consistency checks. It is subtle because both discount and fee calculations appear correct in isolation; only the cross‑function inconsistency creates the over‑payment, making it easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a single referral code per trade by moving the registry lookup and validation into commitBuy, ensuring the same code is used for both discount computation and fee distribution, or by rejecting a purchase if the buyer already has a registered code. This aligns the business logic with the accounting assumption that each trade is linked to exactly one referral entity, eliminating the possibility of double‑code exploitation and preserving the integrity of seller payouts.

title: Whenever There Is a Buyer Discount and a Trade Is Completed Successfully, an Amount of Tokens that Is Equal to the Discount Fee Will Get Stuck in the CSXTrade Contract
description:
Due to the way that the CSXTrade::_distributeProceeds() function calculates the number of payment tokens to be sent out, whenever there is a buyer discount from the referral code used by the buyer, several tokens that are equal to the discount fee will get stuck in the contract forever when that function is used to complete a given trade. That’s because the depositedValue() (which is equal to weiPrice - discountedFee for non-fee-on-transfer tokens) is passed into getNetValue() to calculate the final output amounts.
```solidity
(uint256 buyerNetPrice , uint256 sellerNetProceeds , uint256 affiliatorNetReward , uint256 tokenHoldersNetReward) = getNetValue(
    referralCode , depositedValue);
```
The lost amount itself will come from the sellerNetProceeds, affiliatorNetReward and tokenHoldersNetReward values - i.e. the transferred out amounts will be proportionally less than they could have been, depending on the discount fee.

An amount of tokens that is equal to the discount fee will get lost on some trades.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting miscalculation that occurs in the CSXTrade contract when a buyer applies a discount through a referral code. The contract’s internal function that distributes trade proceeds calculates the amounts to be sent out by calling getNetValue with a variable called depositedValue. DepositedValue is derived from the trade price minus the discount fee, but it does not include the fee that should be accounted for when the token does not charge fees on transfer. As a result, the discount fee is effectively subtracted from the pool of tokens that are later split among the seller, the affiliator and the token‑holder reward. Because the discounted amount is never transferred out, an amount of tokens equal to the discount fee remains locked in the CSXTrade contract forever. The bug is triggered only when a trade is completed successfully and a buyer discount is applied; it does not affect trades without a discount or tokens that implement fee‑on‑transfer logic. Users experience the problem as a shortfall: the seller receives less than expected, the affiliate reward is reduced or zero, and the contract’s token balance silently increases. From the protocol’s perspective, funds that should have been distributed are trapped, breaking the accounting assumptions that total proceeds equal the sum of seller, affiliate and holder rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by the auditor Shiedify, who noticed that the net proceeds calculation ignored the discount fee. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the missing tokens are simply retained in the contract’s balance, which may only be observed by comparing expected versus actual payouts. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a second storage variable that records the deposited value after adjusting for the discount fee (depositedValueWithFees) and to use this corrected value when calling getNetValue in the proceeds‑distribution routine. This change ensures that the discount fee is properly accounted for while preserving support for fee‑on‑transfer tokens. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of fee‑handling or accounting errors where a discount is subtracted from the input amount but not re‑added to the distribution calculation, leading to locked funds and reduced payouts for all parties involved.

title: WrongAddressCheckin receive() Functionin VestedStaking.sol Contract Can Lead to Integrating Contracts Not Being Able to Claim Their Staking Rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the receive() fallback of the VestedStaking contract. The function is intended to reject accidental ETH transfers by ensuring that only the WETH token contract can send ETH to the staking contract. However, the check compares msg.sender against the address of the WETH token, while the legitimate ETH that arrives when a user calls claimRewards() with the convertWethToEth flag set to true is actually sent from the StakedCSX contract. Because the receive() function only permits the WETH address, any ETH transferred from StakedCSX triggers the InvalidSender() revert, causing the claimRewards() transaction to fail. This mismatch means that the convert‑WETH‑to‑ETH feature is effectively broken.
