When the vester of a VestedStaking instance is itself a smart contract that always calls claimRewards() with convertWethToEth set to true, the contract cannot receive the ETH needed to complete the reward conversion, and the accumulated staking rewards become unclaimable. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a pending reward balance, but when the user attempts to claim, the transaction reverts and no ETH is received, leading to the impression that “rewards disappear” or “the refund is missing”. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the receive() logic and the flow of ETH in claimRewards(). It is hard to notice because the receive() guard appears reasonable at a glance and the failure only manifests when the specific flag is true, a path that may not be exercised in basic tests. The root cause is an incorrect address validation – the contract checks for the WETH token address instead of the StakedCSX contract address that actually sends the ETH. The impact is that funds may be permanently locked for any vesting contract that relies on this conversion path, affecting users, protocol revenue, and any third‑party contracts acting as vesters. To remediate, the receive() function should validate that msg.sender is the StakedCSX contract (or otherwise allow the expected sender), ensuring that legitimate ETH transfers are accepted and the reward conversion works as intended. Conceptually, the fix is to align the sender check with the actual source of ETH, restoring the intended business logic that rewards can be claimed and converted to ETH without being blocked by an erroneous guard.

title: SomeTrade-TerminatingFunctionsDoNotCall removeAssetIdUsed() Internally, Potentially Leading The Same Skin Not Being Tradable On CSX Again
description:
Unlike other trade-terminating functions, CSXTrade::buyerCancel(), CSXTrade::sellerTradeVeridict() and CSXTrade::sellerConfirmsTrade() don’t call Users::removeAssetIdUsed() after transferring the committed tokens to the buyer/seller. And since asset IDs are the unique identifiers of Steam items, this means that the same skin won’t be tradable on CSX again. Although asset IDs change, they do so only when the items are traded or changed in some way, so it is unlikely that users will know how or want to change the asset ID of their skin, in order for it to become tradable on CSX again. This can prove to be especially problematic with the CSXTrade::buyerCancel() function, as it can be used to intentionally DoS the trading of concrete user skins.

Some skins will become impossible to trade on CSX for an undefined amount of time.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing internal cleanup step in three trade‑terminating functions of the CSX marketplace contract. After a trade is cancelled by the buyer, or after a seller either rejects the trade or confirms completion, the contract transfers the deposited tokens back to the appropriate party but does not invoke Users::removeAssetIdUsed to clear the asset identifier that represents the traded Steam skin. Asset IDs are unique markers that the platform uses to prevent the same item from being listed multiple times simultaneously. Because the cleanup call is omitted, the asset ID remains flagged as "used" even though the trade has ended and the tokens have been returned. Consequently, the same skin cannot be offered on CSX again until the flag is manually cleared, which the protocol does not provide. This situation creates a denial‑of‑service condition: an attacker who is a participant in a trade can deliberately invoke buyerCancel or trigger the seller‑side cancellation path, causing the skin to become permanently untradeable on the marketplace. Users experience the symptom of a missing or vanished listing – they expect the item to be available for resale after a cancellation, but the UI shows no option to list it, and attempts to add the skin fail silently. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the code paths of all trade‑finalising functions and noticed that only some of them called the removal routine. It is hard to notice because the token balances are correctly restored, so the financial side appears normal, while the asset‑availability logic silently fails. The root cause is an inconsistency in the contract’s state‑management logic: the removal of the used asset identifier is not performed in buyerCancel, sellerTradeVerdict (cancellation branch) and sellerConfirmsTrade. To remediate the problem, each of these functions should call a private helper that invokes Users::removeAssetIdUsed after the token transfer, and the helper should revert if the removal fails. This ensures that the asset identifier is cleared, restoring the ability of the owner to list the skin again and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Add a form of access control to takeFee
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The issue is an unrestricted access control on the fee‑extraction routine of the vault contract. The function takeFee is declared external and contains no checks on the caller, allowing any address to invoke it on behalf of any user. Because the routine reduces the share balance of the supplied user by the calculated fee, an attacker can repeatedly call takeFee for victims, gradually draining their share count (for example from 10 shares to 9.99) while the total share pool remains constant. This dilution increases the relative ownership of any untouched participant, effectively rewarding the attacker or a third party. The vulnerability originates from the missing authorization guard – the contract assumes that only a privileged entity will call the function, but this assumption is not enforced in code. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary supplies the address of a target depositor and a valid pocket identifier, then invokes takeFee; each call silently reduces the target’s recorded shares. The impact is a loss of accounting integrity, where users see their balances shrink without any transaction they initiated, leading to reduced claim on the underlying assets and potential financial loss. The condition under which it occurs is any time the contract is live and the takeFee function is reachable; no special state or timing is required. All depositors, the protocol’s reputation, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate share accounting are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined public entry points and identified the lack of role‑based restrictions. Because the function does not emit obvious error messages or revert on unauthorized calls, the behavior can be hard to notice until users observe unexpected share reductions. The proper mitigation is to enforce access control, such as restricting the function to a designated role (e.g., onlyOwner or a fee‑collector role) or allowing callers to take fees only for themselves, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that fees are collected by the protocol, not by arbitrary users. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “unprotected external function” or “missing access control”, which can lead to unauthorized state changes and financial loss. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a lower share balance after no action was taken, contradicting the expectation that their deposited amount remains unchanged, effectively causing “funds disappear” or “share dilution” symptoms.

title: Circuit breakers are not considered when processing Chainlink's answer
description: Every Chainlink feed has a minimum and maximum price. However, due to the circuit breaker, if an asset's price moves outside these limits, the provided answer will still be capped. This can lead to an incorrect price if the actual price falls below the aggregator's minAnswer, as Chainlink will continue providing the capped value instead of the true one. The Chainlink documentation notes that "On most data feeds, these values are no longer used and they do not prevent your application from reading the most recent answer.". However, this is not the case on Arbitrum, as for most data feeds (including ETH and most stablecoins), these values are indeed used, for example, the ETH/USD aggregator: link
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Chainlink price feeds on Arbitrum enforce a circuit‑breaker range defined by a minimum (minAnswer) and maximum (maxAnswer) price. When the true market price of an asset moves outside this range, the aggregator does not return the actual out‑of‑range value; instead it caps the answer at the configured bound. The examined contract assumes that the value returned by the feed always reflects the real market price and only checks that the answer is greater than zero via an assert statement. Because the contract does not verify that the answer lies between the aggregator’s minAnswer and maxAnswer, it can accept a price that is artificially limited. An attacker or a sudden market move that pushes the price below the minAnswer will cause the feed to keep returning the capped minimum value. The protocol then uses this stale, bounded price for critical calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, and trade execution. As a result, healthy positions may be liquidated, trades may be executed at incorrect rates, and users may see balances that appear unchanged even though the market has moved dramatically. This issue is most likely to appear on Arbitrum feeds for assets like ETH/USD and many stablecoins, where the circuit‑breaker limits are still active despite Chainlink documentation suggesting they are ignored on most networks. The bug was discovered during a security audit of the Cryptex contract when the auditor noticed that the price feed could return a value that does not correspond to the real market price, yet the contract only asserts a non‑zero answer. The problem is subtle because the returned price is still a plausible number and does not trigger obvious errors, making it hard to detect from the UI where users may see a price that seems static or unexpectedly low. To remediate, the contract should explicitly validate that the fetched answer is greater than the known minimum and less than the known maximum before using it, or fall back to an alternative oracle when the value is out of bounds. This class of bug falls under oracle data validation errors, specifically the misuse of circuit‑breaker limits that lead to price capping and accounting inconsistencies, violating the protocol’s assumption that price feeds always provide an accurate market snapshot.

title: Users Can Use the Referral System to Refer Themselves in Order to Buy Skins at a Discount
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the referral system that enables a user to obtain a discount on skin purchases by referring themselves. The contract checks that the owner of a referral code is not the buyer and, if it is, clears the code. However, the function that registers referral codes in the ReferralRegistry contract has no access control, allowing anyone to create a referral code from any externally owned address. Because a malicious actor can generate a referral code from a secondary address that they control, they can then submit that code when buying skins from their primary address. The check sees the code owner as a different address, treats it as a valid external referral, and applies the discount, effectively bypassing the self‑referral restriction. This can be exploited whenever a buyer supplies a referral code whose owner is an address under the same control as the buyer. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol, as users obtain skins at a reduced price without providing a genuine referral, breaking the economic assumptions of the referral incentive program. The issue affects any participant who can create multiple addresses, the protocol’s revenue model, and potentially the trust of legitimate users. It was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the lack of access control on the registration function and the possibility of using multiple wallets to circumvent the check. The bug is subtle because the contract does appear to prevent self‑referral at the point of purchase, so a casual observer may not notice that the registration step can be abused. The flaw belongs to the class of incentive‑manipulation and authorization‑bypass bugs, where business logic assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between a user and a referral code but the implementation does not enforce it. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an unexpected discount or a “referral applied” badge even though the user did not receive a referral from another party, leading to confusion and apparent loss of funds for the protocol. To remediate, the referral code registration should be restricted to eligible participants (for example, only users who have previously bought or sold a minimum number of skins) and should bind a referral code to the caller’s address in a way that cannot be spoofed from another account. Additionally, the contract could enforce that the referral code owner matches the address that originally registered it, or require proof of ownership before allowing the code to be used, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the referral program.

title: Malicious Buyers Can Get Skins Without Paying For Them If The Steam Trade Is Accepted By the Seller After More Than 24 Hours Have Passed Since the Buy Commit Placement
description:
The CSXTrade.sol contract requires sellers to accept the Steam trade of the buyer for the skin they are selling before receiving their desired amount of tokens. After the trade is accepted by the seller, the Keeper Oracle calls the CSXTrade::keeperNodeConfirmsTrade function, which releases the desired token amount from the contract to the seller. However, in some scenarios, this trading approach can be exploited to get the seller’s skin without paying for it.

If more than 24 hours have passed since the buy commit was made, a malicious buyer can front-run the CSXTrade::keeperNodeConfirmsTrade call with a CSXTrade::buyerCancel call. That way, the buyer will be able to get their deposited tokens back, even though the skin was already traded to them.

Skins are going to get stolen from sellers.
Attack Scenario
To illustrate the issue further, let’s take a look at the following example scenario:

1. Bob creates a CSXTrade for his Karambit Fade

2. Alice makes a buy commit on Bob’s trade and sends him a Stream trade offer for the skin

3. Bob decides to wait a little to see whether he won’t be able to get a better offer for his skin from a different marketplace

4. 2 days later, he decides that the trade he received from CSX is the best one he can get, so he accepts the Steam trade Alice sent him

5. The Keeper Oracle sees that the trade has been made, so it sends a transaction that calls CSXTrade::keeperNodeConfirmsTrade

6. Unfortunately for Bob though, Alice has been carefully monitoring the transaction mempool. After she sees the transaction of the Oracle, she front runs it with her one that calls CSXTrade::buyerCancel

7. The transaction of Alice gets successfully executed, while the one of the Keeper Oracle gets reverted. Alice now has both her tokens back and the skin, while Bob is left empty-handed
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that allows a malicious buyer to obtain the seller’s skin without paying when the seller accepts the Steam trade after a 24‑hour timeout. The CSXTrade contract requires the seller to call an accept function before a Keeper oracle calls keeperNodeConfirmsTrade, which releases the buyer’s deposited tokens to the seller. However, the buyerCancel function can be called by the buyer at any time before the keeper call is finalized and the contract does not restrict this call after the seller has accepted the trade. When the seller waits more than 24 hours before accepting, a buyer can monitor the mempool, detect the pending keeperNodeConfirmsTrade transaction, and submit a buyerCancel transaction that is mined first. The front‑run causes the keeper call to revert, the buyer’s token deposit is refunded, and the skin that was already transferred on Steam remains with the buyer. From the seller’s point of view the skin is sent but the token balance stays unchanged, effectively losing the item without compensation. The issue affects any user listing a skin for sale, the escrow logic of the protocol, and the funds held in the contract. It was discovered during a manual security review that examined the trade lifecycle and identified that the cancel path remains open after acceptance, creating a time‑based race window. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to enforce that the seller must accept before funds are released, yet the cancel function can still be triggered by a front‑running transaction, which may not be evident in normal testing. The recommended mitigation is to restrict buyerCancel so it cannot be called after the seller has accepted the trade, or to require an explicit Keeper or other authority to approve a cancellation after acceptance, thereby removing the race condition. In generic terms this is a front‑running and time‑based race condition in an escrow contract where state transitions are not atomically protected, leading to a situation where funds disappear and the seller’s item is transferred without payment.

title: Vested CSX to Regular CSX Conversion Process Enables Potential Unauthorized Withdrawal of Staked Deposits by Malicious Council
description:
Some of the key privileges of the Council role:
• Ability to execute a forced withdrawal of tokens from the contract via cliff() function without any restrictions. In the standard withdraw() method there is a validation check that requires the vesting period (2 years) to pass before the Vester is able to withdraw.
• Ability to change factory and keeper contracts.
Additionally, the Council role can be changed through changeCouncil() function and mistakenly a wrong address can be given resulting in this role being set to an unexpected address.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the contract’s Council role that permits forced withdrawal of staked CSX tokens via the cliff() function without respecting the two‑year vesting period. The root cause is that the cliff() function is protected only by the Council modifier and lacks any time‑based validation, while the contract also allows the Council address to be changed through changeCouncil() without a confirmation or timelock. An attacker who gains control of the Council role—either by being appointed directly or by the existing council mistakenly assigning the role to an unexpected address—can call cliff() and instantly transfer all deposited tokens to an arbitrary address, effectively stealing users’ stakes. This can be exploited at any moment after the contract is deployed, whenever the Council role is held by a malicious entity, and it affects every participant who has locked CSX in the vesting contract. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that their balance becomes zero or they receive no tokens when attempting a normal withdraw, even though the contract’s UI may still indicate a pending withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined privileged functions and noticed the lack of restrictions on cliff() and the insecure changeCouncil() mechanism. The flaw is hard to notice because the privileged function is intended for emergency use and may never be called in normal operation, so its dangerous side‑effects are hidden behind the assumption that the Council is trustworthy. The bug belongs to the class of privileged‑function abuse and unchecked access‑control, violating the business rule that funds should be locked for a defined vesting period. To remediate, the contract should either remove the unrestricted owner privileges, introduce a timelock for council actions, and replace the single‑step role transfer with a two‑step nomination and acceptance process, ensuring that only a verified and active address can become Council and that any emergency withdrawal is subject to appropriate governance checks.

title: Tokens with a Fee-On-Transfer Mechanism Could Break the Protocol
description:
The current transferring implementation is incompatible with tokens that have a fee-on-transfer mechanism. Such tokens for example is PAXG, while USDT has a built-in fee-on-transfer mechanism that is currently switched off.
This will work incorrectly if the token has a fee-on-transfer mechanism - the contract will cache the amount as its expected added balance, but it will actually add the amount - the fee balance. This will result in the inability to withdraw tokens out of the contract.
However, the likelihood is relatively low since there are interface checks for the supported tokens, but still USDT is one of them.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s assumption that a token transfer will deliver exactly the amount specified in the transfer call. This assumption is violated by fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens, which deduct a small portion of the transferred amount as a fee before the recipient receives the tokens. The contract caches the expected added balance based on the amount argument, but the actual balance increase is lower because of the fee. Consequently, the internal accounting records a higher token balance than what is truly held, and subsequent withdrawal functions rely on the cached value. When a user later attempts to withdraw, the contract believes it has enough tokens, initiates a transfer, and the transfer fails or returns less than expected, leaving the user unable to retrieve their funds. The impact is that deposited tokens become effectively locked, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and causing a mismatch between displayed balances and real holdings. This situation occurs only when a whitelisted token implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism, such as PAXG or USDT when its fee feature is enabled, and the contract uses transferFrom or safeTransferFrom without verifying the post‑transfer balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token handling logic and identified the missing balance verification step. It can be hard to notice because the transfer transaction itself succeeds and the fee is deducted silently, so the contract’s state appears consistent at first glance. From a user’s perspective, a deposit appears successful, the UI shows a positive token balance, but later the withdrawal button either reverts or returns zero tokens, contradicting the expectation of receiving the deposited amount. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens” and violates the business logic that token balances are conserved across transfers. To remediate, the contract should record the token balance of the contract before the transfer, perform the transfer, then compute the actual delta between the pre‑ and post‑transfer balances and use that delta for accounting. This approach must be protected with a non‑reentrant guard because some FoT tokens (e.g., ERC777) may trigger callbacks that could be exploited for re‑entrancy. Alternatively, the protocol could exclude known FoT tokens from its whitelist or clearly document that such tokens are not supported until their fee mechanism is disabled.

title: Inaccessible pause and unpause functions
description: The Game contract inherits from PausableUpgradeable, a feature designed to allow the pausing and unpausing of contract functionalities in emergency situations or for maintenance. However, the contract does not expose the pause and unpause functions to contract administrators. As a result, despite inheriting the pausability feature, administrators are unable to utilize these critical controls to pause or resume the contract's operations when needed, potentially leading to issues during periods requiring immediate intervention.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing external interface for the pause and unpause controls in a contract that inherits the PausableUpgradeable module. Although the contract includes the internal _pause and _unpause functions provided by the upgradeable library, it does not expose public wrappers protected by an owner or authorized role. Consequently, the contract owner cannot trigger the emergency stop mechanism, and all functions guarded by the whenNotPaused modifier remain callable even when a critical bug or attack is discovered. The root cause is an omission in the contract’s API design: the developer failed to add external pause() and unpause() functions that call the internal hooks and enforce onlyOwner access. This omission is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the inherited PausableUpgradeable code appears to be present, giving a false impression that the contract can be halted. The impact is a loss of operational control: the protocol cannot be paused to protect users, leaving funds exposed to exploitation, and the business assumption that the owner can intervene in emergencies is violated. The condition exists from the moment the contract is deployed and affects every participant—owner, users, and the broader protocol—because none can stop the contract’s activity. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the inherited interface with the contract’s public functions and noted the absence of pause/unpause entry points. It may be hard to notice in testing because normal operation proceeds normally and no revert occurs, so the missing control is only evident when an emergency response is required. The recommended remediation is to add external pause() and unpause() functions that invoke _pause() and _unpause() respectively and are restricted to the contract owner or a designated role, thereby restoring the intended emergency stop capability and aligning the contract’s behavior with its security design.

title: M-5 AggregateStablePrice EMA can be manipulated
description:
• AggregateStablePrice2.vy#L167-L168
If the pricew() function, which updates lasttimestamp, is not called for a long time, the value of alpha decreases, leading to a risk of EMA manipulation by a hacker. This occurs because the closer alpha gets to zero, the greater the inﬂuence of the new totalSupply() value, which can be manipulated within the current transaction:
alpha: uint256 = 10**18
if last_timestamp < block.timestamp:
alpha = self.exp(- convert((block.timestamp - last_timestamp) * 10**18 / TVLMATIME, int256))
...
if alpha != 10**18:
alpha = 1.0 when dt = 0
alpha = 0.0 when dt = inf
newtvl: uint256 = self.pricepairs[i].pool.totalSupply()
tvl = (new_tvl * (10**18 - alpha) + tvl * alpha) / 10**18
For example, after 10 * TVLMATIME seconds (which is about 5 days in the current implementation), if no one calls the function, alpha becomes 0.0000453999. Ultimately, if alpha=0, new_tvl will simply be equal to totalSupply().
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exponential moving average (EMA) based price aggregator where the smoothing factor alpha is recomputed based on the elapsed time since the last update. If the update function price_w() is not invoked for an extended period, the time delta grows, causing the exponential term exp(-dt/TVLMATIME) to approach zero. As alpha approaches zero, the EMA formula tvl = (new_tvl * (1-alpha) + tvl * alpha) gives almost full weight to the newly observed totalSupply value. Because new_tvl is read from the pool’s totalSupply within the same transaction, a malicious actor who can influence that value (for example by minting or burning tokens just before the call) can drive the reported price to an arbitrary level. The manipulation can be performed in a single transaction after a long inactivity window, effectively allowing the attacker to set the price feed to the manipulated totalSupply. The impact is that downstream contracts that rely on the aggregated price – such as lending, borrowing, liquidation or fee calculations – may accept incorrect valuations, leading to potential loss of funds, unfair liquidations, or over‑collateralisation. The issue manifests only when the price_w() function has not been called for a period comparable to several multiples of TVLMATIME (about five days in the current deployment), which may happen during low activity periods. Users, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the price feed no longer reflects the true market state. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, who noted that the alpha decay logic can be driven to zero and that the EMA becomes fully controlled by the attacker‑controlled totalSupply. The bug is subtle because the EMA calculation appears mathematically sound and the alpha value is hidden inside a fixed‑point exponent, making the extreme case hard to observe in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum bound on alpha, require periodic calls to price_w() (or a fallback update mechanism), limit the influence of a single totalSupply observation, or add monitoring that flags unusually long gaps between updates. In essence, the vulnerability belongs to the class of time‑dependent smoothing‑factor manipulation bugs where a decaying weight can be driven to zero, allowing an attacker to overwrite an aggregated metric with a malicious input.

title: M-1 Raw calls on ETH transfers allow reentrancy
description:
If WETH is used as collateral, users can choose to receive native ETH when it is sent to users. It happens in
function withdraw_collateral().
• Controller.vy#L514-L521
It breaks Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. So, a call to an arbitrary address can be made in the middle
of functions repay() and _liquidate().
• Controller.vy#L731
• Controller.vy#L795
• Controller.vy#L1054
• Controller.vy#L1069
Thus, an attacker can reenter some other smart contract (excluding this Controller). For example, this
attacker can call rate_write() in AggMonetaryPolicy, and the rate will be updated using old
total_debt (not affected by ongoing repay or liquidate).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw caused by the use of raw low‑level calls when transferring native ETH from the protocol. In the withdraw_collateral function the contract sends ETH directly to an address supplied by the caller without first updating the internal accounting state, breaking the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. The same problem appears in the repay and _liquidate functions, where an external call is performed before the protocol’s debt and collateral variables are fully settled. Because the external call can execute arbitrary code, an attacker can re‑enter other contracts that the protocol interacts with – for example the AggMonetaryPolicy contract – and invoke its rate_write function while the original repay or liquidation transaction is still in progress. This re‑entrancy allows the attacker to cause the monetary policy to be updated using a stale total_debt value, leading to an incorrect interest rate or price feed that benefits the attacker. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting can become inconsistent, potentially allowing the attacker to obtain a more favorable rate, avoid liquidation, or extract value from the system. The issue manifests whenever a user withdraws collateral that is backed by WETH and opts to receive native ETH, or when a repayment or liquidation triggers an ETH transfer before state variables are updated. All participants that rely on correct rate calculations – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the stale data can distort the economic model. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the control flow of the Controller contract and identified raw calls placed between state changes. It is hard to notice because the external call is a legitimate ETH transfer and the contract does not emit explicit warnings; the re‑entrancy only becomes visible when the called contract performs a state‑changing operation back in the original contract’s context. To remediate the issue the protocol should follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern by updating all internal balances and debt records before making any external ETH transfer, and should either use a safe transfer wrapper that limits gas or replace raw calls with a pull‑payment model. In generic terms this is a classic reentrancy vulnerability arising from unsafe external calls that allow an attacker to manipulate protocol state during a transaction, leading to funds disappearing or rates being calculated incorrectly, which violates the expected business logic that collateral withdrawals and repayments are atomic and final.

title: Insufficient Input Data Validation
description:
The following state variables are not validated in any regard or missing additional validation:
royaltyFraction, maxClaimableSupply, maxManagerMintableSupply and vendor in the constructor
at initializing phase.
This can lead to the disfunction of the DarkMythosBalinor.sol due to the fact that all of these vari-
ables are immutable so they can not be changed after deployment time.
Example scenarios are:

1. The royaltyFraction parameter is represented as 10 000 (100%). The check asserts that the
variable should be less than 10 000 (100%) which could potentially allow the deployer to set the
royalty fee to 100% for secondary sales, which could impact the economics of the protocol and
disincentivize the community to trade the tokens. This on the other hand could lead to decreased
trading volume and reduced longevity of the project.

2. If the deployer accidentally sets _maxManagerMintableSupply or _maxClaimableSupply to zero,
updateWhitelistClaimAllocations() and mint() function will revert. Note: For mint() func-
tion, it will revert when isManagerMint or isClaimMint parameter is true.

3. The constructor checks if _royaltyReceiver and _vendor addresses are not address(0).
However, there is a missing check if these addresses are identical. After discussion with the
Dark Mythos team, it was deduced that if the _royaltyReceiver and _vendor addresses are
the same, this could lead to unwanted issues in the business logic and incorrect privileges for
these actors.
bug_full: The contract suffers from insufficient validation of critical constructor parameters, creating a class of input‑validation bugs that can be abused at deployment time. The royaltyFraction, maxClaimableSupply, maxManagerMintableSupply and the two privileged addresses (_royaltyReceiver and _vendor) are stored as immutable state variables without comprehensive checks. Because these values cannot be altered after deployment, any mistake or malicious choice made by the deployer becomes permanent. If the royaltyFraction is set to its maximum allowed value of 10 000 (representing a 100 % royalty on secondary sales), the contract will divert the entire sale price to the royalty receiver, effectively preventing any net proceeds for buyers and sellers. This violates the economic assumptions of the protocol, discourages trading, and can lead to a collapse of market activity. Similarly, setting either maxClaimableSupply or maxManagerMintableSupply to zero makes the allocation functions revert whenever they are called, because the minting logic checks that the requested amount does not exceed a non‑zero supply limit. As a result, legitimate users attempting to claim or managers trying to mint will encounter transaction failures, seeing no tokens minted and potentially receiving error messages such as “supply limit exceeded”. The constructor also checks that the royalty receiver and vendor addresses are not the zero address, but it does not ensure they are distinct. When both roles share the same address, the business logic that separates royalty collection from vendor operations collapses, granting a single actor unintended privileges and opening the door to privilege‑escalation or revenue‑misallocation. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the constructor’s parameter checks and identified missing constraints. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and deploys without errors, and the immutable variables appear to be correctly assigned; only the lack of boundary checks reveals the problem when the contract is exercised. Exploitation occurs at deployment: an attacker who controls the deployment transaction can set the royalty fraction to 100 %, set supply limits to zero, or reuse the same address for both privileged roles, thereby breaking the intended accounting and user experience. Affected parties include token holders who expect to receive a fair share of secondary sales, managers who rely on minting caps, and the overall protocol which may suffer reduced liquidity and trust. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are silent: users may see their claim transactions revert, receive no tokens, or notice that every secondary sale they make yields no net proceeds because the full amount is taken as royalty. The issue belongs to the broader class of immutable‑parameter validation errors, where unchecked inputs at contract creation lead to permanent economic or functional defects. The recommended remediation is to introduce explicit upper bounds for royaltyFraction (e.g., 20 % or 2 000 basis points), enforce non‑zero checks for both supply limits, and require that the royalty receiver and vendor addresses differ, applying the same validation in any setter functions that may modify these roles. By adding these checks, the contract restores its intended economic model, prevents accidental or malicious deployment configurations, and aligns with standard best practices for input validation in immutable smart contracts.

title: Centralization Risks
description:
In the current implementation setup, the owner is meant to be a single Externally Owned Account
(EOA) which could potentially introduce security risks regarding single points of failure or misman-
agement.
One possible attack scenario is if the owner is compromised a DoS attack on the protocol can be
executed based on pausing functionality.
Additionally the following functions: updateWhitelistClaimAllocations(), provideSupply(),
setRoyaltyReceiver(), addManagerContract(), removeManagerContract() are dependant solely
on the owner and a single mistake can lead to serious impact.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk caused by the contract being owned by a single externally owned account (EOA) that has exclusive authority over several privileged functions such as updating whitelist claim allocations, providing supply, setting the royalty receiver, and adding or removing manager contracts. The root cause is the design choice to rely on a single private key for governance, without any multi‑signature, timelock, or decentralized decision‑making mechanism. If the owner’s private key is compromised, an attacker can invoke any of these owner‑only functions. By calling the pause function the attacker can deny service to all users, effectively performing a denial‑of‑service (DoS) attack. By altering whitelist allocations the attacker can prevent legitimate claimants from receiving their entitled tokens, or grant themselves excessive allocations. Changing the royalty receiver can divert earned fees to an address controlled by the attacker, and manipulating the supply functions can inflate or shrink the token supply, breaking the economic model. The impact includes loss of trust, potential loss of revenue, inability for users to interact with the protocol, and possible misdirection of funds. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where the owner’s private key is leaked, mis‑used, or the owner makes an inadvertent mistake while executing privileged calls. All participants—token holders, claimants, royalty beneficiaries, and any downstream contracts that rely on the owner’s actions—are affected because the protocol’s core logic can be altered unilaterally. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the single‑owner pattern as a high‑impact design flaw. It can be hard to notice because the contract may function correctly under normal operation, and the centralization is not always obvious from the code without a deeper governance analysis. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as the contract suddenly being paused, claim transactions reverting with no tokens received, royalty payouts disappearing or being sent to an unknown address, and supply‑related functions behaving unexpectedly. The bug violates basic accounting assumptions that only authorized, transparent governance can modify critical parameters. To remediate the issue the ownership should be transferred to a multi‑signature wallet, a decentralized governance contract, or a timelock proxy that enforces a delay and community oversight before any privileged action is executed. This change distributes authority, reduces the attack surface, and aligns the protocol with best practices for decentralized finance security.

title: Insecure Generation of Randomness Used for Token Determination Logic
description:
It generates a uint256 random value that relies on variables like block.timestamp, randomizationNonce
and msg.sender as a source of randomness is a common vulnerability, as the outcome can be
influenced/predicted by miners/validators, but even normal users can easily replicate these three
sources of entropy:

1. block.timestamp can be replicated inside an attacker contract if the attack transaction is in-
cluded in the same block as the PRNG.

2. randomizationNonce can be predicted since the value is deterministically incremented by 1,
and the previous values are publicly accessible (like any state variable of a smart contract on a
public blockchain).

3. msg.sender can be replicated since it’s simply the attacker contract’s address.
bug_full: An insecure randomness generator is used to decide token‑related outcomes. The contract builds a uint256 pseudo‑random number by hashing together block.timestamp, a monotonically increasing randomizationNonce, and msg.sender. Because all three inputs are either fully deterministic or controllable, the resulting value can be predicted or even forced by a miner, validator, or an attacker deploying a contract that submits the transaction in the same block. The nonce increments by one each call and its previous values are stored on‑chain, so anyone can read the exact sequence. The sender address is simply the attacker’s contract address, which can be chosen arbitrarily. Consequently, an adversary can compute the exact “random” number before the transaction is mined and craft a call that yields a favorable token allocation, such as receiving a higher‑value token or avoiding a penalty. This manipulation occurs whenever the contract’s token‑determination logic relies on this PRNG, typically during minting, reward distribution, or loot‑box style functions. Users experience the symptom that the expected chance‑based reward appears to be missing or always goes to the same address, leading to loss of expected tokens or unfair advantage. The issue was identified during a manual security review that flagged the use of block variables and predictable state as a known anti‑pattern. The bug is subtle because the values look random on the surface and no explicit error is thrown; only statistical analysis or repeated exploitation reveals the bias. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “predictable on‑chain randomness” or “insufficient entropy for PRNG”. To remediate, the contract should replace the ad‑hoc PRNG with a source of verifiable randomness, such as Chainlink VRF, which provides a cryptographically secure random number after a configurable number of block confirmations, preventing miners or attackers from influencing the outcome. Proper integration includes handling the asynchronous callback and verifying the proof before using the random value in token logic.

title: Using the transfer function of address payable is discouraged
description:
The transfer() function only allows the recipient to use 2300 gas. If the recipient uses more than
that, transfers will fail. This could, for example, be the case if vendor is the address of a multisig or
payment splitter that is supposed to execute additional logic after the withdrawal. Furthermore, gas
costs might change in the future, increasing the likelihood of that happening. Also, notice that vendor
is immutable after deployment.
Consider the following scenario:

1. During deployment, Dark Mythos is not aware of this “transfer() issue” and sets vendor to a
contract address (e.g., a payment splitter) that consumes more than 2300 gas.

2. Dark Mythos launches the collection.

3. Users mint the entire collection.

4. Dark Mythos tries to withdraw the revenue from the contract. However, all of their attempts
revert because the recipient consumes more than 2300 gas when receiving the funds.
Notice that Dark Mythos cannot reset vendor to another address (e.g., an externally owned ac-
count) because the contract does not provide such functionality. Therefore, all the revenue that
Dark Mythos earned during the mint of the collection is stuck in the contract forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe Ether withdrawal pattern that relies on address.transfer() which forwards a fixed gas stipend of 2300. The root cause is that the Solidity transfer function imposes this stipend to protect against re‑entrancy, but it also prevents the recipient contract from executing any logic that requires more gas. When the contract’s vendor address is set to a contract (for example a payment splitter or multisig) that performs additional operations on receipt, the transfer call reverts because the 2300 gas is insufficient. Because the vendor address is immutable after deployment, the contract cannot be reconfigured to point to an externally owned account that would accept the transfer. Consequently, any Ether accumulated in the contract becomes locked; attempts to withdraw by the owner revert, leaving the revenue permanently inaccessible. This situation occurs after the contract has collected funds (for example after users mint NFTs) and the owner initiates a withdrawal. The affected parties are the contract owner, the protocol that expects to receive the revenue, and any users who assume the funds will be transferred. The issue was identified during a manual security review that noted the use of transfer() with an immutable vendor address. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without warnings and the failure only appears at runtime when the withdrawal is executed, often after a large amount of Ether has been gathered. The bug belongs to the class of gas stipend limitation or unsafe Ether transfer vulnerabilities, where the fixed gas limit breaks compatibility with modern contract wallets. From a user perspective the UI would show a withdrawal failed message, the balance of the contract would remain unchanged, and the expected payout would be zero. The correct mitigation is to replace transfer() with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas and checks the returned success flag, or to redesign the contract so that the payout address can be updated to an EOA. This change removes the 2300‑gas restriction and allows contracts that need more gas to receive the funds safely.

title: Centralization Risk Due to Trusted Owner
description:
The contract has an owner with the privileged right to pause and unpause most of the contract’s
functionality and therefore it needs to be trusted. Currently, the contract owner is not prevented
from renouncing the ownership while the contract is paused, which could cause any user assets
stored in the protocol, to be locked indefinitely.
Both Dark Mythos and Shieldify have been clear from the get-go that this functionality was only im-
plemented because EU law (Article 30 of REPORT on the proposal for a regulation) currently requires
that a mechanism exists to terminate the continued execution of transactions. Nonetheless, Dark Mythos kindly asked Shieldify to incorporate this (hopefully temporary) issue here in the
report to ensure Dark Myhtos’ users enjoy full transparency. Dark Mythos intends to keep this priv-
ileged role only as long as the legal situation is not fully clarified. Furthermore, Dark Mythos has
implemented a dedicated function to revoke their privileged role in the contract as soon as they
are certain that they don’t violate EU law by doing so. Dark Mythos will make an effort to investi-
gate this issue further and stay up to date with the latest legal developments.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization and governance risk that stems from the contract’s owner having unrestricted authority to pause and unpause the majority of the protocol’s functionality while also being allowed to renounce ownership at any time, including when the contract is in a paused state. This design creates a situation where, if the privileged account either deliberately or inadvertently pauses the contract and then renounces its role, there will be no remaining authority capable of unpausing the system. Consequently, any user assets that are held in the protocol become permanently inaccessible, effectively locking funds and breaking the expected withdrawal flow. The root cause is the combination of two logical flaws: (1) the pause mechanism is granted to a single trusted address without any fallback or multi‑party control, and (2) the renounceOwnership function is not gated by a check that prevents execution while the contract is paused. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting in bad faith, can trigger the pause, renounce ownership, and leave the contract in a dead state. The impact is that users see their balances remain unchanged, withdrawal attempts return no tokens, and the UI may display “contract paused” without indicating that the pause is irreversible, leading to confusion and loss of trust. This condition occurs only when the contract is paused; under normal operation the risk is latent but may go unnoticed because pausing is a legitimate feature and the ability to renounce ownership is often considered a harmless administrative convenience. All participants who have deposited assets, as well as the protocol’s reputation and future governance, are affected. The issue was identified during a manual security review that examined the ownership lifecycle and pause logic, and it can be hard to spot because the code does not emit explicit warnings about the irreversible state and the UI does not differentiate between a temporary pause and a permanent lock. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit renouncing ownership while paused, shift the pause authority to a multi‑signature or timelocked governance contract, or introduce an emergency unpause role that remains functional after ownership is renounced. These changes would restore decentralised control, allow users to recover their funds, and align the implementation with the intended legal compliance mechanism without exposing assets to indefinite lock.

title: Merkle Tree criteria can be resolved by wrong tokenIDs
description:
```solidity
[CriteriaResolution.sol#L157](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/4140473b1f85d0df602548ad260b1739ddd734a5/contracts/lib/CriteriaResolution.sol#L157)

The protocol allows specifying several tokenIds to accept for a single offer.
A merkle tree is created out of these tokenIds and the root is stored as the `identifierOrCriteria` for the item.
The fulfiller then submits the actual tokenId and a proof that this tokenId is part of the merkle tree.

There are no real verifications on the merkle proof that the supplied tokenId is indeed **a leaf of the merkle tree**.
It’s possible to submit an intermediate hash of the merkle tree as the tokenId and trade this NFT instead of one of the requested ones.

This leads to losses for the offerer as they receive a tokenId that they did not specify in the criteria.
Usually, this criteria functionality is used to specify tokenIds with certain traits that are highly valuable. The offerer receives a low-value token that does not have these traits.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Seaport protocol validates criteria‑based ERC‑721 offers that rely on a Merkle tree of acceptable token IDs. When a maker creates an offer with a set of token IDs, the contract stores the Merkle root as the identifierOrCriteria and later checks that the fulfiller supplies a token ID together with a Merkle proof. However, the verification logic does not enforce that the supplied token ID corresponds to a leaf of the tree; it only checks that the proof reconstructs the stored root. Because the leaves are the raw token IDs (unhashed) rather than their hash values, an attacker can construct a token whose ID equals an intermediate hash node of the tree – for example, the Merkle root itself – and present an empty or trivial proof that passes the verification. The attack succeeds when the underlying ERC‑721 contract permits minting of arbitrary token IDs, which the ERC‑721 standard explicitly allows. Consequently, the offerer who expected to receive a specific high‑value token (e.g., token ID 1 or 2 with desirable traits) instead receives a token with an unexpected, often large, hash‑like ID that carries little or no value. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the received NFT has no the expected traits and the payment is lost, effectively "funds disappear" or "refund calculation error". The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by building a Merkle tree of two IDs, minting an NFT whose ID equals the Merkle root, and fulfilling the order with that ID, demonstrating that the protocol accepts the intermediate hash as a valid leaf. The problem is subtle because the proof verification does not raise an error – the UI shows a normal successful trade – making it hard to notice that the wrong asset was transferred. The bug belongs to the class of Merkle‑proof injection flaws where leaf validation is missing. To remediate, the protocol should hash token IDs before inserting them as leaves (or otherwise tag leaf nodes) and recompute the leaf hash on‑chain, ensuring that only true leaf hashes can satisfy the proof; this eliminates collisions between leaf and internal node hashes. Implementing such a fix restores the intended business logic that an offerer receives one of the explicitly listed token IDs and protects the protocol’s economic safety.

title: Wrong items length assertion in basic order
description:
```solidity
[BasicOrderFulfiller.sol#L346-L349](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/BasicOrderFulfiller.sol#L346-L349)

When fulfilling a basic order we need to assert that the parameter `totalOriginalAdditionalRecipients` is less or equal than the length of `additionalRecipients` written in calldata.
However in `_prepareBasicFulfillmentFromCalldata` this assertion is incorrect [(L346)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/BasicOrderFulfiller.sol#L346-L349):

        // Ensure supplied consideration array length is not less than original.
        _assertConsiderationLengthIsNotLessThanOriginalConsiderationLength(
            parameters.additionalRecipients.length + 1,
            parameters.totalOriginalAdditionalRecipients
        );

The way the function is written ([L75](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/Assertions.sol#L75-L83)), it accepts also a length smaller than the original by 1 (basically there shouldn’t be a `+ 1` in the first argument).

Interestingly enough, in the case `additionalRecipients.length < totalOriginalAdditionalRecipients`, the inline-assembly for-loop at [(L506)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/BasicOrderFulfiller.sol#L506) will read consideration items out-of-bounds.
This can be a vector of exploits, as illustrated below.
```
poc:
```solidity
Alice makes the following offer: a basic order, with two `considerationItem`s. The second item has the following data:

consideration[1] = {
	itemType: ...,
	token: ...,
	identifierOrCriteria: ...,
	startAmount: X,
	endAmount: X,
	recipient: Y,
}

The only quantities we need to track are the amounts `X` and recipient `Y`.

When fulfilling the order normally, the fulfiller will spend `X` tokens sending them to `Y`. It’s possible however to exploit the previous bug in a way that the fulfiller won’t need to make this transfer.

To do this, the fulfiller needs to craft the following calldata:

calldata pointer | correct calldata | exploit calldata
---|---|---
… | … | …
0x204 | 1 (tot original) | 1 (tot original)
0x224 | 0x240 (head addRec) | 0x240 (head addRec)
0x244 | 0x2a0 (head sign) | 0x260 (head sign)
0x264 | 1 (length addRec) | 0 (length addRec)
0x284 | X (amount) | X (length sign)
0x2a4 | Y (recipient) | Y (sign body)
0x2c4 | 0x40 (length sign) | 0x00 (sign body)
0x2e4 | [correct Alice sign] | …
0x304 | [correct Alice sign] | …

Basically writing `additionalRecipients = []` and making the signature length = `X`, with `Y` being the first 32 bytes. Of course this signature will be invalid; however it doesn’t matter since the exploiter can call `validate` with the correct signature beforehand.

The transaction trace will look like this:

  * the assertion `_assertConsiderationLengthIsNotLessThanOriginalConsiderationLength` passes;
  * the `orderHash` calculated is the correct one, since the for-loop over original consideration items picks up calldata at pointers {0x284, 0x2a4} [(L513)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/BasicOrderFulfiller.sol#L513-L550);
  * the order was already validated beforehand, so the signature isn’t read;
  * at the end, during the tokens transfers, only `offer` and `consideration[0]` are transferred, since the code looks at `additionalRecipients` which is empty.

Conclusion:

Every Order that is “basic” and has two or more consideration items can be fulfilled in a way to not trade the _last_ consideration item in the list. The fulfiller spends less then normally, and a recipient doesn’t get his due.

There’s also an extra requirement which is stricter: this last item’s `startAmount` (= endAmount) needs to be smallish (< 1e6). This is because this number becomes the signature bytes length, and we need to fill the calldata with extra zeroes to complete it. Realistically then the exploit will work only if the item is a ERC20 will low decimals.

I’ve made a hardhat test that exemplifies the exploit. [(Link to gist)](https://gist.github.com/0xsanson/e87e5fe26665c6cecaef2d9c4b0d53f4)
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the length verification performed when a basic order is fulfilled in the Seaport protocol. The contract asserts that the number of additional recipients supplied in calldata is not less than the original number of additional recipients, but the check adds one to the supplied length before comparing it to the stored original count. This means the function incorrectly accepts a calldata array whose length is one element shorter than required. Because the subsequent assembly loop iterates based on the original count, it reads consideration items beyond the end of the calldata array when the actual array is too short. The out‑of‑bounds read allows an attacker to craft a payload where the final consideration item – typically the payment to the last recipient – is never transferred. The attack works only for basic orders that contain at least two consideration items, where the last item is an ERC20 token with low decimals and a small amount (so that the amount can be abused as a fake signature length). The attacker first validates the order with a correct signature, then submits a malicious fulfillment calldata that declares an empty additionalRecipients array while keeping the original total count, causing the contract to skip the transfer of the last consideration item. From the user's perspective the order appears to succeed, but the intended recipient receives zero tokens and the fulfiller saves the amount that should have been paid. This results in a subtle loss of value: the protocol leaks a discount equal to the skipped amount, which in realistic scenarios is limited (for example, up to a few hundred dollars when exploiting low‑decimal tokens such as WBTC). The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BasicOrderFulfiller library, where the incorrect assertion was noticed and the ensuing out‑of‑bounds read was demonstrated with a crafted transaction. The bug is hard to notice because the order does not revert; the only symptom is missing funds for the last recipient, which may be confused with a failed transfer or rounding error. To remediate the problem the assertion must be corrected by removing the extra “+1” added to the supplied length, ensuring that the supplied additionalRecipients array cannot be shorter than the original count. By fixing the length check the assembly loop will never read beyond the calldata bounds, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing the under‑payment exploit.

title: maxTotalFunds() would be inflated during each call
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the public sale contract where the variable that tracks the maximum amount of funds that can be collected (maxTotalFunds) is incremented each time the tier configuration is updated but never reset to zero. This happens because the internal _setTiers function adds the cap of each new tier to the existing maxTotalFunds value without first clearing the previous total, so repeated calls to setTiers cause the stored maximum to be the sum of all caps ever supplied. An attacker or even a legitimate admin can exploit this by calling setTiers after the contract has been deployed, inflating maxTotalFunds and consequently causing the _getRemainingCap calculation (maxTotalFunds minus totalFundsCollected) to report a larger remaining allowance than intended. As a result, users may be able to purchase tokens beyond the advertised hard cap, leading to oversubscription, distorted token economics, and potential loss of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the tier‑setting function is invoked more than once, which is a scenario that may not be covered by basic tests that only exercise the initial deployment. It affects anyone participating in the sale – investors expecting a fixed supply, the protocol owners who rely on the cap for revenue projections, and downstream contracts that assume the cap is enforced. The bug was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the missing reset of maxTotalFunds. It can be hard to notice because the contract still records a non‑zero remaining cap and the sale appears to function, but the underlying limit is silently larger than intended. To remediate, the logic should either reset maxTotalFunds to zero before aggregating the new tier caps or compute the sum of caps in a temporary variable and assign it to maxTotalFunds, ensuring that the maximum fund limit always reflects the current tier configuration. This class of bug is a typical state‑variable accumulation error that violates the business rule that the total funding cap must be immutable after configuration, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential user‑facing symptoms such as being able to buy tokens when the UI shows the cap as reached or seeing unexpected extra tokens allocated to their balance.

title: Content Spoofing
description:
Content spoofing, also known as content injection, arbitrary text injection, or virtual defacement, is an attack targeting a user through a vulnerability in a web application. This occurs when the application improperly handles user-supplied data, allowing an attacker to inject content, typically via a parameter value, which is then reflected back to the user. This results in the user seeing a modified page under the trusted domain’s context. Often, this type of attack is combined with social engineering tactics, exploiting both a code-based vulnerability and the user’s trust.
The impact of a content spoofing attack varies based on context. If user-supplied information is reflected in a way that is correctly escaped and clearly visually marked, such as in error messages, it may be harmless. However, if the input is not clearly visually distinguished from the legitimate content, it can be used in social engineering attacks. Moreover, if the input is not correctly escaped, it may contain active components, enabling attacks similar to Cross-site Scripting (XSS).
In the specific case of dedprz.virtual.tech, parameters url, w and q can be modified to reflect the frontend changes/defacements directly in the response. The parameters can be used initially to self-deface the website as the application allows the user to change the values on the fly while the components are loading.
poc:
Using a proxy intercept the request when browsing to dedprz.virtual.tech. The following GET request will be available:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=640&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
// Other headers not shown.
From the request above, you can see that parameter url, w and q are having predictable values that can be modified in the request and overalls are parsed by the frontend. First of all if we modify the parameter url with different values, the following error messages appear:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2F../../../&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ffoo.png&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
The requested resource isn't a valid image.
For parameters q and w:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=640&q=7500 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
”q” parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=6400&q=750 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
”w” parameter (width) of 6400 is not allowed
It is clear that application response changes according to the url, q and w values which are allowed to be modified on the fly. In this way, when content is loading, it is possible to execute a defacement by changing the values of the images loading:
We modify the tails image for heads on the fly (which will be processed by the application) in this example:
Request: GET /_next/image?url=%2Fheads-button-active.png&w=640&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech

Figure 2: Response (rendered):

Figure 3: Another defacement rendered example:
bug_full: Content spoofing, also known as content injection or virtual defacement, occurs when a web application reflects user‑controlled data back to the client without proper sanitisation, allowing an attacker to replace legitimate visual elements with arbitrary content. In the examined site the image optimisation endpoint (/_next/image) accepts three query parameters – url, w and q – that are taken directly from the request and used to locate and transform an image before it is sent to the browser. The root cause is insufficient validation and lack of output encoding for these parameters; the server trusts the supplied values and does not enforce a whitelist of allowed paths or a strict numeric range for width and quality. An attacker can intercept a request, modify the url parameter to point to a different image (for example swapping a tails button for a heads button) or supply out‑of‑range values for w and q to trigger error messages that are displayed in the page context. The exploit is performed by sending a crafted GET request such as GET /_next/image?url=%2Fheads-button-active.png&w=640&q=75, which the backend processes and returns the attacker‑chosen image under the trusted domain. This results in the user seeing a modified page that appears to originate from the legitimate site, breaking the expectation that the visual assets correspond to the intended content. From the user’s point of view the expected tails button is replaced by a heads button, or an image fails to load and an error message is shown, creating confusion and potentially facilitating social‑engineering attacks. The vulnerability manifests whenever the frontend loads images through the vulnerable endpoint, affecting any visitor of the site and damaging the protocol’s reputation and trustworthiness. It was discovered during a manual security review by intercepting traffic with a proxy and observing that the parameters could be altered on the fly and that the server responded with the altered content. The issue can be hard to notice because the page still renders an image, just not the intended one, and no obvious error is raised unless extreme values are used. The appropriate remediation is to treat the url parameter as untrusted input: enforce a strict whitelist of permissible image paths, validate that w and q are numeric and fall within accepted ranges, and apply output encoding or content‑security policies to ensure that reflected data cannot be interpreted as part of the page’s trusted content. In generic terms this is a content injection vulnerability that enables virtual defacement, a class of bugs where attacker‑controlled data is reflected in a way that changes the visual or textual appearance of a trusted site without executing script code.

title: Denial of Service due to Business Logic Flaw (Authenticated)
description: When a user connects their wallet to dedprz.virtual.tech, the application does not adequately handle the scenario where the user might accidentally or intentionally press the withdraw button as their first interaction. When this happens, all remaining options/buttons become locked, except for the “Get $USA to Play” button. While this functionality may be convenient during an ongoing game, it creates the impression that the entire application is frozen if it occurs during the user’s initial interaction. Although refreshing the page resolves the issue, this situation effectively results in a form of Denial of Service (DoS), as there is no in-app mechanism for recovery.
poc: With the connected wallet, navigate to dedprz.virtual.tech and hit the Withdraw button. After it, the remaining functionality is completely frozen and the user is unable to start a game until it refreshes the page.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by improper business‑logic handling of the withdraw action when it is invoked as the very first interaction after a wallet is connected to the dApp. The front‑end state machine assumes that a withdraw request can only occur after a game session has been initialized; when this assumption is violated, the UI transition logic disables all interactive elements except the “Get $USA to Play” button and never re‑enables them. This occurs because the withdraw handler does not reset or guard the UI state for the initial‑connection scenario, leading to a locked interface. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit the flaw simply by clicking the withdraw button immediately after connecting their wallet, which triggers the faulty state transition and freezes the application. The impact is that the affected user cannot start a new game, cannot interact with any other functionality, and perceives the whole application as frozen; no funds are lost, but the user experience is severely degraded and the service becomes unavailable for that session. The condition manifests only when the withdraw button is the first action taken; subsequent withdrawals after a game has started do not exhibit the problem. All users of the platform are potentially affected because the UI does not differentiate between intentional and accidental early withdrawals. The issue was discovered during manual functional testing where the auditor exercised edge‑case user flows and observed that the interface became unresponsive without any error messages, making it easy to miss in automated tests. The problem is hard to notice because the UI simply appears frozen, offering no explicit indication that a state‑transition error has occurred, and the only visible remedy is a full page refresh. To remediate, the business logic should be revised to detect an early‑withdraw scenario, reset the UI state, and provide an in‑app recovery path (e.g., re‑enabling the main navigation buttons or displaying a clear “reset” option) rather than leaving the interface locked. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of UI state‑lock denial‑of‑service bugs where improper handling of edge‑case inputs leads to a permanent disablement of user controls, violating the expected behavior that a user can always recover from a transaction without needing to reload the page.

title: Improper Error Handling
description:
Improper error handling can introduce numerous security issues for a website. The most common issue arises when detailed internal error messages, such as stack traces, database dumps, and error codes, are displayed to users (potential attackers). These messages reveal implementation details and vulnerabilities in the site. Additionally, such messages can be disturbing for regular users.
Web applications often generate error conditions during normal operation, such as out-of-memory errors, null pointer exceptions, system call failures, database unavailability, and network timeouts. These errors must be managed according to a well-designed scheme that provides meaningful error messages to users, diagnostic information to site maintainers, and no useful information to attackers. Even when error messages lack detail, inconsistencies in these messages can still reveal critical information about a site’s inner workings and the data it contains.
For example, an error message stating “file not found” when a user attempts to access a non-existent file, and “access denied” when trying to access a restricted file, can inadvertently disclose the existence of hidden files or the site’s directory structure. This inconsistency allows users to infer the presence or absence of files they should not be aware of.
In the specific case of dedprz.virtual.tech, the application does not gracefully handle the errors displayed when the user supplies values for the given parameters, as described in the PoC below.
poc:
Using a proxy intercept the request when browsing to dedprz.virtual.tech. The following GET request will be available:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=640&q=75 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
// Other headers not shown.
From the request above, you can see that parameter url, w and q are having predictable values that can be modified in the request and overalls are parsed by the frontend. Similarly as the content spoofing vulnerability from above we are able to modify the parameter with different values and the following error messages appear:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2F../../../&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ffoo.png&w=828&q=011-10 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
The requested resource isn't a valid image.
For parameters q and w:
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=640&q=7500 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
”q” parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100
Request:
GET /_next/image?url=%2Ftails-button-active.png&w=6400&q=750 HTTP/2
Host: dedprz.virtual.tech
Response:
”w” parameter (width) of 6400 is not allowed
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper error handling issue in the image‑serving endpoint of dedprz.virtual.tech. The endpoint accepts the query parameters url, w and q and attempts to locate and resize an image. When the supplied parameters are malformed or reference disallowed paths, the server returns HTTP 400 responses that contain explicit validation messages such as "Unable to optimize image and unable to fallback to upstream image", "The requested resource isn\'t a valid image", "\'q\' parameter (quality) must be a number between 1 and 100" and "\'w\' parameter (width) of 6400 is not allowed". These messages disclose internal validation rules, allowed numeric ranges and the existence of directory‑traversal checks. The root cause is that the application propagates low‑level validation errors directly to the client instead of mapping them to generic user‑friendly messages. An attacker can craft requests with out‑of‑range or path‑traversal values, observe the precise error text, and infer which files exist, what numeric limits are enforced and how the image optimisation pipeline works. This information can be used to enumerate hidden resources, plan further attacks such as directory traversal, or bypass rate‑limiting by targeting only allowed parameter ranges. The impact is information leakage that weakens the security posture of the web service; regular users may also see confusing or alarming messages, reducing usability. The condition occurs whenever the endpoint processes user‑controlled query parameters that fail validation, which is a common path in normal operation (e.g., malformed URLs, extreme width or quality values). The issue was discovered during a manual security review that intercepted HTTP requests and observed the server’s responses. Because the messages are returned in normal HTTP 400 responses, they are easy to miss unless the tester inspects the body of error responses, making the bug subtle. The proper fix is to replace detailed validation strings with generic error messages (e.g., "Invalid image request") while logging the specific reason internally, and to ensure that path validation does not reveal file existence. The bug belongs to the class of "information disclosure through verbose error messages" and violates the principle that error handling should not expose implementation details or internal state to unauthenticated users.

title: Inability to vest and claim saleTokens
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability of participants to initiate the vesting schedule and subsequently claim the sale tokens they purchased during a public token sale. The contract PublicSale provides a function claimAndStartVesting that internally calls a private helper _setVestingHook, which transfers the allocated sale tokens from the treasury and invokes the VestingManager.createVesting function with a set of parameters, including a start timestamp supplied by the caller. The VestingManager validates the start timestamp with the rule that the start must not be earlier than the current block timestamp; if it is, the call reverts with the custom error InvalidStart. This strict validation becomes a problem when the vesting creation is delayed – for example, if a user forgets to call claimAndStartVesting, if the treasury lacks sufficient funds at the moment of the call, or if the admin does not trigger the vesting in the narrow window defined by the sale’s ClaimAndVest stage. In such cases the start time recorded in the vesting parameters ends up being in the past relative to the block timestamp, causing every subsequent attempt to create the vesting schedule to revert.
