Because the PublicSale.setVesting function, which could be used as a manual fallback to set a correct start time, is restricted to the Completed stage, the admin cannot intervene while the sale is in the ClaimAndVest stage. Consequently, affected users are unable to claim their USDC refunds or receive the sale tokens they purchased; from a user’s perspective the UI may show a zero balance or a missing token allocation despite a successful purchase. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the sale contract’s lifecycle logic, where the auditor identified the mismatch between the vesting start validation and the timing of the claim function. The bug is subtle because the revert only occurs after the start time has already passed, making it easy to miss during normal testing where the claim is performed promptly. The root cause is a combination of an overly strict start‑time check in the vesting manager and the lack of a mechanism to adjust or recreate the vesting schedule after the initial window. To remediate, the contract should either relax the start‑time requirement by allowing a start time equal to or later than the current block timestamp, automatically substitute the current timestamp when a past start is supplied, or extend the permission of the setVesting admin function to be callable during the ClaimAndVest stage so that the owner can manually correct vesting parameters for affected users. Implementing any of these fixes would restore the ability of participants to claim their allocated tokens and prevent funds from becoming unintentionally locked.

title: M-4 CONTROLLER.total_debt() may not be up to date
description:
• AggMonetaryPolicy2.vy#L171
The MainController.updaterate() calls the monetary policy rate calculation method which may use a not updated total_debt().
For example, in the adjustloan() method the updaterate() is called before the total_debt update (MainController.vy#L781):
```solidity
debt_adjustment: int256 = MarketOperator(market).adjustloan(account, coll_change, debt_change_final, max_active_band)
self.updaterate(market, c.amm, c.mpidx) // self.total_debt is not updated
total_debt: uint256 = self.uintplusint(self.total_debt, debt_adjustment)
self.total_debt = total_debt
```
In case of large differences, AggMonetaryPolicy2 may not calculate the new rate correctly.
bug_full: During a loan adjustment the MainController calls updaterate before it updates its internal total_debt variable. The monetary policy contract reads total_debt to compute the new interest rate, so it works with a stale value. This ordering flaw means that when a large debt increase or decrease is applied, the rate is calculated on an outdated aggregate debt figure, producing an incorrect rate. An attacker who can trigger a sizable debt adjustment can therefore manipulate the reported rate, potentially causing interest rates to be too low or too high, affecting borrowing costs, liquidation thresholds and overall protocol economics. The bug manifests when adjustloan invokes updaterate and only afterwards adds the debt adjustment to total_debt. Users may notice that after borrowing more, the displayed rate does not reflect the new debt amount, or that their collateral appears to be at risk despite no change in their position. The issue was identified during a systematic audit of the monetary policy integration. Because the rate calculation is a pure function of total_debt, the problem does not raise obvious runtime errors and can remain hidden until a large debt swing occurs. The proper fix is to ensure that total_debt is updated before calling updaterate, or to pass the adjusted debt amount directly to the rate calculation so that the policy always works with the current aggregate debt. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑inconsistency errors where dependent calculations are performed on stale contract state, breaking accounting assumptions and leading to incorrect financial outcomes.

title: M-5 Not reverting on the sequencer downtime
description:
AggregateChainedOracle uses stored prices during the sequencer downtime:
• AggregateChainedOracle.sol#L145-L154
• Layer2UptimeOracle.sol#L31-L38
This is a risky approach, potentially leading to the use of irrelevant prices.
The approach demonstrated in Chainlink's documentation is different:
• https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/l2-sequencer-feeds
The example, it reverts with SequencerDown() or GracePeriodNotOver().
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an oracle contract that continues to provide a stored price even when the underlying Layer‑2 sequencer is offline. The root cause is that the contract does not check the sequencer status before returning the cached price, contrary to the recommended pattern in Chainlink documentation where the call reverts with SequencerDown() or GracePeriodNotOver() during downtime. An attacker who can trigger or wait for a sequencer outage can then cause the oracle to supply stale or irrelevant price data to downstream contracts. Because the price is still returned, the downstream logic proceeds as if the market data were fresh, leading to calculations based on outdated values. This can result in users receiving incorrect trade execution prices, receiving zero or excessive payouts, or experiencing unexpected balance changes. The impact is financial loss for users and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions, as the system relies on accurate, timely price feeds for settlement and risk management. The condition under which the bug manifests is any period when the sequencer is down or within the grace period after it comes back online; the contract will still output the last stored price instead of reverting. All participants that depend on the oracle – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because they trust the price feed to be valid. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against Chainlink’s official guidance. It is subtle because the contract does not throw an error; the UI may display a price that looks normal, making the problem hard to notice until a trade yields an unexpected result. The proper fix is to integrate the sequencer status check and revert the call when the sequencer is down or the grace period has not elapsed, ensuring that downstream contracts never receive stale data during these windows. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of oracle availability checks and stale‑data usage, where a contract fails to enforce freshness guarantees for external data sources, violating the business logic that assumes price feeds are always up‑to‑date.

title: M-6 AggregateStablePrice EMA can be manipulated
description:
• AggregateStablePrice.vy#L156-L157
If the price_w() function, which updates last_timestamp, is not called for a long time, the value of alpha decreases, leading to a risk of EMA manipulation by a hacker.
This occurs because the closer alpha gets to zero, the greater the influence of the new totalSupply() value, which can be manipulated within the current transaction:
```solidity
alpha: uint256 = 10**18
if last_timestamp < block.timestamp:
    alpha = self.exp(- convert((block.timestamp - last_timestamp) * 10**18 / TVL_MA_TIME, int256))
...
if alpha != 10**18:
    alpha = 1.0 when dt = 0
    alpha = 0.0 when dt = inf
new_tvl: uint256 = self.price_pairs[i].pool.totalSupply()
tvl = (new_tvl * (10**18 - alpha) + tvl * alpha) / 10**18
```
For example, after 10 * TVL_MA_TIME seconds (which is about 5 days in the current implementation), if no one calls the function, alpha becomes 0.0000453999. Ultimately, if alpha=0, new_tvl will simply be equal to totalSupply().
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exponential‑moving‑average (EMA) based price aggregator that can be manipulated when its update function price_w() is not invoked for an extended period. The contract computes a smoothing factor alpha that decays as the time since the last update grows; when the elapsed time approaches the configured moving‑average window (TVL_MA_TIME), alpha approaches zero. With alpha near zero the EMA formula gives almost full weight to the freshly read totalSupply() value (new_tvl). Because totalSupply() can be supplied by a pool that the attacker controls within the same transaction, the attacker can force the EMA to adopt an arbitrary price by inflating or deflating the pool’s token supply. The exploit can be triggered simply by waiting long enough for alpha to decay (for example five days in the current parameters) and then submitting a transaction that reports a manipulated totalSupply. From the user’s perspective the protocol may suddenly report a wildly incorrect stable‑coin price, causing liquidations, incorrect collateral valuations, or loss of funds when downstream contracts rely on the price. The issue appears only after a period of inactivity, making it hard to notice because the price feed continues to return a value that looks plausible until the manipulation occurs. The bug belongs to the class of “time‑decay smoothing factor manipulation” or “EMA weight exhaustion” bugs, where a decay parameter becomes too small and lets a single input dominate the average. It was discovered during a manual audit of the AggregateStablePrice contract when the auditor examined the alpha calculation and observed that alpha can become arbitrarily close to zero. To mitigate the risk the protocol should enforce regular calls to price_w(), cap the minimum value of alpha, fallback to a safe price when updates are stale, or replace the EMA with a time‑weighted average that does not allow a single observation to overwrite the history. Implementing monitoring that alerts when price_w() has not been called for a long interval is also recommended.

title: M-7 isMintEnabled blocks extra functionality
description:
• BridgeToken.sol#L290
The isMintEnabled flag blocks the internal _mint() method. This can lead to user transactions getting stuck during cross-chain transfers. For example, if funds are burned on the first chain but cannot be minted on the second chain because the admin disables isMintEnabled midway.
Overall, the inability to mint internally blocks various functionalities:
• Creating and increasing debt.
• Adding liquidity from PegKeeperRegulator: PegKeeperRegulator.vy#L489
• The collect_fees() method: MainController.vy#L827
• There is also a risk of funds getting stuck between chains.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a global boolean flag named isMintEnabled that is consulted by the internal _mint() routine. Because the flag is used as a gate for minting, any administrative action that disables it also blocks every internal operation that relies on minting, including cross‑chain token bridging, debt creation, liquidity addition by the PegKeeperRegulator, and the collect_fees() routine in the main controller. When a user initiates a cross‑chain transfer, the source chain burns the tokens and expects the destination chain to mint the equivalent amount. If the admin disables isMintEnabled after the burn but before the mint, the mint call is rejected, leaving the user’s balance on the destination chain at zero while the source chain has already deducted the funds. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful on the sending side, but the received balance remains unchanged, creating the impression that funds have vanished. The issue occurs whenever the flag is toggled, especially during active bridging or any protocol function that internally calls _mint. All participants that depend on minting – regular users, liquidity providers, borrowers, and fee collectors – are affected because their expected state changes cannot be performed. The problem was identified during a manual audit that traced the flag’s usage across several contracts and recognized that it is not isolated to LayerZero (LZ) bridge features but is also tied to core protocol logic. Because the flag is a single point of control, the bug can be subtle and may not be obvious from the UI; users only see missing tokens or failed operations without an explicit error message. To remediate, the protocol should decouple emergency disabling of bridge‑specific functionality from core minting capabilities, for example by introducing a separate emergency switch for LZ features or by ensuring that minting cannot be globally disabled, and by adding fallback mechanisms that allow manual recovery of stuck funds when minting is temporarily unavailable.

title: M-8 BridgeToken.sendSimple() does not call msgInspector
description:
• OFTCore.sol#L211
• BridgeToken.sol#L153
The OFTCore.send() method calls msgInspector. However, the new BridgeToken.sendSimple() method does not involve such a call.
Thus, if msgInspector is configured, the call to msgInspector will be ignored when sendSimple() is called.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a bypass of the message‑inspection hook in the bridge token contract. The core OFT contract provides a send() function that invokes a configurable msgInspector component before forwarding a cross‑chain message. A newer convenience function sendSimple() was added in BridgeToken and it forwards the message directly without calling msgInspector. If the deployment configures msgInspector to enforce compliance checks, rate limits, black‑list validation or other security policies, those checks are silently skipped when sendSimple() is used. An attacker can therefore craft a transfer that avoids all intended validation, allowing unauthorized token movement or violating accounting assumptions of the bridge. The issue manifests whenever a user or contract calls sendSimple() instead of send(), which may be indistinguishable from the UI perspective because both functions appear to perform a token transfer. Users expect that every outbound transfer is inspected, but the simple path provides no such guarantee, leading to situations where tokens are moved without any audit trail or restriction. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge code when the reviewer noticed that the call to msgInspector present in send() was absent in sendSimple(). Because the two functions have similar signatures, the omission can be hard to notice without a detailed code review, and the functional impact may only become apparent after an unexpected transfer occurs. To remediate, the sendSimple() implementation should be updated to invoke the same msgInspector hook as send(), or the contract should enforce that only the inspected path can be used for cross‑chain transfers. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of security‑critical hook bypasses, where optional validation logic is unintentionally omitted, breaking the intended security model and potentially causing funds to disappear or accounting to become inconsistent.

title: Invariants are not checked after calling calculateDistributeExcessIdleShareProceedsNetLongEdge- CaseSafe
description:
calculateDistributeExcessIdleShareProceedsNetLongEdgeCaseSafe returns:
z_proceed = z_og - ((z_og / P_og) * (sLP / (sLP + sW)) * PV0 - z_flat)
or in other words:
z_og - (1 / P_og) * (sLP / (sLP + sW)) * PV0 - z_flat
1. This scaling is independent of the number of iterations performed in the Newton approximation loop. This is not really an issue just an observation that one the calculation ones picks this specific value only depending on the original point.
2. After one finds z we still need to check that uint256(_params.netCurveTrade) <= maxBondAmount is false on the updated curve C(z, P, y), otherwise the assumption where z + z_curve - z_min = (P_og / z_og) * z would be wrong which would break: PV0 / (sLP + sW) = PV1 / sLP
3. z_proceed is not compared to the idle share reserves to make sure it cannot be greater than that value, we need to check: z_proceed ≤ I
bug_full: The contract contains a logical flaw in the routine that calculates the excess idle‑share proceeds after a net‑long edge trade. The routine computes a value called z_proceed using a scaling factor that depends only on the original curve point (z_og, P_og) and the pool composition (sLP, sW). After the Newton‑approximation loop finishes, the code updates the curve to a new point (z, P, y) but fails to enforce two critical invariants that the protocol’s accounting model relies on. First, it does not verify that the net trade amount on the updated curve, represented by _params.netCurveTrade, stays below the maximum bond amount allowed for the curve (maxBondAmount). If this condition is violated, the derived relationship z + z_curve – z_min = (P_og / z_og) * z no longer holds, breaking the invariant PV0/(sLP+sW) = PV1/sLP that guarantees proportional value distribution between the idle share pool and the liquidity provider pool. Second, the routine never checks that the calculated z_proceed is bounded by the idle‑share reserves I. Without this check, the function could claim more proceeds than actually exist in the idle‑share pool, effectively allowing the protocol to distribute phantom funds. An attacker or a mis‑behaving participant could trigger the function with parameters that cause either of these conditions to be true, resulting in an over‑allocation of assets, a mismatch in the protocol’s accounting, and potentially a loss of funds from the idle‑share reserve. The issue manifests only when calculateDistributeExcessIdleShareProceedsNetLongEdgeCaseSafe is invoked with a state where the Newton iteration converges to a point that would make netCurveTrade exceed maxBondAmount or where the derived z_proceed exceeds the idle‑share balance. Because the function returns a numeric result without any revert or warning, the problem can be hidden from users; the UI may simply show a successful transaction while the internal accounting becomes inconsistent, leading to later failures or unexpected zero balances for users expecting a refund. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the mathematical invariants of the curve‑trading logic. It is subtle because the missing checks are not obvious from the function signature and the calculations appear mathematically sound in isolation. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly assert that _params.netCurveTrade is not greater than maxBondAmount after the point update, and that the computed z_proceed does not exceed the idle‑share reserve I before any token transfers are performed. These checks restore the required accounting invariants and prevent the protocol from distributing more value than it holds, thereby preserving financial integrity.

title: In some cases maxShareReservesDelta can be greater than the idle share reserves in calculateDis- tributeExcessIdle
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that distributes excess idle share reserves in a liquidity pool. The function first computes an initial Newton‑method guess (Δz_guess) for the amount of idle shares that can be reclaimed. When the pool is net short, the formula can produce a guess that is larger than the actual idle share balance (I). The implementation then enters a Newton iteration loop that is allowed to terminate after a single iteration or an early return. Because the initial guess is not clamped before the loop, the early‑exit path can leave the variable maybeMaxShareReservesDelta greater than the idle reserves, bypassing the later safeguard that caps the value to the idle amount. Consequently the contract may record that more idle shares have been distributed than actually exist, breaking the accounting invariants of the pool. From a user’s perspective this can manifest as a mismatch between expected and actual share balances – for example a liquidity provider may see their share count increase unexpectedly or, conversely, later transactions may fail because the pool’s internal accounting believes it has allocated more shares than it holds. The issue only appears under specific conditions: the pool must be net short, the optimal share target must be lower than the current share amount, and the Newton method must exit early. It was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that examined edge‑case arithmetic in the distribution logic. The bug is subtle because the faulty path is rarely exercised; normal operation with multiple Newton iterations would apply the clamp correctly, so the error does not surface in routine tests. The class of bug is an unchecked mathematical guess combined with premature loop termination, leading to a “guess‑overflow” or “clamping‑bypass” error. To remediate, the initial guess should be bounded by the idle share reserves before entering the Newton loop, and the loop’s early‑exit logic should enforce the same bound, ensuring that maybeMaxShareReservesDelta can never exceed the actual idle balance. This restores the invariant that distributed idle shares are always less than or equal to the pool’s idle reserves, preserving correct accounting and preventing unexpected share inflation or loss.

title: After trading on the curve in closeShort and applying the fees, spot price is not check to make sure it is still below 1
description:
In _calculateCloseShort, one checks the following inequality to make sure the non-matured portion of Δy which is trΔy when given back to the pool does not bear negative interest:
(P * (z - P + Δz_curve)) / (y - trΔy) * ts ≤ (1 - φ_c * (1 - p_spot)) ≤ 1
The far right inequality should be right since we need to have checked that before trading on the curve we were in the region with p_spot ≤ 1. Thus the negative interest inequality would guarantee that the point (z - P + Δz, y - trΔy) would also have a spot price of less than 1.
But after trading on the curve we add the LP/curve fees minus the governance fee to the share so:
(z - P, y) → (z - P + Δz, y - trΔy) → (z - P + Δz + (1 - φ_g) * f_c, y - trΔy)
since the share reserves have increased when adding the pool fees, one does not necessarily know that the spot price at this point is still less than 1:
(P * (z - P + Δz_curve + (1 - φ_g) * f_c)) / (y - trΔy) * ts
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the short‑position closing routine of a DeFi protocol that trades against a curve pool. The function that calculates the settlement, _calculateCloseShort, verifies that the spot price of the pool remains below the threshold of one before the trade is executed. This check is intended to guarantee that the non‑matured portion of the delta‑y amount (trΔy) does not incur negative interest, which would otherwise cause the protocol to return more value than it should. However, after the trade the implementation adds the curve fees (minus a governance fee) to the pool’s share reserves and never re‑evaluates the spot‑price condition. Because the fee addition increases the numerator of the spot‑price formula, the resulting price can rise above one, violating the original inequality. The root cause is an incomplete validation: the contract assumes that adding fees cannot push the spot price over the safe bound, an assumption that is not mathematically guaranteed. An attacker can craft a trade that pushes the fee‑adjusted reserves just enough for the spot price to exceed one, causing the protocol to credit the caller with a larger amount of assets than justified. This manifests to users as an unexpectedly high payout when closing a short, or conversely as a loss of funds for the pool when the protocol over‑pays. The issue appears only after the fee‑adjustment step, making it subtle and easy to miss during casual testing because the price may still be close to one and the discrepancy can be small. It was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the mathematical invariants of the closing logic and noticed that the final spot‑price check was omitted. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑condition validation omission” or “invariant breach after state mutation”, where a critical economic invariant is not re‑checked after a state‑changing operation. To remediate, the contract should enforce the spot‑price inequality after the fee addition, for example by requiring P*(z‑P+Δz_curve+(1‑φ_g)*f_c) ≤ y‑trΔy, or by directly checking that the resulting spot price is ≤1. This ensures that the pool never enters a state where the spot price is above one, preserving the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unintended fund transfers.

title: Large vault share price updates can be captured by open/close short
description: When opening a short, the user deposits c / c0 * dy - dz * c, when closing in the same transaction, they receive base proceeds are also c' / c0 * dy - dz * c', where dz * c' dz * c as this represents the bond sell and buyback part of the short. This can lead to a profit when a vault share price transaction increasing c is sandwiched. The trader makes a profit and the loss must therefore come from the LPs in equal terms.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑capture flaw that allows a trader to earn a net profit by opening a short position, forcing a vault share price increase, and then closing the short within the same transaction. The root cause is that Hyperdrive computes the short’s deposit and redemption amounts directly from the current vault share price (c) without applying any smoothing or time‑weighted averaging. When the share price is updated to a higher value (c') before the short is closed, the redemption formula uses c' while the deposit used c, creating a positive differential that translates into extra base tokens for the trader. An attacker can exploit this by sandwiching a large share‑price update between the open and close calls, for example by triggering a large deposit or other state‑changing operation that raises c, then immediately closing the short. The impact is that the profit extracted by the attacker is effectively taken from the liquidity providers, reducing their balances and breaking the accounting invariants of the pool. This condition occurs whenever the protocol permits a short to be opened and closed in the same block or transaction and the vault share price can change non‑linearly between those two calls. The affected parties are short sellers who can gain unintended profit, liquidity providers who lose value, and ultimately the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a test called test_sandwich_vault_share_price_update, which showed a non‑negative profit after a simulated share‑price growth. The bug is subtle because the profit may be modest and can be masked by fees, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. Conceptually, the fix is to decouple short accounting from instantaneous share‑price spikes, for example by using a smoothed or time‑averaged price, enforcing a minimum time delay between opening and closing a short, or redesigning the short mechanics so that both sides of the trade reference the same price snapshot. By doing so the protocol would prevent the capture of artificial price movements and preserve the intended risk‑sharing between traders and liquidity providers.

title: Wrong zeta fee adjustments when closing longs
description:
The z and zeta reserves are expected to update to z' and zeta' as follows (when closing longs):
• z' should reduce by the total trade but include LP fees (gov fees are not reinvested): z' = z - shareProceeds + fees_total - govFees_total.
• The effective reserves z' - zeta' should reduce by the curve trade shareProceedsCurve but reinvest the curve LP fees (fee_c - govFee_c): z' - zeta' = (z - zeta) - shareProceedsCurve + fee_c - govFee_c.
• To get there, the share adjustments need to be updated by the flat trade and the flat LP fees zeta' = zeta - (shareProceeds - shareProceedsCurve) + (fee_f - govFee_f).
Therefore, shareAdjustmentDelta = (shareProceeds - shareProceedsCurve) - (fee_f - govFee_f) but in the code it is shareAdjustmentDelta = (shareProceeds - shareProceedsCurve) - (fee_total - govFee_total) + fee_c.
(dz_c, dy_c, shareProceeds) = HDM.calculateCloseLong(...)
dz_c' = dz_c - fee_c
shareProceeds' = shareProceeds - (fee_c + fee_f) = shareProceeds - fee_total
dz = shareProceeds' + govFee_total = shareProceeds - fee_total + govFee_total = shareProceeds - (fee_total - govFee_total)
dzeta = dz - dz_c' = dz - (dz_c - fee_c) = (shareProceeds - dz_c) - (fee_total - govFee_total) + fee_c
it should be (shareProceeds - dz_c) - (fee_f - govFee_f) where (fee_f - govFee_f) can be obtained by (fee_total - govFee_total) - (fee_c - govFee_c)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee adjustment applied when a user closes a long position. The contract is supposed to update the z and zeta reserves by subtracting the trade proceeds and adding only the flat LP fees while keeping governance fees separate. Instead, the implementation calculates the shareAdjustmentDelta using the total fee amount (fee_total) and then adds the curve fee (fee_c) back, which results in the flat fee component being double‑counted and the governance portion being omitted from the net adjustment. This mis‑calculation occurs in the shareCurveDelta update where the code subtracts curveFee directly instead of subtracting the net curve fee after removing the governanceCurveFee. Because the reserves are updated with the wrong delta, the effective reserve balance (z'‑zeta') can be reduced by an amount that does not reflect the actual trade, causing the protocol’s accounting to diverge from the expected mathematical model. An attacker or any user who closes a long position can trigger the bug and receive a payout that is lower than it should be, while the protocol’s internal accounting records a higher fee collection, effectively siphoning value from users or creating a deficit that may later be covered by other participants. The impact is medium risk: funds may disappear from a user’s balance, refunds may be missing, and the protocol’s invariant that total reserves equal the sum of user balances plus accrued fees is broken. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to the close‑long function that involves both curve and flat fees; the error is hidden because the fee calculations are spread across several internal functions and the discrepancy may be small enough to escape casual testing. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, which compared the intended reserve update formulas with the actual implementation and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the contract’s state variables appear to change normally, and only a detailed accounting audit reveals that the fee components are applied incorrectly. To fix the problem, the shareCurveDelta update should subtract the net curve fee after removing the governance portion, i.e., replace the statement shareCurveDelta -= curveFee with shareCurveDelta -= (curveFee - governanceCurveFee), ensuring that only the intended flat fee is deducted and governance fees are accounted for separately. This correction restores the proper reserve arithmetic, prevents users from receiving less than expected, and maintains the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: LPs are paying twice for governance fees when opening longs
description: The _calculateOpenLong function first computes fees on the bond amount that is paid out to the trader. The governance fee measured in bonds is removed from the bond reserves, then converted to a vault shares amount, and again removed from the share reserves. The governance fees are essentially removed twice, once from the bond and once from the share reserves. Meaning, the LPs are paying twice for it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double‑charging of governance fees when a liquidity provider (LP) opens a long position. The contract's _calculateOpenLong routine first deducts a governance fee from the bond amount that is paid to the trader. That fee is subtracted from the bond reserves, then the same amount is converted into vault share units and subtracted again from the share reserves. Because the fee is removed from both the bond and the share side, the LP effectively pays the governance fee twice. This occurs whenever a long position is opened through the open‑long path, i.e., any call that triggers _calculateOpenLong with a non‑zero bondProceeds. The root cause is the incorrect handling of the governance fee delta: the fee is accounted for in bondReservesDelta and then again in shareReservesDelta, instead of being transferred from bonds to shares. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the protocol itself enforces the double deduction, so any user opening a long suffers reduced net proceeds. The impact is that LPs receive fewer shares for the same amount of bonds, effectively losing a portion of their capital equal to the governance fee percentage. Over time this erodes LP returns and may make the market unattractive. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee calculation logic, where the auditor noticed that the governance fee variable was applied twice. It can be hard to notice because the overall accounting still balances – the total value removed from the system matches the fee amount, but it is taken from two different reserve pools, masking the double charge in simple balance checks. The correct fix is to remove the governance fee only from the share reserves, treating the fee as a conversion from bonds to shares, and to leave the bond reserves unchanged for that portion. In other words, the governance fee should be subtracted from bondReservesDelta only if it is being added back, and the fee amount should not be deducted twice. This class of bug is a fee‑double‑counting or accounting‑misallocation error, where a charge is applied to multiple accounting buckets, violating the intended economic model that each fee is charged once. From a user perspective, a trader opening a long expects to receive a certain amount of vault shares for the bonds supplied, but instead receives fewer shares, effectively seeing “my balance is lower than expected” or “the fee seems higher than advertised”. The protocol’s business logic assumes that governance fees are taken once from the bond side and redistributed as shares; the double removal breaks that assumption and leads to unintended loss of LP capital.

title: checkpoint can be re-entered
description: Most public functions of Hyperdrive have reentrancy guards but the checkpoint function does not. It can change important contract state like reserves. This can interfere with other functions that don't expect state to change during a _deposit call. For example, the following call StEthHyperdrive.openShort -> _openShort -> _deposit performs a refund that happens in the middle of the openShort function. It then continues execution with the _applyShort function. One could re-enter checkpoint during _deposit to apply a checkpoint, changing the market state. This allows calculating a swap that would violate solvency requirements but can pass as solvency is only checked after _deposit. It is also possible that after the market state is updated in _applyCheckpoint there would be some excess idle to be distributed. If so the curve C is scaled down to C. But when we call _applyOpenShort the inputs are from the deltas calculated when we traded on C and not C which might push our point (z, , y) further to the right (not past the solvency or minimum line but more than the amount it should).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the checkpoint routine of the Hyperdrive market contract. Unlike the majority of public functions, checkpoint does not carry a re‑entrancy guard, allowing an attacker to invoke it while the contract is in the middle of executing another operation that expects the market state to remain unchanged. The root cause is the absence of a non‑reentrant modifier (or equivalent checks‑effects‑interactions pattern) on checkpoint, which can be called indirectly through an external call performed during the _deposit step of an open‑short transaction. When a user calls openShort, the contract executes _openShort, then _deposit, which issues a refund to the caller. That external call can be hijacked to re‑enter checkpoint, causing the market’s reserves and the pricing curve C to be updated before the remaining logic (_applyShort) runs. Because the solvency check is performed only after _deposit returns, the contract validates the market state that was true before the re‑entrancy, while the actual state has already been altered. This mismatch enables the calculation of a swap that violates the protocol’s solvency requirements, allowing a trader to obtain a short position that is larger than it should be or to trigger an incorrect distribution of excess idle assets. The impact can be severe: the market may become under‑collateralised, liquidity providers’ funds can be mis‑allocated, and users may see unexpected token balances, such as receiving more short tokens than anticipated or observing a sudden loss of funds after a trade. The issue manifests whenever openShort (or any other function that performs a refund or external call) is executed while checkpoint is callable, i.e., under normal usage conditions. It primarily affects traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the accounting assumptions that the curve C remains constant during a trade are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the presence of re‑entrancy guards across functions and identified checkpoint as the outlier. It is hard to notice because most functions are protected, the re‑entrancy occurs only in a narrow execution window, and the solvency check passes after the state change, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, checkpoint should be protected with a re‑entrancy guard, and the sequence of _calculateOpenShort, _applyOpenShort, and any state‑changing calls should be made atomic so that the pricing curve cannot be altered between the calculation and its application. Additionally, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern to ensure external calls cannot trigger re‑entrancy into critical state‑changing functions.

title: totalSupply / balances accounting invariant will break on transfers to address(0) and address(this)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a design choice that stores the maximum uint256 value in the balance mapping for the zero address and for the token contract’s own address. The intention is to make any transfer to those addresses overflow and therefore revert, protecting users from accidentally burning tokens. However, the contract uses the Solmate ERC20 implementation, which performs balance updates inside unchecked blocks. In an unchecked block, adding a positive amount to a balance that already equals type(uint256).max silently wraps around to zero instead of throwing. As a result, when a mint or transfer targets address(0) or address(this), the balance arithmetic overflows, the stored balance becomes a small value (often zero or a wrapped amount) while the totalSupply variable is still increased by the minted amount. This breaks the fundamental accounting invariant that the sum of all balances must be less than or equal to totalSupply. The bug can be exploited by calling the mint function with the zero address or the contract address as the recipient, causing totalSupply to rise without a corresponding increase in observable balances, effectively allowing the protocol to report a higher supply than actually held by users. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that appears to mint tokens may result in the user’s balance staying at zero or showing an unexpected reduction, leading to confusion such as “my balance didn’t change after minting” or “the token supply looks larger than the sum of all wallets”. The issue occurs only when the contract relies on unchecked arithmetic for balance updates and deliberately sets sentinel max balances, conditions that are easy to miss during testing because the overflow does not generate an exception. The audit discovered the problem by reviewing the balance initialization logic and noting the interaction with Solmate’s unchecked blocks, a subtle combination that is not obvious from a superficial code read. Detecting the bug is difficult because the max‑value sentinel looks intentional and the overflow does not produce a revert, so normal transaction logs appear normal. To remediate, the sentinel assignments should be removed and explicit checks should be added to reject transfers, mints, or approvals involving address(0) or the contract’s own address, ensuring that balance arithmetic never starts from a value that can overflow. This restores the totalSupply‑balances invariant and aligns the contract’s behavior with standard ERC20 expectations, preventing accounting anomalies and protecting users from silent balance loss.

title: calculateSpotPrice(...) should not use _normalizedTimeRemaining
description:
When one trades on the curve, the following share-bond curve is used (with fixed ts):
c (z)^(1-ts) + y^(1-ts) = k
If one calculates the spot price which is the slope of the perpendicular line to the tangent of the curve at a point like (z, y) we would get:
dz / -dy = (1/c) * (z/y)^ts
Instead in calculateSpotPrice(...) the spot price is calculated as:
dz / -dy = (z/y)^(tr * ts)
There are two issues where the first is more important:
1. The (1/c) factor is not considered. This is due to a wrong NatSpec comment that mentions calculateSpotPrice(...) calculates the spot price without slippage of bonds in terms of shares, but it should be the spot price of bonds in terms of the base.
2. tr or _normalizedTimeRemaining does not have a concrete meaning since it is not used in the definition of the curve, but one can apply it to manipulate the price which will be used in fee calculations. But again those fee calculations should not consider the tr in the exponent when calculating fees for non-matured positions.
The spot price is recorded for oracles and is also used in LP and governance fee calculations.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that calculates the spot price of bonds in terms of the base asset. The implementation uses a variable representing the normalized time remaining (often called tr) as part of the exponent and omits a scaling factor (1/c) that is required by the mathematical definition of the share‑bond curve. The curve is defined by the equation c·(z)^(1‑ts)+y^(1‑ts)=k, where the true spot price – the slope of the perpendicular to the tangent at a point (z,y) – should be expressed as (1/c)*(z/y)^ts. Instead, the contract computes the spot price as (z/y)^(tr*ts), ignoring the (1/c) term and inserting tr, which has no meaning in the curve definition. This discrepancy originates from an inaccurate NatSpec comment that misstates the purpose of the function, leading developers to believe the formula was correct. Because the spot price is recorded for on‑chain oracles and fed into liquidity‑provider (LP) fee and governance fee calculations, the erroneous formula can be exploited by manipulating the _normalizedTimeRemaining input or by simply taking advantage of the systematic bias introduced by the missing factor. An attacker can craft trades that cause the contract to report a higher or lower spot price than the true market‑consistent value, resulting in over‑charging of fees for honest users or under‑charging that benefits the attacker at the expense of the protocol’s revenue. The impact manifests as users receiving less than expected returns, LPs seeing reduced fee accruals, and governance fee distributions that do not reflect the actual economic activity. These symptoms are subtle because the spot price is not directly displayed in the UI; users only notice that their balances change unexpectedly or that oracle‑derived prices appear out of line with external market data. The bug occurs every time calculateSpotPrice is invoked, which includes fee calculations for non‑matured positions after each trade. It was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, who compared the contract’s implementation against the theoretical curve and identified the mismatch. The issue is hard to spot in routine testing because the deviation may be small and does not cause outright failures, only economic drift. To remediate, the function should be rewritten to compute the spot price as c*(z/y)^ts, i.e., by multiplying the ratio (z/y) raised to the time‑stretch exponent with the initial share price factor, and must exclude any reference to the normalized time remaining. This correction restores the mathematical integrity of the oracle, ensures fee calculations align with the intended economic model, and eliminates the avenue for price manipulation.

title: Curve part is not reduced by negative variable interest growth when closing longs
description:
When closing longs during a period of negative interest, the trader's proceeds are reduced proportionally to the negative growth. However, this is only done on the shareProceeds variable which represents both flat and curve parts, the curve part shareReservesDelta is not reduced by this amount but it should be.
It also checks the negative interest region compared to the beginning of the deployment (_initialSharePrice) instead of the beginning of opening the longs (_openSharePrice).
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the settlement logic for closing long positions when the protocol’s interest rate becomes negative. During a negative‑interest period the contract is supposed to reduce the trader’s proceeds proportionally to the amount of interest loss. The implementation applies this proportional reduction only to the variable shareProceeds, which aggregates both the flat component and the curve component of the position. The curve component, represented by shareReservesDelta, is left unchanged, meaning the trader receives the full curve value even though the overall position should have been scaled down. In addition, the code determines whether the interest is negative by comparing the current share price to the deployment‑time _initialSharePrice instead of the price that existed when the long was opened (_openSharePrice). As a result, a trader who opens a long, waits for the interest rate to turn negative, and then closes the position can collect an excess amount equal to the unscaled curve part. This excess can be repeatedly exploited by opening and closing longs during negative‑interest windows, draining protocol funds. The bug manifests only when the interest rate moves below zero between the opening and closing of a long, and it is difficult to detect because the overall proceeds may still appear reasonable and the discrepancy is hidden inside the internal accounting of the curve component. Users may notice that they receive more than the expected payout or that the protocol’s reserve balance shrinks unexpectedly after a series of negative‑interest closures. The issue is a classic accounting‑settlement error: an incorrect scaling factor is applied to one part of the payout while another part is omitted, and the reference price used for the check is wrong. To remediate, the contract should apply the same proportional reduction to shareReservesDelta and adjust the flat component (shareProceeds‑shareReservesDelta) accordingly, and it should compare the current share price against the opening price of the long rather than the initial deployment price. This correction restores the intended economic invariants and prevents over‑payment during negative‑interest periods.

title: Removing liquidity does not reduce the shares received by the overestimated amount
description: When redeeming liquidity leads to negative withdrawal shares and the share proceeds are adjusted again, the overestimatedProceeds that are treated as contributing to withdrawal shares are still paid out to the LP.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation in the liquidity removal path where the contract computes withdrawal shares based on an over‑estimated proceeds amount. When the redemption logic determines that the withdrawal shares become negative, the code still adds the previously calculated overestimatedProceeds to the LP’s payout without subtracting them from the final shareProceeds. This logic error originates from the handling of negative share values: the overestimated proceeds are treated as valid contribution to the withdrawal, but the subsequent adjustment step fails to compensate for the over‑estimation. An attacker or any liquidity provider can trigger the condition by redeeming liquidity in a scenario that produces a negative share balance—such as after large price swings, rounding errors, or when the pool’s total assets are insufficient for the requested amount. The contract then pays out more tokens than the LP is entitled to, effectively creating phantom funds that disappear from the pool’s accounting. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal withdrawal amount, but the received token balance is higher than expected, or the pool’s total liquidity drops unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit and was not evident in normal operation because it only manifests under edge‑case share calculations. The bug is hard to notice because the withdrawal transaction succeeds and the excess amount is not flagged as an error. The proper fix is to deduct the overestimatedProceeds from the final shareProceeds whenever the withdrawal shares are negative, ensuring that the payout matches the true entitlement and preserving the pool’s accounting invariants.

title: Sandwich a call to addLiquidity(...) for profit
bug_full: The vulnerability is a sandwich attack on the Hyperdrive pool that exploits the way the protocol calculates the lower bound for the reserve ratio z when a short position is opened. When a user opens a short, the protocol enforces that the updated z must be at least L0 divided by the constant c. If the pool has few or no long positions, or if the total long outstanding L0 is very small, an attacker can open a short with the maximum bond amount that still satisfies the solvency requirement while pushing the point (z, y) extremely close to the y‑axis, making z a tiny value. After this, a liquidity provider calls addLiquidity, which scales the current curve and moves the (z, y) point far from the origin. Because the curve is now scaled, a subsequent flat trade – such as the checkpoint that closes the attacker’s short – experiences a disproportionately large change in the bond reserve y for a small change in z. The attacker then back‑runs the addLiquidity transaction and closes the short, extracting a profit that can be many times the original short size. The attack can also be used as a griefing vector, causing the liquidity provider’s contribution to be de‑valued or the pool’s accounting to become inconsistent. The issue occurs whenever the lower bound for z is only L0/c and the pool state allows z to approach zero, which is typical during addLiquidity calls or when a checkpoint settles a matured short. It was discovered during a formal security review of the Hyperdrive contracts, where the auditors observed that the invariant on z does not prevent it from collapsing to near‑zero values. The problem is hard to notice because the pool may still report a reasonable APR and appear healthy, while the underlying reserve ratio is being manipulated behind the scenes. From a user’s perspective, a liquidity provider may see their LP tokens suddenly appear to earn an unusually high return, only to watch the pool’s share price drop and their effective balance shrink, giving the impression that “funds disappear” after a normal addLiquidity operation. The attack violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that small trades cause proportionate changes in reserves, breaking the expected linear relationship between z and y. To mitigate the issue, the contract should enforce an additional invariant that prevents z from falling below a safe minimum, for example by requiring z ≥ max(L0 / c, zmin), where zmin is a protocol‑defined lower bound derived from risk analysis. This extra check would stop an attacker from pushing the reserve ratio to a dangerous region and eliminate the profit‑making sandwich opportunity.

title: ERC4626DataProvider does not calculate the price per share correctly
description: ERC4626DataProvider does not calculate the price per share correctly. It returns the inverse of the price per share. This hook is implemented correctly in ERC4626Hyperdrive.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC4626DataProvider contract where the internal function that reports the price per share calculates the value incorrectly. Instead of returning the actual share price, the implementation uses the pool’s totalSupply and totalAssets in a way that produces the mathematical inverse – effectively reporting 1/price rather than price. This mis‑calculation stems from an incorrect formula that divides the fixed‑point constant by the share estimate instead of converting a unit of assets to shares (or vice‑versa) using the pool’s conversion helpers. Because the function is exposed through a data‑provider hook, any external component that queries the price per share – such as front‑end UI, off‑chain price oracles, or other contracts that rely on the quoted value for deposit, withdrawal or redemption calculations – will receive a value that is the opposite of what the protocol’s accounting expects. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by submitting transactions that assume the reported price is correct; for example, a user may deposit assets based on the inverted price and receive fewer shares than intended, or a malicious actor could craft a withdrawal that appears to be under‑collateralised and extract excess assets from the pool. The impact is a systematic accounting error that can lead to users receiving less value than they should, potential loss of funds, and a breakdown of trust in the protocol’s pricing logic. The bug manifests whenever the _pricePerShare function is called – typically during quote generation, before a deposit or withdrawal, or when a UI displays the current share price. All participants that rely on the data provider – individual token holders, integrators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the displayed price does not match the true economic value of a share. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit where the auditor compared the data provider’s output against the reference implementation in ERC4626Hyperdrive and observed that the numbers were consistently the reciprocal of the expected price. The problem is subtle because the returned number is still a plausible fixed‑point value; without a direct sanity check, developers may assume the function works correctly, and the error can remain hidden until users notice mismatched balances or unexpected slippage. To remediate the bug, the price per share calculation should be rewritten to use the pool’s conversion functions correctly – either by converting a unit of assets to shares and then taking the reciprocal, or more efficiently by converting a unit of shares directly to assets using the pool’s convertToAsset endpoint, ensuring the result is expressed in the standard 18‑decimal fixed‑point format. This change restores the logical relationship between total assets and total supply, aligns the data provider with the reference implementation, and prevents the erroneous inversion that currently breaks accounting and user expectations.

title: Wrong flat fee when opening longs
description:
When opening longs there should be no flat fee as all newly minted bonds have a maturity time of periodDuration and must therefore be purchased on the curve part of the flat+curve model. When opening longs, updateLiquidity(_baseAmount.divDown(_sharePrice) - _shareReservesDelta) is called where _baseAmount.divDown(_sharePrice) - _shareReservesDelta is the flat part that is supposed to be 0.
However, _baseAmount is set to _baseAmount - totalGovernanceFee when calling _applyOpenLong which is the difference of a base amount and a share amount. The different units can't be subtracted and the mentioned reserves update will not be zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the fee calculation performed when a user opens a long position in the protocol. According to the protocol design, opening a long should not incur any flat fee because newly minted bonds are created with a maturity equal to the period duration and are therefore purchased entirely on the curve portion of the flat‑plus‑curve pricing model. In the implementation, the function that processes a long opening calls updateLiquidity with the argument _baseAmount.divDown(_sharePrice) - _shareReservesDelta, which is intended to represent the flat component and therefore be zero. However, the code first reduces _baseAmount by totalGovernanceFee (a value expressed in base token units) before converting the amount to shares using the share price. This mixes two different units – base tokens and share tokens – and results in a non‑zero value being passed to updateLiquidity. Consequently, a flat fee is unintentionally charged on every long opening. The root cause is the incorrect subtraction of totalGovernanceFee from _baseAmount without scaling it by the current share price, which violates the accounting assumption that the flat part of the fee should be zero for longs. An attacker or any user can exploit this by opening long positions and paying more than expected, effectively losing part of their capital to an unintended fee. The impact is that users receive fewer shares than they anticipate, see a reduction in their balance, and may perceive that “funds disappear” or that the refund calculation is wrong. This condition occurs every time the _applyOpenLong function is invoked with the current fee logic, affecting all participants who open longs, the protocol’s revenue model, and any governance entity that relies on the fee distribution. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Spearbit) by analysing the mathematical relationship between base amounts, share prices, and liquidity updates. It can be hard to notice because the discrepancy may be small and masked by rounding, making the flat fee appear negligible in routine UI displays. To remediate, the calculation should subtract totalGovernanceFee multiplied by the share price before converting to shares, ensuring the flat component is truly zero, or the updateLiquidity call could be removed entirely since the parameter becomes unused. Cleaning up the _baseAmount parameter in _applyOpenLong would also eliminate the erroneous fee path and align the implementation with the intended fee‑free long opening model.

title: Unsafe type-casts
description:
Unsafe type-casts are performed throughout the contracts.
• HyperdriveLong.sol#L259
• HyperdriveLong.sol#L321
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L157
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L320-L321
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L352
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L418
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L418-L441
• HyperdriveLP.sol#L532-L536
• HyperdriveShort.sol#L360
• FixedPointMath.sol#L145
• HyperdriveMath.sol#L388-L389
• HyperdriveMath.sol#L477-L484
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of unsafe type‑casts that are performed in many places across the protocol’s Solidity contracts. An unsafe type‑cast occurs when a value of a larger integer type (for example uint256) is directly converted to a smaller type (such as uint128 or uint64) without any runtime verification that the value actually fits within the destination range. The root cause is the use of Solidity’s built‑in casting syntax instead of a safe casting library that checks for overflow or underflow. Because Solidity silently truncates the high‑order bits when a value exceeds the target type’s capacity, the contract can store a corrupted number that no longer reflects the true amount of tokens, shares, or interest. An attacker can trigger the vulnerable code paths by supplying inputs that cause the intermediate calculation to exceed the smaller type’s maximum, for instance by depositing a very large amount of assets or by manipulating price or time parameters that feed into the cast. When the cast truncates the value, subsequent accounting logic – such as share‑to‑asset conversion, fee calculation, or redemption amount – operates on an incorrect figure. This can lead to a user receiving less than expected, a balance being recorded as zero, or the protocol allowing the withdrawal of more assets than were actually deposited. The impact is therefore a breach of the protocol’s financial invariants: funds may disappear, refunds may be missing, and the overall accounting model can be broken. The issue manifests whenever the contract executes a cast on a value that can grow beyond the destination type’s limit, which is common in functions that handle deposits, withdrawals, interest accrual, or price updates. All participants – liquidity providers, long and short position holders, and any external callers – are potentially affected because the corrupted state propagates through shared storage. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that flagged each explicit cast expression as a high‑risk pattern, noting that no explicit range checks were present. Because the truncation does not revert the transaction, the bug can be subtle and may only be observable through unexpected balance changes or failed refunds, making it hard to detect through normal testing. To remediate the issue, every cast from a larger to a smaller integer type should be replaced with a safe casting routine that verifies the value is within the target type’s bounds and reverts otherwise. Libraries such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast or custom require statements can provide this protection, ensuring that arithmetic overflow cannot silently corrupt the protocol’s state.

title: query's returned price is not accurate
description:
The query(uint256 period) function is supposed to return "the average price between the last recorded timestamp looking a user-determined time into the past". The user-determined time is the period parameter. However, the code looks for the next checkpoint which is period seconds before the last checkpoint. It then just averages these two checkpoints, disregarding the period, meaning the resulting price can have a "time window error" up to the oracle's _updateGap. If the oracle's _updateGap is large (which it probably is to save gas) the TWAP might not really represent the TWAP over period seconds from the last checkpoint.
Example:
• t = 0, sum = 1e18
• t = 100, sum = 2e18
• t = 200, sum = 4e18
With a period = 101, query will look at t = 0 and t = 200, and compute (4e18 - 1e18) / (200) = 1.5e16 but the more accurate value would be much closer to (4e18 - 2e18) / (200 - 100) = 2e16 as only a single second of the period lookback should come from the 0 -> 100 time window with slower growth. It will return the same averaged price for period = 101 and period = 200 even though these have very different averages.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the oracle's query(uint256 period) function, which is intended to return the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) for the exact time window from the current block timestamp back by the user‑specified period. Instead of selecting checkpoints that precisely bound that window, the implementation looks for the checkpoint that occurs exactly _updateGap seconds before the most recent checkpoint and then simply averages the two surrounding cumulative sums. Because the internal _updateGap can be much larger than the requested period, the function effectively ignores the period argument and computes an average over a window that may be up to _updateGap seconds longer than intended. This creates a “time window error” where the reported price can be significantly different from the true average over the requested interval. For example, with checkpoints at t=0, t=100 and t=200 and a period of 101 seconds, the function averages the values at t=0 and t=200, yielding 1.5e16, whereas the correct average over the interval (t=101 to t=200) should be close to 2e16. The bug manifests whenever the oracle’s update gap is large relative to the period supplied by the caller, which is common when the contract is designed to save gas by updating infrequently. Users and downstream protocols that rely on the returned price – such as traders, liquidation engines, or any contract that uses the TWAP for pricing or risk calculations – will receive a price that does not reflect the actual market movement over the requested timeframe. This can lead to unexpected slippage, incorrect liquidation triggers, or arbitrage opportunities for attackers who can craft periods that produce the same stale price despite different market conditions. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the mathematical definition of a TWAP with the contract’s implementation and identified the mismatch between the period argument and the checkpoint selection logic. It is subtle because the returned price often appears plausible and the discrepancy only becomes evident when testing with periods that are shorter than the oracle’s update interval. To remediate, the query function should iterate over all stored checkpoints that intersect the interval (block.timestamp‑period, block.timestamp), weight each segment of cumulative sum by the exact amount of time it overlaps the interval, and optionally extrapolate the partial segment at the interval boundaries. This ensures the computed average truly represents the price over the user‑specified period, restoring correctness for all dependent applications.

title: Late checkpoints will use higher share price, influencing traders' PnL
description:
Calling the checkpoint(_checkpointTime) function for a checkpoint in the past will look for the next checkpoint higher than _checkpointTime, then retroactively apply the later checkpoint's share price to it:
• Under normal circumstances, the earlier checkpoint would have a smaller share price (as the yield source has generated less interest up to this point).
• This closes longs/shorts at the higher share price. For example, in calculateCloseLong, the trader would receive fewer shareProceeds. The protocol essentially stops accruing interest for the trader's long position upon maturity. When closing shorts, this can influence both the openSharePrice and closeSharePrice in closeShort and lead to losses/profits compared to closing them directly at maturity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract’s checkpoint mechanism can be invoked after the scheduled checkpoint time, causing the system to select the next later checkpoint and apply its share price retroactively to the earlier period. Under normal operation each checkpoint records a share price that reflects the cumulative interest earned up to that moment; earlier checkpoints therefore have a lower share price than later ones. When a late call to checkpoint(_checkpointTime) occurs, the contract searches for the first checkpoint whose timestamp is greater than the supplied _checkpointTime and uses that later share price for calculations that close positions that were supposed to be settled at the earlier price. As a result, long positions are closed at a higher share price, which translates into fewer shareProceeds for the trader, effectively reducing the trader’s profit or even turning a profit into a loss. Short positions are also affected because both the openSharePrice and the closeSharePrice are derived from the incorrectly high share price, leading to unexpected gains or losses compared to a direct closure at maturity. The bug manifests only when the checkpoint function is called outside its intended time window – for example, by an operator who forgets to trigger the checkpoint on time or by an automated script that runs late. Traders who rely on the protocol’s accounting to receive the correct PnL see symptoms such as my long position returned less than expected, my short position profit is different from the calculator, or my balance dropped unexpectedly after closing. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the checkpoint logic and its interaction with position settlement. It is difficult to notice because the share price stored in the contract appears consistent at the moment of closing; the discrepancy only becomes visible when comparing the expected interest accrued up to the original checkpoint time with the actual amount received. The vulnerability belongs to the class of time‑window enforcement or retroactive state update bugs, where state that should be immutable after a certain time can be overwritten with a later value. To remediate, the contract should enforce that checkpoint() can only be called within the predefined window for each checkpoint, or it should compute an interpolated share price between the nearest older and newer checkpoints to approximate linear interest growth, thereby preserving the correct accounting for positions settled at the intended time.

title: Updating the factory's implementation will still deploy old data provider
description: While one can set a new deployer in the factories and therefore a new Hyperdrive version, one can't actually change the data provider and it's likely that a new Hyperdrive version will require a new data provider. The reason is that the yield-source-specific deployer is not responsible for deploying the data provider, the yield-source-specific factory is responsible for deploying the data provider.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an upgradeable architecture where a Hyperdrive factory contract is responsible for deploying a yield‑source‑specific data provider while a separate deployer contract handles the deployment of the Hyperdrive implementation itself. When the protocol owner updates the factory to point to a new deployer (for example to upgrade to a newer Hyperdrive version), the factory continues to use its original logic for creating the data provider, which remains unchanged. This mismatch occurs because the data provider deployment is hard‑coded in the factory and not delegated to the deployer, so the upgrade path does not include a mechanism to replace the provider. An attacker or a careless operator can exploit this by deploying a new Hyperdrive implementation that expects a different data interface or newer pricing logic, while the still‑old data provider supplies stale or incompatible data. The resulting impact is that the protocol may calculate yields, fees, or refunds based on incorrect inputs, leading to users receiving zero or unexpectedly low returns, balances appearing unchanged, or accounting invariants being violated. The issue manifests whenever a governance action or admin call updates the factory’s deployer address without also redeploying or migrating the data provider, which is typical during version upgrades. All participants that rely on accurate yield data – including liquidity providers, borrowers, and the protocol’s risk engine – are affected because the core financial calculations become unreliable. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that traced the upgrade flow and identified that the factory, not the deployer, owns the data‑provider creation code. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display successful transactions, while the underlying numbers silently drift, making the bug appear as a subtle performance regression rather than an outright failure. To remediate, the deployment responsibility for the data provider should be moved into the yield‑source‑specific deployer or the factory should expose an upgrade path for the provider, ensuring that a change to the Hyperdrive implementation can also trigger a compatible data‑provider deployment. This aligns the upgrade process with the intended modular design and restores the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Not using safe version of ERC20 transfer/transferFrom/approve can lead to wrong scenarios
description:
Some tokens (like ZRX) do not revert the transaction when the transfer/transferFrom fails and return false, which requires us to check the return value after calling the transfer/transferFrom function. While the code checks for the return value in all other instances of transfer and transferFrom:
• HyperdriveFactory.sol#L205
Additionally note that some ERC20 tokens don't have any return value, for example USDT, BNB, OMG. This will make the expected return value to fail if these tokens are used on the if (!success) revert pattern, which is the predominant case on the code, making these tokens not compatible as base tokens.
Assuming aToken is set to correct address, aToken case can avoid the check as it's known to revert on fail transfer, and therefore not included in the context files.
The AaveHyperdrive contract sets ERC20 approvals by calling token.approve(operator, amount). This comes with several issues:
1. ERC20.approve returns a success boolean that is not checked. Some tokens don't revert and return false instead.
2. Non-standard tokens like USDT return no data at all but the IERC20.approve interface expects the call to return data and attempts to decode it into a boolean. The approval calls will fail for USDT.
3. Non-standard tokens like USDT require approvals to be reset to zero first before being able to set them to a different non-zero value again.
approve instances:
• ERC4626Hyperdrive.sol#L51
• DsrHyperdrive.sol#L52
• AaveHyperdrive.sol#L45
• HyperdriveFactory.sol#L210
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the standard ERC20 interface without using a safe wrapper for transfer, transferFrom, and approve calls. Certain ERC20 implementations, such as ZRX, do not revert when a transfer or transferFrom fails; instead they return a boolean false. Because the code only checks the return value for some calls and omits it for others, a failed token movement can be silently ignored, leaving the contract’s internal accounting unchanged while the external transaction appears successful. In addition, a number of popular tokens (for example USDT, BNB, OMG) deviate from the ERC20 spec by returning no data at all. When the contract attempts to decode a non‑existent return value into a boolean, the call reverts, breaking compatibility with these tokens. The approve function suffers from a similar problem: the contract calls token.approve without verifying the returned boolean, and for tokens like USDT the call returns no data, causing a decode error. Moreover, USDT requires the allowance to be first set to zero before a new non‑zero allowance can be granted; the contract does not perform this reset, so subsequent approvals may fail. These issues manifest when a user deposits a non‑standard token, when the protocol tries to move tokens on behalf of users, or when it sets allowances for downstream contracts. From the user’s perspective the UI may report a successful deposit or approval, yet the token balance remains unchanged or the allowance stays at zero, leading to missing refunds, failed trades, or locked funds. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s token handling logic against known ERC20 edge‑cases. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, so standard testing that only checks for reverts will miss the silent failure. The impact ranges from incorrect accounting (the protocol believes it received tokens it never got) to potential loss of funds if an attacker supplies a token that always returns false, causing the contract to think a transfer succeeded while the attacker retains the assets. To remediate, all external token interactions should be wrapped with a safe transfer library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 or Solady’s SafeTransferLib, which correctly handles missing return data and checks the boolean result. Approvals should be performed with a safeApprove utility that either forces a zero‑reset before setting a new allowance (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s forceApprove) or otherwise guarantees the call succeeds regardless of the token’s implementation. By adopting these patterns the contract will correctly detect failed transfers, maintain accurate balances, and remain compatible with a broader set of ERC20 tokens.

title: Sandwiching removeLiquidity can steal profits from LP
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection for the withdrawalShares component of the removeLiquidity function in a liquidity pool contract. When a liquidity provider calls removeLiquidity they receive two kinds of proceeds: baseProceeds, which are transferred immediately, and withdrawalShares, which represent a claim to future base tokens that can be redeemed later. The contract only checks that baseProceeds meet a user‑supplied _minOutput slippage threshold; it does not enforce any minimum amount for withdrawalShares. Because withdrawalShares are minted based on the pool’s state after the baseProceeds have been taken, an attacker who can front‑run the transaction can add a large amount of liquidity just before the victim’s removal, causing the pool’s share price to shift. The victim’s removal still passes the baseProceeds slippage check, but the number of withdrawalShares minted for the victim is reduced. The attacker then removes his own liquidity and later redeems the extra withdrawalShares for a profit. This attack can be carried out as a classic sandwich: the attacker’s addLiquidity transaction is placed before the victim’s removeLiquidity, and the attacker’s removeLiquidity transaction is placed after. The impact is that the legitimate LP receives fewer withdrawalShares than expected, effectively losing part of the value they intended to withdraw, while the attacker gains additional base tokens. The issue appears only when the pool allows separate withdrawalShares without a minimum‑output guard, and when the attacker can control the timing of liquidity additions. It is difficult to notice because the immediate baseProceeds look correct and the slippage check passes, while the later redemption of withdrawalShares shows a shortfall that may be attributed to normal market variation. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete slippage validation” or “unchecked post‑withdrawal token minting” vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions about invariant preservation during liquidity removal. To remediate, the contract should introduce a slippage parameter for withdrawalShares (e.g., a _minWithdrawalShares argument) and enforce that the minted shares are at least this amount, or redesign removeLiquidity to compute and transfer the full value atomically, ensuring that the total value received cannot be reduced by front‑running actions. Adding proper checks restores the guarantee that a liquidity provider’s expected output cannot be arbitrarily lowered by front‑running actions.

title: LP funds can be locked up cheaply at low-interest rates
description: Opening shorts can be seen as LPs providing the base part of the bonds at the current price and traders paying only the implied fixed interest part on them. The LP funds are locked up (technically removed from the reserves until the shorts are closed) and LP shares cannot directly be redeemed for the base asset anymore, only for withdrawal shares that are slowly converted as LPs receive their proceeds. The ratio of trader funds paid and LP funds locked up is especially large when the fixed interest rate is low. This allows a griefing attack where a large percentage of LP funds can be locked up by opening shorts at low-interest rates.
