The bug appears only when three conditions hold simultaneously: (1) the cached oracle price is stale, (2) the spot price used for the cRatio calculation is lower than the cached price, and (3) the short’s collateral is insufficient to cover the debt computed with the stale price. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the price used for cRatio with the price used for debt calculation and noticed a mismatch that could lead to a negative subtraction. The issue is hard to notice because both prices are fetched from the same library and the underflow only manifests in extreme price swings, which are rare in normal testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of price‑stale mismatch leading to arithmetic underflow and violates the accounting assumption that debt expressed in the same unit as collateral is always less than or equal to the collateral when a liquidation is attempted. A correct fix is to ensure that the same price source is used for both the cRatio and the debt calculation, or to cap the debt amount by the available collateral (for example using the minimum of collateral and ercDebtAtOraclePrice) before performing the subtraction. This prevents the underflow and allows the liquidation to proceed safely.

title: Lack of essential stale check in oracleCircuitBreaker()
description:
The LibOracle::oracleCircuitBreaker() lacks checking the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp". Hence, the function will not be able to verify whether or not the baseChainlinkPrice is stale (2-hour stale heartbeat).

This report raises an issue regarding the lack of stale price check for the base oracle (ETH/USD price) in the oracleCircuitBreaker() only, as the 2-hour stale check and the lack of stale price check for the non-USD asset oracle were flagged as known issues.

The oracleCircuitBreaker() lacks checking the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp" when compared to the baseOracleCircuitBreaker().

Without the check of the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp", the oracleCircuitBreaker() will not be able to verify whether or not the baseChainlinkPrice is stale (2-hour stale heartbeat).

For this reason, the oracleCircuitBreaker() will not revert the transaction as expected if the baseChainlinkPrice is stale.

```solidity
    // @audit -- this report raises an issue regarding the lack of stale price check for the base oracle (ETH/USD price) in the oracleCircuitBreaker() only, as the 2-hour stale check and the lack of stale price check for the non-USD asset oracle were flagged as known issues
    function oracleCircuitBreaker(
        uint80 roundId,
        uint80 baseRoundId,
        int256 chainlinkPrice,
        int256 baseChainlinkPrice,
        uint256 timeStamp,
        uint256 baseTimeStamp
    ) private view { // @audit -- this report raises an issue regarding the lack of stale price check for the base oracle (ETH/USD price) in the oracleCircuitBreaker() only, as the 2-hour stale check and the lack of stale price check for the non-USD asset oracle were flagged as known issues
        bool invalidFetchData = roundId == 0 || timeStamp == 0
            || timeStamp > block.timestamp || chainlinkPrice <= 0 || baseRoundId == 0
            || baseTimeStamp == 0 || baseTimeStamp > block.timestamp
            || baseChainlinkPrice <= 0; // @audit -- lack the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp"

        if (invalidFetchData) revert Errors.InvalidPrice();
    }

    function baseOracleCircuitBreaker(
        uint256 protocolPrice,
        uint80 roundId,
        int256 chainlinkPrice,
        uint256 timeStamp,
        uint256 chainlinkPriceInEth
    ) private view returns (uint256 _protocolPrice) {
        bool invalidFetchData = roundId == 0 || timeStamp == 0
            || timeStamp > block.timestamp || chainlinkPrice <= 0
            || block.timestamp > 2 hours + timeStamp; // @audit -- the baseOracleCircuitBreaker() checks this condition, but the oracleCircuitBreaker() does not check it (for the base oracle (ETH/USD price) only)
        uint256 chainlinkDiff = chainlinkPriceInEth > protocolPrice
            ? chainlinkPriceInEth - protocolPrice
            : protocolPrice - chainlinkPriceInEth;
        bool priceDeviation =
            protocolPrice > 0 && chainlinkDiff.div(protocolPrice) > 0.5 ether;

        ...
    }
```
The oracleCircuitBreaker() lacks checking the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp": https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-09-ditto/blob/a93b4276420a092913f43169a353a6198d3c21b9/contracts/libraries/LibOracle.sol#L120-L123  
Whereas the baseOracleCircuitBreaker() checks that condition: https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-09-ditto/blob/a93b4276420a092913f43169a353a6198d3c21b9/contracts/libraries/LibOracle.sol#L73

This report raises an issue regarding the lack of stale price check for the base oracle (ETH/USD price) in the oracleCircuitBreaker() only, as the 2-hour stale check and the lack of stale price check for the non-USD asset oracle were flagged as known issues.

The oracleCircuitBreaker() lacks checking the condition: "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp". Hence, the function will not be able to verify whether or not the baseChainlinkPrice is stale (2-hour stale heartbeat).

Consequently, the oracleCircuitBreaker() will not revert the transaction as expected if the baseChainlinkPrice is stale. The stale price will be consumed by core functions of the protocol, leading to harming the funds of the protocol and its users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing stale‑price verification in the private view function that validates oracle data before the protocol uses it. The function checks that the round identifiers, timestamps and price values are non‑zero and that the timestamps are not in the future, but it does not enforce the business rule that a price older than two hours must be considered stale. The root cause is the absence of the condition "block.timestamp > 2 hours + baseTimeStamp" for the base ETH/USD price, a check that is present in the analogous baseOracleCircuitBreaker routine. Because this condition is omitted, the contract can accept a baseChainlinkPrice whose timestamp is arbitrarily old. An attacker can exploit the flaw by waiting until the Chainlink feed for ETH/USD stops updating for more than two hours, then triggering a transaction that reads the stale price through oracleCircuitBreaker. The protocol will treat the outdated price as valid, leading to incorrect valuation of collateral, erroneous liquidation thresholds, or mispriced swaps. The impact may be loss of user funds, unexpected liquidations, or the protocol becoming under‑collateralised, while users see balances that drop unexpectedly or receive less than expected from a trade. The bug manifests only when the base price timestamp exceeds the two‑hour freshness window; under normal fresh‑price conditions the function behaves as intended. All participants that rely on the oracle – the protocol itself, its users, liquidity providers and any downstream contracts – are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the logic of oracleCircuitBreaker with the reference baseOracleCircuitBreaker, revealing that the stale‑price guard was missing. The problem is subtle because the function still reverts on many other invalid inputs, so a stale price passes silently and the UI shows no error, making it hard to notice without inspecting the timestamp logic. The correct remediation is to add the missing time‑check condition to the invalidFetchData expression so that any price older than two hours triggers the Errors.InvalidPrice revert, restoring the intended safety guarantees of the oracle circuit breaker.

title: M-1 The owner can manipulate oracles
description: The Oracle contract has a function Oracle.sol#L24 that set an external oracle address for symbols. The owner is able to set a fake external oracle just before the battle end. As a result, it will lead to the incorrect battle settlement.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract that provides price data (the Oracle contract) includes a function that allows the contract owner to change the address of the external oracle that supplies values for a given symbol. Because the function is not restricted after a battle has been created, the owner can replace the legitimate price feed with a malicious contract moments before the battle settlement is executed. When the settlement logic queries the oracle for the final price, it receives a fabricated value, causing the battle to be settled with an incorrect outcome. This can lead to participants receiving less reward, losing their stake, or gaining an unfair advantage, effectively allowing the owner to manipulate the economic result of any ongoing battle. The issue occurs only while a battle is open and before the settlement transaction is called; once the battle is closed the function may still be callable but has no effect on that battle. The affected parties are all users who have entered the battle, the protocol’s token economics, and any third‑party relying on the integrity of the oracle data. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the access control of the oracle‑setting function and noted that the owner role is not removed or time‑locked after battle creation. Because the function is public to the owner and does not emit a distinctive event, the manipulation can be performed silently, making it hard for participants to notice until the settlement result is observed. The bug belongs to the class of “trusted‑oracle substitution” or “privileged address manipulation” vulnerabilities, where a privileged actor can replace a data source after it has been referenced by other contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected battle result, but the final token balance after settlement may be zero or lower than anticipated, contradicting the expectation that the battle settles according to the market price. To remediate the issue the oracle address for a given symbol should be immutable once a battle is instantiated, or the ability to change it should be restricted to a multi‑signature governance process and locked via a time‑delay. Alternatively, the contract could store a snapshot of the oracle address at battle creation and ignore any later changes. Implementing these controls restores the trust model that the price feed cannot be tampered with during an active battle, preventing the owner from influencing settlement outcomes.

title: M-2 Reserve oracle
description: In case of some instability with Chainlink oracle gaps in a price history are probably present. These gaps cause the settle function call to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the protocol’s reliance on a single Chainlink price oracle to provide a continuous price history used by the settle function. When the Chainlink feed experiences instability, such as network congestion, node downtime, or data transmission errors, gaps can appear in the recorded price series. The contract assumes that every price slot contains a valid, non‑zero value and does not include logic to handle missing entries. Consequently, when the settle function attempts to read a price that is absent or zero, the internal arithmetic or validation checks trigger a revert, aborting the transaction. This situation can be triggered unintentionally by natural oracle outages or deliberately by an attacker who forces the feed into a stale state, for example by flooding the network or manipulating the underlying data source. The immediate impact is that settlement operations fail, preventing users from completing trades, claiming rewards, or withdrawing funds, effectively locking assets in the contract until the oracle resumes normal operation. The issue manifests only during periods when the price feed is incomplete; under normal conditions the contract behaves as expected, making the problem hard to detect during routine testing. The affected parties include any user attempting to settle a position, liquidity providers whose capital remains idle, and the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage and loss of confidence. The flaw was identified during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the contract lacks a fallback or reserve price source to cover oracle gaps. Because the revert occurs deep inside business‑logic code, the failure appears as a generic transaction error rather than a clear indication of an oracle problem, complicating debugging. To remediate the issue, the contract should incorporate a reserve price mechanism—such as a secondary oracle, time‑weighted average price, or on‑chain fallback source—and add explicit checks for missing data, allowing the settle function to either use the reserve price or gracefully abort with a user‑friendly error message. This class of bug falls under oracle availability and data‑integrity failures, where insufficient handling of missing external data leads to unexpected contract reverts and potential fund immobilisation.

title: M-3 Public functions for withdrawn assets in the PeripheryPayments contract
description: The PeripheryPayments.sol#L31 and PeripheryPayments.sol#L42 functions allow anyone to withdraw funds from the Manager contract. There are no funds on the contract by design but if someone makes a wrong transfer to the contract by mistake, an attacker can steal it. Also, there is a risk of inheritance of this contract in the future in other cases where funds will be kept on a new contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that two public functions in the PeripheryPayments contract that are intended only for internal accounting are exposed without any access control, allowing any external address to call them and trigger a transfer of Ether or ERC20 tokens held by the contract to an arbitrary recipient. The root cause is that the contract was designed under the assumption that it will never hold a balance, so the developer omitted any onlyOwner or role‑based restriction on the withdraw functions. Because Solidity does not prevent accidental transfers to a contract, a user or another contract may mistakenly send funds to PeripheryPayments. When that happens, any attacker can invoke the public withdraw function, specify the attacker’s address as the destination, and drain the entire balance in a single transaction. The impact is loss of user funds that were sent by mistake, as the victim sees their balance become zero and receives no refund; the protocol itself does not lose intended assets but its reputation may suffer. The condition occurs only when the contract unexpectedly holds a non‑zero balance, which can happen due to user error, a malicious token transfer, or future inheritance where a derived contract does keep funds. All participants who might accidentally send assets to the contract are affected, including end‑users, integrators, and any future contracts that inherit PeripheryPayments. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the public interface of the contract and noted the lack of modifiers such as onlyOwner. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s normal operation never moves funds, so reviewers may assume the withdraw functions are harmless placeholders. The fix is to add proper access control (e.g., onlyOwner, onlyRole, or a withdrawal guard) to the functions, and to include a fallback that rejects unexpected Ether, or to implement a safe‑withdraw pattern that only allows the contract itself to move its own assets. This class of bug belongs to the “unauthorized external withdrawal” or “missing access control on fund‑moving functions” category, which violates the accounting invariant that only the protocol logic may transfer assets out of the contract. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after mistakenly sending tokens to the contract, the balance disappears and no refund is received, contrary to the expectation that the protocol would either reject the transfer or provide a way to recover it. The attack flow is: (1) attacker observes that the contract holds a non‑zero balance, (2) attacker calls the public withdraw function, (3) the contract executes a transfer of the entire balance to the attacker‑controlled address, (4) the original sender’s funds are permanently lost. Because the contract does not emit any special warning and the function is public, the exploit can be performed with a single transaction and without needing any special privileges.

title: Gas Limit Exploitation and Order Book Blockage Due to High-Priced Bids
description:
In scenarios where there are no existing asks or shorts in a specific market order book, a malicious user can disrupt the market. By flooding the market with numerous small bids at an exceptionally high price, this will lead to: prevent new limit asks or limit shorts from being created below their bid price (which is too high) because the matching algorithm will reach the gasLimit matching a bunch of small bids with the incoming sell order. Also, no bids below his price will get matched. And the liquidation process in primaryMarginCall will not be possible for short records.

The vulnerability arises from the way the matching algorithm in function sellMatchAlgo in the LibOrders.sol library matches incoming ask with the highest bid. Here's how the problem unfolds:  
Matching Algorithm Flaw:  
When a new ask is created, it's created in the AskOrdersFacet in function createAsk triggering the sellMatchAlgo() function.

```solidity
   function createAsk(
        address asset,
        uint80 price,
        uint88 ercAmount,
        bool isMarketOrder,
        MTypes.OrderHint[] calldata orderHintArray
    ) external isNotFrozen(asset) onlyValidAsset(asset) nonReentrant {
        uint256 eth = price.mul(ercAmount);
        uint256 minAskEth = LibAsset.minAskEth(asset);
        if (eth < minAskEth) revert Errors.OrderUnderMinimumSize();
        ......
        .......
        LibOrders.sellMatchAlgo(asset, incomingAsk, orderHintArray, minAskEth);//@audit ..
    }
```
If the ask price is less than or equal to the highest bid price and the ask amount is less than the highest bid amount, the ask matches with the bid and doesn't get added to the order book.  
The highest bid matched stays as the highest bid in the bids list with less amount.  
bidOrder.amount = StartingAmount - MatchedAmount.  
and the bidder will get his erc tokens in their virtual balance in the system. as we see in this snippet code:

```solidity
   // when the  : amount  ask < amount bid
    else {
         //update the erc amount of the highest bid ,by sub the ask amount erc
        s.bids[asset][highestBid.id].ercAmount = highestBid.ercAmount - incomingAsk.ercAmount;
        updateBidOrdersOnMatch(s.bids, asset, highestBid.id, false);
       }
       incomingAsk.ercAmount = 0; // set ask ercAmount to zero.
       matchIncomingSell(asset, incomingAsk, matchTotal);
       return;
       .............................................................

   // match highest bid when amount ask < amount bid :
   function matchHighestBid(STypes.Order memory incomingSell,STypes.Order memory highestBid,address asset,
       MTypes.Match memory matchTotal
   ) internal {
       ...
       ...
       s.assetUser[asset][highestBid.addr].ercEscrowed += fillErc;
   }
```
Exploitable Scenario:  
The vulnerability emerges when there are no existing asks or shorts in the order book. (or even if there is but the attacker should buy them all).  
A malicious user can exploit this by:  
creating a bid with an exorbitantly high price. Then, they create an ask with the same price but slightly less in amount (e.g., 10 wei lower). This leaves a tiny highest bid in the order book.  
The user then creates another bid with a slightly higher price than the existing highest bid (1 wei). and another ask that matches with this new highest bid but leaves a tiny amount again. now E.g. we have:  
| Bids Price | Bids Amounts |  
|------------|-------------|  
| 1 | 100 |  
| 2 | 340 |  
| 100 | 0.001 |  
| 100.01 | 0.001 |  
repeating this process in a loop. This results in a bunch of tiny bids with disproportionately high prices in the order book.  
Gas Limit and Reversion:  
When a new regular ask is created with a standard price, due to the existence of these numerous tiny high-priced bids, the matching algorithm starts looping through all these bids to match the incoming ask.  
However, because there are many tiny bids, the transaction reaches the gas limit before the entire ask amount is matched. This premature termination of the transaction leads to a revert.  
NOTICE that the askers can't create an ask that has tiny amount with the same price of the bidder to match with a Reasonable number of bids that not gonna reach the gas limit. that's because there is a minAmountEth which is:

price * amount > minEth

assume the following:  
the Malicious user creates 1000 bid. the highest bid is:  
{price : 1 ether + 1000 wei , amount : 10 wei}  
the price in each previous bid is 1 wei less. so the first bid is:  
{price : 1 ether , amount : 10 wei}  
now let's calculate the minimum amount of erc tokens (pegged asset) that an asker can create ask with it at the highest price (1 ether for each asset which too high).  
assume MinEth is : 0.001 ether.  
we have:  
MinEth = Price * ErcAmount  
ErcAmount = MinEth / price  
so the min erc amount at the price the malicious user set as the highest bid will be:  
ercAmount = 0.001 ether * 1 ether / 1 ether = 1000000000000 wei.  
However, the sum of all the malicious bid amounts from highest to lowest is: 1000 × 10 = 10000 wei. Even if an ask attempts to match the highest bid price, the ask still needs to have a large amount, leading to looping through all these tiny bids. This looping process causes the transaction to reach the gas limit, resulting in a premature termination of the transaction.  
The same is applicable for shorts limits.  
for bidders there is no incentive to create a bid that's higher than this price. (which toooo high)  
the attack will not cost the malicious user too much, since he is matching with itself. the eth amount will cost him for the example provided around: 10000 wei and gas fee.  
by doing this an attacker can set above the highest bid price, an ask order with slightly higher price but with a larger amount that he bought before. forcing the shorters to buy at his price to close their debt. or just lose their collateral in case of secondary call for example.

1. shorters can't close their position: the shorters will be at risk to not be able to close their debt position. only if they buy the ercAsset above the price the attacker set. which likely will be the attacker ask.  
Limited Order Creation: Users are restricted from creating asks (both limit and market) and setting shorts limits below the price set by the attacker. This restriction significantly hampers market activities since there's no incentive for legitimate bidders to buy the pegged asset at an inflated price.  
Blocked Order Book Functionality: Bids placed below the attacker's price will never match with any asks, effectively blocking the entire order book from functioning below the attacker's specified price. This obstruction disrupts the natural trading process and prevents legitimate buyers and sellers from interacting in the market.  
Impaired Liquidation Process: The primary liquidation mechanism becomes impractical because it relies on creating a forceBid, which behaves like a regular bid order. However, these force bids, similar to other bids, won't match due to the artificially inflated price. Consequently, the primary liquidation process is rendered ineffective, preventing the clearing of outstanding positions and increasing the risk of market instability.  
users who tried to create an ask or short limit will pay a high gas fee and the transaction will revert at the end.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the order‑matching engine that can be triggered by an attacker who floods the market with a large number of tiny limit bids priced far above the normal market level. Because the matching algorithm always iterates over the list of bids ordered by price when a new ask is submitted, the presence of many high‑priced, low‑amount bids forces the algorithm to walk through a long sequence of entries before it can either fully satisfy the incoming ask or run out of gas. When the gas limit is reached the transaction reverts, leaving the ask unrecorded and the market state unchanged. This behaviour blocks the creation of any new limit asks or short positions whose price would be below the artificially inflated highest bid, effectively freezing the order book below that price. The problem originates from the sellMatchAlgo routine, which updates the remaining amount of the highest bid after a partial match but does not impose any cap on the number of bids examined in a single call. As a result, an attacker can repeatedly create a high‑price bid, then a slightly lower‑price ask that matches only a tiny fraction of the bid, leaving a residual high‑price bid of minimal size. Repeating this pattern creates thousands of such entries. When a legitimate user later tries to place a normal ask, the matching loop exhausts the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert and the user to lose the gas spent. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are failed ask submissions, out‑of‑gas reverts, and an inability to sell or open short positions at reasonable prices; balances appear unchanged and no refunds are received. The impact is a blocked market, inability to liquidate positions through the primaryMarginCall mechanism, and increased risk of collateral loss for short sellers who cannot close their debt. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that created thousands of high‑price bids and observed gas consumption exceeding the block limit. The bug is subtle because the matching logic itself works correctly for individual matches; the problem only emerges when the cumulative number of bids grows large, a scenario that is not obvious from normal functional testing. To remediate the issue the matching algorithm should enforce a hard limit on the number of orders processed per transaction, or redesign the iteration to stop once the gas consumption approaches the block limit, possibly by batching matches or pruning stale high‑price tiny bids. This class of bug falls under the category of “unbounded iteration leading to gas exhaustion” and violates the protocol’s economic assumptions that any participant can place asks or shorts at market‑reasonable prices without being blocked by malicious order placement.

title: Decreasing and increasing a short's collateral potentially uses an outdated asset price to calculate the collateral ratio
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inaccurate collateral‑ratio calculation that occurs when a short position adds or removes collateral. The contract reads the asset price from a cached oracle value that can be older than fifteen minutes, and it does not refresh the price before checking the minimum margin. Because the getCollateralRatio function multiplies the short's debt by this stale price, the resulting ratio may be higher than the true ratio that would be obtained using the current spot price. An attacker who holds a short can therefore call decreaseCollateral (or increaseCollateral) while the cached price is outdated, withdraw collateral up to the initial‑margin threshold, and end up with a lower real collateralisation than the protocol believes. This divergence can cause the short to become under‑collateralised, potentially triggering liquidation of the position or reducing the overall asset‑level collateral ratio, which harms other participants and the protocol’s solvency. The issue appears only when the oracle price has not been updated for more than fifteen minutes and a short owner interacts with the collateral functions; the UI may still display a healthy margin, leading users to think their withdrawal is safe. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call flow from decreaseCollateral to getCollateralRatio and observed that the oracle update condition is not enforced in this path. It is subtle because the contract emits a revert only when the calculated ratio falls below the initial margin, which may never happen with a stale price even though the real ratio is already below the safe level. To remediate, the protocol should compute the ratio using the current spot price, for example by invoking LibOracle.getSavedOrSpotOraclePrice together with a spot‑price‑aware collateral‑ratio function, or by forcing an oracle refresh before any collateral modification. This change ensures that the margin check reflects the true market value and prevents short owners from extracting more collateral than they are entitled to.

title: Use `safeTransfer`
description:
It is a good idea to add a `require()` statement that checks the return value of ERC20 token transfers or to use something like OpenZeppelin’s `safeTransfer()`/`safeTransferFrom()` unless one is sure the given token reverts in case of a failure. Failure to do so will cause silent failures of transfers and affect token accounting in contract.

However, using `require()` to check transfer return values could lead to issues with non-compliant ERC20 tokens which do not return a boolean value. Therefore, it’s highly advised to use OpenZeppelin’s `safeTransfer()`/`safeTransferFrom()`.
poc:

[L251](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/RubiconRouter.sol#L251): `ERC20(route[route.length - 1]).transfer(to, currentAmount);`

**peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol**

[L114](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L114): `token.transfer(recipient, amountWithdrawn);`

**rubiconPools/BathPair.sol**

**rubiconPools/BathToken.sol**

[L353](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L353): `IERC20(filledAssetToRebalance).transfer(`  
[L357](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L357): `IERC20(filledAssetToRebalance).transfer(msg.sender, stratReward);`  
[L602](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L602): `underlyingToken.transfer(feeTo, _fee);`  
[L605](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L605): `underlyingToken.transfer(receiver, amountWithdrawn);`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked ERC‑20 token transfer pattern that relies on the standard `transfer` and `transferFrom` functions without verifying their outcome. The root cause stems from the ERC‑20 specification allowing implementations to either return a boolean flag, return nothing, or revert on failure. The contract assumes that a failed transfer will automatically revert, but many tokens either return `false` or omit a return value altogether. Because the code does not capture the return value nor enforce a revert, a transfer that silently fails is treated as successful, allowing the contract to continue updating its internal accounting as if the tokens had moved. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a non‑standard token that conforms to the ERC‑20 interface yet deliberately returns `false` or no value on `transfer`. When the contract invokes `transfer` on such a token, the call completes without throwing, the return data is ignored, and the contract proceeds to record the receipt of funds, update balances, or emit events. Consequently, the protocol’s bookkeeping becomes inconsistent: users may see their on‑chain balance unchanged, receive zero tokens after a trade or withdrawal, or experience missing refunds. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction hash, but the expected token amount is absent, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue occurs whenever the contract interacts with an arbitrary ERC‑20 token—especially in the RubiconRouter, BathBuddy, BathPair, and BathToken contracts where multiple raw `transfer` calls are made. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and any party receiving token payouts—are affected because the contract’s token accounting can be corrupted. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that flagged numerous direct `transfer` invocations without any `require` or safety wrapper, highlighting the risk of silent failures. Detecting the problem in runtime is difficult because the transaction does not revert and no error is emitted; only post‑transaction balance checks would reveal the discrepancy. The recommended remediation is to replace each raw `transfer`/`transferFrom` with OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` or `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom`, which correctly handles missing return values and reverts on failure, thereby guaranteeing that token movement succeeds before the contract updates its state. In broader terms, this is a class of unchecked external call bugs where the contract fails to validate the success of a critical token transfer, leading to accounting violations and potential fund loss.

title: RubiconRouter: Excess ether did not return to the user
description: In swapWithETH/buyAllAmountWithETH/offerWithETH/depositWithETH functions of the RubiconRouter contract, when `msg.value > max_fill_withFee/pay_amt/amount/amtWithFee`, the excess ether will not be returned to the user.
bug_full: The RubiconRouter contract contains a set of payable functions—swapWithETH, buyAllAmountWithETH, offerWithETH and depositWithETH—that are intended to accept exactly the amount of Ether required to perform a trade or deposit operation. The vulnerability arises because each of these functions assumes that the caller will pass the precise amount needed, but they do not enforce this assumption with a strict equality check nor do they include logic to return any surplus Ether when msg.value exceeds the calculated max_fill_withFee, pay_amt, amount or amtWithFee. As a result, when a user mistakenly or intentionally sends more Ether than required, the excess value remains locked in the contract. The root cause is a missing refund mechanism and an absent validation that msg.value matches the expected payment amount. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by submitting a transaction with a higher msg.value than necessary; the transaction will still succeed, but the surplus Ether will never be transferred back to the sender. This leads to a direct financial impact: the user loses the over‑paid Ether, which appears to vanish from their balance without any corresponding token receipt or event indicating a refund. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to the affected router functions where the supplied Ether is greater than the exact amount needed for the operation. This bug affects all participants of the Rubicon protocol who interact with the router, including regular traders, liquidity providers, and any smart contracts that forward Ether to these functions. It was discovered during a manual code audit that identified the lack of a require(msg.value == expected) statement and the absence of a transfer back of the surplus. The issue can be subtle because the transaction does not revert; the user receives the expected outcome of the trade but may not notice that part of their Ether balance has been unintentionally retained by the router, especially since no explicit event is emitted for the leftover funds. Conceptually, the vulnerability belongs to the class of "excess payment handling" bugs, where smart contracts fail to either validate the exact payment amount or to safely refund any overpayment. From the user’s perspective, the symptoms can be described as sending Ether to perform a swap, receiving the correct tokens, but seeing the Ether balance reduced by more than expected or the wallet displaying an unexpected zero‑value refund. The expectation that the contract would either accept only the required amount or return the surplus is violated, leading to a loss of funds that appears as “money disappears” or “refund not received”. To remediate the issue, the contract should either enforce msg.value == requiredAmount with a require statement, or after performing the core logic, calculate any excess Ether and transfer it back to msg.sender, ensuring that the contract never retains more Ether than necessary for the operation.

title: Inconsistent Order Book Accounting When Working With Transfer-On-Fee or Deflationary Tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Rubicon Finance records token amounts when creating a new order (the offer function). The contract assumes that the amount of tokens transferred from the user to the protocol exactly matches the amount specified in the transaction. For standard ERC‑20 tokens this assumption holds, but for fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) or deflationary tokens the actual amount received after the transfer can be lower because a portion of the tokens is burned or sent to a fee collector on each transfer. The code in the deposit routine demonstrates awareness of this problem by measuring the token balance before and after the transfer and adjusting the recorded amount accordingly, but the same safeguard is not applied in the order‑book logic that handles offers. As a result, when a user creates an offer with a deflationary token, the orderbook stores the declared pay amount (e.g., 100 XYZ) while only the reduced amount (e.g., 90 XYZ) is actually escrowed. This discrepancy leads to inconsistent internal accounting, where the protocol believes it holds more tokens than it truly does. Under these conditions, later trades that attempt to fill the order may fail because the escrowed balance is insufficient, or the protocol may inadvertently allow partial fills that do not respect the original price, effectively causing a mismatch between the expected and real available liquidity. Users experience symptoms such as seeing a full order appear in the UI, but when the trade is executed the counter‑party receives less than expected or the order is rejected with an "insufficient balance" error. The issue is subtle because the transaction succeeds and the transferFrom call returns true, so there is no immediate revert, making it easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered through code review, where the auditors compared the handling of deflationary tokens in the deposit function with the offer function and noted the missing balance‑delta check. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting bugs that arise from incorrect assumptions about token transfer semantics, specifically fee‑on‑transfer and rebasing token behavior. To remediate the problem, the offer implementation should capture the contract's token balance before the transfer, execute the transferFrom, then recompute the actual received amount by subtracting the pre‑transfer balance from the post‑transfer balance, and finally store this corrected amount in the orderbook entry. Alternatively, the protocol could reject or whitelist tokens that have transfer fees, making the business logic explicit in documentation and preventing users from unintentionally creating orders with unsupported token types. By aligning the recorded amount with the real escrowed amount, the orderbook's accounting integrity is restored, preventing funds from appearing to disappear or orders from being partially fulfilled unexpectedly.

title: Cannot deposit to BathToken if token is Deflationary Token
description: Function `openBathTokenSpawnAndSignal` will alway revert when `newBathTokenUnderlying` or `desiredPairedAsset` is deflationary token
poc: There are ERC20 tokens that may make certain customizations to their ERC20 contracts. One type of these tokens is deflationary tokens that charge a certain fee for every `transfer()` or `transferFrom()` For example, I will assume that `newBathTokenUnderlying` is deflationary token. After [line 163](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathHouse.sol#L156-L163), the actual amount of `newBathTokenUnderlying` that BathHouse gained will be smaller than `initialLiquidityNew`. It will make the [deposit call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/rubiconPools/BathHouse.sol#L168) reverted because there are not enough fund to transfer.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the BathHouse contract’s `openBathTokenSpawnAndSignal` function, which assumes that the underlying ERC20 token used for a new BathToken vault behaves like a standard, non‑deflationary token. The function first transfers an amount defined as `initialLiquidityNew` from the caller to the contract, then reads the contract’s balance via `newBathTokenUnderlying.balanceOf(address(this))` and later calls `IBathToken(newOne).deposit(initialLiquidityNew, msg.sender)`. For tokens that charge a transfer fee (deflationary or fee‑on‑transfer tokens), the amount that actually arrives in the contract is smaller than `initialLiquidityNew`. Because the deposit call requires the exact amount that was approved and transferred, the mismatch causes the call to revert. This logical flaw is a classic transfer‑fee token compatibility issue where the contract’s accounting does not account for token‑level tax or burn on transfer. An attacker does not need to craft a malicious payload; simply supplying any token that deducts a fee on transfer triggers the revert, effectively denying service to users who wish to create a BathToken vault for that asset. The impact is that legitimate users see their transaction fail, receive no funds, and cannot open a vault for the chosen token, which reduces the protocol’s supported asset list and may erode confidence in the platform. The issue occurs each time `openBathTokenSpawnAndSignal` is invoked with either `newBathTokenUnderlying` or `desiredPairedAsset` being a deflationary token, i.e., any ERC20 that implements a fee on `transfer` or `transferFrom`. The affected parties include token holders attempting to create a new vault, the protocol itself because a class of tokens becomes unusable, and any downstream contracts that rely on the BathToken’s existence. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that examined the flow of token transfers and noted that the contract checks balances after the transfer but does not adjust the expected amount for possible transfer deductions. It is hard to notice because standard unit tests typically use vanilla ERC20 tokens that do not levy fees, so the revert only appears with exotic token contracts. The correct remediation is to either prohibit fee‑on‑transfer tokens explicitly or to capture the actual amount received after the transfer (by reading the balance delta) and use that precise value when invoking the deposit function. Conceptually, the fix requires the contract to base its accounting on the net amount transferred rather than the amount approved, thereby eliminating the balance mismatch. In user‑facing terms, a user attempting to create a vault sees a transaction failure with no funds deposited, contrary to the expectation that the vault would be created and their tokens locked. This discrepancy violates the business logic that a deposit should succeed once the user has approved the required token amount, and it breaks the accounting assumption that the transferred amount equals the approved amount. The bug belongs to the broader class of “fee‑on‑transfer token incompatibility” or “incorrect token accounting” vulnerabilities that arise when contracts treat all ERC20 tokens as if they transfer the exact amount specified.

title: No Storage Gap for Upgradeable Contracts
description:
For upgradeable contracts, there must be storage gap to “allow developers to freely add new state variables in the future without compromising the storage compatibility with existing deployments”. Otherwise it may be very difficult to write new implementation code. Without storage gap, the variable in child contract might be overwritten by the upgraded base contract if new variables are added to the base contract. This could have unintended and very serious consequences to the child contracts.

Refer to the bottom part of this article: <https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/1.x/writing-upgradeable>
poc:
As an example, the `ExpiringMarket` contract inherits `SimpleMarket`, and the `SimpleMarket` contract does not contain any storage gap. If in a future upgrade, an additional variable is added to the `SimpleMarket` contract, that new variable will overwrite the storage slot of the `stopped` variable in the `ExpiringMarket` contract, causing unintended consequences.

Similarly, the `ExpiringMarket` does not contain any storage gap either, and the `RubiconMarket` contract inherits `ExpiringMarket`. If a new variable is added to the `ExpiringMarket` contract in an upgrade, that variable will overwrite the `buyEnabled` variable in `ExpiringMarket` contract.
bug_full:
The vulnerability stems from the absence of a reserved storage gap in a hierarchy of upgradeable smart contracts. Upgradeable contracts rely on a fixed storage layout that must remain compatible across implementations, because a proxy forwards calls to the current implementation while preserving the same storage slots. When a contract that forms part of an inheritance chain does not allocate a buffer of unused slots – commonly expressed as `uint256[50] private __gap;` – any future upgrade that introduces new state variables in a parent contract will shift the layout of subsequent variables in the child contracts. This shift causes the newly added variable to occupy a storage slot that was previously used by an existing variable in a descendant contract, overwriting its value. The root cause is therefore a mismatch between the expected storage layout (as defined at deployment) and the actual layout after an upgrade, due to missing reserved storage space.

An attacker (or simply a careless developer) can exploit this by deploying a new implementation that adds a variable to the base contract without having reserved slots. During the upgrade, the new variable is written to a slot that formerly held a critical flag in the child contract, such as a `paused` or `stopped` boolean, or a configuration flag like `buyEnabled`. As a result, the flag may be unintentionally set to true or false, altering the contract’s behaviour. For example, a market contract that should reject trades when paused might suddenly accept them, leading to unauthorized trades, loss of funds, or execution of functions that were meant to be disabled. Because the proxy does not reset storage, the overwritten values persist, and the contract may appear to function normally while its internal accounting is corrupted.

This issue manifests only when a contract upgrade adds new state variables to a parent contract that lacks a storage gap, and the child contracts have already allocated their own variables without padding. The problem is difficult to detect during normal operation because the contract’s external interface may still respond, and only the internal state diverges from expectations. Users may notice symptoms such as trades executing when the UI indicates the market is paused, refunds not being issued, balances unexpectedly becoming zero, or certain functions suddenly reverting without clear cause. From a business‑logic perspective the bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that state variables remain immutable unless explicitly changed, breaking trust in the protocol’s safety mechanisms.

The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the inheritance hierarchy of the Rubicon protocol contracts. The auditor observed that neither `SimpleMarket` nor `ExpiringMarket` included the recommended storage gap, and reasoned that any future addition of variables would overwrite critical flags in descendant contracts. The analysis highlighted concrete scenarios: adding a variable to `SimpleMarket` would overwrite the `stopped` flag of `ExpiringMarket`; adding a variable to `ExpiringMarket` would overwrite the `buyEnabled` flag of `RubiconMarket`. These examples illustrate how the bug can lead to unintended and potentially severe consequences for market operation and user funds.

To remediate the problem, each upgradeable contract in the inheritance chain should reserve a sufficient number of unused storage slots at the end of its state variable list. The conventional approach, as prescribed by OpenZeppelin, is to append `uint256[50] private __gap;` (or a similarly sized array) after the last declared variable. This creates a buffer that can accommodate future variables without shifting the positions of existing slots, preserving storage compatibility across upgrades. Additionally, developers should inherit from OpenZeppelin’s `Initializable` contract and use the standard upgradeable contract templates, which embed the storage gap automatically. By following these practices, future upgrades can safely introduce new state without risking overwrites, ensuring that protocol logic, user balances, and security controls remain consistent.

title: USDT is not supported because of approval mechanism
description:
When using the approval mechanism in USDT, the approval must be set to 0 before it is updated. In Rubicon, when creating a pair, the paired asset’s approval is not set to 0 before it is updated.

Can’t create pairs with USDT, the most popular stablecoin, as the approval will revert.
poc:
[USDT](https://etherscan.io/address/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#code) reverts on approval if previous allowance is not 0:

```solidity
require(!((_value != 0) && (allowed[msg.sender][_spender] != 0)));
```

When creating a pair, Rubicon [approves](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/rubiconPools/BathHouse.sol#L180) the paired asset without first setting it to 0:

```solidity
desiredPairedAsset.approve(pairedPool, initialLiquidityExistingBathToken);
```

Therefore, if desiredPairedAsset is USDT, the function will revert, and pairs with USDT can not be created.

This problem will also manifest in RubiconMarket’s [approval function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconRouter.sol#L157) and BathToken’s [approval function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L256),
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between Rubicon's pair‑creation workflow and the non‑standard approval logic of the USDT token. USDT implements a safety check in its ERC20‑style approve function that rejects any call which tries to change an existing non‑zero allowance to another non‑zero value, requiring the allowance to be reset to zero before a new amount can be set. This pattern deviates from the typical infinite‑approval assumption used by most ERC20 tokens. Rubicon’s smart contracts, specifically the functions that approve a paired asset when a new liquidity pool is created, invoke the token’s approve method directly with the desired allowance amount, without first resetting the allowance to zero. If the caller already has a non‑zero allowance for the USDT token— a situation that commonly occurs after previous deposits or approvals— the call triggers USDT’s revert condition and the entire pair‑creation transaction fails. The exploit scenario is therefore straightforward: a user attempts to create a pool that includes USDT as the paired asset, the contract executes an approve call, the USDT token reverts due to its internal require, and the transaction is aborted. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the operation should succeed, but the transaction simply fails, often with an error such as “approval failed” or a generic revert, leaving the user confused as no pair is created and no liquidity is added. This impacts liquidity providers, traders, and the Rubicon protocol itself because the most widely used stablecoin cannot be paired, limiting market depth and potentially reducing user trust. The issue was identified during a security audit when the auditors attempted to create a USDT pair and observed a deterministic revert caused by the approval logic. It can be hard to notice because many tokens adhere to the standard ERC20 approve behavior, so developers may not anticipate the extra zero‑reset step required by USDT. The proper remediation is to adopt the “reset‑to‑zero‑then‑set” approval pattern for tokens that enforce this rule, or alternatively use the increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance functions where available, or implement a token‑agnostic safe approval library that checks and clears existing allowances before setting a new one. By ensuring the allowance is zeroed out before any new approve call, Rubicon can support USDT and other non‑standard tokens without encountering revert errors, aligning the contract’s behavior with the business logic that expects successful creation of paired assets and preservation of user funds.

title: BathBuddy locks up Ether it receives
description:
The BathBuddy contract is able to receive ETH. But, there’s no way of ever retrieving that ETH from the contract. The funds will be locked up.

Currently, there seems to be no logic in the protocol where ETH is sent to the contract. But, it might happen in the future. So I’d say it’s a MED issue.
poc: `receive()` function: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L69>
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fund‑locking or sink‑hole weakness where the BathBuddy contract can accept Ether through its payable receive() fallback, but it provides no mechanism to transfer that Ether out of the contract. The root cause is the presence of a receive() function without any corresponding withdraw, self‑destruct, or forwarding logic, and without any access‑controlled function that would allow the contract owner or any other actor to retrieve the balance. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit the bug simply by sending ETH to the contract address—either intentionally, by mistake, or via a malicious contract that forwards Ether. Because the contract lacks any outbound ETH logic, the transferred funds become permanently locked inside the contract’s balance. The impact is that any Ether received is effectively lost: users who think they are paying a fee or depositing collateral will see their transaction succeed, but their wallet balance will not decrease in the expected way after the protocol processes the deposit, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. This situation occurs whenever the contract’s address receives Ether, which may happen now or in future protocol upgrades that unintentionally forward ETH. The affected parties include any user who sends Ether, the protocol itself (as it may be forced to hold unusable funds), and developers who rely on the contract’s expected behavior. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the contract’s source files and noted the existence of a receive() function without any complementary withdrawal code. The problem can be hard to notice because Solidity permits a contract to have a receive() function without any compile‑time warnings, and the absence of a withdraw function does not raise errors; only runtime behavior reveals the lock‑up. To remediate, the contract should either remove the receive() function if handling ETH is not required, or implement a safe, access‑controlled withdrawal path (e.g., an onlyOwner withdraw() that uses call() with proper re‑entrancy guards) or a self‑destruct that returns the balance to a designated address. This class of bug—often called "Ether sinkhole" or "fund‑locking"—violates the fundamental accounting assumption that any received value can be reclaimed or redistributed according to the protocol’s logic. From a user’s perspective, they may see a successful transaction receipt, but later notice that the protocol shows no credit or that their deposited amount appears to have vanished, contradicting the expectation that the system would either acknowledge the deposit or return the funds. The discrepancy between expected refund or balance update and the reality of a zero‑return creates confusion and erodes trust in the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Wrong DOMAIN_SEPARATOR
description: The `DOMAIN_SEPARATOR` is wrongly calculated.
poc:
In the `initialize` method of the `BathToken` contract, the `name` of the contract is used to calculate the `DOMAIN_SEPARATOR`, however said name is set later, so it will use an incorrect `name`, making it impossible to calculate the `DOMAIN_SEPARATOR` correctly.

```solidity
DOMAIN_SEPARATOR = keccak256(
    abi.encode(
        keccak256(
            "EIP712Domain(string name,string version,uint256 chainId,address verifyingContract)"
        ),
        keccak256(bytes(name)),
        keccak256(bytes("1")),
        chainId,
        address(this)
    )
);
name = string(abi.encodePacked(_symbol, (" v1")));
```

Affected source code:

  * [BathToken.sol#L199-L210](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/521d50b22b41b1f52ff9a67ea68ed8012c618da9/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L199-L210)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect calculation of the EIP‑712 DOMAIN_SEPARATOR within the BathToken contract. During contract initialization the code builds the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR by hashing the contract name together with other domain fields, but the contract name variable is assigned only after the hash operation. Because the name used in the hash is still the default zero value at that moment, the resulting DOMAIN_SEPARATOR does not reflect the actual token name that will later appear on‑chain. This ordering flaw belongs to a class of initialization‑order bugs where state variables required for cryptographic domain construction are set in the wrong sequence. The impact is that any functionality that relies on the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR—most notably EIP‑2612 permit signatures, meta‑transactions, or off‑chain signed approvals—will fail verification, as signed messages will be validated against a mismatched domain. From a user’s perspective, attempts to approve a token via a signed permit will revert with an "invalid signature" error, leading to a perception that the token is broken or that approvals are silently ignored. The issue manifests whenever the initialize function is called, which is typically during deployment of a new BathToken instance; any subsequent calls that depend on the domain separator inherit the wrong value. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s initialization logic, where the auditor noted that the name assignment occurs after the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR computation. The bug can be subtle because the contract will still compile and appear functional; only signature‑based interactions expose the fault, making it easy to overlook during manual testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should set the name (or any other domain‑relevant fields) before computing the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR, ensuring the hash incorporates the correct values. In broader terms, developers should verify that all inputs to a domain‑separator hash are fully initialized prior to the hash operation, adhering to the EIP‑712 specification and preventing mismatched signatures that break token approval flows.

title: Use `call`
description:
When transferring ETH, use `call()` instead of `transfer()`.

The `transfer()` function only allows the recipient to use 2300 gas. If the recipient uses more than that, transfers will fail. In the future gas costs might change increasing the likelihood of that happening.

Keep in mind that `call()` introduces the risk of reentrancy. But, as long as the router follows the checks effects interactions pattern it should be fine. It’s not supposed to hold any tokens anyway.
poc: See the linked code snippets above.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract using the Solidity built‑in transfer() function to send Ether to external addresses. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient, which is sufficient for a simple fallback that only emits an event, but it is insufficient for any logic that requires more gas, such as writing to storage, calling another contract, or executing complex fallback code. Because the gas amount is hard‑coded, the call will revert if the recipient’s fallback consumes more than 2300 gas, causing the entire transaction to fail and leaving the Ether locked in the sending contract. This situation can be triggered when a legitimate user interacts with a contract that has a fallback requiring additional gas, or when a malicious contract deliberately crafts a fallback that exceeds the stipend, thereby forcing the transfer to revert and potentially freezing funds. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should have resulted in a successful ETH transfer instead completes with no ETH received, or the UI shows a zero balance change despite the operation appearing to succeed. The impact is a loss of usability and, in worst‑case scenarios, permanent loss of funds that cannot be withdrawn because the contract’s withdrawal logic relies on transfer and therefore repeatedly fails. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the router’s ETH handling code and noted the hard‑coded gas limit as a future‑proofing risk, especially given that Ethereum’s gas costs evolve over time and may render the 2300‑gas stipend insufficient for newer contracts. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not necessarily revert with an obvious error message; instead, the transfer silently fails and the contract’s state may not reflect the intended balance change, making debugging difficult. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer() with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas, capture the returned success flag, and explicitly require that the call succeeded. While call() removes the gas‑limit issue, it reintroduces the possibility of re‑entrancy attacks; therefore the contract must follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, ensuring that state changes occur before any external call, and that no sensitive logic is left vulnerable after the call. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “fixed‑gas stipend transfer failures” where using transfer() can cause Ether to become unrecoverable, and the fix is to adopt call() with proper success handling and robust re‑entrancy safeguards.

title: `withdrawForETH` could be used to drain the WETH in `RubiconRouter.sol`
description: In the `withdrawForETH` function in `RubiconRouter.sol`, the `targetPool` may be any contract that implements the `IBathToken` interface and returns `wethAddress` as its underlying token. The `withdrawnWETH` amount could be set to the `RubiconRouter.sol` contract’s WETH balance so that the contract’s entire WETH balance is withdrawn, as long as the `tagetPool` does not transfer any WETH to `RubiconRouter.sol`. The caller of the `withdrawForETH` function would then receive the withdraw amount.
bug_full: The RubiconRouter contract contains a function called withdrawForETH that is intended to let a user redeem a share of a BathToken pool for native ETH. The function assumes that the target pool, which must implement the IBathToken interface and report WETH as its underlying token, will actually transfer the appropriate amount of WETH to the router before the router unwraps it and sends ETH back to the caller. This assumption is not enforced. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that conforms to IBathToken, reports the router's WETH address as its underlying token, and makes its balanceOf function return an arbitrarily large value (for example, uint256.max). Because the withdrawForETH function only checks that the caller owns at least the requested number of shares, the attacker can pass this check by claiming to own a huge number of shares. The subsequent transferFrom call is allowed to be a no‑op, so no WETH is moved into the router. When the attacker then calls the pool’s withdraw method, the malicious pool can be coded to return the full WETH balance currently held by the RubiconRouter contract. The router subsequently calls WETH9.withdraw on this amount, converting all of its WETH into ETH, and finally transfers the obtained ETH to the attacker’s address. As a result, the router’s entire WETH reserve is drained without the attacker having supplied any WETH. This bug occurs whenever the withdrawForETH function is invoked with a crafted targetPool that can lie about its balance and does not actually transfer tokens. It primarily impacts the protocol’s router contract and any user who has mistakenly sent ETH/WETH to the router, as their deposited funds can be unintentionally removed. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the logic of withdrawForETH was examined and the missing verification of token flow was identified. The vulnerability is subtle because the function’s public interface looks legitimate—requiring only that the caller own enough shares—and the lack of a post‑withdraw balance check makes the drain invisible during normal code reviews. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that the amount of WETH withdrawn does not exceed the amount that was transferred into the router during the same call, verify that the router’s WETH balance decreases accordingly, and restrict the targetPool to a whitelist of trusted pool contracts or add explicit checks that the pool’s withdraw function actually reduces the router’s balance. In user‑facing terms, a user might notice that after invoking withdrawForETH they receive ETH even though they never supplied WETH, while the router’s displayed liquidity suddenly becomes zero, indicating a loss of funds.

title: M-4 Lack of incentivization of the battle settlement process
description: There is no specific incentivization of the Battle.sol#L424 function. Though most of the users are interested in battle finalization, but in order to save gas each user would prefer to avoid making the settlement by themselves. It may make sense for some networks where gas is expensive enough. Consecutively, it is expected behavior that users wouldn't make battle settlements, and the project owner will make it in a centralized manner even if it is unprofitable for them. It causes some centralization and an open attack vector for the griefing attack by spamming the project by battles that the project owner is enforced to finalize even if it is unprofitable for them.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing economic incentive for the function that finalizes a battle in the protocol. Because the contract does not reward any caller for executing the settlement step, rational users prefer to avoid the transaction in order to save gas. As a result, the responsibility to call the settlement function falls on the project owner or a single privileged actor, who may be forced to perform the operation even when the gas cost exceeds any potential benefit. This creates a centralization risk: the protocol relies on a trusted party to manually trigger settlement, contrary to the intended decentralized design. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly creating battles that remain unsettled, a form of griefing or denial‑of‑service attack. By spamming the system with many pending battles, the attacker forces the owner to spend increasing amounts of gas to settle each one, potentially making the process economically unviable for the owner. The impact is that the protocol may become unable to progress battles, users see their expected rewards or refunds never materialize, and the overall trust in the system erodes because a single entity must intervene. The issue manifests when a battle reaches the finalization stage but no participant initiates the settlement transaction; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a battle as “completed” while the on‑chain state still indicates it is pending, leading to missing payouts or zero balances where a reward was expected. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the battle lifecycle and noted the absence of any incentive mechanism attached to the settlement call. Because the function executes correctly but simply lacks a reward, the flaw can be subtle and may not be caught by automated tools that focus on re‑entrancy or overflow bugs. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a reward scheme for the caller of the settlement function, possibly combined with a spam‑prevention mechanism such as a minimum stake or a fee, thereby aligning economic incentives with the desired decentralized operation and mitigating the griefing vector.

title: Insufficient input validation
description:
Throughout the codebase, there are couple of functions where important input validation is missing. The inputs are not constrained at all.
setMinimumBid()
setMaxSupply()
setCost()
setPhase()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a lack of input validation in administrative setter functions such as setMinimumBid, setMaxSupply, setCost, and setPhase. Because the contract does not enforce any bounds or sanity checks on the parameters supplied to these functions, an attacker or a careless admin can pass extreme or nonsensical values (for example a minimum bid of zero, a maximum supply of zero or a value that overflows, a cost of zero or an excessively large number, or a phase identifier that is outside the expected enumeration). The root cause is that the code does not include require statements or other checks to ensure that the inputs respect the business rules of the auction or token sale. An attacker who can call these setter functions, either because they are public or because they have been granted the appropriate role, can exploit the missing validation by setting parameters that break the economic model: a zero minimum bid allows anyone to win an auction for free, a zero max supply can freeze minting, an excessively high cost can prevent legitimate participants from buying, and an invalid phase can cause the contract to enter an undefined state where functions revert or behave incorrectly. The impact includes loss of revenue, denial of service for users, potential token supply inconsistencies, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever an authorized account invokes one of the setter functions with an out‑of‑range value; it does not require any special blockchain state and can be triggered at any time after deployment. All participants who rely on the contract’s economic parameters—bidders, token buyers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the contract may behave contrary to the expectations expressed in the UI (for example users see a minimum bid field showing 0, or the UI shows that the sale is in a phase that should not accept purchases). The flaw was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the absence of require checks on critical configuration functions. Because the contract still compiles and the functions execute without reverting, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when abnormal values appear in the UI or when transactions unexpectedly succeed or fail. The proper remediation is to add explicit validation logic to each setter, enforcing that parameters fall within sensible ranges (for example minimum bid must be greater than zero and less than the maximum possible bid, max supply must be a positive integer within the token’s total cap, cost must be non‑zero and reasonable, and phase must be limited to defined enum values). This class of bug—insufficient input validation—breaks the contract’s business logic and accounting assumptions, allowing misconfiguration that can lead to funds disappearing, sales stalling, or the protocol operating in an unintended state.

title: Owners can rug the users and not send anything
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the auction contract where the function that finalises the auction only transfers the highest bid to the contract owner and never transfers the promised NFT to the winning bidder. The root cause is that the endAuction implementation lacks any call to move the NFT and relies solely on a payable call to the owner followed by an event emission. An attacker who is the contract owner can exploit this by invoking endAuction after the auction has been marked active; the call will succeed, the owner will receive the funds, and the winner will receive nothing because no transfer of the token is performed. The impact is that users who win the auction lose the expected reward; from the user’s perspective the UI may show the auction ended and the winner address, but the winner’s wallet will not contain the NFT and the bid amount is gone. This occurs whenever the owner calls endAuction while the auctionActive flag is true, because the function does not verify or enforce prize delivery. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the endAuction logic and noticed the missing NFT transfer. It can be hard to notice because the function emits a correct AuctionEnded event and the transfer to the owner succeeds, giving the impression that the auction completed normally. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑distribution or escrow‑bypass vulnerabilities where the contract pays out one side of a trade without delivering the counterpart asset, enabling a rug‑pull. To remediate, the contract should include a safe transfer of the NFT to the highestBidder before sending the funds, and should revert if the NFT transfer fails, or use a pull‑payment pattern that only releases funds after the prize has been successfully transferred.

title: M-5 The redeemObligation will always be reverted
description: redeemObligation is designed to be called when the state is Outcome.ONGOING. However, it utilizes Manager.sol#L204 which will invariably be reverted under such conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a redemption function that is intended to let users withdraw their obligations while the protocol is in the Outcome.ONGOING state, but the function internally calls a manager routine that unconditionally reverts when the outcome is still ongoing. The root cause is a mismatch between the expected contract state and the actual state check performed in the manager code, resulting in a logical dead‑end: the redeemObligation entry point is reachable, yet any call triggers a revert at Manager.sol line 204. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit this by simply invoking redeemObligation, causing the transaction to fail and preventing the withdrawal of any locked funds. The impact is that users who expect to receive a refund or to close their position see their transaction revert, their balances remain unchanged, and the protocol’s liquidity can become permanently locked for those obligations. This condition occurs whenever the protocol reports an ongoing outcome, which is the normal state during the resolution phase, making the bug appear only in that specific window. All participants holding obligations—individual traders, liquidity providers, or any role that relies on the ability to redeem—are affected because the contract silently refuses to process the request. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined state transitions and function pre‑conditions, and it can be hard to notice because the function signature suggests it is usable, yet the internal revert is not obvious without tracing the manager call. To remediate, the contract should either adjust the manager’s state check to allow calls during Outcome.ONGOING, or replace the call with an alternative withdrawal routine that is compatible with the ongoing state, thereby restoring the intended refund path. In essence, this is a state‑validation bug that breaks the accounting logic of the protocol, leading to missing refunds and funds that appear to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: Platform fees withdrawal will sweep oracle agents earned fees
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract’s platform‑fee withdrawal routine transfers the entire token balance of the LLMOracleCoordinator, including amounts that have only been approved for oracle agents to claim. Oracle agents earn a share of user‑paid fees when their responses satisfy accuracy criteria. Instead of receiving the tokens directly, the coordinator calls approve(responder, amount), giving the agent an ERC‑20 allowance. Because the allowance does not move ownership, the tokens remain in the coordinator’s balance until the agent executes transferFrom. The admin function withdrawPlatformFees() uses a simple token.transfer of the whole contract balance to the protocol treasury. When this function is called before an agent has called transferFrom, the approved amount is swept away, leaving the allowance pointing to a zero balance. As a result the agent’s subsequent transferFrom reverts with an insufficient‑balance error, and the agent never receives the earned fees. The issue occurs whenever the platform‑fee withdrawal is executed while there are pending approved fees for any oracle agent. It affects all oracle agents, the protocol’s revenue accounting, and any user expecting the agent to be compensated. The bug was discovered during a functional test that simulated a generator responding to a request; after the response the coordinator granted an allowance of 0.004 ether, but the admin’s withdrawPlatformFees call emptied the contract, causing the transferFrom to fail. The problem is subtle because the allowance appears to be granted correctly and the contract’s balance shows the expected amount before the admin call, so developers may assume the fees are safe. This class of bug can be described as an allowance‑sweep or fee‑sweeping vulnerability, where a privileged withdrawal function does not account for pending allowances and unintentionally confiscates funds that are earmarked for other parties. From a user perspective the agent receives no payment, the UI may show a zero balance after a successful response, and the expected refund or reward is missing. The business logic that fees earned by agents are reserved for them is violated, breaking the accounting invariant that total fees = platform fees + agent fees. The recommended mitigation is to keep a separate accounting of the amount reserved for agents and subtract that reserve from the amount withdrawn by the admin, or to transfer only the unreserved platform fees, ensuring that approved agent fees remain claimable.

title: Request responses and validations can be mocked leading to extraction of fees and/or forcing other generators to lose their fees by making them outliers
description:
The respond and validate functions can be mocked which will lead to attacker getting the generation and validation fees without providing valid responses, and could also lead to attacks against other generator/validators in order to force them lose their generation/validation fees.
