The LLMOracleRegistry allows any address to register and unregister at any time. An attacker can register multiple generators/validators and call respond and validate with invalid output/scores with as low generatorStakeAmount/validatorStakeAmount whichever is greater. This can be done by calling register -> respond -> unregister for as many generations needed, and then register -> validate -> unregister for as many validations needed.

It will lead to lost generation and validation fees while getting invalid output values. Furthermore, this attack can be used in order to force a legitimate generator/validator appear as an outlier and lose their generation/validation fee.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw in the LLMOracleRegistry where the respond and validate functions can be mocked, allowing an attacker to claim generation and validation fees without providing legitimate oracle outputs. The root cause is the absence of a locking mechanism that prevents a registered generator or validator from unregistering before the request they answered or validated has been finalized, combined with an open registration policy that lets any address join and leave at will and no slashing for misbehaviour. An attacker can register a fake generator or validator, immediately call the respond or validate function with fabricated output or low scores, collect the associated fee, and then unregister before the system has a chance to verify the result. Because the protocol treats the fee payout as unconditional upon the function call, the attacker extracts funds while the oracle receives invalid data. Moreover, by flooding the system with such mock responses, the attacker can cause honest participants to appear as statistical outliers, triggering the outlier‑penalty logic that strips their fees as well. This issue manifests when a user or protocol participant observes that their expected generation or validation rewards vanish after they unregister, or that legitimate generators lose fees despite submitting correct responses. It affects the economic integrity of the entire oracle service, harming honest generators, validators, and any downstream contracts that rely on trustworthy oracle data. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle of registration, response, validation, and fee distribution, noting that the state transition does not enforce any waiting period or penalty for premature deregistration. The problem is subtle because the functions appear to work correctly on the surface – they accept inputs and emit fee transfers – so the loss of funds can be attributed to normal protocol operation rather than a clear exploit. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a lock that disallows unregistering until the associated request is settled, optionally restrict registration to a vetted whitelist, and eventually implement a slashing mechanism that penalises generators or validators that submit falsified data. By enforcing these controls, the system regains its accounting guarantees: fees are only paid for verified, non‑malicious contributions, and honest participants are protected from being falsely flagged as outliers.

title: Unrestricted validation score range for validators in `LLMOracleCoordinator::validate`.
bug_full: The LLMOracleCoordinator contract contains a statistical‑based reward mechanism that selects validators for a fee by filtering submitted scores to the interval mean ± standard deviation. The validate function accepts an arbitrary array of uint256 scores but does not enforce any upper bound on the values that can be submitted. Because the mean and standard deviation are computed over all submitted scores, a validator (or colluding group) can submit extremely high outlier scores, for example values in the range 100‑150 while honest validators submit scores in the normal range 0‑5. These outliers inflate both the arithmetic mean and the variance, which in turn expands the mean ± stddev window. When the finalizeValidation loop later checks each score against this window, the inflated range no longer contains the low, honest scores, so they fail the condition (score >= mean‑stddev && score <= mean+stddev) and are excluded from the “inner mean” calculation. Consequently, only the validators that submitted the high outlier scores satisfy the filter and receive the validator fee, while honest validators see their allowance remain unchanged, effectively receiving zero reward. From a user perspective this appears as a missing or zero reward after a validation round, even though the validator performed a valid submission. The bug is a classic case of unchecked input leading to statistical manipulation, belonging to the class of “unbounded parameter” or “range‑validation” vulnerabilities. It was discovered during a security audit when the test suite demonstrated that validators with low scores received no allowance while high‑scoring validators were rewarded. The issue is subtle because the statistical functions themselves return correct values; the problem lies in the business logic that assumes scores are bounded, so the skewed statistics are not immediately obvious. The impact is unfair reward distribution, loss of incentives for honest participants, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s fairness. The vulnerability manifests whenever the task parameters allow validators to submit scores without a maximum limit, i.e., for any task where the validate function is called. Mitigation consists of introducing a configurable maximum score (e.g., maxScore in the task struct) and adding a check in the validate function that reverts if any submitted score exceeds this bound, thereby preventing outlier manipulation and preserving the intended statistical filtering logic.

title: Users can list assets with price < 1 ERC20 (ETH, WETH), leading to potential DoS vulnerability.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing minimum‑price validation in the asset‑listing functions of the marketplace contract. Because the code only checks that the price is non‑zero, an attacker can create listings with a price that is smaller than one whole ERC20 token (for example 1 wei or 1 unit of the token’s smallest denomination). This flaw originates from the absence of a check that enforces a minimum price based on the token’s decimal precision, allowing any positive amount to be accepted. An attacker can exploit the bug by repeatedly listing their own assets with the minimal allowed price until the per‑buyer, per‑round asset limit (maxAssetCount) is reached. Once the limit is filled, legitimate users attempting to list assets receive the AssetLimitExceeded revert, experience failed transactions, and see no new listings appear in the UI even though they paid the required royalty fee. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden inability to list assets, error messages indicating the asset limit has been hit, and a mismatch between expected listings and actual on‑chain state. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks honest participants from using the marketplace, degrades protocol performance due to a flood of low‑value listings, and undermines the economic assumptions of the platform that each listing carries a meaningful price. The issue occurs only during the sell phase when the buyer agent reports a Sell status, and it is triggered by any call to list or relist that supplies a price lower than the token’s unit. It affects sellers, buyers, and the overall protocol because the asset‑count restriction is a core invariant for market fairness. The problem was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, which included a proof‑of‑concept test that listed multiple assets with a price of 1 and verified that the asset limit could be reached with negligible cost. The bug is hard to notice because the price is technically non‑zero, so fee‑related checks pass, and the low price does not raise obvious red flags in transaction logs. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum price that respects the ERC20 token’s decimal precision (for example at least one‑hundredth of a token or a configurable floor), reject zero or sub‑unit values, and optionally add anti‑spam measures such as rate limiting, deposit requirements, or a separate “free asset creation” guard that prevents Sybil attacks while still allowing legitimate zero‑fee listings.

title: Update state requests or Purchase requests occurring at the end of the phase will not process
poc:
BuyerAgent wants to buy a given item His Round is 10 and we are at the Buy phase know The buying phase is about to end there is just one Hour left BuyerAgent Fired BuyerAgent::oraclePurchaseRequest() Fees got paid and we are waiting for the task to complete Generators and Validators took 6 Hours to complete this task Know, the BuyerAgent Round is 10 and the Phase is Withdraw calling BuyerAgent::purchase() will fail as we are not in the Buy Phase

The problem is that there is no time left for requesting and firing, if the request occur at the end of the Phase, finalizing the request either purach or update state will fail, as the phase will end.

We are doing Oracle and off-chain computations for the given task, and the time to finalize (complete) a task differs from one task to another according to difficulty.

There are three things here that make this problem occur. If the Operator is not active, the BuyerAgent should call the request himself. If Completing the Task process takes too much time, this can occur for Tasks that require a lot of validations, or difficulty is high if there is a High Demand for a given request the Operator may finalize some of them at the end.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of purchase and state‑update requests that are issued close to the end of a protocol phase. BuyerAgent allows a caller to submit an oraclePurchaseRequest or oracleStateRequest during the Buy phase and later to invoke purchase or updateState to finalize the operation. The contract only verifies that the caller is still in the Buy phase at the moment of the final call, but it does not enforce that enough time remains for the off‑chain oracle task (generation and validation) to complete before the phase transitions to Withdraw. Consequently, if a request is submitted with only a short interval left in the Buy phase, the generators and validators may finish after the phase has already changed. When the caller later invokes purchase or updateState, the phase check fails and the function reverts, leaving the previously paid oracle fee unrecoverable. The root cause is a missing time‑window validation: the code checks phase equality but ignores the elapsed time needed for asynchronous off‑chain computation. Exploitation is straightforward – an honest user or a malicious actor can deliberately submit a request at the last minute, causing the protocol to lock the fee without delivering the purchased items or updating the buyer’s state. The impact includes loss of fees, failure to receive purchased assets, and a state that does not reflect the intended transaction, which can be observed by the user as a missing balance, a zero refund, or an unchanged inventory after a purchase attempt. This condition occurs whenever the phase duration is fixed and the off‑chain task duration is variable, especially for complex requests that require many generators or validators. All participants who rely on BuyerAgent – buyers, protocol operators, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that a request made in a phase will be fulfilled within the same phase) are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of a deadline check before the phase transition. It is hard to notice because the initial transaction succeeds and the fee is deducted, yet the later failure produces no explicit error to the user beyond a generic revert, making the loss appear as a silent disappearance of funds. The bug belongs to the class of time‑window or race‑condition errors where state transitions are not synchronized with asynchronous external processes. To remediate, the contract should enforce a safety margin before the end of the Buy phase, reject new oracle requests when the remaining time is insufficient for expected off‑chain processing, or provide a mechanism to refund fees if the request cannot be completed because the phase has changed. Implementing such checks restores the guarantee that fees are only taken when the protocol can actually deliver the requested service, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of reliable purchase and state‑update operations.

title: BuyerAgent Batch Purchase Failure Due to Asset Transfer or Approval Revocation
description:
The vulnerability allows a malicious seller to disrupt the purchase process of the BuyerAgent contract. This occurs when an asset that is supposed to be bought by the BuyerAgent is either transferred away or has its approval revoked, causing the entire batch purchase transaction to fail. As a result, the BuyerAgent becomes unable to complete the intended purchase of other assets, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) scenario.

The vulnerability stems from the flow involving the BuyerAgent's interaction with the Swan contract for purchasing assets. The BuyerAgent first sends an oraclePurchaseRequest to gather the list of assets to be purchased, which is determined by an external oracle. Once the purchase list is available, the user calls BuyerAgent::purchase to buy the assets. During this phase, the BuyerAgent invokes Swan::purchase for each asset in the purchase list. https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-swan-dria/blob/main/contracts/swan/BuyerAgent.sol?plain=1#L237-L252

Each asset listed for purchase creates an ERC721 token, where the seller is the owner of the respective tokenId. https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-swan-dria/blob/main/contracts/swan/SwanAsset.sol?plain=1#L20-L43

The vulnerability is exposed when one of the ERC721 assets in the purchase list is transferred away from the seller to another user, or when the seller revokes the approval for Swan. Since the Swan contract requires the ownership of the asset to remain unchanged and the asset's approval to remain valid, the transfer or revocation leads to the failure of the Swan::purchase call. https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-swan-dria/blob/main/contracts/swan/Swan.sol?plain=1#L294 Consequently, this failure causes BuyerAgent::purchase to revert, preventing the purchase of other assets listed in the transaction.

The impact of this vulnerability is significant as it allows a malicious seller to manipulate the behavior of the BuyerAgent contract, ultimately preventing it from purchasing other legitimate assets. This attack can be used to deceive buyers by causing failed transactions, even if those transactions involve assets from honest sellers. This vulnerability can be exploited repeatedly to create a denial of service, disrupting normal operations of the BuyerAgent and affecting market participants.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the BuyerAgent contract that arises when a batch purchase of ERC721 assets is performed through the Swan marketplace. The contract assumes that every asset listed for purchase remains owned by the original seller and that the seller’s approval for the Swan contract stays valid for the duration of the transaction. This assumption is the root cause: the purchase logic does not verify ownership or approval before invoking Swan::purchase for each token, nor does it catch a revert from an individual call. When a malicious seller transfers one of the listed tokens to another address or revokes the approval for Swan before the BuyerAgent executes its purchase, the call to Swan::purchase reverts with an ERC721InsufficientApproval error. Because the BuyerAgent loops over the entire list without isolating failures, the revert propagates and causes the whole BuyerAgent::purchase transaction to revert. As a result, none of the assets in the batch are bought, even those that are still valid, leading to a denial‑of‑service where legitimate buyers cannot acquire any of the intended assets. This situation occurs during the Buy phase after an oracle has supplied the list of assets, and it affects any user who relies on the BuyerAgent to acquire multiple assets in a single transaction. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails; no assets are transferred, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may only display a generic “transaction reverted” message without indicating which asset caused the problem, making the bug hard to spot. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where a seller transferred an asset before the purchase call, causing the entire batch to revert. The vulnerability belongs to the class of atomic batch operations that lack proper error handling for external calls, allowing a single faulty element to break the whole operation. To remediate, the purchase routine should either pre‑validate ownership and approval for each asset or catch individual reverts and continue processing the remaining assets, thereby preventing a single misbehaving token from aborting the entire batch. This change restores the intended business logic that a buyer should receive all purchasable assets while safely skipping those that are unavailable.

title: Phase calculation inaccuracy will always extend sell phase and cut withdrawal phase time
bug_full: The contract determines the current operational phase (Sell, Buy, Withdraw) by comparing the elapsed time within a round (roundTime) against the configured intervals (sellInterval, buyInterval). The code uses <= for the first two comparisons. Because roundTime is measured in whole seconds, the <= condition causes the Sell phase to be considered active for one second longer than intended and consequently reduces the Withdraw phase by the same amount. This off‑by‑one error propagates to the time‑until‑next‑phase value, which can be reported as zero for Sell or Buy phases. When the Sell interval is supposed to be zero, the contract still treats the first second as Sell, and when the Withdraw interval is set to a single second it may never be reached because the extra second is consumed by the preceding phase. Users interacting during the intended Buy window may see their transactions revert because the contract still reports the Sell phase, and the protocol may skip the Withdrawal window entirely, preventing participants from claiming their funds. The bug does not directly cause loss of ether or tokens; the primary loss is failed transactions and wasted gas. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the phase‑selection logic and observed that the boundary conditions were handled with <= instead of <, leading to a systematic shift of one second. The problem is subtle because a one‑second deviation is easy to miss in normal operation, especially when blocks are produced every two seconds, increasing the probability that a transaction lands in the shifted second. The correct fix is to change the comparisons to strict less‑than (<) for both the sell and buy interval checks, ensuring that each phase occupies exactly its configured duration. This vulnerability belongs to the class of off‑by‑one timing errors in state‑machine implementations, where incorrect boundary conditions break the intended sequencing of protocol phases, violating the business assumption that each phase has a precise, non‑overlapping time window.

title: Using the same hash across games
description: If a hash is revealed in one game its params become public - _number and _salt. This hash must not be used in other games. Otherwise, there is a risk of exploiting a game (guaranteed wins leverage by max available amounts).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay‑style commitment flaw that allows the same cryptographic hash to be reused across independent game instances. In the contract, a player commits to a secret by submitting a hash of a number and a salt, and later reveals the number and salt to prove the commitment. The verification logic only checks that keccak256(_number,_salt) matches the stored hash, but it does not bind the hash to the specific game instance (for example, by including the contract address or a unique game identifier). Consequently, if the same hash is used in more than one game, the reveal of the secret in any one game makes the underlying parameters public. An attacker who observes a reveal can copy the disclosed number and salt and submit a transaction in another game that uses the identical hash. Because the verification does not consider the game context, the contract accepts the commitment as valid, allowing the attacker to guarantee a win and claim the maximum payout available in that game. This breach of the commit‑reveal scheme undermines the fairness of the game, can drain the contract’s balance, and harms honest participants who expect a random outcome. The issue manifests only when a hash is reused and at least one instance reaches the reveal phase, making it easy to miss during casual testing because each individual game appears to function correctly in isolation. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the commitment verification and noticed the absence of a contextual binding. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a unique identifier such as address(this) or a per‑game nonce into the hash calculation (e.g., keccak256(address(this),_number,_salt)) and verify against that value, thereby preventing cross‑game reuse. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a replay or commitment‑reuse vulnerability and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each game’s outcome is independent and unpredictable. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that an opponent consistently wins after a reveal, or that funds disappear from the pool despite correct guesses, contrary to the expectation that a revealed secret only affects the game in which it was disclosed.

title: More rewards than it should be when MONT price is low
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision error in the reward calculation of a gaming contract that distributes MONT tokens based on a USDT‑denominated price feed. The contract queries the price of one whole MONT token (1e18 units) from a Uniswap‑style quoter that returns a USDT amount with only six decimal places. Because USDT uses 6‑decimal precision while MONT uses 18, the returned price is truncated, losing significant fractional information when the MONT price is low. The reward formula multiplies a fixed‑point house fee by a constant and then divides by this truncated price, which inflates the resulting reward by roughly the amount of lost precision – about six percent in the example where MONT trades at $0.0000159. An attacker does not need to manipulate the oracle; the bug is deterministic and occurs whenever the price of MONT is sufficiently low that the truncation error becomes material. Users receive more MONT than the protocol intends, which appears to them as an unexpectedly large payout or a “bonus” that does not match the advertised reward rate. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a higher reward amount than expected, or a balance that jumps unexpectedly after a claim. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain price quote against the expected decimal precision and identified the mismatch between token decimals. It can be hard to notice because the over‑payment is modest at higher prices and only becomes noticeable when the token price drops, making the discrepancy seem like a normal variance. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑mismatch or rounding‑error vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions in financial smart contracts. To fix the problem the contract should either query the inverse price (USDT per MONT) using the USDT’s 6‑decimal base, or perform the calculation with a higher‑precision intermediate representation that aligns both token decimals, ensuring that the reward formula uses an accurately scaled price and eliminates the systematic over‑reward. Properly aligning decimal places restores the intended economic model and prevents unintended token inflation.

title: Free card reveals by choosing all of remaining cards
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract contains a logical flaw in the function that calculates the guessing rate for a card‑reveal game. The function determines a rate by dividing the number of cards that have not yet been revealed (remainingCards) by the number of cards that the player claims to have guessed correctly (remainingSelectedCard). Because the code does not enforce that the player’s guessed set is a strict subset of the unrevealed cards, a player can construct an input where the guessed mask includes every still‑hidden card. In that situation remainingSelectedCard becomes exactly equal to remainingCards, causing the division to evaluate to one. The subsequent reward calculation then multiplies the player’s bet by this rate, resulting in a total winning amount equal to the original bet. After a small ten‑percent fee is subtracted, the net reward equals the bet, leaving the house edge at zero. This allows a user to obtain a free guess, effectively receiving their stake back without any loss, and it also bypasses the maxFreeReveals limit that is supposed to cap the number of free card reveals. The vulnerability is triggered whenever the game has at least one unrevealed card and the player is able to submit a bitmask that marks all those cards as guessed. It primarily affects the protocol’s revenue model and any operator that relies on the house edge for profit, while the attacker (any player) can exploit it to obtain risk‑free bets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between the rate calculation and the enforcement of free‑reveal limits. It is subtle because the arithmetic itself is correct for typical inputs; only the edge case where the divisor equals the dividend produces a rate of one, which the developers did not anticipate. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that remainingSelectedCard is strictly less than remainingCards, for example by adding a require statement that rejects inputs where the two values are equal, thereby guaranteeing a positive house edge for every bet. This class of bug falls under “incorrect business‑logic validation” or “rate calculation edge‑case” where a division yields a neutral multiplier, breaking the intended economic guarantees of the game.

title: Users are penalized when operators are inactive
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the reward‑claiming flow of a betting game where a player can invoke claimWin() even if the game operator has not revealed the card in time. The claimWin() function forwards a call to transferPlayerRewards() with a flag indicating that the player is not a winner. Inside transferPlayerRewards() the contract first computes a house‑edge fee as one‑tenth of the bet amount. When the player is not a winner the code still calculates a burn amount equal to eight‑tenths of that house‑edge and sends it to a burner contract, even though no reward tokens are transferred to the player. Because the house‑edge fee has already been deducted from the player’s stake at the time the bet was placed, the player ends up losing a portion of their funds (80 % of the house‑edge is burnt and the remaining 20 % stays locked in the vault) without receiving any winnings. This situation occurs only when the operator is inactive and fails to call revealCard() before the player’s claimWin() call, meaning the player is penalised for the operator’s fault. The impact is a direct loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees: users expect that if they do not win they at least retain the portion of their stake that is not taken as a house‑edge, yet the contract unintentionally burns part of that stake. The bug is subtle because the burn logic is embedded in the same function that handles reward distribution, so a reviewer focusing only on the reward path may overlook that the burn is executed regardless of the winner flag. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between claimWin() and transferPlayerRewards(). To remediate the issue the contract should either skip the burn when the player is not a winner, or refund the entire house‑edge (or a configurable portion) back to the player instead of sending it to the burner. This change restores the intended accounting model where fees are only applied to successful bets and prevents users from being unfairly penalised by operator inactivity.

title: Some of the expected rewards are not distributed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract contains a reward‑distribution miscalculation that causes a small portion of the expected tokens to remain undistributed when a referral address is present. The function that calculates the player’s reward first reduces the original amount by multiplying it by 9 and dividing by 10, which yields 90 % of the original reward using integer arithmetic. Afterwards the referrer’s share is calculated as reward/10, i.e., 10 % of the already‑reduced amount. Because the division is performed on an integer, any fractional remainder is truncated, so the total amount transferred to the player (90 % of the original) plus the amount transferred to the referrer (9 % of the original) adds up to only 99 % of the original reward. The missing 1 % stays in the contract balance, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. This behaviour contradicts the intended business logic, which states that when a referral exists the full reward should be split 90 % to the player and 10 % to the referrer. The issue is rooted in the order of arithmetic operations and the use of integer division, which silently drops fractions. It is discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented reward scheme with the actual Solidity implementation. The problem may be hard to notice because the loss is small per transaction and only becomes apparent when aggregating many payouts or when a user expects a precise refund amount. From a user’s point of view the UI would show the player receiving slightly less than expected (e.g., 90 000 tokens instead of 90 000 + 1 000) and the referrer receiving a lower amount, leading to confusion such as “my reward is missing a few tokens”. The impact is a gradual erosion of funds that should belong to participants, potentially undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting. The correct fix is to restructure the calculation so that the total distributed amount equals the original reward, for example by computing the player’s share as reward*10/11 and the referrer’s share as reward/11, or by performing the division after the full amount has been allocated, thereby avoiding truncation loss. In general, any reward‑splitting logic that relies on integer division must ensure that rounding errors are compensated or that the arithmetic order preserves the total sum.

title: Centralization Risks
description:
Given a malicious or compromised owner, user assets may be at risk in the following scenarios:
USDT to pay rewards for ongoing games can be withdrawn from the Vault via withdraw() at any time.
The vault can also be depleted by operators playing themselves and making them always win with big guess rate multipliers.
The gameFactory from the Vault can be changed at any time via setGameFactory() to later call transferPlayerRewards() with deceiving game information to claim any amount of rewards.
The montRewardManager from the Vault can be changed at any time via setMontRewardManager() to prevent transferPlayerRewards() from executing and reverting on player wins.
The minimumBetAmount and maximimBetRate values can be modified at any time in the Vault to prevent players from guessing cards.
The gameCreationFee in the GameFactory can be changed right before a game is created to take all the approved USDT from a player when calling createGame(). Other game settings that the player may not agree with can be changed at any time, right before they call createGame().
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a set of centralization risks that arise because the contract owner (or any address that can act as the owner) retains unrestricted authority over critical parameters and external contract references in the vault and game factory components. Because the owner can call a withdraw function that moves the USDT pool used for player rewards at any moment, the pool can be emptied before a pending bet is settled. The owner can also replace the GameFactory address via a setter function, allowing them to invoke transferPlayerRewards with fabricated game data and claim arbitrary reward amounts. Similarly, the reward manager reference can be swapped to a contract that blocks or reverts reward transfers, preventing legitimate winners from receiving payouts. The owner may also modify betting limits such as minimumBetAmount and maximumBetRate, effectively disabling the ability of players to place valid guesses. In addition, the gameCreationFee stored in the GameFactory can be altered immediately before a player creates a game, causing the player to pay an unexpected fee or to be charged the full approved USDT balance. These actions can be performed at any time without delay, meaning that a malicious or compromised owner can silently drain funds, rig games to always win, or change economic parameters in a way that harms users. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include receiving no reward after a win, seeing their balance drop to zero after placing a bet, or being charged a fee that was not disclosed beforehand. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access control of setter functions and the flow of USDT through the vault. The problem is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when these privileged functions are called, and there is no timelock or governance delay to give users a chance to react. The root cause is the lack of decentralised governance and the presence of single‑point‑of‑failure admin functions that can modify critical contract addresses and financial parameters. To remediate the risk the contract should lock reward funds for the duration of a bet, enforce immutable references to the game factory and reward manager, or move privileged changes behind a timelock or multi‑signature governance mechanism that provides a transparent delay before any parameter alteration takes effect.

title: Exploiting referrer bonus to self / controlled address
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the on‑chain referral program of the Dumont game where the contract treats the referrer address as an optional parameter that directly influences the amount of tokens minted for both the referred player and the referrer. The root cause is that the code does not enforce that the referrer must be a distinct third‑party address; it simply checks whether a referrer is set and then applies a 10 % bonus to the referrer while also increasing the player’s reward by 10 % compared to the no‑referral path. Because the referrer can be any address, a malicious user can pass their own externally owned account as the referrer, effectively receiving the player reward plus an additional 10 % of that reward as a “referral” bonus. An attacker can exploit this by invoking the game‑play function with the referrer field equal to their own address, thereby inflating their token balance each time they play. The impact is an unintended increase in the total supply of $MONT tokens, unfair advantage for self‑referring participants, and potential erosion of the token’s economic model, which may harm other users and token holders. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of the reward‑distribution logic where the referrer flag is true; there is no additional guard or validation step, so the flaw is always present when a referrer is supplied. All participants who can control the referrer field are affected, but the protocol itself suffers because the extra tokens are minted without any corresponding economic activity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s reward calculation, where the auditor noticed that the referrer address is not compared against the player address and that the bonus is added on top of the player’s reward. The problem can be subtle because the UI shows a higher reward for referred players, which matches the intended design, so the extra 10 % minted to the referrer may go unnoticed unless the accounting of total minted tokens is examined. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the referrer address is either zero or a distinct third‑party address, or the referral bonus should be accounted for off‑chain rather than minted on‑chain. Alternatively, the referral program could be redesigned so that the presence of a referrer does not increase the total amount of tokens minted, for example by moving the bonus to a separate reward pool or by applying the bonus only to the referrer without augmenting the player’s reward. This would align the implementation with the expected business rule that a referral is optional and should not create extra token inflation.

title: Users will miss some rewards when they add liquidity
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑liquidity accounting bug in the UniswapV3Staking contract. When a user stakes a note, the contract reads the current liquidity of the associated Uniswap V3 position and stores that value in the StakeInfo struct. Later, when rewards are claimed, the calculation multiplies the elapsed time, a fixed rewardsRate, the stored liquidity, and the note’s XP balance. If the user subsequently calls NonfungiblePositionManager.increaseLiquidity to add more liquidity to the same position, the stored liquidity value is not updated. Consequently the reward formula continues to use the original, lower liquidity amount, causing the user to receive fewer tokens than the protocol’s economic model promises. The bug occurs only after a liquidity‑adding transaction; users who never modify their position receive the correct amount. It affects any note holder who stakes a position and later adjusts its size, leading to under‑payment of rewards, which may be perceived as missing funds or a broken incentive mechanism. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s state‑reading logic with the intended accounting rules. Because the contract still emits a Staked event with the correct initial liquidity, the discrepancy is not obvious from the UI; users only notice that the accrued reward balance grows slower than expected after they add liquidity. The problem is hard to spot because the reward numbers are still positive and no revert occurs, so the contract appears to function normally. The bug belongs to the class of “stale state reference” or “out‑of‑date snapshot” errors, where a contract caches a mutable external value instead of reading it on demand. To fix the issue, the reward calculation should query the current liquidity of the position (e.g., via positionManager.positions(tokenId)) each time rewards are computed, rather than relying on the value stored at the moment of staking. This ensures that any subsequent liquidity changes are reflected in the reward amount, preserving the intended economic guarantees and preventing users from missing part of their entitled rewards.

title: Reward time is updated even when no rewards are sent
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming logic of the UniswapV3Staking contract. When a user invokes the claimRewards function, the internal routine _claimRewards calculates the amount of rewards owed and then unconditionally updates the stakeInfo.lastRewardTime to the current block timestamp before checking whether any rewards are actually due. Because the timestamp is written regardless of the reward amount, a situation where the global rewardsRate is temporarily set to zero (or any condition that yields a zero‑reward calculation) allows a staker to call claimRewards, receive no tokens, yet still advance their lastRewardTime. The next time rewards are re‑enabled, the contract will compute rewards starting from the most recent timestamp, effectively discarding the time interval during which the user could have earned rewards. This results in a loss of future accrual, meaning users receive fewer tokens than the protocol’s accounting assumes they are entitled to. The issue manifests only when the reward calculation returns zero – for example during a pause, a rate‑change, or any edge case that temporarily disables reward emission. It affects any address that holds a staked note, i.e., all participants who rely on the contract to correctly track reward periods. The problem was identified during a manual audit that inspected the ordering of state updates and reward transfers. It can be hard to notice because the function does not revert or emit an error when rewards are zero; the only symptom is a subtle reduction in subsequent reward payouts, which may appear as a normal variance. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful claim transaction, but the balance remains unchanged and the next claim yields less than expected, violating the expectation that “if I claim now and get nothing, my future rewards should not be reduced”. Conceptually, this is a classic case of an incorrect state‑update ordering (or “premature timestamp update”) that breaks the accounting invariant that reward time should only advance when rewards are actually distributed. The recommended fix is to move the assignment of lastRewardTime inside the conditional block that checks rewards > 0, ensuring the timestamp is only refreshed when a non‑zero reward transfer occurs, thereby preserving the correct accrual window.

title: MIN_MINT_DYAD_DEPOSIT doesn't enforce any behavior on minters
description:
The public mint() function includes a requirement that users must submit $5k of ETH in order to mint a new dNFT. However, there is no restriction stopping them from immediately redeeming this deposit back into ETH by calling redeemDeposit().

The only requirement is that they keep sufficient balance to avoid being liquidated, which is enforced independently from the MINMINTDYAD_DEPOSIT.

The result is that a user can buy up the full supply of dNFTs for close to free, as they loop through:
mint() => deposit $5k of ETH
redeemDeposit() => cash out up to $5k of ETH

This becomes a greater risk depending how the liquidation() function is changed, based on #4.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic invariant violation that allows any user to mint a new dNFT by depositing a fixed amount of ETH (approximately $5,000) and then immediately withdraw the same amount through the redeemDeposit function. The root cause is that the contract does not enforce any lockup or minimum retained value on the deposited ETH after minting; the only check performed at mint time is the presence of the required deposit, while the redemption logic is completely independent and only ensures that the caller maintains enough balance to avoid liquidation, a condition that is unrelated to the deposit amount. An attacker can exploit this by calling mint, receiving the dNFT, and then calling redeemDeposit to cash out the full deposit, repeating the cycle until the entire supply of dNFTs is acquired at near‑zero cost. This results in the protocol losing the capital it expected to retain, potentially leaving the vault under‑collateralized and breaking the assumptions used by liquidation mechanisms. The issue occurs whenever the public mint function is invoked, because there is no subsequent restriction on withdrawing the exact funds used for minting. All participants—regular users, malicious actors, and the protocol itself—are affected: users may believe they are contributing valuable collateral while the protocol’s economics are eroded, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the mint and redeemDeposit flows and noticed the absence of any state that ties the deposited ETH to the minted token after creation. It can be hard to notice because the requirement to deposit $5k appears to enforce a financial commitment, yet the contract does not prevent that commitment from being instantly reversed, a nuance that may be missed in superficial testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum retained deposit or share balance for each dNFT, introduce a lock‑up period during which the deposited ETH cannot be redeemed, or otherwise tie redemption eligibility to the token’s ongoing collateral requirements. This would preserve the intended economic model, prevent free minting, and ensure that the vault retains sufficient funds to support liquidation and other protocol operations. The bug belongs to the class of “deposit withdrawal bypass” or “free‑mint” bugs where financial invariants are not maintained across contract functions, leading to money disappearing from the system and accounting logic being broken.

title: Check for stale data before trusting Chainlink's response
description:
Much of the math in the protocol is based on the data provided by Chainlink's ETH-USD feed.

According to [Chainlink's documentation](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/price-feeds/historical-data), it is important to provide additional checks that the data is fresh:
If answeredInRound is less than roundId, the answer is being carried over.
A timestamp with zero value means the round is not complete and should not be used.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑oracle data issue. The contract obtains the ETH‑USD price from Chainlink via latestRoundData but does not verify that the returned round is fresh. Chainlink documentation states that if answeredInRound is less than roundId the answer is carried over from a previous round, and a timestamp of zero indicates an incomplete round. Because the contract only reads the price and returns it without these checks, it may accept a price that is outdated or unfinalized. An attacker who can wait for a round where the answer is being carried over, or where the round has not yet been completed, can cause the contract to use a stale price. The protocol’s core calculations – such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, and fee assessments – rely on this price, so using an old value can cause positions to be incorrectly marked as under‑collateralized, trigger premature liquidations, or misprice swaps. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected liquidations, refunds that are zero, or balances that appear to disappear even though market prices have not moved. The issue occurs whenever the _getEthPrice() function is called, which happens on every operation that needs the ETH price, and it affects all users of the protocol as well as the protocol’s overall fund safety. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s logic with Chainlink’s recommended freshness checks. It is hard to notice because the price value itself looks plausible and no transaction reverts; the problem only manifests in downstream accounting errors. The proper mitigation is to add explicit freshness validation – require that the timestamp is non‑zero and that answeredInRound is greater than or equal to roundId – before converting the price to an unsigned integer. This aligns the implementation with the standard oracle‑data‑integrity pattern and prevents the contract from trusting stale or incomplete data.

title: setTVLLimits incorrectly assigns _newMaxTotalDeposits to maxPerDeposit instead of maxTotalDeposits.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the administrative function that updates deposit limits. The function is intended to set two independent constraints: a maximum amount that any single user may deposit (maxPerDeposit) and a maximum aggregate amount that the whole pool may accept (maxTotalDeposits). Due to a copy‑paste mistake the second assignment writes the new total‑deposit limit into the maxPerDeposit variable instead of the maxTotalDeposits variable, and the maxTotalDeposits state variable is never updated. As a result the per‑deposit cap is overwritten with the total‑deposit cap, while the total‑deposit cap remains at its previous value. This mismatch can be exploited by an entity with the onlyCapRaiser role (or a compromised key) to raise the per‑deposit limit arbitrarily, allowing users to deposit amounts far larger than the protocol’s intended risk parameters. Conversely, legitimate users may experience unexpected rejections because the unchanged total‑deposit limit may be reached sooner than expected, even though the per‑deposit limit appears high. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they can enter a large deposit amount, but the transaction either succeeds with an unexpectedly high exposure or fails with a generic “deposit limit reached” error, creating confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual code review where the auditor compared the function body against its specification and noticed that the same state variable was assigned twice. It is subtle because the emitted events still reference both variables, but the MaxTotalDepositsUpdated event reports the old value, making the discrepancy easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect state‑variable assignments, often called “assignment mix‑up” or “parameter mis‑routing”, which violates the business logic that enforces separate per‑deposit and total‑deposit accounting. To remediate, the second assignment must target the maxTotalDeposits variable, ensuring each limit is stored in its proper slot and that the corresponding events reflect the true updated values. Proper testing and code review for variable naming consistency can prevent similar mistakes in future updates.

title: Initial griefing attack possible
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a griefing scenario that stems from the way the vault calculates the conversion between deposited assets and minted shares. The contract adds a constant of one to the conversion formula to mitigate the classic initial‑deposit attack, but it still relies on the total amount of assets held by the contract (totalAssets) when determining how many shares a depositor should receive. Because the vault does not restrict how tokens can arrive in its balance, an attacker can first make a tiny deposit to obtain a small number of shares and then send a large amount of the underlying token directly to the vault address, bypassing the deposit function. This external transfer inflates totalAssets while totalSupply of shares remains unchanged, causing the conversion rate to shift dramatically. When a legitimate user later deposits a normal amount of tokens, the contract’s conversion logic computes that the deposit is worth zero shares, so the user’s balance of shares stays at zero even though the transaction succeeds. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit but the share balance does not increase, and the user later discovers that they cannot withdraw the tokens they just supplied. The attacker can then redeem the few shares they originally received, losing only a small fraction of their own assets (for example 0.1 tokens in the proof‑of‑concept) while the victim’s deposited tokens become locked inside the vault with no way to retrieve them. The impact is that funds are effectively frozen for honest users, the vault ends up in an inconsistent accounting state, and confidence in the protocol may be eroded. The issue occurs whenever the token contract permits direct transfers to the vault and the vault’s accounting does not differentiate between assets received via the official deposit function and those received externally. It was discovered during a security audit by observing the behavior of the convertToAssets function after a manual token transfer. The bug is subtle because the total asset balance appears correct, yet the share balance for a depositor can be zero, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a non‑zero initial deposit that establishes a baseline conversion rate, reject or ignore direct token transfers that bypass the deposit logic, or redesign the conversion calculation to be based on a snapshot taken only when shares are minted, thereby preventing external asset injections from manipulating the share‑to‑asset ratio. This class of issue is an accounting/logic flaw in share‑minting mechanisms that can be exploited for griefing rather than direct profit.

title: Use call() instead of transfer() when sending ETH
description: Couple of functions in the contract are using the transfer method to withdraw accumulated or wrongly sent ETH in the contract to marketingWallet, devTaxWallet. These addresses are possible to be a smart contract that have a receive or fallback function that takes up more than the 2300 gas which is the limit of transfer(). Examples are some smart contract wallets or multi-sig wallets, so usage of transfer is discouraged. report.md More
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s use of Solidity’s transfer() function to forward Ether to the marketingWallet and devTaxWallet addresses. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback or receive function and automatically reverts if the call runs out of gas. This design assumes that the destination is an externally owned account (EOA) with a simple payable fallback, but the addresses may be smart contracts such as wallet contracts or multi‑signature contracts whose fallback logic consumes more than the 2300‑gas stipend. When the contract attempts to withdraw accumulated or mistakenly sent Ether using transfer, the call can fail and revert, leaving the Ether locked in the contract. The failure is silent from the caller’s perspective because transfer throws an exception that aborts the transaction, so the user interface may show a successful withdrawal request while the balance remains unchanged. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: any future attempts to send Ether to the affected address will also revert, effectively freezing the contract’s funds and preventing expected payouts or refunds. This issue occurs whenever the contract executes a transfer, which is triggered by withdrawal functions or any internal logic that redistributes Ether. All parties that rely on the contract’s ability to move funds—such as the protocol operators, token holders expecting refunds, or users awaiting payouts—are affected. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that flagged the use of transfer as discouraged in modern Solidity versions. It can be hard to notice because transfers to regular EOAs succeed, masking the issue until a contract address is used. The proper mitigation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas and checks the returned success flag, for example: (bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: amount}(''); require(success, 'Ether transfer failed'); optionally adding a re‑entrancy guard. This pattern belongs to the broader class of unsafe Ether forwarding bugs where the fixed gas stipend of transfer or send can cause unexpected reverts and fund lock‑up.

title: Not capped array can grow too big and lead to out of gas error
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded dynamic array that stores accounts excluded from reward calculations. Functions that need to know whether an address is excluded – notably the routine that computes the current token supply and the routine that re‑includes an address – iterate over the entire array on each call. Because the array has no explicit size limit, any user or contract that can add an address to the exclusion list can grow the array arbitrarily. When the list becomes large, the linear scan performed by these functions consumes a amount of gas that grows proportionally with the number of entries. If the gas required to complete the loop exceeds the block gas limit, the transaction reverts with an out‑of‑gas error before any state changes are applied. This situation can be triggered during normal operations such as token transfers, balance queries, or reward claims, because the supply‑calculation routine is invoked in most core functions. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to “freeze”: a transaction that previously succeeded now fails with a generic out‑of‑gas message, and users see no tokens transferred or rewards received even though they supplied sufficient gas. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that can affect every participant in the protocol – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on the token’s transfer or reward logic. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined loops over mutable storage structures. It is difficult to notice in early testing because the gas cost only becomes problematic once the exclusion list reaches a substantial size; the contract behaves correctly with a small number of entries, masking the underlying flaw. The root cause is the use of a plain array for membership checks without any cap or alternative data structure, leading to unbounded iteration. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a maximum number of excluded accounts, cache the array length outside of loops to avoid repeated SLOADs, or replace the array with a mapping or enumerable set that provides constant‑time inclusion checks and eliminates the need for costly linear scans. By limiting the growth of the exclusion list or redesigning the data structure, the gas consumption of the affected functions becomes predictable and stays within block limits, restoring normal operation and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: maxTotalDeposits is not checked properly inside _beforeDeposit.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cap‑enforcement logic error in the vault’s deposit flow. The contract is intended to limit the total amount of assets that can ever be held in the vault by a configurable maxTotalDeposits value. To enforce this, the internal function _beforeDeposit checks two conditions: that a single deposit does not exceed maxPerDeposit and that the current token balance of the vault does not exceed maxTotalDeposits. However, the second check only compares the existing balance (_tokenBalance()) with the cap and completely ignores the amount that is about to be added (the assets parameter). As a result, each deposit can succeed as long as the balance before the deposit is below the cap, even though the cumulative total after the deposit may surpass the limit. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the logic of the require statement was examined and found to omit the incoming assets. The issue is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the individual deposit amount is still bounded by maxPerDeposit, so the contract appears to respect its limits on a per‑call basis. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) can repeatedly call deposit with the maximum allowed per‑deposit amount, causing the vault’s total holdings to grow beyond the intended ceiling. The impact is that the vault can hold more assets than the protocol designers assumed, breaking accounting invariants, potentially diluting share value, and exposing downstream logic that relies on the total cap (for example, withdrawal limits or fee calculations). Users who expect the vault to reject deposits once the total cap is reached may see their deposits accepted unexpectedly, leading to confusion when later operations behave incorrectly or when the protocol’s risk parameters are violated. The bug affects all participants of the vault – depositors, token holders, and the protocol itself – because the fundamental guarantee of a maximum total deposit is no longer enforced. To remediate, the cap check must be performed against the projected balance after the deposit, i.e., require(_tokenBalance() + assets <= maxTotalDeposits). This adjustment restores the intended invariant and prevents the vault from exceeding its configured total capacity. The class of bug is a cumulative‑cap enforcement flaw, where a limit is checked against a stale state rather than the future state after the operation, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential financial risk.

title: M-1 EXECUTOR has a full write access to the wallet storage
description:
EXECUTOR has a write access to any storage slots via the executeShortcut function and delegatecall to a
specially crafted library. This allows to trigger
transfer/renounce of the OWNER address and other unintended actions.
EnsoWallet.sol#L57
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted delegatecall that gives the EXECUTOR role full write access to any storage slot of the wallet contract. The root cause is the executeShortcut function, which forwards a delegatecall to an external library address supplied by the caller without any validation or access control. Because delegatecall executes the library code in the context of the calling contract, the library can modify the caller’s storage arbitrarily, including critical variables such as the OWNER address or internal balances. An attacker can craft a malicious library that, when invoked through executeShortcut, writes a new owner address, triggers a transfer of all funds to an attacker‑controlled address, or calls renounceOwnership to leave the contract without a legitimate owner. The impact is loss of control over the wallet, unauthorized fund transfers, and the possibility that the contract becomes unusable because the owner role is removed. This condition occurs whenever any address with the EXECUTOR role can call executeShortcut, which is typically allowed for legitimate shortcut operations but lacks restriction on the target library. All users of the wallet, including the designated owner and any parties relying on the wallet’s security guarantees, are affected because their assets can be drained or the contract’s governance can be hijacked. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the delegatecall pathways and identified that the library address is not whitelisted. The problem is hard to notice because the function appears to be a convenience feature and the delegatecall itself does not revert; the malicious library can silently overwrite storage without emitting obvious events, making the failure mode appear as a normal transaction that simply results in missing funds. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict access control on delegatecall targets, such as maintaining a whitelist of approved library contracts, limiting EXECUTOR privileges, or replacing delegatecall with a safer pattern that does not expose arbitrary storage writes. Conceptually, this is an arbitrary storage write vulnerability caused by unchecked delegatecall, a known class of bugs where external code can corrupt the caller’s state. From the user’s perspective, the wallet UI may show that a transaction succeeded but the balance becomes zero, or the owner field in the UI shows an unexpected address, contradicting the expectation that only the owner can change ownership. The accounting logic of the wallet is broken because the contract assumes that only the owner can initiate transfers or renounce ownership, an assumption violated by this bug.

title: M-2 Admin can bypass the upgrade delay by setDelay
description:
The contract implements a special flow to upgrade the wallet core with delay, but the admin can force an
immediate upgrade by reducing the delay using setDelay().
EnsoBeacon.sol#L208
This will deprive users of the ability to check implementations before applying.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an admin‑controlled bypass of the intended upgrade delay in the wallet core contract. The contract is designed to enforce a waiting period before a new implementation can be applied, giving users time to review the code and react to potentially malicious changes. However, the same privileged admin role that can trigger an upgrade also has permission to call setDelay, a function that arbitrarily changes the delay value. Because the upgrade function checks the current delay at execution time, an admin can first set the delay to zero (or a very short interval) and then immediately perform the upgrade in the same transaction or in rapid succession. This sequence eliminates the safety window, depriving users of the opportunity to inspect the new implementation before it becomes active. The impact is that users of the wallet may be exposed to malicious code without warning, potentially leading to loss of funds, unauthorized transfers, or other harmful behavior. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the admin decides to upgrade the contract and is willing to manipulate the delay parameter; no additional constraints prevent this action. All wallet holders, token holders, and any parties relying on the promised delay are affected because the security guarantee they expect – a period for review – is effectively broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the upgrade flow and identified that setDelay is callable by the admin and can be used to shorten or eliminate the delay. The problem is subtle because the presence of a delay function gives a false sense of protection, and the ability to modify the delay is not immediately obvious from a high‑level view of the contract. To remediate, the upgrade delay should be made immutable or only adjustable through a separate, timelocked governance mechanism that does not share the same authority as the upgrade function. Alternatively, the admin role should be split so that one entity can propose upgrades while another independent entity controls the delay parameter, ensuring that users retain a reliable window to verify new code before it is enforced.

title: M-3 Admin can bypass the upgrade delay by delegate and emergencyUpgrade
description:
The admin can bypass the upgrade delay flow and immediately change the address of the wallet core by
following the sequence:
• transferDelegation (to a new delegate account, controlled by the admin)
• acceptDelegation (from the delegate account)
• upgradeFallback (from the admin account)
• emergencyUpgrade (from the delegate account)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an administrative bypass that allows the privileged account to circumvent the intended upgrade delay mechanism of the wallet core contract. The design specifies a timelocked upgrade path that should give users and the community a window to review and react to any changes to the core logic. However, the contract also supports a delegation model where the admin can transfer delegation rights to a secondary address and later accept those rights. By first calling transferDelegation to a delegate controlled by the admin, then having the delegate accept the delegation, the admin can subsequently invoke upgradeFallback from the original admin account and immediately follow it with emergencyUpgrade from the newly accepted delegate account. The emergencyUpgrade function does not enforce the same delay constraint, so the core contract address can be replaced in a single transaction sequence, effectively bypassing the safety window. This bypass can be exploited by an attacker who controls the admin role to deploy a malicious core contract that redirects funds, disables user functions, or otherwise violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The impact is that users of the wallet may see their balances become inaccessible, experience unexpected zero balances, or have funds transferred to an address controlled by the attacker. The condition under which the bypass occurs is any situation where the admin possesses the ability to invoke the delegation functions and the emergencyUpgrade function, which is typical in the current implementation. All wallet users, the protocol operators, and any third‑party integrations are affected because the core logic governs all state transitions and fund movements. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the upgrade flow and identified that the delay check is omitted for emergencyUpgrade when called by a delegated address. The problem is subtle because the delegation workflow appears legitimate and the emergencyUpgrade function is intended for genuine emergencies, making the missing delay check easy to overlook in code review. To remediate, the upgrade delay should be enforced for all upgrade paths, including emergencyUpgrade, or the emergencyUpgrade function should be restricted to a timelocked role that cannot be delegated, thereby eliminating the possibility of an immediate core replacement. In broader terms, this is a privilege escalation and timelock bypass class of bug where an access‑controlled function unintentionally allows privileged actors to sidestep security controls, leading to potential loss of funds and erosion of trust in the protocol.

title: M-1 Absence of Fee-on-transfer Protection in _deposit Function
description:
An oversight has been detected within the _deposit function of the EnjoyoorsVaultDeposits contract.
The issue arises from the absence of a fee-on-transfer protection mechanism. This could result in incorrect
setting of user amounts. Consequently, users might be in a position to claim more than they are entitled to. It
gravely threatens the contract's integrity since this scenario inevitably leads to a situation where the last user
cannot claim any funds, given there are insufficient funds on the contract due to the over-claims made by the
preceding users.
This issue is classified as Medium severity due to its potential to distort the distribution of deposits and
consequently funds, which could lead to the breakdown of the contract's operation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an absence of fee‑on‑transfer protection in the internal _deposit function of the vault contract. The function assumes that the amount transferred from a user via transferFrom is exactly the amount specified, but it does not verify the actual token balance before and after the call. Tokens that levy a transfer fee (often called tax or fee‑on‑transfer tokens) therefore cause the contract to record a higher deposited amount than the net amount received. This mismatch allows a depositor to claim a larger share of the vault than they are entitled to because the internal accounting inflates their balance. When multiple users exploit this, the vault’s total token pool is depleted faster than expected, and the last user may find that the contract holds insufficient funds to satisfy their claim, resulting in a zero payout. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the deposit logic and identified the missing balance checks for fee‑on‑transfer tokens. It is hard to notice because the external transfer appears successful and no revert occurs, so the contract’s state seems consistent from a superficial view. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal deposit confirmation, yet later the user can withdraw more than they deposited, or later participants see their expected refunds disappear. The root cause is a logical flaw in accounting: the contract assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between the amount argument and the actual token received, violating the fundamental accounting invariant that total deposits equal total token balance. To remediate, the _deposit function should record the token balance before the transfer, execute transferFrom, then record the balance after and compute the net received amount, using that net value for internal accounting. Adding a nonReentrant guard is also recommended to prevent reentrancy attacks that could amplify the accounting error. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of fee‑on‑transfer token handling errors that lead to inflated user balances and incorrect fund distribution.

title: previewWithdraw calculates shares wrongly
description: The fee is wrongly accounted for in `previewWithdraw`.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the pool contract calculates the number of shares that must be burned to withdraw a requested amount of assets. The previewWithdraw function is intended to provide callers with the exact share amount needed to redeem a specified asset quantity, taking the protocol fee into account. However, the implementation mistakenly subtracts the fee from the asset amount before converting it to shares, effectively assuming that the fee has already been removed from the assets. Because the fee is actually deducted later during the _withdraw execution, the previewed share amount is smaller than required. When a user invokes withdraw with a target asset amount, the contract calls previewWithdraw to obtain the expected shares, then burns those shares and applies the fee, which results in fewer assets being transferred to the receiver than originally requested. The subsequent require check (assetsReceived >= assets) fails, causing the transaction to revert. This bug surfaces only when the withdraw pathway that relies on previewWithdraw is used; the alternative redeem function, which calculates shares without the flawed fee adjustment, continues to work. From a user’s perspective, attempts to withdraw a known amount of tokens result in a reverted transaction, often accompanied by an error message such as "You cannot withdraw the amount of assets you expected," and the user’s balance appears unchanged, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the mathematical relationship between assets, fees, and shares and identified that the formula used in previewWithdraw does not correctly incorporate the fee component. The bug is hard to spot because the function is read‑only and appears to return a sensible value; only when the downstream withdrawal logic validates the actual assets transferred does the inconsistency become evident. The root cause is a mis‑applied arithmetic expression: the correct share calculation should add the fee proportionally, e.g., convertToShares(assets + assets * feeBPS / (10000 - feeBPS)), rather than subtracting the fee from assets. This class of bug falls under inaccurate fee accounting or incorrect financial rounding, where the contract’s accounting assumptions are violated, leading to failed withdrawals and a degraded user experience. The recommended remediation is to replace the existing previewWithdraw implementation with the mathematically sound formula that properly accounts for the fee, thereby aligning the share estimate with the actual amount of assets that will be delivered after fee deduction.

title: Admin rug vectors
description:
There are multiple functions that the admin can call to brick various parts of the system, leading to user’s funds being locked

Even if the owner is benevolent the fact that there is a rug vector available may [negatively impact the protocol’s reputation](https://twitter.com/RugDocIO/status/1411732108029181960). See [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards-findings/issues/73) example where a similar finding has been flagged as a high-severity issue. I’ve downgraded these instances to be a medium since it requires cooperation of the admin.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of several privileged admin functions that give the contract owner the ability to permanently disrupt the normal operation of the system and to divert user assets. The root cause is a lack of input validation and unrestricted state mutation in functions that are only protected by an "onlyAdmin" modifier. First, the adminWriteBathToken function allows the administrator to overwrite any entry in the token-to-bath-token mapping with an arbitrary address, effectively redirecting the token handling logic to a contract of the admin’s choosing. Second, the setMarket function lets the admin replace the address of the Rubicon market used by the pool with any address, including a malicious market that can capture or block deposits and withdrawals. Third, the setBonusToken function permits the admin to push an unlimited number of bonus token addresses into an array that is later iterated over in withdrawal logic; because the loop is unbounded, an attacker can fill the array with a large number of entries, causing withdrawals to run out of gas and fail, which locks user funds in the pool. These weaknesses can be exploited when the admin is malicious, when the admin’s private key is compromised, or when a colluding party gains access to the admin role. An attacker could first overwrite the token mapping to point to a contract they control, then set the market address to a contract that refuses to honor withdrawals, and finally flood the bonus token list to make the withdrawal function unusable. The impact is that users may see their balances remain unchanged, receive no refunds or withdrawals, and experience unexpected zero or missing token transfers despite having deposited funds. The problem manifests whenever the privileged functions are called, which may happen rarely in normal operation, making the bug hard to notice during testing because the functions are admin‑only and not exercised in typical user flows. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract source for governance‑related entry points and compared them with known patterns of admin‑induced rug pulls. To remediate, the contract should remove or severely restrict any function that permits arbitrary writes to critical storage, enforce strict validation on addresses being set, limit the size of dynamic arrays used in accounting loops, and replace single‑admin control with multi‑sig or timelocked governance to prevent unilateral, hidden changes. By applying these conceptual fixes, the protocol can restore confidence that user funds will not disappear, withdrawals will succeed, and the system will behave according to its advertised accounting guarantees.

title: Early funds withdrawers can get bonus in multiples of vested bonus tokens
poc:
BathToken.sol, function setBonusToken

1. function setBonusToken allows the same BonusToken to be added more than once to the array.

BathToken.sol, function distributeBonusTokenRewards

2. a. As and when distributeBonusTokenRewards is triggered during a withdraw call, the same bonusToken will be released more than once.

BathBuddy.sol, function release

3. b. The release function is called.
bug_full: The reported issue is a duplicate‑entry vulnerability in the bonus‑distribution logic of the BathHouse protocol. The contract provides a function that lets the BathHouse admin add an ERC‑20 token address to an internal array called bonusTokens. Because the function does not verify that the supplied address is already present, the same bonus token can be pushed into the array multiple times. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract iterates over the entire bonusTokens array and calls the distributeBonusTokenRewards routine for each entry.
