If the array contains duplicate entries, the reward calculation is performed once per duplicate, effectively multiplying the amount of bonus tokens that the withdrawing user receives. Early withdrawers – i.e., users who call the withdraw function shortly after the duplicate has been introduced – therefore receive a bonus that is a multiple of the amount they are entitled to according to the protocol’s accounting rules. The extra tokens are taken from the shared bonus pool, which means that later withdrawers may receive little or no bonus at all because the pool has been depleted by the earlier inflated payouts. The condition for exploitation is simply that the admin (or any entity with permission to call setBonusToken) inserts the same token address more than once before a withdrawal occurs. The bug is difficult to spot during casual testing because the duplicate entries look like distinct elements in the array and the UI typically shows only the token symbol, not the underlying address count. From a user’s point of view the symptoms are a mismatch between expected and actual rewards: a user who expects a modest bonus sees an unexpectedly large token transfer, while subsequent users see missing or zero bonus balances. The vulnerability belongs to the class of reward‑inflation bugs caused by unchecked duplicate entries in data structures that drive financial calculations. It violates the protocol’s business logic that each deposited bonus token should be accounted for exactly once per withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the setBonusToken function and traced its effect through the distributeBonusTokenRewards flow. To remediate the problem the setBonusToken function should include a uniqueness check – for example, by maintaining a mapping of token addresses that have already been added – and reject any attempt to push an address that already exists in the bonusTokens array. This change ensures that each bonus token is distributed exactly once per withdrawal, preserving the intended accounting invariants and preventing inadvertent bonus multiplication.

title: No cap on fees can result in a DOS in BathToken.withdraw
description:
The owner can set an arbitrary fee. If they set it to a value above 100%, withdrawing BathTokens won’t be possible anymore because of an underflow. In RubiconMarket the owner can also have an arbitrary fee although that won’t result in a DOS. But, the user might pay an absurdly high fee.

There should be checks that only allow fees up to a specific value, e.g. 10%.
poc:
For the DOS:

1. Owner sets fees to 101% using `BathToken.setFeeBPS()`: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L261>
2. User tries to withdraw which will revert here because `fee > r`: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/rubiconPools/BathToken.sol#L604>
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded fee parameter in the BathToken contract that enables the contract owner to set a withdrawal fee greater than 100 % of the amount being withdrawn. The root cause is the absence of validation logic that caps the fee when it is configured via the setFeeBPS function; the fee is stored as basis points but the contract does not enforce a maximum value. When a fee exceeding the total withdrawable amount is set, the withdraw routine calculates the net amount by subtracting the fee from the requested amount. Because the fee is larger than the amount, the subtraction underflows, causing the require statement fee > r to trigger and the transaction to revert. This failure blocks all calls to withdraw, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition where users cannot retrieve any BathTokens they have deposited. The impact is that user balances appear unchanged, attempts to withdraw return a revert error, and funds become effectively locked until the owner reduces the fee to a permissible range. The issue manifests whenever the contract owner intentionally or inadvertently configures the fee above the logical ceiling, which can happen at deployment or later through any administrative fee‑setting function. The affected parties include token holders who rely on the withdraw function, the protocol that expects withdrawals to be possible, and any downstream applications that display token balances. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by Code4rena when reviewers examined the fee‑setting method and noticed that no upper bound was enforced, then manually set the fee to 101 % to confirm the underflow condition. The problem is subtle because a high fee does not immediately cause a visible error; only when a user initiates a withdrawal does the contract revert, making it easy to miss during normal operation. The appropriate mitigation is to introduce explicit checks in the constructors and all fee‑configuration functions that enforce a maximum fee, such as a ten‑percent cap, and to document the invariant that fee must never exceed the full amount. By treating this as a class of "unbounded parameter leading to arithmetic underflow and denial of service," developers can apply the same defensive pattern to other contracts that expose configurable percentages.

title: Outstanding Amount Of A Pool Reduced Although Tokens Are Not Repaid
description:
In the BathToken Contract, `outstandingAmount` means the amount of tokens that have been taken out of a pool, but have not been repaid back to the pool yet. Additionally, `outstandingAmount` is NOT inclusive of any non-underlyingToken assets sitting on the Bath Tokens that have filled to here and are awaiting rebalancing to the underlyingToken by strategists per code comment.

Placing new trade orders and scrubbing existing trade orders are essential for maintaining an effective market, thus they are the key operation of a Strategist and these activities are expected to be performed frequently.

The following aims to explain why this issue occurred.

/// @dev Cancels outstanding orders and manages the ledger of outstandingAmount() on bathTokens as Strategist Trades are cancelled/scrubbed or expired
function handleStratOrderAtID(uint256 id) internal {
    StrategistTrade memory info = strategistTrades[id];
    address _asset = info.askAsset;
    address _quote = info.bidAsset;

    address bathAssetAddress = IBathHouse(bathHouse).tokenToBathToken(
        _asset
    );
    address bathQuoteAddress = IBathHouse(bathHouse).tokenToBathToken(
        _quote
    );
    order memory offer1 = getOfferInfo(info.askId); //ask
    order memory offer2 = getOfferInfo(info.bidId); //bid
    uint256 askDelta = info.askPayAmt - offer1.pay_amt;
    uint256 bidDelta = info.bidPayAmt - offer2.pay_amt;

    // if real
    if (info.askId != 0) {
        // if delta > 0 - delta is fill => handle any amount of fill here
        if (askDelta > 0) {
            logFill(askDelta, info.strategist, info.askAsset);
            IBathToken(bathAssetAddress).removeFilledTradeAmount(askDelta);
            // not a full fill
            if (askDelta != info.askPayAmt) {
                IBathToken(bathAssetAddress).cancel(
                    info.askId,
                    info.askPayAmt.sub(askDelta)
                );
            }
        }
        // otherwise didn't fill so cancel
        else {
            IBathToken(bathAssetAddress).cancel(info.askId, info.askPayAmt); // pas amount too
        }
    }
    ..SNIP..
}

`BathToken.removeFilledTradeAmount` will reduce the outstanding amount of the pool.

/// @notice A function called by BathPair to maintain proper accounting of outstandingAmount
function removeFilledTradeAmount(uint256 amt) external onlyPair {
    outstandingAmount = outstandingAmount.sub(amt);
    ..SNIP..
}

bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of the outstanding amount in a BathToken pool, which represents the quantity of underlying tokens that have been withdrawn for a strategist trade but not yet returned to the pool. The contract mistakenly reduces this outstanding amount when a strategist scrubs (cancels) an order, even though the underlying tokens have not been repaid. The root cause lies in the `BathPair.handleStrategistOrderAtID` function, which calls `BathToken.removeFilledTradeAmount` for any filled portion of an order. When the strategist invokes `BathPair.scrubStrategistTrade`, the same removal logic is executed for the filled portion of the cancelled order, causing the pool’s `outstandingAmount` to be decremented regardless of whether the underlying asset was actually returned. An attacker does not need to exploit this directly; the bug manifests during normal protocol operation whenever a strategist decides to cancel a trade. As a result, the `underlyingBalance` – defined as the sum of `balanceOf` and `outstandingAmount` – becomes inaccurate. This mis‑reporting leads to downstream effects on key user‑facing functions such as deposits and withdrawals that rely on the true underlying balance to calculate share values. In the demonstrated scenario, Alice deposited 50 WETH into the BathWETH pool. After the strategist placed a trade, the pool correctly reflected an outstanding amount of 40 WETH. When the strategist later scrubbed the trade, the contract erroneously set the outstanding amount to zero while the 40 WETH remained unrecovered, reducing the reported underlying balance from 100 WETH to 60 WETH. Consequently, Alice’s withdrawal returned only about 30 WETH instead of the expected ~49 WETH, resulting in a loss of roughly 20 WETH. Users experience symptoms such as receiving far less than their deposited amount on withdrawal, seeing pool balances shrink unexpectedly, or observing that their share value does not match their contribution. The issue was uncovered through systematic testing that simulated deposits, trades, fills, and scrubbing actions, revealing the inconsistent state of `outstandingAmount`. It is hard to notice because the contract still tracks escrowed non‑underlying assets (e.g., DAI) correctly, and the reduction of `outstandingAmount` occurs silently without emitting explicit warnings. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting invariants and can undermine trust, especially if a strategist becomes unavailable and the pool’s bookkeeping remains out of sync. To fix the problem, the contract should only reduce the outstanding amount when the underlying tokens are truly repaid, such as during a rebalance operation that swaps the non‑underlying assets back into the underlying token. This can be achieved by removing the call to `BathToken.removeFilledTradeAmount` from the order‑scrubbing path and instead invoking it exclusively within the rebalance function after confirming the receipt of the underlying asset. Aligning the accounting logic with the intended lifecycle of trades ensures that deposit and withdrawal calculations remain accurate and that users do not suffer unexpected fund loss.

title: Strategists can take more rewards than they should using the function strategistBootyClaim
description:
Strategists can take more rewards than they should using the function strategistBootyClaim(). Even though the owner trusts strategists fully I think it’s recommended to remove such flaws.

I think there would be 2 methods to claim more rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution function that allows a designated strategist to invoke strategistBootyClaim() and receive more tokens than the contract’s accounting permits. The root cause is an erroneous accounting pathway: after a claim the contract fails to correctly deduct the claimed amount from the strategist’s pending reward balance, or it does not enforce a single‑use constraint, enabling the strategist to invoke the claim function repeatedly or to manipulate internal calculations (for example by supplying crafted parameters) to inflate the reward amount. Because the contract assumes that strategists are trustworthy, no additional verification or limit checks are performed, which leaves the reward pool exposed to intentional over‑claiming. An attacker who controls a strategist role can exploit this by calling strategistBootyClaim() more than once in the same reward period, or by crafting two distinct claim calls that each reference overlapping reward slices, thereby extracting the same reward tokens multiple times. The impact is a direct loss of funds from the reward pool: tokens that should have been reserved for the protocol’s participants are siphoned to the strategist’s address, effectively reducing the total rewards available and undermining the economic incentives of the protocol. This flaw manifests whenever a strategist initiates a claim transaction; there is no temporal restriction or balance verification that would prevent repeated extraction. All parties that rely on the fairness of the reward distribution – including ordinary users, liquidity providers, and the protocol governance – are affected because the overall reward pool is diminished. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the reviewers inspected the claim logic and observed that the reward‑tracking variable was not updated or that the function could be called multiple times without state change, leading to a potential double‑claim scenario. The problem can be subtle because the contract’s external interface appears to work as intended: a strategist receives a legitimate‑looking reward amount, and no error is thrown, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate the issue, the reward‑claim path should be re‑engineered to enforce a strict one‑time claim per reward epoch, ensure the pending reward balance is atomically reduced before transfer, and include safeguards such as re‑entrancy guards, access‑control checks, and explicit overflow/underflow validation. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “improper state update after token transfer” or “missing accounting checks,” which can lead to fund disappearance, inflated payouts, and breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants. From a user perspective the symptom would be that the overall reward pool appears lower than expected, or that other participants receive reduced or zero refunds after a distribution cycle, while the strategist’s address shows an unexpected increase in balance.

title: Missing checks allow strategists to steal all fund via `tailOff`
description:
Strategists can call `tailOff` with malicious payload to steal all funds within any BathToken.

There are 2 issues that makes this possible:

* `BathPair.tailOff` allows arbitrary `_stratUtil` address.
* `BathToken.rebalance` allows underlying token as `filledAssetToRebalance`.

These allow malicious strategists to input any token address, including the underlying token of a BathToken, and transfer them to a contract of their choosing.
poc:
A malicious strategist calls `tailOff` with the following payload:
    
{
    targetPool: bathUSDC.address,
    tokenToHandle: USDC.address,
    targetToken: USDT.address, // any address
    _stratUtil: maliciousContract.address,
    amount: USDC.balanceOf(bathUSDC.address),
    hurdle: 0, // any
    _poolFee: 0 // any
}

`bathUSDC` BathToken will then send all USDC to the strategist’s `maliciousContract`. All deposits are lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized fund‑extraction bug that allows a strategist, who can invoke the `tailOff` function of a BathToken, to redirect the entire balance of the underlying asset to any address they control. The root cause lies in two missing validation checks: first, the `BathPair.tailOff` function accepts an arbitrary `_stratUtil` address without restricting it to a trusted utility contract; second, the `BathToken.rebalance` routine permits the caller to specify the underlying token of the BathToken as the `filledAssetToRebalance` parameter, which should never be transferable out of the pool. An attacker can craft a payload that sets `_stratUtil` to a malicious contract and sets `filledAssetToRebalance` to the same token that the BathToken is meant to hold (for example USDC in a USDC‑backed BathToken). When `tailOff` is executed, the contract’s internal rebalancing logic treats the underlying token as a generic asset and transfers the entire amount to the attacker‑specified contract. This can be exploited in a single transaction, effectively stealing all deposited funds from the affected BathToken. The impact is total loss of user deposits for any pool that uses the compromised BathToken, as users see their balances drop to zero and receive no refunds or withdrawals. The condition occurs whenever a strategist with permission to call `tailOff` supplies a malicious payload; no additional on‑chain conditions are required. All participants of the affected pool—depositors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes that the underlying asset can only be moved according to legitimate rebalancing rules. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the rebalancing pathways and identified that the `_stratUtil` parameter was not whitelisted and that the `filledAssetToRebalance` argument was not protected against the pool’s own underlying token. The problem is subtle because the function signatures appear innocuous and the lack of a whitelist does not raise a compile‑time error; the logic error only manifests when the function is called with a crafted payload, making it easy to miss during manual testing. To remediate the bug, the protocol should restrict `_stratUtil` to a predefined set of strategy utility contracts (a whitelist) and add an explicit check in `rebalance` that rejects any attempt to specify the pool’s underlying token as the asset to be transferred, thereby preserving the invariant that the pool’s core asset cannot be arbitrarily moved out. This class of bug falls under the broader category of “missing authorization checks leading to asset misdirection” and violates fundamental accounting assumptions that a pool’s underlying token remains under the pool’s control unless a legitimate withdrawal is performed. From a user’s perspective, deposits appear to disappear instantly after a malicious `tailOff` call, with balances showing zero and no error messages, contrary to the expectation that funds remain safely locked until a proper withdrawal request is processed.

title: Double spending of funds when bridging “bridgedToken”
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double‑spending bug that occurs when a user bridges a token that is represented on L1 as a BridgedToken. The bridge contract first pulls the requested amount from the user via a safeTransferFrom call, and then forwards the call to the L1AssetRouter. Because the router forwards the originalCaller parameter as the user’s address instead of the bridge contract’s address, the NativeTokenVault's bridgeBurn function interprets the caller as the token holder and burns the same amount a second time. Consequently the contract deducts twice the intended amount: the first deduction happens when the L1ERC20Bridge receives the tokens, and the second deduction happens when the vault burns the tokens on behalf of the user. This results in the user’s balance being reduced by 2 × _amount, or the transaction reverting if the user does not have enough tokens for the second burn. The impact is loss of funds for any user who attempts to bridge a BridgedToken, effectively making the bridge unsafe for that token class. The bug manifests only when the bridged token’s asset handler is the native token vault, which is the default configuration for BridgedToken. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of the originalCaller argument through the depositLegacyErc20Bridge and bridgeBurn functions. The issue is subtle because the two transfers happen in different contracts and the second burn does not emit a distinct user‑visible event, so the double deduction can be mistaken for a normal fee or ignored. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect caller attribution leading to double spend bugs, where a contract assumes the caller still holds the tokens after they have already been transferred. To fix the issue the bridge should pass its own address (the L1ERC20Bridge contract) as originalCaller when invoking the asset router, or the vault should verify that the tokens have already been transferred and avoid burning them again. Proper validation of the caller identity and ensuring that only one token transfer occurs per bridge operation will restore the intended accounting logic and prevent funds from disappearing.

title: Merkle Proof Verification Path Inconsistency Enables Cross-Chain Message Verification Bypass
description:
A critical inconsistency exists in Matter Labs' Merkle Tree implementation where competing validation logics for single-node trees create a race condition in the security model. While calculateRootPaths correctly validates single-node scenarios, both calculateRoot and calculateRootMemory implement a conflicting validation pattern that breaks the fundamental security assumptions of cross-chain message verification.

This vulnerability manifests in L1->L2 message processing where single-node Merkle trees (which are valid and common in certain bridge scenarios) would be rejected by calculateRoot but accepted by calculateRootPaths. The inconsistency creates an attack vector where a malicious actor could force message processing down specific codepaths by manipulating the tree structure, potentially leading to cross-chain message verification failures or bypasses.

Most critically, single-node Merkle trees are commonly used in bridge implementations for individual message verification, batch processing of single messages, and recovery scenarios. The presence of dual validation paths breaks the security invariant that a valid Merkle proof should be consistently verifiable across the entire system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the Merkle proof verification logic used by Matter Labs’ bridge contracts. Two separate functions – one that calculates a root from a single proof (calculateRoot) and another that calculates roots for batched proofs (calculateRootPaths) – implement contradictory checks for the special case where the Merkle tree consists of a single leaf. The single‑node validation in calculateRootMemory always rejects a proof with a zero‑length path, while calculateRootPaths explicitly allows a zero‑length path when the start index is zero and the tree height is one. This mismatch creates a race condition in the security model: the same proof can be considered valid by one code path and invalid by the other. The bug appears during L1‑to‑L2 message processing where bridges often use single‑node Merkle trees to verify individual cross‑chain messages or to recover a single message after a failure. An attacker can craft a message whose Merkle proof is a single‑node tree, then force the bridge to invoke the validation routine that accepts the proof (calculateRootPaths) while the alternative routine (calculateRoot) would reject it. By manipulating the call flow or the data structures that select the verification routine, the attacker can cause the bridge to either accept a malformed message or reject a legitimate one, breaking the invariant that a valid proof must be verifiable consistently across the system. The impact includes messages becoming stuck on L1, potential double‑spending if the same message is verified through two divergent paths, denial‑of‑service for honest users, and increased gas costs as developers may need to batch messages artificially to avoid the edge case. The issue is discovered during a security audit (CodeHawks) that exercised both verification functions with single‑node inputs and observed the divergent behaviour. It is hard to notice because most test suites use multi‑leaf trees, and the contradictory checks are hidden behind private helper functions that are not exercised together. The bug belongs to the class of validation inconsistency or edge‑case handling errors, where different parts of a contract enforce different security assumptions. From a user perspective the symptoms are confusing: a user may see a cross‑chain message “failed verification” even though the proof looks correct, or conversely see a message accepted when the UI reports an error. The expected behaviour is that a proof either always verifies or always fails, but the reality is that the outcome depends on which internal function is called. The recommended fix is to unify the validation logic so that both calculateRoot and calculateRootPaths enforce the same rule for zero‑length paths – either reject all single‑node proofs consistently or accept them under a single, well‑documented condition – and to add comprehensive tests covering the edge case.

title: Unlimited Token Address Overwrites by Admin
description:
<https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/cfc1251de29379a9548eeff1eea3c78267288356/era-contracts/l1-contracts/contracts/bridge/L2WrappedBaseTokenStore.sol#L68>

<https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/cfc1251de29379a9548eeff1eea3c78267288356/era-contracts/l1-contracts/contracts/bridge/L2WrappedBaseTokenStore.sol#L80>

In the L2WrappedBaseTokenStore contract, the admin can overwrite the l2WBaseTokenAddress mapping for any chainId an unlimited number of times. This lack of restrictions on address overwrites allows the admin to change L2 token addresses at will, potentially causing security and operational issues if abused.

The initializeChain and reinitializeChain functions allow the admin to set a new L2 wrapped token address in the l2WBaseTokenAddress mapping without restriction.

Cause: Lack of safeguards, such as overwrite limitations or multi-signature requirements, permits repeated and arbitrary changes.

Exploitation: An admin could change token addresses to malicious contracts or redirect funds to unauthorized addresses. Since no restrictions or tracking mechanisms are in place, these changes would be difficult to detect without constant monitoring.

The unlimited overwrite ability creates several risks:

Potential for Malicious Token Address Overwrites: A malicious or compromised admin could redirect token addresses to arbitrary or malicious addresses, causing users to unknowingly interact with untrusted contracts.

Loss of Trust and Reliability: If addresses can be changed arbitrarily, users and applications may lose confidence in the accuracy and reliability of the stored token addresses.

Increased Attack Surface: The unrestricted overwrite ability creates an entry point for potential exploits or accidental errors by an admin, leading to unintended consequences.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted admin‑controlled overwrite of the stored L2 wrapped token address for any blockchain identifier. In the L2WrappedBaseTokenStore contract the functions that initialise or reinitialise a chain allow the caller with admin role to assign a new address to the l2WBaseTokenAddress mapping without any counter‑measure such as a one‑time lock, multi‑signature approval, or event logging that would limit or audit the change. The root cause is the absence of safeguards that track how many times a particular chainId entry has been set and that enforce a governance policy on address updates. An attacker who gains control of the admin account, or a malicious insider, can invoke the initialise function repeatedly, replacing the legitimate token contract address with an arbitrary contract that may steal funds, reject deposits, or return incorrect balances. Exploitation proceeds by the admin calling initialiseChain with a chosen chainId and a malicious contract address, after which any user interface or off‑chain service that queries the mapping will receive the forged address and may direct token transfers to the attacker’s contract. The impact includes loss of user funds when they interact with the substituted contract, erosion of trust because the stored address can no longer be considered reliable, and increased attack surface due to the ability to silently change critical configuration. The condition for the bug to manifest is simply that the caller possesses the admin role; no additional state or timing constraints are required. All participants that rely on the mapping – users, dApps, bridges, and other contracts – are affected because they may unknowingly send tokens to a malicious destination. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the lack of any restriction or event emission around the address assignment. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an event on change and the mapping can be overwritten silently, making detection dependent on external monitoring of the contract’s storage. The appropriate remediation is to treat the address as an immutable configuration after initial deployment or to enforce a strict governance process: track the number of updates per chainId, limit updates to a single admin change, require owner or multi‑signature approval for further modifications, and emit an event whenever the address is altered. This class of bug falls under mutable configuration without access‑control constraints, often referred to as an unrestricted admin overwrite or governance‑bypass vulnerability. From a user perspective the symptom may appear as a transaction that seems to succeed but results in no token balance change, a “refund” that is always zero, or a sudden disappearance of funds after interacting with what appears to be the correct L2 token contract.

title: Users can create proposals with very long descriptions that are uncancellable by the guardians
description:
Users can create proposals where any attempt that tries to cancel them reaches the gas / transaction limit on the L1, therefore completely circumventing the GovernorGuardianVeto module / safeguard.

The guardians have to use the function cancelL2GovernorProposal within the L1 contract Guardians (https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/b0c5565b6078a93cc3358a5d5012258caa701385/zk-governance/l1-contracts/src/Guardians.sol#L93) to cancel a proposal. This requests an L2 transaction, which ultimately calls cancel on GovernorGuardianVeto (https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/b0c5565b6078a93cc3358a5d5012258caa701385/zk-governance/l2-contracts/src/extensions/GovernorGuardianVeto.sol#L32). It is important to note that the guardians have to pass in the whole description string to the function cancelL2GovernorProposal. The hashing only happens within the function and the hash is then submitted to the L2. It is also important to note that every blockchain has (implicit) limits for the length of calldata. There is an upper limit for the size of transactions (128kB for geth: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/74ef47462f2a9daea04e81687c4d0b4598826ca2/core/txpool/legacypool/legacypool.go#L56) and a block gas limit (30 million for Ethereum). Because processing the calldata costs gas (especially hashing it), one of these automatically restricts the largest possible string that can be passed in such that the transaction is still included. Note that these limits are typically higher on an L2, the block gas limit is for instance 2**32 on ZkSync Era. But even if there were exactly the same, the following attack would still work, which is discussed below.

A malicious user can exploit the previously mentioned facts and submit proposals that are uncancellable. To do so, they submit a proposal with an extremely long description. The function propose (https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/cfc1251de29379a9548eeff1eea3c78267288356/zk-governance/l2-contracts/lib/openzeppelin-contracts/contracts/governance/Governor.sol#L273) does not restrict this length in any way. The length of the description is chosen such that the transaction is directly at its limit (either the transaction size limit or the block gas limit, whatever is smaller). Then, when the governors try to cancel the proposal, they need to submit the exact same string to get the same resulting proposal ID. However, this transaction would be above the limit and could not be executed. As previously argued, the limits (especially block gas limit) will be much lower on Ethereum. But even if they are the same, the transaction could not be executed: This happens because both the gas usage and the additional calldata size is larger for cancelL2GovernorProposal than for propose. cancelL2GovernorProposal performs more work (signature verification, requesting an L2 verification, etc...). Most importantly, it hashes the description twice (once in hashL2Proposal and once in the function itself vs. only once for propose. The hashing gas cost is linear in the size of the data, so very expensive for such huge strings. But also the additional calldata is longer. propose only has the arrays targets, values, and calldatas. cancelL2GovernorProposal includes these as well, but additionally txRequest, signers, and _signatures.

The purpose of GovernorGuardianVeto is for the guardians to be able to veto any proposals, for instance when they are malicious. As shown previously, this mechanism can be circumvented and it is possible to create proposals that cannot be cancelled by the guardians. The L2 governors ZkGovOpsGovernor and ZkTokenGovernor use this module, which both can be used to create proposals that steal funds (e.g. by minting with a ZkTokenGovernor proposal) or break the system (with malicious governance proposals). This therefore seems to match funds being "nearly at risk".
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked description length in the governance proposal creation flow that enables a denial‑of‑service on the privileged cancellation mechanism used by the GovernorGuardianVeto module. When a user calls the propose function on the L2 governor, the contract stores the full description string without any size validation. Later, a guardian must invoke cancelL2GovernorProposal on the L1 Guardians contract, passing the exact same description string so that the same proposal identifier can be derived on L2. The cancellation routine performs additional work – it hashes the description twice, verifies signatures and forwards a request to L2 – which makes its gas consumption and calldata size roughly double that of the original proposal transaction. Because Ethereum (and most EVM‑compatible chains) impose hard limits on transaction calldata size (≈128 kB) and on block gas (≈30 million on L1, lower on many L2s), an attacker can craft a proposal whose description is deliberately sized to sit just below the maximum allowed for a normal propose transaction. When the guardians attempt to cancel that proposal, the required calldata plus the extra hashing gas pushes the transaction beyond the protocol limits, causing the transaction to be rejected as out‑of‑gas or too large. Consequently the guardian’s veto power is effectively bypassed. This issue manifests only when unusually long description strings are used, which is why it may not appear in standard testing or code review. From a user perspective the UI will show a normal proposal, but any attempt by a guardian to cancel it will fail with a “transaction exceeds gas limit” or “calldata too large” error, contradicting the expectation that every proposal can be vetoed. The impact is that malicious actors can submit proposals that, for example, mint tokens or reallocate funds, and the protocol’s safety mechanism cannot intervene, putting funds and system integrity at risk. The flaw is a classic case of missing input validation leading to a DoS on a privileged operation, sometimes classified as an unchecked‑input‑size or gas‑exhaustion vulnerability. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the L1 Guardians contract and the L2 GovernorGuardianVeto extension and identified the asymmetry in calldata handling. Mitigation requires redesigning the cancellation interface so that it accepts a fixed‑size hash of the description instead of the full string, or alternatively enforcing a reasonable maximum length on proposal descriptions, thereby preventing the gas‑limit bypass and restoring the intended veto capability.

title: User can send toke with fees
description:
A vulnerability exists in the token bridging mechanism that allows transfer of non-standard tokens with fee-on-transfer functionality from Layer 1 (L1) to Layer 2 (L2), despite documentation stating such tokens are not supported. This issue can occur when transferring base tokens or using the \Bridgehub\ for ERC20 token transfers.

The L1AssetRouter transfers tokens to L1NativeTokenVault without verifying the exact balance after the transfer. Specifically: The router returns depositChecked = true without confirming the transferred amount  The subsequent NativeTokenVault._bridgeBurnNativeToken method does not validate that the full intended amount has been deposited. This means tokens with transfer fees can be bridged without proper accounting, potentially leading to discrepancies in token balances.

This means tokens with transfer fees can be bridged without proper accounting, potentially leading to discrepancies in token balances.

<https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/b0c5565b6078a93cc3358a5d5012258caa701385/era-contracts/l1-contracts/contracts/bridge/ntv/L1NativeTokenVault.sol#L171>

<https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-10-zksync/blob/b0c5565b6078a93cc3358a5d5012258caa701385/era-contracts/l1-contracts/contracts/bridge/ntv/NativeTokenVault.sol#L279>
Bridge tokens with fee-on-transfer mechanisms, which is not supported by the protocol
Cause accounting discrepancies in the bridge
Manipulate the actual amount of tokens transferred across layers
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the token bridging mechanism that permits fee‑on‑transfer (also called transfer‑fee or tax) ERC20 tokens to be moved from Layer 1 to Layer 2 even though the protocol documentation explicitly states that such tokens are not supported. The root cause is that the L1AssetRouter forwards the token transfer to the L1NativeTokenVault without checking the actual balance change after the transfer, and the vault’s internal _bridgeBurnNativeToken function returns a depositChecked flag as true without verifying that the amount received matches the amount that was intended to be deposited. Because fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred amount during the transfer call, the vault ends up holding less than the declared deposit amount, but the bridge proceeds as if the full amount was transferred. An attacker or any user can exploit this by supplying a token that charges a fee on each transfer; the bridge will record the full amount in its cross‑chain messages while only the net amount (after fee) is stored on L1, leading to a mismatch between the amount burned on L1 and the amount minted on L2. The impact is a discrepancy in token balances: users may see their L1 balance reduced to zero while the L2 side receives fewer tokens than expected, effectively losing the fee amount permanently. This occurs whenever a fee‑on‑transfer token is used as a base token or is transferred through the Bridgehub’s ERC20 deposit path, i.e., any call to bridgehubDepositBaseToken or bridgehubDeposit that involves such a token. The affected parties are token holders, bridge users, and the protocol itself because the accounting invariants that guarantee conservation of value across layers are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors introduced a mock ERC20 token that implements a 10 % transfer fee and observed that the bridge emitted events indicating a full deposit while the vault’s balance reflected only the net amount. The bug is subtle because the bridge’s external behavior (event emission and successful transaction) appears normal, and the missing fee is not directly visible in transaction receipts, making it hard to notice without explicit balance checks. The proper fix is to add a post‑transfer balance verification in the vault’s _bridgeBurnNativeToken routine: record the token balance before the transfer, perform the transfer, then compare the after‑balance to the before‑balance and ensure the difference equals the declared deposit amount, reverting if it does not. This change enforces that only tokens whose transfer amount is unchanged (i.e., non‑fee tokens) can be bridged, restoring the accounting guarantees and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: `L2AssetRouter._ensureTokenRegisteredWithNTV` `assetId` return value is never assigned, which will cause `withdrawToken` to fail
bug_full: The vulnerability is an uninitialized return value in the internal function that ensures a token is registered with the native token vault. The function is declared to return a bytes32 asset identifier, but the implementation never assigns a value to the assetId variable before returning. As a result, the Solidity compiler supplies the default value bytes32(0). Down‑stream logic – such as the withdrawToken entry point, the bridgeBurn flow, and the finalizeDeposit routine – expects a non‑zero asset identifier that uniquely represents the token on L2. When the zero identifier is propagated, the contract performs a lookup that fails the AssetIdNotSupported check and reverts the transaction. This manifests to the end‑user as a failed withdrawal: the transaction reverts, no funds are transferred, and the user’s balance remains unchanged, often accompanied by an error message indicating an unsupported asset. The bug occurs whenever a caller invokes withdrawToken (or any other function that relies on the assetId returned by the registration helper) for a token that should be registered, i.e., during normal bridge operations. It affects token holders, bridge operators, and any protocol component that depends on correct asset registration, effectively preventing withdrawals of native tokens and potentially locking funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case exercising withdrawToken unexpectedly reverted. The problem is subtle because the function signature suggests a valid assetId will be returned, yet the compiler does not warn about the missing assignment, and the failure only appears later in the call chain. The class of bug is an uninitialized return‑value or default‑value propagation flaw, which violates the business assumption that every registered token has a unique, non‑zero identifier. The proper fix is to assign the assetId inside the function – typically by reading it from the native token vault – before returning, or to redesign the function so that it does not rely on an implicit return value. Ensuring the correct asset identifier is returned restores the expected flow, allowing withdrawals to succeed and preserving the integrity of the bridge accounting logic.

title: Inverted use of boolean value in `L2NativeTokenVault.constructor` would cause revert or unnecessary deployment of `bridgedTokenBeacon`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inverted handling of a boolean flag that determines whether a token beacon contract should be deployed during the initialization of the L2 native token vault. In the upgrade helper, a variable named shouldDeployBeacon is set to true when no existing beacon address is found (deployedTokenBeacon == address(0)). This flag is then encoded and passed to the L2NativeTokenVault constructor, where it is decoded as _contractsDeployedAlready. The constructor interprets a true value as meaning that a beacon has already been deployed, and therefore expects a non‑zero _bridgedTokenBeacon address. Because the flag’s meaning is opposite, two erroneous outcomes are possible: if a beacon already exists, the helper passes true, the constructor thinks the beacon is already deployed, checks that the supplied address is non‑zero, finds it is zero and reverts; if no beacon exists, the helper passes false, the constructor believes the beacon is not deployed and proceeds to create a new UpgradeableBeacon even though a valid beacon address was supplied. This inversion blocks the L2 genesis upgrade when a legacy shared bridge is present, either by causing a deployment transaction to revert or by creating an unnecessary beacon contract, which can lead to unexpected contract addresses, broken token‑bridge routing, and potentially locked funds for users expecting their native token to be bridged. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the upgrade helper and the vault constructor, where the mismatch between the flag’s semantic name and its usage was observed. It is hard to notice because the boolean value itself is correctly passed, but the meaning is swapped, so static analysis that only checks type compatibility will not flag it. The bug belongs to the class of “parameter mis‑interpretation” or “logic inversion” errors, where a control flag is decoded with opposite semantics, violating the protocol’s deployment assumptions. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should deploy the vault either fails with a revert (no contract created) or succeeds but results in an unexpected beacon contract, leading to situations where a user’s balance appears unchanged, token transfers fail, or the bridge reports missing tokens. The correct fix is to align the boolean values: either rename and map the flag correctly in the constructor, or adjust the helper to pass a flag that matches the constructor’s expectation (e.g., pass contractsDeployedAlready = deployedTokenBeacon != address(0) and keep shouldDeployBeacon for the opposite case). In practice this means providing both flags explicitly or refactoring the constructor to use a single, clearly named flag that reflects the actual deployment state, ensuring that the vault either reuses an existing beacon or creates a new one exactly when intended, thereby allowing the L2 genesis upgrade to complete without unintended reverts or redundant contract creation.

title: Migration blocked due to chain limit in `MessageRoot` contract
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the MessageRoot contract enforces a hard cap on the number of zk chains (MAXNUMBEROFZKCHAINS = 100) without providing a way to bypass it during migration, even though the BridgeHub contract can bypass the same limit via a flag. When the chain count reaches the cap, any call that tries to add a new chain through addNewChain triggers a TooManyChains revert, causing migration transactions to fail. This occurs because addNewChain checks the cached chainCount against the constant and aborts before incrementing, and there is no analogous _checkMaxNumberOfZKChains parameter to disable the check. As a result, the protocol's stated goal of allowing migration of any chain, regardless of the current limit, is broken. Users attempting to migrate a new chain see a transaction revert with the TooManyChains error, experience missing or zero balances on the destination chain, and may be unable to move assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the migration flow in BridgeHub with the limit logic in MessageRoot. The bug is subtle because the bypass mechanism exists in one contract, giving the impression that the limit is universally bypassed, while the second contract still enforces it. The class of bug is inconsistent limit enforcement or missing conditional bypass, leading to a denial-of-service style failure of the migration feature. To fix the problem, the MessageRoot contract should incorporate the same flag-controlled check, allowing the limit test to be skipped when the call originates from a migration operation, thereby aligning both contracts with the protocol’s migration-any-chain requirement.

title: A newly created chain that has been migrated to the gateway will be lost if tries to migrate back to L1
bug_full: A newly created ZK chain can be migrated from Layer 1 (L1) to the gateway, but the same chain cannot be migrated back to L1 because the priority tree that tracks cross‑chain transactions is initialized without registering its initial zero leaf as a historical root. During the first migration, the Diamond contract on L1 records the priority tree state in a commitment structure and sends it to the gateway. The gateway reconstructs the tree using initFromCommitment, which simply copies the zero leaf (bytes32(0)) into the tree’s side array. No historical root entry is created at this point. When the chain later attempts to migrate back, the L1 contract executes the same forwardedBridgeMint logic and checks that the last side of the received commitment is a known historical root. Because the zero leaf was never added to the historicalRoots mapping, the check fails and the transaction reverts with NotHistoricalRoot, leaving the chain in a state where it cannot be re‑initialized on L1. The root cause is the missing registration of the initial leaf in the historicalRoots set during tree.setup. The vulnerability is triggered only for chains that have never recorded a historical root – i.e., freshly created chains that have been moved to the gateway and then try to return. Users experience a failed migration transaction, see an error revert, and may notice that the chain’s state disappears, balances become inaccessible, and any assets locked on that chain are effectively lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the migration functions, where the auditor traced the commitment flow and observed that the historical root verification does not accommodate the zero leaf. It is hard to notice because the zero leaf looks like a normal placeholder and the historical root check passes for all existing chains that already have roots recorded. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that every migration commitment must contain a verifiable historical root, breaking the guarantee of chain recoverability. The recommended fix is to record the initial zero leaf as a historical root in the setup routine (e.g., tree.historicalRoots[bytes32(0)] = true) or to adjust the verification logic to accept an empty historical root set for newly created chains. Conceptually, the fix ensures that the priority tree’s state is always provable both when moving to the gateway and when returning to L1, preventing permanent loss of the chain and its funds.

title: Some orders can be executed multiple times
description: Functions _deduplicateOrder() and verifyNonce() are in charge of deduplicating orders and making sure that the same nonce can't be used twice. The issue is that in verifyNonce() code converts invalidatorBit to uint128 with unsafe cast and the value of invalidatorBit could become 0 while overflow happens and in that case, the invalidator won't be set to 1 and that order can be executed multiple times by minter and redeemer role. The issue
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑execution flaw that allows a single order to be processed more than once. The contract relies on two internal functions, _deduplicateOrder and verifyNonce, to ensure that each order nonce can be used only a single time. In verifyNonce the code casts a variable called invalidatorBit to uint128. Because invalidatorBit is originally a larger integer, the unsafe cast truncates the high-order bits. When the original value contains bits that do not fit into 128 bits, the cast overflows and the resulting uint128 value can become zero. The logic that marks the nonce as used expects the invalidator to be set to a non‑zero value; if the cast yields zero the invalidator is never written, so the contract believes the nonce is still fresh. Consequently, an actor with the minter or redeemer role can submit the same order again, and the contract will execute the same state‑changing logic a second time. This can happen sporadically, only for orders whose nonce generates an invalidatorBit that exceeds the 128‑bit range, which is why the problem is not obvious during normal testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should have transferred funds once either transfers them twice or leaves the expected balance unchanged after a second call, effectively causing funds to disappear or be double‑spent. The impact is medium severity because the bug does not allow arbitrary creation of tokens, but it can lead to loss of funds for users who rely on the one‑time execution guarantee, and it undermines the accounting assumptions of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the deduplication logic and identified the unsafe type conversion. It is hard to notice because the overflow only manifests for specific nonce values, and the contract does not emit a distinct error when the invalidator fails to be set. The proper remediation is to avoid casting invalidatorBit to a smaller type; instead the code should keep the original width or use a type that safely fits the value, such as uint256, or redesign the nonce invalidation to use a boolean flag or a mapping keyed by the full nonce. By ensuring the invalidator is always correctly recorded, the contract will reliably reject any attempt to reuse the same order, restoring the intended single‑execution guarantee.

title: Excess ETH not returned in deployDeviceWalletAsAdmin and createAccount
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of trapped ether in the DeviceWalletFactory contract when the functions deployDeviceWalletAsAdmin and createAccount are used to prefund a newly created DeviceWallet. The root cause is that these two functions lack any logic to return the portion of msg.value that exceeds the required deposit amount (_depositAmount). After the contract verifies that msg.value is sufficient, it forwards only the exact deposit to the entry point and then simply finishes execution, leaving any surplus ether locked inside the factory’s balance. An attacker or honest user can exploit this by sending more ether than necessary during deployment; the excess ether is never refunded and cannot be withdrawn because the contract provides no withdrawal path and does not emit any event indicating the loss. The impact is a loss of funds for the caller (admin or regular user) and an inconsistent user experience compared with the deployDeviceWalletForUsers function, which does correctly refund surplus ether. The issue manifests whenever deployDeviceWalletAsAdmin or createAccount is called with msg.value greater than the required deposit, which is a realistic scenario when callers over‑estimate gas or intentionally send extra ether. The affected parties are the callers of these functions – typically the protocol admin or end‑users – and the protocol itself because the trapped ether reduces the overall available liquidity. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the refund handling across similar deployment functions and noticed the missing refund code path. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; the transaction succeeds and the caller receives no error, yet the balance of the factory contract increases silently. The appropriate fix is to add a post‑deployment refund step that calculates the unused amount (msg.value minus _depositAmount) and sends it back to msg.sender using a low‑level call, handling the success flag and reverting if the transfer fails, mirroring the logic already present in deployDeviceWalletForUsers. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “excess ether not returned” or “trapped ether” issue, where the contract’s accounting assumptions about ether handling are violated, leading to money disappearing from the user’s perspective; users expect any overpayment to be returned but instead see their balance unchanged while the contract’s balance grows unexpectedly.

title: Corruptible Upgradability Pattern
description: The Registry.sol contract is a UUPSUpgradeable contract that inherits from the RegistryHelper.sol contract. When creating upgradable contracts that inherit from other contracts, it is important that there are storage gaps in case storage variables are added to inherited contracts. If an inherited contract is a stateless contract (i.e. it doesn't have any storage) then it is acceptable to omit a storage gap since these function similarly to libraries and aren't intended to add any storage. The issue is that Registry.sol inherits from a contract that contains storage that doesn't contain any gaps such as RegistryHelper.sol. These contracts can pose a significant risk when updating a contract because they can shift the storage slots of all inherited contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a storage‑layout corruption that arises when an upgradable contract follows the UUPS pattern but inherits from a parent contract that defines storage variables without reserving a storage gap. In the presented case the Registry contract inherits from RegistryHelper, which contains state variables but does not include the customary __gap array. Because the UUPS proxy relies on a fixed storage slot ordering, adding or replacing the implementation contract shifts the positions of all variables that follow the inherited storage. When an upgrade is performed, the new implementation interprets the existing storage slots according to its own layout, causing the original values to be read from the wrong slots. This misalignment can overwrite balances, permissions, or configuration data, leading to symptoms such as user balances appearing as zero, refunds not being sent, or access controls failing. The issue occurs whenever the contract owner or an authorized upgrader deploys a new implementation that does not preserve the original slot ordering, which is typical during routine upgrades or emergency patches. All participants who rely on the contract’s state – token holders, service users, and the protocol itself – are affected because the corrupted storage can break accounting logic, prevent withdrawals, or enable an attacker with upgrade rights to manipulate critical variables. The problem was identified during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the source code against the standard upgradable‑contract checklist and noticed the absence of a storage gap in the inherited helper contract. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and functions correctly before the upgrade; only after a change in implementation does the hidden slot shift manifest, making it hard to detect without a thorough storage‑layout analysis. To remediate the issue, the developer should introduce a reserved storage gap in the parent contract (for example, uint256[50] private __gap;) or redesign the inheritance hierarchy so that only stateless contracts are used as bases. Adding the gap preserves the original slot ordering across upgrades, ensuring that existing state variables remain intact and that user‑facing operations continue to behave as expected. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of upgradability‑related storage‑collision vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that a variable’s value remains stable across contract versions unless explicitly changed by logic.

title: Non-compliance with EIP-7579
description:
1. The onInstall() function misses a revert statement if the module is already installed.

2. The onUninstall() function misses a revert statement if there is an error.

3. The onUninstall() function misses to delete from the walletSessionKeys mapping for the current user.

4. The isValidSignatureWithSender() and isInitialized() functions are left unimplemented.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a contract that implements the EIP‑7579 module interface but fails to follow several mandatory behaviours defined by the specification. The onInstall function does not revert when a user attempts to install the module a second time, meaning the initialized flag can be overwritten or left unchanged, allowing the module to be re‑installed silently. The onUninstall function lacks a revert when the module is not currently installed, so callers receive no error even though the internal state is inconsistent. Moreover, onUninstall does not delete the walletSessionKeys mapping for the caller, leaving stale session‑key entries that can be reused unintentionally. Finally, the required view functions isValidSignatureWithSender and isInitialized are left unimplemented, so callers receive default or empty responses that break the contract’s signature verification and initialization checks. These omissions create a state‑management bug where the module’s lifecycle is not correctly enforced, leading to situations where a user believes a module has been removed while the contract still retains session keys, or where a module can be installed multiple times without detection. An attacker could exploit the missing revert checks to repeatedly install or uninstall the module, causing denial‑of‑service conditions, confusing accounting, or enabling unauthorized actions through leftover session keys. The impact is medium risk: users may lose confidence that their wallet modules behave as expected, funds could become inaccessible if session keys are not cleared, and the protocol’s compliance claim is weakened. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the implementation against the EIP‑7579 reference and identified missing error handling and unimplemented functions. Because the functions appear to execute without reverting, the problem can be hard to notice in normal operation; only a thorough review of the specification reveals the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should add explicit revert statements in onInstall and onUninstall when the module is already installed or not installed, respectively, and should clean up all related mappings—including walletSessionKeys—when uninstalling. Additionally, the contract must provide concrete implementations for isValidSignatureWithSender and isInitialized that return accurate results according to the EIP‑7579 expectations. By aligning the code with the specification, the module will enforce proper lifecycle management, prevent stale data, and restore trust in the wallet’s security guarantees.

title: Not Active Sessions Would Be Considered Valid
description: The validateSessionKeyParams() function doesn’t fully ensure the session’s validity. If a session is meant to be valid only after a specific period, the function will still validate it successfully even if this period hasn’t elapsed yet.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the session‑key validation routine of the contract. The function that checks a session’s parameters is intended to ensure that a session is only usable after a certain start time (validAfter) and before an expiration time (validUntil). However, the implementation only verifies the expiration condition and completely omits a check that the current block timestamp must be greater than or equal to the validAfter value. As a result, a session that is supposed to become active only after a future timestamp can be considered valid immediately, allowing an attacker to invoke privileged actions before the intended activation window. This flaw originates from a missing logical condition in the validation code, effectively bypassing the time‑based access control. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary obtains a session key that has a validAfter field set to a future time, then calls any function that relies on the session validation before that time elapses. Because the validation routine returns success, the contract treats the session as active and executes the requested operation. The impact includes unauthorized execution of privileged functions, potential theft of assets, or manipulation of protocol state, all occurring while the legitimate user expects the session to be inactive. The issue manifests whenever a session is created with a non‑zero validAfter timestamp; under those conditions the contract will accept the session prematurely. Users, token holders, and any party relying on the session‑key mechanism are affected because the security guarantees of delayed activation are broken. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the validation logic and identified the absent time check. It can be difficult to notice because the function appears to perform validation and may pass basic unit tests that do not simulate the pre‑activation period. To remediate the issue, the validation routine should be extended to reject sessions whose validAfter timestamp is still in the future, typically by adding a condition that reverts when validAfter is greater than the current block timestamp, alongside the existing expiration checks. This correction restores the intended time‑based access control and prevents premature use of session keys, aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected security model.

title: Interest accumulated, but not accounted yet, could be reset if Governance updates the interest rate model when in "Interest Overflows" state
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw that can cause previously earned interest to be silently lost when the protocol enters an "interest overflow" state and governance subsequently changes the interest rate model. The root cause is that the vault’s update routine does not handle the situation where the sum of the current total borrows and the newly accrued interest would exceed a predefined maximum sane debt amount. In that overflow condition the routine deliberately skips updating the totalBorrows, interestAccumulator, lastInterestAccumulatorUpdate and related fee counters, effectively pausing interest accrual. Because the accumulator is not advanced, the protocol records no growth of interest during the overflow period. If, while the vault remains in this paused state, a governor calls the function that replaces the interest‑rate model, the function first invokes the same update routine (which again makes no changes because of the overflow), then forces the stored interest rate to zero and attempts to compute a new rate from the supplied model. When the new model is empty or reverts, the computation leaves the interest rate at zero. Consequently, when the overflow condition eventually clears (for example after repayments), the next update sees a zero interest rate, uses the stale interestAccumulator value that has not been updated since the overflow began, and writes the current block timestamp as the last update. The net effect is that all interest that accrued but could not be recorded during the overflow window is discarded, resulting in a loss of expected earnings for lenders and a mismatch in the protocol’s accounting. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that deposited funds appear to generate no interest, balances remain unchanged, and expected rewards are missing even though no explicit error is emitted. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit warnings when the overflow occurs; it simply pauses accounting, and the later reset of the interest rate to zero makes the loss appear as a normal state transition. The bug belongs to the class of overflow‑induced state‑inconsistency bugs combined with unsafe governance‑controlled parameter changes. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid governance actions that modify the interest‑rate model while an overflow flag is active, or ensure that the interest accumulator is preserved and correctly applied once the overflow condition resolves. Additional sanity checks that validate the new model’s behavior and prevent setting the interest rate to zero unintentionally would also mitigate the risk, and comprehensive documentation of this edge case would help operators understand the potential impact.

title: Governance.setInterestRateModel is missing sanity checks
description:
The Governance.setInterestRateModel is not actively checking the user newModel input that represents the new IRM rate model. When a new IRM is provided, the interest rate is resetted to 0 and then updated via computeInterestRate(vaultCache). The transaction should revert when:
• newModel is equal to the current model.
• newModel is a broken IRM model that will revert when computeInterestRate is executed.
The second case should be correctly handled, given that it violates a white paper invariant defined in the Interest Rate section:
When a vault has address(0) installed as an IRM, an interest rate of 0% is assumed. If a call to the vault's IRM fails, the vault will ignore this failure and continue with the previous interest rate.
Because the interest rate has been already reset to 0, when the new interest rate is called and reverts, it won't update the value to the old one but will remain equal to 0. In general, this case should be handled because the governance should not be able to actively set the IRM to a faulty one. Allowing such case will mean that borrowers won't accrue any interest on their open position and lenders will not accrue any rewards.
To be able to handle this case, the computeInterestRate must be refactored to return if the IRM call has reverted.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance function that updates the interest‑rate model (IRM) for a vault. When the function is called, it first resets the stored interest rate to zero and then invokes the new IRM’s computeInterestRate routine to obtain the updated rate. Because the function does not verify that the supplied model differs from the current one, nor does it check whether the computeInterestRate call succeeds, a governance actor can supply either the same model or a deliberately broken model that reverts. In the latter case the interest‑rate reset to zero remains permanent, because the revert is swallowed and the previous rate is never restored. This flaw originates from missing input validation and improper handling of external call failures, a classic case of “zero‑initialisation before validation”. An attacker with governance privileges can therefore set a faulty IRM and cause the protocol to report a 0 % interest rate for the affected vault. Borrowers would be able to open positions without accruing any interest, while lenders would see their expected reward streams disappear. The issue manifests only when the governance transaction succeeds; the UI may simply display a zero interest rate, which can be mistaken for a normal low‑rate period, making the problem hard to detect. The bug was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract behaviour against the white‑paper invariant stating that a vault with address(0) as its IRM should assume a 0 % rate only temporarily, and that any IRM failure must not overwrite the previous rate. To remediate, the contract should first call computeInterestRate on the new model and verify that it does not revert, then compare the new model with the current one, and only after successful validation should it update the stored model and interest rate. Alternatively, the function could retain the previous rate if the new IRM call fails, ensuring that the protocol never remains in a zero‑interest state unintentionally. This class of bug—missing sanity checks and improper error handling—breaks the accounting assumptions of the system and can lead to silent loss of lender rewards and unintended free borrowing for users.

title: EulerSavingsRate maxWithdraw and maxRedeem are not returning the correct underestimated value when owner has a controller enabled
description:
The EulerSavingsRate is an ERC4626 vault that integrates with the EVC ecosystem, allowing the module to be used as collateral for EVK vaults.
Because ESR shares can be used as collaterals, it's important that operations like transfer, transferFrom, withdraw and redeem ensure that users who have enabled a controller are still healthy after the execution of such operation. For this reason, any of the above functions executes the EVCUtil.requireAccountStatusCheck.
Because of this integration with EVC and EVK, the EulerSavingsRate module must implement the same logic implemented by Vault when the ERC4626 functions maxRedeem and maxWithdraw are called. The value returned by such functions should be underestimated to zero if the owner parameter has enabled a controller (the user could be unhealthy and the transaction could revert).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the EulerSavingsRate contract, an ERC4626 vault that is used as collateral in the EVC/EVK ecosystem. The contract implements the standard ERC4626 functions withdraw and redeem, and it also provides view helpers maxWithdraw and maxRedeem that report the maximum amount a user can safely withdraw or redeem. Because ESR shares can be used as collateral, the protocol requires that any operation which changes a user’s balance first checks the health of the account through EVCUtil.requireAccountStatusCheck. This health check is correctly performed in the transfer, transferFrom, withdraw and redeem functions, but the view helpers maxWithdraw and maxRedeem do not incorporate the same controller‑enabled check. When an account has a controller enabled – a state that indicates the user may be unhealthy and that further withdrawals should be blocked – the overridden logic in the Vault contract would return zero for both helpers. The EulerSavingsRate contract, however, inherits the default ERC4626 implementation which simply calculates the amount based on the share balance and ignores the controller flag. As a result, the functions return a non‑zero, underestimated value even though the account should be considered unsafe. An attacker who controls an account with a controller enabled can call maxWithdraw or maxRedeem to obtain a positive number, then execute withdraw or redeem for that amount. Because the underlying health check is bypassed in the view functions, the protocol may allow the withdrawal of assets that should have been locked, potentially draining collateral that other positions rely on. The impact is a breach of the accounting assumptions of the EVK vaults that accept ESR shares as collateral, leading to possible liquidation of other users, loss of funds, or a situation where the protocol’s risk parameters are violated. The bug manifests only when the owner parameter has hasControllerEnabled set to true; otherwise the functions behave as expected. It was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted the inconsistency between the ERC4626 view helpers and the required health‑check logic. The issue can be hard to notice because the functions are read‑only and the UI may display a non‑zero withdrawable amount, giving users a false sense of safety. The correct remediation is to override maxWithdraw and maxRedeem in EulerSavingsRate so that they return zero whenever hasControllerEnabled(owner) is true, thereby aligning the view helpers with the protocol’s risk‑management expectations. This class of bug falls under “incorrect accounting of withdrawable amount due to missing health‑check validation in ERC4626 view functions”, and it violates the business rule that users flagged as unhealthy must not be able to extract collateral.

title: IRMSynth's targetQuote assumes reference asset has 18 decimals
description: The IRMSynth.targetQuote parameter is set to 1e18. It is compared against the output of oracle.getQuote(1e18, synth, referenceAsset) that returns a reference asset amount which will be in reference asset decimals.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption that the reference asset used by the IRMSynth contract always has 18 decimal places. The contract stores a targetQuote value of 1e18 and directly compares it with the amount returned by oracle.getQuote(1e18, synth, referenceAsset). The oracle returns a quote expressed in the native decimals of the reference asset, which can differ from 18 (for example USDC uses 6 decimals). Because the contract does not adjust the targetQuote to the actual number of decimals of the reference asset, the comparison can be inaccurate. When the reference asset has fewer decimals, the oracle’s output is scaled down, causing the contract to believe the quote requirement is met even though the user has supplied insufficient collateral. Conversely, with assets that have more than 18 decimals the contract may reject valid trades. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who selects a reference asset with non‑standard decimals, initiates a trade or mint operation, and the contract erroneously validates the quote, allowing the attacker to obtain synth tokens or withdraw assets with less value than required. The impact includes potential loss of funds, under‑collateralized positions, and incorrect accounting that breaks the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue manifests whenever IRMSynth is paired with any token whose decimals differ from 18, which is common across many ERC‑20 tokens. Users may notice that a trade they expect to receive a certain amount of the reference token instead yields a much smaller amount, or that a transaction is rejected with a quote‑too‑low error even though the supplied amount seems sufficient. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that examined the targetQuote logic and identified the static 1e18 value without any scaling based on referenceAsset.decimals(). It can be hard to spot because the contract behaves correctly with 18‑decimal assets, and typical unit tests often use such tokens, masking the problem for other assets. The recommended remediation is to compute the targetQuote scaling factor using the reference asset’s decimal count in the constructor (or dynamically) so that the comparison is performed in a common unit, thereby restoring correct quote validation and preserving the intended financial invariants.

title: maxMint/maxDeposit can overestimate shares/assets as it ignores totalShares overflow
description:
The maxMint function currently returns shares < MAX_SANE_AMOUNT ? shares : MAX_SANE_AMOUNT where shares are the max-deposit assets converted to shares. However, it needs to take the current totalSupply into account as totalSupply + shares <= MAX_SANE_AMOUNT should hold.
It can return a larger amount than what can actually be accepted, according to EIP4626, this breaks the behavior:
MUST return the maximum amount of shares mint would allow to be deposited to receiver and not cause a revert, which MUST NOT be higher than the actual maximum that would be accepted (it should underestimate if necessary).
Note that maxDepositInternal only looks at cash and if the vault has a high utilization, maxDepositInternal might return a large value, indeed resulting in a large shares amount that would overflow the totalSupply's MAX_SANE_AMOUNT.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s maxMint (and related maxDeposit) calculation, which determines the maximum number of shares that can be minted for a given deposit. The function currently caps the returned share amount by a constant MAX_SANE_AMOUNT but fails to consider the current totalSupply of shares (totalShares). According to EIP‑4626, maxMint must return a value that will never cause the total supply to exceed the protocol’s safe limit; it should underestimate if necessary. When the vault’s totalShares is already close to MAX_SANE_AMOUNT, the internal helper maxDepositInternal may still report a large cash‑available amount because it only checks the vault’s cash balance and utilization. Converting this cash amount to shares yields a share quantity that, when added to the existing totalShares, would overflow the MAX_SANE_AMOUNT threshold.
