All participants who deposit assets into pools managed by strategists are affected, including ordinary users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the placeMarketMakingTrades and acceptOffer pathways and identified that the same privileged address can appear on both sides of a trade. The problem is subtle because the transaction follows normal market‑making logic; from a user interface perspective the pool appears to execute a regular trade, while the user’s balance silently shrinks, making the bug hard to notice without deep inspection of internal state changes. To remediate the flaw, the protocol would need to overhaul its role model: either separate the ability to propose offers from the ability to fill them, enforce that offers cannot be filled by the same address that created them, introduce caps on the amount of funds a strategist may draw, or require an external approval step before any trade that moves user capital. In essence, the fix must prevent a trusted party from unilaterally deciding trade terms and executing them against the pool, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees and protecting user funds.

title: Strategists can’t be removed
description:
There is no option to revoke strategist’s privilege.

As the strategist is a very strategic role which can effectively steal LP’s funds, this is very dangerous.
poc: There’s a function to [approve](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/rubiconPools/BathHouse.sol#L264) a strategist, but no option to revoke the access.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing revocation mechanism for the strategist role. In the contract a strategist can be approved through an approveStrategist function, but there is no counterpart to set the flag to false. This design flaw means that once an address is granted strategist privileges it retains them for the lifetime of the contract. The root cause is that the access‑control state variable is only ever set to true and never cleared, and no external function is provided to change it. An attacker who obtains the private key of a strategist, or a former team member whose privileges should be withdrawn, can continue to invoke any function protected by the strategist modifier. By repeatedly calling privileged pool‑management functions—such as withdrawing liquidity provider (LP) tokens, adjusting fees, or rebalancing assets—the attacker can siphon funds from the pool. The impact is that liquidity providers may see their deposits disappear, the protocol's capital can be drained, and users lose confidence in the system. The issue manifests whenever a strategist is appointed and later needs to be removed, for example after a role change, key rotation, or suspicion of misconduct; because the contract provides no way to do so, the elevated permissions remain active indefinitely. All participants are affected: LP providers who lose funds, the protocol governance that cannot enforce discipline, and developers who cannot remediate a compromised account. The problem was identified during a manual code review by the auditing team, which noticed the approveStrategist function but could not locate any revocation path. The absence of a revocation function is subtle; the contract otherwise appears functional, so the flaw can be missed unless the reviewer explicitly checks role lifecycle management. The bug belongs to the class of “undeletable privileged role” or “missing access revocation” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes that permissions can be withdrawn but the code does not support it. From a user perspective, the expected behavior is that a malicious strategist could be stripped of rights, preventing further theft; in reality the strategist remains active, leading to symptoms such as unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or complete loss of deposited LP tokens. To remediate, the contract should introduce a function that allows the owner or governance to set the strategist flag to false, emit an event when the role is revoked, and preferably use a well‑tested role‑based access control library that supports both grant and revoke operations. This change restores the ability to enforce the principle of least privilege and mitigates the risk of permanent privileged access.

title: User will loose funds
description: User will lose funds if user accidentally pass route with only 1 value which is route[0]=X WETH while calling swapForETH or swapWithETH/swapEntireBalance/swap function.
poc:
1. User calls swapForETH function with below params:

    pay_amt=500
    buy_amt_min=0
    route[0]=WETH
    expectedMarketFeeBPS=1

2. User will transfer 500+fees amount to the contract

```solidity
    require(
        ERC20(route[0]).transferFrom(
            msg.sender,
            address(this),
            pay_amt.add(pay_amt.mul(expectedMarketFeeBPS).div(10000))
        ),
        "initial ERC20 transfer failed"
    );
```

3. Now _swap function is called. This function will do nothing and loop will not run due to condition failure

```solidity
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < route.length - 1; i++)
```

// here since route.length - 1 is 1-1=0 so loop will not run as i=0 and 0<0 is false

4. Since currentAmount will be 0 and buy_amt_min is also 0 so require(currentAmount >= buy_amt_min, “didnt clear buy_amt_min”); will pass and 0 will be returned back
5. Swap is complete and user will not receive anything
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the swap route length combined with an unchecked minimum‑output parameter, which allows a user to unintentionally lock or lose funds when calling the contract’s swap functions (swapForETH, swapWithETH, swapEntireBalance, or swap). The contract expects a multi‑hop route that describes how the input token should be exchanged for the output token. If a caller supplies a route array that contains only a single element – typically WETH – the internal loop that performs the swaps iterates from 0 to route.length‑1. With a length of one, the loop condition (i < route.length‑1) evaluates to false immediately, so no swap logic is executed. At the same time, the caller can set buy_amt_min (the minimum acceptable amount of output token) to zero, which is interpreted as “accept any amount, even none”. After the contract successfully pulls the user’s input tokens (pay_amt plus the market fee) via ERC20.transferFrom, the swap routine finishes without changing the currentAmount (it remains zero). Because buy_amt_min is also zero, the final require check (currentAmount >= buy_amt_min) passes, and the function returns 0 as the amount of ETH received. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded – the contract emitted no error – but the user receives no ETH and the transferred tokens remain locked in the contract, effectively disappearing from the user’s balance. The issue occurs only when two conditions are met simultaneously: (1) the route array contains exactly one token (the input token itself) and (2) the caller specifies a zero‑slippage or zero‑minimum‑output value. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the swap implementation and identified that the route length was never validated and that a zero buy_amt_min could be used to bypass output checks. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply performs a no‑op swap, making it easy to miss during testing unless the specific edge case is exercised. The flaw belongs to the class of input‑validation errors where insufficient parameter checks allow a function to execute without performing its intended logic, leading to loss of funds. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum route length greater than one (e.g., require(route.length > 1)) and reject zero or unreasonably low buy_amt_min values unless explicitly allowed, thereby ensuring that a swap always involves at least one hop and that the caller cannot accept a zero output. This correction restores the intended business logic that a swap must convert the input token into a non‑zero amount of the target token, preserving user funds and aligning contract behavior with user expectations.

title: Deprecated variables may cause DoS
description: A malicious admin can set the deprecated variables `AqueductDistributionLive` and `AqueductAddress` to deny specific users to buy.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the continued presence of two legacy storage variables, AqueductDistributionLive and AqueductAddress, that remain part of the execution flow of the purchase routine. The contract checks the boolean AqueductDistributionLive and, when true, forwards the trade details to an external Aqueduct contract referenced by AqueductAddress. Because the admin role retains the ability to modify these variables, a malicious or compromised administrator can point AqueductAddress to a contract that deliberately reverts, or set AqueductDistributionLive in a way that triggers the call only for selected users. When the external call fails, the entire purchase transaction reverts, effectively denying the targeted user the ability to buy. This denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition occurs whenever a user initiates a trade that reaches the distribution step, which is a normal part of the business logic that expects funds to be distributed to maker and taker. The impact is that specific users see their transactions fail with no obvious on‑chain indication that the failure is caused by an admin‑controlled flag, leading to loss of expected service and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when reviewers noticed that the variables were marked as deprecated yet still referenced in a conditional block. The problem is subtle because the variables appear unrelated to core functionality and because the external call is wrapped in a plain if statement without any try/catch, making the revert look like a standard execution error rather than an intentional block. To remediate, the deprecated code paths should be eliminated entirely; if storage slot preservation is required for upgradable contracts, the variables can be kept as placeholders but must not be consulted in any logic. Additionally, any external contract interaction should be protected with proper error handling or restricted to trusted addresses, and admin rights over such critical configuration should be minimized or subjected to multi‑signature governance. By removing the unused variables from the active control flow, the protocol eliminates the vector that allows an admin to selectively block users, restoring the intended accounting guarantees where every qualified user receives a successful trade execution and the expected fund distribution.

title: Possible token reentrancy in release
description: If a token with callback capabilities is used as a token to vested, then a malicious beneficiary may get the vested amount back without waiting for the vesting period.
poc:
In the function release, [line](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L87), there’s no modifier to stop reentrancy, in the other contracts it would be the synchronized modifier. If a token could reenter with a hook in a malicious contract (an ERC777 token, for example, which is backwards compatible with ERC20), released token [counter array](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L116) wouldn’t be updated, enabling the withdrawal of the vested amount before the vesting period ends. A plausible scenario would be:

1. A malicious beneficiary contract B calls the release() function with itself as the recipient, everything goes according to the function, and transfer and callback to the malicious beneficiary contract happens.
2. Contract B contains tokensReceived(), a function in the ERC777 token that allows for callback to the victim contract as you can see here <https://twitter.com/transmissions11/status/1496944873760428058/> (This function also can be any function that is analogous to a fallback function that might be implemented in a modified ERC20. As it can be seen, any token that would give the attacker control over the execution flow will suffice.)
3. Inside the tokensReceived() function, a call is made back to the release function.
4. This steps are repeated until vested amount is taken back.
5. This allows for the malicious beneficiary contract to redeem the vested amount while bypassing the vesting period, due to the released token counter array (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L116>) which controls how many tokens are released (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon/blob/8c312a63a91193c6a192a9aab44ff980fbfd7741/contracts/peripheral_contracts/BathBuddy.sol#L101>) being updated only after the transferring of all tokens occurs. As this is the case, malicious beneficiary can get the usual amount that they could withdraw at the time indefinite amount of times (as result of released in line 101 will be 0), thus approximately getting all of their vested amount back without waiting for the vesting period. (fees not included).

There’s also precedents of similar bugs that reported, as seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler-findings/issues/154#issuecomment-1029448627)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a token‑reentrancy flaw in the release function of the BathBuddy contract. The function transfers vested bonus tokens to a beneficiary and only after the transfer updates an internal counter that records how many tokens have been released. If the bonus token implements a callback mechanism – for example an ERC777 token that invokes tokensReceived or a malicious ERC20 that includes a fallback‑style hook – the callback can call release again before the counter is updated. This re‑entrancy allows a malicious beneficiary to invoke the release logic repeatedly within a single transaction, retrieving the same vested amount multiple times and effectively bypassing the intended vesting schedule. The root cause is the absence of a re‑entrancy guard (such as a nonReentrant modifier or the contract’s synchronized modifier) and the violation of the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: the state change (updating the released‑tokens counter) occurs after the external token transfer, giving the external contract control over execution flow. An attacker can craft a malicious token contract that, when received, executes tokensReceived or a fallback function which immediately calls release again. Because the release function does not prevent this recursive call, the loop continues until the full vested balance is drained, while other beneficiaries remain unaffected. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – waiting for the vesting period to elapse before receiving tokens – is broken; users may see their tokens arriving instantly, or conversely may observe that a beneficiary repeatedly calls release and the contract’s internal accounting shows zero remaining releases while the attacker’s balance grows. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the contract’s token handling flow and compared it with other contracts that already employ a synchronization modifier. It is hard to notice because the external token contract appears to behave like a standard ERC20, and the re‑entrancy only manifests when the token implements a callback, a scenario that may not be covered by typical unit tests. The impact is functional rather than direct loss of other users’ funds: the protocol’s vesting guarantees are violated, undermining trust in the reward system. To remediate, the release function should be protected with a re‑entrancy guard and reordered to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern – updating the released‑tokens counter before performing the external token transfer – or alternatively use a pull‑payment model that eliminates external calls during state changes. By applying these mitigations, the contract would prevent malicious tokens from regaining control of execution flow, ensuring that vesting periods are respected and that token releases cannot be replayed to siphon additional rewards.

title: `RubiconMarket.sol#isClosed`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market contract’s closure check. The function that reports whether the market is closed, `isClosed()`, is declared as a pure function and unconditionally returns false. Consequently, any logic that relies on this flag – such as the `can_offer()` and `can_buy()` modifiers that are meant to prevent new offers or purchases after the market has been stopped – will always consider the market open. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended design, which includes a storage variable named `stopped` that is supposed to indicate the paused state, and the actual implementation that never reads this variable and incorrectly marks the function as pure. Because of this, when the protocol administrators set the `stopped` flag (presumably through a separate pause or close function), the contract continues to accept and execute new offers and buys. An attacker or any participant can therefore exploit the bug by interacting with the market after it should have been frozen, potentially draining liquidity, executing trades that were expected to be disallowed, or causing cancellations to be ignored. The impact is a breach of the market’s business logic – users expect that once the market is closed only cancellations are permitted, but the contract silently allows further trading, leading to unexpected loss of assets, trust erosion, and accounting inconsistencies. The issue manifests whenever the `stopped` flag is set to true; under those conditions the UI may still show the market as open, and users may be surprised to see their balances change despite believing the market was paused. All participants – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract no longer enforces its intended state machine. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where reviewers observed the presence of an unused `stopped` variable and a comment indicating that the market should be closed, yet the `isClosed()` function always returned false, a subtle mistake that can be missed without careful review of state‑dependent logic. The bug is hard to notice because the function’s return value is constant and the contract still compiles and runs; only the specific scenario of market closure reveals the discrepancy. To remediate, the `isClosed()` function should be changed to a view function that returns the value of the `stopped` storage variable, and all checks that depend on closure should reference this corrected flag, restoring the intended invariant that no new offers or buys are permitted after closure.

title: Multiple Unsafe Arithmetic Operations
description:
The referenced lines all perform unsafe multiplications using the unitary denominations of either `1 ether` (`1e18`) or `10**9` (`1e9`), both of which can easily lead to overflows when used as a multiplier for large amounts of assets.

Purchasing and selling amounts will be improperly fulfilled as well as improperly tracked as “sold out” / “bought out”.
poc:
Issue is deducible by inspecting the relevant lines referenced in the issue and making note of the raw multiplication (`*`) operations performed.

In order to overflow, you would need `pay_amt` to exceed `type(uint256).max / 1e18`, which would be highly unlikely with majority of the ERC20 tokens.

Possibly arguable with ERC20 tokens of much higher decimals though. Considering that the product is an open orderbook, I’ll let this issue stand.
bug_full: The contract contains an unsafe arithmetic vulnerability that stems from direct multiplication of large numeric values using the Solidity * operator with unit constants such as 1 ether (1e18) or 10**9 (1e9). Because the multiplication is performed without any overflow checks, a malicious actor or a legitimate user supplying an extremely large pay amount can cause the product to exceed the maximum value representable by a uint256, resulting in a wrap‑around overflow. When the overflow occurs, the computed purchase or sale amount is dramatically reduced, which in turn corrupts the internal accounting of the open orderbook. The protocol consequently records orders as "sold out" or "bought out" even though the actual asset transfer was incorrect, leading to mismatched balances. From a user’s perspective, a transaction may appear to succeed while the expected tokens are not received, balances may suddenly become zero or lower than expected, and the UI may indicate that an order is no longer available despite having sufficient funds. The vulnerability is triggered only when the input amount is larger than type(uint256).max divided by the multiplier (approximately 1.15e10 ether or 1.15e27 units of a token with 9 decimals). While such extreme values are unlikely for most ERC‑20 tokens, tokens with very high decimal precision could reach the threshold, making the bug exploitable in edge cases. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the relevant lines of code and noticing raw multiplication operations without safety checks. It is difficult to notice in normal testing because the overflow does not manifest for typical transaction sizes, and the contract does not emit explicit errors when the wrap‑around occurs. The appropriate remediation is to replace the unchecked * operator with a safe multiplication routine such as the mul function from the DSMath library already imported in the codebase, which reverts the transaction on overflow and thereby preserves the integrity of the accounting logic. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unsafe arithmetic or integer overflow vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental business assumption that monetary calculations remain monotonically increasing and never wrap around, ultimately jeopardizing user funds and the protocol’s reliability.

title: Malicious pools can be deployed through `BathHouse`
description: Reentrancy in `BathToken.initialize()` can be exploited and this allows to create a pool which has a legitimate underlying token (even one for which a pool already exists), and has given full approval of underlying Token to an attacker. While this underlying token will differ from the one returned by `BathHouse.getBathTokenfromAsset` for that Pool (since the returned token would be the malicious one which reentered `initialize`), the LPs could still deposit actual legitimate tokens to the pool since it is deployed from the BathHouse and has the same name as a legit pool, and loose their deposit to the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a re‑entrancy flaw in the `BathToken.initialize()` function of the Rubicon BathHouse system. When a new pool is created, `BathHouse.openBathTokenSpawnAndSignal()` deploys a `BathToken` implementation and immediately calls its `initialize()` routine, passing the address of the underlying ERC‑20 token and a market address. Inside `initialize()`, the contract makes an external call to `underlyingToken.approve()` before the internal `initialized` boolean is set to true. Because the approval call is performed on a token supplied by the caller, a malicious token can override the `approve` function and re‑enter `initialize()` during this external call. The malicious token can then call `BathToken.initialize()` again, substitute its own address as the BathHouse role, and set the market to an attacker‑controlled address while still keeping the legitimate underlying token as the pool’s asset. As a result, the pool is created under a name that matches a legitimate pool, but it grants the attacker unlimited approval to transfer the genuine underlying tokens from the pool. Liquidity providers who deposit into what appears to be a normal pool will see their balances reduced to zero or find that withdrawals return no funds because the attacker can pull the tokens out through the rogue approval. The impact is loss of deposited assets for users and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants, breaking the expectation that deposits are safely held in the pool. This condition occurs whenever a pool is spawned with an underlying token that is under the attacker’s control and implements a re‑entering `approve`. The affected parties include liquidity providers, the BathHouse contract, and any downstream contracts relying on the pool’s token balances. The issue was discovered during a code audit that highlighted the approval call at line 214 occurring before the `initialized` flag is set, a classic case of missing the checks‑effects‑interactions (CEI) pattern. The bug can be hard to notice because the malicious token can masquerade with the same name and symbol as a legitimate token, and the UI will display the expected pool name and token details, giving users false confidence. To remediate, the `initialize` function should set the `initialized` flag before any external call, follow the CEI pattern, and restrict calls to only the BathHouse contract via an `onlyBathHouse` modifier. This prevents re‑entrancy and ensures that only authorized pools can be created with verified underlying assets, restoring trust in the accounting logic of the system.

title: M-1 User incurs fee loss when using BURNUNLOCKCODE with a NotSet token status
description:
A user's funds may get stuck when using BURNUNLOCKCODE for a NotSet token.
For example, consider the following scenario:
1. A user locks 1000e18 LP tokens on chain A and mints corresponding synthLp tokens on chain B.
2. As time progresses, the WhitelistV2 contract's owner sets the LP token's status on chain A to NotSet.
3. The user decides to unlock their LP tokens and BURNUNLOCKCODE from chain B to A.
4. While the "burn" operation is successful on chain B, it fails on chain A due to the requirement that the output token must be set as InOut:
```solidity
require(
    IWhitelist(whitelist).tokenState(otoken)
    == uint8(IWhitelist.TokenState.InOut),
    "Portal: token must be whitelisted"
);
```
PortalV2.sol#L87
Therefore, the user loses the commission for the cross-chain transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain state‑validation flaw in the bridge that allows a user to initiate a burn‑unlock operation when the destination token has been moved to a 'NotSet' status in the whitelist. The root cause is that the Synthesis contract does not verify that the output token is currently whitelisted with the InOut flag before performing the burn on the source chain. When the token’s status is changed by the contract owner after the user has locked assets but before they attempt to unlock, the burn transaction on the source chain reverts because of the require check in the Portal contract, while the fee for the cross‑chain operation has already been collected on the destination chain. An attacker does not need to act; the issue can be triggered simply by the protocol’s governance changing the token state. The impact is that the user loses the commission that was charged for the cross‑chain transfer and, in some cases, the locked LP tokens may become unrecoverable until the token status is restored, effectively 'funds disappear' from the user’s perspective. The condition occurs only when the token status is NotSet at the moment of the unlock call, which is a rare but possible scenario in normal protocol operation. All users who rely on the bridge to move LP tokens across chains are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and liquidity. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors noticed that the Synthesis contract lacked the same whitelist‑state guard that exists in the Portal contract. The problem is hard to notice because the UI may report a successful burn on the destination chain, while the source‑chain transaction fails silently, leaving the user with a missing fee and no obvious error message. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check in the Synthesis contract that the token is listed with the InOut state in the Whitelist before allowing any burn‑unlock operation, mirroring the existing guard in PortalV2. This change restores the invariant that a cross‑chain transfer can only proceed when the token is actively whitelisted, preventing fee loss and ensuring that funds cannot become stuck due to a mismatched token state. The bug belongs to the class of 'inconsistent state validation across contract boundaries' or 'cross‑chain whitelist bypass' that violates the accounting assumption that fees are only taken when the full transfer succeeds.

title: M-2 Risk of fee loss due to transactions through a paused router
description: The UnifiedRouterV2 contract can be paused. If the user's path includes a paused router, their transaction can fail, and they might simply lose money on fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑loss condition that arises when a user initiates a token swap or other multi‑step operation through a routing contract that can be paused. The router contract includes a pause flag that, when set, prevents the execution of its core logic. However, the front‑end or calling contract may still construct a transaction path that includes the paused router. When the transaction reaches the paused router, the router reverts its internal processing, but the fee‑collection mechanism may have already deducted a protocol fee from the caller before the revert occurs. As a result, the user’s transaction fails – no tokens are transferred, no expected output is received – yet the fee that was taken is not refunded. This situation typically occurs in a decentralized exchange or liquidity‑aggregation protocol where routes are dynamically selected and the pause state of individual routers is not checked before execution. The impact is that users lose a portion of their funds (the fee) without receiving the intended service, violating the expectation that a failed transaction should be cost‑free aside from gas. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pause functionality of the UnifiedRouterV2 contract and observed that the pause flag is not propagated to the UI layer, allowing users to unknowingly send transactions through a disabled component. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction appears to have been submitted successfully, the blockchain records a revert, and only the fee deduction is visible in the user’s balance – a subtle accounting discrepancy rather than an outright loss of the principal amount. To remediate, the protocol should expose the pause status of each router to the front‑end and prevent path construction that includes a paused router, or alternatively redesign the fee logic so that fees are only collected after the entire operation succeeds. This class of bug falls under “fee‑loss due to improper handling of paused components” and represents a breach of business logic that assumes successful execution before charging fees, leading to unexpected zero‑output swaps and missing balances from the user’s perspective.

title: M-3 Potential loss of funds if msg.value exceeds amountIn + executionPrice
description:
If a user conducts a cross-chain operation with WRAP_CODE, they transfer native currency to the router and, in return, receive WETH. At the same time, the user pays an executionPrice for the cross-chain transaction.
However, there's a risk that users might input a msg.value significantly higher than needed, leading to the excess native currency being stuck on the router.
RouterV2.sol#L213
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment issue that occurs in the router contract when a user invokes the cross‑chain WRAP_CODE operation. In this flow the user sends native cryptocurrency (for example ETH) together with a msg.value that is intended to cover two components: the amount of input tokens to be wrapped (amountIn) and the execution price required for the cross‑chain transaction. The contract does not validate that the supplied msg.value is less than or equal to the sum of amountIn and executionPrice. Consequently, if a caller provides a msg.value that is significantly higher than the required total, the excess native currency is accepted by the router but never forwarded, refunded, or accounted for. The root cause is the missing require statement that would enforce the upper bound on msg.value. An attacker or an unwary user can exploit this by deliberately sending more ether than needed, causing the surplus to become permanently locked in the router’s balance because the contract lacks any mechanism to retrieve or return the extra funds. The impact is a loss of user funds: the user expects to receive wrapped tokens equal to amountIn and to pay exactly executionPrice, but instead sees a reduction in their wallet balance equal to the over‑paid amount, while the transaction otherwise appears successful. This situation can also break the protocol’s accounting assumptions, as the router’s internal accounting will show an unexpected increase in native currency holdings, potentially affecting liquidity calculations and fee distribution. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to the router’s WRAP_CODE path where msg.value exceeds amountIn plus executionPrice. All participants who rely on this function – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bug can lead to silent fund loss and inaccurate balance reporting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the input validation logic of the router’s cross‑chain functions. It may be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no error is emitted, and the UI typically only shows the successful receipt of wrapped tokens, giving no indication that extra ether has been trapped. To remediate the problem the contract should include an explicit check that msg.value is not greater than the sum of amountIn and executionPrice, and optionally implement a refund mechanism that returns any surplus to the caller. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that users should never lose more than the explicitly required fees, restoring confidence in the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: M-4 Lack of user control over maximum bridge fee
description:
• PortalV2.sol#L89
• Whitelist.sol#L90
The PortalV2.unlock() function charges the user a fee specified in the Whitelist contract, which can be increased by the admin up to 100%, affecting transactions already in progress based on lower fees.
Currently, the user cannot set a threshold for the maximum fee, which can lead to situations where a user initiates a bridge transaction expecting a nominal fee, but the admin - without ill intent - increases the fee, resulting in the user receiving less money than anticipated.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the inability for a bridge user to limit the maximum fee that can be charged when unlocking assets on the destination chain. The fee amount is read from a separate contract that can be modified by an admin at any time, up to 100 % of the transferred amount. Because the fee is looked up at the moment the unlock transaction is executed, an admin who raises the fee after a user has already submitted a transaction but before it is mined can cause the user to receive a smaller amount than expected. This can happen even when the admin does not act maliciously; any legitimate fee update can retroactively affect pending transactions. The impact is that users may see a significant portion of their funds deducted, potentially receiving zero or far less than intended, breaking the economic assumptions of the bridge and leading to loss of confidence. The condition occurs whenever the bridge fee variable is mutable and there is no per‑transaction cap or notice period. All participants who rely on the bridge – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting model assumes a stable fee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PortalV2 contract where the fee lookup was traced to a whitelist contract that the admin can change without restriction. The problem is subtle because the fee change is a legitimate state transition and does not revert the transaction, so users may not notice that the fee was higher than the one they anticipated when they signed the transaction. The recommended mitigation is to give users the ability to specify a maximum acceptable fee when they initiate a bridge, or to introduce a time‑locked fee update mechanism that provides a notice period before a new fee becomes effective, thereby preventing retroactive fee increases on pending operations. In generic terms, this is a mutable‑parameter‑without‑user‑guard bug that violates the principle of fee predictability and can be classified as an economic‑logic vulnerability.

title: M-5 Transaction DOS via permit() front-running
description:
The permit() data, once submitted, is publicly accessible in the mempool, allowing anyone to execute the permit by replicating the transaction arguments. Once permit() has been called, the second call with identical parameters will revert.
In a scenario where a signed transaction includes PERMIT_CODE, a malicious actor could frontrun and "activate" this permit, bypassing the router's start() function. As a result, the legitimate user's start() transaction would fail:
• RouterV2.sol#L99-L109
Reference:
• https://www.trust-security.xyz/post/permission-denied
bug_full: The vulnerability is a transaction‑level denial‑of‑service that stems from the public nature of the permit() call used by the router contract. Permit() follows the standard EIP‑2612 pattern where a signed approval is submitted off‑chain and then broadcast in a transaction. Because the signed data is visible in the mempool, any observer can copy the exact arguments and execute the same permit() call before the original sender’s transaction is mined. The router’s start() function expects to invoke permit() once and then continue with the rest of the workflow. When an attacker front‑runs and successfully executes the permit() with the same parameters, the contract records the approval and any subsequent call with identical arguments reverts, as the permit function is designed to reject duplicate executions. Consequently, when the legitimate user’s start() transaction reaches the permit() step, it encounters a revert and the whole transaction fails. This results in a denial of service for the user: the intended operation (e.g., token swap or liquidity provision) does not occur, the user loses the gas spent on the failed transaction, and the protocol may experience stalled interactions. The issue manifests only when the router relies on a single permit() call per user action and does not guard against the possibility that the permit may have already been consumed by an external actor. It primarily affects users of the router, token holders who rely on the permit flow, and the protocol that expects successful execution of start(). The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the call flow of RouterV2.sol and identified that permit() does not have a protective wrapper. It can be difficult to notice because permit() is a standard, seemingly harmless function and the revert only appears when a duplicate call is made, which may be rare in normal testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should handle the permit call in a non‑reverting manner, for example by wrapping the call in a try/catch block and ignoring the error if the permit has already been processed, or by checking the allowance before invoking permit() and skipping the call when the approval already exists. This change prevents the transaction from being aborted solely because the permit was front‑run, thereby eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector while preserving the intended permission semantics.

title: M-6 Unexpected PERMIT_CODE in RouterV2
description:
The PERMIT_CODE is assumed to always be the initial operation in the list. As a result, the checkTo() method does not anticipate this code to follow and consequently returns zero.
• RouterV2.sol#L274
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an implicit assumption in the RouterV2 contract that a PERMIT operation (identified by PERMIT_CODE) will always appear as the first element in a list of batched actions. The checkTo() function, which determines the target address for subsequent operations, is written to treat the first element specially and does not contain logic to handle a PERMIT_CODE that appears later in the sequence. When a caller includes a PERMIT operation after other actions, checkTo() fails to recognise the correct destination and returns the zero address. This mis‑routing can cause the router to attempt to forward funds or execute calls to address(0), effectively burning tokens or causing the intended recipient to receive nothing. The issue is triggered only when the ordering constraint is violated, which may not be obvious during normal usage because most callers place PERMIT first, making the bug hard to detect without targeted testing. It was discovered during a systematic audit by MixBytes, which examined the control‑flow of the router and identified the unchecked assumption. Exploitation does not require privileged access; an attacker can simply craft a transaction that places PERMIT_CODE later in the operation array, causing the router to return zero from checkTo() and leading to loss of funds or failed operations. Affected parties include any user or protocol that relies on RouterV2 for token swaps, cross‑chain transfers, or permissioned actions, as their balances may appear unchanged or tokens may be unintentionally burned. From a user perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should result in a token transfer completes without error but the user’s balance remains unchanged, or the transaction reverts because the contract attempted to interact with the zero address. The bug violates the business logic that assumes a valid destination address for every operation, breaking accounting guarantees. The recommended remediation is to enforce the ordering rule explicitly—reject any batch where PERMIT_CODE is not the first element—or to modify checkTo() so that it correctly resolves the target address regardless of where PERMIT appears, thereby restoring the intended routing semantics.

title: M-1 User cannot deboost after the vote is reset due to
description:
When a user calls EscrowVoteManagerV1.reset(), all data related to their vote is deleted. However, the s_hasVotedByEpochAndTokenId flag remains set to true.
As a result, the user is unable to call EscrowManager.deboost() to retrieve their NFTs until the current epoch ends.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L320-348
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale voting flag that remains true after a user calls the reset function in the EscrowVoteManager contract. The reset function deletes the user's vote data but fails to clear the s_hasVotedByEpochAndTokenId flag. Because the EscrowManager.deboost function checks this flag to determine whether the user is allowed to retrieve their staked NFTs, the function rejects the call while the flag is still true. Consequently, a user who has just reset their vote cannot deboost and retrieve the NFTs until the current epoch finishes, effectively locking the assets. This situation occurs whenever a user invokes reset during an active epoch; the condition is internal to the contract and not exposed in the UI, so users only notice that their attempt to withdraw returns no tokens or that their balance appears unchanged. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state‑cleanup logic of the reset routine. It is hard to notice because the flag is a private storage variable and the contract does not emit an event indicating the failure, leading to a mismatch between the user's expectation (the vote is reset and the NFT can be reclaimed immediately) and the actual behavior (the NFT remains locked). The issue belongs to the class of improper state cleanup or stale flag bugs, which violate the protocol's accounting assumption that resetting a vote also releases any associated escrow constraints. To remediate the problem, the reset logic should explicitly set s_hasVotedByEpochAndTokenId to false (or otherwise clear the voting flag) before exiting, ensuring that deboost can be called immediately after a reset.

title: M-2 Incorrect struct copy leads to unexpected behavior
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect copy of a complex data structure in the EscrowManager contract. The contract stores a snapshot of voting power in a struct called VotingPowerPoint and attempts to keep an immutable reference by assigning it to a second variable m_lastVotingPowerPointCopy using a simple memory assignment. In Solidity, this kind of assignment performs a shallow copy: primitive fields are duplicated, but any nested dynamic arrays, mappings, or other reference‑type members are copied by reference. Consequently, when the original m_lastVotingPowerPoint struct is later updated – for example when a participant’s voting power changes or when the contract records a new voting checkpoint – those updates also mutate the supposedly independent copy. The root cause is the lack of a deep copy operation that would duplicate every nested element. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit this by triggering a state change that modifies the original struct after the snapshot has been taken, thereby corrupting the snapshot used for critical decisions such as escrow release, proposal acceptance, or voting power verification. The impact is that the protocol may make decisions based on stale or altered voting power data, leading to proposals being approved or rejected incorrectly, escrow funds being released to the wrong party, or token holders seeing their voting power reported as zero or inflated. This condition occurs whenever the contract logic relies on the copy as an immutable reference – typically after a voting power update or a checkpoint creation. All participants that depend on accurate voting power calculations – token holders, DAO members, and the escrow mechanism – are affected because the business rule that voting power is fixed at a given point in time is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer noted that the assignment does not guarantee independence and that subsequent state changes appeared to influence the copy. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still function correctly in simple test scenarios, and the symptom – a mismatch between expected and actual voting power – may only surface under specific sequences of updates. From a user perspective the UI may display a sudden drop to zero voting power, or a proposal that should be accepted is rejected, creating confusion and loss of trust. The proper remediation is to implement a deep copy of the struct, manually copying each nested element or using a helper function that returns a new struct with duplicated data, ensuring that the snapshot remains immutable after creation. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a shallow‑copy or reference‑type aliasing issue, where a developer assumes a value copy when only a reference is duplicated, breaking accounting assumptions and leading to incorrect state transitions.

title: M-3 A killed gauge keeps receiving rewards
description:
When the function EscrowVoteManagerV1.killGauge() is called, all claimableRewards associated with the gauge are transferred to the EmissionManager contract, and the sclaimableRewardsByGauge[gauge] mapping is deleted.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L135-137
However, if the EscrowVoteManagerV1.updateRewardIndexForGauge() function is subsequently called with the same gauge address, and if svotesByPool[mpool] is not zero, the sclaimableRewardsByGauge[gauge] mapping will be incremented again.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L356-363
As a result, rewards can still be distributed to the GaugeV1 contract despite it being "killed."
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward accounting logic of a gauge that can be marked as killed. When the EscrowVoteManagerV1.killGauge() function is invoked, the contract transfers any claimable rewards for the target gauge to the EmissionManager and deletes the entry in the sclaimableRewardsByGauge mapping, which gives the appearance that the gauge will no longer accrue any further rewards. However, the updateRewardIndexForGauge() function does not verify whether the gauge has been killed. If this function is called later with the same gauge address and the svotesByPool entry for the associated pool is non‑zero, the function will recompute the reward index and increment the sclaimableRewardsByGauge entry again, effectively recreating a claimable reward balance for a gauge that should be inactive. The root cause is the lack of a state flag or guard that prevents reward index updates after a gauge has been killed, combined with the fact that vote balances are left untouched, allowing the index calculation to succeed. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by first killing a gauge to stop its rewards, then triggering an updateRewardIndexForGauge call (directly or indirectly through normal voting activity) to re‑enable reward accrual. The impact is that rewards continue to be distributed to a gauge that the protocol and its users believe to be disabled, leading to misallocation of funds, potential over‑payment to malicious parties, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions. This condition occurs only after a gauge has been killed and there remain non‑zero votes for the pool; it does not affect gauges that are never killed or that have zero votes. The affected parties include the DAO governance, token holders who rely on correct reward distribution, and any user who expects a killed gauge to stop receiving emissions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the EscrowVoteManagerV1 contract, where the control flow between killGauge and updateRewardIndexForGauge was examined. It can be hard to notice because the mapping entry is deleted, giving the impression that the gauge is fully cleared, yet the later function silently recreates the entry without any explicit warning, and the UI may still show the gauge as killed while rewards keep flowing. To remediate, the contract should update the gauge’s reward indexes when it is killed, set a killed flag, and prevent any further index updates while the gauge remains in the killed state. When a gauge is revived, the indexes must be synchronized again to avoid discrepancies. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent reward accounting” where a termination operation does not fully invalidate subsequent state‑changing functions, allowing unintended fund flow.

title: M-4 Non-zero rebaseEmission_ value from
description:
EmissionManagerV1.calculateRebaseEmission returns 500e18 if currentWeeklyEmission is 7500000e18 as value set in EmissionManagerV1.initialize().
The function EmissionManagerV1._calculateRebaseEmission returns a non-zero value even when totalLocked is zero. For example, with a currentWeeklyEmission value of 7500_000e18, the function returns 500e18.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EmissionManagerV1.sol#L284-287
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the emission calculation routine of the protocol’s reward manager. Specifically, the internal function that determines the amount of tokens to mint during a rebase operation returns a positive, non‑zero value even when the total amount of tokens locked in the system is zero. The root cause is the absence of an explicit guard that checks the totalLocked variable before performing the arithmetic that yields the rebase emission. Because the guard is missing, the function falls through to a default calculation path that produces a constant emission (for example 500 × 10¹⁸ tokens) regardless of the fact that no participants have any stake. An attacker or any caller that can trigger the rebase routine can therefore cause the contract to mint new tokens when there are no locked tokens to justify a distribution. This can be exploited by invoking the rebase function during a period when totalLocked equals zero, causing the protocol to create and potentially allocate tokens that were never earned. The impact includes unintended inflation of the token supply, distortion of accounting assumptions, and possible loss of value for legitimate token holders because the supply expands without corresponding economic activity. The issue manifests whenever the weekly rebase is scheduled or manually triggered while the lock pool is empty – a state that can occur after a mass withdrawal or during the initial deployment before any deposits. All participants, the DAO treasury, and any downstream contracts that rely on the emission amount are affected because the protocol’s monetary policy is violated. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit by MixBytes, which exercised the calculateRebaseEmission function with a zero totalLocked input and observed a non‑zero output. The problem is subtle because the function is only called periodically, and the emitted amount may be relatively small compared to the total supply, making the inflation hard to notice in routine monitoring. To remediate the issue, the emission logic should be updated to return zero whenever totalLocked is zero, or to include a safe‑math guard that prevents any calculation from proceeding when the denominator is zero. This change restores the intended invariant that no emission occurs without locked capital, preserving the protocol’s economic model and preventing accidental token creation.

title: M-5 Execution of a proposal with a blacklisted selector
description:
Users are prohibited from creating proposals with blacklisted selectors in the ProposalManager contract.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/ProposalManager.sol#L150-152
However, if a proposal has already been created and the contract owner adds the selector to the blacklist, the proposal can still be executed despite the selector being blacklisted.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the execution path of governance proposals in a DAO contract that maintains a blacklist of prohibited function selectors. The contract enforces the blacklist only when a proposal is created, rejecting any proposal that contains a selector present in the blacklist at that moment. However, the contract does not re‑evaluate the selector list when the proposal is later executed. Consequently, if a proposal is submitted while its selector is allowed, and the contract owner subsequently adds that selector to the blacklist, the proposal remains eligible for execution and can invoke the now‑blacklisted function. This flaw arises from a missing validation step at the execution stage, effectively decoupling the blacklist from the actual call that is performed. An attacker can exploit the issue by first creating a benign‑looking proposal, then waiting for the governance or owner to blacklist the selector (perhaps as part of a routine update), and finally triggering the proposal execution to perform a prohibited action such as transferring funds, changing critical parameters, or invoking privileged functions. The impact is that funds may be moved without proper authorization, protocol state can be altered in ways that violate the intended governance rules, and token holders lose confidence because the safety mechanism they rely on (the blacklist) is bypassed. The condition under which the bug manifests is any scenario where the blacklist is modified after a proposal has been recorded but before it is executed. All participants of the DAO—proposers, voters, and token holders—are potentially affected because the execution of a malicious proposal can affect the shared treasury and the overall security of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ProposalManager contract when the logic of proposal creation and execution was compared and the inconsistency was observed. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the proposal as valid at creation time, and the blacklist appears to work for new proposals, giving a false sense of security. The proper remediation is to enforce the selector blacklist at the point of execution as well, or to make the blacklist immutable for already‑submitted proposals, ensuring that any prohibited selector always blocks both creation and execution. In generic terms, this is a classic case of insufficient input validation at a later stage of a workflow, leading to a bypass of a security control that was assumed to be enforced throughout the lifecycle of an operation. From a user’s perspective, a DAO member may expect that a proposal containing a blacklisted function will never be executed, yet they may observe the proposal being executed and the associated funds disappearing or protocol parameters changing unexpectedly, violating the expected safety guarantees.

title: Last withdrawal can be DoSed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears when the contract enforces a minimum share threshold after every withdrawal. The contract contains a private check that requires the total supply of shares to be either zero or strictly greater than a constant MIN_SHARES equal to 1e18. When the vault holds only a single depositor, an attacker can front‑run the legitimate user’s final withdrawal by depositing a very small amount of tokens, causing the total supply after the user’s withdrawal to be non‑zero but smaller than the required minimum. The internal _checkMinShares function is called after the core withdrawal logic, so the transaction reverts with a MinSharesViolation error, preventing the user from receiving any assets. Because the attacker’s deposit is tiny, the cost of the attack is negligible, and the attacker can subsequently back‑run their own withdrawal, resetting the total supply to zero and allowing the check to pass for themselves while leaving the legitimate user permanently unable to withdraw. This scenario occurs only when the vault is about to become empty – i.e., when the last user attempts to withdraw all remaining shares. The affected parties are the end‑users who are the final withdrawers from the vault and any protocol that relies on the StakedUSDf contract for staking or liquidity provision. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the post‑withdrawal minimum‑share assertion as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the check is placed after the state‑changing withdrawal call, so the transaction appears to succeed until the revert, and the error message does not directly indicate a DoS condition. The impact is that an attacker can lock funds indefinitely without spending any significant amount of tokens, breaking the expected accounting invariant that users can always retrieve their deposited assets. To remediate the problem, the contract should either remove the minimum‑share validation on withdrawals or move the check to a point where it does not interfere with the final emptying of the vault, ensuring that a zero total supply is a valid and expected state after the last withdrawal. This class of bug falls under post‑condition checks that unintentionally prevent a contract from reaching a zero‑balance state, leading to fund‑locking or denial‑of‑service outcomes.

title: Shares cannot be minted on a deposit attack
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the initial‑state handling ofan ERC4626‑style vault that issues sUSDf shares for deposited USDf assets. The contract calculates the number of shares to mint using the formula assets * (totalSupply + 10**decimalsOffset) / (totalAssets + 1). When the vault is empty (totalSupply == 0) the expected behaviour is that the first depositor receives at least the minimum share amount (MIN_SHARES = 1e18). However, a malicious actor can bypass the public deposit function by transferring USDf tokens directly to the vault address before any legitimate deposit occurs. This direct transfer increases totalAssets while leaving totalSupply at zero. Subsequent calls to deposit trigger the share preview calculation with totalSupply still zero, producing a share amount that is less than MIN_SHARES. The internal _checkMinShares() guard then reverts with a ZeroAmount/MinSharesViolation error, preventing any further share minting. The attack therefore blocks legitimate users from receiving shares, makes the UI show no balance change or zero shares, and can render the vault unusable until the stray assets are manually swept. The issue was discovered during a security audit by testing edge‑case state transitions and noticing that a direct token transfer before the first deposit caused the previewDeposit() function to return zero. It is hard to notice because the contract follows the ERC4626 interface and the deposit function itself appears correct; the problem lies in the implicit assumption that totalSupply will never be zero when assets are present. The bug violates the accounting invariant that each deposited asset must correspond to a non‑zero share, breaking the expected one‑to‑one relationship between USDf and sUSDf. To remediate, the contract should detect the situation where totalSupply == 0 and any stray assets are present, and sweep those assets to a treasury before performing the deposit calculation, typically by overriding the public deposit() function and moving the assets out of the contract when the vault is still empty. This restores the invariant and prevents the share‑minting blockage.

title: M-13 Use general safeTransferFrom
description:
In commit e79ed7dddabc482c56f7828bd9a8725fbbeca2f5, it is required to check the success of the
transfer at the following lines:
• FantiumNFTV1.sol#L372
• FantiumNFTV1.sol#L380.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using a token transfer method that does not verify whether the transfer succeeded, specifically calling a low‑level transfer routine instead of the ERC‑721 safeTransferFrom function. The root cause is the omission of a success check after the call, which means the contract proceeds as if the token moved even when the underlying call returned false or reverted silently. An attacker can exploit this by sending a token to a malicious or non‑compliant contract that does not implement the ERC721Receiver interface; the transfer will fail, but because the caller does not inspect the return value, the contract records the token as transferred while the asset remains locked in the recipient address. The impact is that users may lose access to their NFTs, see their balances drop to zero, or experience refunds that never arrive, effectively causing funds to disappear from the expected holder. This condition occurs whenever the contract executes the transfer at the indicated lines, typically during minting, marketplace sales, or any internal token movement that relies on the unchecked call. All participants who interact with the NFT – owners, buyers, sellers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the system (that a successful transfer updates ownership) are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the code paths were examined and the lack of a require‑style check was noted. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the UI may simply show a successful operation while the token never appears in the recipient’s wallet. The proper remediation is to replace the unchecked transfer with the standard safeTransferFrom function, which includes an internal check that the recipient implements the required interface and reverts on failure, thereby guaranteeing that ownership changes only when the transfer truly succeeds. This class of bug falls under unchecked external calls or unsafe token transfers, a common source of asset loss in smart contracts. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a missing NFT after a purchase – the user expects to receive the token but the balance remains unchanged or shows zero, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The failure mode breaks the accounting logic of the protocol, allowing tokens to become irretrievable without additional recovery mechanisms.

title: M-2 Insufﬁcient constraint checks
description:
Insufﬁcient constraint checks increase the human error probability: a platform manager may enter
incorrect data and break the contract logic.
addCollection() (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L266):
• no zero address check for athleteAddress
• no constraint checks for athletePrimarySalesPercentage,
athleteSecondarySalesPercentage
No check for the collectionId existence:
• updateCollectionName (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L297)
• updateCollectionAthleteAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L308)
• toggleCollectionIsPaused (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L319)
• updateCollectionPrice (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L330)
• updateCollectionMaxInvocations (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L342)
• updateCollectionTier (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L353)
• updateCollectionBaseURI (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L366)
• updateCollectionAthleteName (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L378)
• updateCollectionAthletePrimaryMarketRoyaltyPercentage (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L397)
• updateCollectionAthleteSecondaryMarketRoyaltyPercentage (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L422)
No check maxInvocations < ONE_MILLION check:
• updateCollectionMaxInvocations (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L342)
No zero address check:
• updateCollectionAthleteAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L308)
• updateFantiumPrimarySaleAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L467)
• updateFantiumSecondarySaleAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L479)
• updateFantiumMinterAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L508)
• updateFantiumNFTAddress (FantiumMinterV1.sol#L322)
updateTiers (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L493):
• no check for _priceInWei > 0
• no check for maxInvocations < ONEMILLION
fantiumPrimarySalesAddress in getPrimaryRevenueSplits() (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L600) may be
zero. Consider setting it to a non-zero address in the contract's initializer so it is never zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a series of missing validation checks in the FantiumNFTV1 contract that allow a platform manager to supply malformed or out‑of‑range data when configuring collections. Functions such as addCollection do not verify that the supplied athlete address is non‑zero and they do not enforce that primary and secondary sales percentages fall within a sensible range, for example between 0 and 100 percent. Update functions that modify collection metadata—including name, athlete address, price, maximum invocations, tier information and base URI—do not first confirm that the provided collection identifier actually corresponds to an existing collection, meaning that an administrator could unintentionally or deliberately write to an uninitialized storage slot. Functions that adjust the maximum number of token invocations lack a check that the value stays below the global ONE_MILLION cap, and tier‑update logic does not require a positive price nor respect the same cap. Several address‑update functions also omit zero‑address checks, allowing critical payment or royalty destinations to be set to the burn address. Because these constraints are absent, a manager who enters incorrect data—whether by mistake or with malicious intent—can break the contract’s accounting logic. If a zero address is set for an athlete or for the primary or secondary sale receiver, royalty payments are sent to address(0) and effectively disappear, leaving creators without compensation. Over‑large percentage values or invocation limits can cause arithmetic overflow or exceed gas limits, potentially halting minting or causing unexpected reverts. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include missing or zero refunds, royalty payouts that never arrive, collections that appear paused or unresponsive despite correct inputs, and unexpected transaction failures. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where reviewers inspected each state‑changing function and noted the absence of require statements that enforce basic invariants. This class of bug is known as insufficient input validation or missing constraint checks, a common source of logic errors in smart contracts. To remediate, every external or onlyOwner function that accepts external parameters should include explicit require statements that reject the zero address, ensure percentage values are bounded between 0 and 100, verify that collection identifiers correspond to an existing collection, enforce that maxInvocations does not exceed the defined ONE_MILLION constant, and require non‑zero prices where appropriate. Adding these checks restores the intended business rules, prevents accidental loss of funds, and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations.

title: M-3 DefaultOperatorFiltererUpgradeable initializer is not called
description:
FantiumNFTV1 class inherits DefaultOperatorFiltererUpgradeable but it's initializer is not called together
with other base classes initializers in the initialize() method at FantiumNFTV1.sol#L168.
Due to this, the full functionality related to OperatorFilterRegistry becomes unavailable.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an upgradeable NFT contract that inherits a module responsible for enforcing operator filtering, but the module’s initializer is never invoked during the contract’s own initialization routine. In upgradeable patterns each parent contract that contains state variables or external registrations must have its initializer called explicitly; otherwise the internal storage that tracks the OperatorFilterRegistry address and the subscription to the default filter list remains unset. Because the DefaultOperatorFiltererUpgradeable initializer is omitted, the contract never registers itself with the OperatorFilterRegistry and the modifier that blocks disallowed operators is effectively a no‑op. An attacker can therefore use any address as an operator – for example a marketplace contract that does not honor royalty payments – to call transfer functions such as safeTransferFrom or approve without triggering the expected royalty enforcement checks. The impact is that creators and token holders may lose royalty revenue, and the protocol’s economic assumptions about fee collection are broken. This condition manifests after the contract is deployed and its initialize() function runs; any subsequent operator interaction will bypass the filter. The affected parties include NFT creators, buyers, and any downstream marketplace that relies on the filter to enforce royalty compliance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the initialization sequence was inspected and the missing call to DefaultOperatorFilterer_init() was noted. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and appears functional – token transfers succeed – yet the intended royalty‑blocking behavior is silently disabled, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual behavior that may only be observed when royalties are not received. The proper remediation is to add a call to DefaultOperatorFilterer_init() inside the contract’s initialize() method, ensuring it is executed before or after other base initializers according to the inheritance order, so that the registry address is stored and the operator filter logic becomes active. Conceptually this is a classic case of an uninitialized parent contract in an upgradeable inheritance hierarchy, resulting in disabled security‑critical functionality.

title: M-4 Unsafe Math
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe arithmetic operation performed without validation, specifically an unchecked subtraction that calculates the amount of funds to be collected for a primary sale. The contract assumes that the athlete revenue share is always less than or equal to the sale price, and therefore claims that the subtraction cannot underflow. However, the parameters that determine the athlete revenue share – such as the primary sales percentage, the price of the NFT, and the collection identifier – are not fully validated before the calculation. If an attacker or a misconfigured collection provides a revenue share that exceeds the price, the subtraction will underflow, wrapping around to a very large unsigned integer. This can be exploited by submitting a malicious collection configuration or by manipulating the price input, causing the contract to believe it has collected an enormous amount of funds, which may then be transferred to the attacker or cause accounting inconsistencies. The impact includes incorrect fund distribution, potential loss of legitimate revenue, and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees, effectively making funds disappear or be misallocated. The issue manifests whenever the unchecked block is executed with out‑of‑range parameters, which can happen during NFT minting or secondary sales that rely on the same revenue calculation. All participants who rely on correct revenue splits – buyers, athletes, and the platform – are affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of input validation and the presence of an unchecked arithmetic block. Because the code includes a comment asserting safety, the underflow may be overlooked during testing, especially since Solidity 0.8+ would normally revert on overflow, but the unchecked keyword disables this protection. To remediate, the subtraction should be performed with built‑in overflow checks (by removing the unchecked block) or by using a safe‑math library, and the inputs that influence the revenue share must be validated to ensure the athlete’s share never exceeds the sale price. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the platform never distributes more than it receives, restoring correct accounting and preventing funds from vanishing due to arithmetic wrap‑around.

title: M-5 Use transfer instead of call
description:
If the project work with other contracts is not implied, then the transfer method is safer (this forwards
2300 gas).
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract using a low‑level call to transfer Ether instead of the safer transfer method. Call forwards all remaining gas to the recipient, which means that if the destination address is a contract it can execute arbitrary code before the original function finishes. This creates a re‑entrancy window where a malicious contract can call back into the vulnerable contract, potentially repeating the Ether transfer or manipulating state before the original transaction’s effects are finalized. The root cause is the lack of gas limitation and the absence of a re‑entrancy guard or proper checks‑effects‑interactions ordering. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract with a fallback function that, upon receiving Ether via call, immediately invokes a function on the vulnerable contract that has not yet updated its internal balances, allowing the attacker to drain funds. The impact includes loss of user funds, unexpected zero balances after withdrawals, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, as refunds or payouts may disappear. The issue manifests whenever the contract sends Ether to an address that could be a contract and does not explicitly restrict the gas stipend or enforce re‑entrancy protection. Users, token holders, and the overall protocol are affected because the flaw can be triggered by any participant interacting with the payment function. The problem was identified during a security audit that highlighted the use of call without safeguards as a medium‑severity risk. It can be hard to notice because normal transactions to externally owned accounts succeed, and the call does not revert, so the contract appears to work correctly until a malicious contract is used. To remediate, the contract should replace call with transfer, which limits the gas to 2300 and prevents the callee from performing state‑changing operations, or alternatively employ a re‑entrancy guard, follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, or use call with an explicit low‑gas stipend and proper return‑value checks. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of re‑entrancy vulnerabilities caused by unrestricted external calls.

title: M-6 Broken operatorFilterRegistry may lead to DOS
description:
If the operatorFilterRegistry (OperatorFiltererUpgradeable.sol#L10) is broken and reverts on every
transaction, then all transfers with modifier onlyAllowedOperator
(OperatorFiltererUpgradeable.sol#L32) will be locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an immutable reference to an external Operator Filter Registry contract. The token contract stores the address of a registry (operatorFilterRegistry) and applies the onlyAllowedOperator modifier to every transfer function. The modifier forwards the caller address to the registry to check whether the operator is allowed. If the registry contract is broken, malicious, or simply reverts on any call, the modifier itself reverts, causing every transfer to fail. This situation arises because the token contract does not provide a mechanism for the platform manager or owner to update the registry address or to gracefully handle a failing registry call. Consequently, any user attempting to send, receive, or approve tokens experiences a generic transaction failure, often reported as “transfer failed” without a clear indication of the underlying cause. The impact is that all token holders are effectively locked out of moving their assets, which can halt trading, liquidity provision, and any downstream protocol functionality that relies on token transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the security team examined the onlyAllowedOperator modifier and noted that the external call is unchecked and the registry address is hard‑coded. It can be hard to notice because the revert originates from an external contract, making the error appear as a generic Solidity revert rather than a specific business‑logic violation. To remediate, the contract should allow an authorized manager to update the operatorFilterRegistry address, include a try/catch around the external call, or remove the dependency on an external registry altogether. By adding an admin‑controlled update path or fallback logic, the contract can avoid being permanently locked if the registry becomes unusable, restoring the expected behavior where users can transfer tokens as intended.

title: M-7 Wrong conditions in mint
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a logical condition error in the mint function of the FantiumMinterV1 contract.
