An attacker could deliberately set mismatched BPS values or modify maxInvocations during a payout, causing the arithmetic that determines each holder’s reward to produce an incorrect result. As a consequence, some token holders may receive less than their fair share, while others may receive more, or in extreme cases a holder may receive zero tokens despite the pool containing funds. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a distribution event has been executed and the total pool has been allocated, yet individual balances appear unexpectedly low or empty, violating the expectation that a claim returns the proportional reward. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of the distribution functions and identified missing cross‑contract consistency checks. It is hard to notice because the total amount transferred from the contract can still equal the intended pool size, masking the fact that the internal allocation per holder is wrong. The recommended remediation is to centralize the basis‑point parameters in the Claiming contract, add explicit arithmetic checks that recompute the expected distribution amount from the stored per‑collection shares, prevent changes to maxInvocations while a distribution is active, and persist the share values within each distribution event so that they cannot be altered retroactively. Implementing these safeguards restores the intended business logic that each token holder receives a fair and predictable portion of the rewards.

title: M-9 fantiumFeeBPS should be restricted
description:
fantiumFeeBPS should be <= 10_000, otherwise a claim call will always revert.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L242
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked configuration parameter that represents the fee expressed in basis points (fantiumFeeBPS). The contract assumes that this fee will never exceed 10,000 basis points, which corresponds to a 100 % fee, but it does not enforce this upper bound anywhere in the code. Because the claim function calculates the fee as amount * fantiumFeeBPS / 10,000, setting fantiumFeeBPS to a value greater than 10,000 makes the computed fee larger than the claimed amount. This causes the internal transfer or balance check to fail and the entire claim transaction to revert. The root cause is the missing validation of the fee parameter during contract initialization or any later update, allowing an administrator or attacker to set an out‑of‑range value. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker with permission to modify fantiumFeeBPS can set it to, for example, 20,000. After that, any user calling the claim function will experience a revert, receiving no tokens or refunds, effectively locking their funds in the contract. The impact is that legitimate claimants are unable to retrieve their assets, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol’s users and potentially eroding trust in the platform. The issue manifests whenever the fee parameter is set above the 10,000‑basis‑point threshold, which can happen during deployment, an upgrade, or an administrative fee change. All participants who rely on the claim functionality—individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because their expected outcome (receiving a claim payout) is replaced by a transaction failure and a zero‑balance UI indication. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that reviewed input validation and business‑logic constraints. It can be hard to notice in normal testing because typical fee values are well within the expected range, so the revert only appears under extreme, out‑of‑range configurations that may not be exercised in standard test suites. To remediate, the contract should enforce a hard ceiling on fantiumFeeBPS, for example by adding a require statement that checks fantiumFeeBPS <= 10,000 whenever the value is set or updated. This ensures that the fee calculation never exceeds the total amount, preserving the intended accounting logic and preventing claim‑revert scenarios. The bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or unchecked arithmetic constraints, which can lead to business‑logic violations such as “refund calculation error” or “funds disappear” when the fee exceeds the payable amount.

title: Some functions don't have deadline check
description:
The withdraw() function calls _decreaseLiquidity(), and the deposit() function calls _addLiquidity() and _createLiquidityPosition(). These internal functions set the deadline parameter to block.timestamp:  

Farms_audit.md  

```solidity
INonfungiblePositionManager.DecreaseLiquidityParams({
    tokenId: farm.lp.tokenId,
    liquidity: liquidity,
    amount0Min: minAmount0,
    amount1Min: minAmount1,
    deadline: block.timestamp
});
```

Without a deadline, pending transactions could be left open and later executed under conditions that are unfavorable to the user.  
Users have no way to enforce a time limit on their transactions, meaning their swap could be executed at an unexpected time, which may no longer be beneficial.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing deadline validation in the contract functions that handle liquidity deposits and withdrawals. The withdraw() function internally calls a decrease‑liquidity routine and the deposit() function calls add‑liquidity and create‑position routines, both of which construct a parameter structure that sets the deadline field to block.timestamp. Because the external functions do not expose a deadline argument, users cannot specify a maximum execution time for their transaction. Consequently, a transaction that is submitted to the mempool may remain pending for an arbitrary number of blocks before a miner includes it. When the transaction finally executes, the deadline value will be the current block timestamp, which may be far later than the moment the user intended to act. This opens the possibility for price‑sensitive operations—such as swaps or liquidity removal—to be executed under market conditions that have changed unfavourably, leading to a worse exchange rate, reduced withdrawn amounts, or even a complete loss of expected profit. The issue is a classic example of a time‑bound logic flaw where the contract assumes that the operation will be mined immediately, but the blockchain’s asynchronous nature makes that assumption unsafe. It affects any liquidity provider or trader interacting with the farm contract, because they rely on the contract to enforce the economic assumptions made at the time of submission. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the internal calls and noticed that the deadline parameter was hard‑coded to block.timestamp without any user‑controlled limit. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit any warning or revert when the transaction is delayed; from a UI perspective the user sees a normal transaction submission and later receives a swap result that is unexpectedly poor, or a withdrawal that returns less than anticipated, with no obvious indication that timing was the cause. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a deadline argument in the public deposit and withdraw functions, propagate that value to the internal parameter structures, and enforce that the supplied deadline is greater than the current block timestamp. This change restores the ability for users to bound the execution window and prevents miners or attackers from exploiting arbitrary delays.

title: Fee growth inside could overflow causing a function to revert
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow/underflow bug in the calculation of fee growth inside a Uniswap V3‑style liquidity position. The contract computes feeGrowthInside0X128 and feeGrowthInside1X128 by subtracting fee growth values that are stored outside the current tick range. In Solidity 0.8, which the contract uses, any subtraction that would result in a negative value triggers a runtime revert, whereas the original Uniswap V3 implementation compiled with Solidity 0.6 silently wrapped around on underflow. When the global fee growth is smaller than the sum of the lower and upper outside fee growth values – a situation that can occur after many fee accruals or when the pool’s fee counters wrap – the subtraction underflows, causing the function to revert. This revert propagates to any higher‑level operation that relies on feeGrowthInside, such as minting additional liquidity, collecting accrued fees, or burning a position. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a transaction that should claim or update fees fails with an out‑of‑gas‑like error, leaving the user with “no refund”, “balance stays unchanged”, or “position cannot be closed”. The impact is that liquidity providers may be unable to collect earned fees or withdraw their liquidity, effectively locking funds until the contract is upgraded or the bug is mitigated. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the code to the reference Uniswap V3 library and noted the change in compiler version. It is hard to notice because the arithmetic looks correct and only fails under specific fee‑growth conditions that may not be reproduced in simple tests. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic errors in financial accounting logic where wrap‑around semantics are assumed but not guaranteed by the language version. The proper fix is to perform the subtraction in an unchecked block or to restructure the accounting so that the subtraction cannot underflow, thereby preserving the original wrap‑around behavior while still ensuring correctness of fee distribution.

title: One of the intended functionalities of withdraw() does not work
bug_full: The contract FarmKeeper.sol implements a withdraw() function that is supposed to let a liquidity provider either remove a portion of their deposited liquidity or, when the liquidity argument is set to zero, simply collect any accrued incentive tokens and fee rewards while keeping their position unchanged. The NatSpec documentation explicitly states that passing a liquidity value of zero should trigger a fee and incentive claim without altering the user’s liquidity balance. In practice the function contains a guard clause that checks if the requested liquidity is greater than the user’s current amount or if the supplied liquidity equals zero, and reverts with InvalidLiquidityAmount when either condition is true. Because the second part of the condition (liquidity == 0) is always true for a zero‑withdrawal request, the function never reaches the reward‑distribution logic for that case. The root cause is a logical error in the input validation: the contract treats a zero‑liquidity request as invalid, contradicting the intended business rule. When a user attempts to call withdraw() with liquidity set to 0, the transaction fails, no fees or incentive tokens are transferred, and the user receives an error message. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a “withdraw” button that appears to work for positive amounts but silently rejects a zero‑amount request, leaving the user confused because the expected reward claim does not happen and no funds are returned. This bug does not directly expose funds to theft, but it creates functional friction: users who wish to harvest rewards without changing their position must instead perform a full withdrawal and a subsequent re‑deposit, incurring extra gas costs, possible price impact, and a more complex workflow. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the NatSpec comments were compared against the actual Solidity code and the validation logic was examined. It can be hard to notice because normal withdrawals succeed, and test suites often focus on positive liquidity values, leaving the zero‑liquidity path untested. The appropriate remediation is to relax the guard clause so that only a request exceeding the user’s available liquidity triggers a revert, i.e., replace the condition with if (user.liquidity < liquidity) revert InvalidLiquidityAmount();. This aligns the implementation with the documented behavior, allowing users to claim rewards without modifying their liquidity, restoring the intended user experience and eliminating unnecessary friction.

title: Some functions should be able to overflow
description:
TickMath.sol library is missing unchecked blocks, which causes it to incorrectly revert on phantom overflow. This library was taken from https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/main/contracts/libraries/TickMath.sol, but you can see solidity version is < 0.8.0, meaning that the execution didn't revert when the overflow was reached.  
This library is supposed to handle "phantom overflow" by allowing multiplication and division even when the intermediate value overflows 256 bits as documented by UniswapV3.  
In the original UniswapV3 code, unchecked is not used as solidity version is < 0.8.0, which does not revert on overflow.  
This library is used in many places in the protocol, so it is important that it is properly implemented, or it will lead to unintended results.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow handling error in the TickMath library, which is used throughout the protocol to convert between price ratios and tick values. The library was originally written for Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0, where overflow does not automatically cause a revert. In the audited code the compiler version is 0.8.x, where overflow triggers an exception unless the operation is placed inside an unchecked block. Because the functions getTickAtSqrtRatio and getSqrtRatioAtTick are not wrapped in unchecked, any intermediate multiplication or division that exceeds 256 bits causes the transaction to revert even though the Uniswap specification expects the overflow to be ignored (the so‑called phantom overflow). An attacker or even a regular user can trigger the bug by supplying extreme sqrtPriceX96 or tick values that make the intermediate product larger than 2^256‑1. When this occurs the contract aborts, the user receives a generic revert error, and no state changes are applied. From the user’s perspective the operation appears to fail silently – for example a swap, liquidity addition or price query returns nothing, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show a generic “transaction failed” message without indicating a math problem. The impact is medium because the bug only manifests for edge‑case inputs, but it can prevent legitimate high‑range operations and degrade the reliability of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the library against the reference Uniswap implementation and noticed the missing unchecked blocks. It is hard to notice because normal usage stays within safe numeric ranges, so the overflow condition is rarely exercised in routine tests. The proper fix is to wrap the bodies of the affected functions in an unchecked block, mirroring the implementation used by Uniswap for Solidity 0.8.x, thereby allowing the intended phantom overflow behavior and preventing unintended reverts. This class of bug falls under unchecked arithmetic misuse, where a developer assumes older compiler semantics and forgets to adapt the code for newer Solidity versions that enforce safe math by default.

title: _safeTransferToken() does not check the returned value of tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked return value from the ERC‑20 token transfer call inside the private _safeTransferToken function. The function decides whether to transfer the full balance or a requested amount and then invokes IERC20(token).transfer(to, amount) (or the balance) without verifying the boolean result that the ERC‑20 standard requires to indicate success. Because the contract does not require that the call returns true, it proceeds under the assumption that the tokens were moved even if the token contract returned false or reverted silently. This can happen with non‑standard ERC‑20 implementations, tokens that deliberately reject transfers, or when a rounding error causes the contract to have insufficient tokens. When the transfer fails, the contract’s internal accounting still records the deduction, leading to a mismatch between on‑chain balances and the contract’s state. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the transferred tokens – does not occur; the UI may show a successful transaction receipt while the user’s balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, and the farm may appear to have “missing” or “unclaimed” tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the absence of a require or SafeERC20 wrapper around the transfer call. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the blockchain explorer reports success, so developers may assume the transfer succeeded. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call results, specifically missing validation of ERC‑20 transfer return values, which violates the accounting invariants of the protocol. To remediate, the transfer should be wrapped with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer (or a require statement checking that the returned boolean is true), ensuring that any failure reverts the whole operation and keeps the contract’s state consistent.

title: Checks for solverCalledBack don't cover all situations
bug_full: The contract contains a conditional verification pattern around the solver callback flag that can be bypassed under certain configuration settings. In the function that orchestrates the solver lifecycle, a pre‑solver check asserts that the reconcile routine has not been executed before the PreSolver phase, and a post‑solver check asserts that the callback flag has been set before the PostSolver hook. Both assertions are guarded by config.needsPreSolver() and config.needsSolverPostCall() respectively. When either of these configuration flags is false, the corresponding check is omitted, meaning the contract no longer guarantees that reconcile() is called exactly once and at the correct stage. The root cause is the reliance on optional flags to enforce a critical state transition, rather than enforcing the callback invariant unconditionally. An attacker controlling a malicious solver contract can exploit this by deploying a solver that either skips the callback or triggers reconcile() multiple times when the checks are disabled, causing the internal _solverLock flag to be set incorrectly. This can lead to escrow funds being released prematurely, locked indefinitely, or double‑claimed, which manifests to end users as missing refunds, zero balances after a transaction, or funds that never become withdrawable. The issue appears only in configurations where the pre‑solver or post‑solver phases are disabled, making it easy to miss during testing that focuses on the default configuration where both flags are true. It was discovered during a manual security review that examined the control flow of solverMetaTryCatch and the lock‑state encoding in reconcile(). Because the checks are present but conditionally compiled, the bug can be subtle and may not trigger obvious revert messages; instead the protocol state diverges silently. To remediate, the conditional checks should be removed or replaced with a design that enforces the callback invariant regardless of configuration, such as restricting access to reconcile() to a specific phase via modifiers or a dedicated state machine, and ensuring that the _solverLock flag is only updated in a single, well‑defined location. This eliminates the possibility of bypassing the callback requirement and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the escrow system.

title: ChainlinkAtlasWrapper may break protocol integrations
description:
The ChainlinkAtlasWrapper is intended to be used by integrating protocols as a replacement for the original BASE_FEED Chainlink contract. There are currently two things that would make this integration difficult:
1. The latestRoundData() function does not maintain the behavior from the original Chainlink oracle. This function always returns the current roundId, startedAt, and answeredInRound from the BASE_FEED. This means that an oracle update in the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper will change the overall answer, but will not change the corresponding roundId. This implies that one roundId can have multiple answers, which is not possible in the original Chainlink contracts.
2. There are some functions missing in the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper.
For example, the decimals() and getRoundData() functions are commonly used by protocols, but do not exist in the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper does not preserve the round‑id semantics defined by the standard Chainlink AggregatorV2V3Interface and also omits several required view functions such as decimals() and getRoundData(). In the original Chainlink oracle each roundId uniquely identifies a single answer; the wrapper’s latestRoundData always returns the roundId, startedAt and answeredInRound from the underlying BASE_FEED regardless of how many times the answer is updated. Consequently a single roundId can be associated with multiple different answers. This breaks the assumption that roundId is a monotonic, unique identifier and can cause protocols that rely on the interface to mis‑interpret price data. The root cause is an incomplete wrapper implementation that forwards only a subset of the oracle state and fails to generate or propagate new round identifiers when the answer changes. An attacker does not need to exploit code execution; the bug can be triggered simply by the normal operation of the underlying feed updating its price. When the wrapper reports a new price, a downstream protocol that queries latestRoundData will receive the new answer but the same roundId as before; if the protocol stores the roundId to detect fresh data, it may consider the update stale and ignore it, or it may overwrite previous data under the same identifier, leading to accounting errors. Missing functions such as decimals() prevent callers from correctly scaling the answer, potentially causing the answer to be interpreted with an incorrect number of decimal places, which can make the reported price appear dramatically higher or lower. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a price that jumps unexpectedly, or a liquidation may occur even though the market price has not moved, and balances may appear to be reduced without an obvious cause. The issue affects any smart‑contract system that integrates the wrapper as a drop‑in replacement for a Chainlink feed – for example lending platforms, derivatives, or automated market makers – and consequently the end‑users of those protocols. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the wrapper’s public ABI against the official AggregatorV2V3Interface and observed that the round‑id handling deviated from the specification. Because the wrapper still compiles and returns seemingly valid data, the bug can be subtle and may only surface under edge‑case conditions such as rapid price updates. To remediate the issue the wrapper should either adopt the round‑id generation logic of the original Chainlink contract or expose the underlying feed’s round identifiers unchanged, ensuring that each answer is tied to a unique roundId. Additionally, the missing view functions (decimals(), getRoundData(), etc.) should be implemented to fully conform to the AggregatorV2V3Interface, and the contract should revert with “No data present” when appropriate rather than returning default zero values. Aligning the wrapper with the standard interface restores compatibility with existing integrations and prevents incorrect price handling that could otherwise lead to financial loss.

title: callIndex incremented twice
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract records the number of solver calls using an internal counter called callIndex. The counter is incremented once when a solver lock is obtained in the pure function holdSolverLock, which is the intended place for tracking each solver attempt. However, the same counter is incremented a second time at the end of the internal function _executeSolverOperation after a failed execution. Because _executeSolverOperation is invoked from within a for‑loop in either _bidFindingIteration or _bidKnownIteration, every iteration that does not immediately win the auction increments callIndex twice. This double increment shortens the effective range of callIndex, causing the loop to believe that the maximum number of allowed solver attempts has been reached after roughly half the expected number of iterations. In practice the protocol caps the number of solvers at 83, and the erroneous increment reduces the practical limit, preventing later solvers from being considered and potentially leaving an auction without a winner. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style degradation: users may see their auctions never resolve, bids appear to disappear, or the UI shows zero available solvers even though many are registered. The bug is triggered only when a solver operation fails and the surrounding loop continues, so it is not observable in successful paths and may remain hidden because callIndex is an internal bookkeeping field that is not exposed to external callers. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that traced the flow of callIndex and noticed the redundant ++key.callIndex statement inside _executeSolverOperation. Detecting the problem is difficult because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the state simply diverges from the intended accounting model, leading to subtle functional regressions. The correct remediation is to ensure that callIndex is incremented exactly once per solver attempt—either by removing the increment from _executeSolverOperation or by consolidating the increment logic and resetting the counter appropriately before each new iteration. By aligning the counter with the protocol’s business rule that each solver should consume a single callIndex slot, the contract will correctly honour the full set of solvers, restore expected auction outcomes, and eliminate the inadvertent limitation on solver participation.

title: Winning solver doesn't get gas costs _assign()ed
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract fails to call the internal cleanup function that assigns gas reimbursement when a solver successfully wins an auction. The root cause is an early return in _executeSolverOperation after setting key.solverSuccessful = true, which bypasses the call to _releaseSolverLock that performs the _assign of gas costs. An attacker or honest solver can be affected because the winning solver will not receive the expected gas reimbursement; the protocol assumes that every solver, whether successful or not, will have its gas costs accounted for via _releaseSolverLock. When the success branch returns before invoking this function, the gas spent on the successful operation remains unassigned, effectively disappearing from the solver's balance. This can be exploited by any participant that wins an auction: they will see the transaction succeed, but the ETH used for gas will not be refunded, leading to a net loss. The issue manifests only when result.executionSuccessful() evaluates to true; in failure paths the cleanup function is called correctly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Fastlane contract where the control flow was examined and the missing call identified. Because the function returns normally without reverting, there is no obvious error signal, making the problem easy to overlook. To fix the issue, the contract should ensure that _releaseSolverLock (or an equivalent gas‑reimbursement routine) is executed for both successful and unsuccessful solver outcomes, either by moving the call before the return, adding it after the return via a finally‑style pattern, or by refactoring the logic so that gas assignment cannot be skipped. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where every solver’s gas consumption is reimbursed, preserving economic incentives and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: claims accounting only tracks execution costs
description:
The claims storage variable records the ETH that will be reimbursed to the bundler for paying transaction fees. Currently, this value only tracks the difference between two calls to gasleft(), which implies that the bundler is only reimbursed for execution costs between two markers. However, there are other costs associated with being a bundler, for example, a base 21_000 gas cost for the entire transaction and an additional cost for each byte of calldata. To be more accurate, these costs could be added to the claims accounting.
It appears that this was already intended based on the following commented-out code:
```solidity
uint256 gasMarker = gasleft(); // + 21_000 + (msg.data.length * _CALLDATA_LENGTH_PREMIUM);
```
and also based on the fact that _releaseSolverLock() may charge some solvers for their calldata costs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the claim reimbursement logic of the Fastlane bundler contract. The contract records the amount of ETH to be reimbursed to a bundler by measuring the difference between two calls to gasleft() and using that value as the claim amount. This approach only captures the gas consumed by the contract’s internal execution between the two markers. It ignores the intrinsic transaction cost of 21,000 gas that is always charged for any Ethereum transaction and it also ignores the per‑byte calldata premium that is applied to the size of the calldata. As a result the bundler is reimbursed for only a subset of the total gas it actually pays. The root cause is the omission of these additional cost components from the claim calculation, a mistake that is evident from commented‑out code that intended to add 21,000 plus msg.data.length multiplied by a calldata premium. The bug can be exploited indirectly: a malicious actor can craft transactions with large calldata or trigger many bundler calls, increasing the unaccounted gas cost and causing the bundler to lose ETH on each claim. The impact is economic: bundlers receive less reimbursement than they spend, which can erode their incentives, lead to reduced participation, and potentially cause denial‑of‑service if bundlers stop operating. The condition occurs every time a bundler invokes the claim function, i.e., after executing a bundled transaction. Affected parties include the bundlers themselves, the protocol that relies on their service, and indirectly any users whose transactions depend on active bundlers. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that the claim accounting only used gasleft() and that there was commented‑out code meant to add the missing costs. Because the contract still reimburses some gas, the discrepancy is subtle and may only be visible as a slightly lower balance after each claim, making it hard to notice without detailed accounting analysis. The appropriate fix is to incorporate the base transaction gas and the calldata premium into the claim amount, for example by uncommenting the intended code or by explicitly adding those terms to the reimbursement calculation. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of under‑payment or accounting bugs where a smart contract fails to correctly account for all cost components, leading to systematic financial loss.

title: Incorrect SURCHARGE multiplication
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic mis‑calculation in the way the contract adds and later removes a surcharge on gas costs for a bundler. In the function that records the claimed amount, the code first computes the raw gas cost and then adds a surcharge by multiplying the raw amount by a SURCHARGE factor and dividing by 10_000_000. Later, when the contract settles the transaction, it calculates the unused gas, adds the same surcharge to that remainder, and subtracts the total from the claimed amount. Because the surcharge was applied twice – once when the claim was recorded and again when the remainder was subtracted – the variable that holds the final claim already contains the original gas cost plus the surcharge. The subsequent step that tries to extract the net surcharge mistakenly multiplies this combined value by the SURCHARGE again, effectively taking a percentage of a percentage. For a 10 % surcharge this results in taking 10 % of 110 % of the spent ETH, so the bundler is reimbursed only about 99 % of the amount they actually spent. The bug can be exploited simply by executing any transaction that triggers the settlement path; the bundler will consistently receive slightly less than they are owed, leading to a gradual loss of funds. The impact is financial: bundlers, who are expected to be compensated for the gas they front, receive an under‑payment, which may discourage participation and erode trust in the protocol’s fee model. The condition for the bug to appear is any non‑zero SURCHARGE value; the larger the surcharge, the larger the discrepancy. The affected parties are the bundlers themselves and, indirectly, any users relying on timely transaction inclusion. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the accounting logic of the settlement routine. It is hard to notice because the code appears to follow a reasonable pattern of “add surcharge, then subtract unused gas”, and the double‑counting only becomes evident when the final net surcharge is compared against the original gas cost. The class of bug is a double‑counting arithmetic error, often seen in fee‑calculation or rounding logic where a percentage is applied to a value that already includes that percentage. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the bundler’s balance after settlement is lower than expected – the bundler expects a full reimbursement plus the agreed surcharge but receives a slightly smaller amount, sometimes appearing as a missing or reduced refund. To fix the issue the contract should compute the net surcharge based on the original gas cost, not on the already‑surcharged claim. This can be achieved by dividing the surcharge factor by the sum of the base denominator and the surcharge (i.e., using (_claims * SURCHARGE) / (10_000_000 + SURCHARGE)) so that only the true surcharge portion is removed before the final transfer. The correction restores the intended accounting invariant that the bundler receives exactly the gas they spent plus the agreed surcharge, preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: Call to validateUserOp() won't work
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract’s internal _verifyUser function attempts to validate a smart‑contract wallet by calling the ERC‑4337 method validateUserOp on the address supplied in the UserOperation. The code assumes that a successful validation will return the integer 0 and that the call will succeed only when the wallet is an ERC‑4337 compatible account. In practice this assumption is flawed for several reasons. First, different versions of the EntryPoint contract (v0.6 and v0.7) define the UserOperation struct with different field layouts, so the data passed to validateUserOp does not match the expected format, causing the call to behave unpredictably. Second, most ERC‑4337 wallets restrict validateUserOp calls to originate from the EntryPoint contract; the current check does not enforce this, allowing any external caller to invoke the function. Third, a generic contract that implements a fallback function returning 0 for unknown selectors will satisfy the equality check (==0) even though it does not implement the ERC‑4337 validation logic. Because the call is made with a fixed gas limit of 30 000, the function may silently succeed or fail without propagating an error, further obscuring the problem. An attacker can therefore craft a minimal contract whose fallback returns 0, pass its address as userOp.from, and have _verifyUser treat it as a legitimate smart‑wallet. This bypass enables the attacker to submit user operations that appear to be authorized, potentially leading to unauthorized transfers, loss of funds, or execution of arbitrary logic under the guise of a valid wallet. The issue is subtle because the return value 0 is also the default for a fallback that does nothing, making the validation appear successful even when no real signature or nonce checks have been performed. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect external contract validation” or “trusting return values from untrusted contracts”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that operations that should be rejected (e.g., a transaction from an un‑approved wallet) are accepted, leading to unexpected balance changes or missing signature verification. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s expectations against the ERC‑4337 specification and observed the mismatch in EntryPoint versions and the permissive fallback behavior. To remediate, the contract should stop relying on validateUserOp’s return value and instead use a standard signature verification mechanism such as ERC‑1271.isValidSignature or OpenZeppelin’s SignatureChecker, enforce that validateUserOp can only be called by the official EntryPoint, and remove the hard‑coded gas limit. Proper interface checks and version‑aware handling of UserOperation structures will close the validation bypass and restore the intended security guarantees.

title: V2DAppControl allows both amount0Out and amount1Out to be non-zero
description:
```solidity
V2DAppControl assumes exactly one amount0Out and amount1Out is non-zero, but this isn't enforced. If both these values are non-zero, amount0In and amount1In are calculated incorrectly:
uint256 amount0In =
    amount1Out == 0 ? 0 : SwapMath.getAmountIn(amount1Out, uint256(token0Balance), uint256(token1Balance));
uint256 amount1In =
    amount0Out == 0 ? 0 : SwapMath.getAmountIn(amount0Out, uint256(token1Balance), uint256(token0Balance));
```
This calculation assumes that after the swap, the pool will only transfer out exactly one token.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swap logic of the V2DAppControl contract, which assumes that a swap will transfer out exactly one of the two pool tokens. The code calculates the amount of input tokens required (amount0In and amount1In) based on the condition that either amount0Out or amount1Out is zero. However, the contract does not enforce this exclusivity; it permits a caller to specify non‑zero values for both amount0Out and amount1Out in a single transaction. When both outputs are non‑zero, the conditional expressions used to compute amount0In and amount1In become incorrect because each branch assumes the opposite output is zero. Consequently, the pool’s accounting is mis‑computed: the contract may record an insufficient amount of input tokens while still sending out both output tokens, breaking the constant‑product invariant that underpins the automated market maker. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who crafts a swap request with both amount0Out and amount1Out set to non‑zero values, causing the pool to dispense more assets than the calculated input, effectively draining liquidity or creating arbitrage opportunities. The impact is that liquidity providers may lose funds, users may receive unexpected token amounts (e.g., receiving zero of the expected token or an extra token), and the protocol’s economic guarantees are violated. The issue manifests whenever the swap function is invoked with both output parameters non‑zero, a situation that typical unit tests may not cover because most swaps naturally involve a single output token. It was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the missing validation check. The bug is subtle because the code compiles and appears to work for normal swaps, making it easy to overlook without targeted testing of edge‑case inputs. To remediate, the contract should explicitly reject any swap where both amount0Out and amount1Out are non‑zero, typically by adding a require statement that enforces exactly one non‑zero output. This restores the intended accounting model, preserves the invariant, and prevents unintended token extraction.

title: ChainlinkAtlasWrapper allows retransmitting old reports
description: When transmit() is called on the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper, there is nothing checking that the report and corresponding signatures haven't been used before. While the transmitters are whitelisted and trusted to an extent, this behavior means a single bad actor can exploit the system (which is otherwise secured by multiple independent parties).
bug_full: The vulnerability in the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper contract is a replay weakness that allows an already‑published report to be retransmitted through the transmit() function. The root cause is the absence of any mechanism that records which reports have been processed or that enforces a strictly increasing identifier for each new report. Because transmit() does not verify that the supplied report and its accompanying signatures are unique, a whitelisted transmitter – even though it is trusted to submit data – can resend a previously signed report at any later time. An attacker can exploit this by taking a valid report that was signed by the required set of oracles, storing it, and later calling transmit() with the same data. The contract will accept the replayed report as if it were fresh, update the stored price or other state with stale information, and emit events that appear normal. From a user’s point of view the price feed may suddenly revert to an old price, causing downstream contracts that rely on the feed to make decisions based on outdated data; for example a lending protocol might liquidate a position or a trader might execute a swap at an unexpected rate, leading to loss of funds or failed transactions. The issue manifests whenever a trusted transmitter invokes transmit() with a report that has already been used, which can happen at any time after the original submission. It primarily affects any protocol or user that consumes the AtlasWrapper’s price data, including DeFi applications, automated market makers, and any smart contract that assumes the feed reflects the latest market conditions. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined the wrapper’s logic and noticed the lack of replay protection. Because the signatures are still valid and the transmitter is on the whitelist, the problem can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms; the contract’s state simply appears to update normally, making the regression hard to detect without explicit replay checks. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that each report can be processed only once, for example by storing a hash of processed reports or by requiring a monotonically increasing report identifier, similar to the design used in Chainlink’s BASE_FEED. This change would prevent stale data from being re‑introduced and restore confidence that the feed always reflects the most recent oracle consensus.

title: Solvers don't always reimburse the bundler
description:
In the Atlas system, bundlers pay gas fees upfront and are eventually reimbursed throughout the transaction flow. This is facilitated through the claims storage variable (which tracks the total amount due), the _releaseSolverLock() function (which assigns a reimbursement amount to a specific solver), and finally the _settle() function (which ensures that deposits >= withdrawals + claims).
While this system generally assigns costs fairly, there are two situations where reimbursements are not made as expected. Both situations are the result of an early return that skips a call to _releaseSolverLock(), even though the early return may be caused by a _PARTIAL_REFUND error (which is expected to result in a gas reimbursement).
The first location of this issue is in the _getBidAmount() function, where _releaseSolverLock() is only reached if all validation succeeds and the solverMetaTryCatch() call is made. Also, note that since there are situations where gas is charged, there seems to be a contradiction with the following comment in the function:
```solidity
// NOTE: To prevent a malicious bundler from aggressively collecting storage refunds,
// solvers should not be on the hook for any 'on chain bid finding' gas usage.
```
The second location of this issue is in the _executeSolverOperation() function, where an early return can happen if the _handleAltOpHash() logic fails.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission that prevents solvers from receiving the gas reimbursement they are owed when a transaction aborts early. In the Atlas protocol a bundler front‑loads gas costs and later credits the solver through a claim‑tracking variable and the internal function that releases the solver lock. The root cause is that several code paths return early – for example when the _getBidAmount() routine encounters a _PARTIAL_REFUND error or when the _executeSolverOperation() routine fails inside the _handleAltOpHash() logic – without invoking the _releaseSolverLock() routine that records the reimbursement. Because the claim update is skipped, the protocol’s final settlement check (which verifies that total deposits cover withdrawals plus outstanding claims) still passes, but the solver’s individual claim entry remains unchanged. An attacker controlling a bundler can therefore trigger these early returns deliberately, causing the solver to lose the gas it spent while the transaction otherwise appears successful. The impact is a loss of ether for the solver, a breach of the economic guarantees of the system, and a potential disincentive for honest solvers to participate. The issue manifests only under error conditions; under normal successful validation the reimbursement works as intended, making the bug hard to notice because the UI shows a completed transaction and no explicit error is reported. The affected parties are the solvers who submit bids, the bundlers who pay gas up front, and the overall protocol which relies on correct accounting to maintain trust. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that traced the flow of claim updates and identified the missing call to the reimbursement routine. To fix the problem the contract should ensure that any early‑return branch that originates from a solvable error first records the appropriate gas cost for the responsible solver, either by inserting a call to the lock‑release function before each return or by redesigning the gas‑allocation logic so that reimbursement is guaranteed regardless of where the execution aborts. This change restores the intended invariant that every gas expense incurred by a solver is eventually reimbursed, preserving the protocol’s economic model and preventing silent fund loss.

title: Simulation success may not guarantee on-chain success
description:
Before a bundler submits an Atlas transaction on-chain, they will simulate the transaction off-chain to ensure it succeeds. This will likely be done using the Simulator helper contract, or if the suggestion from the issue "Simulation code path can be kept off-chain" is taken, with some other off-chain method. Regardless of the approach taken, this is an important step of the Atlas process, since bundlers will waste ETH on gas costs if a transaction reverts.
It's important to note that there are situations where off-chain simulation success does not guarantee on-chain success. This is a known concern in systems like ERC4337, which handles this problem with a specific simulation procedure described in ERC7562. For example, this specification disallows certain sections of code from using opcodes that can easily trick simulation (e.g. TIMESTAMP and COINBASE).
In Atlas, there are a few locations where this may be a similar concern. This includes:
• If userOp.from is a smart contract, the _verifyUser() function calls the contract to verify the user's signature. If there aren't any restrictions on the contract's implementation, it may contain malicious logic designed to revert on-chain and waste the bundler's ETH.
• If all solverOps fail, either the UserNotFulfilled() revert happens, or the bundler is treated as the winning solver, and in either case, the bundler is not reimbursed for all gas fees. Since solverOps can contain arbitrary logic, they may revert on-chain even after a successful off-chain simulation.
• If any of the preOpsWrapper(), userWrapper(), or postOpsWrapper() functions revert, then the entire execute() call reverts and the bundler will not be reimbursed any gas. This implies that a userOp or DAppControl could grief the bundler if it's designed to trick simulation.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the reliance on off‑chain transaction simulation to guarantee that an Atlas transaction will succeed when submitted on‑chain. The root cause is that the simulation environment cannot faithfully reproduce all on‑chain state and execution conditions, especially when the transaction involves external contracts whose code may behave differently during a real block execution. For example, the verification step that calls a user contract to check a signature may succeed in the simulated environment but contain hidden logic that deliberately reverts when executed on the blockchain. Similarly, solver operations that appear to succeed during simulation can include arbitrary code that triggers a revert only under the exact gas, block timestamp, or miner address conditions present on‑chain. Wrapper functions that orchestrate pre‑operations, user‑operations, and post‑operations may also be crafted to pass simulation while causing a revert in the live environment, causing the entire execute call to fail. When such a revert occurs, the bundler that submitted the transaction pays the full gas cost without receiving the expected reimbursement, effectively losing ETH. This impact is felt by any entity that acts as a bundler, as well as by users whose transactions are not executed and by the protocol that assumes successful execution for accounting and incentive distribution. The issue manifests when a bundler performs an off‑chain simulation (typically via a helper contract or external tool) and proceeds to submit the transaction based on the positive result, only to see the transaction revert on‑chain. It was discovered during a security review of the Atlas protocol, where auditors identified that the simulation step does not enforce the same restrictions as ERC4337’s ERC7562 specification, which explicitly bans op‑codes like TIMESTAMP and COINBASE that can be used to manipulate simulation outcomes. The problem is subtle because a successful simulation gives a false sense of security; the revert may only be triggered by state that changes between simulation and inclusion, making it hard to detect without exhaustive on‑chain testing. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should consider adding safeguards such as restricting the set of op‑codes that external contracts can use during verification, implementing an on‑chain pre‑check that mirrors the simulation logic, or employing an off‑chain reputation/allowlist system that tracks the historical success rate of user contracts and solver operations. Conceptually, the fix involves ensuring that any code path that can cause a revert is either deterministic across simulation and execution or is explicitly validated before the bundler commits gas, thereby aligning the simulation guarantee with on‑chain reality and protecting bundlers from unexpected gas loss.

title: No quorum requirements for transmit() function
description: In order to transmit() a new oracle update to the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper, a transmitter provides the signatures of other whitelisted signers that are attesting to the oracle update. However, neither of the transmit() or verifyTransmitSigners() functions verify the amount of signatures submitted, and providing an empty array of signatures will technically succeed. This behavior changes the trust assumptions of the ChainlinkDAppControl since a transmitter has full control of each oracle update.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing quorum enforcement in the transmit() workflow of the ChainlinkAtlasWrapper. When a transmitter calls transmit() it is supposed to provide cryptographic signatures from a set of whitelisted signers that attest to the correctness of an oracle update. However, neither transmit() nor the internal verifyTransmitSigners() routine checks how many signatures are supplied. As a result, an empty array of signatures passes the verification step and the contract accepts the update as if it were fully signed. The root cause is a logic flaw: the code only validates the format of each signature but never asserts that the number of signatures matches the required quorum stored in verificationVars[baseChainlinkFeed].signers.length. An attacker who can act as a transmitter can therefore submit arbitrary price data without any signer endorsement. Exploitation is straightforward – the attacker calls transmit() with a crafted report and an empty rs/ss array; the contract treats the report as valid and propagates it to the ChainlinkDAppControl, which then trusts the falsified data. The impact is a breach of the trust model of the oracle system: downstream contracts that rely on the price feed may receive incorrect values, leading to unintended liquidations, loss of collateral, or manipulation of financial logic. This condition occurs every time transmit() is invoked, because the quorum check is absent regardless of the caller. All participants that depend on the oracle – users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that examined the signature verification flow and noticed that the length of the signature arrays was never compared to the expected number of signers. Because the function does not revert or emit an error when signatures are missing, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed through anomalous price movements or unexpected contract behavior. To remediate, the transmit() path should enforce a quorum by requiring that the number of supplied signatures equals the number of authorized signers, for example by adding a require(rs.length == verificationVars[baseChainlinkFeed].signers.length) check in verifyTransmitSigners() or an equivalent validation before accepting the report. This class of bug falls under missing access‑control or quorum enforcement, where a critical consensus check is omitted, allowing a single actor to override multi‑party validation. From a user perspective the symptom may appear as sudden, unexplained price spikes, zero refunds, or funds disappearing after a transaction that relied on the oracle, contradicting the expectation that the price feed is securely signed by multiple parties.

title: Solvers can be unfairly forced into gas refunds
description:
The EscrowBits library defines the circumstances when a solver is required to refund the bundler for gas costs. For example, the SolverOutcome.BidNotPaid flag is part of the _FULL_REFUND value, which means a solver needs to reimburse their gas usage if their solverOp fails due to an insufficient bid. Since these gas costs are forced on the solver, it's important that each error leading to reimbursement is actually something the solver is at fault for. This does not always seem to be the case currently, including the following:
• The SolverOutcome.DeadlinePassed flag is part of the _PARTIAL_REFUND value, although the timestamp when a solverOp is included on-chain is something the bundler controls. So, solvers are unnecessarily punished if the bundler includes their solverOp late.
• The SolverOutcome.GasPriceOverCap flag is part of the _PARTIAL_REFUND value, although the tx.gasprice is something in control of the bundler. So, if the bundler specifies an unreasonably large priority fee, the solver is ultimately punished for not accepting the price. This is also relevant to the SolverOutcome.GasPriceBelowUsers flag when allowsTrustedOpHash() == true, as the solver does not know the userOp.maxFeePerGas ahead of time.
• The SolverOutcome.PreSolverFailed flag is part of the _PARTIAL_REFUND value, although the failure of the preSolverCall() may be due to the DAppControl and not the solver. The SolverOutcome.EVMError similarly punishes the solver but may be caused by an error during the abi.decode() on the preSolverCall() return value (note: this is suggested to be removed in the issue titled "preSolverCall() can revert instead of returning false"). These are contrary to the fact that the SolverOutcome.AlteredControl error can also be caused by unexpected preSolverCall() behavior, but is a part of the _NO_REFUND category.
• The SolverOutcome.PerBlockLimit flag is part of the _PARTIAL_REFUND value, but solvers may not be able to prevent multiple of their solverOps executing in the same block. For example, if a solver interacts with a DAppControl with allowsTrustedOpHash() == true, they may not know exactly when their transactions will be executed on-chain, and may accidentally be included twice in a block.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the EscrowBits library that determines when a solver must reimburse a bundler for gas costs. Certain SolverOutcome flags – such as DeadlinePassed, GasPriceOverCap, GasPriceBelowUsers, PreSolverFailed, EVMError and PerBlockLimit – are currently classified under the _PARTIAL_REFUND category, which forces the solver to pay back gas even though the underlying conditions are controlled by the bundler or the DAppControl contract rather than the solver itself. This mismatch creates a situation where a solver can be unfairly penalised: the bundler can deliberately include a solver operation after the deadline, set an excessively high gas price, or cause a pre‑solver call to revert, all of which trigger the partial‑refund logic and make the solver lose the gas it spent. Because the refund logic is internal to the protocol, solvers typically see only the symptom – a transaction that reverts and a reduction in their balance – without an obvious indication that the loss is not their fault. The impact is economic loss for solvers, reduced incentive to participate, and a breach of the protocol’s intended accounting model where only solver‑controlled errors should result in reimbursement. The issue manifests whenever a solver operation fails and any of the aforementioned flags are set; it is especially pronounced when the bundler manipulates timestamps or gas price, or when the DAppControl’s pre‑solver call behaves unexpectedly. The affected parties are the solvers, who bear unexpected gas costs, and indirectly the users and the protocol’s reputation for fairness. The flaw was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that examined the logical mapping of error flags to refund categories. It is hard to notice because the refund mechanism does not surface in the UI and the loss appears as a generic transaction failure. To remediate, each error flag that is outside the solver’s control should be moved to the _NO_REFUND category, ensuring that solvers are only required to reimburse gas when the failure is directly attributable to their own actions, thereby aligning the refund logic with the business assumption that solvers should not be punished for bundler‑induced conditions.

title: _bidFindingIteration doesn't reset key.callIndex
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the escrow key structure (EscrowKey) is handled across two consecutive loops inside the auction routine. The key is passed as a memory argument to the helper function that calculates each solver's bid amount. Because memory structs are passed by reference, the helper function increments the key.callIndex field each time it is invoked. After the first loop finishes, key.callIndex equals the number of solver operations that were examined. The second loop, which executes the selected solver operations, re‑uses the same key instance without resetting callIndex. Consequently, the callIndex value continues to increase during the execution phase, potentially reaching two or three times the original solver count depending on the winning solver. Since callIndex is stored as a uint8, it overflows after 255, effectively limiting the number of solvers that can be processed to roughly 83 (or even fewer when the increment occurs multiple times). This overflow breaks the contract's accounting assumptions that each solver is invoked exactly once per phase, leading to incorrect solver selection, premature termination of the auction, or silent failure where a user’s bid appears to be accepted but no winner is recorded. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a bid was submitted, yet the auction result is empty, refunds are not issued, or balances remain unchanged, creating the impression that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that traced the flow of the EscrowKey struct and observed that its callIndex field was never restored between loops. It is subtle because the incrementing behaviour is legitimate in the first loop, and the overflow only manifests when the number of solvers approaches the uint8 ceiling, a condition that may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. The proper mitigation is to reset key.callIndex to its original value before entering the second loop, or to use a fresh EscrowKey instance for each phase, thereby preserving the intended one‑to‑one mapping between solvers and call indices. This class of bug falls under improper state reuse and integer overflow due to insufficient type width, which violates the protocol’s business logic that each solver operation must be accounted for exactly once.

title: atlasSolverCall() doesn't check caller
bug_full: AtlasSolverCall suffers from an improper access‑control pattern. The function receives an address parameter named sender and a modifier safetyFirst that requires sender == _owner. Because sender is supplied by the caller, the require statement validates a value that the attacker can choose, not the actual transaction origin. Consequently any external account can invoke atlasSolverCall and pass the owner address as the sender argument, bypassing the intended owner‑only restriction. The vulnerability can be exploited by constructing a transaction that calls atlasSolverCall with sender set to the contract’s owner, allowing the attacker to execute the privileged logic inside the function. Depending on the internal implementation, this may enable unauthorized state changes, fund transfers, or configuration updates, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The issue manifests whenever the function is called directly by an address other than the Atlas contract, because there is no check of msg.sender or of the calling contract’s identity. Users of the protocol may notice unexpected balance reductions, missing refunds, or other anomalous behavior that contradicts the expectation that only the Atlas contract can trigger the solver. The flaw was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the mismatch between the apparent require check and the actual source of authority. It is difficult to spot because the code contains a require statement that appears to enforce ownership, giving a false sense of safety. The correct mitigation is to remove the sender parameter and rely on msg.sender inside the modifier, or to restrict the function with a standard onlyOwner or onlyAtlas modifier that checks the real caller address. In general, this bug belongs to the class of authorization bypass vulnerabilities where user‑controlled inputs are mistakenly used for access control.

title: Circumvent AtlETH unbonding period
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw that allows bonded Ether to be released before the required unbonding period by manipulating the internal _assign function. The contract is designed to keep bonded ETH locked until a predefined delay expires, but _assign subtracts a specified amount from the caller’s bonded balance without checking whether that amount has already been borrowed after the validateBalances check. An attacker who controls all relevant roles – user, auctioneer, bundler, solver and DappControl – can first borrow Ether after validateBalances, then call _assign with an amount smaller than the total bonded balance. The function reduces the stored bonded balance by the borrowed amount while the attacker still retains the borrowed Ether, effectively freeing the funds that should remain locked. This can be exploited whenever the protocol permits a borrow operation followed by a call to _assign, which is typical during auction settlement or solver reward distribution. The impact is that the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken: bonded capital can be drained prematurely, undermining security, slashing mechanisms, and the trust model of the system. The issue occurs only when the attacker can combine multiple privileged roles and execute the borrow‑then‑assign sequence; otherwise normal users see no difference. It primarily affects the protocol itself and any participants relying on the integrity of the bonding mechanism, as well as the overall fund safety. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that traced the flow of balance updates and identified that the bonded field is decremented without a corresponding lock‑time check. Because the reduction happens inside an internal function and the UI still reports a normal unbonding request, the problem can be hard to notice – users may see their bonded balance drop unexpectedly while still receiving the borrowed Ether, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce the unbonding delay for any reduction of bonded Ether, prevent _assign from being called with borrowed amounts, or separate the accounting of borrowed and bonded funds so that a borrow operation cannot later be used to cheat the lock‑time invariant. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “premature release of locked assets due to improper state updates” and violates the accounting assumption that bonded capital cannot be spent until the unbonding period has elapsed.

title: Check with withdrawals in _borrow() is incorrect
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect balance verification in the internal _borrow function of the contract. The function checks whether address(this).balance is less than the sum of the requested amount, pending claims and the cumulative withdrawals variable. After the check passes, the withdrawals counter is increased by the requested amount and the function returns true. The external borrow function then transfers the requested ETH to the caller using SafeTransferLib.safeTransferETH. Because the transfer reduces the contract's ETH balance after the withdrawals variable has already been incremented, the subsequent balance check for a second borrow incorrectly includes the previously increased withdrawals value while the actual ETH balance has already been lowered by the previous transfer. This double‑counting makes the condition appear false even when the contract still holds sufficient ETH, causing legitimate borrow requests to be rejected with an InsufficientAtlETHBalance error. The root cause is the use of a mutable withdrawals accumulator in the same inequality that relies on the current contract balance, without accounting for the fact that the balance will be decreased by the external transfer. An attacker cannot directly steal funds, but the bug can be exploited to create a denial‑of‑service scenario where users are unable to borrow additional ETH despite available liquidity, leading to unexpected reverts and a perception that the protocol is under‑funded. The issue manifests when a user performs a first successful borrow that updates withdrawals, and then immediately attempts a second borrow that would be valid based on the remaining ETH but fails because the check adds the already‑recorded withdrawals to the amount. Users experience a mismatch between expectation (“I should be able to borrow more”) and reality (“the transaction reverts with insufficient balance”). The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the borrowing logic and identified the inconsistent accounting between withdrawals and balance. It is hard to notice because the initial check appears correct before the transfer, and the contract’s balance variable reflects the post‑transfer state only after the external call, obscuring the double counting. The recommended fix is to remove the withdrawals term from the balance comparison, checking only address(this).balance against amount plus claims, or to compute the available liquidity using a separate accounting variable that does not double count already‑withdrawn amounts. This classifies as an accounting or state‑invariant violation where the contract’s internal accounting does not match the external asset state, breaking business logic that assumes withdrawals are deducted from available liquidity only once.

title: Deadline check skipped in simulation mode
description: Deadline check for userOp and dAppOp is skipped in simulation mode. This shouldn't be the case as a successful simulation will lead to an onchain transaction which will then revert wasting gas for the bundler.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing deadline verification when a user operation (userOp) or a dApp operation (dAppOp) is executed in simulation mode. In normal execution the contract checks whether the supplied deadline field is non‑zero and, if the deadline has passed, rejects the operation with a specific error code. However, the conditional logic erroneously excludes the simulation flag, meaning that during a dry‑run the deadline test is bypassed. This occurs because the code uses a guard of the form `if (deadline != 0 && !isSimulation)` instead of simply `if (deadline != 0)`. As a result, a simulation can appear successful even when the operation’s deadline is already expired. When the bundler later submits the same operation on‑chain, the on‑chain execution reaches the deadline check, reverts the transaction, and the gas spent on the simulation and the subsequent on‑chain call is wasted. The impact is that users see a transaction reported as valid in the UI, but the on‑chain transaction fails, leading to lost gas fees for the bundler and potentially delayed or failed user experiences. The bug is triggered only when the operation is simulated before being broadcast, which is a common pattern for bundlers that pre‑validate user ops. All participants that rely on the simulation result – including end users, dApp developers, and the bundler service – are affected because they may assume the operation will succeed after a positive simulation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the validation flow and noticed that the deadline condition was gated by the simulation flag. It can be hard to notice because the simulation path often returns a success flag without performing the same checks as the on‑chain path, and the UI typically mirrors the simulation outcome. The fix is to remove the `!isSimulation` guard so that deadline validation runs unconditionally, ensuring that both simulation and on‑chain execution enforce the same temporal constraints. Conceptually, this is a class of validation‑inconsistency bugs where a safety check is omitted in a test or simulation environment, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual behavior and causing resource waste or denial‑of‑service effects.

title: amount is downcasted to uint112 without overflow protection
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an unsafe down‑casting of a 256‑bit unsigned integer (uint256) to a 112‑bit unsigned integer (uint112) in several core token functions. When a caller supplies an amount that exceeds the maximum value representable by uint112 (type(uint112).max), Solidity silently truncates the higher bits, keeping only the lower 112 bits. This truncation occurs in the internal _deduct routine, the transfer and transferFrom public methods, the unbond helper, and the internal _mint routine. Because the contract does not check that the supplied amount fits into uint112 before casting, the balance bookkeeping can become inconsistent: the sender’s balance may be reduced by the full 256‑bit amount while the recipient’s balance is increased only by the truncated 112‑bit value, or vice‑versa. Moreover, the Transfer and Unbond events are emitted with the original (potentially oversized) amount, which can mislead off‑chain indexers and users who rely on event data for balance displays. An attacker can exploit this by invoking transfer or transferFrom with an amount equal to type(uint112).max + 1 (or any larger value). The contract will accept the call, emit an event showing a huge transfer, but the internal balance update will use the truncated value, potentially allowing the attacker to bypass insufficient‑balance checks or cause a denial‑of‑service situation where balances become out‑of‑sync. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction appears to move a large amount of tokens (as shown in the UI or explorer) while the sender’s or receiver’s on‑chain balance either does not change as expected or becomes unexpectedly low, leading to confusion such as “my balance is zero after I sent tokens”. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the AtlEth.sol contract by the Spearbit audit team. It is hard to notice because Solidity does not raise an error on down‑casting; the truncation is silent and only manifests as accounting mismatches that may only be observed when unusually large amounts are used. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe numeric casts that cause overflow or truncation errors, violating the fundamental accounting invariant that the sum of all balances must equal totalSupply. The recommended remediation is to replace the raw cast with a safe conversion, for example using OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast.toUint112, or explicitly require that amount <= type(uint112).max before performing the cast, thereby ensuring that any oversized input causes a revert instead of silent data loss.

title: Solver bundler doesn't enforce exactly one solverOps
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked array access in the auction verification routine. The function that validates the auctioneer assumes that the list of solver operations (solverOps) always contains at least one element and directly reads solverOps[0]. When the protocol configuration permits zero solvers – a condition exposed by the allowsZeroSolvers() flag – the solverOps array can be empty. In that situation the direct index access triggers an out‑of‑bounds revert, causing the entire verification step to fail. This bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or array‑bounds checks, where a contract relies on an implicit invariant that is not programmatically enforced. An attacker or a mis‑configured deployment can trigger the revert simply by initiating an auction with a bundler that is also a solver but providing no solverOps entry. The exploit does not require malicious code; it only needs to invoke the auction flow under the permissive configuration. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate auction transactions revert, users see their transactions fail without obvious on‑chain error messages, and the auction never records, leaving users with the impression that nothing happened while their funds remain unchanged. From a user perspective the UI may show that the auction did not start, balances stay the same, or refunds are never issued, contradicting the expectation that an auction should be created and funds transferred. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the Fastlane codebase, where the auditor noted that the contract documentation states exactly one solverOps should exist when a solver acts as a bundler, yet the code does not enforce this rule. The problem can be subtle because the revert only occurs under a specific configuration flag, making it easy to miss in standard testing that assumes the invariant holds. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that solverOps.length equals one before any access to solverOps[0], ideally placed in the verifySolverOp() routine where solver operations are validated. Enforcing this invariant eliminates the out‑of‑bounds access, restores correct auctioneer verification, and prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: External calls may use more gas than gasLimit
description:
In the following case, .call copies the entire return data to memory even if it isn't used:
```solidity
(success,) = solverOp.solver.call{ gas: gasLimit, value: solverOp.value }(solverCallData);
```
Since this leads to memory expansion costs, this call may use significantly more gas than just the gasLimit value. The solverGasLimit is used in _validateSolverOperation() to ensure a solver has sufficient funds, so it's likely unexpected for this call to use extra gas. Although data isn't supposed to be returned in this call, it may be done intentionally by an adversarial solver to grief the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑consumption discrepancy caused by an external low‑level call that copies the full return data into memory even when the caller does not need any of that data. In the examined contract a solver is invoked with `solverOp.solver.call{gas: gasLimit, value: solverOp.value}(solverCallData)`. The caller supplies a fixed `gasLimit` that is intended to guarantee the callee cannot exceed a certain amount of gas, and the surrounding validation logic assumes the call will consume at most that amount. However, Solidity’s low‑level `call` automatically copies the entire returned byte array to memory before the caller can discard it. The cost of expanding memory to hold a large return payload is charged to the caller, so a malicious solver can deliberately return a huge data blob – a “return‑bomb” – causing the caller to spend significantly more gas than the declared limit. This extra gas consumption can push the transaction over the block gas limit or cause an out‑of‑gas revert, effectively griefing the protocol and potentially halting further operations. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition where users attempting to interact with the protocol may see their transactions fail, receive no expected outcome, or experience unexpected gas exhaustion, even though the protocol’s accounting logic believes the call is safely bounded. The issue manifests whenever the contract performs the described external call with an assumed “no‑return‑data” expectation, which is common in fast‑lane or solver‑based designs that validate solver gas limits before execution. The affected parties include the protocol itself, any users whose transactions rely on the solver, and any downstream contracts that depend on the successful completion of the call. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that examined the gas‑validation flow and noticed that the call’s return‑data handling was not constrained. It can be hard to notice because the transaction’s gas usage may appear to respect the supplied limit when measured before the memory copy, and the extra cost only appears at runtime when the callee returns a large payload.
