bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an inconsistency in how the contract determines the caller identity for privileged actions. The contract inherits OpenZeppelin's Context contract, which provides the _msgSender() helper to support meta‑transactions – transactions that are submitted by a relayer on behalf of an end‑user. By design, functions that rely on caller authentication should use _msgSender() so that the original user address is propagated through the relayer. However, the onlyDelegate and onlyFundApprover modifiers in the LoanVault contract directly reference msg.sender instead of _msgSender(). This root cause means that when a meta‑transaction is forwarded by a relayer, the modifiers see the relayer’s address rather than the intended user address, causing the access check to fail. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any legitimate user attempting to interact with the contract via a meta‑transaction will have their call rejected because the modifier’s condition is not satisfied. The impact is that the protocol’s intended support for meta‑transactions is effectively broken for the most critical functions, preventing delegated users, wallets, or gas‑sponsor services from performing actions such as delegating authority or approving fund transfers. This condition occurs whenever a function protected by onlyDelegate or onlyFundApprover is invoked through a meta‑transaction, i.e., when msg.sender is a relayer contract rather than the end‑user. Users who rely on relayer services will experience failed transactions, often seeing generic revert messages without a clear indication that the failure is due to an authentication mismatch. The affected parties include end‑users who expect to use meta‑transaction enabled wallets, integrators building on‑top of the protocol, and any delegators whose permissions are checked by these modifiers. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the contract’s use of OpenZeppelin Context against the actual modifier implementations, revealing the inconsistency. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and works correctly for direct calls; only when meta‑transactions are exercised does the bug surface, and typical unit tests may not cover this path. To remediate, the modifiers should be rewritten to call _msgSender() instead of msg.sender, thereby aligning the access control checks with the Context contract’s meta‑transaction semantics. Conceptually, this fixes the class of bug where authentication helpers are mixed with raw blockchain primitives, restoring the intended accounting that the original user is the authority, not the relayer, and re‑enabling the protocol’s meta‑transaction functionality without altering business logic.

title: Multiple centralization attack vectors are present in the protocol
description:
The protocol owner has privileges to control the funds in the protocol or the flow of them.
The mint function in FlorinToken is callable by the contract owner, which is FlorinTreasury, but FlorinTreasury has the transferFlorinTokenOwnership method. This makes it possible that the FlorinTreasury deployer to mint as many FlorinToken tokens to himself as he wants, on demand.
The withdraw method in FlorinStaking works so that the owner can move all of the staked florinToken tokens to any wallet, including his.
The setMDCperFLRperSecond method in FlorinStaking works so that the owner can stop the rewards at any time or unintentionally distribute them in an instant.
The method setFundingTokenChainLinkFeed allows the owner to set any address as the new Chainlink feed, so he can use an address that he controls and returns different prices based on rules he decided.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of privileged admin functions that give the protocol owner the ability to control token supply, withdraw staked assets, manipulate reward distribution and replace the price oracle at will. The root cause is that the contract design places minting rights, token‑ownership transfer, withdrawal of all staked tokens, reward‑rate adjustment and oracle address configuration under a single owner address without any timelock, multi‑sig or governance restriction. Because these functions are callable directly by the owner, an attacker who compromises the owner key or a malicious owner can exploit them by minting an arbitrary amount of the native token and assigning it to themselves, moving every user’s staked tokens to any address, setting the per‑second reward rate to zero or to an extreme value, and swapping the Chainlink feed for a malicious contract that returns fabricated prices. The impact includes inflation of the token supply, loss of user‑deposited funds, disappearance of expected staking rewards, and the ability to manipulate market‑price‑dependent logic, which together can erode user confidence and cause financial loss for token holders and stakers. The attack can be carried out at any time the owner decides to invoke the privileged methods, and it affects all participants who rely on the token’s economic model, the staking rewards, and the price feed. The issue was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the concentration of power in the owner role. It may be hard to notice because the functions appear standard and lack explicit access‑control warnings, and the UI may not surface the underlying changes until users observe missing rewards or empty balances. To remediate, the privileged capabilities should be removed or gated behind a timelock or decentralized governance mechanism, minting should be limited or eliminated, withdrawals should be restricted to the original staker, reward‑rate adjustments should be bounded and transparent, and the price‑oracle address should be immutable or upgradable only through a vetted governance process. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an admin‑centralization or privileged‑function risk, where the protocol’s business logic can be overridden by a single party, leading to fund disappearance, reward calculation errors and broken accounting assumptions.

title: Burned tokens can be re-minted into the totalSupply
description: The FlorenceFinanceMediciToken contract inherits from ERC20CappedUpgradeable and has a max supply limit of "1_000_000_000 * 10 ** 18" token units. The issue is that the contract also inherits from the ERC20BurnableUpgradeable contract, which means that when a user calls the burn method, the totalSupply will be subtracted from, meaning if 10 tokens existed and are all burned, but then 10 new tokens are minted, now totalSupply = 10 which is not the assumption that the protocol has, which is that the total supply of minted tokens can be maximum "1_000_000_000 * 10 ** 18".
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the combination of a capped ERC20 token implementation and an optional burn feature. The contract inherits a supply‑capping mechanism that checks the current totalSupply against a hard‑coded maximum during each mint operation. At the same time it inherits a burn function that reduces totalSupply when tokens are destroyed. Because the cap logic only looks at the current totalSupply, burning tokens effectively lowers the measured supply and opens up space for additional minting up to the original cap. An attacker who can call the burn function – either as a token holder or through a delegated role – can first destroy a portion of the existing supply and then invoke the mint function to create new tokens up to the cap again. This sequence allows the cumulative amount of tokens ever minted to exceed the intended one‑billion‑token limit, inflating the overall token pool. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after burning tokens the totalSupply drops as expected, but later new tokens appear, causing balances to increase unexpectedly and the promised fixed maximum supply to be violated. The impact includes dilution of existing holders, loss of confidence in the token’s economics, and potential financial loss for participants who relied on the capped supply invariant. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed with both the capped and burnable extensions and the burn function is publicly accessible. It was identified during a security audit that examined the inheritance hierarchy and the interaction between _mint and _burn logic. The problem is subtle because the cap appears to be enforced at each mint call, and burning is a standard ERC20 feature, so the violation of the supply invariant may not be obvious without tracing the cumulative supply over time. To remediate the flaw the contract should either remove the burnability feature, override the burn logic to prevent totalSupply from decreasing for cap calculations, or replace the simple cap check with a separate immutable maxSupply variable that never permits the total minted amount to exceed the original limit regardless of burns. This correction restores the guarantee that the token supply cannot surpass the defined maximum, preserving the intended economic model.

title: The Chainlink price feed's input is not properly validated
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the LoanVault contract obtains the exchange rate for a funding token from a Chainlink price feed. The contract calls latestRoundData() and only checks that the returned int256 exchangeRate is non‑zero, reverting otherwise. It does not verify that the price answer is recent nor that the value is positive. Because the price feed can become stale—e.g., if the oracle stops updating due to loss of data, network issues, or a deliberately halted aggregator—the contract may continue to use an outdated price for its share‑allocation calculations. When a stale or negative price is used, the arithmetic that determines how many vault shares a depositor receives, or how much collateral is required for a loan, becomes incorrect. An attacker who can cause the feed to stop updating, or who can submit a malicious round with a manipulated answer, can trigger the contract to compute a dramatically favorable exchange rate. This can lead to users receiving fewer shares than expected, borrowers being under‑collateralized, or the protocol losing funds when positions are liquidated based on the wrong price. The issue manifests only when the feed’s timestamp (updatedAt) is older than a reasonable freshness window (commonly one hour) or when the answer is negative, conditions that are not currently enforced. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be subtle: a depositor may see their balance unchanged after a deposit, a borrower may be able to withdraw more than they should, or the UI may display a price that looks correct while the underlying calculation is using an old value. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the getFundingTokenExchangeRate function and noted the absence of staleness checks. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit any warning when the price is outdated, and the Chainlink interface itself does not automatically reject stale data. The proper mitigation is to validate both the sign and the age of the oracle answer: reject or pause the contract if exchangeRate <= 0 or if block.timestamp - updatedAt exceeds a defined threshold (e.g., one hour). Implementing a pause mechanism or reverting the transaction prevents the protocol from proceeding with incorrect accounting, thereby preserving the intended economic guarantees.

title: Wrong usage of block's timestamp instead of block's number
description:
When code wants to get last block hash it uses blockhash(block.timestamp - 1):

```solidity
bytes32 pseudoRandomness =
    keccak256(abi.encode(blockhash(block.timestamp - 1), msg.sender, nonces[msg.sender])) >> 3;
```

But according to Solidity docs: blockhash(uint blockNumber) returns (bytes32): hash of the given block - only works for 256 most recent blocks. As a result blockhash(block.timestamp - 1) would be calculated for a nonexisting block and would always result in 0 so the pseudoRandomness would be more predictable and not according to the docs.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an incorrect use of the blockchain timestamp where the contract expects a block number to retrieve a recent block hash. The code calls blockhash(block.timestamp‑1) to obtain a pseudo‑random seed, but block.timestamp returns the current Unix time in seconds, not the sequential block number. Because the timestamp value does not correspond to any existing block, the blockhash function receives an out‑of‑range argument and, according to the Solidity specification, returns a value of zero for any block number older than the most recent 256 blocks or for non‑existent blocks. Consequently the pseudoRandomness variable is derived from a constant zero combined with the caller address and a stored nonce, making the resulting hash highly predictable. An attacker who knows the contract address, the caller address and the nonce can compute the exact pseudo‑random value before the transaction is mined, allowing manipulation of any logic that depends on this randomness, such as game outcomes, lottery draws, or reward distribution. The impact is that the contract’s intended fairness and security guarantees are broken; users may consistently lose or win, and the protocol can be drained or manipulated. This condition occurs every time the function that generates the pseudo‑random value is executed, because the faulty expression is evaluated on‑chain regardless of the surrounding logic. All participants who rely on the contract’s randomness – typically players, token holders, or any party receiving a reward – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor compared the code against the Solidity documentation and noticed the mismatch between block.timestamp and block.number. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without errors and the contract does not revert; the bug only manifests as an unexpected deterministic pattern in the output, which may not be obvious without systematic testing. To remediate, the contract should replace block.timestamp‑1 with block.number‑1 when calling blockhash, ensuring the hash is taken from a valid recent block. Even better, the contract should adopt a proven source of randomness such as Chainlink VRF or a commit‑reveal scheme, rather than relying on blockhash, which is only safe for a limited set of use‑cases. In user‑facing terms, a player might notice that the “random” result is always the same for identical inputs, leading to outcomes like always receiving zero reward or always winning, contrary to the expectation of a fair random draw. This bug belongs to the class of improper entropy sources and misuse of blockchain state variables, where a developer confuses timestamp with block number, resulting in predictable or null randomness and a breach of the contract’s business logic.

title: ToyBox.sol contract lacks discountTokens setter
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a price‑discount mechanism for token sales by reading a percentage from a mapping called discountTokens for primary sales and from saleTokenDiscounts for custom sales. The discount value is multiplied by the original price and divided by 10000 to obtain a basis‑point discount, which is then subtracted from the price. However, the contract does not provide any external function that can modify the discountTokens mapping. As a result, the mapping always contains its default value of zero for every payment token. When a user initiates a primary sale, the getFullPrice function reads a zero discount, leaves the price unchanged, and the user pays the full, undiscounted amount. The bug originates from the missing setter – a simple oversight in the contract’s administration interface – and it manifests only for primary sales because custom sales have explicit setter functions (setSaleTokenDiscounts and setSaleTokenDiscount). The vulnerability is discovered during a manual audit that compared the UI‑displayed discount information with the on‑chain price calculation and noticed that the discount was never applied. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still show a discount label, and the price calculation code appears correct at a glance; the problem lies in the inability to actually store a non‑zero discount. The impact is a business‑logic failure: buyers expect to receive a reduced price but are overcharged, leading to potential loss of trust, reduced sales volume, and inaccurate revenue accounting. The issue affects any user purchasing through the primarySale or primarySaleWithPermit functions, as well as the protocol’s economic model that assumes discounts will be honored. To remediate, the contract should either expose a setter function that allows the sale manager to update discountTokens for each payment token, or remove the discount calculation step from the primary‑sale path if discounts are not intended for that sale type. Either approach restores consistency between the advertised discount policy and the actual amount transferred, fixing the accounting discrepancy and aligning user expectations with on‑chain behavior.

title: Excessive msg.value lost when creating an offer
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an input validation flaw in the function that creates a new ETH offer. The contract calculates the exact amount of collateral or value that must be supplied for the offer and then checks that the amount of ether sent with the transaction (msg.value) is greater than or equal to this required amount. Because the check uses a greater‑or‑equal comparison, any excess ether that a user includes in the transaction is accepted without being rejected or refunded. This means that if a user, a trading UI, or any external tool mistakenly includes more ether than necessary, the surplus is silently retained by the contract. The root cause is the use of a non‑strict inequality (>=) instead of an exact equality (==) or a refund mechanism, which constitutes an over‑payment or unchecked value handling bug. An attacker could deliberately send a large msg.value to lock unintended funds in the contract, potentially disrupting accounting, inflating the contract’s balance, or creating a denial‑of‑service condition for other users. The impact is that honest users may see a reduction in their wallet balance that does not correspond to the intended offer amount, leading to lost funds and a mismatch between expected and actual balances. The issue manifests whenever the newOfferETH function is invoked with a msg.value that exceeds the calculated collateral or value, which can happen due to user error, buggy front‑end software, or malicious intent. The affected parties are the users who create offers, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream components that rely on accurate ether accounting. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the require statement and identified that the condition permits overpayment. It can be difficult to notice because the contract does not emit any warning or event about the surplus, and the UI may simply display the intended amount without indicating that more ether was actually transferred. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce an exact match between the required amount and msg.value, or alternatively implement logic that automatically refunds any excess ether back to the sender. This change aligns the implementation with the business rule that an offer must be funded precisely, preserving user funds and maintaining correct accounting throughout the protocol.

title: ETH transfer griefing
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An ETH transfer griefing vulnerability exists in the function that refunds ETH to buyer and seller using a direct low‑level call. The contract attempts to send Ether with (bool success,) = recipient.call{value: amount}(''). If the recipient is a contract whose fallback or receive function reverts, or if the recipient is maliciously crafted to revert, the call returns false and the subsequent require aborts the whole transaction. Because the refund logic is executed inline during order cancellation, a single revert prevents both parties from receiving any of their entitled refunds. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition where either participant can block the other’s refund by deploying a contract that rejects ETH or by deliberately reverting the call. The impact is that funds become locked in the market contract, users see their balances unchanged, refunds appear to be missing, and the protocol may be blackmailed to release the funds. The issue manifests whenever an order involving ETH (exToken == address(0)) is cancelled or settled and the contract tries to transfer ETH directly. Both regular externally owned accounts are safe, but any contract participant can trigger the griefing. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the refund code path and noted the use of a direct call without a pull‑payment fallback. It is subtle because the failure surface is a generic “Transfer Funds to Seller Fail” revert, which does not indicate which side caused the revert, and the contract does not keep a record of pending withdrawals, making the stuck funds hard to trace. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unsafe external call” or “griefable transfer” bugs where the contract pushes Ether to an arbitrary address without handling failures. The correct mitigation is to replace the push pattern with a pull pattern: record the amount owed to each participant in a mapping and let them withdraw it via a separate claim function, ensuring that a failing recipient does not affect other transfers. This approach should be applied to all ETH transfers in the contract, including settleFilled, settle2Steps, and cancelOffer, to guarantee that refunds cannot be blocked and that users receive the expected funds rather than seeing zero or missing balances.

title: Approval in BaseVault reduces over time
description: BaseVault stores users allowances as underlying assets allowances. When a user calls, for example, approve(...), it converts the shares amount in the argument to a corresponding asset amount. This approach means that, over time, due to the value of shares increasing over time (yield from providers), the same amount of shares will be worth more assets. Thus, if users approve a certain allowance, and then a few seconds later, another user tries to use this same allowance amount, it should revert, as this shares amount now equals more assets. The BorrowingVault does not have this issue because it never converts between debt and debtShares and the allowance is stored in debt. Thus, if a user approves another user for, let's say, 100 debt, the other user can always spend 100 debt.
poc: no poc/POCFaillingApproval.t.sol#L32/POCFaillingApproval.t.sol#L32
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way BaseVault records token allowances. When a user calls approve, the contract converts the supplied share amount into an equivalent amount of the underlying asset and stores that asset value as the allowance. Because the vault’s share price increases over time as yield accrues, the same number of shares represents a larger amount of the underlying asset later on. Consequently, an allowance that was sufficient at the moment of approval may become insufficient a short time after, causing any subsequent transfer that tries to consume the originally approved share amount to revert. This problem is a classic case of allowance drift caused by storing a value that is not invariant with respect to the protocol’s accounting model. It occurs whenever the vault’s share‑to‑asset conversion rate changes, which is the normal operation of yield‑generating vaults. Users who have granted permission to another address may see transactions fail unexpectedly, experience “insufficient allowance” errors, or notice that their approved balance appears to have vanished. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the allowance handling logic and compared it with the ERC4626 reference implementation, which stores allowances in shares rather than assets. The bug is subtle because the allowance looks correct at the time of approval; only after the share price moves does the mismatch surface, making it easy to miss during functional testing. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service or user‑experience problem: approved spenders cannot reliably use the permission, potentially breaking integrations that rely on stable allowances. To remediate the issue, the contract should store allowances in share units, matching the ERC4626 OpenZeppelin reference, so that the allowance value remains constant regardless of yield accrual. This change eliminates the conversion drift and restores the expected behavior where an approved amount can be spent at any later time without unexpected reverts.

title: BaseFlasher transfers tokens and then calls xBundle(...), so the sent tokens can't be returned due to the balance check
description: The BaseRouter checks if the balances of the assets remain the same after the xBundle(...) execution. The BaseFlasher, _requestorExecution(...) is implemented in the following way IERC20(asset).safeTransfer(requestor, amount); requestor.functionCall(requestorCalldata); // approve flashloan source address to spend to repay flashloan IERC20(asset).safeApprove(getFlashloanSourceAddr(asset), amount + fee); Thus, when xBundle(...) is called in requestor.functionCall(requestorCalldata);, the initial balance of the BaseRouter will take into account the received funds from the flashloan, such that it will be impossible to return the funds at the end of the call.
poc: no poc/POCCantUseFlashloanFunds.t.sol#L97/POCCantUseFlashloanFunds.t.sol#L97
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the BaseFlasher contract that implements a flash‑loan style workflow. After receiving the borrowed asset, BaseFlasher immediately transfers the requested amount to the caller (the requestor) using safeTransfer and then invokes an arbitrary calldata supplied by the requestor. The requestor’s calldata may call the router’s xBundle function, which expects the router’s token balance to be unchanged after the external call. Because the transfer to the requestor occurs before the external call, the router’s balance at the moment the xBundle check is performed already includes the borrowed tokens. If the requestor’s calldata moves any of those tokens (for example by swapping them inside xBundle), the router’s balance will be lower than the recorded pre‑call balance, causing the balance‑verification logic to fail. As a result the router cannot return the borrowed amount plus fee, effectively locking the funds or causing the flash‑loan transaction to revert. The root cause is a classic check‑effects‑interaction ordering error: the contract checks the balance after it has already altered its own token holdings and after an untrusted external call, allowing the external code to manipulate the balance before the check. The issue manifests whenever BaseFlasher’s _requestorExecution path is used with a requestor that performs any token‑moving operation during the supplied calldata, such as calling xBundle. All participants that rely on the flash‑loan service – the requestor, the flash‑loan provider, and any downstream protocol – are affected because the expected repayment may never happen. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noticed that the balance‑check logic does not account for the fact that the router’s balance already includes the transferred amount before the external call. It is easy to miss because the contract’s state appears correct at the start of the transaction and the failure only surfaces after the external call, making the bug subtle and not obvious from simple unit tests. To remediate, the contract should either move the external call before the token transfer (following the check‑effects‑interaction pattern) or adopt a callback mechanism similar to ConnextRouter’s xReceive, where the router records the balance, invokes the external logic, and only then performs the repayment step. Whitelisting trusted callers for the flash‑loan receive function is another mitigation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a flash‑loan the UI may show the transaction succeeded but the user’s balance is reduced or the expected refund is missing, effectively “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error”. This class of bug is generally known as a balance‑check bypass caused by improper ordering of state changes and external calls, violating the accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: _crossTransfer(...) reverts for smart contracts that don't share the same address on different chains
description: _crossTransfer(...) has a beneficiary check such that the receiver of the funds in the destination chain must be the same as the previous beneficiary (most likely the msg.sender or the ConnextRouter). If the address is a smart contract, the address will probably be different on the different chain, which will make the transaction revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the cross‑chain transfer routine, specifically the internal _crossTransfer function, which enforces a strict beneficiary equality check. The routine requires that the address designated to receive funds on the destination chain be identical to the address that acted as the beneficiary on the source chain, typically the msg.sender or the ConnextRouter contract. This assumption holds for externally owned accounts because the same private key generates the same address on every EVM‑compatible chain, but it fails for smart contracts whose deployment address is derived from the deploying chain’s nonce and therefore differs across chains. When a user attempts to send funds to a contract on another domain, the equality check fails, causing the transaction to revert. The root cause is the hard‑coded comparison of source and destination beneficiary addresses without accounting for cross‑chain address variance. Exploitation is straightforward: any cross‑chain transfer that designates a contract as the recipient will automatically revert, effectively denying service to that class of transfers. The impact is that legitimate users cannot receive funds in contracts on other chains, leading to a user‑facing symptom where a transfer appears to succeed on the source side but the destination transaction reverts, leaving the user with no received funds and potentially a failed transaction fee. This condition occurs whenever the beneficiary is a contract and the destination domain is different from the source domain. The affected parties include end‑users who intend to move assets into contract wallets, protocol developers relying on automated cross‑chain payouts, and any role that expects seamless inter‑chain fund routing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain logic, where the auditor noted the beneficiary equality assertion and recognized that contract addresses are not portable across chains. The problem can be subtle because a revert may be interpreted as a generic network error rather than a logic flaw, and there is no explicit warning that contract beneficiaries are unsupported. To remediate, the contract should decouple the source and destination beneficiary identities and allow callers to register a mapping of source address to a distinct destination beneficiary per domain, for example via an addBeneficiaryToDestDomain function that stores beneficiary[msg.sender][destDomain] = newBeneficiary. This change aligns the implementation with the business expectation that users can specify any address on the target chain, restoring the intended cross‑chain accounting behavior and preventing unnecessary transaction failures.

title: ConnextRouter fails to record failed message if gas sent is not enough
description: The ConnextRouter places the xBundleConnext(...) call on a try/catch block to prevent failed actions to make the transaction revert and the funds being given to Connext. The EVM saves 1/64th of gas before an external call to try to finish execution after the external call. However, if the xBundleConnext(...) transaction inside the try/catch fails, the following execution consumes a non significant amount of gas (transferring and recording the failed message), such that 1/64 of the sent gas could not be enough to finish the execution.
poc: no poc/POCXReceiveGas.t.sol#L34/POCXReceiveGas.t.sol#L34
bug_full: The vulnerability in the ConnextRouter contract is a gas‑shortage failure that prevents the router from recording a message when an external call to xBundleConnext reverts. The contract wraps the external call in a try/catch block so that a failure does not revert the whole transaction and the funds are not automatically transferred to Connext. The EVM, however, reserves only one sixty‑fourth of the remaining gas before performing an external call (the so‑called gas stipend). If the xBundleConnext call runs out of gas or otherwise fails, the catch block must still execute code that transfers the funds back and writes a failed‑message record to storage. This post‑call logic consumes a non‑trivial amount of gas, and because the contract does not check how much gas will be left after the external call, the remaining gas can be lower than the required amount. Consequently the catch block runs out of gas, the transaction finishes without reverting, but the failed message is never recorded. The root cause is the reliance on the implicit 1/64 gas stipend without an explicit gasleft check, combined with the assumption that the catch block will always have enough gas to complete. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the failure by sending a transaction with a gas limit that is just enough for the external call but insufficient for the catch logic, or by crafting a payload that forces the external call to consume most of the gas. When this occurs, the protocol’s accounting is broken: the user expects the cross‑chain message to be logged as failed and possibly refunded, but the UI shows no error, no event is emitted, and the funds may appear to be locked or disappear. The issue is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; only the missing failed‑message record reveals the problem during later audits or when users report missing refunds. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient gas for post‑call cleanup” or “catch‑block out‑of‑gas” vulnerabilities, which violate the business logic that every failed cross‑chain operation must be recorded for later reconciliation. To remediate, the contract should calculate the minimum gas required to finish the catch block before invoking the external call, using gasleft() to ensure enough gas remains, and revert early if the gas budget is insufficient. Alternatively, the recording of the failure could be moved before the external call or the gas stipend increased, guaranteeing that the failure state is always persisted regardless of the external call outcome.

title: Users can claim tokens in ConnextRouter by calling xReceive(...) directly
description: The ConnextRouter allows anyone to call xReceive(...) and the amount of assets the user provided is the balance of the contract. Thus, users can use this functionality to sweep any existing funds into their wallets. In fact, this should also happen when a xReceive(...) call fails at this.xBundleConnext(...), and the balance, including the existing tokens, get attributed to the user. It should not be a likely event given that there are checks to ensure that the ConnextRouter does not end up with funds after xBundle(...) calls. Still, given that the BaseRouter has a sweepTokens(...) function, this might lead to a false sense of security.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ConnextRouter contract where the function xReceive is publicly callable without any access restriction. The implementation determines the amount of tokens to transfer based on the current balance of the contract, assuming that the caller is the authorized xConnect address that initiated a cross‑chain transfer. Because there is no verification of the caller’s identity, any external account can invoke xReceive directly. When invoked, the router sends the entire token balance it holds to the caller, effectively allowing an attacker to sweep all existing funds, including assets deposited by other users. A similar issue appears in the error‑handling path: if the internal call this.xBundleConnext fails, the contract attributes the full contract balance to the user instead of the intended amount, again exposing all tokens to the caller. This flaw is a classic case of missing access control combined with improper use of the contract’s balance as the transfer amount. It can be exploited simply by submitting a transaction that calls xReceive with arbitrary parameters; the router will then transfer its whole token holdings to the attacker’s address. The impact is the loss of user funds stored in the router, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential financial damage to token holders. The condition for exploitation is that the router holds any tokens – which is typical after normal cross‑chain operations – and that an attacker can send a transaction to the router. All users who have deposited tokens through ConnextRouter are affected because their balances can be drained without consent. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the router’s public interface and noticed that xReceive lacks any modifier restricting its caller, and that the fallback logic on failure incorrectly uses the contract balance. The problem may be hard to notice because the normal workflow expects xReceive to be invoked only by the internal xConnect component, and tests may not cover arbitrary external calls; additionally, the presence of a sweepTokens function in the BaseRouter can give a false sense of security that only the contract owner can move assets. To remediate, the router should enforce that only the designated xConnect address can call xReceive, typically by adding an onlyAuthorized modifier or checking msg.sender against a stored authorized address. Moreover, when this.xBundleConnext fails, the contract should revert the transaction or return only the originally intended amount rather than the full balance, preventing accidental asset leakage. Implementing proper access control and correcting the failure handling will align the contract’s behavior with its intended accounting model, ensuring that users receive the correct amount and that no unauthorized sweep of tokens can occur.

title: Connext delegates can perform important actions, make sure smart contract users implement them
description: Connext implements a mechanism of adjusting/forcing parameters in the bridged assets which can be triggered by a delegate. If the delegate is a EOA or wallet, there is no problem, as the delegate can call directly the connext bridge. However, care must be taken if the caller of xBundle(...) is a smart contract, in which it may not implement the necessary Connext function calls. This can be dangerous if the smart contract user set, for example, a low slippage tolerance and did not implement the function forceUpdateSlippage(...) of the connext bridge.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the delegate pattern used by the Connext bridge, where a designated address (the delegate) is allowed to invoke privileged functions that adjust critical parameters of a cross‑chain transfer. When a user interacts with the bridge through a smart contract that calls the xBundle function, the contract must forward certain callback calls such as forceUpdateSlippage or bumpTransfer to the Connext router. If the calling contract does not implement these callbacks, the delegate loses the ability to enforce the user‑specified limits, for example a low slippage tolerance. The root cause is the absence of required interface methods in the caller contract, combined with the bridge assuming that any delegate will correctly forward the calls. An attacker or a misbehaving bridge can therefore execute a transfer with a higher slippage than the user intended, because the contract cannot reject or adjust the transfer after the fact. The impact is that users may receive fewer assets than expected, experience unexpected price impact, or even lose value if the market moves unfavorably during the delayed enforcement. This situation occurs whenever a smart‑contract wallet or protocol integrates Connext via xBundle without explicitly implementing the Connext router functions. The affected parties are end‑users who rely on slippage protection, as well as the protocols that embed Connext for cross‑chain liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected delegate responsibilities with the actual contract code and identified missing method implementations. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and emit no error, while the slippage protection silently fails, leading to subtle financial loss. To remediate, the caller contract should either inherit from or explicitly implement the required Connext interface methods (e.g., forceUpdateSlippage, bumpTransfer) and set the ConnextRouter as the delegate, or the documentation should clearly warn developers that these callbacks are mandatory for contracts. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that any contract acting as a delegate fully complies with the bridge’s callback contract, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing funds from disappearing due to unchecked slippage adjustments.

title: BorrowingVault, if the debt/assets ratio falls too much, liquidators could choose to repay debt equal to the assets at a discount
description: Currently the borrowing vault enables liquidating a user's position 50% if the debt/assets ratio is above liqRatio, but below liqRatio / FULL_LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD. If the ratio debt/assets increases too much, a liquidation might not be profitable for liquidators, because users might not have enough assets. In this scenario, it could be possible to completely close the user position by paying back the debt corresponding to the assets of the user. This will still leave some amount of bad debt, but hopefully much less. In the current implementation, if a specific collateral asset drops too much, it could happen that many liquidations would not be profitable and a lot of bad debt would appear. This bad debt could be limited with this recommendation. In the end, it could prevent a liquidation in a provider. Example: 75 debt, 100 assets asset/debt value falls to 0.74 paying 75 debt, would give the liquidator 100 assets, which is equivalent to 74 debt at 0.74 price, not profitable. This would leave 75 bad debt in the protocol
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the BorrowingVault liquidation mechanism that fails to provide a profitable liquidation path when a borrower’s collateral value drops sharply. The contract only permits liquidators to seize up to 50 % of a position when the debt‑to‑asset ratio exceeds the configured liqRatio but remains below liqRatio divided by FULL_LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD. If the price of the collateral falls enough that the total asset value becomes lower than the outstanding debt, the existing logic forces liquidators to compare the value of the assets they would receive with the amount of debt they must repay. Because the assets are worth less than the debt, the liquidation would be unprofitable, so the liquidator’s transaction is rejected or skipped. As a result, the protocol cannot close the under‑collateralised position, and the bad debt remains on the books. This situation can arise during rapid market downturns or when a specific collateral asset experiences a severe price drop, and it affects any borrower whose debt‑to‑collateral ratio falls into the narrow window between the liquidation trigger and the full‑liquidation threshold. The impact is that the protocol accumulates unrecoverable debt, reducing overall capital efficiency and potentially endangering the solvency of the system. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden loss of collateral value, a zero or near‑zero balance after a price shock, and the absence of any liquidation event despite the position being under‑collateralised. The issue was identified during a systematic audit that examined the liquidation flow and noticed that the profit calculation could become negative, causing the liquidation to be skipped silently. Because the contract does not emit a distinct error for an unprofitable liquidation, the problem can be hard to detect in normal operation. The recommended remediation is to extend the liquidation logic to allow liquidators to “close” the position by repaying an amount of debt that corresponds to the current value of the collateral, applying the standard liquidation penalty as a discount. This discounted full‑close liquidation would let the liquidator receive the remaining assets at a reduced debt cost, thereby limiting the amount of bad debt that remains in the protocol. In conceptual terms the fix adds a fallback liquidation path that is profitable even when collateral value is below debt, aligning incentives and preserving protocol health.

title: Payback can be DoSed in the BorrowingVault, may be profitable for liquidators
description: The borrowing vault enables anyone to payback the debt of another user. Thus, attackers can frontrun a user payback transaction, payback 1 wei and stop users from paying back their debts. This would make sense for liquidators, who are incentivized to do this to liquidate users.
poc: no poc/POCPaybackDoSed.t.sol#L27/POCPaybackDoSed.t.sol#L27
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a borrowing vault that permits any address to submit a repayment on behalf of another borrower. The contract calculates a maximum repayable amount based on the borrower’s current debt and then reverts the transaction if the supplied amount exceeds this maximum. An attacker can exploit this logic by front‑running a legitimate repayment transaction, submitting a tiny repayment (for example 1 wei) just before the victim’s transaction is mined. Because the contract updates the borrower’s outstanding debt immediately after the attacker’s tiny payment, the subsequent legitimate repayment now appears to exceed the newly calculated maximum and the contract reverts. This denial‑of‑service on the payback function prevents the borrower from clearing their debt, potentially forcing liquidation. The issue is triggered only when the payback function is called by a third party and when the blockchain ordering allows an adversary to insert a transaction ahead of the intended repayment. All borrowers, lenders and the overall protocol are affected because blocked repayments can lead to unexpected liquidations and loss of collateral. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, where the interaction between third‑party repayments and the maximum‑payback check was examined. It is difficult to notice because allowing third‑party repayments is a common design pattern in DeFi, and the edge case of a minimal repayment altering the maximum limit is subtle and only manifests under adversarial transaction ordering. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction receipt but the on‑chain state reveals that the debt has not decreased, or the transaction may simply revert with an opaque error, leaving the user confused why their repayment failed. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “front‑runable state‑dependent validation” where a public function’s pre‑condition is recomputed after each call, enabling an attacker to manipulate the condition. The recommended remediation is either to cap the repayment amount to the calculated maximum instead of reverting, or to restrict the payback function so that only the borrower themselves can repay their own debt, thereby eliminating the attack surface for third‑party front‑running.

title: Malicious users can exploit the referral system to always receive extra discounts
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a referral mechanism that grants a referrer a reward and gives the depositor a discount on each node purchase. The logic stores a referrer address the first time a user makes a deposit and then, on subsequent deposits, checks that the supplied referrer either matches the stored value or is zero. Because the validation only ensures that the referrer is non‑zero and not the same as the depositor, an attacker can create an alias address, set it as the referrer on the first deposit, and then reuse that same alias on every later deposit. Each call to the internal deposit function passes the alias through _isValidReferrer, which returns true, so the contract calculates a referralReward and a discountReward, reduces the amount sent to the treasury, and transfers the reward to the alias address. Consequently the attacker receives the referral reward and the discount on every deposit, while the treasury receives less than the full price. The protocol loses funds proportionally to the discount and reward percentages, and the accounting field totalDepositsReferred for the referrer is inflated because it counts each individual deposit instead of a single referral event. This flaw manifests whenever a user calls the deposit function with a non‑zero referrer that is not the caller, which is allowed after the first deposit. It affects any participant who can create an alias address, the protocol’s treasury, and any analytics that rely on the referral count. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and confirmed with a Foundry test that repeatedly called deposit with the same alias, showing that the attacker’s balance grew by the reward amount each time and that the treasury balance was consistently lower than expected. The bug is hard to notice because the reward transfer looks legitimate and the discounted amount still reaches the treasury, so the loss appears as a small reduction rather than a blatant theft. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incentive‑manipulation or referral‑abuse bugs where reward logic can be triggered repeatedly without proper state constraints. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected extra tokens appearing in the attacker’s wallet, a lower than expected treasury receipt, and an inflated referral count that does not reflect unique referrals. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that a referrer can be set only once and cannot be changed to a different address after the initial assignment, rejecting any non‑zero referrer that differs from the stored one. Additionally, anti‑sybil measures such as signature‑based verification of referrers should be introduced to prevent the creation of alias addresses that act as fake referrers.

title: Nodes can be purchased for extremely low price
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a deployment‑time unit mismatch in the script that creates the Fundraiser contract on BSC mainnet. The script reads a variable called usdcBasePrice, which is expressed in the smallest USDC unit (6 decimal places, also known as mwei). However, USDC on BSC uses 18 decimals, the same as native Ether, and the contract expects the price to be supplied with 18‑decimal precision. The code mistakenly passes usdcBasePrice directly to the constructor instead of converting it to 18‑decimal units via finalUSDCBasePrice. As a result the stored base price for USDC is off by a factor of 10^12, making the cost to purchase a node effectively zero or a negligible amount. An attacker can therefore call the node‑purchase function, pay almost nothing, and receive a fully funded node, draining the treasury or preventing legitimate users from acquiring nodes at the intended price. This condition only manifests on BSC mainnet where the token’s decimal count differs from the assumption in the script; on other chains the mismatch does not occur because USDC already uses 6 decimals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the deployment script, which is outside the contract source but critical for correct initialization. It is easy to miss because the contract code itself contains no arithmetic error; the problem lives in the off‑chain deployment parameters, and the price appears reasonable when inspected without considering the decimal conversion. The impact is a financial loss for the protocol, broken tokenomics, and a potential loss of trust from investors who expect nodes to be priced correctly. To remediate, the deployment must pass the correctly scaled price (finalUSDCBasePrice) to the constructor, ensuring the contract stores a value with 18‑decimal precision. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a unit‑conversion or decimal‑handling error, where mismatched token precision leads to under‑pricing or over‑pricing of assets. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a node purchase button that appears to work, but the wallet would be charged an unexpectedly tiny amount, and the user would receive a node for near‑free cost, contrary to the advertised price. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that each node costs a fixed USDC amount are violated, allowing the protocol’s funds to disappear without a corresponding legitimate transaction.

title: Liquidated NFTs can earn more than liquidation incentive
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic mis‑calculation that allows a liquidator to receive more value from seized ERC721 collateral than the protocol’s configured liquidation incentive. The protocol defines a liquidation incentive of 1.08×, meaning that for every unit of debt repaid the liquidator should receive at most 1.08 units of collateral value. During liquidation the contract iterates over each collateral token, multiplies the remaining repayment amount by the incentive and transfers up to that amount. When the collateral token is an NFT, the contract rounds the number of tokens up to the nearest oneNFTAmount and then transfers the full value of the rounded‑up NFTs. Because the rounding can add an entire extra NFT whose market value may be far larger than the 0.08× bonus, the liquidator can obtain a reward that exceeds the intended 1.08× factor. The post‑liquidation check only verifies that the borrower’s debt‑to‑collateral ratio improves; with a collateral factor of 0.85 this check still passes even when the seized value corresponds to a 1.176× incentive. Consequently, any liquidation that involves ERC721 collateral and a collateral factor below 1 can yield excessive rewards. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation logic and the rounding behaviour for NFTs. It is hard to notice because the ratio check appears to protect borrowers and the test suite does not include scenarios where the rounded NFT value overshoots the incentive. Exploitation steps are: (1) a liquidator selects a repayment amount that leaves a small remainder, (2) the contract rounds the required NFT count up, (3) the contract transfers the full rounded‑up NFT value, (4) the borrower loses more collateral than justified while the protocol’s accounting shows a valid debt‑ratio improvement. The impact is that liquidators can earn disproportionate profits, the protocol loses excess collateral, and borrowers may lose NFTs worth more than the debt they repaid. Affected parties include borrowers who provide NFT collateral, liquidators who can exploit the bug, and the protocol that suffers a loss of assets. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑calculation overflow caused by improper rounding and insufficient caps on seized value. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a liquidation the borrower’s NFT balance may drop to zero or an unexpected NFT is taken, while the user expected only a proportional seizure. The fix is to enforce that the value of seized NFTs does not exceed the repayment amount multiplied by the liquidation incentive, or to compute the incentive on a value basis rather than on a token count, and to adjust the rounding logic so that no extra whole NFT is granted beyond the incentive.

title: No check that NFTs aren't being claimed for free in `topUpInterestShortfall()`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interest‑shortfall top‑up routine that liquidators invoke to restore a borrower’s interest balance by seizing a portion of the borrower’s collateral. The function calculates a required top‑up amount (actualTopUpTokens) based on the USD shortfall, price and exchange rate of the interest token, and then determines how many collateral tokens (or NFTs) must be seized (actualSeizeTokens). For NFT markets the code rounds the seize amount up to the nearest whole NFT and proportionally adjusts the top‑up amount. However, the implementation never verifies that the initial top‑up amount is non‑zero before applying the proportional scaling. If, due to integer division or extreme parameter values, actualTopUpTokens evaluates to zero while actualSeizeTokens is positive, the proportional adjustment does nothing and the contract proceeds to transfer the seized NFT to the liquidator without any compensation. This results in a free NFT seizure: the borrower loses ownership of an NFT and receives no tokens in return. The bug is a classic missing‑guard or zero‑value check that can lead to asset loss without payment. It can be exploited by a malicious liquidator who engineers a liquidation scenario where the shortfall conversion yields zero top‑up tokens – for example by using very small shortfall values or by manipulating price or exchange‑rate inputs so that the division truncates to zero. When the condition occurs, the contract’s internal accounting assumes a balanced exchange of value, but the external reality is that the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken: the protocol’s ledger shows a seized NFT but no corresponding increase in the liquidator’s token balance, effectively “money disappears”. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the NFT disappearing from their wallet while no refund or compensation appears, contradicting the expectation that a liquidation always results in a fair trade of assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Fungify contract where the auditor noticed the lack of an explicit revert when actualTopUpTokens equals zero while actualSeizeTokens is greater than zero. The problem is subtle because under normal deployment parameters the shortfall conversion typically yields a non‑zero value, making the bug hard to trigger in routine testing and easy to overlook. The recommended mitigation is to add a guard that reverts the transaction if a zero top‑up amount would accompany a positive seize amount, mirroring checks already present in the redeem functions to prevent free redemptions. By enforcing this check, the protocol restores its accounting guarantees and prevents free NFT seizures, preserving user trust and financial safety.

title: Some NFTs may be incompatible with pools due to `totalSupply()` check
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a compatibility check that was copied from Compound's ERC20 market implementation and placed in the initialization routine of a CErc721 market. During the initialize() call the contract unconditionally invokes the totalSupply() function on the underlying token address, assuming that the token follows the ERC20 interface where totalSupply is mandatory. However, the ERC721 standard does not require a totalSupply function; it is only present in the optional Enumerable extension. Consequently, any ERC721 contract that does not implement totalSupply will cause the initialize() call to revert, preventing the market from being created. This mismatch is the root cause: the code treats an NFT as if it were a fungible token and relies on a function that many NFTs simply do not expose. Exploitation does not involve malicious code execution, but it can be used to deny service to legitimate NFTs. An attacker could deploy a compliant ERC721 that deliberately omits totalSupply and then attempt to list it, causing the market creation to fail and potentially confusing users who expect the pool to accept their NFT. The impact is functional: users attempting to create or interact with a CErc721 market for affected NFTs will see transactions revert, receive no confirmation, and may believe their assets are locked or lost. From the user’s perspective the UI may show an error, the expected pool balance remains zero, or the NFT never appears in the pool despite a successful transaction hash. The issue manifests only at market initialization time, when the underlying address is set; any subsequent operations are unreachable because the contract never reaches a usable state. It affects developers who configure new markets, protocol operators who rely on the market factory, and end‑users who want to trade those NFTs. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the CErc721 code against the ERC721 specification and noticed the inappropriate totalSupply sanity check. Because many popular NFTs implement the Enumerable extension, the bug can remain hidden until a non‑enumerable NFT is used, making it hard to notice in routine testing. The recommended remediation is to remove the totalSupply sanity check entirely or replace it with a proper ERC721 interface detection (for example using ERC165) that only verifies the presence of the required ERC721 functions. By eliminating the unnecessary call, the market can accept any compliant NFT, restoring expected behavior and preventing denial‑of‑service scenarios.

title: All payable calls will revert when sent to CEtherDelegator
description:
The Delegator contracts are intended to pass along any calls to their corresponding implementations.

Some delegators perform this logic by manually implementing each underlying function. Others (such as `CEtherDelegator.sol`) simply use a fallback function which is intended to capture all possible calls to the implementation.

However, the fallback function of this contract contains a check that was taken from the other markets but does not apply to CEther:
```solidity
fallback() external payable {
    if (msg.value > 0) {
        revert CannotReceiveValueGtZero();
    }

    ...
}
```
This will revert in the case that any payable function call are sent to the contract.

Looking at `CEther.sol`, minting, repaying, adding reserves, or WETH withdrawals all require the ability to receive ETH.

Fortunately, there is a payable `delegateToImplementation()` function on the delegator, so all calls from users will be possible by sending their calls to that function, with encoded abi data instead. While this is inconvenient, it is not a security risk.

WETH withdrawals, on the other hand, can only be accepted by a payable `fallback()` or `receive()` function. These will revert when sent to the delegator, and so all liquidations will revert when WETH is attempted to be withdrawn.

Currently, the CEtherDelegator inherits from CEther. This means it is not a delegator. It contains all functionality itself, as well as having an identical implementation that it can delegate call out to.

This inherited contract contains all of the CEther functionality, including the ability to accept payments, so this bug is not currently a problem. However, when the other issue is fixed (which would presumably happen by inheriting an interface from CEther instead of the full functionality), this bug will become a problem.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the CEtherDelegator contract caused by an overly restrictive fallback function that rejects any call carrying a non‑zero ether value. The fallback was copied from other market delegators where receiving ether is not required, and it contains a check that reverts when msg.value > 0. Because CEther and its delegators need to accept ether for core operations such as minting, repaying, adding reserves, and especially for WETH withdrawals that are performed via a plain payable fallback or receive function, the check prevents those payable calls from succeeding. When a user or the protocol attempts to send ether to the delegator – for example during a liquidation that tries to withdraw WETH – the transaction hits the fallback, the condition triggers, and the call reverts with CannotReceiveValueGtZero. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome (receiving a refund, completing a liquidation, or seeing a balance update) does not occur; instead the transaction fails and the ether is not transferred, leaving the user with no change in balance and the protocol with a stalled liquidation. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the delegator’s source code, where the fallback logic was examined and identified as incompatible with CEther’s payable semantics. It is subtle because fallback functions are rarely invoked directly and the contract currently inherits CEther, which provides its own payable fallback, masking the problem. However, if the inheritance is later changed to a pure proxy pattern, the faulty fallback will become active and break all payable interactions. The bug belongs to the class of proxy‑fallback mis‑implementation where a generic check is applied to a contract that must accept ether, leading to a denial‑of‑service or loss of functionality. The impact is that users cannot perform ether‑receiving actions through the delegator, liquidations that rely on WETH withdrawals will revert, and funds may become temporarily inaccessible. The fix is to either remove the proxy pattern for CEther and deploy it as a non‑proxy immutable contract, as Compound does, or modify the fallback (or receive) function to allow non‑zero msg.value and remove the revert condition, ensuring that payable calls are correctly forwarded to the implementation.

title: `beforeRatio` taken before interest accrual in liquidations
description:
In `batchLiquidateBorrow()`, the fundamental check on the liquidation is that the account debt ratio after is less than or equal to what it was before.
```solidity
(err, afterRatio) = getAccountDebtRatio(borrower);

if (afterRatio >= beforeRatio) {
    revert LiquidateSeizeTooMuch();
}
```
Along the pathway to liquidation, all relevant markets have their interest accrued (either in the `liquidateBorrow()` function or the `seize()` function), which increases the value of both the debt and collateral tokens.

These accruals happen after the `beforeRatio` is taken, but before the `afterRatio` is taken. Therefore, the values of the tokens will be shifted between these two checks.

This can lead to a situation where the liquidation takes too much collateral that it actually harms the debt position of the borrower, but is allowed to proceed.

For example, imagine a situation where a borrower has 5 cTokens of collateral worth $1 each (not accrued) and 1 cTokens of debt worth $4.50 (fully accrued). This leads to a `beforeRatio` of `4.5 / (5 * 0.85) = 1.058e18`. If there are interest accruals due that will move the value of the collateral tokens up 25%, and the borrower seizes 1 cToken (unpaid), the resulting `afterRatio = 4.5 / ((5 - 1) * 1.25 * 0.85) = 1.058e18`.

Clearly taking a collateral token without paying any debt off is not good for the borrower, but it will be allowed to pass by this check before the interest accrual mismatch.

Note that in some edge cases, this could also cause the problem of allowing a non-liquidatable position to be liquidated, but this is less likely because it presumes that the position was previously in a liquidatable state but wasn't liquidated.

Because of the logic used to calculate the amount of tokens seized, there is no way for a liquidator to directly choose to seize tokens without paying any debt off. However, this can be combined with issues like [M-01] and [M-04] to lead to additional rewards beyond the `1 / (1 - collateralFactor)` that the liquidator can earn.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the liquidation routine of the protocol where the debt‑to‑collateral ratio is measured before interest is accrued on the involved markets, while the second measurement is taken after interest accrual has already increased the value of the collateral tokens. Because the check compares the after‑ratio to the before‑ratio, the increase in collateral value can mask the fact that no debt has been repaid, allowing the liquidator to seize collateral that does not improve the borrower’s health factor. In practice a borrower whose position is barely liquidatable can lose a token of collateral even though the outstanding debt remains unchanged, resulting in a higher after‑ratio that still satisfies the condition afterRatio < beforeRatio. This can be triggered whenever batchLiquidateBorrow() is called and any of the markets involved have pending interest to be accrued. The affected parties are borrowers, who may see their collateral disappear without a corresponding reduction in debt, and liquidators, who can obtain extra rewards beyond the protocol‑defined incentive. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of accrueInterest() calls relative to the ratio checks. It is subtle because the ratio values appear numerically consistent, and the protocol’s UI may still show the borrower as liquidated without obvious error messages, making the problem hard to spot without inspecting the internal accounting flow. The impact ranges from unfair loss of collateral for users to potential over‑liquidation of positions that should be safe, undermining confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The bug belongs to the class of “interest‑accrual timing” or “state‑inconsistency during liquidation” vulnerabilities, where state changes between validation steps break accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should accrue interest on all relevant markets before taking the initial beforeRatio measurement, or alternatively compute both ratios after all accruals have been applied, ensuring that the comparison reflects the true post‑accrual health of the account. This eliminates the window where collateral value can shift between checks and prevents liquidations that seize assets without reducing debt.

title: `topUpInterestShortfall()` does not accrue interest on tokens
description:
Similar to the above issue, the `topUpInterestShortfall()` function does not explicitly accrue interest for either the interest market token or the collateral token.

This leads to a number of possible problems:
The call to `getAccountLiquidity()` can revert if the user is in shortfall before accrual but would be in good standing after.
The call to `getAccountLiquidity()` can pass if accruing interest on a borrowed token would have pushed the user into a shortfall.
The call to `getAccountLiquidity()` can return an inaccurate interest shortfall if the interest market has not been recently accrued.
The `_adjustTopUpValues()` calculation will use out of date exchange rates for both tokens, skewing results.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing interest accrual step inside the topUpInterestShortfall function. When a borrower calls this function to cover an interest shortfall, the contract does not explicitly invoke accrueInterest on either the interest market token or the collateral token before performing liquidity checks and calculations. The root cause is the omission of these state‑update calls, which leaves the protocol operating on stale exchange rates and outdated account balances. An attacker or a malicious borrower can exploit the omission by timing a top‑up transaction when interest for the borrowed asset has not yet been accrued. Because the contract believes the borrower is still solvent, it may allow the top‑up to proceed, but the subsequent getAccountLiquidity call can either revert unexpectedly (if the user would have been solvent after accrual) or incorrectly report sufficient liquidity (if accrual would have pushed the user into shortfall). Conversely, if the borrowed token would have accrued enough interest to create a shortfall, the missing accrual lets the transaction succeed, leaving the protocol exposed to an under‑collateralized position. From the user’s point of view the symptoms include sudden transaction reverts with no clear explanation, or a successful top‑up that later results in loss of collateral, inability to withdraw funds, or unexpected liquidation because the protocol later discovers an undisclosed shortfall. The impact is a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting invariants, potentially causing lenders to lose funds and eroding confidence in the platform. The condition occurs whenever topUpInterestShortfall is invoked without a prior interest accrual, which is typical for any user attempting to restore solvency. Affected parties are borrowers who rely on the function, lenders whose collateral may be at risk, and the protocol itself which may suffer from inaccurate risk metrics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared expected state transitions with the actual contract code and noticed the missing accrueInterest calls. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed and the UI may display a successful top‑up, while the underlying accounting error only manifests later during liquidation or when getAccountLiquidity is queried. This bug belongs to the class of “missing state update” or “interest accrual omission” errors, where a financial smart contract fails to synchronize its internal accounting before performing critical checks. To remediate the problem the contract should explicitly call accrueInterest on both the interest market token and the collateral token at the beginning of topUpInterestShortfall, ensuring that exchange rates and balances reflect the latest accrued interest before any liquidity calculations are performed. This change restores the intended business logic that a borrower must cover the true, up‑to‑date interest shortfall and prevents the protocol from operating on stale data.

title: Uncollected interest on NFTs not counted in liquidity calculation
description:
When `getHypotheticalAccountLiquidityInternal()` is called to calculate whether a user's overall account is in good standing or has a shortfall, it calculates the value of their collateral (discounted by the collateral factor) and borrows to compare.

In order to ensure we are accounting for the interest owed on NFT borrows, we get the interest balance from `getAccountSnapshot()`:
```solidity
(oErr, vars.cTokenBalance, vars.borrowBalance, vars.exchangeRateMantissa, vars.interestBalance) = asset.getAccountSnapshot(account);
```
We then use this balance to calculate the value of the interest owed:
```solidity
vars.sumInterestOwed = vars.sumInterestOwed + vars.interestBalance * interestOraclePriceMantissa / 1e18;
```
This `sumInterestOwed` balance is used to check whether the account is in an interest market shortfall, which can trigger the `Error.TOOLITTLEINTEREST_RESERVE` and allow other users to top up the interest market and seize collateral.

`sumInterestOwed` is also added to the total borrows that are used to check whether the full account is in shortfall:
```solidity
vars.sumBorrowPlusEffects = vars.sumBorrowPlusEffects + vars.sumInterestOwed;
```
However, we do not perform equivalent logic for the interest earned on NFT collateral. This will cause the balance of interest market tokens owned and overall collateral of the account to both be understated, which could lead to unjustified liquidations.
bug_full: When the protocol evaluates an account's liquidity it calls getHypotheticalAccountLiquidityInternal to compare the value of collateral, discounted by the collateral factor, against the amount borrowed. For NFT‑based borrows the function correctly retrieves the interest balance from getAccountSnapshot and adds the interest owed to the total borrow amount. However, the same routine does not add the interest that has accrued on NFTs supplied as collateral. Consequently the computed collateral value is lower than the true economic value, because the interest earned on the NFT collateral is omitted from the sumCollateral calculation. This under‑statement can cause the protocol to flag a shortfall and allow a liquidation even though the user’s net position is healthy. The bug manifests only for accounts that hold NFT collateral that generates interest; standard token collateral is handled correctly. It was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidity‑checking logic, where the code path for interest earned was missing. Because the discrepancy appears only in internal accounting numbers and does not cause an immediate revert, it can be difficult to notice from the UI; users may see a liquidation event or a warning that their account is under‑collateralized even though their wallet shows the expected NFT balance and accrued interest. An attacker can monitor accounts with NFT collateral, wait for the protocol to compute a shortfall based on the flawed calculation, and then trigger the liquidation or top‑up the interest market to seize collateral. The impact is that honest users can lose collateral or be forced to repay more than necessary, violating the protocol’s business logic that collateral value should include both market value and earned interest. The issue can be remedied by extending the liquidity calculation to include the interest earned on NFT collateral, i.e., adding the accrued interest balance to the collateral sum before applying the collateral factor, ensuring that both sides of the equation (interest owed and interest earned) are symmetrically accounted for. This aligns the accounting with the intended economic assumptions and prevents unjustified liquidations.

title: Collateral token interest is accrued after relative price calculation in liquidations
bug_full: The issue is an inaccurate calculation of the amount of collateral tokens that can be seized during a liquidation because the protocol determines the seize amount before the collateral token’s interest is accrued. The function that computes the seize quantity uses the stored exchange rate of the collateral CToken, which only reflects accrued interest up to the last time the token’s accrueInterest routine was executed. When a liquidation is triggered after a period of inactivity, the exchange rate remains artificially low, causing the denominator in the seize formula to be smaller than it should be. As a result, the numerator divided by this understated denominator yields a larger seize token count than the protocol’s liquidation incentive logic intends. An attacker, typically a liquidator, can exploit this by initiating a liquidation after the collateral market has not accrued interest for a significant time. The liquidator repays the borrower’s debt, the contract calculates the seize amount using the stale exchange rate, and then calls the internal _seize function, which finally accrues interest but after the seize amount has already been determined. Consequently, the liquidator receives more collateral than the 8% incentive that the protocol specifies, potentially up to the full inverse of (1‑collateralFactor), effectively draining the borrower’s remaining collateral.
