This problem manifests when a borrower’s position is liquidated after a long idle period, and it primarily affects borrowers who lose more of their collateral than expected and liquidators who gain an unintended profit. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation flow and noticed that interest accrual was performed after the seize calculation rather than before. It can be hard to notice because the liquidation still succeeds and the protocol does not emit an explicit error; the only symptom is that borrowers see a larger-than-expected reduction in their collateral balance, sometimes ending in a zero balance even though their debt was only partially covered. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state‑dependent values are used out of order, leading to mis‑priced asset transfers. To remediate, the liquidation calculation should first invoke the collateral token’s accrueInterest function (or otherwise ensure the exchange rate reflects up‑to‑date interest) before computing the seize amount, thereby aligning the seized value with the current market price and the intended liquidation incentive. This change restores the correct accounting relationship between debt repayment and collateral seizure and prevents the protocol from unintentionally rewarding liquidators with excess collateral.

title: NFT oracle missing Chainlink liveness checks
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing liveness (stale‑price) checks in the FloorPriceFeedAdaptor that aggregates two Chainlink feeds to compute an NFT floor price in USD. The adaptor calls latestRoundData on the underlying floor‑price and ETH‑price feeds, extracts only the numeric rates, multiplies them, and returns the result together with placeholder values (zeroes) for roundId, startedAt, updatedAt and answeredInRound. Because the adaptor does not forward the updatedAt timestamps and does not perform any stale‑price validation, the composite oracle always reports a timestamp of zero. When a consumer such as getUnderlyingPrice invokes the standard Chainlink stale‑price logic – which compares block.timestamp with updatedAt plus a configured stalePriceDelay – the comparison fails for any non‑instantaneous call, causing the contract to revert with a StalePrice error. The root cause is the adaptor’s omission of the liveness checks that are present in the original Chainlink oracle and its failure to propagate realistic timestamp data. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger the failure simply by calling the price feed; the contract will revert, forcing developers to disable the stale‑price guard in order to keep the oracle usable. Disabling the guard permits outdated or manipulated floor prices to be used in liquidation calculations, potentially allowing liquidations to occur at incorrect values, harming borrowers and undermining the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the FloorPriceFeedAdaptor is queried while a non‑zero stalePriceDelay is configured – essentially any time the price is needed for collateral valuation. Affected parties include borrowers, lenders, and any user relying on accurate NFT pricing for liquidation or margin calls. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the adaptor’s implementation with the recommended Chainlink pattern and noticed the absence of timestamp handling and stale‑price checks. It can be hard to notice because the adaptor still returns a seemingly valid price number, while the failure appears only as a generic revert, which may be misinterpreted as a different bug. To remediate, the adaptor should retrieve the updatedAt values from both underlying feeds, propagate them in its own latestRoundData response, and enforce the same stale‑price validation logic (block.timestamp <= updatedAt + stalePriceDelay) before returning a price. This aligns the composite oracle with the standard Chainlink liveness guarantees and prevents the protocol from accepting stale or manipulated NFT valuations. From a user perspective the symptom is that UI components show a zero or missing price, transactions that depend on the price revert with a StalePrice error, and liquidation attempts may fail or execute with an incorrect price, leading to unexpected loss of collateral. The bug belongs to the class of oracle liveness validation failures, where composite or wrapper contracts omit essential freshness checks, breaking accounting assumptions that prices are up‑to‑date and trustworthy.

title: BaseJumpRateModelV2 uses outdated blockPerYear value
bug_full: BaseJumpRateModelV2 uses a hard‑coded blocksPerYear constant of 2102400, which reflects a 15‑second block time that was valid before the Ethereum merge. After the merge the average block time is about 12 seconds, corresponding to 2628000 blocks per year. The contract converts annual interest parameters to per‑block rates by dividing by this constant. Because the constant is too low, the per‑block rates are inflated by roughly 25 %, causing the protocol to charge borrowers more interest and to credit lenders less than the rates advertised on‑chain or in the UI. The bug manifests in any market that relies on BaseJumpRateModelV2 – essentially all non‑ERC721 money markets – and therefore affects every user who supplies or borrows assets, as well as the protocol’s treasury. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s interest calculation with the expected formula based on the current block time. It is easy to miss because the resulting APR numbers still look reasonable; the discrepancy only becomes apparent when the annualized rate is back‑calculated from the per‑block value or when the protocol’s accounting is audited. Exploitation does not require a separate transaction; the model automatically over‑calculates interest on every block, so the effect compounds over time. The impact is a systematic mispricing of loans: borrowers may pay up to 25 % more interest than intended, and lenders may earn up to 25 % less, potentially leading to fund loss for the protocol if the spread is not compensated elsewhere. From a user’s perspective the UI may display an APR that matches the contract’s parameter, but the actual accrued interest will be higher, resulting in unexpected balance reductions or lower returns. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect time‑base constants” or “static configuration drift” bugs, where a hard‑coded environmental assumption becomes stale after a network upgrade. The recommended remediation is to replace the constant with the correct value (2628000) or, better, compute the blocks‑per‑year dynamically from the current block time, ensuring that future changes to block production do not re‑introduce the error.

title: requestQuery() and verify() Functions Lack Proper Access Control
description: According to the documentation and protocol’s logic, requestQuery() and verify() functions are supposed to be callable only from the Gateway.sol contract. The lack of access controls for these extremely sensitive features could be a serious problem as wrong data can easily be stored.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing access‑control checks on two highly sensitive functions, requestQuery and verify, which according to the protocol specification should only be callable by the dedicated Gateway contract. Because the contract does not enforce any restriction on msg.sender, any external account can invoke these functions directly. The root cause is the absence of an onlyGateway modifier or equivalent authorization logic in the function declarations, meaning the contract never validates that the caller is the trusted gateway address. An attacker can exploit this by sending crafted query requests or verification messages, causing the contract to store incorrect query data, return false verification results, or otherwise corrupt the internal state that downstream logic relies on. This can lead to observable symptoms such as users receiving empty or wrong query responses, refunds not being processed, or balances appearing unchanged when they should be updated. The impact is broad: protocol participants, including users and other contracts that depend on correct query handling, may suffer loss of funds, incorrect accounting, or broken business logic. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed without the intended access control, i.e., under any normal operating condition where the functions are public or external. It was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the discrepancy between the documented design (gateway‑only calls) and the actual implementation (no sender check). The problem can be hard to notice because the functions may not emit events and may appear harmless in isolation, yet they are critical for the protocol’s integrity. To remediate, the contract should store the gateway address as an immutable variable set in the constructor, add a modifier that reverts when msg.sender does not match this address, and apply the modifier to both requestQuery and verify. This restores the intended trust boundary and prevents unauthorized entities from injecting malformed data or influencing verification outcomes.

title: Insufficient Input Data Validation For Gateway.query() Function
description:
The QueryRequest struct and message inputs, which are the parameters of the Gateway.query() function are not sufficiently validated. The missing checks are the following:

1. QueryRequest.dstChainId - This is the chain ID of the destination chain and can be the zero value

2. QueryRequest.height - This is the height of the block when making the query can be the zero value

3. QueryRequest.slot - This is the key used by the Relayer to acquire the storage proof, it can be set to an empty value

4. message - This is the data used when executing callback, it can be set to an empty value
bug_full: The Gateway.query function accepts an array of QueryRequest structs together with a callback address and a calldata message. The implementation does not perform any validation on several fields of the request struct nor on the message payload. Specifically, the destination chain identifier (dstChainId), the block height (height), and the storage slot key (slot) can all be supplied as their zero values, and the message bytes can be empty. Because the contract assumes these inputs are always non‑zero and non‑empty, downstream logic that builds relayer requests, fetches storage proofs, or invokes the callback may operate on invalid data. An attacker can craft a query where dstChainId is zero, causing the relayer to target an undefined chain, or set height to zero, which may be interpreted as the genesis block or trigger division‑by‑zero errors in external libraries. Supplying an empty slot results in the relayer requesting a proof for a null key, which typically returns a default value or fails silently, while an empty callback message leads to the called contract receiving no data, potentially causing it to skip essential state updates or revert. These malformed inputs can therefore cause denial‑of‑service conditions, waste gas, or produce incorrect accounting outcomes such as missing refunds, zero balances, or funds becoming inaccessible. The vulnerability manifests whenever any user can invoke query with arbitrary parameters; there is no guard clause that rejects zero or empty values. All participants that rely on the query result – the relayer, the callback contract, and ultimately end‑users – are affected because the protocol’s business logic assumes valid proofs and meaningful callback data. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by Shiedify, which noted the absence of explicit checks for zero values and empty byte arrays. It can be hard to notice because normal operation with correct inputs does not expose the flaw, and the contract does not revert immediately; the failure only appears later in the proof‑fetching or callback stages. To remediate, the contract should enforce sensible constraints: reject a zero dstChainId, reject a zero height, reject a slot equal to bytes32(0), reject an empty message, and also validate any address fields such as the destination address. Adding explicit revert statements with descriptive error types (for example InvalidInputZeroValue, InvalidInputEmptyBytes32, InvalidInputMessage) ensures that malformed queries are rejected up front, preserving protocol integrity and preventing the described loss of funds or service disruption.

title: The Gateway.query() Function Does Not Return Excess Fees for Executing Query Request
description:
In the query() function, the contract Gateway.sol requires the users to pay a estimateFee() for executing a query.
However, it does not handle the situation where the user pays more msg.value than the required estimateFee(). Currently, if msg.value > estimateFee(), the contract simply accepts the payment without refunding the difference to the user.
The impact is primarily financial, as the current implementation does not return any excess ether msg.value paid beyond the required estimateFee(). Users who pay more than the required estimateFee() will not get their payment back.
The following scenario can happen:

1. Alice wants to make an executing query.

2. Alice calls the query() function from User contract and she sends 0.2 ether, but the estimateFee() is 0.1 ether for example.

3. The estimateFee() is correctly charged at 0.1 ether and Alice makes a query request successfully, but she is not refunded the excess of 0.1 ether.

4. The excess of 0.1 ether price fee will go to the balance of the contract Gateway.sol.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the query function of the Gateway contract, which charges users an estimated fee for executing a data request but does not handle the case where the caller sends more ether than the estimated amount. The root cause is the absence of a validation step that either rejects transactions with an incorrect fee or refunds any excess value; the function simply accepts any msg.value that is greater than or equal to the estimated fee and proceeds without returning the surplus. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by deliberately or accidentally over‑paying the fee: the contract will keep the extra ether in its balance, effectively stealing funds from the sender. This financial impact manifests as a loss of the over‑paid amount, with the contract’s balance growing each time an over‑payment occurs. The condition under which the bug appears is any call to query where msg.value exceeds estimateFee(). All users who interact with the query endpoint are affected, as are the protocol owners who may unintentionally accumulate unearned ether. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee calculation with the actual ether transferred and noticed that no refund logic existed. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the user receives the expected service; the only symptom is a silent reduction of the sender’s wallet balance. Conceptually, this is an economic‑logic flaw commonly classified as an over‑payment handling bug or missing refund mechanism. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful query but the wallet shows a larger-than‑expected deduction, leading to confusion when the expected refund never arrives. The bug violates the accounting assumption that the contract only retains the exact fee required for service provision. The recommended remediation is either to enforce an exact fee check (reverting when msg.value differs from the estimate) or to calculate the excess amount and send it back to the caller using a safe call, thereby ensuring that only the precise fee is retained.

title: Missing Check For callback and lightClient Variables to be Contract Addresses
description:
In Gateway.sol, the query() function accepts callback and lightClient as address variables. The former should be the address of the contract, making the query via the Gateway contract, whereas the latter is the address of the light client, responsible for verification of the queried data, received from the destination chain.
The function contains zero address checks but misses one, validating if the addresses are actually smart contracts implementing the required interfaces (IReceiver and ILightClient). The absence of such a check could allow a user/script/UI to accept an EOA address for both variables or contracts that do not have the required functions, making it impossible to receive and validate the query.
Since the query() function is the core value proposition of the entire protocol, the absence of this check can seriously impact the business logic and result in significant gas costs, especially if a batch query is executed.
Location of affected code
File: contracts/Gateway.sol#L155
```solidity
function query(
QueryType.QueryRequest[] memory queries,
address lightClient,
address callBack,
bytes calldata message
) external payable nonReentrant {
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the core query() function of the Gateway contract, where two address parameters – the callback contract and the light client contract – are accepted without verifying that they actually implement the required interfaces. The function only checks that the addresses are non‑zero, but it does not confirm that the callback address supports the IReceiver interface nor that the light client address supports the ILightClient interface via ERC‑165. This omission means that an externally owned account (EOA) or a contract lacking the expected functions can be supplied. When such an invalid address is used, the gateway will still emit a query transaction, but the subsequent callback that should deliver the result and the verification step performed by the light client will never execute because the expected functions are missing. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, yet no data is returned, no callback is triggered, and any gas spent on the query – especially in batch mode – is effectively wasted. The impact is a breakdown of the protocol’s primary business logic: queries cannot be fulfilled, users may lose confidence, and the protocol may incur unnecessary gas costs. The issue manifests whenever a caller provides arbitrary addresses to query(), which can happen through a malicious UI, a compromised script, or an attacker deliberately passing an EOA. The affected parties include any user or dApp that relies on the gateway to retrieve cross‑chain data, as well as the protocol operators who assume that queries will be processed correctly. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit performed by Shiedify, who noted that the lack of interface validation is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the failure only becomes apparent when the expected callback never arrives. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because there is no explicit error – the contract simply does nothing after the query, making the symptom look like a silent timeout. The recommended remediation is to enforce ERC‑165 checks for both parameters, for example by requiring that the callback and light client contracts inherit IERC165 and implement supportsInterface() returning true for IReceiver and ILightClient respectively. The Gateway should call a helper such as checkSupportedInterface() and revert with a clear error if the interfaces are not supported. Providing example implementations and documentation will help developers supply compliant contracts and prevent the silent failure mode.

title: depositWETHInEtherfi() is limited to depositing only 1e18
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that is intended to move wrapped Ether (WETH) from the contract into an Etherfi liquidity pool. The implementation withdraws the requested amount of WETH, but then deposits a hard‑coded value of 1e18 wei (exactly one ether) into the pool, regardless of the amount supplied. The root cause is the use of a literal constant instead of the caller‑provided _amount when forwarding ETH to the pool. An attacker who controls the contract owner role can invoke the function with a larger amount, for example 2e18 wei, causing the contract to withdraw the full 2 ether from WETH, but only forward one ether to the pool. The surplus ether remains in the contract’s balance with no subsequent code to retrieve or reuse it, effectively locking those funds indefinitely. This situation can be reproduced whenever the owner attempts to deposit more than one ether, leading to a discrepancy between the expected and actual pool contribution. From a user perspective the contract appears to accept the full deposit, yet the UI or subsequent balance checks would show that part of the funds never contributes to yield and simply disappears from the available pool balance. The impact is a loss of capital efficiency: funds that should generate returns are stranded, reducing overall protocol profitability and potentially eroding trust among token holders. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s input parameter with the value passed to the external pool contract and noticed the mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the function does not emit an event indicating the amount deposited, and the constant value looks innocuous in isolation. The proper remediation is to replace the hard‑coded 1e18 with the variable _amount so that the exact amount withdrawn from WETH is forwarded to the liquidity pool, ensuring no ether remains unintentionally locked. Conceptually this bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter forwarding” or “hard‑coded value misuse” that leads to asset loss through unintended residual balances.

title: swapOn1INCH() slippage may be ineffective
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ineffective slippage verification in a token swap function that interacts with the 1inch aggregation router. The function checks that the contract's balance of the output token after the external call is greater than or equal to a user‑provided minimum amount, but it does not consider how many of those tokens were already held before the swap. The root cause is the use of a static balanceOf check instead of measuring the incremental change (delta) caused by the swap. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by supplying a swap that returns fewer output tokens than expected while the contract already possesses a sufficient pre‑existing balance to satisfy the check. For example, if the contract already holds 500 tokenB and the user requests to swap 1000 tokenA for at least 995 tokenB, a malicious swap that only yields 0 tokenB will still pass because the total balance after the call (still 500) is compared against the minimum (995) incorrectly, leading to a false pass. The impact is that users may receive far fewer tokens than anticipated, effectively losing value, and the protocol cannot guarantee that trades respect the quoted minimum output. This condition occurs whenever the contract has a non‑zero balance of the output asset before executing swapOn1INCH, which is common in contracts that hold residual tokens from previous operations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the slippage logic and identified that the balance check does not isolate the swap result. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s balance will often increase after a successful swap, masking the fact that the increase may be insufficient relative to the user’s expectation. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑invariant errors where post‑condition checks ignore prior state, leading to incorrect validation of financial operations. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction but the received amount is zero or far below the expected amount, creating a discrepancy between the expected refund and the actual outcome. To fix the issue, the function should record the output token balance before the external call, perform the swap, then compute the difference between the after‑balance and the before‑balance and compare that delta to the minimum amount. This ensures that only the tokens obtained from the current swap are considered, restoring correct slippage enforcement and aligning the contract’s behavior with its financial guarantees.

title: YieldManager hardcodes slippage to
description:
The current implementation of YieldManager functions moveAssetToYieldManager(), moveAssetToLiquidVault(), and depositYieldIntoLiquidVault() hardcodes the slippage control to 0. This means there is no parameter for slippage control, making all function executions susceptible to significant losses. By setting slippage to 0, these functions accept any amount the relayer returns for swaps or deposits, which can lead to unfavorable outcomes.
The same issue exists in the YieldStrategy.depositToPendle() function.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection in several YieldManager and YieldStrategy functions. The implementation hard‑codes the slippage tolerance to zero, meaning the functions do not accept any amountOutMinimum parameter and therefore accept whatever amount the external relayer reports for a swap or a deposit. This occurs in moveAssetToYieldManager(), moveAssetToLiquidVault(), depositYieldIntoLiquidVault() and YieldStrategy.depositToPendle(). The root cause is a design decision that treats the relayer’s return value as trustworthy and omits a check that the received amount meets a minimum threshold. An attacker controlling or influencing the relayer can deliberately return a smaller amount than expected, or a market participant can front‑run the transaction to shift the price between the quote and execution. Because the functions do not revert on unfavorable rates, the protocol will accept the reduced amount, causing users to receive fewer tokens than they deposited or expected. The impact is a potential loss of user funds and a distortion of the protocol’s accounting, as balances in the YieldManager or LiquidVault may be lower than the deposited value, leading to reduced yields or even a shortfall in the vault. The issue manifests every time any of the affected functions is called, i.e., whenever assets are moved into the YieldManager, transferred to the LiquidVault, or when yield is deposited back into the LiquidVault, as well as when Pendle deposits are made. All participants who rely on these functions – depositors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the function signatures and noticed the hard‑coded zero slippage value. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not fail; the UI may simply show a successful deposit while the resulting balance is smaller than expected, giving the impression that the operation succeeded without error. To remediate, each function should be refactored to accept an amountOutMinimum (or similar) argument supplied by the caller and enforce that the actual amount received from the relayer is at least this minimum; if the condition is not met, the transaction should revert. This restores slippage control, aligns the implementation with typical DeFi best practices, and prevents silent loss of funds due to unfavorable swap rates or malicious relayer behavior.

title: Recovering assets in case of emergency could cause an error in accounting
description:
recoverAsset function is used to withdraw any ERC20 sent to the contract mistakenly. However, this function accepts any address. if the admin passes TRSY address, they can extract TRSY from the contract which is not supposed to happen.
Furthermore, let's say there is an emergency and the admin wants TRSY, cumulativeFees will hold the wrong value as the amount withdrawn is not deducted from it. Thus, causing an accounting error in the overall protocol.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a privileged function that is intended to rescue ERC20 tokens mistakenly sent to the contract. The function accepts an arbitrary token address and transfers the full balance to the caller, who is assumed to be the contract admin. Because the implementation does not discriminate between generic tokens and the protocol’s native token, an admin (or any party that gains control of the admin role) can specify the native token address and withdraw those tokens directly from the contract. The root cause is the lack of a safeguard that excludes the protocol token from the recovery path and the omission of accounting updates when such a withdrawal occurs. When the admin extracts the native token, the internal variable that tracks cumulative fees remains unchanged, so the protocol’s accounting layer continues to report that the fees are still held by the contract. This mismatch can be exploited to hide the theft of funds, as the fee balance appears intact while the actual token balance has decreased. The impact includes loss of user funds, inaccurate fee reporting, and potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s financial integrity. The issue manifests whenever the recoverAsset function is invoked with the native token address, especially during emergency situations where the admin may be motivated to withdraw assets quickly. All participants who rely on the fee accounting – users, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol may distribute rewards based on an inflated fee balance. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined privileged functions for proper access control and state consistency. It can be hard to notice because the function works correctly for arbitrary tokens, and the fee variable is not directly linked to the token transfer logic, so the discrepancy only appears when the native token is recovered. To remediate, the function should either reject the native token address or, if recovery of that token is ever required, explicitly decrement the cumulativeFees variable by the withdrawn amount before completing the transfer, thereby preserving accounting integrity.

title: Updating boost periods could cause loss of rewards
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward‑claiming mechanism of a staking or emission contract that distributes FYDE tokens. The contract calculates a user’s pending reward through an earned view function that multiplies the user’s balance by the difference between the current global reward‑per‑token value and the user’s last recorded reward‑per‑token, then divides by a precision constant. The global reward‑per‑token value is derived from a time‑based formula that incorporates the current boost period parameters. When an administrator changes the boost periods, the contract updates the reward‑per‑token calculation without preserving the portion of rewards that were already accrued under the previous boost configuration. Consequently, any user who has not yet called the claim function after the boost change will see their pending reward recomputed with the new, possibly lower, boost rate, effectively erasing or reducing the amount they were entitled to. This can be exploited by an admin (or any entity with permission to modify boost periods) who deliberately adjusts the boost parameters after users have accumulated rewards but before they claim them, causing a loss of those unclaimed rewards. The impact is that users may see a non‑zero reward balance in the UI, attempt to claim, and receive a smaller amount than expected or even zero tokens, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are monotonically increasing until claimed. The issue manifests only when boost periods are updated while there exist unclaimed rewards; it does not affect users who claim immediately after each update. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the boost‑period setter and the reward‑per‑token view, noting that the stored reward‑per‑token value is not snapshot‑preserved across parameter changes. The problem is subtle because the UI may still display the pre‑update accrued amount, leading users to believe their claim will succeed, while the contract silently applies the new rate during the claim transaction. This class of bug can be described as a state‑inconsistency or accounting race condition caused by mutable global parameters that influence reward calculations. To remediate, the contract should either freeze reward claims while boost periods are being modified, maintain a separate accounting snapshot of pending rewards that is independent of future boost changes, or introduce a grace period that allows users to claim accrued rewards before any boost update takes effect. Implementing such safeguards ensures that reward balances remain accurate and that users cannot lose tokens due to administrative parameter changes.

title: Loss of rewards due to the boostPeriods design
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of boosted rewards in the RewardsDistributor contract. The contract iterates over an array of boost periods and, when a boost period has already passed, substitutes the period’s timestamp with the current block timestamp. This substitution causes the accrued boost multiplier to be computed only for the time between the last update and the current time, discarding any portion of the boost period that elapsed before the user’s last claim. Consequently, if a user does not claim exactly before a boost period expires, the portion of the boost that should have been earned is lost and the user receives rewards based only on the normal rate. Even when a user claims during a boost period, the loop’s break condition and the use of the current timestamp mean that the calculation cannot capture the final fraction of the boost period, leading to a systematic shortfall. The impact is that participants in the staking or reward program receive fewer tokens than the protocol’s economic model promises, creating unfairness and potentially reducing user confidence. The issue manifests whenever a boost period has elapsed without a claim, or when a claim occurs slightly before the period’s end, which is a realistic scenario for most users. All stakers, delegators, or any address that relies on the boosted reward mechanism are affected. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑rate logic and noticed that the algorithm replaces expired timestamps with the current time instead of preserving the elapsed boost interval. The bug is subtle because the contract still distributes rewards; the discrepancy appears only as a slight reduction in the expected boost, which may not be obvious without detailed accounting. To remediate the issue, the boosted portion of rewards should be tracked separately per user, accumulating the exact time spent inside each boost period and applying the multiplier to that precise interval, rather than overwriting expired timestamps with the current block time. This design change restores the intended reward distribution semantics and ensures that users receive the full boost they are entitled to according to the protocol’s specifications.

title: No method to withdraw from EtherFi
description:
The YieldStrategy.sol contract has the method depositWETHInEtherfi that allows the caller to deposit WETH into EtherFi to obtain WEETH.
However, there is currently no method to do the opposite...withdraw the underlying WETH by redeeming the WEETH. As such, the only way to regain the original WETH is to swap via 1INCH, but this depends entirely on the available liquidity in the relevant pools required in the path from WEETH to WETH. I'm not sure why we wouldn't want the withdraw equivalent like we have for sDAI and Pendle.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a functional omission in the YieldStrategy.sol contract: after a user calls the depositWETHInEtherfi method to move Wrapped Ether (WETH) into the EtherFi protocol and receive the interest‑bearing token WEETH, the contract provides no complementary method to redeem WEETH back into the original WETH. The root cause is that the contract developers implemented only the deposit side of the EtherFi integration and omitted the withdraw side, leaving the redemption logic entirely absent. Because of this gap, an attacker or any regular user cannot directly retrieve the underlying WETH from the contract; the only available path is to swap the received WEETH for WETH on an external aggregator such as 1INCH. This external swap depends on the existence of sufficient liquidity in the WEETH‑WETH pool and on the price impact of the trade. If the pool is illiquid, the swap may fail, return a dramatically reduced amount, or consume excessive gas, effectively locking the user’s funds. The impact is that users who expect to be able to deposit and later withdraw their original WETH may find their balance stuck as WEETH, experience zero or near‑zero returns, or be forced to accept unfavorable market rates. The issue manifests whenever a user invokes depositWETHInEtherfi, which records the WEETH balance but provides no function to reverse the operation. All participants who rely on the contract to manage WETH – including end‑users, protocol integrators, and liquidity providers – are affected because the contract violates the basic accounting assumption that every deposit operation should have a matching withdrawal path. The problem was discovered during a manual security review when the auditor examined the EtherFi integration and noticed the presence of a deposit function without a corresponding withdraw function. The omission can be hard to spot because the contract compiles without errors, the deposit works as intended, and there is no explicit revert or warning; the missing functionality is a design‑level flaw rather than a code‑level bug. To remediate the issue, the contract should be extended with a withdrawWETHInEtherfi method that calls EtherFi’s redemption interface, transfers the reclaimed WETH back to the caller, and updates internal accounting accordingly. This addition restores the expected deposit‑withdraw symmetry, eliminates reliance on external swap liquidity, and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations that a deposited asset can be reclaimed on demand.

title: No slippage check when depositing to Pendle
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing slippage protection when the YieldStrategy contract deposits underlying assets into the Pendle protocol. The function depositToPendle forwards the user‑provided amount to the router.swapExactTokenForPt call, but deliberately sets the minPtOut argument to zero. Because minPtOut represents the minimum acceptable amount of PT tokens that must be received from the swap, a value of zero removes any guarantee that the swap will return a reasonable amount of PT. The root cause is that the contract does not calculate or enforce a lower bound based on market price or a user‑defined tolerance, effectively trusting the router to always deliver a fair amount. An attacker can exploit this by manipulating the market price between transaction submission and execution, or by front‑running the transaction with a large trade that pushes the price unfavourably. When the swap executes, the router may return far fewer PT tokens than the user expects, yet the transaction does not revert because the contract accepts any non‑negative output. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears successful in the UI, but the resulting PT balance is much lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as if the funds have vanished or the refund is missing. This discrepancy violates the accounting assumption that a deposit of a given amount of underlying should yield a predictable amount of PT, breaking the protocol’s financial logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review that inspected the parameters passed to the Pendle IPActionSwapPTV3 interface and noticed the hard‑coded zero for minPtOut. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not fail and no explicit error is emitted; only a post‑transaction balance check reveals the loss. The affected parties are any users who interact with the YieldStrategy’s deposit function, as well as the protocol that may suffer reduced liquidity or reputational damage. To remediate, the contract should compute an acceptable minimum PT output based on current market rates and a configurable slippage tolerance, and pass that value as the minPtOut parameter. This change restores the guarantee that the swap will not execute under adverse price conditions, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of preserving user value during deposits.

title: Low-level call is not checked in swapOn1INCH
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swapOn1INCH function, which invokes the 1inch aggregation router through a low‑level call and does not verify the boolean success flag returned by that call. Because the contract only checks that the balance of the output token is greater than or equal to the user‑provided _minAmountOut, a failed call can pass unnoticed when _minAmountOut is set to zero or a very low value. Consequently, the function may continue execution even though the external swap did not occur, leaving the input tokens locked in the contract and providing the caller with no output tokens. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who supplies malicious swap data that forces the router to return false or revert without propagating the error, allowing the contract to retain the input assets while the caller believes a successful exchange took place. The impact is that users who initiate a swap receive no tokens, see a transaction marked as successful, and potentially lose funds because the contract does not revert or emit an error. The issue manifests whenever swapOn1INCH is called with unchecked low‑level call semantics, especially when the caller specifies a zero or negligible _minAmountOut, effectively disabling the slippage safeguard. Affected parties include any user of the YieldStrategy contract, the protocol that relies on accurate accounting of swapped assets, and downstream contracts that assume the swap succeeded. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that flagged the missing require(success) after the low‑level call. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no explicit error event is emitted, and the only symptom is that the expected output token balance does not increase, which can be overlooked in UI displays. To remediate, the code should explicitly check the success flag (e.g., require(success, "Swap Failed")) and optionally decode any revert reason, and enforce a non‑zero minimum amount out or use a safe‑swap interface that reverts on failure. This class of bug is commonly known as an unchecked low‑level call or missing error handling, leading to silent failures and accounting mismatches. From the user's perspective, the UI will show a successful transaction receipt while the target token balance remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation of receiving at least the quoted amount, thereby breaking the business logic that a swap must either succeed or revert.

title: Possible lost msg.value
description:
[GeneralVault.sol#L75-L89](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/78f51a7a74ebe8adfd055bdbaedfddc05632566f/smart-contracts/GeneralVault.sol#L75-L89)  
[LidoVault.sol#L79-L104](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/78f51a7a74ebe8adfd055bdbaedfddc05632566f/smart-contracts/LidoVault.sol#L79-L104)  
[ConvexCurveLPVault.sol#L131-L149](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/78f51a7a74ebe8adfd055bdbaedfddc05632566f/smart-contracts/ConvexCurveLPVault.sol#L131-L149)  

Possible lost value in `depositCollateral` function call
poc:
In call `depositCollateral` can will send value and the asset can be an ERC20(!= address(0)), if `LidoVault` and `ConvexCurveLPVault` contract receive this call the funds will lost.  
Also in **LidoVault, L88** , if send as asset ETH(== address(0)) and send more value than `_amount`(msg.value > _amount), the excess will lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the generic `depositCollateral` routine that is shared by several vault contracts (GeneralVault, LidoVault, ConvexCurveLPVault). The function accepts an asset identifier and an amount, and is also marked payable so that callers may attach native Ether (msg.value). The logic attempts to differentiate between ERC20 tokens and Ether by checking whether the `_asset` address equals address(0). For ERC20 assets the code requires `msg.value == 0`; for Ether it requires `msg.value == _amount`. However, the validation is incomplete and can be bypassed, leading to situations where Ether is sent together with an ERC20 deposit or where the caller supplies more Ether than the declared `_amount`. In the first case the contract does not forward the attached Ether to any downstream protocol nor does it refund it, effectively locking the funds in the vault with no mechanism for retrieval. In the second case the excess Ether is similarly ignored after the internal `_depositToYieldPool` call, leaving the surplus stranded. The root cause is a mismatch between the asset‑type check and the payable handling: the contract treats the two concerns independently and fails to enforce a strict one‑to‑one correspondence between the asset type and the presence of Ether. An attacker—or an unwary user—can exploit this by calling `depositCollateral` with an ERC20 asset while also sending Ether, causing the Ether to disappear from their account. Likewise, a user can unintentionally over‑pay when depositing Ether, expecting the contract to either reject the transaction or return the surplus; instead the extra value is lost. The impact is the loss of user funds without any on‑chain indication other than the `DepositCollateral` event, which records only the asset address, sender, and claimed amount, not the amount of Ether actually received. The bug manifests whenever a contract that inherits `GeneralVault` (such as LidoVault or ConvexCurveLPVault) receives a deposit transaction with mismatched `msg.value`. It is especially insidious because the function is deliberately payable and developers may assume that the require statements fully protect against accidental Ether transfers, leading to false confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault contracts, where the auditor observed that the payable function performed only a superficial equality check but did not handle the case where Ether is sent with an ERC20 asset, nor did it guard against excess Ether when the asset is Ether. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that `msg.value` is zero for all ERC20 deposits and that it equals `_amount` for Ether deposits, and should also reject any transaction where the amount of Ether sent differs from the expected amount. Additionally, any leftover Ether should be explicitly reverted or forwarded to a safe address, and the redundant `require(msg.value > 0, ...)` check in LidoVault should be removed to avoid contradictory logic. By applying these conceptual fixes, the contract will align its accounting assumptions with actual value transfers, preventing silent fund loss and restoring confidence in the vault’s deposit flow.

title: `UNISWAP_FEE` is hardcoded which will lead to significant losses compared to optimal routing
description: In [`YieldManager`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/78f51a7a74ebe8adfd055bdbaedfddc05632566f/smart-contracts/YieldManager.sol#L48), `UNISWAP_FEE` is hardcoded, which reduce significantly the possibilities and will lead to non optimal routes. In particular, all swaps using ETH path will use the wrong pool as it will use the ETH / USDC 1% one due to this [line](https://github.com/sturdyfi/code4rena-may-2022/blob/d53f4f5f0b7b33a66e0081294be6117f6d6e17b4/contracts/protocol/libraries/swap/UniswapAdapter.sol#L50).
poc: For example for CRV / USDC, the optimal route is currently CRV -> ETH and ETH -> USDC, and the pool ETH / USDC with 1% fees is tiny compared to the ones with 0.3 or 0.1%. Therefore using the current implementation would create a significant loss of revenue.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded Uniswap fee constant (UNISWAP_FEE) inside the YieldManager contract’s swap adapter. Instead of dynamically selecting the most liquid pool with the lowest fee tier, the code always assumes a 1 % fee pool when constructing ETH‑based routes. This deterministic choice forces every swap that traverses an ETH hop to use the ETH/USDC 1 % pool, even though Uniswap V3 commonly offers 0.3 % and 0.1 % fee tiers that have far higher liquidity. The root cause is the static constant that bypasses Uniswap’s fee‑tier discovery logic, reducing the set of viable routes to a sub‑optimal subset. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the contract; the flaw is triggered automatically whenever the admin‑only distributeYield function initiates a token‑for‑token swap via the UniswapAdapter. Because the swap still succeeds, the error is subtle: the protocol receives a lower amount of output tokens than it could have achieved, resulting in lost revenue for the protocol and, consequently, reduced yields for all users who rely on the manager to earn interest. The impact manifests as a smaller USDC balance after a CRV → ETH → USDC conversion, for example, where the optimal path would have used the 0.3 % or 0.1 % ETH/USDC pool. Under normal operating conditions—any time the contract performs a swap involving ETH—the loss occurs, and it is not apparent from transaction success status alone. The affected parties include token holders delegating their assets to the protocol, the protocol’s treasury, and ultimately any downstream users who expect a certain return rate. The issue was uncovered during a manual code audit that flagged the constant UNISWAP_FEE as a hard‑coded value and cross‑checked the pool selection against Uniswap’s fee‑tier listings. The problem is hard to notice because swaps do not revert; they merely yield fewer tokens, which can be mistaken for normal market slippage or fee variance. To remediate, the fee parameter should be stored in a configurable mapping per token pair or, preferably, derived dynamically using Uniswap’s best‑pool query functions. Pre‑computing optimal paths, similar to the existing Curve pool mapping, or delegating the routing to an aggregator such as 1Inch or Paraswap would avoid the static fee assumption, improve routing efficiency, and lower gas costs. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded protocol parameters that lead to suboptimal routing and revenue loss, violating the accounting assumption that the contract will always obtain the maximum possible output from a given input swap.

title: `processYield
description: Yields will not be able to be distributed to lenders because attempts to do so will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the yield‑distribution routine of the ConvexCurveLPVault contract, specifically in the `processYield()` function. This function iterates over the entire list of extra reward contracts returned by `extraRewardsLength()` and attempts to transfer each reward token to lenders. Because the iteration has no explicit bound or pagination, the gas consumption can grow linearly with the number of extra rewards and with the complexity of each token transfer. The root cause is the absence of an offset/length limitation that is employed elsewhere in the code base (e.g., `YieldManager.distributeYield()`). Consequently, if the Convex protocol or an attacker adds a large number of extra reward tokens, or if those tokens contain a small amount of dust that forces a transfer, the loop may exceed the block gas limit and cause the transaction to revert. When this revert happens, the entire yield‑distribution process aborts, leaving lenders without any of the expected yield payments. From the user’s perspective, balances that should show newly earned rewards remain unchanged or appear as zero, leading to confusion or panic as their expected refunds or interest never arrive. The issue manifests only when the extra‑reward array grows beyond a certain size or when malicious dust is introduced, making it a conditional denial‑of‑service (DoS) attack against the protocol’s accounting logic. It was uncovered during a manual audit review of the vault’s source code, where the unbounded loop was highlighted as a potential gas‑limit failure. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because normal operation with a modest number of rewards proceeds without error, and the failure only appears under edge‑case conditions that may not be exercised in standard tests. To remediate the flaw, the contract should adopt a bounded iteration scheme similar to `YieldManager.distributeYield()`, adding offset and length parameters to limit each call’s workload, capping the number of extra rewards that can be processed in a single transaction, or otherwise enforcing a gas‑budget check. By doing so, the protocol can guarantee that yield distribution will complete reliably, preserving the expected financial outcomes for lenders and maintaining the integrity of the accounting model.

title: ConvexCurveLPVault’s `_transferYield` can become stuck with zero reward transfer
description:
Now there are no checks for the amounts to be transferred via _transferYield and _processTreasury. As reward token list is external and an arbitrary token can end up there, in the case when such token doesn’t allow for zero amount transfers, the reward retrieval can become unavailable.

I.e. processYield() can be fully blocked for even an extended period, with some low probability, which cannot be controlled otherwise as pool reward token list is external.

Setting the severity to medium as reward gathering is a base functionality for the system and its availability is affected.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution logic of the ConvexCurveLPVault contract, where the internal functions responsible for moving harvested token rewards – _transferYield and the helper _processTreasury – do not verify that the amount to be transferred is greater than zero before invoking a token transfer. Because the vault maintains an external list of incentive tokens, any ERC‑20 token that explicitly rejects a transfer of zero units can cause the entire processYield execution path to revert when the calculated reward for that token is zero. The root cause is the absence of a guard clause checking for a positive yieldAmount prior to calling TransferHelper.safeTransfer and IERC20.safeTransfer. An attacker or simply a benign market condition can trigger this scenario: if a token in the reward list yields no accrual for a given harvest period, the contract attempts a zero‑value transfer, the token contract reverts, and the vault’s yield processing halts. Consequently, the vault becomes unable to deliver any reward to its users until the offending token is manually removed from the reward list or a non‑zero amount is generated, both of which depend on external governance actions and cannot be guaranteed in a timely manner. Users observing the UI will notice that expected rewards remain missing, balances appear unchanged, or the “claim rewards” transaction fails with a generic revert, creating a perception that the system is broken. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where reviewers examined the transfer flow and identified the missing positive‑amount check. It is difficult to spot in routine testing because zero‑value transfers are often considered no‑ops and many ERC‑20 tokens silently accept them; only a subset that enforces a non‑zero amount will exhibit the failure, making the bug intermittent and hard to reproduce. To remediate the problem, the contract should conditionally execute the treasury and yield‑manager transfers only when the computed yieldAmount for a token exceeds zero, thereby avoiding zero‑value calls to external token contracts. Additionally, the vault could filter out or whitelist tokens known to reject zero transfers, or modify the TransferHelper to safely handle such cases, ensuring that reward collection remains reliable and that users receive their entitled yields without unexpected reverts.

title: Withdrawing ETH collateral with max uint256 amount value reverts transaction
description: Withdrawing ETH collateral via the `withdrawCollateral` function using `type(uint256).max` for the `_amount` parameter reverts the transaction due to `_asset` being the zero-address and `IERC20Detailed(_asset).decimals()` not working for native ETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the withdrawal of native ETH collateral through a generic `withdrawCollateral` function that is also used for ERC‑20 assets. The contract treats a special sentinel value – the maximum uint256 (`type(uint256).max`) – as a request to withdraw the entire balance. When a user passes this sentinel for an ERC‑20 token, the code correctly queries the token's `decimals()` function via the `IERC20Detailed` interface and calculates the actual withdrawal amount. However, for native ETH the `_asset` argument is the zero address, and the contract still attempts to call `IERC20Detailed(_asset).decimals()`. Because the zero address does not implement the ERC‑20 interface, the call fails and the transaction reverts. The root cause is the assumption that every collateral asset, including native ETH, conforms to the ERC‑20 `decimals()` method, and the use of a universal sentinel value without a guard for the special case of ETH. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract; the flaw is triggered simply by a legitimate user who tries to withdraw all of their ETH collateral using the maximum‑uint256 sentinel. The impact is that the withdrawal transaction reverts, leaving the user's ETH stuck in the vault until they specify an explicit amount smaller than the sentinel, or until the contract is patched. This condition occurs only when the `_asset` parameter equals the zero address (native ETH) and the `_amount` parameter is set to `type(uint256).max`. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal logic for both ERC‑20 tokens and native ETH. It can be difficult to notice because the same code path is used for all assets and the failure only manifests for the specific combination of ETH and the sentinel value, a situation that may not be covered by standard unit tests. From a user’s perspective the UI may allow the user to request “withdraw all” but the transaction fails with no funds transferred, leading to confusion such as “my balance stays the same” or “the withdraw button does nothing”. This bug belongs to the class of "incorrect handling of sentinel values for native assets" and violates the accounting assumption that the contract can uniformly query token metadata for any collateral type. To remediate, the contract should detect when `_asset` is the zero address and either skip the `decimals()` call or use a hard‑coded 18‑decimal value for ETH, and it should handle the sentinel amount by directly using the vault’s stored ETH balance rather than attempting an ERC‑20 specific calculation. In short, the fix is to treat native ETH as a special case when processing maximum‑withdrawal requests, ensuring that the withdrawal amount is derived from the actual ETH balance without invoking ERC‑20 interface functions.

title: Yield can be unfairly divided because of MEV/Just-in-time stablecoin deposits
description:
[YieldManager.sol#L129-L134](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/YieldManager.sol#L129-L134)  
[YieldManager.sol#L160-L161](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/YieldManager.sol#L160-L161)  

An attacker can use MEV (via gas auction or Flashbots or control of miners) to cause an unfair division of yield. By providing a very large (relative to the size of all other stablecoin deposits combined) stablecoin deposit Just-in-Time before an admin’s call to [distributeYield](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/YieldManager.sol#L118) the stablecoin deposited by the attacker will receive a very large amount of the yield and the attacker can immediately withdraw their deposit after yield is distributed. We assume this allows an attacker to get a lot of the yield reward even though they haven’t provided any deposit that has been borrowed. However, the exact mechanism for how yield is distributed to lenders of a particular stablecoin is in LendingPool.sol, which is out of scope. However it is implied in [the documentation of this repo](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/README.md?plain=1#L52) that it is based on the balance of that asset the lender has provided. We have confirmed that [in LendingPool.sol the yield is distributed based on the proportion of the asset provided](https://github.com/sturdyfi/code4rena-may-2022/blob/d53f4f5f0b7b33a66e0081294be6117f6d6e17b4/contracts/protocol/lendingpool/LendingPool.sol#L182). However, even ignoring this, MEV can still be used to unfairly hurt lenders of other stablecoins.
poc:
1. An attacker watches the mempool for calls to [distributeYield](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/YieldManager.sol#L118) by the admin.
  2. The attacker orders the block’s transactions (most easily using a flashbots bundle) in the following order:  
i. Attacker deposits stablecoins to lend (ideally the stablecoin will be the one with the least volume).  
ii. admin’s call to distributeYield happens.  
iii. Attacker withdraws their deposit.  

The attacker has thus made the asset they deposited (and thus themselves) receive much of the yield even though they provide no value to Sturdy since none of their deposit is ever borrowed so the never do anything to earn yield for sturdy. This attack can be done by a whale or by borrowing (even from sturdy) assets and converting them to a stablecoins accepted by sturdy before i. and returning them after iii. This will essentially be cost free for the attacker, none of their capital will ever be tied up by borrowers.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic front‑running attack that lets an adversary obtain an outsized share of the protocol’s yield by depositing a large amount of a stablecoin immediately before the admin executes the distributeYield function. YieldManager distributes rewards based on the current balance of each stablecoin lender at the moment the distribution call is processed, without taking a snapshot of deposits from the previous period. Because the contract does not lock in the set of eligible deposits, an attacker can monitor the mempool for the upcoming distributeYield call, submit a Flashbots bundle (or otherwise control transaction ordering) that first adds a substantial temporary deposit, then allows the admin’s distribution to run, and finally withdraws the deposit in the same block. The attacker’s temporary balance inflates their share of the proportional yield calculation, letting them capture a large portion of the reward even though their funds were never borrowed and thus contributed no real value to the protocol. Other lenders of the same or other stablecoins receive a reduced portion of the yield, effectively seeing their expected rewards shrink or disappear. This attack can be performed by a whale or by borrowing assets, converting them to an accepted stablecoin, and reverting the conversion after the withdrawal, making the exploit essentially cost‑free. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined YieldManager.sol and LendingPool.sol and identified that yield distribution depends on the instantaneous balance rather than a snapshot, a pattern that is vulnerable to MEV. The problem is subtle because the distribution transaction itself succeeds and emits no error; the loss manifests only as a lower-than‑expected reward, which can be difficult for users to notice unless they closely track their yield accrual. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑allocation manipulation and time‑of‑state dependency vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective, they expect a proportional reward based on the amount they have deposited for the entire period, but after the attack they may see no increase in their balance or a much smaller credit, feeling that “my funds disappeared” or that the “refund calculation is wrong.” To mitigate the issue, the protocol should avoid using the live balance at distribution time, for example by snapshotting eligible deposits, ignoring just‑in‑time deposits for the next reward cycle, or by submitting the distributeYield call through a private channel such as Flashbots to prevent mempool exposure. A more robust design would separate the accounting period from the execution moment, ensuring that only deposits that were present before the start of the period are eligible for rewards, thereby eliminating the incentive for MEV‑driven manipulation.

title: Attacker can inflate share price and cause loss for users
description:
When the share amount is calculated and totalSupply is zero, the code uses the deposit amount and doesn't add extra precision, this will give the attacker the ability to inflate the share price up to 1000 * 1e18 and cause a loss for depositors because of rounding error.
```solidity
function _convertToShares(uint256 _usdValue, uint256 _usdAUM, uint256 totalTrsySupply) {
    return totalTrsySupply == 0 ? _usdValue : (_usdValue * totalTrsySupply) / _usdAUM;
}
```
This is one example that this could happen:
1. Suppose there is one token(T1) with 100% weight in the Fyde token list and there is no tax. T1 price is 1.
2. Attacker deposits 10 * 1e18 T1 tokens into the Fyde and receive 10 * 1e18 shares. The Fyde's AUM will be 10 * 1e18.
3. Now the price of token T1 increased 10% and its 1.1 and Fyde's AUM isn't updated yet and AUM is still 10 * 1e18.
4. Attacker would withdraw 9.1 * 1e18 T1 tokens and it's value with be 1.1 * 9.09 * 1e18 = 10 * 1e18 which is equal to AUM so code would burn 10 * 1e18 share from attacker.
5. Now totalSupply is equal to 0 but real AUM is 1e18.
6. Attacker would deposit 1 wei T1 token and the share price would be about 1e18.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision error in the function that converts a deposited USD value into protocol shares when the total supply of shares is zero. The implementation returns the raw deposit amount instead of scaling it by the protocol’s fixed‑point precision (typically 1e18). Because the conversion omits this factor, an attacker can manipulate the share price after all existing shares have been burned. The attack proceeds as follows: the attacker first deposits a sizable amount of an underlying token, receives a proportional number of shares and inflates the protocol’s assets‑under‑management (AUM). After a price change of the underlying token, the attacker withdraws almost the entire amount, burning all shares so that totalSupply becomes zero while the real AUM remains non‑zero. At this point the conversion function falls back to the zero‑supply branch and assigns shares equal to the raw deposit amount, effectively giving the attacker an astronomically high share price (up to 1000 × 1e18). Subsequent honest users who deposit after this state will receive far fewer underlying assets per share, causing a loss of funds. The issue occurs only when the total supply of shares reaches zero before the AUM is updated, a situation that can arise after a full withdrawal or a forced burn. All participants who later deposit are affected because the accounting invariant that each share represents a constant fraction of the AUM is broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the share‑conversion logic and identified the missing precision factor. It is difficult to notice because the zero‑supply condition is rare and the rounding discrepancy may appear negligible in normal operation, yet it enables a dramatic inflation of share price. To remediate, the conversion should always apply the protocol’s fixed‑point scaling (for example multiplying the USD value by 1e18 when totalSupply is zero) or use a unified formula that never loses precision, thereby preserving the invariant that share price reflects the true value of the underlying assets. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a withdrawal the protocol reports an absurdly high share price, and new deposits receive far fewer tokens than expected – users expect a fair 1:1 value but may see their balance shrink or receive zero tokens despite depositing funds. This class of bug is a share‑price manipulation caused by improper handling of the zero‑supply edge case and rounding errors in financial calculations.

title: Attacker can reenter RelayerV2 with ERC777 tokens and steal funds
description:
There's no reentrancy guard in the RelayerV2 contract and if one of the deposit or withdraw tokens had a hook (ERC777 or ...) then it would be possible to reenter the RelayerV2 contract again and steal the funds while the state is wrong. There are multiple ways that attackers can exploit this, one way is to set previous caching prices for tokens for the current operation. This is the:
1. Suppose token T1 is ERC777 and has a hook in transfers and it's used in the Fyde contract.
2. First Attacker would deposit T1 token by calling deposit().
3. Code would call _enableOracleCache(T1) and OracleModule would set cacheEnabled = true.
4. Now when deposit() wants to transfer T1 token, the hook function will be called and execution will reach the attacker contract.
5. Now attacker would call deposit() and use T2 and T3 tokens to deposit.
6. In this deposit() call when code reaches the OracleModule.useCache(), because cacheEnabled = true so cache price will be used and set for T2 and T3 (getPriceInUSD() would return the cache price)
7. In the end attacker was able to set old cache prices for tokens T2 and T3. Attackers can use this to steal funds whenever the old cached prices show very wrong value (For example a token price was very high in the past and it's still in the cache). There could be other methods to exploit this too.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the RelayerV2 contract that arises when the contract interacts with tokens that implement transfer callbacks such as ERC777. The root cause is the absence of a reentrancy guard combined with the contract’s reliance on an oracle cache that is enabled before an external token transfer is performed. When a token with a hook is deposited, the contract calls an internal function that enables price caching, then initiates the token transfer. The ERC777 hook can invoke arbitrary code in the attacker’s contract before the original deposit call finishes. During this callback the attacker can call deposit or withdraw again, causing the oracle module to read the still‑enabled cache and apply stale or attacker‑controlled prices for other tokens. By supplying tokens whose cached prices were previously high, the attacker can cause the contract to value subsequent deposits at an inflated amount, withdraw more funds than actually deposited, and effectively steal assets. The impact is that funds can disappear from honest users, balances may show zero or unexpected values, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about token valuation are broken. The exploit can be triggered whenever a user deposits an ERC777 (or any token with a transfer hook) while the contract’s cacheEnabled flag is true, which occurs after the first call to _enableOracleCache. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual security review that identified the missing non‑reentrant modifier and the interaction with the OracleModule. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for standard ERC20 tokens and the price discrepancy only appears when the cache is manipulated, which may not be evident in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should be protected with a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or restructure the logic to perform all state changes before any external token call, and ensure the oracle cache is disabled or refreshed after each external interaction. This class of bug falls under reentrancy via token callbacks, a known issue where external calls allow an attacker to re‑enter a contract and corrupt its internal state, leading to loss of funds and broken business logic.

title: Code doesn't validate stale AUM values
description:
In the new design of the system, the value of the AUM should be updated by the off-chain bot. The issue is that there is no validation time for the AUM value and the code assumes that AUM is valid, this would cause issues when the off-chain bot can't update the AUM value for any reason. There are multiple reasons for AUM to not be updated, for example when the Ethereum network is busy when there is a bug in the off-chain bot, or when it's comprised. This is the POC for this issue:
1. Suppose the AUM is $100K and the off-chain bot updated the protocol AUM value.
2. Suppose the off-chain bot is down and real AUM has reached $120K but the AUM value in protocol state is still $100K.
3. Now Attacker can deposit tokens into the protocol and receive more shares (because AUM is lower in the protocol).
4. Protocol allows users to interact with the contracts even when AUM hasn't been updated for a long time.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step for the protocol’s reported Assets Under Management (AUM) value. In the current design the AUM is supplied by an off‑chain bot and stored on‑chain without any timestamp or expiration check, so the contract always treats the stored number as up‑to‑date. This assumption breaks when the bot cannot publish a new value – for example during network congestion, a software bug, or a compromise of the bot. When the on‑chain AUM lags behind the real market value, the conversion formula that mints protocol shares for deposited tokens uses a stale, lower denominator. An attacker can therefore deposit a given amount of tokens while the stored AUM is artificially low and receive more shares than the true value of the assets would justify. Those extra shares can later be redeemed for a larger portion of the real pool, effectively draining funds from honest participants. The impact is a dilution of existing shareholders and a potential loss of protocol capital, which may manifest to users as unexpected reductions in their balances or missing refunds after withdrawal. The issue appears whenever the protocol allows deposits, withdrawals or any share‑minting operation while the AUM timestamp is older than an acceptable window. All users of the protocol, as well as the protocol’s governance and token holders, are affected because the accounting guarantees are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that compared the expected lifecycle of the off‑chain oracle with the contract’s logic and noticed the absence of any freshness check. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the UI continues to display the stored AUM and user balances appear correct until a malicious actor exploits the stale value. The recommended mitigation is to treat the AUM as a time‑sensitive oracle: store a last‑updated timestamp, define a maximum age (e.g., a few minutes), and reject any interaction that relies on an AUM older than that threshold. If the value is stale, the contract should pause deposits or fallback to a safe on‑chain price source, thereby preserving the integrity of share calculations and preventing fund loss.

title: User may lose funds if there are duplicate tokens in the deposit list
description:
RelayerV2 doesn't check that token lists don't have duplicate items and doesn't support duplicate items in the list. If token lists have duplicate items then users may lose funds because some logics won't work as designed. For example when users set _keepGovRights as True, code loops through the tokens list and unstake all the RelayerV2 remaining balance, and it will cause the user to not receive the duplicate amounts. This is POC:
1. User would call deposit() with token list [T1, T1] and _keepGovRights = True.
2. Code would deposit tokens into Fyde contract and receive 2* sharesAfterTax sTrsy tokens.
3. Now code would loop through token list to transfer user sTrsy and also unstake the tax sTrsy.
4. For the first T1 code would transfer sharesAfterTax and also unstake all the remaining balance which is sharesAfterTax.
5. For the second T2 because the balance is 0 code won't transfer any token to the user. So User would receive sharesAfterTax while he should have received 2 * sharesAfterTax.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the RelayerV2 contract’s handling of the token list supplied to the deposit() function. The code assumes that each token appears only once in the list and does not perform any duplicate‑item validation. When a user calls deposit() with a list that contains the same token address more than once and sets the _keepGovRights flag to true, the contract iterates over the list and, for each entry, transfers the user’s share tokens (sTrsy) and then unstakes the remaining balance of that token. Because the unstake step removes the entire remaining balance on the first occurrence, the second (duplicate) entry finds a zero balance and therefore transfers nothing. From the user’s point of view the expectation is to receive twice the amount of sTrsy shares (one for each list entry), but the actual result is only a single share amount, effectively causing a loss of funds. This issue manifests only when duplicate tokens are present and the keep‑governance‑rights option is enabled; normal deposits with unique tokens behave correctly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the loop logic and identified that the contract never checks for duplicates. It can be hard to notice because the UI may allow users to select the same token twice without warning, and the contract does not emit a specific error for the missing transfer, so the discrepancy appears as a silent shortfall. The impact is financial: users receive fewer tokens than they deposited, and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent because the internal balance accounting assumes each token is processed exactly once. To remediate the issue the contract should either reject deposit calls that contain duplicate token addresses, or it should normalize the list by removing duplicates before processing, or it should adjust the unstake logic so that each iteration only withdraws the portion attributable to that specific list entry rather than the entire remaining balance. Implementing any of these fixes restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between deposited tokens and received shares and prevents inadvertent fund loss.

title: Slippage check may be inefficient in deposit() when _keepGovRights=True
description: In deposit() function code checks that slippageChecker with the sum of the minted shares sharesToMint, the issue is that when _keepGovRights = True then the code sends users different sTrsy tokens and there is no slippage check for their values. So even so some of the tokens may be higher than slippageChecker but the user may receive unfavorable sTrsy tokens.
