As a result, a user who receives a signed RFQ order can keep the order off‑chain and wait until market conditions change. When the price moves in a direction that makes the order profitable, the user can submit the stale order to the swapWithRfqOrder function and have it executed, effectively receiving a free option. The root cause is the absence of an on‑chain revocation or nonce system that would allow the order issuer to mark a specific order hash as cancelled. Because the contract only checks the expires field, it assumes the order remains valid for its whole lifetime, which is a flawed business assumption. Exploitation is straightforward: the market maker signs an order, later decides the price is no longer acceptable, but cannot cancel it; the user stores the signed data, monitors the market, and when the price swing makes the quoted price favorable, they call swapWithRfqOrder with the original parameters. The impact is that the market maker may be forced to trade at a price that is no longer aligned with its risk appetite, leading to potential loss of capital or reduced profitability. In extreme cases, a malicious user could create two contradictory RFQ orders – one to buy and another to sell at overlapping price ranges – and execute them sequentially, achieving a risk‑free arbitrage that extracts value from the market maker. The issue appears only when a market maker needs to cancel an order early, which is a common operational requirement in volatile markets. It primarily affects market makers who rely on the RFQ mechanism for liquidity provision, as well as the overall protocol health because the perceived fairness of the order book is compromised. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of RFQ orders and noticed the lack of any cancellation path. It can be difficult to spot because the presence of an expires field gives a false sense of safety, and the contract code does not contain any explicit “cancel” function, so reviewers may assume expiration is sufficient. The recommended remediation is to add an on‑chain invalidation method, such as a mapping of revoked order hashes that the market maker can update, or a nonce‑based scheme that allows selective cancellation. This change restores the ability of the order issuer to withdraw an order immediately, aligning the contract behaviour with the intended business logic that orders should be cancellable at any time before execution.

title: M-4 Paused State Overly Restricts Liquidity Removal and Order Cancellation
description:
This issue arises when _validateLPPriceAndDistributeFees detects a significant drop in the LP token price and triggers _pause().
In this paused state, the removeLiquidity() function is disabled, preventing LP holders from withdrawing their tokens at a time when market conditions could be deteriorating. Moreover, market makers cannot cancel their outstanding orders in the LOB contract, leaving those orders to hang in a potentially volatile situation. This can compound losses if prices move further against them while the contract is paused.
The issue is classified as medium severity because it restricts user access to their funds and prohibits cancelling potentially risky orders during severe market shifts.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑broad pause mechanism that is automatically activated when the system detects a sharp decline in the price of the liquidity‑provider (LP) token. The pause is implemented by calling a global _pause() function inside the _validateLPPriceAndDistributeFees routine. Because the pause flag is applied to the entire protocol, the removeLiquidity() entry point becomes disabled and the order‑cancellation function in the limit‑order‑book (LOB) contract is also blocked. As a result, any LP holder who tries to withdraw their share of the pool during a market downturn receives a reverted transaction or simply sees no change in their balance, while market makers are unable to cancel outstanding orders that may now be deeply out‑of‑the‑money. This situation can exacerbate losses because the market may continue to move against the open positions while they remain locked in the contract. The issue manifests only when the price‑drop detection logic triggers, i.e., during severe market shifts, and it affects all participants who rely on the ability to exit the protocol or manage risk through order cancellation. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between price validation and the pause flag. It is difficult to notice because a pause is generally perceived as a protective measure, yet the implementation unintentionally blocks legitimate user actions that are essential for risk mitigation. Conceptually, the fix is to replace the monolithic pause with a finer‑grained control flag (for example, a slashingAvailableStatus) that allows liquidity removal and order cancellation even when the protocol is in a protective state, while still preventing new order placement or other potentially harmful actions by the primary market maker. This adjustment restores users’ ability to retrieve funds and manage open positions during volatile periods, aligning the contract’s behavior with expected business logic and accounting assumptions about fund accessibility and risk management.

title: M-1 Commission rates can be set to 100%
description: The issue is identified within the OnchainLOB.sol#L90 of the LOB contract. The commissions (admincommission, marketmakercommission, passiveorderpayout) can be set to 100%, which presents a centralization risk. Such a configuration could potentially be exploited by the contract administrator.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted configuration of commission rates in the on‑chain limit order book contract. The contract exposes three fee parameters – an administrator fee, a market‑maker fee and a passive‑order payout – that can each be set by the contract administrator to any unsigned integer value. Because there is no validation that the sum of these rates is bounded below 100 % of the trade value, the administrator can configure the system so that the total fee equals the entire amount transferred in a trade. This situation arises when the admin calls the setter functions for the commission variables and supplies a value representing 100 % (or higher) of the order size. An attacker with administrative privileges can therefore capture the full proceeds of any order, effectively stealing funds that should belong to the trader or market maker. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a successful trade the expected payout is missing; the UI may show the order as filled while the user’s balance remains unchanged or drops to zero. The impact is a centralization risk: the protocol’s economic model assumes that fees are a small fraction of the trade value, and the ability to set fees to 100 % breaks that accounting assumption, erodes trust, and can lead to total loss of user capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑modifying functions, where the lack of a require statement limiting the fee range was noted. Because the contract does not emit a warning or revert when an extreme fee is set, the problem can be hard to notice unless the auditor inspects the setter logic or monitors on‑chain events for unusually high fee values. The recommended mitigation is to introduce explicit checks that enforce a maximum total commission (for example, not exceeding a few percent of the trade value) and to consider moving the control of fee parameters to a decentralized governance process, thereby reducing the single point of failure.

title: M-2 Lack of market maker address check
description: A flaw has been detected within the OnchainLOB.sol#L313 function of the LOB contract. If the market maker is not a smart contract that implements the onTrade function and the shouldinvokeon_trade flag is set to true, calling the placeOrder function will result in a revert. This occurs because the contract attempts to call onTrade on the market maker's address, expecting it to be a valid function call.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the market maker address in the onchainlob contract. The placeorder function assumes that the address stored as market maker is a smart contract that implements an ontrade function. When the shouldinvokeon_trade flag is true the contract performs an external call to ontrade on the stored address. If the address is not a contract, or the contract does not provide the expected function, the call fails and the whole transaction reverts. This situation can occur when the market maker is set to an externally owned account, a contract without the required interface, or a malicious address deliberately supplied by an attacker. The root cause is the absence of any code‑size or interface check in the constructor and in the change market maker address function, allowing an arbitrary address to be accepted. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who can change the market maker address, or who can influence its initial value, can replace it with a non‑compliant address. Subsequent calls to placeorder will revert, causing a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users are unable to submit orders. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails with a revert, often reported as a generic “call to ontrade failed” error, and no funds are transferred, leading to confusion and wasted gas. The impact is medium severity because it does not directly steal funds but can halt trading activity and degrade the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of placeorder and identified the unchecked external call. It may be hard to notice because normal test scenarios use a correct market maker contract, so the failure only appears when an unexpected address is supplied. The proper remediation is to add explicit checks that the market maker address contains contract code and that the contract implements the ontrade function, for example by using the extcodesize opcode together with an ERC165 interface detection or a try‑catch pattern before storing the address. By enforcing these checks the contract will reject invalid market maker addresses, preventing the revert and restoring expected behavior where users can place orders and receive the anticipated trade execution without unexpected failures.

title: M-3 Lack of Upgradeability and Pausable Functionality
description: The issue is identified within the OnchainLOB.sol contract. There is an issue due to the lack of upgradeability and pausable functionality. While adding these features introduces additional centralization risks, they are crucial for handling scenarios where the contract becomes malfunctioned. The pausable function, in particular, allows halting all operations except for order removal, ensuring orderly migration to a new contract version. The issue is classified as medium severity because it impacts the flexibility and maintainability of the contract, potentially leading to prolonged downtime and operational risks in case of malfunctions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any upgradeability or pausable mechanism in the order‑book contract. Because the contract cannot be replaced with a patched version nor temporarily halted, any discovered bug or unexpected behaviour remains active for the lifetime of the deployment. This missing administrative control means that when a flaw is identified, the protocol is forced to continue processing orders with the defective logic, potentially allowing an attacker to repeatedly exploit the flaw, drain liquidity, or lock user funds. The impact is that users may see their balances remain unchanged, orders stay stuck, or withdrawals fail, while the contract continues to accept new orders. The condition occurs because the source code does not inherit OpenZeppelin upgradeable proxy patterns or Pausable contracts and provides no role‑based functions to stop execution. All participants – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol operators – are affected because they rely on the contract’s ability to enforce business rules and to recover from emergencies. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s inheritance hierarchy and noted the lack of any pause or upgrade functions. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation; only when an edge‑case error surfaces does the inability to halt or upgrade become evident, leading to prolonged downtime and operational risk. The recommended remediation is to refactor the contract to use a proxy upgrade pattern (such as UUPS or Transparent) together with AccessControl‑based roles for upgrade and pause, and to renounce the deployer role after the system is battle‑tested. This would allow the team to halt all functions except order removal in an emergency and to migrate state to a new implementation, aligning with the business assumption that the system can be safely stopped during incidents. The class of bug is a missing governance/administrative control, often described as “absence of upgradeability and pausable mechanisms”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a malfunction the UI may still allow order placement but withdrawals return zero, balances appear frozen, and cancellations are ignored, violating the expectation that the protocol can be paused for emergency handling and that bugs can be fixed without redeploying a whole new contract.

title: M-4 Potential Accumulation of Unused Commissions Due to Rounding
description: The issue is pinpointed within the OnchainLOB.sol#L543 function of the LOB contract. There is an issue related to the accumulation of unused commissions due to rounding operations, which can lead to significant residual amounts, especially over prolonged contract operation scaled by tokenyscaling_factor. The issue is classified as medium severity because while the accumulated amounts might seem minor individually, they can sum up to a significant value over time, leading to potential discrepancies and inefficiencies in the commission calculation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑induced dust accumulation in the commission distribution logic of the on‑chain limit order book contract. When the contract splits the total commission into three parts – the admin share, the market‑maker share and the passive‑order payout – each part is calculated using integer arithmetic and a token scaling factor. Because the division truncates fractional units, a small remainder is left unused in each transaction. Over many trades this remainder, often called dust, is not reclaimed but remains locked in the contract’s balance. The root cause is the order of arithmetic: the admin amount is derived from a separate calculation instead of being computed as the residual of total commission minus the other two shares, allowing the rounding error to persist. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the issue manifests automatically as the protocol processes trades, leading to a gradual discrepancy between the expected commission totals and the actual distributed amounts. From a user perspective the symptoms are subtle: the admin dashboard may show a growing unexplained balance, market makers may receive slightly lower payouts than anticipated, and the UI can display zero or negligible commission for the admin even after many transactions. The problem becomes noticeable only after prolonged operation when the accumulated dust reaches a material value, which can affect the protocol’s accounting integrity, reduce efficiency, and potentially erode trust among participants. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the commission‑splitting function and identified the residual term left after integer division. It is hard to notice because each individual rounding loss is tiny and does not trigger alerts, yet the systematic nature of the calculation ensures the loss compounds. The appropriate remediation is to compute the admin amount as the exact residual: adminAmount = totalCommissionAmount – marketMakerAmount – passiveOrderPayout, thereby eliminating the need for a separate rounding‑prone calculation and preventing dust from accumulating. This change restores the intended accounting invariants, ensures that all commission funds are correctly allocated, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the protocol’s financial expectations.

title: M-5 Lack of The Expiry Parameter
description: The issue arises within the OnchainLOB.sol#L199 function of the LOB contract. There is an issue due to the absence of an expiration parameter for orders. Without this parameter, there is no guarantee that an order is added to the blockchain before a specified timestamp, which can be problematic if a transaction remains pending for a long time. This can lead to unintended execution of stale orders, potentially causing financial losses or market disruptions. The issue is classified as medium severity because it affects the timing and validity of order execution, which can impact the reliability and efficiency of the trading platform.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing expiration parameter in the order placement function of the on‑chain limit order book. Because the contract does not record a timestamp after which an order must be included in a block, any order that remains pending in the mempool can be mined at an arbitrary later time. This allows stale orders—orders that were intended to be valid only up to a certain time—to be executed after market conditions have changed. The root cause is the absence of a time‑bound check in the placeOrder logic; the contract assumes that once an order is submitted it remains valid indefinitely. An attacker or even a benign miner can include a delayed transaction after the intended deadline, causing the order to be matched against current prices that may be unfavorable to the original maker. The impact includes unexpected loss of funds for the order creator, distortion of market prices, and potential liquidity disruption for the whole protocol. The condition occurs whenever a transaction stays pending for a long period, for example due to network congestion or low gas price, and there is no on‑chain enforcement of a maximum age. All participants who rely on timely order execution—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LOB contract where the auditor noted that the placeOrder function does not accept an expires argument and that no block‑timestamp validation is performed. Because the bug manifests only when a transaction is delayed, it can be hard to notice in normal testing where orders are mined immediately. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an order that was expected to be cancelled after a deadline is instead filled, resulting in a trade that the user did not anticipate, sometimes showing a zero or negative balance change. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of missing time‑bound validation or stale order execution. To remediate, the contract should be modified to accept an explicit expiration timestamp and to revert the transaction if the current block timestamp exceeds this value, thereby guaranteeing that orders cannot be executed after their intended validity period.

title: M-6 Centralization risks
description: The issue has been identified within the HanjiLOB.sol#L55 and HanjiWatchDog.sol contracts. The current design of the contract grants significant centralized control to the administrator and pauser roles. The administrator has extensive powers, including the ability to upgrade the contract to any arbitrary address, pause or unpause the contract, and configure critical settings. The pauser role can also pause and unpause the contract. This concentration of control introduces centralization risks, as a single compromised or malicious administrator or pauser could disrupt or manipulate the contract, leading to potential security breaches or operational failures. Additionally, allowing the pauser role to unpause the contract could be risky if the contract is in an unstable state, as it could inadvertently enable harmful operations. Moreover, the owner of the HanjiWatchDog contract can upgrade the contract's implementation. If the new implementation is flawed or if the HanjiWatchDog contract is compromised, the creation of new orders in the HanjiLOB contract may be blocked. The issue is classified as medium severity due to the potential impact on the contract's security and operational integrity if these roles are exploited.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from the design of the HanjiLOB and HanjiWatchDog contracts where the administrator and pauser roles hold excessive authority. The administrator can upgrade the contract implementation to any address, pause and unpause the contract, and change critical parameters. The pauser can also pause and unpause the contract. Because these powers are held by a single address, a compromised or malicious admin or pauser can arbitrarily replace the logic, halt the protocol, or resume it while the system is in an unstable state. An attacker who gains control of the admin key could deploy a malicious implementation that blocks the creation of new orders, redirects funds, or inserts back‑doors, while a malicious pauser could repeatedly pause the contract to cause denial‑of‑service or unpause it to allow harmful operations before the protocol has recovered. The impact is that users may see transactions revert, orders fail to be created, balances appear frozen, or unexpected behavior occur, effectively eroding trust and potentially leading to loss of funds if the upgraded logic contains a flaw. The condition occurs whenever the admin or pauser executes their privileged functions, especially during upgrades or when the contract is paused. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and token holders—are affected because the protocol’s core functionality depends on these roles. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which highlighted that the concentration of power is not obvious from the code and may be missed in functional testing because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation. The problem is hard to notice because the privileged functions are standard in many upgradable contracts and the code does not emit warnings about the single‑point‑of‑failure nature of the roles. To remediate, the admin and pauser privileges should be transferred to a multisignature wallet so that multiple parties must approve upgrades, pauses, and unpauses, and the ability for the pauser to unpause should be removed, leaving that capability only to the multisig‑controlled admin. This reduces the attack surface by eliminating a single point of compromise and aligns the governance model with the expectation that no single actor can unilaterally disrupt or manipulate the protocol.

title: M-7 Anyone can set the marketmaker address
description: This issue has been identified within the HanjiLOB.sol#L313 function of the HanjiLOB contract. The function allows the administrator to change the market maker address and includes a flag, shouldinvokeontrade, that determines whether callbacks are invoked after each trade for the marketmaker address. However, the function also permits anyone to change the market maker address if the current market maker address is set to zero. This presents a security risk as it could enable any actor to set a malicious marketmaker address with the shouldinvokeontrade flag set to true. This setup could allow them to engage in sandwich attacks and claim additional fees, thereby manipulating market operations. The issue is classified as medium severity because it introduces a potential vulnerability that could be exploited to interfere with the market's integrity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized address update bug in the market‑maker configuration function of the HanjiLOB contract. The function is intended to allow only the contract administrator to change the market‑maker address and to set a flag (shouldInvokeOnTrade) that controls whether the market‑maker receives callbacks after each trade. However, the implementation contains a conditional check that skips the owner‑only restriction when the current market‑maker address is the zero address. As a result, any external actor can call the function while the market‑maker slot is empty and set themselves as the market‑maker, optionally enabling the callback flag. The root cause is a missing access‑control guard for the zero‑address state, effectively creating an access‑control bypass. An attacker can exploit this by invoking the function, supplying a malicious contract address as the new market‑maker and setting shouldInvokeOnTrade to true. Once registered, the malicious market‑maker receives trade callbacks and can execute sandwich attacks, manipulate price data, or claim extra protocol fees. The impact includes distortion of market pricing, loss of user funds through higher slippage or fee siphoning, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s integrity. The condition under which the bug is exploitable is when the market‑maker address has not been initialized or has been deliberately cleared to zero, which may occur after deployment or after an upgrade that resets the address. All participants who rely on fair market execution – traders, liquidity providers, and token holders – are potentially affected because they may receive worse trade outcomes or see unexplained fee increases. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined function visibility and state‑dependent checks. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be protected by an owner check in the typical case, and the zero‑address path is rarely exercised, leading reviewers to overlook the edge case. From a user perspective, trades may execute with unexpectedly high slippage, fees may appear larger than advertised, or a transaction may be reverted if the malicious market‑maker deliberately blocks execution. The bug belongs to the class of privilege‑escalation or access‑control bypass vulnerabilities where a privileged operation becomes publicly callable under a specific state. To remediate, the contract should enforce the owner‑only restriction unconditionally, for example by applying an onlyOwner modifier or an explicit require(msg.sender == owner) before any address change, regardless of the current market‑maker value. Additionally, the contract should prevent setting the market‑maker to the zero address and consider emitting an event when the address is updated to aid monitoring. By tightening the access control, the protocol can ensure that only authorized entities can become market‑makers, preserving market integrity and protecting user funds.

title: M-8 Potential failure in token permit execution
description: This issue has been identified within the HanjiLOB.sol#L428, HanjiLOB.sol#L552, and HanjiLOB.sol#L754 functions of the HanjiLOB contract. These functions call the permit method on an ERC20 token contract to grant spending approval. However, if the permit function has already been executed in a previous transaction, it may revert, causing the entire transaction to fail. This could lead to significant disruptions, particularly in a high-frequency trading environment where consistent operation is critical. The issue is classified as medium severity because it can cause transaction failures, negatively impacting user experience and potentially resulting in missed trading opportunities.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the order‑placement functions of the HanjiLOB contract that invoke the ERC20 permit method to obtain a spending allowance on behalf of a user. The root cause is that the contract unconditionally calls permit without first verifying whether a valid permit has already been recorded on the token contract. Because the ERC20 permit implementation tracks a nonce for each owner, a second call with the same signature or an expired deadline will cause the token’s permit function to revert. When this revert propagates back to the placeOrder transaction, the entire transaction fails, preventing the order from being recorded. This failure can occur in any high‑frequency trading scenario where the same user repeatedly places orders and the contract attempts to re‑grant allowance on each call. The affected parties are the traders who submit orders, the protocol that loses trading volume, and any liquidity providers whose funds remain idle because orders are not executed. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the control flow of the permit calls. It is subtle because the revert only happens after a successful permit has already been submitted, so the first few transactions appear normal and the problem only surfaces later, making it hard to detect through simple testing. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with no obvious error message, resulting in “order not placed” or “trade missed” despite the user having approved the token. The business logic that assumes a permit can be called repeatedly is violated, breaking the accounting assumption that allowance can be refreshed without error. The recommended remediation is to make the permit call defensive: either wrap it in a try‑catch block and ignore the failure when the permit is already valid, or query the token’s current allowance/nonce and only invoke permit when it is truly needed. This change prevents a single revert from aborting the whole order flow and restores reliable operation of the trading engine.

title: Users Can Block Full Utilization of Vault Capacity
description:
The vulnerability is located in the _deposit() function, which enforces two constraints: a lower-bound check on the deposit amount (require(vaultSetting.minimumSupply <= _amount, "INVALID_AMOUNT");) and an upper-bound check to ensure that the vault’s capacity is not exceeded (require(VaultStore.getNav(fundStorage, vaultKey) + _amount <= vaultSetting.capacity, "INVALID_AMOUNT_CAPACITY");). While these checks are valid in isolation, their interaction introduces a logic flaw when the vault approaches its capacity limit.  
If the remaining capacity in the vault falls below the configured minimumSupply, it becomes impossible for any user to deposit additional funds, even if the remaining space could accommodate a smaller deposit. This occurs because any deposits smaller than minimumSupply are explicitly rejected, while any deposit equal to or greater than minimumSupply will breach the vault’s capacity limit and also be rejected.  
For example, consider a vault with a capacity of 1,000 units and a minimumSupply of 100 units. Suppose the current NAV of the vault is 950 units. This leaves only 50 units of available space. At this point, no further deposit is possible: a deposit of 50 will be rejected for being less than the minimum supply, and a deposit of 100 or more will be rejected for exceeding the vault’s capacity. As a result, the remaining 50 units of capacity become permanently unusable.

This flaw allows users to inadvertently—or maliciously—trigger a state in which part of the vault’s capacity is permanently locked. It prevents full capital deployment and introduces inefficiencies in fund management.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deposit‑capacity deadlock caused by the interaction of a lower‑bound check on the deposit amount (minimumSupply) and an upper‑bound check that prevents the vault’s total net asset value (NAV) from exceeding its configured capacity. The contract requires that any incoming deposit be at least minimumSupply and that the sum of the current NAV and the deposit not surpass capacity. When the vault’s remaining free space becomes smaller than minimumSupply, no amount can satisfy both conditions: any amount smaller than minimumSupply is rejected by the lower‑bound check, while any amount equal to or larger than minimumSupply would push the NAV over the capacity limit and is rejected by the upper‑bound check. As a result, the leftover capacity becomes permanently unusable. This situation can be triggered unintentionally when users deposit amounts that bring the NAV close to the capacity, or it can be induced deliberately by an attacker who deposits a large amount to leave a small remainder, thereby locking the remaining space. The impact is that the vault can no longer accept new deposits, preventing full capital deployment, reducing liquidity, and potentially causing loss of expected earnings for investors. The condition occurs only when the vault is near full, specifically when capacity‑NAV is less than minimumSupply. All participants who wish to deposit – regular users, fund managers, or protocol operators – are affected because their transactions will revert with generic error messages such as 'INVALID_AMOUNT' or 'INVALID_AMOUNT_CAPACITY', giving no indication that the vault is simply out of usable space. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the _deposit() function and identified the edge case where the two constraints intersect. It is hard to notice because each individual check works correctly in isolation and typical test cases use deposit amounts well above the minimum, so the deadlock only appears in a narrow range of states that are not exercised by standard unit tests. The bug belongs to the class of "logic‑based capacity lockout" or "minimum‑deposit deadlock" errors, where validation rules unintentionally prevent legitimate operations. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a failed transaction with an 'invalid amount' error even though the user attempted a reasonable small deposit; the expectation that a small remaining slot can be filled is violated, leading to confusion and the perception that funds have disappeared. To remediate the problem the deposit logic should be adjusted to allow deposits that are less than the configured minimumSupply when the remaining capacity is smaller, for example by dynamically lowering the minimum requirement to the exact free space or by permitting a final partial deposit that exactly fills the vault. This change restores the ability to fully utilize the vault’s capacity and eliminates the permanent lockout.

title: Withdrawal Mechanism Fails When Share Price Declines
description:
The vulnerability manifests in the withdrawal flow between initiateWithdrawal() and withdraw(). When a user initiates withdrawal, the contract records the share amount and equivalent asset value at that time. However, if the share price decreases before execution, withdraw() recalculates the share amount using the new lower price via convertToShares(), resulting in more shares than originally recorded.  
The critical check require(userWithdraw.shares >= _shares, "INVALID_SHARES") then fails because the calculated share amount exceeds the initially recorded value. This creates a deadlock where users cannot withdraw funds despite having initiated the process, as the system compares share amounts from different price epochs without adjustment.

Affected users become unable to complete withdrawals when share prices decline, effectively freezing their funds until prices recover. This violates the expected withdrawal guarantee and damages user trust.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a withdrawal deadlock caused by the contract recomputing the number of shares at the moment of withdrawal instead of using the amount recorded when the user called initiateWithdrawal. When a user initiates a withdrawal the contract stores the requested share amount and the equivalent asset value based on the current share price. If the share price falls before the later withdraw call, the internal conversion function convertToShares uses the lower price and returns a larger share count than was originally recorded. The require check that the stored shares are greater than or equal to the newly calculated shares then fails, causing the transaction to revert with INVALID_SHARES. This mismatch between two price epochs creates a situation where the user cannot complete the withdrawal even though the request was accepted, effectively freezing the funds until the share price rises back to the original level. The issue appears only when the asset price declines between the two calls, so it may go unnoticed during normal operation when prices are stable. It affects any user who relies on the withdrawal guarantee, leading to a user‑visible symptom of a failed withdrawal transaction, a missing or zero balance after the attempt, and an inability to retrieve deposited assets. The bug is a classic example of a price‑dependent accounting error where state is validated against a value that changes over time, violating the assumption that share‑to‑asset conversion is static for a pending withdrawal. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that traced the flow from initiateWithdrawal to withdraw and identified the inconsistent use of the price oracle. Because the failure manifests as a revert only under specific market conditions, it can be hard to reproduce and may be dismissed as a transient network issue. The proper fix is to decouple the share validation from the current price by persisting the exact share amount calculated at initiation and using that immutable value during the withdraw step, or by redesigning the withdrawal logic to lock the price for the pending request. This eliminates the epoch mismatch and restores the expected behavior where a user who initiates a withdrawal can always retrieve the corresponding assets regardless of subsequent price movements.

title: Withdrawal Initiators Suffer Partial Loss When Share Price Increases
description:
The vulnerability manifests in the interaction between initiateWithdrawal() and withdraw(). When share prices increase after initiation but before execution, the proportional calculation in _withdraw() divides the originally recorded withdrawal amount by the new, higher share price. This results in users receiving substantially fewer assets than their initial entitlement.  
The critical flaw occurs in the shares-to-assets conversion, where sharesWithdrawAmount = (_shares * userWithdraw.withdrawAmount) / userWithdraw.shares fails to account for NAV increases. Since userWithdraw.withdrawAmount remains fixed at initiation-time values while share prices appreciate, the equation yields diminished asset payouts despite the fund’s increased value.

Users suffer direct financial losses when share prices rise, as their withdrawals become locked to outdated valuations. The partially withdrawn amount, which is set during initiateWithdrawal(), would be claimed, and the other remaining amount would be lost to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑valuation withdrawal bug that occurs when a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract records the amount of shares to be redeemed, but later, before the withdraw() function is called, the net asset value (share price) of the fund increases. The withdraw logic recomputes the asset amount by dividing the originally recorded share amount by the current (higher) share price, i.e., sharesWithdrawAmount = (_shares * userWithdraw.withdrawAmount) / userWithdraw.shares. Because userWithdraw.withdrawAmount is fixed at the time of initiation while the denominator reflects the new price, the resulting asset payout is smaller than the entitlement calculated at initiation. An attacker (or any user) can trigger this loss simply by waiting for the share price to rise after initiating a withdrawal, then calling withdraw(). The impact is that the user receives only a fraction of the assets they expected; the missing portion is effectively lost, reducing the user's balance and potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The condition required is that the share price must increase between initiateWithdrawal() and withdraw(). All participants who rely on the withdrawal mechanism—individual investors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting invariants (total assets = shares * price) are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal flow, where the auditor noticed that the conversion formula used a mutable price variable instead of the snapshot taken at initiation. The bug is subtle because the contract still transfers some assets, so a casual user may not notice the discrepancy unless they compare the expected amount with the received amount. The class of bug is a stale‑state or price‑oracle mismatch in financial contracts, where calculations use outdated values leading to under‑payment. To fix the problem, the contract should store the exact share amount (or the asset amount) at the moment of initiation and use that immutable snapshot during withdraw(), eliminating any dependence on later price changes. This restores the guarantee that a user who initiates a withdrawal receives the full value they were entitled to at that moment.

title: Users Can Suffer Slippage Losses Due to Missing Slippage Protection in FundContract
description:
The FundContract lacks slippage protection mechanisms in its deposit and withdrawal functions (deposit(), depositNative(), withdraw(), and redeem()), which exposes users to potential financial losses due to unfavourable exchange rates between assets and shares.

The vulnerability arises because the contract implements the ERC-4626 standard but does not provide a way for users to specify minimum acceptable amounts of shares (for deposits) or assets (for withdrawals). While the standard permits direct EOA (Externally Owned Account) interaction, it strongly recommends implementing slippage controls if such access is supported. Currently, users calling these functions directly may receive fewer shares or assets than expected due to price fluctuations between transaction submission and execution.

Users depositing or withdrawing funds may experience unexpected losses if the exchange rate between assets and shares changes unfavorably before their transactions are processed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the FundContract that implements the ERC‑4626 tokenized vault standard. The contract’s deposit, depositNative, withdraw and redeem functions allow a user to exchange assets for shares (or the reverse) without any way to specify a minimum acceptable amount of shares or assets. Because the exchange rate between the underlying asset and the vault shares can change between the moment a transaction is signed and the moment it is mined, a user may receive fewer shares on deposit or fewer assets on withdrawal than expected. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who front‑runs the transaction or by natural market volatility that moves the price unfavourably during the pending period. The impact is that users experience unexpected financial loss: a depositor who expects to receive, for example, 100 shares may end up with only 80, and a withdrawer who expects to get 1 ETH may receive 0.9 ETH. The issue occurs whenever any external account calls the mentioned functions directly, especially in volatile markets or when transaction latency is high. All participants who interact with the vault – individual investors, protocol users and any downstream contracts – are affected because the contract does not enforce the accounting assumption that the asset‑to‑share conversion remains constant during execution. The problem was identified during a security audit that compared the implementation against the ERC‑4626 recommendation to include slippage controls for public functions. It is hard to notice because the transaction succeeds and the UI typically reports only success, while the amount transferred is silently lower; there is no explicit revert or error message. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of slippage or price‑protection vulnerabilities where a contract fails to guard against adverse price movements. To remediate, the contract should be extended with parameters such as minSharesOut for deposits and minAssetsOut for withdrawals, and the logic should revert if the actual amount received falls below the user‑provided thresholds, thereby aligning the on‑chain behavior with user expectations and preserving the intended accounting guarantees.

title: The mint() Functions in NftFactory Do Not Function Properly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the minting workflow of the NftFactory contract. When a user calls publicMint() or preMint() on the factory, the function forwards the request to the corresponding publicMint() or preMint() function in the LendingNFT contract. Those LendingNFT functions attempt to collect payment tokens from the caller by invoking safeTransferFrom(). However, the LendingNFT contract has never been granted an allowance or approval to move the caller’s tokens that are held by the NftFactory contract. Because the factory does not first transfer the payment tokens from the user nor approve the LendingNFT contract to spend them, the safeTransferFrom() call fails and the transaction reverts. The root cause is a missing approval step: the factory assumes the LendingNFT contract can pull tokens directly from the factory’s balance, which is not the case under the ERC‑20/ERC‑721 token standards. An attacker does not need to exploit the bug; any honest user attempting to mint an NFT through the factory will experience a revert, receive no tokenId, and see the transaction fail. The impact is that legitimate users cannot acquire NFTs via the advertised factory interface, leading to a broken user experience and potential loss of revenue for the protocol. The issue manifests whenever publicMint() or preMint() is invoked, i.e., under normal minting conditions. All participants who rely on the factory – end‑users, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts expecting minted NFTs – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that traced the call flow and identified that the token transfer step was never authorized. Because the functions return a tokenId, developers might assume the call succeeds without testing the token transfer path, making the bug easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of authorization or allowance errors where a contract attempts to transfer assets without a prior approval, a common pattern in token‑handling contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a “mint” button, but after confirming the transaction the wallet would display a failure or revert message, and no NFT appears in the user’s wallet, contrary to the expectation that a newly minted token would be received. To remediate, the factory should first pull the required payment tokens from the user (or have the user approve the factory), then explicitly approve the LendingNFT contract to spend those tokens, and only then invoke the LendingNFT mint functions. This ensures the safeTransferFrom() call succeeds and the minting process completes as intended.

title: The Signature of preMint() Can Be Used in Different NFT Contracts
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature replay weakness in the preMint() function of NFT contracts. The function verifies a signature that is computed only over the caller address (msg.sender) and the requested maxMintAmount. Because the signed message does not include the address of the NFT contract itself, the same signature can be presented to any other NFT contract that uses the identical verification routine. The root cause is the absence of a domain separator – the contract address (or another unique identifier) is not bound to the signed data, allowing the signed hash to be reused across contracts. An attacker who obtains a legitimate signature from the authorized signer for one NFT collection can call preMint() on a different collection, supply the same signature, and pass the _verifyAddressSigner check because the hash (msg.sender, maxMintAmount) matches and the recovered signer address is still valid. This enables unauthorized minting of tokens in contracts where the signer did not intend to grant permission, potentially diluting scarcity, stealing revenue, or violating the creator’s expectations. The issue manifests whenever preMint() is invoked on any contract that shares the same signer and verification code, and it is especially dangerous in protocols that deploy multiple NFT contracts under a common signing authority. The affected parties include the NFT creators, buyers who rely on the intended mint limits, and the overall protocol that may lose trust and economic value. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature verification logic and noticed that the contract address was omitted from the signed payload. It can be hard to detect because the signature appears cryptographically valid and the function works as intended for a single contract; only cross‑contract testing reveals the replay possibility. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user can mint NFTs from a second collection using a signature that was meant only for the first, leading to unexpected token allocations or “free” mints that were not authorized. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks caused by insufficient binding of signed messages to a specific contract (missing domain separation). To remediate, the signed message should incorporate the contract’s address (or a unique nonce, chain ID, or EIP‑712 domain separator) so that each signature is valid only for the intended NFT contract, thereby preventing cross‑contract reuse.

title: Users May Lose the Interest They Should Claim When Transferring NFTs
description:
In LendingNFT, claim() is not called in the NFT’s transfer hook.  
This means that the contract cannot guarantee that claim() and transfer of the NFT occur in the same block. If users want to ensure that claiming and transferring an NFT happen in the same block and that claiming occurs before transferring, they can only achieve this by creating a contract themselves to call it or creating a bundle through Flashbots, which is obviously highly difficult for ordinary users.  
Before maturity, interest will increase with the increase of block.timestamp:  
```solidity
// Proportion of time interval from the beginning of the lending period until now to a year, scaled to the 1e18
uint256 proportionOfIntervalTotalScaled = ((Math.min(block.timestamp, maturity) - lendingAt) * 1e18) / year;
```  
If the transfer of the NFT occurs in a block after the claim(), the interest generated during this period cannot be obtained by the previous owner.  
For example:

1. Before maturity, Alice wants to transfer her NFT to Bob.
2. Alice first executes the claim() and then transfers the NFT.
3. Due to this vulnerability, Alice’s two transactions may end up in different blocks, assuming they are separated by one block.
4. Alice cannot receive the interest for that one block, even though it rightfully belongs to her, as she still owned the NFT during this period.
5. Ultimately, the interest in that block, which should have belonged to Alice, ends up belonging to Bob.

Before maturity, if users want to transfer NFTs, they may lose the interest they are entitled to. To avoid this, users must either create their own contracts or use services like Flashbots, which is challenging for regular users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an atomicity flaw in the LendingNFT contract where the claim() function, which withdraws accrued interest, is not invoked automatically inside the NFT transfer hook. Because claim() must be called in a separate transaction, the contract cannot guarantee that the interest claim and the NFT transfer occur within the same block. When a user transfers an NFT before the lending period reaches maturity, the interest that accrues during the block(s) between the claim transaction and the subsequent transfer transaction is calculated based on the new owner’s address. Consequently, the previous owner loses the interest that rightfully belongs to them for that interval, and the new owner receives it instead. This situation arises only when the transfer is performed as two distinct transactions that are mined in different blocks, which is the typical user workflow because the contract does not enforce a bundled call. The affected parties are NFT holders who wish to transfer their positions while still earning interest, as well as the protocol’s accounting logic that assumes interest is always claimed by the current owner before ownership changes. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle of the NFT and identified that the transfer hook does not contain a call to claim(). It can be hard to notice because the missing interest may be a single block’s worth of reward, which appears as a small discrepancy in the user’s balance and may not trigger an obvious error in the UI. From the user’s perspective, they expect to call claim() and then transfer the NFT, seeing their full accrued interest reflected before the hand‑off; instead they may notice that the claimed amount is slightly lower than expected, or that the new owner’s balance includes an unexpected extra amount. This bug belongs to the class of race‑condition or atomicity vulnerabilities where state‑changing operations are not performed atomically, leading to unintended fund redistribution. To remediate the problem, the contract should invoke claim() inside the transfer hook (or otherwise enforce that claim and transfer are executed in a single transaction), ensuring that interest is settled before ownership changes and that the previous owner receives all interest accrued up to the moment of transfer.

title: Admin Cannot Pause Vault Operations to Mitigate Protocol Risk
description:
The VaultSetting struct within the Vault contract includes an isPaused boolean field intended to allow administrators to pause core vault operations such as deposits and withdrawals during abnormal or high-risk scenarios. The setupVaultSetting() function is responsible for initializing and updating vault parameters, including minimumSupply, capacity, and various fee configurations. However, this function hardcodes the isPaused field to false, and there exists no administrative function to set isPaused to true.  
This design omission results in a critical gap in operational controls. Although the contract appears to support a paused state, in practice, there is no mechanism for administrators to activate it. As a result, the pause functionality is entirely unusable.

The inability to pause vault operations undermines the protocol’s resilience to emergency situations. In the event of an exploit or a required upgrade, administrators would be unable to halt deposits and withdrawals, potentially exposing user funds to loss or exploitation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ineffective pause mechanism in the vault contract. The contract defines a boolean isPaused in the VaultSetting struct that is meant to allow an administrator to stop deposits and withdrawals when the protocol is under stress. However, the function that initializes and updates the vault settings unconditionally writes false to this flag and the contract does not expose any external function that can set the flag to true. As a result, the pause state can never be entered. The root cause is the hard‑coded assignment and the absence of an access‑controlled setter. Because the flag never changes, an administrator who tries to invoke a pause operation – either through a UI button or an off‑chain script – will observe no effect; deposits and withdrawals continue as normal even if an exploit is in progress. This situation can be exploited indirectly: if an attacker discovers a vulnerability in the vault logic, the protocol cannot freeze the affected functions, allowing the attacker to continue draining assets or manipulating state while users are still able to interact. The impact is that user funds remain exposed during emergencies, the protocol loses a key risk‑mitigation control, and confidence in the governance model is eroded. The condition under which the bug manifests is any attempt by an authorized role to pause the vault; the contract will silently ignore the request because the state variable is immutable after deployment. All participants – token holders, liquidity providers, and the admin team – are affected because they rely on the pause mechanism to protect assets. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the presence of the isPaused flag with the available external functions and noticed the missing setter. It can be hard to notice because the source code contains the pause variable and may even expose a UI element labeled “Pause”, giving a false sense of safety. The proper remediation is to add an access‑controlled function such as pauseVault() and unpauseVault() that updates the isPaused flag, emits appropriate events, and is protected by the admin role. This change restores the intended emergency stop capability and aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented risk‑management design.

title: Caller Can Permanently Lock Excess ETH in Contract
description:
In the depositNative() function, a user is allowed to send more ETH (msg.value) than the specified _amount they intend to deposit. The function checks that msg.value >= _amount but does not enforce strict equality, nor does it refund any excess ETH. The entire msg.value is passed to the IWETH(asset()).deposit{value: msg.value}() call, which wraps the full amount into WETH.  
However, only _amount of WETH is then deposited via the internal _deposit() function, with the rest of the wrapped ETH remaining in the contract’s balance, potentially without a corresponding accounting mechanism or method to recover or refund the excess.  
This oversight can result in ETH being unintentionally locked within the contract. Users may accidentally overpay and have no means to retrieve the excess, leading to a potential financial loss.

Users who send more ETH than the _amount parameter in depositNative() will have the surplus ETH irretrievably locked in the contract. This leads to unnecessary user losses and undermines trust in the protocol’s handling of native tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an excess‑payment lockup in the depositNative function. The function accepts a parameter _amount that represents the amount of native ETH the caller intends to deposit, but the only check performed is require(msg.value >= _amount). The full msg.value is forwarded to the WETH wrapper contract, which mints an equivalent amount of WETH and stores it in the contract’s balance. Afterwards the internal _deposit routine records only _amount of WETH as a user deposit. The surplus WETH that corresponds to the over‑paid ETH remains in the contract with no accounting entry and no public method to withdraw or refund it. This situation can be triggered whenever a user mistakenly sends more ETH than the declared _amount, either by manual error or by a malicious front‑end that over‑pays. Because the contract does not expose any function to retrieve the leftover balance, the extra ETH becomes permanently locked, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. From the user’s point of view the transaction appears successful, but later the user sees that their wallet balance is lower than expected and the protocol UI shows no deposited amount for the excess funds. The root cause is the lack of strict equality enforcement and the absence of a refund mechanism after wrapping the ETH. The issue was identified during a manual code audit that highlighted the mismatch between the amount sent and the amount recorded. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s ETH balance may contain hidden WETH that is not reflected in any public accounting view. The bug belongs to the class of “unaccounted excess fund” or “over‑payment lock” vulnerabilities, where economic assumptions about one‑to‑one correspondence between input value and recorded balance are violated. The recommended remediation is to require msg.value == _amount, or alternatively to calculate the surplus after the deposit and send it back to the caller, thereby guaranteeing that no ETH can be unintentionally trapped.

title: Claim/Redeem Functionality Is Executed For The Token Owner Instead For the Current User
description: In the TokTokNft contract, the claim(), claimAll(), redeem(), redeemAll() and claimToken() functions can be executed by any user, not just the owner of a specific NFT. This is problematic because these functions transfer the accrued interest and principal, depending on the function, which decreases the contract’s balance of the payableToken. As a result, a malicious user could exploit this by reducing the payableToken balance on behalf of NFT owners without their permission. This vulnerability could severely impact the NFT contract or its owners, especially considering the calculation of claimable interest in claim(), claimAll(), and the principal refunded in redeem() and redeemAll(). Such exploitation could lead to insolvency for the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing ownership verification in the claim, claimAll, redeem, redeemAll and claimToken functions of the TokTokNft contract, allowing any address to invoke these state‑changing methods on any NFT identifier. The root cause is the absence of a check that msg.sender matches the owner of the specified tokenId, so the contract proceeds to transfer the accrued interest or the principal amount based solely on the token identifier. An attacker can exploit this by calling claim or redeem for a token they do not own, causing the contract to move payableToken funds to the attacker or simply reduce the contract’s balance, which deprives the legitimate NFT holder of expected payouts. This can be performed at any point when the functions are callable – claim is typically used after the maturity date to collect interest, while redeem is used before maturity to retrieve principal – meaning the flaw is exploitable both before and after maturity. The impact includes loss of interest or principal for honest owners, unexpected depletion of the protocol’s payableToken reserve, and a risk of insolvency if enough unauthorized claims are made. The affected parties are the NFT owners, any users relying on the contract’s accounting guarantees, and the protocol itself which may become under‑collateralized. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case where a non‑owner attempted to call claim and the transaction succeeded, revealing that the contract does not enforce ownership. The bug is subtle because the functions are public and the UI may not display any warning, leading developers and users to assume that only owners can claim. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a user who expects to receive a refund or interest may receive zero, while the contract balance drops unexpectedly. This class of bug is an access‑control omission that violates the fundamental business rule that only the token holder may withdraw funds associated with that token. The recommended remediation is to introduce an explicit ownership check in each of the affected functions, for example by reverting with a NotAuthorized error when msg.sender is not the owner of the tokenId, and to apply the same check for batch operations to ensure every token in the batch is owned by the caller.

title: Wrong accounting for rebase/fee-on-transfer tokens
description: Currently, anyone can add any tokens from the CurrencyList contract. This means that rebase and fee-on-transfer tokens can be added intentionally or by mistake which will cause errors in the accounting of the balances of such tokens. Rebasing tokens are designed to adjust the supply of tokens automatically based on the market demand while fee-on-transfer tokens charge a fee on each transfer. This would lead to having less tokens than expected in the contract and the accounting of such tokens will be completely wrong.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s ability to add arbitrary ERC20 tokens to its CurrencyList without any validation or access control. The contract assumes that token balances are static and that the amount specified in a transfer call will be exactly the amount received. This assumption fails for two classes of tokens: rebase tokens, which automatically adjust their total supply after each transfer, and fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens, which deduct a fee from the transferred amount. When such a token is added, the contract records the nominal amount it attempted to transfer rather than the actual balance that ends up in the contract. Consequently, the internal accounting shows a higher token balance than what is truly held. An attacker or even an unwitting user can exploit this by adding a rebase or FoT token to the list and then performing deposits or withdrawals. The contract will believe it holds more tokens than it does, leading to under‑payment on withdrawals, missing refunds, or a situation where a user’s UI shows a zero or reduced balance despite a successful deposit. The impact is that users may lose funds, the protocol’s collateral calculations become inaccurate, and business logic that relies on precise accounting (such as fee distribution or liquidity provision) breaks. This issue manifests whenever any address can call the function that registers a new token and later the contract interacts with that token using the naïve transfer amount. It affects all participants who deposit or withdraw the affected tokens, as well as the protocol’s overall financial integrity. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the token handling logic and noted the lack of balance verification and missing access restrictions. It is hard to notice because the token’s balance on‑chain appears correct, while the contract’s internal ledger diverges silently; fee deductions or supply changes are not visible in the UI, leading users to assume their funds are intact. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict access control on the token‑addition function, whitelist only known standard ERC20 tokens, and, importantly, compute the actual amount received by checking the contract’s token balance before and after each transfer, adjusting the internal accounting accordingly. This approach eliminates reliance on the caller‑provided amount and prevents rebase or fee‑on‑transfer tokens from corrupting the accounting model.

title: Missing input sanitization
bug_full: The contract contains several functions that accept numeric parameters without validating their relationship or range, which creates a class of input‑sanitization bugs. In the payoutDelta function the caller provides a startDay and an untilDay that are used to fetch cumulative payout and share values from a storage array. The implementation subtracts the earlier totals from the later ones inside an unchecked block, but it never checks that untilDay is greater than startDay. If a caller supplies a startDay that is later than untilDay, the subtraction underflows, wrapping around the 256‑bit unsigned integer space and producing an astronomically large payout or share value. This incorrect value can be propagated to downstream calculations, breaking the accounting logic of the protocol and potentially allowing an attacker to claim far more tokens than entitled. A similar problem exists in payoutDeltaTrucated, where the same unchecked subtraction is performed and the function also divides by the difference of shares. Supplying an out‑of‑order day range can cause the denominator to become zero or negative, leading to a revert or another underflow, and the multiplier arithmetic can amplify the effect. The third issue appears in collectUnattributedPercent, which accepts a basisPoints argument that should represent a percentage with a maximum of 10 000 (100 %). The function multiplies the unattributed token amount by the supplied basisPoints and then divides by TEN_K. Because there is no upper bound check, a caller can pass a value larger than 10 000, causing the calculation to exceed the intended percentage. Moreover, when the product of unattributed and basisPoints is smaller than TEN_K, integer division rounds the result down to zero, so the caller receives no tokens even though a non‑zero share was expected. From a user’s perspective these bugs manifest as unexpected large payouts, zero refunds, or missing token transfers despite a visible balance that should have decreased. The vulnerabilities were discovered during a manual audit that highlighted missing require statements and unchecked arithmetic. They are subtle because the functions are view‑only or appear harmless, and the underflow only becomes visible when an attacker deliberately reverses the day order, a scenario that may not be exercised in normal testing. To remediate the issues the contract should enforce explicit input constraints such as require(untilDay > startDay) for all range‑based calculations, replace unchecked blocks with safe‑math operations or Solidity 0.8+ built‑in overflow checks, and validate that basisPoints does not exceed TEN_K. Additionally, the rounding logic should be reviewed to ensure that small but legitimate percentages are not truncated to zero, perhaps by using a higher‑precision representation or by adding a minimum‑transfer guard. Implementing these checks restores the intended business logic that payouts and share calculations are monotonic over time and that percentage‑based collections respect the defined maximum, thereby preventing accidental fund loss or malicious over‑allocation.

title: Unsafe downcasts can lead to errors
bug_full: The contract contains an unsafe numeric downcast where a 256‑bit unsigned integer (uint256) supplied by a caller isexplicitly cast to a 40‑bit unsigned integer (uint40) before being forwarded to external functions. This truncation discards any bits above the 40‑bit boundary, so if the original value exceeds 2^40‑1 the higher-order bits are silently lost. The root cause is the lack of range validation and the direct use of a narrower type for a parameter that is originally defined as uint256. An attacker can exploit this by providing a stake identifier (stakeId) that is larger than the maximum uint40 value; the contract will only retain the least‑significant 40 bits, causing the external Hedron contract to receive an incorrect identifier. Because the identifier is used for accounting and minting, the mismatch can lead to duplicate or overwritten stake records, misallocation of minted tokens, and ultimately loss of user funds or incorrect balance reporting. The vulnerability manifests whenever the internal functions _mintHedron or _stakeGoodAccounting are invoked with a stakeId that does not fit into 40 bits, which can happen in normal operation if the protocol allows large identifiers or if an attacker deliberately crafts oversized values. All participants who interact with the staking or minting features—regular users, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the bug breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that each stakeId uniquely maps to a single record. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that flagged the explicit typecast as a potential data‑loss scenario. It is hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not emit a warning for explicit downcasts, and the contract does not revert or emit an error when truncation occurs; the UI may show the original stakeId while the on‑chain logic operates on a different, truncated value, leading to confusing symptoms such as “my stake disappeared” or “my balance is zero after minting”. To remediate, the contract should either accept the correctly sized type (uint40) as the function argument, or perform a safe‑cast that checks the value against the maximum allowed for uint40 and reverts if it is out of range. Using OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library or adding explicit require statements ensures that no data is silently lost, preserving the integrity of stake identifiers and preventing accounting errors. This class of bug is known as an unsafe downcast or integer truncation vulnerability, which violates business logic that relies on precise numeric identifiers for financial operations.

title: Solmate safeTransfer method does not
description:
The Solmate safeTransfer methods are used for transferring ERC20 tokens. However, as we can see
```solidity
/// @dev Note that none of the functions in this library check that a token has code at all! That responsibility is delegated to the caller.
```
doesn't have contract in it, it will always return success, bypassing the return value check. Due to this protocol will think that funds has been transferred and successful, and records will be accordingly calculated, but in reality funds were never transferred.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the Solmate library’s safeTransfer functions, which are intended to provide a convenient wrapper around ERC20 token transfers. The library does not verify that the target address actually contains contract code before performing a low‑level call. When the supplied token address is an externally owned account, an empty address, or otherwise lacks bytecode, the low‑level call succeeds without reverting and returns no data. Because the wrapper interprets the absence of a revert as a successful transfer, the calling protocol records the operation as completed and updates its internal accounting as if the tokens had moved. In reality no token transfer occurs, so the protocol’s state diverges from the true token balances. This discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a non‑contract address or a malicious contract that pretends to be an ERC20 token but never moves funds. The exploit is triggered whenever the protocol relies on safeTransfer for token movement without an explicit code‑existence check, which is common in upgradeable or configurable systems where token addresses can be set by users or administrators. Affected parties include the protocol itself, its users, and any downstream contracts that trust the recorded balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noted the library comment stating that no code‑existence verification is performed and confirmed the behavior by calling safeTransfer with an address that has no contract code; the transaction reported success while the token balance remained unchanged. Because the transaction does not revert and emits no error, the problem can be difficult to notice from the UI – users see a “transfer successful” message but their token balance stays the same, leading to missing refunds or apparent loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “false‑positive transfer confirmation” vulnerabilities, where a wrapper assumes success based solely on the absence of a revert. To remediate, the protocol should either switch to a library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20, which includes a check that the target address contains contract code and validates the returned data, or add an explicit extcodesize check before invoking the token’s transfer function. This ensures that only genuine ERC20 contracts can be interacted with and that failed or non‑existent transfers are correctly detected, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from being silently untransferred.

title: A require check is creating a false sense of security
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a superficial validation performed in the addCurrencyToList function, where the contract checks that the caller holds a non‑zero balance of the token they are trying to register. The check is implemented as a simple equality test against zero and reverts with MustBeHolder if the balance is zero. This logic creates a false sense of security because it assumes that any token for which the caller owns at least one unit is trustworthy and suitable for inclusion in the platform’s supported token list. In reality, an attacker can deploy a custom ERC20 contract, mint a single token to their own address, and satisfy the balance requirement, thereby bypassing the intended safeguard. Once the malicious token is added, the protocol may treat it as a legitimate currency in downstream operations such as deposits, withdrawals, or swaps. Users interacting with the newly listed token may experience unexpected failures, loss of funds, or the inability to retrieve assets because the token’s code can be crafted to behave maliciously (e.g., returning false on transfer, trapping funds, or executing re‑entrancy attacks). The issue manifests whenever any address calls addCurrencyToList with an arbitrary token address; there is no additional verification of the token’s authenticity, total supply, or compliance with standard ERC20 behavior. All participants of the protocol – token holders, traders, and the platform itself – are potentially exposed to financial loss or reputational damage. The flaw was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the logical insufficiency of using a holder‑balance check as a proxy for token legitimacy. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction succeeds and the token appears in the UI as a supported currency, giving users the impression that the platform has vetted it. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the balance check with a robust whitelist mechanism that only permits pre‑approved token contracts, or employ an on‑chain oracle or verification routine that validates critical token properties (such as totalSupply, proper ERC20 interface compliance, and absence of known malicious patterns). This ensures that only vetted, trustworthy tokens can be added, aligning the implementation with the intended security model and preventing attackers from registering counterfeit tokens that could cause funds to disappear or refunds to fail.

title: Bonus Tokens Can Be Claimed Even After The Specified Period Ends
description: The claimToken() function can be executed after the bonusToken valid period has passed and the user will still be able to claim successfully.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing expiration check in the bonus‑token claim logic, allowing the claimToken function to be executed after the predefined bonus period has ended. The root cause is that the contract does not verify that the current block timestamp is less than or equal to the period end (the variable r) before transferring the bonus tokens. An attacker or any user can simply wait until the deadline passes, call claimToken and still receive the allocated bonus amount because the contract proceeds with the transfer unconditionally. This can be exploited by invoking claimToken after the period, causing the contract’s bonus token balance to decrease unexpectedly while the caller’s balance increases, effectively breaking the intended accounting model where bonuses are only distributable within a fixed window. The impact is that funds earmarked for a limited‑time incentive may be drained, users receive tokens they should not obtain, and the protocol’s economic assumptions are violated, potentially leading to unfair advantage and loss of trust.
