Although there is a warning message stating that the input should be a positive number, a user can still input any value (or leave it empty), triggering a zero-value transaction that only consumes gas. Moreover this transaction is occurring without Starting a game which is required before depositing an amount.

Figure 1: In the image: The current implementation allows a user to introduce special characters or an empty string, and the approve button will still process a transaction with a zero value, consuming only gas.

Figure 2: In the image: Details of the 0 value transaction from above. Although the user is required to approve this zero-value transaction, if the application warns the user to use only valid positive numbers, it should enforce this by accepting only valid input for approval.
bug_full: The contract’s deposit routine does not validate the amount supplied by the caller. Because the function lacks a check that the input is a numeric, positive value and also does not verify that a game session has been started before a deposit is accepted, a user can submit an empty string, zero, or arbitrary non‑numeric characters. The transaction is still sent to the blockchain, the approve button succeeds, and the contract records a deposit of zero value while consuming gas. From a technical standpoint the root cause is missing input sanitisation and missing pre‑condition enforcement, which allows the call to pass the require statements that only check for transaction success, not for logical correctness. An attacker can therefore trigger a large number of zero‑value deposits, draining gas from their own wallet or from any account that signs the transaction, and potentially creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the contract’s accounting logic because the contract may assume that every successful deposit increases a user’s balance. The issue manifests when a user interacts with the UI, sees a warning that the amount should be a positive number, but the warning is not enforced; the UI still enables the approve button and the blockchain records a transaction with value 0. This behaviour is hard to notice because the transaction appears normal on explorers – it has a successful status and a gas cost, yet no funds are transferred and the on‑chain state does not change as expected. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the deposit UI with empty and malformed inputs and observed that the contract accepted the call without reverting. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict numeric validation (e.g., using require(amount > 0) and parsing the input safely), reject any non‑numeric or empty values, and add a require that a game session is active before allowing a deposit. By doing so the contract will prevent zero‑value transactions, protect users from unnecessary gas loss, and preserve the integrity of the protocol’s accounting model.

title: Decimals not Required in the Deposit Function
description: When a user deposits an amount into any of the tokens, allowing input of decimal numbers is unnecessary since the wages are fixed in rounded numbers.
poc:
When a user initiates a game and proceeds to deposit, it is possible to enter amounts with decimals.

Figure 3: In the image: The application processes decimals in the Session Balance.  
Figure 4: In the image: The application processes decimals in the Session Balance.  
Although the application seems to manage calculations involving decimal numbers in the rollup/withdrawal process, allowing users to input decimal numbers is unnecessary. This is because the application enforces a fixed wager amount for each available token. Leaving the decimals might cause rounding issues in the backend, in this way the input must be properly constrained.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing users to specify decimal fractions when depositing tokens into a game where wagers are defined as whole units. The contract does not enforce integer‑only deposits, so a user can send 1.5 tokens. Because the backend assumes fixed wager amounts and performs integer arithmetic for accounting, the presence of fractional values can cause rounding mismatches when the session balance is later used for rollup or withdrawal calculations. An attacker could exploit this by depositing a fractional amount that, after rounding, results in a lower effective wager while still being credited with a full wager slot, effectively gaining a free fraction of a token. Conversely, rounding down could cause the contract to think the user has insufficient balance, leading to rejected withdrawals or loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever the deposit function accepts a value with a non‑zero decimal part; it is triggered during normal gameplay when a player initiates a session and supplies a custom amount. All participants who can interact with the deposit endpoint are affected, including regular users and the protocol’s accounting logic. The flaw was discovered during a manual UI/UX audit that observed that the deposit input field accepted decimal numbers despite the protocol’s documentation stating that wagers are whole numbers. Because the contract does not explicitly reject fractions, the problem can be subtle: the UI may display a fractional balance, but the backend may truncate or round it silently, making the discrepancy hard to notice until a withdrawal fails or the accounting totals become inconsistent. The vulnerability belongs to the class of input‑validation and rounding errors, where unchecked numeric precision leads to accounting drift. To remediate, the deposit function should enforce that the amount is an integer multiple of the token’s smallest unit (e.g., require amount % 1 == 0 or use token decimals to validate) and reject any value containing a fractional component. This prevents rounding anomalies and aligns the on‑chain accounting with the protocol’s business rule that wagers are fixed, whole‑number amounts.

title: First loss cover fee investment will fail if it does not exceed minimum deposit amount
description: Fees are invested in two different ways. Whenever an admin account attempts to withdraw accrued income and alternatively via investFeesInFirstLossCover() which is managed by the pool owner and sentinel service accounts. Until the cover reaches max liquidity, fees will be invested. There is important edge case that is not considered which would cause _investFeesInFirstLossCover() to revert, affecting all fee withdrawal functions. When getAvailableCap() < poolSettings.minDepositAmount, then depositCoverFor() will fail and unless cover redeemability is enabled, it will not be possible to withdraw fees because _investFeesInFirstLossCover() will always attempt to deposit an amount that is less than poolSettings.minDepositAmount.
bug_full: The vulnerability isan edge‑case failure in the fee‑investment logic of the first loss cover. When the pool owner or a sentinel service calls the internal function that invests accrued fees into the first loss cover, the contract calculates the amount that can be deposited by calling getAvailableCap(). If this available cap is smaller than the protocol‑wide minimum deposit amount (poolSettings.minDepositAmount) the subsequent call to depositCoverFor() reverts because the deposit amount does not satisfy the minimum‑deposit check. This revert propagates to every external fee‑withdrawal entry point, including the admin‑only withdrawAccruedIncome() function, so any attempt to pull fees results in a transaction failure and the fees remain locked in the contract. The bug occurs only while the first loss cover has not yet reached its maximum liquidity and the cover redeemability flag is disabled, which is a state that can be reached during normal pool growth when only a small amount of fees have been accumulated. The affected parties are the pool owner, sentinel accounts and any admin that expects to receive fee revenue; users of the protocol may notice that their expected fee payouts are missing or that the UI shows a zero balance after a successful fee accrual. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between fee withdrawal functions and the first loss cover investment path. It is hard to notice because the revert only happens when the available cap falls below the minimum deposit threshold, a condition that does not appear in typical test scenarios with larger fee balances. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of minimum‑value enforcement causing unexpected reverts in financial state transitions. To remediate, the contract should either exempt the depositCoverFor() call from the minimum‑deposit requirement when it is invoked from the fee‑investment routine, or add a guard that skips the investment when the calculated amount is below the minimum, thereby allowing fee withdrawals to succeed even when the cover is under‑funded. Fixing the logic restores the intended business rule that accrued fees can always be withdrawn, preserving the accounting integrity of the protocol.

title: Lenders can grief other lenders by depositing on their behalf
bug_full: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑lockout grief vector that arises from the ability of any approved lender to call the deposit() function on behalf of another lender. When a deposit is recorded, the contract stores the timestamp of the last deposit for the receiver. The addRedemptionRequest() function checks that the current epoch start time is greater than lastDepositTime plus the configured withdrawal lockout period; if not, it reverts with WithdrawTooEarly. Because the deposit function can be invoked by a third party for the victim’s address, an attacker can submit a small deposit on the victim’s behalf immediately before the victim creates a redemption request. This action updates the victim’s lastDepositTime, causing the lockout condition to be true and the redemption request to fail. By repeating this pattern at the beginning of each epoch, the attacker can keep the victim’s redemption permanently blocked, effectively griefing the lender and preventing exit from the tranche. The impact is that legitimate users see their redemption requests rejected, their share balances remain locked, and they receive no funds despite expecting a withdrawal. The issue manifests only when both the attacker and the victim are approved LPs, which is a common configuration in the protocol. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the tranche vault’s deposit and redemption logic, where the interaction between deposit timestamps and the lockout check was examined. The bug is subtle because the deposit function does not require the receiver’s explicit consent beyond being an approved LP, and the lockout reset is a side‑effect rather than an explicit permission, making it easy to overlook during testing. The class of bug can be described as an “unauthorized state‑reset” or “deposit‑on‑behalf grief” where an external actor can manipulate a time‑based guard to deny service. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a redemption attempt failing with an error, the expected funds do not arrive, and the balance appears unchanged, leading to confusion. The root cause is the lack of a per‑account deposit authorisation that distinguishes between self‑deposits and third‑party deposits. The recommended mitigation is to introduce an internal approval mechanism that allows each lender to designate which addresses are permitted to deposit on their behalf, thereby restoring the lender’s control over the lastDepositTime update. Until such a change is applied, the attack can be carried out at a low cost equal to the protocol’s minimum deposit amount for each lockout period, making it economically feasible to sustain the grief.

title: Unused function parameters can lead to false assumptions on user side
description: The units parameter in mintClaimWithFractions is used only in the event emission. This is misleading as actually fractions.length number of fractions will be minted. If units != fractions.length this can have unexpected consequences for a user. The same is the problem with the account parameter in both mintClaim and mintClaimWithFractions - it is not used in the method and actually msg.sender is the account to which tokens are minted and is set as the token creator. Again if account != msg.sender this is unexpected from a user standpoint and while in the best case scenario leads to a not so great UX, in the worst case it can lead to faulty assumptions for value received by the account address.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of misleading function parameters that are accepted by the contract but never used in the core logic, creating a gap between the API contract and its actual behavior. In the mintClaimWithFractions function the units argument is only forwarded to an event, while the number of fractions that are minted is derived from the length of the fractions array. Consequently, when a caller supplies a units value that differs from fractions.length, the emitted event reports a quantity that does not match the tokens actually created, leading users to believe they received more or fewer fractions than they really did. A similar issue exists in both mintClaim and mintClaimWithFractions where the account parameter is ignored; the implementation always uses msg.sender as the recipient of the newly minted tokens and also records msg.sender as the token creator. If a caller passes an explicit account address that differs from msg.sender, the contract silently mints to the caller instead of the intended destination. This mismatch can cause false assumptions about token ownership, incorrect accounting in downstream applications, and a poor user experience because the on‑chain state does not reflect the parameters supplied in the transaction. The bug is a classic case of parameter misuse or API‑implementation inconsistency, where unused inputs give a false sense of control. It is exploitable in the sense that a malicious front‑end could display a fabricated units value in the event log, tricking users into thinking they received a larger claim than they actually did, or could mislead auditors and integrators that tokens are being allocated to a specific address when they are not. The impact is primarily informational and financial: users may think they have received a certain amount of claim tokens or that another address has been credited, while the reality is that the tokens are minted to the transaction sender only. This can lead to accounting errors, failed refunds, or disputes over token distribution, especially in protocols that rely on the emitted units value for off‑chain calculations. The condition occurs whenever the mintClaim or mintClaimWithFractions functions are called with a non‑matching units value or an explicit account argument that differs from msg.sender. All participants—token claimants, protocol integrators, auditors, and end‑users—are affected because the contract’s public interface suggests a level of control that does not exist. The issue was discovered during a manual security review where the auditor compared the function signatures with the internal calls and noticed that the parameters were never referenced beyond event emission. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the contract still mints tokens correctly; only the discrepancy between the event data and the actual minted amount reveals the problem. The recommended remediation is to either remove the unused units parameter from mintClaimWithFractions or to incorporate it into the minting logic so that the number of fractions minted matches the reported units, and to replace the use of msg.sender with the supplied account argument in the internal _mintValue calls of both mintClaim and mintClaimWithFractions. Aligning the contract’s external API with its internal behavior restores trust, ensures that users receive the amounts they expect, and prevents accounting mismatches that could otherwise undermine the protocol’s integrity.

title: Input & data validation is missing or incomplete
description:
Multiple methods are missing input/data validation or it is incomplete.  
1. The splitValue method in SemiFungible1155 has the maxIndex[_typeID] += len; code so should also do a notMaxItem check for the index  
2. The createAllowlist method accepts a units argument which should be the maximum units mintable through the allowlist - this should be enforced with a check on minting claims from allowlist  
3. The _createAllowlist of AllowlistMinter should revert when merkleRoot == ""  
4. The _mintClaim and _batchMintClaims methods in SemiFungible1155 should revert when _units == 0 or _units[i] == 0 respectively
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract suffers from insufficient input and data validation across several public and internal functions. The root cause is the absence of explicit checks (require statements) that enforce business rules such as non‑zero mint amounts, non‑empty merkle roots, and adherence to maximum item limits. Because the splitValue function increments the internal maxIndex counter without verifying that the requested index is still below the allowed maximum, a caller can supply an index that exceeds the intended range, potentially corrupting the internal accounting of token splits. The createAllowlist function accepts a units parameter that is intended to cap the total number of tokens that can be minted through the allowlist, yet the contract never validates that each claim respects this cap, allowing an attacker to request more units than authorized. Similarly, the internal _createAllowlist routine does not revert when the merkleRoot argument is an empty string, meaning a malformed allowlist can be created without any cryptographic proof, breaking the security model of merkle‑based claims. Finally, the _mintClaim and _batchMintClaims functions allow a caller to pass a zero value for _units (or any element of the _units array), which results in a mint operation that creates no tokens but still consumes gas and may leave the contract in an inconsistent state. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary can invoke these functions with crafted inputs—zero units, empty merkle roots, or oversized indices—to bypass intended limits, cause accounting mismatches, or waste gas, potentially leading to denial‑of‑service conditions or inflated token supplies. The impact is that users may receive fewer tokens than expected, the protocol’s supply accounting can become inaccurate, and the allowlist mechanism may be rendered ineffective, exposing the system to unauthorized minting. These issues appear only when edge‑case inputs are supplied; normal usage with valid parameters may not reveal the problem, making the bug hard to notice during routine testing. The vulnerability was identified during a manual security audit that inspected function signatures and compared them against the documented business logic. To remediate, each function should include explicit validation: require that indices are below maxIndex, that units are greater than zero, that the merkleRoot is non‑empty, and that cumulative minted units never exceed the allowlist’s declared maximum. Adding these checks restores the intended invariants, prevents accidental or malicious misuse, and aligns the contract with standard defensive programming practices for input validation.

title: Fee calculation uses full instead of net amount for pool impact
description:
In the `_calcAddLiquidity` function, there exists a discrepancy between the amount used for fee calculation (`_amountIn`) and the actual amount added to the pool (`netAmount`). The issue occurs in the following sequence:
```solidity
// In _calcAddLiquidity:
valueChange = (_amountIn * tokenPrice).toDecimals(tokenDecimals + provDecimals, 18);
(, pFee) = _calcFeeRate(
    _token, 
    _amountIn, 
    valueChange, 
    baseSetUp.addRemoveLiquidityFee, 
    true
);
netAmount = _amountIn - pFee;
```
The `valueChange` is calculated using the full `_amountIn` before any fees are deducted. This value is then used in `_calcFeeRate` to determine the pool's token ratio impact through the `_calcDelta` function. However, the actual amount being added to the pool is `netAmount` (which is `_amountIn - pFee`).
This creates a mismatch between:
1. The impact assessment used for fee calculation (based on the full amount).
2. The actual impact on the pool (based on net amount after fees).
For example, if a user adds 1000 Token with a 3% fee:
The fee calculation assesses the pool impact using 1000 Token.
But only 970 token is actually added to the pool.
This leads to incorrect fee calculations as the actual pool impact is less than what was used to calculate the fee.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation mismatch that occurs during the add‑liquidity flow of a decentralized pool. In the internal routine that determines how much of a token a liquidity provider (LP) contributes, the contract first computes a valueChange based on the full input amount (_amountIn) before any protocol fee is deducted. This pre‑fee amount is then passed to the fee‑rate calculator, which uses it to estimate the pool‑impact and derive the fee (pFee). After the fee is calculated, the net amount that actually enters the pool is derived as netAmount = _amountIn - pFee. Because the fee‑rate logic was fed the gross amount rather than the net amount, the pool‑impact assessment is inflated. Consequently the fee charged to the LP is based on a larger token movement than what truly occurs, leading to an over‑charged fee or an inaccurate accounting of the pool’s token ratio. The bug manifests whenever a user adds liquidity through the affected function, regardless of the specific token, and it can be reproduced by adding a known amount (for example 1000 tokens with a 3 % fee) and observing that the fee is calculated as if 1000 tokens were added while only 970 tokens actually increase the pool balance. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that the fee reflects the real change in pool composition, but the reality is that the fee appears higher and the LP receives fewer pool shares than anticipated, effectively causing funds to disappear from the LP’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the mathematical model of fee assessment with the actual state changes in the contract; it is subtle because the fee amount itself may look reasonable, while the underlying pool impact is silently mis‑recorded. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting or fee‑basis errors, where the wrong variable is used as the basis for a financial calculation. The impact is medium severity: it does not directly enable theft of funds, but it erodes trust, creates unfair cost distribution, and can lead to long‑term imbalance in the pool’s pricing. To remediate, the fee calculation should be performed on the net amount that will be added to the pool, or the contract should explicitly charge the LP for the sum of the input amount plus the fee (as suggested), ensuring that the pool‑impact assessment matches the actual token transfer. Properly aligning the fee basis with the net deposit restores accounting integrity and prevents users from being over‑charged.

title: Missing price feed validation in oracle contract
description:
The Oracle contract's `_getLastPrice` function retrieves price data from oracle price feeds without performing critical validation checks, which could lead to stale or invalid price data being used in the protocol.
Link:
https://github.com/Hyperhyperfi/protocol/blob/212acfdcd4066334ff5ea06ce46b0bbca7ca212f/src/core/oracle/Oracle.sol#L96-L101
```solidity
function _getLastPrice(address token) internal view returns (uint256 price, uint256 timestamp) {
    (
        uint80 roundID,
        int256 answer,
        /*uint256 startedAt*/,
        uint256 updatedAt,
        uint80 answeredInRound
    ) = tokenOracle[token].latestRoundData();
    price = answer.toUint256();
    timestamp = updatedAt;
}
```
This vulnerability exists in the following areas:
Staleness Check:
The function does not verify if the price data is fresh by comparing the `updatedAt` timestamp with the current `block.timestamp`.
Stale price data could be used for critical protocol operations.
Price Validity:
No validation of the answer value to ensure it's not going to go below minAnswer defined by the breaker.
L2-Specific Concerns:
When deployed on L2 networks, the contract lacks sequencer uptime validation (To be validated).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step when the Oracle contract reads price information from an external price feed. The internal function that fetches the latest price simply calls `latestRoundData()` on the configured feed and returns the raw answer and the `updatedAt` timestamp without checking whether the data is recent or whether the numeric answer satisfies any sanity bounds. The root cause is that the contract trusts the oracle output unconditionally, treating the returned `answer` as a correct market price and the `updatedAt` field as implicitly valid. Because no freshness check compares `updatedAt` with the current `block.timestamp`, a stale price – for example one that has not been updated for many blocks – can be accepted. Likewise, the contract does not verify that the answer is above a minimum acceptable value defined elsewhere in the protocol, allowing a zero or negative price (after conversion to unsigned) to be used. On Layer‑2 deployments the code also omits any sequencer‑uptime verification, meaning that a paused or out‑of‑sync sequencer could feed outdated data without detection. An attacker who can influence the oracle (or who can wait for the feed to become stale) can therefore cause the protocol to calculate collateral values, liquidation thresholds, or minting amounts based on an incorrect price. This may lead to users being liquidated when their positions are actually healthy, withdrawals failing because the contract believes the user is under‑collateralized, or new tokens being minted at an unfair rate. From the user’s perspective the symptoms appear as unexpected liquidations, balances that suddenly drop to zero, or transactions that revert with “insufficient collateral” even though market prices look fine. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the oracle integration code and noticed the absence of any validation logic. It is hard to notice because the function name `_getLastPrice` suggests a simple getter and the call to a well‑known Chainlink interface looks innocuous; developers may assume the feed itself guarantees data quality. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external data or insufficient input validation, where critical protocol state is derived from an unverified source. To remediate, the function should enforce a staleness check (e.g., require `block.timestamp - updatedAt < MAX_STALENESS`), validate that the price is greater than a protocol‑defined minimum, and on L2 networks also verify that the sequencer is online before accepting the price. Adding these checks restores the intended business logic that price data must be fresh, positive, and reliable, preventing the protocol from acting on outdated or malformed values and protecting user funds from inadvertent loss.

title: Lp token transfer without lock data transfer
description: The LPToken contract allows LP tokens to be freely transferred between addresses. However, the protocol tracks liquidity lock data in the pool contract using the original depositor's address, not the token itself. When LP tokens are transferred to a new address, the lock data remains with the original depositor, making it impossible for the new holder to redeem the underlying assets.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the separation between LP token ownership and the liquidity lock metadata that the protocol uses to control redemption of the underlying assets. The LP token contract permits unrestricted transfers of LP tokens between addresses, but the pool contract records lock information – such as the amount locked, unlock timestamp and the original depositor’s address – only against the address that initially deposited liquidity. Because the lock data is not bound to the token itself, when an LP token holder transfers their tokens to another address, the lock record remains attached to the original depositor. Consequently, the new holder inherits tokens that appear valid on the ERC‑20 interface but lack any associated lock rights, making it impossible for them to call the pool’s withdraw or redeem functions. The root cause is a design flaw where the accounting model assumes that token balance ownership implicitly conveys lock entitlement, while the implementation stores entitlement separately and ties it to a static address. An attacker or an unwary user can exploit this by acquiring LP tokens from a third‑party market, expecting to be able to withdraw the underlying liquidity, only to find that the pool contract rejects the request because the caller’s address does not match the stored lock record. The impact is that funds effectively become locked forever for the new holder, leading to loss of value, user confusion, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s secondary market functionality. This condition manifests whenever LP tokens are transferred after the initial deposit, which is a common operation in DeFi ecosystems that support token trading. All participants who rely on LP tokens as transferable proof of liquidity – including traders, liquidity providers, and protocol integrators – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined the relationship between token balances and lock state, revealing the mismatch between the two data stores. Because the token contract behaves correctly from an ERC‑20 perspective, the problem may not be obvious during casual testing; only when a transfer is followed by a redemption attempt does the failure surface, often appearing as a silent “zero balance” or “nothing to withdraw” response. To remediate, the protocol should either prohibit LP token transfers entirely, ensuring that lock data always aligns with token ownership, or redesign the lock management so that the lock metadata is transferred together with the tokens – for example by storing lock rights within the token contract itself or by updating the pool’s records on each transfer. This would restore the invariant that token ownership confers the right to redeem the underlying assets, eliminating the scenario where transferred tokens become unusable.

title: Unrestricted LP burn enables price inflation to exploit deposits
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted liquidity‑provider (LP) token burn that allows any holder to destroy arbitrary amounts of LP tokens through the public burn() and burnFrom() functions. Because the LP token price is derived from the ratio of total pool value to total LP supply, reducing the supply without a corresponding reduction in pool assets inflates the price of each remaining LP token. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate deposit, mint a large amount of LP tokens, then burn almost all of them, leaving only a tiny residual supply. This manipulation skews the pool state so that the next depositor’s calculation of how many LP tokens to mint yields a value that rounds down to zero. When the depositor supplies a minimum‑LP‑amount (slippage) parameter, the transaction reverts, creating a denial‑of‑service condition; if the slippage check is omitted, the deposit succeeds but the user receives no LP tokens, effectively losing the deposited assets because the protocol records the deposit but does not credit any ownership. The issue occurs whenever the LP token contract permits unrestricted burning and the pool’s accounting logic does not enforce a minimum supply or protect against price distortion caused by supply changes. It affects any user attempting to add liquidity after such a burn, the protocol’s overall accounting integrity, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct LP balances. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the LP token’s burn interface and the liquidity‑addition formula. It can be hard to notice because burning tokens is a standard ERC20 feature and the price inflation is not directly visible in the UI; users only see that their deposit either fails with a slippage error or results in a zero‑balance LP receipt, which may be interpreted as a normal rounding outcome. Conceptually, the fix is to restrict burning to privileged protocol roles (e.g., the pool contract) or to disable public burn functions when the total LP supply falls below a safe threshold, thereby preserving the invariant that LP price reflects the true pool value and preventing price manipulation attacks.

title: Rounding error in put option price reduces safety margin
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding bias in the calculation of put option strike prices that unintentionally reduces the protocol’s safety margin. The contract uses a single helper function to round a computed strike price to the nearest hundred or ten units, rounding upward when the remainder is at least half of the rounding step. This same upward‑rounding rule is applied to both call and put options. For calls, rounding up moves the strike further out‑of‑the‑money, which is favorable to the protocol, but for puts the same upward rounding pushes the strike price closer to, or even into, the money. The root cause is the reuse of a generic rounding routine without considering the opposite risk profile of puts. An attacker can exploit the bug by purchasing put options that appear to be safely out‑of‑the‑money based on the relative discount, only to find that the rounded strike is at‑the‑money or only slightly out‑of‑the‑money, dramatically increasing the probability of a profitable exercise. The impact is a reduction of the intended out‑of‑the‑money buffer, which can lead to higher payouts than the protocol’s risk model anticipates and potentially to loss of collateral held against the options. The condition for the bug to manifest is when the rounding option is set to NEAREST_HUNDRED or NEAREST_TEN and the raw strike calculation leaves a remainder greater than or equal to half of the rounding step; under these circumstances the rounding function adds the rounding step, moving the strike upward. Users who buy puts expect a strike that is safely below the spot price (for example a 5 % discount on a 1000 USD spot should give a 950 USD strike), but they may see a strike equal to the spot price (1000 USD) or only slightly below it, causing the UI to display a higher‑than‑expected payout potential. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that compared the strike‑generation logic for calls and puts and noticed the asymmetric effect of the rounding routine. It can be hard to notice because rounding appears to be a harmless utility function and the same code path is used for both option types, masking the divergent financial consequences. The proper fix is to apply opposite rounding directions: keep rounding up for calls, but round down for puts, or introduce separate rounding logic that ensures the put strike is always rounded away from the spot price, preserving the intended out‑of‑the‑money buffer. This change restores the intended risk profile and prevents the protocol from unintentionally granting traders a more favorable strike price.

title: Weak signature validation allows multiple option mispricing vectors
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a weak signature validation scheme that fails to bind all essential option parameters and does not enforce a signature expiration deadline. Because the signed hash only includes a subset of the data—specifically the underlying asset, option type, period, maturity date and relative strike—but omits the period value in the hash and lacks any deadline field, an attacker can reuse a previously obtained signature with altered parameters. This enables two distinct mispricing vectors. First, period manipulation: a user can request a signature for a longer period (e.g., fourteen days) and later execute the option with a shorter period (e.g., seven days) while the maturity date remains unchanged. The contract validates the position using the implied volatility (IV) associated with the longer period, resulting in a price that is lower than it should be for the actual shorter period, thereby granting the user an unfairly cheap option. Second, stale strike price reuse: a user obtains a signature for a relative strike based on a spot price at the time of signing, then waits for the market to move, and finally executes the option with the same signature. Since the signature does not capture a deadline or the current spot price, the contract applies the IV calculated for the old strike, causing the option to be priced incorrectly. The impact is that the protocol may sell options at a price that does not reflect the true risk, leading to systematic under‑pricing and potential loss of funds for the liquidity providers or the protocol treasury. The issue manifests whenever a user can obtain a valid signature and later submit a transaction with mismatched period or outdated market data, which is possible because the contract’s internal _recoverSigner function does not check a timestamp or deadline. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature hashing logic and identified missing fields. It can be hard to notice because the contract still enforces signature correctness for the fields it does hash, so the transaction appears valid on‑chain, while the subtle economic discrepancy only surfaces in the option payoff calculations. To remediate, the hash function should be extended to include every parameter that influences pricing, such as the period and an explicit deadline, and the contract should reject signatures that are older than the deadline. This aligns the cryptographic commitment with the business logic of option pricing, preventing reuse of stale signatures and ensuring that the IV used matches the actual option terms, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Hardcoded slippage tolerance risks poor trading or DOS
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded slippage tolerance of two percent that is embedded directly in the contract’s internal price‑adjustment routine. Because the value is fixed in code, the contract cannot adapt to changing market conditions, pool depth, or token volatility. When the market moves quickly or a liquidity pool is shallow, the two‑percent buffer may be too small, causing the quoted amount to be exceeded and the transaction to revert; this manifests as a denial‑of‑service condition where users repeatedly lose gas without receiving any tokens. Conversely, in deep, highly liquid pools the same two‑percent buffer is unnecessarily large, so users receive a worse execution price than expected, effectively paying extra slippage that could have been avoided. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the `_applySlippage` function and noted the constant multiplier. It is subtle because the contract still appears to honor the quoted price, yet the hidden addition of a fixed percentage can silently degrade trade outcomes or cause silent failures, making it hard to spot from a casual UI inspection. From the user’s perspective a trade may either complete with a price that is noticeably worse than the quoted rate, or it may fail entirely, leaving the user with a transaction that consumed gas but returned no tokens, creating the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the swap gave me nothing”. The affected parties include any trader interacting with the protocol, the protocol itself which may lose credibility, and liquidity providers whose pools may be under‑utilized due to failed trades. The root cause is the lack of configurability: the slippage tolerance is a magic number rather than a parameter that can be set by governance or adjusted dynamically based on market data. To remediate, the contract should expose the tolerance as an admin‑controlled variable or compute it from on‑chain market indicators, thereby aligning the allowed price deviation with real‑time liquidity and volatility conditions and eliminating both unnecessary price loss and inadvertent transaction reverts.

title: block.timestamp use in dex swap deadlines may cause poor trading
description:
In the PositionInteractionFacet.sol contract, when executing DEX swaps, the deadline parameter is set to `block.timestamp + 30 minutes`:
```solidity
IV3SwapRouter.ExactOutputSingleParams memory params = IV3SwapRouter.ExactOutputSingleParams({
    tokenIn: assetIn,
    tokenOut: assetOut,
    fee: dex.dexFee,
    recipient: address(this),
    deadline: block.timestamp + 30 minutes, // Unnecessary buffer
    amountOut: amountOut,
    amountInMaximum: amountInMaximum,
    sqrtPriceLimitX96: sqrtPriceLimitX96
});
```
This implementation is problematic for several reasons:
1. The 30-minute buffer is unnecessary since the transaction will be executed at the current block.timestamp anyway.
2. This extended deadline window allows malicious MEV bots to potentially withhold the transaction and execute it at a less optimal time.
3. This implementation doesn't provide any real protection against transaction delays since the actual execution time is determined by the network's block production.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the PositionInteractionFacet.sol contract sets the deadline parameter for Uniswap V3 exact‑output swaps. Instead of using a deadline supplied by the caller, the code unconditionally adds a 30‑minute buffer to the current block timestamp (block.timestamp + 30 minutes) and passes this value to the router. This practice creates a time‑based misconfiguration that can be exploited by malicious actors. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the purpose of the deadline field: the deadline is intended to protect a transaction from being executed after a certain time, not to extend the window for execution. Because the transaction is mined in the same block in which it is submitted, the extra 30‑minute window does not provide any real safety; the transaction will either be included immediately or will fail if the block is mined after the deadline. However, the extended window gives MEV bots an opportunity to observe the pending transaction, withhold it, and later submit it at a moment when market prices have moved unfavourably. By waiting up to 30 minutes, a bot can let the price drift, causing the swap to execute at a worse rate, increasing slippage, or even causing the transaction to revert due to insufficient output. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a trade that returns fewer tokens than expected, a sudden loss of value, or a transaction that appears to have been “stuck” before finally being mined with a poor price. The impact is primarily financial: users receive less of the desired asset, their effective price worsens, and in extreme cases the contract may lose value if the swap fails after the deadline passes. The issue affects any participant who relies on the contract to perform swaps – individual traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the overall accounting of assets becomes inaccurate. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction with external DEX routers and identified the unnecessary time buffer as a potential vector for front‑running. It can be hard to notice because the deadline field appears to be a defensive measure; developers may assume that a longer deadline is safer, overlooking the fact that it actually widens the attack surface for time‑sensitive price manipulation. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the hard‑coded block.timestamp + 30 minutes with a deadline value supplied by the user, or alternatively enforce a very short deadline (e.g., a few seconds) that aligns with the expected execution time. This change removes the unnecessary time window, eliminates the opportunity for MEV bots to manipulate execution timing, and restores the intended protection of preventing stale trades. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of time‑parameter misuse and deadline misconfiguration, where a contract incorrectly extends a time‑sensitive operation, leading to economic loss and violation of the expected trade execution guarantees.

title: strategy contracts: exercise window ignored in premium calculation
description:
The protocol currently allows options to be exercised within a window after the maturity date (i.e., exerciseWindowDuration):
```solidity
function isPayoffAvailable
(uint256 positionID, address caller, address /*recipient*/ )
external
virtual
override
returns (bool)
--snip--
return strg.setUp.treasury.manager().isApprovedOrOwner
(caller, positionID)
&& _calculateStrategyPayOff
(positionID) > 0 && block.timestamp >= maturity
&& block.timestamp <= maturity + strg.setUp.base.exerciseWindowDuration;
```
However, the premium calculation does not account for this extended exercise window. This creates an inconsistency, as the price at the maturity date should be used to calculate the value of the option, but the current price after the maturity date is being used instead. An option buyer can wait for the option price to increase after the maturity date, exercise his option at a more favorable price, and gain a positive profit and loss (PnL).
Note: The protocol uses European Options and their pricing model, which assumes options should only be exercised at the maturity date price. However, in the current strategy contracts, exercise is allowed within a window of time (exerciseWindowDuration) after the maturity date. Options are paid off based on the current price, not the maturity date price.
Note: Reducing the exercise window duration will increase the risk of users missing the opportunity to call payOff and losing their potential profit.
Example Scenario (based on tests and scripts numbers):
Option period = 7 days
Exercise window duration = 3 days (extension of 50% of the original period)
A user pays the premium for a 7-day option, but after the maturity date, they are allowed an additional 3-day window to exercise the option. During this period, the user can wait for the price to increase and then exercise the option, maximizing their profit. However, the premium is not adjusted to account for this extra time.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the option exercise window and the premium calculation in the strategy contracts. The contract permits a European‑style option to be exercised not only at the exact maturity timestamp but also within a configurable exerciseWindowDuration after maturity. The payoff function checks that block.timestamp is between maturity and maturity + exerciseWindowDuration and then computes the payoff using the current market price at the time of exercise. However, the premium that the buyer pays is calculated assuming the option can be exercised only at the maturity price, as required by the European pricing model. Because the premium does not incorporate the extra time, a holder can wait until the price moves favorably during the post‑maturity window, call the payoff function, and receive a payout that is higher than the value implied by the premium. This results in an unintended positive PnL for the buyer and a loss for the protocol. The issue occurs whenever the exerciseWindowDuration is non‑zero, the price oracle reports a different price after maturity, and the holder chooses to delay exercising. It is hard to notice because the window is often short and tests may only verify that exercising is possible, not that the price used matches the pricing assumptions. From a user’s perspective the UI shows that the option can still be exercised after maturity, the user expects the payout to be based on the maturity price, but instead receives a larger amount, effectively money disappears from the protocol’s reserves. The bug belongs to the class of pricing‑model mismatches where business logic (European option exercise at a single point) is violated by implementation (allowing a time‑extended exercise with live price). To fix the problem the payoff calculation should be anchored to a historical price snapshot taken at maturity, or the premium formula should be extended to price the additional exercise window, thereby aligning the economic model with the contract’s behavior.

title: StrategyManager functions are not payable
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing payable capability in the StrategyManager contract. The contract exposes a function called executeCall that forwards an arbitrary amount of ether (the value parameter) to a target address using low‑level call syntax. However, none of the external functions of StrategyManager are marked payable and the contract does not implement a fallback() or receive() function. Because of this, the contract cannot accept ether deposits, and its balance will remain zero unless ether is sent via a self‑destruct from another contract. When a user or a strategy tries to invoke executeCall with a non‑zero value, the call attempts to transfer ether from the StrategyManager’s balance. Since the contract holds no ether, the call fails with an out‑of‑gas or insufficient‑balance error, and the require statement may revert the whole transaction if allowRevert is false. From a user’s point of view the expected behaviour – sending ether to fund a strategy and having the call succeed – is not met; the UI may show a transaction pending or successful while the strategy execution does not happen, or the transaction may simply revert with “execution reverted”. This creates a denial‑of‑service style issue: any strategy that requires ether cannot be executed, effectively breaking the business logic that assumes funds can be transferred through the manager. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function signatures and noticed the absence of payable modifiers and a fallback/receive function despite the presence of value‑forwarding logic. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the executeCall function itself does not directly reject a zero‑value call, so only when a non‑zero value is used does the failure surface. To remediate, the contract should mark the functions that forward ether as payable and optionally add a receive() or fallback() function to allow the contract to hold ether, ensuring that the balance is sufficient for the forwarded value and that the intended strategy execution succeeds. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a “missing payable modifier” or “inability to receive ether” and violates the accounting assumption that the manager can hold and forward funds as required by the protocol’s financial flows.

title: Looping.openPosition() insufficient division factor
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the minimum amount out (minAmountOut) inside the openPosition function when a position is opened with the yield asset as the starting token. The code multiplies the flash‑loan amount by a fixed scaling factor of 1e8, divides by the user‑provided _minAmountOut, multiplies by the initial amount, and then divides again by 1e8 to compensate for integer division rounding. This approach assumes that the difference between the decimal precision of the yield asset and the debt asset does not exceed eight places. When the yield asset has more than eight additional decimals compared to the debt asset, the 1e8 factor no longer provides enough granularity, causing the division to round down more aggressively than intended. As a result, the computed minAmountOut can be smaller than the amount the user expects to receive from the swap. In practice, a user who supplies a flash‑loan premium in the yield asset may see the swap execute with a lower output, leaving the position under‑collateralised or causing the protocol to receive insufficient debt asset to cover the loan. This discrepancy can lead to unexpected loss of funds for the user, potential liquidation of the position, or a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants. The issue manifests only when the openPosition call is made with the _startWithYield flag set to true and when the decimal gap between the two assets exceeds eight. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic handling of token decimals. The bug is subtle because the rounding error does not trigger a revert; instead, it silently reduces the amount out, making it hard to detect without detailed balance tracing. To remediate the problem, the scaling factor should be increased to match the maximum possible decimal difference (for example using 1e36) or, more robustly, the calculation should be performed using a library that handles arbitrary‑precision arithmetic or explicitly accounts for the assets’ decimal places. By ensuring that the division factor provides sufficient precision, the protocol can guarantee that the minAmountOut reflects the true expected output, preserving user expectations that the swap will yield at least the quoted amount and maintaining the integrity of the protocol’s financial logic.

title: openPosition() DoS when _initialAmount is _yieldAsset
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the openPosition() function of the Looping contract when a user supplies the initial premium amount (_initialAmount) in the yield asset and chooses to start the operation with that yield asset. The function attempts to swap the supplied yield asset into the debt asset before executing the flash‑loan logic. To protect the swap it calculates a minimum amount out (minAmountOut) using the formula ((flashloanAmount * 1e8) / minAmountOut) * _initialAmount / 1e8. This formula implicitly assumes that the debt asset and the yield asset have identical valuation and decimal scaling, which is not true for assets with different prices or different token decimals (for example USDC versus WBTC). When the assets differ, the computed minAmountOut can become larger than the actual amount of yield asset that the user provided. The swap call then requires at least this inflated amount, causing the internal swap to revert. Because the revert happens before any state changes are committed, the whole openPosition transaction fails, effectively denying service to any user who tries to open a position with a yield‑asset premium under those market conditions. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: legitimate users cannot open positions, their transaction reverts, and they see no change in balances despite having approved token transfers. The bug is triggered only when the user starts with the yield asset and the market price relationship makes the calculated minAmountOut exceed the supplied amount, which can happen with normal price fluctuations or when assets have different decimal conventions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the minAmountOut calculation and identified the unrealistic valuation assumption. It is hard to notice because the code compiles and the arithmetic does not overflow; the error only manifests under specific price ratios, making it appear as a sporadic revert rather than a deterministic bug. The appropriate remediation is to stop deriving the minimum acceptable amount from a formula that assumes equal valuation. Instead, the contract should accept the caller‑provided minimum amount out as an explicit argument, allowing the caller to supply a correctly calculated value based on current market rates, or use an oracle‑based price check. By doing so the swap will no longer demand an impossible amount, preventing the revert and restoring normal operation. This class of bug falls under incorrect financial invariant enforcement, where a contract assumes equal value between heterogeneous assets, leading to impossible swap constraints and a denial‑of‑service condition. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction failure with a generic revert message, the user’s balance remains unchanged, and the expected refund or position opening never occurs, contrary to the expectation that providing the premium should open the position successfully.

title: Unrevoked approvals causing swap failures in UniswapV3Swapper.swap()
description:
The UniswapV3Swapper.swap() function has an issue where it does not revoke tokens approvals from the router after the swap, leading to a potential DoS with tokens like USDT, where this issue arises due to the fact that approvals are not reset after swaps, and if a token like USDT is used, modifying an allowance from a non-zero value to another non-zero value will revert if the allowance of the previous swap is not fully consumed by the router, which will result in reverting the swap transaction.
Similar issue was found with the different impact in the Looping._swap() function.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the swap function of a Uniswap V3 wrapper contract does not clear the ERC‑20 allowance it grants to the router after completing a trade. The root cause is that the code calls approve(router, amountIn) before the swap but never resets the allowance to zero afterwards. For tokens that implement the ERC‑20 standard with a restriction that changing an allowance from a non‑zero value to another non‑zero value must first be set to zero (e.g., USDT), the leftover allowance from the previous trade remains non‑zero. When a subsequent swap attempts to set a new allowance, the token contract reverts the transaction because the existing allowance has not been fully consumed. An attacker can trigger this condition by performing a swap with such a token and then leaving the allowance partially used, causing all later swaps that rely on the same wrapper to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: legitimate users attempting to trade the affected token receive a transaction revert, see no token received, and may be unable to withdraw or move funds through the wrapper. The issue manifests only when the token used in the swap enforces the zero‑before‑non‑zero rule and when the wrapper does not explicitly reset the allowance. Users of the protocol, including traders and liquidity providers, are affected because their expected outcome – a successful swap delivering the desired amountOut – is replaced by a failed transaction with no state change. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the approval flow and compared it against known token behaviours. It can be hard to notice because many ERC‑20 tokens allow direct overwriting of allowances, so tests with standard tokens pass, masking the bug for tokens with stricter allowance semantics. The correct mitigation is to include a call that revokes the router’s allowance (approve(router, 0)) after the swap completes, or to use safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance patterns that respect the token’s allowance rules. By resetting the allowance, the contract ensures that each swap starts from a clean state, preventing the revert and restoring the expected business logic that a swap either succeeds and transfers the output tokens or fails without side effects.

title: liquidityFacet: fenwick tree attack through multiple deposits
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity addition routine that stores each deposit in a Fenwick‑tree based accounting structure. The routine registers a new timestamp key for every deposit without verifying that the caller is the intended beneficiary. Because the tree has a hard‑coded maximum number of entries (maxDepositEntries), an attacker can repeatedly invoke the addLiquidity function on behalf of any address, causing the internal _registerKey routine to push a new key each time until the entry limit is reached. Once the limit is hit, the Fenwick tree rejects further registrations and the contract reverts with a Fenwicks_TooManyKeys error. This behaviour enables a griefing attack: legitimate users attempting to provide liquidity receive a revert or see that their transaction does nothing, effectively locking them out of the protocol. The attack can be carried out as long as the attacker can continue to deposit; the only way to free space in the tree is for all existing liquidity to be withdrawn after the lock duration expires, which may be a long period, extending the denial‑of‑service window. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a deposit transaction fails with an obscure error, or that the “Add Liquidity” button becomes unresponsive, leading users to believe their funds are missing or that the protocol is broken. The root cause is the missing access control on the deposit function – the contract does not enforce that msg.sender matches the beneficiary, nor does it limit the number of entries per user. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the internal bookkeeping logic and noticed that the key registration only checks a global counter. It can be hard to notice because normal deposits succeed and the tree behaves correctly until the global limit is exhausted, at which point the failure appears as a generic “too many keys” revert rather than a clear security problem. To remediate, the contract should validate that the caller is the account for which liquidity is being added, or redesign the accounting to track entries per user and enforce per‑user limits, or increase the tree capacity and provide a safe reset mechanism that does not require a full withdrawal of all funds. In essence, the bug is a classic unauthorized‑action / resource‑exhaustion flaw that allows an attacker to fill a bounded data structure and cause a denial‑of‑service on liquidity provision.

title: liquidityFacet: unauthorized liquidity removal for other users
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized liquidity removal flaw in the removeLiquidity function of a DeFi pool contract. The function accepts a destination address parameter (_to) that determines whose liquidity is withdrawn, but it never verifies that the caller (msg.sender) is the same as the destination address. Because there is no access‑control check, any external account can invoke removeLiquidity and specify another user’s address as the target, causing the contract to treat that user’s unlocked LP tokens as if they were being removed by the owner. The root cause is the missing require statement that would enforce msg.sender == _to before the contract updates lock data, burns the LP tokens and transfers the underlying assets. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a transaction that calls removeLiquidity, passes the victim’s address as _to, and selects an amount up to the victim’s unlocked liquidity. The contract then proceeds to burn the victim’s LP tokens, update lock information for the victim, and send the underlying token amount to the address supplied in _to (which may be the attacker if they also control that address). From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden disappearance of their liquidity balance without any action on their part; the UI may show a zero or reduced LP balance and possibly an unexpected receipt of underlying tokens. The impact is loss of the LP position and any accrued rewards, which cannot be automatically restored, effectively reducing the user’s stake in the pool. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the access patterns of state‑changing functions. It can be hard to notice because the function still performs a legitimate withdrawal and the transferred tokens reach an address, so the transaction appears normal unless the caller’s address is inspected. The flaw belongs to the class of authorization bypass bugs where a privileged operation does not correctly restrict the caller. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the owner of the liquidity can initiate its removal, typically by adding a check that msg.sender equals the _to parameter or by using a dedicated modifier that validates ownership before proceeding with the removal logic.

title: operationalTreasury: assumes 1:1 USD value for base token
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OperationalTreasury component where fees and premium amounts are calculated in USD but the contract implicitly assumes that the base token used for purchases has a constant value of one US dollar. The code converts the USD fee to the token's decimal representation using a generic toDecimals function, yet it never applies the actual market price of the token. Consequently, when the token trades below one dollar, the contract over‑collects tokens from the user because it transfers a larger token amount than the USD‑denominated fee would require. Conversely, if the token depegs and rises above one dollar, the treasury may collect insufficient fees, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This flaw appears in the internal _takeFeesLockLiquidity function, where the calculated fee (in USD) is added to the collectedFees ledger and then transferred from the caller together with the premium, and it also propagates to the payoff logic where profit‑and‑loss values are computed in USD but settled in token units without price adjustment. The root cause is the absence of a price oracle or any external reference that would translate USD values into the correct amount of base token at the time of the transaction. An attacker could exploit the bug by timing a transaction when the base token’s price deviates significantly from one dollar, for example by inducing a depeg of a stablecoin, thereby forcing users to pay excessive fees or allowing the treasury to under‑collect fees and become under‑collateralised. The impact includes users losing more tokens than intended, unexpected balance reductions, and the protocol’s financial model becoming inaccurate, which may eventually lead to insolvency if the discrepancy accumulates. The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a position or receives a payout, i.e., during any fee or premium transfer involving the base token. It affects all participants who interact with the treasury using that token, regardless of their role. The problem was discovered during a manual audit review that highlighted the mismatch between USD calculations and token transfers, a subtle bug because the decimal conversion appears syntactically correct and therefore does not raise immediate red flags. Detecting the flaw in production can be difficult since the contract does not emit explicit warnings about price assumptions, and the symptom—users seeing larger token deductions than expected—may be attributed to normal market volatility. To remediate the issue, the contract should incorporate a reliable price feed for the base token and use that price to convert USD‑denominated fees and premiums into the exact token amount required, or alternatively perform all accounting directly in token units to avoid any implicit 1:1 assumption. This change would align the transferred amounts with the true economic value, restore accurate fee collection, and preserve the integrity of the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: connect() can be called externally in AdminStrategy causing DoS
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized external callable initialization function in the AdminStrategy contract, commonly referred to as a missing‑access‑control or state‑lock bug. The connect() function can be invoked by any address because it lacks any role or sender restriction. When called, it writes the caller’s address into the internal setUp.treasury storage slot. The protocol’s legitimate initialization routine (init()) later checks whether the treasury field is already populated and reverts with TreasuryAlreadySet if it is. Consequently, an attacker who calls connect() before the official AdminOperationalTreasury initialization permanently locks the treasury slot with a malicious or zero address, causing every subsequent legitimate init() or addStrategy call to fail. This denial‑of‑service (DoS) vector prevents the strategy contract from being properly set up, bricks the contract, and stops admins from adding or configuring new strategies. The issue manifests as transaction reverts with the TreasuryAlreadySet error, missing treasury assignments in UI dashboards, and an inability to complete protocol setup steps that users expect to succeed. It affects protocol administrators, strategy developers, and ultimately end‑users who rely on the strategy’s functionality, because the contract becomes unusable and any funds that would have been managed by the strategy remain inaccessible. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s initialization flow and noticed the absence of any onlyRole or msg.sender validation on connect(). It can be hard to notice in routine testing because the normal deployment path uses a trusted admin account, so the function appears to work correctly under expected conditions, while the attack surface is only exposed when an external actor can invoke the function. The proper remediation is to restrict connect() to a trusted caller, for example by applying an onlyRole modifier, checking that msg.sender matches the expected AdminOperationalTreasury address, or otherwise enforcing that only the protocol’s designated controller can set the treasury field. This aligns the function with the intended initialization pattern and eliminates the state‑lock condition that leads to the DoS scenario.

title: Reward Index Inflation Due to Rounding Up Can Trap Rewards
description:
In the _depositPremium function within PositionInteractionFacet.sol, when option premiums are added as rewards for liquidity providers, the rewards.rewardsPerLPQ128 index is updated using mulDivRoundingUp:
```solidity
if (lpSupply > 0) rewards.rewardsPerLPQ128 += upscaledPremium.mulDivRoundingUp
(Q128, lpSupply);
```
Using mulDivRoundingUp causes the calculated reward added per LP token unit (scaled by Q128) to be rounded up to the nearest integer in the fixed-point representation. While seemingly small for individual deposits, these upward rounding errors accumulate in the rewardsPerLPQ128 index with each premium deposit over time.
This leads to the rewardsPerLPQ128 index potentially representing a slightly higher total reward distribution promise than the actual amount of totalRewards physically deposited into the pool.
When a user claims rewards via _claimRewards in LiquidityFacet.sol, their pending rewards (pending) are calculated based on the difference in the (potentially inflated) index relative to their last claim checkpoint. The function then attempts to subtract these pending rewards from the actual totalRewards available:
```solidity
strg.ledger.state.rewardsByToken[token].totalRewards -= pending;
```
If the accumulated upward rounding errors in the rewardsPerLPQ128 index cause the calculated pending amount for a user (especially one claiming later after many premium deposits have occurred) to exceed the actual remaining totalRewards, this subtraction will underflow and revert the transaction.
Consequently, the last users attempting to claim their rewards may be unable to do so, and their legitimately earned rewards become permanently trapped in the contract.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During reward distribution, the contract updates a per‑LP token reward index by multiplying the premium amount and dividing by the total LP supply using a rounding‑up division routine. This causes the index to be slightly larger than the true cumulative premium because each update is rounded upward. Over many deposits the small excess accumulates, so the index eventually promises more reward than the pool actually holds. When a liquidity provider later calls the claim function, the contract computes the provider’s pending reward as the difference between the current (inflated) index and the provider’s last recorded index, then subtracts that amount from the pool’s totalRewards balance. If the pending amount is larger than the remaining totalRewards, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts. As a result the last claimers cannot receive their earned rewards and the excess amount becomes permanently locked in the contract. The bug appears only after several premium deposits have been made and typically affects users who claim late, because earlier claimers reduce the pool balance before the index inflation becomes significant. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑tracking logic, where the auditor noticed the use of a rounding‑up function in a financial accounting context. The problem is subtle because each individual rounding error is tiny and does not affect normal operation, making it easy to miss in testing that only covers a few deposits. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑inflation bugs caused by inappropriate rounding direction in cumulative indices. To fix the issue the reward‑per‑token increment should be calculated with rounding down (or exact integer division) so that the index never exceeds the actual deposited rewards, guaranteeing that totalRewards is always sufficient to cover claimed amounts. Users may observe that after a series of deposits their claim transaction fails with an underflow error, or that the UI shows a reward amount but the transaction reverts, indicating that rewards are trapped. The bug violates the protocol’s assumption that the reward index is a conservative estimate of available funds, breaking the accounting invariant that totalRewards ≥ sum of all pending rewards.

title: Incorrect ERC20 transfer in withdrawFee prevents fee withdrawal
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee withdrawal routine of the treasury contract. The function intended to move accumulated protocol fees from the contract’s own balance to a designated recipient calls the ERC20 safeTransferFrom method instead of the standard safeTransfer. safeTransferFrom requires that the caller (the contract) has been granted an allowance by the token holder (the contract itself) to move the specified amount. Because the contract never approves itself to spend its own tokens, the allowance check fails and the transfer is reverted. This logical error means that whenever the feesReceiver invokes withdrawFee, the transaction reverts and the collected fees remain locked inside the contract. From a user perspective the expected outcome – a positive token transfer to the recipient – does not occur; the UI may display a zero balance change or a failed transaction without an obvious error message. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the treasury’s withdrawal logic, where the auditor noted the misuse of safeTransferFrom. It can be hard to notice because the call compiles and appears syntactically correct, and the failure only surfaces at runtime when the allowance is missing, which may be masked by generic revert messages. The impact is medium severity: protocol fees cannot be withdrawn, leading to funds being effectively frozen and potentially causing accounting mismatches, delayed revenue distribution, and loss of confidence among token holders. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect token transfer patterns, specifically the misuse of transferFrom for self‑owned balances. To remediate, the contract should replace safeTransferFrom with safeTransfer, allowing the contract to move its own tokens without requiring an allowance, and optionally add a check to ensure the amount is non‑zero before attempting the transfer. This aligns the implementation with standard ERC20 transfer semantics and restores the intended fee withdrawal functionality.

title: EmissionScheduler and Minter contracts can't be initialized due to an incorrect startTime check
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the initialization routine of the EmissionScheduler contract that prevents the contract from ever being set up. The initialize() function is supposed to be called once by the Minter contract to record the first emission start time, but the code mistakenly checks if the stored startTime equals zero and reverts with an AlreadyInitialized error when that condition is true. Because the contract’s startTime is initially zero, the guard triggers on the very first call, treating the contract as already initialized and aborting the transaction. This reversed condition is the root cause: the intended guard should reject calls only when startTime is non‑zero, i.e., when the contract has already been initialized. As a result, the EmissionScheduler cannot be initialized, which in turn blocks the Minter contract’s own initialization sequence that depends on a successful call to EmissionScheduler.initialize(). The impact is a denial‑of‑service scenario: the protocol’s emission schedule never starts, token minting is halted, and any downstream logic that expects scheduled emissions will fail. Users looking for newly minted tokens will see no balance changes, front‑ends may display empty or zero‑value fields, and the protocol may appear deadlocked. This condition occurs whenever the deployment script or admin attempts to launch the system with a startTime of zero, which is the normal first‑time value. The affected parties include the protocol administrators, token holders, and any contracts that rely on the emission schedule. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the initialize() logic and noticed the contradictory check. It can be hard to spot because the guard uses a familiar pattern (checking a state variable before allowing re‑initialization) but the comparison operator is inverted, leading to a false positive revert that only manifests on the first call. To fix the problem, the condition should be changed to revert only when startTime is already non‑zero (i.e., if (startTime != 0) revert AlreadyInitialized()), thereby allowing the first initialization while still protecting against subsequent re‑initializations. Conceptually, this is a classic “incorrect initialization guard” or “reversed boolean check” bug that violates the contract’s expected lifecycle and breaks the business logic that assumes emissions will commence after deployment.

title: Dead gauges are not handled correctly in Voter._vote() function
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the voting logic of a decentralized finance protocol where users allocate voting power to liquidity pools through a Voter contract. The core issue is that the internal _vote function does not verify whether a target gauge – the on‑chain entity that receives votes and distributes rewards – is still alive before processing the vote. Because the contract assumes every gauge referenced in the vote array is active, it proceeds to update internal accounting, call reward‑accrual helpers, and deposit bribe tokens even for gauges that have been marked dead. The root cause is the missing isAlive check that should guard the loop iterating over the supplied pool list. When a dead gauge is processed, the _updateFor helper adds accrued reward shares to a temporary variable but, due to the gauge being dead, the share is not recorded in the claimable mapping.
