Because the script fails early in the build process, no runtime code is executed, so the issue is not observable through contract interactions but manifests as a hard failure during compilation. This condition occurs whenever a developer runs the deployment script in a Foundry environment, as the script relies on vm.setEnv and DeployUsdxlFileUtils calls that reference usdxlConfig. The affected parties are developers and protocol engineers who intend to launch the Usdxl component on the Hyper testnet, as well as auditors who cannot verify deployment behavior. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the script for correctness and noticed a comment flagging the missing declaration. The bug can be hard to notice because the surrounding code compiles up to the point of the undefined identifier, and the error message may be dismissed as a minor typo. To remediate, the usdxlConfig variable should be declared with the appropriate type (for example, a struct or contract interface returned by DeployUsdxlFileUtils.readUsdxlInput) and stored as a state variable or local variable before it is used. Adding the declaration resolves the compilation error, allowing the script to execute the intended deployment steps, which restores the expected behavior where the user sees deployed contract addresses and the protocol can progress to production. This class of issue falls under missing variable declarations or undefined identifiers, a common source of build failures that break deployment pipelines and can lead to delays or missed releases if not corrected.

title: Incorrect excessFeeRefundAddress and callValueRefundAddress are provided when bridging tokens to the L2
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of passing the contract’s own address (address(this)) as both excessFeeRefundAddress and callValueRefundAddress when creating a retryable ticket for L1‑to‑L2 token bridging. The bridge expects excessFeeRefundAddress to receive any unused portion of the fee that was supplied for the L2 transaction, and callValueRefundAddress to be the entity that can cancel the ticket and retrieve the call value if the L2 execution fails. By hard‑coding the contract address, any surplus fee is credited to the contract instead of the user, and the only party able to cancel the ticket is the contract itself. If the contract does not implement logic to forward the refund or expose a cancellation interface, the user’s funds become inaccessible. This can be triggered whenever the supplied tokenTotalFeeAmount exceeds the actual gas used on L2, or when the L2 call reverts and a cancellation is required. The impact is that users may see their balance unchanged after a bridge attempt, receive zero refund, or have the bridging ticket stuck, effectively losing the excess fee and possibly the entire call value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the _mintAndBridge function, where the parameters were inspected and found to be hard‑coded to address(this). The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the bridge reports success while the funds are silently redirected to the contract, making the bug easy to miss in functional testing. The proper fix is to make excessFeeRefundAddress and callValueRefundAddress configurable, typically set to the user’s L2 address or a designated treasury, and to ensure that any received refunds are forwarded to the originating caller. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect address handling in cross‑chain messaging, where refund and cancellation destinations are mis‑assigned, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the bridge protocol.

title: Incorrect address provided as the receiver when bridging and minting the Node Key token on the L2
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an address misrouting bug that occurs during the bridging phase of the Node Key token minting process. When a user calls the mint function, the contract internally invokes _mintAndBridge, which is supposed to mint the token to the address supplied by the caller (the _to parameter) and then forward the minting information to the Layer‑2 (L2) contract so that the same amount of tokens is created on L2 for the same recipient. Instead of encoding the _to address into the calldata that is sent to the L2 inbox, the implementation mistakenly uses msg.sender – the address that initiated the transaction on Layer‑1 – when constructing the ABI‑encoded call to the L2 mint function. This mismatch means that the L2 side credits the tokens to the caller’s address rather than to the intended recipient. The root cause is a simple but critical logic error: the developer referenced the wrong variable when building the cross‑chain message. An attacker can exploit this by invoking the mint function on behalf of another user; the L1 token will be minted to the correct address, but the L2 token will be assigned to the attacker’s address, effectively stealing the bridged assets. Even without malicious intent, a legitimate user who is a contract may find that the L2 address does not exist or cannot handle the token, resulting in the token being minted to an unreachable address and disappearing from the expected balance. The impact is a loss of token ownership on L2, broken accounting between the two layers, and a user‑facing symptom where the UI shows a successful mint on L1 but the user’s L2 balance remains zero or the token never appears. The bug manifests every time _mintAndBridge is executed, i.e., for any minting of the Node Key token, and it affects all token holders, the bridging protocol, and any downstream applications that rely on correct cross‑chain token distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the parameters passed to the L2 call with the function’s documented behavior. It can be hard to notice because the L1 transaction succeeds and emits the expected events, while the L2 side silently credits the wrong address, leading to a discrepancy that only becomes apparent when users check their L2 balances. The correct remediation is to replace msg.sender with the _to argument in the abi.encodeWithSignature call, ensuring that the same recipient is used on both layers. Conceptually, the fix aligns the bridging logic with the intended business rule that the recipient of a minted token on L1 must also receive the corresponding token on L2, restoring the integrity of the cross‑chain accounting model.

title: IDOPoolAbstract does not deal with yield and gas accrued on Blast
description: Blast accumulates yield for contracts holding USDB, WETH and ETH and enables contracts to claim some of the gas fees. However, this is not currently dealt with so IDOPoolAbstract will miss out on this.
bug_full: The IDOPoolAbstract contract is designed to hold stablecoins and native assets such as USDB, WETH and ETH for an IDO pool, but it does not contain any logic to interact with the Blast protocol’s reward system. Blast automatically generates yield on any contract that holds those assets and also allows contracts to claim a portion of the gas fees they have spent. Because IDOPoolAbstract never calls Blast’s claim functions, the accrued yield and refundable gas are never transferred to the pool’s balance. The root cause is a missing integration step: the contract assumes that the token balances it tracks are the only source of value, ignoring the external accounting that Blast maintains. This omission can be exploited indirectly by the protocol itself, as the unclaimed rewards remain locked in Blast and are effectively lost to the pool. The impact is financial rather than a classic security breach: participants in the IDO receive less than the expected return, the protocol’s revenue is reduced, and the overall economics of the offering become less attractive. The condition under which the problem manifests is any time the pool holds assets on a chain where Blast is active and accrues yield over time; the longer the assets sit, the larger the missed reward. All parties that rely on the pool’s funds – investors, token buyers, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected because the expected increase in balance never materialises. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the contract’s external dependencies against the documented capabilities of the underlying blockchain, revealing that the contract never invokes Blast’s reward‑claiming API. It is easy to overlook because the on‑chain token balances appear normal; the missing yield is invisible unless one explicitly checks Blast’s pending reward view. To remediate, the contract should be extended with functions that periodically query Blast for any pending yield or gas refunds and then call the appropriate claim methods, updating the pool’s internal accounting to reflect the newly received assets. In broader terms, this is a classic case of incomplete accounting for external incentive mechanisms, where a smart‑contract fails to capture all sources of value that its environment provides, leading to systematic under‑payment of participants.

title: fyToken contribution limits are incorrect as they compare fyToken and buyToken amounts with idoSize in idoToken units
bug_full: The vulnerability is a contribution‑limit mismatch in the IDO pool contract. The contract tracks the total amount funded by adding the amount already contributed in the buy token and the amount contributed in the fyToken, then adds the new contribution amount. This sum, called globalTotalFunded, is expressed in the native units of the buy token or the fyToken. The contract then computes a maximum allowed fyToken funding as (idoSize * fyTokenMaxBasisPoints) / 10000. The variable idoSize represents the size of the IDO in terms of the idoToken, not in fyToken or buyToken units. Consequently the comparison globalTotalFunded > maxFyTokenFunding mixes different units: a value measured in fyToken or buyToken is compared against a limit measured in idoToken. Because the units are not aligned, the check can be bypassed, allowing contributors to exceed the intended fyToken cap. The bug manifests whenever a participant contributes fyToken; the contract may accept a contribution that should have been rejected, leading to over‑funding of the fyToken side of the pool. This can distort the token economics, dilute existing participants, and break the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the total funded amount never exceeds the configured maximum. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the limit‑enforcement logic and noticed the unit mismatch. It is subtle because the code appears to perform a simple arithmetic comparison, and the mismatch does not raise a compiler warning. To remediate, the contract must ensure that both sides of the comparison are expressed in the same unit, either by converting the globalTotalFunded amount to idoToken units before the check or by converting the maxFyTokenFunding limit to fyToken (or buyToken) units using the appropriate price or conversion rate. Aligning the units restores the intended contribution ceiling and prevents unintended over‑allocation.

title: IDOPoolAbstract::withdrawSpareIDO() does not take into account that several rounds may use the same IdoToken
description: IDOPoolAbstract::withdrawSpareIDO() checks if contractBal >= ido.idoSize, where contractBal = IERC20(ido.idoToken).balanceOf(address(this)). When several rounds use the same ido.idoToken, this check is incomplete as ido.idoSize only tracks the tokens of one round.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawSpareIDO function of the IDO pool abstraction. The function attempts to ensure that only tokens that are not required for the current IDO round can be withdrawn by checking that the contract's token balance (the amount of the idoToken held by the pool contract) is greater than or equal to the size of the current round (ido.idoSize). This check is flawed when multiple IDO rounds share the same token because ido.idoSize tracks only the allocation for a single round, while the contract balance aggregates tokens allocated for all rounds that use that token. Consequently, after several rounds have been executed with the same token, the contract may appear to have a surplus according to the per‑round check, even though part of the balance is already reserved for other pending rounds. An attacker, typically the contract owner or any caller with permission to invoke withdrawSpareIDO, can call the function after such a scenario and the contract will incorrectly deem the excess tokens as withdrawable. The attacker can then transfer those tokens out of the pool, reducing the amount available for future participants and breaking the accounting guarantees of the IDO mechanism. From a user perspective, participants may notice that refunds or token allocations are missing, balances become unexpectedly low, or the pool reports zero remaining tokens despite earlier deposits. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token accounting logic across multiple rounds. It is subtle because the balance comparison looks syntactically correct and passes basic unit tests that only consider a single round, making the bug easy to overlook in a multi‑round context. The proper fix is to replace the simple comparison with a calculation that subtracts the total amount of tokens already allocated to all rounds that share the same token, for example by using the globalTokenAllocPerIDORound mapping to compute contractBal - globalTokenAllocPerIDORound[idoToken] and ensuring that only the true surplus can be withdrawn. This change restores the invariant that the pool never releases tokens that are still needed for any active or future IDO round, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: RestrictedFunction could miss come cases
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a function that classifies certain token‑related calls as "restricted" based solely on a hard‑coded list of function selectors. In the examined wallet contract the private helper _isRestrictedFunction returns true only for the ERC20 approve selector and the ERC721/ERC1155 setApprovalForAll selectors. However, many ERC20‑compatible tokens expose additional state‑changing methods such as increaseApproval and decreaseApproval (or similar custom functions) that also modify the allowance mapping. Because these extra methods are not part of the standard selector list, the restriction check does not flag them, allowing a caller to invoke them through the wallet’s session call mechanism. An attacker who can trigger a session call with one of these un‑checked selectors can silently raise or lower a spender’s allowance without the wallet’s internal safeguards detecting the change. This can lead to unauthorized token transfers, effectively draining user balances or preventing legitimate transfers if the allowance is reduced to zero. The issue manifests whenever the wallet processes a transaction that includes a function selector not explicitly listed as restricted, yet the function still alters allowance state. Token holders, delegated operators, and any protocol relying on the wallet’s assumption that only approve/setApprovalForAll can change allowances are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the list of restricted selectors against known allowance‑changing functions in popular token contracts. It is easy to miss because the non‑standard functions look innocuous and are often omitted from documentation, and the restriction logic is encapsulated in a pure function that does not perform any dynamic analysis of the called contract’s ABI. To remediate, the contract should either broaden the selector whitelist to include all functions that can modify allowances (including increaseApproval, decreaseApproval, and any custom allowance‑changing methods) or replace the selector‑based approach with a role‑based access control that limits which callers may invoke any state‑changing token method. Removing the MAGIC_CONTRACT_ALL_FUNCTION_SELECTORS option or restricting it to privileged roles would also close the bypass vector. In short, the bug is a classic case of incomplete input validation for privileged operations, leading to a potential allowance manipulation attack that violates the wallet’s accounting assumptions and user expectations of safe token handling.

title: Working with signatures - nonce and expiry
description:
There are some not protected attack vectors.
if controllers signed two transactions, msg.sender can decide on the ordering of these two transactions, which one to prioritize.
if some signers refused to sign, but some other signers signed - their signatures can be used months later, for some modified set of controller, or signers who refused can find a moment to sign when they see it beneficial.
Some simplified example:
1. We have 3 controllers: A, B, C, each with weights 30, 30, 30
2. New proposal - update the weight of C to 40
3. A signs, B signs, C refuses to sign. Controller C saves the signatures of A and B.
4. After one year, Controller C asks to replace Controller C with his/her other wallet D. All controllers sign the multiple transactions with the result that we have 3 controllers - A, B, and D.
5. Controllers D and C belong to the same signer. Controller D signs the previously saved transaction of updating the weight of C to 40.
6. Now Controller C appears in the list of controllers. Now it is the set of controllers A, B, C, D - with weights of 30, 30, 30, 40.
7. It is not something that controllers A and B signed for.
There are two problems why it is possible:
Currently, nonce in inputs is used as a salt. Multiple verified transactions with the same nonce can exist. Now it is not compared with any storage nonce value. It should be some storage value nonce incremented by one on every call. If a new transaction with the inputted nonce 6 is signed, it means it can only be written when the active nonce in the storage is 6.
There is no Expiry argument in inputs which would be a part of _inputHash. It is a timestamp in the future which is compared to the current block.timestamp. If inputs with the expiry of 1 day are signed by some controllers, their signatures will not be used in one month.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a governance‑level replay and ordering flaw in the controller signature scheme. The contract accepts signed proposals from a set of controllers but does not enforce a unique, monotonically increasing nonce stored on‑chain, nor does it embed an expiry timestamp into the signed input hash. Because the nonce is only used as a salt and is never compared against a persistent storage value, multiple distinct proposals can be signed with the same nonce and later be submitted in any order. Additionally, without an expiry field, a signature that was valid for a short‑lived proposal can be kept and reused months later. An attacker who controls a controller that later adds a new wallet can collect previously saved signatures from other controllers, combine them with a fresh signature from the new wallet, and submit a proposal that was never approved by the original quorum. In the illustrated scenario, controllers A and B sign a weight‑increase proposal for controller C, while C refuses. The signatures of A and B are stored, and a year later controller C adds a new wallet D. D signs the old proposal, causing the weight of C to be increased and an extra controller D to appear in the set, a change that A and B never authorized. This leads to unauthorized modification of controller weights and the composition of the controller set, potentially allowing malicious actors to gain disproportionate voting power or to execute further privileged actions. The issue is hard to notice because the signatures appear cryptographically valid, the contract does not emit explicit warnings about stale or duplicated nonces, and the UI may simply show the updated controller list without indicating that the change originated from an old signature. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature verification flow and identified that the nonce parameter is not persisted and that no expiry check exists. To remediate, a global nonce should be stored in contract storage and incremented on each successful governance call, with every verification function ensuring the supplied nonce matches the stored value. An expiry timestamp should also be added to the signed input structure and incorporated into the hash that is signed, so that signatures become invalid after a reasonable time window. Implementing these controls restores the intended one‑time use of signatures, prevents replay after controller changes, and aligns the contract behaviour with the expected governance model where proposals must be fresh and explicitly approved by the current quorum.

title: ICE-1 | Centralization Risk
description: The owner address, 0xa3056090d5583747ef278f3cb6d599aa0e306e64, is not a multi-sig and has potentially dangerous permissions for renounceOwnership, transferOwnership, reserveForGiveaway, setSaleTime, setCost, setMaxMintAmount, setBaseURI, pause, withdraw, and a modified mint execution where the owner can mint Ice Bear NFTs for free.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from the fact that the contract’s owner address is a single externally‑owned account without any multi‑signature protection and holds a broad set of privileged permissions. These permissions include the ability to renounce or transfer ownership, adjust sale parameters such as start time, price and maximum mint amount, change the base URI, pause the contract, withdraw all collected ether, and execute a special mint path that lets the owner create Ice Bear NFTs without paying the required cost. The root cause is the design choice to grant extensive administrative powers to a single key holder, which eliminates the checks and balances normally provided by multi‑sig wallets or timelocks. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting in bad faith, can exploit these functions by arbitrarily changing sale conditions, pausing the sale to block legitimate users, withdrawing the entire pool of funds, or minting a large number of free NFTs that dilute the value of existing tokens. The impact includes loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, potential de‑valuation of the NFTs, and a breach of the economic assumptions that buyers rely on, such as a fixed price and limited supply. This risk materialises whenever the owner decides to act, or if the owner’s key is compromised, and it affects every participant in the sale – buyers, token holders, and the broader community that expects a fair, decentralized distribution. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the contract’s access control model and noted the absence of any multi‑signature or timelock mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the functions themselves are standard administrative calls and do not emit obvious warnings; the contract appears functional until a privileged action is taken. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be unexpected price changes, a sudden pause of the sale, missing or zero balances after a purchase, or the appearance of free NFTs minted by the owner, all of which contradict the expectation that the sale is transparent and immutable. Conceptually, this is an instance of excessive centralized admin control, a class of vulnerability where a single actor can unilaterally alter contract state and move funds. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single owner with a multi‑signature wallet or to introduce a timelock governance layer, thereby providing community oversight and reducing the chance that a single compromised key can cause irreversible damage.

title: ICE-2 | Uncapped Minting
description: The owner can cause the totalSupply to exceed the maxSupply by calling reserveForGiveaway with an arbitrarily large amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an uncapped minting flaw that allows the contract owner to increase the token totalSupply beyond the declared maxSupply by invoking the reserveForGiveaway function with an arbitrarily large amount. The root cause is the absence of a validation check that compares the amount to be minted with the remaining supply capacity; the function does not enforce the invariant that totalSupply must never exceed maxSupply. An attacker who controls the owner role can exploit this by calling reserveForGiveaway and specifying a huge token amount, causing the internal accounting to record a totalSupply that is larger than the intended cap. This inflationary minting breaks the economic assumptions of the token, dilutes existing holders, and can lead to loss of confidence, price depreciation, or protocol instability. The issue manifests whenever the owner executes reserveForGiveaway without a safeguard, which may be rare in normal operation but can be triggered at any time because the function is publicly callable by the owner. All token holders, users of the platform, and any downstream contracts that rely on the maxSupply invariant are affected, as they may receive fewer relative shares of the token pool or see unexpected supply spikes. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that reviewed the token’s minting pathways and noticed that the reserveForGiveaway routine lacked a require statement limiting the mint amount. Because the function is restricted to the owner, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in routine testing unless the owner’s privileges are exercised with extreme values. To remediate, the contract should include a check such as require(totalSupply + amount <= maxSupply) (or an equivalent conditional) before performing the mint, thereby preserving the maxSupply constraint and preventing arbitrary inflation. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “unbounded minting” or “supply cap bypass” bugs, where privileged mint functions fail to enforce a hard cap, leading to potential token supply overflow and economic distortion.

title: Unauthorized rewardTokens in _marketWeightsByToken
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unauthorized reward allocation that arises from stale data in the internal mapping that tracks how much of each reward token is assigned to each market. The contract stores a weight for every (reward token, market) pair in a structure called _marketWeightsByToken. When a reward token is removed from the system the removal routine does not delete the entries that associate the token with the markets it previously served. Consequently, if the same token is later added again and the governance assigns it to a different market, the old entries remain unchanged and still indicate a non‑zero weight for the original market. An attacker can exploit this by invoking a function that triggers reward calculation for the original market – for example by calling updatePosition on a position that is staked in that market. The reward distribution routine reads the stale weight, treats it as a legitimate allocation and mints or transfers reward tokens to the original market even though the protocol’s business logic states that the token should now only reward the new market. The impact is that liquidity providers in the unintended market receive extra tokens that were never meant for them, inflating their apparent earnings and potentially draining the reward token supply or creating an unfair advantage. This condition only appears after a reward token has been removed and later re‑added with a different market allocation, and it requires that the contract’s removal function does not clear the _marketWeightsByToken entries. Users of the affected market will notice that they receive rewards despite the protocol’s UI or documentation indicating that the token is no longer allocated to that market; they may see a balance increase that they did not expect. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the RewardDistributor contract where the logic of the removeRewardToken and addRewardToken functions was examined and the persistence of the weight mapping was observed. It can be hard to detect because the extra rewards may be small and the mapping appears correct for the newly added market, while the old market silently continues to accrue rewards. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑state or improper‑cleanup vulnerabilities, where leftover configuration data leads to unauthorized asset flows. To remediate the problem the contract should explicitly delete or reset all entries in _marketWeightsByToken for the token being removed, or enforce that adding a token first clears any previous weights, ensuring that reward calculations only consider current, intentional allocations. This conceptual fix restores the invariant that a reward token’s total weight is distributed exclusively among the markets it is actively assigned to, preventing any market from receiving rewards it is not supposed to receive.

title: returnFunds() can be frontrun to profit from an increase in share price
description:
SafetyModule.returnFunds() is used by governance to inject funds back into StakedToken, in the form of underlying tokens. For example, when there are excess funds raised from the auction, they can be returned back to compensate the stakers.
The issue is that anyone can frontrun returnFunds() with a stake() to profit from the share price increase and then redeem shortly once it has reached the unstake window. This will be profitable if a large amount of funds are returned within a transaction.
Furthermore, a return of funds likely indicates there will be no slash event in the near term, which makes it a risk-free transaction to capitalize on it and wait for the unstake window to redeem.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance function that injects excess underlying tokens back into the staking contract, increasing the per‑share value of the staked token. Because the function does not restrict user interactions, an attacker can submit a stake transaction immediately before the returnFunds call is mined. The returned funds raise the share price, so the attacker’s newly minted shares are worth more than the amount they contributed. After the mandatory unstake cooldown expires, the attacker can redeem the inflated shares and extract a profit without any slashing risk, especially when a large amount of funds is returned in a single transaction. This exploit is possible whenever the protocol decides to return excess auction proceeds, which signals that no slash event is imminent, making the attack appear risk‑free. The issue was identified during a manual security review that examined the interaction between the returnFunds and stake logic. It can be difficult to notice because the returnFunds call is intended for governance and does not emit obvious user‑facing events, and the share‑price increase may be perceived as a normal market movement. From a user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected increase in the value of their staked position after a governance return, or conversely a loss of opportunity for other stakers whose relative share is diluted. The flaw belongs to the class of front‑running profit‑extraction bugs where a privileged state‑changing operation can be preceded by a user action to capture the resulting value shift. To remediate the issue the contract should either prevent staking during the window in which returnFunds can be executed, enforce a target raise amount and end the auction before excess funds accumulate, introduce a pause around the returnFunds call, or replace the direct fund return with reward‑token distribution that does not alter the share price. These measures would align the protocol’s accounting assumptions with its business logic and eliminate the incentive for attackers to front‑run the returnFunds operation.

title: addStakedToken() can be griefed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the function addStakedToken in the SafetyModule, which is intended to register a new StakedToken market and initialise its reward‑distribution start time by calling initMarketStartTime. initMarketStartTime contains a guard that reverts if the internal mapping _timeOfLastCumRewardUpdate for the given market is already non‑zero, under the assumption that the start time has never been set before a market is added. However, the internal reward‑distribution contract also updates this mapping in its _updateMarketRewards routine when it detects that a market has never been updated or has zero liquidity. An attacker can exploit this by performing a minimal stake (for example 1 wei) on the target StakedToken and then invoking registerPositions([StakedToken]). The stake call triggers _updateMarketRewards, which sets _timeOfLastCumRewardUpdate[StakedToken] to the current block timestamp even though the market has not yet been added to the SafetyModule. When the legitimate admin later calls addStakedToken for the same StakedToken, initMarketStartTime sees a non‑zero timestamp and reverts with RewardDistributor_AlreadyInitializedStartTime. From the user’s point of view the admin sees a transaction failure when trying to add a new market, with an error that does not mention any staking activity, leading to confusion and the impression that the system is broken or that funds have vanished. The impact is that the protocol cannot onboard new reward markets, effectively halting the expansion of the reward system and potentially preventing users from earning rewards on newly supported assets. The issue occurs only when an attacker can call stake and registerPositions before the market is officially added, which is feasible for any address that can interact with the StakedToken contract. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between initMarketStartTime and _updateMarketRewards and noticed that both functions can initialise the same timestamp variable. It is hard to notice because the revert happens later, during a seemingly unrelated admin operation, and the initial stake of 1 wei does not affect any visible balances. The root cause is a lack of proper isolation between market initialisation logic and reward‑update logic, allowing an external call to set internal state that should be reserved for the SafetyModule. To remediate, the registerPositions function should be removed from the reward distributor as it is not required, or the _registerPosition routine should verify that the market has already been added to the SafetyModule (for example by checking safetyModule.getStakedTokenIdx) before allowing any state‑changing calls. This prevents an attacker from pre‑initialising the start time and ensures that addStakedToken can only be reverted for genuine duplicate additions, preserving the intended business logic of controlled market onboarding.

title: Stakers can activate cooldown during the pause and try to evade slashing
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing pause guard on the function that starts a staker's cooldown period. In the contract, the cooldown() entry point checks only for a non‑zero balance and that the system is not already in a post‑slashing state, but it does not include the whenNotPaused modifier that is applied to most state‑changing functions. Because of this omission, a user can invoke cooldown while the protocol is in an emergency paused state. When the protocol is paused, it is typically a signal that a deficit or other risk is imminent and that a slashing event may be scheduled to penalise staked tokens. By activating cooldown during the pause, a staker can lock in the unstake window before the slash is executed, then attempt to redeem their tokens within that window. If the redemption succeeds before the slash, the staker effectively evades the penalty, while the remaining participants who did not start cooldown during the pause are forced to absorb a larger share of the slash. The immediate impact is a distortion of the intended accounting: the protocol’s slashing mechanism assumes that all eligible stakes are subject to the penalty, but the bug allows a subset of users to opt‑out, leading to an unfair redistribution of losses. From a user perspective, a staker who correctly anticipates a pause may notice that their reward multiplier is reset (as usual when cooldown is called) but their funds are not reduced by the expected slash, creating a mismatch between expected and actual balances. Conversely, other users may see a higher-than‑expected reduction in their rewards because the total slashed amount is spread over fewer participants. The condition under which the issue manifests is any scenario where the contract is paused and a slashing event is either imminent or subsequently executed. It was discovered during a manual security review that flagged the absence of the whenNotPaused modifier on cooldown(). The flaw can be subtle because the function still performs other checks and emits a normal event, so ordinary testing that does not simulate a paused state may not reveal the problem. The bug belongs to the class of missing state‑validation or access‑control errors, specifically the failure to enforce a global pause on a function that changes user positions. To remediate the issue, the cooldown() function should be protected with the whenNotPaused modifier (or an equivalent check) so that it cannot be called while the protocol is paused, thereby preserving the intended slashing semantics and preventing users from gaming the unstake window.

title: Disabling of cooldown during post- slash can be bypassed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a staking contract that disables the cooldown mechanism for a staker who is in the post‑slashing state. After a slash, the contract prevents the staker from directly activating cooldown by setting the internal timestamp mapping to the current block time. However, the contract’s transfer logic does not block the movement of staked tokens from a slashed account to another address that already holds a valid cooldown timestamp. The function that computes the next cooldown timestamp takes the sender’s timestamp (fromCooldownTimestamp) and the receiver’s timestamp (toCooldownTimestamp) and, when the receiver’s timestamp is still within the valid window, applies a weighted‑average formula that can overwrite the receiver’s cooldown value. Because the sender’s timestamp is forced to the current block time when it is expired, the weighted average effectively re‑enables a cooldown for the transferred amount. An attacker can therefore bypass the intended cooldown disablement by first being slashed, then transferring the slashed tokens to a second account that has a non‑zero cooldown timestamp, and finally invoking the cooldown on the receiving account. This allows early unstaking of tokens that should remain locked, undermining the economic deterrent of slashing and potentially causing other stakers to lose expected compensation. The issue manifests only after a slash event, when the sender’s cooldown is marked as disabled but the contract still permits token transfers. Users may notice that the cooldown button appears disabled in the UI, yet after moving tokens to another wallet the cooldown can be activated and the funds become withdrawable earlier than promised. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the getNextCooldownTimestamp routine and observed that the function does not guard against a from‑address that is in a disabled state. The problem is subtle because the contract’s public interface does not expose the internal timestamp manipulation, and typical tests may not cover cross‑account transfer scenarios after a slash. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit transfers of staked tokens while the sender is in the post‑slashing state, or adjust the cooldown calculation to ignore the sender’s timestamp when it is disabled, ensuring that a transfer cannot resurrect a cooldown for the receiver. In essence, the bug is a bypass of a lock‑up enforcement mechanism through indirect state manipulation, a class of vulnerability often referred to as “state‑injection via token transfer”.

title: Extra rewards due to a malfunction with the _cumulativeRewardPerLpToken
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting error in the reward distribution contract where the cumulative reward per LP token accumulator is not cleared when a reward token is removed and later added again. The contract maintains a mapping _cumulativeRewardPerLpToken that records the total reward per unit of liquidity for each market and token. When RewardDistributor::removeRewardToken is called the mapping entry is left unchanged, and the addRewardToken function does not reset it to zero. Consequently, when the market updates rewards after the token has been re-added, the _accrueRewards routine subtracts the stale accumulator value from the user-specific stored value (which is zero because the user has never accrued rewards for the newly added token). The calculation therefore multiplies the user’s LP balance by the old cumulative amount, crediting rewards that were earned before the token was removed. This can be exploited by any holder of LP tokens who claims rewards after the token has been re-added, receiving an amount that can be orders of magnitude larger than intended. The impact is that the protocol may dispense excess tokens, eroding its token economics and potentially causing a loss of value for the treasury. The bug manifests only when a token is removed and later re-added; in normal operation where the token remains continuously active the accumulator behaves correctly. Users experience a sudden increase in their reward balance despite expecting zero new rewards, leading to confusion when their wallet shows an unexpected token influx. The issue was identified during a manual security review that examined the state-reset logic of the reward distributor. It is difficult to notice because the contract emits normal RewardAccrued events and the extra rewards appear as legitimate accruals, not as an explicit error. The problem belongs to the class of stale-state or accumulator reset bugs, where a variable that should be re-initialized after a lifecycle change retains a previous value. The recommended remediation is to explicitly set _cumulativeRewardPerLpToken[token][market] to zero inside the addRewardToken function, and to consider handling any unclaimed rewards before removal to avoid losing them. By resetting the accumulator, the contract will correctly calculate newRewards as zero at the moment of re-addition, aligning the on-chain accounting with the intended business logic that rewards only accrue after a token becomes active again.

title: DoS in all deposits by reaching max. cap in one of the farms
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the AfterMintHook contract selects a farm for depositing assets without verifying that the farm still has available capacity. The root cause is that the internal function responsible for finding the optimal deposit farm (_findOptimalDepositFarm) does not consider the per‑farm cap that is enforced by the farm’s own deposit routine. When a farm’s current asset balance exceeds its configured cap, the farm’s deposit function reverts with a CapExceeded error. Because the hook contract proceeds to call deposit on the selected farm regardless of its state, the revert propagates and aborts the entire transaction. An attacker or even a legitimate user can fill a farm up to its cap, after which every subsequent deposit attempt triggers the same revert, effectively blocking all new deposits across the protocol. The impact is that users attempting to deposit see their transactions fail, their balances remain unchanged, and the protocol’s revenue stream from new deposits is halted until an operator manually adjusts caps or weights. This condition occurs whenever the protocol tries to route a deposit and the selection algorithm picks a full farm, which can happen repeatedly because the algorithm never filters out saturated farms. All participants who rely on depositing – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the hook and farm contracts and identified the missing capacity check as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because the transaction simply reverts with a generic error, offering no clear indication that a capacity limit was the cause, and the UI may only display a generic “deposit failed” message. To remediate, the selection routine should be extended to query each candidate farm’s remaining capacity and skip any farm that would exceed its cap when the incoming assets are added. If no farm can accommodate the deposit, the system should emit a clear error indicating that no capacity is available rather than silently reverting. This class of bug is an unchecked capacity or resource‑exhaustion flaw that leads to a service‑availability failure, violating the business expectation that deposits are always accepted when the protocol reports available farms.

title: Rounding error in partial funding burns fewer receipt tokens than consumed assets
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs when the RedemptionPool contract calculates how many receipt tokens to burn during a partially fulfilled redemption request. The contract uses a fixed‑point conversion ratio between receipt tokens and the underlying asset and performs the division with a function that rounds the result down (divWadDown). Because the division discards any fractional component, the number of receipt tokens that are actually burned is slightly lower than the exact amount that corresponds to the assets transferred. Consequently the remaining request amount is recorded as larger than it should be, inflating the user's pending claim. This discrepancy appears each time the queue processes a partial fill, so the error accumulates over many operations. The root cause is the use of downward rounding in a financial accounting context where the protocol assumes a one‑to‑one correspondence between burned receipt tokens and assets delivered. The issue can be exploited by repeatedly triggering partial fills, allowing an attacker to retain a small surplus of receipt tokens for each fill, which under extreme conditions can translate into free tokens or enable the draining of additional assets from the pool. The impact is an overstatement of user balances, potential loss of assets for honest participants, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants. The bug manifests when the underlying asset has high decimal precision (e.g., 18‑decimal tokens such as WETH or DAI) because the conversion ratio then carries more fractional bits, making the rounding gap larger. Users may notice that after receiving the expected amount of USDC or another asset, a tiny amount of receipt tokens remains in their wallet, contrary to the expectation that all tokens were burned. From a UI perspective the user sees the asset balance increase correctly but also sees a residual receipt balance, leading to confusion and possible over‑claim of future redemptions. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit (Spearbit) by reviewing the redemption logic and spotting the use of divWadDown. It is hard to notice because the error is typically a single unit per partial fill, which is small and only becomes significant after many operations. The appropriate remediation is to change the rounding direction to upward (using divWadUp) or otherwise ensure that the protocol always burns at least the exact number of receipt tokens required for the assets transferred, thereby preserving the accounting invariant and eliminating the precision loss. This class of bug falls under rounding/precision errors that lead to accounting mismatches in tokenized financial contracts.

title: Temporary DoS in redemptions due to incorrect asset withdrawal logic in farms
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporary denial‑of‑service condition that occurs during token redemption and farm rebalancing because the protocol assumes that all assets reported by a farm’s assets() function are instantly withdrawable from the underlying lending protocol. In reality the assets() view aggregates both idle tokens held directly by the farm contract and tokens that have already been supplied to an external protocol such as Aave. When a user initiates a redemption, the controller selects the farm with the highest reported total assets, without checking how much of that total is actually withdrawable. If the selected farm contains a significant amount of idle assets, the subsequent call to IFarm.withdraw requests the full redemption amount from the external protocol. Because the external protocol can only release the portion that has been supplied, the withdrawal reverts, causing the entire redemption transaction to fail. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a failed redemption, the transaction reverts, and the user’s balance remains unchanged, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or that the system is unresponsive. The same logic flaw appears in the rebalancing routine where a max‑uint amount may be interpreted as the farm’s total assets, again ignoring the distinction between idle and supplied funds, leading to stalled rebalances. The impact is that any user attempting to redeem or any automated rebalancing operation can be blocked until the idle assets are manually supplied in a later deposit, which may not happen promptly, effectively locking user funds and breaking the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the redemption hook and the asset accounting logic. It is hard to notice because the assets() function correctly reports the total value under management, and the failure only manifests when the composition of idle versus supplied assets is unfavorable, a situation that may not be exercised in normal testing. To remediate the problem, farms should separate the accounting of withdrawable (supplied) assets from idle holdings and ensure that withdrawal requests never exceed the amount that can be immediately pulled from the underlying protocol, or they should adjust the selection algorithm to consider only the withdrawable portion when choosing a farm for redemption or rebalancing. This change restores the invariant that a redemption request can always be satisfied without reverting, eliminating the temporary DoS condition.

title: First depositor inflation attack in StakedToken contract
description:
The StakedToken contract, inherits from the ERC4626 standard. This contract is susceptible to a well-known exploit referred to as the "first depositor inflation attack." This vulnerability occurs due to the lack of protective mechanisms in the contract's design, allowing the initial depositor to manipulate the share price to their advantage. Such manipulation can enable the first depositor to disproportionately claim assets from the vault, effectively draining value at the expense of subsequent depositors. The problem is worsened by the minMintAmount parameter in the MintController contract being set to 1, which allows extremely small deposits. This low threshold makes the attack both practical and economically viable for an attacker with minimal upfront capital. An attacker could simply:
1. Stake 1 receipt token into the contract. 1:1 share price.
2. Donate 10000 receipt tokens directly to the StakedToken contract. The share price becomes 10001 units per share.
3. Following deposits lower than 10000 receipt tokens will receive no shares and the deposit will be absorbed by the single share in the system that belongs to the first depositor. In the StakedToken contract, no specific safeguards exist to prevent this attack. There is no minimum initial deposit requirement nor use of virtual shares to stabilize the share price and no other mechanisms to ensure fairness.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a first‑depositor inflation attack that can occur in share‑based vault contracts implementing the ERC4626 standard. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum initial deposit or use virtual shares, the first user who deposits a tiny amount of the underlying token creates a single share at a 1:1 price. An attacker can then transfer a large amount of the underlying token directly to the vault, inflating the total asset balance while the share supply remains unchanged. This manipulation raises the share price dramatically; subsequent deposits that are smaller than the inflated asset amount receive no new shares, meaning the deposited tokens are effectively captured by the single share owned by the attacker. The root cause is the lack of protective mechanisms that stabilize the share price at launch, combined with a minMintAmount parameter set to one, which permits deposits of negligible size. The exploit can be carried out by anyone who can make the initial tiny deposit and then donate a large amount of tokens before other users interact with the vault. When it happens, later users see their deposits result in zero share tokens, their balances appear unchanged, and the vault’s accounting shows a disproportionate amount of assets belonging to the first depositor. The impact is a loss of value for subsequent depositors, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential draining of funds from the vault. The issue was identified during a security audit that recognized the pattern as a known class of bug in ERC4626‑style vaults where share price is derived from total assets divided by total shares without an initial seed. It can be hard to notice because the share price looks normal after the first deposit and the large token donation may not be obvious in transaction logs. To remediate, the contract should be seeded with an initial deposit that creates a reasonable share supply, enforce a non‑trivial minimum initial deposit, introduce virtual shares or other price‑stabilizing mechanisms, and prevent direct token transfers that bypass the minting logic. These changes ensure that the share price remains fair for all participants and that no single depositor can inflate the price to capture assets from later users.

title: UnwindingModule users can avoid slashes by withdrawing before the accrue call
description: In the UnwindingModule, users who have begun unwinding and are part of it, still are exposed to any earned yield and losses from accrue calls. However, as accrue is not called upon withdrawals, users could front-run any accrue call that will result in a slash by calling withdraw. The remaining users in the UnwindingModule would absorb the full impact of the negative yield. This could be easily abused by users within the infiniFi protocol to be exposed to yield gains without risking any losses/future slash.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the accounting flow of the UnwindingModule of the InfiniFi protocol. When a participant has entered the unwinding process they remain exposed to the collective yield that is applied by the YieldSharing.accrue function. The contract, however, does not invoke accrue as part of the withdraw routine. Consequently a user can submit a withdrawal transaction that is mined before the next accrue call that would generate a negative yield (a slash). By doing so the withdrawing user receives their full principal and any positive accrued rewards, but avoids sharing the upcoming loss. The remaining participants who stay in the module after the withdrawal are then forced to absorb the entire negative yield, resulting in a disproportionate reduction of their balances. This behavior violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that all active unwinding participants share both gains and losses proportionally. The issue is exploitable whenever an attacker can predict or influence the timing of the next accrue call, for example by monitoring pending transactions or by deliberately delaying the call. The attacker front‑runs the accrue, withdraws, and thereby sidesteps the loss, while honest users see their balances shrink unexpectedly. From a user perspective the symptom is that a user who withdraws sees the expected amount returned, but other users notice a sudden drop in their share of the pool, often described as “my balance fell dramatically after someone withdrew”. The flaw was identified during a manual security review that examined the interaction between UnwindingModule.withdraw and YieldSharing.accrue and noticed the missing accounting step. It can be hard to notice because the withdraw function itself works correctly for the caller, and the loss is only observable in the reduced balances of the remaining participants, which may be attributed to normal market volatility. The proper mitigation is to ensure that the accrue routine is executed (or its effects are accounted for) before any withdrawal is processed, so that every participant shares the outcome of the upcoming yield calculation. In generic terms this is a “withdraw‑before‑accounting” or “front‑runable accrual omission” bug, a class of errors where state updates that affect collective balances are not enforced on individual exit paths, leading to unfair loss distribution and potential fund disappearance for honest users.

title: StakedToken holders can avoid losses
description: Holders of StakedToken are exposed to losses when the accrue function triggers applyLosses. However, they can circumvent these losses by frontrunning the accrue function, redeeming their tokens moments before execution. This vulnerability enables users to sidestep their intended risk exposure entirely.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a loss‑distribution mechanism in a staking contract where a periodic function accrues interest and then applies a proportional loss to all staked token holders. The root cause is that the contract applies the loss after the accrual step without enforcing any lock‑up or ordering constraint on token redemption. Because the loss application is executed in a single transaction that can be front‑run, a holder can submit a redemption transaction that is mined just before the loss‑application step, withdraw their balance, and thereby avoid the intended reduction. Exploitation proceeds by monitoring the pending accrual transaction, broadcasting a redeem call with a higher gas price, and ensuring the redeem is included in the same block prior to the loss calculation. The impact is that the protocol’s risk model is broken: users who should share the loss can escape it, leading to an unfair distribution of risk, potential over‑minting of the underlying asset, and erosion of trust in the staking system. This condition occurs whenever the accrual function is called, typically on a scheduled interval, and there is no minimum unstaking period or re‑entrancy guard. All stakers, especially large token holders, are affected because they can selectively avoid losses while others cannot. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state changes and identified that redemption is permitted before loss application. It may be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation; only when an attacker actively front‑runs does the discrepancy appear, manifesting as users receiving full balances when they expected a reduced amount after a loss event. The fix should introduce a mandatory unstaking delay or a commit‑reveal scheme that prevents immediate redemption after an accrual, or restructure the logic so that loss calculation and token transfer occur atomically, ensuring that any holder who redeems after the accrual also receives the adjusted balance. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “front‑runable state‑transition ordering” vulnerabilities where economic state changes can be bypassed by transaction ordering manipulation, violating the contract’s accounting assumptions that all participants share losses equally. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a normal balance before a loss event, and after the scheduled loss the user still sees the same amount, contrary to the expectation of a reduced balance, effectively making the loss disappear.

title: Validator cutting board weights can disconnect from onchain voting outcomes
description: Infrared.queueNewCuttingBoard() queues new cutting board _weights (BGT receiver address & share percentage) for an Infrared validator with _pubkey and which become active at _startBlock. This method, which is only accessible via Infrared's Keeper role, is a crucial component of the protocol that facilitates to represent the RED onchain voting distribution outcomes as actual cutting board weights for each Infrared validator. However, the provided _weights data and _startBlock in this function has to be fully trusted since it relies on offchain data/analysis by Keeper based on the onchain voting outcomes but without any onchain connection or verification. Impact Explanation: High, because any failure to correctly represent the onchain voting outcomes as cutting board weights leads to losses for specific BGT receivers in addition to reputational damage due to deviation from voting outcomes.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Infrared contract function queueNewCuttingBoard, which allows a privileged Keeper role to submit a list of cutting‑board weights – each consisting of a BGT receiver address and a share percentage – together with a start block for a validator identified by its public key. The function does not perform any on‑chain verification that the supplied weights faithfully represent the results of the on‑chain RED voting process. Consequently, the contract fully trusts data that originates off‑chain, creating a trusted‑data‑injection flaw. An attacker who controls the Keeper role, or who can compromise the off‑chain system that prepares the weight list, can craft arbitrary weight entries that diverge from the actual voting outcome. By queuing manipulated weights, the attacker can allocate a larger share of rewards to chosen addresses or reduce the share of legitimate BGT receivers, causing those users to receive less or even zero tokens despite having voted for a different distribution. The impact is financial loss for the affected BGT holders and reputational damage for the protocol because the on‑chain governance results no longer match the observable reward distribution. The issue manifests each time queueNewCuttingBoard is called – typically at the beginning of a new voting period – and it affects any validator that relies on the queued weights, as well as all token holders expecting rewards according to the published voting outcome. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the absence of any cryptographic link or proof between the voting results and the weight parameters, and the reliance on a single privileged role. Because the function emits no explicit warning and the UI may continue to display the correct voting percentages, users may not notice that their actual rewards are lower, making the bug subtle and hard to detect without deep inspection of the stored weights. To remediate the issue, the protocol should replace the trusted off‑chain submission with a trustless mechanism: either compute the weights directly on‑chain from the voting data, or require a verifiable proof (for example a Merkle‑root or signature) that the submitted weights correspond to the on‑chain results. If gas costs are prohibitive, a public view function that allows anyone to compare the queued weights against the voting outcome should be added, and the Keeper role should be limited or replaced by a decentralized oracle. This would restore the integrity of the reward distribution and align the on‑chain accounting with the governance decisions.

title: Missing call to sweep() before calling collect() in harvestOperatorRewards() may result in inaccurate rewards
description: In harvestOperatorRewards(), there is a potential issue with stale data being used when calculating fees via collect(). Specifically, InfraredBERA.collect() relies on the shareholderFees value, which may not be up-to-date unless a sweep() is performed beforehand. While mint() triggers a sweep, collect() does not. This discrepancy means that when harvestOperatorRewards() is called, it may process rewards using an outdated shareholderFees value, potentially leading to incorrect fee calculations and distribution. Impact Explanation: Medium, because this can result in inaccurate rewards allocation due to outdated fee data, causing mismanagement of protocol fees and discrepancies in the operator rewards distribution, which could negatively affect the trust and reliability of the reward system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑staleness bug in the reward‑harvesting flow of the InfraredBERA contract. The function harvestOperatorRewards() calls InfraredBERA.collect() to transfer accumulated fees to the operator, but it does not invoke InfraredBERA.sweep() beforehand. sweep() is the only routine that updates the internal shareholderFees variable to reflect the most recent fee accruals; mint() calls sweep() automatically, but collect() does not. As a result, when harvestOperatorRewards() is executed, collect() may read an outdated shareholderFees value, causing the fee amount that is transferred to the operator to be lower or higher than the actual amount earned since the last sweep. This mismatch can happen any time harvestOperatorRewards() is called after a fee‑generating event (e.g., a user deposit or a protocol fee accrual) but before a sweep has been performed. The affected parties are the protocol operators who rely on the reported rewards, as well as any users whose fees are ultimately redistributed, because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that fees are distributed exactly as they accrue – are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the state‑update patterns of mint() and collect() and noticed that collect() lacks the sweep() call. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when fees are stale, the problem can be hard to notice; the operator may simply observe that the reward numbers do not match expectations, but the discrepancy may be attributed to normal variance rather than a bug. Exploitation does not require malicious code; an attacker can trigger harvestOperatorRewards() at a moment when shareholderFees is stale, causing the protocol to under‑pay or over‑pay fees. Over‑payment could drain protocol reserves, while under‑payment reduces operator incentives and may erode trust. The attack scenario is: (1) a fee‑generating transaction occurs, increasing the internal fee counter; (2) no sweep() is called, leaving shareholderFees unchanged; (3) an actor calls harvestOperatorRewards(); (4) collect() reads the stale shareholderFees and transfers an incorrect amount; (5) the protocol’s accounting state diverges from the true fee balance. The recommended mitigation is to make harvestOperatorRewards() explicitly invoke sweep() before collect(), ensuring that shareholderFees is refreshed to the latest value. This aligns the reward‑harvesting path with the safe pattern used by mint() and eliminates the stale‑data class of bug, which is generally known as a missing state‑synchronisation or stale‑read vulnerability. From a user perspective, the operator may see rewards that are unexpectedly zero or lower than usual, or conversely, a sudden spike that does not correspond to any activity, indicating that the fee calculation is inaccurate.

title: A malicious reward token can DoS reward claiming for all users in a vault
description: In getRewardForUser(), after the rewards state is updated, the reward tokens earned by the user are transferred to them iteratively in a loop. However, if any of these reward tokens become malicious (or is paused, where pausing is controlled by external token governance), then the reward claiming process can be forced to revert for all users in that particular InfraredVault. While there is a way to remove whitelisting of a reward token from the Infrared system by infrared governance, there is no way to remove a reward token from a vault once it's added to it. In an InfraredVault, governance can only add more reward tokens but not remove any. The entire rewardTokens list is always processed in a getRewardForUser() call. Impact Explanation: High, because the reward claim process cannot succeed for any tokens and any users in an infrared vault with a malicious reward token.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the reward‑claiming function of an InfraredVault. After the contract updates a user’s accrued reward balances, it iterates over the entire list of reward tokens associated with the vault and attempts to transfer each token to the caller. Because the loop processes every token unconditionally, if any token in the list is malicious, deliberately reverts, or is paused by its own governance, the transfer call fails and the whole getRewardForUser transaction reverts. This happens every time a user tries to claim rewards, regardless of how many legitimate tokens are also owed, because the contract does not skip failing transfers nor provide a way to remove a token once it has been added. The impact is that no user can successfully claim any rewards from a vault that contains a problematic token, effectively freezing the reward distribution for all participants. The condition occurs whenever a vault’s rewardTokens array includes at least one token that does not behave as a standard ERC‑20 transfer, which can be introduced by governance adding new tokens without a removal mechanism. All users of the affected vault, as well as the protocol that relies on the vault for incentive distribution, are impacted because they receive no rewards and may see claim transactions revert with no obvious on‑chain indication of the underlying cause. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and identified that the loop does not handle transfer failures. It can be hard to notice because the failure manifests as a generic transaction revert, and the UI may simply show “claim failed” without revealing that a single token is responsible. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unhandled external call failures leading to denial‑of‑service”. The fix should involve adding logic to safely handle failing token transfers—such as skipping tokens that revert, using a safe‑call wrapper like ExcessivelySafeCall, allowing governance to remove tokens from the reward list, and enforcing a strict whitelist of trusted reward tokens. From the user’s perspective the expected behavior is that a claim returns the earned tokens; in reality the user receives nothing, the transaction reverts, and balances remain unchanged, violating the accounting assumption that rewards are always claimable once accrued.

title: Precision loss in reward calculation leads to incorrect accounting for residual amounts
description:
In the previous review, the issue of precision loss in the calculation of reward rate was pointed out. Accounting for "residual amounts" was introduced as a fix. When reward amount is divided by rewardsDuration, any remainder is stored as rewardResidual and utilized in later reward distributions so that it does not get lost. However, the problem still exists in cases where there is a leftover amount from the current running distribution period. We see that the residual amount reward / rewardsDuration is correctly stored as rewardResidual. When there is a leftover amount, it is added into the rewardRate calculation. However, the precision loss there is not considered. Any truncation due to the division leftover / rewardsDuration is not accounted for in rewardRate and neither in the rewardResidual. This can lead to a loss of that reward amount.

Impact Explanation:
Low, because the affected reward amounts leftover % rewardsDuration are small.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the reward‑distribution logic caused by integer division truncation. When a reward period ends, the contract calculates a new rewardRate by dividing the remaining reward amount (leftover) by the duration of the next period. The remainder of this division is not added to the stored rewardResidual, which is intended to capture any fractional amounts that would otherwise be lost. As a result, each time a leftover amount is processed, the fractional part of leftover/rewardsDuration is silently discarded, leading to a small but systematic reduction of the total rewards that can be claimed. This occurs only when there is a non‑zero leftover from the current distribution period and the contract recomputes rewardRate for the next period. Users who stake or claim rewards may notice that their expected payout is slightly lower than the amount advertised, or that a tiny fraction of their reward balance disappears after each cycle. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the residual accounting mechanism; the auditor observed that while the initial reward/residual handling was correct, the subsequent addition of leftover amounts ignored the same rounding loss. Because the lost amounts are typically very small, the bug is hard to notice in normal operation and may be attributed to normal rounding variance. The impact is classified as low to medium because the missing fractions are minor, but over many periods they can accumulate and affect the fairness guarantees of the protocol. The affected parties include any user who earns rewards, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward balances. To fix the problem, the calculation of rewardRate must be revised so that the truncation error from leftover/rewardsDuration is also added to rewardResidual, or the contract should employ a higher‑precision arithmetic library (e.g., fixed‑point math) that avoids integer division loss altogether. By ensuring that every fractional remainder is captured, the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain intact and users receive the full amount of rewards they are entitled to.

title: Incomplete InfraredKeeperScript may lead to unexpected Keeper behavior
description:
Keepers have a special role in the Infrared protocol to automate the calling of several important functions in a timely manner. Such functions include queueNewCuttingBoard(), queueBoosts(), cancelBoosts(), queueDropBoosts(), cancelDropBoosts(), createBribeVault(), registerVault(), harvestBase(), harvestVault() and harvestBribes(). However, InfraredKeeperScript which is intended to capture all such batched keeper jobs is incomplete (with commented code, todo's) and currently has hardcoded testnet addresses.

Impact Explanation:
High, because the incomplete/incorrect calling of important Infrared functions will lead to unexpected protocol behavior.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the automation component that the Infrared protocol relies on to trigger a set of critical state‑changing functions at regular intervals. The keeper script, which is supposed to batch calls such as queueNewCuttingBoard, queueBoosts, cancelBoosts, queueDropBoosts, cancelDropBoosts, createBribeVault, registerVault, harvestBase, harvestVault and harvestBribes, is incomplete: several sections are commented out, there are TODO markers, and the contract addresses embedded in the script are hard‑coded to testnet deployments. The root cause is a development oversight where the off‑chain keeper logic was not fully implemented or validated before being packaged for mainnet release. Because the script runs off‑chain and its failures do not revert on‑chain transactions, the missing calls are silent; the protocol simply does not receive the expected automated updates. An attacker or any keeper operator can invoke the script, but the omitted calls mean that essential protocol actions are never executed. This can lead to a cascade of unintended effects: users may not receive scheduled rewards, boosts may remain unprocessed, bribe vaults may not be created or harvested, and overall accounting can become out of sync with the intended business logic. The impact is considered high because the protocol’s core economic mechanisms depend on timely keeper execution; failure to run them can cause funds to remain locked, reward calculations to be stale, and users to experience missing balances or zero‑value harvests. The issue manifests when the keeper infrastructure is activated on mainnet after deployment, i.e., whenever the automated job is scheduled to run. All participants who rely on the protocol’s automated functions – token holders, liquidity providers, and anyone expecting periodic rewards – are affected. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the keeper script’s source and identified the commented sections, TODOs and hard‑coded testnet addresses. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the contract does not emit explicit errors for the absent calls; the protocol appears to function but silently skips critical steps, leading to subtle accounting drift that may only be observed when expected rewards are missing. To remediate, the script should be completed with all intended batched jobs, the placeholder code removed, and the contract addresses replaced with configurable, validated mainnet addresses. Additional safeguards such as runtime checks that each required function call succeeded, and comprehensive unit and integration testing on a mainnet‑like environment, would ensure that the keeper behaves as intended and that the protocol’s economic guarantees are upheld.

title: Anyone can cause DoS to the updating of a vault's rewardsDuration
description:
The following is the flow for updating the rewards duration for a rewardToken on a specific vault: Infrared::updateRewardsDurationForVault() → VaultManagerLib::updateRewardsDurationForVault() → InfraredVault::updateRewardsDuration() → MultiRewards::_setRewardsDuration(). The _setRewardsDuration() finally checks that the block.timestamp > periodFinish, otherwise it reverts. Because Infrared.addIncentives() is a public function, anyone can come up with a small amount : even 1 wei of a rewardToken and the vault will be notified with 1 wei of a reward and advance the periodFinish value because of the logic in MultiRewards::_notifyRewardsAmount(). The call flow is Infrared::addIncentives() → VaultManagerLib::addIncentives() → InfraredVault::notifyRewardAmount() → MultiRewards::_notifyRewardAmount(). The calculation there does not check if the resultant rewardRate is 0 ⇒ it just advances the periodFinish value forward. This means anyone can notify a reward amount of even 1 wei for a reward token on a vault, which would lead to an increase in the periodFinish timestamp. This can be used to cause DoS to updateRewardsDurationForVault() call forever, and it would become impossible to update the rewardsDuration for any rewardToken on any vault if an attacker kept repeatedly advancing the periodFinish value. Additionally, given that none of the functions in addIncentives() → → notifyRewardAmount() flow have the whenNotPaused modifier, we cannot even pause the vault to perform this update operation.
