The same thing can happen with normal usage via harvestVault() calls because those too notify new rewards to a vault and advance the periodFinish timestamp forward.

Impact Explanation:
Low, because the rewardsDuration is not meant to be regularly updated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows any external account to permanently block the update of a vault’s rewardsDuration by repeatedly pushing the reward period’s finish timestamp forward. The root cause lies in the reward‑notification logic: the public addIncentives function can be called with an arbitrarily small amount of a reward token (for example 1 wei). When this tiny amount is passed through the call chain to MultiRewards._notifyRewardAmount, the contract does not verify that the resulting rewardRate is non‑zero, so it simply records a new reward amount and extends the periodFinish timestamp based on the supplied amount. The subsequent _setRewardsDuration function, which is used to change the rewardsDuration, contains a check that block.timestamp must be greater than periodFinish; because the attacker can keep advancing periodFinish into the future, this check never passes and the transaction reverts. Because none of the functions in the addIncentives → notifyRewardAmount path are protected by a whenNotPaused modifier, the vault cannot be paused to perform a corrective update, and even normal harvestVault calls suffer the same issue. The condition occurs whenever the contract is unpaused and the public addIncentives entry point is reachable, which is the default state of the system. All participants that rely on the ability to adjust reward schedules – protocol operators, liquidity providers, and end‑users – are affected because the rewardsDuration becomes immutable until the contract is redeployed or a privileged upgrade is performed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑management flow, where the lack of a zero‑rate guard and missing pause protection were observed. It is hard to notice because the attacker’s action only moves a timestamp and transfers a negligible token amount, leaving no obvious token balance anomalies, yet the business logic that expects the rewardsDuration to be adjustable is silently broken. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “timestamp‑based reward schedule manipulation” or “reward‑rate zero‑value DoS”. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an error when trying to change the reward period, or the vault may appear frozen with no new rewards being distributed, contrary to the expectation that the reward schedule can be updated. To remediate the issue the contract should recalculate any leftover rewards when a duration change is requested, compute a new rewardRate based on the remaining amount and the new duration, start a fresh reward period with those parameters, and remove the strict block.timestamp > periodFinish requirement. Additionally, the addIncentives and related notification functions should be restricted to authorized roles or guarded with a whenNotPaused modifier so that the vault can be paused to perform maintenance, thereby preventing an attacker from repeatedly extending periodFinish with trivial token amounts.

title: Berachain Consensus Layer implementation and specification not being in-sync and in flux is risky
description:
Berachain Consensus Layer is based on BeaconKit, which is a modular framework for building EVM based consensus clients. Its status says: "This project is work in progress and subject to frequent changes as we are still working on wiring up the final system. Audits on BeaconKit are still ongoing, and in progress at the moment. We don't recommend using BeaconKit in a production environment yet." However, it is not clear which aspects of BeaconKit specification will actually be part of its Berachain implementation. For example, the below two aspects, are mentioned in its README but do not appear to be enforced yet:
1. "EffectiveBalance is capped at MaxEffectiveBalance. Any Balance in excess of MaxEffectiveBalance is automatically withdrawn."
2. "The funds deposited will be locked and the validator will stay inactive until the a minimum staking balance is hit. The minimum staking balance is set to EjectionBalance + EffectiveBalanceIncrement to account for hysteresis." Additionally, InfraredBERADepositor.execute() enforces a deposit amount of INITIAL_DEPOSIT for the first deposit to any Infrared validator. INITIAL_DEPOSIT is hardcoded to a value of 32 ether in InfraredBERAConstants. However, the value of BeaconDeposit.MIN_DEPOSIT_AMOUNT_IN_GWEI was changed from 32 BERA to 10K BERA equivalent in Berachain's recently merged PR 549, which will cause all initial deposits from Infrared BERA liquid staking to always revert with InsufficientDeposit if InfraredBERAConstants are not updated.

Impact Explanation:
High, because any disconnect/deviation between Infrared liquid staking and Berachain Consensus Layer implementation/specification will result in unexpected behavior such as failed/stuck deposits.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a lack of alignment between the Berachain Consensus Layer implementation, which is built on the BeaconKit framework, and the specifications that the Infrared liquid‑staking module expects. BeaconKit is explicitly marked as a work‑in‑progress and its audit is still ongoing, yet Infrared relies on hard‑coded constants and assumed enforcement rules that have not been integrated into the live client. Specifically, the InfraredBERAConstants contract defines an INITIAL_DEPOSIT of 32 ether and assumes that the EffectiveBalance of a validator will be automatically capped at MaxEffectiveBalance and that a validator will remain inactive until a minimum staking balance (EjectionBalance + EffectiveBalanceIncrement) is reached. In the current Berachain codebase the BeaconDeposit contract has been updated so that the minimum deposit amount (MIN_DEPOSIT_AMOUNT_IN_GWEI) is now 10 000 BERA, far higher than the 32 ether constant used by Infrared. Because the Infrared deposit function only checks the hard‑coded INITIAL_DEPOSIT for the first deposit, any attempt to stake through Infrared will hit the BeaconDeposit check and revert with an InsufficientDeposit error. The effective‑balance cap and the minimum‑balance activation rule are also not enforced, meaning validators can hold more than the allowed balance without automatic withdrawal and may stay inactive even after depositing sufficient funds. From a user’s perspective this manifests as transactions that fail with a generic “insufficient deposit” revert, validators that never become active, and balances that appear to be locked or incorrectly reported. The issue was discovered during a security review by Spearbit, which compared the Infrared code against the evolving BeaconKit specification and identified the mismatched constants and missing enforcement logic. The problem is subtle because the code compiles and the mismatches only surface at runtime when a deposit is attempted, and because the specification is still in flux developers may assume the rules are already enforced. The impact is high for users of the liquid‑staking service: funds can become stuck, validators remain inactive, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are weakened. To remediate, the Infrared module must be brought into sync with the final consensus‑layer specification: constants such as the initial deposit amount should be stored as updatable protocol variables governed by the community, the effective‑balance cap and minimum‑balance activation rules should be explicitly enforced in the contract logic, and the deposit check should be applied to every deposit, not just the first one. Renaming INITIAL_DEPOSIT to a more generic DEPOSIT_AMOUNT would also reduce confusion and align the naming with the underlying protocol checks.

title: Rewards harvesting in vaults will be blocked if the RED token is paused
description:
The reward claim process calls RED.mint() in harvestVault() function. The flow is: getRewardForUser() → onReward() → harvestVault() → RED.mint(). Whenever there are new BGT rewards (which means some BGT emissions have accrued and claimed from Bera reward vaults), the harvestVault() function tries to mint a proportional amount of RED tokens. However, token transfers (including mints, burns etc.) can be paused on the RED token. So if RED mint fails, the reward harvesting calls will revert.

Impact Explanation:
High, because this will make all getRewardForUser() calls revert, i.e. this will prevent harvesting of new rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the RED token, which is used as the reward currency in a vault, is placed in a paused state. The reward‑harvesting flow calls RED.mint() inside the harvestVault() function after BGT emissions have been claimed. Because the RED token inherits the pausable pattern, any mint, burn or transfer operation reverts when the contract is paused. Consequently, if an administrator or an attacker pauses RED, the mint call fails and the entire harvestVault() transaction reverts, causing getRewardForUser() to fail as well. This prevents users from claiming newly accrued rewards, effectively making the vault’s reward‑claim interface unusable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that traced the call chain from getRewardForUser() through onReward() to harvestVault() and identified the unchecked external call to a pausable token. It is hard to notice because the revert originates from the token contract, not from the vault logic, and the UI simply reports a generic transaction failure without indicating that the token’s pause state is the root cause. The bug belongs to the class of external‑contract‑state‑dependency errors where a contract assumes that a called contract will always succeed, ignoring possible administrative states such as pausing. From a user’s perspective, clicking the “claim rewards” button results in a transaction that reverts, the UI may show an error or a zero balance, and the user receives no RED tokens despite expecting a proportional reward. The protocol’s accounting assumptions—that rewards can always be minted on demand—are violated, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual token balances. To remediate, the harvestVault() implementation should either catch the failure of RED.mint() using a try/catch construct and handle the error gracefully, or the RED token’s pause mechanism should be adjusted to allow mint operations even when other transfers are paused, for example by modifying the _update() function in ERC20PresetMinterPauser.sol to exempt minting from the pause check.

title: M-1 Lack of supply limit
description: To proﬁt from liquidations, liquidators must be able to sell collateral at a favorable price. However, selling a large amount of collateral may signiﬁcantly impact the selling price, rendering liquidation unproﬁtable and generating bad debt. A supply limit, conﬁgured to match market liquidity, could mitigate this issue. However, the supply limit has not been implemented yet. Although, the borrow limit is in place and may indirectly limit supply, it may not effectively address this issue due to substantial price ﬂuctuations often associated with large volumes of liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a configurable supply limit that caps the amount of collateral a liquidator can sell in a single liquidation event. The root cause is that the contract only enforces a borrow limit, which restricts how much a user may borrow but does not directly restrict how much collateral can be off‑loaded when a liquidation is triggered. When a large volume of collateral is sold without a supply ceiling, the market price of that asset can be pushed down sharply because the sale exceeds the available liquidity. This price impact reduces the proceeds that the liquidator receives, potentially turning a liquidation that should be profitable into a loss‑making operation and creating a shortfall that the protocol must cover as bad debt. The issue manifests during high‑stress scenarios where many positions are liquidated simultaneously or when a single liquidator attempts to sell a substantial amount of collateral. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected zero or near‑zero returns from liquidation transactions, collateral balances that disappear or drop far more than anticipated, and borrowers whose positions are closed without the expected recovery of value. The problem was identified during a systematic audit that examined the economic assumptions of the liquidation engine and noticed that no mechanism exists to align the amount of collateral sold with real‑world market depth. Because price impact is a gradual market phenomenon, the bug can remain hidden until a large liquidation occurs, making it difficult to detect through routine unit tests. To remediate the issue the protocol should introduce a supply limit that is dynamically calculated based on current market liquidity, order‑book depth, or external price‑oracle volatility metrics, and enforce this limit before allowing a liquidation to proceed. By capping the sell volume, the protocol preserves price stability, ensures liquidators receive reasonable compensation, and prevents the accumulation of unbacked debt, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of fair and profitable liquidations.

title: M-2 Insufﬁcient reentrancy protection in FluidVaultT1
description:
Although the FluidVaultT1 smart contract code includes reentrancy protection, some functions remain unprotected:
• admin functions
• read-only functions
Admin functions Admin functions can be called by the DAO. Once the DAO proposal is approved, it can be executed by anyone. Here is a possible attack vector:
• An attacker calls operate().
• The attacker receives a call to their malicious smart contract from FluidVaultT1 while operate() is not ﬁnalized.
• The attacker's contract calls DAO.executeProposal() with, for example, an absorbDustDebt() call.
• The attacker allows the initial operate() to ﬁnish.
The issue is that operate() works with a copy of Variables.vaultVariables: • main.sol#L53 and stores them back at the end of the function: • main.sol#L553. Thus, any modiﬁcations to vaultVariables in absorbDustDebt() will be overwritten by the later update in operate(), as the copied memory value vaultVariables_ in operate() will remain unchanged after the update in absorbDustDebt(). Read-only functions The same vector applies here, but it affects the reading of certain variables like positionData and branchData, which undergo some modiﬁcations before the call to the malicious address. Vulnerabilities in this area typically appear in more complex smart contract integrations, for instance, when external protocols use read-only functions to integrate with Fluid. See an example at https://rekt.news/midas-capital-rekt/. Reentrancy spots The safeTransfer library only requires success on msg.value transfer without gas limitations. As a result, it is possible to receive a call to a malicious smart contract in the line: • safeTransfer.sol#L88. This function is used in the following lines: • main.sol#L515 • main.sol#L1122 • main.sol#L533-L540. Additionally, tokens with hooks (like ERC-777) can open up new spots for reentrancy during fund transfers from a user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete reentrancy guard in the FluidVaultT1 contract that leaves certain privileged and read‑only functions exposed to re‑entrancy attacks. The root cause is that the contract applies a non‑reentrant pattern only to a subset of its entry points, while admin functions that can be triggered through DAO.executeProposal and read‑only view functions such as fetchLatestPosition still perform external calls before finalising their internal state. In particular, the operate() routine copies the vaultVariables struct into a temporary memory variable, performs external interactions (including safeTransfer calls that forward all gas), and only writes the temporary copy back at the end of the function. If a malicious contract is called during the external interaction, it can invoke a DAO proposal that runs absorbDustDebt() or similar admin logic, which mutates the stored vaultVariables. When operate() later writes back its unchanged copy, the modifications made by the admin call are overwritten, effectively discarding legitimate state changes. The same pattern applies to read‑only functions that expose positionData or branchData: a malicious callback can alter those variables before the function returns, causing the caller to receive stale or falsified data. The impact is a breach of accounting integrity – balances may appear unchanged, dust‑debt absorption may be silently ignored, and position information can be corrupted – which can be leveraged to block protocol operations or, in combination with token hooks such as ERC‑777, to siphon funds. The issue manifests whenever operate() or any function that makes an external call (including safeTransfer) is executed while the contract holds a reference to mutable storage that is later overwritten from a stale memory copy. All users, liquidity providers, and the DAO are affected because the protocol’s core accounting and governance actions can be subverted. The flaw was discovered during a MixBytes security audit that examined the contract’s control‑flow and noticed missing nonReentrant modifiers on admin and view functions, as well as the unsafe pattern of copying storage structs before external calls. The problem is subtle because the contract does contain reentrancy protection in many places, leading reviewers to assume the whole contract is safe, and because read‑only functions are typically trusted to be side‑effect free. To remediate, a unified reentrancy status check should be introduced and applied to every external‑call‑making entry point, including admin and view functions, or the contract should be refactored to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: update storage before any external call and avoid keeping stale copies of mutable structs across calls. Additionally, safeTransfer should limit gas or use a token‑standard that does not invoke callbacks, and ERC‑777‑style hooks should be explicitly guarded. By ensuring that no function can be re‑entered before its state is finalised, the protocol will preserve correct accounting, prevent overwriting of legitimate updates, and protect user balances from disappearing or being reported incorrectly.

title: maxBufferSize isnt re-calculated when maxBufferSizePct changes in setMaxBufferSizePct()
description:
When maxBufferSizePct is modified by calling setMaxBufferSizePct(), the function does not re-calculate maxBufferSize according to the new value of maxBufferSizePct. Therefore, if maxBufferSizePct is decreased, maxBufferSize will be temporarily higher than what it should be. This only becomes a problem when slashValidator() is called on a Staking validator immediately after setMaxBufferSizePct(). slashValidator() calls InstitutionalPirexEthDepositLogic.addPendingDeposit() directly without re-calculating maxBufferSize beforehand: InstitutionalPirexEthDepositLogic.addPendingDeposit( ); Since maxBufferSize is still inflated, addPendingDeposit() will then fill up the buffer according to the outdated value of maxBufferSize: uint256 _remainingBufferSpace = ( pirexEthValidatorVars.maxBufferSize > pirexEthValidatorVars.buffer ? pirexEthValidatorVars.maxBufferSize - pirexEthValidatorVars.buffer : 0 ); For example:
• Assume the following:
– buffer = 32 ETH
– maxBufferSize = 64 ETH
– maxBufferSizePct is 30%
• Governance calls setMaxBufferSizePct() to decrease maxBufferSizePct to 15%:
– If maxBufferSize was re-calculated, it would be 32 ETH.
• slashValidator() is called to slash a validator with ValidatorStatus.Staking status. In addPendingDeposit():
– _remainingBufferSpace = 32 ETH, therefore the ETH from the slashed validator is added to the buffer.
• However, if maxBufferSize was updated to 32 ETH, the ETH from the slashed validator would have been added to pendingDeposit and used to stake a new validator.
As seen from the example above, due to the outdated value of maxBufferSize, ETH was wrongly added to the buffer instead of being used to stake a new validator. This will cause the protocol to generate less yield.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the buffer management logic of the Pirex ETH staking module. When the governance function setMaxBufferSizePct() is called, it updates the percentage variable that determines the maximum allowed buffer size (maxBufferSizePct) but it fails to recompute the absolute buffer limit (maxBufferSize) that depends on this percentage. Consequently, if the percentage is reduced, the stored maxBufferSize remains at its previous, larger value. The problem manifests when slashValidator() is invoked immediately after the percentage change. slashValidator() calls InstitutionalPirexEthDepositLogic.addPendingDeposit(), which calculates the remaining buffer space using the stale maxBufferSize value. Because maxBufferSize is temporarily inflated, the function believes there is still buffer capacity and therefore directs the ETH from the slashed validator into the buffer instead of the pendingDeposit pool that would be used to stake a new validator. This misallocation reduces the amount of ETH that can be redeployed for staking, leading to lower yield for the protocol and its participants. The issue occurs only under the specific condition where maxBufferSizePct is decreased and a validator is slashed before any other operation that would refresh maxBufferSize, such as a regular deposit or an explicit recalculation. It affects the protocol’s accounting, stakers who expect slashed ETH to be quickly restaked, and any user relying on the advertised yield. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the governance‑parameter update flow, where the auditor noticed that maxBufferSize was never reassigned after the percentage change. It can be hard to notice because the buffer balance appears normal until a slash event causes an unexpected increase in the buffer and a corresponding lack of pending deposits, which may look like a normal fluctuation to a casual observer. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the buffer balance growing after a slash while the pending‑deposit amount stays unchanged, contradicting the expectation that slashed funds are immediately redeployed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of parameter‑dependency bugs where a derived state variable is not kept in sync with its source, leading to incorrect business‑logic decisions. The recommended remediation is to recalculate and store maxBufferSize in the same transaction that updates maxBufferSizePct, for example by assigning maxBufferSize = totalSupply * pct / DENOMINATOR inside executeSetMaxBufferSizePct(). This ensures that subsequent calls to addPendingDeposit() use the correct buffer limit and that slashed ETH is allocated to pending deposits as intended, preserving the protocol’s yield expectations.

title: Partial redemptions should not be allowed when there are no staked validators left
description:
In InstitutionalPirexEthWithdrawLogic.sol, initiateRedemption() adds pxEthAmount to pendingWithdrawal and proceeds to process pending withdrawals in multiples of DEPOSIT_SIZE. If pxEthAmount is still non-zero afterwards, the function will initiate a partial redemption by minting IUpxEth with the batchId of a future validator: if (pxEthAmount > 0) { pirexEthValidatorContracts.iupxEth.mint( receiver, pirexEthValidatorVars.batchId, pxEthAmount, "" ); } However, allowing partial redemptions for validators that haven't been unstaked might be problematic in an exit scenario where everyone is trying to redeem their institutional pxETH (e.g. migration to a new set of contracts). This is because there might be a case where IUpxEth is minted to a user for a future batchId, but there is no more staked validators to exit. As such, the IUpxEth can never be redeemed for ETH. For example:
• Assume everyone is trying to exit InstitutionalPirexEth:
– There is 1 staked validator left (32 ETH) and 31 ETH in the buffer.
– Alice holds 31 ETH worth of IPxEth, Bob holds 32 ETH worth of IPxEth.
– pendingWithdrawal = 0
• To avoid incurring the instant redemption fee, Alice calls initiateRedemption() with:
– _assets as all her IPxEth
– _shouldTriggerValidatorExit = false, since her 31 ETH is insufficient to trigger a validator exit
• Bob front-runs her transaction and calls initiateRedemption() to withdraw all his institutional pxETH:
– This triggers the exit of the last validator, and his IUpxEth has the batchId of the last validator
• When Alice's transaction is processed:
– pendingWithdrawal + postFeeAmount = 31 ETH, so _requiredValidators = 0 and this check passes
– Her withdrawal is a partial redemption, so the upxEth minted to her has the batchId of the next validator
• However, since there are no more validators to exit, her upxETH can never be redeemed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal logic of an institutional ETH staking contract where a user can trigger a partial redemption even when the protocol has no staked validators remaining. The function that processes redemption requests aggregates withdrawal amounts in multiples of a fixed deposit size and, if a remainder remains, mints a wrapper token (IUpxEth) that is tied to the batch identifier of the next validator that is expected to exit. The root cause is the absence of a guard that checks whether any validators are still staked before minting this wrapper token for a future batch. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate redemption: the attacker redeems a full validator share, causing the last validator to exit, and then the victim’s transaction, which only requests a partial amount, proceeds to mint IUpxEth with a batchId that now refers to a non‑existent validator. Because there are no validators left to be unstaked, the minted IUpxEth can never be exchanged for ETH, effectively locking the user’s funds. This scenario occurs when the pending withdrawal amount is zero, the user’s redemption request is smaller than the deposit size, and the validator set is empty at the moment of minting. Institutional pxETH holders, as well as any participant attempting to exit the protocol, are affected because they receive a token that appears valid but cannot be redeemed, leading to a loss of expected ETH. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the initiateRedemption function and noticed that the code does not verify the existence of validators before issuing a partial redemption token. The bug is subtle because the transaction succeeds, the wrapper token balance increases, and no immediate error is thrown; only later attempts to redeem reveal that the balance remains unchanged, which may be perceived as a UI glitch or a rounding error. From a security taxonomy perspective, this is a business‑logic flaw that creates an orphaned asset – a token that cannot be redeemed due to missing underlying collateral. To remediate the problem, the contract should include a check for the number of active validators before minting a partial redemption token and revert the transaction if none are available, thereby preventing the issuance of unredeemable tokens. The fix restores the invariant that every minted IUpxEth must correspond to an existing validator that can be exited and ensures that users receive the ETH they expect when they redeem their institutional pxETH.

title: User can lose extra rewards
description: rewardManager can at anytime delete the extra Rewards. This impacts the extra rewards earned by existing staker. The existing staker will have no way to claim these extra rewards. Since these extra rewards have been staked for all users making a deposit BaseRewardPool.sol#L215 so basically the extra reward gets locked with no one having access to this fund. Need to be fixed for BaseRewardPool.sol as well
poc:
1. rewardManager adds 2 extra reward token A,B using addExtraReward
2. User X makes a deposit of amount 1000 using stake function
3. This stakes extra rewards A,B for this user
4. rewardManager now calls clearExtraRewards which removes extraRewards object
5. User X has now no way to retrieve the staked extra rewards A,B of amount 1000
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an admin‑controlled function that can delete the contract’s extra reward configuration at any time. When the reward manager invokes the clearExtraRewards routine, the internal data structures that track users’ pending extra reward balances are removed without first withdrawing or allowing those balances to be claimed. As a result, any staker who has already deposited funds and accrued extra rewards finds those rewards locked inside the contract with no available claim path. This occurs after extra rewards have been added through the addExtraReward interface and a user’s stake has been recorded, tying the user’s share of the extra reward tokens to the now‑deleted record. The root cause is a privileged state‑changing operation that does not enforce a safe exit procedure for user‑locked assets, effectively violating the accounting assumption that all accrued rewards remain claimable until withdrawn. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a zero balance for the extra reward token even though the user expects to receive a payout; the contract silently holds the tokens with no observable error, making the problem hard to notice. The impact is a loss of the extra reward tokens for any affected staker, with the funds remaining permanently locked because the contract lacks any sweep or emergency withdrawal function that would let an admin retrieve them. The issue was identified during a formal audit when the code path for clearing extra rewards was examined and it became clear that the function could be executed by a malicious or negligent admin, leaving user funds unrecoverable. To remediate the problem the contract should either remove the clearExtraRewards function entirely or modify it to first iterate over all existing stakes, force a claim or withdrawal of the pending extra rewards, and only then delete the extra reward configuration. This aligns the contract with the generic class of bugs where privileged operations can unintentionally lock user assets, breaking the expected reward distribution logic and causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: Duplicate LP token could lead to incorrect deposits
description:
It was observed that addPool function is not checking for duplicate lpToken which allows 2 or more pools to have exact same lpToken. This can cause issue with deposits.

In case of duplicate lpToken, the first pool calling depositAll will take away all lpToken and deposit them under there own pid. This leaves no balance for 2nd pool.
poc:
1. PoolManager call addPool function and uses lpToken as A
2. PoolManager again call addPool function and mistakenly provides lpToken as A
3. Now 2 pools will be created with lpToken as A
4. depositAll function is called passing first pool.
5. This takes all balance of lpToken A and depsoit it under first pool pid
6. This mean no balance is left for second pool now
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the PoolManager contract’s addPool function failing to enforce uniqueness of the liquidity‑provider (LP) token across pools. Because there is no global check that an LP token is associated with only one pool, an attacker or a mistaken deployment can call addPool twice with the same LP token address, creating two distinct pool identifiers (pids) that both reference the identical token contract. The root cause is the absence of a data structure – such as a mapping – that records which LP tokens have already been registered. When this condition occurs, the first pool that executes a depositAll call will transfer the entire balance of the duplicated LP token from the caller’s wallet into its own accounting, effectively draining the token from the caller’s address. Since the same LP token is also linked to the second pool, that pool now sees a zero token balance and cannot accept further deposits. From a user’s perspective, deposits made to the second pool appear to succeed on the UI, but the token balance remains unchanged, resulting in lost or unavailable funds. The impact includes incorrect accounting, potential loss of liquidity for users who interact with the second pool, and a breakdown of the protocol’s economic assumptions that each LP token maps to a single, isolated pool. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the addPool logic and observed that while duplicate gauge addresses are prohibited, duplicate LP token addresses are not. The bug can be difficult to notice because the UI may list two pools with the same underlying token, yet only one actually receives deposits, and the discrepancy may only surface after a depositAll transaction is executed. To remediate, the contract should maintain a global registry of all LP tokens that have been added, and the addPool function must revert if a supplied LP token already exists in that registry, mirroring the existing validation for gauges. This change ensures that each LP token can be associated with exactly one pool, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unintended token drainage.

title: Incorrectly set `_maxTime` to be in line with the locking `maxTime` of each veToken could render the `deposit` of this contract to be unfunctional or even freeze assets inside the contract
description:
Since _maxTime needs to be manually input in the constructor with no other ways of changing it, if the owner inputs the _maxTime that is higher than the capacity of each vaults of veTokens, it will cause `IVoteEscrow(escrow).increase_unlock_time(_value);` to get rejected.

In the mild case when a user initially locks the asset during depositing, the contract will simply revert the transaction.

In the severe case when a user does not lock the asset during depositing, the asset will end up locked in the contract since noone will be able to succesfully call `lockVeAsset`. This will cause the asset to be locked up with no way of withdrawing it. Even though a user will still get benefits from the minted reward, a contract will not be able to receive any benefits since it can’t utilize the locked asset in `VeAssetDepositor`.
poc:
![Pic 1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63941340/171625668-85834a21-f3c2-4837-b49b-4ed5a975132a.jpg)

1. The owner initially sets _maxTime in constructor to be 126489600 (86400 _366_ 4) instead of 126144000 (86400 _365_ 4) which is the maximum time that a user can deposit in curve

![Pic 2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63941340/171625682-49582795-ed3f-4ae5-8302-57f270376461.jpg)

2. A user `deposit` veAsset but deferring the locking to save gas

3. The veAsset is transferred from a user to the contract and the contract mint a reward token to the user

![Pic 3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63941340/171625696-9d57f982-233e-4f26-8536-a6e8804c6f5e.jpg)

![Pic 4](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63941340/171625706-b8ddf803-1bd4-4aba-89c9-354445168eda.jpg)

![Pic 5](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63941340/171625711-d8c63db6-c962-4150-867d-d51bb15ea055.jpg)  
*Above shows that the deposit will get reverted if lockAmount is more than 4 years in curve’s VotingEscrow

4. The veAsset will not be able to move to the staking contract because when VoterProxy calls `increase_unlock_time` in the targeted vault, the call will get reverted due to exceeded _value of `unlockAt`
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an incorrectly configured immutable parameter called `_maxTime` that is supplied once in the contract constructor and never validated against the maximum lock duration supported by the underlying voting escrow (veToken) contracts. Because the constructor allows any numeric value, an owner can unintentionally set `_maxTime` to a number that exceeds the hard‑coded upper bound of the veToken vaults (for example 126,489,600 seconds instead of the correct 126,144,000 seconds). When a user later attempts to deposit assets and either immediately lock them or defer the lock to a later step, the contract calls `IVoteEscrow(escrow).increase_unlock_time(_value)`. This call checks the requested unlock timestamp against the vault’s maximum permissible lock period. If the supplied `_maxTime` is larger than the vault’s limit, the call reverts. In a mild scenario the revert happens during the initial deposit, causing the whole transaction to fail and the user’s assets to remain in their wallet. In a severe scenario a user may choose to defer the lock, allowing the assets to be transferred to the contract and a reward token to be minted, but the subsequent attempt to lock the asset later fails. The token then becomes permanently locked inside the contract because no further calls to `increase_unlock_time` can succeed, effectively freezing the user’s capital. From a user’s point of view the expected outcome—a successful lock and receipt of a reward—does not happen; instead the transaction either reverts with no visible effect, or the user sees a reward token appear while the underlying asset is stuck, leading to confusion and a perceived loss of funds. The issue is difficult to detect because the contract does not expose any explicit error message for the mis‑configured `_maxTime`; the failure manifests only as a reverted external call, and the assets already transferred into the contract give the false impression that the deposit succeeded. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of configuration‑driven lock‑time validation errors, where an off‑chain or manual parameter determines on‑chain enforcement boundaries. The root cause is the lack of validation and the immutable nature of the `_maxTime` variable, combined with the absence of an emergency mechanism to correct the value after deployment. To remediate, the contract should either compute `_maxTime` dynamically based on the veToken’s actual maximum lock period, or expose a securely gated function (protected by timelock and multi‑signature controls) that allows the owner or governance to update the parameter if a misconfiguration is discovered. Adding explicit checks in the constructor and emitting clear revert messages when the lock duration exceeds the vault’s limit would also improve detectability. Properly fixing the issue restores the intended business logic that deposited assets can always be locked within the allowed time frame, ensuring users receive their expected rewards and can withdraw their funds without unintended freezing.

title: `VE3DRewardPool` and `VE3DLocker` adds to an unbounded array which may potentially lock all rewards in the contract
description:
The function `addReward()` allows the owner to add a new reward token to the list `rewardTokens`.

However, this is an unbounded list that when appended to cannot be shortened. The impact is it is possible to reach a state where the list is so long it cannot be iterated through due to the gas cost being larger than the block gas limit. This would cause a state where all transactions which iterate over this list will revert.

Since the modifier `updateReward()` iterates over this list it is possible that there will reach a state where the we are unable to call any functions with this modifier. The list includes

* `stake()`
* `stakeAll()`
* `stakeFor()`
* `withdraw()`
* `withdrawAll()`
* `getReward()`
* `notifyRewardAmount()`

As a result it would therefore be impossible to withdraw any rewards from this contract.

The same issue exists in `VE3DLocker`. Where rewards can be added by either `Booster` or the owner.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an unbounded dynamic array that stores reward token addresses in the VE3DRewardPool and VE3DLocker contracts. The owner (or an authorized operator) can call addReward to append a new token to this list, but the list has no mechanism for removal or size limitation. Every function that modifies or reads a user's stake – such as stake, withdraw, getReward, or notifyRewardAmount – is wrapped with an updateReward modifier that loops over the entire reward token array to update accounting for each token. As the array grows, the gas required for each iteration increases linearly. When the number of stored reward tokens approaches a threshold – roughly one hundred twenty tokens based on the contract's gas consumption per token – the cumulative gas needed to complete the loop exceeds the block gas limit. At that point any transaction that triggers the updateReward modifier will run out of gas and revert, preventing the contract from processing staking, withdrawals, or reward claims. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a situation where attempts to withdraw or claim rewards simply fail with out‑of‑gas errors, making it appear as though the contract is “bricked” or that funds have vanished. The impact is that all staked assets and accrued rewards become effectively locked, as the protocol can no longer execute the core functions required to release them. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the security team examined the addReward function and observed that the rewardTokens array could be expanded without bound, and that the updateReward logic iterates over this array on every user interaction. The problem is difficult to detect in normal operation because the contract works correctly with a small number of reward tokens; only after an unusually large number of tokens are added does the gas limit breach occur, which may happen only after prolonged use or deliberate malicious addition. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce a hard cap on the number of reward tokens, provide a method to deregister or prune obsolete tokens, or redesign the reward‑distribution logic to operate on a per‑token basis rather than iterating through the entire list in a single transaction. Such changes would restore the ability of users to claim and withdraw rewards and prevent permanent loss of access to funds.

title: Not updating `totalWeight` when operator is removed in `VeTokenMinter`
description:
The `totalWeight` state variable of the `VeTokenMinter` contract is used to work out the amount of `veAsset` earned when the `Booster.rewardClaimed` function is called.

However, while `totalWeight` is modified inside the `VeTokenMinter` contract when function `updateveAssetWeight` is called, the `totalWeight` is not similarly reduced when function `removeOperator` is called.

The impact is that remaining operators do not receive a fair share of the total rewards and a portion of the rewards are not given out at all.
poc:
* Operator 1 is added with weight 9
* Operator 2 is added with weight 1

The `totalWeight` is now 10.

This means that Operator 1 receives 90% of the amount while Operator 2 receives 10%.

If we then call `removeOperator` on Operator 1 then 90% of the reward is no longer minted and distributed. This is unfair to the remaining operators.

The can be seen on lines [607 - 608](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-vetoken/blob/2d7cd1f6780a9bcc8387dea8fecfbd758462c152/contracts/Booster.sol#L607-L608) of the `Booster` contract. Function `rewardClaimed` will never be called for (removed) Operator 1. But for Operator 2 they will still receive 10% of the rewards even though Operator 1 is no longer registered in the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution logic of the VeTokenMinter contract, specifically in the handling of the `totalWeight` accounting variable. `totalWeight` aggregates the weight of all registered operators and is used by the `Booster.rewardClaimed` function to compute the amount of veAsset that should be minted for each operator when rewards are claimed. While the contract correctly updates `totalWeight` when an operator’s weight is changed via `updateveAssetWeight`, it fails to adjust this aggregate when an operator is removed through the `removeOperator` function. As a result, the removed operator’s weight remains counted in `totalWeight` even though the operator is no longer eligible to receive rewards. This mismatch causes the reward calculation to use an inflated denominator, so the remaining operators receive a smaller fraction of the total reward than intended and a portion of the rewards that should have been minted for the removed operator is never created. The flaw can be triggered by any privileged account (typically the contract owner) that calls `removeOperator`. After removal, the system still believes the total weight is unchanged, leading to an under‑minting of veAsset for the active operators. Users observing the protocol may notice that after an operator is deregistered, the expected share of rewards for other operators drops unexpectedly, causing balances to grow slower than anticipated or appear to be missing entirely. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit of the VeTokenMinter code, where the code paths for weight updates and operator removal were compared and found inconsistent. The problem is subtle because the `removeOperator` function itself executes without reverting and does not emit any warning about the stale `totalWeight`, making it easy to overlook in normal operation. To remediate the bug, the `removeOperator` implementation should decrement `totalWeight` by the weight associated with the removed operator before clearing the operator’s entry, ensuring that subsequent reward calculations reflect the current set of operators. Alternatively, the contract could be refactored to always recompute `totalWeight` from the stored weights or expose a dedicated function to synchronize the aggregate after any operator management operation. This fix restores the intended accounting invariant that the sum of operator weights equals the total weight used for reward distribution, thereby preventing loss of yield and preserving fair allocation of veAsset rewards.

title: in notifyRewardAmount
description: Function `notifyRewardAmount()` calculates `rewardRate` for reward token/s in `VE3DRewardPool` and `BaseRewardPool`. to calculate `rewardRate` it divides `reward` amount to `duration` but because of the rounding error in division, some of `reward` amount wouldn’t get distributed and stuck in contract (`rewardRate * duration < reward`). and contract don’t redistributes them or don’t have any mechanism to recover them. This bug can be more damaging if the precision of `rewardToken` is low or token price is high.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the reward distribution contracts calculate the per‑second reward rate. When the function that registers a new reward amount divides the total reward tokens by the fixed reward duration, the operation uses integer division that truncates any fractional part. As a result, the computed rewardRate multiplied by the duration can be slightly lower than the original reward amount, leaving a small leftover amount of tokens that never get scheduled for distribution. This leftover, which can be up to one token unit less than the duration, becomes permanently locked in the contract because there is no subsequent logic to re‑queue or withdraw the undisbursed portion. The issue manifests each time the notifyRewardAmount() function is called – either at the start of a new reward period or when additional rewards are queued – and it persists across multiple periods, especially when the reward token has low decimal precision or a high market price, turning the microscopic dust into a noticeable loss of yield. Users experience the symptom of receiving less reward than expected; in extreme cases a user may observe a zero payout for a claim that should have yielded tokens, leading to the perception that funds have vanished. The bug was uncovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noticed that rewardRate * duration did not equal the supplied reward value – a subtle discrepancy that can be easily missed because the contract does not emit warnings or revert on the shortfall, and the remaining balance simply sits idle in the contract's storage. The root cause is a classic integer‑division rounding error, a class of arithmetic bugs common in smart contracts dealing with fixed‑point values. The impact is a gradual erosion of the reward pool’s total distributable amount, reducing protocol incentives and potentially harming participants’ trust. The vulnerability is hard to detect in routine testing because the loss per period is small and does not cause transaction failures. To remediate the issue, the contract should capture any remainder from the division and add it to a queuedRewards variable for distribution in the next period, or provide an explicit sweep or recovery function that allows the operator to re‑allocate the stuck tokens, thereby ensuring that the total reward promised to users is fully honored.

title: Unable To Get Rewards If Admin Withdraws $VE3D tokens From `VeTokenMinter` Contract
description: It was observed that users will not be able to get their rewards from the reward contract at certain point of time if admin withdraws $VE3D token from the `VeTokenMinter` contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the token balance held by the VeTokenMinter contract and the accounting variables that the contract uses to calculate reward distributions. At deployment the contract is pre‑minted with a fixed amount of VE3D tokens (30 million) and the code assumes that this entire amount will always be available for transfers when users claim rewards. The admin‑only withdraw function, however, transfers tokens out of the contract without updating any of the internal state such as totalSupply or maxSupply. Consequently, if the admin removes a large portion of the pre‑minted tokens, the contract’s balance can fall far below the constant maxSupply value that the mint routine relies on. When a user later triggers a reward claim, the VeTokenMinter.mint function computes the amount to transfer based on the theoretical remaining supply (maxSupply – currentSupply) rather than the actual token balance. If the computed amount exceeds the real balance, the safeTransfer call reverts due to insufficient tokens. This revert propagates through Booster.rewardClaimed and BaseRewardPool.getReward, causing the entire reward‑claiming flow to fail. From the user’s perspective, attempts to claim rewards either revert or result in zero reward being received, even though the protocol reports that they are entitled to a payout. The issue manifests only after an admin withdraws tokens, making it hard to detect during normal operation because the contract’s public supply variables still appear consistent. It affects every project that references the single VeTokenMinter instance, potentially disabling rewards across multiple DeFi strategies. The flaw was identified during a security audit that traced the withdraw function and observed that it does not reconcile the contract’s accounting state. To remediate, the withdraw function should be removed or altered to adjust the internal accounting (e.g., recompute maxSupply or totalSupply) before allowing token transfers, or the mint logic should be changed to base its calculations on the actual token balance, similar to Convex’s on‑the‑fly minting approach. This ensures that the contract never attempts to transfer more VE3D tokens than it holds, preserving reward distribution integrity.

title: Misconfiguration of Fees Incentive Might Cause Tokens To Be Stuck In `Booster` Contract
description: Users will lost their gauge fee if this happens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration risk in the fee allocation logic of the Booster contract, where the two parameters that define how gauge fees are split – the locker incentive and the staker incentive – are not validated to sum to the required 100 % denominator (10 000). The root cause is the absence of a constraint in the setFeeInfo function, allowing the contract owner or fee manager to submit arbitrary values that may be lower or higher than the intended total. An attacker, a careless developer, or even an automated script can call setFeeInfo with values such as 40 and 60 instead of the correct 4000 and 6000. Because the subsequent earmarkFees routine calculates each side’s payout by multiplying the contract’s fee balance by the stored incentive values and then dividing by the denominator, a total below 100 % means that the calculated share for both parties will be far smaller than the actual balance. The remainder of the tokens, in this example 99 % of the collected fees, stays locked inside the Booster contract because the contract never attempts to transfer it elsewhere. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a fee distribution cycle the expected reward is either a tiny fraction of the owed amount or completely missing; the UI may show a zero or near‑zero balance where a substantial reward should appear. The impact is loss of gauge fee revenue for users, effectively “funds disappear” from the perspective of token holders who rely on the Booster to forward their fees to reward contracts. This condition occurs whenever setFeeInfo is called with a mis‑sum, which can happen due to human error (typos, misunderstanding of the fee denominator) or malicious intent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review that noted the lack of a require statement checking the sum of the two incentive values. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit warning; the system continues to operate, but the accounting invariant that total fees are fully disbursed is silently broken. The correct fix is to enforce a validation check in setFeeInfo that requires lockFeesIncentive plus stakerLockFeesIncentive to equal the constant FEE_DENOMINATOR, and to also ensure that neither component exceeds the denominator individually. By restoring the invariant that the fee split always equals 100 %, the contract will reliably forward the full amount of collected fees to the intended reward contracts, preserving user balances and preventing tokens from becoming stuck.

title: updateBuffer() burns pxETH instead of institutional pxETH
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the InstitutionalPirexEthConfigurationLogic contract where the updateBuffer() function invokes batchBurnPxEth(). Inside batchBurnPxEth() the code iterates over a list of burnerAccounts, checks that each account is approved, accumulates the requested amount and then calls burnPxEth(). The burnPxEth() routine is designed to destroy regular pxETH tokens, not the institutional variant that is minted by InstitutionalPirexEth.deposit(). In the institutional version of the protocol only the AutoPxEth contract ever holds regular pxETH, while burner accounts are expected to hold institutional pxETH. Because the function burns the wrong token type, the intended compensation mechanism – burning institutional pxETH from burner accounts to offset deposited ETH – never occurs. The root cause is a mismatch between the token being burned and the token that actually exists in the burner accounts, caused by reusing generic burn logic without accounting for the separate token class. An attacker or, more realistically, a governance actor calling updateBuffer() under the assumption that it will reduce institutional pxETH balances will find that the call either reverts due to insufficient regular pxETH balance or silently succeeds without affecting any institutional pxETH. Consequently the buffer update fails, ETH deposits are not compensated, and the protocol’s accounting between ETH and institutional pxETH becomes inconsistent. Users may notice that after depositing ETH they receive no corresponding reduction in their institutional pxETH balance, or that the protocol’s reported buffer does not change despite governance actions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the configuration logic where the auditor compared the token flows of the institutional and non‑institutional versions and observed that the burn routine referenced the wrong token contract. It is hard to spot because the function names and variable names are generic and the two token contracts have similar interfaces, masking the subtle but critical difference in token class. To remediate the problem the burn routine should be rewritten to operate on institutional pxETH: the contract must first transfer the specified amount of institutional pxETH from each burner account, unwrap it into apxETH, redeem the apxETH for regular pxETH and finally burn that regular pxETH. This ensures that the intended accounting adjustment occurs and that the buffer update reflects the true state of institutional holdings.

title: Rewards might be temporarily stuck in Kodiak adapter
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During the unstake process the contract first calls the reward‑claim function and then updates the staker’s balance. The reward‑claim function transfers the accrued reward tokens to the adapter contract itself. If the external reward‑collection mechanism is paused, the internal call to getReward reverts, so the transfer never completes. As a result the adapter temporarily holds the reward tokens that should have been sent directly to the user or to the locker. This violates the protocol invariant that the adapter must not retain any assets except during an explicit claim. The condition occurs only when a user initiates an unstake while the reward‑collection flag in the underlying Kodiak farm is set to paused. Users observe that after unstaking they receive no reward, their balance in the locker remains unchanged, and the adapter’s internal balance shows a non‑zero amount of reward tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawLocked flow, where the ordering of operations and the pause check were examined. Because the adapter’s balance is not part of the normal UI, the problem can be hard to notice until a user checks the contract’s token holdings or experiences missing rewards. The impact is medium: funds are not lost permanently but are inaccessible until the pause is lifted, breaking the expected accounting guarantees and potentially eroding user trust. The bug belongs to the class of “temporary asset lock due to improper error handling and invariant violation”. A proper fix is to ensure that reward collection is either performed after the pause check or wrapped in a try‑catch so that a revert does not prevent the adapter from forwarding any already‑received tokens, and to consider sending rewards directly to the locker during unstake so the adapter never holds assets. This restores the invariant that the adapter contract should be stateless with respect to user funds.

title: Attacker can DoS lockers from unstaking from Kodiak
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the HoneyLocker staking system that arises when the internal accounting variables that track the total amount of LP tokens staked (totalLPStaked and vaultLPStaked) can be forced into an arithmetic underflow. The root cause is that the locker assumes that only its own functions will modify the token balance of the Kodiak adapter, and it decreases the stored counters by the amount requested for unstaking without verifying that the actual token balance of the adapter matches the recorded amount. An attacker can exploit this by sending a single wei of the LP token directly to the adapter contract – a transfer that bypasses the locker’s stake function. When the attacker later triggers an unstake, the contract attempts to subtract the recorded stake amount from the adapter’s balance, which is now one wei higher than expected, causing the subtraction to underflow and the unstake call to revert. The revert prevents the locker from withdrawing any of the previously staked tokens, effectively freezing user funds. This condition occurs only after an external tiny token donation has been made to the adapter and before any unstake operation is performed. Users who have deposited liquidity through the locker see their withdrawal transactions fail, their UI may display “withdrawal failed” or simply show no change in balance, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a unit test that deliberately transferred one wei to the adapter and observed that the subsequent unstake reverted. Because the underflow happens inside a low-level arithmetic operation, it may not be obvious from the contract’s external behavior until a withdrawal is attempted, making it hard to detect in production. The bug belongs to the class of accounting-state-corruption DoS vulnerabilities where external token transfers break invariant assumptions. To remediate the problem the adapter should maintain its own mapping of stake identifiers to amounts and use those stored values when withdrawing, or it should protect against unsolicited token transfers by rejecting them or by reconciling the actual token balance before performing arithmetic. Upgrading the adapter or the locker to incorporate these checks would restore the ability to unstake and prevent future freezes.

title: ERC20 tokens without return value will DoS reward claiming
description:
Several functions throughout the application use the transfer function to transfer ERC20 tokens. However, some tokens do not return a bool on transfer, and since the ERC20 interface expects the bool return value, calling transfer on tokens that do not return a bool would revert. The following functions suffer from this issue:
- withdrawERC20 in HoneyLocker
- unstake in BeradromeAdapter
- unstake in BGTStationAdapter
- unstake in InfraredAdapter
- unstake in KodiakAdapter
The following functions also call transfer on ERC20, but the call is wrapped in a try-catch block. However, such a call would still revert:
- claim in BeradromeAdapter
- claim in InfraredAdapter
- claim in KodiakAdapter
The impact is rated as medium since the issue can be resolved through a contract upgrade, though users would face a temporary freeze of their assets until the fix is deployed. The likelihood is high given that numerous widely-used tokens in the ecosystem don't strictly follow the ERC20 standard regarding return values.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the ERC20 interface used by the contracts and the actual behavior of some ERC20 tokens. The contracts call token.transfer(...) assuming the function returns a boolean and that a false return indicates failure, but the Solidity interface declares a bool return value. Tokens that implement the older non‑standard ERC20 specification omit the return value and simply revert on failure or return nothing. Because the call is compiled against an interface that expects a bool, the EVM treats the missing return data as an invalid response and automatically reverts the whole transaction. This occurs in several functions that distribute or withdraw rewards such as withdrawERC20, unstake and claim. When a user attempts to claim or unstake rewards that are paid in such a non‑standard token, the transaction reverts, preventing the transfer from completing. From the user’s perspective the reward claim appears to fail silently: the UI shows a pending transaction that never settles, balances remain unchanged, and the user receives no tokens. The protocol’s accounting assumes that rewards can always be transferred, so the freeze breaks the expected flow and effectively locks user funds until the contract code is upgraded or the token is replaced. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected all external token transfers and compared them against the ERC20 specification. It is hard to notice because the revert happens only with specific tokens; with compliant tokens the functions work correctly, so testing with a single token may not reveal the problem. The bug belongs to the class of ERC20 return‑value incompatibility or non‑standard token transfer denial‑of‑service. Exploitation does not require a malicious actor; any user attempting a legitimate claim triggers the revert, causing a denial‑of‑service. The impact is medium because the assets are not stolen, but they become temporarily inaccessible, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer. The condition for the failure is the presence of a token that does not return a bool on transfer and is used in reward distribution. The affected parties are token holders who expect to receive rewards, the protocol’s staking adapters, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful transfers. The recommended mitigation is to replace direct calls to transfer with a safe‑transfer wrapper that does not depend on the return value, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, or to implement a custom pull‑pattern that allows the contract to retry failed transfers after a fix. By handling the lack of return data gracefully, the contract can avoid reverting and keep user balances intact.

title: RewardRecipientGateway.slashValidator() prevents legacy reward recipient from using the buffer with non-zero _amount
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RewardRecipientGateway contract’s slashValidator() function. The function is designed to be invoked either directly by an address that holds the KEEPER_ROLE or indirectly through the legacy RewardRecipient contract’s own slashValidator() wrapper. When the caller sets the _useBuffer flag to true, the code contains a guard that reverts if any ether is sent with the call: if (_useBuffer && msg.value > 0) revert Errors.NoETHAllowed(). This guard assumes that the caller will not forward ether when using the buffer. However, the legacy RewardRecipient contract forwards the sum of msg.value and the _amount parameter to the gateway via pirexEth.slashValidator{value: _amount + msg.value}(). Consequently, when the gateway receives a call with _useBuffer true and a non‑zero _amount, msg.value is no longer zero – it equals the forwarded amount – and the guard triggers, causing the transaction to revert. The result is that the keeper, which relies on the buffer to cover partial penalties, cannot dissolve a validator that has been partially slashed. From a business‑logic perspective, the protocol expects the keeper to be able to use both the validator’s unstaked ETH and the buffer to cover the penalty; the bug prevents this, effectively locking the validator and preventing the intended penalty from being applied. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the legacy contract and the new gateway. It is subtle because the guard appears reasonable in isolation and only fails under the specific combination of using the buffer together with a non‑zero amount via the legacy path – a scenario that may not be exercised in typical unit tests. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for validator slashing: validators that should be dissolved remain active, the protocol may lose expected revenue from penalties, and users relying on timely slashing may see their balances remain unchanged. The affected parties include protocol operators, keepers, validators, and ultimately token holders who depend on correct penalty enforcement. To remediate, the check should be applied only when the call originates directly from a keeper and not when it is routed through the legacy RewardRecipient contract. A conditional exemption such as if (msg.sender != legacyRewardRecipient && _useBuffer && msg.value > 0) revert Errors.NoETHAllowed(); would allow the intended buffer usage while still protecting against accidental ether transfers in other contexts.

title: Function isTargetContractAllowed always returns true
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that is intended to verify whether a target contract is associated with a known protocol. The implementation retrieves a memory string representing the protocol and then uses inline assembly to evaluate the expression not(iszero(protocol)). In the Ethereum Virtual Machine a memory pointer to a string is always non‑zero once the variable is allocated, even if the string’s length is zero. Consequently the assembly check evaluates the pointer rather than the actual content, causing the function to return true for every address, regardless of whether a protocol identifier is stored. This logical flaw originates from a misunderstanding of how Solidity stores dynamic strings in memory and from using a low‑level zero‑check on the pointer instead of inspecting the byte length. An attacker who can influence the address passed to the function can rely on the always‑true result to bypass higher‑level permission checks that assume a false return indicates an unauthorized target. In practice the current codebase also contains a separate selector‑validation routine that prevents unauthorized interactions, so the immediate impact is limited. However, if future versions or extensions replace that routine with the flawed function, locker owners could circumvent the liquidity lock mechanism, withdraw locked tokens without paying the intended fees, and effectively render the lock ineffective. The issue manifests when the function is called with an address that has no protocol entry; the user interface may still display a locked status while the contract internally treats the target as allowed, leading to unexpected zero‑fee withdrawals. The bug is subtle because the assembly expression compiles without warnings and always yields a true boolean, making it easy to overlook during manual review or testing that focuses on functional outcomes rather than internal state checks. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s access‑control logic and identified the misuse of the memory pointer check. To remediate the issue, the function should be rewritten to evaluate the actual length of the stored string, for example by converting the string to bytes and checking that bytes(protocol).length is greater than zero. This change ensures that an empty protocol entry correctly results in a false return, restoring the intended protection against unauthorized contract interactions.

title: HoneyLocker.unstake() can possibly lead to underflow
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An underflow vulnerability exists in the unstake function of the HoneyLocker contract. The contract keeps a double‑mapping staked[LPToken][stakingContract] that records how many LP tokens the owner has deposited in an external staking contract (Kodiak). When the owner calls unstake, the function blindly subtracts the requested amount from this internal accounting variable before forwarding the call to the external contract. If the external contract’s withdrawLockedAll function is invoked before the lock period has expired, it only harvests rewards and does not transfer the locked LP tokens back. Consequently the internal staked balance is reduced to zero even though the tokens remain locked in the external contract. A subsequent attempt to unstake the same amount causes the subtraction to underflow, reverting the transaction and leaving the tokens permanently locked in the external contract. The bug occurs only when the caller uses a selector that triggers a partial withdrawal (rewards only) before the lock expires. It affects the contract owner and any user that relies on the HoneyLocker to correctly track and retrieve their LP tokens. The issue was discovered during manual testing of the interaction between HoneyLocker and Kodiak’s stakeLocked / withdrawLockedAll functions. It can be hard to notice because the first call succeeds and appears to collect rewards, while the missing token transfer is not reflected in the UI; only the second call fails with an underflow error. The impact is loss of liquidity: the user’s LP tokens become irretrievable, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s accounting. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow bugs caused by inconsistent state updates across contract boundaries. The proper fix is to verify that the amount being subtracted does not exceed the recorded staked balance, or to only update the internal accounting after confirming that the external call actually transferred tokens. Adding a conditional check or using SafeMath‑like safeguards prevents the balance from becoming negative and avoids the revert that locks the funds.

title: Users can avoid paying fees to the protocol due to rounding
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down fee calculation in the HoneyQueen contract that allows the contract owner to withdraw ERC20 or BERA tokens without paying the protocol‑defined referral and treasury fees. The computeFees function multiplies the withdrawal amount by a fee rate expressed in basis points and then divides by 10,000 using integer arithmetic. Because the EVM truncates the result toward zero, any withdrawal amount for which amount * fees is smaller than 10,000 yields a fee of zero. An attacker who controls the owner role can therefore split a large withdrawal into many tiny batches, for example repeatedly withdrawing 49 tokens when the fee rate is 2 % (200 bps). The calculation 49 * 200 / 10000 evaluates to 0, so no fee is deducted. This can be executed repeatedly until the desired total amount is withdrawn, effectively bypassing the fee mechanism. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the treasury and referral parties, and it undermines the economic model of the protocol. The issue manifests only when the caller can specify arbitrary withdrawal amounts; it is invisible for typical larger withdrawals where the fee rounds to a non‑zero value, making it hard to notice during normal testing. The affected parties are the protocol’s treasury, referral program, and any stakeholders relying on fee collection. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑computation logic, where the integer division behaviour was examined. Because the fee appears correct for most amounts, the problem may be missed unless edge‑case amounts are tested. To remediate, the fee calculation should be changed to round up (for example by adding the divisor‑1 before division) or a minimum fee threshold should be enforced so that the result can never be zero. This class of bug is a classic rounding‑error or integer‑division truncation issue that breaks the business rule that every withdrawal must incur a non‑zero fee, leading to situations where users see a withdrawal succeed with no fee deducted, contrary to the expectation that a small fee is always taken.

title: Unsafe Downcast Truncation in UniswapOracleLibrary Leading to Invalid Price Data
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe downcast truncation error in the UniswapOracleLibrary that produces invalid price data. The library receives a cumulative tick delta (tickCumulativesDelta) as a signed 56‑bit integer (int56) and then casts it to a signed 24‑bit integer (int24) before dividing by the elapsed time (secondsAgo). Because the cast occurs prior to the division, any tickCumulativesDelta value that exceeds the int24 range is silently truncated without a revert. This truncated value is then used to compute the arithmetic mean tick, which feeds the price calculation of downstream contracts such as SwEthSpotOracle. The root cause is the ordering of operations: casting before arithmetic reduces the magnitude of the operand and discards high‑order bits, violating the mathematical expectation that division should be performed on the full‑precision value. Exploitation is possible when the cumulative tick delta grows large enough – for example after roughly ten consecutive tick updates – causing the int24 cast to overflow. An attacker could trigger or wait for such a state, causing the oracle to return a price that is far from the true market price. The impact is that users see incorrect price quotes, experience unexpected slippage, or receive trades at rates that are too high or too low, potentially leading to loss of funds. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a price that is dramatically different from other sources, or a transaction may settle with a near‑zero or excessively large amount received, contrary to the expectation of a fair market price. The bug occurs only when the cumulative tick delta exceeds the int24 limits, a condition that is rare but not impossible in volatile markets or over long periods. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation to the reference Uniswap code, which correctly performs the division before the cast. The issue is hard to notice because the Solidity runtime does not emit an error on overflow when casting to a smaller signed type; the contract simply continues with the truncated value, making the price deviation appear as a subtle drift rather than an outright failure. To remediate, the arithmetic should be performed on the full‑precision int56 value and only after the division should the result be down‑cast to int24, or alternatively a larger integer type should be used for the final tick value. This aligns the library with the intended Uniswap behavior and restores accurate price data, preventing the oracle from feeding malformed prices into dependent protocols.

title: If a Pool at the Beginning of withdrawQueue() Is Paused, the Depositor Won’t Be Able to Redeem from Other Active Pools
description: When a user wants to withdraw his stakings, he returns his shares by calling withdraw() or redeem(), those two functions calls withdrawFromIonPool(), which is then iterating over withdrawQueue() from the first added pool. The problem here is that if a pool is paused, the tx will revert here, because pool.withdraw() has whenNotPaused modifier and user won’t be able to receive his funds, even if there is available liquidity in next pools in the queue. The impact is a temporary DoS. NOTE The same is valid for deposit().
bug_full: A withdrawal (or redemption) request in the contract triggers a call to withdrawFromIonPool, which walks through an ordered withdrawQueue and invokes each pool’s withdraw function in turn. The implementation assumes every pool in the queue can be called, but it does not verify whether a pool is currently paused. Because each pool’s withdraw method is protected by a whenNotPaused modifier, a paused pool causes the call to revert. The revert aborts the entire loop, so the user never reaches later pools that might have sufficient liquidity. Consequently, a depositor who is positioned behind a paused pool in the queue cannot redeem his shares even though other active pools could satisfy the request. The same logic applies to deposits, where a paused pool blocks the entire deposit flow. This creates a temporary denial‑of‑service condition: funds appear to be locked, users see no balance change, and the UI may show a transaction failure despite available liquidity elsewhere. The bug is triggered only when a pool earlier in the withdrawQueue is paused; if all pools are active the function works as intended. It affects any user trying to withdraw or deposit, as well as the protocol’s reputation because funds can be frozen by simply pausing a single pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of withdrawQueue and noticed the missing pause check.
