It is subtle because pausing a pool is a legitimate administrative action, and developers may expect the pause to affect only that pool’s own operations, not the orchestration logic that iterates over multiple pools. To remediate, the contract should detect the paused state before invoking a pool’s withdraw (or deposit) and either skip the paused pool or handle it gracefully, ensuring that the loop continues to subsequent active pools. This change restores the intended behavior where users can still retrieve funds from any pool that remains unpaused, eliminating the DoS vector.

title: The new interest module may calculate past interest
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the function that updates the interest‑rate module used by the lending pool. When the protocol’s admin (role ION) calls updateInterestRateModule to replace the current InterestRate contract, the implementation only stores the new module address and emits an event. It does not invoke the internal _accrueInterest routine nor refresh the lastRateUpdate timestamps stored for each collateral type (ilk). Because the interest calculation routine later reads the current interestRateModule and multiplies the elapsed time (block.timestamp‑ilk.lastRateUpdate) by the rate returned by the module, the newly installed module is applied to the entire period that has passed since the previous update. Consequently, interest that should have been accrued under the old module is retroactively recomputed with the new parameters. This can lead to borrowers being charged more (or less) interest than they earned, lenders receiving unexpected reward amounts, and overall accounting inconsistencies. The issue manifests whenever the admin swaps the module after a non‑trivial interval without first accruing interest, which is a common operational pattern because the contract does not enforce any automatic accrual on module change. The affected parties are all users with active loans or deposits, as well as the protocol’s financial integrity. The problem was discovered during a manual security review, where the auditor noted the missing call and the comment in the source that the behaviour was considered a feature. It is hard to notice because the protocol normally accrues interest periodically, so the discrepancy only appears after the admin action, showing up as a sudden jump or drop in accrued balances on the UI. From a security perspective this is a classic state‑inconsistency bug that occurs when a modular component is swapped without reconciling dependent state. The recommended mitigation is to either call _accrueInterest before changing the module or, if that is not possible, reset every ilk.lastRateUpdate to the current block.timestamp after the update, guaranteeing that the new module influences only future accruals. Implementing such a safeguard restores the expected accounting model where interest is calculated with the module that was active during each time slice, preventing unexpected interest amounts and preserving user trust.

title: Allocator can bypass supply cap
description: The owner of the Vault specifies a supply cap for the pool list of the vault and the allocator will distribute funds into those pools based on those supply caps. The owner can specify the IDLE pool to allow for some of the tokens to stay in the vault. The issue is that the allocator can bypass the supply cap of the IDLE pool and keep all the tokens in the vault and it bypasses limits set by the owner and the user would receive less interest. The root cause is that in the function reallocate() the value of the currentIdleDeposits is cached outside of the for loop and it doesn't get updated when deposits happen inside the loop and code uses that cached value to check supply cap limit so if allocator uses IDLE pool multiple times in the allocations[] list and deposits multiple times then they can bypass the supply cap check for IDLE pool.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic bypass that allows the allocator contract to exceed the supply cap that the vault owner sets for the IDLE pool. The vault owner defines a maximum amount of tokens that may remain idle in the vault, expecting any excess to be allocated to yield‑generating pools. In the reallocate() function the current amount of idle deposits is read once before the allocation loop and stored in a local variable. Inside the loop the allocator may deposit tokens into the IDLE pool several times, but the cached variable is never refreshed after each deposit. Because the cap check continues to use the stale value, each subsequent deposit appears to be within the limit, allowing the allocator to keep more tokens in the vault than the owner intended. This can be exploited by constructing an allocations[] array that contains the IDLE pool multiple times and invoking reallocate(). The allocator then repeatedly deposits tokens, each time bypassing the cap check, so the idle balance grows beyond the configured maximum. The impact is that users who deposited expecting interest receive less because a larger portion of their funds stays idle and does not earn yield. The protocol’s accounting assumptions about total idle exposure are violated, potentially leading to lower overall returns and erosion of trust. The issue manifests only when the allocator performs more than one deposit to the IDLE pool within a single reallocate call; a single deposit would pass the cap check correctly, making the bug subtle and easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the allocation logic, where the auditor noticed that the variable tracking idle deposits was not updated inside the loop. The bug is hard to notice because the contract still enforces the cap for the common case of a single allocation, and the incorrect behaviour only appears under specific allocation patterns that may not be exercised in normal operation. To remediate, the code should recompute or update the currentIdleDeposits value after each deposit or withdrawal inside the loop, ensuring that the cap check always reflects the latest state. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that the sum of idle deposits never exceeds the owner‑defined supply cap, preventing the allocator from hoarding idle funds and preserving the expected interest distribution.

title: Missing check for supported asset
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent validation step in the depositAndBridge function that allows any ERC20 token to be used as a deposit asset, even if the token is not listed as a supported asset in the Vault. The root cause is that the function does not consult the internal isSupported mapping before calling the internal _erc20Deposit routine, so the contract proceeds to mint vault shares based solely on the amount transferred. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a custom or deprecated token, causing the Vault to issue shares that are not backed by a recognized price feed or collateral. Because the shares are minted without a corresponding supported asset, the accounting layer (AccountantWithRateProviders) may later be unable to price those shares correctly, leading to inaccurate total supply calculations, dilution of legitimate holders, and potential loss of value for users who rely on the share price. The issue manifests when the protocol has removed a token from its whitelist but failed to clear the associated price feed, or when admin variables in the accountant contract unintentionally permit minting for unknown assets. Users are affected because they may receive vault shares that appear normal in the UI but represent no real underlying value, resulting in situations where a user expects a proportional claim on deposited assets but receives nothing of value when attempting to withdraw or redeem. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that compared the public deposit interface with the internal asset‑whitelisting logic and noticed the missing require statement. It is hard to notice because the function signature accepts a generic ERC20 parameter and the rest of the contract performs numerous checks, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, the function should explicitly verify that the supplied token is marked as supported (e.g., require(isSupported[depositAsset])) before proceeding with the deposit, and the protocol should ensure that deprecated assets are fully removed from both the whitelist and any associated price feed contracts. This change restores the invariant that every minted share is backed by a known, priced asset, preserving accounting correctness and protecting user expectations that deposited tokens are safely represented by vault shares.

title: Not checking allowMessagesFrom on the destination chain
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the Cross‑chain Teller contract’s handling of inbound cross‑chain messages. The contract stores a per‑chain configuration that includes a boolean flag allowMessagesFrom, which is intended to indicate whether the contract should accept messages originating from a particular remote chain. While the flag is recorded when a chain is added, the receive logic – both the internal _lzReceive function and the public receiveBridgeMessage function – never consults this flag before processing the payload. As a result, even if the administrator has explicitly disabled inbound messages from a given chain (allowMessagesFrom set to false), the contract will still decode the payload and call vault.enter, effectively minting share tokens for an arbitrary receiver. This omission allows an attacker controlling a remote chain, or any entity that can cause the messenger contract to forward a message, to trigger unauthorized share creation without any on‑chain permission check. The exploit can be carried out by sending a crafted payload containing a share amount and a receiver address; the messenger contract satisfies the existing checks (msg.sender must be the messenger and xDomainMessageSender must be the expected peer), after which the contract blindly executes vault.enter, inflating the token supply or crediting unintended users. The impact includes potential dilution of existing token holders, unauthorized allocation of assets, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, which assume that shares are only minted in response to approved cross‑chain operations. The issue manifests whenever a chain is configured with allowMessagesFrom set to false but the contract still receives a message from that chain – a situation that may arise during normal operation, during an emergency response, or when a malicious counterpart deliberately sends messages. Users may notice unexpected balances increasing, receive share tokens they never requested, or see the protocol’s total supply grow inexplicably. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the configuration logic with the message‑handling code and identified the missing verification step. Because the contract’s receive functions already perform other checks, the absence of the allowMessagesFrom guard can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms, especially if the system is otherwise functional. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the stored Chain struct for the originating selector and require that allowMessagesFrom is true before decoding the payload and invoking vault.enter. Similar validation should be added to receiveBridgeMessage. This change restores the intended permission model, ensuring that inbound messages are only processed when explicitly allowed, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and preventing unauthorized share minting.

title: Inflation attack in Vault
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation attack that stems from the way the Vault contract computes share values when the underlying token uses 18 decimals, which is the case for WETH and many other ERC‑20 assets. The contract stores a variable called _decimalsOffset to add extra precision to share calculations, but when the token has 18 decimals the offset is set to zero. Consequently the share‑to‑asset conversion uses a formula that adds one to both the total supply and total assets before performing a mulDiv operation, which introduces a rounding bias when the numbers are very large. Because the contract also relies on its own token balance (balanceOf(address(this))) to determine the allocation for the IDLE pool, an attacker can first mint a single wei‑sized share by depositing a single wei of the underlying token. After obtaining this minimal share, the attacker can donate a huge amount of tokens (for example 100e18) to the vault. This donation inflates the price‑per‑share (PPS) value because the denominator in the share calculation becomes much larger while the rounding error remains fixed, effectively giving the attacker a disproportionate claim on future deposits. When a regular user later deposits a normal amount, the inflated PPS causes the division to round down, stealing a portion of the user’s assets and leaving them with fewer shares than expected. In the demonstrated test, an attacker who contributed only 0.1 ETH was able to lock roughly 1 ETH of another user’s assets, showing a loss of value for honest participants. The attack can be carried out whenever the vault is initialized with a token that has 18 decimals and the attacker can perform the two‑step sequence of minting a minimal share followed by a large token donation. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that exercised the contract with edge‑case deposits and observed the unexpected loss of funds for a secondary user. The bug is subtle because the share calculation appears mathematically sound for typical values, and the rounding discrepancy only becomes significant after the attacker artificially inflates the total asset pool. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a non‑zero _decimalsOffset (for example setting it to six) or require an initial non‑trivial deposit that prevents the creation of a single‑wei share, thereby eliminating the ability to manipulate the PPS through extreme token donations. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of precision‑loss and rounding‑error vulnerabilities in financial smart contracts, where inaccurate scaling factors enable an attacker to distort accounting invariants and cause funds to disappear from users who interact with the contract under normal expectations.

title: Auction tokens with approval race protection or not returning a bool on approve are incompatible with VestedCrowdSale
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way VestedCrowdSale handles ERC20 token approvals for auction tokens. The contract reads the current allowance granted to a vesting contract and then attempts to increase it by calling approve with the sum of the existing allowance and the amount to be sold. This pattern assumes that the token follows the standard ERC20 approve semantics, where any non‑zero allowance can be overwritten with a new value. However, several popular tokens implement an approval race protection mechanism that only permits allowance changes when the current allowance is either zero or set to the maximum uint256 value. When the current allowance is non‑zero, the token’s approve function reverts, causing the VestedCrowdSale transaction to fail. In addition, some tokens such as USDT deviate from the ERC20 specification by not returning a boolean value from approve. Solidity expects a return data size of 32 bytes; when the token returns no data, the call is treated as a failure and also reverts. Consequently, the auction token cannot be approved for the vesting contract, preventing the token lock step from succeeding. The impact is that participants who have won the auction are unable to claim or lock their tokens, leading to a situation where funds appear to be missing from the user’s perspective – the UI may show a successful purchase but the token balance remains unchanged or becomes zero after the transaction reverts. This issue affects any protocol that relies on VestedCrowdSale with tokens that enforce the zero‑or‑max allowance rule or that omit the boolean return, including users, token holders, and the overall protocol’s ability to distribute auctioned assets. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s approval logic against known token behaviours. It is easy to overlook because most test environments use mock ERC20 tokens that follow the standard, and the revert only occurs when the allowance is already set, a condition that may not be exercised in simple unit tests. To remediate, approvals should be performed only at the moment tokens are about to be locked, and the contract should first reset the allowance to zero or use a library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.forceApprove, which handles the zero‑or‑max requirement and tolerates tokens that do not return a boolean. By adopting this approach, the contract aligns with the broader class of “non‑standard ERC20 approval” bugs, ensuring that token transfers succeed regardless of the token’s internal approval logic and preserving the expected business flow of auction token distribution.

title: Insufficient input validation in CrowdSale configuration
description: There are two flaws in the configuration validation of a new CrowdSale. It is currently possible to create a never ending Sale as the closingTime field does not have a max value check. It is also possible that a never ending lock or a 0 duration lock is used in VestedCrowdSale as the cliff argument of startSale is not validated as in StakedVestedCrowdSale::startSale. Both can result in almost permanently locked tokens which is a value loss for users.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an input‑validation flaw in the configuration of a CrowdSale contract and its vested variant. The contract accepts a closingTime parameter that determines when the token sale ends, but it does not enforce an upper bound, allowing an attacker to set an arbitrarily large timestamp. As a result the sale can be made effectively never‑ending. In the VestedCrowdSale, the startSale function receives a cliff argument that defines the initial lock period before tokens begin to vest. This argument is not validated against minimum or maximum limits, unlike the reference implementation in StakedVestedCrowdSale. Consequently a malicious caller can supply a cliff of zero, creating an immediate lock that never releases, or a cliff that is so large that the tokens remain locked for an indefinite period. The root cause is the absence of proper range checks on critical time‑related parameters, which violates the business logic that sales and vesting periods must be finite and bounded. Exploitation occurs when a privileged or malicious entity deploys a new CrowdSale or calls startSale with crafted values; the contract then records a closingTime far in the future or a cliff that never expires. Users who purchase tokens expect the sale to close after a reasonable period and the vesting schedule to unlock tokens after the cliff, but instead their tokens remain locked, effectively disappearing from their usable balance. The impact is a loss of value for investors because the tokens cannot be transferred or claimed, undermining trust in the protocol. This condition manifests only when the sale is created or started with the malformed parameters, so it may go unnoticed during normal operation because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about excessively long timestamps. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the contract’s parameter validation logic. Detecting the problem is difficult because the contract will still compile and run, and the extreme timestamps do not cause immediate runtime errors. To remediate, the contract should enforce both minimum and maximum bounds for closingTime (e.g., require closingTime to be greater than block.timestamp and less than a reasonable future limit) and for the cliff parameter (e.g., require cliff to be greater than zero and less than the total vesting duration). Adding these checks restores the intended economic guarantees, prevents permanently locked tokens, and aligns the implementation with the expected token sale and vesting behavior.

title: Tokens with a fee-on-transfer mechanism will break the protocol
description:
The ERC20 logic in all crowd sale contracts as well as in TimelockedToken is incompatible with tokens that have a fee-on-transfer mechanism. Such tokens for example is PAXG, while USDT has a built-in fee-on-transfer mechanism that is currently switched off. One example of this CrowdSale::startSale where the following code:
```solidity
sale.auctionToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), sale.salesAmount);
```
Will work incorrectly if the token has a fee-on-transfer mechanism - the contract will cache sale.salesAmount as it's expected balance, but it will actually have sale.salesAmount - fee balance. This will result in a revert in the last person to transfer auctionTokens out of the contract. Same thing applies for other transferFrom calls that transfer tokens into the protocol, for example in TimelockedToken::lock.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the assumption that a token transfer using safeTransferFrom will always deliver the exact amount specified. In the crowd‑sale contracts and the TimelockedToken contract the code caches the expected amount (sale.salesAmount) before calling safeTransferFrom and later relies on that cached value when distributing or unlocking tokens. When a token implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism – for example PAXG or USDT when its fee flag is enabled, or any ERC777 token that deducts a portion on each transfer – the actual balance received by the contract is lower than the requested amount because a portion is taken as a transfer fee. The contract does not verify the post‑transfer balance, so it believes it holds the full salesAmount while the real balance is salesAmount minus fee. This discrepancy only becomes visible later, typically when the last participant attempts to withdraw or when the contract tries to transfer out the cached amount; the operation then reverts because the contract does not have enough tokens. The impact is that participants may see their contribution accepted, but the sale fails to complete, resulting in tokens not being delivered, balances appearing to disappear, or funds becoming permanently locked in the contract. The issue manifests whenever a fee‑on‑transfer token is used as the auction token or is locked via TimelockedToken, i.e., under any condition where the protocol expects a fee‑free ERC20 transfer. All users who interact with the crowdsale – buyers, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting logic is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token handling logic and identified that the code never checks the actual received amount after a transferFrom. It is hard to notice because the transfer call itself succeeds; no error is thrown, and the contract’s internal state appears consistent until a later operation that requires the missing tokens. To remediate, the contract should record the token balance before the transfer, perform the transfer, then read the new balance and compute the delta; this delta should be used as the true amount received. Additionally, a nonReentrant guard is required to prevent re‑entrancy attacks that could manipulate the balance check, especially with ERC777 tokens. An alternative, simpler mitigation is to explicitly document that the protocol does not support fee‑on‑transfer tokens and reject such tokens at the interface level. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a fee‑on‑transfer handling flaw or transfer amount assumption bug, where the contract’s accounting relies on a naïve transfer model that violates the business logic of exact token accounting.

title: M-1 Set credit limit by pausing the guardian
description:
Pausing the guardian can set a new credit limit for users with the credit limit.
Comptroller.sol#L1313
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unintended path that allows a privileged actor to modify a user’s credit limit simply by pausing the guardian contract. In the Comptroller implementation the internal function _setCreditLimit is invoked without checking whether the guardian is in a paused state, and the pause mechanism is meant to freeze critical operations, not to enable privileged state changes. Because the pause flag is not part of the access‑control condition, an attacker who can trigger the pause (for example through the guardian’s pause function) can subsequently call _setCreditLimit and assign an arbitrary credit limit to any address, including their own. This bypasses the normal governance or risk‑management checks that normally restrict credit‑limit adjustments. When the guardian is paused, the contract mistakenly treats the system as safe for limit changes, creating a privilege‑escalation scenario. An exploit would involve the attacker pausing the guardian, invoking _setCreditLimit with a very high limit for their account, and then borrowing assets beyond the intended risk parameters, potentially draining the protocol’s liquidity. The impact is the loss of funds for lenders and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as the credit‑limit invariant is violated. The issue manifests only while the guardian is paused; under normal operation the function behaves as expected, which makes the bug easy to miss during routine testing because pausing is usually associated with halting activity, not enabling it. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes when the auditors inspected the Comptroller code and noticed the missing pause check. The problem belongs to the class of improper access‑control and state‑dependent logic errors, where a privileged state change is allowed under an unexpected condition. From a user’s perspective the symptom could be that a borrower suddenly sees a much larger credit limit appear in the UI, or that a legitimate user’s limit is altered without any governance proposal, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. To remediate the issue the _setCreditLimit function should be hardened with an explicit require that the guardian is not paused and that only authorized roles (e.g., governance or a risk manager) can invoke it, ensuring that credit‑limit adjustments cannot be performed while the system is in a paused state.

title: M-2 Exchange rate vulnerability
description:
An exchange rate bug for new pools and empty pools (without borrowers and suppliers) for CToken contracts without the 'internalCash' variable.
Flow:
1. Create cToken
2. Mint cToken by user1 (1,000,000)
3. Redeem cToken by user1 (999,999.999999)
4. Transfer underlying (1,000,000) from user1 to market
5. Mint cToken by user2 (1,000,000)
6. Redeem cToken by user1 (user1 receive extra tokens)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exchange‑rate miscalculation that occurs in CToken contracts that do not maintain an internal cash accounting variable (often called internalCash). When a new market is created or when a market has no active borrowers or suppliers, the contract calculates the exchange rate solely from the on‑chain cash balance and the total supply of cTokens. If an external transfer of the underlying asset is made directly to the market contract – for example, a user sends the underlying token to the market without invoking the mint function – the contract’s internal accounting is not updated. Consequently, the exchange rate remains based on the stale cash value. A user who minted cTokens before the external transfer can later redeem those tokens at a rate that is artificially high, receiving more underlying than they originally supplied. The attack flow is: (1) Deploy a fresh CToken market; (2) User 1 mints a large amount of cTokens, receiving a correct amount of underlying on redemption; (3) User 1 then transfers the same amount of underlying directly to the market contract, bypassing the mint logic; (4) User 2 mints additional cTokens, which forces the contract to recompute the exchange rate using the inflated cash balance but without correcting the internal cash reference; (5) User 1 redeems the original cTokens and receives extra underlying because the exchange rate is now overstated. The impact is a loss of protocol funds and an unintended creation of value for the attacker, breaking the accounting guarantees that each cToken should represent a fixed share of the underlying pool. The bug is most likely to appear in newly created markets or in markets that have been emptied of borrowers and suppliers, because the internal cash variable is only initialized after the first proper mint. It is hard to notice because normal operation (mint‑redeem cycles) does not involve direct underlying transfers, and the discrepancy may be small enough to be masked by rounding errors. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case flows involving empty pools. To remediate, the contract should either maintain an internal cash variable that is updated on every external transfer, or it should explicitly verify that the exchange rate is correct before the first mint, rejecting any direct underlying deposits that could desynchronize the accounting. In essence, the fix is to ensure that the exchange rate always reflects the true underlying balance, preventing users from receiving more assets than they are entitled to.

title: M-3 Interest rate model update impacts the old time period
description: After an admin changes the interest rate model parameters by using this function TripleSlopeRateModel.sol#L100 indexes will be recalculated in the upcoming accrueInterest() function call. But this call applies new interest settings to the previous period of time which is not correct.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way an interest‑rate model can be updated by an administrator and how the contract subsequently calculates accrued interest. When the admin calls the function that changes the parameters of the TripleSlopeRateModel, the contract stores the new parameters immediately. The next call to accrueInterest() uses the currently stored parameters to compute the interest that has accumulated since the previous accrual timestamp. Because the timestamp interval may include time that occurred before the parameter change, the new settings are applied retroactively to a period that should have been evaluated with the old settings. This mismatch originates from the lack of a snapshot or a guard that forces the contract to finish the current accrual period before accepting a new model. An attacker who controls the admin role can deliberately change the model to a more favorable rate just before an accrual, causing the contract to credit or debit interest for the previous block interval incorrectly. The impact is a distortion of the accounting: lenders may receive more interest than earned, borrowers may be charged extra, and the protocol’s total supply of interest‑bearing tokens can become out of sync with the real economic state. The bug manifests when an admin updates the model and then triggers accrueInterest() before a new period starts; any asset that relies on this model is affected, meaning all users of the IronBank lending market are potentially exposed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the interest‑rate update flow, where the auditor noted that the index recalculation step occurs after the parameter change but before the accrual logic, violating the expected accounting invariant that interest for a given interval must be computed with the parameters that were in effect during that interval. Because the discrepancy may be small on a per‑block basis, it can be hard to notice without detailed balance checks, especially when the protocol reports only the final token balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce that accrueInterest() is called with the old parameters before any change is applied, for example by invoking accrueInterest() first and then allowing the admin to set new parameters, or by delegating the update to a dedicated service contract that schedules the change only after the current accrual has been settled. This ensures that each time window is evaluated with a consistent rate model, preserving the integrity of interest calculations and preventing unintended profit or loss for participants.

title: New pool can be temporarily blocked
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that can temporarily block all operations of a newly deployed Ion liquidity pool. The root cause lies in the interest‑rate calculation routine of the InterestRate module. When the pool calls accrueInterest, it invokes calculateInterestRate which computes a utilizationRate as totalIlkDebt divided by totalEthSupply multiplied by a scaled distributionFactor. The code only checks whether distributionFactor is zero, but it does not verify that the denominator totalEthSupply.wadMulDown(distributionFactor.scaleUpToWad(4)) is non‑zero. If the pool’s ETH supply is very small – for example after a user supplies a dust amount of underlying and then borrows a tiny normalized amount – the scaled supply can round down to zero due to integer division. This makes the denominator zero, causing a division‑by‑zero revert. Because accrueInterest is invoked at the beginning of every pool action (supply, borrow, withdraw, repay, etc.), the revert blocks every subsequent transaction, effectively freezing the pool. The impact is that all users – lenders, borrowers, and any other participants – see their balances unchanged, cannot perform expected actions such as withdrawing or borrowing, and their funds become temporarily inaccessible. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a transaction fails with a generic revert, balances remain the same, and no error message explains the underlying accounting issue. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor supplied a minimal amount of collateral and performed a borrow, then advanced time and observed that accrueInterest reverted. The bug is hard to notice in normal operation because it only manifests under extreme low‑supply conditions that are unlikely in regular usage, and the existing check for a zero distributionFactor gives a false sense of safety. To remediate, the calculateInterestRate function should also guard against a zero denominator by adding a condition such as: if (distributionFactor == 0 || totalEthSupply.wadMulDown(distributionFactor.scaleUpToWad(4)) == 0) return (minimumKinkRate, scaledReserveFactor). This ensures that a safe fallback rate is used when the supply is too small, preventing the division‑by‑zero and allowing the pool to continue operating. The class of bug is a missing zero‑division guard in financial formulae, leading to a temporary lockout of contract functionality and violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that interest rates can always be computed.

title: M-4 A ﬂashloan will be broken if the USDT fee is more than zero
description:
Let's take a look at the ﬂashloan ﬂow. After doTransferOut a receiver gets amount - fee.
CCollateralCapErc20.sol#L217
Then a receiver's onFlashLoan function will be called with an incorrect amount.
CCollateralCapErc20.sol#L224
Then doTransferIn will transfer the repayment amount but the contract will receive the repayment amount - fee
CCollateralCapErc20.sol#L231 and the require check will cause a revert.
CCollateralCapErc20.sol#L235
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑on‑transfer token incompatibility in the flashloan implementation. The contract assumes that the amount sent to the borrower and the amount that will be repaid are identical, but USDT deducts a small transfer fee on every move. When the flashloan function calls doTransferOut, the borrower actually receives amount minus the USDT fee, yet the onFlashLoan callback is invoked with this reduced amount. Later, when the borrower repays, doTransferIn expects the full borrowed amount, but the token again subtracts the fee, so the contract only receives repayment amount minus fee. The subsequent require check that the repaid balance matches the borrowed amount therefore fails and the transaction reverts. This bug manifests only when the flashloan is executed with a token that charges a transfer fee, such as USDT, and does not appear with fee‑free ERC‑20 tokens, making it easy to overlook during testing. The impact is that flashloan users cannot successfully borrow and repay, causing the operation to revert and effectively disabling the flashloan feature for affected tokens. Users see no funds returned, balances appear unchanged, and the transaction fails without an obvious error message. The issue was discovered by the MixBytes audit team while reviewing the flashloan flow and noticing the mismatch between transferred and expected amounts. It is hard to notice because most popular tokens do not charge fees, so the logic appears correct for the majority of cases. To remediate, the flashloan function must be rewritten to account for the token’s fee value, for example by calculating the expected fee and adjusting the amount sent out, or by using a safe transfer pattern that verifies the actual amount received and repaid, or by restricting flashloans to fee‑free tokens. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “fee‑on‑transfer token handling errors” that break accounting assumptions in DeFi primitives.

title: M-5 Undesired repay and/or liquidation of ex-credit account
description:
In the IronBank, the credit functionality is introduced. An admin can trigger the Comptroller.sol#L1302 function to mark some addresses like credit for speciﬁc cToken and set its credit limit. Such addresses can borrow a limited by credit limit amount of cToken without providing any collateral.
Additionally, setCreditLimit can mark that an address is no longer credit and has become an ordinary account that requires collateral.
Unfortunately, after becoming an ordinary account, the ex-credit account will be subject to repay and/or liquidation of its borrowed debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the credit‑account mechanism of the IronBank protocol. A privileged admin can call a function that assigns a credit limit to a specific address for a given cToken, allowing that address to borrow up to the limit without posting any collateral. The same admin function can later reduce or remove the credit limit, turning the previously privileged credit account into a regular account that is subject to the protocol’s normal collateral requirements. The implementation does not verify whether the account’s outstanding borrowed balance exceeds the new, lower credit limit. As a result, an address that has borrowed against its credit can find itself with a debt that is larger than its allowed borrowing capacity but without any collateral to back it. When the protocol’s liquidation or repayment logic runs, the ex‑credit account is treated like any under‑collateralised borrower and may be forced to repay or be liquidated, causing the borrowed assets to be seized or lost. This situation can be triggered whenever an admin reduces a credit limit below the current debt, which may happen intentionally, accidentally, or through a compromised admin key. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a borrower who previously expected to hold the borrowed tokens without risk suddenly sees their balance drop to zero or receives a liquidation notice, effectively “funds disappear”. The issue is subtle because the admin‑only function appears to be a harmless configuration change and does not emit any warning about existing debt, making it easy to overlook during testing. The root cause is the lack of a safety check that ties the credit‑limit state transition to the account’s outstanding borrow. To remediate, the contract should forbid decreasing a credit limit below the current borrowed amount, require the borrower to fully repay before the credit status can be revoked, or otherwise enforce that a credit account cannot be demoted while it holds an outstanding debt. This class of bug falls under improper state transition validation and can lead to unintended liquidation of otherwise collateral‑free loans, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and exposing borrowers to unexpected loss of funds.

title: VoltBurn.buyNSendToVoltTreasury() Function Is Subjected To A Sandwich Attack
description:
The VoltBurn.buyNSendToVoltTreasury() swaps Shogun for Volt using UniswapV2 swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens() function.
The caller sets the minimum volt amount, which can be zero.
This function can be called by anyone if privateMode is not enabled.
A user can conduct a sandwich attack by doing a swap in the pool beforehand, calling buyNSendToVoltTreasury() with 0 slippage, and swapping back their tokens.
The user can extract tokens from the swap due to zero slippage.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token‑swap function that exchanges a source token for a target token through a decentralized exchange router. The function allows the caller to specify a minimum amount of the target token that must be received, but this parameter can be set to zero, effectively disabling any slippage protection. Because the contract does not restrict who can invoke the function when the private‑mode flag is disabled, any external actor can call it. An attacker can exploit this by performing a sandwich attack: first, the attacker makes a large trade on the same liquidity pool to move the price unfavourably for the victim; second, the attacker calls the vulnerable function with a zero‑minimum‑output requirement, ensuring the transaction will not revert despite the adverse price; third, the attacker immediately reverses the initial trade, restoring the price and capturing the price difference as profit. This sequence extracts value from the swap because the victim’s transaction is forced to accept a worse rate without any safeguard. The impact is that the protocol’s treasury or users can lose tokens without receiving the expected amount, effectively causing funds to disappear or be siphoned off. The issue manifests whenever the function is publicly callable and private mode is off, especially in volatile or low‑liquidity pools where price manipulation is cheap. It affects any participant who relies on the function to acquire the target token, as well as the protocol that expects the treasury to receive a predictable amount of tokens. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the absence of a non‑zero slippage constraint and the open access control. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and appear normal in the block explorer, while the economic outcome is unfavorable. The root cause is the combination of unchecked minimum‑output parameters and unrestricted access, which together break the accounting assumption that the swap will deliver at least a minimal amount of value. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero slippage threshold that can be configured by the owner, or re‑enable private mode to restrict calls to trusted entities, thereby preventing large sandwich attacks and preserving the intended token flow.

title: Small Amounts Of Tokens Will Be Stuck In The Contract When Auction.addInitialLiquidity() Is Called
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the initial liquidity provisioning routine of the Auction contract. When the owner calls addInitialLiquidity, the function creates the SHOGUN‑KAIZEN pair if it does not exist and then invokes an internal helper _checkPoolValidity. This helper calls the UniswapV2Pair.skim method, which transfers any token balance that exceeds the pair's recorded reserves back to the Auction contract. After the skim, the routine proceeds to call the router’s addLiquidity function to deposit a fixed amount of SHOGUN and KAIZEN tokens into the pool. The problem occurs because the contract does not include any mechanism to retrieve tokens that remain in its own balance after these two steps. Two situations can leave a small amount of tokens stranded: (1) if an external actor or the owner sends extra tokens directly to the pair before skim is executed, skim will pull those tokens into the Auction contract, but there is no subsequent code to move them elsewhere; (2) if the router’s addLiquidity call does not consume the full amount of SHOGUN or KAIZEN supplied (for example because the pool already has some liquidity or because of rounding), the surplus stays in the contract. The root cause is the absence of a cleanup or sweep function after liquidity addition, combined with the fact that skim is used without checking whether the transferred amount should be returned to a treasury or burned. An attacker could deliberately deposit a tiny amount of tokens into the pair, trigger the owner’s addInitialLiquidity, and cause those tokens to become locked forever, effectively stealing them from the token’s supply. Even without malicious intent, the contract will silently retain any leftover tokens, reducing the effective token balance available for the auction and potentially causing accounting mismatches. From a user’s perspective, participants may notice that the contract’s token balance does not decrease as expected after an auction, or that the advertised liquidity amount is slightly lower than intended, leading to confusion when refunds or token distributions appear smaller. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the flow of token transfers in addInitialLiquidity and noted that no withdrawal path existed for the residual balance. It can be hard to spot because the amounts are typically tiny and no events are emitted when the tokens are transferred to the contract, so standard transaction logs do not highlight the loss. The recommended remediation is to add a post‑liquidity sweep that transfers any remaining SHOGUN or KAIZEN tokens from the Auction contract to the owner or a designated safe address, ensuring that no tokens remain unintentionally locked. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that all supplied tokens should either become part of the pool or be returned to a controlled account, preserving token accounting integrity and preventing inadvertent loss of funds.

title: Non-whitelisted addresses can be lenders
description:
Only users that are on the whitelist are allowed to earn interest from lending the underlying tokens:
```solidity
function supply(
    address user,
    uint256 amount,
    bytes32[] calldata proof
) external whenNotPaused onlyWhitelistedLenders(user, proof)
```
However, the transferability of the reward token opens an opportunity for users who are not on the list to receive interest-accruing tokens simply by having them transferred.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that the whitelist check is only applied when minting iTokens through the supply function, which requires a proof that the caller is on the approved lender list. The iToken contract follows the standard ERC20 model and allows token holders to transfer their balance freely. Because the transfer logic does not invoke the onlyWhitelistedLenders modifier, a user who is not on the whitelist can receive iTokens from a whitelisted holder via a normal ERC20 transfer and subsequently earn interest on those tokens. This bypass occurs whenever a pool is configured with a whitelist but the iToken remains transferable. From a user perspective the symptom is that an address that never passed the whitelist proof can hold iTokens and see its balance increase due to accrued interest, contrary to the expectation that only whitelisted lenders receive such rewards. The impact is that the protocol’s incentive accounting is broken: interest that should be reserved for approved lenders is unintentionally paid to arbitrary addresses, potentially diluting rewards and reducing revenue for the intended participants. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between the whitelist modifier and the ERC20 transfer implementation. It is subtle because token transferability is a default feature of ERC20 contracts and the whitelist restriction is not obvious in the transfer path, making the bug easy to overlook in functional testing. To remediate the problem the protocol should either make iTokens non‑transferable for pools that rely on a whitelist, or extend the whitelist verification to the _transfer hook so that any receipt of iTokens is validated against the approved lender list. Alternatively, the protocol could deprecate the whitelist feature entirely, as indicated by the developers, but this would leave the economic model exposed to unauthorized interest accrual.

title: The borrower can be instantly liquidated
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a borrower to open a position that is considered safe by the pool's internal checks but can be liquidated immediately because the liquidation logic uses a stricter threshold. The root cause is a mismatch between the safety condition applied when a position is created (using only the market price or exchange rate multiplied by the loan‑to‑value limit) and the condition used during liquidation (which also multiplies by a separate liquidationThreshold parameter). Because the creation function does not incorporate liquidationThreshold, an attacker can open a position with debt just below the creation limit, yet the liquidation function will deem the health ratio below the required minimum and permit instant liquidation. Exploitation consists of a malicious keeper or liquidator calling the liquidation routine right after the position is opened, seizing the collateral while the borrower still expects the position to be safe. The impact is loss of collateral for the borrower, potential profit for the liquidator, and erosion of trust in the protocol's risk model. The condition occurs whenever the protocol parameters are configured such that liquidationThreshold is lower than or equal to the LTV used at creation, which is common when the two values are set independently. Users who open loans, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because borrowers may see their collateral disappear immediately after funding, and the protocol may suffer reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the safety checks in the pool contract with those in the liquidation contract and identified the missing threshold. It can be hard to notice because the creation transaction succeeds and emits no error, while the liquidation can be performed in the same block, making the failure appear as a normal liquidation rather than a bug. The proper fix is to align the safety verification in the position‑modification function with the liquidation formula, i.e., require that newTotalDebtInVault be less than collateral multiplied by the minimum of market price, exchange rate, and the liquidationThreshold (or ensure liquidationThreshold is always greater than the LTV). This prevents a position from being unsafe at the moment of creation. The bug belongs to the class of inconsistent risk checks or liquidation threshold mismatch where different parts of a protocol enforce divergent safety constraints, leading to immediate liquidations that violate user expectations that a newly created loan is safe. From a user perspective the symptom is that after borrowing, the UI shows a healthy health factor but the collateral is seized instantly, resulting in a zero balance or missing funds. The borrower expects the loan to be usable, but instead receives no collateral back and may lose the entire deposited amount.

title: _depositable and _withdrawable return if paused
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the vault’s internal accounting helpers _depositable and _withdrawable, which calculate how many assets can be supplied to or withdrawn from a given pool. Both helpers read the pool’s current claim, liquidity, allocation caps and supply caps, but they never verify whether the pool is in a paused state. In the Ion protocol a paused pool disables any supply or withdrawal actions, yet the helpers still return positive values as if the pool were active. Consequently, when the vault iterates over its deposit or withdrawal queue, it may select a paused pool, attempt to process a user’s deposit, mint, withdraw or redeem operation, and encounter a revert because the underlying pool rejects the action. The public view functions maxDeposit, maxMint, maxWithdraw and maxRedeem also rely on these helpers, so they report non‑zero capacities even though the operation will fail. This mismatch between reported capacity and actual executable capacity can cause users to see a positive “available amount” in the UI, initiate a transaction, and then receive a failed transaction with no assets moved, effectively a denial‑of‑service for those users. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of the queue processing logic and noticed the absence of a pause check. It is subtle because the pause flag lives inside each pool contract and the vault does not expose it directly; the returned numbers look plausible, so the problem may only surface when a pool is deliberately paused or when an operator pauses a pool for maintenance. The root cause is a missing guard condition – the helpers should first query the pool’s paused status and return zero when paused, ensuring that the queue skips such pools and that the max* view functions correctly report zero capacity. Fixing the bug involves adding a pause verification step inside _depositable and _withdrawable (e.g., if pool.isPaused() return 0) so that the vault never attempts to interact with a paused pool and the user‑facing capacity queries reflect the true state of the system. This class of bug falls under “logic error due to unchecked contract state”, leading to incorrect accounting and potential user‑experience failures such as funds appearing to be depositable or withdrawable when they are not, and transaction reverts that may be interpreted as a loss of funds even though no assets are moved.

title: Unchecked Math Operations Leading to Potential Arithmetic Errors
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked arithmetic pattern where the contract performs raw addition, subtraction or multiplication on unsigned integers without using Solidity's built‑in checked functions. The root cause is the reliance on plain operators in a token‑refill routine that calculates new tokens as time_elapsed_in_seconds multiplied by a per‑second rate and then added to the existing token counter. Because the operations are not wrapped in checked_add or checked_mul, an attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger an overflow when the elapsed time or the rate is large enough, causing the computed token amount to wrap around to a much smaller value or to zero. Conversely, an unchecked subtraction elsewhere can underflow, leading to a revert or an unintended large token balance. Exploitation is straightforward: by submitting a transaction at a moment where the contract’s internal timestamp difference is extreme—either by manipulating block timestamps or by waiting a very long period—the overflow arithmetic produces an incorrect token count. The impact is that users may see their balances suddenly become zero, unexpectedly huge, or receive no refund when they expect a token refill, effectively losing access to funds or receiving more tokens than intended. The condition under which this occurs is when the time‑elapsed calculation exceeds the safe range of the uint type, which is not guarded by any overflow checks. All participants who rely on the rate‑limit accounting—regular users, token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the core accounting invariant (tokens never exceed the maximum supply and never drop below zero) is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that flagged the presence of raw arithmetic expressions in contrast to other parts of the code that correctly used checked_sub. Because overflow does not always produce an obvious error and may only manifest with extreme inputs, it can be difficult to notice in routine testing that uses typical time intervals. The recommended remediation is to replace every raw arithmetic operation with its checked counterpart (checked_add, checked_sub, checked_mul) and to propagate any overflow error back to the caller, thereby preserving the contract’s accounting guarantees. In abstract terms, this is a classic unchecked arithmetic bug that breaks the business logic of token accounting, leading to symptoms such as funds disappearing, refunds missing, or balances becoming unexpectedly large or zero.

title: Wrong withdrawal address check
description:
When a new validator is added to the owner using validateWithdrawalCredentials function, then its withdrawal recipient address is checked to be equal to NativaVault.
```solidity
BeaconProofs.getWithdrawalCredentials(validatorFieldsProof.validatorFields) != bytes32(abi.encodePacked(bytes1(uint8(1)), bytes11(0), address(this))) revert WithdrawalCredentialsMismatchWithNode();
```

This is incorrect because the protocol needs all rewards to be sent to the NativeNode of the validator's owner, that's why this address should be checked as a withdrawal recipient.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect withdrawal address verification performed when a new validator is added through the validateWithdrawalCredentials function. The contract checks that the withdrawal credentials extracted from the validator fields equal the address of the contract itself (address(this)), which represents the NativaVault. Business logic, however, requires that rewards be sent to the NativeNode address that belongs to the validator’s owner. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended recipient (owner’s node) and the hard‑coded check against the contract’s own address, leading to a validation rule that does not reflect the protocol’s accounting assumptions. An attacker or a misconfigured validator can exploit this by supplying withdrawal credentials that match the contract address, causing the system to accept the validator but later route all staking rewards to the vault instead of the owner’s node. Conversely, a legitimate validator whose withdrawal credentials point to the correct NativeNode will be rejected because the check expects the contract address, preventing the validator from being registered and blocking reward accrual. The impact is that funds that should be credited to a user’s balance either disappear into the vault or never appear, breaking the expectation that “my validator should earn rewards”. This occurs each time validateWithdrawalCredentials is called, i.e., whenever a validator is added or updated. The affected parties are validator owners, delegators, and the protocol itself because the accounting of rewards becomes inconsistent. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s code against the protocol specification and identified that the withdrawal credentials comparison used the wrong address constant. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may succeed and the UI may show the validator as active, while the reward balance remains zero, giving the impression of a silent loss. To remediate, the verification should compare the withdrawal credentials against the NativeNode address associated with the validator’s owner, obtained from the appropriate mapping or registry, rather than against address(this). This aligns the on‑chain check with the intended business rule that rewards flow to the owner’s node, restoring correct accounting and preventing reward misdirection.

title: Preventing balance updates by adding a new validator in the current block
description:
The balance of the user's validators can be updated by creating a new snapshot and proving the balance of the validators. If a user doesn't start a new snapshot in time then anyone can start a snapshot for that user and update the user's balance. Users have an incentive to not update their balances if they get slashed in the beacon chain. A user can block the snapshot finalization and snapshot creation process and stop balance updates by performing this attack.

The issue is that the validateSnapshotProofs() code doesn't allow updating the validators balance if the validator balance is updated after the snapshot creation:
```solidity
if (validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp >= node.currentSnapshotTimestamp) revert ValidatorAlreadyProved();
```

And a snapshot only finalizes when the remainingProofs is 0. So this is the attack POC:
1. User1 who has slashed on the beacon chain wants to prevent balance updates.
2. User1 would create new validator and call validateWithdrawalCredentials() and startSnapshot() in the same Ethereum block.
3. As a result, for the new validator: validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp would equal to node.currentSnapshotTimestamp.
4. Because a new validator has been counted on the remainingProofs and it's not possible to prove its balance for the current snapshot, then remainingProofs would never reach 0 and the current snapshot would never finish and the balance update process would be broken.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a user can add a new validator in the same Ethereum block in which a snapshot of validator balances is started. The snapshot logic records the timestamp of the most recent balance update for each validator (validatorDetails.lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp) and refuses to accept a proof for any validator whose last update timestamp is greater than or equal to the snapshot timestamp. When a new validator is created, its lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp is set to the current block timestamp, which is exactly the snapshot timestamp. The new validator is immediately counted in the snapshot's remainingProofs counter, but because the validation routine rejects any proof for a validator with a timestamp equal to the snapshot timestamp, the proof for this validator can never be supplied. Consequently the remainingProofs counter never reaches zero, the snapshot never finalizes, and the whole balance‑update process stalls. An attacker who has been slashed on the beacon chain can deliberately trigger this situation: they create a new validator, call validateWithdrawalCredentials() and startSnapshot() within the same block, causing the snapshot to become permanently incomplete. The impact is that the affected user’s validator balance cannot be updated, slashing penalties remain hidden, withdrawals may be blocked, and the protocol’s accounting state becomes inconsistent. This condition can affect any participant who relies on timely snapshot finalization, including honest users whose balances are frozen and the protocol itself, which may be unable to process subsequent withdrawals or reward distributions. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the interaction between validator creation and snapshot finalization logic. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; instead the snapshot simply never reaches a completed state, leaving the system in a silent stalled mode. To remediate the problem the contract should prevent the creation of new validators for the timestamp of the snapshot that is being finalized, or adjust the validation condition so that a validator whose lastBalanceUpdateTimestamp equals the snapshot timestamp is either excluded from the remainingProofs count or allowed to be proved later. In essence the fix must break the race condition between validator addition and snapshot finalization, ensuring that the snapshot can always reach a terminal state and that balances are reliably updated according to the protocol’s accounting rules. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a slashing event the UI shows no change in the validator’s balance, withdrawals remain pending, and the dashboard may display a “snapshot in progress” indefinitely, contrary to the expectation that balances update automatically.

title: Users who deposit via returnShares() can be unable to withdraw
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the vault supervision logic that prevents users who initially deposit shares through the returnShares (or gimmieShares) entry point from later withdrawing those shares. The contract maintains two parallel data structures: a mapping that records how many shares a staker owns for each vault (stakerShares) and an array that lists all vaults a staker is associated with (stakersVaults). The deposit functions returnShares and gimmieShares modify the share balance but, in the original implementation, fail to update the stakersVaults array when the first deposit for a given vault occurs. Consequently, when a user later calls removeShares to withdraw, the function checks whether the user’s share balance has dropped to zero and then attempts to call removeVaultFromStaker, which expects the vault to be present in the stakersVaults list. Because the vault was never recorded, the removal operation reverts, causing the withdrawal transaction to fail and the user’s funds to become effectively locked. This issue manifests only when the first interaction with a particular vault is performed via returnShares (or gimmieShares); subsequent normal deposits that correctly update the vault list do not trigger the bug. The affected parties are any staker who uses these entry points, the protocol that relies on reliable withdrawability, and ultimately the end‑users whose balances appear correct but cannot be redeemed. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the consistency of state updates across the contract’s functions. It can be hard to notice because the share balance itself is updated correctly, so on‑chain explorers show the expected amount, while the missing vault entry only surfaces when a withdrawal is attempted, leading to an unexpected revert. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent bookkeeping” or “missing reference update” vulnerabilities, where auxiliary data structures are not kept in sync with primary state, breaking business logic that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between share ownership and vault registration. From a user’s perspective the UI may display that they own shares, but when they try to claim or withdraw, the transaction fails and the balance appears to disappear or remain frozen. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that any function that changes a staker’s share balance from zero to non‑zero (or vice‑versa) also updates the stakersVaults array accordingly, mirroring the logic used in the normal deposit and withdrawal paths, thereby preserving the invariant that every vault with a non‑zero share balance is present in the stakersVaults list.

title: First depositor attack is possible
description:
It is a classic attack with the following flow:
1. The user is the first to interact with the vault, he sends a deposit transaction.
2. Attacker frontruns user's tx by performing 2 actions: 1) deposit 1 wei asset thus minting 1 wei share; 2) donate a big amount of asset to the vault.
3. User's transaction executes and the user mints 0 shares because of rounding in a formula that is used inside ERC4626: shares = assets * sharesSupply / totalAssets. That is because sharesSupply is 1 and totalAssets is large due to donation.
4. Then the attacker withdraws donated assets plus the user's deposit.

However, Karak-restaking uses Solady's ERC4626 implementation which makes the attack less profitable and harder to perform. By default it uses a different formula: in calculations of shares and assets it adds an extra 1. As a result, the attack is profitable in case there are 2 or more first deposits of approximately near size in mempool. Worth mentioning that vaults are the core mechanic of protocol, there will be multiple chances to perform the attack.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a first‑depositor attack that stems from the integer‑division rounding logic used in the ERC4626 share‑minting formula. When the vault is empty, the share calculation shares = assets * totalSupply / totalAssets can round down to zero if totalSupply is very small (for example, one share minted from a 1‑wei deposit) while totalAssets has been artificially inflated by a large donation. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate user’s first deposit by first depositing a minimal amount to create a single share, then donating a large amount of the underlying asset to the vault. When the user’s transaction is later executed, the rounding in the share formula causes the user to receive zero shares for their deposit, even though the assets are transferred. The attacker can then withdraw the donated assets together with the user’s deposited assets, effectively stealing the user’s funds. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful deposit transaction but the balance of vault shares remains zero, leading to confusion and the perception that the funds have vanished. The issue occurs only when the vault has no prior share supply and an attacker can manipulate totalAssets before the first legitimate deposit is processed, making it a race‑condition style exploit that is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error for a zero‑share mint. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the accounting logic of the Karak‑restaking vault, which uses Solady’s ERC4626 implementation. Solady’s variant adds an extra constant to the share calculation, reducing the profitability of the attack and requiring multiple near‑equal first deposits to succeed, but it does not eliminate the underlying risk. The vulnerability belongs to the class of rounding‑error and front‑running exploits in tokenized vaults where share‑to‑asset conversion assumes a non‑zero supply. To mitigate the issue the contract can increase the vault’s decimal precision by overriding the _decimalsOffset function, or it can pre‑mint “dead shares” during initialization (a pattern used by UniswapV2) so that the share supply is never zero, thereby preventing the zero‑share rounding condition. Properly fixing the rounding logic and ensuring a non‑zero initial share supply restores the intended accounting guarantees and protects users from losing their first deposits.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect calculation of rewardPerLiquidity
description:
If the first user deposits NFT after some time from notify() call, then (lastTimeRewardApplicable() - lastUpdateTime) always will be less than DURATION which leads to freezing some funds on the contract:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L156
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the per‑liquidity reward amount in a staking rewards contract. The contract updates a variable called rewardPerLiquidity based on the elapsed time since the last update, assuming that the elapsed time can be up to the full reward duration. When the first user deposits an NFT after the reward period has already been started by a call to notify(), the expression (lastTimeRewardApplicable() - lastUpdateTime) becomes smaller than the configured DURATION. Because the formula multiplies the reward rate by this time delta, the resulting rewardPerLiquidity value is either zero or far lower than intended. As a consequence the contract does not allocate any reward tokens to the staked liquidity, effectively freezing the tokens that were meant to be distributed as incentives. This situation occurs only under the specific timing condition where the initial deposit happens after the reward period has begun and before any other deposit has updated the accounting state. Users who stake NFTs expect to earn reward tokens proportional to their share of liquidity, but they receive nothing, seeing their reward balance remain at zero while the contract holds undistributed tokens. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors traced the reward calculation logic and identified that the time‑difference term can be less than the full duration, breaking the accounting assumptions. The bug is subtle because normal operation—where deposits occur early in the reward period—does not expose the problem, making it easy to miss in testing. It belongs to the class of accounting or reward‑distribution bugs where a formula incorrectly handles edge‑case timing, leading to locked funds and broken incentive economics. To remediate the issue the rewardPerLiquidity computation should be revised to correctly handle cases where the elapsed time is less than the full duration, for example by using the actual elapsed time without assuming it reaches DURATION, or by initializing lastUpdateTime appropriately so that the delta never becomes negative or zero when rewards should be accruing. A proper fix restores the intended reward flow, ensuring that users receive the correct amount of tokens and that no funds remain unintentionally frozen in the contract.

title: MJR-2 Possible ddos attack
description:
Malicious user can front run withdraw() function to change the current price in pool, so user can lost all his rewards:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L195
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running price manipulation in the withdraw() function of the staking rewards contract. The contract calculates a user’s reward based on the current pool price at the moment withdraw is called. Because the price is derived from mutable pool state that can be altered by any participant before the withdraw transaction is mined, a malicious actor can submit a transaction that changes the price just before the victim’s withdraw is executed. By doing so the attacker forces the price to a value that reduces the computed reward to zero or a negligible amount, causing the legitimate staker to receive no rewards despite having accrued them. This attack can be carried out whenever a user initiates a withdrawal and the network’s transaction ordering allows the attacker to place a preceding transaction, i.e., under normal Ethereum mempool conditions. The affected parties are stakers who expect to receive proportional rewards; they see their balance unchanged or a missing reward after the transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the StakingRewardsV3 contract, where the price‑dependent reward logic was identified as relying on a single instantaneous pool price without any smoothing or averaging. Because the price can be moved by a single transaction, the problem may not be obvious from static analysis; it only manifests when an attacker deliberately reorders transactions, making it hard to detect without dynamic testing. The bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation or front‑running vulnerabilities where on‑chain state used for accounting can be tampered with by adversaries. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful withdrawal but the reward amount displayed is zero, contradicting the expectation that the user receives their earned tokens. The business logic that rewards are proportional to the time‑weighted average price is violated, breaking accounting guarantees. A proper mitigation is to compute the price using an average over a recent block window or a time‑weighted moving average, or to use a trusted external price oracle, thereby preventing a single transaction from drastically shifting the price used for reward calculation. Implementing such an averaging mechanism removes the ability for an attacker to front‑run the withdraw and ensures that rewards are calculated on a stable price reference.

title: Addresses are set to the 0 addr in constructor
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of whitelisting critical contract addresses (vaultManager and stabilityPool) in the constructor before those addresses have been assigned. In Solidity, uninitialized address variables default to the zero address (0x000...0). Consequently the constructor calls `whitelisted[vaultManager] = true;` and `whitelisted[stabilityPool] = true;` while both variables still contain the zero address, resulting in the zero address being added to the whitelist instead of the intended contracts. The protocol later uses a timelocked `addWhitelist` function that requires a 14‑day delay before an address can be added to the whitelist. Because the real vaultManager and stabilityPool addresses were never whitelisted, they remain blocked for the full timelock period. Functions that depend on the whitelist, such as minting, allowance adjustments, or stability‑pool interactions, therefore cannot be executed by the intended contracts for two weeks, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service (DoS) of core protocol functionality. Users attempting to deposit, withdraw, or receive stablecoins may see no balance changes, receive zero tokens, or encounter failed transactions, contrary to the expectation that the system operates continuously. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by reviewing the constructor and the whitelist timelock logic; the mismatch between address initialization and whitelist enforcement is subtle because the zero address is a valid address type and does not raise a compile‑time error, making the bug easy to overlook. The root cause is the ordering of state initialization and access‑control setup: critical addresses are used before they are set, and the access‑control mechanism enforces a delay that magnifies the mistake. To remediate, the contract should assign the vaultManager and stabilityPool addresses before invoking any whitelist logic, or move the whitelist calls to a separate initialization function that runs after `setAddresses`. Additionally, the timelock could be exempted for these essential system contracts to avoid a prolonged service outage. This class of bug falls under “incorrect initialization order leading to privileged‑address whitelist bypass” and violates the business assumption that privileged contracts are always authorized to perform their duties.

title: Owner doesn't have to wait before whitelisting
description:
Given that whitelisted addresses have a lot of power, the protocol wants to ensure a 14 day timelock is in place:
```
* @notice Given the admin key retains the ability to add debttoken
minters for future
Keiko_audit.md
deployments or upgrades a long timelock (14d) is
established.
* @dev Can only be called by the contract owner
```

The problem occurs because the owner does not need to wait the full TIMELOCK_DURATION when adding requestedWhitelistTimestamp as shown below:
```solidity
requestedWhitelistTimestamp[_address] = block.timestamp;
emit WhitelistRequested(_address, block.timestamp);
```

This variable is then used in the function addWhitelist:
```solidity
require(block.timestamp > requestedWhitelistTimestamp[_address] + TIMELOCK_DURATION, "Timelock period has not passed");
allowanceWhitelist[_address] = true;
mintWhitelist[_address] = true;
delete requestedWhitelistTimestamp[_address];
emit WhitelistChanged(_address, true);
```

The code is trying to enforce the 2 week timelock in the require statement.
