From a user perspective the symptoms are abrupt: the wallet UI suddenly shows a reduced or zero VeToken balance, voting power disappears, and any rights that depend on token holdings—such as participation in governance proposals or claimable rewards—are lost. This problem manifests whenever the privileged governance entity is exercised, especially if the governing keys are compromised or used maliciously. It impacts all token holders, the governance process, and any protocol components that rely on the accounting integrity of VeToken. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the token’s public interface and identified the absence of a restriction on the burn operation. The vulnerability is subtle because burn functions are common in ERC‑20‑like tokens, and the presence of a burn method does not inherently raise suspicion; however, the combination of privileged access and unrestricted target specification creates a hidden backdoor for token destruction. To remediate, the contract should either delete the burn function entirely or rewrite it so that only the caller can burn their own tokens—e.g., by calling _burn(msg.sender, amount)—thereby restoring the intended token economics and preventing arbitrary loss of user balances. This class of flaw falls under the broader category of unrestricted admin token burn or arbitrary token destruction, where privileged roles can violate accounting assumptions and erode trust in the system.

title: `VE3DRewardPool` claim in loop depend on pausable token
description:
Project veToken is supposed to be a generalized version of Convex for non-Curve token. There is only one contract for all rewards token in the platform.

All ve3Token rewards are bundled together inside `ve3DLocker` and `ve3DRewardPool` in a loop. Instead of having its own unique contract like `VeAssetDepositer` or `VoterProxy` for each token.

If one token has pausable transfer, user cannot claim rewards or withdraw if they have multiple rewards include that pause token.

Right now the project intends to support only 6 tokens, including Ribbon token which has [pausable transfer](https://etherscan.io/address/0x6123b0049f904d730db3c36a31167d9d4121fa6b#code#L810) controlled by Ribbon DAO.

Normally, this would not be an issue in Convex where only a few pools would be affected by single coin. Since, veAsset are bundled together into single reward pool, it becomes a major problem.
poc:
* Token like Ribbon pause token transfer by DAO due to an unfortunate event.
  * `VE3DRewardPool` try call `getReward()`, `VeAssetDepositor` [try deposit token from earned rewards](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-vetoken/blob/2d7cd1f6780a9bcc8387dea8fecfbd758462c152/contracts/VE3DRewardPool.sol#L296-L299) does not work anymore because `IERC20.transfer` [is blocked](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-vetoken/blob/1be2f03670e407908f175c08cf8cc0ce96c55baf/contracts/VeAssetDepositor.sol#L134-L152). This effectively reverts current function if user have this token reward > 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution mechanism of the ve3DRewardPool contract, which aggregates several reward tokens into a single claim function called getReward(). The function iterates over an internal list of reward assets and invokes the standard IERC20.transfer() call for each token. Because the implementation assumes every transfer will succeed, it does not provide a way to skip or isolate a particular token. When one of the bundled reward tokens implements a pausable transfer (as the Ribbon token does, with its transfer function gated by a DAO‑controlled pause flag), a pause event causes its transfer call to revert. Since the loop does not catch this revert, the entire transaction aborts, preventing any of the subsequent or preceding token transfers from executing. As a result, a user who is eligible for multiple rewards, including the paused token, is unable to claim any of their accrued rewards; from the user’s perspective the UI shows no balance increase, or a claim transaction that silently fails with a generic “revert” error. This denial‑of‑service condition occurs only when the external token’s pause flag is active, which is a condition that can be triggered by the token’s own governance or by a malicious DAO action, making it difficult to detect during normal testing because the pause state may be rare. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the reward‑pool logic and identified that the getReward() function does not accept a token filter, thereby creating a tight coupling between the pool and the transfer behavior of each reward token. The flaw violates the protocol’s business assumption that rewards are always claimable independent of one another; it breaks the accounting invariant that a user’s total pending rewards should be withdrawable regardless of individual token state. To remediate the problem, the contract should be refactored to allow callers to specify which reward tokens to claim (e.g., a getReward(address[] tokens) overload) or to process each token transfer in a try/catch‑style pattern that records failures and continues with the remaining tokens. Alternatively, the pool could split each reward into its own claimable contract, eliminating the single‑point‑of‑failure loop. Implementing such a change would restore the ability for users to retrieve unaffected rewards even when a specific token is paused, thereby preserving fund availability and protocol reliability.

title: donateAndClaim() will not work for remote donate and claim
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the combined donateAndClaim function, which is intended to let a user donate native tokens (or supported stablecoins) and immediately claim a ZRO token on a remote chain. The function forwards the entire msg.value only to the donate contract, then calls the claim contract without supplying any native value for the LayerZero (LZ) cross‑chain messaging fee. Inside the claim logic, the internal _claim routine forwards msg.value to endpoint.send, assuming that the caller has provided the required LZ fee. Because donateAndClaim does not pass a separate fee amount, msg.value is zero when the claim is executed, causing the cross‑chain message to be sent without the necessary gas payment. As a result, the remote claim either reverts or silently fails, leaving the user’s donation locked in the donate contract while no ZRO tokens are received. This defect occurs whenever a user invokes donateAndClaim with the expectation of a remote claim, particularly when using native tokens for the donation, but it also affects stablecoin paths because the claim still relies on native fee payment. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the flow of value between the two external calls. It can be hard to notice because the transaction itself does not revert; the donate step succeeds and the overall function returns a receipt, giving the impression of success, yet the user observes that their balance does not increase and the claimed ZRO never arrives. From a user perspective, the UI may show a successful donation but the expected reward is missing, leading to confusion such as “I donated but got nothing.” The root cause is a missing parameter for the LZ fee and an incorrect assumption that msg.value will automatically cover both donation and messaging costs. To remediate, the function should be redesigned to accept an explicit fee argument or to split the supplied msg.value into a donation portion and a fee portion, forwarding the fee to the claim contract’s endpoint.send call. This aligns the implementation with the business logic that a donation and a cross‑chain claim each require separate funds, restoring the guarantee that a user who donates will receive the corresponding ZRO token on the target chain.

title: DonateRemote will fail to deploy when any of the stargate tokens is not set
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the constructor of the remote donation contract, which assumes that the addresses of all three Stargate token bridges (USDC, USDT and the native token) are always provided. The code does not verify that each address is non‑zero before attempting to call the token() function and approve an unlimited allowance. As a result, if any of the token addresses is set to the zero address – a situation that is allowed by the design of the core and local donation contracts – the constructor will revert during deployment. This behavior contradicts the intended flexible architecture where a remote contract should be able to operate with any subset of supported tokens. The root cause is missing input validation (address != 0) for the USDC and USDT token bridges and an unnecessary check for the native token that reverts when the native token bridge is not configured. Because the revert happens at deployment time, the contract never becomes operational, meaning that users attempting to donate through the remote contract will see the contract unavailable, receive no confirmation, and may experience missing or zero balances on the front‑end. The impact is therefore a denial‑of‑service for the remote donation pathway: the protocol cannot accept cross‑chain donations, funds that would have been routed through the remote contract are never collected, and the overall fundraising capability is reduced. The issue manifests only when the constructor is executed with an incomplete token configuration, which may occur during upgrades, test deployments, or mis‑configuration by the protocol owner. It was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the remote contract’s initialization logic with the core and local contracts and identified the inconsistency. The problem can be hard to notice because the same pattern of token approval works correctly in the other contracts, and the redundant native‑token check may appear harmless at first glance. To remediate, the constructor should first verify that each provided token address is non‑zero before invoking IOFT(...).token() and calling forceApprove, and the superfluous native‑token check should be removed entirely. This aligns the remote contract with the intended class of bugs – improper null‑address validation in constructors – and restores the expected behavior where the contract can be deployed with any combination of enabled Stargate tokens, preventing deployment failures and ensuring that donors receive the expected receipt of their contributions.

title: Protocol assumes 1 Stable = 1 USD
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption in the ClaimCore contract that each stablecoin token (USDC, USDT) is always worth exactly one US dollar. In the constructor the contract sets the price numerator to 1 × 10^(decimals‑1) for each supported stablecoin, effectively fixing the exchange rate at 1:1. This design ignores the possibility that a stablecoin can deviate from its peg, a situation that can occur during market stress, de‑peg attacks, or when a less‑trusted stablecoin is used. Because the contract never queries an external price source, the protocol mints ZRO tokens based on the nominal USDC/USDT amount rather than the actual USD value at the time of the donation. An attacker or any market participant can exploit this by donating a stablecoin that is temporarily trading below its peg; for example, if USDC trades at 0.8 USD, a user who contributes 1 000 USDC (worth only 800 USD) will still receive 1 000 ZRO tokens, effectively receiving a 25 % discount. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting becomes inaccurate, ZRO supply can be inflated relative to real USD value, and early donors may suffer dilution of token value while the treasury receives less real‑world value than expected. This condition manifests whenever the stablecoin price diverges from one dollar, which can happen during volatility spikes, oracle outages, or malicious manipulation of the stablecoin market. The affected parties include donors who believe they are paying a fair price, ZRO holders who see their token’s purchasing power erode, and the protocol itself, which may lose credibility and economic security. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s constructor, where the hard‑coded price logic stood out as a potential source of mispricing. It can be difficult to notice because the code appears reasonable for stablecoins that are normally pegged, and typical unit tests may not simulate de‑peg scenarios. The recommended remediation is to replace the static numerator with a dynamic price feed, such as a Chainlink oracle, that provides the current USD price for each stablecoin, or to implement an admin‑controlled price update mechanism that can react to market conditions. By using a reliable oracle, the protocol can ensure that ZRO minting reflects the true economic value of the contributed assets, preserving token economics and protecting users from inadvertent overpayment.

title: Insecure initialization functions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of initialization functionsthat are callable by any address because they lack any form of access control. When a contract or program is first created, these init routines are intended to set critical parameters such as the admin address, treasury destination, fee caps, and references to other system components. The root cause is that the code does not verify the caller’s identity before writing these privileged fields, allowing an arbitrary external account to invoke the function before the legitimate deployer or governance entity does. An attacker can therefore call the init function immediately after the account is allocated, supply their own address as the admin, redirect the treasury to a wallet they control, or set fee limits that benefit them. This can be exploited simply by sending a transaction that calls the vulnerable init with attacker‑controlled arguments; no special permissions or vulnerabilities are required beyond the ability to submit a transaction. The impact is that the attacker gains full administrative control over the contract, which may enable them to withdraw funds, change protocol parameters, or block legitimate users from interacting with the system. The condition under which the bug manifests is the first‑time initialization of the contract – a one‑time step that is often performed automatically by deployment scripts, making it easy to overlook that the function is unrestricted. All participants who rely on the contract’s security model – users depositing assets, other contracts interacting with it, and the protocol’s governance – are affected because the assumed trust boundary is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the source files and noticed that several init_* functions contain no require statements or signer checks. It can be hard to notice in production because the init call succeeds without error and the contract appears to be deployed correctly; the malicious admin assignment may only become visible later when privileged actions behave unexpectedly. To remediate, the init routine should enforce that only a pre‑approved address (for example the deployer’s wallet or a designated upgrade authority) can execute it, using explicit checks such as require(msg.sender == expected) or Anchor’s upgrade_authority_address feature. Alternatively, the contract could be designed so that the admin field is immutable and set at deployment time, eliminating the need for a mutable init step. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked initialization or missing‑access‑control vulnerabilities, where critical configuration can be hijacked, leading to loss of funds, unauthorized parameter changes, and a breach of the protocol’s trust assumptions.

title: LossofRewardsDuetoHardcodedZeroAddressasa _refreral Submitted By atharv_181
description:
Node Operators won’t receive referral rewards for depositing ETH into Lido. When staking ETH with Lido and depositing stETH into the bond, the process calls CSBondCore::_depositETH() to deposit ETH into Lido. However, since the referral address is passed as zero, no referral rewards are earned.
The Lido Rewards Share Program started a referral initiative to increase participation in staking via Lido. Participants can refer others to Lido, earning a share of rewards based on the staked amounts of those they refer.
Participants can earn referral rewards proportional to the staked amount of those they refer. The exact earnings depend on how much ETH the referred users stake and the duration they keep their assets staked.
Let’s say prior to enrollment, the amount of ETH staked through Participant A’s products and services is 60,000 ETH and the Committee agreed to a 25% Rewards Share Percentage.
If as a result of the 60,000 ETH stake a middleware usage fee in the amount of 1,000 ETH is programmatically collected, Participant A would receive 250 ETH as their share (25% of 1000 ETH).
This reward-sharing continues for each ETH staked, starting from the date each ETH is staked, and generally lasts for 12 months. If Participant A decides to stake additional ETH during this period, each new ETH will also earn rewards for 12 months from the date it was staked.
Hardcoding the referral address to address(0), the reward amount is lost.
More info about the referral program - Lido Referral Program
Transaction with Referral Address Provided - Transaction Link
Figure 1: Input Data
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded referral address set to address(0) inside the Lido CSBondCore::_depositETH() function. When a node operator or any participant stakes ETH through Lido and supplies a referral address, the contract ignores the supplied address and records the zero address as the referrer. Because the referral rewards module distributes rewards based on the stored referrer, no rewards are ever credited to the intended participant. The root cause is the use of a literal zero address instead of forwarding the caller‑provided referral parameter, which effectively nullifies the referral incentive mechanism. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any legitimate user who tries to earn referral rewards will automatically lose them. The impact is that the expected share of rewards—calculated as a percentage of the middleware fee collected on the referred stake—simply vanishes, reducing the economic incentive for node operators and potentially lowering participation in the program. The condition under which the loss occurs is any deposit transaction that includes a non‑zero referral address; the contract overwrites it with address(0) before calling the reward distribution routine. The affected parties are the referrers (node operators, participants) and the Lido protocol itself, which may see reduced referral activity and a mismatch between reported fees and actual reward payouts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the referral flow and noticed that the referral argument was never used. It can be hard to notice because the deposit transaction succeeds, no revert occurs, and the user interface shows a normal staking operation, while the reward balance remains unchanged. The correct fix is to remove the hard‑coded address(0) and forward the actual referral address supplied by the caller, and to ensure that the reward distribution logic allocates rewards proportionally to the recorded referrer. In generic terms, this is an instance of an “incorrect default address” or “hard‑coded zero address” bug that breaks incentive accounting, leading to missing rewards and a discrepancy between expected and actual balances.

title: MJR-1 Possible incorrect scaledTotalSupply calculation
description: At the line AStETH.sol#L595 if the shares are below zero then value may overflow and scaled total supply calculation will be wrong.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the scaled total supply in the AStETH contract. The contract stores a variable representing shares as a signed integer. When the share balance becomes negative, the code later casts this signed value to an unsigned uint256 without checking its sign. Because Solidity performs a two's‑complement conversion, a negative number is interpreted as a very large positive integer, causing an overflow. The overflow propagates to the scaledTotalSupply variable, which is used to represent the total amount of stETH that corresponds to the underlying assets. As a result, the reported total supply can be dramatically higher or lower than the actual amount of assets held by the contract. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever a user’s share balance drops below zero, for example after a withdrawal that exceeds the recorded share amount due to rounding errors or edge‑case logic. An attacker who can cause a negative share balance can therefore manipulate the scaled total supply, potentially inflating their own share of the pool or causing other users to receive fewer tokens than expected. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as missing or unexpectedly reduced balances, refunds that are zero, or a total supply displayed in the UI that does not match the sum of individual holdings. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors noted the unchecked conversion at line 595 of AStETH.sol. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the overflow silently corrupts accounting data, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of the supply calculation logic. The class of bug is a signed‑to‑unsigned casting overflow, a common arithmetic error that violates the protocol’s accounting invariants. To remediate the problem the contract should validate that the share value is non‑negative before casting, or use a safe casting library that reverts on negative inputs, thereby ensuring that scaledTotalSupply always reflects the true amount of assets. Proper checks will restore the integrity of the supply accounting and prevent users from experiencing lost or incorrect token balances.

title: MJR-1 Token Bridging doesn't work with Wormhole fees
description:
Line Bridge.sol#L93 has a transferTokens () function of type payable. In the body of this function, on line 133, a call to the internal function logTransfer () is made and one of the parameters msg.value is passed.
At line Bridge.sol#L151 from the logTransfer() function, the publishMessage() function is called.
The publishMessage() function of type payable on the line: Implementation.sol#L21 the condition for payment of the commission must be met. require(msg.value == messageFee(), "invalid fee");
In the checked contract, at line BridgeConnectorWormhole.vy#L49 a call to the transferTokens() function from the transferasset() function is made.
But there is no @payable modifier anywhere and no msg.value value handling.
Therefore, the transferasset() function will not work.
As a result, the submit () and collect_rewards () functions will not work in the AnchorVault.vy contract, because there is no commission fee for the Wormhole system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑handling mismatch in the token bridging flow of the Lido Anchor collateral system. The Bridge contract exposes a payable function transferTokens that forwards the caller‑provided ether (msg.value) to an internal logTransfer routine, which in turn calls a Wormhole implementation’s publishMessage function that enforces a strict fee requirement via require(msg.value == messageFee(),"invalid fee"). However, the higher‑level BridgeConnectorWormhole contract invokes transferTokens from its own transferasset function without declaring the function payable and without forwarding any ether. As a result, when a user or another contract attempts to bridge MJR‑1 tokens, msg.value reaches publishMessage as zero, causing the require check to fail and the transaction to revert with an "invalid fee" error. This failure propagates to the AnchorVault contract, preventing the submit and collect_rewards functions from executing because they depend on a successful bridge that includes the Wormhole commission. The impact is that users cannot move their tokens across chains, cannot claim expected rewards, and may see UI symptoms such as a missing or zero balance after a bridge attempt, or a failed transaction message. The bug occurs whenever transferasset is called through BridgeConnectorWormhole, i.e., any bridging operation that does not supply the Wormhole fee. It affects token holders, the bridging service, and any protocol component that relies on successful cross‑chain transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of payable parameters and identified the missing @payable modifier and fee forwarding. It can be hard to notice because the payable attribute is present on the low‑level function, giving the impression that the system handles fees, while the higher‑level caller silently omits them. Conceptually, this is a classic payable‑mismatch or fee‑forwarding bug, where a contract expects a payment but the caller does not provide it, violating the accounting assumption that the fee will be collected before message publication. To remediate, the transferasset function (or its caller) should be marked payable and should forward the exact amount returned by messageFee() to the Bridge contract, or the internal require should be adjusted to accept a zero fee if the protocol intends to subsidize the Wormhole cost. Proper validation and documentation of fee requirements would prevent the discrepancy and restore the intended bridging and reward‑collection functionality.

title: MJR-1 Changing the shared variable can affect previous votes
description:
At the lines Voting.sol#L126-L133 in the unsafelyChangeVoteTime() method is a change in the common for all voting variable voteTime.
Changing this variable will extend or shorten the voting time on existing voting.
This will affect the voting results, because the process will not go as planned when creating a vote.
So this action is potentially dangerous and may bring the unexpected side effects.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a single mutable contract‑level variable that defines the duration of every voting instance, called voteTime. Because the same variable is read by all active votes, a privileged function named unsafelyChangeVoteTime can modify this value after one or more votes have already been created. The root cause is the design choice to store the voting period as a global parameter instead of embedding it in each Vote struct, which means the contract does not keep a snapshot of the intended duration for a specific proposal. An attacker or any account with permission to call the change function can therefore extend or shorten the remaining voting window of an ongoing proposal. By shortening the period, voters may be cut off before they can cast a vote, causing their preferences to be ignored; by lengthening it, an adversary can keep a proposal open indefinitely to wait for a favorable vote or to stall the decision process. The impact is that governance outcomes can be manipulated, leading to decisions that do not reflect the original community intent, potential misallocation of protocol funds, and loss of trust in the voting mechanism. This condition occurs whenever the contract allows the voteTime variable to be altered while at least one vote is active, and it affects all participants who rely on the voting schedule – token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of vote creation and noticed that the same variable is used for both new and existing votes. It can be hard to notice because the variable appears to be a harmless configuration parameter and typical unit tests may only check the default voting period, not the effect of changing it after a vote has started. To remediate, the contract should store the intended voting duration inside each Vote struct, similar to how supportRequiredPct and minAcceptQuorumPct are handled, and the function that changes the default should only affect future votes. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a proposal that closes earlier than expected or stays open far longer than advertised, resulting in “my vote didn’t count” or “the voting window disappeared” messages, which contradicts the expectation that a vote’s deadline is fixed once the proposal is submitted. This class of bug is a mutable‑state‑shared‑parameter flaw that violates the accounting assumption that a voting period is immutable after creation, thereby breaking the integrity of the governance process.

title: protocol/Gauges/GaugeController.sol: incorrect getRewardsCeiling() logic
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑ceiling calculation of the GaugeController contract. The function getRewardsCeiling(uint256 epoch) is intended to return a decreasing reward amount during an initial loading period and then to apply an inflation‑adjusted formula that caps after a maximum number of inflation periods (MAX_INFLATION_PERIODS). The root cause is that the local variable inflationEpoch is declared but never initialized before it is compared to MAX_INFLATION_PERIODS. Because its default value is zero, the condition if (inflationEpoch > MAX_INFLATION_PERIODS) is never true, and the subsequent else branch always assigns inflationEpoch = epoch / INFLATION_PERIOD. As a result the cap‑checking logic is bypassed and the formula (_initialRewards * (3 ** inflationEpoch)) / (4 ** inflationEpoch) continues to be evaluated for every epoch, even after the intended eight‑year limit. This produces an incorrect rewards ceiling that never reaches the designed maximum, causing the protocol to distribute fewer tokens than expected after the cap should have been applied. The issue can be exploited indirectly: a participant who relies on the advertised reward schedule will receive a lower amount, which can be observed as a missing or zero reward in the UI after the loading period has passed. The impact is primarily economic – users see their expected reward balance stay unchanged or drop, the protocol’s incentive model is broken, and long‑term participants may lose confidence. The bug manifests only after the loading period (six months) and becomes more pronounced once the epoch count exceeds MAX_INFLATION_PERIODS (approximately eight years). It affects any address that claims rewards from the gauge, as well as the overall token emission schedule of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the illogical comparison of an uninitialized variable. Because the function returns a numeric value without emitting events, the mis‑calculation can be subtle and may only be noticed by comparing on‑chain reward data against the published emission schedule. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect state initialization leading to faulty conditional logic” or “logic error in reward‑distribution formulas”. To remediate, the contract should compute inflationEpoch based on the epoch value before performing the cap check, for example by assigning inflationEpoch = epoch / INFLATION_PERIOD first and then clamping it to MAX_INFLATION_PERIODS, or by using a separate variable that correctly reflects the number of completed inflation periods. After fixing, the rewards ceiling will respect the intended cap, and users will receive the promised amount of tokens after the eight‑year horizon.

title: protocol/GenesisNFT.sol: Only 1336 GenesisNFT tokens can be minted
bug_full: An off‑by‑one error in the GenesisNFT minting logic causes the contract toenforce a maximum supply that is one token lower than the documented limit of 1337. The contract stores a counter that starts at 1 and checks that counter + amount is less than or equal to MAX_CAP before minting. Because the counter is initialized to 1 instead of 0, the condition fails when a user attempts to mint the final token, i.e., when amount would bring the total to 1337. The require statement therefore reverts with a cap‑exceeded error even though the total supply would still be within the advertised limit. This bug can be exploited by anyone trying to mint the last token; the transaction will revert, preventing the token from being created. The impact is that the protocol cannot reach its intended total supply, which may break token economics, cause confusion for users who expect to receive a token, and potentially leave allocation slots unused. The condition occurs every time the mint function is called with an amount that would bring the total count to the documented cap, because the internal counter starts at 1. All participants who rely on the advertised cap—collectors, investors, and the protocol’s distribution mechanism—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract constant with the initialization value of the counter and observed the mismatch. It is subtle because the code compiles and the require check looks correct at a glance; the off‑by‑one mistake is hidden by the fact that the counter is incremented after each mint, making the error only visible when the cap is reached. The proper fix is to adjust the cap check to account for the initial offset, for example by adding one to the allowed maximum or by initializing the counter at zero. Adding a dedicated test that attempts to mint the full advertised supply would also prevent regression. In generic terms, this is a classic off‑by‑one boundary condition bug in supply‑limiting logic, leading to a discrepancy between documented and actual maximum token count and causing user‑visible failures such as 'mint failed' or 'no token received' when the last token is requested.

title: Insufficient input validation
description:
The _fee parameter in setFee() is missing any constrains and if we have malicious or compromised owner there might be a serious problem. The comments above the declaration of fee variable says that a value of 100 is 1% fee:
```solidity
* @notice Fee value in basis points.
* @dev Value of 100 is 1% fee.
uint16 public fee;
```
but since we are missing any input validation the fee can be set to uint16 max value which is 65535. This value will be equal to ~ 650% fee. The same can happen in the constructor as well as the setFee() method is called during construction time.
bug_full: The contract defines a public fee variable expressed in basis points, where a value of 100 corresponds to a 1 % fee. The setter function setFee() and the constructor accept an unsigned‑16‑bit integer (_fee) but do not enforce any upper limit on this parameter. Because uint16 can hold values up to 65 535, a malicious or compromised owner can set the fee to the maximum, which translates to roughly a 650 % charge on every transaction that uses the fee. The root cause is the absence of input validation that would restrict the fee to a reasonable range (for example, 5 % or 500 basis points). An attacker who controls the owner role can invoke setFee() after deployment or supply an inflated fee during construction, causing every user‑initiated operation that deducts the fee to lose a disproportionate amount of funds. From a user’s perspective the expected small deduction disappears; instead the user receives far less output or even a negative balance, leading to symptoms such as “my withdrawal returned almost nothing” or “the contract kept most of my funds”. The impact is financial loss for all participants, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential regulatory concerns because the fee mechanism no longer reflects the advertised business logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the comment documentation with the actual code and noticed the missing constraint. It can be hard to notice in testing because normal fee values (e.g., 100‑200) work correctly, and the overflow does not trigger a Solidity error; the contract simply applies an unintended large multiplier. To remediate, the contract should validate the input fee against a predefined maximum (e.g., require(_fee <= 500) or a configurable cap) and optionally enforce a non‑zero minimum. Adding this check both in the constructor and in setFee() restores the intended accounting model and prevents the fee from exceeding the business‑defined limits.

title: CsFeeOracle Can Be Initialized By Anyone Due To Front- Running Submitted By Pelz_Dev
description:
The initialize() function within the CsFeeOracle.sol contract is vulnerable to front-running attacks because it is an external function with no access control. This function allows any external account to call it and initialize the contract with arbitrary parameters, potentially resulting in unau-thorized initialization.

An attacker could front-run the intended owner and initialize the contract with their own parameters. This could lead to unauthorized control over the contract’s administrative functions, misdirecting fees, altering consensus mechanisms, or other critical aspects of the contract’s behaviour.
bug_full: An unprotected initialize function in the CsFeeOracle contract allows any external account to call it after deployment. Because the function is external and lacks any onlyOwner or initializer guard, an attacker observing a pending transaction that intends to set the contract’s parameters can submit their own initialize call with higher gas price, thereby front‑running the legitimate call. The root cause is the absence of access control on the contract’s bootstrap routine, which is a common pattern for upgradeable or proxy contracts but must be restricted to the designated deployer. Exploitation proceeds by broadcasting a transaction that invokes initialize with attacker‑controlled fee recipient addresses, consensus parameters, or other configuration values before the intended owner’s transaction is mined. Once the attacker’s transaction is included, the contract records the malicious parameters, granting the attacker de facto administrative control over fee distribution and any functions that rely on the oracle’s settings. The impact includes misdirection of collected fees to the attacker, alteration of consensus mechanisms, and potential disruption of protocol economics. This condition manifests whenever the contract is freshly deployed and before an authorized initialization transaction is confirmed; it also applies to any scenario where the initialize function can be called again if not protected. All participants that rely on the oracle for fee calculation—stakers, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the oracle may report incorrect fee rates or send fees to an unauthorized address. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that flagged the external initialize function without modifiers. Because the contract may appear correctly initialized after deployment, the vulnerability can be hard to notice unless transaction ordering is examined or the contract’s state is audited after deployment. The proper mitigation is to restrict initialize to a single authorized caller, typically the contract owner or a governance address, using an onlyOwner modifier or a one‑time initializer guard, and to emit an event confirming successful initialization. This class of bug belongs to ‘unrestricted initializer’ or ‘front‑runable bootstrap’ vulnerabilities, where missing access control on a setup function enables an attacker to hijack contract configuration. From a user perspective, fees that should be sent to the protocol may disappear or be sent to an unknown address, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The expectation that the oracle will correctly route fees is violated, resulting in funds effectively disappearing from the protocol’s treasury.

title: M-1 Inconsistent Bond Curve Update Handling
description:
The issue is identified within the function CSAccounting.sol#L168-L173 of contract CSAccounting. When updating a bond curve, there is a potential issue where the unbonded validators amount increases for a specific NO (node operator), but the corresponding depositable amount is not updated accordingly. This inconsistency can lead to unexpected behavior in the system, as the depositable amount should be forced to update, but currently, it is not possible to enforce this.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it can result in inconsistencies within the contract's logic, potentially leading to deposits of NO's keys without appropriate bond.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency that arises when a node operator (NO) updates its bond curve in the accounting contract. The contract tracks two related quantities for each NO: the amount of unbonded validator keys that are currently idle and the amount of keys that are allowed to be deposited (depositable amount). During a bond‑curve update the logic increments the unbonded validator count for a specific NO, but it fails to adjust the corresponding depositable amount. As a result the internal accounting state becomes mismatched: the system believes more keys can be deposited than are actually backed by sufficient bond. This mismatch occurs because the update routine does not enforce a simultaneous change of both variables, allowing one side of the invariant to diverge. An attacker or a careless node operator can exploit the flaw by triggering a curve change (for example through a governance action or a routine NO‑specific transaction) that inflates the unbonded count while leaving the depositable limit unchanged. After the update the contract will accept deposits of validator keys that are not properly bonded, which can lead to funds being locked in an invalid state, potential slashing of those keys, or the protocol accepting more validators than it can safely support. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users expect that a deposit will only succeed when sufficient bond exists, but the contract may record a successful deposit while the underlying bond is insufficient, causing unexpected failures later, loss of staking rewards, or even loss of the deposited ether if the protocol cannot reconcile the state. The condition manifests only when a bond‑curve change is performed for a NO that already has unbonded validators; in all other cases the state remains consistent. The affected parties include the node operators whose keys may be accepted without proper bond, delegators who rely on correct accounting for their stakes, and the overall protocol which could suffer from over‑allocation of validator slots. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors traced the state‑update path and observed that the depositable amount is not forced to update after the unbonded count changes. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error or revert; the inconsistency is hidden in internal storage and only becomes apparent when later operations query the depositable limit or when a deposit is later rejected due to insufficient bond. To remediate the problem the accounting logic should be refactored to perform the bond‑curve update in a two‑step process that atomically synchronises the unbonded validator count and the depositable amount, or to add a mandatory invariant check that forces the depositable amount to be recomputed whenever the curve identifier changes. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑invariant violations where related accounting variables are updated out of sync, leading to logical errors and potential financial loss.

title: M-10 Potential Misallocation of Validators in _getDepositsAllocation Function
description:
The issue is identified within the StakingRouter.sol#L1406-L1434 function of the contract StakingRouter. If a deposit is made before the system updates the status of stuck validators, there is a risk that funds could be allocated to a Node Operator (NO) that has violated an exit request. This can occur because the calculation uses availableValidatorsCount, which may not reflect the true status if stuck validators have not been accounted for yet.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could lead to the misallocation of validators, resulting in staking funds being deposited into a node operator that is not operating properly or has violated an exit request. The most probable scenario is when NO loses private keys for validators and cannot exit them. In this case, the protocol may allocate new deposits for such NO if the deposit is made before the stuck keys update.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking router’s internal allocation routine that determines how newly deposited ETH is distributed among node operators. The routine calculates the number of validators that are available for new deposits by reading a variable that reflects the count of active validators. However, the count is not refreshed after the AccountingOracle reports validators that are stuck because their private keys are lost and cannot be exited. When a user submits a deposit before the protocol finishes updating the status of these stuck validators, the stale count may still include the faulty validators as available. Consequently the allocation logic may assign the new deposit to a node operator that has already violated an exit request. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that the deposit will be delegated to a healthy validator and will start earning rewards, but in practice the funds are locked with a validator that cannot sign blocks, resulting in zero rewards, missing balances in the UI, or the appearance that the funds have disappeared. The bug is a classic case of resource allocation based on stale state, a race condition between state‑update and allocation. It was discovered during a manual audit of the StakingRouter contract by MixBytes. The issue is hard to notice because the allocation transaction succeeds and no explicit error is emitted; only downstream accounting anomalies reveal the problem. The impact is medium severity: funds may be misallocated to a misbehaving node operator, potentially reducing user earnings and requiring governance intervention to recover or re‑assign the stake. The affected parties include any depositor using the router, the node operators whose validators are stuck, and the protocol as a whole. The recommended mitigation is to ensure that the status of all validators, especially those reported as stuck, is fully reconciled before any new deposit is processed. A practical fix is to add a flag in the AccountingOracle that blocks new deposits until the stuck‑validator update is finalized, or to recompute the available validator count after the update. This eliminates the race condition and restores the invariant that only healthy validators receive new stakes.

title: M-2 Potential Mismanagement of Updated Withdrawal Vault Addresses
description:
The issue is identified within the function CSVerifier.sol#L308-L310 of the contract CSVerifier. The current implementation verifies that the withdrawalAddress matches WITHDRAWAL_ADDRESS. However, if the withdrawal vault address is updated through a contract upgrade, this check may fail for old deposits, leading to incorrect handling of those withdrawal processes.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it can cause inconsistencies in withdrawal processing, potentially affecting users' funds and the contract's reliability.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded verification that the address supplied for a withdrawal request exactly matches a single constant called WITHDRAWAL_ADDRESS. This check is performed in the CSVerifier contract when a user attempts to withdraw funds that were previously deposited. The root cause is that the contract does not maintain any history of previous withdrawal vault addresses, nor does it provide a compatibility layer for upgrades that replace the vault address. When the protocol upgrades and changes the withdrawal vault address, deposits that were made before the upgrade still carry the old vault address. Because the verification logic still expects the new constant, those older deposits fail the address check, causing the withdrawal handling logic to reject or misroute the request. An attacker does not directly gain control of funds, but the bug can be exploited by a malicious actor who triggers a contract upgrade to a new vault address while knowing that a large number of pending withdrawals reference the old address; the affected users will see their withdrawal attempts revert or be silently ignored, leading to funds being effectively locked. The impact is inconsistency in withdrawal processing: users may experience missing refunds, zero balances after a withdrawal call, or funds that appear to disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The condition occurs only after a contract upgrade that changes the withdrawal vault address and when there exist pending or historical deposits that reference the previous address. All participants who have deposited before the upgrade—regular users, delegators, or any role that can request withdrawals—are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the CSVerifier source code, where the auditor noted that the verification uses a single immutable constant without any versioning mechanism. The problem is subtle because the contract still compiles and works for new deposits, so the failure only manifests for older data, making it easy to miss in functional testing that focuses on fresh interactions. To remediate, the contract should either store a mapping of allowed vault addresses with timestamps, maintain a list of historical vault addresses, or implement a migration routine that updates pending deposits to the new address. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “address versioning” or “state incompatibility after upgrade” errors, where business logic assumes a static configuration that changes over time, violating the accounting assumption that a withdrawal request will always be routed to the correct vault. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal transaction but the displayed balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, contradicting the expectation that the funds would be transferred to their wallet. This mismatch between expected refund and actual outcome is a direct symptom of the underlying verification flaw.

title: M-3 Unchecked Guardian Quorum Value
description:
The issue is identified within the DepositSecurityModule.sol#L247-L254 function of the DepositSecurityModule contract. The function allows setting a guardian quorum value without checking if it exceeds the number of active guardians.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could lead to operational disruptions and governance issues if the quorum set is greater than the number of available guardians.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked guardian quorum value in the DepositSecurityModule contract. The function that sets the quorum does not verify that the new quorum does not exceed the number of currently active guardians. The root cause is a missing validation check (e.g., a require statement) that should compare the proposed quorum against the count of registered guardians. An attacker or privileged caller can invoke the function with a quorum larger than the available guardians, which means that any governance proposal that requires a majority of guardians will never be able to reach the required number of approvals. This can be exploited by setting the quorum to an impossible value, effectively dead‑locking the governance process: proposals appear to be submitted and even approved by all existing guardians, yet the system reports insufficient confirmations and refuses to execute actions such as withdrawals, upgrades, or parameter changes. The impact is operational disruption and a potential loss of control over the protocol, as critical functions become unexecutable and funds may remain locked until the quorum is corrected. The condition under which this occurs is any call to the _setGuardianQuorum function with a value greater than the current guardian count, which can be performed by an authorized role (e.g., contract owner or governance executor). The affected parties include the protocol itself, token holders, and any users relying on timely governance actions. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of the guardian management functions and noticed the absence of a bounds check. It may be hard to notice because the function compiles and runs without reverting, and the symptom—governance proposals never reaching quorum—can be attributed to other reasons such as network latency or misconfiguration. To fix the issue, the contract should enforce that the new quorum is a positive integer and does not exceed the number of active guardians, typically by adding a require statement that checks newQuorum <= guardianCount && newQuorum > 0 before updating the stored quorum value. This validation restores the intended accounting invariant that the quorum must be achievable, preventing dead‑locks and ensuring that governance actions can be executed as expected.

title: M-4 Reuse of Guardian Signatures for Pausing Deposits
description:
The issue is identified within the DepositSecurityModule.sol#L384 function of the DepositSecurityModule contract. This function checks for guardians' signatures to pause deposits but does not utilize a nonce mechanism. Consequently, a previously used signature could potentially be replayed to initiate another pause, leading to abuse or unintended operational disruptions.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could allow an attacker to repeatedly pause the system by reusing an old, valid signature, thereby disrupting normal operations and potentially causing governance issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replayable guardian signature flaw in the deposit‑pause mechanism of the contract. The pause function accepts a set of guardian signatures to temporarily stop new deposits, but it does not include a unique nonce or any other replay protection. Because the signature verification only checks that the signature is valid for the current message, an attacker who obtains a previously used, still‑valid guardian signature can submit it again at a later time. This allows the same signature to be replayed to trigger additional pause actions without fresh approval from the guardians. The flaw originates from the missing nonce field in the signed payload, which means the contract cannot distinguish a fresh request from a duplicated one. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary records a legitimate pause transaction, extracts the guardian signatures, and later resubmits the same data to the pause function. Each replay will cause the contract to re‑enter the paused state, potentially extending the downtime indefinitely. The impact is operational disruption – users attempting to deposit find the UI reporting that deposits are paused, balances remain unchanged, and expected deposits are rejected. Protocol governance may appear unresponsive because the pause can be repeatedly re‑triggered without new guardian consent, leading to confusion about whether a legitimate governance decision was made. The condition for the bug to manifest is any time a guardian‑signed pause transaction has been executed; the attacker can then reuse the same signatures. All participants who rely on the deposit flow – regular users, delegators, and the protocol’s revenue model – are affected because their funds cannot be deposited during the unintended pause. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DepositSecurityModule contract, where the absence of a nonce field in the signature verification logic was noted. It can be hard to notice because the pause behaviour itself is expected when a valid signature is presented, so repeated pauses may be attributed to legitimate governance actions rather than a replay attack. The appropriate remediation is to introduce a monotonically increasing nonce or a unique identifier into the signed message and to store the highest used nonce, rejecting any signature that does not contain a fresh nonce. This change ensures that each guardian signature can only be used once, aligning the implementation with standard replay‑protection patterns and restoring confidence that pauses are only triggered by fresh, authorized decisions. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks on signature‑based authorization, where missing anti‑replay data allows an attacker to reuse a previously valid cryptographic proof to cause unintended state changes.

title: M-5 Bond Curve is Not Reset Inside the submitInitialSlashing Function
description:
The issue is identified within the CSModule.sol#L1174 function of the CSModule contract, where the initial slashing penalty is applied to the Node Operator bond. While this penalization occurs, the Bond Curve for that Node Operator is not reset to the default.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it may lead to incorrect accounting of the unbonded validator keys count after the Node Operator penalization.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that processes the initial slashing penalty for a node operator. When the protocol applies the penalty to the operator's bond, it updates the amount that is deducted but fails to reset the associated bond curve to its default state. The root cause is a missing call to the accounting module that would re‑initialise the curve after a slashing event. Because the curve remains at the pre‑penalty level, subsequent accounting calculations that rely on the curve – such as the count of unbonded validator keys and the distribution of rewards – become inaccurate. An attacker or a malicious node operator could trigger the slashing function and then exploit the stale curve to create a mismatch between the recorded and actual validator counts, potentially leading to over‑allocation of rewards or under‑penalisation of future infractions. The impact is primarily incorrect accounting: users may see their expected refunds or rewards disappear, balances may appear lower than they should be, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken. This condition occurs every time the submitInitialSlashing function is invoked for a node operator, and it affects any stakeholder that relies on the correct unbonded‑key count – including stakers, the protocol’s governance, and the node operator themselves. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined state transitions after penalty events. It is hard to notice because the bond amount is visibly reduced, giving the impression that the penalty was applied correctly, while the hidden curve state silently stays unchanged. To remediate the problem, the contract should explicitly reset the bond curve for the affected node operator during the slashing routine, typically by invoking accounting.resetBondCurve with the operator’s identifier. This aligns the contract’s internal state with its external accounting expectations and restores the integrity of reward and slashing calculations. The bug belongs to the broader class of state‑inconsistency or missing‑state‑reset vulnerabilities, where a contract updates one piece of data but neglects to synchronise related internal structures, leading to accounting errors and potential financial loss.

title: M-6 Possible missing _updateDepositableValidatorsCount calls
description:
The issue is identified within the CSAccounting.sol#L178 and CSAccounting.sol#L188 functions of the CSAccounting contract.
It is expected that the mentioned functions may be called by an external trusted entity like DAO. The functions change Node Operator bond curve which may lead to unbonded validator keys count change.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it may lead to incorrect accounting of unbonded validator keys count after the Node Operator bond curve update.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of depositable validator slots in the CSAccounting contract. Two functions, setBondCurve and resetBondCurve, are intended to modify the node operator bond curve, which directly influences the number of unbonded validator keys that can be deposited. The contract is designed so that after any change to the bond curve, an internal helper function _updateDepositableValidatorsCount should be called to recalculate the depositable validator count. In the current implementation the calls to _updateDepositableValidatorsCount are missing when setBondCurve or resetBondCurve are invoked directly by an external trusted entity such as a DAO. As a result, the stored count of depositable validators becomes stale and no longer reflects the actual capacity defined by the new bond curve. This mismatch can cause the protocol to report an incorrect number of available validator slots, leading users to believe they can deposit more validators than the system can actually accept, or conversely to think fewer slots are available than exist. The impact is primarily accounting‑related: deposits may be rejected because the contract thinks there are no slots, or excess deposits could be accepted causing over‑allocation and potential loss of funds or protocol instability. The issue manifests only when the bond‑curve functions are called outside the CSModule contract, which normally encapsulates the update logic. Because the discrepancy is internal to a numeric counter, it does not emit explicit events or revert, making it hard to notice without detailed state inspection. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the source code, where the auditor observed that the expected call to _updateDepositableValidatorsCount was absent after the bond‑curve setters. To remediate, the setters should be restricted to be called only through the CSModule contract, which must invoke _updateDepositableValidatorsCount immediately after changing the curve. If future governance mechanisms allow the DAO to call these functions directly, the entry point must be routed through CSModule or an equivalent wrapper that guarantees the accounting update. This fixes the root cause by ensuring the depositable validator count is always synchronized with the bond curve, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and preventing user‑visible symptoms such as missing balances, unexpected zero‑deposit capacity, or rejected validator deposits.

title: M-7 Griefing of CSModule.addValidatorKeysETH() with CSModule.depositETH()
description:
CSModule.addValidatorKeysETH() CSModule.sol#L388-L393 that msg.value is equal to accounting.getRequiredBondForNextKeys(). accounting.getRequiredBondForNextKeys() CSAccounting.sol#L527 that relies on the current node operator's bond. The CSModule.depositETH() CSModule.sol#L471-L481 so anyone can increase the Node Operator's bond. A griefer may front-run a call to accounting.getRequiredBondForNextKeys() and deposit a few weis for 1 bond share. This would cause the initial call to revert. The griefer can do this multiple times, forcing the node operator manager to use another function for adding keys.
Additionally, a potential DoS vector exists if a user deposits 0 wei of ETH. This could block deposits of new keys initiated from the DSM contract because of the nonce update.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interaction between the functions that add validator keys and the function that accepts ETH deposits for a node operator. The addValidatorKeysETH function expects the caller to send exactly the amount of ETH returned by accounting.getRequiredBondForNextKeys, which calculates the bond needed for the next set of validator keys based on the node operator’s current bond balance. Because the depositETH function is public and can be called by any address, an attacker can front‑run the call that queries the required bond, deposit a tiny amount of wei that is sufficient to create one additional bond share, and thereby increase the node operator’s recorded bond. When the original addValidatorKeysETH transaction then executes, the required bond value it previously read is now lower than the actual bond, causing the transaction to revert due to an insufficient msg.value. By repeating this front‑running step, a malicious actor can repeatedly force the node operator manager to abandon the normal key‑addition path and use a fallback mechanism, effectively griefing the operator. A secondary, related denial‑of‑service issue appears when a user calls depositETH with a zero‑wei amount. The function still updates an internal nonce that tracks deposits, but because no ETH is actually added, subsequent calls that rely on a non‑zero deposit to progress (for example, deposits triggered from the DSM contract) become blocked, preventing new validator keys from being funded. The impact is that the node operator’s ability to add new validator keys is disrupted, potentially delaying staking, reducing expected rewards, and harming delegators who rely on the operator’s performance. The affected parties include the node operator manager, the operator’s delegators, and the broader protocol that depends on timely validator onboarding. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the accounting logic and the public accessibility of deposit functions. It is subtle because the contract does not enforce a minimum deposit amount nor restrict who can call depositETH, so the problem may not surface until an attacker deliberately exploits the timing of the bond‑calculation query. To remediate, the depositETH function should be permissioned so that only the authorized node operator manager can increase the bond, a minimum deposit threshold should be enforced to prevent zero‑value calls, and deposits originating from the DSM contract should be routed through private pools that isolate the bond‑update logic from external actors. This fixes the griefing vector by removing the ability for arbitrary accounts to manipulate the bond amount and eliminates the DoS condition caused by zero‑value deposits.

title: M-8 Griefing of CSModule.compensateELRewardsStealingPenalty()
description: CSModule.compensateELRewardsStealingPenalty() CSModule.sol#L1096-L1108. At the same time CSBondLock.sol#L126-L128 to compensate no more than what was locked. A griefer may frontrun a CSModule.compensateELRewardsStealingPenalty() call and compensate 1 locked share, causing the initial call to revert. The griefer can do this multiple times, putting the Node Operator manager at risk of having to settle their lock with a reset of the bond curve.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a grief‑of‑service flaw in the compensation routine of the Lido CSModule contract. The function compensateELRewardsStealingPenalty is intended to reward a node operator manager for losses caused by reward‑stealing attacks, but it can be called by any address. Inside the function the contract checks the amount of locked shares that are still eligible for compensation and limits the payout to that remaining balance. Because there is no access control, an attacker can observe a pending legitimate call from the node‑operator manager, submit a front‑running transaction that consumes one locked share, and thereby reduce the available compensation pool. When the original manager call is executed it finds that the required locked share is no longer available, causing the transaction to revert. The attacker can repeat this pattern, forcing multiple reverts and eventually compelling the manager to settle the lock by resetting the bond curve, which disrupts the protocol’s accounting and may lead to loss of expected rewards. The issue occurs only when the manager attempts to invoke the compensation function and an adversary can submit a higher‑priority transaction; it therefore depends on the attacker’s ability to front‑run and on the mutable state that tracks remaining locked shares. The affected parties are the node‑operator manager, the node operators that rely on the compensation, and indirectly the Lido protocol and its users because the bond‑curve reset can alter reward distribution. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of the compensation routine was examined and the lack of permissioning was noted. It is hard to notice because the function appears harmless and the occasional revert may be attributed to normal runtime errors rather than a deliberate griefing attack. To remediate the issue the function should be permissioned so that only the authorized node‑operator manager can invoke it, or alternatively the contract should enforce a non‑depletable compensation budget or include a re‑entrancy‑style guard that prevents external actors from draining the locked‑share counter. In practice, a user would see the manager’s transaction fail with a revert, the expected refund or reward would be missing, and the protocol might display an unexpected reset of the bond curve, violating the business assumption that compensation is always payable when a penalty is triggered.

title: M-9 Incorrect Check For data.length in the AccountingOracle Contract
description:
The issue is identified within the AccountingOracle.sol#L741 function of the contract NodeOperatorsRegistry.
There is a check whether data.length is smaller than 67 bytes, which is incorrect, because its length should be 72 bytes minimum (nextHash (32 bytes) + itemIndex (3 bytes) + itemType (2 bytes) + itemPayload (moduleId (3 bytes) + nodeOpsCount (8 bytes) + nodeOperatorIds (8 bytes * nodeOpsCount) + validatorsCounts (16 bytes * nodeOpsCount))).
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could lead to processing data in an incorrect format, despite the fact that it is provided in a permissioned way.
bug_full: An incorrect length validation in the AccountingOracle component of the NodeOperatorsRegistry contract allows data payloads that are shorter than the required 72‑byte structure to be accepted. The function currently checks if data.length < 67 and rejects only those smaller than 67 bytes, while the specification of the payload demands at least 72 bytes (32‑byte nextHash, 3‑byte itemIndex, 2‑byte itemType, and a variable‑size itemPayload that itself contains a 3‑byte moduleId, an 8‑byte nodeOpsCount, followed by 8‑byte nodeOperatorIds and 16‑byte validatorsCounts for each operator). Because the guard is off by five bytes, malformed messages that omit part of the itemPayload can pass the check and be processed by the oracle. The root cause is an off‑by‑five error in the length comparison, likely introduced by a miscalculation of the minimum size or a copy‑paste mistake. An attacker who can submit data to the AccountingOracle—either through a compromised node operator or via a permissioned interface—could craft a truncated payload that still satisfies the <67 test. When the contract later parses the payload, it will read beyond the provided bytes, leading to incorrect values being stored, mis‑calculated accounting entries, or even overwriting adjacent memory slots in the EVM stack. The practical impact is that accounting records for node operators may become inconsistent: rewards may be under‑ or over‑paid, validator counts may be reported incorrectly, and the protocol’s total stake accounting could diverge from reality. From a user perspective, a node operator might see their reported validator count drop to zero or receive a smaller reward than expected, while the protocol dashboard could display mismatched totals. The bug was discovered during a manual source‑code audit by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between the documented payload size and the implemented check. Because the contract is permissioned, the issue does not manifest as an obvious runtime error; instead, it silently corrupts data, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of accounting logs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of input‑validation errors, specifically incorrect length checks that allow malformed binary data to be processed. To remediate, the length guard should be updated to require data.length >= 72 before parsing, and additional sanity checks (e.g., verifying that the actual nodeOpsCount matches the remaining payload size) should be added. Proper validation will ensure that only well‑formed accounting messages are accepted, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: MJR-2 Fix gas cost ETH transfer
description: ETH sending at this line Lido.sol#L301 uses 2300 gas amount, but gas price can be vary and it is possible that in future it may exceed gas limit.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of a fixed 2300‑gas stipend when transferring Ether, typically via Solidity's transfer or send functions. This design assumes that the recipient’s fallback or receive function will always fit within the limited gas amount, an assumption that was valid before certain protocol upgrades but is no longer reliable. After hard forks such as Istanbul, the gas cost of several opcodes increased, meaning that even a simple fallback may now exceed the 2300‑gas limit. When the contract attempts to send ETH using this fixed stipend, the call can run out of gas and revert, causing the transfer to fail. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract with a fallback that deliberately consumes more than 2300 gas, causing any ETH sent to it via transfer to revert and effectively locking the funds in the sending contract. The impact is that users expecting to receive a refund, withdrawal, or any ETH payment may see no change in their balance, experience transaction reverts, or observe that their deposited funds remain stuck. This situation occurs whenever the contract sends ETH to an address that is a contract with a non‑trivial fallback, or when network gas costs rise beyond the hard‑coded limit. All participants who interact with the contract – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the business logic that assumes successful ETH transfers no longer holds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the hard‑coded gas amount as a potential future failure point. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the transfer appears to succeed in simple test cases; only when the recipient’s fallback grows or gas costs change does the failure surface. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer/send with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a configurable amount) and explicitly checks the returned success flag, handling failures gracefully. This change aligns the contract with the modern best practice of using call for ETH transfers, eliminating the fixed‑gas limitation and restoring reliable fund movement.

title: MJR-1 Public access to all functions
description: In contract Controller all functions have public access which can be exploited: Controller.sol
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing access control on every external function of the Controller contract. Because each function is declared public without any modifier, any external account can invoke them. The root cause is that the developer did not restrict privileged operations such as setting parameters, pausing the system, or moving assets. An attacker can call these functions directly, for example by invoking the function that changes the address of a critical component or that triggers a withdrawal, thereby altering protocol state, redirecting funds, or disabling safety mechanisms. This can happen at any time after deployment, as there is no role check; the condition is simply that the caller is an EOA or contract. Users of the protocol are affected because the controller may be manipulated to send tokens to an attacker, freeze deposits, or change fee structures, leading to loss of funds or denial of service. The issue was discovered during a manual source‑code audit where the auditor observed that no access modifiers such as onlyOwner, onlyAdmin, or role‑based checks were present on any function. The problem can be subtle because the functions compile and appear to work correctly for legitimate callers, so a casual test may not reveal the over‑exposure. The appropriate remediation is to introduce proper access control, for example by adding OpenZeppelin's Ownable or AccessControl modifiers to restrict privileged functions to authorized accounts, and to review each function to ensure that only intended callers can execute it. In generic terms this is an “unrestricted public function” bug, a class of access‑control flaw that violates the principle that only trusted actors may perform administrative actions. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that a transaction they did not initiate appears to have changed protocol parameters, that their balance suddenly drops to zero, or that a withdrawal they expected never arrives because the controller has been hijacked. The mismatch between the expected behavior (only the protocol owner can change settings) and the actual behavior (anyone can) breaks the accounting assumptions of the system and can lead to funds disappearing or the protocol becoming unusable.

title: MJR-2 Controller can be initialized several times
description: In contract Controller the initialize function can be called several times: Controller.sol#L140
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑initialization flaw in the Controller contract where the public initialize function can be invoked more than once. The root cause is the absence of a protection mechanism such as the OpenZeppelin initializer modifier or an explicit boolean flag that would restrict the function to a single execution. Because the contract relies on an initialize routine to set critical state variables—typically the owner, admin address, fee parameters, or other privileged settings—an attacker who discovers that the function is unrestricted can call it after deployment and overwrite those variables with attacker‑controlled values. Exploitation proceeds by sending a transaction that calls initialize with malicious arguments; the contract accepts the call, updates its storage, and effectively hands over control of the protocol logic to the attacker. The impact includes loss of administrative control, the ability to change protocol parameters arbitrarily, and potential theft or freezing of user funds, as the new controller can redirect withdrawals or disable essential functions. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed without a constructor and expects initialize to be called exactly once, but no guard is present to enforce that expectation. All participants that rely on the controller—protocol governance, token holders, and end‑users—are affected because the security guarantees of the system are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected upgradeable contract patterns and flagged the missing initializer protection as a known anti‑pattern. The flaw can be hard to notice because the initialize function may appear innocuous, emits no special events, and the contract may operate normally until an attacker triggers a re‑initialization, at which point the state change can be subtle or only observable through unexpected behavior such as sudden loss of privileges or zeroed balances.
