To remediate, the initialize function should be marked with the initializer modifier or wrapped in a custom one‑time guard that records whether it has already been executed and reverts on subsequent calls, thereby ensuring the initialization logic runs only once as intended.

title: MJR-3 Incorrect condition
description: The condition is incorrect here that can lead to an infinite loop: Lido.sol#L748
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect logical condition inside a loop of the Lido contract that can cause the loop to never terminate. The root cause is the use of a logical OR (||) where a logical AND (&&) is required, meaning the exit criteria are evaluated incorrectly. When the contract reaches this point, the loop condition remains true for a combination of state variables that should have caused it to stop, so the execution continues indefinitely until the transaction runs out of gas. An attacker or any user can trigger the problematic path by providing inputs that satisfy one side of the OR while the other side never becomes false, causing the contract to enter the infinite loop. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the transaction reverts only after exhausting gas, the caller loses the gas fee, and the contract’s functionality that depends on this loop becomes unavailable for all users until the state is manually corrected. This occurs whenever the function containing the loop is called with values that make the faulty condition true, which can happen in normal operation if the contract’s internal accounting reaches certain edge cases. All participants of the protocol—delegators, node operators, and any external callers—are affected because the contract may become unresponsive, preventing deposits, withdrawals, or reward calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who identified the logical operator mismatch while reviewing the control flow. It is hard to notice because the code compiles and passes basic tests; the loop only fails under specific state combinations that are not exercised in typical unit tests, and the symptom—transactions hanging or consuming all gas—may be attributed to other causes. The proper fix is to replace the OR operator with an AND operator so that the loop exits when either of the intended conditions is no longer satisfied, restoring the correct termination logic. Conceptually, this is a classic infinite‑loop or denial‑of‑service bug caused by an incorrect boolean expression, which violates the contract’s business logic that expects the loop to terminate after processing a bounded set of items. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should complete (for example, a deposit or withdrawal) instead stalls, the UI shows a pending state for an unusually long time, and eventually the transaction fails with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving the user with a lost gas fee and no state change. The expectation that the operation will finish is broken, leading to funds appearing to “disappear” in the sense that the operation never finalizes.

title: MJR-4 Possible burn of zero shares
description: Due to rounding errors a user can burn zero shares: Lido.sol#L522
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑precision error that can cause the burn operation in the staking contract to calculate zero shares to be burned. The root cause is integer division or rounding logic that truncates fractional share amounts, so when a user attempts to burn a very small amount of underlying tokens the computed share quantity may round down to zero. An attacker can invoke the burn function with such a small amount, the contract will accept the call, emit the burn event and possibly transfer the underlying tokens, but the internal accounting will not decrease the caller’s share balance because zero shares were recorded as burned. This mismatch allows the caller to retain the original share balance while the contract believes a burn has occurred, potentially enabling the user to later claim additional rewards or withdraw more assets than entitled. The issue manifests only when the calculated share amount is less than one whole share, which typically happens for tiny withdrawal requests or when the total supply of shares is large relative to the amount being burned. All participants who hold shares are affected because the accounting invariant that total shares equal total underlying assets can be broken, leading to inaccurate reward distribution and possible fund loss for honest users. The bug was discovered during a formal security audit where the auditors examined the burn logic and identified that the rounding could produce a zero‑share result. It is hard to notice in normal operation because most users interact with amounts that round to at least one share, and the contract does not explicitly reject zero‑share burns, so the transaction appears successful even though no state change occurs. To remediate the issue the contract should add an explicit check that the number of shares to be burned is greater than zero before proceeding, or adjust the rounding method to ensure that any positive amount results in at least one share being burned, possibly by using ceiling division or by requiring a minimum burn amount. This class of bug falls under rounding or precision errors that lead to zero‑value operations, a common source of accounting inconsistencies in financial smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after calling the burn function the displayed share balance remains unchanged, the expected reduction does not happen, and the user may see a successful transaction receipt despite receiving no refund or reduction, violating the expectation that burning tokens always reduces the share balance.

title: MJR-5 Possible division by zero
description: In some cases division by zero can take place here: Lido.sol#L658 Lido.sol#L708
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked division operation that can trigger a division‑by‑zero exception in the Lido staking contract. The root cause is a calculation that divides a value representing a user’s stake by the total amount of shares without first verifying that the total shares variable is non‑zero. When the contract’s overall shares balance reaches zero – for example after all participants have withdrawn or a rebase reduces the share count – the denominator becomes zero and the Solidity runtime throws a revert. An attacker or any user can deliberately or unintentionally bring the share total to zero and then invoke the function that performs the division, causing the transaction to fail. This failure can be exploited as a denial‑of‑service vector: legitimate deposits, withdrawals, or reward distributions that rely on the same calculation will revert, preventing users from interacting with the protocol and potentially locking funds in the contract. The impact is that users expect their stake to be calculated and their funds to be transferred, but instead receive no transaction receipt and see no change in balances, effectively experiencing a “funds disappear” symptom because the operation never completes. The condition occurs only in the edge case where the total shares amount equals zero, which is rarely exercised in standard testing, making the bug hard to notice until the edge case is triggered. The issue was discovered by MixBytes during a static analysis audit of the Lido codebase, where the lines performing the division were flagged as potentially unsafe. To remediate, the contract should include a guard that checks the denominator before performing the division and, if the total shares are zero, set the resulting stake to zero or revert with a clear error message. This aligns with the general class of arithmetic‑related vulnerabilities where unchecked division can cause runtime exceptions and break business logic, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a stake must always be derived from a positive share pool.

title: MJR-6 Insufficient xcKSm balance on Lido
description: It is possible that Lido can have less than _readyToClaim : Lido.sol#L563
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient token balance check in the Lido contract when it attempts to transfer xcKSM tokens. The contract maintains an internal counter called _readyToClaim that represents the amount it intends to send to users, but it does not verify that its actual xcKSM balance is at least that amount before performing the transfer. This mismatch can arise when external events such as slashing, token withdrawals, or previous failed transfers reduce the contract's balance without updating the internal accounting. An attacker or any user can trigger the claim function while the contract holds fewer tokens than _readyToClaim, causing the transfer to revert or to send a smaller amount than expected. From the user's perspective the UI may show a pending claim, but the received amount is zero or lower than promised, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue belongs to the classic class of “insufficient balance” or “unchecked external call” bugs, where a contract assumes it has enough tokens without enforcing that invariant. It was discovered during a manual audit of Lido.sol at line 563, where the code reads the internal counter but lacks a require statement that checks the contract's xcKSM balance against _readyToClaim. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract’s internal accounting may still indicate a positive claim even though the token balance is depleted, and the failure only surfaces under specific state conditions. The proper fix is to add an explicit check that the contract’s xcKSM balance is greater than or equal to the amount it is about to transfer, and to handle the case where the balance is insufficient, for example by reverting with a clear error or by adjusting the claim amount. By enforcing this invariant, the protocol restores the guarantee that users receive the full amount they are owed, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from disappearing.

title: MJR-7 Possible zero balance on Lido
description: It is possible that Lido can have zero balance on reward distribution: Lido.sol#L588
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward distribution mechanism of the Lido contract, where the function responsible for allocating accrued rewards can be executed even when the contract’s reward pool holds a zero token balance. The root cause is the absence of a guard condition that verifies the pool contains a positive amount before proceeding with the transfer logic. Because the contract does not check for a non‑zero balance, an external caller can trigger the distribution routine at any time, including moments when the pool is empty due to prior withdrawals, mis‑configuration, or simply because no rewards have been accrued yet. When this occurs, the routine completes successfully but transfers zero tokens to the intended recipients. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded – no revert is emitted, gas is spent, and an event may be emitted – yet the staker’s balance does not increase and the expected reward is missing. This mismatch between expectation (receiving a reward) and reality (receiving nothing) can lead to confusion, loss of trust, and accounting inconsistencies, because the protocol’s internal accounting may record that a distribution event occurred while the actual token flow was nil. The issue was identified during a MixBytes security audit of the Lido KSM implementation, where the auditors noted that the reward distribution code at line 588 lacks a balance‑greater‑than‑zero check. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an explicit error; it simply performs a no‑op transfer, making it easy to overlook during testing unless the specific scenario of an empty reward pool is exercised. To remediate the problem, the contract should include an explicit validation such as require(rewardPoolBalance > 0) before executing the transfer, ensuring that distribution can only occur when there are actual rewards to allocate. This change restores the intended business logic that rewards are only distributed when they exist, prevents users from receiving empty payouts, and aligns on‑chain accounting with the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: MJR-8 Possible underflow
description: It is possible that free balance from the report can be less than free balance from the previous era: Ledger.sol#L297
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can occur when the protocol records the free balance for a new era. The contract assumes that the free balance reported for the current era will never be lower than the free balance recorded for the previous era. Because there is no explicit check enforcing this monotonicity, a situation may arise where the reported free balance is smaller than the prior value. When the contract later calculates the amount to be bonded or transferred using a subtraction that expects a non‑negative result, the subtraction can underflow, wrapping around to a very large unsigned integer. This can be exploited by an attacker who manipulates the reported free balance (for example by triggering a state transition that yields a lower balance) and then initiates a bonding or withdrawal operation that relies on the faulty subtraction. The impact is that the protocol may credit the attacker with an inflated bonded amount or allow withdrawals that exceed the actual holdings, effectively draining funds or breaking the accounting guarantees of the staking system. The condition occurs at the boundary between eras, specifically at the point where the ledger updates the free balance (see Ledger.sol line 297). Any participant whose balance is tracked by the ledger – including regular stakers, delegators, and the protocol itself – can be affected because the accounting error propagates to subsequent reward calculations and bond management. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Lido KSM smart‑contract code, where the auditor noticed that the free‑balance update logic did not enforce a non‑decreasing invariant and that the subsequent bonding calculation performed an unchecked subtraction. The bug can be hard to notice because the underflow only manifests when a rare state transition produces a lower free balance, which may not happen under normal operation, and the resulting huge number may be interpreted as a legitimate value by downstream logic. To fix the problem, the contract should introduce an explicit variable or flag that determines the exact amount to be bonded for the next era and should add a validation step that ensures the new free balance is not less than the previous one, or that uses safe arithmetic (e.g., SafeMath) with proper revert on underflow. In user‑facing terms, a staker might see their balance unexpectedly drop to zero or see a refund that is far larger than expected, contradicting the expectation that their funds are safely accounted for. This class of bug falls under unchecked arithmetic underflow in state‑transition logic, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that balances cannot become negative.

title: M-1 Extra function
description: At lines Lido.sol#L139-L142 and at lines Lido.sol#L158-L165 similar actions are performed. But in one case there is a change in the TOTALMEVTXFEECOLLECTED_POSITION variable, and in the other case there is none. One of these functions is redundant.
bug_full: The contract contains two functions that perform almost identical operations, but only one of them updates the accounting variable that tracks the total MEV transaction fee collected (TOTALMEVTXFEECOLLECTED_POSITION). The other function executes the same core logic without modifying this state variable, making it effectively redundant. This discrepancy originates from a copy‑paste or design oversight where the second function was left without the necessary state mutation. An attacker or any caller who can invoke the redundant function can trigger the intended protocol actions while bypassing the fee accounting update, causing the protocol’s internal accounting to diverge from the actual economic activity. The impact is that the protocol may report lower fee totals than were truly earned, leading to inaccurate revenue distribution, potential underpayment of stakeholders, and a breach of the accounting invariants that users rely on. The issue manifests whenever the redundant function is called, which could happen unintentionally through a user interface that exposes both functions or deliberately by a malicious actor seeking to hide fee collection. All participants that depend on correct fee accounting – such as token holders, delegators, and the protocol’s governance mechanisms – are affected because the reported fee totals no longer reflect reality. The problem was identified during a systematic security audit performed by MixBytes, which flagged the duplicated code paths and the missing state update as a medium‑severity concern. Because the two functions look very similar, the omission is easy to overlook during code reviews and testing, especially if the test suite only checks functional outcomes without verifying internal state changes. To remediate the issue, the redundant function should be removed entirely, or its implementation should be aligned with the primary function to ensure that TOTALMEVTXFEECOLLECTED_POSITION is updated consistently in every execution path. This correction restores the integrity of the fee accounting logic, prevents potential revenue leakage, and eliminates an unnecessary attack surface.

title: M-2 No validation of the address parameter value in the contract constructor
description: The variable is assigned the value of the constructor input parameter. But this parameter is not checked before this. If the value turns out to be zero, then it will be necessary to redeploy the contract, since there is no other functionality to set this variable. At line LidoMevTxFeeVault.sol#L72 the TREASURY variable is set to the value of the _treasury input parameter.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked address parameter in the contract constructor. During deployment the constructor receives an address argument intended to become the immutable TREASURY variable, but the code does not verify that the supplied address is non‑zero. Because the Solidity type address accepts the zero address as a valid value, the contract can be instantiated with TREASURY set to address(0) without any compile‑time or runtime error. The root cause is the absence of a require statement or similar guard that would reject a zero address before assignment. An attacker or a careless deployer can therefore provide the zero address, causing the contract to record a treasury that cannot receive or forward any funds. Since the contract does not expose any function to update TREASURY after construction, the zero address becomes permanent, effectively disabling fee collection or withdrawal logic that depends on a valid treasury destination. When the contract later attempts to transfer collected fees, the transfer fails silently or reverts, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as “no funds are sent to the treasury”, “balance remains zero”, or “refunds are missing”. The impact is medium severity because funds intended for the treasury may become permanently inaccessible, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially causing loss of revenue for token holders or stakers. The condition occurs only at deployment time; any subsequent operation that relies on TREASURY will behave incorrectly if the initial value was zero. The affected parties include the protocol operators, the treasury, and any users expecting fee distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined constructor logic and identified the missing validation. It can be hard to notice because the zero address does not raise an exception and the contract may appear to compile and deploy successfully, while the logical error only manifests later when fee transfers are attempted. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check in the constructor, for example require(_treasury != address(0), "treasury address cannot be zero"), ensuring that only a valid, non‑zero address can be stored. Optionally, providing an administrative function to update the treasury address could mitigate the risk of an accidental zero address deployment. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked input validation errors that lead to immutable misconfiguration and loss of fund flow, violating the business rule that the treasury must always be a reachable address capable of receiving assets.

title: M-3 Max oracle members amount is actually lower
description: Max members are 255 instead of 256 which may affect the quorum: LidoOracle.sol#L432
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the definition of the maximum number of oracle members used by the Lido governance contract. The code limits the member set to 255 entries while the intended design assumes a capacity of 256 members. This discrepancy originates from an incorrect constant or boundary check that truncates the allowed size by one. When the oracle reaches its maximum capacity, the quorum calculation – which depends on the total member count – is performed with the wrong upper bound. As a result, the required number of affirmative votes may be mis‑computed: proposals may be rejected even though enough participants have voted, or conversely, a proposal may pass with fewer votes than the protocol’s specifications dictate. The impact is a distortion of the governance process; token holders and protocol participants may lose confidence because decisions can be made with an unintended quorum, potentially allowing a malicious minority to influence protocol upgrades or fund allocations. The issue manifests only when the member set grows to the limit, making it hard to notice during normal operation because smaller member sets behave correctly. It was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which compared the documented quorum rules with the actual implementation and identified the mismatch. Detecting the bug in production can be difficult because the symptom – a proposal failing or passing unexpectedly – may be attributed to other factors such as voting inactivity. The appropriate remediation is to correct the constant or the conditional check so that the maximum member count matches the intended 256, and to verify that quorum calculations use the accurate member total. This class of bug belongs to boundary‑condition errors that affect access control or consensus thresholds, and it violates the business logic that assumes a fixed quorum based on a known number of participants. From a user’s perspective, the UI may display a quorum of 255, and a user expecting a proposal to succeed with a certain number of votes may instead see it rejected or see an unexpected approval, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust in the protocol’s governance mechanisms.

title: M-4 There is no recovery option for ERC721
description: The transferToVault() function doesn't support ERC721 tokens: Lido.sol#L356
bug_full: The issue is a missing recovery mechanism for ERC721 (non‑fungible) tokens in the Lido contract. The transferToVault() function is designed to move assets to a vault but only implements logic for ERC20‑style tokens, ignoring the ERC721 interface that requires a tokenId and safeTransferFrom call. Because the contract does not implement ERC721Receiver or provide a withdraw function for NFTs, any ERC721 token that is accidentally or intentionally sent to the contract becomes permanently locked. This situation arises whenever a user or a malicious actor transfers an NFT to the Lido contract address, either directly or via a generic token‑transfer call that the contract does not reject. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that the NFT disappears from their wallet, the UI shows no balance for that token, and attempts to retrieve it return nothing. The root cause is the absence of code handling the ERC721 transfer hook and the lack of an administrative function that can call safeTransferFrom to return the token. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s token‑handling functions. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and works correctly for supported token standards, and no tests exercised ERC721 paths. The impact is that users may lose ownership of valuable NFTs, which undermines trust in the protocol and may expose the project to reputational damage. To remediate, the contract should be extended to implement the ERC721Receiver interface, add a function (restricted to an authorized role) that can call safeTransferFrom with a specific tokenId to move the NFT out of the contract, and optionally emit events to track recovery actions. This aligns the recovery logic with the ERC721 standard and ensures that NFTs are not permanently trapped.

title: M-5 Incorrect event
description: In case of cover, stETH doesn't burn StETH.sol#L461
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an inaccurate event emission during the cover operation of the Lido protocol. When a user initiates a cover, the contract is supposed to burn a specific amount of stETH, removing those tokens from circulation. However, the event that is emitted at the end of the transaction still includes the burned stETH amount, as the code at StETH.sol line 461 records the full balance before the burn is applied. This mismatch between the on‑chain state (the tokens are actually destroyed) and the off‑chain observable log (the event suggests the tokens remain) creates a discrepancy in accounting. The root cause is that the event payload is constructed prior to the burn or fails to subtract the burned quantity, resulting in an event that reports a higher stETH balance than the true state. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract directly; the issue can be leveraged by any off‑chain service, analytics dashboard, or wallet that relies on events to infer token balances. Such services may display a non‑zero stETH balance after a cover, leading users to believe their funds are still available, potentially causing confusion, double‑spending attempts, or erroneous financial reporting. The impact is primarily informational: users see an unexpected non‑zero balance, UI shows “refund received” when none exists, and protocol accounting may be out of sync with the actual token supply. The condition under which this occurs is strictly the execution of the cover function where a burn is intended. All participants who depend on event data – token holders, front‑end applications, auditors, and any downstream contracts that listen to these events – are affected. The issue was identified during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who noted that the emitted event does not reflect the state change caused by the burn. It is hard to notice because the contract’s internal state correctly updates; only the emitted log is wrong, and developers often assume events are a faithful representation of state transitions. To remediate, the contract should be changed so that the event either omits the stETH amount entirely or reports the post‑burn balance, ensuring that the emitted data matches the actual token supply after the operation. This correction aligns the event with the intended business logic that burned tokens are no longer part of any user's balance, restoring accurate accounting and preventing misleading UI displays.

title: M-6 There is no recovery for excess stETH
description: It is possible to transfer stETH to wstETH so it will be frozen in the contract. WstETH.sol#L28-L118
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑locking bug in the wstETH wrapper contract. The contract assumes that its internal accounting of wrapped shares matches the amount of stETH held, but it does not provide any mechanism to recover stETH that is sent directly to the contract address without invoking the official wrap function. Because the ERC20 token standard allows anyone to transfer stETH to any address, an attacker or even an unwitting user can call the stETH token’s transfer method and move tokens into the wstETH contract. The contract’s code does not detect this inbound transfer, does not mint corresponding wstETH shares, and lacks a function to withdraw the surplus balance. As a result, the excess stETH becomes permanently frozen inside the contract. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious actor sends a large amount of stETH to the wstETH contract address; the tokens are accepted by the ERC20 transfer, the contract’s balance increases, but the internal share ledger remains unchanged, so the funds cannot be redeemed or transferred out. The impact is that the locked stETH is effectively lost to the protocol and its users, reducing the total assets backing wstETH, potentially skewing redemption ratios and harming confidence in the system. The issue manifests only when stETH is transferred directly to the wrapper contract, a scenario that may not be covered by normal UI flows, making it easy to overlook. Users who mistakenly send stETH to the wstETH address will see their wallet balance decrease while receiving no wstETH tokens, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The bug was identified during a formal security audit by MixBytes, which noted the absence of any recovery path for surplus stETH. Detecting the problem is difficult because the contract’s public view functions report correct share totals, while the underlying token balance appears higher, a discrepancy that is not exposed through standard interfaces. The recommended remediation is to add a controlled recovery function that allows the protocol’s governance to withdraw any excess stETH while preserving the correct number of wrapped shares, or to implement a safeguard that rejects direct ERC20 transfers to the contract, ensuring that all stETH entering the contract goes through the proper wrapping logic. This class of issue falls under “stuck funds” or “asset‑locking” vulnerabilities, where a contract’s accounting does not reconcile with its token balances, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that every deposited asset is represented by a corresponding share token.

title: M-7 Callback verification
description: By mistake a callback which has no implementation of the processLidoOracleReport() method can be added at the line: OrderedCallbacksArray.sol#L60 in case you set the IBeaconReportReceiver address, the execution of the following lines will be reverted. LidoOracle.sol#L644
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing verification step that allows a contract address to be registered as a callback even though it does not implement the required processLidoOracleReport() function. The root cause is that the registration logic does not perform an interface check (for example using EIP‑165) before storing the IBeaconReportReceiver address. When the LidoOracle contract later attempts to invoke processLidoOracleReport() on the stored address, the call fails because the function does not exist, causing the transaction to revert at the point where the oracle tries to forward the report. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a deliberately empty or malicious contract as the callback, which will cause every subsequent oracle report to revert, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol. The impact is that the oracle cannot deliver updated staking data, rewards may not be distributed, and users may see their transactions fail with generic revert messages, leading to confusion and potential loss of expected earnings. The issue occurs whenever the protocol owner or an authorized entity sets the IBeaconReportReceiver address without confirming that the target contract implements the required method. All participants that rely on the oracle – stakers, delegators, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol’s accounting logic is halted. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the Lido codebase, where the auditors noticed that the callback registration line does not include any interface‑support verification. The problem is subtle because a missing function does not raise a compile‑time error; the failure only appears at runtime when the call is made, and the revert message does not indicate the underlying cause. To remediate, the registration routine should explicitly check that the supplied address supports the LidoOracle callback interface, for example by calling supportsInterface() with the appropriate interface identifier as defined in EIP‑165, and reject any address that does not. This ensures that only contracts that implement processLidoOracleReport() can be added, preventing accidental or malicious insertion of non‑functional callbacks and preserving the integrity of the oracle reporting flow. The bug belongs to the class of interface‑implementation verification errors, where a system assumes the presence of a function without confirming it, leading to runtime failures and potential service disruption.

title: M-1 Expired proposals can be executed
description:
An expired proposal can be executed in case of the _gracePeriod extension:
BridgeExecutorBase.sol#L233.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the governance execution contract that allows a proposal that has already passed its deadline to be executed if the global _gracePeriod variable is modified after the proposal was created. The contract checks proposal expiry by comparing the current block timestamp against the proposal’s start time plus the current _gracePeriod value. Because _gracePeriod is stored as a mutable state variable, any later update to this parameter retroactively extends the execution window of all previously created proposals. Consequently, an attacker who can trigger a change to _gracePeriod – for example through another governance action – can wait until a proposal expires, increase the grace period, and then call the execute function to run the proposal’s payload. This defeats the intended safety guarantee that expired proposals are immutable and should never be executable. The impact is that stale or malicious proposals may be executed, potentially altering protocol parameters, moving funds, or performing other privileged actions that were assumed to be blocked after expiry. The issue manifests only when a proposal is marked expired and the _gracePeriod is subsequently altered before an execution attempt, a condition that may be rare but is feasible in a system where governance can modify timing parameters. All participants who rely on the governance process – token holders, protocol users, and developers – are affected because the integrity of the decision‑making timeline is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noticed that the expiration check references a mutable variable rather than a value captured at proposal creation. The bug is subtle because the contract still enforces a time window, and typical tests may only cover the happy path where _gracePeriod remains constant, making the vulnerability easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should store the grace period value as part of each proposal’s immutable data at the moment of creation, or otherwise make the parameter read‑only for the lifetime of the proposal. By using a fixed per‑proposal grace period, later changes to the global setting cannot retroactively reopen execution windows, restoring the intended security property that expired proposals are permanently inert. This class of issue belongs to the broader category of “mutable time‑window parameters” or “expiration logic tampering”, where a contract’s time‑based access control can be altered after the fact, leading to unexpected execution of stale actions and breaking accounting assumptions about when actions are allowed.

title: M-2 The guardian in BridgeExecutorBase can cancel an ActionsSet that changes
description:
The guardian in BridgeExecutorBase can cancel any ActionsSet immediately after an addition. They can also cancel an ActionsSet with a transaction to change the guardian. Thus, if the guardian's address is compromised, there is no way to change it, and redeployment of CrossChainExecutor will be required.
BridgeExecutorBase.sol#L112
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑privileged cancellation mechanism in the BridgeExecutorBase contract. The contract defines a guardian role that is allowed to cancel any pending ActionsSet immediately after it is added to the queue. Because the cancellation right is unconditional, the guardian can also cancel an ActionsSet that contains a single action whose purpose is to replace the guardian address. If an attacker gains control of the guardian’s private key, they can use the guardian’s cancellation power to block the very transaction that would rotate the guardian to a new, safe address. This creates a dead‑end situation where the compromised guardian cannot be removed, effectively locking the governance path for updating the executor. The flaw originates from the contract’s logic that does not differentiate between ordinary actions and the privileged guardian‑update action when evaluating cancellation rights. Exploitation consists of the attacker first compromising the guardian address, then submitting a malicious ActionsSet that attempts to change the guardian, and finally invoking the guardian’s cancel function before the action is executed. Because the cancel call succeeds instantly, the guardian‑update action never reaches execution, leaving the compromised guardian in place. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the contract’s governance and a potential loss of funds if the compromised guardian can later misuse its authority, for example by authorising malicious cross‑chain transfers. The condition under which the bug manifests is any time an ActionsSet is added to the executor while the guardian role is still controlled by an address that may be compromised. All participants that rely on the executor – the protocol, its users, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol can no longer safely rotate the guardian or respond to emergencies. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the cancellation logic of BridgeExecutorBase and identified that the same guard is applied to all actions without exception. It can be hard to notice because the cancellation function appears to be a safety feature, and the special case of a guardian‑update action is not obvious from the code. The recommended remediation is to treat a guardian‑update ActionsSet as a protected operation that cannot be cancelled by the guardian itself; only the executor or a quorum of other actors should be able to veto it, while retaining the ability for the guardian to cancel all other actions. This change restores the ability to rotate the guardian safely and prevents a compromised guardian from creating an irreversible lock‑out. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of “over‑broad privileged cancellation” or “governance dead‑lock” vulnerabilities, where a role that is supposed to provide an emergency stop also blocks the emergency stop from being updated. From a user perspective the protocol may appear to freeze: attempts to submit a guardian change transaction are silently rejected, balances remain unchanged, and no error is shown, leading users to wonder why their governance actions have no effect.

title: MJR-1 Possible blocking of the contract
description: At the line DepositSecurityModule.sol#L123 initializes the owner variable without checking the new value of the variable. If the value of the variable is equal to zero, then the following functions will stop working: setOwner(), setNodeOperatorsRegistry(), setPauseIntentValidityPeriodBlocks(), setMaxDeposits(), setMinDepositBlockDistance(), setGuardianQuorum(), addGuardian(), addGuardians(), removeGuardian(), unpauseDeposits().
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ownership initialization flaw where the contract assigns a new owner address without verifying that the supplied value is non‑zero. Because the code does not include a check such as require(newOwner != address(0)), an attacker or a mistaken transaction can set the owner variable to the zero address. When the owner becomes address(0) the contract’s access‑controlled functions that rely on a valid owner – including setOwner, setNodeOperatorsRegistry, setPauseIntentValidityPeriodBlocks, setMaxDeposits, setMinDepositBlockDistance, setGuardianQuorum, addGuardian, addGuardians, removeGuardian and unpauseDeposits – effectively stop working. These functions either revert due to implicit checks that the caller must be the owner, or they become no‑ops because the contract treats the zero address as an invalid authority. The impact is that the protocol’s administrative controls are frozen, preventing updates to deposit parameters, pausing or unpausing deposits, and managing guardians. From a user’s perspective deposits may suddenly stop being accepted, or previously set limits cannot be changed, leading to a perception that the contract is “blocked” or “broken”. The condition occurs whenever the owner variable is set to zero, which can happen during contract initialization, an upgrade, or a malicious call to setOwner if the function is exposed without proper validation. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, who noted the missing zero‑address guard. It can be hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not reject a zero address assignment and no explicit revert is triggered at the point of assignment; the failure only becomes apparent later when owner‑only functions are called. The proper remediation is to add an explicit validation step before assigning the new owner, for example require(newOwner != address(0)), and to follow a well‑tested Ownable pattern that enforces non‑zero ownership throughout the contract lifecycle.

title: M-1 Rounding errors
description:
Due to rounding errors users will always retain some dust on L2 ERC20RebasableBridged.sol#L86-L94.
This problem can be mitigated by adding a method that allows users to unwrap stETH shares into wstETH shares.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs in the L2 ERC20RebasableBridged contract when converting between stETH shares and the wrapped representation on Optimism. Because the contract uses integer division without proper rounding, a small remainder – often referred to as dust – is left in the user's balance after an unwrap or bridge operation. The root cause is the loss of precision when the rebasing token amount is scaled to the fixed‑point representation required for the L2 bridge, causing the fractional part to be truncated. An attacker does not gain direct control over this dust, but any user who performs the conversion will end up with a non‑zero balance that cannot be withdrawn through the existing interface, leading to a discrepancy between the expected refund amount and the actual amount received. This situation manifests when a user unwraps stETH to wstETH or when the bridge settles a transfer; the UI may display a zero balance because the remaining amount is below the displayed precision, while the on‑chain balance still contains a few wei. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, which identified that the code paths at lines 86‑94 always leave a remainder due to the rounding logic. The problem is hard to notice because the dust is typically very small and may be rounded to zero in front‑end displays, giving the impression that the operation succeeded fully. The impact is primarily financial – users lose the ability to claim the leftover tokens, which over many operations can accumulate to a noticeable loss – and it violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that all transferred value is fully accounted for after a bridge operation. The recommended mitigation is to add a dedicated method that allows users to convert the remaining stETH shares into wstETH shares, effectively enabling them to claim the dust, or to adjust the arithmetic to use rounding up or a higher precision representation so that no remainder is left.

title: M-1 It is possible to vote during the objection time if the proposal was rejected
description: At line Voting.sol#L192 during the objection time, the vote() function checks if the vote is no, if the vote is open for objection and if the voter has balance. But there is no check whether the vote was rejected or not. So it is possible to vote no for a proposal even if it was rejected during the voting time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the governance voting contract that permits a participant to submit a "no" vote during the objection window even after the proposal has already been marked as rejected. The root cause is the absence of a status check that verifies whether the proposal outcome is final before allowing votes in the objection phase. Because the vote() function only validates that the vote is "no", that the objection period is active, and that the caller holds a sufficient token balance, it inadvertently accepts votes on proposals that are no longer open for decision making. An attacker can exploit this by calling vote() with a "no" choice after the proposal has been rejected, thereby inflating the count of negative votes. While the immediate financial impact may be limited, the manipulation can distort governance metrics such as quorum calculations, affect the perceived legitimacy of the decision process, and potentially influence downstream actions that depend on the final vote tally. The issue manifests only when the objection period is still active, the proposal has already been rejected, and the voter possesses a non‑zero balance. Token holders, protocol governors, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate voting outcomes are affected because the governance state no longer reflects the true community consensus. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which identified the missing rejection check as a logical oversight. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display a voting button during the objection window, and the contract does not emit an explicit error for rejected proposals, giving the impression that voting is still valid. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit verification that the proposal status is not "rejected" before permitting a vote in the objection phase, ensuring that once a proposal is rejected, no further votes can be cast and the governance outcome remains immutable. This class of bug falls under improper state validation in multi‑phase voting systems, where transitions between phases are not correctly enforced, leading to potential accounting inconsistencies and violation of the protocol’s business logic that expects a final, immutable decision after rejection.

title: Limits in LIFuelFacet
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LIFuelFacet component, which is designed to handle low‑value bridge operations but does not enforce any upper bound on the amount of assets a caller can submit. The root cause is the absence of a validation step that compares the requested transfer amount against the available liquidity on the destination side or against a protocol‑defined maximum. Because the function proceeds to collect service fees and forward the assets without checking whether the receiving side can actually satisfy the transfer, a user can deliberately or inadvertently send a large sum that exceeds the liquidity pool. When this occurs, the bridge logic attempts to execute the transfer, but the insufficient liquidity causes the assets to become locked in the contract, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. From the user’s point of view the UI may show a successful transaction submission, yet the balance displayed after the operation is unchanged or becomes zero, and no refund or receipt is observed. The impact is that funds may be stuck indefinitely, undermining trust in the protocol and potentially causing financial loss for users and liquidity providers. The issue manifests whenever the _startBridge internal routine is called with either a native asset or an ERC‑20 token, because both branches (native fee collection and token fee collection) lack any amount caps. The problem was identified during a third‑party security audit (Spearbit) that examined the contract’s logic and noticed the mismatch between the intended low‑value use case and the unrestricted amount handling. The bug can be hard to detect in normal testing because small transfers succeed, masking the failure mode that only appears with larger values. To remediate, the contract should introduce explicit limits on the maximum amount that can be processed per call, and it should verify that sufficient liquidity exists on the receiving side before committing the transfer. This aligns the implementation with the business rule that LIFuelFacet is only for small amounts and prevents funds from becoming irretrievable due to liquidity shortfalls.

title: The optimal version _depositAndSwap() isn't always used
description:
The function _depositAndSwap() of SwapperV2 has two versions. The second version keeps _nativeReserve that is meant for fees. Several facets don't use this version although their bridge does require native fees. This could result in calls reverting due to insufficient native tokens left.
```solidity
function _depositAndSwap(...) ... // 4 parameter version
/// @param _nativeReserve Amount of native token to prevent from being swept back to the caller
function _depositAndSwap(..., uint256 _nativeReserve) ... // 5 parameter version
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SwapperV2 contract where the internal helper _depositAndSwap is overloaded. The version with four parameters does not accept a nativeReserve argument that reserves a portion of the native token to cover bridge fees. Several higher‑level facets invoke the four‑parameter overload even though the underlying bridge operation expects a fee to be retained. Because no nativeReserve is set, the bridge may consume all native tokens that were transferred, leaving none for the required fee. When the bridge later attempts to deduct the fee, the call reverts due to insufficient balance. This can happen during cross‑chain swaps that involve native token fees, and it affects any user who initiates a swap through the affected facets. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails; the UI may show a generic “transaction reverted” or “out of gas” error, and the user sees no tokens received despite having approved the operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that some code paths never called the fee‑protecting overload. It is subtle because both overloads have the same name and the missing argument is easy to overlook, especially when the contract compiles without warnings. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect overload usage” or “fee‑reserve omission” bugs, where a function that should preserve a fee buffer is bypassed, breaking accounting assumptions that a certain amount of native token will always be available for fee payment. To remediate, every facet that interacts with a bridge requiring native fees should be updated to call the five‑parameter version of _depositAndSwap, passing an appropriate _nativeReserve value that matches the expected fee amount. Alternatively, the contract could enforce the use of the fee‑protecting overload or add internal checks that revert if the native balance after the deposit is lower than the required fee. Proper testing should verify that fee‑reserve logic is exercised in all execution paths.

title: setContractOwner() is insufficient to lock down the owner
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ownership transfer mechanism of a Diamond proxy contract. The function transferOwnershipToZeroAddress is intended to render the contract immutable by setting the stored contractOwner variable to the zero address. However, the contract also maintains a pendingOwner field (named newOwner in the OwnershipFacet storage) that can later be activated through confirmOwnershipTransfer. When transferOwnershipToZeroAddress is called while a pendingOwner is already recorded, the pendingOwner is not cleared. Consequently, any address that was previously designated as pendingOwner can still invoke confirmOwnershipTransfer, which overwrites the zero address with the pendingOwner and re‑establishes full control over the contract. This occurs because the internal setContractOwner routine simply assigns a new address without checking whether the contract is supposed to be locked, and confirmOwnershipTransfer does not verify that the current owner is non‑zero before performing the transfer. The root cause is the incomplete state cleanup: the pendingOwner slot remains valid after the owner is set to address(0). An attacker who either was previously set as pendingOwner or can induce a pendingOwner entry can exploit this by calling confirmOwnershipTransfer, thereby regaining ownership and executing any privileged functions such as fund withdrawals, configuration changes, or contract upgrades. The impact is a loss of the intended immutability guarantee; the protocol can be taken over, user funds may be drained, and the trust model is broken. The issue manifests only when a pendingOwner exists at the moment the owner is zeroed, which may be hard to notice because the UI or on‑chain view shows the owner as 0x0, giving a false impression of a locked contract while the hidden pendingOwner slot still enables takeover. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete ownership revocation” or “state‑leakage during self‑destruct‑like operations”. It violates the business logic that setting the owner to zero should permanently disable any further ownership changes. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between transferOwnershipToZeroAddress, setContractOwner, and confirmOwnershipTransfer. To remediate, the contract should either clear the pendingOwner field when the owner is set to zero, forbid confirmOwnershipTransfer when the current owner is the zero address, or redesign the ownership model to eliminate a separate pendingOwner variable altogether. Additionally, providing a cancelOwnershipTransfer function that reliably resets pendingOwner, or removing the OwnershipFacet entirely, would prevent the residual ownership path from being exercised.

title: Receiver does not verify address from the originator chain
description: The Receiver contract is designed to receive the cross-chain call from libDiamond address on the destination chain. However, it does not verify the source chain address. An attacker can build a malicious _callData. An attacker can steal funds if there are left tokens and there are allowances to the Executor. Note that the tokens may be lost in issue: "Arithemetic underflow leading to unexpected revert and loss of funds in Receiver contract". And there may be allowances to Executor in issue "Receiver doesn't always reset allowance"
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a cross‑chain Receiver contract that accepts calldata from a bridge router without confirming that the call originated from the expected source chain address. Because the contract does not validate the _sender or the domain identifier supplied by the bridge, an attacker can craft a malicious _callData payload and submit it through the same router interface. When the Receiver contract processes this unauthenticated payload, it may invoke functions that move tokens held by the contract or that have been approved for the Executor contract. If there are leftover token balances and existing allowances, the attacker can trigger token transfers to an address of their choice, effectively stealing funds. The issue manifests only when the contract holds tokens and when an allowance to the Executor has not been cleared, conditions that are common after normal cross‑chain operations. It was discovered during a manual security audit (Spearbit) that highlighted the missing source‑address check and noted that related bugs such as arithmetic underflow and failure to reset allowances could amplify the loss. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external interface appears legitimate; users see a successful cross‑chain receipt and no explicit error, while the underlying logic silently authorises arbitrary calls. From a user perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero balance after a transfer that was reported as successful, or a refund that never arrives. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only the original sender on the source chain may trigger actions on the destination chain. To remediate, the contract should enforce strict verification of the originating address and domain ID, reject fast‑path calls that lack a verifiable sender, and ensure that any token allowance granted to the Executor is cleared after use. Implementing a check similar to the Amarok example—comparing the reported _sender against the known diamond address and handling the special case where _sender is address(0) with a safe fallback—will close the attack surface and restore confidence that cross‑chain calls cannot be hijacked.

title: Arithemetic underflow leading to unexpected revert and loss of funds in Receiver contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a bridge receiver contract that is supposed to return native funds to a user after a cross‑chain swap. The contract decides whether to forward the funds directly or to invoke an external executor by checking the remaining gas with gasleft(). Because gasleft() is called twice – once for the initial reserve‑gas check and a second time to calculate the gas stipend for the executor call – the second value is always smaller than the first as the EVM consumes gas between the two statements. An attacker can deliberately supply just enough gas so that the first check (gasleft() >= _recoverGas) passes, but after subtracting the reserved amount the second query yields a value that is lower than the 2300‑gas minimum required for a low‑level call. Consequently the try‑call to executor.swapAndCompleteBridgeTokens reverts due to insufficient gas, and the catch block, which attempts to forward the amount with receiver.call{value: amount}(''), also reverts because the remaining gas is below the call threshold. The net effect is that the native tokens remain locked in the Receiver contract, violating the expectation that the contract will always refund the user. This situation can be triggered only under a narrow set of gas conditions, making it hard to reproduce in standard testing and easy to overlook during code review. The issue was identified during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted that the dynamic gas calculation creates an implicit arithmetic under‑flow of the gas budget rather than a numeric under‑flow. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful transaction hash, but the balance of the recipient would stay unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of “gas‑budget mis‑management” or “insufficient‑gas forwarding” errors, where contract logic assumes a stable gas amount between checks. To remediate, the contract should cache the result of gasleft() in a local variable before any conditional logic and use that cached value for both the reserve‑gas comparison and the gas stipend supplied to the external call, optionally adding a safety margin to guarantee that the fallback call always has at least 2300 gas. This change eliminates the discrepancy between the two gas queries and ensures that the refund path cannot be unintentionally blocked, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the bridge protocol.

title: Use of name to identify a token
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the bridge function startBridgeTokensViaCelerIM using the token symbol (name) to decide whether a special handling path for the cfUSDC token should be taken. The contract computes the keccak256 hash of the symbol returned by ERC20(_bridgeData.sendingAssetId).symbol() and compares it to the hash of the literal string "cfUSDC". If the hashes match, the code treats the asset as a cfUSDC token and calls a canonical() function on the supplied contract to obtain the underlying ERC20 address that will actually be transferred. Because a token's symbol is mutable and not unique, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract that pretends to be an ERC20 token, sets its symbol to "cfUSDC", and implements a canonical() function that returns the address of any token the attacker controls, such as WETH. When a user initiates a bridge operation and passes the address of this counterfeit token as _bridgeData.sendingAssetId, the bridge logic will mistakenly believe it is dealing with the legitimate cfUSDC token, invoke the attacker‑controlled canonical() function, and transfer the attacker‑chosen token instead of the intended cfUSDC. This can cause user funds to be moved to an address controlled by the attacker, effectively stealing the assets. The issue occurs whenever the bridge function is called with a token whose symbol matches "cfUSDC" but whose address is not the genuine cfUSDC contract. It affects any user attempting to bridge cfUSDC through the CelerIMFacet, the protocol that relies on the bridge for cross‑chain transfers, and any downstream contracts that assume the transferred asset is the correct stablecoin. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the token identification logic and noticed the reliance on a mutable string property rather than a fixed address. The problem is subtle because checking a token's symbol is a common practice for readability, and the code appears to perform a specific check for a known token, leading reviewers to overlook the possibility of symbol spoofing. To remediate the issue, the contract should store the legitimate cfUSDC contract address as an immutable constant and enforce that the _bridgeData.sendingAssetId exactly matches this address, for example by using a onlyAllowSourceToken modifier. This eliminates reliance on mutable metadata and ensures that only the intended token can trigger the special handling path, thereby preventing an attacker from redirecting transfers to an arbitrary token. The bug belongs to the class of token‑identification or authentication bypass vulnerabilities where mutable on‑chain metadata is used for security decisions, leading to incorrect asset routing and potential loss of funds. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should have moved cfUSDC may instead result in a zero balance of cfUSDC and an unexpected increase of another token (or loss of value) in the attacker’s wallet, violating the expectation that the bridge will transfer the selected stablecoin.

title: Unvalidated destination address in Gravity faucet
description:
In the Gravity faucet, there is an issue related to the validation of the _gravityData.destinationAddress address. The code does not validate if the provided destination address is in the valid bech32 format.
This can potentially cause issues when sending tokens to the destination address. If the provided address is not in the bech32 format, the tokens can be locked. Also, it can lead to confusion for the end-users as they might enter an invalid address and lose their tokens without any warning or error message.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Gravity faucet contract where the destination address supplied by a user is not verified to conform to the bech32 encoding used by Cosmos‑based chains. Because the contract trusts the raw string without performing any format check, it may attempt to forward tokens to an address that is syntactically invalid. The root cause is the absence of input validation for the _gravityData.destinationAddress field, which allows any arbitrary byte sequence to be treated as a destination. An attacker or even an unwary user can provide a malformed address; the contract will still execute the transfer logic, resulting in the token transfer being recorded on‑chain but never reaching a valid recipient. Consequently the tokens become locked in an unreachable state, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. This situation occurs each time the faucet’s withdrawal function is called with a destination that does not satisfy the bech32 checksum rules, and it affects any participant who relies on the faucet to receive funds, including end‑users, developers testing the bridge, and the broader protocol that assumes successful payouts. The issue was uncovered during a security audit when the reviewer noted that no validation routine or library call was present to enforce the address format. It can be difficult to detect because the transaction does not revert; the blockchain records a successful transfer, the UI may display a success message, yet the recipient’s balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. From a user‑facing standpoint the symptom is that a user expects a refund or faucet payout but sees no increase in their wallet, sometimes observing a zero balance where tokens should have arrived. This class of bug falls under unchecked external input or address format validation failures, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that every outgoing transfer is directed to a reachable account. The recommended remediation is to integrate a bech32 validation library, such as Bech32.sol, and to reject any transaction where the destination address fails the checksum test, thereby preventing tokens from being sent to an invalid destination and preserving user funds.

title: Hardcode or whitelist the Thorswap vault address
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit function of the router contract, which accepts a user‑supplied vault address as a parameter and forwards assets to that address without any form of validation or whitelist enforcement. Because the contract does not verify that the supplied vault is a trusted Asgard vault, an attacker or a careless user can specify an arbitrary address, including a non‑existent contract, a malicious contract, or an address they control. When a user calls deposit with such an address, the router either sends the supplied ETH via the low‑level send call or credits the ERC‑20 amount to the internal allowance mapping for the chosen vault. If the address is incorrect, the transferred tokens become irretrievable, effectively disappearing from the user’s balance. The impact is a loss of funds for any participant who mistakenly or maliciously directs deposits to an untrusted vault; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all deposits end up in a known vault are broken, leading to mismatched balances and potential liquidity shortfalls. This condition can be triggered whenever a user invokes deposit with any vault argument, which is allowed by the public interface and is not restricted by modifiers or access control. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the function signature and observed the lack of address checks. It is subtle because the function emits a Deposit event that appears normal, and the router does not revert on unknown vaults, so the failure manifests only as missing tokens after a successful transaction. The appropriate remediation is to replace the free‑form vault parameter with either a hard‑coded vault address or a whitelist of known vault contracts, ensuring that only authorized vaults can receive deposits. This change restores the intended business logic that deposits are always routed to a trusted vault, preventing accidental or malicious loss of assets.

title: Remaining tokens can be sweeped from the LiFi Diamond or the Executor
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked asset sweep that allows any native or ERC20 token remaining in the LiFi Diamond contract or its Executor component to be transferred out by the generic swap functions used by the bridges. The root cause is the way the contracts calculate a "startingBalance" before performing a swap and then compare it with the balance after the swap. For native assets the code subtracts msg.value from the contract’s balance, but it does not protect the initial native balance that may already be present, and for intermediate tokens the balance is never recorded at all. Consequently, if the contract holds any dust or if an attacker deliberately deposits a small amount of native token, the post‑swap balance will be higher than the recorded starting balance and the difference is sent to the caller via LibAsset.transferAsset. This logic treats any increase in balance as swap output, even when the increase originates from tokens that were already in the contract, effectively enabling a sweep of leftover funds. An attacker can trigger a swap, cause the contract to think the extra tokens are swap proceeds, and receive them, draining any native token dust or larger amounts that may have been unintentionally left in the contracts. The impact is loss of protocol funds that should remain locked, breaking the accounting assumptions that the contracts never hold native tokens and that only the intended swap output is transferred. The issue manifests whenever any of the listed swap functions (swapAndCompleteBridgeTokensViaStargate, swapAndCompleteBridgeTokens, swapAndExecute, _executeAndCheckSwaps) are called while the contracts have a non‑zero native balance, which can happen due to accidental deposits or malicious funding. It affects the protocol’s treasury, any users relying on the contract to safeguard their assets, and the overall trustworthiness of the bridge. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the asset handling logic and noticed that the balance‑difference check does not differentiate between genuine swap output and pre‑existing funds. The problem is subtle because the contracts are not expected to hold native tokens, so the presence of a small dust balance may be overlooked, and the sweep code appears to be a harmless safety check. To remediate, the contracts should either remove the starting‑balance comparison entirely, enforce that no native tokens are ever held, or explicitly record and protect the initial balance of each token before any swap, ensuring that only the intended swap amount is transferred to the receiver. In other words, the accounting must be tightened so that leftover or intermediate token balances cannot be mistakenly swept away, eliminating the token‑sweep class of bug.

title: Wormhole bridge chain IDs are different than EVM chain IDs
description:
```solidity
According to documentation, Wormhole uses different chain ids than EVM based chain ids. However,
the code is implemented with block.chainid check. LiFi is integrated with third party platforms through API. The
API/UI side can implement chain id checks, but direct interaction with the contract can lead to loss of funds.
function _startBridge(WormholeData memory _wormholeData) private {
if (block.chainid == _wormholeData.toChainId) revert CannotBridgeToSameNetwork();
}
From other perspective, the following line limits the recipient address to an EVM address. If a bridge would be
done to a non EVM chain (e.g. Solana, Terra, Terra classic), then the tokens would be lost.
...
bytes32(uint256(uint160(_wormholeData.recipient)))
...
Example transactions below.
• Chainid 1 Solana
• Chainid 3 Terra Classic
On the other hand, the usage of the LiFi protocol depends largely on off chain APIs. It takes all values, fees, limits,
chain ids and addresses to be called from the APIs. As previously mentioned, the wormhole destination chain ids
are different than standard EVM based chains, the following event can be misinterpreted.
...
emit LiFiTransferStarted(
_lifiData.transactionId,
"wormhole",
"",
_lifiData.integrator,
_lifiData.referrer,
_swapData[0].sendingAssetId,
_lifiData.receivingAssetId,
_wormholeData.recipient,
_swapData[0].fromAmount,
_wormholeData.toChainId, // It does not show correct chain id which is expected by LiFi Data
Analytics
,
true,
false
);
...
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between the chain identifiers used by the Wormhole cross‑chain bridge and the native EVM chain identifiers that Solidity contracts expose via block.chainid. The LiFi integration implements a check that compares block.chainid with the Wormhole‑provided destination chain id (toChainId) and reverts when they are equal. Because Wormhole assigns its own numeric IDs that do not correspond to EVM chain IDs, the equality check is unreliable: a transaction intended for a different network may be incorrectly rejected, or conversely, a transaction may be allowed to proceed when the destination is actually the same network under Wormhole’s numbering scheme. In addition, the contract casts the Wormhole recipient address to an EVM‑style address using bytes32(uint256(uint160(_wormholeData.recipient))). This conversion truncates or misinterprets addresses that belong to non‑EVM chains such as Solana or Terra Classic, effectively sending tokens to an address that does not exist on the target chain. The emitted LiFiTransferStarted event also forwards the raw Wormhole toChainId, which off‑chain APIs and UI components expect to be an EVM chain id. Consequently, the front‑end may display a successful transfer while the underlying bridge has routed funds to an unsupported destination, leading to silent loss of assets. The impact is that users who initiate a bridge to a non‑EVM chain may see their balances unchanged, receive no tokens on the destination, and have no on‑chain mechanism to recover the funds because the tokens are locked on a chain where the contract does not exist. The issue occurs whenever a developer or user interacts directly with the LiFi contract’s _startBridge function, bypassing the off‑chain API validation, or when the contract is used to bridge to any Wormhole‑supported non‑EVM network. It was discovered during a security audit of the LiFi‑Wormhole integration, where the auditor noted the inconsistent use of chain identifiers and the unsafe address casting. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it merely results in missing funds, which can be mistaken for a UI or network delay. To remediate, the contract should maintain a deterministic mapping between EVM chain IDs and Wormhole chain IDs, validate that the destination chain is an EVM‑compatible network before performing the address cast, and emit the correct, mapped chain ID in events so that off‑chain services interpret the transfer accurately. By enforcing these checks, the contract can prevent accidental token loss and align on‑chain logic with Wormhole’s cross‑chain semantics.

title: Facets approve arbitrary addresses for ERC20 tokens
description:
```solidity
All the facets pointed above approve an address for an ERC20 token, where both these values are
provided by the user:
LibAsset.maxApproveERC20(IERC20(token), router, amount);
The parameter names change depending on the context. So for any ERC20 token that LifiDiamond contract
holds, user can:
• call any of the functions in these facets to approve another address for that token.
• use the approved address to transfer tokens out of LifiDiamond contract.
Note: normally there shouldn’t be any tokens in the LiFi Diamond contract so the risk is limited. Note: also see
"Hardcode bridge addresses via immutable"
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked token approval mechanism that allows any caller to designate an arbitrary address as an approved spender for any ERC20 token held by the LifiDiamond contract. The root cause is that several diamond facets expose a helper function (LibAsset.maxApproveERC20) where the spender address (often called router) is taken directly from user‑supplied input without validation against a whitelist of known bridge contracts. Because the contract does not restrict which address can be approved, a malicious actor can invoke any of the exposed facet functions, pass a chosen token address and a malicious spender address, and set an allowance for that spender equal to the amount parameter. Once the allowance is granted, the attacker can call transferFrom on the token contract to move the approved tokens out of the LifiDiamond contract to an address they control. This can be exploited whenever the LifiDiamond contract holds a non‑zero balance of an ERC20 token – for example after a user initiates a cross‑chain swap that temporarily locks tokens in the contract. The impact is the potential loss of user funds: the attacker can drain all tokens of the approved type, leaving the contract balance at zero and users receiving no output from their swap. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a transaction they see their expected token balance disappear or the swap returns zero tokens, even though the transaction appeared to succeed. The issue is discovered during a security audit that inspected the facet implementations and noticed that the spender parameter is not hard‑coded or stored immutably but is instead passed directly from the caller. The bug is subtle because the contract is not intended to retain tokens for long periods, so developers may assume that token loss is unlikely; however, any transient token holding becomes a target. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unrestricted token approval” or “arbitrary allowance grant” bugs, which violate the accounting assumption that only trusted bridge contracts may be authorized to move funds. To remediate, each facet should replace the user‑provided spender address with a pre‑defined, immutable bridge contract address stored in the contract’s state, and the approval logic should only be executed for those whitelisted addresses. This eliminates the ability for an attacker to approve a malicious address and prevents unauthorized token transfers.

title: FeeCollector not well integrated
description:
```solidity
There is a contract to pay fees for using the bridge: FeeCollector. This is used by crafting a
transaction by the frontend API, which then calls the contract via _executeAndCheckSwaps().
Here is an example of the contract Here is an example of the contract of such a transaction Its whitelisted here
This way no fees are paid if a developer is using the LiFi contracts directly. Also it is using a mechanism that isn’t
suited for this. The _executeAndCheckSwaps() is geared for swaps and has several checks on balances. These
(and future) checks could interfere with the fee payments. Also this is a complicated and non transparent approach.
The project has suggested to see _executeAndCheckSwaps() as a multicall mechanism.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way fee payments are handled in the bridge system through the FeeCollector contract. Instead of using a dedicated, transparent mechanism, the fee transfer is performed inside the internal function _executeAndCheckSwaps(), which was originally designed to execute token swaps and enforce balance‑related checks. Because the function contains multiple assertions that verify swap outcomes, those same checks can unintentionally block or skip the fee transfer when the fee logic is mixed with swap logic.
