description: An empty market refers to a market with little or no liquidity, which can occur when a new market is created and listed without initial liquidity from the creator, etc. One of the most common vulnerabilities of empty markets is exchange-rate inflation, i.e., inflating the totalPooled amount while keeping totalSupply as a small number, which can be done through direct donations or stealth donations. Specifically, stealth donations occur due to rounding errors when users mint or redeem tokens, which increases the exchange rate. For example, assuming an attacker holds 1 oToken (in the smallest unit), and the initial exchange rate is 2, i.e., 1 oToken is worth 2 underlying tokens. The attacker can: 1. Mint 0 oToken with 1 underlying token. The exchange rate becomes 3. 2. Mint 0 oToken with 2 underlying tokens. The exchange rate becomes 5. 3. Mint 0 oToken with 4 underlying tokens. The exchange rate becomes 9. and so on. The attacker will be able to inflate the exchange rate exponentially. Although the attacker effectively donates their funds to the market through minting, they do not incur a loss as they hold the only oToken, which can redeem all the underlying tokens afterward. If the markets have an initial exchange rate of 1, the attacker could first mint some oTokens and borrow the underlying tokens with some collateral in the other markets. After one block has passed, interest will be accrued, causing the exchange rate to exceed 1. The attacker then burns all the tokens except 1, resulting in 2 underlying tokens left in the market and, therefore, achieving the initial condition. Exchange-rate inflation could lead to security issues when combined with other vulnerabilities, e.g., incorrect rounding directions. Compound V2 implemented an incorrect rounding direction in the redeem function, which has caused several incidents on Compound V2 forks, i.e., the empty market attack. The attackers were able to inflate the exchange rate first to increase the impact caused by the incorrect rounding direction and, therefore, redeem their donated tokens and left the position with a large debt. For the reviewed protocol, the rounding direction when a user redeems an underlying token is correct. However, we identified an incorrect rounding direction in calculating the seized collateral from a borrower, which can potentially cause a more significant impact when combined with exchange-rate inflation. See the finding "Incorrect rounding direction when calculating the seized collateral from the borrower". Every market should have sufficient liquidity to mitigate exchange-rate inflation attacks. Note that stealth donations are still possible even though the markets have enough liquidity. However, it would be inefficient or impractical for attackers to execute, and they are also more likely to incur a loss due to donations since they do not hold most of the oTokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exchange‑rate inflation attack that becomes possible when a market is launched with little or no liquidity. Because the protocol calculates the price of the interest‑bearing token (oToken) as totalPooled divided by totalSupply, an attacker can increase totalPooled by sending underlying tokens to the pool without receiving any oTokens – a “stealth donation”. Rounding errors in the mint or redeem logic cause the contract to treat the donation as a mint of zero oTokens, which raises the exchange rate. By repeatedly performing such zero‑mint operations the attacker can make the exchange rate grow exponentially while keeping totalSupply unchanged. Once the rate is inflated, the attacker can redeem the single oToken they own for a much larger amount of underlying assets, or combine the inflated rate with an incorrect rounding direction in the collateral‑seizure calculation to create a position that shows a large debt while the attacker walks away with excess funds. The attack works especially on newly created markets that have an initial exchange rate of 1 and no external liquidity, and it can also be triggered after a block of interest accrual when the rate naturally exceeds 1. The impact is that the protocol may lose a significant amount of underlying tokens, borrowers may be left with an artificially high debt, and users may see their balances or redemption amounts become inconsistent with expectations – for example a user expects to receive a proportional amount of underlying tokens but receives far more or far less, or the market’s exchange rate displayed in the UI jumps from 1 to a much higher value without obvious cause. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined rounding behavior and market initialization logic. It is hard to notice because the attacker’s donations do not generate visible token balances and the exchange‑rate change can be attributed to normal interest accrual, especially in low‑liquidity environments. The recommended mitigation is to prevent the market from being usable until sufficient liquidity is provided, for example by setting the collateral factor to zero at launch, minting a protective amount of oTokens and locking them, and only enabling the market after the pool has enough backing. Additionally, the rounding direction in all calculations that involve seized collateral must be verified to match the intended floor/ceil semantics. By ensuring a baseline liquidity and correct rounding, the protocol removes the ability to inflate the exchange rate through stealth donations and protects users and lenders from unexpected loss of funds.

title: Incomplete Validation in isAddress()
description: The isAddress() function in assertions.lua validates the input and returns whether the input is a valid address string. However, there are two issues in the implementation: 1. At assertions.lua#L10, the comparison not type(addr) == "string" should be type(addr) ~= "string" instead since the not operation has higher precedence than ==. 2. At assertions.lua#L12, the regex check should be string.match(addr, "^[A-z0-9_-]+$"), i.e., including the ^ and $ metacharacters, to ensure that all characters are valid.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a utility routine that checks whether a supplied value conforms to the expected format of a blockchain address string. The routine attempts to verify two conditions: that the input is of type string and that it matches a regular‑expression pattern consisting only of alphanumeric characters, underscores or hyphens. Because of a precedence mistake, the type check is written as "not type(addr) == \"string\"". In the language used, the logical NOT operator is evaluated before the equality comparison, so the expression is interpreted as "(not type(addr)) == \"string\"". Since "not type(addr)" always yields a boolean value (false for any non‑nil type), the comparison with the literal string "string" is never true, meaning the guard never rejects non‑string inputs. Consequently, callers can pass numbers, tables or other objects without triggering the intended error. The second flaw is an incomplete regular‑expression match: the code calls string.match(addr, "[A-z0-9_-]+") without anchoring the pattern with ^ and $. Without these anchors the engine returns a match as soon as any substring of the input satisfies the character class, allowing strings that contain illegal characters before or after a valid segment to be accepted. Together, these bugs constitute an incomplete validation routine that may deem malformed or non‑string values as legitimate addresses. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a crafted argument that bypasses the address check, causing downstream contract logic that assumes a well‑formed address to behave incorrectly – for example, invoking a function with a nil or malformed address, triggering unexpected reverts, loss of funds, or bypassing access‑control checks that rely on address validation. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken: users may see transactions fail silently, balances appear unchanged, or funds be sent to an unintended destination because the address was not properly vetted. The issue manifests whenever the isAddress() helper is invoked, which is typically during input sanitisation for user‑provided identifiers, token transfers, or permission checks. Developers and auditors discovered the problem during a systematic code review that highlighted logical operators and pattern‑matching semantics. The bug can be subtle because the function still returns true for many common inputs, so superficial testing with well‑formed strings does not reveal the flaw. To remediate, the type guard should be rewritten using the correct inequality operator (type(addr) ~= "string") and the regular‑expression should be anchored ("^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$") to ensure the entire string complies with the allowed character set. This restores proper validation, preventing malformed inputs from propagating through the system and preserving the intended security and accounting guarantees.

title: Incorrect Update of Auction List after Liquidation
description: When liquidating a position, the removeWhenDone variable indicates whether the position should be removed from the auction list after the current liquidation. According to the comment: The auction needs to be removed if there will be no loans left when the liquidation is complete. Based on this comment, the comparison at L690 should be == nil instead. It is because if the position has no action loan after the liquidation, the util.find() function would return a nil. However, instead of checking if the position has an active loan, a more accurate way is to check if the position would become healthy after liquidation. The position should be kept on the auction list if it is still unhealthy. Otherwise, it should be removed. The current method would still keep a healthy position with an active loan on the auction list.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the logic that decides whether a liquidated position should be removed from the auction list. When a liquidation finishes, a flag called removeWhenDone is set to indicate that the position may be removed if no loans remain. The contract currently checks the result of a util.find() call at line 690 and compares it against nil using an equality that expects a non‑nil value, i.e., it removes the entry only when the find function returns a non‑nil reference. This logic is inverted: if the liquidation makes the position healthy, util.find() will return nil, but the code does not treat this case as a removal condition. Consequently, a position that has become healthy after liquidation can remain on the auction list as long as it still has an active loan record. The root cause is a mistaken comparison and the use of loan existence rather than the health status of the position to decide removal. An attacker or any caller can trigger a liquidation that results in a healthy position staying in the auction list, causing the auction mechanism to repeatedly attempt to auction a position that no longer requires liquidation. This can lead to wasted gas, potential loss of collateral if the auction logic assumes the position is still unsafe, and confusing UI symptoms where users see their position still listed for auction despite having a healthy loan. The issue manifests only after a liquidation where removeWhenDone is true and the contract reaches the faulty comparison; it does not affect positions that remain unhealthy. It was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noted that the comment describing the intended behavior does not match the implemented condition. The bug is subtle because the auction may simply skip execution for a healthy entry, leaving no obvious error, while the list state is incorrect. To remediate, the comparison at line 690 should be changed to check for nil (or equivalently verify that the position would be healthy after liquidation) and the removal logic should be based on the post‑liquidation health status rather than the presence of an active loan. This ensures that only truly unhealthy positions stay in the auction list, aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended business logic and preventing unnecessary auctions and potential fund loss.

title: Position enumeration in sync-auctions handler can lead to DoS when processing large numbers of positions
description: The LiquidOps protocol's sync-auctions handler performs a scan of all market positions to identify underwater positions eligible for liquidation. This handler executes a computationally intensive process that: 1. Fetches all token prices from the oracle. 2. Queries all positions across all markets. 3. Processes and aggregates every user position. 4. Evaluates each position's liquidation eligibility. -- POSITION DATA COLLECTION -- Prepare to query all positions across all markets (oTokens) -- by creating message requests for each market in the system.---@type MessageParam[] local positionMsgs = {} for _, token in ipairs(Tokens) do table.insert(positionMsgs, { Target = token.oToken, Action = "Positions" }) end -- MULTI-MARKET POSITION FETCHING -- Execute all the position queries in parallel and collect responses. -- Each response contains all user positions in a specific market.---@type Message[] local rawPositions = scheduler.schedule(table.unpack(positionMsgs)) This position scanning process scales linearly with the number of positions (O(n) complexity), resulting in performance degradation as the position count increases. An attacker could create numerous small positions across different markets, forcing the system to process each one during liquidation checks. Since the handler iterates through all positions, this could significantly slow down the protocol's operations when the number of positions grows large. Importantly, this scaling issue can arise not only from malicious activity but also naturally as the protocol gains adoption and more users create positions. Additionally, the protocol doesn't clear positions when they're fully repaid, instead keeping them with zero values, which may lead to unnecessary processing of empty positions and wasted storage resources.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a scalability and denial-of-service issue in the sync-auctions handler of the LiquidOps protocol. The handler enumerates every user position across all markets to decide which positions are underwater and should be liquidated. Because the enumeration is performed with a simple linear scan (O(n)) and the code does not discard positions that have been fully repaid, the handler must process even empty entries. When the number of positions grows, either organically as the protocol gains users or artificially because an attacker opens a large number of tiny positions in many markets, the handler consumes excessive computation and gas. This can cause the liquidation routine to become extremely slow, time out, or run out of gas, effectively preventing timely liquidations. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a liquidation transaction is pending for a long time, that no liquidation occurs even though a position is clearly underwater, or that a transaction reverts with an out-of-gas error. The root cause is the lack of pagination, limits, or pruning of zero-value positions, combined with a design that forces a single call to iterate over the entire position set. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the message-passing logic of the sync-auctions handler. It is hard to notice because the function works correctly for small numbers of positions, and the performance degradation appears only as latency, not as an outright failure. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded enumeration or resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities, where a contract processes an unbounded list without safeguards. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum position size or require explicit closure of fully repaid positions, delete zero-value entries from storage, introduce batching or pagination so that only a bounded number of positions are examined per call, move the heavy work to a separate process, and optionally add a modest fee to discourage spamming. These changes would restore predictable execution time, prevent denial-of-service attacks, and reduce unnecessary storage costs.

title: Tokens not always refunded
description: In process.lua tokens are refunded when From ~= CollateralID. However if transfers do have From == CollateralID, the X-tag could be specified incorrectly or could not be forwarded due to a bug in the token contract. In controller.lua there is no code to refund tokens if the X-tag isn't Liquidate. This can happen with the supplied libraries, see finding Tag "X-Action" = "Liquidate" missing in Javascript library. If the tokens aren't returned then they stay stuck in process.lua / controller.lua , although they can be recovery by the protocol via batch-update and other management actions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a conditional refund mechanism that only returns tokens when the sender address (From) differs from the collateral identifier (CollateralID) and when an X‑tag labelled Liquidate is present. When a transfer is initiated with From equal to CollateralID, or when the X‑tag is missing or incorrectly set because of a bug in the supplied JavaScript library or in the token contract’s forwarding logic, the refund path is never executed. As a result the tokens remain locked inside the internal process.lua and controller.lua modules instead of being sent back to the user or the original collateral holder. This situation can arise during normal liquidation workflows, especially when the library fails to attach the required X‑Action=Liquidate metadata. Users experience the symptom of receiving no refund, seeing their balance unchanged or suddenly zero, and may interpret the loss as a scam or a protocol failure. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the refund conditions and the handling of X‑tags. Because the majority of transfers satisfy the From != CollateralID check, the bug only manifests in edge cases, making it difficult to notice without targeted testing. The impact is that funds become effectively inaccessible, breaking the accounting assumptions that collateral must be returned after liquidation. The protocol can eventually recover the stuck tokens through batch‑update or other management actions, but this requires manual intervention and does not restore the expected user experience. The recommended remediation is to extend the refund logic to cover cases where From equals CollateralID and where the X‑tag is absent or malformed, and to ensure that the token contract correctly propagates the X‑tag metadata. By treating the refund as a generic accounting invariant rather than a narrow conditional, the contract can avoid the class of bugs where tokens disappear due to missing metadata or overly specific refund conditions.

title: new deposits be incorrectly rejected due to false "maxCapReached" errors.
bug_full: During the liquidation path of the perpetual vault the contract sets curPositionKey to zero when the position size becomes zero, but it does not clear the accounting variable totalDepositAmount. When a user later calls withdraw, the internal logic detects a liquidated vault (curPositionKey == 0) and calls _handleReturn with a zero collateral balance. Because the balance of the collateral token is zero, the calculation of the withdrawal amount results in zero, so the subsequent call to _transferToken is skipped. The line that reduces totalDepositAmount is placed inside the transfer function, therefore it never executes. As a result totalDepositAmount remains at its pre‑liquidation value even though all assets have been withdrawn. The stale totalDepositAmount makes the contract believe that the maximum deposit cap has already been reached, causing new deposit attempts to be rejected with a maxCapReached error. This bug appears only after a full liquidation followed by withdrawals, and it affects any user trying to deposit or withdraw, as well as the protocol’s accounting of assets under management. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation and withdrawal flow, where the auditors observed that the accounting variable never changed after liquidation. It is hard to notice because no transfer events are emitted and the contract balance is zero, giving the impression that the operation succeeded. The impact is inaccurate protocol accounting, potential denial of service for new depositors, and loss of confidence in the vault’s financial reporting. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting state‑inconsistency bugs caused by conditional execution paths that skip critical state updates. To fix the issue the decrement of totalDepositAmount should be performed unconditionally, for example by moving the subtraction outside the token‑transfer function or by resetting totalDepositAmount when the vault is fully liquidated.

title: No liquidation incentives if the discount interval has passed
description: When a position is liquidated, a discount factor is calculated based on the time that has passed since the start of the auction. The auction follows a Dutch auction design, where the discount factor decreases linearly to zero if a configured period, DiscountInterval has passed. However, it is better to keep a non-zero discount even if the period has passed, which would ensure that liquidators have an incentive to liquidate underwater positions in the system. Otherwise, without being liquidated, the position's debt could increase over time and potentially become bad debt, which puts the protocol at risk of insolvency.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing liquidation incentive once the configured discount interval of a Dutch auction has elapsed. In the protocol, when a borrower’s position becomes under‑collateralised, a liquidator can trigger a liquidation auction. The auction applies a discount factor that linearly decreases over time, reaching zero after the DiscountInterval expires. Because the discount factor is used to calculate the profit that a liquidator receives, a zero discount means the liquidator gains no economic benefit from executing the liquidation. The root cause is the design choice to let the discount decay to exactly zero without a floor, so the contract does not enforce a minimum reward for liquidators. An attacker or a passive borrower can exploit this by allowing the auction to run past the interval; liquidators, seeing no profit, may ignore the liquidation opportunity, allowing the debt to continue accruing interest. Over time the outstanding debt can exceed the value of the collateral, turning into bad debt and potentially pushing the protocol toward insolvency. This condition occurs whenever a position remains underwater for longer than the DiscountInterval, which can happen in normal market downturns or under volatile price movements. All participants who rely on the protocol’s solvency – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the risk of unrecoverable debt increases. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the liquidation logic and noticed that the discount factor is set to zero after the interval, providing no fallback incentive. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit warning; the UI may simply show a zero discount and the liquidator receives no reward, which may be interpreted as a normal outcome rather than a flaw. The appropriate remediation is to introduce a configurable minimum discount factor (a floor) that remains positive after the DiscountInterval, ensuring that liquidators always retain a non‑zero incentive to act. This change restores the economic guarantee that underwater positions will be cleared before they become unrecoverable, aligning the implementation with the intended accounting model where every liquidation yields a reward that compensates the risk taken by the liquidator.

title: UpdateInProgress only checked in a limited number of situations
description: UpdateInProgress is only checked in a limited number of situations: only during "Add-To-Queue", which is send in Borrow(), Transfer() and Redeem(). However the updates are powerful and can perform an arbitrary action on all oTokens. Such an update could influence all actions.
bug_full: UpdateInProgress is a boolean flag that signals that a global configuration change or upgrade is being applied to the protocol. The contract only verifies this flag inside the internal Add‑To‑Queue routine, which is invoked from the public Borrow, Transfer and Redeem functions. Because the flag is not checked in any other entry points, an attacker who can trigger an update while a user is executing a different action can cause the update logic to run concurrently with normal token operations. The update routine is capable of executing an arbitrary call on every oToken, meaning it can modify balances, change permissions or invoke external contracts. If the flag is ignored, the protocol may process a borrow, a transfer or a redemption while the state is being altered, leading to inconsistent accounting, loss of funds or unexpected reverts. The vulnerability manifests when a malicious actor initiates a governance update (or any function that sets UpdateInProgress) and then quickly calls Borrow, Transfer or Redeem before the flag is cleared. From the user’s perspective the transaction may succeed but result in a zero balance, a missing refund, or a silent failure where no error is returned. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that noted the limited placement of the UpdateInProgress check. It can be hard to notice because the flag works correctly for the three functions that explicitly call Add‑To‑Queue, giving a false sense of safety, while other pathways remain unprotected. The bug belongs to the class of incomplete state‑guard checks or partial reentrancy protection. To remediate, the contract should enforce the UpdateInProgress guard on every external‑facing function that mutates state, and also add a guard in the routine that processes queued updates (Check‑Queue‑For). This ensures that no token operation can be performed while a global update is in progress, preserving accounting invariants and preventing arbitrary actions on all oTokens.

title: Potential race condition between repayments and liquidations due to missing queue check, may allow incorrect accounting
description: The LiquidOps protocol has a potential race condition between loan repayments and liquidations that can lead to accounting inconsistencies. The issue exists because the repay.handler function does not check if the user is in the controller's LiquidationQueue before processing a repayment. While the initial transfer handler is wrapped with queue.useQueue() which performs queue checks, the internal repay.handler that processes the Credit-Notice with X-Action = "Repay" lacks this protection: Handlers.advanced({ name = "borrow-repay", pattern = { From = CollateralID, Action = "Credit-Notice", ["X-Action"] = "Repay" }, handle = repay.handler, errorHandler = repay.error }) In the repay.handler function, no queue check is performed: function repay.handler(msg) assert( assertions.isTokenQuantity(msg.Tags.Quantity), "Invalid incoming transfer quantity" ) -- quantity of tokens supplied local quantity = bint(msg.Tags.Quantity) -- allow repaying on behalf of someone else local target = msg.Tags["X-On-Behalf"] or msg.Tags.Sender -- check if a loan can be repaid for the target assert( repay.canRepay(target, msg.Timestamp), "Cannot repay a loan for this user" ) -- execute repay local refundQty, actualRepaidQty = repay.repayToPool( target, quantity, true ) -- Rest of the function... } Meanwhile, the controller's liquidation process adds users to the LiquidationQueue during liquidation: -- Add the target to the liquidation queue to lock further liquidations table.insert(LiquidationQueue, target) -- ... liquidation processing ... -- Remove target from liquidation queue after completion LiquidationQueue = utils.filter( function (v) return v ~= target end, LiquidationQueue ) Impact: This race condition can lead to a an incorrect accounting scenario where both repayment and liquidation succeed simultaneously and is as follows:
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition between loan repayment and liquidation operations in the LiquidOps protocol. The root cause is that the internal repay.handler, which processes a Credit‑Notice with X‑Action set to "Repay", does not verify whether the borrower is currently listed in the controller’s LiquidationQueue. The liquidation workflow explicitly inserts the borrower into this queue before performing any liquidation steps and removes the borrower only after the liquidation completes. Because the repayment handler bypasses this queue check, a repayment transaction can be accepted while a liquidation is still in progress. An attacker (or any user) can therefore submit a repayment on‑behalf of the target either just before or during the liquidation window. The protocol will then execute both the repayment logic (updating the pool balance and marking part of the debt as repaid) and the liquidation logic (seizing collateral and adjusting the pool) as if they were independent, leading to inconsistent accounting where the same debt is considered both repaid and liquidated. The impact includes potential loss of funds for lenders, incorrect pool balances, and unfair penalties for borrowers because the protocol may liquidate a loan that has already been partially or fully repaid. This condition occurs only when a borrower has been added to the LiquidationQueue and a repayment transaction reaches the contract before the queue entry is cleared. The affected parties are borrowers who expect their repayment to stop liquidation, lenders who rely on accurate pool accounting, and the protocol itself which may breach its financial guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the registration of handlers; the audit team noticed that the outer transfer handler is wrapped with queue.useQueue() while the inner repay.handler lacks any such protection. Because both operations succeed without reverting, the bug can remain hidden in normal operation and may only surface as a discrepancy in internal accounting reports or during stress testing. To remediate, the repayment handler should be wrapped with the same queue check used by other position‑modifying handlers, or it should explicitly assert that the caller is not present in the LiquidationQueue before proceeding. Conceptually, the fix restores atomicity between mutually exclusive state transitions, preventing concurrent execution of repayment and liquidation for the same user. This class of bug is a race condition caused by missing synchronization or locking mechanisms, similar to other state‑inconsistent patterns where two mutually exclusive actions can be triggered simultaneously. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as a loan that appears repaid in the UI while the collateral is still seized, or a sudden drop in the borrower’s balance with no clear explanation. Expectations that a repayment stops liquidation are violated, leading to “funds disappear” or “collateral taken despite repayment” scenarios, which break the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Incorrect implementation of supplyRate()
description: The supplyRate() function in interest.lua calculates the supply rate based on the current borrow and utilization rates. However, the implementation is incorrect and has two issues: 1. At interest.lua#L54, borrowRateFloat is calculated as borrowRate / rateMul and, therefore, does not need to be divided by rateMul again at interest.lua#L60. 2. At interest.lua#L61, the utilization rate is incorrectly calculated as TotalBorrows / TotalSupply / 10 ^ CollateralDenomination. It should be TotalBorrows / (TotalBorrows + Cash) by definition.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the supplyRate() routine that determines the interest rate paid to lenders based on the current borrow activity and utilization of the pool. The function contains two mathematical mistakes. First, the intermediate variable representing the borrow rate is derived by dividing the raw borrowRate by a scaling constant (rateMul). The code then mistakenly divides this already‑scaled value by the same constant a second time, which shrinks the effective borrow rate far below its intended magnitude. Second, the utilization ratio – the proportion of assets that are currently borrowed – is computed as TotalBorrows divided by TotalSupply and then further divided by 10 raised to the CollateralDenomination. By definition, utilization must be calculated as TotalBorrows divided by the sum of TotalBorrows and the available cash (TotalBorrows/(TotalBorrows+Cash)). Using the incorrect formula dramatically under‑estimates utilization when cash is present and over‑estimates it when cash is low. Because supplyRate() feeds directly into the accrual of lender rewards, the mis‑calculation leads to an inaccurate APY displayed to users and recorded on‑chain. In practice a lender may see a lower return than promised, while borrowers may benefit from a lower cost of borrowing than the protocol intended. The bug manifests whenever the contract updates interest – typically at each block or on user‑triggered actions such as deposits, withdrawals, or borrows. All participants that rely on the reported supply rate – lenders, borrowers, and any external analytics – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual security review by the Spearbit audit team, who identified the redundant division and the wrong utilization expression as logical errors. Because the rates still appear plausible, the problem can remain hidden unless the numbers are compared against expected financial models or external benchmarks. To remediate, the supplyRate() implementation should be rewritten to remove the second division by rateMul and to compute utilization as TotalBorrows/(TotalBorrows+Cash) using the correct arithmetic precedence. After correction, the reported supply rate will align with the protocol’s economic design, ensuring that users receive the interest they expect and that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.

title: `_harvest` has no slippage protection when swapping `auraBAL` for `AURA`
description: Single swaps of `_harvest` contains no slippage or deadline, which makes it vulnerable to sandwich attacks, MEV exploits and may lead to significant loss of yield.
poc:
When using `BALANCER_VAULT.swap` [here](https://github.com/Badger-Finance/vested-aura/blob/d504684e4f9b56660a9e6c6dfb839dcebac3c174/contracts/MyStrategy.sol#L249) and [here](https://github.com/Badger-Finance/vested-aura/blob/d504684e4f9b56660a9e6c6dfb839dcebac3c174/contracts/MyStrategy.sol#L275), there is no slippage protection. Therefore a call to `_harvest` generating swaps could be exploited for sandwich attacks or other MEV exploits such as [JIT](https://twitter.com/bertcmiller/status/1459175379265073155).

The scenario would be: A authorized actor calls `harvest`, leading to a swap of say x `auraBAL` to `BAL/ETH BPT` and then y `WETH` to `BAL`.

Then while the transaction is in the mempool, it is exploited for example like in <https://medium.com/coinmonks/defi-sandwich-attack-explain-776f6f43b2fd>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the `_harvest` function of the strategy contract, where a single swap operation that converts `auraBAL` tokens into `AURA` is executed without any slippage protection or transaction deadline. The root cause is that the call to `BALANCER_VAULT.swap` is performed with only the input amount specified, leaving the output amount completely uncontrolled. Because the swap does not enforce a minimum acceptable amount of `AURA` to be received, an attacker who can observe the pending transaction in the mempool can front‑run it with a sandwich attack or other MEV technique, such as a just‑in‑time (JIT) arbitrage. In a typical exploitation scenario, an authorized actor triggers `harvest`, which initiates the swap of a certain quantity of `auraBAL` to a Balancer pool token and subsequently swaps the resulting WETH for BAL. While the transaction is pending, a malicious actor submits a preceding transaction that alters the pool price, causing the swap in `_harvest` to execute at a far worse rate. The attacker then follows with a trailing transaction to restore the price, capturing the price difference as profit. The impact is a reduction in the yield that the strategy would otherwise generate, effectively causing funds to be lost or the user’s expected reward to be reduced. This issue manifests whenever `harvest` is called, regardless of the caller, because the function assumes that the caller is trusted and therefore does not implement defensive checks. Users of the protocol experience symptoms such as lower than expected claim amounts, missing rewards, or even outright loss of harvested value when they receive fewer `AURA` tokens than anticipated. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which highlighted the absence of slippage checks as a potential vector for MEV exploitation. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert on unfavorable rates; instead it silently accepts whatever amount the pool returns, making the loss appear as normal variance rather than a security breach. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a slippage tolerance parameter, for example by specifying a minimum amount of `AURA` that must be received from the swap, or by integrating a price‑oracle‑backed limit. Alternatively, using a DEX aggregator such as CowSwap that provides built-in slippage protection can mitigate the risk. Additionally, executing the harvest via private transactions reduces the exposure window for front‑running. Overall, the vulnerability belongs to the class of “unprotected token swaps” where missing slippage safeguards enable sandwich and other MEV attacks, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that harvested rewards are delivered at fair market rates.

title: Badger rewards from Hidden Hand can permanently prevent Strategy from receiving bribes
description: If the contract receives rewards from the hidden hand marketplace in BADGER then the contract tries to transfer the same amount of tokens twice to two different accounts, once with `_sendBadgerToTree()` in `MyStrategy` and again with `_processExtraToken()` in the `BasicStrategy` contract. As it is very likely that the strategy will not start with any BADGER tokens, the second transfer will revert (as we are using safeTransfer). This means that `claimBribesFromHiddenHand()` will always revert preventing any other bribes from being received.
poc:
1. `claimBribesFromHiddenHand()` is called by strategist
  2. Multiple bribes are sent to the strategy including BADGER. For example lets say 50 USDT And 50 BADGER
  3. Strategy receives BADGER and calls `_handleRewardTransfer()` which calls `_sendBadgerToTree()`. 50 BADGER is sent to the Badger Tree so balance has dropped to 0.
  4. 50 Badger is then again sent to Vault however balance is 0 so the command fails and reverts
  5. No more tokens can be claimed anymore
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the Badger strategy’s reward handling routine when the contract receives BADGER tokens from the Hidden Hand marketplace. The function claimBribesFromHiddenHand triggers a transfer of the received BADGER amount twice: first, _sendBadgerToTree() sends the tokens directly to the Badger Tree via a safeTransfer, and then the same amount is handed to _processExtraToken(), which again attempts to forward the Badger tokens to the Vault. Because the first transfer depletes the strategy’s BADGER balance, the second safeTransfer finds a zero balance and reverts, causing the entire claimBribesFromHiddenHand transaction to fail. This logic error manifests only when BADGER rewards are part of the bribe payload; if no BADGER is included, the routine executes without error, making the problem easy to miss during casual testing. The root cause is a developer oversight: the code performs a duplicate token transfer without checking the remaining balance, violating the accounting assumption that token transfers are idempotent. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker or honest participant who triggers a claim that includes any BADGER amount will cause the transaction to revert, permanently blocking any subsequent bribe claims for that strategy. From the user’s perspective the strategy suddenly stops receiving any rewards: the UI shows zero BADGER balance after a claim, and further attempts to claim bribes return with no tokens deposited, contrary to the expectation that rewards should be accumulated. The impact is medium severity because it does not directly lead to loss of already‑held funds, but it effectively silences future revenue streams for strategy operators. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit where the double‑transfer pattern was identified and reproduced in a proof‑of‑concept scenario. Fixing the bug requires removing the redundant transfer: the _sendBadgerToTree function should delegate to _processExtraToken without first sending the tokens directly, ensuring that only a single safeTransfer occurs and that the accounting remains consistent. By correcting the flow, the strategy regains the ability to claim and distribute Badger bribes as intended, restoring the expected financial behavior of the protocol.

title: Withdrawing all funds at once to vault can be DoS attacked by frontrunning and locking dust
description:
All funds can be migrated (withdrawn) at once to the caller vault by using the `BaseStrategy.withdrawToVault` function which internally calls `MyStrategy._withdrawAll`.

The latter function has the following check in place:

[MyStrategy.sol#L184-L187](https://github.com/Badger-Finance/vested-aura/blob/d504684e4f9b56660a9e6c6dfb839dcebac3c174/contracts/MyStrategy.sol#L184-L187)

```solidity
require(
    balanceOfPool() == 0 && LOCKER.balanceOf(address(this)) == 0,
    "You have to wait for unlock or have to manually rebalance out of it"
);
```

Funds can only be withdrawn (migrated) if the balance in `LOCKER` is fully unlocked.

By locking a small amount of want tokens via `AuraLocker.lock` with the `strategy` address, a malicious individual can cause DoS and prevent withdrawing and migrating funds to the vault.

```solidity

```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a strategy attempts to migrate all of its assets back to its vault using the BaseStrategy.withdrawToVault function, which internally invokes MyStrategy._withdrawAll. Within _withdrawAll there is a strict require statement that asserts both the pool balance and the balance held in an external AuraLocker contract (LOCKER) are exactly zero before any funds can be transferred. This invariant assumes that all locked want tokens are fully unlocked, but the contract does not call the LOCKER’s processExpiredLocks method before performing the check. Consequently, any non‑zero amount of want tokens that remains locked—even a single wei of “dust”—causes the require to fail, reverting the entire withdrawal transaction. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a migration or by simply locking a tiny amount of tokens for the strategy address through AuraLocker.lock. When the governance or a trusted operator later calls withdrawToVault, the transaction aborts with the message “You have to wait for unlock or have to manually rebalance out of it”. From a user’s perspective the UI may display that the migration failed, the vault balance stays unchanged, and no funds are moved, even though the operation appears to have been initiated. The impact is that the protocol’s governance loses the ability to replace the strategy, reset the vault, or perform a full migration, effectively freezing any assets that are subject to the lock while still permitting individual users to withdraw via the regular _withdraw path. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test case demonstrated that locking a minimal amount of want caused vault.withdrawToVault to revert, highlighting a subtle state‑dependency that is easy to miss because the failing condition checks a zero balance on an external locker, a value that may be overlooked in typical operation. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or dust‑locking denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities where a small, seemingly inconsequential token amount can lock a contract’s critical functionality. To mitigate the problem the recommended fix is to invoke LOCKER.processExpiredLocks(false) inside MyStrategy._withdrawAll before the balance checks, or to relax/remove the strict zero‑balance requirement, thereby allowing migrations to proceed even when residual dust remains. This change eliminates the attack surface that permits an adversary to block strategy upgrades, restores the protocol’s ability to manage assets freely, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that vault withdrawals should not be hindered by negligible locked balances.

title: Remove splitter will always revert if there are some rewards left on splitter contract
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LSTRewardsSplitterController.removeSplitter function, which is intended to delete a user‑specific splitter and return any remaining token balance to the user. The function reads the total token balance of the splitter contract and the value stored in the splitter’s principalDeposits variable, then attempts to withdraw the full balance. However, when rewards have been accrued, the splitter’s splitRewards routine has already transferred a portion of the balance to the configured fee receivers, while the principalDeposits state variable still reflects the pre‑distribution total. Consequently the balance held by the splitter contract is lower than the principalDeposits value, and the subsequent withdraw call requests more tokens than are actually available. This mismatch triggers a revert, causing the removeSplitter transaction to fail. The bug can be exploited simply by invoking removeSplitter while any rewards are pending; the call will always revert, preventing the splitter from being removed and effectively locking the user’s principal deposit and any undistributed rewards. The impact is that users cannot cleanly deregister their splitter, the protocol’s administrative functions become unusable for affected accounts, and funds may remain inaccessible until the rewards balance is manually cleared to zero. The condition occurs whenever rewards have been accrued but not yet split in the same block, which is a common situation in normal operation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the removeSplitter path with simulated reward deposits and observed a revert. It is subtle because the code appears to check for a non‑zero balance before withdrawing, yet it does not account for the fact that part of that balance may already have been sent out, leading to an accounting inconsistency that is not obvious from the surface logic. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑mismatch vulnerabilities where stored accounting variables diverge from actual contract balances, often resulting in failed transfers or locked assets. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a “Remove splitter” action that suddenly fails with a transaction revert, leaving the user’s funds unchanged and possibly displaying an unexpected error. The expected behavior is that the splitter is removed and the user receives their remaining principal plus any undistributed rewards; the reality is that the transaction reverts and no funds move. To remediate the issue the controller should withdraw only the amount that actually remains after rewards have been distributed, for example by calling splitRewards first and then withdrawing the updated principalDeposits, or by separating the withdrawal of the principal from the withdrawal of any residual balance, ensuring that the amount requested from the splitter never exceeds its current token balance.

title: Removed vaults still remain valid in `OperatorVCS`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vault management logic of the OperatorVCS contract. The contract maintains a mapping (vaultMapping) that records whether a vault address is currently authorized to interact with the strategy. When a vault is removed via the removeVault function, the implementation deletes the vault from the internal arrays but fails to reliably clear the corresponding entry in vaultMapping. As a result, the mapping continues to return true for the removed address, causing the contract to treat the vault as still active. This discrepancy arises because the removal routine updates the vaults array and the vaultsToRemove queue, but the state change that marks the vault as inactive is either omitted or overwritten later, leaving the flag unchanged. An attacker who controls a vault that has been queued for removal can therefore continue to call functions that are restricted to active vaults, such as withdrawOperatorRewards, and successfully extract rewards that should no longer be available. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: funds that were expected to be reclaimed by the staking pool remain withdrawable by the former vault, effectively allowing “funds disappear” from the pool’s perspective and creating a mismatch between deposited balances and actual payouts. The issue manifests whenever the governance or operator initiates a vault removal; under those conditions the contract’s internal validity check (isVaultValid) still reports true, leading to unexpected behavior in the UI where users see rewards being paid out from a vault that should have been de‑registered. The bug was discovered during a security audit that added a test checking the vaultMapping after removal; the test revealed that the mapping still returned true, indicating the vault remained valid. Because the mapping is used only in internal modifiers, the problem can be subtle and may not surface until a removed vault attempts an operation, at which point the transaction succeeds unexpectedly. To remediate the issue, the removeVault function must explicitly set vaultMapping[vault] to false (or delete the entry) after the vault is removed from the arrays, ensuring that any subsequent validity checks fail. This aligns the contract’s state with its business logic, preventing unauthorized reward withdrawals and preserving the integrity of the staking pool’s accounting. The class of bug is an authorization state‑inconsistency where a registry of active participants is not synchronised with removal actions, leading to privilege escalation for entities that should have been revoked.

title: [WithdrawalPool.sol] Prevent efficient return of data in getBatchIds() by blocking updateWithdrawalBatchIdCutoff() update of newWithdrawalIdCutoff
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the WithdrawalPool contract advances its internal cut‑off indices (withdrawalIdCutoff and withdrawalBatchIdCutoff) that are used by the getBatchIds and getFinalizedWithdrawalIdsByOwner view functions to avoid scanning the entire list of queued withdrawals. The updateWithdrawalBatchIdCutoff() routine walks forward from the previously stored cut‑off until it finds the first queued withdrawal that still holds any shares or a partially withdrawable amount. If a user (or a malicious actor) queues a withdrawal and never calls the withdraw() function to clear the entry, that entry will always contain a non‑zero balance. Because the loop stops at the first non‑empty entry, the cut‑off variables never move past the stale index. Consequently, every subsequent call to the view functions must iterate over an ever‑growing prefix of the withdrawals array, leading to linearly increasing gas consumption and computational load. From a user’s perspective the UI may appear to freeze, return empty results after long delays, or cause node providers to hit request quotas, even though the contract’s logic is otherwise correct. The issue is triggered only when a queued withdrawal remains uncleared; it does not require any special permissions and can be caused unintentionally by a forgetful staker or deliberately by an attacker who queues a withdrawal and simply abandons it. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit that added a test case where a queued withdrawal was never withdrawn, after which the stored cut‑off values stopped advancing and the view functions became increasingly expensive. The bug is subtle because the contract still functions for normal withdrawals and does not revert; the degradation manifests only over time as the number of pending entries grows, making it easy to miss in short‑term testing. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable array element to drive the optimisation, without a fallback when that element cannot be cleared. To remediate, the contract should either (i) allow an authorized role (for example the pool owner) to force‑clear stale queued withdrawals after a timeout, (ii) redesign the cut‑off calculation to skip over entries with remaining balances rather than stopping at the first one, or (iii) replace the linear iteration in getBatchIds with a constant‑time mapping or index structure that does not depend on the state of individual withdrawals. Implementing any of these mitigations restores predictable performance and prevents a denial‑of‑service condition that could otherwise exhaust node resources or make the protocol appear unresponsive.

title: Chainlink automation Upkeep can not function because of improper integration
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integration mismatch between the Chainlink Automation (Upkeep) interface and the smart contracts that manage staking and withdrawals, specifically the PriorityPool and WithdrawalPool contracts. The root cause is that the checkUpkeep function in each contract returns data that is encoded as a single uint256 (or an empty byte string) while the corresponding performUpkeep function expects to decode the incoming calldata as an array of bytes (bytes[]). Because the data formats do not match, the abi.decode call in performUpkeep always reverts, causing the upkeep transaction to fail. This mismatch can be exploited by a malicious keeper or by simply triggering the upkeep; the call will revert and the intended automated actions – depositing queued tokens or executing queued withdrawals – will never be performed. The impact is that automated maintenance tasks such as moving queued deposits into the staking pool or processing pending withdrawals are permanently blocked, leading to user funds being effectively locked in the contract. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s internal state satisfies the logical criteria for upkeep (e.g., sufficient deposit room or withdrawal eligibility) and the Chainlink keeper attempts to invoke performUpkeep. All users who rely on the protocol’s automated deposit or withdrawal flow are affected, as they may see their balances unchanged, pending deposits never materialize, or withdrawal requests remain unfulfilled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract code, where the auditor compared the expected Chainlink Upkeep signature with the actual implementation and observed the decoding mismatch. The bug is subtle because the checkUpkeep function still returns true, giving the impression that the upkeep will succeed, while the failure only manifests at runtime when the keeper calls performUpkeep, producing a revert without an obvious error message. To remediate, the contracts must align the data encoding and decoding contracts: either encode the data as a bytes[] array in checkUpkeep or change performUpkeep to decode a single uint256, and ensure that when no additional data is required an empty bytes array is passed consistently. This class of bug falls under improper interface integration or ABI encoding/decoding mismatches, which break the contract’s business logic that assumes automated accounting actions will execute reliably. From a user perspective, the UI may indicate that a deposit or withdrawal is pending, but the on‑chain state never updates, leading to confusion and the perception that “my funds disappeared” or “the refund never arrives.”

title: Griefer can permanently DOS all the deposits to the `StakingPool`
poc:

import { assert, expect } from 'chai'

bug_full: An attacker can permanently deny service to all future deposits in the StakingPool by calling the donateTokens function before any legitimate deposit has been made. The contract tracks totalStaked and totalShares; initially totalShares is zero because no shares have been minted. When a donation is made, totalStaked becomes a positive value while totalShares remains zero. The deposit routine calls getSharesByStake to compute how many shares to mint for the depositor. This function returns (_amount * totalShares) / totalStaked when totalStaked is non‑zero, which evaluates to zero because totalShares is zero. Consequently mintShares is invoked with an amount of zero. Inside mintShares the code checks if totalShares is zero and, in that branch, attempts to subtract a constant DEADSHARES (10**3) from the amount, causing an arithmetic underflow that triggers a panic revert. Because the revert occurs before any state changes for the deposit, every subsequent deposit transaction hits the same path and reverts, effectively locking the pool forever. From a user’s perspective a deposit transaction fails with an underflow error, the expected token balance does not change, and no shares are received, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The issue is discovered during audit testing where a single‑wei donation was front‑run before the first deposit and the deposit call reverted with panic code 0x11. It is hard to notice because the donateTokens function appears harmless and the underflow only manifests after the first deposit logic is exercised. The vulnerability belongs to the class of initialization‑order or accounting‑state bugs where a contract’s internal accounting variables can be set to inconsistent values before the normal lifecycle begins, breaking later calculations. To remediate, the contract should reject donations while totalStaked is zero, or ensure that getSharesByStake correctly handles the case where totalShares is zero without producing a zero share amount, or adjust the mintShares logic to avoid subtracting DEADSHARES when the amount is zero.

title: Vault fee receivers can conditionally block rewards distribution flow
bug_full: The vulnerability is a conditional blocking of the rewards distribution flow caused by fee‑receiver contracts that are invoked through an ERC677 transferAndCallFrom call. In the staking pool, when rewards are minted as share tokens they are sent to each configured fee receiver. The transfer function includes a callback to the receiver contract, and the implementation does not protect the surrounding loop from a revert inside that callback. If a fee receiver deliberately reverts in its token fallback, the transferAndCallFrom call propagates the error, causing the internal _updateStrategyRewards function to revert entirely. Because this internal function is invoked by public entry points that handle strategy removal, fee addition and fee updates, a malicious receiver can block three critical flows: removing a strategy, adding a new fee, and updating an existing fee. The impact is that legitimate rewards are not distributed, strategies cannot be removed, and fee configuration changes are prevented, effectively freezing expected earnings for stakers and breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The issue manifests when at least one fee receiver is a contract with a failing callback; it does not appear when receivers are externally owned accounts, making it hard to detect in standard tests that only use EOAs. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the reward distribution logic, where the auditor noted that the transferAndCallFrom call is made without any try/catch or fallback handling. From a user perspective the symptoms are missing or zero rewards, inability to withdraw or modify strategies, and UI elements that show no balance change despite accrued earnings. The root cause is the lack of defensive programming around external calls that may revert, violating the principle that a single untrusted contract should not be able to halt core protocol operations. A conceptual fix is to isolate fee transfers from the core reward logic, for example by wrapping each transferAndCallFrom in a try/catch block and continuing on failure, by using a non‑reverting transfer method, or by enforcing that only trusted contracts can be registered as fee receivers. This would ensure that a misbehaving receiver cannot block the entire rewards flow and that the protocol’s accounting remains consistent even in the presence of faulty callbacks.

title: Principal amount of removed operator get's stuck in Chainlink's Staking Contract forever
bug_full: The vulnerability is that principal funds of an operator that has been removed from the Chainlink staking system become permanently locked because the required unbonding step is never executed. In Chainlink's OperatorStakingPool the function unbond must be called before unstakeRemovedPrincipal can succeed. Stakelink's FundFlowController builds a list of vaults to unbond by iterating over vault groups and explicitly skips vaults whose isRemoved flag is true. As a result, when an operator is marked as removed the corresponding vault is omitted from the unbond call, so the operator never enters the unbonding period. Later, when OperatorVault.exitVault attempts to call stakeController.unstakeRemovedPrincipal the call reverts with StakeNotFound, preventing the principal withdrawal and leaving the funds trapped inside the OperatorStakingPool contract. The issue occurs only after an operator is removed and the protocol’s regular updateVaultGroups flow runs; normal (non‑removed) operators are unaffected because their vaults are included in the unbond list. Affected parties include the removed operator, any users who delegated to that operator, and the overall protocol because locked capital reduces available liquidity and harms trust. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Stakelink codebase when the auditor noticed that the unbond function is required for removed operators and that FundFlowController deliberately filters out removed vaults. It is hard to notice because the revert happens only on a withdrawal attempt after removal, a path that is exercised rarely in normal operation. From a user perspective the transaction fails, no principal is returned, and the balance of the vault remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the operator can retrieve their stake after removal. This class of bug is an improper state‑transition handling where a required lifecycle step is omitted, leading to locked funds. The recommended fix is to ensure that removed vaults are included in the unbonding process, for example by removing the isRemoved check or by adding an explicit call to stakeController.unbond for removed operators before invoking unstakeRemovedPrincipal, thereby allowing the unbonding period to complete and the principal to be withdrawn.

title: MJR-1 Losses are not taken into account in the strategy
description: The withdrawer from vault should incur the losses from liquidation caused by his own withdrawal. However, the Strategy.sol#L307 is ignoring possible trove liquidation. Currently liquidation will cause revert, but even if not, currently strategy is ignoring the case of trove liquidation. This may lead to improper accounting of user balances and possible locking of vault withdrawals.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the vault’s strategy contract where losses generated by a trove liquidation that is triggered by a user’s own withdrawal are not reflected in the user’s balance. The root cause is that the liquidatePosition function does not consider the scenario in which the withdrawal causes a liquidation; it simply proceeds without adjusting the accounting or, in the current implementation, allows the liquidation to revert without handling the loss. An attacker or any user can exploit this by initiating a withdrawal that pushes the underlying trove into liquidation. Because the strategy ignores the liquidation outcome, the contract either reverts the transaction (leaving the user with no funds) or, if the revert is avoided, records an incorrect balance that does not include the loss. The impact is two‑fold: first, the user’s expected refund may be reduced or disappear entirely, violating the expectation that the vault returns the full deposited amount minus any protocol‑defined fees; second, the vault can become stuck because the internal accounting no longer matches the actual collateral, preventing further withdrawals and potentially locking funds for all participants. This condition occurs whenever a withdrawal request changes the collateralisation ratio of the associated trove enough to trigger liquidation, and the strategy’s logic does not capture that event. All users of the vault, as well as the protocol’s liquidity providers and auditors, are affected because the bug undermines the fundamental accounting guarantees of the system. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the liquidation pathway and identified that the loss handling branch was missing. It is hard to notice because the contract may simply revert on liquidation, giving the impression of a generic failure rather than a subtle accounting drift, and because the vault’s UI may not display internal loss calculations. The correct mitigation is to redesign liquidatePosition so that it explicitly checks for a liquidation event, calculates the loss incurred by the withdrawing user, and updates the user’s balance accordingly before completing the withdrawal. In generic terms, this is a failure to propagate state changes from a dependent contract (the liquidation engine) back to the accounting layer, a class of bug often referred to as “missing state synchronization” or “accounting inconsistency after external call”. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero refund, a balance that appears unchanged despite a successful transaction, or a complete inability to withdraw because the vault reports an internal error. The expectation that a withdrawal returns the correct amount is violated, leading to funds that seem to disappear or become inaccessible.

title: MJR-2 Malfunction of strategy and entire vault on unexpected trove
description:
A liquity trove can be in one of several states: nonExistent, active, closedByOwner, closedByLiquidation, closedByRedemption. When the trove is in state different than active, any call to adjustTrove() will fail. Unfortunately, the strategy does not implement proper handling of trove state. There is some scenarios that will cause trove to be in unexpected state: trove liquidation, full collaterial redemption and trove manual Strategy.sol#L374 by privileged user.
The Strategy.sol#L216 function is expected only two states: zero (which is nonExistent) and other (which is active, closedByOwner, closedByLiquidation, closedByRedemption). However, only active state is valid for Strategy.sol#L237, other three states will cause revert.
The Strategy.sol#L307 function does not handle trove state. When trove is in any state except active, liquidatePosition() will revert on Strategy.sol#L322 call.
This will break harvest() and withdraw() functions so strategy will become broken and should be manually removed from the vault to prevent blocking of any withdrawal from it.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the expected lifecycle of a Liquity trove and the way the strategy contract interacts with it. A Liquity trove can be in one of several states – nonExistent, active, closedByOwner, closedByLiquidation, or closedByRedemption – but the strategy code only anticipates two conditions: a zero value representing a non‑existent trove and any non‑zero value that it assumes to be active. In reality, three of the non‑zero states (closedByOwner, closedByLiquidation, closedByRedemption) are invalid for the strategy’s core functions. When the trove transitions to any of these states, calls such as adjustTrove (used during harvest) and liquidatePosition (used during withdraw) revert because the contract does not perform proper state checks. The reverts propagate up to harvest() and withdraw(), causing those operations to fail and effectively locking the strategy inside the vault. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a failed harvest transaction, a withdraw call that reverts without returning funds, and an apparent disappearance of balances – the user expects a refund or reward but receives nothing and may see a zero balance in the UI. The issue is triggered only under specific conditions: a trove liquidation, a full collateral redemption, or a manual state change performed by a privileged account. These events are relatively rare, which makes the bug hard to notice during normal testing. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by MixBytes, which identified that the strategy does not handle trove states other than active. Because the contract does not guard against closed states, an attacker who can force a liquidation or who has privileged access to manually close the trove can deliberately render the strategy unusable, thereby blocking withdrawals for all users of the vault. The impact is that funds become inaccessible until the strategy is manually removed from the vault, which may require governance intervention or a contract upgrade. To remediate the issue the strategy should explicitly query the trove’s current state and only proceed when the state is active; for any other state it should either skip the operation or safely unwind, ensuring that harvest and withdraw continue to function or fail gracefully without locking the vault. In broader terms this is a state‑management bug where assumptions about external contract state are not validated, leading to unexpected reverts and a denial‑of‑service condition for the vault’s users.

title: M-1 Broken partial liquidations
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the partial‑liquidation mechanism of a lending pool that allows a liquidator to specify an explicit amount of collateral to withdraw instead of using the maximum sentinel value. The contract’s internal liquidation routine calls a helper function twice – once to withdraw locked collateral and once to withdraw unlocked collateral – and passes the same user‑supplied amount to both calls. When a borrower holds locked collateral but has no unlocked collateral, the second call attempts to withdraw a non‑existent amount of unlocked tokens, causing the transaction to revert. This mismatch between the requested amount and the actual unlocked balance is the root cause of the bug. An attacker acting as a liquidator can trigger the revert by submitting a partial‑liquidation request that includes any amount of a collateral asset for which the borrower’s unlocked balance is zero. The exploit flow is: (1) the borrower becomes under‑collateralised after a price shock; (2) a liquidator prepares a liquidation request with a specific amount for a collateral token; (3) the liquidation function invokes the withdrawal of locked and unlocked collateral using the same amount; (4) the unlocked‑withdrawal fails because the borrower has no unlocked tokens, causing the whole liquidation to revert; (5) the liquidator’s repayment funds remain untouched and the borrower stays insolvent. The impact is that liquidators cannot recover the debt, the protocol’s risk‑mitigation mechanism is effectively disabled for affected positions, and funds may become permanently stuck, undermining confidence in the system’s safety guarantees. The issue manifests only when partial liquidation is used and the borrower’s unlocked collateral balance is insufficient for the requested amount; full liquidation (using the maximum sentinel) bypasses the problem because the contract treats the amount specially. The bug was discovered through an integration test that deliberately created a borrower with locked collateral only and attempted a partial liquidation, observing a revert. Because the failure occurs deep inside a helper function and only under specific balance configurations, it can be easy to miss during manual code review or simple unit testing that focuses on successful liquidation paths. Conceptually, the fix is to decouple the amounts used for locked and unlocked collateral withdrawals – for example by passing two separate arrays that specify distinct amounts for each category, or by adding a guard that skips the unlocked‑withdrawal when the borrower’s unlocked balance is zero. This aligns the liquidation logic with the intended business rule that a liquidator may withdraw only the collateral that actually exists, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and ensuring that partial liquidations succeed without unintended reverts.

title: M-10 Missing signature validation in Order structure
description: In the Signing contract, the Order structure includes the fields baseTokenData.toRecipient and quoteTokenData.toTrader. These ﬁelds are currently ignored in the signature veriﬁcation process. They are not included in the data that is signed, meaning they can be altered without invalidating the signature.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing signature validation for two address fields inside the Order structure of the Signing contract. Specifically, the fields that designate the final token recipient (baseTokenData.toRecipient) and the trader that should receive the quote token (quoteTokenData.toTrader) are not part of the data that is hashed and signed when an order is created. The root cause is that the signature verification routine only checks a subset of the order fields, omitting these two mutable addresses. Because the signature does not cover them, an attacker who obtains a valid order signature can arbitrarily change the recipient addresses before calling LiquoriceSettlement.settle without causing the signature check to fail. In practice, an attacker can submit a signed order that originally points to a legitimate recipient, then replace the toRecipient or toTrader values with an address they control. When the settlement function processes the order, the protocol will transfer the base token or quote token to the attacker’s address, effectively stealing funds. The impact is a loss of assets for the original trader or intended recipient, a breach of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and potential reputational damage. This condition occurs whenever an order is settled using the set‑tle method and the contract relies solely on the existing signature verification, which does not include the mutable fields. All participants who rely on the order’s integrity – traders, recipients, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the signed payload against the fields used in settlement and noticed the omission. It can be hard to notice because the user interface may display the correct recipient addresses at the time of signing, yet the on‑chain settlement may use altered values without any visible error, leading to silent fund loss. To remediate, the protocol should incorporate baseTokenData.toRecipient and quoteTokenData.toTrader into the signed message hash, or alternatively require these values to be supplied as explicit arguments to the settlement function and validated against the signed order. This ensures that any change to the recipient addresses would invalidate the signature and prevent unauthorized redirection of funds.

title: M-11 Missing validation on _hooks in settlement contract
description: • LiquoriceSettlement.sol#L65 In the LiquoriceSettlement.sol contract, the settle function calls validateOrder(), which performs necessary checks on the _interactions variable. These checks include validations that ensure secure interactions with the LendingPool, as seen in the Signing.sol#L100. However, the _hooks parameter in settle() is not subjected to the same validation process. This omission allows an attacker to bypass the interactions checks by leveraging the hooks parameter. As a result, the attacker can circumvent critical validations intended to secure the contract's operations, potentially leading to unauthorized actions or exploitation of the LendingPool.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step for the _hooks argument supplied to the settle function of the LiquoriceSettlement contract. The settle routine internally invokes validateOrder(), which checks the _interactions structure to ensure that calls to the external LendingPool follow the protocol’s security rules, such as proper signature verification and allowed function selectors. However, the _hooks parameter – an array of callback specifications that can trigger additional logic after settlement – is passed to the contract without any of the same safety checks. Because the contract trusts the contents of _hooks blindly, an attacker can craft a malicious hook that calls arbitrary functions on the LendingPool or other privileged contracts, effectively bypassing the intended interaction validation. Exploitation requires the attacker to submit a settlement transaction that includes a specially crafted hook payload; the contract will execute the hook after the main settlement logic, allowing the attacker to perform unauthorized actions such as draining funds, altering loan states, or executing re‑entrancy attacks. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken: users may see their balances unchanged or unexpectedly reduced, refunds may not be issued, and the LendingPool can be manipulated in ways that were assumed to be impossible. The flaw manifests whenever the settle function is called with a non‑empty _hooks array, which is a legitimate use‑case for extending settlement behavior. All participants that rely on the settlement process – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the security model assumes that every external interaction is vetted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s control flow, where the auditor noticed that validateOrder() only inspected _interactions and did not address the parallel _hooks input. The problem is subtle because the hook mechanism is designed to be flexible and developers may assume that any data passed to it is harmless, leading to the oversight. To remediate, the contract should apply the same validation logic to each element of the _hooks array as is applied to _interactions, including checks for allowed target contracts, function selectors, and proper authorization signatures. In broader terms, this is an instance of unchecked external callback data, a class of bugs where user‑controlled parameters that trigger further contract calls are not validated, resulting in potential privilege escalation and loss of funds.
