From a user’s perspective, a transaction may appear to settle successfully while the expected token balances remain unchanged or are reduced, contradicting the expectation that a settlement always results in a correct update of their holdings. The bug violates the fundamental business rule that settlement must be atomic and secure, and it opens a path for malicious actors to subvert the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: M-12 Inability to liquidate at high utilization
description: The liquidation function reverts if there aren't enough funds in the pool to perform the transfer: function _liquidation ... (uint256 withdrawnLockedAmount, uint256 lockedAmountToTransfer,) = _withdrawAsset( _withdrawal[i].asset, _withdrawal[i].amount, _borrower, true, protocolLiquidationFee); (uint256 withdrawnAmount, uint256 amountToTransfer,) = _withdrawAsset( _withdrawal[i].asset, _withdrawal[i].amount, _borrower, false, protocolLiquidationFee); ERC20(_withdrawal[i].asset).safeTransfer( _liquidator, lockedAmountToTransfer + amountToTransfer); LendingPool.sol#L667 This can lead to bad debt accumulation. For example, consider a scenario with assets WETH and WBTC. One whale borrows almost all the WETH against WBTC, while another borrows nearly all the WBTC against WETH. Now, both pools lack enough funds for a complete liquidation of both whales. If one of the assets rapidly loses value, no one will be able to liquidate the unhealthy whale, and at some point the level of bad debt will reach an unproﬁtable threshold for liquidators.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a liquidation routine that aborts when the lending pool does not contain enough liquid assets to satisfy the transfer required for a liquidation. The core of the problem lies in the assumption that the pool will always have sufficient balance to cover both the locked portion of the borrower’s collateral and the unlocked portion that is to be transferred to the liquidator. The function first withdraws the locked amount and the unlocked amount via two internal calls, then attempts to send the sum of those amounts to the liquidator using a safe ERC20 transfer. If the pool’s balance for the asset is lower than the required sum, the ERC20 transfer reverts, causing the entire liquidation transaction to revert. This situation typically arises when utilization of the pool is extremely high – for example, when a whale borrows almost the entire supply of one asset against another asset, and a second whale does the opposite, draining both pools. If the price of one of the assets drops sharply, the borrowers become under‑collateralised, but the pool no longer holds enough of the asset to pay the liquidator. Consequently, the protocol cannot liquidate the unhealthy positions, leading to the accumulation of bad debt that may exceed the threshold at which liquidators are willing to act. The impact is that liquidators receive no reward, borrowers remain in an unhealthy state, and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent, potentially resulting in permanent loss of funds and loss of confidence among token holders. The issue is discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of the liquidation function was examined and the revert condition identified. It is hard to notice because under normal utilization the function works as intended; only in extreme edge‑cases does the revert surface, often appearing as a generic transaction failure rather than a systemic flaw. To remediate the problem, the contract should provide an alternative settlement path, such as allowing the liquidator to receive a protocol‑issued CollateralToken that represents the seized collateral, or implementing a partial‑liquidation fallback that does not require the full transfer of underlying assets. This change removes the hard dependency on pool liquidity and restores the ability to enforce liquidation, preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees. From a user’s perspective, a liquidator attempting to execute a liquidation will see the transaction revert and receive no funds, while the borrower’s UI may continue to show an unhealthy loan that cannot be resolved, contradicting the expectation that a liquidation will automatically clear the debt and reward the liquidator. The bug belongs to the class of “liquidation failure due to insufficient pool balance” and violates the fundamental business logic that collateral can always be seized to cover a defaulted loan.

title: M-13 Taker incurs losses when SingleQuote.useOldAmount is set to true
description: When SingleQuote.useOldAmount set to true and SingleQuote.makerAmount less than Single.makerAmount anyone can call LiquoriceSettlement.settleSingle(), as a result trader will receive less tokens. Although this requires the taker to sign such a quote, the process functions incorrectly, potentially causing losses for the taker.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the settlement routine of the Liquorice protocol that allows a taker to receive fewer tokens than were promised in a signed quote. When a SingleQuote is created with the flag useOldAmount set to true, the contract is supposed to settle using the older maker amount only if that amount is equal to or greater than the amount originally quoted to the taker. However, the implementation does not enforce this invariant. If the stored maker amount (SingleQuote.makerAmount) is smaller than the current maker amount (Single.makerAmount), the function LiquoriceSettlement.settleSingle() can be called by any actor. The call succeeds because the contract only checks that the quote is signed, not that the maker amount satisfies the expected minimum. As a result, the settlement proceeds with the lower maker amount and the taker receives a reduced token quantity. The impact is a loss of value for the taker: the user expects to receive a certain amount of tokens based on the signed quote, but the actual transfer may be partially or fully short‑changed, effectively making funds disappear from the taker’s perspective. This condition can be triggered whenever a quote is issued with useOldAmount=true and the market moves such that the newer maker amount exceeds the older quoted amount. Because the UI typically displays the quoted amount and does not reveal the internal check, the discrepancy may only become apparent after settlement, making the bug subtle and hard to detect during normal operation. The issue was identified during a formal audit by MixBytes, which noted that the logic permits a settlement that reduces the taker’s entitlement rather than guaranteeing at least the quoted amount. To remediate, the contract should add explicit validation that when useOldAmount is true the maker amount used for settlement must be greater than or equal to the amount promised to the taker, or the protocol should reject settlements that would cause the taker to receive less than expected, thereby allowing only extra profit for the maker and never a loss for the taker.

title: M-14 LiquoriceSettlement.settle() does not check for upper bound when using
description: When a trader has a non-zero allowance to the BalanceManager contract, the Solver can set SolverData.curFillAmount to a value greater than quoteTokenData.toTrader. As a result, the trader will spend more of token A and receive more of token B than expected. This behavior may be unexpected for the trader.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the settlement function of the Liquorice protocol where the contract does not enforce an upper bound on the amount that a solver can claim to have filled for a trader. When a trader has granted a non‑zero allowance to the BalanceManager contract, a malicious or compromised solver can set the field curFillAmount in the SolverData structure to a value that exceeds the quoted amount that should be transferred to the trader (quoteTokenData.toTrader). Because the contract trusts this value without verification, the settlement logic will debit the trader for a larger quantity of the input token (token A) and credit them with a larger quantity of the output token (token B) than the trade terms specify. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by submitting a crafted settlement transaction that over‑fills the trade, effectively allowing the solver to extract excess tokens from the trader or to manipulate the accounting of the protocol. The impact is that traders may lose more of their input assets than intended while receiving an unexpected surplus of the output asset, breaking the economic assumptions of the market and potentially leading to imbalanced liquidity pools. The condition occurs only when the trader has an active allowance for the BalanceManager and the settlement is performed through the vulnerable settle() path; the alternative settleSingle() function includes a proper upper‑bound check and is not affected. The issue was identified during a formal security audit by MixBytes, which noted that the lack of a bound check is subtle because the contract still appears to transfer tokens, so the over‑fill may not be immediately obvious in transaction logs. Detecting the problem requires inspecting the internal SolverData values or comparing the actual token amounts transferred against the quoted amounts, which many users and even developers may overlook. To remediate, the contract should introduce a validation step that ensures curFillAmount does not exceed quoteTokenData.toTrader, mirroring the logic used in settleSingle(). This change restores the intended accounting invariants, prevents unintended token drains, and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s business logic that a trader should never receive or send more than the quoted trade amounts. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or validation errors where input from an external actor is trusted without proper constraints, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential fund loss.

title: M-15 Repository.setLiquidationThreshold() can unexpectedly change the global
description: When changing the threshold for a speciﬁc asset, the threshold for all default tokens may also change in a way that is unfavorable for the protocol: • Repository.sol#L288-L290 This can lead to bad debt if volatile tokens are assigned a high threshold. The higher the liquidation threshold for an asset, the later users will be liquidated. As a result, if there are two assets—one low-volatility and one high-volatility—and the high-volatility asset uses the default conﬁg, then a reasonable increase in the threshold for the low-volatility asset will also increase the threshold for the high-volatility asset. This may be unexpected for the manager and could lead to the accumulation of bad debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that updates the liquidation threshold for a given asset. Instead of limiting the change to the targeted asset, the implementation also modifies the global default liquidation threshold that is applied to every token that does not have an explicit configuration. This coupling occurs because the function writes to a storage slot that is shared between the per‑asset setting and the protocol‑wide default, so a manager who intends to raise the threshold for a low‑volatility collateral inadvertently raises the threshold for high‑volatility collateral as well. The root cause is the lack of separation between per‑asset and default parameters and the absence of safeguards that prevent the default value from being altered through the same entry point. An attacker does not need to craft a malicious transaction; the risk materialises when an authorized manager calls setLiquidationThreshold expecting a local effect. The protocol then treats volatile assets as if they were safer than they actually are, delaying liquidation events. Consequently, borrowers holding high‑volatility tokens may avoid liquidation even when their collateral value falls sharply, allowing debt to become under‑collateralised and generating bad debt for the system. The impact is financial loss for lenders and a breach of the protocol’s risk‑management assumptions. This condition appears whenever an asset relies on the default configuration – a common scenario for newly added tokens – and the admin adjusts the threshold for any other asset. Users experience the symptom of “my position is not liquidated even though the market moved dramatically” or “the protocol seems to allow larger debt than expected”. From a UI perspective the displayed threshold for the edited asset changes as intended, while the hidden default threshold silently shifts, making the problem hard to notice without deep inspection of storage. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the Repository contract where the code paths for per‑asset and default threshold updates were examined. To remediate, the contract should expose a dedicated function that only modifies the global default threshold, enforce a non‑zero minimum threshold constant, and ensure that per‑asset updates reference a distinct storage slot that does not affect the default. This separation restores the intended accounting model where each asset’s liquidation trigger reflects its own risk profile, preventing unexpected accumulation of bad debt.

title: M-2 Borrowing beyond MaximumLTV
description: LendingPool.borrow() has a limit up to TypeofLTV.MaximumLTV (set at 80% in the project tests). However, LendingPool.withdraw() allows withdrawals up to TypeofLTV.LiquidationThreshold (set at 90% in the tests). An attacker could call borrow() + withdraw() in a single transaction to effectively borrow up to TypeofLTV.LiquidationThreshold, bypassing the MaximumLTV limit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an LTV mismatch that allows a borrower to exceed the configured MaximumLTV by combining borrow() and withdraw() in a single transaction. The contract defines a MaximumLTV of 80% that limits the amount that can be borrowed relative to the supplied collateral. Separately, the withdraw() function uses a higher threshold called LiquidationThreshold set to 90% to determine how much collateral can be removed. Because the two functions perform their checks independently and there is no global invariant enforcing that the total debt after any state change stays below MaximumLTV, an attacker can first call borrow() up to the 80% limit and then immediately call withdraw() to pull additional collateral up to the 90% threshold. This sequence effectively increases the loan‑to‑value ratio to 90%, bypassing the intended safety cap. The exploit works whenever a borrower can execute both calls within the same transaction, for example by using a smart‑contract wallet or a multicall pattern. The impact is that the protocol can become under‑collateralized, leading to premature liquidations, loss of funds for lenders, and erosion of trust in the lending pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the parameter values used in the two functions and identified the lack of a cross‑function consistency check. It is hard to notice because each function individually respects its own limit, so normal single‑action tests appear correct. The bug belongs to the class of inconsistent financial parameter enforcement and invariant violation across contract entry points. From a user’s perspective the contract may allow a borrower to withdraw more collateral than expected or to borrow more funds than the UI indicates, resulting in a situation where “my loan suddenly shows a higher ratio” or “my balance disappears after a combined borrow‑withdraw call”. The correct fix is to enforce a single LTV threshold for all operations that affect the debt‑to‑collateral ratio, or to add a post‑action check that the overall loan‑to‑value never exceeds the MaximumLTV after any combination of borrow and withdraw calls.

title: M-3 Protocol liquidation fee may exceed LTV liquidation gap
description: Repository.setFees() allows setting protocolLiquidationFee > 100% - LiquidationThreshold, making any liquidation unprofitable and potentially leading to bad debt accumulation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's fee‑setting function does not enforce a relationship between the protocol liquidation fee and the liquidation threshold (LTV). Because the function permits the protocol fee to be set higher than the complement of the liquidation threshold (i.e., protocolLiquidationFee > 100% - LiquidationThreshold), the total amount taken from a liquidated position can exceed the collateral value that is supposed to be recovered. This occurs when an admin or governance actor calls setFees with malicious or erroneous parameters. An attacker could deliberately configure the fee so that any liquidation results in a net loss for the liquidator, making liquidation economically unattractive. Consequently, borrowers who become under‑collateralized may never be liquidated, allowing the debt to remain outstanding and eventually turning into bad debt that the protocol must absorb. Users who rely on the protocol for lending may see their expected repayments disappear, and the protocol’s solvency can be compromised. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the fee‑configuration logic, where the lack of a constraint on the sum of fee and threshold was noted. It is subtle because the function itself works as written; only the economic relationship is broken, so normal unit tests that check for successful calls do not reveal the problem. The proper fix is to add a validation that the sum of protocolLiquidationFee and the asset’s liquidation LTV threshold is strictly less than 100%, rejecting any configuration that would violate this invariant. This ensures that after liquidation the protocol can always recover enough collateral to cover the debt, preserving accounting integrity and preventing the scenario where funds disappear due to an unprofitable liquidation.

title: Looping over unbounded array can result in a state of DoS
description: The claimCalculation and getCurrentShareRaw methods both loop over the pool array to do proper calculations. The problem is that there is no way to pop elements out of the array, but there is no upper bound on the length of the array. Each time the currentRewards are more than or equal to the minResetValue, the createPool method will be called, adding a new element to the pool array. If at some point there are now a large number of pools, iterating over them will become very costly and can result in a gas cost that is over the block gas limit. This will mean that a transaction cannot be executed anymore, leaving the contract's main functionalities (withdrawing the staked NFTs and claiming rewards) in a state of DoS.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic array that can lead to a denial‑of‑service condition. The contract maintains a pool array that stores reward pools; each time the accumulated rewards reach a configured threshold the createPool function appends a new element to this array. The claimCalculation and getCurrentShareRaw functions iterate over the entire pool array to compute a user’s claim and share values. Because there is no mechanism to remove or limit the number of pools, the array length can grow without bound. When the array becomes large, the gas required to execute the loops grows linearly and can eventually exceed the block gas limit, causing any transaction that calls these functions to run out of gas and revert. An attacker or even a benign user can trigger many pool creations by repeatedly generating rewards, inflating the array size until the contract’s core operations – withdrawing staked NFTs and claiming rewards – become impossible. The impact is that legitimate users are unable to retrieve their assets or claim earned rewards, effectively locking funds in the contract. This condition occurs only when the pool count reaches a size that makes the loop gas‑intensive; it is not apparent during normal operation with a small number of pools, which makes it hard to notice until the gas limit is breached. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the loops and noted the lack of an upper bound on the array length. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a transaction failure or out‑of‑gas error when attempting to claim or withdraw, contrary to the expectation that the claim succeeds and the NFT is returned. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded iteration or gas‑limit DoS vulnerabilities, where unchecked growth of a data structure leads to excessive computation costs. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum number of pools (for example 25), provide a way to prune or recycle old pools, or redesign the accounting to avoid iterating over the entire collection, thereby ensuring that gas consumption remains bounded and the contract stays usable.

title: Missing constraint on the setter method of a percentage value
description: The setResetShareValue lacks a check that the _newShareResetValue argument is not more than 100%. Since it is expected that the value will be in percentages, setting a value that is bigger than 100 will mess with the important calculations in the contract, one of which is the rewards to claim calculation. This can make users receive a smaller reward than what they have earned since a bigger resetShareValue equals smaller rewards for users.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked setter for a percentage‑based configuration parameter. The contract provides a function that allows an authorized party to update a value representing a share or reset percentage, but it does not verify that the supplied number is bounded by 100 percent. Because the contract treats this parameter as a proportion used in reward‑distribution formulas, any value greater than 100% skews the arithmetic: the larger the reset share value, the smaller the computed reward for each participant. This flaw originates from the absence of input validation in the setter, a classic example of an unchecked arithmetic constraint. An attacker or a careless administrator can invoke the setter with a value such as 150, causing the internal reward calculation to apply a divisor that is too large. When a user later calls the claim function, the contract multiplies the earned amount by the inflated percentage, resulting in a reward that is lower than the user’s entitlement, sometimes even zero. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of users, effectively stealing a portion of the accrued earnings. The condition under which this occurs is any execution path that updates the percentage after deployment; there is no guard preventing values above the logical maximum. All participants who claim rewards after the malicious or erroneous update are affected, while the protocol’s economic model is broken because the accounting assumption that percentages sum to at most 100% no longer holds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected state‑changing functions and noted the missing range check. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and runs, and the symptom—smaller rewards—may be attributed to normal variance or market conditions rather than a code defect. To remediate, the setter should enforce that the new value is less than or equal to 100, typically by adding a require statement that reverts if the argument exceeds the maximum allowed percentage. This restores the invariant that percentages represent a proportion of the whole and ensures that reward calculations remain accurate and users receive the full amount they earned.

title: M-4 No supply limit check in LendingPool.borrowFor()
description: LendingPool.sol#L160 allows users to supply funds without checking the supply limit. LendingPool.sol#L563-L571
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the lending pool contract’s borrowFor function, which permits a caller to supply assets on behalf of another address without enforcing the pool’s configured supply limit. The root cause is a missing validation step that should compare the projected total supplied amount against a predefined cap; the contract simply updates internal accounting regardless of whether the cap would be exceeded. An attacker can exploit this omission by repeatedly invoking borrowFor with large amounts, causing the total supplied balance to grow beyond the intended maximum. As a result, the pool’s accounting becomes inconsistent: later legitimate borrowers may be unable to obtain funds, and lenders may find that their expected withdrawals are blocked because the pool appears to have insufficient liquidity. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal borrowing transaction, but the underlying balance can become unexpectedly high, leading to situations where a user expects to receive a loan or withdraw a deposit and instead receives nothing or a reduced amount. The issue manifests whenever borrowFor is called, regardless of the caller’s role, and therefore any participant in the protocol can trigger it, potentially affecting all lenders, borrowers, and the overall health of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, who noted that the function lacks a supply‑limit check that is present in other entry points. Because the function still works for small amounts, the problem can be hard to notice until the total supplied balance approaches or exceeds the intended cap, at which point the protocol’s business logic—namely that total supplied assets must never exceed the limit—breaks down. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce an explicit require statement (or equivalent guard) that ensures totalSupply + amount does not surpass the configured supplyLimit before updating balances, thereby restoring the intended accounting invariant and preventing over‑allocation of funds.

title: Owner has the power to zero-out user's daily interest on rewards
description: The setDepositsActive method resets startTimestamp and lastGlobalUpdate. The owner can front-run each claimReward transaction and by resetting the startTimestamp this will result in 0 requiredRebases in calculateShareFromTime, so the user will lose on his daily interest. On the other side, by resetting lastGlobalUpdate this will make updateGlobalShares never do a rebase, which will never inflate the overallShare which also shouldn't be possible.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a privileged‑state manipulation bug that allows the contract owner to erase a user’s accrued daily interest on reward tokens. The root cause is the setDepositsActive function, which unconditionally resets two critical accounting timestamps – startTimestamp and lastGlobalUpdate – without any restriction on how many times it can be called. Because the reward calculation (calculateShareFromTime) derives the amount of interest to be paid from the elapsed time since startTimestamp, resetting this value to the current block timestamp makes the required rebases count zero. Consequently, when a user subsequently calls claimReward, the contract computes a reward of zero even though the user expected a positive daily interest. In addition, resetting lastGlobalUpdate prevents the global share updater (updateGlobalShares) from performing any rebases, so the overallShare variable never inflates, further suppressing future reward accruals. The exploit can be performed by the owner front‑running a user’s claimReward transaction: the owner calls setDepositsActive just before the user’s transaction is mined, causing the timestamps to be refreshed and the reward calculation to return zero. The impact is that legitimate users lose the interest they are entitled to, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the perspective of the user – the UI will show a pending reward that, after the transaction, becomes zero, and the user’s balance does not increase as expected. This condition occurs whenever the owner can invoke setDepositsActive after deployment, and there is no safeguard limiting its execution to a single initialization step. All participants who hold deposit positions and rely on daily interest – typically token holders, liquidity providers, or any role that can claim rewards – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the lifecycle of the reward‑distribution logic and identified that the owner‑only function could be abused to tamper with time‑based accounting. The bug is subtle because the function appears innocuous (it merely toggles a “deposits active” flag) and the timestamp resets do not emit obvious error events, making it hard to notice without inspecting the reward‑calculation flow. To remediate, the setDepositsActive function should be restricted to a one‑time call during contract initialization, or its ability to reset timestamps should be removed entirely. Alternatively, the contract could enforce that startTimestamp and lastGlobalUpdate are immutable after the first activation, or require a multi‑signature governance delay before allowing any reset, thereby preserving the integrity of the reward accounting. This class of bug falls under “owner‑controlled state reset leading to reward manipulation” and violates the fundamental business assumption that rewards accrue continuously over time and cannot be arbitrarily nullified by a privileged actor.

title: Constraining approvals only partially limits the NFTs from being sold
description: Constraints on approvals (the onlyApprovedContracts modifier) were added so that the Locked Lizards NFTs can't be sold in marketplaces like OpenSea, Blur etc. This only partially limits selling the NFTs because users can always do OTC trades. Those trades will be scams though, since the original NFT owner can call retractLockedLizard anytime and re-gain ownership of the NFT. Not only sales will be problematic, but for example integrations with NFT games - the games are not expected to work properly with NFTs that can be retracted, as this opens up multiple attack-vectors.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An NFT contract attempts to block marketplace sales by applying a onlyApprovedContracts modifier that restricts the approve function to a whitelist of contracts. The intended business rule is that locked NFTs cannot be transferred through standard ERC‑721 approvals, thereby preventing listings on OpenSea, Blur and similar platforms. However, the contract also provides a retractLockedLizard function that allows the original minter or designated owner to call back the token at any time, regardless of any off‑chain agreement. Because the restriction only covers the approve pathway, a user can still move the token by executing a direct transfer or by arranging an over‑the‑counter (OTC) trade where the buyer receives the token without an on‑chain approval. After the buyer receives the NFT, the seller (or any party with the retract right) can invoke retractLockedLizard and reclaim ownership, effectively stealing the NFT. From the user’s perspective the NFT appears to have been sold or transferred, but shortly afterwards the balance shows zero or the token disappears from the buyer’s wallet, leading to confusion and loss of assets. The flaw is a logical mismatch between the contract’s assumption that limiting approvals is sufficient to block sales and the reality that ownership can be reclaimed through a separate privileged function. The vulnerability is discovered during a security review that examined the interaction between the onlyApprovedContracts modifier and the retract function. It may be hard to notice because the approve restriction works as expected for marketplace contracts, giving a false sense of security, while the retraction path is rarely exercised in normal testing. The impact includes potential scams in OTC trades, broken integrations with NFT‑based games that expect stable ownership, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol. To remediate, the contract should either remove the retractLockedLizard capability and allow normal approvals, or eliminate both approve and transfer pathways entirely, ensuring that ownership cannot be arbitrarily reclaimed after a transfer.

title: M-5 Wrong LTV calculation for duplicate assets
description: If a manager passes two identical assets when calling Repository.newLendingPool(), the pool will be created with an incorrect asset count, and the Loan-to-Value (LTV) calculation will be incorrect, potentially leading to user funds loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect Loan-to-Value (LTV) calculation that occurs when the contract that creates a new lending pool receives a list of collateral assets that contains duplicate entries. The repository function does not verify that each asset address is unique before storing the pool configuration. Because the pool’s internal accounting uses the length of the asset array to determine the total collateral weight or to divide the borrowed amount across assets, a duplicated address inflates the asset count while the actual collateral supplied remains unchanged. As a result the LTV ratio is computed with a larger denominator (or smaller denominator depending on implementation), allowing borrowers to obtain a higher amount of credit than the protocol’s risk parameters permit. An attacker or a careless manager can trigger the bug simply by calling newLendingPool() with the same token address twice. Once the pool is created, users can open loans that appear to be within the allowed LTV, but in reality the pool is under‑collateralised. If the price of the collateral drops or a liquidation is attempted, the protocol may not have enough value to cover the debt, leading to loss of user funds or a shortfall in the pool’s balance. The issue manifests only at pool creation time; any pool that was instantiated with a unique asset list works correctly, making the bug easy to miss during normal operation. It was discovered during a manual audit of the repository contract where the auditor noticed that the asset list was not deduplicated before being stored. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error and the duplicate assets are indistinguishable from legitimate multiple‑asset pools from the outside. The class of bug is an input‑validation flaw leading to arithmetic mis‑calculation, commonly referred to as “duplicate entry causing wrong accounting”. To remediate, the contract should enforce uniqueness of asset addresses, for example by checking a mapping of already‑seen assets or by using a Set data structure, and should recalculate the LTV based on the actual distinct collateral value rather than the raw array length. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a loan can be taken with a seemingly safe LTV, yet later the protocol reports insufficient collateral, the user’s balance may be reduced to zero after liquidation, or the pool may report a deficit. The expectation that the LTV check protects the loan is violated, breaking the core accounting assumption of the lending platform.

title: M-6 Loss of accrued interest on updating InterestRateModel
description: When the InterestRateModel is changed for the LendingPool in the Repository, LendingPool._accrueInterest() is not automatically called, which could lead to a loss of accrued interest for both borrowers and suppliers.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting logic of a lending pool that relies on an external InterestRateModel to calculate accrued interest for both borrowers and suppliers. When the pool administrator updates the InterestRateModel in the repository, the contract does not automatically invoke the internal function that records pending interest, typically named _accrueInterest. As a result, any interest that has accumulated under the previous model remains unrecorded and is effectively lost. The root cause is a missing state transition: the contract assumes that changing a parameter does not require a snapshot of the current financial state, but the interest calculation depends on the elapsed time and the previous rate. An attacker or any actor with permission to change the model can trigger the update without first accruing interest, causing the pool to skip the accounting step. Consequently, borrowers may receive less interest than expected, and suppliers may see reduced returns or even a zero‑interest balance after the change. This issue manifests only when the InterestRateModel is replaced; normal operation without model updates does not expose the bug. Users of the pool—depositors, borrowers, and any third‑party relying on accurate interest accounting—are affected because the protocol’s financial guarantees are broken. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that examined state‑changing functions and identified that the model‑update path does not call the interest‑accrual routine. It can be hard to notice because the pool continues to function, but the missing interest is not reflected in any visible error; only the reduced payouts reveal the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should explicitly call the interest‑accrual routine for the current model before any change to the InterestRateModel is applied, ensuring that all pending interest is captured and transferred to the appropriate balances. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting state‑inconsistency bugs that arise when configuration changes bypass essential state‑update hooks, leading to silent loss of value and violation of the protocol’s economic assumptions.

title: M-7 No pause check in several LendingPool functions
description:
Some methods in LendingPool lack checks to verify whether the contract is paused. In case of an emergency, calling these methods could pose a risk:
• LendingPool.sol#L144.
• LendingPool.sol#L150.
• LendingPool.sol#L183.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing emergency‑stop checks in several core functions of the LendingPool contract. The contract implements a pause mechanism that is intended to block user‑facing operations such as deposits, withdrawals, and loan actions when an administrator signals an emergency. However, the listed functions do not contain the required guard that verifies the paused flag before executing their logic. The root cause is a developer oversight: the pause modifier or explicit require statement was omitted from the function bodies, leaving the contract vulnerable to state changes even after the pool has been marked as paused. An attacker or any user can exploit this gap by invoking the unprotected functions during a pause, thereby bypassing the intended safety barrier. This can lead to unexpected fund movements, such as deposits being accepted, withdrawals being processed, or loan parameters being altered while the protocol is supposed to be frozen. The impact includes potential loss of funds, inconsistent accounting, and violation of the protocol’s risk‑management assumptions, because the emergency stop no longer guarantees that no monetary operations occur. The condition under which the bug manifests is precisely when the contract’s paused flag is set to true; any call to the affected functions will still execute as if the contract were active. All participants who rely on the pause – including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s governance – are affected because their expectations of a halted state are broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that compared the contract’s public interface against its documented pause behavior, revealing that the pause check was absent in the specified lines. The bug can be subtle because the UI may still display a “paused” status, leading users to believe that operations are blocked, while the backend still processes transactions. To remediate, each vulnerable function should be wrapped with the standard pause modifier or an explicit require statement that reverts when the paused flag is true, thereby restoring the intended emergency‑stop semantics. This class of bug falls under the broader category of missing access‑control or state‑validation checks, where critical invariants are not enforced before state‑changing logic is executed.

title: M-8 Potential unhandled exception due to out-of-bounds array access
description:
In the FundingRateConsumer.sol contract, specifically at FundingRateConsumer.sol#L22, there is a potential unhandled exception when processing the sortedRates array retrieved from open-api-v3.coinglass.com. If the length of sortedRates is 1 or less, the following computation causes an error:
const fundingRate = Math.ceil(sortedRates[Math.ceil(sortedRates.length / 2)] * 1e18); Here, Math.ceil(sortedRates.length / 2) returns 1 when sortedRates.length is 1 (since Math.ceil(1 / 2) == 1). This results in an attempt to access sortedRates[1], which is out of bounds for an array of length 1 (as array indices start at 0).
bug_full: The contract attempts to calculate a funding rate by selecting the middle element of a sortedRates array returned from an external API. The calculation uses Math.ceil(sortedRates.length/2) as the index. When the array contains only one element, Math.ceil(1/2) evaluates to 1, which points to sortedRates[1]. Because Solidity arrays are zero‑based, the valid index for a single‑element array is 0, so accessing index 1 triggers an out‑of‑bounds read and causes an unhandled exception that reverts the transaction. This bug belongs to the class of off‑by‑one array‑access errors that lead to runtime failures. It can be exploited simply by supplying a response that contains a single rate – for example, if the API returns only one price point due to market conditions or a temporary outage. When that happens, any call that invokes the funding‑rate computation will revert, meaning the caller sees a failed transaction, receives no funding rate value, and any UI may display an unexpected error or a zero balance. The impact is that legitimate users cannot obtain the expected funding rate, potentially halting downstream logic that depends on this value and causing funds to remain locked or operations to be stalled. The condition occurs whenever the sortedRates array length is less than or equal to one, which may be rare in normal operation but can arise during edge cases, network glitches, or maliciously crafted API responses. All participants that rely on this function – end‑users, protocol operators, and any contracts that call it – are affected because the failure propagates up the call stack. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that inspected the index calculation and identified the off‑by‑one condition. It is hard to notice because typical test data includes multiple rates, masking the boundary case, and the exception is only thrown at runtime when the specific condition is met. To remediate, the contract should first validate that sortedRates.length is greater than one before performing the index calculation. If the length is insufficient, the code should either revert with a clear error message, return a safe default value, or skip the computation, thereby preventing an unhandled exception and preserving expected protocol behavior.

title: M-9 The trader's signature is not considered in nonce
description: In the invalidateOrderNonce method of the Signing contract (Signing.sol#L191), the nonces mapping is set using _trader. It is expected that the trader should be able to cancel their order via the cancelLimitOrder function. However, since the current implementation does not incorporate the trader's signature into the order's signature, the cancelLimitOrder function cannot protect the user from another nonce. This omission allows an unauthorized party to potentially reuse a nonce, making it impossible for the trader to effectively cancel the order.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay‑protection flaw in the order‑cancellation logic of the Signing contract. The contract stores a nonce for each trader in a mapping, but the nonce is recorded using only the trader address and does not incorporate the trader’s cryptographic signature into the order’s signed payload. As a result, when a trader calls cancelLimitOrder the contract checks the nonce without verifying that the cancellation request was signed by the trader who created the order. Because the signature is omitted, an attacker who knows a valid nonce can submit a cancellation or a new order using the same nonce, effectively reusing the nonce and preventing the legitimate trader from cancelling the original order. The flaw occurs whenever a trader attempts to cancel an order through cancelLimitOrder; the function cannot distinguish a genuine cancellation from a malicious reuse of the nonce. This impacts any user who relies on the ability to cancel pending limit orders, allowing an unauthorized party to keep the order alive or to replay it, potentially leading to unintended trades, loss of funds, or locked capital. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the relationship between nonce handling and signature verification. It is subtle because the contract does record a nonce, giving the impression that replay protection is in place, yet the missing signature check means the protection is ineffective. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful cancellation request while the order remains active, balances may stay unchanged, or the order may be executed by an attacker, contradicting the expectation that a cancelled order disappears. The bug belongs to the class of signature‑verification omissions and improper nonce binding, which break the accounting assumption that each order is uniquely authorized by its creator. To remediate, the order‑hash verification should be extended to include the trader’s signature (or the trader address as part of the signed message) so that the nonce is tied to a verifiable authorisation, ensuring that only the genuine trader can invalidate a specific nonce and cancel the associated order.

title: The execution opcode of an action can be changed from call to delegate_call after approval
description: In Llama an action only defines the target address and the function which should be called. An action doesn't implicitly define if the opcode should be a call or a delegate_call. This only depends on whether the target address is added to authorizedScripts mapping. However, adding a target to the authorizedScripts can be done after the approval in a different action. The authorizedScript action could use a different set of signers with a different approval strategy. The change of adding a target to authorizedScript should not impact actions which are already approved and in the queuing state. This could lead to security issues when policyholders approved the action under the assumption the opcode will be a call instead of a delegate call.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way an action’s execution opcode – either a regular external call or a delegate call – is determined in the Llama governance framework. An action only records the target contract address and the function selector, while the actual opcode is inferred at execution time from a separate authorizedScripts mapping. Because this mapping can be modified by a distinct action after the original action has already received the required approvals and entered the queue, the execution mode can silently switch from call to delegate_call. Policyholders approve actions under the expectation that the call will be a simple external invocation that cannot alter the caller’s storage. When the target address is later added to authorizedScripts, the same queued action will be executed as a delegate call, causing the called code to run in the context of the Llama contract and potentially modify its state, withdraw funds, or perform other privileged operations. The impact is that approved actions may be executed with higher privileges than intended, leading to unauthorized state changes, loss of funds, or breach of the protocol’s security guarantees. This condition occurs whenever a target address is not authorized at the moment of approval but becomes authorized through a separate governance action that may involve a different set of signers or an alternative approval strategy. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the relationship between action approval and the authorizedScripts registry and noticed that the opcode is not locked at approval time. It is hard to notice because the user interface typically displays only the target address and function name, not the underlying call type, and users naturally assume a regular call. The bug belongs to the class of “execution mode tampering” or “post‑approval privilege escalation” where the semantics of a transaction change after it has been consented to. From a user’s perspective, an approved transaction that should transfer tokens may instead result in a zero‑balance or an unexpected loss, contradicting the expectation that “my transaction will call the contract, not run its code inside my contract”. To remediate, the protocol should bind the execution opcode to the action at creation or approval, prevent changes to the authorizedScripts mapping that affect already queued actions, or require the same approval quorum for any modification that would alter the opcode. In essence, the system must ensure that the privilege level of an approved action cannot be upgraded without explicit consent from the original approvers.

title: LlamaPolicy.revokePolicy cannot be called repeatedly and may result in burned tokens retaining active roles
description:
Llama has two distinct revokePolicy functions. The first revokePolicy function removes all roles of a policyholder and burns the associated token. This function iterates over all existing roles, regardless of whether a policyholder still holds the role. In the next step the token is burned. If the total number of roles becomes too high, this transaction might not fit into one block. A second version of the revokePolicy function allows users to pass an array of roles to be removed. This approach should enable the function to be called multiple times, thus avoiding an "out-of-gas" error. An out-of-gas error is currently not very likely considering the maximum possible role number of 255. However, the method exists and could be called with a subset of the roles a policyholder. The method contains the following check:
```solidity
if (balanceOf(policyholder) == 0) revert AddressDoesNotHoldPolicy(policyholder);
```
Therefore, it is not possible to call the method multiple times. The result of a call with a subset of roles would lead to an inconsistent state. The token of the policyholder is burned, but the policyholder could still use the remaining roles in Llama. Important methods like LlamaPolicy.hasRole don't check if the token has been burned. (See LlamaPolicy.sol#L250)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency between role revocation and policy‑token burning in the LlamaPolicy contract. Two revokePolicy functions exist: a full‑revoke that iterates over every role a policyholder holds, removes each role and then burns the holder’s policy token, and a partial‑revoke that accepts an explicit list of roles so that the operation can be split into several transactions to avoid a possible out‑of‑gas error when many roles are present. The partial function contains a guard that reverts if the holder’s token balance is zero. Consequently, after the first call – which burns the token – any subsequent call, even if it targets only the remaining roles, fails because the balance check triggers a revert. If a caller supplies only a subset of roles in the first call, the token is burned while the un‑revoked roles stay recorded in the contract’s role mapping. Important role‑checking functions such as hasRole do not verify that the token has been burned, so the policyholder can still satisfy role‑based access checks despite no longer owning a valid policy token. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the policy has been revoked (the token disappears), yet the user can still execute privileged actions, leading to the expectation “my permissions are gone” being violated by the reality “my permissions remain active”. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who, after forcing a token burn, continues to act with the lingering roles to manipulate protocol state or withdraw funds, breaking the accounting assumptions that a burned token equals loss of all associated privileges. The issue manifests when a policyholder holds a large number of roles and the caller attempts to revoke them incrementally, or when any partial revocation is performed. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of both revokePolicy variants and noticed that the balance check prevents repeated calls, yet the role‑removal loop does not guard against a burned token. The bug is subtle because the token burn appears to be a final operation, and developers may assume that once the token is destroyed, all permissions are automatically cleared; however, the contract’s role storage is independent of the token balance. To remediate, the contract should separate role revocation from token burning: introduce a method that only removes roles without burning, allow repeated calls until all roles are cleared, and then perform a final burn, or alternatively make hasRole verify that the holder’s token balance is non‑zero before granting access. Either approach restores the invariant that a burned token implies no active roles, eliminating the possibility of lingering privileges and the associated security risk.

title: Role, permission, strategy, and guard management or config errors
description:
LlamaCore deployment from the factory will only succeed if one of the roles is the BOOTSTRAP_ROLE. As the comments note:
```solidity
// There must be at least one role holder with role ID of 1, since that role ID is initially
// given permission to call `setRolePermission`. This is required to reduce the chance that an
// instance is deployed with an invalid configuration that results in the instance being unusable.
// Role ID 1 is referred to as the bootstrap role.
```
There are still several ways a user can misstep and lose access to LlamaCore.
• Bootstrap Role Scenarios While the bootstrap role is still needed:
1. Setting an expiry on the bootstrap role's policyholder RoleHolderData and allowing the timestamp to pass. Once passed any caller may remove the BOOTSTRAP_ROLE from expired policyholders.
2. Removing the BOOTSTRAP_ROLE from all policyholders.
3. Revoking the role's permission with setRolePermission(BOOTSTRAP_ROLE, bootstrapPermissionId, false).
• General Roles and Permissions Similarly, users may allow other permissions to expire, or remove/revoke them, which can leave the contract in a state where no permissions exist to interact with it. The BOOTSTRAP_ROLE would need to be revoked or otherwise out of use for this to be a problem.
• Misconfigured Strategies A misconfigured strategy may also result in the inability to process new actions. For example:
1. Setting minApprovals too high.
2. Setting queuingPeriod unreasonably high
3. Calling revokePolicy when doing so would make policy.getRoleSupplyAsQuantitySum(approvalRole) fall below minApprovals (or fall below minApprovals - actionCreatorApprovalRoleQty). 1 & 2 but applied to disapprovals. And more, depending on the strategy (e.g. if a strategy always responded true to isActive).
• Removal of Strategies It should not be possible to remove the last strategy of a Llama instance It is possible to remove all strategies from an Ilama instance. It would not be possible to create a new action afterward. An action is required to add other strategies back. As a result, the instance would become unusable, and access to funds locked in the Accounts would be lost.
• Misconfigured Guards An accidentally overly aggressive guard could block all transactions. There is a built-in protection to prevent guards from getting in the way of basic management if (target == address(this) || target == address(policy)) revert CannotUseCoreOrPolicy();. Again, the BOOTSTRAP_ROLE would need to be revoked or otherwise out of use for this to be a problem.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a set of configuration and permission‑management errors in LlamaCore that can permanently lock out all users and render the contract unable to process any actions, effectively freezing the funds held in its Accounts. LlamaCore relies on a special bootstrap role that must always be present because it is the only role initially granted permission to call setRolePermission. The root cause is that the contract allows the bootstrap role, as well as any other role or permission, to be expired, revoked, or removed without any safeguard that guarantees at least one active permission remains. Additionally, the strategy subsystem can be mis‑configured – for example by setting the minimum number of approvals or the queuing period to values that cannot be satisfied, or by revoking a policy that reduces the effective approval supply below the required threshold – and the contract does not prevent the last strategy from being removed. Guard contracts can also be configured to reject every call, and the only built‑in exception excludes calls to the core or policy contracts, which becomes ineffective once the bootstrap role is no longer usable. An attacker or an unwary administrator can exploit these weaknesses simply by performing legitimate management actions: expiring the bootstrap role’s policyholder, removing the bootstrap role from all holders, revoking its permission, revoking other essential permissions, configuring a strategy with impossible approval requirements, or deleting the final strategy. Once any of these steps is taken, subsequent calls to create, approve, or execute actions revert because no role has the required permission, and because adding a new strategy itself requires an action, the contract cannot be restored. The impact is that the protocol instance becomes unusable, users cannot trigger any governance or fund‑movement operations, and the assets locked in the contract remain inaccessible. This condition occurs under normal usage when administrators manage roles, permissions, strategies, or guards without proper checks, and it affects any party that relies on the Llama instance for governance or fund management, including the contract owner, role holders, and end‑users. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the factory deployment requirements and the permission‑checking logic, noting that the bootstrap role’s existence is only enforced at deployment and not protected thereafter. The problem is hard to notice because the contract appears functional after deployment, and the UI may not warn when a role is set to expire or when a strategy is configured with extreme parameters, leading to a silent lockout that only manifests when an action is attempted. The recommended remediation is to make the bootstrap role non‑expirable, to enforce that at least one role with permission to manage the policy always exists, to prevent removal of the last strategy, to add on‑chain validation of strategy parameters such as minimum approvals and queuing periods, and to require that guard contracts cannot block core management calls unless a safe fallback role is present. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of misconfiguration and permission‑management flaws that can cause permanent loss of control over a smart‑contract system.

title: LlamaPolicy.hasRole doesn't check if a policyholder holds a token
description: Incorrect usage of the revokePolicy function can result in a case, where the token of a policyholder is already burned but still holds a role. The hasRole function doesn't check if in addition to the role the policyholder still holds the token to be active. The role could still be used in the Llama system.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the role‑checking routine of the LlamaPolicy contract. The hasRole function is intended to confirm that an address both possesses a specific role and holds an active policy token. However, the implementation only verifies the role mapping and neglects to confirm that the caller still owns a non‑zero balance of the policy token. When a policyholder’s token is burned—typically through an incorrect or malicious use of the revokePolicy function—the token balance becomes zero, but the role entry remains unchanged. Because hasRole does not query the token balance, the contract continues to treat the address as authorized. An attacker who has previously held a token can therefore retain the role after the token is destroyed and invoke any function protected by the role check, effectively bypassing the intended access control. This situation can arise whenever a token is burned without explicitly clearing the associated role, which is not enforced by the contract logic. The impact includes unauthorized execution of privileged actions, potential manipulation of policy parameters, and exposure of the protocol to economic attacks such as unauthorized fund transfers or policy modifications. Users may notice that they can still perform role‑restricted operations even after their policy appears to have been cancelled, leading to confusion when the UI shows a revoked policy but the backend still accepts privileged calls. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the interaction between token lifecycle events and role management. It is subtle because the role mapping persists silently; there is no event indicating that a role has become stale, and the contract does not emit warnings when a balance drops to zero. To remediate the flaw, the hasRole function should be extended to include a check that the caller’s token balance is greater than zero, for example by returning false when balanceOf(policyholder) equals zero, or by explicitly clearing the role entry when a token is burned. This adjustment restores the intended invariant that only active token holders may exercise privileged roles, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic and preventing unauthorized role exploitation.

title: Incorrect isActionApproved behavior if new policyholders get added after the createAction in the same block.timestamp
description: Llama utilizes Checkpoints to store approval quantities per timestamp. If the current quantity changes, the previous values are preserved. The block.timestamp of createAction is used as a snapshot for the approval. (See: LlamaCore.sol#L597) Thus, in addition to the Checkpoints, the totalQuantity or numberOfHolders at the createAction are included in the snapshot. However, if new policyholders are added or their quantities change after the createAction within the same block.timestamp, they are not considered in the snapshot but remain eligible to cast an approval. For example, if there are four policyholders together 50% minimum approval: If a new action is created and two policyholders are added subsequently within the same block.timestamp. The numberOfHolders would be 4 in the snapshot instead of 6. All 6 policyholders could participate in the approval, and two approvals would be sufficient instead of 4. Adding new policyholders together with creating a new action could happen easily in a llama script, which allows to bundle different actions. If a separate action is used to add a new policyholder, the final execution happens via a public callable function. An attacker could exploit this by trying to execute the add new policyholder action if a new action is created
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑estimation of the approval threshold in the Llama governance contract when new policyholders are added after an action has been created but within the same block.timestamp. Llama records the total approval quantity and the number of policyholders at the moment createAction is called by taking a snapshot based on block.timestamp and a checkpoint data structure. Because the snapshot only stores values tied to the timestamp, any subsequent changes to the set of policyholders that occur in the same second are not reflected in the snapshot, yet those newly added holders are still allowed to cast approvals. Consequently the isActionApproved check compares the number of received approvals against a smaller holder count, allowing fewer approvals to satisfy the required percentage. This can be exploited by bundling an add‑policyholder action together with a create‑action call in a single Llama script or transaction batch. An attacker can add extra holders after the action is created, then obtain the minimum number of approvals (for example two out of six instead of four out of six) and cause the action to be considered approved. The impact is that governance actions may be executed with insufficient consent, potentially leading to unauthorized protocol changes, loss of funds, or other malicious outcomes. The bug manifests whenever multiple state‑changing calls are executed in the same block timestamp, which is common because block.timestamp has second‑level granularity and many transactions can share it. All participants that rely on the governance approval mechanism – existing policyholders, the protocol itself, and any users whose assets are controlled by approved actions – are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the checkpoint‑based approval logic and noticed that the snapshot does not account for intra‑timestamp updates. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy only appears when actions are batched in the same block, a scenario that may not be covered by simple unit tests. The recommended fix is to decouple the snapshot from block.timestamp by recording, for each role, the timestamp (or block number) of the last action creation and rejecting any add‑policyholder calls that occur in the same timestamp as an action creation. This ensures that the set of holders used for the approval calculation cannot be altered after the snapshot is taken, preserving the intended approval threshold. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of “snapshot‑inconsistency” or “state‑race” vulnerabilities where a governance state is captured using a coarse time metric that does not guarantee ordering, leading to a reduced quorum requirement and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: LlamaCore delegate calls can bring Llama into an unusable state
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LlamaCore contract’s ability to execute actions via a delegate_call to an external script that has been added as an authorizedScript. Because delegate_call runs the target code in the storage context of the calling contract, the script can write to any storage slot of LlamaCore. The current implementation only protects the first storage slot (slot0) by reading its value before the call and reverting if it changes afterwards. This check does not prevent modifications to other critical variables such as actionsCount, role mappings, or fund pointers. Consequently, a malicious or buggy script can perform arbitrary SSTORE operations that corrupt the core contract’s state. For example, setting actionsCount to the maximum uint value would block the creation of any new actions, effectively freezing the governance workflow and potentially locking any assets held in the associated Account contract. The issue manifests whenever an authorizedScript is executed through the delegate_call path, which is intended for batching multiple tasks. Any user who triggers such an action, or any automated process that relies on the core contract, may experience failures: attempts to create new actions revert silently, withdrawals return zero, or UI dashboards show missing balances despite funds being present on‑chain. The problem was discovered during a security audit that noted the narrow focus on slot0 and recognized that delegate_call grants unrestricted storage access. It is hard to notice because the delegate_call itself appears legitimate and the slot0 check gives a false sense of safety, while the corrupted slots may not be directly observable without deep state inspection. To remediate, the core contract should be refactored to separate mutable logic from delegate‑call scripts, enforce a whitelist of writable slots, or replace delegate_call with a safer call pattern that does not share storage. Additionally, critical variables should be stored in immutable or protected contracts, and any script that performs SSTORE operations must undergo thorough review. By limiting the ability of external scripts to alter core storage, the protocol can prevent the state from becoming unusable and protect user funds from being unintentionally locked.

title: A cap is needed on the amount of Note than can be borrowed
description: The fact that there is no cap on the amount of Note that can be borrowed makes the Oracle Extractable Value unlimited. But as you intend to rely on TWAP, you need to make sure the cost of oracle manipulation is lower than the Oracle Extractable Value.
poc:
By manipulating the TWAPs of the designated proxy used for Note (USDC ?) and its relative price to a given collateral(which would be highly costly), an attacker could borrow Note without limit, and empty all pools related to Note and all Note-related value, instantly killing the stablecoin.

The value extractable by Oracle Manipulations is usually easily computable as it is the size of the lending market, but here, it’s more difficult to evaluate as it could potentially be any value linked to Note. This makes risk management harder and increase significantly the risk of attack.

Therefore a cap on how many Notes can be borrowed needs to be added to mitigate this risk.

The attack would be:

  * Manipulate the USDC / Collateral TWAP to be able to borrow Note with less than 1$ of collateral, which would be costly.
  * Extract all the value possible linked to Note, for example:

    * by buying all the tokens from pools Note / token at a discount
    * by supplying Notes to the lending platform and borrow collaterals for which the Note price is still at 1$
    * etc

Essentially as you have no cap on the amount of Note that could be borrowed in such a scenario, you cannot be sure that the potential attack profits are lower than the attack cost.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any borrowing limit on the Note token within the lending market contract. Because the protocol relies on a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle to determine collateral requirements, an attacker who can manipulate the TWAP for the USDC/underlying pair can artificially lower the perceived price of the collateral. With the collateral appearing cheaper, the attacker can initiate borrow transactions that request arbitrarily large amounts of Note while providing less than the nominal $1 worth of collateral per Note. The contract does not enforce a cap on the total amount of Note that can be minted through borrowing, nor does it limit the rate at which Note may be drawn in a given time window. This design flaw creates an unlimited Oracle Extractable Value (OEV) surface: the attacker can extract value far exceeding the cost of manipulating the price feed, potentially draining all Note‑related liquidity pools, emptying the stablecoin’s reserves, and rendering the token effectively valueless. The issue manifests when the price oracle for cNOTE is fixed to 1, but the fallback price calculation for any other token uses the USDC‑underlying pair, which can be skewed by controlling the TWAP. As a result, the protocol appears to have a stable price for cNOTE while silently allowing a manipulated price for the underlying asset to be used in borrowing calculations. Users affected include lenders who see their deposited collateral devalued, borrowers who may find withdrawals failing or balances suddenly reduced to zero, and token holders who witness the stablecoin lose its peg. The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit through logical reasoning about oracle dependencies and borrowing mechanics, rather than through an on‑chain exploit. It is subtle because the price‑setting code looks innocuous—cNOTE is forced to 1, and no explicit cap is present, so the problem is not obvious from a superficial code review. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a governance‑controlled maximum amount of Note that can be borrowed, possibly supplemented by an hourly or per‑block borrowing limit, and ensure that the mint/burn authority is restricted to a trusted accountant module. Strengthening the oracle by disallowing reliance on a single TWAP or by adding additional sanity checks for price deviations would also reduce the OEV. In summary, the unbounded borrowing privilege combined with a manipulable TWAP creates a scenario where funds can disappear, refunds fail, and the stablecoin’s accounting invariants are broken, necessitating caps and more robust oracle design to protect user assets.

title: Stableswap - Deadline do not work
description:
The `ensure` modifier is commented, so deadlines will not work when passing orders, breaking this functionality.

The warden has shown how, due to a comment, the modifier `deadline` doesn’t work.

Because Front-running is a key aspect of AMM design, `deadline` is a useful tool to ensure that your tx cannot be “saved for later”.

Due to the removal of the check, it may be more profitable for a miner to deny the transaction from being mined until the transaction incurs the maximum amount of slippage.

The lack of deadline means that the tx can be withheld indefinitely at the advantage of the miner.

For those reasons I agree with Medium Severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing time‑based safeguard in the stable‑swap contract: the `ensure` (deadline) modifier, which should reject a transaction after a user‑specified timestamp, is commented out. As a result, the deadline argument supplied by callers is never validated, allowing the transaction to be mined at any later block without triggering a revert. The root cause is a simple developer oversight where the require statement that checks `block.timestamp <= deadline` was disabled through commenting, removing the intended protection against front‑running and delayed execution. An attacker, typically a miner or a validator with ordering power, can exploit this by deliberately withholding the transaction or by waiting until market conditions have shifted, thereby increasing the effective slippage beyond the user’s tolerance. Because the contract still processes the swap after the delay, the user may receive a much worse price, experience higher slippage, or see the swap execute far later than expected, which appears to the user as a “swap taking forever” or a “transaction stuck”. The impact is economic: users lose expected value, liquidity providers may suffer reduced returns, and the protocol’s confidence in time‑sensitive operations is eroded. This condition occurs for every function that accepts a deadline parameter, as the check is globally disabled. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit where the auditors inspected the source code and observed the commented‑out modifier, a logical flaw that does not raise compilation errors and therefore can be hard to notice through ordinary testing. From a user’s perspective, the UI may still display a deadline field, leading users to believe the contract will enforce it, yet the transaction proceeds regardless, violating the business assumption that trades execute within a bounded time window. To remediate, the deadline validation must be restored, either by re‑enabling the `ensure` modifier or by adding an explicit `require(block.timestamp <= deadline, "Deadline passed")` check in each relevant function, accompanied by unit tests that assert proper rejection when the deadline is exceeded.

title: Multiple initialization in `NoteInterest`
description: The `initialize` method of the contract `NoteInterest` can be initialized multiple times.
bug_full: The NoteInterest contract contains an initialization function that can be invoked repeatedly by the admin address. The vulnerability is a classic re‑initialization bug: the contract does not keep any state flag indicating whether it has already been set up, nor does it use a standard initializer guard such as OpenZeppelin’s Initializable pattern. Because of this omission, the function can be called an arbitrary number of times after deployment, each call overwriting the stored cNote token reference and the price oracle address that the interest‑calculation model relies on. The root cause is the missing require statement that would reject subsequent calls once the contract has been initialized. An attacker who gains control of the admin role—or a malicious governance proposal—can exploit this by calling initialize with a malicious oracle or a different cNote address. By swapping the oracle, the attacker can feed false price data, causing the updateBaseRate logic to compute an incorrect base rate, potentially driving the interest rate to zero, to an extreme value, or to a value that redirects accrued interest to an address under the attacker’s control. Changing the cNote address could also redirect token interactions to a contract that does not hold user balances, making user balances appear empty after transactions. The impact is that users may see their interest rewards disappear, their token balances become zero, or the protocol’s accounting invariants break, leading to loss of funds under specific but realistic conditions. The vulnerability manifests whenever the admin calls initialize after the contract has already been set up; there is no temporal restriction preventing repeated calls. All participants who rely on the correctness of the interest calculation—depositors, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the warden highlighted that the initialize function lacks any protection against multiple invocations. It can be hard to notice because the function appears as a normal administrative setter, and the UI typically does not surface a warning when the parameters change, so users may only observe unexpected behavior such as zero interest payouts or missing balances. To remediate, the contract should introduce an immutable initialization flag that is set to true on the first successful call and disallows further calls, or it should move the setup logic into the constructor. Using a well‑tested initialization pattern from a trusted library (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s Initializable) would also ensure the contract adheres to the business logic that the token address and price oracle remain constant after deployment, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Non view function is called with staticcall in `CErc20Delegator`
description:
When using CToken implementation with CErc20Delegator, the functions `borrowRatePerBlock` and `supplyRatePerBlock` will revert when the underlying functions try to update some states.

The v1 of [borrowRatePerBlock](https://github.com/Plex-Engineer/lending-market-v2/blob/443a8c0fed3c5018e95f3881a31b81a555c42b2d/contracts/CToken.sol#L208) and [supplyRatePerBlock](https://github.com/Plex-Engineer/lending-market-v2/blob/443a8c0fed3c5018e95f3881a31b81a555c42b2d/contracts/CToken.sol#L216) were view functions, but they are not anymore. The `CErc20Delegator` is still using `delegateToViewImplementation` for those functions.
