4. The difference between sealedBeforeTimestamp and sealedAfterTimestamp is not more than 500 days for example  
5. The difference between sealedBeforeTimestamp and block.timestamp is not more than 10 days for example  
Also in DropEngine::configureSequence the royaltyBps is not validated that it is not more than 100% (a value of 10000). I suggest you add a lower royaltyBps upper bound.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract exposes a function that lets an authorized node configure a new sequence of operations by supplying a complex data structure. The vulnerability stems from the fact that the supplied fields are not validated against any logical constraints. Specifically, the timestamp that marks when the sequence is sealed before execution is accepted even if it is earlier than the current block time, the timestamp that marks when the sequence is sealed after execution is accepted without guaranteeing it is later than the before‑timestamp, and the allowed time window between the two timestamps is not bounded on either side. As a result a caller can set a before‑timestamp that is already expired, a after‑timestamp that is only a few seconds later, or an interval that stretches for hundreds of days, which breaks the intended scheduling logic of the protocol. In addition, the royalty basis‑points field that determines how much of each sale is paid to the creator is accepted without an upper bound, allowing values that exceed the 100 % maximum (10000 basis points). Because the function is only restricted to authorized addresses, the issue is exploitable by any node that has been granted permission to call the configuration method. An attacker can craft a sequence that either makes a drop immediately unusable (by setting the sealed‑before timestamp in the past), forces the system to wait an unreasonable amount of time before the sealed‑after condition can be satisfied (effectively freezing the drop), or causes the royalty calculation to over‑pay the creator, draining funds from the protocol treasury. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as a drop that never becomes claimable, a claim that reverts with no payout, or a royalty payout that exceeds the purchase price, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The impact ranges from loss of revenue for the protocol, incorrect accounting that violates business assumptions about royalty caps, and potential denial‑of‑service when future operations are blocked by absurd timestamp windows. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the configureSequence entry points and noticed the absence of any require statements checking the logical relationships between the timestamps and the royalty value. The problem is subtle because the function signature accepts a struct, and the lack of explicit checks can be easily overlooked when the code appears to trust the caller’s input. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce sensible constraints: the sealed‑before timestamp must be greater than the current block timestamp, the sealed‑after timestamp must be greater than the sealed‑before timestamp, the interval between them should be limited to a reasonable range (for example at least two days and no more than 500 days), the difference between the sealed‑before timestamp and the current time should not exceed a short horizon (e.g., ten days), and the royalty basis‑points must be bounded between zero and the maximum allowed value of 10000. Adding these checks restores the intended business logic, prevents malformed sequences, and protects the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Using the transfer function of address payable is discouraged
description: The mint function in DropEngine uses the transfer method of address payable to transfer native asset funds to an address. This address is set by a node owner and is possible to be a smart contract that has a receive or fallback function that takes up more than the 2300 gas which is the limit of transfer. Examples are some smart contract wallets or multi-sig wallets, so usage of transfer is discouraged.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of the Solidity built‑in transfer function to send native cryptocurrency to a configurable revenueRecipient address during the mint operation of the DropEngine contract. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback or receive function. If the revenueRecipient is a smart contract – for example a wallet contract, a multi‑signature contract, or any contract that implements a receive/fallback routine requiring more than 2300 gas – the transfer will revert because the gas limit is insufficient. This situation can be triggered by a node owner who is allowed to set the revenueRecipient address, potentially pointing it at a malicious or simply gas‑heavy contract. When the mint function attempts to transfer funds, the call fails, causing the mint transaction to revert or, depending on the surrounding code, to silently skip the payment, leaving the expected funds undistributed. From a user’s perspective the mint may appear to succeed, but the user receives no native asset, balances remain unchanged, or the transaction fails unexpectedly. The impact includes loss of expected revenue, possible denial‑of‑service for the minting process, and a break in the protocol’s accounting assumptions that revenue is always transferred successfully. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that flagged the use of transfer as discouraged in modern Solidity development. It is hard to notice because the failure manifests only when the recipient contract’s fallback consumes more gas, a condition that may not be exercised in typical testing with EOAs. The bug belongs to the class of “gas stipend limitation” or “unsafe Ether transfer” vulnerabilities, where reliance on transfer’s fixed gas stipend violates the assumption that any recipient can accept funds with minimal gas. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a configurable amount) and checks the returned success flag, and to remove the payable qualifier from the revenueRecipient variable since the call pattern no longer requires it. This change eliminates the 2300‑gas restriction, ensures that contracts with complex receive logic can be paid, and restores correct revenue flow without exposing re‑entrancy risks because the mint function already restricts callers to externally owned accounts.

title: M-1 Updating the policy for the existing method will lead to adding unnecessary
description: There is an issue at lines borgCore.sol#L262 and borgCore.sol#L266. paramOffsets is updated even if there is an attempt to change an existing parameter.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the paramOffsets array in the BorgCore contract when an existing method’s parameter constraints are modified. The contract stores the byte‑offset of each method parameter in paramOffsets, which is later used to decode calldata and enforce policy checks. The root cause is a logic error: the update routine unconditionally writes to paramOffsets even when the operation is intended only to change the constraints of a parameter that already exists. Consequently, the stored offset may be shifted, duplicated, or overwritten, breaking the alignment between the expected and actual calldata layout. An attacker who can propose a governance change to alter a method’s parameter constraints can trigger this path, causing the contract to interpret subsequent calls with incorrect offsets. This misinterpretation can lead to policy checks being bypassed, arguments being read from the wrong positions, or even re‑entrancy‑like behavior where funds are transferred based on malformed data. The impact is that legitimate users may experience failed transactions, unexpected zero refunds, or loss of funds because the contract processes malformed inputs without raising errors. The issue manifests only when a transaction attempts to modify an existing method’s parameter constraints; adding a brand‑new method does not expose the bug because the offsets are correctly initialized in that case. All participants that rely on the affected methods – including end‑users, integrators, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the method‑registration logic, where the auditor noticed that paramOffsets was updated without a guard checking whether the parameter was new. The bug is subtle because the paramOffsets array may still contain plausible values, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings, making the failure mode hard to detect until a mismatched call occurs. The correct mitigation is to adjust the update routine so that paramOffsets is only modified when a new parameter is added; when an existing parameter’s constraints are changed, the array should remain unchanged, preserving the original offset mapping. This change restores the integrity of calldata decoding and ensures that policy enforcement remains consistent with the intended method signature, preventing accidental fund loss or incorrect behavior.

title: M-10 Tests do not work
description: Tests do not work, making it impossible to check test coverage and prepare PoCs.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a non‑functional test suite for the smart‑contract system, which prevents developers and auditors from verifying that the contract logic behaves as intended. The root cause is a combination of misconfigured test scripts, missing dependencies, and possibly incorrect test harness initialization that cause compilation or runtime failures when the tests are executed. Because the tests cannot run, any logical errors, arithmetic mistakes, or access‑control flaws remain unchecked, allowing an attacker to interact with the deployed contract under false assumptions about its safety. Exploitation occurs indirectly: an adversary can submit malformed or malicious transactions that would have been rejected by a correct test suite, but because the suite never runs, the vulnerability stays hidden and the contract is deployed with unchecked code. The impact is that users may lose funds, the protocol may behave unpredictably (e.g., refunds not sent, balances becoming zero, or state transitions failing), and the overall trust in the system is eroded. This situation manifests during the pre‑deployment phase when developers attempt to run unit or integration tests, and it persists into production because no automated regression checks exist. All participants who rely on the contract – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol team – are affected because they cannot be assured that the contract adheres to its specification. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors attempted to execute the provided test scripts and observed immediate failures, indicating that test coverage could not be measured. The problem is hard to notice for teams that assume the presence of tests guarantees correctness; without visible test results, the false sense of security can go unnoticed. To remediate, the development team should rebuild the test environment, ensure all required libraries and compiler versions are correctly specified, write comprehensive unit and integration tests that cover critical paths such as fund transfers, access control, and edge‑case arithmetic, and integrate these tests into a continuous‑integration pipeline that blocks deployment if any test fails. In broader terms, this is a testing‑infrastructure defect that undermines the verification process, leading to potential financial loss and broken business logic, such as refunds disappearing or balances being incorrectly updated, contrary to user expectations that their funds will be handled correctly.

title: M-11 Seconds are used instead of days
description: duration is currently not used, but if it were used, it would incorrectly use seconds instead of days: daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L28.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a unit‑conversion error in a time‑based parameter of the DAO veto contract. The code defines a variable called duration that is intended to represent a period measured in days, but the implementation treats the value as a number of seconds. Because the contract currently does not use the duration variable, the problem is latent, yet any future feature that relies on this field will calculate time windows incorrectly. The root cause is the mismatch between the documented unit (days) and the actual arithmetic (seconds) performed when the value is read, a classic mistake of confusing time units. An attacker could exploit this by supplying a duration that appears to be a long waiting period in days, while the contract interprets it as a much shorter interval in seconds. For example, a proposer might think a veto period of 30 days is enforced, but the contract would only enforce 30 seconds, allowing the proposer to bypass the intended governance delay and execute a malicious proposal almost immediately. Conversely, legitimate users could be forced to wait far longer than expected if the contract were to convert a short day‑based value into seconds, causing funds to remain locked or refunds to be delayed. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s business logic: time‑based security guarantees are broken, leading to potential loss of funds, unauthorized state changes, or user confusion when expected waiting periods do not match reality. The condition occurs whenever the duration variable is read and used in a time comparison or deadline calculation, i.e., any function that checks block.timestamp against startTime + duration. All participants who rely on the DAO’s veto mechanism – token holders, proposal submitters, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the security model assumes a correctly sized delay. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the source file where the comment indicated days but the code performed arithmetic in seconds. Because the variable is not currently exercised by tests, the bug can remain hidden; developers may not notice the discrepancy until a feature that uses duration is deployed, making it a subtle, latent risk. The recommended remediation is to align the unit semantics: either store the duration in seconds and rename the variable accordingly, or keep the day‑based representation and explicitly convert days to seconds (e.g., multiply by 86400) before any timestamp arithmetic. This ensures that the contract’s time‑based checks reflect the intended governance policy and prevents premature or excessively delayed actions.

title: M-12 duration is not limited
description: Currently, duration is not saved in proposals (HIGH #2) but is should be saved to proposals, and the value should be limited to avoid breaking the logic: daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L131.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the proposal duration field in the DAO governance contract. The contract creates proposals without persisting the duration value and without imposing any upper bound on the value that can be supplied. Because the duration is not stored, later logic that assumes a valid, bounded duration may read an uninitialized or default value, or may accept an arbitrarily large number supplied at creation time. This omission originates from a missing assignment in the proposal‑initialisation routine and the absence of validation checks on the input parameter. An attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a proposal with an excessively large duration, effectively making the proposal never reach its expiry condition. As a result, the proposal remains permanently active, preventing any veto, execution, or fund release that depends on the expiry event. The impact is a potential governance deadlock: token holders and DAO participants expect proposals to resolve after a reasonable time, but the contract may keep them open indefinitely, causing funds to stay locked, rewards to be withheld, and the overall protocol to lose its ability to progress. The issue manifests whenever a new proposal is created, and it can be triggered by any user who can call the proposal‑creation function, because there is no role‑based restriction on the duration argument. The problem was discovered during a systematic security audit performed by MixBytes, which identified that the duration variable is not saved (as noted in a high‑severity comment) and that the code lacks any limit enforcement. The bug is subtle because the user interface may still display a deadline based on the input value, giving the impression that the deadline is enforced, while the contract’s internal state does not reflect this constraint. To remediate the issue, the duration should be stored as part of the proposal data structure and a maximum allowable duration should be defined and enforced at creation time. Additionally, the contract should reject proposals with zero or negative durations and provide a mechanism to update or correct the duration if needed. By ensuring the duration is persisted and bounded, the governance logic will correctly transition proposals to their terminal state, restoring expected fund flows and preventing indefinite locking of assets.

title: M-13 Proposals do not have an expiration date
description: In the current architecture, proposals do not have an expiration date so they can be executed after a long period of time: • daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L375 • daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L391 • daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L433.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a governance design flaw where proposals created in the DAO have no built‑in expiration mechanism. Because the contract does not store or check a deadline timestamp, a proposal remains executable indefinitely after it is submitted. The root cause is the omission of an expiration field and the corresponding validation in the execution path, which allows the proposal state machine to stay in an "open" state forever. An attacker or any participant can wait arbitrarily long, possibly after the economic or political context of the DAO has shifted, and then trigger the proposal’s execution function. This can lead to actions that were originally approved under different assumptions, such as transferring funds, changing parameters, or granting permissions that are no longer appropriate. The impact is that the DAO’s governance decisions become stale and can be abused to alter the protocol state at an unexpected time, potentially resulting in loss of funds, violation of token‑holder expectations, or a breach of the protocol’s intended business logic. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is created; there is no time‑based guard that prevents later execution, so it can be exploited at any moment after creation. All DAO participants, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the governance process no longer guarantees timely execution, undermining trust in the system. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the DAO’s smart‑contract code, where the absence of an expiration check was noted in the proposal handling functions. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows a proposal as "active" and does not warn that it could be executed months or years later; the contract simply treats the proposal as valid as long as it has not been executed or cancelled. From a user’s perspective, a proposal may appear to be pending forever, and later the DAO may unexpectedly execute an old proposal, causing balances to change or permissions to be granted without recent community consent. The bug belongs to the class of missing time‑bound constraints in governance contracts, often referred to as “unbounded proposal lifetime” or “no expiration date” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should be extended to store an expiration timestamp at proposal creation and enforce that the current block timestamp is less than this deadline before allowing execution. This change restores the expected behavior that proposals must be acted upon within a reasonable window, aligning the implementation with typical governance assumptions that decisions are time‑sensitive.

title: M-14 Too flexible logic
description: updatePolicy can be used to update existing policies or add new ones. The chosen architecture is too flexible, making it harder to control the correctness of parameter updates for the owner. The same issue also applies to the updateMethodCooldown function: • borgCore.sol#L257-L267 • borgCore.sol#L383-L395.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract exposes a single function (updatePolicy) that can both add a new policy and modify an existing one, and similarly updateMethodCooldown can both create a new cooldown entry and change an existing one. Because the implementation does not verify whether the target entry already exists, the owner can unintentionally overwrite previously set parameters or, maliciously, replace them with values that break the protocol's intended accounting or timing rules. This flexibility makes it difficult to enforce invariants such as “a policy can only be added once” or “cooldown periods cannot be reduced below a minimum”. An attacker who gains control of the owner account, or a careless owner, could call the function with a key that already exists and supply a malicious value, causing the protocol to accept incorrect fee rates, permit unauthorized withdrawals, or allow actions to be performed faster than allowed. The impact includes potential loss of funds, disruption of the protocol's economic model, and erosion of trust because users may see unexpected behavior such as transactions being processed without the expected delay, or fees being charged incorrectly. The issue manifests whenever the owner invokes updatePolicy or updateMethodCooldown without first checking the existence of the entry, which is the default behavior of the current architecture. It affects all participants who rely on the correctness of policy parameters, including token holders, liquidity providers, and any external contracts that query these values. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the lack of existence checks and the overly permissive logic. Because the functions appear to work correctly for legitimate updates, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when a parameter change produces an unexpected outcome, making it hard to attribute to the missing guard. The recommended remediation is to split the functionality into two distinct methods: one that adds a new policy or cooldown only if the identifier does not already exist, and another that updates an existing entry only after confirming its presence. This separation enforces proper lifecycle management and prevents accidental or malicious overwrites. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of “inadequate state‑transition validation” or “missing existence checks” that allow unauthorized state mutation. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may be that a transaction that should have been delayed is executed immediately, or that a fee displayed in the UI is suddenly zero or unusually high, contradicting the expected behavior.

title: M-15 Weak condition
description: The token's balance can be easily manipulated by any actor, which makes balanceCondition vulnerable to DoS attacks: balanceCondition.sol#L37.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a weak balance condition that relies on an exact equality comparison of a token balance to decide whether a function may proceed. The contract checks that the token balance of a specific address equals a hard‑coded value using a Comparison.EQUAL operation. Because token balances are mutable and can be altered by any holder of the token, an attacker can change the balance before the check is performed, causing the equality test to fail or succeed unexpectedly. This enables a denial‑of‑service (DoS) scenario: an adversary can transfer tokens into or out of the contract so that the equality condition is never satisfied, causing legitimate calls to revert or be blocked. The impact is that users may be unable to execute expected actions such as withdrawals, trades, or settlements, effectively freezing funds or breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the contract executes the equality‑based balance check, typically during state‑changing operations that depend on a precise token amount. All participants who rely on the contract’s correct accounting – including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract’s logic can be subverted by any token holder. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the unsafe use of Comparison.EQUAL for token balances. It is easy to miss because an equality check looks syntactically correct and may pass tests with static balances, yet it ignores the dynamic nature of ERC‑20 balances. To remediate, the contract should replace the equality comparison with a range or inequality check (e.g., require balance >= expectedAmount) and, where possible, maintain internal accounting that is not directly manipulable by external token transfers. This change restores the intended business logic that a sufficient token amount is present, prevents the DoS vector, and aligns the contract with standard safe‑balance verification patterns.

title: M-16 Backrun of partly set constraints
description: The current version of borgCore.updatePolicy(contracts, methodNames...) doesn't allow setting up all constraints in one call because it doesn't support constraints for UINT and some constraints with multiple exact matches for one parameter. So, multiple calls will be required for some methods. However, the method becomes callable after the first method's constraint is set — the first call of borgCore.updatePolicy(contracts, methodNames...) may be backrun by the Safe, and some partly allowed action will be performed. borgCore.sol#L227 If borgCore.addContract() is intended to add some contract to policy[] before setting constraints, it may be backrun too. borgCore.sol#L196
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporary permission escalation that occurs when the policy‑updating function of the Borg core contract is used to configure method constraints in multiple transactions. The root cause is that borgCore.updatePolicy does not support UINT‑type constraints and cannot handle several exact‑match constraints for a single parameter in one call, forcing callers to split the configuration across separate transactions. After the first transaction sets a subset of the required constraints, the target method becomes callable because the policy entry is considered valid enough for execution. An attacker who can observe the pending transaction can backrun (or front‑run) a call to the method between the first and subsequent updatePolicy calls, thereby performing an action that should only be allowed after the full set of constraints is in place. The same race condition applies to borgCore.addContract, which may be used to add a contract to the policy list before all constraints are defined; the addition can be backrun as well. This issue manifests when a governance or admin process updates permissions for a function that requires multiple, complex constraints, especially those involving unsigned integer limits or multiple exact values. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to have granted access, but the expected safety checks are only partially enforced, leading to situations where a user may see a transaction succeed that should have been rejected, or where funds are transferred without the intended restrictions. The impact includes unauthorized execution of privileged functions, potential loss or misdirection of funds, and a breach of the protocol’s security assumptions about access control. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the policy‑setting workflow and identified that the updatePolicy function does not enforce atomicity of constraint configuration. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit warning when only part of the policy is set; the UI or external observers see the method as enabled, making the temporary window of vulnerability easy to miss. To remediate the issue the updatePolicy function should be extended to support UINT constraints and to allow all required constraints to be supplied in a single atomic call, or the contract should lock the method until the full constraint set is applied. Additionally, the addContract function should be renamed to reflect that it grants unrestricted access (e.g., addFullAccessContract) and should include safeguards that prevent it from being called without the complete policy being established. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “incomplete policy enforcement” or “race‑condition during permission configuration” vulnerabilities, where partial updates create an exploitable gap between intended and actual access control.

title: M-17 Missing boundary check for duration
description: There is an issue at daoVoteGrantImplant.sol#L139. _duration value is not checked which may lead to a significant proposal duration being set. It can lead to proposal creation, which will not be limited by the duration time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing boundary check on the proposal duration parameter in the DAO voting contract. The function that creates a new proposal accepts a _duration argument but does not verify that the value is within a reasonable range. Because there is no validation, an attacker can supply an arbitrarily large or zero duration, causing the proposal to remain open indefinitely. This breaks the expected governance lifecycle where proposals are expected to expire after a predefined time window. The impact is that the DAO’s decision‑making process can be stalled; other users are unable to create or vote on new proposals while a malicious proposal occupies the queue, effectively freezing the protocol’s governance and potentially leading to loss of confidence or financial harm. The condition occurs whenever a user calls the proposal‑creation function; the bug is triggered when the supplied _duration exceeds the intended maximum or is set to a value that the contract treats as no limit. All participants who rely on timely proposal resolution—token holders, governance participants, and any contracts that depend on proposal outcomes—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected line 139 of daoVoteGrantImplant.sol and noticed the absence of any require or assert statement checking the duration. It can be difficult to notice because normal test cases use typical durations, and the UI may simply display a large number without indicating that the proposal will never close. The proper remediation is to introduce a constant such as MAXPROPOSALDURATION and enforce that _duration is less than or equal to this limit before storing it, reverting otherwise. This aligns the implementation with the business rule that proposals must have a bounded lifetime, restoring the intended accounting of voting periods and preventing indefinite lock‑up of governance functions.

title: M-18 The borgMode variable value should be immutable
description: There is a borgMode variable defined at borgCore.sol#L88. It should be impossible to change its value as it will lead to methodConstraint checks performed differently inside isMethodCallAllowed function.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a contract state variable named borgMode that is intended to represent a fixed operating mode of the protocol. In the current implementation the variable is declared as a regular mutable storage variable and is not marked immutable or constant, nor is its value locked after construction. Because the value can be altered after deployment, the internal permission check performed by the isMethodCallAllowed function, which relies on borgMode to select a set of method constraints, may behave inconsistently. An attacker or any account with access to a function that can modify borgMode (directly or indirectly through a setter, upgradeable proxy, or mis‑configured access control) could change the mode to a less restrictive setting, causing the contract to accept calls that should be rejected. This can lead to unauthorized method execution, potential loss or misdirection of funds, and a breach of the protocol’s business logic that assumes a static mode for accounting and security checks. The issue manifests when the variable is changed at runtime; users may observe that operations which previously reverted now succeed, resulting in unexpected state changes such as balances being altered without explicit user intent, refunds not being issued, or privileged actions being performed by unauthorized parties. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s state management and discovered that borgMode lacks the immutable keyword and is not protected against post‑deployment modification. Because the variable appears to be a simple configuration flag, the mutability may not be obvious without a detailed code review, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the borgMode value should be fixed at deployment time, for example by declaring it immutable and assigning it only in the constructor, and by removing any functions that could modify it thereafter. This ensures that methodConstraint checks remain consistent throughout the contract’s lifetime, preserving the intended security guarantees and preventing the described unauthorized behavior.

title: M-19 Parameter constraint is rewritten with empty values in some cases
description: There is an issue at borgCore.sol#L424. If there are such minValue and maxValue which lead to the check failing, the chosen parameter constraint will be rewritten by the empty values at borgCore.sol#L434. The same issue is present at borgCore.sol#L428.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a silent state‑mutation bug in the policy‑update logic of the Borg core contract. When the function that updates a parameter’s constraints receives a minValue and maxValue pair that does not satisfy the internal validation (for example, a minimum that is larger than the maximum or values that are otherwise inconsistent), the contract does not abort. Instead, the code proceeds to call the internal routine that stores the constraint, but it supplies empty (zero) values for the bounds. As a result, the previously defined constraint is overwritten with an empty constraint, effectively removing any range checks for that parameter. This happens because the validation check is performed after the call that writes the constraint, and the failure path does not contain a revert or an explicit error, allowing execution to continue. An attacker or any privileged caller who can invoke the policy‑update function can deliberately supply malformed bounds to trigger the overwrite, thereby stripping the contract of its intended safeguards. The impact is that parameters that were supposed to be limited can now accept arbitrary values, which may break accounting assumptions, allow out‑of‑range trades, cause fee calculations to be bypassed, or otherwise lead to unintended protocol behavior. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a policy update succeeded, but later actions behave incorrectly – for instance, a user may be able to submit a transaction with values that should have been rejected, or they may notice that previously enforced limits are suddenly absent, leading to confusion or potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of the updatePolicy function was examined and the misplaced assignment was identified. It is hard to notice because no error is emitted, no revert occurs, and the contract state change appears legitimate; only a careful inspection of the constraint‑storage logic reveals that empty values are being written. The recommended remediation is to move the validation before any state‑changing call and to make the function revert when the supplied bounds are invalid. Additionally, the helper that adds a parameter constraint should be invoked only for supported parameter types (UINT or INT) and never with empty min or max values, ensuring that malformed inputs cannot silently erase existing constraints.

title: M-6 Chainlink returned data is not checked for being stale
description: There is a call to the Chainlink price feed latestRoundData at line chainlinkOracleCondition.sol#L53. It can return a stale price due to Chainlink lagging in delivering actual data.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on the Chainlink price feed function latestRoundData without verifying the freshness of the returned price. Chainlink oracles publish price updates periodically, but there can be a delay between the actual market price change and the time the oracle writes a new round. Because the contract does not call the updatedAt accessor or compare the timestamp of the returned round with the current block time, it may accept a price that is several minutes or even hours old. An attacker or a market participant can exploit this by triggering contract logic (such as opening a position, executing a trade, or initiating liquidation) during a period when the oracle data is stale. The stale price will be used in calculations that determine collateral requirements, liquidation thresholds, or trade execution rates, causing the contract to behave contrary to the intended business logic. Users may see unexpected outcomes: a trade may execute at a price far from the market, a liquidation may occur even though the market price appears unchanged, or a repayment may be calculated incorrectly, leading to loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever the price feed has not been updated within the expected freshness window, which can happen during network congestion, oracle downtime, or simply because the feed’s update frequency is low. All participants that depend on accurate pricing – lenders, borrowers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the system (that the price reflects the current market) are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the oracle integration code and noted the absence of any timestamp validation. It is subtle because the returned price value looks syntactically correct and the contract does not emit any warning, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. The proper mitigation is to retrieve the updatedAt timestamp from the price feed and enforce a maximum age (for example, require that block.timestamp‑updatedAt be less than a predefined freshness threshold) before accepting the price, or to fall back to an alternative source if the data is stale. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an oracle data freshness or stale‑data vulnerability, where the contract trusts external data without confirming its recency, leading to potential financial mis‑calculations and user loss.

title: M-7 Conditions' order has impact
description: The current implementation of the conditions check relies on the condition order, which makes the system more vulnerable to owner's faults and makes the protocol less flexible. • conditionManager.sol#L62-L74 • conditionManager.sol#L120-L126
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logic flaw where the evaluation of protocol conditions depends on the sequence in which they are stored and checked. The root cause is that the condition manager contracts iterate over a list of conditions and stop processing as soon as a failing condition is encountered, without guaranteeing that all required checks are performed regardless of order. An attacker who controls or can influence the ordering of conditions – typically the contract owner – can deliberately place a benign condition before a critical one, causing the critical check to be skipped when the earlier condition passes. This can be exploited by submitting a transaction that satisfies the first condition while the second, more restrictive condition is never evaluated, allowing actions that should be prohibited, such as unauthorized withdrawals, parameter changes, or execution of privileged functions. The impact is that the protocol’s security guarantees are weakened: users may lose funds, the protocol may behave contrary to its specifications, and the system becomes less flexible because any future addition of conditions must consider ordering constraints. The issue manifests whenever the condition manager’s check function is called, which is during every operation that relies on condition validation – for example, order placement, settlement, or admin actions. All participants that rely on the correctness of these checks – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewers noticed that the condition verification loop used a simple for‑loop over an array and that the order of entries altered the outcome, a pattern that is easy to overlook because the code appears to perform all checks at a glance. The problem is subtle because the contract may work correctly with the current default ordering, masking the risk until an owner intentionally reorders conditions. To remediate, the condition checking architecture should be redesigned to be order‑independent: conditions should be stored in a mapping or set and evaluated independently, or the loop should aggregate results of all conditions before deciding, ensuring that every required rule is enforced regardless of how they are arranged. This change restores the intended security model and prevents owners from bypassing critical checks through manipulation of condition order.

title: M-8 API3 heartbeat
description: API3 heartbeat is 24 hours, which means that the condition is vulnerable to lags in updates: API3OracleCondition.sol#L46.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on a fixed 24‑hour heartbeat interval for the API3 oracle data. The contract assumes that the oracle will provide a fresh value at least once every 24 hours and uses that value in a condition that governs critical protocol logic, such as price verification or state transitions. Because the code does not verify that the timestamp of the latest oracle update is within an acceptable freshness window, a delay longer than the expected 24‑hour period leaves the contract operating on stale data. This situation can be triggered when the API3 oracle experiences network congestion, gas price spikes, or operator downtime, causing the update transaction to be postponed beyond the heartbeat. An attacker who can influence the oracle’s update schedule—or simply wait for a natural delay—can then invoke functions that depend on the condition, causing the protocol to make decisions based on outdated information. The practical impact includes users receiving incorrect outcomes, such as trades executed at obsolete prices, refunds calculated with wrong values, or collateral checks that mistakenly pass, potentially leading to loss of funds or unfair advantage. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as a sudden loss of value, a zero or unexpected balance after an operation, or a missing refund that the UI shows as “0”. The issue was identified during a formal security audit by MixBytes, which noted that the heartbeat logic does not account for occasional lag. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error when the data is stale; it simply proceeds with the last known value, making the bug hard to detect until a delay occurs. To remediate, the contract should treat the oracle value as valid only if its timestamp is within a configurable freshness margin (e.g., 30 hours) and should include fallback logic such as pausing dependent functions, reverting with a clear error, or allowing a manual update when the heartbeat is missed. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “stale oracle data” or “insufficient freshness checks”, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that external data reflects the current state of the world. By enforcing proper timestamp validation and handling missed heartbeats gracefully, the protocol can prevent execution based on outdated information and protect user funds.

title: M-9 The owner can remove themselves
description: The current implementation of role updates allows the owner to remove themselves, which can lead to the full block of the system: auth.sol#L42-L48.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an owner self‑removal flaw in the contract's role‑management logic. The update‑role function does not prevent the current owner from calling the removal routine on their own address, which means the owner can unintentionally or maliciously renounce their privileged role without any fallback administrator being left in place. This occurs because the access‑control check only verifies that the caller is an authorized role, but it does not enforce a rule that at least one owner must remain after the operation. When the owner removes themselves, any function that requires the owner role reverts or becomes a no‑op, effectively halting the protocol's administrative capabilities. From a user's perspective the UI may suddenly stop showing admin buttons, transactions that previously required owner approval start failing, and deposits or withdrawals may be blocked because the contract can no longer execute privileged logic. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the system is blocked, funds may become inaccessible, and the protocol cannot be upgraded or maintained. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the role‑update code where the author noticed that the removal path does not contain a safeguard against zero owners. It can be hard to notice because self‑renunciation is a common pattern in many contracts, yet in this design there is no alternative owner to take over, so the problem only surfaces after the owner actually executes the removal. To remediate, the contract should either forbid the owner from removing themselves, require a multi‑step handover to a new owner, or enforce that at least one owner address remains after any removal operation. This class of bug belongs to privilege‑loss or access‑control misconfiguration where a critical role can be eliminated without a replacement, breaking business logic that assumes an always‑present administrator.

title: M-2 Missing transferred value check
description: There is a check at line borgCore.sol#L154 which passes if there is any calldata specified for the call. It will also pass if there is some value transferred together with the call, which can lead to bypassing the previous check (borgCore.sol#L141) for native token transfers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing transferred value check in a smart‑contract method that is intended to reject native token (e.g., ETH) transfers. The contract contains a guard at line 154 that only verifies the presence of calldata; the condition evaluates to true whenever any calldata is supplied, and it also evaluates to true if the caller attaches a non‑zero value to the call. Because the earlier guard at line 141, which was supposed to block native token transfers, is bypassed when the second guard passes, an attacker can invoke the function with a non‑zero msg.value and arbitrary calldata, causing the contract to accept ether that should have been rejected. This happens whenever a user calls the affected method with both calldata and a value transfer, a scenario that is not covered by the existing checks. The root cause is the logical error of using only calldata length as a proxy for a valid call, neglecting to enforce that msg.value must be zero for functions that are not meant to receive native tokens. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary sends a transaction that includes a small amount of ether together with any calldata; the contract’s check at line 154 returns true, the earlier check at line 141 is skipped, and the ether is accepted. The impact is that funds can be unintentionally deposited into a contract that does not have accounting logic for such deposits, potentially leading to locked or lost ether, broken accounting assumptions, and a mismatch between expected and actual balances. Users of the protocol may notice that their balances appear unchanged while the contract’s internal accounting shows an unexpected increase, or that refunds that should be calculated in tokens are missing because ether was mistakenly accepted. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, which identified that the condition does not consider msg.value. Because the check looks reasonable at a glance—verifying that some calldata exists—it can be easy to overlook the missing value validation, especially if tests focus only on function signatures and not on value transfers. To remediate, the contract should add an explicit requirement that msg.value equals zero (or matches an allowed amount) whenever native token transfers are prohibited, ensuring that both calldata and transferred value are validated before proceeding. This class of bug falls under improper input validation for monetary value, where the contract fails to enforce the intended economic constraints, leading to potential fund loss or accounting errors.

title: M-20 The native token transfer is not supported by borgCore.checkTransaction()
description: There is a zero check of calldata size in borgCore.checkTransaction() in the blacklist branch. So, it's impossible to transfer native tokens in a regular way in this mode. There is also no way to restrict call value similar to what's done in the whitelist branch. borgCore.sol#L168 borgCore.sol#L600
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the transaction validation routine of the core contract when operating in the blacklist mode. The routine performs a check that rejects any transaction whose calldata size is zero. Because a native token transfer (for example, sending ETH) is encoded with an empty calldata payload, the zero‑size check prevents the contract from processing such transfers. Consequently, users attempting to move native tokens through the contract in blacklist mode are unable to do so; the transaction is rejected before execution. In addition, the blacklist branch lacks a mechanism to limit the amount of native token (call value) that can be sent, unlike the whitelist branch which enforces a maximum value. This omission means that, while native token transfers are blocked, there is also no safeguard against accidental or malicious large value transfers when the check is bypassed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes when the auditors inspected the checkTransaction function and noticed the unconditional zero‑calldata requirement and the missing call‑value restriction. It can be hard to notice because most test suites focus on ERC‑20 token flows that include non‑empty calldata, leaving native token paths untested. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a wallet UI shows a transaction being submitted but the contract returns an error or simply does nothing, resulting in “no funds received” or “balance stays the same” after an attempted deposit or withdrawal of the native token. The impact is a functional denial of service: legitimate users cannot deposit, withdraw, or otherwise move native tokens while the contract is in blacklist mode, potentially locking funds or breaking expected business logic such as refunds or fee payments. The affected parties are any participants who rely on native token transfers, including end‑users, liquidity providers, and protocol operators. To remediate the issue the core contract should be extended to recognise empty‑calldata transactions as valid native token transfers in the blacklist branch, mirroring the handling present in the whitelist branch, and a call‑value cap should be introduced to enforce the same limits on the amount of native token that can be sent. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents the accidental blocking of native token flows.

title: M-1 Possible DoS with small transfers
description: A vulnerability exists at the TokenLexscrow.sol#L335, where minor direct deposits to the contract could trigger the check to pass, which will make users' deposits revert.
bug_full: The contract implements an escrow deposit function that first checks whether the amount a user wants to deposit, together with the protocol fee, does not exceed the total amount that the contract currently holds. The check is performed against the contract's raw balance, which can be altered by any direct transfer of tokens or ether to the contract address. Because the code does not distinguish between funds received through the official deposit routine and arbitrary external transfers, a malicious actor can send a very small amount of dust to the contract. This dust increases the contract balance just enough to make the internal check succeed for the wrong reason, causing the subsequent require statement to revert legitimate deposit attempts. In practice, a user initiates a deposit, the transaction reaches the point where the contract validates the available balance, the validation fails due to the unexpected dust, and the whole transaction reverts. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a generic “deposit failed” or “transaction reverted” message, and the expected increase in their escrow balance never occurs. The vulnerability manifests whenever the contract receives unsolicited small transfers – for example, an attacker sending a few wei or token units directly to the address. All regular users of the escrow service are affected because they can no longer add funds, effectively resulting in a denial‑of‑service (DoS) on the deposit functionality. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the balance‑checking logic and noticed that the contract does not filter out external dust. It can be hard to notice because the extra amount is tiny and does not raise obvious alarms in transaction logs, yet it breaks the accounting invariant. The root cause is the reliance on the contract’s external balance as a source of truth for internal accounting, instead of tracking deposits through dedicated state variables. To remediate the problem the contract should compute the expected total using its own accounting records, ignore direct transfers, or require the depositor to send exactly the amount needed to cover the fee, thereby eliminating the influence of unsolicited dust. Conceptually this belongs to the class of “balance‑manipulation DoS” bugs where external value injections corrupt internal invariants, leading to failed operations and loss of service.

title: M-10 rejectDepositor can be front-run
description: rejectDepositor can be front-run by the buyer, so the seller tx will revert: TokenLexscrow.sol#L455-L473, EthLexscrow.sol#L311-L329.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the escrow contracts where the function that allows a buyer to reject a deposit (rejectDepositor) can be executed by the buyer after the seller has submitted a transaction to update the buyer’s status (updateBuyer) but before the seller’s transaction is mined. The root cause is that the contract does not enforce a proper ordering or atomicity between the seller’s acceptance of the buyer and the buyer’s ability to reject the deposit, allowing a malicious buyer to observe the pending seller transaction in the mempool and submit a rejectDepositor call that will be mined first. An attacker (typically the buyer) can monitor the network, detect the seller’s pending updateBuyer transaction, and then broadcast a rejectDepositor transaction with a higher gas price. Because Ethereum processes transactions in the order they are included in a block, the attacker’s transaction can be mined before the seller’s, causing the seller’s updateBuyer call to revert. When the seller’s transaction reverts, the seller loses the gas spent on the call and the escrow state does not progress, effectively resulting in a denial‑of‑service for the seller and potentially locking the escrowed funds until the issue is resolved. This situation occurs only when the seller attempts to finalize the buyer’s participation while the buyer remains able to invoke rejectDepositor, i.e., during the narrow window between the seller’s transaction being broadcast and its inclusion in a block. Both sellers and the overall protocol are affected because the escrow flow can be stalled, funds may remain locked, and users may experience unexpected transaction failures. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined transaction ordering and state‑transition logic. It is hard to notice because the code appears to allow both parties to act independently, and the problem only manifests under specific timing conditions that are not evident from static analysis alone. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a mutual‑consent mechanism that prevents the buyer from calling rejectDepositor after the seller has signaled acceptance, for example by introducing a pause flag, a commit‑reveal scheme, or a mutex that locks the rejectDepositor function once updateBuyer has been called. From the user’s perspective, a seller may see their transaction revert with an “execution reverted” error and a loss of gas, while the buyer may see a deposit being rejected unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or transaction‑ordering vulnerabilities that break business logic assumptions about the sequence of escrow operations, leading to funds appearing to disappear or escrow updates failing.

title: M-11 Incorrect usage of permit
description: In the depositTokensWithPermit function, a user can sign a permit for a specific _amount value, which TokenLexscrow.sol#L320 inside the function which will lead to a revert of the permit call: TokenLexscrow.sol#L342
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the depositTokensWithPermit function of the escrow contract, where the permit operation is executed with an amount that does not match the value originally signed by the token holder. A user signs an EIP‑2612 permit for a specific _amount, expecting the contract to forward that exact amount to the token’s permit function. However, the implementation overwrites or otherwise changes the variable used in the permit call before it is passed to the token contract, causing a mismatch between the signed allowance and the amount supplied to the permit method. Because the permit verification checks that the allowance granted by the signature equals the amount argument, the call reverts when the values differ. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a depositor invokes depositTokensWithPermit with a signed permit, making the transaction fail and the deposit not recorded. The impact is that legitimate users are unable to deposit tokens via the gas‑less permit flow, leading to failed transactions, wasted gas fees, and potential loss of confidence in the escrow service. The issue is discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, where the code path was traced and the inconsistent use of the amount variable was identified. It is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the revert only occurs at runtime, appearing as a generic “permit failed” error without indicating the underlying mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect parameter usage in signature‑based authorisation, where a signed value is not consistently applied throughout the workflow, violating the accounting assumption that the signed allowance equals the transferred amount. To remediate, the contract should retain the original _amount supplied by the user and pass that exact value to the token’s permit function, ensuring that the signed allowance and the amount argument are identical. This change restores the intended behaviour where a user’s signed permit reliably authorises the exact token amount to be transferred into the escrow, eliminating unexpected reverts and preserving user funds.

title: M-2 The buyer address can be set to the seller address
description: There is an issue within the EthLexscrow.sol#L264. Currently, the buyer can alter the buyer variable value to the seller's address. It will lead to the seller's amountWithdrawable value being reduced at the EthLexscrow.sol#L369. The remaining tokens would be stuck on the contract as the balance was accounted in the pendingWithdraw variable.
bug_full: The contract allows the buyer address to be overwritten with the seller address through the updateBuyer (and similarly updateSeller) functions. Because the code does not enforce that the buyer and seller remain distinct, a malicious buyer can call updateBuyer and set the buyer variable to the seller's address. This manipulation changes the internal accounting: the seller’s amountWithdrawable balance is decreased while the total deposited tokens remain recorded in the pendingWithdraw variable. As a result, the tokens that should be claimable by the seller become trapped in the contract because the withdraw logic checks the seller address against the amountWithdrawable mapping, which now reflects a reduced amount. The vulnerability originates from missing validation checks (e.g., require(newBuyer != seller)) in the address‑update functions. It can be exploited at any point after the escrow is funded when the buyer is still permitted to call updateBuyer. The impact is that funds may become permanently locked, violating the expectation that both parties can retrieve their escrowed assets; users may see their balance show zero or missing refunds despite having deposited tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s state‑transition logic and noticed that address updates were unrestricted. Because the functions appear benign and no immediate error is thrown, the problem can be subtle and may only surface when a withdrawal fails. The proper remediation is to add explicit checks that the new buyer address is not equal to the seller address (and vice‑versa), and to ensure that address updates are only allowed before funds are locked or that they are completely disabled after escrow funding. This aligns the contract with the generic class of “improper access control / missing invariant enforcement” bugs that lead to accounting inconsistencies and locked funds.

title: M-3 Random depositor amountDeposited is not cleared
description: There is an issue inside the receive function defined at the EthLexscrow.sol#L230. When openOffer is false and msg.sender is not the buyer, a third party may deposit on behalf of the buyer. After an execute call, the depositor's amountDeposited is not reset to 0. This can lead to a situation where, upon rejection of the depositor, the pendingWithdraw exceeds the address(this).balance. The subsequent buyer deposit could then be less than the actual amount (if the deposit is sufficient not to revert at the EthLexscrow.sol#L231).
bug_full: An amount‑deposited accounting flaw exists in the receive function of the escrow contract. When the offer is marked as closed (openOffer == false) the contract does not restrict who can send ether. A third‑party address that is not the designated buyer can therefore call the receive function and have its contribution recorded in the internal amountDeposited field as if it were the buyer’s payment. After the buyer or seller later calls the execute function, the contract processes the transaction but fails to reset the amountDeposited entry for that third‑party depositor. Consequently, if the transaction is later rejected and the contract attempts to refund the buyer, the pendingWithdraw variable includes the stale amountDeposited value. Because the stale value was never cleared, pendingWithdraw can become larger than the actual ether held by the contract (address(this).balance). When a subsequent buyer deposit is made, the contract may accept a smaller amount than required without reverting, because the internal accounting believes enough funds are already present. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a refund that never arrives, a balance that appears to be zero despite having deposited, or a situation where the contract accepts a deposit but later refuses to release funds. The bug originates from missing state‑reset logic and from allowing arbitrary addresses to deposit when the offer is closed. It was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, and it can be difficult to notice because normal buyer‑only flows do not trigger the stale entry. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect state cleanup after external calls” and “unauthorized deposit handling”. To remediate the issue the contract should either prohibit deposits from any address other than the buyer when openOffer is false, or explicitly clear the amountDeposited entry for the depositor after execute completes, and ensure that pendingWithdraw never exceeds the contract’s ether balance.

title: M-4 Incorrect fee calculation
description: A potential rounding error exists at the TokenLexscrowFactory.sol#L117. The feeDenominatorAdjusted may round down to 0 if a token's decimals are significantly less than 18, leading to the ONE constant being used as _feeDenominatorAdjusted. This results in the fee equating to totalAmount at the TokenLexscrowFactory.sol#L123 Conversely, if decimals exceed 18, feeDenominatorAdjusted does not accurately represent a fraction of totalAmount, resulting in a lower-than-expected _fee. Additionally, tokens with decimals = 0 will encounter a similar issue, as feeDenominatorAdjusted will not reflect the correct proportion of totalAmount.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error in the escrow fee calculation logic. The contract derives a denominator called feeDenominatorAdjusted by scaling a constant with the token's decimal count. Because Solidity performs integer division, when a token has far fewer than 18 decimals – including the extreme case of zero decimals – the scaling factor is rounded down to zero, causing feeDenominatorAdjusted to become the constant ONE (value 1). The fee is then computed as totalAmount multiplied by the fee share divided by this denominator, which effectively reduces to fee = totalAmount. Consequently, a user who expects to receive the escrowed amount minus a modest fee instead receives nothing, as the entire balance is taken as a fee. Conversely, for tokens whose decimals exceed 18, the scaling produces a denominator that is larger than intended, so the fee becomes smaller than the protocol’s business rule, breaking accounting assumptions. The bug manifests during escrow creation when the fee is calculated (lines 117‑123 of TokenLexscrowFactory.sol) and is triggered whenever the token’s decimal precision deviates significantly from the 18‑decimal baseline used by the contract. The affected parties are any users depositing such tokens, the escrow protocol itself, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct fee accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which identified the misuse of token decimals in a financial formula. It is hard to notice because the fee appears as a normal numeric value; only when the fee equals the full deposited amount or is unexpectedly low does the discrepancy become apparent. This violates the core business logic that fees should be a small, predictable fraction of the total amount, leading to either total loss of funds or under‑charging. The recommended remediation is to abandon the decimal‑based scaling and instead use a fixed denominator expressed in basis points (e.g., fee = totalAmount * feeShare / BASIS_POINTS), which provides consistent precision regardless of token decimals and eliminates the rounding problem.

title: M-5 Conditions' order impact
description: The current implementation of the conditions check relies on the condition order, which makes the system more vulnerable to the owner's faults and makes the protocol less flexible. LexscrowConditionManager.sol#L48-L60
bug_full: The vulnerability is an order‑dependent condition evaluation flaw in the contract that manages escrow or similar state transitions. The contract iterates through a list of pre‑defined conditions and decides whether a user action, such as releasing funds, is allowed based on the result of each check. Because the implementation assumes a fixed sequence, the logical outcome changes if the conditions are reordered. This dependency originates from the fact that the code does not treat each condition as an independent predicate; instead, later checks may be skipped, overridden, or incorrectly combined depending on the result of earlier checks. An attacker who controls the ordering – typically the contract owner or any party that can propose a new set of conditions – can manipulate the flow so that a required safety check is never evaluated, or a check that should block a release is bypassed. Exploitation consists of arranging the conditions so that a malicious or faulty condition appears after a condition that already returns true, causing the subsequent checks to be ignored. As a result, funds may be released without satisfying all intended safeguards, or conversely, legitimate releases may be blocked, leading to locked assets. The issue manifests whenever the contract evaluates its condition list, which occurs on every state‑changing operation that depends on those checks, such as escrow settlement, withdrawal, or dispute resolution. All participants who rely on the escrow – users depositing funds, beneficiaries awaiting payment, and third‑party auditors – are affected because the protocol no longer guarantees that every required rule is enforced. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the condition manager’s source code and identified the hard‑coded sequence of checks. It is subtle because the contract may behave correctly under the default ordering used in tests, making the problem easy to miss unless alternative orderings are deliberately tried. The bug belongs to the broader class of “order‑dependent logic” or “state‑machine ordering” vulnerabilities, where the correctness of a system relies on an implicit sequence rather than explicit, order‑agnostic validation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal may succeed even though a prerequisite condition (for example, a dispute resolution or a time lock) was not satisfied, or a legitimate withdrawal may fail with no clear error, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. To remediate the issue the condition evaluation should be redesigned so that each predicate is evaluated independently and the final decision is derived from a deterministic aggregation (e.g., logical AND of all conditions) that does not depend on their position in the list. This makes the protocol resilient to changes in condition ordering, reduces owner‑related risk, and restores the intended security guarantees.

title: M-6 Tests do not work
description: Currently, the protocol's tests do not work, making it impossible to check test coverage and prepare PoCs.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a non‑functional test suite for the protocol. Because the automated tests fail to compile or execute, developers cannot verify that the contract logic satisfies its specifications, nor can they generate reliable proof‑of‑concept attacks. The root cause is that the test files are either missing, incorrectly configured, or depend on unavailable libraries, causing the test runner to abort before any assertions are evaluated. An attacker can exploit this situation by deploying the contract without any prior validation; hidden bugs such as arithmetic errors, access‑control flaws, or re‑entrancy vulnerabilities may remain undetected. The impact is that users may interact with a contract that behaves incorrectly, leading to lost funds, unexpected zero balances, or failed refunds. The condition under which the issue manifests is any development or CI environment where the test command is invoked – the suite immediately exits with errors, providing no coverage metrics. All participants – developers, auditors, and end‑users – are affected because the lack of testing undermines confidence in the protocol’s safety. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors attempted to run the provided test scripts and observed that they never produced results. The issue is hard to notice because a repository may appear complete, yet the absence of passing tests gives a false sense of security. To remediate, the team should create a comprehensive set of unit and integration tests, configure the testing framework correctly, ensure all dependencies are installed, and integrate the suite into a continuous‑integration pipeline so that test failures block deployment. In generic terms, this is a test‑suite failure or missing test coverage bug that violates the fundamental security engineering practice of verifying contract behavior before launch.

title: M-21 Unreachable Code in updateThreshold Function
description: The issue is identified within the multiUseSignCondition.sol#L78-L85 function of the MultiUseSignCondition contract. The function contains a check to ensure that only an owner of the BORG_SAFE can update the threshold. However, this check will always fail because the onlyOwner modifier requires msg.sender to be the BORG_SAFE contract itself, which conflicts with the check inside the function that requires msg.sender to be an owner of BORGSAFE. Since the BORGSAFE contract cannot be an owner of itself, any call to this function will always revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that is intended to let the owner of a safe contract adjust a critical threshold value. The function is protected by an onlyOwner modifier that restricts calls to the safe contract address itself, while an additional inline check requires the caller to be an owner of that same safe contract. Because a contract cannot be its own owner, the two conditions are mutually exclusive and can never be satisfied together. As a result, any attempt to invoke the function triggers a revert, making the code unreachable. The root cause is a contradictory access‑control design where the external modifier and the internal ownership verification enforce incompatible requirements. Exploitation is trivial: a legitimate owner or any external account that tries to call the function will always receive a revert error, preventing the threshold from being updated. The impact is that the protocol’s governance or risk‑management mechanism that relies on dynamic threshold adjustments becomes frozen; users expecting the threshold to change will see no effect, potentially leading to confusion or operational blockage. The issue manifests whenever the function is called, regardless of the caller’s identity, and affects all participants who depend on the ability to modify the threshold, including protocol administrators and token holders. It was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditor examined the access‑control flow and recognized that the onlyOwner modifier already limits calls to the safe contract, making the extra owner check redundant and fatal. The problem can be hard to notice because both checks compile without warnings and appear to enforce security, yet their interaction creates a logical dead‑end that only surfaces at runtime. To remediate, the redundant internal ownership check should be removed or the onlyOwner modifier should be adjusted so that both checks align, thereby restoring the intended permission model. This class of bug falls under contradictory access‑control or unreachable code due to mutually exclusive conditions, and it violates the business assumption that owners can modify protocol parameters, leading to a mismatch between user expectations (the threshold should update) and reality (the transaction always reverts).

title: M-7 Double escrow for one token
description: If tokenContract1 == tokenContract2 in the DoubleTokenLexscrow, all deposited funds will be blocked on the contract: DoubleTokenLexscrow.sol#L243-L244.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical dead‑lock in a double‑escrow contract that is intended to hold two different ERC‑20 tokens, one for each party, and release them when predefined conditions are met. The root cause is the absence of a validation that the two token contract addresses supplied to the escrow are distinct. When the same token contract address is passed for both tokenContract1 and tokenContract2, the contract treats the two escrow balances as separate but they actually reference the same token ledger. During the release phase the contract attempts to transfer each side’s balance using the same token contract, which results in an internal accounting mismatch: the contract believes it still owes tokens to the opposite party while the token balance has already been deducted for the first transfer. Consequently the second transfer fails, the internal state is left inconsistent, and all tokens that were deposited become permanently locked in the escrow contract. This can be exploited simply by a user or an attacker who supplies identical token addresses when creating a new escrow instance; no special privileges or complex interactions are required. The impact is that users who deposit tokens expecting a later refund or swap receive nothing; their UI will show a successful deposit but later attempts to withdraw or claim the counterpart token will return zero, effectively making the funds disappear from the user's perspective while they remain trapped in the contract. The condition occurs whenever the contract is instantiated with tokenContract1 equal to tokenContract2, which may happen unintentionally if a developer reuses the same token for both sides or if a malicious actor deliberately crafts such an escrow. All participants of the protocol who rely on the double‑escrow mechanism are affected, but only those escrows created with identical token contracts suffer the loss. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s initialization logic and identified the missing inequality check. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and runs without reverting, and the failure only manifests later during the release step, which may be exercised infrequently. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit require statement that rejects any escrow creation where the two token contract addresses are the same, thereby preventing the dead‑lock scenario at the source. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect input validation leading to state inconsistency” bugs, where assumptions about distinct assets are not enforced, causing accounting violations and loss of funds.

title: M-8 Centralization risks
description: receiver can front-run escrow creation and change fees: DoubleTokenLexscrowFactory.sol#L192-L204, EthLexscrowFactory.sol#L124-L131, TokenLexscrowFactory.sol#L147-L154
