bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk that allows a privileged receiver to front‑run the creation of a new escrow and modify the fee parameters immediately before the escrow contract is instantiated. The root cause is that the fee‑update function in the escrow factory contracts is callable by a single address without any time‑lock or multi‑step governance, meaning the fee can be changed in the same block as a pending escrow creation transaction. An attacker who monitors the mempool can see a user’s transaction that will create an escrow with a certain fee, then submit a transaction that changes the fee to a higher value before the factory processes the escrow creation. Because the factory reads the fee value at the moment of escrow deployment, the newly created escrow records the malicious fee, causing the user to pay more than expected or, in extreme cases, to lose funds if the fee is set to an amount that drains the escrow balance. This exploit occurs whenever fee updates are unrestricted and can be executed in the same block as escrow creation, affecting any user attempting to lock assets, the protocol’s reputation, and any token holders relying on fair fee calculation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the factory contracts, where the auditor noted that the fee‑changing function was not protected by a delay or governance process and could be invoked by the same address that receives the fees. The problem is subtle because fee changes are legitimate operations and may not raise alarms; the malicious transaction blends with normal fee‑update activity, making it hard to detect without analyzing transaction ordering. To remediate, the fee update should be split into a two‑step process with a mandatory time delay, or restricted to a decentralized governance mechanism, ensuring that any fee change is visible to users before it can affect escrow creation. This would align the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that fees are predictable and cannot be arbitrarily altered at the moment of escrow deployment, thereby preventing users from experiencing unexpected higher fees, missing refunds, or loss of locked assets.

title: M-9 Escrows can be reused
description: Currently, all escrows can be reused. However, the logic of a condition cannot guarantee that it will be correct for two consecutive executions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability to reuse escrow contracts that were intended to be single‑use. The escrow logic includes a condition that determines whether the locked funds may be released to the beneficiary. Because the contract does not enforce a one‑time execution flag or reset the condition safely, the same escrow instance can be invoked a second time. The root cause is the absence of state protection that guarantees the condition is evaluated correctly only once; after the first execution the internal state may remain unchanged or become inconsistent, allowing a subsequent call to bypass the original checks. An attacker or any user who can trigger a second execution can therefore cause the escrow to release funds under an unintended circumstance, such as sending the assets to an address that was not part of the original agreement or keeping the funds locked indefinitely. The impact ranges from partial loss of funds to complete theft, depending on how the condition is mis‑evaluated. This issue manifests when the escrow contract is called more than once, which can happen in normal operation if the contract is reused, or through a malicious re‑entry pattern that deliberately invokes the release function again. All participants that rely on the escrow – the depositor, the intended beneficiary, and the broader protocol that assumes escrow finality – are affected because the financial guarantees of the escrow are broken. The flaw was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined state transitions and identified that the contract does not set a “used” flag or otherwise prevent a second execution. Because the contract still appears to function correctly on the first call, the problem can be hard to notice; only after a second call does the incorrect behavior surface, often showing up as a missing refund or an unexpected zero balance for the depositor. To remediate, the escrow should be redesigned as a single‑use primitive: after a successful release, the contract must mark itself as completed and reject any further calls, or it should be destroyed. Alternatively, the condition logic must be made idempotent and include explicit checks that the escrow has not been previously settled. This class of bug belongs to improper state management in financial primitives, where reuse of a mutable escrow leads to accounting errors, fund disappearance, and violation of the protocol’s trust model.

title: M-22 borgCore._checkDirectorsSignatures() calculates the number of
description: Safe.execTransaction() Safe.sol#L111-L192 to pass more than threshold signatures. SignatureHelper.getSigners() signatureHelper.sol#L50 only first threshold signers. So if some of the directors' signatures go after the first threshold signatures, borgCore.sol#L756 in borgCore._checkDirectorsSignatures() and the total number will be calculated incorrectly.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the Borg core contract validates director signatures for a Safe transaction. When a Safe.execTransaction call includes more signatures than the required threshold, the helper routine SignatureHelper.getSigners extracts only the first *threshold* signatures from the list, discarding any additional signatures that appear later. BorgCore._checkDirectorsSignatures then counts the number of director signatures based on this truncated list. If some legitimate director signatures are positioned after the first threshold entries, they are never considered, causing the total director count to be calculated incorrectly. This mis‑count can allow a transaction to be treated as sufficiently approved even though the required number of distinct director approvals is not actually present, or conversely reject a transaction that does have enough approvals. The flaw originates from an assumption that all relevant signatures will be within the first *threshold* positions, which is not guaranteed by the Safe contract’s signature ordering. An attacker can exploit this by arranging signatures so that the required number of director signatures are placed beyond the threshold slice, while the first threshold slots are filled with non‑director or duplicate signatures. The contract then believes the threshold is met and may execute the transaction, potentially moving funds or changing protocol state without proper governance consent. The issue manifests only when more than the threshold number of signatures are supplied and the ordering places director signatures after the threshold slice; in normal cases with exactly the threshold number of signatures the bug is invisible. All directors, token holders, and any party relying on the governance process are affected because the integrity of multi‑signature approval is broken. The problem was discovered during a MixBytes security audit, and because the contract still reports a successful signature check, the error can be subtle and may not produce obvious UI warnings – users may see a transaction marked as approved while the underlying governance rule has been bypassed. To remediate, the signature extraction logic must be updated to consider the full list of signatures, or the director‑signature verification routine must be rewritten to count director approvals across the entire signature array rather than only the first threshold entries. Documentation should also be updated to clarify the correct ordering expectations for signatures.

title: M-23 Missing Update of lastProposalTime in proposeTransaction
description: The issue has been identified within the proposeTransaction function of the daoVetoImplant contract. The function fails to update the lastProposalTime variable to the current block.timestamp after a proposal is created. This could cause the proposal cooldown logic to malfunction, as it relies on lastProposalTime to enforce proper time intervals between proposals. The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could allow users to bypass the intended proposal cooldown period, potentially leading to system abuse or congestion.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing state update in the DAO governance contract where the proposeTransaction function does not assign the current block timestamp to the lastProposalTime storage variable after a new proposal is recorded. The root cause is an omitted assignment statement, leaving the timestamp that tracks the most recent proposal unchanged. Because the contract’s cooldown mechanism checks the elapsed time since lastProposalTime to decide whether a new proposal may be submitted, the stale value means the time‑difference calculation always evaluates as if the required waiting period has passed. An attacker can therefore call proposeTransaction repeatedly in rapid succession, bypassing the intended delay between proposals. This can be exploited whenever the cooldown check is performed, which is on every call to proposeTransaction; the condition will incorrectly succeed because lastProposalTime still holds the timestamp of the previous proposal (or the default zero). The impact is that the governance process can become congested with spam proposals, allowing malicious actors to flood the DAO with low‑quality or malicious actions, potentially overwhelming voters and degrading the protocol’s decision‑making integrity. The issue manifests when a user expects the UI to display a countdown or a message such as “you can propose again in X minutes,” but in reality the contract permits immediate subsequent proposals, leading to confusion and a perception that the system is broken. All participants who rely on the cooldown for fair proposal spacing—token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the proposal lifecycle logic and noticed that the variable used for timing was never written after a successful proposal. It is subtle because the function otherwise executes successfully and does not revert, so normal testing that only checks for successful proposal creation will not reveal the timing anomaly. To remediate the issue, the contract should update lastProposalTime to block.timestamp immediately after the proposal is stored, ensuring that subsequent calls see the correct reference point for the cooldown calculation. Optionally, the update should be placed before any external calls to prevent re‑entrancy concerns, and the contract should include unit tests that verify the cooldown enforcement under various timing scenarios. This class of bug is commonly known as a state‑inconsistency or missing‑state‑update vulnerability, where a critical bookkeeping variable is not refreshed, leading to logical bypasses of security controls.

title: M-3 Method policies are not cleaned on contract removal
description: There is a removeContract function defined at line borgCore.sol#L203. It sets the allowed and fullAccess struct fields to false, disallowing the contract from any calls. But it doesn't clean the policy[_contract].methods policies mapping. This means it is possible to have that contract allowed in the future with old policies.
bug_full:
The vulnerability is that when a contract is removed from the whitelist using the removeContract function, the function only flips the allowed and fullAccess flags to false but does not delete the entries in the policy mapping that store method‑level permissions. As a result, the stale method policies remain in storage. If the same address is later added back to the whitelist, the old method policies are automatically reinstated, potentially granting permissions that the governance intended to revoke. This is a classic residual‑state or permission‑inheritance bug where cleanup of access‑control data is incomplete.
Root cause: the removeContract implementation updates only two boolean fields in a struct and omits a call to delete or reset the mapping policy[_contract].methods. Solidity mappings do not automatically clear nested mappings when a parent struct field is changed, so the data persists.
Exploitation: an attacker who can influence the whitelist (e.g., via a governance proposal or a privileged role) can first remove a compromised contract, then later re‑add the same address. Because the method policies were never cleared, the contract regains the previous method‑level allowances, allowing it to invoke functions that should have been permanently disabled. Alternatively, an attacker could add a malicious contract that mimics the address of a previously removed contract, causing the system to treat it as having the old permissions.
Impact: the protocol may execute actions that were thought to be prohibited, leading to unauthorized token transfers, state changes, or other business‑logic violations. Users may see unexpected behavior such as transactions succeeding when they should be rejected, or funds being moved without proper approval. The issue affects any role that relies on the whitelist for security, including the protocol’s administrators, token holders, and external users.
Conditions: the bug manifests whenever removeContract is called without a corresponding cleanup of the methods mapping, and later the same address is added back to the whitelist. It also applies if the address is reused by a different contract.
Discovery: identified during a manual code review of the BorgCore contract, where the auditor noticed that the policy mapping was never touched in the removal path.
Why hard to notice: the contract still reports the address as not allowed (allowed flag false), so superficial checks appear to work. However, deeper permission checks that read method policies may still succeed after re‑addition, which can be missed unless the storage layout is inspected.
Fix: modify removeContract to iterate over the stored method identifiers (or use a pattern such as deleting the entire policy entry with `delete policy[_contract];`) so that all method‑level permissions are cleared. Alternatively, redesign the data structure to tie method policies to the allowed flag, ensuring they become inaccessible when the contract is disabled.
Class of bug: residual access‑control state / incomplete cleanup of permission mappings, similar to “stale ACL entries” or “orphaned permissions”.
User‑facing symptoms: a user may attempt to interact with a contract that was supposedly removed and receive a successful transaction, or see that a previously blocked operation now works without any explicit permission grant. Conversely, a user may notice that a contract they thought was fully disabled still has some functions callable after being re‑added.
Overall, the vulnerability violates the protocol’s assumption that removing a contract from the whitelist revokes all its privileges. Failure to purge method policies leaves a backdoor that can be re‑opened unintentionally.

title: M-4 Missing conditionCheck modifers
description: There are two functions: ejectOwner, defined at line ejectImplant.sol#L50, and recoverSafeFunds, defined at line failSafeImplant.sol#L86. Both of them have a call to the checkConditions function inside, but there are no conditionCheck modifiers which check conditions particularly for the callable function.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing conditionCheck modifiers on two privileged functions, ejectOwner and recoverSafeFunds. Both functions invoke an internal checkConditions routine, but the absence of the external conditionCheck modifier means that the contract does not enforce the intended pre‑conditions before the function body executes. The root cause is a developer oversight: the functions were written without attaching the modifier that would normally verify caller permissions, contract state, or other safety constraints. Because the modifier is omitted, any external account that can reach these functions may call them without satisfying the required conditions, potentially bypassing ownership checks, time‑locks, or fund‑locking logic. An attacker could therefore invoke ejectOwner to transfer contract ownership to an address of their choosing, or call recoverSafeFunds to withdraw assets that should be protected by the missing checks. The impact is a loss of control over the contract and possible unauthorized fund extraction, which manifests to users as unexpected ownership changes, missing balances, or refunds that never arrive. The issue appears only when the functions are called; normal operation may seem fine because the internal checkConditions call still runs, but it does not replace the comprehensive validation performed by the modifier. This makes the bug subtle and hard to notice during functional testing, as the contract may still behave correctly under expected usage patterns. The problem was discovered during a systematic security audit performed by MixBytes, which compared the function implementations against the documented security model and identified the missing modifiers. To remediate, the contract should be updated to attach the appropriate conditionCheck modifier to both ejectOwner and recoverSafeFunds, ensuring that all required pre‑conditions are enforced automatically before any state‑changing logic runs. In broader terms, this is an instance of an access‑control or pre‑condition omission bug, where the contract fails to guard privileged entry points, violating the business logic that only authorized parties may trigger ownership transfer or fund recovery.

title: M-5 A threshold check can prevent the owner from self-ejecting
description: There is a owners.length > threshold check at line ejectImplant.sol#L185. There could be some cases when owners.length == threshold, and we are attempting to remove one owner and reduce the threshold by 1. In that case, the mentioned check would always fail and prevent the user from self-ejecting, as the next call to removeOwner would fail because there would be an attempt to set a larger threshold than the updated number of owners.
bug_full: The contract implements a multi‑owner governance model where a numeric threshold defines the minimum number of owners required for privileged actions. When an owner attempts to remove themselves, the implementation first checks that the current number of owners is greater than the threshold before allowing the removal. If the number of owners is exactly equal to the threshold, the check fails, and the removal transaction reverts. The intended flow is to also decrement the threshold by one when an owner leaves, but because the check is performed before the threshold is updated, the contract tries to set a new threshold that is larger than the resulting owner count, causing the call to revert. Consequently, an owner who is at the exact threshold cannot self‑eject, effectively locking their participation and potentially freezing any funds that require their signature. The bug appears only when owners.length == threshold and a removal is attempted; in all other cases the function works as expected. It was discovered during a manual audit of the governance module, where the logical ordering of the length‑check and threshold‑update was examined. The issue is subtle because the condition looks like a reasonable safety guard, yet it prevents a legitimate use‑case and may not surface in normal test scenarios where owners are added before removal. The impact is that a legitimate owner may be unable to withdraw their authority, which can lead to dead‑lock of the contract if the remaining owners cannot meet the threshold without the blocked owner. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect state transition ordering” or “threshold validation logic error”. To fix the problem the check should be removed or moved after the threshold is adjusted, ensuring that the new threshold never exceeds the updated owner count. Proper unit tests covering the edge case where owners count equals the threshold should be added.

title: M-1 Incomplete Check on Milestone Completion in addMetavestMilestone
description:
This issue has been identified in the addMetavestMilestone function of the MetaVesTController.sol#L449-L461 contract.
The logic does not verify whether the _milestone.complete flag is set to false before adding a new milestone. If this check is not enforced, there could be scenarios where a milestone is mistakenly added as already completed, which would prevent its proper execution and awarding process.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could lead to mismanagement of milestone states, affecting the logic of the vesting process.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that registers a new vesting milestone. The code accepts a struct describing the milestone but does not verify that the flag indicating completion is false before storing it. Because the contract assumes a newly added milestone is pending, any milestone that arrives with the completion flag already set to true is treated as finished. This missing validation allows an attacker or a careless caller to inject a milestone that is marked complete at creation time. When later logic checks the milestone state to decide whether tokens can be released or whether a reward should be paid, it will see the milestone as already completed and will skip the normal vesting steps. As a result, legitimate participants may never receive the scheduled token release, or the protocol may record a milestone as done without any work being performed, breaking the accounting assumptions of the vesting schedule. The issue appears whenever the addMetavestMilestone function is invoked, which is typically restricted to project owners or administrators, but if those roles are compromised or if the function is exposed to untrusted input, the bug can be exploited. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a newly added milestone disappears from the list of pending milestones, balances remain unchanged, and expected refunds or token releases never occur, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who noted that the function lacks a require statement checking the _milestone.complete flag. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the state simply reflects an already completed milestone, which can be mistaken for normal operation. The class of bug is an incomplete input validation or state‑initialization flaw, commonly seen in contracts that manage lifecycle states. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that the completion flag is false before accepting the milestone, for example by adding a require(_milestone.complete == false, "Milestone must be incomplete") and by emitting an event that confirms the correct state. Fixing the check restores the intended business logic that a milestone must be pending when added, ensuring that vesting and reward distribution follow the correct schedule and that funds are not unintentionally locked or released.

title: M-2 Incomplete Validation of _callData in
description:
This issue has been identified in the proposeMajorityMetaVesTAmendment function of the MetaVesTController.sol#L570 contract.
The function does not check the length of the _callData parameter before processing, which could allow arbitrary or malformed data to be sent to the function. This lack of validation increases the risk of passing incorrect data that might lead to unintended behavior or errors. Proper validation would help ensure that only well-formed data is used in the proposal.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because improper handling of data could lead to errors in contract execution, impacting the reliability of the voting process.
bug_full: An incomplete validation vulnerability exists in the proposeMajorityMetaVesTAmendment function of the MetaVesTController contract. The function accepts a bytes parameter named _callData that is expected to encode a specific instruction set of exactly 68 bytes. The implementation does not verify the length of this parameter before forwarding it to downstream logic. Because the contract assumes a fixed‑size payload, any caller can supply a shorter, longer, or otherwise malformed byte array. When such data is processed, the contract may read undefined slots, trigger revert conditions, or execute unintended logic paths, potentially causing proposals to be created with corrupted parameters, votes to be counted incorrectly, or the entire voting cycle to stall. The root cause is the absence of an explicit length check, a classic input‑validation omission. An attacker can craft a transaction that calls proposeMajorityMetaVesTAmendment with arbitrary _callData, causing the contract to misinterpret the payload and either reject legitimate proposals or accept malformed ones that bypass governance rules. The impact is a loss of reliability in the voting mechanism, which may lead to governance decisions being based on incorrect data, effectively allowing manipulation of protocol parameters or denial‑of‑service of the voting process. The condition occurs whenever a user or contract invokes the function without the contract enforcing the expected 68‑byte size, which is typical for any external call. All participants that rely on the voting outcome—token holders, protocol modules, and any downstream contracts that act on approved proposals—are affected because the integrity of the decision‑making process can be compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function signature and noted the missing require statement for _callData length. It can be hard to notice because the function may still succeed with well‑formed data, and the failure manifests only when malformed data is supplied, which is not exercised in normal test suites. The appropriate remediation is to add a validation clause that checks _callData.length == 68 and reverts otherwise, thereby enforcing the expected data format before any further processing. This class of bug falls under unchecked input length or missing parameter validation, which commonly leads to unexpected behavior or security breaches in smart contracts. From a user perspective, a proposal may appear to be submitted but later the vote count is zero, or the proposal is never executed, leading to confusion such as user expects refund but receives 0 or the system returns no result. The discrepancy between the expectation that a proposal will be processed correctly and the reality that malformed data can silently break the flow illustrates a violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: M-3 Lack of Validation for _shortStopTime and shortStopDuration in
description:
This issue has been identified in the updateStopTimes function of the RestrictedTokenAllocation.sol#L98-L102 contract and in the updateStopTimes function of the TokenOptionAllocation.sol#L98-L102 contract.
The function does not validate the _shortStopTime parameter before setting its value. If _shortStopTime is set to an extremely large value, it could make it practically impossible to repurchase tokens, as the stop time would be set far in the future. Proper validation should be implemented to ensure that the value is within a reasonable range.
Also, there are no limits set on the value of shortStopDuration, which could potentially be set to an extremely large value, leading to unintended consequences such as infinite delays or a practically unreachable stop time. Without appropriate constraints, this could impact the flexibility of the token repurchase process and cause operational issues.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because an unreasonably large stop time could impact the token repurchase process.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked input validation flaw in the updateStopTimes function of two allocation contracts. The function accepts a parameter called _shortStopTime and a state variable shortStopDuration but does not enforce any upper bound or sanity check before storing them. Because timestamps and durations are stored as unsigned integers, any caller with permission to invoke updateStopTimes can supply an arbitrarily large value that is still syntactically valid. When such a value is written, the calculated stop time is pushed far into the future, potentially beyond any realistic operational horizon. As a result, the token repurchase mechanism, which relies on the stop time to become reachable, may never trigger; users attempting to sell or repurchase their tokens will find the operation permanently blocked. Similarly, an excessively large shortStopDuration can create effectively infinite delays in vesting or repurchase windows, breaking the intended business logic that tokens become eligible for repurchase after a reasonable period. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the reviewers noticed that the updateStopTimes implementation lacked any require statements or range checks for these parameters. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the contract does not revert; the large values simply result in a stop time that appears valid on‑chain but is functionally unreachable, leading to silent failures. The impact is that token holders may be unable to retrieve or sell their tokens, causing loss of liquidity and violating the protocol’s promise of a predictable repurchase schedule. The bug affects any party that relies on the repurchase feature – typically token holders, investors, and the protocol itself – and can be triggered by any account authorized to call updateStopTimes, such as an admin or governance contract. To remediate, the contract should introduce explicit validation that _shortStopTime is less than a reasonable future horizon (for example, a few years from the current block timestamp) and that shortStopDuration does not exceed a predefined maximum duration. These checks enforce the business rule that stop times remain within an operational window, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing the token repurchase process from becoming infeasible.

title: M-4 Incorrect Handling of milestoneUnlockedTotal in
description:
This issue has been identified in the getUnlockedTokenAmount function of all the allocation's contracts.
The current implementation includes milestoneUnlockedTotal in the calculation of unlocked tokens, even when the unlocking process is complete. This can result in an overestimation of the unlocked tokens when all tokens have already been fully unlocked.
The issue is classified as Medium severity because it could lead to inaccurate calculations of unlocked tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the function that reports how many tokens are unlocked for a given allocation. The routine adds the variable that tracks the total amount unlocked by each milestone (milestoneUnlockedTotal) to the calculation of the overall unlocked balance even after the vesting schedule has reached its final milestone. Because the contract does not remove this component once the unlocking process is complete, the reported unlocked amount can be larger than the actual supply that should be available. This over‑estimation occurs only after all milestones have been satisfied, i.e., when the vesting period is finished, and it affects any caller that queries the unlocked token amount or attempts to claim tokens based on that value. The root cause is a logical flaw: the code fails to conditionally exclude milestoneUnlockedTotal once the schedule is fully unlocked, effectively double‑counting tokens that have already been accounted for. An attacker or a regular user could exploit the bug by invoking the claim function with the inflated unlocked amount, thereby withdrawing more tokens than entitled, which may lead to token inflation, loss of economic guarantees, and erosion of trust in the protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the UI or contract call shows a higher unlocked balance than expected, or that a withdrawal succeeds with an unexpectedly large amount, contradicting the user’s expectation of receiving the exact vested amount. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the token allocation contracts and identified the mis‑use of the milestoneUnlockedTotal variable in the getUnlockedTokenAmount logic. Because the bug only manifests after the vesting completes, it can be hard to notice during normal testing that focuses on early‑stage unlocking. The class of bug is a miscalculated accounting or double‑counting error in vesting logic. To remediate, the contract should be updated so that once the final milestone is reached, milestoneUnlockedTotal is excluded from the unlocked‑token formula, ensuring the reported amount matches the true amount that can be claimed. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents users from receiving more tokens than the vesting schedule permits.

title: M-5 Not All the Tests are Passing
description: There are some failing test cases, which make it impossible to check test coverage and prepare PoCs.
bug_full: The issue identified is an incomplete and failing test suite for the smart‑contract protocol. The root cause is that several test cases either do not compile, produce runtime errors, or are missing entirely, which prevents the auditors from measuring test coverage and from constructing reliable proof‑of‑concept attacks. Because the test harness does not execute successfully, developers cannot verify that the contract logic conforms to its specification, nor can they confirm that edge‑case handling (such as re‑entrancy, overflow, or permission checks) behaves correctly. An attacker could therefore interact with the deployed contract in ways that were never exercised during testing, potentially triggering unexpected state changes, loss of funds, or denial of service. The impact is that the protocol may contain hidden bugs that only surface after deployment, exposing users’ assets and undermining confidence in the system. This condition occurs during the pre‑deployment phase when the repository contains failing or absent tests, and it affects anyone who relies on the contract – developers, auditors, and end‑users. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit when the auditors attempted to run the provided test suite and observed multiple failures, making it impossible to generate coverage metrics or PoC scripts. The difficulty in noticing the problem stems from the fact that failing tests can be overlooked if the development team assumes they are non‑critical or if continuous‑integration pipelines are not enforced. To remediate, the team should rewrite or fix the failing tests, add missing test cases that cover all public functions, boundary conditions, and failure paths, and enforce a policy that the entire test suite must pass before any contract is merged or deployed. In generic terms, this is a test‑coverage deficiency that violates the fundamental security practice of exhaustive validation, leading to a situation where “funds disappear” or “transactions revert unexpectedly” because the contract’s behavior under certain inputs has never been verified.

title: M-6 Several Issues with Consents Obtained Through Voting
description:
A consent obtained through voting will also apply to MetaVesTs MetaVesTController.sol#L691 after the voting process finished and MetaVesTController.sol#L625. New set members haven't participated in the voting process, so applying a consent looks unfair in such cases.
Additionally, the consent can be applied to each MetaVesT an unlimited number of times. For example, once the authority receives consent to remove a milestone with index 0, they can remove all milestones from all MetaVesTs in the set.
This issue is classified as Medium, as the consent functionality works incorrectly in certain cases.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the misuse of a consent mechanism that is granted after a voting process. In the current design, once a voting round finishes and a consent flag is set, that consent is applied globally to all instances of the MetaVesT contract, regardless of whether a particular instance participated in the vote. Consequently, an authority can invoke privileged functions, such as removing milestones, on MetaVesTs that never voted, which violates the expectation that only participants are affected by the outcome of the vote. The root cause is an overly broad consent check that does not track the relationship between a consent and the specific MetaVesT instances that contributed to the voting result. Moreover, the consent flag can be reused an unlimited number of times; after a single approval to remove a milestone with a given index, the same consent can be presented repeatedly to delete any or all milestones from any MetaVesT in the set. This effectively creates a replay attack on the consent-protected function. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or a malicious authority obtains a valid consent once, then calls the removal function multiple times, each time targeting a different MetaVesT or a different milestone index, without needing additional votes. The impact is the unauthorized deletion of milestones, which may represent locked funds, progress checkpoints, or governance signals. Users see their milestones disappear, potentially losing access to vested assets or seeing the protocol state diverge from the expected schedule. The issue manifests whenever a consent is recorded after a vote and the contract later executes a function guarded by the consentCheck modifier; it does not discriminate based on participation history. All participants in the protocol, including token holders and project owners, are affected because the integrity of the voting outcome is compromised. The problem was identified during a systematic audit that examined the consent lifecycle and noticed that the consent flag was not scoped to the voting set, and that there were no safeguards against repeated use of the same consent. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract still records a valid consent and the function calls succeed; only the unexpected loss of milestones signals the problem, which may be attributed to normal business logic rather than a security flaw. To remediate, the consent should be bound to the specific MetaVesTs that took part in the vote, and the contract should record whether a particular consent has already been used for a given proposal and MetaVesT, rejecting subsequent calls. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model where consent is a one‑time, participant‑specific authorization, preserving fairness and preventing unauthorized milestone removal.

title: M-7 Inefficient Storage and Iteration Over MetaVesT Sets
description:
In the current implementation of MetaVesT sets, MetaVesTController.sol#L675-L680 during each consentCheck call. The total number of MetaVesTs grows over time, so consentCheck will consume increasing amounts of gas. Eventually, this may lead to reaching the gas hard limit. If, at that moment, setMajorityVoteActive[set] is true for all sets, the contract will require redeployment.
This issue is classified as Medium, as the inefficient approach to set storage will result in higher gas consumption, potentially leading to a contract DoS.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unbounded iteration over a dynamically growing collection of MetaVesT identifiers inside the consentCheck function of the MetaVesTController contract. Each time consentCheck is called, the implementation loops through every stored MetaVesT set to evaluate the setMajorityVoteActive flag. Because the number of MetaVesT sets increases over the lifetime of the protocol, the gas required for a single consentCheck call grows linearly with the set count. When the collection becomes large enough, the gas consumption can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This situation effectively denies service to any user attempting to trigger consentCheck or any downstream functionality that depends on it, resulting in a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s storage patterns, where the auditors observed that the loop does not have a bounded iteration count and that the gas cost is not capped. It is hard to notice in early testing because the initial set count is small, so gas usage appears acceptable; only after many sets are added does the problem surface. The impact is that legitimate users may see transactions fail with out‑of‑gas errors, balances may appear unchanged, and voting or consent mechanisms become unusable, even though the contract’s funds remain intact. The affected parties include any participant who relies on consentCheck, such as token holders, voters, and the protocol itself. To remediate, the contract should replace the custom set storage with a data structure that supports constant‑time membership checks without full enumeration, such as OpenZeppelin’s EnumerableSet, or redesign the logic to avoid iterating over all sets on each call, possibly by maintaining aggregated state or imposing a reasonable cap on the number of tracked sets. This class of bug falls under the category of unbounded iteration leading to gas exhaustion, a common source of availability vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction that never completes or reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, while the user expects the consent check to succeed and their vote or action to be recorded. The discrepancy between expected successful execution and the reality of a silent failure is a hallmark of this inefficiency.

title: M-8 Inability to Repurchase Tokens Due to Low Repurchase Price in
description:
In the RestrictedTokenAward contract, if the repurchase price RestrictedTokenAllocation.sol#L107-L111, RestrictedTokenAllocation.sol#L146 to repurchase tokens after the terminate() function is called. This occurs because the contract calculates the repurchase amount based on the price, and if the price is too low, the resulting repurchaseAmount could end up being zero. This would prevent the authority from repurchasing the remaining tokens, effectively locking them in the contract and making them unrecoverable.
This issue has a Medium severity level due to the potential risk of token loss arising from an error by the authority.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inability of the token repurchase mechanism to retrieve remaining tokens after the contract has been terminated because the calculated repurchase amount can become zero when the repurchase price is set too low. The root cause lies in the contract’s arithmetic that multiplies the number of tokens by a price factor without enforcing a minimum price threshold; when the price drops below a certain level the multiplication yields a value that rounds down to zero. An attacker or even the authorized repurchaser can trigger this condition simply by calling the termination function and then attempting to invoke the repurchase function. Because the repurchase amount is zero, the contract does not transfer any tokens back to the authority, leaving the tokens permanently locked inside the contract. This impact manifests as a loss of recoverable token supply, effectively reducing the circulating token balance and potentially harming token holders who expect to receive their tokens back after termination. The issue occurs only after the terminate() function has been executed and the repurchase price parameter is low enough to produce a zero amount; it does not affect normal operation before termination. The affected parties are the contract authority that is supposed to reclaim the tokens and any users whose tokens become unrecoverable as a result. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the termination and repurchase logic and identified that the price check does not enforce a lower bound. The problem can be hard to notice because the repurchase function may appear to execute without error, yet silently transfers zero tokens, giving the impression that the operation succeeded. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimal repurchase price or include a safeguard that reverts the transaction when the calculated amount would be zero, ensuring that tokens cannot be left stranded. This class of bug falls under arithmetic underflow/zero‑value transfer bugs where business logic assumes a positive transfer amount but the calculation can produce zero, violating accounting assumptions that every terminated token allocation must be recoverable.

title: M-9 Possible reverts due to early vesting termination
description: This issue has been identified in the BaseAllocation.sol#L197 of the BaseAllocation contract. It is possible that there would be an attempt to create a proposal for the set, which has already terminated MetaVesTs (and they were terminated before the vestingStartTime). In the case of VestingAllocation and TokenOptionAllocation contracts, the call to the getAmountWithdrawable would revert. This issue has a severity level of Medium because it may lead to the inability to create a proposal for an entire set.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the governance flow of the BaseAllocation contract where a proposal creation can revert when the underlying vesting set has been terminated before its scheduled start time. The root cause is that the getMajorityVotingPower function does not verify whether the vesting allocation has been marked as terminated before invoking getAmountWithdrawable, a function that assumes an active vesting schedule and reverts if the schedule is already ended. When a set is terminated early, any attempt to create a proposal for that set triggers getMajorityVotingPower, which in turn calls getAmountWithdrawable on VestingAllocation or TokenOptionAllocation contracts. Because the allocation state is inconsistent with the expectations of getAmountWithdrawable, the call throws, bubbling up as a transaction revert. This can be exploited by an attacker who has the ability to terminate a vesting set prematurely; after termination, any user trying to submit a governance proposal for the affected set will experience a failed transaction, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service on that governance path. The impact is that users, token holders, or protocol participants are unable to create proposals for the entire set, breaking the intended voting mechanism and potentially stalling protocol upgrades or parameter changes. The condition occurs only when termination happens before the vestingStartTime, a scenario that may not be covered by standard test suites, making the bug hard to notice during routine audits. The issue was discovered during a manual code review of BaseAllocation.sol, where the auditor observed that getAmountWithdrawable could revert under certain state combinations. From a user’s perspective the UI will report a generic “proposal creation failed” or a transaction revert without a clear reason, leading to confusion and the impression that the system is broken. The bug belongs to the class of missing state validation or unchecked condition errors that cause unintended reverts. To remediate, the getMajorityVotingPower function should first check the termination flag of the vesting allocation and, if terminated, treat the majority voting power as zero and skip the call to getAmountWithdrawable, thereby preventing the revert and preserving the ability to create proposals even for terminated sets.

title: mintGenesis() mints with a push pattern using _mint() which may lead to lost tokens
description: _mint() in mintGenesis() may send tokens to an address that can't deal with ERC721. _safeMint() would be recommended; however, it would introduce additional issues, namely reentrancy and possible malicious reverts.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the mintGenesisfunction using the low‑level _mint operation to create a genesis ERC721 token and directly assign it to a caller‑provided address. Because _mint does not perform the ERC721Receiver check defined by the ERC721 standard, it can transfer a newly minted token to any address, including contracts that do not implement the onERC721Received callback. When such a contract receives the token, the token becomes locked in the contract’s balance because the contract cannot acknowledge or forward ERC721 tokens. This situation is often referred to as an unsafe mint or missing safe‑transfer check. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a malicious contract address that deliberately lacks the ERC721Receiver interface; the contract will accept the mint request, the token will be recorded in the internal ownership mapping, but the token will be unrecoverable and effectively burned. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving a visible NFT in their wallet – does not occur; the UI may show a zero balance or the token may be invisible, leading to confusion and the impression that the funds have disappeared. The problem manifests whenever mintGenesis is called with a recipient that is a contract or an address that cannot handle ERC721 tokens, which can happen unintentionally if a user interacts through a smart‑wallet or deliberately if an adversary crafts a malicious address. The affected parties include any user who receives a genesis NFT, the protocol’s accounting logic (because total supply includes tokens that are effectively inaccessible), and the contract owner who may face reputational risk. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, which noted the push‑style minting pattern and the absence of a safe‑mint alternative. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the token is minted successfully according to the contract’s state, yet the token is unusable, making the loss hard to detect without inspecting ownership mappings or attempting transfers. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the direct _mint call with _safeMint, which enforces the ERC721Receiver check and reverts if the recipient cannot handle the token. Alternatively, a claim‑by‑user design using a merkle tree can be employed, allowing each user to pull their own genesis NFT and eliminating the need for the contract to push tokens to arbitrary addresses, while also reducing storage costs. Implementing either approach restores the guarantee that minted NFTs are always receivable, prevents token loss, and aligns the implementation with ERC721 best practices.

title: In function mint() and lzReceive(), _safeMint() is recommended over _mint(), which performs additional checks
description: Function mint() and lzReceive() mint a nft to a certain address, which may lead to lost tokens if _safeMint() is not used instead. This recommendation should not apply to mintGenesis(), the proposed fixed there is using a Merkle Tree. Note: if lzReceive() reverts due to _safeMint(), the token is already burnt in the source chain, which could mean that the nft is forever lost. However, if this happens, a minter can manually call safeMint() to the user (or another address specified by the user) in the destination chain. Note that the endpoint's behavior is non blocking now by default, such that if the lzReceive reverts, other users may continue sending cross chain nfts https://docs.layerzero.network/explore/layerzero-v2#improved-message-handling. mint() (or safeMint(), if the protocol fixes the usage of _mint()), should have a flag specifying if the nft is a genesis one, so if _safeMint() reverts on lzReceive(), it's still possible to mint the genesis nft. Additionally, if lzReceive() fails, the owner must clear the payload beforehand in the lzEndpoint manually if it wants to call safeMint() separately. If a minter mints the lost token to the user before clearing the payload in the LzEndpoint, the user may act maliciously and send the newly minted token to another chain, burning it in the current chain, and then try to execute the payload again in the LzEndpoint, getting a free nft.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract using the low‑level ERC721 _mint function inside both the public mint() entry point and the cross‑chain lzReceive() handler. _mint assigns ownership without performing the ERC721Receiver check that _safeMint provides. As a result, when a token is minted to an address that is a smart contract lacking a proper onERC721Received implementation, the mint succeeds on the destination chain but the receiving contract cannot acknowledge the token. In the cross‑chain flow, the source chain burns (or marks as transferred) the original NFT before the destination chain completes the mint. If the destination mint reverts because the recipient is not ERC721‑compatible, the source‑chain token is already considered burnt, leaving the NFT permanently lost. The issue can also be abused: an attacker who observes a failed lzReceive can manually invoke safeMint to re‑mint the token to a controlled address, then replay the original payload after clearing the endpoint’s message queue, effectively obtaining a duplicate NFT without paying for it. The problem manifests whenever mint() or lzReceive() is called with a recipient that is a contract not implementing the ERC721Receiver interface, or when the endpoint’s non‑blocking message handling allows the payload to remain pending after a revert. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no NFT after a cross‑chain transfer, seeing their balance drop to zero, or observing that a newly minted token disappears after a transaction reverts. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that a burned token on the source chain will always be recreated on the destination chain – are violated, breaking the one‑to‑one correspondence of NFTs across chains. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit by ThreeSigma, which noted that the use of _mint bypasses essential safety checks and that the current handling of failed lzReceive messages could lead to unrecoverable loss or duplication of assets. Detecting the issue is difficult because the transaction may appear successful on the source chain, and the non‑blocking endpoint permits other users to continue operations, masking the failure. To remediate, the contract should replace every call to _mint with _safeMint, ensuring that the ERC721Receiver check is performed. Additionally, the minting logic should include a flag for genesis tokens so that a failed safeMint does not prevent their creation, and the endpoint payload should be cleared before any manual safeMint is attempted to prevent replay attacks. Proper error handling and explicit checks for contract recipients will restore the intended invariant that each NFT is either safely transferred or remains on its original chain, eliminating the risk of permanent loss or unauthorized duplication.

title: Can not mint 1000 tokens, only 999
description: Only 999 tokens can be limited according to the code, but the comments indicated that
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the token minting logic that restricts the contract to creating only 999 tokens even though the intended maximum supply is 1000. The root cause is the initialization of the internal counter that tracks minted tokens at a value of one instead of zero, combined with a check that stops minting when the counter reaches the declared limit. Because the counter starts one step ahead, the condition becomes true after 999 successful mints, preventing the final token from being minted. An attacker or any user attempting to mint the full advertised supply will be blocked at the last step, receiving a transaction failure or a silent revert. The impact is a supply shortfall: users expecting to receive the full 1000 tokens will receive only 999, which can lead to mismatched accounting, broken token economics, and loss of confidence in the protocol. This situation occurs whenever the mint function is called repeatedly until the supply cap is reached; it does not depend on external inputs beyond the number of mint calls. All participants who rely on the promised token amount—investors, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts—are affected because the actual token balance will be lower than documented. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the contract comments, which stated a limit of 1000, with the actual implementation that enforced a limit of 999. The bug is subtle because the contract still allows many mints and the failure only appears at the final iteration, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem, the genesis counter should be initialized to zero (or the limit check should be adjusted to allow the final mint), ensuring that exactly 1000 tokens can be minted as intended. This class of bug falls under the broader category of off‑by‑one errors in supply‑capped token contracts, where an incorrect initial value or boundary condition leads to an unexpected reduction in total supply, violating the business rule that the token supply must match the advertised amount.

title: A renter can DoS owner from transferring his NFT
description:
The protocols let users rent their NFTs for a price set by them. Renting the NFT lets the renter use it to
breed with his own NFT and give birth to a new one. Until the NFT is rented the owner can NOT transfer it.
Once the NFT is bred or the rented just decides - it can be returned. The problem is in the rentNFT
function because it lets the renter input the rent time in days. Hence a malicious user can input a large
number of days and NOT breed or return the NFT from rent, intentionally griefing the owner from
transferring it. This also locks the NFT from being bred with other NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from the rentNFT function allowing a renter to specify an arbitrary rent duration in days without any upper bound. Because the contract blocks any transfer of the NFT while it is marked as rented, a malicious renter can input an excessively large number of days, then simply refrain from breeding the NFT or returning it. The owner’s subsequent attempts to transfer the NFT, sell it, or use it in another breeding operation will be rejected by the contract’s business logic, effectively locking the asset for the duration of the inflated rental period. This issue occurs whenever the rentNFT function is called because there is no validation that the requested rent time respects a reasonable maximum, nor is there a mechanism for the owner to force early termination of the rental. The root cause is unchecked user input that governs a state variable controlling asset availability, leading to a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that an NFT can be transferred when not actively rented. From a user’s perspective the UI will show the NFT as “currently rented” indefinitely, transfer attempts will revert or do nothing, and breeding functions will report that the token is unavailable, causing confusion and loss of expected revenue. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the rent flow and identified the missing duration cap. It can be hard to notice because normal test cases use short rental periods and the contract does not emit explicit warnings for unusually long rentals. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked input leading to resource‑locking denial‑of‑service bugs. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum rent time (for example one or two days) and optionally provide an owner‑initiated escape hatch that allows the NFT to be reclaimed after a reasonable timeout, thereby restoring the intended transfer and breeding functionality.

title: NFT breeding cooldown is calculated wrong
description:
The protocol lets users breed their NFTs. Two NFTs can only be bred together if their cooldownEndBlock
is less than block.number as seen below:
```solidity
function _isReadyToBreed(NFT storage nft) internal view returns (bool) {
    return (nft.siringWithId == 0) && (nft.cooldownEndBlock <=
        block.number);
}
```
Additionally, an NFT only gives birth if the same cooldown is less than block.number - enforced by the
_isReadyToGiveBirth function.
The problem is how this cooldown is calculated. Taking a look at the only function that it is updated in we
can see that it actually calculates the block that would end the cooldown.
```solidity
function _triggerCooldown(NFT storage _nft) internal { // ok
    _nft.cooldownEndBlock = uint64(
        (cooldowns[_nft.generation] / secondsPerBlock) + block.number
    );
}
```
The problem here, however, is that secondsPerBlock is set 15, while the average block time on the Pume
Network is ~0.5 seconds (This can be verified on the plume testnet's official website: https://plume-
testnet.explorer.caldera.xyz/ ). Having in mind the secondsPerBlock is set to 15 which is around 30 times
more than the network block time this completely breaks the NFT cooldown logic. Also, it is bad in general
to use block.number for time tracking operations as it is certainly NOT constant. Block time may be 0.4
seconds causing the cooldowns to pass faster or 0.6 seconds (if there is less activity) causing cooldown
times to pass slower.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the breeding cooldown for NFTs in the protocol. The contract stores a value called cooldownEndBlock and determines whether an NFT is ready to breed or give birth by checking if this block number is less than or equal to the current block number. The end block is computed by dividing a cooldown duration (expressed in seconds) by a constant called secondsPerBlock and then adding the current block number. The constant is set to 15, which assumes a 15‑second block time, while the actual average block time on the Pume network is about 0.5 seconds. Because the division uses an inflated seconds‑per‑block value, the resulting number of blocks is far smaller than required for the intended real‑time cooldown. Consequently the stored cooldownEndBlock is reached much earlier than the protocol’s business logic expects, allowing NFTs to be bred or to give birth far sooner than intended. The root cause is the use of an inaccurate hard‑coded secondsPerBlock constant together with block.number for time tracking, an anti‑pattern because block times are not constant and can vary between 0.4 and 0.6 seconds. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly breeding NFTs as soon as the contract reports the cooldown as finished, gaining an unfair advantage, inflating token supply, and potentially devaluing the NFTs. The impact is economic: users may lose confidence, the scarcity model breaks, and the protocol’s tokenomics are compromised. The condition occurs every time the _triggerCooldown function is called – after a successful breeding or birth – and persists for the lifetime of the NFT until the next cooldown is set. All participants who interact with the breeding feature are affected, including regular users, developers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s time‑keeping assumptions with the documented block time of the network. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows a countdown timer that appears normal, while the underlying block‑based check silently allows early breeding; users only see the symptom of “breeding works earlier than expected” without obvious error messages. The recommended remediation is to replace the block‑based calculation with a timestamp‑based one: store a cooldownEndTimestamp calculated as block.timestamp plus the required cooldown seconds, and check against block.timestamp instead of block.number. This aligns the contract’s logic with real time and avoids reliance on a static secondsPerBlock value. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of time‑dependency errors where block numbers are used as a proxy for elapsed time, leading to incorrect scheduling and premature state transitions, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a cooldown must enforce a minimum waiting period before further actions can be taken.

title: A user can make a higher bet without increasing the bet price
description:
The protocol lets users auction off their NFTs. The owner can set min bet amount. Users can put bets and
at the end of the auction the highest bidder gets the NFT. The problem is that a user may bet the same
amount as the current highest bet and be the highest bidder. This is possible because of the way the
highestBid is compared:
require(msg.value >= auctionNfts[_auctionId].heighestBid, less
than highest bid price");
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one logic error in the auction bidding function. The contract stores the current highest bid amount and checks incoming bids with a condition `msg.value >= auctionNfts[_auctionId].heighestBid`. Because the comparison allows equality, a participant can submit a bid that is exactly the same amount as the current highest bid and still be recorded as the new highest bidder. The root cause is the use of a non‑strict comparison instead of a strict greater‑than check. An attacker can exploit this by monitoring the auction, waiting until the highest bid is known, and then submitting a transaction with the same ether value. Since the contract updates the highest bidder on any bid that meets the >= condition, the attacker becomes the winner without increasing the total amount paid for the NFT. The impact is that the auction no longer enforces a strictly increasing price, allowing a user to win the NFT for free of additional cost, which can lead to economic loss for honest bidders and undermine the fairness of the marketplace. The issue manifests whenever an auction is active and a new bid is placed that matches the current top bid. All participants, including bidders and the protocol owner, are affected because the auction outcome may be manipulated. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the comparison operator. It can be hard to notice because the condition appears to enforce a minimum bid, and the contract may still accept higher bids correctly; only the edge case of equal bids is problematic, which may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. The correct fix is to replace the >= operator with a strict > operator so that only bids strictly greater than the current highest amount can replace the leader. This belongs to the class of “improper input validation” or “off‑by‑one comparison” bugs that break business logic assumptions about monotonic price increase. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they have placed a winning bid even though they paid the same amount as the previous bidder, leading to confusion such as “my bid was accepted but I didn’t pay more” or “the auction ended with the same price as before”. The expectation that each new bid raises the price is violated, resulting in a scenario where funds appear to disappear from other bidders while the winner gains the NFT without additional cost. The vulnerability does not affect the contract’s ability to transfer ether, but it compromises the economic integrity of the auction mechanism.

title: No way to remove token from being payable
description:
The protocol lets users auction off their NFTs. Users can choose the auction currency - native or some
ERC20/payable token. There is a payable token whitelist that defines the tokens that are allowed to be used
in the auctions. Whitelisted pay tokens can only be added by the admin. However, there is no functionality
that removes a payable token from being allowed. This is a must since the token may get hacked, drained, or
rugged. A good example of this is the TERRA/LUNA stablecoin collapse.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete token whitelist management in the auction contract. The contract maintains a list of ERC20 tokens that are allowed as payment currency for NFT auctions. The list can only be extended by an admin function; there is no corresponding function to remove a token once it has been added. The root cause is that the contract’s access‑control logic implements only an additive whitelist and omits a delisting operation, so the whitelist state is immutable after insertion. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw directly; the risk arises when a token that was previously approved becomes compromised, for example through a hack, a drain of liquidity, or a rug pull such as the Terra/Luna collapse. Because the contract continues to accept the compromised token as a valid payment method, a user who creates or bids in an auction using that token may send funds that are later unrecoverable, or the auction may settle with a token that has lost value, effectively causing the user’s balance to drop to zero. The impact is loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential legal liability for the platform. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time after an admin has added a token to the whitelist and the token’s security status changes; the contract provides no mechanism to pause or disable that token, so the vulnerability is always present once the token is listed. All participants—auction creators, bidders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the protocol’s business logic assumes that any whitelisted token remains safe for payment. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the whitelist management functions and noted the absence of a removal routine. It can be hard to notice because the presence of a whitelist gives a false sense of security; developers may assume that the list can be updated, but the code does not support it. The correct mitigation is to add an admin‑only delist function that removes a token from the payable list, emits an event, and optionally handles any ongoing auctions that reference the removed token (e.g., by pausing them or forcing settlement in a different currency). This class of bug is commonly referred to as an immutable whitelist or missing revocation capability, and it violates the accounting assumption that the set of accepted currencies is static and trustworthy. From a user’s perspective the UI would still show the compromised token as selectable, leading to expectations that the auction will accept the token, but in reality the token may be worthless or the auction may fail, resulting in “my funds disappeared” or “the refund never arrived”.

title: Users can list NFT from other collections if they own ghost NFT
description:
The protocol lets users list their NFTs for sale
```solidity
function listNft(
    uint256 _tokenId,
    uint256 _price
) external
    isPayableToken(_payToken)
    onlyMintedByGhostNFTContract(_tokenId)
    nonReentrant
{
    IERC721 nft = IERC721(_nft);
    // ...
}
```
As per the comment, there would be a few NFT collections that could be listed for sale, the first one being
the Ghost one. The problem with the current listing function is that a user can list an NFT from any other
collection for sale as long as he has an NFT from the GHOST collection with the same id and has approved
it to the marketplace contract.
onlyMintedByGhostNFTContract modifier it is only checked if the user has allowed the marketplace
contract to operate with the NFT in mind. That way a user can just own a GHOST NFT with some id and
_tokenId. The NFT from the fake collection would be transferred to the marketplace contract and up for
sale.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the marketplace contract function that allows a user to list an NFT for sale. The function uses a modifier named onlyMintedByGhostNFTContract which is intended to restrict listings to NFTs that belong to the Ghost collection. However, the modifier only checks that the caller has approved the marketplace to operate on a token with a given identifier, without verifying the actual contract address of the NFT. As a result, any ERC‑721 token from an arbitrary collection can be listed as long as the user possesses a Ghost NFT with the same tokenId and has granted approval. An attacker can therefore acquire a Ghost NFT with identifier X, approve the marketplace for any other ERC‑721 contract, and call listNft with the address of a different collection and tokenId X. The marketplace will transfer the foreign NFT into its custody and publish it for sale under the assumption that it is a legitimate Ghost asset. When a buyer purchases the listed token, the seller may not be able to deliver the expected asset because the marketplace never verified ownership of the foreign token, leading to a situation where the buyer either receives a different NFT than advertised or loses the payment entirely. The impact includes loss of funds for buyers, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential legal liability for the platform. The issue manifests whenever a user lists an NFT while holding a Ghost token of matching id and has set approval for the marketplace; it does not depend on any special state of the foreign collection. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the access control logic of the listing function and noticed that the onlyMintedByGhostNFTContract modifier does not enforce collection whitelisting. The problem is subtle because the function comment suggests that only Ghost NFTs are allowed, yet the code does not enforce this invariant, making the bug easy to overlook in manual testing. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify that the NFT contract address matches the approved Ghost contract (or belongs to a predefined whitelist) and that the caller is the actual owner of the token in that contract before transferring it. This change restores the intended business rule that only approved collections can be listed, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unauthorized assets from entering the marketplace.

title: Winning index can be selected more than once in the raffle
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑winner selection bug in the raffle contract. When the contract chooses the winners it iterates over the number of prizes and computes a winner index as randomResults[i] % ticketOwners.length. Because the array of ticket owners is not modified after a winner is chosen, two or more random results can map to the same three‑digit value and therefore the same array position. As a result the same participant can be added to the winners list multiple times and receive more NFTs than the number of tickets they purchased. The root cause is the lack of a uniqueness guarantee when sampling without replacement; the algorithm treats the selection as with replacement. The exploit works whenever the randomResults array contains values that produce colliding modulo results, which is possible for any raffle that selects more than one winner. An attacker does not need to control the randomness; the mere occurrence of a collision is enough to award extra NFTs. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s fairness guarantees, inflation of the NFT supply, and potential loss of value for other participants because the total number of NFTs distributed exceeds the intended amount. The issue manifests during the winner‑selection loop, i.e., after tickets have been purchased and before the final distribution. All participants are affected because the contract may give away additional NFTs without proper payment, and the project’s reputation may suffer. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the winner‑selection logic and noticed that the selected index is never removed from the pool. It can be hard to notice in testing because collisions are statistically rare and may not appear in a limited test run, so the contract may appear to work correctly most of the time. The correct fix is to sample without replacement: after a winner is chosen, replace the selected entry with the last element of the ticketOwners array and then pop the array, or otherwise keep a set of already‑chosen indices. This ensures each ticket can win at most one prize and restores the intended accounting logic where the number of NFTs minted equals the number of winning tickets.

title: NFT can be stuck in the contract
description:
The protocol lets users create auctions where they can sell their NFTs. Sellers can set minimum bid price
auction start and end times. Sellers can also cancel their auctions, but only if it is before the auction start
time. However, if no one participates in the auction and it has ended the last/highest bidder would be the 0
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the auction module that can cause an NFT to become permanently locked in the contract. When a seller creates an auction they can specify a minimum price, start time and end time, and they are allowed to cancel the auction only before the start time. The contract records the address of the highest bidder during the bidding phase. If no participant places a bid and the auction reaches its end timestamp, the implementation leaves the highest‑bidder variable at its default value (the zero address). Because the settlement logic assumes a valid bidder exists, the contract does not execute the fallback transfer that would return the NFT to the seller. Consequently, the NFT remains owned by the contract with no way for the original owner to retrieve it through the public interface. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the auction lifecycle and noticed that the post‑auction branch does not handle the zero‑bid case. It is easy to miss because the code path is only exercised when an auction ends without any bids, a scenario that may not be covered by typical test suites focused on successful bidding. The impact is that sellers lose access to their token; from a user perspective the UI may show the auction as finished while the token balance in the wallet stays unchanged, leading to confusion such as “my NFT disappeared” or “the auction ended but I never got my NFT back”. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every auction either transfers the NFT to a winning bidder or returns it to the creator. To remediate, the contract should detect the zero‑bid condition at auction finalisation and explicitly set the highest bidder to the seller’s address, then invoke the safe transfer of the NFT back to the creator. This correction aligns the settlement logic with the intended business rule that an unsold item must be returned to its owner, eliminating the risk of assets being irretrievably locked in the contract.

title: resultAuction doesn't correctly validate the _nft param
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auction settlement function that finalises the sale of an NFT. The function receives an external identifier for the NFT contract (the _nft parameter) but never checks that this identifier matches the NFT address stored in the auction record (auction.nft). Because the contract trusts the caller‑supplied _nft value, an attacker who is authorised to call the function (owner, auction creator or last bidder) can supply a different NFT address.
