This hook can trigger an external call back into the DAO, specifically the joinFork() function, before the quit() routine finishes its balance calculations. When the re‑entered joinFork() executes, it mints a new forked noun for the attacker and transfers additional treasury assets into the timelock, thereby increasing the timelock’s balance while the totalSupply variable remains unchanged. Because quit() later uses the stale totalSupply value together with the now‑inflated balances, the attacker receives a larger share of the treasury than entitled, effectively stealing funds from honest participants. The exploit can be carried out only while the fork period is active and the ERC20 token implements the callback, which makes the condition appear rare but still exploitable. Users who call quit expect to receive a proportional amount of ETH and included ERC20 tokens; instead they may receive less than their rightful share, or conversely an attacker may receive more, causing honest users to see missing ETH or token balances. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between quit() and external token callbacks and identified that state variables were read before any external call, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The bug is hard to notice because the external callback is hidden inside the token contract and the quit() function itself appears to follow a straightforward settlement logic. To remediate, the contract should cache all relevant balances (ERC20 token balances and ETH balance of the timelock) before performing any external calls, or move the external token transfers to the end of the function after all state has been finalized. Alternatively, the DAO could prohibit tokens with transfer callbacks from being included in quit, or employ a reentrancy guard that also protects against callbacks triggered by token contracts. In essence, the flaw belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities caused by improper ordering of state reads and external calls, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential loss of treasury funds.

title: A malicious DAO can mint arbitrary fork DAO tokens
description:
The original DAO is assumed to be honest during the fork period which is reinforced in the protocol by preventing it from executing any malicious proposals during that time. Fork joiners are minted fork DAO tokens by the original DAO via claimDuringForkPeriod() which enforces the fork period on the fork DAO side. However, the notion of fork period is different on the fork DAO compared to the original DAO (as described in Issue 16), i.e. while original DAO excludes forkEndTimestamp from the fork period, fork DAO includes forkingPeriodEndTimestamp in its notion of the fork period.
If the original DAO executes a malicious proposal exactly in the block at forkEndTimestamp which makes a call to claimDuringForkPeriod() to mint arbitrary fork DAO tokens then the proposal will succeed on the original DAO side because it is one block beyond its notion of fork period. The claimDuringForkPeriod() will succeed on the fork DAO side because it is in the last block in its notion of fork period. The original DAO therefore can successfully mint arbitrary fork DAO tokens which can be used to: 1) brick the fork DAO when those tokens are attempted to be minted via auctions later or 2) manipulate the fork DAO governance to steal its treasury funds.
In PoS, blocks are exactly 12 seconds apart. With forkEndTimestamp = block.timestamp + ds.forkPeriod; and ds.forkPeriod now set to 7 days, forkEndTimestamp is exactly 50400 blocks (7*24*60*60/12) after the block in which executeFork() was executed. A malicious DAO can coordinate to execute such a proposal exactly in that block.
Low likelihood + High impact = Medium severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch in the definition of the fork period between the original DAO and its forked counterpart, which allows a malicious DAO to mint an arbitrary number of fork DAO tokens after the original DAO’s fork window has officially closed. The root cause is an off‑by‑one logic error: the original DAO treats the forkEndTimestamp as the first block *outside* the fork period, while the fork DAO treats the same timestamp as the *last* block *inside* its fork period. Because claimDuringForkPeriod() on the fork DAO checks only that block.timestamp is less than or equal to forkingPeriodEndTimestamp, a proposal that is executed exactly at forkEndTimestamp is considered out‑of‑bounds for the original DAO (so it can be submitted) but still in‑bounds for the fork DAO (so the claim succeeds). An attacker can therefore submit a malicious proposal that calls claimDuringForkPeriod() in that precise block, causing the fork DAO to mint any token IDs it chooses. This inflation can be used to flood the token auction mechanism, effectively “brick” the fork DAO, or to acquire enough governance weight to approve transfers of the fork DAO’s treasury. The exploit is only possible during the narrow window of a single block at the exact moment the fork period ends, making it low‑likelihood but high‑impact. It affects any participants who rely on the fork DAO’s token accounting, including token holders, governance voters, and anyone expecting a fair distribution of fork tokens after a fork. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the period‑checking logic of the two contracts and identified the inconsistent treatment of the end timestamp. Because the problem manifests only at a precise block boundary, it can be hard to notice in normal testing or simulation, and the symptom from a user’s perspective may be that a claim transaction appears to succeed while the resulting token balance is unexpectedly high or, conversely, that expected refunds or token allocations are missing because the malicious minting has altered the accounting. The bug belongs to the class of time‑boundary or off‑by‑one logic errors that break accounting assumptions about token supply and governance weight. To remediate, the fork period checks in both contracts should be aligned so that the same timestamp is considered either inside or outside the period in both contexts, typically by using a strict “<” comparison on both sides or by sharing a single period‑end constant, thereby preventing any proposal from executing claimDuringForkPeriod() after the original DAO’s fork window has closed.

title: Inattentive fork escrowers may lose funds to fork quitters
description:
Fork escrowers already have their original DAO treasury pro rate funds transferred to the fork DAO treasury (when fork executes) and are expected to claimFromEscrow() after fork executes to mint their fork DAO tokens and thereby lay claim on their pro rata share of fork DAO treasury for governance or exiting. Inattentive fork escrowers who fail to do so will force a delayed governance of 30 days (currently proposed value) on the fork DAO and beyond that will allow fork DAO members to quit with a greater share of the fork DAO treasury because fork execution transfers all escrowers' original DAO treasury funds to fork DAO treasury.
Inattentive slow-/non-claiming fork escrowers may lose funds to quitters if they do not claim their fork DAO tokens before its governance is active in 30 days after fork executes. They will also be unaccounted for in DAO functions like quorum and proposal threshold.
While we would expect fork escrowers to be attentive and claim their fork DAO tokens well within the delayed governance period, the protocol design can be more defensive of slow-/non-claimers by protecting their funds on the fork DAO from quitters.
Low likelihood + High impact = Medium severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting flaw in the fork DAO that allows users who have not claimed their fork DAO tokens to lose their proportional share of the treasury to other members who invoke the quit function after the delayed governance period starts. When a fork is executed, the original DAO treasury funds are transferred to the newly created fork DAO treasury. Escrowers are expected to call claimFromEscrow to mint fork DAO tokens that represent their 1:1 right to the transferred funds. The contract calculates the effective token supply using adjustedTotalSupply, which subtracts the timelock balance but does not add the amount of tokens that remain unclaimed (remainingTokensToClaim). As a result, the reported total supply is artificially low as long as some escrowers have not claimed. After the protocol‑defined delayed governance window of thirty days expires, any fork DAO member can call quit and receive a share of the treasury based on the reduced supply. Because the unclaimed tokens are omitted from the supply, quitters obtain a larger portion of the treasury than they are entitled to, effectively stealing the funds that belong to the inattentive escrowers. Those escrowers also become invisible to quorum and proposal‑threshold calculations, weakening governance and causing unexpected zeros in user balances. The issue manifests only after a fork has been executed, before the escrower calls claimFromEscrow, and within the thirty‑day window before governance becomes active. It affects original DAO participants who escrowed tokens, the fork DAO token holders, and any governance mechanisms that rely on accurate token‑supply data. The flaw was discovered during a security audit of the Nouns DAO fork logic, where the adjustedTotalSupply function was examined and found to ignore remainingTokensToClaim. The problem is subtle because claiming tokens is optional and the supply calculation appears correct for active holders, masking the missing unclaimed balance. From a user perspective, an individual who expects to receive fork DAO tokens after a fork may see no tokens in their wallet, later notice that the treasury balance has shrunk, and be unable to claim any remaining share. The recommended remediation is to modify adjustedTotalSupply to compute nouns.totalSupply() minus nouns.balanceOf(address(timelock)) plus nouns.remainingTokensToClaim(), thereby including unclaimed tokens in the supply calculation. This change freezes the unclaimed share inside the treasury, preventing quitters from draining it and aligning the accounting with the intended 1:1 right of escrowed tokens to fork DAO tokens.

title: Upgrading timelock without transferring the nouns from old timelock balance will increase adjusted total supply
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the accounting logic used to compute the adjusted total supply of Nouns DAO tokens. The function adjustedTotalSupply subtracts the balance of the treasury held by the timelock contract (ds.timelock) and adds the number of tokens owned by the fork escrow. When the DAO upgrades its timelock by deploying a new timelock contract and changes the ds.timelock reference, the migration routine does not transfer any Noun tokens that were still residing in the original timelock address. Because the subtraction still references the new timelock address, the balance of the old timelock is no longer deducted, causing the adjusted total supply to be inflated by exactly the amount of tokens left behind. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever a timelock migration is performed without an explicit step that moves the treasury tokens from the old contract to the new one. The impact is an over‑statement of the token supply that feeds into downstream economic calculations such as reward distribution, voting power, and price‑based valuations. In the concrete scenario examined, a single token left in the old timelock inflates the adjusted total supply, resulting in an estimated loss of about 89 USD per noun and a cumulative loss of roughly 66 300 USD for all holders. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which examined the migration flow and identified that the adjustedTotalSupply formula assumes all treasury tokens are always held by the current timelock. The bug is subtle because the visible totalSupply on‑chain does not change; only the derived adjusted total supply is affected, making the discrepancy easy to miss in routine UI checks. To remediate the problem, the migration proposal should include a step that transfers any Noun tokens held by the old timelock to the new timelock before updating the ds.timelock reference, or the adjustedTotalSupply calculation should be revised to account for tokens held by both the old and new timelock contracts. This class of vulnerability is an accounting or supply‑inflation bug caused by an incomplete state migration, violating the protocol’s invariant that the adjusted total supply equals the real circulating supply after treasury reclassification.

title: MJR-1 Reentry in withdrawAll
description: Malicious token/workerOwner may have a reentry callback to the contract here PoolingStakingContractV2.sol#L236 but the state of the contract changes here PoolingStakingContractV2.sol#L247 it allows to use reentry.
bug_full: During the execution of the withdrawAll function in the PoolingStakingContractV2, the contract performs an external call to a token or workerOwner contract before it updates its internal accounting variables. Because the external call can trigger a fallback or ERC777 hook, a malicious token or a compromised workerOwner can invoke withdrawAll again before the original call finishes. This re‑entrancy allows the attacker to repeat the withdrawal logic while the contract still believes the caller’s balance is unchanged, leading to multiple payouts from the same stake. The vulnerability appears only when the caller controls a contract that implements a callback invoked by the transfer, and when the contract’s state‑change statements are placed after the external call (line 247). From a user’s perspective the function is expected to return the full amount of their stake and rewards once, but an attacker can cause the contract to send additional funds, effectively draining the pool or corrupting accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, who noted that the ordering of operations violates the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and therefore permits re‑entrancy. The problem can be subtle because the external call may succeed silently and the contract does not emit an explicit warning before the state is altered, making the bug easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the flaw the contract should move all token transfers to the end of the function, apply the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, and optionally use a re‑entrancy guard modifier. By ensuring that the internal balance is updated before any external call, the contract prevents a malicious callback from re‑entering the function and preserves the intended accounting guarantees. This class of bug is commonly known as a re‑entrancy vulnerability and violates the fundamental assumption that a contract’s state is immutable during an external call.

title: WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT cannot be too short
description: OwnershipFacet has setWithdrawalRequestTimeout() which sets WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT. WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT is a highly risky parameter. If it is too low, there will be more likely to fall into exodusMode - which means the protocol is disabled (no functions to get back from the exodusMode, the protocol will require deploying a new Diamond or adding new facets).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an adjustable governance parameter called WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT that is stored in the OwnershipFacet contract and can be changed through the setWithdrawalRequestTimeout function. The contract uses this timeout to determine how long a withdrawal request may remain pending before the system automatically switches to an exodus mode, a state in which normal protocol functions are disabled and users are unable to retrieve their assets through the usual interfaces. Because the parameter is not bounded by a minimum value, an owner or a malicious actor with sufficient privileges can set the timeout to an extremely short period, such as a few seconds or minutes. When the timeout expires far sooner than expected, the protocol transitions to exodus mode even though no emergency condition exists. This transition effectively freezes all user‑facing operations: withdrawal calls revert, balance queries may show zero, and the UI often displays a generic “protocol disabled” message. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving a withdrawn token or seeing a pending request – is replaced by an empty balance or a permanent error, violating the core accounting assumption that funds remain accessible after a request is submitted. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the lack of validation on the timeout value. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct warning when the timeout is set to a low value, and the exodus mode may be interpreted as a legitimate emergency shutdown rather than a configuration mistake. The impact is medium severity: the protocol can become unusable, requiring a redeployment of the Diamond architecture or the addition of new facets to restore functionality, which may lead to loss of user confidence and potential financial loss if funds cannot be recovered. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a sensible lower bound on WITHDRAWAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT, for example the default 14‑day period, or to disable further revisions of this parameter entirely, thereby preventing accidental or malicious configuration that could trigger premature exodus mode.

title: The same signature is used for both withdrawal request and subscription cancelling
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract uses a single ECDSA signature scheme for both submitWithdrawalRequest and cancelSubscriptionRequest. Both functions recover the signer from an encoded message that contains only the user address and the current block number. Because the signed payload does not include any identifier that distinguishes the intended action, a signature produced by a user to cancel a subscription can be replayed to the withdrawal function, and vice‑versa. An attacker who can submit a transaction on behalf of the user – for example a relayer, a front‑runner, or a compromised off‑chain service – can take the user’s valid signature and call the other function, causing the contract to transfer the user’s funds even though the user never authorized a withdrawal. This replayable signature flaw appears only when the contract is in exodus mode, because both functions call enforceExodusMode before verifying the signature. The vulnerability therefore affects any user who signs a request for either operation while the protocol is in exodus mode, and it breaks the trustless assumption that a signature is bound to a single operation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a cancellation request results in an unexpected loss of balance, or that a withdrawal appears without the user having initiated it. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the signature verification code of the two functions and noticed the identical message format. It is easy to miss because the require statement checks that the recovered signer matches the user, which looks correct, but the lack of domain separation is subtle. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks caused by missing method‑specific data in signed messages. The proper fix is to add a unique salt or method identifier to the data that is signed – for example by appending a string literal such as submitWithdrawalRequest or cancelSubscriptionRequest to the encoded payload, or by using a full EIP‑712 typed‑data scheme – so that each signature can only be used for its intended function.

title: Setting deposit limit to zero stops all new deposits
description: Deposit limits are managed with functions setDepositsLimit() and setNftDepositsLimit(). They set depositsLimit and nftDepositsLimit without zero input checks. Zero can be inputted either by mistake, or with the intention to disable limits.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract allows an administrator to change the maximum amount that can be deposited by calling functions that set a deposit limit. The implementation does not validate that the new limit is greater than zero. As a result, an attacker or a careless admin can set the limit to zero. When the limit is zero, the deposit‑checking logic treats any positive deposit amount as exceeding the allowed maximum, causing the contract to reject every new deposit. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users attempting to fund the contract receive a transaction revert or a silent failure, and the protocol cannot receive new capital. The bug appears only after the limit variable is updated to zero; prior to that deposits work as expected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s administrative functions, where the lack of a non‑zero guard was noted. Because the contract does not emit a specific error message for a zero limit, the problem can be hard to notice until users report that deposits are no longer accepted. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing input validation” or “parameter misuse” bugs that lead to unintended state changes. To remediate, the setter functions should enforce that the supplied limit is strictly greater than zero, or alternatively provide a separate mechanism for disabling limits that does not interfere with deposit acceptance. Ensuring that a zero value cannot be written to the limit variable restores the expected behavior where users can deposit funds up to the configured maximum.

title: Withdrawal_Stake and pending deposits are returned to wrong address
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect allocation of the withdrawal stake that is meant to be returned to the user who originally submitted a withdrawal request. When the settlement function processes a batch of withdrawals, it transfers the requested amount to the address supplied as the withdrawal receiver, which is correct, but it also sends the fixed WITHDRAWAL_STAKE amount to the same receiver address. The intended business logic is that the stake should be refunded to the initiator of the withdrawal request, not to the party that receives the withdrawn funds. The root cause is a missing reference to the original sender in the payment logic; the function only receives arrays of receiver addresses and therefore cannot distinguish between the party that requested the withdrawal and the party that receives the funds. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by submitting a withdrawal request and specifying a different address as the receiver; the contract will then credit the stake to that receiver, effectively diverting the stake away from the rightful owner. The impact is that the original requester loses the stake that should have been returned, leading to a reduction of their balance and potentially causing funds to disappear from their account. This occurs each time a withdrawal is settled, both for token withdrawals and for NFT withdrawals, because the same payment routine is used in both loops. The affected parties are the users who initiate withdrawals, the protocol that relies on correct accounting of stakes, and any downstream contracts that assume the stake will be reclaimed by the requester. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the settlement routine and noticed that the same address array was used for both the withdrawal amount and the stake payment. It can be hard to notice because the withdrawal amount is correctly transferred, so the user may only observe that the extra stake they expect to receive back is missing, which may be interpreted as a normal fee or a silent loss. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the withdrawal amount arriving in their wallet while the additional stake balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, contradicting the expectation that the stake is refunded. This violates the accounting assumption that every stake deposited for a withdrawal is later reclaimed by the same participant, breaking the protocol’s financial integrity. The recommended remediation is to modify the withdrawal request structure to include the original sender’s address and to use that address when returning the WITHDRAWAL_STAKE, ensuring that the stake is sent back to the correct party regardless of the receiver specified for the withdrawal amount.

title: Staked WITHDRAWAL_STAKE cannot be withdrawn during the exodusMode
description: submitWithdrawalRequest() requires provided msg.value = WITHDRAWAL_STAKE in order to have a pending withdrawal. It is designed to be returned when a withdrawal request is approved via notarizeSettlement(). But during the mass exit scenario, there is no way to return staked WITHDRAWAL_STAKE. Only pending deposits and verified Nume balance can be withdrawn, but not WITHDRAWAL_STAKE if any.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the mandatory withdrawal stake that users must provide when calling submitWithdrawalRequest(). The contract requires the caller to send an amount equal to WITHDRAWAL_STAKE in order to create a pending withdrawal request. Under normal operation this stake is supposed to be returned to the user when the request is approved by notarizeSettlement(). However, when the protocol enters exodusMode – a mass‑exit scenario designed to allow users to pull out their funds – the contract logic does not include the withdrawal stake in the set of assets that can be withdrawn. Consequently, users who have submitted a withdrawal request during or before exodusMode see their pending deposit and verified Nume balance become withdrawable, but the stake they locked remains locked forever. The root cause is a missing or incorrect conditional branch that excludes the WITHDRAWAL_STAKE from the exodus withdrawal path, likely because the settlement routine assumes the stake will be reclaimed only in normal mode. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft any special transaction; simply participating in a normal withdrawal flow and then triggering or waiting for the protocol to enter exodusMode will cause the stake to be permanently unrecoverable. The impact is financial loss for any user who has an active withdrawal request at the time of mass exit – the stake amount disappears from their balance, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual funds. This condition occurs only when exodusMode is active, which may be rare but is a critical state for the protocol. All users who rely on the contract’s guarantee that the stake will be refunded are affected, as the contract silently retains the funds without any UI indication that the stake is unrecoverable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdrawal lifecycle and identified that the exodus withdrawal path does not handle the stake. It can be hard to notice because the stake is typically a small, fixed amount and the UI may only display the larger token balances, making the missing stake appear as a minor rounding error. From a business‑logic perspective the bug violates the accounting assumption that every amount a user deposits, including the withdrawal stake, will either be returned or burned according to explicit rules; instead the stake is unintentionally trapped. To remediate, the contract should be updated so that notarizeSettlement() or the exodus withdrawal routine explicitly includes the WITHDRAWAL_STAKE in the list of refundable assets, ensuring that the stake is either returned to the requester or, if intended, burned in a transparent manner consistent with protocol policy.

title: Unexpected gains&losses for pending withdrawals if WITHDRAWAL_STAKE is changed
description: submitWithdrawalRequest() receives msg.value as WITHDRAWAL_STAKE. However, it does not store the exact value received per request. When withdrawal requests are proceeded in notarizeSettlement(), the current WITHDRAWAL_STAKE is returned. Thus if WITHDRAWAL_STAKE was updated between "submit" and "notarize" (via setWithdrawStake()), the new updated value will be sent back, which is different from initially staked. As a result, pending withdrawals will experience either a loss or a gain. If WITHDRAWAL_STAKE decreases - users will receive less than staked (loss) If WITHDRAWAL_STAKE increases - users will receive more than staked (gain) Gains for such users mean a loss for the whole contract - lack of funds to finalize all withdrawals in case of a mass exit scenario (DoS). Some extravagant scenarios include the frontrun attack: 1. (Frontrun) Withdrawal request, stake a smaller value 2. WITHDRAWAL_STAKE increases 3. waiting for the request to proceed, receive the increased value
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s handling of the global withdrawal stake parameter (WITHDRAWAL_STAKE). When a user calls submitWithdrawalRequest() the function receives msg.value as the stake for that request, but the exact amount is not recorded per request. Later, when the pending request is processed in notarizeSettlement(), the contract reads the current value of the global WITHDRAWAL_STAKE and returns that amount to the user. Consequently, if the contract owner or an authorized party changes WITHDRAWAL_STAKE via setWithdrawStake() after the request has been submitted but before it is settled, the amount returned will differ from the amount originally staked. A decrease in the stake causes the user to receive less than they deposited, resulting in a loss; an increase causes the user to receive more than they deposited, creating an unintended gain. While a gain may appear beneficial to the individual user, it drains the contract’s overall liquidity and can lead to insufficient funds to satisfy a large number of withdrawals, effectively a denial‑of‑service scenario. The issue can be exploited through a front‑running attack: an attacker submits a withdrawal request with a small stake, then quickly raises WITHDRAWAL_STAKE before the request is settled, causing the attacker’s request to be fulfilled with the higher amount and extracting excess funds from the contract. The bug manifests only when the stake variable is altered while there are pending withdrawals, making it easy to miss during routine testing because most withdrawals will succeed with the expected amount when the stake remains unchanged. It affects any user with a pending withdrawal and the protocol as a whole, as the accounting assumptions that each withdrawal returns exactly the staked amount are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of withdrawal requests and identified that the contract does not persist the per‑request stake. Detecting the issue in production can be difficult because occasional correct withdrawals mask the underlying mismatch, and only when the stake is changed does the discrepancy become visible. To remediate, developers should store the exact stake amount for each withdrawal request, prevent changes to WITHDRAWAL_STAKE while any withdrawals are pending, or eliminate the ability to modify the stake altogether, thereby ensuring that the amount returned always matches the amount originally deposited and preserving the contract’s financial integrity.

title: Future fees may be skirted by setting a non-ETH reward token
description:
Fees are planned to be implemented on the `rewardRecipient` splitter by updating to a new fee structure using the `ImmutableSplitController`.

It is assumed that all rewards will flow through the splitter, because (a) all distributed rewards less than 16 ETH are sent to the `rewardRecipient`, and (b) even if a team waited for rewards to be greater than 16 ETH, rewards sent to the `principalRecipient` are capped at the `amountOfPrincipalStake`.

This creates a fairly strong guarantee that reward funds will flow to the `rewardRecipient`. Even if a user were to set their `amountOfPrincipalStake` high enough that the `principalRecipient` could receive unlimited funds, the Obol team could call `distributeFunds()` when the balance got near 16 ETH to ensure fees were paid.

However, if the user selects a non-ETH token, all ETH will be withdrawable only through the `recoverFunds()` function. If they set up a split with their node operators as their `recoveryAddress`, all funds will be withdrawable via `recoverFunds()` without ever touching the `rewardRecipient` or paying a fee.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an implicit assumption that all reward payouts will be denominated in native ETH and therefore must pass through the rewardRecipient splitter where the protocol’s fee logic is enforced. The contract architecture permits the reward token to be any ERC20‑compatible asset, and when a non‑ETH token is selected the only path for withdrawing accumulated ETH becomes the recoverFunds() function. This function transfers the contract’s ETH balance directly to a configurable recoveryAddress without invoking the fee‑collection routine that is tied to the rewardRecipient splitter. Consequently, a malicious actor who can configure a split can choose a non‑ETH token, set the recoveryAddress to an address they control (for example a node‑operator address), and later call recoverFunds() to pull the ETH balance out of the contract. The fee that the protocol expects to collect on every reward distribution is never deducted, allowing the attacker to skirt future fees entirely. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the protocol and a breach of the economic model that relies on fee collection; users may notice that no fee is taken from their withdrawals and that the protocol’s fee accounting shows zero despite ETH being moved. This condition occurs only when the reward token is not ETH and the recoverFunds() path is exercised, which may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to overlook during testing. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the fee‑distribution flow and noticed that the fee logic is gated on the rewardRecipient path rather than on all possible withdrawal mechanisms. The bug belongs to a class of business‑logic bypasses where improper validation of input parameters (the token type) allows an attacker to circumvent accounting rules. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal that should have been reduced by the protocol fee arrives in full, or that the fee balance remains unchanged while ETH disappears from the contract. To remediate the problem the contract should either forbid the use of non‑ETH tokens in the OptimisticWithdrawalRecipient, or enforce that ETH is always treated as a valid reward token and that any ETH withdrawal, including those performed via recoverFunds(), must first pass through the fee‑collection routine. This ensures that fee logic cannot be sidestepped regardless of the chosen reward token.

title: Splits with 256 or more node operators will not be able to switch on fees
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑size truncation bug in the function that packs split controller data. The code stores the number of recipient accounts in a uint256 variable, then downcasts it to a uint8 when encoding the split configuration. Because a uint8 can only represent values up to 255, any split that contains 256 or more operators causes the value to wrap around, effectively storing recipientsSize modulo 256. When the controller later reads the stored size, it only processes the truncated number of accounts, discarding the remainder of the list. As a result, the subsequent call to updateSplit – which attempts to turn on the distributor fee – validates the split using only the truncated set of percent allocations. The sum of the retained allocations no longer equals the required total of 1e6, causing the validSplit check to revert and preventing the fee activation. The bug manifests only when a split is created with more than 255 recipients; splits with fewer recipients behave correctly. Users attempting to enable fees on large splits see a transaction revert with no obvious error, leading to the impression that the contract is broken or that the protocol is refusing to charge fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data‑packing routine and noticed the unchecked downcast. It can be hard to notice because the creation of the split succeeds – the overflow occurs later, when the size is read, and the revert message does not point to the root cause. The impact is that any protocol or DAO that relies on a split with many node operators cannot enable fee distribution, potentially leaving revenue uncollected and breaking business logic that assumes fees are always payable. The affected parties are the split owners, the operator accounts, and any downstream contracts that expect fee revenue. The fix is to validate the number of recipients before casting to uint8 and to reject splits that exceed the supported limit, or to redesign the encoding to use a larger integer type for the size field. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of integer overflow / truncation errors that arise from unsafe type conversions in Solidity.

title: In a mass slashing event, node operators are incentivized to get slashed
description:
When the `OptimisticWithdrawalRecipient` receives funds from the beacon chain, it uses the following rule to determine the allocation:

If the amount of funds to be distributed is greater than or equal to 16 ether, it is assumed that it is a withdrawal (to be returned to the principal, with a cap on principal withdrawals of the total amount they deposited).

Otherwise, it is assumed that the funds are rewards.

This value being as low as 16 ether protects against any predictable attack the node operator could perform. For example, due to the effect of hysteresis in updating effective balances, it does not seem to be possible for node operators to predictably bleed a withdrawal down to be below 16 ether (even if they timed a slashing perfectly).

However, in the event of a mass slashing event, slashing punishments can be much more severe than they otherwise would be. To calculate the size of a slash, we:
take the total percentage of validator stake slashed in the 18 days preceding and following a user's slash
multiply this percentage by 3 (capped at 100%)
the full slashing penalty for a given validator equals 1/32 of their stake, plus the resulting percentage above applied to the remaining 31/32 of their stake

In order for such penalties to bring the withdrawal balance below 16 ether (assuming a full 32 ether to start), we would need the percentage taken to be greater than `15 / 31 = 48.3%`, which implies that `48.3 / 3 = 16.1%` of validators would need to be slashed.

Because the measurement is taken from the 18 days before and after the incident, node operators would have the opportunity to see a mass slashing event unfold, and later decide that they would like to be slashed along with it.

In the event that they observed that greater than 16.1% of validators were slashed, Obol node operators would be able to get themselves slashed, be exited with a withdrawal of less than 16 ether, and claim that withdrawal as rewards, effectively stealing from the principal recipient.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a logic rule in the OptimisticWithdrawalRecipient contract that classifies any incoming amount smaller than 16 ether as a reward and any amount equal to or larger than 16 ether as a withdrawal of principal. This rule was intended to protect against predictable attacks, but it does not account for the effect of large slashing events on the effective balance of a validator. During a mass slashing event the protocol calculates the penalty by taking the percentage of stake slashed in the 18‑day window around the incident, multiplying it by three (capped at 100 %), and applying the resulting figure to the remaining 31/32 of the validator’s stake. If more than roughly 16.1 % of validators are slashed, the penalty can reduce a full 32‑ether withdrawal balance to below the 16‑ether threshold. An operator who monitors the slashing percentage can deliberately trigger a self‑slash once the threshold is crossed, causing the withdrawal amount to fall under 16 ether. Because the contract treats any sub‑16‑ether transfer as a reward, the operator can then claim the reduced withdrawal as a reward, effectively stealing a portion of the principal that should have been protected. The impact is a loss of deposited funds for the operator’s delegators and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are separate from principal. The issue manifests only under extreme slashing conditions, making it rare and therefore easy to overlook during normal testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a surprisingly small “reward” payment – for example a withdrawal of a few ether instead of the expected full principal – which contradicts the expectation that rewards are supplemental and that principal is safe. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Obront through logical analysis of the slashing formula and the reward‑vs‑withdrawal threshold. It is hard to notice because the threshold is low and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a withdrawal is re‑classified as a reward. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a stronger guarantee that funds classified as rewards are indeed generated by protocol incentives, for example by raising the threshold, separating reward and principal flows, or adding cryptographic proof that the transferred amount originates from the reward pool rather than a reduced principal withdrawal.

title: ohmDeployed will become inaccurate if circulatingOhmBurned is used
description:
The OHM deposited to Silo will accure interest over time, which means that the protocol has the potential to withdraw more OHM than is tracked by the `ohmDeployed` value.

This is expected, and the Policy performs valid adjustments to account for it:
```solidity
if (ohmDeployed < amount) circulatingOhmBurned += amount - ohmDeployed;
ohmDeployed -= ohmDeployed > amount ? amount : ohmDeployed;
```
If more OHM is withdrawn than was deployed, `ohmDeployed` is set to 0, and the `circulatingOhmBurned` value is incremented as a sort of negative marker for the amount of surplus OHM that was withdrawn.

However, in the event that OHM continues to be deployed to the Silo, this `circulatingOhmBurned` value is not used to adjust the `ohmDeployed` value to accurately offset for the previous negative value.

Let's walk through an example:
1000 OHM is deployed to the Silo
Additional interest is earned, so this value increases to 1010 OHM
All 1010 OHM is withdrawn, setting `ohmDeployed = 0` and `circulatingOhmBurned = 10`
A new 1000 OHM is deployed
We have no deployed 2000 OHM and withdrawn 1010 OHM, which results in a total mint of `2000 - 1010 = 990 OHM`
However, `ohmDeployed` will be set to 1000

This will cause two problems for the protocol:

1) `_canDeposit` will return false for any deposits that push the `ohmDeployed` over the `maximumToDeploy`, even if the total deployed is not actually greater than `maximumToDeploy`. This will cause all such deposits to revert.

2) Any time `update()` is called in a way that would push us over the `maximumToDeploy` will have the amount automatically reduced to `maximumToDeploy - ohmDeployed`, which will lead to too little OHM being deployed relative to the amount set in `maximumToDeploy`.

While these differences would be small on a short timescale, as the amount of interest earned increases, the difference can become more and more significant.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the Silo module that tracks how much OHM has been deployed to the lending pool. The contract stores two variables: a counter for the total deployed OHM (ohmDeployed) and a marker for surplus OHM that was withdrawn when the pool earned interest (circulatingOhmBurned). When a withdrawal exceeds the current deployment, the code correctly sets ohmDeployed to zero and records the excess as a positive circulatingOhmBurned value. However, the implementation never uses this circulatingOhmBurned value to offset the counter when new OHM is later deposited. As a result, after an interest‑driven over‑withdrawal, the protocol treats the next deposit as if no surplus had ever been withdrawn, leaving the internal accounting out of sync with the real amount of OHM that has passed through the pool. This mismatch occurs whenever interest accrues, a withdrawal larger than the deployed balance is performed, and a subsequent deposit follows before the negative marker is cleared. An attacker or any user can trigger the condition simply by depositing, waiting for interest to accrue, withdrawing the full amount (including interest), and then depositing again. The impact is twofold: the internal check that prevents deposits from exceeding a configured maximum (maximumToDeploy) will incorrectly reject legitimate deposits because ohmDeployed appears larger than it actually is, causing transactions to revert; and any automatic adjustment performed by the update() routine will cap the amount of newly deployed OHM to a value lower than the intended maximum, effectively reducing the protocol’s capital efficiency. From a user perspective the symptoms are deposits that unexpectedly fail with a “cannot deposit” error or succeed but result in less OHM being allocated than expected, leading to lower yields. The bug is subtle because the contract still records a non‑negative balance and the discrepancy only becomes visible after multiple cycles of interest accrual and withdrawal, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the state‑transition logic of the deposit and withdrawal functions and noticed that circulatingOhmBurned is never read when increasing ohmDeployed. The class of bug is an improper state reset or stale negative balance in financial accounting logic, where a corrective offset is recorded but never applied. To fix the problem the deposit routine must first reconcile any existing circulatingOhmBurned amount before adding the new deposit, either by reducing the marker or by applying it to the deployed counter, ensuring that the internal accounting always reflects the true net OHM flow.

title: SiloAMO uses outdated InterestRateModel
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of deploying the SiloAMO policy with a reference to an outdated interest‑rate model contract. The code points to the address 0x7e9e7ea94e1ff36e216a703D6D66eCe356a5fd44, which hosts the original InterestRateModel.sol that contains a comment marking it as deprecated and advises the use of InterestRateModelV2. The root cause is a misconfiguration during deployment: the deployment script or fork‑test suite was not updated to replace the old model address with the newer, intended address (0x76074C0b66A480F7bc6AbDaA9643a7dc99e18314). Because the contract still compiles and the function signatures match, the error is silent and does not raise an exception, making it hard to notice without explicit source‑code verification. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the protocol itself will calculate interest using the deprecated logic, which may have different rate formulas, rounding behavior, or safety checks compared to the V2 implementation. Consequently, users who deposit assets into the SiloAMO may receive interest that is lower or higher than expected, potentially leading to loss of value, mis‑pricing of loans, or unexpected zero accruals. The issue manifests when the SiloAMO policy is instantiated or when the SiloRepository’s getInterestRateModel function is called, returning the old contract address. All participants that rely on accurate interest calculations – depositors, borrowers, and the overall protocol economics – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the deployed address, retrieving the source file from the repository, and observing the deprecation notice. Because the contract still implements the required interface, the bug does not cause immediate failures, which is why it can go unnoticed in normal operation. To remediate the issue, the deployment configuration and any test scripts must be updated to reference the correct InterestRateModelV2 address, ensuring that all interest calculations follow the intended, audited formula and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain valid.

title: If MINTR is paused, SiloAMO will not be able to unwind its position
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a coupling between the SiloAMO contract’s withdrawal routine and the MINTR contract’s burn function. When the AMO needs to unwind its OHM position—either because utilization exceeds the optimal threshold or because an admin triggers an emergency unwind—the internal _withdraw function pulls OHM from the Silo and then calls MINTR.burnOhm to destroy the withdrawn tokens. MINTR implements a pause mechanism guarded by the onlyWhileActive modifier, which reverts any call when the contract is paused. If MINTR is paused before the unwind operation, the call to burnOhm reverts, causing the entire _withdraw transaction to fail. As a result, the AMO cannot complete the withdrawal, leaving the OHM still deposited in the Silo and effectively locked. This situation can arise during a market emergency when the protocol’s governance may pause MINTR to protect the token supply while simultaneously needing to unwind AMOs to reduce exposure. The impact is that assets become inaccessible, users or the protocol cannot reduce a volatile position, and the accounting state diverges from expectations—users see no change in their balances despite initiating a withdrawal, and the protocol’s risk metrics remain inflated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between pause‑controlled contracts and emergency unwind paths. It is subtle because the pause flag is a legitimate safety feature, and the failure only manifests when two independent emergency actions coincide, making it easy to overlook in normal testing. The bug belongs to the class of “cross‑contract pause‑revert” errors where a dependent contract assumes a downstream call will always succeed. To remediate, the burn call should be protected with a try/catch block so that a paused MINTR does not revert the whole unwind; the assets can then be retained in the AMO and later recovered by the admin. Conceptually, the fix decouples the burn step from the withdrawal flow, ensuring that a paused state does not block the ability to move or recover funds. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the business logic that an emergency unwind must succeed even if token burning is temporarily disabled, preserving user expectations that a withdrawal request results in a reduction of the deposited balance.

title: guageBuffered() contains unsafe read of b.buffer
description: b.buffer is passed to guageBuffered() which references the buffer as prices. Access of this buffer should be protected by a mutex, in this case a read lock. This is called periodically in the (b *Buffer) stream ticker cadence. This opens up Omni's fee oracle to memory corruption.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe concurrent read of a shared price buffer inside the fee oracle component. The function that measures buffered prices, referred to as guageBuffered, accesses the buffer directly without acquiring any synchronization primitive such as a read lock or mutex. Because the buffer is also written to by other parts of the contract during the same execution tick, a race condition can occur where guageBuffered reads partially updated or corrupted memory. This race condition arises periodically when the ticker that drives the Buffer stream invokes guageBuffered while a write operation may be in progress. The root cause is the absence of thread‑safety guarantees for a data structure that is intended to be shared across asynchronous updates. An attacker or a malicious transaction could trigger the ticker at a precise moment, causing the oracle to return malformed price data. The immediate impact is that the fee calculation, which relies on the buffered prices, may produce incorrect results – for example, users may be charged excessive fees, receive no refund, or see their balances unexpectedly reduced. From a user perspective the UI may display a fee of zero while the transaction actually deducts funds, or the displayed fee may be dramatically higher than expected, violating the business logic that fees should be proportional to the true market price. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the concurrency model of the oracle and identified the missing lock. Because the bug manifests only under specific timing conditions, it can be intermittent and therefore hard to detect through normal testing or on‑chain monitoring. The appropriate remediation is to make guageBuffered thread‑safe by protecting the buffer with a read‑write lock or by redesigning the data flow so that reads and writes are serialized, ensuring that price data is never read while it is being modified. In broader terms this is a classic data‑race or unsynchronized shared‑state bug that breaks the accounting assumptions of the fee oracle and can lead to financial loss or protocol misbehaviour.

title: cache::Get() unsafely returns a reference to c.network without a lock
description: (c *cache) Get() returns a pointer to c.network and releases its lock upon the function return. This function is called periodically by (k Keeper) getLatestPortals() which will deference the pointer when it calls network.GetPortals(). This makes the node vulnerable to race conditions and thus memory corruption.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic data‑race caused by an unsafe getter in the cache component. The method cache::Get() returns a direct pointer to the internal network object while holding a mutex, but it releases the lock before the function returns. Consequently, the caller receives a reference that is no longer protected by the lock. When the Keeper routine getLatestPortals() invokes cache.Get() and immediately dereferences the returned pointer to call network.GetPortals(), another goroutine may concurrently modify the underlying network structure. Because the pointer is shared without synchronization, the concurrent write can corrupt memory, lead to undefined behaviour, crashes, or incorrect portal data being returned. The bug appears only when multiple threads access the cache at the same time, which is typical in a production node that periodically refreshes portal information. Users of the protocol may notice missing or empty portal lists, unexpected zero‑value responses, or the node becoming unresponsive. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the concurrency model and identified that the lock was released before the reference escaped the function scope. Such race conditions are hard to detect because they may not reproduce consistently in tests and often manifest as sporadic memory corruption or silent data loss. To remediate the problem, the getter should either return a deep copy of the network object or keep the lock held for the entire duration of the caller’s use, or provide a dedicated thread‑safe accessor that performs the required operation while the lock is held. This fixes the root cause by ensuring that no unsafe reference to mutable shared state is exposed, thereby preserving the integrity of the network data and preventing accidental corruption of the node’s state.

title: Potential double-vote if validator runs out of storage
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑persistence flaw that can lead to a double‑vote by a validator when the node runs out of disk space. In the voting routine the in‑memory fields that track the latest attestation (v.latest) and the remaining voting capacity (v.available) are updated before the function attempts to write the new state to persistent storage via v.saveUnsafe(). The save operation uses WriteFileAtomic, which creates a temporary file and swaps it with the existing state file only if the write succeeds. When the filesystem is full, the temporary file cannot be created, WriteFileAtomic returns an error, and v.saveUnsafe propagates that error back to the caller. However, the earlier in‑memory updates are not rolled back, so the validator believes it has recorded the vote even though the on‑disk state remains unchanged. If the node is then restarted, it reloads the stale state from disk, which still reflects the previous latest approved attestation. The validator’s runtime logic will compare the newly received attestation against the outdated on‑disk value, determine that the new attestation is newer, and submit it again, effectively casting a second vote for the same consensus event. This double‑vote violates the protocol’s assumption that each validator votes at most once per epoch or height, potentially causing slashing penalties, undermining consensus safety, and eroding trust in the network. The issue manifests only when storage exhaustion occurs during a vote and the node is allowed to continue running instead of halting; it may be hard to notice because the error is logged but the process does not crash, and the double‑vote only becomes observable after a restart when the validator’s behavior deviates from expected single‑vote semantics. The flaw was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between in‑memory state updates and the atomic file‑write helper. To remediate, the validator should treat a failure to persist state as a fatal condition: it must abort the voting operation, revert any in‑memory changes, and stop the validator process rather than restarting the voting stream. Alternatively, the code could be restructured to write to disk before mutating the in‑memory representation or to employ a transactional approach that guarantees atomicity between memory and storage. In any case, ensuring that a failed persistence does not leave the node in an inconsistent state prevents the double‑vote scenario and preserves protocol integrity.

title: Relayer Will Not Receive Any Fee If `execute` Reverts
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the fee‑payment mechanism for relayers that trigger the BridgeFacet.execute function in the Connext protocol. When a relayer calls execute, the contract records the relayer’s address in a mapping (s.transferRelayer) before attempting to perform a token swap via a StablePool. The swap is subject to a user‑defined slippage limit; if market conditions cause the actual slippage to exceed this limit, the swap call reverts. Because the fee‑payment logic is placed inside the same transaction, the revert from the swap propagates up and aborts the entire execute call. As a result, the earlier state change that stored the relayer’s address is rolled back, and the relayer receives no reimbursement for the gas spent. This situation can be exploited by an adversary who deliberately manipulates the pool to increase slippage or by front‑running a relayer’s transaction with another trade that widens the price impact. Under those conditions the relayer’s transaction will revert, the fee will be lost, and the relayer sees a failed transaction with no compensation, contradicting the expectation that the relayer will be paid for its effort. The impact is primarily economic: relayers incur unrecoverable gas costs, which may discourage participation and weaken the incentive model of the bridge. Users are indirectly affected because a reduced relayer set can increase latency or cause failures in cross‑chain transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BridgeFacet contract, where the auditor noted that the fee is set before the liquidity handling code and that the contract does not contain any “finally”‑style logic to guarantee fee payout after a revert. The problem is subtle because the fee‑recording line appears correct at first glance, and the revert is caused by a downstream swap rather than the fee logic itself, making the loss of fee hard to notice without tracing transaction failures. To remediate the issue, the contract should separate fee attribution from the execution path that can revert, for example by recording the relayer in a persistent storage that is not cleared on revert (using a separate claim contract or an escrow that can be withdrawn later) or by ensuring that fee payment is performed in a distinct transaction that runs after the main execution, regardless of its success. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of "state‑rollback on revert causing loss of reward" and is analogous to situations where fee or reward logic is placed before a potentially failing operation without proper safeguards. The correct design must guarantee that relayers are compensated for the gas they spend, even when the bridge execution fails due to slippage or other runtime errors.

title: Diamond upgrade proposition can be falsified
description:
[DiamondCutFacet.sol#L16-L29](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/main/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/DiamondCutFacet.sol#L16-L29)  
[LibDiamond.sol#L94-L118](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/main/contracts/contracts/core/connext/libraries/LibDiamond.sol#L94-L118)  
[LibDiamond.sol#L222-L240](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/main/contracts/contracts/core/connext/libraries/LibDiamond.sol#L222-L240)  

Diamond is to be upgraded after a certain delay to give time to the community to verify changes made by the developers. If the proposition can be falsified, the contract admins can exploit the contract in any way of their choice.
poc: To determine the id of the proposal, only its facet changes are hashed, skipping two critical pieces of data - the `_init` and `_calldata`. During a diamond upgrade, devs can choose what code will be executed **by the contract using a delegatecall**. Thus, they can make the contract perform **any** actions of their choice.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a falsifiable upgrade proposition in a Diamond proxy pattern used by the Connext protocol. When a governance proposal to upgrade the Diamond is created, the contract computes an identifier for the proposal by hashing only the list of facet cuts—i.e., the new contract modules to be added or replaced. Crucially, the hash omits the two parameters that determine what code will actually be executed during the upgrade: the `_init` address and the `_calldata` passed to it. Because `_init` and `_calldata` are executed via a delegatecall, they can contain arbitrary logic that runs in the context of the proxy. An attacker who can influence or compromise the governance process can therefore craft two distinct upgrade payloads that share the same facet‑cut hash but differ in `_init`/`_calldata`. The first payload can be submitted to obtain a proposal identifier that appears legitimate, and later the attacker can replace the hidden `_init`/`_calldata` with malicious code without altering the hashed facet cuts. This falsification bypasses the intended security delay and community review, allowing the contract admins—or any party that gains control of the proposal—to execute any delegatecall code, such as draining funds, altering state, or disabling critical functionality. The impact is a loss of trust and potential theft of user assets, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions that upgrades are benign are violated. The issue manifests whenever a Diamond upgrade is proposed through the governance flow that relies on the insecure hash computation, which is the default behavior in the current implementation. It affects all users of the protocol, the governance participants, and any contracts that depend on the upgraded logic. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the DiamondCutFacet and LibDiamond libraries, where the missing fields in the hash calculation were identified as a logical oversight. Detecting the bug may be difficult because the hash function appears to provide a unique identifier, leading reviewers to assume that all upgrade data is covered, while in reality the critical execution parameters are excluded. To remediate, the proposal hash must be recomputed to include both `_init` and `_calldata`, ensuring that any change to the execution payload results in a different identifier and that the governance delay and community verification can reliably detect tampering. This fixes the issue at the conceptual level by binding the full upgrade payload to the proposal identifier, preventing falsification and guaranteeing that the upgrade semantics match the community‑approved intent.

title: Malicious relayer could exploit sponsor vaults
description:
[SponsorVault.sol#L234-L263](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/helpers/SponsorVault.sol#L234-L263)  

Sponsor vaults drained.
poc: `reimburseRelayerFees` uses SponsorVault funds to repay users the fees they pay to relayers. A malicious relayer could create a large number of transactions with the max reimbursed relay fee specified in SponsorVault between chains for which they relay all of them. They would receive back the relay fee from the SponsorVault and they would also get the relay fee they paid themselves.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SponsorVault contract’s reimburseRelayerFees routine, which pays back relayers from a sponsor‑funded pool without adequate accounting of how much fee is actually owed. The root cause is that the function trusts a whitelisted relayer to claim a fixed maximum reimbursement amount for each cross‑chain transaction and does not record or limit the total amount a relayer can receive. Because there is no per‑relayer cap, rate‑limiting, or verification that the reimbursed amount matches the fee actually paid, a malicious relayer that is on the whitelist can flood the system with a large number of relayed messages, each specifying the maximum reimbursable fee. For every such message the contract transfers the maximum amount from the sponsor vault to the relayer, while the relayer also retains the fee it originally paid to execute the relay. The net effect is a double‑claim: the sponsor’s vault loses funds equal to the reimbursement, and the relayer profits by the same amount, effectively draining the vault. The issue manifests when a sponsor vault has a positive balance, the maximum reimbursement parameter is set to a non‑zero value, and a whitelisted relayer is able to submit many relay transactions. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the SponsorVault logic and identified that the reimbursement flow lacks any safeguard against excessive claims. The problem is subtle because every reimbursement looks like a legitimate payment for relayer work, so the drain can be hidden among normal protocol activity and may not raise immediate alarms. The impact is financial loss for sponsors who allocate funds to cover relayer fees; users are not directly at risk, but the sponsor’s capital can disappear, violating the business assumption that sponsor funds only reimburse actual relayer costs. To remediate, the contract should implement strict accounting for reimbursable fees, such as per‑relayer limits, tracking of cumulative reimbursements, validation that the reimbursed amount does not exceed the fee actually spent, and possibly a requirement for external proof of fee expenditure. Adding balance checks or removing automatic reimbursement altogether are also viable mitigations. In essence, the bug is a classic case of unchecked reimbursement leading to a double‑spend of sponsor‑funded resources, resulting in unexpected balance reductions, empty vaults, and loss of sponsored liquidity.

title: Funds not always in vault lead to share price calculation mess
description:
At any point, the funds could be outside of OmoVault.sol and still not a UniswapV3 position in dynamic accounts. the funds could be in the agent address, in dynamic accounts as tokens (not UniV3 positions) or UniswapV3 positions but still owned by the agent.
This will affect the return value of the total assets in the vault from OmoVault.so#totalAssets() and it will corrupt all the logic of deposit/mint and redeem.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the OmoVault contract where the totalAssets() view function assumes that every asset belonging to the vault is either held directly in the vault storage or represented as a UniswapV3 position owned by the vault. In practice the protocol allows a separate agent address and dynamic accounts to hold tokens or UniswapV3 positions that are not owned by the vault contract. When funds are transferred to the agent address, stored as raw ERC20 tokens in a dynamic account, or kept in a UniswapV3 position that lists the agent as the owner, the totalAssets() calculation ignores those balances. As a result the reported total assets are lower than the actual amount of capital backing the vault shares. This discrepancy corrupts the share‑price logic used by deposit/mint and redeem functions: the price per share is derived from totalAssets divided by total supply. If totalAssets under‑reports, the share price appears artificially low, allowing a user to mint new shares at a discounted rate, or conversely causing redeemors to receive fewer underlying tokens than expected. The impact is that users may see their balances shrink, refunds become zero or unexpectedly small, and the protocol’s accounting invariants break, potentially leading to loss of funds or unfair profit extraction. The issue manifests whenever the protocol’s dynamic account feature is used or when the agent address is allowed to hold assets, i.e., under normal operation of the vault but only when assets are moved outside the vault’s recognised storage. It was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the totalAssets implementation and identified that it does not enumerate all possible holdings. The bug is subtle because the UI may still display a correct vault balance based on external queries, while the internal share‑price calculation diverges, making the problem hard to notice without deep inspection of accounting code. To remediate, the vault should either lock any transfers that would move assets out of the recognised storage, or, preferably, extend totalAssets() to aggregate all token balances and UniswapV3 positions regardless of ownership, ensuring that the share‑price formula always reflects the true amount of capital. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “incorrect asset accounting” or “share‑price miscalculation due to hidden balances”, which violates the fundamental business logic that each share must represent an exact proportion of the underlying assets.

title: Entry point contract cannot interact with OmoAgent.sol functions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control restriction in the OmoAgent.sol contract. Functions that are meant to be invoked by the ERC‑4337 EntryPoint – such as borrowAsset, repayAsset, topOffToAgent and others – are protected by an onlyAgent modifier that requires msg.sender to equal the address stored in OmoAgentStorage.data().agents[_id]. Because the EntryPoint address is not stored in that list and the modifier does not recognise calls originating from the EntryPoint, legitimate calls from the EntryPoint are rejected with the \"Only agent\" revert. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended architecture (the EntryPoint is the authorized caller) and the concrete implementation (the onlyAgent check only allows a pre‑registered agent address). An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the bug manifests whenever a user tries to perform an account‑abstraction operation through the EntryPoint. The transaction reverts, the user sees no state change, and the expected asset borrow, repayment or top‑up never occurs. From the protocol perspective, funds can become locked because the contract cannot forward the operation to the underlying agent, breaking the accounting flow defined by ERC‑4337. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s permission model, where the auditor noticed that the onlyAgent modifier does not reference the EntryPoint and therefore contradicts the ERC‑4337 specification. The problem can be hard to notice because the functions compile and appear to work in isolation; only when the EntryPoint is used does the revert surface, which may be attributed to a generic \"insufficient gas\" or \"invalid caller\" error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of authorization‑logic bugs where the wrong entity is granted exclusive access, leading to a denial‑of‑service for legitimate users. To remediate, the storage struct should include the EntryPoint address and the onlyAgent modifier (or a separate check) should allow calls from that address, similar to the existing _requireFromEntryPoint pattern used elsewhere in the codebase. After the fix, the EntryPoint will be able to trigger the agent functions, users will receive the expected borrow or repayment outcomes, and the protocol’s accounting will remain consistent.

title: OmoOracle.convertUSDToToken() : missing price staleness validation
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the oracle conversion routine that translates a USD amount into a target token amount. The function retrieves the latest price from an external price feed but fails to verify that the returned price is recent. Because the code only checks that the price is greater than zero, it will accept a price that may be arbitrarily old. The root cause is the omission of a staleness validation step that compares the timestamp of the price update with the current block time and a predefined heartbeat interval. An attacker who can cause the price feed to stop updating, or who can submit a deliberately delayed price, can trigger the conversion function to use a stale price. By doing so the attacker can cause the protocol to undervalue or overvalue assets: for example, if the stale price is lower than the current market price, a user converting USD to the token will receive more tokens than they should, allowing the attacker to extract excess tokens; conversely, a higher stale price can cause users to receive fewer tokens, effectively stealing value from them. The impact is incorrect valuation of assets held by agents, potential loss of funds, and a breach of the accounting assumptions that the oracle always reflects current market conditions. This condition occurs every time convertUSDToToken is called after the price feed has not been refreshed within its expected heartbeat, which may happen after network congestion, feed downtime, or intentional manipulation. The affected parties include any user or contract that relies on the conversion function for deposits, withdrawals, or pricing, as well as the overall protocol that assumes accurate pricing for risk management. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the reviewer noticed that the function performed a positivity check on the price but did not include any freshness check similar to the one used in the getUSDValue helper. Because the function still returns a plausible price, the bug can be hard to notice in normal operation; only a careful review of the timestamp handling reveals the flaw. To remediate, the conversion routine should retrieve the update timestamp from the price feed and assert that block.timestamp minus the update time is less than or equal to the feed’s heartbeat, reverting with a clear error if the price is stale. This aligns the function with the standard oracle freshness pattern and restores confidence that token amounts are calculated using up‑to‑date market data. In user‑facing terms, a user may expect to receive a certain amount of tokens for a given USD amount but instead receives too many or too few, leading to unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or apparent loss of funds, which violates the protocol’s business logic that conversions must be fair and reflect current market rates.

title: OmoOracle.getUSDValue price feed updates may be incorrectly marked stale
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OmoOracle.getUSDValue function, which applies a hard‑coded staleness rule that treats a price as stale when the difference between the current block timestamp and the stored updatedAt timestamp exceeds one hour. This rule assumes that every price feed updates at least once per hour, but in reality each aggregator defines its own heartbeat – the maximum interval it is allowed to go without publishing a new price – and many feeds are configured with heartbeats longer than one hour or update only when a price deviation threshold is crossed. Because the contract does not query the feed‑specific heartbeat, it may incorrectly revert with the StalePrice error for feeds that are still considered fresh by their own schedule. The root cause is the mismatch between a fixed one‑hour timeout and the variable update cadence of external price aggregators. An attacker or even a benign market condition can trigger the bug by simply waiting longer than one hour after the last legitimate price update; subsequent calls to getUSDValue will revert, preventing the contract from returning a USD value. This denial‑of‑service style exploit blocks any downstream logic that depends on the oracle, such as token swaps, collateral valuations, or liquidation checks, leading to failed transactions, potentially locked funds, and a broken user experience where the UI shows missing or zero balances. The issue manifests only for tokens whose price feeds have a heartbeat greater than one hour or that update infrequently due to deviation‑based logic, making it intermittent and hard to spot during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s staleness check against the documented behavior of the underlying aggregators. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a price feed always provides a recent value, breaking the contract’s guarantee that a valid price can be fetched on demand. To remediate, the staleness condition should be rewritten to retrieve the specific heartbeat configured for each price feed and compare the elapsed time against that value, thereby aligning the contract’s freshness check with the feed’s own policy and eliminating unnecessary reverts.

title: OmoAgent.setPositionManager change results in loss of deposited positions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the administrative function that updates the address of the Position Manager contract. The function simply overwrites a storage slot with a new address and does not consider any positions that have already been deposited through the previous manager. Deposited positions are recorded against the specific manager address, so when the address is changed the protocol’s internal bookkeeping continues to reference the old manager while the storage now points to a new contract that has no knowledge of those positions.
