As a result, users who previously deposited positions lose the ability to query or withdraw them; from the user’s perspective the balance appears to be zero or the withdrawal transaction returns no assets. The issue can be triggered whenever the contract owner or a privileged manager calls setPositionManager while there are active deposits. Because the function is gated only by an onlyManager modifier, a malicious or careless manager can deliberately replace the manager address, effectively locking all existing positions. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined state‑changing administrative functions. It is easy to miss because the function does not contain any logic that interacts with the deposited positions, so a superficial test may not reveal any immediate failure. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑binding after address upgrade” or “inconsistent storage after contract reference change” vulnerabilities, where data is tightly coupled to a specific contract instance and the reference is altered without migrating the data. To fix the issue the contract should either forbid changing the manager while any positions are still deposited, or it should maintain a mapping that records the manager address used for each deposit and allow the new manager to access the legacy positions, possibly by migrating the data or by providing a fallback path. Implementing a pre‑condition check such as “require(no active positions)” before updating the address, or redesigning the storage model to decouple positions from a single manager, will restore the expected accounting behavior where users can always retrieve their funds.

title: Incorrect handling of stETH token in OmoRouter.deposit() function
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OmoRouter.deposit() function (and similar entry points in OmoVault) when handling the stETH token, a liquid staking token whose ERC20 transferFrom may return 1‑2 wei less than the amount requested. The router calls safeTransferFrom expecting to receive exactly the assets amount supplied by the caller, then immediately approves the vault for that same amount and forwards it to IOmoVault.deposit(). Because the actual token balance after the transfer is slightly lower, the subsequent deposit call reverts due to insufficient balance. This mismatch between the approved amount and the real token balance causes legitimate deposit transactions to fail, leading users to see a transaction revert, lose gas, and receive no shares in the vault. The issue is triggered only for tokens that do not guarantee exact transfer amounts, such as stETH, and therefore may be missed during generic testing that assumes ERC20 compliance. It affects any whitelisted user attempting to deposit stETH through the router or directly into the vault, as well as internal functions that rely on the same approval pattern (topOff, repayAsset). The problem was discovered during a security audit that exercised the deposit path with stETH and observed the revert. The bug is hard to notice because most tokens transfer the exact amount, so the code appears correct for the majority of cases. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of incorrect handling of token transfer rounding or fee‑deducting tokens, where the contract assumes the transferred amount equals the requested amount without verification. From a user perspective, the UI may show a successful submission but the blockchain transaction fails, resulting in “my deposit returned an error” or “no shares were minted”. The business logic that the vault should receive the exact amount deposited is violated, breaking accounting invariants. The recommended mitigation is to measure the actual token balance received after the transfer (e.g., by recording the contract’s balance before and after safeTransferFrom) and use that precise amount for approval and the subsequent vault deposit, ensuring that the contract never asks the vault to pull more tokens than it actually holds.

title: Missing slippage protection in deposit(), mint(), and redeem() functions
description:
The deposit(), mint(), and redeem() functions in the OmoRouter contract lack a slippage mechanism to safeguard against significant deviations in the assets received or shares minted, which would result in users getting less assets/shares and incur unexpected losses during these operations.
The same issue exists when whitelisted users interact directly with the OmoVault.deposit(), OmoVault.mint(), and OmoVault.redeem() functions.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the deposit(), mint(), and redeem() functions of the OmoRouter contract and the underlying OmoVault contract. Because the functions do not accept a minimum‑out or maximum‑out parameter, they do not verify that the amount of assets received when depositing or the number of shares minted, nor the amount of assets returned when redeeming, stays within an acceptable range. The root cause is that the contract trusts the current on‑chain price or exchange rate at the moment of execution without guarding against rapid price movement or front‑running. An attacker who can influence the price of the underlying asset between the time a user signs a transaction and the time it is mined can cause the user’s transaction to execute at a much worse rate. For example, a user may submit a deposit expecting to receive 1000 vault shares, but a malicious actor can manipulate the pool’s balance or the price oracle so that the same deposit only yields 800 shares. Because the contract does not check a slippage limit, the transaction succeeds and the user receives the lower amount, resulting in an unexpected loss. The same pattern applies to mint() where the user specifies a desired amount of shares and receives fewer underlying assets, and to redeem() where the user expects a certain amount of assets back but receives less. The impact is that any participant—regular users, whitelisted users, or contracts interacting through the router—can suffer reduced balances, effectively “money disappears” from their perspective, even though the transaction does not revert. The issue manifests whenever the functions are called in a volatile market or when an adversary can front‑run or sandwich the transaction. It was discovered during a manual security review that looked for protective checks on output amounts; the absence of a slippage parameter is a classic omission in DeFi vaults. The problem is subtle because the transaction appears successful and no explicit error is emitted; only the post‑transaction balance reveals the loss, making it easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the vault should expose a slippage tolerance argument (e.g., a minimum amount of assets to receive or a maximum number of shares to be burned) and enforce it with a require statement that reverts if the actual outcome falls outside the user‑specified range. This change restores the expected accounting invariant that the amount received is at least what the user anticipated, aligning the contract with standard slippage‑protected patterns used in other DeFi protocols.

title: Unrestricted access in OmoRouter.transfer() function
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access flaw in the OmoRouter.transfer() function that permits any external caller to invoke the function and move an arbitrary amount of vault shares from the router’s own balance to an address of their choosing. The root cause is the complete absence of an access‑control check – the function simply resolves the vault address from the factory and forwards the call to the vault’s transfer method without verifying that the caller is authorized (e.g., the contract owner or a designated manager). An attacker can exploit this by supplying a valid vault identifier, a destination address that they control, and a desired amount, causing the router to execute IOmoVault(vault).transfer(to, amount) on its behalf. Because the router may hold shares collected as fees, rewards, or leftover balances, the attacker can drain those shares, effectively stealing tokens that belong to the protocol or its users. The impact is a loss of assets from the router’s vault holdings, which can reduce overall protocol liquidity, undermine user confidence, and potentially cause financial loss for token holders. This condition occurs whenever the router possesses a non‑zero balance of vault shares; there is no prerequisite beyond the router holding any amount. All participants who rely on the router to safeguard those shares – including the protocol operators, liquidity providers, and end‑users – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined function visibility and permission patterns, and it can be subtle because the transfer function appears benign and does not modify any state directly within the router, making the missing check easy to overlook. To remediate, the transfer function should be restricted to a privileged role such as the contract owner or a designated manager, or the function should be removed entirely if it is not required for protocol operation. In generic terms, this is an unauthorized token transfer vulnerability, a class of access‑control bugs where external actors can invoke privileged token movement functions without restriction, leading to asset disappearance and violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: OmoRouter.approve() function allows unauthorized token approvals
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the OmoRouter contract exposes an approve(...) external function that forwards the call to the underlying vault's ERC20 approve method without any access control. Because the router does not verify that the caller is the token holder or an authorized operator, any address can invoke approve and set itself (or any other address) as an approved spender for the vault's share token balance that the router may hold. This lack of restriction constitutes an unauthorized token approval bug, a classic missing‑access‑control issue in token‑proxy contracts. An attacker can call OmoRouter.approve(vaultId, attacker, amount) where amount may be the full balance of the router’s share tokens in that vault. Once the approval is recorded, the attacker can subsequently call transferFrom on the share token contract to move the router’s shares to an address they control, effectively draining the router’s holdings. The impact is loss of funds that belong to the protocol or its users, as the router’s share tokens represent a claim on underlying assets. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where the router holds a non‑zero balance of vault share tokens – for example after users deposit into a vault through the router. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the router’s public interface and noticed that approve was exposed without any modifier such as onlyOwner or onlyVaultOwner. Because the function simply forwards the call, the problem may be overlooked if reviewers assume that ERC20 approve is harmless, yet it enables a malicious party to grant themselves spending rights over assets they do not own. From a user’s perspective the symptom could be that approvals appear in their wallet for the router’s share token that they never created, or that after a transaction the router’s balance becomes zero unexpectedly. The bug violates the accounting assumption that only the token holder or an explicitly authorized party can grant spend permissions. The recommended remediation is to remove the approve function from the router entirely or to restrict it with proper access control that only allows the legitimate token holder (the router itself) to approve spenders, thereby eliminating the unauthorized approval vector.

title: OmoRouter.mint function unusable due to missing asset handling
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the router contract’s mint function, which is supposed to act as a thin wrapper around a vault’s mint operation. The intended flow is that a user supplies a certain amount of underlying assets, the router transfers those assets from the user, approves the vault to spend them, and then calls the vault’s mint method so that the vault can pull the assets and issue share tokens to the designated receiver. In the current implementation the router skips two critical steps: it never pulls the assets from the caller and it never grants the vault an allowance to spend the assets that might already be held by the router. Because of this omission the vault’s internal mint logic, which expects to be able to transfer the required assets from the router, fails – typically by reverting due to insufficient balance or allowance. Consequently the router’s mint function becomes effectively unusable; callers receive no shares, assets are never moved, and the transaction may appear to succeed from the router’s perspective while the vault silently rejects the operation. The bug manifests whenever any whitelisted address invokes mint, regardless of the vault ID or share amount, and it affects all users who rely on the router to acquire vault shares, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity and accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the router’s interface to the expected ERC‑4626 workflow and noticed the absence of token transfer and approval logic. It can be hard to spot because the function compiles and returns a value, but the underlying vault call fails only at runtime, producing an error that may be attributed to the vault rather than the router. The impact is functional rather than directly financial: users cannot obtain shares through the router, leading to a broken user experience (e.g., “I tried to mint but got no tokens” or “my balance stays at zero”), and the protocol loses a convenient entry point for deposits, potentially reducing capital inflow. To remediate the issue the router’s mint function should be extended to (1) retrieve the exact amount of underlying assets from the caller using safeTransferFrom, (2) compute the net assets received, (3) approve the vault for that amount, and only then forward the call to the vault’s mint method. This restores the intended asset flow, aligns with ERC‑4626 expectations, and ensures that the router can successfully facilitate share issuance.

title: OmoRouter: pendingRedeemRequest() calls a non-existent function
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OmoRouter contract where the function pendingRedeemRequest forwards a call to IOmoVault(vault).pendingRedeemRequest(requestId,owner). The OmoVault implementation, however, does not define a function with this signature. Because the EVM requires the called contract to contain the exact function selector, the external call resolves to a non‑existent function and the transaction reverts with an undefined function error. This mismatch originates from an interface inconsistency: the router assumes the vault contract implements a view method that returns the amount of shares pending redemption, but the vault code never provides it. Exploitation is straightforward – any user or contract invoking OmoRouter.pendingRedeemRequest with a valid vaultId will trigger a revert, causing the whole transaction to fail. In practice, this manifests as a denial‑of‑service condition for the pending‑redeem query: front‑ends display empty values or error messages, users see that their pending redemption amount cannot be retrieved, and higher‑level workflows that depend on this data may abort. The issue affects all participants who rely on the router to read pending redemption information, including end‑users, integrators, and the protocol itself, because the missing data breaks expected accounting visibility. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the router’s external interface against the vault’s actual implementation. It is subtle because the contract compiles without errors; the failure only appears at runtime when the view function is called, making it easy to overlook during testing if the call path is not exercised. To remediate, the OmoVault contract should be extended with a pendingRedeemRequest(uint256 requestId,address owner) external view returns (uint256) function that correctly returns the pending share amount, or the router should be modified to remove or replace the call with an alternative mechanism. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of interface‑mismatch or missing‑function errors that lead to runtime reverts and loss of functionality, violating the protocol’s business rule that users must be able to query pending redemption amounts before confirming a withdrawal.

title: OmoRouter registerAccount does not validate msg.sender as owner
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OmoRouter.registerAccount function, which forwards a registration request to an OmoVault without verifying that the caller (msg.sender) actually owns the account being registered. The function first checks that the supplied account address exists in the AccountFactory, but it never confirms that the caller is the legitimate owner of that account. Consequently, any whitelisted user can invoke registerAccount with an arbitrary account address that is already registered in the factory, and the router will call OmoVault.registerAccount passing msg.sender as the user and the supplied account as the target. OmoVault.registerAccount only restricts callers to the router or the vault owner, and it trusts the user parameter without additional checks. This mismatch creates an access‑control bypass: an attacker can associate any existing account with their own address, effectively hijacking the account registration. Exploitation is straightforward – the attacker calls OmoRouter.registerAccount with a victim’s account address; the router records the attacker’s address as the owner in the vault’s internal mapping (userToAccount) and marks the account as registered for the attacker. The impact includes unauthorized control over accounts that may hold or manage funds, potential theft of assets, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees because the vault now believes the attacker is the rightful user. The flaw manifests whenever a whitelisted entity calls registerAccount with an account that they do not own; it does not depend on any special state beyond the account being present in the factory. All participants who rely on the vault’s registration logic – users, protocol operators, and auditors – are affected because the security model assumes that only the true owner can bind an account to a user. The issue was uncovered during a manual security review that examined the access‑control flow between the router and the vault and noticed the missing ownership assertion. It can be hard to notice because the function does perform a sanity check for account existence, which may give a false sense of safety, and the emitted AccountRegistered event does not reveal the mismatch between caller and account owner. To remediate, the router should explicitly verify that msg.sender matches the owner of the supplied account (for example by consulting the AccountFactory or by requiring a signature from the account owner) before forwarding the registration to the vault. Alternatively, the vault could enforce that the user argument corresponds to the actual owner of the account, adding a second line of defense. This class of bug is an improper authorization or missing access‑control check, where a function trusts caller‑provided data without confirming the caller’s rights, leading to potential fund misallocation and violation of business logic that expects only owners to register their accounts.

title: OmoVault/OmoRouter: no way to remove whitelist restriction
description: Right now, the onlyWhitelisted modifier only allows approved addresses to call vault functions. The documentation says that the whitelist system will be removed in the future, but there is no functionality to do this in the code.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a whitelist that is enforced by the onlyWhitelisted modifier on all vault functions. The modifier checks that the caller address is present in a mapping of approved addresses. The documentation states that the whitelist will be removed in a future version, but the source code does not contain any function that can disable the check or clear the mapping. As a result the whitelist flag is permanently active. This design flaw means that if the owner adds an address to the whitelist by mistake, or if a legitimate user is not added, the user will receive a revert with the message \"Not whitelisted\" whenever they try to call a vault function. Because there is no administrative function to turn off the whitelist, the contract cannot be upgraded to a more open access model, nor can it be used by new participants after a migration. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the contract's access‑control logic. It may be hard to notice because the modifier itself works correctly and the code compiles without warnings; the missing disable function is only apparent when the documentation is compared with the implementation. Exploitation does not require malicious code; simply being absent from the whitelist is enough to block interaction, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service for affected users and potentially locking funds that can only be moved by whitelisted addresses. The impact is that the protocol owner cannot open the vault to the broader community, and users who are not pre‑approved will see no balance changes, receive zero refunds, or be unable to deposit or withdraw. The issue belongs to the class of immutable access‑control restrictions where a back‑door or toggle is omitted. To remediate, the contract should introduce a boolean flag such as whitelistEnabled that the owner can set to false, or provide a function to remove the onlyWhitelisted modifier after a migration, thereby allowing the contract to operate without the whitelist when desired.

title: OmoAgent removeAgent should not remove agent with positive debt
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's removeAgent function permits deletion of an agent record even when the agent has an outstanding positive debt. The root cause is that the function contains no check against the agentDebts mapping before performing a delete operation. An attacker with manager role can call removeAgent with the identifier of any agent that owes tokens; the delete statement erases the stored debt information, causing the protocol's accounting to believe the debt is zero. This can be exploited to hide liabilities, allow the protocol to release collateral or withdraw funds that should be reserved for repayment, and generally break the invariant that total outstanding debt equals the sum of individual agent debts. The impact may be that lenders receive less repayment, funds appear to disappear, or the system becomes inconsistent, potentially leading to liquidation of other participants or loss of trust. The condition under which it occurs is any manager‑initiated call to removeAgent while the target agent's debt balance is greater than zero. All parties that rely on correct debt tracking – the protocol itself, lenders, and other agents – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state‑modifying functions for missing safety checks. Because the function simply deletes a storage slot without emitting an event or reverting, the problem can remain unnoticed until accounting mismatches surface. The fix is to add a validation step that requires the agent's debt to be zero before deletion, or to enforce a settlement process that clears the debt first, or to replace deletion with a deactivation flag that preserves debt information for auditability. This class of bug belongs to unchecked state‑mutation or missing invariant enforcement, where business logic assumes that an entity cannot be removed while it holds a financial obligation.

title: Unbounded loops can lead to out-of-gas errors in contracts
description:
1. The totalAssets() function in OmoVault.sol contains an unbounded loop that iterates through all registered accounts:
2. OmoRouter.registerAccount loops through all accounts, making it susceptible to a DoS attack via createAccount().
3. OmoVaulFactory.getVaultId loops through all vaults...
4. OmoAgent.topOffToAgent has unbounded loop when tries to remove positionId
5. OmoAgent._removeTokenAddress loops through all token addresses
6. AgentSetter.removeAgent loops through all whitelistedAgents which is unbounded
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of several functions that iterate over dynamic arrays without any upper bound. Functions such as totalAssets in OmoVault, registerAccount in OmoRouter, getVaultId in OmoVaultFactory, topOffToAgent and _removeTokenAddress in OmoAgent, and removeAgent in AgentSetter all contain loops that walk through the entire contents of an array (accounts, vaults, token addresses, whitelisted agents). Because the length of these arrays can grow arbitrarily as users create new accounts or the protocol adds new vaults, the gas required for a single call can increase without limit. When the gas needed exceeds the block gas limit, the transaction reverts with an out‑of‑gas error. This behavior can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who registers a large number of accounts or otherwise inflates the array, causing legitimate calls that rely on the same loops to become unusable. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users are unable to query total assets, register new accounts, top‑off positions, or remove agents, effectively freezing protocol functionality and potentially locking user funds behind a failing transaction. The issue appears during normal operation whenever a function that contains the unbounded loop is invoked; it is not limited to a specific caller or role. All participants—regular users, liquidity providers, and protocol administrators—are affected because the core accounting and management functions become inoperable. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the contract source and identified loops that iterate over storage arrays without a maximum size check. The flaw is subtle because the functions work correctly while the arrays are small, giving a false sense of safety; only when the arrays grow does the gas consumption become problematic, which may not be evident in typical test environments. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration leading to gas exhaustion” bugs, a common source of DoS in Ethereum smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show transactions failing with generic out‑of‑gas errors, balances that appear unchanged after an operation, or a “refund” that never arrives, creating confusion and loss of confidence. The expected behavior is that a call returns the correct value or updates state, but the reality is that the call reverts and no state change occurs. To remediate the issue the contract should replace the unbounded arrays with mappings that allow constant‑time look‑ups, or enforce a hard cap on the number of elements that can be stored, and redesign the logic to avoid iterating over the entire collection in a single transaction. Alternative designs such as pagination, off‑chain aggregation, or batch processing can also mitigate the risk while preserving functionality.

title: OmoVault does not enforce supplyCap
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing enforcement of the vault's supply cap in both the deposit and mint entry points. The contract defines a maximum amount of assets that the vault may hold (supplyCap), but the check that would prevent total assets from exceeding this limit is commented out in the deposit function and completely absent in the mint function. As a result, any whitelisted caller can supply an arbitrary amount of assets or request an arbitrary number of shares, causing the internal accounting variable _totalAssets to grow beyond the intended ceiling. This occurs because the developer deliberately disabled the require statement that compares supplyCap with totalAssets() + assets, likely for testing or convenience, and never reinstated it before deployment. An attacker can exploit the flaw by repeatedly calling deposit or mint with large values, inflating the vault's asset balance and share supply without restriction. The impact is a breach of the economic model: the vault may issue more shares than it should represent, leading to dilution of existing shareholders, inaccurate share‑to‑asset ratios, and potential loss of value for users who later withdraw or rely on the share price. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to deposit or mint after the contract is live, provided the caller is whitelisted; there is no runtime guard preventing the vault from exceeding its cap. All participants who hold shares—depositors, investors, and the protocol itself—are affected because the fundamental accounting invariant is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the reviewer noticed a commented‑out require line and the absence of a similar check in mint. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because deposits and mints still succeed and the contract does not emit an explicit error; only when the total assets surpass the intended cap does the discrepancy become visible, often through unexpected share values or reduced withdrawal amounts. To remediate, the supply‑cap verification should be reinstated in deposit and added to mint, ensuring that totalAssets() + incoming amount never exceeds supplyCap before assets are transferred and shares minted. This restores the invariant that the vault cannot hold more assets than its predefined limit, preserving the intended economic guarantees and preventing share dilution.

title: OmoVault first depositor can inflate share price by donating
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑price manipulation flaw in the vault’s accounting logic. The contract computes the total assets of the vault by adding the internal vault balance (_totalAssets) to the summed position values of all registered dynamic accounts. Because the function does not distinguish between genuine vault holdings and externally supplied positions, a user who is the first to interact with the vault can artificially increase the reported total assets by depositing or donating assets to a registered dynamic account without receiving any vault shares. The root cause is that the totalAssets view aggregates values from external accounts that can be controlled by a depositor before any shares exist, and the share price is derived from totalAssets divided by the total supply of shares. An attacker can exploit this by first registering a dynamic account, sending a large amount of the underlying asset to that account, and thereby inflating the totalAssets figure. When the share price is later calculated, it appears higher than the actual backing, allowing the attacker (or later participants) to receive more assets per share than they should. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting is broken: users may receive more tokens than they are entitled to, leading to unfair profit for the manipulator and potential loss of funds for honest participants. The condition for exploitation is that the vault has no or very few shares minted, and that the attacker can register a dynamic account whose position value is counted in totalAssets. All users of the vault, the protocol’s token holders, and any downstream contracts that rely on the share price are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the OmoVault contract when the auditor noticed that totalAssets includes values from external accounts without any safeguard. It is hard to notice because the function appears to correctly sum holdings, and the inflated assets are reflected in a legitimate‑looking total, masking the manipulation. To fix the problem, the accounting should exclude externally supplied position values from the share‑price calculation, or enforce that shares are minted before any external positions are counted, or lock the registration of dynamic accounts after the first deposit, thereby preventing a depositor from inflating the asset pool without receiving proportional shares. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “share‑price inflation via external asset injection” or “accounting manipulation through unguarded external state aggregation”. From a user’s perspective, the vault may show a healthy total balance while the share price is artificially high, leading to expectations of higher returns that are not backed by real assets, and in extreme cases users may see their balances increase unexpectedly or, conversely, later users may receive less value because the inflated price collapses after the manipulation is discovered.

title: OmoAgent: topOffToAgent() does not process and remove all positions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that is intended to transfer a collection of NFT positions from the contract to a designated agent and then clean up the internal bookkeeping. The function iterates over an array that stores the identifiers of all active positions. For each identifier it checks that the contract has been approved to move the token, performs a transfer, and immediately calls a helper routine that removes the identifier from the same array. Because the loop increments its index in a forward direction while the removal routine shifts the remaining elements left, the next element in the original ordering is moved into the slot that has just been processed. The loop then increments the index, causing the shifted element to be skipped entirely. As a result, only a subset of the positions are transferred; the remaining tokens stay locked in the contract even though the caller receives a success indication. The root cause is the mutation of the collection while it is being traversed with a naïve forward index, a classic off‑by‑one/iteration‑skip bug. Exploitation does not require any special permissions beyond calling the function with a non‑empty position list; the attacker can simply trigger the function and watch that some NFTs never leave the contract, effectively causing a loss of assets for the token owners or the protocol. The impact is that users expect all their positions to be handed over to the agent and reflected in their balances, but they observe missing or unchanged balances, “funds disappear”, or “some NFTs are still owned by the contract”. This condition occurs whenever the function is invoked with more than one position in the internal array. The affected parties include the token holders whose positions are being managed, the agent that should receive the assets, and the overall protocol that relies on accurate accounting of transferred positions. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the control flow of the topOffToAgent routine and identified the array‑modification pattern. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is thrown; the contract simply reports success while silently leaving some items untouched. To remediate the problem the removal of identifiers should be performed after the transfer loop has completed, or the loop should iterate backwards, or a separate temporary list should be used so that the original array is not mutated during iteration. Conceptually, the fix is to separate state‑changing operations (transfers) from bookkeeping updates (array deletions) or to adjust the iteration strategy to account for the dynamic size of the collection. This class of bug is commonly known as “modifying a collection while iterating over it”, which leads to skipped elements and inconsistent state.

title: Incorrect condition would cause DoS on subscription and redemption
description: User's effective USD value applicable for fees is determined via _getEffectiveUSDValueAndUpdateUserFeeConfig function. This function will currently fail under certain circumstances for UserFeeMode.NO_FEE_AFTER_LIMIT mode.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic error in the fee‑calculation routine that determines a user’s effective USD value for fee assessment when the fee mode is set to NO_FEE_AFTER_LIMIT. The routine checks whether the user’s accumulated volume plus the incoming transaction amount would exceed the configured limit. Instead of computing the remaining allowance as limitVolume‑currentVolume, the code mistakenly subtracts limitVolume from currentVolume, i.e., currentVolume‑limitVolume. When the sum of currentVolume and the new usdValue is greater than limitVolume, this incorrect subtraction produces a negative number that underflows to a very large unsigned integer, causing the transaction to revert. The revert stops the fee‑calculation function, which is invoked by subscription and redemption pathways, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for any user whose volume crosses the limit. The issue manifests only when a user’s activity pushes the cumulative volume over the limit; normal operations below the threshold behave as expected, making the bug easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a systematic audit where a forged test deliberately drove the volume past the limit and observed an unexpected revert. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a subscription or redemption that should succeed instead fails with no explicit error message, leaving the user unable to add or withdraw assets and seeing balances unchanged or “stuck”. The business logic assumes that once the limit is reached, fees are capped and the transaction proceeds with the remaining allowance; the underflow violates this accounting assumption, causing funds to appear to disappear because the transaction never completes. The fix is to correct the conditional arithmetic so that the effectiveUSDValue is calculated as limitVolume‑currentVolume when the limit would be exceeded, and to ensure the surrounding logic respects the capped fee model. Conceptually this belongs to the class of “incorrect boundary condition” or “signed‑unsigned arithmetic misuse” bugs that lead to underflow/overflow and can be exploited to block contract functionality.

title: CRV claimed as an extraRewardToken will be stuck in Strategy
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the reward‑harvesting routine of a Curve‑based strategy contract. The routine is responsible for claiming both the primary reward token (CRV) and any extra reward tokens from a liquidity gauge and then forwarding the claimed amounts to a reward distributor. The code attempts to handle the primary token specially by aggregating the total CRV claimed across two possible claim paths. However, the amount of CRV that is added to the internal counter is only calculated when the first claim path – a direct call to claim_rewards that sends rewards straight to the strategy – fails. When the direct call succeeds, the flag indicating a successful reward receipt is true and the subsequent block that computes the difference in CRV balance is skipped, leaving the variable that tracks the claimed CRV amount unchanged (zero). As a result, the CRV that was actually received by the strategy is never added to the total that is later deposited into the reward distributor. The CRV therefore remains locked inside the strategy contract instead of being distributed to users or the protocol’s reward pool.

Exploitation is straightforward: any user who triggers a harvest that includes extra rewards while the gauge supports the direct claim path will observe that the newly claimed CRV does not appear in the reward distributor. The funds are silently retained in the strategy’s balance. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a harvest transaction succeeded, but the expected increase in the reward pool’s CRV balance is missing, and the strategy’s own CRV balance grows unexpectedly. This breaks the accounting assumption that all harvested rewards are forwarded to the distributor, leading to apparent “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” symptoms.

The bug manifests only when the gauge’s claim_rewards function succeeds with the strategy as the receiver – a condition that depends on the specific gauge implementation and its support for the direct claim mode. It does not affect gauges that require the fallback path, because in that case the code correctly computes the balance delta and forwards the CRV.

The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a forked mainnet test that harvested CRV from a known gauge. The test showed that after the first harvest (native CRV) the reward distributor balance increased as expected, but after a second harvest that targeted extra rewards the reward distributor balance did not change while the strategy’s CRV balance rose, confirming the accounting gap.

Because the bug is a missing state update rather than a re‑entrancy or overflow, it can be subtle and may not raise obvious runtime errors. The contract appears to function normally, and the transaction does not revert, making the problem easy to overlook without explicit balance checks.

The conceptual fix is to ensure that the CRV amount is accounted for regardless of which claim path succeeds. After a successful direct claim, the contract should read the strategy’s CRV balance before and after the claim (or query the amount transferred) and add the difference to the total claimed amount before depositing to the reward distributor. This guarantees that all harvested CRV, whether obtained via the primary or extra reward path, is correctly forwarded, restoring the intended reward flow and preventing funds from being stranded in the strategy contract.

title: Balancing mechanism will often be imprecise
description:
This is a catch all issue to discuss the areas in which the formulas used for balancing, as well as the implementation realities to lower gas fees, cause the optimizer to misallocate funds between Convex and StakeDAO.

It is clear that the purpose of the protocol is that, on the whole, users will at least be better off than if they simply allocated directly to Convex, and this is largely achieved. However, there are (a) a large number of situations in which funds are overallocated to Convex that would provide a better return on StakeDAO and (b) a small number of situations in which funds would be more profitable on Convex directly.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an imprecise balancing mechanism that allocates deposited assets between two yield platforms, Convex and StakeDAO, using formulas that are deliberately simplified for gas efficiency. The root cause is the combination of rounding errors, integer division, and coarse‑grained thresholds that cause the optimizer to miscalculate the optimal split, leading to systematic over‑allocation to Convex in many market conditions and occasional under‑allocation when StakeDAO would yield more. An attacker or any external participant can trigger the protocol’s rebalance function at moments when the internal state has drifted, causing large and sometimes unpredictable swings in the allocation ratio. This drift does not directly leak funds, but it reduces the effective return for users because the protocol no longer guarantees that a depositor will earn at least the same yield as a direct Convex investment, which is the advertised baseline. The issue manifests when the rebalance function is not called frequently enough, when gas‑saving shortcuts skip precise arithmetic, or when market rates change between calls, allowing the internal accounting to become stale. Users experience symptoms such as lower than expected APY, balances that appear to stagnate despite positive market movements, or occasional periods where the protocol’s yield falls below what could be earned by a simple Convex deposit. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the protocol’s theoretical allocation model with observed on‑chain behavior and identified a pattern of allocation drift. Because the discrepancy is economic rather than a direct loss of funds, it can be subtle and may only be noticed through statistical analysis of returns over time. To remediate, the protocol should replace the gas‑optimized formulas with higher‑precision arithmetic, enforce tighter bounds on allocation ratios, and ensure that the rebalance() routine reliably restores the intended split after any drift. In conceptual terms, the fix is to treat the balancing logic as a deterministic accounting function rather than a heuristic, thereby aligning actual yields with the protocol’s promised performance guarantees.

title: Optimizer will misallocate when StakeDAO is above full boost
description:
On Page 5 of the whitepaper, it says:

We can assume that when this balance is reached for a given gauge, neither Convex nor Stake DAO have maximum boost, which enables us to get rid of the min formula.

The `min` in the formula is intended to cap the boost at 2.5x. If the proportion of veCRV held by a user is greater than their proportion of pool tokens, they will be capped at 2.5x, rather than further increasing the boost.

One example of when this could happen is if both pools have full 2.5x boosts. This example was pointed out in the last audit, and a fix was added to manually send funds to Convex if both pools had maximum boosts.

However, upon further reflection, this fix is not sufficient.

We can simplify the issue with the understanding that, when the `min` is removed from the formula, it allows the formula's perceived boost for a protocol to exceed 2.5x. For example, if StakeDAO holds `10%` of veCRV and only holds `1%` of a given pool, assuming the pool has 100 tokens for simplicity, the boost will be calculated as:
```python
boost = ((0.4 * 1) + (0.6 * 100 * 10%)) / 0.4 = 16x
```
If the min was included, it would have been capped at 2.5x, but instead is allowed to reach 16x. As a result, when the Optimizer calculates the ideal allocation, it will favor this pool more aggressively than it should.

The issue pointed out in the previous audit examines when such an example is matched with a Convex pool at full boost. In this case, the 2.5x from Convex is identical to the 2.5x from StakeDAO, and the Optimizer misattributing StakeDAO a 16x boost would cause funds to flow there, even though the ideal would be allocate to Convex due to the incentives.

But, as we can see from this example, the same issue holds when Convex reaches 2.49x boost, and lower. In fact, calculating precisely, we find the breakeven point. The returns from each protocol are as follows:
```python
convex_return = convex_boost * (1 - 0.17 + 0.05)
sd_return = sd_boost * (1 - 0.16)
```
To calculate the breakeven point for `convex_boost` for when `sd_boost == 2.5x`, we can solve and plug in:
```python
convex_boost * 0.88 == 2.5 * 0.84
convex_boost = 2.386
```
Therefore, in any situation in which Convex has a boost greater than 2.386, it is preferable over StakeDAO with full boost. In these cases, Convex should receive the full deposit.

The same issue exists when Convex is below 2.386x boost, because the optimal balance for StakeDAO will be set too high, so more funds will flow to StakeDAO than should.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect allocation logic inside the Optimizer component that computes the ideal deposit distribution between Convex and StakeDAO pools. The root cause is that the Optimizer’s computeOptimalDepositAmount function removes the minimum‑capping (min) operation from the boost formula, allowing the perceived boost for StakeDAO to exceed the protocol‑defined maximum of 2.5× when the proportion of veCRV held by StakeDAO is larger than its share of pool tokens. Because the formula no longer enforces the cap, a scenario such as StakeDAO holding 10 % of veCRV but only 1 % of the pool tokens yields a calculated boost of roughly 16× instead of the intended 2.5×. The Optimizer then treats this inflated boost as a signal of higher profitability and directs a disproportionate amount of user deposits to the StakeDAO pool, even when Convex offers a comparable or higher real boost (for example any Convex boost above 2.386×). This misallocation can be exploited by any actor that can influence the veCRV distribution or simply by the protocol’s own state, causing funds to flow into a pool that provides lower net returns. The impact is sub‑optimal yield for users, reduced overall protocol efficiency, and potential loss of expected earnings because deposits are sent to a pool with an artificially high boost. The condition under which this occurs is when StakeDAO’s veCRV proportion exceeds its token proportion and the optimizer’s formula omits the min‑cap, which can happen at any time the protocol reaches full or near‑full boost on either side. All users who rely on the Optimizer for optimal deposit routing are affected, as they may see lower returns, unexpected allocation to StakeDAO, or balances that appear unchanged despite a deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the theoretical boost calculations with the optimizer’s allocation decisions and noticed that the optimizer continued to favor StakeDAO even when Convex’s boost should have been preferred. It is hard to notice because the boost numbers themselves look plausible and the UI does not expose the internal calculation, so users only observe the symptom of reduced earnings. The correct fix is to reinstate the minimum‑capping logic inside the optimal deposit computation, ensuring that any calculated boost is bounded by the protocol‑defined maximum before being used to decide allocation. By capping the boost at 2.5×, the optimizer will produce a realistic optimal deposit amount and will no longer over‑allocate to StakeDAO, preserving expected yield and aligning with the business logic that higher real boost pools should receive more capital.

title: Curve gauges with 7+ extra reward tokens cannot be integrated
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the hard‑coded maximum number of reward tokens that a StakeDAO reward distributor can handle and the way the contract copies reward tokens from an existing Curve gauge. The distributor is designed to accept at most eight reward tokens (MAX_REWARDS = 8), a limit inherited from Curve’s own gauge implementation. When a new pool is created, the factory first registers the native CRV token and the SDT token as rewards, and then iterates over the extra reward tokens reported by the target gauge, adding each one until it reaches the hard limit. Because the factory adds two base tokens before the loop, the effective capacity for extra tokens is reduced to six. If the source gauge already contains seven or eight extra reward tokens, the combined total exceeds the eight‑token ceiling, causing the add‑extra‑rewards routine to hit the limit and the transaction to revert. This situation occurs during the pool creation phase, specifically when the factory calls the reward distributor to register all tokens. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to create a pool with a gauge that has many extra rewards see the transaction fail, receive no pool address, and lose the gas spent on the failed call. No funds are stolen, but the protocol cannot support those gauges, breaking the intended business logic that all rewards should be distributed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester deliberately supplied a gauge contract that reported eight extra reward tokens; the creation reverted at the point where the seventh extra token was added. The bug is subtle because the same MAX_REWARDS constant is used in both the original Curve gauge and the forked StakeDAO distributor, leading developers to assume compatibility without accounting for the two additional base tokens. To remediate the problem, the reward distributor’s MAX_REWARDS constant should be increased (for example to ten) or the token‑addition logic should be adjusted to ensure the total number of registered tokens never exceeds the hard limit, thereby aligning the contract’s capacity with the expected reward set.

title: Deployment script mismatches gauges and reward distributors
description:
In Deployment.s.sol, a list of gauges (Curve) and reward distributors (StakeDAO) are provided to migrate.

The gauge list is 162 elements long, but the reward distributor list is only 160 elements long, missing the corresponding reward distributors to the final two gauges.

The match between these two lists is crucial, as funds will be migrated and permissions granted accordingly.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a deployment script that assumes a one‑to‑one correspondence between two parallel arrays: a list of Curve gauges and a list of StakeDAO reward distributors. The script contains 162 gauge addresses but only 160 reward distributor addresses, leaving the last two gauges without a matching distributor. This length mismatch is not validated, so the script proceeds to iterate over the shorter list while still referencing the longer gauge array. As a result, when the migration logic attempts to assign permissions or migrate funds for each gauge, the final two gauges are processed with an undefined or default distributor address. The root cause is an unchecked assumption that the two arrays are equal in length and ordered identically, a classic case of array‑length mismatch and unchecked index correlation. An attacker or a careless operator could exploit this by triggering the migration and causing funds intended for the missing distributors to be sent to an unintended address, remain locked, or be left without proper permission grants. The impact includes potential loss or misallocation of user rewards, incomplete migration of gauge balances, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that each gauge must have a corresponding reward distributor. The issue manifests during the deployment or upgrade phase when the script is executed; it does not appear during normal operation, making it hard to notice because no explicit error is thrown – the script simply skips the last two entries silently. Users may observe that after migration their gauge balances are unchanged or that expected reward streams are missing, leading to confusion when they see zero rewards despite having deposited assets. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the deployment script, where the auditor compared the lengths of the two hard‑coded arrays and noted the discrepancy. Because the script does not emit warnings for mismatched lengths, the problem can remain hidden until a migration is performed. To remediate, the script should enforce a strict equality check between the two arrays before entering the loop and optionally verify that each gauge’s existing distributor matches the intended address. Adding explicit require statements that compare array lengths and per‑index relationships prevents accidental omission of distributors and restores the invariant that every gauge has an associated reward distributor, thereby preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Incorrect Absolute Value Calculation in _abs Function Leads To DoS on Tokens with More Than 18 Decimals
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect implementation of an absolute‑value helper that returns the unsigned magnitude of a signed integer. The function evaluates the ternary expression x >= 0 ? x : -x but never stores the result, so the original signed variable x is cast directly to uint256. When x is negative this cast produces a very large unsigned number (for example uint256(-1) becomes the maximum uint256 value). The bug propagates to the _parseResult logic used by both ChainlinkRelayer and CamelotRelayer contracts. When the MULTIPLIER variable is negative – which occurs when a token reports more than eighteen decimal places – the code calls _abs(MULTIPLIER) to compute the divisor exponent. Because _abs returns an enormous value, the expression 10 ** huge overflows to zero, and the subsequent division by zero triggers a revert. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition: price feeds stop returning values, transactions that rely on the relayer fail, and the protocol appears frozen from the user’s perspective. The issue is most likely to surface for tokens with non‑standard decimal counts, a scenario that is rare in the ChainlinkRelayer (which typically handles 8‑ or 18‑decimal assets) but common in CamelotRelayer where the quote token’s decimals are taken dynamically. The bug was discovered during a manual code audit that examined arithmetic handling of signed multipliers. It can be hard to notice because normal test tokens do not trigger the negative‑multiplier path, so the faulty branch remains unexecuted in typical test suites. The fix is to correctly compute the absolute value by assigning the ternary result back to the variable before casting, ensuring that negative multipliers are turned into their positive magnitude and that the exponentiation does not overflow. Conceptually the problem belongs to the class of signed‑to‑unsigned conversion errors that lead to integer overflow and division‑by‑zero failures, breaking business logic that assumes a well‑behaved scaling factor for token decimals. From a user’s view the symptom is a transaction that reverts with no price data, often described as “price is zero” or “refund missing”, whereas the expectation was that the relayer would return a valid scaled price.

title: Misleading Validity Checks in read Function of ChainlinkRelayer
description:
The read function of the ChainlinkRelayer contract is intended to fetch and return the latest price from a Chainlink feed, reverting if the price is considered invalid. However, the current implementation allows for potentially incorrect behavior due to the misuse of logical operators in the validity check. The function checks that the price _aggregatorResult is either non-zero or the data is fresh, using an OR (||) condition. This allows the function to return a zero price if the data is not stale, and conversely, to return a stale price as long as it is non-zero. Both scenarios are likely unintended and can lead to misleading results being accepted as valid.
The sister function getResultWithValidity uses an AND (&&) condition for similar checks, suggesting that the intention was to require both conditions (non-zero and freshness) to be true for the data to be considered valid.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the read function of the ChainlinkRelayer contract, which is supposed to return the most recent price from a Chainlink oracle only when the price is both non‑zero and based on fresh data. The implementation mistakenly uses a logical OR (||) to combine the two validity conditions – checking that the price is non‑zero OR that the timestamp is recent. Because of this, the function will accept a zero price as long as the timestamp is recent, and it will also accept a non‑zero price even if the timestamp is stale. The root cause is a simple operator misuse that contradicts the intended business rule that a price must satisfy both constraints simultaneously. An attacker or a faulty data source can exploit this by supplying a stale but non‑zero price, or by causing the oracle to emit a zero price while the timestamp remains current. Downstream contracts that rely on read() for pricing will then treat these invalid values as legitimate, leading to incorrect calculations such as minting or burning the wrong amount of tokens, mispricing collateral, or allowing users to receive no value for a transaction. The impact is therefore a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: funds may disappear, users may receive zero or unexpectedly large amounts, and the overall price oracle integrity is compromised. This condition occurs whenever the Chainlink feed returns a zero value or when the feed data becomes outdated, which are both realistic scenarios in live deployments. All participants that depend on the price – token holders, lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract silently accepts malformed data. The issue was discovered during a manual security review when the auditor compared the read function’s logic with the sister function getResultWithValidity, which correctly uses an AND (&&) operator. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert on these edge cases; it simply returns a value that appears valid, making it hard to notice without a detailed code inspection. To remediate, the logical operator should be changed from OR to AND, ensuring that both non‑zero and freshness checks must pass before the price is considered valid. This aligns the function with the intended validation semantics and restores confidence that only correct, up‑to‑date price data is propagated through the system.

title: MJR-1 Invalid owner of token
description: At the line ERC721OBackwardCompatible.sol#L41 ownerOf function returns self contract address probably instead of real token owner, so according that function current contract owns all which exists in that contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect implementation of the ERC721 owner query function. The contract’s ownerOf routine returns the contract’s own address (address(this)) for every token identifier instead of the actual holder stored in the token‑owner mapping. This mistake originates from a logical error in the backward‑compatible ERC721 wrapper where the developer substituted the real owner lookup with a hard‑coded reference to the contract itself. Because ownerOf is the canonical source of truth for token ownership, any external call that relies on it – such as transferFrom, approve, or marketplace listings – will receive a false answer that the contract owns the token. An attacker or any caller can therefore be led to believe that the contract is the legitimate owner, which may allow unauthorized transfers, approvals, or other privileged actions that check ownership against the value returned by ownerOf. The impact is that legitimate token holders lose verifiable ownership; user interfaces may display a zero balance or show that the token is owned by the protocol, causing confusion and potentially preventing owners from transferring or selling their assets. The bug manifests whenever ownerOf is invoked, which is essentially every time a token’s ownership is queried, making it a pervasive condition. All participants who hold or interact with these NFTs – including end users, dApp developers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the fundamental accounting invariant of ERC721 (that each token has a unique external owner) is broken. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditor inspected the source code and identified the hard‑coded return value. It can be hard to notice in testing if the test suite does not explicitly verify ownerOf for a range of token IDs or if UI components do not surface the owner address. To remediate, the ownerOf function must be rewritten to read the owner from the internal mapping that tracks token ownership and return that address, thereby restoring the correct ownership semantics and preventing false ownership reports. In broader terms, this is a classic case of an ownership‑lookup bug that violates the ERC721 specification and undermines the protocol’s accounting guarantees, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as missing balances, zero‑value refunds, or inability to transfer tokens.

title: EIP-1559 parameters are not set in SystemConfig.initialize()
description:
According to the Holocene specs, ConfigUpdate.UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER and ConfigUpdate.EIP_1559_PARAMS should be emitted during initialization:
The following actions should happen during the initialization of the SystemConfig:
• emit ConfigUpdate.BATCHER
• emit ConfigUpdate.FEE_SCALARS
• emit ConfigUpdate.GAS_LIMIT
• emit ConfigUpdate.UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER
• emit ConfigUpdate.EIP_1559_PARAMS
However, SystemConfig.initialize() does not call _setEIP1559Params() to set eip1559Denominator and eip1559Elasticity. As a result, upgraded or newly deployed chains will not have these parameters initialized, causing the EIP-1559 constants declared in the chain's config to be used when calculating gas costs on L2, even after the chain has been upgraded to Holocene.
Additionally, initialize() sets UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER_SLOT directly instead of calling _setUnsafeBlockSigner():
Storage.setAddress(UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER_SLOT, _unsafeBlockSigner);
As such, the ConfigUpdate event will not be emitted for UpdateType.UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER on initialization.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SystemConfig contract’s initialization routine, which fails to correctly configure the EIP‑1559 fee parameters and to emit the expected ConfigUpdate events for the unsafe block signer. According to the Holocene specification, the initialize() function should invoke internal setters that both store the new values and broadcast ConfigUpdate events for a batch of configuration items, including EIP‑1559 denominator and elasticity. Instead, the code omits the call to _setEIP1559Params(), leaving the eip1559Denominator and eip1559Elasticity slots at their default values. Consequently, after a chain upgrade to Holocene or when deploying a fresh chain, the gas‑cost algorithm falls back to the hard‑coded constants defined in the older configuration rather than the intended dynamic EIP‑1559 parameters. This mismatch can cause gas fees to be mis‑calculated: users may be charged higher or lower than expected, transactions might be rejected because the fee does not satisfy the protocol’s accounting rules, and the overall economic model of the L2 can be distorted. In addition, the initialize() function writes the unsafe block signer address directly to storage instead of using the _setUnsafeBlockSigner() helper, which means the ConfigUpdate event for UpdateType.UNSAFE_BLOCK_SIGNER is never emitted. The absence of this event hides the fact that a privileged signer has been set, undermining transparency and making it harder for external observers to verify the signer’s identity. The issue is discovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, where the code was compared against the specification and the missing function calls and event emissions were identified. Because the contract still compiles and appears to work, the problem is subtle and may go unnoticed until users observe unexpected fee behavior or auditors notice the missing events in transaction logs. The bug belongs to the class of initialization‑time configuration omissions and silent state changes that break accounting assumptions. To remediate, the initialize() routine should be updated to call the internal setters _setEIP1559Params() and _setUnsafeBlockSigner(), ensuring that the EIP‑1559 parameters are stored correctly and that the corresponding ConfigUpdate events are emitted, thereby restoring proper fee calculation and observable state changes. Users would then see fees that match the protocol’s advertised rates, and the system would emit clear events indicating the signer configuration, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic.

title: Blacklisted anchorGame in AnchorStateRegistry prevents submitting L2 root claims to L1
description:
AnchorStateRegistry.getAnchorRoot() checks if the current anchorGame is blacklisted, and reverts if so:
if (isGameBlacklisted(anchorGame)) {
revert AnchorStateRegistry_AnchorGameBlacklisted();
}
While this is meant to prevent invalid anchor roots from being used, getAnchorRoot() reverting will break several important functions in the protocol.
anchorGame could be blacklisted if the following sequence occurs:
1. Dispute game incorrectly resolves to DEFENDER_WINS.
2. DISPUTE_GAME_FINALITY_DELAY_SECONDS passes.
3. Guardian calls blacklistDisputeGame() to blacklist the dispute game.
4. Attacker front-runs guardian, calling setAnchorState() to set the dispute game as anchorGame.
When this occurs, due to getAnchorRoot() always reverting when called:
1. New dispute games cannot be created as FaultDisputeGame.initialize() reverts.
2. anchorGame cannot be updated as AnchorStateRegistry.setAnchorState() reverts.
3. The chain cannot be upgraded as OPContractsManager.upgrade() reverts.
(1) is particularly severe as there is no way for Optimism's proposer (or anyone else) to submit root claims to L1 until the situation is manually handled. This violates the L2Beat's Stage 1 requirements.
Additionally, since setAnchorState() cannot be called as outlined in (2), anchorGame is permanently set to the blacklisted dispute game. As such, there is no way for such a situation to be resolved without an upgrade to AnchorStateRegistry.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a logic check in the AnchorStateRegistry contract that refuses to return an anchor root when the currently selected dispute game (anchorGame) is listed in a blacklist. The function getAnchorRoot() unconditionally reverts if isGameBlacklisted(anchorGame) is true. This design is intended to block invalid roots, but it creates a denial‑of‑service condition when an attacker can manipulate the anchorGame after a dispute game has been blacklisted. The root cause is the combination of (1) a delayed guardian action that blacklists a dispute game only after a fixed finality period, (2) the ability for any actor to call setAnchorState() and set the blacklisted game as the new anchor before the guardian’s blacklist transaction is mined, and (3) the getAnchorRoot() function that always reverts for a blacklisted anchorGame. An attacker can front‑run the guardian’s blacklistDisputeGame() call, invoke setAnchorState() to make the just‑blacklisted dispute game the anchor, and thereby cause every subsequent call to getAnchorRoot() to revert. Because many core protocol functions – such as FaultDisputeGame.initialize(), AnchorStateRegistry.setAnchorState(), and OPContractsManager.upgrade() – depend on a successful getAnchorRoot() call, the system becomes permanently unable to create new dispute games, update the anchor, or upgrade contracts. The most severe symptom is that Optimism’s proposer (or any actor) cannot submit L2 state root claims to L1, effectively halting the rollup’s state progression and violating the L2Beat Stage 1 requirement for continuous root submission. From a user’s perspective the UI would show failed transactions when trying to submit a root or upgrade contracts, with messages like “anchor root retrieval failed” or “operation reverted”, leading to confusion as balances appear unchanged and no new blocks are posted. The affected parties include the rollup’s proposers, validators, and ultimately end‑users whose funds remain locked on L2 because the chain cannot progress. The issue was discovered during a security audit that traced the call flow and identified that the blacklist check could be triggered after the anchorGame is set, a scenario that is not covered by existing tests. It is hard to notice because the revert only occurs under a specific timing window involving a blacklisted game, which is rare in normal operation. This class of bug can be described as a denial‑of‑service caused by improper state validation and blacklisting logic that allows a malicious actor to lock critical protocol functionality. To remediate, the blacklist verification should be removed from getAnchorRoot() and performed by callers that need to ensure the anchor is valid, such as OPContractsManager.upgrade(). Additionally, the protocol should enforce that a blacklisted dispute game cannot be set as the anchor, either by adding a guard in setAnchorState() or by requiring the guardian to blacklist before the finality delay expires, thereby eliminating the front‑running window that leads to the lockout.

title: New proposals can be DOS'd by frontrunning
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition in the governance workflow that uses the ApprovalVotingModule. When the governor’s manager calls proposeWithModule, the function computes a proposal identifier (proposalId) by hashing the governor address, the voting module address, the proposal data and the description hash. After storing the proposal metadata, the governor forwards the same proposalId to the module by calling module.propose(proposalId, proposalData). The module’s propose function only checks that the supplied proposalId has not been used before; it does not verify that the identifier matches the hash that the governor calculated, nor does it restrict who may call propose. Consequently, an attacker monitoring the mempool can compute the exact proposalId that the legitimate transaction will use, submit a transaction to the module with the same identifier before the governor’s call reaches the blockchain, and thereby register themselves as the governor for that proposal. When the original proposeWithModule call later reaches the module, the ExistingProposal check fails and the transaction reverts. This race condition can be repeated indefinitely, preventing any new proposals from being created. The impact is that the governance process stalls: users see errors such as “proposal already exists” or experience silent failures where no new proposals appear, breaking the expectation that a manager can always create a proposal after meeting the voting power threshold. The issue affects all participants of the protocol who rely on the ability to submit governance actions, including token holders, developers, and any downstream contracts that depend on timely proposals. It was discovered during a manual audit of the governor‑module interaction, where the lack of validation on the module side was noted as a logical flaw. The problem is subtle because the proposalId appears to be unique and the module’s interface seems to accept a valid identifier, so the failure only manifests when an adversary actively front‑runs the transaction. The bug belongs to the class of authentication‑bypass and race‑condition vulnerabilities where identifiers are not securely bound to the caller. From a user perspective, the UI may show a proposal creation button that appears to work, but the transaction reverts or the new proposal never shows up, leading to confusion and a perception that the system is broken. The correct mitigation is to enforce the uniqueness and correctness of the proposalId inside the ApprovalVotingModule itself. The module should recompute the identifier from the caller (msg.sender), the module address, the proposal data and the description hash, and reject any proposalId that does not match this recomputed value. Additionally, the module should restrict propose calls to the authorized governor contract, preventing arbitrary addresses from registering proposals. By binding the identifier to the caller and verifying it on‑chain, the front‑running attack vector is eliminated and the governance workflow regains its intended reliability.

title: Any address can be passed as a VotingModule, which could lead to abuse
description:
In `OptimismGovernorV5.sol`, the `proposeWithModule()` function has the following signature:
```solidity
function proposeWithModule(VotingModule module, bytes memory proposalData, string memory description);
```
This allows the caller to input a `VotingModule` address, and that module will be used to:
set up the proposal (`module.propose()`)
return the execution data (`module._formatExecuteParams()`)
determine if a user has already voted (`module.hasVoted()`)
determine if quorum has been reached (`module._quorumReached()`)
determine whether a vote succeeded (`module._voteSucceeded()`)

It is assumed that the proposer will enter a valid module that does these things fairly, but there is no check to be sure.

This could be abused in a number of ways, but the most malicious and difficult to catch would be to create a module that operates normally but returns malicious data (unrelated to the proposal) from `module._formatExecuteParams()`. Then one could pass an innocent looking proposal, and when it was executed, a completely different transaction would be run. This could be used to perform unwanted actions or steal funds.

While this risk is diminished at the moment because proposals can only be created by the `manager`, it does add some risk at present and will become Critical when governance is opened up to proposals from the community.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s proposeWithModule function, which accepts an arbitrary address that implements the VotingModule interface. Because the contract does not verify that the supplied module is a trusted or pre‑approved implementation, an attacker can supply a malicious contract that conforms to the interface but returns crafted execution data from its internal _formatExecuteParams function. When the proposal is later executed, the governor calls the module to obtain the calldata that will be sent to the target contract. If the module returns malicious calldata, the execution will perform actions that are unrelated to the proposal description, such as transferring funds to an attacker‑controlled address or calling privileged functions. The flaw occurs whenever a proposal is created via proposeWithModule, which currently is limited to the manager role but will become open to the broader community in future upgrades. The affected parties include any token holders or users who rely on the governance process, as well as the protocol’s treasury, because the unexpected execution can move or lock funds without consent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the parameter validation of the proposeWithModule entry point. It is difficult to notice because the module appears to behave correctly for most queries (e.g., propose, hasVoted, quorum checks) and the UI displays the proposal’s human‑readable description, giving a false sense of safety while the hidden malicious calldata is only revealed at execution time. This class of bug can be described as an “untrusted contract injection” or “module address spoofing” where external code is trusted without verification. An attacker would deploy a malicious VotingModule, call proposeWithModule with a benign‑looking proposal, and later watch the proposal pass and execute, at which point the malicious module supplies calldata that drains funds. From a user’s perspective the proposal seems to promise a harmless change, but after execution the user may see their balance reduced to zero or unexpected token transfers, violating the expectation that a proposal’s description matches its effect. The recommended mitigation is to maintain an allowlist of approved VotingModule contracts and enforce that only modules on this list can be used when creating proposals. Because the module address is hashed into the proposal identifier, a single validation at proposal creation is sufficient, eliminating the need for repeated checks during execution. Implementing this restriction restores the integrity of the governance flow by ensuring that only vetted logic determines execution parameters, thereby preventing arbitrary code injection and protecting protocol assets.

title: Votes can be arbitrarily extended by Manager until they meet quorum
