bug_full: In the OptimismGovernorV5 contract a proposal is created with a fixed snapshot (the block number when voting starts) and a deadline that marks the end of the voting period. All core parameters such as the voting module, quorum, voting delay and voting period are stored immutably at proposal creation, which normally guarantees that the voting window cannot be altered after it begins. However, the contract exposes a public function setProposalDeadline that can be called by any address holding the Manager role and that directly overwrites the stored deadline value. Because the function contains no check that the voting window has already started or finished, the manager can invoke it at any time, even after the vote has been marked Defeated or Executed. By repeatedly calling setProposalDeadline with a later timestamp the manager can extend the voting period indefinitely, reopen a vote that was previously considered final, or move a defeated proposal back to the Active state. This behaviour is especially dangerous when the governance uses an ApprovalVotingModule that only records positive approvals and has no explicit Against option; participants who oppose a proposal can only express dissent by abstaining, so extending the deadline gives the manager more time to attract additional approvals and eventually reach quorum or option thresholds that would not have been met within the original window. The impact is a breach of the fundamental governance assumption that once a vote reaches a terminal state (Defeated, Executed, or Expired) its outcome is immutable. Users may see a proposal they thought was finished suddenly become active again, leading to unexpected token lock‑ups, altered token‑holder expectations, and potential capture of the protocol by a single privileged actor. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the immutability guarantees of the proposal parameters with the actual code and identified that the deadline field is the only mutable element after proposal creation. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the current deadline and may not highlight that it was changed after the vote started, and the emitted ProposalDeadlineUpdated event does not convey the timing context. The recommended mitigation is to restrict deadline changes to the period before voting begins, for example by requiring block.timestamp to be less than the stored voteStart deadline, or by removing the manager’s ability to modify the deadline altogether. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of governance‑parameter mutability flaws where a privileged role can alter a time‑bound condition after the fact, breaking the expected finality of on‑chain voting and allowing manipulation of quorum and outcome calculations.

title: Permitting Multiple Drip Calls Per Block
description: The inline comments correctly note that reentrancy is possible and permitted when state.config.interval is 0. We are currently unaware of use cases where this is desirable. Reentrancy is one risk, flashbot bundles are a similar risk where the drip may be called multiple times by the same actor in a single block. A malicious actor may abuse this ability, especially if interval is misconfigured as 0 due to JavaScript type coercion. A reentrant call or flashbot bundle may be used to frontrun an owner attempting to archive a drip or attempting to withdraw assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s allowance of unlimited drip executions within a single block when the configured interval is set to zero. Because the code does not enforce a minimum interval or an explicit opt‑in flag for zero‑interval drips, an attacker can trigger the drip function repeatedly in the same block, either through a reentrant call or by submitting multiple transactions in a flash‑bot bundle. This behaviour breaks the intended accounting model where each drip is expected to occur only after a defined time gap, and it opens a race condition where the order of transactions directly influences the outcome. An adversary can exploit the situation by front‑running an owner who is trying to archive a drip or withdraw assets, causing the drip to be executed multiple times before the owner’s transaction is processed. The practical impact is that the protocol’s funds may be drained faster than anticipated, the owner may be unable to archive a drip because the state changes repeatedly, and users may see unexpected zero balances or missing refunds after a drip operation. The issue manifests whenever the drip configuration interval is unintentionally set to zero, which can happen due to JavaScript type coercion or developer oversight, and it is especially dangerous in environments that support transaction bundling. The problem was identified during a security audit that highlighted the inline comment about reentrancy and recognized that permitting multiple calls per block provides no clear use case. Detecting the flaw can be difficult because a zero interval does not raise an immediate error and the contract’s external behavior appears normal until an attacker deliberately abuses the timing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a rule that only one drip call can be processed per block, require a positive interval value unless an explicit “allowMultiplePerBlock” flag is set, and clearly document the transaction‑order dependence so owners understand the front‑running risk. By constraining the call frequency and making zero‑interval operation opt‑in, the protocol restores its intended accounting guarantees and prevents malicious actors from exploiting rapid, repeated drips.

title: Balance check in Vault::withdraw() does not take fees into account
description: Vault::withdraw() transfers funds to an user if address(this).balance >= amount, which may transfer funds resulting from fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw routine of a vault contract where the function checks that the contract's total ether balance is greater than or equal to the requested withdrawal amount using the condition address(this).balance >= amount. This check does not subtract any accumulated protocol fees that are stored in a separate accounting variable (totalFees). Because the fee balance is part of the contract's overall ether balance, a caller can request a withdrawal that consumes the entire contract balance, including the portion that should be reserved for fees. The root cause is an incomplete accounting model: the contract treats the raw ether balance as freely withdrawable without accounting for internal liabilities such as fees owed to the protocol. An attacker or any user can exploit this by invoking withdraw with an amount equal to the contract's current ether balance, thereby draining the fee pool together with user funds. The impact is that the protocol loses revenue, fee‑related incentives may be broken, and users may receive less than expected because the fee pool is depleted. This condition occurs whenever totalFees is greater than zero and a withdrawal request is made that does not consider those fees. The affected parties include the protocol operators who rely on fee collection, users expecting correct accounting of their deposits and withdrawals, and any downstream contracts that assume fees remain available. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s accounting logic with its balance checks and noticed that the fee variable was never factored into the withdrawal guard. It can be hard to notice because the balance check appears standard and the contract does not emit explicit events about fee depletion, so the bug may remain hidden until a large withdrawal is performed. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the protocol’s fee balance becomes unexpectedly zero, leading to missing refunds or reduced payouts. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect balance accounting” or “missing liability consideration” bugs, where internal accounting variables are not reflected in external state checks. To remediate the issue the withdrawal guard should be rewritten to ensure that only the net available balance (address(this).balance minus totalFees) is considered withdrawable, for example by replacing the condition with address(this).balance - totalFees >= amount. This change guarantees that fees remain locked in the contract and cannot be unintentionally transferred out during a withdrawal.

title: address.transfer is used in the codebase, which could lead to stuck funds
description: Using address.transfer is not recommended as future gas cost changes can make it no longer work or users might use smart contract wallets. The reason is that it only forwards 2300 gas, which can lead to the 2 problems mentioned before.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of the Solidity built‑in address.transfer function to move Ether out of the contract. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback or receive function. This hard‑coded gas limit was safe when the EVM required very little gas for simple operations, but subsequent protocol upgrades (for example EIP‑1884) increased the cost of certain opcodes, and many modern smart‑contract wallets implement fallback logic that consumes more than 2300 gas. Consequently, when the contract attempts to send Ether to such an address, the call runs out of gas, the transfer reverts, and the execution path that should release the funds is aborted. The result is that the Ether intended for the user or for a downstream protocol remains locked inside the contract, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. Users expect a successful withdrawal or refund, but instead see no change in their balance, receive no transaction receipt of a transfer, or encounter a failed transaction that leaves the contract’s internal accounting out of sync. The issue manifests whenever the codebase uses address.transfer to pay arbitrary addresses – especially external contracts or newly created wallet contracts – without checking the recipient’s gas requirements. It also becomes more likely after network upgrades that raise the gas cost of storage reads or other operations used in fallback functions. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that flagged the use of transfer as a known anti‑pattern. It can be hard to notice because the failure occurs only for certain recipients; normal EOAs with empty fallback functions still succeed, giving a false sense of safety. The bug belongs to the class of “gas‑stipend transfer failures” that lead to stuck funds and broken accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should replace address.transfer with a low‑level call, e.g. address.call{value:amount}(''), optionally specifying a higher gas limit, and must verify the returned boolean to handle failures gracefully. A pull‑payment pattern or an adjustable‑gas forwarding mechanism can ensure that funds are not unintentionally locked and that the protocol’s financial guarantees remain intact.

title: Equality check should be performed for fees, not >= as it can lead to users sending more fees than supposed
description: In BRC20Factory::burn(), Vault::deposit(), it is required that the fee is equal to or exceeds the msg.value. However, this could lead to loss of fees, as the fee can be lowered without users noticing (or frontrunning them), and users would lose this part of the fee. In the case of the Vault, these funds would be left untracked because the fees are tracked in totalFees, so the owner would not be able to withdraw these extra funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment validation flaw in the fee handling logic of two functions, BRC20Factory::burn() and Vault::deposit(). The contract checks that the fee supplied with the transaction (msg.value) is greater than or equal to the required fee, using a >= comparison, instead of requiring exact equality. Because the check allows any amount that meets or exceeds the expected fee, a caller can unintentionally or maliciously send more ether than required. The extra amount is accepted by the contract but is not recorded in the totalFees accounting variable. Consequently, the surplus ether becomes untracked, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective while the contract owner cannot withdraw it because the accounting state does not reflect the additional balance. This issue arises whenever a user calls the affected functions with a msg.value that exceeds the exact fee, which can happen due to user error, a front‑running attacker increasing the required fee, or a malicious UI that over‑pays. The impact is a loss of funds for the user, a mismatch between expected and actual balances, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants – the protocol assumes that totalFees equals the sum of all fees collected, which is violated by the hidden surplus. From the user’s point of view the transaction succeeds, but the wallet shows a larger deduction than anticipated and the contract’s fee ledger shows a lower total, leading to confusion such as “I paid a fee but the contract’s fee total didn’t increase”. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee verification logic and noticed the use of >= instead of ==, a pattern that can be subtle because the contract still accepts the transaction and does not revert, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. The flaw belongs to the class of incorrect input validation bugs, specifically over‑payment or fee‑mismatch vulnerabilities. To remediate the issue the fee comparison should be changed to an equality check (==) so that any deviation from the exact required fee causes the transaction to revert, ensuring that only the intended amount is accepted and correctly accounted for. This change restores the accounting guarantees, prevents accidental loss of user funds, and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations that the fee they see is the fee they actually pay.

title: Withdrawals could be bricked if chain enabled interop before migrating to the SharedLockbox
description:
Upgrading an L2 chain to enable interop (and join the dependency set of its peers) is a distinct process from updating the L1 bridge (and moving ETH to the SharedLockbox). The intention is for these two processes to be decoupled. After interop is enabled on an L2, the possibility exists for more ETH to be withdrawn from the chain than exists in the L1 OptimismPortal. This occurs because ETH can be bridged from other chains. This is the problem that the SharedLockbox solves.
However, if there is a time period where interop is enabled and funds have not been migrated to the SharedLockbox, we can end up with withdrawals that cannot be fulfilled by the balance of the Portal. Ideally, in this situation, these withdrawals would revert. However, the result is actually that withdrawals will be finalized and fail to execute, bricking the user's funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs when an Optimism L2 chain enables cross‑chain interoperability before the L1 bridge has migrated all ETH to the SharedLockbox. After interop is turned on, the L2 can receive ETH from other chains, allowing withdrawal requests that exceed the amount of ETH held in the L1 OptimismPortal. The withdrawal logic calls a low‑level helper SafeCall.callWithMinGas to forward the requested value to the target contract. This helper returns a boolean success flag instead of reverting when the call fails due to insufficient balance. Because the surrounding code does not verify that the portal balance is large enough before invoking the helper, the transaction is marked as finalized even though the ETH transfer never occurs. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction appears successful on‑chain, but the expected funds never arrive and the user’s balance remains unchanged. The funds become effectively “bricked” – they are locked in the portal with no way to replay the withdrawal, resulting in a loss of value for the affected users. The issue is triggered only during the window after interop activation and before the ETH migration to the SharedLockbox, and only for withdrawals whose value exceeds the portal’s current balance. It was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that exercised the finalizeWithdrawalTransaction path and observed that SafeCall.callWithMinGas returned false without causing a revert. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, making it hard to notice without detailed testing. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of insufficient‑funds checks missing in low‑level call wrappers, leading to silent failures and non‑replayable state changes. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit balance check before the low‑level call and revert with a clear error (e.g., NotEnoughBalance) when the portal does not hold enough ETH, thereby preserving replayability and preventing bricked withdrawals.

title: Transaction prevention through invalid message validation
description:
Any contract with flow control privileges can invoke the validateMessage function using an invalid message hash. Since the Supervisor cannot includes such messages on the source chain, it marks these transactions as invalid and excludes them from block inclusion. This allows any contract that receives control flow to block a transaction from occurring. This is typically not the case. If there is a low level call (or a try/catch block) with a specified amount of gas, it is safe to pass control flow to an unsafe contract and be sure they cannot cause the function to revert.
This can make contracts that are safe on other chains because unsafe on Superchain chains, breaking EVM equivalence. As an example, this can be problematic during liquidation or cancellation events, where systems sometimes notify users through a try/catch callback mechanism, allowing them to handle this event without the ability to cause transaction reversion. However, this also enables the user to deliberately prevent liquidations by exploiting the message validation process.
poc:
1. A liquidator initiates a liquidation against a user's loan position.
2. The lending contract notifies the user's designated contract through a try/catch mechanism.
3. The user's contract responds by calling validateMessage with either:
• A non-existent message hash.
• An identifier outside the permitted dependency set.
4. The Supervisor flags the transaction as invalid, preventing its inclusion in the block, and permanently avoiding liquidation.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an ability for any contract that receives control‑flow privileges to invoke the cross‑chain message validation routine (validateMessage) with a deliberately malformed or non‑existent message identifier. The Supervisor on the destination (Superchain) chain treats such a call as an indication that the associated cross‑chain message is invalid and consequently marks the whole transaction as invalid, preventing it from being included in the next block. Because the validation step is performed before the transaction is committed, the attacker can effectively block the execution of any operation that relies on that message, such as a liquidation, cancellation, or user‑notification callback. The root cause is that the validateMessage function does not enforce that the supplied hash corresponds to a message that actually exists on the source chain, and the Supervisor does not distinguish between a genuine validation failure and a deliberately crafted invalid identifier. The exploit works by a contract that is called via a low‑level call or a try/catch callback to submit an out‑of‑range or fake message hash; the Supervisor then flags the transaction as invalid, causing the original operation to be dropped silently. This can happen whenever a protocol uses try/catch or low‑gas calls to notify external contracts about an event and assumes that the callback cannot revert the whole transaction. Users affected are borrowers whose positions are supposed to be liquidated, protocol operators who rely on automated liquidations, and any participant expecting a state change on the Superchain. From the user’s perspective the liquidation simply never occurs: the UI may show a pending liquidation request that never resolves, balances remain unchanged, and no error is reported because the transaction is never mined. The issue was discovered during a security audit of cross‑chain interoperability on Optimism‑based Superchain networks, where the auditors observed that the message‑validation step could be triggered with arbitrary data. The problem is subtle because the transaction appears to be dropped by the consensus layer rather than reverted, so standard debugging tools that look for revert reasons do not surface the failure. The bug belongs to the class of “message‑validation bypass leading to transaction denial” or “cross‑chain message denial of service”. To remediate the issue the validation routine should require proof that the supplied hash corresponds to an existing, authenticated message on the source chain, and the Supervisor should treat invalid‑hash submissions as a regular validation failure that does not automatically discard the whole transaction. Additionally, protocols should avoid granting unrestricted control‑flow to untrusted contracts during callbacks, or they should implement a safe‑fallback path that does not rely on a single validateMessage call to decide transaction inclusion.

title: Native token can be flash minted, breaking protocol expectations
description:
Protocols have been designed with the assumption that there is a fixed amount of ETH in existence. For example, ETH balances are often stored as uint96 on the knowledge that it will be impossible to overflow. The current interop contracts break this invariant by allowing users to "flash mint" ETH by calling relayERC20() before sendERC20() on the SuperchainWETH.sol contract. If they perform this action on two separate chains in the same block, this cycle will net out to being accepted, but will allow the caller to temporarily hold up to type(uint248).max of ETH mid execution.
While flash minting is a common practice with some ERC20s, it is assumed that for ETH, there is an upper bound to flash loans of the total supply in existence.
Because type(uint248).max of ETH will be placed in the ETHLiquidity contract, this assumption is no longer true, and users temporarily hold far more than the total amount of ETH in existence. This can result in important app layer assumptions being broken, breaking composability with L1 contracts.
poc:
We can imagine the following scenario:
• A user uses the L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger to call relayETH() on the SuperchainWETH contract on Chain A. This gives them access to the requested WETH, but requires a sending transaction from Chain B to be valid.
• They perform any actions they would like with this ETH and then call sendETH() to send the funds back to Chain B, all in the same transaction.
• Meanwhile, on Chain B, they perform the same two actions (relay and then send).
• In both cases, ETH was flash minted by calling relay before send, but was valid due to the timestamp invariant.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a flash‑minting flaw in the native ETH handling logic of the SuperchainWETH contract used for cross‑domain messaging. The contract allows a caller to invoke a relay function (relayERC20/relayETH) before the corresponding send function (sendERC20/sendETH) within the same transaction, and this sequence can be performed on two separate L2 chains that are processed in the same block via the L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger. Because the relay function does not enforce any upper bound on the amount of ETH that can be minted, an attacker can request an amount up to type(uint248).max, which is temporarily deposited into the ETHLiquidity contract. The protocol assumes that the total supply of ETH is fixed and that balances stored in uint96 will never overflow; this assumption is broken when the flash‑minted amount far exceeds the real supply. An attacker can therefore hold an astronomically large amount of ETH for the duration of the transaction, use it to manipulate contracts that rely on the fixed‑supply invariant, cause overflow of uint96 balances, or otherwise break composability with L1 contracts that expect realistic ETH amounts. The issue manifests only transiently, making it hard to detect with standard balance checks because the inflated amount never persists on‑chain after the transaction completes. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which traced the call order in the interop contracts and identified that the timestamp invariant used to validate cross‑chain messages does not prevent the relay‑before‑send pattern. The root cause is the lack of accounting for total ETH supply in the relay logic and the use of an excessively large integer type for the amount parameter, combined with the ability to execute matching relay‑send pairs on two chains in the same block. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that the amount relayed cannot exceed the actual minted supply, add explicit checks that prevent relay calls from creating more ETH than exists, restrict the order of operations so that send must precede relay, or redesign the cross‑domain escrow to use a bounded accounting model that respects the fixed‑supply assumption. This would restore the integrity of business logic that depends on ETH being a scarce, non‑inflatable asset and prevent scenarios where users see huge temporary balances that disappear, or where protocol invariants are violated, potentially leading to loss of funds or broken protocol guarantees.

title: Inability to Close Positions with Significant Positive PnL
description: Presently, when there isn't adequate liquidity in the OstiumVault to cover profits for trades with substantial positive PnL, a revert occurs. While this behavior is intended, it's worth considering implementing a solution to partially receive the profit up to a maximum threshold or at least the collateral itself. Otherwise, traders won't be able to exit a position at all.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists ofan inability for traders to close positions that have generated a substantial positive profit‑and‑loss (PnL) when the OstiumVault does not hold enough liquid assets to cover the full profit amount. The contract’s exit routine checks the vault balance before transferring the profit; if the vault balance is lower than the required payout, the function triggers a revert, aborting the whole transaction. This behavior, while deliberately coded to avoid overdrawing the vault, creates a denial‑of‑exit condition because the logic does not provide a fallback path such as a partial profit payout or a guarantee that at least the trader’s collateral can be returned. An attacker or even a benign market event could drain the vault’s liquidity (for example, by large withdrawals or by other profitable trades) and then force a trader with a large unrealized gain to attempt a close. The transaction will revert, leaving the trader’s position and collateral locked in the contract with no way to retrieve it until additional liquidity is supplied. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a failed transaction or a generic “revert” error, while the expected outcome – receiving the profit or at least the original collateral – does not occur. This issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the profit settlement flow and noticed that the contract does not handle the edge case where vault liquidity is insufficient. It can be hard to notice because it only manifests for large‑profit positions, which may be rare in normal testing, and the revert message does not explain the underlying liquidity shortfall. The impact is medium severity: funds can become temporarily inaccessible, user confidence may be eroded, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that profit can always be paid out) are violated. The recommended remediation is to redesign the exit logic to allow a partial payout up to the available vault balance, to enforce a maximum profit cap, or to guarantee that the trader’s collateral is always returned even when the vault cannot cover the full profit. Implementing such a fallback would align the contract with typical financial expectations that a position can be closed and that users will not lose access to their capital because of internal liquidity constraints.

title: Missing Pausability Check in OstiumTrading::executeAutomationOrder() for Opening Orders
description: The execution of a limit order within the OstiumTrading::executeAutomationOrder() function lacks a check to determine if the contract is paused.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent pause guard in the function that processes automated limit orders. When the contract is placed in a paused state – typically to halt trading during emergencies or upgrades – most entry points verify the pause flag before performing state‑changing actions. In this case the executeAutomationOrder routine, which is responsible for opening limit orders, does not check whether the contract is paused. The root cause is a missing require statement or Pausable modifier that would reject calls while the pause flag is true. An attacker or any user can invoke executeAutomationOrder while the contract is paused, causing new limit orders to be opened or existing ones to be executed despite the intended suspension of trading. This can lead to unexpected order fills, mismatched accounting, and potential loss of funds for traders who assume that no trades occur during a pause. The impact is most visible to users who place limit orders; they may see orders being filled when the UI indicates trading is halted, balances changing without consent, or refunds not being processed as expected. The condition occurs only when the contract is paused, which is a state that should block all order‑related functions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the pause checks across the contract’s public functions and identified the omission. Because the function is internal and may be called through automation scripts, the lack of a pause guard can be subtle and may not surface in normal testing unless the pause state is explicitly exercised. To remediate, the function should include a pause verification, either by adding a require(!paused) statement at the start of executeAutomationOrder or by applying the standard Pausable modifier to the function. Additionally, the logic that validates the existence of an open limit order should be retained, ensuring that only legitimate orders are processed. By enforcing the pause check, the contract will honor the emergency stop mechanism, preventing order execution when trading is intended to be disabled and preserving the integrity of user balances and protocol accounting.

title: OstiumTrading::topUpCollateral() is missing pairsStored.groupMaxCollateral(pairIndex) check
description: When opening trades it is checked if the collateral is within limits for each pair in OstiumTradingCallbacks::withinExposureLimits(). The same should be done in OstiumTrading::topUpCollateral().
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the collateral‑top‑up function of the OstiumTrading contract. When a trader opens a new position the system calls withinExposureLimits() to verify that the amount of collateral supplied for each trading pair does not exceed the pair‑specific maximum defined in pairsStored.groupMaxCollateral(pairIndex). However, the same verification step is omitted in the topUpCollateral() routine that allows an existing position to receive additional collateral. The root cause is a missing call to the exposure‑limit check, an oversight in the contract’s business‑logic flow. An attacker or any user can invoke topUpCollateral() with an arbitrarily large amount, bypassing the per‑pair maximum constraint. By doing so the user can push the total collateral for a pair beyond the intended ceiling, potentially distorting the protocol’s risk parameters, creating an imbalance in exposure calculations, and allowing the user to lock more funds than the system is designed to handle. This can lead to scenarios where the protocol appears over‑collateralized for a particular pair while other participants may suffer reduced margin buffers, increasing the chance of liquidation failures or unfair advantage. The issue manifests whenever a trader calls topUpCollateral() after a trade has been opened; the contract does not perform the groupMaxCollateral validation at that point, so the excess collateral is accepted silently. The affected parties include any trader who can top up collateral, the overall protocol that relies on strict exposure limits, and indirectly other users whose positions share the same pair. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the logic of opening‑trade functions with the top‑up path and identified the missing validation call. Because the function appears to simply add funds, the lack of a limit check can be subtle and may not produce obvious on‑chain errors, making it hard to notice without a focused review of the business rules. To remediate, the contract should invoke the same exposure‑limit verification used in withinExposureLimits() before accepting any additional collateral in topUpCollateral(), rejecting the transaction if the new total would exceed pairsStored.groupMaxCollateral for the relevant pair. This aligns the top‑up flow with the intended accounting model, restores the invariant that collateral per pair never surpasses the configured maximum, and prevents the protocol from accepting unintended excess funds.

title: OstiumTrading::closeTradeMarket() and OstiumTrading::topUpCollateral() are missing pending trigger checks
description: OstiumTrading::closeTradeMarket() and OstiumTrading::topUpCollateral() can be used to frontrun liquidation calls whose trigger has already been set, making the liquidation fail in OstiumPriceUpKeep::performUpkeep(), draining fees and gaming the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing checks for a pending liquidation trigger in the functions that close a market trade and that add collateral to an existing trade. When a price‑up keeper schedules a liquidation by setting a trigger, the contract expects that no further state‑changing actions will interfere before the upkeep is executed. Because the closeTradeMarket and topUpCollateral functions do not verify that a trigger is not already pending, an attacker can submit a transaction that either closes the trade or adds collateral after the trigger has been set but before the keeper runs. This front‑running action clears or modifies the trade state so that the subsequent performUpkeep call in OstiumPriceUpKeep fails to liquidate. The failure prevents the protocol from collecting the intended liquidation fees and instead leaves the fees unclaimed, effectively draining them from the system. The issue appears only when a liquidation trigger has already been recorded and a user or bot calls either of the two vulnerable functions before the upkeep executes. It affects any participant who relies on the liquidation mechanism – traders, lenders, and fee recipients – because the expected fee distribution does not occur and the trade may remain in an inconsistent state. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined state transitions around liquidation triggers and identified that the contract lacked a guard such as checkNoPendingTrigger. The bug is subtle because the functions appear to perform legitimate actions (closing a trade or topping up collateral) and the missing guard does not raise an error; only the downstream liquidation fails, which may be observed as missing fees or a trade that does not get liquidated despite price conditions. This class of bug can be described as a missing pre‑condition check leading to a race‑condition‑like exploit, where state changes are allowed after a critical event has been scheduled. From a user perspective the UI may show that a trade was closed or collateral added, but the liquidation that should have happened afterwards does not, resulting in “fees disappear” or “liquidation never occurs”. The expected behavior is that once a liquidation trigger is set, no further modifications to the trade should be permitted until the upkeep processes the trigger. To remediate, each function should invoke a check that ensures no pending liquidation trigger exists, rejecting calls that would interfere with the scheduled liquidation and thereby preserving the integrity of the fee collection and trade lifecycle.

title: Oracle fees should be payed upfront to protect the protocol from failed performeUpkeep() calls
description: At the moment oracle fees are payed after the trades have been finalized, either in registerTrade(), openTradeMarketCallback() or closeTradeMarketCallback(). There are some edge cases in which the trade does not get finalized, but the automation/upkeep is still performed, so the protocol incurs these losses. For example, if there is not a trade in openTradeMarketCallback(), fees will not be charged (this may happen if the user cancels the pending market open order after the timeout, but chainlink triggers the upkeep after closing).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deferred oracle‑fee payment design flaw. In the current implementation the protocol charges the oracle fee only after a trade has been finalized, inside functions such as registerTrade, openTradeMarketCallback and closeTradeMarketCallback. Because the fee collection is performed in a separate callback, the contract does not verify that a trade actually exists before paying the fee. Consequently, if a user cancels a pending market open order after the timeout, the Chainlink keeper may still invoke openTradeMarketCallback. The callback executes the fee transfer to the oracle even though no trade was created, so the protocol pays the oracle fee without receiving any revenue. This edge case can be triggered repeatedly, allowing an attacker to cause the automation to run on non‑existent trades and drain the protocol’s fee reserve. The impact is a loss of funds from the protocol’s treasury; users do not receive any service, yet the protocol’s balance decreases. The issue occurs whenever the upkeep is performed without a corresponding trade, which can happen after order cancellation, timeout, or any situation where the callback is invoked erroneously. The affected party is the protocol itself, as its accounting assumptions that fees are always reimbursed by a completed trade are violated. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the fee flow and noticed that the callbacks lack a guard for trade existence. Because the loss is incurred in a separate transaction that only transfers a small fee, it may be difficult to notice in normal operation. The proper mitigation is to require users to pay the oracle fee upfront when opening a trade, or to add a check that aborts the fee transfer if no active trade is present, thereby aligning fee collection with trade creation and preventing the protocol from paying for a trade that never materialized.

title: Error in OstiumPairsStorage::groupMaxCollateral() calculation
description: The calculation of the maximum deposited collateral per group, erroneously divides by 100, assuming it refers to 100%. However, the maxCollateralP variable, specified here, has a precision of 2 decimals. This means that 100% is expressed as 100_00. This discrepancy results in incorrect checks in OstiumTradingCallbacks::withinExposureLimits(), potentially causing the vault's collateral to be capped at a much larger amount than intended. Furthermore, this miscalculation may dilute the reported profits.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect scaling of the maximum collateral limit for a trading group. In the function that calculates the per‑group collateral ceiling, the code divides the stored percentage value by 100, assuming the value represents a whole‑percentage (e.g., 100 % = 100). In reality the contract stores percentages with two decimal places, using a basis‑point representation where 100 % is encoded as 100_00. This mismatch causes the computed limit to be off by a factor of one hundred, allowing the vault to accept far more collateral than the risk parameters intend. The mis‑scaled limit is later used by the exposure‑checking routine, which therefore fails to reject oversized deposits. As a result, users can deposit amounts that exceed the designed risk ceiling, potentially exposing the protocol to higher liquidation risk and diluting the reported profit figures because the profit calculation assumes a smaller collateral base. The issue manifests whenever the group‑level maximum collateral is queried – typically during deposit or trade execution – and it affects any participant that interacts with the vault, as well as the protocol’s overall risk management. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit when the auditors noticed a division by a literal 100 while the surrounding code treats percentages as basis points. Because the numbers still appear plausible for small deposits, the bug can remain hidden until large positions are opened, making it difficult to detect through routine testing. The proper remediation is to replace the magic divisor with a constant that reflects the actual precision (for example, dividing by 10_000 when using basis points) or to store percentages in a unit‑consistent format such as BPS throughout the contract. By aligning the arithmetic with the declared precision, the exposure checks will correctly enforce the intended collateral caps, preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and preventing unintended fund over‑allocation.

title: updatePair() is missing the pairOk() modifier
description: OstiumPairsStorage::updatePair() updates a pair's attribute but does not check the new values.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that updates a trading pair’s configuration. The function performs the state change but does not invoke the pairOk validation routine that is intended to enforce invariant checks on the new parameters. Because the modifier is omitted, the contract accepts any values supplied by the caller, including ones that violate business rules such as price bounds, fee limits, or token address validity. An attacker or a careless admin can therefore set malformed or malicious attributes, causing the pair to behave incorrectly – for example, returning extreme prices, rejecting legitimate trades, or allowing trades at a rate that drains liquidity. The impact is that users may see unexpected zero balances, failed swaps, or loss of funds when interacting with the affected pair. The flaw manifests whenever updatePair is called, which can be triggered by any account that possesses the update permission; the missing check means the contract does not guard against out‑of‑range or contradictory values. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that compared the function signature against the expected security modifiers and noticed the absence of pairOk. It can be hard to notice because the function executes without reverting and the contract does not emit an explicit warning, so the state appears to change normally while the hidden invariants are silently broken. The appropriate remediation is to attach the pairOk modifier (or an equivalent internal validation call) to the updatePair function so that every new configuration is verified against the protocol’s rules before being persisted. In generic terms this is an input‑validation omission that belongs to the class of unchecked state‑update bugs, where missing constraints allow arbitrary data to corrupt critical accounting logic. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be a trade that returns zero output, a pair that shows absurd price quotes, or a balance that appears to disappear after an update, contrary to the expectation that updating a pair only changes metadata without affecting asset safety.

title: OstiumPriceUpKeep::performUpKeep() does not correctly handle possible reverts
description:
OstiumPriceUpKeep::performUpKeep() should unregister pending market orders or disable triggers and pending limit orders if the execution fails. However, it is not dealing with all the revert scenarios, for example:
1. Not enough value to pay for the verifier.
2. Invalid prices.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upkeep function that is responsible for processing pending market and limit orders. The function attempts to call an external price oracle and, based on the returned price, it should either execute the order or clean up the order state. However, the implementation does not verify that the contract holds enough ether to cover the verifier fee before invoking the oracle, nor does it handle cases where the oracle returns an invalid price. When either of these conditions occurs, the external call reverts and the function exits without unregistering the pending order or disabling the associated trigger. As a result, the order remains in a limbo state: the user’s request appears to have been processed, but the order is still marked as active, and the protocol does not collect the oracle fee that should have been charged. This can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately causes the verifier fee to be insufficient (for example by draining the contract’s balance) or by feeding malformed price data, causing the upkeep to revert repeatedly. Each revert leaves the order untouched, allowing the attacker to create a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users cannot have their orders cleared or their funds released. The impact includes potential loss of funds for users who expect a refund or order cancellation, inaccurate accounting because fees are not recorded, and a breach of the protocol’s business logic that assumes every upkeep either succeeds or cleans up state. The issue manifests only when the upkeep is scheduled and the contract’s ether balance is below the required threshold or when the price data fails validation, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the upkeep routine and noted missing error handling paths. The problem is subtle because a reverted transaction simply returns an error without emitting a specific event, so observers may not notice that the order was never cleared. To remediate, the contract should first check that sufficient ether is available to pay the verifier before calling the oracle, and it should validate the price data. If the call would revert, the function must still unregister the pending order and charge the oracle fee to the user, or at least mark the order as failed, ensuring that the system’s state remains consistent and that users are not left with stuck orders. This pattern belongs to the broader class of improper error handling and insufficient pre‑condition checks in external calls, which can lead to state‑inconsistency and financial loss.

title: Trader Can Set Wrong TP and SL
description: In OstiumTrading::updateSl(), a validation is present for the maximum stop loss (SL) distance. However, there is no validation for the opposite scenario, as seen in OstiumTrading::openTrade() at L202. This absence of validation permits the setting of a stop loss for an amount greater than the open price when initiating a long position and for setting a smaller amount when initiating a short position. Consequently, this issue introduces the potential for errors, whereby automation could mistakenly trigger the closure of a position upon reaching this price, behaving akin to a take-profit order, contrary to its intended function. The same issue arises in OstiumTrading::updateTp(), which lacks validation to ensure that the new take profit (TP) is greater than the open price for long positions and smaller for short positions.
bug_full: The contract allows a trader to set a stop‑loss (SL) or take‑profit (TP) value that contradicts the logical direction of the position because the functions that create and modify a trade do not enforce proper bounds on these parameters. When a long position is opened, the SL should be below the entry price and the TP should be above it; for a short position the opposite holds. The openTrade function and the updateSl and updateTp functions only check the maximum SL distance for one side of the inequality and omit the complementary check, so a caller can supply an SL that is higher than the entry price for a long trade or a TP that is lower than the entry price. This mis‑validation causes the contract to treat the SL as if it were a TP, meaning the position can be closed immediately after opening or updated to a price that triggers an unintended exit. The impact is that users may see their positions close at the wrong price, resulting in unexpected loss of capital, zero or negative profit, or funds that appear to disappear from their account. The bug manifests whenever a trade is created or when the SL/TP is updated, and it affects any participant who interacts with the trading contract, including automated bots that rely on the contract’s guarantees. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the validation logic and confirmed the missing checks by constructing a proof‑of‑concept where a new SL larger than the open price for a long trade caused an immediate closure, and a TP lower than the open price for a long trade was accepted. The issue is subtle because the contract still reverts on obviously out‑of‑range values (e.g., exceeding the maximum SL distance) and normal operation may not trigger the erroneous path unless edge‑case values are supplied, making it easy to miss in standard functional tests. Conceptually, the vulnerability belongs to the class of improper input validation or business‑logic errors where directional constraints are not enforced. To remediate, the contract should add explicit checks that enforce newSl < openPrice for long positions and newSl > openPrice for short positions, and similarly enforce newTp > openPrice for longs and newTp < openPrice for shorts, rejecting any values that violate these directional rules. This ensures that SL always acts as a protective stop and TP always acts as a profit target, aligning contract behavior with trader expectations and preventing premature or unintended position closures.

title: USDC Blacklisting Prevents Trader Liquidation
description:
USDC incorporates a blacklist functionality that reverts any attempt to transfer funds to a blacklisted address, even if the transfer amount is 0. Consequently, during a liquidation, the transfer on L495 within OstiumTradingCallbacks will revert, preventing the liquidation from proceeding and resulting in bad debt for the protocol.
Likewise, other functions such as OstiumTrading::cancelOpenLimitOrder(), OstiumTrading::openTradeMarketTimeout(), and OstiumTradingCallbacks::openTradeMarketCallback() will also revert upon transferring the collateral back to the trader.
poc: no poc is available here.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the USDC token’s built‑in blacklist feature, which automatically reverts any transfer to an address that has been marked as blacklisted, even when the transferred amount is zero. In the Ostium protocol, liquidation and several collateral‑return functions rely on a push‑style transfer of USDC back to the trader after a position is closed or an order is cancelled. When a trader’s address is on the USDC blacklist, the contract attempts to send either a positive amount of collateral or a zero‑value transfer as part of the cleanup step. Because USDC rejects the transfer regardless of the amount, the transaction reverts, causing the liquidation routine (specifically the call at line L495 in OstiumTradingCallbacks) to fail. As a result, the protocol cannot recover the outstanding debt, leading to bad debt accumulation. The same issue appears in functions such as OstiumTrading::cancelOpenLimitOrder, OstiumTrading::openTradeMarketTimeout, and OstiumTradingCallbacks::openTradeMarketCallback, all of which try to return collateral to the trader and therefore revert when the recipient is blacklisted. This problem manifests only when a blacklisted address is involved during the post‑trade cleanup phase; normal trading operations succeed because the blacklist check is not triggered. The affected parties include any trader whose address becomes blacklisted, the lenders who rely on the protocol to liquidate under‑collateralised positions, and the protocol itself, which may suffer financial loss and reduced trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, where the auditors noted that USDC’s blacklist logic applies to zero‑value transfers, a detail that is easy to overlook because developers often assume a zero‑amount transfer is a no‑op and will never revert. From a user’s perspective, a trader may see a liquidation attempt fail silently, their position remain open, and no refund of collateral appear in their wallet, contrary to the expectation that liquidation should close the position and return any remaining funds. This violates the core accounting assumption that collateral can always be reclaimed after a liquidation event. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should either perform a blacklist check before initiating any USDC transfer, preventing blacklisted users from opening positions or triggering a liquidation that cannot be completed, or redesign the liquidation flow to avoid pushing funds to the user. A pull‑over‑push pattern, where the protocol records the amount owed and allows the user to withdraw it after the liquidation process finishes, eliminates the need to transfer to a potentially blacklisted address and removes the failure point entirely. Implementing either of these mitigations restores the guarantee that liquidations can be completed and that collateral can be accounted for, thereby protecting the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Casting from int256 to uint256 won't revert if the number is negative, possibly leading to issues
description: Some instances, namely in OstiumPairInfos::getPendingAccFundingFees(), cast int256 to uint256.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked type conversion where a signed 256‑bit integer (int256) is cast directly to an unsigned 256‑bit integer (uint256) inside the contract logic that calculates pending accumulated funding fees. Because Solidity does not automatically revert when a negative signed value is cast to an unsigned type, the conversion silently wraps the two's‑complement representation, turning a negative number into a very large positive integer (2^256‑|value|). This mismatch between the intended signed arithmetic and the resulting unsigned value can cause the contract to record an inflated fee amount, miscalculate refunds, or deduct an excessive amount from a user's balance. An attacker or a malicious user can trigger a situation where the internal accounting variable becomes negative – for example by causing a funding fee to underflow – and then invoke the function that performs the cast. The contract will then treat the negative fee as a huge positive number, leading to a loss of funds for honest participants, zero or missing refunds for users, or a state where the protocol appears to have more fees than actually accrued. The issue manifests whenever the function that computes pending fees processes a value that can become negative, which may happen under edge‑case market conditions, rapid price swings, or when a user manipulates the funding rate. All participants who rely on accurate fee accounting – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariant is broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected arithmetic operations and identified the unsafe cast in the getPendingAccFundingFees routine. It is subtle because the contract does not emit an error or revert; the incorrect large number may only be observable later as an unexpected fee balance or a missing refund, making it hard to spot without deep inspection of signed‑to‑unsigned conversions. To remediate the issue, the code should avoid direct casts and instead use a safe casting library such as SafeCastUpgradeable, which checks that the signed value is non‑negative before converting, or explicitly add a require statement that the value is >=0. By enforcing this check, the contract will revert when a negative fee is encountered, preserving the intended accounting logic and preventing the accidental creation of massive unsigned values that could drain funds or break the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: Setting maxFundingFeePerBlock to a lower value than abs(lastFundingRate) will brick getPendingAccFundingFees()
description:
getPendingAccFundingFees() computes the number of blocks to the limit by subtracting absLastFundingRate to maxFundingFeePerBlock.
setMaxFundingFeePerBlock() allows setting the max to any value below MAX_FUNDING_FEE.
If maxFundingFeePerBlock is set to a value smaller than absLastFundingRate it will underflow, bricking getPendingAccFundingFees() and it can only be fixed by calling setPairFundingFees().
poc: no poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the function that calculates pending accumulated funding fees per block. The contract stores a maximum fee per block (maxFundingFeePerBlock) and the absolute value of the last funding rate (absLastFundingRate). When getPendingAccFundingFees() determines how many blocks remain before the fee limit is reached, it subtracts absLastFundingRate from maxFundingFeePerBlock. Because both values are unsigned integers, if maxFundingFeePerBlock is configured to a value smaller than absLastFundingRate, the subtraction underflows and wraps around to a very large number. This underflow corrupts the internal accounting used for funding fee accrual, effectively “bricking” the getPendingAccFundingFees() calculation. The issue can be triggered by any caller who invokes setMaxFundingFeePerBlock() with a value below the current absLastFundingRate, which the contract does not validate. Once the underflow occurs, subsequent calls to getPendingAccFundingFees() return nonsensical values, causing funding fee calculations to break, user‑facing interfaces to display zero or astronomically large fees, and potentially preventing positions from being settled or fees from being withdrawn. The impact is medium severity: it does not directly steal funds, but it disrupts the protocol’s accounting logic, can lock user balances, and undermines confidence in fee distribution. The bug manifests only after the malicious or mistaken parameter change and persists until setPairFundingFees() is called to reset the internal state. All participants who rely on accurate funding fee accrual—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, which noted the lack of a guard clause in setMaxFundingFeePerBlock(). Because the underflow does not cause a transaction revert, it can be difficult to notice; the contract continues to operate but produces incorrect fee values that may only be observed through abnormal UI output or failed fee withdrawals. The recommended mitigation is to add a validation check in setMaxFundingFeePerBlock() that reverts if the supplied maxFundingFeePerBlock is less than the current absLastFundingRate, thereby preventing the arithmetic underflow and preserving the integrity of funding fee calculations.

title: Tokens will get stuck if sent to a bot wallet
description: OrdiswapToken allows transfers to a bot address, but not from, such that it would be possible to send tokens to a bot, but the bot can't transfer the tokens out anymore.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asymmetric blacklist restriction in the OrdiswapToken contract that permits tokens to be transferred into an address that has been flagged as a bot, while simultaneously preventing any outbound transfer from that same address. The root cause is a transfer validation routine that only checks the sender against a bot list and does not enforce the same rule on the recipient. Because of this, an attacker or a careless user can send tokens to a blacklisted bot address – for example by using a swap, airdrop, or direct transfer – and the contract will accept the incoming transfer. Once the tokens reside in the bot wallet, any subsequent attempt to move them out fails, as the contract reverts outbound transfers from blacklisted addresses. The impact is that funds become effectively locked: the token holder sees a balance that cannot be spent, the protocol may lose circulating supply, and users experience a mismatch between the expected ability to withdraw or trade tokens and the reality of a zero‑output transaction. This condition occurs whenever an address is added to the bot list and the contract’s transfer function is invoked with that address as the sender, while the same address is allowed as a recipient. The affected parties include token holders who inadvertently send to a bot, any downstream contracts that rely on token movement, and the overall token economics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token’s transfer logic, where the reviewer noticed that the blacklist check was applied only to msg.sender and not to the recipient, a subtle asymmetry that does not raise immediate compile‑time warnings. The bug can be hard to notice because typical test suites focus on preventing transfers to malicious addresses, not on the possibility of locking tokens by sending them to such addresses. To remediate, the contract should enforce symmetric restrictions – either block both inbound and outbound transfers for blacklisted addresses, or provide a safe recovery mechanism (such as an admin‑only forced transfer) that allows tokens to be reclaimed from a bot wallet. Conceptually, this is a blacklist‑logic flaw that results in token lockup, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that any transferred token remains movable by its owner unless explicitly burned. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a balance that appears in their wallet but cannot be spent, leading to situations where “my tokens disappear” or “I cannot withdraw my funds”.

title: setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV2() and setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV3() should be external
description: setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV2() and setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV3() are internal functions but should likely be external.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of two functions that are intended to allow the contract owner or an authorized administrator to register or deregister automated market maker (AMM) pairs, but they are declared with internal visibility instead of external (or public). Because internal functions can only be called from within the same contract or its derived contracts, external callers – including the governance UI, scripts, or other contracts that need to update the AMM pair list after deployment – are unable to invoke them. The root cause is a mistaken visibility modifier, likely introduced by a copy‑paste error or a misunderstanding of Solidity’s access control model. An attacker cannot directly call these functions, however the inability for legitimate actors to update the AMM pair registry can lead to a mismatch between the protocol’s accounting assumptions and the actual state of liquidity pools. For example, when a new liquidity pool is created, the contract expects the pair to be marked as an AMM so that fee‑exempt or special‑tax logic is applied; because the registration function cannot be called externally, the pair remains unmarked, causing trades to be processed with incorrect fee calculations or, in some designs, to be blocked entirely. From a user perspective this may appear as missing or zero fees, unexpected transaction reverts, or funds that seem to be “stuck” because the contract does not recognize the pool as a valid market maker. The issue typically surfaces when the protocol attempts to add or remove AMM pairs after the initial deployment – a step that is common during upgrades, migrations, or when new liquidity is added. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined function signatures and visibility modifiers, noting that the functions were internal despite being referenced in the documentation as callable by the owner. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the internal functions may be called once in the constructor, giving the impression that they work correctly. To remediate, the visibility of setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV2 and setAutomatedMarketMakerPairV3 should be changed to external (or public) and protected with appropriate access control such as onlyOwner, ensuring that authorized external actors can update the AMM pair registry as intended. This correction restores the intended business logic, aligns accounting with actual liquidity pools, and prevents the user‑facing symptoms of missing fees or stuck balances.

title: TCR is overestimated on redemptions
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol calculates the Total Collateral Ratio (TCR) during a redemption operation. The contract fetches the highest market price for the collateral token from the price feed and uses this same price both to determine how much collateral a user can withdraw and to verify that the TCR remains above the Minimum Collateral Ratio (MCR). Because the highest price inflates the perceived value of the collateral, the computed TCR can be larger than the true market‑based TCR. When the real TCR is actually below the required MCR, the inflated value makes the safety check pass, allowing the redemption to proceed. An attacker can trigger a redemption while the protocol is under‑collateralized, withdraw more collateral than should be permitted, and potentially drain assets from the pool. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees: other users may see their balances shrink unexpectedly, the protocol may become insolvent, and the overall trust in the system is compromised. This condition occurs specifically in the redeemCollateral function whenever the price feed returns a peak price and the protocol is close to the MCR threshold. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the price logic used for different operations and noticed that the same conservative price was being reused for a safety check where a more neutral price should be applied. The bug is subtle because the redemption still succeeds and the price feed is expected to provide a high price for user‑friendly withdrawals, so the over‑estimation of TCR does not raise an immediate alarm unless the system is already near its collateral limits. To remediate the problem, the TCR calculation should be performed with the lowest or a weighted‑average price rather than the highest price, separating the price used for user‑facing redemption amounts from the price used for internal safety checks. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that the protocol never allows withdrawals that would push the real TCR below the MCR, preserving users’ funds and the protocol’s economic integrity.

title: DoS due to Chainlink oracle returning wrong data or going offline
description: Chainlink oracle price feed can return wrong data or go offline in extreme cases, which will provoke the EthPriceFeed.fetchEthPrice() function to revert. This function is called to execute the main actions of the system, such as redeeming collateral, opening a position, adding collateral, closing a position, claiming escrow, and liquidating a position. The impact of transaction reverting is especially severe in the case of liquidations, which might cause the system to be uncollateralized, and adding collateral, which might cause users to lose their collateral when the price feed gets back online. In order to prevent this, the system relies on the guardian calling the resetBreaker function to manually provide the new price and set the oracle status to the working state. However, this is not ideal, as: Requires the guardian to act quickly after the oracle goes offline. Until the oracle goes back online, the process has to be repeated after every interaction with the system, as every call will change the oracle status again to not working. Introduces a centralization vector. Another issue is that price movements greater than 50% are considered invalid, which prevents the system from reacting quickly to extreme price movements.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the reliance on a single Chainlink price feed that, when it returns incorrect data or becomes unavailable, triggers a revert in the EthPriceFeed.fetchEthPrice() routine. This routine is invoked by every core operation of the system – opening or closing a position, adding or redeeming collateral, claiming escrow and, critically, liquidating a position. The root cause is the contract’s strict validation logic: it treats any failure to obtain a fresh price, or any price change larger than fifty percent, as an invalid condition and immediately reverts the transaction. Because the contract does not include a fallback oracle or a graceful degradation path, the revert propagates to the caller, preventing the intended state change. An attacker or a network event that forces the Chainlink oracle offline, or that manipulates the reported price beyond the 50 % threshold, can therefore freeze all user interactions. The most severe impact occurs during liquidation, where a revert can leave the protocol under‑collateralized, and during collateral addition, where users may lose the ability to secure their positions and see their funds locked or even forfeited when the feed later recovers. The issue manifests whenever the price feed is stale, corrupted, or deliberately disrupted – conditions that may be rare and therefore easy to overlook during testing. Users experience transaction failures with generic error messages, see no change in their balances, or receive zero refunds when they expected a successful operation. The protocol’s design also introduces a centralization vector: a designated guardian must manually invoke resetBreaker to supply a new price and mark the oracle as operational, which requires rapid response and repeated calls after each failed interaction. This manual intervention is both a performance bottleneck and a trust issue. The problem was identified during a systematic audit that examined the contract’s error‑handling pathways and noted the absence of any alternative data source. Detecting the bug can be difficult because the revert only occurs under extreme oracle conditions, which may not be reproduced in routine test suites. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a fallback oracle or an on‑chain price aggregation mechanism, relax the hard 50 % deviation check, and implement an automated circuit‑breaker that switches to a secondary data source without requiring a privileged guardian, thereby eliminating the single point of failure and reducing the risk of funds becoming inaccessible or the system losing its collateralisation guarantees.

title: getRedemptionHints will revert if _maxIterations is reached
description:
The function getRedemptionHints() in HintHelpers.sol is used to find the right hints to pass to redeemCollateral(). The number of positions to consider for redemption can be capped to _maxIterations to avoid running out of gas. However, there is a flaw in the implementation that will cause the function to revert if _maxIterations is reached.  
File: HintHelpers.sol  
```solidity
while (vars.currentPositionUser != address(0) && vars.remainingStables > 0 && _maxIterations-- > 0) {
```  
The decrement of the _maxIterations variable is done after the condition check, meaning that in the last iteration, when _maxIterations is 0, the condition evaluates to false, but the decrement is still executed, causing an underflow and the function to revert. The original code from Liquity is not subject to this issue, as it intentionally allows the underflow to happen. However, using solc 0.8.0 or higher, the code should be adapted to avoid reverting due to the underflow. The result is that queries that entail a large number of iterations (i.e., the loop is not exited before _maxIterations is reached) will revert.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the getRedemptionHints function of HintHelpers.sol, which is responsible for generating the hint parameters required by redeemCollateral. The implementation uses a while loop with a post‑decrement on the _maxIterations argument: while (vars.currentPositionUser != address(0) && vars.remainingStables > 0 && _maxIterations-- > 0). In Solidity versions 0.8.0 and later, arithmetic underflow triggers an automatic revert. Because the decrement occurs after the condition is evaluated, the loop executes the decrement even when _maxIterations has already reached zero. On the final iteration the condition evaluates to false, but the post‑decrement still subtracts one, causing _maxIterations to underflow from 0 to the maximum uint256 value and immediately reverting the transaction. This off‑by‑one error means that any query that requires more iterations than the supplied _maxIterations limit will cause the function to revert instead of gracefully exiting the loop. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract code, where the loop logic was examined for gas‑optimisation safeguards. It can be hard to notice because the loop appears to respect the iteration cap, yet the subtle ordering of the decrement leads to a failure only at the boundary condition. Exploitation does not require malicious code; an attacker can simply request a redemption that touches a large number of positions, forcing the loop to hit the iteration limit and causing a revert. The practical impact is a denial‑of‑service on the hint‑generation step: users attempting to redeem collateral receive a transaction failure, see no hint data returned, and may be unable to complete the redemption process. From a user’s perspective the UI will display a generic “transaction reverted” or “failed to fetch redemption hints” message, contrary to the expectation that the call returns a list of hints. Funds that are meant to be redeemed remain locked because the subsequent redeemCollateral call cannot be supplied with valid hints. The bug belongs to the class of off‑by‑one loop termination errors that cause arithmetic underflow in modern Solidity compilers. To remediate the issue the loop should be rewritten to avoid the post‑decrement on the external parameter. A common fix is to introduce a local counter (e.g., uint i) and iterate while i < _maxIterations, incrementing i each pass, or to perform a pre‑decrement inside an unchecked block. This ensures the iteration limit is respected without triggering an underflow, allowing the function to exit cleanly and return partial hints when the limit is reached, preserving protocol usability and preventing denial‑of‑service conditions.

title: Max price deviation is too high
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overly permissive price‑deviation guard that allows a large shift in the reported price between two consecutive oracle rounds without triggering the protocol’s anti‑manipulation check. The guard is implemented by comparing the percentage deviation of the current price against a constant named MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION_FROM_PREVIOUS_ROUND. Because the constant is set to a value that permits up to roughly a 49 % change, the function only returns true when the price more than doubles or more than halves. Consequently, any price movement smaller than that threshold – for example a 30 % rise caused by an attacker or market volatility – is considered valid and the protocol proceeds to use the manipulated price for downstream calculations such as collateral valuation, loan‑to‑value checks, liquidation triggers and trade settlements. An attacker who can influence the underlying price feed (for instance by submitting a spoofed Chainlink round) can therefore push the price within the allowed window, causing the system to accept an artificially high or low price. This may lead to under‑collateralisation, unexpected liquidations, users receiving far less than expected from a trade, or the protocol issuing loans against insufficiently valued assets. The issue manifests when the price feed updates, which occurs regularly in normal operation, so the bug can be triggered at any time without any special conditions. All participants who rely on the protocol’s pricing – borrowers, lenders, traders and token holders – are potentially affected because the economic guarantees of the system are weakened. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined the deviation logic and compared the configured threshold against industry‑standard tolerances. It is subtle because a 30‑40 % price swing can appear plausible in volatile markets, making the missing protection easy to overlook during routine testing. To remediate the problem the guard should be tightened, for example by lowering MAX_PRICE_DEVIATION_FROM_PREVIOUS_ROUND to around 20 % or by adopting a more robust multi‑round or statistical sanity check, thereby reducing the window in which price manipulation can occur and restoring confidence that the protocol’s accounting matches its business logic.

title: Current redemption design causes users to be charged a penalty despite doing nothing wrong
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the redemption escrow logic of the protocol, where a timeout penalty is applied automatically once the cooldown and grace period have elapsed, regardless of whether the user actually caused the timeout. The root cause is a missing condition that distinguishes between an idle escrow that has simply expired and an escrow that has been actively used in an attempted redemption but could not be fulfilled due to insufficient collateral. When the contract reaches the branch that sets timedOut to true, it unconditionally charges the fee on the full remaining stable amount and clears the escrow balance. In the normal scenario this penalises a user who abandoned the position, which is intended. However, in a second scenario a user repeatedly calls the redemption function, receives back any unused stable tokens, and the escrow balance is refilled. Because the contract does not record that the user has made an attempt, the same timeout branch later charges the penalty even though the user was actively trying to redeem collateral. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that the redemption request was processed, but after the grace period the user receives less stable tokens than expected or sees a fee deducted with no clear explanation, violating the expectation that fees are only applied to idle positions. The impact is an unfair loss of funds for honest users, potential loss of confidence in the protocol, and a breach of the accounting assumption that penalties are only levied on abandoned positions.
