In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “state‑change‑before‑external‑call” errors that lead to accounting inconsistencies and reward misallocation, breaking the expected business logic that a user who claims a reward should receive the exact amount recorded in the contract.

title: M-4 s_defaultClientBasisPoints should be restricted
description: sdefaultClientBasisPoints should be less than 10000 FeeDistributorFactory.sol#L52 FeeDistributorFactory.sol#L71 otherwise the intialization of the deployed feeDistributors will revert.
bug_full: Thevulnerability originates from an unchecked initialization parameter in the fee distribution factory contract. A state variable that stores the default client basis points – a value that represents a percentage in hundredths of a percent – is expected to be strictly less than 10,000 (the maximum representing 100%). The contract does not enforce this upper bound before using the value in the fee‑distribution logic. Because the basis‑points value is later used in arithmetic that assumes it is a proper percentage, providing a value equal to or greater than 10,000 triggers a division‑by‑zero or overflow condition, causing the constructor of each newly deployed fee distributor to revert. An attacker or a careless operator can supply an out‑of‑range basis‑points value when calling the factory, which results in the fee distributor contract failing to be created. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users attempting to stake or receive fee payouts encounter a transaction that reverts with no explicit error message, and the protocol cannot instantiate the fee distributor needed for fee accounting. This situation affects any participant that relies on the fee distribution mechanism – stakers, delegators, and the protocol’s revenue model – because the expected flow of fee allocation is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the initialization sequence of the fee distributor contracts and noticed the absence of a validation check on the basis‑points parameter. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the variable is internal to the factory and the failure only manifests at deployment time, not during routine fee calculations, so users may only see generic transaction failures without understanding the root cause. To remediate the problem, the contract should include an explicit require statement that enforces s_defaultClientBasisPoints < 10,000 before any arithmetic is performed or before the fee distributor is instantiated. This simple input validation prevents the erroneous state from propagating and restores the expected business logic that fee percentages never exceed 100 %. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked input validation errors that lead to arithmetic exceptions and contract initialization failures, violating the accounting assumption that percentages are bounded between 0 % and 100 %. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with no fee distribution contract being created, leaving balances unchanged and expected refunds or fee shares missing, contrary to the expectation that staking should generate a proportional reward.

title: M-5 Non-existing _feeDistributorInstance can be rejected
description: There is no check that a specific _feeDistributorInstance exists here P2pOrgUnlimitedEthDepositor.sol#L112-L113, so the mapping value can be updated for non-existing address.
bug_full: The vulnerabilityis an unchecked update of a fee‑distributor reference in the P2pOrgUnlimitedEthDepositor contract. When the contract writes a new address into the internal mapping that tracks the fee‑distributor instance, it does not verify that the supplied address corresponds to an already‑initialized contract or a non‑zero address. The root cause is the absence of a validation step – the code simply assigns the value without checking the existence of code at the target address or whether the address has been registered previously. An attacker who can invoke the function that performs this assignment can supply an arbitrary address, including the zero address or a malicious contract, causing the fee‑distribution logic to redirect collected staking fees to an unintended destination. This can be exploited by calling the vulnerable function with a crafted address; if the caller has the required permissions (e.g., owner or any role allowed to update the mapping), the mapping entry is overwritten, and subsequent fee withdrawals are sent to the attacker‑controlled address. The impact is a loss of protocol revenue, broken accounting assumptions (fees that should be credited to the legitimate distributor disappear), and potential user‑facing symptoms such as missing fee payouts, zero balances where fees were expected, or refunds that never arrive. The condition under which it occurs is any execution path that reaches the mapping update without a prior existence check, typically during contract configuration or upgrades. All participants that rely on correct fee distribution – the protocol treasury, stakers, and end‑users – are affected because the financial flows are altered. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noted the missing existence guard. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still compile and function, and the misdirection of funds only becomes apparent when expected payouts are absent, which may be attributed to other causes. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the address being stored is non‑zero and that it points to a contract that has been initialized as a fee distributor, for example by verifying that the address is present in a registry or by checking that the code size at the address is greater than zero before updating the mapping. This class of bug falls under unchecked external address assignment, which violates the business logic that fees must be sent to a valid, pre‑registered distributor and can lead to silent loss of assets.

title: Reduce impact of emergencyUpdatequestPeriod()
description:
Function emergencyUpdatequestPeriod() allows the merkle tree to be updated. The merkle tree contains an embedded index parameter which is used to prevent double claims. When the merkleRoot is updated, the layout of indexes in the merkle tree could become different. Example: Suppose the initial merkle tree contains information for:
- user A: index=1, account = 0x1234, amount=100
- user B: index=2, account = 0x5689, amount=200
Then user A claims => _setClaimed(..., 1) is set. Now it turns out a mistake is made with the merkle tree, and it should contain:
- user B: index=1, account = 0x5689, amount=200
- user C: index=2, account = 0xabcd, amount=300
Now user B will not be able to claim because bit 1 has already been set. Under this situation the following issues can occur:
• Someone who has already claimed might be able to claim again.
• Someone who has already claimed has too much.
• Someone who has already claimed has too little, and cannot longer claim the rest because _setClaimed() has already been set.
• someone who has not yet claimed might not be able to claim because _setClaimed() has already been set by another user.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the emergencyUpdatequestPeriod function, which permits an authorized party to replace the merkle root that backs the claim distribution. The merkle tree stores an index for each beneficiary and a bitmap tracks which indexes have already been claimed. When the root is updated after any claim has been recorded, the ordering of indexes in the new tree can differ from the original ordering. Because the bitmap is not reset or reconciled, a bit that was set for a previous index now corresponds to a different user in the updated tree. This mismatch enables several undesirable outcomes: a user who has already claimed may be able to submit another proof and receive the same allocation again (double claim); a user may receive more tokens than entitled if the new tree assigns a larger amount to the same index; conversely, a user may receive less or be unable to claim because the bitmap already marks the index as claimed even though the user has not received the new amount. The issue manifests only when the emergencyUpdatequestPeriod function is called after at least one claim has been recorded, which is a realistic scenario during a corrective merkle‑tree update. All participants who rely on the claim mechanism – token holders, the protocol’s treasury and any downstream contracts – are potentially affected because the accounting guarantees of the merkle distribution are broken. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the interaction between the merkle‑root update logic and the claim bitmap, noting that the code does not clear or re‑map the bitmap after a root change. It can be hard to notice because successful claim transactions do not revert; instead they silently credit an incorrect amount or reject a legitimate claim, making the bug observable only through mismatched balances or unexpected zero payouts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “claim” button that either returns no tokens, returns the same amount twice, or returns an amount that does not match the displayed entitlement, violating the expectation that a claim yields exactly the allocated balance. Conceptually, the fix is to treat the merkle root as immutable once any claim bitmap bit is set, or to reset the bitmap and pause claims during any root replacement, and to ensure that each beneficiary’s index remains stable across updates or that per‑address claimed amounts are tracked and reconciled with the new tree. Implementing these controls restores the integrity of the claim accounting and prevents funds from disappearing, being over‑paid, or being locked away due to a stale bitmap.

title: Verify the correct merkle tree is used
description: The MultiMerkleDistributor.sol contract does not verify that the merkle tree belongs to the right quest and period. If the wrong merkle tree is added then the wrong rewards can be claimed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MultiMerkleDistributor contract’s claim logic, which validates a Merkle proof without tying the proof to a specific quest identifier (questID) and distribution period. Because the leaf hash and the verification step only include the index, account and amount, an attacker can supply a proof that originates from a completely different Merkle tree – for example a tree that was generated for another quest or a previous period – and the contract will still accept it as valid. This happens because the contract stores a single Merkle root (or a set of roots) but does not enforce that the root corresponds to the questID and period supplied in the claim function. Consequently, when a malicious actor submits a proof that matches a different tree, the contract mistakenly attributes those rewards to the caller, allowing the caller to claim tokens they are not entitled to. The impact is the unauthorized transfer of reward tokens, potentially draining the distribution pool and breaking the economic assumptions of the quest system. The issue manifests whenever a new Merkle root is added without an explicit binding to its questID and period, or when the claim function is called with mismatched parameters that are not cross‑checked against the stored root. All participants of the affected quests, as well as the protocol’s treasury, are at risk because the contract may distribute more tokens than intended. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the claim flow and noticed the absence of questID/period in the leaf construction. It can be difficult to spot in testing because a valid proof from any tree will still pass the cryptographic check, giving the impression that the distribution logic is sound while silently allowing reward leakage. The recommended remediation is to embed questID and period into each leaf node (e.g., keccak256(abi.encodePacked(questID, period, index, account, amount))) and to store a mapping from (questID, period) to the corresponding Merkle root. The claim function must then retrieve the correct root based on the supplied questID and period and verify the proof against that root, ensuring that rewards can only be claimed for the intended quest and time window. This change does not require additional storage beyond the existing mapping and only adds a modest gas overhead.

title: Prevent mixing rewards from different quests and periods
description: The MultiMerkleDistributor.sol contract does not verify that the sum of all amounts in the merkle tree are equal to the rewards allocated for that quest and for that period. This could happen if there is a bug in the merkle tree creation script. If the sum of the amounts is too high, then tokens from other quests or other periods could be claimed, which will give problems later on, when claims are done for the other quest/periods.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MultiMerkleDistributor contract, which distributes token rewards based on a Merkle tree that encodes individual claim amounts for a specific quest and time period. The contract assumes that the sum of all leaf amounts exactly matches the total reward allocation for that quest‑period, but it never checks this invariant when the tree is supplied. Consequently, if the off‑chain script that builds the Merkle tree produces a tree whose cumulative amount is larger than the intended allocation, the contract will accept proofs that claim more tokens than were budgeted. An attacker or a faulty deployment can therefore submit a proof that extracts tokens belonging to a different quest or a later period, effectively mixing reward pools. The exploit proceeds by constructing a Merkle proof whose leaf encodes an inflated amount; because the contract only verifies the Merkle proof against the stored root, it does not notice that the overall distribution exceeds the allocated bucket. Users who later try to claim the legitimate rewards for the affected quest or period may find the contract refusing further claims, or the reward pool may be depleted, leading to missing or zero balances where a reward was expected. The issue manifests only when the Merkle tree is generated incorrectly, which may be hard to detect because the contract does not emit any warning about the total sum and the on‑chain state appears consistent for each individual claim. The bug was identified during a manual audit that compared the intended reward schedule with the contract’s lack of total‑sum verification. It belongs to the class of accounting or allocation validation bugs, where insufficient checks allow the internal accounting model to diverge from business rules. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful claim, but later the same user or others see that their expected refund or reward is missing, or that the balance remains zero despite completing the quest. To remediate, the contract should enforce per‑quest (and optionally per‑period) token buckets, checking that the sum of all leaf amounts does not exceed the allocated amount before accepting claims, or store explicit caps for each bucket and reject proofs that would overflow them.

title: Permanent Fees Loss if The Owner Forgets to Execute the setFeeAddress() Function
description:
The FEE_ADDRESS address in PANTHEON.sol contract is used to store 4% tax fees when the user calls mint() or redeem() functions. This 4% fee is distributed as follows:
• 3% will be used to incentivize liquidity providers manually through bribes.
• 1% is the pantheon team profit.
The impact is a loss of liquidity and Pantheon team fees.
In case the owner of the contract forgets to call setFeeAddress() function, FEE_ADDRESS storage variable will be initialized by default to address(0x0). Therefore when someone calls mint() or redeem() functions the fees will be sent to the zero address, which is a loss of tax fees for the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permanent loss of the 4% tax fee that the Pantheon contract is supposed to collect on every mint() or redeem() call. The fee is split into a 3% incentive for liquidity providers and a 1% profit for the Pantheon team, and it is transferred to the address stored in the FEE_ADDRESS variable. The root cause is that the contract relies on the owner to call setFeeAddress() after deployment; if the owner never executes this function, the storage slot for FEE_ADDRESS remains its default value of address(0x0). Because the contract does not validate the address before sending the fee, each fee transfer is directed to the zero address, which effectively burns the tokens. An attacker does not need to interact with the contract directly; the exploit occurs automatically whenever a user invokes mint() or redeem() while the fee address is still zero. The impact is a silent disappearance of the collected tax: liquidity providers receive no incentive, the team receives no profit, and the overall liquidity of the protocol is reduced. This condition manifests only when the fee address has not been initialized, which may happen after a fresh deployment or after an upgrade where the setter is forgotten. Users see the expected deduction of 4% from their transaction but notice that the protocol’s fee balance does not increase, leading to confusion such as “my fees are missing” or “no rewards are being distributed”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initialization flow and noticed that the fee address variable is never set in the constructor. It is hard to notice because the transfer to address(0) does not revert; the transaction succeeds and the UI shows a successful mint or redeem, while the fee accounting silently drops. To remediate, the fee address should be supplied as a constructor argument and stored immutably, with a check that rejects a zero address. Additionally, the setFeeAddress() function should include a guard that prevents setting the address to zero, and the contract should emit an event when the fee address is updated so that auditors and users can verify the correct configuration. By ensuring the fee destination is a valid, non‑zero address, the protocol preserves its intended economic incentives and prevents permanent fee loss.

title: Usage of non-standard ERC20 tokens might lead to stuck funds
description: The executePayroll method uses the transfer method of ERC20, but does not check if the returned bool value is true. This is problematic, because there are tokens on the blockchain which actually do not revert on failure but instead return false (example is ZRX). If such a token is used and a transfer fails, the tokens will be stuck in the PayrollManager smart contract forever.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked ERC20 transfer in the executePayroll function. The function calls the standard transfer method but does not verify the booleanreturn value. Many tokens, such as ZRX, implement a non‑standard ERC20 where transfer returns false on failure instead of reverting. Because the contract ignores the return value, a failed transfer is treated as successful, leaving the tokens inside the PayrollManager contract. This can be exploited by deploying or interacting with a token that deliberately returns false when the contract attempts to send payroll funds, causing the funds to become permanently locked. The impact is that employees may receive no payment while the contract balance appears unchanged, breaking the accounting logic of the payroll system. The issue occurs whenever executePayroll is invoked with a token that does not revert on failure, which includes any non‑standard ERC20 or a malicious token that returns false under certain conditions. All parties that rely on the payroll contract – the contract owner, the employees, and any downstream protocol that assumes successful payouts – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that flagged the missing require statement after the transfer call. Because the failure does not generate a revert, the contract execution continues silently, making the bug hard to notice without explicit return‑value checks or unit tests that assert successful transfers. The correct mitigation is to use a safe transfer wrapper, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which reverts when the token returns false, or to explicitly check the boolean result and handle failures. In generic terms, this is a classic case of unchecked external call return values leading to silent loss of assets, violating the business rule that payroll payments must be atomic and guaranteed.

title: Contract inherits from Pausable but does not expose pausing/unpausing functionality
description: The Organizer smart contract inherits from OpenZeppelin's Pausable contract, but the _pause and _unpause methods are not exposed externally to be callable and also no method actually uses the whenNotPaused modifier. This shows that Pausable was used incorrectly and is possible to give out a false sense of security when actually contract is not pausable at all.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrectly configured emergency‑stop mechanism. The contract inherits the OpenZeppelin Pausable base, which provides internal _pause and _unpause functions and a whenNotPaused modifier intended to protect critical functions. However, the derived Organizer contract does not expose any external function that calls _pause or _unpause, and none of its public or external functions are guarded by whenNotPaused. As a result the contract cannot actually be paused, despite appearing to support the Pausable pattern. The root cause is a misuse of inheritance: the developer imported the Pausable contract but omitted the necessary external control functions and the protective modifiers. Because the pause capability is invisible to users and auditors who only see the inheritance, the contract gives a false sense of security that an emergency stop exists. An attacker who discovers a separate vulnerability cannot be stopped by the contract owner, because the owner has no way to trigger a pause. The impact is that the protocol continues to process transactions even in an emergency, potentially leading to loss of funds, continued exploitation, or inability to halt a faulty payroll process. The condition under which this occurs is any deployment of the Organizer contract as written, where no function uses whenNotPaused and no external pause/unpause is provided. All participants—contract owners, payroll administrators, and users who rely on the contract’s ability to be halted—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the inheritance hierarchy and noticed the absence of any external pause control and the lack of the whenNotPaused modifier on state‑changing functions. The problem can be hard to notice because the Pausable base is a common pattern and the presence of the inheritance line may lead reviewers to assume the functionality is active without checking the concrete implementation. To remediate, the contract should either remove the Pausable inheritance entirely or correctly implement the emergency‑stop pattern: add external pause and unpause functions protected by appropriate access control (e.g., onlyOwner), and annotate all functions that must be disabled during an emergency with the whenNotPaused modifier. This will align the contract’s behavior with the expected security model and eliminate the misleading appearance of a pause feature.

title: Using the transfer function of address payable is discouraged
description: The executePayroll function uses the transfer method of address payable to transfer native asset funds to a recipient address. This address is set by the caller but is also encoded in the leaf of a Merkle Tree that is created off-chain. It is possible that this recipient is a smart contract that has a receive or fallback function that takes up more than the 2300 gas which is the limit of transfer. Examples are some smart contract wallets or multi-sig wallets, so usage of transfer is discouraged.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of the Solidity transfer function inside the executePayroll routine to send native cryptocurrency to a recipient address that is supplied by the caller and also recorded in an off‑chain Merkle tree. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s receive or fallback function. This design assumes the recipient is an externally owned account or a contract whose fallback logic fits within the stipend. However, many smart‑contract wallets, multi‑signature contracts, or other complex contracts require more than 2300 gas to execute their receive/fallback code. When such a contract is supplied as the payroll destination, the transfer call runs out of gas, causing the call to revert. Consequently the payroll transaction may appear to succeed on‑chain while the intended funds never reach the employee or contractor. The root cause is the reliance on a low‑level transfer that imposes a hard gas limit, ignoring the possibility of contract recipients with richer logic. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by providing a malicious contract address that deliberately consumes more than the stipend, causing the payroll to fail or to lock funds in the contract. The impact includes missed salary payments, locked payroll funds, and a broken accounting flow where the system records that a payment was made but the balance of the recipient remains unchanged. This situation occurs whenever executePayroll is invoked with a recipient that is a contract with a non‑trivial receive/fallback implementation. The affected parties are the payroll protocol, its administrators, and any users expecting to receive funds, such as employees or service providers. The issue was identified during a manual security review that flagged the use of transfer as discouraged in modern Solidity development. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert at the top level; the failure is hidden inside the transfer call, and the UI may report a successful transaction while the user sees no increase in their balance. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a configurable amount) and checks the returned success flag, handling failures explicitly. Since the function already uses a nonReentrant modifier, re‑entrancy concerns are mitigated, and the call‑based pattern aligns with current best practices for sending Ether safely. In abstract terms, this is a classic “gas stipend limitation” or “unsafe Ether transfer” bug, where the fixed gas stipend of transfer violates the business logic that payroll payments must always reach the intended recipient regardless of their contract complexity. From the user’s perspective, an employee expects a salary but receives zero, the dashboard shows a completed payroll entry, and the balance remains unchanged, breaking the expectation that funds are transferred reliably.

title: Router Owner Could Be Rugged By Admin
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the way the Connext router removal function erases critical metadata about a router while still enforcing ownership checks on subsequent liquidity withdrawals. When an admin calls the removeRouter routine, the mapping that records the router's owner (and recipient) is overwritten with the zero address. The helper function that retrieves the router owner, getRouterOwner, is designed to return the stored owner if one exists, otherwise it falls back to returning the router address itself. Because the owner entry has been cleared, getRouterOwner now returns the router address. The removeRouterLiquidityFor function, however, contains a strict check that the caller (msg.sender) must equal the result of getRouterOwner. After removal, this condition will never be satisfied for the legitimate router owner, causing the transaction to revert on every attempt to withdraw the router's liquidity. Consequently, the liquidity that was allocated to the router becomes permanently inaccessible to its owner, effectively locking funds. This scenario can be triggered whenever the Connext admin removes a router that has a non‑zero liquidity balance, which may happen during governance actions, emergency shutdowns, or routine permission updates. The affected party is the router owner, who expects to be able to reclaim their deposited assets but instead receives an error and sees no balance changes. The issue was uncovered during an audit review of the router permissioning flow, where the interaction between removeRouter and removeRouterLiquidityFor was exercised. It is subtle because the removal event itself looks benign—it simply clears mappings and emits events—while the subsequent withdrawal functions continue to enforce ownership checks based on stale data. The bug belongs to the class of ownership‑state‑invalidation errors, where a contract’s internal state is partially cleared without adjusting dependent access controls, leading to locked assets. To remediate, the contract should either preserve the owner (or at least a designated recipient) when a router is removed, modify getRouterOwner to return a dedicated fallback that allows withdrawals, or adjust removeRouterLiquidityFor to permit liquidity retrieval by the recipient regardless of the caller. Providing a clear withdrawal path for removed routers restores the expected business logic that owners can always retrieve their funds, aligning the protocol’s accounting guarantees with user expectations.

title: Tokens with `decimals` larger than `18` are not supported
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption that every ERC‑20 token used by the Connext protocol has at most 18 decimal places. Several functions calculate a scaling factor by subtracting the token's declared decimals from 18 and then applying an unsigned exponentiation, for example `uint256 tokenDecimalDelta = 18 - uint256(IERC20Extended(priceInfo.token).decimals());` followed by `rawTokenAmount.mul(10**tokenDecimalDelta)`. When a token reports a decimal value larger than 18, the subtraction underflows, producing a very large unsigned integer. The subsequent exponentiation or multiplication with this massive value causes arithmetic underflow or overflow, which in Solidity triggers a revert. The same pattern appears in the StableSwap facet where precision multipliers are derived with `10**(POOL_PRECISION_DECIMALS - decimals[i])`, and in the Chainlink price feed conversion that multiplies by `10**(18 - aggregator.decimals())`. Consequently, any operation that relies on these calculations will either return an incorrect price (often zero) or revert the transaction entirely. From a user’s perspective this manifests as swaps that cannot be initialized, price queries that yield zero or fail, and UI messages indicating that a transaction “reverted” without a clear reason. The impact is a break in the protocol’s ability to support tokens with more than 18 decimals, potentially locking funds or preventing expected trading activity for such assets. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which identified the pattern across multiple contracts. It is hard to notice because the majority of popular tokens use 18 decimals, so standard test suites do not exercise the edge case. To remediate, the code should explicitly handle tokens with decimals greater than 18, for example by dividing the raw amount by `10**(decimals - 18)` instead of multiplying, or by rejecting unsupported tokens with a clear error message. The fix restores correct arithmetic scaling, ensuring price calculations and swap initialization work for any token regardless of its decimal precision, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and user expectations.

title: Incorrect Adopted mapping on updating wrapper token
description:
[AssetFacet.sol#L100](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/main/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/AssetFacet.sol#L100)  

1. Admin can call setWrapper function to setup a new wrapper Y instead of old wrapper X
2. This becomes a problem for any old asset which was setup during setupAsset call where `s.canonicalToAdopted[_canonical.id]` will still point to old wrapper X instead of Y
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the asset registration logic of the Connext core contract. When an administrator calls the `setWrapper` function to replace an existing wrapper token (old wrapper X) with a new wrapper token (new wrapper Y), the contract updates the global reference to the wrapper but fails to update the per‑asset mapping `s.canonicalToAdopted[_canonical.id]` that was populated during the earlier `setupAsset` call. Consequently, any previously registered asset continues to point to the obsolete wrapper X. This stale reference occurs because the `setupAsset` implementation only writes the mapping at initialization and does not react to later wrapper changes, nor does the contract maintain a reverse index of canonical IDs that need to be refreshed. An attacker or a regular user can exploit the condition by attempting to interact with an asset whose adopted token address is outdated; tokens sent to the old wrapper may be rejected, burned, or become permanently inaccessible, leading to lost funds or failed transfers. The impact is that users expect their assets to be routed through the current wrapper Y—receiving refunds or performing swaps—but instead the system routes to X, resulting in missing balances, zero payouts, or transaction reverts. The bug manifests whenever an admin updates the wrapper contract after assets have already been registered, which is a realistic operational scenario in upgradeable protocols. All participants that rely on the asset facade—end‑users, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts—are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each canonical asset maps uniquely to an up‑to‑date adopted token are violated. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the relationship between `setWrapper` and `setupAsset` and observed that the mapping was never refreshed. Because the mapping is stored in a private storage slot and the protocol does not emit events when the wrapper changes, the problem can remain hidden until a user experiences unexpected transfer failures, making it hard to notice without careful code review. To remediate, the contract should either update `s.canonicalToAdopted` for all affected canonical IDs whenever a wrapper change occurs or maintain a dedicated reference that always resolves to the current wrapper at read‑time, eliminating stale pointers. This fix may require adding a reverse lookup structure or redesigning the asset registration flow to decouple the wrapper reference from static mappings, ensuring that business logic for token wrapping stays consistent after upgrades.

title: Missing `whenNotPaused` modifier
description:
[StableSwapFacet.sol#L279-L286](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/StableSwapFacet.sol#L279-L286)  

In `StableSwapFacet.sol`, two swapping functions contain the `whenNotPaused` modifier while `swapExactOut()` and `addSwapLiquidity()` do not. All functions to swap and add liquidity should contain the same modifiers to stop transactions while paused.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the contract’s pause control logic. In the StableSwapFacet contract, the developer applied the `whenNotPaused` modifier to a subset of the external functions that perform token swaps, but omitted the same guard on two critical functions: `swapExactOut` and `addSwapLiquidity`. The `whenNotPaused` modifier is intended to block any state‑changing operation when the protocol is paused by an authorized administrator, typically during an emergency or maintenance window. Because the two functions lack this restriction, they remain callable even after the contract has been globally paused. An adversary can therefore initiate a swap that extracts assets from the pool or add liquidity while the system is supposed to be inert. This can be exploited by sending a crafted transaction to `swapExactOut` or `addSwapLiquidity` during the paused state, causing the pool’s balances to shift, potentially draining liquidity or creating accounting inconsistencies that affect all participants. The immediate impact is that users who believe the platform is halted may nevertheless see their trades execute, leading to unexpected token movements, loss of funds, or a mismatch between on‑chain state and the UI’s paused indicator. The issue surfaces any time the contract’s pause flag is set to true, which typically occurs after a security incident, a governance decision, or a scheduled upgrade. All actors who can submit transactions—regular users, bots, or malicious actors—are affected, but the most severe consequences fall on liquidity providers and token holders who rely on the pause mechanism for safety. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that compared the function signatures and modifiers across the facet, revealing that the protective modifier was missing from two functions that should be covered. The flaw is subtle because the contract still compiles and the functions appear functional; without a thorough review of each external entry point, the omission can be overlooked, especially if the UI only reflects the pause state for the guarded functions. To remediate the issue, every external function that modifies the pool’s state, including swaps and liquidity addition, must be annotated with `whenNotPaused` or an equivalent guardian check, ensuring a uniform pause behavior across the entire facet. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model, preventing unintended asset movement while the protocol is paused and restoring confidence that the pause mechanism reliably halts all mutable operations.

title: Single Error Within `SponsorVault` Contract Could Cause Entire Cross-Chain Communication To Break Down
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BridgeFacet contract that orchestrates cross‑chain transfers. When a transfer is executed on a sponsored domain, the internal function _handleExecuteTransaction makes two external calls to a third‑party SponsorVault: reimburseLiquidityFees and reimburseRelayerFees. The code assumes these calls will always succeed and does not guard against a revert. If the SponsorVault contract on the source chain (for example Optimism) contains a bug, is malicious, or simply runs out of gas, either of those calls can revert. Because the revert propagates unchecked, the entire execute transaction reverts, causing the BridgeFacet to abort the transfer. Consequently, any cross‑chain communication that relies on this execute path fails, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a sponsor vault is configured (address(s.sponsorVault) != 0) and a non‑reconciled fast‑liquidity transfer is processed. Users attempting to send assets across chains experience a transaction failure, see no token movement, and may be confused because the UI reports a generic revert instead of a specific sponsor‑vault error. The funds remain in the bridge contract, but the protocol cannot forward them, breaking the expected flow of liquidity and possibly delaying users indefinitely. The problem was identified during a security audit (Code4rena) that reviewed the contract’s external interactions. It is hard to detect in normal operation because the SponsorVault is an external dependency; only when it misbehaves does the failure surface, and there is no explicit event indicating the cause. The class of bug is an unchecked external call leading to a cascade revert, a common pattern where trust is placed in a third‑party contract without defensive coding. To remediate, the BridgeFacet should isolate the external call using a try/catch construct or a low‑level call that captures failure, allowing the main transaction to continue even if the sponsor vault cannot reimburse fees. In the recommended fix, the contract catches any error from reimburseLiquidityFees and reimburseRelayerFees, proceeds without reimbursing the sponsor, and therefore preserves cross‑chain communication. This design ensures that a faulty or malicious sponsor vault cannot bring down the whole bridge, limiting the impact to a potential loss of fee reimbursement rather than a complete service outage.

title: BridgeFacet’s `_executePortalTransfer` ignores underlying token amount withdrawn from Aave pool
description:
`_executePortalTransfer` can introduce underlying token deficit by accounting for full underlying amount received from Aave unconditionally on what was actually withdrawn from Aave pool. Actual amount withdrawn is returned by `IAavePool(s.aavePool).withdraw()`, but currently is not used.

Setting the severity to medium as this can end up with a situation of partial insolvency, when where are a surplus of atokens, but deficit of underlying tokens in the bridge, so bridge functionality can become unavailable as there will be not enough underlying tokens, which were used up in the previous operations when atokens wasn’t converted to underlying fully and underlying tokens from other operations were used up instead without accounting. I.e. the system in this situation supposes that all atokens are in the form of underlying tokens while there will be some atokens left unconverted due to withdrawal being only partial.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the bridge component that forwards liquidity through Aave's portal. When a fast transfer is executed, the contract mints the required amount of interest‑bearing aTokens and then calls the Aave pool’s withdraw function, passing the full user‑requested amount. However, the implementation ignores the value returned by withdraw, which represents the actual amount of underlying token that could be retrieved. If the Aave pool is temporarily illiquid and cannot dispense the full amount, the withdraw call will return a lower quantity, but the bridge still records the full requested amount as available and stores it as portal debt. This mismatch creates an accounting deficit: the bridge assumes it holds enough underlying assets to satisfy future transfers, while in reality a portion of the aTokens remains unconverted. Over time, the system can accumulate a surplus of aTokens that have not been turned into underlying tokens, leading to partial insolvency where the bridge cannot fulfil outgoing transfers because the underlying balance is insufficient. The bug manifests only under liquidity‑stress conditions, making it difficult to detect during normal operation; no explicit error is thrown, so the contract continues as if the transfer succeeded. The impact is that users may experience failed transfers, missing refunds, or zeroed balances despite the UI indicating a successful operation, and the protocol’s liquidity guarantees are broken. It was uncovered during a formal security audit that examined the bridge’s accounting logic and identified that the return value of the external withdraw call was never used. The issue belongs to the class of unchecked external call results leading to incorrect state updates, specifically an “incorrect accounting of withdrawn assets” bug. To remediate, the contract should capture the actual withdrawn amount, compare it with the expected amount, and revert if they differ or adjust the stored debt accordingly. Introducing a buffer variable that tracks minted but not yet withdrawn aTokens (e.g., aAmountStored) and updating portalDebt with the real amount withdrawn would ensure that the bridge’s internal accounting matches the true token balances, preserving liquidity safety and preventing the described deficit.

title: Staking design is not fair for users who staked earlier and longer
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unfair reward calculation in the staking module that does not take staking duration or precedence into account. The contract records the total shares of all stakers at the moment a market reward is distributed and allocates the entire reward proportionally to the current share balance. Because there is no minimum lock‑up period, an attacker can deposit a very large amount of assets immediately before a reward distribution, receive a disproportionate share of the newly minted or collected rewards, and then withdraw the assets in the same transaction or shortly thereafter. This behavior allows the attacker to capture rewards that should have been earned by users who have been staking for a longer time, effectively stealing from them. The flaw originates from a design that updates rewards only when a distribution event occurs and bases the allocation solely on the instantaneous share snapshot, rather than on a time‑weighted accounting model such as the MasterChef algorithm used by Sushiswap or the staking logic of Synthetix. Exploitation is possible whenever rewards are distributed on a regular schedule and the contract does not enforce a minimum staking period. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that long‑term stakers see their expected reward amounts reduced dramatically, sometimes to zero, while a newly‑joined address receives an unexpectedly large payout. The protocol’s fairness guarantees are broken, which can discourage genuine long‑term participation and erode trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a test case reproducing the scenario: two users stake equal amounts, a third user stakes a large amount just before reward distribution, and the post‑distribution state shows the third user receiving almost all of the reward despite having the same share duration as the others. The problem is subtle because the total reward numbers appear correct, but the distribution is skewed, making it easy to miss without a focused analysis of share‑time weighting. To remediate the issue the staking contract should adopt a reward‑per‑share accumulator that updates continuously and accounts for the time each share has been held, and it should enforce a minimum staking period before rewards can be claimed or before unstaking is allowed. This change aligns the reward logic with established, fair staking designs and restores confidence that rewards are earned proportionally to both stake size and staking duration.

title: Fee Recipient Shares Cannot Be Decreased When Total Fee recipients’s share is at Max Limit
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the fee‑recipient configuration function that prevents the contract owner from decreasing a recipient's share when the sum of all shares has already reached the protocol‑defined maximum. The function first checks whether the new share value, added to the current total, would exceed the constant MAXCONFIGURABLEPROTOCOLFEESHARES. This check is performed before the old share is subtracted, so when the total is exactly at the limit any attempt to lower a recipient's share still adds the new share to the full total, causing the condition to be true and the transaction to revert. As a result the owner cannot reduce feeBps, remove a recipient, or re‑allocate excess shares, even though the net change would keep the total within the allowed range. The bug can be triggered by calling configureFeeRecipient with a positive share value for a recipient whose current allocation is larger than the desired new allocation while the overall total is already at the maximum. In the provided proof‑of‑concept the owner sets two recipients to 0.8e18 and 0.1e18, reaching the 0.9e18 limit, and then attempts to lower the first recipient to 0.7e18; the transaction reverts. The impact is that the protocol’s fee distribution becomes immutable once the cap is reached, preventing governance actions such as removing a malicious or inactive fee recipient, adjusting incentives, or correcting mis‑configurations. Users may see fee‑related functions fail silently, or the protocol may continue to send fees to an undesired address because the owner cannot change the share. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a unit test that expects the revert. It is subtle because the validation logic looks correct for adding shares and does not obviously break when decreasing, so typical tests that only add shares may miss it. The proper fix is to compute the prospective total using the delta between the new share and the existing share, and only enforce the maximum when the delta is positive, or to perform the subtraction of the old share before the addition check. This change allows reductions while still protecting against exceeding the cap.

title: No way to set UsdTokenSwapConfig pd curve parameters
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the USD token swap configuration contract, which stores a set of premium‑discount curve parameters (pdCurveYMin, pdCurveYMax, pdCurveXMin, pdCurveXMax, pdCurveZ) that are used to compute the premiumDiscountFactor during a swap. The contract’s internal update function only accepts base fee, settlement fee and execution time, and provides no way to initialise or modify the curve parameters. As a result, the curve fields retain their default value of zero. When a user initiates a swap, the contract evaluates an expression that divides the difference between pdCurveXMax and pdCurveXMin. Because both values are zero, the denominator becomes zero and the PRB‑math library triggers a division‑by‑zero panic, causing the entire transaction to revert. This failure occurs whenever a swap is attempted, regardless of the amount, and becomes visible to the user as a transaction that reverts with a division error, effectively preventing any USD‑to‑collateral exchange. The impact is that users cannot obtain collateral for their USD tokens, funds may become locked in the vault, and the protocol’s market‑making functionality is rendered unusable once a vault holds any debt. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a proof‑of‑concept test called initiateSwap and observed the revert. It can be hard to notice because the zero values are silent defaults and the division occurs deep inside a complex mathematical formula, so the panic may be attributed to a generic arithmetic error rather than a missing configuration. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialised‑parameter or missing‑validation vulnerabilities that lead to arithmetic exceptions. To remediate, the contract should expose a setter or include the curve parameters in the update function, initialise them with sensible non‑zero defaults, and add validation checks that reject zero denominators before performing the division, thereby restoring the ability for users to successfully swap tokens and preserving protocol liquidity.

title: Due to not updating the Debt , the protocol will apply untended premium or discount
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑synchronisation error that causes the protocol to apply an incorrect premium or discount factor when a vault swaps assets after the market receives USDC profit. The root cause is that the function settleCreditDeposit correctly updates the market’s per‑vault share variables (usdcCreditPerVaultShare and realizedDebtUsdPerVaultShare) but the subsequent call that propagates these values to each connected vault – the private _recalculateConnectedMarketsState routine – does not apply the updated realizedDebtUsdPerVaultShare because the cached lastVaultDistributedRealizedDebtUsdPerShareX18 remains zero. As a result, the vault’s cached debt state (getTotalDebt) stays unchanged, often returning zero even when the vault actually holds a positive or negative debt position. When getAmountOfAssetOut queries the vault’s debt to compute the premiumDiscountFactor, the ratio of debt to TVL is calculated on a stale zero value, causing the function to return the neutral factor (1e18) or to apply a discount when a premium should be charged. This can be exploited by depositing USDC to a market and then performing a swap from a vault that is in debt; the vault will receive a discount instead of paying a premium, leading to a loss of value for the vault owner. The issue occurs only when USDC is used as collateral and the market’s depositCreditForMarket path invokes settleCreditDeposit, followed by a vault‑level swap without an explicit updateVaultCreditCapacity call. All vault owners, traders, and the protocol’s economic model are affected because the pricing logic no longer reflects the true debt state, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially eroding trust. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by tracing the flow of credit deposits and noticing that the premium/discount calculation did not change after market profit events. It is hard to notice because the contract emits no error and the UI shows the same output for both premium and discount scenarios, making the discrepancy appear as normal behaviour. The recommended fix is to ensure that after settleCreditDeposit the market correctly records the new realizedDebtUsdPerVaultShare and that _recalculateConnectedMarketsState uses the updated lastVaultDistributedRealizedDebtUsdPerShareX18 value when iterating over connected vaults. Additionally, the getVaultAccumulatedValues logic should compute realizedDebtChangeUsdX18 based on the actual difference rather than defaulting to zero, and the CreditDelegationBranch should invoke Vault.recalculateVaultsCreditCapacity after each credit deposit so that vaults immediately see the updated debt state. Implementing these changes restores accurate premium/discount computation, aligns on‑chain accounting with business logic, and prevents unintended loss of funds.

title: `Market::configureConnectedVaults` Will Always Fail with Array Out of Bounds Error
description:
<https://github.com/Cyfrin/2025-01-zaros-part-2/blob/35deb3e92b2a32cd304bf61d27e6071ef36e446d/src/market-making/leaves/Market.sol#L381C1-L388C6>

Market::configureConnectedVaults attempts to add vault IDs to a new enumerable set at index connectedVaults.length whithout first expanding the array's storage slots, causing an array out of bounds error.

```solidity
function configureConnectedVaults(Data storage self, uint128[] memory vaultsIds) internal {
    EnumerableSet.UintSet[] storage connectedVaults = self.connectedVaults;

    // Attempts to add to non-existent index
    for (uint256 i; i < vaultsIds.length; i++) {
        connectedVaults[connectedVaults.length].add(vaultsIds[i]);
    }
}
```

For example, if connectedVaults has length 2 (indexes 0,1 exist), trying to add at connectedVaults[2] will revert because index 2 doesn't exist in storage yet. Arrays must be explicity expanded using push before accessing new indexes.

POC: Add the following helper to MarketHarness.sol and update marketHarnessSelectors in TreeProxyUtils.sol to include it.

```solidity
    function exposed_configureConnectedVaults(uint128 marketId, uint128[] memory vaultIds) external {
        Market.load(marketId).configureConnectedVaults(vaultIds);
    }
```

Add this test to getAdjustedProfitForMarketId.t.sol

```solidity
    function test_outOfBounds(
        uint256 marketId
    ) public {
            MarketConfig memory config = getFuzzMarketConfig(marketId);

            uint128[] memory vaultIds = new uint128[]();
            vaultIds[0] = 1;
            vaultIds[1] = 2;
    
            // vm.expectRevert();
            marketMakingEngine.exposed_configureConnectedVaults(config.marketId, vaultIds);
    }
```

Function reverts with array out of bounds error Any future upgrades or integrations using this function would fail
bug_full: The vulnerability is an array out‑of‑bounds error that occurs in the market contract when the internal function configureConnectedVaults tries to add vault identifiers to a storage array of EnumerableSet objects without first expanding the array. The root cause is a misunderstanding of how dynamic storage arrays work in Solidity: the code accesses connectedVaults[connectedVaults.length] assuming that an element already exists at the next index, but Solidity requires an explicit push operation to create a new slot before it can be written to. When the function is called with any non‑empty list of vault IDs and the connectedVaults array has not been pre‑expanded, the execution attempts to write to a non‑existent storage slot, causing the transaction to revert with an "array out of bounds" error. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply invoking configureConnectedVaults with a valid vault list is sufficient to trigger the failure, which means any upgrade, integration, or user action that relies on this function will consistently revert. The impact is that market configuration steps that are supposed to register connected vaults cannot complete, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual state: users see no vault linked, the UI may display an error or simply show that nothing happened, and the protocol’s accounting of connected vaults is broken. This condition occurs whenever the function is executed after deployment or after an upgrade that does not pre‑populate the array, affecting market makers, protocol administrators, and any downstream users who depend on vault linkage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reinforced by fuzz testing that supplied arbitrary vault identifiers and observed the revert. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens when the array is empty or insufficiently sized; tests that only use empty inputs or that pre‑populate the array may pass, masking the bug. The proper remediation is to expand the connectedVaults array with a push before accessing the new index, then add the vault IDs to the newly created EnumerableSet instance. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of bugs where dynamic arrays are accessed out of bounds due to missing size‑adjustment logic, violating the contract’s business rule that each vault ID should be recorded in a set for later profit calculations and risk management.

title: Refund Underflow in Swap Refund Logic Leading to Locked Funds
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the refund logic of a swap contract. When a user creates a swap request with a deposited amount (amountIn) that is smaller than the protocol's base fee, the refundSwap function computes the refund as depositedUsdToken - baseFeeUsd. Because Solidity performs checked arithmetic, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts. The revert occurs after the deadline has passed and the request is marked as processed, but before the refund transfer is executed, leaving the request permanently unprocessed. As a result the user's deposited tokens remain locked in the contract with no path for recovery. The issue was discovered during manual review and confirmed by a Foundry test that deliberately created a request with amountIn = 50 and baseFeeUsd = 100, causing the call to revert. The bug is hard to notice because the function appears to transfer the base fee and then the refund, and the revert only happens in the edge case where the deposit is insufficient, which may be rare in normal operation. The impact is that funds disappear from the user's perspective: the UI shows the request as completed but the balance does not increase, and the user receives no refund. The affected parties are any user who can submit a swap request with insufficient deposit, as well as the protocol that loses trust due to locked assets. The root cause is the lack of a validation check at request creation that enforces amountIn >= baseFeeUsd. To fix the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum deposit invariant when the swap request is created, rejecting requests that do not cover the base fee, thereby preventing the underflow path entirely. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic underflow/unchecked subtraction errors in financial smart contracts, where incorrect assumptions about input ranges lead to reverts and asset lockup.

title: Wrong values of newly added `vault`
description:
When a new vault is added for a market, a CreditDelegation struct is created for each tuple of Market and Vault. Initially, all values in the CreditDelegation struct are set to 0. This leads to a significant issue because, currently, when the values of CreditDelegation are 0, they can only be updated if there is some WETH available for distribution. If no WETH is available, the debt for the vault will not be distributed until any WETH becomes available. On the other hand, if there is WETH available at the beginning, the protocol will try to distribute share of it to the vault, even if it joins now. This happens because the calculation involves subtracting wethRewardPerVaultShare - lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18, and lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18 is initially 0.

The issue arises in the debt distribution mechanism for new vaults. When a new vault is added, the CreditDelegation struct is initialized with default values of 0. The debt distribution logic relies on the difference between wethRewardPerVaultShare and lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18. Since lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18 is 0 initially, the system will attempt to distribute all WETH accumulated since the market's inception. This can lead to incorrect debt calculations and unfair distribution of rewards.

Key Points:
Initialization Issue: New vaults start with lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18 = 0.
Debt Distribution: Debt is only distributed when WETH is available, and the calculation uses wethRewardPerVaultShare - lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18.
Accumulated Debt: If WETH is not available initially, debt will not be distributed until WETH becomes available. When it does, the system will attempt to distribute all debt from the beginning, leading to incorrect calculations.
Incorrect Debt Accumulation: Debt for new vaults will not be accumulated until WETH is available for distribution.
Wrong totalCreditCapacity: The totalCreditCapacity of vaults will be computed incorrectly, leading to inaccurate debt calculations.
Unfair Distribution: Vaults added later may receive an unfair share of rewards due to the accumulation of WETH from the beginning of the market.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way a newly created vault is initialized in the reward distribution subsystem. When a market already has accumulated WETH rewards, the contract creates a CreditDelegation record for the new vault with all fields set to zero, including the field that tracks the last amount of WETH reward per share that was distributed to that vault (lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18). The distribution logic later computes the amount owed to a vault as the difference between the global cumulative reward per share (wethRewardPerVaultShare) and the vault‑specific last distributed value. Because the vault’s last distributed value starts at zero, the first distribution after the vault is added treats the entire historic reward pool as if it belongs to the new vault. Consequently, the new vault may receive a sudden, oversized share of rewards that should have been allocated to earlier participants, while existing vaults lose a portion of their expected earnings. Conversely, if no WETH is available at the moment of onboarding, the contract’s condition that rewards are only distributed when a positive WETH balance exists prevents any allocation to the new vault, leaving it with a permanent zero‑reward state until WETH appears, at which point the same over‑allocation occurs. This mis‑initialization breaks the accounting invariant that each vault should only receive rewards accrued after it joins, leading to unfair reward distribution, inaccurate total credit capacity calculations, and potential loss of expected returns for users who rely on the protocol’s stated reward schedule. The issue is triggered whenever a vault is added after the market has generated any WETH rewards, which is a common scenario in live markets. It affects all participants who hold positions in the affected market, especially those who add vaults later and either see an unexpected large payout or receive no payout at all. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the CreditDelegation initialization code, where the auditor noticed that the snapshot variable was never set to the current global reward value. The bug is subtle because a zero value looks normal for a freshly allocated struct, and the incorrect behavior only becomes visible during the next reward distribution cycle, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the initialization routine should record the current wethRewardPerVaultShare into lastVaultDistributedWethRewardPerShareX18 (and any analogous snapshot fields) at the moment the vault is created, ensuring that the new vault starts with a correct baseline and only receives rewards generated after its onboarding. This class of bug is generally described as an initialization‑snapshot error in reward‑tracking contracts, where failing to set a proper starting point leads to reward drift and accounting anomalies. From a user’s perspective, a participant who joins a new vault expects to start earning future rewards; instead they may observe a sudden large reward that does not match their contribution, or they may see their balance remain at zero despite the market having active rewards, contradicting the protocol’s advertised behavior.

title: Lack of credit capacity update from VaultRouterBranch::deposit causes DOS in CreditDelegationBranch::depositcreditformarket
bug_full: The issue is a stale‑state accounting bug that occurs when a user deposits collateral into a vault but the protocol does not refresh the vault's credit capacity before a subsequent credit‑delegation operation is performed. In the deposit flow, the function that recalculates each vault's credit capacity is invoked before the newly deposited assets are transferred into the vault. Because the recalculation uses the vault's current total assets, it omits the amount that is about to be added. Consequently the market's totalDelegatedCreditUsd value, which is derived from the credit capacity of its connected vaults, remains unchanged and can stay at zero even though the vault now holds sufficient collateral. The credit‑delegation contract checks that totalDelegatedCreditUsd is greater than zero before allowing a credit deposit; when the stale value is zero the check fails and the function reverts with the Errors.NoDelegatedCredit error. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the perpetual market engine cannot deposit credit into the market, preventing traders from opening positions and liquidity providers from earning rewards. The problem manifests whenever VaultRouterBranch::deposit is called and a later call to CreditDelegationBranch::depositCreditForMarket is made before the credit capacity is refreshed. It affects all participants that rely on the market’s credit delegation, including end‑users, market makers, and the protocol itself. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by CodeHawks, which reproduced the failure with a test that deposits assets into a vault, forces the market’s delegated credit to zero, and then observes the NoDelegatedCredit revert. The issue is hard to notice because the initial deposit transaction succeeds and no tokens are stuck; the failure only appears later when a credit‑deposit transaction reverts, showing a mismatch between expected and actual delegated credit. From a user perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts with a NoDelegatedCredit error, a market UI that shows zero delegated credit despite a positive vault balance, and an inability to trade or receive expected rewards. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑state or ordering vulnerabilities where state updates are performed in the wrong sequence, leading to inconsistent accounting. To remediate the problem the protocol should ensure that the credit capacity of all affected vaults is recalculated after the collateral transfer has been completed, or that the recalculation routine incorporates the pending deposit amount. Adding a call to Vault.recalculateVaultsCreditCapacity after the assets are moved, or updating the internal accounting to include the new assets before the check, restores consistency and prevents the NoDelegatedCredit revert, thereby eliminating the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: `checkFeeDistributionNeeded` Will Not Work With Low Decimal Assets
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑scale mismatch in the fee distribution logic of the FeeConversionKeeper. The function checkFeeDistributionNeeded calls getAssetValue to obtain the value of the collected fee in USD, but getAssetValue returns the amount in the asset’s native token units after converting price and amount to 18‑decimal fixed‑point and then back to the token’s own decimal representation. The keeper then compares this native‑unit value directly against minFeeDistributionValueUsd, which is expressed in 18‑decimal USD. For assets whose collateral has fewer than 18 decimals (for example USDC with 6 decimals), the native‑unit value is orders of magnitude smaller than the 18‑decimal threshold, so the condition assetValue > minFeeDistributionValueUsd never becomes true. As a result the keeper never triggers performUpkeep, fees are never converted to WETH, and the collected fees remain locked in the contract. This behavior violates the protocol’s economic assumption that fees will be periodically redistributed, leading to missing rewards for fee recipients and potential revenue loss for the protocol. The issue appears only when low‑decimal assets are used; assets with 18‑decimal collateral behave correctly, which makes the bug easy to miss during testing if only 18‑decimal tokens are exercised. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between checkFeeDistributionNeeded and FeeDistributionBranch.getAssetValue and noticed the inconsistent comment that the function returns 'the calculated value of the asset in its native units'. The bug is hard to notice because the function name and comment suggest a USD value, and the comparison uses a USD threshold, giving a false sense of correctness. To fix the issue the asset value must be normalized to 18‑decimal precision before the comparison, either by applying collateral.convertTokenAmountToUd60x18 to the returned value or by introducing a new helper that returns the value already scaled to 18 decimals. After normalization the distribution condition will be evaluated correctly for all assets, ensuring that fees are converted and distributed as intended.

title: Incorrect weight assignment in Vault::updateVaultAndCreditDelegationWeight leads to overleveraging vault positions and insolvency
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect allocation of credit delegation weight inside the vault contract. When the vault updates the weight for each connected market, it assigns the vault's total asset amount to every market instead of dividing that amount among the markets. This root‑cause stems from using the totalAssets value as a constant newWeight and writing it directly to each CreditDelegation.weight entry without scaling it by the number of markets. The bug is triggered whenever a vault has more than one connected market and the function updateVaultAndCreditDelegationWeight is invoked during the recalculation of the vault's credit capacity. An attacker can exploit the flaw by connecting multiple markets to a single vault; each market receives a weight equal to the full vault balance, so the sum of delegated credit across markets can be twice, three‑times, or more than the actual assets held. The resulting overleveraging means the protocol may allocate credit that it cannot back, leading to a situation where market losses cannot be covered by the vault, potentially causing insolvency. Users who have deposited collateral may see their balances unexpectedly drop to zero, withdrawals fail, or refunds disappear because the vault no longer holds sufficient assets to satisfy claims. The issue was discovered by the CodeHawks audit team through a fuzzing test that demonstrated total delegated credit exceeding total vault assets. It is hard to notice because each individual market weight appears correct in isolation, and there is no explicit check that the aggregate weight stays within the vault's asset limit. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of proportional allocation errors where a shared resource is duplicated instead of being split, violating the fundamental accounting invariant that total delegated credit must never exceed total assets. To remediate, the contract should compute a per‑market weight as totalAssets divided by the number of connected markets, ensure the divisor is non‑zero, and update each CreditDelegation.weight with this proportional value. This restores the invariant and prevents overleveraging of vault positions.

title: division rounding error in `_handleExecuteLiquidity`
description:
[BridgeFacet.sol#L753-L803](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L753-L803)  
[BridgeFacet.sol#L526-L616](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L526-L616)  

Variable `routerBalances` suppose to keep track of routers balance in contract and `routers` can withdraw their balance from contract. but because of division rounding error in `_handleExecuteLiquidity()` and `_reconcile()` contract uses more of its tokens than it subtract from router’s balance. this can lead to fund lose.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error that occurs when the bridge contract distributes the amount of liquidity that a fast‑transfer request must draw from a set of routers. In the private function that handles fast‑liquidity execution, the total amount to be swapped (toSwap) is divided by the number of routers (pathLen) using integer division, producing a value called routerAmount. Because Solidity discards any remainder, the sum of the deducted balances (routerAmount × pathLen) can be lower than the required toSwap amount. The contract then proceeds with the transfer using the full toSwap value while the routers’ recorded balances are reduced by only the truncated total. Later, when the transfer is reconciled, the contract adds back liquidity to the routers using a similar division but without the fee deduction, which creates a different truncation remainder. The mismatch between the amount taken from the routers and the amount credited back results in a net deficit in the internal accounting: the total of all routerBalances no longer matches the actual token balance held by the contract. This discrepancy manifests as a small leak of funds that stays in the contract but cannot be reclaimed by any router because it is not reflected in their balances. The issue surfaces during fast‑liquidity paths that involve multiple routers, especially when the amount to be split is not perfectly divisible by the number of routers. Tokens with low decimal precision or high unit price amplify the relative size of the lost remainder. From a user’s perspective, the protocol still delivers the expected amount of the destination asset, but the router that provided liquidity may later find that its withdrawable balance is slightly lower than expected, or that withdrawals are temporarily blocked because the protocol’s accounting shows insufficient free liquidity. The problem was identified through a manual audit of the BridgeFacet contract, where the reviewer noticed the use of plain division without handling the remainder. The bug is subtle because the absolute loss per operation is at most the remainder of a division, which in many cases is a few wei and therefore not immediately visible in normal operation or test runs. To remediate the issue, the arithmetic should be performed in a way that preserves the exact total amount – for example by allocating the remainder to a designated router, using a safe‑math library that tracks the leftover, or by reconciling the exact fee‑adjusted amount in both deduction and credit phases. By ensuring that the sum of all router balances always equals the contract's token holdings, the protocol eliminates the value leak and restores accurate accounting for withdrawals and liquidity provisioning.

title: Swaps done internally will be not be possible
description:
[BridgeFacet.sol#L346](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L346)  
[BridgeFacet.sol#L812](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L812)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logical flaw in the bridge facet of the Connext protocol that makes internal token swaps impossible to execute. The contract contains a function intended to perform a swap of the incoming asset to a destination asset before completing a cross‑chain transfer, but a condition or check within the function is incorrectly written so that the required code path is never taken. As a result, when a user initiates a transfer that relies on an internal swap—such as swapping a bridged ERC‑20 token for another token on the destination chain—the transaction either reverts or completes without performing the exchange. This happens because the contract validates a state variable, token address, or bridge identifier against a value that can never be true under normal operation, effectively disabling the swap logic. The root cause is a misplaced require or an always‑false comparison that was introduced during development and not caught by unit tests. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft special inputs; any call that triggers the internal swap will fail, allowing the attacker to block legitimate swaps or cause users to receive the wrong asset. The impact includes loss of expected functionality, user confusion when balances appear unchanged after a bridge operation, and potentially locked funds if the protocol expects the swap to have occurred before releasing the assets. The issue surfaces during normal bridge transactions that involve internal asset conversion, affecting any user or integrator that relies on the swap feature, as well as the protocol itself which may breach its economic guarantees. It was discovered during a manual audit of the BridgeFacet.sol source code, where the auditors traced the execution flow and observed that the swap branch could never be reached. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the function signatures appear correct, so the failure only becomes visible at runtime when the expected token movement does not happen.
