This mismatch causes the reward calculation formula to apply an outdated share denominator to a new reward rate, leading to an over‑ or under‑allocation of rewards. An attacker or the contract owner can exploit the flaw by adding a token with a high reward rate or by lowering the reward rate after a period of accrual, then allowing users to claim rewards based on the outdated accounting state. The impact is an unfair distribution of incentives: some participants may receive more tokens than their proportional stake warrants, while honest stakers may see their expected rewards reduced or even disappear. The bug manifests when any of the mentioned configuration functions are called – typically before the pool start block or during its lifetime – without a preceding call to _updatePool(). Users experience symptoms such as unexpectedly high reward balances for certain tokens, sudden drops to zero for others, or overall reward amounts that do not match the advertised rate. Because the contract still emits events and appears to function, the issue can be difficult to detect without deep inspection of the accounting logic. The problem was identified during a formal audit by PeckShield, which noted that the lack of timely pool updates violates the core accounting assumptions of proportional reward distribution. To remediate, the contract should call _updatePool() at the beginning of addRewardToken, updateRewardPerBlock, and any other routine that changes reward parameters, ensuring that accTokenPerShare and lastRewardBlock are synchronized before the new configuration becomes effective. This aligns the on‑chain state with the intended business logic and restores fair reward calculations.

title: Suggested Use Of nonReentrant In mint()
bug_full: The contract exposes a public mint function that calculates a number of PUSD tokens to mint, updates several internal accounting variables such as minted amount, bonus amount and staked amount, and then performs a series of external token transfers using ERC20 transferFrom and custom transfer functions. The function violates the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern because the external calls are executed before the contract’s internal state is fully committed, leaving a window in which a malicious contract called by one of the external token contracts can invoke mint again before the first execution finishes. This re‑entrancy possibility allows an attacker to trigger the mint logic multiple times in a single transaction, causing the internal accounting to diverge from the actual token balances and potentially enabling the attacker to receive more minted tokens or bonus tokens than entitled, or to drain the pools that supply the tokens. From a user perspective the symptom may be that after calling mint the expected tokens are not received, balances appear unchanged, or in the worst case the attacker’s address ends up with an inflated balance while the protocol’s reserves are reduced. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that checks for adherence to the checks‑effects‑interactions principle; it can be hard to notice because the code appears to update mappings before the external calls, and typical unit tests do not simulate a malicious contract that re‑enters the function. The vulnerability belongs to the class of re‑entrancy bugs, where external calls allow nested execution of a function that should be atomic. The recommended mitigation is to apply a nonReentrant guard (or restructure the function so that all state changes occur before any external interaction) to ensure that the contract cannot be entered again while a mint call is in progress, thereby aligning the protocol’s accounting assumptions with actual token flows and preventing funds from disappearing or being minted incorrectly.

title: Arbitrary Share Increment in Base Tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arbitrary share increment that occurs when the ERC20‑compatible BTC+ token executes its internal _transfer function with the same address as both sender and recipient. The root cause is that the routine calculates the amount of share to transfer, reads the sender’s current share, subtracts the share, then separately reads the recipient’s share – which, because the sender and recipient are identical, is still the original pre‑deduction value. The contract then writes the reduced share back to the sender slot and adds the same share to the recipient slot, effectively increasing the account’s stored share without a corresponding deduction. This logic flaw is not guarded by a check for the self‑transfer case, so any user can call transfer(address(this), address(this), amount) and cause their userShare balance to grow arbitrarily. An attacker can repeatedly perform self‑transfers with any amount, inflating their share and later withdrawing the excess from the pool, thereby draining the protocol’s funds and breaking the peg to BTC. The issue manifests only when the transfer function is invoked with identical sender and recipient addresses, a condition that is allowed by the ERC20 standard and therefore may go unnoticed during normal operation. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a higher token balance after a self‑transfer, while no corresponding deduction or event indicating a loss is visible, leading to confusion that the system is minting tokens. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the token’s rebasing logic, where the auditor identified that the share update sequence does not handle the corner case of identical addresses. Because the contract does not emit any warning and the totalShares variable remains unchanged, the problem can be subtle and may only be revealed through targeted testing of self‑transfers. To remediate, the _transfer implementation should either early‑return when _sender == _recipient or recompute the recipient’s share after the sender’s balance has been updated, ensuring that the net change is zero for self‑transfers. This correction restores the invariant that totalShares equals the sum of all userShare values and prevents arbitrary minting of tokens, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and user trust.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑centralized administrative control in the BTC+ protocol where a single governance address, currently a multi‑signature wallet, holds unrestricted authority to modify critical system parameters such as account whitelisting, risk settings, reward emission rates and the flow of assets between contract components. This concentration of power originates from the contract design that uses an onlyGovernance modifier on functions that update governance itself, change authorized claimers, and adjust the base reward rate, as well as from the proxy pattern that introduces a separate proxy‑admin key capable of upgrading the implementation. Because the governance address is not governed by a decentralized DAO but by a static multi‑sig, any compromise of the private keys or collusion among the signers gives an attacker the ability to execute these privileged operations. An attacker could, for example, replace the governance address with their own, disable legitimate claimers, whitelist malicious contracts, or set the reward emission to zero or an extreme value, thereby diverting or freezing user funds. The impact is that users may see their expected rewards disappear, deposits become unwithdrawable, or the protocol’s accounting logic be corrupted, leading to loss of confidence and potential financial loss. The issue manifests whenever the privileged functions are called, which is any time the protocol needs to update settings; it does not require a specific transaction pattern beyond the attacker possessing the governance private key. All participants—depositors, claimers, and the broader ecosystem—are affected because the protocol’s security model assumes that governance actions are trustworthy and transparent. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the access control modifiers and the proxy deployment architecture, noting that the admin key is not subject to timelocks or community voting. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation; only a malicious governance action reveals the risk, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a DAO‑style contract with on‑chain voting and timelocked upgrades, and the proxy‑admin should be similarly decentralized or removed, ensuring that no single key can unilaterally change protocol parameters or upgrade the implementation.

title: Possible Sandwich/MEV For Reduced Gains
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the yield‑collection routine that swaps protocol rewards for the underlying asset without enforcing any price protection. When the harvest() function is executed, it claims reward tokens, then uses an AMM router to exchange those tokens for BTCB via a multi‑hop path (reward → WBNB → BTCB). The router call supplies a zero minimum‑out parameter, meaning the transaction will accept any amount of BTCB regardless of the prevailing market price. An attacker who can observe the pending harvest transaction can place a sell order for the same reward token just before the harvest, depressing the pool price, and then place a buy order immediately after to restore the price. This classic sandwich or front‑running pattern forces the harvest swap to execute at a significantly worse rate, delivering fewer BTCB to the contract than would be expected under normal market conditions. The immediate impact is a reduction in the amount of BTCB that is subsequently minted into vBTC+, which translates into lower yield for token holders and a smaller performance fee transferred to the treasury. The issue manifests only when the harvest function processes a non‑zero reward balance and when an adversary can front‑run the transaction, conditions that are common in permissionless blockchain environments where transaction ordering is manipulable. The affected parties include protocol users who rely on the advertised yield, the strategist who calls harvest, and any downstream contracts that depend on the minted vBTC+. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the logic of the harvest routine and noted the absence of a slippage guard, a pattern that is also present in several sibling contracts. Because the transaction does not revert and the swap completes successfully, the loss is subtle and may be mistaken for normal market variance, making it hard to detect without detailed accounting of expected versus actual output. To remediate, the swap should be performed with a defined slippage tolerance (e.g., by specifying a non‑zero minimum‑out amount), or by referencing a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle, splitting large swaps into smaller chunks, or using a router that offers built‑in protection against sandwich attacks. These measures would align the actual received amount with the user’s expectation of a fair conversion rate, preserving the economic guarantees of the protocol while still allowing the harvest operation to function as intended.

title: Missing Authentication for Critical Functions in Strategy Contracts
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthenticated public function that enables arbitrary callers to trigger a full asset conversion inside a strategy contract. In the StrategyPickleUSDC (and similarly in StrategyPickleWBTC) the function withdrawUnderlying is declared as public and performs a series of operations: it approves the Curve pool, removes liquidity from the 3Crv token, exchanges the resulting yDAI and yUSDT tokens for USDC, and finally returns the amount of USDC obtained. Because there is no access control, any external address can impersonate the privileged Controller and invoke this function whenever the contract holds a balance of 3Crv. The root cause is the missing authentication check (e.g., onlyController modifier) and the choice of visibility for a function that should be internal to the strategy’s workflow. An attacker can exploit the bug by simply calling withdrawUnderlying with a non‑zero amount, causing the contract to swap all its 3Crv holdings into USDC and transfer the resulting USDC to the contract itself, effectively locking the funds inside the strategy or allowing the attacker to redirect them if further functions permit withdrawals. The impact is the unauthorized conversion and potential loss of user funds: users who deposited USDC expecting it to be managed by the strategy may see their USDC balance drop to zero, receive no expected returns, or observe that the strategy’s token price collapses. The condition for exploitation is that the strategy contract must hold any amount of 3Crv; once that condition is met, the function can be called at any time. The affected parties include token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol that relies on the strategy to manage assets securely. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed function visibility and access patterns. It can be hard to notice because the function’s logic appears legitimate and there is no explicit event signalling an unauthorized call, so normal monitoring may not flag the conversion as malicious. To remediate, the withdrawUnderlying function should be changed to internal (or private) so it cannot be called from outside, or an explicit access control modifier should be added to restrict calls to the designated Controller address. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that only the protocol’s controller may trigger withdrawals, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unexpected fund disappearance.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Cakepie protocol relies on a single privileged owner address that can call functions guarded by onlyOwner to modify core protocol parameters such as the addresses of MasterChefV3, reward distributor, helper contracts, the vote manager, and the list of allowed operators. Because the owner key is a plain externally owned account (EOA) without any timelock or multi‑signature protection, any compromise of that key or malicious action by the owner can instantly change the protocol’s configuration. An attacker who gains control of the owner key could, for example, replace the reward distributor with a contract that siphons rewards, set a vote manager that votes in favor of a malicious proposal, or disable the protocol by pausing it. The impact is that users may see their expected rewards disappear, deposits become unwithdrawable, or the protocol be halted without warning. The issue manifests whenever the owner executes one of the privileged functions; it does not require a specific transaction pattern beyond possessing the private key. All protocol participants—liquidity providers, stakers, and token holders—are affected because the centralised admin can alter the economic parameters that determine their returns. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the PancakeStakingBaseUpg contract, where the presence of onlyOwner modifiers on critical setters was noted and the lack of a decentralized governance or timelock mechanism was highlighted as a trust issue. The vulnerability can be hard to notice in normal operation because the functions are expected to be called only by a trusted party, and the contract does not emit warnings or enforce community approval before changes. The appropriate mitigation is to replace the single owner key with a governance contract that is controlled by a DAO, optionally protected by multi‑signature and timelock mechanisms, so that any change to protocol parameters must be voted on and delayed, reducing the risk of abrupt or malicious reconfiguration. In generic terms, this is a classic “centralized admin key” or “owner‑controlled configuration” bug, where excessive privileged authority can be abused to violate the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations.

title: Incorrect Redeem Slippage Control Enforcement in Router
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the redeem function of the Cadabra Router contract, where the slippage protection intended to guarantee a minimum amount of tokens received by the designated receiver is incorrectly enforced against the caller (msg.sender) instead of the receiver address supplied to the function. The root cause is a simple but critical mistake: the contract records the token balances of msg.sender before the redemption and then compares the post‑redeem balance of msg.sender against the user‑provided minAmounts array. Because the Balancer.redeem call transfers the redeemed tokens to the receiver argument, the caller’s balance may not change at all when the receiver is a different address. Consequently, the diff calculation (balanceAfter – balanceBefore) will be zero, causing the check to fail and the transaction to revert even though the receiver may have received the expected amount, or conversely, it allows a caller who is also the receiver to bypass the intended protection because the check is performed on the same address that receives the tokens. From a user perspective this manifests as unexpected redemption failures, “no tokens received” messages, or the ability to redeem to an address without the promised minimum amount being enforced. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Router’s redeem logic, where the balance queries were examined and the mismatch of addresses was noted. It is easy to miss because the code pattern of taking a snapshot, performing an external call, and then checking the difference is a common anti‑slippage idiom; the subtle substitution of msg.sender for receiver does not raise compiler warnings. The impact is medium severity: legitimate users may be unable to redeem to third‑party wallets, leading to denial‑of‑service or loss of expected funds, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken because the slippage guard does not protect the intended recipient. To remediate, the balance snapshots and the post‑redeem balance checks should reference the receiver address rather than msg.sender, ensuring that the minimum‑received constraint is applied to the actual token recipient. This aligns the implementation with the business logic that users expect: the receiver should receive at least the amounts specified in minAmounts, otherwise the transaction reverts.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑privileged administrative account that holds the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the Cadabra protocol. This role is able to call functions that change the fee receiver address, add or remove adapters, activate or deactivate adapters and, through the UUPSUpgradeable proxy, perform contract upgrades. The root cause is the design choice to grant a single external account unrestricted authority over protocol‑wide parameters and upgradeability, without any decentralised governance or timelock safeguards. An attacker who gains control of this admin key, or a malicious admin acting intentionally, can exploit the privileged functions by setting the fee receiver to an address they control, inserting a malicious adapter that siphons funds, deactivating legitimate adapters to disrupt service, or upgrading the proxy to a contract with hidden backdoors. The impact includes loss of user fees, unauthorized fund transfers, disruption of adapter functionality, and the possibility of a complete takeover of the protocol logic. The issue manifests whenever the admin key is used – during routine fee updates, adapter management, or contract upgrades – and it affects all participants who rely on the protocol’s fee distribution and adapter ecosystem, including token holders and liquidity providers. The risk was identified during a security audit that examined role‑based access control and noted that the admin role is assigned to a plain externally owned account rather than a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO. Because the privileged actions are gated only by role checks and emit standard events, the malicious changes may blend with legitimate activity and be hard to detect without detailed monitoring of role‑owner addresses and fee‑receiver updates. To remediate, the protocol should transfer the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to a community‑governed contract, introduce timelocks for critical parameter changes, replace the single admin with a multi‑signature or DAO‑based governance model, and consider removing upgradeability or restricting it to a vetted governance process. This class of issue is commonly referred to as an admin‑key or centralisation risk, where excessive trust placed in a single key violates the expected trust‑less and decentralized nature of smart‑contract protocols, leading to potential fund loss, unexpected zero balances, and broken accounting assumptions for users who expect their fees to be sent to the designated receiver.

title: Potential Overﬂow Mitigation in notifyRewardAmount()
bug_full: The ChocolateCash protocol implements a staking reward system that calculates a per‑token reward using the function rewardPerToken. This function multiplies the elapsed time since the last update by the current rewardRate and by a fixed scaling factor of 1e18 before dividing by the total supply of staked tokens. Because rewardRate is derived from the amount supplied to the external function notifyRewardAmount, an attacker who can call notifyRewardAmount with an excessively large reward value can cause rewardRate to become extremely large. When rewardRate is multiplied by the time delta and the scaling factor, the intermediate product can exceed the maximum value representable by a uint256, resulting in an arithmetic overflow. The overflow corrupts the computed reward per token, often resetting it to an incorrect low value or zero. Consequently, subsequent calls that distribute or claim rewards use the corrupted value, causing users to receive no rewards despite having staked tokens. From a user’s perspective the UI may still show the staked balance, but the reward balance stays at zero and claim transactions either revert or return no tokens, giving the impression that funds are locked. The bug manifests whenever the rewardDistribution address – which is the only entity authorised to invoke notifyRewardAmount – supplies a reward amount that, after division by the reward period, yields a rewardRate large enough to overflow the multiplication step. If the contract owner assigns a normal address to rewardDistribution, that address could be compromised or act maliciously, putting all stakers at risk. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the arithmetic operations in the reward calculation routine and identified the lack of explicit overflow protection for the three‑operand multiplication. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because typical reward amounts stay well within safe bounds, so the overflow only appears with extreme inputs that are not exercised in routine testing. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a maximum allowable reward amount, add explicit checks that rewardRate multiplied by the scaling factor does not overflow, and move ownership of the rewardDistribution role to a governance‑controlled address. Using Solidity 0.8’s built‑in overflow checks or a safe‑math library for the entire expression, together with input validation, would prevent the reward per token from being corrupted and ensure that users continue to receive the expected rewards.

title: Potential Overﬂow Mitigation in notifyRewardAmount()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked arithmetic overflow in the reward accounting routine of the ChocolateCash staking protocol. The function that computes the per‑token reward multiplies three uint256 values – the elapsed time, the current rewardRate and a fixed scaling factor of 1e18 – without any overflow protection. Because rewardRate is set by the external notifyRewardAmount function, a caller that can supply an arbitrarily large reward amount can cause rewardRate to become so large that the product rewardRate * 1e18 exceeds the 256‑bit limit and wraps around. This overflow propagates to rewardPerToken, which then stores an incorrect value that can be far smaller than intended or even zero. When the stored reward per token is wrong, subsequent calls that calculate individual user rewards use the corrupted figure, resulting in users receiving no rewards or being unable to withdraw accrued balances. The issue manifests only when the contract has a non‑zero totalSupply and when the rewardDistribution address (or the contract owner, if the owner is a normal externally owned account) calls notifyRewardAmount with an oversized reward argument. Because the overflow does not trigger a revert, the contract continues to operate with silently broken accounting, making the problem hard to detect during normal testing. The impact is that stakers may see their expected reward balance stay at zero, withdrawals may return no tokens, and overall funds can become effectively locked in the pool. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution logic, where the auditor noted the multiplication of three uint256 variables without SafeMath or Solidity 0.8 built‑in checks. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a maximum reward amount, add explicit overflow checks (e.g., using SafeMath or require statements that the multiplication does not overflow), move the ownership of the rewardDistribution role to a governance contract, and apply the same mitigation across all pools that share the same reward calculation pattern. In generic terms, this is an arithmetic overflow bug in a financial accounting routine that violates the invariant that rewards increase monotonically with the supplied reward amount, leading to a loss of accounting integrity and potential fund lockup.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the ChocolateCash contract relies on a single privileged admin address that can queue and execute timelocked transactions. Because the admin is a plain externally owned account (EOA) rather than a multi‑signature wallet or DAO, the contract places trust in a single private key. The root cause is that the contract’s access control checks only that msg.sender equals the stored admin address, without any additional governance or timelock enforcement for critical functions such as executeTransaction. An attacker who compromises the admin private key, or a malicious admin acting intentionally, can invoke executeTransaction to call arbitrary target contracts, transfer value, or change protocol parameters after the required delay has passed. This can be exploited by submitting a malicious transaction to the timelock queue and then, once the eta is reached, calling executeTransaction to execute it, effectively allowing unilateral changes to the protocol state, fund withdrawals, or parameter manipulation. The impact includes loss of user funds, unexpected protocol behavior, and erosion of trust because users expect community‑governed decisions but instead face centralized control. The condition occurs whenever the admin key is used to manage the timelock; there is no fallback or multi‑sig safeguard, so any compromise or rogue action directly translates into execution rights. All participants—token holders, liquidity providers, and any party relying on the protocol’s promised decentralised governance—are affected because the protocol’s security model assumes a trustless DAO but in practice depends on a single key. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined privileged routines and noted the presence of an admin‑only check without multi‑sig or DAO integration. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles correctly, the timelock delay appears to provide protection, and the admin address may be indistinguishable from a normal contract owner in block explorers. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single admin EOA with a governance contract or DAO that enforces collective decision‑making, optionally retain a timelock for queued actions, and consider a multi‑signature wallet as an interim step. By moving the admin role to a decentralized mechanism, the protocol aligns its implementation with its stated trustless model and removes the single point of failure.

title: Trust Issue Of Admin Keys
bug_full: The COGI protocol assigns a privileged admin account the MINTER_ROLE, which authorises the holder of that role to call the public mint function and create new tokens up to the contract's hard‑coded maximum supply. The root cause is that the role is granted to a single externally owned account (EOA) rather than a multi‑signature wallet or a decentralized governance contract. Because the admin key is a plain EOA, the holder can unilaterally invoke mint at any time, bypassing any community oversight or timelock mechanisms. An attacker who compromises the private key, or a malicious insider who controls the account, can call mint with an arbitrary amount (subject only to the maxSupply check) and allocate the newly minted tokens to any address, including themselves. This leads to an inflation of the token supply, dilution of existing holders’ balances, and a loss of confidence in the protocol’s economic model. The issue manifests when the privileged account is used after deployment; the contract itself does not enforce any additional checks, so the exploit can be performed silently and may only be noticed when the total supply unexpectedly jumps or when token prices drop due to perceived oversupply. All token holders, the protocol’s governance participants, and any downstream applications that rely on a fixed supply are affected because the promised scarcity is broken. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined role assignments and noticed that the MINTER_ROLE was bound to a single address without any multi‑sig or DAO guardrails. It is easy to overlook because the mint function follows a standard OpenZeppelin pattern and the role check appears legitimate, masking the centralisation risk. To remediate, the MINTER_ROLE should be transferred to a community‑governed contract, preferably a DAO that enforces proposals, voting, and timelocks before any minting can occur. Alternatively, the role could be assigned to a multi‑signature wallet to distribute control among several trusted parties. In either case, the design must eliminate the single‑point‑of‑failure admin key and align the token’s issuance mechanism with the protocol’s trust‑less and decentralized objectives.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The ChocolateCash contract contains a privileged admin account that is stored as a plain externally owned account (EOA). This admin address is the only entity that can call functions guarded by a require(msg.sender == admin) check, such as executeTransaction, which allows the admin to queue and later execute arbitrary calls after a timelock period. The root cause is the design choice to embed a single, unrestricted admin key directly in the contract code without any additional governance layer, multi‑signature protection, or role‑based access control. Because the admin key is an EOA, anyone who obtains the private key – either through phishing, key leakage, or a malicious insider – can invoke the privileged functions and direct the protocol to perform any state‑changing operation, including transferring assets, modifying fee parameters, or disabling security mechanisms. Exploitation requires only that the attacker be able to send a transaction from the admin address; the timelock does not prevent the attacker from queuing and executing a transaction they control, as the contract only checks that the transaction was previously queued, not who queued it. The impact of such an exploit is a loss of trust in the system, potential theft or misallocation of user funds, and the ability to arbitrarily change protocol dynamics, which can harm all token holders and participants. The vulnerability manifests whenever the admin key is used – for example when a governance proposal is executed – and may be difficult to notice because the require statement simply returns a generic error message and the contract’s UI does not expose the privileged nature of the caller. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined access control patterns across the codebase. To mitigate the risk, the privileged role should be transferred to a decentralized governance contract or a multi‑signature wallet, and all admin‑only functions should be protected by a robust timelock that also records the origin of the queued transaction. By removing a single point of control, the protocol can align with its intended trustless model and reduce the chance that a compromised admin key leads to fund loss or protocol manipulation.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is the existence of a single privileged admin account that is granted exclusive rights to modify critical protocol parameters such as the distribution contract address, the internal bribe address, and the list of allowed tokens. This centralised control originates from the use of the onlyOwner modifier, which ties these functions to a fixed external account rather than a decentralized governance mechanism. An attacker who gains access to the private key of this admin can invoke the privileged functions to replace the distribution address with a malicious contract, redirect bribe funds, or add and remove tokens from the allowed list, thereby altering the economic behaviour of the system. The impact includes potential loss or misdirection of user funds, disruption of token trading, and erosion of trust because the protocol’s assumed permission‑less operation is broken. The exploit can be carried out at any time after the admin key is compromised; no additional conditions are required beyond ownership of the key. All participants who rely on the protocol – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the altered parameters can change fee distribution, block rewards, or token eligibility without notice. The issue was identified during a formal security audit that examined the contract’s access control patterns and noted the lack of DAO‑style timelocks or multi‑sig governance. Because the privileged functions are ordinary external calls guarded only by a single address, the risk may be difficult to detect in production until an unexpected parameter change manifests as missing rewards, zero balances, or sudden denial of token deposits. The bug belongs to the class of centralized admin‑key or privileged‑account vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes a trustless environment but in reality depends on a single trusted entity. From a user perspective the symptoms can appear as refunds that never arrive, token deposits being rejected, or previously available tokens disappearing from the allowed list, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The recommended remediation is to replace the single owner with a DAO‑controlled contract, introduce timelocks for parameter changes, and migrate the admin role to a multi‑signature or governance framework so that no single key can unilaterally modify protocol state.

title: Potential Reentrancy Risk in Coin98Multisig::vote()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that appears in the vote() function of the Coin98Multisig contract. The function is intended to let owners vote on a pending request and, once the required vote threshold is reached, to execute the request by calling an external contract. The root cause is a violation of the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: the external call to req.destination is performed before the contract’s internal state (the stored request and vote progress) is cleared. Because the external contract is invoked with arbitrary data and value, a malicious destination can contain fallback logic that calls back into vote() while the original execution is still in progress. During this re‑entrant call the contract still believes the original request is pending, allowing the attacker to manipulate the voting counters, trigger the execution logic again, or otherwise interfere with the intended flow. Exploitation requires the attacker to be able to set the request destination to a contract they control and to ensure the vote threshold is met so that the external call is reached. Once the external call is made, the attacker’s contract can re‑enter vote(), potentially causing the same request to be executed multiple times or to be executed with altered parameters. The impact includes unauthorized execution of multisig actions, possible loss or misdirection of funds, and corruption of the voting state, which undermines the security guarantees of the multisig governance model. The bug manifests only when a request has gathered enough votes to reach the required threshold and the destination address is malicious; under normal circumstances the function behaves as expected. It affects all owners of the multisig because the state corruption can be observed by any participant, and it endangers the protocol’s funds that are meant to be guarded by the multisig. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the ordering of state updates and external calls. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to update the vote progress before the external call, giving the impression that the state is already settled, while the critical cleanup (deleting the request and vote progress) occurs only after the external call returns. To remediate the problem, the contract should either apply a re‑entrancy guard such as the nonReentrant modifier, or restructure the code so that all state changes—including clearing the request and vote progress—are performed before any external call, thereby adhering to the checks‑effects‑interactions principle. Using a pull‑payment pattern or limiting the external call to a trusted address are additional defensive measures. In short, the bug is a re‑entrancy class vulnerability caused by an out‑of‑order external call that can be exploited to execute a multisig request more than once or with tampered parameters, leading to potential fund loss and governance failure.

title: CPC Fee Collection From Unknowing Users
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee collection logic of the CopycatLeader contract, specifically within the depositTo function that mints pool shares for a user. The function is intended to transfer a user’s assets into the protocol and then charge a leader deposit fee. However, instead of charging the fee from the address that actually initiates the deposit (msg.sender), the code mistakenly calls the fee collector with the user‑provided destination address (the parameter "to"). This misdirection means that whenever a caller supplies an arbitrary address as the recipient of the minted shares, the protocol will attempt to withdraw the fee from that recipient. The root cause is a simple parameter misuse: the contract assumes the fee should be taken from the same address that receives the shares, without verifying that this address is also the one providing the assets. The fee collection is guarded by a condition that checks depositCopycatFee > 0, that the caller is not the factory contract, and that the destination address is not the contract owner. Under these conditions, the fee is deducted from the "to" address via S.collectLeaderFee(to, depositCopycatFee). An attacker can exploit this by calling depositTo with a victim’s address as the "to" argument while the attacker supplies the assets. The victim, if they have previously approved the protocol to pull fees, will see an unexpected reduction in their balance or a missing amount that they did not authorize. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a deposit transaction the expected share balance appears correctly, but the user’s token balance is lower than anticipated, often showing a zero or reduced amount where no explicit fee was displayed. This bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that fees are charged to the party that initiates the transaction, breaking trust in the protocol’s fee model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the share‑minting logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee collection call used the "to" argument instead of msg.sender. The problem can be hard to notice because the fee collection line looks syntactically correct and the function otherwise behaves as expected; only a careful review of the parameter usage reveals the mismatch. To remediate the issue, the fee collection should be revised to charge the fee from msg.sender, or alternatively the contract should enforce that the "to" address is the same as msg.sender before collecting the fee, ensuring that only the transaction initiator is charged. This change restores the intended economic flow and prevents unknowing users from being charged fees they did not trigger.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a privileged administrative key that can unilaterally withdraw all C98 tokens staked in the Coin98 staking contract. The root cause is the presence of a withdraw function that is protected only by an onlyOwner modifier, allowing the address designated as owner to call transfer on the entire token balance without any additional checks, timelocks, or community approval. An attacker who gains control of the owner address – either by compromising the multi‑signature wallet, coercing the signers, or exploiting a flaw in the governance process – can invoke withdraw with any amount up to the contract’s full balance and have the tokens transferred to the attacker’s address. The impact is a total loss of user‑deposited funds: users who have staked expect their tokens to remain locked until a defined release schedule, but the owner can drain the pool at any time, resulting in balances becoming zero, refunds not being issued, and the protocol’s promised trust‑less nature being violated. This condition occurs whenever the owner account is active and the contract holds a non‑zero token balance; it is not limited by any time‑based restriction. All participants who stake – individual users, liquidity providers, and the broader ecosystem – are affected because their assets are held in a contract that relies on a single point of control. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined privileged functions and identified that the withdraw function lacks any governance mediation. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation and the onlyOwner check appears standard; however, the hidden risk lies in the centralization of power rather than a code defect. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a decentralized governance contract, ideally a DAO, with appropriate timelocks, multi‑step execution, and community voting to ensure that no single entity can arbitrarily move user funds. This change would convert the centralised admin key into a distributed decision‑making process, aligning the contract with its intended trust‑less design and preventing the scenario where funds disappear due to an unchecked owner withdrawal.

title: Potential Less Proﬁt From Permissionless unstake()
bug_full: The contract implements a staking system where each stake is represented by an NFT and can be redeemed through the public unstake() function. The function checks that the NFT owner recorded in the stake data matches the owner returned by the ERC‑721 ownerOf() call, but it never verifies that the caller (msg.sender) is the same as that owner. Because the only access control is the owner comparison against a stored value, any external address can invoke unstake() with any tokenId and trigger the redemption logic on behalf of the legitimate holder. When an attacker calls unstake() for a victim’s tokenId, the contract transfers the principal amount plus the accrued profit to the true owner, but it also marks the stake as withdrawn (flag set to false) and emits an Unstake event. This premature withdrawal prevents the victim from keeping the stake locked for the intended period, thereby forfeiting the higher reward rate that would have been earned if the stake had remained until the lock‑time expired. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that their staked position disappears earlier than expected and the received reward is lower than anticipated; the UI may show the NFT no longer owned or the balance suddenly reduced to zero after an unexpected transaction. The vulnerability arises from a missing msg.sender check, a classic authorization flaw where a function is effectively permissionless despite appearing to enforce ownership. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noticed that the require statement only compares two internal values and does not involve the caller. The issue can be subtle because the function still transfers funds to the correct owner, so no direct theft occurs, making the problem easy to overlook during testing. The impact is economic: users lose potential earnings, the protocol’s incentive model is weakened, and trust in the staking service may be eroded. The recommended remediation is to replace the existing owner comparison with a check that the caller is the NFT owner, i.e., require(ownerOf(_tokenId) == msg.sender). This change restores proper access control, ensuring that only the rightful holder can trigger an unstake and that rewards are only realized according to the contract’s intended schedule.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a trust issue arising from a privileged owner account that can execute functions such as invest, pause and resume in the Cygnus protocol. The invest function allows the owner to transfer any amount of the underlying asset to an arbitrary address and then updates the internal buffered and invested asset counters to reflect the transfer. Because these updates are performed without any additional checks, the owner can move user funds to an address of their choice while keeping the protocol’s accounting variables consistent, effectively hiding the loss. The pause and resume functions give the owner the ability to halt all state‑changing operations, preventing users from depositing, withdrawing or interacting with the contract. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious or compromised admin calls invest with a victim’s address as the destination, drains assets, and optionally pauses the contract to stop users from reacting. The impact includes loss of deposited funds, denial of service for all participants, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s claimed trustless nature. The issue manifests whenever the privileged key is exercised, either intentionally or after compromise, and it affects every token holder and any party relying on the protocol’s governance model. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined privileged functions and recognized that the owner’s unchecked powers constitute a counter‑party risk. Detecting the abuse can be difficult because the emitted Invested event shows a normal transfer amount and the internal balances are adjusted to match, giving the appearance of a legitimate operation. The recommended mitigation is to remove the single‑owner model, transfer administrative rights to a DAO‑like governance contract, enforce multi‑signature or time‑locked execution for critical actions, and make any remaining privileges explicit so users are aware of the residual risk.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑centralised administrative key that controls critical asset‑flow functions in the Copycat protocol. The contract defines two privileged functions, toAdapter and toLeader, both guarded only by an onlyOwner modifier. The owner account is a plain externally owned account (EOA) that can arbitrarily transfer protocol tokens to any registered adapter or withdraw them to the contract itself. Because the owner key is not protected by a multi‑signature, timelock, or DAO‑based governance, an attacker who compromises the private key can invoke these functions and move user funds without any additional checks. The root cause is the design choice to place unrestricted asset‑movement authority in a single address and to rely on the proxy‑admin role without additional governance safeguards. Exploitation is straightforward: once the attacker controls the owner address, they call toAdapter with a malicious adapter address and a chosen amount, causing the protocol’s token balance to be transferred to the attacker‑controlled contract, or they call toLeader to withdraw tokens directly to the protocol’s own address and then forward them elsewhere. The impact is a potential loss of user deposits, disruption of reward distribution, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s economic model. This risk materialises whenever the privileged key is an uncontrolled EOA, the proxy‑admin is not hardened, and no timelock or community governance is in place. All protocol participants – token holders, liquidity providers, and end‑users – are affected because their assets may disappear or become inaccessible, contrary to the expectation that the system is trust‑less. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the concentration of power and the lack of decentralised controls. It can be hard to notice because the functions themselves are correctly coded, emit expected events, and the onlyOwner guard appears normal; the problem lies in the governance model rather than a code defect. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a DAO‑governed contract, optionally protected by a timelock, and the proxy‑admin rights should be managed through a multi‑signature or similar decentralised mechanism. This reduces the single point of failure, aligns the protocol with its intended trust‑less design, and prevents arbitrary asset extraction by a compromised admin key.

title: Improved Validation Of Function Arguments
bug_full: The CryptoZoon contract stores each NFT in a collection indexed by a numeric tokenId and uses that identifier as a key for several related state variables such as zoans, isEvolved and latestBlockTransfer. Functions that modify these states – for example exp() which adds experience points and evolve() which records a new DNA and generation – assume that the caller supplies a valid tokenId that already corresponds to an existing NFT. The code does not perform any explicit sanity check on the supplied _tokenId; it merely trusts that the authorized caller will never pass an out‑of‑range value. Because of this missing validation, an attacker who can invoke the authorized functions (or a compromised privileged account) can supply an arbitrary tokenId that is either zero or larger than the current latestTokenId. When such an invalid identifier is used, the contract may read default values from mappings (e.g., isEvolved defaults to false) and may write to storage slots that do not belong to any real NFT, effectively creating phantom entries or corrupting accounting data. In the case of an array‑based zoans storage, an out‑of‑bounds index triggers a revert, causing a denial‑of‑service condition for legitimate users attempting to add experience or evolve a token. From a user’s perspective this manifests as unexpected transaction failures, experience points not being credited, or NFTs that appear not to evolve despite a successful transaction. The impact ranges from loss of functional correctness – users cannot reliably upgrade or reward their tokens – to potential economic distortion if experience or evolution data is recorded for non‑existent tokens, which could be exploited to manipulate on‑chain metrics or reward calculations. The issue was identified during a systematic audit that highlighted the repeated pattern of functions that rely on tokenId without a guard clause. It is subtle because the contract does not immediately revert for every invalid id; mappings silently return default values, making the bug easy to overlook during functional testing. The proper mitigation is to introduce a reusable modifier (for example validTokenId) that checks that the supplied identifier is greater than zero and does not exceed the latest minted tokenId, and to apply this guard to all functions that accept a tokenId, thereby restoring the intended invariant that every operation targets a real NFT and preventing accidental state corruption or denial‑of‑service scenarios.

title: Potential Reentrancy in withdraw()
bug_full: Potential reentrancy in the withdraw function arises because the contract performs external token transfers before it finishes updating the user's balance and reward accounting. The function first calculates pending rewards and, if any, calls safeSkyTransfer which forwards tokens to the caller. Only after this external call does the code modify user.amount, pool token balance and rewardDebt. Because the external token contract (or a malicious caller) can execute code in its fallback that calls withdraw again, the contract can be re‑entered while the internal accounting still reflects the pre‑withdraw state. An attacker can therefore trigger multiple withdrawals of the same LP tokens or reward tokens before the balance is reduced, effectively draining funds from the pool. This issue manifests when a user invokes withdraw with a non‑zero amount and the token being transferred is controlled by an adversary or has a malicious fallback. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the pool balance becomes unexpectedly low or the user receives more tokens than expected, while other users see their rewards disappear. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit that compared the order of operations against the "checks‑effects‑interactions" principle. It can be hard to notice because the external calls are standard ERC20 safeTransfer calls and the state updates appear later in the same function, giving a false sense of safety. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities where effects are applied after interactions. To remediate, the contract should move all state changes (updating user.amount, rewardDebt, and any pool accounting) before any external call, or protect the function with a reentrancy guard such as the "nonReentrant" modifier, or replace the direct transfer with a pull‑payment pattern. Properly applying these fixes restores the invariant that a user’s balance cannot be withdrawn more than once per request and prevents funds from disappearing.

title: Incorrect Liquidity Mining in DackieV3LmPool
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the reward‑growth calculation of the DackieSwap V3 liquidity‑mining module. The function that computes the reward growth inside a position subtracts the reward growth below and above the tick range from the global reward growth using unsigned 256‑bit integers. When the sum of the below‑range and above‑range growth values exceeds the global value, the subtraction wraps around to a very large number, effectively producing a negative (under‑flowed) rewardGrowthInsideX128. Because the value is stored as an unsigned integer, the MasterChef contract later interprets it as a huge positive number and is unable to derive a correct per‑position reward, causing legitimate users to receive no rewards or to have their claim transaction revert. The bug occurs whenever a position’s tick range is such that the stored outside reward growth values are larger than the current global reward growth – a situation that can arise after a series of swaps that move the price outside the position’s bounds or after a reset of the global accumulator. The affected parties are liquidity providers who have deposited NFTs representing V3 positions; from their perspective the UI shows a pending reward amount that never materialises, balances remain unchanged, and claim attempts fail silently or revert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the getRewardGrowthInside routine, where the lack of a check for the condition (rewardGrowthBelowX128 + rewardGrowthAboveX128 > rewardGrowthGlobalX128) was noted. The problem is subtle because the function returns a uint256 value that appears syntactically correct; only when the value is later used in reward distribution does the underflow manifest, making it easy to miss in basic unit tests that do not simulate extreme price movements. The bug belongs to the class of unsigned integer underflow/overflow errors in financial accounting logic, specifically mis‑calculating a delta by assuming the minuend is always larger than the subtrahend. To fix the issue the routine should detect the underflow condition and either clamp the result to zero or handle the negative case explicitly, for example by returning an additional flag indicating that the computed reward growth is negative and adjusting the reward calculation accordingly. By ensuring that rewardGrowthInsideX128 never wraps around, the protocol can correctly credit liquidity providers and maintain the integrity of its reward accounting.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralized administrative key that holds exclusive authority over critical protocol functions in DackieSwap. The contract uses an onlyOwner modifier on functions that can toggle an emergency flag, change the address that receives reward tokens, and replace the pool deployer contract. Because ownership is held by a single external account that is not governed by a DAO or timelocked mechanism, the root cause is the absence of decentralized governance and the reliance on a privileged private key. An attacker who compromises this key can invoke the privileged functions at any time, for example setting a malicious receiver address so that all future reward distributions are sent to an address controlled by the attacker, or disabling the emergency stop to prevent users from pausing the protocol during an incident. The impact includes loss or diversion of user rewards, alteration of system parameters that may affect fee structures or pool behavior, and erosion of trust because the protocol’s design assumes that only a trusted entity can perform these actions. The condition under which the exploit occurs is simply the possession of the owner private key; no additional on-chain conditions are required. All participants—liquidity providers, token holders, and the broader community—are affected because the protocol’s economic guarantees can be silently broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the lack of DAO-like governance and the presence of unrestricted owner functions. It is hard to notice because the contract emits events when parameters change, but there is no on-chain delay or community oversight, so a malicious change can appear as a legitimate administrative update. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a governance contract that enforces multi-signature approval or timelocked proposals, thereby aligning the protocol with a trustless, community-driven model and preventing a single key from unilaterally modifying critical parameters.

title: Potential Underflow For tierId
bug_full: The contract implements a dynamic tax mechanism for the DARK token by storing price thresholds (taxTiersTwaps) and corresponding tax rates (taxTiersRates). A helper function _updateTaxRate is called on every transferFrom to select the appropriate tax rate based on the current DARK price. The function iterates backwards over the tax tier array using a uint8 loop variable tierId, starting from the highest index (getTaxTiersTwapsCount()-1) and decrementing with tierId-- while the condition tierId >= 0 is evaluated. Because tierId is unsigned, the expression tierId >= 0 is always true; when tierId reaches 0 and is decremented, it underflows to 255 and the loop continues indefinitely. The algorithm also assumes that at least the first tier (taxTiersTwaps[0]) will be less than or equal to the supplied price, but this assumption is not enforced. If the price is lower than every threshold, the loop never finds a matching tier, the underflow occurs, and the function enters an infinite loop that consumes all gas and forces every transferFrom transaction to revert. From a user perspective, attempts to send DARK tokens result in a transaction that fails with out‑of‑gas or a revert, effectively making the token non‑transferable and causing balances to appear frozen. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the tax‑calculation logic. It is subtle because the loop syntax looks conventional and static analysis tools may not flag the always‑true condition, especially when test cases use prices that always satisfy a tier. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unsigned‑integer underflow loops that lead to infinite execution and denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the contract should avoid reverse iteration with an unsigned counter, for example by using a signed integer for the index, adding an explicit break when the counter reaches zero, or employing SafeMath’s checked subtraction and a separate termination condition. Ensuring that the price always matches at least one tier or adding a fallback tax rate would also prevent the loop from running without finding a match, thereby restoring normal transfer functionality.

title: Proper Refund of The Excess ETH
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a liquidity‑addition helper that accepts ETH and a token amount, forwards them to a Uniswap‑style router, and is expected to return any unused ETH to the caller. The contract calls the router with the full msg.value, and the router correctly sends back the surplus ETH to the helper contract, but the helper never forwards that surplus to the original sender. The root cause is a missing transfer of the residual ETH after the router call; the function only refunds excess tokens, not excess native currency. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug by supplying more ETH than required for the desired liquidity amount. After the router completes, the contract retains msg.value‑resultAmtFtm wei, effectively stealing the excess ETH from the user. The impact is that users receive fewer ETH than they sent, leading to unexpected balance reductions, potential loss of funds, and accounting inconsistencies where the protocol’s internal ETH balance diverges from the expected state. The issue manifests whenever addLiquidityETHTaxFree is invoked with an amount of ETH larger than the minimum required by the router, which is a common scenario because callers often over‑provide ETH to avoid transaction failure. The affected parties are the end‑users who supply ETH, the protocol that promises tax‑free liquidity addition, and any auditor reviewing the contract’s financial flows. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of funds in convenience routines and noticed that the function returns only token amounts and does not emit any event or code handling the leftover ETH. Because the contract does not emit a warning or revert, the problem can be subtle; users see a successful transaction but their wallet balance is reduced by the unrefunded ETH, which may appear as a “missing refund” or “funds disappeared” symptom. To remediate, the routine should include logic that checks the contract’s ETH balance after the router call and transfers any surplus back to msg.sender, or use the router’s return values to compute and forward the exact excess amount. This class of bug is a typical “unclaimed excess native token” or “refund omission” vulnerability, where a contract fails to return surplus ether, violating the expectation that a function either uses all supplied ETH or refunds the remainder, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Inconsistent Dark Amount Calculation in getBurnableDarkLeft() and redeemBonds()
bug_full: The Treasury contract contains two separate functions that calculate how much DARK token can be released when bonds are redeemed, but they use different formulas, creating an inconsistency that can be exploited. The viewer function getBurnableDarkLeft determines a value called _burnableDarkLeft by taking the minimum of the remaining supply contraction for the current epoch and a maximum burnable amount derived from the number of bonds that can still be minted multiplied by the current DARK price. This calculation is only performed when the DARK price is at or below the peg. In contrast, the redeemBonds function, which actually transfers DARK to a bond holder, computes the amount of DARK to send (_darkAmount) by multiplying the bond amount by a premium rate returned by getBondPremiumRate and dividing by the fixed-point factor. This second calculation is executed when the DARK price is above a small ceiling, and it does not reference the same constraints used in getBurnableDarkLeft. Because the two functions rely on different variables – one on epochSupplyContractionLeft and _maxBurnableDark, the other on a premium rate – the amount reported as available for redemption may differ from the amount that the contract will actually allow. An attacker can observe a lower or higher burnable amount via the view function, then call redeemBonds with a bond amount that triggers a larger DARK payout than the contract’s accounting expects, potentially draining the treasury or causing the contract to mint more DARK than intended. Conversely, legitimate users may see a generous burnable amount but receive less DARK when redeeming, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The issue manifests whenever the price conditions for the two functions overlap across epochs, which is common in volatile markets. It affects any holder of bonds, the treasury’s budget, and the overall monetary policy of the protocol because the accounting invariant that the total amount of DARK minted equals the allowed burnable amount is broken. The inconsistency was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of the two functions and identified that they do not share a common source of truth for the redeemable amount. The bug is subtle because the two functions are not called together in a single transaction, so a simple unit test may not reveal the mismatch, and the UI may display the value from getBurnableDarkLeft, giving users a false expectation. To remediate the problem, the contract should unify the calculation of the redeemable DARK amount, using a single source of constraints (such as epochSupplyContractionLeft and the maximum mintable bonds) and applying the same rate logic in both the view and execution paths. This ensures that the amount shown to users matches the amount that can actually be transferred, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and preventing unintended inflation or treasury depletion.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the DarkCrypto protocol relies on a single privileged Operator account, implemented as a regular externally owned account (EOA), to execute functions that can modify core protocol parameters such as the boardroom contract address, the oracle address, and the price ceiling for the DARK token, as well as to forward operator rights to other contracts. Because the Operator key is not protected by multi‑signature or timelock mechanisms, any holder of the private key can unilaterally change these settings. This centralised control contradicts the intended trust‑less, community‑governed design. The root cause is the use of a single‑owner access control modifier (onlyOperator) without additional governance safeguards. An attacker who compromises the Operator private key, or a malicious operator acting in good faith, can call setBoardroom, setDarkOracle, setDarkPriceCeiling, or boardroomSetOperator to redirect funds, replace the price oracle with a manipulated source, or lower the price ceiling to trigger liquidation or other economic attacks. The impact includes potential loss of user deposits, incorrect price calculations, unauthorized redirection of rewards, and overall erosion of confidence in the protocol. The vulnerability manifests whenever any privileged function is invoked; there is no on‑chain delay or community review, so the change takes effect immediately. All participants—token holders, liquidity providers, and borrowers—are affected because the altered parameters can change the value of their positions or cause funds to be sent to an address they do not control. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Treasury contract, where the auditor noted the presence of onlyOperator‑protected functions and the lack of any DAO or timelock guard. Because the functions appear legitimate and the Operator address is often listed in the contract’s public variables, the problem can be easy to overlook, especially for users who assume that protocol parameters are immutable or governed by a decentralized process. To remediate, the privileged role should be migrated to a governance contract that enforces community voting and timelocked execution, or at minimum be replaced by a multi‑signature wallet with a sufficient number of signers. Removing the single admin key eliminates the single point of failure and aligns the protocol with its stated trust‑less model. In practice, the fix involves replacing the onlyOperator modifier with a governance‑only modifier, adding a delay for parameter changes, and ensuring that any future operator changes are mediated through a DAO or multi‑sig.

title: Inconsistent Handling in Pool::trimExtraToTreasury()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the public trimExtraToTreasury function of the Pool contract, which is responsible for moving excess collateral assets from the reserve to the profitSharingFund when the total collateral value exceeds the total dollar supply value. The function calculates the amount of collateral to transfer (_collateralAmount) based on the difference between the global collateral total value and the dollar supply value, then attempts to cap this amount by a temporary variable _mainCollateralBal. The root cause is that _mainCollateralBal is assigned using _treasury.globalCollateralValue(0).div(10 ** missing_decimals[0]) – a value that represents the USD‑denominated value of the collateral – instead of the actual token balance returned by _treasury.globalCollateralBalance(0). Because the code mixes a value expressed in monetary units with a raw token amount, the cap may be far larger or smaller than the true available balance. When the cap is larger, the contract may request a transfer of more tokens than exist in the reserve, potentially draining the reserve or causing a revert that leaves the system in an inconsistent state. When the cap is smaller, excess collateral remains locked in the reserve, preventing the profitSharingFund from receiving the full amount it is entitled to, which can appear to users as missing refunds or zero balances. The bug is triggered only when the condition _totalCollateralValue > _total_dollar_FullValue holds, i.e., when the protocol holds more collateral value than the issued dollar supply. This situation can arise during periods of over‑collateralisation or after market price changes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the analyst compared the intended accounting logic with the actual variable used and noticed the mismatch in the decimal handling. It is subtle because both globalCollateralValue and globalCollateralBalance have similar names and the missing decimal conversion is easy to overlook, making the problem hard to detect through simple testing. To remediate, the assignment to _mainCollateralBal should be changed to use the correct balance function, i.e., _treasury.globalCollateralBalance(0), ensuring that the cap reflects the true token amount. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that the amount transferred never exceeds the actual reserve balance, preserving user expectations that their refunds are accurate and that no funds disappear unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where value and quantity are confused, leading to incorrect transfer limits and potential financial loss.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of excessive trust placed in two privileged accounts – an owner and a strategist – that control critical protocol functions in the DarkNess Dollar system. The root cause is the use of onlyOwner and onlyStrategist modifiers without any additional governance safeguards such as timelocks, multi‑signature approval, or DAO‑based voting, which concentrates power in a single address or a small set of addresses. Because these accounts can arbitrarily set strategist status, change treasury policy, replace oracle contracts, adjust collateral reserves, add or remove liquidity pools, and modify minting and redemption fees, a malicious or compromised admin can exploit the contract by invoking any of these functions. In particular, when the owner removes an existing pool, the mapping entry is deleted and the address in the pools array is set to zero, leaving a gap that causes the redeem() and collectRedemption() functions of the removed pool to revert. Users attempting to redeem their assets therefore experience transaction failures, see no change in their balances, or even lose collateral if the revert occurs after funds have been transferred. The impact is that token holders, liquidity providers, and any participant relying on stable fee structures or pool availability may suffer asset loss, unexpected fee changes, or a complete inability to redeem, undermining confidence in the protocol. This condition manifests whenever the privileged accounts execute any of the administrative functions, especially during pool removal or fee updates. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the Treasury contract, where the auditor noted that the privileged functions lack any delay or community oversight and that the removal logic leaves a null entry that triggers reverts in downstream pool contracts. The problem is difficult to detect in normal operation because the contract behaves correctly until an admin action, such as pool removal, is performed; at that point the failure appears as a generic transaction revert rather than a clear security flaw. To remediate, the protocol should migrate the owner and strategist roles to a community‑governed DAO, enforce timelock delays on all privileged state changes, replace single‑owner control with a multi‑signature wallet, and ensure that proxy‑admin rights are also governed. Additional safeguards could include preventing removal of pools that have pending redemptions or requiring explicit confirmation before fee adjustments. This class of bug falls under centralized admin control and unsafe upgradeability, leading to trust issues and potential loss of user funds. From the user’s perspective, the expected outcome of a successful redemption is replaced by a transaction that reverts, a balance that remains unchanged, or fees that shift without warning, violating the assumption that protocol parameters are stable and trustworthy.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the DCAv2 protocol relies on a single privileged admin externally owned account that holds the TIME_LOCKED_ROLE, which can call functions to set the swap fee, loan fee, and platform fee ratio. Because the role is assigned to a plain EOA rather than a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO, the protocol’s fee parameters can be altered by any holder of the private key. This centralised control creates a trust issue: if the key is compromised or the admin acts maliciously, fees may be increased arbitrarily, the platform fee ratio may be set above the intended maximum, or other configuration changes could be made that affect the flow of assets. Exploitation would involve an attacker obtaining the admin private key or convincing the admin to execute malicious transactions; once in control, they can call setSwapFee, setLoanFee, or setPlatformFeeRatio to raise fees, causing users to pay higher costs or to divert a larger portion of assets to the protocol owner. The impact is that users may see unexpectedly high fees, receive less value from swaps or loans, and overall trust in the protocol erodes; in extreme cases funds could be drained if the admin also controls proxy‑admin privileges. The condition under which this occurs is any time the privileged account is active; there is no additional on‑chain safeguard such as a timelock or multi‑sig. All users of the protocol, including liquidity providers and borrowers, are affected because the fee parameters apply globally. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected role assignments and noted that the TIME_LOCKED_ROLE is granted to a plain EOA without any governance or timelock mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the functions themselves are correctly coded and emit events, so normal operation appears normal until a fee change is observed. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single admin key with a community‑governed contract or DAO, optionally introduce a timelock for any parameter change, and, if proxies are used, ensure that proxy‑admin rights are also transferred to a decentralized entity. This moves the protocol towards a trustless model and eliminates the single point of failure.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is an administrative key trust issue in the Demeter protocol. The contract defines a privileged owner (or owner/guardian) that can modify critical protocol parameters, assign members, change user permissions, and pause or unpause the entire system and the redemption module. Because the owner is a single externally owned account without any multi‑signature, timelock, or DAO governance, the protocol relies on the honesty and security of that single key. If the key is compromised, an attacker can arbitrarily set new members, alter configuration values, enable or disable user permits, and freeze or unfreeze the protocol at will. By pausing the protocol the attacker can prevent users from redeeming their synthetic stablecoin, effectively locking funds. By changing member addresses the attacker could redirect asset flows or grant themselves privileged roles, leading to loss or misappropriation of user deposits. The impact is that users may see their balances become inaccessible, receive no redemption, or observe unexpected changes in protocol state, violating the expectation that the system operates autonomously and trustlessly. The issue manifests whenever the privileged functions are called, which is any time the owner or guardian decides to act; there is no delay or community oversight, so a malicious or compromised owner can act instantly. The affected parties include all token holders, liquidity providers, and any third‑party services that rely on the protocol’s stability. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the concentration of power in a single address and the lack of governance controls.
