The problem is subtle because the data appears to be encrypted and the keystore JSON is also stored, giving a false sense of security; however, the use of a single‑iteration AES encryption keyed by a low‑entropy password makes the protection ineffective. The vulnerability belongs to the class of insecure local secret storage and weak key‑derivation practices. From a user perspective the wallet UI shows a successful import or creation, but the underlying secrets are persisted in a way that can be silently stolen; the user may later notice unexpected withdrawals or loss of funds without any visible error in the app. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the redundant backup of the private key and mnemonic, relying solely on the standard keystore which already encrypts the secret with a strong KDF, or to apply the same hardened KDF‑based encryption to any additional backup data. In addition, the password hash should not be stored as MD5, and the encryption routine should use a memory‑hard KDF such as scrypt or Argon2 to resist offline cracking.

title: Vulnerability in Outdated Web Plug-in resolve-url-loader
description: It is known that during the web development, it is necessary to import a number of third-party or unoffcial libraries. Therefore, validating the security of dependent libraries is critical and necessary. During our analysis, we found that the imported library resolve-url-loader v3.1.1 contains several known vulnerabilities, the most severe one could lead to denial-of-service to block normal services. More details can be found at https://npmjs.com/advisories/1556.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of an outdated version of the resolve-url-loader package (v3.1.1) in a web development build pipeline. This loader processes relative URLs inside CSS/SCSS files during asset compilation, but the version in question fails to properly validate and sanitize the URLs it resolves. An attacker can craft a malicious stylesheet containing specially crafted url() statements that trigger infinite recursion, excessive file system access, or uncontrolled network requests. When such a stylesheet is processed, the loader enters a resource‑exhaustion state that blocks the webpack compilation, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service condition for the entire front‑end build. The impact is that developers see their build jobs hang or crash, continuous integration pipelines stop, and the resulting web service may become unavailable to end users, who experience blank pages, missing styles, or complete site downtime. The issue manifests only when the build step that invokes resolve‑url‑loader runs, so it may be missed during normal runtime testing and appears as a generic build failure rather than a clear security alert. It was discovered through an npm audit that referenced advisory 1556, which listed the same denial‑of‑service vector for version 3.1.1. Because the failure occurs deep inside the loader’s URL resolution logic, the symptom is often indistinguishable from other compilation errors, making it hard to pinpoint without checking the dependency versions. The appropriate remediation is to upgrade resolve‑url‑loader to at least version 3.1.2, where the URL validation logic has been hardened, and to run npm audit fix afterwards to ensure no other known vulnerabilities remain. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an outdated third‑party library causing a denial‑of‑service due to insufficient input validation, breaking the expected guarantee that asset compilation will complete reliably and that users will receive correctly styled content.

title: Lack of Network Proxy Detection
description: The applications on iOS or Android platforms do not use plain-text communication and all traffic is encrypted by default via HTTPS. Such encryption needs to be enforced to effectively defeat man-in-the-middle attacks. However, there are several network sniffer applications (e.g., Fiddler, Charles) that are able to sniff and capture the packet encrypted by HTTPS, or even modify the packet content (if with the access to the certificate on the mobile device). With that, it is important to reliably detect the presence of a network proxy and avoid it as much as possible in wallet-like applications. Our analysis shows that the detection of the presence of possible network proxies is currently missing.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing detection of network proxies in the mobile wallet application, allowing a man‑in‑the‑middle attacker who can install a custom root certificate on the device to intercept and potentially modify HTTPS traffic. The root cause is that the Android implementation trusts any system‑installed certificate and does not verify that the connection is direct, while the iOS code does not perform any proxy check. An attacker can run a tool such as Fiddler or Charles, install its certificate on the victim’s phone, and then capture or alter JSON‑RPC calls that carry private keys, transaction signatures or balance queries. Because the wallet assumes that HTTPS encryption alone guarantees confidentiality, the user sees no warning; the UI still shows a successful connection and the balance appears unchanged, while the attacker may silently replace a transaction destination or steal credentials. The issue appears whenever the user runs the app on a device that has a user‑installed certificate or is connected through a VPN/proxy that the app does not detect. All users of the wallet, as well as the underlying blockchain protocol, are affected because the attacker can manipulate funds or obtain sensitive data. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that noted the absence of proxy detection logic and the permissive trust manager. The bug is hard to notice because the network traffic still appears encrypted and the app does not expose any error messages. To remediate, the app should reject certificates that are not part of a pinned trust store, abort connections when the system trust manager throws a CertificateException, and actively check the system proxy settings on both Android and iOS, raising an exception or refusing to operate if a proxy or VPN is detected. This aligns the implementation with the security class of man‑in‑the‑middle mitigation via certificate pinning and proxy detection, restoring the expectation that a wallet transaction cannot be altered by an intermediate network device.

title: Possible Privilege Escalation in Plug-in xuexiangjys
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a third‑party utility library that is bundled with the QR‑code scanning feature. The library exposes a public method that builds a command array and then calls the Java Runtime API to execute those commands on the host operating system. The implementation unconditionally selects either a normal shell ("sh") or the super‑user shell ("su") based on a boolean flag, writes each supplied command to the process input stream, and waits for the process to finish. No validation, sanitisation, or permission checks are performed on the command strings, and the caller can request root execution. Because the method is reachable from the scanning component, any code path that can reach the library – including malicious code injected through a crafted QR payload or a compromised module – can trigger arbitrary shell commands, potentially with elevated privileges if the device permits the "su" binary. This constitutes an unsafe command execution flaw that belongs to the class of command‑injection or privilege‑escalation bugs. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker supplies a command such as "rm -rf /data" or "cat /etc/passwd" in the command array, sets the root flag, and the library will execute it directly on the device. If the device is rooted or the "su" binary is present, the attacker gains the same level of access as the operating system’s root user, allowing reading, modification, or deletion of private files, alteration of app state, or installation of persistent backdoors. The impact is a breach of the security model of the wallet application: user data may disappear, confidential keys may be exposed, and the device itself can be compromised. The condition under which this occurs is when the QR‑code scanning feature invokes the vulnerable method, which may happen during normal operation or when a specially crafted QR code is processed. All users of the wallet, as well as the protocol that relies on the integrity of the app, are affected because the compromised device can no longer be trusted to protect funds or private information. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit by PeckShield, where the call to Runtime.exec and the optional use of the "su" command were flagged as unsafe. The flaw can be hard to notice because the method is presented as a generic utility for executing shell commands, a pattern that is common in Android tooling, and the code does not emit warnings or errors when used. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include unexpected device behaviour such as sudden loss of files, unexplained permission changes, or the app performing actions without visible prompts – for example, a user expects a QR scan to return a result but instead observes that files are deleted or that the app requests root access silently. The recommended remediation is to remove the offending third‑party plugin entirely or replace it with a safe alternative that does not invoke Runtime.exec, or at minimum enforce strict command whitelisting and prohibit root execution. In conceptual terms the fix eliminates the ability to run arbitrary operating‑system commands from within the smart‑contract wallet, thereby restoring the intended security boundary between the application and the host device.

title: Possible Private Key Leakage through Clipboard
description: During the process of storing and exporting the private key, we have found a potential risk which may result in the compromise of the private key. Specifically, the wallet allows users to save their private keys to other applications by copying them to the clipboard for easy access. However, a malicious application that has access to the clipboard is able to obtain the private key without being perceived by the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of exposing the user's private key through the system clipboard. When the wallet provides a feature that copies the raw private key string to the clipboard, any other application that has permission to read the clipboard can retrieve the key without the user's knowledge. This occurs because the clipboard is a shared OS resource that does not enforce isolation between processes. An attacker that installs a malicious app or a compromised legitimate app can monitor clipboard changes, detect when a private key is placed there, and store or forward it to an attacker‑controlled server. The impact is that the attacker gains full control over the user's blockchain account, allowing unauthorized transfers, contract interactions, or draining of funds. The condition for exploitation is simply the user invoking the copy‑to‑clipboard function; no additional user interaction is required. All users of the wallet who rely on the copy feature are potentially affected, and the risk extends to any funds held by the compromised accounts. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the wallet's export workflow, where the auditor noted that the private key is written to an insecure global buffer. Because clipboard reads are silent and do not produce visible UI cues, the leakage can be hard to notice; the user may never see any indication that another app accessed the clipboard. The bug belongs to the class of insecure secret handling or clipboard data leakage, where sensitive material is temporarily stored in a location that lacks confidentiality guarantees. From a user perspective, the wallet appears to have exported the key successfully, but later the account may experience unexpected outgoing transactions, balance reductions, or loss of assets without any apparent on‑screen warning. The expected behavior is that the private key remains confidential unless the user explicitly shares it, whereas the reality is that the key can be silently harvested. To remediate, the wallet should avoid copying raw private keys to the clipboard altogether, or at minimum present a clear warning about the risk, require explicit user consent, and provide a function that clears the clipboard immediately after use. Implementing a secure, temporary in‑memory display or QR‑code export can also eliminate reliance on the clipboard.

title: Flawed System Security Validation
description: Once the mobile platform's underlying operating system has been rooted or somehow hooked, the adversary could easily obtain all the local information of device, e.g., the user's password. Moreover, it is also possible to retrieve the private key temporarily stored in the memory through known code injection techniques.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the wallet application’s failure to detect that the user’s mobile device is running in a rooted (Android) or jail‑broken (iOS) state, which allows an adversary who has obtained root privileges or installed a hooking framework to read any data that the app keeps in the device’s memory. The root cause is the absence of runtime checks for elevated system privileges and the practice of temporarily storing the user’s password and private key in clear memory without hardware‑backed protection. An attacker who can gain control of the operating system – for example by exploiting a known rooting exploit, installing a malicious app, or using a physical device that has been compromised – can inject code into the wallet process, dump the process memory, and extract the credentials. Once the private key is obtained, the attacker can sign transactions and move the user’s funds to an address under their control. The impact is the loss of cryptocurrency assets, exposure of the user’s password, and erosion of trust in the wallet. This condition occurs whenever the wallet is launched on a device that has been rooted or jail‑broken, regardless of whether the user is aware of the compromise. All users of the wallet on such devices are affected, as the flaw does not depend on any particular role or permission within the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the client‑side code and noted the lack of any root‑detection logic. It can be difficult to notice because the application behaves normally from the user’s perspective – the UI shows the expected balances and transaction confirmations – while the malicious code silently reads memory in the background. Users may only notice the problem after their balance unexpectedly drops to zero or after a failed login attempt because the password has been changed elsewhere. To remediate the flaw, the wallet should incorporate robust runtime checks that detect rooted or jail‑broken environments and either abort execution or present a clear warning to the user. Additionally, sensitive material such as passwords and private keys should be stored only in secure, hardware‑isolated enclaves or encrypted memory, and the app should minimise the time such data resides in plaintext memory. By aligning the implementation with standard secure‑mobile‑app practices, the wallet can prevent attackers from exploiting the device’s compromised state to steal funds or credentials.

title: Potential Sandwich/MEV Attack For createOption()
bug_full: The contract’s createOption function allows a buyer to purchase a put or call option by first transferring the calculated option price in the buyer’s chosen payment token and then, if the payment token is not the pool’s underlying asset, swapping that token for the underlying token through UniswapV2. The price of the swap is obtained by calling exchange.getAmountsIn, which returns the exact amount of payment token required for the current market rate. This exact amount is stored in the variable optionPrice and is subsequently passed as the amountInMax parameter of the UniswapV2 swapTokensForExactTokens call. The amountInMax parameter is intended to act as a slippage ceiling – it should represent the maximum amount of payment token the caller is willing to spend, allowing the transaction to revert if the market moves unfavourably. By using the same value that was calculated for the current price, the contract effectively disables any slippage protection: if an attacker can move the market price between the time the option price is calculated and the time the swap executes, the swap will consume less than the transferred amount when the price moves in the attacker’s favour, leaving a surplus of payment tokens inside the contract. A front‑runner can therefore execute a sandwich attack, first trading to push the price down, then letting the victim’s transaction swap at the cheaper rate, and finally extracting the leftover payment tokens. This vulnerability manifests only when the payment token differs from the pool’s underlying token (i.e., when swappath.length > 1) and the contract has already transferred the full optionPrice from the buyer before the swap. The affected parties are option buyers, who may see part of their transferred funds disappear without receiving a proportional increase in option value, and the protocol, which may suffer from unintended fund loss and broken accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of token transfers and the parameters supplied to the UniswapV2 router, noticing that the amountInMax argument was set to the exact amount returned by getAmountsIn, thereby nullifying slippage checks. The problem is subtle because the code appears to enforce a precise payment amount, yet it neglects the economic reality that market prices can change between calls, making the surplus invisible to a casual reviewer. To remediate the issue, the function should enforce a slippage tolerance by calculating amountInMax as optionPrice multiplied by (1 + maxSlippage) or by using swapExactTokensForTokens with a minimum amountOut parameter, and any excess payment tokens should be refunded to the buyer after the swap. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage control” or “price‑oracle manipulation” vulnerabilities that allow front‑running attacks to profit from price changes during a multi‑step transaction.

title: Incorrect withdraw Logic In HegicOperationalTreasury
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw logic of the HegicOperationalTreasury contract. The contract exposes an external withdraw function that can only be called by an address holding the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. Inside the private _withdraw routine the code checks require(amount + totalLocked <= totalBalance) before reducing the internal totalBalance and transferring the requested amount to the caller. This check is insufficient because it ignores two additional sources of liability: the lockedPremium amount that must remain reserved for option holders and the available balance held in the external stakeandcoverPool contract. As a result an admin can withdraw tokens that should be kept as a safety buffer for the protocol, potentially draining the treasury below the level required to honor user claims. The flaw originates from an incomplete accounting invariant – the contract assumes that totalBalance alone represents all funds that can be safely spent, while in reality the protocol’s financial model requires that totalBalance minus (totalLocked + lockedPremium) plus the pool’s available balance stay non‑negative. An attacker who controls the admin role, or a compromised admin key, could invoke withdraw with an amount that passes the lax check but exceeds the true safe reserve, causing the treasury to lose funds needed for payouts. Users would experience symptoms such as missing refunds, zero balances after a claim, or failed payouts despite having paid premiums. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by PeckShield, where the logical relationship between locked premiums, the external pool, and the withdraw guard was examined. Because the function appears to perform a standard token transfer, the missing invariant is not obvious from a superficial review, making the bug hard to spot without deep understanding of the protocol’s accounting rules. To remediate, the require statement should be expanded to require(amount + totalLocked + lockedPremium <= totalBalance + stakeandcoverPool.availableBalance()), thereby guaranteeing that after any withdrawal the contract still holds enough tokens to cover locked positions and the pool’s obligations. This class of bug falls under insufficient balance checks or accounting invariant violations, where business logic about reserved funds is not enforced at the code level, leading to potential loss of user funds and breach of protocol guarantees.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of excessive privileges granted to a small set of admin accounts in the Hegic protocol. These accounts – owner, DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, HEGIC_POOL_ROLE, STRATEGY_ROLE and SELLER_ROLE – are able to invoke functions that move or modify the protocol’s treasury, lock liquidity, set benchmark values and add tokens to the total balance. Because the protocol relies on these privileged functions for normal operation, a malicious or compromised admin could withdraw tokens from the operational treasury, replenish the treasury with arbitrary amounts, lock liquidity in a way that prevents users from withdrawing, or change benchmark parameters that affect profit and loss calculations. Such actions can cause user funds to disappear, options to remain locked, or profit calculations to be manipulated, violating the expectation that deposited assets are safe and that payouts follow the protocol’s accounting rules. The issue manifests whenever an account that holds one of the privileged roles calls the corresponding function; there is no additional on‑chain check limiting the amount, purpose or timing of the operation. All users of the protocol implicitly trust that the privileged accounts will act honestly, creating a counter‑party risk. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract source code, where the presence of onlyRole modifiers on critical state‑changing functions was noted and the concentration of power was deemed a concern. The vulnerability is subtle because the functions appear legitimate and are required for protocol operation, making it easy to overlook the centralization of authority. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should make the scope and list of each privileged role explicit to users, consider moving critical actions to multi‑signature or time‑locked governance, and reduce the number of accounts that can withdraw or modify treasury balances. In essence, this bug belongs to the class of “centralized admin key” or “privileged role misuse” vulnerabilities, where excessive authority can be abused to steal or mismanage funds, breaking the business logic that user deposits are protected and that only defined protocol logic determines payouts.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Hegic Herge protocol relies on a set of privileged accounts that hold the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (and EXERCISER_ROLE) to modify core protocol parameters such as the premium calculator contract, the locked limit, the k factor, and the next epoch changing price. These privileged accounts are implemented as regular externally owned accounts (EOAs) without any additional governance safeguards. Because the admin keys are single‑signature EOAs, a compromise of the private key gives an attacker unrestricted ability to call the admin functions and change the values that drive option pricing, payoff eligibility, and overall risk limits. An attacker who obtains the admin key can invoke setPricer to replace the premium calculator with a malicious contract that under‑prices options, call setLimit to raise the locked limit and allow excessive exposure, or alter the k parameter and epoch price to manipulate payoff calculations. The exploitation can be performed at any time after the key is compromised; there is no timelock or multi‑signature check that would delay or require consensus before the change takes effect. As a result, users may see options that appear to have favorable terms but actually provide no real payoff, or the protocol may become under‑collateralized, leading to loss of user funds when positions are exercised. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected zero payouts, sudden changes in displayed premiums, or the inability to exercise options that should be in‑the‑money. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined role‑based access control and noted that the privileged roles are assigned to plain EOAs rather than a multi‑signature wallet or a timelocked governance contract. The problem is subtle because the functions themselves are correctly guarded by role checks, so a superficial test that only verifies that only admins can call them will not reveal the underlying trust assumption. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “centralized admin key” or “privileged key compromise” bugs, where the security of the entire protocol hinges on the secrecy of a single private key. To remediate, the protocol should replace single‑signature admin accounts with a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO‑controlled contract, and introduce timelocks on any parameter change so that stakeholders have a window to review and potentially veto malicious updates. This mitigation reduces the attack surface by requiring multiple parties to collude or by providing a delay that can be used to alert users and halt the change before funds are at risk.

title: Non-Functional Lockup Periods in HegicStaking
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a non‑functional lockup period in the Hegic staking contracts. The protocol is supposed to record a timestamp when a user buys (stakes) tokens and then prevent any transfer or sale of those tokens until a predefined lockup duration has elapsed. In the current implementation the buy function never writes the lastBoughtTimestamp for the caller, leaving the stored value at its default of zero. Because the lockup check in the internal _beforeTokenTransfer hook compares the stored timestamp plus the lockup period against the current block time, a zero timestamp always satisfies the condition, effectively bypassing the lockup restriction. Consequently, a user can transfer or sell freshly minted staking tokens immediately after purchase, even if the receiver has explicitly opted out of receiving funds during the lockup period. The lockupFree modifier, which relies on the same timestamp, also evaluates to true for any account, allowing instant redemption of stakes. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the staking logic where the absence of a timestamp update was noted. It is hard to notice because the contract code appears to enforce a lockup flag and the transfer function does not revert, giving a false sense of security. The impact is that the economic model of the staking pool is broken: rewards that should accrue over the lockup period can be harvested instantly, enabling front‑run or flash‑loan attacks that capture a disproportionate share of rewards, and users may lose confidence when expected lockup constraints are ignored. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that tokens are locked for a certain period, yet the user can sell them right away, leading to confusion and potential loss of expected earnings. The issue belongs to the class of timestamp‑based access‑control bugs where state updates required for time‑locked functionality are omitted. To remediate, the buy function must record the current block timestamp in the lastBoughtTimestamp mapping before minting, ensuring that subsequent transfer and sell operations respect the intended lockup period and that the lockupFree modifier correctly enforces the delay.

title: Denial-of-Service in getReward()
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the reward‑claiming routine of the contract. The function that distributes rewards to option holders does not verify that the supplied option identifier corresponds to a valid, inactive option before marking the reward as claimed. Because the contract stores a boolean flag indicating whether an option has already been rewarded, an attacker can call the function with an identifier that has not yet been created but can be predicted from the sequential assignment logic. The call succeeds, the flag for that future identifier is set to true, and the daily reward accounting is updated, even though no real option exists. When the legitimate holder later creates the option with the expected identifier and attempts to claim the reward, the contract sees the flag already set and aborts the claim, preventing the transfer of the entitled amount. This results in the user seeing a successful transaction that transfers nothing, or a revert with a generic “option was rewarded” error, while the expected reward balance remains unchanged. The issue occurs whenever an option identifier can be guessed, which is typical in systems that allocate identifiers sequentially. Any participant who can predict the next identifier – essentially any external actor – can trigger the condition, affecting all future option holders. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit of the incentivisation logic, where the lack of a state check for the option was noted as a logical omission. It is subtle because the function appears to perform all necessary steps – calculating the amount, checking daily limits, and transferring funds – and the missing validation does not raise a compile‑time warning. The class of bug is an unchecked external identifier or missing input validation that leads to state corruption and denial of service. From a user perspective the symptom is a missing or zero reward where the user expects a payout, breaking the business assumption that every eligible option will receive its reward. The recommended fix is to add a sanity check that the option exists and is in the correct inactive state before proceeding, and to update the daily reward accounting only after the existence check passes, thereby preventing an attacker from pre‑emptively marking a non‑existent option as rewarded.

title: Bypass of Daily Reward Limit in HegicRewards
bug_full: The vulnerability in the HegicRewards contract is a daily‑reward‑limit bypass that allows an attacker to claim more than the intended maximum amount of HEGIC tokens per day. The root cause is that the contract tracks the amount already distributed on a given day in the mapping dailyReward, but the value is never updated after a successful claim. Consequently, the require statement that checks amount.add(dailyReward[today]) < MAX_DAILY_REWARD always evaluates against a stale dailyReward value (typically zero), meaning each individual claim is only limited by the per‑option reward size, not by the aggregate daily cap. An attacker can therefore invoke getReward() repeatedly for many option IDs, each time receiving a legitimate‑looking reward that passes the limit check, and drain the reward pool far beyond the 165,000 HEGIC daily ceiling. The impact is a loss of protocol‑wide incentive funds: users who later try to claim rewards may receive nothing because the pool has been exhausted, breaking the economic model that promised proportional daily distribution. The bug manifests whenever multiple option holders exist and the contract’s getReward() function is called; it does not depend on special inputs beyond a valid optionId. All option holders, the protocol’s reward mechanism, and any investors relying on the promised daily emissions are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noticed that the dailyReward state variable was read but never written. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, the require check passes, and there is no overflow or revert; the contract simply fails to enforce the intended aggregate limit. To remediate, the contract must update dailyReward[today] with the amount actually transferred before completing the reward, thereby ensuring that subsequent calls correctly account for the cumulative daily distribution. This class of bug is an accounting or state‑mutation omission, where a cumulative counter is read but not incremented, leading to a limit‑bypass vulnerability. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that a reward is available, the user expects to receive a certain amount of HEGIC, but after many claims the balance may unexpectedly become zero or the reward claim may fail, contradicting the expectation of a fair daily share. The failure violates the business logic that rewards should be distributed pro‑rata and capped each day, effectively allowing money to disappear from the reward pool.

title: Wrong Reward Rate in HegicWBTCRewards
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑rate misconfiguration in the HegicWBTCRewards contract caused by an incorrect assumption about the token decimal precision. The base rewards contract stores a maximum and minimum rewards rate that are expressed in the token's smallest unit. While WBTC uses 8 decimal places, the HegicWBTCRewards constructor supplies the rates with 18‑decimal scaling (1_000_000e18 and 10e18). This decimal mismatch inflates the intended reward rate by a factor of 10^10, causing the daily reward accounting to believe that far more tokens are available for distribution than actually exist. As a result, the reward pool is depleted almost immediately after deployment, so users who expect to receive WBTC rewards see their balances remain unchanged or receive zero rewards. The issue manifests whenever the contract is instantiated with the wrong parameters, which occurs at deployment time and persists for the lifetime of the contract unless corrected. It affects any participant who relies on the WBTC reward mechanism – option writers, liquidity providers, and end‑users – because the economic incentive promised by the protocol cannot be fulfilled. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the constructor arguments against the known decimal specification of WBTC and identified the mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the numbers appear syntactically correct and the contract compiles without errors; only a careful review of token decimals reveals the problem. The flaw violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are calculated based on the true token precision, leading to an over‑allocation of rewards and eventual exhaustion of the reward fund. The recommended fix is to pass the rates using the correct 8‑decimal scaling (1_000_000e8 and 10e8) or otherwise adjust the calculation to reference the token’s decimals, thereby aligning the reward rate with the actual token units and preventing premature depletion of the reward pool.

title: Potential Sandwich/MEV Attack In HLND
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection in the token‑to‑BNB swap routine of the HLND contract. The function that performs the swap calls PancakeSwap's swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens with the amountOutMin parameter hard‑coded to zero, which means the transaction does not enforce any minimum amount of BNB to be received. This design flaw originates from the contract assuming that the router will always return a reasonable amount of output, ignoring the fact that the price on the automated market maker can be manipulated between the time the transaction is submitted and the time it is mined. An attacker can front‑run the transaction, for example by submitting a large buy order just before the victim's swap and a large sell order immediately after, thereby driving the price down and causing the victim contract to receive far less BNB than expected, potentially even zero. The impact is that token holders or the protocol expecting a fair conversion of HLND to BNB may see their funds disappear or be severely devalued; the user interface may show that the token balance was deducted while the BNB balance remains unchanged, violating the business logic that a swap should yield a proportional amount of BNB. The issue manifests whenever any of the contract's internal functions that invoke the router with amountOutMin set to zero are executed, including addLiquidity, buyBackAndBurn, and swapTokensForDividendToken. It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of slippage checks. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and appears to succeed, making it easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should calculate an acceptable minimum output based on a price oracle or on‑chain quote (e.g., using router.getAmountsOut) and pass that value to amountOutMin, optionally adding a configurable slippage tolerance. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that the amount of BNB received should not fall below a predictable threshold, preventing sandwich or other MEV attacks.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑centralized admin control in the HLND protocol. The contract defines an owner address that is granted a large set of privileged functions: it can change protocol‑wide parameters such as maximum transaction size, fee percentages, enable or disable trading, modify dividend priorities, update addresses of marketing, team, router, and referral contracts, and adjust gas limits for dividend processing. In addition, the owner can exclude arbitrary accounts from fees and dividend distributions, manually trigger buy‑back and burn operations, withdraw any ERC20 tokens held by the contract, and designate authorized accounts that can call internal dividend processing functions. Because these functions are protected only by the onlyOwner or onlyAuthorized modifiers, any compromise of the owner’s private key or malicious behavior by the owner gives the attacker the ability to arbitrarily reconfigure the economic rules, block or exempt users from fees, redirect dividend payouts, and drain tokens from the contract. Exploitation can occur when the owner calls setBoolParameters to disable trading, setSellTransactionMultiplier to inflate sell fees, or withdrawTokens to transfer all contract balances to an address of the attacker. The impact is that users may see their expected refunds or dividend rewards disappear, fees suddenly increase to 100 %, or their token balances become zero after a withdrawal. The issue manifests when a user attempts a normal trade or dividend claim and receives no tokens, or when the UI shows a zero balance despite having previously held tokens. The risk is present for any participant who relies on the protocol’s promised tokenomics, including retail investors and liquidity providers. The problem was identified during a manual audit that listed all functions guarded by onlyOwner and highlighted the breadth of control they confer. Because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation, the excessive privileges are not obvious from on‑chain activity, making the risk hard to detect without source‑code review. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “centralized admin key” or “owner‑controlled parameter manipulation” bugs, where business logic can be overridden by a single address. The recommended mitigation is to reduce the owner’s authority, for example by moving critical parameter changes to a timelocked governance contract, renouncing ownership, or making the list of privileged functions transparent to users through documentation or on‑chain events. By limiting or eliminating the ability of a single key to arbitrarily change fees, withdraw funds, or exclude accounts, the protocol can align with its stated decentralised trust model and protect user assets.

title: User can bypass `entryFee` by sending arbitrary `calldata` to ParaSwap operator
description:
[NestedFactory.sol#L466](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-nested/blob/b4a153c943d54755711a2f7b80cbbf3a5bb49d76/contracts/NestedFactory.sol#L466)  
[ParaswapOperator.sol#L34](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-nested/blob/b4a153c943d54755711a2f7b80cbbf3a5bb49d76/contracts/operators/Paraswap/ParaswapOperator.sol#L34)  

Any user is able to bypass the `entryFee` collection when using `NestedFactory.create()` by passing in arbitrary calldata when using the ParaSwap router. High level, a user can pass in calldata to swap from a miniscule amount of input token to an ERC777 with themselves as the recipient and will gain control of execution, at which time they can send a large amount of output token back to the Nested Factory.

If the user sends `1 wei` of input token, the Nested Factory will return an `entryFee` of `0` due to precision loss. The amount of output token returned to the contract via the direct transfer from the user will then be deposited in the vault.
poc:
**Steps**

  * User calls `NestedFactory.create()` with a single input order. This input order will define the parameters of the call to Paraswap.
  * The single order defines the following in pseudocode:

    1. inputToken: Any token, but we’ll use address(0) ETH
    2. amount: 1 wei
    3. Order(operator=Paraswap, token=USDC, calldata=calldata)

**_The calldata used in the call to paraswap would swap from ETH to any ERC777 (NOT USDC), with an attack contract address set as the`beneficiary`. Upon transferring the swapped ERC777 to the user’s attack contract, the contract would immediately send e.g. 1,000,000 USDC directly back to the Nested Factory contract._**

  * The Paraswap operator checks the balances of the buy and sell tokens. Note that the buy token is defined in the Order token parameter, not the calldata passed to Paraswap. Since the operator will check the balance of USDC, it looks like we’ve swapped 1 wei ETH for 1,000,000 USDC.
  * The Paraswap operator returns the swap amounts back to Nested Factory.
  * Nested Factory deposits the 1,000,000 USDC to the vault for the user without charging any `entryFee`.

NOTE: I use 1 wei as an extreme example. You would have to ensure that you’re swapping at least enough to receive 1 wei of the ERC777 to transfer to the attack contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑bypass flaw in the NestedFactory contract when it creates a new vault through the create() function that forwards an arbitrary order to a Paraswap operator. The factory is designed to charge an entryFee (and similarly an exitFee) based on the amount of the input token that a user sends to the swap router. However, the fee calculation is performed before the swap executes and relies only on the declared input token amount, not on the actual amount of output tokens that are finally transferred back to the factory. By supplying a crafted calldata payload to the Paraswap router, an attacker can request a swap that converts a minuscule amount of ETH (for example 1 wei) into a large amount of a token that the attacker controls, such as an ERC777 or a malicious ERC20, with the attacker’s contract set as the beneficiary. Because the router forwards only the tiny input amount, the entryFee computed from that amount rounds down to zero due to precision loss. When the swapped token is sent back to the factory, the factory records the large token balance and deposits it in the vault without ever deducting the expected fee. From the user’s perspective the UI displays a successful vault creation, a zero fee amount, and an unexpectedly huge token balance, contradicting the expectation that a proportional fee would be taken. The root cause is the mismatch between the token used for fee assessment (the input token) and the token that actually flows through the reserve (the output token), combined with the allowance of unrestricted calldata that gives the caller control over the swap logic. This issue can be reproduced by any user who can call create() with an order that contains arbitrary calldata, and it is not limited to the Paraswap operator; other operators that permit free calldata, such as 0x, are similarly vulnerable. The impact is a loss of protocol revenue because fees can be entirely avoided, and it undermines the accounting assumptions that fees are proportional to the value entering or leaving the reserve. The problem was discovered during a security audit by inspecting the fee‑charging pathway and noticing that the fee is computed prior to the external call and that the contract trusts the operator’s reported token balances. It may be difficult to notice in production because the transaction still succeeds, the fee field shows a value of zero (which appears legitimate), and no explicit error is emitted. A proper remediation strategy is to compute entry and exit fees on the actual amount of output tokens that the reserve receives after the swap, to restrict the calldata that can be passed to known safe function signatures, or to prohibit arbitrary external call data altogether. Whitelisting tokens, enforcing fee collection on any token transferred, and adding post‑swap validation of received balances are also recommended to close the bypass vector.

title: Buyout cannot be rejected when paused
description: While `buy()` and `sell()` are only callable when the system is not paused, `redeem()` and `withdrawERC721()` are also callable when it is not. This means that the `BUYOUT_DURATION` is ignored in such cases and it is possible that users are not able to reject certain buyouts.
poc: A user initiates a buyout via `initiateBuyout()`. Just afterwards, the system is stopped. The token holders now cannot buy new tokens to increase the value. However, after two days, the `bidder` can still withdraw the NFT, i.e. there was no way for the users to reject this buyout.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the interaction between the contract’s pause mechanism and the buyout lifecycle. In the protocol, a buyout can be initiated by a bidder and must remain open for a fixed BUYOUT_DURATION during which token holders may reject the offer by buying additional tokens or otherwise exercising their rights. The contract correctly guards the buy() and sell() functions with a whenNotPaused modifier, preventing new purchases or sales while the system is paused. However, the redeem() and withdrawERC721() functions, which allow a bidder to claim the NFT and retrieve the underlying assets once the buyout period has elapsed, are not protected by the same modifier. As a result, when an admin pauses the contract after a buyout has been started, the countdown toward buyoutEndTime continues unchecked. If the pause persists beyond the original BUYOUT_DURATION, token holders lose the opportunity to reject the buyout because they can no longer call buy() or sell() to increase the token supply or otherwise intervene, while the bidder can still invoke withdrawERC721() to claim the NFT. This creates a scenario where the protocol’s intended safeguard – giving users a temporal window to reject an acquisition – is silently bypassed. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker with pause privileges (or a compromised admin key) initiates a buyout, immediately pauses the contract, and then waits for the buyout deadline to pass. The bidder then withdraws the NFT, and the original token holders receive nothing, effectively losing ownership of the asset without any chance to contest the transaction. The impact is medium severity because it compromises the fairness of the buyout process, potentially causing loss of assets for token holders and undermining confidence in the protocol’s governance guarantees. The condition under which this occurs is any pause triggered during an active buyout window; the bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the pause modifiers on public functions and noted the inconsistency. It may be difficult to notice in practice because pausing is expected to freeze all user interactions, and developers might assume that withdraw-related functions are harmless. However, they directly affect the finalization of a buyout. To remediate, the contract should either apply the whenNotPaused guard to redeem() and withdrawERC721() so that no buyout finalization can occur while paused, or alternatively reset buyoutEndTime to the current block.timestamp when a pause is enacted, thereby restoring the full rejection window once the system resumes. This aligns the implementation with the logical requirement that a paused state should prevent any operation that can change asset ownership, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: `Twav.sol#_getTwav`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that calculates a time‑weighted average valuation (TWAV) by dividing the difference of two cumulative valuation observations by the difference of their timestamps. The contract stores timestamps as a 32‑bit unsigned integer (uint32) and performs a plain subtraction when computing the elapsed time: `_twavObservationCurrent.timestamp - _twavObservationPrev.timestamp`. In Solidity versions prior to 0.8, arithmetic under‑/overflow would wrap around, which was intentionally relied upon by the original Uniswap oracle example. However, the contract is compiled with Solidity 0.8.10, where arithmetic operations automatically revert on underflow or overflow unless placed inside an `unchecked` block. When the global block timestamp exceeds the maximum value representable by uint32 (2^32‑1, corresponding to the year 2106), the subtraction that assumes wrapping will underflow, causing the transaction to revert. Even before the wrap‑around, the use of unchecked arithmetic is inconsistent: the update function uses `unchecked` for the timestamp delta, but the read function does not, leading to a situation where the TWAV calculation can fail precisely at the moment the current observation’s timestamp has overflowed while the previous observation’s timestamp has not. This narrow window results in the contract either reverting or returning an incorrect average valuation, breaking the price‑feed logic that downstream vaults rely on. From the user’s perspective, a vault that depends on the TWAV may appear to stop updating, showing stale or zero prices, and users attempting to interact with the vault may receive unexpected revert messages or see their deposits valued incorrectly. The issue was identified during a formal audit that compared the contract’s logic to the reference Uniswap oracle and noted the change in Solidity's arithmetic semantics. It is easy to miss because the overflow will not occur for more than eight decades, and the contract’s behavior seems correct under normal test conditions. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unchecked arithmetic / overflow handling” errors, where a developer assumes wrap‑around semantics that are no longer guaranteed by the language version. To remediate, the timestamp subtraction in the TWAV getter should be placed inside an `unchecked` block, mirroring the update function, or the contract should migrate to a larger timestamp type (e.g., uint64) and adjust the arithmetic accordingly. By ensuring consistent handling of the timestamp delta, the contract will maintain correct TWAV calculations even after the 32‑bit timestamp rolls over, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unexpected reverts or inaccurate price data.

title: User Could Change The State Of The System While In `Pause` Mode
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a vault contract that manages a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) used to decide whether a buyout proposal should be accepted or rejected. While the contract implements an emergency "Pause" mode that is intended to freeze all mutable state, the function responsible for updating the TWAP, updateTWAV, does not check whether the contract is paused. Consequently, any actor can invoke updateTWAV even when the system is paused. The function first verifies that the vault is currently in the buyout state, then compares the current block timestamp to the last stored timestamp. If they differ, it recalculates the TWAP and immediately calls an internal routine to reject the buyout when the updated TWAP is higher than expected. Because the pause modifier is missing, the TWAP can be altered and the buyout rejected while the contract is supposed to be immutable. An attacker could trigger this function during a pause, causing the buyout to be rejected without giving other participants a chance to challenge the outcome, breaking the economic guarantee that the TWAP provides a fair, time‑averaged valuation. Users who expect a buyout to proceed during a pause – for example, to recover their funds – may instead see the proposal dismissed and their balances remain unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of opportunity. This issue was identified during a manual audit where the auditor noted that state‑changing functions should be guarded by the whenNotPaused modifier. It can be hard to notice because the function does not directly transfer funds and the pause flag is typically assumed to protect all internal state updates. The bug belongs to the class of "pause bypass" or "missing access control" vulnerabilities where emergency controls do not cover all mutable pathways. To remediate the problem, the updateTWAV function should be protected with the whenNotPaused modifier or an explicit require statement checking the paused flag, ensuring that no TWAP updates or buyout rejections can occur while the contract is paused. This aligns the contract's behavior with the intended security model and restores confidence that the pause truly freezes protocol state.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑privileged administrative account (owner) that can invoke a set of setter functions controlling core protocol parameters in the HODL Pool contract. These functions allow the owner to replace the signature verifier, the Uniswap V2 router, the non‑fungible position manager, the operator address, the dead address used for token burns, the tick spacing that influences price granularity, the global fee applied to swaps, and to pause or unpause the entire contract. The root cause is the design choice to grant a single externally owned account unrestricted authority over critical components without any decentralised governance, timelock, or multi‑signature protection. An attacker who gains control of this owner key – either through compromise of the private key or by a malicious insider – can exploit the setters to redirect swaps to a malicious router, replace the verifier with a contract that accepts forged signatures, increase the fee to an arbitrary value, change the dead address to siphon tokens, or pause the contract to freeze user withdrawals. The impact includes loss or misdirection of user funds, unexpected fee hikes, inability to withdraw or claim rewards, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol. The exploit can be triggered at any time the owner decides to call one of the privileged functions; therefore the risk is present continuously as long as the owner remains a single EOA. All participants who deposit assets, provide liquidity, or rely on the protocol’s fee and routing logic are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that fees remain bounded, routing is honest, and withdrawals are always possible – are violated. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s access control and noted the breadth of functions guarded only by the onlyOwner modifier. It can be difficult to notice in normal operation because the setter functions appear benign and may never be exercised in a benign deployment, masking the underlying centralisation risk until a malicious action occurs. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the single‑owner model by transferring control to a community‑governed DAO, optionally protected by a multi‑signature wallet and enforced timelocks for any parameter change, thereby aligning the protocol with a trustless, decentralized governance lifecycle and reducing the counter‑party risk inherent in a privileged admin key.

title: Safe-Version Replacement With safeTransfer() And safeTransferFrom()
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the direct use of ERC20 token functions transfer() and transferFrom() without employing a safety wrapper that normalises the handling of non‑standard token behaviours. In the Holdefi contract two internal functions, transferFromHoldefi and transferToHoldefi, invoke token.transfer and token.transferFrom respectively and then require the boolean return value to be true. While the ERC20 specification defines these functions to return a bool indicating success, many deployed tokens deviate from the standard: some tokens (for example USDT) do not return any value at all, and others may revert on failure instead of returning false. When a token that does not return a bool is called, the Solidity ABI decoder receives an empty data payload; the decoded boolean is interpreted as false, causing the subsequent require statement to revert even though the transfer may have actually succeeded. Conversely, if a token silently fails and returns false, the require correctly reverts, but the contract does not distinguish between a genuine failure and a non‑standard return pattern. An attacker can exploit this inconsistency by supplying a token that deliberately omits the return value, causing the contract to treat a successful transfer as a failure and revert the whole transaction. This can be used to create a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users are unable to deposit or withdraw assets because the contract repeatedly reverts on token transfers. The impact is primarily a loss of usability and potential fund lock‑up: users attempting to move tokens into or out of the protocol may see their transaction fail with the generic “Cannot Transfer” error, leading to frustration and possibly financial loss if the failure occurs after other state changes. The issue manifests whenever the contract interacts with any ERC20 token that does not strictly adhere to the return‑value convention, i.e., any token that either returns no data or uses a different signalling mechanism. All participants who rely on the Holdefi contract – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract cannot reliably accept or send those tokens. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s token handling against known best‑practice patterns and recognised the absence of OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 wrapper. The bug can be subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the require statement appears to protect against failures, yet the underlying assumption about the return data is wrong, making the defect easy to overlook during testing. The recommended remediation is to replace direct calls to transfer() and transferFrom() with the SafeERC20 library’s safeTransfer() and safeTransferFrom() methods, which internally perform low‑level calls, correctly interpret missing return data as success, and revert only on genuine failures. By abstracting away the return‑value handling, the contract regains compatibility with all ERC20 implementations and eliminates the denial‑of‑service vector caused by non‑standard tokens.

title: Owner Address Centralization Risk
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Holdefi protocol relies on a single externally owned account (EOA) designated as the owner and protected by an onlyOwner modifier to execute critical administrative functions such as activating or deactivating market and collateral assets. Because ownership is centralized in one private key, any compromise, loss, or accidental exposure of that key gives an attacker unrestricted access to those privileged functions. An attacker who obtains the owner’s private key can call functions that change the activation status of markets or collaterals, potentially freezing user deposits, preventing withdrawals, or manipulating protocol parameters in a way that harms users. This risk materialises whenever the owner key is exposed, which can happen through phishing, malware, insider error, or insecure key management practices. All participants who rely on the protocol’s ability to add, remove, or manage assets are affected, as the protocol’s operational continuity and governance depend on the owner’s authority. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined access‑control patterns and noted the absence of a multi‑signature governance mechanism; the auditor flagged the single‑owner model as a central point of failure. The problem can be difficult to notice because the onlyOwner modifier appears standard and the contract functions correctly under normal conditions; the vulnerability only becomes apparent when the owner key is compromised, a situation that is not evident from on‑chain activity alone. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single‑owner EOA with a multi‑signature contract or a DAO‑style governance contract that requires multiple approvals before executing privileged actions, thereby eliminating the single point of failure. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a centralized admin key risk or single‑owner access control weakness. From a user’s perspective, an exploit may manifest as markets or collaterals suddenly becoming inactive, withdrawals being blocked, or funds appearing to disappear, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The attack scenario proceeds step‑by‑step: (1) the attacker obtains the owner’s private key; (2) the attacker invokes privileged functions such as deactivateMarket or deactivateCollateral; (3) the protocol state is altered, causing markets to halt and user assets to become inaccessible; (4) the attacker may further exploit any additional privileged functions to move or lock funds. Because the contract does not enforce multi‑signature checks, these malicious actions are accepted without further verification. The impact can range from temporary service disruption to permanent loss of user funds if the attacker also controls functions that transfer assets. Re‑architecting the ownership model to require multiple signatures mitigates the risk by distributing authority and preventing unilateral malicious actions.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is the existence of a single privileged account, referred to as manager or gov, that is able to call a set of functions that change core protocol parameters such as pair configuration, one‑percent depth, rollover fee per block and funding fee per block. The root cause is that the contract does not enforce a decentralized governance mechanism or timelock; the authority is hard‑coded to an address that can be changed only off‑chain. An attacker who gains control of that address can invoke the onlyManager functions and arbitrarily modify fees, depth limits or other parameters. By raising fees to extreme values or setting depth to zero, the attacker can cause trades to be executed with excessive costs, liquidations to trigger incorrectly, or funding payments to be drained, effectively stealing or freezing user funds. The impact is that users may see their balances reduced unexpectedly, receive zero refunds, or be unable to open positions because the protocol parameters no longer reflect market conditions. The exploit can be carried out at any time after the privileged key is compromised, for example through a phishing attack, private key leak, or a malicious upgrade of the manager contract. All participants of the protocol – traders, liquidity providers and the broader ecosystem – are affected because the integrity of the economic model relies on the assumption that only a trusted, community‑controlled entity can adjust these values. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected access control modifiers and noted the absence of a DAO‑style governance or timelock pattern. Because the functions appear normal and emit events, the malicious changes may not be immediately obvious; only a careful review of parameter history or an unexpected shift in fees would reveal the problem. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a decentralized governance contract that enforces proposal voting, quorum and a delay before execution, and the existing manager functions should be protected by a timelock or removed entirely. In short, the bug belongs to the class of centralized admin key risks where a single address can alter critical economic parameters, breaking the trust model and allowing fund loss.

title: Potential Reentrancy Risks
bug_full: The vulnerability is a potential re‑entrancy flaw in the function that processes loan repayments. The contract follows the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern in most places, but when the repayment involves returning excess ETH to the caller, it performs an external call to the caller before updating the borrower’s balance and interest state. Because the external call is made prior to the state‑changing writes, a malicious contract supplied as the caller can execute a fallback function that invokes the repayment function again, before the original execution finishes. This nested call can cause the contract to credit the same repayment amount multiple times or to withdraw additional funds that have not yet been accounted for. The impact is that an attacker could drain ETH from the protocol or manipulate accounting entries, leading to loss of funds for lenders and incorrect interest calculations. The issue manifests whenever a contract calls the repayment function with an amount larger than the outstanding debt, triggering the extra refund path. Users who are regular EOAs are not directly affected, but any contract acting as a borrower or as a proxy can be exploited. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that compared the order of external calls against the checks‑effects‑interactions guideline. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to simply return surplus ETH, and the re‑entrancy only becomes relevant when the caller is a contract with a malicious fallback; normal transactions behave correctly. To remediate, the contract should either move the external transfer after all internal state variables have been updated, or protect the function with a re‑entrancy guard modifier, thereby ensuring that no second entry can occur before the first call completes. This class of bug is known as a re‑entrancy vulnerability caused by violating the checks‑effects‑interactions principle, and it breaks the accounting assumption that balances are settled before any external interaction. From a user’s perspective, a borrower expecting a refund of excess ETH may instead see their balance unchanged while an attacker repeatedly extracts funds, resulting in funds disappear or refund not received symptoms.

title: Incoherent handleGoldGovFees Convention in HSTradingCallbacks
bug_full: The Holdstation protocol contains a callback contract (HSTradingCallbacks) that forwards fee‑related data to a storage contract via the function handleGoldGovFees. The target function is defined to accept five parameters: a pair index, a leveraged position size, a referral fee amount, a trader address, and a boolean flag indicating whether the full fee should be taken. In several callback routines – notably updateSlCallback, openTradeMarketCallback, closeTradeMarketCallback and registerTrade – the fourth argument is supplied as a boolean literal (true or false) instead of the trader’s address. This mismatch means that the storage contract receives an incorrect value for the _trader parameter. Because the fee‑distribution logic inside handleGoldGovFees uses the _trader address to forward agency rewards and to record gold‑fee payments, passing a boolean causes the contract to treat the value as an address (typically the zero address or a low‑value address such as 0x1). Consequently, agency rewards may be sent to an unintended address, gold fee accounting can be distorted, and the final fee amount returned to the caller may be calculated with the wrong full‑fee flag. The vulnerability manifests whenever a trade is processed through the affected callbacks – for example when a user opens a USDC‑collateral trade and the contract executes the true branch of the ternary expression. From the user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected fee deduction: a trader may see a larger fee taken than advertised, or a missing referral reward, and the protocol’s accounting tables will show inconsistent goldFeesUsdc and govFeesUsdc balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑collection logic, where the auditor noticed that the function signature and the call sites did not align. It is subtle because the code compiles and the fee calculation appears to run, but the logical error only becomes visible when tracing fund flows or comparing expected versus actual fee amounts. To remediate the problem the callbacks should be updated so that the fourth argument passed to handleGoldGovFees is the actual trader address and the boolean flag is supplied as the fifth argument, matching the declared parameter order. Alternatively the storage function’s signature could be refactored to accept arguments in the order used by the callbacks, but the essential fix is to ensure type‑consistent and semantically correct argument ordering across all fee‑handling calls, thereby restoring correct fee distribution and preventing inadvertent loss or over‑charging of user funds.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: During the audit of the HoneyFarm protocol we identified that the contract contains a privileged owner account that can invoke functions such as setDevAddress, setFeeAddress, setEarningsReferral and setReferralCommissionRate. These functions allow the owner to change critical addresses that receive protocol fees and to adjust the percentage taken as referral commission. The owner key is a single externally owned account without any multi‑signature or timelock protection. Because the owner can arbitrarily redirect fee flows and modify economic parameters, an attacker who gains control of the private key, or a malicious owner acting intentionally, can divert user funds, increase fees, or lower referral rewards. The vulnerability manifests when the owner calls any of the privileged setters; the contract does not enforce any delay, community vote, or additional checks, so the change takes effect immediately. Users interacting with the protocol expect that fee distribution and referral rates are stable and governed by a decentralized process; instead they may see their expected rewards reduced or their deposits sent to an unexpected address. The issue was discovered through manual code review that highlighted the use of the onlyOwner modifier and the absence of any governance or timelock pattern. Because the functions are simple setters, the risk can be easy to overlook in a UI that does not display the current fee or dev address, making the problem hard to notice until a malicious change occurs. The impact ranges from loss of trust to direct financial loss for users whose assets are routed to a newly set fee address or whose referral commissions are lowered. The vulnerability belongs to the class of centralised admin key or owner‑controlled parameter manipulation bugs, where a single key can alter critical economic variables. To mitigate the issue the privileged role should be transferred to a DAO‑controlled contract, optionally guarded by a timelock that enforces a delay and allows community oversight before any change is applied. Removing the single owner altogether or replacing it with a multi‑signature wallet reduces the attack surface and aligns the protocol with its intended trustless design.

title: Missing Definition of onlyOwner in HoneyToken
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing access‑control definition in the HoneyToken contract. The mint function is marked with the onlyOwner modifier, which is intended to restrict token creation to a privileged owner, but the contract does not declare or inherit such a modifier. The root cause is that the contract neither inherits from a standard Ownable base contract nor defines its own onlyOwner modifier, leaving the identifier undefined at compile time. Because Solidity requires every used identifier to be declared, the contract will fail to compile, preventing deployment and rendering the protocol inoperable. If a developer were to add a placeholder onlyOwner modifier that does nothing, the mint function would become publicly callable, allowing any address to invoke mint and arbitrarily increase the token supply. This could be exploited by an attacker who calls mint with a chosen recipient and a large amount, causing uncontrolled inflation, loss of token value, and breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions. The impact includes potential loss of confidence, dilution of existing holders’ balances, and the inability of the protocol to enforce its token issuance policy. The issue manifests whenever the contract is compiled or when a naive fix removes the modifier without proper access control. All participants who rely on the token – users, liquidity providers, and the governance system – are affected because the token’s supply integrity is compromised. The problem was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the presence of onlyOwner without a corresponding definition. It can be hard to notice because the surrounding code appears otherwise correct and the missing modifier does not generate a runtime warning; the failure only appears at compilation. The correct remediation is to either inherit from a well‑tested Ownable contract (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s Ownable) or explicitly implement an onlyOwner modifier that checks that msg.sender matches a stored owner address, and to ensure that the owner is set correctly in the constructor. This restores the intended restriction on minting, aligns the contract with its business logic that only the protocol operator may create new tokens, and prevents accidental or malicious token inflation.

title: Timely massUpdatePools During Pool Weight Changes
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the set() function allows the pool allocation point to be changed without first updating the accumulated reward state of all pools. The contract provides an optional boolean _withUpdate that, when true, triggers massUpdatePools() before the weight change. If the caller (the contract owner) passes false or ignores the flag, the totalAllocPoint is updated while the per‑pool reward variables (such as accRewardPerShare) remain stale. As a result, the reward distribution for the current period is calculated using an outdated allocation weight, causing an unfair share of newly minted governance tokens. In extreme cases a pool that previously had zero allocation weight can be given a non‑zero weight after the change, and because the reward state was not refreshed, that pool can immediately claim a disproportionate amount of rewards that should have been shared among existing pools. The impact is that legitimate stakers may receive fewer tokens than expected, while the manipulated pool may capture an excessive amount, effectively draining rewards from the protocol. This condition occurs whenever set() is invoked with _withUpdate set to false, or when the owner manually disables the update call. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the HoneyFarm protocol, where the reward accounting logic was examined and the optional update flag was identified as a potential source of inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit warning, and the reward balances appear correct after a later massUpdatePools call, masking the earlier misallocation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “inconsistent state update” or “reward accounting race” bugs, where state changes are applied without synchronizing dependent variables. From a user’s perspective, a staker may notice that their pending reward amount is lower than expected, or that a newly added pool suddenly receives a large reward allocation despite having no prior activity. The expected behavior is that changing a pool’s weight should first bring all pools up to date, preserving the proportional distribution of rewards; the actual behavior without the update violates this accounting assumption. The recommended mitigation is to always invoke massUpdatePools() before modifying any pool’s allocation point, and to remove the optional _withUpdate flag to prevent accidental omission.

title: Revised Selection of bestRouter in HopeSwapBurner::burn()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑conversion routine of the LightDAO governance protocol, specifically in the HopeSwapBurner contract’s burn() function. The function is supposed to swap a received fee token for HOPE by querying a set of candidate swap routers and selecting the router that yields the highest amount of HOPE. The contract calls each router’s getAmountsOut() method, which returns an array where the first element (expected[0]) is the input token amount (the amount that will be spent) and the second element (expected[1]) is the projected output amount of HOPE. The code mistakenly compares expected[0] instead of expected[1] when determining the best router. Because expected[0] is identical for every router – it always equals the spendAmount – the selection logic always picks the first router in the list, regardless of which router would actually provide the most HOPE. This logical error can be exploited by an attacker who can control the ordering of the routers array or insert a malicious router at index zero. The attacker’s router may offer a very poor exchange rate, causing the protocol to receive fewer HOPE tokens than intended, potentially failing the amountOutMin check or simply delivering a lower return to the fee recipient. The impact is a loss of value for the protocol’s fee‑conversion mechanism, reduced HOPE payouts to users, and possible revenue shortfall for the DAO. The issue manifests whenever burn() is called with a token other than HOPE and when more than one router is configured. It affects the feeVault, any user receiving swapped HOPE, and the overall accounting of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit review of the burn() implementation, where the auditor noted the misuse of the return array. The problem is subtle because the code compiles and the swap still succeeds, but the economic outcome is sub‑optimal and may not be obvious from the UI, which only shows a successful transaction without indicating that the received HOPE amount is lower than expected. To remediate, the selection loop should compare expected[1] – the projected HOPE amount – against bestExpected, and update bestRouter accordingly. This change ensures that the router offering the highest HOPE output is chosen, aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended business logic of maximizing fee conversion value.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a trust and centralisation issue arising from the presence of a privileged owner account in the LightDAO governance protocol, specifically within the GaugeController contract.
