Because the contract only checks that the caller has the appropriate role, any holder of the privileged key can arbitrarily add or remove supported assets, change risk parameters, or swap out the index logic contract. An attacker who gains control of this key could, for example, register a malicious index, lower the maxComponents limit to break existing indexes, or point the indexLogic address to a contract that siphons user deposits. Exploitation requires only that the attacker be able to call the privileged functions; no special conditions or complex interactions are needed. The impact is that protocol users may see unexpected behaviour such as their balances becoming zero, refunds failing, or new assets appearing without notice, effectively resulting in loss of funds or a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions. This issue is most relevant when the privileged account is owned by a single entity rather than a decentralized DAO, exposing users to counter‑party risk. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the concentration of power and the lack of transparent governance. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear normal and are protected only by role checks, which may be overlooked in a code review focused on functional correctness rather than governance design. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a DAO‑style governance contract that enforces multi‑signature approval and timelocks for any changes to risk parameters or contract logic, thereby aligning the system with its intended trustless model and reducing the possibility of malicious or accidental misuse.

title: Potential DoS in IndexRouter::mintSwap()
bug_full: The IndexRouter contract of the Phuture protocol contains a minting workflow that ends with a strict invariant check: after processing all asset swaps, the contract requires that its balance of the input token be exactly zero. This invariant is enforced by the statement require(IERC20(_inputToken).balanceOf(address(this)) == 0) at the end of the internal _mint() function. The logic assumes that every token transferred into the contract during mintSwap will be either forwarded to the appropriate vToken or consumed by swaps, leaving no residual amount. However, an attacker can deliberately send a tiny amount of the same input token to the router contract before a legitimate user invokes mintSwap. Because the contract does not restrict arbitrary token transfers into its address, the extra dust remains in the contract’s balance after the normal processing loop. When the final require executes, the leftover balance causes the condition to fail and the transaction reverts with the error message "IndexRouter: INVALID_INPUT_AMOUNT". This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: any user attempting to mint new index tokens will see their transaction revert, receive no index tokens, and lose the gas spent on the call. The issue manifests only when an unexpected token balance exists, which may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors examined the _mint() routine and identified the final balance check as error‑prone. The bug belongs to the class of “dust‑based denial‑of‑service” or “invariant violation due to unexpected token balance”. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a failed mint attempt, often with a generic revert message, and the expected index tokens would never appear in the wallet. Users expect their deposit to be accepted and their share tokens to be minted, but instead the transaction fails and no funds are transferred. To remediate the issue the contract should either remove the strict zero‑balance requirement, explicitly return any leftover input tokens to the caller, or implement a safe accounting mechanism that tracks the exact amount that should be consumed and only reverts on genuine under‑ or over‑payment. By avoiding reliance on a global token balance invariant, the protocol can prevent an attacker from blocking the minting path and ensure that legitimate users can always deposit assets and receive their index tokens.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a trust and centralisation issue arising from privileged admin keys in the PikaPerpV3 protocol. Certain accounts are granted ADMIN_ROLE and MINTER_ROLE, which allow them to call functions that can mint new PIKA or esPika tokens, toggle the global transfer flag, replace the fee calculator contract, change the price oracle, enable or disable position keepers, and modify execution fee and user‑action permissions. The root cause is that these powerful functions are protected only by a simple role‑based access control check without additional safeguards such as multi‑signature approval, time‑locks, or transparent governance. An attacker who gains control of an admin key, or a malicious admin acting intentionally, can exploit these functions by minting arbitrary amounts of tokens, inflating supply and diluting existing holders, or by disabling transfers so users cannot move their tokens, effectively freezing assets. The admin can also replace the oracle with a manipulated source, causing price feeds to be incorrect and enabling profitable liquidations or front‑running. Changing the fee calculator or execution fee parameters can impose excessive fees on users, while toggling user‑execute or user‑cancel flags can prevent users from managing their positions. The impact includes loss of user funds, market manipulation, erosion of trust, and potential regulatory concerns. The issue manifests whenever the privileged functions are invoked, which can happen at any time because there is no delay or community oversight. All token holders, traders, and any party interacting with the protocol are affected because the admin can alter core economic parameters or freeze token movement. The problem was identified during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s access control and enumerated the functions callable by privileged roles. It can be hard to notice in production because the calls are indistinguishable from legitimate admin activity and there is no on‑chain alerting mechanism; users typically only see the downstream effects such as unexpected token balances, disabled transfers, or sudden fee spikes. To remediate, the protocol should make the list of privileged capabilities explicit to users, adopt stronger governance mechanisms (e.g., multi‑sig, timelock, DAO voting) for any admin action, consider removing or limiting minting rights, and provide transparent event logging and user notifications when critical parameters are changed. By reducing the concentration of power and increasing visibility, the protocol can mitigate the risk of abuse and restore confidence in its economic model.

title: Revisited Logic in PikaPerpV3::modifyMargin()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the margin‑adjustment routine of the PikaPerpV3 perpetual contract. The function modifyMargin allows a position owner or an authorized manager to increase or decrease the margin of an existing position. While the code correctly transfers tokens and updates the stored margin value, it only checks that the resulting leverage stays above a minimal threshold (newLeverage >= 1 × BASE). This check prevents leverage from dropping too low but does not enforce any upper bound or verify that the position remains above the liquidation margin after a margin reduction. Consequently, when a user decreases margin, the new leverage can rise dramatically and the position may become under‑collateralised, yet the function will still succeed because the only guard is a low‑leverage requirement. The root cause is a missing health‑check after the margin change – the contract assumes that the simple leverage formula is sufficient to guarantee safety, ignoring the protocol’s liquidation criteria. An attacker or an unwary user could exploit this by deliberately withdrawing margin just enough to push the position into a liquidatable state, after which any third party can trigger liquidation and seize the remaining collateral. The impact is that users may lose a portion of their funds unexpectedly, seeing their balances drop to zero or being forced into liquidation without warning. This condition occurs whenever the shouldIncrease flag is false and the requested margin subtraction brings the position close to the liquidation threshold. The affected parties are position owners, their delegated managers, and any participants relying on the protocol’s risk guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s core logic, where the auditor noted that the function does not call the internal health‑check routine that is used elsewhere for margin updates. Because the function still emits a successful ModifyMargin event, the problem can be subtle and may not be noticed until a liquidation occurs. To remediate, the routine should recompute the position’s health after applying the new margin and enforce that the resulting collateralisation ratio stays above the required minimum, or reject the transaction if the position would become liquidatable. In other words, the function must include the same safety validation that is performed in other margin‑modifying paths, ensuring that decreasing margin cannot render the position unsafe. This class of bug is a missing post‑condition check in financial smart contracts, leading to accounting inconsistencies where the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that positions are always solvent) are violated, causing funds to disappear or be seized unexpectedly.

title: Improved claimable Calculation in claimable()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the contract calculates the amount of PIKA tokens that a user can claim from a vesting deposit. The claimable() function uses a single global variable, vestingPeriod, to determine the proportion of tokens that have vested based on elapsed time. When a deposit is created, the contract records the amount of esPIKA deposited and the timestamps that define the vesting schedule, but it does not store the specific vesting period that was in effect at the moment of creation. If the contract owner later calls setVestingPeriod() and changes the global vestingPeriod, any existing deposit that was created before the change will still be evaluated against the new period. As a result, the claimable amount returned by claimable() can be higher or lower than the amount that should be available according to the original schedule. This mismatch occurs because the calculation is tied to a mutable state variable rather than an immutable per‑deposit parameter, a classic case of using a shared configuration for per‑instance logic. An attacker, or even the contract owner, could manipulate the vesting period after deposits are made to cause users to receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, or conversely to allow premature over‑claiming, which would inflate the token supply. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the UI may show a claimable balance that is unexpectedly zero or significantly different from the expected linear vesting curve; a user who expects to claim a certain amount based on the original schedule may receive nothing or an incorrect amount, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue is difficult to notice because the function appears to perform a straightforward proportional calculation, and the change of a global parameter is a legitimate administrative action, so the discrepancy is not obvious without tracing the relationship between deposit creation time and subsequent period updates. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the vesting logic, where the auditor observed that the claimable() routine does not reference the vesting period that was active at deposit time. To remediate the problem, the contract should record the vestingPeriod value at the moment each deposit is created and use that stored value in the claimable() computation, ensuring that each deposit’s vesting schedule remains immutable regardless of later administrative changes. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that each user’s vesting should be independent and predictable, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unintended token dilution or loss.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a trust and centralisation issue arising from privileged roles that have unrestricted authority over critical contract functions in the Pika protocol. The root cause is the assignment of ADMIN_ROLE, MINTER_ROLE, OWNER, and KEEPER to single accounts without transparent disclosure or additional governance safeguards, allowing those accounts to mint new tokens, toggle the global transfer flag, modify vesting periods, and set token prices arbitrarily. An attacker who gains control of any of these privileged keys can exploit the contract by minting unlimited PIKA or esPika tokens, effectively inflating the supply and diluting existing holders; by disabling transfers, they can freeze user balances and prevent withdrawals; by altering the vesting period, they can accelerate or delay token releases to their advantage; and by manipulating the price feed, they can create artificial price spikes or drops that benefit the attacker in downstream markets. The impact includes loss of token value, potential theft of funds through market manipulation, erosion of user trust, and a systemic risk that the protocol’s economic assumptions are violated. The issue manifests whenever a privileged function is called – for example, when the admin calls setTransfersAllowed(false) and users see their transfers rejected, or when the keeper updates priceMap with malicious values causing price discrepancies. All token holders, liquidity providers, and any participants relying on the protocol’s promised decentralised behaviour are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined access control modifiers and identified that the privileged functions are not explicitly disclosed to users, making the risk subtle and easy to overlook because the functions appear standard and the contracts lack clear warnings. Detecting abuse can be difficult without on‑chain monitoring of role activity, as the contract does not emit events that highlight privileged changes beyond the basic ones. To remediate, the protocol should make the list of privileged accounts and their capabilities visible to users, enforce multi‑signature or time‑locked governance for critical actions, consider decentralising the roles, and provide clear documentation and UI cues about who can perform these operations. By reducing single‑point authority and increasing transparency, the risk of malicious or accidental misuse of admin keys can be mitigated.

title: Incorrect ETH tokenBase Used in OrderBook
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect token base conversion for ETH in the OrderBook contract of the Pika protocol. The contract stores a variable tokenBase that represents the decimal denominator of the collateral token. In createOpenOrder the code correctly multiplies the ETH execution fee by the constant 1e18 (the ETH token base) before transferring, but in cancelOpenOrder the same calculation uses tokenBase instead of the constant. When the collateral token is not ETH, tokenBase will be set to the decimals of that token (for example 1e6 for USDC). As a result the amount of ETH that is refunded to the user when an order is cancelled is scaled by the wrong denominator. The function first transfers the combined execution fee and margin back to the user using the wrong factor, and then sends the execution fee again with the correct factor, creating a mismatch that can leave the user with a shortfall or, conversely, cause the protocol to retain excess ETH. The bug can be triggered simply by creating an order with a non‑ETH collateral token, paying the required ETH execution fee, and then cancelling the order. The user will see the expected fee deducted from their wallet at order creation, but after cancellation the received ETH may be lower than expected, sometimes appearing as zero or a fractional amount that does not match the original fee. This violates the accounting assumption that the execution fee is fully refundable on cancellation and breaks the protocol’s financial invariants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the order lifecycle functions, and it is easy to miss because the two code paths look symmetric and the wrong variable name does not raise a compiler warning. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect denomination or token base usage” bugs, where a constant representing token decimals is substituted with a variable that may hold a different value. To remediate, all ETH‑related calculations should use the fixed 1e18 denominator instead of tokenBase, ensuring that refunds and internal accounting use the same scale as the fee was originally charged.

title: Improved Logic In MainPlayPadContract::withdrawPoolRemainder()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a privileged withdrawal function that allows the contract approver to extract any remaining reward tokens from a staking pool at any moment. The root cause is the absence of a temporal guard that checks whether the staking period has ended; specifically, the function does not verify that the current block number exceeds the predefined finishBlock. Because of this missing condition, an approver can invoke the function before the pool’s reward distribution schedule is complete. When called early, the function calculates the amount to return as the total pool token balance minus the amount already paid and the pending rewards for stakers, then transfers this remainder to the approver. This premature transfer reduces the pool’s balance that would otherwise be allocated to participants, causing stakers to receive fewer tokens than the protocol’s accounting assumes they are entitled to. The impact is a shortfall in user rewards, potentially leading to loss of funds for participants, erosion of trust in the protocol, and a mismatch between expected and actual token distributions. The issue manifests whenever the approver invokes withdrawPoolRemainder before the block number passes finishBlock, which can happen at any time because the function is marked only with an onlyApprover modifier and a nonReentrant guard. The affected parties are the stakers who expect full rewards, the protocol that promises a certain reward schedule, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate accounting. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the logic of the withdrawal routine and noted that the function could be called arbitrarily. It may be hard to notice because the function is restricted to a privileged role and appears to perform a legitimate cleanup of leftover tokens, so developers might assume it is safe to call at any point. To remediate, the contract should enforce a condition that permits withdrawPoolRemainder only after the staking period has officially ended, typically by requiring block.number > finishBlock, thereby ensuring that all earned rewards are fully distributed before any remainder is reclaimed. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards are only reclaimed after the pool’s lifecycle is complete, preventing premature depletion of reward funds and preserving the integrity of the reward accounting.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a trust issue arising from the concentration of privileged authority in a single admin (the approver or contract owner) within the PlayPad‑IDO‑DQ system. The contract design grants this admin the ability to create new IDO contracts, modify the prize limit, withdraw any remaining reward tokens from the staking pool, and alter critical sale parameters such as contract status, sale token address, lock time, maximum and minimum purchase values. The root cause is the reliance on a single address for these high‑impact functions without additional governance safeguards such as multi‑signature approval, timelocks, or transparent role enumeration. An attacker who gains control of the admin key, or a malicious admin acting intentionally, can invoke the privileged functions at any time after deployment. By calling the withdrawPoolRemainder function the admin can siphon the unclaimed reward tokens, leaving stakers with a lower or zero payout. By changing prize limits or sale parameters the admin can manipulate the economics of an IDO, for example reducing the maxBuyValue to exclude participants or raising the minBuyValue to block small investors. The impact includes loss of expected rewards, distortion of token distribution, and erosion of user confidence, potentially resulting in financial loss for investors and damage to the protocol’s reputation. The issue manifests whenever the admin executes any of the privileged calls; it is not tied to a specific transaction pattern but to the existence of unchecked authority. All participants—investors, token sellers, and the broader community—are affected because they rely on the contract to enforce fair and immutable rules. The problem was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the presence of functions protected only by the onlyApprover or onlyOwner modifiers and noted the lack of explicit privilege documentation. Because the contract does not emit detailed events for each privileged change and the UI typically shows only final outcomes, users may not notice that an admin has altered parameters or withdrawn funds, making the bug subtle. To remediate, the protocol should make the full set of privileged actions explicit to users, adopt a role‑based access control model, require multi‑signature or timelocked approvals for critical changes, limit the amount that can be withdrawn from the reward pool, and consider renouncing ownership or transferring it to a governance contract. These measures would reduce centralization risk and align the contract’s behavior with the expected trust model of decentralized finance applications.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract relies on a single privileged account identified by the onlyGovernance modifier to update critical protocol state such as the total volume purchased, per‑user purchase records, and the calculation stage. Because this privileged key is not controlled by a DAO‑like timelocked governance contract, an attacker who compromises the admin key can arbitrarily rewrite purchase amounts and force the protocol into any calculation stage. This breaks the trust model that assumes the protocol’s accounting is immutable and that stage transitions are governed by community consensus. Exploitation is straightforward: once the admin key is obtained, the attacker calls updateCalculatedData with forged user addresses and amounts, or calls setCalculationStage or setCanFinalize to move the pool into the CALCULATED stage prematurely, causing downstream functions that depend on these values, such as finalization and fund distribution, to operate on manipulated data. The impact includes users receiving incorrect allocation, premature finalization of the pool, loss of funds, or the protocol becoming unusable because participants can no longer rely on the recorded purchase totals. The condition occurs whenever the privileged account is active and not protected by multi‑signature or timelock mechanisms; it is especially dangerous in the early deployment phase before DAO governance is wired. All parties that interact with the pool – purchasers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions are violated. The issue was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the mismatch between the intended DAO governance model and the actual single‑key control. It can be hard to notice because the functions themselves perform no validation beyond length checks, and the state changes appear legitimate on‑chain, making the malicious updates blend with normal administrative activity. The recommended remediation is to replace the single privileged address with a proper DAO‑controlled contract, introduce timelocks or multi‑signature for any state‑changing calls, and ensure that the calculation stage can only be advanced through a transparent governance proposal. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of centralised admin key or governance bypass vulnerabilities where critical protocol parameters can be altered by a single entity, breaking the expected trustless behaviour and potentially leading to fund loss or incorrect accounting.

title: Extra Funds Return in swapV2ExactIn()/swapV3MultiHopExactIn()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an extra‑fund retention bug in the swapV2ExactIn (and swapV3MultiHopExactIn) functions of the SwapX contract. When a user swaps native ETH for another token, the function accepts a payable amount and only checks that msg.value is greater than or equal to the required amountIn plus the protocol fee. Because the check uses >= instead of == and there is no logic that returns any surplus ETH, a caller can deliberately or accidentally send more ETH than needed and the contract will keep the excess. The root cause is the missing refund path after the swap and the reliance on a non‑strict inequality. An attacker can exploit this by sending a transaction with a large overpayment; the contract will execute the swap using the exact amountIn‑fee, while the additional ETH remains locked in the contract with no way for the user to retrieve it. The impact is that users may lose the extra ETH they sent, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds, and the protocol’s accounting may show unexplained ETH accumulation, breaking the assumption that all received ETH is either used for the swap or returned. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to swapV2ExactIn (or swapV3MultiHopExactIn) where tokenIn is the native coin (address(0)). Affected parties include regular users who provide ETH, the protocol’s treasury, and any downstream audits that rely on correct fund accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the insufficient validation of msg.value and the absence of a post‑swap refund step. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an event for the retained surplus and the extra ETH does not affect the swap outcome, so the bug is silent from the UI perspective – the user sees a successful swap but the sent ETH amount is higher than expected and the balance of the user is reduced accordingly. To remediate, the contract should either enforce msg.value == amountIn + fee or, after the swap, calculate any leftover ETH (msg.value – amountIn – fee) and transfer it back to the caller using a safe call, ensuring that the protocol never keeps unintended native funds. This class of bug is commonly known as an “over‑payment retention” or “unrefunded excess funds” vulnerability, which violates the business rule that a user’s payment should be fully accounted for or returned.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑centralized administrative key that controls several critical functions of the SwapX protocol. The contract exposes a single owner address that can call pause, unpause, setFeeRate, setFeeCollector, setWETH and setFeeExclude. Because these functions are guarded only by an onlyOwner modifier, the owner can arbitrarily halt trading, change the fee percentage, redirect the fee collector to any address, replace the wrapped ether token reference and whitelist or blacklist accounts for fee exemption. The root cause is the reliance on a single privileged account without any additional governance, timelock, or multi‑signature safeguards. An attacker who compromises the owner key, or a malicious owner acting in bad faith, can exploit the functions by pausing the contract to freeze user withdrawals, setting the feeRate to an extreme value (for example 100 percent) to siphon all incoming swaps, or changing feeCollector to an address they control, causing all fees to be sent to the attacker. The impact is that users may see their trades fail, receive no output, or lose a large portion of their assets to an unexpected fee collector. This situation occurs whenever the contract is live and the owner key is active, which is the default deployment configuration. All participants of the protocol – traders, liquidity providers and any third‑party integrators – are affected because the admin can alter the economic parameters that the protocol promises. The issue was identified during a manual audit that inspected the access control patterns and noted the absence of any decentralized governance or timelock mechanisms. It can be hard to notice from a user’s perspective because the functions are standard OpenZeppelin‑style admin calls and the contract may appear functional until the owner takes a malicious action; there is no on‑chain evidence that the owner is trustworthy. To remediate, the privileged role should be transferred to a community‑governed DAO or a multi‑signature wallet, and any future administrative changes should be subject to a timelock that gives users a window to react. If a proxy pattern is used, the proxy‑admin rights must also be handed over to a decentralized entity. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized admin key” or “owner‑only control” vulnerabilities that break the trust model of decentralized finance by allowing a single party to manipulate fees, pause execution and redirect assets, contrary to user expectations of transparent and immutable protocol behavior.

title: Improved Logic In MainPlayPadContract::stakeTokens()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking function of the MainPlayPadContract where the user’s stakeStartDate is overwritten each time the function is called with an amount that pushes the user’s total staked balance above the vesting threshold (limitForPrize). The root cause is a missing guard that distinguishes between the first crossing of the threshold and subsequent stakes that keep the balance above the limit. Because the code only checks if the new total amount is greater than limitForPrize, it unconditionally updates stakeStartDate whenever a user who is already above the limit adds more tokens. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling stakeTokens with a small additional amount after already exceeding the limit, thereby resetting the vesting start timestamp and extending the vesting period or penalty window each time. This manipulation delays the moment when the user becomes eligible for prize distribution or can withdraw without penalty, effectively reducing the user’s expected reward timing and potentially causing loss of expected earnings. The issue manifests when a staker who has previously crossed the limit performs any further stake; the contract updates stakeStartDate, which the UI may display as a moving vesting end date, leading to confusion as the expected claim date keeps shifting. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the stakeTokens logic, where the conditional update of stakeStartDate was noted as overly broad. It can be hard to notice because the contract still accepts the stake and updates reward debt correctly, so no immediate error is thrown; the problem only becomes apparent when the vesting schedule behaves inconsistently. To remediate, the contract should set stakeStartDate only when the user’s total staked amount transitions from below to above limitForPrize – for example, by checking the previous balance before the addition and only assigning stakeStartDate if the prior balance was ≤ limitForPrize and the new balance > limitForPrize. This change restores the intended one‑time initialization of the vesting timer and prevents malicious extension of the vesting period.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralised admin key that controls privileged functions in the FolioFactory contract. The contract uses a single owner address protected by an onlyOwner modifier to approve new modules and to withdraw arbitrary ERC20 tokens to any recipient. Because the owner is an externally owned account rather than a DAO‑governed contract, the protocol relies on the trustworthiness and security of that single key. If the private key is compromised, an attacker can call approveModule to register a malicious module that may execute arbitrary logic across all portfolios, and can invoke withdraw to transfer any amount of tokens from the contract to an address of their choosing. This breaks the fundamental assumption that module approvals are safe and that funds are locked in the protocol, leading to potential loss of user assets, injection of harmful code, and overall erosion of confidence in the system. The issue manifests whenever the owner account is either malicious or its credentials are exposed, which can happen through phishing, poor key management, or insider threat. All users of the protocol, including portfolio creators and token holders, are affected because the compromised actions apply protocol‑wide. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the presence of privileged functions without any multi‑sig, timelock, or DAO governance layer. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear normal and the owner address may be assumed to be trustworthy, so no on‑chain alerts are emitted when a new module is approved or a withdrawal occurs. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected module approvals, missing token balances, or a sudden zero balance after no interaction. The bug belongs to the class of centralised admin key or single‑point‑of‑failure vulnerabilities, where critical state‑changing operations are not governed by a decentralized mechanism. To remediate, ownership should be transferred to a DAO‑style governance contract, optionally protected by a multi‑signature wallet and timelocks, ensuring that any change to approved modules or token withdrawals requires community consensus and cannot be executed by a single compromised key.

title: Wrong Hardcoded Aave AToken Address
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect hard‑coded mapping between the DAI token and its corresponding Aave aToken (aDAI) inside the tier2Aave contract constructor. The contract stores a series of system‑wide parameters, among them tokenToAToken and aTokenToToken mappings that are meant to translate a base token address (e.g., DAI) to the Aave interest‑bearing token address (aDAI) and vice‑versa. In the deployed code the mapping is populated with the address 0x25550Cccbd68533Fa04bFD3e3AC4D09f9e00Fc50 for both tokenToAToken[DAI] and aTokenToToken[that address]. This address does not correspond to the official aDAI contract on mainnet; instead it is either an unrelated token or a mistaken copy of the DAI address. The root cause is the use of static, hard‑coded addresses without verification, which leads to a mismatched token pair. An attacker or any user interacting with the contract can trigger the bug simply by depositing DAI, expecting the protocol to mint or transfer the correct aDAI. Because the contract references the wrong aToken address, the internal accounting records a transfer to a contract that does not implement the Aave aToken interface, causing the deposited DAI to be sent to an unexpected destination or to be locked in a contract that does not recognize it. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit, but later the balance of aDAI remains zero, refunds are missing, or the user’s DAI balance disappears from the protocol. The impact is a potential loss of user funds and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting logic, as the protocol assumes a 1‑to‑1 relationship between DAI and aDAI for interest calculations. The issue manifests immediately after deployment and persists for any operation that relies on the tokenToAToken or aTokenToToken look‑ups, affecting all users of the tier2Aave contract and the overall Plexus protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the constructor and compared the hard‑coded addresses against known mainnet deployments. The bug is subtle because the addresses are syntactically valid and the contract compiles without warnings, making it easy to overlook without a reference list of correct token contracts. To remediate, the hard‑coded addresses should be replaced with the verified mainnet aDAI address, and the contract should be refactored to accept token addresses as constructor parameters or via an admin‑controlled configuration function that validates the mapping against a trusted source. Additionally, unit tests and runtime checks should be added to ensure that tokenToAToken and aTokenToToken always point to contracts that implement the expected Aave interfaces, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Safe-Version Replacement With safeTransfer(), safeTransferFrom(), And safeApprove()
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of ERC‑20 token contracts that do not follow the official specification for the transfer and transferFrom functions. In the examined implementation, the functions perform a balance and overflow check and simply return false when the check fails, instead of reverting the transaction as required by the ERC‑20 standard. Because the calling code (for example the deposit routine in the Core contract) invokes token.transferFrom without inspecting the returned boolean, a failed transfer is silently ignored and the execution continues as if the tokens had been moved. This mismatch can occur with tokens such as ZRX that return false on insufficient balance, or with tokens like USDT that do not return any value at all, causing the low‑level call to revert unexpectedly. From a user’s perspective the UI will report a successful deposit, the Transfer event may not be emitted, and the protocol’s internal accounting will record an increase in balance that never actually happened. Consequently users may believe their funds were deposited while the contract holds no tokens, leading to lost or locked assets and breaking the accounting invariants of the staking system. The issue is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no error is thrown; developers may assume the ERC‑20 call succeeded based on the lack of a revert. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of token handling logic, where the auditor observed that the transfer functions returned a boolean instead of using require or revert, and that the calling code ignored the return value. To remediate the problem the contract should replace direct calls to transfer, transferFrom and approve with the safe wrappers provided by the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library (safeTransfer, safeTransferFrom, safeApprove). These wrappers enforce a revert on failure, correctly handle tokens that do not return a boolean, and ensure that the calling contract only proceeds when the token transfer has truly succeeded, thereby restoring compliance with the ERC‑20 specification and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Loss of Staked Funds With Wrongly Triggered tier2Farm::kill()
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a contract‑level self‑destruct function (kill) that can be called by the contract owner without first verifying that the contract holds no remaining assets. In the Plexus ecosystem, several tier‑2 farming contracts (tier2Farm, tier2Aave, tier2Pickle, tier2Aggregator) act as intermediaries that stake user deposits into external DeFi protocols. Because the kill() implementation simply executes selfdestruct(owner) and does not attempt to withdraw or check for any staked balances, invoking it while the contract still has active positions permanently locks the underlying funds in the external protocol. The root cause is the absence of a pre‑destruction asset‑cleanup step and the assumption that selfdestruct alone is sufficient for contract termination. An attacker who is the contract owner can trigger kill() at any time, causing the contract code and its storage to disappear while the external protocol still believes the contract address holds the stake. Users who have deposited assets therefore lose the ability to claim their stake; from their perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal request but the balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, and no refund is received. The impact is loss of user‑funds that were intended to be recoverable, effectively “money disappears” from the system. This condition occurs whenever the contract holds any non‑zero staked amount and the owner calls kill(). It affects all participants who have staked through the affected tier‑2 contracts, the overall protocol reputation, and any downstream services that rely on those funds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined contract lifecycle functions and identified that the kill() routine does not perform any asset verification. The problem can be subtle because selfdestruct is a common pattern for contract upgrades or decommissioning, and the presence of external stakes is not obvious from the contract’s public interface. To remediate, the kill() function should first check that the contract’s balance and any external protocol positions are zero, optionally invoking withdrawal functions to retrieve staked assets, and only then proceed with selfdestruct. This ensures that no locked funds remain after the contract is destroyed and aligns the implementation with the expected accounting logic that all user deposits must be either returned or explicitly transferred before termination.

title: Trust Issue Of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Plutos VirtualTrade protocol relies on a single privileged account (owner) to perform critical governance functions such as adding or removing supported assets and configuring the price oracle. This centralised admin key is not controlled by a DAO or timelocked governance mechanism, so if the private key is compromised or the owner acts maliciously, they can arbitrarily change asset listings, disable assets, or point the oracle to manipulated data. The root cause is the use of the onlyOwner modifier without any additional governance checks or multi‑signature protection, which concentrates trust in a single external account. An attacker who obtains the owner’s private key can call remove_asset to delete a legitimate asset, causing users to lose the ability to trade that asset, or call add_asset with a malicious oracle address, causing price feeds to return false values and leading to incorrect trade settlements. From the user’s perspective this may appear as assets disappearing from the UI, trades reverting unexpectedly, or prices that seem wildly off, resulting in refunds that are zero or trades that lose value. The impact includes loss of user funds, market manipulation, and erosion of the protocol’s economic assumptions because the system assumes that asset configuration and price data are trustworthy. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time the privileged account is active; there is no on‑chain safeguard that would prevent a rogue owner from executing these functions. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the asset list and price oracle drive every trade. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the contract’s access control and noted the absence of a decentralized governance layer. Because the functions appear normal and emit legitimate events, the problem can be hard to notice from the outside; the contract will still behave as coded, but the underlying parameters may have been altered maliciously. The recommended remediation is to replace the single owner with a DAO‑style governance contract, optionally protected by timelocks and multi‑signature execution, so that any change to assets or oracle configuration must be approved by the community. In generic terms, this is a privileged‑account or centralised‑admin vulnerability that violates the principle of least privilege and undermines trustless operation.

title: Possible Costly lp_token From Improper Staking Initialization
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the share‑minting logic of an ERC20 staking contract that issues pool‑share tokens (lp_token) when a user stakes a target ERC20 token. When the pool is empty (lp_token totalSupply equals zero), the contract calculates the amount of lp_token to mint by directly scaling the deposited amount with the decimal difference between the two tokens. This calculation does not enforce any minimum granularity or initial supply, allowing the first staker to control the price of the lp_token with a tiny deposit. An attacker can therefore perform a first stake of a single wei, causing the totalSupply of lp_token to become 1 wei. Subsequent deposits are then evaluated with the formula lp_amount = amount * totalSupply / previousBalance, which, because totalSupply is now extremely small, yields a very low or even zero lp_amount after integer division. As a result, later users may deposit a large amount of target_token but receive no or an insignificantly small number of lp_token, effectively locking their assets as dust in the contract. From the user’s perspective the UI would show that a deposit was accepted but the returned pool token balance is zero, contradicting the expectation of receiving a proportional share. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the stake() function where the initialization branch was examined and the lack of a minimum initial mint was noted. It is hard to notice because the first tiny stake appears legitimate and the inflated price of lp_token is not obvious until later deposits produce unexpected zero‑share results. The bug belongs to the class of “initial liquidity price manipulation” or “share token granularity” errors, similar to known problems in early versions of Uniswap that were mitigated by burning a fixed number of LP tokens at launch. To remediate, the contract should enforce a guarded launch: either mint a non‑zero baseline supply (e.g., 1,000 lp_token) and optionally burn it, require a minimum initial deposit, or use a more robust initialization formula that guarantees a reasonable token granularity and prevents a single actor from setting the price arbitrarily low. This change restores the intended accounting relationship between deposited assets and pool shares and prevents loss of funds for subsequent stakers.

title: Improved Liquidation Logic in PluzAccountManager
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the PluzAccountManager contract, specifically in the liquidateCollateral function. The function is intended to allow a liquidator to repay a portion of an underwater borrower’s debt and seize the corresponding collateral. However, the implementation treats the lend asset as a rebasing token and performs an explicit unwrap operation on the token before transferring the repayment amount. Because rebasing tokens automatically adjust balances according to a global index, unwrapping is unnecessary and can lead to an incorrect conversion between the rebasing representation and the underlying asset. This mismatch may cause the liquidator to transfer less value than required to fully cover the debt, leaving the borrower’s position partially under‑collateralised and potentially allowing the liquidator to retain excess collateral. In addition, the function lacks the nonReentrant guard that is applied to other public entry points in the contract. The absence of this modifier opens a reentrancy window: a malicious contract could call back into liquidateCollateral (or other state‑changing functions) during the execution of the external token transfer or the borrower’s repay call, thereby manipulating internal accounting variables such as the liquidation start timestamp or the amount of collateral seized. The issue manifests when a rebasing lend asset is used and when an attacker can trigger a reentrancy cascade, for example by supplying a malicious ERC20 token that executes a callback on transfer. Users affected include liquidators who may receive less collateral than expected, borrowers whose positions remain unsafe, and the protocol overall because the accounting invariants are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the code path involving IERC20Rebasing.unwrap was flagged as redundant and the missing nonReentrant annotation was noted as inconsistent with the rest of the contract. The problem can be subtle because the token balance adjustments happen automatically via rebasing, making the discrepancy hard to observe without detailed accounting checks. To remediate, the unwrap call should be removed and the conversion should rely directly on the rebasing token’s current index, ensuring the repayment amount matches the debt precisely. Moreover, the liquidateCollateral function should be protected with the nonReentrant modifier (or an equivalent reentrancy guard) to prevent nested calls that could corrupt state. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper handling of rebasing assets combined with missing reentrancy protection, leading to potential fund loss, incorrect liquidation outcomes, and violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective, a liquidator may see that the expected collateral is not transferred, or that the borrower’s debt is not fully repaid, resulting in unexpected zero balances or missing refunds, contrary to the expectation that liquidation fully settles the debt and returns the appropriate collateral.

title: Improved Validation of Function Arguments in Pod
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑modification function of the Pod vault, which allows a caller to supply a Settings structure containing a startTime and an endTime for a reward distribution period. The implementation checks that the supplied endTime is not in the past relative to the current block timestamp, but it does not enforce that the startTime must be earlier than the endTime. Consequently, an attacker or a careless administrator can pass a configuration where endTime is smaller than startTime while still satisfying the simple past‑time check. When such an inverted time window is stored, the internal accounting routine _updatePod, which assumes a monotonically increasing time interval, encounters inconsistent state and reverts on every subsequent call. This effectively freezes reward distribution: users attempting to claim or view rewards receive transaction failures, balances appear unchanged, and newly added reward tokens never become claimable. The issue manifests only when modifyRewardToken is invoked with a malformed Settings object; normal operation with correctly ordered timestamps does not trigger the bug. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s logic, where the absence of a startTime < endTime validation was noted. It can be hard to spot because the function already contains several checks (active reward, endTime not in the past, fee handling) that give the impression of thorough validation, masking the missing temporal relationship test. To remediate, the function should explicitly require that the supplied startTime precedes the endTime before persisting the settings, for example by adding a condition require(_settings.startTime < _settings.endTime). This change restores the invariant expected by the reward‑updating logic, prevents the contract from entering a permanently reverted state, and ensures that reward tokens are distributed according to a valid time window, preserving user expectations that deposited rewards become claimable after the announced start time and before the announced end time.

title: Incorrect New Token Addition Logic in Multi-Asset Market
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that adds a new token to a multi‑asset market. The function performs a share reallocation across all supported assets before the newly added token's pool is initialized. Because the pool for the new token does not exist at the moment the allocation logic runs, the accounting step uses uninitialized or zeroed storage for that token. This results in an incorrect distribution of shares: the new token may receive no shares, existing tokens may retain an outdated share balance, or the total accounting may become inconsistent. The bug is triggered whenever a market owner calls the addToken method on a market that supports multiple assets and has not yet reached the maximum asset limit. Under these conditions the contract silently accepts the new token, reallocates shares based on a pool that is still empty, and only afterwards creates the pool with the intended configuration. From a user perspective the symptoms can include unexpected zero balances for the newly added asset, missing or reduced share amounts for existing assets, and overall confusion when the market’s accounting does not match the expected allocation. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the multi‑asset support logic. It is difficult to notice because the function does not revert or emit an explicit error; the state appears to have been updated, yet the internal accounting is subtly wrong. This class of bug is an order‑of‑operations or initialization‑before‑use flaw that violates the fundamental accounting assumption that all assets must be fully defined before any redistribution of shares occurs. To remediate the problem the initialization of the new token’s pool should be performed prior to invoking the share reallocation routine, ensuring that the allocation logic operates on a fully defined and correctly configured pool.

title: Revisited New Asset Support in PriceFeed
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that registers a new asset for the price‑feed oracle. When a new token is added through the supportAsset function, the contract records the pricing strategy using a ticker‑derived identifier, but it fails to store the token's decimal precision in the same identifier space that the rest of the oracle expects. The root cause is a mismatch between the key used for the strategy mapping (a string ticker) and the key used later for price calculations (a bytes32 assetId derived from the ticker). Because the decimal mapping is written under the ticker key while the price‑query logic looks up decimals using the assetId, the newly added token ends up with an undefined base unit. When the oracle later attempts to compute a price, the missing decimal information causes a division by zero or an invalid scaling operation, which reverts the call. An attacker or any user who can trigger the addition of a new asset can therefore cause the price feed for that asset to become unusable, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for trades that rely on that price. The impact is that users attempting to trade the newly supported token see no price, transactions revert, and funds may become temporarily locked in the market contract. This condition occurs only after the supportAsset function is called for a token that has not been previously registered; existing assets are unaffected. The affected parties include the protocol itself, liquidity providers, and end‑users who expect to trade the new token. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by PeckShield, where the auditors noticed that the tokenDecimals mapping was never consulted after asset registration, a subtle oversight that does not produce an immediate error but manifests later during price queries. The bug is hard to notice because the function emits an event indicating that the asset was supported and appears to store the decimals, giving a false sense of correctness. To remediate, the contract should store the decimal value using the same identifier (assetId) that the pricing logic uses, or adjust the price‑query routine to read decimals from the ticker mapping. In conceptual terms, the fix is to ensure that every newly added asset has its decimal precision correctly persisted and accessible to all components that perform arithmetic on token amounts, thereby restoring the invariant that price calculations have a known base unit. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a missing or zero price for a newly added token, leading to failed trades and unexpected “price unavailable” messages, contrary to the expectation that the newly supported asset can be traded immediately after registration.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The PolyJeff protocol uses a single privileged owner address that is granted unrestricted access to a set of administrative functions. These functions include setting the signature verifier, the swap router, the non‑fungible position manager, the operator address, the dead address, the tick spacing parameter, and the ability to pause or unpause the whole contract. The root cause of the issue is the reliance on a traditional onlyOwner modifier without any additional governance, timelock, or multi‑signature protection. Because the owner key is the sole gatekeeper, any compromise of that private key or any malicious intent from the owner gives an attacker the power to reconfigure critical protocol components, redirect asset flows to arbitrary addresses, or halt all user operations. Exploitation can occur simply by obtaining control of the owner account; the attacker can call setVerifier to point to a malicious verifier contract, replace the router with a contract that siphons swaps, change the deadAddress to a wallet they control, or pause the contract to freeze withdrawals. The impact is that users may experience unexpected pauses, see their balances become zero, receive no refunds, or have tokens transferred to an address they did not authorize, effectively losing access to their funds. This situation manifests whenever the privileged account is used, which is during any administrative update or when the contract is paused/unpaused, and it affects every participant in the protocol, including token holders, liquidity providers, and traders. The vulnerability was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the concentration of power in a single address and the lack of any delay or community oversight. The issue can be difficult to notice because the functions appear as normal configuration calls and do not contain overtly malicious code, making the risk invisible to users until an exploit occurs. To remediate, the protocol should replace the single owner with a decentralized governance mechanism such as a DAO, optionally guarded by a timelock to enforce a delay on critical changes, and migrate proxy‑admin rights to a multi‑signature wallet. Removing the privileged key eliminates the central point of failure and aligns the system with its intended trust‑less design, preventing scenarios where funds disappear, refunds fail, or the protocol is arbitrarily halted.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the centralised administrative control exercised by a single externally owned account (EOA) designated as the owner of the Poop token contract and its associated protocol contracts. The owner possesses privileged functions, most notably setVault, which allows the owner to replace the address of the vault that holds and manages protocol assets such as ETH or BNB. Because the owner key is a plain EOA rather than a multi‑signature wallet or a community‑governed DAO, the contract relies on the trustworthiness and security of a single private key. This creates a trust issue: if the private key is compromised, lost, or used maliciously, the attacker can call setVault to point the vault to an address under their control, thereby redirecting incoming funds or withdrawing assets that were intended to be locked in the protocol. Exploitation is straightforward – an adversary who gains control of the owner key simply invokes setVault with a malicious vault address, after which any subsequent deposits or token swaps are funneled to the attacker’s address. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, disruption of protocol operations, and erosion of confidence in the platform’s decentralised claims. The condition for exploitation is the existence of a single‑key owner and the presence of the setVault function guarded only by the onlyOwner modifier; no additional timelocks or governance checks are in place. All participants who interact with the protocol – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on the vault – are affected because the expected flow of assets can be silently altered. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined privileged access patterns and noted the absence of a multi‑sig or DAO‑based governance model. It may be hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the vault address changes, and the UI may continue to display normal operation while funds are being diverted behind the scenes. From a user perspective, a typical symptom would be that a deposit appears to succeed but the user’s balance does not increase, or that withdrawals return zero despite sufficient protocol liquidity. The vulnerability belongs to the class of centralised admin‑key risks and governance bypass bugs, where a single privileged account can override critical protocol parameters. The recommended remediation is to replace the plain owner with a governance contract that enforces community voting, introduce timelocks for parameter changes, and, ideally, migrate the admin role to a DAO‑controlled address, thereby eliminating the single point of trust and aligning the protocol with its intended trustless design.

title: Improper Fee Accumulation Logic in FeeDistributor
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution contract of the PRINT3R protocol, specifically in the accumulateFees function that records newly received WETH and USDC fees and calculates the weekly distribution rate. The contract correctly updates the total accumulated fee balances, but it miscalculates the tokens‑per‑interval values because of an operator‑precedence error: the code assigns wethTokensPerInterval as _wethAmount + wethRemaining / SECONDS_PER_WEEK and usdcTokensPerInterval as _usdcAmount + usdcRemaining / SECONDS_PER_WEEK. Due to Solidity’s left‑to‑right evaluation, the division is performed before the addition, resulting in the remaining amount being divided by the week length while the newly added amount is added unchanged. The intended logic is to add the new amount to the remaining amount first and then divide the sum by SECONDS_PER_WEEK, i.e., ( _wethAmount + wethRemaining ) / SECONDS_PER_WEEK. This flaw causes the per‑week distribution rate to be significantly lower than expected, especially when the newly added fee amount is large relative to the remaining amount. Consequently, users who rely on weekly fee payouts may see little or no reward, balances may appear unchanged after a distribution period, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about equal weekly distribution break down. The issue manifests every time a registered vault calls accumulateFees, which is the normal fee‑deposit workflow, and it affects all participants who are entitled to a share of the accumulated fees. The bug was uncovered during a security audit by Peckshield, who noted the discrepancy between the documented formula and the actual implementation. Because the error is subtle arithmetic, it can be hard to notice in testing unless the distribution amounts are closely inspected over multiple weeks. The proper remediation is to rewrite the two assignment statements to compute the sum of the new fee amount and the leftover amount before dividing by the weekly interval, thereby restoring the correct tokens‑per‑interval calculation and ensuring that fee distribution aligns with protocol expectations.

title: Incorrect ADL Impact Calculation Logic in Execution
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the core Execution contract of the PRINT3R protocol, specifically in the routine that calculates the price impact for an Automatic De‑Leverage (ADL) order. An ADL order is supposed to protect a leveraged position by adjusting the execution price once the position’s profit reaches a predefined threshold, thereby preventing excessive exposure. The contract attempts to compute an acceleration factor and a pool impact using a helper function called percentage, but the arguments are supplied in the wrong order and with an incorrect precision reference. As a result, the accelerationFactor is derived from (_pnlToPoolRatio - TARGET_PNL_FACTOR).percentage(TARGET_PNL_FACTOR) instead of the intended calculation that should scale the difference by the protocol precision and the target factor. Likewise, the pool impact is calculated as pnlImpact.percentage(_poolUsd) rather than applying the precision‑aware percentage operation. Because these formulas are mathematically incorrect, the resulting poolImpact value can be far larger or smaller than intended, which directly skews the priceDelta used to adjust the index price. When an ADL order is triggered – i.e., when a user’s position profit crosses the protocol‑specified threshold – the contract may compute an impactedPrice that is either too aggressive or insufficiently corrective. An attacker or a malicious user could deliberately craft a position that triggers ADL under unfavorable conditions, causing the contract to move the execution price in a way that leaves the user with a reduced profit, an unexpected liquidation, or a situation where the position is not properly de‑leveraged. From the user’s perspective the symptoms appear as a sudden loss of expected profit, a balance that remains unchanged after an ADL event, or a position that remains open despite having reached the de‑leverage trigger, effectively “money disappearing” or “refund calculation error”. The issue is subtle because the code compiles and the percentage function is used elsewhere correctly, making the mis‑ordering of parameters easy to overlook during testing. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑logic errors where scaling factors are applied with wrong precision, leading to incorrect accounting of pool impact and price adjustments. To remediate the problem the routine must be rewritten to compute the accelerationFactor using the proper percentage call that includes the protocol precision and target factor, and the poolImpact must be derived by applying the percentage function with the pool’s USD value as the denominator and the correct precision. In conceptual terms the fix restores the intended linear relationship between realized profit, pool size, and price impact, ensuring that ADL execution respects the defined profit thresholds and does not unintentionally erode user balances or compromise protocol safety.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The Project Chosen protocol relies on a small set of privileged accounts – an owner, an operator and a group of super‑admins – to perform critical management actions such as updating investment levels and adding or removing other super‑admins. The root cause of the issue is that these roles are controlled by single private keys rather than a decentralized governance mechanism, creating a centralization risk. Because the functions updateInvestLevel and updateSupAdmin are protected only by the onlyOperator and onlySuperAdmin modifiers, any holder of the corresponding private key can call them at any time. An attacker who compromises an operator key could invoke updateInvestLevel with malicious parameters, for example setting all yields to zero or extreme values, which would immediately alter the economic behavior of the protocol. Similarly, a compromised super‑admin could call updateSupAdmin to add their own address as a super‑admin and later remove legitimate admins, giving them unchecked authority over future configuration changes. The impact of such abuse includes users receiving far lower returns than expected, assets becoming effectively locked because thresholds are set to unusable values, or, in extreme cases, the protocol’s asset flow being redirected if additional privileged functions exist elsewhere. The vulnerability manifests whenever any of the privileged functions are executed; there is no on‑chain safeguard beyond the simple role check, so the malicious calls appear indistinguishable from legitimate administrative actions in transaction logs. All participants who deposit or interact with the protocol – individual users, liquidity providers and downstream contracts – are affected because the economic assumptions they rely on (stable investment parameters governed by transparent consensus) are violated. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the access‑control design and noted that the privileged accounts are not tied to a trustless governance contract. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the functions behave as intended from a functional perspective; the problem lies in the governance model rather than a coding error. To remediate, the protocol should replace the single‑key admin model with a DAO‑style or timelocked governance contract that requires community voting for any parameter change, thereby eliminating the reliance on undisclosed private keys. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “over‑privileged admin key” or “centralized governance” vulnerability. From a user’s point of view the symptoms may include unexpected zero or dramatically altered returns, inability to withdraw because thresholds have been changed, or simply a mismatch between the advertised yield and the actual payout. Users expect that investment parameters are set by a transparent, decentralized process, but the current design allows a single actor to modify them arbitrarily, breaking the protocol’s trustless promise and its accounting assumptions.

title: Duplicate Pool Detection and Prevention in MasterChef
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the MasterChef contract allows the owner to add a new staking pool without verifying that the LP token address is already used by an existing pool. Because the add() function does not perform any uniqueness check on the _lpToken parameter, the same token can be registered in multiple PoolInfo entries. This duplicate‑pool condition breaks the accounting assumption that each LP token maps to a single reward share. When a duplicate pool is created, the totalAllocPoint is increased again for the same token, causing the scheduled reward emission to be divided among two (or more) pools that reference the same underlying asset. As a result, stakers who deposit into either of the duplicate pools receive a smaller portion of the intended rewards, and the protocol’s reward distribution logic may appear to “lose” tokens or give inconsistent returns. The issue manifests whenever the privileged add() function is called with a token that already exists in poolInfo; it can be triggered unintentionally by a governance mistake or deliberately by a compromised owner who wishes to dilute rewards or redirect them. From a user’s perspective the UI may show two pools with identical token symbols, and a user expecting a certain APY may see a lower or zero reward, leading to confusion. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error and the duplicate pools are indistinguishable except for their internal identifiers, making the misallocation hard to detect without deep inspection of the pool list. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the add() implementation against the protocol’s design specification, which requires each LP token to be unique. To remediate, the contract should enforce a uniqueness check before pushing a new PoolInfo entry, for example by iterating over existing pools and reverting if any pool’s lpToken matches the new one. This simple guard restores the one‑to‑one relationship between LP tokens and reward shares, prevents reward dilution, and aligns the on‑chain state with the intended economic model.

title: Incorrect Average Price Update Logic in MarketUtils
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that updates the weighted average entry price for a trading position when the position size is increased. The contract currently computes the new average price using a simple arithmetic mean formula (prevSize*prevAvg + delta*markPrice) / (prevSize + delta). This formula is mathematically incorrect for weighted averages of price‑size pairs; the correct computation requires dividing the sum of size‑to‑price ratios, i.e., (prevSize + delta) / (prevSize/prevAvg + delta/markPrice). Because the contract applies the wrong formula, the stored average entry price can become artificially low after a size increase. The root cause is a misunderstanding of how to combine two price‑size components into a single weighted average, leading to a mis‑implementation in MarketUtils.calculateWeightedAverageEntryPrice. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by increasing a position with a positive size delta, which is a normal operation. By doing so, the contract records a lower average entry price than should be the case, inflating the apparent unrealized profit for that position. This inflated profit can be harvested later through premature liquidation, margin calls, or by closing the position, effectively allowing the user to extract more funds than entitled or causing the protocol to suffer losses. The issue manifests only when _sizeDelta is greater than zero; decreasing a position or fully closing it follows the intended logic. All traders, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream services that rely on accurate PnL calculations are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that entry price reflects the true cost basis) are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the PRINT3R Positions contract, where the auditor compared the implemented formula against the mathematically correct weighted average expression. It can be hard to notice because the resulting average price still appears plausible and the discrepancy may only become evident after multiple position adjustments or when large price swings occur. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a sudden drop in entry price, unexpectedly high profit, or a loss when closing a position that should have been profitable. To remediate, the routine should be rewritten to implement the correct harmonic‑weighted average formula, using high‑precision arithmetic to avoid overflow or rounding errors, and the contract should be thoroughly tested with edge cases such as very small or very large deltas. In summary, the bug is a miscalculated weighted average entry price that breaks accounting logic, can be exploited to inflate profits, and requires a formula correction to restore correct financial behavior.

title: Trust Issue of Admin Keys
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the PRINT3R protocol relies on a single owner account that possesses a broad set of privileged functions. Because the owner can modify core protocol parameters, replace external contracts such as price feeds, fee distributors, and position managers, and also withdraw ETH that is held for market creation taxes, the protocol’s security depends entirely on the trustworthiness and secrecy of the owner’s private key. The root cause is the use of an unrestricted onlyOwner modifier on functions that affect accounting, fee calculation, and external contract references, combined with the ability to upgrade the proxy implementation. An attacker who obtains the admin key can, for example, change market fees to extreme values, redirect fee distribution to an address they control, replace the price feed with a manipulated contract, and call withdrawCreationTaxes to siphon the contract balance after subtracting only the reserved execution fees. By upgrading the proxy to a malicious implementation, the attacker could also introduce new backdoors or disable existing safeguards. These actions can be exploited at any time the owner key is compromised, either through phishing, key leakage, or a malicious upgrade proposal. The impact includes loss of user funds, incorrect price information leading to unfair trades, altered fee structures that disadvantage participants, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol. Users may notice that their balances are reduced unexpectedly, refunds are missing, or trades execute at prices that do not reflect market reality. The issue was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the concentration of power in a single address and the lack of timelocks or multi‑signature governance. Because the functions are marked onlyOwner, the risk is not immediately obvious to casual observers, making it easy to overlook. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single owner with a DAO‑style governance contract, enforce timelocks on privileged actions, and consider multi‑signature control for upgrades, thereby removing the single point of trust. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized admin key” or “privileged access” vulnerabilities where excessive authority is granted to a single address, allowing arbitrary state changes and fund withdrawals.

title: Incorrect FundingRate And Velocity Update in Funding
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ordering bug in the funding state update routine of the PRINT3R protocol's Funding library. The function updateState calculates the next market skew, then immediately writes the new fundingRateVelocity based on the current market data, and only afterwards updates the fundingRate and fundingAccruedUsd. According to the protocol's design, the velocity should be derived from the freshly computed fundingRate, because the velocity represents the rate of change of the fundingRate. By updating velocity first, the calculation uses the previous fundingRate value, producing a stale or incorrect velocity figure. An attacker or any market participant can trigger updateState through normal contract interactions (for example, opening or closing a position) and cause the protocol to record a mismatched velocity. This mismatch propagates to subsequent funding calculations, leading to inaccurate funding payments: traders may receive too little or too much funding, and the protocol's accounting may diverge from the intended economic model. The issue manifests whenever the pool's state is updated, which is on each trade or price feed update, and it affects all users of the affected market, including long and short positions, as well as liquidity providers who rely on correct funding accruals. The bug was discovered during a manual code review by the audit team, who noted that the comment in the source explicitly states that velocity must be updated after fundingRate, but the implementation does the opposite. Because the discrepancy is a subtle arithmetic error, it may not be immediately visible in the UI; balances may appear correct at a glance, but over time the cumulative funding may drift, causing users to see unexpected reductions or increases in their positions or pool shares. The root cause is a logical ordering mistake rather than a flaw in the arithmetic itself.
