The problem is subtle because the require statement looks correct at first glance, making it easy to miss that the accounting state is incomplete. The recommended remediation is to introduce a mapping that tracks the total pending withdrawal amount per node owner and to subtract this value from the withdrawableWei limit when validating new withdrawals. The pending amount should be increased when a withdrawal is queued and decreased when it is completed, ensuring that the sum of active and queued withdrawals never exceeds the owner’s actual entitlement. This class of bug is an accounting omission that allows infinite queuing of withdrawals, a common pattern in DeFi contracts where pending state is not reflected in limit checks, leading to fund‑drain attacks.

title: assets > withdrawableWei() check in _decreaseBalance() causes NativeVault.finishWithdrawal() to revert when slashing occurs
description:
When finishing a withdrawal, NativeVault.finishWithdrawal() calls _decreaseBalance() to decrease the node owner's asset balance:
```solidity
_decreaseBalance(startedWithdrawal.nodeOwner, startedWithdrawal.assets);
```
_decreaseBalance() checks that startedWithdrawal.assets is not greater than withdrawableWei():
```solidity
if (assets > withdrawableWei(_of)) revert WithdrawMoreThanMax();
```
Note that withdrawableWei() returns the minimum between the node owner's native node balance and the assets equivalent of his shares.
However, if Karak operator or the beacon chain slashes the node owner's ETH balance before a withdrawal is finished, it might become impossible for the withdrawal to be executed using finishWithdrawal() due to this check.
For example:
• Assume that:
– A node owner holds 32e18 shares that corresponds to 32 ETH.
– He is the only node owner in the entire protocol, so totalSupply and totalAssets are both 32e18 as well.
• Node owner calls startWithdrawal() with weiAmount = 32e18 to withdraw his entire balance.
• Karak operator calls slashAssets() to slash 1 ETH, so totalAssets = 31e18.
• Node owner calls finishWithdrawal() to finish the withdrawal. In _decreaseBalance():
– withdrawableWei() returns 31 ETH.
– startedWithdrawal.assets = 32e18 is greater than withdrawableWei(), so the check reverts.
If a withdrawal can never be completed using finishWithdrawal(), as demonstrated above, the node owner will have to go through the full MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY period again to withdraw his assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal finalisation logic of the NativeVault contract. When a node owner initiates a withdrawal, the contract records the amount of native ETH (assets) the user expects to receive. During the final step, finishWithdrawal() calls an internal routine that reduces the owner’s recorded balance. This routine contains a guard that compares the requested amount with the value returned by withdrawableWei(), which represents the maximum amount the owner is currently allowed to withdraw. WithdrawableWei() is defined as the minimum of the owner’s native balance and the ETH equivalent of the owner’s share holdings. The problem occurs when the protocol’s slashing mechanism reduces the total assets after the withdrawal request has been made but before finishWithdrawal() is executed. Because the slashing lowers the total assets, withdrawableWei() can become smaller than the amount originally requested. The guard then triggers a revert (WithdrawMoreThanMax), preventing the withdrawal from completing. An operator or the beacon chain can cause this situation simply by invoking slashAssets() while a withdrawal is pending. From a user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction fails, the UI may show an error or simply no funds arriving, and the user is forced to wait through the full minimum withdrawal delay again before trying another withdrawal. The impact is that legitimate node owners can have their funds effectively locked for an additional delay period, undermining confidence in the protocol’s reliability and potentially leading to financial loss if the user cannot wait. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the Karak Native Restaking system, where the interaction between the slashing path and the withdrawal path was examined. It is subtle because the check appears to protect against over‑withdrawal, yet it does not account for the dynamic nature of the underlying asset pool. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent validation errors” where a condition that is true at request time becomes false later due to external state changes. To remediate the problem the strict revert should be replaced with a safe cap: the contract should compute the current withdrawable amount and, if the pending request exceeds it, reduce the withdrawal amount to the available maximum before decreasing the balance. This ensures that a withdrawal can always be completed, even after a slash, and preserves the accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: YieldManager can claim fewer unstaked tokens than expected resulting in insolvency
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the YieldManager contract that handles unstaking from Lido. When a user initiates an unstake, YieldManager records the full requested amount in its pendingBalance. Later, when the withdrawal queue is claimed, the actual amount that can be retrieved may be lower than the request because Lido’s withdrawal queue can return fewer ether than the number of shares due to negative rebases (the condition batchShareRate > checkpoint.maxShareRate triggers a reduced claim). The contract only subtracts the claimed amount from pendingBalance, leaving the shortfall unaccounted for. As a result, YieldManager continues to believe it will receive the full requested amount, inflating its totalValue and pending balance. This mismatch can cause the protocol to become insolvent for downstream L2 withdrawals because the accounting layer reports more assets than are actually available. The issue is triggered whenever a withdrawal is claimed during a period of negative rebasing, which is a normal but rare state of the Lido system. All users who rely on the YieldManager to retrieve their unstaked funds are affected, as they may see their balances remain unchanged or receive less ether than expected, while the protocol’s internal accounting shows a higher total value. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of YieldManager’s claimPending function with Lido’s WithdrawalQueueBase._calculateClaimableEther implementation. It is difficult to notice because the shortfall may be small and the contract does not emit an explicit event indicating a loss, so the discrepancy only appears in aggregate balance reports. To remediate the issue, the pending balance for a claim must be cleared entirely and the difference between the requested amount and the actually claimed amount must be recorded as a loss. Ideally the same insurance‑fund mechanism used in commitYieldReport should be invoked to absorb the negative yield, updating accumulatedNegativeYields and adjusting totalValue accordingly. In user‑facing terms, a user expects to receive the full amount they unstaked, but instead receives a reduced payout or sees no change in their displayed balance, indicating that the protocol’s accounting has broken and funds may disappear from the system.

title: USDConversions can swap locked funds
description: DAI tokens in the yield manager that are locked for finalized withdrawals can be swapped to other USD yield tokens. User withdrawals can fail after finalization because of this.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the USDConversions component of the yield manager, where DAI tokens that have been locked for a finalized withdrawal can be unintentionally swapped into other USD‑denominated yield tokens. The root cause is that the conversion routine does not verify whether the amount being exchanged includes any portion of the locked balance; the library that performs the swap has no visibility into the locked‑fund accounting and therefore cannot prevent the operation. An attacker or any user with permission to invoke the convert function can trigger a swap after a withdrawal has been marked as finalized but before the user actually claims the funds. By moving the locked DAI to a different token, the protocol’s internal accounting no longer has the expected DAI available for the pending withdrawal, causing the subsequent withdrawal call to revert or return zero. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal request, yet the transaction fails or the user receives no tokens, leading to a perception that funds have disappeared or that a refund is missing. This issue manifests only in the narrow window between finalization of a withdrawal and the actual claim, and it affects any participant who has a pending finalized withdrawal as well as the overall protocol’s financial integrity. The problem was identified during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the USDConversions library lacks a guard against operating on locked balances, a subtle flaw that can be missed because the conversion itself succeeds and only the later withdrawal exhibits the symptom. To remediate the issue the conversion function should include a check that reverts when the amount to be swapped overlaps with any locked balance, or the design should separate locked and free balances so that swaps are only permitted on free assets. Implementing such a guard restores the accounting invariant that finalized withdrawals must be fully redeemable, preventing users from receiving an empty payout and preserving trust in the protocol’s handling of funds.

title: YieldManager can stake locked funds
description: When L2 bridge withdrawals are finalized in the WithdrawalQueue the funds are considered locked as the user can now withdraw these funds from the queue. However, both YieldProvider's stake functions allow staking this locked amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the YieldManager component of a cross‑chain bridge that handles L2 withdrawals. When a withdrawal is finalized in the WithdrawalQueue, the corresponding funds become locked – they are earmarked for the user and should only be withdrawable through the queue. However, the two YieldProvider contracts (DSRYieldProvider and LidoYieldProvider) expose a stake(uint256 amount) function that determines whether the requested amount is available by comparing it to the value returned by YIELD_MANAGER.getTokenBalance() (or the older lockedValue() function). This value represents the total token balance held by the YieldManager, which includes both freely available tokens and the locked tokens that are pending user withdrawal. Because the check does not differentiate between locked and unlocked funds, an attacker or any caller can invoke stake with an amount that consumes the locked portion. The call then forwards the amount to the underlying yield protocol (DSR or Lido), effectively moving user‑reserved tokens into a yield‑earning contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may still display a normal balance, but when they attempt to withdraw they receive nothing or experience a zero‑balance error, as the funds have been re‑allocated. The impact is that users lose immediate access to their withdrawn assets; the funds are not destroyed but become trapped in the yield contract until the protocol implements a recovery path, which may never happen. This breach of accounting logic violates the core business assumption that locked funds remain withdrawable and isolates the protocol from its promised liquidity guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noted that the naming of lockedValue and getTokenBalance is ambiguous and that the stake functions lack a proper “available balance” guard. The flaw is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit errors when locked funds are moved, and the balance‑checking code appears superficially correct. To remediate, the stake functions should compare the requested amount against a dedicated available‑balance metric that excludes locked tokens, revert if the amount exceeds that metric, and the naming should be clarified (e.g., rename lockedValue to totalBalance and getTokenBalance to getAvailableBalance). This change restores the invariant that only free tokens can be staked, preserving user withdrawal rights and preventing accidental or malicious fund capture.

title: Fraud recovery logic is missing
description:
As per documentation, a partial mitigation for fraud is mentioned as:
We can partially mitigate this as the admin by not finalizing withdrawals prior to the fraud period ending.
But if the Admin doesn't finalize the withdrawal, then the withdrawal request will remain stuck in the queue along with other requests, causing DOS on every user's withdrawal request.
In the end, the Admin will be forced to finalize the fraud request (since withdrawal requests in the queue can't be skipped). This means that the ETH for said request will be stuck in lockedAmount forever (an attacker also cannot claim it due to the intervention of the Challenger).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing recovery path for funds that are tied to withdrawal requests that have been marked as fraudulent. In the OptimismPortal contract the withdrawal queue is processed in order and the admin is expected to finalize each request before the next one can be handled. The documentation mentions that the admin may withhold finalization during an active fraud period as a partial mitigation, but the contract does not provide any alternative way to resolve those stuck requests. Consequently, if the admin chooses not to finalize a fraudulent request, the request remains at the head of the queue, preventing all subsequent legitimate withdrawal requests from being processed. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for every user who tries to withdraw, because the queue cannot be skipped. When the fraud period ends, the admin is forced to finalize the fraudulent request; however, the contract logic does not allow the admin or the challenger to release the locked ETH, so the amount stays in the contract’s lockedAmount storage forever. An attacker who submitted the fraudulent request cannot claim the funds either, because the challenger’s intervention blocks the claim. The impact is that user balances appear unchanged while the protocol’s total locked ETH is reduced, effectively causing funds to disappear from the system and breaking the accounting guarantees of the yield manager. The issue occurs only when a withdrawal request is flagged as fraudulent and the admin refrains from finalizing it; it is triggered by the combination of the queue‑first‑in‑first‑out processing and the absence of a recovery function. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain logic with the documented mitigation strategy. It is subtle because the contract behaves correctly for normal withdrawals, so the problem only surfaces under the specific fraud‑handling path, which may not be exercised in routine testing. The recommended fix is to introduce an admin‑only function that can claim the ETH associated with a fraudulent request and transfer it back to the yield manager, thereby allowing the queue to progress and preventing permanent loss of funds. This class of bug can be described as a missing cleanup or reclamation path for locked assets in a FIFO withdrawal queue, which violates the protocol’s expectation that every deposited ETH can eventually be withdrawn or reclaimed.

title: Initial depositor can inflate share to siphon yield of smaller deposits
description:
The initial _totalShares of 1 is insufficient to guard against a share inflation attack that affects yield accrual.
Using the intended config of price() = 1e9 (1 gwei), an initial depositor can:
• Deposit 1 share of 1 gwei.
• Create a contract that selfdestruct() to forcibly send ETH to the contract to inflate _sharePrice(), e.g. 1 ETH.
• _sharePrice() becomes (1e18 + 2e9) / 2 = 0.500000001 ETH.
Because yield doesn't get distributed to remainders, this will prevent small deposits and remainders of <= 0.5 ETH from receiving yield, which is distributed amongst those with shares (>= 0.500000001 ETH), although in the case above, the attacker loses 0.5 ETH as a trade-off.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑inflation attack that stems from initializing the pool with a single share. Because the contract computes the share price by dividing the total ETH balance (including any forced deposits) by the total number of shares, an attacker who is the first depositor can artificially raise the share price by sending ETH to the contract through a self‑destructing contract. In the described scenario the attacker deposits one share worth one gwei, then self‑destructs a contract that transfers one ether into the pool. The share price jumps from the expected one gwei to roughly 0.500000001 ether. Yield distribution logic only rewards holders whose share value meets or exceeds the current share price, so any subsequent small deposits or leftover balances below about half an ether receive no yield. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a tiny deposit yields zero interest, contrary to the expectation that every deposit should accrue proportional yield. The impact is that legitimate users lose expected returns, effectively allowing the attacker to siphon yield from smaller participants while sacrificing a portion of the injected ether. The condition required for exploitation is the presence of an initial totalShares value of one and the ability to force ETH into the contract, which is not prevented by the contract’s interface. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the share accounting logic. It is difficult to notice because the share price appears correct under normal operation and the forced ETH injection does not emit any event, making the manipulation invisible to casual observers. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “share price manipulation via forced value injection” and violates the accounting assumption that share price reflects only legitimate deposits. The recommended mitigation is to initialise the pool with a sufficiently large number of shares (for example 1,000 as used by UniswapV2), which dilutes the effect of any single forced deposit and prevents the share price from being dramatically altered by an attacker.

title: Reinitialization causes metering parameter to be reset
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑initialization flaw in the resource‑metering component of the contract. When the contract’s initializer version constant (Constants.INITIALIZER) is changed, the internal function __ResourceMetering_init is invoked again. This function blindly overwrites the stored ResourceParams structure with hard‑coded defaults (prevBaseFee set to 1 gwei, prevBoughtGas to 0, and prevBlockNum to the current block number). Because the code does not check whether the parameters have already been set, a legitimate upgrade or re‑deployment can reset these values to their defaults. The root cause is the lack of a guard condition that distinguishes a fresh deployment from a re‑initialization, allowing the same initializer logic to run multiple times. An attacker or even an honest developer triggering a re‑initialization can cause the metered modifier, which relies on these parameters to compute gas price and fee calculations, to use stale or incorrect baseline values. As a result, the contract may under‑charge users, over‑charge them, or mis‑report the amount of gas bought, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. This can manifest to users as unexpected zero refunds, gas fees that do not match the transaction cost, or balances that appear to disappear after a transaction. The issue appears only when the initializer version is altered, which may happen during a contract upgrade, a migration script, or a test that resets the version flag. Because the default values are plausible (1 gwei is a reasonable base fee), the bug can be hard to notice without explicit state inspection after an upgrade. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the initializer logic and noticed that the __ResourceMetering_init function does not verify whether the parameters have already been initialized. To remediate, the initialization code should be guarded so that it only runs when the contract has never set the parameters before, for example by checking that params.prevBlockNum is zero before assigning the defaults. This ensures that subsequent upgrades do not unintentionally reset the metering state, preserving correct gas price calculations and protecting user funds.

title: admin in the Insurance contract can never be set
description:
The initialize() function in Insurance.sol does not set admin. As such, it is impossible for the admin to be set as setAdmin() can only be called by the contract's admin.
This makes it impossible for the admin to call coverLoss() should the need arise.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control initialization flaw in the Insurance contract where the admin role is never assigned during the initialize() routine. Because the initialize function does not set the admin variable, the contract starts with the admin address equal to the zero address. The setAdmin() function is protected by a modifier that only allows the current admin to call it, so once the contract is deployed there is no way to assign a proper admin. As a result, any privileged operation that requires admin rights, such as the coverLoss() function used to release funds to policyholders after a claim, cannot be executed. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: users who file a claim expect a payout, but the contract is unable to process the claim and the funds remain locked. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initialization logic and noticed the missing assignment. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the admin‑only functions appear to be correctly guarded, yet they are effectively unreachable. The problem affects the protocol operators who cannot manage the contract, the policyholders whose refunds never arrive, and any stakeholder relying on the insurance mechanism. To remediate, the initialize() function should explicitly assign the admin variable (for example, admin = msg.sender) or provide a secure bootstrap mechanism that allows a trusted address to become admin. This correction restores the intended governance flow and ensures that coverLoss() can be called when needed, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic of paying out insurance claims.

title: YieldManager.finalize can underflow for accumulatedNegativeYields
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the YieldManager.finalize function that updates the accumulatedNegativeYields variable. The function attempts to reduce accumulatedNegativeYields by the difference between the nominal withdrawal amount and the actual amount calculated from a fixed‑point share price. Because the share price is computed with limited E27 precision, the realAmount value can be rounded down. When this rounding occurs, the expression nominalAmount‑realAmount may be larger than the current accumulatedNegativeYields. The code only checks that accumulatedNegativeYields is greater than zero before performing the subtraction, so it does not guard against the case where the subtraction would underflow. An attacker can craft a withdrawal where nominalAmount‑realAmount exceeds the small positive accumulatedNegativeYields (for example, when accumulatedNegativeYields equals one and the share price rounds down by two units). The unchecked subtraction then wraps around to a very large number, corrupting the accounting state. Subsequent calls to finalize will try to subtract from this huge value, causing the function to revert or produce nonsensical results, effectively denying any further withdrawals. From a user perspective the withdrawal transaction may appear to succeed, but the finalization step returns zero or fails, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and giving the impression that funds have vanished. The issue is a classic case of insufficient guard on arithmetic combined with fixed‑point rounding errors, a class of bugs often referred to as underflow due to precision loss. It was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge cases with minimal negative yields and large nominal amounts using property‑based testing. The bug is hard to notice because the guard condition (accumulatedNegativeYields > 0) seems reasonable and the underflow only manifests for very specific numeric relationships that typical unit tests may not cover. The recommended mitigation is to clamp the subtraction so that accumulatedNegativeYields never becomes negative, or to replace the guard with a comparison of nominalAmount and realAmount and use a safe subtraction routine that returns zero when the subtrahend exceeds the minuend. This prevents the underflow and restores correct accounting, ensuring that users can reliably finalize withdrawals and that protocol funds remain accessible.

title: donateETH funds are stuck in OptimismPortal
description: The Blast OptimismPortal inherits the donateETH function from Optimism. It's not needed in Blast as it was used for the migration to bedrock. The donated funds will be stuck in the contract. When withdrawing, the withdrawal transaction's ETH is claimed from the yield manager.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a dead‑ether condition in the Blast OptimismPortal contract. The contract inherits a donateETH function from the original Optimism implementation, but Blast does not need this function because it was only required for the migration to Bedrock. When a user calls donateETH and sends ETH, the function accepts the funds and stores them in the portal’s balance, yet the withdrawal logic of the portal does not draw ETH from that balance. Instead, any withdrawal transaction claims ETH from a separate yield manager contract. Consequently, the ETH that was donated becomes permanently locked in the portal with no accessible path for the donor or the protocol to retrieve it. This situation can be triggered whenever a donor interacts with the donateETH entry point, which appears to succeed on‑chain, leading the user to believe the donation was accepted and later withdrawable. From the user’s perspective the transaction receipt shows success, but subsequent attempts to claim a refund or withdraw result in a zero balance, creating the impression that the funds have vanished. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined inherited functions and identified that the donateETH implementation no longer serves a purpose and lacks any forwarding or accounting logic. The problem is subtle because the function does not revert and does not emit any warning, so the locked funds are not obvious without tracing the withdrawal path. The bug belongs to the class of “stuck ether” or “unreachable funds” vulnerabilities, where ether is sent to a contract that has no mechanism to move it out, violating the expected accounting invariant that all received ETH should be either usable by the contract or refundable to the sender. To remediate the issue the contract should either remove the donateETH function entirely, or modify it to immediately forward the received ETH to the yield manager or another designated address that participates in the withdrawal flow, thereby ensuring that donated funds remain accessible and the accounting model stays consistent.") ,"qna

title: Actual claim rate may be below minClaimRateBips
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the calculation of the minimum staking seconds that are required to satisfy a user‑specified minimum claim rate. The contract computes minSecondsStaked by multiplying the difference between the requested minimum claim rate and the base claim rate with the difference between the ceiling and base gas seconds, then dividing by the difference between the ceiling and base claim rates using ordinary integer division. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the result can be one unit lower than the true ceiling value. Consequently the derived minSecondsStaked may be slightly smaller than necessary, so the subsequent claim rate derived from the consumed ether‑seconds can fall below the user‑requested minClaimRateBips. The bug manifests when a user requests a minimum claim rate that lies between the base and ceiling rates; in the provided example a user with 1 ETH vested for 80 seconds and a minClaimRateBips of 6000 receives a calculated claim rate of 5975, which is below the expected 6000. The root cause is the use of floor division instead of a ceiling division when converting a rate requirement into a time requirement. Exploitation is straightforward: any caller can submit a claim with a minimum rate and receive a lower rate, resulting in fewer ether being claimable than anticipated. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a claim rate lower than the minimum they set, the transaction may return less ether than expected or even zero, and the balance after the claim may appear unchanged. The impact is a breach of the economic guarantee that the protocol promises – users cannot rely on the contract to honour the minimum return they specify, which can lead to reduced earnings or perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by testing the helper contract with concrete parameters and observing the mismatch between the expected and actual claim rates. It is hard to notice because the deviation is small and does not trigger an outright failure; only careful inspection of the returned rate reveals the problem. The bug belongs to the class of financial rounding errors where integer division causes off‑by‑one or under‑allocation of resources. The recommended fix is to replace the floor division with a ceiling division, for example by using OpenZeppelin’s Math.ceilDiv when computing minSecondsStaked, ensuring that the required staking time is never underestimated and that the contract always respects the user‑specified minimum claim rate.

title: L1BlastBridge._initiateBridgeERC20() directly sends _amount of ETH without converting to 18 decimals
description:
L1BlastBridge._initiateBridgeERC20() initiates a L1 -> L2 deposit transaction as shown:
```solidity
portal.depositTransaction(
    Predeploys.L2_BLAST_BRIDGE,
    _amount,
    RECEIVE_DEFAULT_GAS_LIMIT,
    false,
    abi.encodeWithSelector(
        L2BlastBridge.finalizeBridgeETHDirect.selector,
        _from,
        _to,
        USDConversions._convertDecimals(_amount, ethYieldToken.decimals, USDConversions.WAD_DECIMALS),
        _extraData
    )
);
```
It calls L2BlastBridge.finalizeBridgeETHDirect() with USDConversions._convertDecimals(_amount, ethYieldToken.decimals, USDConversions.WAD_DECIMALS), but sends _amount of ETH through OptimismPortal. If a future ethYieldToken has more/less than 18 decimals, this will send the wrong amount of ETH and the following check in finalizeBridgeETHDirect() will fail:
```solidity
require(msg.value == _amount, "StandardBridge: amount sent does not match amount required");
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L1BlastBridge._initiateBridgeERC20 function, which is responsible for forwarding a user’s deposit from Layer 1 to Layer 2 on Optimism. The function builds a cross‑chain message that calls L2BlastBridge.finalizeBridgeETHDirect with a value that has been normalised to 18‑decimal precision using USDConversions._convertDecimals. However, the ETH that is actually sent through the OptimismPortal is the raw _amount supplied by the caller, without applying the same decimal conversion. If the underlying ethYieldToken does not use 18 decimals – for example a token with 6 or 24 decimals – the amount of native ETH transferred to L2 will be either too small or too large compared with the amount that the L2 contract expects. When L2BlastBridge.finalizeBridgeETHDirect executes, it checks that msg.value equals the amount passed in the calldata (the 18‑decimal‑adjusted value). Because the two values differ, the require statement "StandardBridge: amount sent does not match amount required" reverts the transaction. From a user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed on L1 (the UI may show a transaction receipt) but the funds never appear on L2, or the bridge transaction fails silently, leaving the user with a missing balance or a zero‑value refund. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge code where the mismatch between the value sent to the portal and the value encoded for L2 was observed. It is subtle because the same variable name (_amount) is used in two contexts, masking the fact that one side expects a different unit scale. The bug belongs to the class of cross‑chain accounting errors where decimal normalisation is applied inconsistently, breaking the invariant that the amount transferred equals the amount recorded on the destination chain. Exploitation does not require sophisticated tooling; an attacker can simply choose a token with a non‑standard decimal count and trigger a deposit, causing the bridge to reject the transfer and potentially lock funds on L1. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for affected token holders and possible loss of funds if the bridge does not provide a recovery path. The proper fix is to apply the same decimal conversion to the ETH value sent through OptimismPortal as is used for the calldata, ensuring that the amount of native ETH transferred matches the 18‑decimal representation expected by the L2 contract. This restores the accounting invariant and prevents mismatched value checks from reverting deposits.

title: Multiple Methods To Avoid Paying Fees On Withdrawals
description:
Users are intended to pay an annual fee based on deposit size to Brava, this annual fee can be bypassed via various means which remove the liquidity provider tokens from the protocol.
1. Some pool withdraw action contracts include a function called exit(). This function was intended as an escape hatch should a code error cause a DoS situation to occur with fee payments. However, as this function has no access control, it can be used at any time to exit the system without paying accrued interest to Brava.
2. Likewise, the SendTokens action can be used to remove the tokenised representations of liquidity such as aTokens used by Aave. Once removed, these positions can then be exited using the frontend of the underlying protocol, again, avoiding payment of fees to Brava.
3. More advanced users would also be able to design their own calls that make use of the Safe wallet's existing ability to call() or delegatecall() other contracts to achieve the same result of removing supplied assets without paying any fees to Brava.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑bypass mechanism that allows a liquidity provider to withdraw assets from the Brava protocol without paying the annual fee that is supposed to be collected on the deposited amount. The root cause is the absence of proper access control and validation on functions that can move or destroy the tokenised representations of liquidity. Specifically, the pool withdraw contracts expose an exit() function that was intended only for emergency use, but because it is callable by any user at any time it can be invoked to leave the system while leaving the accrued fee unpaid. In addition, the SendTokens action permits the transfer of any token, including the aTokens or other liquidity provider tokens that represent a user’s stake, without checking whether those tokens are part of Brava’s fee‑bearing pools. Finally, the Safe wallet used by users provides a generic call() and delegatecall() capability that can be leveraged to craft custom transactions that strip the supplied assets from the protocol, again bypassing the fee logic. An attacker can therefore follow a simple flow: (1) deposit assets and receive liquidity tokens; (2) invoke exit() or use SendTokens to move those tokens out of the protocol; (3) optionally use a custom call through the Safe wallet to interact directly with the underlying pool’s withdrawal function; (4) retrieve the underlying assets from the external protocol while the Brava contract never records or collects the owed fee. From a user‑facing perspective the protocol appears to allow a normal withdrawal, but the expected fee deduction never occurs, resulting in the user receiving the full amount of assets and Brava losing the revenue it relies on for sustainability. The impact is primarily economic: Brava’s fee model is undermined, leading to reduced earnings and potential imbalance in the accounting of deposited versus withdrawn amounts. The issue manifests whenever a user holds liquidity tokens that can be transferred out and when the exit() function or SendTokens action is available without restriction. It affects all participants of the Brava system, especially the protocol owners and other liquidity providers who rely on the fee to fund operations. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the withdrawal pathways and identified that the emergency exit and generic token transfer mechanisms were not gated by any fee‑payment check. The problem is subtle because the exit() function is a legitimate feature for handling DoS scenarios, and the ability to call arbitrary contracts is a core design goal of the Safe wallet, making the missing checks easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, Brava should either remove the unrestricted exit() function or protect it behind a globally set emergency state that can only be activated by governance, and it should enforce a whitelist of allowed token transfers in the SendTokens action, rejecting any movement of known liquidity provider tokens unless the fee has been settled. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of fee‑evasion or unauthorized asset‑removal vulnerabilities caused by insufficient access control and missing validation of token types in withdrawal‑related functions.

title: Protocol Fees Can Block Further Deposits
description:
Due to system accounting, it is possible for the payment of accrued fees to Brava to cause further deposits to fail. When supplying assets, accrued fees owed to Brava are first removed before processing the deposit. As this occurs after taking the initial share balance, it is possible that the overall share balance may decrease after a deposit, for example, if a user has not interacted with the protocol in a long time, such as 1 year. If the share balance decreases, then the accounting on line [79] will cause an overflow revert, which in turn will cause the deposit to fail.
```solidity
require(
    shares >= _inputData.minSharesReceived,
    Errors.Action_InsufficientSharesReceived(
        protocolName(),
        uint8(actionType()),
        shares,
        _inputData.minSharesReceived
    )
);
```
This check is intended to prevent a supply issuing too few shares for a deposit and so is more likely to occur than the previously mentioned overflow. Note, while only Across can revert due to this issue, the other protocols are affected by this for the accounting aspect only. Other protocols do not revert, but the sharesBefore and sharesAfter emitted by their events do not accurately represent the deposit size.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol accounts for accrued fees when a user attempts to supply assets. When a deposit is processed, the contract first records the user’s current share balance, then deducts any fees that have accumulated for the protocol (Brava) before completing the supply operation. Because the fee deduction occurs after the initial share snapshot, the net share balance can actually decrease if the accrued fees are larger than the amount of new shares that would be minted by the deposit. This situation is most likely to arise after a user has been inactive for an extended period, such as several months, allowing fees to build up to a size comparable to a typical deposit. When the share balance after fee removal is lower than the recorded pre‑deposit balance, the subsequent arithmetic check that validates the number of shares received (require(shares >= _inputData.minSharesReceived,…)) triggers an overflow revert. The revert prevents the deposit from completing, causing the transaction to fail with an “insufficient shares received” error. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful deposit and an increase in their share balance – is replaced by a failed transaction that returns no funds and emits events showing inconsistent share values (sharesBefore and sharesAfter do not reflect the actual deposit size). The impact is that legitimate users are unable to add liquidity, effectively blocking further deposits for the affected account and, in the case of the Across protocol, causing a hard revert that can halt operations. Other protocols that share the same accounting logic do not revert, but they still emit misleading share data, which can confuse downstream analytics and auditing tools. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit of the fee‑taking logic, where the interaction between fee removal and share accounting was examined under edge‑case conditions. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the fee deduction normally represents a small fraction of the deposit, and the overflow only manifests when fees have accumulated to a substantial amount. The bug belongs to a broader class of accounting underflow/overflow errors caused by performing state updates in an order that can invert expected invariants. To remediate the problem the contract should record the share balance after fees have been taken, or enforce regular fee collection so that accrued fees remain negligible relative to typical deposits. By adjusting the accounting flow, the invariant that the post‑deposit share balance is never less than the pre‑deposit balance is restored, eliminating the overflow condition and allowing deposits to succeed as intended.

title: Yearn Vault Withdrawal Amount Discrepancy
description: Users withdrawing tokens from the Yearn Protocol would not receive the exact amount requested. Yearn vaults process withdrawals in yvToken rather than the underlying asset. Therefore, if a user requests an amount to withdraw from a Yearn vault using the Brava protocol, they will end up receiving a different amount due to the exchange rate between the yvToken and the underlying asset. This design differs from other pool designs that Brava is integrating. Moreover, the NatSpec comment for the function ERC4626Withdraw._executeWithdraw() on line [108] states that the parameter amount represents "the amount of the underlying token to withdraw". However, this is inaccurate in the context of the Yearn vault.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a withdrawal amount discrepancy that occurs when a user requests a specific amount of an underlying token from a Yearn vault through the Brava protocol. The root cause is that the Brava YearnWithdraw contract treats the request parameter as an amount of the underlying asset, as indicated by an inaccurate NatSpec comment, but forwards this same value directly to the Yearn vault’s withdraw function, which expects an amount expressed in yvTokens (the vault share token). Because the exchange rate between yvTokens and the underlying asset (pricePerShare) is not applied, the vault returns a different quantity of the underlying token than the user asked for. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the code; any user who initiates a withdrawal will receive a mismatched amount, which may be lower or higher depending on the current share price. The impact is that users see the requested amount in the UI, approve the transaction, and then receive a smaller (or unexpectedly larger) balance, leading to loss of expected funds, broken accounting, and potential erosion of trust in the protocol. This condition occurs whenever the Brava YearnWithdraw contract is used to withdraw from a Yearn vault, i.e., for any pool that integrates Yearn vaults under the current implementation. The affected parties are end‑users who withdraw assets, the Brava protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream contracts that rely on precise withdrawal amounts. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the NatSpec documentation with the actual behavior of the Yearn vault interface. It is hard to notice because the function signature and comment suggest correct behavior, the conversion logic is hidden inside the vault, and the UI typically displays only the requested amount, not the actual amount transferred. To remediate, the YearnWithdraw contract should override the internal _executeWithdraw method to first convert the requested underlying amount into the equivalent number of yvTokens using the vault’s current pricePerShare, then call the vault’s withdraw with that share amount. The helper method _getMaxWithdraw should also be adjusted to reflect the same conversion, ensuring that both maximum and actual withdrawals are calculated in terms of the underlying token. This aligns the Yearn withdrawal flow with other pool designs in Brava and restores the guarantee that a user’s requested underlying amount is the amount they receive.

title: Unbounded iteration over balances in InitGenesis can be exploited to prevent chain start
description: GetAllBalances call in InitGenesis triggers an unbounded iteration over the rewardsPoolBalances address, which any user can deposit an arbitrary number of tokens to. If this is exploited, chain start can be blocked, which would require running an expensive upgrade handler that cleans up the spam token balances prior to chain initialization. Since this would require making direct changes to state and redistributing binaries, the impact is quite high. However, there is no material incentive to do this other than slowing down an upgrade or trying to sneak in a chain halt at upgrade-time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over the rewardsPoolBalances address performed during the InitGenesis routine when the contract calls GetAllBalances. The root cause is that the code retrieves the full list of token balances for a single address without imposing any limit on the number of entries, allowing the list to grow arbitrarily large. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a large number of different token denominations or a huge quantity of tokens to the rewardsPoolBalances address, which any user is allowed to do. When InitGenesis later executes, the GetAllBalances call must iterate over every balance entry, and the subsequent IsAnyGT check processes each element. Because the iteration is not bounded, the gas required can exceed block limits, causing the genesis initialization to fail or stall. The impact is that the blockchain cannot start, effectively halting the upgrade and preventing any transactions from being processed. This denial‑of‑service condition occurs at the moment the chain attempts to start after a governance upgrade, and it affects all participants of the protocol because the entire network remains in a non‑operational state. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the genesis initialization flow and identified the lack of iteration safeguards. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to simply read balances, a common operation, and the problem only manifests when the balance list is artificially inflated, which may not happen in normal testing. To remediate, the logic should avoid calling GetAllBalances on an address that can hold an unbounded number of token types. Instead, the contract should construct the rewardsPoolBalances list denomination by denomination, using GetBalance for each required denomination and performing the IsAnyGT comparison on those limited queries. This change bounds the amount of work performed during InitGenesis, eliminating the possibility of a gas‑exhaustion attack and ensuring that the chain can start reliably. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded iteration or denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities caused by unchecked external data structures, and it violates the protocol’s assumption that genesis initialization will complete within predictable resource limits, leading to a scenario where users see the network never become live, upgrades appear stuck, and no refunds or token transfers can occur because the chain never reaches an operational state.

title: Conditional chain halt vector due to unmetered iteration over unbounded restakable asset under default params
description: In the case where no denoms are allowed as restakable, allowed denom checks are skipped and all denoms are restakable. Due to linear iteration over reward denoms when calculating operator rewards, these circumstances expose a chain halt vector that can be exploited by creating delegations with long lists of spam token denoms. Likelihood: While this bug would be exploitable under default params, the current system has moved off of them and set a list of restakable denoms, so likelihood has been marked as Low. It is still important this is addressed, as the moment there is a reset back to default params (or the list of allowed restakable denoms is reset), a permissionless chain halt will be exposed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that can halt the entire blockchain when a delegation contains an excessively long list of token denominations (denoms). The root cause is that, under default parameters where the contract’s allowed‑restakable‑denom list is empty, the check that restricts which denoms may be restaked is bypassed, causing the system to treat every denom as restakable. When operator rewards are calculated, the contract iterates linearly over the full set of reward denoms attached to each delegation. Because there is no cap on the number of denoms and no additional gas cost that scales with the list size, an attacker can create a delegation with a large number of spam denoms, forcing the reward‑calculation loop to consume more gas than a block can provide. When this happens the transaction runs out of gas, the reward distribution fails, and the chain can become stuck because further blocks cannot be produced while the gas‑heavy operation is attempted. The impact is a chain halt that prevents any further transactions, effectively freezing user activity and halting reward payouts, although user balances themselves are not directly altered. The condition occurs only when the contract is configured with the default, unrestricted restakable‑denom parameters; the current deployment mitigates the risk by explicitly setting a whitelist of allowed denoms, which is why the likelihood is currently low. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined linear iteration patterns over delegation data structures. It is hard to notice because normal usage involves only a few denoms, so the gas consumption stays within limits and the problem only surfaces with deliberately crafted, unusually large denom lists. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum number of denoms per delegation (recommended) or, if a higher limit is required, introduce a gas cost that grows linearly with the number of denoms so that the operation cannot exceed block gas limits. This class of bug is a typical unbounded‑iteration denial‑of‑service flaw that violates the protocol’s assumption that reward calculations remain bounded and inexpensive, leading to unexpected chain freezes and missing rewards from the user’s perspective.

title: Users' funds may be temporarily frozen when the treasury lacks funds
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the burn‑request workflow of the LPExternalRequestsManager contract. When a user submits a request to burn tokens, the request is first marked as processed by an address that holds the SERVICE_ROLE, and later the same role attempts to complete the burn by transferring the required collateral from the protocol treasury to the contract. The contract does not verify that the treasury holds enough balance before attempting the transfer, and once a request has been marked as processed it cannot be reverted. Consequently, if the treasury is under‑funded at the moment of completion, the safeTransferFrom call fails, the burn remains in a processed but incomplete state and the user’s tokens stay locked inside the contract. Users are only allowed to cancel a request while it is in the CREATED state or after it has reached the PARTIALLY_COMPLETED state; a processed request that cannot be completed falls outside these conditions, so the cancellation path is blocked. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the burned tokens or a refund – is replaced by a silent freeze where the UI shows the request as pending forever and the balance appears unchanged. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state transitions and role‑restricted functions. It is difficult to notice because the failure only manifests when treasury liquidity is insufficient, a situation that may be rare and does not raise an explicit error flag in the UI. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent financial flows where a contract moves to an irreversible state without guaranteeing that downstream actions can succeed, violating the accounting assumption that processed burns will always be completed. To remediate the problem the contract should either (i) check treasury balances before marking a request as processed, (ii) allow a processed request to be unprocessed or cancelled when the completion step fails, or (iii) provide a fallback mechanism that refunds the user’s tokens if the treasury cannot satisfy the withdrawal. Implementing any of these measures would restore the ability for users to retrieve their funds and prevent indefinite locking of assets.

title: Incorrect stake limit check
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the stake‑limit verification performed by the LidoTreasuryConnector.deposit() function. The function is intended to allow the treasury to submit any amount of ETH that does not exceed the current Lido stake limit. However, the code uses a less‑than‑or‑equal comparison (if lidoCurrentStakeLimit <= amount) and reverts when the condition is true. As a result, a deposit that is exactly equal to the reported limit triggers a StakeLimit revert even though the business rule permits the deposit. The root cause is an incorrect inequality operator, a classic boundary‑check bug, which was discovered during a manual logical audit of the contract’s staking workflow. The bug manifests only when the amount to be deposited matches the limit value; in most everyday cases the amount is either lower or higher, so the error can be missed by casual testing. When the condition is met, the transaction aborts, no ETH is transferred to the Lido pool, and the treasury receives a revert error. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a failed deposit or a generic “StakeLimit” error, and the expected outcome—funds being staked and earning yield—does not occur. The affected parties include the treasury operator, protocol participants who rely on the treasury’s staking activity, and any downstream users expecting the deposited ETH to generate rewards. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like situation: legitimate deposits at the exact limit are blocked, potentially causing idle capital, reduced staking rewards, and a mismatch between the protocol’s accounting assumptions and actual on‑chain state. Because the revert message only contains the limit and amount, the problem can be hard to spot unless the equality case is explicitly tested. The issue belongs to the class of off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition bugs that violate the intended accounting invariant “deposit amount must be ≤ stake limit”. The correct fix is to change the comparison to a strict less‑than check (if lidoCurrentStakeLimit < amount), thereby allowing deposits that are exactly equal to the limit while still preventing excess staking. After the fix, the contract will align with the business rule, the UI will no longer show unexpected failures for maximum‑size deposits, and the treasury’s funds will be correctly staked.

title: No mechanism to exit isolation mode once entered
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the supply() routine of the AaveV3TreasuryConnector contract, which automatically marks every newly supplied token as collateral by calling setUserUseReserveAsCollateral without regard for Aave v3 isolation rules. In Aave v3, an isolated asset can be used as collateral only if the borrower limits themselves to a predefined list of assets, and while an isolated asset remains enabled as collateral the user is prohibited from enabling any additional assets, including other isolated assets, as collateral. Because supply() forces collateral activation for every token, a user who first supplies an isolated asset triggers isolation mode and then cannot successfully supply any non‑isolated token through the same connector; the internal call to setUserUseReserveAsCollateral reverts or is ignored, leaving the new asset unusable as collateral. The root cause is the lack of a guard that checks whether the user is already in isolation mode and the absence of a mechanism to disable the isolated asset as collateral, which is the only way to exit isolation mode. An attacker does not need to act maliciously – any legitimate user can be trapped by this logic, resulting in a situation where additional funds sent to the connector are effectively locked because they cannot be marked as collateral and therefore cannot be borrowed against. The impact is a loss of flexibility for treasury operations, potential freezing of deposited assets, reduced borrowing capacity and, in worst‑case scenarios, missed revenue opportunities for the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the first asset supplied through the connector is an isolated token; subsequent supply attempts for any other token will hit the faulty collateral‑enabling step. All participants that rely on the TreasuryConnector – including protocol owners, treasury managers and external users – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of collateral management. It is subtle because the function appears to perform a benign convenience action (automatically enabling collateral) and the isolation constraints are not obvious from the code alone, making the bug easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the collateral‑enabling call should be decoupled from the supply logic, allowing callers to decide when to enable collateral, and an explicit function should be provided to disable an isolated asset as collateral so that users can deliberately exit isolation mode. This change restores the expected behavior where users can supply a mix of assets without unintentionally entering a state that blocks further collateralization, aligning the contract with Aave’s isolation model and preserving the treasury’s ability to manage funds safely.

title: Withdrawal of collateral should not be restricted to only allowed providers
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract LPExternalRequestsManager implements a whitelist that limits which addresses are considered allowed providers. The modifier onlyAllowedProviders checks the whitelist flag and reverts if the caller is not listed. This modifier is applied to the functions that create mint and burn requests as well as to the function withdrawAvailableCollateral, which releases the collateral that was locked when a burn request was fulfilled. However, the cancelMint and cancelBurn functions deliberately omit the whitelist check and instead verify that the caller matches the provider stored in the request. Because of this inconsistency, a provider that was originally allowed to create a request can lose the ability to withdraw the associated collateral if the whitelist status changes after the request is created. Two concrete situations illustrate the problem: (1) a provider is removed from the whitelist after his burn request has been completed but before he calls withdrawAvailableCollateral, and (2) the whitelist is enabled after a request was created by an address that was not previously whitelisted. In either case the withdrawAvailableCollateral call will revert with UnknownProvider, leaving the collateral permanently locked in the contract. From a user perspective the provider sees no funds returned, the UI may show a completed burn but the expected collateral balance remains unchanged, creating confusion and potential financial loss. The root cause is the overly restrictive onlyAllowedProviders modifier on the withdrawal path, which contradicts the more permissive cancellation logic and violates the business assumption that a provider who funded a request must always be able to retrieve the locked collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the access control of related functions. It can be hard to notice because the modifier appears reasonable and the function name suggests a simple withdrawal, yet the whitelist check silently blocks legitimate withdrawals. The recommended remediation is to remove the onlyAllowedProviders modifier from withdrawAvailableCollateral or to replace it with a check that allows the original request provider to withdraw regardless of current whitelist status, thereby restoring the intended accounting flow and preventing collateral from becoming unrecoverable.

title: Burning could be DOSed in case a large number of burn requests are processed
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a two‑step burning flow where users submit burn requests that are first recorded by the processBurns function and later finalized by completeBurns. The vulnerability lies in the finalisation step, which iterates over every pending request and, for each item, performs an external ERC20 transfer to retrieve withdrawal collateral. Because the loop length is directly proportional to the number of burn requests accumulated in the current epoch, an attacker or simply a high‑volume batch of legitimate requests can cause the transaction to exceed the block gas limit. When the gas limit is hit, the completeBurns call reverts, leaving the previously processed requests in a half‑finished state. Since the protocol does not provide a mechanism to roll back or discard those processed requests, no new burn requests can be accepted until the stuck batch is somehow completed, effectively denying the burning service. From a user’s point of view, a burn that was expected to succeed ends with no collateral returned and the UI may show the request as “pending” forever, or the user may receive a transaction failure without a clear error message. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the burning functionality, preventing users from converting their tokens and potentially locking collateral in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the LPExternalRequestsManager contract and identified the unbounded for‑loops combined with external token calls as a gas‑heavy pattern. It is hard to notice because the loops appear harmless for small batches and the external calls are assumed to be cheap, yet their gas consumption can vary with token contract logic (e.g., fee on transfer, re‑entrancy guards). The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration with external calls” leading to gas exhaustion and DoS. A proper mitigation is to enforce a strict upper bound on the number of burn items that can be finalised in a single epoch, or to redesign the flow so that each request is completed in a separate transaction or via a pull‑based pattern that does not require iterating over an arbitrarily large array.

title: Lack of instantRedeemWithPxEth support
description: Pirex ETH's redemption process using upxETH (via initiateRedemption and redeemWithUpxEth) requires some time and depends on multiple factors: The number of users wanting to withdraw: if pendingWithdrawal has not reached DEPOSIT_SIZE, need to wait more users need to withdraw until pendingWithdrawal reaches DEPOSIT_SIZE. To withdraw the full balance of a validator, it must first exit entirely. The exiting process takes a variable amount of time, depending on how many others are exiting at the same time. The more exits, the longer a validator has to wait. In addition to being dependent on the exit queue of the Beacon chain, it also depends on Pirex ETH's OracleAdapter, which utilizes an off-chain process that can introduce additional uncertainty regarding the withdrawal finalization time. In case of an emergency where Resolv needs to withdraw assets from the Treasury, the assets in Dinero cannot fulfill the need because the process is not instantaneous.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing instant redemption path for Pirex ETH when users try to withdraw their upxETH holdings. The contract currently relies on a multi‑step process that first aggregates pending withdrawals until a threshold (DEPOSIT_SIZE) is reached, then forces the underlying validator to exit fully before the funds can be released. Validator exits are queued on the Beacon chain and their completion time varies with the number of concurrent exits, so a user may have to wait an indeterminate period for the exit to be processed. In addition, the OracleAdapter that reports the finalization status runs off‑chain, introducing further latency and uncertainty. Because there is no instantRedeemWithPxEth option, the protocol cannot provide immediate liquidity in emergency scenarios where Resolv needs to pull assets from the Treasury. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that a redemption transaction will instantly credit their wallet, but instead the balance remains unchanged, the transaction appears successful, and the user sees a pending withdrawal that may take minutes, hours, or even days to resolve. The impact is that funds become temporarily unavailable, which can undermine confidence, hinder emergency response, and potentially expose the protocol to liquidity stress if many users request withdrawals simultaneously. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the redemption flow and identified the dependence on external validator exit queues and off‑chain oracle updates as a source of delay. This type of problem is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or throw errors; it simply takes longer than expected, which can be mistaken for normal network latency. Conceptually, the fix is to add an instantRedeemWithPxEth function (or option) within the DineroTreasuryConnector that draws from a pre‑funded buffer and charges a higher fee, thereby allowing immediate withdrawals when needed while still preserving the longer‑term redemption mechanism for regular cases.

title: Not supporting IERC1155Receiver interface ID
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ERC‑165 support declaration for the IERC1155Receiver interface in the DineroTreasuryConnector contract. The contract inherits ERC1155HolderUpgradeable, which normally registers the IERC1155Receiver interface ID, and AccessControlDefaultAdminRulesUpgradeable, which registers its own admin‑rules interface ID. Because both parent contracts implement supportsInterface, DineroTreasuryConnector overrides the function and forwards the call to super. Solidity linearizes inheritance from right to left, so the super call resolves to AccessControlDefaultAdminRulesUpgradeable, effectively discarding the ERC1155HolderUpgradeable implementation. As a result, when an external ERC1155 token contract queries DineroTreasuryConnector with ERC‑165 for the IERC1155Receiver interface ID (0x4e2312e0), the call returns false. This causes safeTransferFrom and other ERC1155 safe‑transfer mechanisms to reject the recipient, leading to transaction reverts or tokens not being received. Users attempting to deposit ERC1155 tokens see no balance change, may receive error messages, or experience silent failures where the transfer does not complete. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a test calling supportsInterface on the deployed treasury contract; the test showed a false result for the ERC1155Receiver ID while the admin‑rules ID returned true. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the override appears syntactically correct, making it easy to overlook the inheritance ordering effect. The impact is medium severity: it breaks the intended business logic of accepting ERC1155 assets, potentially causing loss of functionality, user frustration, and downstream protocol failures that rely on ERC1155 token handling. The bug belongs to the class of ERC‑165 interface‑ID omission due to multiple inheritance and improper super calls. To remediate, the supportsInterface function should be modified to explicitly return true for the IERC1155Receiver interface ID before delegating to super, or the inheritance order should be adjusted so that the ERC1155Holder implementation is consulted. This ensures that ERC1155 token contracts recognize the treasury as a valid receiver, restoring correct transfer behavior and aligning with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Griefing attack on claimable rewards
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the reward‑claim calculation of a staking contract. When the contract updates a user’s checkpoint, it computes a new claimable amount as userBalance multiplied by the difference between the global accumulated reward per token and the user’s previously recorded value, divided by a fixed denominator. Because the division is performed with integer arithmetic, any fractional part is discarded. If the resulting value is less than one token unit, the division yields zero and the claimable amount is not increased, even though the contract records that the user’s accumulated rewards per token have advanced. The contract’s updateCheckpoint function can be called by anyone for any address, allowing a malicious actor to repeatedly invoke the checkpoint for a victim’s address. Each call updates the stored accumulated reward per token for the victim but leaves the claimable amount at zero due to the truncation. Over time the victim’s visible reward balance appears to grow, yet any attempt to claim returns nothing, effectively griefing the user by preventing them from withdrawing earned rewards. This situation occurs when reward increments are small relative to the denominator or when the user holds a low balance, conditions that make the integer division round down to zero. All token holders are potentially affected, especially those with modest stakes or low reward rates. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the checkpoint logic and identified that the update function does not enforce caller‑ownership, exposing the rounding bug to external manipulation. The problem is subtle because the UI may display an increasing reward total while the claim transaction silently transfers zero tokens, making it hard to detect without inspecting the contract’s internal state. To remediate, the contract should restrict checkpoint updates so that only the token holder can update their own record, or alternatively adjust the arithmetic to preserve fractional rewards (for example by using a higher‑precision denominator, rounding up, or accumulating remainder values). Either approach eliminates the ability for an attacker to force a state where the accumulated reward per token advances without a corresponding claimable amount, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the staking system.

title: withdraw() allows reward claims when claimEnabled is disabled
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s withdraw function, which permits a caller to request reward distribution even when the global claimEnabled flag has been turned off by the admin role. The contract defines a claim function that checks claimEnabled before allowing rewards to be claimed, but the withdraw routine also invokes the internal checkpoint logic that can distribute rewards and fails to repeat this guard. As a result, a malicious or opportunistic user can initiate a withdrawal of any amount (for example, 1 wei), wait for the mandatory cooldown period, and then call withdraw with the _claimRewards parameter set to true. Because the function does not verify claimEnabled, the checkpoint call will credit the caller with pending rewards despite the protocol’s intention to suspend reward claims. This bypass undermines the admin’s ability to pause reward distribution, leading to unauthorized reward extraction and a reduction of the reward pool that other stakers rely on. The issue appears only when claimEnabled is false and a user is able to trigger a withdrawal; it is difficult to notice because the withdraw path already contains reward logic and developers may assume the claimEnabled check in the separate claim function is sufficient. The impact is a medium‑severity loss of protocol funds and a breach of the intended accounting model, where rewards should be frozen while claimEnabled is disabled. The bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control checks or business‑logic bypasses, where a state variable governing a feature is not consistently enforced across all entry points. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a staker receives reward tokens even though the UI indicates that claiming is disabled, creating confusion and potential distrust. To remediate the issue the withdraw function must enforce the same claimEnabled requirement as the claim function, for example by rejecting calls with _claimRewards true when claimEnabled is false, or by simply forcing _claimRewards to false in that situation. This restores the intended pause mechanism and prevents reward leakage.

title: The returned stUSRAmount from the unwrap operation may be inaccurate due to rounding
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the wrapper contract that converts wrapped stUSR (wstUSR) back into the underlying rebasing token stUSR. When a user calls the unwrap function, the contract calculates the amount of stUSR to return by invoking a conversion routine that rounds down any fractional share. The function then burns the wrapped tokens and transfers the calculated stUSR amount to the receiver, but it returns the pre‑transfer calculation instead of the actual amount that arrived in the receiver’s balance. Because the conversion and the subsequent safeTransfer both apply floor rounding, the real amount received can be one unit (or more) lower than the value reported by the function. This discrepancy becomes visible when the user immediately uses the returned amount as input to the stUSR.withdraw function. The withdraw routine expects the caller to own at least the number of shares indicated, but the caller’s balance is short by the rounding loss, causing the call to revert with an insufficient‑balance error. The issue manifests under normal operating conditions, especially after a rebasing event that changes the conversion rate between wstUSR and stUSR, and it is not limited to edge‑case amounts. All users of the wrapper, as well as any downstream protocol that relies on the returned value for further accounting, are affected because they may see a successful unwrap transaction in the UI while the subsequent withdraw fails, leading to confusion, failed transactions, and potential denial‑of‑service for legitimate withdrawals. The bug was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the unwrap‑then‑withdraw flow in a test suite, where the expected and actual balances diverged by a single token unit. The problem is subtle because the contract emits an event with the calculated amount, which appears correct, and the UI typically displays this value, masking the underlying rounding error. To remediate the issue, the unwrap function should not trust the conversion result alone; instead it should query the receiver’s stUSR balance before and after the transfer and return the exact delta, thereby eliminating any rounding discrepancy. This class of bug falls under inaccurate accounting due to rounding errors in token wrappers, where the contract’s reported state does not match the on‑chain token balances, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that a conversion function’s output equals the transferred amount.

title: mintWithPermit provides the wrong amount to the usrPermit.permit
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract provides a function that lets a user mint wrapped USR tokens (wstUSR) by first authorising the underlying USR token via the ERC‑20 Permit extension and then depositing the tokens in a single transaction. The intended flow is: the user signs a permit for the exact amount of USR that will be transferred, the contract calls the permit method to set an allowance, it calculates how much USR is required for the requested amount of wstUSR using a previewMint helper, and finally it pulls the USR from the user and mints the wrapped tokens. In the current implementation the function passes the user‑supplied _wstUSRAmount directly to the permit call instead of the calculated usrAmount. Because the wrapped amount and the underlying amount are not equal – previewMint applies a conversion rate – the allowance granted by the permit is either too small or unrelated to the actual transfer that will occur later. The try/catch surrounding the permit call silently swallows any revert caused by the mismatched amount, but the subsequent _deposit call still attempts to transfer the correctly calculated usrAmount. Since the allowance for that amount was never set, the transfer fails and the whole transaction reverts. From a user’s perspective the signature appears to be accepted, the UI may indicate that the permit was submitted, yet the mint operation never completes and the user receives no wstUSR; their USR balance remains unchanged and they lose the gas spent on the failed transaction. The bug occurs whenever a caller invokes mintWithPermit, regardless of the specific amounts, because the function always uses the wrong variable when calling permit. It was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted a mismatch between the parameter passed to IERC20Permit.permit and the amount returned by previewMint. The issue is subtle because the try/catch makes the permit failure look harmless, masking the underlying logic error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter usage in authorization flows” or “allowance mis‑calculation bugs”, where a contract authorises a different amount than the one later consumed, breaking the intended business logic of token wrapping. To fix the problem the contract should first compute usrAmount via previewMint, then pass that value to the permit call, and only after a successful (or tolerated) permit should it proceed with the deposit. This aligns the authorized amount with the amount actually transferred, restoring the expected behavior where a user signs a permit, the contract receives the allowance, and the wrapped tokens are minted as intended.

title: Incorrect rounding in previewWithdraw function leads to residual wstUSR balance
description:
