This condition occurs only when at least n‑p+1 owners are malicious and the remaining owners are unable to progress any transaction, a situation that may not be obvious during normal operation. All owners, including honest participants, are affected because they lose access to their funds and the expected security guarantees of a multisig are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by SigmaPrime, and it is subtle because the contract behaves correctly while transactions are being processed; the problem only surfaces after a prolonged deadlock, making it hard to notice without deliberate testing of the recovery path. To remediate, the contract should ensure that the recovery mode cannot be entered by a minority, for example by allowing any owner to extend the lastTransactionTime, by requiring a separate quorum to trigger recovery, or by gradually reducing the required signature count only after a full‑consensus recovery step, thereby preventing a small colluding group from forcing arbitrary withdrawals. This class of bug can be described as a “multisig recovery‑mode abuse” or “threshold reduction attack” where the intended quorum enforcement is bypassed through a time‑based fallback mechanism.

title: An inactive owner can permanently lock tokens.
description:
Fantom tokens become tradeable after the boolean state variable tokensTradeable is set to true. Failure to set this variable to true means that no trading/transferring of tokens is possible. Only the contract owner can modify tokensTradeable by calling the function makeTradeable() at the conclusion of the ICO period.
However, if the owner was unable to access their private key, due to e.g. error or incapacitation, it would not be possible to set tokensTradeable = true and fantom tokens would remain permanently untransferable.
This vulnerability provides a single point of failure that is capable of permanently paralysing all fantoms.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralized activation lock that prevents Fantom tokens from ever becoming transferable if the contract owner is unable to call the function that flips the boolean flag tokensTradeable to true. The root cause is that the only function capable of enabling token transfers – makeTradeable() – is protected by an onlyOwner modifier and there is no alternative mechanism to change the flag after the ICO period. Because the flag remains false, every transfer, trade, or withdrawal call reverts, effectively freezing all token balances. This condition can be triggered when the owner loses access to the private key, is incapacitated, or simply neglects to execute the function before the deadline. The impact is that token holders see their balances locked in the UI, receive error messages when attempting to send or trade, and are unable to realize any economic value from their holdings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the post‑ICO state transition logic and identified the single point of failure. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and works correctly while the flag is true, and the code does not contain explicit warnings about owner inactivity. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a fallback mechanism such as a time‑based permission that allows any user (or a designated set of addresses) to set tokensTradeable after a reasonable delay, replace the onlyOwner guard with a multi‑signature scheme, or redesign the token to be tradeable by default and use a separate pause mechanism. By removing the exclusive reliance on the owner, the protocol ensures that token economics remain functional even if the original privileged key becomes unavailable, preserving user expectations that tokens can be transferred after the sale ends.

title: owner or wallet recipient can mint tokens for free.
description:
The owner has the ability to call the setWallet() function at any time without restriction. The wallet address immediately receives all ether that is deposited into the FantomToken contract.
This allows the owner or the wallet beneficiary to cyclically purchase tokens during the crowdsale. Consider the cycle: wallet user buys tokens using 100 ether. The 100 ether is immediately returned to the user and the user is credited with tokens. The user repeats this process, accumulating tokens for free.
Equivalently, the owner during the crowdsale, can change the wallet address to themselves, purchase tokens a number of times, then change the wallet address back.
Although the owner can already mint tokens for free, they are capped to TOKEN_TOTAL_SUPPLY - TOKEN_MAIN_CAP.
This vulnerability allows the owner to mint tokens for free, including the amount specified by TOKEN_MAIN_CAP.
This is a low likelihood attack as only the owner or designated wallet address can perform this attack.
Note: The level of trust on the owner may be acceptable for the authors of this crowdsale. This issue is raised as potential investors can be diluted in the event of a malicious owner, or if an attacker gains control of the wallet or owner’s private keys.
bug_full: An unrestricted wallet‑address update in the crowdsale contract allows the contract owner (or the designated wallet) to receive the ether that contributors send before the crowdsale is finished. Because the contract immediately forwards the received ether to the current wallet while still minting tokens for the contributor, the owner can set the wallet to an address they control, send a purchase transaction, get the ether back instantly, and keep the newly minted tokens. By repeating this cycle the owner can acquire tokens without any net payment, effectively minting tokens for free up to the total supply limit, including the portion that was intended to be sold during the main crowdsale. The flaw originates from the setWallet() function being callable at any time without access control and from the withdrawal logic not being gated by a crowdsale‑finalized flag. Exploitation requires only that the attacker be the contract owner or control the wallet address; it can be performed during any contribution phase. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept payment and issue tokens, but the ether never stays in the contract, so the token price is effectively zero and investors are diluted. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the crowdsale’s state‑transition logic. It is subtle because the ether transfer to the wallet is an intended feature, so the unexpected free minting is not obvious from the external behavior. The proper fix is to restrict ether withdrawals to after the crowdsale has ended (e.g., by checking a “finalized” flag) and to prevent the owner from changing the beneficiary address while the sale is active, thereby ensuring that each minted token is backed by retained contribution funds.

title: Payloads are not validated during proposal creation
description:
It is possible to create a proposal for a payloadId that does not exist. As a result, an attacker can trick the voter to support a malicious proposal. Additionally, a lack of validation implies the access level of the proposal is not verified.
The documentation states under the section High-level differences V2 vs V3 that "before creation, the proposer or somebody else will need to deploy and register in an Aave contract the payload/s smart contract." However, this logic is not implemented, and a proposer can create a proposal without creating the payload. As a result, it may be possible to trick votingToken holders to support a proposal that contain a malicious payload.
Additionally, there is no check that ensures that the payload access level matches with the proposal access level, so it is possible to execute a Level_2 payload with a Level_1 proposal.
One possible exploit scenario would be as follows:
1. The attacker creates a payload. The attacker is sure that most of the users will support this payload.
2. He creates the proposal with two payloads. The first payload is the one created in the first step. The second one is still not created. The second payloadId should be chosen carefully. The attacker may need to monitor the PayloadsController to figure out the number of payloads created in a period of time.
3. The attacker activates the voting of the created proposal.
4. As the first payload in the proposal created by the attacker is likely to be supported and as the second payload doesn’t exist yet, the users may be tricked and vote for this proposal.
5. When the voting is over, and the proposal is queued, the attacker creates the malicious payload, executes the proposal and finally executes the payload. Note that the payloadId of the malicious payload should match the payload used when creating the proposal.
Such scenario is not likely to happen because a proposal with an empty payload should not be the voted on by users.
Furthermore, the Guardian is able to intervene in such scenario to cancel the proposal.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of payload identifiers when a governance proposal is created. The contract accepts any payloadId supplied by the proposer without checking that the corresponding payload contract has been deployed, that it was created before the proposal, or that its declared access level matches the access level required by the proposal. Because of this omission, an attacker can submit a proposal that references a non‑existent or malicious payload, tricking token holders into voting for a proposal that appears legitimate. After the voting period ends and the proposal is queued, the attacker can deploy a payload with the same identifier and execute it, potentially performing unauthorized state changes or draining funds. The root cause is the absence of existence and access‑level checks in the proposal‑creation logic, as well as the lack of a timestamp comparison to ensure the payload predates the proposal. Exploitation follows a step‑by‑step flow: the attacker creates a benign payload that is likely to receive support, then creates a proposal that lists this payload together with a second payloadId that does not yet correspond to any contract. Voters, seeing only the first payload, approve the proposal. Once voting closes, the attacker deploys the second payload, which matches the previously supplied identifier, and the governance executor runs it under the proposal’s authority. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: the UI shows a proposal with expected payloads, the voter believes they are supporting a safe change, but after execution the protocol state changes unexpectedly, balances may drop, or funds may disappear. The issue is hard to notice because the governance UI typically does not display missing payloads, and the contract does not revert on unknown identifiers. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit of the Aave Governance V3 contracts, where the auditors observed that the documentation required payload registration but the implementation omitted the corresponding checks. To remediate, the governance contract should verify that each payloadId refers to an already deployed payload, that the payload’s creation timestamp precedes the proposal’s creation time, and that the payload’s access level exactly matches the proposal’s required level before allowing the proposal to be created or queued. Enforcing these constraints restores the intended security model, prevents malicious payload injection, and aligns the on‑chain behavior with the documented governance process.

title: Premature Self-Destruct of PoolFactory
description:
PoolFactory may be self-destructed while being sole owner of ACL contract.
During pool deployment, the ownership of ACL contract is transferred to PoolFactory to perform its configuration.
After PoolFactory.configure() is called, the ownership is transferred back to the configurator. Additional
PoolFactory.getRootBack() function is also provided to recover ownership in the case of configuration failure.
The function PoolFactory.destroy() self destructs the PoolFactory contract and there are no check to prevent this
function from being called while PoolFactory is the owner of ACL. If such event occurs, nobody will have ownership
of ACL, which will break many Gearbox functions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a premature self‑destruct of the PoolFactory contract while it remains the sole owner of the Access Control List (ACL) contract. During the lifecycle of a new pool, ownership of the ACL is temporarily transferred to PoolFactory so that the factory can configure the pool. After the configuration step, the ownership is supposed to be handed back to the original configurator, and a helper function getRootBack() exists to recover ownership if configuration fails. However, the destroy() function of PoolFactory contains no safeguard that checks whether the ACL ownership has already been returned. Consequently, an actor who can invoke destroy() while PoolFactory still holds the ACL owner role can trigger self‑destruct, causing the ACL contract to lose its owner entirely. Without an owner, the ACL cannot enforce permissions, and many Gearbox functions that rely on ACL checks become inoperable. This situation can arise after a pool deployment but before the ownership hand‑off completes, or if the configurator forgets to call the ownership‑return step. Users of the protocol experience symptoms such as pools that appear to be created but then refuse any further actions, UI components showing empty responses, or transactions that revert with generic errors because permission checks fail silently. The impact is a loss of functional control over the pool’s access rules, potentially freezing user funds or preventing new pools from being configured, which undermines the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of pool deployment and noted the missing require statement before self‑destruct. It is hard to notice because the destroy() function is rarely exercised in normal operation, and the ownership transfer logic is assumed to be correct. To remediate, the contract should enforce a condition that the ACL’s owner equals the designated configurator (or is otherwise not the factory) before allowing self‑destruct, or restrict destroy() to only be callable by a privileged role after ownership has been safely returned. This change restores the invariant that the ACL always has a valid owner, preserving the intended permission model and preventing accidental or malicious loss of control.

title: Incorrect Token Amounts Used in add_liquidity()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect token amount reference inside the add_liquidity function of a CurveV1StETHPoolGateway wrapper. When a caller supplies a non‑zero amount for token1 (the second element of the amounts array), the contract mistakenly uses amounts[0] – the amount intended for token0 – as the transfer value for token1. This copy‑paste or indexing error causes the contract to attempt to move either too little or too much of token1 from the caller. If the caller does not hold enough token1 to cover the mistakenly referenced amount, the safeTransferFrom call reverts, preventing the liquidity addition and causing the user to lose gas. Conversely, if the caller holds sufficient token1, the contract will transfer an amount that does not match the user’s intention, leading to a mismatch between the deposited amount and the pool’s accounting, potentially breaking invariant checks later in the protocol. The bug manifests only when amounts[1] is greater than zero; the first branch for token0 works correctly. Affected parties include any user trying to add liquidity that includes token1, the liquidity pool that receives an incorrect reserve balance, and the broader protocol that relies on accurate accounting for pricing and slippage calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function parameters with the actual transfer calls and noticed the mismatched index. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without errors and the logic appears symmetric, so the mistake does not raise compiler warnings. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they are depositing X amount of token1, but after the transaction either the token is not transferred at all (revert) or a different amount is taken, resulting in a missing or unexpected balance change. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter indexing” or “mis‑referenced variable” bugs that violate business logic assumptions about token amounts. To remediate, the transfer call for token1 should reference amounts[1] instead of amounts[0], ensuring that the amount specified by the caller is the one actually moved, restoring correct accounting and preventing unnecessary reverts.

title: Incorrect Account Address Results in Missed Rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect handling of the account address supplied to the getReward function. The function receives an address parameter that represents the borrower whose rewards should be claimed, but it forwards this raw address directly to creditManager.executeOrder without first converting it to the corresponding CreditAccount address. As a result, the subsequent call to Convex's BaseRewardPool is made with an address that does not have an associated credit account, causing the reward claim to fail silently. In addition, the first argument passed to creditManager.executeOrder is msg.sender rather than the intended borrower address, which means the order is executed from the caller's credit account instead of the target account. This mismatch prevents the reward pool from locating the correct account balance, so the accumulated rewards remain unclaimed. The issue manifests whenever a user invokes getReward expecting to receive their pending rewards; from the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, no error is thrown, but the reward balance stays unchanged or becomes zero, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The bug was identified during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, who noted that the address conversion step was missing and that the calldata still contained the original borrower address. Because the function does not revert on failure, the problem can be hard to notice unless the user explicitly checks the reward balance after the call. The impact is limited to missed rewards – users do not receive the tokens they have earned, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each credit account’s rewards are claimable on demand. To remediate, the implementation should first resolve the supplied borrower address to its CreditAccount address, rewrite the calldata so that the BaseRewardPool receives the correct credit account, and ensure that the borrower argument passed to executeOrder matches the intended target rather than msg.sender. This correction restores the logical flow of reward distribution and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations that calling getReward will transfer the earned tokens to the caller’s account.

title: Flashloan Protection Bypass Through Debt Increase and Account Closure Within The Same
description:
It is possible to bypass the ﬂashloan attack protection.
Whilst the existing ﬂashloan attack protection mechanism prevents users from opening and closing credit accounts
within the same transaction (block), this check does not prevent users from increasing their debt position beyond the
limits of their collaterization ratio (up to maxBorrowedAmount) and closing the account within the same transaction.
This acts as a fee-less ﬂashloan for borrowers.
Speciﬁcally, there are two ways to exploit this vulnerability:
• by calling functions of adding collateral, increasing debt and closing credit account sequentially, in the same
block (e.g. when called as a single function from an external contract)
• by exploiting lack of collateral checks during the _multicall() operations in
CreditManger.closeCreditAccount(), as the pool is assumed to be repaid, and non-underlying assets are
assumed to be transferred, by the end of the transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan‑style bypass of the protocol’s protection that is intended to prevent a user from opening and closing a credit account within the same transaction. The root cause is that the contract only checks the sequence open‑account → close‑account in the same block, but it does not enforce a separation between a debt‑increase operation (increaseDebt) and the subsequent account closure (closeCreditAccount). Because the check is missing, an attacker can first add collateral, then deliberately push the debt amount beyond the allowed collateralisation ratio up to the maximum borrowable amount, and finally close the credit account in the same block. The close operation assumes that the pool has been repaid and that any non‑underlying assets have been transferred, so the protocol does not verify that the debt was actually covered before the account is removed. This can be performed either by calling the three functions sequentially from an external contract or by abusing the _multicall logic in CreditFacade, which does not perform collateral checks during a multicall that ends with a closeCreditAccount call. Exploiting this flow gives the attacker a fee‑less flash loan: they receive the borrowed amount, the protocol’s accounting records show the debt as repaid because the account is closed, and the collateral is either returned or lost without proper accounting. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a transaction the user’s balance may be reduced to zero or the expected refund is missing, even though the transaction appeared to succeed. The impact includes loss of liquidity, under‑collateralised positions, and potential draining of the pool, affecting borrowers, liquidity providers, and the overall protocol safety. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, and it is subtle because the existing protection appears to work for simple open‑close patterns, making the bypass easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should enforce that increaseDebt and closeCreditAccount cannot be executed in the same block, and the multicall implementation should retain collateral verification when an account is being closed, ensuring that the pool is truly repaid before the account is removed.

title: Chainlink Oracle Data Feeds Lack Validation
description:
Chainlink oracle data feeds lack validation to ensure that the data is fresh and from a complete round. Oracle
malfunctions may lead to large scale liquidation events or alternatively it may put the protocol at risk of insolvency.
bug_full: An insufficient validation of the data returned by Chainlink’s latestRoundData function allows the contract to accept price information that may be stale, zero, or from an incomplete round. The root cause is that the contract does not verify that the answeredInRound identifier is at least as recent as the roundID, that the price value is positive, or that the updateTime field is non‑zero. Because these checks are missing, an attacker or a malfunctioning oracle can supply an old price or a price of zero without causing a revert. When the protocol uses such unvalidated data to calculate collateral ratios, it may incorrectly deem a position under‑collateralised and trigger liquidation, or it may fail to recognise a shortfall and expose the system to insolvency. The vulnerability manifests whenever the contract calls latestRoundData without performing any sanity checks, which is common in many DeFi price‑oracle integrations. Users experience unexpected liquidations, loss of collateral, or see the protocol’s total value locked drop sharply, while the UI may still display a normal price feed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s oracle handling against best‑practice patterns. It is difficult to notice because the returned price can appear plausible while being outdated, and no error is emitted. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit require statements that ensure answeredInRound is greater than or equal to roundID, that the price is greater than zero, and that updateTime is non‑zero before using the data in any financial calculation.

title: Retesting: claimRewards() Reverts Unexpectedly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claimRewards function of the Gearbox ClaimZap adapter. The function attempts to retrieve extra reward contracts by calling extraRewards(0) and extraRewards(1) on each reward pool returned by the caller. The implementation assumes that if an extra reward is not configured the call will simply return the zero address, but the underlying BaseRewardPool contract reverts when the requested index is out of bounds. Consequently, when a reward pool has fewer than two extra rewards, the extraRewards calls trigger an out‑of‑bounds revert, causing the entire claimRewards transaction to fail. This bug occurs during the internal loop that iterates over the supplied rewardContracts array; for each entry the adapter makes two direct calls without any safety checks. Users who try to claim their earned rewards through the ClaimZap adapter experience a reverted transaction, receive no tokens, and are forced to use an alternative claiming method outside the adapter. The impact is a loss of usability and potential confusion for token holders, as they expect a successful claim but instead see a generic “transaction reverted” error. The issue is triggered only when the reward pool does not expose the first or second extra reward, a situation that may be rare in typical deployments and therefore easy to miss during standard testing. It was discovered during a retest of the claimRewards flow, where the auditor observed consistent reverts for pools lacking extra rewards. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not expose the reason for the revert, and the adapter’s logic does not include any fallback or length verification. To remediate, the adapter should either wrap the extraRewards calls in try/catch blocks to gracefully handle reverts and treat missing rewards as a zero address, or eliminate the redundant calls altogether if they are not required for the reward‑enabling logic. In either case, the fix must ensure that the claimRewards function can complete successfully even when extra reward contracts are absent, preserving the expected user experience of receiving their rewards without unexpected failures.

title: Modulo Bias In Randomness
description:
An ideal randomness function has an equal likelihood of producing each possible outcome. Due to the modulo
operations performed between lines [36] and line [39] in the getComponents() function, some values are more
likely to occur than others. This is known as modulo bias [3].
Although there is bias in the quantities rarity, quality, and purity the bias is the most signiﬁcant for the
quality and purity randomness components. For these components, values between 0 and 536 each have
a likelihood of 0.1007%, with all other numbers having a likelihood of 0.0992%. Hence, there is a bias towards
numbers less than or equal to 535.
The rarity value also has a bias, but to a lesser extent, due to the larger range of numbers that a 32-bit
unsigned integer can represent.
bug_full: The contract’s getComponents() routine generates three attributes – rarity, quality and purity – by taking a raw random value and applying a modulo operation to fit the desired range. Because the raw random number is not guaranteed to be a multiple of the divisor, the modulo introduces a statistical skew known as modulo bias. In this specific implementation the divisor is 1000 while the underlying random source is a 16‑bit unsigned integer with a range of 0‑65535. Numbers from 0 to 535 therefore appear with a probability of roughly 0.1007 % each, whereas all other numbers appear with about 0.0992 % each. The bias is most pronounced for quality and purity, where the contract expects a uniform distribution across the full 0‑999 interval. The root cause is the direct use of the % operator on a value whose upper bound is not an exact multiple of the divisor, causing the high‑end values to be under‑represented. An attacker or a participant can exploit this bias by repeatedly interacting with the contract and statistically favoring outcomes that fall in the over‑represented range, effectively increasing the chance of receiving higher‑quality or higher‑purity components. The impact is a deviation from the intended fair randomness, leading to an uneven allocation of valuable attributes, which can erode trust, distort game economics, and give an unfair advantage to users who discover the pattern. The vulnerability manifests whenever getComponents() is called – i.e., during every mint or component‑generation transaction – and affects all users who rely on the randomness for fair outcomes. It was identified during a manual audit that examined the distribution of generated values and compared it against the expected uniform probability. Because the bias is subtle, it may go unnoticed by casual testing or by users who only observe a few samples, making it hard to detect without statistical analysis. To remediate the issue the contract should avoid direct modulo on a non‑aligned range; common approaches include rejection sampling (re‑draw the random number until it falls below the largest multiple of the divisor), re‑hashing the source until a suitable value is produced, or changing the divisor to a power‑of‑two that matches the source range (e.g., using %65536). These methods restore an equal likelihood for each possible outcome, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that each attribute should be equally probable. From a user’s perspective the contract currently promises “random quality and purity” but in practice certain low‑value numbers appear slightly more often, so a user may notice that “my items keep getting the same quality” or “the rarity distribution feels off”, contradicting the expectation of a fair random draw.

title: Tokens Passed in Incorrect Order when Calling fastCollateralCheck()
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of passing token identifiers to the fastCollateralCheck() routine in an order that does not correspond to the order of the balance values supplied alongside them. In the _withdraw() and _withdrawAndUnwrap() paths of the ConvexV1_BaseRewardPool contract, the code first reads the balance of the staked phantom token (balanceInBefore) and the balance of a liquidity‑provider token (balanceOutBefore). It then calls fastCollateralCheck() with the arguments (cvxLPtoken, stakedPhantomToken, balanceInBefore, balanceOutBefore). Because the first token argument (cvxLPtoken) is meant to be paired with balanceInBefore, which actually belongs to stakedPhantomToken, the health‑checking logic receives a mismatched token‑balance pair. In the _withdrawAndUnwrap() variant the mismatch is even worse: the function calculates balanceOutBefore on curveLPtoken but still passes cvxLPtoken as the first token argument, again breaking the token‑balance correspondence. The root cause is a simple developer mistake – swapping the token parameters and referencing the wrong token variable – that propagates into the collateral‑validation step. When fastCollateralCheck() evaluates the credit account’s health using these incorrect inputs, it may report that the account is sufficiently collateralised even though the real token holdings are insufficient. An attacker who controls a credit account that is under‑collateralised can therefore trigger a withdrawal or an unwrap operation, bypass the intended safety check, and extract assets that should have been blocked. The impact is a potential loss of funds for the protocol and its lenders, as the accounting assumptions that guarantee that every withdrawal is backed by adequate collateral are violated. The bug manifests only when the withdrawal functions are invoked by a caller other than the creditFacade, because that is the branch where the fastCollateralCheck() call is executed. Users of the protocol see no explicit error; the UI may still display a healthy account, while internally the health metric is wrong, making the problem hard to notice without deep inspection of the health‑checking code. The issue was discovered during a manual audit performed by SigmaPrime, which identified the mismatched token ordering by reviewing the parameter flow. To remediate the problem, the contract should be updated so that the token arguments are passed in the same order as their corresponding balance values, and the correct token identifiers (e.g., curveLPtoken instead of cvxLPtoken in the _withdrawAndUnwrap path) must be used. This class of bug – parameter misordering leading to accounting errors – is common in financial smart contracts where multiple assets are handled together. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as a withdrawal succeeding despite an apparent lack of collateral, or as a later liquidation that seems unjustified because the account was previously reported as healthy. The fix restores the logical mapping between assets and balances, ensuring that health checks reflect the true state of the account and that protocol safety guarantees are upheld.

title: Incorrect Construction of stakedPhantomToken
description:
In the constructor code of ConvexV1BaseRewardPoolAdapter, the stakedPhantomToken is created with the pool’s
staking token passed in as ﬁrst parameter, instead of the pool address itself.
As such, phantom token will not return correct balances, which will result in unexpected behaviour in other functions.
Affected code:
```solidity
stakedPhantomToken = address(
    new ConvexStakedPositionToken(
        address(IBaseRewardPool(_baseRewardPool).stakingToken()),
        // note, 'stakingToken()' address referenced, instead of pool address
        cvxLPtoken
    )
);
```
Note constructor declaration of ConvexStakedPositionToken - constructor(address _pool, address _lptoken).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect argument supplied to the constructor of the ConvexStakedPositionToken when the ConvexV1BaseRewardPoolAdapter contract is deployed. Instead of passing the address of the reward pool itself, the code passes the address of the pool’s underlying staking token. The ConvexStakedPositionToken expects its first parameter to be the pool contract so that it can correctly map phantom token balances to the actual staked positions. Because the phantom token is bound to the staking token address, any balance query on the phantom token returns values that do not reflect the real amount of LP tokens staked in the pool. This mismatch propagates to all functions that rely on the phantom token for accounting, such as reward calculations, withdrawals, and balance displays. An attacker or any user interacting with the pool may observe that their phantom token balance appears zero or incorrect, leading to confusion when trying to claim rewards or withdraw liquidity. In the worst case, the faulty accounting could be exploited to claim more rewards than entitled or to cause the protocol to under‑pay legitimate claimants, thereby breaking the economic assumptions of the system. The issue manifests immediately after deployment of the adapter and persists for the lifetime of the contract unless corrected. It affects all participants who stake LP tokens through the adapter, including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s reward distribution logic. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit performed by SigmaPrime, where the constructor arguments were examined and found to be mismatched. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the phantom token contract is instantiated without error; only runtime balance checks reveal the inconsistency, making it easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the issue, the adapter’s constructor should be changed to pass the address of the reward pool (address(IBaseRewardPool(_baseRewardPool))) as the first argument to ConvexStakedPositionToken, ensuring that the phantom token correctly tracks staked positions and that all downstream accounting functions operate on accurate balances. This correction restores the intended relationship between the phantom token and the pool, preventing balance mismatches, reward miscalculations, and potential loss of funds.

title: Interest accrual whilst the VaultController is paused
description:
When VaultController is paused, users are unable to repay borrowed funds, but the interest is still accrued, potentially forcing users into liquidation.
VaultController is a pausable contract and amongst its functions which are inaccessible when paused are repayUSDi() and repayAllUSDi(), both of which bear the whenNotPaused modifier. However, calculateInterest() and pay_interest() are both still callable when the contract is paused, with interest accruing as a function of time (and the reserve ratio).
As a result of this, it is possible that a user could mint a vault, deposit into it, borrow USDi against it and then accrue interest, potentially putting the vault on the edge of insolvency.
Consider a situation where, just before this user is about to call repayUSDi(), the protocol is paused (e.g. in a situation where the reserve ratio is very low and so the interest rate is very high). In this situation, the user is locked out from repaying USDi into their vault, but interest keeps accruing over time, eventually forcing the user into insolvency. They are then liquidated as soon as the protocol is unpaused and lose their assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of interest continuing to accrue on borrowed positions while the VaultController contract is in a paused state, even though repayment functions are disabled. The root cause is that the pause mechanism only guards functions marked with the whenNotPaused modifier, such as repayUSDi() and repayAllUSDi(), but the internal accounting functions calculateInterest() and pay_interest() remain callable. Because interest is a time‑dependent function of the reserve ratio, it keeps growing while the contract is paused. An attacker or any external event that triggers a pause – for example a sudden drop in the reserve ratio that forces the protocol to pause to protect liquidity – can therefore lock users out of repaying their debt. As interest keeps adding to the outstanding balance, the collateralisation ratio may fall below the required threshold, putting the vault on the edge of insolvency. When the pause is lifted, the protocol’s liquidation engine detects the under‑collateralised vault and liquidates it, causing the user to lose the deposited assets. The impact is that users who are otherwise able to repay may be forced into liquidation without any opportunity to act, effectively losing their collateral. This condition occurs only when the contract is paused and the interest‑accrual functions are still callable; it affects any borrower with an active vault, regardless of their role. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the pause modifiers and identified that interest‑related functions were not protected. It can be hard to notice because the pause appears to protect the system, yet the hidden accrual silently degrades the health of vaults, and the symptom – a sudden liquidation after a pause – may be attributed to market movements rather than a contract bug. The bug belongs to the class of “business‑logic inconsistency during emergency pause” where state updates that should be frozen continue to run, violating the assumption that pausing halts all financial changes. From a user perspective the UI would show that repayment is unavailable, the debt amount keeps increasing, and eventually the vault is liquidated, contradicting the expectation that pausing protects their position. The recommended fix is to make the interest‑accrual entry point respect the paused flag, either by adding a whenNotPaused guard to pay_interest() or by short‑circuiting the calculation when the contract is paused, while ensuring that the pause operation itself does not depend on the interest calculation to avoid making the contract unpausable.

title: safeTransfer() not used with transfer functions
description:
CappedFeeOnTransferToken, CappedGovToken and SlowRoll do not use safeTransfer() functions:
CappedFeeOnTransferToken calls _underlying.transferFrom() on line [96].
CappedGovToken calls _underlying.transferFrom() on line [84].
SlowRoll calls takeFrom(), which in turn calls _pointsToken.transferFrom() on line [149].
This may cause reverted transactions if the underlying token does not properly implement the ERC20 standard.
Note that the token best known for not complying to this standard is USDT, which does have code capable of implementing a fee on transfer facility, and so could conceivably be contained in one of these token wrappers.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of calling the raw ERC20 transferFrom function directly from wrapper contracts instead of using the safety‑checked safeTransferFrom helper provided by OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20Upgradeable library. The root cause is that the ERC20 specification requires transferFrom to return a boolean indicating success, but several widely deployed tokens, most notably USDT, deviate from the standard by not returning a value and by reverting on failure or by applying a fee on transfer. Because the wrapper contracts (CappedFeeOnTransferToken, CappedGovToken and SlowRoll) invoke _underlying.transferFrom or a similar internal call without any verification of the return data, they assume the call succeeded. When the underlying token does not follow the spec, the call may silently fail, revert, or transfer a different amount than expected due to hidden fees. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by supplying a non‑standard token such as USDT to the wrapper; the wrapper will attempt to move tokens, the call will either revert or succeed with an unexpected balance change, causing the surrounding logic to mis‑calculate fees, caps or rewards. The impact is that legitimate users may see transactions revert unexpectedly, receive no tokens after a deposit, observe their balances unchanged or reduced, or experience missing refunds. In the worst case the protocol may become unable to move tokens at all, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected token pool. The issue manifests whenever the wrapper contracts interact with any ERC20 token that does not strictly implement the standard, which is not covered by typical unit tests that only use compliant mock tokens. All participants who hold or interact with the wrapped token – end‑users, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the wrapper (that transferFrom always succeeds and transfers the exact amount) are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, which identified the direct transferFrom calls and recognized the risk posed by non‑standard tokens. The bug is subtle because the code compiles and works with most tokens, so developers may not notice the missing safety checks until a non‑compliant token is used in production. To remediate the issue, each direct transferFrom call should be replaced with SafeERC20Upgradeable.safeTransferFrom, which performs a low‑level call, checks for a successful return value, and gracefully handles tokens that do not return a boolean, thereby restoring the expected safety guarantees and preventing unexpected reverts or balance mismatches.

title: Denial of Service (DoS) on multi-transaction proposals
description:
Anyone can execute an individual transaction from a multi-transaction proposal via external function executeTransaction(), rendering the overall proposal unusable.
A proposal can consist of multiple transactions (or “calls”) to be executed. Once the proposal successfully passes through and is queued for execution, anyone can execute it through calling execute() function, which will go in sequence through every individual transaction in the proposal and call executeTransaction() on it.
As the executeTransaction() function is external, it is also possible to call it directly to execute any individual transaction separately.
One of the first checks performed in executeTransaction() is if the transaction has been queued for execution:
require(queuedTransactions[txHash], "tx hasn't been queued.");
And the transaction is then removed after successful execution:
queuedTransactions[txHash] = false;
If a proposal with multiple transactions is submitted, an attacker could call executeTransaction() to execute a single transaction from the proposal. Subsequent execute() calls on the proposal will fail and revert, as the previously executed transaction will fail the queued check discussed above, rendering the entire proposal unusable and ‘stuck’.
Note, in such case, it would still be possible to manually call executeTransaction() on every other remaining transaction in the affected proposal to execute it fully. However, it would only be feasible if the proposal does not rely on a specific order of transaction execution.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting proposals that contain multiple sequential transactions. The contract exposes a helper function called executeTransaction as an external entry point, even though it is intended to be invoked only by the internal execute routine that processes a whole proposal. When a proposal passes governance and is queued, any external address can call executeTransaction directly with the hash of one of the proposal’s transactions. The function checks only that the transaction is currently marked as queued, clears the queued flag, and then performs the call. Because the flag is cleared, a later call to the main execute function, which iterates over the remaining transactions, encounters a transaction that is no longer marked as queued and reverts with the message that the transaction hasn’t been queued. As a result the whole proposal becomes stuck and cannot be executed as a batch. This issue arises whenever a multi‑transaction proposal relies on a specific execution order; an attacker can break the order by executing a single transaction out of turn, causing the remaining calls to fail. The impact is that governance actions, upgrades, or fund transfers that depend on the proposal may be blocked, leaving users seeing a proposal that appears ready but never completes, with no funds moving and error messages on execution attempts. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the visibility of internal functions and the state checks surrounding queued transactions. It can be hard to notice because the external function still performs a legitimate call and the state change is subtle; the UI may continue to display the proposal as queued, while the backend reverts on batch execution. The bug belongs to the class of improper function visibility or unintended external access, which enables state manipulation that leads to a denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective the interface shows a proposal ready for execution, the user clicks “execute”, and the transaction fails with a revert, making it look like the protocol is broken or malicious. The correct mitigation is to restrict executeTransaction to internal visibility (or add proper access control) so that only the contract’s own execute routine can invoke it, thereby preserving the atomicity and order of multi‑transaction proposals.

title: The purchase of nomins and/or havvens is vulnerable to front-running
description:
Front-running [1] attacks occur when users watch a blockchain for transactions, then submit transactions with higher gas prices to give their transactions a greater order preference. By modifying the state in some way, the user is able to affect the functioning of earlier-sent transactions.
The IssuanceController contract is vulnerable to front-running attacks as follows. The contract uses an oracle to set the usdToEthPrice via the function updatePrices. The owner of the oracle can watch the blockchain for submitted transactions in which users send eth to purchase nomins. Upon observing submission of such a transaction, the oracle can call updatePrice to change the usdToEthPrice to the disadvantage the user. If the transaction submitted by the oracle is endowed with a large quantity of gas, it will be given priority over the original transaction. Consequently the usdToEthPrice can be changed prior to processing the users transaction, such that the user receives less nomins.
The purchase of havvens by the function exchangeNominsForHavvens is similarly vulnerable to front-running attacks involving an unfavourable change in the value of usdToHavPrice.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running price manipulation bug in the token issuance contract. The contract relies on a single‑owner price oracle to set the conversion rate between ETH and the stable token (nomins) and between the stable token and the secondary token (havvens). Because the price variable can be updated by the oracle at any time, an attacker who controls the oracle – in this case the foundation – can monitor the mempool for a user transaction that attempts to purchase tokens, then submit a transaction with a higher gas price that calls the price‑update function just before the user’s transaction is executed. The updated price is less favorable to the user, so when the purchase is finally processed the amount of tokens calculated from the sent ETH is reduced. The same pattern applies when a user exchanges the stable token for the secondary token: the attacker can lower the usd‑to‑havven price immediately before the exchange, causing the user to receive fewer havvens than expected. The impact is that users receive fewer tokens than the amount they paid for, effectively losing value without any explicit error; from the UI perspective the transaction appears successful but the received balance is lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as a zero or negligible amount. The condition for exploitation is the existence of a single trusted oracle that can be called with higher gas priority, and the contract does not lock the price at the moment the user’s transaction is submitted. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of price updates and token calculations and identified that the price variable is mutable between transaction submission and execution. The issue can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the price change is subtle; only a careful comparison of expected versus actual token amounts reveals the discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or price‑oracle manipulation vulnerabilities where economic state is derived from a mutable external source without commitment. To remediate, the contract should either lock the price for each user request, allow the user to specify the exact amount of tokens they wish to receive and verify that the price yields that amount, or employ a decentralized price feed that cannot be arbitrarily updated by a single party. Implementing a price‑locking mechanism or a commit‑reveal scheme would prevent an attacker from changing the conversion rate after the user’s intent is known, thereby aligning the actual outcome with the user’s expectation of receiving a proportional amount of tokens for their payment.

title: Tokens purchased via IssuanceController may be illegitimate
description:
Within the set of contracts that implement the full functionality of the Havven system, balances for havven and nomin tokens are maintained in associated TokenState contracts. Havven and Nomin contracts interact with these TokenState contracts to, e.g., implement token transfers and modify user balances, while users interact with proxy contracts. This allows the owners to interchange the Havven and Nomin contracts in order to update the system’s functionality in the future.
The owner of IssuanceController can change the addresses of the Havven and Nomin contracts associated with the IssuanceController contract at any stage via the setHavven and setNomin functions. There are currently no checks to ensure that the new Havven and Nomin contracts refer to the associated TokenState contracts. A malicious owner could therefore substitute the Havven and Nomin contracts, such that eth could be collected via IssuanceController without actually issuing valid havven or nomin tokens (i.e., tokens that are registered by the underlying TokenState contracts).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the IssuanceController contract of the Havven system, which allows the contract owner to replace the addresses of the Havven and Nomin token contracts through the setHavven and setNomin functions. The contract does not verify that the new token contract addresses are linked to the correct TokenState contracts, which are the authoritative sources for token balances. Because TokenState contracts expose an associatedAddress that designates the only contract authorised to modify balances, the lack of a check means a malicious owner can point IssuanceController at arbitrary contracts that either do not interact with the TokenState or deliberately return bogus balances. When a user sends ether to IssuanceController expecting to receive newly issued Havven or Nomin tokens, the controller will accept the payment but the substituted contract may simply keep the ether or mint tokens that are not recognised by the TokenState, resulting in tokens that are effectively illegitimate. The exploit can be carried out at any time after deployment, as the owner can invoke the address‑changing functions without any timelock or additional governance safeguard. Affected parties include any purchaser of tokens through IssuanceController, holders of Havven/Nomin, and the broader protocol that relies on accurate issuance accounting. The issue was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, which noted the missing validation of contract topology. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may appear successful on‑chain, the UI may show a “purchase” event, yet the user’s token balance remains unchanged or reflects a token that has no value in the system. The impact ranges from loss of user funds to erosion of trust in the protocol’s issuance mechanism and potential accounting inconsistencies. To remediate, IssuanceController should enforce that any new Havven or Nomin address points to a contract whose associatedAddress matches the address stored in the corresponding TokenState contract, thereby ensuring only contracts authorised to modify balances can be set. Additional mitigations could include restricting the owner’s ability to change these addresses, employing multi‑signature governance, or emitting events that allow external monitoring of contract swaps. Implementing such checks would align the issuance flow with the intended business logic that every ether paid results in a verifiable, state‑backed token allocation, preventing the scenario where funds disappear while no legitimate tokens are issued.

title: get_vault_borrowing_power() could prevent vault’s functionality
description:
External calls from get_vault_borrowing_power() could revert, disabling ability of borrowing against a vault or liquidating a vault.
get_vault_borrowing_power() contains a loop, starting on line [580], which loops through all of the registered tokens and queries the vault for its balance through a call to vault.tokenBalance() on line [589] which in turn makes the external call IERC20(addr).balanceOf(address(this)). It also contains external calls to external oracles for each registered token through _oracleMaster.getLivePrice() on line [594].
There is a chance, with all of these external calls, that one of them might revert. In that case, the entire transaction would revert.
Some potential revert scenarios might be:
• If the anchor oracle and the main oracle are reporting prices too far apart.
• If an oracle is experiencing a problem with its data source and reverts to prevent providing potentially bad data.
• If a token has a complex balance calculation system, akin to uFragments, but containing an error which causes some balance queries to revert.
Consider a situation where an arbitrary token, let’s call it RVRT, is added to the protocol. After a few weeks of normal operation, it experiences the third issue listed above and reverts on all calls to RVRT.balanceOf(). Because this function is called inside get_vault_borrowing_power() for all vaults, even those not containing RVRT, all calls to borrow against a vault, or to liquidate a vault would also revert.
In the event that a vault cannot be liquidated and the asset it contains dropping heavily, it would be possible for it to become heavily insolvent. If this happened to many vaults across the entire protocol, then the entire protocol would become insolvent: the value of the USDC reserve and the assets in vaults would be significantly lower than the total USDi in circulation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by unprotected external calls inside the get_vault_borrowing_power function. The function iterates over every registered token, queries each token's balance via an external call to IERC20.balanceOf and obtains a price from an external oracle through _oracleMaster.getLivePrice. Because each of these calls can revert – for example if an oracle reports a price that diverges too far from a reference, if an oracle encounters a data‑source failure, or if a token implements a complex balance calculation that may throw – the entire get_vault_borrowing_power call will revert. This revert propagates to any higher‑level operation that relies on the borrowing power, such as borrowing against a vault or liquidating a vault. Consequently, a single misbehaving token, even one that is not held by a particular vault, can cause borrowing and liquidation transactions for all vaults to fail. The impact is that users are unable to open new borrowing positions, existing positions cannot be liquidated when they become under‑collateralised, and the protocol may accumulate insolvent vaults, potentially endangering the overall reserve and the value of the stablecoin issued by the system. The condition occurs whenever any external call inside the loop reverts, which can happen at any time after a token is added to the registry or an oracle’s data feed becomes unstable. All vault owners, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the failure blocks core financial actions. The issue was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, which identified the pattern of external calls inside a loop as a classic source of denial‑of‑service bugs. It is hard to notice because the function is internal and the revert only surfaces when a specific token or oracle misbehaves, making the failure appear unrelated to the user’s own vault composition. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls in iterative logic that can lead to protocol‑wide lockout. From a user perspective the UI will show generic transaction failure messages such as “transaction reverted” when trying to borrow or liquidate, with no obvious indication that the problem lies in an unrelated token’s balance query. Users expect to be able to borrow or trigger liquidation and instead receive no action, effectively seeing their funds become inaccessible. To remediate the issue the protocol should eliminate the reliance on external calls inside a loop, for example by redesigning vaults to hold a single asset, by caching price data off‑chain, or by wrapping each external call in a try/catch block and handling failures gracefully. Curating the list of registered tokens and oracles can reduce exposure but does not fully eliminate the risk, so a more structural change is required to restore reliable borrowing and liquidation functionality.

title: Duplicate Node Delegators Not Accounted For
description:
The LRTDepositPool contract does not check for duplicate node delegator addresses when they are added to the nodeDelegatorQueue. This could allow the same node delegator to be added multiple times. As a result, functions that rely on this queue, such as getAssetDistributionData(), will return incorrect values, particularly for the assetLyingInNDCs calculation.
This issue can be illustrated as follows:
1. An admin mistakenly adds the same node delegator address twice to the nodeDelegatorQueue using addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue().
2. An asset is deposited into the LRTDepositPool.
3. The asset is transferred to the first node delegator in the queue.
4. getAssetDistributionData() is called to calculate the asset distribution, including assetLyingInNDCs.
5. Due to the duplicate entry, the calculation for assetLyingInNDCs incorrectly reflects double the real amount transferred.
bug_full: An issue exists in the LRTDepositPool contract where the function that adds node delegator contracts to the internal nodeDelegatorQueue does not verify whether the address being added is already present. Because the queue can contain duplicate entries, any logic that iterates over the queue – for example the getAssetDistributionData() view that aggregates the amount of assets currently held in node delegator contracts (assetLyingInNDCs) – will count the same delegator multiple times. The root cause is the absence of a uniqueness guard or a set‑like data structure when inserting into the queue. An attacker or a careless admin can invoke addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue() with an address that has already been queued, causing the queue to hold two identical entries. When a deposit is made, the contract transfers the asset to the first entry, but the accounting routine later sums the balances of all entries, effectively doubling the reported amount for that delegator. This leads to an inflated assetLyingInNDCs value, which can mislead the protocol’s accounting, reward calculations, and any UI that displays distribution data. Users may see a higher “assets in node delegator contracts” figure than the real amount, potentially causing confusion or incorrect withdrawal amounts. The bug manifests only when duplicate addresses are added; otherwise the system behaves as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, and because the duplicated entry does not cause a transaction revert, the problem can remain hidden until the distribution data is inspected. The issue belongs to the class of “duplicate entry in collection leading to double counting” bugs, common in smart contracts that rely on arrays without uniqueness enforcement. To remediate, the addNodeDelegatorContractToQueue() function should check the existing queue (or maintain a mapping) to ensure an address is not already stored before pushing it, thereby guaranteeing each delegator is represented exactly once.

title: Unexpected Amount of Supported Assets Could Increase rsETH price
description:
If, for any reason, the LRTDepositPool contract or the NodeDelegator contract, received an unexpected amount of supported assets, the rsETH price would increase.
The contract LRTDepositPool could receive intentionally (from a malicious user) or unintentionally (accidentally) an amount of supported assets without the function depositAsset(). Also, the contract NodeDelegator could also get an amount of supported assets without calling the function transferAssetToNodeDelegator().
According to the function LRTOracle.updateRSETHPrice(), rsETHPrice = totalETHInPool / rsEthSupply. So, if one of the LRTDepositPool contracts or the NodeDelegator contract receives an unexpected amount of supported assets, the rsETH price would increase. This is because when getting unexpected amount of supported assets, no new rsETH tokens minted, so the rsEthSupply would not increase. However, the total amount of supported asset would increase and so the totalETHInPool would increase.
An attack scenario that can occur is that the first minter can maliciously manipulate the share price to take a profit from future user’s deposits.
This can be done by first depositing the lowest possible amount of supported assets (1 wei) to the deposit pool, then transferring a large amount of assets to the pool contract directly.
This will artificially inflate the share price of rsETH for future depositors.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic manipulation where the price of the rsETH token can be artificially increased by sending an unexpected amount of the underlying supported asset (ETH) directly to the pool contracts without using the designated deposit functions. The root cause is that the rsETH price is calculated as totalETHInPool divided by rsEthSupply, and the contracts do not enforce that every increase in totalETHInPool is accompanied by a proportional minting of rsETH tokens. Consequently, if ETH is transferred to the LRTDepositPool or the NodeDelegator via a plain transfer, self‑destruct, or any other fallback mechanism, the totalETHInPool grows while rsEthSupply remains unchanged, causing the price per rsETH to rise. An attacker can exploit this by performing a minimal legitimate deposit (for example 1 wei) to become the first minter, then sending a large amount of ETH directly to the pool contract. The inflated price means that future depositors will receive fewer rsETH tokens for the same amount of ETH, effectively allowing the attacker to profit from the price distortion. The impact is a loss of value for honest users who expect to receive a fair amount of rsETH for their deposit; they may see a higher displayed price but receive less token value, leading to reduced returns or even apparent loss of funds. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the pool contracts accept ETH outside the controlled depositAsset() or transferAssetToNodeDelegator() pathways, which is possible because the contracts have payable fallback functions or are vulnerable to forced ETH transfers. All participants who later interact with the pool – depositors, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical relationship between pool balance and token supply was examined and found to be inconsistent. The problem is subtle because the contracts do not emit explicit errors when receiving unexpected ETH, and the price increase may appear as a normal market fluctuation, making it hard to detect without deep accounting checks. To remediate, the protocol should implement strict internal accounting that only updates totalETHInPool through authorized functions, reject or reclaim unsolicited ETH, and consider using virtual shares or an initial mint to align supply with balance. These measures would prevent the price inflation attack and restore the intended economic invariants of the system.

title: initialize() functions are front-runnable
description:
There are no access control checks on initialize() functions used to configure the protocol during the deployment.
An attacker could front-run the deployment process and call initialize() functions to set their own parameters, e.g. set arbitrary implementation and token addresses or modify intended ownerships.
The affected contracts include (note, the list below should not be considered exhaustive):
• VaultController.sol
• USDI.sol
• TokenDelegate.sol
• GovernorDelegate.sol
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing access‑control checks on contract initialization functions that are intended to be called only once during deployment to configure critical protocol parameters such as implementation contracts, token addresses, and ownership. Because the initialize routine does not verify that the caller is the legitimate deployer or owner, any external account can invoke it before the intended party does. This creates a front‑running window: an attacker monitoring the pending deployment transaction can submit their own transaction that calls the same initialize function with malicious arguments, for example setting the implementation address to a contract they control or assigning themselves ownership. The exploit is performed by broadcasting a transaction with higher gas price or earlier nonce so that the network includes the attacker’s call before the legitimate initialization. Once the attacker’s call succeeds, the protocol’s internal state is altered – the attacker becomes the owner, can upgrade the implementation, redirect token flows, or change governance parameters. Consequently, users interacting with the protocol may see unexpected ownership addresses, experience loss of funds, or receive no service because the contract now points to a malicious implementation. The issue manifests only during the brief period after contract deployment but before the intended initialize call is mined; any contract that relies on a one‑time setup without proper authentication is vulnerable. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the source files and noted the absence of require(msg.sender == owner) or similar checks in the initialize functions of VaultController, USDI, TokenDelegate, and GovernorDelegate. The problem can be subtle because the contracts compile and appear functional; only when the deployment transaction is observed or when ownership appears incorrect does the flaw become evident. The recommended remediation is to store the deployer’s address in the constructor and enforce that only this address may invoke initialize, typically by adding a require statement that checks msg.sender against the stored owner before executing the setup logic. This transforms the initialize routine into a protected, single‑use function, eliminating the front‑run vector and restoring the intended trust model where only the protocol’s administrators can configure core parameters.

title: Function getPoints() allows overbuying
description:
The getPoints() function does not ensure the amount of USDC taken from the users is equal to the value of IPT given from the contract.
This can occur if the balance of IPT in the SlowRoll contract is less than _maxQuantity at the final wave.
It is very likely that users will not buy out all the tokens at each wave, making it possible to have a wave where the value of the balance of IPT in the SlowRoll contract is less than the amount of USDC taken from the users.
In this situation, it is also possible to end up overbuying, even when purchasing the exact amount of IPT balance, when another user front-runs a transaction buying smaller amount of IPT with the sum not exceeding _maxQuantity.
An example of this scenario is described below:
1. A new wave starts with 500,000 IPT in balance, _maxQuantity is set to 1,000,000 IPT.
2. Alice pays for 500,000 IPT.
3. Bob front-runs a transaction paying for 499,999 IPT.
4. There is only 1 IPT remaining but Alice ends up paying for 500,000 IPT.
bug_full: During a purchase round (wave) the contract’s getPoints() function calculates how many IPT tokens a user should receive for a given amount of USDC, but it does not verify that the contract actually holds enough IPT to satisfy that calculation. The root cause is the absence of a check that the rewardAmount (the IPT value derived from the USDC payment) is less than or equal to the current IPT balance of the SlowRoll contract. When the contract’s IPT balance is lower than the configured _maxQuantity for the wave, a malicious or even honest user can front‑run a transaction that consumes part of the remaining IPT before another user’s transaction is mined. The second user’s transaction still transfers the full USDC amount based on the original _maxQuantity, while the contract can only deliver the reduced number of IPT tokens that are left. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful purchase, the USDC is deducted, but the received IPT amount is smaller than expected or even zero. This over‑buying scenario leads to a loss of value for the buyer, distorts the token distribution, and breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue appears only when the IPT balance is insufficient for the wave’s maximum quantity and when multiple purchase transactions are processed in the same block, making it easy to miss during normal testing because the contract does not revert on the mismatch. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s purchase logic. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a validation in the takeFrom() (or equivalent) function that the calculated rewardAmount never exceeds the current IPT balance, and should adjust _maxQuantity dynamically or reject purchases that would cause an over‑allocation. By ensuring that the amount of USDC taken is always backed by an equal value of IPT, the protocol restores its accounting guarantees and prevents users from paying for tokens that do not exist.

title: Incorrect sender in Transfer events
description:
The Transfer events in functions withdrawTo() and withdrawAllTo() have an incorrect from value when target is not the same as the message sender.
When a withdrawal is performed by any of these functions, USDC are sent from the protocol to the target and USDi are sent from the message sender to the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Transfer events emitted by the protocol's withdrawal functions incorrectly set the 'from' address when the withdrawal target differs from the caller. In withdrawTo() and withdrawAllTo(), the contract transfers USDC from the protocol to the specified target and simultaneously transfers USDi from the caller to the protocol. However, the emitted ERC-20 Transfer events record the protocol address (or the target) as the sender for the USDi transfer instead of the actual caller. This mismatch originates from using the wrong variable when constructing the event, a typical logging mistake. An attacker or any observer who relies on event logs to reconstruct token flows can be misled: the on-chain record suggests that the protocol sent USDi to itself, while in reality the caller supplied the tokens. This can be exploited to fabricate misleading audit trails, confuse users, or manipulate off-chain analytics that depend on Transfer events, such as balance watchers, portfolio dashboards, or compliance tools. The impact is that users may see a Transfer event showing a zero-amount outgoing from their address or an unexpected incoming transfer from the protocol, leading to confusion about where their funds went. The issue manifests whenever withdrawTo() or withdrawAllTo() is called with a target address that is not the caller, which is a common pattern for delegating withdrawals to a third party. All participants—token holders, auditors, and downstream services that index events—are affected because the recorded data does not reflect the true economic movement. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review by SigmaPrime, who noticed that the parameters passed to the internal _withdraw() helper did not match the arguments used in the emitted Transfer event. Because the token contract itself does not validate the semantics of the event, the problem can remain hidden unless the event fields are cross-checked against the actual token balances after the transaction. The bug belongs to the class of 'incorrect event emission' or 'mis-reported accounting events,' where on-chain logs do not faithfully represent the state transition. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a transaction that appears to send tokens from the protocol to the user while the wallet shows no incoming balance change, or it may show a zero-value transfer from the user’s address, contradicting expectations. To remediate, the contract should emit Transfer events with the caller’s address (_msgSender()) as the sender for the USDi transfer, ensuring that the event data matches the real token flow. Historical events emitted before the fix remain inaccurate and should not be used for accounting or compliance purposes.

title: Circumvention of Checks in validateBorrow()
description:
If a user makes a borrow then repays it in the same transaction, the time difference will be zero as the block timestamp will not have changed between the calls to borrow() and repay(). Therefore users will not pay fees on a loan repaid in the same transaction since the interest accrued is zero, as it is based off time difference. The following check was added to validateBorrow() to prevent users from borrowing and repaying in the same transaction.
```solidity
require(
    lastBorrower == onBehalfOf &&
    lastBorrowTimestamp == uint40(block.timestamp),
    Errors.VL_SAME_BLOCK_BORROW_REPAY
);
```
Here the lastBorrowTimestamp is the timestamp of the most recent call to borrow() on this reserve by any user. It is possible to circumvent this check by using a temporary account to make a borrow before the original account repays the loan. Using two accounts contractA and contractB we may do the following:
1. contractA - borrow()
2. contractB - deposit() (with a very small amount)
3. contractB - borrow() (with an amount of minimal value e.g. 1 WEI)
4. contractA - repay()
The result is that contractA has borrowed and repaid within the same transaction, contractB will be left with a loan of minimal value.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logic flaw in the borrow‑repay validation of a lending pool that allows a borrower to avoid paying accrued interest when the loan is opened and closed within the same block. The contract stores a single timestamp (lastBorrowTimestamp) and a single borrower address (lastBorrower) for each reserve, representing the most recent borrow operation regardless of which user performed it. The check in validateBorrow() only rejects a borrow‑repay pair when the same address that performed the previous borrow also attempts to repay in the same block, i.e. when lastBorrower equals onBehalfOf and lastBorrowTimestamp equals the current block timestamp. Because the timestamp is global, an attacker can introduce a second, temporary account to perform a tiny borrow after the first borrow, thereby updating lastBorrower and lastBorrowTimestamp to the temporary account. The original borrower can then repay the large loan in the same transaction, satisfying the require condition (lastBorrower now matches the temporary account, not the original borrower) and causing the protocol to calculate a zero time difference, which results in zero interest fees. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) Account A calls borrow() for a large amount; (2) Account B deposits a minimal amount of collateral; (3) Account B calls borrow() for a negligible amount (e.g., 1 wei), which overwrites lastBorrower and lastBorrowTimestamp; (4) Account A calls repay() for the large loan within the same transaction. From the user’s perspective the loan appears to be repaid instantly with no fees, while the protocol loses the expected interest revenue and a tiny residual debt remains on Account B. This issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the same‑block borrow‑repay guard and identified that the guard only tracks a single borrower per reserve. It is hard to notice because the check superficially seems to prevent same‑block fee evasion, yet the global state allows a simple two‑account maneuver to bypass it. The bug belongs to the class of “inadequate per‑entity state tracking” or “global timestamp misuse” that can be exploited to subvert accounting assumptions.
