bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of inflationary token minting for the RPL token, which is intended to increase the total supply by 5 % per year, applied as a daily rate. The contract’s inflationCalculate() function attempts to emulate daily minting when the inflationMintTokens() call is delayed for several days. It does this by taking the per‑interval rate, multiplying it repeatedly inside a loop, and dividing by 10**18 after each multiplication. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, each intermediate division loses fractional parts. When the loop runs for more than one interval, the accumulated truncation error makes the computed inflation amount smaller than the amount that would have been minted if the contract had executed the minting every single day. Consequently, the total supply after a period of delayed minting is lower than the theoretical supply, leading to reduced and unpredictable inflation rewards. This discrepancy is only observable when the minting function is not called at every interval, a situation that can occur in production because the RPL contract is immutable and cannot be upgraded. Token holders, protocol incentive mechanisms, and any economic analysis that assumes a steady 5 % annual increase are affected, as users may see their balances grow slower than expected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by SigmaPrime, which highlighted a test case where minting multiple intervals at once produced a different supply than minting each interval individually. The bug is subtle because the loss of fractions is small per interval and only becomes noticeable after many intervals, making it easy to overlook in casual testing. To remediate, the calculation should be performed on the total supply rather than on the rate, iteratively applying the rate to the evolving supply or using a high‑precision exponentiation method, ensuring that delayed minting yields the same total supply as continuous daily minting. In practice, the fix involves rewriting inflationCalculate() so that it compounds the rate on the current total supply inside the loop and then returns the difference, thereby eliminating the truncation discrepancy and restoring the expected inflation behavior.

title: Malicious Actors Can Prevent Non-Owner Distributions
description:
The mechanism that allows any user to distribute capital for a minipool can be subverted by a malicious actor.
The distributeBalance() function is able to be called by users who have previously called beginUserDistribute().
This starts a timer after which a period of time specified by the rocketDAOProtocolSettingsMinipool.isWithinUserDistributeWindow() function, a user can distribute the funds.
This time frame is by default set such that if the function was called between 14 and 16 days ago, a user can distribute the balance.
As beginUserDistribute() is an external function with no modifiers anyone is able to call the function. The function also resets the timer. This means a malicious user can continually reset the timer, or front-run transactions to distribute the funds such that it is never possible for a user to distribute the funds.
The likelihood of this issue is low as funds can still always be distributed by the owner, it's only the feature that non-owners are able to distribute funds that can be prevented.
bug_full: An attacker can prevent non-owner users from distributing the pooled capital by repeatedly calling the public beginUserDistribute function, which resets the distribution timer. The contract is designed so that after a user calls beginUserDistribute, a timer starts and the user may call distributeBalance within a window defined by isWithinUserDistributeWindow, typically between 14 and 16 days after the initial call. Because beginUserDistribute has no access control or state check, any address can invoke it at any time, and each call overwrites the stored timestamp, effectively moving the start of the window forward. A malicious actor can therefore keep invoking beginUserDistribute, or front-run a legitimate user’s distributeBalance transaction, so that the required window never opens for non-owners. The impact is a denial-of-service condition: regular participants expect to be able to trigger distribution of their share, but they receive no funds and may see their balance appear unchanged. The owner of the minipool retains the ability to call distributeBalance directly, so the funds are not permanently locked, but the intended non-owner distribution feature is rendered unusable. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the minipool contract where the lack of modifiers on beginUserDistribute was noted and the timer-reset behaviour was analysed. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract still allows distribution by the owner and no explicit error is thrown; only the absence of expected fund movement is observed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of logic-flaw or race-condition denial-of-service bugs where an unrestricted function can manipulate a time-based access control. To remediate, the beginUserDistribute function should be restricted from resetting the timer once the elapsed time has entered the upper bound of the distribution window, or it should be protected by an access control modifier so that only authorized participants can start the timer. In user-facing terms, a regular participant may attempt to claim a refund or payout and see the transaction succeed but receive zero tokens, contrary to the expectation that the contract will automatically distribute the balance after the waiting period.

title: Behavioural Inconsistencies In Protocol Settings Initialisation Code
bug_full: The vulnerability is an initialization order inconsistency that appears when the RocketPool DAO upgrades add a new protocol settings contract. Each DAO settings contract contains a constructor that writes configuration values to the shared RocketStorage by calling setUint. However, the contract is only allowed to modify RocketStorage after it has been registered in the storage whitelist, a step that is performed by the upgrade transaction itself. Because the constructor executes at deployment time, it attempts to write to RocketStorage before the contract address has been added to the whitelist. This mismatch means the storage write reverts, causing the upgrade to fail. The root cause is the reliance on constructor side‑effects for critical initialization before the contract is authorized, a pattern that violates the assumption that a contract can safely modify shared state immediately upon deployment. An attacker or a mis‑configured DAO could trigger the failure by submitting an upgrade that includes a new settings contract without first ensuring the address is pre‑registered, effectively blocking the upgrade. The impact is that the upgrade process may not complete, leaving the DAO unable to add or update protocol parameters such as auction, deposit, inflation, minipool, network, node, proposal, rewards or security settings. When the upgrade stalls, users see the UI report that the upgrade failed, new settings do not appear, and proposals cannot be created or voted on as expected. The affected parties include DAO members, protocol operators and any users who rely on governance‑controlled parameters. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the RocketUpgradeOneDotThree contract, where the code that adds new contracts to RocketStorage was examined and the constructor of RocketDAOProtocolSettingsProposal was found to call setSettingUint before the contract was whitelisted. The problem is subtle because the constructor code looks innocuous and the failure only manifests during an upgrade transaction, making it easy to overlook. To remediate, the initialization logic should be moved out of the constructor into an initialise function that is called after the contract has been added to RocketStorage, or the upgrade process should use CREATE2 to pre‑compute the contract address and whitelist it before deployment. This eliminates the unsafe constructor side‑effect and restores reliable upgradeability.

title: Incorrect stake.for.allowed Value
description:
Incorrect node address is recorded as allowed to be staked for, which may result in unexpected and unintended results.
On line [305] the address to allow staking for is set as the caller of the function msg.sender, however, it should be a _nodeAddress, as the call may not necessarily come from the node itself, but it may also be a node’s RPL withdrawal address:
```solidity
setBool(keccak256(abi.encodePacked("node.stake.for.allowed", msg.sender, _caller)), _allowed);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect key being stored in the permission mapping that controls which addresses are allowed to stakeon behalf of a node. The contract records the allowed staking relationship by hashing a string identifier together with the caller address (msg.sender) and the address that is being granted permission (_caller). Because the implementation uses msg.sender as the node identifier, the mapping key is built with the address that invoked the function rather than the actual node address that should be referenced. This mismatch occurs when the function is called from a node’s RPL withdrawal address or any other contract that is not the node itself. The root cause is a logical error: the code assumes the caller is always the node, ignoring the fact that staking permissions may be set by a separate authorized address. An attacker or a legitimate user can therefore either be unintentionally granted permission to stake for a node they do not control, or a legitimate node may be denied permission because the mapping was created for the wrong address. Exploitation is straightforward – an adversary can call the permission‑setting function from an address they control, causing the contract to record that address as allowed for a target node. Subsequent staking calls will succeed from the attacker’s address, potentially diverting rewards or causing the node’s intended stake to be blocked. The impact ranges from loss of staking rewards to the possibility of funds being locked or mis‑allocated, depending on how the protocol uses the allowed‑staking flag. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to the permission‑setting routine where the caller is not the node address, which is a common scenario when nodes use a separate withdrawal address. All parties that rely on the staking permission – node operators, delegators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions about who may stake are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, who noted that the mapping key used msg.sender instead of the explicit _nodeAddress parameter. The bug can be subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit warning; the mapping simply stores a value that appears correct when inspected with the wrong key, making it easy to miss during testing. To remediate, the implementation should replace msg.sender with the supplied node address when constructing the mapping key, ensuring that the permission is tied to the intended node rather than the caller. This aligns the contract’s logic with the intended business rule that only the designated node (or its authorized agents) may be granted staking rights, restoring correct accounting and preventing unauthorized stake actions.

title: Challenged Leaf Indices Can Be Left Unverified Onchain
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing on‑chain verification of leaf node data in the Merkle‑tree challenge mechanism used by the Rocket Pool protocol. The contract is supposed to require a proposer to supply a correct hash for each node of the tree as a challenger progresses round by round until the leaf level is reached, at which point the leaf data should be validated on‑chain before the challenge is marked as responded. However, the verification logic contains a condition that only triggers the leaf‑check when the expression indexDepth + depthPerRound >= treeDepth * 2 holds. Because indexDepth can never exceed treeDepth and depthPerRound is limited, this condition is satisfied only for very shallow trees (Merkle depth of five or less) or when the challenge index itself is a leaf node. In practice the network uses deeper trees, so the condition is rarely true and the leaf verification block is skipped. Consequently, when a challenger targets a leaf node, the contract still calls setNode and records the challenge as responded, but it never compares the supplied leaf hash against the expected value. The root cause is therefore an incomplete validation path: the code assumes leaf verification will happen automatically, but the guard clause prevents it for the typical depth configuration. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a challenge on a leaf index, providing arbitrary data that passes the shallow hash check, and having the challenge marked as responded without any on‑chain proof that the leaf data is correct. This allows malicious proposers to hide invalid or manipulated leaf information, potentially corrupting the Merkle representation of Rocket Pool node states, which underpins voting, reward distribution, and other protocol‑critical decisions. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated; users may see voting outcomes that do not reflect the true state, rewards may be allocated incorrectly, and the integrity of the consensus mechanism is weakened. The issue manifests only when the challenge index corresponds to a leaf node and the tree depth is small enough for the guard condition to fail, a scenario that can arise in test environments, future upgrades with multiple pollards, or any sub‑tree that meets the depth bound. It was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime when the auditors examined the submitRoot function and noticed that the leaf verification branch is gated by an inequality that never holds for realistic depths. The bug is subtle because the contract still progresses through the challenge flow and does not revert, so no obvious error is emitted; the UI may simply show a challenge as responded while the underlying data remains unchecked. From a user perspective the symptom is that a challenge appears to be resolved but the expected verification of leaf data never occurs, leading to potential mismatches between displayed balances or voting results and the actual protocol state. The vulnerability belongs to the class of insufficient validation or incomplete verification bugs, where a critical security check is omitted for a subset of inputs. The recommended remediation is to ensure that leaf index challenges are always verified on‑chain, either by removing the restrictive guard condition or by explicitly invoking the verifyLeaves routine for leaf depths, and by only marking a challenge as responded after a successful hash comparison has been performed.

title: Node Operators ETH Can Be Mistakenly Sent To The Deposit Pool
description:
Node operators that have a sufficient deposit credit and additionally send ETH when depositing, lose their additional ETH.
On line [72], the conditional case that an operator has sufficient credit to create a minipool does not check msg.value to see if the node also is sending additional ETH.
It can be the case that a Node Operator forgets, or inadvertently sends a deposit value when it has sufficient credit for a deposit bond. The function accepts the ETH without returning the excess to the node operator.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs when a node operator who already possesses enough deposit credit to create a minipool also includes a non‑zero ether value (msg.value) in the same transaction. The contract’s deposit function contains a conditional branch that checks only the operator’s credit balance and does not verify whether additional ether was sent. Because the code does not validate or return the extra ether, the contract silently accepts the surplus and forwards it to the protocol’s deposit pool, effectively removing the operator’s funds from their control. This flaw is rooted in improper input validation – the function assumes that a positive credit balance guarantees that no ether should be supplied, but it fails to enforce that assumption. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any operator who mistakenly or inadvertently sends ether while already credit‑eligible will lose that ether. The impact is a loss of funds for the affected operator, manifested as a reduction in their wallet balance without any corresponding receipt or refund; the user may see a successful deposit event while their balance drops unexpectedly. The condition is triggered only when the operator’s credit is sufficient and msg.value is greater than zero, so it may go unnoticed during normal operation because the transaction still succeeds and no error is emitted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the deposit logic and identified the missing msg.value check. It is difficult to spot because the contract does not revert or emit a warning, and the UI may simply report a successful deposit, masking the hidden loss. To remediate, the function should either reject any transaction that includes ether when the operator already has enough credit (by reverting if msg.value != 0) or explicitly calculate the excess amount and return it to the sender before proceeding. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of unchecked value handling or improper input validation bugs that lead to unintended fund transfers and accounting inconsistencies, violating the protocol’s expectation that a node operator’s deposit amount matches the required bond and that no extra ether is absorbed silently.

title: Challengers Can Contest Non-Existent Indices To Steal Proposal Bond
description: Due to errors in the getPollardRootIndex() function, users are able to create challenges for indices that exceed the Network Voting Tree length under specific conditions. This issue allows users to directly challenge indices they should not be able to contest, which could lead to lost proposal bonds for valid proposals. When calculating the pollardRootIndex of an index for a Merkle pollard with depth less than 5, the pollard root index will return 1 for all indices of depth at least 5. If we consider a case with 8 nodes, an index depth of 31 will return a pollard root index of 1. However, this exceeds the max depth of our Network Voting Tree’s Merkle pollard. The correct response would be a revert. If the challenger can provide a valid witness for this non existent node, the challenge hash will be updated to the 31st index. This will result in a challenge that cannot be responded to. Note, this issue is only applicable to trees with less than 32 indices, hence a low likelihood of exploitation as there is a significant number of Rocket Pool nodes on the network already.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper bounds check in the function that computes the pollard root index for a Merkle voting tree. Because the implementation returns a constant value of 1 for any index whose depth is greater than or equal to five, it fails to detect when a challenger supplies an index that lies beyond the maximum depth of the Network Voting Tree. As a result, a malicious challenger can create a challenge for a non‑existent node by providing a witness that appears valid for that out‑of‑range index. The contract then updates the challenge hash to reference this illegal index, producing a challenge that the original proposer cannot answer. When the challenge cannot be responded to, the protocol automatically forfeits the proposer’s bond, causing the bond amount to disappear from the proposer’s balance. This bug manifests only when the voting tree contains fewer than thirty‑two leaves (depth less than five), a situation that is rare on the live network but still possible for small proposals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the getPollardRootIndex logic and noticed that the function never reverts when the supplied index exceeds the tree’s maxDepth. The problem is subtle because the function appears to return a plausible root index, so normal operation does not raise an error, and the incorrect index is only observable when a challenge is later attempted on that node. From a user’s perspective, a proposer expects the bond to be returned after a successful challenge resolution, but instead the bond is permanently lost, leaving the proposer’s balance unexpectedly reduced to zero. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect input validation / out‑of‑bounds index handling” in Merkle‑tree based voting contracts. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly compare the supplied index against the tree’s maximum depth and revert with a clear error message when the index is too large, or otherwise correct the pollard root index calculation so that it never yields a valid root for non‑existent nodes.

title: Fee Rates Can Change on Active Products
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a mutable settlement fee rate that is applied when a user burns a previously minted product token. At mint time the protocol displays a fee rate that the minter implicitly accepts, but the actual fee deducted from the payoff is calculated later, during the burn operation, using the feeCollector.settlementFeeRate() value that is current at that moment. Because the fee rate is stored in a separate contract and can be updated by governance or other privileged actors, it may change between the mint and burn events. An attacker or a malicious governance action could raise the fee rate after users have locked capital, causing those users to receive a lower net payoff than expected. The impact is that minters may pay significantly higher fees than they agreed to, effectively losing part of their principal or expected return. This situation occurs whenever a product remains active for a period of time and the fee rate is altered before settlement. The affected parties are the minters, any downstream users relying on predictable fee calculations, and the protocol’s reputation for financial integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee calculation paths for minting and burning and noticed that the fee is not captured in the product identifier or stored at mint time. It can be hard to notice because the fee displayed at mint appears correct, and the discrepancy only surfaces at settlement, often when users see a smaller payout without an obvious cause. The bug belongs to the class of “dynamic fee calculation” or “post‑mint mutable parameter” vulnerabilities, where economic parameters that should be immutable for a given contract instance are instead read from a mutable external source. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected payoff, but after burning the token the received amount is lower, sometimes even zero, leading to confusion and loss of trust. To remediate, the settlement fee rate should be captured and locked at the moment of product creation, for example by including it in the product ID hash or storing it in the product’s state, ensuring that the fee used at burn matches the fee presented at mint. This aligns the contract’s accounting with the business logic that fees are agreed upon up front and prevents unexpected fee inflation.

title: Rounding Issue Causing Dust Amount Being Locked
description:
```solidity
A rounding error in calculating the minter payoff would result in collateral dust amount being locked forever in the
vault.
The minter payoff has the following expression:
LeverageSmartTrendVault.sol
payoff = payoffWithFee - fee + (amount * 1e18 - amount * collateralAtRiskPercentage) / 1e18;
Reducing amount * collateralAtRiskPercentage from amount * 1e18 and then dividing the result by 1e18 will round
down the result by 1 wei. So, for every minter payoff, 1 wei will be locked in the vault.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs when the contract computes the minter payoff for a leveraged vault. The payoff formula first multiplies the deposited amount by a fixed‑point scaling factor (1e18), subtracts the portion of collateral that is at risk, and then divides the result by 1e18. Because Solidity performs integer division, the subtraction is executed before the division, causing the intermediate value to be rounded down by one wei. Consequently, each time a minter withdraws their payoff, exactly one wei of collateral is left behind in the vault and can never be reclaimed. This dust amount accumulates over many transactions, leading to a gradual loss of funds that is invisible to users because the missing amount is extremely small. The issue is triggered whenever the payoff calculation is performed, i.e., on every mint or redemption operation that uses the faulty expression. All participants who interact with the vault – minters, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the locked dust reduces the total assets under management and violates the accounting assumption that the contract should return the full calculated payoff. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the arithmetic order in the payoff function and compared it with a reference implementation that correctly avoids the rounding loss. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the discrepancy is only one wei per operation, which does not cause obvious failures or revert messages, and typical unit tests do not check for exact wei‑level balance equality. To remediate the issue, the arithmetic should be reordered so that the division is applied only to the collateral‑at‑risk term, for example by computing amount - (amount * collateralAtRiskPercentage) / 1e18, which matches the pattern used in the reference vault implementation. This change eliminates the intermediate subtraction before division, preventing the rounding down and ensuring that the contract returns the exact expected payoff without leaving dust behind.

title: COLLATERAL Token Is Not Part of The digest
description:
```solidity
The COLLATERAL token is not part of the digest that the market maker signs. This means that if the vault is upgraded
to a new implementation that allows the admin to change to another collateral token, a user can call mint() function
using a signature intended for the old token, if it has not expired yet.
This scenario, whilst improbable, could be especially impactful if the new collateral token has a different value than the
previous one. For example, Consider an MM signing a transaction for 1e9 USDC and then this being used to trade with
1e9 WBTC.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the collateral token identifier being omitted from the signed message that the market maker uses to authorize minting operations. The market maker creates a digest that includes parameters such as amount, recipient and deadline, but the address or symbol of the collateral token is not part of that digest. Because the digest does not bind the specific token, the signature is valid for any token that the contract later accepts. If the vault contract is upgraded or the admin changes the accepted collateral token, an attacker can present a previously obtained signature that was intended for the original token and call the mint function with the new token. This can be exploited while the original signature is still within its expiration window and after the contract’s collateral configuration has been altered. When the new token has a different market value than the original, the attacker may obtain more economic value than authorized or under‑collateralize a position, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol. Users of the protocol, liquidity providers and any party relying on the market maker’s price guarantees are affected because the signed amount no longer corresponds to the expected collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s signature verification logic, where the auditor noticed that the COLLATERAL variable was never hashed into the message. The bug can be subtle because the transaction still succeeds and the UI may display the expected minted amount, while the underlying economic value is mismatched, making it hard to detect without inspecting the signed payload. To remediate, the contract should include the collateral token identifier in the data that is hashed and signed, ensuring that a signature is bound to a single, immutable token. This change restores the integrity of the authorization and prevents replay of signatures across different collateral assets. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing‑parameter‑in‑signed‑message or signature‑replay‑across‑context‑changes bugs, which violate the principle that a signed statement must fully capture all variables that affect the outcome.

title: Duplicate PoolIds Can Cause Loss Of Funds For Users
description:
Withdrawal vaults handle the distribution of rewards to users, node operators and protocol fee recipients. Due to the use of CREATE2 opcode and contract architectural decisions, accidental or malicious administration can generate the same withdrawal address over two pool registries with identical poolIds.
VaultFactory.deployWithdrawVault() and VaultFactory.computeWithdrawVaultAddress() use the OpenZeppelin Clones Upgradeable contracts to manage the creation of new withdrawal vaults. In turn these use CREATE2 with a salted value that relies on _poolId, _operatorId, _validatorCount. These values are entirely determined by the PoolRegistry contracts, which means that salt hash collisions can occur, resulting in the same withdrawal address being calculated.
If two users share the same withdrawal address across two different pool registry contracts, it is possible for the earlier user to steal funds of the latter user.
Currently PermissionlessNodeRegistry and PermissionedNodeRegistry use the VaultFactory.deployWithdrawVault() which will revert if the same address is calculated twice (since CREATE2 reverts if an address has non-zero nonce, or has extcodesize>0). However, PermissionlessPool.preDepositOnBeaconChain() uses VaultFactory.computeWithdrawVaultAddress which will not be able to differentiate between whether vault is being calculated that matches a different pool with the same poolId.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate withdrawal‑vault address collision that can cause funds to be lost for users of later pools. The factory contracts create withdrawal vaults with CREATE2, using a salt that is derived only from the pool identifier (poolId), the operator identifier and the validator count. Because the poolId is scoped to a single registry contract, two different registry contracts can independently assign the same poolId. When this happens the same salt value is produced, so the CREATE2 algorithm calculates an identical contract address for both pools. In the PermissionlessNodeRegistry and PermissionedNodeRegistry the deployment function (VaultFactory.deployWithdrawVault) will revert if the address already contains code, which prevents the second deployment, but the PermissionlessPool.preDepositOnBeaconChain function calls VaultFactory.computeWithdrawVaultAddress, which merely returns the address without checking whether a contract already exists. Consequently the system may accept a deposit for the second pool and direct the reward tokens to the already‑deployed vault belonging to the first pool. The earlier pool’s operator can then withdraw those tokens, effectively stealing the later user’s funds. The issue manifests when two pools share the same poolId (and identical operatorId and validatorCount) across separate registries, and when the code path uses only the address‑computation function instead of the deployment function. Users see their expected reward balance become zero or see no refund after a deposit, while the protocol’s accounting shows the funds as transferred to a vault that they do not control. The problem was discovered during a logical audit of the VaultFactory and pool‑registry interaction, and it is hard to notice because the address collision does not raise an exception and the UI may display the same vault address for two distinct pools without obvious warning. To remediate the issue the salt should incorporate a globally unique component such as the registry contract address (msg.sender) or the factory should delegate the CREATE2 deployment to each registry so that the same poolId cannot produce the same address in different contexts. Adding an explicit existence check before using a computed address would also prevent silent redirection of funds. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of deterministic‑address collisions caused by insufficient entropy in CREATE2 salts, leading to unintended fund redirection and violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: StaderConfig Cannot Be Updated
description:
StaderConfig serves as a central contract that maintains all protocol settings and access control, crucial for the protocol’s regular operation. Every key contract within the codebase holds the current StaderConfig address as a reference and provides a method for altering the StaderConfig address, namely updateStaderConfig().
However, ETHx.sol and OperatorRewardsCollector.sol contracts lack a function to update the StaderConfig in case of future changes to this address.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that two core contracts, ETHx.sol and OperatorRewardsCollector.sol, store a reference to the central configuration contract (StaderConfig) but do not expose any mechanism to change that reference after deployment. StaderConfig is intended to hold protocol-wide settings and access‑control data, and the rest of the codebase provides an updateStaderConfig() setter so that the address can be migrated if the configuration contract is upgraded or replaced. Because the two contracts lack this setter, the reference becomes immutable once the contracts are deployed. If the StaderConfig address is ever changed – for example during a governance upgrade, a security patch, or a migration to a new version – the ETHx and OperatorRewardsCollector contracts will continue to point to the old, potentially obsolete, configuration contract. This mismatch can cause the contracts to read stale parameters, reject legitimate calls, or fail to emit expected events. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as deposits that never register, rewards that are never distributed, or transactions that revert without a clear error message. The impact is medium severity because the protocol’s core functionality can be partially disabled, leading to loss of expected service and possible financial inconvenience for users, though funds are not directly stolen. The condition occurs only when the StaderConfig address is updated, a scenario that is plausible in a live, evolving protocol. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of contract interfaces, where the auditor compared the presence of updateStaderConfig() across all key contracts and noted its absence in the two mentioned files. The bug is subtle because the contracts compile and operate correctly under the initial configuration, so the problem only surfaces after a configuration change – a situation that may not be covered by standard unit tests. Conceptually, this is a configuration‑reference immutability bug, a subclass of upgradeability or mutable‑state errors where a contract hard‑codes a critical address without a governance‑controlled setter. The recommended remediation is to add an updateStaderConfig() function to both contracts, mirroring the pattern used elsewhere, and to protect it with appropriate access control so that only authorized entities can perform the migration. This change restores the ability to keep the protocol’s settings in sync across all components, ensuring that user actions such as deposits, withdrawals, and reward claims behave as expected after any future configuration upgrade.

title: HasEnoughSDCollateral() Check Is Performed Only Once During Onboarding
description:
The validation of SD token quantity currently only happens during the onboarding of new validators. This process specifically involves the call to addValidatorKeys(), which further invokes checkInputKeysCountAndCollateral(), ultimately calling hasEnoughSDCollateral(). However, this value is only contingent upon the price value during onboarding, allowing users to exploit price volatility and potentially maintain fewer SD tokens than required.
This issue could adversely affect the security offered by SD tokens to users against fraudulent or negligent validators.
There is no assurance that the market value of SD collaterals will suffice over the entire staking duration. A depreciation in the market value of SD collateral could alter the staker’s incentives, making malicious activities potentially more profitable.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a collateral adequacy check that is performed only once, at the moment a validator is onboarded, and never re‑evaluated during the lifetime of the stake. The contract calls addValidatorKeys(), which invokes checkInputKeysCountAndCollateral() and ultimately hasEnoughSDCollateral(). This function compares the amount of SD tokens supplied by the validator against a required threshold that is calculated from the market price of SD at onboarding time. Because the price is captured only once, any subsequent price volatility is ignored. As a result, a validator can initially satisfy the requirement when the price is high, then allow the market value of the deposited SD to fall below the required level without triggering any failure. The root cause is the absence of a periodic or per‑action re‑validation of collateral, creating a classic time‑of‑check‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) economic invariant violation. An attacker can exploit this by staking the minimum required SD tokens during a price peak, then waiting for the price to drop before performing any validator duties. The protocol will still consider the validator sufficiently collateralised, allowing the attacker to behave maliciously, submit fraudulent blocks, or simply abandon the validator while still receiving rewards. From the user’s perspective, rewards may continue to be paid out even though the validator is under‑collateralised, or conversely, rewards may be abruptly stopped when the protocol later detects insufficient collateral, leading to confusion and potential loss of expected earnings. The impact includes reduced security guarantees for delegators, possible loss of funds if a malicious validator exploits the under‑collateralised state, and erosion of trust in the staking mechanism. The issue manifests whenever the market price of SD changes after onboarding and the contract does not re‑run hasEnoughSDCollateral() before critical actions such as reward distribution or validator slashing. It affects all validators, delegators who rely on the collateral as a safety net, and the protocol as a whole. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by SigmaPrime, which noted that the collateral check is tied to a single price snapshot and lacks any ongoing enforcement. The problem can be hard to notice because the onboarding transaction succeeds and no immediate error is raised; only after a price shift does the economic guarantee break, which may not produce explicit on‑chain errors. To remediate, the contract should enforce the collateral requirement at every point where the validator’s economic rights are exercised – for example, before reward calculation, before block proposal, and periodically during the staking period. The protocol could also pause reward accrual until the validator tops up the SD balance to satisfy the current price‑based threshold, thereby restoring the intended security posture.

title: Submit Functions Are Susceptible To Front Running When Trusted Nodes Are Removed
description:
When a trusted StaderOracle node is removed using the removeTrustedNode() they should not be able to vote on balances, withdrawals, or beaconStateRoots. However, since the current voting process allows for submissions if the reporting block is >= to the current block.number with no delay period, it is possible for removeTrustedNode() to be front run with a call to (for instance) submitBalances().
Since both transactions can happen in the same block, and submissions do not allow for delay, there is no way to protect against malicious node removal.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that allows a trusted oracle node to continue influencing protocol state after it has been removed from the trusted set. When the governance function removeTrustedNode() is called, the contract does not enforce any waiting period before the node can still submit voting data such as balances, withdrawals or beaconStateRoots. Because the voting functions only require that the reporting block be greater than or equal to the current block number, an attacker who controls a trusted node can submit a vote in the same block in which the removal transaction is mined. By front‑running the removal transaction with a call to submitBalances (or a similar submit function), the malicious node can have its data accepted before the removal takes effect. This results in the protocol accepting stale or manipulated data from a node that should no longer be trusted, potentially causing incorrect accounting, unauthorized withdrawals, or wrong beacon state updates. The impact is that users may see their balances altered, withdrawals may fail or return incorrect amounts, and the overall security guarantees of the oracle system are weakened. The issue occurs whenever a node removal and a vote submission are included in the same block, which is feasible in high‑throughput environments where miners or validators can order transactions arbitrarily. All participants that rely on the oracle’s data – including token holders, liquidity providers and any downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol’s state may be corrupted. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the interaction between node management and voting logic, noting that the contract only checks block numbers and does not consider the removal timestamp. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to reject submissions from non‑trusted nodes, yet it does not differentiate between a node that was removed earlier in the same block and one that is still trusted. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can be subtle: a user may request a withdrawal and receive zero or an unexpected amount, or see their on‑chain balance suddenly change without any visible transaction from their address. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or timing attacks where state transitions are not atomic across related operations. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a delay or a commit‑reveal scheme that enforces a minimum number of blocks between a node’s removal and the earliest block in which it may submit votes. This ensures that once a node is removed, it cannot influence the protocol state in the same block, eliminating the race condition and restoring the intended trust model.

title: No Minimum Trusted Node Validation
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absence of a safeguard that ensures a minimum number of trusted nodes have been registered before the StaderOracle voting process can start. The contract logic only checks that the number of submissions reaches half of the current trusted node count plus one, and that a newer reporting block number is higher than the stored one. Because there is no requirement that the trusted node set reach a reasonable size, the condition can be satisfied with a single malicious vote when the system is freshly deployed or when only a few nodes have been added. An attacker controlling one of the early trusted nodes can therefore submit a deliberately incorrect exchange rate, cause the submissionCount check to succeed, and have the malicious rate accepted as the official oracle value. This leads to the protocol using a falsified price for downstream calculations, which can result in users receiving incorrect payouts, trades executing at unfavorable rates, or staked assets being valued incorrectly. The issue manifests during the initial setup phase or any period where the trusted node pool is below the intended quorum, and it affects any participant that relies on the oracle’s price feed, including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the voting logic and identified that the trustedNodesCount variable was never validated against a minimum threshold. Because the condition appears syntactically correct, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed when an unexpected price spike occurs. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum trusted node count before allowing any voting, or require a larger quorum (for example, a fixed minimum of three or more trusted nodes) so that a single malicious node cannot dominate the decision. This change restores the intended Byzantine‑fault tolerance and aligns the oracle behaviour with the protocol’s economic assumptions about accurate price reporting.

title: Uninitialized WithdrawDelay
description:
The withdrawDelay value is used in the function claimWithdraw() to calculate the waiting period before operators are able to withdraw their SDCollateral tokens.
However withdrawDelay is uninitialized, so that prior to setWithdrawDelay() being called withdrawDelay will default to zero which results in operators being able to immediately claim their sd collateral tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an uninitialized state variable that controls the mandatory waiting period before an operator can retrieve their SDCollateral tokens. The contract stores a numeric value called withdrawDelay, which is intended to be used by the claimWithdraw() function to calculate how long an operator must wait after depositing collateral before they are allowed to withdraw it. Because withdrawDelay is never assigned a value in the contract’s initializer, the Solidity language automatically sets it to zero. Consequently, the calculation of the waiting period yields zero seconds, allowing any operator to call claimWithdraw() and receive their collateral immediately, even though the protocol’s business logic expects a non‑zero lock‑up time. This flaw can be exploited simply by invoking claimWithdraw() right after a deposit, bypassing the intended security delay. The impact is that the protocol’s economic guarantees, which rely on collateral being locked for a defined period to deter malicious behavior, are effectively nullified; operators can exit the system without any waiting period, potentially leaving the protocol under‑collateralized and exposing it to attacks such as rapid exit or flash‑loan exploits. The condition under which the bug manifests is any state before the owner or governance calls setWithdrawDelay() to assign a proper value; in practice this includes the contract’s deployment and any period before the first administrative configuration. All operators, as well as the protocol’s users who depend on the collateral lock‑up for safety, are affected because the expected protection disappears. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the initialization flow and noticed that withdrawDelay had no explicit assignment. It may be hard to notice because the function call succeeds without reverting, giving the impression that the delay logic is working, while the UI or documentation may still claim a waiting period exists. To remediate, the contract should initialize withdrawDelay to a reasonable non‑zero default in the initializer and enforce that any later updates keep the value above zero, for example by adding a require statement in setWithdrawDelay(). This type of bug belongs to the class of uninitialized state variable vulnerabilities, where default zero values unintentionally bypass critical checks, leading to logical errors such as immediate fund withdrawal, broken accounting assumptions, and a mismatch between user expectations (a delay before withdrawal) and actual behavior (instant withdrawal).

title: Fee Accounting Rounding Favours Users Over Protocol
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting rounding error that occurs in the fee accrual routine of the utility pool contract. When the accrueFee() function updates the total amount of utilized stable‑coins (totalUtilizedSD) and the per‑utilizer index (utilizeIndex), it multiplies the utilization rate per block by the elapsed block count, then divides the product by a fixed decimal constant. Because Solidity uses integer division, any fractional part of the result is truncated. The totalUtilizedSD value is increased by the truncated fee amount, while the per‑utilizer index is increased by a separate truncated calculation that is always slightly smaller because utilizeIndex is less than totalUtilizedSD. This creates a small discrepancy each block: the protocol records a larger fee accumulation in the global pool than it actually distributes to individual users. Over many blocks the discrepancy compounds, causing the protocol’s fee reserve to be under‑funded while users are able to claim slightly more interest than the protocol has earned. The issue is triggered whenever accrueFee() runs, which is typically on every block where the pool is active, and it is more pronounced when the utilization rate per block is low, because the integer division then discards a larger proportion of the intended fee. The affected parties are the protocol itself (its fee balance and solvency), delegators who rely on the protocol’s fee pool to receive their share, and any user who utilizes the pool and later withdraws claimable interest. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, which compared the global fee accounting with the per‑utilizer calculations and observed a persistent shortfall. The bug is hard to notice because the rounding loss per block is tiny and does not manifest in short‑term tests; it only becomes evident after many accrual cycles when the cumulative shortfall grows enough to create bad debt. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the UI may show a higher claimable reward than expected, or that the protocol’s fee balance appears to shrink slower than usage would suggest, effectively giving users “free” interest. This violates the business logic that fees collected from utilization must fully back the interest paid to users. The recommended mitigation is to change the rounding direction so that any fractional fee is rounded up when updating both the global fee total and the per‑utilizer index, ensuring the protocol never under‑collects. Additionally, the repayment function must be hardened to handle possible under‑flows that can arise when the rounded‑up values are later subtracted. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of precision or rounding bugs caused by integer division truncation in financial smart contracts, leading to accounting drift and potential insolvency.

title: Price Inflation Of cTokenShare When Supply Is Zero
description:
If the current supply is zero, an attacker can perform a share inflation attack during delegation.
This can be illustrated through the following steps:
1. Alice wants to delegate 1 SD token (which has 18 decimals) to the utility pool calling delegate().
2. The pool is empty. The exchange rate is the default 1 SD per cTokenShare.
3. Bob sees Alice’s transaction in the mempool and decides to sandwich it.
4. Bob delegates 1 wei of SD and receives 1 wei of cTokenShare in exchange. The exchange rate is now 1 SD per cTokenShare.
5. Bob transfers 1 SD (1e18 wei) to the vault using an ERC-20 transfer. No new cTokenShares are created. Hence, the exchange rate is now 1e18 + 1 SD per cTokenShare, or 1e18 + 1 wei of SD per wei of cTokenShare.
6. Alice’s deposit is executed. Her 1e18 wei of SD tokens are worth less than 1 wei of cTokenShare. Therefore, the contract takes the assets, but does not add shares. Alice has effectively "donated" her tokens.
bug_full: An inflation of the internal share price occurs when the pool's total supply of cTokenShare is zero. The contract calculates the exchange rate as total assets divided by total shares. When total shares is zero, the rate defaults to 1:1. An attacker can submit a tiny delegation transaction (for example 1 wei) immediately before a legitimate large delegation. Because the pool is empty, the attacker receives a share at the default rate. The attacker then transfers a large amount of the underlying token directly to the vault without minting additional shares, which inflates the assets‑per‑share ratio dramatically. When the legitimate user’s delegation is processed, the contract credits the user’s assets but the inflated exchange rate makes the newly minted shares worth far less than the deposited amount, effectively stripping the user of value. The user sees their tokens deducted from their wallet while receiving no or negligible share balance, leading to a loss of funds. This condition only appears when the pool has zero total supply at the moment of delegation, which can happen after deployment, after a complete withdrawal, or after a forced reset. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the delegation logic, where the auditor noticed that the exchange rate calculation does not guard against a zero‑share denominator. The bug is subtle because the contract behaves correctly under normal non‑zero supply conditions, and the inflated rate may not be obvious from the UI, which only shows the amount of tokens transferred. The issue belongs to the class of price‑inflation or share‑dilution attacks that exploit unchecked arithmetic when a denominator can be zero. To remediate, the contract should introduce virtual shares and assets or a minimum share denominator, ensuring that the exchange rate cannot be manipulated when the pool is empty, and should prevent direct asset transfers that bypass share minting. By enforcing a stable exchange rate or requiring a minimum initial liquidity, the protocol can avoid the scenario where an attacker can donate another user’s tokens without providing corresponding shares.

title: Non-Reentrant Modifier Conflict
description:
In the PermissionlessNodeRegistry contract, the function addValidatorKeys() is marked with two nonReentrant modifiers.
This double application of the nonReentrant modifier can lead to unexpected behaviour, causing the function to revert due to the reentrancy guard.
bug_full: In the PermissionlessNodeRegistry contract the function addValidatorKeys is protected by a nonReentrant guard that is applied twice. The nonReentrant modifier works by setting a status flag when the function is entered and checking that flag on every entry. When the same guard is stacked, the first modifier sets the flag to the entered state, and the second modifier immediately sees the flag already set and triggers the built‑in revert that signals a reentrancy violation. As a result any call to addValidatorKeys reverts before any state changes are performed. The root cause is a developer oversight that duplicated the modifier instead of using it once, creating a conflict within the reentrancy protection logic. This can be exploited trivially: an attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply invoking the function causes the contract to reject the call, preventing legitimate validators from being registered. The impact is that the protocol’s node registry becomes unusable for adding new validators, which may halt onboarding, freeze expected upgrades, and frustrate users who see their transaction fail with a generic “reentrancy guard” error. The condition occurs every time the function is called, regardless of whether an external call is made, because the guard checks are performed before any business logic. The affected parties include protocol operators, validator candidates, and any downstream contracts that rely on a populated registry. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the code was inspected for proper use of OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant pattern. It is easy to miss because the Solidity compiler does not warn about duplicate modifiers and the function otherwise compiles and appears safe. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a failed transaction, often with a message like “reentrancy guard: reentrant call”, while the user expects the validator to be added and possibly a fee to be deducted. The bug belongs to the class of modifier misuse or reentrancy‑guard conflicts, where overlapping protective mechanisms interfere with each other and break normal execution. To remediate the issue the redundant nonReentrant modifier should be removed, leaving a single guard that correctly protects against true reentrancy while allowing legitimate calls. Optionally, the contract could be refactored to use a dedicated internal function for the core logic and apply the guard only once at the external entry point. This aligns with standard smart‑contract best practices and prevents unintended reverts.

title: Lost SD Rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one accounting error in the SD incentive controller that causes eligible rewards to be lost when no delegator interaction occurs at the very end of the reward period. The contract’s rewardPerToken() function checks if the current block number is greater than or equal to rewardEndBlock and, if so, returns the previously stored rewardPerToken value without performing any further calculation. Because updateReward() – the function that refreshes rewardPerTokenStored – is only invoked when a user delegates or requests a withdrawal, the stored value is never updated if no such action happens at block rewardEndBlock‑1. Consequently, the reward amount that should have accrued between the last update block and rewardEndBlock‑1 is never added to the delegators’ balances and is effectively lost. This bug manifests when the incentive period reaches its final block and the system is idle; delegators who expected to receive rewards for the last interval instead see their reward balance remain unchanged, contradicting the protocol’s promise of continuous accrual. The issue was identified during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, which noted that the comparison uses ">=" instead of ">" and that there is no fallback logic for blocks after the end of the period. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error – the symptom is simply a missing reward, which may be attributed to normal variance by users. The impact is a loss of SD incentive rewards for any delegator who does not trigger an update at the precise moment before the period ends, potentially reducing overall protocol participation and undermining trust. The affected parties are delegators, the protocol’s reward distribution mechanism, and any stakeholders relying on accurate accounting of SD incentives. To remediate, the comparison should be changed to ">" so that rewards are still calculated for the final block, and additional logic should be added to compute the missing reward portion when the current block exceeds rewardEndBlock and the stored value is stale. This aligns the contract with the intended accounting model where rewards accrue up to and including the last block of the incentive window, ensuring that users receive the full amount they are entitled to.

title: Rounding Error Causing Loss Of Funds
description:
There is a rounding error in the OperatorRewardsCollector.withdrawableInEth() function, such that it can cause a scenario where an operator can lose a small amount of ETH even when not utilizing the SD Utility Pool.
When calculating total collateral in withdrawableInEth(), the collateral value is converted from ETH to SD, then back to ETH. This conversion process, which occur in the getUserData() and withdrawableInEth() functions, will cause withdrawableInEth() to ultimately round down the amount of ETH the operator is entitled to withdraw.
The conversion process is as follows:
In SDUtilityPool.getUserData():
```solidity
uint256 totalCollateralInSD = ISDCollateral(staderConfig.getSDCollateral()).convertETHToSD(
    totalCollateralInEth
);
```
In OperatorRewardsCollector.withdrawableInEth():
```solidity
uint256 availableBalance = ISDCollateral(staderConfig.getSDCollateral()).convertSDToETH(withdrawableInSd);
```
This rounding down effect can lead to scenarios where operators are unable to withdraw their full entitled ETH balance, despite not having any outstanding interest or open liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs when the OperatorRewardsCollector contract calculates the amount of ETH an operator can withdraw. The logic first converts the operator’s total collateral from ETH to the protocol’s native SD token using a conversion function, and later converts the withdrawable amount from SD back to ETH. Both conversion functions truncate fractional values, effectively rounding down at each step. Because the calculation performs an ETH→SD conversion followed by an SD→ETH conversion, the final ETH amount is systematically lower than the true entitlement. This loss manifests even when the operator has no outstanding interest or open liquidations, meaning the operator should be able to withdraw the full balance. The issue is triggered whenever withdrawableInEth() is called, which internally relies on getUserData() to perform the double conversion. Operators of the protocol are affected, as they receive slightly less ETH than expected; the discrepancy may be small per transaction but can accumulate over many withdrawals. The problem was identified during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical flow of conversions was examined and the truncation behavior noted. The bug is subtle because the UI typically displays the pre‑conversion balance, so users see the correct amount on screen but the on‑chain transfer delivers a reduced value, making the loss hard to notice without detailed accounting. This class of bug falls under rounding‑down or precision‑loss errors common in financial smart contracts that perform unit conversions with integer arithmetic. To remediate, the contract should compute the withdrawable amount directly in ETH, avoiding the intermediate SD conversion, and apply a rounding‑up strategy for the interest component so that any rounding bias favours the user. In practice, the fix eliminates the double‑conversion path and ensures that the final ETH amount is at least equal to the operator’s entitlement, preserving the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: updateStream() Is Not Payable
description:
A sender can update a stream using the updateStream() function and deposit the associated stream token into the FuroStream contract.
The _depositToken() function optionally takes native Ether and deposits into bentoBox when the stream token is the wrapped Ether and there is sufficient balance of Ether in the contract.
However, updateStream() is not payable, hence it is not possible to deposit tokens into a stream with the WETH token while paying using native Ether.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the updateStream() function of the FuroStream contract, which is intended to allow a sender to modify an existing token stream and optionally deposit additional tokens. When the stream token is wrapped Ether (WETH), the internal _depositToken() routine can accept native Ether (msg.value) and forward it to BentoBox for wrapping. However, updateStream() is declared without the payable modifier, meaning the EVM will reject any transaction that includes Ether. As a result, a user who attempts to update a WETH‑based stream by sending native Ether will see the transaction revert, even though the contract logic is prepared to handle the Ether deposit. The root cause is a mismatch between the function’s external interface (non‑payable) and its internal token‑deposit logic (payable). This can be exploited by simply sending Ether with the updateStream() call; the call will fail, preventing the stream from being updated or funded. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style issue: users expecting to top‑up or adjust a WETH stream with Ether are unable to do so, leading to missing or delayed payments, zero balances where a positive deposit was expected, and potentially locked funds if the stream cannot be updated. The condition occurs whenever the stream token is WETH and the caller includes a non‑zero msg.value. Affected parties include any user of the protocol who wishes to fund or modify a WETH stream, as well as the protocol itself because the intended business logic of seamless Ether‑to‑WETH conversion is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function signatures with the underlying deposit logic. It may be hard to notice because the UI or documentation might suggest that sending Ether is allowed, yet the transaction simply reverts without a clear error message, giving the impression of a generic failure. To remediate, the updateStream() function should be marked payable so that it can accept msg.value, and the implementation should correctly forward any received Ether to the _depositToken() routine. Conceptually, the fix aligns the external interface with the internal accounting expectations, restoring the intended flow where native Ether can be wrapped and deposited when updating a WETH stream.

title: Unchecked Return Values of ERC20 transfer()
description:
The ERC20 interface definition includes return values for most functions. These values indicate whether the action was successfully executed or not, although most implementations will revert for the case where the execution fails.
The transfer() function will return a bool which is true if execution is successful and false if execution fails.
SushiMakerAuction does not check these return values for token.transfer() and bidToken.transfer() calls.
For ERC20 tokens which instead return false rather than reverting if a transfer fails, this would result in the protocol accounting for transfers which have not happened. If this is the case for the bidToken then the user would not be required to transfer any tokens to place a large bid.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked return value in ERC20 transfer calls within the auction contract. The contract calls token.transfer() and bidToken.transfer() but does not verify the boolean result. According to the ERC20 specification, a transfer may return false instead of reverting when the transfer fails. Because the contract proceeds assuming success, the auction’s internal accounting records a bid that was never actually transferred. An attacker can exploit this by using a token that deliberately returns false on transfer, allowing them to submit a large bid without moving any tokens. The impact is that the auction can be manipulated, other participants may lose the chance to win, and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent, potentially leading to loss of funds or reputation damage. This condition occurs whenever the token implementation follows the “return false” pattern rather than reverting, which is common for some older or custom ERC20 contracts. The affected parties include bidders, the auction contract, and any downstream protocol that relies on the auction outcome. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that noted the absence of any require or SafeERC20 wrapper around the transfer calls. It is hard to notice because most popular tokens revert on failure, so tests that only check for reverts will pass, masking the logical flaw. From a user’s perspective, a participant may see their bid accepted and the auction price increase, yet their token balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion when the auction later settles. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call return values” or “missing success verification” bugs, which violate the business rule that a successful transfer must be guaranteed before state changes. To remediate, the contract should capture the boolean result of each transfer and revert the transaction if the result is false, or use a vetted library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 which automatically reverts on failure.

title: Token Transfers May Fail Locking Auctions
description:
It is possible for token transfers to fail for certain ERC20 tokens. For example, some ERC20 tokens prevent transfers to blacklisted accounts.
If the token.transfer(bid.bidder, bid.rewardAmount); fails during end(), then the entire transaction will fail. The any current or future reward tokens (for this specific token) will be locked in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a failure mode in which an auction contract attempts to transfer reward tokens to a winning bidder during the end() function, but the external ERC20 token transfer can revert or return false for reasons that are specific to the token implementation, such as blacklisting of the recipient address, a paused token contract, or any other custom transfer restriction. The root cause is the contract’s reliance on a direct token.transfer call without any safety checks, fallback handling, or a pull‑based withdrawal mechanism. When the transfer fails, the entire end() transaction reverts, leaving the reward tokens that were supposed to be paid out permanently locked inside the auction contract because no alternative path clears the bid or refunds the tokens. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who either uses a token that deliberately blocks transfers to the contract address or arranges for the token to be blacklisted or paused at the moment the auction is settled. The impact is that bidders who have legitimately won the auction receive no reward, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent (the contract’s internal state records a completed auction while the external token balance remains unchanged), and the locked tokens may be unrecoverable, effectively resulting in a loss of funds for the protocol and its participants. The condition occurs whenever end() is called after the auction period has elapsed and the reward token implements any non‑standard transfer logic that can cause a revert. All participants who expect to receive a reward—bidders, auction creators, and downstream users—are affected. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the flow of token transfers and noted the absence of error handling for external calls. It can be hard to notice because most ERC20 tokens follow the standard transfer‑always‑succeeds pattern, so developers may assume the call cannot fail, and no events are emitted when a revert happens inside end(). To remediate, the contract should adopt a safe‑transfer pattern that checks the return value or catches exceptions, implement a pull‑based reward withdrawal, and provide a clearBid() function that can be invoked within a defined window after an auction ends to allow manual cleanup of stuck tokens. Conceptually, the fix removes the direct dependency on a single successful transfer and ensures that failed transfers do not leave the contract in an unrecoverable state, preserving the intended accounting and user expectations that a winning bid results in a received reward.

title: Re-entrancy Vulnerability Allows Controller To Steal All Tokens
description:
The controller of the UsernameRegistrar contract can withdraw all users’ tokens from the contract by exploiting a re-entrancy vulnerability [2, 3]. Such an attack would require a malicious controller (or an attacker with access to the controller account) which is why the likelihood of this attack vector is classified as Low.
The vulnerability arises in the release() function on lines [142] to [153]. Consider the scenario that 100 token’s have been deposited by users through the standard registration process. Let us also assume the contract has set a price of 10, without loss of generality. A malicious controller could create an attacking contract of the form ReentrancyAttack (given in the appendix) and call the moveRegistry() function with this contract’s address as the parameter. The attacking contract would implement a malicious version of dropUsername(bytes32) which can re-enter the release function a set number of times. This contract would need to be pre-loaded with tokens and would need to have registered a name in the UsernameRegistrar contract.
In our exploitation example, once the moveRegistry() function has been called, the controller would call the stealAllTheTokens() function on the attacking contract. This would re-enter the release() function 10 times (as each time it will withdraw price = 10 tokens, thus withdrawing the full balance of 100 tokens in the contract).
The attacking contract would execute the call on line [142] of UsernameRegistrar.sol which would re-enter release() 10 more times before completing. Once completed, lines [149] - [154] would be executed 10 times, withdrawing 100 tokens to the attacking contract.
See the test: test_attack_controller_steal_all_deposits that accompanies this report for a demonstration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw located in the token release routine of the UsernameRegistrar contract. The function that distributes the stored registration tokens makes an external call to a user‑controlled contract before it updates its internal accounting, allowing a malicious caller to re‑enter the same release logic repeatedly. The root cause is the ordering of operations: the contract transfers tokens (or invokes a callback) and only afterwards clears or reduces the stored balance, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. An attacker who controls the controller role can deploy a malicious contract that implements a specially crafted dropUsername callback. By invoking moveRegistry with the malicious contract address and then triggering stealAllTheTokens, the attacker forces the release function to execute its external call ten times in a row. Each re‑entry withdraws the fixed price amount (10 tokens) until the total deposited balance of 100 tokens is completely drained. This exploitation scenario requires the attacker to have a registered name and to preload the attacking contract with enough tokens to satisfy the price check, but once these conditions are met the contract can be emptied in a single transaction. The impact is that all users who deposited registration fees lose their tokens; from a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – that their registration fee remains locked until a legitimate release – is violated, and the UI may show a successful registration followed by a sudden zero balance or missing refund. The issue occurs only when the controller address is malicious or compromised, and it manifests during any call to the release function that triggers the external callback. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the control flow of release and confirmed the problem with a dedicated test case that repeatedly re‑entered the function. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract’s balance appears correct before the transaction and the external call is legitimate‑looking, so the drain happens atomically without intermediate warnings. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of re‑entrancy bugs in withdrawal or token‑transfer functions. To remediate, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by moving the external call after all state changes, optionally adding a re‑entrancy guard, and ensuring that only trusted contracts can be called during token release. After such a fix, the contract would no longer allow a malicious controller to re‑enter the release logic and therefore would protect user deposits from being stolen.

title: Controller Can Indefinitely Lock Users’ Tokens
description:
The release() function is affected by a denial of service (DoS) vulnerability, which allows the controller (or an attacker who owns the controller account) to permanently prevent users from withdrawing their deposited tokens.
This vulnerability relates to the way the external call on line [143] is executed. A malicious controller can create an attack contract, which implements a false assert (as shown in DOSAttack Contract) that consumes all the gas of the called transaction, causing the global transaction to fail. To execute this attack the controller would migrate the UsernameRegistrar contract to the malicious contract, preventing all users from withdrawing their tokens.
Note: In practice, gas allowance of the CALL opcode varies and is dependent on the total transaction gas allowance.
For transactions with > 3.5M gas, the residue gas after the call is sufficient to complete the release() function.
See the test: test_attack_dos_all_users that accompanies this report for a demonstration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the release() function of the UsernameRegistrar contract that allows the controller, or any attacker who can replace the controller, to permanently block users from withdrawing their deposited tokens. The root cause is an unbounded external call to the controller’s dropUsername(bytes32) method that forwards all remaining gas to the callee. Because the call does not specify a gas stipend, a malicious controller can deploy an attacker contract whose fallback or dropUsername implementation contains a false assert or an infinite loop that consumes the entire gas supplied to the call. When release() attempts to invoke the controller, the external call exhausts the transaction’s gas, causing the whole release() execution to revert. As a result, every user‑initiated withdrawal reverts and no tokens are transferred, leaving user balances unchanged on the UI – users see a failed transaction, receive no tokens, and may observe that their deposited amount appears to be “stuck” or “locked”. The condition occurs whenever release() is called after the controller has been migrated to a malicious contract; under normal circumstances with sufficient gas (>3.5 million) the function may succeed, which makes the issue easy to miss during casual testing. The audit team discovered the flaw by reviewing the external call pattern and by constructing a test contract (DOSAttack) that deliberately reverts and consumes all gas, confirming that the attack can lock all users’ funds. The problem is hard to notice because the function works correctly with typical gas limits, and the failure only manifests when the controller is malicious, a scenario that may not be exercised in standard unit tests. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls that allow a callee to hijack execution flow, violating the protocol’s expectation that deposited tokens remain withdrawable. To remediate, the contract should limit the gas forwarded to the controller by using a fixed gas stipend (e.g., call.gas(gasAmount)) or by adopting a pull‑payment pattern that isolates user withdrawals from untrusted external logic, thereby preventing a malicious controller from consuming all gas and ensuring that token withdrawals remain possible.

title: Users Can Create Unslashable/Non-removeable Subnode Names
description:
