Users can register any name (including unsavoury ones) as a sub-subnode of the ENSNode. These names are irrevocable and can be obtained for free, regardless of the price variable.
The vulnerability exists because there is no functionality in the UsernameRegistrar contract to revoke or deal which is invalid because it includes capitals. Once registered, the user may call setSubnodeOwner() on the ensRegistry contract and create a subnode name of their choosing without restriction (for example, lets use “OwnedSubnode”). The user may then call slashInvalidUsername() in order to have their deposit returned, whilst maintaining ownership of the sub-subdomain. If, for example, ENSNode is set to stateofus (assumed to be a subnode of the Ethereum ENS registry), the malicious user would retain ownership of the stateofus.eth/OwnedSubnode domain.
In this process, the user has obtained this domain for free and the name is irrevocable and unslashable. Although this vulnerability may not affect the front-end application dealing with usernames, it allows malicious users to create names derived from stateofus.eth which could potentially damage status’ reputation.
See the test: test_get_unslashable_subnode that accompanies this report for a demonstration.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an ability for any user to register a top‑level username and then create an arbitrary sub‑subdomain under the ENSNode that cannot be removed or slashed by the protocol. The root cause is that the UsernameRegistrar contract does not enforce naming rules or provide a revocation mechanism for sub‑domains, while the ENS registry’s setSubnodeOwner function is left unrestricted. An attacker can first register a name (even one containing disallowed characters such as capital letters) and then call setSubnodeOwner on the ENS registry to create a child label of their choosing, for example OwnedSubnode, under the registered ENSNode (e.g. stateofus.eth). After the sub‑domain is created, the attacker invokes slashInvalidUsername to retrieve the deposit that was originally required for the username registration. Because the slashing function only refunds the deposit and does not affect ownership of the newly created sub‑subdomain, the attacker retains control of stateofus.eth/OwnedSubnode for free and the name becomes irrevocable. This can be exploited whenever the protocol allows users to call setSubnodeOwner without additional checks, which is the case in the current implementation. The impact includes the creation of unsavoury or malicious domain names that appear to be part of the official namespace, potentially harming the reputation of the service and allowing free acquisition of valuable sub‑domains. The issue manifests when a user expects that an invalid username will be rejected or that slashing will remove any associated sub‑domains; instead the domain remains owned and functional, leading to a mismatch between user expectations and reality. The problem was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, which included a test case (test_get_unslashable_subnode) that demonstrated the flow. The bug is subtle because the front‑end may filter disallowed names, giving the impression that the contract enforces the same rules, while the underlying ENS registry permits unrestricted sub‑node creation. To remediate, the contract should implement a recursive sub‑domain slashing or revocation function that validates each label against the naming policy, restricts setSubnodeOwner to authorized callers, and ensures that slashing an invalid username also resets ownership of any derived sub‑domains, thereby preventing free, unslashable domain acquisition.

title: Amount Values Within BentoBox Can be Inconsistent
description:
If the actions ACTION_DST_DEPOSIT_TO_BENTOBOX and ACTION_DST_WITHDRAW_FROM_BENTOBOX are carried out with the same amount argument, it is possible for the ACTION_DST_WITHDRAW_FROM_BENTOBOX action to revert because the amount of tokens claimed is too high.
This behaviour is caused by the share conversion system within BentoBox, which can create imprecisions in token amounts owing to shares being worth more than one token each. BentoBox does not always round the imprecision in the same way, and so it is possible that the withdrawal action can request a number of shares that is higher than the share balance stored in bentoBox.balanceOf.
The impact of this issue is also mitigated by the checks in sgReceive(). As the withrawal action would revert on the destination chain, the catch block on line [93] should safely transfer the tokens to the user’s address.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns inconsistent handling of token amounts when the BentoBox share conversion mechanism is used in cross‑chain actions. BentoBox stores balances as shares, which represent a fractional amount of the underlying token. When an ACTION_DST_DEPOSIT_TO_BENTOBOX is executed with a specific amount, the contract converts that amount to shares using a rounding rule. Later, an ACTION_DST_WITHDRAW_FROM_BENTOBOX that is called with the same amount argument performs its own conversion back to shares, but the rounding direction may differ. Because shares can be worth more than one whole token, the second conversion can calculate a share quantity that exceeds the actual share balance recorded for the user. When the withdrawal attempts to claim those shares, the call reverts with an “insufficient shares” error. This situation occurs only when the caller supplies a non‑zero amount while leaving the share parameter at zero and requests unwrapping of BentoBox tokens, allowing the rounding discrepancy to surface. Users of protocols that rely on these actions – for example SushiXSwap or StablePool – may see a transaction fail or receive no tokens even though they supplied a valid amount, violating the expectation that a cross‑chain swap will deliver the promised funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, which noted that the share conversion does not round consistently and that the revert can be triggered only under specific amount‑share combinations, making it easy to miss in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit but then display an error or a zero balance after the withdrawal step, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The business logic of accounting for deposited tokens is broken because the protocol assumes that depositing an amount and later withdrawing the same amount will always succeed, which is not true when rounding errors cause share mismatches. A conceptual fix is to ensure that the share conversion uses a deterministic rounding mode for both deposit and withdrawal, or to require callers to provide the exact share value rather than relying on an implicit conversion. Additionally, the contract should validate that the calculated share does not exceed the stored balance before attempting the withdrawal, and fallback mechanisms should be clearly documented so that integrators avoid triggering the edge case. Implementing these changes restores the invariant that deposited tokens can be withdrawn in full, preserving user expectations and protocol safety.

title: Check on Stargate Router Address Could Revert
description:
The development team pointed out that, if the call by Stargate to sgReceive() were to revert, the tokens transferred from Stargate would be left in the SushiXSwap contract on the destination chain, where they could be transferred away freely by any user.
One possible condition under which this transaction could revert is if the Stargate router is redeployed, perhaps as part of an upgrade. The require on line [80] would then cause the transaction to revert, resulting in a loss of funds.
It is difficult to estimate the likelihood of this issue as it is outside the scope of this review to investigate Stargate’s likelihood of redeploying their router. However, whatever their stated policy, there could still be a redeployment and so a risk remains that could result in a loss of user funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a strict address check performed by the SushiXSwap contract when it receives a cross‑chain transfer from the Stargate router. The contract contains a require statement (line 80) that validates the caller against a hard‑coded Stargate router address. If the Stargate router is redeployed – for example as part of an upgrade – the caller address no longer matches the stored value and the call to sgReceive() reverts. Because the revert occurs after the tokens have already been transferred from Stargate to the SushiXSwap contract on the destination chain, the tokens become trapped inside the contract with no automatic refund mechanism. Any user who can invoke a function that moves tokens out of the contract can then withdraw the trapped assets, effectively allowing arbitrary theft of user funds. The issue is triggered only when the router address changes, a condition that is rare but possible and outside the scope of the audit to predict. From a user’s perspective a cross‑chain swap appears to succeed on the source chain, yet the destination balance remains zero and no refund event is emitted, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The problem was discovered during a manual code review by SigmaPrime, which noted that the require check could cause a revert and that the contract does not handle the failure case. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call with irreversible state change” and violates the accounting assumption that a successful token transfer on the source chain guarantees receipt on the destination chain. To remediate the issue the contract should either remove the hard‑coded require, implement a fallback that returns the tokens to the sender when sgReceive reverts, or adopt a pattern that monitors the router address and upgrades the contract when the router changes, thereby ensuring that funds are never left in an unprotected state.

title: sgReceive Could Send Native Tokens to a Contract
description:
The development team pointed out that, if the call by Stargate to sgReceive() were to revert, the tokens transferred from Stargate would be left in the SushiXSwap contract on the destination chain, where they could be transferred away freely by any user.
One possible condition under which this transaction could revert is if the user puts a contract with no receive or fallback function as the to address on line [83]. In this situation, if any native token balance is present in the SushiXSwap contract, then line [98] would cause the entire transaction to revert.
A related situation would be if the receiving contract had a receive or fallback function that uses too much gas, perhaps because of a change in gas fees on the destination chain, and so the transfer call would revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unsafe native token transfer pattern used in the sgReceive function of the SushiXSwap contract on the destination chain. When Stargate invokes sgReceive, the contract attempts to forward any received native tokens to a user‑specified address using the Solidity transfer method. Transfer forwards a fixed 2300 gas stipend and automatically reverts the whole transaction if the callee does not accept the funds or runs out of gas. Consequently, if the destination address is a contract that lacks a receive or fallback function, or if its receive/fallback consumes more than the stipend (for example due to increased gas costs), the transfer call fails and triggers a revert. Because the revert aborts the sgReceive execution, the native tokens that were already moved from Stargate remain locked inside the SushiXSwap contract. The contract does not contain any restriction on who can later withdraw these residual funds, allowing any user to call a withdrawal routine and extract the stranded tokens. This results in a loss of user funds: a user initiates a cross‑chain swap expecting the tokens to arrive on the destination chain, but instead the transaction reverts and the tokens disappear from the user’s perspective while silently accumulating in the SushiXSwap balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of sgReceive and identified the reliance on transfer as a potential failure point. It can be hard to notice because the revert only occurs under specific conditions—namely when the destination address is a contract with an incompatible fallback or when gas dynamics change—so normal test cases with externally owned accounts may pass unnoticed. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe Ether transfer patterns that combine limited‑gas forwarding with automatic reversion, violating the accounting assumption that a failed forward should not leave residual balances. To remediate, the code should replace transfer with a low‑level call using addr.call{value:x}(''), which forwards all available gas, does not revert on failure, and allows the contract to handle the error gracefully, for example by emitting an event or by safely accounting for the leftover balance. Implementing this change eliminates the scenario where funds become trapped and subsequently withdrawable by arbitrary users, restoring the intended business logic that cross‑chain swaps either succeed or safely revert without leaking assets.

title: Unstaking stkAave Extends Cooldown Time
description:
When depositing tokens like USDC into Aave Lending Pool on mainnet, stkAave tokens are rewarded to the depositors.
Staking stkAave should allow relevant parties to unstake and receive AAVE tokens as a result. This behaviour requires the _harvestRewards function to be called twice:
• The first time when the stakerCooldowns is at 0 and needs to be set to the relevant block timestamp.
• The second time to unstake and redeem relevant rewards.
The conditions for unstaking (i.e cooldown + COOLDOWN_SECONDS < block.timestamp and block.timestamp < cooldown + COOLDOWN_SECONDS + UNSTAKE_WINDOW) are difficult to satisfy. This is as a result of Aave’s specific logic, triggered during incentiveController.claimRewards(), which updates the stakerCooldown through STAKE_TOKEN.stake(). Internal logic can then set the stakerCooldown to a value that will not meet the requirements of unstaking.
Each time rewards are claimed, the stakerCooldown is increased proportionally to the amount of new rewards. Therefore, it will take longer before the rewards can be claimed and redeemed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the unstaking flow of stkAave tokens that are obtained as rewards for depositing assets into Aave. In Aave's incentive controller, each time claimRewards is invoked the contract calls stkAave.stake which updates the internal stakerCooldown timestamp. The protocol expects a two‑step process: first a cooldown call that records the current block timestamp, then after a fixed COOLDOWN_SECONDS period and within an UNSTAKE_WINDOW the user may call redeem to receive AAVE. Because claimRewards is executed inside the same transaction that attempts to redeem, the stake operation adds the newly claimed reward amount to the cooldown calculation, effectively pushing the cooldown timestamp forward. As a result the condition cooldown + COOLDOWN_SECONDS < block.timestamp < cooldown + COOLDOWN_SECONDS + UNSTAKE_WINDOW becomes much harder to satisfy, and may never be true if rewards are claimed repeatedly. Users therefore see their rewards locked indefinitely, experience “nothing happens” when trying to unstake, or receive zero AAVE despite having stkAave balance. The issue appears only when the contract’s harvestRewards function is called while a cooldown is already active; otherwise the flow works as intended, which makes the bug subtle and easy to miss during functional testing. The impact is medium severity because funds are not stolen but become inaccessible for the expected period, breaking the economic assumption that rewards can be claimed and immediately redeemed. The problem was identified during a security audit of the BentoBox strategy that integrates Aave staking, where the auditors observed that the incentiveController.claimRewards call was placed inside the unstake window logic. Fixing the issue involves decoupling reward claiming from the cooldown lifecycle – for example, moving claimRewards to a separate step that runs only when no cooldown is active, or resetting the cooldown after a successful claim, ensuring that the cooldown timestamp does not drift forward unintentionally. By aligning the contract’s state transitions with the protocol’s defined cooldown and unstake windows, the contract will honor the intended business logic that users can claim rewards and then promptly unstake their stkAave for AAVE.

title: Delegate call in `Vault#_execute` can alter Vault’s ownership
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Vault contract’s execute mechanism, which forwards arbitrary calls to external contracts using delegatecall. Delegatecall runs the code of the target contract in the context of the Vault, meaning any storage writes performed by the callee affect the Vault’s own storage. The Vault attempts to safeguard ownership by recording the owner address before the delegatecall and reverting if the owner variable changes afterwards. However, the contract also relies on a nonce variable to protect the init function, which can only be called when nonce is zero. Because the post‑call check does not verify the nonce, a malicious or faulty target contract can reset the nonce to zero during the delegatecall. Once the nonce is cleared, an attacker (or any external address) can invoke init, which will set the Vault’s owner to the caller’s address, effectively hijacking ownership. This attack vector is possible when the caller of execute is either the current owner or an address authorized through a merkle‑tree based permission system; the attacker must therefore first be added to the allowed merkle set, but an insider owner could unintentionally approve a malicious contract. The impact includes unauthorized transfer of ownership, potential alteration of other critical storage variables, and the risk that an attacker could later self‑destruct the proxy or steal funds stored in the Vault. From a user’s perspective the symptoms manifest as the Vault reporting a different owner than expected, the ability to re‑initialize the Vault after it was thought to be final, or simply observing that funds become inaccessible because the new owner controls withdrawals. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the post‑delegatecall state only against the owner variable and overlooked other invariants, a common oversight given the subtlety of delegatecall side effects. The issue is hard to detect because the delegatecall does not revert and the owner check passes, giving a false sense of safety while the hidden state change silently prepares the contract for takeover. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of insecure delegatecall patterns where critical contract invariants are not re‑validated after external code execution. The recommended remediation is to snapshot all state variables that guard privileged operations (such as nonce, merkleRoot, and any other access‑control flags) before the delegatecall and to verify that none have been altered afterwards, or to avoid delegatecall for untrusted code entirely, employing staticcall or a well‑audited module system instead.

title: A vault owner can frontrun a plugin call and change its implementation
description:
Each vault owner can manage freely the creation and deletion of plugins at any time if the vault was deployed by calling `VaultRegistry.createFor()`. An owner can simply overwrite a current plugin selector with a new address and change the implementation of that plugin at any time. This can be used to frontrun others and change the logic of a call before it is mined.

This strategy can also be used to bypass the need to uninstall a plugin by overwriting a currently installed one with a different implementation without needing to first remove the old plugin and then install the new one. This can be made just by installing a selector that collides with a previously installed plugin and change the address that is pointing that selector.
poc: There are two scenarios both relying on the fact that plugins can be overwritten which may lead to confusion in one case and to a malicious call in the other one.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted plugin overwrite mechanism in vault contracts that permits a vault owner to replace the address associated with an existing function selector at any time. This occurs because the vault’s plugin registry stores selectors in a mutable mapping without checking whether a selector is already occupied, and the access control for plugin management is based on disparate entry points that grant the owner full authority to add, remove, or replace plugins. An attacker who controls the owner role can front‑run a pending transaction that intends to call a legitimate plugin, overwrite the selector with a malicious implementation, and have the call execute the attacker‑controlled code once the transaction is mined. The exploit can also be used to swap out a plugin without first uninstalling the original, by installing a new contract under the same selector, effectively bypassing any intended de‑registration workflow. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected behavior: a user may submit a request that should yield a payout, but receives zero or a malformed response, or sees their balance unchanged despite a successful‑looking transaction. The impact includes loss of funds, corruption of accounting logic, and a breach of trust because the vault owner can silently redirect logic that users assume to be immutable. The issue surfaces whenever a vault is created through the public factory function (VaultRegistry.createFor) and the owner subsequently calls the plugin installation functions, which lack a guard against selector collisions. It was discovered during a formal audit where the reviewers examined the plugin management flow and identified that the methods mapping could be overwritten without restriction. The problem is subtle because overwriting a selector is a legitimate operation in the contract’s design, making it difficult to distinguish malicious intent from ordinary upgrades. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a selector can only be assigned once unless explicitly cleared, centralize and harmonize the entry points for vault deployment to guarantee consistent access control, optionally introduce a timelock on plugin installation to give users a window to react, and consider an allow‑list of vetted plugins or signature verification to prevent accidental or malicious overwrites. In broader terms, this is a classic instance of an unchecked upgrade path or mutable dispatch table that enables unauthorized logic changes, violating the fundamental accounting assumptions of the vault that its functional behavior remains stable once deployed.

title: A vault owner can also be the controller and arbitraily set the secondary market royalties
description:
The secondary sales of a specific `FERC1155` token can be charged with a certain amount of fees established by the controller of the `FERC1155`. Those royalties are meant to be sent to a receiver according to the current implementation. Currently the protocol intends users to deploy vaults via `BaseVault.deployVault()` which further calls `VaultRegistry.create()` that uses the currently deployed `fNFT` instance which it is controlled by the protocol itself.

However, there is other path that allows users deploying a vault where they are also the controllers of the `fNFT` instance. This allows users to take control over how are the royalty fees changed. A user can easily change maliciously the amount of royalties (which are also uncapped) and steal a considerable (even the whole) amount of `FERC1155` transferred.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an inconsistent privilege model in the fractionalized NFT protocol, where a vault owner can also become the controller of the underlying FERC1155 token contract. When a vault is created through the VaultRegistry.createCollectionFor function, the caller is assigned as both the vault owner and the controller of the token instance. This privileged controller role is allowed to call setRoyalties, which defines the percentage of a secondary‑sale price that is diverted as a royalty. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum cap or any timelock on royalty adjustments, the controller can arbitrarily increase the royalty rate from a modest value (for example 1 %) to the theoretical maximum of 100 % at any moment. An attacker who owns such a vault can therefore front‑run a legitimate secondary‑market transaction, raise the royalty to 100 % just before the sale is mined, collect the entire purchase price as royalty, and optionally revert the royalty back to the original rate after the transaction completes. This exploit is possible only when the vault is deployed via the Registry path, bypassing the intended BaseVault.deployVault flow that would normally keep the controller under protocol control. The impact is that sellers in the secondary market receive no proceeds from their sale, while the malicious vault owner captures the full payment, effectively causing funds to disappear from honest participants. From a user's perspective the UI may show a successful transfer of the token but the expected ether balance remains unchanged or drops to zero, contradicting the user’s expectation of receiving payment. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where a simulated attacker (Alice) changed the royalty to 100 % and verified that the royaltyInfo function returned the entire sale price. The problem is difficult to notice because the royalty configuration is a legitimate feature of the contract and the setRoyalties function does not emit warnings about extreme values, nor does the contract enforce any business‑logic constraints on royalty rates. To remediate, the protocol should separate vault ownership from token control, ensuring that only a designated protocol role can modify royalty parameters. Additionally, a hard ceiling on royalty percentages should be introduced, and a timelock mechanism should be added to any royalty update to provide predictability and prevent instantaneous front‑running. By consolidating vault creation through a single, internally‑restricted entry point and enforcing these constraints, the protocol can restore the intended economic guarantees for token holders and secondary‑market participants.

title: The `FERC1155.sol` don’t respect the EIP2981
description: The [EIP-2981: NFT Royalty Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2981) implementation is incomplete, missing the implementation of `function supportsInterface(bytes4 interfaceID) external view returns (bool);` from the [EIP-165: Standard Interface Detection](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-165).
poc: A marketplace that implemented royalties could check if the NFT has royalties, but if they don’t, add the interface of `ERC2981` on the `_registerInterface`, the marketplace can’t know if this NFT has royalties.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in an incomplete implementation of the NFT royalty standard (EIP‑2981) within the FERC1155 smart contract. Although the contract provides the ERC2981 royaltyInfo getter, it fails to expose the ERC2981 interface identifier through the ERC165 supportsInterface function. This omission means that external callers, such as marketplaces that rely on ERC165 to discover whether a token supports royalties, will receive a false negative and assume the token does not implement royalty logic. The root cause is a missing override of supportsInterface that returns true for the ERC2981 interface ID (0x2a55205a). When a marketplace queries the contract via supportsInterface, the call falls back to the default implementation that only reports ERC1155 and ERC165, so the royalty interface is invisible. An attacker or simply any marketplace that respects ERC165 will therefore be unable to detect royalty information, resulting in royalties not being paid to creators on secondary sales. The impact is primarily financial: creators may lose expected royalty payments, and users may be unaware that the token does not honor royalty specifications, potentially violating the protocol’s economic model. The condition occurs whenever a royalty‑aware platform checks for ERC2981 support; it happens at runtime whenever supportsInterface is called. All holders, royalty recipients, and marketplaces interacting with the token are affected because the contract’s public contract interface does not accurately reflect its capabilities. The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the contract against the EIP‑2981 specification and observed the missing supportsInterface implementation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and the royaltyInfo function works; only the interface detection layer is broken, which is not always exercised in unit tests. The proper mitigation is to add an override for supportsInterface that returns true for the ERC2981 identifier, following the pattern used in well‑audited libraries such as Solmate’s ERC1155 implementation. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of ERC165 registration bugs where a contract implements a feature but does not advertise it via the standard detection mechanism, leading to mis‑reporting of capabilities. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that an NFT listed on a royalty‑supporting marketplace shows no royalty field, the royalty percentage appears as zero, or creators report that they do not receive any royalty payment after a sale, contrary to their expectation that the contract would enforce a royalty fee.

title: Buyout Module: `redeem`ing before the update of totalSupply will make buyout’s current state success
description:
MED - a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements.

Attacker can create a vault with successful buyout status and non zero supply. The attacker can sell the fractions and then simply withdraw the assets.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the buyout module of a fractionalized vault where the redemption function can be invoked before the ERC‑1155 token contract updates its totalSupply. The root cause is that the mint function updates totalSupply only after calling the internal _mint routine, which performs an external call to the recipient address. If the recipient is a malicious contract, its token reception callback can execute redeem() while the totalSupply entry for that token still reflects the old value (often zero). The buyout logic checks the totalSupply to decide whether the buyout has reached a successful state; because the check is performed before the supply is incremented, the module incorrectly marks the buyout as SUCCESS. An attacker can exploit this sequence by deploying an "evil redeemer" contract that receives the freshly minted fractional token, immediately calls redeem, and thereby flips the buyout status. After the state is set to SUCCESS, the attacker can sell the fractions to other users and later invoke the withdraw function of the buyout module to extract the underlying assets at any time, even though the vault’s supply accounting does not yet reflect the minted fractions. The practical impact is the potential theft of assets held in the vault, loss of value for legitimate fraction holders, and a breach of the protocol’s guarantee that a buyout only succeeds after the required supply of fractions is minted. This condition can arise whenever a vault mints tokens to a contract address with non‑zero code size, i.e., any smart contract, and the mint implementation follows the pattern of performing the external call before updating the accounting variable. Users and UI front‑ends may see a vault reported as "buyout successful" while the underlying token supply is still incorrect, making the issue subtle and easy to miss during casual observation. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit where a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated that a crafted contract could trigger redeem in the same transaction as mint. Detection is difficult because the state transition appears legitimate and the totalSupply discrepancy is not directly exposed in the user interface. To remediate the issue, the token contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions principle by updating totalSupply before invoking any external call, or otherwise eliminate the external call from the mint path (e.g., use a safe internal mint without callbacks). Additionally, the buyout module could enforce a re‑entrancy guard or verify that totalSupply reflects the newly minted amount before allowing a state change to SUCCESS, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Migration fails when all tokens are joined
description:
When `proposal.totalFractions` is equal to the total supply (meaning that all token holders want to participate in a migration), there is a division by zero in `_calculateTotal`.

In contrast to a buyout, where it does not make sense to initiate a buyout if all tokens are held (because there is a dedicated method for that), it does make sense to have a migration that all token holders join. Therefore, this case should be handled.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic error that triggers a division‑by‑zero exception during the execution of a token migration when every token holder elects to participate. The migration logic calculates a ratio based on the number of fractions that have voted for the migration (proposal.totalFractions) and the total token supply. The implementation does not guard against the case where proposal.totalFractions equals the total supply, causing the denominator of the division to become zero. This edge case can be reached whenever a proposal is submitted that includes all existing fractions, which is a perfectly valid scenario for a migration unlike a buyout where a separate mechanism exists. When the contract reaches the internal function _calculateTotal, the unchecked division causes the transaction to revert, preventing the migration from completing. As a result, users who expect their tokens to be migrated or redeemed receive no output; from their perspective the migration button appears to do nothing or the transaction fails silently, leaving their balances unchanged yet the migration process is effectively dead‑locked. The impact is that the protocol cannot execute a full‑participation migration, potentially locking funds and breaking the intended upgrade or asset‑exchange flow. This condition occurs only under the specific circumstance of total‑fraction participation, which may not be exercised in standard testing, making the bug subtle and easy to miss. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors inspected the arithmetic expressions and identified the missing zero‑check. Because the failure surface is an internal exception rather than an explicit error message, it can be difficult for developers or users to diagnose without deep code review. The appropriate remediation is to add a safeguard that detects a zero denominator before performing the division, and to handle the full‑participation case explicitly— for example, by routing such proposals through the redeem mechanism or by providing an alternative calculation that does not involve division by a variable that can be zero. In generic terms, this is a classic unchecked arithmetic bug (division by zero) that violates the contract’s accounting assumptions and breaks the business logic that all token holders should be able to migrate safely.

title: Incorrect Token Transfer Pattern to BentoBox
description: Function BentoBox.deposit() is called on line [28] of TridentSwapAdapter.sol to make an initial BentoBox deposit to the Trident pool. This causes BentoBox to attempt a safeTransferFrom from the SushiXSwap contract. This fails because there is no allowance set for BentoBox to spend SushiXSwap’s tokens. This issue will cause a revert. On the source chain, that should only inconvenience the user. On the destination chain, the failed transactions should cause execution to fall into the catch block of sgReceive(). In each case, there should not be a loss of funds but merely a negative user experience.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect token transfer pattern used when the TridentSwapAdapter contract attempts to make an initial deposit into BentoBox. The adapter calls BentoBox.deposit(), which internally invokes a safeTransferFrom on the token contract to move SushiXSwap’s tokens into BentoBox. Because the SushiXSwap contract never grants BentoBox an allowance to spend its tokens, the safeTransferFrom call fails and triggers a revert. This failure occurs both on the source chain, where the user initiates the deposit, and on the destination chain, where the reverted call is caught by the sgReceive() catch block. From a user perspective the transaction simply reverts, showing an error such as “deposit failed” or “transaction reverted”, and no tokens are transferred; the user receives no refund or balance change, contrary to the expectation that the deposit would succeed and the pool would receive the tokens. The root cause is a missing allowance check and the misuse of the deposit function, which assumes that the caller has already approved BentoBox to pull the tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the adapter’s logic, where the auditor noted that the contract never performs an approve before calling deposit. Because the failure manifests only as a revert, it can be easy to overlook in testing if the test suite does not simulate the full token allowance flow, leading to a false sense of correctness. The bug belongs to the class of token‑transfer misuse vulnerabilities, specifically “missing allowance before safeTransferFrom”. It violates the business logic that a user should be able to deposit assets into a pool without manual pre‑approval steps, breaking the accounting assumption that deposited amounts are always credited. The impact is limited to a degraded user experience – transactions revert, users must retry or abandon the operation – but there is no direct loss of funds because the state changes are rolled back. The recommended remediation is to replace the direct deposit call with the skimming mechanism provided by ACTION_DST_DEPOSIT_TO_BENTOBOX: first perform a safeTransfer of the tokens to BentoBox, then let BentoBox deposit the received tokens into the pool. This pattern ensures that BentoBox receives the tokens without requiring a prior allowance, aligning the implementation with the intended token flow and eliminating the revert condition.

title: Bots can set ethReserves and swETHToETHRateFixed to any value
description: Bots are trusted to update not only how many ETH rewards have been generated, but also to update the protocol’s entire supply of ETH. This value is used to calculate the swETH to ETH conversion rate. It is therefore possible for a bot to set the value of swETH to a very high value. Any future withdraw functionality could thus be made to overpay. swETH.reprice() takes a parameter _preRewardETHReserves which it trusts entirely. It uses _preRewardETHReserves to calculate the amount of new swETH to mint for rewards, but it also uses it to reset the contract’s essential ETH bookkeeping values: ethReserves = _preRewardETHReserves + _newETHRewards; swETHToETHRateFixed = wrap(ethReserves).div(wrap(totalSupply())).unwrap(); If _preRewardETHReserves were set to a number, say a hundred times higher than the true reserve amount, then swETH would report a value approximately one hundred times too high when the following functions are called: swETHToETHRate() ethToSwETHRate() getRate() ethReserves() (Solidity automatically generated getter function) Other contracts might rely on these values, which are too easily manipulated. stakeAndVault is one such contract, for example. Furthermore, in future versions, if swETH has a withdraw() function for converting swETH back to ETH, it might reasonably rely on the value of ethReserves. It would also be possible to perform a similar attack by calling reprice() with a very large value for the parameter _newETHRewards. This issue is partially mitigated by security restrictions of the role SwellLib.BOT, which is the only role able to call swETH.reprice().
bug_full: An exploitable accounting flaw exists in the swETH contract where the function reprice can be called by any address that holds the SwellLib.BOT role. The function accepts a parameter _preRewardETHReserves that is assumed to represent the true amount of ETH held by the contract before reward distribution. The implementation trusts this input completely and uses it to recalculate the internal ethReserves variable and the fixed conversion rate swETHToETHRateFixed. Because the contract does not verify that _preRewardETHReserves matches the actual ETH balance, a malicious bot can submit a value that is arbitrarily larger than the real reserve. By inflating ethReserves, the reported swETH‑to‑ETH rate becomes proportionally higher; functions such as swETHToETHRate(), ethToSwETHRate(), getRate() and the public getter ethReserves() will all return values that are many times the true amount. If a future withdraw() function relies on ethReserves to determine how much ETH to send for a given amount of swETH, the contract will over‑pay, effectively allowing the attacker to mint ETH out of thin air. The same effect can be achieved by passing an excessively large _newETHRewards value, which is added to ethReserves during the same calculation. The vulnerability manifests whenever the BOT role is exercised, i.e., during any call to reprice, and it can be triggered repeatedly because the contract does not limit the frequency of reprice calls. Users, liquidity providers, and any downstream protocol that reads the conversion rate (for example the stakeAndVault contract) are affected because they may receive incorrect pricing information or be forced to transfer more swETH than warranted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the bookkeeping logic of swETH and identified that the contract trusts external input for a core accounting variable without any sanity checks. The problem is subtle because the function updates only internal bookkeeping variables; the external balance of the contract remains unchanged, so a casual inspection of ETH holdings may not reveal the manipulation. To remediate, the contract should maintain ethReserves internally based on the actual ETH balance, compute the conversion rate from that immutable source, and enforce bounds on the _preRewardETHReserves and _newETHRewards parameters (for example, rejecting values that exceed the current contract balance by a large factor). Additionally, rate‑updates should be rate‑limited and restricted to a trusted oracle rather than an arbitrary bot. This class of bug falls under untrusted input for on‑chain accounting or price manipulation via mutable reserve variables. From a user’s perspective the symptom would be that the UI shows a swETH price that is far higher than market rates, withdrawals return more ETH than expected, or other contracts report inflated balances, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust.

title: Reentrancy protection is recommended for staking vault
description: The staking vault contract makes external calls, which would allow a reentrant to the contract to steal the assets of the ﬁrst user. It is not within the scope of this review to fully assess whether any of the external calls do contain a reentrancy risk but, as they are not controlled by Swell, it is best to assume that some threat potential is present. The main reentrancy threat occurs during the call to balancerVault.joinPool() on line [132]. If the call to this function passes control ﬂow to an exploit contract after BPT contracts have been transferred to the vault, that contract would be able to call SwellStakeVaultHelper.stakeAndVault() with a very small amount of ETH. During this reentrancy call, the BPT balance of the vault on line [150] would include the BPT tokens of the ﬁrst depositor. These would then be de- posited into aura under the exploit contract’s address. The original depositor’s call to SwellStakeVaultHelper.stakeAndVault() would then resolve, with amount on line [150] being zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy weakness in the staking vault’s helper function that allows an attacker to withdraw or redirect assets that belong to a previous depositor. The root cause is that the contract makes an external call to balancerVault.joinPool before it has fully updated its internal accounting, and it does not protect the surrounding logic with a reentrancy guard. When the external call transfers control to a malicious contract, that contract can invoke SwellStakeVaultHelper.stakeAndVault again with a tiny amount of ETH. Because the vault’s BPT balance has already been increased by the first user’s deposit, the re‑entered call sees the inflated balance and deposits those BPT tokens into the attacker‑controlled Aura contract. After the malicious call finishes, the original transaction resumes and reads a zero amount for the user, effectively leaving the first depositor with no claim to their tokens. This can be exploited whenever the joinPool call can be hijacked – for example if the Balancer vault or any token it interacts with is replaced by a malicious implementation, or if the attacker can craft a contract that receives control during the external call. The impact is loss of deposited assets: users see their balance drop to zero, refunds disappear, and the protocol’s total assets are reduced without any on‑chain error message. The issue occurs during the staking flow, specifically after BPT tokens are transferred to the vault but before the contract records the deposit and before it finalises the stake. All users who deposit through the helper are potentially affected, and the protocol’s reputation is at risk because funds can be silently siphoned. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that flagged the external call as a reentrancy hotspot; it is subtle because the external call is to a well‑known Balancer contract, so developers may assume it is safe and overlook the need for a guard. To remediate, the contract should adopt the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, update internal balances before any external call, and add a non‑reentrant modifier (or equivalent guard) to stakeAndVault so that a second entry cannot occur while the first is in progress. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents an attacker from stealing assets through recursive calls.

title: Updating an operator’s controllingAddress allows the previous operator to maintain control
description: Even after updating the controllingAddress using the function updateOperatorControllingAddress(), the old controllingAddress can still control the Operator and call the function addNewValidatorDetails(). When the controllingAddress is updated using updateOperatorControllingAddress(), the old controllingAddress is still linked to the operatorId, this is because the function do not clear the operatorId from the old controllingAddress. As a result, getOperatorIdForAddress(oldAddress) == getOperatorIdForAddress(newAddress) != 0 and so the old address can still control the Operator that it was controlling. Added to that, it would be impossible in the future to add Operator with an old controllingAddress because of line [293-295]. function addOperator( string calldata _name, address _operatorAddress, address _rewardAddress external override checkRole(SwellLib.PLATFORM_ADMIN) checkZeroAddress(_operatorAddress) checkZeroAddress(_rewardAddress) if (getOperatorIdForAddress[_operatorAddress] != 0) { revert OperatorAlreadyExists(_operatorAddress);
bug_full: The contract allows an operator to be associated with a controlling address stored in a mapping getOperatorIdForAddress. The function updateOperatorControllingAddress is intended to transfer control to a new address, but it only writes the new mapping entry and never removes the entry for the previous address. Consequently both the old and the new address resolve to the same non‑zero operator identifier. Because the old address remains linked, it can still invoke privileged functions such as addNewValidatorDetails, effectively retaining full control over the operator after the supposed hand‑over. This bug appears whenever an operator’s controlling address is changed, which is a normal administrative operation. The affected parties are the platform administrators who expect the old address to lose authority, and any users relying on the operator’s integrity, as unauthorized actions could be performed by the former controller. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the updateOperatorControllingAddress logic and noticed that the mapping entry for the previous address was never cleared. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an event indicating the stale link, and the state change appears successful, making it easy to miss during functional testing. The impact includes potential unauthorized validator additions, manipulation of rewards, and the inability to re‑register the old address as a new operator because the duplicate mapping triggers a revert. This class of bug falls under improper access‑control revocation or stale reference in address‑to‑identifier mappings. To remediate, the update routine should delete or overwrite the old mapping entry (e.g., delete getOperatorIdForAddress[oldAddress]) before assigning the new address, and emit an event confirming the revocation. After the fix, only the new controlling address would be able to call privileged functions, restoring the intended security model.

title: Contract Owner Can Arbitrarily Change Minting Fees and Interest Rates
description: The issueFeeRate and interestRate variables can both be changed by the EtherCollateral contract owner after loans have been opened. As a result, the owner can control fees such as they equal/exceed the collateral for any given loan.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a privileged parameter manipulation flaw in which the contract owner is able to modify the minting fee (issueFeeRate) and the interest rate (interestRate) after a loan has already been opened. The root cause is that the setter functions for these economic parameters are not restricted to a pre‑loan phase and are protected only by an owner‑only modifier, allowing the owner to change them at any time. An attacker who controls the owner address can exploit this by calling the fee‑adjustment functions after a borrower has taken a loan, raising the fee or interest to a level that equals or exceeds the collateral posted for that loan. When the borrower later attempts to repay or withdraw collateral, the contract will calculate a repayment amount that is dramatically higher than originally quoted, often consuming the entire collateral or causing the transaction to revert due to insufficient funds. The impact is that borrowers can lose the full value of their collateral, the protocol’s economic assumptions are broken, and user trust is eroded because the fee structure is no longer predictable. This condition occurs whenever a loan is active and the owner decides to change the parameters, affecting any user who has taken a loan, as well as the overall health of the lending platform. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mutability of economic variables and identified that the owner could invoke the setters after loan creation. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s UI may display the current fee rates without indicating that they can change retroactively, and the increased cost only becomes apparent at repayment time. To remediate, the minting fee should be made immutable after deployment or locked once the first loan is issued, and any changes to the interest rate should be governed by a multi‑signature or time‑locked mechanism rather than a single owner. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a privileged parameter change or mutable economic parameter vulnerability, which violates the business logic that fees should be fixed or at least predictable for the duration of a loan, leading to scenarios where funds disappear or refunds are unexpectedly reduced.

title: Staking Before Operator Leads To No swETH Minted
description: The ﬁrst staking call to a validation node is intended to be done by the operator, in which the operator sends a 1 or 16 ETH deposit (assuming they are not in the super whitelist). However, no validation is done to check the ﬁrst user staking is the operator. This means a naive end user, Bob, can stake to a new validation node and their funds will become stuck, misinterpreted as the operator’s deposit. This is because when an operator makes their initial deposit, it is intended as a bond to ensure good behaviour, and so they mint no swETH. In addition because Bob lacks the private key related to the validator’s public key, this transaction will be rejected on the Beacon chain as there is no way for his signature to match the validator’s public key. This will lead to his funds becoming stuck as they will be sent to the deposit contract but not recorded on the Beacon chain and so be unclaimable in the future. Then as a knock-on eﬀect, this also leads to the operator being able to bypass their required deposit bond as subsequent calls will now always mint swETH, allowing them to sell this to oﬀset their ETH deposit. This breaks behavioural assumptions as now the operator has no funds inside the validator and so has less incentive to fear being slashed. This can therefore risk all funds deposited with this validator. Bob must still deposit the correct amount of 1 or 16 ETH exactly, else the call to stake() will reject this as the initial validator deposit. Bob must also directly call stake(), having generated his own incorrect signature and deposit data information. As most users would leverage the user interface that automates this process, the likelihood of this issue with deemed Low.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract does not enforce that the first call to the staking function is performed by the validator operator. The protocol expects the operator to provide an initial deposit of 1 or 16 ETH that serves as a bond and does not result in any swETH tokens being minted. Because there is no check, any external user can submit the first deposit. When a regular user such as Bob sends the initial deposit, the contract forwards the ETH to the Ethereum deposit contract but does not record a corresponding validator on the Beacon chain, because the user does not possess the validator’s private key required to sign the deposit data. Consequently the deposit is rejected on the Beacon chain, the ETH remains locked in the deposit contract, and no swETH is minted for the user. From the protocol’s perspective the operator’s bond appears to be satisfied, allowing the operator to skip the intended bond requirement for subsequent deposits, which now mint swETH. This breaks the incentive model: the operator holds no stake that can be slashed, while users’ funds are effectively lost. The issue manifests only on a newly created validator where no operator deposit has yet been recorded; it is triggered when a non‑operator calls the staking entry point with the exact required amount. The affected parties are the end‑users who attempt to stake, the operator who loses the bonding guarantee, and the overall protocol which may suffer from under‑collateralised validators. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the staking workflow, where the lack of a first‑caller‑is‑operator guard was observed. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically hides the operator‑only step and most users interact through a front‑end that automatically performs the correct sequence, so the erroneous path is rarely exercised. The correct mitigation is to enforce that the initial deposit can only be made by the entity that controls the validator’s private key, for example by requiring a proof‑of‑possession signature or by adding an explicit flag that the caller is the operator, and by ensuring the bond logic is executed before any swETH minting. In short, the bug is a missing access control / initialization check that leads to a deposit‑locking and incentive‑bypass scenario, causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective and breaking the accounting assumptions of the staking system.

title: Lack Of Safe Transfer In ERC20 Prover Payment
description:
AssignmentHooks are used to pay a prover’s fee via calling onProposedBlock() and transferring the specified asset
from the proposer. A prover can choose to be paid in ETH or any ERC20 token.
Certain ERC20 tokens vary from the ERC20 specifications, which cause the following transfer to the assigned prover
to either always fail or to fail silently.
```solidity
IERC20(assignment.feeToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, blk.assignedProver, proverFee);
```
The first issue is that certain tokens such as USDT will not return a bool. The IERC20 interface expects a boolean
to be returned and will attempt to decode the return value. If there is no return value, such as in the USDT case the
transaction will be reverted. It is therefore not possible to call these tokens.
The second issue is that some ERC20 implementations, such as BAT, do not revert when there is insufficient balance
or allowance. Instead, these tokens return false and expect the calling contract to handle this case. These tokens are
rare and not often used.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s use of the standard IERC20.transferFrom function to pay a prover’s fee during the onProposedBlock hook. The code assumes that every ERC20 token conforms to the original ERC20 specification, which requires the transferFrom call to return a boolean indicating success. In practice, several widely‑deployed tokens deviate from this expectation. Tokens such as USDT do not return any value; the Solidity ABI decoder therefore attempts to read a boolean that does not exist, causing the whole transaction to revert. Other tokens, for example BAT, return a boolean but do not automatically revert when the transfer fails due to insufficient balance or allowance; they simply return false. Because the contract does not inspect the return value, a false result is ignored and the contract proceeds as if the fee had been transferred. An attacker controlling the proposer can exploit this by selecting a non‑standard token that either reverts silently or returns false, thereby preventing the fee from being paid while the protocol believes the payment succeeded. The impact is two‑fold: (1) honest provers may never receive their compensation, breaking the economic incentives of the protocol; (2) the protocol’s accounting assumes fees have been collected, which can lead to inaccurate accounting, potential over‑allocation of rewards, or denial‑of‑service if the transaction reverts and blocks cannot be proposed. The issue manifests whenever onProposedBlock is executed and the fee token is an ERC20 that does not follow the strict specification, i.e., during any block proposal that uses USDT, BAT or similar tokens. The affected parties are the proposer (who may unintentionally cause a revert), the prover (who may be under‑paid), and the overall protocol (which may suffer accounting inconsistencies). The problem was identified during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, which noted that the contract does not use a safe wrapper for ERC20 transfers. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the ERC20 interface appears correct; only at runtime with non‑standard tokens does the failure become visible, and silent false returns produce no event or error message. The recommended remediation is to replace direct calls to transferFrom with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom, which internally handles missing return data and enforces that a true value is returned, reverting otherwise. This change ensures that fee transfers either succeed or cause a clear revert, preventing silent loss of funds and aligning the contract with the broader class of “non‑standard ERC20 transfer handling” bugs.

title: AssignmentHook Does Not Sign Over metaHash
description:
The function hashAssignment() does not hash over assignment.metaHash, allowing it to be arbitrarily set by the pro-
poser.
```solidity
function hashAssignment(
    ProverAssignment memory assignment,
    address taikoAddress,
    bytes32 blobHash
) public pure returns (bytes32) {
    return keccak256(
        abi.encode(
            "PROVER_ASSIGNMENT",
            taikoAddress,
            blobHash,
            assignment.feeToken,
            assignment.expiry,
            assignment.maxBlockId,
            assignment.maxProposedIn,
            assignment.tierFees
        )
    );
}
```
The metaHash is required to determine the execution of a block. Changes to the metaHash will vary the block execution
and therefore also the proof generation time. It is an optional field which may be set to zero, if the prover allows any
metaHash.
A prover signs over hashAssigment() to validate they will be the assigned proposer for the block. Without a prover’s
signature for the metaHash, the proposer is able to set this field in the assignment to an arbitrary value, mostly likely
the zero hash.
Additionally, the fields address(this) and block.chainId are not included in the assignment hash. As a result, it
would be possible to replay transactions on other deployed contracts or the same contract on alternate chains.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the function that computes the assignment hash used for prover signatures. The hash is built from a fixed list of fields but deliberately omits the assignment metaHash as well as the contract address and the chain identifier. Because the metaHash determines how a block is executed, a proposer can set this field to any value after the prover has signed the hash, most commonly to the zero hash, without breaking the signature. The omission also means the same signed assignment can be replayed on a different deployment of the contract or on another blockchain, since the hash does not bind the assignment to a specific contract instance or chain. An attacker who controls the proposer role can therefore manipulate block execution, alter proof generation time, or cause verification failures, potentially leading to stalled block production, loss of rewards, or economic damage to users relying on the protocol. The issue manifests when a prover signs the assignment hash; the signature appears valid because the signed data matches the computed hash, yet the unsigned metaHash can be changed later. From a user perspective the block may be produced with unexpected state, proofs may fail verification, or rewards may be missing, creating the impression that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is not honoring commitments. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fields used in the hash with the full assignment structure and identified the missing bindings. It is hard to notice because the hash function itself is deterministic and the signature verification succeeds, so the problem only becomes visible when the altered metaHash influences downstream logic. The recommended remediation is to adopt an EIP‑712 typed‑data hashing scheme that includes every field of the assignment, including metaHash, the contract address and the chain ID, thereby cryptographically binding the assignment to a single contract instance on a specific chain and preventing replay or arbitrary metaHash manipulation.

title: L2 Proposer Can Significantly Bias Difficulty
description:
A L2 block proposer can repeatedly rearrange transactions before proposing a block to bias difficulty.
The proposer calls the function proposeBlock() with either a transaction list or a blob if EIP-4844 has been imple-
mented. In either case the value is set by the proposer which will be recorded as meta.blobHash.
```solidity
unchecked {
    meta.difficulty = meta.blobHash ^ bytes32(block.prevrandao * b.numBlocks * block.number);
}
```
The issue occurs in that difficulty is directly based off the value meta.blobHash which can be set by the block proposer.
Furthermore, the block proposer knows the fields block.prevrandao, b.numBlocks and block.number ahead of time.
By using a guess and check method the proposer is able to heavily influence the value of meta.difficulty.
To perform the attack, the proposer will first create a transaction list and set the last transaction as a no-op with calldata
0x01. The proposer then calculates meta.difficulty using the remaining fields. If the difficulty meets some required
threshold, the proposer will accept the block. Otherwise, the proposer will increment the no-op transaction calldata to
0x02 and again check if the difficulty meets the required threshold.
The proposer will repeat the process until they have found a transaction list with the required conditions for difficulty.
There are two impacts of having a non-random difficulty. The first is that it is used to calculate meta.minTier. Thus,
a proposer can determine exactly what proof level to achieve. Second, programs on L2 may be using difficulty as a
partial form of randomness, similar to how Taiko uses difficulty to select the proof tier. A non-random difficulty allows
for manipulation of smart contracts which use difficulty as a source of randomness.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a difficulty‑biasing flaw in the L2 block‑proposer logic. The contract computes the block difficulty by XOR‑ing a value that the proposer can set (meta.blobHash) with a deterministic expression that depends on block.prevrandao, the number of blocks in the batch (b.numBlocks) and the current block number. Because the proposer supplies the transaction list or blob that determines meta.blobHash, they can repeatedly modify a harmless last transaction (changing its calldata from 0x01 to 0x02, 0x03, etc.) and recompute the resulting difficulty until it satisfies a chosen threshold. This guess‑and‑check loop is possible because the proposer knows all the other inputs ahead of time. When the difficulty meets the required condition the proposer finalises the block; otherwise they iterate again. The root cause is the direct dependence of difficulty on a proposer‑controlled field, which breaks the assumption that difficulty is an unpredictable, pseudo‑random value. Exploitation consists of the proposer crafting a transaction list that yields a difficulty value that gives them a desired proof tier (meta.minTier) or that manipulates any smart contract that uses difficulty as a source of randomness. The impact is twofold: first, the proposer can force the block to be classified in a higher or lower proof tier, potentially gaining economic advantage; second, contracts that rely on difficulty for randomness (for example, selecting a validator or determining a lottery winner) can be steered, undermining fairness and security. This condition occurs whenever a proposer is able to set meta.blobHash, which is true for every block they propose, and when the protocol does not enforce an immutable source of randomness for difficulty. The affected parties include the protocol itself (its security guarantees), any L2 applications that depend on difficulty‑derived randomness, and users who trust the protocol’s fairness. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, which identified that the difficulty formula uses a mutable input. The flaw can be subtle because the difficulty value still appears to change each block, giving the illusion of randomness, and there is no explicit error or revert that would flag the manipulation. To remediate, the difficulty calculation should be based solely on immutable, unpredictable data such as a hash of block.prevrandao, b.numBlocks and block.number (e.g., keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...))) or an external verifiable random function, removing any proposer‑controlled component. This change restores the intended randomness property and prevents the proposer from biasing proof tier selection or contract behaviour.

title: Pausing Proving For Longer Than cooldownWindow May Skip Contesting
description:
There is a pausing mechanism specifically to prevent proving and verifying blocks. If there are pending state transitions
and the proving is paused for longer than cooldownWindow, then when unpaused these transitions will be instantly
verifiable.
The pauseProving() function is an onlyOwner function which can prevent calling proveBlock() and verifyBlocks().
A pending state transition is one which a prover has called proveBlock() but not yet verifyBlock(). Each pending
state must elapse cooldownWindow seconds before it is possible to call verifyBlocks(). During this pending state is
when other users are able to call proveBlock() to contest an invalid state transition.
An edge-case exists where a faulty prover or malicious user submits an invalid state transition just before the owner
calls pauseProving(). The state transition will now be pending and no users are able to call proveBlock() to contest
this state transition. If the pause period elapses more than cooldownWindow, when the unpause occurs it will be possible
to call verifyBlocks() on the invalid state transition without allowing sufficient time for users to contest.
Furthermore, the owner of TaikoL1 is the TaikoTimelockController governance contract. The governance contract
has a timelock which requires a delay before the transaction can be executed. The security council must also adhere
to the delay, although the security council is able to skip voting.
Second interesting case occurs when proving is paused for longer than provingWindow. If there is a block proposed
before or during the pause which does not have state transition then the assigned prover may miss the provingWindow.
Any prover who does not submit a proof within provingWindow will not be able to prove a block and lose their liveness
bond.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the pause mechanism that blocks the functions responsible for proving and verifying blocks in a roll‑up protocol. When the contract owner (which is a timelocked governance contract) invokes pauseProving, any pending state transition – a block that has been submitted with a proof but not yet verified – becomes frozen. The protocol requires each pending transition to remain in a contestable state for at least cooldownWindow seconds before it can be verified, giving other participants a chance to submit a competing proof if the original one is invalid. However, the pause logic does not record the moment when proving is resumed. If the pause lasts longer than cooldownWindow, the unpause operation allows verifyBlocks to be called immediately, bypassing the contest period entirely. An attacker or a faulty prover can therefore submit an invalid state transition just before the pause, and when the owner later unpauses after the cooldownWindow has elapsed, the invalid transition can be verified without any opportunity for others to contest it. A second edge case appears when the pause exceeds the provingWindow: a block that was proposed but has no associated state transition may miss the window in which a prover must submit a proof, causing the assigned prover to lose their liveness bond. The impact is that the protocol may accept and finalize incorrect state transitions, breaking the integrity of the chain, and honest provers can lose bonded funds unexpectedly. This condition occurs only when the governance timelock delay allows the pause to be extended beyond the defined windows, and because the pause/unpause flow does not enforce a timestamp check against the pause duration, the bug can be subtle and easy to miss during normal operation. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of the pauseProving function and its interaction with cooldownWindow and provingWindow constraints. From a user’s perspective, a block may appear to be finalized normally, but the underlying state could be wrong, and provers may see their bond disappear without a clear reason. The bug belongs to the class of time‑based access‑control flaws where state‑dependent windows are not correctly enforced after a privileged pause. To remediate, the contract should store the exact time when proving is resumed (unpauseTime) and require verifyBlocks to ensure that the current block timestamp exceeds the later of the original state timestamp and unpauseTime by at least cooldownWindow. Additionally, the ability to pause proving should be granted to a dedicated pausing role that is not subject to the timelock, preventing governance delays from unintentionally extending the pause beyond safe limits.

title: Gap Between Periods Can Lead to Erroneous Rewards
description:
The SNX rewards are earned each period based on reward and duration as specified in the notifyRewardAmount()
function.
The "rate per second" at which rewards are distributed is given by:
rewardRate = reward / duration.
Rewards are paid out for all stakers following the formula:
rewards_distributed = rewardRate * (lastTimeRewardApplicable - lastUpdateTime)
However, lastUpdateTime includes the time between periods and therefore, if there is a gap between periods:
(lastTimeRewardApplicable - lastUpdateTime) > duration
Therefore, resulting in:
rewards_distributed > reward
Where reward is the amount from notifyRewardAmount() and rewards_distributed is the total amount earned
by all stakers.
The result is the contract will output more rewards than it receives. Therefore if all stakers call getReward()
the contract will not have enough SNX balance to transfer out all the rewards and some stakers may not receive
any rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the reward distribution logic of a staking contract that pays SNX rewards per period. The contract calculates a constant rewardRate as the total reward amount divided by the declared duration of the period, and then distributes rewards based on the elapsed time measured as (lastTimeRewardApplicable - lastUpdateTime). The root cause is that lastUpdateTime is not reset when a new reward period begins; it retains the timestamp of the previous period’s update. If there is any idle time between the end of one period and the start of the next, the elapsed time used in the formula becomes larger than the intended duration, causing rewardRate * elapsedTime to exceed the original reward amount. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger this situation simply by allowing a gap—either by not calling the function that starts a new period promptly or by manipulating the timing of period notifications. When the contract later processes getReward calls, it attempts to transfer more SNX than it actually holds, resulting in some stakers receiving zero or partial rewards while the contract balance is depleted. This issue manifests to users as a missing reward: a staker expects a positive SNX payout after a period ends, but the UI shows no change in balance or a failed transaction. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward accounting equations and identified that the time delta could exceed the declared duration. It is hard to notice because the per‑period rewardRate calculation appears correct in isolation; only when periods are not contiguous does the over‑distribution become apparent. The bug belongs to the class of “time‑window accounting” or “reward over‑mint” vulnerabilities, where improper handling of period boundaries leads to inflation of payouts and violation of the protocol’s economic assumptions. To remediate, the contract should enforce that each new period starts exactly at the previous period’s end, or it should clamp the elapsed time used in the reward calculation to the declared duration, ensuring that rewards_distributed never exceeds the reward amount supplied by notifyRewardAmount. Proper checks on period continuity and adjustments to lastUpdateTime would restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent users from losing expected rewards.

title: Potential Economic Gain When Submitting False Proofs
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic incentive flaw that allows a malicious actor to submit a fabricated zero‑knowledge and SGX proof in order to contest a previously accepted optimistic transition and receive a net token reward. The root cause lies in the reward logic of the contest mechanism: when a contester is recorded as the zero address the contract treats the caller (who may also be the original prover) as the winner and pays out a reward calculated as one quarter of the original validity bond plus the contest bond. Because the contract does not prevent the contester from being the same entity that submitted the optimistic proof, an attacker can immediately submit a higher‑tier false proof, pay a relatively small validity bond (250 TKO), win the contest, and collect a larger reward (500 TKO). This yields a net gain of 250 TKO per successful fake proof. The exploit can be carried out whenever an optimistic transition is posted and the protocol permits an external address to submit a higher‑tier proof without a waiting period or a chance for the original prover to respond. The attack assumes the attacker can generate a proof that passes verification for the TIER_SGX_AND_PSE_ZKEVM tier, which would require breaking both the zero‑knowledge scheme and the SGX enclave; while this is cryptographically difficult, the economic model makes repeated attacks financially attractive if such a proof can be forged. The impact is a gradual drain of protocol funds, distortion of the incentive structure, and loss of confidence for honest provers who may see their expected rewards disappear or their bonds reduced without justification. From a user perspective, an honest prover may notice that after submitting a valid optimistic proof they receive no reward, their balance is reduced, or the transition they expected to be finalized is overwritten, leading to confusion and potential panic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, and it is subtle because the reward flow appears legitimate and the contester address check only filters out the zero address, not the case where the prover re‑enters as contester. To remediate, the contract should prevent a contester from immediately submitting a higher‑tier proof, enforce a challenge window that gives the original prover an opportunity to submit a stronger proof, and ensure that rewards are only paid to external challengers distinct from the prover. This would close the economic loophole and align the protocol’s accounting with its intended security guarantees.

title: Reentrancy Vector In depositEtherToL2()
description:
The function depositEtherToL2() does not have the nonReentrant modifier. It is therefore possible to reenter into depositEtherToL2().
