The problem can be hard to notice because the contract correctly reverts on a reused nonce, which may be interpreted as a normal user error rather than an attack, and there is no explicit warning that another authorized party could have consumed the nonce. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce nonce uniqueness per signer, for example by storing used nonces keyed by both accountId and signer address, or by requiring each signer to maintain its own ordered nonce sequence. This change would prevent one authorized user from invalidating another’s signed messages and restore the intended protection against replay and double‑spending while preserving the ability for multiple users to interact safely with the same account.

title: Stork Oracle price can be arbitrated
description: StorkERC7412WrapperModule.fulfillOracleQuery is used to update the price of the Stork oracle. Given that the oracle works with a push model, this opens the opportunity to arbitrage a price update by performing a trade, setting the new price, and closing the position, all in the same transaction. What is more, the price can be updated multiple times in the same block, so the following conditions: The initial price timestamp is equal to or greater than the previous price timestamp. This increases the chances of performing a profitable arbitrage, especially in moments of high volatility. Note that while FeatureFlagSupport.ensureExecutorAccess() ensures that the caller is allowed to perform the price update, and the protocol will start restricting the update of the price to trusted entities, it is planned to allow anyone to perform this action in the future, which can be done by setting allowAll to true for the executor feature flag.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation weakness in the Stork oracle integration where the function that fulfills an oracle query can be called multiple times within the same block, allowing an attacker to arbitrarily overwrite the reported price. The root cause is that the oracle uses a push model and only checks that a new price timestamp is not older than the previous one, without enforcing a single update per block or preventing stale data from being accepted. Because the contract records the latest price but does not record whether the price has already been refreshed in the current block, an adversary who can invoke the price‑update function (currently restricted by a feature‑flag executor but planned to be opened to anyone) can execute a trade based on the old price, then immediately call the price‑update function to set a more favorable price, and finally close the position—all inside one transaction. This sequence creates a profitable arbitrage loop, especially during periods of high volatility when price swings are large. The impact is that traders can extract value from the protocol, liquidity providers may lose funds, and the overall market price feed becomes unreliable, breaking the accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on for margin, liquidation, or fee calculations. The issue manifests when the price is refreshed more than once per block or when a stale payload is accepted; from a user’s perspective the UI may show a price that jumps instantly, but their trade executes at the previous price, resulting in unexpected profit or loss and a perception that “the price changed out of nowhere”. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle wrapper module and identified that the timestamp comparison alone does not prevent intra‑block price overwrites. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct event for multiple updates in the same block and the price appears to be valid on‑chain. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that a new price cannot be written if the latest update already occurred in the current block, reject payloads that are older than the stored timestamp, and reject stale data that exceeds a reasonable delay. Additionally, when the price is consumed by downstream logic, the code should verify that the price was refreshed in the same block, ensuring freshness before any financial calculation. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an oracle update race condition or price manipulation via unrestricted oracle writes.

title: Stork and Pyth prices can be arbitrated
description: The `fullfillOracleQueryStork` and `fullfillOracleQueryPyth` functions are used to update the price of the Stork and the Pyth oracles, respectively. Given that both oracles work with a pull model, this opens the opportunity to arbitrage a price update by performing a trade, setting the new price, and closing the position, all in the same transaction. What is more, the price can be updated multiple times in the same block, so the following conditions: The initial price timestamp is greater than the previous price timestamp. This increases the chances to perform a profitable arbitrage, especially in moments of high volatility. Note that while FeatureFlagSupport.ensureExecutorAccess() ensures that the caller is allowed to perform the price update, and the protocol will start restricting the update of the price to trusted entities, it is planned to allow anyone to perform this action in the future, which can be done by setting allowAll to true for the executor feature flag. Also, in the case of the Pyth oracle, it is possible to update the price by calling directly the Pyth contract.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle price manipulation flaw that allows an attacker to arbitrage the Stork and Pyth price feeds by updating the price multiple times within a single block and even within the same transaction. The root cause is that the fulfilOracleQueryStork and fulfilOracleQueryPyth functions operate under a pull model without any restriction on update frequency, and the contract only checks that the new timestamp is greater than the previous one. Because the executor access control can be relaxed in the future by setting the allowAll flag to true, or because the Pyth price can be set directly on the Pyth contract, any actor who can call these functions may submit a fresh price that deviates from the market price. An attacker can exploit this by opening a position based on the current on‑chain price, then calling the price‑update function to push the price in a favorable direction, and finally closing the position in the same transaction, pocketing the price difference. This sequence can be repeated as many times as the attacker can fit into a block, especially during periods of high volatility when price swings are large. The impact is that traders and liquidity providers may suffer unexpected losses, balances may appear to drop to zero, refunds may be missing, and the overall market integrity of the protocol is compromised. The issue occurs whenever the price‑update functions are callable by an untrusted entity, when the allowAll flag is enabled, or when the attacker can interact directly with the Pyth contract. It affects all users who rely on the oracle for accurate pricing, as well as the protocol itself because the manipulated price can be used to settle trades, liquidations, or fee calculations. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle integration logic and noticed that the contract does not enforce a single update per block nor a freshness check for the submitted price. The problem is subtle because price updates are expected behavior and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a price is overwritten, making the manipulation hard to detect from the UI where users only see the final price. To remediate the issue the protocol should enforce that a price can be updated at most once per block, reject stale or out‑of‑order timestamps, and restrict price updates to a trusted set of executors. Additional safeguards such as a commit‑reveal scheme, a push‑based oracle, or a minimum time interval between updates would further reduce the attack surface and align the implementation with the intended business logic that prices reflect the current market and cannot be arbitraged within a single transaction.

title: InitiateOrUpdateSession typehash is encoded incorrectly
description: According to the ERC-712 standard: The type of a struct is encoded as name ‖ "(" ‖ member₁ ‖ "," ‖ member₂ ‖ "," ‖ … ‖ memberₙ ")" where each member is written as type ‖ " " ‖ name. In SessionUpdateHashing.sol, the _INITIATE_OR_UPDATE_SESSION_TYPEHASH constant does not follow the standard, as it includes an extra space between the deadline and session members. As a result, SessionPermissionModule.verifySignature will fail to verify a correct signature for the given session data.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ERC‑712 type‑hash encoding error in the SessionPermissionModule. The contract defines a constant _INITIATE_OR_UPDATE_SESSION_TYPEHASH that is supposed to be the keccak256 hash of the struct type string InitiateOrUpdateSession(uint256 verifyingChainId,uint256 deadline,InitiateOrUpdateSessionDetails session). However the actual string used in the source contains an extra space before the last member, i.e. ... deadline, InitiateOrUpdateSessionDetails session). According to the ERC‑712 specification the type string must be constructed without any superfluous whitespace; each member is concatenated as type name and members are separated only by commas. The extra space changes the resulting hash, so the on‑chain typehash does not match the hash that off‑chain tools compute when signing the data. When a user signs a correctly formed InitiateOrUpdateSession struct, the signature is generated against the proper typehash. During verification, SessionPermissionModule.verifySignature recomputes the hash using the incorrect constant and therefore the recovered signer address does not match the expected one. As a result, a valid signature is rejected as invalid. This manifests to users as transactions that revert with an “invalid signature” error, UI messages indicating that a session update failed, or simply no change in the expected state despite a successful signing step. The bug is triggered any time the contract attempts to verify a signature for an InitiateOrUpdateSession operation, which includes both initiating a new session and updating an existing one. All participants that rely on this permission module – including regular users, protocol operators, and any automated agents – are affected because they cannot perform the intended action. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain constant against the ERC‑712 encoding rules. It is hard to notice because the hash mismatch does not produce a compile‑time error; the contract compiles and runs, but the logical verification fails, leading to confusing runtime reverts. The class of bug is an ERC‑712 type‑hash mismatch caused by incorrect struct type string formatting. To fix the problem the constant must be recomputed using the exact type string without the stray space, aligning the typehash with the specification and restoring correct signature verification, allowing legitimate users to update sessions and preventing potential misuse where an attacker could craft a signature that matches the wrong hash to bypass intended checks.

title: Confidence interval of Pyth price is not validated
description: PythOffchainLookupNode.process does not validate the confidence interval of the Pyth price. As stated in the Pyth documentation, it is important to check this value to prevent the contract from accepting untrusted prices.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the contract accepting price data from the Pyth oracle without validating the confidence interval that accompanies each price update. Pyth documentation explicitly advises that callers should check the confidence value because a large confidence interval indicates that the price is uncertain and could be manipulated. In the current implementation the function that processes the off‑chain lookup simply reads the price and confidence fields and proceeds to use the price in downstream calculations, regardless of how wide the confidence interval is. This omission creates a logical flaw: an attacker who can influence the oracle feed, or who can supply a crafted price with an artificially inflated confidence interval, can cause the contract to accept a price that does not reflect the true market value. When such a low‑confidence price is used, calculations for swaps, liquidations, or reward distributions become incorrect, leading to outcomes such as users receiving far less than expected, balances being reduced unexpectedly, or the protocol settling trades at unfavorable rates. The issue manifests whenever the Pyth price update contains a non‑zero confidence that exceeds a reasonable threshold, which the contract does not check. All participants that rely on the price – traders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts – are potentially affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price reliability are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit where the reviewer noted the absence of any confidence‑interval validation logic in the PythOffchainLookupNode.process function. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically displays only the price value, not the confidence metric, so users see a seemingly normal price and assume it is trustworthy. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum confidence‑to‑price ratio (or reject prices whose confidence exceeds a configurable bound) before using the price, as illustrated in the recommended Solidity snippet. This check ensures that only price updates with an acceptable level of certainty are accepted, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol and preventing scenarios where funds disappear or refunds are calculated incorrectly due to unreliable oracle data.

title: Incorrect parameters length check
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect validation of the size of the parameters field used when registering a Pyth off‑chain lookup node. The contract checks that the byte array nodeDefinition.parameters has a length equal to 32*4 (128 bytes) before accepting the registration. In reality the parameters consist of only two 32‑byte words – the oracle adapter address and a bytes32 pair identifier – which together occupy exactly 64 bytes. Because the length check is too strict, a correctly formed registration request is rejected, preventing legitimate nodes from being added to the system. Conversely, an attacker can append an arbitrary 64‑byte padding to the valid 64‑byte payload, making the total length 128 bytes and satisfying the faulty check. This allows the same logical node to be registered multiple times with different padding values. The impact is that the registry can become polluted with duplicate entries that appear distinct to the protocol, potentially causing the oracle aggregation logic to treat them as separate sources, leading to double counting of price data, inconsistent state, or denial‑of‑service if the registry fills up. Users who rely on the oracle may see unexpected price fluctuations or missing data because the protocol may select a duplicated node that returns stale or manipulated values. The issue occurs whenever a contract or off‑chain service attempts to register a Pyth node, i.e., during the node onboarding flow, and it affects any participant that depends on the correctness of the node registry – developers, auditors, and end‑users of the protocol. It was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the expected ABI encoding size with the contract’s hard‑coded constant. The bug is subtle because a length check is a common defensive pattern, and the mismatch does not produce an obvious runtime error; instead, legitimate registrations simply fail silently, and the padding trick does not alter the visible behavior of the node, making it hard to spot without inspecting the raw byte array. To remediate, the contract should validate that the parameters length equals 32*2 (64 bytes) and optionally verify that the content matches the expected ABI‑encoded address and pair id, rejecting any extra padding. This aligns the check with the actual data layout and prevents duplicate registrations caused by arbitrary padding, restoring the integrity of the node registry and the reliability of the oracle data it provides.

title: Lack of signature cancellation functionality
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements an off‑chain order flow where a user signs a message and later calls executeSessionOrdersBySig to have the order processed on‑chain. The code checks that the signer still has an active permission but it never provides a way to invalidate a previously signed message. Because the signed payload contains a nonce that is only marked as used when the order is executed, the contract lacks a mechanism to mark the nonce as cancelled. Consequently, if a user decides to withdraw the order – for example after a change of intent or after suspecting that their private key has been compromised – the signature remains valid and can be replayed by anyone who still possesses it. An attacker who obtains the signed data (or the user themselves, unintentionally) can submit the same signature at a later time, causing the contract to execute the order again. This replay can lead to unintended trades, loss of assets, or other state changes that the original signer did not authorize. The vulnerability appears when a signed order is stored off‑chain and the signer expects to be able to cancel it without revoking the whole permission set; the contract’s only mitigation is revoking the signer’s permission, which is a coarse‑grained action that does not address the specific need to cancel a single order. Users experience a mismatch between expectation (“my order is cancelled”) and reality (the order can still be executed), often manifested as unexpected token transfers, balances that change without any new on‑chain activity, or refunds that never arrive. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the order execution path and noticed the absence of any function that records a cancelled nonce. It can be hard to spot because the contract otherwise appears to enforce permission checks correctly, and the missing cancellation logic does not raise compile‑time warnings. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑or‑cancellation‑missing vulnerabilities for signed messages. To remediate, the contract should introduce a cancellation function that records the nonce of a signed order as used, restricting future execution of the same signature. Access to this function must be limited to the original signer or the owner of the associated account identifier, preserving the intended permission model while providing fine‑grained revocation of individual orders.

title: Potential loss of Ether due to overpayment
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overpayment of Ether when the fullfillOracleQueryPyth function forwards the entire msg.value to the Pyth price‑feed contract without first verifying the exact fee required for the update. The root cause is that the function does not call the Pyth contract’s getUpdateFee method or otherwise compare the supplied value with the fee calculated by the Pyth contract, and the Pyth contract itself does not return any excess Ether. An attacker or an unwary user can trigger the issue simply by sending more Ether than necessary when invoking fullfillOracleQueryPyth; the contract will forward the whole amount, the Pyth contract will accept the payment as long as it meets the minimum fee, and any surplus remains locked in the Pyth contract with no refund mechanism. This leads to a loss of funds for the sender, manifested as a balance that is lower than expected or a transaction that succeeds while the user receives no refund of the extra amount. The problem occurs whenever the function is called, especially in scenarios where the fee required by Pyth may change between the time the off‑chain data is signed and the time the transaction is executed, because the contract does not recalculate the fee at execution time. Users, developers, and the protocol’s treasury are affected because funds can disappear silently, breaking accounting assumptions that the fee paid equals the fee required. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined fee handling logic and noticed that msg.value is passed unchecked to an external payable function. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful, yet the sender’s balance is reduced by more than anticipated. The recommended remediation is to query the exact fee using the Pyth contract’s getUpdateFee function, compare it with msg.value, and either require an exact match or refund any excess Ether before forwarding the payment, thereby aligning the transferred amount with the contract’s fee expectations and preventing unintended loss of Ether.

title: Misconfiguration of pythAddress causes failure in dependent contracts
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing configuration of the oracle address used by contracts that depend on the Pyth price feed. In the Configuration library a struct stores a field called pythAddress, but the internal set function only copies the storkVerifyContract field and never writes the supplied pythAddress into storage. As a result the stored value remains the default zero address. When any downstream contract calls getPythAddress, the function reads the zero address, detects the condition and reverts with a PythAddressNotSet error. This behaviour can be exploited simply by invoking a function that triggers an oracle query; the call will always revert because the required address is unavailable. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for any feature that relies on Pyth data, such as price calculations, collateral valuations or liquidation triggers. Users experience failed transactions, missing price updates in the UI, or complete freezing of protocol actions that expect a valid oracle response. The condition occurs whenever the configuration is initialized or upgraded without explicitly providing a non‑zero pythAddress, which is common during deployment scripts that only set the storkVerifyContract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the storage library: the auditor noticed that the set function omitted the pythAddress assignment and that the unit test confirmed the address stayed zero after configuration. Because the failure manifests as a revert rather than an obvious incorrect value, it can be hard to notice until a dependent contract attempts to read the oracle. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialized or missing configuration parameters, where a critical address is left at its default value, breaking business logic that assumes the oracle is always reachable. To remediate, the set function should be updated to store the supplied pythAddress alongside the other fields, ensuring that getPythAddress returns a valid contract address and that oracle queries succeed, restoring expected functionality and preventing silent denial of service.

title: Unauthorized signature cancellation in ExecutionModule
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ExecutionModule contract where the cancelSignature function is intended to let an authorized user invalidate a specific signed message by marking its nonce as used. The function checks only that the caller is authorized to trade for the given accountId, using the isAuthorizedToTrade check, and then unconditionally marks the nonce as used. Because the contract does not record which address originally created the nonce, any address that holds the MATCH_ORDER permission for the same accountId can invoke cancelSignature on any nonce belonging to that account. This creates an improper authorization flaw: the access control verifies a generic permission rather than the specific right to cancel a particular signature. An attacker who is also authorized for the account can therefore cancel a legitimate order signed by another user. The exploit scenario is straightforward: the account owner grants MATCH_ORDER to Alice and Bob; Alice signs an order with nonce 1; before the order is executed, Bob calls cancelSignature with the same accountId and nonce 1, causing the nonce to be marked as used. When the ExecutionModule later attempts to execute Alice’s order, the nonce is already consumed and the signature is rejected, resulting in a failed transaction. The impact is that legitimate trades become impossible, leading to missed execution opportunities and potential financial loss for the affected user. The bug manifests only when multiple users share the same accountId with the MATCH_ORDER permission, a situation common in collaborative or delegated trading setups. Users may notice that their signed orders disappear or that execution reverts with an “invalid signature” error even though they did not cancel anything themselves. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a unit test demonstrating that a different authorized user could cancel another’s nonce. It is hard to notice because the function appears to enforce proper access control at a high level, masking the fact that it does not differentiate between nonce owners. The flaw belongs to the class of improper authorization or privilege‑escalation bugs, where a function grants broader rights than intended. To remediate, the contract should track the creator of each nonce and restrict cancelSignature so that only the nonce creator or the account owner can invoke it, or alternatively remove the ability for non‑owners to cancel signatures altogether. This change aligns the implementation with the business logic that a user should be able to cancel only their own orders, preserving expected behavior where a signed order remains executable until its author explicitly revokes it.

title: Admin role evasion risk
description:
```solidity
The function AccountModule::revokeAccountPermission is designed to
remove permissions from a user. However, a malicious admin could
preemptively execute a front-run by calling
AccountModule::grantAccountPermission to assign admin permissions to
another controlled account before their own permissions are revoked. Consider
this scenario:
1. Permissions are being revoked for an admin using the function
AccountModule::revokeAccountPermission.
2. The malicious admin performs a front-run, executing the function
AccountModule::grantAccountPermission to assign admin privileges to
another controlled user.
3. The transaction from step 1 completes, but the malicious admin retains
access through the newly empowered user.
```
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An admin role evasion risk exists in the permission management module of the contract. The function that revokes a permission can be front‑run by a malicious admin who, before the revocation transaction is mined, calls the function that grants permissions to assign the admin role to a second address they control. Because the grant operation is executed in a separate transaction that precedes the revocation, the original admin retains privileged access through the newly created admin account even after their own rights are removed. This race condition arises from the lack of atomicity between revocation and any subsequent grant, and from the fact that any address with admin rights can also call the grant function. An attacker can exploit this by monitoring the mempool for a revocation transaction, submitting a higher‑gas transaction that grants admin rights to a controlled address, and then allowing the revocation to proceed. The impact is that the intended removal of an admin does not actually reduce the attack surface; the attacker continues to control privileged functions, potentially modifying contract state, withdrawing funds, or altering protocol parameters. The vulnerability manifests whenever an admin role is being revoked and the contract does not enforce that only a trusted owner can assign admin rights. Users of the protocol, the protocol itself, and any funds guarded by admin‑only functions are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined role‑management flows. It can be hard to notice because the revocation transaction appears successful and the contract state shows the original admin address no longer has the role, while the newly created admin address silently gains the same privileges. The bug belongs to the class of race‑condition privilege‑escalation or role‑evasion vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should restrict the ability to grant admin permissions to a single immutable owner or use a two‑step commit‑reveal scheme that makes granting and revoking atomic, or enforce that an address cannot grant a role to another address after a revocation of its own role is pending. In user‑facing terms, an admin who thinks they have been removed may still be able to perform admin actions through a hidden account, breaking the expectation that revoking a role fully disables privileged access.

title: Inadequate Verification of tokenAmount Leads to Potential Dust Theft
description:
```solidity
The Periphery's functionality allows bridging of funds between the source
chain and the protocol, encompassing integration with the deposit, withdrawal,
and transfer functionalities of the Core and Passive Pool. An issue arises when
the deposit action fails on the destination chain; the DepositsFallbackModule
is designed to catch this failure and refund the user on the source chain via the
Socket bridge. The problem occurs when the tokenAmount is lower than the
tokenFees (a static fee), leading to a transaction revert due to insufficient fees,
consequently trapping the tokenAmount in the periphery. This scenario
becomes exploitable due to the absence of verification between the user-input
tokenAmount and the bridgeAmount in the BridgingUtils::executeBridging
function. Attackers can exploit this by calling
DepositsFallbackModule::depositPassivePool with a tokenAmount equating
to the Periphery's balance (accumulated from previous users' dust) and a
different bridgeAmount, causing a revert in the
DepositsModule::depositPassivePool that triggers the
BridgingUtils::executeBridging function, thereby bridging the Periphery's
balance back to the attacker in the other chain. This issue allows attackers to
siphon accumulated dust amounts from the Periphery.
```
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inadequate verification of the amount of tokens that a user claims to bridge (tokenAmount) against the amount that the bridging logic actually forwards (bridgeAmount). Because the Periphery contract does not enforce that tokenAmount equals bridgeAmount, a situation can arise where tokenAmount is smaller than a static fee required for the cross‑chain transfer. When a deposit on the destination chain fails, the DepositsFallbackModule attempts to refund the user by invoking the Socket bridge. The fee check then reverts due to insufficient fees, leaving the tokenAmount locked inside the Periphery contract. Over time this locked amount accumulates as dust from many users who experienced failed deposits. An attacker can exploit the missing verification by calling DepositsFallbackModule.depositPassivePool with a tokenAmount that matches the entire Periphery balance (the accumulated dust) while supplying a different bridgeAmount. This mismatch triggers a revert in DepositsModule.depositPassivePool, which in turn calls BridgingUtils.executeBridging with the attacker‑controlled bridgeAmount, causing the Periphery’s dust balance to be bridged to the attacker’s address on the other chain. The impact is that small but potentially valuable amounts of tokens that should have been refundable become siphoned by a malicious actor, effectively stealing the dust. The issue occurs only when a bridging failure happens, the fee is higher than the tokenAmount, and an attacker can invoke the fallback deposit function. All users of the protocol are affected because any user’s failed deposit can contribute to the dust pool, and any external actor can trigger the exploit. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the fallback logic and noticed the lack of a tokenAmount‑bridgeAmount equality check. It is hard to notice because the failure path is rarely exercised in normal operation and the amounts involved are small, making the loss appear as normal rounding or fee variance. To remediate, the bridging utility should enforce that the amount the user supplies matches exactly the amount forwarded to the bridge, and a recovery mechanism should be added so that users can reclaim tokens on the destination chain when a bridging operation fails. This class of bug falls under improper input validation and unchecked arithmetic leading to asset misdirection, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that deposited funds are either successfully transferred or safely returned to the sender.

title: Stale Price Data in DivReducer Due to Average Timestamp Calculation
description:
```solidity
The DivReducer function within the system is designed to calculate the
quotient of the prices from two input nodes, typically used for deriving asset
prices in alternative currency terms when direct feeds are not available. A
critical part of this functionality is the calculation of the updated_at
timestamp for the output, which currently averages the timestamps of the two
input nodes. This approach introduces a significant risk; if one input node
provides a very recent timestamp and the other is significantly stale, the
averaged timestamp could misleadingly pass staleness checks, thus presenting
the output as more current than it actually is. This can lead to the use of
outdated price data in critical financial calculations, potentially affecting all
dependent systems relying on the accuracy of this feed for timely decision-
making.
```
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price aggregation component that computes a derived price by dividing the values reported by two independent price nodes. To indicate how recent the derived price is, the contract records an updated_at timestamp that is calculated as the arithmetic mean of the timestamps supplied by the two input nodes. This averaging logic is flawed because it can mask the presence of a stale source: if one node reports a very recent timestamp while the other reports a timestamp that is far in the past, the average may still satisfy any freshness check that only verifies that the timestamp is newer than a configured threshold. Consequently, the system may treat the derived price as up‑to‑date even though it is partially based on outdated data. An attacker or a misbehaving oracle can exploit this by ensuring that one of the input feeds remains stale while the other feed supplies a fresh timestamp, thereby causing the averaged timestamp to appear valid. When the derived price is subsequently used in downstream financial calculations—such as collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or trade execution—participants may receive incorrect pricing information. From a user perspective this can manifest as unexpected liquidation, trades executed at unfavorable rates, or balances that appear to change without a corresponding market move. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of timestamp handling. It is difficult to notice because the timestamp field contains a plausible value and no explicit error is raised; only the subtle interaction between two timestamps leads to the mis‑representation of freshness. The bug belongs to the class of “timestamp aggregation” or “stale data acceptance” vulnerabilities, where the method of combining freshness indicators allows outdated information to slip through. The proper mitigation is to replace the averaging operation with a conservative approach, such as taking the minimum (oldest) timestamp of the two inputs, ensuring that the derived price is considered fresh only when both sources are fresh. This change restores the intended security invariant that the output timestamp must never be newer than any of its inputs, thereby preventing the use of stale price data in critical protocol logic.

title: Lack of Price Freshness Verification in Oracle Price Data
description:
```solidity
The getOraclePrice and getCollateralExchangeInfo functions retrieve
NodeOutput.Data containing price information and a timestamp indicating the
freshness of this price. An issue has been identified wherein these functions use
the price data directly without verifying the freshness of the data based on the
timestamp. This oversight could lead to scenarios where stale or outdated price
data is used in significant financial calculations or decision-making processes.
```
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing verification of the timestamp that accompanies price data returned by the oracle. The getOraclePrice and getCollateralExchangeInfo functions read NodeOutput.Data, which includes a price value and a freshness timestamp, but they forward the price to downstream calculations without checking whether the timestamp is within an acceptable freshness window. The root cause is the absence of any logic that compares the timestamp to a predefined threshold, allowing stale or outdated price information to be treated as current. An attacker who can influence the oracle or who can replay old NodeOutput.Data can cause the contract to use a price that no longer reflects the market. By submitting a transaction that triggers a collateral valuation, liquidation check, or exchange rate computation, the stale price may cause a user’s collateral to be undervalued, leading to premature liquidation, incorrect exchange amounts, or loss of funds. The impact is financial mis‑calculation: users may receive less than expected, collateral may be seized, or trades may settle at unfavorable rates. The condition occurs whenever the contract calls getOraclePrice or getCollateralExchangeInfo, which happens for every operation that depends on market price, such as deposits, withdrawals, trades, or liquidation checks. All participants who rely on price‑dependent logic—traders, lenders, borrowers—are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the data flow from the oracle and noticed that the timestamp field was never used. Because the contract still compiles and the price values appear syntactically correct, the bug can be hard to notice in normal testing unless the oracle is deliberately fed stale data. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be a sudden liquidation despite a stable market, a trade that returns far less than expected, or a balance that drops to zero after an operation that should have been neutral. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of 'missing data freshness validation' or 'stale oracle data usage'. To remediate, the contract should introduce a check that compares the oracle timestamp against a configurable freshness threshold and revert the transaction if the data is older than the allowed window, thereby ensuring that only up‑to‑date price information is used for financial decisions.

title: Invalid Nodes can be registered due to an incorrect check
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the registration of a special node type that is expected to have two valid parent nodes. During registration the contract calls an internal validation routine that is supposed to verify that each parent node is itself valid. However the routine that checks parent validity returns a boolean result which is never examined, and the outer validation function does not assign or return any value based on that result. Consequently the check effectively does nothing; an invalid parent node passes the registration gate and the new node is recorded as if it were correctly formed. This logical flaw originates from an incorrect handling of the return value of the helper function and the absence of an explicit return statement for the overall validity flag. An attacker or careless developer can therefore register a node whose parent references are malformed, missing, or deliberately crafted to break later processing. When the protocol later attempts to use the node for its intended arithmetic reduction, assumptions about the existence and correctness of the parent nodes are violated. This can lead to erroneous calculations such as division by zero, incorrect reduction results, or even a halt of the processing pipeline, effectively causing funds to be mis‑allocated, payouts to be zero, or the protocol to become unusable for downstream users. The issue manifests only when a DIV_REDUCER node is created; normal nodes are unaffected. Users who rely on the node graph for financial logic – typically node creators, liquidity providers, or any participant whose rewards are derived from the reduction – are exposed to potential loss or denial of service. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the validation flow and noticed that the boolean result of the parent‑validation helper was ignored. Because the function silently returns the default false value without being used, the problem can be subtle and may not surface until a malformed node is actually processed, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests. The proper fix is to propagate the result of the parent‑validation check and to return a definitive boolean indicating overall validity, ensuring that registration aborts when any parent node fails its own validation. In abstract terms, this is an input‑validation omission that allows malformed hierarchical data to enter the system, breaking the contract’s accounting invariants and leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds.

title: Inability to cancel signed commands
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract implements a signed‑command execution flow where the replay‑preventing nonce is automatically increased only when the ExecutionModule.executeBySig function is called. Because there is no separate mechanism for an account owner or an administrator to manually bump the nonce, a signed command that has been created but not yet executed cannot be cancelled or invalidated. The root cause is the absence of a nonce‑reset or cancel function in the contract’s permission model. An attacker or even the legitimate user cannot prevent a previously signed command from being replayed later, especially if the original transaction fails (for example due to out‑of‑gas) and the nonce remains unchanged. Consequently, a stale withdrawal, transfer or order may be executed at a later time, leading to unexpected fund movement, loss of assets, or execution of orders that the user intended to abort. This situation arises whenever a user signs a command and then wishes to withdraw it, when an urgent cancellation is required, or when a transaction reverts without advancing the nonce. All account owners, administrators, and the broader protocol are affected because the inability to cancel undermines the expected safety guarantees of signed off‑chain instructions. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the lifecycle of signed messages and identified that the only path to increment the nonce is through successful execution, leaving no fallback for cancellation. The problem can be subtle because normal operation appears correct; only edge‑case flows involving failed executions or user‑initiated cancellations expose the flaw. To remediate, the contract should expose a privileged function that allows the owner or a designated admin to manually increment the nonce or explicitly mark a command as revoked, thereby providing a reliable way to invalidate pending signed messages and restore the intended security posture. This class of bug falls under “missing cancellation mechanism for replay‑protected signed commands” and violates the business logic that users should be able to rescind pending orders before they are processed.

title: Nonce reset vulnerability on Owner change
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unintended reset of the replay‑protection nonce when the ownership of an account is transferred. In this design the nonce, which is bound to the current account owner and is incremented for each signed command, is set back to zero by the ownership‑change routine. Because the nonce is used as part of the signed message digest, resetting it erases the history of used nonces and allows a signature that was valid before the owner change to become valid again. An attacker who obtains a previously signed command – for example a withdrawal or an administrative action – can replay that command after the owner has been changed, because the contract will recompute the digest with the reset nonce and accept the old signature. The impact is that funds or privileged actions can be executed without the new owner's consent, effectively bypassing the intended access control. This condition occurs whenever the contract’s owner‑transfer function is called; any subsequent signed transaction that was generated under the former owner may be replayed until the nonce is incremented again. The affected parties are the account holders who change ownership and any downstream users who rely on the integrity of signed messages, such as token holders or protocol participants. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the signature verification flow and noticed that the nonce‑increment function is called after the owner address is read, but the owner‑change routine resets the stored nonce to zero. Because the reset happens silently and does not emit a warning, it can be difficult to notice in normal operation – the contract appears to function correctly until a replayed message is submitted. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑nonce mis‑management vulnerabilities, where nonce state is not preserved across critical state changes, breaking the assumption that a nonce monotonically increases for a given signer. From a user perspective the symptom may be that a transaction that should be rejected (because it was signed by a previous owner) is accepted, leading to unexpected loss of funds or actions being performed without the new owner's approval. The correct mitigation is to keep the nonce tied to the signer’s address and never reset it on ownership transfer, or to migrate the nonce to the new owner in a way that preserves its monotonic property, ensuring that previously signed messages cannot become valid again.

title: Incorrect principle tracking due to fee inclusion
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the deposit routine where the contract's principal state variable is increased by the full amount supplied by the user, including the staking fee and the bridging fee, instead of only the net amount that is actually staked. The root cause is that the code adds the variable amount directly to principal before subtracting any fees, conflating gross deposits with net stake. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by calling deposit with any positive amount; the function calculates fees, transfers the staking fee to the protocol vault, and then incorrectly records the entire deposit as principal. Because the principal value is used for reward distribution, liquidation thresholds and other financial logic, the over‑statement leads to rewards being calculated on a larger than real stake, which can later cause the protocol to allocate more tokens than it holds or to under‑pay users when they withdraw. The impact is a mismatch between on‑chain accounting and actual token balances, potentially resulting in users receiving less than expected, the protocol appearing to have more capital than it truly does, and increased risk of insolvency. The condition occurs whenever the deposit function is executed while the contract is not paused. All users who deposit are affected, as are the protocol’s reward mechanisms and any third‑party integrations that rely on the principal value. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the state updates in the deposit flow. It is hard to notice because the principal variable may be displayed as the total deposited amount, which matches the user’s expectation, while the hidden fee transfers are not reflected in that number, masking the discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of financial state mis‑tracking or fee double‑counting errors. To fix the problem the contract should update the principal with only the net staked amount (for example principal += mintedAmount) after fees have been deducted, ensuring that accounting reflects the true amount that is actually locked in the staking mechanism. This correction restores the invariant that principal equals the sum of all tokens that are actually locked in the staking mechanism, aligning user expectations with on‑chain reality.

title: Decimals discrepancy causes the incorrect pegging
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑precision mismatch between the staking token and its underlying asset wTAO. The contract is supposed to issue a staking token that is pegged 1:1 to wTAO, meaning that one unit of wTAO (which uses 9 decimal places) should correspond to one whole staking token (which uses 18 decimal places). Because the implementation assumes the two tokens share the same number of decimals, the deposit function copies the raw amount of wTAO into the staking token balance without applying a scaling factor. Consequently, when a user deposits 1 wTAO (1 × 10⁹ base units) they receive only 1 × 10⁹ staking‑token units, which represent 0.000000001 of a full staking token under the 18‑decimal scheme. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a balance of zero or an unexpectedly tiny amount, leading to the impression that funds have vanished. The bug manifests whenever the contract converts amounts between the underlying token and the staking token – typically during deposits and any function that relies on the same conversion logic, such as withdrawals. All participants who interact with the staking contract – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariants that assume a 1:1 peg are broken, potentially causing incorrect reward calculations, cap enforcement, and overall economic imbalance. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case logged a staking‑token balance of 1 000 000 000 after depositing what should have been a full token, revealing the mis‑scaled result. The problem is subtle because both tokens store balances as large integers and the discrepancy is hidden unless the values are interpreted with the correct decimal precision; many front‑ends simply format the number according to the token’s own decimals, which masks the error. To remediate the flaw the contract must either align the staking token’s decimal count with that of wTAO (setting decimals to 9) or explicitly scale the amount in the deposit and withdrawal functions by a factor of 10⁹ to bridge the 9‑decimal gap. Either approach restores the intended 1:1 peg and ensures that users receive the correct amount of staking tokens for the underlying assets they provide.

title: Users can frontrun rebase to extract profits at the expense of long-term stakers
description: The StakingToken contract is susceptible to a frontrunning attack during the rebase process. Users who monitor on-chain events can detect when a rebase is imminent, especially if they can predict or observe an increase in the total supply in the calldata. They can exploit this by: Front-running the Rebase: Depositing a significant amount of tokens just before the rebase occurs, thereby increasing their share of the total supply. Benefiting from the Rebase: When the rebase increases the total supply, these users receive a disproportionate share of the newly minted tokens relative to their short-term stake. Back-running with Withdrawal: Immediately requesting an unstake after the rebase, capturing the rebase rewards without a long-term commitment. This behavior allows opportunistic users to extract undue profits, effectively diluting the value of long-term stakers' holdings. It undermines the fairness and intended reward distribution of the staking mechanism.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running rebase exploitation in the staking token contract. During a scheduled rebase the contract mints additional tokens proportionally to each staker’s share of the total supply. Because the contract does not enforce any minimum staking period, an attacker who watches pending transactions or event logs can submit a large deposit just before the rebase transaction is executed. By increasing the attacker’s share of the total supply at the moment the supply is expanded, the attacker receives a disproportionate amount of the newly minted tokens. Immediately after the rebase the attacker can call the withdraw function and retrieve the inflated balance, leaving the newly minted tokens in their wallet while the long‑term stakers see their relative ownership diluted. The impact is that short‑term opportunistic users can extract profit without providing the intended long‑term commitment, effectively reducing the value of holdings for honest participants. The condition for exploitation is the existence of a rebase that changes total supply and the ability to submit a transaction in the same block before the rebase is processed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward distribution logic and noticed the absence of a lock‑up period. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for normal staking flows and the profit extraction only appears as a sudden increase in the attacker’s balance and a subtle decrease in the per‑share value for other users, which may be attributed to normal market fluctuations. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a sudden profit for some accounts and a lower effective share or zero reward for others after a rebase, contradicting the expectation that rewards accrue proportionally over time. This class of bug belongs to timing or front‑running attacks on economic state updates, specifically rebase‑aware reward manipulation. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a minimum staking duration or a lock‑up period before withdrawals are allowed, thereby preventing immediate exit after a rebase and preserving the fairness of the reward distribution.

title: [Buyout module] Fraction price is not updated when total supply changes
description: Lines: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-fractional/blob/8f2697ae727c60c93ea47276f8fa128369abfe51/src/modules/Buyout.sol#L118-L138>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the buyout module of the Fractional protocol where the price of each fractional token (fraction price) is calculated once at the moment a buyout auction is started and stored in the auction struct. The contract assumes that the total supply of fractions remains constant for the duration of the auction, but it never validates that assumption. When a vault’s total supply changes after the auction begins— for example through a split, mint, or any other supply‑inflating operation— the stored fraction price no longer reflects the actual value of a single token. Because the contract continues to use the stale price when a seller calls sellFractions, the ether that the buyer sent for the whole vault is multiplied by the outdated price, resulting in an under‑payment to the seller and an over‑payment loss for the buyer. In the demonstrated exploit, Bob initiates a buyout for 1 ETH based on an initial supply. Alice then calls the split module twice, quadrupling the total supply, and subsequently sells only a quarter of the new supply. The contract computes the payout using the original fraction price, so Bob loses his 1 ETH while receiving only 25 % of the intended fractions. The issue occurs whenever the total supply changes between the start of a buyout and a subsequent sell, and it affects any participant who relies on the buyout price—both buyers and sellers—as well as the overall accounting integrity of the protocol. The bug was uncovered during a security audit by Code4rena through a handcrafted test that simulated the split operation and verified the mismatch between ether transferred and fractions received. It is subtle because the auction appears to proceed normally, there is no explicit event indicating a supply change, and the price discrepancy only becomes visible after the transaction is executed, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should recompute the per‑fraction price at the time of each sell (and buy) using the current total supply, store the last observed supply alongside the auction data, and revert or emit an event when a supply mismatch is detected. This ensures that the ether transferred always matches the true market value of the fractions, preserving financial correctness and preventing loss of funds.

title: Migration.join
description: `Migration.join()` and `Migration.leave()` can still work after unsucessful migration. As I submitted with my high-risk finding “Migration.`withdrawContribution()` might work unexpectedly after unsuccessful migration.”, withdraw logic after unsuccessful migration is different from the initial `leave()` logic and the withdrawal logic would be messy if users call `join()` and `leave()` after unsuccessful migration.
poc:
According to the [explanation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-fractional/blob/8f2697ae727c60c93ea47276f8fa128369abfe51/src/modules/Migration.sol#L23), join() and leave() functions must be called for 7 days before commition.

Currently, such a scenario is possible.

  * Alice creates a new migration and commits after some joins.
  * The migration ended unsuccessfully after 4 days.
  * Then users can call `leave()` or `withdrawContribution()` to withdraw their deposits but it wouldn’t work properly because we should recalculate eth/fractional amounts with returned amounts after unsuccessful migration.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migration module of the fractional vault contract, where the functions that allow participants to add liquidity (join) or remove it (leave) remain callable even after a migration attempt has failed. The root cause is the absence of proper state checks – the code does not verify that the migration proposal has either been successfully committed or that the 7‑day window preceding commitment has expired. Consequently, users can still invoke join() and leave() after the migration period ends unsuccessfully, and the withdrawal path (withdrawContribution) that is executed in this edge case follows a different calculation routine than the original leave() logic. This mismatch leads to an inconsistent recomputation of the ETH and fractional token amounts that should be returned to each contributor. An attacker or a curious user can exploit the bug by calling join() or leave() after the migration has been marked unsuccessful, causing the contract to attempt to process withdrawals with stale or incorrect accounting data. The impact is that participants may receive an incomplete refund, see their balances incorrectly reduced to zero, or have their funds become permanently locked in the contract because the refund calculation does not reflect the actual state after failure. The issue manifests specifically when a migration proposal finishes without being committed – for example, after four days of a seven‑day proposal period – and participants subsequently try to withdraw their contributions. All users who have contributed to the migration are affected, as the bug violates the core business logic that guarantees a fair and accurate return of assets when a migration does not succeed. The problem was uncovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) that examined the migration flow and identified that the withdrawal logic diverges from the leave() path and lacks protective modifiers. Because the functions still appear to execute without reverting, the defect may be difficult for casual observers to notice; the contract does not emit explicit error messages about the failed migration, and the UI may simply show a transaction success while the user’s balance is unexpectedly reduced or remains unchanged. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce two additional constraints: (1) disallow any call to join() or leave() once the migration proposal has been committed or the proposal period has elapsed, and (2) ensure that the withdrawal routine used after an unsuccessful migration mirrors the original leave() accounting logic, correctly recalculating the proportion of ETH and fractional tokens to be returned. By adding these checks and aligning the accounting paths, the contract will restore the expected behavior that users receive their rightful refunds and that funds cannot be trapped or misallocated after a failed migration.

title: `fallback
description:
Vault owners can install plugins via `Vault.install()`, with calls to the installed plugins made through the vault’s fallback function. Unlike the vault’s external `Vault.execute()` function, `fallback()` imposes no checks on the permissions of the caller, assuming proper installation of the plugin by the owner at install time.

While this design seems intentional given `NFTReceiver.sol`, it can lead to unintended vulnerabilities, like loss of vault NFTs, if the vault owner:

  * Mistakenly installs a plugin not intended for unpermissioned use or installs a malicious plugin
  * Is transferred vault ownership from a prior owner who misconfigured vault plugin installations
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a vault contract that forwards calls to external plugin contracts through its fallback function. Unlike the explicitly permissioned execute() entry point, the fallback does not perform any checks on the caller’s identity or the plugin’s required authorisation, assuming that the owner installed only trustworthy plugins. This design decision creates a class of unauthorized‑call bugs where any external address can trigger a plugin function simply by sending a low‑level call to the vault’s address. The root cause is the absence of a per‑plugin permission flag in storage and the lack of enforcement of that flag inside the fallback handler. When a vault owner installs a plugin that implements a sensitive operation—such as an ERC‑721 transfer—and then transfers ownership of the vault to another user, the original owner can still invoke the plugin via the unguarded fallback. By crafting a call that matches the selector of the transfer function, the former owner can cause the vault to move NFTs out of its custody without the new owner’s consent. The impact is a loss of assets: deposited NFTs disappear from the vault and appear in the attacker’s account, violating the expectation that only the current owner can manage vault contents. This situation can arise in any workflow where ownership changes after plugin installation, or where a developer mistakenly installs a plugin that was never intended to be called without authentication. Users who deposit NFTs see their balances drop to zero and receive no error, leading to confusion and a breach of trust. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit and demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept test that installed a transfer plugin, transferred ownership, and then used the fallback to steal the NFT. The problem is subtle because fallback functions are a common pattern for extensibility, and developers may overlook the need for explicit access control on those delegated calls. The recommended mitigation is to maintain a mapping that records whether each installed plugin requires authentication and to enforce this check inside the fallback before delegating the call. By doing so, only authorised callers (typically the current vault owner) would be able to trigger privileged plugin functionality, preventing the described asset‑drain scenario.

title: Migration total supply reduction can be used to remove minority shareholders
description:
As new total supply can be arbitrary, setting it significantly lower than current (say to 100 when it was 1e9 before) can be used to remove current minority shareholders, whose shares will end up being zero on a precision loss due to low new total supply value. This can go unnoticed as the effect is implementation based.

During Buyout the remaining shareholders are left with ETH funds based valuation and can sell the shares, but the minority shareholders that did contributed to the Migration, that could have other details favourable to them, may not realize that new shares will be calculated with the numerical truncation as a result of the new total supply introduction.

Setting the severity to Medium as this is a fund loss impact conditional on a user not understanding the particulars of the implementation.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a migration mechanism that permits the contract owner or a governance proposal to set an arbitrary new total supply for fractional shares during a vault migration. The calculation that distributes new shares to each participant is performed as (userContribution * newTotalSupply) / totalContribution, using integer division. When the newTotalSupply is set significantly lower than the previous supply—for example, reducing a supply of 1 × 10⁹ to 100—the division can truncate the result to zero for any user whose proportional share is below the granularity of the new supply. As a consequence, minority shareholders who contributed a small amount of ETH or who hold a small fraction of the vault end up receiving no new fractions after migration. This situation becomes critical during a buyout, where the contract requires the vault to be in an INACTIVE state before a user can call leave() or withdrawContribution(). If the buyout proceeds while the minority shareholder’s share has been reduced to zero, the user cannot withdraw any funds, effectively losing their contribution. The impact is a loss of funds for those minority participants, a violation of the economic expectation that shares scale proportionally with contributions, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol's fairness. The issue manifests only when a migration proposal includes a total‑supply reduction and the migration logic does not enforce any monotonicity constraint on the supply value. It may go unnoticed because the on‑chain state shows a valid total supply and the arithmetic appears correct at a high level; only the rounding effect hides the loss. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit that examined the migrateFractions() and commit() functions and identified that the supply parameter can be lowered without checks. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that any new total supply is greater than or equal to the existing supply, or alternatively redesign the share‑allocation algorithm to use a high‑precision representation or rounding mechanism that guarantees every contributor retains at least a proportional claim. By enforcing a monotonic increase or by using a safe allocation scheme, the protocol can prevent the accidental or malicious reduction of minority shareholders’ balances, preserving the intended accounting guarantees and protecting user funds.

title: Use of `payable.transfer
description:
The use of `payable.transfer()` is heavily frowned upon because it can lead to the locking of funds. The `transfer()` call requires that the recipient has a `payable` callback, only provides 2300 gas for its operation. This means the following cases can cause the transfer to fail:

  * The contract does not have a `payable` callback
  * The contract’s `payable` callback spends more than 2300 gas (which is only enough to emit something)
  * The contract is called through a proxy which itself uses up the 2300 gas

If a user falls into one of the above categories, they’ll be unable to receive funds from the vault in a migration wrapper. Inaccessible funds means loss of funds, which is Medium severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the built‑in payable.transfer function to return ether to a caller during migration and withdrawal operations. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback function and automatically reverts the call if the recipient does not implement a payable fallback or if the fallback consumes more than the allotted gas. Because the migration wrapper unconditionally uses transfer, any user whose address is a contract without a suitable payable fallback, or whose fallback performs actions that exceed the gas stipend (such as emitting events or interacting with other contracts), will cause the transfer to fail. The failure is silent from the caller’s perspective – the transaction appears to succeed but the ether remains locked inside the vault contract. This situation can also arise when the call passes through a proxy that consumes part of the 2300‑gas stipend, leaving insufficient gas for the final recipient. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the leave and withdrawContribution functions and noted the absence of any alternative payout mechanism or owner‑change logic. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the transfer fails; the only symptom is that the user’s balance in the UI shows zero or that a migration reports success while the user receives no funds. The impact is a loss of accessibility to deposited ether – users may be unable to retrieve their funds, effectively freezing assets in the contract. This affects any participant who attempts to withdraw or migrate their escrowed ether, including EOAs and contracts, and can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately supplies a malicious contract as the recipient to trigger the gas‑limit failure and lock funds for other users. The root cause is the use of a low‑level, gas‑restricted ether transfer primitive without a fallback path. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (address.call{value:x}('')) and to check the returned success flag, optionally providing a pull‑payment pattern or an admin‑controlled escape hatch so that locked funds can be recovered. By adopting a more flexible payout method, the contract aligns with standard best practices and prevents the accounting inconsistency where the protocol’s internal ledger shows a deduction but the external balance of the user remains unchanged.

title: An attacker can DoS vault’s buyout with as little as 1 wei per 4 days
description:
The underlying issue here is:

  * A user can create a buyout with as little as 1 wei (which is basically nothing, it’s worth about 1e-15 USD), without any fractions
  * Once a buyout is created, nobody else can create another buyout on the same vault till the previous buyout ends (even if he’d like to offer a much higher price)

This leads to the fact that with as little as 1 wei a user can block a vault from holding a buyout for 4 days.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition in the vault buyout mechanism that allows any participant to initiate a buyout with an effectively negligible amount of ether—specifically 1 wei—without holding any fractional tokens. Because the protocol enforces a rule that only one buyout can be active for a given vault at any time, the tiny buyout monopolizes the buyout slot for the full duration of its proposal period (approximately four days). This happens because the contract does not validate the buyout price against a minimum threshold or against the proposer’s share of the vault fractions, and it does not permit competing higher offers to replace an existing proposal. An attacker can exploit this by calling the start function with a minuscule value, thereby locking the vault in an "invalid state" where subsequent attempts to start a buyout immediately revert with an IBuyout.InvalidState error. The impact is that legitimate users who wish to purchase the vault at a fair market price are unable to do so for the remainder of the proposal window, effectively freezing the marketplace for that asset. The condition occurs whenever a buyout is created; there is no additional guard that checks price realism or proposer stake, so the attack can be repeated indefinitely, each time resetting the timer and extending the blockage. Users, protocol participants, and any party that relies on timely vault liquidation are affected, as they experience missing buying opportunities and potentially lost revenue. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when a test case demonstrated that a user with a zero fraction balance could start a buyout with 1 wei and that another user was prevented from initiating a higher‑priced buyout until the first one expired. The bug is subtle because the contract’s logic appears to allow any positive ether amount, and the price of 1 wei is too small to raise immediate suspicion, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate, the buyout initiation should enforce a minimum price relative to the vault’s value or require the proposer to hold a minimum percentage of fractions, and the contract should allow higher‑priced buyouts to supersede an existing one, optionally with a required minimum increase (e.g., 5%). This adjustment would restore the intended competitive buyout process and prevent griefing attacks that block legitimate market activity.

title: The fee calculation is inconsistent
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent fee calculation in the unstaking workflow of the RivusCOMAI contract. When a user submits a request to unstake, a manager with a specific role approves the request and transfers a calculated amount of wrapped COMAI (wCOMAI) to the contract based on the current unstaking and bridging fees. The contract computes these fees using a view function that multiplies the requested amount by fee percentages stored in contract state. Because the fee percentages are mutable, a manager can change them after the approval step but before the user calls the unstake function. The unstake function recomputes the required wCOMAI amount using the same view function, now with the updated fee values. As a result, the amount of wCOMAI that was previously deposited by the manager may be insufficient to cover the newly calculated fee‑adjusted amount. When the user later calls unstake, the contract attempts to transfer the calculated amount to the user; if the contract’s balance is lower than required, the transfer fails and the user receives no tokens. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful unstake request but the transaction reverts or the user receives zero tokens, contradicting the expectation of receiving the full amount minus fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of fee calculations across approveMultipleUnstakes and unstake and observed that the fee variables are mutable and used at two different points. The bug is subtle because the same helper function is called in both places, giving the impression that the amounts will match, yet the state change between calls breaks that assumption. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for users who cannot retrieve their assets and a potential loss of confidence in the protocol’s accounting, as funds may become locked until a manager manually reconciles the shortfall. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “state‑dependent calculation inconsistency” or “mutable‑parameter race” bugs, where a contract relies on a value that can be altered between two dependent operations. To remediate, the fee‑adjusted amount should be fixed at the time the unstake request is created (or at approval) and stored immutably with the request, ensuring that both the approval transfer and the later user withdrawal use the same numbers regardless of later fee changes. Alternatively, the contract could prohibit fee changes while there are pending unstake requests. This fix restores accounting integrity and prevents users from experiencing failed withdrawals or receiving less than expected.

title: Missing input validation on createAuction function parameters can lead to loss of value
description:
There are some problems with the input validation in createAuction, more specifically related to the timestamp values.
1. endTimestamp can be equal to startTimestamp, so duration will be 0
2. endTimestamp can be much further in the future than startTimestamp, so duration will be a huge number and the auction may never end
3. Both startTimestamp and endTimestamp can be much further in the future, so auction might never start
Those possibilities should all be mitigated, as they can lead to the initial reserves and/or the bids being stuck in the protocol forever.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing input validation on the parameters of the auction creation function, specifically the startTimestamp and endTimestamp values. Because the contract does not enforce any relationship between these timestamps, an auction can be created with a start time equal to the end time, resulting in a zero‑second duration, or with an end time set arbitrarily far in the future, producing a duration that may exceed practical limits. Likewise, both timestamps can be placed far ahead of the block time at which the auction is created, causing the auction to never become active. The root cause is the absence of business‑logic checks that enforce a minimum duration, a maximum duration, and a reasonable offset between the creation time and the start time. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by submitting a transaction that creates an auction with a zero or excessively long duration. Once such an auction is on‑chain, any initial reserve funds deposited by the creator and any subsequent bids become locked in the contract because the auction never reaches a state where it can be settled or closed. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that an auction appears in the UI but never receives bids, or that a bid is accepted but never results in a win or a refund, effectively making the funds disappear from the user’s accessible balance. The impact is that value can be trapped indefinitely, harming both the auction creator and participants, and undermining confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The issue manifests whenever the createAuction function is called without proper timestamp constraints, which can happen at any time during normal operation. It was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted logical gaps in the auction lifecycle. The problem is subtle because the contract may appear to work correctly for typical timestamps, making the bug hard to notice unless edge‑case values are tested. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimal duration (for example one day) and a maximal duration (for example twenty days), and also require that the startTimestamp is not more than a defined number of days after the transaction that creates the auction.
