The EnhancedSportsPrediction::setHouseFee function allows the owner to change the global house fee, which affects all existing bets. This can lead to unexpected changes in payout calculations for users who have already placed bets. More critically, the house fee calculation occurs in two separate places (EnhancedSportsPrediction::resolveCondition and EnhancedSportsPrediction::claimPayout), creating a potential inconsistency when the fee changes between these operations. This creates two significant impacts:
1. Users receive less than expected: If the house fee increases between condition resolution and payout claiming, users will receive lower payouts than they should based on the fee at the time of resolution.
2. Funds get trapped in the contract: The inconsistency creates a situation where totalFeesCollected doesn't match the actual fees collected from users. This breaks the economic integrity of the protocol and can result in funds permanently locked in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s design where the house fee is stored as a single mutable global variable that can be altered by the contract owner at any time. The fee is consulted in two distinct functions – one that resolves a betting condition and another that allows a user to claim their payout – but the contract does not snapshot the fee value at the moment a bet is created. Consequently, if the owner changes the global fee after a bet has been placed but before the payout is claimed, the two functions may apply different fee percentages. This creates a mismatch between the fee that was effectively taken when the condition was resolved and the fee that is deducted when the payout is finally transferred. An attacker with owner privileges can deliberately raise the fee after resolution, causing bettors to receive a smaller amount than the contract originally promised. Additionally, because the contract tracks total fees collected based on the global fee, a discrepancy can arise where the recorded fees do not match the actual amount taken from users, leading to leftover ether that becomes permanently locked in the contract. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as a payout that is lower than expected – for example, a user who expects a 10 % fee may receive a payout calculated with a 15 % fee, or may see their balance reduced to zero while the contract still holds unclaimed funds. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined the flow of fee calculations and identified that the fee is not immutable per betting condition. It is difficult to notice because the fee change is a legitimate owner action and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the fee used for resolution differs from the fee used for claim. The bug belongs to the class of mutable‑global‑parameter inconsistencies that break economic invariants and can be described as a “fee race condition” or “global fee drift”. To remediate the issue, the contract should store the house fee inside each betting condition at the time the bet is created, and both the resolve and claim functions should reference this stored value, ensuring that the fee applied remains constant for the lifetime of the bet and that fee accounting stays consistent.

title: Lack of reimbursement mechanism for incorrect bets leads to fund locking
description: In the EnhancedSportsPrediction::claimPayout function, if all users bet on the wrong outcome, the funds remain locked in the contract due to the line if (outcomePool == 0) revert NoBetsOnOutcome();. Currently there is no mechanism to reimburse users or collect the funds as house fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claimPayout function of the EnhancedSportsPrediction contract where the logic assumes that at least one bet will be placed on the winning outcome. When the outcomePool variable, which represents the total amount bet on the correct result, is zero the function executes a revert with the error NoBetsOnOutcome(). This revert prevents any further execution, meaning that the total ether held by the contract remains permanently locked because there is no alternative path to either distribute the funds to the house or reimburse the participants. The root cause is a missing edge‑case handling for the situation in which every participant wagers on the losing side, an outcome that is logically possible but rarely exercised in testing. An attacker does not need to perform any special action; the condition is triggered naturally when the collective betting pattern results in zero correct bets. The impact is that users who try to claim a payout receive a transaction revert, see no change in their wallet balance, and are left without any way to retrieve the funds they originally deposited. From the protocol’s perspective the locked capital reduces liquidity, undermines trust, and may render the contract unusable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the payout flow and identified the unconditional revert on a zero outcomePool. It can be hard to notice because typical test scenarios include at least one correct bet, so the zero‑pool branch is not exercised. To remediate, the contract should include a fallback mechanism that either allows the contract owner or a designated house address to claim the locked ether as a fee, or implements a reimbursement path that returns each bettor’s stake (potentially minus a small house commission). This class of bug falls under improper handling of edge cases leading to dead‑locks and fund‑locking due to unconditional reverts in financial smart contracts. Users experience the symptom of “balance stays the same after claiming” or “claim transaction fails with no payout”, contrary to the expectation that a claim either pays out or refunds the stake.

title: Race condition with initiatingAdminSettleDebt() could under- compensate participants
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During a deposit operation the contract checks that the admin‑settle‑debt process has not been initialized (require(!isAdminSettleDebtInitialized())) . This check is intended to stop new deposits once the admin has decided to cancel the vault and settle debt with zero earnings. However the check is performed only at the beginning of the deposit transaction and there is no atomic relationship with the admin’s initiatingAdminSettleDebt() call. If a participant’s final deposit is mined in the same block before the admin’s transaction, the vault can be started even though the admin expected it to remain un‑started. In that race condition the admin records a settle‑debt amount that is smaller than the fixed side capacity because the vault has not yet reached its full fixed supply. When the vault later ends with zero earnings the fixed‑side participants receive a payout based on the smaller adminSettleDebtAmount, while the variable‑side participants receive nothing because the vault’s ETH balance does not match the expected stETH backing. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or reduced refund, a balance that becomes zero after the vault ends, and an inability to claim the full amount that was originally deposited. The issue occurs only when the admin initiates the settle‑debt process before the vault is started and a competing deposit transaction is front‑run into the same block, a situation that can be triggered by MEV bots or natural transaction re‑ordering. All participants of the vault – both fixed and variable – are affected because the accounting assumptions of ‘total fixed supply equals settled debt amount’ are violated, leading to under‑compensation. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state changes and identified that the require statement does not provide a guarantee against concurrent deposits. The bug is hard to notice because the require passes in normal operation and the loss only appears under a specific timing edge case. The recommended mitigation is to make the admin’s expectation explicit by passing a boolean flag expectedVaultStarted to initiatingAdminSettleDebt() and requiring that it matches the actual vault start state; if the expectation is wrong the call reverts, preventing the under‑compensation scenario. More generally the class of bug is a race condition caused by non‑atomic checks that allow state to change between verification and execution, leading to financial mis‑allocation.

title: Cross SeaDrop reentrancy
description:
The contract that implements IERC721SeaDrop can work with multiple Seadrop implementations, for example, a Seadrop that accepts ETH as payment as well as another Seadrop contract that accepts USDC as payment at the same time. This introduces the risk of cross contract re-entrancy that can be used to circumvent the maxMintsPerWallet check. Here's an example of the attack:
1. Consider an ERC721 token that that has two allowed SeaDrop, one that accepts ETH as payment and the other that accepts USDC as payment, both with public mints and restrictedFeeRecipients set to false.
2. Let maxMintPerWallet be 1 for both these cases.
3. A malicious fee receiver can now do the following:
• Call mintPublic for the Seadrop with ETH fees, which does the _checkMintQuantity check and transfers the fees in ETH to the receiver.
• The receiver now calls mintPublic for Seadrop with USDC fees, which does the _checkMintQuantity check that still passes.
• The mint succeeds in the Seadrop-USDC case.
• The mint succeeds in the Seadrop-ETH case.
• The minter has 2 NFTs even though it's capped at 1.
Even if a re-entrancy lock is added in the SeaDrop, the same issue persists as it only enters each Seadrop contract once.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑contract reentrancy flaw that allows a malicious fee receiver to bypass the per‑wallet mint limit enforced by SeaDrop implementations attached to a single ERC‑721 token. The ERC‑721 contract is designed to work with multiple SeaDrop contracts, each handling a different payment token (for example ETH and USDC). Each SeaDrop enforces its own maxMintsPerWallet check, but the check is scoped only to the individual SeaDrop instance. When a user initiates a public mint on a SeaDrop that pays fees in ETH, the SeaDrop first validates the mint quantity, then transfers the ETH fee to the configured fee receiver. Because the fee transfer is an external call, a malicious fee receiver can re‑enter another SeaDrop contract during this callback and invoke its mintPublic function before the first mint finishes. The second SeaDrop again performs its own quantity check, which still passes because the limit is applied per contract, not globally. As a result the attacker receives two NFTs while the protocol intended to allow only one per wallet. The issue manifests only when the ERC‑721 token is configured with more than one SeaDrop contract and when a fee receiver is under the attacker’s control. It is difficult to notice because each individual SeaDrop appears to respect its own limits and a typical reentrancy guard placed inside a SeaDrop only protects against re‑entry into the same contract, not across different SeaDrop instances. The impact is that users can acquire more tokens than permitted, undermining scarcity, revenue calculations, and fairness of the sale. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the ERC‑721 token and its allowed SeaDrop contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a wallet received two NFTs even though the sale rules advertised a maximum of one per wallet, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. To remediate the issue the ERC‑721 contract should enforce the maxMintsPerWallet constraint centrally, or implement a global reentrancy lock that blocks any mint operation while another is in progress, thereby preventing cross‑contract re‑entry. Alternatively, the protocol could restrict fee receivers to trusted addresses or redesign the fee‑payment flow to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, ensuring that state changes occur before external calls.

title: Lack of replay protection for mintAllowList and mintSigned
description: In the case of mintSigned (minting via signatures) and mintAllowList (minting via merkle proofs) there are no checks that prevent re-using the same signature or Merkle proof multiple times. This is indirectly enforced by the _checkMintQuantity function that checks the mint statistics using IERC721SeaDrop(nftContract).getMintStats(minter) and reverting if the quantity exceeds maxMintsPerWallet. Replays can happen if a wallet does not claim all of maxMintsPerWallet in one transaction. For example, assume that maxMintsPerWallet is set to 2. A user can call mintSigned with a valid signature and quantity = 1 twice. Typically, contracts try to avoid any forms of signature replays, i.e., a signature can only be used once. This simplifies the security properties. In the current implementation of the ERC721Seadrop contract, we couldn't see a way to exploit replay protection to mint beyond what could be minted in a single initial transaction with the maximum value of quantity supplied. However, this relies on the contract correctly implementing IERC721SeaDrop.getMintStats.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing replay protection mechanism for two minting pathways – mintSigned, which relies on off‑chain signatures, and mintAllowList, which uses Merkle proofs. Because the contract does not record whether a particular signature or proof has already been consumed, the same authorisation data can be submitted in multiple transactions. The root cause is that the only enforcement of per‑wallet limits is performed by the external getMintStats call, which checks the total quantity minted against a configured maxMintsPerWallet. If a wallet does not exhaust its allowance in a single transaction, it can split the allowed quantity across several calls, each using the same signature or proof, and the contract will treat each call as a fresh mint. Exploitation consists of an attacker (or any user) re‑submitting a valid signature or Merkle proof multiple times, each time requesting a portion of the allowed quantity, thereby obtaining more tokens than intended. The impact is that the economic assumptions of the protocol – that each address can mint only a bounded number of NFTs – are violated, leading to an inflated token supply, potential loss of scarcity value, and unfair advantage for the attacker. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the minting function does not store a nonce, digest, or tokenId tied to the authorisation data, and where the external mint statistics function is either incorrectly implemented or can be bypassed. All participants who rely on the per‑wallet cap – users, the protocol’s token economics, and downstream marketplaces – are affected because the cap no longer guarantees fairness. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of mintSigned and mintAllowList and noted the absence of any state‑ful replay guard. It can be hard to notice because the contract still reverts when the total minted quantity exceeds the limit, so a single large mint behaves correctly; only when the quantity is split does the flaw become apparent, which may not be covered by typical test cases. To remediate, the contract should record a unique identifier for each authorisation (such as the hash of the signature or Merkle proof, possibly combined with a nonce or tokenId) and reject any subsequent use of the same identifier. Additionally, the signature payload should include immutable data like the tokenId to prevent reuse after a burn‑and‑re‑mint scenario, and the contract should avoid relying on mutable external statistics for enforcement. In user‑facing terms, a user may observe that they can mint two NFTs by sending two separate transactions each requesting one token, even though the UI or documentation states that only one token per wallet is allowed. This discrepancy between expectation (single mint) and reality (multiple mints) constitutes a breach of the intended business logic and accounting guarantees of the NFT drop.

title: adminSettleDebtLockPeriod might not be long enough
description: admin has the ability to end the vault early in case of unforeseen circumstances. This is done by first calling initiatingAdminSettleDebt which triggers a timelock before adminSettleDebt can be called. This so that users can chose to withdraw before all stETH and pending withdraw requests are transferred to AdminLidoAdapter. The timelock, adminSettleDebtLockPeriod, is set in VaultFactory to 3 days. This might however not be enough. Looking at what lido says the withdrawal requests can take anything between 1-5 days: https://blog.lido.fi/ethereum-withdrawals-overview-faq/#:~:text=How%20does%20the,1%2D5%20days. How does the withdrawal process work? The withdrawal process is simple and has two steps: Request: Lock your stETH/wstETH by issuing a withdrawal request. ETH is sourced to fulfill the request, and then locked stETH is burned, which marks the withdrawal request as claimable. Under normal circumstances, this can take anywhere between 1-5 days.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the administrative settlement mechanism of a vault that holds stETH and wstETH. The contract allows an admin to end the vault early by first calling initiatingAdminSettleDebt, which starts a timelock, and then, after the lock expires, calling adminSettleDebt to transfer all stETH and any pending withdrawal requests to an AdminLidoAdapter. The timelock duration, adminSettleDebtLockPeriod, is hard‑coded in the VaultFactory to three days. Lido’s withdrawal process, however, can take between one and five days to become claimable after a request is made. Because the lock period is shorter than the maximum withdrawal latency, an admin could trigger the early settlement after only three days while some user withdrawal requests are still pending. In that situation the contract will move the underlying assets to the admin adapter before the external Lido protocol has had time to fulfil the requests, effectively preventing users from receiving the ETH they expect. From a user’s point of view the balance shown in the vault may drop to zero, a withdrawal attempt returns no funds, or a claim transaction reverts, contradicting the expectation that a submitted request will be honoured within the usual 1‑5 day window. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the admin settlement flow and compared the timelock value against Lido’s documented withdrawal timeline. It is hard to notice because the three‑day lock appears to provide a safety window, and the asynchronous nature of Lido’s withdrawal means that pending requests are not visible on‑chain until they become claimable. The bug belongs to the class of premature finalisation or insufficient timelock bugs, where an on‑chain action is allowed before an off‑chain or cross‑protocol process has reached its final state, creating a race condition. The impact is medium: users may lose access to their funds, the protocol’s trustworthiness is questioned, and the admin could be perceived as acting maliciously. To remediate, the timelock should be extended to at least the maximum withdrawal period (five days) plus a safety buffer (for example six days), or the contract should enforce that no pending withdrawal requests exist before allowing adminSettleDebt, or make the lock period configurable based on the external protocol’s latency guarantees.

title: adminSettleDebt() could be called multiple times leading to the loss of funds
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the adminSettleDebt function of the vault contract. The function is intended to be called once by the admin after a lock period to settle outstanding debt and distribute remaining staking earnings and fixed‑deposit funds. However, the implementation does not verify whether it has already been executed; it only sets a boolean flag adminSettledDebt but never checks that flag on subsequent calls. Consequently, an admin can invoke the function multiple times. The first call records correct values for vaultEndedStakingEarnings and vaultEndedFixedDepositsFunds based on the total supply of the fixed‑ETH deposit token at that moment. If users withdraw some of their positions after this call, the total supply changes. A second call recomputes the same variables using the new total supply, which can produce incorrect, often lower, amounts. Users who have not yet withdrawn may therefore receive less than their entitled balance or see their funds disappear entirely. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal withdrawal request but the received amount is zero or unexpectedly small, violating the expectation that the contract will return the full deposited value plus earned interest. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the function’s logic and noticed the missing idempotency guard. It is subtle because a single execution appears correct; only repeated execution under altered state reveals the accounting error, which many test suites may not cover. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent re‑execution or missing‑guard vulnerabilities, where a privileged function can be called more than once, breaking invariant assumptions. To remediate, the contract should enforce a one‑time execution check, such as require(!adminSettledDebt) or a mutex, ensuring that the settlement logic cannot be run again after the first successful call, thereby preserving the integrity of the accounting and preventing fund loss.

title: Admin could call adminSettleDebt anytime without previous call initiatingAdminSettleDebt
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic flaw in the adminSettleDebt function that allows the privileged admin to settle the vault’s debt without ever having started the required timelock. The function is intended to be called only after the admin has first invoked initiatingAdminSettleDebt, which sets a non‑zero timestamp in the variable adminSettleDebtLockPeriodEnd. However, the only guard present is a require statement that checks block.timestamp > adminSettleDebtLockPeriodEnd. Because the default value of a uint256 is zero, if the timelock was never initiated the comparison becomes block.timestamp > 0, which is true as soon as the contract is deployed. Consequently the admin can call adminSettleDebt at any time, bypassing the intended delay. When executed prematurely the function marks vaultEndedWithdrawalsFinalized and adminSettledDebt as true and calculates vaultEndedStakingEarnings and vaultEndedFixedDepositsFunds based on the current token supply. If the timelock was never started, these calculations resolve to zero, effectively breaking the withdrawal flow for all users: balances appear unchanged, expected refunds are missing, and the UI may show that withdrawals are disabled or that earnings are zero. The impact is medium severity because it does not directly steal funds, but it can lock user assets and violate the protocol’s accounting guarantees, leading to loss of confidence and potential financial loss if users cannot withdraw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended lifecycle of the settlement process with the actual code and noticed the missing check for a non‑zero lock period. It is subtle because the require statement looks correct at a glance, and the default zero value is a silent failure mode that does not raise an explicit error. To remediate, the require should also enforce that adminSettleDebtLockPeriodEnd is greater than zero (or that a specific flag indicating the timelock was initiated is set) before allowing settlement. This adds an explicit state validation, ensuring the function can only be called after the proper initiation step and preserving the intended timelock behavior. The bug belongs to the class of missing state validation or uninitialized‑variable misuse, where a function assumes a prerequisite has been satisfied without verifying it, leading to unintended privileged actions and broken business logic.

title: Accrual before vault start can be used as honeypot
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that the fixed‑side participant in the vault can withdraw their principal together with any staking rewards before the vault officially starts. When a fixed‑side staker deposits, the contract immediately forwards the funds to Lido and begins accruing staking rewards. Because the withdrawal function does not enforce a start‑time lock, the same participant can call the claimWithdrawals routine at any moment prior to the vault start, receiving both the original deposit and the accrued earnings. This creates a situation where an attacker can open a vault, deposit the entire fixed premium, and let the Lido rewards accumulate. The vault UI will then display a large amount of earnings, making the vault appear highly profitable despite a high premium. A victim, seeing the attractive earnings, may decide to join the variable side, assuming the earnings offset the premium cost. The attacker can then front‑run the victim’s variable deposit, withdraw their own fixed‑side deposit together with the accrued rewards, and optionally re‑enter the vault with a fresh deposit in the same transaction. From the victim’s perspective the vault seems to offer a fair trade, but the attacker extracts the earnings risk‑free, effectively using the pre‑start accrual as a honeypot. The impact is an unfair premium for the variable‑side participant and a loss of expected profit, while the protocol’s economic model is subverted because the accounting assumption that earnings are only realizable after the vault start is violated. The issue occurs whenever the vault start timestamp has not been reached and the contract permits early withdrawals; it affects any user who joins the variable side after seeing pre‑start earnings, as well as the overall integrity of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of deposits and withdrawals. It can be hard to notice because the UI correctly shows growing rewards, which users interpret as legitimate profit rather than a manipulable state. The recommended mitigation is not a technical on‑chain fix but clear documentation stating that earnings accumulated before the vault start are not guaranteed and may be withdrawn by the fixed‑side participant, thereby warning users against relying on those numbers when deciding to join the vault.

title: ongoing withdrawals from variable side hurts variable earnings
description:
When the vault is active, a variable side staker can chose to withdraw their share of the, so far, accrued earnings:
```solidity
(
    uint256 currentState,
    uint256 ethAmountOwed
) = calculateVariableWithdrawState(
    (lidoStETHBalance - fixedETHDeposits) + withdrawnStakingEarnings + totalProtocolFee,
    variableToWithdrawnStakingEarnings[msg.sender]
);
```
On L584 this unstakes from lido, meaning it will lessen the rewards gained by other variable stakers (and themselves) going forward. This mainly makes it difficult for variable side stakers to calculate expected earnings as accounting for how many early withdrawals might be made is hard.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: Variable‑side early withdrawals allow a staker to claim a portion of the accumulated staking earnings while simultaneously triggering an unstake operation on the underlying Lido position. Because the vault calculates each variable staker’s share based on the total Lido balance minus the fixed deposits, any reduction of that balance directly lowers the amount of future rewards that remain to be distributed among the remaining variable participants. The root cause is that the withdrawal routine does not isolate the accounting of earned rewards from the underlying asset’s principal; it treats the withdrawal as a reduction of the shared staking pool. An attacker or any user can exploit this by repeatedly withdrawing small amounts, causing the pool’s effective stake to shrink and consequently diminishing the reward rate for all other variable stakers. The impact is a deviation between the expected earnings (as advertised by the protocol) and the actual earnings received, leading to lower returns, unpredictable profit calculations, and potential loss of confidence in the vault’s accounting model. The condition occurs whenever the vault is active and the variable side is permitted to withdraw; each withdrawal invokes the Lido unstake call, which reduces the pool’s future reward generation. All participants who rely on the variable side – typically users seeking flexible exposure to staking rewards – are affected, as their future yield becomes dependent on the withdrawal behavior of others. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s withdrawal logic, where the auditor noted that the state‑transition function calculateVariableWithdrawState uses a balance that includes the variable stake itself, and that the subsequent unstake call on Lido reduces the shared capital. Because the symptom is a gradual erosion of expected returns rather than an outright loss of funds, it can be hard to notice without detailed accounting or simulation. The bug belongs to the class of “shared‑pool accounting distortion” or “withdrawal‑induced reward dilution” defects, where a user‑initiated state change unintentionally modifies the reward base for other participants. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal, but later the dashboard displays lower than projected earnings, or even zero growth, contradicting the expectation that “my earnings should continue to accrue after I withdraw”. To remediate the problem the contract should decouple the withdrawal of earned rewards from the underlying staking principal, for example by imposing an early‑withdrawal fee on the variable side, or by adding a configuration flag that disables ongoing variable withdrawals altogether, thereby preserving the integrity of the reward pool for remaining stakers.

title: The digest in SeaDrop.mintSigned is not calculated correctly according to EIP-712
description: mintParams in the calculation of the digest in mintSigned is of struct type, so we would need to calculate and use its hashStruct , not the actual variable on its own.
bug_full: The SeaDrop contract implements a signed mint function (mintSigned) that relies on an EIP‑712 typed data signature to authorize minting parameters such as price, time window, per‑wallet limits and fee configuration. The vulnerability stems from an incorrect construction of the EIP‑712 digest: the code feeds the entire MintParams struct directly into the outer abi.encode call instead of first hashing the struct according to the EIP‑712 hashStruct rule. Because the struct contains several uint256 fields and a boolean, the resulting byte layout differs from the canonical hashStruct representation, so the final digest does not match the one that the off‑chain signer produced. As a consequence, the contract validates signatures against a malformed digest. An attacker who understands the mistake can craft a signature that satisfies the incorrect digest, or reuse an existing signature, thereby bypassing the intended checks on mint price, start/end times, per‑wallet caps, stage limits and fee restrictions. This can lead to unauthorized minting, free token acquisition, or the ability to mint beyond the configured supply limits, ultimately draining funds or breaking the economic model of the drop. The flaw manifests every time mintSigned is invoked, because the digest calculation is performed inside the function without any conditional guard. It affects any user or contract that relies on the signed mint path, including legitimate minters, the protocol’s revenue model, and downstream marketplaces that assume the minting constraints are enforced. The issue was discovered during a manual security review where the auditor compared the on‑chain digest generation with the EIP‑712 specification and noticed that the MintParams struct was not hashed. The problem is subtle because the existing unit tests reuse the same faulty digest routine, so they pass even though the contract would accept signatures that should be invalid. To remediate, the contract must compute a hashStruct for MintParams using a type hash that enumerates each field, then include that hash in the outer encoding as prescribed by EIP‑712. After correcting the digest, signatures will only be accepted when they correspond to the exact parameters signed off‑chain, restoring the intended economic safeguards. In user‑facing terms, the bug can cause a situation where a user expects a paid mint but receives a free token, or where the contract appears to allow unlimited mints despite configured caps, breaking the expected balance and supply accounting.

title: Token gated drops with a self-allowed ERC721SeaDrop or a variant of that can lead to the drop getting drained by one person.
description:
There are scenarios where an actor with only 1 token from an allowed NFT can drain Token Gated Drops that are happening simultaneously or back to back.

• Scenario 1 - An ERC721SeaDrop is registered as an allowedNftToken for itself  
This is a simple example where an ERC721SeaDrop N is registered by the owner or the admin as an allowedNftToken for its own token gated drop and during or before this drop (let's call this drop D) there is another token gated drop (D0) for another allowedNftToken N0, which does not need to be necessarily an IERC721SeaDrop token.  
Here is how an actor can drain the self-registered token gated drop:  
1. The actor already owns or buys an N0 token t0 with wallet w0.  
2. During D0, the actor mints an N token t0 with wallet w0 passing N0, t0 to mintAllowedTokenHolder and transfer t0 to another wallet if necessary to avoid the max mint per wallet limit (call this wallet w1 which could still be w0).  
3. Once D starts or if it is already started, the actor mints another N token t1 with w1 passing N, t0 to mintAllowedTokenHolder and transfers t1 to another wallet if necessary to avoid the max mint per wallet limit (call this wallet w2 which could still be w1).  
4. Repeat step 3 with the new parameters till we hit the maxTokenSupplyForStage limit for D.

```solidity
// during token gated drop D'
t = seaDrop.mintAllowedTokenHolder(N, f, w, {N', [t']})
// during token gated drop D
while (have not reached maxTokenSupplyForStage) {
    if (w has reached max token per wallet) {
        w' = newWallet()
        N.transfer(w, w', t)
        w = w'
    }
    t = seaDrop.mintAllowedTokenHolder(N, f, w, {N, [t]})
}
```

• Scenario 2 - Two ERC721SeaDrop tokens are doing a simultaneous token gated drop promotion  
In this scenario, there are 2 ERC721SeaDrop tokens N1, N2 where they are running simultaneous token gated drop promotions. Each is allowing a wallet/bag holder from the other token to mint a token from their project. So if you have an N1 token you can mint an N2 token and vice versa. Now if an actor already has an N1 or N2 token maybe from another token gated drop or from an allow list mint, they can drain these 2 drops till one of them hits maxTokenSupplyForStage limit.

```solidity
// wallet <w> already holds token <t> from N1
while (have not reached N1.maxTokenSupplyForStage or N2.maxTokenSupplyForStage) {
    w = newWalletIfMaxMintReached(N1, w, t) // this also transfers t to the new wallet
    w = newWalletIfMaxMintReached(N2, w, t) // this also transfers t to the new wallet
    t = seaDrop.mintAllowedTokenHolder(N2, f, w, {N1, [t]})
    t = seaDrop.mintAllowedTokenHolder(N1, f, w, {N2, [t]})
}
```

This scenario can be extended to more complex systems, but the core logic stays the same.  
Also, it's good to note that in general maxTotalMintableByWallet for token gated drops and maxMintsPerWallet for public mints are not fully enforceable since actors can either distribute their allowed tokens between multiple wallets to mint to their full potential for the token gated drops. And for public mints, they would just use different wallets. It does add extra gas for them to mint since they can't batch mint. That said these limits are enforceable for the signed and allowed mints (or you could say the enforcing has been moved to some off-chain mechanism).
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns token‑gated drops that rely on ownership of an allowed ERC721 token to grant minting rights. The contract checks only that the caller holds a qualifying NFT, but it does not prevent the same NFT from being reused after each mint by moving it to a new wallet. When a drop registers its own ERC721 contract as an allowed token (self‑allowed) or when two separate ERC721SeaDrop contracts cross‑allow each other's tokens, an attacker who possesses a single qualifying token can repeatedly call the mintAllowedTokenHolder function, receive a newly minted token, transfer that token to a fresh address to reset the per‑wallet mint counter, and repeat the process until the stage’s maxTokenSupplyForStage is exhausted. This loop drains the entire allocation that was intended for a broad community, leaving legitimate participants unable to obtain any tokens. The root cause is the lack of a mechanism that tracks usage per token ID or locks the qualifying token for the duration of the drop, combined with per‑wallet limits that are easy to circumvent by simply switching wallets. The issue manifests when a token‑gated drop is configured with self‑allowance or mutual allowance between contracts, and when the drop enforces a maximum number of mints per wallet rather than a global per‑holder limit. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit through logical analysis of the mintAllowedTokenHolder flow and the ability to transfer the qualifying NFT after each mint. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to enforce reasonable limits, yet an attacker can exploit the transferability of the NFT to bypass those limits, making the drain difficult to detect until the supply is depleted. To remediate, the protocol should forbid registering the same ERC721 as an allowed token, disallow cross‑allowance that creates circular dependencies, and implement a usage counter tied to each token ID or lock the qualifying token for the duration of the drop. Alternatively, the drop could use a Merkle‑proof based allowlist or enforce a global per‑address mint cap that aggregates across all wallets owned by the same entity. By ensuring that a single qualifying token cannot be reused indefinitely, the drop’s intended distribution model is preserved and the risk of supply exhaustion is mitigated.

title: The spent offer amounts provided to OrderFulfilled for collection of (advanced) orders is not the actual amount spent in general
description:
When Seaport is called to fulfill or match a collection of (advanced) orders, the OrderFulfilled is called before applying fulfillments and executing transfers. The offer and consideration items have the following forms:  
C = (It, T, i, acurr, R, acurr)  
O = (It, T, i, acurr, acurr)  
Where  

parameter | description  
--- | ---  
It | itemType  
T | token  
i | identifier  
acurr | the interpolation of startAmount and endAmount depending on the time and the fraction of the order.  
R | consideration item's recipient  
O | offer item.  
C | consideration item.  

The SpentItems and ReceivedItem items provided to OrderFulfilled event ignore the last component of the offer/consideration items in the above form since they are redundant.  
Seaport enforces that all consideration items are used. But for the endpoints in this context, we might end up with offer items with only a portion of their amounts being spent. So in the end O.acurr might not be the amount spent for this offer item, but OrderFulfilled emits O.acurr as the amount spent. This can cause discrepancies in off-chain bookkeeping by agents listening for this event.  
The fulfillOrder and fulfillAdvancedOrder do not have this issue, since all items are enforced to be used.  
These two endpoints also differ from when there are collections of (advanced) orders, in that they would emit the OrderFulfilled at the end of their call before clearing the reentrancy guard.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the OrderFulfilled event emitted by Seaport when a collection of (advanced) orders is fulfilled. The event is emitted before the contract applies the fulfillments and executes the token transfers. At that point the contract uses the static offer amount field O.acurr, which represents the full start‑or‑end amount of the offer item, even though only a portion of that amount may actually be transferred in a partial fill. Consequently the spentOfferAmount reported in the event can be larger than the amount that was really moved. This discrepancy is invisible to on‑chain observers because the event data itself is syntactically correct, but off‑chain agents that rely on the event for bookkeeping – such as analytics dashboards, aggregators, or wallet UI – will record an incorrect spend, leading to mismatched balances, unexpected zero‑balance warnings, or apparent loss of funds. The problem only occurs for the collection endpoints (e.g., matchOrders, fulfillAvailableOrders) where the event is emitted prior to the reentrancy guard being cleared; single‑order functions like fulfillOrder or fulfillAdvancedOrder enforce full usage of items and therefore do not exhibit the issue. The root cause is the ordering of state changes and event emission, combined with the omission of the actual transferred amount in the event payload. Because the event appears to contain the correct fields, developers may not notice the bug until they compare on‑chain token balances with the logged amounts after a partial fill. The impact is primarily accounting inconsistency rather than direct loss of assets, but it can undermine trust in the protocol’s reporting and may be exploited by malicious actors to create misleading audit trails. The recommended fix is to move the OrderFulfilled emission to the end of the execution flow, after all transfers have been performed, and to populate the spent offer amount with the actual transferred quantity. This aligns the event with the true state change and restores reliable off‑chain accounting.

title: ERC721A has mint caps that are not checked by ERC721SeaDrop
description:
ERC721SeaDrop inherits from ERC721A which packs balance, numberMinted, numberBurned, and an extra data chunk in 1 storage slot (64 bits per substorage) for every address. This would add an inherent cap of 2^64 - 1 to all these different fields. Currently, there is no check in ERC721A's _mint for quantity nor in ERC721SeaDrop's mintSeaDrop function.  
Also, if we almost reach the max cap for a balance by an owner and someone else transfers a token to this owner, there would be an overflow for the balance and possibly the number of mints in the _packedAddressData. The overflow could possibly reduce the balance and the numberMinted to a way lower number and numberBurned to a way higher number.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way ERC721A stores per‑address accounting data in a single 256‑bit slot, packing balance, numberMinted, numberBurned and an auxiliary field as four 64‑bit unsigned integers. Because each field is limited to 2^64‑1, the contract implicitly imposes a hard cap on the number of tokens an address can own or have minted. ERC721SeaDrop inherits this storage layout but does not add any explicit checks in its mintSeaDrop function or rely on ERC721A’s internal _mint routine to enforce a quantity limit. Consequently, an attacker or a legitimate user can repeatedly mint tokens to a single address until the stored balance or numberMinted approaches the 64‑bit maximum. If, after reaching a value close to 2^64‑1, another token is transferred to the same address—or an additional mint is performed—the packed uint64 field overflows, wrapping around to a low value. This overflow silently reduces the recorded balance and numberMinted while potentially inflating numberBurned, breaking the contract’s accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as a sudden loss of tokens, a balance that unexpectedly drops to zero or a very small number, and refunds or royalty calculations that become incorrect because the contract believes the holder owns fewer tokens than actually does. The impact includes loss of confidence in token ownership, possible double‑spending if the contract later allows re‑minting of the “missing” tokens, and disruption of any business logic that relies on accurate token counts, such as airdrop eligibility or royalty distribution. The issue manifests only when an address accumulates an astronomically large number of tokens, which is why it can remain unnoticed during normal testing. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which identified the missing quantity check and the inherent 64‑bit overflow risk in the packed address data. Mitigation requires adding explicit require statements in mintSeaDrop (and any other minting paths) to ensure that quantity plus the current balance and numberMinted do not exceed type(uint64).max, or redesigning the storage layout to use a larger integer size or separate variables, thereby preventing silent overflow and preserving the integrity of token accounting.

title: ERC721SeaDrop owner can choose an address they control as the admin when the constructor is called.
description:
The owner/creator can call the contract directly (skip using the UI) and set the administrator as themselves or another address that they can control. Then after they create a PublicDrop or TokenGatedDrop, they can call either updatePublicDropFee or updateTokenGatedDropFee and set the feeBps to  
• zero  
• or another number and also call the updateAllowedFeeRecipient to add the same or another address they control as a feeRecipient.  
This way they can circumvent the protocol fee.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the ERC721SeaDrop contract allows the contract owner or creator to specify an administrator address in the constructor without any validation. This administrator is granted permission to call fee‑related functions such as updatePublicDropFee, updateTokenGatedDropFee and updateAllowedFeeRecipient. Because the admin can be an address controlled by the owner, the owner can later set the fee basis points (feeBps) to zero or any arbitrary value and add themselves as a feeRecipient. By doing so they can bypass the protocol‑defined marketplace fee, diverting the fee revenue to an address they control. The issue occurs whenever a new ERC721SeaDrop token contract is deployed; the malicious admin can be set at deployment time and later exercised after a public or token‑gated drop is created. Users who purchase NFTs from such a drop expect the standard protocol fee to be deducted and sent to the marketplace, but instead they receive no fee deduction or a reduced fee, and the owner receives the fee amount. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the constructor and admin‑only functions and noticed that the admin role is not restricted to an internal allow‑list. The flaw is subtle because the UI typically hides the admin selection and the fee parameters may appear normal in the contract’s public view, making it difficult for a user or a third‑party auditor to notice that the fee can be set to zero. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unauthorized fee manipulation” or “admin‑controlled economic parameter tampering”. Exploitation steps are: (1) deploy the ERC721SeaDrop contract and pass an address controlled by the attacker as the admin; (2) create a PublicDrop or TokenGatedDrop; (3) call updatePublicDropFee or updateTokenGatedDropFee to set feeBps to zero or a low value; (4) call updateAllowedFeeRecipient to add the attacker’s address as the feeRecipient; (5) collect the fee revenue that should have gone to the protocol. The impact is loss of protocol revenue, unfair advantage for the malicious token creator, and potential erosion of trust in the marketplace. The issue can be mitigated by enforcing that the admin address must belong to a whitelist maintained by the SeaDrop protocol, by separating the admin role of the token contract from the fee‑setting role, or by moving fee configuration entirely into the SeaDrop contract where only protocol‑controlled admins can modify it.

title: ERC721SeaDrop's admin would need to set feeBps manually after/before creation of each drop by the owner
description: When an owner of a ERC721SeaDrop token creates either a public or a token gated drop by calling updatePublicDrop or updateTokenGatedDrop, the PublicDrop.feeBps/TokenGatedDropStage.feeBps is initially set to 0. So the admin would need to set the feeBps parameter at some point (before or after). Forgetting to set this parameter results in not receiving the protocol fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a configuration omission in the ERC721SeaDrop contract that allows a newly created public or token‑gated drop to start with a fee basis‑point value (feeBps) of zero. The root cause is that the functions used by a token owner to initialise a drop – updatePublicDrop and updateTokenGatedDrop – set the feeBps field to the default value 0 and do not enforce any later update by the protocol admin. Because the contract does not check that feeBps is non‑zero before the drop becomes active, the protocol fee collection step silently skips, meaning the admin never receives the expected protocol fees for that drop. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; the issue can be triggered simply by the owner forgetting to call the corresponding fee‑update function (updatePublicDropFee or updateTokenGatedDropFee) or by the admin overlooking the need to set the fee after the drop is created. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol or any party that relies on the fee mechanism; users of the drop may still be able to purchase tokens, but the protocol’s accounting will show zero fees collected, breaking the business assumption that each sale generates a fee. The condition under which this occurs is any drop that is created via the aforementioned update functions without a subsequent fee‑setting transaction before the drop is opened for minting. Both token owners and the protocol admin are affected – owners may assume fees are being collected automatically, while admins may discover missing fees only after the drop has completed. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the lifecycle of a drop and noticed that feeBps is left at its default value with no guard clause. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the drop proceeds normally, and the missing fees are only visible in accounting reports. To remediate, the contract should enforce that feeBps is set to a non‑zero value before a drop can be activated, either by combining the fee‑setting call with the drop‑creation call, adding a validation check in updatePublicDrop/updateTokenGatedDrop, or by providing an admin‑only modifier that requires the fee to be configured. Alternatively, a default protocol fee could be baked into the contract, or a flag could be introduced to waive fees explicitly, ensuring that the business logic of fee collection cannot be bypassed unintentionally.

title: owner can reset feeBps set by admin for token gated drops
description:
Only the admin can call updateTokenGatedDropFee to update feeBps. However, the owner can call updateTokenGatedDrop(address seaDropImpl, address allowedNftToken, TokenGatedDropStage calldata dropStage) twice after that to reset the feeBps to 0 for a drop.  
1. Once with dropStage.maxTotalMintableByWallet equal to 0 to wipe out the storage on the SeaDrop side.  
2. Then with the same allowedNftToken address and the other desired parameters, which would retrieve the previously wiped out drop stage data (with feeBps equal to 0).
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of the contract owner to override a fee percentage (feeBps) that is intended to be set exclusively by an admin for token‑gated drops. The protocol defines an admin‑only function updateTokenGatedDropFee that writes the feeBps value into storage on the SeaDrop side of the system. However, the owner role also possesses permission to call updateTokenGatedDrop, a function that creates or replaces a drop stage for a specific allowed NFT token. By invoking updateTokenGatedDrop twice, the owner can first pass a dropStage with maxTotalMintableByWallet set to zero, which the implementation treats as a removal operation and consequently clears the entire drop‑stage storage, including the feeBps field. In a second call the owner supplies the same allowedNftToken address together with the desired drop parameters but does not specify a non‑zero feeBps, causing the previously cleared storage to be re‑initialized with feeBps equal to zero. This sequence effectively resets the fee that the admin had previously configured, allowing the owner to bypass any fee collection logic for that drop. The issue manifests whenever the owner has the ability to call updateTokenGatedDrop and chooses to reuse an existing allowedNftToken address after a removal. It may be difficult to notice because the fee appears correctly set after the admin’s transaction, yet later the owner’s transaction silently overwrites the fee without emitting a distinct warning or event. From a user perspective, minting a token from the affected drop may show a 0 % fee or result in no fee being deducted, contrary to the expectation that a fee should be charged. The impact is primarily economic: the protocol loses expected revenue, and the integrity of the fee model is compromised. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between admin‑only fee updates and owner‑controlled drop stage updates, revealing that the storage reset logic does not preserve feeBps. To remediate, the contract should either restrict updateTokenGatedDrop to the admin role, make feeBps immutable once set, or add explicit checks that prevent feeBps from being cleared or set to zero except when the intention is to remove the entire drop stage. Such changes would enforce the intended separation of duties and protect the fee mechanism from being unintentionally or maliciously overridden.

title: The spent offer item amounts shared with a zone for restricted (advanced) orders or with a contract offerer for orders of CONTRACT order type is not the actual spent amount in general
description:
When Seaport is called to fulfill or match a collection of (advanced) orders, there are scenarios where not all offer items will be used. When not all the current amount of an offer item is used and if this offer item belongs to an order which is of either CONTRACT order type or it is restricted order (and the caller is not the zone), then the spent amount shared with either the contract offerer or zone through their respective endpoints (validateOrder for zones and ratifyOrder for contract offerers) does not reflect the actual amount spent. When Seaport is called through one of its more complex endpoints to match or fulfill orders, the offer items go through a few phases:

parameter
description
It
itemType
T
token
i
identifier
as
startAmount
ae
endAmount
acurr
the interpolation of startAmount and endAmount depending on the time and the fraction of the order.
O
offer item.

• Let's assume an offer item is originally O = (It, T, i, as, ae)
• In _validateOrdersAndPrepareToFulfill, O gets transformed into (It, T, i, acurr, acurr)
• Then depending on whether the order is part of a match (1, 2. 3) or fulfillment (1, 2) order and there is a corresponding fulfillment data pointing at this offer item, it might transform into (It, T, i, b, acurr) where b ∈ [0, 1). For fulfilling a collection of orders b ∈ {0, acurr} depending on whether the offer item gets used or not, but for match orders, it can be in the more general range of b ∈ [0, 1).
• And finally for restricted or CONTRACT order types before calling _assertRestrictedAdvancedOrderValidity, the offer item would be transformed into (It, T, i, acurr, acurr).

So the startAmount of an offer item goes through the following flow:
as → acurr → b ∈ [0, 1) → acurr
And at the end acurr is the amount used when Seaport calls into the validateOrder of a zone or ratifyOrder of a contract offerer. acurr does not reflect the actual amount that this offer item has contributed to a combined amount used for an execution transfer.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the amount of an offer item that is reported as spent to a zone (via validateOrder) or to a contract offerer (via ratifyOrder) when Seaport processes advanced orders. In the normal flow an offer item is defined by a startAmount and an endAmount that may be interpolated over time to produce a current amount (acurr). During order validation the code transforms the startAmount through several intermediate representations, eventually passing acurr to the external endpoint. When an order is restricted or of the CONTRACT type and the caller is not the zone, the protocol may not use the full amount of the offer item; a portion of the item can remain unused (represented by a factor b that can be any value in [0,1)). The implementation, however, continues to forward acurr – the original current amount – instead of the actual amount that was transferred (acurr‑b). As a result the zone or contract receives a value that does not reflect the real amount spent. This discrepancy can be triggered whenever a collection of advanced orders is fulfilled or matched and not all offer items are consumed, which is common for fulfillAvailableOrders, fulfillAvailableAdvancedOrders, and for matched orders where the b factor may be arbitrary. The affected parties include the protocol’s accounting logic, the contract offerer, the zone, and ultimately end‑users who rely on correct balance updates. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as a missing refund, a balance that stays unchanged after an order is supposedly executed, or a situation where the UI shows that an order succeeded while the underlying token transfer did not occur for the full amount. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the transformation pipeline of offer items and identified that the value sent to external validation callbacks does not incorporate the unused portion. It is hard to notice because the contract still reports a successful order execution and the mismatch only appears in the internal accounting that is not directly exposed. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑mismatch or state‑propagation errors where an intermediate variable is forwarded without being adjusted for actual usage. To remediate the problem the protocol should compute the true spent amount (originalAmount minus unusedAmount) before invoking validateOrder or ratifyOrder for non‑matched orders, and redesign the handling of the b factor for matched orders so that the correct spent amount can be derived or the external callbacks are supplied with a reliable representation of the transferred value. This correction restores consistency between the protocol’s internal accounting and the values observed by zones and contract offerers, preventing erroneous balance calculations and potential loss of funds.

title: Empty criteriaResolvers for criteria-based contract orders
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of criteria‑based items in contract orders on the Seaport marketplace. In a normal advanced order that uses a Merkle‑based criteria, the fulfiller can supply a CriteriaResolver struct that specifies the concrete token identifier it wishes to receive. The marketplace logic checks that the resolver matches the original item whose identifierOrCriteria field is zero (meaning the offer applies to an entire collection) and then resolves the identifier during execution. However, for contract‑based offers the internal function _compareItems contains a special case: when the offerer is a contract and the identifierOrCriteria is zero, the function rewrites the order’s itemType to a non‑criteria type and does not expect a CriteriaResolver. Consequently, the fulfiller is unable to provide an explicit identifier, and any attempt to include a resolver causes the transaction to revert. This asymmetry creates a situation where a malicious contract can present a preview of an order that appears to resolve to a rare or valuable NFT, while the actual execution delivers a different, possibly worthless token because the fulfiller cannot enforce the identifier. From the user’s point of view the UI may show that a specific NFT should be received, but after settlement the user’s wallet shows a different token or no token at all, violating the expectation of receiving the advertised asset. The impact is that users can lose value or receive unintended assets without any obvious error message, undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case was modified to replace a criteria‑based offer with an empty criteriaResolvers array, causing a revert, and when the opposite case (providing a resolver for a contract offer) also reverted. The bug is subtle because the code path for contract offers appears to work correctly for other scenarios, and the special‑case logic is hidden inside _compareItems, making it easy to overlook. To remediate the problem the special case should be removed so that contract offers must return the same itemType and identifierOrCriteria as regular offers, and a CriteriaResolver must be supplied for every criteria‑based item regardless of whether the offerer is a contract. This aligns the behaviour of contract orders with regular orders, restores the ability for fulfillers to enforce the desired identifier, and prevents contracts from silently swapping assets. The fix restores consistency in the order‑matching logic and eliminates the possibility of receiving an unexpected NFT, thereby preserving the protocol’s intended accounting model.

title: Advance orders of CONTRACT order types can generate orders with less consideration items that would break the aggregation routine
description: When Seaport gets a collection of advanced orders to fulfill or match, if one of the orders has a CONTRACT order type, Seaport calls the generateOrder(...) endpoint of that order's offerer. generateOrder(...) can provide fewer consideration items for this order. So the total number of consideration items might be less than the ones provided by the caller. But since the caller would need to provide the fulfillment data beforehand to Seaport, they might use indices that would turn to be out of range for the consideration in question after the modification applied for the contract offerer above. If this happens, the whole call will be reverted. This issue is in the same category as Advance orders of CONTRACT order types can generate orders with different consideration recipients that would break the aggregation routine.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of advanced orders that use the CONTRACT order type in the Seaport protocol. When a caller submits a batch of advanced orders, it first builds fulfillment data based on the order information it receives. For CONTRACT orders the protocol invokes the contract offerer’s generateOrder(...) function to obtain the final order details. The contract is allowed to modify the order, and in particular it can return fewer consideration items than were present in the original order supplied by the caller. Because the caller has already calculated indices that point to the original consideration items, the reduction in the number of items makes those indices point outside the actual array after generateOrder finishes. When the aggregation routine later tries to access the out‑of‑range items, the whole transaction reverts. The root cause is that the protocol does not enforce a consistency rule between the previewOrder (or the caller’s view) and the generateOrder output, allowing a contract offerer to shrink the consideration list without signalling the change. An attacker could craft a CONTRACT order that deliberately drops consideration items, causing any downstream caller that pre‑computes fulfillment data to experience a revert, effectively a denial‑of‑service for that order batch. The impact is that users attempting to fulfill or match the order see a failed transaction, lose the gas spent on the call, and receive no assets – the UI may show “order fulfillment failed” or “no items received”. This situation occurs only when advanced orders of type CONTRACT are used and the caller relies on static order data before calling Seaport. All participants that interact with such orders – traders, marketplaces, aggregators – are affected because they cannot reliably predict the shape of the order. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between generateOrder and the aggregation logic. It is hard to notice because the reduction of consideration items happens inside a contract call that is not visible to the caller until the revert occurs, and the protocol does not emit a specific error indicating a mismatch. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that a contract offerer cannot return fewer consideration items than were originally advertised; if fewer items are needed the contract should either revert or replace the missing items with zero‑amount placeholders. Additionally, the previewOrder function should be required to return data that matches generateOrder for the same inputs, and the documentation of ContractOffererInterface should be updated to clearly describe this invariant. By guaranteeing a stable consideration count, callers can safely compute fulfillment indices and the aggregation routine will no longer encounter out‑of‑range accesses, eliminating the denial‑of‑service risk and restoring confidence in order execution.

title: AdvancedOrder.numerator and AdvancedOrder.denominator are unchecked for orders of CONTRACT order type
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the handling of the numerator and denominator fields of an advanced order when the order type is CONTRACT. In the normal flow for most advanced order types the contract validates that the supplied fraction is well‑formed – the numerator must be non‑zero and not larger than the denominator – and reverts otherwise. For CONTRACT orders this validation step is omitted. Later in the execution path the contract uses the numerator only as a flag: a zero numerator causes the engine to skip applying criteria resolvers, to skip aggregating offer and consideration amounts, and to bypass the final validity check that would normally call the ratifyOrder endpoint of the offerer. Despite these skips, the contract still emits an OrderFulfilled event that lists the offerer, zone, recipient and the full set of offer and consideration items. Consequently, an attacker can craft a CONTRACT order with numerator set to zero (and denominator also zero, as returned by _getGeneratedOrder) and cause the transaction to succeed while no actual token transfers or criteria checks occur. From the blockchain’s point of view the transaction is successful and an OrderFulfilled event is logged, but the logical state of the order is effectively a no‑op. Off‑chain services that index events – such as explorers, analytics dashboards, or automated accounting bots – will record the order as fulfilled and may assume that assets moved, leading to discrepancies between on‑chain reality and off‑chain records. Users interacting through a UI may see a confirmation that their order was fulfilled yet their balances remain unchanged, creating confusion and potential loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) by noticing that the fraction checks are conditionally compiled out for CONTRACT orders, a subtle omission that does not raise a revert and therefore can be missed during functional testing. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked input validation combined with inconsistent event emission, where a contract emits a success event despite skipping core business‑logic steps. To remediate, the validation of numerator and denominator should be performed before any logic that depends on the flag, or the contract should enforce that for CONTRACT orders the numerator and denominator are both equal to one, ensuring that the flag never triggers the skip path. By guaranteeing that the fraction is always valid, the engine will not bypass critical checks and the emitted OrderFulfilled event will accurately reflect a genuine fulfillment, restoring consistency between on‑chain state and off‑chain indexing.

title: Calls to PausableZone's executeMatchAdvancedOrders and executeMatchOrders would revert if unused native tokens would need to be returned
bug_full: The PausableZone contract used as a zone controller for Seaport order matching does not implement a payable receive or fallback function. When a match (or matchAdvanced) order includes native token (ETH) items, the caller supplies msg.value to the Seaport marketplace. In several realistic scenarios – such as rounding errors when the start and end amounts of an item differ, an accidental over‑payment of ETH, or a CONTRACT‑type offerer that provides a different amount than expected – the Seaport router may end the execution with a surplus of native tokens that need to be sent back to the caller. Because PausableZone cannot accept incoming ETH, the attempt to transfer the unused amount triggers a revert, causing the entire match transaction to fail. This bug was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately sent an extra 1 wei with the order and observed a revert. The failure is subtle: it only manifests when the execution path leaves leftover ETH, which may not happen on every order, making it easy to miss in normal testing. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should succeed and possibly refund excess ETH instead reverts, leaving the user with a failed transaction and lost gas, while the protocol cannot complete the intended trade. The affected parties include any user or contract that relies on PausableZone to facilitate ETH‑based trades, the Seaport marketplace (which cannot complete matches), and the overall protocol’s reliability. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “non‑payable contract receiving ether” bugs, where a contract lacking a payable fallback rejects incoming native token transfers, leading to denial‑of‑service or unexpected reverts. The recommended mitigation is to add a payable receive() external function (or a fallback payable function) to the PausableZone contract so that it can safely accept and forward any unused ETH back to the caller, thereby preserving the intended accounting logic of the trade.

title: ABI decoding for bytes: memory can be corrupted by maliciously constructing the calldata
description:
In the code snippet below, size can be made 0 by maliciously crafting the calldata. In this case, the free memory is not incremented.
```solidity
assembly {
    mPtrLength := mload(0x40)
    let size := and(
        add(
            and(calldataload(cdPtrLength), OffsetOrLengthMask),
            AlmostTwoWords
        ),
        OnlyFullWordMask
    )
    calldatacopy(mPtrLength, cdPtrLength, size)
    mstore(0x40, add(mPtrLength, size))
}
```
This has two different consequences:  
1. If the memory offset mPtrLength is immediately used then junk values at that memory location can be interpreted as the decoded bytes type. In the case of Seaport 1.2, the likelihood of the current free memory pointing to junk value is low. So, this case has low severity.  
2. The consequent memory allocation will also use the value mPtrLength to store data in memory. This can lead to corrupting the initial memory data. In the worst case, the next allocation can be tuned so that the first bytes data can be any arbitrary data.  

To make the size calculation return 0:  
1. Find a function call which has bytes as a (nested) parameter.  
2. Modify the calldata field where the length of the above byte is stored to the new length 0xffffe0.  
3. The calculation will now return size = 0.  
Note: there is an additional requirement that this bytes type should be inside a dynamic struct. Otherwise, for example, in case of function foo(bytes calldata signature), the compiler will insert a check that calldatasize is big enough to fit signature.length. Since the value 0xffffe0 is too big to be fit into calldata, such an attack is impractical. However, for bytes type inside a dynamic type, for example in function foo(bytes[] calldata signature), this check is skipped by solc (likely because it's expensive). For a practical exploit we need to look for such function. In case of Seaport 1.2 this could be the matchAdvancedOrders(AdvancedOrder[] calldata orders, ...) function. The struct AdvancedOrder has a nested parameter bytes signature as well as bytes extraData. In the above exploit one would be able to maliciously modify the calldata in such a way that Seaport would interpret the data in extraData as the signature. Here is a proof of concept for a simplified case that showcases injecting an arbitrary value into a decoded bytes. As for severity, even though interpreting calldata differently may not fundamentally break the protocol, an attacker with enough effort may be able to use this for subtle phishing attacks or as a precursor to other attacks.
bug_full: An ABI decoding flaw exists in contracts that decode a bytes value located inside a dynamic struct or array. The assembly routine reads the length field from calldata, masks it, adds a constant and then copies that many bytes into memory. Because the length is only masked and not validated against the actual calldata size, an attacker can supply a crafted length value such that after the mask the computed size becomes zero. When size is zero the calldatacopy copies no data, but the free‑memory pointer (mload(0x40)) is not advanced. Subsequent writes that rely on this pointer therefore overwrite whatever data previously occupied that memory region. If the overwritten region is later interpreted as a decoded bytes variable – for example the signature or extraData field of an AdvancedOrder struct in Seaport’s matchAdvancedOrders function – the contract will treat arbitrary garbage as a valid signature. This can cause orders to be fulfilled without a genuine authorisation, enable subtle phishing attacks, or serve as a stepping stone for more complex exploits. The issue appears only when the bytes type is nested inside a dynamic struct or array, because the Solidity compiler skips the automatic calldata‑size check for such parameters. From a user’s perspective a transaction may appear to succeed while the UI shows an empty or nonsensical signature field, and assets may be transferred without the expected consent. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the low‑level size calculation and noticed that a zero size does not move the free‑memory pointer. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; the corrupted memory is only observed later when the decoded value is used, which may manifest as unexpected behaviour rather than an explicit error. To remediate the problem the contract should validate that the decoded length is non‑zero and does not exceed the remaining calldata size, and it should always increment the free‑memory pointer even when no bytes are copied. Using Solidity’s built‑in abi.decode or a vetted decoding library eliminates the need for manual assembly and prevents the pointer misuse. In short, the vulnerability is an unchecked length field leading to memory‑pointer misuse, a class of bugs that can corrupt memory and break the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Attempted Out Of Bound Array Access On TWAP Result When Zero Address >= Target Address
description:
Situation:
zeroi can be either 0 or 1, dependant upon the zero address being smaller or equal/larger than its corresponding target address. In the latter case, out of bounds array access is attempted on the results variable, which only returns 1 result. This matches the requested number of queries, which is 1. This out of bounds access leads to a panic code-path and will revert the transaction.
This means any Zero address that has a larger bytes20 representation than its target would be DoS’d from accessing the Zero oracle. Thereby, a number of functionalities for it would never be able to work. In the case of non-deterministic address being used, the chance of this occurring is equivalent to a coin toss, i.e. 50/50.
If it had been deployed in the wild, this may not initially be noticed. Due to the probabilistic nature of this problem, it may go unnoticed, even with some initial successful deployment of Zero contracts. However, when it has been discovered, it would require a pause and redeploy with fix.
References Balancer v2 test snippet confirming behaviour of getTimeWeightedAverage returning 1 result per query: PoolPriceOracle.test.ts#L521-L540.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑bounds array access that occurs in the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle when the zero address used for a price query is larger in its 20‑byte representation than the target address. The contract determines a flag zeroi that can be either 0 or 1 based on the comparison of the zero address with the target address. When zeroi equals 1 the code attempts to read results[1] from the results array, but the array is populated with only a single element (index 0) because the oracle returns exactly one price per query. Accessing index 1 therefore triggers a Solidity panic (array‑out‑of‑bounds) and causes the whole transaction to revert. This bug manifests only for the subset of zero addresses that are greater than their corresponding target addresses, which for uniformly random addresses happens with roughly a 50 % probability. From a user’s perspective the call to the oracle may sometimes succeed and return a price, while other times it reverts with no price, leading to confusing UI behaviour such as “price not available” or “transaction failed”. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: any functionality that relies on the Zero oracle for those address pairs becomes unusable, potentially halting trades, liquidations, or other protocol actions that depend on price data. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle’s getTimeWeightedAverage implementation and confirmed the single‑result behaviour via Balancer v2 test code. Because the failure is probabilistic, early deployments may appear to work correctly and the problem can remain hidden until a failing query is observed, making it hard to notice without exhaustive testing. The root cause is the incorrect assumption that the results array always contains an element at the index indicated by zeroi; the contract does not validate the array length before indexing. To fix the bug the contract should only ever read results[0] and, if a reciprocal price is required, compute it mathematically rather than accessing a non‑existent second element. Adding comprehensive unit tests and fuzzing that cover both ordering cases of the zero and target addresses would prevent similar out‑of‑bounds errors in the future.
