title: Checks In issue() And redeemZero()
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overly restrictive caller validation in the issue() and redeemZero() functions of the Divider contract. When the internal flags level.issueRestricted() or level.redeemZeroRestricted() are true, the code requires that msg.sender be exactly the adapter address, otherwise the call reverts with IssuanceRestricted or RedeemZeroRestricted. The root cause is that the restriction logic does not recognise the Periphery contract, which is also an authorized caller for these operations, as a valid source. Consequently, whenever the flags are enabled – for example after a governance action or an internal state change – any attempt to issue new tokens or redeem zero through the Periphery contract is blocked. An attacker who can trigger the flag (or who relies on the flag being set by design) can cause a denial‑of‑service condition, preventing legitimate users from minting or redeeming via the standard UI. The impact is that users see their transactions revert, receive no newly minted tokens, or get no refund when trying to redeem, contrary to the expectation that the Periphery should always be able to perform these actions. This situation occurs only when the restriction flags are true, which may be a rare path not exercised in normal testing, making the bug hard to notice. The affected parties include token holders, liquidity providers, and any integrator that relies on the Periphery contract for issuance or redemption. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Divider contract by Spearbit, where the extra require statements were flagged as potentially too strict. The bug belongs to the class of overly restrictive access‑control checks, where the allowed caller set is incorrectly narrowed. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction failure with an error message, a missing token balance after a mint attempt, or a zero refund after a redeem attempt, violating the business logic that assumes issuance and zero‑redeem are always possible through the Periphery. The recommended fix is to broaden the require condition to include the Periphery address (or any other authorized contract) or to replace the direct address comparison with a role‑based access control that explicitly lists all permitted callers.

title: Defining Bytes Literals With A String Literal Causes Malformed Bytes
description:
Situation:
The bytes variable is set by a string literal. The variable’s data in this case will be equivalent to the ASCII encoded data of the string, not a hex literal version of it.
This causes the variable to contain malformed bytes which the developer likely didn’t expect. In the best case, it causes unnecessary extra gas cost. Worst case scenario, it could lead to undefined and unexpected effects during contract interaction, especially in the case of said bytes being passed onto other contracts as calldata.
e.g. PoolManager.sol#L185
```solidity
bytes memory constructorData = abi.encode(
    target,
    comptroller,
    targetParams.irModel,
    ERC20(target).name(),
    ERC20(target).symbol(),
    cERC20Impl,
    "0x00", // calldata sent to becomeImplementation (currently unused) L185
    targetParams.reserveFactor,
    adminFee
);
```
The developer would appear to expect bytes as 0x00 to be sent along as calldata, but in fact this would send 0x30783030 as the calldata, the ASCII encoded bytes equivalent of 0x00. The prospective contract this would call out to, for now, appears to essentially ignore these bytes. However, future implementations could end up depending on it which would lead to adverse effects and issues.
One of the on-chain contracts within this call-chain that may use this calldata is an unverified contract on chain, which could lead to issues, but cannot be confirmed due to lack of source code availability.
If this ought to be 0x00, define it using a hex literal as hex'00'.
Periphery.sol#L465
userData: ""
It is an exception from the other mentioned context lines, since it’s just an empty string literal and won’t cause malformed bytes. However, it would still be best practice to define with a hex literal. The malformed bytes issue is why hex literals should be preferred over even hex escaped strings for bytes.
bug_full: The issue originates from using a plain string literal to initialise a variable of type bytes. In Solidity a string literal is interpreted as a sequence of ASCII characters, so the literal \"0x00\" is stored as the four ASCII bytes 0x30, 0x78, 0x30, 0x30 rather than the single zero byte 0x00 that the developer intended. This mismatch produces malformed bytes that are silently accepted by the compiler but change the actual calldata that is forwarded to other contracts. The root cause is a misunderstanding of how Solidity treats string literals versus hex literals, leading to an encoding bug where the contract logic assumes raw byte values while the runtime data contains their textual representation. When such a bytes variable is passed as part of an abi.encode call and later used as calldata for an external contract, the receiving contract sees unexpected data. In the best case the extra bytes only increase gas consumption; in the worst case the receiving contract may reject the call, execute an unintended code path, or mis‑interpret the parameters, potentially causing funds to be locked, transferred to the wrong address, or otherwise mishandled. The vulnerability manifests whenever a developer writes a bytes assignment like \"0x00\" or any other hex‑looking string instead of using a proper hex literal (hex'00') or an explicit escape sequence (\"\\x00\"). Users of the protocol experience symptoms such as transactions that appear to succeed but result in no state change, missing or zeroed return data, or unexplained reverts when interacting with downstream contracts. Because the code compiles without warnings and the visual representation of the literal looks correct, the problem can be hard to notice during testing, especially when the downstream contract currently ignores the malformed calldata. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the construction of calldata in PoolManager.sol and identified that the developer’s intention (sending a single zero byte) did not match the actual bytes emitted. To remediate the issue, all bytes literals should be expressed with hex literals (e.g., hex'00') or, if a string must be used, with proper hex escape sequences (\"\\x00\"). This ensures that the byte sequence matches the intended protocol semantics and prevents accidental data corruption, unnecessary gas costs, and potential downstream contract failures. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of byte‑encoding mistakes where developers confuse textual representations with raw binary data, violating the contract’s accounting assumptions about exact calldata formats and leading to subtle but potentially costly failures.") ,"qna

title: Beware Of Malicious Adapters
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked external adapter pattern in the Periphery contract that allows any address to be passed as an adapter and then grants that adapter unlimited ERC20 allowance. Because the contract does not maintain a whitelist of trusted adapters and does not protect the functions that call the adapter with a nonReentrant guard, a malicious adapter can be supplied by an attacker. When the Periphery contract executes one of the listed functions (such as sponsorSeries, swapTargetForZeros, addLiquidityFromTarget, migrateLiquidity, etc.) it calls safeApprove on tokens whose address is derived from the supplied adapter and often sets the allowance to type(uint256).max. This creates two attack vectors. First, the malicious adapter can immediately call back into the Periphery contract during the same transaction, exploiting the missing reentrancy protection to manipulate internal state or trigger additional token transfers. Second, after the approval is recorded, the adapter can invoke transferFrom at any later time and drain any ERC20 tokens that the Periphery contract holds, including tokens that may be deposited in future operations because the allowance persists. The root cause is the combination of (i) lack of validation of the adapter argument, (ii) granting unlimited token allowance without revoking it, and (iii) absence of a reentrancy guard on functions that interact with the adapter. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract that conforms to the expected adapter interface but contains malicious logic, such as calling back into Periphery or simply pulling the approved tokens. The impact is the potential loss of all tokens stored in the Periphery contract, which translates to users receiving no refunds, swaps completing with zero output, or liquidity being removed without compensation. The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a transaction that passes a malicious adapter address, which can happen both now and in the future because the allowance is not cleared. The affected parties are the protocol participants who rely on Periphery for swaps, liquidity provision, and migration, as well as the protocol itself, whose accounting assumptions are broken when tokens disappear. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the adapter handling code and noticed the missing whitelist and the pattern of approving the adapter for the maximum amount. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when an allowance is set, and the token balances may appear normal until the malicious adapter executes the theft. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a whitelist of vetted adapters, add a nonReentrant modifier to all functions that interact with an adapter, limit the allowance to the exact amount needed for each operation, and avoid keeping any ERC20 tokens in the Periphery contract after an operation completes. By reducing the trust surface and tightening token approvals, the protocol can prevent a malicious adapter from stealing funds and restore confidence in the swap and liquidity flows.

title: Admin Can Always Update lscales Levels
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an administrative backdoor that allows a privileged account to arbitrarily overwrite the per‑user scaling factor (lscale) used by the protocol’s accounting logic. The root cause is the combination of two functions: setAdapter, which can disable an adapter, and backfillScale, which contains a require statement that only checks the adapter flag. When the admin calls setAdapter with isOn set to false, the adapters[adapter] flag becomes false, causing the require(!adapters[adapter] || block.timestamp > cutoff) condition in backfillScale to evaluate to true regardless of the timestamp. This permits the admin to invoke backfillScale and write any values into the lscales mapping for any user and any maturity. Because the collect() function later reads these lscale values to compute how much a user can withdraw, the admin can inflate or deflate a user’s entitled amount at will. The exploit can be performed at any time the admin chooses to turn the adapter off, call backfillScale with crafted arrays of addresses and lscale values, and then re‑enable the adapter. The impact is that users may receive less than their rightful rewards, see their pending balances drop to zero, or conversely be granted excessive payouts, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially leading to fund loss or unintended inflation. The vulnerability affects all participants who rely on the collect() mechanism, including depositors, lenders, and any role that expects the protocol to honor previously accrued balances. It was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the unusual ability of a trusted role to bypass a time‑based guard and directly mutate internal accounting state. The issue can be hard to notice because the functions are protected by a requiresTrust modifier, giving the impression that only a trusted party can call them, and the adapter flag is a binary switch that does not raise alarms when toggled. To remediate, the protocol should either remove the admin’s ability to disable the adapter, restrict backfillScale to immutable or bounded updates, add multi‑signature or timelock controls, or enforce that lscale values cannot be set arbitrarily after deployment. In essence, the bug is a privileged state‑mutation flaw that violates the expectation that lscale values reflect genuine user activity and not admin discretion, leading to potential reward manipulation and loss of trust in the system.

title: Force Claim Collection For Any Address
bug_full: The vulnerability is a forced claim collection mechanism that allows an arbitrary actor to trigger the claim logic of a user’s balance without the user’s consent. It originates from the Claim token contract’s transferFrom function, which unconditionally calls Divider.collect before executing the ERC‑20 transfer. Because the call passes a transfer amount of zero, the ERC‑20 allowance check (allowance == 0 and amount <= allowance) succeeds, and the transfer itself does nothing. However, Divider.collect receives uBalTransfer == 0, interprets this as a request to collect the full balance of the caller (the "from" address) by substituting uBal for the amount parameter in the internal _collect routine. Consequently, any caller can invoke transferFrom with a zero amount and any destination address, causing the Divider contract to execute the claim on behalf of the victim and potentially route the collected funds to an address chosen by the attacker. The exploit works whenever the token contract permits zero‑value transfers, which is a common pattern in ERC‑20 implementations. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a claim is processed at an unexpected time; the user may see a balance change or a claim event they did not initiate, or they may notice that a claim was sent to an address they did not authorize. The business logic assumes that a claim can only be initiated by the token holder or by a trusted contract, but this assumption is broken because the Claim contract delegates claim execution to an external Divider contract without proper access control. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the interaction between Claim.transferFrom and Divider.collect. It can be hard to notice because the zero‑value transfer appears harmless and the collect call does not revert, so normal testing may not surface the unintended side‑effect. To remediate, the contract should separate the concerns of token transfer and claim collection, ensuring that collect can only be called by the token holder or an explicitly authorized entity, and that a zero‑value transfer does not trigger claim logic. Adding explicit checks on the amount parameter, restricting the caller of collect, or removing the collect call from transferFrom would close the attack surface and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Disabled Adapters Should Stay Disabled
description:
Situation:
Anyone can enable an adapter again as soon as someone has disabled the adapter (in whenPermissionless). This circumvents the reason to disable the adapter.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permission‑logic flaw that allows any address to re‑enable an adapter that has previously been disabled through the whenPermissionless entry point. The root cause is that the contract does not keep a permanent record that an adapter has been removed, nor does it enforce a check that prevents a disabled adapter from being added again. An attacker can simply call the enable function after a legitimate disable action, causing the adapter to become active again without any governance or owner approval. This can be exploited by observing a transaction that disables an adapter—often done for security or upgrade reasons—and then immediately submitting a transaction that calls the same function to add the adapter back. Because the enable function is permissionless, the attacker does not need any special role. The impact is that the protocol’s intended safety barrier is bypassed; a compromised or malicious adapter can be re‑introduced, potentially allowing unauthorized token transfers, price manipulation, or other harmful actions that affect all users and the overall integrity of the system. The issue manifests whenever an adapter is disabled in a permissionless context; under those conditions the contract’s state machine treats the adapter as if it were never removed. Users may notice that an adapter they thought was disabled suddenly appears active again in the UI, leading to unexpected behavior such as transactions being routed through a faulty module or funds being processed by a contract that should no longer be trusted. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that examined the lifecycle management of adapters and identified the missing guard. It can be hard to notice because the enable function works correctly for fresh adapters, so the re‑enable path looks identical to a normal addition, masking the fact that a previously disabled component has been resurrected. To remediate, the contract should maintain an immutable “removed” flag for each adapter and reject any attempt to add an adapter that has been marked as removed, or require explicit governance approval for re‑adding. This change restores the intended invariant that once an adapter is disabled, it stays disabled unless a privileged process explicitly overrides the restriction, thereby aligning the implementation with the protocol’s security model and preventing accidental or malicious re‑activation of unsafe modules.

title: Composability of GClaimManager
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the GClaimManager contract depends on the Claim token's transfer and transferFrom functions, which internally invoke Divider.collect. Divider.collect contains a conditional revert that triggers when the claim series is not settled and the current block timestamp exceeds the maturity timestamp plus a sponsor window. Because GClaimManager's join() and exit() functions use safeTransferFrom and safeTransfer to move Claim tokens, any revert inside Divider.collect propagates back and causes the entire join or exit transaction to fail. This breaks the intended composability of GClaimManager, preventing users from joining a claim or exiting their position when the series is in an unsettled state past the sponsor window. The root cause is the coupling of token transfer logic with external accounting logic that can fail, combined with the lack of defensive handling of that failure in GClaimManager. An attacker does not need to actively exploit; the condition can be triggered simply by attempting to join or exit after the sponsor window without the series being settled, causing the transaction to revert and funds to remain locked. The impact is that legitimate users see their transactions revert, receive no tokens, and may lose the ability to retrieve their balances until the series is settled, effectively making funds inaccessible. This occurs whenever join() or exit() is called while the underlying claim series is unsettled and the block timestamp is greater than maturity+SPONSOR_WINDOW. All participants—users, liquidity providers, and the protocol—are affected because the composability promise is broken and the protocol cannot progress. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the call flow from GClaimManager through Claim to Divider and identified the conditional revert in _collect. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens under a specific time‑based condition and the token transfer appears to succeed in normal cases, so tests that do not simulate the post‑window state may miss it. The proper fix is to decouple token transfer from accounting logic, for example by moving the collect call out of the token's transfer functions, adding a non‑reverting fallback, or having GClaimManager handle the potential revert with try/catch and provide a graceful failure path. In general this is a composability‑break bug where external calls in ERC20 transfer can cause unexpected reverts, violating the expectation that token transfers are atomic and always succeed when sufficient balance is present.

title: Reentrancy Safeguards Needed In GClaimManager
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw in the exit function of the GClaimManager contract. The function performs several external calls – collecting a claim, calculating a token balance, transferring tokens from an adapter contract, and transferring the underlying claim token – before it updates the internal accounting by burning the caller’s gclaim tokens. Because the state change (the burn) occurs after these external interactions and the function lacks a nonReentrant guard, a malicious adapter contract can invoke a callback during one of the external calls and re‑enter the exit function. By re‑entering, the attacker can repeat the token transfers while the original burn has not yet reduced the user’s balance, allowing the attacker to withdraw more tokens than entitled. This can be exploited whenever a user calls exit with an adapter that the attacker controls, or in any scenario where an external call triggers code that can call back into GClaimManager. The impact is that funds belonging to honest users may be drained, resulting in missing balances, zero refunds, or unexpected token loss from the protocol’s treasury. The issue manifests under conditions where the exit function is invoked with a crafted adapter address; from a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful claim but the protocol’s token reserves are reduced unexpectedly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that checked for adherence to the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern and noted the absence of a reentrancy guard. It can be hard to notice because the external calls appear legitimate and the final burn seems to happen “at the end,” masking the fact that state is not protected during the earlier calls. The proper mitigation is to apply the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions principle by moving the burn (or any state‑changing operation) before any external call, and to protect the function with a nonReentrant modifier or a mutex. This class of bug – reentrancy – violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a contract’s internal balances cannot be altered by external code during a transaction, leading to money disappearing or refunds failing. Users may experience a situation where they expect to receive their claim tokens but receive zero or less than expected, indicating a breach of the protocol’s financial logic.

title: Do collect() First In GClaimManager
bug_full: The GClaimManager contract contains a logical ordering flaw in its join() function. The function is designed to pull a certain amount of the protocol's target token from the caller in order to back‑fill any excess that should have been returned by previous calls to Divider.collect(). However, the code performs the back‑fill transfer before it invokes Divider.collect(), assuming that the caller already holds enough target tokens to satisfy the back‑fill. If a user has not called collect() for an extended period, or has never called it, their wallet will not contain the required target balance. When join() attempts the safeTransferFrom of the target token, the transfer fails or succeeds with an insufficient amount, leaving the caller unable to complete the join operation. This can cause the transaction to revert, lock the user’s claim tokens inside the contract, or result in a state where the user’s expected refund never arrives. The impact is that legitimate users may lose the ability to join a new adapter, see their claim balances disappear, or experience a denial‑of‑service where the contract refuses further interactions. The issue manifests only after a period of inactivity, making it easy to miss in standard testing that typically exercises the happy‑path where collect() is called immediately before join(). It was identified during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted that the business logic assumes a pre‑existing target balance without enforcing it. The bug belongs to the class of token‑accounting ordering errors, where the sequence of state‑changing calls violates the protocol’s accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “join” button that appears to work, but after confirming the transaction the wallet shows no change in balance and the claim tokens remain stuck, contrary to the expectation that the join will succeed and the user will receive their target refund. To remediate the issue the contract should invoke Divider.collect() at the very start of join() (or otherwise ensure the caller receives any pending target before the back‑fill transfer), thereby guaranteeing that the required target balance is present and preserving the intended accounting flow.

title: Do Not Use abi.encodedPacked With Multiple Dynamically-Sized Types
description:
Situation:
The abi.encodePacked method is called where there are multiple dynamically-sized types. Trying to pack these dynamically-sized types leads to ambiguity in unpacking. This makes it difficult to impossible to unpack, especially in a safe manner. It is made more difficult, in a case like this, because users have some limited input control over the contents passed via the name and symbol parameters. This could present a danger, when the contract becomes permissionless for adding custom zero/claim adapters.
```solidity
bytes memory constructorDataZero = abi.encodePacked(
    zero,
    comptroller,
    zeroParams.irModel,
    ERC20(zero).name(),
    ERC20(zero).symbol(),
    cERC20Impl,
    "0x00",
    zeroParams.reserveFactor,
    adminFee
);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using abi.encodePacked to concatenate several dynamically‑sized values (address, string name, string symbol, etc.) into a single bytes array that is later decoded by another contract. Because abi.encodePacked does not insert length information for dynamic types, the resulting byte stream is ambiguous: the boundary between the name and the symbol cannot be reliably determined when both are variable‑length strings. An attacker who can influence one of the dynamic inputs (for example the ERC20 name or symbol supplied to a zero/claim adapter) can craft a payload where the concatenated bytes are interpreted differently by the decoder, causing the downstream contract to read incorrect parameters. This can lead to the registration of a malicious adapter, misrouting of funds, or execution of unintended logic. The issue appears whenever the constructor or any function builds a packed payload that contains more than one dynamic type and later relies on abi.decode or manual slicing to extract the original values. It is especially dangerous in permission‑less contexts where anyone can supply the name and symbol fields, because the attacker does not need privileged access to trigger the malformed packing. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Sense protocol’s adapter registration code, where the auditor noted that the packed data included two strings and that no length delimiters were present, making safe unpacking impossible. The bug is hard to notice because the packed call does not revert and the resulting bytes look syntactically correct; only when the data is decoded does the ambiguity manifest, often silently producing wrong values. From a user perspective the contract may appear to accept a new adapter but later refunds or claims fail, balances may stay unchanged, or unexpected zero‑address calls may occur, leading to the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the claim returned nothing”. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “packed‑encoding ambiguity” or “dynamic‑type collision” bugs, which violate the assumption that encoded data can be uniquely decoded. The recommended mitigation is to replace abi.encodePacked with abi.encode, which prefixes each dynamic element with its length, and to decode the payload with abi.decode, ensuring that each field can be safely extracted regardless of its size. Using the safer encoding eliminates the ambiguity and prevents an attacker from manipulating the byte layout to hijack adapter registration or fund flow.

title: Imported Trust Contract Has Poor Access Controls
description:
Situation:
This contract gives blanket authority to any and every single account that is trusted. This means full access to any privileged contract functions. It also allows any trusted account to unilaterally set or remove trusted users.
Therefore, if any single trusted account were to ever be compromised, the malicious accounts could lock out all other trusted accounts, including the compromised account, leaving control only in the hands of the malicious actors.
Based on the work-in-progress deployment scripts inspected within the project, the Divider contract would be deployed by an EOA (externally owned account, i.e. regular Ethereum address behind a private key) named deployer, and subsequently another EOA named Dev would be added as an additional trusted user.
If either were to be compromised, which is very well likely to occur with an EOA, it would lead to a compromise of the Divider contract with its privileged functions. The more EOAs are added as trusted users, the greater the risk with this Trust contract.
Additionally, TokenHandler and PoolManager are insofar deployed by an EOA, which becomes their trusted account. Periphery will also depend on a trusted account.
These contracts expose a number of privileged actions to trusted users.
In some cases, the Trust contract is utilized to set the contract that deployed it as its trusted user. In many cases, this will be safer with the assumption that the contract does not have some ability or vulnerability of adding other trusted users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an overly permissive trust model that grants every address listed as a trusted user full authority over all privileged functions of the imported Trust contract and any contracts that rely on it, such as Divider, TokenHandler, PoolManager and Periphery. The root cause is the absence of fine‑grained role based access control; the contract implements a single “trusted” role that can both execute high‑value operations and unilaterally add or remove other trusted addresses. Because the initial deployment is performed by an externally owned account (EOA) and additional EOAs are later added as trusted users, the system relies on the secrecy of private keys that are inherently vulnerable. If any trusted EOA is compromised, an attacker can call the privileged functions, replace the trusted set, and lock out legitimate operators, effectively taking control of the contract. This can be exploited by submitting a transaction from the compromised address that calls the function to remove all other trusted accounts and then adds the attacker’s address as the sole trusted user. Once in control, the attacker may change critical parameters, withdraw funds, or prevent honest users from interacting with the protocol, leading to loss of funds, denial of service, and erosion of trust in the platform. The issue manifests when a trusted account’s private key is leaked, when many EOAs are added as trusted users, or when the contract is used in a context that assumes the trusted entity cannot add new users. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: legitimate users may see transactions revert, expected actions such as deposits or withdrawals failing, or balances appearing unchanged despite successful calls, because the contract’s privileged logic is being hijacked. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined deployment scripts and the Trust library’s access control logic, noting that the same “root” permission is granted to every trusted address without restriction. The flaw is hard to notice because all trusted addresses appear legitimate and the contract does not emit warnings when the trusted set is altered. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to use a robust role‑based access control system where only a multisignature wallet holds the ultimate “admin” role, and separate, limited roles are assigned to other participants. The ability to add or remove trusted users should be restricted to the admin role, and EOAs should be used only for low‑privilege calls. Alternatively, the Trust library could be limited to contract‑to‑contract relationships where the trusted contract cannot modify the trusted set, thereby eliminating the single point of failure.

title: Move The safeApprove() Stake to BaseAdapter.sol and Update the Inheritance in Periphery.sol
description:
Situation:
The inheritance of the BaseAdapter.sol isn’t quite right, which results in a few issues:
Periphery.sol imports Adapter from CropAdapter.sol, while WstETHAdapter.sol inherits directly from BaseAdapter.sol.
The safeApprove() of stake in the constructor for CropAdapter isn’t called for WstETHAdapter.sol.
This means that the Divider cannot transfer the stake, which it tries to do in settleSeries() and backfillScale().
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect inheritance structure among the adapter contracts used by the protocol. The periphery contract imports an adapter implementation (CropAdapter) that inherits from BaseAdapter, while another adapter (WstETHAdapter) inherits directly from BaseAdapter and bypasses CropAdapter. The constructor of CropAdapter contains a call to safeApprove() for the stake token, which grants the Divider contract permission to transfer the staked assets. Because WstETHAdapter does not inherit from CropAdapter, its constructor never executes the safeApprove() call. Consequently, when the Divider attempts to move the stake during the settleSeries() or backfillScale() functions, the transfer fails due to missing allowance. From a user perspective this manifests as series settlement not completing, expected rewards not being distributed, or the protocol appearing to “freeze” the staked balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the inheritance chain and noticed that the safeApprove() logic was not present in all adapters. It is subtle because the contracts compile and run without reverting; the failure only becomes visible when a settlement operation tries to move the stake and the allowance check silently blocks the transfer. The root cause is a design flaw: the approval logic is placed in a subclass constructor rather than in the shared base class, violating the assumption that all adapters will have the same permission setup. The impact is medium‑risk: funds may remain locked in the adapter, users may not receive expected payouts, and the protocol’s accounting can become inconsistent. To remediate, the safeApprove() call should be moved to BaseAdapter so that every adapter, including WstETHAdapter, grants the Divider the required allowance. Additionally, Periphery.sol should be updated to inherit directly from BaseAdapter instead of CropAdapter, ensuring a consistent inheritance hierarchy and eliminating the missing approval path.

title: New 0x transformers are allowed by default, which could lead to unexpected problems
description:
When the controller checks `canCall()` for calls to the 0x contract, it begins by checking that `sig == 0x415565b0`.

If this check fails (ie if any other function is called), the call is not allowed. However, if it passes, all possible calls are allowed. There is no further validation.

The `transformERC20()` function being called takes in some assets, as well as transformer nonces (which are translated to addresses) and calldata to pass to these addresses. The 0x contract then executes these calls and returns the assets to the caller.

The 0x contract has its own logic to ensure that only valid 0x transformers can be called, so there is no risk of malicious addresses being passed. However, because each of these transformers performs a different function, and more transformers can be added at any time, there is a risk that a new transformer will be added that causes unexpected behavior.

As an example, one could imagine a transformer that allows a user to approve an Operator. This Operator could then make calls to 0x on their behalf. If this was possible, all of Sentiment could be drained with the following exploit:
Take a flash loan and deposit a large amount of funds into Sentiment (> 20% of protocol's TVL).
Borrow the maximum amount of funds against it and convert all funds into one token.
Approve 0x to transfer this token on behalf of the Sentiment account.
Call `transformERC20()` with the transformer that sets another Operator.
After the `exec()` call, the account is still healthy, so it's permitted.
From the Operator account, call `transformERC20()` with to pull funds from the Sentiment account, with another non-Sentiment account as the receiver.
Since the call is not coming from Sentiment, there is no way to check account health after it is executed, and the pulled funds represent all of Sentiment's TVL.

While I do not think adding such a feature is likely, it is clear that allowing calls to a contract that implements arbitrary logic is very dangerous. The current architecture leaves the door open for 0x to make changes down the road that will be accepted automatically by the Sentiment protocol without being analyzed and approved by the Sentiment team.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the Sentiment protocol's controller logic that validates calls to the external 0x contract. The controller first checks that the function selector equals 0x415565b0, which corresponds to the transformERC20 entry point. If this selector matches, the controller grants permission for the call without performing any additional checks on the specific transformer that will be executed. Consequently, any transformer that the 0x contract knows about becomes callable, including transformers that may be added in the future. The root cause is an overly permissive allow‑list that relies solely on a single function signature instead of inspecting the concrete transformer address or its intended behavior. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a new transformer that, for example, grants an operator the ability to move tokens on behalf of the Sentiment account. By taking a flash loan, depositing a large amount of assets, borrowing against them, and then invoking transformERC20 with the malicious transformer, the attacker can set an operator, keep the account health check satisfied, and later use the operator to pull the entire protocol TVL to an external address. The impact is a potential total loss of user funds, where balances appear to drop to zero and users receive no tokens after a transaction that seemed legitimate. This scenario occurs whenever the controller’s canCall function sees the approved selector and the 0x contract is instructed to execute an unvetted transformer. All Sentiment users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that only safe, pre‑approved transformations are executed – are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the controller’s permission checks and identified that the signature check does not constrain the downstream logic. The problem is subtle because the presence of a single valid selector gives the impression of a strict whitelist, yet the actual execution path allows arbitrary code, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate, the protocol should implement a granular allow‑list of transformer addresses that have been reviewed and approved, rejecting any unknown transformer by default. This approach restores the intended safety boundary, ensures that only known, safe transformations can be performed, and prevents future additions from introducing unexpected behavior that could drain funds or break accounting invariants.

title: Duplicate Chunk IDs
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑size mismatch in the ChunkProcessor component of the SFT418 contract. Chunk identifiers and owner‑index values are stored as uint32 even though the public ERC‑721 interface uses uint256 for token IDs and balances. When the total number of minted NFTs exceeds the maximum value of a 32‑bit unsigned integer (2^32‑1 ≈ 4.29 billion), the contract silently truncates the higher bits of the token ID and the index during the down‑cast performed in functions such as _pushChunk. This truncation creates duplicate chunk IDs because two distinct uint256 IDs that differ only in the high 224 bits are reduced to the same 32‑bit value. The root cause is the inappropriate down‑casting of IDs and indexes, which violates the ERC‑721 specification that expects each token ID to be globally unique up to type(uint256).max. Exploitation occurs when an attacker or a legitimate user attempts to mint or transfer NFTs beyond the 32‑bit limit; the contract will accept the operation, assign a truncated ID, and may overwrite or collide with an existing token record. The impact includes loss of the non‑fungible property, potential overwriting of ownership data, and a supply cap that is far lower than the protocol advertises, leading to user confusion when expected unique tokens appear duplicated or missing. The condition under which the bug manifests is any minting or chunk‑push operation that results in a token ID greater than type(uint32).max; in typical deployments this threshold is rarely reached, making the issue hard to notice during normal testing. Affected parties are token holders, developers building on SFT418, and any protocol relying on the contract’s claim of ERC‑721 compliance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the chunk manipulation logic, where the down‑cast annotations were flagged as non‑compliant with the ERC‑721 standard. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after a large minting operation the UI may show the correct token count but the displayed token IDs repeat, or a user may receive a token that appears to be a duplicate of an existing one, contradicting the expectation that each NFT is unique. This bug constitutes a supply‑capping and ID‑truncation class of vulnerability, breaking accounting assumptions that each token ID maps to a distinct asset. The recommended remediation is to store chunk IDs and owner indexes using uint256 throughout the contract, or to enforce a hard supply limit that never exceeds the 32‑bit maximum, thereby restoring full ERC‑721 compliance and preventing duplicate identifiers.

title: Reroll becomes unfunctional after all tokens have been minted
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the _reroll function of the SFT418 Native contract, which is intended to give a token holder a 50 % chance of receiving a newly minted chunk when they request a reroll, otherwise swapping the requested chunk with a random one from the pool. The function first checks whether the total number of minted chunks is still below the maximum allowed (maxChunks > mintedChunks). If this condition holds, a random number determines whether a new chunk is minted or a pool swap occurs. However, when the supply is exhausted (mintedChunks equals maxChunks), the outer condition fails and the code falls through to the else‑branch that always attempts a pool swap. This branch unconditionally requires that the pool contain at least one item (require(_poolOwnedLength > 0, "NO_ITEMS_TO_REROLL")). After all chunks have been minted, the pool is often empty because all items have been transferred to users, causing the require statement to revert. Consequently, any attempt to invoke _reroll after the supply cap is reached results in a transaction revert, effectively denying the reroll functionality. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to “do nothing” or to return zero value: a user expects a new chunk or a successful swap, but instead the transaction fails and no tokens are transferred, leaving the user’s balance unchanged while the operation appears to have been accepted by the UI. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents legitimate users from exercising the reroll feature once the token supply is exhausted, breaking the intended game‑like economics and potentially causing confusion or loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a stress test that repeatedly transferred tokens back and forth until mintedChunks reached the maximum value; the test logged a successful run but highlighted that the reroll logic could no longer function, indicating a logical flaw rather than a runtime error. This bug is subtle because the reroll path is rarely exercised after the supply limit is hit, making it easy to miss in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should separate the mint‑and‑swap logic: first evaluate the random chance, then only attempt a mint when the supply limit permits, otherwise fall back to a pool swap only if the pool contains items, and provide a graceful fallback or disable reroll when neither option is viable. In essence, the fix requires restructuring the conditional flow so that the pool‑swap branch is not executed when the supply is exhausted without a valid pool, thereby eliminating the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Missing slippage parameter in buyToken()
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage tolerance in the buyToken function of a token sale contract. The function calculates the exact amount of ETH required for a purchase by calling a pricing routine and then checks that the caller sent at least that amount. Because the contract does not accept a maximum acceptable price deviation, any change in the token price between the moment the user obtains the quote (typically via a UI) and the moment the transaction is mined will cause the require statement to fail and the transaction to revert. The root cause is the absence of a user‑controlled slippage parameter that would allow the transaction to proceed as long as the price stays within an acceptable range. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a front‑running transaction that slightly moves the price upward (or downward) just before the victim’s transaction is included. This sandwich attack creates a price deviation that triggers the revert, causing the victim’s purchase to fail while the attacker profits from the price movement. The impact is that users attempting to buy tokens may see their transactions revert with a “Not enough Ether sent” error even though they supplied the exact amount indicated by the UI. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a failed purchase, no tokens received, and loss of gas fees, which can be confusing and may appear as if the contract is refusing to sell. The issue occurs whenever the sale is active and the contract is deployed on a blockchain with a public mempool that reveals pending transactions, allowing adversaries to observe and react to price queries. All participants who rely on the exact quote – typically early buyers during the initial sale phase – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the buy and sell pathways and noted that the sell function includes a slippage argument while the buy function does not. The problem is subtle because the revert message mentions insufficient ETH rather than a price‑change condition, making it hard to diagnose without inspecting the pricing logic. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “price‑oracle without tolerance” or “missing slippage protection” vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions about deterministic trade execution. To remediate, the contract should be modified to accept a maximum slippage value from the caller, compute the acceptable upper bound for the ETH amount, and revert only if the required amount exceeds that bound, mirroring the safety checks present in the sellToken implementation.

title: Latest tokens bought in the market are more expensive than in the pool
description: The price of the tokens bought in the market increases as the number of tokensSold approaches tradeableSupply. This means that the last tokens bought in the market are ~1% more expensive than the first tokens bought in the pool. Given that the pool is created once all the tradeableSupply is bought, there is an incentive to wait until other users buy the last tokens in the market and buy them in the pool at a lower price.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a pricing misalignment between the on‑chain market and the associated liquidity pool. As the market sells tokens, the contract increases the token price proportionally to the number of tokens already sold, approaching the total tradeable supply. Because the price rises continuously, the final tokens purchased on the market end up roughly one percent more expensive than the first tokens that can be obtained directly from the pool after it is created. The root cause is an arithmetic formula that ties the market price to the cumulative tokensSold without accounting for the pool’s initial pricing model, creating a gap between the market’s last‑stage price and the pool’s entry price. An attacker can exploit this gap by waiting for other participants to purchase the last, overpriced tokens on the market and then immediately acquiring the same amount from the pool at the lower initial pool price, effectively buying the tokens at a discount. This results in a loss of revenue for the protocol and an unfair advantage for users who can time their purchases, potentially draining the market’s intended profit margin. The condition occurs whenever the market reaches near‑full token allocation, i.e., when tokensSold is close to tradeableSupply, and the pool is subsequently instantiated with its original price. All users of the market and pool are affected, especially those who expect a consistent price curve; they may see the price spike unexpectedly and then notice that the same tokens are cheaper in the pool, violating the expectation that later purchases should not be cheaper than earlier ones. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the pricing logic, where the auditor observed the price curve and compared it against the pool’s initialization parameters. It can be hard to notice because the price difference is relatively small (about one percent) and only manifests at the tail end of the sale, a point that many tests may not cover. To remediate, the initial pool price should be calibrated so that the market’s final price does not exceed the pool’s entry price, or the pricing formula should be adjusted to ensure monotonicity and parity between market and pool pricing throughout the sale. This class of bug falls under “price oracle inconsistency” or “pricing curve misalignment,” where the contract’s economic assumptions about token value are broken, leading to arbitrage opportunities and potential loss of trust in the protocol’s fairness.

title: Risk of unaccounted asset removal
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset accounting omission that occurs when a token is removed from the MarginAccount.availableErc20 list. The list is used by the liquidation routine to enumerate which ERC20 balances are considered for debt settlement. If a token is deactivated and removed, its balance remains in the erc20ByContract mapping but is never included in the liquidation loops. As a result the protocol attempts to cover the outstanding debt using only the remaining active tokens. When the remaining collateral is insufficient, the shortfall is transferred from the InsurancePool, effectively shifting user loss to the pool. This can happen whenever the contract owner or an authorized role calls setAvailableErc20 to delete a token before a liquidation is triggered. The affected parties are the margin account owners, who may be liquidated despite holding sufficient assets, and the InsurancePool, which may incur unexpected losses. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the relationship between the availableErc20 array and the liquidation logic. It is subtle because the token balance still appears in the UI and in storage, so users see their tokens but the liquidation calculation ignores them, leading to unexpected zero‑out or partial liquidation. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or whitelist removal bugs where state changes are not reflected in downstream calculations. To fix the problem the contract should either forbid removal of tokens from the availableErc20 list, or modify the liquidation routine to iterate over all stored token balances regardless of their presence in the list, ensuring that every asset remains accountable throughout the account lifecycle. In practice the expected behavior is that a user’s token balance contributes to the liquidation valuation; the actual behavior is that the balance is omitted, causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective and the insurance pool to pay out unexpectedly.

title: Lack of incentives for Liquidation calls
description:
The liquidation operates as follows:
1. All collateral balances owned by the marginAccount are retrieved in the code line MarginAccount#L221-L231.
2. Assets are liquidated for USDC through the ModularSwapRouter::liquidate function, converting the account's holdings into a more liquid form. Code line MarginAccount#L233.
3. Debts in corresponding LiquidityPools are cleared in the code line MarginAccount#L237, using the USDC acquired from liquidation (step 2). If debts exceed the liquidation proceeds, additional funds are drawn from the insurancePool to cover the shortfall (MarginAccount#L293).
The problem is that there is no incentive for calling the MarginTrading::liquidate function, which is crucial for maintaining the financial health of the system. The lack of incentives for initiating liquidation poses several risks:
1. If the value of collateral within a margin account sharply declines, and liquidation is not triggered in a timely manner, the account may become insolvent, threatening the solvency of the InsurancePool contract.
2. Delayed liquidation increases exposure to financial risk, particularly as market conditions fluctuate, potentially degrading the collateral's value further.
3. Simultaneous insolvencies across multiple accounts could destabilize the entire system, highlighting the critical nature of proactive liquidation management.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing economic incentive for callers of the liquidation routine in the margin trading contract. The contract provides a function that can be invoked to liquidate a margin account’s collateral, convert it to USDC, and repay the account’s debt, with any shortfall covered by an insurance pool. However, the code does not reward the caller for performing this operation. Because the caller receives no fee or profit, there is no natural motivation for external actors—such as arbitrage bots, liquidators, or other users—to invoke the function when a position becomes under‑collateralised. The root cause is the absence of a reward‑or‑fee mechanism in the liquidation flow, which leaves the liquidation step economically neutral. An attacker can exploit this by allowing the price of the collateral to drop sharply, creating an under‑collateralised margin account. Since no party is incentivised to call the liquidation function, the account may remain insolvent for an extended period. During this time the insurance pool must continuously cover any debt shortfall, draining its reserves. If multiple accounts become insolvent simultaneously, the insurance pool can be exhausted, leading to a systemic loss of funds and potentially halting the protocol. The impact is that users may see their positions remain open despite being under‑collateralised, they may receive no refund or partial liquidation, and the protocol’s insurance fund can be depleted, jeopardising all participants’ assets. The condition under which the issue manifests is when collateral value falls rapidly and no external actor is willing to trigger liquidation because there is no profit to be earned. The affected parties include margin account owners, the insurance pool, and any users relying on the protocol’s solvency. The problem was identified during a manual security review that examined the liquidation workflow and noted the lack of any fee transfer to msg.sender. Because the function can be called by anyone, the missing incentive is subtle and may not be obvious from a superficial code inspection; the contract appears to have a liquidation path, but the economic model that drives actors to execute it is incomplete. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incentive‑misalignment” or “missing reward for critical maintenance operation” bugs. It violates the business assumption that liquidations will be performed promptly by profit‑seeking participants, breaking the accounting invariant that collateral value plus insurance pool must always cover outstanding debt. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a reward scheme for the caller, such as allocating a configurable percentage of the liquidated assets or a fixed fee in USDC. The reward must be sufficient to cover gas costs and provide a profit margin, thereby aligning participants’ incentives with the protocol’s need for timely liquidation.

title: Potential avoidance of liquidation
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract allows users to supply ERC721 tokens as collateral through the provideERC721 function, but it does not verify whether the supplied token is still a valid option within the protocol. A token is considered valid only if it has a positive payoff amount, is marked as active, and has not expired. Because the function skips this check, a malicious actor can deposit tokens that are expired, inactive, or otherwise worthless. When the margin account becomes eligible for liquidation, the liquidate routine iterates over every stored ERC721 identifier, regardless of its validity, and forwards each ID to the HegicModule liquidate function. The module then performs the same validity test for each token, but the loop has already been executed, meaning that the liquidator must process a potentially large list of useless IDs. This extra processing increases gas consumption and can cause the liquidation transaction to run out of gas or become prohibitively expensive, effectively preventing the liquidation of an under‑collateralised position. Moreover, once an exercised token is re‑deposited, it remains in the account but cannot be withdrawn because the withdrawERC721 function reverts with “token id is not valid”. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that a deposited NFT can be either used to obtain a payoff or withdrawn later, yet the reality is that the token may be locked forever and the account holder sees no balance change or receives a revert when trying to withdraw. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that an exercised ERC721 could be provided again and then become non‑withdrawable, highlighting a logical flaw in the collateral acceptance logic. The vulnerability is subtle because the contract does not outright reject the token at deposit time, and the invalidity only manifests later during liquidation or withdrawal, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The root cause is the absence of a pre‑deposit validity check, which should be enforced by calling a function such as checkValidityERC721 that confirms payoff, activity, and expiration before the token is accepted as collateral. Fixing the issue involves adding a require statement that validates the token ID against the protocol’s rules before it is stored, thereby preventing the introduction of dead collateral and preserving the expected accounting behaviour of the margin trading system.

title: Liquidity pool interest accrual can be manipulated
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the LiquidityPool contract updates its interest accrual state each time the borrow function is executed. When borrow is called, the private routine _fixAccruedInterest recomputes the total borrowed amount and immediately overwrites totalBorrowsSnapshotTimestamp with the current block.timestamp. Because the timestamp is refreshed on every call, even when the caller requests a zero‑amount loan, the variable ownershipTime – defined as block.timestamp minus totalBorrowsSnapshotTimestamp – can be reduced to the smallest possible value (often a single second). The total interest owed is calculated by raising a rate factor to the power of ownershipTime divided by the number of seconds in a year. When ownershipTime is near zero, the exponent approaches zero, the power function evaluates to a value close to one, and the resulting interest increment becomes severely understated. An attacker who can repeatedly invoke borrow with a zero amount, for example through a MarginTrading contract, can therefore keep resetting the timestamp and prevent the pool from accruing the expected interest. When the attacker later takes a genuine loan, the recorded interest to be repaid is lower than it should be, allowing the borrower to repay less than the protocol’s economic model predicts. Liquidity providers experience a loss of expected return because the pool’s interest pool grows more slowly than intended. The issue manifests only under a pattern of frequent, zero‑value borrow calls; under normal usage the interest calculation appears correct, making the problem hard to notice without targeted testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the worst‑case ownershipTime of one second and the resulting precision loss. The bug belongs to the class of economic manipulation bugs where state variables that drive accounting are updated on every call without validating the economic relevance of the call, leading to precision loss and under‑accrual of interest. From a user perspective the symptoms are a borrower receiving a repayment amount that is lower than expected, and pool participants seeing their accrued interest or rewards remain stagnant despite time passing. The recommended mitigation is to reject borrow requests with a zero amount, or to decouple the timestamp update from calls that do not change the net debt, thereby ensuring that interest accrual reflects actual elapsed time and genuine borrowing activity.

title: Free flashloans due to the lack of fee or interest charges
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a free‑flash‑loan condition that arises when the liquidity pool’s interest‑accrual logic depends exclusively on the elapsed time between a borrow and the next snapshot. The pool records a timestamp at the moment the total debt snapshot is taken and calculates accrued interest by multiplying the outstanding principal by a rate that is exponentiated over the time difference (block.timestamp – snapshotTimestamp). If a borrower takes a loan and repays it within the same transaction, the elapsed time is effectively zero, causing the interest formula to evaluate to one and the additional interest term to be zero. Consequently, the debt reported for the borrower and the total pool debt both return the principal amount without any fee or interest charge. An attacker can therefore borrow any amount that the pool holds, use it for arbitrage or other profit‑making actions, and return it in the same transaction while paying nothing. From the user’s perspective the pool appears to lend assets for free; a liquidity provider may see their pool balance unchanged after a large flash loan, but the protocol loses the expected revenue from fees, and the economic model that assumes borrowers pay interest is broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case executed a borrow followed immediately by a repay in a single transaction and observed that the total interest snapshot remained zero. The bug is subtle because the interest calculation works correctly for normal loan durations, and the zero‑time edge case is not obvious from a casual code review. The flaw belongs to the class of “zero‑time interest bypass” or “fee‑less flash loan” bugs, where a contract’s accounting assumes a positive time delta to generate revenue. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a minimal non‑zero fee or interest charge that applies even when the loan is repaid in the same block, or it should prevent the borrow and repay functions from being called within the same transaction, or update the snapshot before the borrow so that any subsequent repayment still incurs a fee. Implementing any of these mitigations would close the free‑flash‑loan loophole and restore the intended economic incentives for liquidity providers and the protocol as a whole.

title: Uniswap V3 quoter contract should not be called on-chain
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the Uniswap V3 quoter contract being invoked directly on‑chain. The two public functions getInputPositionValue and getOutputPositionValue call quoter.quoteExactInput and quoter.quoteExactOutput respectively to obtain an estimated amount of tokens for a swap. These quoter calls are designed for off‑chain price estimation and involve complex path parsing and pool state reads, which consume a large amount of gas. Because the functions are callable from multiple places in the codebase, a single transaction can trigger them repeatedly, inflating the gas consumption of that transaction. When the accumulated gas usage approaches or exceeds the block gas limit, the transaction reverts, effectively denying service to legitimate users. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately invokes the quoting functions many times within a single transaction, causing the contract to hit the gas ceiling and preventing other users from executing swaps. The impact is primarily economic: users experience unexpectedly high transaction fees, swaps may fail with out‑of‑gas errors, and the protocol can be rendered unusable under heavy load, constituting a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue manifests whenever any caller invokes the quoting functions, which includes regular users, liquidity providers, or automated bots that rely on the contract’s price estimation. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditor noted the NatSpec warning that the functions are gas‑intensive and should not be called on‑chain, and subsequent gas profiling confirmed the excessive cost. The problem is subtle because the functions return correct numerical estimates, so the logical correctness appears sound; however, the hidden gas cost only becomes apparent under repeated calls or in a congested network. To remediate the issue, the protocol should be redesigned to avoid on‑chain quoting entirely. A typical mitigation is to replace the quoter calls with an off‑chain price oracle that supplies token valuations, or to rely on the actual output of executed swaps rather than an estimated quote. This eliminates the heavy on‑chain computation, reduces gas consumption, and removes the avenue for a DoS attack based on quote spamming. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a transaction that suddenly consumes a large amount of gas or fails with an out‑of‑gas error, contrary to the expectation that the contract simply returns a swap estimate. The discrepancy between expected low‑cost estimation and the reality of high gas usage breaks the protocol’s accounting assumptions and can lead to funds being locked in failed transactions.

title: Partial repayment is not possible in liquidation if no funds on the insurance pool
description: At the end of the liquidation process, all debts of the account being liquidated are cleared. This is done by repaying the debt in each liquidity pool with the account's funds. If the account is underwater, the remaining funds required to repay the debt are taken from the insurance pool. If the insurance pool does not have enough funds to cover the debt, none of the debt is repaid, and the account collateral can only be used to repay the debt partially if the account's owner calls the repay function. However, there is no incentive for the account owner to do so, as the collateral is locked in the contract.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During the liquidation routine the protocol attempts to clear every outstanding debt of the liquidated account by pulling funds from the account itself and, if necessary, from a shared insurance pool. The implementation assumes that the insurance pool can always cover any shortfall that remains after using the account's own balance. When the insurance pool holds insufficient tokens, the code aborts the repayment for that particular liquidity pool but still proceeds to mark the debt as cleared for the whole account. As a result the account’s collateral remains locked in the contract while the protocol records the debt as repaid even though no funds were transferred. This logical flaw creates a situation where partial repayment is impossible; the protocol either repays the full amount or, if it cannot, repays nothing and leaves the borrower with an unrecoverable shortfall. An attacker can trigger liquidation of an under‑collateralised position at a moment when the insurance pool is depleted, causing the protocol to record a zero debt while the borrower’s collateral stays immobilised. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the debt has been cleared, yet the collateral cannot be withdrawn and the account balance appears unchanged or zero, leading to confusion and loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow where the conditional handling of the insurance‑pool shortfall was examined. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and emits no explicit error; the state change looks successful, but the accounting invariants are violated – the sum of outstanding debts no longer matches the actual assets held. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete repayment” or “partial settlement” errors where a financial protocol fails to correctly account for insufficient backing assets. To remediate the problem the liquidation logic should be altered to allow whatever amount can be covered by the account’s balance and the remaining insurance pool to be applied, updating the debt amount accordingly, or to skip clearing the debt for pools that cannot be fully repaid and leave the debt outstanding. This ensures that the protocol’s accounting stays consistent, that borrowers can still retrieve any unlocked collateral, and that bad debt is either absorbed transparently or recorded for later handling.

title: Borrowers can be left with debt shares after full repayment
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting inconsistency that can leave a borrower with a non‑zero debt‑share balance even after the borrower has repaid the full principal amount. The root cause is the integer division used to compute the variable shareChange inside the repay function. The expression (amount * debtSharesSum) / newTotalBorrows truncates any fractional part, effectively rounding the result down. Because the contract tracks both absolute debt amounts and proportional debt shares, the rounded‑down shareChange may be slightly smaller than the exact proportional reduction that the repayment should represent. Consequently, after the state updates – totalInterestSnapshot, debtSharesSum and the borrower’s shareOfDebt – the borrower’s shareOfDebt entry can retain a tiny positive value. This leftover share can continue to accrue interest or be considered outstanding debt by downstream logic, such as liquidation checks. The issue manifests whenever a repayment amount does not divide evenly into the total debt share pool, which is common for most realistic repayment sizes. From a user’s perspective the UI may still display a small debt balance or show that the borrower is still liable for interest, contradicting the expectation that the loan is fully settled. The impact includes potential over‑charging of interest, inaccurate liquidation triggers, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, which could erode user trust and lead to financial loss if the leftover shares are later seized. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the repay logic and identified the rounding down behaviour as a source of discrepancy. It can be hard to notice because the residual share is often very small and may only appear after multiple repayments or when inspecting low‑value accounts. The class of bug is a rounding error caused by integer division in financial accounting, a common issue in smart contracts that track proportional ownership or debt shares. To remediate the problem the protocol should either eliminate the dual tracking of absolute debt and debt shares, or replace the truncating division with a rounding‑up or exact arithmetic method (for example using a higher‑precision library or adjusting the formula to ensure the shareChange fully covers the repaid amount). Ensuring that after a full repayment the borrower’s debt‑share balance is forced to zero restores the intended business logic that a repaid loan leaves no residual obligations.

title: Borrowers can leave unpaid dust
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the debt valuation logic of the MarginTrading protocol that can leave a borrower with a non‑zero amount of debt that is valued as zero in the base token (USDC). The contract calculates the portfolio ratio by dividing the total value of the account’s assets by the total debt with accrued interest, both expressed in USDC. Debt is obtained by iterating over each borrowed token and converting the owed amount to USDC via the getInputPositionValue function. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, a very small amount of a borrowed token can be converted to a USDC value of zero. When this happens, debtWithAccruedInterest becomes zero, the require statement in _calculatePortfolioRatio only checks that the asset value multiplied by a coefficient is greater than zero, which is always true, and the function returns a ratio that appears healthy. Consequently, functions such as withdrawERC20, withdrawERC721, borrow and liquidate believe the account is fully collateralised and allow the user to withdraw all collateral without repaying the residual debt. An attacker can deliberately borrow a tiny amount of a token, wait for the conversion to round down, and then extract the entire collateral, leaving a “dust” amount of unpaid debt that continues to accrue interest. The impact is loss of protocol funds, under‑collateralised positions, and erosion of lender confidence. The issue manifests only when the borrowed amount is small enough that its USDC valuation rounds to zero, which can be hard to notice because the residual debt is invisible in the UI and the portfolio ratio check seems to pass. The bug affects any user who can open a margin account, the protocol’s risk model, and any party relying on the correctness of the collateralisation check. It was discovered during a manual audit of the ratio calculation and the token‑to‑USDC conversion routine. The problem is subtle because the code appears to enforce a strict >0 relationship, yet the rounding hides the debt. To remediate, the contract should verify that the raw debt amount in the original token is zero before allowing a full withdrawal, or use a rounding method that never yields zero for non‑zero debt (e.g., ceiling division or a minimum debt threshold), and ensure that debtWithAccruedInterest reflects any outstanding token balances regardless of conversion size. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that collateral can only be removed when all debt is fully repaid, preventing funds from disappearing due to rounding‑induced dust.

title: New liquidity providers are unfairly charged
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the liquidity pool that causes new liquidity providers to receive fewer assets than they are entitled to. The contract computes the total liquidity as the sum of the pool token balance and the total amount borrowed, where total borrows includes both the net debt and the accrued interest. However, a portion of the accrued interest is automatically transferred to an insurance pool as a fee. Because the fee is not subtracted from the total liquidity value, the getTotalLiquidity view returns a figure that is artificially inflated by the amount that will later be removed. When a provider calls the provide function, the share of LP tokens they receive is calculated using this inflated totalLiquidity, effectively diluting their ownership share. Later, when the provider withdraws, the withdraw calculation again uses the inflated totalLiquidity, causing the provider to receive less than the proportional amount of underlying assets. The impact is that later providers lose a fraction of their deposited capital, as illustrated by the example where Provider B loses 0.5 WETH. The issue occurs whenever interest has accrued and part of that interest is sent to the insurance pool, i.e., after any borrowing activity that generates interest. All liquidity providers, especially those who add liquidity after interest accrual, are affected, as are borrowers who rely on correct pool accounting. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between totalBorrows, interest accrual, and the insurance fee, noticing that the fee was not accounted for in the liquidity denominator. It can be hard to notice because the totalLiquidity value appears reasonable and the fee transfer is a separate internal operation, so the discrepancy is hidden from a superficial view of balances. The flaw belongs to the class of fee‑double‑counting or share‑dilution bugs, where a fee is counted both as part of the pool’s assets and then removed, breaking the invariant that each LP token represents a fixed proportion of the pool. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a withdrawal amount that is lower than the deposited amount despite no explicit fee, and an unexpected loss of a small fraction of capital. The contract violates the business logic that liquidity providers should receive a share of the pool proportional to their contribution after accounting for any fees. The correct mitigation is to exclude the insurance fee from the totalLiquidity calculation used in both the provide and withdraw functions, ensuring that only the assets that remain in the pool are used to determine share ratios. This restores the accounting invariant and prevents new providers from being unfairly charged.

title: Option NFTs that go in the money after liquidation can be locked
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of option NFTs during the liquidation process in a modular swap router and a margin account contract. When the liquidation function in the router iterates over a list of option token IDs, it only transfers the NFT back to the holder if three conditions are simultaneously true: the payoff amount is greater than zero, the option is still marked as active, and the expiration timestamp has not been reached. If any of these checks fails—most commonly because the option is out‑of‑the‑money at the moment of liquidation—the function skips the transfer step and leaves the NFT inside the MarginAccount contract.
