The root cause is the assumption that the try‑catch block surrounding the lockbox.withdrawTo call will always have enough gas to execute the catch branch, even when the try statement fails after consuming most of the allotted gas. If the external lockbox contract reverts at the last possible moment – for example because the token is paused or the withdrawal logic runs out of gas itself – the catch clause must perform a safeTransfer and emit an event, which together require additional gas that the stipend does not provide. When the gas runs out, the entire cross‑chain call reverts and cannot be retried, leaving the tokens that were minted to the bridge contract effectively locked and unrecoverable. From a user’s point of view, a sender initiates a bridge transfer expecting the wrapped tokens to appear on the destination chain, but the balance remains unchanged and no refund is received, violating the expectation that “my funds arrive on the other side”. The impact is a loss of funds for any user whose transfer triggers the failure path, as well as a breach of the bridge’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only when a lockbox address is set and the withdrawal fails under high‑gas consumption scenarios; it does not appear when the lockbox is absent or when withdrawals succeed. It was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime when a test case (test_receiveToken_succeeds_insolvent_lockbox) was modified to use the 180 000 gas stipend and the transaction reverted. The problem is hard to notice because the out‑of‑gas revert does not emit a distinct error message – it simply fails, making debugging ambiguous. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑stipend underestimation errors, where a contract assumes a fixed gas amount for a downstream call and its error handling, ignoring variability in external contract implementations and opcode pricing. To remediate, the bridge should increase the gas stipend for the receiveToken call, preferably making it configurable by an admin so it can be adjusted for different token contracts or chain upgrades. Alternatively, the contract could use a low‑level call with a dynamic gas amount or implement a retry mechanism for failed withdrawals, ensuring that the catch logic always has sufficient gas to execute and that funds are either transferred or safely refunded.

title: Empty Committee Is Accepted In Validium Setup
description: Setting up the Validium rollup signing committee is achieved by calling setupCommittee(). Due to a lack of input validation it is possible to register an empty committee. An empty committee occurs when following parameters are submitted. _requiredAmountOfSignatures = 0 urls.length = 0 addrsBytes.length = 0 Any existing members will be removed and no new members are added. The result is that any sequenced batches will pass the Validium signatures checks without the need for a committee to sign the message. The issue may be exploited since CDKDataCommittee.verifySignatures() is called with requiredAmountOfSignatures = 0. Thus, passing an empty signaturesAndAddrs will successfully verify the signedHash.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an improperly validated committee configuration in a Validium rollup contract. When the function that creates or updates the signing committee is called, it accepts three parameters – the required number of signatures, a list of member URLs and a list of member address bytes – without checking that any of these values are non‑zero. Consequently an attacker can invoke the setup routine with requiredAmountOfSignatures set to 0 and both the URLs and address arrays empty, which causes the contract to delete any previously stored committee members and replace them with an empty set. Because the signature verification routine later checks the required amount of signatures against the supplied signatures, a required amount of zero means that an empty signatures array is considered valid, allowing any sequenced batch to pass the CDKDataCommittee.verifySignatures check without any real signatures. This bypass can be exploited by an adversary who first clears the committee and then submits malicious batches that are accepted as if they were properly signed. The impact is that the rollup loses its core integrity guarantee: unauthorized state transitions, fund transfers or data updates can be recorded without any cryptographic endorsement, effectively letting an attacker rewrite the rollup history. The condition occurs whenever the committee‑setup function is called with zero‑length inputs, which may happen during contract initialization, upgrades or administrative re‑configuration. All participants that rely on the rollup’s security – users, relayers, and the bridge that moves assets between layers – are affected because they assume that batches have been signed by a quorum of trusted committee members. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the input validation of administrative functions and noticed that the requiredAmountOfSignatures parameter was not constrained. It is easy to miss because the function appears to succeed and emits no error, and the contract’s normal operation (batch acceptance) continues without obvious visual cues; the missing signatures are not logged or displayed in the UI. From a user’s perspective, transactions that should have required a delay for signature collection are confirmed instantly, leading to confusion when expected safeguards do not appear. The bug belongs to the class of “missing authority validation” or “empty authority bypass” where a critical access‑control list can be cleared, allowing operations to proceed unchecked. To remediate, the setupCommittee routine should enforce that the member list is non‑empty and that requiredAmountOfSignatures is greater than zero before overwriting the stored committee, thereby preserving the invariant that at least one signature is required for batch verification.

title: Aggregator Rewards Are Averaged Across Forced Batches & Rollups
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a design where a single batch fee is shared across every rollup that the sequencer processes, and aggregator rewards are calculated by dividing the total POL balance of the contract by the number of sequenced batches without distinguishing which rollup contributed the fee. Because the batch fee is adjusted according to overall network throughput, a rollup that generates a large volume of transactions pushes the fee upward for all other rollups, even those with very low activity. When the fee rises, the sequencer raises the L2 gas price that users must attach to their transactions, so a user on a low‑throughput rollup may see an unexpectedly high gas cost or may have their transaction rejected because the supplied fee is insufficient. At the same time, the reward function `calculateRewardPerBatch` simply returns `currentBalance / totalBatchesToVerify`, meaning that the amount an aggregator receives for verifying a batch is an average of all fees collected, not the exact fee that was paid for that specific batch. Consequently, when a forced batch is sequenced with a higher fee, the aggregator does not receive the full amount that was paid, and if the batch fee later drops, the aggregator may be over‑rewarded relative to the original cost. This misalignment breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol: users expect to pay a fee that directly funds the aggregator who secures their batch, and aggregators expect to be compensated proportionally to the work they perform. The issue manifests whenever there is heterogeneous throughput among rollups, when forced batches are used, or when the batch fee fluctuates between sequencing and verification. All participants—regular users, rollup operators, and aggregators—are affected because users experience higher-than‑expected transaction costs and aggregators receive rewards that do not reflect the actual fees they helped collect, potentially discouraging participation and reducing overall security. The problem was identified during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, which noted that the averaging logic masks the per‑rollup fee contribution and makes the reward calculation appear correct while actually being economically inaccurate. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit per‑rollup accounting events, and the fee increase is reflected only in the L2 gas price, which can be attributed to normal market dynamics. To remediate, the fee and reward mechanisms should be modularised so that each rollup maintains its own batch fee and POL contribution accounting, and aggregators are rewarded based on the exact fee associated with the batch they verify. If full modularisation is too costly, the protocol should at least document the averaging behaviour so aggregators are aware that forced batch rewards may be lower than the fee paid, thereby aligning expectations with reality.

title: Batch Fees Multiplier Cap Bypassed With Multiple Calls
description: The aggregators who verify batches by posting zero-knowledge proofs on-chain are compensated by a fee paid by the sequencer. This fee is updated when a non-trusted aggregator verifies a batch so that it remains competitive. Depending on if more batches are late or early the _batchFee will be adjusted down or up. There is a maximum multiplier size to prevent the batch fee moving too much in one verification call. However, it is trivial to bypass this maximum multiplier. An attacker will check if the number of new batches to be verified exceeds _MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER in size, if so they split the total batches to verify into _MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER segments. By splitting verification into segments with _MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER batches, an aggregator can ensure they receive the maximum increase in batch fees. However, the L1 gas fees will increase for the aggregator as the FFLONK verification must occur for each new segment. When more than _MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER are available for sequencing and are late, the aggregator has the option to pay more L1 gas fees and increase the batch fee. This would increase future rewards for all aggregators. Likewise, when an aggregator detects that early batches have occurred which will decrease batch fee they may include the maximum possible number of batches in one transaction to limit the decrease. However, in a decentralised aggregator environment, delaying submitting batches to limit the fee decrease may result in other aggregators first calling verifyBatches() to claim the rewards. This will result in less control over batch fees paid by the sequencer and may lead to the sequencer not realising a profit in extreme cases. As a knock-on effect the sequencer is then less financially motivated to batch user transactions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the mechanism that adjusts the batch fee paid by the sequencer to aggregators when a non‑trusted aggregator verifies a batch of transactions. The contract stores a maximum multiplier (_MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER) that is intended to limit how much the fee can change in a single verification call. However, the logic only enforces the cap on a per‑call basis and does not track the cumulative effect across multiple calls. An attacker can therefore split a large set of new batches into several verification transactions, each containing exactly _MAX_BATCH_MULTIPLIER batches. Because each call is evaluated independently, the fee is increased by the maximum allowed amount each time, effectively bypassing the intended overall cap. This can be exploited whenever the number of pending batches exceeds the multiplier limit; the attacker repeatedly invokes the verifyBatches function with appropriately sized segments, paying additional L1 gas for each verification but receiving a proportionally larger fee increase. The impact is a systematic inflation of the batch fee, which reduces the sequencer’s net profit and may distort the economic incentives for both aggregators and end‑users. Users may notice higher transaction costs or lower rewards than expected, while aggregators see unexpectedly large fee payouts. The issue manifests only under conditions where many batches are late or early and the attacker can control the size of each verification segment. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑adjustment logic and identified that the cap was not enforced globally. The problem is subtle because each individual fee change appears legitimate and stays within the documented limit, making it hard to detect through simple monitoring. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a cumulative cap on fee adjustments, for example by limiting the total multiplier increase per block, per timestamp, or per a fixed number of verified batches, thereby preventing repeated maximal increases from a single batch set. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “per‑operation limit bypass” where a constraint intended to protect a global invariant is applied only locally, allowing an attacker to achieve the same effect through repeated actions.

title: Missing ifNotEmergencyState Modifier
description: The system contains an emergency mode which pauses functionality across multiple contracts. This emergency mode can be activated manually or through the discovery of a soundness bug to protect assets during a security incident. Most importantly, functionality for the claimAsset() and claimMessage() functions is paused when the emergency state is active. For consistency, bridgeAsset(), bridgeMessage() and bridgeMessageWETH() are also meant to be paused. However, for these latter two functions the ifNotEmergencyState modifier is missing, meaning that they will continue to function when the emergency state is active.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an omission of the emergency‑state guard on two bridge functions, allowing them to be executed while the system is in emergency mode. The contract implements an emergency flag that, when set, should pause all user‑facing operations that move assets or messages across the bridge. The pause is enforced by the ifNotEmergencyState modifier, which is correctly applied to claimAsset(), claimMessage() and bridgeAsset(). However, the bridgeMessage() and bridgeMessageWETH() functions lack this modifier, so they remain callable even when the emergency flag is active. This oversight originates from a simple coding mistake: the developer forgot to attach the same protective modifier to the latter two functions, creating an inconsistency in the contract’s access control logic. An attacker or any user can invoke bridgeMessage() or bridgeMessageWETH() during an emergency, thereby bypassing the intended safeguard and potentially moving messages or associated funds while the protocol is supposed to be frozen. The impact is that assets that should be protected by the emergency pause may be transferred out of the bridge, undermining the security guarantees promised to users and exposing the protocol to loss of funds or manipulation of state. The condition under which this occurs is any scenario where the emergency flag has been triggered, either manually by governance or automatically after detection of a critical bug. All participants who rely on the emergency pause – including token holders, message senders, and the protocol’s governance – are affected because the pause no longer provides comprehensive protection. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit performed by SigmaPrime, which compared the modifier usage across related functions and identified the missing guard. Because the pause appears to work for most functions, the inconsistency can be subtle and may not be noticed during routine testing or by users who only observe the UI indicating a paused state. From a user’s perspective, the interface may display that the bridge is paused, yet a transaction to bridge a message still succeeds, leading to confusion such as “my bridge still works even though it says paused” or “funds disappear after I try to bridge during emergency”. This violates the business logic that emergency mode should freeze all cross‑chain activity, breaking accounting assumptions that no state changes occur while the system is in a protected state. The recommended remediation is to add the ifNotEmergencyState modifier to both bridgeMessage() and bridgeMessageWETH() so that they respect the emergency flag, thereby restoring uniform pause behavior across the entire bridge contract.

title: Rollups Can Be Overwritten Without Checks
description: It is possible to overwrite an existing rollup by calling addExistingRollup() with a rollup address relating to an existing rollup. This then allows the user to arbitrarily overwrite the other parameters stored about a rollup in PolygonRollupManager. If done on an existing rollup, then rollupAddressToID will be overwritten for this address and cannot be reset to its original value without a contract upgrade. It is worth noting that this is an access-controlled function that is normally only accessible to the timelock contract and requires a different chainId to the existing value to succeed. Hence, the risk of this bug occurring is low.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the addExistingRollup() function of the PolygonRollupManager contract. This function is intended to register a new rollup by storing its address, chain identifier and a set of configuration parameters. However, the implementation does not verify whether the supplied rollup address is already present in the rollupAddressToID mapping. As a result, an attacker who can invoke addExistingRollup() with a rollup address that already exists can overwrite the stored parameters for that rollup, including the mapping from address to internal rollup identifier. The root cause is the missing existence check – the function assumes that the caller will only provide previously unseen addresses, but the contract does not enforce this invariant. Exploitation proceeds by calling addExistingRollup() with a valid existing rollup address while providing a different chainId value; the function updates the mapping, replacing the original rollupID with a new one. Because the mapping is overwritten, the original rollupID becomes inaccessible and cannot be restored without redeploying or upgrading the contract. The impact is that the bridge’s accounting for that rollup becomes corrupted: deposits, withdrawals or cross‑chain messages that rely on the original rollup identifier may be routed to the wrong rollup or rejected, effectively causing funds to become stuck or mis‑attributed. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as missing balances, zero refunds, or transactions that never complete when interacting with the affected rollup. The condition under which the bug can be triggered is when the caller has permission to execute addExistingRollup() – in the current design this is limited to the timelock contract – and supplies a chainId that differs from the stored value. Although the access control reduces the likelihood of accidental misuse, any compromise of the timelock or a malicious governance proposal could enable the overwrite. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined state‑modifying functions for proper validation of input data. It is subtle because the function succeeds without reverting, and the overwritten mapping does not emit an explicit event indicating a conflict, making the problem hard to notice in routine testing. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing existence checks leading to state overwrite” vulnerabilities, where a contract fails to protect unique identifiers from being reassigned. The recommended remediation is to add a guard that checks rollupAddressToID[providedAddress] == 0 before performing the registration, and to reject calls that attempt to reuse an existing address. Optionally, emitting an event on successful registration and enforcing that the chainId matches the stored value would further harden the logic and provide visibility into any attempted overwrites.

title: Empty Forced Batch Event Will Look Like It Came From An EOA
description: If a batch is forced with transactions.length = 0, it will emit the same event with the same data whether msg.sender == tx.origin is true or false. Since the msg.sender is not equal to tx.origin the batch data will not be available in the transaction calldata. Instead, any attack controlled data will exist in the transaction calldata. The comments around line [632-636] indicate that this may cause issues with the off-chain monitoring. When attempting to fetch the batch transaction data from the transaction calldata it will return incorrect results causing the aggregators to halt.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract function that allows a batch of transactions to be forced without validating that the batch actually contains any transactions. When an attacker calls this function with an empty transaction array (transactions.length == 0), the contract still emits the standard batch event. Because the caller is a contract (msg.sender) and not an externally owned account (tx.origin), the batch data that would normally be placed in the transaction calldata is absent. Instead, any attacker‑controlled payload ends up in the raw calldata of the transaction, which off‑chain monitoring tools expect to contain a well‑formed batch payload. These tools therefore attempt to decode the calldata, receive incorrect or empty results, and consequently halt aggregation or processing of further batches. The issue was identified during a security audit (SigmaPrime) where comments near lines 632‑636 highlighted the mismatch between the emitted event and the missing calldata. It is subtle because the emitted event looks identical to a legitimate batch event, so on‑chain observers see no anomaly, while off‑chain services silently fail. The impact is primarily on protocol reliability: aggregators and monitoring services stop working, which can delay or prevent the processing of legitimate batches and affect users who rely on timely bridge operations. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation failures where empty or malformed data is accepted, leading to a breakdown in off‑chain accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the forced batch contains at least one transaction (transactions.length > 0) before emitting the event, thereby guaranteeing that the expected calldata is present and that off‑chain components can correctly reconstruct the batch data.

title: Token Wrapped Creation Code Is Not Deterministic
description: The creation code for the smart contract TokenWrapped will change when using a new compiler or modifying any metadata associated with the contract. The variable type(TokenWrapped).creationCode is used to deterministically calculate the address of wrapped ERC20 tokens. However, when upgrading to version 2 of the bridge the value of type(TokenWrapped).creationCode will change. This occurs due to two reasons, first a new compiler is used which outputs different bytecode and second, the smart contract metadata such as directory structure has changed and this will be included in the bytecode. The impact is that wrapped token addresses on other chains can no longer be pre-calculated. Furthermore, precalculatedWrapperAddress() will not return the correct address.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the non‑deterministic creation code of the TokenWrapped contract used by the cross‑chain bridge. The bridge relies on the Solidity expression type(TokenWrapped).creationCode to compute a deterministic address for each wrapped ERC20 token via CREATE2, allowing the address to be pre‑calculated off‑chain. After upgrading the bridge to version 2 a new compiler version was used and the contract metadata (such as directory layout) changed, both of which alter the bytecode emitted by the compiler. Because type(TokenWrapped).creationCode reflects the compiled bytecode, its value changed, causing the address derived from CREATE2 to differ from the one that was originally expected. This mismatch means that the function precalculatedWrapperAddress() returns an incorrect address and any off‑chain calculations of wrapped token addresses become invalid. The impact is that users and bridge operators can no longer locate the correct wrapped token contract on the destination chain; deposits may be sent to a non‑existent address, withdrawals may fail, and the UI may show missing tokens or zero balances even though funds were locked on the source chain. The issue manifests only after the bridge upgrade or any change that modifies the compiled bytecode, affecting anyone who interacts with wrapped tokens – token holders, bridge relayers, and protocol developers. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the address‑derivation logic and noticed the reliance on a value that is not guaranteed to stay constant across compiler versions. The bug is subtle because developers often assume that the creation code of a contract is immutable once the source is written, and the discrepancy only appears when the address is calculated off‑chain rather than during on‑chain deployment, making it easy to miss in functional testing. Conceptually, this is a class of deterministic‑address bugs where the inputs to CREATE2 are not stable, breaking the accounting assumption that a token’s wrapped contract address can be derived solely from its source token identifier. To remediate the issue the contract should store the original version‑1 creation bytecode in a constant bytes variable and use that constant when deploying new TokenWrapped instances via assembly and the CREATE2 opcode, thereby decoupling the address calculation from compiler‑specific bytecode generation. This approach restores predictability of wrapped token addresses and prevents future mismatches caused by compiler upgrades or metadata changes.

title: Service fees should depend on asset
description: Service fees are fixed, but they should depend on the asset, as their price differs significantly. Users are likely to arbitrage this.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a service fee that is applied as a constant amount regardless of which asset a user interacts with. The root cause is that the contract stores a single fixed fee value instead of a per‑asset fee structure, ignoring the fact that different tokens have widely varying market prices. When a user submits a transaction using a low‑value asset, the fixed fee represents a much larger proportion of the transaction value than when a high‑value asset is used, creating a price‑based arbitrage window. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly performing operations with assets whose market price makes the fixed fee disproportionately cheap, effectively extracting value from the protocol or other users. The impact is economic: the protocol may lose revenue, users may receive less service for the same fee, and the overall token economics can become distorted. This condition occurs whenever the contract supports multiple assets with differing USD values while still charging a single static fee. All participants who rely on the service – end‑users, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the fee model does not reflect the true cost of processing each asset. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the fee calculation logic, where the auditor noted that the fee does not reference any price feed or asset‑specific mapping. Because the contract still executes successfully and does not revert, the problem can be hard to notice without a detailed economic analysis; the code appears functional, yet the business rule of proportional fees is violated. To remediate, the contract should replace the fixed fee with a mapping that stores a distinct fee for each supported asset, ideally derived from a reliable price oracle or a configurable table, ensuring that the fee scales with the asset’s market value. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that fees reflect the value of the processed asset, eliminating the arbitrage opportunity and restoring economic fairness.

title: CurveAddLiquidityAssetManager::curveAddLiquidity() does not deal correctly with isLegacy = 0b10 and ETH
description:
If isETH, but args.isLegacy is 1, it wraps to weth and allows pool, see here. 
if args.isLegacy is 0b10 and the asset is ETH, it does not send ETH to the pool, here. 
Additionally, it seems that it expects the ether balance to increase, which is unexpected, 
mintAmount = address(this).balance - initAmount;, as can be seen here.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CurveAddLiquidityAssetManager contract, specifically in the curveAddLiquidity() function when the caller supplies native Ether and sets the isLegacy flag to the binary value 0b10 (decimal 2). The function is designed to forward the supplied asset to a Curve pool and then calculate the amount of LP tokens minted by subtracting the pool’s initial LP balance (initAmount) from the contract’s post‑call balance (mintAmount). For ERC20 assets and for the legacy flag values 0 and 1, the code correctly wraps Ether to WETH or forwards the token, and the balance‑based calculation works as intended. However, when isLegacy equals 0b10 and the asset is Ether, the implementation fails to actually send the Ether to the Curve pool. Instead, it mistakenly relies on the contract’s Ether balance increasing after the call – it computes mintAmount as address(this).balance‑initAmount. Because no Ether is transferred, the contract’s balance does not change, resulting in mintAmount being zero or otherwise incorrect. This mismatch means that the user who expected to add liquidity receives no LP tokens, while the transaction may still be considered successful from a blockchain perspective. The root cause is an incorrect handling of the isLegacy flag combined with an assumption that the pool will increase the contract’s Ether balance, which is not true for this flag value. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) can invoke curveAddLiquidity() with isLegacy set to 0b10 and attach Ether. The function will execute without reverting, but the pool will not receive the Ether and the LP token accounting will be wrong, leading to a loss of expected liquidity and potentially confusing accounting for the protocol. The impact is that users adding liquidity with Ether under this flag receive no LP tokens, their funds appear to be locked or vanished, and the protocol’s accounting tables become inconsistent. This condition only occurs when the asset is native Ether and the isLegacy flag is exactly 0b10; all other asset types or flag values behave correctly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noticed that the code path for isLegacy==0b10 does not contain a payable call to the pool and that the balance‑based mintAmount calculation relies on an unexpected Ether balance increase. The bug is subtle because the function otherwise appears to succeed, and the missing Ether transfer is not obvious without tracing the call. To remediate, the function should either forward the Ether to the Curve pool using a proper payable call (e.g., pool.add_liquidity{value:msg.value}(...)) or, more robustly, compute mintAmount based on the LP token balance before and after the pool interaction (using IERC20(lpToken).balanceOf) rather than the contract’s Ether balance. Additionally, the handling of the isLegacy flag should be clarified and validated so that each flag value follows a well‑defined asset‑transfer path. In summary, the bug is a legacy‑flag‑specific Ether forwarding error that leads to incorrect LP token minting, causing users to receive no liquidity tokens despite sending Ether, and it can be fixed by correcting the asset transfer logic and using token‑balance based accounting.

title: Uniswap asset managers are missing slippage checks
description:
All Uniswap interactions are missing a deadline argument and are not setting the following slippage protection arguments in UniswapLiquidityAssetManager:
- amount0Min and amount1Min in MintParams.
- amount0Min and amount1Min in DecreaseLiquidityParams.
UniswapSwapAssetManager sets the minAmountOut value, but is not signed by the user in the circuit, so it could be gamed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the contract components that interact with the Uniswap V3 router. When adding liquidity, removing liquidity, or swapping assets, the code does not provide a deadline parameter that limits the time window for execution, nor does it set the minimum acceptable amounts for each token (commonly known as amount0Min and amount1Min) in the parameters that are passed to Uniswap. In the swap manager, a minimum output amount is calculated but the value is not included in the user‑signed proof, allowing an attacker to replace it with a lower figure. The root cause is the omission of these safety fields from the cryptographic proof that the user signs, meaning the contract trusts whatever values are supplied by the caller without user verification. An attacker can front‑run or manipulate the market price between the time the user signs the transaction and when it is executed, causing the contract to accept a trade or liquidity operation that yields far fewer tokens than the user expects. The impact is that a user may receive a dramatically reduced amount of tokens, potentially ending with zero tokens received while still paying gas and any transferred assets, effectively losing funds. This condition occurs whenever a user initiates a liquidity add, liquidity removal, or token swap through the affected asset managers, regardless of the user’s intended slippage tolerance. All participants who rely on these managers – regular users, liquidity providers, and protocol integrators – are exposed. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the contract’s interface against Uniswap’s recommended safety parameters and identified the missing fields. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and appear normal on the surface; only when market conditions shift or an attacker deliberately manipulates the price does the loss become evident. To remediate, the contract should include the deadline, amount0Min, and amount1Min values in the data that the user signs, ensuring that the on‑chain execution cannot deviate from the user’s slippage expectations. By making these parameters part of the proof, the contract regains the standard slippage protection guarantees of Uniswap, preventing unexpected token shortfalls and preserving the intended accounting logic of the protocol.

title: No support for fee on transfer tokens
description: Fee on transfer tokens are not correctly dealt, as the transferFrom() call is expected to transfer exactly the requested amount. However, this is not the case for tokens that charge a fee on transfer.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns contracts that assume the ERC20 transferFrom (or safeTransferFrom) call moves exactly the amount specified by the caller. Fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a percentage or fixed amount from each transfer, so the actual amount received by the contract is lower than the requested amount. This mismatch is not checked, causing the contract’s accounting to record that the full amount was transferred while only a reduced amount arrived. The root cause is the reliance on the ERC20 specification that transfer functions return a boolean indicating success but do not provide the net amount transferred, combined with the contract’s omission of a post‑transfer balance verification. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a fee‑on‑transfer token to a function that expects a precise amount, causing the contract to believe it has received sufficient tokens and to proceed with subsequent logic such as releasing rewards, minting shares, or updating user balances. The impact includes under‑funded pools, users receiving no reward or a zero payout, and potential loss of funds if the contract later attempts to transfer out more tokens than it actually holds. The condition occurs whenever the contract interacts with a token that implements a transfer fee, which is common in many DeFi projects. Users, token holders, and the protocol are affected because expected balances do not match reality; from a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction while the displayed token balance remains unchanged or drops unexpectedly, leading to confusion such as user expects a refund but receives 0 or balance becomes zero after sending tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditors tested the contract with a known fee‑on‑transfer token and observed the discrepancy. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the ERC20 event still reports the requested amount, so standard logs appear normal. The proper mitigation is to treat fee‑on‑transfer tokens as a special case: record the contract’s token balance before the transfer, execute the safeTransferFrom, then read the new balance and compute the actual amount received, using that value for all subsequent calculations. This pattern ensures that accounting reflects the true net transfer and prevents the contract from assuming more tokens than it actually holds, thereby preserving the intended business logic of accurate refunds, reward distribution, and fund safety.

title: Some ETH transfers don't revert if they fail
description: ETH transfers should revert if they fail. Although this issue alone will not lead to exploits, it increases the attack surface.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of ETH transfers that are performed without checking the success flag of the low‑level call, so a failed transfer does not cause the surrounding transaction to revert. This situation occurs in several functions that handle liquidity removal and token exchanges, where the contract attempts to send Ether to a user or another contract using a raw call or an outdated transfer pattern. The root cause is the omission of a require statement or a safe‑send utility after the call, which means that if the recipient contract reverts, runs out of gas, or otherwise refuses the Ether, the call simply returns false and the execution continues. An attacker can trigger such a failure by supplying a malicious contract as the recipient, causing the Ether transfer to fail while the protocol’s internal accounting still records that the user should have received the funds. From the user’s perspective the transaction is reported as successful, the UI shows a completed withdrawal or exchange, but the user’s wallet balance remains unchanged or becomes zero, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have disappeared. The issue is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; only a discrepancy between expected and actual balances reveals the problem. Although the bug does not directly enable theft of assets, it expands the attack surface by allowing denial‑of‑service or accounting inconsistencies, which could be leveraged in more complex exploits. The appropriate remediation is to treat the result of every Ether‑sending call as critical: either use OpenZeppelin’s Address.sendValue, which reverts on failure, or explicitly check the returned boolean and revert with a clear error message. By ensuring that any failed ETH transfer aborts the whole operation, the protocol’s accounting invariants are preserved and users receive the funds they expect, restoring confidence in the system.

title: Self liquidations are profitable under certain collateralization ratios
bug_full: The vulnerability is a profit‑making self‑liquidation flaw that arises from the way the protocol calculates the debt amount expressed in collateral tokens. The eligibility check for a self‑liquidation compares the assigned collateral of a credit position with a value called debtInCollateralToken, which is derived from state.debtTokenAmountToCollateralTokenAmount(debtPosition.getTotalDebt()). Because getTotalDebt includes the principal, accrued interest, repay fees and overdue liquidator rewards, the resulting debtInCollateralToken can be larger than the actual face value of the loan. Consequently, a creditor who is also the lender can satisfy the condition assignedCollateral < debtInCollateralToken even when the position is not truly under‑collateralised. In practice, when there is a single lender, the inequality state.debtTokenAmountToCollateralTokenAmount(creditPosition.credit) < assignedCollateral < debtInCollateralToken can hold, allowing the lender to invoke the self‑liquidate function and claim the collateral that would otherwise be reserved for covering the repay fee and the overdue liquidator reward. The exploit proceeds as follows: the lender calls validateSelfLiquidate, the contract confirms that the caller is the lender, that the credit position is marked self‑liquidatable, and that the assigned collateral is lower than debtInCollateralToken. The call then triggers the liquidation logic, which transfers a portion of the borrower’s collateral to the lender as profit. The profit is bounded by the converted value of the repay fee plus the overdue liquidator reward, but it is strictly positive, meaning the borrower loses collateral that should have remained locked. This breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol: borrowers expect their collateral to be protected unless a third‑party liquidator steps in, and the system assumes that self‑liquidations only occur when the position is genuinely under‑collateralised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation module, where the mismatch between total debt and face value was observed. It can be hard to notice because the self‑liquidation check appears to enforce a safety margin, yet the underlying conversion uses a value that inflates the debt side of the equation. To remediate the problem, the calculation of debtInCollateralToken should be based on debtPosition.faceValue rather than debtPosition.getTotalDebt(), ensuring that self‑liquidation is only permitted when the actual loan principal exceeds the collateral. Alternatively, the eligibility logic could be tightened to require a true under‑collateralisation check that excludes fees and rewards, thereby preserving the intended liquidation incentives and preventing lenders from extracting extra value from borrowers.

title: LiquidateWithReplacement might not be available for the big enough debt positions
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the liquidateWithReplacement function, which is designed to liquidate a borrower’s debt position by finding a single replacement borrower that can cover the entire outstanding debt with its free collateral. The implementation assumes that for any debt size there will always be at least one borrower whose collateral is sufficient to replace the liquidated position in a single atomic step. This assumption is the root cause of the issue. When a debt position becomes very large, the pool of potential replacement borrowers may not contain any single account with enough free collateral to satisfy the whole amount. Because the function validates the existence of such a borrower before proceeding, the call will fail and the protocol will fall back to a standard liquidate‑then‑withdraw flow. The fallback path does not generate the liquidatorProfitBorrowAsset that would normally be earned when a replacement borrower is found, effectively depriving the protocol of a source of revenue. The impact is that, for prolonged periods during which large debt positions exist, the protocol loses the extra profit that could be captured from liquidators, potentially reducing incentives for liquidators and altering the expected economic model. This situation occurs only under specific conditions: the debt position must be sufficiently large, the market must lack a single borrower with enough free collateral, and the liquidation cannot be performed via a flash‑loan style replacement because the new debt position must remain on‑chain. The affected parties include the protocol itself (loss of revenue), liquidators (expected profit disappears), and borrowers (liquidation may still occur but with different mechanics). The issue was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noted that the validation step state.validateUserIsNotBelowOpeningLimitBorrowCR assumes the existence of a suitable borrower, an assumption that does not hold for extreme cases. The bug is subtle because the function works correctly for the majority of typical positions; only edge cases with very large debts expose the flaw, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should be modified to allow multiple replacement borrowers to collectively satisfy the debt, similar to the multi‑receiver logic used in BorrowAsMarketOrder, thereby removing the single‑borrower requirement and ensuring that liquidator profit can still be captured even for the biggest positions. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that liquidations should always be able to generate the expected profit, preserving protocol economics and preventing silent revenue loss.

title: Unexpected fee deduction on self-liquidations
description: The selfLiquidate function is designed to allow lenders to liquidate their positions without external liquidator involvement, improving protocol health by ensuring timely collateral recovery without profitability for the liquidator. According to the technical documentation 3.5.3.2 Self Liquidation, no fees should be charged during this process. However, the current implementation incorrectly charges a repay fee before computing the collateral to be assigned to the lender, thereby reducing the collateral amount available contrary to the documentation.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the self‑liquidation routine of the lending protocol, where the function intended to let a lender close its own position without involving a third‑party liquidator incorrectly applies a repay fee before the collateral that should be returned is calculated. The root cause is the call to chargeRepayFeeInCollateral inside executeSelfLiquidate, which deducts a fee from the collateral pool even though the protocol documentation explicitly states that self‑liquidations must be fee‑free. An attacker or any user who initiates a self‑liquidation can be exploited by receiving less collateral than expected because the fee reduces the amount assigned to the lender. This results in a shortfall for the user: instead of recovering the full value of their deposited collateral, they obtain a reduced amount, potentially leaving a balance that is lower than anticipated or even zero in extreme cases. The issue manifests whenever a credit position invokes the self‑liquidate function, i.e., under the condition that the lender calls executeSelfLiquidate on its own debt. It primarily affects lenders who rely on the fee‑free guarantee for self‑liquidation, undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting logic and violating the business rule that no fees should be charged in this scenario. The bug was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, which compared the implementation against the technical specification and noted the discrepancy. Because the fee deduction is performed silently within the contract logic, users may not see an explicit fee line in the UI, making the problem hard to notice until they compare the expected versus actual collateral returned. To remediate the issue, the fee‑charging call must be removed from the self‑liquidation flow so that the collateral assignment is computed without any prior fee deduction, thereby aligning the code with the documented fee‑free behavior and restoring correct accounting of user funds.

title: Maximum capital checks may prevent deposits
description:
The deposit functions performs two validation checks after depositing either the collateral or borrow token. These two validations attempt to ensure that the maximum amounts defined by the Size team of each token on the protocol are not exceeded. The functions that perform the checks are:
• validateCollateralTokenCap
• validateBorrowATokenCap
The maximum amounts are initially designed to avoid an excessive amount of funds entering the protocol. Nevertheless there are certain scenarios where these checks may arise functional problems.
The exposed scenario for illustrating this issue starts with a user attempting to deposit ETH as collateral. But the amount of borrow token, calculated as the total balance of aToken from funds deposited on Aave has increased over the maximum amount, the transaction reverts.
This can also have a higher impact when depositing collateral to avoid liquidation, as identified by Size team.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the protocol enforces a maximum capital limit on each token after a deposit, but the check uses the total amount of the borrow token (aToken balance) rather than the amount of newly minted debt. When the total aToken balance already exceeds the configured cap, any subsequent deposit— even a pure collateral deposit— triggers a revert. This can happen when other users have previously filled the protocol up to the cap, or when the aToken balance grows due to interest accrual. As a result, legitimate users attempting to add collateral to protect themselves from liquidation are blocked, leading to possible liquidation and loss of collateral. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the deposit flow and the two validation functions validateCollateralTokenCap and validateBorrowATokenCap. The problem is subtle because the revert occurs after the token transfer, and the error message does not clearly indicate that the cap is being exceeded, making it hard for users to understand why their transaction failed. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect cap enforcement” or “post‑deposit validation overflow” where business rules are applied on a global state rather than on the incremental change. From a user perspective the expected outcome is that a collateral deposit succeeds and protects the position, but in reality the transaction reverts and the user sees no change in balance, sometimes appearing as if the funds disappeared. This violation of accounting assumptions can cause money to disappear from the user’s perspective and prevent the protocol’s liquidation‑avoidance mechanism from working. To fix the issue, the protocol should enforce the maximum amount on the amount of debt token that is minted in the current operation, or adjust the validation to consider only the new debt rather than the total aToken balance. This change would allow users to deposit collateral even when the protocol’s overall borrow token balance is at its limit, preserving the intended safety mechanisms without unintentionally blocking legitimate deposits.

title: Operator might be unable to withdraw rewards due to gas limit
description: The PoolGovernance:withdrawRewards method allows operators to withdraw their yield, which happens with this external call: (bool sent, ) = msg.sender.call{value: rewards, gas: 2300}(""); The 2300 gas limit might not be enough for smart contract wallets that have a receive or fallback function that takes more than 2300 gas units, which is too low (you can't do much more than emit an event). If that is the case, the operator won't be able to claim his rewards and they will be stuck in the contract forever.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient‑gas stipend in the withdrawRewards function of the pool governance contract. When an operator calls withdrawRewards, the contract attempts to send the accumulated reward amount to the caller using a low‑level call with an explicit gas limit of 2300 units. This gas amount is historically enough only for a simple external account that has no fallback logic, but it is too small for smart‑contract wallets that implement a receive or fallback function requiring more than 2300 gas to execute (for example, to emit an event or perform bookkeeping). Because the call is forced to use this limited gas, the transfer can fail with an out‑of‑gas error, causing the call to revert silently while the rewards remain locked inside the pool contract. The root cause is the developer’s decision to constrain the gas forwarded to the recipient, a pattern that was safe when using Solidity’s transfer but is now unsafe for contracts that need more gas to accept ether. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any operator using a contract wallet will be unable to claim their rewards, effectively resulting in a denial‑of‑service on the reward withdrawal path. The impact is that legitimate operators may see their expected reward balance stay unchanged, receiving no funds despite a successful transaction receipt, which violates the business logic that rewards should be claimable after accrual. The condition occurs whenever the withdrawRewards function is invoked and the caller is a contract with a non‑trivial fallback, which is a common pattern for smart‑contract wallets and DeFi aggregators. The affected parties are the operators of the pool and any users who rely on contract wallets to receive rewards; the protocol’s overall accounting remains correct but the user‑visible balance for those operators appears empty. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the external call pattern and recognized the fixed gas stipend as a potential blocker for contract wallets. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may appear successful on‑chain, and the failure only manifests as missing funds for certain wallet types, which may not be exercised in typical test suites. The recommended remediation is to remove the explicit gas limit from the call, allowing the EVM to forward all available gas, or to replace the call with a safer pattern such as using a pull‑payment mechanism or a trusted escrow that does not impose a restrictive stipend. This class of bug falls under the broader category of “insufficient gas stipend for external calls” leading to denial‑of‑service and locked funds, and it breaks the expectation that a user can withdraw earned rewards without encountering hidden gas constraints.

title: The stake fees are not tracked on chain
description:
Every validator who joins the SmoothlyPool should register by paying a STAKE_FEE (with the size of 0.065 ETH) to the contract. The pool does not track how much of a stake fee balance a validator has, which is problematic for the following reasons:
1. The pool has no guarantee that it holds at least numValidators * STAKE_FEE ETH in its balance - the ETH might have been mistakenly distributed as rewards or claimed as fees from operators
2. It is possible for a validator to deposit more than STAKE_FEE if he calls SmoothlyPool::addStake multiple times
3. The slashing/punishment mechanism can't be enforced on chain
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of on‑chain accounting for the fee that each validator must pay when joining the staking pool. When a validator registers, a fixed amount of ether (0.065 ETH) is transferred to the pool, but the contract does not store any record of how much fee each validator has contributed. This lack of tracking originates from a design omission: the contract never updates a mapping or any other state variable that reflects the cumulative stake‑fee balance per validator. Because the fee balance is not recorded, the pool cannot guarantee that its total ether holdings are at least the product of the number of active validators and the required fee. Consequently, the pool may unintentionally spend or distribute ether that should be reserved for stake fees, for example when rewards are allocated or when operators claim fees. An attacker or a careless operator could also cause a validator to overpay the fee by invoking the registration function multiple times, since each call transfers the fee without checking prior contributions. The missing accounting also prevents the slashing or punishment mechanism from being enforced on chain, because the contract has no knowledge of how much fee is available to be deducted from a misbehaving validator. In practice, a user who expects their 0.065 ETH stake fee to be held securely may see the pool balance drop, receive no refund when withdrawing, or observe that slashing events do not result in any loss of funds. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s state variables and found no mapping or balance tracking for stake fees. It can be hard to notice because the contract still accepts ether and appears to function, while the accounting error only manifests when the pool’s total ether becomes insufficient or when slashing is attempted. The proper remediation is to introduce a dedicated on‑chain data structure, such as a mapping from validator address to fee balance, and to update this structure on every fee payment, while also enforcing that a validator cannot pay more than the required amount. This change restores correct accounting, ensures that the pool always holds enough ether to cover all required fees, and enables on‑chain enforcement of slashing penalties.

title: MJR-1 "Sandwich attack" on user withdrawal
description: In some rare conditions, the strategy is using AMM DEX to Strategy.sol#L348 inside of the user-handled transaction. This is vulnerable to the "sandwich attack".
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic sandwich attack that can be triggered during a user‑initiated withdrawal when the strategy contract performs an automated market maker (AMM) token swap inside the same transaction. The root cause is that the swap is executed without any slippage protection or price verification, allowing an attacker who observes the pending withdrawal to place a trade that moves the market price just before the user’s swap (front‑run) and then reverse the trade immediately after (back‑run). By doing so the attacker inflates the price the user receives, causing the user’s withdrawal to be settled at an unfavorable rate. This can result in the user receiving less of the expected token, or in extreme cases the protocol losing value because the swap extracts value from the pool. The attack can only be carried out when the withdrawal path includes a direct AMM swap and when the attacker can monitor the mempool and act within the same block, conditions that are relatively rare but not impossible. All users who request a withdrawal are affected, as they may see their balance reduced unexpectedly, and the protocol’s overall liquidity can be eroded over time. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of funds in the withdrawal function and identified the lack of slippage checks. It is hard to notice because the failure manifests only under specific market conditions and the user interface typically shows a successful transaction without indicating that the received amount is lower than expected. To remediate the problem the swap operation should be protected with a maximum slippage parameter, use a trusted price oracle, or be moved out of the user‑controlled transaction so that the price cannot be manipulated by a front‑runner. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation vulnerabilities caused by unchecked AMM interactions within privileged functions, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual refund amounts and breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: Base contracts inherited by the upgradeable Vault contract need storage gaps
description:
For upgradeable contracts, there must be a storage gap to allow the addition of new state variables in the future without compromising the storage compatibility with existing deployments. Without a storage gap, if there are any new variables in the DivaBeaconOracle contract, they will override variables in the Vault contract, since Vault extends DivaBeaconOracle.
OpenZeppelin Reference here.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing storage gap in an upgradeable contract hierarchy. The Vault contract inherits from DivaBeaconOracle, which is intended to be used behind a proxy and therefore must preserve its storage layout for future upgrades. Because DivaBeaconOracle does not reserve a storage gap, any new state variables added to that contract in a later implementation will be placed in storage slots that are already occupied by variables defined in Vault. This creates a storage collision where the new variables overwrite existing Vault state, such as balances, validator mappings, or access control flags. The root cause is the omission of the OpenZeppelin‑recommended uint256[50] __gap; placeholder in the base contract, which is required to keep a buffer of unused slots. An attacker or even an honest developer could trigger the issue by deploying a new implementation that adds variables to DivaBeaconOracle; when the proxy is pointed to the new implementation, the overwritten slots cause the Vault’s internal accounting to become corrupted. The impact may include loss of user funds, failed withdrawals, incorrect validator status reporting, or any business logic that relies on the corrupted state. The condition occurs whenever the contract is upgraded after the initial deployment without a storage gap, especially if the upgrade adds new storage variables to the base contract. All users of the Vault, the protocol that relies on accurate validator data, and any role that can trigger upgrades are affected because the corrupted state can lead to unexpected zero balances or failed operations. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that referenced OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable contract guidelines. It can be hard to notice because the contract may continue to function correctly until a specific upgrade introduces new variables, at which point the failure manifests as subtle accounting errors rather than an outright revert. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a correct balance before the upgrade, then after the upgrade the balance appears as zero or withdrawals revert without explanation, violating the expectation that a deposited amount remains available. The bug belongs to the class of storage layout incompatibility errors common in proxy‑based upgradeable contracts. To remediate, the base contract should be modified to include a storage gap array (e.g., uint256[50] __gap;) placed after the last declared state variable, ensuring that future upgrades can add new variables without colliding with existing storage slots. After adding the gap, the contract should be redeployed via a proper upgrade path and thorough testing performed to confirm that state is preserved.

title: In Vault.purchase() the denomination of premium is ambiguous
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Vault.purchase function where the premium amount is supplied as a raw uint256 without an explicit indication of whether it represents a value in native ETH or in the underwriting token (for example wstETH). The function decides how the payment is processed by comparing msg.value with the premium: if msg.value is less than the premium it assumes the user will pay with the underwriting token and pulls that amount via transferFrom, otherwise it treats the payment as ETH and, if the sent ETH exceeds the premium, refunds the excess. Because the denomination of the premium is ambiguous, a user who believes the premium is quoted in ETH may send the exact ETH amount, but the contract could interpret the same numeric value as a token amount, causing the contract to pull a larger value of wstETH whose market price exceeds the ETH sent. Conversely, a user who expects to pay in the token may send ETH, and the contract will accept the ETH as payment, effectively giving the user a discount because the token price is higher than ETH. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who crafts transactions that trigger the undesired payment path, leading to users over‑paying in the higher‑valued asset or receiving an unintended discount, both of which break the protocol’s accounting assumptions and can result in loss of funds or unfair advantage. The issue manifests whenever purchase is called with a premium value that is not accompanied by a clear denomination flag, and it affects any participant attempting to buy coverage – the user, the protocol’s risk pool, and any downstream insurers that rely on correct premium accounting. The problem was discovered during a manual audit review of the purchase logic, where the lack of documentation and the simplistic msg.value comparison raised suspicion. It is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit events indicating which asset was used, and the refund logic can mask the underlying mismatch, making it appear as a normal over‑payment refund. To remediate, the premium should be defined with a fixed denomination in the off‑chain specifications, and the contract should use a conversion factor (such as convertToEthFactor) to translate token‑denominated premiums into ETH equivalents or vice‑versa, enforcing a single, explicit payment method and rejecting mismatched asset submissions. This eliminates the ambiguity, aligns the on‑chain accounting with the intended business logic, and prevents users from unintentionally losing value or receiving unintended discounts.

title: Vault.withdrawServiceFee() should reset totalServiceToken and totalServiceEth.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee withdrawal routine of the Vault contract. The function withdrawServiceFee is intended to transfer the accumulated service fees, both in the underwriting token and in native ether, to an address chosen by the contract owner. However, after performing the transfers the function never clears the accounting variables totalServiceToken and totalServiceEth that record how much fee has been collected. Because these counters remain unchanged, the contract continues to believe that the same amount of fee is still pending. As a result, the owner can invoke withdrawServiceFee repeatedly and receive the same amount of tokens and ether each time, effectively draining any funds that remain in the contract. Even if the owner behaves honestly, a second call after the vault has expired or after users have withdrawn their balances will cause the transaction to revert, since the contract still reports a non‑zero fee balance while the actual balance may be insufficient. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state updates after external calls. It is easy to miss because the function is restricted to the owner and the code appears to perform a straightforward transfer, giving the impression that the state is correctly handled. The impact includes potential loss of funds for the protocol, broken accounting assumptions, and a poor user experience where expected refunds or fee withdrawals fail unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑reset errors, where mutable storage is not updated after a critical operation. To remediate, the function should capture the fee amounts in local variables, perform the transfers, and then set totalServiceToken and totalServiceEth to zero, ensuring that the contract’s internal accounting matches the external state after each withdrawal.

title: Total coverage is not reduced in Vault.claim()
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting error in the Vault contract where the totalCoverage variable is not decreased after a successful claim. When a validator is slashed, a user who purchased coverage can call Vault.claim() and receive a payout. The claim function correctly reduces the underwriter ETH and token balances, but it omits the line that subtracts the coverage amount from the global totalCoverage counter. As a result, the contract’s view of the amount of coverage that is still available remains artificially high. The purchase function checks that totalPossibleCoverage * leverage / basisPoints is greater than or equal to totalCoverage + requestedCoverage; because totalCoverage is inflated, the check can fail even though the contract still holds enough free capital. Consequently, legitimate users attempting to buy new coverage may encounter a NotEnoughFundsForCoverage revert, effectively locking the vault from accepting new policies. The issue manifests whenever a claim is processed; each claim leaves the totalCoverage counter larger than the actual covered amount, and the problem compounds with multiple claims. The affected parties are policy buyers, underwriters, and the protocol itself, as the inability to sell new coverage reduces revenue and may break promised service level agreements. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the claim logic, where the auditor noticed that the state updates for underwriter balances were present but the totalCoverage update was missing. Because the contract does not emit an explicit event for the totalCoverage change, the discrepancy is not visible on‑chain without inspecting the storage directly, making it easy to overlook. This class of bug falls under 'inconsistent state accounting' or 'missing state mutation after external interaction'. To remediate, the claim routine must subtract the coverage amount from totalCoverage, mirroring the reductions applied to the underwriter balances, and optionally emit an event to reflect the updated totalCoverage. After the fix, the purchase check will correctly reflect the remaining capacity, allowing new users to acquire coverage as intended. The failure mode appears to users as a sudden inability to purchase coverage, with transactions reverting and error messages indicating insufficient funds, even though the vault still holds the required capital.

title: Using the same signature multiple times
description: Private sales require a signature from createSigner for a given wearablesSubject+amount, with different signatures for buy and sell. But once signed the signature can be used many times. As a result, in fact, createSigner has no power to control amount for buy and sell operations. It is even possible to arrange a secondary market, where only one signature is used to access anyone to a sale, so the private market will be not so private.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay weakness in the private‑sale signature verification logic. The contract expects a cryptographic signature from a designated signer that authorises a specific wearablesSubject together with a concrete amount for a buy or sell operation. However, the verification routine does not record whether a particular signature has already been consumed, nor does it incorporate a unique nonce or timestamp. Consequently the same signature can be presented repeatedly and will be accepted each time. This occurs because the contract only checks that the signature matches the expected signer and payload, without any state that would invalidate the signature after one use. An attacker can therefore reuse a legitimate signature to perform unlimited buy or sell actions, effectively bypassing the intended per‑transaction amount restriction. From a user perspective the private market that should be limited to a single participant becomes public: users see that anyone can acquire the item with the same signature, balances may be deducted unexpectedly, and the promised exclusivity disappears. The impact includes loss of control for the signer, erosion of market privacy, potential financial loss for parties that assumed a bounded amount, and the ability to create a secondary market where a single signature grants access to all participants. The flaw is discovered during a manual audit of the signature handling code, where the absence of a used‑signature mapping or nonce was noted. It can be hard to notice because the contract still validates the cryptographic proof correctly; the failure is logical rather than syntactic, and normal testing may not exercise repeated use of the same signature. To remediate, the contract should track used signatures, for example by storing a hash of each processed signature or by requiring an incrementing nonce that is part of the signed message. This ensures that each authorisation can be consumed only once and restores the intended private‑sale semantics.

title: Excessive msg.value lost when buying
description:
msg.value is considered incorrect only in this equation:
msg.value < price + protocolFee + creatorFee
As a result, msg.value above price+fees will pass, but never return and thus lost. It can happen in case of a mistake from users if they provide the wrong msg.value. This mistake can be either from fee calculations, or it can be some sell operations before the user, so the total price is less than expected.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment loss bug that occurs in the purchase function of the contract. The code validates the incoming ether amount with a condition that only checks whether msg.value is less than the required total (price plus protocol fee plus creator fee). Because the check uses a strict less‑than comparison, any amount that is greater than the required total passes the require statement, but the contract does not contain logic to return the surplus. As a result, when a user mistakenly sends more ether than the exact price plus fees—whether due to a miscalculation, a UI rounding error, or a preceding sell operation that changes the expected price—the transaction succeeds and the excess ether remains locked in the contract with no event or refund. This leads to a situation where the user’s balance is reduced by more than the advertised cost, effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue is triggered whenever the payable function is called with an amount that exceeds the calculated total; it does not depend on any special state, only on the value sent. All buyers who interact with the function are affected, and the protocol’s overall fund accounting becomes inconsistent because the contract assumes that the received ether equals the sum of price and fees. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the require statements and noticed the asymmetric validation. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the UI may show a successful purchase while the user later sees an unexpected reduction in their wallet balance. The class of bug is an improper input validation and missing refund mechanism, commonly referred to as an over‑payment or unchecked excess value vulnerability. To remediate, the contract should either enforce that msg.value equals exactly price plus fees, or implement a safe refund path that returns any surplus ether to the sender after the purchase logic completes. Either approach restores the expected invariant that the amount received matches the cost, preventing silent loss of user funds.

title: Balance going below BASE_WEARABLE_UNIT
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing post‑operation balance validation in the wearable token contract. The contract defines a constant BASE_WEARABLE_UNIT equal to 0.001 ether and enforces that any transferWearables or sellPrivateWearables call must specify an amount that is at least this base unit. However, the logic only checks the amount being moved, not the user’s remaining balance after the operation. When a user holds a balance only slightly above the base unit—for example 0.002 ether—and initiates a transfer of 0.0015 ether, the transaction succeeds because the amount meets the minimum requirement. The user’s balance is then reduced to 0.0005 ether, which is below BASE_WEARABLE_UNIT. Because subsequent calls to transferWearables or sellPrivateWearables also require the amount to be at least the base unit, the leftover balance can no longer be transferred, sold, or otherwise interacted with. From the user’s perspective the funds appear to disappear: the UI shows a reduced balance, but attempts to move the remaining amount fail silently or revert with an InsufficientBaseUnit error. This situation effectively locks the residual ether in the contract, violating the expectation that any owned balance can be freely transferred or sold. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the amount checks but did not consider the resulting balance after state changes. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific warning about low residual balances, and the error only surfaces when a user later tries to act on the stuck amount. The impact is medium severity: users may lose access to a small portion of their funds, which can accumulate to a significant amount across many accounts, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about token liquidity are broken. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑condition balance underflow” or “minimum unit enforcement only on input amount” errors, where business logic assumes that satisfying a minimum transfer amount guarantees a usable remaining balance. To remediate, the contract should verify that after any transfer or sell operation the sender’s balance remains greater than or equal to BASE_WEARABLE_UNIT, or alternatively allow operations on balances below the base unit by adjusting the rounding or providing a withdrawal path for the residual amount.

title: Last user can't sell all his wearables
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the price calculation logic used for both purchasing (buy) and liquidating (sell) wearable assets. The contract computes the unit price by performing integer division and then truncates any fractional component, effectively rounding the result toward zero. Because the same rounding rule is applied to both directions, a user who splits a single intended purchase into multiple smaller batches can end up paying a lower average price than the contract later credits when the same assets are sold. This discrepancy arises from the fact that each division discards the remainder, so the sum of rounded‑down buy prices can be less than the rounded‑down sell price for the same total quantity. An attacker can exploit the bug by first buying a large amount of wearables in several small transactions, thereby reducing the effective purchase cost, and then selling the accumulated wearables in a single transaction that yields a higher per‑unit payout. The immediate impact is an unintended profit for the attacker, which can drain the contract’s reserve of funds or distort the intended economic incentives of the platform. The condition under which the exploit works is when the contract’s pricing formula uses floor division for both sides of the trade and when the total quantity is divisible into batches that each generate a rounding loss on the buy side but not on the sell side. All participants who interact with the wearable marketplace – buyers, sellers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the pricing invariant that should keep buy and sell rates symmetric is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic expressions in the pricing functions and verified them with unit tests that demonstrated a scenario where the sell price exceeded the buy price.
