However, the setSAM (Supply Adjustment Mechanism) function is protected only by the onlyBeforeMintConcluded modifier, which allows the owner to enable or modify SAM at any point before the final token is minted. Because SAM can be configured with a very low price and an early inflection point, invoking setSAM after most tokens have been sold causes the contract to mint a large number of additional tokens, effectively inflating the supply. This behavior violates the expectation that the supply is fixed once minting starts, leading users to believe they are purchasing a scarce asset while the owner can later dilute it. The exploit can be carried out by an owner who first markets the edition as having no SAM, lets the community mint the majority of the intended supply, and then calls setSAM and SAM.create with parameters that trigger massive token creation. The impact is a sudden devaluation of existing holdings, loss of confidence, and potential financial loss for token buyers. The condition for the attack is that at least one token has been minted but the minting process has not yet concluded; under these circumstances the owner retains the ability to modify SAM. All participants who rely on the fixed‑supply guarantee—collectors, investors, and the broader protocol—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended supply‑locking logic with the actual access control on setSAM, revealing a mismatch between business rules and code enforcement. It can be hard to notice because the UI may not prominently display SAM changes, and the contract does not emit a clear warning when the supply‑adjustment mechanism is activated after minting has started. To remediate, the contract should restrict setSAM to be callable only when no tokens have been minted (i.e., _totalMinted() == 0) or move SAM configuration into the initialization phase, ensuring that the supply cannot be altered after the mint begins. This class of bug falls under “post‑mint supply manipulation” where a privileged function can modify economic parameters after users have formed expectations about scarcity, breaking accounting assumptions and leading to potential rug pulls.

title: Edition owner can manipulate Golden Egg by ending auction early
description:
The Golden Egg is intended to be chosen randomly, without the ability to be influenced by users or the edition owner. The pseudorandom function is incredibly thorough at stopping an attacker from predicting the randomness in advance to manipulate it in their favor.

However, the edition owner does have one major lever that can allow them to have influence over the randomness: they can use the `setEditionMaxMintableRange()` function to decide when the minting period ends.

Here's a basic POC:
Edition owner sets `editionMaxMintableLower` to a low value and `editionMaxMintableUpper` to a high value.
For each mint after the lower threshold has been crossed, they can calculate `(keccak256(_mintRandomness) % totalMinted()) + 1` to determine the tokenId that would win the Golden Egg if minting was shut down now.
Once they see a value they are happy with, they can call `setEditionMaxMintableRange()` with a `editionMaxMintableUpper` value that is equal to or below the current `totalMinted()`. This will shut down fixed price minting and transition the project to the SAM.

(An alternate version of this exploit would require setting both `editionMaxMintableLower` and `editionMaxMintableUpper` to a high value, and waiting until after `editionCutoffTime` is passed to lower `editionMaxMintableLower` and end the fixed price sale.)

While at present, the benefits of this amount to just 1% of sales and may not be worth the lost revenue, it is clear that great lengths have been taken in this system to ensure that the Golden Egg is immune to manipulation, presumably so it can be safely bestowed with great value.

This exploit gives an owner the opportunity to break the fairness of the selection mechanism, which may be abused in these high-value cases.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of the edition owner to influence the selection of the so‑called Golden Egg, which is supposed to be awarded to a randomly chosen token after the fixed‑price minting phase ends. The contract uses a pseudorandom function that hashes internal minting data and then takes the remainder modulo the total number of minted tokens, a method that on its own prevents anyone from predicting the winner in advance. However, the function setEditionMaxMintableRange, which is intended only to adjust the allowable supply range, also permits the owner to close the minting period at an arbitrary moment by lowering the editionMaxMintableUpper bound to a value that is equal to or lower than the current totalMinted count. When the owner does this after the lower threshold has been crossed, they can compute the token identifier that would be selected by the randomness formula ((keccak256(_mintRandomness) % totalMinted()) + 1) for the present state, and then immediately end the sale, freezing the randomness with that token as the winner. This manipulation breaks the fairness guarantee of the Golden Egg, allowing the owner to bias the outcome toward a token they control, potentially extracting additional value from a high‑value reward. The issue manifests only when the owner has permission to call setEditionMaxMintableRange and chooses to set the upper bound at or below the current total minted, effectively ending the sale before the full randomness space has been exhausted. Users and participants expect a transparent, unbiased random draw; instead they may see the same address repeatedly winning or the draw never finalizing because the owner is deliberately timing the termination. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between supply‑range controls and the randomness finalization logic; it is easy to miss because the function appears innocuous and the randomness itself looks cryptographically sound. To remediate, the contract should prevent the owner from lowering the lower bound to the current totalMinted value; a safe approach is to require that the new lower bound be at least totalMinted plus a configurable offset, ensuring that additional unpredictable minting events occur before the Golden Egg is locked in. More robust designs would decouple the sale termination from the randomness source, for example by using a commit‑reveal scheme or an immutable random beacon, thereby eliminating any owner‑controlled timing advantage.

title: Artist can set GoldenEggFee to zero, rugging winner
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that allows the edition owner or an authorized admin to modify the Golden Egg fee at any point in the contract's lifecycle. The function checks only that the caller is the edition owner or an admin, but it does not verify whether the minting phase has already finished or whether a winner has already been declared. Because of this missing temporal guard, an artist can invoke the function after a user has been announced as the Golden Egg winner and set the fee to zero, effectively disabling the prize that was promised. This can be exploited by the artist calling setGoldenEggFee with a value of zero after the mint concludes, which causes the contract to treat the Golden Egg reward as having no value. The impact is that the winner, who expects to receive a monetary or token reward, receives nothing; the UI may still display that a Golden Egg was won, creating a discrepancy between the displayed reward and the actual payout. The issue occurs whenever the contract permits fee adjustments after the minting period, and it affects all participants who rely on the guarantee that a declared winner will receive the prize, as well as the overall trustworthiness of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the permission model of the fee‑setting function. It is subtle because the function appears to be a harmless administrative setter, and there is no explicit event or error indicating that the prize has been nullified. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑condition state‑change” vulnerabilities where critical economic parameters can be altered after a condition that should lock them in has been satisfied. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or zero payout despite a visible winning announcement, violating the expectation that a winner receives a non‑zero reward. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict changes to the Golden Egg fee to the period before the mint ends, or make the fee immutable once a winner has been recorded, thereby preserving the economic guarantee promised to participants.

title: All fees accrue to minters, which can be forked to use platform without fees
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass design flaw that allows an edition owner to mint tokens on the Sound platform without the platform receiving its configured fees. The root cause is that the logic that calculates, records and withdraws platform fees lives in the minter contract rather than in the core SoundEdition contract, and the core contract exposes a public grantRoles function that lets the edition owner assign any address to the MINTER_ROLE. Because there is no on‑chain validation that the address granted as a minter is the official Sound minter, the owner can deploy a forked minter that overrides or disables the fee‑accrual code, grant it the MINTER_ROLE, and attach it to their edition. When users mint through this forked minter, the transaction follows the same flow as a normal mint – the caller sends msg.value, the contract computes totalPrice and platformFlatFee, checks that the payment is sufficient, and then calculates platformFee. However, the forked minter can simply set platformFee to zero or omit the increment of platformFeesAccrued, causing the platform fee variable to remain unchanged. The exploit can be carried out at any time after an edition is created, as the owner can call grantRoles at will. The affected parties include the Sound platform (loss of revenue), artists who rely on the fee model, and users who may be unaware that the platform is not receiving its expected compensation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑handling code and the role‑granting mechanism, noting that the front‑end UI assumes the minter attached to an edition is the official one and therefore does not verify fee accrual. The problem is hard to notice because the UI displays normal minting behavior – users receive their tokens and see no error – while the missing fee is not reflected in any visible balance or event, making the revenue loss silent. To remediate, the protocol should enforce fee accrual in the immutable core contract, restrict the MINTER_ROLE to only the authorized Sound minter address (or a whitelist of approved contracts), and add on‑chain checks that any granted minter emits the correct fee‑accrual events. Additionally, the front end should verify that each edition’s minter matches the official contract before displaying it, preventing users from interacting with fee‑free forks.

title: Potentially unsafe use of forceSafeTransferETH
bug_full: The contract implements a refund mechanism for NFT minting that uses the library function forceSafeTransferETH. After a successful mint, if the caller sent more ether than the required amount, the excess is sent back to msg.sender with a call that, on failure, creates a temporary contract and self‑destructs it to force the ether into the destination address. This pattern assumes that msg.sender is an address capable of receiving ether via a normal transfer. The root cause is that the fallback logic does not check whether the recipient can actually accept ether; instead it relies on the self‑destruct fallback, which bypasses the receive() and fallback() restrictions of Solidity. When a user mints through an intermediate contract that does not implement a payable receive function (for example a Multicaller proxy), the normal call would revert, but forceSafeTransferETH forces the ether into the proxy’s balance via self‑destruct. The proxy now holds the refunded ether without any way for the original user to retrieve it directly, creating a race condition where the user or a front‑running MEV bot can extract the funds before the proxy’s balance is drained. The impact is that users who overpay and use a non‑payable forwarding contract may see their expected refund disappear, the protocol may unintentionally lock ether in contracts, and malicious actors can profit by front‑running the forced transfer. This situation occurs only when an over‑payment triggers the refund path and the caller is a contract without a payable fallback. It affects any participant that uses an intermediate contract to interact with the mint function, including end‑users, developers of proxy contracts, and the NFT protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the refund logic and identified the unsafe use of forceSafeTransferETH. It can be hard to notice because the forced transfer succeeds silently; the transaction does not revert and the UI may show a successful mint, while the refunded ether is silently deposited into a contract that the user does not control, leading to missing funds from the user’s perspective. To remediate, the protocol should avoid using forced transfers for refunds; instead it should either require the exact payment amount, revert when a normal transfer fails, or use a safe transfer that respects the recipient’s ability to receive ether. By doing so, users will either receive the refund directly or be forced to send the correct amount, eliminating the possibility of ether being forced into contracts that cannot handle it. This vulnerability belongs to the class of forced‑ether‑transfer bugs where self‑destruct is misused to bypass payable checks, breaking accounting assumptions that a refund will always reach the intended recipient and potentially causing funds to disappear from the expected balance.

title: Artist can frontrun transactions to extract additional fees
description:
The artist has a number of vectors to increase the fees they receive, all of which can be adjusted while the SAM is live:
increase `artistFee` to max value
increase `affiliateFee` to max value
set `affiliateMerkleRoot` to a random value so proofs are rejected (because rejected proofs don't cause an error, and instead default to the artist)

These changes can result in up to 15% of the mint price being forwarded to the artist.

An artist looking to maximize fees might watch the mempool for `buy()` transactions, and use Flashbots to perform the following attack:
1) Adjust fees to the values that maximize the artist's payout
2) Execute the `buy()` transaction
3) Adjust fees back to their previous state

While the `msg.value` of the `buy()` function is used as slippage protection, there are three events in which an artist would still be able to exploit this:

1) In a period of high volatility, users will need to send higher `msg.value`s in order to ensure their transactions get through.
2) If a `buy()` tx is submitted in the same block as a large `sell()` tx, the artist could use Flashbots to create a bundle that goes `sell > change fees > buy`, with the sell creating extra buffer for the additional fees.
3) An artist may not increase the total cost at all, and may perform the attack by simply changing the affiliate root in order to steal the affiliate's fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic manipulation vector that allows the artist, who controls mutable fee parameters in the contract, to capture additional fees from user buy transactions. The root cause is that the contract permits the artist to adjust the artistFee, affiliateFee and the affiliateMerkleRoot while the contract is live, and the fee calculation uses the values that are current at the moment the buy function is executed. Because there is no protection against fee changes between the moment a user submits a transaction and the moment it is mined, an artist can monitor the mempool, submit a Flashbots bundle that first raises the fee percentages to their maximum, then includes the user’s buy transaction, and finally restores the original fee settings in the same block. In addition, the contract defaults to sending affiliate fees to the artist when an affiliate proof is rejected, and it does not revert the transaction in that case. This means the artist can also replace the affiliateMerkleRoot with a random value, causing every affiliate proof to be rejected and silently diverting the affiliate’s share to the artist without increasing the total amount the user pays. The attack can be executed especially when users set loose slippage parameters, during periods of high market volatility that require higher msg.value, or when a large sell transaction creates a buffer that the artist can exploit by ordering sell‑>fee‑change‑>buy. The impact is that up to fifteen percent of the mint price may be redirected to the artist, users may overpay or lose the affiliate portion they expected, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are violated. The vulnerability affects any user who purchases through the buy function, affiliates who rely on their fee share, and the overall trustworthiness of the platform. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mutability of fee‑related state variables and the fallback logic for invalid affiliate proofs. The issue is hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds, the slippage protection based on msg.value still passes, and the fee changes are not visible to the end‑user; the contract silently redirects the extra amount to the artist. To remediate, fee‑related parameters should be made immutable or only changeable through a time‑locked governance process, and the contract should revert when an affiliate proof is invalid instead of defaulting the fee to the artist. Requiring users to explicitly set address(0) as the affiliate when they do not wish to use an affiliate, or adding a check that prevents fee adjustments in the same block as a user‑initiated buy, would also mitigate the attack. In summary, the bug is a class of MEV‑style front‑running and economic manipulation caused by mutable fee configuration and unsafe fallback handling, leading to unexpected fee extraction and loss of expected affiliate rewards.

title: MEV risk in periods of high volatility
description:
Bonding curves are particularly susceptible to MEV. Any transaction along the curve can be sandwich attacked by a bot that creates the following Flashbots bundles:

`buy X tokens => ORIGINAL BUY TX => sell X tokens` (where X is the maximum number of tokens that can be bought without causing the original transaction to revert).

The protocol implements protections against this. Namely:
the `buy()` function uses `msg.value` as a max slippage parameter
the `sell()` function has an explicit `minimumPayout` parameter

In periods of high volatility, it is likely that users will need to add sufficient buffer to these slippage parameters to get their transactions through.

This may be acceptable, as these users are explicitly accepting this slippage in setting these parameters. But the current situation allows MEV bots to capitalize on all of the consumer surplus between what a user is willing to pay and what the market requires they pay. In an ideal world, this surplus should belong to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a market‑making mechanism that uses a bonding curve to price token purchases and sales. The contract allows callers to specify a maximum slippage for buys (via msg.value) and a minimum payout for sells. In periods of high price volatility users often increase these parameters to ensure their transaction does not revert. This creates a predictable price window between the user‑defined tolerance and the actual market price. A malicious bot can observe a pending buy transaction, calculate the maximum amount of tokens that can be purchased without exceeding the user’s slippage limit, and then submit a Flashbots bundle that first buys that amount, lets the original user transaction execute at the inflated price, and finally sells the same amount back to the market. The bot captures the consumer surplus – the difference between what the user was willing to pay and the price the market required – without the user’s knowledge. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the effective purchase price is higher than expected, resulting in fewer tokens received or a higher cost, and the subsequent sell may yield a lower payout than anticipated. The issue manifests especially when volatility is high and users set generous slippage buffers; under normal conditions the gap may be small enough to go unnoticed. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the economic assumptions of the bonding curve and the interaction of the slippage controls with front‑running opportunities. Because the slippage parameters are user‑controlled, the contract’s existing checks (max slippage and minimum payout) do not prevent a third‑party from exploiting the price gap, making the bug subtle and easy to miss in functional testing. The core class of bug is a sandwich‑attack vector on a price‑oracle‑less AMM where user‑provided tolerance parameters create an exploitable price band. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should introduce a temporal separation between buying and selling actions, such as enforcing a one‑block freeze after a purchase before a sell can be executed, thereby eliminating the zero‑time arbitrage window that MEV bots rely on. Additional defenses could include commit‑reveal schemes, price smoothing, or dynamic slippage limits that adapt to volatility, but the primary fix is to remove the immediate back‑to‑back transaction possibility that enables the profit‑free sandwich attack.

title: The `digest` calculation in `deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature` does not follow EIP-712 specification
description:
The calculation of the digest done in ProxyFactory.deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature() does not follow the EIP-712 specification. It is missing the function's corresponding typeHash, as well as the hashStruct calculation of the data signature parameter, which are both defined in the EIP.

Not following the EIP specification will end up in unexpected integration failures with EIP712-compliant wallets or tooling that perform the encoding in the appropriate way.

In ProxyFactory.deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature(), the digest is calculated as follows:

```solidity
bytes32 digest = _hashTypedDataV4(
    keccak256(
        abi.encode(contestId, data)
    )
);
```

The EIP-712 specification defines the encoding of a message as:

"\x19\x01" ‖ domainSeparator ‖ hashStruct(message)

In the current implementation, "\x19\x01" and domainSeparator are correctly calculated and appended as per OpenZeppelin's _hashTypedDataV4() function, but hashStruct(message) is not respected. 

The EIP defines that the hashStruct of a message is calculated from the hashing of the typeHash and the encoding of the data; and the former is currently missing in the digest calculation.

Additionally, the data parameter which is being included as part of the signature, is a bytes type, which the EIP defines as Dynamic. Dynamic types are encoded as the hash of the contents; and currently the data parameter is being encoded as-is.

The data being signed is not being encoded as per the EIP-712 specification, which will result in unexpected integration failures with EIP712-compliant wallets or tooling that perform the encoding in the appropriate way.

After looking at the tests, I would say this error was not caught since the tests themselves follow the same exact implementation for creating the data being signed. Usage of external libraries such as Ethers.js would have likely revealed this issue earlier.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect EIP-712 digest construction in the function that deploys a proxy and distributes assets by signature. The contract builds the message hash by calling OpenZeppelin’s _hashTypedDataV4 on keccak256(abi.encode(contestId, data)) but omits the required type hash for the function and does not hash the dynamic bytes parameter as defined by EIP-712. Because the specification mandates that the hashStruct be computed from keccak256(abi.encode(typeHash, contestId, keccak256(data))) the resulting digest differs from the one produced by compliant wallets or libraries such as ethers.js. The root cause is a misunderstanding of how EIP-712 encodes structured data: the developer used a simple abi.encode instead of the full type-hash-based encoding. This can be exploited by an attacker who can craft a signature that matches the contract’s malformed digest but would be rejected by external tools, or conversely, a legitimate user may sign a message that the contract cannot verify, causing the distribution transaction to revert with an "invalid signature" error. The impact is that legitimate participants may be unable to claim or receive funds, and a malicious actor could potentially replay or forge signatures that the contract accepts, leading to unauthorized token distribution or loss of funds. The condition occurs whenever deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature is called, i.e., during proxy deployment and fund distribution, and affects any user, wallet, or integration that relies on standard EIP-712 signing. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit where the reviewer compared the implementation against the EIP-712 spec; the test suite did not catch it because the tests generated the same malformed hash. The bug is subtle because the contract still produces a deterministic hash, so unit tests that mirror the same logic pass, making the problem easy to overlook. To fix the issue, the contract should define a constant type hash for the DeployAndDistribute function, include that type hash in the abi.encode call, and hash the dynamic data field with keccak256 before encoding, thereby producing a compliant hashStruct that OpenZeppelin’s _hashTypedDataV4 can combine with the domain separator. This change restores compatibility with standard wallets, prevents signature mismatches, and eliminates the risk of unauthorized fund distribution.

title: Blacklisted STADIUM_ADDRESS address cause fund stuck in the contract forever
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded commission transfer to a fixed STADIUM_ADDRESS that cannot be changed after deployment. Because the address is immutable, the contract assumes it will always be able to receive USDC rewards. The root cause is that the token used for rewards (USDC) allows its operator to blacklist arbitrary addresses, and the Distributor contract does not check for or handle a blacklist rejection. When the contest is closed and the Organizer calls deployProxyAndDistribute, the internal function _commissionTransfer attempts to move the entire token balance of the Proxy contract to STADIUM_ADDRESS via token.safeTransfer. If STADIUM_ADDRESS has been blacklisted, the safeTransfer call reverts, causing the whole distribution transaction to fail. As a result, the USDC that was already deposited into the Proxy contract remains locked there forever because the Proxy’s implementation is immutable and no rescue function can bypass the failing transfer. This situation occurs only after the blacklist is applied and a contest is being settled; it does not affect earlier stages of the contest. The parties affected include the Organizer who sent the rewards, the participants who expect to receive a share, and the protocol that relies on successful reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of funds and identified the hard‑coded address and the unconditional transfer. It can be hard to notice because the blacklist is an external condition that does not appear in the contract source, and the failure only manifests at the final distribution step, making the symptom look like a generic transaction revert. The impact is that funds disappear from the user’s perspective – rewards are never credited, balances stay at zero, and the UI may show a pending or failed reward indefinitely. To remediate, the STADIUM_ADDRESS should be stored in a mutable variable controlled by an admin role, allowing it to be updated if a token operator blacklists the current address. Additionally, the contract should handle transfer failures gracefully, for example by using a pull‑payment pattern or by checking the return value and providing an alternative rescue path, while also considering storage‑collision risks introduced by making the address updatable.

title: Malicious/Compromised organiser can reclaw all funds, stealing work from supporters
description:
The contest details state that 'If a contest is created and funded, there is no way to refund. All the funds belong to the persons who wants to help solve the problem, we call them "supporters".' (see More Context section). This is untrue, as the organizer is able to refund all of the contest funds.

In Distributor#distribute, there is no input validation on the winners array. A malicious or compromised organizer can, with little effort, simply pass an array of length one containing a wallet address that they control as the winners parameter, and [10000] as the percentages parameter in order to receive 100% of the funds initially deposited to the contract. Due to the design of the protocol, they would have 7 days after the contest ends (the value of the EXPIRATION_TIME constant in the ProxyFactory contract) to perform this action without the owner being able to prevent it.

Malicious/Compromised organizer can refund 100% of the contest funds, stealing work from sponsors.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked distribution mechanism that allows the contest organiser to claim the entire pool of funds deposited by supporters. The root cause is the absence of input validation in the Distributor contract’s distribute function: the winners array and the corresponding percentages are accepted without any checks on who the winners are or whether the percentages sum to the expected total. Because the contract’s logic does not restrict the organiser from being listed as a winner, a malicious or compromised organiser can invoke distribute after the contest has ended, supplying a single address that they control and a percentage value of 10000 (representing 100 %). The protocol’s design gives a seven‑day window after the contest expiration (the EXPIRATION_TIME constant in the ProxyFactory) during which this call can be made, and there is no owner or admin guard that can block it. An attacker can therefore redirect all deposited ether to their own wallet, effectively “refunding” the contest funds to themselves while the supporters receive nothing. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden disappearance of the expected reward pool, a zero balance for supporters, and the organiser receiving the full amount despite the public statement that refunds are impossible. The impact is financial loss for supporters, loss of trust in the platform, and the theft of work that was funded by those supporters. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s advertised behaviour with its actual code paths. It is hard to notice because the contract’s UI and documentation claim that refunds are not possible, leading reviewers to assume the distribution logic is safe, while the code silently permits arbitrary winner selection. To remediate the problem the distribution process should be split into two steps: the organiser submits the intended winners and percentages, which are stored in contract state, and a trusted admin (the owner of the ProxyFactory) must review and approve the allocation before any funds are transferred. Additional safeguards such as prohibiting the organiser from being a winner, enforcing that percentages add up to 100 %, and limiting the distribution window would also close the attack surface. This class of bug falls under “missing access control / unchecked input validation in fund distribution”, a common pattern where business‑logic assumptions are not enforced at the contract level, leading to unauthorized fund transfers.

title: TRANSFER_FROM_WITH_PERMIT command is vulnerable to DOS via frontrunning
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition that arises when the router’s TRANSFER_FROM_WITH_PERMIT command attempts to execute an ERC20Permit call and a token transfer in the same transaction. The command first calls permit(...) with the signature supplied by the user, then proceeds to transfer the approved amount. Because the permit function consumes a nonce, any other transaction that calls permit with the same parameters before the router’s transaction is mined will increment the nonce and render the signature invalid. An attacker who monitors the mempool can extract the signature and deadline from the pending calldata, submit a separate permit transaction, and thereby consume the nonce. When the original router transaction is later executed, the internal permit call reverts due to an invalid nonce, causing the whole execute() call to revert. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails; no tokens are transferred, the user’s balance remains unchanged, and the user may need to resend the transaction, incurring additional gas costs. The issue occurs only when the router includes the permit call inside the same execute() call; it does not affect plain token transfers that use a pre‑approved allowance. The affected parties are token holders who rely on the router for gas‑less approvals, the router contract itself, and any downstream protocol that assumes the transfer will succeed. The problem was discovered during a security audit by observing that the permit signature could be front‑run, and it is subtle because the revert does not explicitly indicate a nonce mismatch, making it appear as an unexplained failure. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running‑induced denial-of-service vulnerabilities in meta‑transactions that combine signature verification and state‑changing calls. To mitigate the issue, the router should not assume that a permit call will always succeed; it can use a try/catch around the permit invocation and, if it fails, verify that the required allowance is already present before proceeding, or separate the permit step into a distinct transaction, or enforce that only the signature owner can call permit. By ensuring that the final allowance state matches the intended transfer amount, the router can continue execution even when the permit call is front‑run, eliminating the denial-of-service condition.

title: Code doesn't work with fee on transfer tokens
description:
There are some places in the code that assume the ERC20 transfer function will transfer a specified amount and this is not true for tokens with fee. This will cause wrong calculation results in those cases. Some of the places where this issue happens:
1. In _addInitialLiquidity() code assumes it transfers _initialLiquidityInIBT tokens and tries to transfer them to the Curve pool.
2. In _dispatchPreviewRate() code assumes it would transfer value from the user.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect assumption about ERC20 transfer semantics. The contract treats the transfer function as if it always moves the exact amount specified, but fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens deduct a percentage or fixed fee on each transfer, so the recipient actually receives less than the amount sent. This mismatch appears in two critical paths: when the contract adds initial liquidity it calls transfer to move a declared amount of the token to a Curve pool, assuming the pool receives the full amount; and when the contract previews a rate it transfers tokens from the user, assuming the transferred value equals the user‑provided amount. Because the actual received balance is lower, the subsequent calculations for liquidity provisioning and rate preview are based on an incorrect token balance. An attacker or an unwary user can trigger the bug simply by using a fee‑on‑transfer token with the protocol; the transaction will not revert, so the error can go unnoticed. The impact is that liquidity may be under‑funded, rate previews become inaccurate, and users may see smaller balances than expected, potentially leading to loss of funds or mispricing of trades. The issue manifests whenever a fee‑on‑transfer token is supplied to functions that rely on exact transfer amounts, i.e., during initial liquidity addition or any preview‑rate operation. All participants—liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions are broken. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the reliance on transfer return values without checking the actual post‑transfer balance. It is hard to notice because the ERC20 transfer call succeeds, no error is thrown, and the contract does not verify the amount received, so the discrepancy is silent. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit fee‑on‑transfer tokens, or it must measure the real amount received by checking token balances before and after the transfer and use that value for all subsequent calculations. Alternatively, the code can be refactored to work with the token’s transfer fee logic, for example by using a pull‑based model (allowance) and accounting for the fee explicitly. In short, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer ERC20 tokens” and leads to wrong accounting, unexpected zero or reduced balances, and potentially incorrect financial outcomes.

title: Attack surface in the middle of the execute()
description:
Users can execute multiple commands through Router contract's execute() function. These commands allow to transfer funds from msg.sender which is set as msgSender in the first execute() call. The issue is that if during the execute() execution, the execution reaches a malicious address, the attacker can perform a variety of actions leading to funds stolen.
The condition "execution flow reaches a malicious address" can happen in various ways, for example with hook functionality that some ERC20 tokens have(ERC777, ERC677 and ...), the execution will reach the recipient address that is defined in the commands.
1. The address can reenter the Router contract and execute arbitrary commands like transferring the initial transaction sender's funds.
User1 -> Router.execute() -> .... -> malicious address -> Router.execute() -> USDT.transferFrom(User1, malicious address, )
2. onFlashLoan() function doesn't check the caller and the operator and so it would be possible to call it from an arbitrary address with arbitrary data.
Users can execute multiple commands through Router contract's execute() function. The malicious address can reenter the Router contract through onFlashLoan() function and steal the original msgSender funds.
User1 -> Router.execute() -> .... -> malicious address -> Router.onFlashLoan() -> Router.execute() -> USDT.transferFrom(User1, malicious address, )
3. Users can set approval of Router's tokens for malicious address by setting arbitrary address in the execute() function's command (for example using DEPOSIT_ASSET_IN_IBT command and setting malicious address as ibt's value). The malicious address can transfer Router contract's balance and steal the original msgSender funds.
A. Malicious_address -> Router.execute() -> USDT.approve(malicious address, uint256.max)
B. User1 -> Router.execute() -> .... -> Malicious_address -> USDT.transferFrom(Router, malicious address, )
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Router contract’s execute() function, which allows a caller to batch multiple arbitrary commands that may interact with external token contracts. Because execute() does not restrict which addresses can be called during the command sequence, the execution flow can be redirected to a malicious contract through mechanisms such as ERC777/ERC677 token hooks, custom onFlashLoan callbacks, or approval commands. When control reaches a malicious address, that contract can re‑enter the Router (or its Dispatcher) and issue additional commands on behalf of the original msg.sender. For example, a malicious token hook can invoke a fallback that calls Router.execute() again and triggers a transferFrom that moves the original user’s USDT to the attacker, or the attacker can exploit an unchecked onFlashLoan function to re‑enter and drain funds, or set an unlimited allowance for itself and later transfer the Router’s token balance. The root cause is the absence of a whitelist or re‑entrancy guard for external calls inside execute(), the lack of caller validation in onFlashLoan(), and the failure to reset token allowances after command execution. An attacker can craft a transaction that appears benign to the user, but once the Router processes the malicious command, the attacker’s contract executes a callback that steals the user’s or Router’s assets. The impact is the loss of user funds or protocol liquidity; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction while the token balance becomes zero or the expected refund never arrives. This condition occurs whenever a command triggers an external call to a contract that can execute code, which is common with tokens that implement transfer hooks or flash‑loan interfaces. All users of the Router, as well as the protocol that relies on its asset management, are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that traced the execution path of execute() and identified unchecked external interactions. Because the problem is hidden behind token callbacks and allowance settings, it can be difficult to notice without deep analysis of the call graph. To remediate, the Router should enforce a whitelist of addresses that are allowed to be called from within execute(), add a re‑entrancy guard, validate msg.sender and operator in onFlashLoan(), and ensure that any token allowance granted during a command is cleared or limited to trusted contracts such as known Curve pools. These measures restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent malicious contracts from hijacking the execution flow and stealing funds.

title: High decimal tokens will lead to loss of precision in oracle results
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic routine that converts a Chainlink price, expressed with 18 fixed‑point decimals, into a quote amount for arbitrary token pairs. The routine first divides the product of the price and the base amount by 10**baseDecimals and only afterwards adjusts the scale to match the quote token’s decimals. When either the base or the quote token uses more than 18 decimals – a situation that occurs with high‑precision tokens such as those with 24 decimals – the intermediate division truncates the result because Solidity integer division discards any fractional part. The subsequent multiplication that attempts to restore the missing precision cannot recover the lost digits, so the final amount may be rounded down dramatically, often to zero for modest input amounts. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a high‑decimal token pair and a small baseAmount; the oracle will return a quote amount of zero, causing the user to receive no tokens despite having supplied a non‑zero amount. The impact is that users see their expected balances disappear, the protocol under‑pays or fails to credit the correct amount, and accounting assumptions that a price conversion is lossless are violated. This condition manifests only when token decimals exceed the oracle’s 18‑decimal baseline, which is uncommon for most ERC‑20 tokens and therefore easy to overlook during testing. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test using two mock ERC‑20 contracts with 24 decimals; the test demonstrated that converting an amount of 1 000 000‑1 resulted in a zero quote amount. The bug is hard to notice because typical token pairs have 18 or fewer decimals, so the rounding error does not appear in standard test vectors. To remediate, the conversion logic should be reordered so that the multiplication of price and baseAmount occurs before any division, and the scaling for token decimals should be applied after the full‑precision product is computed. Using a larger intermediate type or a fixed‑point library can also prevent truncation. In essence, the flaw is a classic precision‑loss arithmetic bug caused by improper ordering of integer division and multiplication in a financial calculation, leading to unexpected zero or reduced payouts for users of high‑decimal assets.

title: Tokens with extreme price differences along the path could round price to zero
description:
In the unlikely event that the price ratio between two tokens is more than `1e18:1`, the oracle will round the price down to zero.

While the largest price ratio I can currently find is `BTC/SHIB` (which can be calculated using [SHIB/ETH](https://etherscan.io/address/0x8dD1CD88F43aF196ae478e91b9F5E4Ac69A97C61#readContract) and [ETH/BTC](https://etherscan.io/address/0xdeb288F737066589598e9214E782fa5A8eD689e8#readContract) to be approximately `1e11:1`), that puts us close enough to the range that this is something we should be prepared for.

Based on the use for this oracle with swappers, a `0` price would allow the bot executing the swap to steal all of a user's tokens for free.

Note that this `0` price could occur as an intermediate step along a longer path, and the `0` value would carry through to the final price, leading to the theft of tokens with closer values as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑division underflow in the price oracle used by the swapping module. When the price ratio between two tokens exceeds the 18‑decimal precision limit (approximately 1e18:1), the fixed‑point division truncates the result to zero. This occurs because the oracle stores prices with 18 decimals of precision and performs a downward rounding division; if the numerator is far smaller than the denominator, the quotient becomes zero. An attacker can exploit this by constructing a swap path that includes an intermediate token pair with an extreme price disparity, causing the oracle to return a zero price for that step. The swap logic then treats the zero price as a valid quote, allowing the bot executing the swap to acquire the user’s input tokens without paying any output tokens, effectively stealing the funds. The impact is the loss of user balances: a user expects to receive a certain amount of tokens but receives none, and the user’s balance may be reduced to zero. The condition under which this occurs is rare but possible when trading pairs such as BTC/SHIB, which have a ratio on the order of 1e11:1, or any path where an intermediate price exceeds the 1e18:1 threshold. All participants that rely on the oracle for price information – including end‑users, swapping bots, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariant that input value equals output value times price is broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle’s handling of extreme price ratios. It is difficult to notice because the zero price may only appear as an intermediate value in a multi‑hop swap, not as an obvious final price, and the contract does not currently check for a zero result. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑to‑zero or underflow errors in fixed‑point arithmetic. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify that the computed price is non‑zero before using it, reverting with an appropriate error if the check fails, or alternatively employ higher‑precision arithmetic or a minimum‑price safeguard. This change restores the expected behavior that a user receives a non‑zero amount of tokens and prevents the protocol from allowing free token extraction.

title: Splits with too many recipients can lead to locked funds
description:
When calling `distribute()` for a given Wallet, it is required to send assets to all recipients. In the event that a Split is initialized with too many recipients, the gas cost of such a transaction can get so high that it will not fit within the block gas limit. In such a case, all funds will be stuck (unless there is an owner set who can recover them via `execCalls()`).

While a split this large seems unlikely, some of the larger current Splits (like Protocol Guild) have upwards of 100 recipients, so it seems in the range of possibility that larger Splits could be used at some point (especially with liquid Splits, where use cases like distributing to owners of a ~10k NFT collection might be common).

Based on gas estimates, it appears that ~1100 recipients is the point where such a failure would occur.

There are multiple other "safety check" validations that are not included when Splits are validated. These include checking for an empty Split (which won't send any payments), checking for duplicate addresses, etc. However, all of these boil down to user error. The user is getting the reasonably expected behavior, even if we think this behavior is unwanted.

This issue is different, because the result the user gets is not what they would reasonably expect. For this reason, I am submitting this as an issue to be fixed, while leaving the others for the Splits team to handle on the front end.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a Split contract is configured with an excessively large number of recipients and the distribute() function is called. The root cause is that distribute() iterates over the entire recipient list and performs a token transfer for each entry, but the contract does not enforce any upper bound on the list length. When the number of recipients grows beyond the amount of gas that can fit in a single block – roughly 1,100 recipients for typical ERC20 transfers – the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, leaving the contract’s balance untouched. Because the function requires sending assets to every recipient in one atomic call, the failure prevents any payout from being executed, so users see no funds arriving, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may simply show a pending or failed transaction without an explicit error message. The impact is that funds become effectively locked; only an owner with access to execCalls() can manually recover them, otherwise the assets remain inaccessible. This situation can arise whenever a split is created with many participants, such as distributing to owners of a large NFT collection or a protocol guild with hundreds of members. The issue was discovered during an audit by measuring gas consumption in a test that created a split with 1,100 recipients and observed that more than 30 million gas was required, exceeding typical block limits. The problem is hard to notice because the contract behaves as documented – it attempts to send to all recipients – but the out‑of‑gas failure is silent from a business‑logic perspective, leading users to assume the distribution succeeded when it actually did not. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded loop gas‑limit exhaustion, a form of denial‑of‑service that violates the expectation that a split payout will always deliver each participant’s share. To remediate, the contract should include a validation step that caps the number of recipients to a safe threshold (for example fewer than 250), or redesign the payout mechanism to use a pull‑based model, batch processing, or other techniques that avoid a single transaction needing to cover an arbitrarily large list. By enforcing such limits, the contract can guarantee that distribute() will complete within the block gas limit, preserving the expected behavior that each user receives their allocated amount and preventing funds from becoming locked.

title: Denial of Service Attacks on Router Permit Functions
poc: See here for a deeper dive.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises in the router contract when it uses external permit functions to set token allowances before performing a deposit or repayment. The root cause is that the permit() function in the lender contract and the permitTransferFrom() function in the Permit2 contract are public, external calls that advance a nonce each time they are executed. An attacker who can monitor the mempool can extract the owner, spender, value, deadline and signature parameters from a legitimate user’s transaction and submit a front‑run transaction that calls the same permit function with identical parameters before the user’s call is mined. This front‑run consumes the current nonce, so when the user’s transaction later invokes the router’s depositWithPermit2 or repayWithPermit2 function, the permit call inside the router fails because the signature no longer matches the updated nonce. The router does not catch this failure and proceeds assuming the allowance was granted, causing the subsequent transfer or repayment step to revert. The impact is that a user’s attempt to deposit collateral or repay a loan silently fails; from the user’s perspective the transaction reverts or emits no event, the expected balance update does not occur, and the user may see their token balance unchanged or even a temporary reduction with no refund. In time‑sensitive repayment scenarios this can lead to missed deadlines, potential liquidation, or loss of borrowing capacity. The condition occurs whenever the router relies on a single‑transaction permit flow without handling a failed permit, and when an adversary can front‑run the transaction, which is feasible on public blockchains with transparent mempools. All users of the router, lenders, and the protocol as a whole are affected because the denial‑of‑service can be repeatedly triggered to block legitimate operations. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of the router’s permit‑based functions and noticed that the external permit calls were not protected against nonce manipulation. It is hard to notice because the transaction simply fails with a generic error (for example “insufficient pre‑pay”) rather than an obvious indication that a permit was front‑run. To remediate, the contract should wrap the permit call in a try‑catch block, verify that the allowance is sufficient after the call, and continue with a fallback safeTransferFrom if the permit fails. Alternatively, the logic used for deposits – a boolean flag indicating whether a pre‑pay has occurred – can be applied to repayments, ensuring that the contract does not depend exclusively on a successful permit. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of front‑runable external call vulnerabilities where a dependent state change (nonce increment) can be hijacked to cause a denial of service.

title: Lack of deadline Check in the BadDebtProcessor::uniswapV3FlashCallback() Could Lead To Loss of Funds to the User
description:
The UNISWAP_POOL().swap() is performed in the FrontendManager::callback() when the action == 6 and in the BoostManager::_action2Burn() functions. In both those occasions, the deadline check is performed in addition to the slippage checks. This is to ensure that the transaction is not executed after a delay at an unfavourable price point to the user. The slippage check alone can not mitigate this issue since slippage applies to the derived swap value at the time of the transaction execution.

But the UNISWAP_POOL().swap() performed in the BadDebtProcessor::uniswapV3FlashCallback() only performs the slippage check but does not perform a deadline check.

The BadDebtProcessor::process() transaction can be executed after a significant delay, which could prompt the asset ratios in the UniswapV3Pool to have changed considerably. Hence the swapped and recovered asset amounts are calculated based on the highly altered price points. As a result, the provided slippage is stale and will not provide the required protection to the user, thus incurring loss to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing deadline verification in the BadDebtProcessor::uniswapV3FlashCallback function, which performs a Uniswap V3 flash swap without checking whether the transaction is still within a user‑specified time window. In other parts of the system, such as FrontendManager::callback and BoostManager::_action2Burn, a deadline check is combined with slippage checks to protect users from price movement after a delay. The root cause is that the flash‑swap callback relies solely on a slippage check, assuming the price at execution will be close to the price at the time the slippage limit was set. Because the deadline is not enforced, the BadDebtProcessor::process transaction can be executed long after the user submitted it, allowing the pool’s asset ratios to drift significantly. An attacker, a miner, or a network congestion event can cause this delay, resulting in the flash swap being settled at a much worse price than expected. The stale slippage limit no longer provides protection, so the swapped amount that must be repaid may exceed the amount recovered, causing the user to lose part or all of the intended refund. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful transaction, but the balance after the call is lower than expected, sometimes even zero, contrary to the expectation that the process will recover the full amount without loss. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the implementation of deadline checks across different contract entry points. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the slippage check passes, yet the economic outcome is unfavorable, making the loss appear as a normal market result. The bug belongs to the class of deadline‑missing or time‑bound validation errors, where a contract fails to enforce a temporal constraint that is essential for preserving economic invariants. To remediate, a deadline parameter should be passed from the user to BadDebtProcessor::process and enforced inside uniswapV3FlashCallback before invoking the pool swap, ensuring that the flash swap is aborted if the current block timestamp exceeds the supplied deadline, thereby restoring the intended protection against stale price data and preventing inadvertent fund loss.

title: Unfair Liquidation of Healthy Accounts
description:
A borrower can be unfairly liquidated even after becoming healthy if borrowing is paused and modification is restricted, and a liquidator front-runs the borrower’s Borrower::clear() transaction. The Borrower.liquidate() function does not check if the borrower is currently healthy BalanceSheet.isHealthy(), relying solely on the warnTime being greater than zero.

Furthermore, the Borrower::clear() can be called after the LIQUIDATION_GRACE_PERIOD to make an account healthy again. This allows a depositor to make their account healthy again by depositing directly to the lender and replenishing their ante even after the LIQUIDATION_GRACE_PERIOD has passed.

But the issue here is that a liquidator who doesn’t immediately liquidate an unhealthy account (until 7 minutes have passed) since there is no incentive could observe this Borrower::clear() transaction and decide to front-run it with liquidate() transaction setting the CloseFactor == 10000. This will enable the liquidator to liquidate a healthy position maliciously and gain the ante as an incentive.

The vulnerability occurs in the following scenario:

1. A borrower’s account becomes unhealthy and is warned via Borrower.warn().

2. Borrowing is paused via Factory.pause(). This prevents the borrower from using Borrower.modify().

3. The LIQUIDATION_GRACE_PERIOD expires.

4. The borrower decides to make his account healthy by directly depositing to the Lender contract and replenishing the ante in the Borrower contract. This would make the BalanceSheet.isHealthy() true again.

5. The borrower attempts to call Borrower.clear() to remove the warning status.

6. A liquidator observes the pending clear transaction and front-runs it with a Borrower.liquidate() transaction with CloseFactor == 10000.

7. Because Borrower.liquidate() only checks warnTime > 0 and not BalanceSheet.isHealthy(), the liquidation proceeds.

8. The liquidator receives the borrower’s full ante amount as a liquidation incentive, even though the borrower’s account was healthy at the time of liquidation.

• Unfair Liquidation: Borrowers who have taken steps to become healthy can be liquidated, losing their ante.
• Liquidators making unfair profit: Liquidators can profit by liquidating healthy accounts, exploiting a race condition.
• Loss of Funds: The borrower loses funds (up to the full ante value) unfairly.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unfair liquidation condition that allows a liquidator to seize the full ante of a borrower even after the borrower has restored the account to a healthy state. The root cause is that the liquidation routine only verifies that a warning timestamp (warnTime) is set, without checking the current health of the borrower’s balance sheet via the isHealthy() predicate. When borrowing is paused, the borrower cannot use the normal modify() path to resolve the warning, so they resort to a direct deposit to the lender contract and then call clear() to remove the warning flag after the liquidation grace period has elapsed. Because clear() can be executed after the grace period, a pending clear transaction can be observed in the mempool. A malicious liquidator can front‑run this transaction by submitting a liquidate() call with a maximum close factor (CloseFactor == 10000) before the clear transaction is mined. The liquidate() function sees warnTime > 0, assumes the account is still unsafe, and proceeds with liquidation, awarding the liquidator the entire ante as incentive. This scenario occurs only when borrowing is paused, the grace period has expired, and the borrower attempts to clear the warning after manually replenishing collateral. The affected parties are borrowers who have taken steps to become healthy, liquidators who can profit from the race condition, and the protocol itself, which loses trustworthiness. The issue was discovered during a security review of the StackingSalmon contracts, where the logical flow of warning, pause, grace period, and clear was examined and the missing health check identified. It is hard to notice because the warning flag remains set, giving the impression that the account is still unsafe, and the front‑running window is short and depends on transaction ordering. From a user perspective the UI may show a healthy balance but a liquidation event still occurs, resulting in the borrower’s ante disappearing and the liquidator receiving an unexpected profit. The bug belongs to the class of race‑condition and state‑validation errors where a function relies on stale or incomplete state checks. To remediate, the liquidation function should perform an explicit isHealthy() verification before proceeding, and the protocol should consider restricting clear() calls after the grace period or requiring the warning flag to be cleared only when the account is truly healthy. This change restores the intended business logic that only unhealthy positions may be liquidated, preserving borrower funds and protocol integrity.

title: Rounding issues could allow majority shareholders to steal funds
description:
When distributions are calculated (using either push or pull), the `_split.calculateAllocatedAmount()` function is used to determine the amount.

```solidity
allocatedAmount = amount * split.allocations[index] / split.totalAllocation;
```

In the situation where one user holds a majority position in a Split, and the decimals of the token being distributed are very low, it is possible that an amount could be distributed such that minority positions are rounded down to zero and all funds are sent to the majority position.

Of course, with most normal tokens, the values required are so small that this doesn't present a risk. However, when tokens with very low decimals (such as [Gemini's GUSD](https://etherscan.io/token/0x056Fd409E1d7A124BD7017459dFEa2F387b6d5Cd?a=0x5f65f7b609678448494De4C87521CdF6cEf1e932)) are combined with a low cost chain, the risk presents itself.

(Note that, while GUSD is a rarer token with wei valued at $0.01 USD, more common tokens like WBTC could face a similar risk, with wei valued at $50,000 / 108 = 1/20th of a cent.)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the calculation of each recipient’s share during token distribution. The contract multiplies the total amount by the recipient’s allocation and then divides by the total allocation. When the token has very few decimal places (for example two‑decimal stablecoins) and a split is heavily weighted toward one address, the integer division can truncate the minority’s share to zero. As a result, each distribution sends the full amount to the majority holder while the minority’s portion is silently dropped. This can be triggered repeatedly by distributing small chunks of value (e.g., $9.99 of a 2‑decimal token) so that the minority’s computed share is less than one token unit and is rounded down. The impact is that minority participants see no increase in their balance, the contract’s residual balance grows, and the majority address accumulates the entire pool, effectively stealing funds from other shareholders. The condition occurs only when the token’s granularity is coarse and the allocation percentages are extreme; with typical 18‑decimal ERC‑20 tokens the effect is negligible, which makes the bug easy to overlook during testing. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where a split of 101 receivers with a 90 % majority and a 0.1 % minority was fed 2‑decimal GUSD; after many small distributions the minority balances remained zero. The problem is hard to notice because the total distributed amount matches the input amount, and the missing fractions are hidden in the contract’s residual balance. To remediate, the protocol should either warn users when a split involves low‑decimal tokens and extreme allocation ratios, or modify the allocation algorithm to use a rounding‑up scheme or a minimum allocation check that prevents a share from being rounded to zero. In business terms the bug violates the assumption that every shareholder receives a proportional payout; instead the accounting logic discards fractional shares, causing money to disappear from minority accounts.

title: Front-Running Vulnerability in enrollCourier() Function
description:
The enrollCourier() function allows users to enroll in a referral program by associating their address with a unique courierId and a cut value, which represents the portion of the interest they will receive, from the interest earned by the referrer. The function includes a requirement that the cut for a given courierId must be zero before enrollment as shown below:
```solidity
require(couriers[id].cut == 0);
```
The above check is in place to ensure that once a particular id has been enrolled its information can not be changed. This requirement further ensures that each courierId can only be used once. However, it also opens up the possibility for an attacker to front-run a enrollCourier() transaction. By monitoring the network for transactions attempting to enroll a specific courierId, an attacker can quickly submit their own transaction with the same id and a cut > 0 value, causing the original transaction to revert since the courierId is already taken. Since the protocol is implemented on the Berachain this vulnerability is easy to exploit due to low gas fees.

Denial of Service: Genuine users can be prevented from enrolling with their desired courierId, as the attacker can claim the id first. Loss of Incentives: Users may lose the opportunity to earn incentives through the referral program if they cannot register.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the enrollCourier() function of the referral program. The function allows a caller to register a courierId together with a cut value that determines the share of interest the courier will receive. Before writing the record the contract checks require(couriers[id].cut == 0) to guarantee that an identifier that has already been used cannot be overwritten. Because the identifier is supplied by the caller, an attacker who watches the mempool can see a pending transaction that tries to enroll a particular id, and can immediately submit another transaction with the same id but a non‑zero cut. The attacker’s transaction is mined first, the state entry for that id is created, and when the original transaction is later executed the require statement fails, causing the call to revert. The bug occurs whenever the network fee is low enough to allow rapid submission, as on Berachain, and when the contract does not enforce any ordering or uniqueness beyond the simple cut‑zero check. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for legitimate users: they receive a revert and never obtain the courierId they expected, losing the chance to earn referral incentives. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a “transaction failed” message without explaining that the identifier was already taken, leading to confusion. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the enrollment logic. It can be hard to notice because the revert is indistinguishable from other failure reasons and the contract does not emit an explicit event indicating that the id is already occupied. The vulnerability belongs to the class of front‑running or race‑condition bugs where user‑controlled identifiers are not protected against pre‑emptive claims. To remediate, the contract should generate courierIds internally (e.g., by incrementing a counter) or otherwise restrict how many times a single address can request a custom id, possibly by charging a small fee or imposing per‑address limits. By removing the ability for an external actor to choose the identifier, the race condition disappears and legitimate users can reliably enroll and receive their expected cut of interest.

title: Front-Running Vulnerability in Lender::redeem() Function Leading to Denial of Redemption
description:
The Lender::redeem() function is used to burn shares from the owner and send the amount of underlying tokens to the receiver. In the redeem function, after the respective shares are burnt, the following check is performed on the cache.totalSupply value.
```solidity
cache.totalSupply = _burn(owner, shares, inventory, cache.totalSupply);
require(cache.totalSupply == 0 || cache.totalSupply > 1e5);
```
The transaction will only proceed if the cache.totalSupply is either 0 or >1e5. Now let’s consider the following scenario:

1. User A has amount1 shares and the totalSupply is also equal to amount1.

2. User A decides to redeem his amount1 shares and calls the Lender::redeem() function.

3. The transaction should proceed since now the cache.totalSupply == 0.

4. But an attacker front-runs the redeem Tx and deposits an amount equaling 1 wei of shares into the Lender contract.

5. Now User A Tx executes and after the _burn execution the cache.totalSupply == 1 and it is != 0 and < 1e5. Hence the UserA redeems Tx reverts.

A genuine user is unable to redeem his total amount of shares when he is the final redeemer of the Lender contract, even though the protocol logically allows the redemption. This will degrade the user experience and will waste gas due to revert if the user calls the redeem multiple times. The user will either have to redeem fewer shares than his total eligible share amount or wait for subsequent deposits to increase the totalSupply > 1e5 (after the user redemption is accounted for). This is a loss of opportunity for the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑redemption bug in the Lender contract’s redeem function. The function burns a caller’s shares and then checks the cached totalSupply, requiring that the value be either exactly zero or larger than 100 000 shares. When a user holds the entire share supply and attempts to redeem all of it, the totalSupply becomes zero after the burn and the transaction would normally succeed. However, an attacker can front‑run the user’s transaction by depositing a single wei of shares just before the redemption is executed. This tiny deposit changes the post‑burn totalSupply from zero to one, which fails the require condition because one is neither zero nor greater than the 100 000 threshold. Consequently the user’s redeem call reverts, preventing the expected transfer of underlying tokens. The root cause is the reliance on a totalSupply invariant that can be manipulated by arbitrarily small deposits, creating an edge case that only appears when the supply is very low. Exploitation requires only the ability to submit a transaction with a minimal share deposit before the victim’s redemption, a realistic scenario in public mempools where front‑running is possible. The impact is a denial of service for legitimate users who are the final redeemer: they receive no tokens, see a transaction revert, waste gas, and must either redeem a smaller amount or wait for additional deposits that raise totalSupply above the threshold. This condition occurs specifically when the user’s share balance equals the entire contract supply and an attacker injects dust before the burn. All users of the Lender contract are affected, as any final redeemer can be blocked, undermining the protocol’s promised ability to fully withdraw funds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of the redeem function and identified the unexpected interaction between the burn operation and the totalSupply check. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears to enforce a sensible safety margin, yet it does not account for the edge case where totalSupply is reduced to a non‑zero dust amount. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑invariant manipulation” or “dust‑induced revert” vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal accounting invariant can be broken by minimal value changes. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful redeem request but then display an error, no tokens received, and possibly a message about the totalSupply requirement, contradicting the expectation that redeeming all shares should always work. To fix the issue, the contract should remove the totalSupply == 0 || totalSupply > 1e5 check, replace it with a minimum‑deposit rule that prevents dust deposits, or adjust the logic to allow redemption when totalSupply becomes a small non‑zero value after burning. The correction must ensure that the invariant cannot be violated by front‑running tiny deposits and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions about full withdrawal remain intact.

title: Swap Callback Rejects Current Time as deadline
description:
In FrontendManager.sol’s callback() function, if the action is 6, a swap action is supposed to take place. The function, however, rejects the deadline check if the current block time is less than the deadline.

This violates the common DeFi practice of including the current time with the deadline. Also, since the function is used in Borrower.sol’s liquidate function, the caller may be a bot, keeper or a contract programmed to scan for borrowers to liquidate. Many of these external contracts are designed to use the current block.timestamp as deadline, therefore, this check will break integration.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the callback function of FrontendManager.sol, which is invoked when a swap action (identified by the numeric code 6) is requested. The function performs a deadline validation that is inverted: it rejects the transaction whenever the current block timestamp is less than the supplied deadline, effectively requiring the deadline to be in the past or exactly equal to the current time. In typical DeFi contracts, the deadline represents the latest acceptable block time for the operation, and the validation should allow execution while the current time is less than or equal to the deadline. The root cause is a reversed comparison operator that checks block.timestamp < deadline instead of block.timestamp <= deadline (or the opposite logical condition). This mistake can be exploited by any caller that supplies a future deadline, which is the normal practice for swaps and liquidations. An external bot, keeper, or liquidation contract that follows the common pattern of passing block.timestamp plus a safety margin as the deadline will trigger the reject path, causing the swap to fail. Because Borrower.sol’s liquidate function relies on this callback, a failed swap prevents the liquidation from completing, potentially leaving collateral unclaimed and exposing the protocol to increased risk. From a user perspective, the UI may show that a liquidation attempt returns no result, the expected token exchange never occurs, and balances remain unchanged despite a successful transaction submission. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the callback routine and compared it against standard deadline handling patterns. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles and the check appears to enforce a deadline, yet the logic is opposite to the intended behavior, and the failure only manifests when a deadline greater than the current block time is used. To remediate, the deadline comparison should be corrected to accept transactions while the current time is less than or equal to the deadline, typically by replacing the strict less‑than check with a less‑than‑or‑equal operator or by inverting the condition. This aligns the contract with the common DeFi expectation that a deadline defines an upper bound on execution time, restores compatibility with liquidation bots, and prevents denial‑of‑service scenarios where swaps cannot be performed.

title: UniswapPositionFeesAreNotIncludedinAssetCalculationFor Warnings and Liquidation
description:
Uniswap LPs earn fees for providing liquidity to Uniswap pools. These fees are, however, not taken as a part of the position’s assets when the assets are being tallied for warning via the _getAssets() function. The function only returns the borrower’s balance and pool liquidity at price points a and b as seen in the Assets struct.

Since the user’s fees are not considered, a borrower could technically have enough assets, both in liquidity and fees, but will still be deemed unhealthy and prime for liquidation. Worse, when a user is liquidated, their Uniswap positions are burned, and their fees are collected to Borrower.sol where it is eventually considered as part of the assets to put up for auction, in a way, sending the fees to the liquidators instead.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑valuation omission that occurs when a borrower holds Uniswap liquidity provider (LP) positions with accrued but unclaimed fees. The protocol’s internal health‑check routine, implemented in the _getAssets() function, aggregates only the borrower’s raw token balance and the current pool liquidity at two price points, deliberately ignoring any fees that have accumulated on the LP position.
