The issue is subtle because events do not modify on‑chain state and are often assumed to be reliable logs; the code path that emits them looks legitimate, making the problem hard to spot during casual review. The bug was identified during a security audit when the auditor noticed the automatic EMITTER role grant and the generic call function in the DAO, realizing that the two together form an unrestricted event‑emission vector. The impact is medium severity: while no ether or tokens are directly stolen, the ability to fabricate trusted events can undermine accounting, reward distribution, or any off‑chain process that relies on the emitted logs. The vulnerability can be mitigated by preventing the DAO’s generic call function from targeting the Emitter contract, by removing the EMITTER role from DAO proxies, or by adding stricter access control (e.g., only a designated trusted address may emit events). Since events are immutable, any fabricated logs already emitted cannot be erased, so the primary remediation is to stop further misuse and to adjust off‑chain consumers to validate event sources.

title: Admin can't increase claim balance when hasAllowanceMechanism has been set in Claim contract
description: When users creates DAO they specify the claimBalance and later they can increase it. The issue is that when hasAllowanceMechanism is set there's no way to increase claimBalance because depositTokens() won't allow it. This would cause constant claimBalance that admin set during the DAO creation and it won't be possible to increase airdrop total amount.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical restriction that prevents an authorized administrator from increasing the claim balance of a DAO when the contract’s hasAllowanceMechanism flag is enabled. During DAO creation the admin sets an initial claimBalance that represents the total amount of tokens available for an airdrop. The contract is supposed to allow the admin to later increase this amount by calling depositTokens, but the depositTokens implementation contains a guard that blocks any balance increase if hasAllowanceMechanism is true. As a result, once the allowance mechanism is activated, the claimBalance becomes immutable; any attempt by the admin to top‑up the airdrop silently fails and the on‑chain state remains unchanged. This occurs because the function’s conditional logic does not differentiate between regular token deposits and admin‑initiated balance adjustments, treating both the same and rejecting the latter under the flag. Exploitation is straightforward: an admin who follows the intended workflow to increase the airdrop total will see the transaction succeed (no revert) but the claimBalance will not change, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual token availability. Users attempting to claim tokens after the admin’s failed increase will observe that no additional tokens are available – the UI will display the original claim amount, and claimants may receive less than anticipated or see the airdrop run out prematurely. The impact is functional rather than directly malicious: the protocol cannot scale its airdrop, potentially causing denial‑of‑service for future claimants and breaking business assumptions that the admin can replenish the pool. The issue manifests only when hasAllowanceMechanism is set and the admin invokes the increase function; in configurations where the flag is false, the balance can be raised normally. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the Claim contract’s state‑management functions, where the reviewer noted that the depositTokens path lacked an exception for privileged callers. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert, so developers may assume the increase succeeded, and the contract emits no explicit error indicating the restriction. To remediate, the contract should separate the logic for regular token deposits from admin‑controlled balance adjustments, either by adding an admin‑only bypass for the hasAllowanceMechanism check or by providing a dedicated function that updates claimBalance when the flag is active. This change restores the intended mutable nature of the claim pool while preserving the allowance mechanism’s security guarantees.

title: mintGTToAddress() in ERC20DAO doesn't check distributionAmount limit
description: While mintGTToAddress() in ERC721 and Factory contract check for distributionAmount limit the ERC20DAO doesn't check for distributionAmount limit and it would be possible for admins to mint unlimited amount of tokens.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked mint operation in the ERC20DAO contract’s mintGTToAddress() function. Unlike the ERC721 and Factory contracts, this function does not enforce the distributionAmount limit that caps how many governance tokens may be created for a given distribution round. The root cause is the absence of a require statement that compares the amount to be minted against the remaining distributionAmount, allowing any caller with the admin role to invoke the function with an arbitrary token amount. An attacker who controls the admin role can repeatedly call mintGTToAddress() and mint an unlimited number of tokens, inflating the total supply. This inflation dilutes existing token holders, undermines the token’s economic model, and can erode confidence in the DAO’s governance because voting power becomes meaningless when supply is unbounded. The issue manifests whenever an admin initiates a token distribution; there is no safeguard to stop the supply from exceeding the intended cap. It affects all participants who hold or expect to receive GT tokens, as their relative share and the value of their holdings may drop dramatically. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the implementation of mintGTToAddress() across contracts and noticed the missing limit check. Because the function signature and surrounding code appear normal, the problem can be easy to overlook without a side‑by‑side comparison. To remediate, the mintGTToAddress() implementation should include a check that the amount being minted does not exceed the remaining distributionAmount and should update the distributionAmount state accordingly, restoring the intended supply cap and preventing unlimited minting. In user‑facing terms, a token holder might notice that after a distribution event their balance seems smaller than expected, or that the token price drops sharply because new tokens appear out of thin air, contrary to the expectation that only a fixed amount would be minted for that round.

title: Owner's share should be deducted from total payment in governance buy functions
description: When users wants to buy governance token code calculates the total amount and then calculates the owner's share. The issue is that code transfers totalAmount + ownerShare from user. So as result users pays more than real price of the tokens because code doesn't subtract owner's share from total amount.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑charging arithmetic error in the governance token purchase functions. When a user initiates a buy, the contract first computes the nominal total price for the requested amount of tokens and then separately computes the owner’s fee (ownerShare). Instead of deducting the owner’s fee from the nominal total, the implementation adds the fee on top of the total and transfers totalAmount + ownerShare from the buyer’s wallet. The root cause is a misplaced addition operation and a failure to treat the owner’s share as part of the total cost rather than an extra amount. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any user calling the buy function will automatically be charged more than the advertised price, effectively losing the owner’s fee twice. The impact is monetary loss for users, who see the token price displayed correctly in the UI but receive a higher debit on their balance, leading to unexpected zero‑balance or reduced funds after a purchase. The condition under which it occurs is any execution of the governance token purchase path that uses the flawed calculation, typically the public buy function. All participants who attempt to acquire governance tokens – regular users, investors, and downstream contracts – are affected, while the protocol owner unintentionally receives excess funds. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the on‑chain transfer amount with the price calculation logic. It can be hard to notice because the UI may only show the token price, not the exact amount transferred, and the extra fee is hidden in the contract’s internal arithmetic. To remediate, the contract should compute a single total that already includes the owner’s share and transfer exactly that amount, or alternatively subtract the owner’s share from the nominal total before performing the transfer. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “incorrect payment aggregation” or “price calculation mismatch”, where the contract’s accounting assumptions about how fees are incorporated are violated, causing users to pay more than the intended cost and breaking the expected financial invariants of the system.

title: Cross-chain deployments failure
description: When code wants to create cross-chain DAO deployment message it divides the total ETH amount equally between cross-chain messages. The issue is that different destination chains may require different cross-chain fee. Code should allow user to specify bridge fee amount for each cross-chain message. In the current design user have to pay based on maximum bridge fee amount.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way a cross‑chain DAO deployment contract allocates the ETH that a user supplies for bridge fees. When a deployment is intended for several destination chains, the contract simply divides the total ETH amount equally among the individual cross‑chain messages and assumes that each chain will require the same bridge fee. In reality, bridge fees differ per destination chain because of varying gas costs, validator fees, or protocol parameters. The root cause is the hard‑coded assumption of uniform fees and the absence of a mechanism for the caller to specify a distinct fee for each chain. An attacker or a careless user can be forced to overpay: the contract requires the user to provide enough ETH to cover the highest fee among the target chains, then spreads that amount evenly, causing the excess portion to be locked in the contract or wasted on chains where the fee is lower. This can be exploited by deploying to a set of chains that includes at least one chain with a high bridge fee, thereby inflating the total amount the user must send even though the other chains would need far less. The impact is economic: users see their balance reduced more than expected, may receive a DAO deployment with insufficient funds on some chains, or experience unexpected fee deductions that appear as “missing” ETH. The issue manifests whenever a multi‑chain deployment is performed and the fee schedule is heterogeneous. It affects any participant who initiates a cross‑chain deployment, including developers, token holders, and the protocol itself, because the protocol may appear to charge unfair fees and could lose trust. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the fee‑handling logic and identified the equal‑division calculation as a mismatch with real‑world bridge fee variability. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about overpayment, and the UI may simply show the total amount required without breaking down per‑chain fees, making the overpayment hard to notice. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to accept an explicit fee amount for each destination chain, compute the exact required ETH per message, and only charge the sum of those precise fees. This change aligns the implementation with the business logic that each chain may have a different cost, restores accurate accounting, and prevents users from unintentionally losing funds due to a blanket maximum‑fee assumption. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect fee allocation” or “miscalculated cross‑chain payment distribution” bugs, where a generic assumption about uniform costs leads to over‑charging and potential fund loss.

title: Tokens with more than 18 decimals are not supported
description: The current design of the amountToSD() and amountToLD() functions limits compatibility to tokens with 18 or fewer decimals. If a DAO is created using a token with more than 18 decimals as the depositTokenAddress, the DAO creation will fail due to an underflow issue during the convertRate calculation. While this poses no financial risk, it restricts the factory's adaptability within the broader DeFi ecosystem, preventing its use with such tokens. For instance, tokens like YAMv2, which has 24 decimals, would cause the computation to attempt 18 - 24, resulting in an underflow and unsuccessful DAO creation.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from two helper functions that convert token amounts between standard and scaled representations. These functions assume that the token used as a deposit token has at most 18 decimal places. Internally they compute a conversion rate by subtracting the token’s decimal count from the constant 18. When a token with more than 18 decimals – for example a token with 24 decimals such as YAMv2 – is supplied, the subtraction 18‑24 underflows because the operation is performed on an unsigned integer. The underflow produces a very large positive number, which is then used in further arithmetic and ultimately causes the DAO creation routine to fail. The failure manifests as a reverted transaction or a silent abort during the factory’s createDAO call, leaving the user with no newly created DAO and no clear error message. This issue does not expose user funds to theft, but it prevents the factory contract from being used with any token that exceeds the 18‑decimal limit, reducing its interoperability across the DeFi ecosystem. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the factory’s token handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the conversion functions did not guard against a negative exponent. Because the underflow only triggers when a high‑precision token is used, it can be easy to miss in standard testing that typically employs 18‑decimal ERC‑20 tokens. The class of bug is an unchecked integer underflow caused by improper handling of token decimal metadata, a common pattern in contracts that perform arithmetic on token amounts without validating input ranges. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a DAO creation transaction that should succeed instead reverts or completes without creating the DAO, leading to confusion such as “my DAO never appeared” or “the transaction failed for no obvious reason”. The expected behavior is that any ERC‑20 token, regardless of its decimal count, can be used as a deposit token, but the reality is that tokens with more than 18 decimals are rejected by the contract logic. To remediate the issue the conversion routine should first check whether the token’s decimals exceed 18 and, if so, normalize the amount by dividing by 10^(decimals‑18) or by adjusting the conversion rate accordingly. Adding explicit validation and safe arithmetic (e.g., using SafeMath or Solidity 0.8’s built‑in overflow checks) will prevent the underflow and restore compatibility with high‑precision tokens.

title: Cross-Chain and KYCed users will only pay a portion of the fees
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee calculation in the factory contract that handles deposits for DAOs. The contract is supposed to charge a base deposit fee and, when a DAO is cross‑chain, an additional platform fee calculated as depositFees * platformFeeMultiplier / 100. It is also supposed to add the same extra fee when KYC is enabled. The implementation uses a single conditional with an OR (||) and applies the multiplied fee only once, even if both conditions are true. As a result, when a DAO is both cross‑chain and KYC‑enabled, the required fee is under‑charged by one multiplied fee unit. An attacker or a user can exploit this by depositing through a DAO that satisfies both conditions and sending only the lower amount of ether; the transaction will pass the require check and the contract will accept the deposit while the platform receives less revenue than intended. The impact is a systematic loss of fees for the platform, potentially amounting to a significant amount of value if many cross‑chain, KYC‑enabled DAOs are used. The bug manifests only when the DAO’s depositChainIds array contains more than one chain identifier and the KYC flag is true; in all other cases the fee calculation behaves as expected. The affected parties are the protocol operators who rely on the fee model for revenue, the sponsors who may be unaware of the shortfall, and any users who might notice that their deposits cost less than advertised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the business specification (fees should be additive) with the actual Solidity code. It is easy to miss because the code appears to guard the fee with a single require statement and the arithmetic looks correct in isolation; the logical operator hides the fact that the two fee‑increasing conditions are not combined. To fix the problem the contract should explicitly test for the case where both flags are true and add the multiplied fee twice, or compute the fee as a sum of separate components (base fee + cross‑chain fee + KYC fee). This class of bug belongs to the category of “incorrect conditional logic leading to under‑payment” or “fee calculation error due to missing additive term”. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected total amount (e.g., 100 + 125 = 225) but the transaction succeeds with only 200 wei sent, resulting in a discrepancy where the user pays less than the displayed fee. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that each enabled feature adds a fixed surcharge are violated, breaking the intended revenue model.

title: Unchecked Low-level Call when buying tokens
description: In the _buyGovernanceTokenERC20DAO() and _buyGovernanceTokenERC721DAO() functions, the success of low-level calls to both gnosisAddress and ownerAddress is not verified. This oversight means that when these calls fail, the failure will go unnoticed, leaving the funds in the factory without being distributed to gnosisAddress or ownerAddress. This results in neither party receiving their share of the payment.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked low‑level call in the token purchase functions that forward payment to the DAO treasury (gnosisAddress) and to the contract owner (ownerAddress) without verifying the success of those calls. The root cause is the use of the low‑level .call syntax without checking the boolean return value, which means a failed external call – for example due to a revert, out‑of‑gas, or a malicious fallback that consumes all gas – is silently ignored. An attacker or a misbehaving recipient can cause the call to fail, causing the funds that were meant to be split between the DAO and the owner to remain locked in the factory contract. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed: the buyer receives the purchased tokens, but the expected distribution of the payment does not occur, leading to a situation where the DAO’s balance stays unchanged and the owner receives nothing. This breaks the accounting assumptions of the protocol, as the total amount collected does not match the recorded shares, potentially affecting future token economics and governance decisions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the implementation of _buyGovernanceTokenERC20DAO and _buyGovernanceTokenERC721DAO and noted the missing require or revert on the call result. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the only symptom is the missing funds in the treasury, which may only be observed by reviewing balances after a purchase. The appropriate remediation is to capture the boolean returned by each low‑level call, require that it is true, and revert the transaction if the call fails. Additionally, the gas stipend supplied to the ownerAddress call should be limited to a safe amount to prevent a gas‑griefing attack that could deliberately cause the call to fail. By enforcing proper error handling and safe gas limits, the protocol can ensure that payment distribution either succeeds or the whole purchase is rolled back, preserving the intended financial invariants.

title: Users can grief the owner by buying in chunks
description:
The factory contract supports all ERC20 tokens, allowing DAO creators to add any token as a payment method for their DAO. When users buy tokens using the buyGovernanceTokenERC20DAO() function, the owner takes a portion of the payment as a fee:
```solidity
uint256 _totalAmount = (_numOfTokensToBuy * _daoDetails.pricePerToken) / 1e18;
if (_totalAmount == 0) {
    revert AmountInvalid("_numOfTokensToBuy", _totalAmount);
}
uint256 ownerShare = (_totalAmount * _daoDetails.ownerFeePerDepositPercent) / (FLOAT_HANDLER_TEN_4);
```
However, users can exploit this calculation by making small, fragmented purchases, causing the ownerShare to round down to zero. This issue is particularly problematic for tokens with low decimal precision, such as GUSD, which has 2 decimals. Consider the following scenario:
DAO Settings:
Dao.depositTokenAddress = GUSD
Dao.ownerFeePerDepositPercent = 100
pricePerToken = 10e2
Exploit Execution:
Bob, a malicious user aware of the bug, aims to exploit the system.
Bob calls buyGovernanceTokenERC20DAO() with numOfTokensToBuy = 9.9e16.
Calculation:
_totalAmount = (9.9e16 * 10e2) / 1e18 = 99
ownerShare = (99 * 100) / 10000 = 0
The ownerShare rounds down to zero, meaning the owner receives no fees for each purchase of 9.9e16 tokens. The trick is that _totalAmount * _daoDetails.ownerFeePerDepositPercent must be less than FLOAT_HANDLER_TEN_4 (i.e. 10_000).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑division rounding error in the fee calculation of a DAO token‑sale factory that supports arbitrary ERC20 payment tokens. When a user purchases governance tokens, the contract computes the total payment amount by multiplying the requested token quantity by a price and dividing by a fixed‑point scaling factor (1e18). It then derives the owner’s fee by multiplying this total amount by a fee‑percentage and dividing by a constant representing 100 % with four decimal places (FLOAT_HANDLER_TEN_4). Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, any fractional part of the division is discarded. If the product of the total amount and the fee percentage is smaller than the divisor, the result of the fee calculation becomes zero. This situation can be deliberately triggered by buying in very small, fragmented chunks, especially when the payment token has low decimal precision (e.g., a stablecoin with two decimals). In the illustrated scenario, a malicious user purchases a quantity that yields a total amount of 99 units; with a 1 % fee (ownerFeePerDepositPercent = 100) the fee formula evaluates to (99 * 100) / 10000 = 0, so the owner receives no fee for that transaction. The bug manifests whenever the product of the computed payment amount and the fee percentage does not reach the scaling constant, which is more likely for tokens whose smallest unit is large relative to the price. The affected parties are the DAO owner, who loses expected revenue, and the protocol, whose economic model assumes that each deposit contributes a fee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the factory’s payment logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee check only validates that the total amount is non‑zero, but does not ensure that the fee itself is non‑zero. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error when the fee rounds to zero; the transaction succeeds and the buyer receives the tokens, making the loss invisible to the owner unless they monitor fee receipts. Exploitation consists of repeatedly calling the purchase function with carefully chosen small amounts so that each call yields a zero fee, effectively griefing the owner by draining the DAO of fee income while still allowing token distribution. The impact is a reduction or complete elimination of the owner’s fee revenue, which can undermine the DAO’s funding model and may be used to manipulate governance power if fees are tied to voting weight. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the fee calculation does not underflow to zero, for example by adding a check that the product of the total amount and the fee percentage is at least the scaling constant before performing the division, or by using a rounding‑up division method. This change ensures that any purchase that would result in a zero fee is rejected, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Invariant violation (funds could remain in the vault and a depositor could benefit from it)
bug_full: The contract defines a strict invariant that after any vault operation – deposit, withdraw, rebalance or compound – the vault must hold no token balances. The compound() routine is intended to reinvest reward tokens received from an external source (for example GMX airdrops) by first pulling tokenA and tokenB from a linked trove and then performing a compound step only when the balance of a designated tokenIn is greater than zero. The implementation checks the tokenIn balance, but it does not verify that tokenA or tokenB have been fully cleared before exiting the function. Consequently, if tokenIn is zero while tokenA or tokenB still hold a non‑zero amount after the trove withdrawal, the function terminates without moving those residual tokens back to the trove. Moreover, the function resets the vault status to a compound state inside the same conditional block, allowing the status to be inconsistent with the actual operation. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a scheduled compound transaction: the attacker initiates a withdraw that changes the vault status to Withdraw, then lets the compound call proceed with a tokenIn that has zero balance. The compound call leaves the previously withdrawn tokenA/B in the vault, and the attacker’s subsequent withdraw callback can claim those leftover tokens, effectively siphoning rewards that should have been redistributed to all depositors. The impact is a breach of accounting guarantees – funds disappear from the protocol’s pool and are captured by a malicious participant – and the protocol’s users receive less than expected returns. The issue manifests only when the vault contains a mix of token balances and the compound is invoked with a tokenIn that is empty, a situation that can be triggered by timing attacks or by the natural arrival of airdropped tokens. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the invariant enforcement logic and identified that the compound path lacked an else clause to enforce the empty‑vault rule. The bug is subtle because the function appears to guard against empty tokenIn amounts, leading reviewers to assume that no assets remain, while in reality other token balances may persist unnoticed. To remediate, the contract should enforce that after any compound execution the vault’s tokenA and tokenB balances are explicitly transferred back to the trove (or otherwise cleared) regardless of the tokenIn amount, and the vault status should be set only after confirming the invariant holds. Adding an else branch that returns any residual tokens and resetting the status accordingly restores the intended invariant and prevents the front‑run profit scenario.

title: Setter functions for core GMX contracts
description:
GMX docs state that their ExchangeRouter and GMXOracle contracts will change as new logic is added. Therefore setter functions should be added to GMXVault.sol to be able to update the state variables storing those addressed when the need arises.

From the GMX docs:

If using contracts such as the ExchangeRouter, Oracle or Reader do note that their addresses will change as new logic is added

Not being able to use the ExchangeRouter and GMXOracle contracts the protocol would effectively be unusable given their importance.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the GMXVault contract storing the addresses of the ExchangeRouter and GMXOracle contracts in immutable state variables without any administrative function to modify them after deployment. The GMX documentation explicitly states that the ExchangeRouter, Oracle and Reader contracts may change as new logic is added, but the vault code lacks setter functions that would allow the protocol owner to point the vault to the new contract instances. This design oversight creates a configuration immutability problem: when the external contracts are upgraded, the vault continues to reference the old addresses, which may become obsolete, unresponsive, or even malicious. An attacker could exploit this situation by deploying a counterfeit contract at the old address before the legitimate upgrade, causing the vault to interact with a malicious router or oracle and potentially misroute trades or feed incorrect price data. Even without an active attacker, the protocol becomes effectively unusable because core functionality such as trade execution and price discovery relies on those contracts; users attempting to trade will see transactions revert or receive no response, balances may appear unchanged, and expected refunds or position updates will never occur. The issue manifests only when the GMX team updates the router or oracle addresses, a condition that is documented and expected in production environments. All participants—protocol owners, liquidity providers, traders, and end‑users—are affected because the inability to update the addresses can halt trading, freeze funds, and erode confidence in the platform. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public interface with the official GMX documentation and noticed the absence of any function guarded by onlyOwner that could change the stored addresses. Because the contract compiles and passes basic tests, the missing setters are not obvious during routine testing, making the bug subtle and easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the vault should expose owner‑only setter functions that safely update the stored ExchangeRouter and GMXOracle addresses and emit corresponding events, thereby aligning the on‑chain configuration with the off‑chain documentation and preserving the protocol’s ability to adapt to future upgrades. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an immutable configuration or missing admin update vulnerability, where hard‑coded dependencies prevent proper maintenance of external contract references, leading to functional breakdowns and potential financial loss.

title: The protocol will mint unnecessary fees if the vault is paused and reopened later.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unintended fee minting mechanism that activates when a vault contract is paused and later reopened. The root cause lies in the fee‑accrual formula, which calculates pending fees as the product of the vault token total supply, a per‑second fee rate and the elapsed time since the last fee collection (block.timestamp‑lastFeeCollected). When the vault is paused, the contract does not update the lastFeeCollected timestamp, so the elapsed time continues to grow even though no user activity occurs. Upon reopening, the first deposit triggers the fee‑minting logic, which interprets the entire pause duration as active fee‑earning time. Consequently, the protocol mints an excessive amount of fee tokens to the treasury – for example, a one‑month pause can generate billions of wei in fees – and these tokens are deducted from the shares that would otherwise belong to the depositing user. The impact is a dilution of user holdings and an unfair transfer of value to the treasury, potentially eroding trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This condition occurs only when the vault enters a paused state and is later resumed without resetting the fee timestamp; it affects any user who interacts with the vault after the pause, as well as the protocol’s overall token economics. The issue was uncovered during testing that simulated a long pause and observed the pendingFee function returning a large value. It can be hard to notice because the fee calculation appears correct during normal operation, and the pause flag does not visibly alter the fee‑minting code. To remediate, the contract should either disable fee accrual while paused or explicitly reset the lastFeeCollected timestamp to the current block time when the vault is reopened, ensuring that only time spent in an active state contributes to fee generation. This fix restores the intended accounting behavior where fees are proportional to actual usage rather than idle time, preventing unnecessary minting and protecting user shares from inadvertent loss.

title: `emergencyPause` does not check the state before running && can cause loss of funds for users
bug_full: An emergencyPause function that can be invoked by a privileged keeper at any moment without checking whether any critical operation such as a deposit callback is pending. The function simply sets the vault status to Paused. When a user initiates a multi‑step deposit, the contract first transfers the underlying asset and then expects a callback (afterDepositExecution) to mint the corresponding svToken. If the keeper calls emergencyPause before the callback runs, the vault status is no longer Deposit, so the callback’s conditional checks fail and no minting occurs. The beforeProcessDepositChecks also revert because the status is not Deposit. As a result the user’s assets have been transferred out of their wallet but no tokens are credited, effectively losing the funds. The issue appears only when an emergency pause is triggered during an in‑progress transaction; normal operation is unaffected. It was discovered during a targeted audit test that simulated a pause between the deposit transaction and its callback. The bug is subtle because the pause function itself does not revert or emit an error, so the transaction appears successful from the caller’s perspective, while the internal accounting is broken. This is a classic example of an unchecked state transition that violates the invariant that a deposit must either complete fully or be rolled back. To fix the problem the contract should enforce a pre‑condition that prevents emergencyPause while any deposit, rebalance, compound or withdrawal operation is pending, or it should queue the pause until those operations finish, ensuring that callbacks can still execute or that the state is safely rolled back. The impact is loss of user funds, stuck balances, and erosion of trust, as users may see their token balance remain zero while their underlying asset balance has decreased.

title: Emergency Closed Vault Can Be Paused Then Resume
bug_full: The contract provides an emergencyClose function that is advertised as a one‑way irreversible shutdown of a vault, intended to repay all debt and prevent any further operations. In practice the vault can be reopened because the same contract also exposes emergencyPause and emergencyResume functions that modify the vault's status without checking whether the vault has already been permanently closed. The root cause is the absence of a permanent closure flag or any guard in the pause and resume functions that would reject calls after emergencyClose has been executed. An attacker or any caller with access to these functions can first call emergencyClose, which sets the vault status to a closed state, and then invoke emergencyPause to set the status to Paused and subsequently call emergencyResume to set the status to Resume, effectively re‑enabling liquidity addition and other vault operations. This sequence can be performed immediately after the close, under any condition where the caller can reach the external functions, and it subverts the expectation that funds are locked and no further actions are possible. Users, token holders, and protocol participants are affected because they rely on the guarantee that an emergency close protects their assets; the ability to resume operations may expose the vault to further attacks, unintended withdrawals, or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, who created a test that called emergencyPause, then emergencyClose, and then called emergencyPause and emergencyResume again, observing that the vault status changed back to a paused and then resumed state. The bug is hard to notice because the status variable changes silently and the UI may still display the vault as active, giving the impression that the emergency close did not take effect. To fix the problem, the contract should introduce an immutable closed flag that is set when emergencyClose is called and never cleared, and all functions that alter the vault status, including emergencyPause and emergencyResume, must check this flag and revert if the vault has been permanently closed. This ensures that the business logic of an irreversible shutdown is enforced and that users’ expectations of a locked vault are met, preventing accidental or malicious reopening of the vault after an emergency closure.

title: Chainlinks oracle feeds are not immutable
bug_full: The vulnerability is an immutable configuration flaw in the oracle module where price feed addresses, once added, cannot be updated or removed. The root cause is a restrictive check in the addTokenPriceFeed function that reverts if a feed for a token is already set, effectively preventing any later modification of the mapping. Because the contract uses this mapping both to retrieve price data and to validate that a token is supported, an outdated, incorrect, or deprecated Chainlink feed will continue to be considered valid, causing the consult function to return a stale address or to revert only when the address is zero. If Chainlink deprecates a feed, the owner mis‑enters an address, or the protocol decides to stop supporting a token, the immutable entry prevents the contract from pointing to a new feed or deleting the entry, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for that token. Users experience symptoms such as missing price information, transactions that fail with a “NoTokenPriceFeedAvailable” error, or unexpected zero values where a price should appear, contradicting the expectation that the protocol will always provide a current price. The impact includes loss of functionality for the affected token, potential liquidation or trade failures, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol’s pricing mechanism. This issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the oracle’s management functions and identified that the only administrative entry point forbids updates. The flaw is subtle because the function name suggests adding a feed, yet the protective check silently blocks any future change, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should allow the owner or a designated governance role to update or delete existing feed entries, for example by removing the revert that checks for an existing address and adding a separate function with proper access control to modify the mapping. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of immutable configuration or hard‑coded address vulnerabilities that break upgradability and can be exploited to render a token’s price feed unusable, violating the business logic that assumes price feeds remain accurate and replaceable over time.

title: The transfer of ERC-20 tokens with blacklist functionality in process functions can lead to stuck vaults
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe token transfer pattern inside the vault’s process functions that can cause the entire strategy vault to become permanently stuck when an ERC‑20 token with blacklist capabilities, such as USDC, is used. The root cause is the assumption that a token transfer will always succeed; the code transfers tokens directly to the user and only afterwards updates the vault status back to Open. If the recipient address is blacklisted, the token contract reverts the transfer, the subsequent status update is never executed, and the vault remains in a Withdraw (or DepositCancellation) state. An attacker – or an accidental blacklisted user – can trigger this by calling the withdraw function, after which a keeper bot invokes processWithdraw. The transfer to the blacklisted address fails, the try‑catch does not catch the revert, and the status stays locked. As a result, no further deposits or withdrawals can be processed, effectively a denial‑of‑service for all participants. This occurs only when the token implements a blacklist feature and the vault is not in an Open state during the keeper’s call. All users of the strategy vault, the protocol owners, and any keepers interacting with the contract are affected because the vault cannot progress to a usable state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the process functions and identified direct safeTransfer calls without handling possible reverts from blacklisted addresses. It is hard to notice because the token conforms to the ERC‑20 interface and blacklist behavior is rarely exercised in normal testing, so the failure only appears under the specific condition of a blacklisted recipient. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a withdraw request that appears to succeed, but the user receives no tokens, their balance remains unchanged, and the vault status stays in a pending withdraw state, contrary to the expectation of receiving the funds. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls that can lock contract state, often described as a “transfer‑failure‑induced state lock”. To remediate, the contract should avoid sending tokens directly in the process functions; instead it should adopt a two‑step escrow pattern where funds are first deposited into a dedicated holder contract together with an entitlement record, allowing the vault to reset its status regardless of transfer success, and enabling blacklisted users to be handled separately without halting the whole system.

title: Wrong hardcoded PnL factor is used in all GMXVault add liquidity operations
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the deposit and rebalanceAdd pathways of the GMXVault contract where the call to GMXOracle.getLpTokenValue is made with the boolean flag isDeposit set to false. According to GMX documentation, the oracle expects a different PnL factor constant for deposit operations (MAXPNLFACTORFOR_DEPOSITS) than for withdrawals (MAXPNLFACTORFOR_WITHDRAWALS). By hard‑coding the withdrawal flag, the contract retrieves a market token price that is calculated with the wrong PnL factor. When the two factors differ, which is the normal case, the price used for the deposit calculation is either too low or too high. If the withdrawal factor is lower than the deposit factor, a user attempting to deposit the maximum allowed amount will see the transaction revert because the oracle reports a price that makes the deposit exceed the permitted limit. Conversely, if the withdrawal factor is higher, the oracle returns an overly favorable price, allowing a user to deposit more value than the protocol intends. This discrepancy breaks the accounting assumptions of the vault, leading to either denial of service for legitimate depositors or unintended over‑allocation of liquidity, which can affect the fairness of the market and potentially expose the protocol to economic loss. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract code against the GMX deposit notes and identified the mismatched boolean argument. It is subtle because the flag appears to be a simple true/false parameter, and the price deviation only manifests under edge‑case deposit amounts, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. The proper remediation is to pass true for the isDeposit argument in all calls to getLpTokenValue originating from GMXVault.deposit and GMXRebalance.rebalanceAdd, ensuring the oracle uses the correct MAXPNLFACTORFOR_DEPOSITS constant. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a deposit either fails with a revert error despite meeting the apparent limits, or the UI shows a higher deposited amount than expected, violating the expectation that the protocol will enforce the documented maximum deposit limit.

title: Incorrect depositable shortToken amount calculation in Delta neutral vaults
description:
When calculating the maximum possible depositable amount for delta neutral vaults, _maxTokenBLending is calculated incorrectly.
```solidity
    if (self.delta == GMXTypes.Delta.Neutral) {
      (uint256 _tokenAWeight, ) = tokenWeights(self);

      uint256 _maxTokenALending = convertToUsdValue(
        self,
        address(self.tokenA),
        self.tokenALendingVault.totalAvailableAsset()
      ) * SAFE_MULTIPLIER
        / (self.leverage * tokenAWeight / SAFEMULTIPLIER);

      uint256 _maxTokenBLending = convertToUsdValue(
        self,
        address(self.tokenB),
        self.tokenBLendingVault.totalAvailableAsset()
      ) * SAFE_MULTIPLIER
        / (self.leverage * tokenAWeight / SAFEMULTIPLIER)
        * 1e18;
```

https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-10-SteadeFi/blob/0f909e2f0917cb9ad02986f631d622376510abec/contracts/strategy/gmx/GMXReader.sol#L254-L270

If a user wants to deposit v value to a l leveraged delta neutral vault with token weights a and b, the calculation of required lending amount would be as follows:

Total value to deposit to GMX = lv
Value of tokens to short = lva
Hence this value will be borrowed from the tokenA lending vault
Remaining value to borrow (from tokenB lending vault) = lv - lva - v (deposit value provided by user)
Hence if there is Tb value of tokens in tokenB lending vault, v <= Tb / (l - la - 1)

Deposit attempts can revert even when there is enough tokens to lend causing inefficiency, loss of gas for depositors and deviation from the protocol specification.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the maximum depositable amount for tokenB in delta‑neutral vaults, caused by a formula that reuses the tokenA weight when determining the tokenB lending capacity. The contract assumes that the same weight applies to both sides of the neutral position, so the denominator of the _maxTokenBLending expression is computed as (leverage * tokenAWeight / SAFEMULTIPLIER) instead of accounting for the portion of leverage already allocated to the short tokenA position and the proper tokenB weight. As a result, the computed _maxTokenBLending value can be lower than the true amount of tokenB that is available in the lending vault. When a user attempts to deposit an amount that is actually supported by the vault, the contract’s check against the underestimated limit fails and the transaction reverts. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that sufficient tokenB balance exists, yet the deposit transaction is rejected and the user loses the gas spent on the failed call. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition where legitimate depositors cannot add liquidity to delta‑neutral vaults, leading to inefficiency, potential loss of user confidence, and deviation from the protocol’s specification that deposits should be possible whenever the underlying lending vault holds enough assets. The bug manifests only when the vault is configured for a neutral delta position; other vault types use a correct calculation. It was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who noted that the deposit capacity logic did not match the documented formula for the remaining value to borrow from tokenB. The issue is subtle because the two calculations for tokenA and tokenB look almost identical, and the contract compiles without warnings, making the error easy to overlook without targeted testing of edge cases where tokenB liquidity is abundant but deposits still fail. To fix the problem the denominator must be changed to reflect the remaining leverage after subtracting the portion already allocated to tokenA, for example (leverage - (leverage * tokenAWeight / SAFEMULTIPLIER) - 1e18), or alternatively use the correct tokenB weight in the formula. This adjustment restores the intended business logic that the maximum depositable amount is limited only by the actual available tokenB assets, ensuring that users can deposit when the vault has sufficient liquidity and that the protocol behaves according to its specifications.

title: `emergencyClose()` may fail to repay any debt
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the emergencyClose function of the strategy contract, which is intended to repay all outstanding tokenA and tokenB debt after the contract has been paused and all GMX liquidity withdrawn. The function calculates the total debt amounts, determines whether a token swap is required to obtain the missing amount of one token, performs the swap if needed, and then calls repay to transfer the full debt back to the lending vault before marking the contract as closed. The root cause is an incorrect assumption that the balance of the non‑deficient token will always be sufficient to cover the shortfall of the deficient token after the swap. The code does not verify that the token used as input for the swap actually holds enough value to obtain the required output amount, nor does it re‑evaluate the debt amounts after the swap. Consequently, when the contract is paused under adverse conditions such as bad debt, a hack, or extreme market volatility, the balances of tokenA and tokenB may both be insufficient to satisfy the repayment calculation. The swap then either reverts due to insufficient input balance or succeeds but leaves the contract with a remaining shortfall, causing the subsequent repay call to revert because the contract no longer holds the full debt amount. This failure path is triggered only when a swap is required, which is common in emergency scenarios where one token balance is below its debt. From the user’s perspective the contract status changes to Closed, but attempts to withdraw svToken shares return zero or fail, and lenders see their debt remain unpaid, effectively losing the funds they expected to be repaid. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who identified the logical flaw in the repayment assumptions. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to complete successfully in normal operation and emits an EmergencyClose event, masking the underlying revert that only occurs under specific balance conditions. The bug violates the business logic that emergency closure must guarantee full debt repayment before allowing user withdrawals, breaking the accounting invariant that total assets equal total liabilities. To remediate, the contract should either settle the debt during the pause step, enforce strict checks on swap input balances, allow partial repayment with proportional adjustments, or redesign the emergencyClose flow to guarantee that the required token amounts are available before attempting any swap or repayment, thereby ensuring that the contract can always close without leaving outstanding debt.

title: Missing minimum token amounts in the emergency contract functions allows MEV bots to take advantage of the protocols emergency situation
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked slippage condition in the emergency control functions of a vault that interacts with the GMX liquidity pool. When the protocol owner calls the emergencyPause function the contract attempts to remove all of its LP tokens but does not populate the minTokenAAmt and minTokenBAmt fields of the RemoveLiquidityParams structure, leaving them at their default value of zero. Because the minimum acceptable amounts are zero, the GMX manager will accept any amount of tokenA or tokenB returned from the pool, even if the price has moved dramatically. The same omission occurs in the emergencyResume function, which adds liquidity back to GMX without specifying minimum token amounts, again defaulting to zero. This design flaw allows a malicious MEV bot to front‑run the pause or resume transaction, manipulate the market price, and cause the vault to receive far fewer tokens than expected, effectively stealing value from the vault. The impact is that all funds deposited in the strategy vault can be drained or severely devalued, leading to users seeing their balances drop to zero or receiving far less than they deposited when the vault is resumed. The issue manifests only during the brief window when the contract is in an emergency state, i.e., when the pause or resume functions are executed, and it affects any user who has assets in the vault as well as the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the parameter handling of the emergency functions and noticed the missing minimum‑amount checks. The problem is subtle because the functions appear to succeed without reverting, giving the impression that the emergency operation completed safely, while in reality the slippage protection is completely disabled. To remediate, the contract should enforce a sensible minimum‑token‑amount check based on current market rates or a configurable slippage tolerance, ensuring that the vault never accepts a zero‑or‑excessively‑low return. This change restores the accounting invariant that assets withdrawn from a liquidity pool must be at least equal to the expected market value, preventing money from disappearing due to unchecked slippage.

title: re-entrency possible on processWithdraw since external call is made before burning user's shares in Vault
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that occurs in the withdraw processing routine of a vault contract. The function first performs an external call – either a low‑level call that sends native ether to the user or an ERC‑20 safeTransfer – and only after those transfers does it update the internal accounting by burning the caller’s share tokens. Because the state change (burning shares) happens after the external interaction, a malicious caller can trigger a recursive call back into the same withdraw function before its share balance is reduced. In practice the router or keeper that orchestrates the withdrawal may expose a public entry point that the attacker can manipulate, allowing the attacker’s contract to re‑enter the withdraw routine via the user‑controlled address supplied to the call. By re‑entering, the attacker can repeat the token transfer step multiple times while the original share amount remains unburned, effectively draining more assets than the share entitlement permits. The impact is a loss of user funds and a reduction of the protocol’s total assets, potentially compromising the economic integrity of the vault. The issue manifests only when the withdraw function is invoked – typically by a keeper contract – and when the caller’s address is a contract capable of executing a fallback that calls back into the withdraw logic. It is hard to notice because the external call is placed after a seemingly harmless token transfer, and the code follows a linear flow that appears to respect the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern at a glance, yet the ordering of effects is inverted. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the sequence of state changes and external calls. To remediate, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions principle by burning (or otherwise reducing) the user’s share balance before any external transfer, or by adding a re‑entrancy guard that blocks recursive entry. This change ensures that even if a re‑entrant call occurs, the user’s share balance will already be accounted for, preventing excess withdrawals. The bug belongs to the broader class of re‑entrancy vulnerabilities where external calls are made before critical state updates, leading to inconsistent accounting and potential fund loss. From a user’s perspective the symptom would be that after initiating a withdrawal they receive more tokens than expected, or that the vault’s total balance suddenly drops, while the user’s share balance may still appear unchanged. The expectation that a withdrawal returns exactly the proportional amount is violated, resulting in “money disappears” for the protocol and “extra funds appear” for the attacker.

title: min max price on getMarketTokenPrice is not utilized such that deposit and withdrawal can use the same price, leading to free tx for cost-free manipulation
description:
min max price on getMarketTokenPrice is not utilized such that deposit and withdrawal can use the same price, leading to free tx for cost-free manipulation

GMX provides getMarketTokenPrice on its synethicReader which leverages MarketUtils. It allows passing in index/long/short token price with min/max. The isDeposit flag would then be used to determine whether the min or max price would be used for calculating marketTokenPrice, this is important to always favor the protocol and prevent MEV.

However on the getMarketTokenInfo implemented in GMXOracle, it passes in the same price from the oracle to the min/max price for all long&short/lpToken. This implies the same pricing is used for both deposit and withdrawal, enabling user to freely deposit/withdraw without cost or slippage. Malicious users can use this to trigger rebalance, and hence deposit or withdrawal directly on GMX that benefit the attacker with the use of bundled tx.

```solidity
    function getMarketTokenPrice(
        DataStore dataStore,
        Market.Props memory market,
        Price.Props memory indexTokenPrice,
        Price.Props memory longTokenPrice,
        Price.Props memory shortTokenPrice,
        bytes32 pnlFactorType,
        bool maximize
    ) external view returns (int256, MarketPoolValueInfo.Props memory) {
        return
            MarketUtils.getMarketTokenPrice(
                dataStore,
                market,
                indexTokenPrice,
                longTokenPrice,
                shortTokenPrice,
                pnlFactorType,
                maximize
            );
    }
```

https://github.com/gmx-io/gmx-synthetics/blob/613c72003eafe21f8f80ea951efd14e366fe3a31/contracts/reader/Reader.sol#L187-L206

Impact
free deposit and withdrawal due to the same token price is used for min or max price, which leading to the same marketTokenPrice calculation for deposit and withdrawal.

free deposit and withdrawal due to the same token price is used for min or max price, which leading to the same marketTokenPrice calculation for deposit and withdrawal.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑retrieval routine used by the GMX synthetic market oracle. The contract exposes a function that calculates a market token price by calling a library routine with a flag that indicates whether the price should be taken from the minimum side (for deposits) or the maximum side (for withdrawals). In the current implementation the oracle forwards the same raw price value for both the minimum and maximum arguments, effectively ignoring the flag that would normally bias the price in favor of the protocol. Because the same price is used for both deposit and withdrawal calculations, the resulting marketTokenPrice is identical regardless of the operation. This flaw allows an attacker to perform a deposit and an immediate withdrawal at the same quoted price, incurring no slippage or fee, and thereby extracting value from the protocol without cost. The attacker can also combine this free‑swap with a rebalance transaction, using the cost‑free manipulation to shift positions or capture arbitrage opportunities. The issue manifests whenever the getMarketTokenPrice function is invoked through the GMXOracle reader, which is the standard path for price queries in the synthetic market. All participants that rely on the oracle – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the economic invariant that deposits should be priced slightly less favorably than withdrawals is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the GMXOracle code when the auditor noticed that the isDeposit flag was never used and that the same price value was passed for both min and max parameters. The bug is subtle because the function still returns a plausible price, so normal UI displays show no error and users may see a perfectly normal transaction receipt, while the underlying accounting silently allows free value extraction. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a deposit appears to succeed with zero cost, the balance after withdrawal is unchanged or even higher, and no slippage or fee is reported – essentially “funds disappear” from the protocol but not from the attacker’s wallet. This class of bug can be described as an improper handling of price bounds leading to a price manipulation vulnerability that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions. To remediate the issue the oracle should correctly apply the minimum price when isDeposit is true and the maximum price when it is false, or alternatively introduce a small fee buffer (for example five basis points) on both sides of the price calculation to ensure that deposits are always slightly less favorable than withdrawals, thereby restoring the intended economic protection against MEV and free‑tx attacks.

title: Incorrect state transition may cause vault in stuck
description:
When keeper execute compound action and GMXCallback return afterDepositCancellation action, then protocol will call GMXCompound#processCompoundCancellation function to change vault status.

However, vault status is changed to GMXTypes.Status.Compound_Failed instead of GMXTypes.Status.Open by GMXCompound#processCompoundCancellation function, which is different with document described below:

https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-10-SteadeFi/blob/main/docs/sequences/strategy-gmx-compound-sequence-detailed.md

and All scenarios should be handled to ensure vault eventually returns to an Open status. Consider how a scenario might lead to a stuck vault (other statuses).

Vault may stuck in unexpected state after processCompoundCancellation action.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect state transition that can leave a vault permanently stuck after a compound cancellation operation. When a keeper triggers a compound action and the GMXCallback returns the afterDepositCancellation signal, the protocol invokes the GMXCompound.processCompoundCancellation function to update the vault's lifecycle status. Instead of resetting the vault to the expected Open state, the function mistakenly assigns the status Compound_Failed. This deviation from the documented sequence causes the vault to remain in a failed state, preventing further deposits, withdrawals, or any other user interactions that require an Open status. The root cause is a logic error in the state‑update routine: the contract uses the wrong enum value when handling the cancellation path. Exploitation does not require an external attacker; it occurs automatically under the normal execution flow whenever a compound cancellation is processed. The impact is that users may see their vault appear active in the UI but encounter transaction reverts, missing balances, or error messages indicating the vault is not open. Funds remain locked because the protocol logic blocks any operation that depends on an Open status, effectively freezing user assets until an administrator manually corrects the state. The condition arises only when the specific callback sequence is executed, making the bug hard to notice during routine testing because the vault does not revert to a clearly broken state; instead it silently stays in a non‑operational status. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the contract implementation against the official strategy‑gmx‑compound sequence documentation and identified the mismatch in status handling. To remediate, the processCompoundCancellation function should be modified to set the vault status to Open, aligning with the intended recovery path and ensuring that the vault can resume normal operations after a cancellation. This class of bug falls under improper state management or incorrect lifecycle transition, which violates the accounting assumptions that a vault must always return to an operational state after a cancellation event.

title: GMXVault can stop working in case if GMX will change `Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT` to smaller than 2 millions
description:
Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT is configurable param inside GMX protocol, which can be changed to value that is smaller than 2 millions. As Steadefi callback gas limit is hardcoded, deposits and withdraws can fail.

GMXWorker library is used to send requests directly to GMX protocol. It contains addLiquidity and removeLiquidity functions that will create request on GMX and will be waiting for execution. Both these functions set 2 millions of gas as callbackGasLimit.

When deposit or withdraw request is handled on GMX side, then callbackGasLimit is validated to be not bigger than it's allowed. Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT value is configurable and can be changed by GMX team. And in case if it will be less than 2 million, then all deposits and withdraws requests from steadefi will be reverted.

I leave this as medium severity, because of the fact that callback limit should be decreased first in order to create problems.

Deposits and withdraws from steadefi will be blocked.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption in the Steadefi integration with the GMX protocol. The Steadefi GMXWorker library implements addLiquidity and removeLiquidity functions that submit deposit and withdraw requests to GMX and specify a callback gas limit of exactly two million gas units. GMX, however, exposes a configurable parameter called Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT that defines the maximum gas that a callback may consume. Because the Steadefi code does not read this parameter and instead always uses the fixed value of two million, the system implicitly trusts that GMX will always allow at least that amount. If the GMX governance or any party with authority over the protocol reduces Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT to a value lower than two million, every subsequent deposit or withdraw request generated by Steadefi will fail the validation performed on the GMX side. The GMX contract will reject the request and revert the transaction, causing the user‑facing operation to appear as a failed deposit or withdrawal. From the user’s perspective the UI may show an error, the transaction reverts, and the expected funds never arrive in the vault; balances may appear unchanged or the user may see a “deposit failed” message with no obvious reason. The impact is that the entire deposit/withdraw flow of the Steadefi protocol becomes inoperable, effectively locking users out of adding or removing liquidity until the gas limit mismatch is resolved. This class of bug is a configuration‑driven hard‑coded constant mismatch, where an external protocol parameter can be changed without the dependent contract adapting, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between Steadefi’s GMXWorker and the GMX protocol’s callback gas limit logic. It can be difficult to notice because the parameter is not part of the Steadefi source code and may only be altered in a future governance action, making the failure appear intermittent or only after a protocol upgrade. The recommended remediation is to make the callbackGasLimit value configurable in Steadefi, or to query the current Keys.MAX_CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT from GMX at runtime and use a value that is guaranteed to be within the allowed range, thereby eliminating the hard‑coded assumption and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Rewards from GMX are sent to Trove only in deposit and withdraw functions
description:
As protocol doesn't collect rewards from GMX in each function, these rewards can be sent to the user.

Each deposit, tokenA and tokenB balance is sent to the Trove. The same is done for the withdraw.

This is because protocol expects to receive rewards from GMX in form of these tokens. So amount is sent to the Trove function, so later it can be compounded.

The problem is that deposit and withdraw functions are not the only entry point that can send these rewards to user. For example, processDepositFailureLiquidityWithdrawal function will send whole balance to the user after repay is done.
Another example inside processDepositCancellation function, in case if depositParams.token is native, then whole balance is sent to user.

As after deposit or withdraw request was done, there is some delay, then during that delay rewards can come and they can be sent to the user.

Rewards are not sent to the Trove, but to the user.
bug_full: The contract assumes that GMX reward tokens are only collected during the explicit deposit and withdraw calls, where the received token amounts are immediately forwarded to the Trove for compounding. In reality GMX can credit reward tokens to the contract at any time, including while a deposit or withdrawal request is pending. Because the contract does not treat reward tokens as a separate accounting class, other internal pathways – such as processDepositFailureLiquidityWithdrawal and processDepositCancellation – transfer the entire token balance back to the caller without first routing the newly arrived rewards to the Trove. This means that if rewards arrive during the waiting period, a user can trigger one of these alternative functions and receive the full balance, which now contains both the original principal and the accrued rewards. The root cause is the lack of a unified reward‑collection mechanism and the use of raw balance transfers in functions that were not designed to handle extra reward tokens. Exploitation consists of depositing or withdrawing, waiting for GMX to send rewards, and then invoking a cancellation or failure‑withdrawal function to pull out the whole balance. The impact is that the protocol loses the expected yield, users receive more tokens than intended (which may be considered a “free” reward but actually represents a misallocation of protocol funds), and the accounting model that assumes rewards are always compounded is broken. The issue manifests only after a deposit or withdraw request has been submitted and before it is finalized, i.e., during the asynchronous delay window. All participants who rely on the protocol’s yield – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s economic model – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reward‑handling logic across different entry points and noticed that only deposit and withdraw functions forward rewards to the Trove, while other functions send the raw balance to the user. Because the extra tokens are indistinguishable from the principal, the bug can be subtle and may go unnoticed until a user observes an unexpected increase in their withdrawn amount or a missing reward in the Trove. To remediate, the contract should centralise reward collection so that any incoming token, regardless of the caller, is first accounted for and sent to the Trove before any user‑facing transfer. Functions that return funds to users must cap the transferred amount to the original principal (for example, using the cached deposit amount) and never include unaccounted reward balances. Alternatively, a separate accounting variable for rewards could be introduced and deducted from user transfers, ensuring that rewards are always compounded and never unintentionally sent to users.

title: In case if withdraw has failed, then processWithdrawFailure will decrease exchange rate of GMXVault shares
description:
In case if user has executed withdrawal and it was not accepted by Steadefi, then processWithdrawFailure will then put withdrawn amount back to GMX and will loose on slippage, however user will still have same shares amount.

When user withdraws, then he provides shares amount, and the appropriate lpAmt is calculated to be withdrawn from GMX. Then in case if such withdrawal will fail, for example because user is not happy with amount that was received after withdrawal, then call will revert, which means that system will go to Withdraw_Failed state. Note, that in this case, user's shares will not be burnt, as it's done only, when withdraw has succeeded.

So what we have now. We have executed withdrawal with some slippage, so our total assets has decreased a bit.
What will be done next. We will call processWithdrawFailure function, which will deposit back all received funds and we will again face some slippage. But user will still have same shares amount.
As result we have lost funds on 2 actions with slippage, which means that all stakers of GMXVault had a loss.

Stakers of the pool have a loss in case of failed withdrawals.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way Steadefi handles awithdrawal that fails to be accepted by the GMXVault. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract calculates the amount of underlying liquidity (lpAmt) that corresponds to the supplied share amount and attempts to transfer it from GMX. If the transfer reverts – for example because the user rejects the received amount or because of a slippage check – the contract moves to a Withdraw_Failed state but does not burn the user’s shares, because share burning is only performed on successful withdrawals. The processWithdrawFailure routine is then invoked; it deposits the returned funds back into GMX, incurring another round of slippage before the liquidity is restored. Because the user’s share balance remains unchanged while the total pool assets have been reduced by two instances of slippage, the exchange rate of each share drops, effectively diluting the value of every staker’s holdings. This loss is not visible to the individual user who sees the same number of shares after the failed attempt, but the overall pool value is lower, meaning that all participants suffer a reduction in their claimable assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the failure path of the withdrawal function and observed that the accounting invariant – that total assets equal shares multiplied by the exchange rate – is violated after a failed withdrawal. The bug can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows the unchanged share balance and does not highlight the decrease in the pool’s net asset value. An attacker could deliberately trigger withdrawals that are expected to fail, causing the contract to repeatedly re‑deposit funds with slippage and thereby erode the vault’s capital over time. The proper mitigation is to treat a failed withdrawal as a redemption event: the contract should burn the corresponding shares and recalculate the exchange rate after the liquidity is returned, or otherwise ensure that the accounting remains consistent and no extra slippage is incurred.

title: All functions that burn or mint shares for user's should mintFee for protocol before
description:
In case if GMXVault mints/burns shares for users, then it should call mintFee before in order to get correct portion of fee.

Steadefi protocol takes management fee from stakers. This fee accrues each second and is some percentage of totalSupply. In order to mint fees, GMXVault.mintFee should be called. Once, it's done, then _store.lastFeeCollected is updated up to date.

Currently mintFee is called only in 2 places in the code. Once in the deposit and once in the withdraw function. However, minting and burning is not done in any of them. For example, minting of shares is done in the processDeposit function and this function is called after some time, when deposit is called. As result some time already has passed and fees should be accrued. But in current implementation, new shares will be added to the totalSupply and fees will be taken out of them for the time when this shares were not even minted.

Same for the withdraw. When withdraw is called, then shares are not burnt. They are burnt inside processWithdraw function. So in case if burn is done before feeMint is called, then this removed shares doesn't pay management fee.

And last place is GMXEmergency.emergencyWithdraw. This function also burns shares, which means that mintFee should be called before it.

Incorrect fee payment is done, depending on the situation users or protocol will suffer.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect ordering of fee accrual and share accounting in the Steadefi protocol. The protocol charges a management fee that accrues every second as a percentage of the total supply of shares. To update the fee balance, the contract provides a mintFee function that records the fee amount and updates the lastFeeCollected timestamp. However, mintFee is invoked only in the external deposit and withdraw functions, while the actual minting of new shares occurs later in an internal processDeposit function and the burning of shares happens in internal processWithdraw and GMXEmergency.emergencyWithdraw functions. Because the fee is not minted before these internal share adjustments, the protocol either retroactively extracts fees from shares that did not exist at the time of accrual or fails to collect fees on shares that have just been burned. This timing mismatch leads to an inaccurate fee distribution: users may lose a portion of newly minted shares to fees that should not apply, while the protocol may miss fees that should have been collected on burned shares. The issue manifests when a user deposits funds, waits for some time, and then the contract processes the deposit; the elapsed time is not accounted for before minting new shares, causing the fee calculation to be applied to shares that were not yet minted. Similarly, when a user withdraws or triggers an emergency withdrawal, shares are burned before mintFee is called, so the management fee is not deducted from the burned amount. The impact is a distortion of the intended fee model, potentially resulting in users receiving fewer shares than expected or the protocol collecting less revenue than designed. The bug is subtle because the external functions appear to handle fees correctly, while the internal accounting steps hide the missing fee update, making it difficult to detect through casual testing. The proper remediation is to ensure that mintFee is called immediately before any minting or burning of shares, i.e., at the start of processDeposit, processWithdraw, and emergencyWithdraw, or to integrate fee accrual directly into the share accounting logic so that fee updates are always synchronized with supply changes. This adjustment restores the intended accounting invariants, guaranteeing that fees are calculated on the correct share supply and that users receive the expected net balances after deposits or withdrawals.

title: Inaccurate Fee Due to missing lastFeeCollected Update Before feePerSecond Modification
description:
