From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after confirming a trade the NFT disappears from their wallet while the received ether or token amount is zero or dramatically reduced, contrary to the expectation of a fair market price. The impact is loss of assets for users, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential financial damage to the ecosystem. The issue occurs whenever the owner has the ability to call the price‑changing functions and there is no enforced delay between announcing a new price and its activation; it can be triggered in any block where a trade is pending. The affected parties include any user attempting to trade through the pool, the protocol’s reputation, and any downstream applications that rely on the pool’s pricing integrity. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined privileged functions and identified that the immediate effect of price changes could be abused for front‑running. The problem is hard to notice because the price adjustment happens atomically within the same block, leaving no visible window for users to react, and the contract does not emit a pre‑change event that could be monitored. Conceptually, the fix is to introduce a timelock or announcement mechanism for any change to pricing parameters, such as an announce(newSpotPrice) function that records the intended price together with a future timestamp, and only permits the actual change after one or two blocks have elapsed, thereby preventing same‑block front‑running. This class of bug belongs to privileged‑parameter manipulation and front‑running vulnerabilities common in automated market makers that lack proper governance or delay controls.

title: Pair may receive less ETH trade fees than expected under certain conditions
description: Depending on the values of protocol fee and royalties, if _feeRecipient == _assetRecipient, the pair will receive less trade fees than expected. Assume a scenario where inputAmount == 100, protocolFee == 30, royaltyTotal == 60 and tradeFeeAmount == 20. This will result in a revert because of underflow in saleAmount -= tradeFeeAmount; when _feeRecipient != _assetRecipient. However, when _feeRecipient == _assetRecipient, the pair will receive trade fees of 100 - 30 - 60 = 10, whereas it normally would have expected 20.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑distribution miscalculation in the Sudoswap LSSVM2 pair contract that can cause the pair to receive fewer ETH trade fees than the protocol’s accounting expects. The root cause lies in a conditional branch that checks whether the fee recipient address (_feeRecipient) is the same as the asset recipient address (_assetRecipient). When the two addresses are identical, the contract skips the external transfer of the trade fee but also omits the subtraction of the trade fee amount from the sale amount. As a result, the sale amount is reduced only by the protocol fee and royalty totals, leaving the trade fee unaccounted for. In a typical scenario with an input amount of 100 ETH, a protocol fee of 30 ETH, royalty total of 60 ETH and a trade fee of 20 ETH, the pair should receive 20 ETH as trade fees. However, because the subtraction is bypassed, the pair ends up with only 10 ETH (100 - 30 - 60) instead of the expected 20 ETH. If the trade fee amount exceeds the remaining balance after protocol and royalty deductions, the subtraction operation can underflow, causing the transaction to revert when _feeRecipient and _assetRecipient differ. The issue manifests only when the fee recipient and asset recipient are the same address and when a non‑zero trade fee is configured. It affects the pair contract’s revenue accounting, liquidity providers who rely on accurate fee distribution, and the overall economic incentives of the protocol. The bug was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noted that the symptom is subtle: transactions may succeed but the pair’s fee balance is lower than expected, and in some configurations the transaction may revert with an underflow error, which can be hard to spot without detailed fee‑flow tracing. To remediate, the contract should always perform the subtraction of the trade fee amount from the sale amount, allowing the operation to revert on underflow, while only skipping the external transfer when the recipient addresses coincide. This ensures that fee accounting remains correct and that the pair receives the full amount of trade fees it is entitled to, preserving protocol revenue and liquidity‑provider expectations.

title: Swapping tokens/ETH for NFTs may exhibit unexpected behavior for certain values of input amount, trade fees and royalties
description: The _pullTokenInputAndPayProtocolFee() function pulls ERC20/ETH from caller/router and pays protocol fees, trade fees and royalties proportionately. Trade fees have a threshold of MAX_FEE == 50%, which allows 2*fee to be 100%. Royalty amounts could technically be any percentage as well. This allows edge cases where the protocol fee, trade fee and royalty amounts add up to be > inputAmount. In LSSVMPairERC20, the ordering of subtracting/transferring the protocolFee and royaltyTotal first causes the final attempted transfer of tradeFeeAmount to either revert because of unavailable funds or uses any balance funds from the pair itself. In LSSVMPairETH, the ordering of subtracting/transferring the tradeFees and royaltyTotal balance funds from the pair itself.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the swap functions calculate and transfer protocol fees, trade fees and royalty amounts when a user exchanges ERC20 tokens or ETH for NFTs. Each fee component is computed correctly in isolation, but the contract allows the sum of protocolFee, royaltyTotal and tradeFeeAmount to exceed the total amount supplied by the caller. The trade fee is capped at a maximum of 50 % of the input, which means the protocol fee and royalty can together push the combined fee over 100 % of the input amount. In the ERC20 implementation (LSSVMPairERC20) the contract first subtracts and transfers the protocol fee and the royalty total, and only afterwards attempts to transfer the trade fee. When the combined fees are larger than the input, the contract no longer has enough tokens to satisfy the trade fee transfer. This either causes the transfer to revert due to insufficient balance, or, if the transfer function falls back to using the pair’s own token balance, it unintentionally drains funds from the liquidity pool. The ETH implementation (LSSVMPairETH) follows a different ordering, subtracting trade fees before royalties, which leads to a different failure mode but the same underlying problem: the contract may end up moving funds that were not intended to be part of the user’s trade. The issue manifests when a trader supplies an amount that is small relative to the configured fees, or when royalty percentages are set unusually high. Users experience symptoms such as a swap transaction reverting unexpectedly, receiving no NFTs, or observing that the pool’s token balance has decreased without a clear reason. Liquidity providers may notice unexplained reductions in their pool’s holdings. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined fee handling logic and identified that the contract does not enforce the invariant protocolFee + royaltyTotal + tradeFeeAmount < inputAmount. Because each fee is calculated separately, the problem is not obvious from a superficial review and may only appear under specific fee configurations, making it hard to detect through standard testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should validate that the total of all fees is strictly less than the input amount before any transfers occur, and the ordering of fee deductions should be unified between the ERC20 and ETH pair contracts so that their behavior and failure modes are consistent. This change restores the accounting guarantees expected by the protocol, prevents accidental depletion of pool balances, and ensures that users receive the assets they paid for without hidden fee overruns.

title: NFTs may be exchanged for 0 tokens when price decreases too much
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error that occurs when a user attempts to sell a batch of NFTs through a linear bonding curve where the spot price decreases with each item sold. The contract calculates the total price decrease as delta multiplied by the number of items requested. If this total decrease would push the spot price below zero, the function getSellInfo adjusts the variable numItems to the smallest number of NFTs that would bring the price exactly to zero (spotPrice/delta + 1). However, the subsequent transfer logic still uses the original request amount instead of the adjusted value, causing the contract to take the full set of NFTs from the caller even though the last few NFTs have a theoretical value of zero. This mismatch means the seller loses NFTs without receiving any compensation for them. The issue is triggered only when the spot price is lower than the cumulative price decrease, i.e., when the sale would drive the price into negative territory. Any participant who initiates a sell operation under these conditions can be affected, leading to unexpected loss of assets and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that each transferred NFT is paid for. The problem was identified during a manual security review that examined the interaction between getSellInfo and the token transfer routine. It can be hard to notice because the UI may simply display the total amount of NFTs being sold and the overall proceeds, without highlighting that part of the batch is valued at zero, making the discrepancy subtle. To remediate, the contract should either reject sell requests that would cause the price to fall below zero, enforce a floor price, or ensure that the number of NFTs actually transferred matches the rational number computed by getSellInfo, thereby preventing zero‑value NFTs from being taken from the user. This class of bug falls under the broader category of “price floor violation” or “zero‑value asset transfer” errors, where accounting logic fails to align transferred assets with their calculated value.

title: _pullTokenInputAndPayProtocolFee() doesn't check that tokens are received
description:
```solidity
The function _pullTokenInputAndPayProtocolFee() doesn't verify that it actually received the tokens
after doing safeTransferFrom(). This can be an issue with fee on transfer tokens. This is also an issue with
(accidentally) non-existing tokens, as safeTransferFrom() won't revert on that, see POC below.
Note: also see issue "Malicious router mitigation may break for deflationary tokens".
function _pullTokenInputAndPayProtocolFee(...) ... {
    ...
    _token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, _assetRecipient, saleAmount);
    ...
}
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token‑pulling routine that assumes a successful ERC20 safeTransferFrom call guarantees that the exact amount of tokens has been moved to the contract. The function does not verify the recipient’s balance after the transfer, so when the token implements a transfer fee, a deflationary mechanism, or simply does not exist, the call can succeed while the contract receives fewer tokens—or none at all. This mismatch occurs because safeTransferFrom only checks the low‑level call’s return value and does not compare pre‑ and post‑transfer balances. An attacker can exploit the flaw by supplying a fee‑on‑transfer token or a token address that points to a non‑contract; the marketplace will record that the sale amount was received and will continue with fee calculation, while the protocol fee is effectively unpaid. The impact is a breach of the accounting invariants of the protocol: the fee collector receives less than expected, users may acquire assets without paying the required fee, and the overall economic model can be skewed, potentially allowing profit extraction or causing funds to disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The issue manifests whenever the contract interacts with arbitrary ERC20 tokens without performing a balance delta check, which is common in generic marketplace implementations. Users see a transaction that appears successful in the UI, but the protocol’s internal accounting shows a shortfall, leading to confusion when expected refunds or fee deductions do not occur. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who demonstrated a proof‑of‑concept using a dummy token address that does not implement ERC20, showing that safeTransferFrom does not revert and the contract proceeds as if tokens were transferred. Because the function lacks explicit verification, the bug can be subtle and may only be revealed through careful balance inspection or by observing unexpected fee shortfalls. To remediate, the routine should record the token balance of the recipient before the transfer, execute the safeTransferFrom, then read the balance again and assert that the increase is at least the intended amount. Additional safeguards include whitelisting known fee‑on‑transfer‑compatible tokens, checking that the token contract exists, or using a library that handles fee‑on‑transfer semantics. Implementing these checks restores the guarantee that the protocol fee is truly paid and aligns the contract’s state with the expected business logic of fee collection and asset accounting.

title: balanceOf() can be circumvented via reentrancy and two pairs
description: A reentrancy issue can occur if two pairs with the same ERC1155 NFTid are deployed. Via a call to swap NFTs, the ERC1155 callback onERC1155BatchReceived() is called. This callback can start a second NFT swap via a second pair. As the second pair has its own reentrancy modifier, this is allowed. This way the balanceOf() check of _takeNFTsFromSender() can be circumvented. If a reentrant call, to a second pair, supplies a sufficient amount of NFTs then the balanceOf() check of the original call can be satisfied at the same time. We haven't found a realistic scenario to abuse this with the current routers. Permissionless routers will certainly increase the risk as they can abuse isRouter == true. If the router is malicious then it also has other ways to steal the NFTs; however with the reentrancy scenario it might be less obvious this is happening.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy bypass that allows an attacker to circumvent the balanceOf() verification performed when NFTs are taken from a sender in a swap operation. The root cause is that each LSSVM pair maintains its own reentrancy guard, while the balance check is executed before the external call that triggers the ERC1155 callback. When two pairs are deployed that share the same ERC1155 token identifier, a swap on the first pair invokes onERC1155BatchReceived, and the callback can initiate a second swap on the other pair. Because the second pair has an independent reentrancy modifier, the reentrant call is permitted. If the attacker supplies enough NFTs in the second call, the balanceOf() condition of the original _takeNFTsFromSender function becomes satisfied after the reentrant execution, effectively allowing the original swap to complete without the sender actually owning the required NFTs. This can be exploited by a malicious or permissionless router that is marked as isRouter==true, which can orchestrate the two‑pair sequence. The impact is that NFTs can be transferred out of a user’s account without proper ownership verification, leading to loss of assets and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests when a user initiates a swap expecting to receive an NFT, but after the transaction the NFT is missing or the user’s balance appears unchanged, contradicting the expectation that the contract would have deducted the correct amount. It affects any participant using the affected pairs, especially those relying on the default router, and undermines trust in the protocol’s safety guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that traced the flow of the ERC1155 callback and identified that the reentrancy guard was scoped per pair rather than globally. The problem is subtle because the balance check passes after the reentrant call, making the exploit hard to detect from transaction logs alone. To remediate, the reentrancy state variable should be moved to a shared location such as the LSSVMPairFactory so that a reentrant call across any pair is blocked, and routers should be thoroughly vetted before being whitelisted. Additionally, applying the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern or performing balance verification after external calls would close the loophole and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Function call() is risky and can be restricted further
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a generic proxy function that allows the contract owner to forward an arbitrary call to any address that the factory marks as allowed. The function checks only the target address against a whitelist, but it does not validate the calldata that is sent. Because the calldata contains the function selector, a whitelisted contract can be instructed to execute any of its public functions, including those that move assets or change critical state. This design flaw arises from trusting the factory’s callAllowed check to be sufficient, while ignoring the fact that a contract can expose multiple entry points. An attacker who can influence the calldata – for example by submitting a malicious transaction through the owner or by compromising the owner’s signing key – can craft a selector for a dangerous function such as pairTransferERC20From, pairTransferNFTFrom, pairTransferERC1155From, or onOwnershipTransferred. By invoking these selectors, the attacker can cause the target pair contract to transfer tokens or NFTs out of the pool, effectively draining funds or altering ownership without the intended permission checks. The impact is the potential loss of user deposits, unexpected token transfers, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls the proxy with calldata that includes a prohibited selector, even though the target address passes the whitelist test. All participants who rely on the pool’s integrity – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because their assets may be moved without consent. The problem was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the mismatch between address whitelisting and function‑level access control. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction may succeed (the low‑level call returns true) and the logs only show a generic “Call succeeded” message, while the underlying state change is hidden inside the called contract. To remediate, the proxy should implement selector filtering, explicitly rejecting calls whose first four bytes match known dangerous functions, or adopt a more granular permission model that validates both the target address and the intended operation. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked‑calldata proxy vulnerabilities where a whitelist of contracts is insufficient without also restricting the functions that can be invoked, leading to unintended asset movement and violation of business logic that assumes only safe operations are permitted.

title: Incorrect newSpotPrice and newDelta may be obtained due to unsafe downcasts
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe downcast from a 256‑bit unsigned integer to a 128‑bit unsigned integer when the contract updates its virtual reserves after a buy or sell operation. The contract stores the spot price and the NFT reserve (delta) as uint128 values, but the intermediate calculations for the new reserves are performed in uint256. The result is then cast to uint128 without any overflow check. If the computed value exceeds the maximum representable by uint128 (2^128‑1), the cast silently wraps around, producing a much smaller number than intended. This happens in the getBuyInfo function when newSpotPrice is set to uint128(spotPrice + inputValueWithoutFee) and in the getSellInfo function when newDelta is set to uint128(nftBalance + numItems). The root cause is the lack of a safety check before the downcast, a pattern that is otherwise guarded elsewhere in the code but omitted here. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a trade with a large number of items or a large input value so that the addition overflows the 128‑bit limit. The overflow causes the new virtual token reserve or NFT reserve to be drastically lower than it should be, which in turn skews the pricing curve used by the automated market maker. As a result, subsequent trades can be executed at prices far from the intended market price, allowing a malicious actor to buy assets for far less than their true value or to sell assets for far more, effectively draining funds from the pool or causing liquidity providers to lose value. The impact is a breakdown of the accounting assumptions of the protocol: the invariant that reserves reflect the true state no longer holds, leading to incorrect price calculations, potential loss of user funds, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The condition occurs only when the trade size pushes the intermediate sum beyond the uint128 ceiling, which may not be obvious during normal operation with modest trade sizes. Any user interacting with the pool, including regular traders and liquidity providers, can be affected because the price displayed in the UI may appear normal while the underlying reserve values are corrupted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the direct cast without overflow protection as a high‑risk pattern. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the overflow is silent, so the blockchain records a successful trade even though the internal state is wrong. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include receiving far fewer tokens than expected, seeing their balance drop unexpectedly, or observing that a trade that should have cost a certain amount instead costs almost nothing. To remediate the bug, the contract should check whether the computed 256‑bit value fits within the uint128 range before casting, or it should keep the reserves in uint256 throughout the calculation. Using OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library or an explicit overflow guard (e.g., if (_newValue > type(uint128).max) revert) will prevent the silent wrap‑around and preserve the integrity of the pricing algorithm.

title: Fewer checks in pairTransferNFTFrom() and pairTransferERC1155From() than in pairTransferERC20From()
bug_full: The router contract provides three helper functions – pairTransferERC20From, pairTransferNFTFrom and pairTransferERC1155From – that forward token transfers from a caller to a liquidity pair. The ERC20 helper includes a strict validation that the caller contract is a registered pair (factory.isPair) *and* that the pair variant matches the expected ERC721‑ERC20 configuration. By contrast, the NFT and ERC1155 helpers only verify that the caller is a registered pair, omitting any check of the pair variant. This missing check means the router does not confirm that the pair actually supports the token standard being transferred. As a result, a caller can invoke pairTransferNFTFrom on a pair that is not an NFT‑ERC20 pair, or pairTransferERC1155From on a pair that does not support ERC1155, and the call will still succeed if the pair contract implements both ERC721 and ERC1155 interfaces. An attacker could craft a call that targets a mismatched pair, causing tokens to be moved into a contract that does not correctly handle them, effectively locking or burning the assets. The vulnerability manifests whenever the router is used to route NFT or ERC1155 transfers without the variant guard, especially in environments where a single pair contract implements multiple token standards. Users of the protocol – token owners, liquidity providers, and any front‑end that relies on the router to correctly transfer assets – are affected because they may see their NFTs or ERC1155 tokens disappear, become inaccessible, or be transferred to an unintended address. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the three functions and noticed the inconsistent validation logic. It can be hard to spot because the factory.isPair check passes for any registered pair, giving a false sense of safety, and the functions otherwise have identical signatures. To remediate, the router should add a variant check to pairTransferNFTFrom and pairTransferERC1155From that mirrors the require statement in pairTransferERC20From, ensuring the pair variant matches the expected token standard before proceeding with the transfer. This aligns the functions with the intended business logic that each helper only operates on pairs supporting the corresponding token type, preventing accidental or malicious misuse that could break accounting assumptions and lead to loss of user funds.

title: A malicious collection admin can reclaim a pair at any time to deny enhanced setting royalties
description: A malicious collection admin can forcibly/selectively call reclaimPair() prematurely (before the advertised and agreed upon lockup period) to unilaterally break the settings contract at any time. This will effectively lead to a DoS to the pair owner for the enhanced royalty terms of the setting despite paying the upfront fee and agreeing to a fee split in return. This is because the unlockTime is enforced only on the previous pair owner and not on collection admins. A malicious collection admin can advertise very attractive setting royalty terms to entice pair owners to pay a high upfront fee to sign-up for their settings contract but then force-end the contract prematurely. This will lead to the pair owner losing the paid upfront fee and the promised attractive royalty terms. A lax pair owner who may not be actively monitoring SettingsRemovedForPair events before the lockup period will be surprised at the prematurely forced settings contract termination by the collection admin, loss of their earlier paid upfront fee and any payments of default royalty instead of their expected enhanced amounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a premature termination path that allows a collection administrator to call the reclaimPair() function before the lockup period that was advertised to the pair owner has elapsed. The root cause is that the contract only checks the unlockTime constraint for the previous pair owner, while the collection admin, who is authorized through authAllowedForToken, is exempt from this time check. Consequently, a malicious admin can invoke reclaimPair() at any moment, causing the Settings contract associated with the pair to be removed. This action effectively denies the enhanced royalty terms that were promised in exchange for an upfront fee, resulting in a denial‑of‑service for the pair owner. The exploit can be carried out by an admin who advertises attractive royalty splits, convinces a pair owner to pay a high upfront fee, and then, before the agreed lockup expires, calls reclaimPair() to dissolve the settings. The pair owner loses the prepaid fee and any future enhanced royalty revenue, receiving only the default royalty rate or nothing at all. The issue manifests when a pair owner does not actively monitor SettingsRemovedForPair events during the lockup period; the unexpected event appears as a sudden termination of the royalty settings, often without any on‑chain warning. The affected parties are the pair owners who rely on the enhanced royalty agreement, as well as any downstream users who expect the promised fee split. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the access control and time‑lock logic of the settings management functions. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s public interface does not emit a distinct warning before the admin‑initiated call, and the unlockTime check is silently bypassed for admins. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce the unlockTime restriction for all callers, including collection admins, or otherwise require a consensus mechanism before a settings contract can be reclaimed. In broader terms, this is a privilege‑escalation and time‑lock bypass bug that breaks business logic assumptions about immutable royalty agreements, leading to lost funds and broken expectations for users who anticipate a guaranteed royalty enhancement over a defined period.

title: PropertyCheckers and Settings not sufficiently restricted
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LSSVMPairFactory’s handling of external contract addresses that provide critical protocol logic. When a new ERC‑721/ETH pair is created, the factory function accepts arbitrary addresses for the bonding curve, property checker and settings contracts without performing any validation of their origin or integrity. The same lack of checks appears in the toggleSettingsForCollection function, which also allows any address to be supplied as a settings contract. Because the factory does not enforce that these contracts were deployed by the authorized PropertyCheckerFactory or StandardSettingsFactory, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract that implements the expected interfaces, register its address, and pass it to the factory. Once the malicious contract is linked, its code will be executed during core operations such as price calculation, property validation, or configuration changes. This can lead to unauthorized fee manipulation, incorrect property checks, or arbitrary configuration changes that may cause user funds to be locked, transferred to unintended parties, or result in zero refunds where a user expects a payout. The issue is exploitable whenever a user or liquidity provider creates a new pair or when the protocol toggles settings for a collection, because the functions accept any address without sanity checks. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the missing validation logic. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the function signatures accept generic address parameters and the contract emits no warning when a malicious address is used; the malicious contract can mimic the expected interface, making the failure appear as a regular logic error. The root cause is the absence of a whitelist or factory‑origin verification for the property checker and settings contracts, combined with the possibility of later replacement via proxy or self‑destruct patterns. To remediate, the factory should maintain a registry of contracts created by the authorized factories and verify that any supplied address is present in that registry before accepting it. Additionally, the bonding‑curve whitelist should be extended to cover all external logic contracts, and interface checks (e.g., ERC‑165) could be added as a secondary safeguard. By restricting the accepted contracts to those generated by trusted factories, the protocol can ensure that only vetted logic is executed, preserving accounting assumptions, preventing fund loss, and aligning user expectations with actual behavior.

title: Possible incorrect utilization rate
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the utilization rate used by the lending market. The function takes three unsigned integers – cash, borrows and reserves – and returns the ratio of borrowed assets to the total liquidity (cash plus borrows minus reserves). The implementation assumes that the cash amount is always greater than or equal to the reserves, an assumption that is not enforced anywhere in the protocol. When the reserves grow larger than the cash balance, which can happen over time as fees are accrued to reserves, the denominator (cash + borrows – reserves) becomes smaller than the borrows amount. Because the function only checks for borrows equal to zero, it proceeds to compute borrows * 1e18 / (cash + borrows – reserves). If reserves > cash while borrows > 0, the denominator is reduced enough that the division yields a value greater than 1e18, meaning the reported utilization rate exceeds 100%. This incorrect utilization rate can be exploited by influencing the reserve accumulation (for example, by depositing large amounts that are later transferred to reserves through protocol fee mechanisms) so that reserves surpass cash. An inflated utilization figure may cause downstream calculations – such as interest rate models, borrowing limits, or liquidation thresholds – to behave unexpectedly, potentially allowing borrowers to obtain more credit than intended or causing lenders to receive incorrect interest. The impact is a breach of the core accounting invariant that utilization must be bounded between 0 and 1, leading to possible over‑issuance of loans, mispriced interest, and ultimately loss of funds for users or destabilisation of the protocol. The bug manifests only when borrows are non‑zero and reserves exceed cash, a state that is not prevented by any guard condition and may be hard to notice because most front‑ends display utilization as a percentage and do not flag values above 100%. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BaseJumpRateModelV2 contract, where the formula was examined and the missing cap was identified. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or throw; it simply returns a mathematically valid but semantically incorrect number. To remediate, the utilization calculation should be constrained to the maximum possible value (1e18) when reserves are greater than cash, or the denominator should be clamped to a minimum of borrows to ensure the ratio never exceeds one. This change restores the invariant that utilization is always between 0 and 1, preserving correct interest rate behavior and protecting user funds.

title: Borrow rate calculation can cause CToken.accrueInterest() to revert SumerMoney_report.md
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by a hard‑coded upper bound on the borrow interest rate (BORROW_RATE_MAX_MANTISSA) that is enforced with a require statement inside CToken.accrueInterest(). The contract calculates the current borrow rate dynamically based on market conditions, but the calculation does not take the hard‑coded cap into account. When the dynamically computed borrowRateMantissa reaches or exceeds the maximum mantissa, the require check (borrowRateMantissa <= BORROW_RATE_MAX_MANTISSA) triggers and the function reverts with the message 'borrow rate is absurdly high'. This revert propagates to every CToken function that calls accrueInterest(), such as mint, redeem, borrow, repay, and transfer, effectively halting all core protocol operations. The impact is that users attempting legitimate actions see their transactions fail, receive no token balance changes, and may be unable to withdraw or repay, which contradicts the expectation that the protocol will process these actions smoothly. The condition occurs only when market parameters drive the borrow rate to an extreme value, making it difficult to observe during normal testing and easy to miss in a code review that focuses on typical paths. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interest‑rate logic and identified the mismatch between the dynamic calculation and the static cap. Because the failure is triggered by a single require statement, it may appear as a simple error message rather than a systemic problem, obscuring the broader denial‑of‑service effect. The bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded threshold checks that cause contract reverts instead of graceful degradation. A proper fix is to replace the revert with logic that caps the borrowRateMantissa at BORROW_RATE_MAX_MANTISSA, allowing accrueInterest() to continue execution with the maximum allowed rate and restoring normal operation once the market rate falls below the cap. This change aligns the contract’s behavior with business expectations that interest rates may spike but should not stop the protocol from functioning.

title: Insufficient input validation
description:
Throughout the codebase there are couple of places where important input validation is missing. The inputs are not constrained at all or only partly.  
The newCloseFactorMantissa param in Comptroller:_setCloseFactor().  
The supplySpeed and borrowSpeed params in CompLogic:_setCompSpeedInternal().  
The _rewardsDuration param in StakingRewardsMultiGauge:setRewardsDuration() is only partly validated but it is missing an upper constrain.  
The new_rate param in StakingRewardsMultiGauge:setRewardRate().  
SumerMoney_report.md
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing or incomplete input validation on several privileged setter functions across the protocol. In the Comptroller contract the function that updates the close factor (newCloseFactorMantissa) does not enforce any upper or lower bound, allowing an administrator to set a value that could be zero, negative (if unsigned underflow is possible) or arbitrarily large. Similarly, the CompLogic contract’s internal routine that sets the supply and borrow reward speeds (supplySpeed and borrowSpeed) accepts any uint256 without checking that the rates are within a reasonable range. In the StakingRewardsMultiGauge contract the function that defines the rewards duration (_rewardsDuration) only performs a partial check and lacks an upper limit, while the function that sets the per‑second reward rate (new_rate) also omits bounds checking. Because these parameters directly control economic variables such as liquidation thresholds, reward emission rates and the time window over which rewards are distributed, an attacker with the ability to call the setter functions can manipulate them to extreme values. For example, setting the close factor to 100 % would allow liquidators to seize an entire collateral position in a single transaction, effectively wiping out borrowers’ balances. Inflating supplySpeed or borrowSpeed to huge numbers could cause the protocol to mint excessive COMP tokens, diluting existing holders and draining the reward pool. An unbounded rewards duration could keep rewards flowing indefinitely, while an excessively high reward rate could exhaust the staking contract’s token balance in seconds, leaving stakers with no future earnings. These effects manifest whenever a privileged account (owner, admin or governance) invokes the affected functions, which may happen during routine upgrades or parameter adjustments. Users experience symptoms such as sudden loss of collateral, unexpected zero balances after a liquidation, reward payouts that are either missing or absurdly large, and staking contracts that stop distributing rewards because the token reserve has been emptied. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that flagged the absence of require statements or explicit range checks in the setter implementations. It is difficult to notice because the functions execute without reverting and appear to work under normal values; only extreme inputs reveal the flaw. The proper mitigation is to introduce explicit validation logic that enforces sensible lower and upper bounds for each parameter, for instance requiring the close factor to be between 0.05 and 0.5 (5 %–50 %), reward speeds to be capped at a maximum emission rate, rewards duration to be limited to a reasonable number of seconds, and reward rates to stay within a predefined range. Adding these checks ensures that economic assumptions remain intact and prevents malicious manipulation of protocol incentives.

title: Use call() instead of transfer() when sending ETH
description:
The repayBorrowBehalf() is using the transfer method to send ETH to the caller of the function. This than the 2300 gas which is the limit of transfer. Examples are some smart contract wallets or multi-sig wallets, so usage of transfer is discouraged.  
More
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of the Solidity transfer() function to forward Ether in the repayBorrowBehalf() routine. Transfer imposes a hard gas stipend of 2300 gas on the callee, which is sufficient for a simple externally owned account but insufficient for many contract wallets, multi‑signature wallets, or any contract whose fallback or receive function performs additional logic such as logging, state updates, or external calls. Because the protocol assumes that the transfer will always succeed, it does not check for a failure condition, and the repayment logic proceeds as if the Ether had been delivered. When the caller is a contract that requires more than 2300 gas to accept the payment, the transfer reverts, causing the entire repayBorrowBehalf() transaction to fail or, if the failure is not properly propagated, to silently drop the Ether. This results in users seeing a successful transaction on the blockchain but receiving no funds, or in the repayment being blocked entirely, which can prevent borrowers from clearing debt and may lead to unintended liquidations. The issue is discovered during a manual security audit that flagged the use of transfer() as a known anti‑pattern. It is difficult to notice in testing because most test suites use simple EOAs that accept Ether with the default gas stipend, masking the problem. The bug belongs to the class of “gas‑stipend transfer failures” and violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that repayments are always delivered. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer() with a low‑level call{value: amount}('') and verify the returned boolean, handling any failure explicitly, thereby allowing the full gas amount to be supplied to the recipient contract and preventing denial‑of‑service or silent loss of funds.

title: Assumption that all tokens have 18 decimals will lead to wrong calculations
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption that every reward token used by the farm contract has 18 decimal places. In the reward‑per‑token and earned calculations the code multiplies by 1e18 and later divides by 1e18, treating the token amount as if it were expressed in 18‑decimal units. This assumption is false for tokens such as USDC and USDT, which use only 6 decimals. Because the contract does not query the token’s decimals() function, the scaling factor is applied uniformly, causing the arithmetic to be off by a factor of 10^(18‑tokenDecimals). When a 6‑decimal token is used, the reward amount is understated by a factor of 1,000,000, effectively draining the reward pool or giving users far fewer tokens than they expect. The issue can be exploited simply by staking or depositing a supported low‑decimal token; the contract will compute rewards using the wrong scale, and users will receive a dramatically reduced payout. The impact is a systematic loss of funds for any pool that distributes rewards in tokens with fewer than 18 decimals, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and violating the expectation that rewards are proportional to stake and time. The bug manifests whenever the reward calculation functions are invoked while a non‑18‑decimal token is part of the rewardTokens array – a condition that is true for the intended USDC and USDT rewards. It affects all participants who stake, all pools that rely on these reward tokens, and ultimately the protocol’s financial integrity. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the reward math and noticed the hard‑coded 1e18 factor. It is hard to notice because the numbers may still appear plausible for a short test, and the discrepancy only becomes evident over many reward cycles or when users compare on‑chain balances with expected values. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a reward balance that is zero or far lower than anticipated, leading to confusion when “I should have earned X tokens but I got almost nothing”. The root cause is a classic scaling‑factor bug, a class of errors where fixed‑point arithmetic assumes a uniform decimal precision across heterogeneous tokens. The correct mitigation is to retrieve each token’s decimals via the ERC20 decimals() view, compute a token‑specific scaling factor (10**decimals), and replace the hard‑coded 1e18 with that dynamic value in both the multiplication and division steps. This change restores proper proportional reward calculations regardless of token precision and aligns the contract’s accounting with the business logic that rewards should be accurately distributed based on actual token units.

title: Use of transferFrom is dangerous for non-compliant ERC 20 tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of calling the ERC-20 transfer (or transferFrom) function without verifying the boolean return value. The ERC-20 specification defines that these functions must return true on success and revert on failure, but several widely-used tokens such as USDC and USDT deviate from the standard and simply return false or omit a return value while leaving the transaction non-reverting. In the contract, the reward distribution routine invokes IERC20(token).transfer(recipient, amount) and then emits a RewardPaid event, assuming the transfer succeeded. Because the return value is ignored, a failed transfer is treated as successful; the contract's internal accounting records the reward as paid, the event is emitted, and the user interface shows that the user received the reward, while the token balance of the contract remains unchanged. This can happen whenever the token is non-compliant, when the contract lacks sufficient balance, when the token is paused, or when the token's internal logic rejects the transfer (for example, due to blacklisting). The immediate impact is that users may not receive their expected rewards, leading to funds disappearing from the protocol's perspective, and the protocol's accounting becomes inconsistent, potentially causing further logic errors or loss of trust. The issue is difficult to detect because the transaction does not revert, no error is thrown, and the emitted event gives the false impression of success. It was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the missing safety wrapper around ERC-20 transfers. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked ERC-20 transfer or non-compliant token handling vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should use OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeTransfer (or safeTransferFrom) which checks the return value and reverts on failure, or explicitly verify that the call returned true. This ensures that rewards are only marked as paid when the token transfer truly succeeded, preserving correct accounting and preventing funds from becoming stuck.

title: A malicious/compromised owner or TokenManager can rug rewards SumerMoney_report.md
bug_full: The contract implements a recoverERC20 function that is supposed to let privileged roles retrieve tokens that were sent to the contract by mistake. The intended design is that the contract owner may withdraw any non‑reward token, while a designated reward manager may only withdraw the specific reward token it controls, and the staking token is explicitly protected from withdrawal. In practice the function is guarded only by a modifier that restricts callers to token managers, and the internal logic checks the caller against a reward‑manager mapping only when the token is identified as a reward token. Because the token manager role is allowed to invoke the function and the code does not enforce a separate check that prevents token managers from withdrawing reward tokens, a token manager can call recoverERC20 with the address of a reward token and have the contract transfer an arbitrary amount of that token to themselves. The root cause is a missing access‑control condition: the function assumes that only reward managers will be token managers for reward tokens, but this assumption is not enforced, allowing a malicious or compromised token manager to bypass the reward‑manager check. An attacker who controls the token manager role can therefore rug the entire pool of reward tokens, draining funds that were meant to be distributed to users. This vulnerability manifests whenever a token manager invokes recoverERC20 with a reward token address; the transaction succeeds and the reward balance of the contract drops to zero or an unexpectedly low value. Users observing the UI would see their expected rewards disappear, balances showing zero, or refunds that never arrive. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s withdrawal logic, where the reviewer noted that the only restriction was against the staking token, not against reward tokens for token managers. The bug can be subtle because the function emits a generic “Recovered” event and does not differentiate between legitimate owner withdrawals and malicious token‑manager withdrawals, making it easy to miss in routine monitoring. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the owner may withdraw non‑reward tokens and that only the designated reward manager may withdraw its associated reward token, while explicitly denying token managers from withdrawing any reward token. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model and prevents unauthorized draining of reward assets.

title: withdrawAssets will always revert
poc: No poc.
bug_full: withdrawAssets is intended to let the contract admin pull out any ERC20 tokens that might have been sent to the contract by mistake after the sale has finished. The function is protected by the fromStage modifier, which is supposed to ensure that the contract is in the Completed stage before allowing a withdrawal. However the modifier contains a condition that reverts not only when the required stage is higher than the current stage, but also when the current stage is exactly Completed. Because withdrawAssets passes Stages.Completed as the required stage, the second part of the condition is true and the call always reverts with WrongStage. The root cause is an incorrect logical expression in the stage‑checking modifier. An attacker does not need to exploit the function; the bug is a denial‑of‑service for the admin: any attempt to call withdrawAssets will fail, leaving tokens that were accidentally transferred to the contract permanently locked. This situation occurs only after the contract reaches the Completed stage, which is the normal final state of the sale. The affected parties are the contract administrators and any users who rely on the ability to recover mistakenly sent assets; from a user perspective the UI may show a withdraw button but the transaction reverts, resulting in “no funds received” or “balance remains unchanged”. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the stage‑checking logic. It can be hard to notice because the modifier appears to enforce the correct stage, yet the extra equality check unintentionally blocks the very stage it is meant to allow. To fix the problem the modifier should be rewritten to allow calls when the current stage equals the required stage, or the withdrawAssets function should perform its own explicit check that only reverts when the contract is not in Completed. In conceptual terms this is a stage‑validation logic error that leads to a permanent asset lock, a class of bugs where access‑control conditions are inverted or overly restrictive, breaking the expected business rule that admins can recover stray tokens after a sale ends.

title: Wrong calculation of tokens to transfer will break deposit flow
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the number of tokens that should be transferred to a depositor in a tiered‑sale contract. The private function that determines the token amount iterates over the sale tiers and decides whether the remaining deposit amount fits within the current tier by checking if the remaining amount is less than or equal to the tier’s cap. Tier caps are defined as cumulative values, but the logic treats them as if they were the marginal capacity of each tier. Consequently the contract compares the remaining amount to the wrong threshold and also passes the full cumulative cap to the token‑computation routine instead of the incremental amount that actually belongs to that tier. When a deposit spans multiple tiers, the contract therefore credits the depositor with tokens priced at a lower tier than should apply, effectively allowing a purchase at a cheaper price. In addition, because the total funds collected are increased by the full deposit amount, the next deposit may cause an arithmetic underflow when the contract computes the remaining capacity of the next tier as tier.cap minus totalFundsCollected, since totalFundsCollected can already exceed the cumulative cap of that tier. The impact is twofold: users can obtain more tokens than intended, leading to revenue loss for the protocol, and the sale flow breaks because subsequent deposits revert, freezing the contract and preventing further participation. The bug manifests only when a deposit pushes the total collected amount across a tier boundary; for small deposits that stay within a single tier the logic appears to work, making the problem easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the tier‑iteration loop and identified the misuse of cumulative caps. The issue belongs to the class of tier‑pricing accounting errors where cumulative limits are treated as incremental limits, resulting in mis‑priced token allocation and a potential underflow condition. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a large deposit yields more tokens than expected and that after such a deposit any further attempt to deposit fails with a revert error, often reported as an “underflow” or “insufficient funds” failure. The contract violates the business assumption that each tier has a fixed amount of funds that can be sold at its price; the logic incorrectly assumes the tier cap is the amount still available in that tier. To fix the problem the calculation must compare the remaining deposit amount to the marginal capacity of the tier (tier.cap minus the previous tier’s cap) and pass that marginal amount to the token‑computation function. The remaining amount should then be reduced by the marginal capacity, and the total funds collected must be updated accordingly, eliminating the underpricing and preventing the underflow on subsequent deposits.

title: The onERC721Received() Is Not Implemented Correctly
description: The PositionManager.onERC721Received() function intends to accept liquidity positions sent only by the admin to the PositionManager contract. It performs some validations regarding the liquidity position type that is being transferred and records the pair so other liquidity positions in the same pair are not accepted. An attacker can exploit the safeTransferFrom() function by front-running the admin’s transaction and invoking the PositionManager.onERC721Received() function with crafted arguments. Specifically, the attacker can set the from parameter to the admin’s address to bypass the require(hasRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, from), "...") check, which validates the sender’s role. By specifying a tokenId corresponding to the same pair the admin is attempting to transfer—one that the admin does not control—the attacker causes the admin’s safeTransferFrom() call to revert. This effectively prevents the admin from transferring a liquidity position for the targeted pair, creating a denial-of-service scenario for this specific operation. The admin, and indeed anyone, can still send liquidity positions to the PositionManager using the transferFrom() function instead of safeTransferFrom(). However, doing so will result in the _uniV3NftByToken0Token1 and _uniV3NftIds mappings not being updated, rendering them inaccurate and effectively useless.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrectly implemented ERC721 receiver hook in the PositionManager contract. The onERC721Received() function is supposed to accept liquidity position NFTs only when they are transferred by an address that holds the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. However, the function validates the sender by checking the "from" argument rather than the actual caller of safeTransferFrom(). Because the ERC721 standard passes the original owner as the "from" parameter, an attacker can front‑run the admin’s transaction, call safeTransferFrom() themselves, and set the from field to the admin’s address. This tricks the require(hasRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, from)) check into believing the transfer is authorized. The attacker also supplies a tokenId that belongs to the same token pair the admin intends to deposit but that the attacker does not own. When the admin later executes safeTransferFrom() for that pair, the onERC721Received() hook reverts due to the mismatched tokenId, causing the admin’s transaction to fail. The result is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents the admin (or any user) from depositing a liquidity position for the targeted pair via safeTransferFrom(). Although the same NFT can still be moved using the lower‑level transferFrom() function, doing so bypasses the hook and leaves the internal bookkeeping mappings (_uniV3NftByToken0Token1 and _uniV3NftIds) unchanged. Consequently, the contract’s view of which NFTs are associated with which token pairs becomes stale, breaking downstream logic that relies on those mappings, such as addLiquidity(), collectFees(), and collectFeesOnly(). The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the role‑based checks in the ERC721 receiver implementation and identified that the check could be spoofed by manipulating the from argument. It is hard to notice because the contract still accepts transfers and the revert only occurs under a specific front‑running scenario, which may not be reproduced in routine testing. The impact includes blocked admin operations, inaccurate accounting of deposited positions, and potential loss of functionality for users who rely on the contract’s bookkeeping. The affected parties are the protocol administrators, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that assume the mappings are correct. To remediate, the contract should remove the onERC721Received() override entirely and replace it with an explicit, admin‑only deposit function that internally calls safeTransferFrom(), performs proper access control based on msg.sender, and updates the bookkeeping mappings atomically. This redesign eliminates reliance on the mutable from parameter, prevents role‑check bypass, and restores reliable accounting of liquidity positions.

title: Staking and Reward Token Overlap Can Risk User Stakes
description: The StakingVault.acceptPositionManagerRewards() can be called by anybody and uses transferFrom with an arbitrary from value. This means that an attacker can use this function and transfer reward tokens from anybody that has given allowance to the StakingVault. This is problematic since if the staking and the reward token are both $VOLT then users will first approve the StakingVault and then they will call stake(). An attacker can front-run the stake call of the user and use this approved amount as a reward via the acceptPositionManagerRewards(). A user could lose their tokens when they attempt to stake.
bug_full: The contract contains a function that allows any caller to invoke acceptPositionManagerRewards which internally calls transferFrom with a caller‑supplied from address. Because the function does not restrict the source of the tokens, an attacker can specify any address that has previously granted an allowance to the vault. In typical usage the staking token and the reward token are the same ERC‑20 (VOLT). Users first approve the vault to spend their VOLT tokens and then call stake(). An attacker observing the pending stake transaction can front‑run it, call acceptPositionManagerRewards and pass the victim’s address as the from argument. The vault then pulls the approved amount from the victim and treats it as reward tokens, effectively stealing the user’s stake before it is locked. The impact is that a user may see a reduction or complete loss of their token balance after attempting to stake, with no error shown in the UI; the stake may appear to succeed while the tokens have been transferred away. The vulnerability manifests whenever the same token is used for both staking and rewards and the contract relies on an unchecked transferFrom source. It was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑handling logic, where the lack of a msg.sender check was noted as a deviation from standard allowance patterns. The issue can be hard to notice because the function does not emit a distinct error and the front‑run transaction can be executed in the same block, making the loss appear as a normal staking operation. The bug belongs to the class of unrestricted transferFrom or allowance abuse vulnerabilities, often combined with front‑running opportunities. The correct mitigation is to restrict the transferFrom source to the caller (msg.sender) or to a known trusted address, and to ensure that reward collection cannot be triggered by arbitrary parties. By enforcing that only the contract itself or the intended reward manager can pull tokens, the protocol preserves the accounting invariant that a user’s approved balance is only used for their own stake.

title: Incorrect chainId used for permit EIP712 domain separator
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect EIP‑712 domain separator construction in the token contract that implements the permit() function. The contract’s constructor builds the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR by hard‑coding the chain identifier to the constant value 1 using inline assembly. This value corresponds to the Ethereum mainnet chain ID, while the contract is intended to run on a different network (for example the TRON network) that uses a distinct chain ID. Because the domain separator embeds a mismatched chainId, any wallet or user‑agent that follows the EIP‑712 specification will detect the discrepancy between the embedded chainId and the active chain it is connected to. According to the specification, the signing UI must refuse to produce a signature when the chainId does not match, so the permit() call cannot be signed. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the bug itself causes a denial‑of‑service condition for the permit functionality. When a user attempts to approve a token transfer via a signed permit, the wallet will reject the signing request, often displaying an error such as “signature rejected” or simply refusing to proceed. The user expects a gas‑less approval but receives no signature, leading to failed transactions and potentially blocked token transfers that rely on permit. This issue manifests only on chains whose identifier differs from 1, i.e., any deployment that is not on Ethereum mainnet. It affects all token holders, dApps, and protocols that depend on the permit() method for off‑chain approvals, reducing usability and possibly causing loss of functionality for users who cannot fall back to on‑chain approvals. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the hard‑coded assembly line was examined and flagged as a deviation from the EIP‑712 recommendation to use the dynamic chainid opcode. The bug can be subtle because the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR appears syntactically correct and the contract compiles without warnings; the failure only becomes visible at runtime when a signing request is made. To remediate the issue, the constructor should retrieve the current chain identifier using the EVM’s chainid opcode (or accept it as a constructor argument) and incorporate that value into the domain separator calculation, ensuring that the embedded chainId always matches the network on which the contract is deployed. This change restores compliance with EIP‑712, allowing wallets to sign permits correctly and re‑enabling the intended gas‑less approval flow.

title: Abuse of permit functionality to block legitimate transactions
description:
The removeLiquidityWithPermit function in the SushiSwapV2Router02 contract allows users to remove liquidity from a liquidity pool by leveraging the permit function to approve the transfer of liquidity tokens. However, this mechanism introduces a potential front-running vulnerability. An attacker can observe the transaction containing the permit call in the mempool and issue their own transaction with the same permit parameters but a different function call before the legitimate transaction is mined. This could result in the legitimate transaction failing due to the altered state. Similarly, the user who created the signature will end up approving tokens to SushiSwapV2Router02 without them being used, requiring the signer to execute the transaction manually.

```solidity
function removeLiquidityWithPermit(
    address tokenA,
    address tokenB,
    uint liquidity,
    uint amountAMin,
    uint amountBMin,
    address to,
    uint deadline,
    bool approveMax,
    uint8 v,
    bytes32 r,
    bytes32 s
) external virtual override returns (uint amountA, uint amountB) {
    address pair = SushiSwapV2Library.pairFor(factory, tokenA, tokenB);
    uint value = approveMax ? uint(-1) : liquidity;
    ISushiSwapV2ERC20(pair).permit(msg.sender, address(this), value, deadline, v, r, s);
    (amountA, amountB) = removeLiquidity(
        tokenA,
        tokenB,
        liquidity,
        amountAMin,
        amountBMin,
        to,
        deadline
    );
}
```

Once the permit is executed by an attacker, the nonce for the user will be incremented, causing the legitimate permit call to fail with a "INVALID_SIGNATURE" revert error. Consider the next scenario:
1. UserA intends to call SushiSwapV2Router02::removeLiquidityWithPermit with specific parameters.
2. Attacker observes the pending transaction from UserA and he sends a transaction to call the permit function with the same parameters as UserA transaction.
3. The nonce for the permit is now used.
4. When UserA transaction is executed, it reverts due to the invalid nonce. Additionally, the same issue occurs in SushiSwapV2Router02::removeLiquidityETHWithPermit and SushiSwapV2Router02::removeLiquidityETHWithPermitSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition affecting the permit‑based liquidity removal functions of the SushiSwapV2Router02 contract. The router exposes a removeLiquidityWithPermit (and similar ETH variants) that internally calls the ERC‑20 permit method to approve the router to transfer the caller’s liquidity tokens using a signed EIP‑2612 signature. Because the permit call is executed inside the same transaction as the liquidity removal, an attacker who monitors the mempool can copy the exact permit parameters (owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) and submit a separate transaction that invokes only the permit function before the legitimate transaction is mined. The attacker’s transaction consumes the user’s current nonce for that token, incrementing it on the token contract. When the original user’s transaction later executes, the internal permit call fails with an INVALID_SIGNATURE revert because the nonce no longer matches the signed message. As a result, the subsequent removeLiquidity call never runs, the user’s liquidity remains locked in the pool, and the user sees a transaction that reverts after paying gas. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the router was approved but no tokens were withdrawn, leading to confusion and a perception that funds have disappeared. The issue affects any user who relies on the permit shortcut to avoid a separate approve transaction, and it can affect any token that implements the permit interface. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of permit usage and identified that the nonce is mutable and can be pre‑empted by a front‑runner. The problem is subtle because the permit call is hidden inside the router’s function, so developers may not anticipate that the signature can be replayed by a third party before the intended transaction is mined. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or race‑condition vulnerabilities on mutable state (the nonce) combined with off‑chain signatures. To mitigate the issue, the contract should handle a failing permit gracefully, for example by wrapping the permit call in a try/catch block as recommended by OpenZeppelin, or by separating the approval step from the liquidity removal, using a short deadline, or employing a nonce‑checking mechanism that ensures the signature cannot be reused by an attacker. Proper handling prevents the transaction from reverting due to an invalid signature and preserves the expected user experience where a signed permit reliably authorises the router to move the liquidity tokens.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect events parameter
description:
At the lines below:
LendingPair.sol#L252
LendingPair.sol#L267
LendingPair.sol#L282
LendingPair.sol#L291
LendingPair.sol#L306
LendingPair.sol#L321
there are places where we have events which require an affected user address as a parameter, however in these cases msg.sender is wrongly used as a parameter. These functions accept special user parameter that should be used in events instead of msg.sender. The issue marked as major since it can fatally affect the user's side code that is based on events.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of emitting events with an incorrect address parameter. Several functions in the LendingPair contract accept an explicit user address argument that identifies the account whose balance is being modified, but the corresponding events are built using msg.sender instead of this supplied user argument. The root cause is a simple coding mistake: the developer assumed the caller of the function is always the affected user, ignoring cases where the function is called on behalf of another address (for example, depositFor, withdrawFor, or any delegated operation). When the contract emits an event, off‑chain services, user interfaces, and other contracts that rely on those events to track balances or trigger further actions will associate the action with msg.sender rather than the intended beneficiary. Consequently, a user who initiates a transaction for a different address will not see the expected event, leading to missing updates in dashboards, inaccurate accounting in analytics, and potential failures in downstream logic that expects the event to contain the beneficiary address. The impact is primarily on the user‑side code and any ecosystem component that indexes events for state reconstruction; funds are not lost on‑chain, but the visibility of state changes is compromised, which can cause confusion, missed refunds, or incorrect balance displays. The issue manifests whenever the affected‑user functions are called with a non‑msg.sender target, which is a common pattern in lending or vault contracts that support third‑party interactions. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared function signatures with emitted event arguments and noted the mismatch. The bug can be hard to notice because the events still fire and the transaction succeeds, so developers may not see an immediate failure, only a discrepancy between expected and observed event data. To remediate, the contract should emit the user argument supplied to the function rather than msg.sender, ensuring that the event accurately reflects the account whose state changed. This correction aligns the on‑chain state with off‑chain observers and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Fee-on-Transfer Tokens Can Cause Accounting Errors in Swappee Contract
description: The Swappee contract contains a vulnerability in its handling of Fee-on-Transfer (FOT) tokens. The issue manifests in the swappee function, where the contract assumes the actual received amount of tokens will equal the transferred amount, without accounting for potential transfer fees. Specifically, when processing token transfers via IERC20(inputToken).transferFrom(), the contract uses the pre-transfer amount (amountsClaimedPerWallet[inputToken][msg.sender]) for all subsequent calculations and approvals, rather than checking the actual received balance. This assumption breaks for FOT tokens, where the received amount may be less than the transferred amount due to built-in transfer fees. When users attempt to swap FOT tokens, the contract will: incorrectly calculate fees based on the pre-fee amount, potentially approve more tokens than necessary to the aggregator, and may trigger reverts when attempting to swap the full pre-fee amount that isn’t actually available.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Swappee contract’s handling of tokens that charge a fee on each transfer, commonly known as fee‑on‑transfer (FOT) tokens. The contract assumes that the amount it requests to transfer from a user will be the exact amount it receives, and it bases all subsequent calculations, including fee assessment and token approval for the downstream aggregator, on this pre‑transfer amount. In reality, FOT tokens deduct a portion of the transferred value as a built‑in fee, so the balance that actually arrives in the contract is lower than the amount recorded in the internal accounting mapping. This mismatch leads the contract to over‑estimate the available token balance, approve more tokens than it truly holds, and attempt to swap an amount that does not exist, which can cause the swap transaction to revert or to execute with incorrect fee calculations. The impact is that users attempting to swap FOT tokens may see their transaction fail, receive fewer output tokens than expected, or inadvertently approve excess tokens that could be drained by a malicious aggregator. The issue manifests only when a user swaps a token that implements a transfer fee; normal ERC20 tokens without such a fee are unaffected. The bug was discovered during a manual security review by the Shiedify audit team, who noticed that the contract never checks the post‑transfer balance and relies solely on the amount stored before the transfer. Because the fee is deducted silently by the token contract, the problem can be hard to notice in normal testing unless the specific fee‑on‑transfer behavior is exercised. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction submission, but the on‑chain receipt reveals a revert or a zero balance change, leading to confusion when the expected tokens do not appear in the wallet. The root cause is a missing verification step that measures the actual amount received after the transfer. To remediate, the contract should record the token balance of the contract before the transfer, perform the transferFrom call, then read the new balance and compute the delta; this delta represents the true amount received and should be used for all fee calculations and approvals. By treating the received amount as the authoritative value, the contract aligns its accounting with the token’s fee‑on‑transfer semantics and prevents over‑approval and failed swaps, restoring correct business logic for token swaps.

title: Use safeTransfer() and safeTransferFrom() Instead of transfer() and transferFrom()
description: Tokens that do not comply with the ERC20 specification could return false from the transfer function call to indicate the transfer fails, while the calling contract would not notice the failure if the return value is not checked. Checking the return value is a requirement, as written in the EIP-20 specification: “Callers MUST handle false from returns (bool success). Callers MUST NOT assume that false is never returned!” Some tokens do not return a bool (e.g. USDT, BNB, OMG) on ERC20 methods. This will make the call break, making it impossible to use these tokens. It would not revert even though the transaction failed.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on the raw ERC20 transfer and transferFrom functions without verifying the boolean return value that indicates success. According to the ERC20 specification, a token contract may return false to signal a failed transfer, and callers are required to handle this case. In practice, many popular tokens such as USDT, BNB and OMG deviate from the spec by either returning false on failure or not returning any boolean at all. When a calling contract invokes transfer or transferFrom and ignores the return data, a failed token movement is silently ignored; the transaction continues as if the transfer succeeded. This can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a non‑standard token that deliberately returns false or no value, causing the contract to believe that funds were moved while they remain unchanged. The impact is that user balances appear to be updated in the UI, but the underlying token balances stay the same, leading to missing refunds, zero‑amount swaps, or apparent loss of funds. The condition occurs whenever the contract interacts with any ERC20 token that does not strictly follow the EIP‑20 return‑value contract, especially in functions that assume a successful transfer without a require statement. All participants who rely on the contract – end users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because accounting assumptions are broken and the protocol may think it holds more assets than it actually does. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s token handling code against the ERC20 specification and identified missing checks for the return value. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the blockchain records a successful transaction, yet the token balances are unchanged, which may only be observed through post‑transaction balance queries or UI discrepancies. The proper remediation is to replace raw transfer and transferFrom calls with wrappers that enforce a revert on failure, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library or a custom SafeTransferLib, thereby ensuring that any false return or missing return triggers an exception and preserves the integrity of the protocol’s accounting logic.

title: Lack of two-step role transfer
description: The contracts lack two-step role transfer. All of the contracts use the onlyOwner modifier which shows that this role is important for the project. Especially the DepositContract where the funds deposited by receiving the role is inaccessible is not covered properly. Also, it can be seen in the documentation that this is one of the main security concerns of the team. The ownership transfer should be done with great care and two-step role transfer should be preferable.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insecure ownership handover pattern where the contracts rely on a single‑step transferOwner function guarded only by the onlyOwner modifier. Because the transfer is immediate and does not require the new address to explicitly accept the role, any mistake, compromised key, or malicious substitution of the owner address can instantly give full control of the contract to an unintended party. This problem is especially critical in the DepositContract, where the owner is responsible for managing deposited funds; if ownership is transferred to an address that cannot or does not execute the withdrawal logic, the funds become effectively locked and users receive no refunds. The root cause is the absence of a two‑step (push‑pull) role transfer mechanism, which means there is no verification step that the new owner is aware of and willing to assume responsibility.
