```solidity
if (_action.id == TOFT_REMOVE_AND_REPAY) {
    HelperTOFTRemoveAndRepayAsset memory data = abi.decode(
        _action.call[4:],
        (HelperTOFTRemoveAndRepayAsset)
    );
    _checkSender(data.from);
    IUSDOBase(_action.target).removeAsset(
        data.from,
        data.to,
        data.lzDstChainId,
        data.zroPaymentAddress,
        data.adapterParams,
        data.externalData,
        data.removeAndRepayData,
        data.approvals,
        data.revokes
    );
}
```
Since no gas is forwarded to the external call, the external call will have msg.value of 0.
However if we check the removeAsset function in BaseUSDO.sol, we see a subsequent layerzero call via the USDOMarketModule.
```solidity
bytes memory lzPayload = abi.encode(
    PT_MARKET_REMOVE_ASSET,
    externalData,
    removeAndRepayData,
    approvals,
    revokes,
    airdropAmount
);
_checkAdapterParams(
    lzDstChainId,
    PT_MARKET_REMOVE_ASSET,
    adapterParams,
    NO_EXTRA_GAS
);
_lzSend(
    lzDstChainId,
    lzPayload,
    payable(from),
    zroPaymentAddress,
    adapterParams,
    msg.value
);
```
The issue here is that msg.value is 0, hence no gas will be sent to the layerzero endpoint, failing the cross-chain call.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing gas forwarding bug that occurs when the MagnetarV2 contract processes the TOFT_REMOVE_AND_REPAY action. In this flow the contract decodes a HelperTOFTRemoveAndRepayAsset structure and calls the external removeAsset function on a USDO market contract. The call is made without attaching any ether value, so msg.value received by removeAsset is zero. Inside removeAsset the contract builds a LayerZero payload and then invokes the internal _lzSend function, passing msg.value as the amount of native gas to forward to the LayerZero endpoint. Because msg.value is zero, the cross‑chain message is sent without any gas, causing the LayerZero call to fail. The root cause is that MagnetarV2 does not propagate the caller‑provided gas when invoking removeAsset, breaking the assumption that the downstream function will have enough native currency to pay for the cross‑chain transmission. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any user who attempts to exit a position using the TOFT_REMOVE_AND_REPAY action will experience a silent failure of the cross‑chain removal. From the user’s perspective the transaction may appear successful on‑chain, but the position remains open, collateral is not removed, and the expected refund or repayment never arrives, effectively locking funds. The issue is discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the call chain and noticed that msg.value was never forwarded. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the failure occurs in an off‑chain LayerZero endpoint, leaving no obvious on‑chain error flag. The impact is medium severity: users lose the ability to close positions, the protocol’s cross‑chain accounting becomes inconsistent, and overall trust in the system may be eroded. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient gas forwarding” or “cross‑chain call gas omission” vulnerabilities, where a contract forwards a call that requires native gas but does not supply it. The recommended fix is to modify the MagnetarV2 call to forward the original msg.value (or an appropriate amount) to removeAsset, for example by using the Solidity syntax IUSDOBase(_action.target).removeAsset{value:_action.value}(...), ensuring that the LayerZero send receives the necessary gas to complete the cross‑chain operation.

title: Not maximizing Glp in GlpOracle miscalculates _minGlp when adding liquidity
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑retrieval logic of the GlpOracle contract, which calls the GLP manager with the maximisation flag set to false (glpManager.getPrice(false)). This flag instructs the manager to return a price that is deliberately lower than the maximum possible price for the same underlying assets. The returned price is then used to compute the expected amount of GLP tokens that should be minted when a user adds liquidity, after applying a slippage adjustment. Because the price is understated, the calculated minimum GLP amount (_minGlp) is also lower than it would be if the maximisation flag were true. Consequently, the require check that enforces mintAmount >= _minGlp can be satisfied even when the GLP manager mints fewer tokens than the user reasonably expects. The impact is that users receive a smaller GLP balance than anticipated, effectively losing value on the transaction; the protocol’s accounting assumptions about token issuance are violated, and the discrepancy may go unnoticed because the transaction does not revert and the UI simply shows a successful deposit. The issue occurs whenever liquidity is added through the Yieldbox module that relies on this oracle, i.e., under normal operation of the protocol. It affects any participant who supplies assets for GLP minting, including regular users and the protocol’s liquidity pool. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s price‑oracle integration, where the auditor observed the use of the false flag and traced its effect on the slippage calculation. The problem is subtle because the transaction succeeds and no explicit error is emitted, making the loss of GLP tokens appear as a normal outcome rather than a failure. This class of bug can be described as an oracle misconfiguration leading to incorrect slippage or minimum‑output calculations, a common issue in DeFi contracts that rely on price feeds for minting or swapping logic. To remediate the issue, the oracle should request the maximised price by calling glpManager.getPrice(true), ensuring that the computed _minGlp reflects the highest realistic price and that the mintAmount check protects users from receiving fewer tokens than expected. In summary, the contract under‑estimates the GLP price, lowers the slippage threshold, and permits minting of insufficient GLP, resulting in users seeing a smaller balance than they anticipated after adding liquidity.

title: Any tokens or eth in Magnetar can be drained
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked external contract address injection that allows a malicious actor to approve and transfer any ERC20 token or ETH held by the Magnetar contract. The root cause is that several public functions accept addresses for YieldBox, market contracts, and asset contracts directly from the caller without any validation or whitelist enforcement. Because the contract subsequently grants token approvals to these supplied addresses and invokes functions on them, a malicious contract can be supplied that receives those approvals and executes arbitrary token transfers or receives ETH sent during an unwrap operation. An attacker can exploit this by calling withdrawToChain with a crafted YieldBox address that returns a malicious asset address, setting the unwrap flag to true, and providing a gas amount that is forwarded as ETH. The malicious asset contract then simply accepts the ETH, effectively draining the contract’s balance. Similarly, functions that handle collateral deposits retrieve collateral token addresses from a user‑provided market contract; the attacker can supply a market that returns a malicious token address, after which the contract calls an internal token extraction routine that transfers the tokens out and approves the malicious YieldBox to move them. The impact is that any ETH reserved for gas or any ERC20 tokens that happen to be stored in Magnetar can be taken by the attacker, violating the expectation that the contract does not hold user funds. This condition occurs whenever the affected functions are invoked with attacker‑controlled addresses, which is possible for any user of the protocol. The parties affected include the protocol itself, its users who might rely on the contract’s internal accounting, and any downstream contracts that assume Magnetar’s balances are safe. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of external contract parameters and noticed that approvals were granted to addresses that were never verified. Because the contract is not intended to store assets, reviewers may overlook the risk, making the bug subtle. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist of known, trusted YieldBox and market contracts, or replace user‑provided addresses with immutable references set at deployment, thereby preventing arbitrary contracts from receiving approvals and executing token transfers. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked external address or authorization bypass, where malicious contracts can be injected to drain funds. From a user perspective the symptom is a missing balance: after interacting with the protocol the user may see that their tokens or ETH have vanished, receiving no refund or transfer, contrary to the expectation that the contract would retain or correctly forward the assets.

title: Magnetar _depositRepayAndRemoveCollateralFromMarket can fail due to rounding errors
poc: No poc.
bug_full: An arithmetic rounding inconsistency occurs in the function that removes collateral and optionally withdraws it to another chain. When a user specifies a non‑zero collateralAmount, the contract first converts the token amount to internal shares using YieldBox.toShare with the rounding‑down flag set to false. If the conversion does not result in an integer number of shares, the function truncates the value, for example 100 tokens may become 49 shares. Later the same amount of tokens (100) is passed to a withdraw call where YieldBox.toShare is invoked internally with the rounding‑up flag, causing the contract to require 50 shares to be burned. Because only 49 shares were removed earlier, the withdraw step reverts due to an insufficient share balance. The bug is a classic rounding‑error or arithmetic‑precision flaw that leads to a mismatch between the number of shares deducted during removal and the number required during withdrawal. It can be triggered whenever the token‑to‑share conversion yields a fractional share, i.e., for many token amounts that are not exact multiples of the share unit. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to reject the withdrawal, returning an error and leaving the expected collateral unchanged, which looks like my balance stays zero or the transaction fails even though I supplied enough tokens. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users cannot successfully remove or withdraw collateral for affected amounts, potentially locking funds in the protocol and breaking business logic that assumes a 1‑to‑1 correspondence between deposited tokens and withdrawn tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the rounding direction used in the two YieldBox calls. It is hard to notice because the two calls are separated by several lines and the rounding flag is a boolean that defaults to false, making the inconsistency subtle. The proper fix is to use the same rounding direction for both operations, typically by rounding up when calculating the collateralShare before removal, ensuring that enough shares are available for the subsequent withdraw. This aligns the internal accounting, restores the expected behavior that a user who deposits X tokens can later withdraw exactly X tokens, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Using only DEX swappers is suboptimal
description:
Currently, most of the actions that need tokens to be swapped across Tapioca's codebases use the swappers, which currently, they are 3.
Each swapper uses a different DEX, UniV2, Univ3 and Curve DeFi pools. This is not the ideal scenario for most cases as when you are swapping you are trying to maximize the amountOut that you get in exchange for the tokens you swapped. To accomplish this and get better rates for your swaps, at least one aggregator should be added to the list of swappers.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s reliance on a fixed set of three DEX‑specific swappers – Uniswap V2, Uniswap V3 and Curve – for every token‑to‑token conversion performed by the system. Because each swapper queries only a single liquidity source, the contract does not compare alternative market offers before executing a trade. The root cause is a design decision that treats these three DEXes as the sole execution paths, ignoring the existence of price‑aggregation services that can route a swap through multiple venues to obtain the best possible amountOut. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit this by initiating a swap when the selected DEX offers a sub‑optimal rate compared to what an aggregator could have found; the contract will dutifully execute the trade at the worse price, causing the user to receive fewer output tokens than expected. The impact is financial loss: users may see their balances shrink, receive less than the quoted amount, or experience lower returns on liquidity provision because the protocol pays more input tokens for a given output. This condition occurs any time a swap is performed through the existing swappers, which is the default behaviour across the codebase. All participants who rely on the protocol’s swapping functionality – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the DAO itself – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes optimal market execution. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the token‑exchange pathways and identified the lack of rate optimisation as a deviation from best‑practice DeFi design. It can be hard to notice because the swaps still succeed and the returned amounts may appear reasonable on the surface; only a detailed comparison with aggregator‑derived quotes reveals the inefficiency. To remediate, the contract should be extended to include at least one reputable aggregator such as 1inch or 0x, allowing the system to query multiple DEXes and select the highest amountOut before finalising the trade. This change aligns the implementation with the expected business logic of maximizing user value and preserving protocol capital, turning the current sub‑optimal swapping pattern into a rate‑optimal aggregation strategy.

title: Lack of sequencer uptime check for TapOracle can cause stale prices
description:
TapOracle takes an average of 3 TWAP prices from UniswapV3 pool with an interval of at least 4 hours (based on FETCH_TIME ). The 3 TWAP prices are stored in lastPrices[] and updated when get() is called to retrieve TAP price.
The issue is that when the L2 sequencer is down for an extended period, there will be no interaction with the oracle via get() , preventing lastPrices[] from being updated with the latest prices. This will cause TapOracle to return stale prices when the sequencer recovers.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑price oracle condition caused by the absence of a sequencer‑uptime verification step in the TapOracle contract. TapOracle computes a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) from a UniswapV3 pool by sampling three price points spaced by a configurable FETCH_TIME, which must be at least four hours. These three samples are stored in the lastPrices[] array and are refreshed only when the public get() function is invoked. Because get() is the sole trigger for updating lastPrices[], the contract implicitly assumes that the underlying L2 sequencer is continuously operational and that calls to get() will occur regularly. When the sequencer experiences an extended outage, no transactions can be processed on the L2, which means get() is never called and the lastPrices[] array remains unchanged. Once the sequencer recovers, the contract resumes normal operation but continues to return the outdated values that were cached before the outage. An attacker who can predict or induce a sequencer downtime can exploit the stale price by submitting trades or liquidations that rely on the oracle, receiving a price that is no longer reflective of the market. This can lead to users receiving too few tokens, over‑paying for assets, or the protocol suffering unintended losses because the accounting logic assumes the price is up‑to‑date. The issue manifests only when the sequencer is down for a period longer than FETCH_TIME and no external actor calls get() during that window, which is a realistic scenario for L2 networks that occasionally experience downtime. All participants that depend on the TAP price – including traders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that use the oracle for collateral valuation – are affected. The problem was identified during a manual security review that examined the oracle’s update path and noticed the missing heartbeat check. It is subtle because the contract still returns a numeric price that appears valid; without external monitoring of the sequencer’s health, developers may not notice that the price is stale. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a sequencer‑beat verification call (for example, _sequencerBeatCheck()) inside get() and to enforce a grace period after sequencer recovery during which the contract forces an update of all three TWAP samples. Adjusting FETCH_TIME to be no more than one‑third of the grace period ensures that the three price slots can be refreshed promptly after the sequencer resumes. In generic terms, this is an oracle‑staleness bug arising from a missing liveness guard, and the fix consists of adding a heartbeat or timeout mechanism that forces price refresh when the underlying data source becomes available again.

title: UniswapV3Swapper should not use the same poolFee for all token pairs
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic error in the UniswapV3Swapper contract where a single hard‑coded pool fee (poolFee) is used for every token pair that the contract attempts to swap. Uniswap V3 pools are identified by the two token addresses *and* the fee tier, so a pool only exists at a specific fee. Because the Swapper does not allow the fee to be specified per swap, it calls the internal getPool function with the same fee for all pairs. If a particular token pair does not have a pool at that fee, the computed pool address points to a non‑existent contract. When the swap logic then tries to interact with this address, the call fails, the transaction reverts, or the contract silently receives no output. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the destination token – does not happen; the UI may show a successful transaction hash while the balance remains unchanged, or the transaction may revert with an obscure error. The impact is that users cannot reliably swap arbitrary token pairs through the Swapper, leading to failed trades, potential loss of gas fees, and a broken user experience. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to swap a pair that only exists at a different fee tier (for example, a 0.05 % pool when the contract is hard‑coded to 0.3 %). It affects any participant relying on the Swapper, including end‑users, integrators, and the protocol that assumes the Swapper can handle all pairs. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s interaction with Uniswap V3, where the auditor noted that the getPool call always uses a constant fee and did not verify the existence of the returned pool. The problem can be subtle because many popular pairs do have a pool at the default fee, so tests that only cover those pairs pass, masking the bug for less common assets. To remediate, the contract should expose the fee tier as a parameter of the swap function (or determine the correct fee dynamically) and verify that the returned pool address contains code before proceeding. This change aligns the Swapper with Uniswap V3’s design, ensuring that each swap targets a valid pool and that users receive the expected token output.

title: UniswapV3Swapper and UniswapV2Swapper will fail when depositing received ETH into YieldBox
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the UniswapV3Swapper (and similarly in UniswapV2Swapper) when the caller requests a swap that should automatically deposit the output token into YieldBox (depositToYb set to true) and specifies the native ETH placeholder address (address(0)) as the tokenOut. In this scenario the contract first swaps the input token for WETH, then immediately unwraps the WETH into raw ETH. After unwrapping, the code calls yieldBox.depositAsset to place the received ETH into YieldBox. However, depositAsset is designed to accept ERC‑20 tokens and explicitly rejects native ETH, causing the transaction to revert. The root cause is a mismatch between the asset type being deposited (native ETH) and the function used for the deposit (ERC‑20‑only depositAsset). An attacker or a careless user can trigger this path by supplying tokenOut = address(0) while also enabling depositToYb, causing the swap to fail and the transaction to revert. The impact is that users expecting their swapped ETH to appear in YieldBox receive no funds; the transaction fails, gas is spent, and the protocol’s automated liquidity‑routing logic may be blocked, potentially leading to denial‑of‑service conditions for other users. The bug manifests only when the specific combination of parameters is used, making it easy to overlook during casual testing because most swaps involve ERC‑20 tokens. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the swapper contracts, where the code path for native‑asset handling was examined and found to call the wrong YieldBox entry point. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful swap request, but after confirmation the balance in YieldBox would remain unchanged and the transaction would be marked as reverted, creating confusion and loss of gas. The issue belongs to the class of “incorrect asset handling” bugs, where a contract assumes a function can accept any asset type without verifying the asset’s nature. To remediate, the swapper should either avoid unwrapping WETH when depositToYb is true, allowing the WETH ERC‑20 token to be deposited directly via depositAsset, or it should call the dedicated yieldBox.depositETHAsset function that is built to handle native ETH. Both approaches ensure that the asset type matches the deposit function, preventing the revert and restoring the expected flow of funds into YieldBox.

title: Using buildSwapData() with tokenIn/tokenOut will cause swap to fail when depositing into/withdrawing from YieldBox
description:
When buildSwapData(address tokenIn, address tokenOut, ...) is used to populate SwapData , both tokenInId and tokenOutId will be set to zero.
However, when using swap() with depositToYb = true , it will deposit to YieldBox based on the tokenOutId . That will fail as tokenOutId is zero.
Same issue for withdrawToYb = true , which will fail as tokenInId will be zero as well.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the helper function buildSwapData that constructs the SwapData structure for token swaps. When the caller supplies tokenIn and tokenOut addresses, the function incorrectly leaves the internal identifiers tokenInId and tokenOutId at their default value of zero. The swap() routine can be instructed to deposit the output token directly into the YieldBox vault (depositToYb = true) or to withdraw the input token from YieldBox (withdrawToYb = true). Both paths rely on the token identifier fields to locate the correct asset inside YieldBox. Because the identifiers are zero, the vault lookup fails and the swap transaction reverts. This situation occurs only when the swap is performed with the YieldBox integration enabled; a normal swap without YieldBox works as expected. The affected parties are users who attempt to execute a swap that should automatically move assets into or out of YieldBox, as well as the protocol that expects these operations to succeed. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails or reverts, often with no obvious error message, leading to confusion and potentially lost time. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the swap helper functions, where the auditor noticed that the identifier fields were never populated. The bug is subtle because the function signature suggests that tokenIn and tokenOut are sufficient, and the zero identifiers do not cause a compile‑time error; only at runtime does the vault reject the operation. The root cause is a missing mapping from token address to YieldBox asset ID in the buildSwapData implementation. To remediate, the helper should either correctly resolve tokenInId and tokenOutId from the YieldBox registry or, as recommended, disable the YieldBox flags (withdrawFromYb and depositToYb) for this helper and remove the unsupported parameters. By preventing the function from being used with YieldBox integration, the swap will no longer attempt an invalid deposit or withdrawal, eliminating the failure mode. The vulnerability can be classified as an integration‑parameter mismatch leading to an invalid asset identifier, which results in a failed external call and a reverted transaction.

title: FETCH_TIME is too large and this can lead to a stale price
description:
The FETCH_TIME value in the TapOracle.sol contract is set to 4 hours, which determines the minimum interval between updates of the oracle price.
```solidity
uint32 public FETCH_TIME = 4 hours;
```
But this interval is too large and can lead to an outdated price. In highly volatile markets, price data can become outdated quickly. A 4-hour interval may not be sufficient to capture important market movements, potentially leading to the oracle providing stale or inaccurate data.
Change it to 1 hour exactly as you described it in the NatSpec and in the documentation.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an excessive oracle update interval. In the TapOracle.sol contract the constant FETCH_TIME is set to 4 hours, which defines the minimum time that must pass before the price can be refreshed. Because the interval is long, the oracle may continue to return a price that was fetched up to four hours earlier. In fast‑moving markets the true market price can diverge significantly within minutes, so the contract can provide a stale or inaccurate price to downstream logic such as swaps, lending, or liquidation. An attacker or even an honest user can exploit this by initiating a transaction after the price has moved but before the oracle is allowed to update, causing the transaction to be evaluated against an outdated price. The impact includes users receiving less favorable rates, potential liquidation of positions that would otherwise be safe, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol's pricing mechanism. The condition occurs whenever the market experiences volatility within the four‑hour window and the contract relies on the oracle for price decisions. All participants that depend on the oracle—traders, lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the business logic assumes the price reflects the current market. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the documented fetch interval (1 hour) with the actual constant (4 hours) and recognized the mismatch as a risk. Because the contract still functions and does not revert, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when users observe unexpected trade outcomes or liquidation events. The bug belongs to the class of “stale data” or “insufficient refresh rate” vulnerabilities, where a time‑based guard prevents timely updates of external information. From a user perspective the UI may show a price that looks correct but the transaction settles at a rate that is too low or too high, leading to perceived loss of funds or missing refunds. The correct mitigation is to align the FETCH_TIME constant with the intended one‑hour interval, or to redesign the oracle to allow on‑demand updates or shorter minimum intervals, thereby ensuring that price data remains fresh enough for the protocol’s risk assumptions.

title: Missing implementation of the quoteLayerZeroFee() in StargateLbpHelper.sol
description:
We use the participate() function when we want to do a cross-chain transfer. The function calls the swap method using Stargate router:
```solidity
router.swap{value: msg.value}(
    stargateData.dstChainId,
    stargateData.srcPoolId,
    stargateData.dstPoolId,
    payable(msg.sender), // refund address
    stargateData.amount,
    amountWithSlippage,
    IStargateRouterBase.lzTxObj({
        dstGasForCall: 0,
        dstNativeAmount: 0,
        dstNativeAddr: "0x0"
    }),
    abi.encodePacked(
        // msg.sender), // StargateLbpHelper.sol destination address
        abi.encode(lbpData, msg.sender)
    )
);
```
To pay fee we send msg.value :
```solidity
swap{value:msg.value}
```
From Stargate documentation we see that we have to call quoteLayerZero() to calculate the fee.
For the native gas fee required for swap() you need to call quoteLayerZero() on the Router.sol contract to get the amount you should send as msg.value.
But such a function is missing. Because of this, we don't know how many fees to send for the transfer to be successful. If we send more than needed it will refund, but if we send less than needed the cross-chain transfer will fail.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing fee‑quotation routine in the helper contract that orchestrates cross‑chain swaps via the Stargate router. The contract’s participate() function forwards a user’s request to the router’s swap() method and supplies msg.value as the native gas payment, assuming that the caller knows the exact amount required for the LayerZero messaging fee. However, the helper does not implement the quoteLayerZeroFee() call that the router documentation specifies for estimating the fee. Because the fee is not calculated, the contract cannot determine the minimum native amount that must accompany the swap. If a caller provides less than the required fee, the router will reject the transaction and the cross‑chain transfer will revert, leaving the user’s assets locked in the contract or causing the transaction to fail without a clear error. If a caller over‑pays, the router will refund the excess, but the over‑payment may be unexpected and could be perceived as a loss of efficiency. The issue arises during any cross‑chain transfer initiated through participate(), affecting all users who rely on the helper for token swaps, as well as the protocol that depends on successful cross‑chain liquidity provisioning. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against the official Stargate integration guide and noted the absence of the fee‑quotation call. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction may simply revert without an explicit “insufficient fee” message, and developers might assume that the router will accept any msg.value. The impact is a potential denial‑of‑service for cross‑chain operations and a degraded user experience where users see their swaps fail or receive unexpected refunds. To remediate, the helper contract should implement a call to the router’s quoteLayerZeroFee() (or the current equivalent) before invoking swap(), capture the returned fee amount, and forward exactly that amount as msg.value, optionally adding a small buffer for safety. This aligns the contract with the expected fee‑calculation pattern, restores reliable cross‑chain functionality, and prevents inadvertent transaction failures due to insufficient native gas payment.

title: _withdrawToChain() will refund excess gas for LZ call to the wrong address
description:
As MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain() allows withdrawal to another chain, it requires refundAddress to be specified so that excess gas can be refunded to an address on the source chain. However, refundAddress is incorrectly set as it does not handle all cases.
```solidity
// build LZ params
bytes memory _adapterParams;
ICommonOFT.LzCallParams memory callParams = ICommonOFT.LzCallParams({
    refundAddress: msg.value == gas ? refundAddress : payable(this), // @audit this does not handle all cases
    zroPaymentAddress: address(0),
    adapterParams: ISendFrom(address(asset)).useCustomAdapterParams()
        ? adapterParams
        : _adapterParams
});
```
I have determined 4 different cases of how _withdrawToChain() can be called, and the following shows that cases 2/3/4 are incorrect.
Case 1: Direct call
gas == msg.value and refundAddress will be from parameter This is correct, assuming no user error.
EOA -> MagnetarV2.withdrawToChain()
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain() // delegatecall
Case 2: Cross-chain direct call
gas == msg.value and refundAddress will be payable(to) due to BaseTOFTMarketDestinationModule.sol#L247 This is incorrect as refundAddress should be a user provided address on the source chain.
LZ (dest) -> BaseTOFT._nonblockingLzReceive()
-> BaseTOFTMarketDestinationModule.remove() // delegatecall
-> MagnetarV2.withdrawToChain()
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain() // delegatecall
Case 3: Cross-chain indirect call
gas == msg.value and refundAddress will be payable(this) due to MagnetarMarketModule.sol#L858 This is incorrect as refundAddress should be a user provided address on the source chain.
LZ (dest) -> BaseTOFT._nonblockingLzReceive()
-> BaseTOFTMarketDestinationModule.borrowInternal() // delegatecall
-> MagnetarV2.depositAddCollateralAndBorrowFromMarket()
-> MagnetarMarketModule.depositAddCollateralAndBorrowFromMarket() // delegatecall
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdraw()
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain()
Case: 4. Multicall using burst()
gas == _action.value and refundAddress will be payable(this) due to MagnetarMarketModule.sol#L800 This is incorrect as refundAddress should be msg.sender .
EOA -> MagnetarV2.burst()
-> MagnetarV2.depositAddCollateralAndBorrowFromMarket()
-> MagnetarMarketModule.depositAddCollateralAndBorrowFromMarket() // delegatecall
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdraw()
-> MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain()
poc: No poc.
bug_full: During a withdrawal that is intended to move assets to another blockchain, MagnetarMarketModule._withdrawToChain builds a LayerZero call parameter structure. The code decides the refundAddress with the expression msg.value == gas ? refundAddress : payable(this). This logic assumes that when the amount of ether sent equals the gas limit, the caller‑provided refundAddress can be used, otherwise the contract itself should receive any leftover gas. The assumption breaks in several realistic execution paths. When the function is invoked directly by an externally owned account, the condition holds and the correct address is used, but when the call originates from a cross‑chain message, from an internal borrowing flow, or from a multicall burst, the msg.value comparison still succeeds while the context of msg.sender is no longer the original user. Consequently the fallback branch selects payable(this) or, in one case, the destination address on the target chain, causing the excess gas to be sent to the contract or to an address that the user does not control on the source chain. Users therefore see a transaction that reports success but receive no gas refund; the UI may show the withdrawal completed while the expected “refund” field remains zero, and the user’s balance on the source chain is reduced by the amount that should have been returned. The root cause is the reliance on a gas‑equality check and an implicit fallback to the current contract address instead of explicitly propagating the user‑provided refund address through all call layers. An attacker could trigger a withdrawal on behalf of a victim, causing the refund to be directed to a contract they control, effectively stealing the leftover gas. The impact is a loss of potentially valuable gas refunds and, in extreme cases, a reduction of the user’s available funds on the source chain. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the refund logic across the four identified call patterns and verified that cases 2, 3 and 4 use an incorrect refund destination. Because the contract still performs the primary asset transfer, the bug can remain unnoticed unless the developer or auditor checks the post‑transaction balances or the event logs for the refund amount. The recommended remediation is to make the refundAddress an explicit parameter that is passed from the initial public function down through every internal call, ensuring that the same user‑controlled address is used regardless of the execution path. This eliminates the need for the gas‑equality heuristic and guarantees that excess gas is always returned to the intended recipient, aligning the implementation with the expected business logic that refunds should never be lost or sent to an unrelated address.

title: TapOracle TWAP duration for Uniswap Oracle should be at least 30 mins
description:
TapOracle uses a single price feed based on Uniswap V3 TWAP oracle for TAP/USDC pool.
However, the deploy script for TapOracle indicates a TWAP duration of 600 secs (10mins), which is lower than typical 1,800 secs (30mins) that is used by Euler[1] and Uniswap[2] in their studies. This puts TapOracle at a higher risk of price manipulation when liquidity of the TAP/USDC pool is not spread over a wide range. This could occur during protocol launch where the Uniswap pool has limited liquidity.
One may argue that such price manipulation is risky for the attacker, as the attacker has to use their own capital (instead of flash loan) to keep the price manipulated for more than a block, making them vulnerable to arbitrage. But that is not a total deterrence as shown in Rari's Fuse hack[3], where the attacker risked their capital and waited for multiple blocks.
The root cause of that hack was due to price manipulation of the Uniswap V3 TWAP oracle, which had a TWAP duration of 600 secs and the Uniswap pool did not have liquidity over a wide range.
```javascript
const args: Parameters<Seer__factory['deploy']> = [
    'TAP/USDC', // Name
    'TAP/USDC', // Symbol
    18, // Decimals
    ARGS_CONFIG[chainID].TAP_ORACLE.TAP_ADDRESS, // TAP
    ARGS_CONFIG[chainID].MISC.USDC_ADDRESS, // USDC
    ARGS_CONFIG[chainID].TAP_ORACLE.TAP_USDC_LP_ADDRESS, /// LP TAP/USDC
    [1], // Multiply/divide Uni
    600, // @audit Uniswap V3 TWAP duration 600 seconds is lower than typical 30 mins
    10, // Observation length that each Uni pool should have
    0, // Whether we need to use the last Chainlink oracle to convert to another
    // CL path
    [], // Multiply/divide CL
    86400, // CL period before stale, 1 day
    [deployer.address], // Owner
    hre.ethers.utils.formatBytes32String('TAP/USDC'), // Description,
    ARGS_CONFIG[chainID].MISC.CL_SEQUENCER, // CL Sequencer
    deployer.address, // Owner
];
```
References
[1] https://docs.euler.finance/euler-protocol/eulers-default-parameters#twap-length
[2] https://blog.uniswap.org/uniswap-v3-oracles
[3] https://cmichel.io/replaying-ethereum-hacks-rari-fuse-vusd-price-manipulation/
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an oracle configuration that uses a Uniswap V3 time‑weighted average price (TWAP) window of only ten minutes for the TAP/USDC price feed. Because the TWAP period is shorter than the thirty‑minute window commonly recommended by Uniswap and Euler, the price reported by the TapOracle can be influenced by short‑term market manipulation. The root cause is the deployment script that hard‑codes a TWAP duration of 600 seconds together with a liquidity pool that may have limited depth and a narrow price range, especially during the early stages of the protocol when liquidity is not yet widely distributed. An attacker who controls a modest amount of TAP or USDC can shift the pool price for a few blocks, and the short TWAP will still reflect this manipulated price when the TapOracle queries it. This manipulated price can be used to under‑price collateral, over‑price loans, or otherwise break the accounting assumptions of the protocol, potentially leading to loss of funds, unexpected liquidations, or incorrect token swaps. The issue manifests when the protocol relies on the oracle for critical decisions such as loan issuance or liquidation; users may see their positions liquidated at seemingly fair market rates while the on‑chain price feed is actually distorted. The problem was identified during a security audit that compared the configured TWAP length with industry best practices and cited the Rari Fuse hack, where a similar short TWAP allowed price manipulation over multiple blocks. Because the price feed appears normal on a per‑block basis, the manipulation can be hard to detect without deeper analysis of the TWAP window. To remediate, the TWAP duration should be increased to at least thirty minutes, and the TAP/USDC pool should be seeded with liquidity across a wide price range to raise the cost of manipulation. Adding a secondary fallback oracle or longer observation periods would also mitigate the risk. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation vulnerabilities caused by insufficient averaging periods and thin liquidity, leading to inaccurate price data that violates the protocol’s financial logic and can cause users to receive zero or incorrect amounts during withdrawals or trades.

title: Not upadting `_totalAuctionTokenAllocation` when removing last auction config at cooldown leads to wrong accounting of `_totalAuctionTokenAllocation` and permanent lock of auction tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when the contract removes the configuration of the most recent auction while the auction is still in its cooldown period. The function that deletes the auction configuration fails to adjust the global variable that tracks the total amount of tokens allocated to all active auctions. Because this decrement is omitted, the contract continues to record a higher allocation than the actual tokens held for future epochs. When a new auction is started, the contract calculates the amount of tokens available for the epoch by subtracting the recorded allocation from the contract's token balance. The inflated allocation value makes this calculation yield zero, causing the startAuction call to revert with a NotEnoughAuctionTokens error. Even if the required extra tokens are supplied to satisfy the calculation, the global allocation variable is then updated with the sum of the old stale value and the new epoch amount, effectively double‑counting the tokens. As a result, a surplus of tokens becomes permanently locked in the contract because the recoverToken function also relies on the same faulty accounting and refuses to release any amount that would exceed the (incorrect) available balance. The bug is triggered only when the DAO executor removes the last auction configuration during the cooldown phase – a scenario that is rare but possible during governance actions. It affects the protocol’s ability to run successive auctions, locks auction tokens that should be recoverable, and breaks the expectation that token balances can be reused across epochs. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed the contract reverting on startAuction and being unable to recover the excess tokens after the auction ends. The problem is hard to notice because the external token balance of the contract appears correct, while the internal accounting variable silently diverges, leading to subtle failures only when new auctions are initiated. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑cleanup or accounting bugs where invariant updates are omitted during a removal operation. To fix the issue, the removal logic must decrement the total allocation counter by the amount recorded for the deleted epoch before clearing the configuration, ensuring that the global allocation accurately reflects the tokens still reserved for active auctions. Additionally, any recovery or start‑auction calculations should reference the corrected allocation value to prevent permanent token lockup.

title: Changes to vesting period is not handled inside `_getVestingRate`
bug_full: The contract stores a single global vesting period that determines how quickly a stake becomes fully vested. When a user creates a stake, the contract records the start timestamp and a fullyVestedAt timestamp that is calculated using the current global vesting period at that moment. The function that computes the vesting rate, however, always divides the elapsed time by the current global vesting period instead of the period that was in effect when the stake was created. Consequently, if the protocol owner shortens the vesting period after a stake has been made, the denominator becomes smaller while the numerator (elapsed time) continues to grow, producing a vestingRate that can exceed the theoretical maximum of 1e18. This inflated rate translates into higher than intended reward calculations for the staker, effectively giving the user more tokens than the protocol intended to distribute. Conversely, if the vesting period is lengthened, the denominator grows and the vestingRate can drop sharply below the expected value, causing reward claims to revert because the stored userRewardPerTokenPaid value, which was based on the earlier higher rate, underflows when the contract attempts to update it. The vulnerability is triggered only when the vesting period is changed while there are active stakes that have not yet reached their fullyVestedAt timestamp, a situation that can occur during a draw or any period where the protocol allows the owner to adjust the vesting schedule. Users are affected because they may see rewards that are unexpectedly large at first, or later experience failed claim transactions that revert and leave their reward balance unchanged. From a protocol perspective, the bug can lead to over‑payment of rewards, draining treasury funds, or to a denial‑of‑service where legitimate claims cannot be processed. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that added a public getter for the vesting rate and observed that after reducing the vesting period from 16 weeks to 8 weeks, the computed rate for a stake created earlier exceeded 1e18, confirming the arithmetic overflow. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the rate surpasses the maximum, and the arithmetic still fits within uint256, so the abnormal value can go unnoticed without targeted testing. To remediate the flaw, the calculation should either cap the vestingRate at 1e18 or, preferably, use the original vesting period that was captured at stake time for each individual stake, ensuring that subsequent changes to the global parameter do not affect already‑vested positions. This aligns the accounting logic with the business rule that a stake’s vesting schedule is immutable once created, preventing inflated rewards and claim reverts.

title: Interface definition error
description:
`MarketPlace.authRedeem()` call interface `ISwivel.authRedeem()` but Swivel contract does not have this method only method “authRedeemZcToken()“.

The result will cause `MarketPlace.authRedeem()` to fail forever, thus causing `ZcToken.withdraw()` to fail forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interface definition mismatch between the MarketPlace contract and the Swivel core contract. MarketPlace.authRedeem() invokes ISwivel.authRedeem(), assuming that the Swivel contract implements a function named authRedeem. In reality the Swivel contract only provides authRedeemZcToken(). Because the called selector does not exist in the deployed Swivel contract, the external call reverts every time it is executed. The root cause is a faulty interface declaration: the ISwivel interface lists a method that the implementation never defines, and the contracts that import the interface do not inherit from it (i.e., they do not declare "is ISwivel"). This mismatch can be exploited simply by triggering the redemption flow that relies on the broken call path – for example, a user or a third‑party contract attempting to redeem a ZcToken through MarketPlace.authRedeem() will cause the transaction to fail, leaving the user’s redemption request unfulfilled. The impact is that, for the specific redemption path that bubbles through MarketPlace → Swivel → ZcToken, funds become effectively locked: the ZcToken.withdraw() call never succeeds, the underlying assets are not transferred, and the user sees no change in balance, contrary to the expectation that a redemption request returns the underlying token. The condition under which this occurs is any invocation of MarketPlace.authRedeem() – typically when a user or the protocol initiates a redemption via the marketplace interface. All participants that rely on this path – end users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s accounting layer – are affected because the accounting invariant that redeemed tokens are burned and underlying assets are returned is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Swivel codebase when the auditor noticed that the ISwivel interface referenced a non‑existent function and that MarketPlace.authRedeem() failed to compile against the actual Swivel implementation. Because the failure manifests only when the specific authRedeem path is taken, it can be easy to miss in functional testing that mainly exercises the primary redemption flow directly on Swivel.sol. The bug belongs to the class of interface contract mismatch or missing function implementation, often caused by typographical errors or outdated interface specifications. From a user’s perspective, the UI may display a successful redemption request, but the on‑chain transaction reverts, resulting in “no funds received” or “withdrawal stuck”. Users expect their balance to decrease and the underlying asset to be transferred, yet the reality is that the balance remains unchanged and the transaction fails. To remediate, the Swivel contract should either implement the authRedeem() function defined in ISwivel or the interface should be corrected to reference the existing authRedeemZcToken() method, and the MarketPlace contract should be updated to call the correct selector. Additionally, all contracts should explicitly inherit from the appropriate interface (e.g., "contract Swivel is ISwivel") to let the compiler catch such mismatches early. Aligning the interface with the implementation restores the EIP‑5095 compliance path and eliminates the risk of locked funds in the secondary redemption flow.

title: Users Can Transfer Tokens to Blacklisted Addresses Causing Fund Locking
description:
The contract’s transfer() function in BeraBitcoin.sol fails to verify whether the recipient address (to parameter) is blacklisted before executing the transfer. While the function properly checks that the sender (msg.sender) is not blacklisted through the notBlacklisted() modifier, it omits this critical check for the receiving address. This oversight exists despite the contract maintaining a comprehensive blacklisting system intended to restrict token movements for flagged addresses. The vulnerability stems from incomplete validation in the transfer authorization logic, specifically in the inherited ERC20 transfer() function implementation.

This vulnerability can lead to locking of tokens when users transfer tokens to blacklisted addresses. Once tokens are transferred to a blacklisted address, they become effectively frozen since the recipient cannot transfer them out.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete blacklist enforcement in the token contract’s transfer function. The contract maintains a blacklist that is intended to prevent any blacklisted address from participating in token movements, and it correctly checks that the sender (msg.sender) is not blacklisted via a notBlacklisted modifier. However, the function does not perform the same validation on the recipient address (the to parameter). As a result, a user can call transfer and send tokens to an address that has been flagged as blacklisted. When tokens arrive at a blacklisted address, the contract’s other functions that enforce the blacklist (such as subsequent transfers) will reject any outgoing operation from that address, effectively freezing the received tokens. This creates a situation where the sender’s balance decreases as expected, but the recipient is unable to move the funds, leading to locked or “disappearing” tokens from the user’s perspective. The issue occurs whenever the transfer function is invoked with a blacklisted destination, which can happen unintentionally (e.g., a user mistypes an address that is already blacklisted) or maliciously (an attacker encourages victims to send tokens to a blacklisted wallet). The affected parties include any token holder who initiates a transfer, the protocol because the total circulating supply may be reduced by locked tokens, and the overall trustworthiness of the token’s accounting logic. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that compared the blacklist checks applied to the sender against those applied to the recipient and found the latter missing. It can be hard to notice because the UI may not warn users about the blacklist status of the destination address, and the contract still appears to enforce blacklisting for outgoing transfers, giving a false sense of safety. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control or validation checks, often described as a blacklist bypass. To remediate, the transfer implementation should include a require that the recipient address is not blacklisted, mirroring the existing sender check, and revert the transaction if either party is blacklisted, thereby preventing tokens from being sent into a frozen state.

title: Stack-based call stack may overflow the stack
description: EVM execution requires a call stack to store all information of sub-calls as they happen. Etherlink uses a custom implementation of its call/create routines. Within it, the sub-call execution directly happens on the (native) stack. This will likely lead to (native) stack overflow, because the depth limit of EVM sub-calls is 1024.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's call handling logic implements sub‑call execution directly on the EVM's native call stack instead of using a heap‑based structure. Because the EVM enforces a hard limit of 1024 nested calls, each additional sub‑call pushes a new frame onto the native stack. When the custom implementation does not check this limit, a sequence of legitimate calls that reaches or exceeds the depth limit will cause the native stack to overflow. This overflow manifests as an unexpected revert or out‑of‑gas error, and can prevent the contract from completing its logic, leading to funds being locked or refunds not being sent. The issue occurs whenever a user or another contract triggers a function that performs many internal calls, for example batch operations, recursive token transfers, or complex multi‑step workflows. The affected parties are any users of the protocol that rely on these functions, as well as the protocol itself because the failure breaks its accounting and may halt progress. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the call and create routines, where the auditor noticed that the implementation directly used the native stack without any guard. It is hard to notice because the overflow only appears after a deep call chain, which may not be exercised in normal testing, and the error surface looks like a generic out‑of‑gas or stack‑too‑deep exception. The root cause is the misuse of the EVM's call stack as a storage mechanism instead of a proper heap‑based call stack. To remediate, the contract should replace the native‑stack based call handling with the heap‑based call stack provided by SputnikVM or another well‑tested library, and add explicit checks that prevent exceeding the 1024‑call depth. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of call‑stack overflow or stack‑exhaustion vulnerabilities, where the program assumes unlimited recursion depth. In practice a user may see a transaction that appears to succeed but then receives no tokens, or a UI that shows a pending operation that never completes, because the contract silently reverted due to the overflow. The violation is of the protocol's business logic that expects every sub‑call to complete and update balances; the overflow breaks that guarantee and can cause loss of funds or denial‑of‑service.

title: Blacklisted Addresses Can Still Mint and Redeem Tokens Despite Restrictions
description:
The contract fails to implement blacklist checks in critical token operations including custodianMint(), excessStakeMint(), and redeem() functions. While the contract maintains a blacklist mapping and implements checks for standard transfers via the notBlacklisted() modifier, these critical administrative functions lack similar protections. The custodianMint() and excessStakeMint() functions allow privileged roles to mint tokens to any address without verifying if the recipient is blacklisted. Similarly, the redeem function permits any caller to burn tokens without checking if their address is blacklisted.

This vulnerability severely compromises the effectiveness of the blacklisting mechanism. Malicious actors who have been blacklisted can still receive newly minted tokens through the custodian or excess stake minting functions, allowing them to maintain token holdings despite sanctions. Additionally, blacklisted users can continue redeeming tokens, potentially enabling them to extract value from the system even after being flagged.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing blacklist enforcement in privileged token operations. Although the contract stores a blacklist mapping and applies a notBlacklisted modifier to normal transfer functions, the administrative mint functions (custodianMint and excessStakeMint) and the redeem function do not verify whether the target or caller address is listed as blacklisted. The root cause is an oversight in access‑control logic: the developer assumed that the existing modifier would protect all token movements, but failed to include the same check in functions that bypass the standard transfer path. An attacker whose address appears on the blacklist can still receive newly minted tokens because a privileged role can call custodianMint or excessStakeMint with the blacklisted address as the recipient, and the contract will not reject the call. Likewise, the redeem function allows any caller, including a blacklisted address, to burn tokens and receive the underlying asset without a blacklist guard. Exploitation is straightforward: once an address is flagged, the adversary can either wait for a mint event or actively invoke redeem, thereby retaining or extracting value that the protocol intended to freeze. The impact is that the blacklist mechanism, which is meant to sanction malicious participants, is effectively bypassed, allowing sanctioned accounts to continue holding and moving value. This compromises compliance, may lead to regulatory exposure, and erodes trust for honest users who expect blacklisted funds to be frozen. The condition for the bug to manifest is simply that the blacklist contains the address and a mint or redeem transaction is executed; no special state or timing is required. The affected parties are the blacklisted users themselves (who can still receive and withdraw tokens), the protocol (which loses the ability to enforce sanctions), and any other participants who rely on the integrity of the blacklist. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the presence of blacklist checks across the contract’s public functions and identified the omission in the admin paths. It can be hard to notice because the contract does appear to enforce blacklist rules on regular transfers, giving a false sense of completeness, and test suites often focus on transfer scenarios rather than privileged minting or redemption. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit require statement or reuse the notBlacklisted modifier inside custodianMint, excessStakeMint, and redeem so that any address involved in receiving or burning tokens is first verified against the blacklist. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incomplete access‑control enforcement” or “missing authorization check” where a security policy is applied inconsistently across code paths, leading to unintended fund flow and violation of business rules that assume blacklisted accounts are frozen.

title: Missing Minimum Output Validation in HODL Token Purchase
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing minimum‑output validation in the internal token‑purchase routine of the HODL contract. The contract determines the amount of HODL tokens a buyer should receive by calling getBuyAmount based on the current price, which is derived from the contract’s beraBTC balance. After each purchase the safetyCheck function updates the price and enforces a monotonic increase (lastPrice <= newPrice). Because the _buyHodl function does not accept a minOut argument or otherwise verify that the calculated receiveHodl meets a user‑defined lower bound, a buyer cannot guarantee that the number of tokens they receive will not fall below an acceptable threshold. This omission becomes exploitable when the contract’s state changes between the moment a transaction is submitted and when it is executed, for example when a donate() call precedes a buy() call in the same block. The donate transaction raises the beraBTC balance, causing safetyCheck to increase the price before the subsequent buy is processed, which reduces the amount of HODL tokens minted for the same BTC input. From the user’s perspective the transaction succeeds, but the UI shows fewer tokens than expected or even a zero balance increase, leading to the impression that funds have vanished or that the purchase was overpriced. The impact is a loss of economic value for buyers, potential over‑payment in a rising market, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s pricing guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s price‑adjustment logic runs after a state‑changing operation that affects the underlying reserve, i.e., any time a donate or similar function modifies the beraBTC balance before a buy. It affects all participants who rely on the public buy() function, especially those who cannot set a maximum price or a minimum token amount. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of price updates and token minting. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the contract simply mints fewer tokens, which can be mistaken for normal market variation. To remediate the problem the contract should introduce a minOut parameter (or equivalent slippage protection) that is compared against receiveHodl before minting, and revert the transaction if the output falls below the user’s expectation. Additionally, exposing a max‑price or slippage‑limit field would allow buyers to protect themselves against price spikes caused by intervening state changes. This class of bug is commonly known as a missing minimum‑output or slippage‑protection vulnerability in automated market‑making or token‑sale contracts.

title: Inconsistency between hardcoded gas limit and actual gas left in smart contract execution
description: During the execution of a smart contract function a() in contract A, an inconsistency was observed between the hardcoded maximum gas limit defined in the code and the actual remaining gas reported by the gasleft() function. In the code snippet provided, the MAXIMUM_GAS_LIMIT constant is set to 30_000_000, which represents the maximum amount of gas allowed for a transaction. This value is derived from the block gas limit defined in EIP-1559 as 2 times the gas target. However, when executing the a() function using the cast call command with a specified gas limit of 999999999, the gasleft() function returned a value of 999978817, which is significantly higher than the hardcoded MAXIMUM_GAS_LIMIT. This inconsistency raises concerns about the accuracy and reliability of the gas limit enforcement in the smart contract execution environment. If the actual gas left exceeds the defined maximum gas limit, it suggests that the gas limit is not being properly enforced or that there may be issues with the gas accounting mechanism.
bug_full: During execution of function a in contract A, the contract returns the value of gasleft(). The source code also defines a constant MAXIMUM_GAS_LIMIT set to 30_000_000, which the author intended to represent the maximum gas that a transaction may consume. When the function is called with a transaction gas limit of 999,999,999, the value reported by gasleft() is 999,978,817, which is far above the hard‑coded constant. This mismatch reveals a logical inconsistency: the contract assumes that the constant accurately reflects the amount of gas that can be used, but the EVM does not enforce this value. The root cause is the use of a static, hard‑coded gas limit that is derived from an outdated interpretation of the block gas limit (EIP‑1559 target × 2) and the fact that gasleft reports the remaining gas after intrinsic costs, not a capped value. An attacker or any caller can therefore supply a transaction with a gas limit that exceeds the constant, and the contract’s internal checks that compare gasleft() to MAXIMUM_GAS_LIMIT will either be bypassed or produce incorrect results. The impact is that the contract may allow operations that were intended to be blocked by the gas cap, leading to higher than expected gas consumption, unexpected fees for users, or potential denial‑of‑service if expensive logic is executed without proper limits. The condition occurs whenever the contract relies on the hard‑coded constant for gas accounting, which can happen on any network where the actual block gas limit differs from the assumed 30 million value. Users experience symptoms such as transactions succeeding when they should have been rejected, or paying more gas than anticipated, creating a discrepancy between expected and real costs. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by executing the function with a very high gas limit and observing the returned gasleft value. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit events or revert, and the large numeric values can be mistaken for normal operation. The proper remediation is to remove the static MAXIMUM_GAS_LIMIT and instead rely on the transaction gas limit enforced by the node, or dynamically query the block’s gas limit (block.gaslimit) and compare it to gasleft() if a custom cap is required. By aligning the contract’s logic with the actual gas accounting mechanism, the inconsistency disappears and the intended gas‑usage constraints are correctly enforced.

title: Inconsistant stack in execute_fa_withdrawal
description:
In the new logic of execute_fa_withdrawal, on L207, a new execution stack is pushed by handler.begin_inter_transaction. It then enters inner_execute_withdrawal with Rust's ? syntax. Later lines we also calls inner_execute_proxy also with Rust's ? syntax.
If an error happens in either function, the function returns directly without any further clean up code, meaning that the handler.end_inter_transaction will not be called. In this case, the "transaction stack" will become inconsistent. At this stage, SputnikVM can guarantee nothing, not even correctly returning an ExitFatal error.
We rate this as medium severity, as we believe that there's a particularly high risks that some forms of the bug may be exploitable during a system upgrade. From the author's experience with other blockchains of similar stacks, it's particularly likely, even in production environment, that some small amount of storage values may become unparsable due to incorrect migrations. At that moment, read_u256_le_default in the TicketTable will trigger this bug.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistent transaction stack in the execute_fa_withdrawal routine. When the function begins, it pushes a new execution context onto a handler-managed stack via begin_inter_transaction. The core logic then calls inner_execute_withdrawal and inner_execute_proxy using Rust's ? operator, which automatically propagates any error to the caller. If either inner call fails, the ? operator causes an early return, bypassing the explicit cleanup step that would normally invoke handler.end_inter_transaction. As a result, the previously pushed execution context remains on the stack, leaving the transaction stack in an inconsistent state. This inconsistency can corrupt the internal bookkeeping of the virtual machine, causing undefined behavior such as unparsable storage values, unexpected ExitFatal errors, or failure to correctly process subsequent transactions. The issue manifests only when an error occurs inside the inner functions, which may happen during a system upgrade or migration when new code paths are exercised. Users are affected because transactions that appear to succeed may later result in missing balances, zeroed accounts, or failed reads from storage tables like TicketTable, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the error‑handling flow and identified that the automatic ? propagation prevented the required cleanup code from executing. It is difficult to notice because normal operation does not trigger the error path, and the missing cleanup does not produce an immediate visible symptom; the failure only becomes apparent under rare error conditions. To remediate the problem, error handling should be performed manually so that handler.end_inter_transaction is guaranteed to run, or the stack entry and exit logic should be encapsulated in a dedicated function that uses the ? operator only within its own scope, ensuring the stack is always correctly unwound.

title: Insufficient Authentication Controls on Critical Services
description:
Critical services should use FIDO2 hardware security key authentication, instead of relying on less secure methods.
FIDO2 hardware keys provide stronger security against phishing and account takeover compared to SMS or authenticator app 2FA.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of insufficient authentication controls on a set of critical services such as cloud infrastructure, CI/CD platforms, domain registrars, and communication tools. The contracts or configuration rely on traditional password‑based login, SMS one‑time passwords, or mobile authenticator apps, which are vulnerable to phishing, SIM‑swap, and credential‑stuffing attacks. Because these mechanisms do not provide cryptographic proof of possession of a hardware token, an attacker who obtains a user’s credentials or intercepts a one‑time code can successfully authenticate and gain privileged access. Exploitation typically follows a social‑engineering flow: the attacker sends a convincing phishing message, the victim enters their password and the SMS or app code, the attacker captures the credentials, and then logs into the target service using the same weak factor. Once inside, the attacker can modify DNS records, deploy malicious infrastructure on AWS, read or delete messages on Slack, alter incident‑response settings in PagerDuty, or impersonate the organization on Twitter and Discord. The impact ranges from loss of control over critical infrastructure, potential data exfiltration, service disruption, to reputational damage and financial loss. The condition occurs whenever an account with administrative privileges is protected only by these weaker factors, which is common for single‑admin or high‑value accounts. All users who rely on the affected services are at risk, especially administrators and operators who assume that two‑factor authentication provides sufficient protection. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the authentication methods used by each service against best‑practice recommendations for high‑value assets. It can be hard to notice because the login experience appears normal, no error messages are shown, and the compromised activity may blend with legitimate actions, making the breach subtle until a critical change is observed. The recommended remediation is to disable password, SMS, and authenticator‑app based second factors for the listed services and enforce FIDO2 passkey authentication using hardware security keys. For accounts with a single login, a secondary backup key should be provisioned and stored separately to avoid lock‑out. This change aligns the authentication model with a cryptographic proof‑of‑possession scheme, eliminating the phishing vector and reducing the risk of account takeover. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “weak multi‑factor authentication” or “insufficient authentication” flaws, where the chosen factors do not provide strong assurance of user identity, leading to potential unauthorized control over critical resources.

title: Missing Security Vulnerability Reporting Process
description:
The project lacks a clear process for security researchers to report vulnerabilities and has no defined bug bounty program to incentivize responsible disclosure.
Not having a published security contact information or bug bounty program, makes it difficult for security researchers to responsibly disclose vulnerabilities. Sometimes, a quick way to contact the development team can make a big difference in defending against hacks.
The lack of a public bounty program may incentivize black hats to conduct a hack instead of reporting the issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an organizational security weakness: the project does not provide a documented, public process for security researchers to disclose vulnerabilities and it lacks a defined bug bounty program. The root cause is the absence of any published security contact information, such as a security.txt file, and the failure to establish incentives for responsible disclosure. Because there is no clear channel, a researcher who discovers a flaw cannot easily reach the development team, and the project does not outline response time expectations or reward structures. An attacker can exploit this gap by choosing to keep the vulnerability private and launch an exploit rather than reporting it, since there is no guaranteed compensation or safe avenue for disclosure. The impact may include increased likelihood of successful attacks, loss of user funds, erosion of trust, and reputational damage to the protocol. The condition occurs whenever a security issue is discovered, whether through internal testing, external audit, or independent research, and persists until a formal reporting mechanism is put in place. All stakeholders are affected: users may see their assets disappear, developers may face unanticipated attacks, and the broader ecosystem loses confidence in the protocol’s security posture. The issue was identified during a third‑party audit that noted the missing security.txt file and the lack of any bounty scope. It can be hard to notice because the contract code itself may be sound; the problem lies in the surrounding governance and operational processes, which are not visible in the codebase. To remediate, the project should publish a security.txt file at the well‑known location containing encrypted contact details, add security contact information to the website and documentation, define a bug bounty scope and reward schedule, consider using a platform such as Immunefi to manage submissions, and establish service level agreements for initial response. This transforms the missing reporting process into a structured vulnerability disclosure program, aligning with industry best practices and reducing the incentive for malicious exploitation. From a user’s point of view the failure mode appears as unexpected loss of funds or lack of communication after an incident – users expect a quick response and possibly a refund, but instead receive silence or zero compensation because the team had no formal way to receive and act on the report. The bug belongs to the class of governance or operational security gaps, where the absence of a responsible disclosure pathway creates a higher risk of exploitation and undermines the accounting assumptions that all security issues will be reported and mitigated promptly.

title: Unconstrained Vercel Spending Limits
description: Spend monitoring and control mechanisms are not configured in Vercel, creating risk of unexpected charges or potential abuse. Currently, spending is monitored manually on a monthly basis without automated alerts or controls. Automatic controls would provide better oversight and early warning of unusual activity that could indicate security issues or resource abuse.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absence of automated spend monitoring and control mechanisms for Vercel deployments. Because the account configuration relies solely on manual, monthly review of invoices, there is no real‑time enforcement of a maximum spend threshold, no automatic pausing of services when usage exceeds a predefined limit, and no alerting system to warn of abnormal consumption. The root cause is that Vercel’s built‑in spend management features are left disabled, leaving the billing logic unconstrained. An attacker who gains access to the Vercel project, or even a legitimate user who unintentionally triggers a runaway build or deployment, can cause the service to continue consuming resources indefinitely. This can be exploited by repeatedly invoking build pipelines, spawning large numbers of serverless functions, or uploading heavy assets, thereby inflating the compute and bandwidth usage without any automatic stop. The impact is financial: the organization may receive an unexpectedly large invoice, potentially exhausting its budget or causing cash‑flow issues. The condition occurs whenever the account is active and no spend limits are set, which is typical for many teams that rely on manual oversight. All stakeholders who depend on the Vercel‑hosted application—developers, product owners, finance teams, and end‑users—are affected because the cost overrun can lead to service interruption if funds run out, or to a loss of trust in the platform’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined operational controls and identified that the free spend management options were not enabled. Because the problem manifests only as a billing surprise rather than a functional failure, it can be hard to notice until the monthly statement arrives, especially when usage patterns appear normal on dashboards. To remediate, the account should enable Vercel’s spend management features: define a maximum spend threshold that exceeds typical usage, configure automatic pausing of deployments when the threshold is reached, and set up tiered alert notifications (e.g., at 25%, 50%, and 75% of the limit) with webhook integration to monitoring channels such as Slack. This aligns the system with the principle of defensive budgeting, ensuring that unexpected resource consumption is detected and halted before it translates into financial loss. The bug belongs to the class of “unconstrained resource consumption” or “missing operational guardrails” vulnerabilities, where the lack of runtime limits permits unchecked usage that violates business assumptions about cost predictability and budget enforcement.
