From a user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden, unexplained charge or a zero balance after a period of normal activity, contrary to the expectation that the service will stop or warn before exhausting funds.

title: Single Bot Design in Liquidation System
description: The protocol's liquidation process currently relies on a single bot implementation. When this bot failed due to an interface change, the team successfully fell back to manual liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a single point of failure in the protocol’s liquidation workflow. The system relies on one automated bot to detect under‑collateralised positions and execute liquidations. Because the bot is the only executor, any disruption – such as a contract interface change, a deployment error, or an external denial‑of‑service – prevents the liquidation logic from running. When the bot failed after an interface upgrade, the team had to intervene manually, using a run‑book and flash‑loan assistance to clear the positions. The root cause is the lack of redundancy, health monitoring, and automated fallback mechanisms. An attacker could deliberately trigger a contract upgrade, block the bot’s transaction, or flood the network to stall the bot, causing liquidations to be delayed or omitted. This delay allows borrowers to remain under‑collateralised longer than intended, potentially leading to bad debt, loss of funds for lenders, and erosion of confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the bot stops working; under normal operation the problem is invisible, making it hard to notice until a failure occurs. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation architecture and noted the absence of multiple bots, monitoring alerts, and test coverage for interface changes. The bug belongs to the class of “single‑point‑of‑automation failure” and violates the business assumption that liquidations are always executed promptly to preserve solvency. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see their position remain open despite being flagged, or a lender may observe a sudden drop in collateral value without any liquidation event, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The recommended remediation is to document the manual process, add health checks and alerts, deploy redundant bot instances, and maintain comprehensive test suites that cover interface modifications, thereby ensuring that liquidation can continue automatically even if one executor fails.

title: node.js Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
description:
Current dependency management practices expose the protocol to potential supply chain attacks.
The front-end repository shows frequent commits of yarn.lock with caret (^) version ranges, indicating dependencies are being updated automatically when developers install packages locally. This creates risk of malicious code being introduced through compromised dependencies.
Supply chain attacks have become increasingly common as attackers sometimes find it easier to take over some obscure dependency rather than hack protocols directly.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a supply‑chain risk caused by lax dependency management in the front‑end repository. The project’s package.json uses caret (^) version ranges, which tell the package manager to automatically accept any newer semver‑compatible release when developers run install commands or when CI builds pull dependencies. This practice means that the exact code of third‑party libraries is not fixed, allowing a malicious actor who compromises an upstream package to inject harmful code without any explicit change in the repository. The root cause is the absence of strict version pinning and insufficient vetting of each dependency’s provenance, activity, and security history. An attacker can exploit this by publishing a compromised version of a widely used but low‑profile library, then relying on the caret range to have the vulnerable project automatically fetch the malicious release during the next install or CI run. Once the malicious code is executed in the front‑end, it may exfiltrate private keys, tamper with transaction data, or display falsified information, leading to loss of user funds, incorrect protocol state, or erosion of trust. The impact manifests as users seeing unexpected behavior such as empty balances, failed refunds, or UI elements that do not reflect the true on‑chain state, effectively making funds disappear or transactions be rejected. The issue occurs whenever a developer or CI pipeline installs dependencies without a locked lockfile, especially after a new version of a dependency is published. All participants who interact with the front‑end – end users, protocol operators, and auditors – are affected because the compromised code runs in the client’s browser and can manipulate user interactions with the blockchain. The problem was discovered during a security audit that inspected the repository’s dependency declarations and noticed the presence of caret ranges and frequent yarn.lock commits, indicating that versions were being updated automatically. The vulnerability is hard to notice because the source code of the front‑end does not change, yet the behavior of imported libraries can shift silently, and typical testing may not cover the malicious payload. To remediate, the project should lock every dependency to an exact version, remove caret and tilde ranges, optionally pin critical libraries to specific commit hashes, enforce strict review of any lockfile changes, and implement continuous monitoring through tools such as Dependabot, security mailing lists, and periodic manual audits. By treating dependency versions as immutable assets and establishing a disciplined review process, the protocol can prevent supply‑chain attacks that would otherwise allow malicious code to infiltrate the front‑end and compromise user assets.

title: Multisig Security Enhancements
description:
Current multisig setup uses 3/5 threshold (60%) with all internal signers. While functional, this configuration could be strengthened with a goal of 70% for medium and high risk operations.
For further discussion, see this article, The Right Way To Multisig.
bug_full: The issue identified is an insufficient multisignature (multisig) security configuration for medium and high risk operations. The current setup uses a three‑of‑five (3/5) threshold, meaning that any three internal signers can approve a transaction, which represents only 60 % of the total signer set. This threshold is lower than the recommended 70 % quorum for high‑value or critical actions, creating a governance weakness. The root cause is the combination of a relatively low quorum and the fact that all signers are internal to the organization, providing no external oversight or diversification of trust. Because only three colluding or compromised signers are needed, an attacker who gains control of a subset of internal keys – through phishing, insider threat, or key leakage – can authorize malicious transfers without detection. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker submits a transaction, obtains signatures from the required three internal accounts (which may be coerced or compromised), and the multisig contract executes the operation. The impact can be the unauthorized movement of funds, loss of protocol assets, and erosion of user confidence, as users may see their balances reduced or transactions they did not approve being processed. This condition manifests whenever a medium‑ or high‑risk operation is performed under the existing 3/5 rule, especially for large transfers where a higher security margin is expected. All protocol participants, including token holders, developers, and the governing team, are affected because the security guarantees of the protocol are weakened. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit that examined governance parameters and compared them against industry best‑practice thresholds for multisig wallets. It can be hard to notice because the multisig contract functions correctly – transactions are executed as intended – and the low threshold does not raise immediate errors; the risk only becomes apparent when considering threat models involving insider collusion. To remediate, the quorum should be increased to at least four out of six signers (≈66.7 %) by adding a trusted external signer, and eventually to a five‑of‑seven configuration to approach the 70 % target. Formal key‑management procedures, periodic review of signer composition, documented replacement processes, and emergency revocation criteria should be instituted. Additional safeguards such as out‑of‑band transaction hash verification, mandatory cool‑down periods for large transfers, and predefined transaction templates can further reduce the chance of unauthorized execution. In essence, the vulnerability belongs to the class of authorization‑policy misconfigurations where the required approval threshold is too low, allowing a minority of compromised parties to bypass intended security controls, leading to potential fund loss and breach of trust.

title: Comprehensive Application Security Review of Front-End System
description:
Thala’s front-end system has not undergone a comprehensive application security (AppSec) review.
This system handles user interactions, displays sensitive data, and integrates with backend services, making it a prime target for attacks such as cross-site scripting (XSS), client-side logic manipulation, or phishing exploits.
Without a thorough assessment, latent vulnerabilities could persist, increasing the risk of exploitation that could compromise user trust, funds, or system integrity.
The absence of a prior AppSec review is notable given:
• Dependency management risks identified in M-05, which are only one aspect of front-end security.
• Lack of Content Security Policy (CSP) noted in L-06, suggesting broader front-end security gaps may exist.
• SQL injection vulnerabilities in an API route (L-05), highlighting potential weaknesses in systems interacting with the front-end.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a systematic application security (AppSec) review for the front‑end component of the system. Because no formal assessment of the user‑facing code, dependencies, and security headers has been performed, the front‑end may contain latent weaknesses such as cross‑site scripting (XSS), cross‑site request forgery (CSRF), client‑side logic manipulation, and phishing vectors. The root cause is a process gap: the development lifecycle omitted a dedicated security review step, leaving missing controls like a Content Security Policy (CSP), secure HTTP headers, and thorough dependency vetting. An attacker could exploit this gap by injecting malicious scripts into pages that render user‑controlled data, bypassing client‑side validation to alter business logic, or leveraging outdated third‑party libraries that contain known vulnerabilities. Exploitation would typically occur when a victim interacts with the UI—submitting forms, viewing dynamic content, or loading external resources—allowing the attacker’s payload to execute in the victim’s browser. The impact includes disclosure of sensitive information, unauthorized actions on behalf of users, potential loss of funds through deceptive UI flows, and erosion of user trust in the protocol. The issue manifests under normal operating conditions whenever the front‑end processes external input or displays data without proper sanitisation, making it difficult to notice because the symptoms may appear as benign UI glitches, unexpected pop‑ups, or missing balances rather than explicit code failures. The vulnerability was identified during a broader security audit that highlighted the lack of any prior AppSec assessment, and it is hard to detect without dedicated testing because the front‑end may appear functional while silently exposing attack surfaces. To remediate, the project should conduct a comprehensive AppSec review that includes secure coding practices, rigorous input validation and output encoding, implementation of a strict CSP and other security headers, verification that client‑side business logic cannot be tampered with, systematic dependency analysis and updates, and targeted penetration testing to validate that the front‑end resists common web‑based attacks. This approach aligns the front‑end with standard security baselines and mitigates the risk of funds disappearing, refunds failing, or accounting logic being subverted due to client‑side vulnerabilities.

title: Call of FA bridge proxy contract not respecting the depth limit
description: After inner_execute_proxy, handler.execute_call takes over and starts to execute the proxy contract. It notes the call stack depth but does not enforce it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the proxy contract used by the FA bridge does not enforce the configured call‑stack depth limit when executing delegated calls. After the internal function inner_execute_proxy finishes, the handler.execute_call routine takes control and forwards the call to the target proxy. Although the code records the current depth, it never checks whether the depth exceeds the maximum allowed value. Consequently an attacker can craft a sequence of calls that repeatedly invoke the proxy, causing the call stack to grow arbitrarily. This can be exploited by submitting a transaction that triggers the proxy to call itself (or another contract that calls back) many times, eventually exhausting the gas limit or hitting the protocol‑defined maximum call depth, which results in a transaction failure or a state where the bridge logic is bypassed. The impact includes denial‑of‑service for legitimate bridge users, potential loss of funds if the bridge relies on the depth limit to prevent re‑entrancy or to enforce accounting invariants, and a breach of trust in the protocol because the bridge may appear to process transfers while actually failing silently. The condition occurs whenever a user or a contract invokes the bridge proxy through the standard entry point; there is no special flag that triggers the bug, only the presence of a nested call chain. All participants that rely on the bridge – token holders, relayers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bridge may stop processing or may process an incomplete transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the bridge’s proxy implementation, where the auditor noticed that the depth counter was incremented but never compared against a limit. Because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error when the limit is exceeded, the problem can be subtle and may only surface under heavy load or crafted attack patterns, making it hard to detect in normal testing. The proper fix is to introduce a dedicated transaction‑data structure that carries the current depth and to add a check in handler.execute_call that reverts when the depth would exceed the predefined maximum. This enforces the intended recursion guard and restores the bridge’s safety guarantees. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of missing bounds check on recursion depth or unlimited call‑stack growth vulnerabilities, which violate the business rule that a bridge operation must complete within a bounded number of internal calls. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a bridge transfer may appear to be submitted but later results in no tokens being received, or the UI may show a pending transaction that never finalises. Users expect the bridge to either succeed or fail with a clear error, but instead the transaction may silently run out of gas or be dropped, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds.

title: Users can not remove some amount of collateral from contract because of wrong implementation of "canRemoveCollateral()"
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect implementation of the canRemoveCollateral() check in the SmartVault contract. The function is intended to decide whether a user may withdraw a specified amount of collateral while keeping the vault sufficiently collateralised. Instead of evaluating the health of the vault after the proposed removal, the code compares the current maximum mintable euro amount (maxMintable) with the euro value of the collateral the user wants to remove (eurValueToRemove) and also checks that the already minted euro amount is less than or equal to maxMintable minus eurValueToRemove. Because maxMintable is calculated from the *current* collateral, removing a large portion of collateral can make eurValueToRemove larger than maxMintable even though the remaining collateral would still support the minted euros. This causes the first condition to fail and the second condition to underflow, resulting in a revert with an "err-under-coll" error. The bug manifests when a user who has minted any euros (minted > 0) attempts to withdraw a substantial but not total amount of collateral; the transaction is rejected despite the vault remaining healthy after the removal. From the user’s perspective the UI reports that collateral cannot be removed, the expected balance does not change, and no funds are returned, leading to confusion and the impression that the protocol is stealing or locking funds. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit test that simulated a user depositing 10 WBTC, minting 1 000 EUR, and then trying to withdraw 9.5 WBTC; the test logged that the euro value of the collateral to be removed exceeded the current max mintable amount, causing the failure. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not expose the internal health‑factor calculation and the error message does not explain that the check is performed on pre‑removal values. The impact is medium: affected users cannot retrieve part of their collateral and must either close the vault or wait for a fix, potentially leading to loss of liquidity. The root cause is the misuse of maxMintable for a pre‑withdrawal check and an incorrect second condition that can underflow. The recommended fix is to reverse the order of operations: first transfer the requested collateral back to the user, then verify that the vault remains sufficiently collateralised (e.g., by checking that minted <= maxMintable after removal). A simplified canRemoveCollateral() should only ensure that when minted is non‑zero, the current minted amount does not exceed the maximum mintable amount based on the *remaining* collateral, eliminating the faulty comparison and underflow condition.

title: Missing deadline check allow pending transactions to be maliciously executed
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing deadline parameter in the swap function of the SmartVaultV3 contract. The function builds a Uniswap ExactInputSingle call and sets the deadline field to block.timestamp. Because block.timestamp is the timestamp of the block that eventually includes the transaction, the deadline condition is always satisfied regardless of when the transaction is finally mined. Consequently a malicious miner or a relayer can postpone the execution of a pending swap, or reorder it, causing the swap to be performed at a later time when market prices have moved. This allows the vault owner to receive fewer output tokens than expected, or even to trigger a liquidation if the price shift is severe. The issue appears only when the swap is called by the contract owner; the contract does not expose any way for the caller to provide a custom deadline, so the business logic that expects a user‑defined deadline to protect against price volatility is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function signature with typical Uniswap usage patterns. It is subtle because the code compiles and the deadline field is populated, giving the impression that a deadline check exists, yet the check is ineffective. To remediate, the contract should accept a deadline argument supplied by the caller, validate that it is greater than the current block timestamp, and optionally enforce an upper bound on how far in the future the deadline may be set. This change restores the intended protection against delayed execution and price manipulation, ensuring that users receive the expected amount of tokens and that the vault cannot be unintentionally liquidated due to a stale swap.

title: Fees are hardcoded to 3000 in ExactInputSingleParams
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded swap fee of 3000 (representing 0.3%) in the ExactInputSingleParams structure that is used by the SmartVaultV3.swap function when routing trades through Uniswap V3. The root cause is that the fee tier is fixed in the source code instead of being derived from the pool with the best liquidity or being supplied as an argument, which forces the router to select only the 0.3% pool even when lower‑fee pools such as the 0.05% tier exist. An attacker can exploit this limitation by creating a malicious 0.3% pool with insufficient liquidity or by manipulating the pool’s price, causing the swap to either execute with excessive slippage or to fail entirely. The impact is that users of the vault receive less output token than expected, experience higher transaction costs, or see swaps revert, effectively reducing the value of their holdings. This condition occurs each time the contract owner calls the swap function, because the fee value is embedded in the transaction parameters at compile time. The affected parties include token holders, the vault owner, and any protocol relying on the SmartVault for asset management. The issue was identified during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who noted that the constant fee contradicts Uniswap V3’s design of multiple fee tiers and that the symptom of sub‑optimal pricing can be subtle, appearing only as slightly higher slippage rather than an outright failure. The problem is hard to notice because the fee field is a numeric literal that does not raise warnings, and the contract still performs swaps, albeit inefficiently. To remediate the bug, the fee tier should be made configurable – for example by adding a fee parameter to the swap function or by querying the manager for the optimal pool fee – allowing the router to select the pool with the lowest fee and highest liquidity, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with expected market conditions and preventing potential exploitation.

title: No incentive to liquidate small positions could result in protocol going underwater
description:
The protocol allows to create vaults and provide collateral for minting EUROs with no lower limit. As such, multiple low value vaults can exist. However, there is no incentive to liquidate low value vaults because of gas cost.

Liquidators liquidate users for the profit they can make. If there is no profit to be made than there will be no one to call the liquidate function. For example a vault could exist with a very low collateral value. This user is undercollateralized and must be liquidated in order to ensure that the protocol remains overcollateralized. If a liquidator wishes to liquidate this user, they will first need to stake some TST/EUROs which involves gas cost. Because the value of the collateral is so low, after gas costs, liquidators will not make a profit liquidating this user. In the end these low value vaults will never get liquidated, leaving the protocol with bad debt and can even cause the protocol to be undercollateralized with enough small value accounts being underwater.
The protocol can go underwater, complete loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic incentive gap in the liquidation mechanism of a collateralized stable‑coin vault system. Because the protocol permits the creation of vaults with arbitrarily small amounts of collateral, it is possible to open under‑collateralized positions whose total collateral value is lower than the gas cost required to execute a liquidation. The root cause is the absence of a minimum collateral threshold or any other compensation that would make liquidating such tiny vaults profitable. An attacker (or any user) can therefore open many low‑value vaults, deliberately under‑collateralize them, and rely on the fact that rational liquidators will ignore these positions since the expected profit after paying transaction fees is zero or negative. As a result, the protocol is unable to purge bad debt from these accounts; the accumulated under‑collateralized debt remains on‑chain, gradually eroding the overall collateralisation ratio. When enough of these small, un‑liquidated vaults exist, the system can become under‑collateralised, leading to a situation where the protocol’s liabilities exceed its assets, effectively causing a loss of all user funds. This condition manifests to users as vaults that remain in an insolvent state without being liquidated, unexpected reductions in the protocol’s health metrics, or even a complete halt of minting operations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the economic assumptions of the liquidation flow and identified that the profit‑making model for liquidators does not cover the gas overhead for tiny positions. It is hard to notice because each individual vault appears to be a normal, low‑value account, and the aggregate risk only becomes apparent when many such vaults accumulate. To remediate the problem, the protocol should enforce a minimum collateral value required for minting, introduce a baseline liquidation bounty that covers gas costs for small positions, or redesign the liquidation incentive structure so that every under‑collateralized vault can be profitably liquidated regardless of size. This class of bug falls under the broader category of incentive‑misalignment or economic‑logic flaws that allow bad debt to persist, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that every debt position can be reclaimed through liquidation.

title: Anyone can call the burn function in SmartVaultV3.sol
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized‑access bug in the SmartVaultV3 contract where the public burn() function is only protected by an ifMinted modifier and lacks any owner or role restriction. Because the function is external, any address that already holds minted EUR tokens can invoke burn() on any SmartVault instance, causing the internal minted counter of that vault to be set to zero. The root cause is the missing access control: the contract assumes that only the vault owner will call burn, but the ifMinted check only verifies that the caller has previously minted tokens, not that they are the vault’s owner. When minted becomes zero, the calculation of requiredCollateralValue inside calculateMinimumAmountOut() collapses to zero. Consequently the function returns a minimum amount out of zero for a swap operation. The swap routine then passes this zero value to the Uniswap‑style router as amountOutMinimum, which according to the router documentation removes the price‑protection safeguard. An attacker can therefore trigger a swap where the protocol accepts any output amount, enabling front‑running or sandwich attacks that drain the vault’s collateral. From a user’s perspective the swap appears to succeed but the received token amount may be zero or far below expectations, effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue manifests whenever a malicious user who possesses minted EUR tokens calls burn() on a vault they do not own; it is not tied to a specific transaction size and can be reproduced repeatedly. All participants that rely on the vault – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are at risk of losing value. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by CodeHawks, who noted that the burn function’s visibility and modifier combination did not enforce proper ownership checks. The problem is subtle because the burn function does not directly transfer funds, and the zero‑minimum‑out value may pass unnoticed in normal operation, especially if UI components do not display the expected minimum output. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a strict onlyOwner (or equivalent role‑based) modifier on burn(), ensure that minted cannot be arbitrarily reset by external callers, and add validation that calculateMinimumAmountOut never returns zero when a swap is intended. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a vault’s collateral must always back the minted tokens and that swaps must enforce a minimum acceptable output to protect against price manipulation.

title: Divergence in the pricing method for collateral within the `calculateMinimumAmountOut()` may result in vaults transitioning into an uncollateralized state after executing swaps.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a pricing divergence bug in the calculation of the minimum amount out for a swap in SmartVaultV3. The function calculates collateralValueMinusSwapValue by subtracting the current token price (tokenToEur) from the euro‑denominated collateral, while the euroCollateral helper itself uses an averaged price (tokenToEurAvg) for the existing collateral. This mismatch means that when the market price of the input token moves sharply, the subtraction uses a stale or too‑recent price, producing an inaccurate collateral balance after the swap. If the recent price is lower than the four‑hour average, the contract underestimates the remaining collateral and may set a minAmountOut that is too small; the swap can then deliver less value than required to keep the vault above the collateralisation ratio, instantly putting the vault in an uncollateralised state. The issue occurs during on‑chain swap execution, especially when a vault owner swaps one collateral asset for another in a volatile market. Users, vault owners, and the protocol are affected because the vault may become liquidatable or incur penalties despite the owner’s intention to protect it. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the price‑oracle calls used in the calculation and noticed the inconsistent use of tokenToEur versus tokenToEurAvg. Because the mis‑calculation only manifests under rapid price swings, it can be hard to notice in normal testing where prices are stable; the contract will still appear to respect the collateral rate most of the time. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a swap the displayed collateral balance may drop unexpectedly, the vault may be flagged as under‑collateralised, or a transaction that should succeed reverts with an “insufficient collateral” error, even though the user swapped a sufficient amount of assets. The bug belongs to the class of “price oracle inconsistency” or “average‑price vs spot‑price mismatch” bugs that break accounting assumptions. To remediate the issue the calculation should consistently use the same price source – replacing the call to calculator.tokenToEur with calculator.tokenToEurAvg when computing collateralValueMinusSwapValue – so that the estimated collateral after the swap reflects the same averaging window as the collateral valuation used elsewhere. This alignment restores the intended safety margin and prevents swaps from unintentionally de‑collateralising a vault.

title: Wrong Implementation of `LiquidationPool::empty` excludes holder with pending stakes when decreasing a position, resulting in exclusion from asset distribution
description:
If a holder has withdrawn from a previous consolidated position but still has pending stakes eligible for consolidation, they will not be included in the asset distribution. This is due to their prior exclusion from the LiquidationPool.holder array through LiquidationPool::deletePosition, given that the position will be considered as empty when position.TST == 0 && position.EUROs == 0.

Pending stakes that are consolidated during asset distribution will be excluded from rewards if there is no previous consolidated position due to a prior complete withdrawal, leading to wrong asset distribution when a liquidation occurs
poc:
Bob has a position of (TST = 100, EUROS = 100).
Alice has a position of (TST = 100, EUROS = 100).
Alice increases her position by (TST = 100, EUROS = 100). Consequently, a pending stake in her favor is added to the LiquidationPool.pendingStake array.
Immediately after step 3, Alice does a complete withdrawal of her consolidated position. Given that 24 hours have not passed since step 3, the pending stake created during the previous step is not consolidated. Her current position is considered empty; therefore, she is excluded from holders.
After 24 hours, a vault is liquidated. Now, Alice's pending stake is consolidated, but since she is not included in holders, she is not considered for asset distribution. All assets go to Bob.

Coded POC
bug_full: During liquidation the contract builds a list of holders from the LiquidationPool.holder array. A holder is removed from this array when the internal function empty determines that the holder's position is empty, i.e. both TST and EUROs are zero. The implementation of empty only inspects the stored position and ignores any pending stake that may belong to the same address. Consequently, if a user withdraws their consolidated position before a pending stake is automatically consolidated (for example within the 24‑hour waiting period) the holder is marked as empty and deleted from the holders list. When the pending stake later consolidates during a liquidation event, the holder is no longer present in the distribution loop and receives no share of the liquidated assets. From the user’s point of view the expected refund or reward is missing – the UI shows a zero payout even though the user had a pending stake that should have been credited. The bug originates from a logical flaw in the empty check, which treats a zero balance as sufficient to remove the holder without verifying outstanding pending stakes. It can be exploited by any participant who can trigger a full withdrawal, wait for the pending stake to remain un‑consolidated, and then cause a liquidation after the stake becomes eligible. The impact is an incorrect asset distribution where funds that belong to the excluded holder are effectively transferred to the remaining participants, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and fairness assumptions. The condition only occurs when a holder has a pending stake and the position is considered empty at the moment of withdrawal; it does not affect holders with only active positions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, and it is subtle because the distribution routine still works for all holders that remain in the array, making the missing payout easy to overlook. The proper fix is to extend the empty function so that it scans the pendingStake collection for any entry belonging to the same holder before returning true, thereby preventing premature removal from the holders array. This change restores the intended behavior that every holder with either an active position or a pending stake participates in the liquidation reward calculation.

title: Incorrect calculation of amount of EURO to burn during liquidation
description:
In order to maintain a peg, we must ensure that when a position is liquidated, we liquidate more than or equal to the amount of stablecoin that is borrowed.

Let us say Alice locks up 12000 EURO worth of collateral into her vault and borrows 10000 EURO, with a minimum collateralisation rate of 120%. For simplicity, we assume a single staker owns the entire LP containing 10000 EURO. Now, assume that Alice's collateral value locked falls to 11000 EURO due to rapid price action (but it is still above 100% collateralisation rate).

During liquidation, the amount of EURO to burn is computed in https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-12-the-standard/blob/main/contracts/LiquidationPool.sol#L220

```solidity
uint256 costInEuros = portion * 10 ** (18 - asset.token.dec) * uint256(assetPriceUsd) / uint256(priceEurUsd) * hundredPC / _collateralRate;
```

A high level explanation of this code is:

Asset Value in EURO * 100 / Collateral Rate

So computing the costInEuros we receive

11000 * 100 / 120 = 9166 EURO

Which results in 9166 EURO being burnt which is much lower than the 10000 EURO Alice borrowed. This can cause the EURO to depeg.

The fundamental assumption that is wrong here is that the developers have assumed that liquidation immediately occurs when the asset value falls below 120% collateralisation rate (or in the example above 12000 EURO, which results in the correct EURO to be burnt 12000 * 100 / 120 = 10000 EURO).

EURO depegging.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the amount of EURO stablecoin that must be burned when a vault is liquidated. The contract derives the burn amount from the current euro‑denominated value of the collateral multiplied by a factor of 100 divided by the required collateralisation rate, rather than using the exact amount of EURO that was originally minted (the debt). This assumption works only if liquidation is triggered precisely at the moment the collateral value falls to the minimum ratio, but in practice rapid price movements can cause the collateral value to drop while still remaining above the threshold. When a liquidation is executed under those conditions, the formula under‑estimates the debt, burning fewer EURO than were borrowed. An attacker can exploit this by forcing a price swing that leaves the vault just above the collateralisation limit, then calling the liquidation function; the protocol will burn an insufficient amount of EURO, leaving a residual debt that is not covered by the seized collateral. The impact is that the EURO stablecoin can lose its peg because the system’s accounting no longer guarantees that every borrowed EURO is fully backed after liquidation, potentially leading to de‑pegging, loss of confidence, and under‑collateralisation of the protocol. The bug manifests whenever a liquidation occurs after a rapid price drop but before the collateral ratio falls below the required level, affecting any borrower whose position is liquidated, as well as lenders and token holders who rely on the peg. It was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who noticed that the liquidation calculation used the collateral value instead of the minted amount and that the resulting burn amount could be lower than the outstanding debt. The issue is subtle because the on‑chain computation appears mathematically sound for converting collateral value to a euro amount, so UI dashboards may report a successful liquidation while the debt remains partially unpaid, making the problem hard to spot without deep inspection of the accounting logic. To remediate, the protocol should compute the burn amount directly from the position’s outstanding EURO debt (the amount of tokens minted for that vault) and ensure that the burned amount is at least equal to the debt, possibly adding a safety margin. This class of bug falls under liquidation accounting errors where the settlement amount is derived from an incorrect state variable, leading to under‑payment, loss of collateral coverage, and potential stablecoin de‑pegging. From a user perspective, a borrower may see their vault marked as liquidated but still owe EURO, or notice that the stablecoin price drifts below 1 €, effectively causing funds to disappear or the peg to break, contrary to the expectation that liquidation fully repays the loan.

title: M-4 Insufficient quality of the _collateralERC20 check in BAMM
description:
It is possible to provide the wrong address in the _collateralERC20 parameter's value to the BAMM constructor:  
• value that is different from StabilityPool,  
• value that is not an ERC20 token,  
• address of a token with the wrong decimals value (not 18)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient validation of the _collateralERC20 address supplied to the BAMM contract constructor. Because the constructor does not verify that the provided address corresponds to the expected StabilityPool token, is a genuine ERC20 contract, or uses the required 18‑decimal precision, an attacker or a careless deployer can pass an arbitrary address. The root cause is the lack of runtime checks on the collateral token’s interface and properties, allowing a mismatched or malicious token to be registered as collateral. An exploit can be carried out by deploying a BAMM instance with a deliberately wrong token address – for example, a non‑ERC20 contract, a token with fewer or more than 18 decimals, or a completely unrelated ERC20. Once the contract is initialized with this incorrect token, all subsequent accounting that assumes 18‑decimal precision will produce erroneous collateral valuations. Users who deposit what they believe to be the correct collateral may see their balances reported incorrectly, experience failed withdrawals, or find that their deposited funds appear to disappear because the contract’s internal math under‑ or over‑estimates the token amount. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees: under‑collateralization can lead to liquidation of positions, loss of user funds, and erosion of trust in the system. The condition under which the bug manifests is at deployment time, when the constructor argument is set; any party with permission to deploy the contract can trigger it. The affected parties include the protocol itself, any users who interact with the BAMM contract, and the StabilityPool that relies on correct collateral accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors noted the absence of explicit checks for the collateral address and token decimals. It can be hard to notice because the contract will compile and run without reverting, and the wrong token may still implement the ERC20 interface superficially, masking the problem until financial calculations produce unexpected results. To remediate, the constructor should either remove the _collateralERC20 parameter and fetch the token address directly from the trusted StabilityPool contract, or add explicit validation steps: confirm that the address implements the ERC20 interface, call the decimals() function and require a return value of 18, and optionally compare the address against a whitelist of approved collateral tokens. This ensures that only the intended token can be used as collateral, preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and preventing funds from disappearing due to mismatched token specifications.

title: M-1 An incorrect collateral value with decimals <> 18
description: The PriceFeed.sol#L124 in PriceFeed.sol is not suitable for the ERC20 tokens with decimals() not equal to 18. If the decimals() value is less than 18, the collateral value will be underestimated, which can result in a trove creation failure due to the BorrowerOperations.sol#L588 requirement. On the other hand, in the rare case where decimals() is greater than 18, the collateral value will be overestimated, which may allow minting of THUSD with an unreasonably low collateral value.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded assumption that every ERC‑20 token used as collateral has 18 decimal places. In the price‑feed contract the collateral value is calculated by multiplying the token amount by its price without first normalising the amount to the token’s actual decimals. When a token reports fewer than 18 decimals, the calculation divides the amount by a larger factor than intended, causing the protocol to underestimate the true value of the supplied collateral. As a result, a borrower attempting to open a trove may see the transaction fail because the contract believes the collateral is insufficient, even though the user supplied enough assets. Conversely, if a token reports more than 18 decimals, the same formula inflates the perceived value, allowing a borrower to mint THUSD with far less real collateral than required. This over‑valuation can leave the system under‑collateralised and expose it to liquidation attacks that drain funds. The issue manifests only when a token with a non‑standard decimal count is used; the rest of the protocol behaves as expected. Users experience symptoms such as “my trove creation failed despite providing enough tokens” or “I was able to mint THUSD with a tiny amount of collateral and later the system liquidated my position”. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the price‑feed logic against the ERC‑20 interface and identified the missing decimals handling. It is subtle because the UI typically shows token balances in human‑readable format, masking the scaling error, and because most popular tokens do use 18 decimals, the bug does not appear in common test scenarios. To remediate, the price‑feed should query the token’s decimals() function and apply the appropriate scaling factor before performing valuation, or the contract should explicitly assert that only 18‑decimal tokens are permitted, rejecting any token with a different precision. This change restores correct accounting, ensures that collateral requirements match economic reality, and prevents both inadvertent trove creation failures and the possibility of minting stablecoins with insufficient backing.

title: M-2 A cross-check of contract parameters
description: If contracts ActivePool, CollSurplusPool, DefaultPool, StabilityPool and BorrowerOperations are deployed with the misconfigured _collateralAddress parameter, they will be unable to withdraw the deposited collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑contract parameter mismatch where the _collateralAddress value stored in ActivePool, CollSurplusPool, DefaultPool, StabilityPool and BorrowerOperations is not forced to be identical. Because each contract uses its own copy of the address to locate the collateral token, a deployment in which any of these contracts receives a different address causes the withdrawal functions to reference an unexpected token contract. When a user initiates a collateral withdrawal, the call reaches a pool that looks for the token at the mismatched address, fails to locate the deposited balance and therefore does not transfer any assets. The root cause is the absence of an explicit equality check or invariant enforcement for the _collateralAddress parameter during deployment or upgrade. Exploitation consists of deploying the system with inconsistent addresses, either accidentally or maliciously, which results in a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users see a successful transaction receipt but receive no tokens, their on‑chain balance remains unchanged and the UI may report a zero or unchanged collateral amount. The impact is that deposited collateral becomes effectively locked, preventing borrowers from reclaiming their assets and potentially undermining confidence in the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the contracts are instantiated with different _collateralAddress values, which can happen due to manual deployment errors or a compromised deployment script. All participants who have deposited collateral—borrowers, lenders and any role that can trigger a withdrawal—are affected. The issue was discovered by the MixBytes audit team through a systematic review of contract constructors and the lack of cross‑contract validation logic. It is hard to notice because the withdrawal transaction does not revert; it simply results in no token transfer, leading to silent failures that may be interpreted as a UI glitch. The recommended remediation is to enforce that the _collateralAddress supplied to each system contract is equal, for example by adding a require statement that compares the value against a canonical source or by initializing all contracts from a single factory that passes the same address. By establishing this invariant, the contracts will correctly reference the same collateral token and withdrawals will succeed as intended, restoring the expected business logic that deposited collateral can be reclaimed as expected.

title: M-3 Privileges granted to accounts as system contracts cannot be revoked
description: Accounts can be marked as THUSDToken.sol#L58-L61. Such accounts have privileged access to some functionality: burn and arbitrary transfer between accounts. However, once granted, this privilege can't be revoked. If one of these accounts become compromised, there is no way to revoke its privileges.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract allows certain addresses to be marked as privileged system contracts, granting themthe ability to invoke burn functions and perform arbitrary token transfers on behalf of any user. The marking is performed by a function in THUSDToken.sol (lines 58‑61) and once an address is added to the privileged list there is no corresponding function to remove it. The root cause is that the access‑control data structure does not provide a revocation path; the code only sets a boolean flag to true and never checks for a false state or provides an admin function to clear it. An attacker who gains control of a privileged address – for example through a compromised private key, a malicious upgrade, or a phishing attack – can continue to call the privileged functions indefinitely. By invoking the burn function the attacker can destroy tokens belonging to other users, and by using the arbitrary transfer function they can move tokens from any account to an address they control. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected loss of balance, tokens disappearing from their wallet, or transfers that they never initiated. The impact is loss of funds for any user whose tokens are burned or transferred, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, because the system assumes that only trusted contracts can perform these operations. The condition under which the bug manifests is any time a privileged address is added; there is no time‑bound or emergency stop that can be triggered to disable its rights. The affected parties are token holders, borrowers, and any participant that relies on the stability of the THUSD token, as well as the protocol operators who cannot mitigate the damage once the address is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token contract where the auditors noted the absence of a revocation function for privileged accounts. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the privileged accounts are expected to be trusted system contracts, and the contract does not emit events when a privileged address is added, nor does it provide any on‑chain evidence that the privilege can be removed. The bug belongs to the class of “non‑revocable privileged access” or “immutable role assignment” vulnerabilities, which violate the principle of least privilege and the ability to respond to key compromise. To remediate, the contract should introduce admin‑controlled functions that can pause or permanently revoke the privileged status of any address, emit events on grant and revocation, and optionally enforce a multi‑signature or timelock mechanism before removal. This would allow the protocol to disable a compromised system contract, prevent further unauthorized burns or transfers, and restore confidence that token accounting cannot be subverted.

title: Removing assets in the `TokenManager` leads to major issues
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol manages the list of accepted collateral tokens. The TokenManager contract allows the owner to add and remove token entries, and several core functions – liquidation, asset removal and reward claiming – iterate over the current accepted token array to decide which assets to process. When a token is removed, the array entry is simply replaced by the last element and the length is reduced, but the liquidation routine still assumes that every token that ever backed a vault will be present in the list. Consequently, if a vault holds collateral in a token that has been removed, the liquidate function will set the minted amount to zero, emit a liquidation event and transfer only the tokens that remain in the accepted list. The removed token stays locked inside the vault because the loop never reaches it. The canRemoveCollateral check later permits the borrower to call removeAsset because it returns true whenever minted equals zero, ignoring the fact that collateral still exists. This lets the attacker walk away with both the borrowed EURO stablecoins and the original collateral, effectively stealing an arbitrary amount of value. A similar problem appears in the LiquidationPool reward claim function, which also loops over the accepted token list; if a token with pending rewards is removed, those rewards become permanently frozen, depriving stakers of funds they have already paid for. The issue is triggered only when a token that is actively used as collateral or has pending rewards is removed from the accepted list, either before or after a liquidation event. Users see a vault reported as liquidated while their collateral balance remains unchanged, or they notice that reward claims return zero despite having accrued amounts. The bug is subtle because the removal operation itself does not revert or emit an error, and the liquidation appears to succeed from a contract‑level perspective, making the loss easy to miss in UI dashboards. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable array for security‑critical accounting without guarding against removal of tokens that are still referenced elsewhere, combined with a collateral‑removal check that only looks at the minted counter. To remediate, the protocol should forbid removal of any token that currently backs a vault or has outstanding rewards, or redesign the liquidation and claim logic to reference a stable identifier (for example a mapping of token address to a boolean flag) rather than iterating over a mutable list. Adding a modifier that blocks asset‑removal functions after liquidation, or implementing per‑token liquidation and reward‑claim pathways that do not depend on the global accepted‑token array, would close the attack surface and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Attacker can force reduce `minAmountOut` from vault swaps, making they vulnerable to being sandwiched.
description:
The attacker has the ability to burn EURO tokens on other users' vaults, thereby decreasing the required collateral for those users. This manipulation can be exploited, particularly during swaps, where the calculation of minAmountOut is based on the required collateral. Consequently, attackers can take advantage of this EURO burn to diminish the target user's swap minAmountOut, enabling them to execute a sandwich attack and "steal" part of the collateral used in the swap.

Consider SmartVaultV3.burn() function, it allows any holder of EURO tokens to burn EURO tokens, reducing that vault minted value, even if they are not the owner of such vault. This reduction in minted also decreases the required collateral for the vault. The required collateral plays a crucial role in various vault methods, particularly the SmartVaultV3.swap() method. The calculated minAmountOut in the swap method is influenced by the difference between the vault collateral (after deducting tokens spent on the swap) and the required collateral to maintain the vault as overcollateralized.

If an attacker frontruns the vault's swap transaction and burns EURO tokens in that vault, the resulting minAmountOut will be smaller than intended by the vault owner. The attacker can exploit this situation to frontrun and sandwich the vault swap (SmartVaultV3.swap()) in a way that wouldn't be possible otherwise.

Consider both examples below. For simplification fees will be ignored, the price EURO and both accepted tokens (A and B) are $1 and the vault collateral ratio is set to 120%.

Normal vault swap:  
Initial vault state (minted: 100, collateral: 120 token A ($120)).  
Vault owner calls SmartVaultV3.swap(A, B, 10) to swap 10 token A for token B.

As expected from the code logic, in order for the vault to maintain collaterization, the minAmountOut calculated on-chain will be 10 token B.

Now consider the alternate scenario where attacker exploit the burn function.  
Initial vault state (minted: 100, collateral: 120 token A ($120)).  
Vault owner calls SmartVaultV3.swap(A, B, 10) to swap 10 token A for token B.  
Attacker sees that swap transaction on the mempool and frontruns it by burning 10 EURO on that vault.

Intermediate vault state: minted: 90, collateral: 120 token A ($120).

Therefore, when the SmartVaultV3.swap(A, B, 10) transaction is executed, the on-chain calculated minAmountOut will be zero. This occurs because the required collateral ($108) is smaller than the collateral minus the swap amount ($110), opening up the possibility for this swap to be sandwiched.

It is important to note that due to the overcollateralization of the vaults (for instance, the collateralization ratio is set to 120% in the test suite), the collateral ratio will always be greater than 1. As a result, for every EURO burned, the reduction in minAmountOut is more substantial. This means that the reduction in the minAmountOut value exceeds the value spent to burn EURO, creating a potential for the sandwich attack to be profitable. Therefore an attacker can gain more value from the sandwich than the EURO tokens spent to decrease the target vault's collateral. However, the exact profit will depend on the Uniswap pool balances and how much the attacker can unbalance the pool during the sandwich.

By burning tokens on target users' vault, the attacker can reduce the minAmountOut from swaps, allowing them to sandwich and steal part of the collateral involved in the swap.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted token‑burn function that lets any holder of the EURO token destroy EURO tokens that are accounted to a vault belonging to another user. The burn operation reduces the vault’s recorded minted amount, which in turn lowers the amount of collateral the vault is required to hold in order to stay over‑collateralised. The swap routine of the vault calculates the minimum amount of output tokens (minAmountOut) based on the difference between the current collateral after the swap and the required collateral. Because the required collateral is derived from the minted amount, an attacker who front‑runs a pending swap can call the burn function on the target vault, shrink the required collateral, and consequently force the on‑chain minAmountOut to drop dramatically – in the extreme case to zero. When the victim’s swap transaction is then executed, the protocol believes the swap satisfies the collateral constraint and allows it to proceed, but the attacker can place a preceding trade that moves the price in their favour and a following trade that extracts part of the collateral that would otherwise have been protected. The impact is that the vault owner receives far fewer output tokens than expected, possibly none, and the attacker can profit by stealing a portion of the collateral that was meant to back the swap. This situation occurs whenever a vault is over‑collateralised, a swap is submitted, and an adversary can observe the transaction in the mempool and execute a burn on the same vault before the swap is mined. The affected parties are the vault owners, any users relying on the swap functionality, and the protocol itself because the accounting guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SmartVaultV3 contract when the burn function was found to lack any access control and its effect on the required‑collateral calculation was traced to the swap logic. The bug is subtle because the swap does not revert when minAmountOut becomes zero; the transaction appears successful, yet the user’s balance may be unchanged or reduced, which can be missed without careful inspection of the output amounts. To remediate the problem the burn operation should be restricted to the vault owner or to a privileged role, and the swap’s minAmountOut calculation should be based on the pre‑burn state or include a safeguard that prevents the value from falling below a safe threshold. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of “unauthorised state mutation leading to incorrect economic invariants”, where an external actor can manipulate accounting variables that downstream functions rely on for security checks, resulting in loss of funds and broken business logic.

title: M-1 The swap function doesn't check insufficient liquidity
description: It's common practice to check that the protocol has enough amount of tokens to make a swap. The minCollateralReturn parameter has to be used only for preventing sandwich attacks (price manipulation) but in BAMM smart contract this parameter is also used as a liquidity check. Let's suppose that an attacker is the biggest depositor of the BAMM contract. The attacker can always front-run swap function calls and keep the given minCollateralReturn collateral amount on the contract. Calling the BAMM.sol#L250 function with minCollateralReturn is a way to lose money even if the price has not been changed. As a result, users will always get minCollateralReturn tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swap routine of the BAMM contract where the function does not verify that the pool holds enough tokens to satisfy the requested exchange. Instead of performing an explicit liquidity check, the implementation re‑uses the minCollateralReturn argument, which is intended only as a safeguard against price manipulation, as a proxy for available balance. This misuse creates a logical flaw: an attacker who is also the largest token depositor can front‑run legitimate swap calls, deliberately keep the amount specified by minCollateralReturn locked in the contract, and then invoke the swap. Because the contract never confirms that the remaining pool balance can cover the swap, it proceeds and returns exactly the minCollateralReturn amount to the caller, regardless of the actual token reserves. The exploit can be carried out whenever a swap transaction is pending and an attacker can insert a transaction with higher gas price before it. The impact is that users receive a fixed amount of collateral that may be larger than the pool can actually provide, effectively draining the pool’s liquidity and causing users to lose value. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful swap but the received token amount is unexpectedly low or zero, or the user may notice that their balance does not change despite the transaction confirming. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended purpose of minCollateralReturn with its actual usage in the code. It is subtle because the function still returns a value and does not revert, so the failure does not raise an exception and can be missed by simple testing. The bug belongs to the class of “missing liquidity validation” or “incorrect use of input parameters for state checks”, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a pool cannot dispense more assets than it holds. To remediate, the contract should include a dedicated check that the pool’s token balance is greater than or equal to the amount to be transferred before executing the swap, and the minCollateralReturn parameter should be limited to its original purpose of protecting against price slippage, not as a liquidity guard.

title: M-2 The Trade function doesn't use minCollateralAmount
description: BAMM.sol#L268 can be used by mistake by someone and according to the M-1 it leads to losing money because the minCollateralAmount parameter is always zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the trade function of the BAMM contract, where the required minimum collateral amount (minCollateralAmount) is never validated because the parameter is hard‑coded to zero. As a result, the function can be invoked without any guarantee that the caller supplies sufficient collateral for the trade. This omission stems from a missing access control check and an absent assertion that minCollateralAmount > 0 before executing the trade logic. An attacker or any external account can call the trade function directly, bypassing the intended Kyber protocol gateway, and trigger a trade with zero or insufficient collateral. When this occurs, the contract may execute a swap that moves assets out of the pool while the caller provides no backing, effectively draining liquidity and causing users to lose funds. The issue manifests only when the trade function is called outside the trusted Kyber contracts; normal operation through Kyber does not expose the flaw because the protocol enforces its own checks. Users affected include liquidity providers and any participant expecting their deposited collateral to be protected; they may see their balances shrink unexpectedly or receive no tokens after a trade. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that compared the trade implementation against the documented minimum collateral requirement (M‑1). It is subtle because the function signature appears standard and the missing check does not raise compiler warnings, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should restrict calls to the authorized Kyber protocol contracts and explicitly require that the supplied collateral meets or exceeds the defined minCollateralAmount before proceeding with the trade, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unauthorized fund extraction.

title: M-3 The Receive function revert
description: The BAMM contract supports only one collateral token. If it is set to ERC20 tokens the BAMM.sol#L289 function has to revert all ETH transfers to the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s receive function, which is intended to reject plain Ether transfers when the protocol is configured to use an ERC‑20 token as its sole collateral. Because the receive function does not contain a conditional revert, any Ether sent to the contract – whether through a direct transfer, a self‑destruct, or a fallback call – is accepted even though the business logic assumes only ERC‑20 tokens will be held. This mismatch creates a situation where Ether can be deposited unintentionally and then become invisible to the contract’s accounting mechanisms, as the contract’s internal bookkeeping only tracks ERC‑20 balances. An attacker or an unwitting user can exploit the flaw by sending a small amount of Ether to the contract address; the transaction succeeds, but the Ether is not credited to any user balance and cannot be withdrawn through the existing functions. The impact is that funds may become permanently locked, the protocol’s invariant that collateral equals the declared ERC‑20 balance is broken, and users may experience symptoms such as “my transaction succeeded but my balance shows zero” or “the contract shows no Ether even though I sent some”. The issue manifests only when the collateral token is set to an ERC‑20 address; if the collateral were native Ether, the receive function would be appropriate. All parties that interact with the contract – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the hidden Ether distorts the overall asset pool. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the receive function and noted the absence of a revert condition for the ERC‑20 collateral mode. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit events on Ether receipt, the UI typically displays only ERC‑20 balances, and the receive function is silent, giving no immediate feedback. To remediate the issue, the contract should include an explicit check that reverts any incoming Ether when the collateral is an ERC‑20 token, for example by requiring msg.value == 0 or by disabling the receive/fallback functions entirely, thereby aligning the contract’s external behavior with its internal accounting assumptions.

title: Wrong yield accumulation in claimYieldAndEnter
description: The claimYieldAndEnter function does not accrue yield to the Gate contract itself (this) in case xPYT was speciﬁed. The idea is to accrue yield for the mint recipient ﬁrst before increasing/reducing their balance to not interfere with the yield rewards computation. However, in case xPYT is used, tokens are minted to the Gate before its yield is accrued. Currently, the transfer from this to xPYT through the xPYT.deposit call accrues yield for this after the tokens have been minted to it (userPYTBalance * (updatedYieldPerToken - actualUserYieldPerToken) / PRECISION) and its balance increased. This leads to it receiving a larger yield amount than it should have.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the claimYieldAndEnter function, which is responsible for crediting accrued yield to a user before adjusting their token balance. The function is intended to first accrue yield for the eventual recipient of newly minted tokens and only then modify the balance, ensuring that the yield calculation uses the correct pre‑mint state. However, when the optional wrapped token (xPYT) is supplied, the implementation mints the new PYT tokens to the Gate contract itself before invoking the xPYT.deposit wrapper. The yield accrual routine is then executed after the mint, using the updated balance of the Gate contract (userPYTBalance * (updatedYieldPerToken - actualUserYieldPerToken) / PRECISION). Because the balance has already been increased by the mint, the contract records a larger yield amount than it should have. The root cause is the misplaced order of operations: yield is accrued after token minting instead of before, and the accrual target address is incorrectly set to the Gate contract rather than the final recipient when xPYT is involved. An attacker or a careless user could trigger claimYieldAndEnter with a non‑zero xPYT address, causing the protocol to credit excess yield to the Gate contract. This over‑allocation distorts the accounting of the vault, potentially leading to loss of funds for other participants, inflated yield reports, and a breach of the economic assumptions that each token holder receives yield proportional to their true stake. The issue manifests only when claimYieldAndEnter is called with xPYT specified; normal calls without xPYT behave correctly. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of yield accrual and token minting. The bug is subtle because the contract still emits a successful transaction and the extra yield may appear as a harmless increase, making it hard to detect without detailed balance tracing. To remediate, the code should accrue yield to the address that will ultimately receive the minted tokens before any mint occurs, and the conditional logic must correctly handle the case where xPYT is present, as illustrated in the recommended patch. In essence, the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting order” or “yield accrual timing” bugs, where financial state updates are performed in the wrong sequence, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and leading to unexpected fund distribution.

title: TickMath might revert in solidity version 0.8
description: UniswapV3’s TickMath library was changed to allow compilations for solidity version 0.8. However, adjustments to account for the implicit overﬂow behavior that the contract relies upon were not performed. The UniswapV3xPYT.sol is compiled with version 0.8 and indirectly uses this library through the OracleLibrary. In the worst case, it could be that the library always reverts (instead of overﬂowing as in previous versions), leading to a broken xPYT contract. The same pragma solidity >=0.5.0; instead of pragma solidity >=0.5.0 <0.8.0; adjustments have been made for the OracleLibrary and PoolAddress contracts. However, their code does not rely on implicit overﬂow behavior.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the TickMath library used by Uniswap V3 relies on the implicit overflow semantics of Solidity versions prior to 0.8. In those versions arithmetic overflow wraps around, allowing the library to compute tick‑to‑sqrtPrice conversions using unchecked math. When the library was upgraded to compile with Solidity ^0.8.0, the code was not modified to place the arithmetic inside unchecked blocks. Solidity 0.8 introduces automatic overflow checks that cause a revert whenever an intermediate result exceeds the type’s range. As a result, functions in TickMath that previously overflowed and returned a wrapped value now revert. The OracleLibrary and the xPYT contract import TickMath indirectly; when they call TickMath functions with inputs that trigger an overflow, the call reverts, causing the whole transaction to fail. This can happen during normal price‑range calculations, especially at the extreme ends of the tick space, and therefore may break price oracle queries, liquidity provision, or token redemption in the xPYT contract. Users attempting to read a price or withdraw funds may see the transaction revert with no obvious error, leading to a perception that the contract is frozen or that funds are missing. The impact is a loss of functionality rather than direct theft, but it can effectively lock user assets because essential operations cannot be completed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the pragma version of TickMath with its implementation and noticed the missing unchecked blocks. It is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the revert only occurs for specific edge‑case inputs, making it easy to miss in standard testing. The proper fix is to adopt the official TickMath implementation for Solidity 0.8, which wraps all arithmetic in unchecked blocks, or to maintain two separate versions of the library: one for <0.8 that relies on implicit overflow and one for >=0.8 that uses explicit unchecked. By doing so the library regains its original behavior and the dependent contracts resume normal operation.

title: Rounding issues when exiting a vault through shares
description:
When exiting a vault through Gate.exitToVaultShares the user speciﬁes a vaultSharesAmount. The amount of PYT&NYT to burn is determined by a burnAmount = _vaultSharesAmountToUnderlyingAmount(vaultSharesAmount) call. All implementations of this function in derived YearnGate and ERC4626 contract’s round down the burnAmount. This means one needs to burn fewer amounts than the value of the received vault shares. This attack can be proﬁtable and lead to all vault shares being stolen If the gas costs of this attack are low. This can be the case with vault & underlying tokens with a low number of decimals, highly valuable shares, or cheap gas costs. Consider the following scenario:
• Imagine the following vault assets: totalAssets = 1.9M, supply = 1M. Therefore, 1 share is theoretically worth 1.9 underlying.
• Call enterWithUnderlying(underlyingAmount = 1900) to mint 1900 PYT/NYT (and the gate receives 1900 * supply / totalAssets = 1000 vault shares).
• Call exitToVaultShares(vaultSharesAmount = 1), then burnAmount = shares.mulDivDown(totalAssets(), supply) = 1 * totalAssets / supply = 1. This burns 1 "underlying" (actually PYT/NYT but they are 1-to-1), but receive 1 vault share (worth 1.9 underlying). Repeat this for up to the minted 1900 PYT/NYT.
• Can redeem the 1900 vault shares for 3610 underlying directly at the vault, making a proﬁt of 3610 - 1900 = 1710 underlying.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the function that converts a requested number of vault shares back to the amount of underlying tokens to be burned when a user calls exitToVaultShares. The contract uses a floor division (shares * totalAssets / supply) which always rounds down, so the burnAmount is slightly smaller than the true value of the shares being redeemed. Because the vault shares are worth more than the burned underlying amount, a user can repeatedly request a single share, burn only one unit of underlying, and receive a share that is worth 1.9 underlying in the example. By repeating this operation up to the amount of underlying initially deposited, the attacker can extract more underlying tokens than they supplied, effectively stealing value from the vault. The issue appears when the vault and its underlying token have low decimal precision or when the share price is not an integer, and the gas cost of the loop is low enough to make the attack profitable. It affects any participant who can call exitToVaultShares, the vault protocol itself, and ultimately the funds of honest users. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic used in the share‑to‑underlying conversion and noticed the use of a down‑rounding helper. The problem is subtle because the contract still respects the mathematical relationship between total assets and total shares; the discrepancy is only a few fractional units that may be invisible in normal usage and only becomes apparent when the attacker repeatedly exploits the rounding bias. The correct mitigation is to use an upward‑rounding conversion (round‑up) or to enforce that the burned amount is at least the exact value of the shares being redeemed, preventing the creation of excess shares. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic precision errors, specifically floor‑division rounding bugs in financial smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that they are burning a small amount of tokens but receiving a full share, leading to unexpected profit; a normal user would expect the amount burned to match the value of the share they receive, not to be lower. The attack flow is: (1) deposit underlying tokens to receive proportional vault shares, (2) call exitToVaultShares with a small share amount, (3) the contract calculates burnAmount with floor rounding, burning fewer underlying tokens than the share’s value, (4) the attacker keeps the share, (5) repeat until all deposited shares are exchanged for more underlying than originally supplied, (6) finally redeem the accumulated shares for the underlying asset, realizing a net gain. This violates the accounting assumption that each share represents an exact claim on the underlying pool, breaking the invariant that total assets equal total shares multiplied by the share price.

title: Multiple centralization vulnerabilities can break the protocol
description: Multiple methods in TopiaLpStaking are centralization vulnerabilities and some can be used to break the protocol for users: setRewardsToken can be used to update the rewardsToken address to a random one, making all reward claims revert, leading to stuck funds. setUniswapPair can be used to update the uniswapPair address to a random one, making all stakes/unstakes revert, leading to stuck funds. addLockupInterval can be used to add strange lockup intervals with huge multipliers. The setRewards method has multiple problems in itself: can be called multiple times, pushing the reward period away with every call. the _start value can be too further away in the future. the _end value can already have passed. the duration between _start and _end might be too large (for example 70 years). the contract balance of reward tokens is not validated - this can mean users won't be guaranteed to be able to claim their rewards.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract TopiaLpStaking contains several admin‑only functions that allow the privileged account to change core protocol parameters after deployment.
