The functions setRewardsToken, setUniswapPair, addLockupInterval and setRewards modify the address of the token used for rewards, the address of the Uniswap pair used for staking, the lock‑up schedule and the timing of the reward distribution respectively. Because these variables are mutable and there is no validation of the new values, an attacker who can call the admin functions – either the contract owner or a compromised key – can replace the rewards token with an arbitrary contract, replace the Uniswap pair with a non‑existent or malicious address, or insert lock‑up intervals with extreme multipliers. When the rewards token address is changed, every subsequent call to claimRewards reverts, causing users’ pending rewards to become inaccessible and effectively locking the funds in the contract. Changing the Uniswap pair address makes the stake and unstake functions revert, preventing users from depositing or withdrawing LP tokens and also locking their principal. Adding lock‑up intervals with huge multipliers can distort the reward calculation, potentially granting excessive rewards or, conversely, making the reward amount zero. The setRewards function can be invoked repeatedly; each call overwrites the start and end timestamps without checking that the start is in the future, that the end has not already passed, or that the duration is reasonable. An attacker could push the start far into the future or set an end date many decades away, effectively pausing reward distribution indefinitely. Moreover, the contract does not verify that the balance of the rewards token held by the contract is sufficient to cover the promised rewards, so even if the timing is correct users may receive less than expected or nothing at all. These issues manifest when the privileged functions are exercised, which may happen during normal upgrades, governance actions, or if the owner’s key is compromised. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or reverted reward claims, inability to stake or unstake, and balances that appear to be frozen with no way to retrieve them. The vulnerabilities belong to the class of centralization‑induced protocol‑break bugs where mutable critical parameters and missing sanity checks allow an admin to sabotage the economic flow. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s state‑changing functions. The bugs are subtle because the functions are intentionally permissioned and therefore may not be exercised frequently, making the lack of validation easy to overlook. To remediate, the rewards token address, the Uniswap pair address and the lock‑up schedule should be declared immutable or only set once through a secure governance process, the setRewards function should be restricted to a single execution with strict validation of start, end and duration, and the contract should enforce that the reward token balance is at least equal to the total outstanding rewards before allowing claims.

title: Rewards can possibly be left stuck in contract
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The contract allows an administrator to set a rewards schedule before any liquidity provider has deposited LP tokens. The setRewards function contains only a comment stating that it should be called after at least one LP position is staked, but there is no on‑chain enforcement of this precondition. When the rewardsPeriod.start timestamp passes while the total staked weight is still zero, the internal accounting for rewards per weight is never updated because the stake() function calls updateRewardsPerWeight before recording the new staker’s checkpoint. As a result, any reward tokens that were transferred to the contract before the first stake become permanently locked in the contract and cannot be claimed by later users. The issue is a logical precondition flaw: the contract assumes that a non‑zero stake exists at the start of the rewards period, but this assumption is not validated. An attacker or even an honest user could trigger the condition simply by waiting until the start time without staking, causing the rewards to be trapped. The impact is that the protocol loses the allocated reward funds, reducing the incentive for participants and potentially harming the economic model. The problem manifests only when the start timestamp is reached before any stake is recorded; if at least one LP is staked beforehand, the accounting works as intended. All users who later stake after the start will see zero accrued rewards because the per‑weight reward factor was never advanced, leading to a user‑facing symptom of “my rewards are always zero” or “the contract balance never decreases despite rewards being funded”. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review where the comment in setRewards was noted but not backed by a require statement. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the funds simply sit idle, and normal staking operations appear to work. The recommended fix is to enforce the precondition on-chain, for example by requiring that the total staked weight is greater than zero before allowing setRewards or by checking that the start timestamp is in the future and that at least one stake has occurred. This moves the assumption from documentation to executable code, preventing the reward‑locking scenario. The bug belongs to the class of “missing state validation” or “precondition enforcement” vulnerabilities that lead to locked assets due to incorrect accounting initialization.

title: Staking won't work correctly with non-standard ERC20 tokens
description: Some tokens do not revert on failure in transfer or transferFrom but instead return false (example is ZRX). While such tokens are technically compliant with the standard it is a common issue to forget to check the return value of the transfer / transferFrom calls. With the current code, if such a call fails but does not revert it can result in users unstaking without claiming their rewards, even though they wanted to. Those rewards will be forever stuck in the contract. Some tokens also implement a fee-on-transfer mechanism, meaning on stake, the actual value transferred to the contract's balance won't be _lpAmount but _lpAmount - fee. This will be problematic on unstake as the last users to call it will get their transactions reverted because of insufficient balance in the contract. Low decimals tokens won't work with setRewards, as the method requires at least 10e18 worth of the reward token as a reward per second, which in the case of just a stable coin would be a crazy daily reward rate, which is close to impossible to fulfill for a prolonged period of time. Using highly valued tokens as ETH or BTC would make it even worse. While those are expected to not be a problem since the README suggests the staking token will be TOPIA/ETH Uniswap V2 LP tokens and the reward token will be TOPIA, currently the contract has a mechanism to update both tokens and it opens up the attack vector to use ones that are not compatible with the staking contract.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the staking contract assumes ERC20 transfer and transferFrom calls will either revert on failure or that the caller will check the boolean return value. Many compliant tokens, such as ZRX, return false instead of reverting, and the contract does not verify the return value. As a result, a stake or unstake operation that silently fails leaves the contract state inconsistent: users can call unstake, the contract believes the tokens were transferred back, but the actual token balance does not change. Consequently the user’s pending reward balance is cleared while the reward tokens remain locked in the contract, effectively making the rewards disappear. In addition, the contract does not account for fee‑on‑transfer tokens, where a portion of the transferred amount is taken as a fee. The contract records the intended amount (_lpAmount) but the actual amount received is lower, so later unstake calls may try to withdraw more tokens than the contract holds, causing the transaction to revert. The setRewards function also requires a minimum reward rate of 10^18 units per second, which is unrealistic for low‑decimal stablecoins or high‑value assets, leading to a situation where the contract cannot sustain the advertised reward rate and rewards become permanently unavailable. The issue manifests whenever the staking token or reward token is replaced with a non‑standard ERC20 that either returns false on failure or implements transfer fees, or when the reward token has a small number of decimals. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no tokens after an unstake, seeing their reward balance reset to zero while the contract still holds the reward tokens, or encountering transaction reverts due to insufficient balance. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted missing SafeERC20 usage and the ability to update token addresses without additional compatibility checks. The bug is subtle because the ERC20 standard permits silent failures, and the contract’s logic does not emit explicit error messages for the failed transfer, making the loss of rewards hard to detect. To remediate, the contract should employ OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library to enforce revert on failure, verify the actual amount received for fee‑on‑transfer tokens by comparing pre‑ and post‑balance, and either restrict token updates to known compatible tokens or add runtime checks that reject tokens that do not conform to the expected behavior. Reducing the minimum reward rate or removing the ability to arbitrarily change the reward and staking tokens would also mitigate the economic impact.

title: VestingMaster: Banning account causes future rewards in RevenueSharingVault to get lost and tokens are stuck
description: It is possible for the owner of VestingMaster to ban accounts from calling IndividualVestingVault.claim(). As a result of this, the shares that belong to the banned account, are never withdrawn and just remain owned by IndividualVestingVault. This means that any revenue earned on these shares is lost forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interaction between the VestingMaster contract and each IndividualVestingVault that holds a beneficiary’s share tokens. When the owner of VestingMaster invokes the banAccount function, the contract marks the beneficiary as prohibited from calling the claim() method on its vault. However, the ban logic only flips a boolean flag and does not trigger any redemption of the underlying vault shares. As a result, the shares remain locked inside the IndividualVestingVault, and the vault’s accounting continues to treat them as owned by the banned address. Because the vault’s claimableTokenAmount function returns zero for a banned account, the beneficiary can no longer withdraw any accrued revenue, and any future revenue generated on those shares is effectively lost. This situation occurs whenever an account is banned while still holding unredeemed shares; the owner can ban an account at any time, and the bug will manifest regardless of the amount of revenue already accrued. Users are affected because they see a zero balance or receive no tokens when attempting to claim, yet the underlying shares still exist and continue to generate revenue that never reaches anyone. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the banAccount implementation and noticed that the vault’s redeem step was missing. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows a “no claimable tokens” message, which is expected for a banned account, masking the fact that the shares are still present and revenue is being wasted. Conceptually, the bug is a failure to clean up state and reclaim assets when access is revoked, a class of asset‑locking or “orphaned balance” bugs. The proper fix is to have the IndividualVestingVault redeem its vault shares for the underlying token (TRNDO) and transfer those tokens back to VestingMaster before marking the account as banned, ensuring that no tokens remain stuck and that future revenue can still be accounted for or redistributed. This change restores the accounting invariant that all shares either belong to an active claimant or are returned to the protocol, preventing silent loss of funds.

title: TWAP price manipulation
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) manipulation risk that arises when a contract queries a Uniswap V3 pool for a price over a time window that is longer than the pool’s stored observation history. The code falls back to the oldest available observation without verifying that the pool’s observation cardinality is sufficient. In pools that have just been created or that have a cardinality of one, the oldest observation can be the price recorded in the same block as the query, because Uniswap V3 only writes an observation when the first swap or liquidity change occurs in a block. An attacker can front‑run the contract’s call, perform a swap that moves the price, and then the contract’s fallback will use this freshly written, potentially manipulated price as the TWAP. The contract therefore executes a token swap or liquidity provision based on a price that does not reflect the intended averaging period, leading to an inaccurate quote, higher slippage, or a loss of value for the user. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a fair exchange rate or a successful liquidity addition – is replaced by a worse rate, a smaller amount of tokens received, or a failed transaction due to unexpected slippage. The issue appears only when the requested TWAP period (secondsAgo) exceeds the oldest observation stored, which commonly occurs in newly deployed pools or pools with low cardinality. It affects any participant that relies on the FarmKeeper or UniversalBuyAndBurn contracts for swapping or providing liquidity, including token holders and the protocol’s revenue mechanisms. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the fallback logic and observed that the code does not enforce a minimum observation count. The bug is subtle because the fallback to the oldest observation is a legitimate safety measure in many contexts, and the low cardinality condition is not obvious from the contract’s interface. To remediate, the contract should reject a quote request when the pool does not contain enough historical data – for example by reverting if oldestObservation is less than the requested secondsAgo – or by enforcing a minimum observation cardinality (e.g., ten) before allowing TWAP‑based operations. This ensures that the TWAP truly reflects an averaged price over the intended interval and prevents price manipulation attacks.

title: Initial mint amount of TRNDO is wrong
description:
```solidity
_mint(msg.sender, 10e8 * 10 ** decimals()); // 100 million
```
In the constructor of TornadoBlastBotToken, 100 million tokens should be minted to the owner: However, the code specifies 10e8, which is one billion and not 100 million.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect initial token minting amount in the constructor of the TornadoBlastBotToken contract. The code uses the literal 10e8 multiplied by the token decimals to mint tokens to the deployer, intending to create a total supply of one hundred million tokens. However, in Solidity the notation 10e8 is interpreted as the floating‑point literal ten times ten to the power of eight, which evaluates to one billion (1,000,000,000) rather than one hundred million (100,000,000). This mis‑calculation originates from a misunderstanding of scientific notation and the fact that Solidity treats the expression as a decimal value before scaling by the decimals factor. Because the constructor runs only once at deployment, the owner receives an excess of nine hundred million tokens. The over‑minted supply can be exploited by the owner or any party that gains control of the owner’s private key to sell or transfer the surplus tokens, diluting the value of legitimate holders, breaking the intended token economics, and potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The impact is a supply inflation that may lead to market manipulation, reduced confidence, and financial loss for users who expected a fixed 100 million token cap. The issue manifests immediately after deployment: users inspecting the total supply or their balances will notice a larger-than‑expected number of tokens, and the share of each holder will be smaller than anticipated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor compared the comment “// 100 million” with the actual minted amount and identified the discrepancy. It can be hard to notice because the literal 10e8 visually resembles a concise representation of 100 million, and typical unit tests may not verify the exact supply value. To remediate, the mint expression should be replaced with an explicit integer literal representing the intended amount, such as 100_000_000, multiplied by the decimals factor, thereby aligning the on‑chain supply with the documented token economics and preventing unintended inflation.

title: DoS attack on initialization is possible
description:
The initializeDistributor method in TokenDistributor has the following check:
```solidity
require(token.balanceOf(address(this)) == _totalTokensToDistribute, "totalTokensToDistribute must match token balance of contract");
```
This gives the expectation that the owner will pre-transfer let's say 10 tokens to the contract and then set the _totalTokensToDistribute argument to 10 when calling initializeDistributor. The problem with this is that if a malicious user front-runs the owner call with a transfer of 1 wei worth of token to the contract, the check and the transaction will revert as the balance will not be equal anymore.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs during the initialization of a token distribution contract. The contract’s initializeDistributor function checks that the contract’s token balance exactly matches the _totalTokensToDistribute argument supplied by the caller. This check assumes that the contract owner will first transfer the intended amount of tokens to the contract and then call initializeDistributor with the same amount. The root cause is the reliance on an external token balance as a source of truth instead of pulling the tokens inside the initialization routine. Because the balance can be altered by any external transfer, a malicious actor can front‑run the owner’s transaction and send a small amount of the same token to the contract just before the owner calls initializeDistributor. The extra token changes the contract’s balance, causing the require statement to fail and the transaction to revert. As a result, the contract never reaches its initialized state, the distribution logic remains locked, and no users can receive the expected tokens. The impact is that the owner’s deployment process is blocked, users see no token distribution, and the protocol’s intended token‑airdrop or reward mechanism is effectively halted. This condition occurs only when the contract relies on a pre‑funded balance and the initialize function is called after that funding; any token transfer to the contract before the call can trigger the failure. The affected parties are the contract owner, any participants awaiting token distribution, and the broader protocol that depends on the distributor’s operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the initialization logic and identified that the balance check could be manipulated by a front‑running transaction. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears to enforce a sensible invariant, yet it does not consider that token balances are mutable by external actors. The recommended mitigation is to eliminate the pre‑funding step and have the initializeDistributor function pull the required amount of tokens from the caller using a safeTransferFrom call, thereby guaranteeing that the contract’s balance matches the intended distribution amount at the moment of initialization. This change moves the source of truth to an internal accounting step and removes the external balance dependency, preventing the front‑run denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Fee and profit payments into RevenueSharingVault can be sandwiched
description:
TRNDO transfer fees and trading profits are sent to RevenueSharingVault where the shares of stakers appreciate. Rewards to stakers are paid out immediately. As a result, if large payouts are made, it can be profitable to make a flash-deposit to earn rewards without having staked TRNDO for any considerable amount of time.
Such behavior acts as a net transfer of rewards from unsophisticated to sophisticated stakers. Consider that the buy and sell fee payments to the Vault can be sandwiched within a single transaction by constructing a transaction consisting of:
1. deposit into the Vault
2. buy or sell TRNDO and incur the buy / sell fee
3. withdraw from the Vault
Payments of trading gains are harder to sandwich because they can only be triggered by an external transaction, and Blast has no mempool that allows front-running. Still, the same considerations apply that users that have staked for a short period of time can earn an outsized portion of rewards.
bug_full: The issue is a reward manipulation flaw in the RevenueSharingVault where fee and profit payments are distributed to stakers immediately after each deposit or withdrawal. Because rewards are paid out instantly, an attacker can perform a flash‑deposit, trigger a fee‑generating trade, and then withdraw within the same transaction, capturing a disproportionate share of the newly minted rewards without holding the underlying token for any meaningful period. The root cause is the lack of a time‑based vesting or delayed distribution mechanism; the vault treats every incoming fee as instantly claimable, and the accounting does not enforce a minimum staking duration before rewards become eligible. An exploit proceeds by (1) depositing a large amount of tokens into the vault, (2) executing a trade that incurs a buy or sell fee which is immediately sent to the vault, (3) withdrawing the original deposit in the same transaction, thereby receiving the full reward allocation that was generated by the fee. The impact is a net transfer of rewards from regular, long‑term stakers to sophisticated actors who can execute flash‑deposit attacks, effectively draining expected earnings from honest participants. This condition occurs whenever the vault processes fee payments and rewards in a single block and allows immediate withdrawal, which is typical for ERC4626‑style vaults without reward lock‑up. All users who stake tokens in the vault are affected, as their share of the reward pool is diluted by the attacker’s temporary stake. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward payout flow and identified that the reward calculation does not consider the time a user’s assets have been locked. The problem is subtle because the vault appears to function correctly for normal users; only when a flash‑deposit is combined with a fee‑generating trade does the reward distribution become abnormal, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate, rewards should be routed through a separate distributor contract that snapshots available rewards and releases them linearly over a configurable period, preventing immediate full claim after a single transaction. This introduces a vesting schedule that aligns reward eligibility with actual staking duration, thereby closing the sandwich attack vector and preserving the intended economic incentives of the protocol.

title: The value of lastExecutionPrice fails to update if pool.poolUpkeep() reverts
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the PoolKeeper contract where the stored execution price for a pool is updated before an external call to the pool’s poolUpkeep function. The contract reads the current price (lastExecutionPrice), writes the new price (latestPrice) into the executionPrice mapping, and then invokes pool.poolUpkeep with both the old and new prices. If poolUpkeep reverts – for example because a modifier such as checkInvariantsBeforeFunction in mintTokens throws – the try/catch block catches the error but the earlier assignment to executionPrice[_pool] remains. As a result the most recent price is recorded even though the price‑difference processing never succeeded, causing the previous price value to be lost. This leads to inaccurate accounting in subsequent upkeeps: the protocol will calculate price differences against a stale or incorrect baseline, potentially minting or burning the wrong amount of leveraged tokens. The impact is that users may receive incorrect token amounts, see balances that do not reflect the true market price, or experience unexpected zero‑value refunds. The bug manifests only when poolUpkeep fails, which may be rare and therefore hard to notice during normal operation; the UI may still show the updated price, giving a false impression that the upkeep succeeded. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the ordering of state changes and external calls. It is difficult to detect because the revert is caught silently and no event is emitted to signal that the price update was rolled back. The proper fix is to move the assignment of executionPrice[_pool] inside the successful branch of the try block, or to let the pool contract update its own price after it has verified that its internal logic succeeded. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “update‑before‑call” vulnerabilities where a contract writes to storage before invoking an external function that may revert, violating the principle of atomic state changes and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Pools can be deployed with malicious or incorrect quote tokens and oracles
description:
```solidity
The deployment of a pool via deployPool() is permissionless. The deployer provides several parameters that have to be trusted by the users of a specific pool, these parameters include:
• oracleWrapper
• settlementEthOracle
• quoteToken
• invariantCheck
If any one of them is malicious, then the pool and its value will be affected.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the ability for any address to call deployPool() and specify the quote token, the oracle wrapper, the settlement ETH oracle and the invariant check contract. Because the deployment function does not enforce any validation or allow‑list, a malicious actor can supply a token that behaves incorrectly (for example, a token that always returns zero balance, reverts on transfer, or has a malicious transfer hook) or an oracle that reports fabricated prices. The pool logic trusts these external contracts for price discovery and for verifying that the pool invariant holds after each trade. When a fake or compromised oracle is used, the pool will accept trades based on false price data, allowing an attacker to extract value or cause the pool’s internal accounting to diverge from reality. Similarly, a malicious quote token can cause swaps to fail, burn user balances, or redirect funds to the attacker. The invariantCheck contract, if altered, can skip or falsify the safety checks that normally prevent the pool from entering an unsafe state. The issue manifests when users interact with a newly deployed pool that appears legitimate but was created with these untrusted components. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected loss of funds, swaps that return zero or extremely unfavorable amounts, or a pool that suddenly reports a zero or negative reserve. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the Tracer protocol where the permissionless nature of deployPool() was examined and the lack of constraints on critical parameters was noted. The bug is hard to notice because the pool contract itself does not contain any logic that validates the supplied addresses; the malicious behavior is hidden inside the external contracts, which may appear benign at first glance. The class of bug is a trust‑boundary misconfiguration in permissionless contract deployment, often referred to as ‘unrestricted external dependency injection’ or ‘oracle/ token injection attack’. To remediate, the protocol should restrict the set of acceptable quote tokens and oracle contracts, for example by maintaining an on‑chain allow‑list, using a governance‑approved registry, or by verifying that the oracle implements a known interface and returns reasonable price ranges. Additionally, the invariantCheck contract should be immutable or limited to a vetted implementation, and the deployment function should emit events that allow users to audit the chosen components before interacting with the pool. By enforcing these controls, the protocol can prevent attackers from deploying pools that silently manipulate pricing or break accounting, thereby protecting user funds and preserving the economic guarantees of the system.

title: pairTokenBase and poolBase template contracts instances are not initialized
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the PoolFactory constructor deploying three template contracts – a pair token template, a leveraged pool template, and a pool committer template – but only initializing the pool committer. The pair token (PoolToken) and leveraged pool (LeveragedPool) templates remain uninitialized, meaning their internal initializer functions have never been called. Because these contracts inherit from OpenZeppelin’s Initializable pattern, the first call to their initialize() function can be made by any external address. An attacker can therefore invoke initialize() on the uninitialized templates, supplying an address they control as the owner or governance parameter. Once the attacker becomes the owner of the template contracts, they gain access to privileged functions such as minting new ERC20 tokens, changing governance settings, or pausing the pool. This can be exploited by directly interacting with the template instances, which are publicly addressable, and calling their initialize() functions with malicious arguments. After gaining ownership, the attacker can mint arbitrary tokens that appear to be legitimate pool tokens, potentially deceiving users who see a valid‑looking ERC20 contract and assume it is backed by the protocol. The impact includes unauthorized token creation, dilution of legitimate token holders, possible loss of trust in the protocol, and financial loss for users who interact with the counterfeit tokens. The issue manifests whenever the factory is deployed, because the templates are created at construction time and never receive dummy initialization values. All participants who rely on the pool’s token contracts – investors, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that reference the token address – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the factory’s constructor and noticed the missing initialization calls. It can be hard to notice because the templates are not used in normal operation; they sit idle and their functions are not exercised in typical test flows, giving a false sense of safety. The proper remediation is to call the initialize() function on both the pair token and leveraged pool templates during factory construction, passing harmless dummy parameters, or to replace the contracts with OpenZeppelin upgradable ERC20 implementations that do not rely on constructors. By ensuring the templates are initialized, the ownership slot is set to a known, non‑controllable address, preventing an attacker from hijacking the templates and minting tokens.

title: Oracles are not updated before use
description:
```solidity
The PoolKeeper contract uses two oracles but does not ensure that their prices are updated. The poll() function should be called on both oracles to get the first execution and the settlement / ETH prices. As it currently is, the code could operate on old data.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the PoolKeeper contract relying on two external price oracles without guaranteeing that the oracle values are refreshed immediately before they are consumed. The contract reads the first execution price and the settlement/ETH price by calling getOraclePrice() and other internal functions, but it never forces the oracle wrappers to execute their poll() method, which is the only mechanism that updates the underlying price data. Because poll() may revert when the oracle does not have enough data to compute a simple moving average or when the required update interval has not elapsed, the developers omitted the call entirely, assuming the data would be up‑to‑date. As a result, the contract can operate on stale price information that may be arbitrarily old. An attacker who can influence the oracle feed or who knows the timing of price updates can trigger a pool operation (such as creating a new leveraged pool or performing a keeper upkeep) while the oracle still holds a previous price. The contract will then settle trades, calculate fees, or adjust collateral based on this outdated price, potentially causing users to receive less than expected, experience unexpected liquidations, or see their balances reduced without a corresponding market movement. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a normal price, but the transaction outcome shows a zero or reduced payout, leading to confusion and loss of funds. The issue is most likely to appear during the first execution of a pool (newPool) or during periodic upkeep (performUpkeepSinglePool) when the code does not invoke poll() before reading the price. All participants that interact with the leveraged pools – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that prices are current are violated. The problem was identified during a manual security audit that examined the control flow and noticed the missing poll() calls. It is difficult to detect in testing because the oracle may return a plausible price that simply happens to be old, and the contract does not emit any warning when stale data is used. The recommended mitigation is to explicitly call poll() on each oracle wrapper before any price read, and to wrap the call in a try‑catch block to handle possible reverts caused by insufficient data or premature updates. If poll() fails, the contract should abort the operation or fall back to a safe default rather than proceeding with stale data. This pattern addresses the broader class of “stale oracle data” bugs where contracts assume external feeds are fresh without enforcing freshness checks, which can lead to financial mis‑calculations and loss of user funds.

title: getPendingCommits() underreports commits
description:
```solidity
When frontRunningInterval > updateInterval, the PoolCommitter.getAppropriateUpdateIntervalId() function can return updateInterval IDs that are arbitrarily far into the future, especially if appropriateIntervalId > updateIntervalId + 1.
Therefore, commits can also be made to these appropriate interval IDs far in the future by calling commit(). The PoolCommitter.getPendingCommits() function only checks the commits for updateIntervalId and updateIntervalId + 1, but needs to check up to updateIntervalId + factorDifference + 1.
Currently, it is underreporting the pending commits which leads to the checkInvariants function not checking the correct values.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PoolCommitter contract's getPendingCommits function. The function is intended to enumerate all commits that are pending for the current update interval and the immediately following interval, so that the protocol's invariant checks can verify that no unexpected commitments exist. However, when the configured frontRunningInterval parameter is larger than the regular updateInterval, the helper function getAppropriateUpdateIntervalId may return an interval identifier that is many periods ahead of the current updateIntervalId. This occurs because the calculation does not cap the interval offset, allowing appropriateIntervalId to exceed updateIntervalId + 1. As a result, users or an attacker can submit a commit to a far‑future interval by calling commit with the large interval id. The getPendingCommits implementation still only scans the two intervals (updateIntervalId and updateIntervalId + 1). Consequently, any commit placed in a later interval is invisible to the pending‑commit enumeration. The checkInvariants routine, which relies on getPendingCommits to detect outstanding commitments, therefore operates on incomplete data and may incorrectly deem the system healthy. From a user's perspective, a transaction that appears to have been accepted may later be rejected by the protocol, or the user may see their balance unchanged while the contract believes no pending work exists. The impact is that the protocol's accounting assumptions are broken: funds locked for future intervals are not accounted for, potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate the timing of commits, bypass slashing conditions, or cause a mismatch between expected and actual token reserves. The bug manifests only when frontRunningInterval > updateInterval, a configuration that can be set by the protocol owner or derived from market parameters. It was discovered during a manual audit of the PoolCommitter logic, where the auditor noticed that the interval‑selection function could return values far beyond the range that getPendingCommits checks. The issue is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning when a commit is placed in a distant interval, and the invariant check still passes, giving a false sense of security. The class of bug is an under‑reporting or incomplete enumeration flaw, similar to off‑by‑range errors in accounting loops. To remediate, getPendingCommits must be extended to iterate over all intervals up to the appropriateIntervalId (or at least up to updateIntervalId + factorDifference + 1) and include any pending commits found there. Alternatively, the contract could enforce that commits may only be made for intervals within the range that getPendingCommits inspects, thereby preventing the mismatch. Proper validation and comprehensive enumeration will restore the integrity of the invariant checks and ensure that all locked funds are visible to the protocol's accounting mechanisms.

title: Authenticity check for oracles is not effective
description:
```solidity
The deployPool() function verifies the authenticity of the oracleWrapper by calling its deployer() function. As the oracleWrapper is supplied via deploymentParameters, it can be a malicious contract whose deployer() function can return any value, including msg.sender.
Note: this check does protect against frontrunning the deployment transaction of the same pool. See Undocumented frontrunning protection.
function deployPool(PoolDeployment calldata deploymentParameters) external override returns (address) {
    ...
    require(IOracleWrapper(deploymentParameters.oracleWrapper).deployer() == msg.sender, "Deployer must be oracle wrapper owner");
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an ineffective authenticity check for oracle contracts used during pool deployment. The deployPool function attempts to verify that the supplied oracleWrapper is owned by the caller by calling its deployer() function and requiring the returned address to equal msg.sender. Because the oracleWrapper address is provided as an arbitrary parameter, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract that implements deployer() to return any value, including the caller’s address, thereby satisfying the require statement without actually being the legitimate oracle owner. This logical flaw allows a malicious oracle to be injected at the moment a pool is created, bypassing the intended ownership verification. Once the fake oracle is accepted, it can feed arbitrary price data to the pool, causing incorrect pricing, unintended liquidations, or loss of user funds. The impact is that users of the compromised pool may see their balances shrink, trades execute at unfavorable rates, or their positions be liquidated unexpectedly, effectively making funds disappear. The condition under which the bug manifests is any deployment of a pool where the deployer supplies an untrusted oracleWrapper address; the check does not enforce any external allowlist, code hash verification, or trusted registry. The affected parties include the pool deployer, all participants who interact with the pool, and the broader protocol that relies on accurate oracle data. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of the deployment function and identified that the authenticity check can be spoofed. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears to enforce ownership, giving a false sense of security, while the underlying assumption that the oracleWrapper’s deployer() function is trustworthy is unfounded. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “authentication bypass via untrusted contract callbacks” and represents a failure of the protocol’s trust model for external data sources. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show normal operation but later display unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or sudden liquidation events, contradicting the expectation that the oracle provides correct price information. To remediate, the protocol should replace the direct deployer() check with a robust allowlist of vetted oracle contracts, verify the code hash of the oracleWrapper, or integrate with a trusted oracle registry, ensuring that only authorized oracle implementations can be used during pool creation.

title: Incorrect calculation of keeper reward
description:
```solidity
The keeper reward is calculated as (keeperGas * tipPercent / 100) / 1e18. The division by 1e18 is incorrect and undervalues the reward for the keeper. The tip part of the keeper reward is essentially ignored.
The likely cause of this miscalculation is based on the note at PoolKeeper.sol#244 which states the tip percent is in WAD units, but it really is a quad representation of a value in the range between 5 and 100.
The comment at PoolKeeper.sol#L241 also incorrectly states that _keeperGas is in wei (usually referring to ETH), which is not the case as it is denominated in the quote token, but in WAD precision.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect arithmetic expression used to compute the keeper reward in a liquidity pool contract. The code multiplies the gas amount allocated to the keeper by the tip percentage, divides by 100 to obtain the tip portion, and then divides the whole result by a fixed‑point constant (1e18). Because the tip percentage is already expressed in WAD (fixed‑point) format and the keeper gas amount is also stored with WAD precision in the quote token, the additional division by 1e18 removes the tip component entirely and reduces the base reward. The root cause is a misunderstanding of unit conventions: a comment in the source incorrectly states that the gas amount is in wei and that the tip percent is a plain integer, while in reality both values are stored in WAD precision. When the contract executes the reward calculation, the extra division causes the tip to be effectively ignored, so the keeper receives a reward that is lower than the protocol’s economic model expects. This can be exploited by any keeper who relies on the advertised tip incentive; the keeper will consistently be under‑paid, which may discourage participation, weaken the pool’s security, and ultimately lead to reduced liquidity or higher costs for users. The issue manifests whenever the keeper reward function is called with a non‑zero tip percent – the tip portion disappears and the transferred amount may be far smaller than anticipated. Affected parties include keepers who perform maintenance tasks, the protocol that assumes proper incentive alignment, and indirectly the users who depend on a well‑secured pool. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented unit conventions with the actual implementation and identified the mismatched division. It is subtle because the contract still transfers a non‑zero amount, so a superficial test may not reveal the missing tip; only a detailed accounting of expected versus actual reward values exposes the discrepancy. To remediate the problem the division by the fixed‑point constant should be removed and the formula rewritten to operate entirely in WAD arithmetic, and the misleading comments should be corrected to reflect the true units of _keeperGas and _tipPercent. In conceptual terms the fix restores the intended reward calculation, ensuring that the tip percentage contributes correctly to the keeper’s compensation and that the economic incentives of the protocol are preserved.

title: performUpkeepSinglePool() can result in a griefing attack when the pool has not been updated for many intervals
description:
```solidity
Assuming the pool has not been updated for many update intervals, performUpkeepSinglePool() can call poolUpkeep() repeatedly with _boundedIntervals == true and a bounded amount of gas to fix this situation. This in turn will call executeCommitments() repeatedly.
For each call to executeCommitments() the updateMintingFee() function will be called. This updates fees and changes them in an unexpected way. A griefing attack is possible by repeatedly calling executeCommitments() with boundedIntervals == true and numberOfIntervals == 0.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a grief‑grinding logic flaw that appears when the upkeep routine for a single liquidity pool is invoked after the pool has fallen behind for many scheduled intervals. The function performUpkeepSinglePool is designed to catch up the pool by repeatedly calling an internal poolUpkeep routine with the flag _boundedIntervals set to true and a limited gas budget. Each invocation of poolUpkeep triggers executeCommitments, and executeCommitments unconditionally calls updateMintingFee. Because the code does not check whether any intervals were actually processed, an attacker can repeatedly trigger performUpkeepSinglePool with _boundedIntervals true and a request for zero intervals (numberOfIntervals == 0). Each call still runs updateMintingFee, causing the minting fee state variable to be recomputed and altered many times without any real work being done. Over a large number of iterations the fee can drift far from its intended value, inflating costs for honest participants or rendering the pool economically unusable. The issue manifests when the pool is out‑of‑sync and an external actor repeatedly invokes the upkeep function, for example via a bot or a malicious contract. All users who rely on the pool’s fee schedule – liquidity providers, borrowers, and token holders – may see unexpectedly high fees, failed transactions, or reduced returns. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that traced the call chain and observed that updateMintingFee is executed on every bounded‑interval call regardless of actual interval count. It is hard to notice because the fee change may be small per call and only becomes apparent after many repetitions, and because a zero‑interval request looks harmless at first glance. The recommended mitigation is to ensure that updateMintingFee is invoked only once per series of bounded‑interval calls, or to guard the call with a condition that at least one interval has been processed before updating fees. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “repeated state‑update without progress” or “fee‑recalculation loop” vulnerabilities, where a state‑changing function is called repeatedly in a loop that performs no meaningful work, leading to unintended economic side effects.

title: MJR-1 Wrongly increased participants amount
description:
```solidity
At line StakingPool.sol#L120 contract increases participants amount, that happens if user.amount is zero, however if user will provide zero _amountToStake participants also will increased. So somebody can increase participants infinitely by calling stakeTokens with zero stake.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the staking contract where the counter that tracks the number of participants is incremented even when a user stakes zero tokens. The root cause is a condition that only checks whether the caller’s existing stake amount is zero before increasing the participants count, without verifying that the amount being added (_amountToStake) is greater than zero. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling the stakeTokens function with a zero stake while their current balance is also zero, causing the participants counter to grow indefinitely. This inflated participant count can break downstream assumptions that rely on an accurate number of active stakers, such as reward distribution formulas, governance voting weight calculations, or any logic that divides rewards by the participant count. When the counter is artificially high, legitimate participants may receive a smaller share of rewards, or the protocol may encounter division‑by‑zero or overflow errors if the count exceeds expected limits. The issue manifests only when a user with no prior stake invokes stakeTokens with a zero amount; under normal staking operations with a positive amount the counter behaves correctly. All users of the protocol are affected because the displayed number of participants may be misleading, and the economic outcomes for stakers can be altered without any visible transaction. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit by MixBytes, where the logic of the participant‑incrementing statement was examined and found to lack a proper amount check. It can be hard to notice because a zero‑value stake appears to be a no‑op, yet the contract still records a new participant, making the discrepancy subtle in UI dashboards that only show total participants. To remediate, the contract should only increase the participants counter when the incoming stake amount is strictly greater than zero, ensuring that the counter reflects only accounts that actually hold a positive stake. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that participants are users who have contributed funds, preserving correct accounting, reward calculations, and governance integrity.

title: MJR-2 Potentially differentiating message senders
description:
```solidity
This warning is about inconsistent message sender address source (msg.sender and _msgSender()) usage in here: FeeToken.sol#L37, FeeToken.sol#L39, FeeToken.sol#L40.
This can lead to the incorrect message sender address choice in case, for example, particular function call was a relayed call or meta-transaction-related call.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent use of the Ethereum transaction origin identifier, where some functions read the caller from the built‑in variable msg.sender while other functions obtain the caller through a wrapper such as _msgSender(). This inconsistency creates a class of access‑control bugs that appear when the contract is used with relayed calls or meta‑transactions. The root cause is that msg.sender always returns the immediate caller (for example a relayer contract), whereas _msgSender() is designed to return the original user that signed the meta‑transaction. When a function that protects a privileged operation checks msg.sender but the surrounding logic or inherited contracts expect _msgSender(), the contract may grant or deny rights to the wrong address. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a transaction through a trusted relayer or a meta‑transaction forwarder, causing the contract to treat the relayer as the authorized sender. This can lead to unauthorized minting, fee collection, or ownership changes, effectively allowing the attacker to move or lock funds that belong to honest users. The issue manifests only when the contract is called via a forwarding mechanism; direct calls from an EOA will appear normal, making the bug hard to notice in standard unit tests. Users may experience symptoms such as fees not being deducted, withdrawals appearing to succeed while balances remain unchanged, or unexpected loss of token control. The affected parties include token holders, the protocol’s governance, and any role that relies on correct sender verification. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted lines where msg.sender and _msgSender() were mixed. Because both identifiers are valid addresses, the inconsistency does not raise compiler warnings and can remain hidden until a meta‑transaction is used. To remediate, the contract should adopt a single, consistent method for retrieving the caller—preferably the context‑aware _msgSender() provided by an AccessControl or Context base contract—and replace every direct msg.sender reference. This eliminates double‑ownership or mis‑ownership scenarios and restores the intended security model.

title: `increaseUnlockTime` missing `_checkpoint` for delegated values
description:
In the VotingEscrow contract, users can increase their voting power by:

  * Adding more funds to their delegated value
  * Increasing the time of their lock
  * Being delegated by another user

Specifically, when users are delegated by other users through the `delegate` function, the delegated user gains control over the delegate funds from the delegating user.

The delegated user can further increase this power by increasing the time that the delegated funds are locked by calling `increaseUnlockTime`, resulting in ALL the delegated funds controlled by the delegated user, including those that do not originate from the delegated user, being used to increase the voting power of the user.

The issue lies in the following scenario: If user A delegates to user B, and then user B delegates to user C, user B loses the ability to extend his or her voting power by `increaseUnlockTime` due to a missing `_checkpoint` operation. If user B calls the `increaseUnlockTime` function, the `_checkpoint` operation will not proceed, as user B is delegating to user C. However, B still owns delegated funds, in the form of the funds delegated from user A. Therefore, user B should still gain voting power from `increaseUnlockTime`, even though user B is delegating.
poc:
Assume three users, Alice, Bob, and Carol, who each possess `locks` with 10 units of `delegate` value. Also assume that the unlock time is 1 week.

  * Alice delegates her 10 units to Bob.
  * Bob then delegates his 10 units to Carol.
  * At this point, Alice has 0 `delegate` value, Bob has 10 `delegate` value, and Carol has 20 `delegate` value.
  * Carol calls `increaseUnlockTime` to 2 weeks, resulting in `_checkpoint` raising her voting power accordingly.
  * Bob calls `increaseUnlockTime` to 2 weeks, resulting in no change in his voting power, even though he has 10 units of `delegate` value.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the VotingEscrow contract’s increaseUnlockTime function, where the internal bookkeeping step known as _checkpoint is conditionally skipped when the caller is simultaneously a delegatee and a delegator. In the normal flow, increaseUnlockTime should record the new lock expiry and update the delegated voting power for all funds under the caller’s control. However, when a user (e.g., Bob) receives delegated voting power from another user (Alice) and then delegates his own voting power to a third party (Carol), the contract’s logic treats Bob as a delegatee and therefore bypasses the _checkpoint call. As a result, the delegated tokens that originated from Alice are not accounted for in the vote‑weight recalculation even though Bob still controls them. This omission means that Bob’s voting power remains unchanged after extending the unlock time, contrary to the expectation that a longer lock multiplies all controlled voting power. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately creates a delegation chain and then attempts to boost governance influence by extending lock periods; the contract will silently ignore the boost for the intermediate delegate, potentially distorting quorum calculations or enabling a malicious delegatee to retain disproportionate influence while intermediaries cannot recover their expected power. The bug manifests only when a user has both incoming delegations and outgoing delegations at the same time; pure delegators or pure delegatees are unaffected. All participants in the delegation graph—delegators, delegatees, and the protocol’s governance mechanisms—are impacted because the accounting of voting power becomes inconsistent, leading to a mismatch between the on‑chain state and the perceived voting weight shown in UI dashboards. The flaw was uncovered during a code audit that inspected the control flow of increaseUnlockTime and noted that the checkpoint logic was wrapped inside an if‑statement that omitted the case where the caller is delegating out. The problem is subtle because the function executes without reverting, and the user interface still displays a successful transaction, making the missing power increase difficult to notice without explicit state verification. Conceptually, this is a state‑synchronization bug where a crucial side‑effect (updating delegated balances) is conditionally omitted, breaking the invariant that lock extensions affect all controlled tokens. The recommended fix is to move the _checkpoint call outside of the conditional block so that it always runs for any caller, regardless of delegation direction, thereby restoring the proper update of voting power for delegated assets. Once corrected, extending an unlock time will consistently raise voting power for both direct and delegated holdings, aligning on‑chain accounting with user expectations and preserving the integrity of the governance protocol.

title: The current implementation of the VotingEscrow contract doesn’t support fee on transfer tokens
description:
Some ERC20 tokens implemented so a fee is taken when transferring them, for example `STA` and `PAXG`. The current implementation of the `VotingEscrow` contract will mess up the accounting of the locked amounts if `token` will be a token like that, what will lead to a state where users won’t be able to receive their funds.

This will happen because the value that is added to the locked amount is not the actual value received by the contract, but the value supplied by the user (the value which the fee is taken from).
poc:
The `STA` token burns 1% of the value provided to the `transfer` function, which means the recipient gets only 99% of the transferred asset. Let’s assume that `token` is the address of the `STA` token.

  1. Bob wants to lock 100 STA tokens and calls `createLock(100 * 10**18, unlockTime)`.
  2. The addition to the locked amount variable is done with `100 * 10**18`, while the actual amount that was received by the contract is `99 * 10**18`.
  3. When the lock expires Bob will try to withdraw his tokens, and the transfer function will be called with the accounted locked amount (which is `100 * 10**18`). This might succeed due to other users locking too, so the transferred tokens will be taken from “their tokens”, but in the end there will be users left without an option to withdraw their funds, because the balance of the contract will be less than the locked amount that the contract is trying to transfer.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the VotingEscrow contract records the amount of tokens that a user locks when using tokens that deduct a fee on each transfer. The contract assumes that the number of tokens supplied by the caller is the exact amount that will be received, and it stores this supplied value directly in its internal accounting. This assumption is false for fee‑on‑transfer (also called deflationary) ERC‑20 tokens, where the token contract deducts a percentage of the transferred amount and sends only the remainder to the recipient. Because the contract does not verify the actual balance change after the transfer, the recorded locked amount can be larger than the real balance held by the contract. An attacker or any user holding such a token can lock, for example, 100 tokens, while the contract only receives 99 tokens due to a 1 % fee. When the lock expires, the contract will attempt to transfer the previously recorded 100 tokens back to the user. If the contract’s balance is insufficient, the transfer will fail, leaving the user unable to withdraw their funds. The impact is that users may lose access to the tokens they intended to lock, effectively causing their assets to become unrecoverable within the escrow system. This condition materializes only when the token used with VotingEscrow implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism; with fee‑free tokens such as Balancer V2 pool tokens, the issue does not manifest. The affected parties are any token holder who locks a deflationary token through the VotingEscrow contract, as well as the protocol that relies on accurate escrow accounting for voting power and reward distribution. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s handling of token transfers and identified that the amount added to the locked balance is derived from the user‑provided value rather than the actual incoming balance. The problem can be subtle because the transaction appears to succeed and the user receives no immediate error, making the discrepancy hard to notice until withdrawal time. To remediate the issue, the contract should determine the exact amount received by measuring its token balance before and after the transfer (or by using the Transfer event’s actual value) and use that delta for accounting. Additionally, an invariant check can be added to require that the balance delta matches the declared amount, thereby rejecting fee‑on‑transfer tokens outright. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches caused by unchecked external token behavior, where a contract’s internal state diverges from the on‑chain token balances due to token‑specific transfer logic. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after locking tokens they later see a “withdrawal failed” or “insufficient balance” error, or they simply receive nothing when attempting to claim their locked assets, contrary to the expectation that they would retrieve the same amount they deposited. This breach of the expected deposit‑withdrawal symmetry undermines the trust in the escrow mechanism and can lead to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective.

title: Attacker contract can avoid being blocked by BlockList.sol
bug_full:
The vulnerability stems from a block‑listing mechanism that decides whether an address is allowed to interact with the protocol by calling a private helper _isContract(address). This helper simply returns true when extcodesize(addr) is greater than zero, i.e., when the address contains contract bytecode at the moment of the check. Because the check is performed only at the time of the call, the system assumes that once an address is identified as a contract it will remain a contract forever. An attacker can break this assumption by deploying a contract at a deterministic address using CREATE2, interacting with the protocol, then invoking selfdestruct to erase the bytecode. After self‑destruction the address reports a code size of zero, so any subsequent block‑list check that relies on extcodesize will treat the address as non‑contract and allow it to bypass the blacklist. The attacker can then redeploy a new contract at exactly the same address (again via CREATE2 with the same salt) and continue interacting with the protocol while the original address remains marked as blocked. This attack flow—deploy, self‑destruct, recreate—lets a malicious contract avoid detection by the block‑list.

The impact is that an adversary can circumvent restrictions that are meant to prevent certain contracts from locking LP tokens, delegating permissions, or increasing unlock times. By evading the block‑list, the attacker may lock tokens, later self‑destruct, and then re‑enter to withdraw or manipulate tokenized positions, effectively undermining the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially leading to loss of funds for honest participants. The issue manifests whenever the block‑list modifier is applied to functions such as createLock, increaseAmount, increaseUnlockTime, or delegate, and the attacker has the ability to use CREATE2 and selfdestruct. All users of the protocol, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the security guarantee that blocked contracts cannot interact is broken.

The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noticed that the block‑list relied solely on extcodesize and did not maintain any persistent state about blocked addresses. The problem is subtle because extcodesize checks are a common and generally reliable way to distinguish contracts from externally owned accounts, and the ability to recreate a contract at the same address is not obvious in typical development workflows. Consequently, the bypass may go unnoticed in routine testing.

To remediate the issue, the block‑listing logic should not depend exclusively on the presence of bytecode. Instead, a persistent on‑chain registry that records addresses as blocked regardless of their code status should be used, or the protocol should explicitly prohibit self‑destruct or CREATE2‑based redeployment for addresses that have been blocked. By storing a boolean flag in a mapping (e.g., blocked[address] = true) and checking that flag in addition to or instead of extcodesize, the protocol can ensure that an address once blacklisted remains blocked for the lifetime of the contract, thereby preserving the intended security guarantees.

title: Inconsistent logic of increase unlock time to the expired locks
description: Can not prevent expired locks being extended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the voting escrow contract that permits an expired token lock to be extended when the lock is delegated to another address. The root cause is that the increaseUnlockTime() function contains a check that rejects extensions only when the caller’s lock is not delegated; the delegated execution path skips the expiration validation entirely. As a result, an attacker (or any user) can let their lock expire, delegate the lock to a third‑party address, and then invoke increaseUnlockTime() to set a new unlock timestamp. After the lock has been extended, the user can undelegate or re‑delegate back to themselves, thereby restoring voting power that should have been lost at expiry. This exploitation flow proceeds as follows: (1) create a lock with a defined end time; (2) allow the lock to pass its expiry; (3) delegate the expired lock to another address; (4) call increaseUnlockTime() with a future timestamp, which succeeds because the delegated branch does not enforce the "lock expired" requirement; (5) re‑delegate back to the original address, causing the balanceOf() query to report a positive voting balance again. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumption – that expired locks yield zero voting power – is broken, enabling manipulation of governance decisions, vote‑weight inflation, and a breach of trust in the voting escrow mechanism. The issue manifests only under the specific condition where a lock’s end timestamp is earlier than the current block timestamp and the lock has an active delegatee; otherwise the function reverts as expected. Users experience an unexpected return of vote power after a lock has supposedly expired, seeing a zero balance disappear and then reappear without any additional token transfers, which can be confusing and may be interpreted as a bug or malicious behavior. The problem was discovered through automated testing that exercised both delegated and non‑delegated paths, revealing that the former incorrectly permits the operation. The bug is hard to notice because the primary revert message "Lock expired" is present in the non‑delegated branch, giving the impression that the contract uniformly protects against extending expired locks. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce the expiration check uniformly, regardless of delegation status, or explicitly disallow any increaseUnlockTime() calls on expired locks. Removing the line that skips the check for delegated locks (as suggested in the original report) restores the intended invariant that expired locks cannot be extended, thereby preserving correct vote‑weight accounting and protocol integrity.

title: Error in Updating `_checkpoint` in the `increaseUnlockTime` Function
description:
The potentiel impact of this error are :

  * Give wrong voting power to a user at a given block.
  * Give wrong total voting power at a given block.
  * Give wrong total voting power.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that extends the unlock time of a locked voting escrow token. When a user calls the increaseUnlockTime entry point, the contract builds a snapshot of the previous lock (oldLocked) and the new lock (newLocked) and forwards both to the internal _checkpoint routine, which updates the per‑address bias, slope and the global point history used to calculate voting power. The implementation mistakenly sets oldLocked.end to the newly calculated unlock_time instead of preserving the original lock expiration (oldUnlockTime). As a result the old and new lock snapshots share the same end timestamp. Because the bias for a point is computed as slope multiplied by the remaining lock duration (end‑block.timestamp), the old point’s bias becomes identical to the new point’s bias. This corrupts the arithmetic that adjusts the user’s voting power, the aggregate bias, and the slopeChanges mapping that tracks when locks expire. Consequently the contract may report an incorrect voting power for the caller at a given block and may also misreport the total voting power of the protocol. The error only manifests when the lock is delegated (owner.delegated == msg.sender) and the unlock time is being increased, i.e., when the oldLocked snapshot is created. Users are affected because they may see a higher or lower voting weight than expected after extending a lock, and the protocol’s governance calculations (balanceOfAt, totalSupply, totalSupplyAt) become unreliable, potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate voting outcomes or disrupt quorum calculations. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which compared the contract’s behaviour against the specification in CheckpointMath.md and identified the mismatch between the intended old lock end timestamp and the implementation. The issue is subtle because the contract still updates the lock and no obvious revert occurs; the mis‑calculated bias only becomes visible in derived voting power queries, making it hard to detect through simple functional tests. To remediate, the oldLocked.end field must be assigned the previously stored oldUnlockTime rather than the new unlock_time, thereby preserving the correct historical state for the _checkpoint calculation. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect state snapshot during lock modification” bugs, where a contract records an outdated version of a variable with a fresh value, leading to arithmetic errors in time‑dependent tokenomics and governance accounting.

title: Unsafe casting from int128 can cause wrong accounting of locked amounts
description: The unsafe casting to int128 variable can cause its value to be different from the correct value. For example in the createLock function, the addition to the locked amount variable is done by `locked_.amount += int128(int256(_value))`. In that case, if `_value` is greater than `type(int128).max` which is `2**127 - 1`, then the accounting will be wrong and the amount that will be added to `locked_.amount` will be less than the amount of token that will be transferred from the user. Then the user won’t be able to withdraw the tokens that he transferred, and they’ll be stuck in the contract forever.
poc:
1. Alice tries to lock `2**128` tokens. She calls `createLock(2**128, unlockTime)` with the time she wants to lock for.
  2. The addition of the given value is done by `locked_.amount += int128(int256(_value))`, which actually does nothing to the `locked_.amount` variable and it remains 0. That’s because when casting `int128(int256(2**128))` truncates to 0, and that leaves the locked amount unchanged but the tokens are transferred.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unsafe down‑cast of a token amount from a 256‑bit integer to a signed 128‑bit integer within the lock creation routine. When a caller supplies a value larger than the maximum representable signed 128‑bit number (2^127‑1), the cast `int128(int256(_value))` truncates the high bits and may produce a drastically smaller value or zero. The contract then adds this truncated value to the stored locked amount (`locked_.amount += …`). Consequently, the amount recorded in the contract’s accounting state is smaller than, or even equal to, zero while the full token amount has already been transferred from the user’s wallet to the contract. This mismatch means that, later, when the user tries to withdraw the locked tokens, the contract believes the user has no locked balance and refuses the withdrawal, effectively locking the tokens forever. The flaw is triggered only when the input amount exceeds the int128 ceiling, a condition that rarely occurs with typical ERC‑20 tokens but is theoretically possible for tokens with very large supplies or for malicious actors deliberately supplying an oversized value. It was identified during a formal audit by examining the arithmetic operations and testing boundary values such as 2^128. The issue can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the transfer succeeds, but the internal accounting silently records an incorrect amount, leading to a silent loss of funds. To remediate, the contract should either keep the locked amount in a 256‑bit unsigned type, perform an explicit overflow check (`require(_value <= type(int128).max)`) before casting, or use a safe casting library that reverts on overflow. This class of bug belongs to integer truncation or unsafe type conversion errors, which break the fundamental accounting invariants of the protocol: the amount of tokens transferred into the contract must equal the amount recorded as locked. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior (“I lock 100 tokens and can withdraw them later”) is violated; instead the UI shows a zero locked balance and the withdrawal function returns nothing, creating a situation where funds appear to disappear despite the contract holding them.

title: It is not possible to call executeCommitments() for multiple old commits
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑timing flaw in the pool upkeep routine where the contract updates its lastPriceTimestamp after the first execution of poolUpkeep in a block, even when there are still pending commitments that need to be processed. The root cause is that the function poolUpkeep sets lastPriceTimestamp to the current block.timestamp before it has called executeCommitments for all old commitments. Because intervalPassed checks whether block.timestamp is greater than or equal to lastPriceTimestamp plus the configured update interval, any subsequent call to poolUpkeep in the same block sees the interval as not having passed and aborts at the require statement. As a result, executeCommitments is invoked only once per block, leaving the remaining commitments unexecuted and causing the updateIntervalId to fall behind the actual state of the pool. This can be exploited by a keeper or any actor that repeatedly triggers performUpkeepSinglePool with the boundedIntervals flag set, effectively starving the contract of the opportunity to process older commitments. The impact is that users’ pending actions – such as token swaps, withdrawals, or refunds – never get executed, leading to balances that appear unchanged, expected refunds that are missing, or swaps that never complete. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a pending transaction that never resolves, or a balance that stays at zero despite having deposited funds. The issue occurs whenever the pool has accumulated several update intervals without being refreshed and the keeper attempts to catch up using bounded intervals. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between intervalPassed, lastPriceTimestamp, and the bounded‑interval processing logic. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; it simply stops processing further commitments, which can be mistaken for normal inactivity. To remediate the problem the contract should defer updating lastPriceTimestamp until after all old commitments have been processed, and ensure that executePriceChange is called only once for a batch of old commitments, thereby preventing premature interval gating and guaranteeing that every pending commitment is eventually executed. This class of bug is generally described as an early state update or timing inconsistency that breaks logical progression of scheduled operations, leading to accounting mismatches and user‑visible failures such as funds appearing to disappear or refunds not being delivered.

title: DealManager::initiatePrincipalPayout unbounded slippage on burnt tokens
description:
A total payout amount is computed off-chain and an amount proportional to the on-chain only payment is passed as an argument to the call on DealManager::initiatePrincipalPayout. During execution, the total payout amount is reconstructed from the values of onChainTotalBalance, fiatTotalBalance and on chain payout. This total amount is used to determine the quantity of deal tokens to burn, but if the ratio has changed since the payoutAmount has been precomputed (some tokens are burnt or transferred), more tokens than needed will be burnt.
Scenario:
• Initial state:
onChainTotalBalances = 1000
fiatTotalBalances = 1000
1. The originator computes a payout amount for a total payout of 1000, since onChainTotalBalances/totalSupply == 1/2, payoutAmount passed as an argument to initiatePrincipalPayout is 500.
2. The state changes, and 500 tokens are burnt from a on chain account. As a result the state is:
• Intermediate state
onChainTotalBalances = 500
fiatTotalBalances = 1000
– The originator emits the computed transaction and as the ratios have changed, the total reconstructed payout is 1500 instead of 1000, and instead of half the tokens, all of the tokens are burnt.
Note that the scenario likelihood is yet to determine, since only an originator can do all of the operations outlined above (initiatePrincipalPayout, burn or forceTransfer).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded slippage bug in DealManager::initiatePrincipalPayout where the contract reconstructs the total payout amount from on-chain balances and uses it to calculate how many deal tokens to burn. Because the payout amount is pre‑computed off‑chain and passed as a parameter, any change to the on‑chain balances between the off‑chain calculation and the execution (for example a token burn or a forced transfer performed by the same originator) changes the ratio used in the reconstruction.
