The contract does not enforce a maximum deviation, so it may burn more tokens than the proportional share that corresponds to the intended payout. An attacker who controls the originator role can first compute a payout assuming a certain balance, then deliberately burn or move tokens before calling initiatePrincipalPayout, causing the reconstructed total to be larger and resulting in an excessive burn that can wipe out all remaining tokens. The impact is that token holders see their balances drop unexpectedly, potentially to zero, and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent because the amount of fiat that should be paid out no longer matches the burned token supply. This situation can occur only when the originator can execute both the payout function and token‑burning or forced‑transfer operations in the same transaction or in close succession. The issue was identified during a manual security review that compared the off‑chain payout logic with the on‑chain reconstruction code. It is hard to notice because the burn operation itself is permitted by the contract and no explicit error is emitted when the amount exceeds the expected proportion; the discrepancy only appears as a sudden loss of tokens. The proper mitigation is to treat the off‑chain amount as a maximum slippage bound, verify that the calculated burn does not exceed the expected proportional amount, and revert the transaction if the deviation is larger than an acceptable threshold. In other words, the contract should either compute the payout entirely on‑chain or enforce a slippage parameter that limits how many extra tokens may be burned, thereby preserving the intended accounting relationship between fiat payouts and token supply.

title: Investors cannot receive their deposited principal or due interest if their deal requirement checks start failing
description:
In PayoutManager contract the investor's eligibility check is performed when principal or interest is claimed for an investor.
• The claimPayout reverts if checkAccountEligibility(msg.sender) reverts.
• In _pushPayout the investor is skipped when isEligibleAccount(account) returns false.
There could be scenarios where an investor was eligible when he deposited principal in a deal but going forward some of his quadrata attributes become invalid as per the deal's requirement.
A simple example could be when a deal was set up to allow investors whose AML score is upto 3. An investor with AML score of 3 invests into the deal. After a while the investor's AML score increases to 4. Now neither that investor nor the protocol admin can pull out the investor's deposited principal and due interest. This leads to loss of funds for the investor.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the payout logic of the PayoutManager contract where an investor’s eligibility is re‑checked at the moment a principal or interest claim is executed. The contract calls checkAccountEligibility(msg.sender) inside claimPayout and filters accounts with isEligibleAccount(account) inside the internal _pushPayout routine. Because these checks are performed on every claim, an investor who satisfied the deal’s requirements at the time of deposit can become ineligible later if any of the dynamic attributes used by the deal (for example an AML score, KYC status, or other quadrata attributes) change beyond the allowed threshold. When the eligibility check fails, claimPayout reverts and _pushPayout simply skips the account, meaning that neither the investor nor the protocol admin can pull out the deposited principal or the accrued interest. From a user’s perspective the claim transaction fails with an error, the UI shows no payout, and the displayed balance remains unchanged, giving the impression that the funds have disappeared. The root cause is the coupling of eligibility verification with payout execution without providing a fallback or recovery path, effectively locking funds when business‑logic conditions evolve after the initial investment. This class of bug can be described as an eligibility‑gating lock or a state‑dependent access‑control flaw that violates the accounting assumption that deposited assets remain withdrawable regardless of later attribute changes. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of claim functions and identified that eligibility checks are not limited to the investment entry point. It may be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for compliant investors and the failure only appears after an external attribute change, which is not obvious from static analysis. To remediate, the eligibility check should be removed from the payout path, or a separate recovery mechanism should be introduced that allows eligible‑once investors to retrieve their funds even if they later fail the attribute test, such as an admin‑override or a grace‑period withdrawal function. This ensures that the protocol’s financial guarantees are upheld and that investors are not unintentionally locked out of their own assets.

title: payoutPeriodStartTime skips 1 second for payouts
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one timing error in the calculation of the start of a new interest payout period. The contract determines the next period start by taking the timestamp of the most recent period end (latestInterestPeriodEnd) and adding one second. Because each period is defined as a closed interval, the extra second creates a gap – the interval [latestInterestPeriodEnd, latestInterestPeriodEnd+1] is never accounted for. This gap occurs every time the PayoutManager initiates a new interest payout, so the timeline is not perfectly contiguous. The root cause is the use of a “+1” offset when returning payoutPeriodStartTime, which was intended to avoid overlapping periods but instead skips a one‑second slice of time. An attacker or simply a regular participant can exploit the bug by joining or exiting a deal during the skipped second. For example, if a holder is entitled to yield from time t to t+200 and a new investor joins at t+101, the first distribution covers up to t+100, while the second distribution starts at t+101 instead of t+100. The new investor receives the same amount of yield as an existing holder for the interval t+101‑t+200, depriving the existing holder of the extra yield that should have accrued during the missing second (t+100‑t+101). In environments with a one‑second block time such as zkSync, the effect is even more pronounced: an investor who enters at t and exits at t+1 may receive no yield at all if the previous payout ended at t, because the skipped second contains the entire holding period. The impact is unfair distribution of accrued interest, potentially resulting in a loss of expected yield for long‑standing participants and an unintended advantage for newcomers who time their entry to the gap. The issue manifests whenever a payout is executed, i.e., during each call to _initiateInterestPayout, and affects all token holders whose balances change around the period boundary. It was discovered during a manual security review by the Spearbit audit team, who noted that the period start logic did not align with the accounting assumptions of continuous, non‑overlapping intervals. The bug can be hard to notice because a one‑second discrepancy is tiny compared to typical DeFi timeframes, and the contract’s UI may simply show that a user’s balance or accrued interest is lower than expected without indicating a calculation error. To remediate, the payoutPeriodStartTime function should return the exact timestamp of the previous period end (latestInterestPeriodEnd) rather than adding one second, and fall back to the overall yield generation start when no prior payouts exist. This aligns the period boundaries, eliminates the missing interval, and restores correct, fair accounting of interest across all participants. The class of bug is a period‑boundary off‑by‑one error that violates the protocol’s accounting invariants, leading to missing yield and potential fund loss for users who rely on precise interest calculations.

title: QuadrataKYCVerifier::verifyEligibility wrong expiration check for businessAttribute
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the KYC verification routine of the QuadrataKYCVerifier contract. During the eligibility check the contract is supposed to ensure that the business attribute of an account has not expired before granting business‑only privileges. Instead of passing the business attribute to the internal expiration helper, the code mistakenly passes the investor attribute. As a result the contract validates the expiry of the wrong attribute, allowing an account whose business attribute is stale or revoked to be treated as a valid business entity. This happens because the developer referenced the wrong variable when calling the _isExpired function, a classic copy‑and‑paste or naming mistake. An attacker can exploit the flaw by presenting an expired business attribute while keeping the investor attribute fresh; the verification will succeed, the contract will record the account as a business, and the attacker can then access functions that are restricted to verified businesses, such as privileged trading, fund allocation, or governance actions. The impact includes unauthorized access to business‑only features, potential regulatory non‑compliance, and the risk that funds could be moved by parties that should have been blocked by KYC rules. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to verifyEligibility where the entityType requirement is Business (or Individual with a contradictory check) and the business attribute has passed its allowed age while the investor attribute has not. All users of the protocol that rely on the KYC gate are affected, as are the protocol operators and any downstream participants who assume that only current business entities can interact. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, which identified the mismatched parameter in the expiration check. It can be hard to notice because the function still performs an expiry check, so superficial testing that only verifies a non‑expired investor attribute will pass, and the UI may continue to display a “business verified” badge even though the underlying attribute is out of date. The proper remediation is to replace the investorAttribute argument with businessAttribute in the _isExpired call, ensuring that the correct attribute’s timestamp is validated. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of attribute‑validation errors where a wrong data field is used for a security‑critical check, leading to a mismatch between business logic (the contract expects a fresh business attribute) and implementation (the contract checks a different field). From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an account that should be rejected because its business verification has expired is still accepted, resulting in unexpected access to business‑only functions, missing compliance warnings, or funds being transferred to an entity that should have been blocked. The failure mode can be described as “business status bypass” or “expired KYC attribute accepted”, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that only up‑to‑date KYC attributes grant certain privileges.

title: Rewards for wrapping NFTs can be gamed
description: The prize structure for wrapping an NFT is restarted everyday. The first user to wrap his NFT will receive 0.1 ETH, the second 0.05 ETH, and all users after that will get 0.015 ETH. However, as this is restarted each day, users will be incentivized to wait for the next day and get the higher reward. This could lead to users intentionally waiting and not wrapping their NFTs, slowing the whole process (which is expected to take place for 1-2 weeks), or alternatively many users missing the period to wrap their NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a design flaw in the reward mechanism for wrapping NFTs where the prize distribution is reset every calendar day. The first participant who wraps an NFT on a given day receives a higher payout (0.1 ETH) followed by a smaller second‑place reward (0.05 ETH) and a flat amount (0.015 ETH) for all subsequent wrappers. Because the schedule restarts at midnight, rational users are incentivised to postpone their wrapping transaction until the next day in order to claim the larger first‑place reward. This creates a game‑theoretic incentive misalignment: instead of continuously wrapping NFTs over the intended 1‑2‑week window, participants may deliberately wait, causing a slowdown or even a halt in the wrapping process. The impact is that the protocol’s expected throughput and liquidity provision are reduced, users may miss the limited wrapping period, and the overall reward distribution becomes uneven and unpredictable. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s daily reset logic is executed, i.e., at the start of each UTC day, and it affects any user who wishes to wrap an NFT, the protocol operators who rely on timely wrapping, and any downstream services that depend on the wrapped assets. It was identified by the CD Security audit team while reviewing the incentive model; the problem is subtle because the daily reset appears benign and the reward amounts are modest, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. Detecting the flaw requires analysing user behaviour over multiple days rather than a single transaction. To remediate, the reward schedule should be decoupled from a daily reset – for example by using a cumulative pool, a time‑weighted decay, or a non‑resetting tiered system that rewards early wrappers without encouraging deliberate delays. In user‑facing terms, a participant may notice that after wrapping an NFT they receive a lower or zero reward because they wrapped later in the day, or they may see that many NFTs remain unwrapped for days, contrary to the expectation that wrapping proceeds continuously. This misalignment violates the business logic that rewards should encourage prompt participation rather than strategic waiting, leading to a potential loss of expected earnings and a slowdown of the protocol’s core functionality.

title: TradableStaking: Users cannot unstake all their shares
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the unstake function of the TradableStaking contract that prevents a user from withdrawing the full amount of their staked shares. The function first checks require(userShares < _stakes.shares, \"!insufficient-shares\"); which enforces that the amount the user wants to unstake must be strictly less than the total shares recorded for the stake. Immediately after, the code computes a boolean isFullRedeem = userShares >= uint256(_stakes.shares); and, if true, sets userShares to the total shares. Because the require forces userShares to be smaller than _stakes.shares, the condition userShares >= _stakes.shares can never be satisfied, making the full‑redeem branch unreachable. As a result, when a user attempts to unstake an amount equal to their entire share balance, the transaction reverts with the \"!insufficient-shares\" error. This contradicts the expected business logic where a user should be able to withdraw all of their stake. The bug was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the contradictory inequalities. It is easy to miss because the require statement appears reasonable at a glance and the subsequent if‑statement seems harmless, yet the combination creates an impossible condition. The impact is that users are unable to fully redeem their tokens, effectively locking part of their funds in the contract until the bug is fixed. The issue affects every participant who uses the staking feature, and it undermines trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To fix the problem the require should allow equality (userShares <= _stakes.shares) and the full‑redeem flag should be based on equality (userShares == _stakes.shares). The extra if‑statement is unnecessary and can be removed, restoring the intended behavior where a user can unstake any amount up to and including their total shares.

title: Stuck tokens due to not using SafeTransfer
description: reclaimToken() does not use SafeERC20.safeTransfer(), which could lead to stuck tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a token reclamation function that transfers ERC20 tokens out of the contract without employing the SafeERC20.safeTransfer wrapper. By calling the raw token.transfer method and ignoring its return value, the contract assumes a successful transfer even when the token contract deviates from the ERC20 specification, returns false, or imposes transfer restrictions such as fees or pausing. This mismatch creates a situation where the reclaimToken routine may appear to complete without reverting, yet the tokens remain locked inside the contract. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a non‑standard or malicious ERC20 token that deliberately causes transfer to fail silently; when the owner later invokes reclaimToken, the call will not revert, the function will not detect the failure, and the assets become unrecoverable. The impact is loss of funds for the contract owner and any users who trusted the protocol to handle those tokens, effectively breaking the accounting guarantees of the system. The issue manifests whenever reclaimToken is used for tokens that do not strictly follow the ERC20 return‑value convention or that implement additional logic in their transfer function. It was discovered during a manual audit where the code path was inspected and the absence of SafeERC20 usage was noted. Because the failure does not emit an error event and the UI may simply show that the contract balance is unchanged, the problem can be hard to spot without deep testing. The proper remediation is to replace the direct transfer call with SafeERC20.safeTransfer, or at minimum to check the boolean return value and revert on false, thereby ensuring that any transfer failure aborts the transaction and prevents tokens from becoming permanently stuck. This class of bug falls under unsafe ERC20 handling, where missing safety checks lead to token loss and broken business logic, such as users expecting a refund or withdrawal but receiving nothing, or seeing their balance unexpectedly drop to zero.

title: Swaps should use the deadline argument on top of minimumAmountOut
description:
Swapping with block.timestamp as deadline means validators may do MEV up to the minimumAmountOut.
https://github.com/TrestleProtocol/Audit-Contracts/blob/main/src/Trestle.sol#L441
https://github.com/TrestleProtocol/Audit-Contracts/blob/main/src/Trestle.sol#L709
https://github.com/TrestleProtocol/Audit-Contracts/blob/main/src/Trestle.sol#L727
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the swap function determines its execution deadline. The contract sets the deadline argument to the current block timestamp (block.timestamp) instead of allowing a user‑provided future time. Because block.timestamp can be adjusted by validators within a small but permitted range, a validator can manipulate the timestamp or reorder transactions to ensure the swap executes at a moment that maximises their profit while still satisfying the minimumAmountOut check. In practice, a user initiates a swap expecting to receive at least a certain amount of output tokens; the contract enforces this lower bound but also requires the transaction to be mined in the same block. A validator can therefore set the block timestamp to the highest value allowed, or place their own transaction immediately before the user’s, causing the market price to shift just enough that the user still receives the minimum amount but the validator captures the difference between the expected market price and the actual execution price. This results in the user receiving fewer tokens than anticipated, effectively losing value that is transferred to the validator. The issue manifests whenever a swap is called with the deadline equal to block.timestamp, which is the default in the examined code paths. All participants who rely on the swap – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the hidden MEV window can erode trust and reduce overall protocol revenue. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noted that the deadline parameter does not provide a protective time buffer and that the reliance on block.timestamp opens a subtle miner‑extractable‑value (MEV) vector. The bug is difficult to spot because the transaction passes the deadline check and the minimumAmountOut condition, giving the appearance of correct behavior while silently allowing profit extraction. To remediate, the contract should accept a deadline supplied by the caller that is strictly greater than the current block timestamp, enforce a minimum future window (e.g., several seconds or minutes), and optionally use a more immutable time source or incorporate a slippage check that accounts for possible timestamp manipulation. By ensuring the deadline cannot be satisfied by the current block alone, the protocol removes the validator’s ability to manipulate execution timing for profit, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations that a swap will deliver at least the quoted amount without hidden losses.

title: On tax sells, swaps are vulnerable to MEV
description: Tax sells specify a minimumAmountOut of 0, which is vulnerable to MEV. Keep in mind that this is usually a design choice of tax tokens to avoid other issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing a token swap operation to proceed with a minimumAmountOut parameter set to zero. This design choice, common for tax‑bearing tokens that deduct a fee on transfer, removes any slippage protection from the transaction. Because the contract does not enforce a lower bound on the amount of output tokens that must be received, a malicious actor can observe the pending transaction in the mempool and submit a competing transaction that changes the price or consumes the liquidity before the victim's swap is executed. The attacker can therefore force the victim’s swap to execute at an unfavorable rate, often resulting in the victim receiving far fewer tokens than expected or even zero tokens, while the attacker captures the value difference. The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a sell or swap of a tax token through a function that hard‑codes minimumAmountOut to 0, typically in decentralized exchanges or router contracts that support taxed assets. It affects any user who relies on the swap to receive a predictable amount of tokens, as well as the broader protocol that may suffer from reduced trust and potential loss of liquidity. The problem was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of slippage checks for taxed token swaps. It can be difficult to notice because a zero minimum amount out is sometimes justified as a workaround for tax‑related rounding errors, and the contract may still appear to function correctly under normal market conditions. To remediate the issue, the contract should calculate an appropriate minimumAmountOut based on current market rates, incorporate a configurable slippage tolerance, or use a price oracle to enforce that the output amount cannot fall below a reasonable threshold, thereby preventing front‑running exploitation and preserving user expectations of receiving a non‑zero amount of tokens.

title: createAmmPairWith() in initialize() will revert if the pair already exists
description: createAmmPairWith() in initialize() reverts if the pair exists, which means that the contract could be DoSed.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the initialization routine of the AMM contract where the function createAmmPairWith is called without first verifying whether the token pair already has an associated liquidity pool. The contract assumes that the pair does not exist and attempts to create it unconditionally. In Solidity, the pair‑creation call reverts if a pair for the given token addresses is already registered. Because the code lacks a guard clause, any subsequent invocation of initialize – either directly or indirectly through functions such as addLiquidityETH – will trigger a revert when the pair has been created previously, either by a legitimate user or by an attacker who pre‑creates the pair. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the contract becomes unusable for further liquidity provision or swaps, and users experience transaction failures with no funds transferred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s initialization flow, where the auditor observed that the pair‑creation step did not include an existence check. The bug is subtle because the revert only occurs after the pair exists, a state that may not be encountered during normal operation where the pair is created only once, making it easy to overlook. The impact is that an attacker can pre‑create the pair, or a user can inadvertently trigger the condition, causing the contract to reject further interactions and effectively freezing the ability to add liquidity, which harms liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol’s overall functionality. The affected parties include anyone trying to add liquidity, withdraw funds, or trade through the AMM. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a generic transaction failure or a revert message, while the expected outcome – a successful liquidity addition and updated balance – does not occur. The root cause is a state‑dependent initialization flaw that violates the business logic assumption that liquidity can be added at any time. To remediate, the contract should first query the pair registry to determine whether the pair already exists and skip the creation step if it does. Because addLiquidityETH relies on the pair being present, the fix must also introduce slippage‑control parameters to protect against price manipulation when the pair already exists. In summary, the bug is an unchecked duplicate‑pair creation that leads to a denial‑of‑service by reverting on existing state, breaking accounting expectations and user experience.

title: Amounts to distribute are added directly to tokenPerShare, skipping using rewardPerToken
description: Rewards are emitted at a rate of rewardTokenPerBlock. However, when distributing, the received reward tokens are added directly to rewardPerToken, instead of being left in the contract and letting rewardTokenPerBlock distribute the amounts over time.
bug_full: The contract implements a reward distribution scheme where a fixed amount of reward tokens is supposed to be emitted over time at a rate defined by rewardTokenPerBlock. The intended design is that newly received reward tokens remain in the contract balance and are gradually accounted for through the rewardPerShare (also called rewardPerToken) variable as each block passes. In the current implementation, however, the distribution function adds the incoming reward tokens directly to the rewardPerShare variable at the moment they are received, bypassing the time‑based accrual mechanism. This direct addition skips the rewardPerToken calculation that would normally spread the tokens across future blocks. The root cause is a logical error in the accounting code: the amount to be distributed is summed into the per‑share counter instead of being left untouched in the contract so that the per‑block emission logic can apply. An attacker or any caller who can trigger the distribution can supply a large amount of reward tokens, causing the rewardPerShare value to jump instantly. As a result, all stakers see an inflated per‑share reward, which may later be corrected when the contract runs out of balance, leading to either over‑payment (inflation of rewards) or under‑payment (missing rewards) for users. The impact is that users may receive more tokens than intended in a single transaction, breaking the economic model, or conversely may see their expected rewards disappear, with balances becoming zero or lower than expected. This condition occurs each time the distribution routine is executed, especially after a token swap that changes the contract’s balance. The affected parties are the protocol’s stakers, any downstream applications that rely on accurate reward accounting, and the overall token economics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that the emittedRewards() function was never called before the swap and that the amountToDistribute variable was added directly to rewardPerShare. The bug is subtle because the rewardPerShare variable still updates, so on‑chain explorers and UI dashboards may show a higher reward rate, masking the fact that the underlying accounting no longer respects the per‑block emission rate. From a user’s perspective, the UI may display a large pending reward, but after claiming the reward the user’s balance may be unexpectedly low or even zero, contradicting the expectation that rewards accrue steadily over time. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “reward accounting bypass” or “incorrect accrual” bugs, where a contract’s intended time‑based distribution is circumvented by an immediate state change. To remediate the issue, the contract should retain incoming reward tokens in its balance, compute the amount of rewards that have been emitted up to the current block using the rewardPerBlock rate, and only then update rewardPerShare. The swap operation should be performed before any reward calculation so that the contract’s balance accurately reflects the tokens available for distribution, preventing the per‑share counter from being artificially inflated or truncated.

title: TradableSideVault.sol: users can grief sideVaults by spending their funds on LZ messages
description:
Any user can spam function marginAccountDeposit() on a sideVault with an amount of 0 tokens and drain the contract of ether (they would also receive the LZ gas refunded, if any).
They could call this function several times within a single transaction, which would result in a cheap call to grief the vault, but a big cost to the protocol.
This would also prevent other users in the same chain from interacting with the sideVault, not allowing them to make deposits, withdrawals, etc.
Note: Before spamming this function, the griefer would need to run createUserFundingAccount() once, but at a small gas cost.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the marginAccountDeposit function of a tradable side vault contract. The function accepts a deposit amount but does not enforce a lower bound, allowing callers to submit a deposit of zero tokens. When the function is executed, it triggers a LayerZero cross‑chain message that consumes ether from the vault’s balance to pay for the message transmission. Because the contract refunds the caller for the gas used by the LayerZero message, a zero‑amount deposit results in a net loss of ether from the vault while the caller receives a refund. An attacker can invoke marginAccountDeposit repeatedly, even multiple times within a single transaction, draining ether from the side vault without providing any value. The attack requires only a single call to createUserFundingAccount, which costs a negligible amount of gas, after which the attacker can spam the deposit function indefinitely. This behavior creates a denial‑of‑service condition: as the vault’s ether balance diminishes, other legitimate users on the same chain are unable to perform deposits, withdrawals, or other interactions because the contract no longer has the funds needed to cover LayerZero messaging. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by ThreeSigma, where the lack of input validation and the unexpected refund mechanism were identified as logical flaws. The problem is subtle because a zero‑value deposit appears harmless and the contract does not revert; the loss of ether is hidden behind the gas refund, making it difficult to notice until the vault’s balance is significantly reduced. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum non‑zero deposit amount or require the depositor to cover the cost of the LayerZero message directly, thereby preventing the net ether drain and restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the side vault. This class of bug can be described as an unchecked input leading to a resource‑draining external call, which violates the business logic that deposits must increase the vault’s balance and that the contract should not lose funds on empty operations.

title: Possible to mint or burn infinite shares, stealing all rewards or making transfers fail
description:
Increasing shares infinitely allows an attacker to steal all rewards. It’s possible by doing:
1. In _isExcludedFromRewards(), the condition addr.code.length > 0 && !isOptin[addr] will return false if the contract is in the constructor, enabling - 1. transfer Trestle no a new contract, 2. after the constructor, move the funds to another address, which won't reduce shares as the contract has not opted in.
2. Calling rewardOptIn() with a blacklisted address will increase shares infinitely as _isExcludedFromRewards() will always return true, increasing shares every time (not possible anymore as addresses can not be blacklisted post dead block period).
3. Removing from the blacklist a smart contract that has not opted in will keep increasing shares every time, as _isExcludedFromRewards() will always return true.
Decreasing shares to 0 will mean reward eligible accounts (EOAs or smart contracts that have opted in) with previous non 0 balance will always revert when transferring shares (either from or to). It’s possible to do this in the 2 following aways:
1. rewardOptout() will keep decreasing shares if called by an EOA or in the constructor of a smart contract, as _isExcludedFromRewards() will always return false.
2. _addToBlacklist() will keep decreasing shares if addr is an EOA or a smart contract that has opted in, as will always return false (not possible anymore as the dead block period is over).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that allows an attacker to manipulate the share accounting of a reward‑bearing token, effectively minting or burning an unlimited number of shares. The root cause lies in the _isExcludedFromRewards() helper, which decides whether an address is treated as excluded from reward calculations based on two conditions: the address must contain contract code (addr.code.length > 0) and must not have opted‑in ( !isOptin[addr] ). During a contract’s constructor the code size is still zero, causing the first condition to evaluate to false. Consequently, a contract that receives tokens while still in construction is mistakenly considered non‑excluded, and later, after construction finishes, the contract can move the received tokens to another address without the share balance being reduced. By repeatedly performing a transfer to a freshly deployed contract in its constructor and then moving the tokens out, the attacker can increase its share balance without bound, allowing it to claim all future reward distributions. A similar effect can be triggered by calling rewardOptIn() with an address that is blacklisted; because the blacklist check forces _isExcludedFromRewards() to always return true, each call inflates the share count indefinitely. Removing a blacklisted contract from the blacklist after it has never opted‑in also leaves _isExcludedFromRewards() permanently true, producing the same infinite‑mint effect. Conversely, the share balance can be driven to zero, causing any subsequent transfer involving reward‑eligible accounts (EOAs or contracts that have opted‑in) to revert. This can be achieved by invoking rewardOptOut() from an EOA or from a contract’s constructor, where _isExcludedFromRewards() stays false, or by adding an address to the blacklist after it has opted‑in, which forces the share subtraction logic to run repeatedly. The impact is two‑fold: an attacker can either drain all reward tokens by inflating its share share, or they can create a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate transfers fail because the sender’s share balance is zero. The issue manifests only under specific edge‑cases – during contract construction, when interacting with blacklisted addresses, or when using the opt‑in/opt‑out functions after the dead‑block period has elapsed. All token holders, reward participants, and the protocol itself are affected because the reward distribution logic no longer reflects the true ownership of shares. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward eligibility checks and identified that the combination of code‑size detection and blacklist/opt‑in state could be abused. It is hard to notice because the normal execution path (non‑constructor calls) behaves correctly, and the blacklist logic appears to be a one‑time safeguard, masking the hidden state transition during construction. To remediate the issue, the contract should treat contracts in construction as excluded from rewards, either by checking the deployment flag or by deferring reward eligibility until after construction completes. The blacklist should be immutable after the dead‑block period, and rewardOptIn/OptOut should enforce that share adjustments cannot be performed on addresses that are currently excluded. Additionally, the share accounting functions should include explicit safeguards that prevent share balances from growing or shrinking beyond logical limits, and any share change should be validated against the actual token balance to ensure consistency.

title: address(0) can be added as a pair, triggering taxes on burn
description: A pair with zero address may be added to the pairs mapping which means burns will be taxed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the ability to register the zero address (address(0)) as a liquidity pair in the contract's internal pairs mapping. The root cause is that the function that records a new AMM pair does not validate that the supplied address is non‑zero before inserting it into the mapping. Because the contract later treats any entry in the pairs mapping as a taxable pair, a burn operation that sends tokens to address(0) is mistakenly identified as a transfer to a taxable pair, causing the burn to be subject to the contract's tax logic. An attacker or a careless user can trigger this by calling the pair‑registration function with address(0) or by exploiting a public interface that allows arbitrary pair addition. Once the zero address is present, any subsequent token burn will incur the same tax that would normally be applied to a regular trade, reducing the amount of tokens that are actually destroyed and effectively diverting a portion of the burned amount to the tax collector. This leads to unexpected loss of funds for token holders who expect a full burn, and it breaks the accounting assumption that burning tokens does not generate tax revenue. The issue manifests whenever a burn is performed after the zero address has been added to the pairs mapping; it does not require any special permissions beyond the ability to add a pair. Users see a discrepancy between the amount they intended to burn and the amount that is deducted from their balance, often observing that their balance decreases by less than the burn amount while the tax address receives an unexpected transfer. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the pair‑registration logic, where the lack of a non‑zero address check was noted. Because the zero address is a valid Solidity value and the contract does not emit a specific warning, the bug can remain hidden until a burn is executed and the tax is observed. The appropriate fix is to add an explicit require statement that reverts if the supplied pair address is address(0) before writing to the pairs mapping, or to use a modifier that validates all external addresses used in pair registration. This falls under the broader class of input‑validation errors where unchecked zero addresses lead to unintended state changes and financial mis‑calculations.

title: SideMarginFundingAccount: Unreachable functions changeAdminUser() and allocateFundingAccount()
bug_full: The contract SideMarginFundingAccount contains two public functions, changeAdminUser() and allocateFundingAccount(), that are intended to be called by an administrator or by the designated user to modify the account’s admin address or to allocate a funding balance. However, the constructor of the contract assigns the admin role to msg.sender, which is the SideVault contract that creates the SideMarginFundingAccount instance, and also sets the vault variable to the same SideVault address. Because the SideVault is the deploying contract, it never gains the privileges required by the internal access‑control checks of changeAdminUser() and allocateFundingAccount(), which expect a distinct admin or user caller. As a result, those functions become effectively unreachable: any transaction sent from the SideVault will fail the require statements, and calls from the intended user are rejected because the contract still records the SideVault as the sole admin. This misconfiguration is a classic access‑control bug where the privileged role is bound to the wrong address at deployment time. An attacker does not need to exploit a vulnerability; the protocol itself cannot perform essential management actions, leading to a situation where a user cannot allocate funding or change the admin, and the protocol may be unable to recover or reassign funds that become locked in the account. The issue manifests whenever a SideMarginFundingAccount is instantiated by the SideVault, which is the normal operational flow, so the bug is always present in production deployments. It primarily affects the protocol’s administrators, the end‑users who expect to manage their margin accounts, and any funds that should be allocated through allocateFundingAccount(). The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the constructor and the access‑control logic of the two functions. Because the functions exist and compile without errors, the bug can be subtle and may only be noticed when a user attempts to call them and receives a generic “unauthorized” revert, which could be mistaken for a temporary issue rather than a design flaw. To remediate the issue, the constructor should assign the admin role to the intended administrator address (for example, a separate governance address or the user itself) instead of msg.sender, or the admin variable should be removed entirely and the functions should be protected by a modifier that allows the designated user to call them. Adding unit tests that verify successful calls to changeAdminUser() and allocateFundingAccount() after deployment would also prevent regression. In summary, the bug is an access‑control misassignment that renders critical management functions unreachable, causing potential fund lock‑up and breaking expected business logic around margin account administration.

title: `TSender.huff` and `TSender_NoCheck.huff` contracts will transfer funds to wrong addresses when called with specific calldata.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a calldata‑offset mismatch in the Huff implementations of the TSender contract. The contract hard‑codes static positions for the recipients and amounts arrays (for example RECIPIENTONE_OFFSET = 0xa4) and then computes the distance between those two offsets to locate each recipient element. In Solidity and Vyper the ABI does not guarantee a fixed order for the dynamic‑type offsets, so a caller can supply the same logical arguments with the offsets swapped. When the calldata is formatted with the amounts offset before the recipients offset (Calldata B), the hard‑coded subtraction yields zero, causing the code to read the amount value as if it were an address. Consequently the transfer function is invoked with the amount as the recipient address and the correct amount as the value, e.g. transfer(0x64, 0x64) instead of transfer(0x4dba…108c, 0x64). From the user’s point of view the airdrop appears to succeed – the transaction does not revert – but the intended recipient receives no tokens while an unexpected address (the numeric amount interpreted as an address) receives the funds. This breaks the business logic that the contract should distribute tokens to a list of recipients, leading to loss or misallocation of funds. The issue occurs whenever the Huff contracts are called with dynamic‑array arguments whose calldata offsets are not in the exact order expected by the hard‑coded values. It affects any user or protocol that relies on the TSender.huff or TSender_NoCheck.huff contracts for token airdrops, potentially causing unrecoverable loss of tokens. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by constructing two equivalent calldata payloads and observing that the Huff contracts behaved differently from the reference Solidity/Yul implementations. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an error; the only symptom is an unexpected token balance change. The proper fix is to remove all hard‑coded offsets for dynamic types and instead parse the calldata at runtime using the standard ABI decoding logic, ensuring that the offsets are read from the calldata itself rather than assumed. This eliminates the reliance on a specific ordering and prevents the wrong address from being used in the transfer call.

title: Malicious actors can grief the LP contribution
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The ULTI protocol's deposit() function accepts a deadline parameter that is intended to limit the time window for a deposit transaction. The function forwards this deadline through several internal calls, ultimately to the nonfungiblePositionManager.increaseLiquidity() call. However, the contract does not check whether block.timestamp exceeds the supplied deadline before invoking the liquidity addition. As a result, an attacker can submit a deposit with a deadline that is already in the past. When the internal increaseLiquidity call is executed, it reverts, but the surrounding try/catch block swallows the error and continues execution. The catch block deliberately ignores the failure, leaving the tokens that were meant for liquidity (inputTokenForLP and ultiForLP) locked inside the contract instead of being added to the pool. From a user's perspective the deposit succeeds, the contract emits the usual events, but the expected LP tokens are never minted and the contributed assets remain idle. This effectively allows a malicious actor to grief other participants by preventing the protocol from increasing its liquidity, which can reduce the effectiveness of future price‑pump mechanisms that rely on that liquidity. The issue occurs whenever a deposit is made with an expired deadline; it does not depend on the amount deposited or the caller’s role. Anyone can trigger it, but the impact is felt by all users who rely on the protocol's liquidity provision, as the pool may become under‑funded and price impact may increase. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of the deadline parameter and noticed the missing validation. Because the failure is caught and ignored, there is no on‑chain error or revert that would alert developers or users, making the problem subtle and easy to miss in testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unchecked time‑bound parameters leading to silent failure” and is similar to other bugs where a contract silently discards a critical operation. The recommended fix is to add an explicit require statement that reverts when block.timestamp > deadline before any liquidity‑adding call, ensuring that deposits with expired deadlines are rejected. This restores the intended accounting invariant that every deposit either results in a proportional increase in liquidity or is rejected, preventing funds from being stranded and preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: Wrong rounding of TWAP when tickCumulativeDelta is negative
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding bias in the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) calculation used by the contract’s price oracle. The oracle computes a signed tick cumulative delta as the difference between two cumulative tick values and then divides this delta by the elapsed time (secondsAgos[0]) to obtain a time‑weighted average tick. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the result is rounded down for positive deltas but rounded up for negative deltas, effectively increasing the tick value when the price has moved down. This asymmetry creates a systematic over‑estimation of the average tick whenever the tickCumulativeDelta is negative and not an exact multiple of the time interval. The over‑estimated tick is then fed into the price conversion routine, causing the quoted price to be higher than the true market price during downward price movements. Users who rely on the oracle for trade execution, collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or any protocol logic that assumes accurate pricing may receive unfavorable rates, experience unexpected slippage, or see their positions liquidated prematurely. The issue manifests only when the price trend is negative and the division leaves a remainder, which can be hard to notice because the deviation may be small and only apparent over many observations or in edge‑case market conditions. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the oracle implementation, where the auditor observed that the code does not apply a corrective adjustment for negative deltas. It belongs to the class of signed integer division rounding errors, a subtle arithmetic flaw that violates the accounting assumption that the average price should be unbiased regardless of direction. From a user’s perspective the contract may return a price that seems too high, leading to trades that receive less output than expected or collateral that appears over‑valued. The recommended fix is to detect when tickCumulativeDelta is negative and the division has a non‑zero remainder, then decrement the resulting average tick by one to achieve a floor division that rounds down consistently for both signs, or replace the division with a custom function that always rounds toward negative infinity. This adjustment restores the intended mathematical behavior and eliminates the price distortion, ensuring that the oracle’s output matches the true time‑weighted average tick irrespective of market direction.

title: Referrer's contributions are not updated correctly for non-native deposits
description:
On deposits, the _updateReferrals function processes the referral bonuses. In
step 3 of the process, the _updateContributors function is called to update the
referrer's contributions.
```solidity
_updateContributors(cycle, effectiveReferrer, 0, msg.value, referrerBonus);
```
The fourth argument of the _updateContributors function is the
inputTokenReferred which is the amount of tokens deposited by the referred
user. However, the msg.value is passed as the argument, which will be zero if
the deposit is made using the deposit function and not the depositNative
function.
As a result, the totalInputTokenReferred mapping will not be updated for the
referrer. While this value is currently not used in the contract, it is exposed
through view functions, so it could be used to calculate the distribution of
additional rewards via external implementations. In this regard, it is also worth
noting that the whitepaper mentions a "reputation system based on contribution
(deposits, referrals, streaks)" for future implementations.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way referral contributions are recorded when a user deposits a non‑native token. During a deposit the contract calls an internal function that updates referral bonuses and then invokes another internal routine to increase the referrer’s contribution counter. The routine expects the amount of tokens that the referred user actually deposited, but the code passes msg.value, which is only non‑zero for native ETH deposits. Consequently, when the deposit function that handles ERC20 tokens is used, msg.value is zero and the referrer’s totalInputTokenReferred entry is never increased. This discrepancy does not break any on‑chain logic because the mapping is currently only read by view functions, yet it is exposed to external callers and could be used by off‑chain or future on‑chain modules that calculate reputation, streaks or additional reward distributions as described in the protocol’s whitepaper. An attacker could repeatedly refer users who deposit ERC20 tokens, causing the referrer’s contribution metric to stay at zero while still receiving any direct bonuses, thereby potentially inflating their reputation score or preventing competitors from earning reputation‑based rewards. The issue manifests only when the non‑native deposit path is taken, leaving native‑ETH deposits unaffected. It was discovered through manual code review that identified the mismatched argument passed to the contribution‑updating function. The bug is subtle because the affected state variable is not used in core token accounting, so no immediate failure or loss of funds is observable; only the displayed contribution numbers are wrong, which may be missed unless the view data is inspected. To remediate, the contract should forward the actual deposited token amount (the inputTokenAmount variable) to the contribution‑updating routine instead of msg.value, ensuring that the referrer’s contribution statistics accurately reflect all deposit types. This correction restores consistency between the protocol’s accounting assumptions and the data exposed to users and external reward calculators, preventing inaccurate reputation calculations and preserving trust in the referral system.

title: Wrong assumption that the input token will be WETH
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded assumption that the input token used for the ULTI launch is WETH, i.e., an ERC20 with 18 decimals and a value equivalent to ETH. Although the constructor records the token’s decimals, the stored value is never used in any calculation. Constants such as MINIMUM_DEPOSIT_AMOUNT (0.000001 ether) and INITIAL_RATIO are expressed in wei units and multiplied by 1e18, which only makes sense for an 18‑decimal token. When a token with a different decimal count, for example USDC with 6 decimals, is supplied, the contract interprets the amount as if it had 18 decimals. Consequently the required deposit becomes astronomically large (e.g., 33 trillion USDC) and the launch transaction reverts due to the minimum‑deposit check. Conversely, using a low‑value token with 18 decimals but a price far below ETH causes the ULTI token to be severely under‑priced, breaking the intended economic model. The issue manifests during contract deployment and any subsequent deposit or launch function that relies on the hard‑coded ETH‑based thresholds. It affects the contract owner, any user attempting to provide the initial liquidity, and the overall protocol because the token economics become invalid. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the stored inputTokenDecimals with the actual calculations and noticed that the variable is never referenced. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without warnings and the constants appear reasonable in isolation; the mismatch only surfaces when a non‑WETH token is used. Exploitation does not require malicious code, merely selecting a token with a different decimal precision, which can render the contract unusable or cause severe mispricing. The impact ranges from preventing the contract from launching to creating a scenario where users receive far fewer ULTI tokens than expected, effectively losing value. The recommended remediation is to make the minimum deposit amount, the initial ULTI‑to‑token ratio, and any other token‑dependent constants configurable at construction time and to base all token‑amount calculations on 10 ** inputTokenDecimals instead of the hard‑coded 1e18 factor. This aligns the arithmetic with the actual token precision and restores the intended economic guarantees.

title: DoS on the deposit function due to excessively low slippage tolerance
description:
On deposits, part of the input tokens and newly minted ULTI tokens are added
to the pool as liquidity. As a slippage protection mechanism, adding liquidity
reverts when the difference between the TWAP and the spot price is greater
than MAX_ADD_LP_SLIPPAGE_BPS basis points.
The value of this constant is set to 33 basis points. This means that for very
small variations in the spot price, the transaction will revert, not allowing users
to deposit input tokens.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the deposit (add‑liquidity) function of the ULTI pool. The contract protects users from excessive price impact by comparing the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) with the current spot price and reverting the transaction if the difference exceeds a constant called MAX_ADD_LP_SLIPPAGE_BPS. This constant is hard‑coded to 33 basis points (0.33%). Because the market price of the underlying assets can naturally drift by more than 0.33% between the TWAP window and the spot price, legitimate deposit attempts are frequently rejected. The root cause is an overly strict slippage tolerance that does not account for normal price volatility, effectively making the slippage check a bottleneck. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply waiting for a modest price movement or submitting a transaction during a volatile period triggers the revert, preventing any user from adding liquidity. The impact is that liquidity providers cannot deposit tokens, the pool may become stagnant, and users see their deposit transactions fail with no state change, leading to a loss of confidence in the protocol. This condition occurs whenever the spot price deviates from the TWAP by more than 33 bps, which can happen in normal market conditions, especially on low‑liquidity or volatile pairs. All participants who rely on adding liquidity – individual users, automated bots, and the protocol itself – are affected because the pool cannot grow or rebalance. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the slippage logic and compared it against realistic price movement scenarios. It is hard to notice because a revert looks like a generic “price slippage too high” error, which developers may assume is rare, while in practice it happens often enough to block deposits. To remediate, the slippage tolerance should be increased to a value that reflects expected market volatility, or made configurable or dynamic based on recent price variance, ensuring that normal price fluctuations do not cause unnecessary reverts. Conceptually, this is a mis‑configured slippage protection mechanism that turns a safety feature into a denial‑of‑service vector, breaking the accounting assumption that deposits will succeed as long as the user supplies sufficient tokens.

title: TWAP can be manipulated
description:
The contract uses the TWAP oracle to calculate the price for deposits and
swaps performed through the pump mechanism. The observation window is set
to 18.15 minutes.
However, two issues cause the TWAP to be easily manipulated:
1. Uniswap V3 pools are initialized with an observation cardinality of 1, which
means that the TWAP oracle will only consider the last price update.
2. Even if the observation cardinality is high enough for the observation
window, the number of observations recorded might not be enough.
This means that an attacker could manipulate the price of the ULTI token.
Given that both the deposit and the pump functions have slippage protection
mechanisms, the outcome of the attack would be the DoS for these functions.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a manipulable time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle that the contract relies on to compute the price for deposits and swaps executed through the pump mechanism. The root cause is a misconfiguration of the Uniswap V3 pool: it is initialized with an observation cardinality of only one, meaning the TWAP calculation only incorporates the most recent price update, and even when the cardinality is increased the contract does not guarantee that enough price observations are recorded to cover the 18.15‑minute observation window. Because the TWAP can be based on a single or very few data points, an attacker can trade against the ULTI token to shift the price, wait for the observation window to elapse, and then cause the TWAP to reflect the manipulated price. The attacker can then trigger the deposit or pump functions, which contain slippage protection, to either revert or accept an unfavorable price, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service (DoS) for those functions. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are failed deposit transactions, swaps that revert with slippage errors, or UI messages indicating that the price is out of range or that liquidity is unavailable, even though the on‑chain price appears normal. The impact is that legitimate users cannot deposit or swap, freezing new liquidity and potentially harming the protocol’s revenue and reputation. The issue occurs whenever the contract is used with the current pool settings, i.e., under any normal operation of the deposit or pump functions, and it affects all participants who rely on those functions – depositors, traders, and liquidity providers. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle configuration and identified that the observation cardinality and the number of stored observations were insufficient for the intended window. The bug is hard to notice because the TWAP still returns a price value, so superficial checks may not reveal that the price is based on an inadequate history. Conceptually, the fix is to increase the pool’s observation cardinality to a value that can store enough price points to span the observation window (for example, observationWindow divided by the average block production rate) and to ensure that the contract records a sufficient number of observations before using the TWAP for pricing. This aligns the oracle’s statistical assumptions with the protocol’s accounting logic, preventing price manipulation and restoring reliable deposit and swap functionality.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Poor Practices
description:
Throughout the contracts there are myriad instances of:
Lack of camelcase
Unnecessary local variables which waste gas
Redundant boolean checks e.g. == true
Typos in the comments
Unnecessary for-loops which waste gas and enable DoS
Ineﬃcient computations e.g. feeBalance -= feeBalance
Many functions can be declared external
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a collection of poor coding practices that lead to unnecessary gas consumption and potential denial‑of‑service vectors. The root cause is that the contracts were written without adhering to standard Solidity style guidelines: variables and functions use inconsistent naming, many local variables are declared but never used, boolean expressions are compared to true or false, and loops iterate over fixed ranges even when the work could be done in constant time. Inefficient arithmetic such as feeBalance -= feeBalance is used instead of a direct assignment to zero, and most functions are declared public even though they are only called from outside the contract. These patterns increase the amount of bytecode executed per transaction, raise gas fees for users, and in the case of unbounded for‑loops they allow an attacker to craft inputs that cause the loop to run for a large number of iterations, exhausting the block gas limit and effectively blocking legitimate calls. The impact is that ordinary users may see higher than expected gas costs, refunds may be delayed or fail because a transaction runs out of gas, or the contract appears unresponsive. The issue manifests whenever any of the affected functions are invoked; the symptoms from a user’s perspective are higher than expected gas costs, transactions reverting with out‑of‑gas errors, or the contract appearing to freeze. The audit team discovered these problems during a systematic code review that highlighted deviations from best‑practice guidelines and measured gas usage. Because the problems are subtle style issues rather than explicit logical errors, they can be missed by functional testing and may only become apparent when the contract is deployed at scale. To remediate, the code should be refactored to follow Solidity naming conventions, eliminate unused local variables, replace redundant boolean checks with direct conditionals, collapse inefficient arithmetic to direct assignments, convert loops that have a deterministic small bound into constant‑time operations, and mark functions that are never called internally as external. Applying these changes reduces gas consumption, removes a potential DoS surface, and aligns the contract with industry‑standard security and efficiency expectations.

title: UBT-3 | Payment Pushed Back
description:
Admin can just keep calling createAllocation so the allocation for a particular address cannot be
withdrawn as payoutday keeps getting pushed back.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a privileged‑function manipulation where an account with admin rights can repeatedly invoke the createAllocation routine for the same beneficiary address. Each invocation resets or extends the payoutDay timestamp that governs when the allocated funds become withdrawable. Because the contract does not enforce a single allocation per address or limit the number of times the payout schedule can be altered, the admin can keep pushing the payoutDay further into the future, effectively preventing the intended recipient from ever meeting the withdrawal condition. This occurs whenever the admin role is exercised, typically through a function that accepts an address and an amount and then records a future payout timestamp. The root cause is the lack of state‑guardrails: the contract does not check whether an allocation already exists for the target address, nor does it lock the payoutDay after the first assignment. An attacker with admin privileges can therefore exploit the logic by calling createAllocation in a loop or at regular intervals, each time updating the payoutDay to a later block time. The impact is that users who are supposed to receive a payout see their expected balance remain locked, often appearing as a zero or unchanged amount in the UI, despite the contract holding the funds. From the user’s perspective the interface may show a pending reward that never materialises, violating the business rule that rewards become claimable after a fixed period. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined privileged functions and noticed that the allocation logic lacked idempotency checks. It can be hard to notice because a single call behaves correctly; only repeated calls reveal the delay effect, which may not be exercised in normal testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a one‑time allocation per beneficiary, make the payoutDay immutable after the first set, or require a multi‑signature approval for any admin‑level changes that affect payout schedules. Adding explicit checks that prevent overwriting an existing allocation or limiting the number of admin calls per address would close the manipulation vector and restore confidence that allocated funds will become withdrawable as promised.

title: CA-1 | Inaccurate Comment
description:
In reportResult the for loop that loops through each bettor in the playersSide mapping is gas
expensive and unnecessary.
bug_full: The contract contains a function reportResult that iterates over the entire playersSide mapping to set an isWinner flag for each bettor. This loop is executed on-chain and its gas consumption grows linearly with the number of participants. Because the winner status can be derived directly from the stored result variable, maintaining a separate isWinner mapping and looping through every bettor is unnecessary. The root cause is the design choice to perform an on-chain enumeration of a dynamic mapping, which Solidity does not provide an efficient way to traverse, leading to a gas‑intensive operation. An attacker or any user who triggers reportResult when the participant set is large can cause the transaction to exceed the block gas limit, resulting in a failed transaction and preventing the contract from finalising the betting round. Consequently, legitimate bettors may be unable to claim rewards, and the protocol suffers from increased costs and potential denial‑of‑service. The issue appears only when reportResult is called after a betting round with many bettors; small rounds may not exhibit noticeable gas waste. It affects all participants, the contract owner, and any downstream contracts that rely on the result being recorded. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined gas usage patterns and identified an unnecessary for‑loop over a mapping. Because the loop does not produce visible state changes beyond what can be inferred, the inefficiency can be easy to overlook, especially if the contract is not exercised with a large number of bettors. The appropriate fix is to remove the isWinner mapping entirely and compute winner status off‑chain or by a simple comparison with the result variable inside the claim function, thereby eliminating the costly enumeration. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “unnecessary on‑chain iteration over dynamic data structures” which leads to excessive gas consumption and potential denial‑of‑service. From a user perspective, a transaction that should settle a betting round may revert with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving users with no payout despite having placed a winning bet. The expectation that the contract will automatically mark winners is not met; instead the contract consumes a large amount of gas and may fail, breaking the business logic that winners receive their funds.

title: (Out of scope) Missing unchecked block in TickMath library
description:
Uniswap math libraries rely on wrapping behavior for conducting arithmetic
operations. Solidity version 0.8.0 introduced checked arithmetic by default
where operations that cause an overflow would revert.
Since the lib/uniswap/TickMath.sol library was adapted from Uniswap and
written in Solidity version 0.8.24, these arithmetic operations should be
wrapped in an unchecked block.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing unchecked arithmetic blocks in the TickMath library that Uniswap relies on for price‑tick conversions. In Solidity versions prior to 0.8, arithmetic overflow wrapped around silently, which the original Uniswap code assumes. Starting with Solidity 0.8, arithmetic is checked by default and any overflow causes an automatic revert. Because the adapted TickMath.sol file was compiled with Solidity 0.8.24 but the overflow‑prone operations were not placed inside an unchecked block, the functions getSqrtRatioAtTick and getTickAtSqrtRatio may revert when supplied with tick values that approach the protocol‑defined limits. This happens during normal price calculations when extreme market conditions push the tick parameter close to its minimum or maximum bound, or when a malicious actor deliberately supplies such extreme values. When the overflow occurs, the transaction aborts with a generic execution‑reverted error, preventing the contract from returning a price ratio or tick value. From a user perspective the UI may show a failed transaction, a missing price, or a zero return where a valid ratio was expected, leading to confusion and potentially a denial‑of‑service situation for traders and liquidity providers who rely on these calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the library against the original Uniswap implementation and noted the absence of unchecked blocks after the Solidity version upgrade. It is hard to notice because normal operation with typical tick values does not trigger overflow, and standard unit tests often omit edge‑case inputs. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked‑arithmetic omissions that break compatibility when porting code that depends on wrapping semantics. To remediate, the arithmetic sections in getSqrtRatioAtTick and getTickAtSqrtRatio should be wrapped in unchecked { … } blocks (or otherwise use explicit wrapping functions) so that overflow behaves as originally intended, restoring correct price‑tick calculations and preventing unexpected transaction reverts.

title: Potential overflow risk due to not using mulDiv in _getSpotPrice()
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the internal function that computes the spot price of ULTI when ULTI is token0. The code multiplies a 192‑bit fixed‑point price value (priceX192) by 1e18 and then right‑shifts by 192 bits. Because Solidity does not automatically check for overflow on intermediate 256‑bit values, the multiplication can exceed the 2^256‑1 limit if priceX192 grows beyond 2^256/1e18, which can happen when the ULTI price spikes dramatically. When the overflow occurs the transaction reverts, preventing any call that relies on _getSpotPrice – for example deposit functions that validate the current spot price, automated price‑pumping mechanisms, or any other routine that queries the spot price. The impact is that users attempting to deposit or interact with the pool see their transactions fail with no obvious error message, effectively freezing funds that would otherwise be accepted and breaking the protocol’s pricing logic. The condition required for the bug to manifest is that ULTI is token0 and the market price reaches a level where priceX192 is extremely large; under normal market conditions the overflow may never be observed, which makes the issue hard to notice during routine testing. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that inspected the arithmetic operations used for price calculation and compared them with Uniswap v3’s recommended FullMath.mulDiv pattern. The root cause is the use of unchecked multiplication instead of a safe mul‑div routine that can handle intermediate overflow while preserving precision. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that simply reverts, often reported as “deposit failed” or “price calculation error”, while the user expects the deposit to succeed and the pool balance to increase. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of fixed‑point arithmetic overflow errors in smart contracts, where an intermediate product exceeds the 256‑bit word size. The recommended remediation is to replace the direct multiplication and shift with FullMath.mulDiv (or an equivalent safe‑math library) so that the intermediate product can overflow without causing a revert, ensuring accurate spot‑price computation even under extreme price conditions.

title: Referral bonus cap will be lower than what was intended
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the maximum referral bonus that a referrer can earn. The protocol documentation states that a referrer may accumulate up to ten times the amount of ULTIs they have deposited directly, and the implementation enforces this limit by comparing the total of claimable bonuses against a cap derived from the referrer's own deposits. The code obtains the cap (skinInAGameCap) and then computes the remaining allowance as the difference between the cap and the value stored in claimableBonuses[effectiveReferrer]. The problem is that claimableBonuses aggregates several distinct bonus categories – referral bonuses, streak bonuses, top‑contributor bonuses, and others – in a single array. Consequently, when a user earns a large amount of non‑referral bonuses, those amounts are subtracted from the same pool that is used to determine how much referral bonus can still be granted. The logic therefore mistakenly treats those unrelated bonuses as if they were already part of the referral allowance, causing the remainingReferralBonus to be reduced or even to become zero prematurely. An attacker does not need to craft a transaction; the condition occurs naturally whenever a high‑earning user also participates in the referral program. The impact is that legitimate referrers receive less than the advertised maximum, potentially receiving zero additional referral reward despite meeting the deposit criteria. This undermines the incentive structure, may discourage top contributors from referring new users, and could lead to user complaints or loss of trust in the protocol’s reward system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented referral cap with the actual on‑chain accounting logic and noticed the mismatch between the intended “referral‑only” cap and the implementation that uses a generic claimableBonuses array. The bug is subtle because the cap check itself appears correct – it does compare against a limit – but the variable being checked mixes unrelated values, making the problem invisible unless the interaction of multiple bonus types is examined. To remediate, the contract should maintain a dedicated storage variable that tracks only referral‑earned bonuses, and the cap comparison should be performed against that variable. Alternatively, the calculation of remaining allowance could subtract only the portion of claimableBonuses that originates from referral rewards, leaving other bonus types out of the equation. This change restores the intended economic guarantee that a referrer can earn up to ten times their own deposited amount, regardless of other bonus streams.

title: SQPR-1 | Winners Can’t Get Prize
description: winnersClaimPrizePool uses a push pattern such that it loops over all winners and sends them their funds. If there are too many equal winners then no one would be able to claim due to the for loop exceeding the block gas limit. Furthermore, if a winner is a contract that is unable to receive ether upon .transfer(), no one would be able to receive their prize money.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service caused by a push‑based prize distribution function that iterates over the entire list of winners and sends each winner their share using a direct ether transfer. Because the function uses a for‑loop that processes every winner in a single transaction, the total gas required grows linearly with the number of winners. When the number of equal winners is large enough, the loop exceeds the block gas limit, causing the whole transaction to run out of gas and revert. In addition, the function relies on the .transfer() primitive, which forwards a fixed 2300 gas stipend and reverts if the recipient is a contract whose fallback or receive function consumes more than that stipend or deliberately reverts. If any winner is such a contract, the transfer to that winner fails, the entire loop reverts, and consequently no winner receives any prize. The impact is that legitimate winners are unable to claim their funds; from a user’s perspective the claim transaction either fails silently or appears successful while the balance remains unchanged, leading to expectations of a payout that are not met.
