The issue manifests whenever the claim function is invoked with a winner set that is large or contains at least one non‑payable contract, conditions that can be triggered by normal game outcomes or by an attacker registering a malicious contract as a winner. The bug was identified during a manual audit that examined the prize‑payout logic and recognized the classic push‑over‑pull anti‑pattern. It can be hard to notice because a single successful claim may work for a small number of winners, masking the problem until the winner list grows or a malicious contract is introduced. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “mass‑payout DoS” and “unsafe external call” bugs, violating the accounting assumption that the contract can always distribute the total prize pool to all entitled parties. The recommended remediation is to replace the push pattern with a pull‑over‑push design: each winner should be able to call a dedicated function that transfers only their own share, eliminating the need for a loop over all winners and removing the reliance on .transfer(). This change prevents gas‑limit exhaustion and isolates failures to the individual recipient, ensuring that a single problematic contract cannot block the entire distribution.

title: SQPR-2 | Arbitrary Prize Distribution
description: Anyone can call the function winnersClaimPrizePool and end the prize pool as long as some winners have been added.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the prize‑distribution mechanism of the contract. The function that finalises the prize pool, typically called winnersClaimPrizePool, can be invoked by any address once the contract has recorded at least one winner. Because the function lacks a check that the caller is an authorised winner or that the full set of winners has been added, an attacker can trigger the distribution arbitrarily. Exploitation proceeds by monitoring the contract state until a winner is added, then calling winnersClaimPrizePool. The contract will treat the call as a legitimate claim, close the prize pool and execute the payout logic, which may transfer the remaining funds to the caller or to an empty winner list, effectively allowing the attacker to capture the prize pool or to end the pool without proper payouts. The impact is that legitimate participants may receive no reward, their expected balances remain unchanged, and the total prize amount disappears from the contract. This situation occurs under the condition that the contract has entered a state where at least one winner exists but the winner‑addition process is not yet complete. All users of the betting platform, especially the intended winners, are affected because the promised prize may never be delivered. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the absence of any modifier such as onlyWinner or onlyOwner on the claim function. It can be hard to notice because the UI may simply show a “Claim prize” button without indicating that any address can press it, and the contract may still emit events that look normal. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only addresses that have been explicitly recorded as winners can invoke the claim function, and it should verify that the winner list is finalised before allowing the pool to be closed. In broader terms, this is a classic case of missing access control leading to arbitrary execution of a privileged operation, breaking the accounting assumptions that only authorised parties receive funds and that the prize pool is distributed according to the game rules.

title: UF-1 | Centralization Risk
description: The owner address, 0x3e522051a9b1958aa1e828ac24afba4a551df37d, is not a multi-sig and has potentially dangerous permissions for renounceOwnership, transferOwnership, setRoyaltyAddress, setSpiritRouter, updatePaintRouter, setBaseURI, setMintSize, sweepEthToAddress.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk caused by the contract assigning a single externally owned account (EOA) as the owner with unrestricted authority over a set of privileged functions. Because the owner address is not a multi‑signature wallet and no timelock or governance delay is enforced, the root cause is an overly permissive ownership model that concentrates critical administrative powers in one key holder. The owner can invoke functions such as renounceOwnership, transferOwnership, setRoyaltyAddress, setSpiritRouter, updatePaintRouter, setBaseURI, setMintSize and sweepEthToAddress. By exercising any of these functions, the owner can arbitrarily change royalty payout destinations, redirect router contracts that handle token transfers, modify the base URI that defines token metadata, alter the maximum number of tokens that can be minted in a batch, or withdraw all Ether held by the contract to an address of their choosing. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting in bad faith, can exploit these permissions to divert funds, rewrite token metadata, or otherwise manipulate the protocol’s economic parameters. The impact includes loss of user funds through unauthorized sweeps, unexpected changes to token metadata that break user interfaces, altered royalty distribution that deprives creators of earnings, and erosion of trust in the protocol because the community has no oversight or delay before critical changes are applied. The condition under which this risk materialises is any moment the owner decides to act, since there is no multi‑sig approval or timelock to provide a window for community review. All token holders, creators, and users of the platform are affected because they rely on stable royalty addresses, correct metadata, and secure handling of contract balances. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s access control patterns and identified that the sole owner holds dangerous permissions without any decentralised safeguard. This type of risk is often hard to notice because the functions themselves appear legitimate and are common in many contracts, yet the lack of a multi‑sig or timelock means there is no built‑in protection against insider abuse or key compromise. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may manifest as a sudden loss of funds when a sweep function is called, a token’s image or metadata suddenly changing, royalty payments being sent to an unknown address, or mint limits being altered without announcement. Users expect the contract to behave predictably and for royalties to be paid to the declared address, but the reality is that a single owner can override those expectations. The vulnerability belongs to the class of centralisation and privileged‑function abuse bugs, where excessive authority is granted to a single key without appropriate checks. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the single owner with a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO‑controlled governance contract, and introduce a timelock mechanism for any state‑changing administrative call, thereby providing community oversight and reducing the chance of unilateral malicious actions.

title: UF-2 | Denial-of-Service With Failed Call
description: publicMint relies on multiple external calls which can fail accidentally or deliberately. If just one consistently fails, users will not be able to mint.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the publicMint function caused by unguarded external calls. The function attempts to transfer or allocate wFTM to external addresses as part of the minting process. Because the contract does not isolate these calls or handle their failure, a single external call that reverts or returns false will cause the entire mint transaction to revert. An attacker can deploy a contract that deliberately rejects the incoming wFTM transfer or otherwise forces the call to fail, and then trigger the minting flow repeatedly. When this occurs, every user who tries to mint experiences a transaction that consumes gas but returns no newly minted token, effectively blocking access to the service. The issue appears only when the external call fails; under normal conditions the mint succeeds, making the problem hard to notice during routine testing. The impact is that legitimate users cannot obtain the token, revenue streams tied to mint fees are halted, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer. The bug belongs to the class of external‑call‑failure denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes successful external interactions without proper fallback. It violates the accounting assumption that token allocation will always succeed, leading to a mismatch between expected mint receipt and actual outcome. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the reliance on multiple external calls within a single transaction. To remediate, the external interactions should be moved to a separate transaction or replaced with a pull‑over‑push pattern, allowing users to claim their allocations independently and ensuring that a failing external call does not block the core minting logic.

title: UF-3 | Random Manipulation
description: The random function relies on weak sources of pseudo-randomness from only on-chain attributes. A validator node can manipulate the block.timestamp and therefore the random number. Therefore, the _sendTo address can be manipulated in favor of the validator.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a predictable‑randomness flaw. The contract generates a random number by hashing only on‑chain attributes such as block.timestamp. Because block.timestamp can be set within a bounded range by the miner/validator that proposes the block, the validator can influence the resulting hash and therefore control the output of the random function. The contract uses this random output to select the destination address (_sendTo) for a transfer of funds. By adjusting the timestamp, a validator can bias the selection so that the chosen address is one they control, allowing them to divert funds that should have been distributed to other participants. This issue occurs whenever the function that computes the random number is executed in a block that the validator can produce, i.e., during normal operation of the protocol. Any user who expects a fair random allocation, such as participants awaiting a reward or a lottery winner, may receive nothing or see their balance reduced because the contract sends the amount to the manipulated address instead. The problem was identified during a manual audit that flagged the use of block.timestamp as a sole entropy source and recognized that validators have the ability to manipulate it. The flaw is subtle because the contract still appears to execute successfully; there is no revert or error, only an unexpected transfer destination, which can be mistaken for a normal outcome. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “predictable on‑chain randomness” or “timestamp manipulation” bugs, where insufficient entropy allows a privileged actor to influence contract logic. To remediate, the contract should replace the weak source with a secure randomness pattern, such as using a commit‑reveal scheme, a verifiable random function (VRF) provided by an oracle, or another source that cannot be controlled by a single validator. Implementing a trusted randomness oracle removes the ability of a validator to steer the random output, restoring the intended fair distribution of funds.

title: UF-4 | Mint Failure
description: In publicMint, when performing _earnTo = random() % (_tokenIdCounter.current() +1), there is a possibility _earnTo is equivalent to _tokenIdCounter.current() which yields a tokenID for a token that does not exist yet. Therefore, the subsequent call to ownerOf will fail and the mint will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the publicMint function that can cause the minting transaction to revert. The code selects a token identifier for a reward by computing _earnTo = random() % (_tokenIdCounter.current() + 1). Because the modulo operand includes the current counter value plus one, the random result may equal the counter itself, which corresponds to a token ID that has not been minted yet. When the contract subsequently calls ownerOf(_earnTo) it expects the token to exist, but the call fails for the non‑existent ID and the whole mint operation reverts. The root cause is the incorrect range used for the random index; the developer assumed that the highest existing token ID is _tokenIdCounter.current(), but in most ERC‑721 implementations the counter points to the next token ID to be minted, so the valid IDs are 0 … _tokenIdCounter.current()‑1. The bug can be triggered by any user invoking publicMint; when the random number happens to produce the maximum value, the transaction aborts, wasting gas and preventing the user from receiving the newly minted NFT. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure for minting and potential loss of funds sent with the transaction, as the revert returns the ether to the sender but the user experiences a failed mint and may be confused. The condition occurs sporadically – with probability roughly 1/(currentSupply+1) – and becomes less frequent as the collection grows, which makes it easy to miss during testing because the failure is rare. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the logic of the reward selection and identified the off‑by‑one calculation. It is hard to notice because typical test suites may not cover the exact random outcome that triggers the edge case. To remediate, the random modulo should be performed against the current token count without the extra increment, i.e., _earnTo = random() % _tokenIdCounter.current(), ensuring the selected ID always refers to an existing token. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “index out‑of‑bounds” or “invalid reference” bugs where a contract assumes the existence of an element that may not be present. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction that reverts with no NFT appearing in the wallet, or the balance of owned tokens remains unchanged despite paying the mint fee, contradicting the expectation that a successful mint adds a new token to the account. The bug violates the business logic that every mint should result in a newly owned token and that reward distribution should never reference a non‑existent token.

title: UF-5 | Price Inconsistency
description: In the getPrice function the stepwise price jumps do not account for the following tokenIds: 101, 301, 601, 1001, 1501, and 2301. This is because each if statement utilizes > instead of >= when referring to these tokenIds. Therefore a mint for one of these tokenIds will mistakenly go to the else branch and charge 6 FTM.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the price‑selection logic of the getPrice function. The contract determines the mint price by checking the tokenId against a series of thresholds, but each conditional uses a strict greater‑than (>) comparison instead of a greater‑than‑or‑equal (>=). As a result, tokenIds that sit exactly on the defined boundaries – 101, 301, 601, 1001, 1501 and 2301 – are not matched by any of the intended price tiers. When a user attempts to mint an NFT with one of these boundary IDs, the execution falls through to the final else clause, which applies the highest price of 6 FTM. This mispricing occurs only when the tokenId equals the boundary values, so it is easy to miss during casual testing because most other IDs receive the correct price. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the pricing function, where the auditor noticed that the stepwise price jumps did not cover the listed IDs. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the UI may display the expected lower price, but the transaction reverts or succeeds with a charge of 6 FTM, leading to unexpected overpayment and a perception that the protocol is overcharging or even malicious. The impact is financial loss for users who mint at those specific IDs and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, which expect a monotonic price schedule. The problem is hard to notice because the price tiers appear correct for the majority of IDs and the off‑by‑one condition only affects a small set of values. To remediate, the comparison operators should be changed to >= so that the boundary IDs are included in the correct tier, or the lower bounds of each range should be decremented by one. This correction restores the intended price schedule, prevents users from being overcharged, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented pricing model.

title: UB-3 | Report Result Twice
description: reportResult does not require the event to be finished. Therefore, the result can be reported multiple times and the winner and loser swapped while the treasury fee is taken multiple times.
bug_full: The contract contains an idempotency flaw in the function that records the outcome of a betting event. The function does not verify that the event has already been marked as finished before accepting a new result, so it can be called repeatedly. Because the state variable indicating event completion is never checked, an attacker or any caller can invoke the function multiple times, each call overwriting the previously stored winner and loser and triggering the fee‑withdrawal logic again. This allows the treasury fee to be deducted more than once from the same pool of funds and can cause the declared winner to be swapped with the loser, resulting in an incorrect payout distribution. The vulnerability manifests whenever a participant or a malicious actor calls the result‑reporting function after the first successful report, which is typically after the event has logically concluded. Users who expect to receive a single payout based on the true outcome may instead receive nothing, a reduced amount, or an amount that belongs to the opposite side, while the protocol’s treasury may unintentionally collect multiple fees from the same bet. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state transitions of the betting lifecycle and noticed the absence of a guard such as require(!isEventFinished) before recording the result. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the function is called a second time, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed through unexpected balance changes or missing payouts after an event has ended. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑state‑validation or double‑spend vulnerabilities, where a function that should be executed only once can be replayed, breaking accounting assumptions and allowing funds to disappear from users’ balances. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a check that the event is not already finished before accepting a new result, making the reporting operation idempotent and preventing repeated fee extraction and outcome swapping.

title: Hook address is not correctly represented in the SVG
description: The generateSVGPositionDataAndLocationCurve of the SVG library generates the SVG for the position data. This data includes the address of the hook contract, which is not represented in full, but only the first and last characters with an ellipsis in between. To process the hook address, first, the toHexString function is called to transform the address into a string, so the hookStr variable is 42 characters long and the range of its bytes indexes is from 0 to 41. Then the sliced address is generated by concatenating the first 5 characters, the ellipsis, and the last 3 characters of the hookStr variable. However, the values passed to the substring function are incorrect for the last characters, as endIndex should be 42 instead of 40. function generateSVGPositionDataAndLocationCurve( string memory tokenId, address hook, int24 tickLower, int24 tickUpper ) private pure returns (string memory svg) { string memory hookStr = (uint256(uint160(hook))).toHexString(20); string memory tickLowerStr = tickToString(tickLower); string memory tickUpperStr = tickToString(tickUpper); uint256 str1length = bytes(tokenId).length + 4; string memory hookSlice = string(abi.encodePacked(substring(hookStr, 0, 5), "...", substring(hookStr, 37, 40))); This means that if the hook address is 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48 , the SVG will show the following text: Hook: 0xa0b...6eb This will result in users not being able to identify the hook contract.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate visual representation of a hook contract address in the SVG generated by the library function that builds position data. The root cause is an off‑by‑two error in the substring parameters used to extract the trailing characters of the hexadecimal address string. The address is first converted to a 42‑character hex string, but the code slices characters 37 to 40 instead of the correct range 39 to 42, so the final three characters displayed are wrong. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a hook contract whose true address differs from the truncated version shown in the UI; because users only see the first five characters and an incorrect suffix, they may mistakenly believe the hook is a known or trusted contract. The impact is primarily informational: users are unable to verify the identity of the hook contract, leading to confusion, potential phishing, or loss of trust in the protocol. This occurs every time the generateSVGPositionDataAndLocationCurve function is called, such as when a position token’s metadata is rendered on a marketplace or explorer. The affected parties are token holders, UI users, and any participant relying on the displayed address to assess contract safety. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the string manipulation logic and compared the displayed address with the actual hook address. It is hard to notice because the UI intentionally abbreviates long addresses, so the incorrect suffix can appear as a benign formatting mistake rather than a security flaw. To remediate, the substring indices must be corrected to capture the true last three characters, or the implementation should avoid truncating the address altogether and display the full address or a verifiable checksum. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect data sanitisation and UI misrepresentation, where off‑by‑one or off‑by‑two errors lead to misleading output. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a hook label that reads something like "Hook: 0xa0b...6eb" while the real address ends with "...eb48", causing the user to see a missing or wrong suffix and potentially assume the hook is different from what it actually is. The discrepancy violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that displayed metadata accurately reflects on‑chain data, breaking trust in the visual representation of contract relationships.

title: UB-4 | Same Winner and Loser
description: reportResult does not prevent the oracle from setting the winner and loser to the same side which can lead to loss of funds for many users. Consider a 100 ether bet on one side and 10 ether bet on another, but the 100 ether side is chosen as both the winner and loser. From the calculation in withdrawGain, the contract will attempt to payout a total of 200 ether while it only holds 110. Therefore the users who claim first will deplete the contract and the ones who claim later will experience a complete loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the result reporting mechanism of a binary betting contract. The function that records the outcome does not enforce that the declared winner and loser must be different sides. Because of this missing invariant, an oracle (or any caller with permission to set the result) can submit a result where the same side is marked as both winner and loser. The contract’s payout routine assumes the two sides are distinct and calculates the total amount to be withdrawn by summing the total stakes of the winner side and the loser side. When the same side is supplied for both parameters, the calculation effectively doubles the amount of that side’s stake. For example, if 100 ether is bet on side A and 10 ether on side B, and the oracle reports side A as both winner and loser, the withdrawal logic will attempt to pay out 200 ether while the contract only holds 110 ether. The first users who invoke the withdrawal receive the available funds, depleting the contract balance, and subsequent claimants receive nothing, resulting in a complete loss of their expected gains. This issue manifests whenever the result‑setting function is called with identical winner and loser arguments, which can happen due to a faulty oracle, a malicious actor, or a programming mistake. All participants who place bets are affected because the accounting guarantees of the protocol are broken; users expect a correct distribution of winnings based on distinct outcomes, but instead experience missing refunds or zero balances. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the result‑handling logic and identified the absence of a safety check. It can be hard to notice because the contract may appear to work correctly when the oracle behaves as intended, and the over‑payment only becomes evident when the edge case is triggered. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit validation that the winner and loser identifiers differ before proceeding with any payout calculations, thereby preserving the invariant that the two sides are mutually exclusive and preventing the double‑counting of stakes. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “invalid state transition” or “incorrect invariant enforcement” that leads to accounting errors and fund loss.

title: Fee can be set to 100%
description: In the Vault docs we can see the following: The vault fee is 8% of the rewards earned by the vault. Now let's look at the code: function setFee(uint32 newFee) external onlyOwner { if (newFee > _FEE_BASIS) { revert InvalidAmount(newFee); _FEE_BASIS is equal to 100% meaning that the newFee can be set to be up to 100%. Plus there is not a lower constraint, meaning the fee can be set to 0% as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted fee parameter in a vault contract that can be modified by the contract owner through the setFee function. The documentation states that the vault charges an 8% fee on rewards, but the implementation only checks that the new fee does not exceed a constant _FEE_BASIS, which represents 100% of the reward amount. Because there is no lower bound either, the owner can set the fee to any value between 0% and 100%. This mismatch between the advertised fee and the on‑chain logic creates a situation where a malicious or careless owner can arbitrarily increase the fee to the maximum, effectively diverting the entire reward pool to themselves, or lower it to zero, depriving the protocol of any revenue. The exploit is straightforward: the owner calls setFee with a value of 10000 (representing 100% in basis points) and the contract accepts it, causing all future reward distributions to be taken as fees. The impact is that users who deposit into the vault expect to receive a net reward after an 8% deduction, but instead receive nothing, or receive a much smaller amount than anticipated, leading to loss of trust and potential financial loss. The condition for the bug to manifest is simply that the caller is the contract owner; no additional checks or governance constraints are required. All participants who rely on the vault’s reward mechanism—depositors, token holders, and the protocol’s revenue model—are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the public documentation with the source code and identified the missing fee bounds. It can be hard to notice because the UI may display the current fee value, but users may not monitor changes, and the documentation’s static claim of an 8% fee gives a false sense of security. To remediate, the contract should enforce both upper and lower limits that reflect the intended business policy (for example, a minimum of 2% and a maximum of 15%) and should emit an event whenever the fee is changed. Additionally, the documentation should be updated to clearly state that the fee is configurable within these bounds, and any governance process for fee changes should be made transparent to users.

title: SQDF-1 | Report Result Twice
description: isResultReported is not set to true after the call to reportResult. Therefore, the result can be reported multiple times with varying arguments. Furthermore, line 119 isVotingClosed = false can be used to prevent a winner from ever getting picked in pickWinner().
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical state‑management flaw in the betting contract where the boolean flag that should indicate that a game result has already been reported is never set to true after the reportResult function executes. Because the flag remains false, the function can be called repeatedly with different arguments, allowing an attacker to overwrite the previously recorded outcome. In addition, the contract contains a statement that resets the voting‑closed flag (isVotingClosed = false) which can be triggered after a result is reported, preventing the pickWinner routine from ever reaching the condition that selects a winner. The combination of these two issues enables a malicious actor to manipulate the final result, block winner selection, and potentially divert payouts. Exploitation occurs when the attacker invokes reportResult multiple times, each time supplying a favorable result, and optionally calls the function that reopens voting to keep the winner selection loop from terminating. As a result, users may see the game marked as finished in the UI but receive no payout, balances may remain unchanged, or the contract may repeatedly emit events indicating a winner without actually transferring funds. The bug manifests only after a result has been reported; before that point the contract behaves as intended. Anyone who can call the reporting functions—typically the contract owner or a privileged role—can trigger the flaw, affecting all participants who placed bets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state transitions and noticed that the isResultReported flag was never updated, and that the voting‑closed flag could be reset, a pattern that is easy to miss in automated analysis because the code compiles and the functions appear to work in a single‑run scenario. Detecting the problem in production is difficult because the contract may still emit a result reported event and appear to function correctly on the surface, while the underlying state can be silently altered. The proper remediation is to set isResultReported to true at the end of the reportResult function and to remove or protect any logic that can reset isVotingClosed after a result has been finalized, ensuring that the winner selection path can only be executed once per game. This class of bug falls under incomplete state flag handling and logical reset where missing or mutable state variables allow repeated execution of functions that should be one‑time only, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and leading to funds disappearing or being withheld from rightful winners.

title: SQDF-2 | Arbitrary Voting Results
description: In the resultVote function, the if statements that determines which finalVoteDecision to return are placed inside of the for loop that counts the votes. Therefore the finalVoteDecision will be arbitrarily based on whichever votes happen to be first in the votes list.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the voting result calculation routine. In the function that aggregates individual votes, the conditional statements that decide which finalVoteDecision value to return are placed inside the loop that iterates over the votes array. Because the decision logic is evaluated on each iteration, the final result is overwritten repeatedly and ultimately reflects the outcome of the first few votes processed rather than the true majority. This happens because the loop does not first count all votes before applying the decision rule; instead it applies the rule prematurely, making the final decision arbitrarily dependent on the order in which votes appear in the list. An attacker or a malformed transaction can exploit this by submitting votes in a specific order, causing the contract to return a result that does not match the actual consensus. The impact is that governance proposals, bet outcomes, or any protocol state that relies on a correct majority vote may be decided incorrectly, potentially leading to misallocation of funds, unauthorized state changes, or loss of trust in the system. The condition occurs whenever the resultVote function is called, i.e., during any vote tallying operation, and it affects all participants who rely on the voting outcome, including token holders, bettors, and protocol administrators. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditor examined the control flow of the resultVote function and noticed that the decision branches were inside the counting loop. The bug is subtle because the code still compiles and appears to count votes, so superficial testing may not reveal the discrepancy unless the vote distribution is examined against the reported result. To remediate, the decision logic should be moved outside and executed after the loop has completed counting all votes, or the entire voting mechanism should be refactored to separate counting from decision making, ensuring that the finalVoteDecision is derived from the aggregated totals rather than from intermediate state. This class of bug is a mis‑placed conditional within an aggregation algorithm, often referred to as an early‑exit or premature‑decision logic error, and it violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the final outcome must be based on the complete set of inputs.

title: SQDR-1 | No Check For Max Players
description: registerPlayer does not check if registration exceeds the maxNumberOfPlayers. As a result, contracts that loop over the winners such as SquidBetPrizePool may face a DoS attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the player registration function of the betting contract. The function registerPlayer allows any address to be added to the list of participants without checking whether the current number of registered players has already reached the contract‑defined maximum (maxNumberOfPlayers). Because the contract does not enforce this upper bound, an attacker can submit an arbitrary number of registrations, causing the internal array of players to grow without limit. Functions that later iterate over the player list, such as the prize‑distribution routine in SquidBetPrizePool, will then have to process a potentially unbounded number of entries. When the array becomes large enough, the gas required for a single iteration exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate winners cannot be paid, the prize pool cannot be settled, and the protocol appears to be stuck. The issue manifests when the contract is used under normal conditions but an adversary deliberately floods the registration phase. Users experience symptoms such as “my winnings are not paid out” or “the prize claim transaction runs out of gas and fails”, even though they have correctly placed bets. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the registration logic and noted the absence of a comparison against maxNumberOfPlayers. It can be hard to notice because the registration function itself succeeds and does not revert, giving the impression that everything works, while the problem only appears later during payout. The root cause is a missing input validation check, a classic example of an unchecked limit leading to resource exhaustion. To remediate, the contract should enforce the maximum player count by adding a require statement that compares the current length of the player array with maxNumberOfPlayers before pushing a new entry. This simple guard prevents the array from growing beyond the intended size and eliminates the DoS vector. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unbounded array growth” or “missing bounds check” bugs that break business logic assumptions about participant limits and can cause accounting failures and loss of service.

title: SQDR-2 | Can’t Update Betting Fee
description: The betting fee is unable to be updated because updateBettingFees updates the maxNumberofPlayers rather than bettingFee.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic error in the administrative function intended to modify the betting fee. The function, named updateBettingFees, receives a new fee value but assigns it to the variable that stores the maximum number of players instead of the variable that stores the betting fee. As a result, any attempt by the contract owner or authorized role to change the fee silently fails; the fee value stored in the contract remains the original amount. This bug originates from a simple copy‑paste or naming mistake, where the wrong state variable is written to. Exploitation does not require malicious code; an attacker can simply invoke the function (or rely on the owner’s call) and observe that the fee does not change, leading to a mismatch between the expected fee and the actual fee used in bet calculations. The impact is that the protocol cannot adjust its economic parameters, potentially causing users to overpay or underpay betting fees, breaking the intended revenue model, and making future fee adjustments impossible without redeploying the contract. The condition occurs whenever the owner calls updateBettingFees with a new fee value; the contract will instead modify maxNumberofPlayers, which may be unrelated to the fee logic. Users experience the symptom that the fee displayed in the UI remains unchanged despite the admin’s action, or that bets are accepted with an unexpected fee amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the function body with its specification and noticed the mismatched assignment. Because the function does not revert or emit an error, the bug can be hard to notice unless the fee value is explicitly read after the call. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect state variable updates or miswired assignments, a common logical flaw that bypasses intended governance changes. To remediate, the function should assign the incoming parameter to the bettingFee storage variable (e.g., bettingFee = _newBettingFee) and optionally emit an event confirming the update. This correction restores the ability for the protocol to modify its fee and aligns on‑chain state with off‑chain expectations.

title: Users can't request to withdraw at any time like the docs say
description: In the Vault documentation page, we can see the following answer to the FAQ "How do I withdraw?": You can withdraw your LYX and rewards at any time. But that is not 100% true. There is a pause functionality controlled by the owner present in the contract. Meaning if there is a malicious or compromised owner, he can pause the contract which will affect exactly the withdraw function (other ones as well) and it will become not callable due to the whenNotPaused modifier in this function.
bug_full: Users expect to be able to withdraw their LYX tokens and accrued rewards at any moment, as stated in the Vault FAQ. In reality the withdraw function is protected by a whenNotPaused modifier that checks a pause flag controlled exclusively by the contract owner. When the owner calls the pause function, the flag is set and any subsequent call to withdraw reverts, preventing the transfer of funds. This design creates a situation where a malicious, compromised, or simply over‑cautious owner can freeze user withdrawals, effectively locking assets until the contract is unpaused. The impact is that users see a withdraw button in the UI, click it, and receive no tokens or an error message, contrary to the documented guarantee. The vulnerability is discovered during a security review that compared the public documentation with the source code and identified the mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the pause mechanism is a common pattern and the FAQ wording gives a false sense of unconditional availability. The issue belongs to the class of “pausable contract” bugs where critical user‑facing functions are gated by owner‑controlled state, violating the business assumption that funds are always accessible. To remediate, the documentation should be corrected to reflect that withdrawals are only possible while the contract is not paused, or the contract should remove or restrict the pause capability, add an emergency withdrawal path, or transfer pause authority to a decentralized mechanism.

title: Insufficient input validation
bug_full: The vulnerabilityis an insufficient input validation in the function that allows the contract owner to change the global deposit limit. The function accepts a uint256 parameter without any checks for minimum or maximum values. Because the parameter is stored directly into the state variable used by many deposit‑related functions, an owner who is malicious, compromised, or who makes a typing error can set the limit to an extremely large number, to zero, or to any value that violates the business assumptions of the protocol. When the limit is set to zero, subsequent deposit attempts are rejected, causing users to see no balance change or receive an error, effectively blocking legitimate participation. When the limit is set to an excessively high value, arithmetic operations that assume the limit fits within a reasonable range may overflow or cause accounting mismatches, potentially allowing deposits that exceed intended caps, leading to fund misallocation or loss of accounting integrity. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls setDepositLimit, which is unrestricted apart from the onlyOwner modifier. All participants—depositors, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the deposit limit is a core invariant that protects against over‑exposure and ensures predictable token economics. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the lack of require statements or other constraints on the newDepositLimit argument. Because the function does not emit any warning beyond the DepositLimitChanged event, the problem can be hard to notice until abnormal behavior such as blocked deposits or unexpected large balances appears in the UI. The correct mitigation is to enforce both a sensible lower bound (e.g., greater than zero) and an upper bound that reflects the maximum amount the protocol can safely handle, using require statements or a configurable cap defined by governance. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unchecked input validation leading to invariant violation, which can break business logic, cause denial‑of‑service, or corrupt financial accounting.

title: Signature Malleability in RunaAGI.sol
description:
In RunaAGI.sol the functions whitelistMint(), claimPreSale() and FCFSMint() used ECDSA.recover from OpenZeppelin. We can see from package.json that the version used is 4.6.0. The functions ECDSA.recover and ECDSA.tryRecover are vulnerable to a kind of signature malleability due to accepting EIP-2098 compact signatures in addition to the traditional 65-byte signature format. This is only an issue for the functions that take a single bytes argument, and not the functions that take r, v, s or r, v, s as separate arguments. Reference The functions whitelistMint(), claimPreSale() and FCFSMint() used _salt variable. This variable plays an essential role in the cryptographic scheme, primarily to ensure that each signature is unique, even if the same user requests it multiple times.

The _salt makes it harder for attackers to generate valid signatures unless they know the exact parameters, including the salt, that were used to create the signature. If a malicious actor sees the _salt in the Мempool, they could attempt to submit a similar transaction with the same parameters but a higher gas price to have it processed before the original.

The potentially affected contracts are those that implement signature reuse or replay protection by marking the signature itself as used rather than the signed message or a nonce included in it. A user may take a signature that has already been submitted, submit it again in a different form, and bypass this protection.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature‑malleability flaw that arises because the contract uses OpenZeppelin ECDSA.recover (version 4.6.0) to verify signatures that are supplied as a single bytes argument in the whitelistMint, claimPreSale and FCFSMint functions. ECDSA.recover accepts both the traditional 65‑byte (r,v,s) signature format and the newer EIP‑2098 compact format, meaning the same signed message can be represented by two different byte strings. The contract’s replay‑protection logic records the raw signature bytes as used, rather than the underlying signed message or a nonce, so when an attacker submits the alternative representation of a previously used signature the contract does not recognise it as a replay and accepts the transaction again. The _salt variable, which is included in the signed payload to make each request unique, is emitted in the transaction’s calldata and can be observed in the mempool. An attacker who sees a pending transaction can copy the _salt, create the compact version of the same signature, and front‑run the original by offering a higher gas price. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) a legitimate user creates a signature over a message that includes the _salt and submits a transaction; (2) the attacker monitors the mempool, extracts the _salt and the original signature; (3) the attacker converts the signature to its compact EIP‑2098 form, which has a different byte representation but verifies to the same signer; (4) the attacker submits a transaction with the compact signature before the original is mined, and because the contract only checks the stored raw signature, it treats the compact version as new and processes the mint or claim again. The impact is that an attacker can obtain an additional whitelist mint, presale claim or FCFS mint, effectively stealing the opportunity that should be limited to one per user, and the protocol may issue extra tokens, leading to economic loss and erosion of trust. Users affected are those trying to mint or claim through the affected functions, as well as the protocol that relies on the uniqueness of each signed request. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the OpenZeppelin version and the way signatures were stored for replay protection. It can be hard to notice because both signature formats are valid and the contract appears to reject duplicate signatures only when the byte strings are identical, so the UI may show a successful transaction while the underlying accounting is compromised. To remediate, the contract should be upgraded to a newer OpenZeppelin release (>=4.7.3) where ECDSA.recover no longer accepts compact signatures for the single‑bytes overload, or the replay‑protection mechanism should be changed to track the hash of the signed message or an explicit nonce instead of the raw signature bytes. This class of bug is known as signature malleability leading to replay bypass, and from the user’s perspective the expectation of receiving a single token per signed request may be violated, resulting in either no token received or unexpected token balances appearing for the attacker.

title: Choosing winner can be manipulated
description:
The protocols offers users the ability to enter a raffle by buying tickets. The problem is that the winners of the raffle are input by the owner.
```solidity
uint256 id)
    public
    onlyOwner
{
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < _raffleWinners.length; i++) { // iterate over input array
        isWinnerOf[_raffleWinners[i]][id] = true; // set winner to true
    }
}
```
This is problematic since the owner can chose winners.
bug_full: The contract implements a raffle where participants purchase tickets and expect a winner to be chosen randomly. The contract contains a function that can only be called by the owner and accepts an array of addresses together with a raffle identifier. Inside the function the contract iterates over the supplied array and marks each address as a winner for the given raffle by setting a mapping entry to true. Because the function is restricted to the owner, the owner can arbitrarily decide which addresses are recorded as winners after tickets have been sold. This design creates a manipulation vector: the owner can replace the intended random selection with a pre‑selected list that may include the owner’s own address or addresses of collaborators. An attacker who controls the owner role can therefore guarantee that the chosen winners receive the prize, while honest participants receive nothing despite having paid for tickets. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s fairness guarantees, loss of trust, and potential financial loss for users who expect a chance to win. The vulnerability manifests whenever the owner invokes the winner‑setting function, typically after the ticket‑sale period and before the payout phase. All participants in the raffle are affected because the outcome no longer reflects a random process. The issue was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the owner‑only winner selection as a deviation from standard decentralized raffle designs. The problem can be difficult to notice because the function may be presented as an administrative utility and does not contain obvious arithmetic errors; the malicious behavior is logical rather than syntactic. To remediate the issue the contract should remove any owner‑controlled winner assignment and instead use a verifiable randomness source such as Chainlink VRF to compute winners on‑chain in a trust‑less manner. This change restores the intended probabilistic selection, ensures that no single party can dictate the outcome, and aligns the contract with the expected business logic that each ticket holder has an equal chance of winning.

title: When The Owner Uses mintToWallet() , saleSupplyMinted Is Not Incremented
description:
The mintToWallet() function in RunaAGI.sol is used only by the owner to mint NFT to the wallet but in the for loop where NFTs are minted, it is forgotten to add a saleSupplyMinted update. The function increases _totalSupply each time a token is minted but does not adjust the saleSupplyMinted counter. This counter tracks how many tokens have been sold or allocated during specific sale events. Additionally, because of this, the admin can accidentally set the sale supply lower than the minted supply.

By not increasing saleSupplyMinted when minting tokens through mintToWallet, the contract might inaccurately represent how many tokens are left for sale under the sale-specific conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑tracking inconsistency in the owner‑only mintToWallet function of the RunaAGI contract. The function loops to mint a number of NFTs, correctly increasing the global _totalSupply counter for each token, but it fails to update the saleSupplyMinted counter that records how many tokens have been allocated during a sale event. The root cause is a missing increment statement inside the minting loop, so the contract’s accounting for tokens sold or reserved for a sale becomes inaccurate. An attacker who controls the owner role can mint tokens to any wallet without this activity being reflected in the saleSupplyMinted metric. Because the saleSupplyMinted value remains lower than the actual number of minted tokens, the admin may later configure the sale supply limit to a value that is unintentionally lower than the already minted supply, causing the sale logic to believe the supply is exhausted or to permit additional minting beyond the intended cap. This can lead to several impacts: the protocol may block legitimate buyers because the UI shows zero tokens left while tokens actually exist, or conversely it may allow overselling, breaking the token economics and undermining trust. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls mintToWallet, which is intended for administrative distribution of NFTs. Users affected include the protocol’s buyers who may see missing refunds or unavailable purchases, and the project team who may be unable to enforce the advertised sale limits. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the behavior of the saleSupplyMinted variable against the total supply after owner minting operations. It is subtle because the overall token count appears correct, so typical balance checks do not reveal the discrepancy; only the sale‑specific counter is off, which may only be visible in internal accounting or UI elements that display remaining sale inventory. To remediate, the mintToWallet loop should include a saleSupplyMinted++ (or equivalent) for each minted token, ensuring that both total supply and sale‑specific supply remain synchronized. This aligns the contract’s accounting with its business logic that saleSupplyMinted must always reflect the number of tokens allocated through any minting path.

title: Refunds for losing tickets aren't registered
description:
When users buy tickets for a raffle and don't win, 90 % of the loosing tickets value is paid back to users in the form of XP. This is done be calling the returnLoserTicketXPs function. The function checks if the losing tickets for the raffle are already paid and if they are the transaction reverts.
```solidity
require(losersPaidBack[id] == false, "Ticket prices already paid back");
```
Varonve.md The problem is that the losersPaidBack is never set to true when the refund is done.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw in the raffle contract where the state variable that records whether losing tickets have already been refunded, losersPaidBack, is never updated after the refund operation. The function returnLoserTicketXPs is intended to distribute 90 % of the ticket value as XP to each address that held a losing ticket. It begins with a require check that reverts if losersPaidBack[id] is true, but because the flag remains false, the require condition never blocks subsequent calls. Consequently, any caller – typically the contract owner – can invoke the function repeatedly for the same raffle identifier and receive the same XP payout each time. This can be exploited by repeatedly calling the function to inflate XP balances, effectively creating XP out of thin air and draining the contract’s XP reserve. The impact is that users may receive multiple refunds for a single loss, breaking the intended economic model, giving unfair advantage to attackers, and potentially destabilising the XP economy of the protocol. The issue manifests after a raffle has concluded and the owner calls returnLoserTicketXPs; under these conditions the contract believes the losers have not been paid back, even though they have, because the flag is never set. All participants, especially those who lose tickets, are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that each losing ticket is refunded exactly once – are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the refund logic and noticed the missing state update. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly on the first call and no explicit error is raised on subsequent calls; only repeated observations of unexpected XP gains reveal the problem. To remediate, the contract should set losersPaidBack[id] to true after processing the refunds, and optionally add additional safeguards such as emitting an event, limiting calls to a single execution per raffle, and protecting against re‑entrancy. This correction restores the intended one‑time refund behavior and preserves the integrity of the raffle’s accounting model.

title: Large Centralization Risk
description: The withdrawFunds() Function within the RunaAGI.sol file poses a significant centralization risk. This function permits the contract owner to withdraw the entire balance of funds to any specified address. This capability grants the owner excessive control over the contract’s funds, potentially leading to misuse or exploitation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted withdrawal mechanism that gives the contract owner the ability to move the entire ether balance of the contract to any address at any time. The root cause is the absence of any governance, timelock, multi‑signature, or withdrawal limit checks in the withdrawFunds() function, which means the owner’s private key alone controls the full pool of funds. An attacker who compromises the owner’s key, or a malicious owner acting intentionally, can simply invoke withdrawFunds and drain the contract, causing the on‑chain balance to drop to zero. This can happen whenever the function is called because there is no delay, no review process, and no restriction on the destination address. All participants who have deposited funds or rely on the contract’s escrow functionality are affected: users see their expected balances disappear, refunds that should be available become unavailable, and the protocol’s reputation is damaged. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the centralization of fund control as a design flaw. Because the function signature looks like a normal administrative call, the risk may be overlooked by developers who assume owner privileges are acceptable, making the problem subtle until an exploit occurs. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct owner withdrawal with a timelocked withdrawal request, require multiple signatures, enforce withdrawal caps, or move the authority to a decentralized governance contract, thereby aligning the implementation with the expected trust model and preventing a single party from unilaterally emptying the contract’s funds.

title: Missing disableInitializers() call in the constructor
description: When using Initializable.sol, it's a good practice calling disableInitializers() in the constructor, such that the implementation itself can't be initialized. The call is missing in the Clearinghouse.sol, Endpoint.sol, OffchainExchange.sol, PerpEngine.sol, SpotEngine.sol, ClearinghouseLiq.sol and Verifier.sol (commented out). ClearingHouse may be selfdestructed via the delegateCall().
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the omission of a call to _disableInitializers() in the constructor of several upgradeable contracts that inherit from OpenZeppelin's Initializable.sol. When a contract is designed to be used as an implementation behind a proxy, the implementation itself must be locked against direct initialization; otherwise, an attacker can invoke the public initializer function on the implementation contract. Because the constructor does not invoke the disabling function, the implementation remains in an uninitialized state after deployment. An adversary can therefore call the initializer, supply arbitrary parameters such as a malicious admin address, and gain control over the contract’s storage layout. This control can be leveraged to execute privileged functions, alter critical protocol parameters, or even trigger a self‑destruct via a delegatecall that points to a malicious implementation. The impact is that the protocol’s core components – including clearinghouse, exchange engines, and verification modules – may be taken over, leading to loss of funds, disruption of trading, or unauthorized contract termination. The issue manifests whenever the implementation contract is deployed without the disabling call and before any proxy has been pointed to it; it is especially dangerous in environments where the implementation address is publicly known. All affected parties – users depositing assets, liquidity providers, and the protocol operators – are at risk because the attacker can manipulate accounting logic, block withdrawals, or destroy contracts that hold escrowed funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected constructor bodies and compared them against best practices for upgradeable contracts. It can be hard to notice because the contracts compile and function correctly when accessed through a proxy, masking the fact that the implementation itself is still callable. The proper remediation is to add a constructor that invokes _disableInitializers(), ensuring the implementation cannot be initialized directly. This aligns the contracts with the standard upgradeable pattern and prevents unauthorized initialization, preserving the intended trust model and protecting user assets.

title: Input is insufficiently validated in multiple methods
description: The input validation of multiple methods throughout the codebase is insufficient: In RewardDistributor::setScanPeriod if the _newScanPeriod argument is too big of a number it can result in a DoS in the _distribute method, and if it is too small it can result in lost unclaimed yield for validators In GaugeProxy::setValidatorFee if the _fee argument is more than FEE_BASE it will result in a DoS in distributeToken and also if it is equal to FEE_BASE it will result in the whole rewardAmount getting sent to the validatorFeeRecipient address In TenetVesting::initialize the cliff , vestingPeriod and startTime inputs are not properly validated and can contain too big values which can result in stuck funds in the contract if revocable == false
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of insufficient validation of several public configuration functions across the contract suite. In the reward distributor, the function that sets the scan period accepts any uint256 value; if a caller supplies an excessively large period the subsequent _distribute routine iterates over a range that exceeds block gas limits, causing the distribution transaction to run out of gas and effectively denying any further reward payouts (a denial‑of‑service condition). Conversely, if the period is set to a very small value the contract may skip the accounting step that credits unclaimed yield to validators, resulting in permanent loss of those rewards. In the gauge proxy, the function that sets the validator fee does not enforce that the fee be strictly lower than the defined fee base constant. Supplying a fee greater than the base again triggers a gas‑exhaustion path in distributeToken, while supplying a fee exactly equal to the base causes the reward calculation to evaluate to zero for the protocol and to transfer the entire reward amount to the fee‑recipient address, effectively diverting all earnings. Finally, the vesting contract’s initialization routine accepts cliff, vesting period and start‑time parameters without upper‑bound checks. When these timestamps are set to values that are far in the future or exceed the maximum representable range, and the contract is marked as non‑revocable, the vesting schedule never reaches a point where tokens become claimable, leaving user funds permanently locked in the contract. The root cause across all three cases is the absence of explicit range checks (require statements) that enforce business‑logic limits such as maximum scan period, maximum fee percentage, reasonable cliff length and start time constraints. The issues were discovered during a manual audit that inspected the setter functions and identified missing validation clauses. They are hard to notice because normal operation with typical parameter values behaves correctly; only extreme or malicious inputs trigger the failure modes. From a user perspective the symptoms are missing or zero rewards after a distribution, unexpected transfer of the full reward amount to a fee address, and balances that remain at zero despite a vested amount being recorded. The impact includes loss of earned yield for validators, potential diversion of funds to an attacker‑controlled fee recipient, and permanent locking of tokens for users who rely on the vesting contract. Mitigation requires adding proper bounds checks: cap the scan period to a value that guarantees the distribution loop fits within block gas limits, enforce fee < FEE_BASE and preferably limit it to a small percentage (e.g., 10 %), and validate that cliff, vesting period and start time are within sensible ranges and that start time is not set in the past or an unreasonably distant future. These fixes restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent denial‑of‑service, reward misallocation and fund‑locking bugs.

title: Non-standard ERC20 tokens will be stuck in contracts
description: Tokens like USDT do not return a bool on ERC20::transfer call, while others do not revert on a failed transfer but just return false . Those types of tokens are not properly supported in VestRewardReceiver::sendTokens and TenetVesting::rescueFunds , as the code in those methods uses the normal ERC20::transfer method without accounting for them. This can result in inability to call rescueFunds for USDT for example in TenetVesting , which will result in stuck funds.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract's reliance on the standard ERC20 transfer interface, which assumes that the transfer function returns a boolean value and reverts on failure. Certain widely used tokens, such as USDT, deviate from this specification: they either do not return any value or they return false without reverting when a transfer fails. The VestRewardReceiver.sendTokens and TenetVesting.rescueFunds functions invoke the plain ERC20.transfer method and do not handle these non‑standard behaviours. As a result, when the contract attempts to move or rescue tokens that follow the non‑standard pattern, the call appears to succeed (no revert is thrown) but the transfer either silently fails or returns an unchecked false value. Consequently, the intended token movement does not occur and the funds remain locked inside the contract. From a user perspective, a participant expecting a refund or a rescue of vested tokens may see their balance unchanged, receive no tokens, or observe a zero payout despite a successful transaction receipt. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the token handling logic and compared it against known token implementations. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, making the failure appear as a normal execution path. The bug belongs to the class of token compatibility or unsafe ERC20 handling vulnerabilities, where assumptions about the token interface break accounting guarantees and allow funds to become unrecoverable. To remediate the problem, the contract should adopt a safe token transfer pattern, such as OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 library, which wraps the transfer call and correctly handles tokens that do not return a boolean or that signal failure via a false return value. By using safeTransfer, the contract will detect failed transfers and revert, preventing silent loss of funds and ensuring that rescue mechanisms work for all ERC20 tokens, including non‑standard ones.

title: Validator fee will be lost if recipient is not set
description: In GaugeProxy::distributeToken rewards are distributed to gauges based on validator activity. Also some fee is taken, called a validatorFee , and sent to a different recipient for each validator. The problem is that the code doesn't check if a validatorFeeRecipient has been set - if it hasn't been then the fee would be burned (sent to the zero address).
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution routine of the GaugeProxy contract, specifically in the function that allocates validator fees after token rewards are split among gauges. For each validator the contract calculates a validatorFee and attempts to transfer that amount to a stored address called validatorFeeRecipient. The root cause is that the code does not verify whether the recipient address has been initialized; if the mapping entry for a given validator is the zero address, the ERC20 transfer call succeeds and silently burns the fee by sending it to address(0). This situation can be triggered whenever a validator is added to the system without first setting a fee recipient, or if the recipient is later cleared inadvertently. An attacker or a careless governance action could cause the distribution loop to include such a validator, resulting in the fee being lost for every distribution cycle. The impact is a direct loss of funds that should have been credited to the validator’s fee recipient, leading to lower-than-expected balances for fee earners and a mismatch in the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are always collected. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the expected fee never arrives – the user may see their reward balance reduced, or notice that the fee portion of the reward is missing, while the gauge itself reports the correct total reward. Because the transfer to address(0) does not revert, the bug can remain unnoticed during normal operation and only become apparent when fee recipients report missing payments. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward distribution logic and identified the missing zero‑address check. It belongs to the class of unchecked address vulnerabilities where a contract assumes a stored address is always valid, leading to unintended token burns. To remediate, the contract should explicitly verify that validatorFeeRecipient[validator] is not the zero address before performing the transfer, and either skip the fee or redirect it to a safe fallback address when the check fails. This change restores the intended accounting flow and prevents silent loss of validator fees.

title: The owner of AddressRegistry can take over the protocol
description: Currently most contracts have critical methods only callable by the GOVERNANCE account. This account can be set or updated at anytime by the owner of the AddressRegistry contract, which allows him to set an address that he controls and then exploit all protected methods' functionality for his own gain, for example making him the only recipient of rewards in the protocol.
poc: No poc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ownership‑controlled address registry that holds the reference to the GOVERNANCE account used by most contracts to restrict critical functions. Because the owner of the AddressRegistry contract can update the stored governance address at any time, an attacker who gains control of the registry—or the current owner—can replace the legitimate governance address with an address they control. This replacement gives the attacker permission to call any function that is protected by the onlyGovernance modifier, such as reward distribution, parameter updates, or emergency pauses. The exploit can be performed in a single transaction after the attacker changes the address, allowing them to redirect all protocol rewards to themselves, freeze or modify protocol state, and effectively take over the protocol. The impact is that users may see their expected rewards disappear, balances may remain unchanged while the protocol sends funds to an attacker‑controlled address, and the overall trust model of the protocol is broken. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where the AddressRegistry owner is able to call its setAddress function; there is no timelock or multi‑signature safeguard, so the change can happen instantly. All participants that rely on the governance‑only checks—stakers, liquidity providers, and token holders—are affected because the privileged role can be hijacked. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access‑control flow and identified that the governance address is not immutable and is sourced from a single‑owner contract. Because the change is a legitimate state transition from the contract’s perspective, it does not raise an exception and can be hard to notice without explicit monitoring of the governance address. The bug belongs to the class of “centralized admin takeover” or “privileged address hijack” vulnerabilities, where a mutable reference to a high‑privilege role is controlled by a single owner. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that no rewards are being received, or that rewards are being sent to an unknown address, contradicting the expectation that the protocol distributes rewards to the staker’s address. To remediate the issue the AddressRegistry owner should be replaced with a timelocked contract governed by a multi‑signature wallet or a DAO governor, ensuring that any change to the governance address is delayed and requires consensus, thereby preventing instantaneous takeover.

title: Blocking Through Change of Blocklist Could Trap Tokens
description:
In the normal flow, an account that is blocked is protected from having its funds locked by a call to `forceUndelegate()`, as occurs on line 27 of `Blocklist.sol`.  
However, this protection could potentially be circumvented if the value of `blocklist` is changed to an address which returns `True` for `isBlocked()` (as tested in the modifier `checkBlocklist()`) and if this account was not previously blocked (ie. `forceUndelegate()` was never called on it).  
In this situation, if the account has delegated, its tokens will be rendered irretrievable.
poc:
The blocked account would not be able to call `withdraw()` successfully because of the check on line 531.  
The blocked account would not be able to call `quitLock()` successfully because of the check on line 637.  
The blocked account would not be able to call `delegate()` to undelegate and thereby allow it to make these calls because `delegate()` uses the `checkBlocklist` modifier.  
`Blocklist` has no unblock functionality, so the only way to release the tokens would be through a redeployment of `Blocklist`.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the way the protocol manages a dynamic blocklist that determines whether an account is considered blocked. In normal operation, when an account is added to the blocklist the contract calls forceUndelegate() to lock the account’s delegated tokens, preventing further withdrawals or state changes. This protection assumes that the blocklist address remains constant once an account is blocked. However, because the blocklist contract address is stored in a mutable variable, an administrator can replace it with a new contract that implements isBlocked() to return true for an address that was never previously blocked. When this happens, the checkBlocklist modifier – which queries the current blocklist contract – will reject calls from the newly blocked account, even though forceUndelegate() has never been invoked for that address. As a result, any tokens that were delegated by the affected account become effectively irretrievable: the user cannot call withdraw(), quitLock(), or delegate() to undelegate and unlock the funds because each of those functions is guarded by the same blocklist check. The issue manifests only after a blocklist migration or any update that changes the blocklist reference to a contract with a different blocking policy. Users experience symptoms such as “my balance shows zero”, “withdraw fails”, or “quitLock reverts”, despite having previously delegated tokens. The impact is a loss of accessibility to the locked tokens for the affected accounts, though the total amount of funds at risk is limited because the blocklist contract does not provide an unblock operation and the admin can redeploy a new blocklist to restore access. The root cause is the combination of a mutable blocklist reference and the lack of an explicit unblock pathway, which together allow a newly blocked address to bypass the initial forceUndelegate protection. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the interaction between the blocklist modifier and the delegation logic and noting that the blocklist address can be changed without resetting the protection state. This type of bug belongs to the class of “access-control state inconsistency” or “blocklist migration trap” where state‑dependent guards become out‑of‑sync after a contract upgrade. To remediate the issue, the protocol should either make the blocklist immutable after deployment, add an explicit unblock function that safely restores delegation rights, or ensure that any address newly marked as blocked undergoes the same forceUndelegate flow before the blocklist reference is altered. By aligning the blocklist state with the token‑locking mechanism, the protocol can prevent tokens from becoming permanently trapped.

title: Attackers can abuse the `quitLock` function to get a very large amount of votes
description: An attacker can use a flashloan and the quitLock function to achieve a large amount of votes for one transaction. It can, depends on the implementation of the modules that will use this contract, be used to pass malicious proposals or exploit any feature that depends on the voting balance.
bug_full: The issue revolves around an abuse of the contract’s quitLock function, which permits a user to create a token lock that grants voting power and then terminate that lock within the same transaction or block. The root cause is the lack of a temporal barrier that separates the acquisition of voting rights from the release of the underlying tokens, allowing both actions to be performed atomically. An attacker can obtain a flash‑loan of the governance token, lock the borrowed amount for a very short period (for example, one week), thereby receiving a large amount of voting power proportional to the lock duration, and immediately call quitLock to retrieve the tokens after paying a penalty that is calculated based on the remaining lock time. Because the penalty scales linearly with the remaining lock duration, the attacker can still end up with a net increase in voting influence for the block in which the lock was created, even though the economic cost of the penalty may offset the benefit for larger attacks. This pattern can be exploited in a single transaction: (1) acquire a flash‑loan, (2) create a lock with the borrowed tokens, (3) use the inflated vote balance to push a malicious proposal, and (4) quit the lock to return the tokens (minus penalty) before the flash‑loan must be repaid. The impact is that proposals which would otherwise fail due to insufficient voting weight may pass, potentially leading to unauthorized parameter changes, fund transfers, or other governance actions that depend on the vote tally. The vulnerability manifests whenever the governance module allows the creation and termination of a lock in the same block and does not enforce a minimum lock‑to‑quit interval. It primarily affects the protocol’s governance integrity and any participants relying on the correctness of vote accounting; token holders are not directly at risk of losing funds, but the collective decision‑making process can be subverted. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by a security researcher who constructed a flash‑loan based proof‑of‑concept contract that demonstrated the lock‑and‑quit sequence and measured the resulting vote balance.
