The root cause is a logical flaw: the strategy does not enforce the invariant that the withdrawal amount must be less than or equal to the available assets before delegating the transfer. An attacker or any user can exploit this by deliberately specifying an oversized withdrawal request; the external call will revert, and the strategy contract may become stuck in a state where further withdrawals are blocked, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the requested tokens – is replaced by a transaction that reverts, often showing no error message other than a generic “call failed” or simply returning no funds, leading to confusion and the impression that the protocol is broken. The impact is that legitimate users may be unable to retrieve their deposits, funds can appear to disappear from the UI, and the protocol’s reliability is questioned. The issue manifests whenever the withdrawal function is called with an amount greater than the contract’s current holdings, regardless of the caller’s role. It affects all participants who rely on the strategy to manage stablecoin assets, including liquidity providers and end‑users. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which compared the code paths of the DAI and USDC strategies against the USDT strategy where a proper balance check is already implemented (StrategyUSDT.sol line 163). Because the failure only occurs under an edge‑case input, it can be easy to miss during normal testing. The recommended remediation is to introduce an explicit validation step that mirrors the USDT implementation: before invoking any external transfer, the contract should verify that the requested withdrawal amount does not exceed the strategy’s available asset balance, and revert with a clear error message if the check fails. This class of bug falls under insufficient pre‑condition validation or “missing balance check” vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that a contract cannot dispense more tokens than it holds.

title: MJR-2 Incorrect transfer of parameter values
description: At the lines: StrategyUSDC.sol#L222 StrategyUSDT.sol#L224 the parameters are not passed correctly.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect transfer of parameter values inside the strategy contracts that manage USDC and USDT assets. In the affected functions (around line 222 in StrategyUSDC.sol and line 224 in StrategyUSDT.sol) the code passes arguments to internal calls or external contracts in the wrong order or with mismatched types, causing the called routine to receive unintended data. The root cause is a simple programming mistake: the developer mixed up the positions of the amount and address parameters, or omitted a required conversion, so the callee interprets the supplied value as a different variable. An attacker or any user can trigger the faulty path simply by invoking the public strategy functions (for example, deposit, withdraw or harvest) that eventually reach the mis‑parameterized call. Because the amount parameter is corrupted, the contract may transfer an incorrect token quantity – either sending too few tokens to the vault, sending excess tokens to an external protocol, or even attempting to move zero tokens while still updating accounting records. This leads to a mismatch between the on‑chain accounting and the actual token balances, causing users to see missing or reduced balances, unexpected zero refunds, or share prices that do not reflect the true value of the underlying assets. The issue manifests whenever the strategy executes its core asset‑movement logic, which typically occurs during regular harvest cycles or when users interact with the vault. All participants who rely on the strategy – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting error can erode trust and potentially result in permanent loss of funds if the mis‑sent tokens become unrecoverable. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noticed that the arguments supplied to the low‑level call did not match the function signature defined in the target contract. Because the bug does not cause an immediate revert, it can be hard to notice without detailed tracing of token flows or balance checks after each operation. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated so that each external or internal call receives parameters in the exact order and type defined by the callee, and thorough unit tests should be added to verify that the transferred amounts match the intended values under all execution paths. In broader terms, this is a classic case of an argument‑ordering or type‑mismatch bug that breaks the integrity of financial transfers, violating the fundamental accounting assumptions of the protocol and leading to funds disappearing or being allocated incorrectly.

title: MJR-1 No check _amt value under withdraw
description: At the lines: StrategyDAIypool.sol#L207 StrategyTUSDypool.sol#L207 StrategyUSDCypool.sol#L207 StrategyUSDTypool.sol#L207 there are not valid available balance on the contract. This will lead to the fact that the _WithDRAWSome() function will not always work. At the lines: StrategyDAIypool.sol#L265 StrategyTUSDypool.sol#L265 StrategyUSDCypool.sol#L265 StrategyUSDTypool.sol#L265 the same in the forceW() function.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the withdrawal amount in the Yearn stablecoin y‑pool strategy contracts (StrategyDAIypool, StrategyTUSDypool, StrategyUSDCypool, StrategyUSDTypool). The internal function that processes withdrawals (_WithDRAWSome) and the forceW helper accept a parameter _amt but do not verify that the contract’s current token balance is at least that amount. Consequently, when a user or another contract requests a withdrawal larger than the actual balance—such as after previous withdrawals, slashing events, or external token transfers—the function attempts to transfer more tokens than are available. Because the ERC‑20 transfer will fail or the contract will revert, the withdrawal call may silently fail, return zero, or leave the transaction in a reverted state. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome (“I should receive X tokens”) is not met; the UI may show no tokens received or a zero balance, creating the impression that funds have disappeared or are locked. The issue is a classic example of missing input validation or unchecked arithmetic in financial smart contracts, where the business logic assumes that the requested amount is always bounded by the contract’s holdings. The bug is hard to notice during normal testing because most withdrawals occur when the contract is fully funded, so the missing check does not trigger. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the strategy contracts, where the auditor observed that the balance variable “before” is read but never used to cap the withdrawal amount. The impact is a potential denial‑of‑service on withdrawals, loss of user confidence, and possible fund lock‑up if the contract’s balance becomes insufficient. To remediate, the withdraw logic should compare the requested amount with the actual token balance and, if the request exceeds the balance, either reduce the amount to the available balance or revert with a clear error message. Adding a guard such as “if (amt > before) { amt = before; }” restores the invariant that withdrawals never exceed available funds and aligns the contract’s behavior with expected accounting rules.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect use of a library function
description: At the lines BaseWrapper.sol#L117 BaseWrapper.sol#L198 use the safeApprove() function from the SafeERC20 library. But before giving permission for a certain amount of tokens, you first need to zero this value. Now the safeApprove() function is called only once with a specific value. After the first call, everything will work, but after the second call, the function will be blocked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect usage pattern of the ERC20 safeApprove function from OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 library. The contract calls safeApprove(address, amount) directly without first resetting the allowance to zero. According to the ERC20 standard and many token implementations, changing an existing non‑zero allowance to another non‑zero value can be rejected or can lead to a race condition where the second approval is ignored. As a result, after the first successful approval, any subsequent attempt to increase or change the allowance fails, leaving the contract unable to transfer tokens on behalf of the user. This can be exploited by an attacker who triggers a second approval (for example, by calling a function that re‑authorises a larger amount) and causes the safeApprove call to revert, effectively blocking further token withdrawals or deposits. The impact is that users may see their balances unchanged, refunds may not be sent, or vault operations that rely on token transfers become stuck, leading to loss of liquidity or inability to claim rewards. The condition occurs whenever the contract attempts to set a new allowance without first clearing the previous one, which is common in functions that allow users to deposit more tokens or adjust allowances. The affected parties are token holders interacting with the Yearn Vault, the vault protocol itself, and any downstream contracts that depend on successful token transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noted the missing zero‑reset step. It can be hard to notice because the first approval works as expected and no immediate error is thrown; only subsequent calls fail, which may only surface under repeated usage or after a user tries to increase allowance. The proper fix is to follow the two‑step pattern: first call safeApprove(spender, 0) to clear the existing allowance, then call safeApprove(spender, newAmount). This aligns with the ERC20 allowance change best practice and prevents the approval from being blocked. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect allowance reset” or “non‑compliant ERC20 approve pattern” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes that approve can overwrite an existing allowance safely. From a user perspective, the UI may show a successful deposit but later actions such as withdrawals or reward claims return zero tokens, or the transaction reverts with an approval error, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The business logic that assumes unlimited or adjustable token transfer rights is violated, breaking accounting assumptions that the vault can always move the user's tokens.

title: MJR-2 Outdated _cachedVaults after registry changing
description: Each registry has own vaults variable. It is possible that new registry contains different set of Vaults. In allVaults function we always copy old _cachedVaults BaseWrapper.sol#L71-73. The cache is updated with allVaults produce BaseWrapper.sol#L148-149. So we will never update _cachedVaults prefix part.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑cache bug in the wrapper contract that maintains a list of vault addresses in a private array called _cachedVaults. Each registry instance owns its own set of vaults, and the wrapper provides an allVaults() view that copies the current registry’s vault list into the cache. When the contract’s setRegistry() function is called to point to a new registry, the implementation only updates a subset of the _cachedVaults entries (the suffix part) and never refreshes the prefix part that was copied earlier. As a result, after a registry change the cache still contains vault addresses from the previous registry. This happens because the cache‑update logic in BaseWrapper.sol lines 71‑73 copies the old array and the later code at lines 148‑149 only appends or modifies the tail, leaving the leading entries untouched. An attacker or a careless user can exploit the stale cache by invoking functions that rely on the allVaults() list, such as depositing, withdrawing, or querying balances, and the contract will interact with outdated vault addresses. If those old vaults have been deprecated, migrated, or compromised, funds may be sent to contracts that no longer honor withdrawals, effectively causing a loss of assets or incorrect accounting. The impact is that users may see vaults listed in the UI that no longer exist, attempt a deposit and see no change in their balance, or experience silent failures where the transaction succeeds but funds are locked in an unintended vault. The condition required for the bug to manifest is a registry change via setRegistry() while the wrapper’s cache is not fully cleared or rebuilt. All participants that rely on the wrapper – end‑users, protocol operators, and auditors – are affected because the contract’s business logic assumes the cached list is always up‑to‑date. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the cache handling code and noticed that only part of the array is refreshed. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the UI may still display the stale vault names and no explicit error is thrown; the contract simply operates on wrong addresses. The proper remediation is to invalidate the entire _cachedVaults array when setRegistry() is called and repopulate it with the complete set of vaults from the new registry, or to redesign the function to fetch vaults directly from the registry each time without caching, thereby eliminating the stale‑cache risk.

title: M-1 Security and sanity check bypass in MultiCallOptimizedSwapper
description: As well as similar functions, TradeFactoryExecutor.sol#L126 performs several sanity and security checks: • provided swapper is required to be in _swappers enumerable set • exchange path tokenIn and tokenOut is required to be enabled for given strategy • output token amount is required to be greater or equal to provided minAmountOut. However, the actual code executed by MultiCallOptimizedSwapper.sol#L27 is arbitrary and can accidentally or intentionally bypass these checks. Although MultiCallOptimizedSwapper can be only invoked by the trusted actor onlyMechanics, arbitrary code execution can probably lead to loss of funds in case of accidental bug at off-chain bot. Also, single compromised Mechanic account key can lead to "rug pull" from all connected strategies.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MultiCallOptimizedSwapper contract, which exposes a low‑level call that can execute arbitrary calldata supplied by the onlyMechanics address. In the normal workflow the TradeFactoryExecutor contract performs several sanity and security checks before a swap is executed: it verifies that the provided swapper is part of an enumerable whitelist, that the token pair (tokenIn, tokenOut) is enabled for the selected strategy, and that the amount of output tokens is at least the caller‑specified minAmountOut. Because MultiCallOptimizedSwapper forwards the calldata without re‑applying these checks, an attacker who controls the onlyMechanics account or who triggers a bug in the off‑chain bot that constructs the calldata can bypass all three protections. The bypass allows the caller to invoke any function on any contract, move tokens arbitrarily, or force a swap that returns zero or a very small amount while still reporting success. This can lead to loss of user funds, empty balances, or swaps that do not meet the expected minimum output, effectively breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the onlyMechanics address invokes MultiCallOptimizedSwapper; if that key is compromised or the bot sends malformed data, the arbitrary execution path is taken and the whitelist and minAmountOut constraints are ignored. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes when the auditors noticed that the sanity checks in TradeFactoryExecutor were not enforced by the downstream MultiCallOptimizedSwapper implementation. The problem is subtle because the call chain hides the missing validation behind a trusted actor, making it easy to miss in functional tests that only use honest callers. To remediate the issue the contract should disallow arbitrary calldata execution, enforce a strict whitelist of allowed target contracts and functions, and explicitly validate that the token pair is enabled and that the output amount satisfies the minAmountOut requirement. In other words, the design should follow the same white‑listing pattern used by other swappers in the async directory, removing the ability to bypass security checks. This class of bug is an unchecked external call leading to a security‑check bypass, which violates the business logic that swaps must respect minimum output guarantees and that only approved swappers may be used. From a user’s perspective a transaction may appear to succeed while the received token amount is zero or far below expectations, resulting in missing refunds or balances that unexpectedly drop to zero.

title: M-2 Unnecessary and unrestricted trade() at sync/BancorSwapper
description: BancorSwapper.sol#L52 function has no use and most likely remains in contract by an accident. However, it is unrestricted and can be called by anyone.
bug_full: The contract contains a public function named trade() that does not appear in any execution path and therefore serves no legitimate purpose for the protocol. Because the function is declared without any access control modifiers, any external account can invoke it at any time. The root cause is an accidental inclusion of dead code that was never removed during development, leaving an unrestricted entry point into the contract’s logic. If an attacker calls this function, the contract may execute token transfer or swap logic that was intended to be triggered only by internal mechanisms, potentially moving assets out of the contract, altering internal accounting, or causing unexpected state changes. The impact can range from loss of funds to corrupted balances, making user balances appear zero or refunds missing, and breaking the economic assumptions of the BancorSwapper module. This condition manifests whenever an external actor discovers the function signature and sends a transaction to it, which is possible at any time because there are no guards such as onlyOwner or onlyAuthorized. The vulnerability was identified during a manual source‑code audit where the function was found to be orphaned and publicly callable. Because the function does not affect any visible UI element and does not emit events that would raise suspicion, the issue can remain unnoticed until an exploit is attempted or funds disappear. The appropriate remediation is to delete the unused function entirely or, if it must remain for future use, to protect it with strict access control and ensure that its logic cannot be abused. In generic terms, this is an example of an unrestricted dead‑code entry point, a class of bugs where leftover functions expose contract state to arbitrary callers, violating the principle of least privilege and potentially leading to unauthorized token movements or accounting errors.

title: M-3 Incompatibility with fee-on-transfer tokens
description: Several parts of code have assumption that transferFrom(..., amount) will result in receiving of exact amount of tokens: • TradeFactoryExecutor.sol#L82-L88 • TradeFactoryExecutor.sol#L111-L117 However, actual amount of received tokens can be less for fee-on-transfer tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incompatibility between the contract logic and fee‑on‑transfer (also called deflationary) tokens. The code assumes that calling transferFrom with a given amount will result in the contract receiving exactly that amount of tokens. This assumption is made in several places where the contract later uses the transferred amount for calculations such as trade execution and fee distribution. In reality, fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred value as a built‑in fee, so the actual amount that arrives in the contract can be lower than the amount specified in the call. The root cause is a missing verification step: the contract never checks the token balance before and after the transfer to determine the real amount received. Because the contract proceeds with the originally requested amount, subsequent arithmetic – for example, computing how many output tokens to send back to the user – is based on an inflated figure. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a fee‑on‑transfer token, causing the contract to think it has more input than it actually does. The trade may then produce a smaller output, revert due to insufficient balance, or leave a residual amount of tokens locked in the contract. The impact is that users may receive fewer tokens than expected, see their balances unexpectedly reduced to zero, or experience failed trades without a clear error message. This situation occurs whenever a user trades a token that implements a transfer fee through the affected functions, which are used by the TradeFactoryExecutor component. All participants who rely on the contract – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the transfer logic and identified the hard‑coded expectation of a 1:1 transfer. It can be hard to notice because the ERC‑20 transferFrom call does not revert when a fee is taken; the transaction appears successful, and the UI typically only shows that the trade was executed, not that the received amount was lower. To remediate the problem, the contract should measure the token balance before and after the transferFrom call (or use a safeTransferFrom pattern that returns the actual amount received) and base all subsequent calculations on that real amount. This change aligns the contract with the generic class of bugs known as fee‑on‑transfer incompatibility, where accounting logic assumes exact token transfers and therefore violates the business rule that a user should receive the amount they are promised. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the expected output (for example, “I should get 100 tokens”) and the actual result (often “I got 95 tokens” or “my balance is now zero”). The contract’s failure to account for the fee breaks the expected accounting invariants and can lead to loss of funds or failed trades.

title: M-4 Incorrect slippage check
description: Condition in slippage check is logically reversed: TradeFactoryExecutor.sol#L150
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect slippage validation in the trade execution component of the protocol. The contract is supposed to compare the observed price impact of a swap against a user‑provided maximum slippage limit and reject the trade if the impact exceeds that limit. However, the logical condition is reversed: the code treats a slippage value that is greater than the allowed maximum as acceptable and may reject trades that are actually within the limit. This reversal stems from a simple operator mistake in the slippage check, causing the contract to approve trades with excessive price impact. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a swap request with a deliberately high slippage value; the contract will consider the request valid and execute it, resulting in the user receiving far fewer output tokens than expected. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden loss of value: the transaction completes, but the received amount is much lower than the quoted price, sometimes appearing as if the funds have vanished or the balance becomes unexpectedly small. The impact includes direct financial loss for users, distortion of the protocol’s accounting, and potential arbitrage opportunities for malicious actors. The bug manifests whenever the TradeFactoryExecutor component processes a trade and evaluates the slippage condition, affecting any participant who relies on that contract for token swaps. It was discovered during a security audit performed by the developers, who noticed that the slippage guard behaved opposite to its intended purpose. The issue can be hard to notice because the surrounding code may appear to perform a standard safety check, and typical test cases that use modest slippage values may not trigger the faulty branch. To remediate the problem the slippage comparison must be inverted so that the contract only proceeds when the observed slippage is less than or equal to the user‑specified maximum, restoring the intended protection against unfavorable price movements. In broader terms this is a classic example of a reversed conditional check that undermines input validation and leads to financial mis‑execution.

title: Missing Vesting Period Verification in unstake() Method Puts Users at Risk
bug_full: The contract provides two public functions, unstake and rageQuit, that both forward to the same internal routine _unstake. The business model expects rageQuit to be callable before a vesting schedule ends and to apply a penalty that partially burns the user’s stake, while unstake is intended to be used only after the vesting period has fully elapsed and therefore should return the entire locked amount. Because the unstake implementation does not contain any check of the vesting end timestamp, it behaves exactly like rageQuit. This missing validation is the root cause: the developer reused the internal function without adding a time‑based guard, violating the intended accounting rule that funds become fully withdrawable only after the vesting deadline. An attacker or any regular user can exploit the flaw simply by calling unstake before the recorded end time, believing they are performing a normal withdrawal. The contract will then apply the same penalty logic as a rage quit, resulting in a partial loss of the staked tokens. The impact is a reduction of user balances that is unexpected; users may see their token balance drop after an unstake transaction, or they may receive less than the amount they thought they were entitled to. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user invokes unstake during the vesting window, regardless of the amount or index, and affects every participant who has an active vesting entry. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended semantics of the two functions with their actual code paths. The issue can be hard to notice because the user interface often presents a single “unstake” button and does not highlight the penalty, leading users to assume the operation is safe after the vesting period, while the contract silently applies the penalty. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing state validation or business‑logic enforcement errors, where a function fails to verify a required condition before executing critical state changes. To remediate, the unstake function should include a require statement that checks block.timestamp against the vesting end timestamp, ensuring that the full amount is only released after the vesting period has truly finished. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents accidental or malicious premature withdrawals that would otherwise burn user funds.

title: MJR-1 Losses are not taken into account in the strategy
description: At line: Strategy.sol#L264-L277 the liquidatePosition() function does not take into account the value of the _loss variable accounting in prepareReturn() function. In this case the liquidatePosition() function will always return liquidatedAmount = amountNeeded excluding losses. This implementation may lead to revert when the Vault call the function withdraw function (at line BaseStrategy.sol#L681) by reason of the insufficient balance. Also the withdrawer from vault should incur the losses from liquidation caused by his own withdrawal. However, the Strategy.sol#L264 is ignoring any losses from underlying DAI vault. This may lead to improper accounting of user balances and possible locking of vault withdrawals.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the strategy's liquidation path. The prepareReturn function calculates a variable _loss that represents the amount of underlying DAI that was lost during previous operations. However, the liquidatePosition function, which is invoked when the vault requests funds, ignores this _loss value and always reports that it can provide the full amountNeeded. Consequently, when the vault calls withdraw, the strategy may not actually hold enough DAI to satisfy the request because the previously incurred losses have reduced the real balance. The vault then receives insufficient funds, causing the withdraw call to revert. This situation also violates the intended business rule that the user who triggers a withdrawal should bear the proportional share of any liquidation loss; the current implementation shields the withdrawer from those losses. The bug manifests whenever a withdrawal triggers liquidation while there is a non‑zero _loss from earlier operations, which can happen in normal usage of the YFI‑Maker strategy. Users experience symptoms such as failed withdrawals, unexpected revert messages, or their reported vault balance remaining unchanged while the underlying DAI appears to be missing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by MixBytes, which traced the call flow from BaseStrategy.withdraw through Strategy.liquidatePosition and observed that the loss variable was never incorporated into the returned liquidatedAmount. Because the omission does not produce an obvious on‑chain event, it can be hard to notice until a withdrawal fails or funds become locked. The impact includes potential loss of liquidity, inability to withdraw funds, and inaccurate accounting of user balances, which undermines trust in the protocol. To remediate, the liquidation logic should be rewritten so that the amount returned to the vault is reduced by any outstanding _loss, and the loss should be allocated to the withdrawing user according to the protocol’s accounting rules. This aligns the implementation with the expected accounting model and prevents reverts caused by insufficient balance.

title: Significantly Decreased Entropy in draftWinners() Method
description: In the draftWinners method of the Yeet contract, the initial entropy randomNumber is meant to be split 10 times into smallNumbers which are subsequently hashed to randomData. This randomData is meant to provide randomness for determining the winner in each iteration. However, it’s currently unused and randomNumber is directly used without hashing. Consequently, the entropy for drafting 10 winners is significantly reduced compared to the intended implementation. Currently, the only measure preventing all 10 winners from being the same is that the randomNumber is downshifted by 16 bits in each iteration, i.e. randomNumber >>= 16.
bug_full: The contract includes a function that selects winners by deriving a series of pseudo‑random values. The intended design splits a large random seed into ten smaller pieces, hashes each piece to produce a new random value (randomData), and then uses that hashed value to pick a winner for each iteration. In the current implementation the hash step is never used; the original seed (randomNumber) is shifted and fed directly into the winner selection logic. Because the same seed is only right‑shifted by 16 bits between iterations, the amount of independent entropy available for each of the ten selections is dramatically lower than expected. This reduction in entropy means that the ten winners are highly correlated and may often be identical or follow a predictable pattern. An attacker who can influence or observe the original seed can therefore increase the probability of being selected repeatedly, or can manipulate the outcome by submitting transactions at specific block numbers to align the shifted seed with a favorable value. The impact is that the fairness guarantees of the draft are broken: users may receive no reward even though they were supposed to be eligible, or a single address may receive multiple payouts, leading to an uneven distribution of funds and potential loss of trust in the protocol. The condition occurs each time the draftWinners method is called, which is typically after a funding round or a game round ends. All participants of the protocol are affected because the winner selection is part of the core economic model. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the intended entropy‑splitting algorithm with the actual implementation and noticed that the hashed randomData variable was never used. Because the contract still produces a seemingly random number, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in simple testing; only statistical analysis of many drafts would reveal the bias. To remediate the bug, the contract should replace the direct use of the original seed with the hashed small‑number value (randomData) for each iteration, ensuring that each winner is derived from fresh, high‑entropy data. This change restores the intended randomness, aligns the implementation with the documented design, and prevents predictable or repeated winner selection. The vulnerability belongs to the class of insufficient entropy or weak randomness bugs, where deterministic or low‑entropy sources are used for security‑critical decisions.

title: MJR-1 Correct migration
description: In constructor, rights are granted to spend tokens, which should be canceled when migrating the strategy. Strategy.sol#L171
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the strategy contract’s constructor, where it grants unlimited spend allowances (approve) for external token contracts such as CRV and USDC. These allowances are intended to enable the strategy to manage its assets while it is active. However, when the strategy is migrated to a new implementation, the migration routine does not revoke or reset those allowances. As a result, the old strategy contract retains the right to move the tokens that remain in its balance after migration. An attacker who can trigger a transferFrom call on the token contracts, or a malicious new strategy that re‑uses the old allowance, can drain the assets that were supposed to be transferred to the new strategy. The impact is that users who have deposited funds into the vault may see their balances reduced or completely emptied after a migration that appears to have succeeded. The issue manifests only during or after a migration operation, specifically when the prepareMigration function is executed without clearing the previously granted approvals. Token holders, the vault’s governance, and any downstream protocol that relies on the migrated strategy are affected because the accounting assumptions that the old contract no longer has control over the assets are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the constructor’s approve calls were never paired with a corresponding reset in the migration path. Because approvals are stored on the token contracts and not reflected in the strategy’s UI, the problem can be difficult to notice; the migration may look successful while the hidden allowance still exists. To remediate the issue, the migration routine should explicitly set the allowances for all previously approved tokens back to zero, claim any pending rewards, transfer any residual token balances to the new strategy, and finally revoke the vault’s own approvals. This ensures that after migration the old contract no longer possesses any authority to move user funds, restoring the intended accounting invariants and preventing unauthorized token transfers.

title: Dysfunctional Instantiation of the Yeetback.sol Contract
bug_full: The Yeetback contract is designed to be instantiated with two external contracts: an entropy contract that implements the IEntropy interface and an entropyProvider contract that supplies randomness. The constructor stores the supplied addresses in internal variables and later core functions such as restart, addYeetback and getEntropyFee call methods defined in IEntropy. In the deployed version the constructor receives address(this) for the entropy parameter and a plain address for the provider that does not implement any required functions. Because the Yeet contract itself does not implement the IEntropy interface, any internal call to entropy.someMethod reverts or returns default values. Consequently every function that depends on entropy fails silently or reverts, so users see no refund, no fee calculation, and the contract appears to do nothing even though transactions are mined. The bug originates from an incorrect instantiation pattern: the contract is wired to itself instead of to a dedicated entropy contract, which is a classic case of interface mismatch or misconfiguration. The issue is discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the constructor arguments with the expected IEntropy implementation described in the Pyth Network documentation. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the constructor does not enforce any interface checks, so the deployment succeeds and the UI may show successful transaction receipts while the business logic never executes. The impact is that the protocol cannot perform its core randomness‑dependent operations, leading to loss of functionality, potential lock‑up of funds that rely on entropy‑driven refunds, and a broken user experience where expected payouts are zero. The affected parties include any user interacting with the Yeet contract, the protocol operators who rely on the entropy fee, and any downstream contracts that expect correct entropy data. To remediate, the deployment script must be updated to pass the address of a contract that implements IEntropy and a valid entropyProvider contract as documented by the Pyth Network, and the constructor should include a runtime check that the supplied addresses support the required interface.

title: Incomplete Validation
description:
In the NFTVesting.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- In constructor() if _startTime is set in the past the getTimePassed() function will revert on every call and there claim() will be unusable. The same applies for _vestingPeriod and _tokenAmount to be greater than 0.
- In claim() function check whether the vesting period has started and whether the vesting period has ended. A zero-value check for claimable should be applied as well.

In the Stake.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- stake() and startUnstake() functions are missing zero-value checks.

In the OnlyYeetContract.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- setYeetContract() function missing zero address check for _yeetContract parameter.

In the Reward.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- addYeetVolume() function missing zero address check for user parameter.
- In the addYeetVolume() function there is a require statement which must not allow zero amount to be sent for the tx but the comparison allows zero value to pass.

In the Yeet.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- constructor() missing zero address check for _publicGoodsAddress, _lpStakingAddress and _teamAddress.
- restart() function missing empty bytes check for userRandomNumber parameter.
- setPublicGoodsAddress(), setLpStakingAddress(), setTreasuryRevenueAddress(), setYeetardsNFTsAddress() functions are missing zero address checks.

In the Yeetback.sol contract the following validation checks are missing:
- constructor() missing zero address check for _entropy and _entropyProvider parameters.
- addYeetsInRound() function missing zero-value check for round and zero address check for user parameters.
- addYeetback() function missing empty bytes check for userRandomNumber and zero-value checks for round and amount parameters.
- claim() function zero-value check for the round parameter.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a systematic lack of input validation across several contracts that manage token vesting, staking, reward distribution and game‑related logic. In the vesting contract the constructor accepts a start time that may already be in the past, a vesting period of zero and a token amount of zero. Because the getTimePassed function assumes a future start time, any call to claim after deployment reverts, making the claim function unusable for legitimate users. The claim function itself does not verify that there is any claimable amount, so a user may invoke it and receive no tokens while the transaction succeeds, violating the expectation that a vested balance can be withdrawn. In the staking contract the stake and startUnstake functions lack checks that the supplied amount is non‑zero, allowing zero‑value stakes that waste gas and can be used to manipulate accounting or trigger edge‑case bugs. The OnlyYeetContract, Reward, Yeet and Yeetback contracts all miss zero‑address checks for critical parameters such as contract addresses, user addresses and entropy providers, meaning that a caller could pass address(0) and cause funds to be sent to an irretrievable destination or cause the contract to reference an uninitialized external contract. Several functions also omit empty‑bytes checks for random‑number parameters, allowing callers to submit a zero hash that may bypass intended randomness checks. The combined effect is that under certain input conditions – zero amounts, zero addresses, past timestamps or empty byte values – the contracts either revert unexpectedly, silently do nothing, or accept invalid state changes. From a user perspective this manifests as transactions that revert with generic errors, claim operations that return zero tokens despite a vested balance, staking attempts that appear to succeed but do not increase the staked amount, and balances that remain unchanged after reward‑adding calls. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected each external‑facing function for proper require statements; the missing checks are subtle because they do not affect normal operation with valid inputs and therefore may not be caught by standard unit tests. The bug classifies as an incomplete validation or missing input sanitisation vulnerability, which is often hard to notice until edge‑case inputs are exercised. To remediate, each function that receives external parameters should enforce that numeric values are greater than zero, timestamps are not in the past, addresses are not the zero address, and byte‑array inputs are not empty. Adding explicit require statements with clear error messages restores the intended business logic, prevents funds from being locked or sent to invalid destinations, and aligns contract behaviour with user expectations of successful vesting, staking and reward distribution.

title: NFT of NFT collection or NFT drop collection can be locked when calling _mint or mintCountTo function to mint it to a contract that does not support ERC721 protocol
poc:
The following steps can occur when minting an NFT of a NFT collection or NFT drop collection.

1. The [`_mint`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-foundation/blob/main/contracts/NFTCollection.sol#L262-L274) or [`mintCountTo`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-foundation/blob/main/contracts/NFTDropCollection.sol#L171-L187) function is called with `msg.sender` or the `to` input corresponding to a contract.
2. The OpenZeppelin’s `ERC721Upgradeable` contract’s [`_mint`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721Upgradeable.sol#L284-L296) function is called with `msg.sender` or `to` used in Step 1 as the receiver address.
3. Since calling the OpenZeppelin’s `ERC721Upgradeable` contract’s [`_mint`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721Upgradeable.sol#L284-L296) function does not execute the same contract’s [`_checkOnERC721Received`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721Upgradeable.sol#L400-L422) function, it is unknown if the receiving contract inherits from the `IERC721ReceiverUpgradeable` interface and implements the `onERC721Received` function or not. It is possible that the receiving contract does not support the ERC721 protocol, which causes the minted NFT to be locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of OpenZeppelin's low‑level _mint function when minting ERC721 tokens to an arbitrary address. Unlike _safeMint, _mint does not invoke the internal _checkOnERC721Received hook, which verifies that the recipient contract implements the IERC721Receiver interface and correctly returns the onERC721Received selector. Consequently, if the "to" address supplied to the _mint or mintCountTo functions is a contract that does not support the ERC721 protocol, the token is transferred to that contract's balance map, but the contract lacks any mechanism to acknowledge or forward the token. The result is a locked NFT: the token exists on‑chain and is owned by the contract address, yet it cannot be moved, displayed, or otherwise interacted with by the intended recipient. From a user's perspective the symptom is that after a successful mint transaction the NFT either does not appear in their wallet or appears as owned by an address that they cannot control, effectively rendering the asset inaccessible and potentially causing a loss of value. This situation occurs whenever the collection's minting logic permits specifying an arbitrary recipient, such as in airdrop or batch‑mint scenarios, and the caller mistakenly or unintentionally provides a contract address without ERC721Receiver support. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit that inspected the contract's minting pathways and noted the deviation from OpenZeppelin's recommendation to prefer _safeMint for external recipients. The bug is subtle because the mint transaction does not revert; the contract's state changes as expected, so standard transaction logs do not reveal the problem, making it easy to miss during testing. The underlying class of bug is an improper handling of token receipt verification—a missing safety check that permits tokens to be sent to non‑compliant contracts. The recommended mitigation is to replace every call to _mint (or its looped variant in mintCountTo) with _safeMint, which enforces the ERC721Receiver check and reverts the transaction if the target does not implement the required interface, thereby preventing tokens from becoming permanently locked. This fix preserves the intended business logic of token creation while ensuring that the accounting invariant—that every minted NFT is owned by an address capable of managing it—remains intact.

title: Penalty rate is used for pre-maturity date as well
description: When `_addInterest()` is called post maturity, the penalty rate is applied since the last time `_addInterest()` was called, including the period before maturity.
bug_full: The contract implements a borrowing mechanism that accrues interest over time and switches to a higher penalty rate once the loan matures. The vulnerability lies in the way the interest‑accrual function calculates the amount to be added after the maturity date. When the public addInterest() function is invoked after maturity, the implementation multiplies the elapsed time by the penalty rate for the entire interval since the previous addInterest() call, without distinguishing the portion of that interval that occurred before the maturity date. Consequently, borrowers who do not call addInterest() before the loan expires are charged the penalty rate for days that should have been subject to the normal interest rate. This mis‑calculation occurs because the contract does not split the elapsed period at the maturity boundary before applying the two different rates. An attacker, or simply a borrower who forgets to trigger interest accrual on time, can be exposed to an inflated debt balance: the outstanding principal plus an excessive interest amount that can be several tens of percent higher than expected. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a surprising increase in the debt figure, often seen as a near‑zero or negative payoff after repayment, or a loan that appears to be far more expensive than advertised. The impact is financial loss for borrowers, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential reputational damage for the platform. The bug manifests whenever the contract’s addInterest() function is called after the loan’s maturity timestamp while the previous call was made before that timestamp. It is discovered during a targeted test that compares two scenarios: one where addInterest() is omitted for a month before maturity, and another where it is called a day before maturity. The test shows a discrepancy of roughly 50% in the final debt amount, confirming that the penalty rate is being applied to the pre‑maturity period. The issue is subtle because the contract’s public interface encourages callers to invoke addInterest() at any time, and the calculation uses a single cumulative formula that hides the boundary condition. Detecting the over‑charging requires either inspecting the interest‑accrual logic or performing a side‑by‑side comparison of the debt under different timing conditions, which is not obvious from normal operation. To remediate, the interest‑accrual routine should first compute the normal interest for the sub‑interval that ends at the maturity timestamp, then separately compute the penalty interest for any remaining time after maturity, and finally sum the two results. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce a mandatory addInterest() call before maturity or provide incentives for users to do so, but the core fix is to split the time interval at the maturity point before applying the respective rates. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of "rate‑boundary miscalculations" where different financial rates are incorrectly applied over a single elapsed period, leading to over‑charging or under‑charging of interest.

title: `mintFromFixedPriceSale` for a custom contract can lead to users losing funds
description:
`NFTDropMarketFixedPriceSale.createFixedPriceSale` allows creators to create a sale drop. A creator can create a drop sale for their custom NFT Contract that adheres to `INFTDropCollectionMint`.

`INFTDropCollectionMint.mintCountTo` must return the `firstTokenId` being minted, but it is not clear as to what should be returned upon all tokens being minted. A valid implementation could for instance return `0` if called after the last token has been minted.

But the drop market [expects the call to mintCountTo](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-foundation/blob/792e00df429b0df9ee5d909a0a5a6e72bd07cf79/contracts/mixins/nftDropMarket/NFTDropMarketFixedPriceSale.sol#L207) to revert upon the last token being minted, meaning a user calling it afterwards would lose the ETH they sent.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interaction between NFTDropMarketFixedPriceSale and a custom NFT contract that implements the INFTDropCollectionMint interface. The market contract expects the function mintCountTo, which reports the first token identifier to be minted, to revert when the collection has been exhausted. In practice, a compliant custom contract may instead return a valid numeric value such as 0 after the last token has been minted, because the interface does not explicitly require a revert. This mismatch of expectations means that when a buyer calls mintFromFixedPriceSale after all tokens are sold out, the market contract proceeds to accept the buyer's Ether, believes the mint operation succeeded, and does not perform any further checks on the returned token identifier. Consequently, the buyer pays ETH but receives no NFT, effectively losing the funds. The defect is triggered only after the sale reaches its maximum supply; any transaction submitted thereafter can trigger the loss. All participants who attempt to purchase a token after the supply is depleted – typically end‑users, but also the protocol’s revenue model – are affected because their payments are accepted without delivering the promised asset. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors compared the assumed revert behavior of mintCountTo with typical implementations that simply return 0 on exhaustion. It is hard to notice because the interface documentation does not clarify the required revert semantics, and normal testing may stop once the sale is sold out, overlooking post‑exhaustion calls. The bug violates fundamental accounting assumptions: users expect to receive an NFT in exchange for their payment, but the contract’s logic allows the payment to be taken while the accounting state indicates no asset can be minted. To remediate the problem, the market contract should explicitly verify the return value of mintCountTo and reject payments when the returned identifier indicates no mintable token (e.g., zero), or the custom NFT contract should be required to revert on exhaustion. Either approach restores the invariant that funds are only transferred when a token can be successfully minted, preventing silent ETH loss and aligning the contract’s behaviour with user expectations.

title: Insufficient checks to confirm the correct status of the sequencerUptimeFeed
description:
The ChainlinkUtil.sol contract has sequencerUptimeFeed checks in place to assert if the sequencer on Arbitrum is running, but these checks are not implemented correctly. Since the protocol implements some checks for the sequencerUptimeFeed status, it should implement all of the checks.

The chainlink docs say that sequencerUptimeFeed can return a 0 value for startedAt if it is called during an "invalid round".
startedAt: This timestamp indicates when the sequencer changed status. This timestamp returns 0 if a round is invalid. When the sequencer comes back up after an outage, wait for the GRACEPERIODTIME to pass before accepting answers from the data feed. Subtract startedAt from block.timestamp and revert the request if the result is less than the GRACEPERIODTIME.

Please note that an "invalid round" is described to mean there was a problem updating the sequencer's status, possibly due to network issues or problems with data from oracles, and is shown by a startedAt time of 0 and answer is 0. Further explanation can be seen as given by an official chainlink engineer as seen here in the chainlink public discord:

Chainlink Discord Message (must be a member of the Chainlink Discord Channel to view)

Bharath | Chainlink Labs — 03/03/2024 3:55 PM:

Hello, @EricTee An "invalid round" means there was a problem updating the sequencer's status, possibly due to network issues or problems with data from oracles, and is shown by a startedAt time of 0. Normally, when a round starts, startedAt is recorded, and the initial status (answer) is set to 0. Later, both the answer and the time it was updated (updatedAt) are set at the same time after getting enough data from oracles, making sure that answer only changes from 0 when there's a confirmed update different from the start time. This process helps avoid mistakes in judging if the sequencer is available, which could cause security issues. Making sure startedAt isn't 0 is crucial for keeping the system secure and properly informed about the sequencer's status.

Quoting Chainlink's developer final statement:
"Making sure startedAt isn't 0 is crucial for keeping the system secure and properly informed about the sequencer's status."

This also makes the implemented check below in the ChainlinkUtil::getPrice to be useless if its called in an invalid round:

```js
uint256 timeSinceUp = block.timestamp - startedAt;
if (timeSinceUp <= Constants.SEQUENCERGRACEPERIOD_TIME) {
    revert Errors.GracePeriodNotOver();
}
```

as startedAt will be 0, the arithmetic operation block.timestamp - startedAt will result in a value greater than SEQUENCERGRACEPERIOD_TIME (which is hardcoded to be 3600) i.e block.timestamp = 1719739032, so 1719739032 - 0 = 1719739032 which is bigger than 3600. The code won't revert.

Imagine a case where a round starts, at the beginning startedAt is recorded to be 0, and answer, the initial status is set to be 0. Note that docs say that if answer = 0, sequencer is up, if equals to 1, sequencer is down. But in this case here, answer and startedAt can be 0 initially, till after all data is gotten from oracles and update is confirmed then the values are reset to the correct values that show the correct status of the sequencer.

From these explanations and information, it can be seen that startedAt value is a second value that should be used in the check for if a sequencer is down/up or correctly updated. The checks in ChainlinkUtil::getPrice will allow for successful calls in an invalid round because reverts don't happen if answer == 0 and startedAt == 0 thus defeating the purpose of having a sequencerFeed check to assert the status of the sequencerFeed on L2 i.e if it is up/down/active or if its status is actually confirmed to be either.

There was also recently a pull request to update the chainlink docs sample code with this information, because this check should clearly be displayed there as well.

Inadequate checks to confirm the correct status of the sequencerUptimeFeed in ChainlinkUtil::getPrice contract will cause getPrice() to not revert even when the sequencer uptime feed is not updated or is called in an invalid round.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the ChainlinkUtil contract validates the sequencer uptime feed before returning a price. The contract attempts to protect against a down sequencer by checking the answer field (0 means up, 1 means down) and by enforcing a grace period using the startedAt timestamp. However, Chainlink documentation states that during an "invalid round" the startedAt value is zero and the answer may also be zero until the round is confirmed. Because the code only checks that the time since startedAt exceeds the configured grace period, a zero startedAt causes block.timestamp‑startedAt to be a very large number, which always exceeds the grace period threshold. Consequently the revert never triggers, and getPrice() proceeds even when the sequencer status is unconfirmed or the feed is in an invalid round. This flaw originates from an incomplete validation of the sequencer feed – the contract does not verify that startedAt is non‑zero nor that the answer has been updated after the initial zero state. An attacker who can cause the sequencer feed to enter an invalid round (for example by inducing network delays or oracle failures) can make the contract accept price data while the L2 sequencer is actually down, potentially exposing the protocol to stale or manipulated price information and resulting in incorrect settlements, loss of collateral, or unintended liquidations. The issue manifests when the sequencer uptime feed is configured and a call to getPrice occurs during an invalid round; users see transactions succeed but later discover that the price used was not reliable, leading to unexpected balance changes or failed withdrawals. The problem was identified by the CodeHawks audit team through review of Chainlink documentation and the contract’s logic, and it is subtle because the existing check appears syntactically correct yet is logically ineffective when startedAt equals zero. To remediate, the contract should explicitly require that startedAt is greater than zero before applying the grace‑period comparison, and it should ensure that the answer field reflects a confirmed status after the round has been finalized. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model of rejecting price queries while the sequencer status is uncertain, thereby restoring the integrity of the price feed validation.

title: A malicious User can DOS all offchain orders making them unexecutable and leaving the protocol in an insolvent state. Also all offchain Trades can also be DOSed for honest parties that do not meet the fillorder requirements (no try and catch)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition affecting the batch execution of off‑chain orders in the perpetual market contract. The root cause is that the fillOffchainOrders function validates each order inside a single for‑loop without any error handling; any validation failure – such as an order with a sizeDelta of zero, a mismatched marketId, an invalid nonce, a non‑existent trading account, or a previously filled order – triggers a revert that aborts the entire transaction. Because off‑chain orders are collected into a batch and processed atomically, a malicious actor can submit a large number of deliberately malformed orders (for example, zero‑size orders) that satisfy the signature requirements but fail the size check. When the keeper later calls fillOffchainOrders, the first malformed order causes the whole batch to revert, preventing all legitimate orders in the batch from being executed. This can be repeated at low cost, effectively locking the off‑chain order pipeline. The impact is that honest users see their orders remain unfilled, balances stay unchanged, and the protocol may become insolvent if a significant volume of valid orders is consistently blocked, leading to missed fee collection and potential liquidity shortfalls. The condition occurs whenever off‑chain orders are batched and the contract lacks try‑catch or per‑order error skipping. All market participants who rely on off‑chain order execution are affected, including traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of the fillOffchainOrders routine and identified that validation reverts are not isolated. It is hard to notice because zero‑size orders appear innocuous and the contract does not emit explicit error events for each failure, making the batch failure look like a generic transaction revert. The recommended mitigation is to introduce per‑order error handling: emit an OrderError event and continue to the next order when a validation check fails, and wrap the internal _fillOrder call in a try‑catch block so that a failure in one order does not revert the whole batch. Additionally, the contract should enforce sizeDelta > 0 before batching and consider pre‑filtering invalid orders off‑chain. This transforms the batch processing from an all‑or‑nothing model to a resilient, best‑effort execution, eliminating the DoS vector and preserving protocol solvency.

title: An Uninitialized Variable In The `MarketConfiguration::update` Function Causes The `PrepMarket::getIndexPrice` Function To Revert
description:
The update function within the MarketConfiguration library fails to update the priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds variable, which is essential for the getIndexPrice function to operate correctly. This oversight causes the getIndexPrice function to always revert due to an uninitialized heartbeat check.

In the MarketConfiguration library, the update function is designed to update various market configuration parameters. However, it neglects to update the priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds variable. Consequently, this variable remains uninitialized, defaulting to zero.

The getIndexPrice function relies on the priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds variable to validate the timeliness of the price feed data from Chainlink oracles. When it checks if (block.timestamp - updatedAt > priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds), the comparison always results in true (since priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds is zero), causing the function to revert every time it is called.

This vulnerability significantly impacts the functionality of the protocol by making the price checking mechanism always revert. As a result, it effectively halts the correct operation of any process relying on the getIndexPrice function. Specifically, it renders the entire price validation mechanism inoperative, potentially disrupting market operations.

These are the list of functions that got affected by this vulnerability includes:
PerpMarket::getIndexPrice
TradingAccountBranch::getAccountEquityUsd
TradingAccountBranch::getAccountMarginBreakdown
TradingAccountBranch::getAccountTotalUnrealizedPnl
TradingAccountBranch::getAccountLeverage
TradingAccountBranch::withdrawMargin
SettlementBranch::fillMarketOrder
SettlementBranch::fillOffchainOrders
OrderBranch::simulateTrade
OrderBranch::getMarginRequirementForTrade
LiquidationBranch::liquidateAccount
LiquidationBranch::checkLiquidatableAccounts
bug_full: The vulnerability is an uninitialized storage variable that breaks the price‑feed heartbeat validation logic. In the MarketConfiguration library the update function is supposed to copy all configuration fields, including the priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds parameter that defines how many seconds may elapse before a price feed is considered stale. The function forgets to assign this field, leaving it at its default value of zero. The getIndexPrice routine later checks the freshness of the Chainlink price by evaluating if (block.timestamp - updatedAt > priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds). Because priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds is zero, the inequality is always true, causing the function to revert with an OraclePriceFeedHeartbeat error every time it is called. This denial‑of‑service condition appears whenever any contract component attempts to read the index price – for example margin calculations, liquidation checks, order simulation, and order execution – effectively halting market operations. Users experience symptoms such as “price fetch failed”, “order cannot be placed”, or “account equity returns zero”, contrary to the expectation that the system will provide a current price. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a Forge test deliberately called exposed_getIndexPrice and observed a consistent revert. It is easy to miss in normal usage because the contract does not expose the missing assignment directly; the failure only surfaces when the price‑validation path is exercised. The root cause is a simple oversight in the configuration update logic, classifiable as an uninitialized variable leading to a logic error and denial‑of‑service. The fix is to ensure the update function writes the supplied priceFeedHeartbeatSeconds value into storage, restoring the intended heartbeat check and allowing getIndexPrice to succeed, which in turn re‑enables all dependent accounting and trading functions.

title: Incorrect liquidatable checking for market order creation
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect liquidatable check that is performed when a market order is created. During the simulation of a new order the contract calculates the required initial and maintenance margin and also obtains the account's unrealized PnL for the hypothetical trade. It then calls getMarginBalanceUsd with the unrealized PnL that already includes the sizeDelta of the pending order, producing a marginBalanceUsdX18 that represents the margin balance after the trade would be executed. The code subsequently compares this post‑trade margin balance with the current required maintenance margin (obtained with a zero sizeDelta) to decide whether the account is liquidatable. Because the comparison mixes a future state value with a present‑state requirement, an account that is actually healthy can appear liquidatable and the transaction is reverted with AccountIsLiquidatable. The root cause is the use of the simulated unrealized PnL instead of the current unrealized PnL when computing the margin balance for the safety check. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any trader whose order would change the mark price in a direction that reduces their unrealized profit may be blocked, as the simulated margin balance becomes lower than the maintenance margin. The impact is that legitimate orders are rejected, preventing users from adjusting positions, potentially leading to missed profit or forcing a later liquidation if the position cannot be reduced. The condition occurs only during the market order creation path, specifically in the simulation block before the trade is applied. Affected parties are traders who attempt to open or reduce positions and the protocol because order flow is artificially constrained. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic where the auditor noticed that the same function used for liquidation was being called with a different PnL input. It is hard to notice because the code pattern mirrors the correct liquidation check and the revert message is identical, giving the impression that the check is functioning as intended. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails with an AccountIsLiquidatable error even though the displayed margin ratio is above the maintenance threshold, leading to confusion and a missing trade. The bug violates the accounting assumption that the margin balance used for a safety check must reflect the current state of the account, not a projected state after a hypothetical trade. The recommended fix is to obtain the current margin balance by calling getMarginBalanceUsd with the unrealized PnL calculated using a zero sizeDelta, and compare that current margin balance against the current required maintenance margin, exactly as the liquidation routine does. Aligning the check with the liquidation path restores the correct invariant that an account is only prevented from trading when it is truly liquidatable.

title: User can withdraw all collateral when a position has enough profit so if liquidated no collateral can be deducted
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the margin‑withdrawal logic of a perpetual trading contract. The function that allows a user to withdraw collateral only checks that the account’s margin balance remains greater than the required initial margin after the withdrawal. When a trader’s open position is in profit, the unrealised profit can exceed the maintenance‑margin requirement, causing the total margin balance to be larger than the required amount. Because the check does not consider that the profit is not locked collateral, the trader can withdraw the entire deposited amount, leaving the account with zero actual collateral while the position remains open. If the market then moves against the position and the unrealised profit falls below the maintenance margin, the position becomes liquidatable. During liquidation the protocol attempts to seize collateral to cover the required maintenance margin and the liquidation fee, but because the account holds no collateral, the seized amount is zero. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal margin balance before liquidation, then after liquidation the account shows a negative margin balance while the withdrawn funds are already in the user’s wallet, effectively making the protocol’s funds disappear. The impact is that the protocol cannot enforce its risk parameters, may suffer under‑collateralisation, and loses the liquidation fee that should have been collected. The issue occurs whenever a position has sufficient unrealised profit to satisfy the margin check and the user initiates a full‑withdrawal before the price reverses. It affects any trader with an open position and any party relying on the liquidation mechanism to protect the system’s solvency. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when a test case was added that withdrew the full collateral after the position became profitable and then forced a liquidation, revealing that the emitted liquidation event reported zero liquidated collateral. The problem is subtle because the margin‑check logic appears correct at first glance; it does not differentiate between locked collateral and profit that can be freely withdrawn. The bug belongs to the class of “margin‑withdrawal under‑collateralisation” or “liquidation bypass due to profit‑driven withdrawal”. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a minimum amount of actual collateral – at least the required initial (or maintenance) margin – remains locked in the account for the lifetime of any open position, preventing a full withdrawal while a position is still open. This ensures that liquidation can always seize sufficient funds and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions about locked collateral remain valid.

title: User might be unfairly liquidated after L2 Sequencer grace period
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the price‑retrieval routine that blocks both order creation and order filling during the sequencer grace period after a Layer‑2 sequencer outage. The contract reads the sequencer uptime feed and, if the feed reports that the sequencer is up, it calculates the time elapsed since the last up‑timestamp. If this elapsed time is less than or equal to the constant SEQUENCERGRACEPERIOD_TIME, the function reverts with a GracePeriodNotOver error. Because this check is applied to the same internal function that is used for normal trading operations, users are unable to submit new orders or have existing orders matched while the grace period is active. On Arbitrum, price updates from Chainlink become available almost instantly after the sequencer recovers, so market prices can shift dramatically within the short grace window. Users who hold positions that become under‑collateralised during this window cannot react by adding collateral or executing a trade, yet the liquidation engine may still trigger a liquidation. The result is an unfair liquidation where the user’s collateral is removed and the balance appears to drop to zero, while the UI only shows a generic GracePeriodNotOver revert. The issue occurs only after a sequencer downtime event and only while the defined grace period is in effect, affecting any account with an open position that relies on timely order execution. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the ChainlinkUtil contract and noticed that the same revert logic used to protect against stale price data also prevents legitimate order activity. The problem is subtle because the revert message does not indicate a liquidation risk, and the sequencer downtime scenario is relatively rare, making the bug easy to overlook in normal testing. To remediate, the protocol should separate the sequencer‑grace check from the order‑creation path, for example by adding a flag that skips the grace‑period validation when creating or filling orders, or by moving the check to only guard liquidation‑specific calls. This change would allow users to react to rapid price changes after the sequencer recovers, preventing unexpected loss of funds and aligning the contract behaviour with the intended business logic that liquidations should be disabled during the grace period while trading operations remain available.

title: when fillOrder() , small pnl can cause orderFee/settlementFee to not be fully collected
bug_full: During the execution of fillOrder the contract deducts settlementFee, orderFee and pnl from the trader’s collateral by calling withdrawMarginUsd for each component. withdrawMarginUsd converts the USD amount to a collateral amount using requiredMarginInCollateralX18 = amountUsdX18.div(marginCollateralPriceUsdX18). Because the division is performed with integer arithmetic that rounds down, a very small pnl (dust) can produce a required collateral value of zero. When this happens the condition marginCollateralBalanceX18.gte(requiredMarginInCollateralX18) evaluates to true, the function returns isMissingMargin = false and the outer loop in deductAccountMargin interprets the fee as fully satisfied, breaking out of the collateral‑priority loop. Consequently the remaining settlementFee or orderFee that should have been taken from the next collateral type is never deducted. The protocol therefore collects less fee than intended, leading to a shortfall in revenue and a mismatch between expected and actual fee balances. The bug appears only when the pnl amount is smaller than the price‑per‑collateral unit, a situation that is easy to miss because the loop exits silently and no error is emitted. It was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑deduction logic. The issue belongs to the class of rounding‑error and dust‑loss bugs where floor division causes under‑allocation of resources. To fix the problem the conversion should use a rounding‑up division (divUp) so that any non‑zero USD amount maps to at least one unit of collateral, ensuring isMissingMargin remains true until the fee is fully collected. This change restores the invariant that all fees are deducted before the order is considered settled, aligning the contract’s accounting with the business rule that fees must be fully collected.

title: Liquidating positions of different accounts for the same market on the same block.timestamp uses the same fundingFeePerUnit regardless of the computed MarkPrice based on the size of the position been liqudiated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error that occurs during batch liquidation of perpetual positions when several accounts are liquidated in the same transaction. The contract computes a fundingFeePerUnit for each position based on the elapsed time since the last funding update, the average funding rate and the current mark price. Because the liquidation loop runs within a single block, block.timestamp is identical for all accounts, causing the function getProportionalElapsedSinceLastFunding to return zero for every account after the first. Consequently the pendingFundingFeePerUnit becomes zero and the currentFundingRate collapses to the lastFundingRate, so the nextFundingFeePerUnit for the second and subsequent positions is equal to the value calculated for the first position. This logic flaw means that positions with different sizes or mark prices are charged the same funding fee, leading to an incorrect accrued funding amount that is added to unrealized PnL. The impact is that liquidated traders receive a PnL that is either higher or lower than the protocol’s economic model predicts, effectively causing funds to disappear or be over‑charged. The bug manifests only when multiple accounts are liquidated in the same block, a scenario that is common for liquidators who batch calls to reduce gas costs. Users, liquidators and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting invariants that guarantee fair funding distribution are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that logged fundingFeePerUnit values before and during liquidation, showing identical values for different positions. It is hard to notice because the funding fee is a small component of the overall PnL and the discrepancy may be masked by market volatility, making the error appear as normal loss. The vulnerability belongs to the class of time‑dependent accounting bugs where a zero‑time delta leads to division‑by‑zero or nullified terms, similar to rounding or stale‑state errors. From a user perspective the expectation is that each liquidated position is charged a fee proportional to its size and market price, but the reality is that the fee is constant, causing unexpected zero or negative balances after liquidation.
