It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit event with the price used for each purchase, and the price mapping is internal, so users see no discrepancy in transaction receipts. The appropriate mitigation is to make the price an explicit parameter of the purchase function – for example, by adding a purchasePrices array – and to enforce that each supplied price is greater than or equal to the stored price at execution time. This transforms the bug from a mutable‑state race condition into a deterministic check, aligning the contract’s behavior with the business rule that a buyer should never pay more than the price they agreed to. The issue belongs to the broader class of front‑running or race‑condition vulnerabilities where mutable on‑chain state is read after it can be altered by another transaction within the same block, violating the accounting assumption that price data remains stable between user intent and contract execution.

title: Builders must pay more interest when the system is paused.
description:
[Community.sol#L455](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L455)  
[Community.sol#L484](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L484)  
[Community.sol#L509](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L509)  

Builders can’t repay when the system is paused so they must pay more interest for the paused period.
poc:
Builders can repay to lenders using 3 functions, [repayLender()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L455), [reduceDebt()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L484), and [escrow()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L509).

But they all don’t work when the system is paused and builders have no way to avoid it.

Furthermore, the HomeFi admin is the main lender of builders and there is no assurance that the admin would pause the community for a while to get more interest.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the repayment flow of the HomeFi Community contract where three distinct functions—repayLender, reduceDebt, and escrow—are responsible for allowing builders to settle their outstanding loans. When the protocol enters a paused state, these functions are deliberately disabled to prevent state changes while severe bugs are being addressed. However, the interest calculation logic that runs on each block continues to accrue interest on the builder's debt during the pause. Because the repayment functions cannot be invoked, builders are forced to wait until the contract is unpaused before they can make any payment, and the accrued interest for the entire pause period is added on top of the original principal. This creates a situation in which builders end up paying more than expected, violating the business rule that pausing should be a neutral maintenance operation rather than a mechanism to increase lender earnings. The flaw is triggered whenever the admin (currently a centralized entity that also acts as a lender) pauses the community, which may happen during emergency upgrades or bug fixes. Builders attempting to repay during this window experience failed transactions or silent reverts, see no change in their debt balance, and later discover that the amount owed has grown unexpectedly. From a user perspective the symptom is a missing or zero repayment response, a sudden increase in the displayed debt, and an inability to clear the loan when they need to, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the interaction between the pause modifier and the interest accrual routine, noticing that the pause check is applied to the repayment functions but not to the interest update, creating an asymmetry that can be abused or cause unintentional over‑charging. The problem is subtle because pausing is generally assumed to freeze all state changes, so developers may not expect interest to keep ticking while repayments are blocked. Conceptually, this is a "paused state accrual mismatch" bug, a class of defect where economic state continues to evolve despite functional shutdown, breaking accounting assumptions that balances remain static during maintenance windows. To remediate the issue, the contract should either (i) also suspend interest accrual while paused, (ii) allow repayment functions to operate in a limited fashion that settles the principal without further interest, or (iii) redesign the interest formula to exclude the paused interval from the calculation. Any of these approaches would align the protocol's operational semantics with the expectation that pausing does not impose additional cost on borrowers and would restore fairness for builders and confidence in the protocol’s governance.

title: `Project.changeOrder`
description:
[Project.sol#L402](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L402)  

The `changeOrder()` function will revert when it’s called for the tasks that don’t have subcontractors.

As a result, the project builder and contractor can’t change the cost of a task until the subcontractor is confirmed.
poc:
The `changeOrder()` is used to change the cost or subcontractor of a task and there is no documentation that this function must be called only after a subcontractor is confirmed.

Also, it’s reasonable to be able to change the cost when a subcontractor isn’t confirmed yet.

But when it checks signature [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L402), it assumes the task has a confirmed subcontractor already and `checkSignatureTask()` will revert in other cases.

So this function will be useless for non SCConfirmed tasks.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Project contract’s changeOrder() function, which is intended to allow a project builder or general contractor to modify the cost or subcontractor assignment of a specific task. The function unconditionally invokes a signature verification routine that assumes the task already has a confirmed subcontractor. When a task has not yet received subcontractor confirmation, the internal checkSignatureTask() function receives a zero‑address subcontractor and an invalid or missing signature, causing the call to revert. Consequently, the changeOrder() operation becomes unusable for any task that is still awaiting subcontractor confirmation. The root cause is a missing conditional branch that distinguishes between confirmed and unconfirmed subcontractor states, combined with an insufficient signature‑validity check that does not reject zero or malformed signatures. An attacker can exploit this logic error by deliberately leaving a task in an unconfirmed state, thereby preventing legitimate parties from adjusting the task’s cost or subcontractor information; the transaction will consistently revert, effectively locking that aspect of the project. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑style failure: the builder and contractor experience failed transactions, the UI may display generic “transaction failed” or “update not applied” messages, and the expected business logic—being able to renegotiate task pricing before a subcontractor signs off—is violated. This malfunction affects all participants who rely on dynamic task pricing, potentially stalling project progress and leading to financial losses if costs cannot be corrected before work begins. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor attempted to call changeOrder() on tasks that had not yet been confirmed and observed an unexpected revert, a behavior that was not documented in the contract’s specification. It is difficult to notice because the function operates correctly for already‑confirmed tasks, and the lack of explicit pre‑condition checks or clear documentation obscures the requirement that a subcontractor must be confirmed beforehand. To remediate the problem, the contract should first query the task’s confirmation status and then invoke either the existing checkSignatureTask() path (for confirmed subcontractors) or a generic checkSignature() path (for unconfirmed tasks). Additionally, the signature‑validation helper must be hardened to revert on any invalid or zero‑address signature, ensuring that a missing subcontractor cannot bypass authentication. By separating these two verification flows and tightening signature checks, the changeOrder() function will behave as intended across all task states, restoring the ability of builders and contractors to modify task parameters safely and preserving the protocol’s economic workflow.

title: Missing upper limit definition in `replaceLenderFee`
description:
[Community.sol#L392-L394](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Community.sol#L392-L394)  
[HomeFi.sol#L184-L197](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/HomeFi.sol#L184-L197)  

The admin of the `HomeFi` contract can set `lenderFee` to greater than 100%, forcing calls to `lendToProject()` to all projects created in the future to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑setting mechanism of the HomeFi protocol. The contract provides an admin‑only function called replaceLenderFee that allows the administrator to write an arbitrary unsigned integer into the lenderFee storage slot. Because the function does not enforce any upper bound, the admin can assign a value that exceeds the logical maximum of 100% (the protocol represents 100% as 1000 in the fee formula). The lenderFee value is later used in the lendToProject function, where the payable amount for a lender is calculated as (_lendingAmount * lenderFee) / (lenderFee + 1000). If lenderFee is set to an extremely large number, such as type(uint256).max, the multiplication overflows the 256‑bit integer range, causing the entire expression to revert. As a result, any attempt by a community member to lend to a newly created project fails at runtime, and the transaction is rolled back, leaving the user with no funds transferred and no receipt of a loan. This situation can be reproduced by an admin calling replaceLenderFee with a huge value, then a regular user invoking lendToProject, which will consistently revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style griefing attack: future projects become unusable for lenders, user confidence erodes, and the protocol’s advertised functionality is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the fee‑replacement logic and identified the missing constraint on fee magnitude. It may be hard to notice in normal testing because typical fee values are within expected ranges, and overflow only manifests when the fee is set to an out‑of‑bounds value that normal users would never choose. To remediate the problem, the replaceLenderFee function should include a bounds check that restricts the fee to a sensible maximum (e.g., require(_newLenderFee <= 1000) to enforce a maximum of 100%, or a slightly lower ceiling to allow protocol fees). Using safe‑math libraries or Solidity ^0.8's built‑in overflow checks would also prevent silent overflow. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked input validation leading to arithmetic overflow, which breaks business logic that assumes lenderFee is a percentage not exceeding 100%. From the user’s perspective, a lender sees a transaction fail with no refund, expecting a successful loan but receiving an error instead, effectively experiencing “funds disappear” or “loan never happens”. The protocol’s integrity is compromised because the core accounting assumption – that fees are a percentage of the loan amount – no longer holds, allowing an admin to grief the ecosystem.

title: Signature Checks could be passed when `SignatureDecoder.recoverKey`
description:
[Project.sol#L887](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L887)  
[Project.sol#L108-L115](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L108-L115)  

It is possible to pass Signature Validity check with an SignatureDecoder.recoverKey() returns 0 whenever the builder and /or contractor have an existing approved hash for a data.

With occurrence of above, any user can call changeOrder or setComplete functions successfully after user approves data hashes.
bug_full: The contract contains a signature verification flaw that allows an attacker to bypass the intended authentication check. The function that validates a signature calls `SignatureDecoder.recoverKey`, which returns the address that signed the data, but the implementation does not verify that the returned value is non‑zero. When the builder or contractor has previously stored an approved hash for a particular payload, `recoverKey` can return the zero address (0x0) for a crafted input. Because the contract only checks that the recovered address matches an approved signer and does not assert that the address is valid, the zero address is treated as a successful match. Consequently, any user can invoke privileged functions such as `changeOrder` or `setComplete` after a hash has been approved, without possessing a legitimate signature. The vulnerability emerges during normal operation when a hash is recorded as approved and the contract later attempts to validate a signature for that hash. It affects all participants in the protocol—builders, contractors, and end users—because it permits unauthorized state changes, potentially leading to incorrect order updates, premature completion flags, and downstream financial consequences like mis‑allocation of escrowed funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature verification pathway and noticed the missing require statement guarding against a zero‑address result. It is subtle because the contract does not explicitly reject a zero address, and the zero address can superficially satisfy the equality check against an approved mapping, making the bug easy to overlook in testing. The flaw belongs to the class of “missing validation of cryptographic primitive output” or “unchecked return value leading to authentication bypass.” From a user’s perspective the UI may show that an order was changed or marked complete even though they never signed anything, creating confusion and loss of trust. The business logic assumes that only parties who have signed the data can trigger these state transitions; the bug violates that accounting assumption by allowing anyone to produce a false signature that the contract accepts. To remediate, the signature checking routine should explicitly require that the recovered address is not the zero address before comparing it to the approved signer list, thereby ensuring that only genuine, non‑zero signatures are accepted. This change restores the intended security model and prevents unauthorized state manipulation.

title: Hash approval not possible when contractor == subcontractor
description:
[Project.sol#L859](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/f2498c86dbd0e265f82ec76d9ec576442e896a87/contracts/Project.sol#L859)  

When a contractor (let’s say Bob) is also a subcontractor (which can be a valid scenario), it is not possible to use the hash approval feature for `checkSignatureTask`. The first call to `checkSignatureValidity` will already delete `approvedHashes[address(Bob)][_hash]`, the second call therefore fails.

Note that the same situation would also be possible for builder == contractor, or builder == subcontractor, although those situations are probably less likely to occur.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the hash‑approval mechanism used by the Project contract when validating task signatures. The contract stores a boolean approval for each hash under a two‑dimensional mapping approvedHashes[account][hash]. When the function checkSignatureValidity is called, it first verifies that the hash has been approved and then immediately deletes the entry approvedHashes[account][hash]. This design assumes that each hash will be used only once per account. However, when a single address plays multiple roles – for example, a contractor who is also a subcontractor – the same hash must be checked twice: once in the contractor role and once in the subcontractor role. The first call to checkSignatureValidity correctly clears the approval entry, but the subsequent call for the same address finds no entry and therefore fails the signature check. As a result, the hash‑approval feature cannot be used for checkSignatureTask in this role‑overlap scenario. The issue arises only when the same Ethereum address appears in two distinct role mappings (contractor == subcontractor, builder == contractor, or builder == subcontractor), a situation that is valid but relatively rare, making the bug hard to spot during normal testing. The impact is that a legitimate participant who holds both positions cannot complete the required signature verification, potentially preventing tasks from being marked as completed, escrowed funds from being released, or refunds from being processed. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a hash was approved initially, but subsequent actions result in “signature verification failed” or “task cannot be completed,” leading to confusion and stalled workflows. The bug belongs to the class of premature state‑mutation or double‑use errors where a resource is deleted before all dependent operations have finished. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit of the Project contract’s task‑handling logic. To remediate the issue, the contract should defer the deletion of the approvedHashes entry until after all role‑specific checks have been performed, or it should maintain separate approval records per role to avoid accidental removal on the first check. In short, the contract currently deletes the approval too early, breaking the expected business logic that a single hash can be validated in multiple roles performed by the same address.

title: Anyone can create disputes if `contractor` is not set
description:
[Project.sol#L498-L502](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L498-L502)  
[SignatureDecoder.sol#L25](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/libraries/SignatureDecoder.sol#L25)  

Disputes enable an actor to arbitrate & potentially enforce requested state changes. However, the current implementation does not properly implement authorization, thus anyone is able to create disputes and spam the system with invalid disputes.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the dispute‑creation workflow of the Project contract. The function `raiseDispute` recovers a signer address from a supplied signature and then checks that the recovered address matches either the builder, the contractor, or (for a specific task) the task’s subcontractor. However, when the contract does not have a contractor set (i.e., `contractor == address(0)`) and the supplied signature is malformed, the signature‑decoder returns the zero address. Because the authorization check compares the recovered signer directly to the allowed roles, the comparison `signer == contractor` succeeds when both are the zero address, causing the require statement to pass. Consequently, any caller can invoke `raiseDispute` with an arbitrary `_data` payload and an invalid signature, and the contract will forward the call to the external Disputes contract, creating a dispute record without any legitimate party involvement. This can be exploited by constructing a transaction that supplies a signature of incorrect length (e.g., 66 bytes) which triggers the decoder’s length‑mod‑65 guard and returns `address(0)`. The attacker then calls `raiseDispute` with any project address and task identifier; if the task is zero or the task’s subcontractor is also unset, the authorization logic is bypassed. The impact is that an adversary can spam the dispute system with bogus disputes, inflating storage usage, increasing gas costs for honest participants, and potentially causing denial‑of‑service conditions for legitimate dispute resolution. The issue occurs whenever the contract is instantiated without a contractor or when a task’s subcontractor is not defined, which are legitimate states in the platform’s lifecycle. All participants—builders, contractors, subcontractors, and end users—are affected because the integrity of the dispute mechanism is compromised, undermining trust in the protocol’s arbitration process. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit review of the `raiseDispute` implementation, where the interplay between signature recovery and role checks was examined and the edge case of a zero‑address contractor was identified. It is subtle because the code appears to enforce role‑based restrictions, yet the special case of a zero address silently satisfies the equality test, making the problem easy to miss in testing that only uses valid signatures. To remediate, the contract should explicitly reject a zero‑address signer after recovery, for example by adding `require(signer != address(0), "Zero‑address signer");` before any role checks, or by ensuring that a contractor is always set before disputes can be raised. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model where only authenticated parties can create disputes, preventing unauthorized users from flooding the system with fake disputes and preserving the economic and functional assumptions of the platform.

title: Attacker can drain all the projects within minutes, if admin account has been exposed
description:
[HomeFi.sol#L156-L169](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFi.sol#L156-L169)  
[HomeFi.sol#L199-L208](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFi.sol#L199-L208)  

In case where the admin wallet has been hacked, the attacker can drain all funds out of the project within minutes. All the attacker needs is the admin to sign a single meta/normal tx.  
Even though the likelihood of the admin wallet being hacked might be low, given that the impact is critical - I think this makes it at least a medium bug.

Examples of cases where the attacker can gain access to admin wallet:

* The computer which the admins are using has been hacked

    * Even if a hardware wallet is used, the attacker can still replace the data sent to the wallet the next time the admin has to sign a tx (whether it’s a meta or normal tx)
* The website/software where the meta tx data is generated has been hacked and attacker modifies the data for tx
* A malicious website tricks the admin into signing a meta tx to replace the admin or forwarder

Since the forwarder has the power to do everything in the system, once an attacker manages to replace it with a malicious forwarder, he can do whatever he wants within minutes:

* The forwarder can replace the admin
* The forwarder can drain all funds from all projects by changing the subcontractor and marking tasks as complete, or adding new tasks / changing task cost as needed.

Even when signatures are required, you can bypass it by using the `approveHash` function.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authentication bypass that arises from the combination of an over‑privileged trusted forwarder and the use of the meta‑transaction helper _msgSender() in admin‑only functions. Because the contract treats any call that passes through the forwarder as coming from the real sender, an attacker who obtains control of the admin’s signing authority can replace the forwarder with a malicious contract in a single transaction. Once the forwarder is under the attacker’s control, the forwarder can invoke admin‑only functions on behalf of the admin, including replaceAdmin and setTrustedForwarder, effectively hijacking the administration of the HomeFi system. This allows the attacker to change the subcontractor address, mark tasks as complete, or alter task costs, which in turn enables the draining of all DAI held by any project in the system. The impact is the complete loss of user‑funds, as the attacker can redirect payments intended for contractors and builders to addresses they control, resulting in balances that appear to vanish from the user interface. The flaw manifests only when the admin’s private key or signing device is compromised, which can happen through typical attack vectors such as malware on the admin’s computer, manipulation of the meta‑transaction generation website, or social engineering that tricks the admin into signing a malicious meta‑transaction. Because the forwarder is trusted and the contract does not differentiate between a genuine admin call and one relayed through the forwarder, the issue is subtle and may not be obvious during routine testing; the contract still enforces signature checks, but those checks are bypassed by approveHash, which authorises arbitrary function calls when invoked by the forwarder. The bug belongs to the class of "trusted forwarder misuse" or "meta‑transaction impersonation" vulnerabilities, where delegating authentication to a third‑party contract expands the attack surface. From the user’s perspective, a project that previously displayed a healthy DAI balance may suddenly show zero, and tasks that were thought to be pending may appear completed without any payouts, violating the business logic that funds are released only after proper completion. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined the admin replacement flow and the approveHash function, revealing that a single signed transaction from the compromised admin is sufficient to replace the forwarder and then drain assets. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict approveHash to be callable only by contracts, replace the use of _msgSender() with msg.sender for admin‑only checks, and introduce a multi‑step, time‑delayed process for changing the admin or the trusted forwarder, providing a window for detection and response. Additionally, eliminating the reliance on meta‑transactions for critical admin functions would reduce the attack surface and align the contract’s authentication model with the principle of least privilege.

title: `Project.raiseDispute`
description:
[Project.sol#L493-L536](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L493-L536)  

In case users are using a contract (like a multisig wallet) to interact with a project, they can’t raise a dispute.

The sponsors have added the `approveHash()` function to support users who wish to use contracts as builder/GC/SC. However, the `Project.raiseDispute()` function doesn’t check them, meaning if any of those users wish to raise a dispute they can’t do it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical authorization omission in the Project contract’s dispute‑raising flow. When a participant interacts with the system through a smart‑contract wallet (for example a multisig, a builder contract, a guarantor contract or a service contract), the protocol requires the participant to first register the action hash with the approveHash() function. This registration signals that the contract‑based caller is authorized to perform privileged operations on the underlying project. However, the raiseDispute() function that creates a dispute over a previously submitted action does not verify whether the caller’s hash has been approved. Consequently, any contract that relies on the approveHash() mechanism cannot successfully invoke raiseDispute(), even though the off‑chain user expects to be able to dispute the action. The root cause is a missing check of the approvedHashes mapping inside raiseDispute(), which contrasts with other privileged functions that correctly enforce this guard. An attacker does not need to exploit a classic re‑entrancy or overflow; the bug is a denial‑of‑service‑type logic error that blocks legitimate users from exercising a core governance right. The impact is that builders, guarantors, or service contracts that act on behalf of users are unable to raise a dispute when they detect a malicious or erroneous task addition, leaving the protocol vulnerable to undisputed incorrect state changes and potential fund loss for the affected parties. The condition under which the issue manifests is when the caller is a contract address that has previously called approveHash() and then attempts to call raiseDispute() with the same encoded action data. The affected parties include any project participant that uses a contract as their execution layer, the protocol’s dispute resolution mechanism, and ultimately the funds that could be frozen or wrongly allocated because no dispute can be opened. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors extended an existing test suite to include a contract‑based builder and observed that the raiseDispute() call reverted despite a prior approveHash() call, indicating the missing verification step. The problem can be hard to notice because external callers using EOAs (externally owned accounts) do not require approveHash(), so the function appears to work for normal users, masking the defect for contract users. To fix the issue, raiseDispute() should be updated to incorporate the same approved‑hash validation that other privileged functions use, ensuring that the contract checks the approvedHashes mapping before processing the dispute. This adjustment restores the intended access control, re‑enables dispute rights for contract‑based participants, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic that requires explicit approval before privileged actions. From a user’s perspective, a builder trying to dispute a task addition sees the transaction fail or the dispute event never emitted, contradicting the expectation that "I can raise a dispute and see a DisputeRaised event". Instead they experience a silent denial, which can be described as "the dispute never registers" or "my refund attempt does nothing".

title: It should not submit a project with no total budget. Requires at least one task with cost > 0
description:
[Community.sol#L206-L282](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Community.sol#L206-L282)  

When publishing a project, there is still possibility the project doesn’t have any task or 0 budget.
poc:
According to contest guideline, there is information that says:

_“Note that you cannot submit a project with no total budget. Therefore it requires at least one task with a budget > 0.”_

Meanwhile, on `publishProject()` in Community.sol, there is no check of this condition.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation check in the community contract’s publishProject function that allows an author to submit a new project without any tasks or with a total budget of zero. The underlying cause is the absence of a require statement that enforces the business rule defined in the protocol documentation – a project must contain at least one task whose cost is greater than zero. Because the contract does not verify the cost of the first task (or the aggregate budget) before registering the project, an attacker can create a project that appears valid on‑chain while internally having no allocated funds. This can be exploited by calling publishProject with a project contract whose tasks mapping returns a cost of zero for the first task (index 1). The transaction succeeds, the project is recorded, and subsequent logic that assumes a positive budget – such as reward distribution, task funding, or accounting calculations – operates on a zero value. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions: users may see projects listed with no budget, tasks cannot be funded, and any downstream functions that calculate payouts based on the total budget may produce incorrect or zero results, effectively causing funds to disappear or rewards to be granted without proper payment. The condition manifests whenever a project is created without meeting the documented minimum‑budget rule, which can happen unintentionally by a careless developer or deliberately by a malicious actor seeking to manipulate the system. All participants – project creators, task assignees, and the broader community – are affected because the protocol’s integrity and trust model rely on accurate budgeting. The issue was discovered during a static audit that compared the contract implementation against the official protocol documentation, noticing the discrepancy between the stated rule and the actual code. It is subtle because the contract compiles and runs without errors, and the missing check does not produce an immediate revert, making it easy to overlook during normal testing. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit validation such as require(_projectInstance.tasks[1].cost > 0, "First task must have a positive cost"); or a loop that aggregates all task costs and ensures the total exceeds zero before accepting the project. This belongs to the broader class of input‑validation or business‑rule enforcement bugs, where essential domain constraints are not enforced at the smart‑contract level, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential loss of trust in the platform.

title: Possible DOS in `lendToProject`
description:
[Project.sol#L710](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L710)  

In `Project` contract, the `lendToProject()` function might not be available to be called if there are a lot of Task in `tasks[]` list of project. It means that the project cannot be funded by either builder or community owner.

This can happen because `lendToProject()` used `projectCost()` function. And the loop in `projectCost()` did not have a mechanism to stop, it’s only based on the length `taskCount`, and may take all the gas limit. If the gas limit is reached, this transaction will fail or revert.

Same issue with `toggleLendingNeeded()` function which also call `projectCost()` function.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded‑gas denial‑of‑service condition that appears when the Project contract calculates the total funding requirement through the public view function projectCost(). The function iterates over every task stored in the tasks mapping, using the current taskCount as the loop bound. Because there is no safeguard limiting the number of tasks that can be added, an attacker or even a benign user can create a large enough task list that the gas required to sum all task costs exceeds the block gas limit. When lendToProject() or toggleLendingNeeded() invoke projectCost() to verify that a new total lent amount does not exceed the required project cost, the call triggers the full iteration. If the iteration runs out of gas, the transaction reverts, meaning the lending function becomes effectively unavailable. This situation can be reproduced simply by adding many tasks and then attempting to fund the project; the user sees a revert error instead of a successful funding transaction, and the UI may show that the project cannot be funded or that the lend button is disabled. The impact is that the project’s funding flow is halted: builders, community owners, or any lender cannot provide capital, potentially freezing the project's lifecycle and causing loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract code, where the auditor noticed that projectCost() performs a linear scan over an unbounded collection without any early‑exit condition or gas‑saving mechanism. It is hard to notice because the function is declared as view and therefore appears safe, yet it is invoked inside state‑changing functions where gas limits apply. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration leading to out‑of‑gas denial of service” and violates the business assumption that the project’s cost can always be computed on‑chain regardless of the number of tasks. From the user’s perspective, the expectation is that submitting a lend transaction will increase the total funded amount, but in reality the transaction fails and no funds are transferred, giving the impression that the protocol is broken or possibly malicious. To remediate the issue, the contract should maintain an aggregate cost variable that is updated whenever a task is added, removed, or its cost changes, thereby eliminating the need for a full loop at each call. Alternatively, the contract could enforce a maximum number of tasks, or redesign the cost calculation to use a more gas‑efficient data structure, ensuring that the cost can be retrieved within the block gas limit and that lending functions remain callable.

title: Owner of project NFT has no purpose
description:
Creating a new project mints a NFT to the `_sender` (builder). The `builder` of a project has special permissions and is required to perform various tasks.

However, if the minted NFT is transferred to a different address, the `builder` of a project stays the same and the new owner of the transferred NFT has no purpose and no permissions to access authorized functions in Rigor.

If real-world use-cases require a change of the `builder` address, there is currently no way to do so. Funds could be locked in the project contract if the current `builder` address is unable to perform any more actions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a mismatch between ownership of a project NFT and the privileged builder role required to manage a project on the Rigor platform. When a new project is created, the contract mints a unique NFT and assigns the address that called createProject (the builder) as the entity that holds special permissions for the project's lifecycle. These permissions are stored independently of the NFT ownership and are never updated after deployment. Consequently, if the NFT is transferred to another address, the new holder acquires a token that visually represents the project but does not inherit any of the builder's authorisation rights. The contract continues to recognise the original builder address as the only account capable of invoking privileged functions such as funding, configuration changes, or project finalisation. From a user’s point of view, the transferred NFT appears in their wallet, leading them to expect that they can manage the project, but attempts to interact with the contract are rejected, leaving the project potentially inoperative. If the original builder becomes inaccessible—for example, if the private key is lost, the address is a contract that self‑destructs, or the builder is otherwise unable to act—funds locked within the project contract become irretrievable because no other account possesses the required permissions. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared token ownership checks against role‑based access control and identified that the NFT transfer event does not trigger any update to the builder mapping. The problem is subtle because the NFT is the sole visible indicator of project ownership, and the UI does not expose the underlying builder address, making it easy to assume that token holders have full control. This class of bug can be described as an "authorization decoupling" or "ownership‑privilege mismatch" where token transfer does not propagate associated rights. The impact includes loss of functional control over a project, inability to withdraw or re‑allocate funds, and potential financial loss for users who acquire the NFT under the false impression of having management capabilities. The vulnerability manifests whenever the project NFT is transferred, which can happen at any time after project creation, and it affects any party that receives the NFT without also being the original builder. To remediate, the contract should either (1) prohibit transfers of the project NFT while a builder role is required, thereby ensuring that only the original builder can hold the token, or (2) redesign the access control to bind privileged actions to the current NFT owner, updating the builder reference on each transfer, or (3) provide an explicit administrative function that allows a verified, KYC‑ed builder to delegate or change the builder address in a controlled manner. By aligning token ownership with functional authority, the protocol restores the expected business logic that owning a project NFT confers the ability to manage the associated funds and operations.

title: `updateProjectHash` does not check project address
description:
[Project.sol#L162](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L162)  

In Project.sol, function `updateProjectHash` L162, `_data` (which is signed by builder and/or contractor) does not contain a reference to the project address. In all other external functions of Project.sol, `_data` contains the address of the project, used in this check:  
`require(_projectAddress == address(this), "Project::!projectAddress");`.  

The lack of this verification makes it possible to reuse the same `_data`, and the same `_signature` on another project, in the case the latter has the same builder and/or contractor, and the same `_nonce`. In pratice, if the same group of people starts a new project, when `_nonce` reaches the correct value, anyone can change the hash of a task (if we suppose that that `updateTaskHash()` was used in the previous project).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that updates a project’s task hash. The contract accepts a signed data payload, but the payload does not embed the address of the project that is being updated. All other external functions in the same contract include a check that the supplied project address matches the contract’s own address, asserting `require(_projectAddress == address(this))`. In the `updateProjectHash` function this check is missing, which means that the same signed payload—containing a builder or contractor address, a nonce, and a task hash—can be replayed on any other instance of the Project contract that shares the same builder or contractor and reaches the expected nonce value. An attacker who controls or knows the signature from a previous project can submit it to a newly created project, causing the task’s hash to be overwritten without the project participants’ consent. This breaks the business logic that each project’s metadata should be immutable unless updated by its own participants, potentially leading to incorrect task identifiers, wrong payment calculations, or a denial of service where the task cannot be referenced correctly. The issue manifests only when a new project is deployed with the same parties and the nonce aligns, a condition that is plausible in environments where the same builder and contractor repeatedly create projects. It is difficult to notice because the signature verification itself succeeds, giving the false impression that the update is legitimate, while the missing address binding silently allows cross‑project replay. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the handling of signed data across functions. To remediate, the signed payload should be required to include the project’s address and the contract should enforce that the address extracted from the payload matches `address(this)` before accepting any hash update, thereby binding the signature to a single project instance. This class of bug is a replay‑attack vulnerability caused by insufficient domain separation in signed messages, and it violates the expectation that a user’s signed command applies only to the intended project.

title: In `Project.setComplete`
description:
[Project.sol#L330](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L330)  

`setComplete()` function might be called successfully using the past signature when it shouldn’t work.

As a result, a task might be completed when a builder doesn’t want it.
poc:
[approveHash() function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L108) can set only true so there is no method to cancel already approved hash without [passing validation here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L891).

So the below scenario would be possible.

  * A builder, GC, and SC started a task and SC finished the task.
  * They are approved to complete the task and signed the signature.
  * But right before to call [setComplete()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L330) using the signature, the SC felt the cost is too low and raised a dispute to change the order using [raiseDispute()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L493).
  * As I suggested with another medium issue, the task can’t be completed when there is an ongoing dispute from [this document - “If there is no ongoing dispute about that project, task status is updated and payment is made.”](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor#tasks-completion-and-payment). So `setComplete()` might revert.
  * Even if it doesn’t check active disputes as now, `setComplete()` might revert when the funds haven’t been allocated and a builder signed by fault.
  * After that, the HomeFi admin accepted the dispute, and the cost of the task was increased as SC wanted.
  * Then the builder would hope to get more results (or scores) from this task as the cost is increased rather than completed right away.
  * But SC can call `setComplete()` using the previous signature and complete the task without additional work.
  * A builder might know about that before and try to update task hash but it will revert because SC doesn’t agree to [updateTaskHash()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L283).
  * In this case, it’s logical to cancel the approved hash [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L108) but there is no such option.

I don’t know if there would be similar problems with other functions that use signature and I think it would reduce the risk a little if we add an option to cancel the approved hash.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Project contract handles task completion signatures. The contract stores a boolean flag for each approved hash using the approveHash function, but the implementation only ever sets the flag to true and never provides a mechanism to revoke or reset an already approved hash. Consequently, once a hash has been signed by the required parties, that signature remains valid indefinitely. The setComplete function relies solely on the presence of a true flag for the supplied hash to authorize the completion of a task, without checking the current state of the project such as whether a dispute is active or whether the funds for the task have already been allocated. This omission creates a replay‑style flaw: after a dispute is raised, or after the payment amount for a task is altered, an attacker can reuse the previously approved hash to invoke setComplete and force the contract to mark the task as finished and release payment based on the old, lower amount. From a user's perspective the builder may see a task appear as completed even though they have opened a dispute expecting a higher payment, leading to unexpected zero or reduced refunds, missing score updates, and a breach of the expected business logic that disputes must block task finalisation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature workflow and noticed that approveHash does not allow cancellation and that setComplete does not query the dispute status. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract superficially appears to enforce multi‑party consent through signatures, yet it silently trusts stale signatures regardless of later state changes. To remediate, the contract should either allow approved hashes to be revoked (e.g., by setting the flag to false or removing the entry) and/or incorporate a nonce or expiry into the signed data, and setComplete must verify that no active dispute exists and that the task’s funds have been correctly allocated before honouring the signature. This class of issue falls under the broader category of “signature replay after state change” and violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions by permitting premature or under‑paid task settlement.

title: Incorrect initialization of smart contracts with Access Control issue
description:
[HomeFiProxy.sol#L216-L230](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFiProxy.sol#L216-L230)  
[Community.sol#L102-L119](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L102-L119)  
[DebtToken.sol#L43-L58](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/DebtToken.sol#L43-L58)  
[Disputes.sol#L74-L81](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Disputes.sol#L74-L81)  
[HomeFi.sol#L92-L120](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFi.sol#L92-L120)  
[Project.sol#L94-L105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L94-L105)  
[ProjectFactory.sol#L45-L55](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/ProjectFactory.sol#L45-L55)  

All next Impact depends on actions and attention from developers when deployed

  * Loss of funds
  * Failure of the protocol, with the need for redeploy
  * Loss of control over protocol elements (some smart contracts)
  * The possibility of replacing contracts and settings with harmful ones

And other things that come out of it…
poc:
For a proper understanding of Proof of Concept, you need to understand the following things:

  1. Hardhat does not stop the process with a deploy and does not show failed transactions if they have occurred in some cases
  2. Malicious agents can trace the protocol deployment transactions and insert their own transaction between them

Reason:

  * [During deploy TransparentUpgradeableProxy’s](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFiProxy.sol#L216-L230) initialize method for initializing contracts not called. The third parameter responsible for this is an empty string. This causes the initialization process itself to be **delayed**
  * Contract initialization methods have no check over who calls them

Example [ProjectFactory.sol#L45-L55](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/ProjectFactory.sol#L45-L55)

**Also suitable for other contracts, strings are attached in Links to affected code**

**Failure of the protocol, with the need for redeploy** && **Loss of control over protocol elements (some smart contracts)** :

  1. User listen transaction in mempool, etherscan, transaction in block etc
  2. Finds the moment of deployment and sends the transaction for setup his HomeFi address in Disputes contract: Just he call initialize method and put his _homeFi parameter
  3. In the event that hardhat tracked a failed transaction, the deployment will stop and you will need to start over. If the hardhead misses it and the developers do not check the result and the setting, access to this part will be lost and fix is needed

**Loss of funds** :

  1. User listen transaction in mempool, etherscan, transaction in block for listne when HomeFi will deployed
  2. Send transaction for initialize [HomeFi](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/HomeFi.sol#L92-L120) with his _treasury address
  3. Transfer the admin ownership the right to the real address to divert the eyes
  4. The address of the treasury remains with the attacker
  5. The protocol fees (fee) will be [transfered](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L443) to the attacker’s address until it is detected
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an incomplete and insecure initialization flow used when deploying a suite of upgradeable contracts with TransparentUpgradeableProxy. The proxy constructor accepts an optional third argument – a calldata payload that is supposed to invoke the implementation’s initialize function atomically with the deployment transaction. In the examined contracts this payload is left empty, so the implementation contracts are deployed but never automatically initialized. The initialize functions themselves contain only a check that supplied address parameters are not the zero address, but they lack any access‑control modifier that restricts who can call them. Consequently, after the proxy deployment transaction is mined, the implementation contracts remain in an uninitialized state and any external account can invoke the initialize entry point at any later time. An attacker monitoring the mempool can detect the exact moment when the proxy deployment transaction is broadcast, and insert a front‑running transaction that calls the vulnerable initialize function with attacker‑controlled parameters, such as setting the admin or treasury address to their own wallet. Because the contracts do not verify the caller, the malicious transaction succeeds, granting the attacker ownership or fee‑collection rights. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that funds that should flow to the protocol treasury are instead transferred to an unknown address, or that administrative actions become unresponsive because the real owner lost control. The impact includes loss of funds, loss of control over core protocol components, and the need to redeploy the affected contracts, effectively halting the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the proxy deployment code and the initialize functions, noting the missing access‑control checks and the empty initialization payload. It is easy to overlook because the contracts compile and appear functional, and the deployment scripts may not report failed initialization calls, especially when using tools like Hardhat that continue execution after a reverted transaction. To remediate, developers should either supply a proper initialization calldata to the proxy constructor so that the implementation is securely initialized in the same atomic transaction, or they should add explicit access‑control checks (e.g., onlyOwner or onlyProxyAdmin) to the initialize functions and enforce a one‑time initialization guard. Additionally, deployment scripts should verify that the initialize call succeeded before proceeding, and consider using OpenZeppelin’s Initializable pattern that prevents re‑initialization. In short, the bug belongs to the class of “unprotected contract initialization” vulnerabilities, where the lack of caller verification combined with delayed or missing init calls enables front‑runner attacks that hijack contract roles and divert protocol fees.

title: New subcontractor can be set for a SCConfirmed task without current subcontractor consent
description:
Malicious builder/contractor can change the subcontractor for any task even if all the terms was agreed upon and work was started/finished, but the task wasn’t set to completed yet, i.e. it’s `SCConfirmed`, `getAlerts(_taskID)[2] == true`. This condition is not checked by inviteSC().

For example, a contractor can create a subcontractor of her own and front run valid setComplete() call with a sequence of `inviteSC(task, own_subcontractor) -> setComplete()` with a signatory from the `own_subcontractor`, stealing the task budget from the subcontractor who did the job. Contractor will not breach any duties with the community as the task will be done, while raiseDispute() will not work for a real subcontractor as the task record will be already changed.

Setting the severity to be high as this creates an attack vector to fully steal task budget from the subcontractor as at the moment of any valid setComplete() call the task budget belongs to subcontractor as the job completion is already verified by all the parties.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized subcontractor reassignment bug that allows a builder or contractor to replace the currently confirmed subcontractor of a task with a new address, even after the subcontractor has accepted the invitation and the task is in the SCConfirmed state. The root cause is that the inviteSC() function does not verify whether the task’s SCConfirmed alert (alerts[2]) is true, nor does it invoke the checkSignatureTask() routine that would require signatures from all parties for such a change. Because the only guard in _inviteSC() is a non‑zero address check and the internal inviteSubcontractor() function is protected only by an onlyInactive modifier, a malicious actor can call inviteSC() with a self‑owned subcontractor while the original subcontractor’s work is already underway. The attacker can then immediately invoke setComplete(), which marks the task as completed and transfers the task budget to the newly invited subcontractor. The original subcontractor, who performed the work, loses the expected payment, sees no refund, and cannot raise a dispute because the task record now reflects a different subcontractor. This attack vector is triggered only when a task has been marked SCConfirmed (getAlerts(_taskID)[2] == true) but has not yet reached the final completed state; in that window the contract incorrectly permits a subcontractor swap. The parties affected include the honest subcontractor who forfeits payment, the builder/contractor who may be malicious, and the overall protocol whose reputation and trust assumptions are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined state transitions and signature checks, revealing that the contract’s state‑machine mixes the SCConfirmed flag with the Active flag, allowing an unintended transition. The bug is hard to notice because the UI and event logs show a task progressing normally, and the only visible symptom is that the subcontractor receives no payment after completing the work. Conceptually, this is a privilege‑escalation / unauthorized state‑change flaw where a role can alter critical payment destinations without consent. The recommended fix is to enforce signature verification when alerts[2] is true, to prevent inviteSC() from executing in that state, and to redesign the task lifecycle so that SCConfirmed and Active flags are independent, using modifiers such as onlyUnconfirmed for subcontractor invitation and employing unConfirm or deActivate functions instead of unApprove to keep the task active while disallowing subcontractor changes. By aligning the business logic with the accounting assumptions that a confirmed subcontractor must retain payment rights until the task is formally completed, the protocol can restore its intended security guarantees.

title: Malicious delegated contractor can block funding tasks or mark tasks as complete
description:
[Project.sol#L219](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L219)  
[Project.sol#L655](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L655)  
[Project.sol#L807](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L807)  

A malicious delegated contractor can add a huge number of tasks (or one task with a huge cost). This would then pose problems in `allocateFunds()` as tasks could not be funded. Builder could remove delegation for the contractor but couldn’t replace the contractor and so couldn’t remove the malicious contractor. The contractor is required to sign various state changes in `Project.sol`. A delegated contractor can also for example complete tasks which results in transferring funds to subcontractors.

This sounds very problematic and would be critical, but reading through the documentation and the code, I’m assuming there is certain trust incorporated and required for the system to work. Hence I’m assuming the system considers a delegated contractor is trustworthy as is the builder. So while the impact may be big I consider the likelihood quite small.
poc:
When a contractor is delegated, various operations only need his signature.  
[Project.sol L807](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/main/contracts/Project.sol#L807)
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from an insecure delegation model in the Project contract where a delegated contractor holds the authority to submit, modify, and complete tasks on behalf of the builder. Because the contract does not provide a mechanism to replace or fully revoke a contractor once delegated, a malicious contractor can exploit this privilege by inserting an excessive number of tasks or a single task with an inflated cost. When the allocateFunds() function attempts to distribute the project’s budget across the task list, the artificially large task set exhausts the available funds, causing the allocation loop to fail and preventing legitimate tasks from receiving any payment. In addition, the delegated contractor can mark tasks as complete, which triggers fund transfers to subcontractors, potentially draining the project's escrow without the builder’s consent. This situation can occur whenever a builder delegates authority to a contractor and later wishes to remove or replace that contractor; the contract only allows revocation of delegation but not substitution, leaving the builder unable to eject a malicious actor. The impact includes a denial‑of‑service style blockage of funding, unauthorized disbursement of funds to parties controlled by the contractor, and the inability of the builder to recover or reallocate the locked resources. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of signatures and delegation logic, noting that the contractor’s signatures are sufficient for critical state changes. It is hard to notice because the system’s documentation assumes the contractor is trusted, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the task list grows beyond reasonable bounds. The bug belongs to the class of privileged delegation and access‑control flaws, where an entrusted party can manipulate accounting data and trigger fund movements that violate the intended business logic of escrow management. From a user’s perspective, a builder may see that newly added tasks never receive any allocated budget, or that tasks are marked complete and funds disappear from the project’s balance despite no legitimate work being performed. The contract should be hardened by adding explicit controls that allow the builder or a designated dispute contract to update the internal pointer used for allocation, and by permitting the removal or replacement of a delegated contractor to prevent a single malicious actor from monopolising task management. In essence, the design must enforce the principle that delegation does not grant unchecked authority over financial flows, and that the system should be able to recover from or mitigate a contractor that attempts to sabotage funding or siphon funds.

title: Task Functionality completely sidestepped via `autoWithdraw`
description:
[Project.sol#L770](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L770)  

`autoWithdraw` will send funds to the `builder`, we can use this knowledge to drain all funds from `Project` to the builder contract. Completely sidestepping the whole Task based logic.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a privileged withdrawal routine called autoWithdraw that is accessible to the contract’s builder. The routine is intended to refund excess tokens when a task’s allocated cost is reduced, but it contains no accounting distinction between funds contributed by the builder and those supplied by the broader community. Because the builder alone can invoke addTasks, allocateFunds and changeOrder, the contract implicitly trusts the builder with full control over the project’s balance. When a task is created and funded, the builder can subsequently invoke changeOrder with a lower cost, triggering the condition _newCost < _taskCost. The contract then computes the difference between the original and reduced cost, subtracts that amount from the internal totalAllocated counter, and immediately calls autoWithdraw with the difference as a parameter. Since autoWithdraw simply transfers the supplied amount to the builder’s address, the builder can repeatedly create new tasks, allocate funds, and repeatedly lower their costs to extract the entire contract balance, completely bypassing the intended task‑based logic that should govern fund release. This exploitation can be performed solely with the builder’s signature, without any additional permissions or checks, allowing the builder to drain all tokens held by the Project contract. From a user perspective the symptoms are stark: deposited funds vanish, the project’s balance drops to zero, and participants expecting refunds or task payouts receive nothing. The issue was discovered during a security audit where a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated the iterative reduction of task costs and the subsequent autoWithdraw calls that funneled all tokens to the builder’s wallet. The flaw is subtle because the autoWithdraw function appears legitimate—its purpose is to return over‑allocated funds—so a casual review might not spot the missing restriction on the source of those funds. The bug belongs to the class of privileged withdrawal or logic‑bypass vulnerabilities where a contract trusts a single role to manage monetary flows without proper safeguards. To remediate, the autoWithdraw mechanism should either be removed entirely or rewritten so that it can only return funds that were originally contributed by the builder, while community contributions remain locked until the intended task outcome is reached. An alternative mitigation is to replace the single‑signer withdrawal model with a multi‑signature or governance‑controlled withdrawal path, ensuring that no single party can unilaterally empty the contract. Proper accounting must be introduced to track the origin of each deposited token and prevent unauthorized extraction, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic and protecting participants’ assets.

title: `changeOrder` requires subcontractor signature when the subcontractor address is 0
description:
[Project.sol#L402](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/f2498c86dbd0e265f82ec76d9ec576442e896a87/contracts/Project.sol#L402)  
[Project.sol#L485](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/f2498c86dbd0e265f82ec76d9ec576442e896a87/contracts/Project.sol#L485)  

Via `changeOrder`, it is possible to set the subcontractor address to 0 (and it is zero when no one is invited). However, when it is updated later again, a signature of the “current subcontractor” (in this case `address(0)`) is still required. This is in contrast to contractors, where the signature is only required when the contractor address is non-zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract's order‑modification logic, specifically in the `changeOrder` function that handles updates to a project's subcontractor address. The function permits the subcontractor field to be set to the zero address, which represents an empty or uninitialized subcontractor. However, the same function later enforces a signature check against the "current subcontractor" regardless of whether that address is zero. Because the zero address cannot produce a valid ECDSA signature, any subsequent attempt to change the subcontractor again is blocked by an impossible authentication requirement. This inconsistency stems from a missing guard that should bypass the signature verification when the stored subcontractor address equals `address(0)`. An attacker—or even an honest participant—can trigger the issue by calling `changeOrder` and deliberately setting the subcontractor to zero. Once the subcontractor is zero, any future call that tries to replace it must present a signature from `address(0)`, which cannot be generated, effectively locking the subcontractor slot. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the project owner or a future legitimate subcontractor cannot be added, payments intended for a subcontractor may be stalled, and the overall workflow of the protocol is broken. This problem manifests whenever the subcontractor field is initially empty or is explicitly cleared, and it affects all parties that rely on the ability to appoint or replace a subcontractor, such as project owners, contractors, and downstream users expecting work to be performed. The flaw was identified during a systematic code audit that compared the signature requirements for contractors and subcontractors and noticed the asymmetric handling of a zero address. The issue can be subtle because the contract compiles and runs without reverting; the failure only appears as an unexpected inability to update the subcontractor, which may be interpreted as a business‑logic error rather than a security bug. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit check that skips the subcontractor signature verification when the stored subcontractor address is zero, mirroring the existing logic for contractors. Conceptually, this aligns the contract with the intended access‑control model where only a non‑zero participant must authorize a change, preventing the impossible signature requirement and restoring the ability to manage subcontractor assignments.

title: `Project.sol` and `Community.sol` have no way to revoke a hash in approvedHashes
description:
[Community.sol#L501-L506](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L501-L506)  
[Project.sol#L108-L115](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Project.sol#L108-L115)  

User is unable to revoke previously approved hash.
poc: If user reconsiders or notices something malicious about the hash after signing, they should be able to revoke the hash. For example the user approves a hash only to find out later that the hash has been spoofed and they weren’t approving what they thought they were. To protect themselves the user should be able to revoke approval, otherwise it may lead to loss of funds or access.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an immutable approval mechanism for cryptographic hashes in the Project and Community contracts. Both contracts store a mapping approvedHashes[user][hash] that can be set to true when a user signs off on a given hash, but they provide no function for the user to later set the flag to false. The root cause is the omission of a revocation routine in the contract's access‑control design, which assumes that once a hash is approved it will never need to be invalidated. An attacker can exploit this by inducing a user to approve a malicious or spoofed hash—through a deceptive user interface, phishing, or off‑chain signature manipulation. Because the user cannot revoke the approval, the contract continues to treat the compromised hash as valid, allowing the attacker to trigger functions that rely on the approved‑hash check, potentially causing unauthorized transfers, loss of funds, or unintended state changes. The impact is that users may have their assets drained or lose control over protocol actions they believed to be safe, and the protocol’s security guarantees are weakened. This condition manifests whenever a user signs a hash without fully verifying its content, or when the hash’s meaning changes after approval. All participants who rely on the hash‑based permission model—regular users, project owners, and the broader protocol—are affected. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that inspected the contract’s permission logic and noted the absence of a revocation path. It can be subtle to notice because the contracts otherwise function correctly for legitimate approvals, and test suites often only cover the happy‑path of approving and using a hash. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing revocation or immutable approval vulnerabilities, where an access‑control flag cannot be cleared after being set. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that once a hash is approved, even if the user later realizes the hash was wrong or malicious, the contract provides no way to cancel that approval, leading to situations where "my funds disappear" or "the contract performs actions I didn’t authorize". The proper remediation is to introduce a revocation function, for example a public or external method that allows the hash owner to set approvedHashes[msg.sender][hash] = false, protected by appropriate access control and accompanied by an event to signal the change. This restores the ability for users to correct mistaken approvals and aligns the contract’s behavior with expected permission‑revocation semantics.

title: Possible centralization issue around RandProvider
description:
[ArtGobblers.sol#L560-L567](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-artgobblers/blob/d2087c5a8a6a4f1b9784520e7fe75afa3a9cbdbe/src/ArtGobblers.sol#L560-L567)

While it is very common for web3 projects to have privileged functions that can only be called by an admin address, special thought should be given to functions that can break core functionality of a project.

One such function is `ArtGobblers.upgradeRandProvider()`. If this is called passing a non-compatible contract address or EOA, requesting new seeds will be bricked and as a consequence reveals will not be possible. Also the seed could be controlled using a custom contract which would allow a malicious actor to set seeds in his favor.

Naturally, the assumption that the deployer or a multisig (likely that ownership will probably be transferred to such) go rogue and perform a malicious action is unlikely to happen as they have a stake in the project (monetary and reputation wise).

However, as this is a project that will be unleashed on launch without any further development and left to form its own ecosystem for many years to come, less centralized options should be considered.
bug_full: The contract contains a privileged upgrade mechanism that allows the owner to replace the source of randomness used for token reveals. The function that performs the upgrade does not enforce any compatibility checks on the new provider and only blocks the change while a seed request is pending. Because the randomness provider is the sole entity authorized to submit a random seed that unlocks the reveal process, swapping it for a contract under the attacker’s control or for an address that does not implement the expected interface effectively bricks the reveal workflow. An attacker who gains control of the owner role, or a malicious owner acting deliberately, can set the provider to a malicious implementation that returns deterministic or attacker‑chosen seeds, or to an address that never returns a seed at all. When this occurs, users attempting to mint or reveal their assets receive no output: the UI shows a pending reveal, balances remain unchanged, and expected legendary tokens never materialize. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑style griefing attack that prevents the core economic activity of the protocol—revealing minted tokens—thereby eroding user trust and potentially reducing protocol utility. The vulnerability manifests whenever the owner calls the upgrade function while no seed request is in flight; it does not depend on external market conditions. All participants who rely on the randomness for fair token distribution—collectors, minters, and the protocol itself—are affected. The issue was identified during a security audit that inspected privileged functions and noticed that the upgrade logic lacked validation of the new provider’s behavior. It can be difficult to detect in routine testing because the contract operates correctly with a legitimate provider, and the failure only surfaces after the upgrade to a faulty address, which may not be exercised in normal test suites. The root cause is the combination of unrestricted admin control over a critical component and the absence of a governance or fallback mechanism to ensure that the new provider conforms to the expected randomness contract interface. To remediate, the upgrade path should be protected by a decentralized decision process such as token‑weighted voting, a timelocked multisig with clearly defined signers, or a whitelist of vetted randomness contracts. Additionally, the contract could include runtime checks that verify the new provider can deliver a seed before accepting the upgrade, or retain a fallback provider to avoid a complete bricking of reveals. By limiting the ability of a single actor to unilaterally change the randomness source, the protocol can preserve its intended fairness and availability guarantees.

title: Hackers can deploy token with respective name as the stable one to impersonate the stable token
description: Hackers can deploy tokens with respective names as the stable ones to impersonate the stable token. Then hackers can get profit from the malicious price oracle.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an impersonation flaw in the price‑oracle component of a lending market that relies on the token symbol – a non‑unique string – to identify stablecoins such as cNOTE, cUSDT and cUSDC. The oracle obtains the symbol from the supplied cToken contract, compares it with hard‑coded strings, and if a match is found it either returns a fixed price of 1e18 (treating the token as a stable asset) or calculates a price based on the underlying token’s decimals. Because the comparison is performed on the symbol rather than on a verified contract address, an attacker can deploy a malicious ERC‑20 token that bears the same symbol as any of the protected stablecoins. When the protocol’s Comptroller queries the price of this attacker‑controlled token, the string comparison succeeds, the oracle mistakenly treats the token as a stablecoin and returns the static price. Consequently the oracle publishes an inaccurate price that can be exploited by the attacker to borrow against inflated collateral, swap assets at a favorable rate, or otherwise siphon value from the protocol. The exploit works whenever the oracle code path that uses string comparison is executed – typically during price retrieval for lending, liquidation or repayment – and it requires only that the attacker’s contract implements the ERC‑20 interface and returns the targeted symbol.
