Since the sender’s vote balance is already zero, the subtraction causes an under‑flow check to revert, making any subsequent transfer or burn of the affected token IDs impossible. This bug can be triggered at any moment by the token holder simply calling delegate(address(0)) or delegateBySig with a zero‑address _to parameter, effectively locking the token and stripping the owner of governance power. From the user’s point of view, a previously transferable NFT suddenly reverts with a generic “transfer failed” or “burn failed” error, and the owner observes that their voting power has vanished despite holding the token. The issue was uncovered during a manual code audit that inspected the delegation logic and the after‑transfer vote adjustment. It is subtle because delegating to address(0) is technically allowed by the ABI and the contract does not explicitly guard against it, so the problem does not manifest until a transfer is attempted, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The root cause is a missing validation that the delegate address must be non‑zero, leading to an incorrect accounting path that treats a valid delegation as a vote burn without a corresponding mint. The bug belongs to the class of “null‑address delegation / vote under‑flow” flaws that break token accounting and can be used to freeze assets. To remediate, the contract should reject zero as a delegate target—by reverting in _delegate when _to == address(0)—or otherwise ensure that any vote movement always includes a matching addition, preserving the invariant that total voting power remains constant. This change restores the ability to transfer and burn tokens and prevents owners from arbitrarily disabling the protocol’s governance mechanisms.

title: Delegation should not be allowed to address
description:
[ERC721Votes.sol#L179-L190](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/lib/token/ERC721Votes.sol#L179-L190)  
Assuming an existing bug in the `_delegate` function is fixed (see my previous issue submission titled ”[Delegating votes leaves the token owner with votes while giving the delegate additional votes](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder-findings/issues/198)”):  
if a user delegates to address(0) that vote gets lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the delegation mechanism of an ERC‑721 based voting token where the contract permits a token holder to delegate voting power to the zero address (address(0)). The root cause is an incorrect accounting of the previous delegate during the `_delegate` function: the code reads the previous delegate from the raw `delegation` mapping instead of using the `delegates()` helper, which already reflects any prior delegation. When a holder delegates to address(0), the contract treats the zero address as a legitimate delegate and removes the holder’s votes, effectively burning them. Because the previous delegate value is still reported as the holder’s own address, a subsequent delegation to address(0) causes the subtraction logic to underflow, wrapping the holder’s vote count to the maximum value of a uint192 (2^192‑1). This overflow grants the holder an unrealistically large amount of voting power. The impact is two‑fold: an honest user who mistakenly delegates to address(0) loses all voting rights, and a malicious actor can repeatedly delegate to address(0) to inflate their vote balance to the maximum, potentially hijacking governance decisions. The issue manifests only when the contract’s delegation function is called with address(0) as the delegate, a scenario that may not be obvious because delegating to the zero address is often assumed to be a no‑op or disabled. Users experience symptoms such as their vote count dropping to zero after a delegation transaction, or unexpectedly jumping to an astronomically high number after a second delegation to the same address. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, reproduced with a Forge test that shows the vote count changing from 1 to 0 and then to `type(uint192).max`. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error for delegating to address(0), and the overflow result may appear as a valid large number. To remediate, the contract should either reject any delegation attempt to address(0) by adding an explicit require check, or fallback to delegating back to the token owner when address(0) is provided. Additionally, the `_delegate` implementation should correctly retrieve the previous delegate via the `delegates()` view to ensure proper vote accounting. By fixing these issues, the system will preserve the integrity of vote distribution, preventing vote loss and the possibility of vote inflation, thereby maintaining the intended security guarantees of the governance protocol.

title: Index out of bounds error when properties length is more than attributes length breaks minting
description:
[MetadataRenderer.sol#L188-L198](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/token/metadata/MetadataRenderer.sol#L188-L198)  

When a token is minted, the `MetadataRenderer.sol` `onMinted` function is called which will set the particular token’s attributes to a random item from one of the properties. A token has a maximum of 16 attributes, the first one being the total number of properties. The properties from which the token receives its attributes are supplied by the owner of the `MetadataRenderer.sol` contract by calling `addProperties`. The issue is that the number of properties the owner can supply is not limited. If the number of properties is more than 15 then the `onMinted` function will revert due to the limit on the number of attributes a token may have.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an index‑out‑of‑bounds error that occurs during the minting process of a token when the metadata renderer is configured with more properties than the token can hold. Each token is allowed a maximum of sixteen attribute slots, where the first slot stores the total number of properties and the remaining fifteen slots store the selected items for each property. The contract’s addProperties function, which can be called by the contract owner, does not enforce any limit on how many properties may be added. When the owner adds sixteen or more properties, the onMinted callback iterates over all supplied properties and attempts to write a value to tokenAttributes[i + 1] for each one. Because the underlying array only has sixteen entries, the loop writes to an index beyond the array bounds (e.g., tokenAttributes[16]), causing the transaction to revert with an “index out of bounds” error. This error can be triggered simply by configuring the metadata renderer with an excessive number of properties and then calling the mint function, which any user or the auction contract may do. From the user’s point of view, a mint transaction that should deliver a new NFT instead fails, the user receives no token, pays gas for a reverted transaction, and may see a generic runtime error without immediate indication of the underlying cause. The impact is that token creation is blocked, potentially freezing a sale or auction, leading to loss of expected revenue and damage to protocol reliability. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately added sixteen properties and observed the revert. It is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings; the failure only appears at runtime when the property count exceeds the hard‑coded attribute limit, making it easy to overlook during regular development. The correct remediation is to enforce a maximum property count that is less than the token’s attribute capacity (for example, fifteen properties) or to redesign the token attribute storage to accommodate an arbitrary number of properties, thereby aligning the metadata configuration with the token’s structural constraints.

title: The quorum votes calculations don’t take into account burned tokens
description:
Because the following happens:

  1. Burned tokens votes are effectively deleted in `token._moveDelegateVotes()` when called by `token.burn()`
  2. When an auction gets settled without bidders the function burns the token by calling `token.burn()`
  3. When `_createAuction()` is called an amount of tokens >= 1 is minted, of which 1 is kept in the auction contract
  4. The functions `governor.proposalThreshold()` and `governor.quorum()` both depend on `token.totalSupply()` for their calculations.

We can derive that the protocol calculates the `quorumVotes` taking into account burned tokens and tokens held in the auction contract, which don’t have any actual voting power. In other words the actual `quorumThresholdBps` is equal or higher than the setted `quorumThresholdBps`.
poc:
I wrote a test that’s expected to revert a `proposal.queue()` even if all possible votes available are cast in favor.

The test comes with two parameters to set: `auctionsToRun` and `tokensToBidder`. The test runs `auctionsToRun` auctions, of which the first `tokensToBidder` are bidded upon and the rest are not. Then:

  1. Creates a proposal
  2. Cast all possible votes in favor
  3. Tries to queue a proposal
  4. Reverts

The default parameters are set to `auctionsToRun = 130` and `tokensToBidder = 10`. Also `quorumThresholdBps = 1000`. This test results in `121 tokens burned` and `133 token minted`. It’s quite an unrealistic scenario, but it can get more real if `quorumThresholdBps` is setted lower. Keep in mind that this is the case in which everybody shows up to vote and averybody votes for.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect calculation of the governance quorum and proposal threshold because the protocol relies on the token contract’s totalSupply value without accounting for tokens that have lost voting power. When a token is burned, the internal delegate‑vote mapping is cleared, yet the totalSupply variable is not decreased; similarly, tokens that are minted and immediately locked in an auction contract remain counted in totalSupply even though they cannot be used to cast votes. Both the quorumVotes and proposalThreshold functions read totalSupply to derive the required number of votes, assuming that every unit of supply represents an active vote. Consequently, the effective quorum threshold is treated as if additional voting power exists, which inflates the required quorum percentage. This flaw can be triggered whenever the auction settlement process burns tokens (by calling token.burn()) and when new tokens are minted for auction purposes, situations that occur regularly in the system’s lifecycle. An attacker or a misbehaving participant could intentionally cause many token burns—such as by repeatedly triggering empty auctions—thereby raising the quorum requirement to a level that cannot be reached by the remaining circulating voters. Even in a benign scenario where all eligible token holders cast votes in favor, the proposal may still fail to reach the calculated quorum and revert when attempting to queue, effectively stalling governance actions. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the protocol’s upgrade and decision‑making mechanisms, leading to delayed or impossible proposal execution and potentially loss of trust among token holders. The issue was uncovered during a targeted test that simulated a large number of auctions, intentionally burning a substantial portion of the token supply while also minting tokens for the auction contract. The test demonstrated that, despite all available votes being cast for a proposal, the queue operation reverted because the on‑chain quorum calculation still included the burned and locked tokens. This bug is hard to notice because the token’s totalSupply appears to match the expected supply at a given block, and the governance contracts do not expose the circulating supply directly, masking the discrepancy between actual voting power and the value used for quorum. To remediate, the protocol should either adjust totalSupply whenever tokens are burned—ensuring that the variable truly reflects the amount of voting‑eligible tokens—or modify the quorum and proposal threshold calculations to subtract burned tokens and tokens held by non‑voting contracts (such as the auction contract) from the supply figure used. Restoring a checkpointed totalSupply mechanism, as seen in reference implementations, would allow accurate accounting of circulating voting power and prevent the quorum from being unintentionally inflated.

title: Loss of Veto Power can Lead to 51% Attack
description:
[Governor.sol#L76](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L76)  
[Governor.sol#L596-L602](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L596-L602)  

The veto power is important functionality for current Nouns DAO logic in order to protect their treasury from malicious proposals. However there is lack of zero address check and lack of 2 step address changing process for vetoer address.  
This might lead to DAO owner losing their veto power unintentionally and open to 51% attack which can drain their entire treasury.

<https://dialectic.ch/editorial/nouns-governance-attack>  
<https://dialectic.ch/editorial/nouns-governance-attack-2>
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the governance contract’s veto mechanism, which is intended to act as a safety valve preventing malicious proposals from draining the DAO treasury. The root cause is two‑fold: during contract initialisation the vetoer address is assigned without a check that the address is non‑zero, and the function that updates the vetoer allows the owner to replace the address in a single transaction without a pending‑approval step. Because there is no protection against setting the vetoer to the zero address or to an arbitrary address, the DAO can unintentionally lose its veto power. When the vetoer address becomes zero or is set to an address controlled by an attacker, the contract no longer has an entity that can block proposals, effectively removing the only on‑chain safeguard against a majority (51 %) voting attack. An attacker who can acquire or purchase 51 % of the voting power can then submit a proposal that passes unchecked and execute it, resulting in the treasury being transferred out or otherwise drained. The impact is the potential loss of the entire treasury, which affects all token holders, users that rely on the DAO’s services, and the overall trust in the protocol. This condition occurs whenever the owner calls the updateVetoer function with an address that is zero or malicious, or when the contract is deployed with a zero‑address vetoer due to the missing check in initialise. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the governance factory code and identified the lack of a zero‑address guard and the single‑step update pattern. The issue is subtle because the contract’s normal operation does not emit an obvious error; the contract simply records a new vetoer value, so the loss of protection can go unnoticed until a malicious proposal is executed and funds disappear. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “admin‑controlled privilege loss” bugs, where a critical authority can be unintentionally revoked, leading to governance takeover. From a user’s perspective, a proposal that should have been blocked is accepted, and after execution the DAO’s balance may appear to drop to zero or the expected refund may not be received. To remediate, the initialisation routine should enforce that the vetoer address is never zero, and the updateVetoer function should be redesigned to a two‑step process: first the current vetoer designates a pending new vetoer, and then the pending address must claim the role in a separate transaction, ensuring that accidental or malicious overwriting of the vetoer is avoided.

title: Try-catch block at `Auction._createAuction
description:
[Auction.sol#L234](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/auction/Auction.sol#L234)  

The `_createAuction` function wraps the `token.mint()` call in a try-catch block, however this will only catch reverts that comes from the require keyword and not the reverts with custom errors or other kinds of errors (arithmetic over/underflow etc.)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the `_createAuction` function handles errors that arise from the `token.mint()` call. The function wraps the minting operation inside a `try‑catch` block, but the catch clause is written as `catch Error(string memory)` which only intercepts revert messages generated by the `require` statement or by explicitly reverting with a string. Solidity also allows contracts to revert using custom error types (e.g., `error MyError(); revert MyError();`) as well as low‑level failures such as arithmetic overflow, division by zero, or out‑of‑gas conditions. Because the catch clause is limited to `Error(string)`, any revert that does not produce a string payload bypasses the handler entirely. Consequently, when `token.mint()` fails with a custom error or any non‑string revert, the catch block is never executed, the `_pause()` call is omitted, and the contract remains in an un‑paused state while the auction creation process aborts. This leaves the contract effectively bricked: future calls to create auctions will fail, user interactions such as placing bids or retrieving refunds become impossible, and funds already locked in the contract may become inaccessible. The bug can be exploited by an attacker who induces a minting failure that triggers a custom error—for example, by providing a malicious token address or manipulating token state—to cause a denial‑of‑service condition without the contract automatically pausing. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that an auction was supposed to start, but afterwards no bids are accepted, balances appear frozen, or the expected auction events never fire, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit test that deliberately invoked a contract emitting a custom error; the test demonstrated that the `catch Error(string)` clause did not capture the revert, confirming the flaw. The problem is subtle because developers often assume a generic `try‑catch` will handle all revert types, overlooking the newer custom error mechanism introduced in Solidity 0.8.4. To remediate, the catch clause should be written without specifying an error type—simply `catch { … }`—so that it captures any revert, regardless of its encoding, and then invokes `_pause()` or an equivalent safety mechanism. This adjustment aligns the error handling with the intended defensive pattern and prevents the contract from becoming permanently unusable when minting encounters unexpected failures.

title: Compromised or malicious vetoer can veto any proposals with unrestricted power
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted veto authority granted to a single address defined as the ``settings.vetoer``. This privileged role can invoke the ``veto`` function on any proposal that has not yet reached the Executed state, regardless of the proposal’s lifecycle stage – whether it is Pending, Active, Succeeded, or Queued. The root cause is a governance design decision that gives one founder, potentially an externally owned account (EOA), absolute power to block proposals without any additional checks, time limits, or multi‑signature safeguards. Because the vetoer’s private key can be lost, compromised, or the holder can become malicious, the system lacks any mitigation against misuse. An attacker who gains control of the vetoer address can simply call ``veto(proposalId)`` at any moment, causing the contract to set the proposal’s ``vetoed`` flag to true and, if the proposal was already queued in the treasury, to invoke ``cancel`` on the treasury, thereby removing the proposal from the execution queue. This effectively freezes the governance process for any critical actions such as contract upgrades, parameter changes, or treasury withdrawals. The impact is a denial‑of‑service against the DAO’s decision‑making, loss of ability to upgrade or withdraw funds, and potential centralization where a single actor can arbitrarily halt progress, undermining token‑holder expectations of decentralized governance. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is awaiting execution; the UI will display a proposal as "Vetoed" even though voting may have already succeeded, leading users to see that their votes did not result in any action, balances remain unchanged, and expected treasury disbursements never occur. This vulnerability was identified during a security audit by reviewing the governance contract’s access control and by writing tests that demonstrated the vetoer’s ability to block proposals in all states. It can be hard to notice because the veto functionality is deliberately intended as a safety mechanism against 51 % attacks, so its presence appears benign, yet the lack of constraints makes it a powerful single point of failure. To remediate, the contract should replace the single‑address vetoer with a more robust governance model, such as a token‑supply‑threshold rule that limits veto power until the DAO is sufficiently decentralized, a time‑bound veto window after voting ends, voting‑based conditions for veto (e.g., only when support and opposition margins are narrow), or a multi‑signature/role‑based control that distributes the authority among several trusted parties. By adding these constraints, the protocol can retain the intended protective function while preventing a compromised or malicious vetoer from arbitrarily stopping proposals.

title: Creating a new governance proposal can be prevented by anyone
description: When creating a new governance proposal, the `proposalId` is generated by hashing the proposal data (`_targets, _values, _calldatas, descriptionHash`). To prevent duplicated proposals, the current `Governor` implementation checks if the `proposalId` exists already. If it exists, the call will revert with the `PROPOSAL_EXISTS` error.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted ability for any address to block the creation of future governance proposals that share an identical set of parameters. In the Governor contract a proposal identifier is derived by hashing the proposal payload – the arrays of target addresses, ETH values, calldata payloads, and a description hash. Before a new proposal is stored, the contract checks whether a proposal with the same identifier already exists by inspecting the stored struct’s voteStart field; if voteStart is non‑zero the transaction reverts with the PROPOSAL_EXISTS error. Because the hash is deterministic and the check does not incorporate any proposer‑specific information (such as the caller address or a nonce), an attacker can submit a proposal with the exact same data as any legitimate proposal before the intended proposer does. Once the attacker’s proposal is recorded, the voteStart field is populated, and any subsequent attempt to submit a proposal with the same payload will be rejected. The cancel function only flips a boolean flag (canceled) but leaves voteStart unchanged, meaning a cancelled proposal still occupies the identifier slot and continues to trigger the existence check. Consequently, an adversary can deliberately create a “placeholder” proposal – even with empty or trivial actions – and thereby prevent any other user from proposing the same set of actions. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition for the governance process: users expect to be able to submit proposals, but instead receive a revert with PROPOSAL_EXISTS and see no effect on the UI other than an error message. The impact is that the protocol’s governance mechanism can be stalled, preventing community voting on upgrades, parameter changes, or fund movements, which could indirectly affect protocol safety and fund accessibility. The issue was uncovered during a static audit of the Governor contract’s propose function and its interaction with the cancel routine. It is subtle because the revert appears to be a normal safeguard against duplicate proposals, yet the lack of a proposer‑bound uniqueness constraint makes it exploitable by any external account. The bug belongs to the class of “identifier collision denial‑of‑service” or “unprotected proposal ID reuse” flaws, where deterministic identifiers are used without including a source identifier, enabling malicious pre‑emptive registration. To remediate, the contract should incorporate the proposer’s address, a nonce, or a timestamp into the proposal identifier, or enforce that only authorized accounts can register a proposal identifier, and ensure that cancellation clears the identifier’s occupancy (e.g., resetting voteStart) so that the same payload can be re‑proposed after a legitimate cancellation.

title: Malicious pausing the contract
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the auction contract’s private function that creates a new auction for each newly minted token. The function invokes an external mint operation on a separate token contract using Solidity’s try/catch syntax. If the mint call runs out of gas, the catch block executes a pause on the auction contract. Because of EIP‑150’s restriction that a called contract receives at most 63/64 of the caller’s remaining gas, the mint operation can be forced to revert when its gas consumption exceeds the forwarded stipend. The token’s mint implementation walks through an array up to one hundred times, which under certain state conditions can require more than 1.5 million gas. When this happens, the call reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, the catch clause is triggered, and the auction contract is paused. From a user’s perspective the auction interface suddenly stops accepting bids, displays no active auctions, or returns an error message indicating that the contract is paused; users expect to place bids or see ongoing auctions but receive nothing, effectively a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue affects any participant or integrator relying on the auction mechanism, the protocol’s revenue stream, and potentially the governance process that hinges on successful auction execution. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined gas forwarding semantics and identified that the pause logic could be unintentionally activated by a predictable gas‑exhaustion scenario. The flaw is subtle because pausing is a legitimate response to a failed mint, so developers might assume any revert is harmless, making the denial of service hard to spot in testing. To remediate, the contract should validate that sufficient gas remains before invoking the external mint, possibly by checking gasleft() against a safe threshold, or by restructuring the logic so that a mint failure does not automatically trigger a contract‑wide pause. Alternatively, the token contract could be designed to guarantee bounded gas usage, or the auction contract could catch specific error types rather than any revert, thereby preventing a malicious or accidental out‑of‑gas situation from disabling the entire system.

title: Auction parameters can be changed during ongoing auction
description:
[Auction.sol#L307-L335](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/auction/Auction.sol#L307-L335)  

The auction parameters can be changed anytime, even during ongoing auctions, and take effect immediately. Users may need time to react to the changes. The impacts maybe followings:

  * some sudden changes may cause bidder’s transaction fail, such as `setReservePrice()` and `setMinimumBidIncrement()`
  * some changes may change users expectation about the auction, such as `setDuration()` and `setTimeBuffer()`, with different time parameters, bidders will use different strategy
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auction contract’s parameter management logic, which permits the contract owner to modify core auction settings such as duration, reserve price, time buffer, and minimum bid increment while an auction is already in progress. Because the contract immediately applies any change to the current auction state, the underlying business rules that bidders rely on can be altered without warning. The root cause is the absence of any safeguard—such as a timelock, state check, or deferred‑application mechanism—to prevent mutable parameters from affecting an active auction. An attacker who can call the owner‑only setters, or a malicious owner, can exploit this by adjusting the reserve price to a value higher than the highest bid, shrinking the time buffer so that a pending out‑bid transaction is rejected, or shortening the duration to end the auction before a participant can submit a valid bid. These actions can cause a bidder’s transaction to revert, result in unexpected auction termination, or force the auction to settle at an unintended price, effectively causing participants to lose the opportunity to win the token or, in the worst case, leaving the auction unsettled. The issue manifests whenever a parameter change transaction is mined during the execution window of an ongoing auction, a condition that can occur at any time because the contract exposes the setters without any temporal restriction. Users are affected directly: a bidder may see their transaction fail with no clear indication that the failure is due to a mid‑auction parameter shift, or they may observe the auction ending earlier than expected, receiving no token despite having placed a qualifying bid. From the auditor’s perspective the problem was identified during a manual review of the contract’s setter functions, which revealed that each setter updates the shared settings structure instantly, regardless of the auction’s lifecycle state. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows only the current auction timer and does not surface a pending parameter change, making it difficult for participants to understand why their transaction failed or why the auction behavior deviated from the advertised rules. Conceptually, this flaw belongs to the class of "state‑dependent configuration mutations" where mutable configuration is allowed to change during a critical operation, breaking the invariants that the operation assumes. To remediate the issue, the contract should either reject any parameter modification while an auction is active or store the requested changes in a pending buffer and apply them only at the start of the next auction, optionally guarded by a timelock to give participants sufficient notice. Such a redesign restores the expectation that auction rules remain stable throughout the bidding period, preventing surprise failures, protecting user funds, and preserving the integrity of the auction’s economic model.

title: MetadataRenderer contract raise error when minting
description:
[MetadataRenderer.sol#L194](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/token/metadata/MetadataRenderer.sol#L194)  

It is not possible to mint a ERC721 token if its properties has different length than its items.
poc:
I run the following test to reproduce the error:
```solidity
    deployMock();

    vm.prank(address(governor));
    string[] memory _names = new string[](1);
    _names[0] = "propertyName"; //fill _names with some value
    MetadataRendererTypesV1.ItemParam[] memory _items; //define empty array
    
    MetadataRendererTypesV1.IPFSGroup memory _ipfsGroup; 
    _ipfsGroup.baseUri = "";
    _ipfsGroup.extension = "";
    MetadataRenderer(token.metadataRenderer()).addProperties(_names, _items, _ipfsGroup); //call add property with _items array empty.

    vm.stopPrank();
    vm.prank(address(auction));

    uint256 success = token.mint();//error happens inside here
    assert(success != 0);

    vm.stopPrank();
```
    
Log from Foundry console:
```
    ├─ [736] TOKEN::metadataRenderer() [staticcall]
    │   ├─ [353] Token::metadataRenderer() [delegatecall]
    │   │   └─ ← METADATA_RENDERER: [0x7076fd06ec2d09d4679d9c35a8db81ace7a07ee2]
    │   └─ ← METADATA_RENDERER: [0x7076fd06ec2d09d4679d9c35a8db81ace7a07ee2]
    ├─ [78618] METADATA_RENDERER::addProperties(["propertyName"], [], ("", ""))
    │   ├─ [78172] MetadataRenderer::addProperties(["propertyName"], [], ("", "")) [delegatecall]
    │   │   ├─ emit OwnerUpdated(prevOwner: FOUNDER: [0xd3562fd10840f6ba56112927f7996b7c16edfcc1], newOwner: TREASURY: [0xf8cf955543f1ce957b81c1786be64d5fc96ad7b5])      
    │   │   ├─ emit PropertyAdded(id: 0, name: "propertyName")
    │   │   └─ ← ()
    │   └─ ← ()
    ├─ [0] VM::stopPrank()
    │   └─ ← ()
    ├─ [0] VM::prank(AUCTION: [0x9a1450e42d752b8731bc88f20dbaa9154642f1e6])
    │   └─ ← ()
    ├─ [121037] TOKEN::mint()
    │   ├─ [120650] Token::mint() [delegatecall]
    │   │   ├─ emit Transfer(from: 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000, to: FOUNDER: [0xd3562fd10840f6ba56112927f7996b7c16edfcc1], tokenId: 0)
    │   │   ├─ emit DelegateVotesChanged(delegate: FOUNDER: [0xd3562fd10840f6ba56112927f7996b7c16edfcc1], prevTotalVotes: 0, newTotalVotes: 1)
    │   │   ├─ [25762] METADATA_RENDERER::onMinted(0)
    │   │   │   ├─ [25372] MetadataRenderer::onMinted(0) [delegatecall]
    │   │   │   │   └─ ← "Division or modulo by 0"
    │   │   │   └─ ← "Division or modulo by 0"
    │   │   └─ ← "Division or modulo by 0"
    │   └─ ← "Division or modulo by 0"
    └─ ← "Division or modulo by 0"
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the metadata rendering component used by the ERC‑721 token contract. The renderer accepts two parallel arrays – one describing property names and the other containing the corresponding item parameters – and assumes that both arrays have the same length. No explicit validation is performed when the addProperties() function stores these arrays. Later, during the onMinted() callback that is invoked when a token is minted, the contract iterates over the stored properties and performs arithmetic that divides by the length of the items array. If the lengths differ, the items array can be empty while the properties array is not, causing a division or modulo by zero. This arithmetic exception propagates up the call stack and makes the mint() transaction revert with the generic error "Division or modulo by 0". From a user’s perspective, attempting to mint a token results in an immediate failure: no token is transferred, no balance changes, and the auction that relies on successful minting cannot proceed, effectively halting the protocol’s core functionality. The bug is triggered when the governance address (or any entity with permission to call addProperties) supplies mismatched arrays, for example by providing a non‑empty list of property names together with an empty list of items. The issue was discovered during a functional test that deliberately called addProperties with an empty items array and observed the subsequent revert during mint. Because the failure occurs deep inside a delegatecall chain, the root cause – a missing length check – is not obvious from the revert message, making the problem hard to spot during normal operation. The defect belongs to the class of input‑validation bugs where unchecked array length mismatches lead to arithmetic exceptions, a pattern that can cause denial‑of‑service conditions in many smart‑contract systems. To remediate the issue, the addProperties() method should enforce that the two arrays have identical lengths before storing them, reverting with a clear message if they differ. Moving this validation to the beginning of the function also saves gas. By guaranteeing consistent array sizes, the onMinted() logic will never encounter a zero divisor, allowing minting to succeed and auctions to run as intended.

title: A proposal can pass with 0 votes in favor at early DAO stages
description:
It’s possible to create a proposal for a DAO as soon as it’s deployed and the proposal can pass even if nobody votes.

This possibility of doing so is based on the following assumptions:

  1. The vetoer doesn’t veto the proposal
  2. `proposal.quorumVotes` is 0, which happens when `token.totalSupply() * settings.quorumThresholdBps < 10_000`
  3. `proposal.proposalThreshold` is 0, which happens when `token.totalSupply() * settings.proposalThresholdBps < 10_000`

The amount of time necessary to create and execute a proposal of this kind is dictated by `governor.settings.votingDelay + governor.settings.votingDelay + treasury.delay()`, the lower the time the higher the risk.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a governance logic flaw that allows a newly‑deployed DAO to approve and execute a proposal without any affirmative votes. The root cause lies in the way the contract calculates the minimum number of votes required for a proposal to be considered valid. Both the quorum threshold (the total number of votes needed for a proposal to be valid) and the proposal threshold (the minimum voting power needed to create a proposal) are derived by multiplying the token total supply by a basis‑point setting and then implicitly rounding down via integer division. When the total supply is small enough, the product can be less than the divisor (10 000), causing both thresholds to evaluate to zero. The contract’s state‑transition logic only checks whether the number of for‑votes is lower than the number of against‑votes or lower than the quorum, but it never enforces that at least one for‑vote exists. Consequently, a proposal with zero for‑votes, zero against‑votes, and a zero quorum is treated as having met the voting requirements and can move to the Succeeded state. An attacker can exploit this by becoming the vetoer, lowering the voting delay, voting period, and treasury execution delay to zero or a minimal value, and then submitting a proposal immediately after deployment. Because no one votes against and the thresholds are zero, the proposal is queued and executed almost instantly, allowing the attacker to drain the treasury funds that exist at that early stage. The impact is limited to the amount of treasury balance at deployment, which is typically low, but the flaw demonstrates that the protocol’s fundamental accounting assumptions— that a proposal must receive at least one affirmative vote before execution—are violated. This issue was discovered during an audit by reproducing the attack path in a test contract that manipulates voting parameters and submits a proposal with no votes. It can be hard to notice because the contract code appears to perform the usual quorum and threshold checks, and the zero values are a side‑effect of integer rounding rather than an explicit misconfiguration. To fix the problem, the governance contract should enforce a non‑zero minimum for both quorum and proposal thresholds, or explicitly require that proposal.forVotes > 0 before a proposal can be marked as Succeeded. Adding a check that at least one vote is cast, or preventing the voting delay and period from being set to zero during deployment, would close the attack vector and align the contract behaviour with the expected business logic that proposals need active support before funds can be moved.

title: Precision is not enough for `proposalThreshold` and quorum. Collections with at least 20000 NFTs in total supply may have some trouble.
description:
[Governor.sol#L465-L477](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L465-L477)  

Precision is not enough for proposalThreshold and quorum. Collections with at least 20000 NFTs in total supply may have some trouble. These collections can’t be set proposalThreshold = 1 or quorum = 1.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the governance contract calculates the number of votes required to submit a proposal (proposalThreshold) and the number of votes needed to reach quorum. Both values are derived by multiplying the total token supply by a basis‑point setting (proposalThresholdBps or quorumThresholdBps) and then dividing by a fixed divisor of 10,000. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional part of the result is discarded. When the total supply of NFTs is large – for example 20,000 tokens – and the threshold settings are at their minimum (1 basis point), the expression (totalSupply × 1) / 10,000 yields exactly 2, and it cannot be reduced to 1. For smaller supplies the same computation can round down to zero, meaning that the contract would accept a proposal or consider a quorum reached with no votes at all. This rounding error is a classic precision‑loss bug caused by using an insufficient scaling factor for fractional percentages. An attacker who holds only a handful of tokens can therefore satisfy the proposal or quorum requirement unintentionally, allowing the creation or approval of malicious governance actions. The impact is a compromised governance process: proposals may be submitted by anyone, and votes may be counted as sufficient even when the community has not expressed explicit support. The issue appears only under specific conditions – namely when the token totalSupply multiplied by the basis‑point setting is less than the divisor – and is hard to notice because the contract still returns a non‑zero integer for many typical supply sizes, masking the fact that the threshold cannot be set to the intended granularity of "one vote". The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the Governor.sol source code, where the arithmetic was examined and test values demonstrated the rounding to zero or an unintuitively low value. To remediate the problem, the division should use a much larger scaling constant (for example 1e18) so that the fractional component is retained with sufficient precision, and the stored threshold values should be expressed in the same high‑precision unit. Conceptually, the fix is to increase the precision of the percentage calculation, thereby preventing the threshold from being rounded down to zero or an undesired minimum value. This change restores the intended business logic that a proposal requires a meaningful amount of voting power and that a quorum reflects a true majority of token holders, eliminating the scenario where "funds disappear" from the governance model or where "refund calculation" (i.e., vote counting) is wrong due to rounding errors.

title: `Governor` - Quorum could be less than intended
description: There could be tokens minted between the `quorum` computation and the vote, which would lead to a quorum lower than intended. It could be an issue at the beginning of the `Token` lifecycle, when the total supply is still low.
poc: When creating a proposal in the `Governor` contract, [`proposal.quorumVotes`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L168) is computed during the `propose` tx. However tokens could be minted after the `propose` in the same block. In this case, they’ll still have a vote during the proposal due to how [`token.getPastVotes`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L462) works, therefore the quorum will be lower than intended given the actual total supply.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Governor contract determines the quorum required for a proposal to pass. During the proposal creation transaction, the contract captures the current total token supply and computes a quorum threshold based on that snapshot. However, the token contract permits new tokens to be minted in the same block after the proposal transaction has been executed. Because the Governor later checks a voter’s past voting power using the token’s getPastVotes function, any tokens minted after the proposal but before the vote are counted toward a voter’s weight, while the quorum value remains anchored to the earlier, lower supply figure. This mismatch means the effective quorum – the amount of voting power needed to approve a proposal – can be lower than the protocol’s intended level, especially when the token is at the beginning of its lifecycle and the total supply is still small. An attacker who can trigger token minting (or exploit a burn‑then‑mint pattern) after a proposal is submitted can acquire enough voting power to push a proposal through with fewer legitimate votes. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a proposal that seems to reach quorum despite only a handful of votes being visible, or a situation where the on‑chain quorum calculation reports a lower number than expected based on the displayed total supply. The impact includes the possibility of governance actions being approved without the proper community consensus, opening the door to value leakage, malicious parameter changes, or outright theft. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the logical flow of quorum computation and token supply dynamics, and it can be hard to notice because the discrepancy occurs within the same block and the contract does not explicitly surface the supply change. To remediate the flaw the quorum should be calculated from a supply snapshot taken at vote time, or the proposal timestamp should be adjusted (for example using proposal.timeCreated ‑ 1) so that any token minting in the same block is excluded from voting power. A broader refactor of the token’s mint/burn mechanisms may also be required to guarantee that the totalSupply used for quorum remains immutable throughout the voting period. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of governance quorum mis‑calculation vulnerabilities where a mutable supply metric is used to derive a fixed threshold, violating the assumption that total supply is constant during a proposal’s lifecycle.

title: Attackers can increase voting power by incentivizing
description: If the benefit to be gained from the outcome of the vote is less than the cost of obtaining the right to vote, the outcome of the vote is influenced.
poc:
* [Governor.sol#L248-L297](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L248-L297)  

  * [Vampire Attack Explained](https://finematics.com/vampire-attack-sushiswap-explained)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation of the governance module that allows an attacker to artificially increase their voting power and sway the outcome of proposals. The root cause lies in the absence of a blacklist enforcement step inside the internal `_castVote` routine, which means that even addresses that should be excluded from voting can still submit votes and have their weight counted. Because the contract does not provide a mechanism to revoke or reduce the voting weight of blacklisted participants, an adversary can acquire a small amount of voting tokens, incentivize additional accounts to delegate or transfer tokens cheaply, and then cast votes that outweigh the honest community's preferences. Exploitation proceeds by the attacker first obtaining a token stake whose expected benefit from a proposal exceeds the modest cost of acquiring that stake. The attacker then either directly votes or forces the contract to treat their stake as higher than it truly is, because the system does not verify that the voter is not on a blacklist and does not adjust the stored vote totals when a blacklist entry is added. When a proposal is executed, the manipulated vote totals can cause the decision to be opposite to the genuine intent of the community, leading to misallocation of funds, unintended contract upgrades, or other governance actions that harm the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is being voted on and any address that should be barred from participating is either not prevented from calling `_castVote` or its previously allocated voting power is not removed after blacklisting. All token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself are affected because the governance outcome no longer reflects the true distribution of stake, breaking the trust model of the system. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, which identified the missing `isBlacklisted` guard and the lack of a function to delete voting power for blacklisted addresses. The problem can be subtle because the contract correctly tracks vote counts for legitimate voters, so the additional malicious votes blend in with normal activity and may not raise immediate red flags. To remediate, the contract should enforce a blacklist check at the beginning of the voting function, reject any vote from a blacklisted address, and provide a privileged function that can reduce the stored `forVotes`, `againstVotes`, or `abstainVotes` associated with a blacklisted participant, effectively removing their influence from the tally. This aligns the implementation with the intended governance model where only eligible participants can affect proposal outcomes, preserving the accounting invariants that the total votes equal the sum of individual voting powers. In user‑facing terms, users may notice that proposals they expected to pass based on their stake instead fail, or that the on‑chain vote counts appear inconsistent with the visible token distribution, indicating that "funds disappear" from the governance decision process due to hidden, incentivized voting power.

title: Truncation in casting can lead to a founder receiving all the base tokens
description:
The initialize function of the `Token` contract receives an array of `FounderParams`, which contains the ownership percent of each founder as a `uint256`. The initialize function checks that the sum of the percents is not more than 100, but the value that is added to the sum of the percent is truncated to fit in `uint8`. This leads to an error because the value that is used for assigning the base tokens is the original, not truncated, `uint256` value.

This can lead to wrong assignment of the base tokens, and can also lead to a situation where not all the users will get the correct share of base tokens (if any).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unsafe type conversion performed during the token contract's initialization routine. The contract receives an array of founder parameters, each containing an ownership percentage stored as a uint256. When the initialize function aggregates these percentages into a running total, it casts each founderPct to a uint8 before adding it to totalOwnership. Because a uint8 can hold a maximum value of 255, any percentage larger than this value is silently truncated to the lower 8‑bit representation – for example, a value of 256 becomes 0. The contract then checks that totalOwnership does not exceed 100, but the check is applied to the truncated sum, allowing malicious input where the real percentages far exceed the allowed bound while the truncated sum remains within the limit. This flaw allows the schedule calculation, defined as 100 divided by founderPct, to evaluate to zero when founderPct is larger than 100, because the division is performed using integer arithmetic. A zero schedule prevents the base token identifier from advancing during the allocation loop, causing every base token (identified by tokenId % 100) to be assigned to the first founder in the list. As a result, the second and any subsequent founders receive no base tokens, effectively giving a single founder control over the entire base token supply. The impact is a complete misallocation of ownership: users expecting a proportional distribution see only one address receiving all tokens, while other founders’ balances remain at zero. The bug manifests only at contract deployment, when the initialize function is called, and only the deployer (or any party that can influence the founder array) can trigger it. It may be difficult to notice because the initialization succeeds without reverting, and the truncation does not emit an error – the contract’s state appears consistent with the (incorrect) truncated values. The issue was uncovered through a targeted audit that included a Foundry test reproducing the scenario with two founders each assigned an ownershipPct of 256; the test confirmed that all base token ids up to 99 were owned by the first founder. To remediate the problem, the contract should avoid casting founderPct to a smaller integer type when performing arithmetic checks, or it should enforce an explicit bound that founderPct does not exceed 100 before any cast. A safe approach is to keep the percentages as uint256 throughout the validation logic, ensure the cumulative ownership never surpasses 100, and revert on any input that would violate this invariant. This class of bug falls under integer truncation and unchecked casting errors, which can lead to logic bypasses and unintended allocation outcomes, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and eroding trust in the token distribution mechanism.

title: Owners receive more percentage of total nft if some nfts were burned
description:
According to Nouns Builder, founder can have percentage of created nft. This is set in `Token::_addFounders` function. When new nft is minted by `mint` function then total supply of tokens is incremented and assigned to tokenId using `tokenId = settings.totalSupply++`. Then this token is checked if it should be mint to founder(then again increment total supply of tokens) or should be mint to auction using `while (_isForFounder(tokenId))`.

If token wasn’t sold during the auction then auction burns it using `burn` function. And this function doesn’t decrement `settings.totalSupply` value. But total supply has changed now, it has decreased by one.

So suppose that we have 1 founder of dao that should receive 2% of nft, that means that if 100 nft are available(for example), then 2 of them belongs to that founder. If we have minted 100 nft and 10 of them were not sold(they were then burned), then there are 90 nft available now. And in current implementation founder has ownership of 2 of them, however 2 is not 2% of 90. So in case when nft are not sold on auction the percentage of founder’s tokens is increasing and the increasing speed depends on how many tokens were not sold. Also founder gets more power in the community(as he has more percentage now).
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an accounting mismatch in the NFT mint‑and‑burn lifecycle of the Nouns Builder DAO. When a new NFT is minted, the contract stores the current total supply in a counter (settings.totalSupply) and uses this value to determine the founder’s entitlement as a fixed percentage of the overall supply. The founder’s share is allocated by checking each tokenId against a founder‑allocation predicate and minting the appropriate number of tokens. However, when an NFT fails to sell at auction and is subsequently destroyed via the burn function, the implementation does not decrement the totalSupply counter. Consequently, the recorded totalSupply remains higher than the actual number of existing NFTs. Because the founder’s allocation logic continues to reference the stale totalSupply, the founder retains the same absolute number of tokens while the denominator (the real supply) shrinks, causing the founder’s relative ownership percentage to increase. This effect is observable to users as a sudden increase in the founder’s voting power or influence without any additional tokens being minted to the founder’s address. The issue manifests only after unsold NFTs are burned; it does not arise during normal minting or transfers. It was discovered during a systematic audit that examined token accounting and the interplay between minting, auction, and burn pathways. The bug can be difficult to notice because the burn operation appears harmless and does not emit any obvious warnings, while the totalSupply variable still reports a larger number, masking the inflated founder share. The impact is a breach of the intended governance economics: community members expect the founder to hold a constant proportion (e.g., 2% of all NFTs) regardless of market outcomes, but the faulty accounting grants the founder a disproportionate and dynamically increasing share, undermining decentralization and potentially allowing the founder to acquire majority control if many NFTs are burned. To remediate the flaw, the burn routine should correctly update the totalSupply counter (e.g., settings.totalSupply--) or the allocation logic should be refactored to base founder percentages on a immutable maximum supply or to explicitly account for burned tokens, thereby preserving the intended fractional ownership distribution.

title: Changing treasury owner through `transferOwnership
description:
[Governor.sol#L21](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/governance/governor/Governor.sol#L21)  
[Ownable.sol#L63](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/lib/utils/Ownable.sol#L63)  
[Auction.sol#L22](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/7e9fddbbacdd7d7812e912a369cfd862ee67dc03/src/auction/Auction.sol#L22)  

`governor.transferOwnership()` and `Auction.transferOwnership()` is exposed to `Treasury.sol` and can be called in a governance proposal. If this is used then it causes an inconsistency between the owner of these contracts and `settings.treasury` which would prevent governance from ever modifying its own parameters and Ethereum from auctions will be sent to the wrong address.

I believe medium severity is suitable because we lose partial control of governance and/or ETH from auctions, assuming that a proposal (malicious or not) is passed which changes contract ownership.
poc:
1. A proposal which calls `governor.transferOwnership()` is executed and transfers ownership to a new treasury address
  2. When subsequent proposals are passed, `Governor.sol` will make an external call to `settings.treasury` which is not modified when ownership is passed
  3. Therefore, `settings.treasury` is not able to modify any governance parameters such as `proposalThreshold`

The same issue applies to `Auction.sol`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between contract ownership and the stored treasury address in the governance system. The Governor and Auction contracts inherit a generic `transferOwnership` function that updates the internal `owner` variable but does not adjust the `settings.treasury` reference used by the protocol for critical operations. Because the treasury address is a separate configuration stored in a settings struct, changing the owner through a governance proposal leaves `settings.treasury` pointing to the original address. This decoupling allows an attacker who can pass a proposal to call `governor.transferOwnership()` or `auction.transferOwnership()` to redirect the contract’s ownership to an address they control without updating the treasury reference. Consequently, subsequent governance actions that rely on `settings.treasury` – such as modifying proposal thresholds, executing timelocked functions, or receiving ETH from auctions – will interact with the stale, incorrect address. From a user’s point of view, proposals that should adjust parameters appear to be accepted, yet the protocol silently ignores them, and users see no ETH arriving in the intended treasury. The impact is a partial loss of control over the governance process and a risk of funds being sent to an unintended contract, effectively draining auction proceeds or preventing legitimate governance changes. This condition can be triggered whenever a proposal successfully calls the ownership transfer function; it is not prevented by any access control beyond the usual governance voting, making it exploitable by a malicious proposer or by an inadvertent honest proposal that unintentionally corrupts the system state. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between ownership management and the treasury settings. It is subtle because the contract’s `owner` field updates correctly, and standard UI tools display the new owner, giving a false sense of security while the underlying treasury address remains unchanged. To remediate, the `transferOwnership` implementation should be extended to also update the `settings.treasury` entry, or the architecture should be refactored to eliminate the ability to change ownership independently of the treasury configuration, possibly by making the system immutable and handling migrations through a full redeployment and explicit fund transfer proposals. This aligns the on‑chain authority with the protocol’s accounting assumptions and restores the guarantee that governance actions affect the correct treasury address.

title: Token: Founder percentages not always respected
description:
[Token.sol#L110](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/debe9b792cc70510eadf9b3728cde5b0f2ec9a1f/src/token/Token.sol#L110)  

Because of the “greedy” minting scheme for founders (tokens to founders are minted until `_isForFounder` returns `false`, i.e. until there is an unset `tokenRecipient[tokenId % 100]`), it can happen that the actual percentages of tokens that the founders receive deviate significantly from the desired percentages:
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way founder token allocations are performed in the Token contract. Instead of assigning founder shares at fixed intervals, the contract uses a "greedy" minting loop that continues to mint tokens for founders until the internal helper function `_isForFounder` returns false, which happens when an entry in the `tokenRecipient` mapping for the current `tokenId % 100` slot is empty. Because the loop stops at the first free slot rather than at a predefined schedule, the actual percentage of tokens received by each founder can drift away from the percentages declared in the contract configuration. The root cause is that the allocation logic relies on the dynamic availability of slots in a circular buffer rather than on a deterministic, per‑hundred‑token schedule. An attacker or a malicious founder can craft a particular `founderPct` array that causes the greedy loop to repeatedly fill the same slot, effectively giving one founder a larger share while starving another. This mis‑allocation can be triggered during normal minting operations whenever the contract mints a batch of tokens that crosses a multiple of 100, and it becomes especially pronounced when the founder percentage configuration is deliberately skewed. From a user perspective, a founder may notice that after a series of mints the expected share of tokens (e.g., 10 % of every 100 tokens) does not materialize; instead, the balance may be higher or lower than anticipated, leading to confusion such as "my token balance is lower than it should be" or "I received far more tokens than my agreed share". The impact is a violation of the business logic that each founder should receive a fixed proportion of the total supply, which can undermine trust in the protocol’s token economics and potentially cause financial loss for founders who receive fewer tokens than owed. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the minting flow and identified that certain founder percentage arrays produce unfair reward distributions. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about deviation and the overall token supply still grows as expected, making the discrepancy subtle. To remediate the problem, the allocation mechanism should be changed to a deterministic schedule: mint founder tokens only when `tokenId % 100 == 0`, ensuring that exactly one token per hundred is allocated according to the predefined percentages. This guarantees that the realized percentages match the intended ones, eliminating the greedy slot‑search behavior and preventing any configuration‑driven imbalance.

title: Minting is not possible when a property has no items
description:
[MetadataRenderer.sol#L194](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/token/metadata/MetadataRenderer.sol#L194)  

If a property without items was added, minting becomes impossible. To enable minting again, an item must be added to the property, which is only possible through a new governance proposal.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an input‑validation defect in the metadata rendering component that makes the token minting function revert whenever a property is added to the contract without any associated items. The root cause is that the renderer assumes every property has at least one item and performs arithmetic (such as division for random selection or weight calculation) based on the number of items. When the items array is empty, the division denominator becomes zero, triggering a Solidity division‑by‑zero error and causing the mint transaction to fail. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit this by calling the addProperties function with a non‑empty list of property names but an empty items array. After the empty property is recorded, any subsequent call to the token's mint function will revert, preventing new tokens from being issued. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to mint receive a transaction that reverts with a generic "division error", the user interface shows no token minted, and the protocol’s supply growth stalls. This condition occurs the moment a property without items is recorded, which can happen during contract initialization, governance‑driven upgrades, or any off‑chain script that adds properties. All participants who rely on the token – token holders, prospective minters, and the protocol’s governance – are affected because the expected behavior (minting a new NFT) does not happen. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case intentionally added a property with an empty items array and observed that minting reverted with a division error. The bug can be hard to notice because the addProperties call itself succeeds; the contract does not emit a warning about the empty collection, and only the later mint operation fails, presenting an unexpected runtime error rather than a clear validation message. To remediate, the contract should enforce that each newly added property includes at least one item, either by rejecting empty items in the addProperties function or by adding a guard that prevents the renderer from executing division when the items list is empty. In broader terms, this is a classic case of missing input validation leading to a division‑by‑zero vulnerability, which violates the business logic that every minted token must have complete metadata and that the token supply can be increased without error. From the user's viewpoint, the expectation is that calling mint results in a new NFT being transferred to their address; instead, the transaction reverts, leaving the user with no token, no balance change, and an unexplained error message.

title: Tokens without properties can be minted and cannot be rendered
description: It’s possible to mint tokens when properties haven’t yet been set in `MetadataRenderer`. Such tokens won’t be possible to render due to [this check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/token/metadata/MetadataRenderer.sol#L222) in the `getAttributes` function of `MetaRenderer` contract. There’s no way to fix such tokens after they were minted since the number of properties of each token [is stored individually](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-nouns-builder/blob/main/src/token/metadata/MetadataRenderer.sol#L216-L219), thus a patched `MetadataRenderer` and a proxy contract need to be deployed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the ability to mint a token when the metadata renderer has not yet been configured with any property definitions. The root cause is a missing guard in the MetadataRenderer contract: the onMinted() callback does not verify that the array of properties stored for the token has a non‑zero length, and the getAttributes() function later assumes that at least one property exists before attempting to build the attribute string. Because of this omission, a token can be successfully minted (the mint transaction does not revert) while the internal propertiesCount for that token remains zero. When a client later calls getAttributes() to retrieve the visual or descriptive data for the token, the function hits a require statement that checks for a non‑empty property list and reverts with a TOKEN_NOT_MINTED error. From a user’s point of view the token appears to have been acquired – the balance and totalSupply counters are updated – but the UI shows no artwork, no attributes, or a cryptic error message. The expected behavior is that each minted token immediately has a valid set of attributes that can be rendered; instead the token is in a limbo state where it exists on‑chain but cannot be displayed. This bug is exploitable by any actor who can call the mint function before the DAO or protocol owners have added the required properties to the renderer. By deliberately minting a token in this window, the attacker can create a token that is effectively useless – it cannot be sold, displayed, or used in governance actions that rely on token metadata, potentially undermining confidence in the protocol. The issue arises only when the contract is freshly deployed or upgraded and the properties have not yet been populated; once properties are added, subsequent mints behave correctly. The problem was discovered through an audit test case that deliberately omitted the property‑setting step, observed that minting succeeded, and then verified that getAttributes() reverted. The bug is subtle because the mint transaction itself shows no error, so developers and users may not notice the failure until they attempt to view the token in a marketplace or wallet. To remediate the issue, the onMinted() function should enforce that properties.length > 0 before allowing a mint, or the contract should provide a default property set that ensures every token has renderable metadata. Deploying a patched renderer via a proxy and updating the implementation is also required to address already‑minted tokens that lack properties, because the number of properties for each token is stored individually and cannot be retroactively set without a contract upgrade. Overall the vulnerability constitutes a medium‑risk flaw in the token’s accounting logic, breaking the contract’s guarantee that every minted token will have usable metadata, and may lead to user confusion, loss of confidence, and potential financial impact if the token cannot be sold or used in governance.

title: State function does not require majority of votes for supporting and passing a proposal
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s `state` function, which decides whether a proposal has been defeated, succeeded, or is in another terminal state after the voting period ends. The function checks if a proposal is defeated with the condition `else if (proposal.forVotes < proposal.againstVotes || proposal.forVotes < proposal.quorumVotes)`. Because the operator is a strict less‑than (`<`), a situation where `proposal.forVotes` equals `proposal.againstVotes` but both values satisfy the quorum requirement is not captured by the defeat branch. Consequently, the function falls through to the `Succeeded` branch, treating the proposal as successful even though it did not obtain a strict majority of supporting votes. The root cause is an off‑by‑one logical error: the equality case is omitted, so a 50 %‑plus‑zero tie is considered a passing outcome.

An attacker can exploit this by coordinating votes so that the number of "for" and "against" votes are identical and the total reaches the quorum threshold. After the voting deadline, the contract will report the proposal as `Succeeded`, allowing it to be queued and eventually executed. This permits critical governance actions—such as upgrading the contract implementation, re‑allocating treasury assets, or changing protocol parameters—to be approved without genuine majority consent. From a user’s perspective the UI will display “Proposal succeeded” while the vote tally shows an exact tie, violating the expectation that a proposal needs more supporting votes than opposing votes to pass. Token holders, treasury managers, and any participants relying on the DAO’s governance integrity are therefore exposed to unexpected fund withdrawals or malicious upgrades.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case was added that deliberately created a tie (two for, two against) with quorum reached. The test proved that the contract returned `Succeeded` instead of `Defeated`. The bug is subtle because tie outcomes are rare in practice, and the code appears to follow a typical pattern for checking defeat, making the missing equality condition easy to overlook.

To remediate, the defeat condition should be changed to include the equality case, for example by using `proposal.forVotes <= proposal.againstVotes` or adding a configurable governance flag that asserts a strict majority is required. This adjustment ensures that proposals with exactly equal support and opposition are classified as defeated, aligning the contract’s behavior with standard democratic principles and preventing unintended execution of proposals.

In summary, the flaw is an off‑by‑one logical error in the voting outcome calculation, classified as a majority‑vote handling bug. It can cause proposals with a perfect 50/50 split to be incorrectly marked as successful, leading to potential loss of funds or unauthorized protocol changes. The recommended fix is to modify the comparison operator to include equality or to make the majority requirement explicit in the contract’s governance configuration.

title: Attacker can list an NFT they own and inflate to zero all users’ contributions, keeping the NFT and all the money
description:
Crowdfunds split the voting power and distribution of profits rights according to the percentage used to purchase the NFT. When an attacker lists his own NFT for sale and contributes to it, any sum he contributes will return to him once the sell is executed. This behavior is fine so long as the sell price is fair, as other contributors will receive a fair portion of voting power and equity. Therefore, when maximum price is defined, it is not considered a vulnerability that an attacker can contribute `maximumPrice - totalContributions` and take a potentially large stake of the Crowdfund, as user’s have contributed knowing the potential maximum price.

However, when maximum price is zero, which is allowed in BuyCrowdfund and CollectionBuyCrowdfund, the lister of the NFT can always steal the entirety of the fund and keep the NFT. Attacker can send a massive contribution, buy the NFT and pass a unanimous proposal to approve the NFT to his wallet. Attacker can use a flash loan to finance the initial contribution, which is easily paid back from the NFT lister wallet.

It is important to note that there is no way for the system to know if the Crowdfund creator and the NFT owner are the same entity, and therefore it is critical for the platform to defend users against this scenario.
poc:
1. Suppose totalContributions=X. Attacker will prepare flashloan callback which does:

     * `contribute()` with the borrowed funds
     * call BuyCrowdfund’s `buy()` with a contract that will purchase the NFT using the large sum
     * call NFT lister contract’s sendProfit() function which will send attacker the NFT sell amount
     * pay back the flash loan
  2. Attacker will call flashloan(10,000X) to buy his own NFT and take unanimous holding of created party
  3. Attacker will create ArbitraryCallsProposal with a single call to token.approve(ATTACKER, token_id). It is immediately ready for execution because attacker has > 99.99% of votes. Precious approve() is allowed in unanimous proposals.
  4. Attacker calls NFT’s `transferFrom()` to take back control of the NFT, leaving with the Crowdfund’s contribution and the listed NFT.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in crowd‑funding contracts that allow an NFT to be listed for sale with a maximum price of zero. In these contracts the voting power and the share of profits are calculated from the amount each participant contributes to purchase the listed NFT. Because the system does not distinguish between the creator of the crowd‑fund and the current owner of the NFT, an attacker who already owns the NFT can list it, contribute an arbitrarily large amount (often using a flash‑loan), and then execute a purchase at the zero‑price ceiling. After the contribution, the attacker holds virtually all voting weight, enabling a unanimous proposal that calls the NFT contract’s approve function for the attacker’s address. The proposal passes immediately because the attacker controls more than 99.99 % of the votes. Once approved, the attacker invokes transferFrom to move the NFT back to their wallet and keeps the full pool of contributed ether. From the user’s point of view, contributors see their balances reduced to zero while no NFT is delivered; the UI may indicate a successful purchase, yet the funds have vanished. The impact is a complete loss of all contributions in the affected crowd‑fund, a breach of the expected profit‑sharing model, and erosion of trust in the platform. The flaw is triggered only when the maximumPrice parameter is set to zero, which is permitted by the BuyCrowdfund and CollectionBuyCrowdfund contracts, and when the NFT owner also participates as a contributor. The audit uncovered this logical oversight by analyzing the relationship between contribution handling, voting power calculation, and proposal execution. The issue is difficult to spot because the same code path works correctly for non‑zero maximum prices, and there is no explicit check that the listing creator and contributor are distinct entities. Mitigation requires disabling the ability to set an unlimited (zero) maximum price for these crowd‑fund contracts, or adding explicit constraints that prevent the NFT owner from both listing and contributing sufficient funds to achieve unilateral control. More generally, the bug belongs to the class of “economic manipulation via unchecked auction ceiling” where a participant can inflate contributions to capture the entire pool, violating the intended accounting and fairness assumptions of the system.

title: Previously nominated delegate can reset the delegation
description:
`burn()` allows for previously recorded delegate to set himself to be contributor’s delegate even if another one was already chosen.

This can be quite material as owner choice for the whole voting power is being reset this way to favor the old delegate.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a delegation‑reset bug that allows an attacker to overwrite a contributor’s chosen delegate and redirect the entire intrinsic voting power to a previously recorded delegate. It originates from the mint() function, which is invoked during the _burn() process, assuming that every mint operation is the first one for the owner. Consequently, mint() unconditionally calls _adjustVotingPower with the delegate argument supplied by the stored delegationsByContributor mapping, without checking whether the owner already has an active delegate.
