This class of bug falls under the broader category of insufficient input validation or missing guarantee enforcement, where financial calculations are performed without safeguarding against adverse market movements. From a user’s standpoint, the symptom is that a swap that should have yielded a certain amount of tokens instead returns a much smaller amount or even zero, contrary to the user’s expectation of receiving at least the quoted minimum. The failure violates fundamental accounting assumptions that the protocol will preserve value parity for participants and that trades will be executed within acceptable price ranges.

title: A malicious user can send tokens to the `TribeRedeemer` contract to make the redeem function work, and other users may lose assets as a result
poc: [TribeRedeemer.sol#L44-L61](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-tribe/blob/769b0586b4975270b669d7d1581aa5672d6999d5/contracts/shutdown/redeem/TribeRedeemer.sol#L44-L61)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an early‑redeem flaw in the TribeRedeemer contract where the redeem function only checks that the contract holds a non‑zero balance of each reward token before allowing a user to exchange their redeemedToken for rewards. This minimal check assumes that the contract will be fully funded before any redemption can occur, but it does not enforce a minimum amount or a time lock. Consequently, a malicious actor can deposit a small quantity of reward tokens into the contract, satisfying the non‑zero balance requirement. When an uninformed user later calls the redeem function, the transaction succeeds and the user receives a proportionally tiny amount of reward tokens, far less than they would have obtained once the full reward pool is later transferred to the contract. From the user’s point of view, they expect to receive a meaningful reward for their redeemedToken, but instead they may see a near‑zero payout or a balance that appears to disappear, leading to disappointment and potential loss of value. The issue occurs only when the contract has not yet been fully funded and an attacker can both send a minimal amount of reward tokens and convince users to redeem before the intended funding window, typically after contract deployment but before the DAO vote funds the contract (a lag of at least three days). The affected parties are token holders who attempt to redeem, especially those unaware of the funding schedule, and the protocol’s reputation because the premature redemption leaks value that should have been distributed later. The flaw was identified during a security audit by analyzing the redeem logic and noting that the sole require statement `require(balance != 0, "ZERO_BALANCE")` does not guarantee sufficient assets, making the problem subtle and easy to miss because the function executes successfully and does not revert when a small balance exists. The bug falls into the class of under‑funded contract redemption or premature execution vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes a certain state that is not programmatically enforced. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum funding threshold, pause redemption until the expected reward pool is deposited, or incorporate a governor‑controlled start flag, thereby aligning the contract’s state with the intended economic assumptions and preventing users from receiving unintentionally low rewards.

title: `TribeRedeemer` will start redeeming incorrectly if someone transfer redeem tokens directly to it
description:
`TribeRedeemer` contract has one goal. It should take `_redeemedToken` (token that contract will accept from users), `_tokensReceived` - list of exchange tokens (these are created exactly to be exchanged for redeemedToken) and `_redeemBase` amount of tokens that should be redeemed (this actually should be `IERC20(_redeemedToken).totalSupply()`). After that it will start redeeming `_redeemedToken` in exchange for `_tokensReceived` tokens.

Suppose we have redeemed token `tokenA` with total supply of `10000` and `redeemBase == 10000`. And in `_tokensReceived` list we have only 1 token `tokenB` with total supply of `10000` (all tokens are controlled by `TribeRedeemer`). According to logic of `TribeRedeemer`, if user wants to redeem X tokens then he will receive `(x * tokenB.balanceOf(address(this))) / redeemBase` that in our case will be just amount X. So user send X `tokenA` and receive back X `tokenB`. Now because `redeemBase == 10000` and contract balance of `tokenB` is `10000` the exchange ratio is `1:1`.

However, if someone will transfer some amount of `tokenA` to `TribeRedeemer` contract directly using `ERC20.transfer`, for example `500` tokens, then it does not call `redeem` function and `redeemBase` value will not be decreased with amount sent. That means that right now the exchange ratio should not be `1:1` as `TribeRedeemer` contract received more `500` tokens and didn’t pay user for them (it should redeem that amount then with the next users, their share should be increased). So the next users will receive less amount than they should (`TribeRedeemer` should spend all `tokenB` amount in exchange of all `tokenA` tokens).

```solidity
uint256 redeemedAmount = (amountIn * balance) / base;
```

where balance is

```solidity
uint256 balance = IERC20(tokensReceived[i]).balanceOf(address(this));
```
poc:
Here is where `amountOut` is calculated.  
[TribeRedeemer.sol#L58](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-tribe/blob/main/contracts/shutdown/redeem/TribeRedeemer.sol#L58)

This is where the `redeemBase` is decreased with redeem amount, but is not called because of direct transfer.  
[TribeRedeemer.sol#L70](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-tribe/blob/main/contracts/shutdown/redeem/TribeRedeemer.sol#L70)
bug_full: The TribeRedeemer contract is designed to exchange a specific redeem token for a set of pre‑allocated exchange tokens at a rate that is calculated from the current balance of the exchange tokens divided by a constant called redeemBase. In the intended flow users call the redeem() function, which atomically transfers the user’s redeem tokens to the contract, decreases redeemBase by the amount redeemed, and then computes the user’s payout as (amountIn * exchangeTokenBalance) / redeemBase. The vulnerability arises because the contract does not distinguish between redeem tokens that arrive via the redeem() function and those that are transferred directly to the contract using the standard ERC‑20 transfer() method. When a user (or any address) sends redeem tokens directly, the contract’s balance of the redeem token increases, but the internal redeemBase value is not reduced because the internal accounting logic is only executed inside redeem(). Consequently, the ratio used for subsequent redemptions becomes skewed: the denominator (redeemBase) remains unchanged while the numerator (exchange token balance) is unchanged, but the total supply of redeem tokens held by the contract is now larger. This means that later users receive a smaller amount of exchange tokens than they are mathematically entitled to, effectively diluting their reward. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who redeems a given amount of the redeem token may receive fewer exchange tokens than expected, or in extreme cases may receive nothing while the contract holds a surplus of redeem tokens that were sent directly. The impact is a loss of value for legitimate redeemers because the contract over‑counts the redeemable supply and under‑pays users, and the directly transferred redeem tokens become locked and are effectively burned because the contract has no mechanism to redistribute them. The issue occurs whenever any address transfers the redeem token to the TribeRedeemer contract outside of the redeem() function, which can happen unintentionally (e.g., a user mistaking the contract address for a normal wallet) or deliberately by an attacker looking to manipulate the payout ratio. The flaw was discovered during a code audit that examined the accounting of redeemBase and observed that the variable is only updated in redeem(), while ERC‑20 transfer events are not intercepted. It is subtle because the contract’s public functions appear to work correctly when used as intended, and the imbalance only becomes evident when the contract’s token balance deviates from the expected accounting, a condition that is not directly exposed in UI or events. To fix the issue the contract should compute the redeemable amount based on the actual outstanding redeem tokens rather than a static redeemBase, for example by using totalSupply() minus the contract’s current balance of the redeem token, or by making redeemBase a constant and adjusting the formula to subtract the contract’s redeem token balance from the denominator. This change ensures that any tokens sent directly to the contract are either accounted for in the redemption formula or otherwise prevented, thereby preserving equal claim rights and preventing inadvertent token burning.

title: Supply cap of `VariableSupplyERC20Token` is not properly enforced
description:
[VariableSupplyERC20Token.sol#L36-L46](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/main/contracts/token/VariableSupplyERC20Token.sol#L36-L46)  

The admin of the token is not constrained to minting `maxSupply_`, they can mint any number of tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token contract that allows an administrator to increase the total supply without respecting the declared maximum supply limit. The contract stores a variable representing the amount of tokens that can still be minted (mintableSupply). The logic treats a value of zero for this variable as a special case, interpreting it as "infinite minting" rather than as the actual exhaustion of the supply cap. Consequently, once the admin has minted the exact amount allowed by the cap, mintableSupply becomes zero and the contract mistakenly believes there is no limit, allowing the admin to mint any additional amount thereafter. This flaw originates from an incorrect assumption about the semantics of a zero value in the supply‑tracking variable; the intended design was to use zero to signal that the supply cap is disabled, but the implementation conflates the cap‑exhausted state with the unlimited‑mint state. An attacker, who in this case is the privileged admin, can exploit the flaw by first minting up to the maximum allowed quantity and then invoking the mint function again with an arbitrary large amount, because the require check that enforces amount ≤ mintableSupply is bypassed when mintableSupply equals zero. The impact is severe for any ecosystem that relies on the token’s scarcity: the token can be arbitrarily inflated, eroding holder value, disrupting economic incentives, and potentially allowing the admin to drain value from protocols that assume a fixed supply. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s mint function is called after mintableSupply has been reduced to zero, i.e., after the prescribed cap has been reached. All token holders, users of the protocol, and any downstream contracts that depend on the token’s supply invariants are affected. The issue was discovered during a code review that highlighted the inconsistent handling of the mintableSupply variable and the absence of a guard preventing further minting after the cap is hit. The bug is subtle because the contract behaves correctly up to the point where the supply cap is reached, after which the behavior changes silently, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should treat a sentinel value such as the maximum uint256 (2**256‑1) as the representation of an unlimited supply, and keep zero as a legitimate indicator that no more tokens may be minted. Additionally, the mint function should always enforce that the total supply never exceeds the configured maxSupply, regardless of the mintableSupply value. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents arbitrary inflation of the token.

title: `_baseVestedAmount`
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L183-L187](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L183-L187)  
[VTVLVesting.sol#L198](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L198)  

As the comments in `_baseVestedAmount()` explain, once there is any `_claim.amountWithdrawn`, it will be returned if it is greater than the calculated value `vestAmt`. However, `vestAmt` takes account of time, `_referenceTs`, whereas `_claim.amountWithdrawn` is always the amount withdrawn to date. Therefore, for all historical values below `_claim.amountWithdrawn`, including timestamps before `_claim.startTimestamp` and before `_claim.cliffReleaseTimestamp`, `_claim.amountWithdrawn` will be returned.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal helper that computes the base vested amount for a token claim. The function is intended to return the amount that has become vested based solely on the passage of time, the start timestamp, the cliff, and the linear vesting schedule. However, the implementation also compares the already‑withdrawn amount stored in the claim and, when that withdrawn amount is greater than the time‑derived vested amount, it returns the withdrawn amount instead. Because the withdrawn amount is a cumulative absolute figure that never decreases, this comparison causes the function to report a non‑monotonic value for any historical timestamp that lies before the moment when the withdrawn amount first equals the vested amount. In practice, queries for vesting amounts at timestamps prior to the claim’s start or cliff can return a positive number that actually represents tokens already taken out, even though no vesting should have occurred yet. This discrepancy arises from the root cause that the view logic mixes a dynamic, time‑dependent calculation with a static cumulative counter, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that vested amounts must increase monotonically over time. An attacker or confused user can exploit the bug by calling the public vestedAmount view with a past timestamp to obtain a misleading figure, potentially influencing downstream logic that relies on this view – for example, revocation or reward distribution functions that assume the returned value reflects the real amount that can be withdrawn. The impact is primarily informational: users may see a vested balance that is larger than expected before vesting begins, leading to false expectations of available tokens, UI components that display erratic graphs, or protocol mechanisms that make incorrect decisions based on the inflated number. The condition occurs whenever a claim has a non‑zero amountWithdrawn and a query is made for a timestamp earlier than the point where vestAmt caught up to that withdrawn amount. All claim holders, the contract owner, and any external system that reads the vesting status are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors examined the comments of the _baseVestedAmount function and created a test that printed vested amounts before, during, and after a withdrawal, revealing the inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the function is a read‑only view and does not directly affect token transfers, so the contract still behaves correctly when actually withdrawing, making the error easy to overlook in normal operation. The recommended remediation is to separate the concerns: for active claims, ignore the amountWithdrawn entirely and return only the time‑derived vested amount; for inactive (revoked) claims, return the minimum of the time‑derived amount and the withdrawn amount, thereby preserving monotonicity without distorting historical values. This conceptual fix restores the invariant that vested amounts never decrease and aligns the view with the intended business logic of linear vesting with a cliff, eliminating the misleading user‑facing symptom where a balance appears to be available before the vesting schedule starts.

title: Possible DoS on `vestingRecipients` due to lack of disposal mechanism
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L224](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L224)  
[VTVLVesting.sol#L245](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L245)  
[VTVLVesting.sol#L302](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L302)  
[VTVLVesting.sol#L317](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L317)  

When the smart contracts start to be used, the variable in storage vestingRecipients will start to be filled with addresses, as there is no mechanism to eliminate elements, this will cause the `allVestingRecipients()` function to generate a DoS yes has many addressess.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unbounded, append‑only storage array that records every address that ever receives a vesting schedule. The contract populates the array `vestingRecipients` each time a new vesting entry is created, but it never provides a method to remove an entry after the vesting is fully claimed or cancelled. Because the array can only grow, the public helper function `allVestingRecipients()` will eventually attempt to return a list that contains a very large number of addresses. When the size of the array approaches the block gas limit, the EVM will run out of gas while trying to copy the entire array into memory, causing the call to revert. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: any off‑chain tool, explorer, or on‑chain logic that relies on fetching the complete list of recipients will be unable to do so, effectively making the data unavailable. The problem manifests only after the contract has been in use for a sufficient period for the array to accumulate many entries; the exact point of failure depends on how quickly entries are added and the prevailing block gas limit. Users are affected because they may observe that calls to retrieve the list return out‑of‑gas errors or incomplete data, leading to confusion when they expect to see all vesting participants. Auditors discovered the issue during a routine source‑code review, noting the absence of any deletion logic and the fact that the array is never trimmed. The defect is subtle because the function that returns the array is not used by the core token‑vesting flow, so the contract continues to operate correctly for vesting releases, making the problem easy to overlook. Conceptually, this is an instance of an unbounded dynamic array that lacks a disposal mechanism, a known class of DoS bugs related to gas‑exhaustion when returning large collections. To remediate, the contract should either introduce a way to prune entries whose vesting schedules are finished, or redesign the getter to support pagination (e.g., returning a slice of the array) so that the amount of data copied fits within the block gas limit. By ensuring the array does not grow unchecked or by limiting the size of each query, the denial‑of‑service risk is eliminated and users can reliably retrieve recipient information.

title: not able to create claim
description:
If admin revoked any recipient’s claim, admin can not create claim for the same recipient because `startTimestamp` is not updated to initial value on revoke claim.  
There will be a need to create a claim again for any reason like: 1) mistakenly revoked claim, 2) wrong info provided to claim, 3) new vesting period starts, etc.
poc:
1. Alice creates claim for Bob
2. Alice revokes claim of Bob
   * On `revokeClaim()`, claim’s `isActive` will be false, but `startTimestamp` will remain as it is
   * [VTVLVesting.sol#L418-L437](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L418-L437)
3. Alice tries to create claim for Bob but claim will not create because it has modifier `hasNoClaim()` which is checked for claim should not active and it checks for `require(_claim.startTimestamp == 0, "CLAIM_ALREADY_EXISTS");`
4. [VTVLVesting.sol#L245-L253](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L245-L253)
5. [VTVLVesting.sol#L123-L140](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L123-L140)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the lifecycle management of a vesting claim in a token vesting contract. When an administrator revokes an existing claim, the contract correctly marks the claim as inactive by setting its `isActive` flag to false, but it fails to reset the claim’s `startTimestamp` field. The creation routine for a new claim checks that `startTimestamp` is zero as an indication that no claim currently exists for the beneficiary. Because the timestamp remains unchanged after revocation, the `hasNoClaim` modifier rejects the new request with the error message “CLAIM_ALREADY_EXISTS”. Consequently, an admin who has revoked a claim – for instance to correct a mistaken address, wrong amount, or to start a new vesting period – cannot re‑create a claim for the same recipient within the same vesting contract. This logical inconsistency becomes apparent only when the revocation path is exercised; the contract appears to have deactivated the claim, yet the underlying state still signals an existing claim, making the bug easy to overlook during casual testing. The impact is primarily an availability issue: the intended recipient cannot receive the corrected vesting schedule, leading to a mismatch between business expectations (the user expects a new claim to be created) and reality (the transaction reverts). No funds are directly stolen or lost, but the protocol’s functionality is impaired and may require the deployment of a fresh vesting contract to work around the problem. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised the revoke‑and‑recreate workflow and observed the unexpected rejection. It belongs to the class of state‑reset bugs where a function does not fully clean up mutable storage, causing stale data to block legitimate future operations. From a user perspective, the UI may display an empty balance or a generic error, while the user expects a new vesting schedule to be established. The recommended remediation is to reset `startTimestamp` to zero (or otherwise clear the claim’s identifying fields) within the `revokeClaim()` function, ensuring that the contract’s state correctly reflects the absence of any claim after revocation. This change restores the intended ability to recreate claims and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic.

title: Tokens with lower number of decimals can result in postponed linear vesting for user
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L174](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/69da6e96f94ff3e02b9bb6175e6de2b3e71d3eb0/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L174)  

In the `_baseVestedAmount` of `VTVLVesting.sol` we see the following code:

```solidity
uint40 finalVestingDurationSecs = _claim.endTimestamp - _claim.startTimestamp; // length of the interval
uint112 linearVestAmount = _claim.linearVestAmount * truncatedCurrentVestingDurationSecs / finalVestingDurationSecs;
```

Let’s look at `truncatedCurrentVestingDurationSecs` as just the duration passed from the start of the vesting period for the PoC (this doesn’t omit important data in this context).

Now think of the following scenario:

We have a token `$TKN` that has 6 decimals (those are the decimals of both USDT & USDC). We want to distribute 10,000 of those tokens to a user vested over a 10 year period.

10 years in seconds is 315360000 (this is `finalVestingDurationSecs`)

This means that we will distribute 10,000 * 10^6 = 10000000000 fractions of a token for 315360000 seconds, meaning we will distribute 310 fractions of a token each second - this is `linearVestAmount`

Now, since `finalVestingDurationSecs` is so big (315360000) it will almost always round `linearVestAmount` to zero when dividing by it, up until `_claim.linearVestAmount * truncatedCurrentVestingDurationSecs` becomes a bigger number than 315360000, but since `_claim.linearVestAmount` is 310 we will need the current vesting duration to be at least 1017290 seconds which is **12** days postponed vesting. 12 days in a moving market can make a big difference if the user was expecting the tokens to start vesting from the first day.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the linear‑vesting calculation that can postpone the release of tokens for the first days of a vesting schedule. The contract computes the amount that should be vested at a given moment by multiplying the total linear vesting amount by the elapsed seconds and then dividing by the total vesting duration, all using Solidity's integer arithmetic. Because the division is performed without any scaling factor, the result is truncated toward zero. When the token involved has a low number of decimals (for example six‑decimal USDC or USDT) and the total vesting period is long (several years), the per‑second vesting amount becomes a small integer (often less than one token fraction). Consequently, the product of the per‑second amount and the elapsed seconds remains smaller than the denominator for a substantial period, causing the division to evaluate to zero. In the concrete example, a 10‑year vesting of 10 000 six‑decimal tokens yields a per‑second amount of roughly 310 token fractions; the integer division only becomes non‑zero after about 1 017 290 seconds, or roughly twelve days. This means that a user who expects tokens to start vesting from day one will see no tokens become claimable for almost two weeks, effectively postponing the linear vesting schedule. The impact is a delay in token availability, which can be financially material in a volatile market because the user loses the opportunity to sell or use the tokens during the postponed window. The issue manifests whenever the contract is used with tokens that have fewer than 18 decimals and a long vesting duration; it does not appear with 18‑decimal tokens because the per‑second amount is larger and the integer division yields a non‑zero result much earlier. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the VTVLVesting.sol source code, where the auditor noticed that the calculation uses plain uint arithmetic without any fixed‑point scaling. It can be hard to detect because standard unit tests often use mock tokens with 18 decimals and short vesting periods, masking the truncation problem. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum token precision (e.g., require 18 decimals) or, preferably, adopt fixed‑point arithmetic with an explicit scaling factor (such as using 1e18 as a multiplier) before performing the division. Alternatively, the vesting logic could be re‑implemented to distribute amounts in discrete chunks that guarantee at least one token fraction per interval. From the user’s perspective, the UI would show a zero balance or a “nothing to claim” message even though time has passed, contradicting the expectation that a linear vesting should have released some tokens each day. This discrepancy violates the business logic that tokens are supposed to become gradually available, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially eroding trust in the protocol.

title: Variable balance token causing fund lock and loss
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L295](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L295)  
[VTVLVesting.sol#L388](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L388)  

Some ERC20 token’s balance could change, one example is stETH. The balance could become insufficient at the time of `withdraw()`. User’s fund will be locked due to DoS. The way to take the fund out is to send more token into the contract, causing fund loss to the protocol. And there is no guarantee that until the end time the balance would stay above the needed amount, the lock and loss issue persist.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on a token’s on‑chain balance to guarantee that sufficient funds are available for withdrawals. The contract assumes that the ERC‑20 token balance reported by `balanceOf(address(this))` remains stable after a claim is created, but this assumption is violated when the token implements a variable supply mechanism such as rebasing, fee‑on‑transfer, or any other feature that can change the holder’s balance without an explicit transfer. Because the contract records the required amount only at claim‑creation time and later checks the current balance only in a `require` statement, a reduction in the token balance after the claim is recorded can cause the subsequent `safeTransfer` in `withdraw()` to revert due to an "INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE" condition. When this revert occurs, the user’s claim cannot be executed, effectively locking the user’s funds in the contract (a denial‑of‑service). The only way to release the locked funds is to deposit additional tokens into the contract, which results in a net loss for the protocol because the original amount allocated for the vesting schedule is no longer fully recoverable. This issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the handling of external ERC‑20 tokens and identified that the contract does not account for tokens whose total supply can fluctuate, such as stETH, which calculates balances based on internal share accounting. The problem is subtle because the `require` check passes at the moment of claim creation, giving a false sense of safety, and the balance may only drop later, making the failure non‑deterministic and hard to reproduce in testing. The impact is that users expecting to receive their vested tokens may see the transaction revert, receive a zero payout, or find their contract balance unchanged despite having a valid claim, breaking the business logic that vesting guarantees delivery of the promised amount. To mitigate the issue, the contract should either restrict accepted tokens to those with a fixed supply and no transfer fees, or redesign the accounting to use a share‑based system that tracks proportional ownership rather than absolute token quantities, thereby insulating the vesting logic from external balance changes. In essence, this is a classic case of assuming token immutability in the presence of rebasing or fee‑on‑transfer tokens, leading to balance‑validation failures, denial‑of‑service, and potential fund loss.

title: Vesting Schedule Start and End Time can be Set in the Past
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L245-L304](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L245-L304)  

There is no check whether `_startTimestamp` and `_endTimestamp` is greater than `block.timestamp` at `VTVLVesting.sol` `_createClaimUnchecked` function. Therefore it is possible for administrators to accidentally create vesting schedule that starts and ends in the past without noticing it. When administrators does this and this transaction goes through, then the vesting recipients can withdraw their entire vest amount which is not what administrators intended to do. Add require check that force `_startTimestamp` to be greater than `block.timestamp`.

Team comments as below on line 260

    // -> Conclusion: we want to allow this, for founders that might have forgotten to add some users, or to avoid issues with 
    transactions not going through because of discoordination between block.timestamp and sender's local time

However this is not an issue by adding `require(_startTimestamp > uint40(block.timestamp))` since this will revert transaction if _startTimestamp is less than block.timestamp so administrators can simply try again with correct time. On the other hand, it is more dangerous to not include this check because transaction will simply succeed even though _startTimestamp is set to past which means that there is a chance of administrators not noticing this.
poc:
1. Admin creates new vesting schedule using `createClaim` function. However admin mistakenly set `_startTimestamp` and `_endTimestamp` in the past.
2. Since there is no check of `require(_startTimestamp > uint40(block.timestamp))`, this transaction is valid and claim is created.
3. Vesting recipients calls the `withdraw` function and receive entire vest amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vesting contract’s schedule creation routine, which does not enforce that the supplied start and end timestamps are in the future relative to the current block time. Because the `_createClaimUnchecked` function lacks a `require(_startTimestamp > block.timestamp)` (and a similar check for the end time), an administrator can unintentionally define a vesting schedule whose start and end moments are already elapsed. When such a back‑dated schedule is recorded, the contract’s accounting logic treats the vesting period as already completed, allowing any designated recipient to call the `withdraw` function and obtain the full allocated token amount immediately. The root cause is a missing validation of time‑dependent input parameters, a classic example of insufficient input validation for business‑logic constraints. Exploitation follows a simple flow: (1) an admin calls `createClaim` (or an equivalent function) and provides `_startTimestamp` and `_endTimestamp` that are earlier than `block.timestamp`; (2) the transaction succeeds because no check rejects the stale timestamps; (3) a beneficiary invokes `withdraw`, which sees that the vesting schedule is already “finished” and releases the entire balance. The impact is that funds become claimable far earlier than the intended vesting schedule, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol, potentially destabilising token distribution plans, and causing loss of trust among token holders, employees, or investors who expected a delayed release. This condition occurs whenever an administrator mistakenly uses local clock values, mis‑calculates offsets, or simply forgets to adjust timestamps during deployment, and it is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and the UI may simply display the schedule without flagging that the dates are in the past. The issue was discovered during a formal audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditors observed the absence of a temporal guard and flagged it as a medium‑severity logic flaw. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a recipient who expects a gradual vesting schedule can withdraw the total grant instantly, leading to an unexpected zero balance for the contract’s vesting pool and a sudden increase in the user’s token holdings. The bug belongs to the broader class of “missing validation of time‑based constraints” which can cause accounting inconsistencies and violate business logic that assumes future‑dated events. To remediate, the contract should enforce that `_startTimestamp` is strictly greater than the current block timestamp and that `_endTimestamp` is greater than `_startTimestamp`, preferably with clear error messages. Additional layered checks, such as role‑based approvals or off‑chain validation, can further reduce the risk of accidental back‑dating.

title: Two address tokens can be withdrawn by the admin even if they are vested
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L446-L451](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/f68b7f3e61dad0d873b5b5a1e8126b839afeab5f/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L446-L451)  

Two address tokens exist in the blockchain. For example, Synthetix’s `ProxyERC20` contract is such a token which exists in many forms (sUSD, sBTC…). Tokens as such can be vested, but the admin can withdraw them even if they are vested by providing the other address to the `withdrawOtherToken` function. The only check in this function is that `_otherTokenAddress != tokenAddress`, which is irrelevant in the case of two address tokens.

This can make the admin be able to withdraw the vested funds and break the system, because the balance of the contract can be less than the vested amount.
poc:
1. The `VTVLVesting` is deployed with the `sUSD` contract, using its main (proxy) address - `0x57Ab1ec28D129707052df4dF418D58a2D46d5f51`.
2. A claim is created for Alice, vesting 1000 sUSD in linear vesting. Assuming this is the only claim currently, the balance of the contract is 1000 sUSD and the value of `numTokensReservedForVesting` is `1000e18`.
3. The admin calls the `withdrawOtherToken` for 1000e18 sUSD, providing its second address - `0x57Ab1ec28D129707052df4dF418D58a2D46d5f51`. The value of `numTokensReservedForVesting` is still `1000e18`, but the balance of the contract is now 0 sUSD.
4. Alice waits for her vest to end, calls the withdraw function, but the function reverts on the call to `safeTransfer()` because there is insufficient balance of sUSD. Alice can’t receive her funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a weak validation in the withdrawOtherToken function of the VTVLVesting contract. The function is intended to prevent the admin from withdrawing the token that is being vested by checking that the supplied token address is not equal to the primary token address stored in the contract. However, certain ERC‑20 implementations, such as Synthetix’s ProxyERC20 pattern, expose the same logical token through two distinct contract addresses: a proxy address used by callers and an underlying implementation address. Because the check only compares the supplied address against the proxy address, an admin can supply the implementation address and bypass the restriction, effectively withdrawing tokens that are earmarked for vesting. The root cause is the reliance on a simple address inequality test instead of verifying that the contract’s token balance remains unchanged after the withdrawal. An attacker with admin privileges can invoke withdrawOtherToken with the secondary token address, transfer the full amount of vested tokens out of the contract, and leave the recorded vesting reserve (numTokensReservedForVesting) untouched. This creates a mismatch between the contract’s internal accounting and its actual token balance. When a beneficiary later attempts to claim their vested tokens, the safeTransfer call reverts due to insufficient balance, resulting in a user‑visible symptom where the expected refund is missing, balances appear as zero, and the withdrawal transaction fails. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed with a token that follows the two‑address proxy pattern and there are active vesting claims; it is exploitable by any admin or privileged account able to call withdrawOtherToken. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the function’s logic and demonstrated the exploit using the sUSD proxy token. The subtlety of the proxy pattern makes the bug difficult to detect, as developers often assume a single token address and may not consider that the token can be transferred via an alternate address. To remediate, the contract should replace the address check with a balance consistency verification: record the contract’s token balance before the transfer, execute the withdrawal, then assert that the post‑transfer balance is equal to the pre‑transfer balance, ensuring that vested tokens cannot be removed. Alternatively, the function could be restricted to a whitelist of non‑vested tokens or completely disabled for the vested token type. By enforcing proper accounting, the protocol can preserve the integrity of vesting schedules, prevent accidental or malicious fund loss, and align actual token holdings with the recorded vesting commitments.

title: `_releaseIntervalSecs` is not validated
description:
VTVLVesting.sol has `_createClaimUnchecked` function to create the claims internally while validating parameters with the users’ allocations.  
However, `_releaseIntervalSecs` is not validated comparing to user’s `_linearVestAmount` and `_startTimestamp` `_endTimestamp`. Theoretically, `_linearVestAmount` should be equal to `((_endTimestamp - _startTimestamp) / _releaseIntervalSecs)` so the `_releaseIntervalSecs` = `_linearVestAmount / ((_endTimestamp - _startTimestamp)`.  
But this check was never done.

If the `_releaseIntervalSecs` is validated either to a higher or to a lower amount, it will create unfair distributions amongst the users during withdrawals due to being higher/lower than it should be. And also it may end up with the last withdrawals can be reverted due to the calculation board not matching.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vesting contract’s internal claim‑creation routine, which accepts a release interval (the number of seconds between each linear vesting tranche) without checking that this interval is mathematically consistent with the amount that is supposed to be released per interval and the overall vesting schedule. In a correctly configured linear vest, the total duration (endTimestamp – startTimestamp) must be exactly equal to the product of the release interval and the number of linear vesting steps, which is derived from the linear vest amount. The contract only verifies that the interval cleanly divides the total duration, but it never validates that the linearVestAmount corresponds to that interval. As a result, an administrator who creates a claim with a mismatched _releaseIntervalSecs value can unintentionally or deliberately cause the vesting math to be off. If the interval is set too high, each withdrawal will dispense fewer tokens than intended, leading to users receiving less than their promised allocation; if set too low, users may receive more than they should, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. Moreover, because the final withdrawal logic assumes the interval matches the vest amount, a mismatch can cause the last withdrawal to revert, effectively freezing the remaining tokens for the affected recipient. This flaw manifests only when the private _createClaimUnchecked function is invoked with inconsistent parameters – a path that is reachable by the contract’s admin role and, according to the audit, is also driven by front‑end validation. The issue is subtle because the contract still passes all other sanity checks, the token balance remains sufficient, and no re‑entrancy or access‑control problems are present, making the incorrect distribution visible only after a user attempts to withdraw the final tranche. The impact is an unfair distribution of vested assets, potential loss of funds for users whose final claim reverts, and a breach of the business rule that vesting schedules must be linear and predictable. The audit discovered the problem by reviewing the claim‑creation logic and noticing the missing cross‑field validation. The bug belongs to the class of “parameter consistency” or “cross‑field validation” errors, where related input variables are not jointly constrained, leading to arithmetic mismatches. From a user’s perspective, a participant may see that their balance does not increase as expected after a scheduled release, or that a withdrawal transaction fails with a revert, even though the contract reports sufficient token balance. To remediate the vulnerability, the contract should enforce a relationship such as linearVestAmount * _releaseIntervalSecs == (endTimestamp – startTimestamp) (or an equivalent integer division check) before storing the claim, ensuring that the interval, amount, and timestamps are coherent and that the vesting schedule remains fair and executable.

title: Reentrancy may allow an admin to steal funds
description:
[VTVLVesting.sol#L394-L411](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-09-vtvl/blob/main/contracts/VTVLVesting.sol#L394-L411)  

If the token is reentrant, an admin can steal all tokens locked in the `VTVLVesting` contract while having active locks.

In other words, due to this exploit possibility, the contract may be insolvent with respect to _active_ vestings. Note that revoking claim doesn’t break this invariant since the vesting is closed in that case.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the administrative withdrawal routine of a vesting contract. The contract tracks a reserve amount (numTokensReservedForVesting) that represents tokens locked for active vestings and allows an admin to withdraw any surplus tokens that are not currently reserved. The function first computes the surplus by subtracting the reserved amount from the contract’s token balance, checks that the requested amount does not exceed this surplus, and then transfers the requested tokens to the admin. Because the function does not update any internal state after the transfer and relies on the external token contract’s transfer implementation, a malicious admin can exploit a reentrant token (for example an ERC777 token that invokes a callback during the safeTransfer call). By hijacking execution before the token balance is decremented, the admin can re‑enter the withdrawAdmin function multiple times, each time seeing the same pre‑transfer balance and therefore passing the surplus check repeatedly. This permits the admin to drain the entire token balance, including tokens that are meant to be locked for vesting, rendering the contract insolvent with respect to active vestings. The issue manifests whenever the contract holds tokens earmarked for vesting and the token implementation allows re‑entrancy during transfer. It affects any user relying on the vesting schedule because their locked funds may disappear, and it violates the core business assumption that reserved tokens are untouchable until vesting is complete. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdrawAdmin logic and considered the possibility of a re‑entrant token transfer. It can be hard to notice because the function follows the usual checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and does not modify any storage variables, so a superficial code review may miss the external call’s re‑entrancy risk. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after an admin initiates a withdrawal, the contract balance suddenly drops to zero or to an unexpectedly low amount, and expected vesting payouts no longer occur. The expected behavior is that only surplus tokens can be withdrawn while reserved tokens remain safe; the reality under exploit is that the admin can siphon all tokens. This class of bug belongs to reentrancy vulnerabilities where external calls are made before internal accounting is updated, allowing an attacker to repeat the call and corrupt accounting invariants. The recommended mitigation is to protect the withdrawAdmin function with a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or to move the balance update to occur before the external token transfer, thereby breaking the re‑entrancy window. Implementing such a guard restores the invariant that reserved tokens cannot be withdrawn and ensures the contract remains solvent for all active vestings.

title: Oracle is tracked per token instead of per pair, leading to surprise results
description: Oracles are tracked by individual token, instead of by pair. Because for some tokens (ie BTC) it is unclear which implementation is the canonical one to compare others to, this can result in a situation where different pairs (ie ibBTC-wBTC and ibBC-renBTC) using the same oracle, which will be incorrect for one of them.
poc:
The protocol assumes that there is a canonical asset to compare pegged assets to, so oracles are tracked only by the pegged asset. However, for some assets (like BTC), there is no clear canonical asset, and the result is that tracking `tokenToOracle` is not sufficient.

When there is a conflict in `tokenToOracle`, the protocol responds by skipping the assignment and keeping the old value:

```solidity
if (tokenToOracle[_token] == address(0)) {
    tokenToOracle[_token] = _oracle;
}
```

The result of this is that the protocol may define a new pair with a new oracle, and have it silently skip it and use a non-matching oracle. As an example:

  * The admins start with an implementation of ibBTC-wBTC, deploying the oracle
  * This is set as `tokenToOracle[ibBTC]`
  * Later, the admins create a new pair for ibBTC-renBTC, deploying a new oracle
  * The protocol silently skips this assignment and uses the ibBTC-wBTC oracle

This can produce incorrect results, for example if wBTC appreciates relative to the other two, or if both ibBTC and renBTC depeg.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the protocol stores price feed contracts (oracles) in a mapping that is keyed only by a single token identifier (tokenToOracle[token]) instead of by the full trading pair. The design assumes that each pegged asset has a single canonical counterpart to which its price can be compared, but for assets such as Bitcoin there are several equivalent representations (e.g., wBTC, renBTC) and no universally accepted canonical token. When the protocol creates a new market pair that shares one of these ambiguous tokens, it attempts to register a new oracle only if the token entry is still empty. Because the earlier pair has already populated tokenToOracle for that token, the conditional assignment (if tokenToOracle[_token] == address(0)) prevents the new oracle from being stored, causing the contract to silently reuse the previously registered oracle. This results in the ibBTC-renBTC market, for instance, unintentionally querying the ibBTC‑wBTC oracle. Consequently, price calculations for the second pair are based on inappropriate reference data, leading to inaccurate quotes, faulty de‑peg detection, and potential mis‑pricing of trades. Users interacting with the affected pair may observe unexpected outcomes such as receiving far less of the output token than expected, seeing a zero or unusually low return, or experiencing trades that appear to execute at a wildly favorable or unfavorable rate. The impact is medium‑severity because the bug does not directly enable theft of funds, but it can cause financial loss to traders and liquidity providers, undermine the protocol’s collateralization assumptions, and erode trust in the system’s pricing integrity. The issue occurs whenever a token that appears in multiple pairs does not have a unique, universally accepted reference asset, and the contract attempts to add a new pair after an oracle for that token has already been set. It primarily affects users of the affected markets, the protocol’s risk management layer, and any party relying on accurate price feeds. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit that examined the oracle registration logic and identified that the mapping’s granularity was insufficient for assets with multiple equivalents. The problem is subtle because the UI typically shows a price feed without indicating which pair it belongs to, and the contract does not emit an explicit error when the assignment is skipped, making the misconfiguration hard to detect in routine operation. To remediate the issue, the oracle storage should be reshaped to index by the full token pair—either by defining a composite Pair struct as the key or by nesting a second mapping (e.g., tokenToOracle[base][quote])—ensuring each market can reference its own dedicated price oracle. Additionally, the conditional that skips oracle assignment should be removed or replaced with logic that updates the mapping appropriately, and events should be emitted when an oracle is set or changed to aid monitoring and debugging. This correction restores proper isolation of price data between markets, aligns with expected business logic that each pair has its own pricing source, and eliminates the risk of silent price mismatches.

title: Fee-on-Transfer tokens cause problems in multiple places
description:
Certain tokens (e.g., STA or PAXG) charge a fee for transfers and others (e.g., USDT or USDC) may start doing so in the future. This is not correctly handled in multiple places and would lead to a loss of funds:

1. `SemiFungibleVault.deposit`: Here, less tokens are transferred to the vault than the amount of shares that is minted to the user. This is an accounting mistake that will ultimately lead to the situation where the last user(s) cannot withdraw anymore, because there are no more assets left.
2. `Controller.triggerDepeg` & `Controller.triggerEndEpoch`: `sendTokens` tries to send the whole asset balance to the other contract, which will fail when less tokens are available at this point (because the previous accounting was done without incorporating fees). This will mean that the end can never be triggered and all assets are lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s assumption that token transfers are fee‑free. Fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens such as STA, PAXG or potentially USDT/USDC deduct a percentage of the transferred amount and send the remainder to the recipient. The SemiFungibleVault.deposit function calculates the number of shares to mint based on the amount parameter supplied by the caller, then calls safeTransferFrom to move that amount from the user to the vault. Because the token applies a transfer fee, the vault actually receives fewer tokens than the amount used for share accounting. This creates an accounting inconsistency: the vault records more shares than it holds underlying assets. When later users try to withdraw, the vault can run out of tokens and the final users receive zero or an incomplete amount, violating the expectation that a share represents a proportional claim on the underlying balance. The problem propagates to the Controller contract: both triggerDepeg and triggerEndEpoch call an internal sendTokens routine that attempts to forward the entire asset balance to another contract, assuming the balance equals the amount previously accounted for. Since the vault’s internal accounting over‑states the true token balance, the sendTokens call may revert because the contract does not have enough tokens after fees, preventing the de‑peg or epoch termination logic from executing. Consequently, assets become locked forever and effectively lost. The issue only manifests when a fee‑on‑transfer token is used; with fee‑free ERC‑20 tokens the logic works as intended. It was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed token handling paths and noticed that the code never checks the actual amount received after a transfer. Because the discrepancy is hidden inside internal accounting and the contract does not emit explicit error messages about missing funds, it can be difficult to notice until withdrawal failures occur. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens” or “accounting mismatch due to transfer fees”. To remediate, the contract should either forbid FoT tokens or, if support is required, measure the pre‑ and post‑transfer balances (or use the returned amount from the transfer call) and base share minting and subsequent transfers on the net amount actually received. Documentation should clearly state which token types are supported. Affected parties include users who deposit fee‑on‑transfer tokens, the protocol that relies on accurate accounting for epoch transitions, and any downstream contracts that expect the full balance to be available. The impact ranges from partial withdrawals to total loss of deposited assets.

title: StakingRewards reward rate can be dragged out and diluted
poc:
Imagine the current rewardRate is 1000 rewards / rewardsDuration.

20% of the rewardsDuration passed, i.e., now = lastUpdateTime + 20% * rewardsDuration.

A malicious actor notifies the contract with a reward of 0: notifyRewardAmount(0).

Then the new rewardRate = (reward + leftover) / rewardsDuration = (0 + 800) / rewardsDuration = 800 / rewardsDuration.

The rewardRate just dropped by 20%. This can be repeated infinitely. After another 20% of reward time passed, they trigger notifyRewardAmount(0) to reduce it by another 20% again: rewardRate = (0 + 640) / rewardsDuration = 640 / rewardsDuration.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a staking rewards contract that recalculates the per‑second reward rate each time the admin invokes the notifyRewardAmount function. When a new reward amount is supplied, the contract extends the current reward period to the current block timestamp plus a fixed rewardsDuration, and recomputes rewardRate as (newReward + leftover) / rewardsDuration, where leftover represents the portion of the previous reward still unclaimed (remaining × oldRewardRate). Because the function allows a reward amount of zero, an attacker with admin privileges can repeatedly call notifyRewardAmount(0) after a fraction of the reward period has elapsed. Each call reduces the remaining time factor (remaining / rewardsDuration) and therefore proportionally lowers rewardRate. Over successive calls the rate can be dragged down arbitrarily, effectively diluting the expected yield and extending the payout schedule indefinitely. This manipulation is subtle: the contract’s external interface does not expose the new rate directly, and the UI may simply show a slower accrual of rewards, leading users to believe the protocol is underperforming rather than being actively sabotaged. The issue manifests whenever the contract is not yet past periodFinish and the admin can supply any reward value, including zero. All stakers, token holders, and any downstream protocols that rely on the advertised yield are affected because their earned rewards are permanently reduced. The flaw was identified during a formal security audit that compared the implementation to a known pattern of reward‑rate dilution. Detecting the problem in the wild is difficult because the contract continues to function and does not revert; only the decreasing rewardRate and the resulting lower returns hint at the exploit. To remediate, the rewardRate calculation must be changed so that it never decreases as a result of a notifyRewardAmount call. One approach is to keep periodFinish immutable and simply increase rewardRate by reward / (remainingTime) without recomputing a lower rate. Alternatively, the contract could maintain a constant rewardRate and only extend periodFinish by an amount proportional to the newly added reward. In any case, the admin should not be able to overwrite or dilute existing rewards, and appropriate access controls or checks must be added to enforce monotonicity of the reward distribution curve.

title: After the vault expires, users may still receive rewards through the StakingRewards contract
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the lifecycle of the insurance vault (insrVault) and the reward distribution logic in the associated StakingRewards contract. When the Controller contract executes triggerEndEpoch, it transfers the assets from the insrVault to the riskVault and explicitly sets the claimable total value locked (TVL) for that epoch to zero. This action renders the insrTokens held by users effectively worthless for any future claim, because the accounting formula that determines entitled rewards now multiplies by a zero TVL. However, the StakingRewards contract continues to use its own periodFinish timestamp to decide whether staking is still permitted. If periodFinish remains greater than the epoch end time (_epochEnd) after the vault has been closed, the contract does not block further deposits of the now‑devalued insrToken, and it still distributes rewards based on the original rewardsDuration. An attacker or any user can therefore stake these expired tokens after the vault expiration and receive additional rewards that were intended only for valid epochs. The impact is a leakage of protocol value: rewards that should have been unavailable are minted or transferred to users holding tokens with no underlying claim, effectively “stealing” future reward allocations. This condition occurs whenever the Controller ends an epoch but the StakingRewards contract is not synchronously updated to reflect the new epoch boundary. The affected parties include token holders who may be misled into believing they can still earn legitimate rewards, as well as the protocol itself, which loses the economic value of the rewards pool. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that examined the interaction between the vault expiration logic and the reward distribution schedule. It can be difficult to detect because the staking interface remains functional, showing normal UI elements (e.g., stake buttons, reward balance updates), while the underlying token has lost its claim value, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual economic outcomes. To remediate the problem, the reward contract should enforce that its reward period does not extend beyond the current epoch identifier. A practical fix is to update the notifyRewardAmount function to reset lastUpdateTime to the current block timestamp, recompute periodFinish as the present time plus rewardsDuration, and add a require statement that ensures periodFinish does not exceed the epoch identifier supplied by the Controller. This guarantees that once the vault expires, staking of its tokens is disabled and no further rewards can be accrued, aligning the contract’s accounting with the intended business logic that rewards are only payable for active, claim‑worthy epochs.

title: StakingRewards: Significant loss of precision possible
description: In `notifyRewardAmount`, the reward rate per second is calculated. This calculation rounds down, which can lead to situations where significantly less rewards are paid out to stakers, because the effect of the rounding is multiplied by the duration.
bug_full: The reported vulnerability is a loss‑of‑precision error that occurs when the contract computes the per‑second reward rate inside the notifyRewardAmount function. The calculation uses integer division that rounds the result down (floor division). Because the reward rate is applied repeatedly for each second of a staking period, the small truncation error introduced at the moment of rate calculation is multiplied by the total duration of the stake. Consequently, stakers receive fewer tokens than the economic model promises; in extreme cases, especially for tokens with low decimal precision (for example a token with only two decimal places such as EURS), the rounding can reduce the effective reward to near zero. The root cause is the use of an imprecise arithmetic operation for a financial formula that assumes exact proportional distribution of rewards over time. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers examined the reward distribution logic and noticed that the rounding could accumulate a non‑trivial deficit. This kind of bug is often hard to detect because the per‑second discrepancy is tiny—often less than one token unit—so individual transactions appear correct, while the cumulative effect becomes evident only after many seconds or days of staking. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between expected and actual reward payouts: a user expects to earn, for example, 0.5% of their stake over a month but receives a much smaller amount, or sees their balance increase by only a few cents instead of the advertised reward. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees, loss of trust, and potential financial loss for all participants who rely on the advertised reward rate. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of precision‑loss / rounding bugs in smart contracts that handle periodic financial calculations. To remediate the issue, the contract should avoid floor division when determining the per‑second rate. Instead it can keep the fractional remainder in a separate accumulator and distribute it over time, or compute rewards using a high‑precision fixed‑point library, ensuring that any discarded fractional part is eventually accounted for and claimed by users according to their share of the pool. By preserving the residual differences and allowing users to claim them at the end of the staking period, the protocol can maintain correct accounting and prevent systematic under‑payment of rewards.

title: It is possible that receiver and treasury can receive nothing when calling `withdraw` function due to division being performed before multiplication
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the calculation of the amount a user is entitled to withdraw from a vault. In the beforeWithdraw function the contract computes entitledAmount by first dividing the requested amount by the final total value locked (idFinalTVL) and then multiplying the result by the claimable TVL (idClaimTVL) using fixed‑point helper functions divWadDown and mulDivDown. Because the division is performed before the multiplication, the intermediate result is rounded down to zero whenever the requested amount is smaller than idFinalTVL, even if the product of amount and idClaimTVL would be non‑zero. Consequently entitledAmount becomes zero, and the subsequent withdraw routine transfers zero tokens to both the user (receiver) and the protocol treasury, despite the caller having supplied a positive assets value. This situation can happen in any market, regardless of whether a depeg event has occurred, and affects both risk and hedge participants as well as the fee‑collecting treasury. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit when the analysts added a test that exercised a small withdrawal amount and observed that the user’s balance remained unchanged. The flaw is subtle because the code expresses a mathematically correct formula, yet the order of operations together with integer‑only arithmetic introduces a loss‑of‑precision bug that is not obvious from a superficial reading. From the user’s perspective the UI would show a successful transaction, but the reported amount received would be zero, contradicting the expectation that a positive withdrawal yields a positive payout. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that assets deposited can be reclaimed proportionally and may erode trust in the protocol, potentially leading to funds being effectively locked in the contract if users repeatedly trigger zero‑payout withdrawals. The recommended remediation is to reorder the arithmetic so that multiplication precedes division (e.g., entitledAmount = (amount * idClaimTVL) / idFinalTVL) to preserve precision, and to add an explicit check that the computed entitledShares is greater than zero before proceeding with the transfer, thereby preventing zero‑value withdrawals.

title: StakingRewards.sol#stake is intended to be pausable but isn’t
description: Staking is unable to be paused as intended.
poc: StakingRewards.sol inherits pausable and implements the whenNotPaused modifier on stake, but doesn’t implement any method to actually pause or unpause the contract. Pausable.sol only implements internal functions, which requires external or public functions to be implemented to wrap them. Since nothing like this has been implemented, the entire pausing system is rendered useless and staking cannot be paused as is intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing external pause/unpause interface in a staking contract that was designed to be pausable. The contract inherits a Pausable abstract contract that only provides internal functions for changing the paused state, yet no public or external function is implemented to expose those internal calls. Consequently, the whenNotPaused modifier applied to the stake function never actually prevents staking because there is no way for an authorized party (typically the contract owner or governance) to set the paused flag. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended business logic – the ability to halt staking during emergencies – and the technical implementation that omitted the wrapper functions required to manipulate the pause flag. An attacker cannot directly exploit the missing pause functionality to steal funds, but the lack of a usable pause mechanism means that, in the event of a discovered vulnerability or an operational emergency, the protocol cannot freeze staking activity. This inability may allow continued deposits and reward calculations while the system is compromised, potentially leading to loss of funds, inaccurate accounting, or a state where users cannot rely on the promised safety guarantees. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time the protocol operators attempt to invoke a pause: the transaction will do nothing, and staking will remain active, contrary to operator expectations. Users are affected because they may assume that the contract can be halted during attacks or maintenance, and they may see their stakes remain exposed when they expected the contract to be paused. The problem was discovered during a formal code audit when the auditor examined the contract inheritance hierarchy and noted that the Pausable implementation from OpenZeppelin lacks a public setPaused method, unlike the custom Synthetix version that the developers originally based their design on. The issue can be subtle because the contract compiles and the stake function includes the whenNotPaused modifier, giving the false impression that pausing works, yet the flag can never be toggled. To remediate, the contract should implement explicit external (or public) pause and unpause functions, guarded by an onlyOwner or similar access control, that internally call the _pause() and _unpause() functions provided by the Pausable base contract. This aligns the contract's behavior with the intended emergency stop pattern and restores the ability to protect user funds in critical situations. The flaw belongs to the class of improper access control or incomplete interface implementation, where a critical control mechanism is present in the code base but not exposed for activation, leading to a functional security control that is effectively disabled.

title: Fees are taken on risk collateral
description: Fees are taken on funds deposited as collateral.
poc:
```solidity
uint256 feeValue = calculateWithdrawalFeeValue(entitledShares, id);
```

In L226 of Vault.sol#withdraw the fee is taken on the entire collateral deposited by the risk users. This is problematic for two reasons. The first is that the collateral provided by the risk users will likely be many many times higher than the premium being paid by the hedge users. This will create a strong disincentive to use the protocol because it is likely a large portion of the profits will be taken by fees and the risk user may unexpectedly lose funds overall if premiums are too low.

The second issue is that this method of fees directly contradicts project [documents](https://medium.com/@Y2KFinance/introducing-earthquake-pt-2-6f206cd4b315) which clearly indicate that fees are only taken on the premium and insurance payouts, not when risk users are receiving their collateral back.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic‑logic error where the protocol charges a withdrawal fee on the full amount of collateral that risk providers have locked, rather than restricting fees to the premium paid by hedgers and any insurance payouts as described in the project’s documentation. This mis‑calculation originates from the fee function being invoked with the total entitled shares (the entire collateral) during a withdrawal call, causing the fee value to be derived from a much larger base than intended. An attacker does not need to craft a special exploit; any risk user who attempts to retrieve their collateral will automatically trigger the over‑charged fee. When the premium collected from hedgers is small compared to the collateral size, the fee can exceed the premium, effectively reducing the risk provider’s net return and, in extreme cases, turning a profitable position into a loss. The impact is a direct financial loss for collateral providers, a breach of the protocol’s stated fee model, and a strong disincentive for participants to supply risk capital, which threatens the overall liquidity and trust in the system. The condition under which this occurs is any standard withdrawal transaction performed after the collateral has been pledged; it does not require any abnormal state or special permissions. The affected parties are the risk users who lock collateral, the protocol’s economic model, and any external participants relying on the documented fee structure. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the discrepancy between the code and the public fee policy was noted. Because the fee appears as a regular withdrawal deduction, it may be hard to notice without comparing the actual withdrawn amount to the expected amount based on the premium, especially for users unfamiliar with the fee specifications. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑miscalculation or economic‑logic vulnerabilities, where the scope of fee application is incorrectly defined. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a withdrawal that returns less than the deposited collateral, often prompting a message such as “I expected my full collateral back but received a smaller amount” or “my balance dropped unexpectedly after withdrawing”. The expected behavior is that only the premium and insurance payouts be subject to fees, while the reality is that the full collateral is reduced by an additional fee, violating the business assumption that risk providers receive their entire collateral back less only the intended charges. To remediate the issue the fee calculation should be refactored so that it references only the premium amount and any payout on insurance, excluding the collateral principal from fee consideration, thereby aligning the implementation with the documented economic model.

title: User funds lost because they can’t `withdraw
description: Users deposit their funds in `Vault` when epoch is not started but as other users deposit funds too or price of pegged token changes, users get different risk to reward. And they may want to withdraw their funds before epoch start time to get out of bad position, but there is no logic in code to give them ability to withdraw their funds before epoch start time.
poc:
`Withdraw()` function in `Vault` only allows users to withdraw after epoch ends and there is no logic in the contract to allow users to withdraw their funds before epoch start time.

After users deposit their funds, the risk to reward ratio of their investment changes as other users deposit funds in one of the Vaults and user may wants to withdraw their funds if they saw that position is bad for them or maybe the price of that token has been changed dramatically before epoch startTime and users wants to withdraw. But, there is no functionality that gives users the ability to withdraw their funds before epoch start time and users lose control of their funds after depositing and before epoch start time. As epoch is not started yet, users should be able to withdraw their funds but there is no such functionality in the code.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a vault contract that locks user deposits until an on‑chain epoch finishes, without providing any mechanism to retrieve the funds before the epoch begins. The root cause is the absence of an early‑withdrawal or emergency‑exit path in the contract’s state machine; the only withdraw function checks that the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to the epoch end time and reverts otherwise. Consequently, a user who deposits while the epoch is still pending cannot invoke the withdrawal function, even if market conditions shift dramatically, other participants add large amounts that alter the risk‑to‑reward profile, or the price of the underlying pegged token spikes or crashes. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker does not need to craft any special transaction; simply depositing funds before the epoch start time and then waiting for the market to move will cause the victim’s capital to become inaccessible until the epoch concludes. The impact is that users lose control over their assets during the lock‑up period, potentially missing the chance to exit a losing position, experience opportunity cost, or face liquidity constraints if they need the funds urgently. This condition occurs whenever a vault’s epoch has been initialized but not yet started, which may be a frequent state in protocols that batch deposits into discrete time windows. All participants who rely on the vault for investment—retail users, liquidity providers, and protocol‑level risk managers—are affected because their deposited balances appear in the contract but cannot be transferred out on demand. The issue was discovered during a formal audit review of the contract’s public interface, where the absence of a withdraw‑before‑epoch function was noted as a gap between documented expectations and actual implementation. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without error, the withdraw function works as coded after the epoch, and the documentation may implicitly suggest that funds are always retrievable, creating a false sense of security. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a conditional branch that permits users to call a withdrawal routine when the current time is earlier than the epoch start timestamp, possibly with proportional penalties or lock‑up fees if the business model requires them. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “emergency withdrawal omission” or “missing early exit path” and violates basic accounting assumptions that deposited capital remains liquid on user request unless explicitly locked by a consensus‑level decision. From a user’s perspective, the UI would show a deposited balance but the “Withdraw” button would remain disabled or revert with an error, leading the user to believe their funds are missing or the contract is broken. Expectations are that a user can pull out their money at any time before the epoch begins, but reality is that the contract refuses the request, resulting in funds that appear to disappear from the user’s control until the epoch ends.

title: `timewindow` can be changed unexpectedly that blocks users from calling `deposit` function
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the use of a mutable `timewindow` variable in the `epochHasNotStarted` modifier that guards the `deposit` function. The modifier checks `block.timestamp <= idEpochBegin[id] - timewindow` and reverts with `EpochAlreadyStarted` when the condition is false. Because `timewindow` can be altered by an admin through the `VaultFactory.changeTimewindow` function, the guard can be changed after a user has verified that the condition holds but before the user’s transaction is mined. In practice, an attacker with admin privileges (or a dishonest admin) can submit a transaction that increases `timewindow` moments before a user’s deposit transaction is executed. The increased `timewindow` shortens the allowed window for deposits, causing the previously valid condition to become false, and the deposit transaction reverts. This creates a race condition where the contract’s state that determines eligibility is altered retroactively, violating the expectation that once a user observes a valid window, their deposit will succeed.
