It also violates the fundamental business logic that ownership and access control should be immutable after deployment, breaking the accounting assumptions that only the designated controller can authorize token movements.

To remediate, the `initialize` functions must be protected by the `initializer` (or `reinitializer` with a version) modifier so that they can be executed only once. Additionally, the contracts should use OpenZeppelin’s `Initializable` pattern which includes a guard variable that prevents re‑entrance. Applying this guard to `BridgeEscrow`, `L1GraphTokenGateway`, `L2GraphTokenGateway` and `L2GraphToken` eliminates the ability for a compromised implementation to reset ownership, thereby restoring the intended security model where only the legitimate governance process can change privileged roles.

title: If L1GraphTokenGateway’s `outboundTransfer` is called by a contract, the entire `msg.value` is blackholed, whether the ticket got redeemed or not
description:
[L1GraphTokenGateway.sol#L236](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-thegraph/blob/309a188f7215fa42c745b136357702400f91b4ff/contracts/gateway/L1GraphTokenGateway.sol#L236)  

The outboundTransfer function in L1GraphTokenGateway is used to transfer user’s Graph tokens to L2. To do that it eventually calls the standard Arbitrum Inbox’s createRetryableTicket. The issue is that it passes caller’s address in the `submissionRefundAddress` and `valueRefundAddress`. This behaves fine if caller is an EOA, but if it’s called by a contract it will lead to loss of the submissionRefund (ETH passed to outboundTransfer() minus the total submission fee), or in the event of failed L2 ticket creation, the whole submission fee. The reason it’s fine for EOA is because of the fact that ETH and Arbitrum addresses are congruent. However, the calling contract probably does not exist on L2 and even in the rare case it does, it might not have a function to move out the refund.

The docs don’t suggest contracts should not use the TokenGateway, and it is fair to assume it will be used in this way. Multisigs are inherently contracts, which is one of the valid use cases. Since likelihood is high and impact is medium (loss of submission fee), I believe it to be a HIGH severity find.
poc: Alice has a multisig wallet. She sends 100 Graph tokens to L1GraphTokenGateway, and passes X ETH for submission. She receives an L1 ticket, but since the max gas was too low, the creation failed on L2 and the funds got sent to the multisig address at L2. Therefore, Alice loses X ETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the L1GraphTokenGateway’s outboundTransfer function, which is responsible for moving a user’s Graph tokens from Layer 1 to Arbitrum Layer 2. To fund the retryable ticket that carries the transfer, the function forwards the caller’s Ether (msg.value) to the Arbitrum Inbox’s createRetryableTicket method, while also supplying the caller’s address as both the submissionRefundAddress and the valueRefundAddress. This design works when the caller is an externally owned account (EOA) because the EOA’s address is directly usable on L2 and any leftover Ether can be returned to the same address. However, when a contract—such as a multisig wallet or any other smart‑contract account—invokes outboundTransfer, the contract’s address does not automatically resolve to a payable account on L2, and the contract may not implement a function to withdraw the refunded Ether. Consequently, any surplus Ether that is not consumed by the retryable ticket’s submission fee, as well as the entire submission fee in the rare event that ticket creation fails, becomes permanently locked (blackholed) in the L2 system. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a missing or zero balance after a bridge operation: the user expects the unused Ether to be returned or at least to see the refund reflected in their wallet, but instead the funds disappear. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the token bridge’s handling of the refund addresses and identified that the existing documentation does not warn contract callers about this behavior. The problem can be subtle because the outboundTransfer transaction does not revert; it merely succeeds, making the loss of Ether appear as an unexpected accounting discrepancy rather than a blatant failure. This violates the accounting assumptions of the bridge, where the amount of Ether supplied must either be fully consumed for ticket submission or be safely refunded to the initiator. The vulnerability fits the class of “refund address misuse” or “failed refund handling” bugs, where the contract assumes the caller can always receive a refund on the destination chain. To remediate, the gateway should either enforce that only EOAs can call outboundTransfer, or require callers to explicitly provide a valid L2‑compatible refund address through an additional parameter, or implement a flag that forces contracts to acknowledge the risk and handle refunds via a separate withdraw flow. By decoupling the refund destination from the caller’s address, the bridge can guarantee that any unused Ether is recoverable, restoring the expected economic behavior and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: Governor can rug pull the escrow
description:
[BridgeEscrow.sol#L28-L30](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-thegraph/blob/309a188f7215fa42c745b136357702400f91b4ff/contracts/gateway/BridgeEscrow.sol#L28-L30)  

Governor can rug pull all GRT held by BridgeEscrow, which is a severe undermining of decentralization.
poc:
The governor can approve an arbitrary address to spend any amount from BridgeEscrow, so they can steal all escrowed tokens. Even if the governor is well intended, the contract can still be called out which would degrade the reputation of the protocol (e.g. see here: <https://twitter.com/RugDocIO/status/1411732108029181960>). This is especially an issue as the escrowed tokens are never burnt, so the users would need to trust the governor perpetually (not about stealing their L2 tokens, but about not taking a massive amount of L1 tokens for free for themselves).

This seems an unnecessary power granted to the governor and turns a decentralized bridge into a needless bottleneck of centralization.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BridgeEscrow contract, which holds a pool of GRT tokens that are meant to be escrowed for cross‑chain transfers. The contract exposes a public function, approveAll(), that can be called by the Governor role. This function unconditionally grants an arbitrary address an unlimited allowance to transfer the escrowed GRT. Because the only access control on approveAll() is the Governor modifier, any entity that can act through the Governor – a Gnosis Safe controlled by The Graph Council – can invoke the function and set a spender’s allowance to the maximum possible value. Consequently, a malicious or compromised Governor can approve a rogue address and subsequently drain all tokens from the escrow. The root cause is an overly permissive privileged operation that bypasses the bridge’s intended accounting logic and does not limit token movements to the designated bridge contract or to a controlled recovery pathway. Exploitation is straightforward: the Governor calls approveAll(attacker, type(uint256).max), the attacker then calls the GRT token contract’s transferFrom() to pull the entire balance, leaving the escrow empty. The impact is severe for users who trust that escrowed funds are safely locked: their balances appear to vanish, refunds or cross‑chain transfers fail, and the protocol’s claim of decentralization is undermined. This can occur whenever the Governor decides to act maliciously, is coerced, or its multi‑signature process is compromised, making the entire escrow a single point of failure. All token holders, bridge users, and the broader Graph ecosystem are affected because the loss of escrowed GRT compromises liquidity and damages reputation. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined function visibility and role restrictions. It may be difficult to notice because approveAll() is intended for emergency fund recovery, and its presence does not immediately suggest a vector for theft, especially when the governance model already trusts the Council’s Safe. To remediate, the approval mechanism should be confined to the bridge contract itself or to a dedicated recovery function subject to stricter multi‑sig thresholds, or the function should be removed entirely. In general, this is a classic case of an admin‑controlled token approval that creates centralization and allows unchecked withdrawal, violating the accounting assumption that escrowed funds cannot be moved without a legitimate bridge operation.

title: After proposed 0.8.0 upgrade kicks in, L2 `finalizeInboundTransfer` might not work
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the address aliasing logic used by the L2 Graph Token Gateway to restrict the `finalizeInboundTransfer` function to calls originating from its L1 counterpart. The contract employs a modifier that compares `msg.sender` against the result of `AddressAliasHelper.applyL1ToL2Alias(l1Counterpart)`. This helper function adds a fixed offset (0x1111000000000000000000000000000000001111) to the L1 address, casts the sum to a uint160 and then to an address, relying on the natural wrapping behavior of unsigned integer arithmetic in Solidity versions prior to 0.8.0. With the planned upgrade to Solidity 0.8.0, arithmetic operations are checked by default; the addition of the offset to certain L1 addresses can overflow the uint160 range, causing a runtime exception instead of the intended wrap‑around. The overflow probability is roughly one in fifteen for random L1 addresses because the offset pushes the value close to the uint160 maximum. When the overflow occurs, the modifier reverts with "ONLY_COUNTERPART_GATEWAY", preventing the L2 gateway from accepting the inbound transfer finalization call. Consequently, legitimate cross‑chain token transfers become stuck: users who bridge tokens from L1 to L2 observe that their balances do not increase, refunds are not issued, and the UI may show a transaction that appears successful on L1 but yields no token credit on L2. The issue was identified during a security audit that compared the compiler‑specific semantics of arithmetic operations and recognized that the existing code assumes unchecked overflow. It is subtle because the overflow is intentional for address aliasing, a pattern that historically succeeded without explicit unchecked blocks, making the bug easy to miss in code review. The affected parties include any token holder attempting to bridge through the Graph Token Gateway on Arbitrum, the protocol operators who rely on correct inbound finalization, and downstream applications that display token balances. To remediate, the addition should be placed inside an `unchecked { ... }` block, which restores the original wrap‑around behavior under Solidity 0.8.0. Alternatively, a dedicated aliasing routine that performs the addition using low‑level assembly without overflow checks could be used. Fixing the bug ensures that `finalizeInboundTransfer` can be called by the correctly aliased L1 contract, preserving the intended business logic that inbound transfers are accounted for and users receive their tokens as expected.

title: `LBRouter.removeLiquidity` returning wrong values
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the LBRouter.removeLiquidity function, which is intended to withdraw liquidity from a pair and return the amounts of each token that were transferred back to the caller. The function accepts two token addresses, tokenX and tokenY, and internally checks whether the supplied order matches the canonical order of the underlying LBPair (the pair stores its tokens in ascending address order). If the order does not match, the implementation swaps the local variables _tokenX and _tokenY as well as the minimum‑amount parameters so that the internal removal operation works correctly. However, after the liquidity removal is performed, the function returns the variables amountX and amountY directly, without correcting for the earlier swap. Consequently, when the input token order is reversed, amountX actually contains the amount of tokenY that was returned, and amountY contains the amount of tokenX. This mismatch is not visible in the function signature or in the event logs, so callers receive values that appear syntactically correct but are semantically inverted.

The root cause is an inconsistent handling of token ordering: the input parameters are reordered to match the pair’s expectations, but the corresponding output values are not reordered to reflect that change. This logical inconsistency produces a return‑value swap bug, a class of vulnerability where a function’s output does not align with its documented contract because of an internal reordering step.

An attacker can exploit the flaw simply by invoking removeLiquidity with the token addresses in the non‑canonical order. A third‑party contract that assumes amountX corresponds to the first token argument will record the received amount under the wrong token balance. For example, a protocol may call LBRouter.removeLiquidity(address(tokenA), address(tokenB), …) and then add amountAReceived to its internal tokenA balance and amountBReceived to its tokenB balance. If tokenA and tokenB are supplied in the wrong order, the protocol will credit tokenA’s balance with the amount of tokenB that was actually received, and vice‑versa. The immediate symptom from the protocol’s perspective is a mismatch between expected and actual token holdings: balances appear to be missing, become unexpectedly large, or an operation that depends on the precise amounts (such as a subsequent swap or settlement) may fail or produce incorrect results. Users may observe that after withdrawing liquidity, their contract reports that it received zero of one token while the other token balance has jumped unexpectedly.

The impact is indirect but potentially severe. Although no ether or token value is lost within the LBRouter call itself, the downstream contract may perform further financial operations based on the incorrect accounting, leading to loss of funds, failed trades, or exploitable state inconsistencies. Any protocol that integrates LBRouter without enforcing the canonical token order is vulnerable, and the bug could be propagated to multiple third‑party contracts that rely on the router as a library.

The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit of the Trader Joe contracts, where the auditor noticed that the function performed a conditional swap of input parameters but omitted a corresponding swap of the returned amounts. The problem is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns values that look plausible, making it easy to overlook during testing, especially when the caller supplies tokens in the expected order.

To remediate the bug, the contract should ensure that the returned values match the order of the input arguments presented to the caller. This can be achieved by adding a final conditional that swaps amountX and amountY when the original token order was reordered, or by enforcing that callers always provide tokens in the canonical order and documenting this requirement clearly. By aligning the output with the caller’s perspective, the function’s behavior will once again satisfy the contract’s accounting assumptions and prevent downstream mis‑accounting.

title: `beforeTokenTransfer` called with wrong parameters in `LBToken._burn`
description:
[LBToken.sol#L237](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-traderjoe/blob/37258d595d596c195507234f795fa34e319b0a68/src/LBToken.sol#L237)  

In `LBToken._burn`, the `_beforeTokenTransfer` hook is called with `from = address(0)` and `to = _account`:
```solidity
_beforeTokenTransfer(address(0), _account, _id, _amount);
```
Through a lucky coincidence, it turns out that this in the current setup does not cause a high severity issue. `_burn` is always called with `_account = address(this)`, which means that `LBPair._beforeTokenTransfer` is a NOP. However, this wrong call is very dangerous for future extensions or protocol that built on top of the protocol / fork it.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect invocation of the `_beforeTokenTransfer` hook inside the token burn routine of the LBToken contract. In a standard ERC‑1155 implementation, the hook is expected to receive the address of the token holder as the `from` argument and the zero address as the `to` argument when tokens are being destroyed. The LBToken code, however, calls the hook with `from = address(0)` and `to = _account`, effectively swapping the arguments. This mistake originates from a simple typographical error in the `_burn` function, where the parameters are passed in the wrong order. The immediate impact is mitigated in the current deployment because the `_burn` function is only ever called with `_account` set to `address(this)`, the pair contract itself. The LBPair implementation of `_beforeTokenTransfer` performs no action for this particular call, so the swapped parameters do not trigger a visible failure. Nevertheless, the flaw creates a hidden inconsistency in the contract’s accounting logic. If a future extension, a fork, or an external contract were to rely on the hook for validation, event emission, fee collection, or any side‑effect that distinguishes minting from burning, the reversed arguments could cause the protocol to treat a burn as a mint, bypassing security checks, or emitting misleading events. An attacker who can trigger `_burn` with a custom `_account` could thus exploit the hook to manipulate the contract’s internal state, potentially creating tokens out of thin air or avoiding restrictions that are only enforced on legitimate burns. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as an unexpected disappearance of balance updates or missing transfer events after a burn operation, contradicting the expectation that a burned amount is deducted from the holder’s balance and recorded as a burn to the zero address. The bug belongs to the class of hook‑parameter mis‑ordering errors, a subset of logical mistakes that break the contract’s accounting invariants. It was discovered during a formal code audit by Code4rena, where the auditor traced the execution flow of `_burn` and identified the swapped arguments. The problem is subtle because the faulty call does not generate an error or revert, and the hook implementation does nothing in the current context, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the issue, the hook should be invoked with the correct ordering: `_beforeTokenTransfer(_account, address(0), _id, _amount)`. This restores the intended semantics of a burn operation, ensuring that any hook logic that depends on the source and destination addresses functions correctly and that accounting, events, and security checks remain consistent with the protocol’s design.

title: Flashloan fee collection mechanism can be easily manipulated
description: [`LBPair.flashLoan()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-traderjoe/blob/79f25d48b907f9d0379dd803fc2abc9c5f57db93/src/LBPair.sol#L415-L456) utilizes an "unfair" fee mechanism in which the whole pair liquidity can be loaned but only the liquidity providers of the active bin receive the fees. Although one can argue that this unfair structure is to incentivize greater liquidity around the active price range, it nonetheless opens up a way to easily manipulate fees. The current structure allows a user to provide liquidity to an active bin right before a flashloan to receive most of the fees. This trick can be used both by the borrower themselves, or by a third party miner or a node operator frontrunning the flashloan transactions. In either case, this is in detriment to the liquidity providers, who would be providing the bulk of the flashloan, but receiving a much less fraction of the fees.
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the flash‑loan fee accounting of the LBPair contract. When a flash loan is issued, the contract permits the borrower to withdraw the entire liquidity of the pair, but the accrued fees are recorded only for the liquidity providers (LPs) that belong to the currently active price bin. This design creates a fee‑distribution bias: LPs that supplied capital to other bins, which may still constitute the majority of the borrowed amount, receive no portion of the fees, while the small set of LPs in the active bin receive the whole fee pool. The root cause is that the fee‑per‑share variables (accTokenXPerShare and accTokenYPerShare) are incremented solely for the active bin's _id, without any aggregation across the full set of bins. Consequently, any entity that can place liquidity in the active bin immediately before the flash‑loan execution will capture almost the entire fee reward, regardless of how little of the total liquidity they contributed.

An attacker can exploit this by either (1) front‑running a pending flash‑loan transaction: the miner or a bot adds a modest amount of liquidity to the active bin, lets the flash‑loan proceed, receives the fee credit, and then removes the added liquidity in the same block; or (2) the borrower themselves performing an atomic add‑then‑remove operation around the flash‑loan call, effectively borrowing the full pool while paying only a fraction of the intended fee. Because the fee is credited per‑share to the active bin, the attacker’s small liquidity stake translates into a disproportionately large fee share.

The impact is economic loss for honest LPs whose capital is used by the flash‑loan but who see no corresponding increase in accrued fees. From a user’s perspective, an LP monitoring their fee earnings will notice that their balance remains unchanged or even appears to decrease relative to the amount of liquidity that was borrowed, creating a mismatch between expected yield and actual returns. The protocol also suffers a weakened incentive model: liquidity that is not placed in the active bin becomes unattractive, potentially reducing overall depth and capital efficiency. The issue manifests whenever a flash‑loan is executed, especially when the active bin represents only a small slice of the total liquidity pool.

The bug was discovered during a manual security audit by Code4rena, where the fee‑distribution code was examined and the mismatch between borrowed amounts and fee allocation was identified. It is subtle because the flash‑loan function correctly transfers the token amounts, and the fee calculation appears benign at first glance; only a deeper analysis of the per‑bin accounting reveals the bias. Detecting it in routine testing is difficult unless the test suite explicitly checks fee accrual across all bins during flash‑loan operations.

To remediate the issue, the fee mechanism should be decoupled from the active bin and made global for the entire pair, recording token‑X and token‑Y fees per share across all liquidity regardless of bin placement. Alternatively, fees could be spread over a configurable range of bins surrounding the active bin (the "n‑th" bins) to dilute the incentive for a single bin, though this introduces higher gas costs. If a fair distribution cannot be achieved, the most drastic mitigation would be to remove the flash‑loan feature altogether, eliminating the avenue for fee manipulation. In any case, the fix must ensure that every LP whose tokens are borrowed receives a proportionate share of the fees, preserving the intended economic incentives and preventing fee‑stealing attacks.

title: Very critical `Owner` privileges can cause complete destruction of the project in a possible privateKey exploit
description:
[PendingOwnable.sol#L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-traderjoe/blob/main/src/libraries/PendingOwnable.sol#L42)  

Typically, the contract’s owner is the account that deploys the contract. As a result, the owner is able to perform certain privileged activities.

However, Owner privileges are numerous and there is no timelock structure in the process of using these privileges. The Owner is assumed to be an EOA, since the documents do not provide information on whether the Owner will be a multisign structure.

In parallel with the private key thefts of the project owners, which have increased recently, this vulnerability has been stated as medium.

Similar vulnerability;  
Private keys stolen:

Hackers have stolen cryptocurrency worth around `€552` million from a blockchain project linked to the popular online game Axie Infinity, in one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Security issue : PrivateKey of the project officer was stolen: <https://www.euronews.com/next/2022/03/30/blockchain-network-ronin-hit-by-552-million-crypto-heist>
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an overly powerful owner role that is protected only by a simple `onlyOwner` modifier without any time‑delay or multi‑signature safeguard. In the examined contracts, the owner can invoke a wide range of privileged functions such as changing the flash‑loan fee, swapping the pair implementation, locking the factory, adding or removing quote assets, modifying fee recipients, and even forcing a pair to decay. Because there is no timelock, each of these calls takes effect instantly and without public warning. The root cause is the combination of a single‑key externally owned account (EOA) being designated as the owner and the absence of any validation mechanism that would either delay the execution or require multiple signatures. If an attacker manages to obtain the owner’s private key—a scenario that has become increasingly common—the attacker can instantly execute any of the owner‑only functions. Exploitation could proceed by, for example, raising the flash‑loan fee to 100 %, redirecting fee revenue to an address controlled by the attacker, or locking the factory so that no new pairs can be created. Such actions would either steal user funds directly (through fee diversion) or cripple the protocol’s core functionality, leaving users unable to interact with the platform, see their balances freeze, or receive zero returns on expected operations. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms might appear as suddenly higher fees, missing or zero‑balance withdrawals, or an inability to create or trade pairs that previously worked, creating a perception that the system has broken or that refunds are missing. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that inspected the ownership pattern in the `PendingOwnable.sol` library and identified the lack of any timelock or multi‑sig requirement. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the privileged calls are legitimate for the intended owner, and no on‑chain alerts are emitted when they are executed. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the single `onlyOwner` gate with a governance mechanism that includes a time‑locked delay for all critical changes and, ideally, require a multi‑signature wallet to be the owner. This would give users and auditors a window to detect and react to suspicious changes, reduce the attack surface associated with private‑key compromise, and align the contract with best practices for high‑value DeFi protocols. The class of bug can be described as an "improper access control with missing delay and centralization" that creates a single point of failure and enables an attacker with the owner’s private key to perform destructive or fund‑draining actions.

title: Attacker can keep fees max at no cost
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the fee calculation logic of Trader Joe’s FeeHelper library, specifically in the updateVariableFeeParameters function that maintains the volatile fee component. The protocol computes a volatility accumulator Va as the sum of a volatility reference Vr and a bin delta. Vr is supposed to decay over time according to the elapsed time since the last swap: if the elapsed time Δt is less than the filter period Tf, Vr should remain unchanged; if Tf ≤ Δt < decay period Td, Vr should be reduced proportionally; otherwise Vr resets to zero. The implementation, however, updates the stored timestamp (_fp.time) on every call regardless of whether Vr is actually decayed. When a swap occurs with Δt < Tf, the function skips the decay branch, leaving Vr at its previous high value, but still records a new timestamp. Consequently, an attacker can execute a series of minimal‑size swaps spaced just under Tf seconds apart, keeping Vr permanently high. Because Va is calculated as Vr plus the absolute bin offset, Va remains elevated, which drives the variable fee component to its maximum for all subsequent trades. The attacker incurs essentially no cost for each swap (transaction fee of a few cents on AVAX), yet the protocol continuously charges exorbitant fees—potentially dozens of dollars per day—making the market uncompetitive and draining users’ funds. This issue impacts any market participant: traders experience unexpectedly high fees, liquidity providers see reduced net returns, and the protocol’s revenue model is compromised. The bug was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test reproducing rapid low‑volume swaps demonstrated the fee escalation. The problem is subtle because a single trade still shows normal fees; the abnormal behavior only emerges after a pattern of timed swaps, making it easy to overlook during casual testing. To remediate, the fee logic should either decay Vr linearly with the actual elapsed time even when Δt < Tf, avoid updating the timestamp when Vr is not decayed, or conditionally allow the skip of Vr decay only for swaps that are truly negligible, thereby ensuring that high volatility cannot be sustained without corresponding economic activity. In essence, the bug is a state‑update inconsistency that allows economic manipulation of the fee mechanism, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees reflect recent market volatility.

title: Calling `swapAVAXForExactTokens` function while sending excess amount cannot refund such excess amount
bug_full:
The vulnerability resides in the AVAX‑for‑exact‑token routing function, which is intended to allow callers to provide more AVAX than strictly required and automatically receive a refund of the surplus. The contract checks whether msg.value exceeds the calculated input amount (amountsIn[0]) and, if so, attempts to transfer the difference back to the caller using the expression `_safeTransferAVAX(_to, amountsIn[0] - msg.value)`. Because the subtraction is performed in the wrong order, the expression evaluates to a negative value when msg.value is larger than amountsIn[0]. In Solidity versions with built‑in overflow/underflow checks, this negative result triggers an arithmetic underflow error and causes the whole transaction to revert. The root cause is therefore an incorrect arithmetic operation that flips the refund calculation, leading to a self‑inflicted revert whenever excess AVAX is supplied.

An attacker does not need to perform any special actions; any user or front‑end that follows the documented expectation of sending a small buffer of AVAX for slippage will unintentionally trigger the underflow. The exploitation flow is straightforward: the caller invokes `swapAVAXForExactTokens` with a value slightly higher than the exact amount needed, the contract reaches the refund branch, computes `amountsIn[0] - msg.value` (a negative number), the arithmetic check fails, and the transaction reverts before any token transfer occurs. The immediate impact is a failed swap, loss of the gas spent on the transaction, and no tokens being received or refunded. From a user’s perspective the UI will report a transaction failure or “revert”, often without an explicit reason, leading to confusion as the user expected a refund of the extra AVAX.

The condition occurs every time the function is called with msg.value > amountsIn[0], which is a common pattern when users rely on the “refund any excess” comment. Consequently, the majority of realistic use‑cases that involve any slippage tolerance are impaired, reducing the practical usability of the protocol. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit where a test case deliberately sent `amountIn + 1` AVAX and observed an `arithmeticError` revert, confirming the faulty refund logic.

Because the problem is purely logical—an arithmetic under‑flow—it does not expose user funds to theft, but it is hard to notice because the code superficially appears to implement a refund mechanism and the revert message is generic. The correct mitigation is to reverse the subtraction order so that the contract transfers `msg.value - amountsIn[0]` back to the caller, thereby eliminating the underflow and restoring the intended refund behavior. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect financial calculation or refund logic errors that break accounting assumptions, leading to failed transactions and degraded user experience.

title: Incorrect fee calculation on LBPair
description: LBPair contracts consistently collect less fees than their FeeParameters.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee calculation in the LBPair contract, which is responsible for handling swaps in a liquidity pool. The contract references a set of FeeParameters that define the rate at which fees should be collected from each trade, but due to a logical error in the arithmetic – such as misplaced scaling factors, integer division ordering, or rounding down – the amount of fees actually taken from every swap is consistently lower than the configured rate. This discrepancy originates from the way the fee amount is derived from the input amount; the code applies the fee percentage incorrectly, resulting in a systematic under‑collection. An attacker or any user can exploit this by simply performing trades, because each trade automatically triggers the faulty fee routine, allowing the attacker to accrue a larger share of the pool’s value or, for the protocol, to lose expected revenue over time. The impact is economic: liquidity providers receive fewer fees than they are entitled to, the protocol’s treasury accrues less revenue, and the overall accounting of the pool becomes inaccurate, potentially leading to imbalanced token reserves. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of the swap function – essentially every trade performed on the pair – making the issue persistent and pervasive. All participants who rely on the fee mechanism – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s governance token holders – are affected because the fee shortfall reduces expected returns and may distort incentive structures. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where testers compared the on‑chain fee amounts against the documented FeeParameters and observed a consistent shortfall. The bug can be hard to notice because fee amounts are generally small relative to trade size, and rounding errors may mask the discrepancy, especially when users only see the net trade amount and not the explicit fee breakdown. To remediate the issue, the fee computation should be rewritten to follow a clear fixed‑point arithmetic pattern: multiply the input amount by the fee rate first, then divide by the scaling factor using a rounding method that matches the protocol’s economic model (e.g., round up rather than down), and validate that the resulting fee never exceeds the configured percentage. This aligns the collected fee with the intended FeeParameters and restores correct accounting. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of "fee miscalculation" or "incorrect financial accounting" vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal math diverges from the declared economic policy, leading to lost revenue, inaccurate balances, and broken trust in the protocol's incentive mechanisms.

title: `diamondCut` is not protected in case of governor’s key leakage
description:
When the governor proposes a diamondCut, governor must wait for `upgradeNoticePeriod` to be passed, or security council members have to approve the proposal to bypass the notice period, so that the governor can execute the proposal.
    
```solidity
require(approvedBySecurityCouncil || upgradeNoticePeriodPassed, "a6"); // notice period should expire
require(approvedBySecurityCouncil || !diamondStorage.isFrozen, "f3");
```

If the governor’s key is leaked and noticed by zkSync, the attacker must wait for the notice period to execute the already proposed diamondCut with the malicious `_calldata` based on the note below from zkSync, or to propose a new malicious diamondCut. For, both cases, the attacker loses time.

NOTE: proposeDiamondCut - commits data associated with an upgrade but does not execute it. While the upgrade is associated with facetCuts and (address _initAddress, bytes _calldata) the upgrade will be committed to the facetCuts and _initAddress. This is done on purpose, to leave some freedom to the governor to change calldata for the upgrade between proposing and executing it.

Since, there is a notice period (as zkSync noticed the key leakage, security council member will not approve the proposal, so bypassing the notice period is not possible), there is enough time for zkSync to apply security measures (pausing any deposit/withdraw, reporting in media to not execute any transaction in zkSync, and so on).

But, the attacker can be smarter, just before the proposal be executed by the governor (i.e. the notice period is passed or security council members approved it), the attacker executes the proposal earlier than governor with the malicious `_calldata`. In other words, the attacker front runs the governor.

Therefore, if zkSync notices the governor’s key leakage beforehand, there is enough time to protect the project. But, if zkSync does not notice the governor’s key leakage, the attacker can change the `_calldata` into a malicious one in the last moment so that it is not possible to protect the project.
poc:
[Diamond.sol#L277](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-zksync/blob/4db6c596931a291b17a4e0e2929adf810a4a0eed/ethereum/contracts/zksync/libraries/Diamond.sol#L277)  
[DiamondCut.sol#L46](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-zksync/blob/4db6c596931a291b17a4e0e2929adf810a4a0eed/ethereum/contracts/zksync/facets/DiamondCut.sol#L46)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upgrade mechanism of the ZkSync diamond architecture, where a governor can propose a diamondCut operation that consists of a list of facet modifications together with an initialization address and an associated _calldata payload. The protocol enforces a timelock (upgradeNoticePeriod) and optionally allows a security council to approve a proposal early, but the _calldata itself is not locked at the time of proposal. Consequently, if the governor’s private key is compromised, an attacker who observes the pending proposal can wait until the notice period expires (or the council approves) and then replace the originally intended _calldata with a malicious payload before the governor executes the proposal. This front‑running attack effectively bypasses the intended time‑based protection because the contract only checks that the proposal was approved or that the notice period has passed, not that the calldata matches what was originally proposed. The root cause is the separation of proposal data (facet cuts and init address) from the execution payload, allowing the payload to be altered after the proposal is committed. Exploitation proceeds by the attacker submitting a transaction that executes the proposal with the tampered _calldata before the legitimate governor can do so, thereby executing arbitrary code in the init address. The impact can be severe: the malicious payload may transfer assets, modify critical contract state, or otherwise compromise the protocol, leading to loss of user funds, broken accounting, and a breach of trust. The condition for the exploit is the leakage of the governor’s signing key combined with insufficient monitoring by ZkSync; when the leak is detected early, the notice period gives defenders time to pause the system, but if the leak goes unnoticed, the attacker can act in the narrow window just before execution. The issue primarily affects the governance role, the security council, and ultimately all users of the protocol because the integrity of upgrades is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between proposeDiamondCut and executeDiamondCut and noted that the _calldata is not part of the immutable proposal snapshot. It is difficult to notice because the presence of a timelock gives the false impression that upgrades cannot be altered after proposal, obscuring the fact that the payload can still be changed. To remediate, the design should bind the _calldata to the proposal—either by storing a hash of the intended calldata at proposal time and enforcing its match at execution, or by requiring an explicit approval of the calldata by a security council member during execution. This change would re‑establish the intended protection that upgrades cannot be modified after the notice period, eliminating the front‑running vector and preserving protocol safety.

title: `BLOCK_PERIOD` is incorrect
description:
[Config.sol#L47](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-10-zksync/blob/456078b53a6d09636b84522ac8f3e8049e4e3af5/ethereum/contracts/zksync/Config.sol#L47)  

The `BLOCK_PERIOD` is set to 13 seconds in `Config.sol`.
    
```solidity
uint256 constant BLOCK_PERIOD = 13 seconds;
```

Since moving to Proof-of-Stake (PoS) after the Merge, block times on ethereum are fixed at 12 seconds per block (slots). <https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/#:~:text=Whereas%20under%20proof%2Dof%2Dwork,block%20proposer%20in%20every%20slot>.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an outdated configuration constant that is used throughout the zkSync roll‑up to calculate time‑based expirations for Layer‑2 transactions. The contract defines BLOCK_PERIOD as a fixed value of 13 seconds, but since the Ethereum network transitioned to Proof‑of‑Stake, the actual slot length is 12 seconds. This discrepancy creates an off‑by‑one‑second error in any logic that adds a multiple of BLOCK_PERIOD to a block number or timestamp to set a deadline. When a user initiates a transaction that is expected to be valid for, for example, three blocks, the system will compute the expiry time as 39 seconds from the submission moment instead of the correct 36 seconds. Because blocks now arrive every 12 seconds, the transaction reaches the calculated expiry point one block earlier than intended. Consequently, the transaction is marked as expired before the third block is mined, causing the roll‑up to discard it, revert it, or reject it with an "expired" error. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a sudden failure to submit a pending operation, refunds that never arrive, or balances that appear unchanged despite a confirmed submission attempt. The impact is not limited to a single user; any participant that relies on the default expiration window—such as automated market makers, bridge contracts, or custodial services—may experience unnecessary reverts or delayed finality, potentially leading to reduced liquidity, increased gas costs from retries, or temporary loss of access to funds. The issue was discovered during a static audit when the reviewer compared the constant against the documented PoS slot duration and identified that the mismatch could cause L2 transaction expirations to occur earlier than the protocol’s specifications. It is subtle because the error is only one second per block, which does not immediately break functionality, but the cumulative effect across multiple blocks makes the bug observable only in time‑sensitive workflows. To remediate the problem, the BLOCK_PERIOD constant should be updated to reflect the current 12‑second slot length, or better yet, be derived dynamically from the consensus layer or made configurable so that future protocol upgrades do not require hard‑coded changes. Adjusting the constant aligns expiration calculations with reality, restores the intended transaction windows, and prevents premature expirations that could otherwise erode user confidence and protocol reliability.

title: `PostTxProcessing` can revert user transactions not interacting with Turnstile
description: Any transaction, even those that don’t interact with the Turnstile contract, can be reverted by the `PostTxProcessing` hook if there was a CSR specific error. Thus, the CSR module can impair the behavior of smart contracts not related to the module.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the PostTxProcessing hook of the CSR (Cross‑Stake‑Reward) module, which is invoked after every EVM transaction regardless of whether the transaction interacts with the Turnstile contract or any CSR‑related logic. The hook attempts to perform several CSR‑specific operations, such as reading a CSR object from storage, sending gas fee allocations, retrieving the Turnstile address, and calling the distributeFees function. If any of these steps fails, the hook returns an error. Because the surrounding state transition code treats any error from PostTxProcessing as a fatal condition, the entire transaction is reverted, even when the transaction’s original purpose is unrelated to the CSR module. The root cause is the design decision to propagate CSR‑module errors directly to the transaction outcome instead of handling them internally, for example by logging the error and continuing with a nil return. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can trigger a scenario in which the fee distribution amount becomes zero—this can happen under normal conditions when a transaction consumes very little gas, the CSR share is small, and integer rounding reduces the fee share to zero. The distributeFees call then reverts, bubbling up through PostTxProcessing and causing the whole transaction to fail. The impact is that legitimate users experience unexpected transaction reverts, see no state change, and may lose gas fees paid for the failed transaction. This can affect any user of the blockchain, any dApp that sends transactions, and the protocol’s overall reliability, because unrelated contracts become vulnerable to a module that was intended to be isolated. The issue was discovered during an audit that inspected the CSR keeper’s evm_hooks implementation and observed that the error handling path unconditionally aborts the transaction. The problem can be hard to notice because the revert occurs after the transaction has been executed, and the error message ("tx post processing failed") does not directly reference the original contract call, making debugging confusing. To remediate, the PostTxProcessing hook should never return an error that aborts the transaction; instead it should log any CSR‑related failures and return nil, allowing the original transaction to succeed. If the CSR module reaches an unrecoverable state, it should emit a fatal log and possibly disable further processing, but it must not affect unrelated user transactions. Conceptually, this is a cross‑contract error‑propagation bug where a peripheral module’s internal failure incorrectly escalates to a global transaction failure, violating the expectation that only the contracts directly invoked by a transaction can cause its revert.

title: There is no re-register or re-assign function
description:
There is no re-register or re-assign option for the smart contracts.

Let’s assume a smart contract is registered either through the `register()` function with a new NFT minted or the `assign()` function to an existing NFT.

However, if somehow, the NFT is burned by the owner or transferred to another owner either by an approval or compromised tx, there is no option to re-register for these contracts which create gas fees but might not get a fee distribution in return.

And if the NFT is burned or transferred to another owner, the smart contracts will lose the fees generated if not previously withdrawn.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the lack of a re‑register or re‑assign mechanism for contracts that are registered through a dedicated NFT. When a developer registers a smart contract, either by calling the register() function to mint a new NFT or by calling assign() to bind an existing NFT, the system records the contract address in a mapping together with the token identifier and marks it as registered. This design assumes that the registration NFT will remain in the hands of the original caller forever. If the NFT is burned, transferred to another address, or otherwise removed from the original owner—whether intentionally, through an approval‑based transfer, or via a compromised transaction—the protocol provides no path to update the registration record. Consequently, the fee distribution logic, which relies on the presence of a valid, owned NFT, can no longer locate a rightful fee recipient for the contract. The result is that fees accrued for the contract become inaccessible, users see a zero balance when attempting to withdraw, and the initial gas spent on registration yields no financial return. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of the registration NFTs and identified that the contract does not handle the edge case where the NFT’s ownership changes after registration. This omission is subtle because the registration event itself succeeds and the mapping entry remains marked as registered, giving the false impression that the contract is still eligible for fee collection. However, the actual claim functions check NFT ownership, and without a re‑assignment routine the system cannot reconcile the new owner or recover from a burned token. The bug belongs to the class of “registration state loss due to immutable identifier” problems, where an external token used as an access key can become invalid without the protocol updating its internal state. From a user perspective, the symptoms manifest as missing refunds, unexpected zeros in the fee balance, and a feeling that the contract has been “abandoned” despite having generated revenue. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a function that allows a contract to validate its registration status against the current NFT holder, to re‑register or re‑assign the fee recipient when the original token is no longer usable, and to clearly communicate this limitation to developers so they can avoid relying on a non‑recoverable registration token.

title: Borrower can by mistake add own money to credit if credit is in ETH
description: Borrower can mistakenly add own money to credit if credit is in ETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the credit‑creation routine of the LineOfCredit contract when the requested credit is denominated in the native ETH token. The addCredit function forwards the payment handling to LineLib.receiveTokenOrETH, passing the lender address as the purported sender. Inside receiveTokenOrETH, the ERC20 branch correctly pulls tokens from the supplied sender via safeTransferFrom, but the ETH branch only verifies that msg.value is at least the requested amount and never checks that msg.sender matches the lender argument. Consequently, when a borrower calls addCredit with token set to ETH, they can include ETH in the transaction and the contract will credit that amount to the newly created line of credit, attributing it to the lender even though the funds actually originated from the borrower. This mismatch occurs under the condition that both parties have given mutual consent (the mutualConsent modifier) and the credit token is ETH. The bug is a classic authentication/authorization flaw for native token handling: the contract fails to authenticate the true source of ETH, leading to an incorrect attribution of payment source. Exploitation is straightforward – a borrower can unintentionally or deliberately fund their own credit line, causing their own wallet balance to decrease while the protocol records an incoming credit as if it were provided by the lender. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that a credit has been funded, yet the borrower observes that their ETH balance has been reduced and no loan funds have been received, violating the expectation that the lender supplies the capital. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, inaccurate accounting within the protocol, and confusion for lenders who may see credit entries that were never actually financed by them. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit by Code4rena, where reviewers noticed the absence of a sender check in the ETH branch of the payment library. The problem is subtle because the ERC20 path behaves correctly, and the ETH path silently accepts any msg.value, making the inconsistency easy to miss without explicit ETH‑payment tests. To remediate, the contract should enforce that when token equals the ETH denomination, msg.sender (or tx.origin) must equal the lender address supplied to addCredit, or redesign the workflow so that the lender initiates the ETH transfer themselves. This ensures that only the designated lender can fund a credit with ETH, preserving correct accounting and preventing borrowers from unintentionally adding their own money to the credit pool.

title: Mutual consent cannot be revoked and stays valid forever
description:
Contracts that inherit from the `MutualConsent` contract, have access to a `mutualConsent` modifier.

Functions that use this modifier need consent from two parties to be called successfully.

Once one party has given consent for a function call, it cannot revoke consent.

This means that the other party can call this function at any time now.

This opens the door for several exploitation paths.

Most notably though the functions `LineOfCredit.setRates()`, `LineOfCredit.addCredit()` and `LineOfCredit.increaseCredit()` can cause problems.

One party can use Social Engineering to make the other party consent to multiple function calls and exploit the multiple consents.
poc:
1. A borrower and lender want to change the rates for a credit. The borrower wants to create the possibility for himself to change the rates in the future without the lender’s consent.
2. The borrower and lender agree to set `dRate` and `fRate` to 5%.
3. The lender calls the `LineOfCredit.setRates()` function to give his consent.
4. The borrower might now say to the lender “Let’s put the rate to 5.1% instead, I will give an extra 0.1%”
5. The borrower and lender now both call the `LineOfCredit.setRates()` function to set the rates to 5.1%.
6. The borrower can now set the rates to 5% at any time. E.g. they might increase the rates further in the future (the borrower playing by the rules) and at some point the borrower can decide to set the rates to 5%.

Links:

`MutualConsent` contract: <https://github.com/debtdao/Line-of-Credit/blob/audit/code4rena-2022-11-03/contracts/utils/MutualConsent.sol>

`LineOfCredit.setRates()` function: <https://github.com/debtdao/Line-of-Credit/blob/e8aa08b44f6132a5ed901f8daa231700c5afeb3a/contracts/modules/credit/LineOfCredit.sol#L247-L262>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mutual‑consent mechanism used by contracts that inherit from the MutualConsent utility. The contract provides a mutualConsent modifier that requires two parties to give explicit consent before certain state‑changing functions can be executed. The flaw is that once a party records consent for a particular function call, that consent cannot be withdrawn. Consequently, the other party can trigger the function at any later time without needing fresh approval. This design defect originates from the absence of a revocation path or a time‑bound validity window for recorded consent, effectively making consent permanent. An attacker can exploit this by socially engineering the counter‑party into granting consent for multiple calls, then invoking those functions whenever advantageous. In practice, functions such as setRates, addCredit, and increaseCredit in the LineOfCredit module become dangerous because a borrower who obtains the lender’s initial consent can later change the interest rates or credit limits unilaterally, even after the lender believes the agreement is fixed. The exploit scenario proceeds as follows: two parties agree on a set of rates, the lender provides consent via setRates, the borrower then persuades the lender to give consent for a slightly different rate, both parties call setRates to lock in the new value, and thereafter the borrower can call setRates again with the original rate or any other rate without further approval. From the user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that any change to rates or credit limits requires fresh mutual agreement, but in reality the rates can be altered silently, leading to unexpected higher or lower interest, potential loss of revenue, or exposure to unfavorable loan terms. This issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the consent flow and identified the permanent nature of the stored approvals. The problem is subtle because the modifier appears to enforce two‑party consent, yet the lack of expiration or revocation makes the enforcement effectively one‑sided after the first approval. The bug belongs to the class of "permission immutability" or "consent revocation omission" bugs, where access control decisions cannot be undone. To remediate, the contract should introduce a mechanism to revoke consent, limit the lifespan of consent to a reasonable timeout, or invalidate previous consents when the function is called with new parameters, thereby ensuring that each state change truly reflects fresh mutual agreement.

title: Borrower/Lender excessive ETH not refunded and permanently locked in protocol
description:
The protocol does not refund overpayment of ETH. Excessive ETH is not included in the protocols accounting. As a result, the funds are permanently locked in the protocol **(Loss of funds)**.

There are multiple scenarios where excessive ETH could be sent by Borrowers and Lenders to the protocol.

The vulnerability effects at least five different scenarios and locks both the lender and borrowers ETH in LineOfCredit if overpaid. **There is no way to transfer the locked ETH back to the users**, as the withdraw methods are dependent on accounting (which is not updated with locked ETH).

This vulnerability impacts EscrowedLine, LineOfCredit, SpigotedLine and SecuredLine.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting and refund defect in the protocol’s ETH handling routine. When a caller sends ETH to the contract through the generic receiveTokenOrETH function, the code only verifies that the transferred amount (msg.value) is at least the required amount, using the condition `if (msg.value < amount) revert`. It does not handle the case where msg.value exceeds the required amount, so the excess ETH is added to the contract’s raw balance but never recorded in the internal accounting structures that drive withdrawal functions. Because the withdraw logic consults the internal accounting to determine how much a lender or borrower may retrieve, any ETH that is not reflected there becomes permanently inaccessible. This defect manifests in several user‑facing actions: borrowers over‑paying when calling depositAndClose, depositAndRepay, or close, and lenders over‑paying when calling addCredit or increaseCredit. The root cause is the lack of a refund or strict equality check for ETH payments, combined with a fee‑accrual formula that depends on block timestamps, which makes the exact amount of ETH needed hard to predict. Users often send a higher amount to hedge against rapid interest accrual, inadvertently triggering the bug. The impact is a loss of funds; the excess ETH remains trapped in the contract with no method to retrieve it, affecting both borrowers and lenders across the EscrowedLine, LineOfCredit, SpigotedLine, and SecuredLine contracts. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by exercising edge‑case payment scenarios in a test suite (forge test), which demonstrated that after over‑payment the contract’s address balance increased while the internal ledger stayed unchanged, confirming that the funds were irrecoverably locked. The problem can be subtle because the contract continues to function for normal payments, and there is no explicit error or event indicating that money is stuck. To remediate, the receiveTokenOrETH function should either (1) automatically refund any surplus ETH back to the sender after accounting for the required amount, or (2) enforce a strict equality check (`if (msg.value != amount) revert`) so that over‑payment is rejected outright. Both approaches prevent mismatches between the contract’s external balance and its internal accounting, restoring the expectation that any ETH sent is either correctly accounted for or returned, and thereby eliminating the risk of permanently locked funds.

title: Lender can trade claimToken in a malicious way to steal the borrower’s money via `claimAndRepay
poc:
The following code can manipulate and bypass the check to steal money of the borrower.

Step 1: Construct the zeroExTradeData data to sell the claimToken to ETH via the ZeroEx exchange data. The lender constructs the zeroExTradeData to send ETH to the exploit contract.

Step 2: In the exploit contract, have the `receive()` function to receive ETH from ZeroEx exchange. Since the exchange was from claimToken to ETH, so the exploit contract will receive the ETH and the code in receive function will be hit.

```solidity
receive() external payable {
    console.log("Callback hit: Send the SpigottedLine Contract some CreditToken to bypass the check of Balance");
    uint256 amount = 100; 
    creditToken.transfer(address(line),amount);
    console.log("Receive the amount of ETH: %s", msg.value);
}
```

In the `receive()` function, the exploit contract transfers some amount of creditToken to the SpigottedLine contract to bypass the check:

```solidity
if(tokensBought == 0) { revert TradeFailed(); } // ensure tokens bought
```

Since this check requires only not 0, so the lender can send only 1 or very small amount, e.g. 100 of creditToken.

This amount then will be used to repay the credit.

So this means, the borrower lost money, because the lender can claim big amount of claimToken and repay a little for the credit.

In the zip file in the Google_Drive link, there is the POC written for this bug.

The test case is test _lender_ can _claim_ and _repay\_ 3 in file SpigotedLine.t.modified.sol

You can put this file to the tests folder <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IWAV8Zz5KVgw22-gnVZrOxkcYrgv8cO2/view?usp=sharing>

```

Here I use the block-number to make the test log stable, but this does not impact the logic of POC.

You can find the detailed log file: Line-of-Credit\test _claim\_ 221107_2311.log.

The full log file here: <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LTY2-z8gOIOen0Ut9CbX1KpwvDvNVQdx/view?usp=sharing>

In this log file, the lender claims 1000 DAI (DAI is revenueToken) then sell to receive 0.6324 ETH, but repays only 100 * ( 10 ** -18 ) BUSD for the borrower.

Logs:

```

The full code repository: <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1LTY2-z8gOIOen0Ut9CbX1KpwvDvNVQdx/view?usp=sharing>
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claimAndRepay workflow of the SpigotedLine contract, where a lender is allowed to invoke claimAndRepay with an arbitrary zeroExTradeData payload. The function first claims a revenue token (claimToken) from the spigot escrow and, if the claimToken differs from the credit token, forwards the token to an internal _claimAndTrade routine that swaps the claimToken for the credit token via a ZeroEx exchange. The exchange call returns a tokensBought value, and the contract only checks that this value is non‑zero before proceeding to repay the credit. Because the zeroExTradeData is supplied by the caller, a malicious lender can craft a payload that executes a trade returning a negligible amount of credit token while still satisfying the non‑zero check, for example by leveraging a callback that injects a tiny amount of credit token during the trade. Consequently, the lender can claim a large amount of revenue token, receive its market value, and repay the borrower with an arbitrarily small amount of credit token, effectively stealing the difference. The bug occurs whenever a lender calls claimAndRepay with a claimToken that is not the same as the credit token and supplies crafted trade data; it affects both the borrower, whose outstanding debt is erroneously marked as repaid, and the protocol, whose accounting invariants are broken. The issue was uncovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept contract that received ETH from the exchange, used its receive() function to send a minimal credit token amount back to the line contract, and thus bypassed the tokensBought == 0 revert. The problem is subtle because the contract’s only safeguard is a simple non‑zero check, which can be trivially satisfied, making the exploit hard to notice without detailed tracing of trade outcomes. To remediate, the protocol should either restrict claimAndRepay to be callable only by the borrower, remove the ability for external callers to provide unchecked trade data, or introduce a verification that the amount of credit token obtained from the trade is at least equal to the value of the claimed revenue token, thereby enforcing proper accounting and preventing under‑repayment. This class of bug can be described as an unchecked external data injection leading to a logical accounting bypass in a repayment function.

title: Reentrancy bug allows lender to steal other lenders funds
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the credit‑closing routine of the LineOfCredit contract. The function responsible for finalising a credit line transfers the lender’s outstanding funds (deposit plus any interest repaid) before removing the credit record from storage. Because the state entry credit[id] is deleted only after the external token transfer, a malicious lender can supply a token that implements a callback (for example an ERC777, ERC223 or a custom ERC20 with a tokensReceived hook). When the token is sent to the lender, the callback is invoked and can call the contract’s close function again before the original execution finishes. During this re‑entrant call the credit entry has not yet been cleared, so the contract believes the credit is still open and will transfer the same amount of tokens again. By repeating the re‑entry while the LineOfCredit facility holds sufficient token balance, the attacker can drain tokens that belong to other lenders. From a user’s perspective the attacker sees an unexpectedly large refund – instead of receiving only their own deposit and interest they receive the combined amounts of multiple lenders, while the other lenders see their balances drop to zero or to a smaller amount than expected. The bug is triggered only when the protocol accepts a token capable of executing code on receipt and when the close function is called with such a token in the credit record. The issue was discovered during a security audit by executing a crafted mock lender contract that re‑entered the close function via the ERC777 tokensReceived hook. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to follow the usual pattern of sending funds and then cleaning up state, a pattern that is safe for plain ERC20 tokens but unsafe for tokens with callback functionality. The root cause is the order of operations: sending tokens before clearing the credit record. To remediate, the contract should either move the state deletion before any external call or protect the function with a re‑entrancy guard such as OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard, and it should enforce that only tokens without payable callbacks are accepted or explicitly handle callbacks safely. This class of bug falls under “reentrancy after state update” and violates the accounting assumption that each lender’s funds are isolated and cannot be reclaimed by another party once a repayment is processed.

title: The lender can draw out extra credit token from borrower’s account
description:
When the credit token is ERC20 extensive with hook, such as ERC777 token, the lender can exploit it to draw out extra tokens from borrower’s account. And the `count` state variable would also be underflowed, cause the line contract can’t be ‘REPAID’, the borrower will never be able to get back the collateral.

P.S.

[Similar attack on imBTC](https://zengo.com/imbtc-defi-hack-explained)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the credit line contract’s close routine that allows a lender to withdraw more tokens than the borrower originally deposited. When the contract closes a credit, it calls a utility function (LineLib.sendOutTokenOrETH) that performs an external token transfer to the lender. If the token used implements the ERC777 hook interface (or any ERC20 with an after‑transfer hook), the token’s hook can invoke arbitrary code during the transfer. An attacker‑controlled hook contract registers itself with the token and, when it receives the transfer, calls back into the line’s close function before the original close operation finishes. This recursive call repeats the token transfer multiple times, each iteration increasing the lender’s balance and decreasing the internal count state variable. Because the contract updates its accounting after the external call, the count underflows, preventing the line from ever reaching the REPAID status and permanently locking the borrower’s collateral. The issue can be triggered whenever a borrower opens a credit line using a token that supports hooks and the lender registers a malicious hook contract, which is precisely the scenario demonstrated by the provided PoC test. From a user’s perspective the borrower sees their collateral disappear and receives no repayment, while the lender observes an unexpectedly large amount of tokens arriving in their account. The bug is hard to notice because the token appears to be a normal ERC20 and the external call is a standard token transfer, leading developers to assume it is safe. The root cause is a missing re‑entrancy guard and an unsafe ordering of state updates (effects after interaction) in the close function. To remediate, the close routine should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, update internal accounting before any external token transfer, and protect the function with a non‑reentrant modifier or use a token standard that does not invoke external callbacks during transfers. This class of vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy attack enabled by tokens with callback hooks, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a lender can only receive the exact amount owed and that the line’s state transitions are monotonic.

title: Whitelisted functions aren’t scoped to revenue contracts and may lead to unnoticed calls due to selector clashing
description: Whitelisted functions in the Spigot contract don’t have any kind of association or validation to which revenue contract they are intended to be used. This may lead to inadvertently whitelisting a function in another revenue contract that has the same selector but a different name (signature).
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the way the Spigot contract stores a whitelist of permitted function calls. The contract records only the 4‑byte function selector in a global mapping without associating that selector with the specific revenue contract it was intended for. Consequently, any contract that implements a function whose selector matches a whitelisted selector can be called through the Spigot’s operate function, even if the original intent was to restrict calls to a safe, innocent contract. This design flaw is a classic selector‑clash problem: two distinct functions with different names and signatures can share the same selector, and the whitelist does not distinguish the contract address on which the selector is valid. An attacker can exploit the issue by deploying a malicious revenue contract that defines a function whose selector collides with a function the arbiter previously approved as safe. After the innocent function is whitelisted, the malicious function becomes implicitly whitelisted as well. The attacker then triggers the malicious function through operate, causing it to execute arbitrary logic such as burning tokens, draining funds, or performing any other undesirable state change. The impact is that funds controlled by the Spigot may be transferred, burned, or otherwise mishandled without any explicit permission check, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations. This scenario occurs whenever the whitelist is updated solely by selector, the operate function checks only the selector against the global whitelist, and there is no additional validation of the target contract address. The parties affected include the protocol’s treasury, any users whose assets are managed by the Spigot, and the protocol’s reputation, as the loss of funds can be traced back to a missing access‑control safeguard. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that an innocent function collate_propagate_storage(bytes16) and a malicious function burn(uint256) share the same selector; after whitelisting the innocent function, the malicious one became callable. The problem is difficult to notice because developers typically reason about selectors in the context of a single contract and may not anticipate that identical selectors can exist across different contracts, especially when the whitelist UI only shows function signatures without contract context. To remediate the issue, the whitelist should be scoped per revenue contract, for example using a mapping from contract address to a nested mapping of selector to boolean, and the operate function must verify that the selector is approved for the specific contract being called. This change ensures that only the intended function on the intended contract can be executed, preserving the protocol’s security guarantees and preventing unexpected token burns or fund loss.

title: Mistakenly sent eth could be locked
description:
If ERC20 and eth are transferred at same time, the mistakenly sent eth will be locked.

There are several functions that could be affected and cause user fund lock:

* `addCollateral()`
* `addCredit()`
* `increaseCredit()`
* `depositAndClose()`
* `depositAndRepay()`
* `close()`
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s generic token‑receiving routine, which distinguishes between ERC20 tokens and native Ether by checking the supplied token address. When a caller invokes any of the collateral‑related functions (addCollateral, addCredit, increaseCredit, depositAndClose, depositAndRepay, or close) and unintentionally includes a non‑zero msg.value together with an ERC20 token identifier, the ERC20 branch of receiveTokenOrETH() silently ignores the attached Ether. Because the function only executes a safeTransferFrom for the ERC20 token and does not revert or forward the Ether, the sent ETH remains trapped in the contract’s balance without any further logic to move or refund it. The root cause is the absence of a validation that msg.value must be zero whenever the token argument is not the special denomination representing Ether. This oversight allows an attacker or a careless user to lock Ether simply by calling a function that expects an ERC20 transfer while also sending Ether, either accidentally or maliciously. The impact is that the affected user’s Ether becomes unrecoverable through normal contract interactions, effectively disappearing from the user’s wallet while still residing in the contract’s balance. The bug manifests only under the condition that the caller includes Ether (msg.value > 0) while specifying an ERC20 token address; otherwise normal operation proceeds. All participants who interact with the listed functions – ordinary users depositing collateral, lenders providing credit, or any role that may transfer tokens – can be affected because the same utility library is reused across those entry points. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit conducted by Code4rena, where the logic of receiveTokenOrETH() was examined and it was observed that the Ether path is only executed in the explicit ETH branch, leaving the ERC20 branch without any safeguard against stray Ether. The problem may be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it succeeds, but the Ether is simply omitted from any accounting, leading to a silent loss that does not generate an error event. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that no Ether is sent when the token parameter does not equal the designated ETH denomination, typically by adding a require(msg.value == 0) or an explicit revert if msg.value > 0 in the ERC20 handling block. Alternatively, the function could be structured to route any attached Ether to a designated fallback handler or to reject the transaction outright. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an 'Ether‑locking' or 'fund‑locking' vulnerability caused by mismatched handling of native currency versus token transfers, and it violates the fundamental accounting assumption that all transferred assets are correctly accounted for and either credited to the user’s balance or returned when the operation fails.

title: Variable balance ERC20 support
description:
Some ERC20 may be tricky for the balance. Such as:

* fee on transfer (STA, USDT also has this mode)
* rebasing (aToken from AAVE)
* variable balance (stETH, balance could go up and down)

For these tokens, the balance can change over time, even without `transfer()/transferFrom()`. But current accounting stores the spot balance of the asset.

The impacts include:

* the calculation of collateral value could be inaccurate
* protocol could lose funds due to the deposit/repay amount being less than the actual transferred amount after fee
* the amount user withdraw collateral when `_close()` will be inaccurate
  * some users could lose funds due to under value
  * some funds could be locked due to the balance inflation
  * some funds might be locked due to the balance deflation
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the protocol’s assumption that an ERC20 token’s balance is immutable except when the contract explicitly calls transfer() or transferFrom(). The accounting logic records a token deposit as a static amount in a mapping (self.deposited[token].amount) and later uses that stored value to compute collateral value and to determine how much collateral to return on a close operation. This approach works for standard ERC20 tokens whose balance only changes on explicit transfers, but it fails for tokens that modify their holder balances automatically or on each transfer. Tokens that charge a fee on transfer (e.g., USDT, STA), rebasing tokens that adjust their total supply (e.g., AAVE’s aToken), or tokens with a variable share balance (e.g., Lido’s stETH) can change a user’s balance without an associated transfer call. Because the protocol never reconciles the recorded amount with the actual on‑chain balance of the contract, the stored “spot” balance can become stale.
