The contract implements the onERC721Received callback and enforces a strict check that the sender of any incoming NFT must be the specific Moonbird underlying asset (msg.sender == _underlyingAsset). This requirement, placed on line 70, causes the function to revert whenever an ERC‑721 token that is not the exact Moonbird NFT is transferred to the pool. As a result, any airdropped NFTs – for example Moonbirds Oddities or future airdrops targeting nested Moonbird positions – cannot be received by the pool and the transfer fails. The root cause is the hard‑coded validation that treats the pool as a whitelist for a single token type, ignoring the fact that airdrops are delivered by third‑party contracts that send a different ERC‑721 token. An attacker or an honest airdropper who attempts to send a supplemental NFT to the pool will trigger the require statement, causing the transaction to revert. The impact is that users who have supplied Moonbird NFTs as collateral lose the opportunity to claim airdropped assets, effectively reducing their expected rewards and breaking the protocol’s promised airdrop mechanics. This situation occurs whenever an external contract initiates a safeTransfer of any non‑Moonbird ERC‑721 to the reserve pool, which includes scheduled community airdrops or malicious attempts to flood the pool with unsupported tokens. The affected parties are the token holders who stake Moonbirds, the protocol’s accounting layer that assumes airdrops can be collected automatically, and any third parties relying on the pool to act as a sink for supplemental NFTs. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit through manual code review of the onERC721Received implementation. It can be hard to notice because the revert happens only on receipt of an unexpected token type, which may be interpreted as a generic failure rather than a deliberate whitelist. To remediate, the contract should relax the sender check and allow any ERC‑721 to be accepted, then handle the token appropriately – for example by forwarding it to the pool’s supply function without reverting, or by adding a separate handling path for airdropped assets. This change restores the intended business logic that the reserve pool can act as a collector of all NFTs related to Moonbird staking, preserving users’ entitlement to airdrops and aligning the contract’s behavior with protocol expectations.

title: Adversary can force user to pay large gas fees by transfering them collateral
description: Adversary can DOS user and make them pay more gas by sending them collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an automatic collateral‑enable mechanism that is triggered when a user receives a transfer of an asset that was previously used as collateral by the sender. The contract checks whether the recipient’s balance before the transfer is zero; if it is, the code unconditionally calls setUsingAsCollateral for the recipient, marking the newly received asset as collateral. This logic is the root cause: the health‑factor calculation treats every enabled asset as part of the borrower’s collateral, and the calculation is performed on every operation that requires a health check (e.g., borrowing, repaying, or even disabling collateral). Because the health check iterates over all enabled collateral types, each newly enabled asset adds extra storage reads, arithmetic, and external price‑oracle calls, which significantly increases the gas consumption of subsequent transactions for the recipient. An adversary can exploit this by sending a tiny amount of collateral to a victim who currently has no balance of that asset. As soon as the transfer is processed, the victim’s account now has the asset flagged as collateral, inflating the gas cost of any future operation that triggers a health‑factor check. By repeating the process with multiple assets or by forcing the victim to hold many different collateral types, the attacker can drive the gas cost so high that the victim’s transactions run out of gas, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service (DoS) on the user’s ability to interact with the protocol. The impact is that honest users may experience unexpected, large gas fees, see their transactions revert due to out‑of‑gas errors, and may become unable to manage their positions, jeopardising the usability of the platform. The condition under which this occurs is specific: the sender must have the asset enabled as collateral, and the receiver must start with a zero balance for that asset. The affected parties are the recipients of such transfers, any lenders or borrowers whose positions depend on the health factor, and the protocol itself, which may suffer from degraded performance and reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a systematic code audit that highlighted the automatic call to setUsingAsCollateral inside the transfer routine and recognized that the flag change has downstream gas‑cost implications that are not obvious from the UI. The problem is hard to notice because the collateral flag change happens silently, and the UI typically shows only the transferred amount, not the fact that the asset is now counted in health‑factor calculations. From the user’s perspective, after receiving a small amount of collateral, they may see a message such as "transaction failed: out of gas" when trying to repay or withdraw, even though they expected the operation to be cheap. The bug belongs to the class of "automatic state‑change side effects that increase downstream computational cost", similar to other flaws where a benign‑looking update triggers expensive checks later. To remediate, the protocol should remove the implicit enable‑as‑collateral call; collateral should only be enabled explicitly by the recipient through a separate user‑initiated transaction or after an explicit consent step. Additional safeguards, such as checking that the recipient has opted in or limiting the number of collateral types that can be auto‑enabled, would also mitigate the gas‑inflation attack vector.

title: User collateral NFT open auctions would be sold as min price immediately next time user health factor gets below the liquidation threshold, protocol should check health factor and set auctionValidityTime value anytime a valid action happens to user account to invalidate old open auctions
description: Attacker can liquidate users NFT collaterals with min price immediately after user health factor gets below the liquidation threshold for NFT collaterals that have old open auctions and `setAuctionValidityTime()` is not get called for the user. Whenever user’s account health factor gets below the NFT liquidation threshold attacker can start auction for all of users NFTs in the protocol. User needs to call `setAuctionValidityTime()` to invalidated all of those open auctions whenever his/her account health factor is good, but if user doesn’t call this and doesn’t close those auctions then next time user’s accounts health factor gets below the threshold, attacker would liquidate all of those NFTs with minimum price immediately.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the auction‑based liquidation of NFT collateral in a lending protocol. The protocol relies on a per‑user timestamp called `auctionValidityTime` to decide whether an active auction for a given NFT is still valid. An auction is considered valid only if its start time is greater than the user’s `auctionValidityTime`. However, the only way to update `auctionValidityTime` is through an explicit call to `setAuctionValidityTime()`, which the user must perform manually when their health factor improves. If the user never invokes this function, old auctions remain open indefinitely. When the user’s health factor later falls below the liquidation threshold, an attacker can trigger the liquidation process, start (or continue) an auction for each NFT, and, because the auction has been running for a long period, the price‑decay algorithm in `calculateAuctionPriceMultiplier()` drives the price down to the minimum multiplier. Consequently, the attacker can liquidate the NFTs for essentially zero value. The root cause is a missing automatic reset of the `auctionValidityTime` whenever a user’s health factor changes or any account‑affecting action occurs, allowing stale auctions to be reused maliciously. Exploitation requires the attacker to monitor a user’s health factor, detect the moment it drops below the threshold, and then invoke the liquidation function while the auction is still considered valid. The impact is that users lose their NFT collateral without receiving a fair market price; from the user’s perspective the NFT disappears from their wallet, balances show zero, and no refund or compensation is received. This issue is especially hard to notice because the UI may only alert the user to a health‑factor breach without indicating that an old auction is still active, and most users do not watch their health factor continuously. The bug belongs to the class of “stale state‑dependent access control” or “auction invalidation race” issues, where business logic assumes a manual state update that is not enforced. To remediate, the contract should automatically update `auctionValidityTime` (or otherwise invalidate existing auctions) on every user‑triggered action that can affect health, such as collateral supply, withdrawal, or repayment, and it should provide incentives for anyone to start or end auctions safely. By ensuring that old auctions are promptly invalidated, the protocol restores the intended economic guarantees of the liquidation process and prevents NFTs from being sold at the minimum price without proper bidding.

title: Users can be locked out of providing Uniswap V3 NFTs as collateral
description: A malicious actor can disallow supplying of Uniswap V3 NFT tokens as collateral for any user. This can be exploited as a front-running attack that disallows a borrower to provide more Uniswap V3 LP tokens as collateral and save their collateral from being liquidated.
bug_full:
The vulnerability allows a malicious participant to prevent legitimate users from adding Uniswap V3 NFT positions as collateral in the lending protocol. The root cause lies in the protocol’s enforcement of a hard cap on the number of Uniswap V3 NFTs that any single address may hold as collateral – a balance limit of 30 tokens – without any validation of the actual liquidity represented by each NFT. Because Uniswap V3 NFTs can be minted at zero liquidity, an attacker can cheaply create or acquire a large collection of such empty NFTs and transfer them to a victim’s address. Each transferred NFT increments the victim’s collateral‑token count, quickly exhausting the 30‑token quota. Once the limit is reached, any further attempt by the victim to supply a genuine liquidity‑bearing NFT is rejected by the _checkBalanceLimit_ guard, even though the victim’s existing NFTs contribute no value to the collateral pool.

The exploit proceeds in a straightforward step‑by‑step fashion: (1) the attacker obtains or mints a batch of zero‑liquidity Uniswap V3 NFTs; (2) the attacker sends those NFTs to the target borrower’s address (or to a contract acting on the borrower’s behalf); (3) the protocol’s internal accounting updates the borrower’s NFT balance, hitting the predefined balance limit; (4) when the borrower subsequently tries to deposit a real LP position to avoid liquidation, the protocol rejects the transaction with an NTOKEN_BALANCE_EXCEEDED error; (5) the borrower is left unable to increase collateral, exposing the loan to liquidation or forced repayment.

From a user’s perspective the symptoms are puzzling: a user who expects to add more collateral sees the transaction revert, receives an error about exceeding a balance limit, and may notice that their collateral balance remains unchanged even though they attempted a deposit. The UI may display a generic “transaction failed” message without clarifying that the underlying issue is a token‑count restriction, leading the user to think the protocol is malfunctioning or that they are being scammed.

The impact is primarily financial: borrowers cannot protect their positions, potentially leading to forced liquidation and loss of assets. The protocol’s reputation is harmed because users perceive the system as unreliable or deliberately obstructive. This class of bug falls under “resource‑quota abuse” where an attacker exhausts a per‑account resource limit (here, the number of collateral tokens) using assets that carry no economic weight.

The issue was discovered during a security audit that initially focused on a front‑running gas‑exhaustion attack related to unlimited NFT minting. The mitigation introduced a token‑count limit, but the audit team later identified that the limit could itself be weaponized because it does not consider the actual liquidity of each NFT. The problem is subtle and may go unnoticed because zero‑liquidity NFTs are syntactically valid and the balance‑limit check is a simple numeric comparison, offering no visibility into the economic value of the tokens counted.

To remediate the vulnerability, the protocol should replace the pure count‑based restriction with a value‑based one. Possible fixes include requiring a minimum amount of underlying liquidity for any NFT accepted as collateral, aggregating total liquidity across all NFTs rather than counting tokens, or rejecting NFTs that report zero liquidity at the time of deposit. Additionally, the protocol could implement per‑user liquidity thresholds or introduce a separate whitelist for NFTs that have been verified to contain a non‑zero amount of assets, thereby eliminating the attack surface while still protecting against gas‑related abuses.

title: LooksRare orders using WETH as currency cannot be paid with WETH
description: Users won’t be able to buy NFTs from LooksRare via the Paraspace Marketplace and pay with WETH when `MakerOrder` currency is set to WETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in the Paraspace Marketplace when it attempts to fulfil a LooksRare order whose MakerOrder specifies WETH as the payment currency. In the LooksRare adapter the code treats WETH specially: it rewrites the consideration item to use the native token type (ItemType.NATIVE) and clears the token address, effectively converting the expected payment from an ERC20 (WETH) to ETH. Later, in the buyWithCredit flow, the contract determines whether the supplied credit token is native by checking if the token address equals address(0). Because the user supplies WETH (a non‑zero address) the isETH flag remains false, and the credit token variable is set to the WETH contract address. When the contract validates the compatibility between the consideration item and the supplied credit token, it requires that either the item type be ERC20 or, if the item type is NATIVE, that the credit token be native (isETH true). Since the consideration item was forced to NATIVE but the credit token is still identified as WETH, the validation fails and the transaction reverts with an INVALID_ASSET_TYPE error. This mismatch prevents users from purchasing NFTs on LooksRare through the Paraspace Marketplace using WETH, even though the external exchange advertises WETH support. The impact is a functional denial‑of‑service for any user who attempts to pay with WETH: the transaction fails, no NFT is transferred, and any prepared credit or borrowed funds remain unused, potentially leaving the user confused as their balance appears unchanged while the order cannot be completed. The bug occurs only when the MakerOrder's currency field is set to the WETH contract address and the buyer supplies WETH as the credit token; all other currency combinations work as intended. It affects all participants of the protocol who rely on WETH for purchases, including regular users, liquidity providers, and third‑party integrators, and it undermines the marketplace’s promise of seamless cross‑protocol trading. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated the revert. It can be hard to notice because the adapter’s conversion logic appears legitimate – converting WETH to ETH is a common pattern – and the error surface is a generic asset‑type check that only triggers under this specific combination. To resolve the problem, the adapter should stop substituting the native token type when the order specifies WETH, treating WETH as a standard ERC20 asset, or the credit‑handling logic should recognise that a WETH‑derived order can be satisfied with native ETH, aligning the isETH flag with the consideration item. In essence, the bug is a mismatch between currency representation (ERC20 versus native) caused by an incorrect conditional conversion, leading to a failed payment path and a broken user experience where funds appear to disappear without completing the intended purchase.

title: Oracle does not treat upward and downward price movement the same in validity checks, causing safety issues in oracle usage
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price validity logic of the NFTFloorOracle used by the ParaSpace protocol. The oracle stores a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) for a collection of ERC‑721 tokens and limits how much this price may change between successive updates using a configurable parameter called maxPriceDeviation. The implementation calculates a deviation value by taking the larger of the two prices, multiplying it by 100 and dividing by the smaller price, then checks whether this ratio exceeds the configured limit. While this formula yields the same numeric result for a price increase of 10→15 and a price decrease of 15→10 (both produce a deviation of 1.5), the economic meaning of those moves is very different: the increase represents a 50 % rise while the decrease corresponds to a 33 % fall. Because the oracle treats both directions as identical, upward price movements are permitted far more aggressively than downward movements. As a result the protocol may accept inflated price feeds that artificially raise the collateral value of NFTs, allowing borrowers to obtain more credit than warranted, while simultaneously rejecting legitimate price drops that would otherwise protect lenders. This asymmetry can lead to over‑collateralized loans, unexpected liquidations, or stale high prices that remain visible in the UI, causing users to see their collateral valued incorrectly or their borrowing capacity change without explanation. The issue was discovered during a static audit of the contract code where the deviation calculation was examined and found to mis‑represent percentage change. It can be difficult to spot because the code uses a familiar “*100 /” pattern that superficially resembles a percent calculation, yet the absence of a signed difference hides the directional bias. The proper fix is to compute a true percentage change by measuring the signed difference between the new and prior TWAP, applying an absolute value, and comparing that to maxPriceDeviation, or to maintain separate upward and downward thresholds. In short, the oracle currently violates the business logic that price deviations should be symmetric, leading to potential financial mis‑valuation and security concerns for all participants in the protocol.

title: Pausing assets only affects future price updates, not previous malicious updates
description:
NFTFloorOracle retrieves ERC721 prices for ParaSpace. It is pausable by admin on a per asset level using setPause(asset, flag). setPrice will not be callable when asset is paused:

```solidity
function setPrice(address _asset, uint256 _twap)
    public
    onlyRole(UPDATER_ROLE)
    onlyWhenAssetExisted(_asset)
    whenNotPaused(_asset)
```

However, getPrice() is unaffected by the pause flag. This is really dangerous behavior, because there will be 6 hours when the current price treated as valid, although the asset is clearly intended to be on lockdown.

Basically, pauses are only forward facing, and whatever happened is valid. But, if we want to pause an asset, something fishy has already occured, or will occur by the time setPause() is called. So, “whatever happened happened” mentality is overly dangerous.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the NFTFloorOracle handles the pause mechanism for individual assets. The contract provides a setPause(asset, flag) function that, when invoked by an admin, prevents any further calls to setPrice for the paused asset by applying the whenNotPaused modifier on the setter. However, the complementary getter function getPrice does not check the pause flag and continues to return the most recent TWAP value even after the asset has been marked as paused. This discrepancy creates a situation where a malicious updater can submit a manipulated price, immediately pause the asset, and the stale, incorrect price will remain observable by any downstream protocol component that relies on getPrice for six hours (the typical update interval). The root cause is a missing guard in the read‑path; the contract assumes that pausing an asset implicitly invalidates its current price, but this assumption is not enforced in code. An attacker with UPDATER_ROLE—or a compromised updater account—can exploit this by setting an artificially high or low price, then calling setPause to freeze further updates, thereby preserving the malicious price for the duration of the oracle’s validity window. Consumers of the oracle, such as lending or liquidation modules, will treat the returned price as trustworthy despite the asset’s paused status, leading to potential under‑collateralisation, wrongful liquidations, or loss of value for borrowers and lenders. The issue manifests when an asset is paused after a price update, which may be done as an emergency response or as part of routine maintenance; users see the asset flagged as paused in the UI, yet the price displayed remains unchanged, violating the expectation that pausing freezes all price activity. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interplay between the pause modifier and the oracle’s public interfaces, noting that the read‑only function lacked the same restriction as the write‑only function. It can be hard to notice because the UI often only highlights the pause flag, and the price value appears normal, leading developers and users to trust it implicitly. To remediate, the getter should also be protected by the whenNotPaused modifier, or the contract should explicitly invalidate or revert price reads for paused assets, ensuring that no stale data can be consumed while the asset is in a locked state. This class of bug—an inconsistent access control between state‑modifying and state‑reading functions—breaks the fundamental accounting invariant that a paused asset should not provide a usable price, thereby exposing the protocol to financial loss.

title: During oracle outages or feeder outages/disagreement, the `ParaSpaceFallbackOracle` is not used
description:
If the feeders haven’t updated their prices within the default six-hour time window, the floor oracle will revert when requests are made to get the current price, and these reverts are not caught by the wrapper oracle which handles the fallback oracle, so rather than using the fallback oracle in these cases, the calls will revert, leading to liquidations to fail (see my other submission for the full chain from the floor oracle to the liquidation function).

Additionally, the code uses the deprecated chainlink `latestAnswer()` API for its token requests, which may revert once it is no longer supported.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑feed architecture of the protocol, where a primary floor oracle provides asset prices and a secondary fallback oracle is intended to supply a price when the primary source is unavailable. The primary oracle rejects requests if the stored price data is older than a six‑hour expiration window; it does this by executing a require statement that reverts the transaction when the price is considered stale. Because the wrapper contract that coordinates the two oracles directly calls the primary source without surrounding the call with a try‑catch clause, any revert generated by the primary oracle propagates up to the wrapper and prevents the fallback oracle from being consulted. Consequently, when feeders are down, price updates are delayed, or a price deviation exceeds the configured threshold, the getAssetPrice function reverts instead of returning a secondary price. This failure manifests itself during liquidation attempts, where the protocol expects a valid price to calculate collateral value. If the price request reverts, the liquidation transaction itself fails, leaving an under‑collateralised position un‑liquidated, potentially exposing the protocol to credit loss. The issue is triggered only under conditions where the primary price data has not been refreshed within the configured expiration period or when the primary source returns a zero value due to stale or divergent data. Affected parties include borrowers whose positions may become unsafe, liquidators who are unable to execute their functions, and the protocol as a whole because the accounting assumption that a price is always available is broken. The problem was identified during an audit that traced the call flow from the NFTFloorOracle through the ParaSpaceOracle to the liquidation routine, observing that the wrapper does not handle the revert and therefore never reaches the fallback oracle. The bug is subtle because the wrapper’s logic appears to provide a safety net—checking for a zero price and then querying the fallback—but that logic is never reached when the primary call reverts rather than returns zero. To remediate the issue, the wrapper should catch any exception raised by the primary price source, for example using Solidity’s try‑catch construct, and fall back to the secondary oracle when a revert occurs. Additionally, the contract should migrate away from the deprecated Chainlink latestAnswer() function to a more stable interface such as latestRoundData(), ensuring that future deprecation does not cause unexpected reverts. By handling stale data gracefully and guaranteeing that a price is always returned, the protocol restores its liquidation guarantees and aligns with its financial model that assumes continuous price availability.

title: Interactions with AMMs do not use deadlines for operations
description:
From a judge’s comment in a previous [contest](https://code4rena.com/reports/2022-06-canto-v2/#m-01-stableswap---deadline-do-not-work):

Because Front-running is a key aspect of AMM design, deadline is a useful tool to ensure that your tx cannot be “saved for later”.

Due to the removal of the check, it may be more profitable for a miner to deny the transaction from being mined until the transaction incurs the maximum amount of slippage.

Most of the functions that interact with AMM pools do not have a deadline parameter, but specifically the one shown below is passing `block.timestamp` to a pool, which means that whenever the miner decides to include the txn in a block, it will be valid at that time, since `block.timestamp` will _be_ the current timestamp.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from the omission of a deadline parameter in functions that interact with automated market maker (AMM) pools, specifically when decreasing liquidity on Uniswap V3. The contract passes the current block timestamp (block.timestamp) directly to the AMM's decreaseLiquidity call, which means the transaction is considered valid at the exact moment a miner includes it in a block. Because there is no future‑looking deadline, a malicious miner can withhold the transaction, reorder it, or wait until market conditions have deteriorated before mining it. By delaying the transaction, the miner can force the operation to execute under higher slippage than the caller anticipated, potentially turning a profitable liquidity withdrawal into a loss or causing a liquidation that benefits the miner. This exploit can be carried out whenever a user submits a transaction to reduce their position and the protocol does not enforce a maximum execution time; the miner simply chooses the block in which to include the transaction. Affected parties include liquidity providers who expect their liquidity to be withdrawn within a known price range, the protocol that assumes safe reduction of exposure, and any downstream contracts that rely on the proper execution of the decreaseLiquidity call. The issue was highlighted during a Code4rena audit where a judge noted that front‑running is a core risk of AMMs and that a deadline is required to bound execution time. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert – it appears successful, but the received token amounts may be far below the user‑specified minima, leading to unexpected loss of capital. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the withdraw request was submitted, yet the balance remains unchanged or a liquidation event occurs shortly after, contradicting the expectation that the liquidity was safely removed. The bug belongs to the class of time‑bound omission vulnerabilities where lack of an explicit deadline permits miners to manipulate execution timing. To remediate the issue, every function that calls an AMM should accept a deadline argument supplied by the caller, and this deadline should be forwarded to the AMM call so that the transaction will revert if it is mined after the specified time, thereby protecting users from excessive slippage and front‑running attacks.

title: Centralization Risks
description: **Note: per discussion with the judge, instead of highlighting only one submission related to centralization risks, all related findings are being compiled together under M-14 to provide a more complete report.**
bug_full: The reported issue is a centralization risk inherent in the contract’s governance and control structures. At its core, the vulnerability stems from an overly concentrated authority model in which a single address, role, or small group possesses the ability to modify critical protocol parameters, upgrade the contract, pause or unpause functionality, and potentially transfer or freeze user assets without broader community oversight. Because the privileged entity can unilaterally execute these high‑impact actions, an attacker who compromises that entity, or a malicious insider, can exploit the design to alter fee structures, redirect withdrawals, or halt service, thereby causing loss of funds, erosion of user trust, and disruption of the protocol’s economic incentives. The impact manifests when a user attempts a normal operation—such as withdrawing a deposit or expecting a promised yield—but the centralized controller intervenes to block the transaction, change the calculation, or reroute the payout, leading to symptoms like empty balances, missing rewards, or complete denial of service. This condition materializes whenever the contract’s privileged functions are invoked, especially in scenarios where a single private key is used for governance, the contract is upgradable via an admin‑only proxy, or emergency stop mechanisms lack a timelock or multi‑signature safeguard. The risk was identified during a systematic audit that examined the ownership model, upgrade pathways, and access control lists, noting that the concentration of power was not mitigated by decentralized voting, quorum requirements, or external audits. Detecting this problem can be difficult because the contract may function correctly under normal conditions, masking the hidden power held by the central authority until an exploit occurs or a key is compromised. To address the issue, the protocol should shift to a more decentralized governance framework—such as multi‑signature wallets, timelocked upgrades, or token‑based voting—ensuring that no single actor can unilaterally alter protocol state or financial flows. By distributing decision‑making authority and introducing transparent, community‑driven checks, the contract can align with its expected trust model and prevent scenarios where funds disappear, refunds are blocked, or the system can be shut down by a single point of failure.

title: NFTFloorOracle’s assets will use old prices if added back after removal
description:
`assetFeederMap` mapping has elements of the `FeederRegistrar` structure type, that contains nested `feederPrice` mapping. When an asset is being removed with _removeAsset(), its `assetFeederMap` entry is deleted with the plain `delete assetFeederMap[_asset]` operation, which leaves `feederPrice` mapping intact.

This way if the asset be added back after removal its old prices will be reused via _combine() given that their timestamps are fresh enough and the corresponding feeders stay active.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the NFTFloorOracle contract handles the removal of an asset from its internal registry. When the internal function _removeAsset() is called, the contract executes a plain delete on the assetFeederMap entry that stores a FeederRegistrar struct. In Solidity, deleting a struct clears all of its value‑type fields but deliberately leaves any nested mappings untouched. Because FeederRegistrar contains a mapping called feederPrice that holds the historical price information supplied by each feeder, the deletion of the struct does not erase those price entries. Consequently, if the same asset address is later re‑added through _addAsset(), only the index field of the struct is re‑initialized while the feederPrice mapping still contains the previously recorded prices. The oracle’s price aggregation function _combine() reads from feederPrice and, provided the timestamps of those stale entries are still within the configured expirationPeriod and the feeders remain active, it will treat the old values as fresh data. An attacker who can influence the price feed before the asset is removed can therefore craft a scenario where a manipulated price persists after removal and is unintentionally reused when the asset returns to the system. This leads to incorrect floor price calculations, which can cause under‑valuation or over‑valuation of NFTs, potentially triggering wrongful liquidations, incorrect collateral valuations, or users receiving zero or unexpected refunds. The issue manifests only after an asset has been removed and then added again; it is invisible in the UI because the asset appears to have been freshly registered, while the price data behind the scenes remains stale. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the delete semantics of structs containing mappings. It can be difficult to detect because the contract does not emit any warnings or events regarding the retained mapping data, and the UI does not display the hidden price entries. To remediate the flaw, the contract should explicitly clear the feederPrice mapping for each feeder when an asset is removed, for example by iterating over the known feeder list and deleting each entry, or by resetting the entire FeederRegistrar to a fresh instance that has an empty mapping. This ensures that when an asset is re‑added, no obsolete price information can be inadvertently reused, preserving the integrity of the oracle’s price calculations and protecting user funds from misvaluation.

title: When users sign a credit loan for bidding on an item, they are forever committed to the loan even if the NFT value drops massively
bug_full: The vulnerability is an indefinite credit commitment bug in the ParaSpace marketplace bidding flow. When a maker signs a credit structure to finance the purchase of an NFT, the signed data includes the token address, amount, order identifier and the maker’s signature components, but it lacks any temporal restriction such as a deadline or expiration timestamp. The contract validates the signature using verifyCreditSignature and then proceeds to accept the bid via validateAcceptBidWithCredit as long as the resulting health factor remains positive. Because the credit struct has no expiration, the maker remains bound to the loan forever, even if the market value of the underlying NFT collapses. An attacker, or even the original maker, can wait until the NFT price drops, then reuse the previously signed credit to claim a larger loan amount than was originally intended, effectively over‑paying for the asset or forcing the borrower to repay a higher debt. This abuse is possible because the signed message does not contain a time‑bound clause and there is no on‑chain mechanism to revoke or cancel the signature after it has been issued. The impact is that users who rely on the credit to acquire NFTs can be permanently locked into an unfavorable loan, leading to loss of capital, inability to withdraw funds, and potential liquidation if the health factor later turns negative. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature verification logic and the data structures used for credit‑based bids. It is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a health‑factor check, which may give a false sense of safety, while the missing deadline is not obvious from the function signatures. To remediate, the credit structure should be extended with a deadline timestamp that is included in the signed hash, and the contract should reject any credit whose deadline has passed. Additionally, a revocation or cancellation mechanism should be added to allow borrowers to withdraw their commitment before execution. This class of bug falls under the broader category of “missing expiration in signed authorization,” which can lead to stale or outdated approvals being replayed to the detriment of users. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms include an inability to cancel a bid, unexpected persistence of a loan obligation, and potentially seeing their balances locked or receiving no refund when attempting to close the position, contrary to the expectation that a signed loan can be managed or cancelled after a reasonable period.

title: Attacker can abuse victim’s signature for marketplace bid to buy worthless item
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way credit‑based bids are validated in the ParaSpace marketplace. When a maker creates a bid that can be fulfilled using a credit loan, the contract stores the bid information in a Credit struct that contains only the token address, amount, orderId, and the signature components (v, r, s). The validation function verifyCreditSignature hashes this struct and checks the signature against the maker’s address, but the struct does not include any identifier of the marketplace to which the order belongs. Because the marketplace address is omitted from the signed data, the same signature can be replayed on a different marketplace adapter that implements the same credit‑loan API. An attacker can therefore take a legitimate signature that the maker issued for a high‑value item on Marketplace A, replace the orderId with one that points to a cheap or worthless item on Marketplace B, and still pass the signature check. The contract then authorises a credit loan for the attacker, who purchases the low‑value item while the maker’s credit line is consumed. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving a valuable NFT in exchange for a loan – is replaced by a scenario where the loan is granted for a trivial asset, leading to an imbalance between borrowed funds and received value. The impact is that the maker’s credit line can be drained for essentially nothing, causing loss of collateral or debt for the maker and potentially harming the protocol’s accounting assumptions about loan‑backed purchases. The flaw manifests whenever a marketplace adapter that supports matchBidWithTakerAsk (such as SeaportAdapter currently, and likely LooksRareAdapter or X2Y2Adapter in the future) processes a credit‑based bid, because the same signature verification logic is reused without a marketplace binding. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the credit‑loan integration, where the absence of a marketplace field in the signed data was noted as a replay vector. It is hard to notice because the signature verification itself succeeds, and no immediate error is thrown; only the mismatch between the intended asset and the asset actually bought reveals the problem. To remediate, the Credit struct should be extended to include a MarketplaceAddress (or a unique marketplace identifier) that is incorporated into the hash used for signature verification. This binds each signature to a specific marketplace, preventing cross‑marketplace replay attacks and ensuring that the loan is only used for the item the maker originally authorized.

title: Bad debt will likely incur when multiple NFTs are liquidated
description:
_getUserBalanceForERC721() in GenericLogic gets the value of a user’s specific ERC721 xToken. It is later used for determining the account’s health factor. In case `isAtomicPrice` is false such as in ape NTokens, price is calculated using:

```solidity
uint256 assetPrice = _getAssetPrice(
    params.oracle,
    vars.currentReserveAddress
);
totalValue =
    ICollateralizableERC721(vars.xTokenAddress)
        .collateralizedBalanceOf(params.user) *
    assetPrice;
```

It is the number of apes multiplied by the floor price returns from _getAssetPrice. The issue is that this calculation does not account for slippage, and is unrealistic. If user’s account is liquidated, it is very unlikely that releasing several multiples of precious NFTs will not bring the price down in some significant way.

By performing simple multiplication of NFT count and NFT price, protocol is introducing major bad debt risks and is not as conservative as it aims to be. Collateral value must take slippage risks into account.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the protocol evaluates the value of ERC‑721 collateral during health‑factor calculations. When the contract retrieves a user's balance of a specific NFT‑based xToken, it multiplies the number of owned NFTs by the price returned from the oracle, assuming a linear relationship. This approach disregards the market impact that selling multiple high‑value NFTs would cause; in reality, each additional NFT sold would push the floor price lower due to limited liquidity, a phenomenon known as slippage. Because the calculation does not apply any discount or slippage model, the reported collateral value can be substantially higher than the amount realistically realizable in a liquidation event. If a user's position becomes under‑collateralized and the protocol initiates liquidation, the system may attempt to liquidate a batch of NFTs based on the inflated valuation, sell them at the optimistic oracle price, and consequently incur a shortfall. The shortfall manifests as bad debt: the protocol owes more to lenders than the proceeds obtained from the liquidated NFTs. This risk materialises particularly when the flag `isAtomicPrice` is false – as is the case for ape NTokens – and the user holds several copies of the same high‑value NFT. From the user’s perspective, the expectation that their collateral will be liquidated at a fair price is violated; after liquidation the user may see their balance reduced dramatically, or the protocol may report a loss without an obvious on‑chain event, leading to confusion. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the collateral‑valuation function and recognised that the simple multiplication model does not reflect realistic market dynamics for illiquid assets. It is hard to notice because oracle feeds reliably report per‑unit prices, giving an impression of accuracy, while the aggregated impact of multiple units is hidden in the contract logic. The proper remediation is to incorporate a slippage‑aware valuation, for example by applying a discount factor that grows with the number of NFTs, using tiered thresholds, or by simulating the expected price impact of selling the given quantity. In addition, conservative loan‑to‑value and liquidation‑threshold parameters should be selected to provide a safety margin. The bug belongs to the class of "collateral over‑valuation due to missing slippage modeling" and breaks the accounting assumption that collateral value scales linearly with quantity, potentially causing funds to disappear or debt to accrue unexpectedly.

title: Rewards are not accounted for properly in NTokenApeStaking contracts, limiting user’s collateral
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the NTokenApeStaking contract suite that is responsible for exposing a user's effective ApeCoin balance to a lending protocol. The core issue is an incomplete accounting of reward earnings when a BAYC or MAYC NFT is paired with a BAKC token. The function getTokenIdStakingAmount() aggregates three components: the amount of ApeCoin directly staked by the primary NFT, the pending rewards for that primary NFT, and the amount of ApeCoin staked by the paired BAKC token. However, it omits the pendingRewards that accrue on the BAKC token itself. This omission stems from a logical oversight: the code adds the BAKC staked amount but never queries or adds the BAKC's pending rewards. The function’s return value is subsequently used by the PTokenSApe balanceOf() implementation, which is intended to represent the total collateral a user has supplied to the lending platform. Because the pending BAKC rewards are invisible to balanceOf(), the protocol underestimates the user's collateral. In practice, a user who has paired a BAKC token will see a lower balance than they are actually entitled to, meaning that the extra rewards cannot be used as collateral for borrowing or debt repayment. This can lead to unintended loan rejections, higher liquidation risk, or mis‑aligned debt‑to‑collateral ratios. The bug is triggered whenever the paired BAKC token has accrued pending rewards, which is a normal condition for any active staking position. Affected parties include any user of the staking wrapper who pairs BAKC tokens, the lending protocol that relies on the reported balance for credit decisions, and consequently any counterparties involved in loans backed by these NFTs. The issue was discovered through a manual audit of the staking logic, where the auditor identified that the pendingRewards call was made only for the primary NFT and not for the secondary BAKC token. Detecting the problem is difficult because the returned amount still reflects a plausible total—only it is systematically lower than the true value, and the discrepancy may not be obvious from a UI that shows a single aggregated balance. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or reward‑calculation errors where not all accrued incentives are incorporated into a financial state variable. To remediate the problem, the getTokenIdStakingAmount() function should be modified to also fetch and add the pendingRewards for the BAKC token when a pair exists, ensuring that the balanceOf() view reflects the full economic value of the staked position, including all pending rewards. This correction restores the integrity of the collateral calculation and aligns protocol behavior with user expectations that "my total staked amount plus all earned rewards" is accurately represented.

title: Price can deviate by much more than maxDeviationRate
poc:
maxDeviationRate = 150  
Currently 3 oracles in place, their readings are [1, 1.1, 2]  
Oracle #2 can call setPrice(1.5), setPrice(1.7), setPrice(2) to immediately change the price from 1.1 to 2, which is almost 100% growth, much above 50% allowed growth.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑validation logic of an oracle contract that checks a new time‑weighted average price (TWAP) against the previously stored TWAP. The function calculates a percentage deviation for a single update and rejects the update only if the deviation exceeds a configured maximum. Because the check is performed per transaction without considering the elapsed time since the previous update, an attacker who controls or can influence one of the oracle sources can repeatedly call the price‑setting function with a series of small, individually acceptable changes. By chaining these updates—each respecting the per‑call deviation limit—the cumulative price can drift far beyond the intended maximum deviation, effectively allowing the price to double or grow by a large factor over a short period. This manipulation is possible whenever the oracle permits multiple successive price submissions, which is typical in systems that aggregate readings from several independent sources. The issue was discovered during a formal audit, where the auditors noted that the contract’s TWAP validation only addresses a single‑step jump and does not enforce a bound on the rate of change over time. It is difficult to spot in casual testing because every individual price update appears legitimate; the contract’s state transitions look normal, and no error is emitted. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a price that appears to respect the advertised deviation limit but nevertheless moves dramatically, causing unexpected outcomes such as lower than expected payouts, premature liquidations, or trades executing at severely off‑market rates. Users expect the oracle to keep the price within a bounded window; instead the price may “disappear” from its true value, breaking accounting assumptions and undermining confidence in the protocol’s financial logic. The impact affects any participant relying on the oracle—traders, lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself—because mispriced assets can lead to loss of funds, unjust liquidations, or exploitation of downstream contracts. The root cause is the lack of a temporal constraint on price changes; the contract records a timestamp for each update but does not use it to limit how much the TWAP may change per unit of time. A proper fix is to incorporate the elapsed time since the last update into the deviation calculation, enforcing a maximum allowable price movement per time window (for example, a percentage change per hour). By bounding the TWAP drift over time, administrators gain a window to detect and react to abnormal behavior before the price can be driven to extreme values. In summary, this is a class of oracle manipulation vulnerability where incremental updates bypass per‑call deviation checks, leading to excessive cumulative price deviation and breaking the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: Oracle will become invalid much faster than intended on non-mainnet chains
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Paraspace price oracle determines whether a cached price is still fresh. The contract calculates the age of a price entry by subtracting the block number at which the price was last updated (priceInfo.updatedAt) from the current block number (currentBlock) and comparing the result to a constant called EXPIRATION_PERIOD that is set to 1800. This constant was chosen based on the assumption that blocks on Ethereum mainnet appear roughly every 12 seconds, making 1800 blocks equivalent to six hours. The root cause is that the logic mixes a block‑based counter with a time‑based expectation, ignoring that block times differ dramatically across EVM‑compatible chains. On networks such as Binance Smart Chain (≈3 seconds per block) or Avalanche (≈1 second per block), 1800 blocks elapse in 15 minutes or 30 minutes respectively, causing the oracle to deem a price stale far earlier than the intended six‑hour window. When the stale‑price condition is triggered, the contract refuses to add the price to the list of valid prices, effectively cutting off price feed data. An attacker does not need to manipulate any contract state; the bug is deterministic and can be exploited simply by operating on a chain with a faster block time. The impact is that legitimate price updates are rejected, leading to scenarios where users attempting to open, modify, or liquidate positions receive errors such as "price unavailable" or experience silent failures where no price can be fetched. Borrowers may be unable to repay loans, lenders may see their collateral unable to be evaluated, and overall protocol functionality can grind to a halt on the affected chains. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed on a network whose average block time is less than the 12‑second baseline, which includes many popular testnets and alternative layer‑1s. It primarily affects users, liquidity providers, and any party that relies on timely price information from the oracle. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented intention (six‑hour expiration) with the actual implementation, noting the mismatch between block count and real‑world elapsed time. The problem is difficult to spot because the code appears to perform a conventional freshness check; only a deeper understanding of block‑time variability reveals the mis‑alignment. The appropriate remediation is to replace the block‑number based check with a timestamp comparison using block.timestamp, ensuring that the difference between the current timestamp and the stored update timestamp is bounded by 6 × 3600 seconds. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of temporal logic bugs where time is measured using a proxy that does not reliably correlate with real time, leading to premature expiry of time‑sensitive data. From the user's perspective, the UI may show messages like "price data stale" or simply refuse to proceed with a transaction, contradicting the expectation that price data remains valid for several hours. In summary, the contract should measure elapsed time with wall‑clock timestamps rather than block height to align the expiration behaviour with the intended six‑hour window across all supported networks.

title: MintableIncentivizedERC721 and NToken do not comply with ERC721, breaking composability
bug_full: The contract implements an ERC‑721 style token but its ERC165 supportsInterface function only reports support for the optional ERC721Enumerable and ERC721Metadata extensions. According to EIP‑721, a compliant contract must also claim support for the core ERC721 interface (interface ID 0x80ac58cd). The root cause is a logical omission: the supportsInterface implementation checks only two extension identifiers and never returns true for the ERC721 identifier itself. Because ERC165 is the standard mechanism for external contracts and tooling to discover a token's capabilities, any contract, marketplace, or wallet that queries supportsInterface(0x80ac58cd) will receive false and therefore treat the token as non‑ERC721. This breaks composability; callers that expect standard ERC721 functions such as transferFrom, safeTransferFrom, approve, or ownerOf will either reject the token or be unable to invoke those functions via generic interfaces. From a user’s perspective the token may appear to exist, but attempts to transfer it through a marketplace UI result in errors like “token does not implement ERC721” or the transaction simply reverts, leading to a situation where the user cannot move or sell their asset. The vulnerability was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a minimal test contract that invokes supportsInterface on the deployed token with the three known ERC165 identifiers. The test showed that the ERC721 identifier returned false while the others returned true. The issue can be subtle because the contract still compiles, and the token may work in isolated tests that call only the enumerable or metadata functions, making the non‑compliance hard to notice without explicit interface probing. To remediate, the supportsInterface function should be extended to return true when the queried interfaceId matches type(IERC721).interfaceId, typically by adding an OR clause for the ERC721 identifier or by delegating to a parent ERC721 implementation that already includes the correct check. This change restores full ERC721 compliance, ensuring that any external component can correctly recognize the token as a standard NFT and interact with it according to the expected business logic.

title: `SWAP_ROUTER` in `AutoPxGmx.sol` is hardcoded and not compatible on Avalanche
description:
I want to quote from the doc:

- Does it use a side-chain? Yes
- If yes, is the sidechain evm-compatible? Yes, Avalanche

This shows that the projects is intended to support Avalanche side-chain.

`SWAP_ROUTER` in the AutoPxGmx.sol is hardcoded as:

```solidity
IV3SwapRouter public constant SWAP_ROUTER =
	IV3SwapRouter(0x68b3465833fb72A70ecDF485E0e4C7bD8665Fc45);
```

But this address is the Uniswap V3 router address in arbitrium, but it is a EOA address in Avalanche,

<https://snowtrace.io/address/0x68b3465833fb72a70ecdf485e0e4c7bd8665fc45>

Then the AutoPxGmx.sol is not working in Avalanche.

```solidity
gmxAmountOut = SWAP_ROUTER.exactInputSingle(
	IV3SwapRouter.ExactInputSingleParams({
		tokenIn: address(gmxBaseReward),
		tokenOut: address(gmx),
		fee: fee,
		recipient: address(this),
		amountIn: gmxBaseRewardAmountIn,
		amountOutMinimum: amountOutMinimum,
		sqrtPriceLimitX96: sqrtPriceLimitX96
	})
);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded address for the Uniswap V3 swap router in the AutoPxGmx contract. The contract was designed to run on both Arbitrum and Avalanche, but the address 0x68b3465833fb72a70ecdf485e0e4c7bd8665fc45 is the router on Arbitrum and an externally owned account on Avalanche. Because the address is stored as a constant, the contract does not allow the router address to be supplied per‑network. When the contract executes its compound() function on Avalanche, it calls SWAP_ROUTER.exactInputSingle(...). Since the target address is not a contract that implements the IV3SwapRouter interface, the call fails and the transaction reverts. The root cause is the assumption that the same router address works on every EVM‑compatible chain, a classic configuration‑hardcoding bug. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the contract; the bug manifests automatically when any user triggers the auto‑compounding flow on Avalanche. The impact is that users attempting to compound their pxGMX rewards receive a revert, their gas is spent, and the expected reward token (GMX) is never received, effectively breaking the business logic that rewards should be automatically swapped and minted. The issue appears only on Avalanche; on Arbitrum the call succeeds because the address points to a valid router contract. Users see no change in their balances, may notice that the “compound” transaction fails with an “execution reverted” error, and may think the protocol is broken or malicious. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented supported chains with the hard‑coded address and verified the code on Snowtrace, revealing that the address resolves to an EOA. Because the failure occurs at runtime and the contract does not emit a clear error message, it can be hard to notice until a user attempts the function. The proper fix is to remove the constant and make the router address a constructor or initializer parameter, allowing each deployment to supply the correct router address for its target network, or to use a registry that resolves the router address per chain. This class of bug falls under “hard‑coded external contract address” or “network‑specific configuration mismatch”, which can cause contract calls to non‑existent code and lead to silent reverts, breaking expected accounting and user experience.

title: Assets may be lost when calling unprotected `AutoPxGlp::compound` function
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AutoPxGlp contract where the compound function is publicly callable and does not enforce any access control. The function forwards two caller‑controlled parameters, a minimum amount of USDG and a minimum amount of GLP, to the GMX reward router’s deposit routine. The only validation performed on these parameters is that they are non‑zero, which means an attacker can supply values that are effectively zero relative to the token’s decimal precision (for example 1 wei on a token with 18 decimals). When compound is invoked, the contract calls PirexGmx.depositGlp, which in turn calls GlpManager.addLiquidityForAccount. This internal call uses the supplied minimums to determine the acceptable amount of GLP and USDG to receive from the vault swap. Because the caller can set the minima arbitrarily low, the vault may execute the swap at an unfavorable price or with a manipulated oracle, and the contract will accept the result even if the actual amount received is far below the expected value. In a volatile market or during price‑oracle manipulation, the swap can yield almost no GLP or USDG, effectively burning the assets that were meant to be compounded. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the underlying balance of compounded assets is reduced dramatically, often to zero, leading to the symptom “my balance shows nothing after compounding” or “the refund I expected is missing”. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the lack of access restrictions and the minimal validation of the minUsdg and minGlp arguments. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply delivers a negligible amount of tokens, which may not be obvious without detailed accounting. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external input leading to economic loss, specifically an under‑protected function that trusts caller‑provided minimum thresholds for token transfers. To remediate, the contract should stop relying on caller‑supplied minima, instead compute acceptable thresholds using a trusted price feed such as the GMX oracle cross‑checked with an independent source like Chainlink, and enforce reasonable bounds. Additionally, restricting the compound function to an authorized role or to internal calls would prevent arbitrary actors from triggering the vulnerable path, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Deposit Feature Of The Vault Will Break If Update To A New Platform
poc: No data
bug_full: The vault contains a function that allows the contract owner to replace the external platform contract responsible for pulling GMX tokens during a deposit. The original implementation grants an unlimited ERC20 allowance to the platform address at construction time, enabling the platform to transfer GMX tokens from the vault. However, the subsequent setPlatform function only updates the stored platform address and emits an event; it does not re‑establish the token allowance for the new address nor revoke the allowance from the previous contract. As a result, when the owner calls setPlatform, the new platform is unable to call transferFrom on the GMX token because its allowance remains zero. Deposit operations that rely on the platform pulling GMX therefore fail silently: users submit a deposit transaction, the vault records the intent, but the platform call reverts or returns false, leaving the user's balance unchanged and the transaction appearing to succeed while no assets are actually moved. This breaks the core business logic that expects the vault to forward deposited tokens to the platform for staking, violating accounting assumptions that each deposit results in a corresponding token transfer. The issue manifests only after a platform upgrade, making it easy to miss during routine testing because the setPlatform function itself does not revert and the contract compiles without warnings. It was discovered during a security audit that examined state‑changing functions and noticed the missing safeApprove call. The impact is medium severity: funds are not lost, but users cannot deposit, effectively freezing the primary user flow and potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The affected parties include all vault users, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts that expect deposits to be processed. To remediate, the setPlatform function should first reset the allowance of the old platform to zero, then grant an unlimited allowance to the new platform address, mirroring the logic performed in the constructor. This ensures that after any platform change the vault retains the ability to transfer GMX tokens as intended, restoring normal deposit functionality.

title: `PirexGmx.initiateMigration` can be blocked
poc:
PirexGmx was designed with the thought that the current contract can be changed with another during migration.

`PirexGmx.initiateMigration` is the first point in this long process.

As you can see the main condition to start migration is that PirexGmx doesn’t control any gmxVester and glpVester tokens.

So attacker can [deposit](https://arbiscan.io/address/0xa75287d2f8b217273e7fcd7e86ef07d33972042e#code#F1#L117) and receive such tokens and then just transfer tokens directly to PirexGmx.

As a result migration will never be possible as there is no possibility for PirexGmx to burn those gmxVester and glpVester tokens.

Also in the same way, the migration receiver can also be blocked.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migration initiation routine of the PirexGmx contract. The function initiateMigration is intended to signal the GMX reward router that the current contract will transfer its entire account to a new contract. To do this, it calls the external function signalTransfer on the GMX reward router. SignalTransfer contains two require statements that check that the caller (the PirexGmx contract) holds zero balance of the gmxVester and glpVester tokens. If either balance is non‑zero, the call reverts with a generic error, preventing the pendingReceivers mapping from being set and effectively halting the migration process. The root cause is the reliance on a strict zero‑balance condition for two vesting token contracts that are, by design, non‑transferable but can theoretically be acquired and forced into the PirexGmx contract. An attacker who can obtain vGMX or vGLP tokens – for example by depositing into a vulnerable vesting contract and then transferring the tokens directly to PirexGmx – would cause the balance checks to fail. Consequently, any subsequent call to initiateMigration would revert, leaving the contract unable to signal a transfer and locking the funds in place. From a user perspective, the migration transaction would appear to fail silently; the UI would show no progress, the expected migration event would not be emitted, and the user would see that their assets remain in the original contract despite attempting to move them. The impact is that the protocol’s upgrade path can be blocked, potentially freezing user funds and breaking the promised ability to migrate to newer contracts. This condition can only be triggered when the contract holds vested tokens, which normally should never happen because the vesting tokens are non‑transferable and the depositForAccount function is restricted to a privileged handler. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the migration flow, where the auditor noted the require statements and reasoned about possible token balances. The problem is subtle because the non‑transferable nature of the vesting tokens masks the risk; developers may assume that no external party can ever place such tokens into the contract, making the check appear harmless. To remediate, the migration logic should either remove the strict zero‑balance requirement, implement a safe burn or reclaim mechanism for any vesting tokens that might be present, or add a fallback path that allows migration to proceed even if vesting balances exist. In broader terms, this is a classic case of a state‑dependency lock where a contract’s ability to perform a critical operation is gated by an invariant that can be violated by external token transfers, leading to a denial‑of‑service style blockage of contract upgrades.

title: Preventing any user from calling the functions `withdraw`, `redeem`, or `depositGmx` in contract `AutoPxGmx`
description:
It is possible that an attacker can prevent any user from calling the functions `withdraw`, `redeem`, or `depositGmx` in contract `AutoPxGmx` by just manipulating the balance of token `gmxBaseReward`, so that during the function `compound` the swap will be reverted.

The attack is unlikely: there is no real reason to do it as the attacker would have to pay gas, you need conditions on the price, and conditions on the reward amounts, as if rewards are accruing you won’t be able to do it, so downgrading to Medium severity.

However it’s true that it may be good to set a minimum amount for the swaps that depends on the `amountIn`, or remove entirely the `minAmountOut` requirement.

Hi @Picodes, this is going to be resolved as a side effect of issue [#321](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel-findings/issues/321) being fixed (i.e. `compound` will be updated to consider token balances w/o dependence on external factors to prevent DoS’ing of users). Wanted to flag it for your attention but ultimately up to you re: awarding. Thanks for your help ser.
bug_full: An attacker can cause a denial‑of‑service on the AutoPxGmx vault by exploiting the hard‑coded minimum output amount in the internal swap that is executed during the compound routine. The contract’s compound function always calls Uniswap V3’s exactInputSingle with amountOutMinimum set to 1 token of GMX, regardless of how many gmxBaseReward tokens are supplied. If the vault holds a non‑zero but very small balance of gmxBaseReward – for example a single token whose market value is less than one GMX – the swap will return zero GMX. Because the router is required to deliver at least one GMX, the transaction reverts. The compound function is invoked by the public entry points withdraw, redeem and depositGmx, so any call that triggers compound will fail when the condition is met. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that a withdrawal or redemption transaction reverts with no funds transferred, leading to the impression that the contract is broken or that their balance has vanished. The root cause is the use of a static, absolute minimum‑output parameter instead of a value derived from the input amount or a slippage tolerance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call flow from the public functions to the swap and observed the fixed amountOutMinimum. It is difficult to notice because the revert only occurs when the reward token balance is unusually low, a state that does not happen under normal reward accrual conditions. The impact is a potential denial‑of‑service: legitimate users cannot withdraw or redeem their assets while the attacker maintains the small reward balance, effectively freezing funds. The attack requires the attacker to send a tiny amount of gmxBaseReward to the vault and to pay gas for the transaction; it does not provide direct profit, which is why the severity is assessed as medium. To remediate, the contract should replace the constant amountOutMinimum with a dynamic threshold based on the amountIn (for example amountIn multiplied by a price feed or a reasonable slippage factor) or remove the requirement entirely and rely on the router’s built‑in slippage protection. This change eliminates the ability to force a revert by manipulating the reward balance and restores normal operation of withdraw, redeem and depositGmx.

title: Anyone can call AutoPxGmx.compound and perform sandwich attacks with control parameters
description:
AutoPxGmx.compound allows anyone to call to compound the reward and get the incentive.

However, AutoPxGmx.compound calls `SWAP_ROUTER`.exactInputSingle with some of the parameters provided by the caller, which allows the user to perform a sandwich attack for profit.

For example, a malicious user could provide the fee parameter to make the token swap occur in a small liquid pool, and could make the amountOutMinimum parameter 1 to make the token swap accept a large slippage, thus making it easier to perform a sandwich attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AutoPxGmx.compound function, which is intended to compound accrued rewards and distribute an incentive to the caller. The function forwards a call to the external SWAP_ROUTER.exactInputSingle method, but it accepts several critical parameters—such as the pool fee and the amountOutMinimum—from the transaction sender without any validation or restriction. Because these parameters directly influence which liquidity pool is used and how much slippage is tolerated, a malicious actor can deliberately select a low‑liquidity pool by setting a small fee and can set amountOutMinimum to a trivial value (e.g., 1) to allow the swap to execute even under extreme price movement. By doing so, the attacker can position their own trades before and after the victim’s compound call, performing a classic sandwich attack: they front‑run the victim’s transaction to push the price, let the victim’s swap execute at the manipulated price, and then back‑run to capture the price reversal. This exploitation is possible whenever any user invokes compound, because the contract does not enforce that the fee corresponds to a known, liquid pool nor does it compute a realistic minimum output based on an on‑chain price oracle. The impact is that honest users who call compound may receive far fewer reward tokens than expected, or may see their effective reward value reduced, effectively losing value to the attacker. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal reward claim but the received amount is unexpectedly low or zero, contradicting the expectation that the reward should increase. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s external calls and identified that user‑controlled swap parameters could be abused. It is difficult to notice because the function appears benign—simply “compounding rewards”—and the parameters look like ordinary configuration options, masking the economic risk. To remediate, the contract should hard‑code the pool fee to a known, sufficiently liquid pool, restrict swaps to whitelisted pools, and calculate amountOutMinimum using a reliable on‑chain price oracle or a conservative slippage bound, thereby preventing arbitrary manipulation of swap economics and eliminating the sandwich attack surface.

title: AutoPxGmx.maxWithdraw and AutoPxGlp.maxWithdraw functions calculate asset amount that is too big and cannot be withdrawn
description:
The ERC-4626 Tokenized Vault Standard requires the `maxWithdraw` function to be implemented (<https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/standards/tokens/erc-4626/#maxwithdraw>).

This function is supposed to return “the maximum amount of underlying assets that can be withdrawn from the owner balance with a single withdraw call”.

The `PirexERC4626` contract implements this function (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/PirexERC4626.sol#L225>).  
It is implemented correctly when `PirexERC4626` is used on its own.

However in this project, the `PirexERC4626` contract is not used on its own but inherited by `AutoPxGmx` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGmx.sol#L14>) and `AutoPxGlp` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGlp.sol#L14>).

`AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` implement a `withdrawalPenalty` i.e. a fee that is paid when a user wants to withdraw assets from the vault.

`AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` do not override the `maxWithdraw` function.

This causes the `maxWithdraw` function to return an amount of assets that is too big to be withdrawn.

So when `maxWithdraw` is called and with the returned amount `withdraw` is called, the call to `withdraw` will revert.

This can cause issues in any upstream components that rely on `AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` to correctly implement the ERC4626 standard.

For example an upstream wrapper might only allow withdrawals with the maximum amount and determine this maximum amount by calling the `maxWithdraw` function. As this function returns a value that is too big, no withdrawals will be possible.
poc:
1. The `maxWithdraw` function in a `AutoPxGmx` contract is called
2. Now the `withdraw` function is called with the value that was returned by the `maxWithdraw` function (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGmx.sol#L315>)
3. The `withdraw` function in turn calls the `previewWithdraw` function (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGmx.sol#L199>)
4. The `previewWithdraw` function will increase the amount of shares to include the `withdrawalPenalty` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGmx.sol#L215-L216>) which causes the amount of shares to burn to be too large and the call to `burn` will revert (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-redactedcartel/blob/03b71a8d395c02324cb9fdaf92401357da5b19d1/src/vaults/AutoPxGmx.sol#L332>)
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect implementation of the ERC‑4626 maxWithdraw function in vault contracts that inherit from a base ERC4626 implementation but add a withdrawal penalty. The base contract correctly reports the maximum amount of underlying assets that can be withdrawn, but the derived AutoPxGmx and AutoPxGlp contracts introduce a fee that is deducted when a user withdraws. Because these contracts do not override maxWithdraw, the function continues to return the gross asset amount without subtracting the penalty. When a caller queries maxWithdraw and then passes the returned value to the withdraw function, the internal previewWithdraw calculation adds the penalty to the required share amount, causing the contract to attempt to burn more shares than the user actually holds. This mismatch triggers a revert in the burn step, preventing the withdrawal from completing. From a user perspective the UI may display a non‑zero withdrawable balance, the user initiates a withdrawal, and the transaction fails with no assets transferred, leading to confusion and a perception that funds have disappeared. The issue manifests whenever the vault is used through any component that relies on maxWithdraw to determine the allowable withdrawal amount, such as wrappers that automatically withdraw the maximum possible amount. It affects all users of the AutoPxGmx and AutoPxGlp vaults, as well as any downstream protocols that integrate these vaults, potentially causing denial‑of‑service or loss of expected liquidity. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit that compared the contract behaviour against the ERC‑4626 specification and exercised the withdrawal path with the penalty in place. The problem is subtle because the maxWithdraw function appears to comply with the interface, yet the business logic of the penalty is omitted, making the bug easy to miss without thorough testing of the full withdrawal flow. The correct fix is to override maxWithdraw in the derived contracts and compute the net withdrawable amount by converting the user's share balance to assets and then subtracting the proportional penalty, ensuring that the returned value matches what the withdraw function can actually process. This aligns the contract with the ERC‑4626 standard, restores accurate user expectations, and prevents unexpected reverts during withdrawals.
