When this happens, collateralValueCached becomes zero even though the vault still holds one or more NFTs (count != 0). Consequently the contract treats the vault as having no collateral, sets maxDebt to the current debt, and later clears any remaining debt without burning the NFTs. An attacker who triggers a liquidation under these conditions can purchase the NFT at the auction price, receive the asset, and have the protocol write off the associated debt, effectively allowing the withdrawal of collateral for free. The impact is loss of protocol funds and violation of the accounting invariant that debt must be backed by collateral. The bug manifests only when the price feed returns zero while the vault still contains NFTs, a situation that can arise due to oracle downtime, missing floor data, or malicious manipulation of the external price source. It was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the auditor noted the unsafe equality check and verified that the Reservoir oracle documentation explicitly warns that zero values are possible. The issue is subtle because a zero price is rare and may be interpreted as a failure rather than a valid value, making the bug easy to overlook in testing. The proper fix is to determine the last‑collateral condition based on the actual NFT count (e.g., count == 0) rather than on the derived price, or to add explicit handling for zero‑price responses. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect assumption about external data validity and can lead to funds disappearing, refunds not being applied, or collateral being withdrawn without repayment.

title: User fund loss because function `purchaseLiquidationAuctionNFT
description:
Function `purchaseLiquidationAuctionNFT()` purchases a liquidation auction with the controller’s papr token. The liquidator pays the papr amount which is equal to price of the auction and receives the auctioned NFT. Contract would transfer paid papr and pay borrower debt and if there is extra papr left, it would be transferred to the user. 

For extra papr that is not required for brining user debt under max debt, contract gets liquidation penalty but in some cases (when the auctioned NFT is user’s last collateral) contract take penalty from all of the transferred papr and not just the extra. So users would lose funds in those situations because of this and the fund could be big because the penalty is 10% of the price of the auction and in most cases user would lose 10% of his debt (the value of the NFT).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation‑auction purchase routine that accepts a PAPR payment, settles the borrower’s debt and, if any payment remains, returns the surplus to the borrower. The logic correctly distinguishes between the amount needed to bring the vault under its maximum allowed debt and any excess that should be refunded after applying the liquidation penalty. However, when the auctioned NFT is the borrower’s last piece of collateral, the contract mistakenly treats the entire payment as excess. This happens because the code sets the maximum‑debt cache to the current debt when the collateral value is zero, which makes the “needed to save vault” amount zero. Consequently, the excess variable becomes equal to the full price paid, and the penalty (10 % of the price) is deducted from the whole payment instead of only from the true surplus (price minus debt). An attacker (or any liquidator) who purchases a last‑collateral auction where the price exceeds the outstanding debt therefore causes the borrower to lose the full 10 % penalty on the entire price, rather than the intended 10 % of the surplus. For example, with a debt of 900 PAPR and an auction price of 1000 PAPR, the borrower should receive 100 PAPR (price‑debt) minus a 10 % penalty on that 100 PAPR, i.e., 90 PAPR. The buggy implementation instead applies the 10 % penalty to the full 1000 PAPR, leaving the borrower with only 0 PAPR after the debt is cleared. This results in a direct loss of funds that can be as large as ten percent of the auction price, especially common because many users hold a single NFT as collateral. The issue manifests only when the vault has no remaining collateral after the liquidation, making it an edge‑case that is easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) by inspecting the debt‑reduction and excess‑handling logic. The bug is subtle because the same code path works correctly for non‑last‑collateral liquidations, and the erroneous branch is only taken when a specific condition (collateral value equals zero) is true. To remediate, the contract should treat the maximum‑debt cache as zero when the vault is being emptied, ensuring that the “needed to save vault” amount equals the full debt and that only the true surplus is subject to the liquidation penalty. In conceptual terms, the fix requires separating the calculation of required repayment from the surplus refund logic for the last‑collateral case, thereby preventing the protocol from confiscating more than the intended penalty amount and preserving the borrower’s expected refund.

title: Missing deadline checks allow pending transactions to be maliciously executed
description: The `Pair` contract does not allow users to submit a deadline for their action. This missing feature enables pending transactions to be maliciously executed at a later point.
poc:
Omitted in this case, since the exploit is solely based on the fact that there is no limit on how long a transaction is allowed to be pending, which can be clearly seen when looking at the mentioned functions.

Fixed in <https://github.com/outdoteth/caviar/pull/6>

Add a deadline check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing time‑bound validation in the Pair contract, meaning that functions which should be limited by a user‑specified deadline have no deadline parameter and therefore no check that the transaction is executed within an expected time window. The root cause is the absence of a deadline argument and the corresponding require statement that would compare the current block timestamp against the user‑provided deadline. Because the contract does not enforce any maximum pending period, a transaction that a user signs and broadcasts can remain in the mempool for an arbitrarily long time. An attacker who observes the pending transaction can wait until market conditions change, then submit the same transaction with a higher gas price so that it is mined later, or can even replay the transaction after the user’s intended window has passed. This manipulation can lead to users receiving unexpected results, such as swaps executing at unfavorable rates, liquidity being removed at a loss, or fees being taken when the user expected a different outcome. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a pending operation that later completes with a zero or dramatically reduced output, or the user may see that a trade they thought would be executed at a certain price instead yields a much worse price or no output at all. The impact is therefore financial loss for any participant who relies on timely execution, and it undermines the economic assumptions of the protocol that trades are performed within a bounded time frame. The issue appears only when a transaction is delayed; if the transaction is mined immediately the contract behaves as intended, which makes the problem easy to miss during normal testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function signatures and noticed the lack of a deadline field, and the exploit does not require any special code execution beyond the natural transaction‑pending mechanism. To remediate the issue the contract should be updated to accept a deadline parameter for each time‑sensitive function and include a require statement such as require(block.timestamp <= deadline, "deadline passed"); this forces the transaction to revert if it is mined after the user’s intended window, preventing malicious delayed execution. The fix restores the expected business logic that operations are bounded in time, protecting users from price‑slippage attacks and ensuring that the protocol’s accounting remains consistent.

title: Price will not always be 18 decimals, as expected and outlined in the comments
description:
The `price()` function is expected to return the price of one fractional tokens, represented in base tokens, to 18 decimals of precision. This is laid out clearly in the comments:

`/// @notice The current price of one fractional token in base tokens with 18 decimals of precision.`  
`/// @dev Calculated by dividing the base token reserves by the fractional token reserves.`  
`/// @return price The price of one fractional token in base tokens * 1e18.`  

However, the formula incorrectly calculates the price to be represented in whatever number of decimals the base token is in. Since there are many common base tokens (such as USDC) that will have fewer than 18 decimals, this will create a large mismatch between expected prices and the prices that result from the function.

```solidity
return (_baseTokenReserves() * ONE) / fractionalTokenReserves();
```

We know that `fractionalTokenReserves` will always be represented in 18 decimals. This means that the `ONE` and the `fractionalTokenReserves` will cancel each other out, and we are left with the `baseTokenReserves` number of decimals for the final price.

As an example:

* We have `$1000` USDC in reserves, which at 6 decimals is 1e9
* We have 1000 fractional tokens in reserve, which at 18 decimals is 1e21
* The price calculation is `1e9 * 1e18 / 1e21 = 1e6`
* While the value should be 1 token, the 1e6 will be interpreted as just 1/1e12 tokens if we expect the price to be in 1e18
poc: No data
bug_full: The contract implements a price() view that is documented to return the price of one fractional token expressed in base tokens with 18 decimal places of precision. In reality the function computes the price by multiplying the raw base‑token reserve amount by a constant ONE (1e18) and dividing by the fractional‑token reserve, assuming that both reserves are expressed with 18 decimals. This assumption is false for many common base tokens such as USDC, USDT or other ERC‑20 assets that use fewer than 18 decimals (for example USDC uses 6). Because the fractional token always uses 18 decimals, the ONE factor cancels the fractional‑token scaling and the result inherits the decimal precision of the base token instead of being normalised to 18. Consequently the returned value is off by a factor of 10^(18‑baseTokenDecimals). For a USDC‑based pool the price that should be 1e18 (representing one whole token) is returned as 1e6, which would be interpreted as 1/1e12 of a token if the caller expects 18‑decimal precision. The bug can be exploited by any participant that relies on the price() output for valuation, swaps, or accounting: an attacker could trigger trades based on the mis‑scaled price, causing the protocol to sell or buy assets at a dramatically incorrect rate, leading to loss of funds or unfair arbitrage opportunities. The impact is a systematic mis‑pricing of fractional tokens, broken accounting, and user‑facing symptoms such as displayed prices that appear far too low, zero‑value refunds, or balances that seem to disappear. The condition occurs whenever the base token does not have 18 decimals, i.e., on any call to price() in those pools. All users, traders, and the protocol itself are affected because the price feeds downstream logic. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the comment stating the expected 18‑decimal output conflicted with the actual arithmetic. It is hard to notice because the function returns a numeric value that may look plausible in isolation, and UI formatting can hide the magnitude error. The correct mitigation is to scale the base‑token reserve by an additional factor that compensates for the difference between 18 and the token’s native decimals, for example multiplying by 10^(36‑baseToken.decimals()) before dividing by the fractional reserve, thereby guaranteeing that the final price always carries 18 decimals as documented.

title: Rounding error in `buyQuote` might result in free tokens
description:
In order to guarantee the contract does not become insolvent, incoming assets should be rounded up, while outgoing assets should be rounded down.

The function `buyQuote()` calculates the amount of base tokens required to buy a given amount of fractional tokens. However, this function rounds down the required amount, which is in favor of the buyer (i.e. he/she has to provide less base tokens for the amount of receiving fractional tokens.

Depending on the amount of current token reserves and the amount of fractional tokens the user wishes to buy, it might be possible to receive free fractional tokens.

Assume the following reserve state:

* base token reserve: 0,1 WBTC (=`1e7`)
* fractional token reserve: 10.000.000 (=`1e25`)

The user wishes to buy 0,9 fractional tokens (=`9e17`). Then, the function `buyQuote()` will calculate the amount of base tokens as follows:

`(9e17 * 1000 * 1e7) / ((1e25 - 9e17) * 997) = 0,903`

As division in Solidity will round down, the amount results in `0` amount of base tokens required (WBTC) to buy 0,9 fractional tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the price‑calculation routine that determines how many base tokens (e.g., WBTC) a buyer must provide to receive a requested amount of fractional tokens. The function computes the required base token amount using integer arithmetic and then divides, which in Solidity always rounds down. Because the contract does not explicitly round the result up, the calculated quote can be truncated to zero when the true value is less than one wei. This happens when the reserves are such that the product of the desired fractional amount, the scaling factor and the base‑token reserve is only slightly larger than the denominator, causing the division to yield a value between 0 and 1 wei. An attacker can exploit this by selecting a small fractional‑token purchase that triggers the rounding‑down path, submitting a transaction that requires zero base tokens, and receiving the fractional tokens for free. The impact is a direct loss of value from the protocol: tokens are minted or transferred without any payment, eroding the reserve backing and potentially allowing unlimited free minting if the attacker repeats the operation with varying amounts. The condition under which the bug manifests is when the reserve ratio and the chosen purchase size make the exact quote smaller than one wei; it is not limited to a single hard‑coded amount but can occur for any combination that satisfies the inequality. Users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting assumptions that every token issued is backed by a proportional amount of base asset are broken. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the auditors examined the rounding behavior of the quote function and identified that the contract only rounds down incoming asset calculations, contrary to the design principle that incoming amounts should be rounded up to preserve solvency. The bug is subtle because the contract still transfers the correct number of fractional tokens and the transaction succeeds, giving the impression that the price calculation is correct; only a careful inspection of the quoted amount reveals that no base tokens were deducted. To remediate the problem, the quote calculation should be performed with a rounding‑up operation (for example using a mulDivUp helper) so that the required base‑token amount is never less than the mathematically exact value, guaranteeing that at least one wei is required for any non‑zero purchase. This aligns the implementation with the intended economic model where buyers always pay a positive amount and prevents the protocol from unintentionally issuing free tokens.

title: It’s possible to swap NFT token ids without fee and also attacker can wrap unwrap all the NFT token balance of the Pair contract and steal their air drops for those token ids
description:
Users can `wrap()` their NFT tokens (which id is whitelisted) and receive `1e18` fractional token or they can pay `1e18` fractional token and unwrap NFT token. there is two issue here:

  1. anyone can swap their NFT token id with another NFT token id without paying any fee(both ids should be whitelisted). it’s swap without fee.
  2. attacker can swap his NFT token(with whitelisted id) for all the NFT balance of contract and steal those NFT tokens airdrop all in one transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the design of the wrap and unwrap functions in a fractional NFT pair contract. When a user calls wrap, the contract checks only that the supplied token identifiers belong to a whitelisted merkle tree and then mints a fixed amount of fractional tokens proportional to the number of identifiers, without recording which specific NFT ids were deposited. Conversely, the unwrap function simply burns the same amount of fractional tokens and transfers any NFT ids supplied by the caller from the contract to the caller, again without verifying that those ids were originally supplied by that caller. Because the amount of fractional tokens required to unwrap is independent of the actual NFT id, any holder of a single whitelisted NFT can wrap it, obtain the corresponding fractional tokens, and then repeatedly unwrap other ids that are already held by the contract. This creates a fee‑less swap mechanism where the attacker can exchange one NFT for any other whitelisted NFT without paying any additional cost. The root cause is the lack of binding between wrapped NFTs and the caller’s ownership, combined with the absence of any fee or lock‑up logic on unwrapping. Exploitation proceeds by wrapping a single attacker‑owned NFT, then looping over all ids stored in the pair contract, unwrapping each one by paying the standard fractional token amount, calling the external airdrop function that rewards the current NFT holder, and optionally re‑wrapping the newly obtained NFT to repeat the process. The attacker can therefore claim airdrop tokens that were intended for all original NFT holders, effectively stealing the entire airdrop distribution in a single transaction. The impact includes loss of airdropped assets, potential theft of staking rewards tied to the NFTs, and erosion of trust for liquidity providers who expected their fractional tokens to represent a proportional claim on the underlying NFTs. The issue manifests when the contract is open for wrapping, the merkle root includes the relevant ids, and an external airdrop function can be called by any current NFT owner. It affects all users who deposit NFTs into the pair, the protocol that relies on fair distribution of airdrops, and any downstream applications that assume ownership cannot be transferred without explicit consent. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of wrap/unwrap and identified the missing ownership check. It can be difficult to notice because the functions appear to work correctly for honest users and no explicit fee is expected, making the fee‑less swap seem benign. To remediate, the contract should bind each wrapped NFT id to the address that supplied it, enforce that only the original depositor can unwrap that specific id, introduce a fee or time‑locked period for unwrapping, and optionally allow an admin to claim airdrops before they become available to users. Additional safeguards such as delaying unwrapping or restricting airdrop claims to the original owner would also mitigate the attack surface. In user terms, a participant may wrap an NFT expecting to receive the same token back after providing fractional tokens, but instead receives a different token or sees their fractional balance reduced without obtaining the expected NFT, while the airdrop rewards that should have been theirs disappear from the system.

title: Pair price may be manipulated by direct transfers
description: An attacker may manipulate the price of a pair by transferring tokens directly to the pair. Since the `Pair` contract exposes the `price` function, it maybe be used as a price oracle in third-party integrations. Manipulating the price of a pair may allow an attacker to steal funds from such integrations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a price oracle that is derived directly from the token balances held by a liquidity pair contract instead of from internally tracked reserve variables. Because the contract’s public price function reads the current ETH balance (or ERC20 balance) of the pair and the balance of the fractional token via a simple mapping, any external account can alter those balances by sending tokens or ETH directly to the contract address. This direct transfer bypasses the pair’s normal swap and liquidity‑addition logic, which enforces the constant‑product invariant (K) and updates reserves in a controlled manner. As a result, an attacker can inflate or deflate the apparent reserves, causing the price function to return a manipulated price. When third‑party protocols rely on this price as an oracle—for example to price collateral, trigger liquidations, or calculate fees—the manipulated value can be used to extract funds, cause incorrect liquidations, or otherwise break accounting assumptions. The attack can be carried out in a single transaction: the attacker first transfers an arbitrary amount of the base or fractional token to the pair, then calls the vulnerable price function (or any dependent function) to obtain the falsified price, and finally interacts with the dependent protocol to execute a trade, liquidation, or loan settlement that benefits the attacker. The impact is that users may see unexpected swap rates, receive less output than expected, or see their collateral liquidated unfairly, effectively causing funds to disappear from the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the pair contract’s address can receive tokens outside of its defined addLiquidity or swap functions, which includes normal ERC20 transfers, self‑destruct transfers, or direct ETH sends. All participants that trust the pair’s price—liquidity providers, traders, and any external contracts using the price as an oracle—are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the implementation of the price calculation and noticed that it relied on address(this).balance and ERC20.balanceOf rather than on stored reserve state, a pattern that is easy to overlook because the function is read‑only and appears harmless. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit events or revert when balances are altered externally, making the manipulation invisible to casual observers. To remediate, the contract should maintain its own reserve variables that are only updated inside the controlled swap and liquidity functions, mirroring the design of Uniswap V2. Additionally, a time‑weighted cumulative price mechanism should be introduced to prevent short‑term manipulation, and direct token transfers to the pair should be either prohibited or ignored in price calculations. By decoupling the oracle price from raw token balances, the protocol restores correct accounting and protects users from price‑manipulation attacks.

title: `selfdestruct
description:
`selfdestruct()` will not be available after EIP-4758. This EIP will rename the SELFDESTRUCT opcode and replace its functionality. It will no longer destroy code or storage, so, the contract still will be available.

In this case it will break the logic of the project because it will not work as expected:

FixedPrice.sol

* After calling the [cancel() function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L50), the contract still will be available. Users will be able to buy a number of NFTs even if the current sale is cancelled.

OpenEdition.sol

* After calling the [cancel() function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L75), the contract still will be available. Users will be able to buy a number of NFTs even if the current sale is cancelled.
poc:
According to [EIP-4758](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4758):

* The SELFDESTRUCT opcode is renamed to SENDALL, and now only immediately moves all ETH in the account to the target; it no longer destroys code or storage or alters the nonce.
* All refunds related to SELFDESTRUCT are removed.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the SELFDESTRUCT opcode to terminate an active NFT sale. In the original design, calling the cancel() function triggers SELFDESTRUCT, which both transfers any remaining ether to a designated address and permanently removes the contract’s bytecode, storage and nonce, effectively disabling further interactions. EIP‑4758 changes this behaviour by renaming the opcode to SENDALL and restricting its effect to an immediate transfer of all ether, while leaving the contract’s code and storage intact. Consequently, after the network upgrades to EIP‑4758, the cancel() function no longer destroys the contract; the contract remains callable and its state variables (such as sale status) are not automatically reset. An attacker or any user can therefore continue to invoke purchase functions even though the UI or off‑chain logic reports the sale as cancelled. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a situation where the sale appears closed, yet minting transactions succeed, leading to unexpected token issuance and potential revenue loss for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the cancellation logic and cross‑checked it against the EIP‑4758 specification. It can be hard to notice because the cancel() call still succeeds and may emit expected events, giving the impression that the sale has been terminated, while the underlying contract remains functional. The impact is medium severity: the protocol’s business logic is broken, allowing sales to continue against the intended policy, which can erode trust and cause financial discrepancies. The flaw belongs to the class of “opcode‑dependency” bugs where contract behaviour assumes a particular EVM instruction semantics that later change. To remediate, the architecture should be refactored to avoid using SELFDESTRUCT for control flow. Instead, an explicit pause or cancelled flag should be introduced, with proper access control, and any ether handling should be performed via dedicated withdrawal functions. This ensures that sale termination is enforced by contract state rather than by the destruction of the contract itself.

title: Sale contracts can be bricked if any other minter mints a token with an id that overlaps the sale
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the sale contracts mint ERC‑721 tokens sequentially within a predefined identifier range. Each sale assumes it is the exclusive minter for the IDs from currentId+1 up to finalId, and the buy function simply loops over this range calling the NFT contract’s mint method. The underlying ERC‑721 implementation rejects any attempt to mint an identifier that already exists, reverting with the message "ERC721: token already minted". If an external account – for example the creator, another minter role holder, or a different sale contract – mints any token ID that belongs to the sale’s range before a buyer invokes buy, the loop will encounter the already‑existing ID and the whole transaction will revert. This condition effectively bricks the sale: no further purchases can be processed because the contract cannot advance past the colliding identifier. The impact is that legitimate buyers see their purchase transactions fail, receive no NFT, and only lose gas costs; the protocol loses potential revenue and the user experience is broken. The issue appears only when the sale contract shares minting privileges with other entities and does not reserve or validate exclusive ownership of its ID range. It was discovered during an audit by constructing a test where a separate minter pre‑minted an ID inside the sale interval, causing the buy call to revert. The bug can be hard to notice because the sequential minting logic looks correct in isolation and the error surfaces only under the specific circumstance of an overlapping mint, which may not occur in normal testing. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce exclusive control over the identifier range – either by reserving the range for the sale contract, limiting minting to a single minter role at a time, or by minting tokens to the sale contract itself and then transferring them to buyers, thereby preventing external interference. This class of flaw is a token‑ID collision caused by shared minting authority, similar to a race condition where multiple parties compete for the same resource, violating the business assumption that each token ID is minted exactly once during the sale.

title: Escher721 contract does not have setTokenRoyalty function
description:
On the Code4rena page of this contest there is a “SALES PATTERNS” section that describes the flow of how to use Sales:

<https://code4rena.com/contests/2022-12-escher-contest>

It contains this statement:

If the artist would like sales and royalties to go somewhere other than the default royalty receiver, they must call setTokenRoyalty with the following variables

So an artist should be able to call the `setTokenRoyalty` function on the `Escher721` contract.

However this function cannot be called. It does not exist. There exists a `_setTokenRoyalty` in `ERC2981.sol` from OpenZeppelin. This function however is `internal` (<https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/3d7a93876a2e5e1d7fe29b5a0e96e222afdc4cfa/contracts/token/common/ERC2981.sol#L94>).

So there is no `setTokenRoyalty` function that can be called by the artist. So an artist cannot set a royalty individually for a token as is stated in the documentation.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing external interface for configuring per‑token royalty information in the Escher721 contract. The contract inherits OpenZeppelin’s ERC2981 implementation, which provides an internal function named _setTokenRoyalty that updates the royalty receiver and fee for a specific token identifier. However, the public documentation for the sales pattern explicitly instructs artists to call a function called setTokenRoyalty to change the royalty destination for an individual token. Because the contract does not expose any external or public wrapper around the internal _setTokenRoyalty, the setTokenRoyalty selector does not exist in the compiled bytecode. Consequently, when an artist or a developer attempts to invoke setTokenRoyalty, the call fails at compile time or reverts due to the missing function signature. The root cause is a mismatch between the documented API and the actual contract code: the developer assumed that the internal function would be callable externally, but OpenZeppelin deliberately marks it internal to restrict access. This oversight can be exploited by simply attempting to call the non‑existent function, which results in a transaction that cannot be executed, preventing the artist from assigning a custom royalty receiver. The impact is that all royalty payments for token sales default to the contract’s global royalty receiver, contrary to the expectation that each token could have an independent royalty address. Users—specifically artists and token owners—are affected because they receive no royalty revenue from secondary sales, leading to missing funds and a breach of the business logic that royalties should be payable to the designated creator. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors compared the sales pattern documentation with the contract’s ABI and observed that the expected setTokenRoyalty entry was absent. It may be hard to notice in a live deployment because the contract compiles and functions otherwise, and the missing function only becomes apparent when an artist attempts to configure royalties, which may be a rare operation. To remediate the problem, the contract should expose a public or external function—typically named setTokenRoyalty—that forwards the caller’s parameters to the internal _setTokenRoyalty routine, optionally guarded by appropriate access control such as onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE). This change aligns the contract’s interface with its documentation, restores the ability for artists to set per‑token royalty receivers, and ensures that royalty accounting behaves as intended, preventing funds from disappearing or being sent to an unintended default address.

title: Use of `payable.transfer
description:
The protocol uses Solidity’s `transfer()` when transferring ETH to the recipients. This has some notable shortcomings when the recipient is a smart contract, which can render ETH impossible to transfer. Specifically, the transfer will inevitably fail when the smart contract:

* does not implement a payable fallback function, or
* implements a payable fallback function which would incur more than 2300 gas units, or
* implements a payable fallback function incurring less than 2300 gas units but is called through a proxy that raises the call’s gas usage above 2300.
poc:
[File: LPDA.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol)
```solidity
            ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(fee);
            temp.saleReceiver.transfer(totalSale - fee);
    
        payable(msg.sender).transfer(owed);
```

[File: FixedPrice.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109)
```solidity
        ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(address(this).balance / 20);
```

[File: OpenEdition.sol#L92](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92)
```solidity
        ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(address(this).balance / 20);
```
Issues pertaining to the use of `transfer()` in the code blocks above may be referenced further via:

* [CONSENSYS Diligence’s article](https://consensys.net/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/)
* [OpenZeppelin news & events](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/reentrancy-after-istanbul/)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on Solidity’s built‑in transfer() function to send Ether to external parties. Transfer forwards a fixed gas stipend of 2300 units and automatically reverts if the call runs out of gas or if the recipient does not implement a payable fallback function. When the recipient is a smart contract whose fallback or receive function requires more than 2300 gas – for example because it performs storage writes, emits events, or calls other contracts – the transfer will fail and the whole transaction reverts. The same failure occurs if the contract is called through a proxy that adds extra gas overhead, pushing the effective gas available to the fallback above the stipend. Consequently, legitimate ETH payouts such as fee withdrawals, seller refunds, or user‑claimed balances may become impossible, leaving funds locked in the contract. From a user’s point of view the expected outcome – receiving a refund or seeing an increased balance – does not materialise; the UI may show a pending transaction or a zero balance change, creating the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the code paths where transfer() is used (e.g., feeReceiver().transfer(fee) and payable(msg.sender).transfer(owed)). It is subtle because transfer() does not expose a return value; the failure manifests only as a reverted transaction, which can be mistaken for a generic bug or network issue rather than a systematic inability to pay contracts with non‑trivial fallback logic. The root cause is the outdated assumption that 2300 gas is sufficient for any payable contract, an assumption that was invalidated by EIP‑1884 and subsequent hard‑forks that increased gas costs for certain opcodes. The impact ranges from denial‑of‑service – preventing the protocol from paying fees or refunds – to potential loss of user confidence, as users may believe the protocol is unsafe. The class of bug is commonly referred to as “transfer gas stipend limitation” or “inflexible Ether forwarding”. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer() with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas, checks the returned success flag, and reverts with a clear error if the call fails. Using OpenZeppelin’s Address.sendValue() or a pattern such as (bool success, ) = payable(recipient).call{value: amount}(''); require(success, "Transfer failed"); together with a re‑entrancy guard and the check‑effects‑interactions pattern mitigates both the gas‑stipend issue and the associated re‑entrancy risk. As an additional safety net, the contract could attempt to send Ether via call and, if that fails, fallback to sending an equivalent amount of wrapped Ether (WETH) to ensure the intended party still receives value.

title: `OpenEdition.buy
description: `OpenEdition.buy()` might revert due to uint overflow when it should work.
bug_full: The OpenEdition contract implements a public buy function that accepts an amount of tokens to purchase and validates that the caller sent exactly amount multiplied by the edition price. The function stores the requested amount in a uint24 variable and the price of the edition is stored as a uint72. The validation line performs amount * sale.price and relies on Solidity’s built‑in overflow checking (introduced in version 0.8) to revert if the multiplication overflows. Because the multiplication is evaluated in the uint72 domain, any combination where amount * sale.price exceeds the maximum value representable by a uint72 (2**72‑1) triggers an overflow, causing the require statement to revert with the generic "WRONG PRICE" error. This means that a perfectly valid purchase – for example buying 64 units when the price is 73 × 10¹⁸ wei – will fail even though the caller supplied the correct ether amount. The bug manifests only when the product of amount and price is large enough to overflow, which may not be obvious during normal testing with small values, making it hard to notice. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts, the UI may display a generic price‑mismatch error, and the buyer receives no tokens despite sending the correct funds, effectively losing the opportunity to acquire the edition. The affected parties are any buyer attempting large‑scale purchases, the protocol that loses legitimate sales revenue, and any downstream services that assume the buy function always succeeds when the price is correct. The issue was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) where the overflow annotation was added to the require line. It belongs to the class of arithmetic overflow vulnerabilities that break business logic by violating the assumption that price × amount fits within the chosen integer type. To remediate the problem the multiplication should be performed in a wider type (e.g., uint256) or explicitly cast the operands before multiplication, and the require should compare the full‑precision product against msg.value, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This change eliminates the overflow check failure and restores the intended behavior where a correct payment always succeeds.

title: Editions should be checked if they are actually deployed from the legitimate Escher721Factory
description:
For all kinds of sales, the creators create new sales contracts with arbitrary sale data, and the edition is not properly checked.

Malicious creators can create fake contracts that implemented `IEscher721` and fake buyers to get free earnings.
bug_full: An issue exists in the sale creation flow where the contract does not verify that the edition address supplied by a creator originates from the authorized Escher721Factory. The function only checks that the edition contract reports a specific role via IEscher721.hasRole, but a malicious creator can deploy a contract that implements the interface and returns true for any caller. Because the protocol trusts the edition address without confirming its provenance, a creator can pass a counterfeit edition address when calling createFixedSale. When a buyer later pays into the sale, the payment is routed to the fake edition which either does not mint or transfer the expected NFT, or simply discards the funds. From the buyer’s perspective the transaction succeeds, but the expected token never arrives and the paid ether is effectively lost. The vulnerability is triggered whenever any creator is allowed to call createFixedSale with arbitrary _sale data, which is the case for all sales types. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the role check and noticed the absence of a factory‑based validation step. The problem can be subtle because the presence of a role check gives the impression of proper authorization, yet the check can be spoofed by a contract that pretends to implement the interface. The bug belongs to the class of untrusted external contract reference or inadequate source verification vulnerabilities, where a system accepts an address without confirming that it was created by a trusted entity. To remediate, the protocol should maintain a registry of legitimate Escher721 contracts emitted by the factory and require that sale.edition be present in that registry, or directly query the factory to confirm that the edition address was deployed by it. Additional safeguards such as using ERC‑165 to ensure the contract truly implements IEscher721 and restricting edition registration to the factory can also close the attack surface. By enforcing these checks, buyers will receive the promised NFTs and their payments will not disappear into a counterfeit contract.

title: Inconsistency in fees
description: If the seller cancels before the sale startTime then all funds should be moved to saleReceiver without any deduction (Assuming seller has sent some ETH accidentally before sell start). But in `FixedPrice.sol` contract, fees are deducted even when seller cancels before the sale startTime which could lead to loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in fee handling when a seller aborts a fixed‑price sale before the scheduled start time. The contract’s cancel function reuses the internal _end routine, which unconditionally transfers a fixed percentage (1/20) of the contract balance to the protocol’s fee receiver before self‑destructing and sending the remaining ether to the designated saleReceiver. Because the fee transfer is performed without checking whether the sale has actually begun, any ether that was accidentally sent to the FixedPrice contract prior to the sale start – for example through a mistaken self‑destruct of a personal contract – is partially siphoned off as a fee even though the sale never commenced. An attacker (or the honest seller) can trigger this by calling cancel while block.timestamp is still less than sale.startTime. The contract then emits an End event, deducts the fee, and self‑destructs, leaving the seller with only 95 % of the mistakenly deposited funds. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that a pre‑sale cancellation returns the full balance, but the reality is a missing amount equal to the protocol fee, which appears as a sudden reduction of the seller’s ether balance or a “refund” that is lower than expected. The impact is a loss of funds for the seller and a breach of the business logic that fees should only be collected when a sale actually occurs. This issue was discovered during a manual audit when the researchers constructed a proof‑of‑concept that deliberately sent 20 ETH to the contract before the sale start and then cancelled, observing a 1 ETH fee deduction. The bug is subtle because the same _end function is used for both normal sale termination and owner‑initiated cancellation, making the fee logic appear correct at first glance. To remediate, the cancel path should be refactored to skip the fee transfer entirely, for example by emitting the End event and directly self‑destructing to the saleReceiver without invoking the fee‑sending line, or by adding an explicit condition that only allows fee collection after the sale has started. Conceptually the fix separates the accounting of fees from the cancellation flow, ensuring that no fee is taken when the sale never began and preserving the seller’s full balance.

title: `buy
description: A buyer could plan on buying early at higher prices to make sure he would secure a portion (say 50%) of NFTs he desired. When the number of NFTs still available got smaller and that `sale.endTime` were yet to hit, he would then watch the mempool and repeatedly attempt to thwart the final group of buyers from successfully completing their respective transactions amidst the efforts to prolong the Dutch auction till `sale.endTime` was reached.
poc:
Assuming this particular edition pertained to a 100 NFT collection that would at most last for 60 minutes, and Bob planned on minting 10 of them. At the beginning of the Dutch auction, he would first mint 5 NFTs at higher prices no doubt. At 50th minute, `sale.currentId == 95`. Alice, upon seeing this, made up her mind and proceeded to buy the remaining NFTs. Bob, seeing this transaction queuing in the mempool, invoked `buy()` to mint 1 NFT by sending in higher amount of gas to front run Alice. Needless to say, Alice’s transaction was going to revert on line 68 because `newId == 101`:

[File: LPDA.sol#L68](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L68)
```solidity
    68:        require(newId <= temp.finalId, "TOO MANY");
```
Noticing the number of NFTs still available had become 4, Alice attempted to mint the remaining 4 NFTs this time. Bob, upon seeing the similar queue in the mempool again, front ran Alice with another mint of 1 NFT.

These steps were repeatedly carried out until Bob managed to get all NFTs he wanted where the last one was minted right after `sale.endTime` hit. At this point, every successful buyer was happy to get the biggest refund possible ensuring that each NFT was only paid for the lowest price. This intended goal, on the contrary, was achieved at the expense of the seller getting the lowest amount of revenue and that the front run buyers minting nothing.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition and allocation overflow in the Dutch‑auction style NFT sale contract. The buy() function calculates a new token identifier (newId) by adding the amount of NFTs a caller wants to purchase to the current amountSold. A simple require statement checks that newId does not exceed the final token identifier (temp.finalId). Because this check is performed after the addition, two or more buy transactions that are mined in close succession can each see the same pre‑update amountSold value. An attacker can monitor the mempool, submit a buy transaction with a higher gas price, and cause newId to be computed as larger than the remaining supply. The require then reverts the legitimate buyer’s transaction, while the attacker’s transaction succeeds and reduces the remaining supply. By repeatedly front‑running pending transactions, the attacker can capture a disproportionate share of the NFTs, deny other participants the ability to buy the last few tokens, and force the auction to finish with lower revenue for the seller. The issue manifests only when the auction is close to its end time and the number of remaining NFTs is small, creating a narrow window where concurrent calls can overshoot the finalId. It affects any buyer attempting to purchase the remaining NFTs, the protocol’s revenue model, and overall fairness of the auction. The bug was discovered during a security audit that simulated mempool competition and identified that the require check does not prevent oversubscription under race conditions. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears correct in isolation and typical unit tests do not emulate simultaneous transactions. The proper mitigation is to cap newId at temp.finalId, compute the excess amount (diff), and adjust amountSold and the payment amount accordingly, ensuring that no transaction can allocate more tokens than are actually available. This change prevents the overflow, eliminates the front‑running advantage, and restores the intended economic behavior where each buyer receives the correct number of NFTs at the price dictated by the auction schedule.

title: ETH will get stuck if all NFTs do not get sold.
poc:
Consider this scenario:

* The sale contract deployer deploys a sale contract (FixedSale) to sell 100 NFTs ranging from id 1 to 100 with price 1 ETH per NFT.
* Users only buy the initial 10 NFTs. So the sale contract now has 10 ETH and currently 90 NFTs are unsold.
* No more users buy anymore NFTs from the sale contract.
* The 10 ETH are in stuck state as the `saleReceiver` cannot pull them out even though some NFTs have been already legitimately sold.
* To recover those 10 ETH, the contract deployer or `saleReceiver` has to come up with 90 ETH and buy the unsold 90 NFTs.

The scenario for the LPDA sale contract is similar. ETH can get stuck for partial batch NFT sales and upfront capital will be needed to recover the ETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logic error in the sale contracts that only forwards the accumulated ether to the designated receiver when the last token identifier of the batch is sold. Both the FixedPrice and the LPDA implementations check if the newly minted token id equals the finalId before calling an internal _end routine that performs the transfer of the total sale proceeds and the protocol fee. Because the transfer is gated by this equality, any situation where only a subset of the NFTs is purchased leaves the ether that was sent by the buyers locked inside the contract. The root cause is the absence of a fallback or claim mechanism for partial sales and the reliance on a single condition to trigger the payout. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; simply purchasing a few tokens and then stopping further purchases creates a state where the contract holds ether that cannot be withdrawn. The impact is that the saleReceiver, the contract owner, and the buyers lose access to the funds; the buyers have paid for NFTs but the seller cannot retrieve the proceeds, and the ether remains trapped until someone supplies enough capital to buy the remaining unsold tokens, thereby satisfying the finalId condition. This situation occurs whenever the sale is configured as a fixed‑price batch and the market demand does not exhaust the full range of token ids. It affects any party that relies on the contract to forward payments – typically the project team receiving the revenue and the end users expecting their purchase to be reflected in the receiver’s balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of ether in the buy function and noticed that the transfer logic is placed inside an if‑statement that only executes on full batch completion. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error or provide a visible “withdraw” function, the locked ether can be hard to notice until the sale is considered finished or the owner attempts to retrieve the balance. The bug belongs to the class of “conditional payout” or “funds‑locking” vulnerabilities where business logic assumes a final state before releasing assets. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the purchase succeeded, but later the seller’s dashboard reports zero revenue despite having sold items, and the buyers see no refund when the sale is aborted. To remediate the problem the contract should include a pull‑based claim function that allows the designated receiver (or the contract owner) to withdraw the accumulated ether at any time, or implement a cancellation path that settles pending balances when the sale is terminated before all tokens are sold. Using a safe transfer method such as call with proper checks‑effects‑interactions pattern is also recommended.

title: Unsafe downcasting operation truncate user’s input
description: Unsafe downcasting operation truncates user’s input.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe downcasting operation where values supplied by users are cast from a larger unsigned integer type (uint256) to a smaller type (uint48 or uint80) without any safety checks. This truncates the high‑order bits of the original value, causing the contract to record a smaller amount than the user actually provided. The root cause is the direct use of Solidity’s implicit casting syntax (e.g., uint48(_amount) or uint80(msg.value)) in the buy functions of FixedPrice.sol and LPDA.sol, as well as in the refund calculation of LPDA.sol, instead of employing a safe‑casting library or explicit range checks. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug by sending a purchase amount or payment that exceeds the maximum representable value of the target type (2^48‑1 for uint48, 2^80‑1 for uint80). When this occurs, the contract silently truncates the value, allowing the transaction to succeed while the internal accounting records a lower amount. Consequently, the user may receive fewer NFTs than paid for, or later be unable to claim the full refund because the stored balance or price has been reduced to the truncated value. The impact is a loss of funds for the buyer and incorrect revenue accounting for the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to buy or refund where the amount, msg.value, or computed price exceeds the respective type’s limit; normal‑sized purchases do not trigger it, making the issue hard to notice. Affected parties include any buyer interacting with the sale contracts, the protocol’s revenue distribution logic, and any role that relies on accurate balance tracking. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which added console logs and a test that demonstrated a large msg.value being truncated from a 256‑bit number to a 80‑bit value, resulting in a mismatch between the amount sent and the amount recorded. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: a transaction appears successful, the UI shows a purchase or refund, but the user receives fewer tokens or a smaller refund than expected, often seeing a zero or unexpectedly low balance. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of integer truncation or unsafe casting errors that violate the contract’s accounting assumptions. To remediate, the code should replace direct casts with OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library or add explicit require statements that ensure the value fits within the target type before casting, thereby preventing silent truncation and preserving the intended economic guarantees.

title: Creator can still “cancel” a sale after it has started by revoking permissions in `OpenEdition` contract
description:
```solidity
The `OpenEdition` type of sale has a start time and an end time. The creator (or owner of the contract) can cancel a sale using the `cancel` function only if it hasn’t started yet (i.e. start time is after current block timestamp).

However, the NFT creator can still revoke the minting permissions to the sale contract if he wishes to pull out of the sale. This will prevent anyone from calling the `buy` and prevent any further sale from the collection.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the OpenEdition sale contract, which is intended to allow a creator to cancel a sale only before the configured start time. The contract enforces this rule by checking that the current block timestamp is earlier than the sale start timestamp when the cancel function is called. However, the sale contract relies on the NFT contract’s MINTER_ROLE to mint tokens for each purchase. Because the creator (or contract owner) retains the ability to grant and revoke this role on the NFT contract at any time, the creator can revoke the MINTER_ROLE after the sale has already begun. When the role is revoked, the OpenEdition contract loses the permission to mint new NFTs, causing every subsequent call to the buy function to revert. From a user’s perspective, a buyer who attempts to purchase during the active sale receives a transaction failure and receives no tokens, even though the sale window is still open and the price appears correct. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style interruption: legitimate buyers are unable to acquire the NFTs, the sale cannot progress, and the creator can effectively “cancel” the sale without using the designated cancel function. This situation occurs whenever the creator decides to pull out after the start time, which is possible because the role revocation is not restricted by the sale’s timing logic. The affected parties are the buyers who expect to receive NFTs in exchange for payment, as well as any downstream participants who rely on the sale’s completion (e.g., royalty receivers). The issue was discovered during a functional audit that simulated a mid‑sale scenario, revoked the minter role, and observed the buy transaction revert. It can be hard to notice because the sale contract itself reports no error; the failure originates from an external permission check on the NFT contract, which may not be obvious from the sale’s UI. Conceptually, this is a privilege‑escalation / permission‑revocation bug that breaks the assumed invariant that the sale contract can always mint during its active window. To remediate, the design should either remove the creator’s ability to revoke the minter role once the sale has started, enforce that the cancel function can be called at any time (making the explicit cancel path the only way to stop the sale), or introduce a safeguard in the sale contract that checks the minter role before each purchase and fails gracefully with a clear error message. The fix must ensure that the sale’s lifecycle cannot be subverted by external role changes, preserving the guarantee that buyers can obtain NFTs throughout the advertised sale period.

title: NFTs mintable after Auction deadline expires
description:
```solidity
The `buy` function on the `LPDA.sol` contract is not validating if the auction is still running, allowing a purchase to be made after the stipulated time. The `endtime` variable used to store the end date of the auction is not used at any point to validate whether the purchase is being made within the deadline.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent validation of the auction deadline in the purchase function of alinear price decreasing auction contract. The contract stores an endTime value that marks when the auction should stop, but the buy function never checks the current block timestamp against this value. As a result, any caller can invoke buy after the scheduled end, receive a newly minted NFT and transfer ether to the contract even though the auction is supposed to be closed. The flaw originates from a missing require statement that would enforce block.timestamp <= endTime, allowing the logical condition that the sale is still active to be bypassed. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) simply waits until after the deadline or manipulates the blockchain timestamp in a test environment and then calls buy, receiving the token at the final price or at a price that may no longer be intended. The impact is that the auction’s economic model is broken – late buyers can obtain NFTs that should no longer be available, potentially at a discounted price, undermining fairness, revenue expectations, and the protocol’s promised scarcity. This issue manifests when the contract’s buy function is called after the endTime, which can happen naturally as time passes or artificially via timestamp manipulation. All participants who rely on the auction schedule – sellers, legitimate early bidders, and the protocol’s revenue accounting – are affected because the contract may collect funds for a sale that is supposed to be finished, and the token distribution no longer matches the intended rules. The problem was discovered during a security audit that included a test case warping the blockchain time three days beyond the configured endTime; the test still succeeded in minting a token and receiving ether, demonstrating the missing deadline check. The bug can be hard to notice because the UI may only display the auction end time without enforcing it on-chain, and the contract’s other logic (price decay, start time) appears correct, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, the contract should include a guard at the beginning of the buy function, such as require(block.timestamp <= sale.endTime, "TOO LATE"), which enforces the auction window and restores the intended economic guarantees. This class of issue is a typical time‑bound access control omission, where a critical temporal condition is not enforced, leading to unintended state changes after the prescribed period.

title: Ownership of EscherERC721.sol contracts can be changed, thus creator roles become useless
description:
```solidity
( creator = has a CREATOR_ROLE in Escher.sol

non-creator = doesn’t have a CREATOR_ROLE in Escher.sol )

Currently creating an ERC721 edition via the `Escher721Factory.sol` contract requires a user to have the `CREATOR_ROLE` in the main `Escher.sol` contract.

This requirement would mean that only users with the aforementioned role can be admins of editions. This requirement can be bypassed by having a ‘malicious’ creator create an edition for someone who doesn’t have the `CREATOR_ROLE` set by creating the edition and granting the `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` to the non-creator via AccessControl.sol’s `grantRole()` function. This way the non-creator can revoke the original creator’s roles in this edition and gain full ownership. Now this non-creator admin can create sales and operate as if he/she was a creator.

This defeats the point of having a role for creators and makes this function of the protocol not as described == faulty.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control design in the EscherERC721 edition contracts that allows the ownership of an edition to be transferred after it has been created. The contract inherits AccessControlUpgradeable, whose grantRole function is unrestricted and can be called by any address that holds a role with the admin privilege. Because the creator of an edition holds the CREATOR_ROLE, the creator can call grantRole to assign the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to an arbitrary address. Once the new address becomes the admin, it can revoke the original creator’s roles, effectively stripping the creator of any authority over that edition. This flaw occurs whenever an edition is instantiated through the Escher721Factory and the creator decides to grant the admin role to a third party, which may be a malicious payer. An attacker can therefore take over the edition, create sales, withdraw payments, or otherwise operate the contract as if they were the legitimate creator. From the user’s perspective the expected behaviour – that only the creator can manage the edition – is violated; users may see that they no longer have admin rights, that balances become inaccessible, or that sales are controlled by an unknown party. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a test where a creator granted the admin role to address 9, after which that address revoked the creator’s permissions and assumed full control. The problem is subtle because AccessControl’s grantRole is designed to be flexible, so the ability to change admins is not flagged as an error by the compiler, and there is no on‑chain registry of edition owners to detect the change. The bug belongs to the class of role‑escalation or mutable‑admin access‑control vulnerabilities, where privileged roles can be reassigned after deployment, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only creators can manage sales and funds. To remediate, the contract should make the admin role immutable after initialization, for example by overriding grantRole to always revert, or by restricting admin‑role grants to the contract’s constructor only. Additionally, storing each created edition in a mapping would provide a reliable source of truth for ownership and simplify audits of role assignments.

title: `RuniverseLand.sol#mint`
bug_full: The contract defines two minting entry points: a public mint() function that automatically assigns the next token identifier by reading the internal counter numMinted, and an internal‑facing mintTokenId() function that accepts an explicit tokenId argument. The root cause of the vulnerability is that mintTokenId() increments the same counter numMinted regardless of the tokenId supplied, while mint() assumes that the counter value always matches the identifier of the next unminted token. Because mintTokenId() can be invoked with any tokenId, a caller can deliberately or inadvertently mint a token with an identifier that is larger than the current counter, causing numMinted to advance while the explicit tokenId remains unrelated. When mint() is later called, it will compute tokenId = numMinted, which may already be occupied by the earlier mintTokenId call. The ERC‑721 _mint routine then reverts due to a duplicate tokenId, effectively bricking the minting process. This scenario can be reproduced by having the primaryMinter call mintTokenId(recipient,1,…) when numMinted is zero, followed by the secondaryMinter invoking mint(recipient, size). The second call attempts to mint tokenId 1 again, triggering a failure. The impact is that legitimate users or the protocol may be unable to mint new land NFTs, leading to a loss of expected functionality, potential revenue loss, and a broken user experience where a transaction reverts with no token minted. The bug affects any party that relies on the mint() interface – typically end‑users expecting to receive a newly minted plot, as well as the protocol’s economic model that assumes continuous token issuance. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementations of mint() and mintTokenId() and identified the inconsistent handling of the token identifier counter. The issue can be subtle because both functions appear to work in isolation; only a specific ordering of calls reveals the collision, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should either eliminate the mint() wrapper and force all callers to use mintTokenId with a strict check that tokenId equals the current counter, or redesign mintTokenId so that it does not modify numMinted when an explicit tokenId is supplied, and instead centralize tokenId allocation in a single, well‑defined function. Aligning the token identifier generation logic removes the possibility of duplicate IDs and restores reliable minting behavior.

title: Raffle creator might not start raffle draw
description: The raffle creator is not required to actually give the NFT away. The NFT that is used for the raffle is transferred to the contract when `startDraw` is executed. Before that, the NFT is in the hands of the creator. This means that he might create a raffle to make users buy NFTs required to participate and then refuse to draw a winner and keep the NFT to himself. Furthermore, he might not even be the owner of the NFT in the first place, which he can achieve by flash loaning the NFT in order to pass the `ownerOf` check in `initialize` function.
poc:
**Example 1**

  1. User U creates an NFT collection C
  2. He buys a BAYC NFT
  3. He creates a raffle with it, and requires `drawingToken` to be from collection C
  4. Users buy tokens from his collection C
  5. He then refuses to execute `startDraw` function and rather sells the BAYC NFT

**Example 2**

  1. User U creates an NFT collection C
  2. User U uses an NFT flash loan to borrow a very expensive NFT
  3. In the same transaction he creates a raffle with this NFT, and requires `drawingToken` to be from collection C
  4. The check that he is the owner will pass, because for the duration of the transaction he in fact is
  5. Users see that there is a raffle for a very expensive NFT, so they buy tokens C
  6. The winner is never drawn, because the creator does not even own the NFT

**Example 3**

  1. User U has an NFT X
  2. He puts X on a sale on some NFT marketplace (which does not require him to lock it in contract)
  3. He forgets about it and creates a raffle with it
  4. Users buy the tokens necessary for the raffle
  5. User U wants to execute the `startDraw` function, but just before it the NFT X is bought from him through the marketplace
  6. The winner cannot be drawn
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the raffle contract does not escrow the prize NFT at the moment the raffle is created and relies on the creator to call startDraw to transfer the NFT. Because the NFT remains in the creator’s wallet, the creator can simply refuse to execute startDraw, sell or transfer the NFT elsewhere, or even use a flash‑loan to temporarily satisfy the owner‑of‑NFT check during initialization. As a result participants who have paid for raffle tickets never receive the promised prize and their funds remain locked in the contract with no guarantee of a winner being drawn. The root cause is the missing transfer of the prize token during the makeNewDraw/initialization flow and the fact that startDraw is restricted to the creator and does not verify that the contract actually holds the NFT. An attacker can exploit this by creating a raffle, advertising a valuable NFT, collecting ticket payments, and then either keeping the NFT, selling it on a marketplace, or borrowing it via a flash loan to pass the ownership test and never calling startDraw. The impact is financial loss for ticket buyers, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential regulatory concerns because the contract effectively allows a creator to run a lottery without delivering the prize. The condition under which the bug manifests is any raffle where the prize NFT has not been transferred to the contract before startDraw is invoked, and where startDraw can only be called by the creator. Users see the raffle listed, purchase tickets, but later observe that no winner is announced, their ticket balances remain unchanged, and the prize NFT disappears from the contract or never appears. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of a raffle and identified that the ownerOf check is performed only at initialization and that the NFT transfer is performed inside startDraw rather than at creation. The problem is subtle because the UI shows an active raffle and the contract does not emit an explicit error when the prize is missing, making it appear as a normal waiting period. To remediate, the prize NFT should be transferred to the raffle contract at creation (e.g., via an approved transfer in makeNewDraw), the contract should enforce that it holds the NFT before allowing a draw, and the startDraw function should be callable by anyone after a predefined time window to remove reliance on the creator. Additional safeguards such as preventing the creator from reclaiming the NFT after a draw, and providing a recovery mechanism for participants if a draw never occurs, would close the escrow and trust gaps. This class of bug is an escrow‑or‑ownership enforcement flaw that allows a privileged actor to withhold the prize and break the expected accounting logic of a lottery.

title: VRFNFTRandomDraw admin can prevent created or started raffle from taking place
description:
The admin/owner of `VRFNFTRandomDraw` can `startDraw()` a raffle, including emitting the `SetupDraw` event, but in a way that ensures `fulfillRandomWords()` is never called. For example:

  * `keyHash` is not validated within `coordinator.requestRandomWords()`. Providing an invalid `keyHash` will allow the raffle to start but prevent the oracle from actually supplying a random value to determine the raffle result.

    * <https://github.com/smartcontractkit/chainlink/blob/00f9c6e41f843f96108cdaa118a6ca740b11df35/contracts/src/v0.8/VRFCoordinatorV2.sol#L407-L409>
    * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgeries/blob/fc271cf20c05ce857d967728edfb368c58881d85/src/VRFNFTRandomDraw.sol#L163>
  * The admin/owner could alternatively ensure that the owner-provided chain.link VRF subscription does not have sufficient funds to pay at the time the oracle attempts to supply random values in `fulfillRandomWords()`.

    * <https://github.com/smartcontractkit/chainlink/blob/00f9c6e41f843f96108cdaa118a6ca740b11df35/contracts/src/v0.8/VRFCoordinatorV2.sol#L594-L596>

In addition, the owner/admin could simply avoid ever calling `startDraw()` in the first place.
poc: Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an admin‑controlled denial‑of‑service condition in the VRFNFTRandomDraw contract that allows the contract owner to start a raffle while guaranteeing that the Chainlink VRF callback, fulfillRandomWords(), will never be executed. The root cause is that the contract does not validate the keyHash supplied to the coordinator when requesting random words and does not enforce that the VRF subscription has sufficient LINK balance at the moment the oracle attempts to fulfill the request. Because the startDraw() function merely emits a SetupDraw event and forwards the request to the VRFCoordinatorV2 without any sanity checks, an admin can provide an invalid keyHash or deliberately under‑fund the subscription, causing the coordinator to reject the request or to be unable to pay for the randomness. As a result, the raffle is marked as started, participants can enter, but the random number that determines the winner is never generated. The impact is that users who entered the raffle see their tickets recorded, may expect a reward NFT, but the contract never resolves the draw, leaving funds locked and the promised reward never distributed. This situation occurs whenever the privileged admin calls startDraw() with malformed parameters or insufficient subscription balance, or simply never calls startDraw() after creating a raffle. All participants, the protocol’s reputation, and any downstream contracts that rely on the reward distribution are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of startDraw() and fulfillRandomWords() and noticed the lack of validation and the reliance on external oracle state. It can be hard to notice because the SetupDraw event is emitted, giving the appearance that the raffle is live, and no error is thrown at the time of startDraw(); the failure only becomes visible when the expected winner is never announced. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the keyHash matches a known, whitelisted value, verify that the subscription holds enough LINK before making the request, and make the successful execution of fulfillRandomWords() a precondition for any subsequent reward claim or admin state transition. Additionally, the contract could revert the startDraw() call if the VRF request is rejected, or move the draw initiation to a trusted, non‑admin entity, thereby eliminating the possibility for the owner to intentionally block the randomness and protect participants from a raffle that never pays out.

title: Protocol safeguards for time durations are skewed by a factor of 7. Protocol may potentially lock NFT for period of 7 years.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect definition of the constant representing the number of seconds in a month. The contract defines HOUR_IN_SECONDS correctly as 60*60, defines WEEK_IN_SECONDS as 3600*24*7, and then defines MONTH_IN_SECONDS as (3600*24*7)*30. The extra multiplication by 7 copies the week constant, resulting in a value that is seven times larger than the true number of seconds in a typical 30‑day month. This mis‑calculation is used in the initialize() function to validate two configurable parameters: drawBufferTime, which must be less than one month, and recoverTimelock, which must be less than one year from the current block timestamp. Because the month constant is inflated, the checks actually allow drawBufferTime up to roughly seven months and recoverTimelock up to roughly seven years. An attacker or a careless deployer can therefore set these values within the apparent limits while unintentionally (or maliciously) extending the lock period far beyond the protocol’s intended behavior. The impact is that an NFT that should become recoverable within a year may remain locked for up to seven years, and periodic redraws that are expected to occur monthly may be delayed for up to seven months, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol. The bug manifests when the contract is initialized; any user who relies on the advertised timing will experience a discrepancy between the UI countdown (showing a maximum of one year) and the actual on‑chain lock (which may be seven years). The affected parties are NFT owners, participants who expect timely refunds or draws, and the protocol itself, whose business logic assumes monthly cycles and yearly recovery. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where reviewers compared the constant definitions and identified the copy‑paste error. It can be hard to notice because the variable name MONTH_IN_SECONDS appears correct, and typical unit tests may only cover short durations, missing the long‑term effect. The proper fix is to redefine MONTH_IN_SECONDS as (3600*24)*30, i.e., the number of seconds in 30 days, and to ensure that any time‑related checks use correctly calibrated constants. This correction restores the intended one‑month and one‑year limits, aligning on‑chain behavior with user expectations and preserving the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Extensive permissions for owner
description:
[contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L358](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/00a247e70de35d7a96d0ce03d66c0206b62e2f65/contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L358)  
[contracts/RuniverseLand.sol#L195](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/ea5fce62baeabf3f9d067ad747cee521d7be3a8a/contracts/RuniverseLand.sol#L195)  
[contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L513](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/00a247e70de35d7a96d0ce03d66c0206b62e2f65/contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L513)

Some privileged functions are often unavoidable in smart contracts. However, in these contracts, the privileges are (unnecessarily) very extensive and without checks on the smart contract side:

  1. He can use `ownerMint` (or `ownerMintUsingTokenId`) to mint an arbitrary number of tokens. While these functions should be used for private minting, there is nothing restricting the owner from minting more than 10,924 plots and using the function later on to mint additional plots.
  2. He can use `setVestingStart` / `setVestingEnd` / `setLastVestingGlobalId` to change the vesting configuration at any point. This can cause already vested tokens to suddenly become unvested (and therefore untransferable). Furthermore, there is no restriction on the parameters, so an owner could for instance set a vesting end that is 100 years in the future.
