  3. He can change the plots that are available per size at any time with `setPlotsAvailablePerSize`. Therefore, a user might think that he buys a rare plot size, but the plot size becomes very common afterwards, destroying the value of his NFT.

Therefore, the user currently has to trust the owner that he does not perform any of the previously described actions.
bug_full: An extensive permission set granted to the contract owner allows the owner to modify core economic parameters of the Runiverse land NFT system without any on‑chain constraints. The owner can call a minting function that creates new plot tokens and there is no check that the total number of minted plots stays within the intended cap of 10,924. Because the function is unrestricted, the owner could mint an arbitrary number of additional NFTs at any time, diluting the supply and devaluing existing holders. In addition, the contract exposes functions that let the owner change the vesting start time, vesting end time and the global identifier that marks the last vested token. By moving the vesting end far into the future, tokens that were previously vested become locked again, preventing their transfer and breaking the expectation that a vested token is freely tradable. Finally, the owner can alter the mapping that defines how many plots are available for each size category. This means a buyer who purchased a rare plot size can later see that size re‑classified as common, destroying the perceived rarity and market value of the NFT. The vulnerability stems from missing access‑control checks and mutable state variables that should be immutable once the sale phases begin. It can be exploited simply by the owner invoking the privileged functions; no special conditions or external contracts are required. The impact is a loss of economic trust: users may receive no token, see their token become non‑transferable, or watch the rarity of their asset disappear, leading to potential financial loss and reduced confidence in the protocol. The problem is observable from a user’s perspective as a missing NFT after purchase, an unexpected transfer not allowed error on a supposedly vested token, or a sudden drop in the rarity label of a plot. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that inspected privileged functions and noted the absence of invariant checks. Because the functions are only callable by the owner, the risk can be easy to overlook unless the code is examined for governance‑related constraints. To remediate, the minting function should enforce the total supply cap and be callable only before the public sale phases, vesting parameters should be made immutable after deployment, and the function that changes plot availability per size should be removed or locked, thereby preserving the intended scarcity model.

title: `ownerMintUsingTokenId` can brick the whole contract
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the privileged function ownerMintUsingTokenId, which allows the contract owner to mint an ERC721 token by supplying an arbitrary token identifier. Because the function does not verify that the supplied identifier is distinct from identifiers that will later be generated by the internal counter used in ownerGetNextTokenId, the owner can create a token whose ID collides with a future automatically‑assigned ID. When a regular user later attempts to purchase land, the contract calls mintTokenId, which internally invokes _mint. The ERC721 _mint implementation contains a require(!_exists(tokenId)) check, causing the transaction to revert with \"ERC721: token already minted\". This revert prevents the minting of the new token and, because the same counter is used for every subsequent sale, all further mint or buy operations fail, effectively rendering the contract unusable – a state often described as "bricking" the contract. In addition, the token identifier encodes plotSize information; the owner can embed any plotSize value, including sizes that are not offered for sale, thereby violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and allowing the creation of tokens that should be unavailable. The root cause is the absence of validation that the provided tokenId does not overlap with future sequential IDs and that its encoded fields respect the allowed ranges. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditors noticed that the privileged mint function bypasses the normal counter logic and that no guard clauses prevent identifier collisions. Because the function is restricted to the owner, the problem may not be obvious during normal user testing, and the failure only becomes visible when a regular mint operation reverts, which can be mistaken for a generic transaction error. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for all participants: users attempting to buy land receive a transaction revert, see no token transferred, and may lose confidence in the protocol. Funds sent with the transaction are returned by the EVM on revert, but the contract’s state remains locked, preventing any future sales. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked identifier collisions and privileged‑function misuse that leads to inconsistent contract state. To remediate, the ownerMintUsingTokenId function should be removed entirely or augmented with strict checks that decode the tokenId, verify that its global and local counters cannot be generated by the normal minting flow, and ensure that any embedded plotSize falls within the permitted range. By enforcing these constraints, the contract can guarantee that token identifiers remain unique and that the business logic governing land sales remains intact.

title: `setPlotsAvailablePerSize` does not work correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a configuration function that adjusts the number of land plots available for each size category. The function permits the contract owner to both decrease and increase the per‑size supply, but it lacks any validation that the new values respect two critical invariants: (1) the available count for each size must never be lower than the number of plots that have already been minted for that size, and (2) the sum of all size‑specific supplies must not exceed the global maximum token supply defined in the land token contract (MAX_SUPPLY = 70000). Because these checks are missing, an attacker with owner privileges can set a size’s available count below its minted count. When the contract later computes the remaining plots with the expression "plotsAvailablePerSize[i] - plotsMinted[i]", the subtraction underflows, producing a very large unsigned integer. This underflow corrupts the accounting of available lands, potentially allowing further minting operations to succeed against an incorrect supply view or causing the UI to display nonsensical numbers such as a huge available balance. Conversely, if the owner raises the per‑size totals so that their aggregate exceeds 70000, the minting logic that enforces the global cap will reject new tokens even though the per‑size counters suggest they are still available. From a user’s perspective this manifests as mint transactions that revert with “max supply reached” or as a dashboard that suddenly shows zero or negative plot availability, breaking the expectation that a user can always purchase a plot when the contract reports availability. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the invariants governing supply accounting; the flaw is subtle because the erroneous values are only produced inside internal calculations and do not immediately surface as explicit errors. The bug belongs to the class of invariant‑breakage or arithmetic‑underflow vulnerabilities that arise from unchecked state updates. To remediate, the contract should enforce that every new entry in the size‑specific supply array is greater than or equal to the already minted count for that size, and that the total of all entries never exceeds the immutable MAX_SUPPLY (or, if a supply reduction is intended, that the new total is less than or equal to the previous total). An alternative safe approach is to remove the mutable configuration function entirely, thereby preserving the supply invariants for the lifetime of the contract.

title: `RuniverseLandMinter._mintTokensUsingTokenId` does not verify that the `tokenId` matches the corresponding `plotSize`
poc: [contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L362-L393](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L362-L393)
bug_full: RuniverseLandMinter._mintTokensUsingTokenId is intended to mint a land NFT of a specific plot size while respecting a hard cap on the number of plots available for each size. The contract encodes the plot size in the first eight bits of the tokenId, and the public minting path validates that the tokenId matches the requested size. However, the private helper _mintTokensUsingTokenId does not verify that the plotSize argument corresponds to the size encoded in the supplied tokenId. As a result, an account with owner privileges can call ownerMintUsingTokenId and pass a small plotSize (for example 8x8) while providing a tokenId that encodes a much larger size (for example 128x128). The function only checks the plotsMinted counter for the supplied plotSize, increments that counter, and then mints the tokenId. Because the counter for the larger size is never updated, the contract’s invariant that plotsMinted[size] ≤ plotsAvailablePerSize[size] is broken and the total supply of large plots becomes larger than the advertised limit. This can be exploited to create more high‑value land NFTs than the protocol intended, inflating supply, distorting marketplace pricing, and undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting. The issue manifests whenever the privileged owner uses the admin mint function; regular users are not able to trigger it directly. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an NFT appears with a size that should be unavailable, while the on‑chain statistics still report that the size is scarce. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the tokenId encoding logic with the minting implementation and noticed the missing cross‑validation. It is hard to notice because the UI shows the correct size derived from the tokenId, while the internal counters remain consistent with the smaller size argument, creating a silent discrepancy. The proper fix is to add a check that extracts the plot size from the tokenId and ensures it matches the plotSize parameter, or to remove the privileged mint path entirely and rely on the standard minting function that already enforces the invariant. In generic terms the vulnerability is an invariant‑violation bug caused by missing validation of correlated parameters, allowing privileged minting to bypass supply caps.

title: `secondaryMinter` may break `plotsAvailablePerSize`
poc:
[contracts/RuniverseLand.sol#L88-L102](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/RuniverseLand.sol#L88-L102)  
[contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L323-L341](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/RuniverseLandMinter.sol#L323-L341)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of the secondaryMinter address to bypass the per‑size supply limits that are enforced for RuniverseLand NFTs. The contract defines a public array plotsAvailablePerSize that records the maximum number of NFTs that may exist for each PlotSize (8x8, 16x16, 32x32, 64x64, 128x128). These limits are checked inside the private function _mintTokens, which validates that plotsMinted for a given size does not exceed the corresponding entry in plotsAvailablePerSize before minting new tokens. However, the external function mintTokenId, which is callable by either primaryMinter or secondaryMinter, does not invoke _mintTokens nor does it perform any size‑specific accounting. It simply increments the global counter numMinted, emits a LandMinted event, and calls the ERC721 _mint routine. Because secondaryMinter can call mintTokenId directly with any tokenId and PlotSize, it can create NFTs of a particular size without updating plotsMinted or respecting the plotsAvailablePerSize caps. This breaks the invariant that the total number of NFTs of each size must stay within the predefined limits. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of mintTokenId with the checks present in _mintTokens and noticed that the secondaryMinter path lacks the size validation. The issue may be hard to notice because the public interface appears to work correctly – a LandMinted event is emitted and the token is transferred to the recipient – while the internal accounting variables remain inconsistent, leading to a silent over‑minting of certain plot sizes. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who controls the secondaryMinter address can repeatedly call mintTokenId with a chosen PlotSize, minting more tokens than the protocol intended. The impact includes dilution of scarcity, potential loss of value for existing holders, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s economic model. The bug manifests whenever secondaryMinter is authorized and used, affecting the protocol, its investors, and any users expecting the advertised limited supply. To remediate, the contract should enforce the per‑size checks for all minting entry points, either by restricting mintTokenId to the primaryMinter only, by having secondaryMinter call a wrapper that includes the same checks as _mintTokens, or by moving the size validation into a shared internal function that both minters must use. Restoring the invariant ensures that the number of minted plots for each size never exceeds the values defined in plotsAvailablePerSize, preserving the intended scarcity and economic guarantees of the system.

title: Grief on `transfers` due to `vestingStart` during vesting
description:
[contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L99-L101](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L99-L101)  
[contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L44](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L44)  
[contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L65](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-forgotten-runiverse/blob/dcad1802bf258bf294900a08a03ca0d26d2304f4/contracts/ERC721Vestable.sol#L65)

Past similar finding with the same severity: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-runes-findings/issues/30>

While centralization risk is acknowledged by the team & the C4udit tool: this may lead to loss of functionality (grief).
bug_full: The contract implements a time‑based vesting mechanism for ERC‑721 tokens. A vesting schedule is defined by two timestamps, vestingStart and vestingEnd, and a boolean flag vestingEnabled. The vulnerability stems from the internal function that updates vestingStart: it does not enforce that the new start time is earlier than the current end time. In contrast, the function that updates vestingEnd correctly requires the end to be greater than the start. Because of this asymmetry, an administrator (or any privileged caller) can set vestingStart to a value that is greater than vestingEnd, creating an invalid state where vestingDuration = vestingEnd - vestingStart underflows and becomes a very large unsigned integer. During a token transfer, the _beforeTokenTransfer hook checks that the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to (chunk * globalId) + vestingStart, where chunk = vestingDuration / lastVestingGlobalId. When vestingDuration underflows, chunk becomes huge, making the right‑hand side of the comparison far larger than any realistic block.timestamp. Consequently, the require statement "Not vested" reverts for every transfer that occurs while vestingEnabled is true and the token identifier is within the vesting range, even though the vesting period has technically already ended. From a user’s perspective the token appears to be permanently locked: attempts to transfer result in a generic "Not vested" error, balances remain unchanged, and the UI shows no movement of the asset. The issue also corrupts view functions such as vestsAt, which compute vestingDuration using the same subtraction and therefore return nonsensical timestamps. This bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the setter logic for the two timestamps and identified the missing validation. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific event for the misconfiguration and the arithmetic underflow does not throw; the only symptom is a transfer failure that looks like a normal vesting restriction. The impact is griefing – token holders may lose the ability to move their NFTs during the intended vesting period, effectively freezing assets. The affected parties are token owners, the protocol that relies on the vesting schedule, and any downstream applications that assume tokens can be transferred after the vesting end. The recommended remediation is to make vestingStart immutable after deployment, or at a minimum add a require(_newVestingStart < vestingEnd) check in the _setVestingStart function so that the two setters enforce the same invariant. Aligning the setter logic eliminates the possibility of creating an invalid vesting window and restores the intended transfer behaviour.

title: `RewardsPool.sol` : It is safe to have the `startRewardsCycle` with `WhenNotPaused` modifier
description:
When the contract is paused, allowing startRewardsCycle would inflate the token value which might not be safe.

Rewards should not be claimed by anyone when all other operations are paused.

I saw that the `withdrawGGP` has this `WhenNotPaused` modifier.

Inflate should not consider the paused duration.

Let’s say, when the contract is paused for the duration of 2 months, then the dao, protocol, and node validator would enjoy the rewards. This is not good for a healthy protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing the rewards cycle to be started while the contract is in a paused state, because the startRewardsCycle function does not include the WhenNotPaused guard that other privileged operations use. The root cause is an inconsistency in the pausing logic: the pause flag is checked for functions such as withdrawGGP but omitted for the function that initiates a new rewards period and triggers token inflation. When an attacker or any caller invokes startRewardsCycle during a pause, the internal inflate call mints new GGP tokens according to the daily inflation schedule, regardless of the fact that the protocol is supposed to be halted. These newly minted tokens are then distributed to the DAO, multisig and node‑operator claim contracts, resulting in unexpected reward payouts. From a user perspective the protocol appears to be paused, yet balances may increase, rewards may be claimed, and the token supply expands, violating the expectation that no economic activity occurs while paused. The impact includes token value dilution, unfair gains for privileged parties, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions, potentially harming token holders and undermining confidence in the system. The issue manifests whenever the guardian or governance pauses the contract for any duration, such as a planned maintenance window of two months, because startRewardsCycle remains callable. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit that highlighted the missing WhenNotPaused modifier and the resulting inconsistency. The bug can be hard to notice because the function does not interact directly with users and the inflation occurs silently in the background. To remediate, the startRewardsCycle function should be protected by the WhenNotPaused modifier or otherwise restricted to authorized callers, ensuring that token inflation and reward distribution only happen when the protocol is active, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended pause semantics.

title: Coding logic of the contract upgrading renders upgrading contracts impractical
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract upgrade mechanism that registers a new implementation before removing the old one. The upgrade function writes the new contract address to a storage mapping keyed by the contract name, then immediately calls the unregister routine which clears the entry for the same name. When the upgraded contract keeps the original name, the second call overwrites the freshly stored address with a zero value, because both operations use the identical name key. Consequently the system loses the reference to the new implementation and any subsequent lookup of the contract address returns address(0). This design forces the upgrader to change the contract name for every upgrade. In a codebase where many contracts reference each other by hard‑coded names – for example modifiers that check onlySpecificRegisteredContract("ClaimNodeOp") – a name change in one contract breaks the references in all dependent contracts. The cascade effect requires every cross‑referencing contract to be redeployed with a new name, leading to a complex, error‑prone upgrade process that may never be completed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the upgrade function with identical and different names and observed the storage state after each call. It is subtle because the function compiles and executes without reverting; the failure manifests only when another contract attempts to resolve the upgraded name, resulting in unexpected reverts or silent no‑ops. Users experience the problem as a contract that appears to have been upgraded but no longer responds to calls that rely on the original name – for instance reward distribution functions revert with an InvalidOrOutdatedContract error, or UI components show missing balances because the underlying contract cannot be located. The impact is not an immediate loss of funds, but it can halt protocol functionality, prevent reward accrual, and make future upgrades impractical, undermining the system’s upgradability guarantee. The root cause is the ordering of register and unregister calls combined with the reliance on contract names as unique identifiers. A proper fix is to unregister the existing contract before registering the new one, or to decouple the name from the address lookup so that the same name can be reused. Removing the name parameter from the upgrade function or ensuring that the storage update does not overwrite the new address would also resolve the issue, restoring the ability to upgrade contracts without cascading name changes.

title: NodeOp funds may be trapped by a invalid state transition
description:
The Multisig can call `MinipoolManager.sol::recordStakingError()` if there is an error while registering the node as a validator. Also the Multisig can call [MinipoolManager.sol::finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/MinipoolManager.sol#L528) in order to “finish” the NodeOp’s minipool proccess.

If the Multisig accidentally/intentionally calls `recordStakingError()` then `finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig()` the NodeOp funds may be trapped in the protocol.

The `finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig()` has the next comment: _Multisig can move a minipool from the error state to the finished state after a human review of the error_ but the NodeOp should be able to withdraw his funds after a finished minipool.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑machine flaw in the MinipoolManager that can permanently lock a node operator’s deposited funds. When a minipool encounters a staking error, the protocol’s multisig is allowed to call recordStakingError to mark the minipool as errored and subsequently call finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig to move the minipool into a finished state after a human review. The withdrawMinipoolFunds function, however, only permits withdrawals from a limited set of states and does not recognise the finished‑after‑error combination as a valid withdrawal state. As a result, the withdrawal call reverts with an InvalidStateTransition error, leaving the AVAX that the node operator deposited in the vault inaccessible. The bug occurs only when the multisig invokes both recordStakingError and finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig, either accidentally or maliciously, after a staking error has been recorded. It affects node operators who rely on being able to reclaim their funds and, indirectly, the protocol because trapped capital reduces available liquidity. The issue was uncovered during a targeted audit test that simulated the exact sequence of calls and observed the revert. It is subtle because the minipool appears to be in a normal finished state, so a user interface may show the minipool as completed while the withdraw function silently fails, leading users to see no balance returned and possibly assume the protocol is withholding funds. The root cause is an incomplete validation of state transitions in the withdrawal logic; the finite‑state machine does not include a transition from the error‑finished state to a withdrawable state. To remediate, the withdrawal function should be extended with an additional requireValidStateTransition check that explicitly allows withdrawals when the minipool is in the finished state after an error, or the multisig‑only finishFailedMinipoolByMultisig method should be removed or altered so that it cannot create a state from which funds cannot be withdrawn. This class of bug—incorrect state transition handling leading to locked assets—is common in contracts that rely on complex FSMs for fund management.

title: `requireNextActiveMultisig` will always return the first enabled multisig which increases the probability of stuck minipools
description:
For every created minipool a multisig address is set to continue validator interactions.

Every minipool multisig address get assigned by calling `requireNextActiveMultisig`.

This function always return the first enabled multisig address.

In case the specific address is disabled all created minipools will be stuck with this address which increase the probability of also funds being stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical allocation flaw in the function that selects the next active multisig address for newly created minipools. The function always returns the first enabled multisig address instead of rotating or randomly picking among all enabled addresses. Because the selection does not advance, every minipool created while the first multisig is enabled is bound to that address. If that multisig later becomes disabled, all minipools that were assigned to it cannot progress, causing validator interactions to fail and funds to appear locked. The root cause is the absence of a stateful index or fallback mechanism; the code simply scans the list and returns the first enabled entry. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or even a benign operator can disable the first multisig after a number of minipools have been created, resulting in those minipools being stuck. The impact is that users see their minipool balance remain unchanged, withdrawals are rejected, and the protocol’s liveness is compromised. The condition under which this occurs is when the system has more than one multisig configured and the first enabled one is later disabled. All participants who rely on minipool operations—validator operators, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the multisig selection logic, and it is hard to notice because normal operation appears correct as long as the first multisig stays active. To remediate, the selection routine should implement a round‑robin or provably random algorithm, maintain a pointer to the last used multisig, and revert if no enabled multisig exists. This change ensures that minipools are distributed across all active multisigs and prevents a single point of failure that can cause funds to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: Bypass `whenNotPaused` modifier
description: The `whenNotPaused` modifier is used to pause minipool creation and staking/withdrawing GGP. However, there are several cases this modifier could be bypassed, which breaks the intended admin control function and special mode.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent application of the emergency‑stop mechanism that is implemented through the whenNotPaused modifier. The contract is designed to block creation of new minipools, staking of GGP tokens and withdrawal of GGP when the admin calls pause(). The pause flag is checked only in functions that are explicitly marked with whenNotPaused, such as stakeGGP() and withdrawGGP(). However, other external entry points – notably restakeGGP() in the Staking contract, claimAndRestake() in the ClaimNodeOp contract and the guardian‑only spend() function – do not include the pause guard. Because these functions are not protected, they can still be invoked while the system is paused, allowing token transfers to and from the vault and additional staking actions. The root cause is a missing whenNotPaused check on functions that move funds, combined with reliance on other modifiers (onlySpecificRegisteredContract, onlyGuardian) that do not consider the paused state. An attacker or any user who can call claimAndRestake can trigger a sequence where the contract withdraws GGP from the vault, optionally restakes it via restakeGGP, and then forwards a claim amount to the caller, all while the protocol is supposed to be in a halted state. This bypass defeats the intended admin control, potentially enabling unintended token movement, reward manipulation, or draining of the vault if the caller is able to repeatedly claim and restake. The issue manifests only when the pause flag is active; under normal operation the functions behave as expected, which makes the bug easy to miss in routine testing that focuses on the primary stake and withdraw functions. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the presence of the whenNotPaused modifier across related functions and identified the inconsistency. From a user’s perspective the UI may display “paused” while the user can still submit a claim or restake transaction, leading to confusion because the expected behavior is that all token‑moving actions are blocked. This class of bug falls under inconsistent access‑control or emergency‑stop bypass, where some code paths unintentionally ignore the global pause state. The recommended remediation is to add the whenNotPaused modifier to restakeGGP(), claimAndRestake() and, if appropriate, to the spend() function, ensuring that every external function that can transfer tokens respects the paused flag and restores a uniform security posture.

title: Inflation rate can be reduced by half at most if it gets called every 1.99 interval
poc:
Consider the scenario:

1. Assume last inflation time is `InflationIntervalStartTime = 100`. `InflationIntervalSeconds = 50`.
2. At `timestamp = 199`, function `getInflationAmt()` will calculate

```solidity
inflationIntervalsElapsed = (199 - 100) / 50 = 1
// Compute inflation for total inflation intervals elapsed
for (uint256 i = 0; i < inflationIntervalsElapsed; i++) {
    newTotalSupply = newTotalSupply.mulWadDown(inflationRate);
} // @audit only loop once.
```

3. And then in `inflate()` function, `InflationIntervalStartTime` is still updated to current timestamp, so `InflationIntervalStartTime = 199`.
4. If this sequence of actions are repeatedly used, we can easily see

    InflationIntervalStartTime = 199, inflated count = 1
    InflationIntervalStartTime = 298, inflated count = 2
    InflationIntervalStartTime = 397, inflated count = 3
    InflationIntervalStartTime = 496, inflated count = 4
    InflationIntervalStartTime = 595, inflated count = 5

While at `timestamp = 595`, inflated times should be `(595 - 100) / 50 = 9` instead.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation‑schedule miscalculation that stems from two closely related logic errors. First, the contract determines how many inflation intervals have elapsed by dividing the time difference between the current block timestamp and the stored start time by the configured interval length. Because Solidity uses integer division, any fractional part of an interval is discarded, so a time span of 1.99 intervals is counted as only one interval. Second, after performing the inflation step the contract updates the stored start time to the current block timestamp instead of advancing it by the exact number of whole intervals that have been accounted for (intervalLength × intervalsElapsed). When the inflation function is called slightly before a full interval has elapsed, the rounding down causes the contract to recognise fewer intervals than actually passed, and the incorrect start‑time update discards the missed fractional interval permanently. Over repeated calls this leads to a cumulative shortfall in the number of inflation periods that are applied; for example, after five calls spaced just under the interval boundary the contract may have applied only five intervals instead of the nine that should have been applied. The impact is a reduction of token emissions – users receive less newly minted tokens than the protocol’s economic model promises, resulting in lower rewards, diminished yield, and a deviation from the intended supply curve. The issue does not enable theft of existing funds, but it harms token holders and any downstream incentives that rely on the expected inflation rate. It manifests only when the inflation function is invoked at sub‑optimal timing, which can happen unintentionally or be deliberately exploited by an attacker who schedules calls to maximise the rounding loss. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that balances increase slower than advertised, rewards appear missing, or the protocol’s “inflation” dashboard shows a lower rate than expected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the inflation logic, where the auditor noticed the integer division and the start‑time update pattern. Because the effect is a gradual under‑inflation rather than an outright failure, it can be hard to spot without precise accounting checks. The proper fix is to compute the elapsed intervals using a method that accounts for the fractional part (for example, rounding up or using a ceiling function) and to update the stored start time by adding intervalLength × intervalsElapsed instead of overwriting it with the current timestamp, thereby preserving any leftover time for the next inflation cycle.

title: Rialto may not be able to cancel minipools created by contracts that cannot receive AVAX
description: A malicious node operator may create a minipool that cannot be cancelled.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the Rialto contract attempts to cancel a minipool using the function cancelMinipoolByMultisig. The cancellation logic follows a push‑payment pattern: it transfers the node operator’s AVAX balance to the recorded owner address with a direct call (owner.safeTransferETH). The root cause is the assumption that the owner is always able to receive AVAX. If the owner is a contract that does not implement a payable fallback or deliberately reverts on ETH receipt, the low‑level call fails and the entire cancel transaction reverts with an ETH_TRANSFER_FAILED error. An attacker who controls the node operator can therefore create a minipool whose owner is a contract that blocks ETH, causing any subsequent cancellation attempt by Rialto to fail. This can be exploited by deploying a malicious contract as the node operator, staking the required GGP, creating a minipool, and then refusing ETH transfers. When Rialto later tries to cancel the minipool—either as part of a multisig governance action or an automated cleanup—the transfer to the owner fails, the revert aborts the state change, and the minipool remains in its pre‑launch status. The impact is that the protocol loses the ability to cancel that specific minipool, effectively locking the associated AVAX and preventing the protocol from freeing resources or enforcing its intended lifecycle. Users (node operators, delegators, and the protocol itself) may see the minipool stuck in an active state, UI elements indicating cancellation succeeded while on‑chain the status is unchanged, and funds that appear to disappear from the protocol’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the warden demonstrated that checking the return value of a call can be used as a grief vector, and a proof‑of‑concept test reproduced the failure by using a contract that cannot receive AVAX. The problem is subtle because ETH transfers are often assumed to succeed, and the code does not include a fallback mechanism or a pull‑payment alternative, making the failure easy to miss in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should adopt a pull‑over‑push pattern: instead of sending AVAX directly during cancellation, it should record the amount owed and allow the owner to withdraw it via a separate function, or it should handle failed transfers gracefully (e.g., by emitting an event and marking the funds as claimable). This change removes the reliance on the recipient’s ability to accept ETH and eliminates the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Recreated pools receive a wrong AVAX amount due to miscalculated compounded liquid staker amount
description: After recreation, minipools will receive more AVAX than the sum of their owners’ current stake and the rewards that they generated.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the minipool recreation logic of the protocol’s MinipoolManager contract. When a minipool finishes a validation cycle and is recreated, the function `recreateMinipool` compounds the AVAX amount by adding the node operator’s reward to the previously deposited AVAX and then writes the same compounded value to both the node‑operator amount (`avaxNodeOpAmt`) and the liquid‑staker amount (`avaxLiquidStakerAmt`). The code comment explicitly states a "1:1 nodeOp:liqStaker funds ratio" and the implementation assumes that the rewards earned by the node operator and the liquid stakers are identical. In reality the protocol charges a commission fee on the liquid‑staker share, so the liquid‑staker reward is smaller than the node‑operator reward. Because the function adds the full node‑operator reward to the liquid‑staker amount, the stored `avaxLiquidStakerAmt` becomes larger than the actual liquid‑staker entitlement. Consequently the contract believes that more AVAX has been supplied by liquid stakers than truly exists, leading to an inflated assigned AVAX balance (`increaseAVAXAssigned`) and an over‑draw from the liquid‑staker pool when the minipool is recreated. This mis‑calculation can occur whenever a minipool is recreated after a validation period in which the node operator and liquid stakers received unequal rewards – a condition that is common because of the commission fee. The impact is primarily accounting‑related: the protocol’s “high‑water” value for liquid‑staker AVAX is falsified, the equality check that triggers `recordStakingEnd` may never succeed, and the system may attempt to pull more AVAX from the liquid‑staker reserve than is available, potentially stalling the staking lifecycle or causing unexpected failures when users try to withdraw. From a user’s perspective the pool appears to have a higher AVAX balance than expected, refunds may be missing, or withdrawals may revert with no clear error, creating confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors wrote a unit test that demonstrated the liquid‑staker amount being increased by the node‑operator reward instead of the correct liquid‑staker reward. The bug is subtle because the contract still respects the overall AVAX supply – no funds are directly stolen – but the invariant that node‑operator and liquid‑staker balances remain equal after compounding is broken, making the problem easy to overlook in routine testing. The recommended mitigation is to stop assuming equal rewards and either use an average of the two reward amounts or, more safely, apply the liquid‑staker reward amount when updating both balances. This ensures that the compounded AVAX amount never exceeds the actual liquid‑staker contribution, preserving accounting integrity and allowing the staking lifecycle to complete correctly.

title: State Transition: Minipools can be created using other operator’s AVAX deposit via recreateMinipool
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑transition flaw in the MinipoolManager that allows a minipool to be recreated after the node operator’s AVAX deposit has already been returned to the operator. The contract tracks AVAX deposits at the vault level rather than per‑operator, and the FSM permits the sequence Prelaunch→Launched→Staking→Error→Finished→Prelaunch. When a minipool reaches the Finished state, the operator’s AVAX is withdrawn, leaving the vault empty of that operator’s funds but still holding AVAX that belongs to other pending minipools. If the Rialto (or any privileged caller) subsequently invokes recreateMinipool on the finished minipool, the manager creates a new minipool in the Prelaunch state without requiring a fresh operator deposit. The new minipool then consumes AVAX that was intended for a different operator’s pending pool, causing the second pool to fail to launch with an InsufficientContractBalance error. This can be exploited by an attacker who front‑runs the Rialto’s claimAndInitiateStaking call or deliberately triggers recreateMinipool after a withdrawal, effectively stealing or mis‑allocating AVAX from other operators and creating a denial‑of‑service condition for honest participants. The impact is that funds disappear from the vault for legitimate minipools, users see their expected launch fail, balances remain zero, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about per‑operator AVAX guarantees are broken. The issue occurs only in the specific combination of states that allow recreation after a Finished transition; it is not triggered in normal Prelaunch→Launched→Staking flows. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test case reproduced the sequence and observed the vault balance dropping from 2 × depositAmt to depositAmt after recreation, followed by a revert when a second operator attempted to launch. The bug is subtle because the contract’s overall AVAX balance appears correct, but the per‑operator accounting is lost, making the problem easy to miss without state‑specific checks. The proper fix is to enforce that any state that can transition back to Prelaunch must first ensure the operator’s deposit is either retained or explicitly returned, and to tie AVAX accounting to the specific minipool rather than a shared vault, preventing recreation without a fresh deposit. In essence, the contract should treat the recreateMinipool transition as a fresh creation that requires a new AVAX deposit, or disallow the transition altogether for pools that have already withdrawn their funds.

title: Functions `cancelMinipool`
description: The value of `RewardsStartTime` shows when node runner started the minipool and validation rewards are generated by node runner. It is used to see if node runners are eligible for ggp rewards or not and node runners should run their node for minimum amount of time during the rewarding cycle to be eligible for rewards. But right now node runner can create a mimipool and cancel it (after waiting time) and even so the minipool generated no rewards and cancelled the value of `RewardsStartTime` won’t get reset for node runner and in the end of the cycle node runner would be eligible for rewards (node runner can create another minipool near the end of cycle). So this issue would cause wrong reward distribution between node runners and code doesn’t correctly track `RewardsStartTime` for node runners and malicious node runners can use this issue and receive rewards without running validation nodes for the minimum amount of required time.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s handling of the per‑node‑runner timestamp called RewardsStartTime, which is set when a minipool is created and later used to decide eligibility for GGP rewards based on the amount of time the node has been active during a reward cycle. The cancelMinipool function permits a node runner to cancel a minipool after the mandatory moratorium, but it does not reset or clear RewardsStartTime when the minipool is cancelled. As a result, a malicious node runner can create a minipool at the beginning of a reward cycle, cancel it without ever running a validator, and then create a new minipool near the end of the same cycle. Because RewardsStartTime still reflects the original creation time, the eligibility check (ClaimNodeOp.isEligible) treats the runner as having satisfied the minimum active‑time requirement, granting GGP rewards despite no actual validation work. This leads to incorrect reward distribution, allowing users to earn rewards without providing the required service. The bug manifests whenever a node runner cancels a minipool and later creates another minipool within the same reward cycle; it affects all node runners, the protocol’s reward accounting, and ultimately token holders who expect fair distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the cancelMinipool logic and noticed that the rewardsStartTime variable is never cleared or recomputed after a cancellation. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit any event indicating a change to the rewards timestamp, and the UI may still show the runner as eligible for rewards, giving the impression that everything is functioning correctly. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent accounting bugs where a lifecycle operation fails to clean up time‑based eligibility data. To remediate, the contract should either clear RewardsStartTime when a minipool is cancelled or recompute it only after a minipool has successfully entered the active state, and it should prevent cancellation of a minipool that would affect reward eligibility. From a user perspective, a node operator expects that cancelling a minipool removes any claim to future rewards, but instead they may see “eligible for GGP rewards” in the dashboard even though they never ran a validator, effectively receiving funds that should not exist. This violates the protocol’s business logic that rewards are earned proportionally to the time a node is actively validating.

title: MultisigManager may not be able to add a valid Multisig
description: When more than 10 multisig, it is impossible to modify or delete the old ones, making it impossible to create new valid ones.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MultisigManager component, which enforces a hard‑coded limit of ten registered multisig addresses. The contract tracks the total number of entries using a simple counter and does not distinguish between active (enabled) and inactive (disabled) multisigs when evaluating this limit. Consequently, once ten distinct multisig addresses have been registered, the internal counter reaches the maximum and any subsequent call to register a new address triggers a MultisigLimitReached revert. Because the contract provides no function to delete, deregister, or replace an existing entry, even if all previously registered multisigs are later disabled, the counter remains at ten and the system is permanently unable to accept new, valid multisig contracts. This logic flaw means that the protocol can become locked into using an outdated or compromised set of guardians, violating the expectation that governance can evolve its signing authority over time. From a user perspective, the UI may stop offering the option to add a new multisig, and attempts to do so result in a transaction failure with no obvious indication that the underlying issue is the static limit. The impact is that the protocol’s control plane may be rendered inoperable or forced to rely on a disabled multisig, exposing funds to risk if the remaining guardians are compromised. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors observed that the count of multisigs is never decremented after a disable operation, leading to a permanent cap. The bug is subtle because the limit is relatively high for initial deployment, so it may not surface until the full set of multisigs is exhausted or deliberately disabled. To remediate, the contract should either (a) provide a method to replace or delete an existing multisig entry, (b) adjust the counting logic to consider only enabled multisigs when enforcing the limit, or (c) increase the limit and implement proper governance for managing the multisig set. Implementing any of these fixes restores the ability to rotate guardians and aligns the contract’s behavior with standard governance expectations.

title: Cancellation of minipool may skip `MinipoolCancelMoratoriumSeconds` checking if it was cancelled before
description: When canceling a minipool that was canceled before, it may skip `MinipoolCancelMoratoriumSeconds` checking and allow the user to cancel the minipool immediately.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the minipool lifecycle management that allows a node operator to bypass the mandatory cancellation waiting period when a minipool is recreated after an earlier cancellation. The contract stores a rewards start timestamp for each operator when the first minipool is created. The cancelMinipool function checks the elapsed time against the protocol‑defined MinipoolCancelMoratoriumSeconds by comparing the current block timestamp with this stored rewards start time. When a minipool is cancelled, the stored rewards start time is not cleared. Consequently, if the operator creates a new minipool using the same address, the contract reuses the old rewards start timestamp. The moratorium check therefore sees a large elapsed interval and permits immediate cancellation, even though the new minipool has just been created. This bypass occurs because the state transition logic does not reset the timing variable on recreation, and the cancellation logic relies on the wrong reference point (rewards start time instead of the minipool creation time). An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly creating and cancelling minipools without waiting, effectively evading the intended lock‑up period. While the exploit does not directly steal funds, it undermines the protocol’s economic assumptions, allowing operators to avoid penalties, manipulate reward calculations, or flood the system with short‑lived minipools, potentially degrading liquidity and fairness. The issue manifests when a user attempts to cancel a freshly created minipool; the UI may incorrectly enable the cancel button immediately, leading to confusion as the expected waiting period (e.g., five days) is ignored and funds are returned instantly. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a second cancellation succeeded without the required time skip. It is subtle because the same function is used for both initial creation and recreation, and the timestamp variable is only set once, making the oversight easy to miss in code review. The proper fix is to reset the rewards start time (or store a separate minipool creation timestamp) each time a minipool is (re)created, and to base the moratorium check on that timestamp rather than the persistent rewards start time. This ensures that every new minipool must respect the configured cancellation delay, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Slashing fails when node operator doesn’t have enough staked `GGP`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs during the slashing of a node operator's GGP collateral when the calculated slash amount exceeds the operator's actual staked GGP balance. The protocol determines the required GGP collateral as 10% of the AVAX stake using the current GGP‑AVAX price from an oracle. When a minipool finishes and the operator has low availability, the contract computes the amount of GGP to slash based on the expected AVAX rewards and the same price oracle. If the GGP price has moved down since the minipool was created, the conversion can produce a slash amount larger than the operator’s remaining GGP stake. The core logic in MinipoolManager calls calculateGGPSlashAmt, which returns a value that is then passed to Staking.slashGGP. Inside Staking, decreaseGGPStake blindly subtracts the slash amount from the stored staked balance using subUint without first checking that the balance is sufficient. When the subtraction would underflow, the internal arithmetic reverts, causing the entire slash transaction to fail. Because the slash cannot be executed, the protocol is unable to penalise the misbehaving operator and the liquid stakers who were supposed to receive the slashed funds receive nothing. This failure only manifests when the oracle price changes unfavourably after the minipool is created, making it easy to miss during normal testing where prices remain stable. The issue was discovered by an audit test that deliberately altered the GGP price and observed a revert on recordStakingEnd, confirming that the underflow prevents the slash. From a user perspective the transaction to end staking reverts, the operator’s GGP collateral remains untouched, and liquid stakers see zero reward where they expected a payout. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or balance‑validation errors that break economic invariants. To remediate, the contract should verify that the operator’s staked GGP is at least the slash amount and, if not, slash the entire remaining stake (or otherwise handle the shortfall) before attempting the subtraction, thereby preventing underflow and ensuring the protocol can enforce penalties as intended.

title: Any duration can be passed by node operator
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing validation check on the staking duration supplied by a node operator when a minipool is created. The contract stores the caller‑provided duration value without enforcing the protocol‑defined bounds of fourteen to three hundred sixty‑five days. Later, the stored duration is used in the slashing logic to compute the expected AVAX rewards and consequently the amount of GGP that will be deducted from the node operator in case of a slash. Because the duration directly scales the reward calculation, a node operator can pass a very small value – for example one day – which drives the expected reward and the derived slash amount to the minimum possible. The vault prevents a zero‑duration value, but it does not stop a duration of one day, which is sufficient to reduce the penalty to a negligible figure. This flaw can be exploited by a malicious node operator who deliberately creates a minipool with an artificially short duration, stakes the required AVAX, and then, if a slash event occurs, receives an almost zero penalty while still receiving the full stake back. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s economic incentives: the node operator avoids the intended penalty, other participants see reduced rewards, and the protocol may lose the expected slashing revenue, potentially leading to a non‑trivial loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever a minipool is created and the duration parameter is not checked, which is the case in the current implementation of MinipoolManager.sol. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that created a minipool with a duration of one day and verified that the slash amount was effectively zero. The problem is subtle because the duration field is stored and later read, but the contract does not otherwise expose the value, making the abnormal low slash amount easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the supplied duration lies within the protocol‑specified range (≥14 days and ≤365 days) before persisting it, thereby aligning the slashing calculation with the intended economic model and preventing grief attacks that exploit an artificially short staking period.

title: Wrong reward distribution between early and late depositors because of the late `syncRewards`
description: Function `syncRewards()` distributes rewards to TokenggAVAX holders, it linearly distribute cycle’s rewards from `block.timestamp` to the cycle end time which is next multiple of the `rewardsCycleLength` (the end time of the cycle is defined and the real duration of the cycle changes). when a cycle ends `syncRewards()` should be called so the next cycle starts but if `syncRewards()` doesn’t get called fast, then users depositing or withdrawing funds before call to `syncRewards()` would lose their rewards and those rewards would go to users who deposited funds after `syncRewards()` call. contract should try to start the next cycle whenever deposit or withdraw happens to make sure rewards are distributed fairly between users.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract advances reward cycles through the public function syncRewards(). The function is intended to be called at the exact moment a rewards cycle ends, resetting the cycle end timestamp to the next multiple of the configured rewardsCycleLength and linearly releasing the accumulated rewards between the current block timestamp and that new end time. Because syncRewards() can only be triggered manually, if it is not executed promptly after a cycle finishes, the contract continues to treat the old cycle as active. During this lag, any deposits or withdrawals that occur before syncRewards() is finally called are accounted for in the wrong cycle: early depositors who added funds before the delayed call do not receive any portion of the upcoming rewards, and users who withdraw before the call receive zero reward for the time their funds were actually staked. Conversely, users who deposit after the delayed call are treated as if they participated for the whole new cycle and therefore capture the entire reward pool. This timing mismatch creates an unfair distribution of yield, effectively stealing expected rewards from early participants and granting them to later participants. The issue manifests when a rewards cycle ends (block.timestamp >= rewardsCycleEnd) but the contract owner or any external actor fails to invoke syncRewards() for an extended period, such as several days. Under these conditions, the linear reward schedule is compressed into a shorter interval once syncRewards() finally runs, causing the reward rate to spike and rewarding only the balances that exist after the call. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept deposits and show normal balances, yet the expected reward calculation (e.g., “I should earn X AVAX for 8 days of staking”) is not honored; the user may see a zero or dramatically reduced reward after withdrawal, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The flaw was identified during a security audit that examined the reward accounting logic and noticed that the syncRewards() revert prevents automatic cycle progression, leaving the system vulnerable to timing‑based reward skew. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the contract still emits rewards events and the total reward amount is unchanged; only the per‑user allocation is incorrect, which may only be observed by comparing expected versus actual payouts. The class of bug is a reward‑epoch timing or state‑transition race condition, where the contract’s accounting assumes a deterministic cycle boundary that is not enforced. To remediate, the contract should ensure that a new rewards cycle is started automatically on any state‑changing operation (deposit, withdraw) that occurs after the previous cycle’s end, or provide an incentive mechanism that guarantees syncRewards() is called promptly. Removing the revert that blocks early calls and integrating the sync logic into deposit/withdraw functions would align the reward distribution with the actual time each user’s funds were locked, restoring fairness and preventing loss of yield.

title: `maxWithdraw
description: Functions `maxWithdraw()` and `maxRedeem()` returns max amount of assets or shares owner would be able to withdraw taking into account liquidity in the TokenggAVAX contract, but logics don’t consider that when user withdraws the withdrawal amounts subtracted from `totalReleasedAssets` (in `beforeWithdraw()` function) so the maximum amounts that can user withdraws should always be lower than `totalReleasedAssets` (which shows all the deposits and withdraws) but because functions `maxWithdraw()` and `maxRedeem()` uses `totalAssets()` to calculate available AVAX which includes deposits and current cycle rewards so those functions would return wrong value (whenever the return value is bigger than `totalReleaseAssets` then it would be wrong).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency between the view functions that report the maximum amount a holder can withdraw (maxWithdraw and maxRedeem) and the actual accounting performed when a withdrawal is executed. The contract tracks two separate aggregates: totalReleasedAssets, which records the net amount of assets that have been deposited and actually released to users, and totalAssets, which also includes pending rewards that have not yet been released. The maxWithdraw function calculates the available AVAX as totalAssets minus the amount locked for staking, and then caps this value by the holder's share balance. Because totalAssets counts pending rewards, the computed available amount can be larger than totalReleasedAssets. When a user attempts to withdraw the amount returned by maxWithdraw, the beforeWithdraw hook subtracts the requested amount from totalReleasedAssets. If the requested amount exceeds totalReleasedAssets, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts. This mismatch can happen whenever the protocol has accrued rewards that are not yet part of totalReleasedAssets, a situation that is common when liquidity is low or rewards are high. The bug affects any token holder who relies on the maxWithdraw view, front‑end interfaces that display the maximum withdrawable balance, and other contracts that call maxWithdraw before performing a withdrawal. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by exercising edge‑case scenarios with low liquidity and large pending rewards. The issue is subtle because the view function appears to return a sensible number, so users only see a failure at the point of execution, making it hard to detect without thorough testing. The impact is that users may be shown a withdrawable amount that they cannot actually receive, leading to transaction reverts, a degraded user experience, and a breach of the ERC4626 specification that expects view functions to reflect real limits. To remediate, the maxWithdraw and maxRedeem calculations should be constrained by totalReleasedAssets (or the minimum of the current formula and totalReleasedAssets) so that the returned value never exceeds the amount that can be safely deducted from the contract’s accounting. This adjustment restores consistency between the view and state‑changing functions and brings the implementation back into compliance with the ERC4626 standard.

title: NodeOp can get rewards even if there was an error in registering the node as a validator
description:
The [documentation](https://multisiglabs.notion.site/Architecture-Protocol-Overview-4b79e351133f4d959a65a15478ec0121) says that the NodeOps could be elegible for GGP rewards if they have a valid minipool. The problem is that if the MiniPool [has an error](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/MinipoolManager.sol#L484) while registering the node as a validator, the NodeOp can get rewards even if the minipool had an error.

When the Rialto calls `recordStakingError()` function the `AssignedHighWater` is not reseted. So the malicious NodeOp (staker) can create pools which will have an error in the registration and get rewards from the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑eligibility accounting flaw in the MinipoolManager contract. When a minipool fails during the validator registration step, the Rialto contract calls recordStakingError, but this function does not clear the avaxAssignedHighWater value that was set by recordStakingStart. Because the high‑water mark remains at the amount that was originally assigned to the node operator, the protocol later treats the node operator as if it still has an active staking position and allows the nopClaim contract to consider the operator eligible for GGP rewards. An attacker who controls a node operator can deliberately trigger a registration error, withdraw the deposited AVAX, and later claim GGP rewards that were never earned. The impact is that the protocol distributes free GGP tokens, diluting token value and breaking the economic assumptions that rewards are only paid for successful validator participation. The bug occurs only when the state machine permits a transition from Staking to Error, which is currently allowed by the code even though such a transition cannot happen on Avalanche under normal operation. The affected parties are node operators who can exploit the flaw, the reward pool that loses tokens, and any token holder whose holdings are de‑valued. The issue was uncovered by an audit test that simulated the sequence: create minipool, call claimAndInitiateStaking, then recordStakingStart followed by recordStakingError, withdraw funds, and finally invoke the reward claim. Because the high‑water variable is internal and not reflected in external balances, the problem is subtle and may go unnoticed until a reward distribution is observed for a node that never successfully validated. The proper fix is to reset avaxAssignedHighWater inside recordStakingError or to forbid the Staking‑to‑Error transition altogether, ensuring that only minipools that have completed staking can accrue rewards. In user‑facing terms, a node operator expects to receive no rewards after a registration failure, but instead sees a positive GGP balance, indicating that the accounting logic incorrectly credits rewards despite the error.

title: Users may not be able to redeem their shares due to underflow
description:
The `totalReleasedAssets` variable is updated on the [syncRewards()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/TokenggAVAX.sol#L88) function if someone calls the function before `rewardsCycleEnd` the [redeemAVAX()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/TokenggAVAX.sol#L191) will be reverted because the `totalReleasedAssets` may not include all the rewards.

The ggAvax holder can not redeem his funds until the `rewardsCycleEnd`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can block ggAVAX token holders from redeeming their shares. The contract updates the totalReleasedAssets counter in the syncRewards function, but if syncRewards is called before the rewardsCycleEnd timestamp the counter does not yet reflect the full amount of rewards that will be distributed. When a user later calls redeemAVAX, the redeem logic compares the requested share amount against the totalReleasedAssets value and performs a subtraction that can underflow because the assets available are lower than the amount implied by the user’s share balance. The ERC4626 specification requires redeem to revert when the full share amount cannot be withdrawn, and the implementation follows this rule, causing the transaction to revert with an arithmetic error instead of returning a partial amount. This situation can be triggered deliberately by calling syncRewards early or can happen unintentionally at the very start of a ggAVAX pool when the first reward sync occurs before the cycle ends. The impact is that users see a failed redemption transaction, their UI shows no change in balance, and they cannot withdraw their principal or earned rewards until the rewards cycle finishes, effectively locking funds. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit where a reproducible test case demonstrated that after syncing rewards early, previewRedeem reported a higher asset amount than maxRedeem, and the subsequent redeem call reverted. The bug is hard to notice because it only appears under a specific timing condition and the contract otherwise behaves correctly; normal users would not see the mismatch unless they inspect the preview values or encounter a revert. The problem belongs to the class of rounding‑related accounting errors in ERC4626‑style vaults where state variables tracking released assets become inconsistent with share balances. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction that fails with an arithmetic error and a missing refund – the user expects to receive AVAX but receives nothing and the balance stays the same. To fix the issue the contract should either adjust the syncRewards logic to postpone updating totalReleasedAssets until the cycle end, or modify redeemAVAX to allow redemption of the maximum available amount rather than reverting, or otherwise ensure that the previewRedeem and maxRedeem values are always consistent and that rounding does not cause an underflow. Such a change would restore the ability for users to withdraw their funds at any time while still respecting the ERC4626 specification.

title: MinipoolManager: `recordStakingError` function does not decrease `minipoolCount` leading to too high GGP rewards for staker
description:
The `MinipoolManager.recordStakingError` function (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/MinipoolManager.sol#L484-L515>) does not decrease the `minipoolCount` of the staker.

This means that if a staker has a minipool that encounters an error, his `minipoolCount` can never go to zero again.

This is bad because the `minipoolCount` is used in `ClaimNodeOp.calculateAndDistributeRewards` to determine if the `rewardsStartTime` of the staker should be reset (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/ClaimNodeOp.sol#L81-L84>).

Since the `minipoolCount` cannot go to zero, the `rewardsStartTime` will never be reset.

This means that the staker is immediately eligible for rewards when he creates a minipool again whereas he should have to wait `rewardsEligibilityMinSeconds` before he is eligible (which is 14 days at the moment) (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/ClaimNodeOp.sol#L51>).

To conclude, failing to decrease the `minipoolCount` allows the staker to earn higher rewards because he is eligible for staking right after he creates a new minipool and does not have to wait again.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑management bug in the MinipoolManager contract where the function recordStakingError fails to decrement the minipoolCount associated with a staker after a minipool enters an error state. The root cause is that the function does not invoke the staking contract’s decreaseMinipoolCount method, leaving the counter permanently at a non‑zero value. Because the ClaimNodeOp contract uses minipoolCount to decide whether to reset the rewardsStartTime, a non‑zero count prevents the reset logic from running. Consequently, when the same staker creates a new minipool after the error, the rewardsStartTime is still set to the original value, making the staker immediately eligible for GGP rewards instead of having to wait the protocol‑defined rewardsEligibilityMinSeconds (currently fourteen days). This can be exploited by a staker who deliberately triggers a minipool error, calls recordStakingError, and then opens a fresh minipool to collect rewards without the intended waiting period, effectively inflating their reward earnings. The impact is an unfair increase in rewards for the affected staker, which distorts the protocol’s accounting and could lead to overall reward over‑distribution. The condition for the bug to manifest is any scenario where a minipool encounters an error and recordStakingError is executed; under normal successful staking the counter is correctly managed. The affected parties are the stakers (node operators) who receive extra rewards and the protocol itself, which suffers from inaccurate reward accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which added a test that logged the minipoolCount after each state transition and observed that the count remained at one even after recordStakingError was called. The bug is subtle because the counter is only used in a downstream eligibility check, so the discrepancy does not immediately surface in most view functions, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate the problem, the recordStakingError function should call staking.decreaseMinipoolCount(owner) so that the counter correctly reflects the removal of the failed minipool, allowing rewardsStartTime to be reset when the count reaches zero and restoring the intended waiting period before new rewards can be earned. This fix aligns the contract’s state with its business logic, ensuring that reward eligibility respects the defined time lock and preserving fairness in the reward distribution mechanism.

title: TokenggAVAX: maxDeposit and maxMint return wrong value when contract is paused
description:
The `TokenggAVAX` contract (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/TokenggAVAX.sol#L24>) can be paused.

The `whenTokenNotPaused` modifier is applied to the following functions (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/TokenggAVAX.sol#L225-L239>):  
`previewDeposit`, `previewMint`, `previewWithdraw` and `previewRedeem`

Thereby any calls to functions that deposit or withdraw funds revert.

There are two functions (`maxWithdraw` and `maxRedeem`) that calculate the max amount that can be withdrawn or redeemed respectively.

Both functions return `0` if the `TokenggAVAX` contract is paused.

The issue is that `TokenggAVAX` does not override the `maxDeposit` and `maxMint` functions (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/upgradeable/ERC4626Upgradeable.sol#L156-L162>) in the `ERC4626Upgradable` contract like it does for `maxWithdraw` and `maxRedeem`.

Thereby these two functions return a value that cannot actually be deposited or minted.

This can cause any components that rely on any of these functions to return a correct value to malfunction.

So `maxDeposit` and `maxMint` should return the value `0` when `TokenggAVAX` is paused.
poc:
1. The `TokenggAVAX` contract is paused by calling `Ocyticus.pauseEverything` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/Ocyticus.sol#L37-L43>)
2. `TokenggAVAX.maxDeposit` returns `type(uint256).max` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/upgradeable/ERC4626Upgradeable.sol#L157>)
3. However `deposit` cannot be called with this value because it is paused (`previewDeposit` reverts because of the `whenTokenNotPaused` modifier) (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-gogopool/blob/aec9928d8bdce8a5a4efe45f54c39d4fc7313731/contracts/contract/tokens/upgradeable/ERC4626Upgradeable.sol#L44>)
bug_full: The TokenggAVAX contract implements the ERC‑4626 tokenized vault standard and includes a pause mechanism that blocks any deposit or withdrawal operation when the contract is paused. The pause is enforced by the whenTokenNotPaused modifier, which is applied to previewDeposit, previewMint, previewWithdraw and previewRedeem, causing those calls to revert while the contract is paused. The ERC‑4626 specification requires the view functions maxDeposit, maxMint, maxWithdraw and maxRedeem to report the maximum amount that can be safely deposited, minted, withdrawn or redeemed in the current state. In TokenggAVAX the developers correctly overrode maxWithdraw and maxRedeem so that they return 0 when the contract is paused, but they omitted the same override for maxDeposit and maxMint. Consequently, the inherited implementation from ERC4626Upgradeable returns type(uint256).max (the largest possible uint256) regardless of the paused flag. When an external component queries maxDeposit or maxMint it receives a value that suggests an unlimited amount can be deposited or minted, yet any actual deposit or mint transaction will revert because the preview functions reject the operation. This discrepancy violates the ERC‑4626 accounting assumptions, breaks UI expectations (users see a large allowance but receive a transaction failure or a zero‑amount deposit), and can cause dependent contracts or front‑ends to malfunction, leading to user confusion, failed transactions and a denial‑of‑service style disruption. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s compliance with the ERC‑4626 spec; the inconsistency is subtle because the faulty functions are view‑only and do not directly revert, making the problem easy to overlook unless the pause state is exercised. The recommended remediation is to override maxDeposit and maxMint in TokenggAVAX, mirroring the logic used for maxWithdraw and maxRedeem, and return 0 when the contract is paused. This aligns the contract with the standard, ensures that all maximum‑value queries accurately reflect the operational state, and prevents misleading information from being presented to users or other contracts.

title: Division by zero error can block `RewardsPool#startRewardCycle` if all multisig wallet are disabled
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error that occurs in the RewardsPool.startRewardsCycle function when the contract attempts to distribute GGP tokens to multisig wallets. The internal helper distributeMultisigAllotment calculates tokensPerMultisig as allotment / enabledCount without first verifying that enabledCount, the number of enabled multisig contracts, is greater than zero. If all multisig wallets have been disabled or none have been added, enabledCount equals zero, the division triggers a runtime exception and the entire startRewardsCycle transaction reverts. This situation can be reproduced by disabling every multisig wallet (or by deploying the system without any multisig) and then calling startRewardsCycle, as demonstrated in the test suite where the transaction fails with “Division or modulo by 0”. The impact is that the rewards cycle cannot be started, so protocol participants – the DAO, node operators and any users expecting GGP rewards – receive no tokens and the protocol’s incentive mechanism is effectively frozen. The bug is hard to notice because the normal operating path always has at least one enabled multisig, so the edge case is not exercised in routine testing.
