It belongs to the class of arithmetic errors where unchecked division leads to a revert, a common source of denial‑of‑service failures in smart contracts. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails, the UI may show an error or no reward transfer, and balances remain unchanged even though the user expected a payout. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit check that enabledCount > 0 before performing the division, or to skip the multisig distribution step when there are no enabled wallets, thereby preventing the revert and allowing the rest of the reward cycle to proceed.

title: Inaccurate estimation of validation rewards from function `ExpectedRewardAVA` in `MiniPoolManager.sol`
description: The validation rewards can be inaccurately displayed to user and the slashed amount can be wrong when slashing happens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that estimates validation rewards for Avalanche validators, named getExpectedAVAXRewardsAmt, which is used both to display expected AVAX earnings to users and as an input to the slash calculation in the MiniPoolManager contract. The implementation simplifies the reward calculation to a linear formula: rate multiplied by the staked AVAX amount and the validation duration, divided by 365 days. This approach ignores the sophisticated reward model defined by Avalanche, which incorporates remaining token supply, the proportion of existing supply, the proportion of staking duration relative to a maximum, and a dynamic minting rate. Because the contract relies on a single rate obtained from the ProtocolDAO, the estimated reward can be significantly inaccurate, especially for durations that differ from a full year or for varying stake sizes. When a slash event occurs, the contract calls calculateGGPSlashAmt with the estimated reward amount; an incorrect estimate leads to an incorrect slash amount, causing either an under‑slashing (allowing a validator to retain more GGP than intended) or an over‑slashing (penalising a validator more than justified). From the user’s perspective the UI may show a reward that is lower or higher than the actual expected earnings, and after a slash the user may notice an unexpected GGP deduction or, conversely, a smaller penalty than anticipated. The issue is discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the contract’s formula with the official Avalanche reward specification and noticing the mismatch. It is hard to detect because the displayed numbers appear plausible and the discrepancy only manifests under specific duration or amount scenarios, which may not be exercised in routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑logic errors where a reward or interest formula is implemented incorrectly, violating accounting assumptions that rewards scale with both stake size and time in a non‑linear fashion. To remediate, the ExpectedRewardAVA implementation should be aligned with the full Avalanche reward algorithm, either by fetching a duration‑adjusted rate from the DAO or by reproducing the complete calculation (including remaining supply, portion of existing supply, and dynamic minting rate) inside the contract, ensuring that both reward display and slash calculations reflect the true economic model.

title: An attacker can make users unable to cancel their L1 calls on Ethereum To Arbitrum
description:
[EthereumToArbitrumRelayer.sol#L118-#L127](https://github.com/pooltogether/ERC5164/blob/5647bd84f2a6d1a37f41394874d567e45a97bf48/src/ethereum-arbitrum/EthereumToArbitrumRelayer.sol#L118-#L127)  

When someone wants to make calls to Arbitrum from Ethereum, first they call `relayCalls` to fingerprint their data and then anyone else can call `processCalls` to process the calls. According to the doc in Inbox source code <https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/blob/1f32bec6b9b228bb2fab4bfa02867716f65d0c5c/contracts/src/bridge/Inbox.sol#L427>, function `createRetryableTicket` has one parameter called `callValueRefundAddress` and this is the address that is granted the option to `cancel` a `Retryable`. In `EthereumToArbitrumRelayer.sol` it’s currently set as `msg.sender` (5th parameter) which is whoever makes the call to function `processCall`:
```solidity
uint256 _ticketID = inbox.createRetryableTicket{ value: msg.value }(
      address(executor),
      0,
      _maxSubmissionCost,
      msg.sender,
      msg.sender,
      _gasLimit,
      _gasPriceBid,
      _data
    );
```

This implementation allows an attacker to remove the possibility of a user to cancel their calls, which is an important mechanism to be properly implemented. This scenario demonstrates how this could happen:

* User A calls `relayCalls` to fingerprint their calls
* User B calls `processCalls` to process user A’s calls.
* User A now changes his mind and wants to cancel his calls but he’s unable to since `callValueRefundAddress` is set to user B’s address, now user B is the one who decides whether to cancel user A’s calls or not, which should be user A’s option.
* Another common case is when users’s calls failed, anyone can try to `redeem` it, according to the doc <https://developer.arbitrum.io/arbos/l1-to-l2-messaging>. So if someone calls `processCalls` to process others’s calls and it fails, the owner of the calls now cannot cancel their calls and anyone else can redeem (reexecute) them.

It should be noted here that `EthereumToArbitrumRelayer.sol` provides no other functionality to cancel users’s calls, but it seems to rely only on Arbitrum’s Retryable cancel mechanism to do so.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the EthereumToArbitrumRelayer contract where the function that creates an Arbitrum retryable ticket passes msg.sender as the callValueRefundAddress parameter. This address is granted the exclusive right to cancel the retryable ticket on L2. Because processCalls can be invoked by any external account, an attacker who processes another user’s queued calls becomes the refund address and therefore the only party able to cancel the ticket. The original user, who originally fingerprinted the calls via relayCalls, loses the ability to cancel their own request. Exploitation proceeds by a malicious actor calling processCalls for a victim’s pending calls; once the ticket is created, the attacker can either cancel the ticket or prevent the victim from cancelling it, and may also redeem a failed ticket, forcing execution of unwanted logic. The impact is a denial‑of‑service or griefing scenario where users cannot withdraw or reverse their L1‑to‑L2 messages, potentially locking funds or causing unwanted state changes on Arbitrum. The issue manifests whenever processCalls is called by an address different from the original sender, which is a common situation because the relayer does not restrict who may invoke the function and provides no separate cancellation interface. Affected parties include any user of the relayer service, the PoolTogether protocol that relies on the ability to cancel retryable tickets, and any funds locked in the retryable ticket. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the relayer’s interaction with the Arbitrum Inbox contract and noticing that the refund address was incorrectly set to the caller rather than the original sender. The bug is subtle because the contract itself does not expose a cancel function, leading developers to assume that the Arbitrum cancel mechanism will work as intended for the original user. Conceptually, this is a privilege‑escalation or authority‑misassignment bug where the wrong address is granted cancellation rights, a class of errors often seen when refund or callback addresses are taken from msg.sender without proper validation. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a request has been processed but the “cancel” button is missing or ineffective, and the user may see their funds remain locked with no way to retrieve them. The expected behavior—being able to cancel a pending L1‑to‑L2 call—is violated, breaking the accounting assumption that a sender can always reverse a pending transaction. The recommended fix is to pass the original sender’s address (stored as _sender) as the callValueRefundAddress, or to add an explicit cancellation function that restricts the right to the user who originally submitted the call, thereby restoring the intended cancellation capability.

title: When a smart contract calls `CrossChainRelayerArbitrum.processCalls`, excess submission fees may be lost
description:
When the user calls CrossChainRelayerArbitrum.processCalls, ETH is sent as the submission fee.

According to the documentation : <https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum/blob/master/docs/L1_L2_Messages.md#retryable-transaction-lifecycle>
```
Credit-Back Address: Address to which all excess gas is credited on L2; i.e., excess ETH for base submission cost (MaxSubmissionCost - ActualSubmissionCostPaid) and excess ETH provided for L2 execution ( (GasPrice x MaxGas) - ActualETHSpentInExecution).
...
Submission fee is collected: submission fee is deducted from the sender’s L2 account; MaxSubmissionCost - submission fee is credited to Credit-Back Address.
```

The excess submission fee is refunded to the address on L2 of the `excessFeeRefundAddress` provided when calling `createRetryableTicket`.
```solidity
 * @notice Put a message in the L2 inbox that can be reexecuted for some fixed amount of time if it reverts
 * @dev all msg.value will deposited to callValueRefundAddress on L2
 * @param destAddr destination L2 contract address
 * @param l2CallValue call value for retryable L2 message
 * @param  maxSubmissionCost Max gas deducted from user's L2 balance to cover base submission fee
 * @param excessFeeRefundAddress maxgas x gasprice - execution cost gets credited here on L2 balance
 * @param callValueRefundAddress l2Callvalue gets credited here on L2 if retryable txn times out or gets cancelled
 * @param maxGas Max gas deducted from user's L2 balance to cover L2 execution
 * @param gasPriceBid price bid for L2 execution
 * @param data ABI encoded data of L2 message
 * @return unique id for retryable transaction (keccak256(requestID, uint(0) )
 */
function createRetryableTicket(
    address destAddr,
    uint256 l2CallValue,
    uint256 maxSubmissionCost,
    address excessFeeRefundAddress,
    address callValueRefundAddress,
    uint256 maxGas,
    uint256 gasPriceBid,
    bytes calldata data
) external payable virtual override onlyWhitelisted returns (uint256) {
```

In `CrossChainRelayerArbitrum.processCalls`, `excessFeeRefundAddress == msg.sender`.
```solidity
uint256 _ticketID = inbox.createRetryableTicket{ value: msg.value }(
  address(executor),
  0,
  _maxSubmissionCost,
  msg.sender,   // @audit : excessFeeRefundAddress
  msg.sender,  // @audit: callValueRefundAddress
  _gasLimit,
  _gasPriceBid,
  _data
);
```

For EOA accounts, the excess submission fees are correctly refunded to their address on L2. However, for smart contracts, since there may not exist a corresponding address on L2, these excess submission fees will be lost.

Also, since the `callValueRefundAddress` is also `msg.sender`, according to the documentation, if the Retryable Ticket is cancelled or expired, then the smart contract caller may lose all the submission fees
```
If the Retryable Ticket is cancelled or expires before it is redeemed, Callvalue is credited to Beneficiary.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way CrossChainRelayerArbitrum.processCalls forwards the submission fee refund addresses when creating a retryable ticket on Arbitrum. The function passes msg.sender as both the excessFeeRefundAddress and the callValueRefundAddress, assuming that the caller has a corresponding L2 address that can receive the refunded ETH. This assumption holds for externally owned accounts (EOAs) because an EOA has a direct L2 counterpart, but it fails for smart contracts, which do not have an automatic L2 address mapping. Consequently, when a contract invokes processCalls and supplies more ETH than required for the base submission cost, the excess portion is sent to a non‑existent L2 address and is effectively lost. The same issue applies to the call value refund: if the retryable ticket is cancelled or expires before being redeemed, the callValueRefundAddress (again msg.sender) receives no refund, causing the contract to lose the entire amount it forwarded as msg.value. The root cause is an improper handling of refund destinations – the code hard‑codes msg.sender without providing a way to specify an alternative address that can actually receive funds on L2. Exploitation does not require a sophisticated attack; any contract that calls processCalls with an over‑payment will experience the loss, and an attacker could deliberately trigger ticket cancellation to increase the impact. The impact is a silent drain of ETH from the calling contract, visible to the user as a balance reduction or a transaction that appears successful but leaves the contract with less funds than expected. This situation occurs whenever a non‑EOA contract calls processCalls, especially when the caller over‑estimates maxSubmissionCost or when the retryable ticket fails to be redeemed. Affected parties include any contracts that rely on the relayer for cross‑chain messaging, their owners, and ultimately the protocol that assumes refunds will be returned. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the Arbitrum documentation on retryable ticket lifecycle and comparing it with the implementation of processCalls, revealing the mismatch between expected refund behavior and actual code. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the loss happens after the call completes, and there is no explicit error indicating that the refund address is invalid. To remediate, the contract should either restrict processCalls to EOAs only or, preferably, expose parameters that allow the caller to provide explicit excessFeeRefundAddress and callValueRefundAddress values that point to an address capable of receiving L2 refunds, such as an EOA or a designated treasury. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees that excess fees are returned and prevents unintended ETH loss, aligning the implementation with the documented refund mechanism.

title: `CrossChainExecutor` contracts do not update the necessary states for failing transactions
description:
[EthereumToOptimismExecutor.sol#L45-L59](https://github.com/pooltogether/ERC5164/blob/5647bd84f2a6d1a37f41394874d567e45a97bf48/src/ethereum-optimism/EthereumToOptimismExecutor.sol#L45-L59)  
[EthereumToArbitrumExecutor.sol#L31-L45](https://github.com/pooltogether/ERC5164/blob/5647bd84f2a6d1a37f41394874d567e45a97bf48/src/ethereum-arbitrum/EthereumToArbitrumExecutor.sol#L31-L45)

The `CrossChainExecutorArbitrum` and `CrossChainExecutorOptimism` contracts both use `CallLib` library to invoke `Call`s on external contract. As per the `CallLib` library implementation, any failing `Call` results in the entire transaction getting reverted.

The `CrossChainExecutor` contracts does not store whether the calls in `CallLib.Call[]` were already attempted which failed.

This creates several issues for `CrossChainExecutor` contracts.

1. Offchain components can be tricked to submit failing `Call[]`s again and again. This can be used to drain the offchain component of gas.
2. Once a failing `Call[]` was invoked (which failed) and if again the same `Call[]` is invoked, the transaction should revert with `CallsAlreadyExecuted` error but it reverts with `CallFailure` error.
3. It is difficult to determine whether a to-be executed `Call[]` is pending or the invocation was already tried but failed.

PoCs for the above issues are listed below.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CrossChainExecutor contracts used for cross‑chain message delivery on Arbitrum and Optimism. These contracts rely on the CallLib library to execute an array of external calls (Call[]). CallLib is designed so that if any individual call fails, the entire transaction reverts. However, the executor contracts do not persist any information about whether a particular Call[] batch has already been attempted and failed. Consequently, when a batch contains a failing call, the transaction reverts with a generic CallFailure error and no on‑chain flag is set to indicate that this batch was already processed. Off‑chain relayer components, which monitor pending messages, cannot distinguish between a batch that has never been tried and one that has already failed. This ambiguity allows an attacker or a malicious relayer to repeatedly submit the same failing Call[] batch, causing the relayer to waste gas on each attempt. Moreover, because there is no expiration or nonce mechanism, a previously failed batch can be replayed at a later time when the contract state has changed, potentially causing unintended side effects such as re‑enabling a paused system. The impact is primarily economic for the relayer service (gas drain) and logical for the protocol (risk of non‑idempotent state changes). The issue manifests when a batch includes a call that reverts; the executor does not record the failure, the transaction reverts with CallFailure, and the off‑chain component may continue to treat the message as pending. Users observing the UI will see a transaction revert with a generic error and may be confused why the same message keeps failing without any indication that it was already attempted. The root cause is the combination of CallLib’s all‑or‑nothing revert behavior and the executor’s lack of state tracking for attempted batches. This makes the problem hard to notice because the on‑chain logs do not differentiate a first‑time failure from a repeated one, and the off‑chain service receives no explicit signal. A proper fix involves persisting a flag (e.g., a mapping from message hash to execution status) that records whether a batch has been attempted, emitting distinct events for CallSuccess and CallFailure, and adjusting CallLib to return a boolean status instead of reverting outright. Adding an expiration or nonce scheme would further prevent replay of stale failed messages, eliminating the gas‑drain attack vector and ensuring that protocol state changes cannot be unintentionally triggered by replayed calls.

title: Bypass `userWithdrawLimitPerPeriod` check
description: User can bypass the `userWithdrawLimitPerPeriod` check by transferring the balance to another account.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a per‑period withdrawal limit that is enforced only against the address that initiates the withdraw call. The contract records how much each address has withdrawn during the current period (userToAmountWithdrawnThisPeriod) and compares it with a fixed cap (userWithdrawLimitPerPeriod). Because the limit is tied to the caller’s address, an attacker can split his holdings across multiple addresses and withdraw the full amount from each address in the same period. The root cause is that the accounting of withdrawn funds does not follow the logical user identity; it relies solely on msg.sender and does not consider token transfers that move balance between accounts. An exploit proceeds as follows: a user deposits a large amount, calls the withdraw function and extracts the maximum allowed amount (for example 1,000 tokens). The contract updates the per‑address counter and blocks any further withdrawal from that address for the remainder of the period. The user then transfers the remaining balance (the other 1,000 tokens) to a second address that has not withdrawn anything yet. Because the limit check in the withdraw hook is performed against the new address, the contract sees a fresh counter of zero and permits another full‑limit withdrawal, effectively allowing the user to extract more than the intended per‑period total. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the withdrawal limit has been reached for the first account, but the funds are still available after a simple transfer, leading to a mismatch between the displayed limit and the actual amount that can be taken. The impact is that the protocol’s economic safeguards are bypassed, potentially draining funds, breaking accounting assumptions, and allowing malicious actors to exceed rate‑limiting protections. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the withdraw path together with token transfers and observed that the limit counter was not shared across accounts. It can be hard to notice because the transfer function appears benign and the limit check is only present in the withdraw hook, giving the impression that the limit is globally enforced. To remediate, the contract should track the total withdrawn amount per logical user across all addresses, or restrict transfers of withdraw‑eligible balances, or only allow a transfer of the remaining unused limit. In conceptual terms the fix requires moving the limit enforcement from an address‑scoped check to a user‑scoped or global period counter, ensuring that moving tokens does not reset the withdrawal quota.

title: The recipient receives free collateral token if an ERC20 token that deducts a fee on transfer used as baseToken
description:
* There are some ERC20 tokens that deduct a fee on every transfer call. If these tokens are used as baseToken then:

    1. When depositing into the **Collateral** contract, the recipient will receive collateral token more than what they should receive.
    2. The **DepositRecord** contract will track wrong user deposit amounts and wrong globalNetDepositAmount as the added amount to both will be always more than what was actually deposited.
    3. When withdrawing from the **Collateral** contract, the user will receive less baseToken amount than what they should receive.
    4. The treasury will receive less fee and the user will receive more `PPO` tokens that occur in **DepositHook** and **WithdrawHook**.
poc:
Given:

  * baseToken is an ERC20 token that deduct a fee on every transfer call.
  * **FoT** is the deducted fee on transfer.
  * The user deposits baseToken to the **Collateral** contract by calling `deposit` function passing **_amount** as 100e18.
  * `baseToken.transferFrom` is called to transfer the amount from the user to the contract.

    * https://github.com/prepo-io/prepo-monorepo/blob/feat/2022-12-prepo/apps/smart-contracts/core/contracts/Collateral.sol#L49
  * The contract receives the _amount - **FoT**. Let’s assume the FoT percentage is 1%. Therefore, the actual amount received is 99e18.
  * When the **DepositHook** is called. the **_amount** passed is 100e18 which is wrong as it should be the actual amount 99e18.

    * https://github.com/prepo-io/prepo-monorepo/blob/feat/2022-12-prepo/apps/smart-contracts/core/contracts/Collateral.sol#L53
  * Calculating **collateralMintAmount** is based on the **_amount** (100e18- the fee for treasury) which will give the recipient additional collateral token that they shouldn’t receive.

    * https://github.com/prepo-io/prepo-monorepo/blob/feat/2022-12-prepo/apps/smart-contracts/core/contracts/Collateral.sol#L57
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s assumption that the amount specified in the deposit or withdraw call is the exact number of base tokens that will be transferred. Certain ERC20 tokens implement a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism, automatically deducting a percentage of the tokens on each transfer. When such a token is used as the baseToken, the transferFrom call delivers fewer tokens to the Collateral contract than the _amount argument supplied by the caller. Because the contract records and uses the original _amount for minting collateral tokens, updating DepositRecord, and calculating fees, the internal accounting becomes inconsistent: the recipient receives more collateral tokens than they should, the global net deposit amount is overstated, and during withdrawal the user receives fewer base tokens than expected while the treasury collects a reduced fee. This mismatch also causes the DepositHook and WithdrawHook to emit incorrect PPO token amounts. The issue is triggered whenever a fee‑on‑transfer token is deposited or withdrawn, affecting any user interacting with the protocol, the protocol’s treasury, and the overall token economics. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of token transfers and identified that the contract never verifies the actual amount received after the transfer. The bug is subtle because the transfer succeeds and no revert occurs, so the discrepancy is hidden from the user interface and standard event logs. It belongs to the class of “fee‑on‑transfer token handling errors” where contracts fail to account for tokens that modify the transferred amount. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately using a fee‑on‑transfer token to inflate their collateral balance, effectively receiving free collateral and extra PPO tokens while the protocol loses fee revenue. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected: after a deposit the wallet shows more collateral tokens than the deposited amount, and after a withdrawal the returned base token amount is lower than anticipated, sometimes accompanied by a smaller treasury fee. The proper mitigation is to measure the actual token balance change by recording the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer, computing the real amount received, and using that value for all subsequent calculations and hook calls, thereby ensuring accurate accounting regardless of token transfer mechanics.

title: Frontrunning for unallowed minting of Short and Long tokens
description:
The documentation states that minting of the Short and Long tokens should only be done by the governance.
    
File: apps/smart-contracts/core/contracts/interfaces/IPrePOMarket.sol
73:    * Minting will only be done by the team, and thus relies on the `_mintHook`
74:    * to enforce access controls. This is also why there is no fee for `mint()`
75:    * as opposed to `redeem()`.

The problem is, that as long as the **_mintHook** is not set via **setMintHook**, everyone can use the mint function and mint short and long tokens. At the moment the **_mintHook** is not set in the constructor of PrePOMarket and so the transaction that will set the **_mintHook** can be front run to mint short and long tokens for the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an uninitialized access‑control hook that is supposed to restrict the creation of Short and Long tokens to the governance address. In the PrePOMarket contract the mint function relies on an internal _mintHook to verify that only the authorized entity can call mint, but the hook is not set during construction. Consequently, until the governance explicitly calls setMintHook, the mint function is effectively open to any caller. An attacker can therefore front‑run the governance transaction that sets the hook by first providing collateral, approving the market contract, and invoking mint to receive the full amount of newly minted Short and Long tokens. After the hook is finally set, subsequent mint attempts revert, but the tokens already minted remain in the attacker’s account, diluting the token supply and potentially disrupting market pricing and valuation. This flaw is observable from a user’s perspective as unexpected token balances appearing after a mint call that should have been restricted, or as a sudden inability to mint once the hook is in place. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a fake mint hook could be front‑run, allowing the attacker to mint before the hook was enforced. The problem is subtle because the contract documentation states that minting is governance‑only, yet the code does not enforce this invariant until after deployment, making the risk easy to overlook. To remediate, the mint hook should be initialized atomically at deployment—either by passing the hook address through the factory or by deploying a default hook that reverts until replaced—ensuring that no window exists where unrestricted minting is possible. This class of bug falls under improper initialization of access‑control mechanisms, leading to unauthorized asset creation and economic distortion of the protocol.

title: PrePO NFT holders will not be able to redeem collateral
description:
The protocol has set a limitation on who can participate in the protocol activities.

1. Users who are included in an allowed list: `_accountList`.
2. Users who own specific NFTs that are supported by NFTScoreRequirement. These NFTs are PrePO NFTs that were minted to accounts that historically participated in PrePO activities.

Users who are #2 that deposited funds into the protocol are not able to redeem collateral tokens and withdraw their profits/funds from the market. (Loss of funds).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control mismatch between the deposit and redeem pathways of the PrePO market. During a deposit the contract checks two conditions: the sender must be on an allowed account list or must own a PrePO NFT that satisfies the NFTScoreRequirement. This logic is implemented in the DepositHook and therefore NFT holders are permitted to mint collateral and trade in the Uniswap V3 pools. However, when the same user later calls the redeem function, the RedeemHook only verifies that the caller is present in the same account list and does not perform the NFTScoreRequirement check. As a result, a user who entered the system solely because of NFT ownership passes the deposit check but fails the redeem check, causing the transaction to revert with redeemer not allowed. The impact is that the user’s collateral tokens and any accrued profit remain locked in the contract; from the user’s perspective the balance appears unchanged and the expected refund is missing. This situation occurs whenever the protocol uses separate AccountList instances for deposit and redeem hooks and does not synchronize the NFT eligibility logic. The affected parties are NFT‑holding participants and, indirectly, the protocol’s reputation because funds can become effectively inaccessible until governance manually updates the redeem AccountList or removes the redeem hook. The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the hook implementations and noted the inconsistency. It can be hard to notice because the deposit flow works correctly and the failure only manifests at the later redemption step, which may be exercised infrequently. The correct mitigation is to align the access‑control checks: either add the NFTScoreRequirement verification to the RedeemHook, use the same AccountList for both hooks, or deactivate the redeem hook after the market is closed so that all users can withdraw. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent whitelist enforcement” or “mismatched ACL between entry and exit functions”, leading to a loss‑of‑funds scenario where expected refunds do not occur.

title: `PrePOMarket.setFinalLongPayout
description: If `finalLongPayout` is changed twice by admin fault, the market would be insolvent as it should pay more collateral than it has.
poc:
If `finalLongPayout` is less than `MAX_PAYOUT`, it means the market is ended and `longToken Price = finalLongPayout, shortToken Price = MAX_PAYOUT - finalLongPayout`.

So when users redeem their long/short tokens, the total amount of collateral tokens will be the same as the amount that users transferred during `mint()`.

Btw in `setFinalLongPayout()`, there is no validation that this function can’t be called twice and the below scenario would be possible.

1. Let’s assume there is one user `Bob` in the market for simplicity.
2. `Bob` transferred 100 amounts of `collateral` and got 100 long/short tokens. The market has 100 `collateral`.
3. The market admin set `finalLongPayout = 60 * 1e16` and `Bob` redeemed 100 `longToken` and received 60 `collateral`. The market has 40 `collateral` now.
4. After that, the admin realized `finalLongPayout` is too high and changed `finalLongPayout = 40 * 1e16` again.
5. `Bob` tries to redeem 100 `shortToken` and receive 60 `collateral` but the market can’t offer as it has 40 `collateral` only.

When there are several users in the market, some users can’t redeem their long/short tokens as the market doesn’t have enough `collaterals`.
bug_full: The contract allows the market owner to set the final payout for long positions through the function setFinalLongPayout. The function does not contain a guard that prevents it from being called more than once after the market has been settled. Because the only check is that finalLongPayout must be greater than a constant MAX_PAYOUT, the owner can overwrite the previously recorded payout value after some users have already redeemed their tokens. When the payout is changed a second time, the accounting of the remaining collateral no longer matches the amount that must be paid out to the outstanding short (or long) tokens. As a result the market can become insolvent: users who try to redeem their remaining tokens receive less collateral than expected, or the transaction reverts because the contract does not hold enough funds. The vulnerability is triggered when the owner calls setFinalLongPayout, users redeem a portion of their tokens, and then the owner calls setFinalLongPayout again with a different value that reduces the remaining pool of collateral. Any token holder – long or short – is affected because the protocol’s guarantee that the total collateral equals the sum of payouts is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that simulated a scenario with a single user (Bob) who first redeemed long tokens at a payout of 60 % of the collateral, leaving 40 % in the contract, and then the owner reduced the finalLongPayout to 40 %, causing the short token redemption to request 60 % of collateral while only 40 % remained. The problem is subtle because the function is owner‑only and appears to be a one‑time finalisation step, so developers may assume it cannot be abused. To remediate, the contract should enforce a one‑time finalisation rule, for example by checking that finalLongPayout is still set to a sentinel value (e.g., MAX_PAYOUT) before allowing an update, or by introducing a boolean flag that is set after the first successful call and prevents any further modifications. This ensures that once the market is settled, the payout values cannot be altered, preserving the invariant that total collateral equals the sum of long and short payouts and preventing users from receiving less than the promised amount or seeing funds disappear.

title: Manager can get around min reserves check, draining all funds from Collateral.sol
description:
When a manager withdraws funds from Collateral.sol, there is a check in the `managerWithdrawHook` to confirm that they aren’t pushing the contract below the minimum reserve balance.
    
```solidity
require(collateral.getReserve() - _amountAfterFee >= getMinReserve(), "reserve would fall below minimum");
```

However, a similar check doesn’t happen in the `withdraw()` function.

The manager can use this flaw to get around the reserve balance by making a large deposit, taking a manager withdrawal, and then withdrawing their deposit.
poc:
Imagine a situation where the token has a balance of 100, deposits of 1000, and a reserve percentage of 10%. In this situation, the manager should not be able to make any withdrawal.

But, with the following series of events, they can:

* Manager calls `deposit()` with 100 additional tokens
* Manager calls `managerWithdraw()` to pull 100 tokens from the contract
* Manager calls `withdraw()` to remove the 100 tokens they added

The result is that they are able to drain the balance of the contract all the way to zero, avoiding the intended restrictions.
bug_full: During a manager‑initiated withdrawal from the Collateral contract a safety check is performed that ensures the contract's reserve after the withdrawal remains above a configured minimum. The check is implemented in managerWithdrawHook with a require statement that compares collateral.getReserve() - _amountAfterFee to getMinReserve(). However the public withdraw() function, which also moves tokens out of the contract, does not repeat this invariant check. Because the manager role can call both deposit() and withdraw(), the manager can first increase the contract's balance by depositing additional tokens, then invoke managerWithdraw() to take a permitted amount, and finally call withdraw() to retrieve the tokens they just deposited. The second call bypasses the reserve validation, allowing the total outflow to exceed the reserve and ultimately drain the contract to zero. The root cause is the missing reserve‑balance verification in withdraw(), a classic example of an unchecked state transition that violates the accounting assumption that a minimum buffer must always be preserved. The vulnerability manifests only when a privileged manager performs the sequence of calls; regular users see no direct way to trigger it, which makes the bug easy to overlook during code review. From a user perspective the contract balance unexpectedly drops to zero, refunds that should be available disappear, and funds that were thought to be secured as collateral are lost. The impact is a complete loss of user funds and a breakdown of the protocol's collateralisation guarantees. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised manager functions and compared the behaviour of managerWithdrawHook with withdraw(). Because both functions appear to perform similar withdrawals, the missing check can be missed if the auditor only inspects one path. To remediate, the same minimum‑reserve validation must be added to withdraw() (and any other external outflow functions), or the contract should centralise all token removals through a single internal hook that enforces the invariant. Reducing the manager's ability to arbitrarily move funds, for example by limiting the role or adding multi‑sig approval, also mitigates the risk. In summary, the bug is a business‑logic invariant bypass where the contract fails to enforce its minimum reserve requirement on all withdrawal paths, allowing a malicious or compromised manager to drain all collateral.

title: Users do not receive owed tokens if `TokenSender` contract cannot cover their owed amount.
poc:
Bob wants to redeem his long and short tokens via `PrePOMarket.redeem()`. However, Alice’s redemption prior to his, significantly drained the `TokenSender` contract of its tokens. As a result, Bob’s redemption fails to benefit him in the amount of the outputToken he should have received in compensation for the fees paid.

Because the quantity of tokens paid to Bob is partially dependent upon the token’s price at the time of redemption, the protocol might shoulder more downside loss (token price dropped compared to when Bob redeemed, must pay out more tokens) or Bob might suffer upside loss (price went up compared to time of redemption, Bob loses the difference).

Bob’s recourse is to contact the project administrators and try to have his tokens sent to him manually. Agreeing to a value adds friction to the process.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the TokenSender contract that is responsible for sending a compensation token to users when they withdraw or redeem assets from the protocol. The send function first checks that the price of the output token is above a configurable lower bound and that the calculated output amount is non‑zero. After those checks it verifies that the contract’s own balance is sufficient to cover the amount. If the balance is lower than the required amount the function simply returns without transferring any tokens and without emitting an event or reverting the transaction. This silent early return means that a user who is entitled to a rebate based on the fee they paid receives nothing, even though the surrounding protocol logic treats the operation as successful. The root cause is the lack of accounting for shortfalls: the contract does not record that a user is owed tokens when the balance is insufficient, nor does it provide a mechanism for later claim. Exploitation occurs when another actor, either through normal usage or by front‑running, drains the TokenSender contract of its token reserve before a victim’s redemption is processed. When the victim’s transaction reaches the send function, the balance check fails and the function exits, leaving the user with no rebate. The impact is a financial loss for the user who expected a fee refund; from the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful withdrawal but the balance does not increase, creating a mismatch between expectation (“I should receive a rebate”) and reality (“I receive zero”). The issue manifests whenever the output token price is above the lower bound, the calculated amount is positive, but the TokenSender contract does not hold enough tokens – a condition that can be triggered by prior redemptions, malicious draining, or simply insufficient funding of the contract. All participants who rely on the rebate mechanism – regular users, auditors, and the protocol’s reputation – are affected. The problem was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge cases where the contract’s balance was deliberately reduced. It is hard to notice because the function does not revert or log an error; the transaction appears successful and no explicit failure is reported. The appropriate remediation is to treat the compensation as an owed liability: the contract should record any shortfall in a mapping and expose a claim function that allows users to retrieve their tokens after the contract is replenished, or alternatively enforce that the contract always holds enough balance before allowing withdrawals, or revert the operation when the balance is insufficient. This class of bug can be described as an insufficient‑balance silent‑failure in a payment‑distribution routine, leading to lost or unclaimed funds and breaking the accounting assumption that every fee‑refund obligation is fulfilled.

title: `Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity` can be frontrunned which leads to price manipulation
description: `Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity` can be frontrunned which allows the setting of a different initial price.
poc:
When new Pool is created, it is already initialized with active tick (`Pool.sol#L76`). This allows the pool creator to provide price for assets. So when first LP calls `Pool.addLiquidity`, this active tick is used to determine how many assets LP should deposit.

`Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity` function allows caller to add liquidity to the pool that can be not created yet. In such case it will create it with initial active tick provided by sender and then it will provide user’s liquidity to the pool. In case the pool already exists, function will just add liquidity to it.

`Router.sol#L277-L287`

```solidity
function getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity(
    PoolParams calldata poolParams,
    uint256 tokenId,
    IPool.AddLiquidityParams[] calldata addParams,
    uint256 minTokenAAmount,
    uint256 minTokenBAmount,
    uint256 deadline
) external payable checkDeadline(deadline) returns (uint256 receivingTokenId, uint256 tokenAAmount, uint256 tokenBAmount, IPool.BinDelta[] memory binDeltas) {
    IPool pool = getOrCreatePool(poolParams);
    return addLiquidity(pool, tokenId, addParams, minTokenAAmount, minTokenBAmount);
}
```

1. Pool of tokenA:tokenB doens’t exist.
2. User calls `Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity` function to create pool with initial active tick and provide liquidity in same tx.
3. Attacker frontruns tx and creates such pool with different active tick.
4. `Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity` is executed and new Pool was not created, and liquidity was added to the Pool created by attacker.
5. Attacker swapped provided by first depositor tokens for a good price.
6. First depositor lost part of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Router.getOrCreatePoolAndAddLiquidity function, which merges pool creation and liquidity provision into a single transaction. When a caller invokes this function for a token pair that does not yet have a pool, the router forwards the caller‑supplied pool parameters, including the initial active tick, to the internal getOrCreatePool routine and then immediately calls addLiquidity on the resulting pool. Because the transaction does not verify whether the pool already existed, an attacker can submit a front‑running transaction that creates the same pool just before the victim’s transaction, but with a deliberately chosen active tick that sets an unfavorable initial price. When the victim’s transaction is mined, the router finds that the pool already exists, skips the creation step, and adds the victim’s liquidity to the attacker‑controlled pool. The attacker can then swap the newly supplied assets at the manipulated price, extracting value from the victim. The root cause is a race condition caused by combining two state‑changing operations—pool creation and liquidity addition—without atomic protection or a check that the pool was freshly created. Exploitation requires the pool to be absent at the time the victim sends the transaction and the attacker to be able to front‑run with a higher gas price. The impact is that the liquidity provider receives fewer tokens than expected, may lose part of the deposited assets, and the protocol’s price oracle can be temporarily skewed, undermining trust in the pool’s pricing mechanism. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that liquidity was added successfully, but the subsequent token balance appears reduced or the swap price is unexpectedly poor, contradicting the expectation that the deposit would be valued at the quoted initial price. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined transaction ordering and the handling of pool parameters. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and the price discrepancy only becomes apparent after the attacker’s follow‑up swap. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running and race‑condition vulnerabilities where multiple dependent actions are bundled in a single call, allowing an adversary to manipulate intermediate state. Mitigation involves separating pool creation from liquidity addition into two distinct transactions, enforcing that the active tick cannot be overridden when a pool already exists, or requiring the caller to set isDelta to false, thereby preventing the attacker from influencing the initial price. Implementing these controls restores the intended business logic that a liquidity provider should set the initial price themselves and should not be exposed to external manipulation.

title: Pool address is not deterministic, the actual Pool address deployed may be different from the address computed in advance
description: Users and contracts associated with Maverick may result in errors or token losses due to using a wrong Pool address.
poc:
Pools are deployed in a `create2` manner just like Uniswap. This is used to ensure that the pool contract address is deterministic and guaranteed, because in some scenarios it is necessary to know the address of the pool in advance and perform some operations.

However, the address of the Pool contract in the current implementation is not fully deterministic.

Let’s see the code of `Deployer#deploy()`(`Deployer.sol#L24`):

```solidity
function deploy(
    uint256 _fee,
    uint256 _tickSpacing,
    int32 _activeTick,
    uint16 _lookback,
    uint16 _protocolFeeRatio,
    IERC20 _tokenA,
    IERC20 _tokenB,
    uint256 _tokenAScale,
    uint256 _tokenBScale,
    IPosition _position
) external returns (IPool pool) {
    pool = new Pool{salt: keccak256(abi.encode(_fee, _tickSpacing, _lookback, _tokenA, _tokenB))}(
        _fee,
        _tickSpacing,
        _activeTick,
        _lookback,
        _protocolFeeRatio,
        _tokenA,
        _tokenB,
        _tokenAScale,
        _tokenBScale,
        _position
    );
```

Any change in `_fee, _tickSpacing, _activeTick, _lookback, _protocolFeeRatio, _tokenA, _tokenB, _tokenAScale, _tokenBScale, _position` will result in a different contract address.

This is because they are all used as the Pool’s constructor arguments which will be used to calculate the contract address.

see [Salted contract creations / create2](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/control-structures.html#salted-contract-creations-create2)

Of these parameters, only `_fee, _tickSpacing, _lookback, _tokenA, _tokenB` are used to determine a pool:

* They are used to lookup (`Factory.sol#L46`) a pool

```solidity
function lookup(uint256 _fee, uint256 _tickSpacing, uint16 _lookback, IERC20 _tokenA, IERC20 _tokenB) external view override returns (IPool pool) 
```

* They are the keys of the pools mapping (`Factory.sol#L16`)

```solidity
mapping(uint256 => mapping(uint256 => mapping(uint32 => mapping(IERC20 => mapping(IERC20 => IPool))))) pools;
    
pools[_fee][_tickSpacing][_lookback][_tokenA][_tokenB] = pool;
```

Other parameters are the properties or state of the pool. They do not determine a pool.

Some of them may be set to or modified to any value, which leads to the loss of determinism and guarantee of the pool address:

* `_activeTick`: may be set to any value by creator when `create()`(`Factory.sol#L58`)
* `_protocolFeeRatio`: may be set to any value at any time by factory owner. See setProtocolFeeRatio (`Factory.sol#L33`)
* `_tokenAScale, _tokenBScale`: may be set to any value at any time by token owner (if the token is settable or upgradable)
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the deterministic calculation of a pool contract address in the Maverick protocol. The factory creates pools using CREATE2 with a salt that is derived from all constructor arguments, including parameters that are meant to be mutable such as _activeTick, _protocolFeeRatio, and token scale values. Because these mutable values are part of the salt, any change to them – either at creation time or later through governance actions – results in a different contract address than the one that can be predicted from the immutable identifiers (fee, tick spacing, lookback, tokenA, tokenB) used by the factory’s lookup function. Consequently, users and other contracts that rely on the address being known in advance may compute an address that does not correspond to the actual deployed pool. When they send tokens or invoke functions on the expected address, the transaction either fails or the funds are transferred to an unintended contract, leading to apparent loss of assets. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a pool they believe exists at a certain address shows a zero balance, refunds do not arrive, or calls revert with “address not found”. The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the keys used in the factory’s mapping with the arguments supplied to the CREATE2 deployment and noticed the mismatch. It is hard to notice because CREATE2 is generally assumed to guarantee address determinism, and the extra arguments are not obvious in the deployment flow. The root cause is the inclusion of mutable state in the address‑deriving salt, violating the principle that only immutable identifiers should influence deterministic contract addresses. To fix the problem the factory should store mutable parameters in its own storage and have the pool constructor read them via a getter, while the CREATE2 salt should be computed solely from the immutable identifiers, mirroring the approach used by Uniswap. This change restores true determinism, prevents users from interacting with the wrong address, and eliminates the risk of token loss due to address mismatches.

title: Trader can manipulate price because bin only moved after swap
description:
In Maverick, liquidity bin is only moved after a swap:

`Pool.sol#L305-L306`

```solidity
emit Swap(msg.sender, recipient, tokenAIn, exactOutput, amountIn, amountOut, currentState.activeTick);
_moveBins(currentState.activeTick, startingTick, lastTwa);
```

If the pool does not have a lot of activity (which is very common for newer DEX / tail asset), the bin will not be moved to the expected position. 

Trader will have a free option to manipulate price in their favor.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation edge case that stems from the order in which Maverick updates its internal liquidity bin position relative to the execution of a swap. In the current implementation the contract emits the Swap event, performs the token transfer calculations, and only afterwards calls the internal _moveBins function that shifts the active bin to reflect the new time‑weighted average price (TWAP). When a pool has very little activity – a common situation for newly launched or low‑volume assets – the bin may remain at its previous position for the duration of the block. An attacker can exploit this timing gap by first submitting a zero‑amount swap (or any swap that does not change the token balances) to force an update of the TWAP without triggering the bin movement. Because the bin is still anchored at the old price, the subsequent genuine swap is priced against a stale bin, allowing the trader to obtain a more favorable rate, often crossing a bin boundary and receiving more tokens than the market price would dictate. The exploit is only possible when the attacker’s trade is the first swap of the block, the price movement of the previous block was in the opposite direction of the intended trade, and the pool’s liquidity is thin enough that the bin does not automatically shift. From a user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly good execution price – for example, buying tokens at a price that appears too low or receiving a larger token amount after a trade that should have been neutral. Liquidity providers suffer because the pool’s accounting is distorted: they effectively sell assets at a price below the true market value, eroding their capital. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that inserting a zero‑token swap between two regular swaps resulted in a significant excess of tokens for the trader. The bug is subtle because the external price feed (TWAP) appears correct, and the Swap event does not reveal that the bin has not moved, making the manipulation hard to detect without inspecting internal state. The recommended mitigation is to move the bin immediately after updating the TWAP, i.e., before the token transfer calculations, ensuring that the price used for the swap always reflects the most recent bin position. Conceptually, this aligns the price calculation and bin migration steps, eliminating the window where a stale bin can be abused and restoring the intended economic invariants of the DEX.

title: `exactInput` allows stealing of funds via a malicious pool contract
description:
`Router.sol#L151`

`Router.sol#L128`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the router contract that implements the exactInput function used for multi‑hop swaps. The function receives a byte‑encoded path that contains a sequence of token‑pool‑token tuples, and for each hop it extracts the pool address and calls its swap method. Because the router does not verify that the pool address belongs to a pool created by the official factory, an attacker can insert a malicious contract that pretends to be a pool. When the router invokes the swap on this contract, the malicious code can call back into the router and sweep the input token to the attacker’s address, then return a fabricated output amount. This allows the attacker to drain the user’s funds while the transaction appears to have succeeded. The exploit is triggered whenever a user relies on a front‑end to build the path automatically, which is the common case because the path is a binary blob that users cannot easily inspect in their wallet UI. From the user’s perspective the transaction completes, the input token balance is reduced, but the expected output tokens are not received – the user sees a missing refund or a zero balance where tokens should have arrived. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept malicious pool contract and a test that demonstrated the loss of tokens after a call to exactInput. The problem is subtle because the router contract itself is trusted, the path encoding hides the malicious address, and the swap callback is a standard part of the protocol, making the malicious behavior blend in with legitimate swaps. Conceptually, this is an instance of an unchecked external call to an untrusted contract, leading to a “untrusted pool” or “malicious callback” class of bug. The impact is loss of user funds and erosion of confidence in the protocol’s routing logic. Mitigation requires the router to enforce that every pool address in the path is verified against the factory (for example by calling factory.isFactoryPool) before invoking swap, or to restrict routing to only factory‑created pools. If the protocol intentionally supports third‑party pools, additional safeguards such as explicit user confirmation of each hop or on‑chain validation of pool code would be needed to prevent fund theft.

title: Unused ETH is not refunded when a limit price is set
description:
```solidity
Router.sol#L90-L91
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a situation where a user who sends native ETH to the Router contract for a token swap that includes a price limit ends up losing the portion of ETH that is not actually consumed by the swap. The Router’s internal pay function blindly deposits the full amount of ETH supplied by the caller into the WETH9 contract and transfers it to the pool, assuming the entire value will be used. When the downstream Pool contract enforces a sqrtPriceLimitD18, the swap may stop early, consuming only a fraction of the input ETH while still returning the full amount of tokens that correspond to the spent portion. Because the Router does not track how much ETH was really spent, it never refunds the unused remainder to the original sender. The leftover ETH remains in the Router’s balance and can be withdrawn by anyone through the public refundETH function, which any MEV bot can call. An attacker can therefore extract the unrefunded ETH after a partial fill, as demonstrated by the PoC where a user intended to sell 1 ETH, the swap stopped after 0.7 ETH, and the remaining ~0.3 ETH was later withdrawn by a bot. The impact is a direct loss of user funds and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol, since users expect that the amount of ETH they send will either be fully spent on the swap or returned if not used. The issue occurs only when three conditions are met simultaneously: the caller supplies native ETH, the Router forwards the full amount to the pool, and the pool’s limit‑price logic causes a partial execution. It primarily affects users of the Router contract, but any party can benefit from the leaked ETH, making it a systemic risk for the protocol’s economics. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite observed that the Router’s ETH balance increased after a limited‑price swap and that the refundETH function could be called by a third party to drain it. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning or error about the leftover balance, and the refund function is intentionally public, so the extra ETH can disappear silently. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “partial‑fill input asset leakage” bugs, where a contract fails to reconcile the actual amount of input tokens consumed with the amount initially transferred. To remediate the issue, the Router should compute the exact amount of ETH spent by the pool (for example by reading the pool’s balance change or by having the pool return the spent amount) and then transfer any surplus back to the caller, or at minimum document that callers must perform a separate multi‑call to retrieve leftover ETH. This would align the contract’s behavior with user expectations that unspent ETH is either refunded automatically or can be reclaimed safely, eliminating the opportunity for external actors to siphon the funds.

title: `Pool._amountToBin`
description:
```solidity
Pool._amountToBin()
```
returns a larger value than it should when `protocolFeeRatio = 100%`.

As a result, bin balances might be calculated incorrectly.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal helper function that converts an ERC‑20 amount plus fee into a bin‑scaled amount. When the protocol fee ratio is set to its maximum (100 %), the function adds an extra unit to the fee calculation because the conditional expression adds +1 after multiplying the fee basis by the fee ratio. As a result the returned bin amount is one unit larger than it should be, which makes the internal delta that updates the pool’s bin balances smaller than the actual deposited amount. This off‑by‑one error propagates to the balance‑update logic, causing the pool to record a lower inbound balance and a higher fee than intended. Users who deposit tokens may see their balance reduced or receive a smaller share when withdrawing, while the protocol may collect an unintended extra fee. The bug appears only when the protocol fee ratio equals the maximum scaling constant; in all other configurations the function behaves correctly. It was discovered during a static audit that compared the expected fee calculation with the implementation and noticed that the fee basis is incremented by one. The issue is subtle because the deviation is a single unit, which may be hidden by rounding or large transaction amounts, making it hard to detect in normal operation. The proper fix is to treat the maximum‑ratio case as a special branch that returns deltaInErc‑feeBasis without the extra +1, or to adjust the clipping logic so that no additional unit is added. This class of bug is an off‑by‑one arithmetic error in fee accounting that breaks the invariant that total inbound amount equals sum of user amount and protocol fee.

title: TWA update is not correct
description: Time-warped-price is updated incorrectly and this affects moving bins.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) that the pool updates on every swap. The contract builds the TWAP by adding a fractional component derived from the end square‑root price of the swap. In the current implementation the endSqrtPrice value is first passed through a clipping function before the division that produces the fractional part. The clipping function forces the value to stay within the lower tick bound, which makes the division result always positive. Consequently the endSqrtPrice can only increase the active tick and can never decrease it, even when the true price movement should pull the tick downward, a logical error that originates from using Math.clip on endSqrtPrice, a misuse that discards the sign of the price delta. An attacker can trigger the condition by performing a swap where tokenAIn is false, a sqrtPriceLimit is used, and there is a gap between price bins. By crafting the swap so that the real end price lies below the lower tick, the contract still adds a positive contribution to the TWAP, skewing the average price upward. The protocol then uses the distorted TWAP to decide how to move bins, causing bins to shift in the wrong direction. Users consequently receive trades at prices that are worse than expected, liquidity may be re‑allocated incorrectly, and the accounting assumptions of the pool (that the TWAP reflects the true time‑weighted price) are violated. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a normal price but the subsequent swap may return less token than anticipated or the pool may appear to lose balance. The issue appears only during swaps that update the TWAP; normal reads of the price do not reveal the problem, making it hard to notice without detailed audit. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit where the auditor observed that the second term of the TWAP sum is always positive and therefore cannot contribute negatively to the active tick. To remediate the bug the clipping should be removed and the fractional component should be calculated directly from endSqrtPrice relative to the lower and upper tick bounds, preserving its sign. Additionally the log‑TWAP calculation for swaps that hit a sqrtPriceLimit must be corrected to handle gaps between bins accurately. Implementing these changes restores the intended behavior where the TWAP can move both up and down, aligning bin movement with the true market price and preventing mispricing or loss of funds.

title: The calculation of LP token amount and deposit amount is wrong for edge cases
description:
```solidity
Bin.sol#L35
```
```solidity
Bin.sol#L38
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect conditional check in the liquidity‑provision routine that determines how many LP tokens are minted when the current price lies outside the bin’s defined price range. The contract uses two inequalities to decide which side of the reserve (token A or token B) should be set to zero for edge cases where the active price p is lower than the lower tick p_l or higher than the upper tick p_u. In the implementation the signs of these inequalities are reversed, so the branch that should be taken for p<p_l is executed for p>p_u and vice‑versa. As a result, when a user adds liquidity while the market price is below the bin’s lower bound, the code incorrectly zeroes the reserve of token A instead of token B, and when the price is above the upper bound it zeroes the wrong reserve. This leads to a mis‑calculation of the pro‑rata liquidity (the amount of LP tokens) – the contract may mint too few tokens, sometimes even zero, despite the user having supplied a non‑zero amount of assets. The impact is that liquidity providers receive fewer LP tokens than they are entitled to, which translates into a smaller share of future fees and can appear to the user as a missing or zero balance after a successful deposit. The bug manifests only under the edge‑case conditions p<p_l or p>p_u, which are relatively rare in normal operation, making it easy to miss during routine testing. It was discovered during a formal audit that compared the on‑chain implementation with the white‑paper formula presented in Table 1 of the protocol documentation; the audit team noticed that the inequalities in the code did not match the intended mathematical model. Because the error only affects extreme price scenarios, it may not be obvious from standard UI feedback – a user might see a transaction succeed but later find that their LP balance is unexpectedly low or zero, contradicting the expectation that the deposited amount is fully represented by minted tokens. The class of bug is a conditional‑logic error that violates the accounting invariant that the total minted LP tokens should be proportional to the value of assets deposited. To remediate the issue, the two inequality checks should be inverted so that the correct reserve side is zeroed for each edge case, thereby restoring the intended proportional minting logic. Conceptually, the fix restores the alignment between the contract’s state updates and the economic model defined in the protocol’s specification, ensuring that LP token supply accurately reflects the value of deposited liquidity across all price ranges.

title: GroupBuy may purchase NFT not in the allowed list
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the GroupBuy contract’s purchase function where the validation of a Merkle proof is incorrectly implemented for the case of an empty proof array. When the caller supplies a purchaseProof with length zero, the code compares the raw tokenId directly against the stored merkleRoot (if (bytes32(_tokenId) != merkleRoot) revert InvalidProof()). Because the merkleRoot is a hash of the whitelist tree and not a legitimate token identifier, an attacker can simply set the tokenId to the numeric value of the merkleRoot and satisfy the equality check. This bypasses the intended allow‑list enforcement, allowing any tokenId that matches the merkleRoot – even tokens that were never included in the whitelist – to be purchased. The root cause is a logical flaw: the contract treats an empty proof as a special case and uses a direct equality comparison instead of hashing the tokenId and verifying it against the Merkle root, or rejecting empty proofs altogether. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious user calls purchase with an empty proof array and supplies a tokenId equal to uint256(merkleRoot). The contract believes the proof is valid and proceeds with the purchase logic, potentially transferring funds or minting an NFT that was not authorized. The impact includes unauthorized acquisition of NFTs, loss of funds from legitimate buyers, and a breach of the protocol’s whitelist guarantees. This condition triggers only when the proof array is empty, which is a scenario that can be deliberately crafted by an attacker. All participants who rely on the whitelist – the protocol, its users, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the economic assumptions about who may buy are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a Foundry test demonstrated that providing an empty proof with a tokenId equal to the merkleRoot caused the contract to behave differently than expected. The bug is subtle because the check appears to guard against empty proofs, yet the equality comparison is nonsensical and may not be caught by casual code review or simple unit tests. To remediate, the contract should always hash the tokenId and compare the resulting leaf to the merkleRoot, regardless of proof length, or reject empty proofs outright. In other words, the Merkle verification logic must be applied uniformly, ensuring that only tokenIds explicitly included in the whitelist can be purchased, thereby restoring the intended security guarantees.

title: Attacker can delay proposal rejection
poc:
1. Attacker proposes a 10000 collateral at a very low price
2. Bob tries to reject it by purchasing the 10000 collateral
3. Attacker sees Bob’s tx in the mempool, frontruns it to reject 1 unit
4. The proposedListing.collateral is now 9999
5. Bob’s call reverted
6. This keeps happening until PROPOSAL_PERIOD passes or Bob gave up because of gas paid on failing tx
7. Attacker buys the NFT at a very low price
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the rejectProposal function of the OptimisticListingSeaport contract. The function checks whether the collateral attached to a proposed listing is lower than the amount that a caller wants to reject, and if so it reverts with InsufficientCollateral. Because the check and the subsequent subtraction of the amount are performed in separate steps, an attacker can manipulate the collateral value between the check and the subtraction by front‑running the transaction. In practice the attacker first creates a proposal with a large collateral amount but at a very low price. When a legitimate user (for example Bob) submits a rejectProposal call that would consume the full collateral, the attacker watches the mempool, inserts a transaction that rejects only a single unit of collateral just before Bob’s transaction, thereby reducing the stored collateral from the exact required amount to one unit less. When Bob’s transaction executes, the condition proposedListing.collateral < _amount becomes true, the call reverts, and the proposal remains active. By repeatedly repeating this front‑run step the attacker can delay or completely prevent the rejection until the proposal deadline expires, after which the attacker can acquire the NFT at the originally low price. The impact is a denial‑of‑service against honest rejectors and a potential loss of value for users who expected the proposal to be rejected; gas is wasted on failing transactions and the protocol’s economic guarantees are undermined. The issue occurs only when a rejectProposal call attempts to consume the full remaining collateral and an adversary can observe and front‑run that call, which is feasible in a public mempool environment. Anyone who tries to reject a proposal – regular users, market makers, or automated bots – can be affected, while the attacker benefits by keeping the under‑priced proposal alive. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the logical flow of the rejectProposal function was examined and the lack of atomicity between the balance check and the state update was identified. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens when the collateral is exactly one unit less than the requested amount, a situation that may not be reproduced in normal testing and appears as a simple “InsufficientCollateral” error without obvious malicious intent. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running‑prone race conditions and denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities caused by state‑dependent checks that are not protected against transaction ordering attacks. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a transaction failure with an “InsufficientCollateral” message, no change in the proposal status, and repeated gas costs, contrary to the expectation that the reject would succeed and the proposal would be removed. To remediate the issue the contract should not revert when the requested amount exceeds the available collateral; instead it should cap the amount to the current collateral, perform a safe subtraction, and refund any excess to the caller. Alternatively, the function could be redesigned to use a check‑effects‑interaction pattern or to lock the proposal state during the reject operation, ensuring that the collateral value cannot be altered between the check and the update. Such changes would eliminate the race condition and restore the intended economic behavior of the protocol.

title: Users that send funds at a price lower than the current low bid have the funds locked
description:
If a user contributes funds after there is no more supply left, and they don’t provide a price higher than the current minimum bid, they will be unable to withdraw their funds while the NFT remains unbought.

Ether becomes stuck until and unless the NFT is bought, which may never happen.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs when a participant calls the payable contribute() function after the fractional pool has already been filled and provides a bid price that is not higher than the current lowest bid in the priority queue. In this situation the contract calculates a fillAtAnyPriceQuantity of zero, skips the insertion of the bid into the queue and proceeds to the processBidsInQueue() routine. Because the supplied price is lower than the lowest existing bid, the while‑loop in processBidsInQueue() breaks immediately and the function never updates the pendingBalances mapping that records refundable amounts. Consequently the ether sent with the contribution is recorded only in the totalContributions variable and becomes owned by the GroupBuy contract without any path for the contributor to retrieve it. The root cause is a missing revert or balance‑recording step when the price is insufficient and the queue is already full, which allows the transaction to succeed silently while effectively locking the funds. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately submitting a low‑price contribution after the pool is full; the transaction will not revert, the UI will show a successful contribution event, but later attempts to call withdrawBalance() will revert with InsufficientBalance because pendingBalances remains zero. The impact is that users see their ether disappear – they expect a refund or a claim of excess funds, yet their balance reads zero and they cannot withdraw, potentially forever if the NFT is never purchased. This condition only manifests when the pool’s supply is exhausted, the contribution quantity exceeds the remaining supply, and the offered price does not meet or exceed the lowest queued bid. All contributors to the pool are affected, as the contract’s accounting assumptions that every successful contribution either fills the queue or creates a refundable entry are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised edge‑case scenarios where the queue is full and the price check fails; it is subtle because the transaction does not revert and emits a Contribute event, making the loss of funds easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of logic errors in bid‑queue handling that lead to funds‑locking, similar to unchecked price conditions in auction contracts. To remediate, the contract should either revert the transaction when the supplied price is lower than the minimum bid while the queue is full, or ensure that any ether transferred is always recorded in pendingBalances so that a later withdraw can succeed. In short, the contract must enforce that no contribution can be accepted without either being queued or being refundable, thereby preserving the expected invariant that contributors can always retrieve their funds if their bid is not accepted.

title: Priority queue min accounting breaks when nodes are split in two
description: The README states `If two users place bids at the same price but with different quantities, the queue will pull from the bid with a higher quantity first`, but the data-structure used for implementing this logic, is not used properly and essentially has its data corrupted when a large bid that is the current minimum bid, is split into two parts, so that a more favorable price can be used for a fraction of the large bid. The underlying issue is that one of the tree nodes is modified, without re-shuffling that node’s location in the tree.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a corruption of the minimum‑priority queue used to order bids in a group‑buy contract. The queue is implemented as a binary heap stored in an array and its ordering rule is price first, and when prices are equal the larger quantity is considered smaller (i.e., should appear closer to the root). The root cause is that the contract modifies a heap node in place – specifically when a large bid that is currently the minimum is partially filled and its quantity is reduced – without first removing the node from the heap and re‑inserting it or otherwise restoring the heap invariant. Because the heap property is violated, the internal ordering no longer reflects the intended price‑and‑quantity ranking. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the bug by submitting a bid that is split into two parts: the original minimum bid is decreased in quantity, and a new bid with a slightly larger quantity is inserted. The heap still thinks the modified node is the minimum, so the new bid is incorrectly promoted and the original sibling with the larger quantity remains hidden deeper in the tree. Consequently, bids that should be visible as the lowest‑price, highest‑quantity offers become invisible to the queue logic, preventing their owners from being selected for partial fills or from withdrawing pending balances. From the user’s point of view the symptom is that a bid that was previously at the front of the queue disappears, the expected refund or pending balance never arrives, and the UI may show a zero balance even though the user’s funds are still locked in the contract. The impact is a breakdown of accounting: funds become effectively stuck, the protocol’s guarantee that the cheapest, biggest bid is always processed first is violated, and overall financial correctness is compromised.
