The issue occurs only when a minimum bid is altered without re‑heapifying, which is a subtle condition that can be missed during normal testing because the queue still returns a value and no explicit error is thrown. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the GroupBuy.processBidsInQueue function and the underlying MinPriorityQueue implementation. The bug belongs to the class of heap‑invariant violations caused by mutable priority‑queue misuse. To remediate, any modification of a node’s key fields (price or quantity) must be preceded by removing the node from the heap and then re‑adding it, or by performing a proper swim/sink operation after the change, thereby restoring the correct ordering and ensuring that all bids remain visible to the selection algorithm.

title: Orders may not be fillable due to missing approvals
description: Not all `IERC20` implementations `revert()` when there’s a failure in `approve()`. If one of these tokens returns false, there is no check for whether this has happened during the order listing validation, so it will only be detected when the order is attempted.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked ERC20 approval step performed when an order is listed on the marketplace. During the on‑chain validation routine the contract iterates over each offer item and calls IERC20(token).approve(conduit, type(uint256).max) for ERC20 tokens, but it does not examine the boolean return value of approve. While many ERC20 implementations revert on failure, a subset merely returns false, meaning the call can silently fail while the surrounding transaction continues. As a result the order is recorded as valid even though the required allowance for the conduit has not been granted. This mismatch is discovered only later when a taker attempts to fill the order; the transfer of the ERC20 token fails, the fill transaction reverts or does nothing, and the order remains unfillable. From the user’s perspective the order appears in the UI as available, but attempting to execute it yields no token movement, leaving the proposer’s funds locked in the contract. The issue is a classic case of missing validation of an external call’s return value, specifically the ERC20 approve pattern, and it violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that a listed order always has sufficient allowance for the conduit. The bug is hard to notice because no immediate error is emitted during listing, and the order signature validation passes, giving a false sense of correctness. It was identified during a Code4rena audit that inspected the validateListing function and observed the lack of a safeApprove wrapper. Exploitation can be performed by submitting an order that includes a token known to return false on approve, effectively preventing the order from ever being filled and potentially holding the proposer’s funds hostage unless they cancel the order (which requires proposer permission or an expensive buy‑out of the pooled assets). The recommended remediation is to replace the raw approve call with OpenZeppelin’s safeApprove, which checks the return value and reverts on failure, thereby ensuring that only orders with a confirmed allowance are accepted. Conceptually, any contract that relies on ERC20 approve must verify the call’s success to avoid silent allowance failures that break downstream logic.

title: Only one `GroupBuy` can ever use USDT or similar tokens with front-running approval protections
description: Calling `approve()` without first calling `approve(0)` if the current approval is non-zero will revert with some tokens, such as Tether (USDT). While Tether is known to do this, it applies to other tokens as well, which are trying to protect against [this attack vector](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YLPtQxZu1UAvO9cZ1O2RPXBbT0mooh4DYKjA_jp-RLM/edit).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the SeaportLister contract manages ERC20 token allowances for its conduit. The contract unconditionally calls approve(conduit, type(uint256).max) for every ERC20 token that appears in an order, assuming that the allowance can be overwritten at any time. However, a number of popular tokens, most notably Tether (USDT), implement a non‑standard safety check that rejects an approve call when the current allowance is non‑zero and the new allowance is also non‑zero. These tokens require the allowance to be first set to zero before it can be changed to a different value. Because the contract never resets the allowance to zero, any subsequent attempt to re‑approve after a partial spend will revert, preventing the contract from granting the conduit the permission it needs. The conduit address itself is stored in an immutable variable set in the constructor, so once the contract is deployed it cannot be swapped for a fresh conduit that might have a clean allowance state. Consequently, after the first successful listing that consumes part of the allowance, the contract is effectively locked out of handling that ERC20 token for any further listings. From a user’s perspective, a listing that previously worked now fails with a transaction revert, and the expected behavior of “the contract can always sell my token” is broken; users may see their orders rejected, balances unchanged, and may be unable to list or sell the token again. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any ERC20 that enforces the zero‑to‑non‑zero rule, which contradicts the protocol’s claim of a maintenance‑free hyperstructure. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the approval logic and the immutable conduit design. It is subtle because many ERC20 tokens follow the standard that allows direct allowance updates, so the problem only surfaces with tokens that implement the extra check, making it easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should first set the allowance to zero before granting a new maximum allowance, and the conduit address should be configurable per call or updatable via governance so that a fresh conduit can be used if an allowance becomes irrecoverable. This change restores the expected accounting logic where the contract can always approve the conduit to transfer the full token balance, preventing funds from becoming inaccessible and preserving the protocol’s promised uninterrupted operation.

title: Loss of ETH for proposer when it is a contract that doesn’t have fallback function.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a helper routine that attempts to send native ETH to an arbitrary address using a low‑level call with a fixed gas stipend of 30 000. If the destination is a contract that does not implement a payable fallback or receive function, the call returns false and the routine falls back to wrapping the ETH into WETH and transferring the ERC‑20 token instead. Because the receiving contract was written to interact with the OptimisticListingSeaport protocol only through ETH payments, it is unlikely to include logic for handling incoming WETH tokens. Consequently, the WETH transfer succeeds on the token contract side but the recipient contract cannot recognise or withdraw the tokens, effectively locking the funds. This situation can be triggered whenever a proposer or any other participant is a smart‑contract wallet that lacks a payable fallback, or when the gas limit is insufficient for the fallback execution. The impact is that the proposer loses the expected ETH payout; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful proposal rejection or cash‑out, yet the balance of the proposer remains unchanged or shows a zero‑value WETH that cannot be accessed. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the OptimisticListingSeaport contract suite, where the code path of _sendEthOrWeth was examined and the fallback behaviour noted. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the protocol does not emit an explicit error, making the loss appear as a silent accounting discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of “failed ETH transfer to non‑payable contracts with token fallback”, a pattern where an assumed safe conversion to a token masks the inability of the recipient to handle that token. To remediate, the protocol should either restrict proposers to externally owned accounts, enforce that the recipient address implements a payable fallback, or avoid the automatic WETH fallback altogether and instead revert the transaction when the ETH transfer fails, thereby preventing silent fund loss.

title: Earlier bidders get cut out of future NFT holdings by bidders specifying the same price.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the GroupBuy contract’s bid‑processing routine, specifically the loop that iterates over the priority queue of existing bids. When a new contribution is submitted, the code retrieves the lowest‑price bid from the queue and decides whether to stop processing based on the condition `if (_price < lowestBid.price) { break; }`. Because the comparison uses a strict less‑than operator, bids that have exactly the same price as the current lowest bid are not considered a break condition. Consequently, the algorithm treats an equal‑price bid as if it were higher, proceeds to modify the existing lowest bid, reduces its quantity, adjusts contribution accounting, and inserts the new bid ahead of the older one. The documentation for the module states that when two bids share the same price, the queue should prioritize the bid with the larger quantity, preserving the earlier bidder’s allocation. The implemented logic violates this rule, allowing a later participant to overwrite an earlier bidder’s position simply by submitting a bid at the same price, regardless of quantity. This flaw originates from an off‑by‑one logical error in the price comparison, a classic case of an incorrect boundary condition in a priority‑queue algorithm. An attacker can exploit the issue by submitting a bid with a price equal to that of an existing lower‑quantity bid; the contract will erroneously remove the older bid, credit the attacker’s pending balance, and decrement the original bidder’s contribution. The impact is that earlier contributors may lose their expected NFT share, see their pending balance increase unexpectedly, or receive zero holdings despite having funded the pool. The problem manifests only when two bids have identical prices, a scenario that may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the GroupBuy module where the code path handling equal‑price bids was examined against the specification. The subtlety of the bug—appearing as a harmless comparison—makes it difficult to detect without careful review of edge‑case conditions. To remediate the issue, the price check should be changed to `if (_price <= lowestBid.price) { break; }`, ensuring that equal‑price bids trigger the break and preserve the original ordering. Additionally, the queue implementation should explicitly enforce a tie‑breaker based on quantity, matching the documented behavior. By correcting the boundary condition and reinforcing the ordering rule, the contract will prevent newer bidders from displacing earlier participants, thereby preserving fairness and preventing unintended loss of NFT holdings.

title: GroupBuys that are completely filled still don’t raise stated target amount
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes the minimum bid price for a group purchase of an NFT. When a pool is created, the code divides the declared initial price of the NFT by the total number of fractional tokens (Raes) that will be minted, storing the result as minBidPrice. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the division rounds down whenever the initial price is not an exact multiple of the total supply. Consequently the per‑token price is set slightly lower than required, and the total amount collected when all tokens are sold (minBidPrice multiplied by totalSupply) falls short of the target initial price. The contract later uses this underestimated minReservePrice to validate purchases, checking that the offered price does not exceed minReservePrice times the number of filled tokens. When the pool is completely filled, the check still fails because the accumulated funds are insufficient, causing the purchase function to revert with InvalidPurchase. From a user’s perspective the pool appears 100 % filled, yet the NFT is never acquired, their contribution may be locked, and no refund is automatically provided. The issue is hard to notice because participants normally assume that a fully filled pool guarantees enough capital to buy the NFT; the shortfall is hidden in the rounding error. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic rounding or precision errors in financial smart contracts, where integer division leads to under‑collection of funds. It was discovered during a formal audit that examined the relationship between the target price, token supply, and the reserve‑price update logic. To remediate the problem the calculation should be performed with a ceiling operation (rounding up) or by using a formula that guarantees minBidPrice * totalSupply ≥ initialPrice, for example (initialPrice + totalSupply ‑ 1) / totalSupply. This change ensures that the pool always gathers at least the declared amount, preventing the purchase from reverting and aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic of fully funded NFT acquisition.

title: Lock.sol: claimGovFees function can cause assets to be stuck in the Lock contract
description:
When calling [`Lock.claimGovFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L110), assets that are set to be not allowed or assets that don’t have any shares yet in the `BondNFT` contract will cause a silent failure in [`BondNFT.distribute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/BondNFT.sol#L215).

The funds from the `GovNFT` contract will get transferred into the `Lock` contract and then will be stuck there. They cannot be recovered.
poc:
1. An asset is added to the `BondNFT` contract by calling [`BondNFT.addAsset`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/BondNFT.sol#L349)
2. There are no bonds yet for this asset so the amount of shares for the asset is zero
3. [`Lock.claimGovFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L110) is called
4. Funds are transferred from the `GovNFT` contract to the [`Lock` contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L115)
5. The call to `BondNFT.distribute` now fails quietly without reverting the transaction:

```solidity
if (totalShares[_tigAsset] == 0 || !allowedAsset[_tigAsset]) return;
```

6. The funds are now stuck in the `Lock` contract. They cannot be recovered.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interaction between the Lock.claimGovFees function and the BondNFT.distribute function. When claimGovFees is executed, it transfers governance fee tokens from the GovNFT contract into the Lock contract and then attempts to forward those tokens to the BondNFT contract by calling distribute. BondNFT.distribute contains a guard clause that checks whether the asset is allowed and whether the total number of shares for that asset is greater than zero. If either condition fails, the function executes a plain return statement instead of reverting. Because the return is silent, the transaction that called claimGovFees does not revert and appears successful, but the subsequent transferFrom that would move the tokens to BondNFT never occurs. As a result the fee tokens remain locked inside the Lock contract with no mechanism to retrieve them. This situation occurs only for assets that are either not listed as allowed or that have zero shares at the time of the claim, which can happen when a new asset is added but no bonds have been minted yet, or when an asset is deliberately marked as disallowed. Users who expect to receive a fee claim see no change in their balance; the UI may report a successful claim while the underlying token balance stays unchanged. The impact is a loss of expected yield and potentially unrecoverable funds, affecting token holders, governance participants, and the overall protocol economics. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena through analysis of the claimGovFees flow and the early‑return pattern in BondNFT.distribute. It is hard to notice because no revert or error event is emitted, making the failure appear as a normal execution. The bug belongs to the class of silent‑failure or asset‑locking vulnerabilities caused by improper error handling. A proper fix would replace the early return with a revert, or redesign the distribution logic to skip only the offending asset while still processing others, and optionally add an owner‑only rescue function that can withdraw only the excess balance from the Lock contract without touching legitimately locked amounts.

title: Must approve 0 first
description: Some tokens (like USDT) do not work when changing the allowance from an existing non-zero allowance value. They must first be approved by zero and then the actual allowance must be approved.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑reset bug that occurs when the contract attempts to set a new non‑zero ERC20 allowance without first clearing the existing allowance to zero. Certain token implementations, most notably USDT, deliberately reject a direct change from a non‑zero allowance to another non‑zero value as a protective measure against the well‑known ERC20 race condition. In the affected function the contract calls IERC20(token).approve(address(bondNFT),type(uint256).max) on each iteration without first calling approve(address(bondNFT),0). When the token enforces the zero‑first rule, the approve call reverts, causing the entire claimGovFees transaction to fail. As a result the protocol cannot transfer the newly claimed governance fees to the bondNFT for distribution, leaving user balances unchanged and fees effectively stuck in the contract. The issue manifests only when the contract interacts with tokens that implement the non‑standard approve behaviour; standard ERC20 tokens that allow direct allowance updates are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor observed that the approve call could always revert for some tokens and reproduced the failure with a proof‑of‑concept that called approve(max) directly. The bug is subtle because most developers assume the ERC20 specification permits any allowance change, and the contract’s logic does not check the return value or catch the revert, making the problem easy to overlook in testing. Conceptually, the fix is to follow the safe‑approval pattern: reset the allowance to zero before setting a new non‑zero allowance, or use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance functions when available. Implementing this pattern ensures compatibility with all ERC20 variants, prevents transaction reverts, and guarantees that claimed fees are correctly transferred to users, preserving the intended accounting and business logic of the protocol.

title: Bypass the delay security check to win risk free funds
description: The current implementation uses `_checkDelay()` function to prevent profitable opening and closing in the same tx with two different prices in the “valid signature pool”. But the protection is not enough, an attacker can long with low price and short with high price at the same tx but two orders to lock profit and take risk free funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an insufficient delay validation that allows an attacker to open a long position at a low price and a short position at a high price within the same transaction by supplying two distinct, still‑valid price signatures. The contract only checks that the price data is recent (via a timestamp) but does not enforce that only one price level can be used per block or that the price cannot move in opposite directions before the trade is settled. Because the delay check does not compare the actual price values, a trader can submit two orders that lock opposite exposures, later close both positions when the market price is favorable, and capture the spread as risk‑free profit. This works whenever the spread between the two supplied prices, amplified by leverage, exceeds the sum of spread and funding fees that would otherwise offset the arbitrage. The attack is executed by constructing two market orders with different price data, signing each with a valid oracle signature, and submitting them in the same block; the contract records both positions, and the attacker later closes them at a common exit price, realizing a net gain while the protocol’s liquidity providers lose the corresponding amount. The issue appears only under conditions where the oracle provides price updates fast enough for two distinct signatures to be valid in the same block and where the protocol’s fee model does not fully absorb the price differential. Users of the protocol may notice unexpected profit without any market risk, while LPs may see their balances shrink without a clear cause. The flaw was discovered during a security audit through a crafted test case that demonstrated the dual‑order exploit. It is hard to notice because the delay mechanism seems to protect against same‑transaction arbitrage at first glance, yet it does not enforce price monotonicity or a single‑price constraint. The proper mitigation is to cache the lowest and highest price observed in the current block and reject any new order that would create a price range larger than the allowed spread, or to enforce that only one side of the market can be opened per block per user, effectively strengthening the delay check to guarantee that a single price cannot be used to open opposing positions in the same transaction.

title: Approved operators of Position token can’t call Trading.initiateCloseOrder
description: Approved operators of owner of Position token can’t call several function in Trading.
poc:
Functions that accept Position token in Trading are checking that the caller is owner of token using `_checkOwner` function.

```solidity
function _checkOwner(uint _id, address _trader) internal view {
    if (position.ownerOf(_id) != _trader) revert("2"); //NotPositionOwner   
}
```

As you can see this function doesn’t allow approved operators of token’s owner to pass the check. As a resul, functions are not possible to call for them on behalf of owner.

For example [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/contracts/Trading.sol#L235), there is a check that doesn’t allow to call initiateCloseOrder function.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an inconsistency between the ERC‑721 operator model and the internal permission check used by the Trading contract. Functions that accept a Position token, such as initiateCloseOrder, call an internal helper _checkOwner that simply compares the token owner returned by position.ownerOf(id) with the address supplied as the trader. This equality test does not consider addresses that have been granted operator rights through ERC‑721 approve or setApprovalForAll, so an approved proxy is treated as a non‑owner and the call reverts with error code "2" (NotPositionOwner). As a result, any user who relies on an approved operator – for example a trading bot, a delegated wallet, or a third‑party service – cannot invoke the intended trading actions on behalf of the token holder. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the proxy is approved, the user initiates a close order, but the transaction fails and the position remains open, leading to confusion such as “my position won’t close” or “I get a mysterious error”. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service for delegated users: they cannot close positions, claim refunds, or perform other lifecycle actions, which may cause missed market opportunities or locked capital. The issue occurs whenever a Trading function invokes _checkOwner, i.e., for any operation that requires ownership verification of a Position token. It affects token owners, their approved operators, and ultimately the protocol’s usability and trustworthiness. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s intended delegation model with the actual code, revealing that the check does not align with ERC‑721’s approved‑operator semantics. The problem can be hard to notice because normal owner‑only paths work correctly and unit tests may not cover operator scenarios. To remediate, the _checkOwner logic should be expanded to accept either the token owner or any address that is authorized as an operator for that token, using position.getApproved(id) or position.isApprovedForAll(owner, operator). This change restores the intended delegation capability without altering the existing owner‑only checks for direct calls. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of authorization bypass or improper permission checks where a contract fails to honor standard token operator mechanisms, leading to functional denial rather than a direct security breach.

title: Failure in `endpoint` can cause minting more than one NFT with the same token id in different chains
description:
In the contract `GovNFT`, it is possible to bridge the governance NFT to other chains. It is also stated in the document that:

NFT holders only earn the profits generated by the platform on the chain that the NFT is on.

It is assumed that there is only one unique NFT per token id. But there is a scenario that can lead to more than one NFT with the same token id on different chains.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the cross‑chain bridging logic of the GovNFT contract, where the function that receives messages from the LayerZero endpoint (lzReceive) does not mark a message as consumed when the call to the internal non‑blocking handler fails. Because the failure path only records the payload in a failed‑messages map and does not set a consumed flag, an attacker – or an honest user acting maliciously – can later invoke the retry mechanism and cause the same payload to be processed a second time. In a typical bridge operation a user burns an NFT on the source chain and expects it to be minted exactly once on the destination chain. If the endpoint supplies insufficient gas, the call to nonblockingLzReceive reverts, the message is stored as failed, and the NFT is still minted on the destination chain because the minting step is performed before the revert is detected. Later, when the user retries the failed message, the contract again executes the minting logic, creating a second NFT with the identical tokenId on the original chain while the first copy already exists on the destination chain. The result is that the same tokenId can exist simultaneously on multiple chains, violating the fundamental assumption that each tokenId is globally unique. From the user’s perspective the expected behavior – a single NFT that moves between chains – is replaced by a situation where the user sees the same NFT appear in their wallet on both chains, can sell one copy while still earning platform profits on the other, and generally experiences duplicated balances that were never intended. The impact includes double ownership, double profit extraction, and a breakdown of the platform’s accounting model that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between tokenId and chain. The issue is triggered only when the endpoint call fails (e.g., due to low gas, network lag, or other execution errors) and the contract does not record the message as consumed before attempting the mint. It was discovered during a security audit that exercised failure scenarios of the LayerZero messaging flow. The bug is subtle because the contract still emits the expected mint event on the successful path, making the duplicate creation invisible until the retry is performed. The proper mitigation is to introduce a consumed‑message tracking mapping that is set to true before any processing of the payload, and to ensure that the retry logic checks this flag and aborts if the message has already been handled, thereby making the bridge operation idempotent and preventing replay of the same tokenId across chains.

title: BondNFTs can revert when transferred
description:
`BondNFT`s should be transferrable. According the the proposal and the sponsor, `BondNFT`s should could be sold and borrowed against.

The proposal for context: <https://gov.tigris.trade/#/proposal/0x2f2d1d63060a4a2f2718ebf86250056d40380dc7162fb4bf5e5c0b5bee49a6f3>

The current implementation limits selling/depositing to only the same day that rewards are distributed for the `tigAsset` of the bond.

The impact if no rewards are distributed in the same day:

  1. `BondNFT`s listed on open markets will not be able to fulfill the orders
  2. `BondNFT`s deposited as collateral will not be able to release the collateral

Because other market/platforms used for selling/depositing will not call `claimGovFees` to distribute rewards, they will revert when trying to transfer the `BondNFT`.

Realistic examples could be `BondNFT`s listed on OpenSea.

Example of reasons why rewards would not be distributed in the same day:

  1. Low activity from investors, rewards are distributed when users lock/release/extend
  2. `tigAsset` is blacklisted in `BondNFT`, rewards will not be distributed in such case.
bug_full: The BondNFT contract implements a transfer hook that requires the reward epoch for the underlying asset to be exactly equal to the current day (block.timestamp/DAY) and the bond to be marked as not expired before allowing the NFT to move between owners. This check is intended to prevent a bond that should have expired from being transferred while the epoch has not been updated. However, the epoch value is only advanced when the distribute function is called, which happens when rewards are actually distributed. If no reward distribution occurs on a given day – for example because investor activity is low, because the asset is blacklisted, or because an external marketplace such as OpenSea does not invoke claimGovFees – the stored epoch remains behind the current day. When a holder then attempts to sell or use the BondNFT as collateral, the transfer logic detects a mismatch, triggers the "Bad epoch" require, and reverts the transaction. From the user’s point of view the NFT appears to be stuck: a sale order on an open market fails, no funds are received, and the NFT cannot be deposited as collateral, even though the user expects a normal transfer. The impact is that listed NFTs cannot be fulfilled and collateralized positions cannot be released, effectively freezing user assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the transfer path and identified the overly strict epoch equality check. It is subtle because the revert message does not explain the business‑logic reason, making it look like a generic contract error rather than a missing reward distribution. The bug belongs to the class of state‑dependency transfer restrictions, where a function’s ability to execute depends on an auxiliary state that is not guaranteed to be refreshed in all usage scenarios. A proper fix is to replace the equality check with a condition that only blocks transfers after the bond’s official expiration epoch, for example require(bond.expireEpoch >= block.timestamp/DAY), thereby decoupling transferability from the reward‑distribution schedule while still preventing transfers of truly expired bonds.

title: Trading will not work on Ethereum if USDT is used
description:
Traders will not be able to:

  1. Initiate a market order
  2. Add margin
  3. Add to position
  4. initiate limit order

If USDT is set as the margin asset and protocol is deployed on Ethereum.

(Note: this issue was submitted after consulting with the sponsor even though currently there are no plans to deploy the platform on Ethereum).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance handling flaw that appears when the Trading contract uses USDT (or any token that implements the non‑standard ERC20 approve logic requiring a zero‑to‑non‑zero change) as the margin asset on Ethereum. USDT’s approve function contains a require that rejects a call which tries to set a non‑zero allowance while a non‑zero allowance already exists, forcing callers to first set the allowance to zero. The Trading contract’s internal _handleDeposit routine unconditionally calls IERC20(_marginAsset).approve(_stableVault, type(uint).max) each time a user deposits margin for actions such as initiating a market order, adding margin, adding to a position, or creating a limit order. On the first deposit the allowance is zero, so the approve succeeds, but on any subsequent deposit the allowance is already non‑zero, causing the USDT approve call to revert. Because the approve call is executed after the transferFrom but before the stable vault deposit, the whole transaction reverts, so the user’s trade does not execute, no funds are transferred, and the UI typically shows a generic “transaction failed” or “reverted” message while the user expected the order to be placed and their margin to be locked. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the allowance pattern used by the protocol and compared it against the USDT token source code on Ethereum. It is easy to miss because most ERC20 tokens allow allowance overwrites, leading developers to assume the same behaviour for all tokens. The impact is that any trader who selects USDT as the margin asset on Ethereum is unable to perform core trading functions, effectively rendering the platform unusable for that asset and potentially causing loss of confidence. The affected parties include the traders, the protocol’s liquidity providers, and the protocol owners who may need to address the bug. The bug belongs to the class of “non‑standard ERC20 approve” or “allowance race‑condition” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should either reset the allowance to zero before setting a new value, use a safeApprove pattern that checks the current allowance, store a flag indicating that the maximum allowance has already been granted and skip further approve calls, or provide an owner‑controlled function that pre‑approves the stable vault once. Using ERC20Permit (EIP‑2612) where available or switching to increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance can also avoid the problem. Implementing one of these fixes will allow USDT margin deposits to succeed without reverting, restoring expected trading functionality.

title: GovNFT: maxBridge has no effect
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unused state variable maxBridge that is intended to cap the number of GovNFT tokens that can be transferred across a bridge in a single operation. The contract provides a setter setMaxBridge that can be called by the owner, but the bridge implementation never reads the variable, so the limit is never enforced. As a result, any user can request to bridge an arbitrary number of GovNFTs in one transaction. The root cause is a logical omission: the developer declared and exposed the variable but omitted the check in the bridging function. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker calls the bridge function with a quantity larger than the intended maximum; the contract processes the request without rejecting it. This can lead to several impacts. First, the protocol’s economic model assumes a bounded flow of NFTs; unlimited bridging can cause accounting mismatches, overflow of internal counters, or exhaustion of gas when processing very large batches, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for honest users. Second, users expecting a safeguard may be surprised when their bridge transaction succeeds with far more NFTs than advertised, violating trust. The condition occurs whenever the bridge function is invoked, regardless of the value set via setMaxBridge, because the check is absent. All participants who interact with the bridge—regular users, token holders, and the protocol’s governance—are affected, as the missing limit can be abused to flood the system. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where the code was inspected and the maxBridge variable was found to be assigned but never referenced in any require or conditional statement. Because the variable is public, its presence may give a false sense of security, making the bug hard to notice without reviewing the execution path. The appropriate remediation is to integrate the maxBridge variable into the bridge logic, adding a condition that rejects any request exceeding the stored limit, and to ensure that the limit is correctly updated and respected across all relevant functions. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “unused state variable / missing enforcement” where a security‑critical parameter is declared but never applied, leading to logic errors and potential DoS or economic abuse. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a “max 20 NFTs per bridge” notice, yet the transaction proceeds with 100 NFTs, resulting in unexpected behavior such as unusually high gas costs or empty balances after a failed attempt to enforce a limit that does not exist. The discrepancy between expectation (a capped bridge) and reality (no cap) breaks the protocol’s accounting assumptions and can be exploited to undermine the system’s integrity.

title: `safeTransferMany`
description: Both `BondNFT` and `GovNFT` are an ERC721 implementation, and they both also have a function named `safeTransferMany()` which its name implies is supposed to safe transfer many tokens at once. However the function doesn’t actually safe transfer.
bug_full: The contract implements two ERC721 tokens, BondNFT and GovNFT, each exposing a function named safeTransferMany that is intended to transfer multiple token IDs in a single call while performing the safety checks defined by ERC721. In reality the function calls the internal _transfer routine instead of _safeTransfer, so the required check that the recipient contract implements IERC721Receiver is omitted. The root cause is a mismatch between the function name and its implementation: the developer copied the single‑token safeTransferFrom logic but replaced the internal call with the non‑safe variant, possibly to avoid the receiver check, but left the name unchanged. An attacker or any user can exploit this by invoking safeTransferMany to send NFTs to a contract that does not implement onERC721Received. Because the transfer succeeds without a revert, the tokens become locked in a contract that has no way to acknowledge or forward them, effectively removing the assets from the owner's control. The impact is loss of ownership or inability to retrieve the NFTs, which may represent voting power, governance rights, or financial value. The vulnerability manifests whenever safeTransferMany is called with a recipient that is not an ERC721Receiver, i.e., any regular address or a contract without the required interface. Users, token holders, and the protocol that relies on the NFTs for governance are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit when test cases expected a revert for transfers to a non‑receiver contract; the single‑token safeTransferFrom behaved correctly, but safeTransferMany did not revert, confirming the discrepancy between intent and behavior. Because the function name suggests safety, developers and auditors may overlook the missing check, especially if they rely on naming conventions rather than reviewing the internal call. The bug belongs to the class of “unsafe token transfer” or “missing receiver validation” bugs common in ERC721 implementations. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful transfer, but later the NFT no longer appears in the wallet and cannot be displayed, leading to confusion such as “my token disappeared” or “the transfer succeeded but I cannot see the NFT”. The expected behavior is that the contract reverts when the recipient does not implement IERC721Receiver; the actual behavior is that the transfer succeeds, violating the ERC721 safety guarantees and breaking accounting assumptions about token custody. The recommended remediation is to replace the internal _transfer call with _safeTransfer for each token ID, or to rename the function to reflect that it performs an unsafe transfer, thereby aligning implementation with intent and restoring the ERC721 safety checks.

title: `BondNFT.extendLock` force a user to extend the bond at least for current bond.period
description:
The current implementation forces a user to extend their bonds for at least they current bond period. This means that, for instance, a bond which was initially locked for 365 can never be extended, even after a week of being created.

If we consider that a bond should have at least a 7 days lock and at the most 365 days, then the current `BondNFT.extendLock` function should be refactored.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the lock‑extension mechanism of the BondNFT contract. The extendLock function calculates the new lock period by adding the remaining epochs of the existing bond (pendingEpochs) to the user‑requested extension (_period). Because pendingEpochs already represents the time left until the original expiry, the resulting newBondPeriod always includes the full remaining original duration, effectively forcing the bond to be extended for at least the current period rather than the incremental amount the user intended. This mistake violates the business rule that a bond may be extended by a small number of days (for example three days) after a partial lock time has elapsed. The bug is triggered whenever a user calls extendLock with a period that is shorter than the remaining lock time, which is a common scenario when users wish to add a few extra days after the bond has partially matured. As a result, the contract records a longer expiry epoch than expected, preventing the user from releasing the bond at the anticipated time. From the user’s perspective the bond remains locked beyond the promised date, the UI shows an unchanged or increased period, and attempts to release the bond revert with an “!expire” error, effectively trapping the principal. The impact is a loss of usability and potential financial loss because the user receives fewer rewards for the unintended longer lock and cannot access their funds when they expected to. The issue was discovered during a functional test that simulated a lock of ten days, waited five days, then attempted to extend by three days; the contract extended the lock to thirteen days, causing the release call to fail. The flaw is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit warning; the only symptom is that the lock duration is longer than the user requested, which can be mistaken for a normal longer lock. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect state update due to misuse of remaining time in period calculations” and is a specific instance of a lock‑extension logic error. To remediate, the implementation should compute the new period based solely on the user‑requested increment, validate that the resulting total period respects the minimum and maximum bounds, and avoid adding the remaining epochs to the extension. In other words, the contract must enforce newBondPeriod = bond.period + _period (or similar) after confirming that the bond is not expired and that pending rewards are zero, rather than using pendingEpochs in the calculation. Proper checks for minimum and maximum lock durations should remain, but the core arithmetic must be corrected to reflect the intended incremental extension, thereby restoring the expected release timeline and reward calculation.

title: `_handleOpenFees` returns an incorrect value for `_feePaid`. This directly impacts margin calculations
description:
Formula for `fee paid` in [Line 734](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/contracts/Trading.sol#L734) is incorrect leading to incorrect margin calculations. Since this directly impacts the trader margin and associated fee calculations, I’ve marked as HIGH risk.

On initiating a market order, `Margin` is adjusted for the `fees` that is charged by protocol. This adjustment is in [Line 178 of Trading](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/588c84b7bb354d20cbca6034544c4faa46e6a80e/contracts/Trading.sol#L178). Fees computed by `_handleOpenFees` is deducted from Initial margin posted by user.

Formula misses to account for the `2*referralFee` component while calculaing `_feePaid`.
poc:
Note that `_feePaid` as per formula in Line 734 is the sum of `_daoFeesPaid`, and sum of `burnerFee`&`botFee` . `_daoFeesPaid` is calculated from `_fees.daoFees` which itself is calculated by subtracting `2*referralFee` and `botFee`.

So when we add back `burnerFee` and `botFee` to `_feePaid`, we are missing to add back the `2*referralFee` which was earlier excluded when calculating `_daoFeesPaid`. While `botFee` is added back correctly, same adjustment is not being done viz-a-viz referral fee.

This results in under calculating the `_feePaid` and impacts the rewards paid to the protocol NFT holders.
bug_full: The contract contains an accounting bug in the function that computes the fee amount for opening a market order. The variable that represents the total fee paid, _feePaid, is calculated using a formula that adds the DAO fee component and the sum of the burner and bot fees, but it fails to re‑include the referral fee that was previously subtracted when the DAO fee was derived. Because the referral fee is multiplied by two in the DAO fee calculation, omitting the 2*referralFee term causes the final fee value to be lower than it should be. This under‑calculation propagates to the margin adjustment logic, where the fee amount is deducted from the trader’s initial margin. As a result, the trader’s effective margin appears larger than the protocol’s accounting expects, allowing positions to be opened with insufficient collateral or causing the protocol to collect less revenue than intended. The issue manifests whenever a market order is opened and a non‑zero referral fee is configured, which is the normal path for most trades. Users experience a discrepancy between the margin shown in the UI and the actual risk they are taking; they may notice that their positions can be opened with more leverage than expected, or that protocol‑issued NFT rewards are lower because the fee pool is under‑funded. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditor traced the fee flow and identified that the referral component was omitted from the final fee aggregation. Because the error is hidden inside a multi‑step fee calculation, it does not produce an obvious runtime exception and can easily be missed during testing, especially if the UI only displays the final margin figure. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑calculation or accounting errors where a component of a composite fee is unintentionally dropped, leading to an under‑estimation of required fees. To remediate, the fee formula should be amended to add back the missing 2*referralFees term, ensuring that the total fee paid reflects all constituent parts before being deducted from the trader’s margin. This correction restores the intended economic guarantees of the protocol, aligns the on‑chain accounting with the expected fee revenue, and prevents potential exploitation where an attacker could open over‑leveraged positions or cause the protocol to lose fee income.

title: Centralization risks: owner can freeze withdraws and use timelock to steal all funds
description:
The project heavily relies on nodes/oracles, which are EOAs that sign the current price.

Since all functions (including withdrawing) require a recently-signed price, the owner(s) of those EOA can freeze all activity by not providing signed prices.

I got from the sponsor that the owner of the contract is going to be a timelock contract. However, once the owner holds the power to pause withdrawals - that nullifies the timelock. The whole point of the timelock is to allow users to withdraw their funds when they see a pending malicious tx before it’s executed. If the owner has the power to freeze users’ funds in the contract, they wouldn’t be able to do anything while the owner executes his malicious activity.

Besides that, there are also LP funds, which are locked to a certain period, and also can’t withdraw their funds when they see a pending malicious timelock tx.
poc:
* The fact that the protocol relies on EOA signatures is pretty clear from the code and docs
  * The whole project relies on the ‘StableVault’ and ‘StableToken’

    * The value of the ‘StableToken’ comes from the real stablecoin that’s locked in ‘StableVault’, if someone manages to empty the ‘StableVault’ from the deposited stablecoins the ‘StableToken’ would become worthless
  * The owner has a few ways to drain all funds:

    * Replace the minter via `StableToken.setMinter()`, mint more tokens, and redeem them via `StableVault.withdraw()`
    * List a fake token at `StableVault`, deposit it and withdraw real stablecoin
    * List a new fake asset for trading with a fake chainlink oracle, fake profit with trading with fake prices, and then withdraw

      * They can prevent other users from doing the same by setting `maxOi` and opening position in the same tx
    * Replace the MetaTx forwarder and execute tx on behalf of users (e.g. transferring bonds, positions and StableToken from their account)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk where the contract’s owner (initially a timelock or multisig) retains the ability to halt all user withdrawals and manipulate oracle data. The protocol requires a freshly signed price from external EOAs for every state‑changing operation, including withdrawals. Because the owner controls those EOAs, they can simply stop signing, causing the contract to reject any request that depends on a recent price. In addition, the contract includes an admin‑only pause function that can be invoked by the owner to freeze the withdraw function directly. This combination defeats the intended safety mechanism of the timelock, which is supposed to give users a window to react to a pending malicious proposal. When the owner exercises the pause or withholds oracle signatures, users see no balance updates, attempts to withdraw return zero or revert, and LP tokens remain locked even though the lock period has elapsed. The impact is that the owner can effectively seize control of all deposited stablecoins, mint additional protocol tokens via a privileged setMinter call, list fake assets, or replace the meta‑transaction forwarder to act on behalf of users, leading to a total drain of funds. The condition occurs whenever the owner decides to withhold price data or invoke the pause, which can be done at any time because the privilege is not time‑locked. All participants—regular users, liquidity providers, and any party relying on the protocol’s price feed—are affected because their assets become inaccessible or can be stolen. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the dependency on external EOAs for price signatures and identified admin functions that bypass the timelock’s delay. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves normally when signatures are provided, and the pause function may be assumed to be a harmless safety switch rather than a tool for theft. To remediate, the protocol should replace the EOA‑based oracle with a decentralized on‑chain price source (e.g., Chainlink or Uniswap TWAP), remove or restrict the admin pause of withdrawals, and ensure that any fallback price mechanism can be triggered by users after a reasonable timeout. In general, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized oracle and admin‑controlled freeze” vulnerabilities, where excessive privileged control breaks the trust model and enables fund confiscation.

title: One can become referral of hash 0x0 and because all users default referral hash is 0x0 so he would become all users referral by default and earn a lot of fees while users didn’t approve it
description: By default the value of `_referred[user]` is 0x0 for all users and if one set 0x0 as his referral hash then he would become referral for all the users who didn’t set referral by default and he would earn a lot of referral funds that users didn’t approve it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a default‑value misuse in the referral system where the contract treats the zero hash (0x0) as a regular referral identifier. By default the mapping that stores a user’s referred hash returns 0x0 for any address that has not explicitly set a referral. The contract’s createReferralCode function does not forbid registering a referral code with the zero hash, so the first caller can execute createReferralCode(0x0) and become the owner of the zero‑hash entry. When a trader who has not set a referral invokes a trade, the getRef function queries the referred hash, receives 0x0, and then looks up the address associated with that hash, which is now the attacker’s address. The fee‑handling functions (_handleOpenFees and _handleCloseFees) use the result of getRef to transfer the referral portion of the fee, unintentionally sending it to the attacker. This flaw occurs whenever a user trades without specifying a referrer and the attacker has previously claimed the zero hash. All traders, the protocol’s revenue model and any legitimate referrers are affected because a portion of fees that should either remain with the protocol or be unassigned is diverted to the attacker without the users’ consent. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the assumptions around the default referral value and demonstrated that the first claimant to the zero hash receives fees from all non‑referred users. It is hard to notice because the zero address is commonly used as a sentinel value and the UI does not display any referral information for users who have not set one, so the trade appears normal while the referral fee silently disappears. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that no referral fee is taken when no referrer is set, yet the reality is that the fee is transferred to an unknown address, leading to missing referral rewards or reduced net proceeds. The bug belongs to the class of “default value or null identifier misuse” and can be mitigated by rejecting zero‑hash referrals, treating the zero hash as a special case that returns address(0) and does not trigger fee transfers, or by requiring a non‑zero hash at creation time. Conceptually the fix is to enforce that the null identifier cannot be used as a legitimate referral code, thereby restoring the intended accounting logic where only explicitly chosen referrers receive fees.

title: `BondNFT.sol#claim
description:
In `BondNFT.sol#claim()`, `accRewardsPerShare[][]` is amended to reflect the expired shares. But only `accRewardsPerShare[bond.asset][epoch[bond.asset]]` is updated. All the epochs between `bond.expireEpoch-1` and `epoch[bond.asset]` are missed.

However, some users claimable rewards calculation could be based on the missed epochs. As a result, the impact might be:

  * `accRewardsPerShare` is inaccurate for the epochs in between.
  * Some users could lose reward due to wrong `accRewardsPerShare`, some users might receive undeserved rewards.
  * Some rewards will be locked in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claim logic of the BondNFT contract where the accumulated rewards per share (accRewardsPerShare) are only updated for the most recent epoch when a bond is marked as expired. The function calculates a pending delta based on the current epoch index but does not iterate over or adjust the entries for any epochs that lie between the bond's last recorded expiry epoch (bond.expireEpoch‑1) and the current epoch for the asset. This omission creates a mismatch between the stored accRewardsPerShare values for those intermediate epochs and the actual rewards that should have been accrued. As a result, when a user later calls claim, the pending reward is derived from a stale or incorrect accRewardsPerShare entry, causing the contract to either under‑pay the holder, over‑pay them, or lock a portion of the rewards inside the contract. The issue manifests only after a bond has expired and multiple epochs have elapsed without an intermediate claim, which is a common scenario for long‑term holders. It affects any bond holder, the protocol’s overall yield distribution, and any party that can trigger the claim function, including the manager role. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that the accRewardsPerShare array was amended only at index epoch[asset] while the loop over the missing epochs was absent, leading to inaccurate accounting. The problem is subtle because the contract still transfers some reward amount, so users may not notice a small shortfall, and there is no explicit error or event indicating the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should either iterate over all missed epochs and update accRewardsPerShare for each, or redesign the accounting to store cumulative rewards that can be correctly referenced for any epoch, ensuring that the pending calculation always reflects the true accrued amount. Such a fix restores the invariant that rewards are neither lost nor granted erroneously, preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees and preventing locked funds.

title: `_checkDelay` will not work properly for Arbitrum or Optimism due to `block.number`
description: Trade delay will not work correctly on Arbitrum allowing users to exploit multiple valid prices.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on block.number to enforce a minimum number of blocks between opening and closing a position. On roll‑up chains such as Arbitrum and Optimism, block.number does not increase with every L2 block in the short term; instead it reflects the most recent L1 block that has been synchronised, which typically happens only once per minute. Because of this, a contract that expects a delay of, for example, twelve seconds by adding a fixed number of blocks may actually see the delay collapse to a single L2 block when the transaction occurs just before the synchronisation point. An attacker can therefore open a position in the block immediately preceding the sync, wait for the synchronisation to occur, and then close the position in the next L2 block, satisfying the apparent block‑based delay while only a few seconds have elapsed. This bypass allows the attacker to reuse a price that should have become stale, execute multiple trades at the same oracle price, and potentially capture arbitrage profits that the protocol intended to prevent. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions: users expect a waiting period that protects against rapid price manipulation, but the contract may allow immediate execution, leading to unfair advantage, loss of confidence, and possible financial loss for other participants. The issue manifests only when the delay is measured in a short time window (seconds to a few minutes) on L2 networks; longer delays of minutes to hours remain reliable because the synchronisation lag becomes negligible. The bug was identified during a security audit by reviewing the delay logic and cross‑checking the Arbitrum and Optimism documentation, which explicitly warn that block numbers are unreliable for fine‑grained timing. It is difficult to notice because the block number appears to increase as usual, yet it is stale relative to the actual L2 block progression, so developers may assume the delay works as on Ethereum mainnet. The proper mitigation is to replace block.number with a time‑based metric such as block.timestamp, or to use an L1‑derived block number that updates each L2 block, thereby ensuring that the enforced waiting period reflects real elapsed time. In user‑facing terms, a trader who expects their order to be delayed for about a minute may see the trade execute instantly, receiving no warning and potentially losing the opportunity to act on a stale price, which contradicts the protocol’s intended behavior and breaks the accounting model that relies on a minimum time gap between actions.

title: `distribute`
description:
Function `BondNFT.createLock()` creates a bond and it sets bond’s mint epoch as `epoch[asset]`. Function `Lock.lock()` first calls `claimGovFees()` which calls `BondNFT.distribute()` for all assets and updates the `epoch[assets]` for all assets. So during normal bond creation, the value of `epoch[asset]` would be updated and bond would be created from `today` epoch to `today+period` epoch. But if `totalShares[tigAsset] == 0` for an asset, then `distribute()` won’t update `epoch[asset]` for that asset and `epoch[asset]` will be some old epoch (will be the start time where asset is added or the time where `totalShares[_tigAsset] != 0`). This would make `createLock()` set very wrong values for bond’s mint epoch when `totalShares[tigAsset] == 0`.

This would happen for the first bond that has been created for that asset always and it will happen again if for some period `totalShares[asset]` become 0, then the next bond would have wrong mint epoch. or `setAllowedAsset(asset, false)` has been called for that asset.
bug_full: The contract suffers from an epoch‑update logic flaw in the reward distribution routine. The function that records incoming rewards, distribute, only advances the stored epoch for a given asset when the total amount of shares for that asset is non‑zero. If totalShares for the asset equals zero – which occurs for the very first bond of a newly added asset, after all bonds have been withdrawn, or after an asset has been temporarily disabled – the early‑return prevents the epoch index from being moved forward to the current day. Consequently, when a user later calls lock, the lock routine invokes claimGovFees which triggers distribute, but because the epoch value remains stuck at an old timestamp, the subsequent call to createLock records a mint epoch that is far in the past. The bond therefore receives an expire epoch that is calculated from this stale mint epoch, granting the locker an artificially long reward period while the actual lock duration may be only a few days. An attacker can exploit this by waiting until the asset is re‑enabled, creating a lock with a short period, and still receiving reward shares as if the lock had lasted the full (incorrectly extended) period, allowing them to claim excess yield. The impact is a theft of protocol rewards: honest participants receive less than their fair share, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about linear reward accrual per day are violated. The bug manifests as users seeing unexpectedly high reward balances or receiving rewards for a lock that has already expired, while the UI may show normal lock durations. It is hard to notice because the epoch variable is not directly exposed and the contract still enforces period limits, so the abnormal reward amounts may be attributed to normal variance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow from lock through claimGovFees to distribute and observed that epoch was never updated when totalShares was zero. To remediate, the distribute function should always increment the epoch index up to the current day regardless of share balance, while skipping only the division‑by‑zero and token transfer when totalShares is zero. This ensures that mint epochs are always based on the actual current time, preserving correct reward calculations and preventing inflated share allocation.

title: User can close an order via `limitClose`
description:
Bot fees are used when a position is opened/closed via a bot. In that case a bot fee is subtracted from the DAO fee and sent to the closing bot. A user can use that to reduce the DAO fees for closing an order and keeping it to themselves.

Instead of closing the order via `initiateClose()`, the user can use a proxy contract to update the stop-loss value and then `limitClose()` the order. Since that is done in one function call, no bot can run the `limitClose()` and the bot fee will go to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an economic bypass that lets a trader capture the fee normally reserved for a closing bot by executing a stop‑loss or take‑profit update and a limit‑close in the same transaction. In the protocol, when a position is closed by a bot the bot fee is subtracted from the DAO fee and transferred to the bot that called limitClose. Because the contract does not enforce a separation between the price‑limit update (updateTpSl) and the actual limitClose call, a user can deploy a proxy contract, approve it, and invoke a function that first updates the stop‑loss or take‑profit and then immediately calls limitClose. Since both actions occur in the same block, no external bot has the opportunity to run limitClose, and the fee that would have been paid to the bot is instead sent to the caller of the proxy – the user themselves. This reduces the DAO’s fee revenue and gives the trader an unintended discount, violating the protocol’s fee accounting assumptions. The issue appears only as a subtle reduction in expected DAO earnings; the transaction succeeds and the user’s balance reflects the received fee, making it easy to miss during functional testing. It was discovered during a security audit by constructing a minimal MyTrader contract that reproduces the flow. The root cause is the lack of a temporal or state guard that prevents updating sl/tp and executing limitClose within the same block, combined with the fee logic that credits the caller of limitClose. The recommended mitigation is to disallow calling limitClose in the same block as an sl/tp update, for example by recording the timestamp of the last limit‑order modification and refusing a limitClose if it occurs before a defined delay, thereby ensuring that only an independent bot can earn the fee and preserving the intended fee distribution model.

title: StopLoss/TakeProfit should be validated again for the new price in `Trading.executeLimitOrder`
description:
The open price of a stop order might be changed during execution but it doesn’t validate StopLoss/TakeProfit for the changed price.

As a result, the executed market order might be closed immediately and there would be an unexpected loss for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of stop‑loss (SL) and take‑profit (TP) thresholds after the contract overwrites the open price of a stop order during execution in the Trading.executeLimitOrder function. The root cause is that the code updates trade.price with the current verified market price (_price) for stop orders (orderType 2) but does not re‑evaluate whether the new price still satisfies the SL/TP conditions that were originally set by the trader. Because the SL/TP checks are performed only against the original price, a large price movement or a manipulated price feed can cause the updated price to fall outside the allowed SL/TP range. An attacker or a volatile market can therefore trigger the SL or TP immediately after the order is opened, causing the market order to be closed in the same transaction. This results in an unexpected loss for the user: the trade is opened and then instantly closed, often leaving the user with a zero or reduced balance, no profit, and a perception that funds have disappeared. The issue occurs only for stop orders whose price is not guaranteed; limit orders are safe because their price is fixed. It affects any trader who relies on SL/TP protection, the protocol’s accounting logic, and ultimately the overall trustworthiness of the platform. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that the price variable was reassigned without a subsequent SL/TP check, and a warden demonstration showed that a limit order could pass the initial validation yet be executed with an invalid SL/TP configuration. The bug is subtle because the price change is a legitimate operation for stop orders, so the missing check does not raise an obvious error flag, making it hard to notice during normal testing. To fix the issue, the contract should re‑validate both SL and TP (or at least TP, as the mitigation later applied) after any modification of trade.price, or avoid modifying the price for stop orders altogether, ensuring that the final execution price always respects the trader‑specified protection levels. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that SL/TP thresholds must guard against adverse price movements throughout the entire order lifecycle.

title: `_handleDeposit` and `_handleWithdraw` do not account for tokens with decimals higher than 18
description:
In `Trading.sol` a [deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/contracts/Trading.sol#L675) or [withdrawal](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/contracts/Trading.sol#L700) of tokens with decimals higher than 18 will always revert.

This is the case e.g. for `NEAR` which is divisible into 10e24 `yocto`
poc:
Change [00.Mocks.js#L33](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/deploy/test/00.Mocks.js#L33) to:

```solidity
args: ["USDC", "USDC", 24, deployer, ethers.utils.parseUnits("1000", 24)]
```

Then in [07.Trading.js](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/main/test/07.Trading.js):

Opening and closing a position with tigUSD output
Opening and closing a position with <18 decimal token output

are going to fail with:

Error: VM Exception while processing transaction: reverted with panic code 0x11 (Arithmetic operation underflowed or overflowed outside of an unchecked block)
bug_full: The contract contains a mathematical handling error in the internal deposit and withdrawal routines that assumes every ERC20 token uses at most 18 decimal places. The code scales token amounts by a constant factor derived from 10**18, and when a token reports a larger decimal count (for example NEAR with 24 decimals) the scaling operation attempts to multiply or divide by a negative exponent, which underflows the unsigned integer arithmetic. This underflow triggers Solidity’s built‑in panic with code 0x11, causing the entire transaction to revert. The vulnerability is discovered during a security audit when a mock token with 24 decimals was used in a test that exercised the deposit and withdraw paths; the test consistently failed with an arithmetic underflow panic. From a user’s point of view, attempting to deposit or withdraw a high‑precision token results in an immediate transaction failure, often reported as “transaction reverted” without any change to balances, contrary to the expectation that the operation would succeed and the token balance would be updated. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for any token whose decimal precision exceeds 18: users cannot add liquidity, open positions, or retrieve funds using such tokens, effectively locking the functionality for those assets. The issue is subtle because the majority of popular tokens conform to the 18‑decimal convention, so standard test suites may not expose the bug. The root cause is the hard‑coded assumption about token decimals rather than querying the token’s `decimals()` value and adjusting the arithmetic accordingly. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the token’s decimal count at runtime and perform scaling using a dynamic factor, or explicitly reject tokens with more than 18 decimals with a clear error message. By correcting the scaling logic, the contract will honor the accounting assumptions for all ERC20 tokens, preventing unexpected reverts and preserving expected user experience.

title: Trading#initiateMarketOrder allows to open a position with more margin than expected due to _handleOpenFees wrong calculation when a trade is referred
poc:
The output of `_handleOpenFees` is `_feePaid`, which is calculated [once](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/588c84b7bb354d20cbca6034544c4faa46e6a80e/contracts/Trading.sol#L734-L738), and it does not consider referralFees:

```solidity
// No refferal fees are considered
_feePaid =
    _positionSize
    * (_fees.burnFees + _fees.botFees) // get total fee%
    / DIVISION_CONSTANT // divide by 100%
    + _daoFeesPaid;
```

Then we can notice that, if the output of `_handleOpenFees` did not consider referral fees, neither would `\_marginAfterFees` do:

```solidity
uint256 _marginAfterFees =
    _tradeInfo.margin-
    _handleOpenFees(
        _tradeInfo.asset,
        _tradeInfo.margin*_tradeInfo.leverage/1e18, 
        _trader,
        _tigAsset,
        false);
 
// @audit Then _positionSize would be greater than what is supposed to be, allowing to create a position greater than expected
uint256 _positionSize = _marginAfterFees * _tradeInfo.leverage / 1e18;
```
bug_full:
The vulnerability originates from an incorrect fee accounting path in the Trading contract when a market order is initiated with a referrer attached. The function initiateMarketOrder computes a temporary variable _marginAfterFees by subtracting the result of _handleOpenFees from the trader's supplied margin, and then derives the final _positionSize by multiplying _marginAfterFees with the requested leverage. The root cause is that _handleOpenFees calculates the total fee to be paid based solely on burnFees and botFees, completely ignoring any referralFees that should be deducted when a referrer address is present. Because the referral fee is omitted, the fee amount returned by _handleOpenFees is lower than it should be, which means the subtraction from the trader's margin is smaller, leaving a larger _marginAfterFees value. Consequently, the subsequent multiplication by leverage yields a _positionSize that exceeds the size a trader expects given the original margin and fee schedule.

An attacker can exploit this by ensuring that a non‑zero referrer address is supplied in the trade data, thereby triggering the fee‑omission path. The protocol will then credit the trader with a larger position than the economic model predicts, effectively allowing the trader to open a position with more effective margin than intended. This can lead to over‑leveraged positions, distort the protocol’s risk calculations, and give the attacker an unfair advantage that may result in higher profits or reduced liquidation risk. The impact is primarily on the protocol’s accounting integrity and on other market participants who rely on correct fee deductions; the protocol may suffer from unexpected exposure, and the DAO’s fee revenue could be reduced.

The condition under which the bug manifests is any market order that includes a referrer (i.e., _referrer != address(0)) while the contract’s fee configuration defines a non‑zero referralFees percentage. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors traced the fee calculation flow and observed that the referral component never contributed to the feePaid variable. Because the resulting position size still appears mathematically consistent – the contract simply uses a larger margin after fees – the problem can be subtle and may not be immediately visible in UI screens; users see a larger position and may assume they received a better deal, while the protocol’s internal accounting is silently out of balance.

From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after submitting a trade the displayed position size is larger than expected, and the margin that appears to be deducted from the wallet is smaller than it should be. A trader might expect a certain amount of collateral to be locked, but observes that more leverage is granted for the same collateral, leading to confusion. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑calculation or accounting errors where a component of the fee schedule is omitted, causing an inflated effective margin.

The recommended remediation is to modify _handleOpenFees so that the feePaid calculation incorporates the referralFees component alongside burnFees and botFees. By adding the referral fee percentage to the total fee multiplier, the fee amount will correctly reflect the full fee schedule, ensuring that _marginAfterFees is reduced by the proper amount and that the derived _positionSize matches the protocol’s economic expectations. This change restores accurate accounting, prevents unintended leverage inflation, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic.

title: `executeLimitOrder`
description:
The `PairsContract` registers the total long/short position that’s open for a pair of assets, whenever a new position is created, the total grows accordingly.

However at `executeLimitOrder()` the position size that’s added is wrongly calculated - it uses margin before fees, while the actual position is created after subtracting fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the limit‑order execution path of the trading contract. When a limit order is executed, the protocol records the new open interest (OI) for the asset pair by multiplying the supplied margin by the requested leverage. However, the calculation mistakenly uses the raw margin amount before any protocol fees are deducted, while the actual position that is created later in the same transaction applies the fee deduction first. As a result, the OI value stored in the PairsContract is larger than the true economic exposure of the trader. This discrepancy becomes visible in tests where a 100× leveraged order reports an OI that is about 11 % higher than the position’s real size. The root cause is a mismatch between the accounting of fees and the OI update logic inside executeLimitOrder. An attacker can exploit the bug by opening large‑leverage limit orders, artificially inflating the reported OI. Because funding rates, liquidation thresholds and other risk parameters are derived from OI, an inflated figure can lead to incorrect funding payments, premature liquidations or mis‑priced funding that harms honest traders and liquidity providers. The impact is therefore a distortion of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, potentially causing users to lose funds or receive unexpected fees. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of a limit order where fees are charged – it does not affect market orders that bypass the same path. All participants who rely on accurate OI – traders, protocol governance, and anyone holding positions that are funded by the protocol – are affected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the OI value returned by the contract with the margin × leverage formula and observed a systematic over‑statement. It is hard to notice in production because OI is an internal metric not displayed in the UI; only indirect symptoms such as abnormal funding rates or unexpected liquidation behavior may hint at the problem. The correct fix is to adjust the OI calculation to use the net margin after fee deduction, ensuring that the recorded position size matches the economic reality of the trade. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches where fees are applied inconsistently across related state updates, leading to a divergence between on‑chain accounting and business logic expectations.
