From a user’s perspective the contract may appear to open a position with the expected leverage, yet the protocol’s internal bookkeeping shows a larger exposure, causing the user to see funding charges that do not align with the actual trade, or to see their position liquidated earlier than anticipated.

title: Unreleased locks cause the reward distribution to be flawed in BondNFT
description:
After a lock has expired, it doesn’t get any rewards distributed to it. But, unreleased locks cause other existing bonds to not receive the full amount of tokens either. The issue is that as long as the bond is not released, the `totalShares` value isn’t updated. Everybody receives a smaller cut of the distribution. Thus, bond owners receive less rewards than they should.

A bond can be released after it expired by the owner of it. If the owner doesn’t release it for 7 days, anybody else can release it as well. As long as the owner doesn’t release it, the issue will be in effect for at least 7 epochs.

Since this causes a loss of funds for every bond holder I rate it as HIGH. It’s likely to be an issue since you can’t guarantee that bonds will be released the day they expire.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the reward distribution mechanism of the BondNFT contract where expired bonds that have not been released continue to be counted in the global share pool (totalShares). The root cause is that the contract only updates totalShares when the release function is called, subtracting the shares of a bond at that moment. When a lock expires, its rewards are not automatically released; instead the bond remains in the system for up to seven days before the owner or any external actor can invoke release. During this window the expired bond’s shares are still part of totalShares, so the proportion of rewards allocated to active bonds is reduced. An attacker does not need to act maliciously; the bug can be triggered simply by allowing a bond to expire and remain unreleased. Exploitation consists of letting one or more bonds sit expired without calling release, then performing a distribution; active bond owners receive a smaller slice of the tokens than the contract’s accounting assumes. The impact is that bond holders receive less reward than they are entitled to, effectively causing a temporary loss of funds. This situation occurs whenever a bond expires and the release function is not invoked within the seven‑epoch grace period, which can happen because users may forget to release or may be unable to act promptly. All participants who hold active bonds are affected, as each suffers a reduced payout. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the scenario in a test that locked two bonds, distributed rewards, let one bond expire, and observed that the remaining bond’s pending reward was lower than expected. The bug is subtle because the contract still emits a distribution event and the amounts appear plausible, making the shortfall easy to miss without precise accounting checks. To fix the problem, the distribution logic should consider only shares belonging to currently active bonds, either by updating totalShares automatically on expiration or by excluding expired‑but‑unreleased bonds from the share calculation. This change restores the intended invariant that the sum of distributed rewards equals the total amount allocated to active participants, ensuring that users receive the full amount of tokens they are owed and that the protocol’s reward guarantees are upheld.

title: Governance NFT holder, whose NFT was minted before `Trading._handleOpenFees` function is called, can lose deserved rewards after `Trading._handleOpenFees` function is called
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing ERC20 allowance when the Trading contract processes open‑position fees. In the internal function that handles opening fees, the contract mints DAO fee tokens to its own balance and then calls the Governance NFT contract’s distribute function, which attempts to pull the minted tokens via IERC20.transferFrom. Because the Trading contract never calls approve for the Governance NFT before this pull, the transferFrom call fails silently inside a try‑catch block, leaving the DAO fees locked in the Trading contract. This omission only manifests when an open‑position fee is processed before any close‑position fee has been handled, because the close‑fee function does include an approve call. As a result, any Governance NFT that was minted before the first open‑fee call does not receive the rewards it is entitled to; the pending reward for the holder remains zero even though the FeesDistributed event shows that fees were generated. The impact is a loss of expected reward tokens for early NFT holders, breaking the accounting assumption that DAO fees are automatically credited to the reward pool. The bug is discovered during a security audit by observing that the approve call is absent in the open‑fee path and confirming the behavior with a test that mints an NFT before calling initiateMarketOrder. It is hard to notice because the contract still emits the correct event and mints the tokens, so a UI that only reads the event may appear correct while the reward balance stays empty. The issue belongs to the class of token‑allowance omission bugs where a contract attempts to pull tokens without having been granted an allowance. The fix is to add an approve call for the Governance NFT before invoking distribute, or to set a permanent allowance on deployment, ensuring that transferFrom succeeds and the reward accounting matches the emitted fees. This correction restores the expected behavior where a user who holds a Governance NFT sees a positive pending reward after a trade, aligning the protocol’s business logic with its accounting of DAO fees.

title: Chainlink price feed is not sufficiently validated and can return stale price
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

  1. Alice calls the `Trading.initiateMarketOrder` function, which eventually calls the `TradingLibrary.verifyPrice` function, to initiate a market order.
  2. When the `TradingLibrary.verifyPrice` function is called, the off-chain price is compared to the price returned by the Chainlink price feed for the position asset.
  3. The price returned by the Chainlink price feed is stale, and the off-chain price has less than a 2% difference when comparing to this stale price.
  4. Alice’s `Trading.initiateMarketOrder` transaction goes through. However, this transaction should revert because the off-chain price has more than a 2% difference if comparing to a more current price returned by the Chainlink price feed.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract validates the price returned by a Chainlink oracle. The verification routine calls the deprecated latestAnswer function, which only returns the most recent price value without any information about when that price was reported or whether it belongs to the current round. Because the code never checks the round identifier or the timestamp associated with the answer, a stale price – a price that was reported in a previous round and has not been updated – can be accepted as fresh. When a trader submits an off‑chain price that differs by more than two percent from the current market price, the contract is supposed to revert the transaction. However, if the Chainlink feed is stale, the stale price may still be within the two‑percent window, causing the require statement to succeed and the trade to be processed. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who either waits for the feed to become outdated or manipulates the off‑chain price source, allowing trades to execute at a price that is significantly worse than the true market price. The impact is that users may receive an unfavorable execution price, potentially losing funds, while the protocol may suffer value extraction or unintended accounting errors. The issue occurs whenever the contract’s price verification path is enabled (the _chainlinkEnabled flag is true and a non‑zero feed address is supplied) and the Chainlink feed has not been updated for the latest round. All participants who rely on the price check – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the documented oracle validation logic with the actual implementation and noted the use of the deprecated function and the absence of freshness checks. Because the transaction does not revert and the UI shows a successful trade, the bug can be hard to notice; users only see a trade that appears to have executed normally but may notice an unexpected loss or a price that seems off. The class of bug is an oracle‑staleness validation failure, where the contract accepts outdated data without proper verification. To remediate, the contract should replace latestAnswer with latestRoundData, compare answeredInRound with the current roundId to ensure the answer is fresh, and verify that the returned timestamp is non‑zero (and optionally recent). This ensures that the price used for the two‑percent tolerance check reflects the latest market data, restoring the intended security guarantees.

title: Griefing attack by front-running to prevent user withdrawals.
description: An attacker can revert a user’s withdrawTo by front-running to deposit a dust amount of collateral in the user’s account. The collateralInvariant modifier is used to check whether the account is either empty or above the minimum collateral at the end of each withdrawTo. Meanwhile, depositTo allows deposits to an arbitrary address with no minimum deposit amount required. This opens a griefing attack vector where an attacker can frontrun any user’s withdrawTo to deposit a dust amount of collateral for the victim and make the victim's withdrawTo revert because the account is not empty after the withdrawal and the amount of remaining funds cannot meet the minimum collateral. Example scenario: 1. Alice has 1M collateral 2. Alice submits withdrawTo 1M (all the collateral) 3. Attacker frontruns Alice’s transaction to deposit 1 Wei in her account 4. Alice's withdrawal will revert with CollateralUnderLimitError The attacker can repeatedly front-run Alice's withdrawAl and effectively prevent Alice from withdrawing her collateral. This causes a denial-of-service to users’ withdrawals.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running griefing attack that exploits a mismatch between the contract's deposit logic and a collateral invariant check, allowing an attacker to prevent a user from withdrawing their entire collateral. The root cause is that the depositTo function permits deposits of any amount, including a single wei, to an arbitrary address without enforcing the protocol's minimum collateral requirement. After a withdrawal, the collateralInvariant modifier asserts that the account must be either empty or hold at least the minimum collateral defined by the controller. When a user initiates a withdrawTo that would empty the account, an attacker can observe the pending transaction and front‑run it by depositing a dust amount (for example, 1 wei) into the victim’s account. This tiny deposit makes the account non‑empty but still below the required minimum, causing the invariant check to fail and the withdrawal to revert with a CollateralUnderLimitError. The attack can be repeated indefinitely, resulting in a denial‑of‑service where the victim’s funds remain locked despite having sufficient balance. The issue manifests when a user attempts to withdraw all of their collateral and the protocol allows arbitrary, zero‑minimum deposits to other accounts. Any holder of collateral who wishes to empty their position is affected, as the attacker can target any such withdrawal. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditor noticed that the invariant logic did not account for dust deposits and that depositTo lacked a minimum amount check. It is hard to notice because a one‑wei deposit appears negligible and does not raise alarms, yet it triggers a contract‑level revert only after the withdrawal completes. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “dust‑based front‑running griefing” or “minimum‑balance enforcement bypass” bugs, where an adversary injects a minimal amount of value to violate a business rule that assumes either zero or a threshold balance. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction failure with an error message, the expected full withdrawal does not occur, and the displayed balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that any deposit to an address other than the sender must be at least the controller’s minimum collateral, or the invariant should be rewritten to allow a non‑zero balance that is below the threshold only when the withdrawal is not intended to empty the account. Additional mitigations could include commit‑reveal schemes or preventing front‑running through transaction ordering guarantees. Implementing a proper minimum‑deposit check eliminates the dust attack vector and restores the intended withdrawal functionality.

title: Protocol owner is a single point of failure.
description: Protocol owner can arbitrarily and unilaterally create coordinators/products, update product/incentivizer/collateral addresses and change the various fees and minimum collateral requirements used by all the products and users of the protocol. This presents a critical single point of failure. If a protocol owner becomes malicious or compromised, the entire protocol is immediately at risk for all existing/future products and users. While the updation of critical parameters emit events, that only lets product owners and users react after the fact because these changes are not time-delayed. A scenario that affects future products/users is the updation of product/incentivizer/collateral contract addresses to malicious ones and creation of malicious/biased products/coordinators. A DoS scenario, for existing products/users, is the protocol owner increasing the minimum collateral to a high enough value which prevents deposits and withdrawals for certain accounts/products. The owner may increase the protocol fee split to 100% taking away the incentives for existing product owners. The owner may decrease the liquidation fee to a very low value making it uneconomical to liquidate under-collateralized accounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralized administrative control flaw where a single protocol owner possesses unrestricted authority to create new coordinators and products, modify critical contract addresses (product, incentivizer, collateral), and alter fee structures and minimum collateral requirements for every product and user in the system. This centralization creates a single point of failure because the owner can unilaterally change protocol parameters without any time‑delay or governance oversight. The root cause is the design choice to grant an externally owned account (EOA) or equivalent single authority full permission to invoke privileged functions that affect the economic rules of the protocol. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or a malicious owner acting intentionally, can exploit this by, for example, replacing legitimate contract addresses with malicious ones, deploying biased or fraudulent products, inflating the minimum collateral threshold to a level that blocks deposits and withdrawals, setting the protocol fee split to 100 % and stripping incentives from product owners, or lowering liquidation fees to make liquidations uneconomical. These actions can be performed instantly because the contract emits events but does not enforce a timelock, meaning users only become aware after the harmful change has taken effect. The impact includes loss of access to funds (users cannot withdraw or deposit), reduction or elimination of expected rewards, exposure to malicious contract code that could steal assets, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol’s economic model. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of the privileged admin functions by the owner, which can happen at any time and affect both existing and future products. All participants—individual users, product owners, liquidity providers, and token holders—are affected because the protocol’s core accounting assumptions are overridden. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the ownership model and the lack of multi‑signature or timelock mechanisms. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the contract’s events appear legitimate and there is no on‑chain safeguard that forces a waiting period or community approval before changes are applied. To remediate, the protocol should replace the single owner with a threshold multisignature wallet (e.g., 4‑of‑7 or 5‑of‑9) that requires multiple independent signers, enforce timelocks on any parameter updates, and eventually migrate control to token‑holder governance. This reduces the risk of unilateral malicious actions, provides a window for users to react to proposed changes, and aligns the protocol’s security posture with decentralized finance best practices.

title: Product owner can collude to force liquidations.
description: A malicious/compromised product owner can collude with liquidators to force liquidations by suddenly increasing maintenance. Product owners are semi-trusted in the protocol (per protocol design) because they can provide custom code and arbitrarily change their product parameters. While this is recognized in the protocol to implement safeguards against fee ranges of funding, maker and taker, the maintenance and maker limits are not protected against malicious/compromised owners of products whose providers allow modifications of product parameters. A malicious/compromised product owner can collude with liquidators to force liquidations by suddenly increasing maintenance requirements for their product. Given that this change can be effected immediately without any time-delay, users may not have the time to react to increase their collateral deposits and prevent liquidations of their positions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation risk that arises because a product owner – a semi‑trusted entity that can supply custom code and modify product parameters – is allowed to increase the maintenance‑margin requirement of a product instantly and without any timelock. The root cause is that the protocol’s design protects fee‑related parameters but does not enforce any delay or bounded step for the maintenance and maker‑limit settings. An attacker who controls or compromises a product owner can collude with external liquidators: the owner raises the maintenance requirement in a single transaction, which immediately makes many open positions under‑collateralised. Liquidators can then submit liquidation calls that succeed because the positions now violate the new margin rule. The impact is that users who trusted the product’s stability see their positions liquidated without warning, their collateral is seized, and they may receive far less than expected or even lose the entire position. This situation occurs the moment the owner executes the parameter change; there is no window for traders to add more collateral or to close positions safely. All traders holding positions in the affected product are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and overall security guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the privilege model and identified that the maintenance‑margin setter lacks any protective mechanism. Because the change is a legitimate state transition from the contract’s perspective, it does not raise an obvious error flag, making it hard to notice without explicit monitoring of parameter updates. The bug belongs to the class of privileged‑parameter‑manipulation vulnerabilities that can be used to force liquidations or otherwise disrupt accounting assumptions. From a user’s point of view the UI may suddenly show a liquidation event, a balance dropping to zero, or a refund that is far lower than anticipated; the user expects the maintenance requirement to stay stable, but instead the protocol forces a loss. To remediate the issue the protocol should restrict how much the maintenance margin can be increased in a single step, enforce that any increase does not immediately trigger liquidation, and introduce a timelock or governance delay on the function that changes the maintenance parameter so that traders have sufficient time to react by adding collateral or closing positions.

title: Malicious/compromised product owners can manipulate users.
description: Malicious/compromised product owners can create products with payoff functions, parameters and oracles which deceive users taking a position in those products to benefit product owners or a subset of product users. contain custom code from the product owners." While the protocol owner technically has an opportunity (as part of the initial guarded launch) to check the implementation/effects of custom code and allowlist a provider adding a product via createProduct, the extent of these due-diligence checks possible and enforced is not clear beyond the dynamic safe range checks for fundingFee, makerFee and takerFee. The provider can provide custom code including the provision of a custom oracle (which may even be changed later) which is a risk. Moreover, a misbehaving product can only be paused by its product owner or, in the case of a malicious/compromised product owner, by the protocol owner only by pausing the entire protocol. A malicious/compromised product owner can deceive users via rigged payoff functions, manipulated values of maintenance/fees/limit or use of untrustworthy oracles. A malicious product that misbehaves to deceive users under certain conditions may be hard to detect apriori and once deployed within the protocol may require the protocol owner to pause the entire protocol to stop it from cheating its users and damaging protocol reputation. The risk of interacting with potentially malicious untrusted products is taken by product users who typically are not informed enough to make a judgement on a product's trustworthiness without the availability of any data, tools or techniques to help them with this decision-making.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the ability for a product owner (or a compromised coordinator) to embed arbitrary payoff logic, fee parameters and custom oracle contracts when creating a product on the Perennial protocol. Because the protocol only enforces generic range checks on fundingFee, makerFee and takerFee, it does not validate the semantic correctness of the payoff function or the trustworthiness of the oracle. Consequently, a malicious product can be launched with a payoff that always routes any positive outcome to the product owner, can manipulate fee or maintenance parameters to extract excessive value, or can replace its oracle after users have taken positions so that price data is falsified. The exploit is carried out by the product owner submitting a crafted ProductProvider contract through the createProduct entry point; users who interact with the product are unaware that the underlying logic is hostile because the front‑end does not expose any risk metrics and the protocol does not provide per‑product pause capability. If the product behaves maliciously, the only recourse for the protocol owner is to pause the entire protocol, which halts all unrelated products as well. This situation leads to users seeing their balances reduced to zero, receiving no expected payout, or observing fees that are far higher than advertised, while the product owner extracts the lost funds. The issue manifests whenever a new product is added without thorough manual review of its custom code, and it is especially dangerous because the custom oracle can be swapped later, making post‑deployment detection difficult. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the privilege model of the product creation flow and noted the lack of constraints on arbitrary code execution. The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the fact that the protocol only checks numeric ranges, not the business logic of the payoff calculation, and because the custom code is opaque to ordinary users. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should introduce explicit vetting of product provider contracts, expose risk indicators to users, enforce immutable or whitelisted oracle sources, and provide a mechanism for pausing or disabling individual products without affecting the whole system. In essence, the flaw belongs to the class of “untrusted third‑party code execution” or “malicious contract injection” vulnerabilities, where a privileged actor can embed harmful logic that violates the expected accounting guarantees of the platform.

title: Centralization risk of Feed contracts' VALIDATOR_ROLE
description: Any address that is granted the VALIDATOR_ROLE will bypass the aggregation and validator group signature process. DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can be granted to any address by the admin of the FluxP2PFactory, and VALIDATOR_ROLE can be granted by addresses with the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. Any address that is given the VALIDATOR_ROLE can submit any answer to the price feed, thus bypassing the aggregation and validator group signature process. The price feed can be fed malicious answers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from the VALIDATOR_ROLE in the price feed contracts. Any address that holds this role is allowed to call the transmit function and provide a price answer directly, skipping the normal aggregation of multiple validator signatures. The root cause is that the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, which can be granted by the admin of the FluxP2PFactory, is also authorized to assign VALIDATOR_ROLE to arbitrary addresses. Because the role assignment is not limited to a trusted set, an attacker who obtains the admin role or convinces an admin to grant VALIDATOR_ROLE can submit malicious price data. Exploitation consists of the privileged address calling transmit with a fabricated answer, which the system accepts as the official price without any consensus check. This can cause the protocol to use a false price, leading to incorrect liquidations, erroneous collateral valuations, or loss of funds for users who rely on the feed. The condition occurs whenever the transmit function is invoked by a VALIDATOR_ROLE holder; there is no additional verification step. All participants that depend on the feed—traders, lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the economic assumptions of the system are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined role relationships and the flow of price data. It is subtle because the presence of a role-based permission may appear normal, yet it silently disables the intended multi‑validator security model, making the problem easy to overlook in testing. The appropriate mitigation is to remove the ability for arbitrary VALIDATOR_ROLE holders to bypass aggregation, for example by restricting transmit to be callable only by the P2PFactory contract or by eliminating the VALIDATOR_ROLE entirely and enforcing a strict validator group signature process. In generic terms this is an access‑control bypass that undermines the consensus mechanism of a price oracle, resulting in potential fund loss and protocol misbehavior.

title: Duplicate signature should be checked in the first round as well
description: The duplicate signature check for the first round is skipped. This is partially caused by a mismatch in _roundId and latestAggregatorRoundId. _roundId has to be 0 for the first round, to match latestAggregatorRoundId = 1. However, the duplicate check only occurs when _roundId is greater than zero. Thus, the check is skipped for the first round. Duplicate signatures and answers can be submitted for the first round.
bug_full: During the first aggregation round the contract is supposed to reject any price update that carries a signature already seen in a previous round. The implementation compares the supplied _roundId with the latestAggregatorRoundId+1, but the check that enforces uniqueness is guarded by an if (_roundId > 0) condition. Because the first round uses _roundId = 0 while latestAggregatorRoundId is initialized to 1, the condition evaluates to false and the duplicate‑signature verification is never executed. As a result an attacker can submit the same signed price data multiple times in the initial round, effectively overwriting the legitimate price or inflating the feed without being detected. The impact is that the price oracle can be manipulated at deployment or during the first update, causing downstream contracts that rely on the feed to receive incorrect pricing information, which may lead to loss of funds, incorrect liquidations, or unfair trades. The bug appears only when the contract processes the very first round; later rounds are protected because _roundId > 0 holds true. Users of the protocol, the protocol itself, and any third‑party contracts that consume the price feed are affected because they trust the feed to be unique and tamper‑free. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the round‑id handling logic with the intended specification and noticed that the duplicate‑signature guard was never reached for the initial round. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves normally after the first update and no obvious error is emitted; the price appears to change but the underlying validation is missing. The proper fix is to align the round identifiers so that the first round uses a positive identifier (e.g., start counting from 1) and remove the redundant _roundId > 0 guard, or explicitly require priceFeed.latestRound() + 1 == _roundId before performing the duplicate check. This ensures that every submitted price, including the first one, is subject to the same uniqueness verification, restoring the intended security guarantees of the oracle.

title: Validators will be unable to validate current round after priceFeed.transmit() fails
description: Validators used for the current round cannot submit for the same round should the transmission fail. Should transmission fail, the transaction will not revert, but an error log is emitted. This means that the validators’ last signed round will still be updated to the latest round, but price feed’s latestAggregatorRoundId remains unchanged. Existing validators who participated in the failed update will then be unable to participate in the current round because of the condition require(fluxPriceFeeds[id].lastSignedRound[recoveredSigner] < _roundId, "Duplicate signature"); A new, mutually exclusive, set of validators is required to sign the current round.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability of the current set of validators to submit a price update for the same round after a call to priceFeed.transmit() fails. The root cause is that the transmit function updates each validator’s lastSignedRound mapping before the price feed’s latestAggregatorRoundId is successfully incremented. When the transmission fails – for example because the caller lacks VALIDATOR_ROLE, the round counter overflows, or the transaction runs out of gas – the function does not revert; instead it emits an error log and leaves the validator state advanced while the feed round remains unchanged. Consequently the require check that enforces fluxPriceFeeds[id].lastSignedRound[recoveredSigner] < _roundId triggers a “Duplicate signature” error for any subsequent attempt by the same validators to sign the unchanged round. This lock‑out forces the protocol to recruit a new, mutually exclusive validator set before the next round can be processed. An attacker or a misconfiguration that deliberately revokes the VALIDATOR_ROLE from the proxy, or any of the other failure conditions, can therefore stall the price feed without any obvious on‑chain revert, making the problem hard to notice because only an error log is emitted. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that the price has not changed, validators report “duplicate signature” errors, and downstream contracts that rely on fresh price data may operate on stale values, potentially leading to incorrect settlements or loss of opportunities. The issue is a classic example of a non‑atomic state update combined with improper error handling and insufficient access control, where partial state changes are persisted even though the overall operation failed. It was discovered during an audit by reproducing a scenario in which the proxy’s VALIDATOR_ROLE was revoked before a transmit call, causing the transaction to succeed superficially while the price feed round stayed the same. The bug can be mitigated by restricting priceFeed.transmit() to be callable only by the factory, removing the try‑catch block, and ensuring that validator state is updated only after a successful round increment, thereby preserving atomicity and preventing validator lock‑out.

title: Uninitialized Strike is allowed to be used
description:
A Strike can either be added when a board is added with createOptionBoard or later
on with addStrikeToBoard. When a Strike is initialized, its id is derived from the
nextStrikeId variable, which is incremented by one for every Strike that is added.
nextStrikeId is set to 1 when the OptionMarket is created. Strike ids are checked for
their validity by comparing Strike.id with the id from the user input that is used to
retrieve the struct from the ​strikes mapping. This check is insufficient for Strike id 0
because, by default, Strike.id is 0, so the check can be bypassed and the Strike is valid
even though it is uninitialized.
The code in _composeTrade performs checks to make sure it only uses a valid Strike.
An invalid Strike can be submitted, though with the id 0. The data structure has not
been initialized as the nextStrikeId starts at 1. So using the id 0 bypasses the check
and then composes TradeParameters based on the uninitialized Strike and
subsequently OptionBoard. While during testing, it was not possible to create a
position with the uninitialized Strike it might be possible under certain circumstances.
The setStrikeSkew function has a similar issue and the Strike id 0 is not rejected.
The owner could accidentally call setStrikeSkew with id 0. With the strike skew set, it
might be possible to create or update a position with invalid Strike values.
bug_full: An uninitialized strike vulnerability exists in the OptionMarket contract where the first strike identifier (id 0) is never created but is still accepted as a valid strike. The contract initializes nextStrikeId to 1, so the mapping entry for strike id 0 remains empty and its struct fields retain default zero values. Validation logic checks only that the stored Strike.id equals the user‑supplied id; because the default value of an uninitialized struct is also 0, the check succeeds for id 0 even though the strike has never been added. Consequently functions that compose trade parameters, set strike skew, or otherwise rely on a valid strike can be called with id 0. The code then reads uninitialized data, builds TradeParameters based on a zeroed strike and its associated board, and may allow the owner or an attacker to set a skew on a non‑existent strike. Under certain conditions this can lead to the creation or modification of positions with incorrect pricing, zero or negative premiums, or other accounting anomalies. The impact is that funds may be locked, positions may be created with unintended terms, or the market’s pricing model can be corrupted, potentially causing loss of user confidence and financial loss. The issue appears only when a caller supplies strike id 0; normal operation using valid ids (>=1) is unaffected. It affects any user or contract that interacts with the market, as well as the protocol’s overall integrity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the strike‑initialisation flow and noticed that the validation does not explicitly reject id 0. Because the contract does not revert or emit an error when id 0 is used, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in routine testing unless a transaction is crafted to target the zero identifier. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “default‑value bypass” or “uninitialized entity acceptance” bugs, where a default zero value is mistakenly treated as a legitimate object. To remediate, the contract should either start nextStrikeId at 0 and treat id 0 as a valid strike that is properly initialized, or more safely, add an explicit require that rejects any strikeId (or boardId) equal to 0 in all public and internal functions that manipulate strikes. This ensures that uninitialized strikes cannot be referenced, preventing malformed trade composition and protecting the market’s accounting logic.

title: Failing withdrawals could permanently freeze the queue
description:
Withdrawals are done in a two-step process. First, a user starts the withdrawal and if
the initial validation succeeds, the withdrawal is added to queuedWithdrawals. After a
withdrawal delay, a user can then call processWithdrawalQueue. This function does
not allow a user to process the withdrawal based on an id but processes withdrawals
in chronological order. So if a user wants to withdraw funds, all other withdrawals that
were initiated before need to be processed first. This can be problematic if one of the
withdrawals fails for an unforeseen reason because then, the withdrawal queue is
stuck and no other withdrawals after the failing one can take place.
Deposits have the same two-step process and the design of the queue could lead to a
similar issue where a processing failure for a deposit could freeze the deposit queue.
The withdrawal queue returns without processing the withdrawal if
totalTokensBurnable is 0. The withdrawal can not be processed until the condition
changes. There could be other undiscovered issues that might cause failures or
reverts, in which case the withdrawal queue could become stuck as well.
The withdrawal queue could become permanently stuck and users will not be able to
withdraw their funds anymore from the LiquidityPool contract. This will cause a DoS.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a queue‑sticking flaw in the LiquidityPool contract’s two‑step withdrawal (and deposit) mechanism. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the request is placed in a chronological queue called queuedWithdrawals. After a mandatory delay the user calls processWithdrawalQueue, which iterates over the queue in order and attempts to settle each pending request. The implementation does not allow processing by identifier and will stop at the first entry that cannot be completed. A typical stop condition is totalTokensBurnable being zero; in that case the function returns without advancing the queue. Because the queue cannot skip the failing entry, every later withdrawal remains blocked indefinitely. The root cause is the rigid ordering logic combined with a lack of fallback or administrative override for failed entries. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger the failure by creating a withdrawal that leaves totalTokensBurnable at zero (for example by withdrawing the last burnable tokens) or by causing any other revert inside the processing loop. Once the queue is stuck, any subsequent user who tries to withdraw sees their transaction succeed but receives no funds, their UI shows a pending withdrawal that never resolves, and their balance appears unchanged. The same problem exists for deposits, which use a similar queued design, meaning a single failing deposit can freeze the entire deposit pipeline. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition where the protocol’s liquidity becomes inaccessible, harming all participants who rely on the pool for trading or yield. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the queue processing logic and identified the early‑return path when totalTokensBurnable equals zero. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the queue processes correctly until the rare condition occurs; the contract simply returns silently without emitting an error, giving the impression that processing succeeded. To remediate, the design should be changed so that each withdrawal can be processed independently of others, for example by allowing users to specify the request ID, by skipping over failed entries, or by granting a privileged guardian the ability to force‑process or purge stuck items. Removing the strict chronological dependency or adding a robust fallback mechanism would prevent the queue from becoming permanently frozen and restore the expected behavior that users can always retrieve their funds when they meet the contract’s withdrawal criteria.

title: Updating BoardCachedGreeks does not check if a board is expired
description: A function in the OptionGreekCache contract that updates the cached greeks for an OptionBoardCache misses expiration checks for the board. The _updateBoardCachedGreeks function only checks if the board id is 0 but misses a check if the board is expired. Various parameters of the GlobalCache and the OptionBoardCache can be updated based on the expired board values.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that refreshes the cached option Greeks for a board within the OptionGreekCache contract. The routine, named _updateBoardCachedGreeks, validates that the supplied board identifier is non‑zero but fails to verify whether the board has already reached its expiration timestamp. Because the contract does not enforce an expiration guard, an attacker or any caller can invoke the update on a board that is no longer active. When this occurs, the function proceeds to write new values into the GlobalCache and the OptionBoardCache based on data that belongs to an expired board. Consequently, downstream pricing logic, collateral calculations, and risk metrics may be derived from stale or invalid Greeks. Users who rely on the on‑chain price feed – for example, traders executing swaps or liquidity providers assessing exposure – may see option prices that are too high or too low, leading to unexpected slippage, potential loss of capital, or misallocation of collateral. The issue manifests only when a caller supplies an identifier of a board that has already expired; otherwise the function behaves as intended. It was uncovered during a systematic security audit that examined state‑update pathways and identified the missing expiration check as a logical oversight. The problem is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an error; it silently overwrites cache entries, making the bug hard to detect from normal UI interactions where users simply see price quotes that appear plausible. To remediate the flaw, the contract should include an explicit require that the board’s expiration timestamp is greater than the current block timestamp before performing any cache updates, thereby preventing stale data from contaminating the pricing engine. This class of bug falls under the broader category of missing state‑validation checks, where a contract updates critical on‑chain data without confirming that the underlying entity is still valid, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only active boards contribute to price calculations.

title: Interchanged from-to addresses cause loss of user funds
description: The from and to addresses are interchanged in _returnBase and _returnQuote leading to an excess amount of base/quote asset in the contract being transferred again from the user (to contract) instead of being sent back to the user (from the contract). When a user closes or force closes their position via OptionMarketWrapperWithSwaps, the user's excess base assets in the contract are expected to be sent back to the user via a call to _returnBase. However, when _returnBase makes a call to _transferAsset, it incorrectly uses msg.sender as the from address and address(this) as the to address, instead of the other way around. A similar issue exists in _returnQuote, which affects both the opening and closing of positions. This leads to the loss of user funds whose excess quote/base asset while opening/closing a position is transferred again from the user to the contract leading to twice the amount of the user's initial excess base asset getting stuck in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an address‑swap bug in the internal asset‑return functions of the OptionMarketWrapperWithSwaps contract. When a trader closes or force‑closes a position, the wrapper is supposed to send any excess base or quote tokens that remain in the contract back to the trader. The helper function _returnBase calls a generic _transferAsset routine, but it passes msg.sender as the source address and address(this) as the destination, which is the opposite of the intended direction. The same mistake exists in _returnQuote. Because the source and destination are interchanged, the contract attempts to pull the excess tokens from the user again instead of pushing them back, effectively locking twice the amount of the user’s surplus assets inside the contract. The root cause is a simple parameter ordering error in the internal transfer call, which goes unnoticed because the transaction itself does not revert and the UI may simply show a successful close. Exploitation does not require any special privileges; any user who triggers a close or an opening that generates a surplus will lose those tokens, as the contract will retain them. The impact is a loss of user funds – the excess base or quote balance that should have been refunded remains stuck, leading to a lower wallet balance than expected, often appearing as “funds disappear” or “refund missing”. The condition occurs whenever the wrapper’s _returnBase or _returnQuote paths are executed, i.e., during normal position closure, force‑closure, or opening when a surplus of quote assets is created. The affected parties are the traders using the Lyra protocol and, by extension, the protocol’s reputation for safe asset handling. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Sherlock, who identified the swapped arguments as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the only symptom is that the user’s balance does not increase after a close, which may be attributed to market movement rather than a bug. To remediate, the transfer call should be corrected to use address(this) as the source and msg.sender as the destination, i.e., _transferAsset(asset, address(this), msg.sender, amount). This change restores the intended refund flow and prevents assets from being unintentionally retained by the contract. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect asset direction” or “parameter ordering” errors that violate accounting assumptions that assets leaving the contract must be credited back to the user.

title: Event emitted with incorrect value
description: Event PositionUpdated is always emitted with a value of PositionUpdatedType.ADJUSTED, which is incorrect for positions being opened. The check for _positionId == 0 in the emission of event PositionUpdated will always return false because _positionId is always updated to a non-zero value earlier. This would cause the PositionUpdated event emission to always say PositionUpdatedType.ADJUSTED and never PositionUpdatedType.OPENED. Frontend or offchain monitoring tools could be affected because they would never see new positions being opened but only positions being adjusted (even when they are being newly opened). This could negatively impact UI & UX to cause confusion and perhaps even a DoS vulnerability.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect event payload emitted by the contract when a new trading position is created. The contract always emits the PositionUpdated event with the enum value PositionUpdatedType.ADJUSTED, even in the case where a position is being opened for the first time. The root cause is that the function reassigns the _positionId parameter to a non‑zero identifier before it checks whether the identifier was originally zero. Because the check "if (_positionId == 0)" is performed after the assignment, the condition can never be true, so the branch that would emit PositionUpdatedType.OPENED is never taken. An attacker does not need to interact directly with the contract; the bug can be exploited simply by opening a position, after which off‑chain listeners, front‑end applications, or monitoring tools that rely on the PositionUpdated event will never see the OPENED signal. Consequently they will interpret every new position as an adjustment of an existing one. From a user’s perspective the UI may never display a “new position opened” notification, showing only “position adjusted” messages, which can lead to confusion, the impression that a trade failed, or even a denial‑of‑service scenario if the front‑end blocks further actions waiting for an OPENED event that never arrives. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s function that creates a position is called, i.e., when a trader opens a fresh position. All participants that depend on accurate event data – traders, front‑end developers, analytics services, and auditors – are affected because the accounting assumptions about position lifecycle are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the OptionToken.sol source, where the logic of the event emission was examined and the premature update of _positionId was identified. It is subtle because the contract still emits a valid event; only the enum value is wrong, making it easy to miss in functional testing that does not verify the exact event type. The proper remediation is to preserve the original identifier before it is overwritten, for example by caching the incoming _positionId in a local variable or using a separate variable for the updated identifier, and then basing the event‑type decision on the cached original value. This ensures that the PositionUpdated event correctly reports PositionUpdatedType.OPENED for newly created positions and PositionUpdatedType.ADJUSTED for subsequent modifications, restoring the intended business logic and preventing UI/UX inconsistencies and potential denial‑of‑service conditions.

title: Interchanged function arguments
description: The positions of arguments totalPoolValue and exchangeParams.spotPrice in the function call _getLiquidity are accidentally interchanged compared to what is expected by the parameters of _getLiquidity. The first two arguments of _getLiquidity within _getTokenPriceAndStale are interchanged. Instead of: _getLiquidity(exchangeParams.spotPrice, totalPoolValue,...) _getLiquidity(totalPoolValue, exchangeParams.spotPrice,...) This will break the liquidityThresholdCrossed constraint in the circuit-breaker _updateCBs and would cause a DoS with the protocol unable to make progress because CBTimestamp check in _canProcess will always fail while processing deposit/withdrawal queues. This would then require the guardian to take over and
bug_full: The contract contains a logic error where the two numeric arguments passed to an internal liquidity‑calculation routine are swapped. The routine expects the first argument to be the current spot price of the asset and the second argument to be the total value locked in the pool, but the caller provides them in the opposite order. Because the routine also updates a circuit‑breaker that checks whether the pool’s liquidity has crossed a predefined threshold, the swapped values cause the threshold‑crossed flag to be set incorrectly. Consequently the timestamp‑based guard that prevents processing of deposit and withdrawal queues never becomes satisfied; every call to the queue‑processing function fails the CBTimestamp check and the protocol cannot advance the queue. From a user perspective deposits appear to be rejected or remain pending indefinitely and withdrawals never complete, effectively a denial‑of‑service condition. The bug is triggered whenever the price‑oracle‑driven price update path executes, i.e., during normal price‑feed updates or when a user triggers a price‑dependent operation. All participants that rely on the queue – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol’s guardian – are affected because funds become locked in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit when the auditor noticed that the argument order in the call to _getLiquidity did not match the function signature. The problem is subtle because the two arguments are of the same type (uint256) and the compiler does not emit a warning, so the contract behaves normally for most inputs and only fails when the swapped values cause the liquidity threshold condition to be evaluated incorrectly. The proper fix is to align the call with the function definition, passing the spot price first and the total pool value second, and to add a compile‑time check or unit test that validates the ordering of arguments for critical internal calls. More generally, the bug belongs to the class of “argument‑order” or “parameter‑misplacement” errors that can break business‑logic invariants such as circuit‑breaker thresholds, leading to denial‑of‑service or loss of liveness in financial protocols.

title: Accurate price at board expiry is not ensured
description: The expiration date for a board can be set by settleExpiredBoard function. It queries the spot price from the Synthetix contracts and sets the boardToPriceAtExpiry assuming the price is close to the expiration time. There is no on-chain mechanism take on the responsibility of calling the function at board expiration and that they will implement a mechanism to incentivize users (i.e. keepers) to call the function. If no one calls settleExpiredBoard function at board expiration and it’s only later called after a longer period has been passed, then it is possible that the current spot price deviates significantly from the one at board expiration. The settlement of the expired board could lead to financial loss for some users.
bug_full: An inaccurate settlement price may be recorded for a board after its expiration because the contract relies on an external call to settleExpiredBoard that fetches the current spot price from Synthetix and stores it as the expiry price. The contract does not enforce that this function is executed exactly at the expiration timestamp, nor does it provide an on‑chain incentive or automated trigger to guarantee timely execution. Consequently, if no keeper or external actor calls settleExpiredBoard at or shortly after the expiry, the function may be invoked much later, at which point the spot price can have moved substantially from the true price at expiry. An attacker or simply a passive market condition can therefore cause the recorded boardToPriceAtExpiry to be stale, leading to settlements that credit or debit participants based on an incorrect price. Users who expect to receive payouts that reflect the market price at the moment of expiry may instead receive too little, too much, or even see their positions liquidated unexpectedly. The loss manifests as missing or reduced payouts, balances that appear lower than anticipated, or trades that settle at a price far from the market at expiry. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the settlement logic, where the lack of a deterministic on‑chain trigger for the expiry function was noted. Because the bug is timing‑related, it may not be obvious during normal testing where calls are made promptly; only when the function is delayed does the price deviation become apparent. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle staleness or delayed settlement bugs, where a contract assumes that an off‑chain actor will provide fresh data at a precise moment. To remediate, the protocol should introduce an on‑chain mechanism—such as a keeper incentive, a time‑locked callback, or an automated trigger—that forces settleExpiredBoard to be executed as close as possible to the expiration time, and optionally includes a fallback source (e.g., a Chainlink price feed) for cases where the primary oracle is unavailable. By ensuring the expiry price is captured accurately, the protocol can preserve the intended accounting guarantees and prevent users from suffering unexpected financial loss.

title: Incorrect collateral transferred leads to loss of user funds
description: setCollateralWrapper transfers the entire collateral from the user instead of transferring only the differential amount when there is already some previously deposited collateral. If setCollateralTo > currentPosition.collateral, then instead of transferring the differential collateral (i.e. setCollateralTo - currentPosition.collateral) amount from the user, setCollateralWrapper transfers the entire collateral amount of setCollateralTo again from the user. At a minimum, the user is surprised (could affect their protocol engagement) and the transaction could revert if the user doesn't have the unexpected amount of collateral funds. If transferred, it leads to the loss of the user's additional collateral to the protocol wrapper, which may be claimed by the next user engaging with the wrapper contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the collateral handling routine of the protocol wrapper, specifically the function that adjusts a user’s deposited collateral. When a user already has collateral on the contract and requests to increase it, the wrapper is supposed to pull only the additional amount (the difference between the desired total and the current balance). Instead, the implementation mistakenly transfers the full target amount again from the user’s wallet. This mis‑calculation causes the contract to request more funds than necessary. If the user does not possess the extra tokens, the transaction reverts, which can be confusing and may discourage further participation. If the user does have enough tokens, the contract deducts the entire target amount, effectively stealing the differential amount and depositing it into the wrapper’s internal pool. The excess collateral becomes part of the wrapper’s balance and can later be claimed by another participant, leading to an unintended loss of the original user’s funds. The root cause is an arithmetic error where the code uses the absolute target collateral value rather than the net increase, violating the accounting assumption that only the net change should be transferred. This bug was discovered during a manual audit of the LiquidityPool contract. It is hard to notice because the user interface typically shows the new total collateral, not the amount actually transferred, so users may not realize that more tokens were taken from their wallet than they expected. The impact includes unexpected balance reductions, possible transaction failures, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s collateral management. To remediate the issue, the transfer logic must be changed to compute and send only the difference between the desired collateral and the current collateral, ensuring that the protocol never pulls more than the net amount required. This class of bug falls under incorrect amount calculation or over‑transfer vulnerabilities, which break fundamental business logic around collateral accounting and can cause funds to disappear from a user’s perspective.

title: CEI pattern violations and cross-function reentrancy
description: Checks-effects-interactions (CEI) pattern is violated in a few places. If there is a reentrancy possibility in quoteToken or baseToken, an attacker could steal funds by exploiting cross-function reentrancy. An attacker could potentially split their OptionToken in the middle of a settleOptions call. The attacker would be fully paid for the settleOptions call, and they would be minted another OptionToken that can be settled for its full value minus one wei. Attacks can be repeated to drain the contract. Although there are individual nonReentrant guards on the settleOptions (within ShortCollateral.sol) and split (within OptionToken.sol) functions, these functions exist in different contracts, so an attacker might be able to call split in the middle of a settleOptions call (e.g. perhaps _sendLongCallProceeds transfers control flow to the position’s owner due to the implementation of quoteToken/baseToken). At the beginning of each iteration of the main for loop in settleOptions, a memory copy of the position is taken. An attacker can simply call split on this position after the memory copy is taken, and this won’t affect the memory copy of position.amount. This will create a new OptionToken that can also be settled later on, while the original OptionToken will be burned at the end of the settleOptions call. A small detail here is that the attacker can’t call split to create an OptionToken of equal value, but this doesn’t prevent the attack, since the attacker can just subtract one wei which is essentially the same value. If there is a reentrancy possibility in quoteToken or baseToken, an attacker could steal funds. This is a hypothetical risk at the moment because there are no actual control flow transfers to the user in settleOptions despite the nonReentrant guard suggesting there could be. However, Synthetix tokens are upgradable, and so it is not impossible that quoteToken/baseToken are upgraded by Synthetix in the future and this issue becomes exploitable. Code Snippet: reclaimInsolventQuote (CEI pattern violation) settleOptions (CEI pattern violation) split
bug_full: The vulnerability is a violation of the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions (CEI) pattern across multiple contracts, which enables a cross‑function reentrancy attack. The contract that settles option positions copies the position data into memory, then later transfers tokens (quoteToken or baseToken) to an external address. Because the transfer occurs after the memory copy and before the original OptionToken is burned, a malicious caller can re‑enter the contract through the token’s transfer callback and invoke the split function in a different contract that creates a new OptionToken based on the same position amount. The split call sees the original amount unchanged in the copied memory, so it can mint a new token that is worth almost the full value of the original (the attacker may lose only one wei). After the re‑entered split finishes, the original settleOptions call continues and burns the original token, effectively allowing the attacker to receive the payout for the settled position twice, minus a negligible amount. This can be repeated for each iteration of the settlement loop, draining the contract’s funds. The issue arises only if the quoteToken or baseToken contracts allow a callback that transfers control flow back to the attacker, which is currently not the case but could appear if those tokens are upgraded (as they are upgradable in the Synthetix ecosystem). The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that flagged CEI violations and noted that the nonReentrant modifiers are applied to individual functions but not across contract boundaries, creating a potential reentrancy window. The problem is subtle because the settleOptions function does not directly call external code, and the presence of a nonReentrant guard gives a false sense of safety, making the risk easy to overlook. The impact is that an attacker could repeatedly split and settle options, extracting almost the full value of each option and ultimately draining the protocol’s collateral pool, affecting all option holders and the overall liquidity of the platform. To remediate, the settlement logic should follow the CEI pattern strictly: burn or otherwise update the internal state before performing any external token transfer, and consider adding a contract‑wide reentrancy guard that spans the entire settlement flow across contracts. Additionally, the split function should be protected against being called during settlement, either by checking a reentrancy lock or by redesigning the flow so that no external calls occur after state changes. Implementing these changes eliminates the cross‑function reentrancy window and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: NFTs may get locked in MultiVaults leading to loss of user tokens.
description: NFTs with tokenId > type(uint32).max will cause corresponding NFTs with colliding tokenIds to get locked in MultiVaults with their original beneficial owners unable to withdraw them anymore. Hook project documentation says: “The multi vault does not support any collection with token ids that overflow uint32. Uint32 is used to reduce the number of storage slots that must be allocated to add an asset to the vault; very few NFT projects based on ERC-721s actually utilize tokenIds outside this range” with the assumption that authorized ALLOWLISTER_ROLE will never list a MultiVault for an NFT project with tokenIDs in that range. However, instead of checking received NFTs with tokenId > type(uint32).max and reverting, the current implementation forces a downcast in onERC721Received via uint32(tokenId). If tokenId > type(uint32).max then the forced downcasting will make this tokenId collide with the corresponding NFT whose tokenId is within the type(uint32).max range, if it were to have been vaulted earlier. ENS uses hash(name) as its uint64 tokenId which is greater than type(uint32).max. Another NFT project Artblocks uses tokenId = (projectNumber * 1000000) + mintNumber, which could be greater than type(uint32).max. NFT projects may also get creative after the initial mint to issue new ones with tokenIds outside the initially planned type(uint32).max. Example scenario: 1. ALLOWLISTER_ROLE lists BAYC NFT series in a MultiVault assuming that its tokenId will never exceed type(uint32).max 2. BAYC approves a change to mint many more BAYC NFTs with randomized tokenIds that now can exceed type(uint32).max 3. Alice creates an option for her BAYC with tokenId 0 4. Mallory creates an option for her BAYC with tokenId 0x000000001 which when forcibly downcasted to uint32 becomes 0x0 and collides with Alice’s BAYC 5. Mallory is made the beneficial owner for Alice’s NFT and depending on the option status of Alice there could be other unexpected behavior 6. Alice loses access to her BAYC which gets locked in the MultiVault The worst case scenario is that NFTs with colliding tokenIds may get locked in MultiVaults leading to loss of such user tokens. There could be other unexpected behavior depending on different scenarios.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑overflow handling flaw in the MultiVault contract that stores NFT identifiers in a 32‑bit unsigned integer slot. The contract blindly downcasts any incoming ERC‑721 tokenId to uint32 inside onERC721Received, without verifying that the original tokenId fits within the 32‑bit range. When a tokenId larger than 2^32‑1 is received, the high bits are discarded and the value wraps to a lower 32‑bit number that may already be used by another NFT that was previously vaulted. This creates a collision in the vault’s internal accounting: two distinct NFTs are mapped to the same storage key, causing the vault to treat them as the same asset. An attacker can exploit this by minting or transferring an NFT with a deliberately large tokenId that collides with an existing low‑value tokenId already stored in the vault. By depositing the colliding NFT, the attacker can become the recorded beneficial owner of the victim’s NFT, or cause the vault to reject withdrawals because the internal record now points to the attacker’s token. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are that a previously deposited NFT disappears from the vault, the withdrawal function reverts or returns no asset, and the user’s balance appears to be zero even though they still own the NFT on the underlying ERC‑721 contract. The impact is loss of access to the original NFT, potential misallocation of options or other derivative positions tied to that NFT, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol because assets become permanently locked. The condition under which this occurs is when a MultiVault is listed for a collection whose tokenIds are not guaranteed to stay within the uint32 range – for example ENS, ArtBlocks, or any ERC‑721 that later expands its tokenId space beyond 2^32‑1. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit (Sherlock) that compared the contract’s documentation, which states that collections with tokenIds exceeding uint32 are not supported, with the actual implementation that performs an unchecked cast. The issue is hard to notice because the downcast does not generate an error; the contract silently accepts the token and overwrites the existing entry, making the problem only visible when a user attempts to retrieve the asset. The correct mitigation is to replace the raw cast with a safe conversion such as SafeCast.toUint32, which reverts if the tokenId exceeds the 32‑bit maximum, or to add an explicit require statement that checks tokenId <= type(uint32).max before proceeding. By enforcing this check, the vault will reject out‑of‑range NFTs, preventing collisions and ensuring that each deposited NFT retains a unique identifier within the vault’s storage model.

title: Protocol admin is a single point of failure.
description:
Protocol admin can arbitrarily and unilaterally list vaults/options, update vault/call factory addresses, configure the market/collection parameters and pause/unpause the markets/protocol. This presents a critical single point of failure.
Hook protocol uses OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl.sol to implement role-based access control (RBAC) with seven different roles: ADMIN_ROLE, ALLOWLISTER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE, VAULT_UPGRADER, CALL_UPGRADER, MARKET_CONF and COLLECTION_CONF. specific timelocks or other safety measures. The roles are granted with the principal of least privilege. As the protocol matures, these additional measures can be layered by granting these roles to other contracts. In the extreme, the upgrade and other roles can be burned, which would effectively make the protocol static and non-upgradeable.”
However, the initial configuration assigns the admin address to all the seven roles thereby defeating the motivation behind separation of roles. If a protocol admin becomes malicious or compromised, the entire protocol is immediately at risk for all existing/future markets/participants. While the updation of many critical parameters emit events, that only lets market participants react after the fact because these changes are not time-delayed.
A scenario that affects future markets/participants is the updation of vault/call factory addresses to malicious ones. Neither of these actions emit events and will go unnoticed by option writers/holders/bidders.
A DoS scenario, for existing markets/participants, is the protocol admin, in the MARKET_CONF role, setting the minimumOptionDuration, newSettlementStartOffset or minBidIncrementBips to unreasonable values which prevents the expected functioning of covered call option markets. The admin in the COLLECTION_CONF role can disable airdrops, flash loans and execTransaction capability of solo vaults which may cause DoS for certain assets and actions.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a centralized administration model where a single address is granted all seven privileged roles defined by the protocol’s AccessControl implementation: ADMIN_ROLE, ALLOWLISTER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE, VAULT_UPGRADER, CALL_UPGRADER, MARKET_CONF and COLLECTION_CONF. Because the same account holds every permission, the intended separation of duties and principle of least privilege are completely bypassed, creating a single point of failure. The root cause is the initial contract configuration that assigns the admin address to every role instead of using distinct addresses or a multisignature governance contract. This design allows the privileged account to arbitrarily list new vaults or options, replace the vault and call factory contracts with malicious implementations, modify market configuration parameters such as minimum option duration, settlement start offset or minimum bid increment, pause or unpause the entire protocol, and disable auxiliary features like airdrops, flash‑loan support or transaction execution on solo vaults. Exploitation does not require any special conditions beyond the admin’s ability to invoke the privileged functions; no timelocks or event emissions are present for many of the critical actions, so changes can be made instantly and silently. An attacker who controls the admin address—or whose private key is compromised—can replace factory addresses with contracts that siphon user deposits, set market parameters to values that make trading impossible (for example, an excessively high minimum bid increment), or pause the protocol, effectively denying service to all participants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include being unable to place bids or write options, seeing expected markets disappear, observing that balances remain locked or become zero after a market update, or noticing that previously available features such as flash loans or airdrops are no longer functional. The impact ranges from loss of funds due to malicious contract upgrades to denial‑of‑service conditions that halt all economic activity on the platform, undermining trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined role assignments and identified that the admin address was granted every role, contradicting the intended least‑privilege model. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and functions correctly; only a careful review of role distribution reveals the centralization risk. To remediate, the protocol should replace the single admin address with a threshold multisignature wallet (for example a 4‑of‑7 or 5‑of‑9 arrangement) and assign each privileged role to a distinct address or contract, enforce checks that prevent duplicate role owners in the constructor, and eventually transition control to token‑holder governance. Adding timelocks and emitting events for critical configuration changes would also mitigate the risk of silent malicious updates.

title: Reclaiming asset will fail when the option writer is also the highest bidder.
description:
Hook allows for the option writer to reclaim i.e. withdraw the underlying asset from an active option if certain conditions are met. However, this will fail if the option writer is also the highest bidder.
Protocol documentation states that: “If the writer wishes to withdraw the underlying asset from an active option, they first must obtain the option instrument NFT and transfer it to the writer account. Then, they may call the reclaim function, which will release the entitlement on the vault, return any active bids to the bidder, and burn the option NFT. They may then either withdrawal the asset from the vault or mint a new option with it.”
However, the implementation does not account for the scenario where the option writer is also the highest bidder at the time of reclaiming. _returnBidToPreviousBidder and settleOption handle this scenario by subtracting the call strike amount during _safeTransferETHWithFallback to the option writer. This is because the option writer is allowed to bid by only paying the difference between their bid and strike price.
Therefore, if call.writer is also the call.highBidder at the time of attempting to reclaim then _safeTransferETHWithFallback(call.highBidder, call.bid) will revert because the option contract will only have ETH amount equal to the spread but not the strike part of call.bid.
Option writer is unable to reclaim the underlying asset in the scenario when the writer is also the highest bidder.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reclaim function of an options protocol that allows the option writer to withdraw the underlying asset from an active option after obtaining the option NFT. The contract assumes that the highest bidder of the option is a different address from the writer. When the writer also happens to be the current highest bidder, the reclaim logic attempts to return the full bid amount (call.bid) to the writer via a low‑level ETH transfer. However, the contract’s balance only contains the spread amount (call.bid minus the strike price) because the writer’s bid was recorded as the difference between the strike and the bid. Consequently, the transfer of the full bid amount exceeds the available ETH and the call to _safeTransferETHWithFallback reverts, preventing the writer from reclaiming the underlying asset. This edge‑case arises during the execution of _returnBidToPreviousBidder and settleOption, which correctly handle the spread for normal bidders but are not consulted by the reclaim path. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the writer themselves experiences a failure when they try to withdraw the asset, resulting in a transaction that reverts and leaves the underlying token locked in the vault. The impact is that the writer’s expectation to retrieve their collateral is unmet, potentially reducing liquidity and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the writer has placed a bid that is also the highest at the moment of reclamation, a scenario that may be rare and therefore omitted from standard test suites, making it hard to notice. The bug belongs to a broader class of role‑collision accounting errors where a single address holds multiple responsibilities and the contract’s accounting does not correctly reconcile the overlapping balances. To remediate, the reclaim routine should detect when the high bidder equals the writer and return only the spread amount (highBid‑strike) instead of the full bid, or otherwise prevent the writer from becoming the highest bidder. This adjustment restores the invariant that the contract always has sufficient ETH to satisfy the refund and allows the writer to successfully withdraw the underlying asset as documented.

title: hedgingTwapPeriod can exceed pool maximum
description: hedgingTwapPeriod can exceed pool maximum twap period. On the Oracle contract’s getTwap function, _period means that number of seconds in the past to start calculating time-weighted average. In the CrabStrategyV2 contract, the period is set with hedgingTwapPeriod with _checkPeriod: true. However, if hedgingTwapPeriod exceeds the pool’s maximum twap period, that period is used, but hedgingTwapPeriod is ignored. Unexpected twap price calculation without hedgingTwapPeriod. CrabStrategyV2.solL786,Oracle.solL45 ```solidity function _isPriceHedge() internal view returns (bool) { uint256 wSqueethEthPrice = IOracle(oracle).getTwap(ethWSqueethPool, wPowerPerp, weth, hedgingTwapPeriod, true); uint256 cachedRatio = wSqueethEthPrice.wdiv(priceAtLastHedge); uint256 priceThreshold = cachedRatio > 1e18 ? (cachedRatio).sub(1e18) : uint256(1e18).sub(cachedRatio); return priceThreshold >= hedgePriceThreshold; } ```
bug_full: During the execution of the CrabStrategyV2 contract the function _isPriceHedge reads a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) from the Uniswap V3 oracle by calling getTwap with a parameter called hedgingTwapPeriod. The oracle expects the period argument to be no larger than the pool’s configured maximum TWAP window. If the supplied hedgingTwapPeriod exceeds that maximum, the oracle silently falls back to the pool’s maximum value and ignores the caller‑provided period.
