The root cause is that the contract’s accounting function totalAssets deliberately subtracts the reserve amount from the reported asset balance, while the lending function lendTo does not enforce any check that the remaining vault balance stays above the reserve after a loan is issued. Consequently, as long as a borrower provides enough collateral to keep their health factor above the required threshold, the lendTo function will transfer the requested amount of the underlying asset without verifying that the vault still holds the required reserve. An attacker can therefore borrow up to the full amount of assets held by the vault, including the portion earmarked as reserve, by repeatedly calling lendTo with small increments or a single large request. The impact is that the protocol loses its liquidity safety net: if the reserve is drained, the protocol may become ill‑liquid, cannot compensate for losses, and liquidity providers who expect their deposits to be protected may find the vault unable to honor redemptions. Users may see their LP tokens redeem for less than expected, balances appear to drop to zero, or refunds fail without an obvious error. The issue manifests whenever a borrower with sufficient collateral interacts with the vault, and it is not prevented by any pause or guard condition. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reserve‑aware totalAssets view with the actual transfer logic in lendTo, revealing the inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the public view hides the reserve, making the vault appear fully liquid while the internal state permits draining. To remediate, the lending function should include a post‑transfer check that the vault’s asset balance remains at least equal to the computed reserve, or it should abort lending entirely when the available liquidity is less than or equal to the reserve. This ensures the reserve stays intact and the protocol’s backstop function is preserved, aligning the contract’s accounting with its intended business logic of protecting protocol funds.

title: Unsafe casting of user amount from uint256
description: The unsafe casting of the recovered amount from uint256 to uint128 means the users’ funds will be lost. logIncomingERC20() has the recovered amount as type uint256, but amountStored is of type uint128. There is an unsafe casting when incrementing amountStored: _erc20WithdrawalAllowances[_originalAddress][_erc20Address].amountStored += uint128(_amount). It is thus possible for the amount recorded to be less than the actual amount recovered. Loss of funds.
poc: The user's balance is type(uint128).max=2**128, but the incremented amount will be zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe down‑casting of a recovered token amount from a 256‑bit unsigned integer to a 128‑bit unsigned integer. The function that records incoming ERC‑20 withdrawals stores the amount in a mapping field called amountStored which is declared as uint128. When the contract adds the recovered amount, it explicitly casts the uint256 value to uint128 before the addition. If the recovered amount is larger than the maximum value that fits in 128 bits (2**128‑1), the cast truncates the high‑order bits. As a result the amount recorded in amountStored can be smaller than the actual amount transferred, and in the extreme case the addition may become zero. This discrepancy means that the protocol’s internal accounting believes fewer tokens have been received than were actually sent, causing user balances to appear reduced or zero while the tokens are effectively locked in the contract with no way for the user to claim them. The bug can be triggered whenever a token with a total supply or a withdrawal amount that exceeds the uint128 limit is processed, which is rare for most ERC‑20 tokens but possible for tokens with very large supplies or for an attacker deliberately crafting an oversized transfer. The impact is loss of funds for any user whose deposit exceeds the limit, a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees, and a mismatch between on‑chain balances and the UI that shows a missing or zero balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the variable types did not match and that the cast could overflow. It is hard to notice because typical token amounts stay well below the 128‑bit ceiling, so the contract appears to work for ordinary cases. The proper remediation is to store the amount in a uint256 variable, or to keep the uint128 type but use a safe‑casting library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast that reverts on overflow, thereby preventing silent truncation. By ensuring that the recorded amount always matches the actual transferred amount, the protocol restores correct accounting, prevents funds from disappearing, and aligns user expectations (a user expects their deposited tokens to be reflected in their balance) with reality.

title: reduceERC721Fee function can not set fee
description: reduceERC721Fee function can not set fee when the NFT token ID is more than type(uint128).max. The NFT token ID can be any value within uint256. As the reduceERC721Fee takes the _id argument as uint128, when the reduceERC721Fee function is called with an NFT id that has above type(uint128).max, the fee can not set to the expected NFT id. High: RC721Fee can not set fee when the NFT token ID value is more than type(uint128).max
bug_full: The vulnerability is a type‑mismatch bug in the reduceERC721Fee function of an ERC721 fee‑management contract. The function is declared with a parameter _id of type uint128, but ERC721 token identifiers are defined as uint256 and can take any value up to 2^256‑1. When the function is invoked with a token ID that exceeds the maximum value of a uint128 (2^128‑1), the supplied ID is silently truncated or rejected by the Solidity type conversion, causing the internal fee‑reduction logic to address a different (or zero) token identifier. As a result the fee associated with the intended NFT is never updated. This occurs only when the NFT’s token ID is larger than type(uint128).max; for the vast majority of tokens with smaller IDs the function works as expected, which makes the problem easy to miss during testing. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the bug by submitting a reduceERC721Fee call for a high‑value token ID, leading to a situation where the fee remains at its original amount, potentially causing over‑charging or preventing legitimate fee reductions. Users experience the symptom of seeing no change in the displayed fee after a reduction request, or receiving a higher fee than expected, while the contract state shows that the reduction transaction succeeded. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function signature and compared it against the ERC721 specification. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the ID is out of range, the failure is silent and can be mistaken for a successful operation. The proper fix is to change the _id parameter type from uint128 to uint256, aligning it with the ERC721 token ID type, and to add validation that the provided ID exists before attempting to modify its fee. This adjustment restores the intended business logic that each NFT’s fee can be reduced independently, prevents accidental fee omission, and ensures accounting consistency across the protocol.

title: Nonces not used in signed data
description: Nonces are not used in the signature checks. A nonce can prevent an old value from being used when a new value exists. Without one, two transactions submitted in one order, can appear in a block in a different order. If a user is attacked, then tries to change the recipient address to a more secure address, initially chooses an insecure compromised one, but immediately notices the problem, then re-submits as a different, uncompromised address, a malicious miner can change the order of the transactions, so the insecure one is the one that ends up taking effect, letting the attacker transfer the funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing nonce in the data that is signed by the contract before a state‑changing operation is executed. Because the signed message does not contain a unique, monotonically increasing identifier, an attacker who controls block ordering – typically a malicious miner – can submit two otherwise valid transactions that target the same logical operation but specify different parameters, such as two different recipient addresses. When the first transaction (for example, an address that was chosen quickly and later discovered to be compromised) is broadcast, the user may immediately submit a second transaction that corrects the address to a secure one. Without a nonce, the two signed messages are indistinguishable from the protocol’s point of view, so the miner can place the second transaction before the first in the block. The blockchain then processes the corrected transaction first, but the later transaction – still signed and valid – overwrites the state with the insecure address, causing the funds to be transferred to an attacker‑controlled destination. This reordering attack is possible whenever the contract relies solely on signature verification without a replay‑prevention mechanism. The impact is that a user who believes they have secured a transfer may unintentionally send assets to a compromised address, effectively losing the funds. The issue is subtle because the contract appears to accept correctly signed messages and the UI may show a successful transaction, yet the final state reflects the attacker‑chosen address. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature verification flow and noted the absence of a nonce field. Detecting the problem in testing can be difficult because normal transaction ordering on a testnet may not trigger the reordering scenario. The proper mitigation is to include a unique, incrementing nonce (or a timestamp combined with a nonce) in the data that is signed, and to enforce that each signed message can only be used once, thereby preventing old or reordered messages from being accepted. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of replay and ordering vulnerabilities in off‑chain signed authorizations, where missing anti‑replay data allows an adversary to manipulate the execution order and subvert business logic that assumes a single, latest update will be applied.

title: Can register a non-allowed collateral as collateral
description: Some external interactions send tokens to the account, and the token address is not checked before being registered as a collateral for the account. This allows using an arbitrary token as a collateral as long as there is a corresponding oracle. In the following controllers, at the line referenced UniV2Controller.sol #L189 AaveV2Controller.sol #L91 AaveV3Controller.sol #L79 BalancerController.sol#L137 There is an operation with a return value that can be an arbitrary token. No check is made to verify that the tokens in tokensIn are activated in controllerFacade.isTokenAllowed. No check is made either in AccountManager.exec() when calling _updateTokensIn() (AccountManager.sol#L305), so the tokens are added as a collateral as long as the oracle for the token in OracleFacade is active. This can be clarified with an example using UniV2Controller.sol: 1. Admin sets the oracle for token XYZ, but does not activate yet the token in controllerFacade.isTokenAllowed or in AccountManager.isCollateralAllowed waiting to clear some security concerns with the token (vulnerabilities, high volatility, low liquidity, ...) 2. Attacker opens an account 3. Attacker provides liquidity to XYZ / ETH pool on UniswapV2 4. Attacker transfers the LP to the account 5. Attacker removes liquidity from the UniswapV2 pool through the account by tokens exiting the account are allowed (UniV2Controller.sol#L175-L190). No checks are performed on tokens sent from the pool to the account, so account receives WETH + XYZ and also XYZ is registered as an account collateral (AccountManager.sol#L305). An oracle was set for XYZ so the call to riskEngine.isAccountHealthy(account)(AccountManager.sol#L310) does not revert and the transaction succeeds. 6. Attacker can take advantage of the aforementioned security concerns to manipulate the price of XYZ, inflate his collateral balance and drain funds from the protocol. The same behaviour can be reproduced with the other integrations listed above by transfering LP tokens of that particular protocol directly to an account and then removing liquidity through AccountManager.exec() to get the pair tokens registered into the account as collateral. See point 6. of section above.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an asset‑injection flaw that allows an arbitrary token to be registered as collateral even when the token has not been approved by the protocol’s whitelist. The root cause is the absence of a validation step that checks whether a token is listed in controllerFacade.isTokenAllowed or the isCollateralAllowed mapping before the token is added to an account’s collateral set. This missing check appears in several controller contracts (UniV2Controller, AaveV2Controller, AaveV3Controller, BalancerController) and in the AccountManager._updateTokensIn function, which is invoked by AccountManager.exec when tokens are transferred into an account. Because the only requirement for the risk engine to accept the new collateral is that an oracle for the token exists, an attacker can first have an oracle registered for a token that the admin has not yet whitelisted, then provide liquidity to a pool, transfer the resulting LP tokens to an account, and finally remove liquidity through the controller. The removal operation sends the underlying assets (for example WETH and the unapproved token XYZ) back to the account, and the AccountManager adds those assets to the account’s collateral list without verifying their whitelist status. Consequently the risk engine perceives the account as healthy, the transaction succeeds, and the attacker can manipulate the price of the unapproved token to artificially inflate the reported collateral value and drain funds from the protocol. The issue manifests when an oracle is active for a token but the token is not marked as allowed, and when external interactions return token addresses that are not filtered. All users, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting assumptions that only approved assets back positions are broken, leading to potential under‑collateralisation and loss of funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that traced the token flow from controller calls to the AccountManager and noticed the missing whitelist guard. It is hard to notice because the protocol does not revert on receipt of the tokens, the health check passes due to the oracle, and the unexpected assets appear as normal collateral in the UI, giving the impression that everything is functioning correctly. The proper remediation is to enforce the whitelist check inside _updateTokensIn (or an equivalent gate) so that only tokens flagged as allowed can be added as collateral, and to ignore or separately track non‑whitelisted reward tokens rather than treating them as collateral. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that only vetted assets may secure loans, preventing asset‑injection attacks and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s risk model.

title: AccountManager: Liquidations not possible
description: When the transfer of one asset fails, liquidations become impossible. _liquidate calls sweepTo, which iterates over all assets. When one of those transfers fails, the whole liquidation process therefore fails. There are multiple reasons why a transfer could fail: 1.) Blocked addresses (e.g., USDC) 2.) The balance of the asset is 0, but it is still listed under asset. This can be for instance triggered by performing a 0 value Uniswap swap, in which case it is still added to tokensIn. Another way to practice the assets of an account should not contain any tokens with zero balance) Some tokens revert for zero value transfers (see https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20) 3.) Paused tokens 4.) Upgradeable tokens that changed the implementation. See above, an account cannot be liquidated. In certain conditions, this might even be triggerable by the user. For instance, a user could try to get on the USDC blacklist to avoid liquidations.
bug_full: During a liquidation the contract calls sweepTo which loops over every token recorded for the borrower and attempts to transfer the full balance to the liquidator. The loop does not handle a transfer that reverts; instead the revert propagates and aborts the entire liquidation function. Consequently, if any token in the borrower’s asset list cannot be transferred – for example because the address is on a blacklist (USDC), the token reports a zero balance but is still present in the list, the token contract reverts on zero‑value transfers, the token is paused, or the token implementation has been upgraded to a non‑compatible version – the liquidation transaction fails and the borrower remains un‑liquidated. This behaviour can be triggered intentionally by a user who adds a deliberately failing token to his portfolio, effectively shielding the position from liquidation. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome (the position being closed and collateral transferred) does not occur; the UI may show a pending transaction that eventually reverts or simply no change in balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow where the lack of error handling around sweepTo was observed. It is hard to notice because the failure only appears when the borrower holds an exotic or mis‑configured token, and the contract does not emit a specific error indicating which asset caused the problem. The impact is that the protocol may retain under‑collateralized debt, risking loss of funds for lenders and undermining the economic guarantees of the system. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unhandled external call failures” that break batch processing logic. The recommended mitigation is to catch any revert from the token transfer, skip the offending asset, and optionally keep it in the list for a later retry, thereby allowing the rest of the assets to be liquidated safely.

title: Accounts with ETH loans can not be liquidated
description: Setting address(0) as LEther's underlying is allowed, and the logic in AccountManager.settle() and RiskEngine._valueInWei() handles address(0) specially, which implies that address(0) can be an asset. However, if LEther's underlying is set to address(0), the accounts with ETH loans will become unable to be liquidated. https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/AccountManager.sol#L318-L326 https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/RiskEngine.sol#L178-L188 Given that at AccountManager.sol#L100 in settle() and RiskEngine.sol#L186 in _valueInWei(), they both handled the case that the asset==address(0), and in Registry.sol#L95-L105 in setLToken(), underlying==address(0) is allowed: https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/Registry.sol#L95-L105 We assume that address(0) can be set as the underlying of LEther. In that case, when the user borrows native tokens, address(0) will be added to the user's assets and borrows list. https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/AccountManager.sol#L203-L217 ```solidity function borrow(address account, address token, uint amt) external whenNotPaused onlyOwner(account) { if (registry.LTokenFor(token) == address(0)) revert Errors.LTokenUnavailable(); if (!riskEngine.isBorrowAllowed(account, token, amt)) revert Errors.RiskThresholdBreached(); if (IAccount(account).hasAsset(token) == false) IAccount(account).addAsset(token); if (ILToken(registry.LTokenFor(token)).lendTo(account, amt)) IAccount(account).addBorrow(token); emit Borrow(account, msg.sender, token, amt); } ``` This will later prevent the user from being liquidated because in riskEngine.isAccountHealthy(), it calls _getBalance() in the for loop of all the assets, which assumes all the assets complies with IERC20. Thus, the transaction will revert at L157 when calling IERC20(address(0)).balanceOf(account). https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/AccountManager.sol#L250-L255 ```solidity function liquidate(address account) external { if (riskEngine.isAccountHealthy(account)) revert Errors.AccountNotLiquidatable(); _liquidate(account); emit AccountLiquidated(account, registry.ownerFor(account)); } ``` https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/src/core/RiskEngine.sol#L150-L161 ```solidity function _getBalance(address account) internal view returns (uint) { address[] memory assets = IAccount(account).getAssets(); uint assetsLen = assets.length; uint totalBalance; for(uint i; i < assetsLen; ++i) { totalBalance += _valueInWei( assets[i], IERC20(assets[i]).balanceOf(account) ); } return totalBalance + account.balance; } ``` We noticed that in the deployment documentation, LEther is set to init with WETH as the underlying. Therefore, this should not be an issue if the system is being deployed correctly. https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/4e45871e4540df0f189f6c89deb8d34f24930120/protocol/deployments/ArbiDeploymentFlow.md#L47-L53 But considering that setting address(0) as LEther's underlying is still plausible and the potential damage to the whole protocol is high (all the accounts with ETH loans can not be liquidated), we believe that this should be a medium severity issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the protocol allowing the native ETH token to be represented by address(0) as the underlying asset of the LEther lending token. The Registry contract does not prevent an LToken from being configured with address(0), and both AccountManager.settle and RiskEngine._valueInWei contain special‑case code that treats address(0) as a valid asset. When a borrower takes out an ETH loan, the borrow function adds address(0) to the borrower’s list of assets and borrows. Later, the risk engine evaluates account health in isAccountHealthy by iterating over every asset returned by the account and calling IERC20(asset).balanceOf(account). This loop assumes every asset implements the ERC20 interface. Because address(0) does not implement balanceOf, the call reverts at runtime, causing the health check to fail and the subsequent liquidate function to revert with an out‑of‑gas or revert error. As a result, any account that holds an ETH loan becomes permanently non‑liquidatable; the protocol cannot seize collateral, leaving the position open even if it is under‑collateralised. From a user perspective the liquidation transaction simply fails, no liquidation event is emitted, and the borrower’s balance appears unchanged while the protocol’s risk metrics remain inaccurate. The issue is hard to notice because the official deployment script initializes LEther with WETH, so most test deployments never hit the address(0) path, and the special handling in settle and _valueInWei may give the impression that address(0) is safely supported. The bug belongs to the class of asset‑type handling errors where a contract assumes all assets conform to a common interface (ERC20) without guarding against native token representations. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid address(0) as an underlying asset in setLToken, or modify the risk engine to treat native ETH separately—using the account’s native balance instead of an ERC20 call—and remove the misleading special‑case logic that pretends address(0) behaves like an ERC20 token. This prevents the revert and restores the ability to liquidate ETH‑loan positions, preserving protocol solvency.

title: Balances of rebasing tokens aren't properly tracked
description: Rebasing tokens are tokens where balanceOf() returns larger amounts over time, due to the addition of interest to each account, or due to airdrops. Sentiment doesn't properly track balance changes while rebasing tokens are in the borrower's account. The lender will miss out on gains that should have accrued to them while the asset was lent out. While market-based price corrections may be able to handle interest that is accrued to everyone, market approaches won't work when only subsets of token addresses are given rewards, e.g. an airdrop based on a snapshot of activity that happened prior to the token being lent.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the Sentiment lending protocol tracks balances of rebasing tokens – tokens whose total supply changes over time and whose balanceOf() value can increase due to interest accrual, airdrops, or other supply‑adjusting mechanisms. The protocol records a borrower’s position using a static share‑to‑balance conversion that is calculated when the asset is deposited. Because the accounting logic assumes token balances remain constant, it never updates the stored share amount when the underlying token rebases. Consequently, when a rebasing event occurs while the token is held by a borrower, the protocol does not credit the lender with the additional tokens that should have been earned. An attacker can exploit this by borrowing a rebasing token, waiting for a rebasing event (for example, an airdrop that rewards only a subset of addresses), and then repaying the loan. The repayment calculation uses the original balance snapshot, so the lender receives fewer tokens than they are entitled to, effectively losing the rebasing gains. This issue manifests whenever a rebasing token is used as collateral or is borrowed and a supply‑adjusting event happens before the position is closed. It affects any user who supplies such tokens to the protocol, as well as the protocol itself because the accounting invariants become inaccurate and could lead to under‑collateralisation of other positions. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the share conversion routine does not incorporate balance changes caused by rebasing or fee‑on‑transfer behaviour. The bug is subtle because the token’s balanceOf() call returns a higher value, yet the internal accounting still reports the old share amount, making the discrepancy easy to miss in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after repaying a loan the expected interest or airdrop reward is missing – the user may see “my balance is lower than it should be” or “the funds I expected to receive never arrived”. This class of bug falls under dynamic‑supply token accounting errors, where the protocol fails to reconcile share‑based accounting with tokens whose supply changes after deposit. The recommended remediation is to adjust the stored share amount whenever the on‑chain balance of a rebasing token diverges from the share‑derived amount, or to prohibit rebasing and fee‑on‑transfer tokens from being used in the protocol altogether, ensuring that share‑to‑balance conversions remain correct throughout the lifecycle of a loan.

title: ERC4626Oracle Vulnerable To Price Manipulation
bug_full: The vulnerability is an on‑chain price manipulation flaw in the ERC4626Oracle contract. The oracle’s getPrice function calculates the LP token price by calling ERC4626.previewRedeem, which in turn calls convertToAssets. ConvertToAssets derives the asset‑per‑share ratio from the vault’s totalAssets and totalSupply, both of which can be altered in the same transaction or block by invoking deposit, mint, withdraw or redeem on the vault. Because the price is computed from a mutable state that an attacker can change immediately before the oracle query, the reported price can be artificially inflated or deflated within a single block. An attacker can therefore present a collateral value that is far higher than its true market value, allowing them to borrow more assets than the protocol intends, or they can depress the value of another user’s collateral to trigger premature liquidation. The impact is that borrowers may obtain excess credit, lenders may suffer losses from under‑collateralized positions, and the overall protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken. The issue occurs whenever the oracle relies on previewRedeem for price discovery without any time‑averaging or state snapshot, i.e., during any block where a malicious actor can execute a vault state‑changing operation followed by a price query. It affects all participants that rely on the oracle – borrowers, lenders, and any user whose collateral is evaluated by the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that traced the data flow from getPrice through previewRedeem to convertToAssets and identified that the underlying variables are mutable within a single transaction. The problem is subtle because the price returned by a view function appears correct at the moment of the call, yet it can be manipulated instantly, making it hard to detect from off‑chain monitoring. The recommended mitigation is to stop using previewRedeem for price calculation and instead employ a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or an external immutable price feed that cannot be altered within the same block, thereby preventing flash‑style price distortion. This class of bug is a typical oracle manipulation vulnerability where the price source depends on mutable on‑chain state rather than a stable reference, leading to scenarios where funds disappear, borrowing limits are bypassed, or liquidations occur unexpectedly.

title: Delisted assets can still be deposited and
description:
Delisting an asset does not prevent accounts, that already contain the asset from depositing more. It blocks the deposit function but users can sidestep by sending tokens directly to their account.
AccountManger.sol#deposit attempts to block deposits from assets that are not on the list of supported collateral. When calculating the health of the account, the total balance of the account address is considered. An account that already has the asset on its assets list doesn't need to use AccountManger.sol#deposit because they can transfer the tokens directly to the account contract. This means that these accounts can continue to add to and use delisted assets as collateral.
One of two scenarios depending on actions taken by the protocol. If the asset is delisted from accountManager.sol and the oracle is removed then all users with loans taken against the asset will likely be immediately liquidated, which is highly unfair to users. If the asset is just delisted from accountManager.sol then existing users that already have the asset would be able to continue using the asset to take loans. If the reason an asset is being delisted is to prevent a vulnerability then the exploit would still be able to happen due to these accounts sidestepping deposit restrictions.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises from a mismatch between the asset whitelist enforcement in the deposit function and the way the protocol evaluates an account's collateral value. When an asset is removed from the supported collateral list, the deposit() routine in AccountManager.sol correctly rejects new deposit calls for that token. However, the health calculation later aggregates the total token balance of the account contract without checking whether each token is still whitelisted. Consequently, a user who already holds the delisted token can simply transfer additional tokens directly to the account contract—bypassing the deposit() guard—and those tokens will be counted as collateral. This enables continued borrowing against a token that the protocol intended to disable, or, if the oracle for the token is also removed, causes the protocol to instantly consider the account under‑collateralised and trigger liquidation. The impact is two‑fold: borrowers may be unfairly liquidated the moment the asset is delisted, and malicious actors can continue to exploit the asset as collateral despite the protocol’s intention to block it. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the whitelist check in the deposit function with the health‑calculation logic and noticed that token balances were still included regardless of whitelist status. It is subtle because the UI may still show the deposit button disabled, giving the impression that the asset cannot be used, while the underlying contract still accepts token transfers and counts them toward collateral. To remediate, the health‑calculation should be split into two distinct paths: when assessing post‑action health for new borrowing, assets that are no longer supported must be excluded from the total value; when assessing liquidation eligibility, only assets that were part of the account’s original asset list should be considered. This separation prevents new borrowing against delisted assets while avoiding mass liquidations of existing positions. The bug belongs to the class of whitelist bypass or accounting inconsistency vulnerabilities, where state updates are enforced in one entry point but ignored in another, leading to a mismatch between expected business rules and actual on‑chain accounting.

title: M-05 Yearn withdraw(uint) selector may back-
description:
The YearnController is using:
```solidity
/// @notice withdraw(uint256) function signature
bytes4 constant WITHDRAW = 0x2e1a7d4d;
```
Which is the selector for withdraw(amount, msg.sender, 1) where the max_loss is 1bps
See Yearn Code: https://github.com/yearn/yearn-vaults/blob/efb47d8a84fcb13ceebd3ceb11b126b323bcc05d/contracts/Vault.vy#L1010
On one hand the selector will allow for loss, if you'd want to have no loss you should change it to a function call with a hardcoded 0 value for maxLoss
On the other hand, if the account has too big of a position in a Yearn Vault (e.g. more than 10% of the vault), then a withdrawal may simply not be possible as the function will always revert.
You can monitor the limits on https://yearn.watch/, per the Yearn withdraw code, the function will go through the withdrawal queue, adding up losses (if any) to the caller.
Because the hardcoded selector will not offer any flexibility to the maxLoss parameter, in any scenario in which the losses are above 1 bps, the function will simply revert, preventing any withdrawal.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded function selector used by the YearnController contract to invoke the Yearn Vault withdraw(uint256) entry point. The selector 0x2e1a7d4d corresponds to the overloaded withdraw(amount, receiver, maxLoss) signature where the maxLoss argument is fixed to 1 basis point (0.01%). Because the selector does not expose the maxLoss parameter, callers cannot request a withdrawal with a different loss tolerance. The root cause is the use of a constant selector instead of a dynamic call that passes a configurable maxLoss value. An attacker or any user interacting with the controller can trigger a withdrawal that will automatically revert whenever the vault would need to incur a loss greater than 1 bps. This situation commonly occurs when a single account holds a large share of the vault (for example more than 10 % of total assets) or when the vault’s internal accounting queue reports a cumulative loss above the hard‑coded threshold. When the revert happens, the user’s transaction fails, no funds are transferred, and the user’s balance in the vault remains unchanged, giving the impression that the withdrawal request was ignored. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a “withdraw” button that appears to work, but after confirming the transaction the wallet displays a failed transaction and the expected funds never arrive, effectively “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. The impact is medium severity because it does not allow an attacker to steal assets, but it can lock legitimate users out of their own funds or cause unexpected slippage, violating the business assumption that a user can always withdraw their share of the vault with a configurable loss tolerance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Yearn integration code, where the constant selector was identified and cross‑checked against the Yearn Vault source showing the hard‑coded maxLoss of 1 bps. The bug is subtle because the selector itself looks like a normal withdraw function and the revert only occurs under specific loss conditions, making it easy to miss in functional testing that only covers successful withdrawals. The recommended remediation is to replace the constant selector with a call that includes a configurable maxLoss argument, allowing callers to set maxLoss to zero for no loss or to a higher value when necessary, or to expose a dedicated withdraw interface that forwards the caller‑specified maxLoss. This change restores flexibility, prevents unnecessary reverts, and aligns the contract with the expected withdrawal semantics of the Yearn Vault.

title: Reserves should not be considered part of the
poc:
Given:
• asset.address(this)+borrows=10000
• reserves=1500,borrows=7000
Expected result:
When calculating getRateFactor(), available liquidity should be asset.balanceOf(address(this))-reserves=1500,util=7000/8500=0.82, getBorrowRatePerSecond()=9114134329
Actual result:
When calculating getRateFactor(), asset.balanceOf(address(this))=3000,util=0.7e18, getBorrowRatePerSecond()=7763863430
The actual interest rate is only 7763863430/9114134329=85% of the expected rate.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the utilization ratio that drives the borrow interest rate. According to the protocol documentation the utilization should be computed as borrows divided by the sum of available liquidity and borrows, where available liquidity excludes any amount set aside as reserves. The implementation, however, treats the entire token balance of the LToken contract as liquidity and does not subtract the reserves before calling the rate model. As a result the utilization value is lower than it should be, which in turn reduces the borrow rate per second returned by the rate model. This discrepancy was discovered during a security audit when the auditor compared the documented formula with the actual Solidity code in getRateFactor and the DefaultRateModel contract and observed that the reserves parameter was never used. The bug is subtle because the resulting interest rates still appear plausible; they are simply about 85 % of the expected value in the provided example, making it easy to miss without a precise benchmark. Exploitation occurs whenever a borrower triggers an interest accrual – for example when a loan is taken or when time passes and getRateFactor is called – because the protocol will charge a lower rate than intended. The impact is a systematic under‑charging of interest, which reduces the protocol’s revenue and can distort risk metrics that rely on accurate pricing. Users who expect a certain rate may see a lower cost, but the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated: the protocol assumes that reserves are not part of the liquid pool, yet the code treats them as such, breaking the economic model. The issue affects any participant that interacts with the lending market – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – because the mis‑priced rates affect all interest calculations. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the final rate or accrued interest, not the intermediate utilization, and the deviation may be within normal market fluctuations. The proper fix is to adjust the liquidity argument passed to the rate model by subtracting the reserves, or to modify the utilization function to exclude reserves from the total assets before dividing. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of accounting or formula‑implementation errors where a financial invariant is violated by an incorrect inclusion of a reserve balance in a liquidity metric. After correcting the formula, the protocol will charge the intended interest rate, restoring revenue expectations and aligning on‑chain calculations with the documented economic model.

title: LToken's implmentation is not fully up to EIP-
description:
contest. This scope was only reviewed by WatchPug and relates to these three PRs:
1. Lending deposit cap
2. Fee accrual modification
3. CRV staking
LToken's implmentation is not fully up to EIP-4626's specification. This issue is would
https://github.com/sentimentxyz/protocol/blob/ccfceb2805cf3595a95198c97b6846c8a0b91506/src/tokens/utils/ERC4626.sol#L185-L187
```solidity
function maxMint(address) public view virtual returns (uint256) {
    return type(uint256).max;
}
```
MUST return the maximum amount of shares mint would allow to be deposited to receiver and not cause a revert, which MUST NOT be higher than the actual maximum that would be accepted (it should underestimate if necessary). This assumes that the user has infinite assets, i.e. MUST NOT rely on balanceOf of asset.
maxMint() and maxDeposit() should reflect the limitation of maxSupply.
Could cause unexpected behavior in the future due to non-compliance with EIP-4626 standard.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the token contract’s implementation of the EIP‑4626 vault interface, specifically the maxMint (and consequently maxDeposit) function. According to the standard, maxMint must return the maximum number of vault shares that can be minted for a given receiver without causing a revert, and it must never exceed the true limit imposed by the vault’s maxSupply. The current code simply returns type(uint256).max, which assumes the caller has an infinite amount of the underlying asset and ignores the vault’s supply cap. This mismatch between the contract’s reported capacity and the actual enforceable limit creates a logical inconsistency. An attacker or any user can query maxMint and be told that an arbitrarily large amount can be deposited, then attempt to mint or deposit that amount. When the vault’s totalSupply approaches or reaches maxSupply, the mint or deposit transaction will revert because the underlying logic enforces the cap, while the UI or other off‑chain components may have displayed that the operation was allowed. From the user’s perspective this appears as a sudden failure: the user expects the transaction to succeed, sees no error until the revert, and may lose gas or, in worst cases, have funds locked if the contract does not handle the revert cleanly. The impact is medium severity because it does not directly enable theft of assets, but it can cause denial‑of‑service for legitimate users, unexpected transaction failures, and inaccurate accounting in dashboards that rely on maxMint to show available capacity. The issue manifests whenever maxMint or maxDeposit is called, which is typically during deposit or mint UI flows, and it affects any participant who interacts with the vault – depositors, liquidity providers, and downstream protocols that rely on the vault’s capacity guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of three pull‑requests that introduced a lending deposit cap, fee accrual changes, and CRV staking, where the auditor noticed that the implementation deviated from the EIP‑4626 specification. It can be hard to notice because the function returns a value that is syntactically correct and does not cause immediate failures; only when the supply limit is reached does the inconsistency surface. The proper fix is to make maxMint respect the maxSupply constraint by returning maxSupply‑totalSupply (or zero if the cap is already reached) and to compute maxDeposit based on the convertible asset amount of that share limit. This brings the contract back into compliance with the standard, ensures that capacity queries reflect reality, and prevents users from being misled about how much they can safely deposit or mint.

title: originationFee may result in the borrower ac-
description:
contest. This scope was only reviewed by WatchPug and relates to these three PRs:
1. Lending deposit cap
2. Fee accrual modification
3. CRV staking
originationFee may result in the borrower account becoming liquidatable immediately.
When checking riskEngine.isBorrowAllowed(), the originationFee of the borrow is not considered. Thus, when originationFee is large enough, the borrower account becomes liquidatable immediately.
For example:
Let's say USDC's originationFee is 30%;
Alice has 100USDC, and 0 debt in her account; Alice borrowed 400USDC, received only 280USDC after the originationFee; Alice's account is now liquidatable. Actually, in the case above, Alice's account won't even get liquidated as all the assets are worth (380 USDC) less than the total debt (400USDC).
originationFee may result in the borrower account becoming liquidatable immediately.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the lending protocol calculates and validates a borrower’s health after a loan is taken. When a user initiates a borrow, the contract first calls riskEngine.isBorrowAllowed to ensure the account is eligible for the requested amount. However, this check is performed before the protocol deducts the origination fee from the amount that the borrower actually receives. The fee is sub‑tracted from the disbursed funds, but the recorded debt remains the full requested amount. Consequently, the borrower’s collateral value after the fee may be insufficient to cover the debt, yet the protocol does not re‑evaluate the account’s health after the fee is applied. If the origination fee is large enough – for example a 30 % fee on a USDC loan – a user who deposits 100 USDC and borrows 400 USDC will receive only 280 USDC while the debt stays at 400 USDC. The account’s net asset value (280 USDC) is lower than the liability (400 USDC), making the position immediately liquidatable. This condition can be triggered any time a borrower takes a loan on a token with a high origination fee, and it affects any user who relies on the protocol’s risk checks to prevent under‑collateralisation. The issue was discovered during a focused audit of three pull‑requests related to deposit caps, fee accrual, and staking logic, where the auditor noticed that riskEngine.isBorrowAllowed ignored the fee impact. It is subtle because the borrow transaction succeeds and the user receives funds, so the failure only becomes apparent when the liquidation engine flags the account or when the user sees that their balance is lower than expected and their position is closed. The impact includes immediate liquidation of healthy‑looking accounts, loss of collateral, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s risk model. To remediate, the contract should perform a post‑borrow health verification, such as calling riskEngine.isAccountHealthy after the loan is recorded, and reject the transaction if the account is not healthy. The redundant riskEngine.isBorrowAllowed call can be removed, and the health check should consider the net amount after fees, ensuring that borrowers cannot be liquidated solely because of an unaccounted origination fee.

title: First user can inflatepointsPerShare and cause
description:
pointsPerShare can be manipulated by the first user and cause _correctPoints() to revert later.  
POINTS_MULTIPLIER is an unusually large number as a precision fix for pointsPerShare: type(uint128).max = 3.4e38.  
This makes it possible for the first user to manipulate the pointsPerShare to near type(int256).max and a later regular user can trigger the overflow of _shares * _shares * in _correctPoints().  
By manipulating the pointPerShare precisely, the attacker can make it possible for the system to run normally for a little while and only to explode after a certain amount of deposits, as the pointsPerShare will be too large by then and all the _mint and _burn will revert due to overflow in _correctPoints().  
The users who deposited before will be unable to withdraw their funds.
bug_full: An attacker can manipulate the global accounting variable pointsPerShare by being the first minter. The contract uses a very large constant POINTS_MULTIPLIER (type(uint128).max ≈ 3·10^38) to achieve fixed‑point precision. Because there is no lower bound on the first update of pointsPerShare, a depositor who contributes a negligible amount can trigger distributeRewards with a large reward amount, causing pointsPerShare to be set to a value close to the maximum signed 256‑bit integer. Later, when a regular user deposits and the contract calls _correctPoints(), the calculation involves multiplying the user’s share amount by pointsPerShare (and sometimes by the share amount again). This multiplication exceeds the range of int256, causing an arithmetic overflow that makes the internal _mint or _burn revert. The revert prevents the user’s withdrawal transaction from completing, effectively locking the previously deposited funds. The bug appears only after a certain volume of deposits because the overflow condition is not reached immediately; it is therefore easy to miss during normal testing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the reward‑distribution logic and identified that the precision multiplier could be driven to extreme values. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unchecked arithmetic overflow due to unbounded scaling factor” and violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that pointsPerShare remains within a safe range. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal balance after deposit, but when trying to withdraw the transaction fails and the balance appears unchanged, leading to confusion and loss of funds. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum initial mint amount, allocate a portion of the first shares to a trusted reserve, and replace the gigantic POINTS_MULTIPLIER with a reasonable fixed‑point base (for example 1e12). Additional safeguards such as explicit overflow checks or using unsigned arithmetic for the whole calculation would also prevent the overflow from being triggered.

title: dispute() can only be called by root
bug_full: The contract implements a dispute() function that is intended to be callable by any participant who wishes to challenge an oracle answer. Internally dispute() calls _settleDispute() which in turn calls blockCaller(). The blockCaller() function is defined with the callerIsRoot modifier, meaning only an address that holds the root role can invoke it. Because blockCaller() is invoked from within dispute(), the external dispute() entry point inherits the same restriction: only the root address can successfully execute dispute(). As a result, the function is no longer permissionless; regular users attempting to call dispute() will encounter a revert or a silent failure, depending on how the modifier is implemented. The root cause is an overly restrictive access control on an internal helper that was not intended to be exposed to external callers. An attacker who controls the root address can arbitrarily block or unblock callers, and honest participants are unable to raise disputes, effectively centralising the dispute mechanism and opening a denial-of-service vector. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the OptimisticOracle contract when the auditor traced the call chain from dispute() to blockCaller() and observed the callerIsRoot requirement. Because the restriction is hidden behind an internal call, it may not be obvious from the public interface, making it easy to miss during testing. The impact is that users expecting to be able to dispute an oracle answer receive no response or a transaction revert, leading to loss of confidence and potential financial loss if a wrong answer cannot be challenged. The bug belongs to the class of improper access control or privilege escalation where an internal function inherits a stricter modifier than intended, breaking the contract’s business logic that assumes open dispute participation. To remediate, the contract should either remove the callerIsRoot modifier from blockCaller() when it is called from dispute(), or invoke blockCaller() via this.blockCaller() after granting the contract itself root privileges, ensuring that the external dispute() remains permissionless. In practice, granting the contract root role and calling the internal function through the contract’s own context restores the intended open-access behavior while preserving the ability to block specific callers when needed. Until fixed, any user trying to dispute will see their transaction fail, the UI may show “dispute failed” or simply no change in state, and the protocol’s dispute resolution process is effectively disabled for non-root participants.

title: rate should be updated before modifyCollater
description:
If the user is not calling through VaultActions, vaults[vault].rate will not be updated before modifyCollateralAndDebt(), thus repayment can be made at a lower rate than expected.  
At L124 in VaultActions.sol, publican.collect(vault) will be called to update vaults[vault].rate of codex with codex.modifyRate().  
However, the user may not repay their debt using VaultActions but interact with the codex contract directly.  
By doing so, codex.modifyCollateralAndDebt() will use the old rate, which should be updated with publican.collect(vault).  
If vaults[vault].rate is not updated by others, then the user can avoid the interests since the last updated time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the interest rate associated with each vault is only refreshed when the publican.collect (or drip) function is called, which in the current implementation occurs inside the VaultActions contract before modifyCollateralAndDebt is executed. When a borrower interacts directly with the Codex contract and calls modifyCollateralAndDebt without first invoking publican.collect, the function reads the stale vaults[vault].rate value that has not been updated to reflect accrued interest since the last collection. As a result the borrower can repay the principal using a lower effective interest rate than the protocol has accrued, effectively avoiding the interest that should have been charged for the elapsed time. This situation can be triggered whenever time has passed since the last rate update and no external keeper or user has called the rate‑updating function. The affected parties are borrowers, who may unintentionally receive a discount, and the protocol, which loses the interest revenue it is entitled to. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the repayment flow, where the call chain from VaultActions to Codex was examined and the missing rate update in the direct‑call path was identified. The bug is subtle because the rate variable appears to be kept up‑to‑date in the usual workflow, and there is no explicit check inside modifyCollateralAndDebt that the stored rate matches the current accrued rate, making the problem easy to overlook. From a user's perspective the UI may show the expected interest amount, but after repayment the balance may be higher than anticipated, or the transaction may succeed with a lower interest charge than displayed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “stale state usage” or “interest accrual bypass” bugs, where a contract relies on an external function to refresh accounting data before performing a critical operation. To remediate, the contract should either (i) invoke the rate‑updating function internally at the start of modifyCollateralAndDebt, (ii) make the rate a view that always computes the up‑to‑date value on‑chain, or (iii) enforce that any call that changes collateral or debt must be routed through a wrapper that guarantees the rate has been collected. Such a fix would close the gap that allows borrowers to repay with an outdated, lower rate and would ensure that the protocol consistently captures the accrued interest.

title: Malicious proposers can frontrundispute() and
description:
dispute() is a permissionless function that anyone can call to claim all the bonds from an invalid proposal. This allows the malicious proposers to claw back their bond by front-running dispute() and minimizing the penalty.  
When a malicious proposal front run dispute() on their own invalid proposal, the real cost is the gas cost of the dispute transaction.  
A very sophisticated attacker can deliberately create a few invalid proposals, frontrun others' dispute() transactions, and waste their gas.  
As a result, the other dispute bots will be pushed out as they often get front run, resulting in those bots wasting gas costs on failed transactions.  
After a while, the attacker can casually add an invalid proposal, and there is a chance that no other bots will dispute(), and even if they do, the attacker will just frontrun them again, with very minimal cost.  
Even if the bondSize is very large, say $5000, it becomes insufficient to prevent malicious proposals. As the front run cost can be as low as $50, and the potential gains with a malicious price proposal can be >$500k.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running abuse of the permissionless dispute() function in the OptimisticOracle contract. dispute() is intended to allow any participant to challenge an invalid price proposal and, as a reward, claim the full bond that the proposer posted. Because the function does not differentiate between the original proposer and an external challenger, a malicious proposer can submit an invalid proposal and then submit a dispute transaction that is mined before any honest dispute bot. By doing so, the proposer reclaims the entire bond while only paying the gas cost of the dispute call, effectively minimizing the penalty. This attack can be repeated: the attacker creates several deliberately invalid proposals, watches for honest bots to broadcast dispute transactions, and front‑runs them, causing the bots to waste gas on failed transactions that revert. Over time the attacker can continue to insert low‑value invalid proposals, relying on the low front‑run cost (often a few dollars) to outweigh the bond size (even if the bond is set to several thousand dollars). The issue arises from the lack of access control or economic deterrent on who may receive the bond payout, combined with a gas‑inefficient ordering of checks that makes honest dispute calls expensive. The impact includes loss of economic incentive for honest dispute bots, increased gas waste, potential manipulation of price data, and erosion of trust in the oracle’s dispute mechanism. It affects any participant that runs a dispute bot, the protocol’s price integrity, and ultimately users who rely on accurate pricing. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the dispute flow and identified that the proposer could be the caller of dispute() and that the contract performed costly validation after the bond transfer. The problem is subtle because the function appears to reward dispute callers, and the front‑running behavior is not obvious without analyzing transaction ordering. To mitigate the issue, the contract should limit the bond payout to a fraction of the total bond, allocate the remainder as a reward for honest proposers, and enforce that the caller of dispute() is not the original proposer or is otherwise restricted. Additionally, moving validation logic earlier in the function to revert before costly state changes would reduce gas consumption for honest bots, making the system less vulnerable to front‑running attacks. These changes restore the intended economic penalties and protect the protocol from profit‑driven manipulation.

title: Lack of price freshness check in ChainlinkOra
description:
ChainlinkOracle should use the updatedAt value from the latestRoundData() function to make sure that the latest answer is recent enough to be used.  
In the current implementation of ChainlinkOracle.sol getPrice(), there is no freshness check. This could lead to stale prices being used.  
If the market price of the token drops very quickly ("flash crashes"), and Chainlink's feed does not get updated in time, the smart contract will continue to believe the token is worth more than the market value.  
Chainlink also advise developers to check for the updatedAt before using the price:  
Your application should track the latestTimestamp variable or use the updatedAt value from the latestRoundData() function to make sure that the latest answer is recent enough for your application to use it. If your application detects that the reported answer is not updated within the heartbeat or within time limits that you determine are acceptable for your application, pause operation or switch to an alternate operation mode while identifying the cause of the delay.  
And they have this heartbeat concept:  
Chainlink Price Feeds do not provide streaming data. Rather, the aggregator updates its latestAnswer when the value deviates beyond a specified threshold or when the heartbeat idle time has passed. You can find the heartbeat and deviation values for each data feed at data.chain.link or in the Contract Addresses lists.  
The Heartbeat on Arbitrum is usually 1h.  
Source: https://docs.chain.link/docs/arbitrum-price-feeds/  
A stale price can cause the malfunction of multiple features across the protocol:  
1. _valueInWei() is using the price to calculate the value of the loan and collateral; A stale price will make the price calculation inaccurate so that certain accounts may not be liquidated when they should be, or be liquidated when they should not be.  
2. ChainlinkOracle.sol getPrice() is used to calculate the value of various LPTokens (Aave, Balancer, Compound, Curve, and Uniswap). If the price is not accurate, it will lead to a deviation in the LPToken price and affect the calculation of asset prices.  
3. Stale asset prices can lead to bad debts to the protocol as the collateral assets can be overvalued, and the collateral value can not cover the loans.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing freshness validation when the contract retrieves token prices from Chainlink price feeds. The getPrice function calls latestRoundData but never checks the updatedAt timestamp against a reasonable time window, such as the feed’s heartbeat. Because the contract trusts the returned answer regardless of its age, a stale price can be used for critical calculations. In a scenario where the market experiences a rapid price drop – for example a flash‑crash – the Chainlink aggregator may not update its answer for up to an hour on Arbitrum. The protocol, however, continues to believe the token is worth its previous higher value. This stale valuation propagates through the loan‑to‑value logic, the collateral‑valuation routine (_valueInWei) and the pricing of various LP tokens. As a result, borrowers may avoid liquidation even though their positions are under‑collateralised, or conversely, healthy accounts may be liquidated based on an inflated price. The downstream effect is that the protocol can accrue bad debt because collateral is over‑valued and cannot cover outstanding loans. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s logic with Chainlink’s recommended practice of checking the latestTimestamp or updatedAt field. It is difficult to notice because the price feed still returns a numeric answer and no transaction reverts; the problem only becomes visible under extreme market conditions, when users observe unexpected liquidation behaviour, missing refunds, or a sudden loss of protocol funds. The bug belongs to the class of oracle‑staleness vulnerabilities, where the lack of a timeliness guard allows outdated data to drive financial decisions. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see that their collateral appears to retain value despite a market crash, or a lender may notice that liquidations are not triggered when they should be, leading to confusion and potential loss of capital. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a freshness check by comparing block.timestamp with the updatedAt timestamp and rejecting answers older than a predefined validPeriod (typically the feed’s heartbeat). This ensures that only recent, reliable price data is used for accounting, liquidation and LP‑token valuation, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Curve points should be guaranteed to be mono-
description:
Lack of checks to ensure the points in the curve are monotonic increasing, which can result in a malfunction of deposit() / extendLock() due to underflow when the curve is not set properly.  
In the current implementation, getMultiplier() assume the later point in the curve is always bigger than the previous point, otherwise curve[n+1] - curve[n] will revert due to underflow.  
However, since there is no check in __TimeLockPool_init() / setCurve() / setCurvePoint() to guarantee that, a lower point can actually be set after a higher point.  
deposit() / extendLock() may revert due to underflow.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s handling of a time‑based multiplier curve that is expected to be strictly monotonic increasing. The implementation of getMultiplier assumes that each successive point in the curve array is larger than the previous one, and it computes the difference curve[n+1] - curve[n] without any safety check. Because the initialization function (__TimeLockPool_init), the administrative setters (setCurve and setCurvePoint) do not enforce that new points must be greater than earlier points, an attacker or a mis‑configured admin can insert a lower value after a higher one. When deposit() or extendLock() later calls getMultiplier with such a malformed curve, the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. This underflow does not manifest at the time the curve is set, making the bug hard to notice until a user attempts to deposit or extend a lock and experiences an unexpected revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users cannot create or extend locked positions, which may appear as “funds disappear” or “my deposit fails with no clear reason”. The issue affects any participant who relies on the multiplier curve – typically token holders locking assets for rewards – and it undermines the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the multiplier is always non‑decreasing. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of getMultiplier and noticed the missing monotonicity check. To remediate, the contract should include a validation routine that checks the curve length is at least two and that each subsequent element is greater than or equal to the previous one, reverting with a clear error if the condition is violated. By guaranteeing a monotonic curve, the underflow risk is eliminated, restoring correct multiplier calculation and allowing deposits and lock extensions to succeed as intended.

title: Expired locks should not continue to earn re-
description:
Expired locks should be considered as same as the deposits with no lock.  
The current implementation allows the deposits with expired locks to continue to enjoy the original high multiplier rate, while they can withdraw anytime they want.  
The multiplier of shares amount is essentially a higher reward rate (APR) for longer period of locks.  
For example:  
If the regular APR is 2%; Locking for 4 years will boost the APR to 10%.  
• Alice deposited 1M $MC tokens and got 10% APR;  
• 4 years later, Alice's deposit's lock was expired.  
Expected result:  
The new APR for Alice's deposit is 2%;  
Actual result:  
Alice can continue to enjoy a 10% APR while she can withdraw anytime.  
Users with expired locks will take more rewards than expected, which means fewer rewards for other users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the reward‑distribution logic of a lock‑based staking contract. When a user creates a time‑locked deposit, the contract assigns a multiplier to the deposited amount that raises the effective share balance and therefore the annual percentage rate (APR) for the duration of the lock. The root cause is that the contract never resets or reduces this multiplier once the lock period has elapsed. Consequently, an expired lock is treated the same as an active lock: the user can withdraw at any time but continues to earn rewards at the higher, lock‑specific APR instead of the baseline APR that should apply after expiry. An attacker can exploit this by simply waiting for the lock to expire, then leaving the deposit untouched while it keeps generating the inflated reward rate. The impact is a systematic over‑payment of rewards to the holder of the expired lock, which reduces the reward pool available to all other participants and can erode the protocol’s economic model. This condition occurs whenever a deposit’s end timestamp is in the past and the contract does not contain a mechanism to adjust the share amount or to “kick” the excess multiplier. All users who lock tokens are potentially affected because the excess rewards taken by one expired lock are deducted from the collective reward pool, harming other stakers and the protocol’s tokenomics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Merit Circle contracts, where the auditor observed that the multiplier field was never cleared after the lock expiry and that the UI displayed no warning despite the continued high APR. The problem is subtle because the contract still allows withdrawals, so there is no obvious failure; the only symptom is that rewards keep accruing at an unexpectedly high rate, which may be missed unless the reward calculations are compared against the expected baseline APR. To remediate the flaw, the contract should implement a post‑expiry adjustment similar to Curve’s gauge “kick” function: after the lock end time, the extra shares granted by the multiplier must be burned or the multiplier reset to 1, ensuring that the effective APR reverts to the standard rate. This change restores correct accounting, prevents unfair reward extraction, and aligns the protocol’s incentives with its intended design.

title: escrowedReward will be frozen in the contract if
description:
A portion of users' reward, which is expected to be "escrowed", will be frozen in the pool contract if escrowPool == address(0) but escrowPortion > 0.  
Setting _escrowPool to address(0) is allowed in __BasePool_init():  
ining/contracts/base/BasePool.sol#L75-L77  
However, when escrowPortion > 0, if escrowPool == address(0), claimRewards() will still only transferring nonEscrowedRewardAmount to the _receiver and left the escrowedRewardAmount in the contract.  
As a result, a portion (escrowPortion) of the rewards will be frozen in the contract, and there is no way for the users or even the admin to retrieve these rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑escrow locking defect that occurs when a pool contract is configured with a non‑zero escrow portion but the escrow pool address is set to the zero address (address(0)). The claimRewards function calculates an escrowedRewardAmount based on the escrowPortion, but it only transfers the non‑escrowed portion to the receiver. Because the escrowPool address is zero, the subsequent call to escrowPool.deposit never executes, leaving the escrowedRewardAmount permanently stored in the pool contract. This situation arises during initialization when __BasePool_init allows _escrowPool to be address(0) while still permitting escrowPortion > 0. An auditor discovered the issue by reviewing the initialization logic and the reward‑claim flow. The bug is subtle because the function emits a successful claim event and transfers some tokens, so users may not notice that a fraction of their expected reward is missing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a lower-than‑expected reward or, in extreme cases, a completely empty payout when the entire reward is earmarked for escrow. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that escrowed rewards will be deposited elsewhere are violated, breaking the intended financial flow. The impact is that a portion of each user’s reward becomes irretrievable; neither the user nor the contract admin can withdraw the locked tokens, effectively freezing those funds. The condition for exploitation is simply calling claimRewards when escrowPortion is positive and escrowPool is zero, which can happen for any participant. The class of bug is an “optional external contract address misuse” that leads to locked assets, similar to zero‑address escrow or treasury misconfiguration errors. The recommended mitigation is to guard the escrow calculation with a check that both escrowPortion is non‑zero and escrowPool is a valid non‑zero address before attempting a deposit, and to skip or revert the escrow portion when the pool address is unset, ensuring that all reward tokens are either transferred to the receiver or correctly handled.

title: Front run distributeRewards() can steal the
description:
A surge of pointsPerShare on each distributeRewards() call can be used by the attacker to steal part of the newly added rewards.  
Every time the distributeRewards() gets called, there will be a surge of pointsPerShare for the existing stakeholders.  
This enables a well-known attack vector, in which the attacker will deposit a huge amount of underlying tokens and take a large portion of the pool, then trigger the surge, and exit right after.  
While the existence of the MIN_LOCK_DURATION prevented the usage of flashloan, it's still possible for the attackers with sufficient funds or can acquire sufficient funds in other ways.  
In which case, the attack is quite practical and effectively steal the major part of the newly added rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑run exploitation of the distributeRewards function that allows an attacker to capture a disproportionate share of newly added rewards. The root cause lies in the way pointsPerShare is increased in a single step each time distributeRewards is called; the increase is applied to all existing stakeholders before the contract records any new deposits. An attacker can deposit a large amount of the underlying token, wait for the next distributeRewards call which creates a surge in pointsPerShare, and then withdraw immediately after the distribution while still holding the inflated share. Because the reward allocation is calculated based on the attacker’s enlarged balance at the moment of the surge, the attacker receives a large portion of the freshly minted rewards, effectively stealing them from other participants. This attack can be carried out by any entity that can acquire sufficient capital, even though the MIN_LOCK_DURATION prevents flash‑loan attacks; the attacker simply needs to lock the funds for the required duration and then exit after the reward distribution. The impact is that legitimate stakers receive far less reward than expected, their reward balances may appear unchanged or lower after a distribution, and the protocol loses a significant amount of newly added rewards. The issue occurs whenever distributeRewards is invoked while a large, newly‑locked stake exists, and it affects all users of the staking pool, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward accounting. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who recognized the pattern as a known front‑run reward‑distribution flaw. It can be hard to notice because the pointsPerShare surge is a normal part of the contract’s accounting logic, and the reward distribution appears to succeed from a transaction‑status perspective, masking the fact that the reward share has been unfairly skewed. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a rewardRate‑based gradual release model similar to Synthetix’s StakingRewards, where rewards accrue continuously over time rather than being allocated in a single burst, thereby eliminating the incentive for an attacker to manipulate the timing of deposits and withdrawals. In user‑facing terms, a participant may see their expected reward balance stay at zero or increase only marginally after a distribution, contrary to the expectation that the reward should grow proportionally to their stake. This mismatch violates the core business logic that rewards are distributed fairly based on each user’s share of the pool.

title: LeverEPTActions#buyCollateralAndIncreaseLeve
description:
Because of the precision loss in the conversion of borrowed amount (addDebt) to deltaNormalDebt with wdiv(addDebt, rate), the newly generated internal credit for FIAT (deltaDebt) will most certainly always be 1 Wei less than addDebt.  
As a result, the buyCollateralAndIncreaseLever() will fail due to insufficient credit in codex.transferCredit().  
When buyCollateralAndIncreaseLever() is called, it will take a flashloan from flash which will callback and call the internal function addCollateralAndDebt() with the amount of addCollateral and borrowed (as addDebt).  
codex.modifyCollateralAndDebt() will then be called with deltaNormalDebt = wdiv(addDebt, rate); In codex.modifyCollateralAndDebt(), the deltaNormalDebt will be convert back as int256 deltaDebt = wmul(v.rate, deltaNormalDebt);.  
The back and forth conversion will most certainly incur a precision loss, resulting in the deltaDebt to be 1 Wei smaller than addDebt.  
Thus, the transaction will revert in exitMoneta(creditor, addDebt); as the credit will be insufficient (by 1 Wei).  
LeverEPTActions#buyCollateralAndIncreaseLever() will most certainly fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one rounding error that occurs when the contract converts a borrowed amount (addDebt) into an internal credit representation (deltaNormalDebt) using a fixed‑point division function wdiv that rounds down. Because the division discards fractional wei, the resulting deltaNormalDebt, when multiplied back by the current rate with wmul, yields a deltaDebt that is typically one wei smaller than the original addDebt. The buyCollateralAndIncreaseLever function relies on this internal credit to transfer the exact borrowed amount via codex.transferCredit. When the credit is one wei short, the transfer fails and the transaction reverts in exitMoneta, causing the whole leverage operation to abort. This issue manifests whenever a user attempts to open a leveraged position through the flash‑loan‑based buyCollateralAndIncreaseLever flow, which first obtains a flash loan, then calls addCollateralAndDebt, and finally attempts to settle the borrowed credit. The affected parties are any users of the protocol who try to increase leverage, as well as the protocol itself because failed transactions waste gas and may undermine confidence in the system. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic pathways of debt accounting and noticed the mismatch between addDebt and the credit transferred. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is only one wei, which may not be caught by typical unit tests that use larger amounts or ignore exact equality checks. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: users cannot successfully execute leveraged purchases, leading to lost opportunities and potentially higher gas costs. Conceptually, the fix is to use a rounding‑up division (wdivUp) when calculating deltaNormalDebt so that the multiplied credit never falls short, ensuring that the internal credit matches or exceeds the borrowed amount.
