This change eliminates the precision loss and allows the credit transfer to succeed, restoring the intended business logic of accurate accounting for leveraged positions.

title: Aer.lock only locks itself.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incomplete shutdown mechanism in the Aer contract. The lock() function is intended to halt all protocol activity during the Tenebrae global settlement process by setting the live flag to zero, clearing queued debt, resetting debt on auction, and invoking lock() on the surplusAuction and debtAuction contracts. However, only the lock() entry point checks the live flag; the rest of Aer’s external and public functions do not verify whether the contract is still live. As a result, after a successful call to lock(), the Aer contract remains callable for any functionality that does not contain an explicit live check. This allows privileged or authorized callers to continue interacting with the contract, resetting surplus or debt auctions, or performing other state‑changing operations that should be prohibited after shutdown. The root cause is the missing live‑state guard in functions that are expected to be disabled during settlement. An attacker who can invoke those unprotected functions after lock() can manipulate auction parameters, alter debt accounting, or otherwise interfere with the intended settlement flow, potentially leading to incorrect distribution of funds, loss of user balances, or a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue manifests only after the lock() function has been executed, i.e., during the shutdown phase, and it affects any participant that relies on the protocol’s guarantee that no further state changes will occur – typically creditors, token holders, and the protocol itself. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer observed that the live flag is only consulted in lock() and not elsewhere, a pattern that can be easily missed because the contract still emits a Lock event and appears to have entered a halted state. From a user’s perspective, the UI may indicate that the system is “locked” while underlying functions still accept transactions, leading to confusion such as “my balance did not change after shutdown” or “the contract still processes actions”. The bug belongs to the class of incomplete pause or shutdown implementations where the global guard is not uniformly applied. To remediate, every function that must be disabled after a lock should include a check that live != 0 (or use a reusable modifier) so that no state‑changing operation can be performed once the contract is marked as not live. This ensures that the protocol’s settlement logic remains sound and that users’ expectations of a frozen system are met.

title: Base interest can change while there is uncol-
description:
baseInterest can be modified at any time, while there may be uncollected interest.  
The interestPerSecond setter has a check to ensure that there is all interest has been collected prior to changing its value.  
```solidity
if (block.timestamp != vaults[vault].lastCollected) revert Publican__setParam_notCollected();
```  
"Global, per-second stability fee contribution", so it seems that it should only be modified when all interest has been collected too.  
Base interest rate update is retroactively applied to uncollected interest, which may be undesirable.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability to modify the global base interest rate while there is still uncollected accrued interest in the protocol. The contract stores a per‑second stability fee (interestPerSecond) and a separate baseInterest parameter that contributes to the overall rate. The setter for interestPerSecond includes a guard that reverts if the lastCollected timestamp does not match the current block timestamp, ensuring that all pending interest has been harvested before the rate can be changed. The setter for baseInterest, however, lacks this safeguard. As a result, an administrator or DAO can call the baseInterest update function at any moment, even when the vault still holds interest that has not been collected. Because the protocol calculates accrued interest retroactively using the current baseInterest value, the new rate is applied to the period that has already elapsed but whose reward has not yet been distributed. This leads to a mismatch between the amount users expect based on the rate that was in effect when they deposited and the amount they actually receive after the rate change. The impact is a potential loss or gain of interest for users, typically small because interest is collected only every three days or when a user interacts with the contract, but it violates the accounting assumption that interest accrues at a fixed rate until it is explicitly harvested. The issue manifests when the DAO or privileged account updates baseInterest between collection cycles; users may notice that their pending reward is lower (or higher) than anticipated, or that a final depositor cannot fully cover accrued fees because the rate was altered after their deposit. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of the two rate setters and identified the missing check. It can be hard to notice because the discrepancy only appears after the next collection event, and the per‑second accrual model masks the retroactive effect. To remediate, the baseInterest setter should incorporate the same conditional check used by the interestPerSecond setter, or the contract should force a collection of pending interest before any rate modification. This ensures that the protocol’s accounting remains consistent, users receive the interest they earned under the original rate, and the protocol cannot silently rewrite historical accruals.

title: Users can push any value to Collybus immedi-
description:
Users can push any value to Collybus immediately if disputeWindow is less than proposeWindow.  
If disputeWindow is less than proposeWindow, users can bypass conditions (canShift) called by shift function in OptimisticOracle.sol.  
Suppose:  
• current block.timestamp = 1000  
• disputeWindow = 10  
• proposeWindow = 100 (disputeWindow is less than proposeWindow)  
• Nonce of current proposal is 0, or it's unable to dispute (proposeWindow exceeded)  
Alice can push any value to Collybus immediately:  
1. Because any users can craft nonce, Alice crafts a nonce that decodeRoundTimestamp(nonce) = 980 and calls shift.  
2. shift function will check nonce by calling canShift, but the nonce crafted by Alice will pass canPropose(nonce) because (block.timestamp - decodeRoundTimestamp(nonce) <= proposeWindow) (1000 - 980 <= 100). Thus Alice updated the proposal with a malicious value.  
3. Then Alice call shift again, now canShift will check that the nonce (it's prevNonce now) should be unable to dispute. But the nonce can pass the condition: !canDispute(prevNonce): !(block.timestamp - decodeRoundTimestamp(nonce) <= disputeWindow) (!(1000 - 980 <= 10))  
Finally, the proposal will be pushed to Collybus.  
If disputeWindow is less than proposeWindow, attacker can push any malicious value to Collybus immediately in the same block. Users may get a wrong price when calling the read function in Collybus.sol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked relationship between the dispute window and the propose window in the OptimisticOracle contract that governs the shift operation for price proposals. The root cause is that the contract does not enforce the invariant disputeWindow >= proposeWindow, allowing a situation where the dispute period is shorter than the time allowed for proposing a new value. When this condition holds, an attacker can craft a nonce whose decoded round timestamp falls within the propose window but outside the dispute window. The shift function first calls canShift, which internally checks canPropose for the new nonce and !canDispute for the previous nonce. Because the dispute window is shorter, the crafted nonce satisfies both checks in the same block, letting the attacker call shift twice and push an arbitrary value directly into the Collybus price feed without any opportunity for a challenger to dispute it. This can be exploited by any user who can generate a suitable nonce; the attacker simply submits a shift transaction with the malicious value, and the contract immediately records it as the official price. The impact is that the price oracle may return a completely wrong price when other contracts or users call the read function of Collybus, leading to incorrect calculations, potential loss of funds, or execution of trades at unintended rates. The flaw manifests only when the disputeWindow parameter is configured to be less than the proposeWindow parameter, which may happen during deployment or through an upgrade that changes these timings. All participants that rely on the oracle – traders, lenders, protocol logic – are affected because they receive a price that does not reflect the true market. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the OptimisticOracle shift logic, where the auditor noticed that the two time‑based checks could be satisfied simultaneously under certain parameter configurations. It is subtle because each individual check appears correct; only their combination under a mis‑configured window creates the bypass, making it easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce that disputeWindow is greater than or equal to proposeWindow at construction (or during any parameter update) and/or adjust the canShift logic to require that a proposal cannot be shifted until the full dispute period for the previous round has elapsed, regardless of the propose window. This ensures that no value can be injected without giving honest participants a chance to dispute, preserving the integrity of the price feed and preventing users from seeing a zero or wildly inaccurate price where they expect a correct market rate.

title: Unsafe casting to uint88
description:
fCashAmount is unsafely casted to uint88 in when buying and selling collateral in VaultFCActions.sol.  
In both buying and selling collateral, the respective functions take fCashAmount as uint256. It is unsafely casted to uint88 in the _buyFCash() and _sellFCash() functions.  
Even though _sellfCash() checks for the casting overflow, the casting has already performed, making it redundant.  
The deltaCollateral calculated would be impacted as it retains the original value that could exceed type(uint88).max. As a POC, if we take fCashAmount to be type(uint88.max) + 1, we would have vastly different values for deltaCollateral and fCashAmount:  
• deltaCollateral = 3094850098213450687247810560000000000  
• fCashAmount = 0  
The collateral to be credited / deducted can be made to be much greater / smaller than the fCashAmount. The likelihood of an exploit is low, because the collateral has to be transferred into and from the vault, which, in practice, would be too large an amount for most collateral tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe down‑casting of a 256‑bit unsigned integer (uint256) to an 88‑bit unsigned integer (uint88) inside the VaultFCActions contract when buying or selling fCash collateral. The functions _buyFCash() and _sellFCash() receive fCashAmount as a uint256 but immediately cast it to uint88 before any overflow validation. Because Solidity truncates values that exceed the target type, a value larger than type(uint88).max is silently reduced modulo 2^88, effectively turning, for example, type(uint88).max+1 into zero. Although _sellFCash() contains an overflow check, the cast has already occurred, making the check ineffective. The deltaCollateral variable is calculated using the original fCashAmount before the cast, so when an oversized amount is supplied the contract records a massive deltaCollateral while the stored fCashAmount becomes zero. An attacker can trigger this by submitting a fCashAmount equal to type(uint88).max+1, causing the contract to credit or debit an astronomically large amount of collateral (e.g., deltaCollateral = 3094850098213450687247810560000000000) while the internal fCash balance appears as zero. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal transaction but the resulting collateral balance could suddenly jump to an unexpected huge value or disappear entirely, violating the expectation that the amount of collateral received matches the fCash amount supplied. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s arithmetic logic. It is hard to notice because the overflow does not revert; it merely wraps, and the redundant overflow check gives a false sense of safety. The impact is a breach of accounting invariants: the protocol’s accounting assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between fCash and collateral, which this bug breaks, potentially allowing loss or unintended gain of funds. The exploit requires moving an extremely large amount of the underlying collateral token, which limits practical risk, but the logical flaw remains. The recommended fix is to keep fCashAmount as a uint256 throughout the workflow, add proper overflow checks before any casting, and avoid casting to uint88 altogether, thereby preserving the correct relationship between fCash and collateral and preventing mis‑calculation of deltaCollateral.

title: Proposer can submit malicious data that can prevent disputes
description:
A proposer can submit malicious data that forces dispute attempts to be reverted, thus preventing disputes (and is therefore able to submit a malicious value unless push() is called).
Oct 3rd to Oct 5th.
There are 2 ways in which a malicious proposer can force a dispute transaction to revert.
1. ABI Decoding
The data cannot be decoded to uint80 dataRoundId and uint64 dataRoundTimestamp.
(Eg. data = 0x).
```solidity
// Retrieve the round data from Chainlink
(uint80 dataRoundId, uint64 dataRoundTimestamp) = abi.decode(
    data,
    (uint80, uint64)
);
```
2. Malicious dataRoundId
The dataRoundId used is out of range (eg. a future dataRoundId or low dataRoundId).
```solidity
(
    ,
    int256 roundValue,
    ,
    uint256 roundTimestamp,
) = AggregatorV3Interface(feed).getRoundData(dataRoundId);
```
Proposals with malicious dataRoundId cannot be disputed. While this can partially be nevertheless be able to continue submitting these malicious proposals as his bond cannot be removed, causing DoS of the shift() and dispute() functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that a proposer can submit malformed or out‑of‑rangedata that causes the dispute() function to revert, effectively preventing any dispute from being processed. The root cause is that the contract assumes the data field can always be decoded into a uint80 round identifier and a uint64 timestamp, and that the Chainlink AggregatorV3Interface.getRoundData call will never revert. When the data is empty or otherwise not ABI‑compatible, the abi.decode statement throws, and when the supplied round identifier is outside the valid range (for example a future round or a very low round), the external call to the price feed reverts. Because the dispute logic does not catch these exceptions, the whole transaction reverts, leaving the malicious proposal in place and the proposer’s bond locked. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a proposal with either an empty data payload (e.g. 0x) or a round identifier that the price feed rejects. The attacker then repeatedly calls push() to add more proposals, but any attempt by honest participants to call dispute() or shift() will fail with a revert, resulting in a denial‑of‑service of the dispute mechanism and potentially freezing the protocol’s ability to correct incorrect proposals. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is created with invalid data and the contract later attempts to dispute it; it affects all users who rely on the dispute process, the protocol’s integrity, and any funds that are supposed to be slashed from a malicious proposer. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the handling of the data field and the external price‑feed call, noting that no try‑catch or validation was present. Because the revert occurs inside a low‑level external call, the failure can be subtle: the UI may simply show that the dispute transaction 'failed' without indicating that the underlying data is malformed, and users may see no change in balances or bond status, leading to confusion. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call and ABI‑decoding errors that allow malformed input to break contract logic. To remediate, the decode and the getRoundData call should be wrapped in a try‑catch (or equivalent low‑level call with success flag) and the proposal marked as invalid if either operation fails; the dispute function should then treat the proposal as disputable and allow the bond to be slashed. In user‑facing terms, a user attempting to dispute a proposal may receive a transaction revert, see no refund of their dispute fee, and observe that the proposal remains active despite being obviously incorrect. This violates the protocol’s expectation that any submitted value can be challenged and corrected, breaking the accounting guarantees of the system.

title: _settleDispute() does not block the proposer
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the dispute‑settlement flow of the OptimisticOracle contract. When a dispute is settled, the internal function blockCaller is invoked with the intention of preventing the proposer from making any further bond calls. However, blockCaller only clears the root flag for the proposer – a flag that the proposer never possessed – and does not remove the generic ANY_SIG permission that actually grants the ability to call the bond method. The canCall view function determines call rights by checking three mappings: a specific signature entry, a wildcard ANY_SIG entry, and a universal caller entry. Because blockCaller only sets _canCall[sig][who] to false for the supplied signature, the proposer remains authorized through the ANY_SIG entry, making the block operation effectively a no‑op. Consequently, a malicious proposer can bond again after a dispute is settled and continue to submit new proposals, potentially manipulating the oracle’s outcome or draining funds. The issue manifests whenever a dispute is settled and the contract attempts to revoke the proposer’s bonding rights; it does not depend on external inputs beyond the normal dispute‑settlement path. The affected parties are the protocol’s users and any participants relying on the oracle’s integrity, as the continued bonding ability of a malicious proposer can lead to incorrect price feeds or financial loss. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the permission‑revocation logic and noticed that the root‑only modifier on blockCaller does not align with the actual permission model used by canCall. The problem is subtle because the function emits a BlockCaller event, giving the impression that the proposer is blocked, while the underlying permission check still permits bonding. To remediate, the contract should either revoke the ANY_SIG entry for the proposer, replace the wildcard with the concrete bond function signature when calling blockCaller, or redesign the canCall logic so that revoking a specific permission truly disables the corresponding action. In essence, this is a classic case of insufficient permission revocation leading to an authorization bypass, where the expected behaviour (proposer cannot bond after dispute) diverges from reality (proposer can still bond).

title: new loans "max duration" is not restricted
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the enforcement of the maximum loan duration in a public vault that operates on a time‑based epoch schedule. The protocol is designed so that a newly created loan may not extend beyond the end of the next epoch; for example, if a vault is halfway through a 30‑day epoch, the loan length should be limited to 45 days. However, the implementation that checks the allowed epoch does not correctly restrict durations that exceed two epochs. The test suite demonstrates that a loan with a 50‑day duration is accepted even though it should be rejected, indicating that the validation logic either miscalculates the target epoch or applies an insufficient bound (epoch <= currentEpoch + 1). As a result, borrowers can request loans that remain outstanding for longer than the protocol’s accounting window, which can cause liquidity to be locked unexpectedly, break the assumption that repayments will be settled within the next epoch, and distort the vault’s risk metrics. The issue is triggered when a loan’s duration is longer than the remaining time in the current epoch plus one full epoch, i.e., when the duration spans more than two epochs. It primarily affects users who rely on the advertised loan window, the strategists who configure vault parameters, and the protocol itself because the accounting model assumes all loans finish within the next epoch. The flaw was discovered during a targeted audit test that attempted to create a loan with a duration greater than the allowed maximum; the test passed, revealing the missing restriction. The problem is subtle because the epoch calculation uses a ceiling division and an offset that can mask the overflow for certain start times, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly compare the proposed loan end timestamp against the timestamp of the next epoch boundary and reject any loan that would finish later, or adjust the epoch calculation so that the require statement enforces epoch <= currentEpoch + 1 correctly. In practice, fixing the bug restores the guarantee that loans cannot outlive the next epoch, preserving expected liquidity flow, preventing funds from being locked indefinitely, and aligning the smart contract’s behavior with the documented business logic.

title: If an auction has no bidder,the NFT ownership
description:
The lenders in principal have the claim for the loan collateral, but current rule will let the liquidation caller get the collateral for free. Effectively take advantage from the vault LP, which is not fair. After the endAuction(), the collateral will be released to the initiator. Essentially, the initiator gets the NFT for free. But the lenders of the loan take the loss. However, the lenders should have the claim to the collateral, since originally the funds are provided by the lenders. If the collateral at the end is owned by whoever calls the liquidation function, it is not fair for the lenders. And will discourage future users to use the protocol.  
• Lenders could suffer fund loss in some cases.  
• The unfair mechanism will discourage future users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an auction settlement flaw that allows the caller of the liquidation function to receive the NFT collateral without paying for it when the auction finishes with no bidders. The root cause is a missing safeguard that checks whether any valid bid was placed before transferring ownership of the collateral. Because the contract unconditionally releases the NFT to the transaction initiator after endAuction(), the protocol treats the caller as the new owner even though no payment was made. An attacker can exploit this by invoking the liquidation routine on a loan whose collateral is put up for auction, waiting for the auction timer to expire without submitting a bid, and then calling endAuction(). The contract will transfer the NFT to the attacker for free, while the lenders who funded the loan lose their claim to the collateral. The impact is a loss of the underlying asset for the lenders, effectively stealing the NFT and reducing confidence in the lending platform. This condition occurs only when an auction ends with zero bids, which can be deliberately engineered by the attacker or happen naturally if the market is illiquid. All parties that provide liquidity to the loan pool are affected because their collateral backing is stripped away without compensation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the auditor noticed that the final ownership transfer did not verify the presence of a winning bid. The bug is subtle because the auction appears to complete successfully and no explicit error is thrown, making it easy to miss during testing unless the edge case of an empty auction is exercised. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a successful bid exists before releasing the NFT, or alternatively, if no bids are received, the collateral should be returned to the pool of lenders or re‑auctioned rather than handed to the caller. This class of bug belongs to improper handling of empty‑auction states and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that collateral remains claimable by the lenders until a legitimate purchase occurs. From a user perspective, lenders would see their expected collateral disappear, while the caller unexpectedly receives a valuable NFT without any payment, contradicting the expectation that a liquidation either transfers the asset to a buyer or returns it to the pool.

title: Buyouts of shorter duration liens can lead to
description: Liens whose duration is equal to (or maybe less than) minDurationIncrease cannot be bought out to be replaced by newer liens with lower interest rates but the same duration. This locks the borrower out of better-termed liens, effectively resulting in the loss of their funds. Liens whose duration is equal to (or maybe less than) minDurationIncrease cannot be bought out to be replaced by newer liens with lower interest rates but the exact duration because it results in an underflow in _getRemainingInterest(). Example scenario: if the strategyliendetails.duration is <= 14 days, then it's wait minDurationIncrease, which is set to 14 days. However, if the buyer waits 14 days, the lien is expired, which triggers the earlier mentioned underflow. The borrower gets locked out of better-termed liens, effectively resulting in the loss of their funds because of extra interest paid on older liens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an underflow error in the buyout logic for short‑duration liens. When a lien’s total duration is less than or equal to the protocol‑defined minDurationIncrease (14 days in the current configuration) the contract prevents the lien from being bought out and replaced by a new lien with a lower interest rate but the same term. The check that blocks the buyout also leads to a call to _getRemainingInterest() after the original lien has technically expired. Because the elapsed time equals the full duration, the remaining‑interest calculation attempts to subtract a larger value from a smaller one, causing an unsigned integer underflow. This underflow either reverts the transaction or returns an incorrect (typically very large) interest amount, which in practice stops the borrower from refinancing the loan. The borrower therefore remains locked into the original high‑rate lien, continues to accrue interest at the old rate, and may see no way to obtain a better‑priced loan. The issue manifests only for loans whose duration is at most the minimum duration increase; longer loans are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Astaria protocol where the logical flow of the buyout function was examined and the edge case of short‑duration loans was found to be mishandled. The bug is subtle because the duration check appears reasonable and the underflow occurs only after the lien has expired, a state that is rarely exercised in normal testing. To remediate the problem the contract should either allow buyouts for short‑duration liens or adjust the remaining‑interest calculation to safely handle the case where the elapsed time equals the total duration, for example by capping the remaining interest at zero or by redefining minDurationIncrease logic. In broader terms this is a classic example of a boundary‑condition arithmetic error that breaks the intended refinancing workflow, leading to funds being effectively trapped and borrowers receiving no refund or lower‑rate loan as they expected.

title: Loan duration can exceed the end of the next
description:
epoch
Loan duration can exceed the end of the next epoch, which deviates from the protocol specification. From the specs: "The duration of new loans is restricted to not exceed the end of the next epoch. For example, if a PublicVault is 15 days into a 30-day epoch, new loans must not be longer than 45 days." However, there's no enforcement of this requirement. The implementation does not adhere to the spec: Loan duration can exceed the end of the next epoch, which breaks protocol specification and therefore lead to miscalculations and potential fund loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the smart‑contract loan module does not enforce the rule that a newly created loan must finish before the end of the next epoch. According to the protocol specification, if the current epoch is 15 days into a 30‑day period, the maximum loan duration is 45 days, i.e., the loan must not extend beyond the start of the following epoch. The implementation lacks any check on the requested loan term, allowing borrowers or malicious actors to request a duration that runs past the next epoch boundary. This mismatch between the on‑chain logic and the off‑chain accounting model causes the protocol’s epoch‑based interest and repayment calculations to become inaccurate. When a loan spans into a later epoch, the system may apply the wrong interest rate, mis‑report the loan’s maturity, or fail to trigger scheduled liquidation or repayment events that are tied to epoch transitions. As a result, lenders may see their expected returns reduced, borrowers may be unable to repay on schedule, and the vault’s accounting can show negative or missing balances, effectively leading to fund loss. The issue manifests whenever a loan is created after the epoch has progressed beyond the midpoint, because the contract does not compare the requested term with the remaining time until the next epoch. It was discovered during a manual audit of the loan creation flow, where the specification was cross‑checked against the code and the missing validation was noted. The bug is subtle because the contract still accepts the loan and appears to function normally; only the downstream epoch‑based accounting reveals the discrepancy, which may not be obvious during routine testing. To remediate, the contract should include a validation step that computes the epoch end timestamp and rejects any loan whose duration would exceed that point, or the protocol specification should be revised to match the actual behavior. In essence, this is an epoch‑boundary enforcement flaw, a class of bug where time‑based constraints are not correctly validated, leading to accounting errors and potential loss of funds.

title: First ERC4626 deposit can break share cal-
description: The first depositor of an ERC4626 vault can maliciously manipulate the share price by depositing the lowest possible amount (1 wei) of liquidity and then artificially inflating ERC4626.totalAssets. This can inflate the base share price as high as 1:1e18 early on, which force all subsequence deposit to use this share price as a base and worst case, due to rounding down, if this malicious initial deposit front-run someone else depositing, this depositor will receive 0 shares and lost his deposited assets. Given a vault with DAI as the underlying asset: Alice (attacker) deposits initial liquidity of 1 wei DAI via deposit() Alice receives 1e18 (1 wei) vault shares Alice transfers 1 ether of DAI via transfer() to the vault to artificially inflate the asset balance without minting new shares. The asset balance is now 1 ether + 1 wei DAI -> vault share price is now very high (= 1000000000000000000001 wei ~ 1000 * 1e18) Bob (victim) deposits 100 ether DAI Bob receives 0 shares Bob receives 0 shares due to a precision issue. His deposited funds are lost. The shares are calculated as following return supply == 0 ? assets : assets.mulDivDown(supply, totalAssets()); In case of a very high share price, due to totalAssets() > assets * supply, shares will be 0. ERC4626 vault share price can be maliciously inflated on the initial deposit, leading to the next depositor losing assets due to precision issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑price manipulation and precision bug in ERC4626‑style vaults that rely on a simple share‑to‑asset conversion formula. The root cause is that the vault allows an attacker to make the first deposit with the minimum possible amount (1 wei) and then increase the reported total assets by transferring additional underlying tokens directly to the vault without minting corresponding shares. Because the share price is calculated as assets multiplied by the current supply divided by totalAssets, inflating totalAssets while keeping supply tiny creates an extremely high share price. When a subsequent user deposits a normal amount, the contract computes the number of shares using a rounding‑down division (mulDivDown). With the inflated denominator, the division result can round down to zero, so the depositor receives no vault shares even though their tokens have been transferred into the vault. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed, but the UI shows no increase in balance and the funds are effectively lost. The impact is that honest users can lose their deposited assets without receiving any representation of ownership, and the attacker can front‑run deposits to either capture the inflated share price or cause victims to receive zero shares. The condition for exploitation is that the vault’s supply is initially zero or very low and that the contract does not enforce a minimum initial deposit or prevent direct asset transfers that bypass share minting. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined edge cases of the ERC4626 share calculation, noting that similar problems have appeared in other protocols such as Uniswap when the supply is zero. The bug is hard to notice because the contract’s public functions appear to work correctly for normal deposits, and the loss only manifests when the share price becomes extreme, a situation that may not be exercised in typical testing. Conceptually, the fix is to prevent the share price from being artificially inflated: enforce a minimum initial deposit, require that any increase in total assets be accompanied by proportional share minting, or use a more robust share‑price calculation that caps the effect of extreme asset‑to‑supply ratios and avoids rounding‑down to zero. This class of bug falls under “share price manipulation via asset injection” and “precision loss in integer division”, both of which break the accounting invariants of the vault and violate the expectation that a deposit always yields a non‑zero amount of shares proportional to the deposited assets.

title: LiquidityProvider can also lend to Private-
description: Insufficient access control for lending to PublicVault found by yawn-c111 Docs says as follows https://docs.astaria.xyz/docs/intro Any strategists may provide their own capital to fund these loans through their own PrivateVaults, and whitelisted strategists can deploy PublicVaults that accept funds from other liquidity providers. However, Liquidity Providers can also lend to PrivateVault. This is because lendToVault function is controlled by mapping(address => address) public vaults, which are managed by _newVault function and include PrivateVaults. This leads to unexpected atttack. Unexpected liquidity providers can lend to private vaults
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient access‑control check in the lending entry point of the Astaria protocol. The function that allows a liquidity provider to deposit capital, lendToVault, validates the target vault only by confirming that the address exists in a public mapping of vault identifiers. This mapping is populated by the internal _newVault routine, which registers both PublicVault contracts (intended for open‑access lending) and PrivateVault contracts (intended to hold only strategist‑provided capital). Because the lendToVault logic does not differentiate between the two vault types, any external liquidity provider can invoke the function with the address of a PrivateVault and successfully transfer funds into a vault that is supposed to be isolated from public participants. The root cause is a missing authorization rule that should restrict lending operations to PublicVaults only. An attacker or an unwary user can exploit this by simply calling lendToVault with a PrivateVault address, causing their deposited assets to be locked in a contract that does not expose the usual withdrawal or reward mechanisms for public providers. The impact includes loss of expected returns, potential permanent loss of capital if the PrivateVault does not implement a public exit path, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that private vault balances are not part of the public liquidity pool. This condition occurs whenever a liquidity provider interacts with the lending interface without the protocol enforcing a vault‑type check, i.e., under any normal usage of lendToVault. The affected parties are external liquidity providers who assume they are depositing into a public, open‑access vault, as well as the protocol itself, which may present inaccurate total liquidity figures. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the access‑control model of the vault registry and identified that the mapping includes PrivateVault entries without additional guards. The flaw can be hard to notice because the function signature and event logs appear normal, and the contract does not revert or emit an error when a private vault is used, giving the false impression that the deposit succeeded as intended. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction, but the expected reward or balance update never materialises, leading to a situation where “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. Conceptually, this is an authorization or privilege‑escalation bug where a function intended for a specific class of contracts is inadvertently exposed to a broader class. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit requirement that the target vault be registered as a PublicVault, for example by maintaining a separate whitelist or flag that is checked before accepting a deposit, thereby preventing private vaults from receiving external liquidity.

title: LiquidationAccountant.claim may revert for
description: LiquidationAccountant.claim may initiate a transfer with the amount 0, which reverts for some tokens. Some tokens (e.g., LEND -> see https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20#revert-on-zero-value-transfers) revert when a transfer with amount 0 is initiated. This can happen within claim when the withdrawRatio is 100%. In such a scenario, the funds are not claimable, leading to a loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claim function of the LiquidationAccountant contract, where the routine may attempt to execute an ERC20 token transfer with an amount of zero. This situation arises when the withdrawRatio parameter reaches 100%, causing the calculated payout to be exactly zero. Certain ERC20 implementations, such as the LEND token, explicitly reject zero‑value transfers by reverting the transaction. Consequently, when claim triggers a zero‑amount transfer, the whole call reverts, preventing any funds from being transferred to the claimant. From a user perspective, the interface may indicate that a claim was submitted, yet the expected tokens never arrive, or the transaction appears to have failed with a generic revert message. The root cause is a missing guard that checks whether the transfer amount is greater than zero before invoking the token’s transfer method. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case arithmetic in the liquidation accounting logic. It can be hard to notice because zero‑value transfers are uncommon and many token contracts do not enforce a non‑zero check, leading auditors to assume that a transfer of zero is a no‑op. The impact is that users who are entitled to a full liquidation payout (withdrawRatio = 100 %) are unable to claim their funds, effectively locking or losing those assets. The affected parties include any holder of the vulnerable token who interacts with the liquidation module, as well as the protocol that relies on the accountant for correct fund distribution. To remediate the issue, the contract should include a conditional that skips the transfer call when the computed amount is zero, or alternatively enforce a minimum transfer amount of one token unit before proceeding. This class of bug falls under improper handling of edge‑case values in financial calculations, specifically zero‑value token transfers that violate the expected accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: LienToken._payment function increases users
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal _payment function of the LienToken contract, where the line lien.amount = _getOwed(lien) overwrites the stored principal amount with the total amount currently owed, which already includes accrued interest. The root cause is a logical misuse of the _getOwed helper: it returns principal plus interest, but the contract treats lien.amount as the original borrowed principal. By assigning the full owed value back to lien.amount before the payment comparison, the contract inflates the recorded debt each time a partial repayment is made. An attacker or even an honest borrower can trigger the bug simply by calling makePayment with any non‑zero paymentAmount while the lien is still active. The function first updates lien.amount, then checks if lien.amount > paymentAmount to decide whether to reduce the balance or delete the lien. Because lien.amount now contains interest that was already accounted for, the subsequent subtraction either reduces the principal by less than intended or, when the payment covers the inflated amount, causes the lien to be considered fully repaid while the borrower has actually over‑paid. On the next repayment attempt the interest is calculated again on the already‑inflated principal, leading to a compounding of interest on interest. From the user’s point of view the expected behaviour – “I repay 0.5 ETH and my debt drops by 0.5 ETH” – is violated; instead the displayed debt may stay the same or even increase, and the borrower ends up losing funds because extra interest is charged repeatedly. The issue manifests whenever a partial payment is processed (paymentAmount > 0) and the lien has not expired, which covers the normal borrower repayment flow as well as the liquidation path used by the AuctionHouse. Borrowers, lenders, and the overall protocol are affected because the accounting invariants are broken and funds can be unintentionally drained from borrowers. The bug was discovered during a manual audit review of the payment logic, where the auditor noticed that the principal field was being overwritten with a value that already includes accrued interest – a subtle mistake that does not raise an immediate revert but leads to incorrect accounting over time. The problem is hard to spot because the assignment appears to “refresh” the debt amount, a pattern that is common in interest‑bearing contracts, yet the surrounding code assumes lien.amount represents only the principal. To remediate the issue the contract should stop mutating lien.amount with the result of _getOwed. Instead, the function should compute the total owed in a temporary variable, compare it with paymentAmount, and only adjust lien.amount by the principal portion or clear the lien when fully repaid. This preserves the invariant that lien.amount tracks the original borrowed amount and prevents interest from being double‑counted, thereby aligning the contract’s behaviour with the expected repayment semantics and protecting users from inadvertent fund loss.

title: LienToken.createLien doesn't check if user
description: LienToken.createLien doesn't check if user should be liquidated and provides new loan if auction do not exist for collateral. LienToken.createLien relies on AuctionHouse to check if new loan can be added to borrower. It assumes that if auction doesn't exist then user is safe to take new loan. The problem is that to start auction with token that didn't pay the debt someone should call AstariaRouter.liquidate function. If no one did it then auction for the NFT will not exists, and LienToken.createLien will create new Lien to user, while he already didn't pay debt and should be liquidated. New loan will be paid to user that didn't repay previous lien.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan creation routine of the LienToken contract. When a borrower requests a new loan, the function createLien assumes that the absence of an active auction for the borrower’s collateral means the borrower is not subject to liquidation and therefore is eligible for additional credit. In reality, liquidation eligibility is determined by whether any of the borrower’s existing liens are past due, not by the presence of an auction. The protocol relies on the AstariaRouter.liquidate function to start an auction for overdue debt; if no external actor calls this function, the auction never materialises. Consequently, createLien proceeds to mint a new lien and transfers the new loan amount to the borrower even though the borrower has already defaulted on a previous lien. This logical flaw allows a delinquent borrower to obtain fresh funds without first settling the outstanding debt, effectively bypassing the protocol’s liquidation safeguards. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken: collateral that should be seized remains with the borrower, and the total outstanding debt exceeds the value of locked collateral, exposing lenders to loss. The issue manifests whenever a borrower has an overdue lien and no liquidation auction has been triggered – a situation that can arise simply because the liquidation function is permission‑less and may not be called promptly. All participants who rely on the protocol’s guarantee that loans are fully collateralised—lenders, other borrowers, and the protocol itself—are affected. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between LienToken and AuctionHouse and noticed that createLien does not perform an explicit liquidation eligibility check. Because the check is indirect (looking for an auction) rather than explicit, the problem can be subtle and may only surface under specific timing conditions, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enumerate all active liens of the borrower and verify that none are in a liquidatable state before permitting a new lien to be created. This explicit validation removes the reliance on the existence of an auction and restores the intended safety guarantees of the lending protocol.

title: Strategist nonce is not checked
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that the smart contract does not verify the strategist's nonce when a commitment is submitted to the VaultImplementation.commitToLien function. In the AstariaRouter.validateCommitment routine the contract checks that the deadline has not passed, that the strategy type is valid, and that the Merkle proof matches the supplied leaf, but it never inspects the nonce that was included in the off‑chain signature of the strategist. Because the nonce is never incremented – the increaseNonce function is never called – the strategist is forced to reuse the same nonce for every signed commitment. This omission makes it impossible for the strategist to cancel a previously signed commitment, and it allows any user who possesses the signed commitment data to replay it multiple times. In practice a borrower can present the same commitment up to five times, each time borrowing against the vault under the same terms, effectively draining funds that were intended for a single loan. The issue is triggered whenever a strategist creates a commitment off‑chain and relies on the contract to enforce uniqueness through the nonce; the contract’s logic assumes the nonce will change, but it never enforces that assumption. The affected parties include the strategist (who loses the ability to revoke a deal), the vault owner or delegate (who may see unexpected multiple loans), and any users of the protocol whose funds could be depleted. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the off‑chain signing flow with the on‑chain validation code and noticed the missing nonce check. It can be hard to spot because the nonce is an off‑chain construct and the on‑chain code appears to perform all other required checks, giving a false sense of completeness. To remediate the problem the contract should incorporate the strategist’s nonce into the validation logic and provide a mechanism for the strategist to increment the nonce after a commitment is used or cancelled, for example by exposing the increaseNonce function or by directly checking that the nonce in the commitment matches the current stored nonce. By doing so the protocol restores the intended one‑time use property of commitments, prevents replay attacks, and re‑enables the strategist to cancel or replace commitments safely.

title: _validateCommitment fails for approved op-
description: If a collateral token owner approves another user as an operator for all their tokens (rather than just for a given token), the validation check in _validateCommitment() will fail. another user: • Approve them to take actions with a given token (approve()) • Approve them as an "operator" for all your owned tokens (setApprovalForAll()) However, when the _validateCommitment() function checks that the token is owned or approved by msg.sender, it does not accept those who are set as operators. if (msg.sender != holder) { require(msg.sender == operator, "invalid request"); } Approved operators of collateral tokens will be rejected from taking actions with those tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper authorization check in the _validateCommitment function of a protocol that uses ERC‑721 collateral. The function is intended to ensure that the caller is either the token holder or an address that has been granted approval for the specific token via ERC721.approve. However, it does not recognise the ERC721.isApprovedForAll operator mechanism, where a token owner can designate an operator to manage all of their tokens with a single call to setApprovalForAll. The root cause is that the validation logic only compares msg.sender to the token holder and to the per‑token approved address, ignoring the global operator flag. When an operator that has been approved for all tokens attempts to perform an action that triggers _validateCommitment, the check fails and the transaction reverts with the message "invalid request". This can be exploited by any legitimate operator who expects to act on behalf of the token owner; instead of being able to move or lock collateral, the operator is blocked, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service condition for that collateral. The impact is that collateral may become unusable, withdrawals or other protocol actions that rely on operator permissions are impossible, and users may lose access to their funds until the contract is patched or the owner manually revokes the operator and uses a different workflow. The condition occurs only when the token owner has granted operator rights via setApprovalForAll rather than per‑token approval. Affected parties include token owners who rely on delegated management, the approved operators, and the protocol itself because the locked collateral can affect liquidity and risk calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s access‑control flow, where the auditor noticed that the require statement only checks msg.sender against the holder and a single approved address. It is easy to miss because ERC‑721 specifications provide two distinct approval mechanisms, and developers often assume they are interchangeable. From a user’s perspective, an operator attempting to withdraw collateral sees a transaction failure with an "invalid request" error, contrary to the expectation that the operator can act on behalf of the owner. This bug belongs to the class of authorization bypass or missing permission checks, where a legitimate permission (global operator) is not accounted for in the contract logic. To remediate, the validation should be extended to also accept msg.sender when ERC721.isApprovedForAll(holder, msg.sender) returns true, thereby aligning the contract’s permission model with the ERC‑721 standard and preventing legitimate operators from being unintentionally blocked.

title: _makePayment is logically inconsistent with
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency between the payment loop and the lien‑removal routine. `_makePayment` creates a temporary memory copy of the list of open liens and iterates from index 0 up to the original length, calling `_payment` for each position. When a lien is fully repaid, `_payment` invokes `_deleteLienPosition`, which shifts all higher‑indexed liens down one slot and then pops the last element, thereby shortening the storage array. If the payment amount is sufficient to clear more than one lien, the array length is reduced during the iteration but the loop counter continues to increase based on the original length. As a result, on the iteration that references the next index the contract reads a position that no longer exists, triggering a Solidity index out of bounds revert. This occurs whenever a user attempts to settle multiple liens in a single transaction, for example paying 150 units against two liens of 100 and 50. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails; no funds are transferred and the UI may show that the payment was submitted but the balance remains unchanged. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Astaria LienToken contract when the auditor noticed that the loop variable i was not adjusted after the array was compressed. The bug is subtle because the code appears to handle each lien sequentially and the revert only happens for larger payments, making it easy to miss in basic testing that only single‑lien payments succeed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like condition: users cannot clear their debt in one step, must manually pay each lien, and any automated process that assumes batch payment will fail. The affected parties are borrowers who interact with the payment function, as well as any integrators that rely on batch settlement. To remediate, the payment routine should avoid mutating the lien array while iterating. Common fixes include iterating over a copy of the array, iterating backwards, or collecting the indices to delete after the loop and performing the deletions afterwards. Aligning the logic with the proven pattern used in AuctionHouse.sol, which does not modify the array during iteration, will eliminate the out‑of‑bounds condition and restore correct batch payment behavior.

title: timeToEpochEnd calculates backwards,break-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect implementation of the timeToEpochEnd function, which is intended to return the remaining time until the current epoch finishes. The code mistakenly returns zero whenever the epoch has not yet ended because it checks if epochEnd is greater than or equal to the current block timestamp and then returns zero, whereas the correct logic should return the difference epochEnd - block.timestamp when the epoch is still active. As a result, any liquidation that should be settled in the current epoch is mistakenly classified as a future‑epoch liquidation. The liquidate() routine uses the condition timeToEpochEnd() <= auctionWindow to decide whether to route the payout through a liquidation accountant and adjust protocol accounting for a later epoch. Because timeToEpochEnd incorrectly yields zero, the condition is always true, causing the protocol to invoke the liquidation accountant, decrease the epoch lien count, set the payee to the accountant, and increase the expected liquidation count at the epoch boundary. These side‑effects corrupt the accounting model: the epoch may be considered finished earlier than intended, funds that should remain in the vault are redirected to the accountant, and the withdrawal ratio applied to the accountant can lead to unexpected shortfalls or excesses. From a user’s perspective, a borrower or lender expecting an immediate payout after liquidation may see no funds arrive, or the vault balance may appear lower than expected, creating confusion and loss of trust. The issue manifests only when a lien is liquidated during an active epoch, which is the normal operating condition for the protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit by the security team, and its subtle nature makes it hard to notice because the function returns a plausible value (zero) and the downstream accounting errors only surface later in the epoch processing logic. To remediate the problem, the timeToEpochEnd function must be rewritten to return the correct remaining time (epochEnd - block.timestamp) when the epoch is still ongoing and zero only after the epoch has passed, thereby ensuring that the liquidation path and accounting adjustments are applied only for true future‑epoch liquidations. This correction restores the intended business logic that liquidations settle in the current epoch, preserves vault balances, and prevents premature epoch termination and inaccurate liquidation accounting.

title: Underlying With Non-Standard Decimals Not
description: Arithmetic operations are performed with the assumption that the token always has 18 decimals. LiquidationAccountant.claim Arithmetic operations assume the token has 18 decimals. Not all tokens use 18 decimals, such as Tether. • The addition of underlying capital that does not use 18 decimals will not be possible.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑precision assumption bug in the LiquidationAccountant contract. The contract performs arithmetic on the underlying token amount assuming the token uses 18 decimal places, which is the default for most ERC‑20 tokens. The root cause is that the code does not query the token’s decimals() function nor apply scaling based on the actual number of decimals, and instead hard‑codes 10^18 as the unit. When a token with a different decimal count, such as USDT (6 decimals), is used as underlying capital, the addition, subtraction and liquidation calculations produce values that are off by several orders of magnitude. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the bug simply by depositing or claiming liquidation rewards in a non‑standard‑decimal token. The contract will either reject the addition because the computed amount underflows/overflows, or it will record an incorrect amount that appears as zero in the UI. Consequently, users may see their balance unchanged after a deposit, receive a zero refund from a liquidation claim, or experience failed transactions when trying to add capital. The impact is medium severity: funds may become inaccessible, accounting invariants break, and liquidation processes may be inaccurate, potentially leading to under‑collateralisation of positions. The condition occurs whenever the protocol interacts with an ERC‑20 token whose decimals differ from 18, which includes popular stablecoins like USDT, USDC (6 decimals) and others. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected arithmetic expressions and noted the hard‑coded 18‑decimal scaling factor. Because the bug manifests as a silent mis‑calculation rather than an explicit revert, it can be hard to notice unless balances are compared against expected values or the token’s decimals are examined. The bug belongs to the class of “fixed‑precision assumption” or “decimal handling” vulnerabilities, where contracts assume a uniform token precision. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the token’s decimals at deployment or via an interface call and apply a dynamic scaling factor, or refactor the accounting logic to use a universal base unit (e.g., using a library that normalises amounts to a common precision). This change would allow the addition of capital for tokens with any decimal configuration and ensure that liquidation claims and balance updates reflect the true token amount.

title: Outstanding debt is not guaranteed to be cov-
description: The best-effort one-time English auction for borrower collateral is not economically efficient to drive auction bids towards reaching the total outstanding debt, which leads to loss of LP funds. When any lien against a borrower collateral is not paid within the lien duration, the underlying collateral is put up for auction where bids can come in at any price. The borrower is allowed to cancel the auction if the current bid is lower than the reserve price which is set to the total outstanding debt. The reserve price is not enforced anywhere else. If there are no bids, the liquidator will receive the collateral. This auction design of a best-effort one-time English auction is not economically efficient to drive auction bids towards reaching the total outstanding debt which effectively leads to loss of LP funds on unpaid liens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the one‑time English auction used to liquidate borrower collateral does not enforce the reserve price equal to the total outstanding debt. The auction allows any bid price, and the borrower can cancel the auction whenever the current highest bid is below the reserve. Because the reserve price is only a reference for the borrower’s cancellation right and is not enforced as a minimum sale price, the auction may close with no bids or with a bid lower than the debt. In that case the liquidator receives the collateral for less than the amount owed, and the shortfall is absorbed by the liquidity providers (LPs) that funded the loan. The root cause is a design flaw in the auction logic: the contract checks only the borrower’s cancellation condition and never validates that the final sale price covers the debt. An attacker (or any participant) can simply refrain from bidding, or submit a low bid, knowing the borrower can abort the auction and the protocol will still transfer the collateral to the liquidator at the low price. The impact is a loss of capital for LPs, potentially reducing the protocol’s solvency and eroding trust. The condition occurs whenever a lien expires and the collateral is put up for auction; it is triggered by the lack of a mandatory reserve‑price enforcement. All parties that rely on the auction to recover the debt—LPs, borrowers, and the protocol—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation module, where the auditor observed that the reserve price is only used for a cancellation check and not as a hard floor. Because the auction still proceeds even when no bids meet the reserve, the problem may be subtle and not evident from normal operation unless a liquidation event occurs with low participation. To remediate, the auction should be redesigned so that the sale price cannot be lower than the outstanding debt, for example by using a Dutch auction that starts at the reserve price and only decreases, or by adding a mandatory check that rejects any final bid below the debt and forces a re‑auction or alternative liquidation path. This class of bug is an economic‑logic flaw where the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that collateral sale will fully cover the debt) are violated, leading to “funds disappear” symptoms: LPs see their balances reduced after a liquidation, borrowers may see their collateral taken without covering the loan, and users may notice that the protocol’s total assets shrink unexpectedly.

title: Extension logic incorrectly extends the auc-
description: Incorrect auction extension logic extends the auction by an additional amount of the previous duration instead of extending it by 15 minutes. The calculation of newDuration incorrectly adds duration in the auction extension logic. This causes the new duration to be extended by an additional amount of the existing duration, instead of an additional 15 minutes (timeBuffer), when a bid is created in the last 15 mins of the existing auction duration. Delayed payout of funds/collateral upon auction completion only after the newly extended duration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect auction extension calculation that causes the auction to be prolonged by an amount equal to the current remaining duration instead of the intended fixed time buffer (typically fifteen minutes). The root cause is a faulty arithmetic expression in the extension logic that adds the existing duration to the new deadline rather than adding a constant timeBuffer. When a participant places a bid within the last fifteen minutes of the current auction window, the contract computes a newDuration using the previous duration value, effectively doubling or otherwise inflating the remaining time. This miscalculation can be exploited by submitting a last‑minute bid, which triggers an unintended large extension, keeping the auction open far longer than users expect. The impact includes delayed payout of the winning bid and any associated collateral, as the contract will not settle until the erroneously extended period expires. The condition occurs only when a bid is placed in the final timeBuffer window; otherwise the auction proceeds normally. All participants in the auction—bidders, sellers, and any protocol that relies on timely settlement—are affected because funds remain locked and the market price may become stale. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the time‑based extension code and compared the intended business rule (add fifteen minutes) with the actual implementation (add the remaining duration). It is subtle because the contract still extends the auction, so the behavior appears functional, but the extension length is much larger than documented, making it hard to notice without precise timing tests. The bug belongs to the class of time‑buffer miscalculation or arithmetic logic errors that violate the protocol’s accounting assumptions about auction length and settlement timing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an unexpectedly long countdown, the auction may appear to never finish, and the expected refund or payout may be missing after the original end time. To remediate, the calculation should be changed to add the constant timeBuffer to the current block timestamp (or to the first bid timestamp) and then safely cast the result, ensuring the new deadline is exactly fifteen minutes beyond the current time rather than an additional copy of the existing duration. This correction restores the intended auction lifecycle, guarantees timely payouts, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented specifications.

title: AstariaRouter.commitToLiens will revert if the
description: The function commitToLiens() will revert in getProtocolFee(), which prevents borrowers from depositing collateral and requesting loans in the protocol. If the protocol fee is enabled by setting feeTo to a non-zero address, then getProtocolFee() will revert because of division-by-zero given that protocolFeeDenominator is 0 without any initialization and no setter (in file()) for setting it. The function commitToLiens() will revert if the protocol fee is enabled thus preventing borrowers from depositing collateral and requesting loans in the protocol thereby failing to bootstrap its core NFT lending functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AstariaRouter contract where the function commitToLiens triggers a revert when the protocol fee mechanism is activated. The root cause is an uninitialized protocol fee denominator; the contract stores a numerator and a denominator for the fee but never sets the denominator and provides no setter function to modify it. When the feeTo address is set to a non‑zero value, indicating that the protocol fee is enabled, the internal helper getProtocolFee attempts to calculate the fee by dividing the numerator by the denominator. Because the denominator is still zero, a division‑by‑zero exception is thrown, causing the entire commitToLiens transaction to revert. An attacker does not need to perform any special actions – simply enabling the fee (or the protocol owner enabling it) is sufficient to make the contract unusable for borrowers. The impact is that any user trying to deposit collateral or request a loan will see their transaction fail, often manifested in the UI as a generic “transaction reverted” or “loan request failed” message with no funds transferred. This condition occurs whenever feeTo is non‑zero, which is a legitimate configuration path for the protocol, so the bug blocks the core NFT lending functionality under normal operating conditions. The affected parties are borrowers, lenders, and any participants relying on the router to manage liens, effectively halting the protocol’s primary revenue stream. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation path and noticed that the denominator variable had no initialization or setter in the file() configuration. Because the revert only happens after the fee is enabled, it can be easy to miss in basic unit tests that keep feeTo at the default zero address. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialized state variable errors that lead to arithmetic exceptions, specifically division‑by‑zero bugs in fee or interest calculations. From a user perspective the expectation is that after approving a loan request the contract will lock collateral and issue a loan; instead the transaction reverts, the UI shows no change in balances, and the user receives no loan or receipt of collateral. To remediate the issue the protocol should initialize both the fee numerator and denominator to sensible non‑zero defaults and expose setter functions through the file() interface so that the parameters can be updated safely. Proper validation should also be added to prevent setting the denominator to zero in the future, thereby restoring the ability of borrowers to deposit collateral and obtain loans as intended.

title: LienToken.createLien may prevent liens that
description: The potentialDebt calculation in createLien is incorrect. The calculated potentialDebt is effectively (impliedRate + totalDebt) * params.terms.duration because getImpliedRate() returns impliedRate = impliedRate.mulDivDown(1, totalDebt);. The calculated potentialDebt because of multiplying totalDebt by duration is significantly higher than it actually is and so will fail the params.terms.maxPotentialDebt check and revert. This will cause DoS on valid lien creation.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the lien creation routine where the contract computes a value called potentialDebt to enforce a maximum‑debt limit. The function that derives the implied interest rate mistakenly divides the rate by the current totalDebt, which inflates the impliedRate value. When the contract later multiplies this inflated rate by the totalDebt and by the loan duration, the resulting potentialDebt becomes far larger than the true amount owed. Because the contract checks potentialDebt against a configurable maxPotentialDebt threshold, the over‑estimated figure triggers a revert even for otherwise valid lien parameters. This mis‑calculation therefore blocks legitimate users from creating liens, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. The bug appears only during the execution of the createLien function when totalDebt is non‑zero and the loan term is greater than zero, and it is discovered through static analysis and logical review of the financial formulas. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with an error indicating that the maximum potential debt was exceeded, the UI may show no lien created or a zero balance, and the user receives no confirmation that the lien was recorded. The issue is hard to notice because the arithmetic looks plausible and the revert message can be mistaken for other validation failures. Conceptually the problem is an arithmetic logic error in a financial formula that leads to an over‑estimation of debt and a subsequent denial‑of‑service. The correct fix is to remove the division of the implied rate by totalDebt and to compute potentialDebt using the standard formula: totalDebt multiplied by (1 plus impliedRate times duration divided by the interest denominator). This restores the intended accounting behavior, ensures that only truly excessive debt is rejected, and prevents the protocol from unintentionally blocking legitimate lien creation.

title: Incorrect LienToken.changeInSlope calculation
description: The calculation of newSlope in changeInSlope() is incorrect which can lead to vault insolvency. Contrary to the changeInSlope function, the calculateSlope function uses the _getOwed function to calculate the owed amount (incl. the interest). The interest is calculated with the _getInterest function. This function takes care of the lien.last and also if a lien is expired already. This logic is completely missing in the changeInSlope for the newSlope calculation which makes it incorrect. Also, very importantly, in the changeInSlope function, the INTEREST_DENOMINATOR is missing which makes the value inflated causing an underflow error in the last line of changeInSlope function: slope = oldSlope - newSlope;. oldslope, which accounts for the INTEREST_DENOMINATOR, is less than newSlope. The incorrect changeInSlope() calculation can lead to reverts and vault insolvency because users cannot determine the implicit value of vaults while interacting with it as borrowers or lenders.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that updates the interest slope of a lien, specifically the changeInSlope routine. Instead of using the same interest accounting logic as the calculateSlope helper, changeInSlope builds the new slope value without calling the internal _getOwed or _getInterest helpers and omits the INTEREST_DENOMINATOR scaling factor. As a result the newSlope is dramatically inflated. When the contract later computes the adjusted slope as oldSlope‑newSlope, the inflated newSlope can exceed oldSlope, causing an unsigned integer underflow and a revert. This arithmetic error can leave a vault without a valid slope, making the vault appear insolvent and preventing borrowers or lenders from correctly estimating the value of their positions. The flaw manifests whenever a lien is modified, especially when a lien has accrued interest or has already expired, because the missing interest calculation fails to account for the time‑dependent component of the debt. Users of the protocol – lenders providing capital and borrowers taking loans – are affected because their transactions may unexpectedly revert, balances may appear to disappear, and the vault may become unable to honor withdrawals or repayments. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the two slope‑calculation paths and noticed the discrepancy in the handling of interest and denominator scaling. Because the slope values are internal bookkeeping figures, the problem does not surface as an obvious UI bug; it only appears as a silent revert or a vault that reports zero available liquidity, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of the arithmetic. To remediate the issue the contract should extract the interest‑adjusted slope computation into a shared helper that incorporates _getOwed, _getInterest and the INTEREST_DENOMINATOR, and then reuse that helper in both calculateSlope and changeInSlope. This ensures that the newSlope is calculated consistently, prevents underflow, and restores correct accounting for vault solvency.

title: Auctions run for less time than intended
description: Auctions run for less time than intended causing them to be not economically efficient for the lenders, thus causing a suboptimal credit of liquidation funds to them. The time of the first bid and duration is supposed to be the length of time to run the auction for, after the first bid was made. However, when an auction is created in createAuction(), the auction's firstBidTime is incorrectly initialized as block.timestamp.safeCastTo64() instead of 0. This is premature initialization because the auction was only created here and no bid has been made yet via createBid(). The code in createBid() which check for firstBidTime == 0 is more evidence that the initialization in createAuction() is incorrect. This causes auctions to run for less time than intended if the first bid comes at a much later time after the auction was created. A shorter auction time could potentially allow fewer bids and cause it to be not economically efficient for the lenders, thus causing a suboptimal credit of liquidation funds to them.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑based logic error in the auction module of the protocol. When an auction is created, the contract stores the timestamp of the first bid in a variable called firstBidTime. The implementation incorrectly initializes this variable with the current block timestamp at the moment the auction is created, instead of leaving it at the sentinel value zero. The surrounding code, especially the createBid function, treats a zero value as an indicator that no bid has been placed yet and only sets firstBidTime to the block timestamp when the first bid arrives. Because the timestamp is already populated, the contract believes a bid has already occurred and therefore calculates the remaining auction duration based on the elapsed time since creation rather than since the first actual bid. If the first real bid is submitted long after the auction was created, the remaining time is reduced by that delay, causing the auction to close earlier than the intended duration. This premature termination can limit the number of participants, reduce competition, and ultimately lower the liquidation proceeds that lenders expect to receive, leading to sub‑optimal credit of liquidation funds. The issue manifests whenever an auction is created and the first bid does not happen immediately; it affects lenders, borrowers and any user relying on the auction to liquidate collateral. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the initialization in createAuction with the guard condition in createBid (firstBidTime == 0). The bug is subtle because the auction still functions and may appear to work correctly on the surface; only the shortened time window reveals the economic inefficiency, which can be hard to notice without inspecting timestamps. The proper remediation is to initialize firstBidTime to zero when the auction is created and only assign the current block timestamp when the first bid is recorded, thereby ensuring the auction runs for the full configured duration after the first bid. This class of bug belongs to premature sentinel initialization or incorrect time‑window calculation, where a contract uses a non‑zero default value that conflicts with later logic, breaking expected business rules such as “auction runs for X seconds after the first bid”.
