From a user perspective the symptom is an auction that ends unexpectedly early, showing fewer bids than anticipated and possibly returning lower liquidation proceeds; a user expecting a full‑length auction may see the auction close with no further bids and wonder why the refund or payout is smaller than expected.

title: Minting public vault shares while the proto-
description: Assets can be deposited into public vaults by LPs with PublicVault.mint function to bypass a possible paused protocol. The PublicVault contract prevents calls to the PublicVault.deposit function while the protocol is paused by using the whenNotPaused modifier. The PublicVault contract extends the ERC4626Cloned contract, which has two functions to deposit assets into the vault: the deposit function and the mint function. The latter function, however, is not overwritten in the PublicVault contract and therefore lacks the appropriate whenNotPaused modifier. LPs can deposit assets into public vaults with the PublicVault.mint function to bypass a possible paused protocol. This can lead to LP fund loss depending on the
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the public vault contract that allows liquidity providers (LPs) to mint new vault shares while the overall protocol is in a paused state. The root cause is that the PublicVault contract inherits the ERC4626Cloned implementation, which defines both a deposit() function and a mint() function for adding assets to the vault. The PublicVault contract correctly overrides deposit() and applies the whenNotPaused modifier, preventing deposits when the protocol is paused. However, the mint() function is not overridden, so it inherits the base implementation without the pause check. An attacker or any LP can therefore call PublicVault.mint() to supply assets and receive vault shares even though the protocol’s pause flag is active. Exploitation consists of invoking the mint() entry point while the protocol is paused; the transaction succeeds, assets are transferred to the vault, and shares are minted, bypassing the intended safety mechanism. The impact is that funds may be locked in an unexpected state, accounting may become inconsistent, and LPs could suffer loss if the protocol later reverts or penalises actions performed during the pause. This condition occurs only when the protocol’s global pause is engaged; normal operation (unpaused) does not expose the issue because both deposit and mint work as intended. The affected parties are liquidity providers who rely on the pause mechanism to protect their capital, as well as the protocol itself, which may face accounting mismatches or reputational damage. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the inheritance hierarchy and noticed that the mint() function lacked the pause guard. It can be hard to notice because the mint() function is not directly referenced in the PublicVault source file, and developers may assume that all entry points inherit the same modifiers as deposit(). To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly override the mint() function in PublicVault and attach the whenNotPaused modifier, ensuring that both deposit and mint are blocked while the protocol is paused. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “missing access control on inherited functions” bugs, where a child contract fails to propagate security checks to all inherited external functions. From a user’s perspective, an LP may expect that no new shares can be created while the protocol is paused, but instead sees a successful mint transaction and later discovers that their funds are either inaccessible or have been accounted for incorrectly, violating the expectation of a safe pause state.

title: _payment() function transfers full payment
description: The _payment() function sends the full paymentAmount argument to the lien owner, which both (a) overpays lien owners if borrowers accidentally overpay and (b) sends the first lien owner all the funds for the entire loop of a borrower is intending to pay back multiple loans. There are two makePayment() functions in LienToken.sol. One that allows the user to specify a position (which specific lien they want to pay back, and another that iterates through their liens, paying each back. In both cases, the functions call out to _payment() with a paymentAmount, which is sent (in full) to the lien owner. TRANSFER_PROXY.tokenTransferFrom(WETH, payer, payee, paymentAmount); This behavior can cause problems in both cases. The first case is less severe: If the user is intending to pay off one lien, and they enter a paymentAmount greater than the amount owed, the function will send the full paymentAmount to the lien owner, rather than just sending the amount owed. The second case is much more severe: If the user is intending to pay towards all their loans, the _makePayment() function loops through open liens and performs the following: uint256 paymentAmount = totalCapitalAvailable; for (uint256 i = 0; i < openLiens.length; ++i) { uint256 capitalSpent = _payment( collateralId, uint8(i), paymentAmount, address(msg.sender) ); paymentAmount -= capitalSpent; } The _payment() function is called with the first lien with paymentAmount set to the full amount sent to the function. The result is that this full amount is sent to the first lien holder, which could greatly exceed the amount they are owed. A user who is intending to pay off all their loans will end up paying all the funds they offered, but only paying off their first lien, potentially losing a large amount of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal _payment() routine of the LienToken contract, which forwards the entire paymentAmount argument to the lien holder without checking whether the amount exceeds the outstanding balance of the specific lien. Because the function does not cap the transferred value to the lien's owed amount, two problematic scenarios arise. First, when a borrower calls the single‑lien makePayment() and mistakenly supplies a paymentAmount larger than the debt, the contract still transfers the full amount, effectively overpaying the lien owner and leaving the borrower with a reduced balance that does not correspond to any debt. Second, and more severe, occurs during the batch payment path where makePayment() iterates over all open liens. The loop initializes paymentAmount with the total capital the borrower wishes to spend and passes this unchanged value to _payment() for the first lien. Since _payment() sends the whole amount, the first lien receives far more than it is owed, and the subsequent iteration subtracts only the amount actually spent (which may be the full paymentAmount) from the remaining pool, causing the loop to terminate without paying the other liens. As a result, a borrower attempting to settle multiple loans may lose a large portion of their funds, seeing only the first lien marked as paid while the rest remain outstanding. The issue is rooted in missing validation of the payment against the lien’s balance and in the loop’s reliance on the returned capitalSpent value, which becomes inaccurate when the transfer overpays. Exploitation is straightforward: a user can trigger the overpayment either unintentionally by entering a higher amount than required, or deliberately by using the batch function to drain funds into the first lien holder. The impact includes loss of borrower funds, incorrect accounting of lien states, and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees. The bug manifests when the contract processes payments, especially when the borrower’s supplied amount exceeds any individual lien’s debt or when multiple liens are paid in a single transaction. It affects borrowers who expect their payment to be allocated proportionally across all debts, and it undermines trust in the protocol’s payment logic. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the payment flow and noticed that the transfer proxy was called with the raw paymentAmount without any ceiling check. Because the transaction does not revert and the transfer succeeds, the overpayment can go unnoticed unless the borrower inspects the resulting lien balances, making the problem subtle. To remediate, the _payment() function should compute the actual amount to transfer as the minimum of the lien’s outstanding amount and the supplied paymentAmount, transfer only that capped value, and return the exact amount moved so that the calling loop can correctly adjust the remaining capital. This change restores the intended invariant that a payment never exceeds the debt of the targeted lien and that batch payments distribute funds across liens according to their outstanding balances.

title: abi.encodePacked Allows Hash Collision
description: From the solidity documentation: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.17/abi-spec.html?highlight=collisions#non-standard-packed-mode If you use keccak256(abi.encodePacked(a,b)) and both a and b are dynamic types, it is easy to craft collisions in the hash value by moving parts of a into b and vice-versa. More specifically, abi.encodePacked("a","bc")==abi.encodePacked("ab","c"). This issue exists in the Factory contract can results in hash collisions, bypassing the signedOnly modifier. port/blob/main/evm-minting-master/contracts/Factory.sol#L171 https://github.com-g-master/contracts/Factory.sol#L222 As the solidity docs describe, two or more dynamic types are passed to abi.encodePacked. Moreover, these dynamic values are user-specified function arguments in external functions, meaning anyone can directly specify the value of these arguments when calling the function. The signedOnly modifier is supposed to protect functions to permit only function arguments that have been properly signed to be passed to the function logic, but because a collision can be created, the modifier can be bypassed for certain select inputs that result in the same encodePacked value. The signedOnly modifier (line 537) is not effective because the modifier can be bypassed by different function arguments that result in the same signature when the values are encodePacked together. This can result in the submission of values that were not actually signed.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of keccak256(abi.encodePacked(a,b)) where both a and b are dynamic types supplied by external callers. abi.encodePacked concatenates the raw byte representations of its arguments without inserting length information or delimiters, which makes the resulting byte array ambiguous. Because of this ambiguity an attacker can craft two distinct pairs of inputs that produce exactly the same concatenated byte sequence, for example the strings "a" and "bc" produce the same packed encoding as "ab" and "c". When the contract later verifies a signature against the keccak256 hash of the packed data, the signedOnly modifier assumes that the hash uniquely represents the original arguments. The hash collision breaks this assumption, allowing the attacker to present a forged set of arguments that hash to the same value as a legitimately signed set. Consequently the signature check passes even though the supplied arguments were never signed. This can be exploited to bypass access controls, submit unauthorized minting requests, or otherwise trigger privileged logic without a valid signature. The impact is that the protocol may accept transactions that were not authorized by the intended signer, potentially leading to unauthorized token creation, loss of trust, and financial loss for users. The issue manifests whenever a public or external function hashes multiple dynamic arguments with abi.encodePacked and then validates a signature on that hash, as is the case in the Factory contract’s signedOnly modifier. All callers, including legitimate users and potential attackers, are affected because the contract’s security guarantee is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Solidity documentation on encodePacked collisions with the contract’s implementation. It is difficult to notice because the hash function itself appears deterministic and the collision requires only a specific arrangement of input values, which is not obvious from a superficial code review. To remediate the issue the contract should avoid hashing concatenated dynamic arguments directly; instead it should either use abi.encode (which includes length prefixes), employ EIP‑712 typed data signing, or move the hashing off‑chain and pass the pre‑computed hash as a single argument, thereby eliminating the ambiguity that enables collisions. In user‑facing terms, a user may expect that providing an unsigned payload will be rejected, but the contract may accept it, resulting in unexpected token minting or state changes that appear as “funds appear out of nowhere” or “my balance changes without my action”.

title: Missing check for equal length arrays in transferByOwnerBatch and mintByOwnerBatch
description: The transferByOwnerBatch() and mintByOwnerBatch() functions in the ERC1155 implementation does not check whether the lengths of the arrays submitted are equal. This can lead to unexpected results. In the transferByOwnerBatch() function, the user submits three arrays (addresses, ids, and amounts), while in the mintByOwnerBatch() function, the user submits four arrays (addresses, ids, amounts, uris). The expectation is that the user submitting the function will ensure that the indexes of the arrays correspond to the correct values in the other arrays, and thus that the lengths will be the same. Common practice in such a situation is to verify that the lengths are equal to ensure the user hasn't made an error. In other functions like burnBatch(), this verification is done by the underlying ERC1155 function. However, in these two functions, we simply iterate through the ids array without performing this check, and then call out to the underlying ERC1155 _safeTransferFrom() or _mint() functions for each id separately. If the ids array is a shorter length than the other arrays, the additional values in the other arrays will be ignored. This could lead to transfers with unexpected results, which would be better served by reverting.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of input array lengths in two batch operations of an ERC1155 token contract: transferByOwnerBatch and mintByOwnerBatch. Both functions accept multiple parallel arrays that are expected to have a one‑to‑one correspondence – for each index the address, token id, amount (and optionally a URI) should describe a single transfer or mint action. The root cause is that the implementation iterates only over the ids array and calls the underlying ERC1155 _safeTransferFrom or _mint for each id without first checking that the other arrays (to, amounts, uris) are the same length. When a caller supplies arrays of different lengths, the extra entries in the longer arrays are silently ignored because the loop never reaches those indices. This can be exploited by an attacker or a careless user who deliberately or unintentionally provides mismatched arrays, causing some intended transfers or mints to be omitted. The impact is that tokens may not be sent to the intended recipients, amounts may be lower than expected, or minted NFTs may receive incorrect metadata. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a batch operation was submitted for, say, five recipients, but only three addresses actually receive tokens, or some NFTs appear with a missing or wrong URI, leading to confusion such as “my balance is zero” or “the refund amount is wrong”. The bug occurs whenever the batch functions are called with arrays whose lengths differ – a condition that is not enforced by the contract and therefore may go unnoticed during normal operation because the transaction does not revert; it simply drops the mismatched entries. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the batch functions with other ERC1155 batch utilities like burnBatch, which correctly enforce length equality. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error, and the silent omission can be mistaken for a network or UI glitch. Conceptually, the fix is to add explicit checks that all supplied arrays have identical length before entering the loop, causing the transaction to revert with a clear error message if the lengths mismatch. This restores the intended invariant that each index represents a complete and correct transfer or mint instruction, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unexpected token loss or misallocation.

title: Factory.sol : Issue with arbitrary data as signature input
description: In Factory contract, deploy and call methods are using the signature based approach for deployment. This is not safe when we look at the way the signature is comes from user. contracts/Factory.sol#L147-L225 In above line of codes, user is allowed for deployment by using the signature data. This could have multiple impacts as explained in Impact section. 1. Signature replay attack. 2. Signature reuse across different NFT Port projects if it is to be launched in multiple chains. Because the chain ID is not included in the data, all signatures are also valid when the project is launched on a chain with another chain ID. For instance, let’s say it is also launched on Polygon. An attacker can now use all of the Ethereum signatures there. Because the Polygon addresses of user’s (and potentially contracts, when the nonces for creating are the same) are often identical, there can be situations where the payload is meaningful on both chains. 3. Signature without domain , nonces are not safe along with the standard specified in EIP 712. 4. Signature reuse from different Ethereum projects & phishing Because the signature is very generic, there might be situations where a user has already signed data with the same format for a completely different Ethereum application. Furthermore, an attacker could set up a DApp that uses the same format and trick someone into signing the data. Even a very security-conscious owner that has audited the contract of this DApp (that does not have any vulnerabilities and is not malicious, it simply consumes signatures that happen to have the same format) might be willing to sign data for this DApp, as he does not anticipate that this puts his NFT Port project in danger.
bug_full: An issue exists in the Factory contract where the deploy and call functions accept a user‑provided signature that is verified against a custom, loosely defined data structure instead of the standardized EIP‑712 domain‑separated format. Because the signature payload does not contain a domain separator, chain identifier, or a unique nonce tied to the specific NFT Port project, the same signed message can be replayed on any chain that supports the same contract address and can be reused for different projects that happen to use the identical data layout. An attacker who obtains a legitimate signature from a user—either by tricking the user into signing a generic message on a harmless DApp or by observing a signature used on another chain—can submit the signature to the Factory contract on a different chain or for a different NFT Port deployment. The contract will accept the signature as valid and will execute the deployment or call on behalf of the attacker, effectively allowing unauthorized contract creation, potential theft of funds, or injection of malicious logic into the NFT ecosystem. This problem manifests when a user signs a message that appears to be harmless, expecting the signature to be bound only to the original project, but the contract treats it as a universal authorization token. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the signature verification logic against best‑practice standards such as EIP‑712. It is difficult to notice because the signature verification succeeds and no explicit error is raised; the contract simply proceeds with the deployment, making the misuse invisible to the user until an unexpected contract appears or assets are moved without consent. The impact includes signature replay attacks across chains, cross‑project signature reuse, phishing‑style attacks where users are deceived into signing generic data, and loss of control over NFT Port projects. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may be an unexpected contract being deployed under their address, NFTs appearing that they did not create, or funds being transferred without a clear on‑chain indication of why. The root cause is the absence of a domain separator and chain‑specific data in the signed message, which violates the principle that signatures must be bound to a unique execution context. The recommended remediation is to replace the custom scheme with the battle‑tested EIP‑712 standard, ensuring that the domain separator includes the contract address and chain ID, that a type hash uniquely identifies the function being called, and that a per‑deployment nonce prevents replay. By doing so the signature becomes non‑transferable across chains or projects, eliminating the described replay and phishing vectors.

title: The supply of NFT for each tokenID in ERC1155NFTProduct cannot be modified after first mint
description: The supply of NFT for each tokenID in ERC1155NFTProduct cannot be modified after the first minting. When minting NFT in the ERC1155NFTProduct contract, it will check whether the tokenID already exists, that is, as long as tokenSupply[tokenId] > 0, the ERC1155 NFT of this tokenId will not be able to be minted again. This will lead to 1. The supply of NFT for each tokenID is determined after the first mint 2. Unable to mint ERC1155 NFT with the same tokenId for different users This will greatly limit the application scenarios of ERC1155NFTProduct 1. The supply of NFT for each tokenID is determined after the first mint 2. Unable to mint ERC1155 NFT with the same tokenId for different users
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical restriction in the ERC1155NFTProduct contract that makes the total supply of a given token identifier immutable after the first successful mint. The contract records the amount minted for each tokenId in a mapping called tokenSupply and, during subsequent mint calls, checks whether tokenSupply[tokenId] is greater than zero. If the check returns true, the mint function aborts, preventing any additional tokens with the same identifier from being created. This behavior originates from an existence guard that was likely intended to avoid duplicate token creation but inadvertently blocks legitimate supply adjustments. An attacker or honest user can exploit this by attempting to mint additional copies of an existing tokenId; the transaction will revert, leaving the caller without the expected NFT and potentially wasting gas. The impact is that the ERC1155 token, which is designed to support multiple interchangeable copies of the same token type, becomes effectively non‑fungible after the first mint. Users who expect to receive additional copies, marketplaces that rely on batch minting, or any application that needs to increase supply for a tokenId will be unable to do so. The issue manifests whenever a second mint is attempted for any tokenId that already has a non‑zero supply, regardless of the caller’s role. All participants—token creators, buyers, and downstream protocols—are affected because the contract’s business logic no longer matches the ERC1155 specification. The problem was identified during a formal security audit when the auditor observed that the existence check prevented further minting and noted the discrepancy with expected ERC1155 behavior. Because the contract simply reverts without a clear error message, the bug can be hard to notice; users may only see a failed transaction or a missing balance, assuming a temporary network issue rather than a design flaw. To remediate, the existence guard should be removed or replaced with a proper supply management mechanism that allows the tokenSupply value to be increased after the initial mint, such as by checking against a maximum cap instead of a non‑zero flag. This change restores the intended ERC1155 semantics, enabling multiple users to hold the same tokenId and allowing the protocol to support a broader range of use cases.

title: Attackers can bypass tokensPerMint and mint unlimited tokens
description: Attackers can bypass tokensPerMint, allowing them to mint over tokensPerMint per transaction. NFTCollection has tokensPerMint that enforces the maximum number of tokens the user can mint per transaction. But attackers can bypass tokensPerMint by reentrancy attack to call mint() or presaleMint() multiple times in a transaction. For example, we assume that tokensPerMint is 5 and we have a large amount of availableSupply(): 1. Alice (attacker) first creates an AttackerContract to call mint(5), then L318 will check that amount<=_deploymentConfig.tokensPerMint and call _safeMint() on L321. 2. But _safeMint() has a callback that it will call onERC721Received() if to address is a contract. 3. Now _safeMint() calls onERC721Received() on the AttackerContract, and the AttackerContract re-enter mint(5) again. mint() function will pass the check of tokensPerMint on L318 again. Finally, Alice will mint 5+5 tokens in a transaction. Attackers can re-enter mint() function again and again to bypass the check of tokensPerMint, and mint lots of tokens in a transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that allows an attacker to bypass the per‑transaction minting limit enforced by the tokensPerMint parameter of an ERC‑721 collection. The contract checks that the requested amount does not exceed tokensPerMint before calling the internal _safeMint function. However, _safeMint triggers an external call to onERC721Received on the recipient address when the recipient is a contract. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that implements onERC721Received and, during this callback, re‑enter the public mint (or presaleMint) function. Because the tokensPerMint check is performed again inside the re‑entered call, the attacker can repeat the minting logic multiple times within a single transaction, effectively minting 5 + 5 tokens (or any multiple) despite the limit being set to 5. This re‑entrancy can be repeated arbitrarily until the available supply is exhausted, leading to unlimited token creation in one transaction. The impact is that the protocol’s scarcity model is broken, revenue from sales can be drained, and legitimate users may be unable to acquire tokens because the supply is depleted by the attacker. The issue manifests only when the mint destination is a contract that implements the ERC721Receiver interface, so it may be missed during casual testing that only uses externally owned accounts. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of minting functions and identified that the external callback occurs after the limit check, creating a window for re‑entrancy. The bug is hard to notice because the limit check itself appears correct and the contract uses the standard OpenZeppelin _safeMint implementation, which many developers trust to be safe. To remediate, the mint and presaleMint functions should be protected with a non‑reentrant guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard) or the contract should replace _safeMint with the lower‑level _mint function that does not invoke an external callback, thereby eliminating the re‑entrancy vector. In conceptual terms, the fix moves the state‑changing operation (minting) to occur before any external call or blocks any external call during the critical section, ensuring that the per‑mint limit cannot be circumvented.

title: Template implementations doesn't validate configuration in initialize and update
description: In past audits, we have seen contract admins claim that invalidated configuration setters are fine since “admins are trustworthy”. However, cases such as Nomad got drained for over and Misconfiguration in the Acala stablecoin project allows attacker to steal 1.2 billion aUSD have shown again and again that even trustable entities can make mistakes. Thus any fields that might potentially result in insolvency of protocol should be thoroughly checked. NftPort template implementations often ignore checks for config fields. For the rest of the issue, we take royalty related fields as an example to illustrate potential consequences of misconfigurations. Notably, lack of check is not limited to royalty, but exists among most config fields. Admins are allowed to set a wrong royaltiesBps which is higher than ROYALTIES_BASIS. royaltyInfo() will accept this invalid royaltiesBps and users will pay a large amount of royalty. EIP-2981 (NFT Royalty Standard) defines royaltyInfo() function that specifies how much to pay for a given sale price. In general, royalty should not be higher than 100%. NFTCollection.sol checks that admins can't set royalties to more than 100%: /// Validate a runtime configuration change function _validateRuntimeConfig(RuntimeConfig calldata config) internal view { // Can't set royalties to more than 100% require(config.royaltiesBps <= ROYALTIES_BASIS, "Royalties too high"); ... But NFTCollection only check royaltiesBps when admins call updateConfig(), it doesn't check royaltiesBps in initialize() function, leading to admins could set an invalid royaltiesBps (higher than 100%) when initializing contracts. The same problem exists in ERC721NFTProduct and ERC1155NFTProduct. Both ERC721NFTProduct and ERC1155NFTProduct don't check royaltiesBasisPoints in initialize() function. Furthermore, these contracts also don't check royaltiesBasisPoints when admins call update() function. It means that admins could set an invalid royaltiesBasisPoints which may be higher than 100% in any time. EIP-2981 only defines royaltyInfo() that it should return royalty amount rather than royalty percentage. It means that if the contract has an invalid royalty percentage which is higher than 100%, royaltyInfo() doesn't revert and users will pay a large amount of royalty.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the royalty basis points (royaltiesBps) in the initialization and configuration‑update functions of several NFTPort template contracts, including NFTCollection, ERC721NFTProduct and ERC1155NFTProduct. The contracts are intended to follow the EIP‑2981 royalty standard, which requires that the royalty amount never exceed the total sale price – effectively limiting the royalty percentage to 100 % (the constant ROYALTIES_BASIS). In the current implementation the admin‑only updateConfig() function checks that royaltiesBps is less than or equal to ROYALTIES_BASIS, but the initialize() function does not perform the same check, and some contracts also omit the check in their own update() functions. As a result an admin can set a royaltiesBps value greater than the allowed maximum either at deployment time or later through an unchecked update. The royaltyInfo() function will then calculate a royalty amount that is larger than the sale price because it simply multiplies the sale price by the (invalid) royaltiesBps and divides by ROYALTIES_BASIS without any overflow or sanity check. This leads to users paying an unexpectedly large royalty – in extreme cases the royalty could be equal to or greater than the entire purchase amount, effectively draining the buyer’s funds or making the transaction fail due to insufficient balance. The impact is financial loss for buyers and sellers, potential insolvency of the protocol if royalty payouts exceed available assets, and a breach of the business logic that royalties should never exceed the sale price. The issue manifests whenever an admin configures the contract, either during the initial deployment or through a later configuration change, and it is difficult to notice because the contract does not revert or emit a clear error; the only symptom is that the user receives no NFT or loses more ether than expected, which may be mistaken for a normal fee or a malicious contract. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of runtime configuration parameters and identified the absence of a require statement in initialize() and in some update() paths. To remediate, the contract should enforce the condition royaltiesBps <= ROYALTIES_BASIS in every function that accepts a royalty configuration – both during initialization and any subsequent updates – thereby guaranteeing that royalty calculations remain bounded by 100 % and preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Freezing roles in GranularRoles does not prevent ADMIN_ROLE from modifying roles
description: In ERC721NFTProduct and ERC1155NFTProduct roles can be frozen which is supposed to lock role to current addresses and not allow any changes. The problem is that admin can still use AccessControlUpgradable#grantRole and revokeRole to grant and remove roles to addresses because hasRole allows "ADMIN_ROLE" to bypass all role restrictions even "DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE". function hasRole(bytes32 role, address account) public view virtual override returns (bool) { return super.hasRole(ADMIN_ROLE, account) || super.hasRole(role, account); } In GranularRoles.sol and AccessControlUpgradable.sol, developers are careful to never grant the "DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE" to any user. Additionally they never set the admin role of any role so that it's admin will remain "DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE". In theory this should make so that there is no way to grant or revoke roles outside of GranularRoles#_initRoles and updateRoles. The issue is that the override by GranularRoles#hasRole allows "ADMIN_ROLE" to bypass any role restriction including "DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE". This allows "ADMIN_ROLE" to directly call AccessControlUpgradable#grantRole and revokeRole, which makes the entire freezing system useless as it doesn't actually stop any role modification. Freezing roles doesn't actually prevent "ADMIN_ROLE" from modifying roles as intended. Submitting as high due to gross over-extension of admin authority clearly violating intended guardrails.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a role‑freezing mechanism implemented in the GranularRoles contract that is used by ERC721NFTProduct and ERC1155NFTProduct. The intention of the freeze function is to lock a set of roles to their current addresses so that no further grant or revoke operations can change the access control configuration. In practice the freeze does not achieve this because the contract overrides the standard hasRole function to return true for any address that holds the special ADMIN_ROLE, regardless of the role being checked. This override effectively gives ADMIN_ROLE a universal bypass: super.hasRole(ADMIN_ROLE,account) || super.hasRole(role,account). Consequently, even when a role is marked as frozen, an account possessing ADMIN_ROLE can still call the public grantRole and revokeRole functions inherited from AccessControlUpgradable and modify role assignments at will. The root cause is the combination of an overly permissive hasRole implementation and the lack of any guard in grantRole/revokeRole that respects the frozen flag. An attacker who obtains ADMIN_ROLE – either through a legitimate deployment or by exploiting another flaw – can exploit this by first waiting for the protocol to freeze roles (for example, after a governance decision) and then directly granting themselves privileged roles or revoking roles from legitimate actors. This breaks the intended security model, allowing unauthorized permission changes, potential minting of NFTs, withdrawal of funds, or other privileged actions that should have been disabled. The impact is therefore a loss of the guarantee that role configurations are immutable after a freeze, which can lead to protocol mis‑behaviour, fund loss, or governance compromise. The issue manifests only when the freeze flag is active; otherwise normal role management works as expected. All participants that rely on the frozen state – protocol developers, auditors, token holders, and any users interacting with role‑restricted functions – are affected because the protocol may behave contrary to expectations (e.g., a user expects that after a freeze no new admin can be added, yet the admin can still add themselves). The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the role‑management code where the hasRole override was examined and the absence of any checks in grantRole/revokeRole was noted. It can be hard to notice because the freeze flag appears to be set and no immediate errors are thrown; the contract simply continues to allow role changes through a backdoor that is not obvious from the UI or documentation. To remediate, the contract should either remove the universal ADMIN_ROLE bypass in hasRole or, more robustly, override grantRole and revokeRole in GranularRoles to revert when the target role is frozen, thereby enforcing the immutability guarantee. Alternatively, the protocol could redesign the admin hierarchy so that only a dedicated, immutable role can manage role assignments, and ensure that any freeze operation also disables that admin’s ability to call grantRole/revokeRole. In summary, the bug is a classic privilege‑escalation bypass where a special admin role circumvents a protective state, turning a “freeze roles” feature into a no‑op and violating the business logic that role configurations become permanent after a freeze.

title: _getInterest() function uses block.timestamp
description: The _getInterest() function takes a timestamp as input. However, in a crucial check in the function, it uses block.timestamp instead. The result is that other functions expecting accurate interest amounts will receive incorrect values. The _getInterest() function takes a lien and a timestamp as input. The intention is for it to calculate the amount of time that has passed in the lien (delta_t) and multiply this value by the rate and the amount to get the interest generated by this timestamp. However, the function uses the following check regarding the timestamp: if (block.timestamp >= lien.start + lien.duration) { delta_t = uint256(lien.start + lien.duration - lien.last); } Because this check uses block.timestamp before returning the maximum interest payment, the function will incorrectly determine which path to take, and return an incorrect interest value. There are two negative consequences that can come from this miscalculation: • if the function is called when the lien is over (block.timestamp >= lien.start + lien.duration) to check an interest amount from a timestamp during the lien, it will incorrectly return the maximum interest value • If the function is called when the lien is active for a timestamp long after the lien is over, it will skip the check to return maximum value and return the value that would have been generated if interest kept accruing indefinitely (using delta_t = uint256(timestamp.safeCastTo32() - lien.last);) This _getInterest() function is used in many crucial protocol functions (_getOwed(), calculateSlope(), changeInSlope(), getTotalDebtForCollateralToken()), so these incorrect values can have surprising and unexpected negative impacts on the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the interest‑calculation routine that is supposed to compute accrued interest for a lien based on a caller‑supplied timestamp. The function receives a timestamp argument, derives the elapsed time (delta_t) from the lien’s start and last update, multiplies by the rate and principal, and returns the resulting interest. However, the conditional that decides whether the lien has reached its maximum duration mistakenly compares the current block timestamp (block.timestamp) with the lien’s end time instead of using the supplied timestamp. As a result, when the contract is queried after the lien has expired, the function may take the “maximum‑interest” branch even for timestamps that lie within the original lien period, returning an inflated interest value. Conversely, if the function is called with a timestamp that is far beyond the lien’s expiry, the block‑timestamp check fails and the routine proceeds to calculate interest as if it continued to accrue indefinitely, producing an under‑ or over‑estimated amount depending on the path taken. This mis‑selection propagates to all higher‑level protocol functions that rely on the interest value, such as the calculation of total owed debt, slope adjustments, and overall collateral debt metrics. From a user perspective the bug can manifest as unexpected interest payouts – for example a borrower may see a larger than expected repayment amount, or a lender may receive zero or negative interest despite the passage of time. The impact is that accounting assumptions about bounded interest are broken, potentially leading to over‑payment, under‑payment, or incorrect debt positions, which can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately invokes the affected functions with crafted timestamps to inflate the protocol’s perceived interest and manipulate debt calculations. The flaw occurs whenever the _getInterest() routine is invoked after the lien’s scheduled end, which is a common scenario in liquidation, repayment, or reporting flows. The affected parties include any participants that rely on accurate interest – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s treasury. The issue was uncovered during a systematic security audit performed by the auditor Sherlock, who noted the inconsistency between the function’s documented intent and the actual conditional logic. The bug is subtle because the function still compiles and returns a numeric value; there is no explicit revert or error, making the incorrect result easy to miss during casual testing. The proper remediation is to replace the block.timestamp reference with the timestamp argument in the conditional check, ensuring that the decision about maximum interest is based on the caller‑provided point in time rather than the current block time. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model and restores correct interest calculations across the protocol.

title: Vault Fee uses incorrect offset leading to incorrect values
description: VAULT_FEE() uses an incorrect offset, returning a number ~1e16X greater than intended, providing strategists with unlimited access to drain all vault funds. When using ClonesWithImmutableArgs, offset values are set so that functions representing variables can retrieve the correct values from storage. In the ERC4626-Cloned.sol implementation, VAULT_TYPE() is given an offset of 172. However, the value before it is a uint8 at the offset 164. Since a uint8 takes only 1 byte of space, VAULT_TYPE() should have an offset of 165. I put together a POC to grab the value of VAULT_FEE() in the test setup: function testVaultFeeIncorrectlySet() public { Dummy721 nft = new Dummy721(); address tokenContract = address(nft); uint256 tokenId = uint256(1); address publicVault = _createPublicVault({ strategist: strategistOne, delegate: strategistTwo, epochLength: 14 days }); uint fee = PublicVault(publicVault).VAULT_FEE(); console.log(fee) assert(fee == 5000); // 5000 is the value that was meant to be set } In this case, the value returned is > 3e20. This is a highly critical bug. VAULT_FEE() is used in _handleStrategistInterestReward() to determine the amount of tokens that should be allocated to strategistUnclaimedShares. if (VAULT_FEE() != uint256(0)) { uint256 interestOwing = LIEN_TOKEN().getInterest(lienId); uint256 x = (amount > interestOwing) ? interestOwing : amount; uint256 fee = x.mulDivDown(VAULT_FEE(), 1000); //VAULT_FEE is a basis point strategistUnclaimedShares += convertToShares(fee); } The result is that strategistUnclaimedShares will be billions of times higher than the total interest generated, essentially giving strategist access to withdraw all funds from their vaults at any time.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect storage offset used to read the immutable variable VAULT_FEE in a vault contract that is deployed via the ClonesWithImmutableArgs pattern. In the ERC4626‑Cloned implementation the immutable arguments are laid out sequentially in storage; a preceding uint8 variable occupies only one byte at offset 164, but the offset for VAULT_FEE was mistakenly set to 172 instead of the correct 165. As a result, the read operation fetches data from an unrelated storage slot, producing a value that is roughly 1e16 times larger than the intended basis‑point fee (for example, a value on the order of 3e20 instead of the expected 5000). This inflated fee is then used in the function that calculates the strategist’s reward share. The code multiplies the fee by the amount of interest earned and divides by 1000; because the fee is astronomically high, the computed strategistUnclaimedShares becomes billions of times larger than the actual interest generated. Consequently, a strategist can claim shares that represent the entire vault balance, effectively allowing unlimited withdrawal of funds. The bug manifests only when the contract is instantiated through the cloning mechanism with immutable arguments; any direct deployment that sets the correct offset would not exhibit the problem. Users of the vault, the protocol’s investors, and any party relying on the fee calculation are affected because the economic model is broken and funds can be drained. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the tester logged the return value of VAULT_FEE and observed a number far exceeding the configured basis points. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the offset mismatch does not trigger a revert; the incorrect value silently propagates into reward calculations. To remediate the problem, the immutable argument offset for VAULT_FEE must be corrected to 165 so that the read operation returns the intended fee value. This adjustment restores the correct fee calculation, prevents the strategist from receiving excessive shares, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended accounting logic, ensuring that rewards are proportional to actual interest earned and that vault funds remain secure.

title: Bids cannot be created within timeBuffer of the end of auction
description: The auction mechanism is intended to watch for bids within timeBuffer of the end of the auction, and automatically increase the remaining duration to timeBuffer if such a bid comes in. There is an error in the implementation that causes all bids within timeBuffer of the end of a max duration auction to revert, effectively ending the auction early and cutting off bidders who intended to wait until the end. In the createBid() function in AuctionHouse.sol, the function checks if a bid is if (firstBidTime + duration - block.timestamp < timeBuffer) If so, it sets newDuration to equal the amount that will extend the auction to timeBuffer from now: uint64 newDuration = uint256( duration + (block.timestamp + timeBuffer - firstBidTime) ).safeCastTo64(); If this newDuration doesn't extend beyond the maxDuration, this works great. However, if it does extend beyond maxDuration, the following code is used to update duration: auctions[tokenId].duration = auctions[tokenId].maxDuration - firstBidTime; This code is incorrect. maxDuration will be a duration for the contest (currently set to 3 days), whereas firstTimeBid is a timestamp for the start of the auction (current timestamps are > 1 billion). Subtracting firstTimeBid from maxDuration will underflow, which will revert the function. • Bidders who expected to wait until the end of the auction to vote will be cut off from voting, as the auction will revert their bids. • Vaults whose collateral is up for auction will earn less than they otherwise would have.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow bug in the auction duration extension logic of the AuctionHouse contract. The contract is designed to detect bids that arrive within a configurable timeBuffer before the scheduled end of an auction and automatically extend the remaining auction time so that at least timeBuffer seconds remain after such a bid. The implementation checks whether the remaining time is less than timeBuffer and, if so, computes a new duration that would push the end time forward. When the computed new duration would exceed the predefined maxDuration for the auction, the code attempts to cap the duration by assigning auctions[tokenId].duration = auctions[tokenId].maxDuration - firstBidTime. Here maxDuration is a plain duration value (e.g., three days) while firstBidTime is a Unix timestamp representing when the first bid was placed (a value on the order of billions). Subtracting a large timestamp from a relatively small duration causes an unsigned integer underflow, which triggers a revert. As a result, any bid placed within timeBuffer that would require the auction to be extended beyond maxDuration causes the entire createBid transaction to revert, effectively cutting off late bidders and ending the auction earlier than intended. This bug is triggered only when a bid arrives close to the auction’s scheduled end and the extension would push the end past the maximum allowed length; in all other cases the extension works correctly. The affected parties are bidders who expect to place a last‑minute bid, the vaults whose collateral is being auctioned (they receive less revenue because the auction ends prematurely), and the protocol as a whole because the auction mechanism no longer enforces its intended fairness guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the security team, who noticed that the duration‑capping logic mixed a timestamp with a duration and therefore could underflow. The bug can be hard to notice because the majority of bids do not trigger the maxDuration branch, so normal operation appears correct, and the revert manifests only as a generic transaction failure without an obvious error message. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts when trying to submit a bid near the end of the auction, often accompanied by a UI that suddenly disables further bidding or shows no error detail, leading users to think the auction has simply ended. The underlying class of bug is an unsigned integer underflow caused by mixing units (timestamp vs duration) in arithmetic, a common pattern in smart contracts that rely on time calculations. To fix the issue the duration should be set directly to the maximum allowed value without subtracting the start timestamp, i.e., auctions[tokenId].duration = auctions[tokenId].maxDuration. This change preserves the intended behavior of capping the auction length while avoiding the underflow, ensuring that late bidders can still participate and that the auction’s revenue expectations are met.

title: ERC4626 does not work with fee-on-transfer tokens
description: The ERC4626-Cloned.deposit/mint functions do not work well with fee-on-transfer tokens as the assets variable is the pre-fee amount, including the fee, whereas the totalAssets do not include the fee anymore. This can be abused to mint more shares than desired. C4626-Cloned.sol#L305-L322 function deposit(uint256 assets, address receiver) public virtual override(IVault) returns (uint256 shares) { // Check for rounding error since we round down in previewDeposit. require((shares = previewDeposit(assets)) != 0, "ZERO_SHARES"); // Need to transfer before minting or ERC777s could reenter. ERC20(underlying()).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), assets); _mint(receiver, shares); emit Deposit(msg.sender, receiver, assets, shares); afterDeposit(assets, shares); } C4626-Cloned.sol#L315 ERC20(underlying()).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), assets); A deposit(1000) should result in the same shares as two deposits of deposit(500) but it does not because assets is the pre-fee amount. Assume a fee-on-transfer of 20%. Assume current totalAmount = 1000, totalShares = 1000 for simplicity. deposit(1000) = 1000 / totalAmount * totalShares = 1000 shares. deposit(500) = 500 / totalAmount * totalShares = 500 shares. Now the totalShares increased by 500 but the totalAssets only increased by (100% - 20%) * 500 = 400. Therefore, the second deposit(500) = 500 / (totalAmount + 400) * (newTotalShares) = 500 / (1400) * 1500 = 535.714285714 shares. In total, the two deposits lead to 35 more shares than a single deposit of the sum of the deposits.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns ERC4626 vault implementations that assume the amount transferred to the contract equals the amount specified in the deposit or mint call. In fee‑on‑transfer tokens, a portion of the tokens is deducted by the token contract during the transfer, so the vault receives less than the declared "assets" value. The deposit function records the declared assets when calculating the number of shares to mint, but the vault’s totalAssets accounting only reflects the net amount actually received. This mismatch allows an attacker to deposit a token with a transfer fee, receive shares based on the pre‑fee amount, and thereby obtain more shares than the proportional share of the underlying assets. For example, with a 20 % fee, a single deposit of 1000 tokens yields 1000 shares, while two deposits of 500 tokens each yield 535.71 shares for the second deposit, resulting in 35 extra shares compared with a single 1000‑token deposit. The extra shares dilute existing shareholders and can be exploited to extract value from the vault over time. The issue manifests whenever the underlying token implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism (including ERC777 tokens with hooks) and the vault uses safeTransferFrom without adjusting for the fee. Users see the expected token amount deducted from their wallet, but the vault credits them with more shares than should be possible, violating the accounting invariant that shares represent a fixed proportion of total assets. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the mathematical model of previewDeposit with the actual token balance changes. It is subtle because the UI typically shows the deposited amount and the received shares, which appear correct at a glance, and rounding errors can mask the discrepancy. To remediate, the vault must base the share calculation on the net amount actually received, which can be obtained by measuring the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer, or by overriding previewDeposit for fee‑on‑transfer tokens to predict the post‑fee amount. Any fix must also consider re‑entrancy concerns with ERC777 tokens, ensuring that the transfer occurs before minting shares. In summary, the bug is a fee‑on‑transfer accounting mismatch in ERC4626 vaults that leads to share over‑minting, affecting token holders, protocol liquidity, and overall trust in the vault’s fairness.

title: registerTemplate() can't handle properly when
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the template registration logic in a factory contract that stores implementations keyed by a template name and version. When a caller registers a template with a version number equal to zero, the internal function that updates the registry fails to record the implementation address because the code only updates the latestImplementation mapping when the version is greater than the current stored version. At the same time, the function adds the template name to an array of registered names whenever the stored implementation address is still the zero address. Because a version of zero never triggers the address update, the condition that checks for a zero address remains true, causing the same template name to be pushed into the array repeatedly. This results in duplicate entries in the list of template names and leaves the latestImplementation entry at address(0). External contracts that rely on the existence of a non‑zero implementation address interpret the missing address as an uninitialized template, leading them to attempt registration again. Each subsequent attempt fails or creates further duplicates, causing the system to appear stuck, with users seeing the same template name appear multiple times and receiving no functional implementation when they request it. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the factory’s registration flow, where the auditor observed that registering a version‑zero template did not set the implementation and that the name array grew with repeated entries. The bug is subtle because version zero is a valid uint256 value and the code does not explicitly forbid it, so the problem does not manifest for typical positive versions. It violates the business assumption that each template name maps to a single latest implementation, breaking accounting of available implementations and potentially preventing legitimate upgrades. To remediate, the registration logic should treat version zero like any other version, updating the latestImplementation mapping whenever the supplied version is greater than or equal to the stored version, and should only push a new name into the registry when the name has not been recorded before. This eliminates duplicate entries and ensures that the implementation address is always stored, restoring correct template lookup behavior.

title: DnGmxJuniorVaultManager#harvestFees can
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fee‑harvesting routine of the junior vault manager, which converts senior‑tranche WETH rewards into USDC and supplies the resulting aUSDC directly to Aave. This conversion increases the junior vault's aUSDC balance, which is later interpreted by the accounting function that calculates the amount of USDC borrowed by the junior vault. Because the conversion is performed without checking the vault's borrow cap, the reported borrowed amount can exceed the configured cap. When the vault is already at its maximum allowed borrow, the subtraction borrowCap‑borrowed in the availableBorrow view underflows, producing a very large unsigned integer that causes the function to revert. The revert propagates to the deposit and withdraw entry points, which call harvestFees on every user interaction, so any subsequent deposit or withdrawal transaction fails with a generic revert error. From a user perspective the symptoms are a transaction that instantly reverts, no change to the displayed balance, and an inability to add or remove funds, giving the impression that the contract is broken or possibly malicious. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the logic of fee conversion was examined and the interaction with the borrow‑cap check was traced. It is hard to notice because the fee conversion appears beneficial – it increases senior‑vault value – and the underflow only manifests when the cap is already reached, producing a silent revert without a clear error message. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow and accounting‑logic errors where indirect state changes (fee conversion) are not reconciled with existing limits (borrow cap). The impact is that users cannot interact with the junior vault, effectively locking their assets, and the protocol’s business logic that guarantees borrowing limits is violated. The recommended mitigation is to guard the subtraction by checking whether the borrowed amount exceeds the cap and, if so, return zero available borrow or otherwise prevent the fee conversion from pushing the vault over its limit, thereby eliminating the underflow condition.

title: Wrong price calculation in DnGmxJuniorVault-
description:
in DnGmxJuniorVaultManager.sol at line:647: usdcPrice should be on denominator and MAX_PRECISION on numerator (cf pricing in Vault: uint256 redemptionAmount = _usdgAmount.mul(PRICE_PRECISION).div(price);)
In the case usdcPrice is higher than 1$ (which already happened in reasonable market circumstances). Min amount expected will be higher than swap result under 0% slippage conditions. The call will revert, which will delay rebalances until usdcPrice comes back to 1$, and causing potential loss to the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculated price formula inside the DnGmxJuniorVaultManager contract. The code uses the USDC price (usdcPrice) as the numerator when it should be the denominator, while the constant MAX_PRECISION (or PRICE_PRECISION) is placed on the wrong side of the division. Because the contract expects USDC to be pegged at exactly $1, the incorrect formula works only when the price is exactly one. When market conditions cause USDC to trade above $1 – a situation that has occurred in real markets – the division yields a redemption amount that is smaller than the amount that would be obtained from the actual swap. The contract checks that the amount received meets a minimum threshold (often expressed as 0 % slippage). Under the wrong formula the calculated minimum is higher than the real swap result, causing the internal call to revert. The revert stops the rebalance routine, meaning the vault cannot adjust its exposure until the USDC price returns to $1. During this pause the protocol may miss profitable arbitrage opportunities or suffer from an imbalanced asset allocation, which can translate into lost yield or even a reduction of the total value locked. The bug is triggered only when the USDC price deviates above the peg and the rebalance function is executed, so it may remain hidden during normal operation when the price is stable. It was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s pricing logic, where the auditor compared the formula with the one used elsewhere in the system and noticed the inversion. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error message; it simply reverts, and the surrounding code does not log the reason, making the failure appear as a generic transaction failure. To remediate the problem the pricing expression must be rewritten so that the USDC price is placed in the denominator and the precision constant in the numerator, matching the pattern used in the main vault (redemptionAmount = _usdgAmount.mul(PRICE_PRECISION).div(price)). This change restores the correct minimum‑receive calculation, prevents unnecessary reverts, and allows the rebalance process to continue under normal market fluctuations. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑order‑of‑operations errors that break financial invariants, leading to situations where users expect a refund or redemption but receive nothing, or where protocol funds become temporarily inaccessible.

title: WithdrawPeriphery#_convertToToken slippage
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect slippage protection calculation in the WithdrawPeriphery contract when converting GLP to a token other than USDC. The function assumes the output token has six decimals because the estimated amount is expressed in USDC units. It multiplies the estimated token amount by a slippage factor and compares it with the actual amount received, but it does not adjust for tokens that have eighteen decimals such as WETH or WBTC. As a result the minTokenOut value is off by a factor of 10^(tokenDecimals‑6). When a user withdraws to a high‑decimal token the contract may accept a far smaller amount than expected, effectively providing no protection against price manipulation or MEV. An attacker or a market move can cause the rewardRouter.unstakeAndRedeemGlp call to return far fewer tokens than the user anticipates, yet the transaction will not revert because the minTokenOut check is satisfied due to the decimal mismatch. The impact is that users can lose a large portion of their withdrawn value, seeing their balance reduced to near zero or receiving far fewer tokens than expected. The bug manifests whenever the withdraw function is called with a token whose decimals differ from six, which includes most tokens on GMX. The affected parties are the end‑users who hold junior share vault tokens and the protocol that promises safe redemption. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the slippage logic against token decimal specifications. Because the contract does not emit any warning and the calculation appears syntactically correct, the problem can be hard to notice unless the auditor checks the decimal assumptions. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect unit handling” or “decimal‑mismatch slippage protection” bugs, where a financial formula is applied using an assumed token precision. To fix the issue the contract should scale the minTokenOut value by 10^(tokenDecimals‑6) or compute the slippage threshold using the token’s actual decimals, ensuring that the protection works for any token. In practice a user expecting a USDC‑like refund may instead receive almost nothing, violating the business logic that the withdrawal should return at least the quoted amount minus a small, configurable slippage.

title: WithdrawPeriphery uses incorrect value for
description:
WithdrawPeriphery accidentally uses an incorrect value for MAX_BPS which will allow for much higher slippage than intended.
```solidity
uint256 internal constant MAX_BPS = 1000;
```
BPS is typically 10,000 and using 1000 is inconsistent with the rest of the ecosystem contracts and tests. The result is that slippage values will be 10x higher than intended. Unexpected slippage resulting in loss of user funds, likely due to MEV
bug_full: WithdrawPeriphery contract defines a constant that represents the maximum basis points (MAX_BPS) used to calculate allowed slippage on withdrawals. The constant is set to 1000, which corresponds to 10 % when interpreted as basis points, whereas the ecosystem standard is 10 000 (100 %). Because the contract later treats the value as if it were expressed in basis points, the slippage tolerance is effectively multiplied by ten. As a result, a user who specifies a 1 % slippage limit will actually be allowed up to 10 % slippage. This mismatch originates from a simple copy‑and‑paste or misunderstanding of the unit convention and is not caught by unit tests that assume the standard 10 000 value. An attacker or a malicious miner can exploit the inflated tolerance by front‑running or sandwiching a withdrawal transaction, causing the contract to accept a trade at a price that deviates far beyond the user’s expectation. The impact is that users may receive far fewer assets than anticipated, effectively losing funds to market price movement or MEV extraction. The condition occurs whenever a user initiates a withdrawal through WithdrawPeriphery with a slippage parameter that is interpreted against the incorrect MAX_BPS constant. All participants who rely on the contract for safe withdrawal – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions about price protection are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the constant against the rest of the codebase and test suite, noticing the inconsistency. Because the contract still compiles and the error does not trigger a revert, it can be difficult to notice without explicit inspection of the constant or observing abnormal price deviations in production. The proper fix is to align the constant with the ecosystem standard by setting MAX_BPS to 10 000 (or 10_000 in Solidity) so that slippage calculations reflect the intended percentage limits. This change restores the invariant that the maximum allowed slippage expressed in basis points matches the protocol’s risk model, preventing unintended fund loss. From a user’s perspective, the bug manifests as a withdrawal that completes but returns significantly less value than expected, often appearing as a “balance drops to zero” or “my refund is much smaller than I set”. Users expect the contract to honor their specified slippage ceiling, but due to the bug the reality is a ten‑fold higher tolerance, breaking the business logic that guarantees price protection.

title: Early depositors to DnGmxSeniorVault can ma-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way DnGmxSeniorVault (and the analogous DnGmxJuniorVault) computes the exchange rate between deposited aUSDC assets and minted vault shares. The contract’s convertToShares function returns assets multiplied by the current totalSupply divided by totalAssets, using a mulDivDown operation that truncates any fractional part. When the vault is empty, the first depositor can mint a single share (or any minimal amount) because totalSupply is zero, establishing a 1:1 ratio. After this initial mint, an attacker can donate a large amount of aUSDC – for example 1e8 units – without receiving additional shares. This donation inflates totalAssets while totalSupply remains extremely low, causing the share‑to‑asset ratio to collapse to 1:1e8. Any subsequent user who deposits an amount smaller than the inflated totalAssets experiences severe rounding loss: the mulDivDown calculation rounds down to zero or a negligible number of shares, so the user receives far fewer shares than expected. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the deposit was accepted but the share balance increases only marginally or not at all, leading to the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The attacker can later withdraw the previously minted share at the manipulated price, effectively extracting value from later depositors. The issue occurs only when the vault starts from a zero supply state and the first deposit is tiny; it is hard to notice because the share price appears correct for large deposits, while small deposits silently suffer precision loss. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the share conversion logic and identified the division‑by‑totalAssets pattern as a precision‑loss vector. To remediate, the vault should be initialized with a non‑zero baseline deposit that locks the exchange rate, for example by minting a small amount of shares to a dead address before any user deposits, or by enforcing a minimum totalSupply before allowing external deposits, or by using a rounding‑up method or a different formula that does not allow the supply to be arbitrarily small relative to assets. This would prevent an attacker from establishing a manipulable share price and protect users from losing value due to rounding errors.

title: DnGmxJuniorVaultManager#_totalAssets cur-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal NAV estimation routine of the DnGmxJuniorVaultManager contract, specifically the _totalAssets function that accepts a boolean flag named maximize. The function is intended to return either the highest possible net asset value (NAV) when maximize is true, or the lowest possible NAV when maximize is false. However, the implementation inverts the price direction for both the asset side (unhedgedGlp) and the debt side (borrowValueGlp) by always calling the price oracle with the opposite of the maximize flag. Consequently, when the caller requests a maximized NAV, the function uses a minimized GLP price for both assets and debt, which reduces the reported value of the assets at the same time as it reduces the reported debt, resulting in a NAV that is not truly maximized. The slippage adjustment is also applied incorrectly: for the debt component the code subtracts the slippage threshold when it should add it, meaning the estimated cost to repay the debt is artificially low. This logical inconsistency can be triggered whenever _totalAssets is invoked, which occurs during share price calculations, withdrawal limits, fee assessments and other critical protocol parameters. An attacker who can influence the GLP price oracle or the slippageThresholdGmxBps variable can cause the contract to report a NAV that is higher than the actual collateral value, allowing the attacker to mint or withdraw more shares than should be permitted, or conversely cause legitimate users to see a lower share price and receive less value than expected. From a user perspective the symptoms may include withdrawals that return zero tokens despite a positive balance, share prices that appear unusually low or high, or unexpected failures when trying to redeem assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the maximize flag was used with a logical NOT operator in both price queries and that the slippage factor was subtracted on the debt side. The bug is subtle because the function is internal and its output is used only for accounting; the mis‑calculation does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to overlook during testing. The root cause is a mix‑up of the intended maximization/minimization semantics and an incorrect sign on the slippage adjustment. To remediate the problem the code should query the GLP price with the maximize flag for the asset side, use the opposite flag for the debt side, and apply slippage as an addition to the debt estimate rather than a subtraction. By aligning the price direction and slippage handling with the intended financial model, the NAV calculation will correctly reflect the best‑case or worst‑case scenario, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and protecting user funds.

title: In "maxWithdraw" for Senior Vault, the calcu-
description: In "maxWithdraw" for Senior Vault, the calculation for "maxAvailable" was incorrect. Could result in unexpected behavior
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the senior‑tranche vault’s maxWithdraw function, where the internal calculation of the maximum amount a holder may withdraw (referred to as maxAvailable) is implemented incorrectly. The root cause is a faulty arithmetic expression – typically an omitted scaling factor, an integer‑division mistake, or a misuse of total assets versus total shares – that produces a value that does not faithfully represent the holder’s actual entitlement. Because maxWithdraw is used as a guard before a withdrawal is executed, an inflated maxAvailable can allow a user to request and receive more tokens than the vault actually holds, while an understated value can prevent legitimate users from withdrawing their full share. An attacker can exploit the bug by calling maxWithdraw, observing the erroneous high limit, and then invoking the withdraw routine to pull out the excess amount. This drains senior‑tranche assets, breaks the accounting invariants of the vault, and may leave junior‑tranche participants under‑collateralised. The issue manifests whenever the vault’s balance changes – for example after deposits, rewards, or partial withdrawals – and the faulty formula is evaluated. All senior‑tranche token holders, the protocol’s risk model, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct accounting are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the expected withdrawable amount (based on share‑to‑asset conversion) with the value returned by maxWithdraw and noticed a discrepancy. Because the function is not directly exposed in the UI and the numbers can appear plausible for small balances, the bug can remain hidden until a large withdrawal is attempted. To remediate, the maxAvailable computation should be rewritten to use the precise share‑to‑asset conversion, apply proper rounding (e.g., using SafeMath’s rounding‑up or down as required), and include a final sanity check that caps the result at the vault’s current token balance. Adding unit tests that cover edge cases such as zero balance, full depletion, and rounding scenarios will help prevent regression. In essence, the vulnerability is a classic accounting‑logic error that violates the fundamental business rule that a vault cannot dispense more assets than it holds, leading to potential fund loss and broken financial guarantees.

title: Auctioneer Cannot Be Removed From The Pro-
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an immutable whitelist for auctioneer contracts in the BondAggregator component. When an auctioneer address is added through the registerAuctioneer function, the contract sets a boolean flag in a private mapping and pushes the address onto an array, but it never provides a complementary mechanism to clear that flag or remove the entry. The root cause is the absence of a deregistration function and the lack of logic to delete or deactivate a previously authorized auctioneer. Because the whitelist can only grow, an attacker who compromises a whitelisted auctioneer, or an administrator who mistakenly authorises a malicious contract, cannot be removed from the protocol. Exploitation is straightforward: once the vulnerable auctioneer is active, it can continue to receive bids, manipulate auction outcomes, or divert funds, while the protocol has no on‑chain way to block its participation. The impact is that the protocol remains exposed to ongoing malicious behavior, potentially leading to loss of user funds, failed refunds, and erosion of trust, especially when every second counts during an active exploit. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time after an auctioneer has been added to the whitelist; there is no guardrail to reverse that decision. All participants—bond holders, bidders, and the protocol’s governance—are affected because they rely on the auctioneer to enforce correct auction logic. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle management of privileged contracts and noted that only an add‑only path existed. The omission is subtle because the whitelist appears to work for onboarding new auctioneers, and developers may assume removal is unnecessary, making the bug easy to overlook until a real‑world exploit occurs. To remediate, the contract should implement a revocation function that clears the whitelist entry, optionally removes the address from the array, emits an event, and enforces the same access control as the registration function. This pattern belongs to the class of “missing revocation of privileged roles” or “inability to de‑authorize a whitelisted contract”, which violates the business assumption that administrators can react quickly to compromised components. From a user perspective the symptoms may include auctions that never settle, refunds that never arrive, or balances that appear to disappear because the compromised auctioneer continues to process transactions without a way to be blocked.

title: _validateDeploymentConfig function in NFT-
description: Due to not thoroughly checking all conditions of the deployment config, users might not be able to mint certain amount of tokens. In NFTCollection.sol, there is a function called _validateDeploymentConfig, which checks whether the deploymentConfig input to initialize function is valid. The function checks whether the maxSupply and tokensPerMint are greater than zero. But it never checks if the tokensPerMint is less than or equal to maxSupply. Suppose maxSupply < tokensPerMint. Then if the user calls a function which in-turn calls the _mintTokens function with an amount equal to tokensPerMint, it will revert. Even though he is technically trying to mint as per the rules. This is because the availableSupply() won't be greater than amount. 1. Dissatisfaction and Frustration of the user along with loss of his gas fees. 2. The contract would need redeployment as deployment config cannot be changed once its set.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the contract’s deployment configuration routine. When the contract is initialized, a function called _validateDeploymentConfig checks that the maximum token supply (maxSupply) and the number of tokens that can be minted in a single call (tokensPerMint) are both greater than zero.
