However, it does not verify that tokensPerMint does not exceed maxSupply. If the deployer sets a configuration where maxSupply is smaller than tokensPerMint, the contract will later reject any mint request that tries to mint the allowed batch size because the internal availableSupply() check will see that the requested amount is larger than the total supply that can ever exist. This logical inconsistency causes the _mintTokens call to revert, even though the user is following the documented minting rules. The bug manifests when a user initiates a mint transaction that should succeed according to the UI or documentation, but the transaction fails and the user loses the gas spent on the call. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that they can mint the advertised number of tokens, but the reality is that the transaction reverts with no tokens transferred and no refund of gas. The impact is limited to user frustration, loss of gas fees, and the need to redeploy the contract because the deployment configuration is immutable after initialization. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the validation logic of the initialization parameters and noticed the absence of a comparison between tokensPerMint and maxSupply. It can be hard to notice because both parameters are individually positive, satisfying the existing checks, so a superficial test may not trigger the failure unless the specific edge case of maxSupply < tokensPerMint is exercised. The bug belongs to the class of configuration validation errors where inter‑parameter constraints are omitted, leading to a denial‑of‑service style failure where legitimate mint operations are blocked. To remediate the issue, the validation routine should include a require statement that enforces tokensPerMint to be less than or equal to maxSupply, thereby guaranteeing that any allowed mint size can always be satisfied by the total supply. This change restores the intended business logic that the contract can always fulfill a mint request of size tokensPerMint without violating supply constraints.

title: Factory uses signature that do not have expi-
description:
NftPort can't remove license from user, once the signature was provided to it, without changing SIGNER_ROLE address. In Factory contract there are few methods that are called when signed by trusted signer. This is how the signature is checked:
```solidity
signedOnly(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, instance, data), signature)
```
As you can see there is no any expiration time. That means that once, the signer has signed the signature for the user it can use it for the end of life. It's like lifetime license. The only option to remove the license from user is to revoke SIGNER_ROLE and set it to another account. But it's possible that the NFTPort will have a need to do that with current signer. License can't be removed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an indefinite‑validity signature used by the Factory contract to grant a license to a user. The contract verifies the signature by hashing the caller address, an instance identifier and arbitrary data, then calling signedOnly with that hash and the supplied signature. Because the signed payload does not contain any timestamp, block number, or explicit expiration field, the signature remains valid forever. The root cause is the omission of a time‑bound parameter in the signed message, which makes the authorization effectively a lifetime license. An attacker who obtains a legitimate signature from the trusted signer can reuse it at any later point to call the privileged factory methods, even after the business logic intends to revoke the license. Exploitation consists of presenting the previously issued signature to the contract after the intended revocation period; the contract will accept it because the signedOnly check only validates the signer role, not the age of the signature. The impact is that the platform cannot remove or expire a user’s license without replacing the entire signer address, which may be operationally costly or impossible. This prevents the protocol from enforcing subscription‑style access, limits compliance with regulatory or policy changes, and could allow a malicious user to retain privileged actions indefinitely. The condition occurs whenever a license is granted via a signed message and the signer role remains unchanged; it is triggered when the contract owner attempts to revoke a license by any means other than changing the signer. All users who rely on time‑limited access, as well as the protocol operators, are affected because the contract’s accounting assumes that a license can be withdrawn. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Factory contract’s access‑control functions, where the absence of an expiration field in the signed payload was noted. It can be hard to notice because the signature verification itself succeeds and the contract does not emit any warning when a license is expected to be expired; the problem only becomes visible when an operator tries to revoke a license and finds it still active. The appropriate fix is to include a deadline (e.g., block.timestamp or a block number) in the data that is signed, and to enforce that the current time is less than the deadline before accepting the signature. This turns the authorization into a time‑bounded permit rather than a perpetual one, aligning the contract behaviour with the intended business logic of expiring licenses. The bug belongs to the class of “missing expiration in signed authorization” or “unbounded replayable signature” vulnerabilities, where a signed message can be replayed indefinitely because no freshness check is performed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a license that should have been removed or expired remains active, leading to unexpected continued access or privileges. The expectation that the platform can revoke a license is violated; instead the user continues to receive the same rights, effectively making the license “non‑revocable”.

title: exchangeFee can be escaped
description:
Comparing the before and after balance of the swap call for the swapped amount can be exploited to escape the exchangeFee by wrapping the actual swap inside a fake swap. The attacker can reenter with another CardTopupPermit()->_processTopup()->IExchangeProxyexecuteSwapDirect() at L174 to claw back the fee:
1. Swap minAmount with 1inch, inside the 1inch swap at ExchangeProxy.solL174, reenter and HardenedTopupProxy.solCardTopupPermit();
2. The inner swap is the actual amount: 1M; whichshouldpayfor
As a result, the user successfully escaped most of the exchangeFee. User can escape the exchangeFee.
bug_full: An attacker can bypass the exchange fee that is supposed to be deducted during a token swap by exploiting a re‑entrancy flaw in the HardenedTopupProxy contract. The proxy exposes three non‑view functions (CardTopupPermit, CardTopupTrusted and CardTopupMPTProof) that internally call IExchangeProxy.executeSwapDirect. Because these functions lack a re‑entrancy guard, an adversary can trigger a swap with a minimal amount through a 1inch router, and while the external router is still executing, re‑enter the proxy via CardTopupPermit. The inner call performs the real swap for the full amount, causing the fee calculation that occurs after the first call to be applied to the minimal amount only. As a result the contract records that only a tiny fee was owed, while the attacker receives the full proceeds of the larger swap, effectively escaping most of the intended exchange fee. This behaviour is observable from a user’s perspective as a swap transaction that completes successfully but leaves the user’s balance higher than expected, or conversely shows no fee deduction where one should appear. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared pre‑ and post‑swap balances and identified that the fee could be manipulated by wrapping the genuine swap inside a fake one. The issue is subtle because the contract’s external interface reports a successful swap and the fee appears to be collected, yet the internal accounting is corrupted only when re‑entrancy occurs, making it hard to detect through simple event logs. The root cause is the absence of a non‑reentrant guard on the functions that forward swap calls, allowing nested execution paths that bypass the fee logic. To remediate, the contract should protect the three entry points with a nonReentrant modifier or an equivalent re‑entrancy lock, ensuring that a second call cannot be made until the first swap finishes and the fee is correctly accounted for. By enforcing this guard, the protocol restores its economic assumptions that every swap pays the declared exchange fee, preventing fee‑escape attacks and preserving the integrity of user balances.

title: Denial of Service on Batching Manager
description: In case there is significant amount (like $1M) of USDC deposited into Batching Manager then after conversion of usdc into sGLP would work fine (executeBatchStake) but from sGLP to shares (executeBatchDeposit) would fail due to slippage tolerance checks. This would lead to batching manager being stuck in this state since batch deposit cannot go through and users would not be able to withdraw the sGLP. Users would not be able to withdraw the sGLP from the Batching Manager.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the Batching Manager component that handles the conversion of deposited USDC into sGLP and subsequently into protocol shares. The root cause lies in the slippage‑tolerance validation performed during the second conversion step (sGLP → shares). When a very large amount of USDC (for example, around one million dollars) is deposited, the first conversion to sGLP succeeds, but the resulting sGLP amount is so large that the calculated share amount falls outside the pre‑configured slippage tolerance. The contract therefore reverts the executeBatchDeposit transaction. Because the batch deposit cannot complete, the manager remains in a partially processed state: the sGLP tokens are locked inside the Batching Manager and no further batch operations can be executed. An attacker does not need to interact directly with the contract; the condition can be triggered simply by a legitimate user depositing a sufficiently large USDC amount, causing the slippage check to fail. The impact is that all users who have deposited through the Batching Manager lose the ability to withdraw their sGLP; their balances appear unchanged in the UI, but attempts to claim or withdraw return zero or revert, effectively freezing the funds. This situation occurs whenever the deposited volume pushes the sGLP‑to‑share conversion outside the allowed tolerance, which is more likely with high‑value deposits or during periods of market volatility that affect price ratios. The affected parties are the end‑users of the protocol who rely on the Batching Manager for liquidity provision, as well as the protocol itself because locked assets reduce available capital and damage trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the batch processing logic, where the auditor observed that the slippage check could reject large conversions and that there was no fallback path to recover the locked sGLP. The bug is subtle because the contract behaves correctly for typical deposit sizes, and the failure only manifests under extreme but plausible conditions, making it easy to miss in standard testing. To remediate, the slippage tolerance logic should be redesigned to handle large deposits gracefully, for example by using a dynamic tolerance, splitting large batches into smaller sub‑batches, or allowing a manual override/recovery path that lets users withdraw locked sGLP even when the batch deposit fails. Conceptually, the fix removes the hard stop that freezes assets and restores the ability for users to retrieve their balances, aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that deposited funds remain withdrawable at any time.

title: executeBatchDeposit() will revert under cer-
description: DnGmxBatchingManager.executeBatchDeposit() will always revert if _convertAUsdcToAsset is called within DnGmxJuniorVault.deposit sub call because it will again call DnGmxBatchingManager.depositToken() and this will revert due to glp 15 mins cooldown. DnGmxBatchingManager.executeBatchDeposit() will revert under certain conditions
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batch deposit workflow of the DnGmxBatchingManager contract. When a user calls DnGmxJuniorVault.deposit, the function may invoke an internal helper named _convertAUsdcToAsset. This helper, in turn, triggers a second call to DnGmxBatchingManager.depositToken. Because the GLP token used by the protocol enforces a 15‑minute cooldown between successive deposits, the second depositToken call violates the cooldown rule and causes the entire executeBatchDeposit transaction to revert. The root cause is a state‑dependent revert: the contract assumes that a deposit operation can be safely re‑entered from within the conversion routine, but it does not account for the external cooldown restriction on GLP. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit this by simply depositing through the junior vault while the cooldown is active, causing the batch to fail and preventing any funds from being recorded. The impact is that legitimate depositors may see their transaction revert with no funds transferred, leading to a loss of expected deposit opportunity and potentially eroding confidence in the protocol. This condition occurs only when the conversion path is taken during a deposit and the GLP cooldown window has not elapsed, which can happen frequently in a live system where deposits are batched. All users of the DnGmxJuniorVault and any downstream contracts that rely on successful batch deposits are affected because their balances remain unchanged and the UI may show a “deposit failed” or simply no change in their asset holdings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call stack of executeBatchDeposit and identified the hidden re‑entrancy into depositToken under cooldown constraints. It is hard to notice because the revert originates from an external token contract’s cooldown logic, not from an explicit require statement in the batching manager, making the failure appear as an unexplained transaction revert. To remediate, the batching manager should either defer the conversion step until after the cooldown has passed, add a guard that prevents depositToken from being called recursively, or redesign the workflow so that GLP cooldown checks are performed before any nested deposit attempts. In generic terms, this is a state‑dependent re‑entrancy bug where an internal call violates an external time‑based restriction, leading to unexpected transaction failure and broken accounting logic. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a generic error, the expected increase in deposited balance never materializes, and the user may wonder why “my funds disappeared” when in fact the transaction simply reverted without state changes.

title: Debt Decay Faster Than Expected
description:
The debt decay at a rate faster than expected, causing market makers to sell bond tokens at a lower price than expected. The following definition of the debt decay reference time following any purchases at time t taken from the whitepaper. The second variable, which is the delay increment. However, the actual implementation in the codebase differs from the specification. At Line 514, the delay increment is rounded down instead. A.sol#L514 File: BondBaseSDA.sol
```solidity
513: // Set last decay timestamp based on size of purchase to linearize decay
514: uint256 lastDecayIncrement = debtDecayInterval.mulDiv(payout_, lastTuneDebt);
515: metadata[id_].lastDecay += uint48(lastDecayIncrement);
```
When the delay increment (TD) is rounded down, the debt decay reference time increment will be smaller than expected. The debt component will then decay at a faster rate. As a result, the market price will not be adjusted in an optimized manner, and the market price will fall faster than expected, causing market makers to sell bond tokens at a lower price than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the calculation of the debt‑decay reference timestamp for bond purchases. According to the protocol specification, the increment that advances the last‑decay time should be rounded up so that the decay schedule matches the linearised model described in the whitepaper. In the actual implementation the code uses a floor division (mulDiv) which truncates any fractional part, producing a smaller increment than intended. Because the increment is smaller, the stored lastDecay timestamp advances more slowly, which means the debt component decays faster than expected. This accelerated decay causes the market price of bond tokens to fall more quickly than the economic model predicts, leading market makers to sell bonds at a lower price than users anticipate. The issue manifests whenever a purchase triggers the update of lastDecayIncrement; each such call applies the rounded‑down value, so the effect compounds over time. Affected parties include the protocol itself (its pricing oracle becomes inaccurate), market makers (who may incur losses or gain unfair advantage), and token holders who see their bond value drop unexpectedly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the white‑paper formula with the Solidity implementation and noticed the discrepancy in the rounding direction. It is hard to notice because the contract still functions and no transaction reverts; the problem only appears as a gradual drift in price, which may be attributed to market volatility. The impact is a deviation from the intended accounting assumptions, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the perspective of users expecting a stable price. The recommended remediation is to compute the increment with a ceiling operation (mulDivUp) so that the decay interval is never underestimated, thereby aligning the on‑chain behaviour with the protocol’s economic design.

title: Market Price Lower Than Expected
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic miscalculation caused by rounding the market price down instead of rounding it up as required by the protocol specification. The root cause lies in the internal function that derives the current market price; it uses a plain multiplication‑division operation that truncates any fractional component, whereas the whitepaper mandates a ceiling division to guarantee that the integer price is never lower than the true market value. Because the price is rounded down, makers who sell tokens receive a price that is smaller than the minimum price they expect, leading to a loss of value for sellers. The lower price also feeds into the decay routine, producing a higher payout token amount, inflating the last decay increment and consequently reducing the total debt. A reduced total debt then causes subsequent price calculations to be even lower, creating a feedback loop that further erodes maker returns. This condition occurs whenever the internal price function is invoked, which includes the regular decay and price‑query pathways. All participants who rely on the market price – primarily token makers – are affected, as they may see their balances decrease unexpectedly or receive fewer proceeds from a sale. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the specification’s rounding requirement was compared against the actual implementation. It is subtle because the price still respects the minimum price bound and therefore does not raise an obvious error flag; the discrepancy only becomes visible through economic analysis or by observing unexpectedly low sale proceeds. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the expected refund or sale price and the actual amount received, often appearing as “my tokens sold for less than advertised” or “my balance dropped more than it should”. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions in financial smart contracts. To remediate the problem the internal price calculation must be changed to use a ceiling division (mulDivUp) so that the computed integer price is always greater than or equal to the real market price, thereby restoring the intended protection for makers and preventing the cascade of debt reduction and price distortion.

title: Teller Cannot Be Removed From Callback Con-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing revocation mechanism for the whitelist of Teller contracts inside the Callback contract. When the owner calls the whitelist function, the address of a Teller and its market identifier are stored in the approvedMarkets mapping and are permanently marked as true. Because there is no complementary function to set the entry back to false, the contract cannot remove a Teller once it has been approved. This design flaw originates from an incomplete access‑control implementation: the contract only defines an add‑to‑whitelist path (onlyOwner) but omits a remove‑from‑whitelist path. If a whitelisted Teller becomes compromised or is discovered to be malicious, an attacker can continue to invoke the Teller’s callbacks and drain assets that are held by the Callback contract. The exploit works by the attacker using the already‑approved Teller to trigger callback logic that moves funds out of the Callback contract; the owner has no way to block the Teller because the whitelist entry cannot be cleared. The impact is that funds may be siphoned away, users may see their balances become zero or experience failed withdrawals, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only trusted Tellers can interact are violated. The condition under which this issue manifests is any situation where a Teller that has been added to the whitelist is later found to be vulnerable or was added by mistake. The parties affected are the Callback contract owner, the protocol that relies on the Callback contract for market operations, and ultimately the end‑users whose assets are stored in the Callback contract. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the contract’s permission model and noticed the absence of a removal function. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the whitelist addition appears to work correctly; the missing revocation path only becomes apparent when a security incident occurs. To remediate, the contract should implement a removeFromWhitelist function guarded by onlyOwner that sets approvedMarkets[teller][id] to false, emits an appropriate event, and optionally includes checks to ensure the entry exists before clearing it. This change restores the ability to revoke trust in a Teller, aligns the contract with standard whitelist management patterns, and prevents permanent exposure to a compromised Teller.

title: Create Fee Discount Feature Is Broken
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a fee‑discount mechanism that is intended to reduce the protocol fee when a user creates a new bond. The contract stores the discount amount in a state variable (createFeeDiscount) and later compares the configured protocol fee against this discount to decide how much fee to deduct. However, the variable is never initialized or updated because the contract lacks any function that can set its value. As a result, createFeeDiscount remains at its default value of zero for the lifetime of the contract. Consequently, the conditional check "if (protocolFee > createFeeDiscount)" is always true, causing the full protocol fee to be applied on every create operation. Users therefore receive no discount; the fee amount is calculated as if the discount were zero, and the minted bond token amount is reduced by the full fee. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – a lower fee and a larger token allocation – does not materialize; instead the user sees the same or slightly lower token balance than anticipated, leading to the impression that the protocol is overcharging. The impact is primarily economic: users overpay fees, which can erode trust and affect the protocol’s perceived fairness, although no direct loss of funds beyond the higher fee occurs. The bug manifests on every call to the create function, regardless of the protocol or underlying asset, because the discount variable is globally zero. It affects all participants who rely on the advertised discount, including token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that assume a reduced fee. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit when the auditor noted the absence of any setter or initializer for the discount variable and observed that the discount logic always evaluates to zero. The problem can be subtle because the contract still functions – it mints tokens and records fees – so the missing discount does not cause a runtime error, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a controlled setter (or constructor initialization) for the createFeeDiscount variable, enforce that the discount does not exceed the protocol fee or a reasonable maximum, and optionally emit an event when the discount is changed. This change restores the intended economic behavior, aligns the implementation with the protocol’s documentation, and prevents users from unintentionally paying the full fee.

title: BondAggregator.liveMarketsBy eventually will
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a read‑only function that enumerates all markets stored in the BondAggregator contract. The function iterates over the entire marketCounter range and, for each index, performs two external calls to the associated auctioneer contract – one to check if the market is live and another to verify ownership. Because the loop size grows with every new market, the total number of external calls scales linearly and can reach four calls per market when all markets are live and owned by the caller. Although the function is marked view, the EVM still executes the code and must pay for the gas consumed by those external calls. As the number of markets increases, the gas required to complete the loop eventually exceeds the block gas limit (estimated around 50 million gas). When this limit is hit, the transaction reverts, causing the function to always fail and return no data. The root cause is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic collection that performs external calls without any pagination, pruning, or early exit conditions. An attacker or even a benign user can trigger the denial‑of‑service condition simply by creating enough markets, inflating the loop until the gas budget is insufficient. The impact is that any off‑chain service, UI component, or other contract that relies on liveMarketsBy (or the related findMarketFor, marketsFor, liveMarketsFor functions) will be unable to retrieve the list of markets, leading to missing or empty results, users seeing no markets, or dashboards showing zero balances where markets should appear. This bug is hard to notice because view functions are often assumed to be free and safe, yet they still consume gas on the node executing the call, and the gas cost grows silently as the protocol expands. The issue violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that market data can always be queried, breaking transparency and user trust. To remediate, the contract should avoid iterating over the full market set in a single call; instead it can store live market identifiers in a separate list, implement pagination with start and end indices, prune inactive markets, or expose events for off‑chain indexing. By limiting the amount of work per call, the function will remain within the block gas limit and reliably return data.

title: meta.tuneBelowCapacity param is not up-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the BondBaseSDA contract where the meta.tuneBelowCapacity field is not refreshed when the market owner calls setIntervals to modify the tuning interval and related parameters. The root cause is that setIntervals updates meta.tuneInterval, meta.tuneIntervalCapacity, meta.tuneAdjustmentDelay and meta.debtDecayInterval, but it never recomputes meta.tuneBelowCapacity, a value that represents the amount of capacity that has already been sold relative to the current tuning interval capacity. Because meta.tuneBelowCapacity is used in the conditional that decides whether a price tuning step should be executed, a stale value can cause the tuning logic to either skip a necessary price adjustment or perform an adjustment when it is no longer required. An attacker who controls the market owner role can invoke setIntervals with a smaller tuneIntervalCapacity, causing meta.tuneBelowCapacity to remain artificially high; the contract will then believe the market is still under‑capacity and will not lower the control variable, allowing the market to become oversold at an inflated price. Conversely, increasing the capacity while leaving meta.tuneBelowCapacity unchanged can trigger unnecessary tuning, potentially driving the price down too quickly. The impact is that bond prices may diverge from the intended economic model, users may receive payouts that are higher or lower than expected, and the market may become unbalanced, leading to loss of trust and possible financial loss for participants. The bug manifests after any successful call to setIntervals and persists until the next tuning event that overwrites meta.tuneBelowCapacity, meaning the issue can remain hidden for the entire remaining duration of the market. All participants who buy or sell bonds in the affected market are affected, while the protocol’s overall pricing integrity is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the setIntervals function does not touch meta.tuneBelowCapacity despite the comment that this variable depends on tuneIntervalCapacity. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the incorrect behaviour only appears as a deviation in price dynamics, which can be hard to attribute to a missing state update. The correct remediation is to recalculate and store meta.tuneBelowCapacity inside setIntervals, using the same formula that is applied after a successful tuning step: meta.tuneBelowCapacity = market.capacity > meta.tuneIntervalCapacity ? market.capacity - meta.tuneIntervalCapacity : 0; This ensures that the tuning condition always reflects the current capacity state. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of missing state‑synchronisation errors where a dependent variable is not updated after a related parameter change, leading to logical inconsistencies and economic misbehaviour.

title: Solmate safetransfer and safetransferfrom
description: The safetransfer and safetransferfrom don't check the existence of code at the token address. This is a known issue while using solmate's libraries. Hence this may lead to miscalculation of funds and may lead to loss of funds, because if safetransfer() and safetransferfrom() are called on a token address that doesn't have a contract in it, it will always return success, bypassing the return value check. Due to this protocol will think that funds have been transferred successfully, and records will be accordingly calculated, but in reality, funds were never transferred. So this will lead to miscalculation and possibly loss of funds. llback.sol#L143 'token_.safeTransfer(to_, amount_);' llback.sol#L152 'token_.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount_);' ller.sol#L108 'token.safeTransfer(to_, send);' ller.sol#L187 'quoteToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount_);' ller.sol#L195 'quoteToken.safeTransfer(callbackAddr, amountLessFee);' ller.sol#L210 'payoutToken.safeTransferFrom(owner, address(this), payout_);' ller.sol#L214 'quoteToken.safeTransfer(owner, amountLessFee);' ller.sol#L89 'underlying_.safeTransfer(recipient_, payout_);' ller.sol#L114 'underlying_.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount_);' ller.sol#L152 'underlying.safeTransfer(msg.sender, amount_);' er.sol#L90 'payoutToken_.safeTransfer(recipient_, payout_);' er.sol#L114 'underlying_.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount_);' er.sol#L151 'meta.underlying.safeTransfer(msg.sender, amount_);' k.sol#L42 'payoutToken_.safeTransfer(msg.sender, outputAmount_);'
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the library functions safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom from Solmate do not verify that the target address implements contract code before performing a low‑level call. Because the functions only check the boolean return value of the call, a call to an address that contains no contract (or a contract that does not implement the ERC‑20 interface) will still return true, causing the caller to assume the token transfer succeeded. This occurs whenever the protocol interacts with an ERC‑20 token using these helpers without first ensuring the token address points to a deployed contract. An attacker can supply a malicious token address that is either an externally owned account or a contract that deliberately returns success without moving tokens. When the protocol invokes token_.safeTransfer(to, amount) or token_.safeTransferFrom(...), the call will succeed, the protocol will record the transfer in its internal accounting, and downstream logic will treat the funds as received. In reality, no tokens are moved, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual balances. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful deposit or withdrawal, but the on‑chain balance of the protocol remains unchanged, causing missing funds, zero payouts, or refunds that never arrive. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Bond Protocol code where multiple calls to safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom were identified without any preceding code‑size check. Because the failure manifests as a silent loss of tokens rather than a revert, it can be hard to notice without explicit balance verification after each operation. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “missing contract existence validation” vulnerabilities, which break the assumption that a successful call guarantees token movement. To remediate, the code should either switch to OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which includes an address‑code check, or add an explicit require that the token address contains contract code (e.g., using extcodesize) before performing the transfer. Proper error handling and post‑transfer balance assertions would also mitigate the risk. Until fixed, any user who interacts with the protocol using a malicious or non‑contract token address may experience funds that appear to be transferred but are actually never received, potentially resulting in financial loss.

title: Transferring Ownership Might Break The Mar-
bug_full: During a bond market operation the contract stores a mapping callbackAuthorized that lists addresses allowed to use a callback. The purchaseBond function checks that the current market.owner is authorized before allowing a purchase. When ownership is transferred via pushOwnership, the function only updates newOwners mapping and does not verify that the new owner is present in callbackAuthorized. Consequently, if the market uses a callback (callbackAddr != 0) and the new owner is not whitelisted, every subsequent call to purchaseBond reverts with Auctioneer_NotAuthorized. This denial-of-service condition appears only after an ownership transfer, making it easy to miss during testing because the transfer itself succeeds and no explicit error is emitted at that moment. An attacker could exploit the situation by acquiring ownership of a market that relies on a callback and then either keeping the market non-functional or selling it to a party that is unaware of the missing whitelist entry, resulting in loss of sales and inability for users to buy bond tokens. Users experience a transaction that fails with an authorization error, receiving no bond tokens and potentially losing gas, contrary to the expectation that a purchase should succeed. The issue affects market makers, bond purchasers, and the overall protocol revenue because the market becomes unusable. The root cause is an incomplete invariant: the contract does not enforce that the owner remains authorized after a state-changing operation. The bug belongs to the class of improper access-control updates after ownership transfer. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between pushOwnership and the callback authorization check. Fixing the problem requires adding a validation step in the ownership transfer function that, when a callback is configured, ensures the new owner is present in the callbackAuthorized whitelist, or alternatively updating the whitelist together with the ownership change.

title: Fixed Term Bond tokens can be minted with
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency between the way token expiry timestamps are rounded in the internal payout handling logic and the way they are processed in the public deploy() function of the Fixed Term Bond protocol. Internally, when a bond is minted through the standard flow, the contract rounds the calculated expiry down to the nearest whole day (using ((vesting+block.timestamp)/1 days)*1 days) before encoding it into the token identifier. This rounding guarantees that all tokens that share the same day share a single tokenId and that the expiry stored in the token metadata matches the day encoded in the identifier. However, the external deploy() function accepts an arbitrary expiry value, computes the tokenId by hashing the underlying asset address together with expiry/1 days (effectively using the unrounded expiry), and then stores the raw expiry value in the token metadata without applying the same rounding step. As a result, a tokenId can be created whose identifier represents a different day than the actual expiry stored on‑chain. This mismatch can manifest to users as a bond that appears to expire at a certain date in the UI but actually expires at a later or earlier timestamp, breaking user expectations and front‑end calculations. The issue can be exploited by a malicious actor who calls deploy() with a future timestamp that is not aligned to the daily bucket, thereby pre‑creating a token for that day with an arbitrary expiry. Because the protocol only creates a token if the tokenId does not already exist, the attacker can “take over” the daily slot, lock the expiry at a time that benefits them, and prevent the protocol from issuing correctly‑rounded tokens for that day. This can lead to funds being locked in a token that cannot be redeemed until the unexpected expiry, causing loss of liquidity, confusing balances, and potential financial loss for honest users. The bug appears only when the deploy() function is invoked directly; normal minting paths remain unaffected, which makes it easy to overlook during casual testing. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the bond contract’s token creation logic, where the auditor noticed that the rounding step present in the internal payout routine was absent from the public deploy entry point. The difficulty in spotting the problem stems from the fact that both code paths ultimately call the same internal _deploy routine, and the tokenId calculation looks superficially identical, masking the subtle difference in how expiry is handled. To remediate the issue, the deploy() function should apply the same rounding logic used elsewhere before computing the tokenId and storing the expiry, ensuring that the token identifier and the stored expiry are always aligned to the daily granularity. This correction restores the invariant that each day corresponds to a unique tokenId with a matching expiry, preserving the protocol’s accounting assumptions and preventing malicious pre‑deployment attacks. The vulnerability belongs to the class of time‑rounding or timestamp‑validation bugs, where inconsistent handling of temporal data leads to mismatched state and exploitable conditions.

title: Read-only reentrancy in BondFixedTermTeller
description: supply of this specific bond is updated after the new bonds are sent to the recipient, which introduces a reentrancy attack. through _handlePayout() or create(), the total supply is updated after the bond has been minted. ERC1155 tokens will perform a callback to the recipient in case the recipient implements the ERC1155TokenReceiver interface. Therefore, the recipient (msg.sender in create() or recipient_ in _handlePayout()) is able to perform a call to an arbitrary contract before the total supply of the bonds is updated. function, there is no interesting function which might result in financial loss in case it gets called in the callback. Alternatively, the recipient could enter a smart contract late the current bond price based on the supply. As the supply is not yet updated, but the tokens are minted, this might result in a miscalculation of the price. calculate the price, might come at risk.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy in the BondFixedTermTeller contract. The contract mints ERC1155 bond tokens and then updates the internal total‑supply counter. Because ERC1155 mint triggers a callback to the recipient if it implements ERC1155TokenReceiver, a malicious recipient can execute arbitrary code before the supply variable is incremented. The price of a bond is calculated from the current supply, so during the callback the contract still sees the old supply value while the newly minted tokens already exist. An attacker can therefore call back into the contract (for example via _handlePayout or create) and trigger a second price calculation that uses the stale supply, obtaining a more favorable price or causing the protocol to issue bonds at an incorrect rate. This can lead to financial loss for the protocol or other users because bonds may be sold cheaper than intended or payouts may be under‑ or over‑paid. The issue occurs whenever a bond is minted or a payout is handled, i.e., any function that mints tokens before updating the supply. It affects any user who purchases or redeems bonds, as well as the protocol’s accounting logic. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the order of state updates and recognized that the ERC1155 callback provides a reentrancy window. It is hard to notice because the callback does not directly transfer ether and the contract does not contain an obvious external call that changes balances, so the reentrancy is “read‑only” and may not raise immediate red flags. The class of bug is an unsafe state‑update order combined with a callback‑enabled reentrancy, a pattern common in token contracts that mint before adjusting accounting variables. From a user’s perspective the symptom can appear as a bond price that is unexpectedly low, a payout that returns less than expected, or a balance that seems to disappear after a transaction. The expected behavior is that the supply is increased first, then tokens are minted, ensuring that price calculations use the up‑to‑date supply. To fix the issue the contract should update the supply counter before calling the ERC1155 _mint function, or otherwise use a reentrancy guard that blocks callbacks during the critical section. By moving the supply update ahead of the external call, the price calculation will always reflect the correct state, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Existing Circuit Breaker Implementation Al-
description:
The current implementation of the circuit breaker is not optimal. Thus, the market maker will lose an excessive amount of payout tokens if a quoted token suddenly loses a large amount of value, even with a circuit breaker in place. When the amount of the payout tokens purchased by the taker exceeds the term.maxDebt, the taker is still allowed to carry on with the transaction, and the market will only be closed after the current transaction is completed. A.sol#L427 File: BondBaseSDA.sol
```solidity
426: // Circuit breaker. If max debt is breached, the market is closed
427: if (term.maxDebt < market.totalDebt) {
428:     _close(id_);
429: } else {
430:     // If market will continue, the control variable is tuned to to expend remaining capacity over remaining market duration
431:     _tune(id_, currentTime, price);
432: }
```
Assume that the state of the SDAM at T0 is as follows:
• term.maxDebt is 110 (debt buffer = 10%)
• maxPayout is 100
• market.totalDebt is 99
Assume that the quoted token suddenly loses a large amount of value (e.g. stablecoin depeg causing the quote token to drop to almost zero). Bob decided to purchase as many payout tokens as possible before reaching the maxPayout limit to maximize the value he could extract from the market. Assume that Bob is able to purchase 50 bond tokens at T1 before reaching the maxPayout limit. As such, the state of the SDAM at T1 will be as follows:
• term.maxDebt = 110
• maxPayout = 100
• market.totalDebt = 99 + 50 = 149
In the above scenario, Bob's purchase has already breached the term.maxDebt limit. However, he could still purchase the 50 bond tokens in the current transaction. In the event that the price of the quote token falls to almost zero (e.g. 0.0001 dollars), then the fastest taker will be able to extract as many payout tokens as possible before reaching the maxPayout limit from the market. The extracted payout tokens are essentially free for the fastest taker. Taker gain is maker loss. Additionally, in the event that a quoted token suddenly loses a large amount of value, the amount of payout tokens lost by the market marker is capped at the maxPayout limit instead of capping the loss at the term.maxDebt limit. This resulted in the market makers losing more payout tokens than expected, and their payout tokens being sold to the takers at a very low price (e.g. 0.0001 dollars). The market makers will suffer more loss if the maxPayout limit of their markets is higher.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a circuit‑breaker enforcement flaw that allows a taker to purchase bond tokens that push the market’s total debt above the configured term.maxDebt limit within a single transaction. The contract checks the maxDebt condition only after the purchase logic has already executed; if market.totalDebt exceeds term.maxDebt, the code simply calls the internal _close function but does not revert the current purchase. Consequently, when a quoted token experiences an abrupt loss of value (for example a stablecoin depeg to near zero), a fast taker can submit a large order that exhausts the remaining payout capacity before the circuit breaker closes the market. In the illustrated scenario, the market started with totalDebt 99 and maxDebt 110. The taker bought 50 bond tokens, raising totalDebt to 149, well above the limit, yet the transaction succeeded because the maxDebt check was performed after the purchase. The market then closed, but the taker obtained payout tokens at a negligible price, effectively receiving free value while the market maker lost payout tokens far beyond the intended maxPayout cap. This bug impacts market makers and any protocol participants who rely on the circuit breaker to cap exposure; they may see their payout balances drop dramatically, refunds missing, or the market closing unexpectedly after a trade. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Bond protocol’s market‑closing logic. It is hard to notice because the transaction appears successful from the user interface, and the circuit‑breaker trigger is not visible until after the state change, making the loss seem like a normal market outcome rather than a contract defect. The root cause is a race‑condition‑like design where the debt limit is enforced post‑execution instead of pre‑validation, allowing the debt to overshoot within the same call. To remediate, the contract should enforce the term.maxDebt ceiling before any bond tokens are minted or transferred, reject or partially fill orders that would exceed the limit, refund the excess quote tokens, and trigger the circuit breaker immediately when the limit is reached. This change restores the intended protection that caps maker loss at the maxDebt threshold rather than at the higher maxPayout amount, preventing free‑token extraction during extreme price drops.

title: BondAggregator.findMarketForFunction Will Break
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market‑selection routine of the BondAggregator contract. The findMarketFor function iterates over all markets that match a given payout and quote token, calling the BondBaseSDA.payoutFor view function for each market to compute the expected payout. payoutFor contains a safety check that reverts the call when the calculated payout exceeds the market‑specific maxPayout limit. Because the call to payoutFor is performed without any error handling, a single market whose maxPayout is lower than the computed payout triggers a revert that propagates out of the for‑loop, aborting the entire findMarketFor execution. This occurs when the caller supplies a minAmountOut value of zero (or any value that satisfies the minAmountOut_ <= maxPayout test) and passes the full amountIn_ to payoutFor, which is the normal case for most callers. Under those conditions, any market with a restrictive maxPayout will cause the whole view function to fail, preventing the contract from returning a list of viable markets. From a user perspective the UI may display an empty market list or report that no markets meet the criteria, even though suitable markets exist. Market makers lose the opportunity to sell their bond tokens because their markets are silently excluded by the revert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the logical flow of the loop was examined and the unchecked revert path was identified. It is subtle because the revert only happens for specific market configurations and the function is marked view, so developers may assume it cannot fail. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call failures that break iteration logic, similar to unhandled exceptions in loops. To remediate, the contract should catch the revert from payoutFor—using Solidity try‑catch on external calls or a low‑level call that returns a success flag—or pre‑filter markets to ensure the payout calculation cannot exceed maxPayout before invoking the function. Proper handling will allow the loop to continue evaluating remaining markets and return a correct set of candidates, preserving the intended market discovery behavior.

title: Use safeMint instead of mint for ERC721
description:
Use safeMint instead of mint for ERC721. The msg.sender will be minted as a proof of staking NFT when _stakeToken() is called. However, if msg.sender is a contract address that does not support ERC721, the NFT can be frozen in the contract. As per the documentation of EIP-721: A wallet/broker/auction application MUST implement the wallet interface if it will accept safe transfers. Ref: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721 As per the documentation of ERC721.sol by Openzeppelin Ref: https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L274-L285
```solidity
/**
 * @dev Mints `tokenId` and transfers it to `to`.
 *
 * WARNING: Usage of this method is discouraged, use {_safeMint} whenever possible
 *
 * Requirements:
 *
 * - `tokenId` must not exist.
 * - `to` cannot be the zero address.
 *
 * Emits a {Transfer} event.
 */
function _mint(address to, uint256 tokenId) internal virtual {
```
Users possibly lose their NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from using the internal _mint function of an ERC‑721 token to issue a staking proof NFT directly to the caller of the staking function. _mint transfers the newly created token to the supplied address without verifying whether the recipient implements the ERC721Receiver interface required for safe transfers. When the caller (msg.sender) is a contract that does not implement onERC721Received, the token is still recorded as owned by that contract, but the contract has no mechanism to acknowledge or forward the NFT. As a result the NFT becomes permanently locked inside the contract’s balance, effectively disappearing from the user’s view. This situation can be triggered whenever the staking entry point calls _stakeToken, which internally invokes _mint(msg.sender, tokenId). If a malicious or simply non‑compliant contract stakes on behalf of a user, the NFT is minted to that contract and cannot be transferred out, leading to a loss of the proof‑of‑stake token. The impact is that users expect to receive a visible NFT representing their stake, but their wallet shows no new token, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting may show a missing NFT, potentially breaking downstream logic that relies on token ownership. The condition for exploitation is any call to the staking function where the caller address is a contract lacking ERC721Receiver support; no special permissions are required. The affected parties include individual stakers, the protocol that relies on the NFT for reward distribution, and any downstream applications that query token ownership. The issue was identified during a manual audit by comparing the contract’s minting logic against the EIP‑721 specification and OpenZeppelin’s documentation, which explicitly warns that _mint should be avoided in favor of _safeMint. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the token is successfully minted, yet the token is effectively unusable, making it easy to overlook during testing. The recommended remediation is to replace the call to _mint with _safeMint, which performs the ERC721Receiver check and reverts if the recipient contract cannot handle ERC721 tokens, or to add an explicit interface check before minting, or to restrict staking to externally owned accounts only. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unsafe token transfer or token lock due to missing safe transfer validation, and it violates the business assumption that every minted NFT will be immediately accessible to the recipient.

title: Hardcoded monsterMultiplier in case of stake
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency between the governance‑controlled monsterMultiplier and the value used when calculating the stakedTimeBonus for Frankenmonster NFTs. The contract defines a mutable variable monsterMultiplier that can be changed through a governance proposal, and the getTokenVotingPower function correctly applies this variable when determining voting power. However, the internal _stakeToken function that records a time‑based bonus for staked tokens contains a hard‑coded expression that divides the full bonus by two for monster tokens, effectively fixing the multiplier at 50% regardless of any later updates. The root cause is the use of a constant division instead of referencing the mutable monsterMultiplier, leading to a business‑logic violation where the intended weighting of monster votes is ignored. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by staking monster NFTs after a governance change, knowing that their voting power will remain capped at half of what the protocol specification promises, thereby skewing governance outcomes in favor of parties holding Frankenpunk NFTs. The impact is a systematic under‑allocation of votes to monster holders, which may cause proposals to pass or fail incorrectly, erode trust in the DAO’s voting fairness, and break accounting assumptions that each token type contributes a predictable share of voting weight. This condition occurs whenever a token is staked with a non‑zero unlock time, because the stake function unconditionally applies the hard‑coded divisor. Affected parties include monster NFT owners, the DAO’s governance process, and any downstream decisions that rely on accurate vote tallies. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the getTokenVotingPower implementation with the staking logic and noticed that the latter did not reference the mutable multiplier. It is subtle because both functions appear to compute voting power, yet only one respects the configurable parameter, making the discrepancy easy to miss in testing. From a user’s perspective, a monster holder may see their expected voting power reduced to roughly half, leading to confusion such as “my votes are missing” or “the UI shows a lower score than before”. The bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded constants that bypass updatable state, violating the protocol’s intended accounting model. The recommended remediation is to replace the hard‑coded division with a reference to the monsterMultiplier variable, ensuring that any governance‑approved change is reflected consistently across all voting‑power calculations.

title: Using ERC721.transferFrom() instead of safeTr
description: There are certain smart contracts that do not support ERC721, using transferFrom() may result in the NFT being sent to such contracts. In unstake(), _to is param from user's input. However, if _to is a contract address that does not support ERC721, the NFT can be frozen in that contract. As per the documentation of EIP-721: A wallet/broker/auction application MUST implement the wallet interface if it will accept safe transfers. Ref: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721 The NFT may get stuck in the contract that does not support ERC721.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of the standard ERC721 transferFrom function in the contract’s unstake routine instead of the safety‑checked safeTransferFrom. transferFrom simply moves the token from the caller to the destination address without verifying that the recipient contract implements the ERC721Receiver interface defined in EIP‑721. Because the unstake function accepts an arbitrary _to address supplied by the user, an attacker or an unwitting user can specify a contract that does not implement the required onERC721Received callback. When the NFT is sent to such a contract, the token is recorded as owned by the contract but the contract has no logic to handle or forward ERC721 assets, effectively freezing the NFT. From the user’s perspective the token disappears from their wallet, the UI may show a zero balance or a missing NFT, and attempts to retrieve the asset through the usual unstake flow fail silently because the transfer does not revert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the unstake implementation, where the lack of a safety check was noted as a deviation from the EIP‑721 recommendation that any wallet, broker, or auction application that accepts safe transfers must implement the ERC721Receiver interface. The problem is subtle because the transaction succeeds, no error is emitted, and the contract’s state appears consistent, making it easy to miss during testing. The impact is that users lose access to their NFTs, potentially losing valuable assets, and the protocol may end up with locked tokens that cannot be re‑issued or accounted for correctly, breaking accounting assumptions about token availability. The vulnerability can be mitigated by replacing transferFrom with safeTransferFrom, which performs the ERC721Receiver check and reverts if the recipient does not support the interface, or by adding an explicit interface check or restricting the _to address to externally owned accounts or whitelisted contracts. In short, the bug belongs to the class of unsafe token transfer patterns that allow assets to be sent to contracts lacking the required receiver logic, leading to token lock‑up and loss of user funds.

title: queue() should increase proposalsPassed in-
description: proposalsCreated will be increased in verifyProposal(), queue() should increase proposalsPassed. Based on the context, queue() should increase userCommunityScoreData[proposal.proposer].proposalsPassed and totalCommunityScoreData.proposalsPassed instead. Due to the presence of setProposalsCreatedMultiplier() and setProposalsPassedMultiplier(), the multiplier of both scores can be different, when that's the case, the proposer's voting power bonuses will be wrongly calculated because proposalsPassed is not correctly increased in queue().
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the queue() function of the governance contract, which is responsible for moving a proposal that has reached the Succeeded state into the execution queue. According to the protocol’s accounting rules, queuing a successful proposal should increment two counters: the proposer’s personal proposalsPassed count stored in userCommunityScoreData and the global proposalsPassed count stored in totalCommunityScoreData. These counters are later used together with configurable multipliers (setProposalsCreatedMultiplier and setProposalsPassedMultiplier) to calculate community voting‑power bonuses that reward proposers for successful governance actions. However, the current implementation of queue() fails to update either of these counters. As a result, when a proposal is queued, the proposer’s personal score and the protocol‑wide score remain unchanged, causing the bonus calculation to rely on stale or incorrect data. This discrepancy becomes especially problematic when the two multipliers differ, because the intended proportional reward for proposalsCreated versus proposalsPassed is no longer respected, leading to either an under‑allocation or over‑allocation of voting power. The impact is that proposers may receive fewer voting‑power bonuses than they are entitled to, or conversely, the protocol may distribute bonuses based on inaccurate community metrics, undermining the incentive model and potentially allowing malicious actors to manipulate the multiplier settings to gain an unfair advantage. The bug manifests only after a proposal transitions to the Succeeded state and queue() is invoked; proposals that remain pending or are rejected are unaffected. Users experience the issue as a missing increase in their community score or a zero reward after a proposal that visibly succeeded and was queued, which can be confusing because the UI shows the proposal as queued but the expected boost in voting power never appears. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting flow with the actual contract code, and it is subtle because the missing increments do not revert or throw errors, making the bug silent and easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the queue() function should be amended to explicitly increment both userCommunityScoreData[proposal.proposer].proposalsPassed and totalCommunityScoreData.proposalsPassed before removing the proposal from the active list, thereby restoring the correct accounting of passed proposals and ensuring that the voting‑power bonuses are calculated as designed.

title: Staking#changeStakeTime and changeStakeAmount
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the staking contract stores a per‑token voting bonus at the moment a token is locked. When a user stakes a token, the contract calculates a fullStakedTimeBonus based on two mutable protocol parameters: maxStakeBonusAmount and maxStakeBonusTime. This calculated bonus is written into a mapping (stakedTimeBonus) and never recomputed. Consequently, any later call to the administrative functions changeStakeTime or changeStakeAmount that modifies those parameters does not retroactively adjust the bonuses of already‑locked tokens. The root cause is the separation of immutable stored bonus values from mutable global multipliers, creating a state inconsistency between the protocol’s current economic rules and the persisted voting power of existing stakes. An attacker or governance actor can exploit this by first allowing a set of users to lock tokens under a low bonus, then increasing maxStakeBonusAmount (or decreasing maxStakeBonusTime) to grant new stakers a higher voting multiplier while the earlier stakers remain stuck with the lower, outdated bonus. Conversely, decreasing the bonus after a token has been locked gives the early staker a permanent advantage because newer participants can only earn the reduced multiplier. The impact is a skewed distribution of voting power that can be leveraged to capture governance decisions, undermine protocol fairness, and potentially lock out legitimate participants from influencing proposals. This condition occurs whenever the contract permits parameter changes after tokens have been staked, and it affects all existing stakers, prospective stakers, and the overall governance mechanism. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the stakingSettings struct and the stored stakedTimeBonus values. It is subtle because the UI typically displays the stored bonus correctly for each token, giving the impression that the system is consistent, while the underlying voting weight calculation used by governance contracts diverges from the displayed values. Users may notice symptoms such as “my voting power stays the same while others suddenly have more influence,” “new stakers receive a higher bonus than I expected,” or “my locked token seems disadvantaged after a parameter change.” The bug belongs to the class of economic‑parameter‑tampering or state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where mutable configuration data is not propagated to dependent persisted state. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit changes to the bonus parameters after any token is locked, or implement a mechanism that recomputes and updates the voting bonus for all affected tokens whenever the parameters are altered. A recommended approach is a public “poke” function that any user can call to iterate over specified tokens and recalculate their voting power based on the current multipliers, thereby normalising the voting distribution and preventing permanent advantage or disadvantage.

title: castVote can be called by anyone even those
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s internal voting routine, which permits any address to invoke the vote function even when the caller holds zero voting power. The function only validates that the proposal is active, that the support flag is within the allowed range, and that the voter has not already voted; it never checks whether the calculated vote weight returned by the staking contract is greater than zero. Because the refund mechanism is tied to the voter’s address rather than the amount of voting power, an attacker can create a large number of fresh addresses, call the vote function with zero votes, and still trigger a refund for each address. By repeating this process, the attacker can systematically drain the vault that holds the refund funds. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is in the Active state and an adversary can submit a transaction to the vote function; it does not depend on any special conditions beyond the existence of an active proposal. All participants in the protocol, including token holders and governance participants, are affected because the vault’s balance can be depleted, undermining the economic incentives and the integrity of the voting process. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the vote‑handling logic and noticed the absence of a non‑zero vote check, a subtle omission that can be easily missed because the function otherwise appears to update vote tallies correctly. The problem is a classic case of insufficient input validation leading to an economic denial‑of‑service style attack, where funds disappear despite the user’s expectation that only holders of voting power can claim refunds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show votes being recorded while the vault balance unexpectedly drops to zero, and users may receive a refund even though they never owned any votes, contradicting the expected behavior that refunds are proportional to actual voting weight. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the retrieved vote count is greater than zero and revert the transaction otherwise, thereby ensuring that only addresses with genuine voting power can participate in the refund flow and preserving the accounting assumptions of the governance system.

title: Adversary can abuse delegating to lower quo-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the quorum calculation in a governance contract that relies on community voting power delegation. When a user delegates their community votes to another address, the contract reduces the total community voting power, which in turn lowers the overall voting power used to compute the quorum threshold for new proposals. The quorum value is locked at the moment a proposal is created, based on the current total voting power. After creating a proposal, a user can self‑delegate, which restores their previously forfeited community votes and updates the total voting power upward, but the quorum value remains the lower figure that was recorded earlier. This sequence allows a group of colluding users to artificially shrink the total voting power before proposal creation, thereby reducing the required quorum, and then regain their votes to meet the artificially lowered quorum and push through a proposal that would not have succeeded under normal conditions. The impact is that proposals can be approved with far fewer genuine votes than intended, breaking the intended security and fairness of the governance process, potentially leading to malicious parameter changes, fund misallocation, or other harmful protocol actions. The issue occurs whenever the contract permits self‑delegation to restore voting power after a proposal has been instantiated and when the quorum is calculated solely from the total voting power at proposal creation without accounting for subsequent delegation changes. All token holders and participants in the protocol’s governance are affected because the integrity of collective decision‑making is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the delegation logic and the quorum‑locking mechanism, noticing that the two behaviours could be combined to lower the quorum threshold. The problem is subtle because delegation and quorum calculation are implemented in separate functions, making the temporary reduction of total voting power easy to overlook, and the self‑delegation appears as a legitimate action from a user’s perspective. To remediate, the contract should either prevent delegation changes from influencing the total voting power used for quorum after a proposal is active, enforce a cooldown period before a delegator can vote on newly created proposals, or adopt a checkpointing system that records immutable snapshots of total voting power for each proposal. By ensuring that the quorum requirement reflects a stable, unalterable voting power total, the protocol can restore the intended security guarantees and prevent collusive quorum‑lowering attacks.

title: Delegate can keep can keep delegatee trapped
bug_full: The contract implements a delegation mechanism where token holders can assign their voting power to another address. Because the staking module does not keep historical vote checkpoints, the code adds a modifier called lockedWhileVotesCast to the unstake and delegate functions. This modifier iterates over every currently active governance proposal and checks two conditions for the caller’s delegate: (1) whether the delegate has already cast a vote on that proposal, and (2) whether the delegate is the proposer of that proposal. If either condition is true, the transaction reverts with a TokenLocked error, preventing the caller from unstaking or changing their delegate. The root cause is the combination of (a) the lack of vote checkpointing, which forces a runtime check of every active proposal, and (b) the overly strict rule that any activity by the delegate – voting or proposing – permanently locks the delegator’s tokens while the proposal remains open. A malicious delegate can exploit this by continuously creating new proposals, either directly or by alternating between multiple accounts, so that there is always at least one active proposal in which they have voted or are listed as proposer. As a result, any delegator whose delegate is this attacker will see every attempt to unstake or re‑delegate fail with a TokenLocked revert. From the user’s point of view the UI shows the usual balance, but when the user clicks “unstake” or “change delegate” the transaction reverts and no tokens are released, contrary to the expectation that they can withdraw at any time. The impact is that funds become effectively frozen for the delegator, governance power cannot be re‑assigned, and the protocol’s voting dynamics can be manipulated by a single actor who can keep a perpetual proposal chain alive. This condition only occurs while there is at least one active proposal involving the delegate; if the attacker stops proposing, the lock is lifted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the delegation logic and identified that the modifier does not differentiate between a single proposal and a series of proposals, allowing an attacker to keep the lock indefinitely. The bug is subtle because the revert message is generic and the logic appears to protect against double voting, making it easy to overlook the possibility of a denial‑of‑service style lock. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “delegation lock” or “proposal‑driven token freeze” bugs, where business rules intended to preserve voting integrity unintentionally give a delegate the ability to trap delegators. To remediate, the contract should provide an emergency ejection function that allows a delegator to withdraw their staked tokens even when the delegate is locked, and optionally blacklist the token from being restaked for a cooldown period equal to the current voting duration. Additional mitigations include implementing vote checkpoints so that the lock check can be performed against a snapshot rather than iterating over live proposals, or relaxing the modifier to allow delegators to override the lock after a reasonable timeout.

title: Veto function should decrease proposalsPassed
description: When a proposal that has passed is vetoed, the proposer still has the bonus of proposalsCreated and proposalsPassed related to the proposal. Both should be decremented because veto is intended to be used for malicious proposals. The function getCommunityVotingPower returns a bonus to users for voting, creating. The veto function is supposed to the malicius proposer should not keep a bonus based in this proposal's creation and/or passing, and the function should decrease both the values of proposalsCreated and proposalsPassed. Malicious proposer keeps bonus after his proposal is vetoed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the governance contract’s veto mechanism, which is intended to penalise proposers of malicious proposals by removing the reputation bonuses they earned for creating and successfully passing a proposal. In the current implementation, when a proposal that has already been marked as verified and subsequently queued is vetoed, the contract does not adjust the proposer’s counters for proposalsCreated and proposalsPassed. These counters feed into the getCommunityVotingPower function, which awards extra voting power based on the number of proposals a user has created and had pass. Because the veto function fails to decrement these values, a malicious proposer retains the full bonus even after the proposal is nullified. The root cause is a missing state‑update branch in the veto logic: the code checks the proposal’s verification status but never reduces the proposer’s contribution to the community score, nor does it update the global totals. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a proposal, ensuring it reaches the passed state, and then triggering a veto (either by an authorized party or through a governance action). The attacker’s voting power remains inflated, allowing them to influence future votes with an unfair advantage. The impact is a distortion of the governance incentive model, where honest participants see their relative voting weight diluted while the malicious actor retains an undeserved boost. This condition occurs whenever a proposal transitions from the Queued state to a vetoed state without the corresponding decrement logic. The affected parties include any proposer whose proposal is vetoed, the overall community scoring system, and the protocol’s governance integrity because the voting power distribution no longer reflects actual contributions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s scoring functions, where the auditor noted that the bonus calculation did not account for vetoed proposals. It is subtle because the counters are internal and not directly exposed in the UI; users may only notice that their voting power does not drop after a veto, which can be mistaken for a UI glitch. To remediate, the veto function should include explicit decrements of both the proposer’s proposalsCreated counter (when the proposal was verified) and the proposalsPassed counter (when the proposal was in the Queued state), as well as the corresponding global totals, thereby restoring the intended penalty and preserving the fairness of the community voting power model.

title: getCommunityVotingPower doesn't calculate voting power correctly due to precision loss
bug_full: The function getCommunityVotingPower is intended to return a user’s total voting weight by applying three separate multipliers (for votes, proposals created and proposals passed) and dividing each product by a constant PERCENT. Because the implementation performs the division on each term individually using Solidity’s integer arithmetic, any fractional remainder from each multiplication is truncated before the results are summed. This per‑term truncation causes a systematic loss of precision, especially when the individual components are small relative to the divisor, leading to an under‑estimation of the overall voting power. The root cause is the classic fixed‑point rounding error that occurs when integer division is applied repeatedly instead of once on the aggregated numerator. An attacker can exploit this by presenting a low but non‑zero score that, after rounding, yields a smaller reported voting power than the protocol’s accounting expects, potentially affecting quorum calculations or the outcome of proposals. The impact is that legitimate participants may see their voting power reduced, causing proposals that should succeed to fail, while a malicious actor could manipulate the relative share of voting power among participants. The bug manifests whenever getCommunityVotingPower is called for any address, including the special sentinel address used to query the total community voting power, because the same per‑term division logic is applied in all cases. All users, delegators, and the governance protocol are affected because voting power is a core input to decision‑making. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s output against a reference calculation and observed a consistent shortfall that grew with the number of components. It is hard to notice because the contract still returns a plausible integer and the loss may be only a few units, which can be mistaken for normal variance in small scores.
