bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability of the payer to retrieve excess amounts of the streaming token that are accidentally transferred to the streaming contract. The contract provides a rescueERC20 function that allows the payer to withdraw any ERC20 token that is not the designated streaming token, but it deliberately blocks withdrawals of the streaming token itself. Consequently, if the payer sends more of the streaming token than required for the stream, the surplus becomes locked inside the contract. The root cause is a missing rescue path for the streaming token; the contract logic treats the streaming token as immutable and only permits its removal through stream cancellation. An attacker or honest user can exploit this by simply over‑funding the contract, after which the only way to recover the surplus is to invoke the cancel‑stream function, which terminates the entire payment flow. This action may disrupt the receiver’s expected cash‑flow, especially in a governance‑driven protocol where restarting a cancelled stream may require a vote that the receiver cannot pass. The impact includes locked funds, interruption of scheduled payments, potential loss of trust, and operational delays for the receiver. The issue manifests whenever the payer mistakenly transfers an amount larger than the intended stream balance, a scenario that is realistic because users often interact with token contracts using generic transfer interfaces. It was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the rescue capabilities for generic ERC20 tokens against the special‑case handling of the streaming token. The problem is subtle because the rescue function works for all other tokens, giving a false sense of safety, while the special‑case restriction is easy to overlook. To remediate, the rescueERC20 function should be extended to allow the payer to withdraw a limited amount of the streaming token that exceeds the remaining stream balance, while still protecting the portion that is owed to the receiver. This change restores the ability to recover accidental over‑deposits without having to cancel the entire stream, preserving both fund availability and protocol continuity.

title: GLOBAL-4 | Centralization Risk
description: The exchange keeper and other permissioned addresses have the power to do nearly anything: Execute any order or liquidation at any arbitrary price Defer execution of any arbitrary deposit, withdrawal, order, or liquidation Select the order of execution for all incoming deposits, withdrawals, and orders Power to shut off any feature – including withdrawals and closing positions Change out the protocol-wide variables used in the dataStore There are many assumptions made on the form of the price input from the keeper. Adding validation for the expected format and range of acceptable inputs would reduce the risk of high-cost mistakes, and assist in limiting the scope of the internal exploits available to the keeper. The keeper must diligently execute orders, for example stop loss orders must be executed with the correct range of prices while staying within the MAX_ORACLE_PRICE_AGE limit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from the design that grants the exchange keeper and other privileged addresses unrestricted authority over core protocol actions. Because the keeper can execute any order or liquidation at any price, defer or reorder deposits, withdrawals, orders, and liquidations, and even disable features such as withdrawals or position closing, the protocol relies on the honesty and correctness of a single party. The root cause is the absence of on-chain validation and governance constraints on the inputs and actions performed by the keeper, as well as the lack of multi-signature or timelock mechanisms for changes to protocol-wide variables stored in the data store. An attacker who compromises the keeper’s private key, or a malicious insider, could submit malformed price data, arbitrarily delay or reorder user operations, or shut down withdrawal functionality, causing users to receive no funds, experience unexpected liquidation at unfavorable prices, or see their positions frozen. The impact includes loss of user funds, erosion of trust, and potential market manipulation. The condition occurs whenever the keeper is required to act – for order execution, liquidation, deposit/withdrawal processing, or protocol parameter updates – and there is no secondary check on the price format, range, or timeliness (MAX_ORACLE_PRICE_AGE). All users of the platform, including traders, liquidity providers, and anyone holding synthetic assets, are affected because the centralized authority can alter the outcome of their transactions. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that highlighted the breadth of privileged functions and the lack of defensive checks. Because the behavior is controlled off-chain and only visible through transaction outcomes, it can be difficult to notice until a mis-execution occurs, especially when the keeper behaves correctly most of the time. To mitigate the risk, the keeper’s private keys should be protected with hardware security modules, multi-party signatures, and strict operational procedures. Additionally, the contract should enforce validation of price inputs (format, range, freshness), require timelocked governance for changes to protocol variables, and introduce fallback mechanisms that allow users to contest or revert suspicious executions. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized authority over critical state transitions” and violates the expected decentralized, trust-less accounting model of the protocol.

title: ERTR-1 | Any Address May Rescue Trapped ETH
description: The sendWnt function can be called by anyone to collect any ether that may find itself in the ExchangeRouter contract. Meanwhile, the FundReceiver contract that the ExchangeRouter extends stipulates that the controller is the only address that can recover these funds using the recoverNativeToken function.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unrestricted ether‑recovery function in the ExchangeRouter contract. The sendWnt function is publicly callable and forwards any ether held by the contract to the caller without checking the caller’s identity. The contract inherits from FundReceiver, which defines a recoverNativeToken function that is explicitly limited to the controller address, creating the expectation that only the controller can retrieve trapped native tokens. The root cause is the absence of an access‑control check (e.g., onlyController modifier) on sendWnt, allowing any external account to invoke it. An attacker can exploit this by simply calling sendWnt when the contract holds ether—such ether may accumulate from failed swaps, accidental transfers, or refunds. Upon invocation, the contract’s entire ether balance is sent to the attacker’s address, effectively draining the funds. This can happen at any time the contract contains ether, regardless of the intended recovery policy, and affects all parties that rely on the contract’s accounting, including users, token holders, and the protocol’s controller. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the access restrictions of recoverNativeToken with the implementation of sendWnt and identified the mismatch. Because the function may appear to be an internal utility, tests that do not simulate external calls with ether present can miss the problem, making it hard to notice in routine testing. The impact is a loss of ether that was presumed to be safely locked, breaking trust in the protocol’s financial guarantees and potentially causing accounting inconsistencies where the protocol reports higher balances than are actually available. To remediate, the sendWnt logic should be refactored to either restrict calls to the controller, remove the function entirely if unnecessary, or ensure it only forwards the exact amount of ether supplied by the caller rather than the contract’s full balance. This aligns the implementation with the intended access‑control model and prevents unauthorized rescue of trapped ether.

title: GLOBAL-5 | Execution Fee DoS
description: There is a potential DoS with createDeposit, createWithdrawal, and createOrder as a malicious address may send a miniscule amount of WNT to the deposit/withdrawal/order store such that another user’s WNT deposit no longer matches the executionFee in their deposit. Thus, the deposit execution reverts and is unable to be created.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises in the deposit, withdrawal and order creation pathways of the protocol when a strict equality check is used to verify that the stored WNT amount for a user exactly matches the required execution fee. The root cause is that the contract assumes only its own functions can modify the accounting entry for a user, but an attacker can send a minuscule amount of WNT directly to the contract’s internal store (for example by transferring tokens to the contract address or exploiting a fallback that credits the store). This external transfer increases the recorded balance for a victim’s deposit without the victim’s consent, causing the equality comparison between the stored balance and the expected execution fee to fail. When the check fails, the createDeposit, createWithdrawal or createOrder transaction reverts, preventing the legitimate user from completing the operation. The impact is that honest users are unable to create new deposits, withdraw funds or place orders, effectively locking their ability to interact with the protocol and potentially freezing funds that depend on those actions. The condition occurs whenever the contract relies on an exact match between the stored amount and the execution fee and does not protect the accounting entry from arbitrary token transfers. All participants who attempt to use the affected functions are affected, while the attacker can selectively block specific users by targeting their deposit identifiers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the strict equality logic and the lack of access control on the underlying token balance storage. It can be hard to notice because token transfers to a contract are generally allowed and the contract’s public interface does not expose the internal balance manipulation, making the failure appear as an unexplained “execution fee mismatch” error. To remediate, the strict equality should be replaced with a more tolerant comparison (e.g., require the stored amount to be at least the execution fee) or the accounting should be isolated so that only authorized contract functions can modify a user’s deposit amount, preventing external addresses from inflating the stored balance. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state manipulation DoS vulnerabilities where external inputs can corrupt internal invariants that the contract relies on for correct operation, leading to unexpected reverts and loss of service.

title: GLOBAL-6 | Missing Validation
description: When creating a deposit, there is no validation that the longToken or the shortToken are valid for the supplied market. If WBTC is accidentally used as the long token in an ETH/USDC market, the user would lose their WBTC in the depositStore. Furthermore, there is no validation that either the long token amount or short token amount is non-zero. This check should be added to prevent the keeper from executing trivial deposits. Additionally, when creating an order, there is no validation that the initial collateral token is valid for the provided market, which can lead to invalid orders stored in the orderStore.
bug_full: Missing validation in deposit and order creation functions allows users to submit deposits or orders with tokens that do not belong to the specified market and with zero amounts. The contract does not check that the longToken or shortToken supplied for a deposit matches the market's token pair, nor that the initial collateral token for an order is part of the market. Consequently, a user can unintentionally or maliciously deposit an unrelated token such as WBTC into an ETH/USDC market. The depositStore records the amount under the market identifier, but later settlement logic expects ETH or USDC, causing the WBTC to become inaccessible and effectively lost. Similarly, zero‑amount deposits pass the checks, creating entries that a keeper may later process, wasting gas and potentially opening avenues for denial‑of‑service. The vulnerability stems from absent whitelist or sanity checks in the contract’s input handling, a classic case of insufficient input validation. An attacker can craft a transaction that calls the deposit function with a mismatched token address and a non‑zero amount, causing the contract to accept the deposit and lock the tokens in a storage slot that is never referenced by any withdrawal or settlement routine. The impact is loss of user funds and disruption of the market’s accounting, as the protocol’s invariant that each market only holds its two designated tokens is broken. The issue manifests whenever a deposit or order is created; it does not depend on any special state, only on the caller providing wrong token parameters. All participants—depositors, order makers, keepers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the protocol may hold tokens it cannot later transfer or settle. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public interface with the market definition and noticed the absence of require statements checking token compatibility and non‑zero amounts. Because the contract does not emit explicit error messages for these cases, the problem can be hard to notice; a transaction may succeed while the funds are silently trapped. The recommended remediation is to add explicit validation that the longToken and shortToken supplied to a deposit belong to the market’s token pair, that the collateral token for an order is one of the market’s tokens, and that at least one of the token amounts is greater than zero. These checks should revert with clear error messages, restoring the invariant that each market only contains its designated assets. This class of bug is commonly referred to as missing input validation or token whitelist enforcement, and it violates the business logic that deposits must correspond to the market’s underlying assets, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential fund loss.

title: ERTR-2 | Weak Referrals
description: A trader is allowed to specify a different referral code each time an order is created. Only one affiliate is permitted per trader account, so when an order is created with a different affiliate, the affiliate associated with the trader’s account is updated. This can lead to affiliates missing out on rewards if a trader decides to use another affiliate’s referral code even if they were the one to bring the trader onto the platform.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the referral mechanism of a trading platform where each trader is allowed to provide a referral code when creating an order. The contract stores a single affiliate identifier per trader account and updates this identifier every time a new order is submitted with a different referral code. Because the logic does not enforce immutability of the first referrer, a trader can arbitrarily replace the original affiliate with another one simply by specifying a different code on a subsequent order. This behaviour violates the expected business rule that the affiliate who initially brings a trader to the platform should continue to receive rewards for all of that trader’s activity. The root cause is the lack of a guard that locks the affiliate mapping after the first association, combined with per‑order acceptance of a referral code without validation against the existing affiliate. An attacker – in this case the trader themselves or a colluding party – can exploit the flaw by submitting an order with a competitor’s referral code, causing the contract to overwrite the stored affiliate. The immediate impact is that the original referrer loses commission that would otherwise be earned, leading to inaccurate reward accounting, reduced incentive for affiliates, and potential loss of trust in the platform’s fairness. The issue manifests whenever a trader places more than one order and chooses to change the referral code; it does not require any special permissions. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the referral handling logic and noticed that the affiliate address is written on every order without a check for prior assignment. The problem can be subtle because the UI may simply show the referral code field on each order, giving the impression that changing it is normal, while the backend silently rewrites the affiliate mapping. To remediate, the referral logic should be refactored so that the first affiliate linked to a trader is immutable, or alternatively the system should support multiple affiliates with a defined split, but in any case it must prevent arbitrary overwriting of the original referrer. This class of bug falls under mutable state misuse and reward‑allocation logic errors, where a critical mapping is unintentionally mutable, leading to loss of earned rewards and broken accounting assumptions.

title: GLOBAL-7 | Cannot Cancel Deposits/Withdrawals
description: A user does not have the capability to cancel their deposit or withdrawal like with an order. As a result, if the keeper for some reason does not execute their deposit/withdrawal, their funds are locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing cancellation mechanism for pending deposit and withdrawal requests. In the contract, when a user initiates a deposit or withdrawal, the request is stored and later executed by a designated keeper. The code does not provide any function that allows the originating user to withdraw the request before the keeper processes it. Consequently, if the keeper fails to execute the request—because of network congestion, gas limits, a bug, or malicious behavior—the user's funds remain locked in the contract with no way to retrieve them. This situation violates the expected business logic that users should retain control over their assets until the operation is completed. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the order lifecycle, where the absence of a cancel path was noted. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows a pending status and does not display an error, leading users to assume the operation will eventually succeed. The impact is that users lose access to the deposited amount, potentially for an indefinite period, reducing confidence in the protocol and affecting overall liquidity. The problem occurs whenever a deposit or withdrawal request is in the pending state and has not yet been executed by the keeper. Affected parties include any user who relies on the ability to reverse a pending operation and the protocol itself, which may accumulate unrecoverable balances. The bug belongs to the class of stuck‑funds or non‑reversible state transition vulnerabilities, where asynchronous actions lack a user‑initiated rollback. To remediate, the contract should introduce a cancel function that checks the request’s execution status, returns the locked amount to the user, and clears the pending record, thereby restoring the expected invariant that users can always reclaim unprocessed funds.

title: ORDU-4 | Unnecessary Execution Fee
description: A user can cancel an order on their own without the need of a keeper. Even if a user cancels an order on their own accord, the executionFee is paid to the keeper which doubles the amount of gas a user expends.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic misallocation where the protocol pays the executionFee to a keeper even when the order cancellation is initiated directly by the order owner. The root cause is a logic path that unconditionally transfers the executionFee to the keeper on every cancellation, without checking whether the caller is the user who placed the order or an authorized keeper. An attacker does not need to exploit a flaw; any regular user can trigger the condition simply by calling the cancel function themselves. When this happens the user’s transaction pays the normal gas cost for the cancellation and, in addition, the contract transfers the predefined executionFee to the keeper. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome is that the order is removed and only the gas used by the transaction is deducted, but in reality the user sees a larger deduction from their balance, often appearing as a “double fee” or “extra charge”. This extra cost reduces the economic efficiency of the protocol and can discourage users from managing their own orders. The issue occurs whenever a user calls the cancellation method directly, regardless of the order state, and it affects all participants who rely on self‑service order management. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee handling logic and noticed that the executionFee transfer is not gated by the caller’s role. The problem can be subtle because the fee transfer looks like a normal part of the contract’s operation, making it easy to overlook that the same fee is being paid twice. To remediate, the contract should include a condition that skips the executionFee payment when the caller is the order owner, reserving the fee only for external keepers that perform automated cancellations. This change restores the intended accounting model where users only pay for the gas they consume, aligning the protocol’s incentives with its economic design and preventing unnecessary fund loss.

title: GLOBAL-8 | Unintelligible Revert Reasons
description: In every catch (bytes memory _reason) case, the reason is parsed with string(abi.encode(_reason)) However, parsing the bytes reason like this results in unintelligible revert strings. The first 4 bytes of the _reason bytes represent the selector for the error that caused the revert, and the rest represent the data that accompanies the error. There ought to be a way (perhaps off-chain) to map from these 4 bytes to the error type and decode the data. Additionally, panic reverts will be caught in this case and should not be parsed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of unintelligible revert messages that are produced whenever a contract catches a low‑level error using a catch clause that receives the raw bytes of the revert reason (bytes memory _reason) and then attempts to turn those bytes into a string by calling string(abi.encode(_reason)). This approach concatenates the 4‑byte selector that identifies the error type with the encoded error data, and then treats the whole blob as UTF‑8 text. Because the selector and the data are not valid character data, the resulting string is a series of unreadable characters that provide no useful information to developers, auditors, or users. The root cause is the misuse of abi.encode for decoding revert data instead of extracting the selector and decoding the payload according to the error’s ABI. The problem manifests whenever any catch block in the contract follows this pattern, including cases where a Solidity panic (e.g., arithmetic overflow) is caught; panic errors are also encoded with a selector and data, and the same faulty conversion hides the actual panic reason. An attacker does not directly profit from this bug, but the lack of clear error messages makes debugging difficult, can mask underlying logic failures, and may lead to mis‑interpretation of contract state during incident response. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a blank error field, a string of random symbols, or simply “transaction reverted” without any hint of why, contrary to the expectation that a revert reason such as “Insufficient collateral” or “Invalid signature” would be shown. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s error‑handling code and noted that the conversion produced gibberish. It is hard to notice because the transaction still reverts correctly and funds are returned, so the contract appears to function, yet developers lose visibility into the cause of failures. The bug belongs to the class of error‑handling and revert‑reason decoding flaws, where raw revert data is mishandled. To remediate, the contract should avoid converting the raw bytes directly to a string. Instead it should extract the first four bytes, map them to the corresponding custom error or Solidity error identifier (potentially using an off‑chain lookup table), and then decode the remaining data with abi.decode according to the identified error’s parameter types. Alternatively, the contract can re‑throw the original error or emit a custom event with a human‑readable message, thereby preserving the original revert reason. Proper handling also requires distinguishing panic errors and either propagating them unchanged or decoding them with the known Panic(uint256) signature. Implementing these changes restores transparent error reporting, aids debugging, and prevents confusion caused by garbled revert strings.

title: OBU-3 | Unexpected Frozen Order
description: When a limit order is executed with an invalid increasing/decreasing price range, the order reverts with a bespoke revert string–which results in the order getting frozen. But this is unexpected as all other order price-related errors simply revert and will be retried. This might lead to a poor execution of limit order types or a complete lack of execution of limit orders.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a limit‑order execution path where the contract validates the price range of an incoming order. When the price range is invalid—specifically when the increasing or decreasing bounds do not satisfy the expected relationship—the contract triggers a revert using a bespoke revert string instead of the standard error handling used for other price‑related failures. Because the order manager only recognises a predefined error key (for example UNACCEPTABLE_PRICE_ERROR_KEY) to mark an order as retryable, the custom revert string is not interpreted, causing the order to be marked as frozen rather than being automatically retried. This behaviour is unexpected: most price‑validation errors cause the order to revert and then be resubmitted by the execution engine, but the bespoke revert bypasses that logic. The root cause is the mismatch between the error signalling mechanism and the order‑state machine, i.e., the contract emits an error that the surrounding infrastructure does not handle. An attacker or a careless user can craft a limit order with a deliberately malformed price range, causing the transaction to revert with the custom string and leaving the order in a frozen state. The impact is that the user’s order never executes, funds remain locked in the order contract, and the user sees a “Frozen” status in the UI with no further activity. From a protocol perspective, a large number of frozen orders can reduce liquidity, degrade the reliability of limit‑order types, and potentially lead to missed trading opportunities. The condition occurs only when the price‑range validation fails and the bespoke revert path is taken; normal price errors continue to be handled correctly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the handling of different revert paths and noted the inconsistency. It is hard to notice because the transaction simply fails with a custom message, and the UI does not surface a clear error, only a frozen order flag. To remediate, the contract should emit a custom error that is registered with the order manager in the same way as UNACCEPTABLE_PRICE_ERROR_KEY, or otherwise map the revert to the existing retry logic, ensuring that invalid price ranges trigger a retryable failure rather than a permanent freeze. Conceptually, this is a mismatch between error signalling and state‑transition handling, a class of bug where custom revert messages are not integrated into the surrounding orchestration layer, leading to unintended order immobilisation.

title: GLOBAL-9 | Possible Loss of Funds
description: When creating a decrease order or a swap order, there is no validation that the receiver address is not the zero address. In this case, when the order is executed and a swap takes place, the user’s funds will be left in the MarketToken, otherwise if no swap is executed during the decrease, the funds would be sent to the zero address.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step for the destination address when a user creates either a decrease order or a swap order in the market contract. The contract assumes that the provided receiver address is a valid, non‑zero address, but it does not enforce this rule. As a result, if a user (or an attacker) supplies the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) as the receiver, the execution path diverges depending on whether a swap occurs. When a swap is performed, the contract transfers the user’s funds into the internal MarketToken balance instead of sending them to an external address, effectively locking the assets inside the contract with no public withdrawal function for that specific flow. If no swap happens during a decrease operation, the contract attempts to transfer the funds to the zero address, which causes the tokens to be burned and permanently removed from circulation. This flaw can be exploited by submitting a crafted order that includes the zero address as the receiver; the attacker does not need any special privileges because the contract does not check the address. The impact is a loss of user funds: users expect their tokens to be returned to their wallet after a decrease or swap, but instead they see their balance unchanged, receive nothing, or notice that the tokens have vanished from their account. The condition occurs whenever an order is created without proper input sanitisation, i.e., any call to the decrease or swap functions that passes an unchecked address. All participants who interact with the market – traders, liquidity providers, and any external callers – are potentially affected because the bug resides in a core accounting routine. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed input validation and fund flow logic; the auditor noted the absence of a require statement checking that the receiver is not address(0). The problem is subtle because the transaction may still succeed and emit normal events, giving the impression that the operation completed correctly, while the funds are silently trapped or burned. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero address check for any parameter that designates a recipient of transferred assets, and it should ensure that fallback paths route funds back to a valid user‑controlled address rather than the contract’s internal token balance or the zero address. This class of bug falls under “missing input validation leading to asset loss” and is analogous to other cases where unchecked addresses cause funds to be irretrievably locked or destroyed. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful trade, but the wallet balance would either stay the same or drop to zero, contradicting the expectation that the trade would return the appropriate amount of tokens. The violation is of basic accounting invariants: the sum of user balances should be conserved, yet the bug creates a sink where tokens disappear, breaking the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: FR-1 | Lack of Access Control For Events
description: Anyone can call notifyFeeReceived as there is a lack of access control, which leads to a depreciation of the authenticity of the event.
bug_full: An unauthenticated public function named notifyFeeReceived can be invoked by any address. The function emits a FeeReceived event that external services and user interfaces rely on to display that a fee has been transferred to the protocol. Because there is no access control, an attacker can call the function with arbitrary parameters, causing the contract to emit events that do not correspond to any real token transfer. This falsifies the on‑chain log, depreciates the authenticity of the event, and can mislead off‑chain accounting, dashboards, or reward distribution mechanisms that trust the event as proof of payment. The issue occurs whenever the contract is deployed with the function marked public and no modifier restricting callers. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s public interface and noticed the absence of any onlyOwner or role‑based checks. The problem is subtle because the contract’s internal state does not change; therefore the bug does not cause a revert or obvious on‑chain error, making it easy to overlook. Users may see a fee notification in the UI but their wallet balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing‑access‑control bugs that affect event authenticity. To remediate, the function should be protected by an appropriate access‑control modifier (e.g., onlyOwner, onlyFeeManager) or made internal and called only from authorized code paths, ensuring that only legitimate fee transfers can generate the corresponding event.

title: MKTU-4 | Lack of Funding Fees When OI Is Stacked
description: When computing funding fees in the getNextFundingAmountPerSize function, the cache.oi.longOpenInterest == 0 || cache.oi.shortOpenInterest == 0 condition stipulates that when all of the open interest is stacked on one side no funding fees are charged to the users who have positions on the stacked side. This means there is a lack of disincentive for the users with stacked positions to switch sides. In such a case, the funding fees could be redirected to the poolAmount for the benefit of LPers. Exchanges like Binance have a minimum funding fee that is held at all times to properly disincentivize such imbalances.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an edge‑case fee exemption that occurs when the market’s open interest (OI) is completely stacked on one side. In the function that calculates the next funding amount per size, the code checks whether the long or short OI equals zero and, if so, skips the funding fee calculation entirely. This logic assumes that fees are only needed when both sides have exposure, but the root cause is a business‑logic flaw: the contract treats a zero‑interest side as a condition to waive fees rather than enforcing a minimum fee or redirecting the fee to the pool. An attacker or any trader can exploit this by ensuring that the opposite side has no open positions—either by closing all opposing positions or by opening a dominant position that drives the other side’s OI to zero. Once the condition is met, the protocol does not deduct any funding fee from the positions on the stacked side, allowing those traders to hold large positions without paying the periodic financing cost that would normally be charged. The impact is twofold: users on the stacked side receive an unintended free‑funding benefit, and liquidity providers lose the fee revenue that should have been collected, potentially eroding the incentive structure that keeps the market balanced. This situation occurs whenever the market reaches a state where either long or short OI is zero, which can happen after large trades or coordinated position closures. The affected parties include any trader with positions on the dominant side, the protocol’s fee pool, and ultimately all participants who rely on fair funding mechanics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed the conditional check that returns zero fees when one side’s OI is zero. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display a funding rate, yet the on‑chain transfer of fees is silently omitted, leading to a mismatch between displayed rates and actual balance changes. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to always compute a funding fee regardless of the OI distribution, possibly enforcing a minimum fee or routing the fee to a designated pool or fee receiver, thereby restoring the intended disincentive for one‑sided market positions. This class of bug is a conditional fee exemption or minimum‑fee omission, which violates the accounting assumption that funding fees are always collected to balance long and short exposure and to compensate liquidity providers. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after a funding interval the expected deduction from their balance does not occur, even though the protocol shows a non‑zero funding rate, leading to confusion and potential unfair advantage.

title: OCL-1 | Chainlink Feed Validation
description: Extra validation checks should be added on the result from the Chainlink price feed to ensure non-stale data. The price from the data feed influences the execution of orders and liquidations so it is imperative the data is up to date and correct.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of the Chainlink price feed data before it is used to drive order execution and liquidation logic. The contract trusts the raw price returned by the external oracle without checking whether the reported round is the most recent one or whether the round has been fully populated, i.e., it does not verify that answeredInRound is greater than or equal to the expected round identifier and that the timestamp of the round is non‑zero. Because of this omission, a stale or incomplete price can be accepted as current. An attacker who can influence the oracle or wait for a delay in the feed can cause the contract to read an outdated price, which may be significantly different from the market price at the time of the transaction. When the stale price is used, orders may be filled at an unfavorable rate, and liquidations may be triggered incorrectly, potentially wiping out user collateral or causing unnecessary liquidations. The impact is therefore loss of funds for traders, incorrect accounting for the protocol, and erosion of trust in the system. The issue manifests whenever the Chainlink feed fails to update within the expected interval, such as during network congestion, oracle downtime, or when the feed returns a round that has not yet been completed. All participants who rely on accurate pricing – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the absence of sanity checks on the feed data. It can be hard to notice because the price value appears syntactically correct and the contract does not emit any warning when the data is stale, so normal operation seems unchanged while the underlying accounting is wrong. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce explicit checks that the answeredInRound is at least the current round identifier and that the timestamp of the round is greater than zero before using the price, causing the transaction to revert if the data is stale. This aligns the implementation with the standard Chainlink best practices for feed validation and restores confidence that only fresh, complete price information influences critical financial actions.

title: MKTF-1 | Malicious Backing Token
description: In the future, GMX hopes to enable permissionless MarketToken creation. However, a MarketToken can use an arbitrary malicious backing token that performs mischievous actions such as cancelling orders on the exchange during execution when the token is transferred. Additionally, it is possible for contracts of the existing tokens on the exchange to be upgraded with new logic that is able to maliciously exploit the exchange.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the ability for a MarketToken created on the GMX synthetic exchange to specify any ERC20 token as its backing asset. Because the exchange does not restrict the behaviour of the backing token, a malicious token can execute arbitrary code during its transfer callback (e.g., via ERC777 hooks or a token that overrides transfer to call external contracts). When the exchange attempts to move the backing token as part of order execution or settlement, the malicious token can re‑enter the exchange contract and perform actions such as cancelling the order, modifying the order state, or draining funds. In addition, because the exchange supports upgradeable token contracts, an attacker who controls the implementation of an existing token can upgrade it to a version that contains the same re‑entrancy logic, thereby affecting all users that trade that token. The issue arises from the lack of a re‑entrancy guard around token transfer operations and the assumption that transferred tokens are benign. An attacker can exploit the flaw by deploying a token that, in its transfer function, calls back into the exchange's order‑matching function and triggers a cancellation before the original transfer completes. The impact is that legitimate users may see their orders disappear, trades fail, or funds become temporarily locked, leading to loss of confidence and potential financial loss if the malicious token also manipulates balances. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user places or settles an order that involves a token whose contract contains malicious logic, or when an existing token is upgraded to a malicious implementation. All participants of the exchange—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the exchange’s accounting assumes that token transfers are atomic and side‑effect free. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the token handling path and identified that the contract does not prevent re‑entrancy from external token contracts. It can be difficult to notice because the token appears to conform to the ERC20 interface and the unexpected order cancellation occurs only during the narrow window of a transfer, making the behaviour look like a normal market event. The proper mitigation is to treat token transfers as untrusted external calls: use a checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, add a non‑re‑entrant modifier around any function that moves tokens, and optionally whitelist only known safe backing assets or enforce that tokens cannot be upgraded after being listed. By isolating token transfer logic and preventing re‑entry, the exchange can ensure that malicious backing tokens cannot interfere with order execution or cancel trades.

title: OCL-2 | Median Price Validation
description: There should be validation that the medianMaxPrice is greater than the medianMinPrice. Otherwise, many critical exchange values such as poolValue, pnlToPoolFactor, and many others could be adversely affected.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation check that allows the median maximum price to be set lower than or equal to the median minimum price. This logical error originates from the contract’s price‑range handling code, which accepts two oracle‑derived values – medianMinPrice and medianMaxPrice – without enforcing the fundamental invariant that the maximum must be greater than the minimum. When the invariant is violated, downstream calculations that depend on a proper price interval, such as the pool value, profit‑and‑loss‑to‑pool factor, and other accounting metrics, produce incorrect results. An attacker or a faulty data source can supply a price update where medianMaxPrice ≤ medianMinPrice, causing the contract to compute negative or zero pool values, mis‑price synthetic positions, and potentially allocate insufficient or excessive payouts. From a user’s perspective this may appear as a missing refund, a balance that unexpectedly drops to zero, or a payout that is far lower than expected. The issue is triggered whenever the oracle update routine writes the two price bounds without a guard clause, which can happen during volatile market conditions, data feed glitches, or deliberate manipulation. All participants who rely on the contract’s pricing – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that the pool is fully collateralised and that payouts are correctly derived from market prices are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit review that identified the absence of a require statement enforcing medianMaxPrice > medianMinPrice. It is subtle because the contract may still operate with seemingly reasonable numbers, and the error only manifests when the price bounds cross, a scenario that may be rare in normal operation. To remediate the issue, the contract should include an explicit validation step (e.g., require(medianMaxPrice > medianMinPrice)) before any calculations that use these values, ensuring that the price interval is always well‑formed and that downstream financial formulas remain sound.

title: A user can use the same proof for a commitment more than 1 time
description: A user can use the same commitment signature and merkleData more than 1 time to obtain another loan.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay flaw in the loan commitment mechanism of the Astaria protocol. Aborrower can reuse the same signed commitment and Merkle proof to obtain more than one loan against the same NFT collateral. The root cause is that the signature verification performed in the vault’s _validateCommitment function hashes only the strategy data that excludes the strategy.vault address and the strategy version, and the contract does not maintain any nonce or one‑time‑use marker for a commitment. Because the signed hash does not bind the commitment to the specific vault that processes the loan, an attacker can modify the strategy.vault field and the stack data, call commitToLien directly on the vault after transferring the NFT to the CollateralToken contract, and pass all signature and Merkle checks. The exploit can be carried out by first taking a legitimate loan through the AstariaRouter, then re‑using the same commitment with altered fields to request a second loan either through the router again or by invoking the vault directly. When successful, the protocol issues a second payout while the same collateral remains recorded only once, effectively creating an under‑collateralized position and causing the protocol’s funds to disappear. The issue occurs whenever a valid commitment exists and the attacker can control the strategy.vault and stack parameters; it is not prevented by any existing checks because the contract only validates ownership, signature, Merkle proof, and rate/amount limits, none of which consider replay protection. Users are affected because they may receive a loan they did not intend to request, and the protocol is affected because its accounting assumptions—one loan per collateral—are violated, leading to potential loss of funds. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of commitToLien and identified that the encoded strategy data used for ecrecover omitted critical fields, allowing the same proof to be accepted multiple times. The problem is subtle because the signature appears valid and all other validation steps succeed, making it easy to miss without inspecting the exact data that is signed. To remediate, the protocol should bind the commitment to the specific vault (and optionally the strategy version) in the signed message, introduce a per‑user or per‑commitment nonce that is incremented after each successful loan, and reject any commitment that has already been used. This would enforce a one‑time‑use policy and prevent replay attacks that cause multiple loans against a single NFT.

title: `_buyoutLien`
description: Illegal liquidationInitialAsk, resulting in insufficient bids to cover the debt.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic flaw in the internal function that processes a lien buyout. When a caller attempts to purchase a lien, the function iterates over the existing stack of liens, accumulates the total debt that would be owed (potentialDebt) and checks that this amount does not exceed the liquidationInitialAsk value associated with each lien. However, the comparison is performed against the liquidationInitialAsk stored in the original (old) stack that was supplied as input, not against the stack that will exist after the new lien is inserted (the newStack). Because the function later replaces part of the stack with a new lien, the liquidationInitialAsk of the affected position can change, but the validation step never sees the updated value. Consequently, a malicious actor can craft a buyout where the accumulated debt is higher than the true liquidationInitialAsk of the resulting stack, bypassing the intended safety check. The exploit proceeds by calling the buyout function with a stack that contains an expired or near‑expiry lien, causing the loop to compute a potentialDebt that exceeds the real liquidation threshold. Since the contract checks the old threshold, the transaction succeeds and the buyer acquires a lien that is under‑collateralised. When the protocol later attempts to liquidate the position, the bids collected may be insufficient to cover the outstanding debt, leading to a shortfall of funds. Users observing the UI may see that their expected refund or payout is zero or far lower than anticipated, while the protocol’s accounting shows a mismatch between debt and available collateral. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where reviewers noted a comment marking the use of the old stack as a potential bug. It is difficult to spot because the code appears to perform a sensible check, and typical test cases may not exercise the path where the new stack’s liquidationInitialAsk differs from the old one. The proper remediation is to perform the liquidationInitialAsk validation against the stack after the replacement (newStack) or to recompute the threshold based on the new lien’s details before finalising the buyout, ensuring that the debt never exceeds the actual liquidation ask. This class of bug falls under “state‑inconsistent validation” where a contract validates against stale state, breaking accounting invariants and allowing economic loss.

title: `settleAuction`
description: ClearingHouse.safeTransferFrom() to execute successfully even if there is no bid.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic error in the settleAuction function that determines whether an auction can be settled. The function is supposed to revert when there is no active auction (collateralIdToAuction == 0) or when the underlying NFT is not owned by the clearing house. However the code uses a logical AND (&&) between the two checks and also uses a negated comparison, which means the revert is only triggered when both conditions are true simultaneously. Consequently, if an auction exists but receives no bids, the condition evaluates to false and the function proceeds to call ClearingHouse.safeTransferFrom, transferring the collateral to the clearing house without any payment. This allows an attacker or any caller to settle an empty auction and cause the collateral to be moved out of the user's control. The impact is that users may lose ownership of their NFT or see their collateral disappear without receiving any compensation. The bug manifests at the end of an auction when settleAuction is invoked, typically by anyone. It affects all participants who lock collateral in the protocol, including borrowers and lenders. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the auction flow, where the conditional logic was compared against the intended specification and found to be inverted. Because the function does not emit an explicit error when no bid is present, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed when a user’s NFT is unexpectedly transferred after an auction with zero bids. The correct fix is to replace the && with a logical OR (||) and to ensure the ownership comparison uses equality rather than inequality, matching the intended guard: if (auctionId == 0 || owner != clearingHouse) revert. This restores the intended safety check and prevents unauthorized transfers. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper conditional checks leading to authorization bypass, often referred to as “logic flaw in access control” or “incorrect auction settlement guard”. From a user perspective, the UI may show that an auction has ended, but the user’s balance shows the NFT is no longer in their wallet, and no refund or payment is recorded. Users expect the auction to either award the highest bid or revert if there are no bids; instead the contract silently moves the asset, violating the accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: `LienToken.transferFrom` There is a possibility of malicious attack
description: Corrupt multiple key properties of public vault, causing vault not to function properly.
poc:
When LienToken.makePayment()/buyoutLien()/payDebtViaClearingHouse()  
If it corresponds to PublicVault, it will make multiple changes to the vault, such as: yIntercept, slope, last, epochData, etc.

If LienToken corresponds to PublicVault, then ownerOf(lienId) = PublicVault address

When the LienToken is a private vault, it is possible to transfer the owner of the LienToken.

As the above seems, if the private vault is transferred to the PublicVault address will result in the wrong modification of the yIntercept, slope, last, epochData, etc.

So we restrict the to in transferFrom to not be a PublicVault address

```solidity
function transferFrom(
  address from,
  address to,
  uint256 id
) public override(ERC721, IERC721) {

  if (_isPublicVault(s, to)) {  //***@audit when to == PublicVault address , will revert
    revert InvalidState(InvalidStates.PUBLIC_VAULT_RECIPIENT);  
  }  
```

However, such a restriction does not prevent an attacker from transferring PrivateVault’s LienToken to PublicVault.  
Because the address is predictable when the vault contract is created, a malicious user can predict the vault address, front-run, and transfer PrivateVault’s LienToken to the predicted PublicVault address before the public vault is created, thus bypassing this restriction

Assumptions:

  1. alice creates PrivateVault, and creates multiple PrivateVault’s LienToken
  2. alice monitors bob’s creation of the PublicVault transaction, i.e., AstariaRouter.newPublicVault(), and then predicts the address of the newly generated treasure chest

Note: newPublicVAult() although the use of create(), but still can predict the address

see：<https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/760/how-is-the-address-of-an-ethereum-contract-computed>

The address for an Ethereum contract is deterministically computed from the address of its creator (sender) and how many transactions the creator has sent (nonce). The sender and nonce are RLP encoded and then hashed with Keccak-256.

  3. front-run , and transfer LienToken to public vault predict address
  4. bob’s public vault created success and do some loan
  5. alice do makePayment() to Corrupt bob’s public vault
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ERC‑721 LienToken used by the Astaria protocol to represent liens on vaults. When a LienToken is transferred, the contract checks the destination address and reverts if the address is currently a PublicVault. This check is performed at the moment of transfer, using the ownerOf function to infer the vault type. However, the protocol creates PublicVault contracts with deterministic addresses that can be predicted from the creator’s address and nonce. An attacker can therefore predict the address of a future PublicVault, front‑run the transaction that creates the vault, and transfer a PrivateVault’s LienToken to that predicted address before the PublicVault contract exists. Because the address is not yet a contract, the transfer passes the runtime check and succeeds. When the PublicVault is later deployed at the predicted address, the protocol treats the token as belonging to a PublicVault and allows functions such as makePayment, buyoutLien, and payDebtViaClearingHouse to modify critical accounting variables (yIntercept, slope, last, epochData, etc.) based on the assumption that the token is linked to a legitimate public vault. Since the token was originally tied to a private vault, these modifications corrupt the public vault’s state, breaking its accounting logic, potentially causing loan repayments to fail, balances to become zero, or funds to disappear from the vault. The issue is triggered only when an attacker can predict the future contract address and successfully front‑run the creation transaction, a scenario that is subtle because the transfer looks normal to users and the revert condition is only evaluated after the vault exists. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the transferFrom implementation and recognizing that the deterministic address generation of CREATE contracts allows the recipient check to be bypassed. It is hard to notice because the token transfer does not raise an error and the subsequent state corruption only manifests later when the public vault is used. To remediate, the contract should not rely on ownerOf to decide whether a destination is a public vault; instead it should use the immutable originOwner stored in s.lienMeta[id] or maintain an explicit registry of public vault addresses and reject any transfer to an address that is or could become a public vault. By enforcing the correct vault association at transfer time, the protocol can prevent the malicious pre‑deployment transfer and preserve the integrity of public vault accounting.

title: Users are unable to mint shares from a public vault using `AstariaRouter` contract when share price is bigger than one
bug_full: The issue is a denial‑of‑service style bug that appears when a public vault’s share price rises above one and a user tries to mint new shares through the AstariaRouter contract. The router’s mint function first calls safeApprove on the underlying asset token, approving the vault to pull an amount equal to the number of shares the caller wants. However, the ERC4626 vault’s previewMint calculation multiplies the requested shares by the ratio of total assets to total supply, rounding up. When the share price is greater than one, this calculation yields an asset amount that is larger than the share amount. Consequently the vault’s mint implementation attempts to transfer more asset tokens from the router than the router has approved, causing the ERC20 transferFrom to revert with a TRANSFER_FROM_FAILED error. The root cause is the mismatch between the approved allowance (based on shares) and the actual asset amount required (based on the previewMint result), which only becomes visible when the share price exceeds one. An attacker can trigger this condition by borrowing from the vault and then repaying after a period, which inflates the share price, and then legitimate users who rely on the router’s slippage protection are blocked from minting. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails, they receive no shares, and any expected deposit or slippage‑controlled mint does not happen, leading to confusion and potential loss of opportunity. The bug affects any participant that uses the router to interact with public vaults – lenders, borrowers, and anyone trying to acquire shares through the router – and it undermines the protocol’s promised minting flow. It was discovered during a systematic audit that included a test reproducing the scenario: after a borrow‑repay cycle the share price exceeds one, and a subsequent router‑based mint reverts. The problem is subtle because the router’s approve call looks correct under normal conditions; only the edge case of a share price greater than one reveals the insufficient allowance. The appropriate fix is to compute the exact asset amount required for the requested shares (using previewMint) and approve that amount for the vault, rather than approving the share amount. This aligns the allowance with the actual transfer needed and restores the ability to mint with slippage control regardless of the share price. The vulnerability belongs to the class of allowance‑miscalculation bugs in ERC4626‑compatible tokenized vault interactions, where an incorrect approval leads to failed asset transfers and blocked functionality.

title: Improper Approval Mechanism of Clearing House
description:
The `ClearingHouse` implementation performs a `@solmate`-based `safeApprove` instruction ([1]) with the remaining `balanceOf(address(this))` but contains code handling any remainder of funds that may remain in the contract [2]. Investigation of the `payDebtViaClearingHouse` function will indicate that the function may not consume the maximum approval that was set to the `TRANSFER_PROXY` [3].

As a result, any consequent invocation of `_execute` via `safeTransferFrom` from OpenSea with a `paymentToken` (i.e. `identifier`) such as USDT would fail. Given that the `ClearingHouse` of a particular `collateralId` is created only once, this vulnerability will impact consequent listings and cause them to fatally fail for a token that has been used in the past and is part of the non-compliant EIP-20 tokens, with USDT being the prime and most popular example.

The code in USDT that causes this complication is as follows:

```solidity
require(!((_value != 0) && (allowed[msg.sender][_spender] != 0)));
```
poc:
The vulnerability is clearly defined above, however, for testing purposes, the `ClearingHouse::safeTransferFrom` function of a particular clearing house instance can be invoked twice with the same arguments. The second invocation will fail provided that the first invocation provided a token balance that exceeds the number of funds necessary for the debt payment which should be denoted in USDT.

On an important note, if the code used `safeApprove` from `@openzeppelin` this issue would affect any token, however, it is limited to non-standard tokens due to the usage of the `@solmate` implementation of `safeApprove`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the ClearingHouse contract manages ERC20 token approvals for the TransferProxy. Instead of resetting an existing non‑zero allowance before granting a new one, the contract calls the Solmate‑based safeApprove with the remaining token balance. Certain ERC20 implementations, most notably USDT, contain a non‑standard check (require(!((_value != 0) && (allowed[msg.sender][_spender] != 0)))) that rejects an approve call when the spender already has a non‑zero allowance. Consequently, when the ClearingHouse attempts to approve the TransferProxy a second time – for example during a subsequent debt payment or NFT listing – the approve transaction succeeds silently but the allowance is not updated, leaving the previous allowance unchanged. When OpenSea later invokes the internal _execute function via safeTransferFrom, the TransferProxy tries to pull the required USDT amount but the allowance is insufficient, causing the transfer to revert. From a user’s perspective a listing that previously succeeded now fails with no error message, the expected refund or payment never arrives, and balances appear unchanged or zero. The issue manifests only after a token that has already been used with the ClearingHouse and that follows the non‑standard ERC20 pattern; fresh tokens or tokens that follow the standard ERC20 specification are not affected. The bug was uncovered during a formal audit that examined the payDebtViaClearingHouse flow and identified that the maximum approval set for the TransferProxy was not always consumed. It is difficult to notice because the approve call does not revert, and the contract’s state appears correct until a later transfer attempt fails, breaking business logic that assumes a successful payment will always be possible. The root cause is an improper approval handling pattern – failing to clear a prior non‑zero allowance before setting a new one – which violates the accounting assumption that the contract can always pull the exact amount owed. The recommended remediation is to check the current allowance, reset it to zero when it is non‑zero, and then set the desired allowance, or to switch to an approval library that implements this safety pattern for non‑standard tokens. By ensuring the allowance is correctly refreshed, subsequent listings and debt repayments will succeed, preserving user funds and protocol reliability.

title: Public vault strategist reward is not calculated correctly
description:
Strategist interest reward is not calculated correctly. The reward will almost always be calculated with interestOwed, regardless of the amount paid.

As a result, the strategist gets paid more than they are supposed to. Even if the borrower hasn’t made a single payment, the strategist can make a tiny payment on behalf of the borrower to trigger this calculation.

This also encourages the strategist to maximize interestOwed and make tiny payments on behalf of the borrower. This can trigger a compound interest vulnerability which I’ve made a separate report about.
poc:
As confirmed by the sponsor, the strategist reward is supposed to be “paid on performance and only@on interest. if the payment that’s being made is greater than the interest owing we only mint them based on the interest owed, but if it’s less, then, mint their shares based on the amount”

However, this is not the case. When LienToken calls beforePayment, which calls _handleStrategistInterestReward, the amount passed in is the amount of the lien (stack.point.amount), not the amount paid.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the strategist’s interest reward in the public vault contract. The reward logic is intended to mint strategist shares based on the smaller of the actual payment amount and the interest that is currently owed (interestOwed). However, the implementation mistakenly uses the remaining debt amount stored in the loan’s stack point (stack.point.amount) instead of the amount that the borrower actually paid. This root‑cause stems from a mismatch between the variable that tracks the loan principal and the variable that represents the payment being processed. Because the contract always references the larger debt figure, the reward calculation almost always falls back to interestOwed, even when the payment is tiny or zero. An attacker who holds the strategist role can therefore trigger a payment of an arbitrarily small amount on behalf of a borrower, causing the contract to mint reward tokens as if the full interest amount were being paid. The impact is that the strategist receives more reward tokens than entitled, draining protocol funds and creating an incentive for the strategist to repeatedly make minimal payments to inflate their earnings. This behavior can also amplify a separate compound‑interest vulnerability, as the inflated rewards increase the apparent interest balance. The flaw manifests whenever the beforePayment hook calls _handleStrategistInterestReward, which forwards stack.point.amount instead of the actual payment amount. All parties that rely on the vault’s accounting – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions about interest distribution are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented reward policy with the on‑chain implementation and identified the mismatched variable usage. It is subtle because the reward function still appears to respect the “pay on interest” rule at a glance, but the hidden variable substitution causes the rule to be bypassed. To remediate, the contract should replace the use of stack.point.amount with the true payment amount (often named amount) and ensure the reward is minted based on the minimum of that amount and interestOwed. Conceptually, this is a reward‑calculation bug where an incorrect state variable is used, leading to over‑minting of tokens and violation of the protocol’s financial logic. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see no change to their balance while the strategist’s wallet unexpectedly receives extra tokens, contradicting the expectation that rewards are proportional to actual interest paid.

title: Tokens with fee on transfer are not supported in `PublicVault.sol`
description:
Some tokens take a transfer fee (e.g. `STA`, `PAXG`), some do not currently charge a fee but may do so in the future (e.g. `USDT`, `USDC`).

Should a fee-on-transfer token be added to the `PublicVault`, the tokens will be locked in the `PublicVault.sol` contract. Depositors will be unable to withdraw their rewards. In the current implementation, it is assumed that the received amount is the same as the transfer amount. However, due to how fee-on-transfer tokens work, much less will be received than what was transferred.

As a result, later users may not be able to successfully withdraw their shares, as it may revert at <https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-astaria/blob/main/src/PublicVault.sol#L148> when `WithdrawProxy` is called due to insufficient balance.
bug_full: The PublicVault contract assumes that the amount of ERC20 tokens transferred into the vault equals the amount specified by the caller. This assumption is invalid for fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens, which deduct a portion of the transferred amount as a fee and therefore deliver fewer tokens than requested. When a user deposits a FoT token, the vault records the full requested amount as received and mints a corresponding number of shares, while the actual token balance of the contract is lower. Subsequent withdrawals calculate the amount of assets to return based on the recorded share balance, but the contract’s token balance is insufficient to satisfy the transfer. The withdrawal routine therefore reverts when it attempts to move more tokens than are available, effectively locking the deposited tokens and preventing users from receiving their expected rewards or principal. This issue manifests only when a token that implements a transfer fee is added to the vault, either because the token already charges a fee (e.g., STA, PAXG) or because a token that currently has no fee may introduce one in the future (e.g., USDT, USDC). The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined the deposit and redemption logic of the ERC4626‑cloned implementation and identified the missing balance verification step. It can be hard to notice because the transfer call itself succeeds and no error is emitted at deposit time; the discrepancy only appears later during withdrawal when the contract’s internal accounting no longer matches its actual token holdings. The impact is that users who deposit FoT tokens may see their balances disappear from the UI, receive zero assets on withdrawal, or experience transaction reverts, effectively losing access to their funds. To remediate the issue, the contract should either measure the actual amount received by checking the token balance before and after the transfer, or explicitly reject tokens that implement a transfer fee, thereby ensuring that the accounting model remains consistent with the token’s behavior.

title: Public vault owner
description: By calling buyoutLien before transferWithdrawReserve() is invoked (front-run if necessary), Public vault owner (strategist) can indefinitely prevent liquidity providers from withdrawing. He now effectively owns all the fund in the public vault.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the public vault’s withdrawal lifecycle. In the current design the function that moves available funds from the vault to the withdraw proxy – transferWithdrawReserve() – is called only after a liquidity provider signals a withdrawal and after the epoch has been processed. However, the contract does not enforce that this transfer must happen before a strategist can invoke buyoutLien, a function that refinances an existing lien by purchasing it from the vault. Because the ordering check is missing, a strategist who controls the vault (the public vault owner) can front‑run the withdrawal by calling buyoutLien as soon as funds become available, but before transferWithdrawReserve() is executed. The buyout consumes the reserve that would otherwise be sent to the withdraw proxy, leaving the proxy with little or no balance. The withdraw proxy then waits for funds that will never arrive, effectively blocking the liquidity provider’s withdrawal. The attack can be repeated indefinitely; the only mechanism that could release the stuck funds is a liquidation, but the strategist can avoid liquidation by only buying out liens from vaults they control and lending to themselves. This creates a denial‑of‑service or griefing scenario where the strategist, by abusing transaction ordering, can lock all user deposits and appear to own the entire public vault balance. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a pending withdrawal, the user expects to receive the full amount they deposited, but the withdraw proxy returns zero or a fraction of the expected ether, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test reproduced the scenario: after a buyoutLien call placed before transferWithdrawReserve(), the withdraw proxy balance was less than one third of the expected 60 ether. The problem is subtle because buyoutLien is a legitimate operation and the missing prerequisite call is not obvious in the contract’s flow, making the bug hard to spot without targeted testing. The appropriate mitigation is to enforce the execution of transferWithdrawReserve() (or a state flag indicating that the reserve has been transferred) before any buyoutLien can be performed, mirroring the existing commitLien flow. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that funds earmarked for withdrawal are locked and cannot be re‑allocated by a refinancing transaction, thereby preventing the strategist from permanently denying withdrawals.

title: Users are forced to approve Router for full collection to use commitToLiens
poc:
The check above allows the following situations pass:

* caller of the function == owner of the NFT
* receiver of the loan == owner of the NFT
* receiver of the loan == address approved for the individual NFT
* caller of the function == address approved for all

This is inconsistent and doesn’t make much sense. The approved users should have the same permissions.

More importantly, the most common flow (that the address approved for the individual NFT — the Router — is the caller) does not work and will lead to the function reverting.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the authorization logic of the Router#commitToLiens workflow. When a user invokes Router#commitToLiens, the Router forwards the call to the underlying commitToLien function, which checks whether the caller is allowed to act on a specific NFT used as collateral. The check compares the caller (msg.sender) against the NFT holder, the loan receiver, and the address approved for the individual token (operator), but mistakenly validates the receiver against the operator instead of the caller. As a result, the contract only accepts a call if the caller is either the NFT owner, the loan receiver, an address approved for all tokens via setApprovalForAll, or if the receiver matches the operator. Because the Router is typically approved only for the individual NFT using approve, it does not satisfy the isApprovedForAll condition, causing the transaction to revert with InvalidRequest. Users therefore must grant the Router a blanket approval for all of their NFTs, a level of permission many are uncomfortable with, in order to bypass the faulty check. The root cause is a logical error in the authority verification: the code uses receiver != operator where it should compare msg.sender with operator. Exploitation is straightforward: a user who follows the documented flow (approve the Router for a single token) attempts to commit a loan, the call fails, and the user sees a revert without receiving the expected loan or collateral lock. The impact is functional: legitimate users cannot use the commitToLiens feature unless they relax their approval settings, potentially exposing other assets to the Router and undermining trust in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever commitToLien is called through the Router with only per‑token approval, which is the common usage pattern. Affected parties include NFT owners, borrowers, and any participant relying on the Router to manage loans. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract comments (which state that router approval is sufficient) with the actual code logic. It can be hard to notice because the revert message is generic and the comment misleads developers into believing the check is correct. The recommended fix is to replace the receiver != operator comparison with msg.sender != operator, thereby granting the same permissions to the approved address as to the loan receiver and eliminating the need for a blanket setApprovalForAll. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper access‑control checks where the wrong variable is used, leading to unintended permission requirements and broken functionality.

title: Users can liquidate themselves before others, allowing them to take 13% above their borrowers
description:
The `canLiquidate()` function allows liquidations to take place if either (a) the loan is over and still exists or (b) the caller owns the collateral.

In the second case, due to the liquidation fee (currently 13%), this can give a borrower an unfair position to be able to reclaim a percentage of the liquidation that should be going to their lenders.
poc:
* A borrower puts up a piece of collateral and takes a loan of 10 WETH
  * The collateral depreciates in value and they decide to keep the 10 WETH
  * Right before the loans expire, the borrower can call `liquidate()` themselves
  * This sets them as the `liquidator` and gives them the first 13% return on the auction
  * While the lenders are left at a loss, the borrower gets to keep the 10 WETH and get a 1.3 WETH bonus
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic‑logic flaw that permits a borrower to initiate the liquidation of their own under‑collateralised loan before any external participant can do so. The contract’s canLiquidate() check treats a loan as liquidatable not only when it is overdue, but also when the caller is the owner of the collateral. Because the liquidation process awards a fixed liquidation fee – currently 13 % of the repaid amount – to the entity that calls liquidate(), a borrower who calls the function themselves captures that fee instead of the lenders who are supposed to receive it. This occurs when the loan is close to its expiration, the collateral value has fallen, and the borrower still holds the borrowed assets. In that narrow window the borrower can submit the liquidation transaction, become the liquidator, and receive the first 13 % of the auction proceeds as a bonus. From the lender’s perspective the expected repayment is reduced by the fee, resulting in a loss; from the borrower’s perspective the user sees an unexpected extra amount (for example, borrowing 10 WETH and receiving an additional 1.3 WETH). The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation eligibility logic and identified that ownership of the collateral alone is sufficient to trigger liquidation.
