However, both functions are marked with the onlyOwner modifier, which restricts calls to the wallet’s owner address only. Inside each function the code also calls a helper _requireFromEntryPointOrOwner() that would normally allow either the EntryPoint or the owner to proceed, but the external onlyOwner modifier overrides this check and blocks any call that does not originate from the owner. As a result, when a bundler or the EntryPoint tries to forward a UserOperation to the wallet, the transaction reverts because the caller is not the owner. This breaks the expected workflow described in EIP‑4337, where the EntryPoint must be able to trigger arbitrary calls on behalf of the user. The impact is a functional denial‑of‑service: legitimate users cannot have their meta‑transactions executed, balances may appear unchanged, and funds that should be transferred or refunded remain locked in the wallet. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a transaction was submitted but no change occurs, or that a refund amount is always zero despite a correct request. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s public interface against the EIP‑4337 specification and noticed the contradictory onlyOwner restriction. It can be hard to spot because the contract compiles without errors and the internal check seems correct; only runtime testing through the EntryPoint reveals the mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect access control for delegated execution” or “owner‑only guard on functions that must be callable by a trusted system contract”. To remediate, the onlyOwner modifier should be removed from both execute and executeBatch, allowing the internal _requireFromEntryPointOrOwner() logic to enforce the proper permission model. This aligns the contract with the intended design, restores the ability of the EntryPoint to process UserOperations, and prevents the denial‑of‑service condition where funds appear to disappear or refunds fail.

title: DoS of user operations and loss of user transaction fee due to insufficient gas value submission by malicious bundler
description:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L68-L86](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L68-L86)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L168-L190](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L168-L190)

An attacker (e.g. a malicious bundler) could submit a bundle of high gas usage user operations with insufficient gas value, causing the bundle to fail even when the users calculated the gas limits correctly. This will result in a DoS for the user and the user/paymaster still have to pay for the execution, potentially draining their funds. This attack is possible as user operations are included by bundlers from the UserOperation mempool into the Ethereum block (see post on ERC-4337 <https://medium.com/infinitism/erc-4337-account-abstraction-without-ethereum-protocol-changes-d75c9d94dc4a>).

Reference for this issue: <https://github.com/eth-infinitism/account-abstraction/commit/4fef857019dc2efbc415ac9fc549b222b07131ef>
poc:
In innerHandleOp(), a call was made to handle the operation with the specified mUserOp.callGasLimit. However, a malicious bundler could call the innerHandleOp() via handleOps() with a gas value that is insufficient for the transactions, resulting in the call to fail.

The remaining gas amount (e.g. gasLeft()) at this point was not verified to ensure that it is more than enough to fulfill the specified mUserOp.callGasLimit for the user operation. Even though the operation failed, the user/payment will still pay for the transactions due to the post operation logic.

[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L176](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/aa-4337/core/EntryPoint.sol#L176)
    
    (bool success,bytes memory result) = address(mUserOp.sender).call{gas : mUserOp.callGasLimit}(callData);
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service and fee‑loss condition that arises in the ERC‑4337 EntryPoint contract when a bundler submits a batch of user operations with a gas amount that is lower than the limits declared by the operations. The root cause is that the EntryPoint’s innerHandleOp function does not verify that the remaining gas after its own bookkeeping is sufficient to satisfy the user operation’s callGasLimit and verificationGasLimit before performing the external call to the user’s contract. Because this check is missing, a malicious bundler can deliberately invoke handleOps with an artificially low gas stipend. The contract then attempts to execute the user operation using the declared callGasLimit, runs out of gas, and the external call fails. The failure is not propagated as a revert; instead the EntryPoint records the operation as processed and still charges the paymaster or the user for the gas that was consumed up to the point of failure. From the user’s perspective the expected action – such as a token transfer or state change – never occurs, yet the wallet balance is reduced by the transaction fee, creating the impression that funds have disappeared. This situation can be reproduced whenever a bundler includes high‑gas‑usage operations from the mempool into a block and supplies an insufficient gas value, which a malicious actor can do repeatedly to block many users. The affected parties are the end‑users of the smart‑contract wallet, any paymaster that sponsors the operation, and the broader protocol that relies on correct accounting of fees. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the flow of gas handling in EntryPoint and noticed the absence of a post‑call gas‑sufficiency assertion. It is hard to notice because the transaction receipt may show success while the intended state change is missing, and the fee loss appears as a normal cost rather than an exploit. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked gas validation or “gas griefing” attacks, where insufficient gas is supplied to an external call, causing a silent failure and economic loss. The recommended remediation is to upgrade to the latest Account Abstraction implementation that adds an explicit check ensuring that the remaining gas is greater than the sum of the declared callGasLimit and verificationGasLimit before invoking the user contract, and to revert the operation if the check fails. This prevents a bundler from forcing a failure while still extracting fees, thereby eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector and protecting user funds.

title: Doesn’t Follow ERC1271 Standard
description: As Per [EIP-1271](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1271) standard `ERC1271_MAGIC_VAULE` should be `0x1626ba7e` instead of `0x20c13b0b` and function name should be `isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)` instead of `isValidSignature(bytes,bytes)`. Due to this, signature verifier contract go fallback function and return unexpected value and never return `ERC1271_MAGIC_VALUE` and always revert `execTransaction` function.
poc:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/interfaces/ISignatureValidator.sol#L6](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/interfaces/ISignatureValidator.sol#L6)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/interfaces/ISignatureValidator.sol#L19](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/interfaces/ISignatureValidator.sol#L19)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L342](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L342)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a non‑compliant implementation of the ERC1271 signature verification interface. According to EIP‑1271 the contract must expose a function named isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes) that returns the constant magic value 0x1626ba7e (ERC1271_MAGIC_VALUE) when a signature is valid. The examined smart‑account contract instead declares isValidSignature(bytes,bytes) and uses the constant 0x20c13b0b. Because the function selector does not match the standard, external callers that expect the ERC1271 interface invoke the fallback function of the validator contract. The fallback returns an unexpected value and never emits the required magic constant, causing the calling execTransaction routine to treat the signature as invalid and to revert the transaction. This defect can be exploited by any user or attacker who attempts to submit a transaction that relies on signature validation; the transaction will always fail, effectively locking the wallet’s funds or preventing legitimate operations. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected smart‑account, where users see their transactions revert with no obvious error, balances remain unchanged, and expected actions such as token transfers or contract calls never occur. The issue manifests whenever execTransaction is called with a signature, i.e., for any operation that requires authorisation through the ERC1271 validator. All users of the wallet, as well as any protocol that integrates the wallet for meta‑transactions, are affected because the contract does not honour the standard verification flow. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s ABI against the EIP‑1271 specification and observed the mismatched selector and magic constant. It is subtle because the fallback does not throw an explicit error; instead it silently returns a wrong value, making the failure appear as a generic transaction revert rather than a signature‑validation bug. To remediate, the contract should be updated to implement the exact ERC1271 function signature isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes) and return the correct magic constant 0x1626ba7e on successful verification, ensuring that execTransaction receives the expected success indicator and can proceed with the intended state changes. This correction aligns the contract with the standard, restores proper signature verification, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service risk caused by the faulty implementation.

title: `SmartAccount.sol` is intended to be upgradable but inherits from contracts that contain storage and no gaps
description:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/base/ModuleManager.sol#L18](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/53c8c3823175aeb26dee5529eeefa81240a406ba/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/base/ModuleManager.sol#L18)

SmartAccount.sol inherits from contracts that are not stateless and don’t contain storage gaps which can be dangerous when upgrading.
poc: When creating upgradable contracts that inherit from other contracts is important that there are storage gap in case storage variable are added to inherited contracts. If an inherited contract is a stateless contract (i.e. it doesn’t have any storage) then it is acceptable to omit a storage gap, since these function similar to libraries and aren’t intended to add any storage. The issue is that SmartAccount.sol inherits from contracts that contain storage that don’t contain any gaps such as ModuleManager.sol. These contracts can pose a significant risk when updating a contract because they can shift the storage slots of all inherited contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a storage‑layout incompatibility that arises because SmartAccount.sol is designed to be upgradeable through a proxy but inherits from base contracts such as ModuleManager that declare storage variables without reserving a storage gap. In upgradeable Solidity contracts, each state variable occupies a fixed slot in storage, and the order of declaration determines the slot index. When a contract is upgraded, the new implementation must preserve the exact slot ordering of the existing storage layout; otherwise, newly added variables shift the positions of existing ones. Because the inherited contracts lack the reserved 50‑slot gap that OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable base contracts normally provide, any future addition of variables to those bases would move the slots of all downstream variables. This can happen when the proxy owner (who may be any user) initiates an upgrade to a newer implementation that unintentionally or maliciously adds storage to a base contract. An attacker could exploit the situation by deploying an implementation that inserts a new variable in a base contract, causing critical fields such as the account owner, module registry, or balance pointers to be overwritten with attacker‑controlled data. The impact includes loss of ownership, unauthorized transfer of funds, or complete corruption of the wallet state, leading to a user seeing a zero balance, missing transaction history, or an unusable account interface. The condition occurs only during an upgrade; the contract functions correctly before the upgrade, making the bug hard to notice during normal operation. The affected parties are all users of the SmartAccount wallet and any protocol that relies on its correct state, because the proxy can be upgraded by the owner, who may not be a developer and could be tricked into applying a broken implementation. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) that examined the inheritance chain and identified the lack of storage gaps as a medium‑risk upgradeability flaw. It is difficult to detect because the contract behaves normally until an upgrade is performed, at which point the storage corruption may manifest as subtle bugs rather than immediate failures. The recommended remediation is to introduce a reserved storage gap in every contract that defines state variables, preferably by inheriting from OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable base contracts, and to add a safe‑rail upgrade pattern such as UUPS with access control that prevents arbitrary owners from deploying malicious implementations. By ensuring that each base contract reserves enough empty slots, future upgrades can add new variables without shifting existing ones, preserving the integrity of critical fields and preventing the described loss of funds or account malfunction.

title: Transaction can fail due to batchId collision
description:
The protocol supports 2D nonces through a `batchId` mechanism.  
Due to different ways to execute transaction on the wallet there could be a collision between `batchIds` being used.

This can result in unexpected failing of transactions
bug_full: The vulnerability is a nonce‑collision bug in the smart‑account contract that uses a two‑dimensional nonce identified by a batchId. The protocol reserves batchId 0 exclusively for transactions that originate from the EntryPoint contract, and the EntryPoint’s validateUserOp function increments and checks the nonce in that slot. However, the execTransaction function, which can be called directly by a user, does not enforce any restriction on the supplied batchId and will happily increment nonces[0] when batchId 0 is passed. When a user invokes execTransaction with batchId 0 before the EntryPoint processes a UserOperation, the nonce in the reserved slot is incremented out of sync with the value expected by the EntryPoint. Subsequent EntryPoint calls then fail the nonce validation check and revert, causing the transaction to fail unexpectedly. From a user’s perspective the wallet appears to reject otherwise valid operations, showing generic 'transaction failed' messages or empty revert reasons, while the user expects the operation to succeed and the funds to be transferred. The impact is limited to denial‑of‑service for the affected smart account: legitimate AA transactions cannot be executed until the nonce mismatch is resolved, effectively freezing the account’s ability to move funds through the EntryPoint path. The issue is discovered during a code audit that compared the nonce handling in both execution paths and noticed the missing guard in execTransaction. It is hard to notice because each function works correctly in isolation; the failure only manifests when the two entry points are mixed, a scenario that may not be covered by simple unit tests. The bug belongs to the class of 'shared nonce space misuse' or 'nonce collision' vulnerabilities, where multiple transaction pathways share a single counter without proper isolation, violating the accounting assumption that each batchId represents an independent sequence. The recommended fix is to add an explicit requirement that batchId is not zero in execTransaction, or to redesign the nonce scheme so that each execution path uses a distinct namespace, thereby preventing the collision and restoring the expected behavior.

title: DOS when using `addPriorityStakers`
description: DOS when using `addPriorityStakers` with two consecutive addresses badly ordered `(address a2 < address a1)`, which can be quite frequent (50% chance).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the addPriorityStakers function that can cause a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition. Inside a for‑loop the contract checks `if (i > 0 && staker < _priorityStakers[i‑1]) revert DuplicateArrayElements();`. This condition compares the numeric value of two consecutive addresses and reverts when the later address is numerically smaller than the previous one. Because Ethereum addresses have no natural ordering requirement, any unordered pair of addresses has roughly a 50 % chance of triggering the revert. The custom error name suggests a duplicate‑array check, but the code actually enforces an unnecessary ascending order. The root cause is a misplaced comparison that was likely intended to detect duplicate entries, yet duplicates are harmless – writing the same address to `isPriorityStaker` multiple times only wastes gas. When the condition is met, the transaction aborts before any `isPriorityStaker[staker] = true` assignments or `PriorityStakerRegistered` events occur, leaving the priority‑staker list unchanged. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – successful registration of priority stakers – is replaced by an unexpected revert with the error `DuplicateArrayElements`, consuming gas without any state change. This can be exploited by submitting a list of addresses deliberately ordered to fail, or even unintentionally by a legitimate caller whose address order happens to be descending, effectively blocking the addition of priority stakers and degrading protocol availability. No assets are directly at risk, but the protocol’s ability to manage privileged participants is impaired, which may affect downstream reward distribution or governance mechanisms. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced on Remix by feeding two random addresses; the transaction succeeded only when the first address was greater than the second. The bug is subtle because the revert occurs only for certain permutations, making it appear intermittent and hard to reproduce without systematic testing. The recommended remediation is to remove the ordering check entirely, as duplicates do not affect correctness, or replace it with a proper duplicate detection that does not rely on address ordering. By eliminating the faulty revert, the function will always succeed in registering the supplied priority stakers, restoring expected behavior and preventing the DoS scenario.

title: Deregistering inactive knot via calling deRegisterKnots directly
description:
Deregistering inactive knot via calling deRegisterKnots directly by the Syndicate owner always reverts.

**Actual Behaviour & Impact**  
The liquid staking manager (Syndicate owner) calls `deRegisterKnots` function to deregister knots. However, if any of those knots is inactive, the transaction will revert. This means in order to deregister an inactive knot, one should call `updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH` function since it calls internal `_deRegisterKnots`.

**Expected Behaviour**  
Deregistering knots by Syndicate owner should succeed especially if the knot is inactive.

**Cause**  
There is a circular dependency between deRegisterKnots and `_updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersLiabilitySnapshot` functions which leads to this behaviour.

`deRegisterKnots` always calls internally `_updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersLiabilitySnapshot`, and `_updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersLiabilitySnapshot` calls `_deRegisterKnot` in case the knot is inactive. So when the knot is deregistered the first time, the second time it reverts.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the deregistration flow of a staking position, referred to as a knot, in the liquid‑staking manager contract owned by the Syndicate. When the Syndicate owner invokes the public deRegisterKnots function to remove a knot that has become inactive, the transaction reverts instead of succeeding. The root cause is a circular dependency between the deRegisterKnots function and the internal liability‑snapshot routine. Specifically, deRegisterKnots always calls an internal helper that updates the collateralized slot owners’ liability snapshot. That helper, in turn, checks each knot’s activity status and, for inactive knots, calls another internal routine that attempts to deregister the knot again. Because the knot has already been deregistered once, the second call hits a state where the knot is no longer present, causing a revert. This logic error means that the contract cannot directly deregister an inactive knot; the only path that works is to invoke updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH, which internally performs the deregistration as part of a broader snapshot update. The impact is that users or the protocol cannot cleanly remove inactive positions through the intended public interface, potentially leaving stale entries in storage, inflating accounting data, and preventing the recovery of any remaining ETH associated with the knot. The issue manifests only when the knot is inactive at the time of the call and only when the caller is the Syndicate owner using deRegisterKnots directly. It was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the deregistration path with both active and inactive knots and observed a revert in the latter case. The bug is subtle because the revert occurs only under a specific combination of state (inactive knot) and function call order, making it easy to miss in standard unit tests that focus on successful paths. Conceptually, the fix requires breaking the circular dependency: either avoid calling the liability‑snapshot update from deRegisterKnots, or modify the snapshot routine so that it does not attempt a second deregistration of an already removed knot. By decoupling these operations, the contract can correctly handle inactive knots without reverting, restoring the expected behavior where the owner can deregister any knot and the protocol’s accounting remains consistent. This class of bug falls under improper state transition handling caused by recursive internal calls, leading to unintended reverts and accounting inconsistencies.

title: A comment in Syndicate.sol states
description: A comment in Syndicate.sol states that “Basically, under a rage quit or voluntary withdrawal from the beacon chain, the knot kick is auto-propagated to syndicate”. However, when a KNOT is inactive, the KNOT can still remain part of the syndicate and isn’t automatically removed from the syndicate.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑consistency defect in the Syndicate contract where the on‑chain logic does not honour the documented behaviour for inactive KNOTs. The contract’s comment claims that when a KNOT performs a rage quit or a voluntary withdrawal from the beacon chain, the “knot kick” is automatically propagated to the syndicate, meaning the KNOT should be removed from the syndicate’s membership list. In practice, however, the implementation fails to delete the inactive KNOT from the syndicate data structures, allowing the KNOT to remain listed as an active participant even though it is no longer operational. This discrepancy arises from a missing or incorrect conditional check that should trigger the removal routine during the inactivity transition. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit the bug by deliberately triggering a KNOT’s inactivity (for example by calling the withdrawal function) and then relying on the fact that the contract still treats the KNOT as a member. Because the syndicate’s accounting, reward distribution, and voting mechanisms assume that all listed members are active, the stale entry can cause rewards to be allocated to a non‑existent address, inflate the apparent size of the syndicate, or allow the inactive KNOT to be re‑activated in an unintended way. The impact includes potential loss of funds for honest participants (rewards may be siphoned away), inaccurate accounting that could break economic guarantees, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s governance model. The condition occurs whenever a KNOT becomes inactive – either through a rage quit or a voluntary withdrawal – and the contract’s internal state update does not execute the removal logic. All users who rely on the syndicate’s membership list – delegators, reward claimants, and governance participants – are affected because they may see incorrect member counts, receive zero rewards, or be unable to withdraw because the system believes the KNOT is still present. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit where the auditor compared the contract’s comments with the actual code paths and observed that the removal function was never called for inactive KNOTs. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit events for the missing removal, and the UI may still display the KNOT as part of the syndicate, masking the underlying state inconsistency. To remediate, the contract should be updated to include a reliable state transition that checks for KNOT inactivity and invokes the syndicate‑kick routine, ensuring that the membership list is pruned accordingly. This fix aligns the implementation with the documented contract behaviour and restores the invariant that only active KNOTs are counted in syndicate operations. The bug belongs to the class of documentation‑implementation mismatches and state‑invariant violations, where business logic assumes a certain lifecycle that the code fails to enforce, leading to accounting errors such as “funds disappear” or “rewards are missing”. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may appear as a syndicate showing members that cannot claim rewards, or a user expecting a refund after a withdrawal but seeing no change in their balance because the system still thinks the KNOT is active.

title: When staking on a given knot
description:
When staking on a given knot, the protocol prevents staking amounts fewer than 1 gwei. Additionally, when unstaking, there’s a check against unstaking amounts greater than the amounts allowed (at [263](https://github.com/pvgo80/2023-01-blockswap-fv-private/blob/certora/contracts/syndicate/Syndicate.sol#L263)), but there’s no check on the remaining amount. Thus, this leaves open scenarios where the user may leave less than 1 gwei on a knot. In such cases, the user cannot claim additional earnings due to the following calls: [679](https://github.com/pvgo80/2023-01-blockswap-fv-private/blob/certora/contracts/syndicate/Syndicate.sol#L679) \- [693](https://github.com/pvgo80/2023-01-blockswap-fv-private/blob/certora/contracts/syndicate/Syndicate.sol#L693) \- [370](https://github.com/pvgo80/2023-01-blockswap-fv-private/blob/certora/contracts/syndicate/Syndicate.sol#L370).

The user could “restake” his position on a knot, but there’s a (short) limit of 12 eth that could be filled by anyone.  
A Knot could become inactive, making future rewards forever inaccessible.  
The user could recover the smalls staked amounts, but he’ll not be compensated by accrued earnings.  
Property violated.

Rule `issue2_unstakingLeavesSmallAmountsBehind` in `M002.spec`, regarding the possibility of small stakes.  
Rule `issue2_ifTheUserHasClaimableAmountsHeShouldBeAbleToClaimIt` in `M002.spec` regarding the rewards unclaimable.
bug_full: During staking the contract enforces a minimum stake of 1 gwei. When a user later unstakes, the code checks that the amount being withdrawn does not exceed the user's share, but it does not verify that the remaining balance on the knot stays above the minimum. Consequently a user can deliberately or accidentally withdraw almost all of their stake, leaving a residual balance smaller than 1 gwei. The claim functions that distribute earned rewards require the caller to have at least the minimum stake; they read the stake amount and, if it is below the threshold, skip reward calculation and return without transferring any earnings. As a result the tiny leftover amount becomes permanently locked on the knot, the user cannot claim accrued rewards, and the knot may become inactive if its total stake falls below the operational threshold. The issue is observable from the user interface as a situation where the displayed balance shows a non‑zero amount (for example 0.000000001 ETH) but the claim button either does nothing or reverts, and attempts to restake fail because the contract caps the additional stake that can be added to a knot at 12 ETH, which is unrelated to the tiny leftover. The vulnerability was discovered through formal specification testing that flagged a property violation where unstaking could leave small amounts behind and where claimable rewards were not accessible. It is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error for the small remainder, and the UI may simply show a negligible balance, leading users to assume everything is fine. The impact is a loss of earned rewards for the affected user and a potential reduction of total active stake for the protocol, which can affect reward distribution and protocol health. The bug belongs to the class of minimum‑balance enforcement or dust‑locking errors, where insufficient validation of post‑operation balances allows dust to become unrecoverable. To remediate, the unstake function should include a check that the remaining stake after withdrawal is either zero or at least the minimum required amount, or it should automatically round down the withdrawal to leave no dust, and the claim logic should handle tiny balances gracefully or allow users to withdraw the residual amount together with any earned rewards.

title: An inactive KNOT can successfully stake
description:
An inactive KNOT can successfully stake.

Expected behaviour of the system: The stake function should revert if an inactive KNOT is trying to stake.

Actual behaviour of the system: The stake function succeeds and the inactive KNOT stakes.

Property Violated: `cannotStakeIfKnotIsInActive`

In this rule, the `isActive` state of the `blsPubKey` is set to `false`. The stake function is then called with this `blsPubKey` and the expected behaviour is that the function would revert because the KNOT is inactive. However, the stake function succeeds and an inactive KNOT can therefore successfully stake. The stake function checks if KNOT is not registered (`!isKNOTRegistered`) and if it is no longer part of the syndicate (`!isNoLongerPartOfSyndicate`) and reverts accordingly but does not check whether the KNOT is inactive.

Lines of code: <https://github.com/Certora/2023-01-blockswap-fv/blob/certora/contracts/syndicate/Syndicate.sol#L216>
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step in the staking routine of a syndicate contract that permits a participant identified by a BLS public key (referred to as a KNOT) to deposit stake even when the KNOT is marked as inactive. In the intended design, the contract should reject any staking attempt from an inactive KNOT because the business logic assumes that only active participants are eligible to contribute capital and receive subsequent rewards. The root cause is that the stake function checks only two conditions – whether the KNOT is registered and whether it is still part of the syndicate – and does not verify the isActive flag that indicates the operational status of the KNOT. Consequently, when an attacker or a careless user supplies a BLS public key whose isActive state is false, the function proceeds without reverting, allowing the stake transaction to succeed. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary can call the stake function with an inactive KNOT, lock funds in the contract, and later claim rewards that were meant exclusively for active participants. The impact includes distortion of the reward distribution, potential dilution of legitimate stakers’ earnings, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that active status correlates with stake eligibility. This condition manifests whenever the contract’s internal state marks a KNOT as inactive but the other registration checks pass, which can happen after a KNOT is deliberately deactivated or after a governance action that changes its status. All users who rely on the contract to enforce participation rules – including delegators, token holders, and the protocol’s governance layer – are affected because the system may allocate rewards to entities that should not be entitled to them. The issue was uncovered during a formal verification audit that asserted the property cannotStakeIfKnotIsInActive; the property failed, indicating that the contract does not enforce the intended invariant. The bug can be hard to notice in manual testing because the transaction does not revert and the UI may display a successful stake, while the underlying accounting error only becomes visible later in reward calculations. To remediate the flaw, the staking function should include an explicit require statement that checks the isActive flag of the supplied KNOT and reverts if the flag is false, thereby restoring the intended invariant that only active participants may stake. This change re‑establishes the correct relationship between participant status and economic rights, preventing inactive KNOTs from entering the staking pool and preserving the integrity of reward distribution.

title: Whenever a knot is deregistered
bug_full: The issue is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a knot is deregistered without first bringing the global accumulator of ETH rewards per free‑floating share up to date. The contract stores the current value of accumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare in a mapping called lastAccumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare at the moment a knot is marked as noLongerPartOfSyndicate. This snapshot is required so that later claims or unstaking operations can correctly calculate the rewards owed to the knot’s stakers based on the accrued ETH up to the deregistration point. However, two public functions – updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH and batchUpdateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH – can trigger the internal deregistration logic via _updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersLiabilitySnapshot without first calling updateAccruedETHPerShares, which is the only routine that refreshes accumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare. As a result, when these functions deregister a knot, the stored lastAccumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare reflects an outdated, lower value. Stakers who later claim or unstake receive less ETH than they are entitled to, because the reward calculation uses the stale snapshot. The bug manifests only when a knot becomes inactive and is deregistered through the aforementioned functions without any intervening call that updates the global accumulator. Users experience the symptom of receiving a smaller reward amount or even zero when they expect the full share of newly earned ETH. The problem was discovered by a formal verification rule that asserts the equality of lastAccumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare and the current accumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare after a deregistration event; the rule failed for calls to the two functions, indicating the missing update. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error – the reward shortfall is silent and only observable through reduced balances. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of stale‑state‑snapshot or missing‑state‑update errors, where a critical accounting variable is not refreshed before a state transition that relies on it. To fix the problem, the contract should invoke updateAccruedETHPerShares inside both updateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH and batchUpdateCollateralizedSlotOwnersAccruedETH (or otherwise guarantee that accumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare is current before any deregistration), ensuring that the snapshot stored in lastAccumulatedETHPerFreeFloatingShare accurately reflects all earned rewards. By doing so, the protocol restores the intended accounting guarantees, preventing loss of rewards for stakers and aligning the actual reward distribution with the protocol’s business logic.

title: Adding NFTS with AssociationType ORDERED or PRIMARY may cause overwriting
description:
**_Note: Prior to this audit, a group of wardens added test coverage. While auditing was not the purpose of the testing phase, relevant and valuable findings reported during that timeframe were eligible to be judged. As such, this finding [M-01] was discovered during the “testing squad” phase and is being included here for completeness._**

Subprotocol NFTs may be trapped in contract CidNFT forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CidNFT contract’s add() function when handling subprotocol NFTs that are associated with a CID NFT using the AssociationType ORDERED or PRIMARY. The function writes the supplied NFT identifier directly into a mapping slot (ordered[key] for ORDERED or primary for PRIMARY) without first checking whether that slot already contains a previously added NFT. Because there is no guard against overwriting, a caller can add a second NFT with the same key (for ORDERED) or a second primary NFT, which silently replaces the earlier entry. The earlier NFT remains transferred to the CidNFT contract but its identifier is no longer stored in the mapping, so subsequent calls to remove() can only retrieve the most recently stored NFT. When the owner attempts to remove the first NFT, the contract reverts with OrderedValueNotSet or PrimaryValueNotSet, indicating that the expected value is missing. From the user’s perspective the NFT they transferred to the contract appears to be lost: the contract’s balance shows the NFT is still owned by the contract, yet the remove operation returns an error and the user receives only the second NFT. This results in assets being permanently trapped, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each added NFT can be later reclaimed. The issue occurs whenever the same CID NFT identifier, subprotocol name, and (for ORDERED) key are reused without first removing the existing association. It affects any holder of subprotocol NFTs who interacts with CidNFT, as well as the overall protocol because locked NFTs represent unrecoverable value. The bug was discovered during a dedicated testing phase when unit tests added two NFTs sequentially and observed that the first NFT became unrecoverable after the second addition. The problem is subtle because the contract emits successful add events for both NFTs and does not emit any warning about the overwrite, making it easy to miss during casual inspection. The vulnerability belongs to the class of storage‑slot overwriting bugs that lead to asset lock or loss. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit checks in add() that revert if the target ordered key or primary slot is already occupied, as shown in the provided diff, thereby preventing accidental overwrites and ensuring that each NFT can be safely removed after being added.

title: Multiple accounts can have the same identity
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a lack of uniqueness enforcement for on‑chain identity registrations in the AddressRegistry contract. The contract stores a single mapping from a user address to a CID NFT identifier, but it does not keep a reverse mapping or any check that prevents the same NFT identifier from being associated with more than one address. When a user registers an NFT, the contract simply writes cidNFTs[msg.sender] = _cidNFTID. If the NFT is later transferred to another wallet, the original address still retains the stale entry, and the new owner can also register the same identifier. Consequently, two or more distinct accounts can point to the identical CID NFT, creating duplicate identities. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who either transfers a registered NFT to a controlled address or registers the same NFT after a legitimate user has done so, thereby gaining the same identity privileges that the protocol assumes are unique. The impact includes potential bypass of access‑control checks, voting manipulation, and confusion in any business logic that relies on a one‑to‑one relationship between an address and an identity. The issue manifests whenever a CID NFT is transferred after registration or when multiple registrations of the same NFT occur, affecting all participants that depend on the registry for authentication, including users, the protocol itself, and any downstream contracts. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑management logic of the registry and noticed that the mapping is only one‑directional. The problem is subtle because the contract emits events that appear correct and the UI may still display the expected NFT ID for each address, making the duplicate mapping hard to spot without inspecting the reverse relationship. To remediate, the contract should maintain a secondary mapping from NFT identifier to the owning address, enforce that an NFT can be linked to at most one address at any time, and clear the previous association when the NFT is transferred or re‑registered. This change restores the intended invariant that each identity is uniquely bound to a single wallet, preventing the described accounting and permission inconsistencies.

title: Griefing risk in mint
poc:
* The next CidNFT mint ID is `1000`.
  * Alice wants to mint and prepares `_addList` with the expected `_cidNFTID` of `1000`.
  * Bob saw Alice’s transaction and frontran her, incrementing the next minting ID to `1001`.
  * Alice’s transaction tries to add subprotocol NFTs to ID `1000` which is owned by Bob. This causes the transaction to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability isa race‑condition griefing issue in the mint function of the CID NFT contract. The function accepts an optional parameter _addList that contains identifiers of sub‑protocol NFTs which the caller expects to associate with the newly minted token. The implementation trusts the caller‑provided _cidNFTID values inside this list and checks ownership against those IDs before the mint operation has definitively assigned the token ID. Because the next token identifier is determined only at execution time, a malicious actor can submit a higher‑fee transaction that mints a token before the victim’s transaction is mined. This front‑runs the pending mint, increments the internal token counter, and causes the victim’s _addList to reference an ID that now belongs to the attacker or does not exist. When the contract reaches the ownership check (ownerOf[_cidNFTID] …) the condition fails and the transaction reverts with NotAuthorizedForCIDNFT. The impact is that users attempting to mint with a non‑empty _addList experience failed transactions and lose the gas spent, effectively a denial‑of‑service or griefing attack. The issue occurs only when the mint includes sub‑protocol registration and when there is competition for the next token ID, such as during periods of high traffic or when an attacker deliberately front‑runs. All users who rely on the add‑list feature are affected, while the rest of the protocol remains functional. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of token ID generation and noticed that the contract does not bind the minted ID to the subsequent add loop. It is subtle because normal mint calls without an add list succeed, and the failure appears intermittent, making it easy to attribute to network congestion rather than a logical bug. To remediate, the contract should capture the actual token ID returned by the mint operation and use that exact identifier for any subsequent sub‑protocol registration, ensuring atomicity between creation and association. Alternatively, the add logic could be moved into a separate, explicitly authorized call after the mint, or the contract could enforce that the add list cannot reference external IDs. This class of bug falls under “incorrect assumption about mutable state between sequential operations” and violates the business rule that a newly minted NFT should be owned by the caller and immediately available for further configuration without external interference.

title: CidNFT: Broken tokenURI function
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the tokenURI function of an ERC721 implementation where the numeric token identifier is concatenated directly into the URI string without first converting it to its decimal representation. Because Solidity’s abi.encodePacked treats a uint256 as a 32‑byte binary value, the raw bytes of the identifier are inserted into the resulting string. Consequently, the generated URI contains non‑printable or control characters (for example, the byte sequence for token ID 1 becomes the invisible start‑of‑heading character) or other ASCII symbols that are not valid in a URL path (such as an asterisk for token ID 42). This malformed URI breaks the expected pattern baseURI/<id>.json, causing metadata look‑ups to fail, images to disappear, and user interfaces to display empty or corrupted data. The issue occurs whenever tokenURI is called for an existing token, as the function first checks ownership and then returns the concatenated string. It affects all token holders, marketplaces, and any downstream services that rely on the token metadata URL. The bug was discovered during a security audit when test cases compared the actual output of tokenURI against the expected human‑readable URI and observed a mismatch caused by the raw byte encoding. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the function executes without reverting, yet the output is silently incorrect, making it easy to overlook without explicit string comparison. The root cause is a missing conversion of the uint256 identifier to a decimal string before concatenation, which is a classic string‑handling error in smart contracts. To remediate, the identifier should be transformed into its textual representation (for example using a library such as LibString.toString) before being passed to abi.encodePacked, thereby restoring the correct URI format and ensuring that token metadata can be reliably retrieved. This fix aligns the implementation with ERC721 expectations that tokenURI returns a valid, human‑readable URL pointing to a JSON metadata file.

title: `unauthorize`
description:
The `Caller` contract enables users to authorize other users to execute tx on their behalf. This option enables the authorized/delegated user to add more users to the authorized users list. In case the original user is trying to remove an authorized user (i.e. run `unauthorize()`), the delegated user can simply front run that tx to add another user, then after `unauthorized()` is executed the delegated can use the added user to gain his authority back.

This would allow the malicious delegated user to keep executing txs on behalf of the original user and cause them a loss of funds (e.g. collecting funds on their behalf and sending it to the attacker’s address).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the delegation mechanism of the Caller contract, where an original user can grant another address the ability to execute transactions on their behalf. The contract’s authorize function relies on the internal _msgSender() value, which reflects the caller of the delegated call rather than the original transaction sender. Because of this design, any address that has already been authorized can invoke authorize() while acting as the original user, effectively adding new authorized addresses without the original user’s consent. When the original user attempts to revoke a malicious delegate by calling unauthorize(), the malicious delegate can front‑run that transaction by submitting an authorize() call with a higher gas price (or by bribing the block producer) that adds a fresh authorized address before the revocation is mined. After the unauthorize() transaction is executed, the newly added address can be used to re‑authorize the malicious delegate, restoring its authority. This race condition allows the attacker to maintain continuous control over the original user’s account, enabling repeated execution of privileged calls such as withdrawing drips or transferring funds to the attacker’s address. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: after attempting to remove a delegate, the user may notice that expected refunds are missing, balances become unexpectedly low, or funds are transferred without any visible authorization. The issue is hard to detect because the contract appears to provide a working revocation mechanism, yet the underlying ordering of transactions can silently bypass it. The root cause is the misuse of _msgSender() in authorize(), which does not differentiate between a direct call from the original user and a delegated call from an already‑authorized address. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that front‑runs an unauthorize() transaction and re‑adds the malicious delegate via an intermediate address. To remediate the problem the authorize function should be restricted to only accept calls from the original user (using msg.sender) or be replaced with a dedicated signed‑authorization flow that validates an off‑chain signature from the original user. Additional mitigations include preventing already‑authorized users from invoking authorize() on behalf of the original user, introducing a revokeAll or unauthorizeAll function to clear the authorization list atomically, or adding a time‑lock mechanism that makes front‑running ineffective. By ensuring that only the true owner can extend the list of trusted addresses, the contract regains its intended security guarantees and prevents the attacker from continuously stealing funds.

title: Fee on transfer tokens will not behave as expected
description:
In Numoen, it does not specifically restrict the type of ERC20 collateral used for borrowing.

If fee on transfer token(s) is/are entailed, it will specifically make `mint()` revert in Lendgine.sol when checking if `balanceAfter < balanceBefore + collateral`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the assumption that every ERC‑20 token used as collateral behaves like a standard token that transfers the exact amount specified. In the Numoen Lendgine contract, the mint() function records the token1 balance before invoking the external mintCallback, then checks that the post‑callback balance is at least the pre‑balance plus the declared collateral amount. This check (balanceAfter < balanceBefore + collateral) is intended to guarantee that the contract received the full collateral. However, fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) or deflationary tokens deduct a percentage of the transferred amount as a fee, so the actual amount received is lower than the amount sent. Consequently, the balance comparison fails and the transaction reverts with InsufficientInputError, even though the token transfer succeeded from the user’s perspective. The root cause is the reliance on a static input amount rather than the dynamic amount actually credited to the contract. The issue can be triggered by any token that implements a transfer fee, such as typical “tax” tokens, by simply supplying such a token as the collateral argument to mint(). When a user attempts to open a position with a FoT token, the transaction aborts, the user’s funds remain in their wallet, and the protocol appears to reject the token silently. From a user‑facing standpoint the UI would show a failed mint operation, often with a generic error message, while the user expects their collateral to be deposited and a share token to be minted. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service for borrowers who wish to use fee‑on‑transfer tokens, and it may also lead to confusion or loss of confidence in the protocol because the contract does not support a class of tokens that are otherwise ERC‑20 compliant. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Lendgine.sol source, where the balance check was identified as incompatible with non‑standard token behavior. It is easy to miss because most ERC‑20 tokens do not charge a fee, making the check appear correct under normal testing. To remediate, the protocol should either whitelist only tokens that are known to be fee‑free, or replace the static collateral parameter with a dynamic calculation that uses the actual balance delta (balanceAfter – balanceBefore) as the effective collateral amount. This change would align the accounting with the real amount received and prevent unnecessary reverts, while still allowing the protocol to reject tokens that do not meet its economic assumptions. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect token balance accounting for fee‑on‑transfer tokens”, where a contract assumes a one‑to‑one transfer relationship that does not hold for deflationary ERC‑20 tokens, leading to failed mint operations and a degraded user experience.

title: First liquidity provider will suffer from revert or fund loss
description:
[src/periphery/LiquidityManager.sol#L135](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/2ad9a73d793ea23a25a381faadc86ae0c8cb5913/src/periphery/LiquidityManager.sol#L135)

The first liquidity depositor should supply three input values `amount0Min, amount1Min, liquidity` via `AddLiquidityParams` but these three values should meet an accurate relationship, or else the depositor will suffer from revert or fund loss
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the initialization of a new liquidity pool when the total liquidity is zero. In this state the contract LiquidityManager.addLiquidity trusts the caller to provide three values – amount0Min, amount1Min and the desired liquidity – without any on‑chain verification that these numbers satisfy the mathematical relationship required by the pool invariant defined in Pair.invariant. The invariant checks that a+b‑c‑d is never strictly positive, where a and b are scaled versions of the supplied token amounts and c and d are functions of the upper bound parameter. If the caller supplies amounts that do not respect this relationship, two bad outcomes are possible. First, the internal check if (amount0 < params.amount0Min || amount1 < params.amount1Min) may trigger a revert, causing the transaction to fail and the user to lose the gas spent. Second, if the mismatched values happen to pass the AmountError test, the invariant becomes strictly positive, meaning a+b‑c‑d > 0. In that case any participant can later call swap and extract token0 from the pool without paying anything, effectively draining the funds that the first liquidity provider deposited. The impact is therefore a loss of the deposited assets for the first LP and a potential total drain of the pool, breaking the economic guarantees of the protocol. This condition only occurs during the very first deposit, i.e., when totalLiquidity equals zero, and it affects anyone who attempts to be the initial liquidity provider as well as downstream users who rely on the pool’s integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined how the invariant is calculated and noticed that the contract does not compute the correct liquidity amount from the supplied token amounts for an empty pool. The problem is subtle because the function signature suggests that the caller can freely choose the three parameters, and the revert message does not explain that the values are mathematically linked, so developers may assume any reasonable numbers will work. To remediate the bug the contract should calculate the required liquidity on‑chain from the provided token amounts (or vice‑versa) and enforce the invariant before accepting the deposit. Adding preview functions that return the correct liquidity for given token amounts would also help users avoid off‑chain guesswork. In generic terms this is an initialization‑parameter validation flaw that allows the pool invariant to be violated, leading to potential fund loss or a complete drain of the pool.

title: Economical games that can be played to gain MEV
description: Disclaimer from warden: Developers did an extremely good job writing the protocol, however, these are some aspects that I think are missed in the design stage and can be considered. Look at it as a food for thought in future designs.
poc:
Lets consider several cases: (These also happen in other markets, but can get exaggerated here)

* Imagine a liquidity market which has up to a considerable percentage of its liquidity borrowed, if the safe `upperbound` for the liquidators starts to move down the protocol allows the earliest liquidators to opt-out, creating a certain kind of MEV for the fastest liquidators. While the remaining providers will get more fees, the protocol favors the fastest actors to decide when to opt-out. In the extreme case of base token crashing down, there would be a race between borrowers to lock the money and the earliest liquidity providers to get out.
* Liquidity providers might mint some shares for themselves in times of uncertainty, just to have the option to quickly opt-out of the protocol if they need. They can give back the borrowed amount and withdraw the said amount in one transaction. while if they do not lock the funds, they either have to take the funds out or someone else might come and get lock the funds.
bug_full: The reported issue is an economic design flaw that enables participants to extract miner extractable value (MEV) by exploiting timing advantages in the protocol’s liquidation and liquidity‑withdrawal mechanisms. The root cause lies in the protocol allowing liquidators to opt‑out of liquidation when the safe upper‑bound for liquidations is reduced, and permitting liquidity providers to mint additional share tokens that can be redeemed in a single transaction during periods of market stress. Because the protocol does not enforce a uniform withdrawal window or restrict the creation of redeemable shares, actors who can submit transactions faster than others can lock in higher fees or protect their capital while slower participants suffer reduced returns or even loss of deposited assets. An attacker can monitor the market for rapid price drops or high borrowing ratios, then submit a high‑gas transaction that either opts‑out of liquidation first or mints and redeems shares before the protocol updates its state, thereby capturing the extra fee margin or avoiding a forced liquidation. The impact is a distortion of fee distribution, potential capital erosion for ordinary liquidity providers, and a loss of confidence in the fairness of the system. This situation occurs most prominently when a market experiences a sharp decline in the base token price, when a large proportion of liquidity is borrowed, or when the protocol’s upper‑bound parameter is adjusted downward, creating a race between borrowers trying to lock funds and early liquidators seeking to exit. The vulnerability affects all roles that interact with the market – liquidity providers, borrowers, and liquidators – and ultimately the protocol’s economic integrity. It was identified during a design‑stage audit that examined the incentive structures and edge‑case behaviours rather than through a concrete exploit. Because the flaw does not manifest as a contract revert or a visible code error, it can be difficult to notice; the symptoms appear as subtle, unexpected profit capture by fast actors and lower than expected fee earnings for regular participants. To remediate the issue, the protocol should redesign the liquidation and withdrawal logic to eliminate early opt‑out privileges, enforce a standardized withdrawal period, prevent on‑the‑fly minting of redeemable shares during volatile periods, and consider aggregating multiple markets with weighted incentives that favour larger, more stable markets. Such changes would align incentives across participants, reduce the opportunity for MEV extraction, and restore confidence that the protocol’s accounting assumptions hold under stress.

title: Wrong init code hash
description: An init code hash is used to calculate the address of UniswapV2 pair contract. But the init code hash is not same as the latest UniswapV2 repository.
poc:
UniswapV2Library.pairFor uses the following value as the init code hash of UniswapV2Pair.

```solidity
hex"e18a34eb0e04b04f7a0ac29a6e80748dca96319b42c54d679cb821dca90c6303" // init code hash
```

But it is different from the [init code hash](https://github.com/Uniswap/v2-periphery/blob/master/contracts/libraries/UniswapV2Library.sol#L24) of the uniswap v2 repository.

I tested this using one of the top UniswapV2 pairs. DAI-USDC is in the third place [here](https://v2.info.uniswap.org/pairs).

The token addresses are as follows:

DAI: 0x6B175474E89094C44Da98b954EedeAC495271d0F

USDC: 0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48

And the current UniswapV2Factory address is 0x5C69bEe701ef814a2B6a3EDD4B1652CB9cc5aA6f [here](https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v2/reference/smart-contracts/factory).

The pair address calculated is 0x6983E2Da04353C31c7C42B0EA900a40B1D5bf845. And we can’t find pair contract in the address.

So I think the old version of UniswapV2Factory and pair are used here. And it can cause a risk when liquidity is not enough for the pair.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using an incorrect init code hash when calculating the deterministic address of a UniswapV2 pair contract. The init code hash is a constant that represents the bytecode of the UniswapV2Pair contract and is combined with the factory address and token addresses to derive the pair address via the CREATE2 algorithm. In the examined library the hard‑coded hash corresponds to the SushiSwap implementation rather than the current UniswapV2 implementation. Because the hash does not match the actual bytecode deployed by the official UniswapV2Factory, the address produced by the pairFor function points to a location where no contract exists. This mismatch can be reproduced by feeding known token addresses (for example DAI and USDC) into the library; the resulting address (0x6983E2Da04353C31c7C42B0EA900a40B1D5bf845) does not contain a pair contract. The root cause is a stale constant that was not updated when the library was copied or when the upstream repository changed. An attacker or a careless developer may rely on the calculated address to perform swaps, add liquidity, or query reserves, assuming the pair exists. When a transaction is sent to the wrong address the call fails, funds may be transferred to an address with no code, and the user sees no receipt of tokens, effectively losing the assets. From the user’s perspective the UI may still display the pair as available (because off‑chain indexes list the correct pair) but on‑chain interactions return empty balances or revert, leading to confusion such as “my balance is zero after adding liquidity” or “the swap transaction never completes”. The issue is hard to notice because the address format looks valid and the error only appears at runtime. It was discovered during a security audit by testing the library against top‑ranked UniswapV2 pairs and observing that the computed address did not resolve to a contract. The bug belongs to the class of deterministic address miscalculation due to outdated init code hashes, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a pair address uniquely identifies a deployed liquidity pool. The recommended remediation is to replace the hard‑coded hash with the correct value from the official UniswapV2Factory (or retrieve it dynamically) and to ensure the library is kept in sync with the upstream repository. After updating the hash, pairFor will generate the proper address, enabling correct interaction with the intended liquidity pool and preventing accidental loss of funds.

title: Borrower can lose partial fund during minting of Power Token as excess ETH are not refunded automatically
description:
[src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L142](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/main/src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L142)  
[src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L87-L124](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/main/src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L87-L124)  
[src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L119-L123](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/main/src/periphery/LendgineRouter.sol#L119-L123)  
[src/periphery/Payment.sol#L44-L46](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/main/src/periphery/Payment.sol#L44-L46)

When the collateral/speculative token (Token1) is WETH, a borrower could mint Power Tokens and deposit the collateral tokens by sending ETH while calling the payable mint() function in LendgineRouter.sol.

The exact collateral amount required to be deposited by the borrower is only calculated during minting (due to external swap), which could be lesser than what the borrower has sent for the mint. This means that there will be excess ETH left in LendgineRouter contract and they are not automatically refunded to the borrower.

Anyone that sees this opportunity can call refundETH() to retrieve the excess ETH.

The borrower could retrieve the remaining ETH with a separate call to refundETH(). However, as the calls are not atomic, it is possible for a MEV bot to frontrun the borrower and steal the ETH too.

Furthermore, there are no documentation and test cases that advise or handle this issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability arises in the payable mint function of the LendgineRouter contract when the collateral token is WETH. During minting the contract performs an external swap to obtain the required token1 amount, and only after the swap does it calculate the exact amount of ETH (collateralIn) that must be transferred from the caller. Because the caller supplies the full msg.value up front, the actual collateralIn can be lower than the amount sent if the swap yields more token1 than anticipated. The surplus ETH remains locked in the router contract because the mint function does not automatically return the excess. A separate refundETH function can be invoked to withdraw any remaining balance, but this call is not atomic with mint. Consequently a malicious actor or MEV bot can monitor the transaction, front‑run the borrower and call refundETH before the borrower does, stealing the leftover ETH. The issue occurs whenever the external swap results in a collateralSwap value that exceeds the borrower’s expectation, which is common when market conditions change between the time the transaction is signed and when it is executed. The affected parties are borrowers who intend to mint Power Tokens and any user of the protocol who supplies ETH as collateral; they may see part of their ETH disappear, receive fewer tokens than expected, or notice that the contract balance has increased unexpectedly. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of ETH through mintCallback, identified that the collateralIn calculation can be smaller than msg.value, and observed that no automatic refund or event is emitted for the leftover balance. The bug is subtle because the contract’s UI does not display the intermediate ETH balance and the refund must be called explicitly, so users may assume the transaction handled all funds correctly. This class of bug is an “excess fund handling” or “unclaimed ether” issue, where a payable function accepts more value than needed and fails to return the surplus within the same transaction, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol. To remediate, the contract should either compute the required ETH before accepting payment and reject over‑payment, or automatically transfer any surplus back to the caller before the function returns. Alternatively, the protocol can enforce the use of its multicall feature to combine mint and refundETH in a single atomic call, ensuring that no third party can intercept the leftover ETH. Implementing an explicit check and refund mechanism would align the contract’s behavior with user expectations that all supplied ETH is either used as collateral or returned, eliminating the risk of funds disappearing due to front‑running.

title: Division before multiplication incurs unnecessary precision loss
description:
[src/core/Pair.sol#L56](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/2ad9a73d793ea23a25a381faadc86ae0c8cb5913/src/core/Pair.sol#L56)  
[src/core/Pair.sol#L57](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/2ad9a73d793ea23a25a381faadc86ae0c8cb5913/src/core/Pair.sol#L57)  
[core/Lendgine.sol#L252](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/2ad9a73d793ea23a25a381faadc86ae0c8cb5913/src/core/Lendgine.sol#L252)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss bug that stems from performing integer division before multiplication in several core financial calculations. In the interest‑accrual routine the code computes dilutionLPRequested as (FullMath.mulDiv(borrowRate,_totalLiquidityBorrowed,1e18) * timeElapsed) / 365 days, which is equivalent to (borrowRate * totalLiquidityBorrowed / 1e18 * timeElapsed) / 365 days. Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the intermediate division borrowRate * totalLiquidityBorrowed / 1e18 truncates any fractional part, potentially reducing the value to zero when the product is smaller than the scaling factor. A similar pattern appears in the invariant function where amount0 and amount1 are first multiplied by 1e18 and divided by liquidity before being scaled by token0Scale and token1Scale. When liquidity is large, amount0 * 1e18 / liquidity can also truncate to zero. This ordering error causes the protocol to underestimate dilution, reward distribution, and invariant checks, leading to lower interest accrual for lenders and inaccurate accounting of collateral. The impact is that users may receive less interest or rewards than expected, balances can appear stagnant, and over many blocks the cumulative rounding error can erode protocol economics, potentially exposing funds to loss or mispricing. The bug manifests whenever the scaled product is smaller than the divisor, which is common for high‑precision tokens or large liquidity pools. It affects all participants – lenders, borrowers, and token holders – because the core accounting logic is flawed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the order of operations in FullMath.mulDiv calls was examined and found to truncate values unnecessarily. The problem is subtle because the loss per transaction may be tiny and the use of FullMath hides the intermediate steps, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the calculations should be reordered so that multiplication occurs before division, or a single mulDiv call should be used with the full numerator and denominator to preserve precision (for example, mulDiv(borrowRate, _totalLiquidityBorrowed * timeElapsed, 365 days * 1e18)). Additionally, token amounts should be normalized by their respective scales before dividing by liquidity. This class of bug is a rounding or truncation error caused by improper fixed‑point arithmetic ordering, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards and interest are calculated exactly according to the defined formulas.

title: Admin should be able to refund or redeem the sanctioned users
description: Sanctioned user’s funds are locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic and access‑control flaw that prevents the privileged MANAGER_ADMIN role from refunding or redeeming assets belonging to users whose KYC or sanction status has become invalid. The contract’s completeRedemptions function is restricted to the admin role, but it still invokes internal checks that require every redeemer and refundee address to pass a KYC verification step. When a user’s KYC expires, is revoked, or the user is placed on a sanctions list after they have submitted a mint or redemption request, the _checkAddressesKYC modifier rejects the address even though the caller is the admin. As a result the admin cannot execute the redemption flow, the _processRefund and _processRedemption steps are never reached, and the collateral that should be returned or burned remains locked in the contract. This situation occurs whenever the user’s compliance status changes between the request and the epoch‑service time, which is a realistic scenario in regulated environments. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the CashManager.sol source where the code path was traced and it became clear that the admin role does not have an override for the KYC check. The problem is subtle because the function is protected by onlyRole(MANAGER_ADMIN), giving the impression that the admin can always intervene, yet the internal compliance guard silently aborts the transaction without an explicit error message, making the lock appear as a normal “no‑action” outcome. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – receiving a refund or seeing their balance reduced after a redemption – is replaced by a silent failure where the UI shows no change, the user receives nothing, and the funds seem to disappear from the protocol’s active pool. This violates the core accounting assumption that assets can always be reclaimed by the protocol or its administrators. The bug belongs to the class of privileged‑role authorization bypass where compliance checks are applied indiscriminately, preventing legitimate administrative recovery actions. To remediate the issue the contract should either allow the admin to bypass the KYC verification for redemption and refund operations, or provide a separate admin‑only function that can force‑unlock or manually process refunds for non‑compliant addresses, ensuring that funds are never permanently inaccessible due to a change in KYC status.

title: First Deposit Bug
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mint‑rate rounding error in a CToken‑style yield token that allows an attacker to steal underlying assets by front‑running a deposit. The contract mints new CToken tokens based on an exchange rate that is calculated from the contract's cash balance, total borrows and reserves divided by the total supply of CTokens. For the very first deposit the total supply is zero, so the contract returns a fixed initial exchange rate. After the first mint the total supply becomes a small non‑zero value (often just one token). If an attacker transfers a large amount of the underlying token directly to the CToken contract before another user calls mint, the cash balance used in the exchange‑rate formula inflates dramatically while the total supply remains tiny. The resulting exchange rate becomes larger than the amount the second user is trying to mint, and because the mint calculation uses integer division, the division of the deposited amount by the huge exchange rate rounds down to zero. Consequently the mint call succeeds, the user’s underlying tokens are transferred into the contract, but the user receives zero CToken tokens. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, yet their balance stays at zero and their funds disappear. The attacker can then redeem the single CToken they hold, withdrawing not only their own original deposit but also the underlying that was taken from the second user, effectively stealing the funds. The bug occurs only after the first mint when totalSupply is low and can be triggered whenever an attacker can increase the contract’s cash balance before another user’s mint. It was discovered through a targeted test that performed a front‑run transfer of underlying tokens before a second mint, observing that the second user’s balance remained zero while the contract’s cash grew. The issue is subtle because the mint function does not revert on a zero‑mint result, and the exchange‑rate value, although large, is not directly exposed to users. This class of bug belongs to the category of “division‑by‑large‑value rounding to zero” or “minting underflow due to inflated exchange rate”. It violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each deposited unit of underlying should yield a positive amount of protocol tokens. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the computed mint amount is greater than zero and revert otherwise, or adjust the exchange‑rate calculation to prevent extreme values (for example by using a minimum totalSupply threshold, capping cash growth, or employing rounding‑up arithmetic). Adding explicit checks for zero‑mint results and ensuring the exchange rate cannot exceed the deposited amount are the conceptual fixes required to stop the exploit.

title: `CashManager.setEpochDuration` functions has inconsistent output
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract that manages time‑based epochs. An administrative function allows a privileged role to change the length of an epoch (the epochDuration variable) but does not first finalize the current epoch by calling the routine that records the transition (transitionEpoch). Because the contract does not enforce a call to transitionEpoch before the duration is altered, the state that tracks how many epochs have passed becomes dependent on the order in which external transactions are mined. An attacker who can front‑run or back‑run the admin transaction can therefore cause the contract to record a different number of elapsed epochs for the same period of time. In a front‑run scenario the attacker invokes transitionEpoch first, then the admin changes epochDuration; the contract records the old duration for the just‑completed epoch and the new duration for subsequent epochs, resulting in a higher epoch count than expected. In a back‑run scenario the admin changes epochDuration first and the attacker invokes transitionEpoch afterwards; the just‑completed epoch is recorded with the new duration, causing the epoch count to be lower than it should be. The impact is that any logic that relies on the epoch number – such as reward distribution, vesting schedules, interest calculations or protocol governance – may use an incorrect epoch index, leading to users receiving too little or too much reward, funds being locked or released at the wrong time, or governance proposals being counted in the wrong period. From a user’s point of view the UI may show an epoch number that does not match the elapsed time, balances may appear unchanged after a period where they should have accrued interest, or a claim transaction may revert because the contract believes the user is still in a previous epoch. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the state simply diverges from the intended accounting model, making it hard to detect without explicit epoch‑transition tests. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when test cases that warped block timestamps revealed that calling setEpochDuration before or after transitionEpoch produced different values for currentEpoch.
