The condition occurs whenever stake(), unstake() or rebalanceToWeights() is executed and at least one derivative contract reverts. All users who rely on the protocol, as well as the protocol owner, are affected because their balances appear unchanged and the UI reports a failed transaction, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or are permanently locked. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case scenarios for each derivative and observed that a single revert propagates to the whole call. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract works correctly when all derivatives behave as expected; only rare external failures expose the problem. The bug belongs to the class of external‑call‑failure denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where unchecked external calls break atomicity and accounting assumptions. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with no change to their balance, often described as “my stake failed and my funds are stuck”. To remediate the issue the contract should catch individual call failures, skip the failing derivative, optionally redistribute the intended amount among the remaining derivatives, and record any shortfall so that users can later claim the missing funds. This changes the logic from an all‑or‑nothing approach to a resilient, partial‑success model that preserves overall functionality even when a single external contract misbehaves.

title: In de-peg scenario, forcing full exit from every derivative & immediately re-entering can cause big losses for depositors
description:
In a de-peg scenario, there will be a general flight to safety (`ETH`) from users across the board. All pools will have a uni-directional sell-pressure where users prefer to exchange derivative token for WETH.

There are 3 sources of losses in this scenario
* Protocol currently doesn’t localize exit & force-exits all positions. So even non de-pegged assets are forced to exit causing further sell-side pressure that can further widen slippages
* Protocol immediately tries to re-enter the position based on new weights. Since de-peg in one asset can trigger de-peg in another (eg. USDT de-pegged immediately after UST collapse), immediately entering into another position after exiting one might cause more. A better approach would be to simply exit stressed positions & waiting out for the market/gas prices to settle down. Separating exit & re-entry functions can save depositors from high execution costs.
* Protocol is inefficiently exiting & re-entering the positions. Instead of taking marginal positions to rebalance, current implementation first fully exits & then re-enters back based on new weights (see POC below). Since any slippage losses are borne by depositors, a better implementation can save losses to users
poc:
* Assume positions are split in following ratio by value: 10% frax-Eth, 70% stEth and 20% rEth
* Now frax-Eth starts to de-peg, forcing protocol to exit frax-Eth and rebalance to say, 80% stEth and 20% rEth
* Current rebalancing first exits 70% stEth, 20% rEth and then re-enters 80% stEth and 20% rEth
* A marginal re-balancing would have only needed protocol to exit 10% frax-Eth and divert that 10% to stEth

By executing huge, unnecessary txns, protocol is exposing depositors to high slippage costs on the entire pool.
bug_full: In a de‑peg scenario the protocol’s rebalanceToWeights function forces a full exit of every derivative position and immediately re‑enters based on the new target weights. The root cause is that the implementation does not localize exits, does not separate the exit and entry steps, and always exits the entire pool before rebuilding the new composition, even when only one asset is under stress. When a derivative such as frax‑Eth loses its peg, the contract is instructed to sell the frax‑Eth tokens and then, in the same transaction, sell all other positions (for example stEth and rEth) before buying back the new target allocation. This creates a massive sell‑side pressure on the market, inflates slippage, and forces depositors to absorb the loss because the slippage is deducted from the pool balance. An attacker or a governance caller can trigger this behavior simply by invoking rebalanceToWeights during a rapid market move, causing the protocol to liquidate assets at unfavorable rates and then repurchase them at higher prices. The impact is that users see their share value shrink, often receiving far less than expected when they later withdraw; the UI may show a sudden drop in balance or a zero‑return on a withdrawal that should have yielded a normal amount. The condition required is a black‑swan event where at least one derivative de‑pegs, combined with a decision by the owner or DAO to call the rebalancing function. All depositors, the protocol’s treasury, and any downstream contracts are affected because the loss is distributed across the entire pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit that simulated a de‑peg of frax‑Eth and observed that the contract first exited 70 % of stEth and 20 % of rEth before re‑entering the new allocation, whereas a marginal re‑balance would have required only the 10 % of frax‑Eth to be moved. The bug is hard to notice because the function appears to achieve the intended weight adjustment, yet the hidden cost of full‑pool slippage is not obvious from the code alone. The recommended fix is to redesign rebalanceToWeights so that exits are localized to the stressed asset, to split the logic into separate exit and entry functions, and to implement marginal re‑balancing that only adjusts the net change in positions, allowing the protocol to wait for market conditions to stabilise before re‑entering. This class of vulnerability belongs to inefficient rebalancing or over‑aggressive liquidation bugs, where the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional asset weights are violated by unnecessary full‑pool trades, leading to unexpected fund loss for users.

title: Possible DoS on `unstake`
description:
RocketPool rETH tokens have a [deposit delay](https://github.com/rocket-pool/rocketpool/blob/967e4d3c32721a84694921751920af313d1467af/contracts/contract/token/RocketTokenRETH.sol#L157-L172) that prevents any user who has recently deposited to transfer or burn tokens. In the past this delay was set to 5760 blocks mined (aprox. 19h, considering one block per 12s). This delay can prevent asymmetry protocol users from unstaking if another user staked recently.

While it’s not currently possible due to RocketPool’s configuration, any future changes made to this delay by the admins could potentially lead to a denial-of-service attack on the `ùnstake()` mechanism. This is a major functionality of the asymmetry protocol, and therefore, it should be classified as a high severity issue.
poc:
Currently, the delay is set to zero, but if RocketPool admins decide to change this value in the future, it could cause issues. Specifically, protocol users staking actions could prevent other users from unstaking for a few hours. Given that many users call the stake function throughout the day, the delay would constantly reset, making the unstaking mechanism unusable. It’s important to note that this only occurs when `stake()` is used through the `rocketDepositPool` route. If rETH is obtained from the Uniswap pool, the delay is not affected.

A malicious actor can also exploit this to be able to block all `unstake` calls. Consider the following scenario where the delay was raised again to 5760 blocks. Bob (malicious actor) call `stakes()` with the minimum amount, consequently triggering deposit to RocketPool and resetting the deposit delay. Alice tries to `unstake` her funds, but during rETH burn, it fails due to the delay check, reverting the `unstake` call.

If Bob manages to repeatedly `stakes()` the minimum amount every 19h (or any other interval less then the deposit delay), all future calls to `unstake` will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a potential denial‑of‑service on the unstake function of the asymmetry protocol that relies on RocketPool’s rETH token. RocketPool implements a deposit‑delay mechanism that blocks any transfer or burn of rETH that was minted within a configurable number of blocks (historically 5 760 blocks, about 19 hours). The contract checks the timestamp of the most recent deposit and reverts any burn operation – which the unstake routine performs – if the token is still within the delay window. Because the delay is stored globally, each new stake that routes through the RocketDepositPool resets the delay for the entire token contract. An attacker can repeatedly call stake with the minimum allowed amount at intervals shorter than the delay, constantly refreshing the lockout period. Consequently, any honest user who attempts to unstake will see the transaction revert, receive no tokens, and their balance will appear unchanged, effectively locking their funds for the duration of the delay. The issue manifests only when rETH is obtained via the RocketPool deposit path; acquiring rETH from the Uniswap V3 pool bypasses the delay, which is why the current configuration (delay set to zero) does not expose the bug. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between the protocol’s stake/unstake flow and RocketPool’s token contract. It is difficult to notice because the delay is currently disabled and the revert occurs deep inside the burn call, presenting as a generic “unstake failed” error without obvious indication of a time‑based lock. The bug belongs to the class of time‑based lockout or state‑dependent denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where a mutable global parameter can be abused to prevent legitimate state transitions. To remediate, the protocol should avoid relying on a token that enforces a deposit delay, for example by sourcing rETH exclusively from a Uniswap V3 pool or by redesigning the unstake logic to use a token without such a lock, or by adding a separate per‑user delay that cannot be reset by other users. Fixing the issue restores the expected behavior where a user who initiates an unstake receives the corresponding assets promptly, aligning with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that deposits and withdrawals are symmetric and that funds are always recoverable.

title: Non-ideal rETH/WETH pool used pays unnecessary fees
description:
rETH is acquired using the Uniswap rETH/WETH pool. This solution has higher fees and lower liquidity than alternatives, which results in more lost user value than other solutions.

The Uniswap rETH/WETH pool that is used in Reth.sol to make swaps has a liquidity of `$5 million`. In comparison, the Balancer rETH/WETH pool has a liquidity of `$80 million`. Even the Curve rETH/WETH pool has a liquidity of `$8 million`. The greater liquidity should normally offer lower slippage to users. In addition, the fees to swap with the Balancer pool are only 0.04% compared to Uniswap’s 0.05%. Even the Curve pool offers a lower fee than Uniswap with just a 0.037% fee. [This Dune Analytics dashboard](https://dune.com/drworm/rocketpool) shows that Balancer is where the majority of rETH swaps happen by volume.

One solution to finding the best swap path for rETH is to use RocketPool’s [RocketSwapRouter.sol contract `swapTo()` function](https://etherscan.io/address/0x16d5a408e807db8ef7c578279beeee6b228f1c1c#code#F19#L64). When users visit the RocketPool frontend to swap ETH for rETH, this is the function that RocketPool calls for the user. RocketSwapRouter.sol automatically determines the best way to split the swap between Balancer and Uniswap pools.
poc:
Pools that can be used for rETH/WETH swapping:

  * [Uniswap rETH/WETH pool](https://etherscan.io/address/0xa4e0faA58465A2D369aa21B3e42d43374c6F9613): `$5 million` in liquidity
  * [Balancer rETH/WETH pool](https://app.balancer.fi/#/ethereum/pool/0x1e19cf2d73a72ef1332c882f20534b6519be0276000200000000000000000112)
  * [Curve Finance rETH/ETH pool](https://curve.fi/#/ethereum/pools/factory-crypto-210/deposit): `$8 million` in liquidity

[Line where Reth.sol swaps WETH for rETH](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L101) with the Uniswap rETH/WETH pool.
bug_full: The issue is an economic inefficiency in the Reth.sol contract where swaps from ETH (or WETH) to rETH are performed exclusively through the Uniswap rETH/WETH pool. This pool holds roughly five million dollars of liquidity, which is significantly lower than the Balancer pool (about eighty million) and the Curve pool (about eight million). Because liquidity is lower, the Uniswap pool incurs higher price impact and a higher swap fee of 0.05% compared with Balancer’s 0.04% and Curve’s 0.037%. The root cause is a hard‑coded reference to the Uniswap pool and the absence of any routing logic that would select a better‑liquidity, lower‑fee pool or split the trade across multiple pools. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by simply executing a swap and receiving less rETH than the market would otherwise provide; the contract does not protect users from the extra slippage or fee loss. The impact is a loss of user value: users expect to receive a certain amount of rETH for their ETH, but the transaction completes with a smaller amount, effectively “money disappears” from the user’s perspective. This situation occurs every time a user invokes the swap function in Reth.sol, i.e., when they use the RocketPool frontend to acquire rETH. The affected parties are the end‑users who perform the swap, the RocketPool protocol which may be perceived as inefficient, and any sponsor that relies on accurate value transfer. The problem was discovered during a code audit that compared the liquidity and fee structures of available AMM pools and noted that the contract’s choice was sub‑optimal. Because the transaction does not revert and no error is emitted, the inefficiency can be hard to notice; the UI simply shows a successful swap, while the user’s rETH balance is lower than expected. To remediate, the contract should adopt the same routing logic used by RocketPool’s frontend – namely the RocketSwapRouter.swapTo() function – which automatically determines the optimal split between Balancer and Uniswap (or other pools). Alternatively, the hard‑coded Uniswap reference can be replaced with a call to the Balancer rETH/ETH pool, thereby reducing both slippage and fee costs and preserving user value. This class of bug falls under “value leakage” or “sub‑optimal AMM routing”, where the business logic assumes optimal market conditions that are not enforced by the code.

title: Stuck ether when use function `stake` with empty `derivatives`
description: After `initialize` the contract `SafEth`, if someone call `stake` before `addDerivative`, the function `stake` skip the two for cycles because the `derivativeCount` is equal to `0` and don’t `deposit` in the `derivative` contract also mint `0` tokens to the sender. Finally the amount of `msg.value` will stuck in the contract
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the staking entry point of the SafEth contract when the contract has been initialized but no derivative contracts have been registered. The contract stores a counter called derivativeCount that tracks how many derivative contracts are available for deposit. The stake function iterates over the list of derivatives to forward the incoming ether and mint corresponding staking tokens. Because there is no explicit guard that derivativeCount must be greater than zero, calling stake while derivativeCount equals zero causes both for‑loops to be skipped. Consequently the function does not forward the ether to any derivative contract and it mints zero staking tokens to the caller. The ether sent in msg.value remains locked in the SafEth contract because no withdrawal path is provided for this situation. This bug was discovered during a security audit when a test case called stake before any derivative was added; the transaction succeeded, the contract balance increased by the deposited amount, and the caller’s token balance stayed at zero, indicating that funds were silently trapped. The issue is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and emits no error, giving the impression that staking succeeded while the accounting state is inconsistent. The impact is that any user who stakes before a derivative is added loses access to the deposited ether, effectively causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective and reducing the protocol’s available liquidity. The problem affects all participants who might interact with the staking function, the protocol’s overall capital efficiency, and any downstream accounting that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between deposited ether and minted tokens. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a requirement that derivativeCount be greater than zero before allowing a stake, or otherwise handle the zero‑derivative case by reverting the transaction or providing a fallback mechanism that returns the ether to the sender. This change restores the expected business logic that a stake must result in a deposit to a derivative and the issuance of a positive amount of staking tokens, preventing ether from becoming permanently stuck.

title: Residual ETH unreachable and unutilized in SafEth.sol
description:
Unlike the other three contracts in scope, SafEth.sol does not have a measure in place to utilize the residual ETH, be it:

  * accidentally received,
  * zero ETH output from `unstake()` arising from recipient non-contract existence, or
  * ETH sent in via `stake()` fails to deposit into a derivative due to uninitialized derivatives and weights, as I have explained in a separate submission.

In the derivative contracts, the above issue is wiped clean via `address(this).balance` every time `withdraw()` is predominantly invoked in [`unstake()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L118) of SafEth.sol:

[File: WstEth.sol#L63-L66](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L63-L66)  
[File: SfrxEth.sol#L84-L87](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/SfrxEth.sol#L84-L87)  
[File: Reth.sol#L110-L114](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L110-L114)  

```solidity
            (bool sent, ) = address(msg.sender).call{value: address(this).balance}(
                ""
            );
            require(sent, "Failed to send Ether");
```
bug_full: The contract SafEth.sol contains a logic error that can leave ether permanently locked inside the contract. The root cause is the way the functions `unstake()` and `rebalanceToWeights()` calculate the amount of ether to redistribute. Both functions record the contract balance before and after calling the derivative contracts, then compute a delta (`ethAmountAfter - ethAmountBefore`). When the derivative contracts withdraw their entire balance back to SafEth, the contract balance does not change, so the computed delta is zero. Any ether that arrived in SafEth for reasons such as accidental transfers, a zero‑value output from `unstake()` when the recipient is not a contract, or a failed deposit into an uninitialized derivative remains in the contract but is never considered for redistribution because the delta is zero. As a result, users who expect a refund or a proportional share of the residual ether receive nothing, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated: the total ether held by the contract is assumed to be fully allocated to stakers, but a hidden remainder persists. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the balance‑before and balance‑after logic with the actual ether flows and identified that the residual amount is never used. The bug is subtle because the contract successfully sends ether back to the caller in most cases, so the presence of a small leftover balance does not raise an immediate error, and the `require(sent, "Failed to send Ether")` check passes. However, over time the hidden ether can accumulate, effectively disappearing from users’ perspectives. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or balance‑delta miscalculation bugs, where a contract relies on a change in balance to determine the amount to process, ignoring the absolute balance that may contain residual funds. To fix the issue, the contract should use the total current balance (`address(this).balance`) when calculating the amount to rebalance, as shown in the recommended patch, thereby ensuring that any residual ether is harvested and redistributed to stakers. This change eliminates the hidden stash of ether and restores correct accounting semantics, preventing users from seeing their expected refunds turn into zero and protecting the protocol from unintended fund loss.

title: No slippage protection on `stake`
description: `mintAmount` is determined both by `totalStakeValueEth` and `preDepositPrice`. While the former is associated with external interactions beyond users’ control, the latter should be linked to a slippage control to incentivize more staker participations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the stake function of the SafEth contract. When a user calls stake() and sends ETH, the contract calculates the amount of derivative tokens to mint (mintAmount) based on two variables: totalStakeValueEth, which aggregates the value of all underlying derivatives, and preDepositPrice, which is derived from the ratio of the aggregated underlying value to the current total supply of the derivative token. Because totalStakeValueEth is obtained from external derivative contracts whose balances can change at any time, and because preDepositPrice is recomputed on‑chain without any user‑controlled bound, a rapid change in the value of the underlying assets between the moment a transaction is signed and the moment it is mined can cause the computed mintAmount to deviate from the amount the user expected. In practice this means that two users staking the same amount of ETH a few minutes apart may receive different numbers of derivative tokens, and a malicious actor could manipulate the underlying derivative balances (for example by front‑running or by feeding a volatile oracle) to force the price down, inflating the mintAmount for an attacker or, conversely, reducing the amount received by honest stakers. From the user’s perspective the UI may display an expected token amount, but after the transaction is mined the wallet shows a smaller balance or even zero tokens, leading to the symptom “my stake tokens disappeared” or “I received far fewer tokens than I paid for”. The issue is hard to notice because the contract assumes the price of each derivative is stable and close to a 1:1 peg, an assumption that can be broken by market volatility or by deliberate de‑pegging attacks similar to recent stablecoin de‑peg events. The bug belongs to the class of “price‑oracle manipulation / slippage‑absence” vulnerabilities, where a contract relies on a price that can change between transaction submission and execution without providing a minimum‑output guarantee. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the stake() implementation and identified that the mintAmount calculation does not include any user‑specified minimum output parameter. To remediate the issue the stake function should accept a minMintAmountOut argument supplied by the caller and enforce require(mintAmount >= minMintAmountOut, "mint amount too low"); this creates a slippage guard similar to those used in AMM swaps. Additionally, the front‑end should expose a slippage tolerance selector (e.g., 0.1 %) so users can set an acceptable deviation before confirming the transaction. By adding this check, the contract will revert if the price moves unfavourably, protecting users from unexpected token loss and preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants.

title: ProfilePicture subprotocol is immutably linked by `subprotocolName` to the CID protocol
description: Besides having to re-register the protocol, it will also have to be redeployed.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the ProfilePicture subprotocol stores its registration identifier, subprotocolName, as an immutable variable that is assigned only once during contract construction. The contract later uses this stored name to query the CID protocol for the primary CID NFT identifier. Because the name is fixed at deployment, the contract assumes that the same identifier will be successfully registered in the SubprotocolRegistry. However, registration is performed in a separate transaction after deployment, and there is no mechanism to update subprotocolName if the registration fails. An attacker who can front‑run the registration transaction can register the same name before the legitimate owner does. In that case the original registration call reverts or fails, and the deployed ProfilePicture contract is left with a subprotocolName that no longer matches any entry in the registry. The contract’s logic then cannot retrieve a valid cidNFTID, causing the internal checks to reset nftContract and nftID to zero and effectively disabling the profile‑picture functionality. From a user’s perspective the profile picture appears missing or the contract seems to do nothing when they try to set or view it, even though the contract is deployed and holds funds for the registration fee. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the subprotocol and a loss of the registration fee because the owner must redeploy the contract with a new name before it can be registered again. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the constructor and the later use of subprotocolName, noticing the mismatch between deployment and registration phases. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert on a failed registration; it simply becomes non‑functional, which may be interpreted as a benign bug. The proper mitigation is to make deployment and registration atomic – for example by performing both actions in a single transaction – or to allow the subprotocolName to be set after deployment by a temporary owner, ensuring that the name stored in the contract always matches the name under which it is registered. This aligns the contract’s state with the business logic that each subprotocol must be uniquely registered and prevents an attacker from hijacking the name and rendering the contract unusable.

title: The range of `iteratePRNG` limits the number of Zalgo distortions
description: Only a tiny fraction of all Zalgo distortions are accessible.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Zalgo distortion generator derives its pseudo‑random values. When a character is rendered with font class 7, the contract uses a 256‑byte seed called _characterModifier and feeds it through the internal function iteratePRNG three times to decide how many diacritic symbols appear above, over, and below the base letter. iteratePRNG multiplies the current state by a constant, cubes the result and then applies a modulus of 2038074743. Because of this modulus, after the first iteration the state space collapses to at most 2,038,074,743 distinct values, regardless of the original 256‑bit seed. Consequently the total number of distinct Zalgo modifications that can ever be produced per letter is limited to 7 × 2038074743, roughly 1.4 × 10^10, which is a tiny fraction of the mathematically possible 1.38 × 10^24 variations. The root cause is therefore an insufficient entropy source: the PRNG’s output range is far smaller than required to cover the combinatorial space of diacritic selections. This limitation can be exploited by an attacker who can enumerate the entire reachable set of distortions, predict the visual output for any given input, and potentially craft characters that look identical to legitimate ones, undermining the protocol’s claim of randomness and uniqueness. The impact is primarily on user experience and trust – users may notice that Zalgo characters repeat far more often than expected, leading to a perception of low quality or even manipulation. The issue manifests only when the Zalgo font class is used, and it is invisible in normal operation because the characters still appear distorted, just not with the full diversity the design intended. It was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the theoretical number of possible modifications with the actual number generated by the contract’s PRNG. The bug is hard to spot because the visual output still looks random at a glance; only a statistical analysis of the output space reveals the truncation. To remediate, the contract should replace iteratePRNG with a generator that provides at least 1.98 × 10^23 distinct states – for example by using a larger modulus, a cryptographic hash‑based PRNG, or by expanding the seed size – and also increase the allowed range of _characterModifier beyond 0‑255. This would restore the intended entropy and ensure that each letter can exhibit the full spectrum of Zalgo modifications, aligning the implementation with its design specifications.

title: `characterModifier` is `uint8` but encodes `1.38e24` different Zalgo distortions
description: Only 256 Zalgo distortions are possible, which is a miniscule fraction of the actual combinations possible.
bug_full: The issue originates from the way Zalgo distortions are encoded in the contract. A Zalgo tile is defined by a letter together with a modification that can combine up to seven diacritic characters above the letter, optionally one over‑letter character, and up to seven characters below the letter. Mathematically this yields roughly 1.38e24 distinct modifications per letter. However the contract stores the modifier in a variable called characterModifier that is declared as a uint8. Because a uint8 can only represent 256 distinct values, the contract can generate at most 256 different distortions for any Zalgo tile. The root cause is an insufficient integer size for representing a combinatorial space that is many orders of magnitude larger than the type can hold. This mismatch is introduced in the _drawing function where a pseudo‑random seed is reduced modulo 256 and cast to uint8 before being used to derive the numbers of above, middle and below diacritics. When a user purchases a tray that contains a Zalgo tile, the contract deterministically selects a distortion based on this limited characterModifier. As a result, many theoretically possible distortions are never reachable, some expected combinations of diacritics are missing entirely, and different users frequently receive identical distortions or even duplicate distortions within the same tray. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a Zalgo character but the variety is far lower than advertised; users may notice that the same distorted letter appears repeatedly, that they cannot obtain a specific style they expected, or that the protocol appears to promise billions of variations while only a few hundred are actually possible. The impact is primarily on user experience and trust: the protocol gives the impression of offering a vast space of unique visual effects, but the limited encoding leads to repeated patterns, perceived cheating, and potential loss of confidence in the platform. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the mathematical description of the Zalgo space with the actual implementation of characterModifier and observed the narrowing of the range to a uint8. The problem is subtle because the visual output still looks random, making the limitation hard to detect without inspecting the underlying combinatorial logic. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient‑range integer encoding, sometimes described as a type‑size mismatch or encoding bottleneck. To remediate the issue the contract should store characterModifier in a type large enough to cover the full combinatorial space, such as uint256 or at least a sufficiently wide unsigned integer (e.g., uint88). Alternatively, the design could be changed to generate a subset of distortions in a way that matches the advertised range, or to hard‑code a fixed list of 256 variations if that is the intended limit. In any case, the fix must align the declared capabilities of the protocol with the actual number of distinct Zalgo distortions that can be produced, thereby eliminating the discrepancy between promised and delivered functionality.

title: Bio Protocol - `tokenURI` JSON injection
description:
The Bio Protocol allows users to mint Bio NFTs that represent user’s bio. Once NFT is minted anyone can trigger `tokenURI` to retrieve JSON data with the bio and generated svg image. Example JSON content (decoded from Base64):
    
    {"name": "Bio #1", "description": "Test", "image": "data:image/svg+xml;base64,"}

The issue is that function `Bio.tokenURI` is vulnerable to JSON injection and it is possible to inject `"` character into bio completely altering the integrity of JSON data. User sends following data as `bio`:
    
    Test\", \"name\": \"Bio #999999999

This is will result in following JSON data (new `name` key was injected):
    
    {"name": "Bio #1", "description": "Test", "name": "Bio #999999999", "image": "data:image/svg+xml;base64,"}

Depending on the usage of Bio Protocol by frontend or 3rd party applications this will have serious impact on the security. Some examples of the attacks that can be carried:

  1. Attacker might create a Bio NFT that mimics copies the name of different Bio NFT.
  2. Attacker might change the generated svg `image` to completely different one.
  3. Attacker might point `image` to external `URL`.
  4. Attacker might trigger cross-site scripting attacks if the data from JSON is not properly handled.
bug_full: The Bio Protocol tokenURI function returns a JSON document that contains the fields name, description and image. The JSON is assembled by concatenating the user‑provided bio string directly into the JSON text without any escaping. Because the double‑quote character is not filtered, an attacker can include an escaped quote in the bio, close the original string value and inject additional key‑value pairs. For example, submitting the bio string Test\", \"name\":\"Bio #999999999 results in a JSON object that contains two name entries and can replace the image field with an attacker‑controlled value. The contract does not validate the resulting JSON, so the tokenURI call still returns syntactically valid data but the content no longer reflects the original user input. This is a classic JSON injection vulnerability, similar to cross‑site scripting when the metadata is rendered in a web UI. The flaw can be exploited whenever any front‑end or third‑party service reads the tokenURI output and trusts the fields for display, linking, or rendering the SVG image. An attacker could impersonate another NFT by copying its name, replace the SVG with malicious graphics, point the image to an external URL, or embed script tags that trigger XSS if the consumer does not sanitise the data. From the user’s perspective the NFT may show an unexpected name, a blank or wrong picture, or cause the browser to load unexpected resources, violating the expectation that the bio they entered is shown unchanged. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the string construction in tokenURI and identified the lack of escaping. It can be hard to notice because the JSON remains well‑formed; only the values are altered, so a quick visual check may not reveal the injection. The proper mitigation is to encode or escape all user‑controlled characters before inserting them into the JSON document, or to move the sanitisation to the client side and treat the on‑chain metadata as untrusted. In any case, the contract should enforce a whitelist of safe characters or use a library that safely builds JSON to prevent injection attacks.

title: If the underlying NFT is burned, getPFP may return incorrect results
bug_full: The ProfilePicture contract exposes a view function getPFP that is intended to return the address of the underlying NFT contract and the token identifier associated with a given profile picture token. The function first reads the stored nftContract and nftID from its internal mapping, then obtains a CID NFT identifier and checks that the address registered for that CID NFT matches the current owner of the underlying NFT via ERC721.ownerOf. If the CID identifier is zero or the registered address does not match the owner, the function clears the returned values to zero. The vulnerability arises when the underlying NFT has been burned. Some ERC721 implementations return the zero address for ownerOf on a burned token instead of reverting, and the AddressRegistry also returns zero when a CID NFT has not been registered. In this situation the equality check (addressRegistry.getAddress(cidNFTID) != ERC721(nftContract).ownerOf(nftID)) evaluates to false because both sides are zero, causing the function to skip the safety branch and return the stale nftContract and nftID values. An attacker who controls the underlying NFT can transfer it away, sell it, or burn it, and later callers of getPFP will receive a contract address and token ID that no longer correspond to a valid asset. From a user perspective the UI may still display a profile picture or claim ownership of an NFT that no longer exists, leading to confusion such as “my profile picture shows a token but I cannot view its metadata” or “the contract reports an NFT but the token is missing”. Integrators that rely on getPFP for access control, royalty distribution, or cross‑protocol verification may mistakenly treat the returned data as proof of ownership, potentially allowing unauthorized actions or causing accounting mismatches. The bug is an edge case that is hard to detect because most ERC721 contracts follow the standard and revert on burned tokens, so typical tests pass; only non‑standard NFTs that return address(0) expose the flaw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of getPFP and considered the behavior of ownerOf on burned tokens. To remediate, the function should explicitly treat a zero address returned from ownerOf as an invalid state and reset the output values, or better yet, catch the revert from non‑standard implementations and handle it uniformly. Adding a direct check for ERC721(nftContract).ownerOf(nftID) == address(0) before the registry comparison, or requiring that the CID NFT be registered before any lookup, eliminates the false‑positive scenario and restores the intended invariant that getPFP only returns valid, existing NFT references.

title: Incorrect emoji displaying
description: Possible to split bio incorrectly, this leads to incorrect display of generated image. This image will be impossible to modify. This might lead to integration problems.
poc:
Let’s consider tokenURI function of the Bio contract.

Here implemented corner case for some emojis, but current implementation doesn’t handle all cases. I suppose handling all cases is redundant, erroneously, complicated and unnecessary.

Let’s consider part of tokenURI code in python, this part just rewritten on Python part of Solidity code:
    
    import binascii
    
    def sol_func_same(bio):
        bioTextBytes = str.encode(bio, "utf-8")
        lengthInBytes = len(bioTextBytes)
        lines = (lengthInBytes - 1) // 40 + 1
        strLines = [None for _ in range(lines)]
        prevByteWasContinuation = False
        insertedLines = 0
        bytesLines = []
        bytesOffset = 0
        for i in range(0, lengthInBytes):
            character = bioTextBytes[i]
            bytesLines.append(character)
            bytesOffset += 1
            if ((i > 0 and (i + 1) % 40 == 0) or prevByteWasContinuation or i == lengthInBytes - 1):
                nextCharacter = 0
                if (i != lengthInBytes - 1):  # 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿
                    nextCharacter = bioTextBytes[i + 1]
                if (nextCharacter & 0xC0 == 0x80):
                    prevByteWasContinuation = True
                else:
                    if (
                            (nextCharacter == 0xE2 and bioTextBytes[i + 2] == 0x80 and bioTextBytes[i + 3] == 0x8D) or
                            (nextCharacter == 0xF0 and
                             bioTextBytes[i + 2] == 0x9F and
                             bioTextBytes[i + 3] == 0x8F and
                             int(bioTextBytes[i + 4]) >= 187 and
                             int(bioTextBytes[i + 4]) <= 191) or
                            (i >= 2 and
                             bioTextBytes[i - 2] == 0xE2 and
                             bioTextBytes[i - 1] == 0x80 and
                             bioTextBytes[i] == 0x8D)
                    ):
                        prevByteWasContinuation = True
                        continue
    
                    strLines[insertedLines] = binascii.unhexlify(''.join([hex(x)[2:] for x in bytesLines])).decode("utf-8")
                    insertedLines += 1
                    bytesLines = []
    
                    prevByteWasContinuation = False
                    bytesOffset = 0
    
        for idx, i in enumerate(strLines):
            print(idx, i)
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        sol_func_same("0🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿")
        print("===" * 20)
        sol_func_same("000000000000000000000000000000🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿")

The result is:
    
    0 0🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿
    ============================================================
    0 000000000000000000000000000000🏴󠁧󠁢
    1 󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

In the second line present 31 character.

but correct answer for the second case is:
    
    000000000000000000000000000000🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

This happened because Eng flag presented with combination of different emojis, this case isn’t handled by contract.

Similar test might be added to the Bio.t.sol contract:
    
    function testSmallLine() public {
        string memory text = unicode"000🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿";
        bio.mint(text);
        string memory result = bio.tokenURI(1);
        console.logString(result);
    }
    
    function testLongLine() public {
        string memory text = unicode"000000000000000000000000000000🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿";
        bio.mint(text);
        string memory result = bio.tokenURI(1);
        console.logString(result);
    }

You need to decode them and you’ll receive the same incorrect result.
bug_full: The contract generates an SVG image from a user‑provided biography string and splits the string into lines of 40 bytes before embedding it in the tokenURI metadata. The implementation assumes that a line break can be inserted after every 40 bytes without considering that many Unicode characters, especially emojis and composite flag symbols, occupy multiple bytes. The root cause is a simplistic byte‑based line‑splitting algorithm that only checks a limited set of continuation‑byte patterns and does not correctly handle grapheme clusters formed by sequences such as regional indicator symbols. When a multi‑byte emoji straddles a 40‑byte boundary, the algorithm may cut the emoji in half, treat the remaining bytes as a separate line, or skip them entirely. As a result, the generated SVG contains truncated or missing emoji glyphs, leading to an image that does not display the intended characters. From a user’s perspective the token’s visual representation may show a broken flag, missing symbols, or an empty space where the emoji should be, contradicting the expectation that the full biography, including all emojis, is rendered correctly. This defect can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately includes specially crafted emoji sequences in the bio field; the malformed SVG can cause UI rendering errors, break integrations that rely on the tokenURI, or obscure information in the metadata. The issue was discovered during a security audit when test cases containing a flag emoji composed of several code points produced an incorrectly split line and a malformed SVG. The problem is subtle because the tokenURI still returns a valid base64 JSON payload, so the error is only visible when the SVG is rendered, making it easy to overlook. To remediate the bug, the contract should avoid manual byte‑wise splitting and instead use a view function that constructs the SVG with proper Unicode‑aware line breaking, or store explicit byte offsets supplied by the caller to guarantee that line breaks occur only at safe boundaries. Implementing a Unicode‑compliant splitter or leveraging existing libraries to handle grapheme clusters will ensure that emojis are kept intact, preserving the visual integrity of the generated image and preventing integration failures.

title: Users can end up buying and paying for a different Tray than the one they were trying to acquire
description:
Trays and their tiles are the building blocks for fusing a Namespace NFT. The tiles in a tray are generated based on a hash of the previous mint.

Users will need specific tiles to be able to create the name they want, so it is of utter importance for them to get the trays they want with their corresponding tiles. The users should be able to precompute this, [as the documentation states](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-canto-identity/blob/main/canto-namespace-protocol/README.md#tray):

“The 7 tiles per tray are then generated according to a deterministic algorithm. A user can therefore precompute which trays he will get.”
bug_full: Thecontract allows users to purchase a deterministic set of tiles called a Tray, where each tile is derived from a hash that is updated on every mint. The vulnerability arises because the buy() function does not verify that the hash used to generate the tiles matches the hash the user pre‑computed off‑chain. Consequently, if another transaction (for example a malicious front‑runner) is mined just before the user’s purchase, the stored lastHash will change, the contract will compute a new sequence of tiles, and the user will receive a Tray with different tile data than the one they intended to buy. This is a classic front‑running race condition: the protocol assumes that the hash is immutable between the user’s off‑chain calculation and the on‑chain execution, but the code provides no safeguard. An attacker can simply submit a transaction that triggers a mint, thereby advancing lastHash, and then let the victim’s transaction execute, causing the victim to pay the full price for a Tray that does not contain the required tiles. From the user’s point of view the UI will show a successful purchase, but the resulting Tray may lack the expected characters, making the desired Namespace NFT impossible to assemble; the user may see missing or incorrect tiles, or a completely different Tray ID than anticipated. The impact is loss of funds and failure to obtain the intended name, which undermines the economic model of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s logic with the documentation stating that tiles are deterministic and pre‑computable. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the contract does not emit an explicit warning; the only symptom is that the acquired Tray does not match the user’s expectation. The proper mitigation is to make the hash part of the transaction input and enforce a strict equality check against the contract’s stored lastHash before generating tiles, causing the transaction to revert if the hash has changed. This commit‑reveal style check prevents front‑running and ensures that users receive exactly the Tray they pre‑computed, restoring the deterministic guarantee of the system.

title: Bio lines will overflow the buffer for repeated “continuation” characters
bug_full: The vulnerability is a line‑buffer overflow that occurs in the tokenURI function when it formats a biography string into fixed‑size lines. The implementation builds each line in an 80‑byte temporary buffer (bytesLines) and attempts to avoid splitting Unicode characters by checking for continuation bytes, zero‑width joiners and skin‑tone modifiers. The root cause is that the algorithm treats a sequence of continuation bytes as a single logical unit and keeps the flag prevByteWasContinuation set, which prevents the buffer from being flushed even when the 80‑byte limit is reached. If an attacker supplies a bio consisting of many valid continuation characters – for example a skin‑tone modifier codepoint repeated many times – the buffer never reaches the split condition, the 80‑byte array is written past its capacity and the Solidity runtime throws an out‑of‑bounds exception, causing the whole tokenURI call to revert. Exploitation is straightforward: during minting the attacker includes a specially crafted Unicode string (e.g., 21 repetitions of the U+1F3FE skin‑tone emoji) and later any caller of tokenURI for that token triggers the overflow, resulting in a reverted transaction. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on metadata retrieval: users and marketplaces see no token metadata, the UI may display a missing image or an error, and the token appears broken even though the token itself and its funds remain intact. The condition occurs only when the biography contains a long run of continuation characters, an edge case that passes normal UTF‑8 validation and therefore can be overlooked during casual testing. The issue was discovered by the Code4rena audit team through a targeted test that deliberately constructed such a string and observed the revert. It is hard to notice because the offending characters are visually normal emojis and the overflow only manifests after an unusually long repetition, which is unlikely in typical usage. To remediate, the line‑splitting logic should enforce a hard limit on the buffer size and start a new line when the current buffer reaches 80 bytes, or switch to a dynamically sized buffer that does not rely on a fixed‑size array. This change ensures that even pathological Unicode sequences cannot cause an out‑of‑bounds write, restoring reliable tokenURI generation and preserving the protocol’s guarantee that token metadata is always accessible.

title: Bio NFT incorrectly breaks SVG lines and doesn’t support more than 120 characters effectively
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the Bio NFT contract builds the SVG image that displays a user‑provided biography. The contract attempts to insert line breaks after every 40 characters by checking the byte index (i+1) % 40 == 0, but it treats the biography as a raw byte array and does not account for multi‑byte Unicode characters such as emojis or zero‑width joiners. Because many emojis occupy two or more bytes, the simple modulo calculation can split a character in the middle of its UTF‑8 encoding, causing the line‑break logic to trigger at the wrong position. The rendering code also always uses a fixed dy value for each line and does not reset dy for the first line, which prevents proper vertical centering, and the x attribute is not consistently applied to achieve horizontal centering. As a result, when a user mints a Bio NFT containing emojis or a biography longer than about 120 characters, the generated SVG may display truncated or garbled text, missing characters, or mis‑aligned lines. From the user’s perspective the NFT image can show an empty line, unexpected zeros, or a biography that looks different from the input, violating the expectation that the on‑chain metadata faithfully represents the submitted text. The issue appears during the tokenURI generation, which is called whenever the NFT metadata is queried, and it is triggered only for biographies that contain multi‑byte characters or exceed the simple 40‑byte threshold, making it easy to miss in basic tests that use only ASCII. The bug was discovered through manual testing with long strings and emojis, where the visual output differed from the expected line breaks. Because the problem manifests as a visual defect rather than a contract‑level security flaw, it can be overlooked unless the SVG output is inspected. The impact is primarily on user experience and protocol reputation: users may lose confidence if their biographies are displayed incorrectly, and third‑party services that rely on the SVG may propagate wrong information. The fix requires changing the line‑break algorithm to operate on Unicode grapheme clusters or rune length rather than raw bytes, handling continuation bytes and zero‑width joiners correctly, and adjusting the SVG generation to set dy to zero for the first line and ensure the x attribute centers each line. Expanding the viewBox or limiting biographies to 120 characters are temporary mitigations, but a proper solution involves Unicode‑aware splitting and correct SVG attribute handling to guarantee that the displayed text matches the stored biography.

title: Award is still distributed when there aren’t any stakers, allowing users to get reward without staking
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unearned reward distribution flaw that allows a participant to claim the full reward that accumulated during a period when no tokens were staked. The contract’s update modifier only updates the reward accounting when totalStake() is greater than zero. When the staking period begins and the total stake is zero, the variable _mostRecentValueCalcTime is not advanced, leaving the reward accumulator _totalWeight unchanged. If an attacker stakes a single token and immediately withdraws in the same transaction, the stake function records the user’s weighted entry as the stale _totalWeight. On the subsequent withdraw, totalStake() becomes non‑zero, the update modifier runs, calculates the elapsed time since the stale _mostRecentValueCalcTime, multiplies it by the per‑second reward rate, and adds the resulting value to _totalWeight. Because the elapsed interval includes the entire idle period, the attacker receives all rewards that should have been distributed only when genuine stakers were present. From the user’s perspective the dMute balance jumps from zero to a large amount even though the user never actually provided liquidity, violating the expectation that rewards are earned proportionally to time staked. The impact is that malicious actors can drain the reward pool without contributing value, reducing the earnings of honest participants and potentially exhausting the incentive budget. The bug manifests whenever the staking contract is entered after the start time, no other address has a positive stake, and a user performs a stake‑and‑withdraw sequence within a single block. It affects any holder of the LP token who interacts with the amplifier, the protocol’s economic model, and the overall token distribution. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when a test case showed that a user could “get reward without staking” by staking and withdrawing immediately. It is subtle because the contract state appears consistent – the reward calculation uses legitimate arithmetic and the user receives a valid token amount, making the flaw easy to miss without targeted testing of zero‑stake intervals. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where reward accrual is not correctly gated by the presence of a stake, similar to “zero‑balance reward accrual” or “unprotected reward claim” bugs. To remediate, the contract should ensure that reward accounting is only performed when a non‑zero stake existed throughout the elapsed interval, for example by always updating _mostRecentValueCalcTime regardless of totalStake, enforcing a minimum staking duration, or resetting firstStakeTime when totalStake returns to zero. Additionally, any rescue or token‑retrieval functions must be adjusted to handle undistributed rewards that would otherwise be lost. Implementing these changes restores the intended economic guarantees that rewards are earned only by actual stakers and prevents users from extracting tokens without providing liquidity.

title: A user can ‘borrow’ dMute balance for a single block to increase their amplifier APY
description:
The amplifier’s APY is calculated based on the user’s dMute balance (delegation balance to be more accurate) - the more dMute the user holds the higher APY they get.

However, the contract only checks the user’s dMute balance at staking, the user doesn’t have to hold that balance at any time but at the staking block.

This let’s the user bribe somebody to delegate them their dMute for a single block and stake at the same time.

Since the balance checked is the delegation balance (`getPriorVotes`) this even makes it easier - since the ‘lender’ doesn’t even need to trust the ‘borrower’ to return the funds, all the ‘lender’ can cancel the delegation on their own on the next block.

The lender can also create a smart contract to automate and decentralize this ‘service’.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the amplifier contract determines a user’s reward multiplier. The contract computes the multiplier by reading the user’s delegated dMute balance (the voting power returned by getPriorVotes) at a single point in time – the block in which the user initially stakes, stored as staked_block. Because the contract never re‑examines the balance after that block, an attacker can temporarily increase the recorded voting power by borrowing delegation from another address for exactly that block, stake, and immediately receive a higher APY multiplier. dMute itself is a soulbound token that cannot be transferred, but it can be delegated, and the delegation can be revoked by the delegator in the following block without any further consent. Consequently, the attacker can coordinate with a willing delegator or automate the process through a smart contract that delegates for one block, stakes, and then lets the delegator cancel the delegation. From the user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly large APY or reward that appears to be earned without holding the required dMute balance; honest participants may notice that their own rewards are reduced because the pool’s total reward is being siphoned by the attacker. The issue was discovered during an audit that inspected the calculateMultiplier function and observed that it only queries getPriorVotes with the staked block (or block.number‑1 when enforce is false). The root cause is the reliance on a single‑block snapshot of delegated voting power, which can be manipulated through the delegation mechanism. This design flaw is subtle because the delegation change occurs after the reward has already been calculated, so the contract’s state appears consistent and the exploit does not leave an obvious on‑chain trace. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the user’s dMute balance is measured over a longer window of blocks, for example by sampling several random blocks between staking and reward distribution and using the minimum observed balance, or by disallowing delegated voting power from influencing the multiplier altogether. Alternatively, the protocol could require a minimum holding period for dMute before it can affect rewards, thereby preventing a one‑block “borrow‑and‑stake” attack and preserving the intended economic incentives.

title: `MuteAmplifier.rescueTokens
description:
There will be 2 impacts.

  * The reward system would be broken as the rewards can be withdrawn before starting staking.
  * Some rewards would be locked inside the contract forever as it doesn’t check `totalReclaimed`
bug_full: The MuteAmplifier contract contains a flaw in the rescueTokens function that governs the withdrawal of the muteToken used as staking rewards. The function is intended to prevent the contract owner from taking tokens that belong to stakers, but the implementation fails in two ways. First, when the contract reports zero stakers (totalStakers == 0) the function does not perform any balance check before allowing a rescue, which means an attacker can call rescueTokens and withdraw any amount of muteToken even while the staking period is still active. Second, when there are active stakers the require statement subtracts only totalRewards minus totalClaimedRewards from the contract balance, ignoring the amount already reclaimed to the treasury (totalReclaimed). Because totalReclaimed is part of the reward pool, the missing subtraction permits the caller to withdraw more than the unclaimed portion, and it also leaves a portion of rewards permanently locked because the rescue logic never accounts for them. The root cause is an incomplete accounting model and a missing conditional branch for the zero‑staker case. An attacker who can invoke rescueTokens can therefore drain rewards before users have earned them, or withdraw an amount that exceeds the true unclaimed reward pool, causing the reward distribution to break. Stakers may see their expected payouts reduced to zero or notice that their balances do not increase after the staking period, while the protocol may retain a residual amount of muteToken that can never be claimed. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the rescueTokens checks with the accounting variables used elsewhere in the contract. It is subtle because the function contains a require statement that appears to protect the rewards, yet the condition is mathematically incorrect and the special case of zero stakers is omitted, making the bug easy to overlook in testing. The appropriate fix is to extend the balance check to subtract totalReclaimed as well, and to add a safeguard that, when totalStakers is zero, the amount rescued cannot exceed the remaining reward pool (totalRewards – totalClaimedRewards – totalReclaimed) or is prohibited until the staking end time. This brings the rescue logic in line with the contract’s accounting model and prevents unauthorized or excessive withdrawals, preserving the integrity of the reward system.

title: An edge case in amplifier allows user to stake after end time, causing reward to be locked in the contract
bug_full: The vulnerability is an edge‑case logic flaw in the staking module of the amplifier contract that permits a user to place a stake after the declared staking period has ended, but only when no one has previously staked during that period. The contract records the timestamp of the first stake in a variable called firstStakeTime. The code checks the end of the staking window with a require statement only when firstStakeTime is already set; if firstStakeTime is still zero, the require is skipped and the timestamp is set to the current block time, even if that time is later than endTime. Because the first stake occurs after the period, the internal reward‑distribution routine uses a variable called _mostRecentValueCalcTime that is initialized to firstStakeTime. The reward‑drip logic only executes when _mostRecentValueCalcTime is less than endTime, a condition that is false for the late stake. Consequently, no rewards are ever calculated or released for the staker, and the reward balance remains locked inside the contract. At the same time, the rescue function that the protocol could use to withdraw unclaimed muteToken rewards is blocked by a check that prevents withdrawing tokens while any staker exists and while totalRewards minus totalClaimedRewards is non‑zero. Since the late staker is counted as a staker, the rescue path fails, leaving the reward pool permanently inaccessible. This bug can be exploited by a malicious actor who deliberately stakes after the period ends, thereby freezing the reward pool and preventing the protocol from rescuing the tokens. The impact is that users see no reward payout (their balance stays at zero), the protocol cannot recover the locked funds, and the overall token economics are disrupted. The condition only manifests when the staking window closes with zero participants and a subsequent stake is made after endTime, making it easy to miss in standard testing that assumes at least one early staker. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logical flow of the staking and rescue functions was examined. To remediate, the require that enforces block.timestamp < endTime should be applied unconditionally, i.e., moved outside the else block that depends on firstStakeTime, or the contract should reject any stake that would set firstStakeTime after endTime. Additionally, the reward‑drip condition should be robust to a first stake occurring after the period, either by allowing a final reward calculation or by preventing the stake entirely. In short, the bug belongs to the class of time‑window validation errors that allow state changes outside of intended periods, leading to locked assets and broken accounting assumptions.

title: MuteBond is susceptible to DOS
bug_full: The contract contains a denial‑of‑service flaw that originates from the token‑minting calculation in the internal function that converts a locked amount and lock duration into dTokens. The function multiplies the deposited amount by the lock time, divides by the maximum lock period (52 weeks) and then truncates the result using integer division. When the lock time is the minimum allowed value (1 week) and the deposited amount is smaller than 52 tokens, the division yields zero, so the function returns 0 tokens. The public LockTo function checks that the returned token amount is greater than zero and reverts otherwise. The deposit routine of the bond contract forwards the payout amount (computed from the bond price) to LockTo as the amount argument. Because the bond contract enforces that the payout does not exceed maxDeposit(), an attacker who can manipulate the bond parameters so that maxDeposit() becomes less than 52 can force every deposit to produce a zero‑token mint and therefore trigger the revert. This makes the deposit function unusable, effectively locking out all users from buying bonds and halting the protocol’s revenue stream. The issue is subtle because the calculation works correctly for larger amounts; only small amounts that fall below the integer‑division threshold cause the failure, which may not be obvious during normal testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic‑truncation bugs that lead to under‑minting and unintended reverts. It can be exploited by adjusting the bond’s price range or max payout so that the computed payout is forced below the 52‑token threshold, after which any call to deposit will revert with “INSUFFICIENT_TOKENS_MINTED”. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that a deposit transaction fails immediately, with no tokens minted and no balance change, even though the input amount appears valid. The contract should enforce a minimum mintable amount, adjust the formula to avoid zero results (for example by using ceiling division or scaling), or add a safeguard that starts a new epoch or rejects deposits when maxDeposit() falls below a safe threshold. Implementing such a check restores the ability of users to deposit and prevents the protocol from being rendered inoperable.

title: Amplifier users might not get all the LP fees they are entitled to
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a time‑bounded fee‑harvesting logic in the Amplifier contract. The contract calls the external claimFees function only inside an update modifier that is guarded by the condition `_mostRecentValueCalcTime < endTime`. When a user withdraws after the staking period has ended, the modifier sets `_mostRecentValueCalcTime` to the current block timestamp, which is greater than `endTime`. From that point onward the condition is permanently false, so the claimFees call is never executed again. As a result, any LP fees that accrue after the first post‑period withdrawal remain locked inside the underlying mute‑switch pair and are never distributed to stakers. Users who withdraw later, especially large LP providers, receive less than the fee share they are entitled to; from the user’s perspective the balance appears unchanged or the expected refund is missing, effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the update modifier and noticed that fee collection was placed inside the same conditional block that stops executing after the end time. The root cause is an incorrect placement of the fee‑claiming code, violating the assumption that fee accrual continues after the staking window and breaking the accounting invariant that all earned fees must eventually be harvested. Exploitation does not require malicious intent – any normal withdrawal after the period ends unintentionally locks the fees for all subsequent withdrawals. The impact is a loss of LP fee revenue for affected stakers and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The bug is subtle because reward weight calculations still work, making the missing fees hard to notice without inspecting the fee‑claim path. The recommended remediation is to move the claimFees invocation out of the `if (_mostRecentValueCalcTime < endTime)` block, or to add a separate mechanism that ensures fees are claimed on every update regardless of the time condition, thereby restoring the intended continuous fee distribution behavior.

title: `MuteAmplifier.sol`: multiplier calculation is incorrect which leads to loss of rewards for almost all stakers
description:
This report deals with how the calculation of the `multiplier` in the `MuteAmplifier` contract is not only different from how it is displayed in the [documentation on the website](https://wiki.mute.io/mute/mute-switch/amplifier) but it is also different in a very important way.

The calculation on the website shows a linear relationship between the `dMUTE / poolSize` ratio and the `APY`. The `dMUTE / poolSize` ratio is also called the `tokenRatio`.

By “linear” I mean that when a user increases his `tokenRatio` from `0` to `0.1` this has the same effect as when increasing it from `0.9` to `1`.

The implementation in the `MuteAmplifier.calculateMultiplier` function does not have this linear relationship between `tokenRatio` and `APY`.

An increase in the `tokenRatio` from `0` to `0.1` is worth much less than an increase from `0.9` to `1`.

As we will see this means that all stakers that do not have a `tokenRatio` of exactly equal `0` or exactly equal `1` lose out on rewards that they should receive according to the documentation.

I estimate this to be of “High” severity because the issue affects nearly all stakers and results in a partial loss of rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect reward multiplier calculation in the MuteAmplifier contract that deviates from the linear relationship described in the official documentation. The contract computes a multiplier by subtracting a token‑ratio‑scaled difference from a fixed stakeDivisor, which creates a non‑linear, diminishing‑returns curve. As a result, any staker whose dMUTE‑to‑pool ratio (tokenRatio) is greater than zero but less than one receives a lower percentage of the maximum possible rewards than the specification promises. The root cause is a mis‑implemented financial formula: instead of adding a proportion of the tokenRatio to a base percentage, the code subtracts a proportion from a divisor, producing a convex curve that under‑rewards users. Exploitation is not active; the bug simply causes legitimate reward amounts to be lower than expected. When a user stakes dMUTE, the contract calls calculateMultiplier, which returns a value that, when used in the reward formula reward = lpTokenOut * weightDifference / multiplier, yields a smaller reward. This effect is observable whenever tokenRatio is not exactly 0 or 1, which includes the overwhelming majority of participants. Affected parties are all stakers of the MuteAmplifier pool, the protocol’s APY guarantees, and any downstream users who rely on the advertised reward rates. The issue was discovered during a security audit by comparing the on‑chain multiplier function against the documented linear model, plotting both curves, and noticing the systematic shortfall. Because the contract still distributes rewards, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when users compare actual APY to the advertised figures or when they perform manual calculations. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑calculation or financial‑formula errors, where the implementation does not match the specification, leading to accounting inconsistencies. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a certain APY boost, but the actual token balance after a claim is lower than expected, sometimes appearing as if the reward is missing or zero for low tokenRatio values. The expected behavior is a linear increase in rewards proportional to tokenRatio, but the reality is a curved, sub‑optimal reward curve. To remediate, the contract should replace the stakeDivisor mechanism with a percentageMin parameter and compute the multiplier as percentageMin + tokenRatio * (1 − percentageMin), applying the result multiplicatively rather than divisively. This change restores the linear scaling and aligns on‑chain rewards with the documented model, eliminating the systematic loss of rewards for most stakers.

title: `MuteAmplifier.sol`: `rescueTokens` function does not prevent fee tokens from being transferred
bug_full: The MuteAmplifier contract contains a rescueTokens function that is intended to let the contract owner withdraw tokens that are not required for the protocol’s core operation. The function explicitly protects the liquidity‑provider token (lpToken) and the native muteToken by checking that only amounts exceeding the stake‑related balances can be rescued. However, the contract also holds two fee tokens, fee0 and fee1, which are accumulated during reward calculations and later paid out to stakers when they call payout or withdraw. Because rescueTokens does not include any special handling for these fee tokens, the owner can specify fee0 or fee1 as the tokenToRescue and transfer any amount out of the contract. The root cause is the missing accounting check for fee0 and fee1 in the rescueTokens logic, which treats them like any other ERC‑20 token. When the owner rescues fee tokens, the internal accounting variables (totalFees0, totalFees1, _totalWeightFee0, _totalWeightFee1) still assume that the fees are available, so the subsequent payout calculation computes a non‑zero fee amount based on the recorded weight. The actual token balance, however, is now insufficient, causing the ERC‑20 transfer inside the payout or withdraw flow to revert due to an out‑of‑balance error. From a user’s perspective, a call to payout or withdraw that previously would have returned fee rewards now fails with a revert, or the user receives zero fee tokens while the rest of the withdrawal succeeds. This situation can leave stakers unable to claim their earned fees, effectively “stealing” the fee rewards from them, and may force users to manually send fee tokens back to the contract to restore functionality – an unintended and undesirable user experience. The vulnerability manifests only when there are active stakers (totalStakers > 0) and fee tokens have been accrued, i.e., after the update modifier has recorded fees. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the rescueTokens implementation and noticed that only lpToken and muteToken were protected. The issue is subtle because the function appears to safeguard the main assets, and fee tokens are less obvious, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the rescueTokens function should be extended with explicit checks for fee0 and fee1, ensuring that only excess fee tokens beyond what is owed to stakers can be rescued. Additionally, the payout logic should verify that the contract’s actual fee token balances are sufficient before attempting a transfer, using the real balance rather than the recorded totalFees variables. This aligns the on‑chain accounting with the contract’s business logic and prevents the owner from unintentionally or maliciously depriving stakers of their fee rewards.

title: `MuteBond.sol`: When `maxPayout` is lowered the contract can end up DOSed
description:
The [`maxPayout`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-mute/blob/4d8b13add2907b17ac14627cfa04e0c3cc9a2bed/contracts/bonds/MuteBond.sol#L34) variable in the `MuteBond` contract specifies the amount of `MUTE` that is paid out in one epoch before the next epoch is entered.

The variable is initialized in the constructor and can then be changed via the [`setMaxPayout`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-mute/blob/4d8b13add2907b17ac14627cfa04e0c3cc9a2bed/contracts/bonds/MuteBond.sol#L119-L123) function.

The issue occurs when `maxPayout` is lowered.

So say `maxPayout` is currently `10,000 MUTE` and the `owner` wants to reduce it to `5,000 MUTE`.

Before this transaction to lower `maxPayout` is executed, another transaction might be executed which increases the current payout to `> 5,000 MUTE`.

This means that calls to [`MuteBond.deposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-mute/blob/4d8b13add2907b17ac14627cfa04e0c3cc9a2bed/contracts/bonds/MuteBond.sol#L153-L200) revert and no new epoch can be entered. Thereby the `MuteBond` contracts becomes unable to provide bonds.

The DOS is not permanent. The `owner` can increase `maxPayout` such that the current payout is smaller than `maxPayout` again and the contract will work as intended.

So the impact is a temporary DOS of the `MuteBond` contract.

The issue can be solved by requiring in the `setMaxPayout` function that `maxPayout` must be bigger than the payout in the current epoch.
bug_full: The MuteBond contract defines a variable called maxPayout that limits the total amount of MUTE that can be paid out during a single epoch. The variable is set in the constructor andcan be changed later through the setMaxPayout function. The vulnerability arises because setMaxPayout does not verify that the new value is at least as large as the amount already paid out in the current epoch. If the contract owner lowers maxPayout to a value that is smaller than the current epoch's payout, any subsequent call to the deposit function will hit a require check that compares the accumulated payout with maxPayout and will revert. This reversion prevents new deposits from being accepted and also blocks the transition to the next epoch, effectively putting the bond issuance mechanism into a temporary denial‑of‑service state. The issue can be triggered when an owner transaction that reduces maxPayout is executed after another transaction that increases the current payout beyond the new limit. From a user’s perspective, a deposit that previously succeeded now fails with no tokens received, leading to a situation where a user expects a bond but receives nothing and may see a zero balance change. The impact is limited to the inability to create new bonds; existing bonds and already‑distributed payouts remain intact, and the contract can be restored by the owner raising maxPayout above the current payout again. The bug was discovered during a security audit that exercised the setMaxPayout path and observed the revert behavior. It can be hard to notice because the contract continues to function normally until the specific sequence of lowering maxPayout after a large payout occurs, at which point the failure appears only as a generic revert without an obvious link to the maxPayout change. The root cause is a missing invariant check in the setter function.
