The proper fix is to add a requirement that the new maxPayout value must be greater than the total payout already recorded for the active epoch, thereby preserving the invariant that payout never exceeds the configured limit and preventing the temporary DOS condition.

title: Exchange Rate can be manipulated if positions are big enough for a long enough time
description:
If exchangeRate can be manipulated, then this can be used to extract value or grief withdrawals from the `KangarooVault`.

From my experimentation, the values to manipulate the share price are very high, making the attack fairly unlikely.

That said, by manipulating `markPrice` we can get manipulate `getTokenPrice`, which will cause a leak of value in withdrawals.

This requires a fairly laborious setup (enough time has passed, from fairly thorough testing we need at least 1 week).  
And also requires a very high amount of capital (1 billion in the example, I think 100MLN works as well)
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exchange‑rate manipulation flaw in the KangarooVault system. The contract derives the value of vault shares from a token price that is calculated using the exchange’s mark price. Because the mark price is updated based on the funding rate, which in turn depends on the size and duration of open positions, an attacker who opens a sufficiently large long (or short) position can shift the funding rate and therefore the mark price. By keeping the position open for a long enough period—approximately one week in the observed tests—and by committing a very large amount of capital (on the order of hundreds of millions to a billion units), the attacker can cause the token price returned by getTokenPrice to deviate from its true market value. When users later withdraw their shares, the vault uses the manipulated token price to compute the amount of underlying assets to return, resulting in a loss of value for honest participants or allowing the attacker to extract excess funds. The issue manifests as withdrawals that are lower than expected, share balances that appear correct but translate to fewer assets, or a sudden drop in the reported share price. It is difficult to detect because the price shift may be modest relative to normal market fluctuations and requires an unusually large position, so ordinary monitoring may not flag it as abnormal. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by creating a test contract that opened a large position, advanced time, and observed the change in funding rate and mark price, confirming that the exchange rate can be altered. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle or price‑feed manipulation bugs, where internal accounting relies on a variable that can be influenced by market participants. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should decouple share valuation from manipulable variables, for example by using a time‑weighted average price, limiting the impact of any single position on the funding rate, or adding sanity checks that prevent extreme price deviations before processing withdrawals.

title: Users can receive less collateral than expected from liquidations
description: Users might receive very little or no collateral when liquidating extremely unhealthy short positions.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the liquidation routine of a perpetual exchange where a short position can be liquidated without the liquidator receiving any of the pledged collateral. The root cause lies in the liquidation algorithm that determines the amount of collateral to return solely from the proportion of debt being repaid, without enforcing a lower bound on the collateral output. When the underlying asset price rises sharply – for example a 50 % increase in the sUSD price used in the test – the short position becomes extremely unhealthy and the value of the locked collateral can drop to zero relative to the outstanding debt. Because the contract does not check that the calculated collateral amount is greater than zero (or a user‑specified minimum), the liquidate() call succeeds and the debt is reduced while the collateral transferred to the caller is nil. An attacker can exploit this by opening a short position with a very small collateral amount, waiting for a large adverse price movement, and then triggering one or more liquidation calls. Each liquidation removes a slice of the debt but returns no sUSD to the caller, effectively allowing the attacker to strip the protocol of collateral without compensation. The impact is that users who expect to be rewarded for liquidating unhealthy positions receive nothing, leading to loss of funds for liquidators and a breakdown of the economic incentives that keep the system solvent. The issue manifests only under extreme price swings and when the collateral ratio is low; under normal market conditions the returned collateral may be non‑zero and the problem remains hidden. It affects short position owners, liquidators, and ultimately the protocol’s overall collateralisation health. The flaw was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through fuzzed tests that deliberately increased the base asset price by up to 50 % and observed that the liquidate() function still succeeded while the collateral balance of the liquidator stayed at zero. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, so a developer inspecting only the transaction success may miss the fact that no value was transferred. To remediate, the liquidation function should require a minimum collateral amount – either passed as a parameter or derived from a protocol‑wide safety margin – and revert if the calculated payout falls below this threshold. Adding such a sanity check prevents zero‑output liquidations and restores the intended incentive structure, ensuring that liquidators receive a meaningful amount of collateral proportional to the debt they retire. This class of bug can be described as an insufficient output validation or missing lower‑bound check in economic‑critical functions, leading to scenarios where funds disappear from the user’s perspective despite a successful transaction.

title: `KangarooVault.initiateDeposit`, `KangarooVault.processDepositQueue`, `KangarooVault.initiateWithdrawal`, and `KangarooVault.processWithdrawalQueue` functions do not use `whenNotPaused` modifier
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

1. An emergency, such as a hack, occurs in which further withdrawals can cause users and the protocol to lose funds.
2. The protocol team is able to pause the `LiquidityPool.withdraw`, `LiquidityPool.queueWithdraw`, and `LiquidityPool.processWithdraws` functions.
3. However, the protocol team is unable to pause the `KangarooVault.initiateWithdrawal` and `KangarooVault.processWithdrawalQueue` functions.
4. As a result, funds can be lost from the `KangarooVault`.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing pause guard on four core functions of the KangarooVault contract: initiateDeposit, processDepositQueue, initiateWithdrawal and processWithdrawalQueue. Although the contract inherits the PauseModifier utility, the developer never applied the whenNotPaused modifier to these entry points. As a result, when the protocol’s emergency pause is activated – typically via a call to the PauseModifier pause function after a hack or other critical event – the LiquidityPool functions are correctly blocked, but the KangarooVault functions remain callable. An attacker or any external actor can therefore continue to submit deposit or withdrawal requests, or trigger the processing of queued deposits and withdrawals, even while the system is advertised as paused. This can lead to unexpected fund movements: users may see their balances decrease or disappear, withdrawals may be processed despite a UI indicating that the protocol is halted, and overall accounting assumptions that no state changes occur during a pause are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the pause usage of KangarooVault with the analogous LiquidityPool implementation, which consistently applies whenNotPaused. The bug is subtle because the contract imports the pause library and the surrounding code appears similar to the correctly protected pool, making it easy to assume the pause is enforced everywhere. Exploitation requires only that the contract be in a paused state; no additional permissions are needed to call the unprotected functions. The impact is a medium‑severity risk: funds can be drained or lost during an emergency, users may lose confidence, and the protocol cannot reliably enforce its own safety mechanisms. The recommended remediation is to add the whenNotPaused modifier to each of the four vulnerable functions, ensuring that all state‑changing operations respect the global pause flag and that the protocol’s emergency controls function as intended.

title: `LiquidityPool._getDelta` and `LiquidityPool._calculateMargin` functions should execute `require
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

1. Calling the `perpMarket.assetPrice` function returns a positive `spotPrice` and a true `isInvalid` at this moment.
2. Calling the `LiquidityPool._getDelta` and `LiquidityPool._calculateMargin` functions would not revert because `require(!isInvalid || spotPrice > 0)` would be passed.
3. Trades, such as for closing a long position through calling the `LiquidityPool.closeLong` function, can go through even though the used `spotPrice` is invalid and untrusted.
4. In this case, such trades should not be allowed but are still made.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from inconsistent validation of the oracle price data used by the liquidity pool. Two high‑level functions in the vault contract – transferPerpMargin and _openPosition – correctly require that the price returned by the liquidity pool is both valid (isInvalid is false) and non‑zero before proceeding. In contrast, the internal pricing helpers _getDelta and _calculateMargin in the LiquidityPool contract use a logical OR condition (require(!isInvalid || spotPrice > 0)). This means that if the underlying perp market reports a positive spotPrice while simultaneously flagging the price as invalid (isInvalid true), the require statement still passes because the spotPrice > 0 clause is satisfied. As a result, the pool will compute deltas and margins based on a price that the oracle itself has marked as unreliable. An attacker or a faulty market can trigger this state, causing trades – such as opening or closing long or short positions – to be executed with an untrusted price. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a normal price value, but the contract treats the price as valid, leading to unexpected outcomes like receiving an incorrect margin, losing funds, or having a position closed at an unfavorable rate. The impact is medium: funds can be mis‑allocated, traders may suffer losses, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price integrity are broken. The issue occurs only when the perp market’s assetPrice function returns a non‑zero spotPrice together with isInvalid set to true, a condition that can arise during oracle failures or manipulation. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it is subtle because the price value itself looks correct, masking the invalid flag. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent input validation” or “oracle flag bypass” where a boolean safety check is incorrectly combined with a numeric check using OR instead of AND. To remediate, the require statements in _getDelta and _calculateMargin should be changed to require(!isInvalid && spotPrice > 0), ensuring that both the validity flag and the price value must be acceptable before any financial calculation is performed.

title: Some functions that call `Exchange.getMarkPrice` function do not check if `Exchange.getMarkPrice` function’s returned `markPrice` is 0
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

1. The `KangarooVault.removeCollateral` function is called with `collateralToRemove` being 100e18.
2. `markPrice` returned by `LIQUIDITY_POOL.getMarkPrice()` is 0 because a 0 `spotPrice` is returned by `perpMarket.assetPrice()`.
3. Due to the 0 `markPrice`, `minColl` is 0, and `positionData.totalCollateral >= minColl + collateralToRemove` can be true even if `positionData.totalCollateral` is also 100e18 at this moment.
4. Calling the `KangarooVault.removeCollateral` function does not revert, and 100e18 collateral is remove from the Power Perp position.
5. However, a 0 `spotPrice` returned by `perpMarket.assetPrice()` and a 0 `markPrice` returned by `LIQUIDITY_POOL.getMarkPrice()` should be considered as invalid and should not be used. In this case, removing 100e18 collateral from the Power Perp position should not be allowed or succeed but it does.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an invalid‑price usage bug in the KangarooVault contract where functions that rely on Exchange.getMarkPrice do not verify that the returned markPrice is non‑zero. The root cause is that Exchange.getMarkPrice forwards the spot price from perpMarket.assetPrice through pool.baseAssetPrice, and when the underlying spot price is zero the function returns a zero markPrice. Some internal functions such as transferPerpMargin and _openPosition already guard against a zero baseAssetPrice, but other callers like removeCollateral omit this check. An attacker or a faulty market condition can cause perpMarket.assetPrice to return zero, which propagates to a zero markPrice. The removeCollateral function then computes the minimum required collateral (minColl) by multiplying the short amount with the zero markPrice, resulting in minColl equal to zero. The subsequent require statement (positionData.totalCollateral >= minColl + collateralToRemove) becomes trivially true, allowing the caller to withdraw the specified collateral even though the price data is invalid. From a user perspective the UI may show a normal position balance, but after invoking removeCollateral the collateral disappears unexpectedly, violating the expectation that collateral can only be removed when sufficient margin is maintained. The impact is a potential loss of collateral from positions that should be protected by price validation, effectively allowing funds to be drained when the market price feed is temporarily zero. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the validation logic across functions and noticed the missing zero‑price check. It is subtle because a zero price may be rare and the contract does not emit explicit error messages, making the failure mode appear as a normal collateral removal. The bug belongs to the class of price‑validation or oracle‑sanity‑check failures, where a contract trusts a price value without confirming its validity. To remediate, every function that consumes Exchange.getMarkPrice should add an explicit require that the returned markPrice is greater than zero (or that the accompanying isInvalid flag is false), reverting the transaction when the price is invalid, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: `KangarooVault._resetTrade`, `LiquidityPool.rebalanceMargin`, and `LiquidityPool._getTotalMargin` functions should check `isInvalid`, which is returned by external perp market contract’s `remainingMargin` function, and revert if such `isInvalid` is true
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

1. The `LiquidityPool.deposit` function is called to deposit some sUSD tokens.
2. When the `LiquidityPool.getTokenPrice` function is called, `_getTotalMargin()`’s returned `totalMargin`, which is `margin` returned by `perpMarket.remainingMargin(address(this))`, is invalid. However, such invalid `totalMargin` does not cause calling the `LiquidityPool.getTokenPrice` function to revert.
3. The deposit action succeeds while the used liquidity token’s price that depends on the invalid `totalMargin` is inaccurate. Such deposit action should not be allowed but it is.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from three internal functions – KangarooVault._resetTrade, LiquidityPool.rebalanceMargin and LiquidityPool._getTotalMargin – that query the external perpetual market contract for the remaining margin of the vault or pool. The external call returns a tuple (margin, isInvalid) where the boolean flag indicates whether the reported margin value is trustworthy. In the affected functions the code extracts only the numeric margin and completely ignores the isInvalid flag, proceeding to use the possibly corrupted value in subsequent accounting logic. This omission constitutes a classic “missing validation of external data” bug: the contract assumes that the external market will always return a valid number, even though the market contract explicitly signals failure through the flag. When the market is in a state that causes isInvalid to be true – for example during a market pause, liquidation, or internal error – the returned margin may be zero, extremely large, or otherwise nonsensical. Because the functions do not revert, the invalid margin is fed into the pool’s price calculation in LiquidityPool.getTokenPrice, which in turn influences deposit, withdrawal and token‑minting operations. From a user’s perspective the pool appears to accept deposits and issue liquidity tokens, but the token price is derived from a wrong margin value, so users may receive fewer tokens than expected, or the protocol may credit them with more value than it actually holds. This mismatch breaks the fundamental accounting invariant that total pool value equals the sum of underlying assets plus correctly accounted margin, leading to potential fund loss, mis‑pricing of liquidity tokens, and the ability to perform actions (such as deposits or withdrawals) that should be blocked when the margin is invalid. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation of KangarooVault.getTokenPrice – which correctly checks isInvalid and reverts – with LiquidityPool.getTokenPrice, which omits the check. The bug is subtle because the functions execute without reverting and the price deviation may be small enough to escape casual observation, yet it undermines the economic safety of the protocol. The proper remediation is to propagate the isInvalid flag through each call that relies on remainingMargin and to add an explicit require(!isInvalid) (or equivalent revert) before using the margin value, thereby ensuring that any invalid external data aborts the transaction and preserves the integrity of the pool’s accounting.

title: `usedFunds` can be greater than `totalFunds` in contract `KangarooVault`, which leads to `KangarooVault` being unable to close its trades and users being unable to withdraw
description: `KangarooVault` contract can’t close the trades and users can’t withdraw from it, then users and `KangarooVaults` will lose a lot of funds.
poc:
1. In contract `KangarooVault`, `usedFunds` is the uint256 variable which tracks the funds utilitized from the vault. And `totalFunds` is the uint256 variable which tracks the funds claimed by vault from profits and users’ depositing.
2. Contract `KangarooVault` has no check if `totalFunds` >= `usedFunds` when `usedFunds` is increased (transfer from vault) or `totalFunds` is decreased (transfer to vault).
3. If someone transfers funds directly into the vault, `usedFunds` can be greater than `totalFunds` because the vault can transfer out more than `totalFunds`.
4. When `usedFunds` > `totalFunds`, KangarooVault can not close its trades because it will revert on underflow in function `_resetTrade`:

```solidity
function _resetTrade() internal {
    ...
    totalFunds -= usedFunds;
    ...
}
```

5. When `usedFunds` > `totalFunds`, user can’t not withdraw by function `processWithdrawalQueue` because it will revert on underflow.

```solidity
function processWithdrawalQueue(uint256 idCount) external nonReentrant {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < idCount; i++) {
        ...

        uint256 availableFunds = totalFunds - usedFunds;

        ...
```

**Scenario:**

* A deposit 1000 SUSD, then `totalFunds` = 1000 SUSD, `usedFunds` = 0
* B transfer directly 1000 SUSD to the KangarooVault, that doesn’t change `totalFunds` and `usedFunds`
* KangarooVault opens a short position and uses 2000 SUSD to increase the margin, then `usedFunds` = 2000
* After that, `usedFunds` > `totalFunds` (2000 > 1000) then KangarooVault can’t close its position
bug_full: The vulnerability in the KangarooVault contract stems from an invariant violation where the internal accounting variable usedFunds can become larger than the recorded totalFunds. The contract tracks totalFunds as the amount of tokens that have been deposited or claimed from profits, while usedFunds records the amount currently allocated to open trades. No check is performed when usedFunds is increased (for example when a trade borrows margin) or when totalFunds is decreased, and direct token transfers into the vault do not update totalFunds. Consequently, an attacker or any external account can send tokens directly to the vault without invoking the deposit function, leaving totalFunds unchanged while the contract may later increase usedFunds based on internal logic. When usedFunds exceeds totalFunds, functions that assume totalFunds >= usedFunds underflow: the internal _resetTrade function subtracts usedFunds from totalFunds, causing a revert, and the processWithdrawalQueue function computes availableFunds as totalFunds - usedFunds, also reverting. From a user’s perspective the vault appears to be stuck: trades cannot be closed, the UI shows that the position is still open, and withdrawal attempts fail with a transaction revert, leaving balances appearing unchanged or zero. The impact is that funds become effectively locked in the vault, users cannot retrieve their deposits, and the protocol may lose liquidity or be unable to settle positions. This issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic relationships between the two accounting variables and identified the missing safety checks. It is hard to notice because the contract operates correctly until the moment a trade is closed or a withdrawal is processed, at which point the underflow manifests as a generic revert rather than an explicit error. The bug belongs to the class of accounting invariant violations where state variables that should maintain a monotonic relationship are not enforced, leading to arithmetic underflow and denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the contract should enforce the invariant totalFunds >= usedFunds on every state change: require statements should be added before increasing usedFunds or decreasing totalFunds, and direct token transfers should be captured (for example by using ERC20’s transfer hook or by updating totalFunds in a fallback function). Using safe‑math libraries or custom accounting that automatically rebalances the two variables can also prevent the condition from ever arising, restoring the ability to close trades and allow users to withdraw their funds.

title: LiquidityPool can be DoS when a complete withdrawal is performed
description: `LiquidityPool` can be DoS when all funds are withdrawn from the pool, causing `getTokenPrice()` to revert due to zero `totalSupply()`.
bug_full: LiquidityPool contains a function that calculates the token price by dividing the pool's total funds by the total supply of liquidity tokens. When all liquidity is withdrawn, the totalSupply becomes zero. Subsequent calls to getTokenPrice perform a division by zero, causing the transaction to revert. Because many core operations – such as deposit, price queries, and margin rebalancing – invoke getTokenPrice, the pool enters a state where no further deposits or withdrawals can be processed. An attacker or any user can trigger this situation simply by withdrawing the entire balance, after which any attempt to interact with the pool fails with a revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: funds already in the pool remain locked, new users cannot add liquidity, and the protocol’s market mechanisms stop functioning. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by adding a test that performs a complete withdrawal and then attempts a deposit, which reverts due to the division by zero. The issue is subtle because normal operation never reduces totalSupply to zero, so the error only appears in the edge case of a full withdrawal, making it easy to overlook during regular testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic errors – specifically unchecked division by zero – that lead to contract‑wide DoS. To remediate, the contract should explicitly check whether totalSupply is zero before performing the division and handle that case, for example by returning a price of zero or by preventing price‑dependent operations until liquidity is restored. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that suddenly reverts with no obvious reason, or a UI that shows a zero balance after a withdrawal and then refuses further deposits, contrary to the expectation that the pool should continue to accept liquidity.

title: Short positions with minimum collateral can be liquidated even though `canLiquidate`
description: Frontends or contracts that rely on `canLiquidate()` to determine if a position is liquidatable could be incorrect. Users could think their positions are safe from liquidation even though they are liquidatable, leading to them losing their collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an off‑by‑one error in the liquidation safety check for short positions that are exactly at the minimum required collateral. The contract computes a safetyRatio that represents the proportion of collateral to the required amount. The function canLiquidate() returns false when safetyRatio is greater than 1e18 (i.e., strictly above the 100 % threshold). However, the liquidation logic that determines the maximum liquidatable debt treats a safetyRatio equal to 1e18 as liquidatable. Consequently, when a short position’s collateral is precisely the minimum needed (safetyRatio == 1), canLiquidate() incorrectly reports that the position is safe while maxLiquidatableDebt() reports a positive amount that can be seized. An attacker or any other user can therefore call the liquidate() function on such a position, causing part of the short amount and a portion of the collateral to be removed. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the position cannot be liquidated, yet the collateral disappears or is reduced after another participant triggers liquidation, leading to unexpected loss of funds. This edge case occurs only when the collateral amount exactly matches the minimum required, making it hard to notice during normal testing because most positions operate with a safety margin. The issue was discovered through a targeted audit test that opened a short position with the smallest possible collateral, verified that canLiquidate() returned false, and then demonstrated that liquidation was still possible. The bug belongs to the class of logical boundary errors where equality conditions are mishandled, breaking the intended accounting invariant that a position with safetyRatio ≥ 1 should be immune to liquidation. To remediate the problem the safety check should be adjusted to treat equality as unsafe, for example by changing the comparison from ‘> 1e18’ to ‘>= 1e18’, or by aligning the canLiquidate() logic with the liquidation calculation so that both use the same threshold. This correction ensures that positions with exactly the required collateral are correctly flagged as liquidatable, preventing false‑negative warnings and protecting users from unexpected collateral loss.

title: Malicious users can exploit deposit and withdrawal queueing in `KangarooVault` and `LiquidityPool` contracts to force exorbitant transaction fees
description: Direct loss of money for users who have deposited funds and wish to withdraw them, as they would be required to pay extremely high gas fees due to the queuing mechanism exploited by the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style griefing issue caused by the sequential processing of queued deposits and withdrawals in the KangarooVault and LiquidityPool contracts. When a user initiates a deposit while the vault has active positions, or when a regular trader uses the queueDeposit function, the request is stored in a depositQueue data structure and assigned an incremental identifier. The contract later processes these entries with a for‑loop that iterates from the current queuedDepositHead up to a caller‑specified count, minting tokens and updating accounting for each entry in order. Because the loop must handle every pending request before reaching the caller’s own entry, an attacker can flood the queue with a very large number of tiny deposits or withdrawals at negligible cost. Once the queue is filled, any legitimate user who calls processDeposits (or the analogous withdrawal processing function) is forced to iterate through all preceding malicious entries, causing the transaction’s gas consumption to grow dramatically – potentially into the billions of gas units. The impact is that users who have deposited funds and wish to withdraw them must pay exorbitant gas fees, which may make the operation economically infeasible, effectively locking their assets behind an unaffordable transaction cost. The issue manifests only when the queue is active – i.e., when there are active positions in KangarooVault or when the queueDeposit path is used in LiquidityPool – and when the caller attempts to process more entries than are currently at the head of the queue. All depositors and withdrawers are affected, as the contract does not differentiate between malicious and honest requests. The problem was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that queued 100 000 tiny deposits followed by a single large deposit, then called processDeposits with a count large enough to include the entire queue, observing gas usage in the millions. The bug is subtle because normal operation with a modest number of queued requests incurs reasonable gas, so the excessive cost only becomes apparent under adversarial queue saturation. Mitigation requires redesigning the queue handling: users should be able to execute their own deposits or withdrawals without processing earlier entries, or the contract should provide a cancellation mechanism for queued requests, or impose strict limits on queue length or per‑address entry counts. Simply raising the minDepositAmount only raises the attacker’s cost marginally and does not eliminate the underlying sequential processing flaw. In summary, the contract’s design allows a malicious actor to create a massive backlog of low‑value queued operations, forcing honest participants to bear extreme gas costs to access their own funds, which violates the protocol’s expectation of affordable withdrawals and undermines user trust.

title: The Liquidity Pool will lack margin of Synthetix perpetual market, if `liquidationBufferRatio` of contract `PerpsV2MarketSettings` from Synthetix is updated
description: The Liquidity Pool can lack the margin of PerpMarket if `liquidationBufferRatio` of contract `PerpsV2MarketSettings` from Synthetix is greater than 1e18. Then the delay orders of the pool can not be executed and the position of the pool might be liquidated.
bug_full: The issue originates from the way the LiquidityPool contract determines the amount of collateral it must hold for a position opened on the Synthetix perpetual market. The pool uses a simple formula that divides the absolute position size multiplied by the spot price by a fixed futuresLeverage value, producing a margin that is roughly 1/futuresLeverage of the position value. However, the perpetual market enforces an additional safety requirement called the liquidation buffer ratio, which is stored in the PerpsV2MarketSettings contract and can be changed by an admin at any time. The liquidation margin that the market expects is calculated as the absolute position value multiplied by this buffer ratio plus a fixed liquidation fee. Because the LiquidityPool does not read the current buffer ratio when it computes its margin, it may supply a margin that is lower than the market‑required liquidation margin whenever the buffer ratio is increased above the pool’s implicit 1/futuresLeverage threshold. When this happens, the internal check in _updatePositionMargin reverts with an InsufficientMargin error, causing delayed orders to fail and leaving the pool’s position exposed to liquidation. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a previously pending order never executes, the pool’s position is liquidated, and the user may see their balance drop unexpectedly or become zero, effectively losing funds that appeared to be safely deposited. The vulnerability is triggered only when the admin raises liquidationBufferRatio to a value greater than the margin fraction supplied by the pool – for example, with a futuresLeverage of 5 the pool supplies about 20 % margin, so a buffer ratio above 20 % (e.g., 30 % as demonstrated in the proof‑of‑concept) will cause failure. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the margin calculation in LiquidityPool with the liquidation margin logic in PerpsV2MarketBase and identified that the former never queries the mutable buffer ratio. The problem is subtle because the default buffer ratio is low (1 %) and therefore the pool operates correctly under current settings, making the risk easy to overlook until the parameter is changed. To remediate the issue the pool should retrieve the current liquidationBufferRatio from PerpsV2MarketSettings and incorporate it into the minimum margin calculation, ensuring that the margin it provides is always at least the market‑required liquidation margin. This change aligns the pool’s accounting with the perpetual market’s risk model and prevents unexpected order failures and forced liquidations.

title: Attacker can transfer all SUSD’s balance of LiquidityPool as margin to Synthetix perpetual market, and break the actions of users until the pool is rebalanced by the authority
description: Contract `LiquidityPool` will transfer margin of size delta for every trade, and this margin is always > 0. Then attacker can repeat open and close a position in 1 transaction, to make the pool transfer all its SUSD tokens to Synthetix perpetual market as margin, even the perpetual size of `LiquidityPool` will not change after that. Then many actions of users which need SUSD of the pool such as withdrawing liquidity tokens, opening short positions, closing long positions… can’t be executed until the pool is rebalanced by the authority.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the LiquidityPool contract that causes it to always transfer a positive amount of SUSD as margin to the Synthetix perpetual market whenever a trade triggers the internal _hedge function. The root cause is that the marginRequired value is calculated solely from the absolute size of the hedging position and is never allowed to be negative, even when the net sizeDelta of the pool’s perpetual position decreases or returns to its original value. Consequently, each call to _hedge adds marginRequired to the usedFunds counter and unconditionally calls perpMarket.transferMargin with a positive int256, regardless of whether the pool actually needs to provide additional collateral. An attacker can exploit this by opening a position and immediately closing it within a single transaction, causing two consecutive positive margin transfers while the pool’s perpetual size remains unchanged. By repeating this open‑close cycle many times, the attacker can drain the entire SUSD balance of the LiquidityPool, leaving the pool with insufficient funds for any subsequent operation that depends on its SUSD reserve. This includes withdrawing liquidity tokens, opening short positions, or closing long positions, all of which will fail or revert because the pool no longer holds the required collateral. The attack can be front‑run to target specific high‑value users, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service or grief attack. The issue manifests only when the pool’s margin accounting is invoked; because the perpetual size does not change, the abnormal loss of SUSD may not be immediately obvious, making the bug hard to notice until user actions start failing. The affected parties are all liquidity providers and traders that rely on the pool’s ability to supply SUSD for margin, as well as the protocol’s overall reliability. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditor observed that the margin calculation always yields a positive value and that the contract does not handle the case where a reduction in position size should release margin back to the pool. The bug belongs to the class of improper collateral accounting or over‑allocation of margin, where sign handling is missing and the contract transfers more collateral than necessary. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or zero balances in the pool, failed withdrawals, and error messages indicating insufficient pool funds, contrary to the expectation that the pool should always have enough SUSD to cover trades. To remediate the issue the marginRequired calculation should be adjusted to reflect the net change in required collateral, allowing negative or zero values when the position size shrinks, and the transferMargin call should be guarded by a check that prevents moving more SUSD than the pool actually holds. Aligning the logic with the existing rebalanceMargin function, which correctly computes the delta margin, would eliminate the over‑transfer and stop the grief attack vector.

title: Possible spamming attack in opening or closing Long or Short Positions in `Exchange.openTrade`
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing a user to open a short position with a zero token amount and without providing any collateral, and then using the resulting short‑token balance to block other users from opening long positions. The contract checks only that a user does not hold an opposite‑type position before opening a trade, but it does not verify that the amount of the short position being opened is greater than zero. Consequently, the function Exchange.openTrade accepts a request where isLong is false and the amount parameter is zero, creates a short position record, mints a short‑token identifier to the caller and skips any collateral transfer. Because the short‑token balance of the caller is now non‑zero, the later check that a user must have zero short holdings before opening a long will always revert, even though the short position carries no economic value. An attacker can therefore spam the contract by repeatedly calling openTrade with amount 0, accumulating many zero‑value short tokens, and optionally transferring those tokens to other accounts. The affected parties are any participants of the exchange who wish to open long positions; they experience a denial‑of‑service where their transaction reverts with the message “Short position must be closed before opening” despite having no visible short exposure. From a user‑interface perspective the symptom is that a user sees a short‑token balance increase while their collateral and perp balance remain zero, and attempts to open a long result in an unexpected revert. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that loops 1000 times opening zero‑amount shorts and observing the resulting blockage of long trades. The bug is subtle because a zero‑amount position does not move funds, so it can be overlooked during casual testing, yet it violates the business rule that a trader cannot simultaneously hold long and short positions. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum non‑zero amount (or a positive collateral requirement) when opening a short, and add a guard in the position‑adjustment logic to reject zero‑amount adjustments. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that a user’s position is either long or short with a meaningful amount, preventing the spam attack and ensuring that users can open the positions they expect.

title: First Depositors will incurr a rebalancing Loss
bug_full: The vulnerability is a token‑price dilution bug that occurs when the vault’s token price is calculated as totalFunds divided by totalSupply without accounting for fees that reduce totalFunds. After an initial deposit, the vault opens a position and pays a trading or hedging fee; this fee permanently lowers totalFunds while the totalSupply of vault tokens remains unchanged. Because the price formula uses the reduced totalFunds, the resulting token price drops slightly. A later depositor who calls the deposit function after the fee has been taken can purchase vault tokens at this lower price, receiving more tokens per unit of underlying asset than the first depositor. This creates an unfair advantage: early depositors suffer a rebalancing loss, while subsequent depositors obtain a discount that translates into a higher share of future yield. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately triggers fee‑incurring actions (such as opening a position) and then deposits a large amount, acquiring a disproportionate number of vault tokens that can later be redeemed at a higher effective value. The impact is a loss of value for early participants, distortion of accounting assumptions, and potential profit for malicious actors, undermining the fairness and economic integrity of the protocol. The condition for the bug to manifest is any operation that reduces totalFunds (fees, slippage, or other costs) without a corresponding adjustment to totalSupply or token price logic. All users who deposit before the fee event are affected, while later depositors benefit. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by observing that getTokenPrice returned a lower value after openPosition and that a second test depositor received roughly five times more vault tokens than the first. The bug is subtle because the price function appears to be a simple division, and fee deductions are expected in many financial contracts, making the resulting price drop easy to overlook. To remediate, the token‑price calculation should incorporate fee adjustments, for example by reducing totalSupply proportionally, applying a deposit/withdrawal fee that offsets the fee impact, or redesigning the accounting model so that fees are reflected in the token’s net asset value rather than silently decreasing totalFunds. This aligns the token price with the true value of assets held and prevents dilution of early participants.

title: Users’ collateral could get stuck permanently after fully closing short trades
description:
When completely closing a short trade, a user is supposed to input `TradeParams` such that:

`shortPosition.shortAmount == params.shortAmount`  
`shortPosition.collateralAmount == params.collateralAmount`

However, if cares have not been given particularly when inputting `params.collateralAmount` via a non-frontend method such as <https://optimistic.etherscan.io/>, a zero or a value smaller than `shortPosition.collateralAmount` could be accidentally entered. After the transaction has succeeded, the user’s collateral would be permanently locked in contract `ShortCollateral`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of collateral when a user fully closes a short position on the exchange contract. The contract expects the caller to provide TradeParams where the short amount and the collateral amount exactly match the values stored in the position. However, the _closeTrade function does not enforce that the collateralAmount supplied by the caller equals the full collateral when the short amount is reduced to zero. If a user (or an attacker) supplies a collateralAmount of zero or any value smaller than the position’s collateralAmount—something that can happen when the transaction is sent directly through a tool such as Etherscan rather than through the front‑end UI—the contract will transfer only the supplied amount back to the user and then burn the ERC‑721 token that represents the short position. Because the token is burned, the subsequent ownership check (shortToken.ownerOf(positionId) == msg.sender) fails for any remaining collateral, preventing the contract from ever releasing the leftover funds. The root cause is the missing validation that, when totalShortAmount becomes zero, the contract should automatically return the entire collateral or reject a partial amount. Exploitation is straightforward: an adversary calls closeTrade with a deliberately low collateralAmount, the transaction succeeds because the minimum collateral requirement becomes zero, and the remaining collateral becomes permanently locked in the ShortCollateral contract. The impact is that users lose part or all of the collateral they posted for a short trade, effectively causing funds to disappear from their perspective. This occurs only when a position is fully closed and the caller provides an insufficient collateralAmount, a scenario that is easy to trigger when interacting with the contract off‑chain or via raw transaction submission. All users who open short positions are affected, as the protocol’s accounting assumes that collateral is either fully returned or correctly accounted for, and the bug breaks that invariant. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the _closeTrade logic, where the auditor noticed that the require statement uses a minimum collateral value that becomes zero when the short amount is zero, allowing the transaction to pass even with an under‑payment. The bug is subtle because typical front‑end interfaces enforce the correct values, so the problem only surfaces when the contract is called directly, making it hard to notice in normal usage. To remediate, the contract should add a check that overrides params.collateralAmount to the full position collateral when totalShortAmount is zero, or explicitly require that the supplied collateralAmount equals the position’s collateralAmount for a full close, thereby guaranteeing that no collateral remains locked after the token is burned. This fix restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents permanent loss of user funds.

title: Lack of price validity check from Synthetix results in loss of funds while liquidating
description: Lack of a validity check while liquidating results in loss of funds, as the price could be invalid momentarily from Synthetix due to high volatility or other issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step for the price data returned by the Synthetix oracle when a liquidation is performed. The liquidation logic calls the exchange to obtain a mark price and the Synthetix adapter to obtain a collateral price, but it never checks the boolean flag isInvalid that the oracle returns to indicate that the price is stale, zero, or otherwise unreliable. Because the contract proceeds with the calculation even when isInvalid is true, a liquidation can be executed with an invalid or zero price. This can happen during periods of extreme market volatility or when the oracle experiences a temporary failure, situations in which Synthetix deliberately marks the price as invalid. When such a price is used, the amount of collateral that is seized or the fee that is charged is computed incorrectly. The result may be an under‑liquidation, where the borrower receives less than the amount required to cover the debt, or an over‑liquidation, where the protocol seizes more than it should, both leading to a loss of funds for the user or the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared liquidation functions with other parts of the code where the isInvalid flag is correctly required; the absence of the check stood out as an inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the oracle normally returns valid data, so the contract appears to work correctly under normal conditions, and no explicit error is emitted when an invalid price is used. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that appears to succeed but results in a zero or unexpectedly low payout, a sudden drop of the user’s balance after liquidation, or a protocol accounting entry that shows an unexplained loss. The expected behavior is that liquidation settles at the current market price, but the reality is that it may settle at an invalid price, effectively making funds disappear. The flaw belongs to the class of missing external data validation bugs, where a contract trusts an oracle output without confirming its integrity. The recommended remediation is to add a require(!isInvalid) check after each price fetch, or to abort the liquidation entirely when the price is flagged invalid, thereby ensuring that only reliable price data is used for settlement calculations.

title: Collateral removal not possible
description: If an approved collateral has later started say taking fees on transfer then protocol has no way to remove such collateral. The current deposit logic cannot handle fee on transfer token and would give more funds to user then actually obtained by contract
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inability for the protocol to remove a previously approved collateral token once that token starts charging a fee on each transfer. The deposit routine assumes that the amount transferred from the user to the contract is received in full; it calls safeTransferFrom, then records the supplied amount directly in the position’s accounting without verifying the actual balance that arrived. When a token such as USDT changes its policy to deduct a fee on transfer, the contract will receive less than the declared amount, but the internal accounting will still reflect the full amount. This mismatch creates an over‑statement of collateral, meaning the protocol believes a user has supplied more security than is truly held. The root cause is the lack of a verification step for fee‑on‑transfer tokens and the absence of a governance mechanism to disapprove or de‑list a collateral that becomes unsuitable. Exploitation is straightforward: any user can deposit the affected token after the fee is enabled, and the contract will record a higher collateral balance than it actually possesses. Subsequent actions that rely on the recorded balance—such as withdrawals, liquidation checks, or interest calculations—will operate on incorrect data, potentially leading to under‑collateralisation, failed withdrawals, or loss of funds for the protocol and its users. The issue manifests only after the token’s fee policy changes, and it affects all participants who interact with the affected collateral, including depositors, lenders, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the collateral management flow and identified that the code never checks the post‑transfer balance. The problem can be subtle because the transfer itself succeeds, no revert occurs, and the UI may still display the expected deposited amount, hiding the shortfall until a later operation reveals the discrepancy. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a disapproval or de‑listing function that allows governance to remove a collateral token from the whitelist, coupled with a phased withdrawal or wipe‑out of existing positions. Additionally, the deposit logic must be hardened by measuring the actual token balance received (for example, by recording the contract’s balance before and after the transfer) and using that real amount for accounting, or by rejecting tokens that implement fee‑on‑transfer behavior. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that collateral amounts are fully transferred and ensures that users receive the funds they expect when withdrawing, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Unsafe casting from `uint256` to `uint16` could cause ticket prizes to become much smaller than intended
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe numeric cast that occurs when the lottery contract packs fixed reward amounts into a single 256‑bit word. The function that performs the packing divides each reward by a token‑specific divisor and then casts the resulting uint256 value to a uint16 before shifting it into the packed word. If the division result is larger than the maximum value that fits in 16 bits (65535), the cast silently truncates the high‑order bits, leaving only the low 16 bits. As a result the stored prize for that win tier becomes dramatically smaller than the amount originally supplied. This happens during the initialization of a lottery when the `rewards[]` array contains values that, after division by the token‑decimals‑based divisor, exceed the 16‑bit limit – effectively any reward larger than roughly 6553.5 tokens for a typical 18‑decimal ERC20. The bug was discovered through a formal audit and reproduced with a unit test that initialized the contract with rewards of [0, 6500, 7000] tokens; the second tier was stored correctly, but the third tier was truncated to 446 tokens. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a ticket that should earn a large payout instead receives a much lower amount, or even zero, leading to confusion when the UI displays a reward that does not match the advertised prize. The impact is an under‑payment of winners, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially eroding trust in the lottery’s fairness. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; the truncation is silent and the packed value still fits the expected bit‑width, so only a careful inspection of the casting logic or a discrepancy in observed payouts reveals the problem. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of unsafe casting or integer truncation errors that arise when down‑casting a larger integer type to a smaller one without range checks. To fix the problem the contract should either avoid packing rewards into a 16‑bit field—e.g., by storing each reward in a mapping—or enforce a safe cast using OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library, reverting when a reward does not fit into 16 bits. Either approach restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between the configured reward amounts and the values actually paid out, preserving the lottery’s economic guarantees.

title: Undermining the fairness of the protocol in `swapSource`
description:
This issue will demonstrate how the current implementation of `swapSource()` and `retry()` goes directly against Chainlink’s Security Consideration of **Not re-requesting randomness** (<https://docs.chain.link/vrf/v2/security#do-not-re-request-randomness>).

Returning two random numbers clearly breaks the intent of the protocol, and I would consider it to meet the Medium-risk criteria.
> 2 — Med: Assets not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted, or leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements.

For the severity criteria, see <https://docs.code4rena.com/awarding/judging-criteria/severity-categorization>
poc:
1. `retry()` is called enough times to reach `maxFailedAttempts`, attacker starts monitoring the mempool for the `swapSource()` call.
2. Admin decides to swap Source. Admin waits for `maxRequestDelay` time to pass and calls `swapSource()`.
3. Attacker notices the `swapSource()` call and front-runs a `retry()` call before the `swapSource()` invocation.
4. The introduced code bug displays that `swapSource()` is not invalidated by the front-ran `retry()` and both `retry()` and `swapSource()` request a random number from Chainlink VRF.
5. Attacker now scans the mempool for the callbacks from the requests to VRF, inspects the random numbers and front-runs the transaction with the random number that favors him.

1. Assume Lottery configuration with a short `drawPeriod` e.g 1 hour.
2. `retry()` is called enough times to reach `maxFailedAttempts`, attacker starts monitoring the mempool for the `swapSource()` call.
3. Admin decides to swap Source. Admin waits for `maxRequestDelay` time to pass and calls `swapSource()`.
4. Attacker notices the `swapSource()` call and front-runs a `retry()` call before the `swapSource()` invocation thus achieving 2 callback RN requests as in Issue #2 PoC.
5. Attacker uses front-running suppression after one of the callback requests is picked up by the protocol and therefore current draw is finalized. 
6. Attacker registers a ticket with the winning combination generated from the suppressed RN.
7. After `drawPeriod` is past attacker or other user calls `executeDraw()`.
8. Attacker front-runs the “suppressed RN” to be picked by miners first.
9. ‘fulfillRandomWords()’ is called with the RN known by the attacker thus winning a jackpot.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between the contract functions that manage randomness sources and the retry mechanism used when a randomness request fails. In the current design, an administrator can call swapSource() to replace the contract’s randomness provider after a certain number of failed attempts have been recorded. The retry() function is allowed to be invoked up to maxFailedAttempts, and the code mistakenly checks for equality rather than a greater‑than‑or‑equal condition, allowing an extra retry call to be executed just before the source is swapped. Because swapSource() does not invalidate any pending randomness requests, a front‑runner can observe the admin’s intention to change the source, submit a retry() transaction that triggers a new Chainlink VRF request, and then let the admin’s swapSource() transaction issue a second VRF request for the same draw. This results in two independent random numbers being generated for a single lottery round, directly violating Chainlink’s security recommendation that a contract must not re‑request randomness for the same logical operation. An attacker who monitors the mempool can capture the callback containing the first random number, front‑run the transaction that consumes the second random number, and thereby influence the outcome of the draw. In practice the attacker can ensure that the random number used to select the winning ticket is one they have already observed, allowing them to purchase a ticket that matches the known winning combination and claim the jackpot. The impact is a breach of fairness: participants expect a truly random draw, but the protocol can be manipulated to consistently favor the attacker, leading to loss of funds from the lottery pool and erosion of trust in the system. The issue manifests only when the admin initiates a source swap after the maximum number of retry attempts has been reached and when an adversary can front‑run transactions in the narrow window between the retry and the swapSource call, which is more likely in configurations with short draw periods. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logic of swapSource() and retry() was compared against Chainlink VRF security considerations. It is subtle because both randomness requests succeed and the contract does not emit an explicit error, so the protocol appears to operate normally while the underlying fairness guarantee is broken. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that a source swap invalidates any outstanding randomness requests, prevent additional retry calls once the maximum threshold is reached by using a >= comparison, and restrict source changes to trusted governance processes that include checks against re‑requesting randomness. Following the Chainlink VRF documentation and adding explicit state flags to ensure only one random number is generated per draw will restore the intended security properties and protect users from manipulated outcomes.

title: An attacker can leave the protocol in a “drawing” state for extended period of time
poc:
1. Ticket registration closes, attacker calls `executeDraw()` with insufficient gas and Lottery is put in the Executing Draw State (drawExecutionInProgress = true).
2. Attacker front-runs the transaction if there are other `executeDraw()` transactions.
3. `RNSourceController.sol` calls `VRFv2RNSource.so` in a `try{} catch{}` block, VRF transaction reverts and `lastRequestFulfilled` remains equal to `false`.
4. After “maxRequestDelay” time has past retry() becomes available that relies on the same `try{} catch{}` block in `requestRandomNumberFromSource()`.
5. Attacker calls `retry()` with insufficient gas and front-runs the transaction if there are other `retry()` transactions.
6. Attacker repeats steps 4 and 5 leaving the system in a Drawing state for extended period of time (5 hours for every `retry()` in the example implementation).

Moreover, the attacker doesn’t have any incentive to deposit LINK himself since VRF will also revert on insufficient LINK tokens.

This Proof of Concept was also implemented and confirmed in a Remix environment, tested on the Ethereum Sepolia test network. A video walk-through can be provided on my behalf if requested by judge or sponsors.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows an attacker to keep the lottery contract in a perpetual "drawing" state. The root cause is the misuse of Solidity’s try‑catch construct when calling the Chainlink VRF source. In the RNSourceController contract the function requestRandomNumberFromSource records a timestamp, sets lastRequestFulfilled to false and then invokes source.requestRandomNumber() inside a try‑catch block. If the external VRF call reverts – for example because the transaction is sent with insufficient gas or the contract lacks enough LINK – the catch clause only emits an event and does not revert the state change, leaving lastRequestFulfilled false. Because drawExecutionInProgress remains true until a successful callback sets it back to false, the protocol cannot progress to the next draw. An attacker can trigger the condition by calling executeDraw with deliberately low gas, causing the VRF request to fail, and then repeatedly calling the retry function with low gas after the maxRequestDelay (five hours) expires. Each retry restarts the delay timer, effectively extending the locked state indefinitely. The impact is that users see the UI indicate that a draw is in progress, they cannot register new tickets, no winner is selected, and any funds that would be distributed remain frozen. This affects every participant in the lottery, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts that rely on the draw outcome. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and confirmed with a proof‑of‑concept on Sepolia, where the attacker was able to keep the contract in the drawing state for multiple five‑hour intervals. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not revert, the state variables simply show a pending request, and the emitted events may be ignored by monitoring tools. To remediate, the contract should avoid swallowing errors from the VRF call; it should either propagate the revert, enforce a require that the request succeeds, or implement a fallback that resets the state after a configurable timeout. Additionally, validating that sufficient gas and LINK are available before making the request, and providing an admin‑only reset mechanism, would prevent the protocol from being held hostage by a malicious low‑gas transaction.

title: The buyer of the ticket could be front-runned by the ticket owner who claims the rewards before the ticket’s NFT is traded
description: If the ticket owner lists the winning ticket on the secondary market and initiates their own claiming transaction before the trade transaction takes place, the NFT buyer could lose funds as a result.
bug_full: An attacker can front‑run a ticket transfer by invoking the claimWinningTickets function before the buyer’s transfer transaction is mined. The contract allows a ticket owner to list a winning ticket on a secondary market and does not prevent the owner from calling the claim function while the ticket is still owned. Because the claim function does not check whether the NFT has been transferred or mark the ticket as claimed, the owner can submit a claim transaction with a higher gas price, have it included first, receive the full reward amount, and then transfer the NFT to the buyer. When the buyer later calls claimWinningTickets, the call reverts with a NothingToClaim error, leaving the buyer with an NFT that yields no reward and with the expectation of a profit that never materializes. This race condition occurs whenever a winning ticket is tradable and the contract lacks a mechanism to lock or burn claimed tickets. The impact is a loss of claimable funds for the buyer, a double‑dip profit for the seller, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue was discovered during an audit when a test case reproduced the scenario by having the original owner claim before transferring the ticket. The problem is subtle because the UI may show that the buyer owns the ticket, yet the underlying reward balance is already zero, making the failure hard to notice without inspecting transaction ordering. The vulnerability belongs to the class of front‑running and improper state‑management bugs where mutable assets can be claimed after they have been transferred. To remediate, the contract should either burn the NFT after a successful claim or prohibit transfers of tickets that have already been claimed, for example by adding a claimed flag and checking it in the transfer function.

title: Possibility to steal jackpot bypassing restrictions in the `executeDraw`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the time‑based restrictions that govern when a lottery draw can be executed and when tickets may be purchased. The contract’s executeDraw function checks that the current block timestamp is strictly less than the scheduled draw start (block.timestamp < drawScheduledAt(currentDraw)). Because the comparison uses a strict “<”, the function can still be called at the exact moment the draw is scheduled, which should be prohibited. A similar mistake exists in the beforeTicketRegistrationDeadline modifier, which uses a strict “>” to reject ticket purchases after the registration deadline, allowing purchases when the timestamp is exactly equal to the deadline. When the cool‑down period between draws is set to zero, these boundary conditions line up so that an attacker can call executeDraw at the last second of the draw period, trigger a request for a random number, receive the random number in the same block (or immediately via the Chainlink callback), read the winning ticket value, and then purchase a ticket with that exact number before the contract’s deadline check blocks the action. After buying the ticket, the attacker can immediately call claimWinningTickets and collect the entire jackpot. The exploit works because the contract assumes the random number is unpredictable and that ticket purchases are impossible once the draw has started, both of which are invalidated by the faulty comparisons. The impact is that the jackpot can be drained by a single malicious participant, causing other users to lose expected winnings and reducing confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The issue manifests only when the draw schedule allows a zero‑length cool‑down period and when an attacker can synchronize actions within the same block, making it difficult to detect in ordinary testing that does not cover exact‑timestamp edge cases. The bug belongs to the class of boundary‑condition timestamp comparison flaws that create race‑condition‑like opportunities. To remediate, the executeDraw check should be changed to block.timestamp <= drawScheduledAt(currentDraw) and the deadline modifier should use block.timestamp >= ticketRegistrationDeadline(drawId), thereby preventing execution or ticket purchase at the exact boundary and closing the window for the described attack.

title: Insolvency: The `Lottery` may incorrectly consider a year old jackpot ticket as unclaimed and increase `currentNetProfit` by its prize while it was actually claimed
description:
According to the [documentation](https://docs.wenwin.com/wenwin-lottery/the-game):

“This means that at worst you could directly use...
What the finding also implies, is that if...

Winning tickets have up to 1 year to claim their prize. If a prize is not claimed before this period, the unclaimed prize money will go back to the Prize Pot.”

As part of this mechanism, the `Lottery.executeDraw()` function (which internally calls `Lottery.returnUnclaimedJackpotToThePot()`) increases `Lottery.currentNetProfit` by the prize of any 1 year old unclaimed jackpot ticket. At this point, the contract thinks it still holds that prize and it’s going to include it in the prize pot of the next draw. This function can only be called when `block.timestamp >= drawScheduledAt(currentDraw)`.

On the other side, the `Lottery.claimWinningTickets()` function (which internally calls `Lottery.claimWinningTicket()` and `Lottery.claimable()`) sends the prize to the owner of a jackpot ticket only if it isn’t 1 year old (if `block.timestamp <= ticketRegistrationDeadline(ticketInfo.drawId + LotteryMath.DRAWS_PER_YEAR)`).

However, if `Lottery.drawCoolDownPeriod` is zero, both of these conditions can pass on the same time - when the `block.timestamp` is exactly the scheduled draw date of the draw that takes place exactly 1 year after the draw in which the jackpot ticket has won.

In this edge case, the owner of the jackpot ticket can call `Lottery.executeDraw()`, letting the `Lottery` think the prize wasn’t claimed, followed by `Lottery.claimWinningTickets()`, claiming the prize, all in the same transaction.
poc:
Let’s say Eve buys a ticket to draw #1 in a `Lottery` contract where `Lottery.drawCoolDownPeriod` equals zero, and wins the jackpot. Now, Eve can wait 1 year and then, when `block.timestamp` equals the scheduled draw date of draw #53 (which is also the registration deadline of draw #53), run a transaction that will do the following:
    
    lottery.executeDraw()
    lottery.claimWinningTickets([eveJackpotTicketId])

This will send Eve her prize, but will also leave the contract insolvent.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the lottery contract that can cause a jackpot prize to be counted twice, leading to a potential insolvency condition. The root cause is the use of a non‑strict deadline check (<=) in the claimable logic combined with the ability to set the draw cooldown period to zero. When the cooldown is zero, the timestamp that marks the end of the one‑year claim window is exactly the same as the scheduled time for the next draw. At that precise moment the contract’s executeDraw function treats the one‑year‑old ticket as unclaimed and adds its prize to the currentNetProfit, while the claimWinningTickets function still considers the ticket claimable because the timestamp comparison allows equality. An attacker who holds a winning jackpot ticket can wait until the exact block where block.timestamp equals the registration deadline, call executeDraw to make the contract think the prize is unclaimed, and immediately call claimWinningTickets to withdraw the prize. The contract therefore pays out the prize to the user and, because the prize was also added to currentNetProfit, it remains in the prize pot for the next draw. This double inclusion reduces the contract’s overall balance and can render it insolvent if the prize size is large relative to the pot. The issue occurs only when drawCoolDownPeriod is configured to zero and the transaction is executed at the exact scheduled draw time, a condition that is rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing. It affects jackpot ticket owners, the lottery protocol, and any participants who rely on the integrity of the prize pool. The bug was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the interaction between executeDraw and claimWinningTickets and noticing the overlapping timestamp condition. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a winner receives the expected jackpot amount, but the contract’s balance appears lower than expected and subsequent draws may have an unexpectedly high prize pool or even fail due to insufficient funds. The vulnerability violates the business rule that unclaimed prizes should either be claimed by the owner or returned to the pot, never both. To remediate the issue the claimable check should require a strict less‑than comparison to the registration deadline, or the contract should enforce a non‑zero cooldown period, ensuring that the two functions cannot be executed in the same block for a one‑year‑old ticket. This change restores the intended accounting flow where a prize is either paid out or returned, but never both, preventing the contract from becoming insolvent.

title: Locking rewards tokens in Staking contract when there are no stakes
description:
Blocking rewards assigned to stakes from the sale of lottery tickets when stakes are absent in the `Staking` contract.

So, the situation is unlikely, but it can happen.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a reward‑locking condition in the staking module of the lottery protocol. When the staking contract has a total supply of zero – meaning no user has any tokens currently staked – the internal accounting variable that tracks the cumulative reward per token (rewardPerTokenStored) is left unchanged. As a result, any reward tokens that are transferred to the staking contract by the lottery’s claimRewards function are recorded but never attributed to any staker, because the calculation that distributes rewards divides by the total supply, which is zero, and the contract deliberately returns the previously stored value instead of updating it. This situation can be triggered in two realistic ways: (1) immediately after deployment, before any user has performed a stake, a user may call claimRewards for the staking reward type, causing the first batch of reward tokens to be deposited while totalSupply is still zero; (2) later in the lifecycle, after all existing stakers have withdrawn their positions, the totalSupply again becomes zero, and any subsequent reward distribution will suffer the same locking effect. The impact is that the deposited reward tokens become permanently inaccessible – they remain in the staking contract balance but are never claimable by any participant, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s economic flow. Users experience symptoms such as seeing a non‑zero token balance in the staking contract while their own reward balance stays at zero, or receiving no payout despite the protocol indicating that rewards were generated. From the protocol’s perspective, accounting assumptions that rewards are always distributable to active stakers are violated, breaking the expected invariant that rewardPerToken increases with each distribution. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by reproducing the edge case in a test suite that logged the contract’s internal state before and after staking, reward claims, and withdrawals, revealing that rewardPerTokenStored remained at zero while the contract’s token balance grew. Because the condition only occurs when totalSupply is zero, it may go unnoticed in normal operation where at least one staker is always present. To remediate, the contract should implement a fallback flow for periods with zero totalSupply – for example, redirecting undistributed rewards to a treasury, allowing an emergency withdrawal function, or updating rewardPerTokenStored using a safe divisor or a placeholder value so that rewards are not stranded. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “zero‑balance accounting” or “division‑by‑zero reward distribution” flaws that cause funds to become locked when the expected participant set is empty.

title: User transactions can call system contracts directly
description: User transaction can call system contracts directly, which shouldn’t be allowed to not invoke potentially dangerous operations.
poc:
The [DefaultAccount.executeTransaction](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/DefaultAccount.sol#L117) executes a user transaction after it was validated. The function calls [_execute](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/DefaultAccount.sol#L140) under the hood. The `_execute` function makes two different calls depending on the destination address of a transaction:

  1. if the `ContractDeployer` is called, it’ll [pass the call to the contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/DefaultAccount.sol#L149) via the system call (`ContractDeployer` is a system contract and can be executed only via system calls);
  2. if any other contract is called, it’ll [execute the call via `EfficientCall.rawCall`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/DefaultAccount.sol#L151).

`EfficientCall.rawCall` in its turn also makes two different calls:

  1. If `msg.value` of the transaction is 0, it’ll [make a regular call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/libraries/EfficientCall.sol#L131).
  2. If there’s some ETH sent with the transaction (i.e. `msg.value` is positive), it’ll [pass the call to the `MsgValueSimulator` contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/libraries/EfficientCall.sol#L144). `MsgValueSimulator` is a system contract, thus the `isSystem` flag will be set in the far call ABI (notice the `true` in the [last argument of `_loadFarCallABIIntoActivePtr`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/libraries/EfficientCall.sol#L134)). However, it’ll also [set the forward mask](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/libraries/EfficientCall.sol#L141) to 1 (the value of [MSG_VALUE_SIMULATOR_IS_SYSTEM_BIT](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/Constants.sol#L71)). `MsgValueSimulator` will [extract the mask and will set the `isSystemCall` flag to true](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/MsgValueSimulator.sol#L27)–it’ll then pass the `isSystemCall` flag to the [subsequent call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-zksync/blob/21d9a364a4a75adfa6f1e038232d8c0f39858a64/contracts/MsgValueSimulator.sol#L62), making the call a system one.

To sum it up, if a transaction calls a contract that’s not `ContractDeployer` and sends ETH, the call will be a system one, which will let it call the system contracts. However, users shouldn’t be allowed to call system contracts directly to not invoke potentially dangerous operations. As per the documentation:

Some of the system contracts can act on behalf of the user or have a very important impact on the behavior of the account. That’s why we wanted to make it clear that users can not invoke potentially dangerous operations by doing a simple EVM-like call. Whenever a user wants to invoke some of the operations which we considered dangerous, they must explicitly provide isSystem flag with them.
