To remediate, the contract should employ a robust ERC165 checker such as OpenZeppelin’s ERC165Checker, which first confirms that the target contract supports ERC165 before querying for a specific interface. Alternatively, the protocol could enforce ERC165 implementation as a prerequisite for any resolver, ensuring that the supportsInterface call never reverts. Fixing the check restores the intended resolution flow, allowing the fallback staticcall to execute and preventing unnecessary reverts, thereby improving composability and developer experience.

title: Incorrect implementation of `RecordParser.readKeyValue
description:
`RecordParser.readKeyValue()` returns a wrong `value` if the terminator not found.  
This is a fundamental library and any contract using it may experience unexpected errors and problems due to this bug.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RecordParser.readKeyValue library function, which extracts a key‑value pair from a byte array given an offset and a length. The function searches for the '=' separator and then looks for a space character that marks the end of the value. If the space is not found, the implementation sets the terminator to input.length, ignoring the length constraint supplied by the caller. Consequently the function returns a value that extends beyond the intended slice (offset..offset+len) and also reports a nextOffset that points past the end of the allowed range. This occurs whenever the last key‑value entry in the supplied segment does not end with a space, a situation that is common when the data format omits a trailing delimiter. The root cause is an incorrect boundary check: the terminator is allowed to exceed offset+len because the code does not cap it to the query range. An attacker or a malformed data source can craft input such that the missing space forces the parser to read into subsequent fields, for example pulling a URL into the value of the preceding key. From a user’s perspective the contract may return a value that contains extra characters (e.g., "18;https://tether.to" instead of "18"), the nextOffset may become larger than the buffer, and subsequent parsing loops can fail or produce corrupted state. The impact is that any contract relying on this library – such as ENS DNS registrar contracts – may store incorrect configuration data, mis‑route requests, or reject legitimate operations, potentially leading to loss of funds or denial of service. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that parsing a string without a trailing space produced an oversized value and an out‑of‑bounds offset. The bug is subtle because normal inputs that include a space after each value work correctly, so the failure only appears in edge cases that are easy to overlook. To remediate, the parser must enforce that the terminator never exceeds offset+len, update nextOffset accordingly, and ensure that the returned value is confined to the specified range. This aligns the implementation with the intended contract of the function – to safely extract a key‑value pair within the caller‑provided bounds – and prevents accidental data leakage and malformed state updates.

title: Unintentionally register a non-relevant DNS name owner
description:
If a user proves and claims a DNS name using a wrong address format, it executes successfully without getting any error and the DNS name owner will be changed to a new unknown address.

I considered this as medium severity, as it is high impact finding with low likelihood. Cause the person who owns the new address can take control of the ENS name and transfer its ownership to another account. But because if a person finds out, she can immediately replace the correct address, the probability of such an event is low.
bug_full: An unintended ownership change can occur in the ENS registrar when a caller invokes proveAndClaim with an address argument that does not conform to the expected 0x‑prefixed 40‑character hexadecimal format. The underlying hexToAddress helper only verifies that the supplied byte slice contains at least 40 hex characters and then converts the last 20 bytes of the slice into an address, silently discarding any leading characters. Because the function does not enforce an exact length or reject extra data, a user can supply a longer byte string; the contract will truncate it and register the truncated value as the new owner of the DNS name. An attacker who knows this behaviour can craft an arbitrary 22‑byte value, cause the contract to accept it without reverting, and thereby set the ENS name owner to an address under the attacker’s control. The impact is that the legitimate owner loses control of the name and the attacker can later transfer or sell the name, violating the protocol’s ownership guarantees. The condition occurs only when the caller provides a malformed address; normal, correctly sized addresses are processed as intended, which makes the bug low‑probability but high‑impact. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised proveAndClaim with non‑standard inputs and observed that the contract accepted the call and recorded an unexpected owner. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the contract emits no warning; the only symptom is that the ENS name’s owner field shows an address that the caller did not intend, leading to confusion such as my name is now owned by a random address. This class of bug belongs to insufficient input validation and unsafe parsing, where truncation of user‑supplied data leads to incorrect state changes. The recommended fix is to enforce strict validation of the address string: require the 0x prefix, ensure the length is exactly 40 hexadecimal characters, and revert the transaction if the check fails, rather than silently truncating. By adding these checks the contract will prevent accidental or malicious registration of a non‑relevant DNS name owner and preserve the intended ownership model.

title: `validateSignature
description: Currently not exploitable because this bug is cancelled out by another issue (see my Gas report). If the other issue is fixed `validateSignature` will return completely incorrect values.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the validateSignature routine of the EllipticCurve contract used by the DNSSEC oracle. The function mixes affine and projective coordinate handling incorrectly: after adding two affine points it converts them to projective form but then immediately applies an inverse modulo on the Z coordinate even though the Z coordinate is always 1. The code also squares the inverse (mulmod(Px, Px, p)) which is redundant because Px equals 1. As a result the final comparison uses Px % n == rs[0] where Px is effectively the X coordinate multiplied by 1, but the extra operations mask a logical flaw: if the surrounding bug that forces Z to be zero is removed, the function would compute an incorrect X value and reject every signature. The root cause is a misunderstanding of coordinate systems and unnecessary modular inverses, leading to a validation routine that can return false for all inputs once the compensating bug is fixed. Exploitation would consist of an attacker triggering the fix of the compensating bug (or deploying a patched version) and then submitting valid signatures that are incorrectly rejected, causing the protocol to consider legitimate actions unauthenticated. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on any functionality that relies on DNSSEC signatures, such as name resolution or oracle updates, potentially halting the protocol’s operation. The condition occurs only after the other issue that forces the Z coordinate to zero is eliminated; otherwise the bug is effectively neutralized. All users, contract callers, and the protocol itself are affected because they would receive error responses instead of successful verification, leading to missing updates or failed transactions. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the redundant conversion chain and the constant‑one Z coordinate. It is hard to notice because the function still returns true for test vectors when the compensating bug is present, and the redundant arithmetic does not change the result, so unit tests may pass. The proper fix is to remove the unnecessary inverse and squaring, and to compare the X coordinate directly against the signature component, i.e., return P[0] % n == rs[0], and to refactor the point addition to stay in projective form until the final conversion. This aligns the implementation with standard elliptic‑curve verification logic and eliminates the hidden dependency on a separate bug. In user‑facing terms, a user would expect a valid signature to be accepted but would instead see the transaction revert or receive a “signature verification failed” error, effectively making the service unavailable. The bug belongs to the class of cryptographic verification logic errors caused by incorrect handling of coordinate representations.

title: Missing recursive calls handling in `OffchainDNSResolver` CCIP-aware contract
description:
The `resolveCallback` function from `OffchainDNSResolver` is used as part of the EIP-3668 standard to properly resolve DNS names using an off-chain gateway and validating RRsets against the DNSSEC oracle.

The issue is that the function lacks proper error handling, specifically, a try/catch block to properly bubble up `OffchainLookup` error from the `dnsresolver` extracted from the RRset. As the EIP specifies,

> When a CCIP-aware contract wishes to make a call to another contract, and the possibility exists that the callee may implement CCIP read, the calling contract MUST catch all`OffchainLookup` errors thrown by the callee, and revert with a different error if the `sender` field of the error does not match the callee address.  
> […]  
> Where the possibility exists that a callee implements CCIP read, a CCIP-aware contract MUST NOT allow the default solidity behaviour of bubbling up reverts from nested calls.
poc:
1. Client calls `OffchainDNSResolver.resolve`, which reverts with `OffchainLookup`, and prompts the client to execute `resolveCallback` after having fetched the necessary data from the `gatewayURL`
2. The RRset returned by the gateway contains a `dnsresolver` that is a CCIP-aware contract, and also supports the `IExtendedDNSResolver.resolve.selector` interface
3. Calling `IExtendedDNSResolver(dnsresolver).resolve(name,query,context);` could trigger another `OffchainLookup` error, but with a `sender` that does not match the `dnsresolver`, which would be just returned to the client without any modifications
4. As a result, the `sender` field would be incorrect as per the EIP
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the OffchainDNSResolver contract that implements the EIP‑3668 CCIP‑read flow for DNSSEC‑validated name resolution. When a client calls the resolve function, the contract reverts with an OffchainLookup error that contains a gateway URL. After the client fetches the required data and invokes resolveCallback, the callback extracts a dnsresolver address from the returned RRset and calls IExtendedDNSResolver(dnsresolver).resolve. If that nested resolver also implements CCIP‑read, it may revert with its own OffchainLookup error. The OffchainDNSResolver callback does not wrap this external call in a try/catch block nor does it verify that the sender field of the propagated OffchainLookup error matches the address of the dnsresolver that generated it, as required by EIP‑3668. Consequently the contract forwards an unmodified OffchainLookup error with an incorrect sender field. This mismatch violates the specification that a CCIP‑aware contract must catch all OffchainLookup errors from a callee and either re‑throw a different error or ensure the sender field is correct. The root cause is the missing error‑handling logic for recursive CCIP reads. An attacker can supply a malicious dnsresolver that deliberately triggers an OffchainLookup error with a forged sender value; because the parent contract does not validate the sender, the client receives the malformed error and cannot complete the DNS resolution. From the user’s perspective the lookup simply fails – the UI shows no address, an empty result, or a generic “resolution failed” message, contrary to the expectation that the ENS name resolves to a valid address. The impact is a denial‑of‑service or potential redirection attack, breaking the trust model of DNSSEC validation and affecting any dApp or user that relies on ENS name resolution through this contract. The issue appears only when the RRset returned by the off‑chain gateway contains a dnsresolver that itself supports CCIP‑read, a condition that is not obvious during normal testing and therefore easy to miss. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which compared the implementation against the EIP‑3668 requirements. Because the faulty behaviour manifests as a normal revert without explicit logging, it can be difficult to detect without deliberate inspection of nested error handling. The recommended remediation is to follow the example provided in EIP‑3668: wrap the call to the nested resolver in a try/catch, verify that any caught OffchainLookup error’s sender field equals the address of the resolver that was called, and if it does not, revert with a distinct error or re‑emit a correctly‑formatted OffchainLookup. In broader terms, this is a class of bug where recursive CCIP‑read calls are not properly guarded, leading to incorrect error propagation and violation of protocol safety guarantees.

title: Function `restructureCapTable
description: Incorrect typo in function `restructureCapTable()` leading to only burning tokens of first address of `addressToWipe` array argument.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that is intended to wipe the token holdings of a list of addresses during a cap‑table restructuring. The code iterates over the addressesToWipe array but mistakenly reads the element at index 0 on every iteration (address current = addressesToWipe[0];). As a result, only the first address in the array is actually burned, while the remaining addresses are ignored. The root cause is a typographical error that substitutes the loop variable i with a constant index, a classic off‑by‑one/incorrect‑index bug. An attacker or a careless operator can trigger the function with an array containing multiple addresses, expecting all of them to be cleared. Because the contract only burns the first address repeatedly, the other participants retain their token balances. From a user perspective the expected outcome – a zero balance for every address supplied – does not materialise; some users still see their tokens, leading to confusion such as 'my balance should be zero after the restructure but it isn’t'. The impact is primarily accounting‑related: the cap table no longer reflects the intended ownership distribution, which may affect voting rights, dividend calculations, or downstream protocol logic that assumes those addresses hold no tokens. The bug manifests whenever restructureCapTable is called with an addressesToWipe array longer than one element, which is a normal scenario for a multi‑party restructuring. The affected parties are token holders whose balances should be cleared, the protocol that relies on accurate equity calculations, and any downstream contracts that read the token supply. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that inspected the loop logic and noticed the constant index. It can be hard to notice because the function may still succeed (the first burn works) and no explicit revert occurs; the problem only becomes visible when checking the balances of the other addresses after the call. The bug belongs to the class of 'incorrect loop indexing' or 'logic error in array handling'. The correct fix is to replace the constant addressesToWipe[0] with the loop variable addressesToWipe[i], ensuring each address in the array is processed exactly once. After the fix, the function will burn the full balance of every supplied address, aligning the on‑chain state with the intended cap‑table restructuring and preventing residual token holdings.

title: POSITION LIMIT COULD BE FULLY REDUCED TO ZERO BY CLONES
description: A newly opened position could have its limit fully reduced to zero as soon as the cooldown period has elapsed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a position contract that tracks a minting limit for a newly opened position. The contract exposes a function that allows a clone of the position to request a reduction of the remaining limit by supplying a parameter called _minimum. The implementation computes a reduction value as (limit‑minted‑_minimum)/2 and then subtracts reduction+_minimum from the stored limit. Because the code only checks that the subtraction does not underflow, a caller can set _minimum equal to the current limit when the position has minted zero tokens. In that case the reduction term becomes zero, the subtraction becomes limit‑limit and the stored limit is set to zero. The function then returns the full amount that was transferred to the caller, effectively allocating the entire remaining capacity to the clone. This logic flaw occurs after the cooldown period has elapsed, when the position is alive and no challenge is active, and it can be invoked by any address that satisfies the onlyHub modifier (typically a clone contract). As a result the original position owner loses all remaining minting capacity; from the user’s perspective the UI will show that the position has no available limit, minting attempts return zero, and the expected ability to issue more Frankencoin disappears. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the original position’s revenue stream and a potential loss of trust in the protocol, especially for popular positions that many clones may target. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the arithmetic in reduceLimitForClone and noticed that the _minimum argument is not bounded away from the current limit, allowing a full‑limit drain. It is easy to miss because the division by two appears to halve the reduction, giving a false sense of safety, and the underflow check does not trigger when the reduction is zero. To remediate, the contract should enforce that _minimum is strictly less than the remaining limit (limit‑minted), preserve a non‑zero reserve for the original owner, or charge a fee to clones that compensates the original position. In general, the bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted parameter leading to full resource exhaustion” where a caller can force a contract’s accounting variable to zero through unchecked arithmetic, violating the business assumption that a position always retains some mintable capacity after opening.

title: Manipulation of total share amount might cause future depositors to lose their assets
bug_full: An issue exists in the Equity contract where the internal share calculation function contains a special case that forces the total number of shares to reach 1,000 × 10¹⁸ whenever the current totalSupply is below that threshold. The function returns newTotalShares‑totalShares as the amount of shares to mint. Because the redeem function can burn shares, the totalSupply can be reduced below 1,000 × 10¹⁸ after the first depositor has already received the initial 1,000 × 10¹⁸ shares. When this happens, any subsequent deposit triggers the fallback branch and receives exactly the difference between 1,000 × 10¹⁸ and the current totalSupply, regardless of the amount of Frankencoin supplied. An attacker who holds at least one share can deliberately redeem a small number of shares to drop the totalSupply below the threshold, causing the next depositor to obtain only a single share for a large deposit. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a deposit that appears to succeed but results in an almost empty share balance, or a balance that is far lower than expected, leading to a situation where the deposited tokens can be reclaimed by the earlier holder. The impact is a loss of economic value for the victim depositor and a potential unfair gain for the attacker, effectively breaking the accounting assumption that shares represent a proportional claim on the underlying assets. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between calculateSharesInternal and redeem, and it is subtle because the fallback condition is only triggered after a burn, a state that may not occur in normal operation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect threshold handling” or “share‑minting logic error” where a constant is used instead of the minimal safe bound, leading to disproportionate token‑to‑share conversion. The recommended fix is to replace the 1,000 × 10¹⁸ threshold with the minimal invariant of 1 × 10¹⁸, ensuring that the special‑case minting only applies when the total supply would otherwise drop to zero, thereby preserving proportionality for all future deposits.

title: `anchorTime
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s use of the block number as a proxy for elapsed time when calculating the internal anchorTime value. The function shifts the current block number left by a fixed number of bits and casts the result to a 64‑bit integer, assuming that each increment of block.number corresponds to a predictable amount of real‑world time. On Optimism, block numbers are assigned to batches of transactions that can be produced much faster than one‑second intervals, and the relationship between block.number and wall‑clock time is not constant. Consequently, any logic that relies on anchorTime for time‑based actions such as vesting schedules, reward accrual, or lock‑up periods will compute incorrect timestamps. An attacker or even a regular user could experience premature unlocking of funds, delayed reward distribution, or funds appearing to be permanently locked because the contract believes the required time has not yet passed. The issue manifests only when the contract is deployed on Optimism (or similar L2s) where block.timestamp reflects L2 time but block.number does not. Users may notice that expected balances remain zero, that vesting periods end earlier or later than advertised, or that refunds are missing despite meeting the stated time conditions. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s time‑keeping mechanisms and recognized that block.number is unsuitable for measuring time on L2 networks. It can be hard to detect because the code compiles and works correctly on Ethereum mainnet, where block intervals are roughly constant, giving a false sense of correctness. The proper remediation is to replace the block‑number‑based calculation with a timestamp‑based one, using block.timestamp (or an L2‑compatible time oracle) and adjusting any resolution constants accordingly. This change restores the intended accounting assumptions that time progresses linearly and ensures that user‑facing expectations—such as receiving a refund after a certain number of days—match the actual contract behavior.

title: Owner of Denied Position is not able to withdraw collateral until expiry
description:
Denying a position puts it into perma cooldown state ie. cooldown ends at expiry. It’s impossible to withdraw collateral in the cooldown state.

Locks owner funds until expiry, expiry time is not capped and can be expected to be long. There is no benefit to the owner to set it shorter and be forced to repay the position at an inconvenient time. Hence a high risk exists to lock the collateral semi permanently
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper lock‑up of the owner’s collateral when a position is denied. When the deny function is called, the contract sets a cooldown timestamp equal to the immutable expiration time of the position. The withdrawCollateral function is protected by a noCooldown modifier that reverts with the error Hot if the current block timestamp is less than or equal to the stored cooldown value. Because the cooldown is set to the expiration, which can be arbitrarily far in the future and is not capped, the owner is unable to call withdrawCollateral until that far‑away expiry is reached. This creates a situation where the owner’s funds remain locked in the contract even though the position has been denied, violating the expectation that a user can retrieve their collateral after closing a position. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a positive collateral balance, but any attempt to withdraw results in a transaction failure and the user receives no funds, effectively seeing “my funds disappear” or “withdrawal returns nothing”. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the deny call followed by a withdrawCollateral call, which consistently reverted due to the noCooldown check. The bug belongs to the class of denial‑of‑service or improper access‑control bugs where a contract’s own logic prevents a legitimate actor from accessing their assets. It is hard to notice because the contract does not explicitly lock funds; instead the lock is enforced indirectly through a timestamp comparison that appears correct at a glance. The root cause is the combination of setting cooldown to an immutable expiration and the strict noCooldown guard that does not make an exception for the owner after a deny. To fix the issue the contract should either allow the owner to withdraw collateral after a deny, reset or clear the cooldown, or modify the noCooldown condition to exclude the owner’s withdrawal path, thereby restoring the expected business logic that collateral can be reclaimed once a position is closed.

title: Challengers and bidders can collude together to restrict the minting of position owner
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic denial‑of‑service that stems from the contract’s ability to accept an unlimited number of challenges with arbitrarily small collateral and to reward the challenger with no penalty when a challenge is averted. The root cause is the absence of any minimum collateral requirement, per‑auction challenge limit, or economic cost for a challenger who launches a challenge that later gets averted. Because the tryAvertChallenge function calls restrictMinting whenever a bid is high enough, each successful avert extends the minting cooldown for the position owner. An attacker can therefore collude with a bidder: the challenger opens a challenge with a tiny amount of collateral, the colluding bidder immediately submits a bid that satisfies the price condition, the contract transfers the collateral to the bidder, and restrictMinting is invoked, suspending the owner’s ability to mint for an additional day. By repeating this process in rapid succession, possibly within the same block, the attacker can keep pushing the cooldown horizon forward, effectively preventing the position owner from minting any new positions. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a cooldown timer or simply refuse to mint, leading to a situation where “the owner cannot mint” or “my transaction does nothing”. The protocol’s business logic assumes that challenges are a risk for the challenger; here that assumption is broken because the challenger loses nothing, while the owner suffers repeated minting restrictions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the challenge lifecycle and identified that launchChallenge does not enforce any size or frequency constraints and that tryAvertChallenge unconditionally calls restrictMinting on success. The flaw can be hard to notice because each individual challenge appears legitimate, the collateral amounts are tiny, and the only visible symptom is a delayed minting operation, which may be attributed to normal network latency. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum collateral amount, impose a fixed fee that is transferred to the position owner when a challenge is averted, prevent a challenge from being averted in the same block it was launched, and limit the number of concurrent challenges per auction. These changes would restore the intended economic balance where challengers bear risk and prevent colluding parties from repeatedly extending the minting cooldown, thereby protecting the position owner’s ability to interact with the protocol.

title: Need alternative ways for fund transfer in `end`
description: The `end()` function to conclude a challenge involves several fund transfers, including the return of challenger’s collateral, challenger’s reward transfer, the bidder’s excess return, position owner’s excess fund return. Further, in `Position.sol#notifyChallengeSucceeded()`, underlying collateral withdrawal. If any transfer of the above fails and reverts, all the other transfer calls will fail. The funds could be stuck temporarily or forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the end() function that finalises a challenge by performing a series of token transfers: returning the challenger’s collateral, paying the challenger’s reward, refunding any excess bid to the bidder, and sending any surplus funds back to the position owner. All of these transfers are executed in a single transaction using direct ERC20 transfer calls. Because the calls are not guarded against failure, any one of them reverting causes the entire end() call to revert, leaving all pending transfers undone. The root cause is the use of an atomic, push‑based payment model without fallback mechanisms, combined with assumptions that every transfer will succeed. Edge cases such as a zero‑amount transfer to a token that reverts on zero (e.g., some ERC20 implementations), a position owner address that has been set to address(0), or an insufficient balance of the protocol’s reward token (zchf) trigger a revert. Additionally, concurrent challenges can cause the total challenged amount to exceed the position’s collateral, resulting in a calculated transfer amount of zero for the collateral withdrawal. When any of these conditions occur, the transaction fails and the collateral, reward and excess funds become locked in the contract, potentially forever if no alternative withdrawal path exists. From a user perspective the symptoms are a failed transaction, no refund received, balances that remain unchanged, and an inability to complete a challenge. The affected parties are challengers, bidders and position owners who expect to receive their funds back, as well as the protocol that relies on the proper accounting of collateral and rewards. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of end() and identified that the function does not separate the accounting of owed amounts from the actual token transfers. The bug is hard to notice because normal operation with non‑zero amounts and valid owners proceeds without error; only rare edge cases expose the failure. Conceptually, the fix is to replace the push model with a pull‑based withdrawal pattern: record the amount owed to each participant during end(), emit events, and allow each party to claim their funds later via a dedicated withdraw function. The implementation should also guard against zero‑amount transfers, enforce that the total challenge amount never exceeds the available collateral, and use safe transfer wrappers that handle tokens that revert on zero or insufficient balance. By decoupling the accounting from the external token calls, the protocol avoids a single point of failure and ensures that funds cannot be permanently locked due to an unexpected revert.

title: `initializeClone`
description: `initializeClone()` Price calculations use `round down`, which only works if divisible. If precision is lost, it will revert
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error in the clone initialization routine of a DeFi position contract. The function calculates the price of a cloned position as price = _mint * ONE_DEC18 / _coll, which in Solidity performs integer division and therefore rounds the result down to the nearest integer. When the mint amount and the collateral amount are not perfectly divisible, the computed price is slightly lower than the true rational price. The contract later validates the collateral by checking collateralReserve * atPrice >= minted * ONE_DEC18 in checkCollateral(). Because the rounded‑down price is smaller, the left‑hand side of the inequality can become smaller than the right‑hand side by exactly one unit of the fixed‑point base, causing the require to fail and the transaction to revert with InsufficientCollateral. This situation occurs only during the clonePosition operation, when the caller supplies arbitrary initial collateral and mint values that are not cleanly divisible. Users attempting to clone an existing position therefore see the transaction revert, receive no new position, and their token balances remain unchanged, which is contrary to the expectation that cloning should succeed with the same economic parameters as the original. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that deliberately used non‑divisible values (e.g., 1000e18 mint and 1001 collateral), causing the price to round down to 0.999…e18 and triggering the revert. The bug is subtle because the rounding loss is only a single unit of the 18‑decimal fixed‑point representation, making the price appear correct when printed, and the failure only manifests in the internal collateral check, not in any external view. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: legitimate users cannot clone positions unless they carefully choose divisible amounts, and an attacker could deliberately craft values that cause the rounding error, preventing clones and potentially forcing users to adjust their parameters. The root cause is the use of integer division without handling the remainder. The recommended fix is to adjust the price calculation to round up when a remainder exists, for example by adding one unit if _mint * ONE_DEC18 % _coll != 0, ensuring that the price is never lower than the exact rational value and that the collateral check cannot under‑flow. This change restores the intended business logic that the collateral supplied must be sufficient for the minted amount, eliminates the unexpected revert, and aligns the contract’s accounting with the protocol’s expectations.

title: Unable to adjust position in some cases
description: The `adjust` function in `Position.sol` is designed to adjust the outstanding amount of ZCHF, the collateral amount, and the price in a single transaction. However, there are certain cases where this function always reverts. Assuming the new price is greater than the current price, if the value of `newCollateral` is less than `colbal` or the value of `newMinted` is greater than `minted`, the `adjust` function will always revert with a customized error message reading `Hot`.
bug_full: The Position contract provides an adjust() entry point that is intended to let the contract owner change three state variables – the amount of ZCHF that has been minted, the amount of collateral held, and the market price – in a single transaction. The function checks the current collateral balance (colbal) and the current minted amount (minted) and then performs a series of conditional transfers, burns, withdrawals and mints before optionally updating the price. The logic assumes that the caller will only request changes that move the system in a direction that satisfies the ordering of these operations. However, when the new price is higher than the current price, the contract’s internal cooldown mechanism (enforced by the noCooldown modifier on withdrawCollateral and mint) is triggered. If the caller also requests a reduction of collateral (newCollateral < colbal) or an increase of minted ZCHF (newMinted > minted) at the same time, the function reaches a state where the cooldown has not yet elapsed, causing both withdrawCollateral and mint to revert with the custom error Hot. Consequently, the entire adjust transaction reverts, preventing the owner from performing the desired update. This bug manifests only under the specific combination of a price increase together with a collateral reduction or a mint increase, which makes it easy to miss during casual testing because the function works correctly for many other parameter combinations. From a user perspective the contract appears to “freeze” – attempts to adjust a position result in a transaction that fails with no obvious indication other than the Hot error, leaving the position unchanged while the owner expects the new price and balances to be applied. The impact is primarily a loss of usability: the protocol cannot react to market movements in the affected scenarios, potentially leading to stale pricing, over‑collateralisation or under‑collateralisation that the protocol’s risk model does not anticipate. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised adjust() with a matrix of price, collateral and minted values and observed a deterministic revert. The root cause is the rigid ordering of state changes combined with a cooldown guard that does not account for simultaneous collateral withdrawal and minting when the price moves upward. To resolve the problem the adjust logic should be reordered or split into separate steps that respect the cooldown, for example by first handling collateral deposits, then performing any necessary burns, then withdrawing collateral, and finally minting new ZCHF, as shown in the recommended code snippet. By aligning the sequence of operations with the cooldown constraints, the function can succeed in all legitimate adjustment scenarios, restoring the intended flexibility of the protocol.

title: No slippage control when minting and redeeming FPS
description:
When minting and redeeming FPS in Equity, there is no slippage control. Since the price of FPS will change with the zchf reserve in the contract, users may suffer from sandwich attacks.

Consider the current contract has a zchf reserve of 1000 and a total supply of 1000.

Alice considers using 4000 zchf to mint FPS. Under normal circumstances, the contract reserve will rise to 5000 zchf, and the total supply will rise to (5000/1000)**(1/3)*1000 = 1710, that is, alice will get 1710 - 1000 = 710 FPS.

Bob holds 400 FPS, and bob observes alice’s transaction in MemPool, bob uses MEV to preemptively use 4000 zchf to mint 710 FPS.

When alice’s transaction is executed, the contract reserve will increase from 5000 to 9000 zchf, and the total supply will increase from 1710 to (9000/5000)**(1/3)*1710 = 2080, that is, alice gets 2080-1710 = 370FPS.

Then bob will redeem 400 FPS, the total supply will drop from 2080 to 1680, and the contract reserve will drop from 9000 to (1680/2080)**3*9000 = 4742, that is, bob gets 9000-4742 = 4258 zchf.

Bob’s total profit is 310 FPS and 258 zchf.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any slippage protection when users mint or redeem the FPS token in the Equity contract. The contract determines the FPS price solely from the ratio of the ZCHF reserve to the total FPS supply, and the mint and redeem functions do not accept a minimum‑output parameter or otherwise enforce a bound on how much the price may move during the execution of a single transaction. Because the price is a function of the reserve, a large transaction that changes the reserve can dramatically shift the price for subsequent transactions that are included in the same block. An attacker can monitor the mempool, detect a victim’s pending mint or redeem, and submit a front‑running transaction that consumes a large amount of ZCHF to inflate or deflate the reserve before the victim’s transaction is processed. In the example, Alice intends to mint FPS with 4000 ZCHF and expects to receive about 710 FPS based on the current reserve. Bob observes Alice’s pending transaction, front‑runs with his own 4000‑ZCHF mint, which raises the reserve and the FPS price. When Alice’s transaction is finally executed, the price has already moved, so she receives only 370 FPS instead of the expected amount. Bob then redeems his FPS at the new, more favorable price and extracts a profit of both FPS and ZCHF. The impact is that honest users receive fewer tokens than anticipated, while the attacker gains extra FPS and ZCHF, effectively stealing value from the protocol’s liquidity pool. This issue manifests whenever the mint or redeem functions are called without a slippage limit, which is the default behavior of the contract as written. All participants who interact with the Equity contract – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the pool’s accounting can be manipulated, leading to loss of funds and erosion of trust. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the economic invariants of the contract and noticed that the price‑impact calculation had no guard against adverse price movement. The problem is subtle because price changes are expected as reserves shift, so developers may assume that the formula alone is sufficient; however, without explicit minimum‑output checks, the contract cannot distinguish legitimate price movement from malicious front‑running. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated to accept minFPSout and minZCHFout arguments (or equivalent slippage caps) and revert the transaction if the actual output falls below the caller‑specified threshold. Additional mitigations may include using time‑weighted average pricing, limiting the size of a single mint/redeem, or integrating a commit‑reveal scheme to hide transaction intent. By enforcing a bound on acceptable price deviation, the protocol can prevent sandwich attacks, ensure that users receive the amount of FPS or ZCHF they expect, and preserve the integrity of its accounting model.

title: Later challengers can bid on the previous challenge to extend the expiration time of the previous challenge, so that their own challenge can succeed before the previous challenge and get challenge rewards
bug_full: The contract allows a challenger to extend the expiration time of an existing challenge when the remaining time drops below a 30‑minute threshold. This extension logic does not preserve the chronological order of pending challenges. As a result, a challenger who submits a later challenge can deliberately out‑bid an earlier challenge just before its deadline, causing the earlier challenge’s end time to be pushed forward while the later challenge retains its original, earlier expiration. The later challenger can then call the end function first, claim the challenge reward, and later the original challenger attempts to end their challenge only to find the position’s collateral already drained and the reward unavailable. The root cause is the unconditional update of the challenge.end timestamp based solely on the current block time, without checking whether other challenges with later timestamps exist or enforcing a FIFO queue. Exploitation requires a scenario with multiple concurrent challenges, a short remaining window (less than 30 minutes), and the ability to place a higher bid on the earlier challenge to trigger the time bump. When successful, the victim sees their expected reward disappear, the position’s collateral becomes zero, and any bid they placed is either returned or lost, violating the protocol’s economic assumptions that challenges are resolved in the order they were created. This bug is subtle because the time‑extension behaviour mimics familiar auction patterns (e.g., eBay) and only manifests under specific race‑condition timing, making it easy to overlook during testing. The issue belongs to the class of “challenge ordering and deadline manipulation” bugs, where state updates break the intended sequencing of operations. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a challenge queue that only permits the end function on a challenge after all earlier challenges have either succeeded or expired, or prohibit extending a challenge’s deadline beyond the expiration of any subsequently submitted challenge. Additionally, requiring a minimum bid increment (e.g., 0.5 %) can make the attack economically unattractive, but the primary fix is to preserve ordering rather than rely on cost deterrence.

title: Auctions fail to account for network and market conditions
description: Under certain extreme, but inevitable, network conditions, auctions will not be effective in covering the bad debt of a challenged position. Worse, certain position parameters under these conditions can lead to extremely small bids winning large amounts of collateral. More details follow in the next section, but it should be noted that this same design oversight was responsible for almost destroying Dai in March of 2020—the closest MakerDAO has ever been to utilizing its emergency shutdown module.
poc:
When the Ethereum network becomes highly congested, the price of gas can skyrocket to incredible levels. During times like these, users of the network will limit their activity to only the most urgent matters—in the case of March 12th, 2020, for example, the only people paying the exorbitant network fees were rushing to exit their positions as the price of ETH (and everything else) began to free fall.

On that day, MakerDAO’s collateral auctions were slipping by unnoticed, as the bots that would typically compete in the majority of these auctions saw failing transactions, hit cost limits defined by their owners, or were simply deactivated. An attacker noticed them, however, and began winning auctions on liquidated collateral with bids of zero ETH.

This exact vulnerability exists in the Frankencoin system, and it can be exploited under exactly the same circumstances. If a challenge only has a single bid when the challenge period ends, and that bid is near zero, the bid will still win the collateral regardless of how much it is actually worth.

At first glance, Frankencoin developers might be tempted to believe that the dynamic challenge period on its positions will allow for the system to rely primarily on auctions that can outlast abnormally volatile days. In practice, however, this is unlikely to be true, since “safe” positions will likely end up with very short challenge periods. This is unavoidable, because the vast majority of ZCHF will be backed by these types of collateral, and the system risks carrying untenable amounts of bad debt ever more the longer these challenge periods are extended. And extending these windows does not actually solve the problem anyways, since the bad debt cannot be covered until they end.

Consider, as well, that Frankencoin has a significant additional barrier to liquidating its positions when compared with MakerDAO: challenging requires collateral. I’ll actually discuss this piece of the challenge design in more detail in a separate report, but it bears mentioning that such a requirement will only make it less likely that positions will be challenged under extreme network and market conditions in the first place. If huge swaths of positions against a highly trusted collateral type all violate their liquidation prices concurrently, the amount of capital required to challenge all unsafe positions at once is unlikely to materialize quickly. This will lead to a severe loss of confidence in the ZCHF peg, as the system’s bad debt balloons, auctions clear for pennies on the dollar, and large, undercollateralized positions remain unchallenged. The peg likely could not withstand the ZCHF panic selling that would doubtlessly occur alongside this.

In fact, this vulnerability does not even require a malicious actor to make the protocol insolvent in market conditions such as these. Since a challenge with no bids will determine the collateral to be worthless, the protocol will fail to liquidate any collateral from some or all of its unsafe positions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an auction design flaw that allows a liquidation auction to close with a near‑zero winning bid, causing the protocol to receive far less value than the market price of the seized collateral. The root cause is that the auction starts at a price of zero and accepts the highest bid without enforcing a minimum price floor or a Dutch‑style decreasing price curve. Because the system relies on external bidding bots to compete, extreme network conditions such as very high gas fees or congestion can prevent those bots from submitting transactions, causing the challenge period to end with only a single, low‑value bid. When this happens, the protocol records the collateral as sold for the tiny bid amount, leaving the bad debt of the liquidated position largely uncovered. An attacker can deliberately wait for a congested block, submit a zero‑or‑near‑zero bid, and win the collateral, while honest participants are unable to outbid due to gas limits or cost caps. The impact is that the protocol may accumulate large amounts of bad debt, the peg of the stable token can break, and users may see their balances shrink unexpectedly or receive no compensation for liquidated positions. This scenario occurs when the network is under stress, market prices are falling rapidly, and the challenge period for a position is short, which is typical for “safe” positions that have limited time to be challenged. The affected parties include the protocol itself, token holders, sponsors, and any users whose positions are liquidated under these conditions. The issue was discovered by comparing the March 2020 MakerDAO emergency event, where bots failed to bid and zero‑price auctions were observed, with the Frankencoin implementation that exhibits the same logic. It is hard to notice because the auction completes successfully on‑chain, but the sale price is far below market value, and logs may not highlight the abnormal price. The recommended mitigation is to replace the current ascending‑from‑zero auction with a Dutch auction that starts above the liquidation price and gradually decreases, thereby guaranteeing a price floor and preventing near‑zero bids from winning. Additional safeguards such as enforcing a minimum bid amount or extending the challenge window can also reduce the risk. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “price‑floor‑missing auction” or “under‑bidding liquidation” vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions about collateral recovery and can lead to funds disappearing from the protocol’s balance sheet.

title: Can’t pause or remove a minter
description:
The project is supposed to be self-governing. Token owners are able to suggest new minters and collateral. The auction mechanism allows participants to remove collateral from the system if it’s deemed unhealthy. But, there’s no way to remove a registered minter.

Why would you want to remove a registered minter? Because they can have bugs that could break the whole system. The current minter, MintingHub, for example, implements a novel auction mechanism to price collateral instead of choosing the industry standard Chainlink oracles. While I support the idea of having a fully decentralized system, it does add additional risk to the project. A risk that’s taken not only by the protocol team but every ZCHF holder as well.

Obviously, these are just hypotheticals. But, the system is not equipped to handle a scenario where the minter malfunctions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is the inability of token holders or governance to pause or completely remove a registered minter once the initial proposal period has elapsed. The contract only permits a denial of a minter during a ten‑day window after the minter is suggested; after that, the denyMinter function reverts because the block timestamp exceeds the stored deadline, leaving the minter permanently active. This design flaw arises because the system does not include any revocation or emergency stop mechanism for minters, treating them as immutable once accepted. An attacker or a buggy minter can therefore continue to call its minting routine indefinitely, potentially issuing tokens at an uncontrolled rate, inflating the total supply, diluting existing holders, and breaking the accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on for collateral valuation and auction pricing. The exploit scenario is straightforward: a malicious or faulty minter is proposed, passes the ten‑day denial period, and then begins to mint tokens according to its own logic – for example using a non‑standard auction mechanism instead of a trusted price oracle. Because there is no pause or removal function, the protocol cannot halt the minting, and users may observe unexpected increases in total supply, reduced token value, or transactions that fail due to supply caps being exceeded. The impact is medium severity, affecting all ZCHF holders, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream applications that assume a bounded token supply. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewer examined the denyMinter implementation and noted that the timestamp check makes the function unusable after the deadline, effectively locking in the minter. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the minter may behave correctly initially, and the lack of a revocation path does not generate an explicit error; only when the minter misbehaves does the problem surface, often as subtle inflation rather than an outright failure. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a governance‑controlled pause flag and a removal function that can be invoked at any time, or require that every minter contract implements its own pause and volume limits that can be triggered by token holders. This aligns the system with standard upgradeability and emergency‑stop patterns, ensuring that a faulty or malicious minter can be safely disabled, preserving the integrity of the token supply and protecting holder assets.

title: Re-org attack in factory
description:
The `createClone` function deploys a clone contract using the create, where the address derivation depends only on the `PositionFactory` nonce.

Re-orgs can happen in all EVM chains. In ethereum, where currently Frankencoin is deployed, it is not “super common” but it still happens, being the last one less than a year ago:

<https://decrypt.co/101390/ethereum-beacon-chain-blockchain-re-org>

The issue increases the chances of happening because Frankencoin is thinking about deploying also in L2’s/rollups, proof:

<https://discord.com/channels/810916927919620096/1095308824354758696/1096693817450692658>

where re-orgs have been much more active:

<https://protos.com/polygon-hit-by-157-block-reorg-despite-hard-fork-to-reduce-reorgs/>

being the last one, less than a year ago.

The issue would happen when users rely on the address derivation in advance or try to deploy the position clone with the same address on different EVM chains, any funds sent to the new clone could potentially be withdrawn by anyone else. All in all, it could lead to the theft of user funds.

As you can see in a previous report, the issue should be marked and judged as a medium:

<https://code4rena.com/reports/2023-01-rabbithole/#m-01-questfactory-is-suspicious-of-the-reorg-attack>
poc: Imagine that Alice deploys a position clone, and then sends funds to it. Bob sees that the network block reorg happens and calls `clonePosition`. Thus, it creates a position clone with an address to which Alice sends funds. Then Alice’s transactions are executed and Alice transfers funds to Bob's position contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑org attack that stems from the factory contract deploying clone contracts with the CREATE opcode, where the resulting address is derived solely from the factory’s transaction nonce. Because the address depends on a mutable nonce, a chain reorganization that removes the original deployment can cause the same address to become available again. An attacker can then invoke the same createClone function after the reorg, obtain a contract at the previously expected address, and withdraw any funds that users have already sent to that address. This scenario unfolds when a user pre‑computes or relies on the clone address before the transaction achieving finality, sends funds to that address, and a subsequent block reorg discards the original deployment. The attacker, observing the reorg, calls createClone, recreates the contract at the identical address, and can then call any withdrawal functions to move the funds to themselves. The impact is the potential theft of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as balances that users believe are held by their position contract may suddenly become zero or be transferred to an unauthorized party. The issue is most relevant for deployments on L2s or roll‑ups where re‑orgs are more frequent, but it also exists on Ethereum where occasional re‑orgs have been observed. All parties that depend on deterministic address generation—users, the protocol’s position management logic, and any external services that reference the address—are affected. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit that referenced a similar issue in a previous report. It can be hard to notice because the address appears valid and the transaction to send funds succeeds; only after the reorg does the balance disappear, presenting as an unexplained zero balance or missing refund in the UI. To remediate, the factory should deploy clones using CREATE2 with a salt that incorporates unique data such as msg.sender and the target address, thereby making the address independent of the factory’s nonce and resistant to re‑org‑induced collisions. Additionally, users and integrators should wait for sufficient block confirmations before interacting with a newly created clone to ensure finality. This class of bug is a deterministic address generation flaw that enables address collision after a chain reorganization, violating the protocol’s expectation that a contract address remains immutable once created.

title: `notifyLoss` can be frontrun by redeem
description:
`notifyLoss` immediately transfer zchf from reserve to the minter, reducing the amount of reserve and hence the equity and zchf to claim per share.

While the deposit has 90 days cooldown before depositor can withdraw, current depositor that passed this cooldown can take advantage of a `notifyLoss` event by first frontrunning the `notifyLoss` by redeeming, then re-depositing into the protocol to take advantage of the reduced value per share.

`notifyLoss` can only be called by MintingHub::end, current depositor can bundle `redeem + end + deposit`, when they see a challenge that is ending in loss for the reserve.
bug_full: The contract exposes a function called "notifyLoss" that is intended to move a portion of the reserve to the minter when a challenge ends with a loss. The function is called by MintingHub::end and immediately reduces the total reserve, which in turn lowers the equity per share that each depositor can claim. Because the protocol allows a depositor who has already passed the 90‑day cooldown to redeem their shares at the current share price, an attacker can observe a pending loss, submit a transaction that redeems their full balance, then let the public call to "notifyLoss" execute, and finally deposit the redeemed amount back into the protocol. By performing redeem → end → deposit in a single block, the attacker captures the reduced share price for the newly deposited amount, effectively extracting value from the reserve while other users see their claim per share shrink. The vulnerability arises from the lack of ordering protection between the redemption step and the loss notification; the protocol does not lock the share price or prevent new deposits until the loss has been fully accounted for. Exploitation is possible whenever a challenge is about to be settled with a loss and there are eligible depositors who have completed the cooldown period. The impact is a reduction of the overall equity for honest participants, causing funds to disappear from the reserve and leading to lower payouts for all remaining shareholders. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the interaction between MintingHub::end, redeem and deposit functions. It can be difficult to notice because the individual functions appear correct in isolation and the loss accounting logic seems sound, yet the combination of calls in a single transaction creates a front‑running window. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a protected window for calling end, for example by allowing only a whitelisted bot to invoke the function before it becomes public, to amortise the loss over multiple periods instead of applying it instantly, or to implement a withdrawal queue that bases the final withdrawal price on pending equity changes. These approaches prevent an attacker from capturing the loss before it is distributed to all shareholders, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Use of `_mint` in `ReraiseETHCrowdfund#_contribute` is incompatible with `PartyGovernanceNFT#mint`
description: Misconfigured receiver could accidentally DOS party.
poc:
[ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol#L238](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol#L238)

```solidity
if (previousVotingPower == 0) _mint(contributor); <- @audit-issue standard minting here
```

[ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol#L374](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol#L374)

```solidity
uint256 tokenId = party.mint(contributor, votingPowerByCard[i], delegate); <- @audit-issue uses party.mint
```

[PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L162](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L162)

```solidity
_safeMint(owner, tokenId); <- @audit-issue PartyGovernanceNFT#mint utilizes _safeMint
```

The issue at hand is that ReraiseETHCrowdfund#_contribute and PartyGovernanceNFT#mint use inconsistent minting methods. PartyGovernanceNFT uses safeMint whereas ReraiseETHCrowdfund uses the standard mint. This is problematic because this means that a contract that doesn’t implement ERC721Receiver can receive a CrowdfundNFT but they can never claim because safeMint will always revert. This can cause a party to be inadvertently DOS’d because CrowdfundNFTs are soul bound and can’t be transferred.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the way ERC721 tokens are minted inside the ReraiseETHCrowdfund contract and the PartyGovernanceNFT contract. In the contribution function of ReraiseETHCrowdfund, the code calls the low‑level _mint function to create a new NFT for the contributor. Later, when the party attempts to issue the same NFT through PartyGovernanceNFT.mint, the implementation uses _safeMint, which performs the ERC721Receiver check and reverts if the recipient does not implement the required interface. Because _mint does not perform this safety check, a contributor that is a smart contract without ERC721Receiver support can still receive the token at contribution time. However, when the party later tries to claim or interact with the NFT using the safe‑mint path, the transaction reverts, preventing the NFT from being transferred or claimed. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the party’s governance token becomes effectively soul‑bound to an address that cannot hold it, blocking further governance actions and potentially locking the funds raised. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the minting calls and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the initial mint succeeds and no error is emitted; the failure only appears later when a claim is attempted, making the symptom appear as a missing or zero balance from the user’s perspective. Users expect to receive a usable NFT after contributing, but instead they may see no token appear in their wallet or a claim transaction that always fails. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe ERC721 minting patterns where the contract does not enforce receiver compatibility, violating the accounting assumption that every minted token can be transferred or claimed. To remediate, the contribution function should use _safeMint consistently, or the protocol should allow the contributor to specify an alternative receiver address that implements ERC721Receiver, thereby ensuring that every minted NFT can be safely transferred and claimed.

title: `MaxContribution` check can be bypassed to give a card high voting power
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the enforcement of a per‑card voting‑power ceiling in the ReraiseETHCrowdfund contract. The contract is designed to limit the voting power attached to each PartyGovernanceNFT by checking that the contribution equivalent of the requested voting power falls between a configurable minimum and maximum (minContribution and maxContribution) inside the claim and claimMultiple functions. This check is intended to ensure a “one card = one vote” style governance where each card cannot exceed a predefined amount of voting power. However, after a card is minted, the contract contains a separate code path that allows the owner of the card to increase its voting power directly via party.addVotingPower when party.ownerOf(tokenId) equals the caller. This path does not repeat the maxContribution verification, so an attacker can bypass the original limit. By contributing the maximum allowed amount from two separate contributor addresses that they control, claiming a card with the first address, transferring the PartyGovernanceNFT to the second address (the NFT is transferable while the crowdfund NFT is not), and then invoking claim again, the attacker can add the second contribution’s voting power to the same card, effectively doubling the voting power beyond the intended cap. The flaw arises because the contract only validates the contribution size at the moment of minting and does not enforce a cumulative voting‑power bound on the card after transfers or subsequent additions. It is exploitable whenever the partyGovernanceNFT is transferable and the flag disabling contributions to existing cards is not set. The impact is that a malicious participant can acquire disproportionate voting influence, potentially steering governance decisions in their favor and undermining the protocol’s security assumptions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the claim logic and identified the missing check in the addVotingPower branch. It can be difficult to notice because the maxContribution guard appears to be present in the claim functions, giving a false sense of safety, while the later ownership‑based branch silently skips the same validation. To remediate, the contract should enforce the maximum voting‑power constraint at the PartyGovernanceNFT level before any increase, either by checking the card’s total voting power in addVotingPower, disabling contributions to existing cards, making the governance NFT non‑transferable, or redesigning the claim flow to mint a fresh card per contribution and ensure the transferred voting power never exceeds the configured limits.

title: Contributions can be smaller than `minContribution` and may receive no voting power
description: Valid contribution is awarded no voting power.
bug_full: The contract implements a crowdfunding mechanism where each contribution must be at least a configured `minContribution` and no more than a `maxContribution`. When the cumulative contributions approach the overall `maxTotalContributions` limit, the code reduces the incoming amount so that the total does not exceed the cap, then refunds the excess. The vulnerability stems from the fact that the check against `minContribution` is performed **before** this reduction. Consequently, a contributor can send an amount that initially satisfies the minimum, but after the excess is subtracted the effective contribution becomes smaller than `minContribution`. Because the contract does not re‑validate the reduced amount, the contribution is accepted even though it violates the minimum‑contribution rule. In practice this edge case occurs only when the contribution would push the crowdfund over its hard cap, i.e., when `totalContributions + amount >= maxTotalContributions`. The attacker (or any user) can deliberately craft a contribution that exceeds the cap by a tiny margin, causing the post‑refund amount to fall below the minimum threshold. The contract then calculates voting power based on the final contribution amount; if the reduced amount is less than the exchange‑rate denominator (`exchangeRateBps`), the resulting voting power can be zero. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful contribution transaction, but the user receives no voting power, may be unable to claim a party card, and sees a refunded amount that does not match the original intent. This violates the economic assumptions of the protocol, where every contribution above the minimum is expected to grant proportional voting rights. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contribution handling logic and noticed that `amount` is decreased after the minimum‑contribution revert, as highlighted by the audit comment. The bug is subtle because it only manifests in a narrow state‑space (near the funding cap) and the refund path is rarely exercised in normal operation, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce the `minContribution` rule **after** any reduction of the contribution amount, or alternatively reject contributions that would become smaller than the minimum after the overflow adjustment. Additionally, a sanity check that the computed voting power is non‑zero before finalizing the contribution would prevent users from ending up with a contribution that yields no governance weight.

title: `ReraiseETHCrowdfund#claimMultiple` can be used to grief large depositors
description: User can be grieved by being force minted a large number of NFTs with low voting power instead of one with high voting power.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claimMultiple function of the ReraiseETHCrowdfund contract. The function is publicly callable and accepts an arbitrary votingPowerByCard array that determines how a contributor’s total voting power is split into individual NFTs. Because the implementation does not verify that the caller is the contributor nor enforce a minimal number of NFTs, any external user can invoke claimMultiple on behalf of another address and supply a deliberately fragmented array. This allows an attacker to break a large contributor’s voting power into a very high number of low‑voting NFTs. The root cause is the lack of validation on the caller’s authority and on the length or composition of the votingPowerByCard array, which the contract trusts blindly. An exploit proceeds by the attacker calling claimMultiple for a target contributor, passing an array that divides the target’s voting power into many small pieces (for example, 100 NFTs of 1 vote each instead of a single NFT of 100 votes). The contract then iterates over the array, minting a separate NFT for each entry, which dramatically inflates gas consumption and can cause the transaction to run out of gas or become prohibitively expensive. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a single NFT representing the full voting power – is replaced by a flood of tiny NFTs, leading to unexpected high gas fees, possible transaction failure, and a degraded governance experience. The issue is triggered whenever claimMultiple is used with a low minContribution and a high maxContribution, conditions that permit many small contributions to be represented as separate NFTs. All contributors, especially large ones, are affected because their voting power can be fragmented without consent, undermining the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each NFT’s voting power reflects a meaningful share of the total. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the loop in claimMultiple and noticed that the votingPowerByCard array is supplied by the caller without any checks. The flaw is subtle because the function is intended to enable third‑party claims for convenience, so the lack of restriction may not be obvious at first glance. To remediate, the contract should either restrict claimMultiple to the contributor themselves, enforce that the array length matches the minimal number of NFTs required by the maxContribution limit, or, preferably, compute the allocation of voting power internally rather than trusting external input. Refactoring the claim logic to mint NFTs per contribution and to perform a 1:1 conversion of a crowdfund NFT into a party card would also eliminate the ability to arbitrarily split voting power, thereby fixing the underlying class of fragmentation and gas‑griefing bug.

title: Possible DOS attack using dust in `ReraiseETHCrowdfund._contribute`
description: Normal contributors wouldn’t contribute to the crowdfund properly by a malicious frontrunner.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises in the ReraiseETHCrowdfund contract when the function that processes contributions mints a crowdfund NFT solely based on the contributor’s previous voting power being zero. The root cause is that the minting guard does not verify whether the new contribution actually yields a positive amount of voting power; if the exchange rate is low enough, a tiny contribution (dust) can produce zero voting power even though ether was transferred. Because the pendingVotingPower remains zero after the first dust contribution, the contract still believes the contributor has never received a meaningful contribution and attempts to mint the NFT again on the next legitimate contribution. The second mint attempt triggers the AlreadyMintedError and reverts the transaction, preventing any further contributions from that address. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running an honest user’s transaction, sending a minimal amount of wei that converts to zero voting power, thereby forcing the NFT to be minted with no voting rights. When the honest user later tries to contribute a substantial amount, the contract reverts, effectively locking the user out of the crowdfund. The impact is that legitimate contributors are unable to add funds, the funding round may fail to reach its target, and users see an NFT in their balance but with no associated voting power, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The condition occurs whenever the exchangeRateBps is set such that the smallest unit of contribution yields zero voting power, which is common when the rate is 5 000 basis points (0.5 %). The affected parties include any contributor to the crowdfund, the protocol’s governance mechanism that relies on voting power, and the overall health of the fundraising campaign. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a fuzz test reproducing the dust front‑run scenario. It can be hard to notice because a zero‑voting‑power contribution does not immediately break the contract; the problem only surfaces on a subsequent contribution when the mint guard fires again. The proper mitigation is to only mint the NFT when the resulting voting power after the contribution is positive, or to reject contributions that would result in zero voting power, thereby preventing duplicate mint attempts and the associated revert. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper state‑based access control where minting logic relies on stale or insufficient conditions, leading to unintended re‑entrancy of minting and denial‑of‑service attacks.

title: `PartyGovernanceNFT.sol`: burn function does not reduce `totalVotingPower` making it impossible to reach unanimous votes
description:
With the new version of the Party protocol the [`PartyGovernanceNFT.burn`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L201-L224) function has been introduced.

This function is used to burn party cards.

According to the sponsor the initial purpose of this function was to enable the [`InitialETHCrowdfund`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/InitialETHCrowdfund.sol) contract (the `burn` function is needed for refunds).

Later on they decided to allow any user to call this function and to burn their party cards.

The second use case when a regular user burns his party card is when the issue occurs.

The `PartyGovernanceNFT.burn` function does not decrease `totalVotingPower` which makes it impossible to reach an unanimous vote after a call to this function and it makes remaining votes of existing users less valuable than they should be.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance NFT contract where the burn function removes a holder’s token and its associated voting power but fails to adjust the global totalVotingPower counter. The root cause is that the implementation only updates mintedVotingPower and the owner’s individual voting balance, while deliberately leaving totalVotingPower unchanged for the special case of the InitialETHCrowdfund refund path. However, the same code path is also reachable by any regular user after the governance phase has started, because the only guard is a check that totalVotingPower is non‑zero or the caller is an authority. When a regular participant burns their NFT, the contract’s accounting still reports the original total voting supply, even though the actual supply has shrunk. An attacker can simply call burn on their own token, reducing the effective voting mass without any on‑chain warning. The immediate impact is that the percentage of votes required for a unanimous decision is calculated against a stale total, making it mathematically impossible for the remaining voters to ever reach 100 % agreement. For example, with three equal voters (300 total votes) if one burns half of their power, the real supply drops to 250 but the contract still uses 300, so the maximum achievable unanimity is 83 %. From a user’s perspective the UI may still display a “unanimous” requirement, yet even when every active member votes “yes” the proposal is rejected, leading to confusion such as “my vote seems to count less than before” or “the proposal can never pass”. This breaks the business logic that assumes totalVotingPower accurately reflects the sum of all active voting rights, undermining governance integrity and potentially freezing protocol upgrades or fund releases that depend on unanimous consent. The issue was uncovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that after burning a token the totalVotingPower value remained unchanged and the _isUnanimousVotes check could never succeed. The bug is subtle because burning tokens is an expected operation and the contract does correctly adjust individual balances, so the discrepancy is not obvious without inspecting the global counter. The proper remediation is to decrement totalVotingPower by the burned token’s votingPower for non‑authority calls (i.e., regular users) while preserving the current behaviour for the InitialETHCrowdfund path, typically by adding a conditional update after the token is burned. This restores the invariant that totalVotingPower always equals the sum of all active votingPower values, allowing unanimous votes to be reachable again.
