title: `totalVotingPower` needs to be snapshotted for each proposal because it can change and thereby affect consensus when accepting / vetoing proposals
description:
This issue does not manifest itself in a limited segment of the code.

Instead it spans multiple contracts and derives its impact from the interaction of these contracts.

In the PoC section I will do my best in explaining how this results in an issue.

I discussed this with the sponsor and they explained to me that this issue is due to a PR that has unintentionally not been merged.

![Discord message](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/118979828/231990051-b9f731f1-1678-43e3-81e4-7ec0164bdc10.png)

So they have already written the code that is necessary to fix this issue. It’s just not been merged with this branch. So since the sponsor knows about this already and it’s just the PR that has gone missing it’s not necessary for me to provide the full Solidity code to fix this issue.

In short, this issue is due to the fact that the `totalVotingPower` is not snapshotted when a proposal is created.

The votes that are used to vote for a proposal (or veto it) are based on a specific snapshot (1 block prior to the proposal being created).

When the `totalVotingPower` changes this leads to unintended consequences.

When `totalVotingPower` decreases, votes become more valuable than they should be.

And when `totalVotingPower` increases, votes become less valuable than they should be.
poc:
When a proposal is created via the [`PartyGovernance.propose`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L527-L548) function, the proposal’s `proposedTime` is set:

[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L537-L543)
    
    ProposalStateValues({
        proposedTime: uint40(block.timestamp),
        passedTime: 0,
        executedTime: 0,
        completedTime: 0,
        votes: 0
    }),

When users then vote in order to accept the proposal or veto the proposal, their votes are based on the snapshot at the `proposedTime - 1` timestamp.

We can see this in the `PartyGovernance.accept` function:

[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L592)
    
    uint96 votingPower = getVotingPowerAt(msg.sender, values.proposedTime - 1, snapIndex);

And we can see it in the `VetoProposal.voteToVeto` function:

[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L37-L41)
    
    uint96 votingPower = party.getVotingPowerAt(
        msg.sender,
        proposalValues.proposedTime - 1,
        snapIndex
    );

However the `totalVotingPower` to determine whether enough votes have been collected is the current `totalVotingPower`:

[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L598-L605)
    
    if (
        values.passedTime == 0 &&
        _areVotesPassing(
            values.votes,
            _governanceValues.totalVotingPower,
            _governanceValues.passThresholdBps
        )
    ) {

[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L46-L51)
    
    if (
        _areVotesPassing(
            newVotes,
            governanceValues.totalVotingPower,
            governanceValues.passThresholdBps
        )
    )

The `totalVotingPower` is not constant. It can increase and decrease.

Now we can understand the issue. The `totalVotingPower` must be based on the same time as the votes (i.e. `proposedTime - 1`).

Let’s look at a scenario:
    
    At the time of proposal creation (proposedTime - 1):
    
    Alice: 100 Votes
    Bob: 50 Votes
    Chris: 50 Votes
    
    totalVotingPower=200

Let’s say 80% of votes are necessary for the proposal to pass.

Now the `totalVotingPower` is increased (e.g. by a `ReraiseETHCrowdfund`) since David now has 100 Votes:
    
    Alice: 100 Votes
    Bob: 50 Votes
    Chris: 50 Votes
    David: 100 Votes 
    
    totalVotingPower=300

Now it is impossible for the proposal to pass.

The proposal needs 80% of 300 Votes which is 240 Votes. But the votes are used from the old snapshot and there were only 200 Votes.

The old `totalVotingPower` should have been used (200 Votes instead of 300 Votes).

Similarly there is an issue when `totalVotingPower` decreases:
    
    Alice: 100 Votes
    Bob: 50 Votes
    Chris: 0 Votes
    
    totalVotingPower=150

If 60% of the votes are necessary for the proposal to pass, Alice can make the proposal pass on her own because `totalVotingPower=150` is used even though the old `totalVotingPower=200` should be used.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent state inconsistency in the governance module where the aggregate voting power (totalVotingPower) used to decide whether a proposal has reached its acceptance or veto threshold is taken from the live contract state instead of the snapshot that was taken when the proposal was created. The root cause is that the contract records each voter’s voting power at block N‑1 (the snapshot moment) but continues to read the global totalVotingPower at the current block when evaluating the quorum. Because totalVotingPower can change after a proposal is opened – for example when new tokens are minted, a crowdfund raises additional ETH, or tokens are burned – the quorum calculation can become either too high or too low. An attacker who can increase the total voting power after a proposal is opened can make the required quorum unattainable, effectively dead‑locking the proposal, while an attacker who can decrease the total voting power can allow a proposal to pass with far fewer votes than intended. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are proposals that never reach the “passed” state despite receiving the expected amount of votes, or proposals that pass instantly with a single large holder’s vote, contradicting the expectation that a certain percentage of the total voting power is required. The impact is a broken governance process: decisions may be blocked or hijacked, leading to loss of protocol control, potential fund misallocation, and erosion of trust among participants. The issue manifests whenever the total voting power is mutable between proposal creation and the voting period – i.e., any token mint, burn, or transfer that changes the aggregate supply. It affects all participants who rely on the governance mechanism, including token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol itself. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit of the governance contracts when the reviewer noticed that the function _areVotesPassing compared the vote tally against _governanceValues.totalVotingPower, which is not frozen at proposal time. The bug is subtle because the per‑voter snapshot appears correct, so the discrepancy is not obvious from simple vote counts; only a careful inspection of the quorum calculation reveals the mismatch. The correct mitigation is to snapshot the totalVotingPower at the same block used for individual voting power (proposedTime‑1) and store that value with the proposal, then use the stored snapshot for all quorum checks. This belongs to the broader class of snapshot‑related governance bugs where state used for decision making is not consistently frozen, leading to logical errors in consensus thresholds.

title: `ETHCrowdfundBase.sol`: All funds are lost when fee recipient cannot receive ETH
description:
In the [`ETHCrowdfundBase`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol) contract a [`fundingSplitRecipient`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L142) address is configured which receives a percentage of the funds in case the crowdfund is won.

Neither the `fundingSplitRecipient` address nor the `fundingSplitBps` percentage can be changed.

The issue is that the `_finalize` function can only succeed when the fees can be transferred to the recipient.

However the recipient contract may revert when it receives ETH. This causes all ETH in the `ETHCrowdfundBase` contract to be stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑transfer lockup that occurs when the ETHCrowdfundBase contract attempts to pay a configured fundingSplitRecipient during the finalisation of a successful crowdfund. The contract stores a fixed recipient address and a fixed basis‑point percentage that represent the protocol fee. In the internal _finalize function the fee amount is calculated, the contract calls fundingSplitRecipient_.transferEth(feeAmount) and only after that transfers the remaining ETH to the party. Because the call uses a plain transfer that propagates any revert, if the recipient contract rejects the incoming ETH – for example by having a fallback function that reverts or by being a non‑payable address – the whole _finalize transaction reverts. As a result the crowdfund remains in the Won state, the finalize call cannot succeed, and all ETH that was collected stays locked inside the contract forever. Users who contributed expect their funds to be transferred to the party and to receive voting power, but instead they see no change in their balances, no voting power, and the UI reports a failed transaction. The impact is that contributors lose access to their funds and the protocol cannot distribute the intended fee, effectively breaking the accounting assumptions of the crowdfund. The issue is triggered only when the crowdfund is won and the finalize function is called while the fee recipient is unable to receive ETH. It was discovered during a security audit that examined edge cases where external calls could fail. The problem is hard to notice because the transfer is performed with a standard call and the contract does not check for or handle a failure, so the revert simply bubbles up and appears as a generic transaction failure. To remediate the bug the fee payment should be decoupled from the finalisation logic, for example by moving the fee transfer to a separate pull‑based function that can be retried, by using a try/catch block to ignore a failing fee transfer, or by sending the fee to the party if the recipient fails. In any case the contract must ensure that a failure to pay the fee does not prevent the remaining ETH from being released, thereby preserving contributors’ funds and the intended voting power distribution.

title: `InitialETHCrowdfund` + `ReraiseETHCrowdfund`: Gatekeeper checks wrong address
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect access‑control check in the contribution functions of the InitialETHCrowdfund and ReraiseETHCrowdfund contracts. Both contracts call a gatekeeper contract to decide whether a contribution is allowed, but they pass the address stored in the local variable "contributor" to the gatekeeper’s isAllowed function instead of the transaction sender (msg.sender). The gatekeeper is designed to restrict which external accounts may initiate a contribution; it expects the caller’s address so that only whitelisted participants can fund the campaign. Because the contract checks the beneficiary address rather than the caller, any address can submit a contribution on behalf of a whitelisted contributor, effectively bypassing the whitelist. An attacker can therefore trigger a contribution from an unauthorized account, causing the campaign to accept funds that should have been rejected. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that contributions appear to be accepted from accounts that are not on the whitelist, or that a user can contribute for a whitelisted address without being authorized, leading to unexpected balances and potential accounting mismatches. The bug manifests whenever the gatekeeper is configured (i.e., not the zero address) and the contribute function is executed; the faulty check is performed inside the internal contribution logic before the funds are recorded. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the code path that invokes gatekeeper.isAllowed was examined and the argument mismatch was identified. It can be hard to notice because the contribution transaction itself succeeds and the only failure would be a revert from the gatekeeper, which does not occur under the buggy logic; therefore the contract behaves as if the whitelist were ineffective. The proper fix is to replace the "contributor" argument with "msg.sender" in the call to isAllowed and to adjust the revert parameters accordingly, ensuring that the gatekeeper validates the actual caller of the contribution. This correction restores the intended security property that only authorized participants may initiate contributions, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and preventing unauthorized fund inflows.

title: `OperatorProposal.sol`: Leftover ETH is not refunded to the `msg.sender`
description:
The [`OperatorProposal`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/OperatorProposal.sol#L7-L63) contract is a type of proposal that allows to execute operations on contracts that implement the [`IOperator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/operators/IOperator.sol) interface.

Upon execution of the proposal it might be necessary that the `executor` provides ETH.

This is true especially when `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=false`, i.e. when ETH cannot be spent from the Party’s balance. So it must be provided by the `executor`.

The amount of ETH that is needed to execute the operation is sent to the operator contract:
[Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/OperatorProposal.sol#L45)
```solidity
data.operator.execute{ value: data.operatorValue }(data.operatorData, executionData);
```

The operator contract then spends whatever amount of ETH is actually necessary and returns the remaining ETH.

For example the [`CollectionBatchBuyOperator`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/operators/CollectionBatchBuyOperator.sol#L14-L224) contract may not spend all of the ETH because the actual purchases that are made are not necessarily known at the time the proposal is created. Also not all purchases may succeed.

So it is clear that some of the ETH may be returned from the `operator` to the `OperatorProposal` contract.

The issue is that the remaining ETH is not refunded to the `executor` and therefore this results in a direct loss of funds for the `executor`.

I discussed this issue with the sponsor and it is clear that the remaining ETH needs to be refunded when `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=false`.

However it is not clear what to do when `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=true`. In this case ETH can be spent from the party’s balance. So there should be limited use cases for the `executor` providing additional ETH.

But if the `executor` provides additional ETH what should happen?

Should the ETH be taken from the `executor` first? Or should it be taken from the Party balance first?

The sponsor mentioned that since there are limited use cases for the `executor` providing additional ETH it may be ok to not refund ETH at all.

I disagree with this. Even when `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=true` there should be a policy for refunds. I.e. the necessary ETH should either be taken from the Party’s balance or from the `executor` first and any remaining funds from the `executor` should be returned.

However since it is not clear how to proceed in this case and since it is less important compared to the case where `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=false` I will only make a suggestion for the case where `allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth=false`.

The sponsor should decide what to do in the other case and make the appropriate changes.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing refund of leftover native ether after an OperatorProposal is executed. When a proposal is submitted with allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth set to false, the executor must provide the exact amount of ether required for the operator call via the operatorValue field. The operator contract (for example CollectionBatchBuyOperator) may spend only a portion of the supplied ether and deliberately returns the unused portion to the calling OperatorProposal contract. However, the OperatorProposal contract does not forward this returned ether back to the original executor (msg.sender). As a result, the executor’s transaction appears to succeed, but a portion of the ether they supplied is permanently retained by the Party contract, effectively disappearing from the executor’s balance. This occurs because the proposal code only records the party’s balance before the call and, after execution, returns an empty string without any transfer of the surplus ether. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of funds between the executor, the operator, and the proposal contract and noticed that the operator’s refund logic was never mirrored in the proposal. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an event or revert; the transaction completes normally, making the loss of funds easy to overlook unless the executor checks their post‑execution balance. The impact is a direct monetary loss for any executor who supplies more ether than the operator ultimately uses, violating the expectation that any unused ether will be returned. The affected parties are the executor (who may be a user or a bot) and, indirectly, any protocol participants who rely on accurate accounting of proposal costs. The root cause is an incomplete handling of the operator’s returned ether – the proposal contract assumes no leftover funds or that the party’s balance will cover the cost, which is not true when allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth is false. To remediate, the proposal should calculate the surplus after the operator call and explicitly transfer that surplus back to the executor, or define a clear policy for how surplus ether is sourced and refunded when allowOperatorsToSpendPartyEth is true. This class of bug falls under “missing refund / improper handling of returned value” and can lead to money disappearing from the caller’s wallet, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: `CollectionBatchBuyOperator.sol`: `tokenIds` array is not shortened properly which makes execute function revert when not all NFTs are purchased successfully
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect shortening of the tokenIds dynamic array in the CollectionBatchBuyOperator contract. The execute function iterates over tokenIds to transfer purchased NFTs after attempting batch purchases. When a purchase fails, the contract skips the failed call but does not correctly reduce the length of tokenIds, leaving trailing entries that contain the default value 0. The code attempts to adjust the length using assembly: mstore(mload(ex), tokensBought). However mload(ex) loads a pointer to the first field of the execution data struct, not the storage location of the tokenIds array, so the length field of tokenIds remains unchanged. Consequently the subsequent loop calls safeTransferFrom with tokenId 0, which either reverts or transfers an unintended token, causing the whole execute transaction to revert. This occurs only when at least one NFT purchase in the batch fails, i.e., when the market price changes or the seller rejects the offer. The affected parties are the executor of the proposal and any user expecting the batch purchase to succeed; they see the transaction fail and receive no NFTs despite some purchases having succeeded. The issue was discovered during a security audit where the test suite incorrectly passed, masking the bug. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit errors for the zero tokenId and the revert happens deep in the transfer loop. The bug belongs to the class of array‑length mismanagement or memory‑corruption bugs caused by misuse of low‑level assembly to modify dynamic arrays. The proper fix is to write the new length directly to the tokenIds array slot (mstore(tokenIds, tokensBought)) or to use high‑level Solidity array slicing. Fixing the length ensures that only actually purchased token IDs are transferred, allowing the execute function to succeed even when some purchases fail, preserving funds and expected behavior.

title: `VetoProposal`: proposals cannot be vetoed in all states in which it should be possible to veto proposals
description:
The [`VetoProposal`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L8-L69) contract allows to veto proposals with the [`voteToVeto`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L19-L60) function.

The proposal can only be vetoed when it is in the `Voting` state, otherwise the `voteToVeto` function reverts.

The issue is that the `Voting` state is not the only state in which it should be possible to veto the proposal. It should also be possible to veto the proposal in the `Passed` and `Ready` states.

(We can see this by looking at the downstream [`PartyGovernance.veto`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L617-L637) function)

It has been confirmed to me by the sponsor that the `voteToVeto` function should not restrict the situations in which vetos can occur.

The impact of this issue is that the situations in which vetos can occur is more limited than it should be. Users should have the ability to veto proposals even in the `Passed` and `Ready` states but they don’t.
bug_full: The VetoProposal contract implements a wrapper function voteToVeto that is intended to forward a veto request to the PartyGovernance contract. The wrapper checks the current proposal status and only permits the call when the status equals Voting. Business rules and the downstream PartyGovernance.veto implementation, however, allow a veto not only during the Voting phase but also after a proposal has been marked as Passed or Ready, i.e., before execution. The root cause is an overly restrictive state validation: the wrapper compares the proposal status against a single enum value instead of the three allowed values, causing a mismatch between the wrapper and the core governance logic. An attacker or any legitimate participant who tries to veto a proposal that has already passed or is ready will trigger the revert ProposalNotActiveError, meaning the veto request is silently rejected. This limitation reduces the set of situations in which a veto can be exercised, breaking the protocol’s expectation that stakeholders retain the right to cancel a proposal up until execution. From a user perspective the transaction fails or appears to succeed without effect, leading to confusion such as “my veto did nothing” or “the contract rejected my veto”. The impact is that proposals that should be cancelable remain executable, potentially resulting in unwanted state changes or fund transfers that participants cannot stop. The issue manifests whenever a proposal transitions from Voting to Passed or Ready and a user calls voteToVeto; it affects all participants who rely on veto rights, including proposal creators, voters, and token holders. The problem was discovered during a security audit by comparing the state checks in VetoProposal.voteToVeto with those in PartyGovernance.veto and noticing the inconsistency. It can be hard to notice because the wrapper appears to delegate the core logic, leading developers to assume the same state constraints apply. The appropriate remediation is to broaden the status check to include Passed and Ready, or to remove the check entirely and let PartyGovernance enforce the correct constraints. Conceptually this is a state‑validation bug that results in improper access control based on proposal lifecycle, violating the governance model that veto should be possible until execution.

title: Rewards for initial period may be lost in `BathBuddy` contract
bug_full: The BathBuddy contract allows the owner to start a reward cycle by calling notifyRewardAmount, which records a start timestamp, a finish timestamp and a per‑second reward rate. The implementation assumes that at the moment the reward period begins there is at least one holder of the BathToken, because the earned reward for each participant is calculated as rewardRate multiplied by the time elapsed divided by the total supply of BathTokens. If the total supply is zero when the period starts, the division yields zero distribution and the contract never records any claimable balance for that interval. Consequently, any reward tokens that accrue during the initial period are effectively locked in the contract because no participant can call getReward to claim them. The bug is triggered when the owner initiates the reward cycle before any BathToken has been minted or transferred to a user, and then a participant joins only after some time has passed. In the proof‑of‑concept test, the owner starts a 10 000‑second reward period, waits half of the duration, mints BathTokens to Alice, and after the full period Alice can claim only half of the promised reward; the remaining half stays in the BathBuddy balance. From a user’s point of view the expectation is to receive the full reward amount, but the actual outcome is a missing portion of tokens and a residual balance that appears “stuck” in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the reward lifecycle and observed the leftover balance. It is hard to notice because the contract emits the correct RewardAdded event, the rewardRate looks reasonable, and the leftover tokens are not transferred out, so the contract state appears normal. The vulnerability belongs to the class of reward‑distribution edge‑cases where the accounting logic does not handle a zero‑participant set, leading to unclaimed reward accumulation. The impact is financial: users receive less than advertised rewards and the protocol loses incentive value, which may erode trust. The affected parties are token holders, the protocol’s incentive mechanism, and any downstream contracts that rely on the full distribution of rewards. A proper fix is to defer the start of the reward period until the first participant stakes (i.e., when total supply becomes greater than zero) or to adjust the accounting so that rewards accrued while the supply is zero are either redistributed later or refunded to the owner. This eliminates the initial‑period loss and aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that every rewarded token should be claimable by a participant.

title: `BathBuddy` contract should implement methods to pause and unpause contract
bug_full: The contract inherits the OpenZeppelin Pausable module but never provides any external function that can change the paused state, leaving the internal _pause and _unpause methods unreachable after deployment. The getReward function is guarded by the whenNotPaused modifier, which assumes that an authorized party can pause the contract in an emergency. Because no public pause or unpause function exists, the paused flag can never be set, meaning the whenNotPaused check always passes and reward claims continue unabated. This design omission creates a missing access‑controlled pause mechanism: the protocol administrators cannot halt reward distribution even if a vulnerability is discovered, allowing an attacker to keep calling getReward and potentially drain token balances. The impact is that funds may continue to be transferred out despite expectations that the contract can be frozen, breaking the intended emergency‑stop business logic and exposing users and the protocol to financial loss. The condition occurs at any time after deployment, as the internal pause functions are never exposed. Affected parties include the protocol owners who lose the ability to protect the system, token holders who expect rewards to be stoppable, and the overall ecosystem that relies on the pause safety net. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the inherited Pausable contract with the derived contract’s public interface and noticed the absence of pause/unpause functions. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the presence of the Pausable base gives a false impression of a functional emergency stop. The recommended remediation is to add public pause and unpause functions protected by an onlyOwner (or appropriate admin) modifier that invoke the internal _pause and _unpause methods, thereby restoring the intended ability to freeze contract operations. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an incomplete Pausable implementation or missing access‑controlled pause mechanism, and it violates the business assumption that the protocol can be halted to safeguard assets, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as rewards being paid out when they should be frozen and balances decreasing unexpectedly.

title: No deadline parameter in `sellAllAmount`
description: There is no deadline parameter in these two functions. This missing feature enables pending transactions to be maliciously executed at a later point.
poc:
Consider following scenario:

1. Alice wants to create order of 1000DAI for 1 ETH. She signs the transaction with `minOutputAmount = 0.99 ETH` to allow for some slippage.
2. The transaction is submitted to the mempool; however, Alice chose a transaction fee that is too low for miners to be interested in including her transaction in a block. The transaction stays pending in the mempool for extended periods, which could be hours, days, weeks, or even longer.
3. The average gas fee dropped far enough for Alice’s transaction to become interesting again for miners to include it. In the meantime, the price of ETH could have drastically changed. She will still at least get 0.99 ETH due to `minOutputAmount`, but the DAI value of that output might be significantly lower. She has unknowingly performed a bad trade due to the pending transaction she forgot about.

An even worse way this issue can be maliciously exploited is through MEV:

1. The swap transaction is still pending in the mempool. Average fees are still too high for miners to be interested in it. The price of `___` has gone up significantly since the transaction was signed (lets say its not dai now and some other token), meaning Alice would receive a lot more ETH when the swap is executed. But that also means that her `minOutputAmount` value is outdated and would allow for significant slippage.
2. A MEV bot detects the pending transaction. Since the outdated `minOutputAmount` now allows for high slippage, the bot sandwiches Alice, resulting in significant profit for the bot and significant loss for Alice.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a deadline parameter in the sellAllAmount functions of the automated market maker contract. Because the function does not record an expiration time, a transaction that is signed and broadcast can remain in the mempool indefinitely if the attached gas fee is too low or network congestion is high. When the transaction finally becomes attractive to miners, the market price of the traded assets may have moved substantially. The contract only checks that the output amount is above a user‑provided minOutputAmount, which was calculated at the time of signing. Consequently, the transaction can be executed at a price that is far worse for the user, resulting in a trade that yields far less value than expected, or in the worst case, a loss caused by a front‑running or sandwich attack performed by a MEV bot that exploits the outdated slippage tolerance. The impact is that users may receive far fewer tokens than anticipated, see their balances shrink unexpectedly, or experience a trade that appears to have been executed at an unfair rate. The issue manifests whenever a transaction is pending for an extended period, which can happen on L2 networks with variable gas pricing, during airdrop spikes, or when users deliberately set low fees. All participants who rely on the AMM – individual traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the economic guarantees of the swap are broken. The problem was identified during a formal audit that examined the function signatures and noticed the missing deadline field, a common safeguard in AMM designs to prevent delayed execution. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the function succeeds and returns a valid amount; the loss only becomes apparent after the price shift, which may be attributed to market volatility rather than a contract flaw. The recommended remediation is to introduce a deadline argument that is compared against the block timestamp at execution, rejecting any transaction whose deadline has passed, thereby restoring the intended time‑sensitivity of the trade and preventing malicious re‑ordering or unintended slippage. This class of bug is a time‑bound execution flaw, where the lack of an expiration check allows pending transactions to be replayed under changed market conditions, violating the business logic that a trade should be executed at roughly the price expected at signing time.

title: Fee inclusivity calculations are inaccurate in `RubiconMarket`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑inclusivity logic of the RubiconMarket contract. When a taker calls the buy function with a desired amount that is supposed to include both the protocol fee and the maker fee, the contract first reduces the supplied amount by the two fees using a simple subtraction (calcAmountAfterFee). The reduced amount is then used again to calculate the actual fees that will be transferred. Because the fees are subtracted twice – once before the trade and once after – the final sum of trade amount plus fees is lower than the original amount the user intended to spend. This arithmetic error originates from an incorrect algebraic formulation: the function treats the fee‑inclusive amount as amount‑fee rather than solving for the pre‑fee amount that satisfies amount = trade + fees. The bug can be exploited by any user who relies on fee‑inclusivity, for example a taker who specifies a total spend of 1,000 tokens expecting the contract to automatically allocate the appropriate portion for fees. In practice the contract will only deduct 850 tokens for the trade, then compute fees on 850, resulting in a total outflow of 977 tokens, leaving 23 tokens unspent. From the user’s perspective the trade appears to have executed, but the taker’s balance shows a leftover amount (e.g., unspent BTC) and the maker and protocol receive less fee revenue than intended. The issue manifests whenever calcAmountAfterFee is called with a non‑zero maker fee, i.e., in markets that have both protocol and maker fees enabled. All participants – takers, makers, and the protocol – are affected because accounting records become inconsistent and fee revenue is understated. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that a buyer (Bob) retained a small amount of BTC after purchasing USDC due to the mis‑calculation. The flaw is subtle because the discrepancy is relatively small and can be masked by rounding, making it hard to notice in normal operation. The correct remedy is to compute the fee‑inclusive amount by dividing the desired total by (1 + totalFeeRate) or, equivalently, using the formula amount - (amount * (totalFeeBPS) / (100 000 + totalFeeBPS)). This ensures that the sum of the trade amount and the fees exactly equals the user‑specified total, restoring proper accounting and preventing leftover balances.

title: Low level calls to accounts with no code will succeed in `FeeWrapper`
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the FeeWrapper contract forwards calls to an arbitrary target using Solidity low‑level .call and .call{value:…} without verifying that the target address actually contains contract code. In the EVM, a low‑level call to an account with no code always returns a success flag (true) and, if value is sent, transfers the ether to that address. Because the wrapper does not perform an extcodesize check or validate that the returned data is non‑empty, a call to a non‑contract address is treated as a normal successful execution. An attacker or a mistaken user can supply an address that has no deployed bytecode; the wrapper will charge the fee, forward the call, and the transaction will appear to have succeeded, while the fee amount (or any attached ether) is simply deposited into an empty account that cannot execute any logic. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a successful transaction, the fee is deducted from their balance, but no expected action occurs – for example a trade does not happen or a refund is never received, leading to “funds disappear” or “refund missing” symptoms. This issue is discovered during an audit by constructing a test where the target address’s code length is zero and observing that feeWrapper.rubicall{value:…} completes without revert. The problem is subtle because low‑level calls do not automatically revert on missing code, unlike regular Solidity function calls that include a built‑in contract‑existence check, so developers may assume a successful call implies a valid implementation. The impact is loss of ether or tokens sent as part of the fee, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are transferred to a contract that will handle them. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls or missing contract‑code validation. To remediate, the wrapper should verify that the target address contains code (e.g., using OpenZeppelin’s Address.functionCall or Address.functionCallWithValue) or ensure that the returned data is non‑empty before accepting the call as successful. Adding such checks prevents accidental or malicious transfers to empty accounts and aligns the observed behavior with user expectations that a successful call results in the intended state change.

title: The `_matcho()` function is not implemented properly
description: The `_matcho()` function is not implemented properly. It might revert while the taking amount is greater than the best offer’s amount, which leads to order a matching failure.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal order‑matching routine used by the RubiconMarket contract, specifically the `_matcho()` function that processes taker‑maker trades. The function assumes that the amount a taker wants to acquire (`t_buy_amt`) can be satisfied by the best maker offer (`m_pay_amt`) without taking the protocol fee into account. When the taker’s requested amount is larger than the maker’s available amount, the function calculates the transfer amount using `min(m_pay_amt, t_buy_amt)` and then recomputes the remaining taker payment with the expression `t_pay_amt = mul(t_buy_amt, t_pay_amt) / t_buy_amt_old`. Because the fee is deducted from the maker’s payout but the fee is not added back into `m_pay_amt`, the actual amount transferred (`take_amt`) becomes slightly smaller than the expected full amount (for example 0.9999e18 instead of 1e18). This tiny discrepancy triggers a rounding mismatch that causes the subsequent arithmetic to produce a zero or negative value, leading the function to hit the `if (t_pay_amt == 0 || t_buy_amt == 0) { break; }` guard or to revert outright. As a result, a valid taker order that should have partially filled the maker’s offer instead fails, the transaction reverts, and no trade is recorded. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that the order submission failed or that the expected trade did not occur, even though the taker supplied sufficient funds; the maker’s offer appears to be stuck and the taker receives no tokens. The issue manifests whenever a taker order attempts to consume more than the best maker’s amount and the protocol fee is non‑zero, which is a common scenario in a fee‑charging order book. It affects any participant trying to trade on the market – both makers and takers – and can lead to liquidity being unusable, potential loss of fee tokens without a corresponding trade, and a degraded user experience. The flaw was discovered during a unit‑test audit where a deliberately crafted scenario caused the `offer` call to revert, and the logs revealed that the `take_amt` was off by exactly the fee amount. The problem is subtle because the mismatch is only a fraction of a percent, making it easy to miss in manual inspection, and the revert occurs deep inside the matching loop rather than at the entry point. The root cause is an incorrect fee handling and rounding logic in the matching algorithm; the fix requires adjusting the calculation of `m_pay_amt` to include the fee (e.g., `m_pay_amt + fee`) or redesigning the arithmetic to use ceiling division or safe rounding that guarantees the taker’s requested amount is fully satisfied before fee deduction. In broader terms this is a classic order‑matching rounding bug where fee adjustments are applied after the core amount comparison, violating the invariant that the trade amount must be consistent with both parties’ expectations and the protocol’s accounting rules.

title: Missing a check for minimum sell amount at the `make` function
description:
There is a check for `_dust` amount inside offer function at [L835](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L835) but not inside the other offer function being called by the `make` function at [L511](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L511).

The `make` function will not avoid dust offers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the minimum sell amount, commonly referred to as a dust check, in one of the internal offer functions that is invoked by the public make function. In the contract, a global mapping _dust stores the smallest acceptable amount for each token. The primary offer implementation (the one at line 835) correctly enforces require(_dust[address(pay_gem)] <= pay_amt) to prevent offers that are smaller than the dust threshold. However, the secondary overload of offer, which is called indirectly by make (line 511), omits this require statement. As a result, the make function can create offers with a pay_amt that is lower than the protocol‑defined dust limit. This omission occurs because the developer duplicated the offer logic but failed to copy the dust‑check line, leaving a logical gap in the code path. An attacker can exploit the gap by submitting a make transaction that creates a dust offer, thereby polluting the order book with offers that are effectively worthless or that may cause rounding errors during trade execution. Because the contract still accepts the offer and transfers the tiny amount of tokens, subsequent trades may result in the counter‑party receiving an amount that rounds down to zero, or the protocol may waste gas processing meaningless offers. From a user’s perspective, a trader may see an order appear in the market that promises a sell of a token, but when the trade is executed the buyer receives nothing or an unexpectedly small amount, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue manifests only when the make function is used, i.e., when a user creates an offer through the high‑level API; direct calls to the other offer function remain safe. All participants who rely on the market’s accounting assumptions – including liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the invariant that every offer meets a minimum size is broken. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the two offer implementations and noticed the missing dust check. It is subtle because the presence of the check in one function gives a false sense of security, and the missing line does not cause a compilation error or an obvious runtime failure. The recommended remediation is to add the same dust validation to the overloaded offer function, i.e., require(_dust[address(pay_gem)] <= pay_amt), thereby restoring the invariant that every sell order meets the minimum amount and preventing dust‑related accounting anomalies.

title: REENTRANCY ATTACK POSSIBLE IF THE `_feeTo` IS A MALICIOUS CONTRACT IN `FeeWrapper._chargeFeePayable`
description:
Reentrancy attack could happen if `_feeTo` is a `malicious` contract and has `recieve()` function implemented in `_feeTo` contract. `FeeWrapper._chargeFeePayable()` function is used to send the `_feeAmount` of ETH to the `_feeTo` address.

Consider that `FeeWrapper._chargeFeePayable()` is called by the `FeeWrapper._rubicallPayable()` function with the necessary `_feeParams` input parameter, and the following scenario can occur:

  1. The call to `(bool OK, ) = payable(_feeTo).call{value: _feeAmount}("")` is made. Lets assume the `_totalAmount` = 1ETH and `_feeAmount` = 0.1ETH initially.
  2. `_feeTo` contract has the `recieve()` function implemented in it.
  3. It reenters the `FeeWrapper` contract by calling the `rubicallPayable()` function by sending 0.01ETH as `msg.value`.
  4. It sets the `_feeParams.totalAmount` = 0.01ETH and `_feeParams.feeAmount` = 0.1ETH in the call to `rubicallPayable()`.
  5. `FeeWrapper.chargeFeePayable()` will be called again by the `rubicallPayable()` function.
  6. `(bool OK, ) = payable(_feeTo).call{value: _feeAmount}("");` will be called and `Tx will pass` since there is enough ETH in the contract from the previous deposit.
  7. Again `_feeParams.feeAmount` = 0.1ETH will be transferred to the `_feeTo` address.
  8. This can be continued till there is enough ETH in the contract.
  9. This happens as there is `no check` to make sure `msg.value > _feeAmount` before the low level `call` to the `_feeTo` address.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw that appears when the fee‑receiving address (_feeTo) is a contract capable of executing code on receipt of Ether. The function that charges the protocol fee, FeeWrapper._chargeFeePayable, forwards the fee amount to _feeTo using a low‑level call before any state is updated and without any reentrancy protection. Because the call is made with payable(_feeTo).call{value:_feeAmount}(''), a malicious _feeTo contract can implement a receive() function that immediately invokes FeeWrapper._rubicallPayable again, supplying a small msg.value and manipulated fee parameters. Each recursive entry repeats the fee transfer because the contract never checks that the incoming msg.value exceeds the fee amount, allowing the attacker to drain the contract’s ETH balance until the contract no longer holds enough to cover the fee. The attack can be triggered whenever a user sends ETH to the wrapper contract, expecting the fee to be deducted and the remaining amount forwarded to a target router. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the expected output may be missing, balances may become unexpectedly low or zero, and refunds may not be received. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the interaction between fee charging and the external call path and noticed the absence of a reentrancy guard and the missing msg.value > _feeAmount validation. It is hard to notice because the low‑level call does not revert on reentrancy and the contract’s logic seems correct at a glance; the problem only manifests when the fee recipient is malicious. The bug belongs to the broader class of reentrancy attacks caused by external calls before state changes (Checks‑Effects‑Interactions violation). To remediate, the contract should either apply a reentrancy guard such as OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier to both _chargeFeePayable and _rubicallPayable, or enforce that msg.value is strictly greater than the fee amount before performing the external call, thereby eliminating any profit for a reentering attacker. Additionally, moving the fee transfer after the external call or using a pull‑payment pattern would further reduce the attack surface.

title: Use of `block.number` leads to incorrect interest calculations
description:
The interests that need to be paid upon closing a position are computed as follows:

```solidity
File: contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol
322: function _calculateDebt(
323:         address _bathToken,
324:         uint256 _startBlock,
325:         uint256 _borrowedAmount
326:     ) internal view returns (uint256 _debt) {
327:         uint256 _blockDelta = block.number - _startBlock;
328: 
329:         uint256 _interest = (
330:             (_borrowedAmount).mul(borrowRate(_bathToken).mul(_blockDelta))
331:         ).div(10 ** 18);
332:         _debt = _borrowedAmount.add(_interest);
333:     }
```

The interest rate is computed using the block delta, between `block.number` and the starting block.

The issue is that the block production on Optimism is currently [not fixed](https://community.optimism.io/docs/developers/build/differences/#block-numbers-and-timestamps):

    each transaction on L2 is placed in a separate block and blocks are NOT produced at a constant rate
poc:
Run the following command several times in the repo, using an optimism rpc url:

    cast block-number --rpc-url YOUR_OPTIMISM_RPC_URL

You will see that the blocks are not produced at a constant rate.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on block.number to measure the elapsed time for interest accrual. The code calculates a block delta (current block minus the block at which a position opened) and multiplies the borrowed amount by a per‑block borrow rate to derive interest. This approach assumes that blocks are produced at a regular interval, an assumption that holds on Ethereum mainnet but not on Optimism, where each transaction creates its own block and block times are highly variable. Because the block production rate on Optimism is not fixed, the block delta can grow much faster or slower than real elapsed time, causing the interest formula to over‑ or under‑estimate the amount owed. An attacker or any user can exploit this by opening a position and then triggering a series of transactions that generate many blocks in a short period, inflating the block delta and consequently the interest charged. Conversely, a period of low activity could reduce the block delta, leading to insufficient interest collection. The practical impact is that borrowers may be charged more than the agreed‑upon rate, resulting in unexpected fee spikes, reduced refunds, or even a situation where the protocol’s accounting no longer matches its economic model. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the expected repayment amount and the actual amount required – for example, a user expects to receive a modest interest‑adjusted balance but sees a much lower amount or a zero refund. This issue manifests only when the contract is deployed on L2 networks with non‑constant block times, such as Optimism or Arbitrum, and it affects any participant that interacts with the borrowing functionality, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol treasury. The problem was uncovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that calling `cast block-number` against an Optimism RPC returned irregular intervals, highlighting the mismatch between block‑based accounting and real‑world time. The bug is subtle because the calculation appears mathematically correct on a per‑block basis; the error only becomes evident over multiple blocks where the time distortion accumulates, making it easy to miss in unit tests that run on a single block. To remediate the issue the interest calculation should be refactored to use block.timestamp (or a per‑second rate) instead of block.number, ensuring that the elapsed time reflects actual wall‑clock seconds. This may require redesigning the rate model from “per block” to “per second” and updating all dependent contracts, but it restores the intended economic guarantees and prevents the unintended fee inflation or deflation caused by variable block production.

title: Incorrect reward duration extension in notifyRewardAmount function
description: This issue can lead to extending the reward duration beyond the intended time period, causing rewards to be distributed over a longer duration than initially planned. This could result in users receiving smaller rewards over time, which may not align with the project’s goals or user expectations.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution contract’s notifyRewardAmount function, which is responsible for topping up a staking reward pool and updating the schedule for when rewards cease. The function unconditionally adds the configured rewardsDuration to the stored periodFinish timestamp each time it is called, regardless of whether the current reward period has already elapsed. This logic flaw causes the reward period to be extended whenever new rewards are supplied during an active distribution window. As a result, the total reward amount is spread over a longer time span than originally advertised, diluting the per‑second reward rate. An attacker or any participant who can trigger notifyRewardAmount while the reward window is still open can therefore extend the distribution window, causing legitimate users to receive smaller incremental rewards than they expect. The impact is primarily economic: stakers see their accrued balances grow more slowly, the protocol may distribute the same token supply over a longer horizon, and the promised incentive model is broken, potentially undermining user confidence and the protocol’s tokenomics. The bug manifests only when the function is invoked before periodFinish has been reached; if the call occurs after the period has ended, the logic behaves as intended. The issue was identified during a formal audit by examining the state updates in the function and confirming that periodFinish is always incremented by rewardsDuration, a behavior that contradicts the documented reward‑top‑up semantics. Because the function also correctly updates the reward rate, the extension can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms, making it hard to detect through casual testing. To remediate, the contract should conditionally extend periodFinish only when the existing reward period has expired, or recompute the new finish time based on the remaining time rather than always adding the full duration. This change restores the intended fixed‑duration reward schedule, ensuring that added rewards increase the rate rather than lengthening the distribution window, and aligns the on‑chain behavior with user expectations of consistent reward payouts.

title: Calling `ExpiringMarket.stop` and `ExpiringMarket.isClosed` functions cannot pause any functionlities of the market
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

  1. The protocol is hacked so the `RubiconMarket` contract’s owner calls the `ExpiringMarket.stop` function as an attempt to pause the functionalities of the market.
  2. After the `ExpiringMarket.stop` function is called, none of the market’s functionalities are paused because `stopped` is not used at all in the protocol for pausing any of the market’s functionalities and the `ExpiringMarket.isClosed` function always returns `false`.
  3. As a result, the attacker can transfer user funds out from the protocol, and such user funds are lost.
bug_full: An ineffective pause mechanism exists in the ExpiringMarket contract. The stop function sets a storage variable named stopped, but the variable is never consulted by any other part of the protocol, so calling stop does not actually pause any market operation. In addition, the isClosed function is declared as a pure function that always returns false, meaning the market is never reported as closed. Both the can_offer, can_buy and can_cancel modifiers contain require(!isClosed()) or require(isClosed() || ...) checks that therefore always evaluate to true for the open‑market path. As a result, even when the RubiconMarket owner invokes stop during an emergency, new offers, buys and cancellations remain permitted, allowing an attacker to continue moving funds out of the contract. The vulnerability stems from missing integration of the stopped flag into the business logic and from a placeholder isClosed implementation that does not reflect the actual market state. It was discovered during a code audit that examined the pause‑related functions and their usage in modifiers. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract exposes a stop function that appears to provide an emergency stop, yet no tests or UI cues verify that the flag influences behavior, leading to a false sense of security. The impact is that users cannot rely on the market being halted; they may see transactions succeed when they expect the market to be closed, potentially resulting in loss of funds if the protocol is compromised. The bug belongs to the class of ineffective state enforcement or dead‑code pause mechanisms. A correct fix requires making stopped a persistent state variable, having isClosed return the value of stopped, and adding require(!stopped) checks (or using isClosed) in all functions that should be disabled when the market is paused. Removing the pure isClosed function and ensuring that the pause flag is consulted throughout the contract would align the implementation with the intended emergency‑stop semantics.

title: User can possess less value than before when `V2Migrator.migrate` function is called to give up `bathTokenV1` tokens and hold `bathTokenV2` tokens
poc:
The following steps can occur for the described scenario.

1. The `bathTokenV1` tokens owned by Alice are worth 1000 USDC.
2. Alice calls the `V2Migrator.migrate` function to migrate her `bathTokenV1` tokens to `bathTokenV2` tokens.
3. When the `V2Migrator.migrate` function is called, a fee of 10 USDC is transferred to `feeTo` so the `bathTokenV2` tokens minted to Alice are worth only 990 USDC.
4. As a result, Alice loses 10 USDC because of the migration, even though she should own the same value either holding the `bathTokenV1` tokens before the migration or `bathTokenV2` tokens after the migration.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migration workflow that moves a user’s bathTokenV1 holdings to bathTokenV2. The migrate function first withdraws the underlying asset from the V1 token by calling bathTokenV1.withdraw, which internally calculates a fee (feeBPS) and transfers that fee to a designated address (feeTo). The net amount after fee deduction, called amountWithdrawn, is then used as the input to the V2 mint operation. Because the fee has already been subtracted, the newly minted bathTokenV2 represents a smaller amount of the underlying asset than the original V1 tokens represented. From the user’s perspective the migration transaction succeeds without error, but the user receives fewer underlying tokens than they started with – for example a user holding 1000 USDC worth of bathTokenV1 may receive bathTokenV2 worth only 990 USDC after migration. The root cause is that the migration logic does not account for the withdrawal fee; it assumes the withdrawn amount equals the full underlying balance, while the V1 contract’s withdraw function deliberately reduces that amount by the fee. This issue manifests whenever the V1 token has a non‑zero feeBPS and feeTo is set to a non‑zero address, i.e., under normal operating conditions of the protocol. All users who invoke migrate are affected because the contract does not differentiate between callers. The impact is a loss of value for users, violating the expectation that migration preserves economic equivalence. The problem was identified during a formal audit (Code4rena) by tracing the flow of funds through the withdraw and mint calls and noticing the fee subtraction. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the user’s balance of bathTokenV2 appears correct relative to the mint call, masking the hidden reduction in underlying value. To remediate, the migration routine should either temporarily set the V1 fee to zero before calling withdraw, or adjust the amount minted on V2 to compensate for the fee, or refund the fee to the user. In essence, the fix requires eliminating the fee deduction from the amount that determines the V2 token supply, thereby restoring the intended one‑to‑one value transfer across versions.

title: Calling `Position._marketBuy` and `Position._marketSell` functions that calculate `_fee` by dividing by `10000` can cause incorrect calculations
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation mismatch between the Position contract and the RubiconMarket contract. In the Position._marketBuy and Position._marketSell internal functions the fee is computed as amount multiplied by the market fee basis points and then divided by 10000. The RubiconMarket.buy (and the corresponding sell logic) computes the same fee but divides by 100000. Because the denominator differs, the fee value used by Position is ten times larger than the fee actually charged by the market. This discrepancy originates from an inconsistent scaling factor for basis points, a classic arithmetic‑precision bug. When a user invokes Position.buyAllAmountWithLeverage or any function that routes through _marketBuy or _marketSell, the Position contract reserves a larger fee amount, reduces the effective spend, and consequently the user receives fewer asset tokens than expected. The impact is that users lose a portion of the tokens they are entitled to; the protocol’s accounting becomes inaccurate and the user‑facing UI may show a smaller received balance without an obvious error. The bug manifests whenever the Position contract calls the market’s buy or sell functions, i.e., during leveraged long or short operations. It affects any holder of the Position contract who attempts to trade through these entry points, potentially draining funds over many trades. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test compared token balances before and after a trade and observed a shortfall caused by the mismatched fee formula. The problem is hard to spot because both contracts use the same feeBPS variable and similar arithmetic, so the error is hidden in the constant value of the divisor. To remediate, the Position contract should use the same denominator as RubiconMarket, i.e., divide by 100000 when calculating the internal fee, thereby aligning the fee logic and restoring correct token accounting. This class of bug falls under inconsistent financial‑calculation constants, which can lead to under‑ or over‑charging fees and breaking business logic expectations such as "user expects to receive X tokens but gets less".

title: Incorrect calculations can occur when calling `Position._marketBuy` and `Position._marketSell` functions that do not include maker fee in `_fee`
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the internal Position contract functions that perform market trades, specifically _marketBuy and _marketSell. These functions compute a fee variable (_fee) using only the taker fee returned by rubiconMarket.getFeeBPS() and a divisor of 10000, while completely ignoring the maker fee that the RubiconMarket contract may charge when makerFee() > 0. Because the RubiconMarket.buy (and sell) implementation later deducts both the taker fee and the maker fee from the user, the amount of fee subtracted in the Position contract does not match the total fee actually taken on chain. This mismatch causes the Position contract to request a larger net trade amount than it should, resulting in the user receiving more asset tokens than they are entitled to. The excess tokens are effectively taken from the liquidity pool, so other participants lose value and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken. The flaw is triggered whenever a trade is executed through Position.buyAllAmountWithLeverage (or the analogous sell function) while the market’s maker fee is non‑zero. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the user observes an unexpectedly high amount of received tokens, while the pool balance shrinks and other users may later notice missing funds. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by comparing the fee calculation in Position with the fee logic in RubiconMarket and confirming the discrepancy with unit tests that showed different asset token outputs depending on whether the maker fee was accounted for. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert; the over‑payment is silently absorbed by the market, making it easy to miss in casual testing. It belongs to the class of fee‑miscalculation or accounting bugs where a component of the fee (maker fee) is omitted and the scaling factor is incorrect (division by 10000 instead of the market’s 100000 basis points). To remediate, the Position functions should be updated to (1) use the same divisor as the market (100000), (2) add the maker fee to the _fee calculation when rubiconMarket.makerFee() > 0, and (3) ensure the total fee passed to the market matches the amount actually deducted, thereby preserving the intended economic balance of the protocol.

title: Calling `Position._marketSell` function compares `fill_amt` that includes fee to `min_fill_amount` that does not include fee
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the amount that is checked against the user‑provided slippage limit and the amount that actually includes the protocol fee. In the Position._marketSell function the caller supplies a _minFill value that represents the smallest acceptable amount of the quote token after the trade, and the function calculates a fee based on this value. However, when the function forwards the trade to RubiconMarket.sellAllAmount it passes the original _minFill unchanged, while the market contract computes a fill_amt that already contains the fee before the final fee deduction step. The require statement inside sellAllAmount therefore compares fill_amt (fee‑inclusive) with min_fill_amount (fee‑exclusive). Because the fee is a positive amount, fill_amt is almost always greater than or equal to min_fill_amount, causing the slippage check to be effectively bypassed. An attacker or a careless user can therefore trigger a trade that appears to satisfy the minimum‑fill condition but actually delivers less net quote tokens after the fee is taken. From the user’s perspective the transaction succeeds, the UI shows that the position was closed, yet the received amount is lower than expected – sometimes even zero – leading to a loss of value. The bug manifests whenever Position._marketSell is used, i.e., for any leveraged position that relies on the market’s sellAllAmount function and when the market fee basis points are non‑zero. It affects all users of the Position contract, the protocol’s leverage offering, and any downstream contracts that assume the min_fill_amount guarantee. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors logged the values of min_fill_amount, fill_amt (including fee) and fill_amt after fee deduction, observing that the latter equals the former while the former is larger than the limit, proving the slippage control is ineffective. The problem is subtle because the require does not revert, so the transaction looks successful, and the fee accounting is hidden inside the market contract, making it hard to spot without explicit instrumentation. The proper fix is to ensure that the amount compared to min_fill_amount is fee‑exclusive – either by adding the fee to the min_fill_amount argument passed to sellAllAmount, or by performing the fee deduction before the require check, or by redesigning the market function to expose a fee‑neutral fill amount for slippage validation. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of mismatched accounting units in invariant checks, where fee‑inclusive and fee‑exclusive values are unintentionally mixed, breaking guarantees about minimum received amounts and allowing unintended loss of funds.

title: `BathBuddy` rewards DoS
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) attack on the BathBuddy reward distribution mechanism that can block reward accrual for liquidity providers (LPs) holding a small amount of bathToken. The root cause lies in the way the contract calculates earned rewards: the earned amount is derived from a global rewardPerToken value that is updated on every call to rewardPerToken, which in turn depends on the time elapsed since the last update, the global reward rate and the total supply of bathToken. Because the calculation uses integer arithmetic with division by the total supply, frequent updates – for example one call per block – make the incremental reward per token extremely small. When an LP’s bathToken balance is tiny relative to the total supply, the product of the balance and the incremental reward per token rounds down to zero, causing the earned function to return zero rewards. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling getReward (or claimRewards, which internally calls getReward) at short intervals, constantly refreshing the global lastUpdateTime. Each refresh reduces the per‑block reward increment, so small LPs never accumulate enough reward to surpass the rounding threshold. The impact is that affected users see no reward tokens transferred to their address; their UI shows a zero balance or no increase despite having deposited liquidity, violating the expectation that rewards accrue over time. This condition occurs especially on low‑cost L2 networks such as Optimism, where an attacker can afford to send a transaction every block. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which reproduced the scenario with a test that repeatedly called claimRewards from a large LP while a small LP attempted to claim and received zero each time. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error – it simply returns zero, making the symptom appear as a normal “no reward yet” state. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑distribution rounding or accounting DoS bugs, where global state updates can be abused to suppress earnings for low‑balance participants. To mitigate the issue, the contract should decouple per‑user reward accrual from the global lastUpdateTime, introduce per‑user checkpoints, use a higher‑precision arithmetic or a minimum reward threshold, and prevent frequent global updates from being triggered by any user claim. By redesigning the accounting so that small balances can still earn a non‑zero amount or by limiting how often the global rewardPerToken can be refreshed, the protocol can restore fairness and prevent indefinite griefing of small LPs.

title: The return value of `buyAllAmount` is incorrect
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the return value of the exchange function that purchases a target token using a source token. The function is expected to report the total amount of source tokens that were spent to acquire the desired amount of the target token. Internally the contract accumulates the raw amount of source tokens required for each matched offer in the variable fill_amt. After the loop, the code checks that fill_amt does not exceed a caller‑provided maximum and then applies a fee calculation by calling calcAmountAfterFee(fill_amt). The result of this fee deduction overwrites fill_amt, and the overwritten value is returned to the caller. Because the fee is subtracted from the amount that was actually transferred, the returned value is lower than the real amount of source tokens that left the caller’s wallet. For example, with a 10 % fee a user who spends 10 000 USDC to receive 0.9 WBTC will see the function return 9 000 USDC, even though the contract has taken the full 10 000 USDC. The root cause is the misplaced fee adjustment after the accumulator has already been used as the function’s output, violating the contract’s accounting assumptions. An attacker or a downstream contract that relies on the returned amount to enforce limits or to update balances may be misled into believing that less capital was consumed, potentially allowing double‑spending, over‑allocation of credit, or incorrect accounting in the protocol’s treasury. The bug manifests whenever a non‑zero fee is applied and the user purchases a non‑trivial amount, i.e., when fill_amt is greater than zero. All participants that interact with the exchange – regular users, liquidity providers, and any smart contracts that call buyAllAmount – are affected because they receive an inaccurate spend figure. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain token transfers with the value returned by the function and noticed a discrepancy. It is subtle because the function name and the surrounding require statement suggest that the returned value already accounts for the fee, and typical unit tests may only verify that the trade succeeds, not that the reported amount matches the transferred amount. To remediate the problem the fee deduction should be performed on a separate variable used for internal accounting, while the function should return the original fill_amt representing the total source tokens transferred, or the contract should clearly document that the return value excludes fees and provide an additional output for the fee‑adjusted amount. This correction restores consistency between the contract’s state changes and its public interface, preventing misleading information from propagating through the protocol’s financial logic.

title: Cannot close leveraged positions
bug_full: An leveraged position is opened by repeatedly supplying collateral and borrowing, resulting in a borrowed amount that exceeds the liquid asset held by the contract. The function closePosition is designed to unwind the position by calling an internal _repay routine that attempts to repay the entire borrowed quote token balance in a single step, then redeems the remaining bath tokens. Because the borrowed amount is larger than the available asset tokens, the _repay routine first tries to swap asset tokens for the full quote amount. When the contract does not hold enough asset tokens, the swap fails and the subsequent transferFrom call attempts to pull the shortfall from the caller, which reverts if the caller has no extra balance. Consequently, the transaction reverts and the position remains open. This behavior is triggered whenever a user tries to close a leveraged position without providing additional liquid assets, which is a common scenario when the leverage factor is greater than one and the user expects the contract to unwind automatically. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a unit test that opened a leveraged position, revoked the user's asset allowance, and then called closePosition, observing a revert. The bug is subtle because the closePosition function succeeds for small leverages or when the user still holds enough collateral, making the failure appear only under specific conditions. From the user's perspective the UI indicates a request to close the position, but the transaction fails, leaving the balance unchanged and the position still listed as open, which contradicts the expectation that the position can be closed in the same block without extra capital. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incomplete unwind or single‑step repayment bugs, where a contract assumes sufficient assets to settle the full debt in one operation instead of iteratively repaying, redeeming, and swapping. The impact is a poor user experience and the potential for funds to become effectively locked until the user supplies additional assets, though no direct loss of funds occurs. To remediate the issue the contract should implement a repayment loop that repeatedly repays a portion of the debt, redeems collateral, and swaps assets until the borrowed balance reaches zero, or it should allow partial closing of positions so that users can unwind as much as their current assets permit.

title: A liquidated position possibly cannot be closed
description:
The `Compound V2` protocol is a lending protocol that allows users to supply collaterals in order to borrow other assets (possibly the collateral itself). If a user’s position gets undercollateralized, the user will get liquidated (i.e. a liquidator can seize some of their collateral, while repaying also part of their debt.)

The problem is that, if a user’s created margin position gets liquidated, it is not possible to close said position, at least not without disrupting other positions alongside that.

This is because the function `closePosition()` will attempt to close the position _using the full amount_ it has been provided when opening. In other words, the contract never got the info that any liquidations happened, and will attempt to explicitly undo the position in addition to closing it.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability of the Position contract to be closed after a liquidation event in the Compound V2 based margin system. When a user opens a leveraged position, the contract records the original borrow amount and later expects to close the position by repaying that exact amount via the closePosition() function. However, if the position becomes under‑collateralized and a liquidator seizes part of the collateral while repaying a portion of the debt, the contract does not update its internal accounting to reflect the reduced debt and altered collateral balance. Consequently, closePosition() still attempts to repay the full original amount, which no longer matches the outstanding debt, causing the transaction to revert. This state inconsistency arises because the contract never receives or processes information about external liquidations, leading to a mismatch between on‑chain reality and the contract’s stored expectations. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the mere occurrence of a legitimate liquidation triggers the failure. The impact is that users are unable to close their positions through the intended UI flow, receive a revert error, and are left with residual cTokens and a remaining debt balance. From the user’s perspective the “Close” button appears to do nothing, the transaction fails, yet the contract still holds tokens and shows a non‑zero debt, creating confusion and potential mis‑management of the margin portfolio. This condition occurs whenever a position has been liquidated and the owner subsequently attempts to invoke closePosition(). It affects any trader using the Position contract, the protocol’s risk model, and potentially other positions that share the same collateral pool because the stuck assets may interfere with subsequent liquidations. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a Hardhat test that deliberately forced a liquidation and then called closePosition(), which reverted while the contract still owned cTokens and owed debt. The bug is hard to notice because the contract’s balances appear non‑zero, but the UI does not surface the underlying accounting mismatch, and the failure only manifests after a liquidation, a relatively rare event.
